depth.title: Truth functions, normal forms, and completeness

blocks.body: Every connective in this section is a **truth function**: a map $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ assigning each of the $2^n$ input rows an output bit. Counting fixes the landscape before any proof is written: each row can independently carry 0 or 1, so there are exactly $2^{2^n}$ connectives of arity $n$ — four unary ones, sixteen binary ones, 256 ternary ones, and already $2^{32}$ of arity five. The connectives $\lnot, \land, \lor, \to, \leftrightarrow$ therefore sample a vanishing corner of the possible functions, and the graduate theory of this section asks two sharp questions about them: which sets of connectives can express **every** truth function (functional completeness), and how large must the expressions be? The first question has a complete classical answer, proved below; the second is the seed of circuit complexity, pursued at Level III.

blocks.heading: Disjunctive normal form
blocks.body: Every truth function $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is computed by a formula using only $\lnot, \land, \lor$. Explicitly, let $S$ be the set of rows on which $f$ takes the value 1, and for each row $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ write the **minterm** $m_a = \bigwedge_{i=1}^n L_i(a)$, where $L_i(a)$ is $p_i$ if $a_i = 1$ and $\lnot p_i$ if $a_i = 0$. Then $f$ is computed by $\varphi = \bigvee_{a \in S} m_a$. In particular the set $\{\lnot, \land, \lor\}$ is **functionally complete**: every connective of every arity is definable from it, and so is any connective yet to be invented.

A minterm $m_a$ is true under an assignment $v$ exactly when $v = a$: if the two agree in every coordinate, every literal $L_i(a)$ is true and the conjunction stands; if they differ in coordinate $i$, the literal $L_i(a)$ is false and the conjunction collapses. A disjunction, in turn, is true exactly when some disjunct is true. So $\varphi$ is true under $v$ precisely when the disjunct $m_v$ was included, that is, precisely when $f(v) = 1$ — the formula computes $f$ on all $2^n$ inputs. If $S$ is empty, take any contradiction such as $p_1 \land \lnot p_1$, which represents the constant-0 function. Read backwards, the construction is exactly the algorithm for converting an arbitrary truth table into a formula, and dualizing every connective in the argument yields the conjunctive normal form theorem for free.

blocks.heading: Post's completeness criterion
blocks.body: A set $B$ of connectives is functionally complete if and only if $B$ is **not** contained in any one of the five classes: $T_0$ (functions with $f(0,\dots,0) = 0$), $T_1$ (functions with $f(1,\dots,1) = 1$), the **monotone** functions, the **affine** functions (those of the form $a_0 \oplus a_1 p_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus a_n p_n$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$), and the **self-dual** functions (those with $f(\lnot p_1, \dots, \lnot p_n) = \lnot f(p_1, \dots, p_n)$). These are the maximal **clones** in the lattice of closed classes of truth functions that Emil Post classified completely in 1941, and functional completeness is precisely escape from all five.

Necessity first. Each of the five classes is closed under composition — plugging monotone (or affine, or 0-preserving, …) functions into one another cannot leave the class — and each is a proper subclass of all truth functions, so a connective set inside one class generates only that class, never everything. For sufficiency, choose connectives $f_1, \dots, f_5$, one escaping each class. Identify all arguments of the $T_0$-escape to get a unary $u$ with $u(0) = 1$, and of the $T_1$-escape to get $v$ with $v(1) = 0$; working the cases, either one of them is a negation, or $u$ and $v$ are the two constants 1 and 0. If we hold the constants, a non-monotone function takes the values 1 and 0 on comparable inputs, and a chain between them that flips one coordinate at a time yields, after the fixed coordinates are replaced by constants, a negation. If instead we hold negation, a non-self-dual function has $f(a) = f(\lnot a)$ for some $a$, and feeding each argument $x$ or $\lnot x$ according to the bits of $a$ yields a constant. Either way we obtain $\lnot$, 0 and 1. The final step is a finite case check: with negation and the constants available, any non-affine function generates conjunction or disjunction — each of the eight non-affine binary truth functions does. With $\lnot$ and $\land$ in hand, the normal-form theorem finishes the construction.

blocks.heading: The Sheffer stroke and the Peirce arrow
blocks.body: Functional completeness from a **single** connective was observed by Sheffer (1913), with an unpublished anticipation by Peirce. Write $p \mid q = \lnot(p \land q)$ (NAND, the Sheffer stroke) and $p \downarrow q = \lnot(p \lor q)$ (NOR, the Peirce arrow). Negation and conjunction — hence, by the normal-form theorem, everything — reduce to NAND: $$\lnot p \;\equiv\; p \mid p, \qquad p \land q \;\equiv\; (p \mid q) \mid (p \mid q).$$ For NOR the mirror identities hold: $$\lnot p \;\equiv\; p \downarrow p, \qquad p \lor q \;\equiv\; (p \downarrow q) \downarrow (p \downarrow q).$$ The remaining connectives follow by De Morgan, for instance $p \to q \equiv \lnot p \lor q$. This is why physical hardware concentrates on one robust gate type — a chip built only from NAND gates is logically universal — and Post's criterion confirms that among all sixteen binary connectives, exactly the two dagger-shaped ones manage the trick alone.

depth.title: SAT at the frontier: NP-completeness and beyond

blocks.body: The decision problem **SAT** — given a formula, decide whether some assignment satisfies it — is the computational heart of this chapter: the satisfiability testing of the equivalence section was its baby case. The **Cook–Levin theorem** (1971; Levin independently, 1973) makes SAT the canonical intractable problem: SAT is **NP-complete**, so every problem whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time reduces to it. The proof encodes a polynomial-time verifier as a giant propositional formula asserting “this computation is legal and accepting,” clause by clause, over variables that name tape cells at each time step; the verifier has an accepting run exactly when the formula is satisfiable. Every theme of this chapter — translation, normal forms, consistency checking — is downstream of that one encoding idea, which is why a logic course is secretly a computational complexity course.

blocks.heading: From DPLL to CDCL
blocks.body: The Davis–Putnam–Logemann–Loveland procedure (1960; the tree-search revision, 1962) decides SAT by branching on a variable, simplifying, and backtracking on conflict. Its modern descendant, **conflict-driven clause learning** (GRASP, 1996; Chaff, 2001), converts each dead end into a learned clause that prunes the entire remaining search space, and Chaff's **VSIDS** heuristic — branch on variables active in recent conflicts, with scores decayed exponentially — lets the solver discover the instance's structure on the fly. Restarts, watched literals and aggressive clause deletion complete the engine. The empirical outcome transformed the field: industrial instances with millions of variables — hardware verification, planning, scheduling, cryptographic puzzles — now fall routinely, although carefully constructed worst cases remain exponential. SAT solving has become a general-purpose reasoning backend embedded in production systems at Google, Intel and Amazon, and the mathematical analysis of these algorithms (proof lengths, restart policies, heuristics) is itself a research area.

blocks.heading: The random k-SAT threshold
blocks.body: Fix $k \ge 2$ and draw a formula from $m$ independent random $k$-clauses over $n$ variables, with density $\alpha = m/n$. There is a **critical density** $\alpha_k$: below it the formula is satisfiable with probability tending to 1 as $n \to \infty$, and above it unsatisfiable with probability tending to 1. Friedgut (1999) proved that such a sharp threshold exists for every fixed $k$, and Ding, Sly and Sun (2016) confirmed the location predicted by statistical physics — the replica-symmetry value — for all sufficiently large $k$. For $k = 3$ the exact threshold, believed to be near $4.267$, is still open; the transition's fine structure is precisely where the CDCL solvers of the previous block struggle hardest.

blocks.heading: The P versus NP problem
blocks.body: Is every problem whose solutions can be verified efficiently also solvable efficiently — does $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}$? Open since 1971, a Clay millennium problem carrying a million-dollar prize, and the deepest single question about the material of this chapter, since SAT is its pivot. The known barriers are themselves theorems: relativization (Baker–Gill–Solovay, 1975) shows that diagonalization alone cannot settle it; natural proofs (Razborov–Rudich, 1997) show that the standard method for circuit lower bounds cannot settle it; algebrization (Aaronson–Wigderson, 2008) extends both obstructions. Between the undergraduate truth table and the answer there is, at present, no known bridge.

prerequisites: Declarative sentences and propositional truth valuation (True / False)
Elementary truth tables for negation ($\neg$), conjunction ($\land$), and disjunction ($\lor$)
Concept of logical equivalence ($\equiv$): identical truth value under all interpretations
intro: Logic is the grammar of mathematics: every definition, theorem and proof you will ever read is built out of propositions stitched together by connectives. This section defines propositions, the connectives ¬, ∧, ∨, ⊕, → and ↔, and the truth tables that give each of them exact meaning.
objectives: Recognize propositions and distinguish them from commands, questions and open sentences
Translate English statements into compound propositions using ¬, ∧, ∨, ⊕, → and ↔
Build and read truth tables, including multi-variable tables
Apply operator precedence to parse compound propositions correctly
Compute bitwise AND, OR and XOR on bit strings

concepts.statement: A **proposition** is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both. Its **truth value** is T (true) or F (false).
concepts.detail: Commands (“Close the door.”), questions (“What time is it?”), opinions and open sentences with unbound variables (“x + 1 > 5”) are not propositions. Paradoxes like “This sentence is false” fail the definition because they can be neither true nor false.

concepts.statement: The **negation** of a proposition p is the proposition ¬p (“not p”), which is true exactly when p is false.
concepts.detail: If p is “Today is Friday,” then ¬p is “Today is not Friday” (equivalently, “It is not the case that today is Friday”). The negation of a negation returns the original: ¬¬p has the same truth value as p.

concepts.statement: The **conjunction** p ∧ q (“p and q”) is true exactly when both p and q are true. The **disjunction** p ∨ q (“p or q”) is the **inclusive** or: it is false exactly when both p and q are false.
concepts.detail: Inclusive or means “one, the other, or both.” Natural language “or” is sometimes inclusive (“experience with Java or C++”) and sometimes exclusive (“soup or salad”), so translation must respect the intended meaning.

concepts.statement: The **exclusive or** p ⊕ q is true exactly when precisely one of p and q is true; it is false when p and q have the same truth value.
concepts.detail: It can be built from the other connectives: p ⊕ q ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q). It is also exactly the negation of the biconditional: p ⊕ q ≡ ¬(p ↔ q).

concepts.statement: The **conditional** p → q (“if p, then q”) is false only in the single case where p is true and q is false. Here p is the **hypothesis** (antecedent) and q is the **conclusion** (consequent).
concepts.detail: Many phrasings mean p → q: “p only if q,” “p is sufficient for q,” “q is necessary for p,” “q whenever p,” “q follows from p.” The **converse** is q → p, the **inverse** is ¬p → ¬q, and the **contrapositive** is ¬q → ¬p — only the contrapositive is equivalent to the original. A conditional with a false hypothesis is true (vacuously).

concepts.statement: The **biconditional** p ↔ q (“p if and only if q”) is true exactly when p and q have the same truth value.
concepts.detail: Read it as “p if and only if q,” “p iff q,” or “p is necessary and sufficient for q.” It decomposes into the two conditionals: p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p).

concepts.statement: A **truth table** lists all 2ⁿ combinations of truth values of the n propositional variables in a compound proposition, together with the resulting truth value of the compound for each row.
concepts.detail: Build columns from the inside out: variables first, then sub-expressions, then the whole formula. A one-variable table has 2 rows, two variables give 4 rows, three give 8 — the table doubles with each added variable, which is why algebraic methods (Section 1.3) eventually replace tables.

concepts.statement: From highest to lowest precedence: ¬, then ∧, then ∨, then →, then ↔.
concepts.detail: So ¬p ∨ q parses as (¬p) ∨ q, and p ∨ q → r parses as (p ∨ q) → r. When in doubt — or to be unambiguous to a reader — write parentheses.

concepts.statement: A **bit** is a symbol with two values, 0 (false) and 1 (true); a **Boolean variable** has 0 or 1 as its value; a **bit string** is a sequence of bits. The bitwise operations AND, OR and XOR apply ∧, ∨, ⊕ to corresponding positions of two equal-length bit strings.
concepts.detail: For example, the AND of the 8-bit strings 01 1010 11 and 11 0001 10 is 01 0000 10, and their XOR is 10 1011 01. Computers store truth values exactly this way, which is why logic and hardware meet in Chapter 12.

derivations.title: Logical Equivalence of the Conditional Proposition
derivations.statement: The conditional statement $p \to q$ is logically equivalent to the disjunctive proposition $\neg p \lor q$: $$ (p \to q) \equiv (\neg p \lor q) $$
prerequisites: Truth valuation of conditional statement: $p \to q$ is false if and only if $p = T$ and $q = F$
Truth valuation of negation ($\neg$) and disjunction ($\lor$)
Truth table equivalence criterion

steps.label: Step 1: Formal truth valuation of p → q
steps.formula: $$ v(p \to q) = \begin{cases} F & \text{if } v(p) = T \text{ and } v(q) = F \\ T & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$
steps.explanation: In propositional logic, a conditional assertion is a promise: "if the condition holds, the consequence follows". The only circumstance under which this promise is broken is when the premise $p$ is fulfilled (True) yet the outcome $q$ fails to materialize (False). In all other three possibilities, the statement remains unbroken (True).

steps.label: Step 2: Valuation of the negation ¬p
steps.formula: $$ v(\neg p) = 1 - v(p) \implies \text{Row 1: } F, \quad \text{Row 2: } F, \quad \text{Row 3: } T, \quad \text{Row 4: } T $$
steps.explanation: Negation inverts truth values: for input rows $(T, T)$ and $(T, F)$, $\neg p$ evaluates to False ($F$). For rows $(F, T)$ and $(F, F)$ where hypothesis $p$ is false, $\neg p$ evaluates to True ($T$).

steps.label: Step 3: Valuation of the disjunction ¬p ∨ q
steps.explanation: A disjunction is True whenever at least one disjunct is True. Computing row-by-row: Row 1 ($F \lor T = T$), Row 2 ($F \lor F = F$), Row 3 ($T \lor T = T$), and Row 4 ($T \lor F = T$).

steps.label: Step 4: Exhaustive truth vector comparison
steps.formula: $$ [v(p \to q)] = \begin{pmatrix} T \\ F \\ T \\ T \end{pmatrix} = [v(\neg p \lor q)] $$
steps.explanation: Comparing the resulting truth columns demonstrates complete identity across all $2^2 = 4$ rows of the truth table. Since the truth values match under all possible interpretations, the two propositions are logically equivalent by definition.

The derived equivalence $(p 	o q) \equiv (

A conditional proposition $p 	o q$ is logically equivalent to its contrapositive $
eg q 	o 
eg p$, while not equivalent to its converse or inverse: $$ (p 	o q) \equiv (
eg q 	o 
eg p) $$

Double negation law: $\neg(\neg A) \equiv A$
Commutative law of disjunction: $(A \lor B) \equiv (B \lor A)$

We substitute the hypothesis $

steps.label: Step 3: Applying commutativity of disjunction
steps.explanation: Disjunction is an abelian (commutative) logical connective: the order of disjuncts does not alter the truth value of the compound proposition.

The resulting formula $

This purely algebraic derivation establishes the validity of Proof by Contraposition: to prove "if $p$ then $q$", one may instead prove "if not $q$ then not $p$". In contrast, the converse $q 	o p \equiv

examples.title: Spotting propositions
examples.problem: Which of the following are propositions, and what are their truth values? (a) Toronto is the capital of Canada. (b) 1 + 1 = 2. (c) What time is it? (d) x + 1 = 2.

steps.label: Step 1: Test (a) for declarative form and definite truth value
steps.text: It is a declarative sentence with a definite truth value — it is false, since Ottawa is the capital. So it is a proposition.

steps.label: Step 2: Test (b)
steps.text: 1 + 1 = 2 is a declarative sentence that is true — a proposition.

steps.label: Step 3: Test (c)
steps.text: A question has no truth value — not a proposition.

steps.label: Step 4: Test (d)
steps.text: “x + 1 = 2” depends on the value of x; it is a predicate (propositional function), not a proposition — until x is fixed.

examples.result: Only (a) and (b) are propositions: (a) is false, (b) is true.

examples.title: A two-variable truth table
examples.problem: Use a truth table to show that (p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (¬p ∨ q) is logically equivalent to p ↔ q.

steps.label: Step 1: List the four rows
steps.text: (p, q) over T T, T F, F T, F F, and add columns for ¬p and ¬q.

steps.label: Step 2: Compute the two disjuncts
steps.text: p ∨ ¬q gives T, T, F, T (rows 1–4) and ¬p ∨ q gives T, F, T, T.

steps.label: Step 3: Conjoin them
steps.text: (p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (¬p ∨ q) gives T, F, F, T.

steps.label: Step 4: Compare with the biconditional
steps.text: p ↔ q is true exactly when p and q agree: T, F, F, T — identical columns.

examples.result: The two propositions have the same truth value on every row, so (p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (¬p ∨ q) ≡ p ↔ q. Note each disjunct is itself a conditional in disguise: p ∨ ¬q ≡ q → p and ¬p ∨ q ≡ p → q.

examples.title: Translating and transforming a conditional
examples.problem: Let p be “It is raining this afternoon” and q be “The match will be cancelled.” Express the following in symbols: (a) If it is raining this afternoon, then the match will be cancelled. (b) its converse, (c) its contrapositive, (d) its inverse, and (e) “The match will be cancelled only if it is raining this afternoon.”

steps.label: Step 1: The conditional
steps.text: (a) is p → q.

steps.label: Step 2: Swap hypothesis and conclusion
steps.text: (b) The converse is q → p: if the match is cancelled, it is raining.

steps.label: Step 3: Negate and swap
steps.text: (c) The contrapositive is ¬q → ¬p: if the match is not cancelled, it is not raining.

steps.label: Step 4: Negate without swapping
steps.text: (d) The inverse is ¬p → ¬q: if it is not raining, the match is not cancelled.

steps.label: Step 5: Translate “only if”
steps.text: (e) “q only if p” means q → p — the same shape as the converse, not the original conditional.

examples.result: Only the original statement (a) and its contrapositive (c) are logically equivalent; the converse (b), inverse (d) and statement (e) say something different.

keyTakeaways: A proposition is a declarative sentence with a definite truth value, T or F.
∧ is true only when both parts are true; ∨ (inclusive) is false only when both are false; ⊕ is true exactly when exactly one part is true.
p → q is false only in the single case T → F; a false hypothesis makes the conditional vacuously true.
The contrapositive ¬q → ¬p is equivalent to p → q, but the converse q → p and inverse ¬p → ¬q are not.
Operator precedence: ¬ before ∧ before ∨ before → before ↔ — parentheses remove all doubt.
Bit strings store truth values, and bitwise ∧, ∨, ⊕ mirror the propositional connectives — the hardware bridge to Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Which of these sentences is a proposition?
quiz.explanation: A proposition must be a declarative sentence with a definite truth value. “3 + 5 = 8” qualifies (it is false). The others are an imperative, a question, and an open sentence whose truth depends on x.

quiz.q: If p is true and q is false, then p → q is:
options: True only because p is true
quiz.explanation: The conditional is false in exactly one situation: a true hypothesis with a false conclusion. That is precisely this case.

quiz.q: The exclusive or p ⊕ q is true exactly when:
options: both p and q are true
p and q have the same truth value
exactly one of p and q is true
neither p nor q is true
quiz.explanation: Exclusive or demands exactly one true operand: it is false both when both are true and when both are false.

quiz.q: The bitwise OR of the bit strings 01 1010 and 10 1001 is:
quiz.explanation: OR column by column: 0∨1 = 1, 1∨0 = 1, 1∨1 = 1, 0∨0 = 0, 1∨0 = 1, 0∨1 = 1, giving 11 1011. (00 1000 would be the AND, and 01 1001 the XOR.)

depth.title: Boolean algebras: the algebra behind the circuits

blocks.body: The connectives of Section 1.1 obey equational laws, and abstracting them yields a **Boolean algebra**: a set $B$ carrying operations $\land, \lor$, a complement $\lnot$, and constants $0, 1$, satisfying the commutative, associative, distributive and identity laws together with $x \land \lnot x = 0$, $x \lor \lnot x = 1$ and absorption. The truth values $\{0,1\}$ under the truth-table operations form the smallest nontrivial example, and every powerset $\mathcal{P}(S)$ under intersection, union and complementation forms another. Huntington (1904) proved that strikingly small equational bases suffice, and this corner of algebra became a benchmark for machines too: the Robbins conjecture — whether associativity, commutativity and the single Robbins equation already force Boolean structure — resisted mathematicians for sixty years until McCune's theorem prover EQP settled it in 1996. Boole's 1854 “algebra of thought” is thus both a theory with theorems of its own and a permanent test case for what automated reasoning can do.

blocks.heading: The duality principle
blocks.body: Let $e$ be any equation between terms of Boolean algebra that holds in every Boolean algebra. Then its **dual** $e^\ast$ — obtained throughout by exchanging $\land$ with $\lor$ and $0$ with $1$ — also holds in every Boolean algebra. Duality halves the equational workload: each proved identity manufactures a partner for free, so absorption $x \land (x \lor y) = x$ begets $x \lor (x \land y) = x$, and the two De Morgan laws of the equivalence section are duals of one another. What the truth-table section did by computing two columns, the duality principle does by pure symmetry.

Given a Boolean algebra $B$, form its **opposite** $B^{\mathrm{op}}$: the same underlying set, but with $x \land^{\mathrm{op}} y = x \lor y$ and $x \lor^{\mathrm{op}} y = x \land y$, the two constants exchanged, complementation unchanged. Each axiom of the Boolean-algebra axiomatization is carried by these exchanges onto another axiom — the axiom list is closed under duality — so $B^{\mathrm{op}}$ is again a Boolean algebra. Now let $e$ be an identity valid in every Boolean algebra, and let $C$ be an arbitrary one; we must show $e^\ast$ holds in $C$. Interpret the terms of $e$ in the Boolean algebra $C^{\mathrm{op}}$: the operation symbols of $e^\ast$, evaluated in $C$, behave exactly as those of $e$ behave in $C^{\mathrm{op}}$, so the truth of $e$ in $C^{\mathrm{op}}$ is precisely the truth of $e^\ast$ in $C$. Since $e$ holds in every Boolean algebra, $C^{\mathrm{op}}$ included, $e^\ast$ holds in $C$; and $C$ was arbitrary, so the dual identity holds universally.

blocks.heading: Finite Boolean algebras are powerset algebras
blocks.body: Every finite Boolean algebra $B$ is isomorphic to the powerset algebra of its set of **atoms** — its minimal nonzero elements. Consequently the cardinality of $B$ is a power of two; two finite Boolean algebras are isomorphic exactly when they have equally many atoms; and there is no Boolean algebra with 6 or 12 elements. The algebra with $k$ atoms has exactly $2^k$ elements, so the two-element truth-value algebra is the one-atom case and the eight-element algebra is the powerset of a three-element set in disguise.

Order $B$ by $x \le y$ iff $x \land y = x$. Call $a 
e 0$ an **atom** if $x \le a$ forces $x = 0$ or $x = a$. Every nonzero element dominates an atom: descending from any non-atom, $0 < x < b$, must terminate in a finite algebra, and it terminates at an atom below $b$. For an atom $a$ and any element $b$, either $a \le b$ or $a \le \lnot b$: the meet $a \land b$ lies below $a$, so it equals $0$ or $a$; if it is $a$ then $a \le b$; if it is $0$, then $a = a \land (b \lor \lnot b) = (a \land b) \lor (a \land \lnot b) = a \land \lnot b$, so $a \le \lnot b$. Now send each element to its atom set, $\pi(b) = \{a 	ext{ atom} : a \le b\}$. **Injectivity**: if $b 
e c$, say $b \land \lnot c 
e 0$; an atom below it lies below $b$ but not below $c$, so the atom sets differ. **Surjectivity and structure**: for a set $X$ of atoms with join $b =  igvee X$, the either/or lemma and distributivity show the atoms below $b$ are exactly the members of $X$; and meets, joins and complements act on atom sets by intersection, union and complementation. The map is an isomorphism onto the powerset algebra of the atoms of $B$.

blocks.heading: Logic synthesis
blocks.body: A combinational circuit's specification is a truth function, and the designer must realize it in gates: two-level logic realizes a disjunctive normal form directly, as an OR layer over an AND layer. Exact minimization — the Quine–McCluskey tabulation that generalizes Karnaugh maps — is itself exponentially costly, so industrial tools such as Espresso iterate safe local algebraic rewrites; modern flows rewrite circuits into **AND-inverter graphs** and hand equivalence checking to SAT solvers and binary decision diagrams against the specification. Behind the pipeline stands this section's mathematics: the specification is a Boolean function, the circuit is a term, and “does the implementation meet the spec?” is a propositional validity question — the consistency checking of the system-specifications subsection, scaled to millions of variables. Gate libraries are bases of a Boolean algebra, and technology mapping is a change of basis.

depth.title: Boolean function complexity: the lower-bound frontier

blocks.heading: Shannon's counting bound
blocks.body: Fix the binary basis $\{\land, \lor, \lnot\}$, negations on inputs free. As $n \to \infty$, the fraction of $n$-variable truth functions computable by circuits of size below $2^n/(c\,n)$ — for a suitable absolute constant $c$ — tends to $0$. Almost every truth function needs circuits of size proportional to $2^n/n$: exponential size is the norm, and the small, friendly formulas of this chapter are the freaks. Shannon's 1949 observation founded circuit complexity by proving that hard functions are not rare but overwhelmingly typical.

Count descriptions instead of functions. A circuit with $s$ two-input gates is described by choosing, for each gate, its operation and the two earlier sources feeding it — at most $(c(s+n))^{2s}$ descriptions in all, for an absolute constant $c$ — and this over-counts, since many descriptions are invalid or describe the same circuit. The number of $n$-variable truth functions is $2^{2^n}$. Choosing $c$ large and setting $s = 2^n/(c\,n)$, the number of descriptions is at most roughly $2^{2^n/4}$, an exponentially small fraction of the functions for large $n$. So all but a vanishing fraction of truth functions need more than $s$ gates: hard functions are not exotic, they are the overwhelming norm. What counting cannot do is **name** a hard function — it proves existence without exhibition — and that is exactly the gap that makes the next block a frontier rather than a settled chapter.

Against Shannon's guarantee, the best lower bound proved for any **explicitly presented** function over the full binary basis remains about $3n$ — Blum's 1984 construction, improved only marginally in four decades. The frontier therefore advances under restrictions. For constant-depth, unbounded-fan-in circuits of AND, OR and NOT gates ($\mathrm{AC}^0$), Håstad's switching-lemma analysis (1986) proves that parity requires size $2^{\Omega(n^{1/(d-1)})}$ at depth $d$ — exponential for every fixed depth — with matching quasipolynomial upper bounds nearby. For threshold circuits ($\mathrm{TC}^0$), no super-polynomial lower bound is known at all; for depth two the best bounds are barely super-linear (Kane–Williams, 2016). The natural-proofs barrier of Razborov and Rudich (1997) explains much of the stall. Every result here is a theorem about the truth functions of Section 1.1; every open gap is one.

blocks.heading: Ordered binary decision diagrams
blocks.body: A **BDD** is a directed acyclic graph of decision nodes — each tests one variable along two edges — whose shared subgraphs compress the truth table of a function; with a fixed variable order and a merge-equal-children reduction, the representation becomes **canonical** (Bryant, 1986), so equivalence and satisfiability reduce to graph comparison and the search for a path to the 1-terminal. Canonical BDDs power **symbolic model checking**: sets of states are stored as their characteristic functions, and the fixpoint computation of reachable states is executed entirely on BDDs, with image operations carried out on Boolean matrices. This is the technology with which the model checkers of Clarke, Emerson and Sifakis (Turing Award, 2007) reached industrial scale, and the variable-order sensitivity of the representation — an art as much as a theorem — remains a live research topic.

Over $\mathbb{F}_2$, every truth function has a unique **algebraic normal form** — a polynomial $f = \bigoplus_{S} a_S \bigwedge_{i \in S} p_i$, with one coefficient per subset of the variables — computed by the Möbius transform on the subset lattice. This is the working language of stream-cipher design, where filter and combining functions on register states are specified, and attacked, through their ANFs: algebraic degree governs higher-order differential attacks, and **bent functions** — those at maximal Hamming distance from the affine functions — are sought exactly through this normal form. The same representation underlies the SAT-encoding of XOR constraints, where it explains why resolution struggles with parity reasoning.

intro: Propositional logic is not an abstract game — it is a working tool for software engineers, search engines, puzzle solvers and chip designers. This section trains you to translate English (including slippery phrases like “only if” and “unless”) into logic, to check that a list of system specifications is consistent, and to see how logic powers Boolean searches, famous puzzles and digital circuits.
objectives: Translate nuanced English sentences, including “only if” and “unless”, into compound propositions
Test a list of system specifications for consistency
Write Boolean search queries using AND, OR and NOT
Solve knights-and-knaves puzzles with case analysis
Explain how digital circuits implement propositional connectives

concepts.statement: To translate an English sentence into logic: **(1)** identify the atomic propositions and name them p, q, r, …; **(2)** combine them with the connective matching the English wording — “and” → ∧, “(inclusive) or” → ∨, “exclusive or” → ⊕, “if … then” → →, “if and only if” → ↔, “not / it is not the case that” → ¬.
concepts.detail: Translation is the hard part: natural language is ambiguous, logic is not. Once a sentence is translated, everything that follows (equivalence checking, satisfiability, reasoning) becomes mechanical.

concepts.statement: A **system specification** is a compound proposition describing required behavior of a system. A collection of specifications is **consistent** if there is at least one assignment of truth values to the variables that makes every specification true simultaneously.
concepts.detail: If no such assignment exists, the specifications are inconsistent and no system can implement them — a disaster if discovered after the system is built. This is why spec lists are checked with logic before code is written.

concepts.statement: To check consistency: assign a variable to each atomic claim, translate every specification, then determine (for example with a truth table) whether at least one row makes all of them true.
concepts.detail: One satisfying assignment is enough to prove consistency; every row failing some specification proves inconsistency.

concepts.statement: Web and database searches use Boolean operators that mirror the connectives: **AND** matches pages containing all terms (∧), **OR** matches pages containing at least one term (∨), **NOT** excludes pages containing a term (¬), and parentheses group.
concepts.detail: A query like (Utah OR Arizona) AND hiking AND NOT Colorado retrieves pages mentioning hiking and one of the two states, but excludes any page mentioning Colorado — propositional logic with a search engine.

concepts.statement: In knights-and-knaves puzzles every inhabitant is either a **knight**, who always tells the truth, or a **knave**, who always lies. Translate each statement, then run a case analysis: assume a speaker is a knight (statement true) or a knave (statement false) and keep only the consistent assignments.
concepts.detail: The power of the method is that contradictions prune possibilities quickly — often one or two case checks are enough to pin down every inhabitant's type.

concepts.statement: Digital circuits realize propositional logic: signals are bits (0 = false, 1 = true) and gates compute connectives — the **inverter** (NOT gate) outputs ¬p, the **OR gate** outputs p ∨ q, the **AND gate** outputs p ∧ q.
concepts.detail: Any compound proposition can be built as a circuit of these gates, and every circuit computes a compound proposition. Chapter 12 develops this correspondence into Boolean algebra and circuit minimization.

concepts.statement: “q is necessary for p” means p → q; “q is sufficient for p” means q → p; “p only if q” means p → q; “p unless q” means ¬q → p (equivalently p ∨ q); “neither p nor q” means ¬p ∧ ¬q.
concepts.detail: Watch the direction: “You can graduate only if you complete 120 credits” translates as graduate → credits, *not* credits → graduate. Mixing up the direction of “only if” is the single most common translation error.

examples.title: Are these specifications consistent?
examples.problem: Specifications: (1) The diagnostic message is stored in the buffer or it is retransmitted. (2) The diagnostic message is not stored in the buffer. (3) If the diagnostic message is stored in the buffer, then it is retransmitted. Are they consistent?

steps.label: Step 1: Assign variables and translate
steps.text: Let p = “the message is stored in the buffer,” q = “the message is retransmitted.” The specs are: p ∨ q; ¬p; p → q.

steps.label: Step 2: Use the strongest constraint first
steps.text: Spec 2, ¬p, forces p = F.

steps.label: Step 3: Propagate
steps.text: With p = F, spec 1 (p ∨ q) forces q = T.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify the remaining spec
steps.text: Spec 3 becomes F → T, which is true.

examples.result: Yes — the assignment p = F, q = T satisfies all three specifications, so the system can be built.

examples.title: The island of knights and knaves
examples.problem: You meet two islanders, A and B. A says: “We are both knaves.” What are A and B?

steps.label: Step 1: Case 1 — suppose A is a knight
steps.text: Then A's statement is true, so both are knaves — contradicting A being a knight. This case is impossible.

steps.label: Step 2: Case 2 — suppose A is a knave
steps.text: Then A's statement is false: it is not the case that both are knaves.

steps.label: Step 3: Finish the deduction
steps.text: Since A is a knave, the only way “both are knaves” can be false is that B is a knight.

examples.result: A is a knave and B is a knight.

examples.title: Designing a Boolean search query
examples.problem: You want web pages about hiking trails in Utah or Arizona, but nothing about Colorado. Write the query.

steps.label: Step 1: Identify the alternatives
steps.text: Utah or Arizona — a disjunction: (Utah OR Arizona).

steps.label: Step 2: Add the mandatory term
steps.text: AND hiking AND trails — conjunctions narrow the result.

steps.label: Step 3: Add the exclusion
steps.text: NOT Colorado removes every page mentioning Colorado.

examples.result: (Utah OR Arizona) AND hiking AND trails NOT Colorado — AND narrows, OR broadens, NOT excludes, exactly like ∧, ∨, ¬.

keyTakeaways: Translate first, reason second: name the atomic propositions, then connect them.
“p only if q” is p → q; “p unless q” is ¬q → p (i.e., p ∨ q).
A specification list is consistent exactly when some truth assignment makes all specs true at once.
Boolean search operators AND, OR, NOT behave like ∧, ∨, ¬ with parentheses for grouping.
Knights-and-knaves puzzles are solved by case analysis: assume each speaker's type and discard contradictory cases.
Inverters, OR gates and AND gates physically implement ¬, ∨, ∧ — logic is the blueprint of hardware.

quiz.q: A list of system specifications is consistent when:
options: at least one truth assignment makes every specification true at once
no two specifications mention the same variable
all specifications can be false simultaneously
quiz.explanation: Consistency means the conjunction of all specifications is satisfiable — one row of the joint truth table where everything is true. Tautologies are irrelevant, and all-false says nothing about all-true.

quiz.q: The specifications “p ∨ q”, “¬p”, and “p → q” are simultaneously satisfied when:
quiz.explanation: ¬p forces p = F; then p ∨ q forces q = T; and p → q becomes F → T, which is true. No other assignment works (with p = F, q = F the first spec fails).

quiz.q: “You will pass the course unless you skip the final exam” (p: you pass; q: you skip the final) translates as:
quiz.explanation: “p unless q” means that when the “unless” condition fails, p must hold: ¬q → p, equivalently p ∨ q. The other options reverse the direction or claim equivalence where none exists.

quiz.q: An islander says “I am a knave.” On an island where knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie:
options: the situation is impossible — neither type could truthfully or falsely say this
the speaker's type cannot be determined
quiz.explanation: A knight saying it would be asserting a falsehood (impossible for a knight); a knave saying it would be asserting a truth (impossible for a knave). No inhabitant can ever make this statement, so the scenario is impossible.

depth.title: Equational logic, resolution, and satisfiability

blocks.body: Section 1.3 works equivalences by hand; the graduate reading makes the tool precise. Logical equivalence is a **congruence** on formulas: it is an equivalence relation, and it is preserved in every context — if $\varphi \equiv \psi$ then $C[\varphi] \equiv C[\psi]$ for any formula $C$ with a hole — which is precisely the license an algebraic derivation uses when it rewrites one subformula at a time and leaves the rest alone. The same frame exposes the deep symmetry of the subject: **satisfiability and validity are duals**, since $\varphi$ is valid exactly when $\lnot\varphi$ is unsatisfiable, so a refutation engine for one is a decision engine for the other. That design decision powers every theorem prover, and the two technologies that follow — resolution and Horn propagation — are the two exploitations of it that survive into modern practice.

blocks.heading: Resolution is sound and refutation-complete
blocks.body: A **clause** is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is read as its set of clauses. From clauses $A \lor p$ and $B \lor \lnot p$, resolution infers the **resolvent** $A \lor B$. Resolution is sound — every resolvent is a logical consequence of its parents — and, as a refutation system, complete: an unsatisfiable clause set has a resolution derivation of the empty clause, and a satisfiable one never derives it. Refutation by resolution is therefore a complete alternative to truth tables: to prove $\varphi$ a tautology, refute the clause set of $\lnot\varphi$.

Soundness is a two-case check: at any assignment satisfying both parents, if $p$ is false then the clause $A \lor p$ is satisfied through some literal of $A$, and if $p$ is true then $B \lor \lnot p$ is satisfied through $B$; either way $A \lor B$ holds. Completeness follows by induction on the number of variables, the Davis–Putnam elimination. Let $\Sigma$ be an unsatisfiable clause set; close it under resolution on the single variable $p$, and delete every clause containing $p$ or $\lnot p$, obtaining $\Sigma'$ over the remaining variables. Every clause of $\Sigma'$ is derivable from $\Sigma$, so suppose toward contradiction that some assignment $\sigma$ satisfies $\Sigma'$. Split the clauses of $\Sigma$ into those containing $p$, those containing $\lnot p$, and the rest — the rest survive into $\Sigma'$, so $\sigma$ satisfies them. If setting $p$ true falsifies $\Sigma$, some clause $B \lor \lnot p$ has $B$ false under $\sigma$; if setting $p$ false also fails, some clause $A \lor p$ has $A$ false under $\sigma$; then the resolvent $A \lor B$ — which the closure placed in $\Sigma'$ — is falsified by $\sigma$, contradicting that $\sigma$ satisfies $\Sigma'$. So one of the two settings satisfies $\Sigma$: an unsatisfiable $\Sigma$ forces $\Sigma'$ unsatisfiable, and by induction the empty clause is derivable from $\Sigma'$, hence from $\Sigma$. A satisfying set can never derive the empty clause — soundness again — so refutation exactly characterizes unsatisfiability.

blocks.heading: Unit propagation solves Horn-SAT
blocks.body: A **Horn clause** is a disjunction of literals with at most one positive literal, equivalently an implication $p_1 \land \cdots \land p_k \to q$ — a **fact** when $k = 0$, a **goal** when the head is falsity. A Horn formula is satisfiable if and only if the following fixpoint computation succeeds: start with the set $U$ of facts; whenever all premises of a clause have entered $U$, add its conclusion; if a goal clause's premises all enter $U$, report unsatisfiable. If the process stops without failure, $U$ is the **least model** of the definite clauses — contained in every other model — and the whole computation runs in time linear in the formula size (Dowling and Gallier, 1984). This fixpoint is exactly how logic-programming interpreters execute queries, and why pure Prolog programs are tractable.

Let $U^\ast$ be the closure the propagation computes, and let $M$ be any model of the formula. By induction on the stages, every stage is contained in $M$: the facts are clauses with empty bodies, which $M$ must satisfy outright; and if all premises of $p_1 \land \cdots \land p_k \to q$ lie in $M$, then $M$ satisfies the clause only if $q \in M$. Hence $U^\ast \subseteq M$ for every model $M$ — the propagation computes the least model of the definite clauses, which is where linear-time satisfiability comes from: only one candidate needs testing. Now both directions are immediate. If the process stops without a goal firing, then $U^\ast$ itself is a model: each definite clause either had its conclusion added, or some premise is forever absent, hence false in $U^\ast$; and each goal clause has a premise forever absent, so it holds vacuously. If instead a goal fires, all its premises lie in $U^\ast$, hence in every model, so every model falsifies that goal clause — the formula is unsatisfiable. A linear-time implementation keeps a counter of unsatisfied premises per clause and a queue of newly derived atoms.

blocks.heading: Two-SAT as an implication graph
blocks.body: A 2-SAT instance is a graph problem in disguise. For each clause $(\lnot p \lor q)$ add the implications $p \to q$ and $\lnot q \to \lnot p$ — a clause is false exactly when the corresponding implication is violated — producing the **implication graph**, which is skew-symmetric: whenever it contains the edge $l \to m$ it also contains $\lnot m \to \lnot l$. An assignment satisfies the formula exactly when the set of literals it makes true is closed under the edges. **The criterion (Aspvall–Plass–Tarjan, 1979)**: the formula is satisfiable if and only if no variable has $p$ and $\lnot p$ in the same strongly connected component. Necessity is immediate: a cycle through both forces any consistent assignment to make both true — an impossibility. For sufficiency, topologically order the components of the condensation and set each variable true exactly when its literal's component comes **after** its negation's; skew-symmetry guarantees the choice is consistent, because an edge from a chosen-true literal leads to another chosen-true one, and any contradiction inside the ordering would collapse the two complementary components into a single cycle. The result: satisfiability of 2-CNF in linear time by depth-first search — structure in the clause set buys algorithms that brute force cannot see.

depth.title: Proof complexity: resolution and its limits

blocks.heading: Haken's pigeonhole bound
blocks.body: Let $\mathrm{PHP}_n$ — the pigeonhole principle for $n$ holes and $n+1$ pigeons — be written as an unsatisfiable CNF over variables $p_{ij}$ reading “pigeon $i$ sits in hole $j$,” with clauses asserting that every pigeon sits somewhere and that no hole holds two pigeons. Every resolution refutation of $\mathrm{PHP}_n$ has length at least $2^{\Omega(n)}$, although the formula itself has only polynomially many clauses. Resolution — the complete rule of the Level II notes — is nonetheless **exponentially weak** on this most combinatorial of tautologies: the first super-polynomial lower bound in proof complexity (Haken, 1985), and still the textbook exhibit of the gap between completeness and efficiency.

Haken's technique is **bottleneck counting**. Call an assignment of the pigeon variables *critical* when it comes from an injective placement of $n$ of the pigeons into the $n$ holes, the last pigeon left homeless; such an assignment satisfies every clause but one, and a refutation must kill every critical assignment by deriving some clause it falsifies. The counting shows that any clause of moderate width kills only a few critical assignments — an isoperimetric fact about partial matchings — so exponentially many clauses are needed to cover them all. Later work systematized the phenomenon: Ben-Sasson and Wigderson (2001) proved a general **width–size tradeoff**, converting lower bounds on the width of any refutation into lower bounds on its length, and the pigeonhole formulas remain the laboratory in which the field tests its instruments. The exact resolution complexity of the *onto* variant — where every hole must be occupied — is a subtler quantity tied to matching structures.

The broader program is **proof complexity**, posed by Stephen Cook in the 1970s: is there a propositional proof system in which every tautology has a polynomial-size proof? Such a “super” system exists exactly if $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{coNP}$, making the question the natural dual of the P versus NP problem of the first section's Level III notes. The known map is ragged: resolution and its refinements fall to exponential bounds, and constant-depth Frege systems fall on counting principles (Beame–Pitassi–Impagliazzo; Krajíček–Pudlák–Woods, 1990s). But for **Frege systems** — ordinary Hilbert-style propositional calculi — no super-polynomial lower bound is known at all, only quadratic ones, and separating Frege from **extended Frege**, which merely adds definitional abbreviations, is a recognized open problem. Each lower bound is a theorem about the limits of an inference style; each gap is a theorem about the limits of current mathematics.

intro: Two propositions that always share the same truth value are logically equivalent, and the algebra of such equivalences is what makes logic computable. This section builds the complete law toolkit — De Morgan's laws, the distributive laws, the conditional-biconditional rewrites — and applies it to classifying tautologies and testing satisfiability.
objectives: Classify propositions as tautologies, contradictions, or contingencies
Prove equivalences with truth tables and with algebraic derivations
Use De Morgan's laws and the standard equivalence laws fluently
Rewrite conditionals and biconditionals in terms of ∧, ∨, ¬
Determine whether a compound proposition is satisfiable

concepts.statement: A compound proposition is a **tautology** if it is true for every assignment of truth values to its variables, a **contradiction** if it is false for every assignment, and a **contingency** otherwise.
concepts.detail: p ∨ ¬p is a tautology; p ∧ ¬p is a contradiction; p ∨ q is a contingency (its truth depends on the facts). Only tautologies and contradictions are independent of how the world actually is.

concepts.statement: Propositions p and q are **logically equivalent**, written p ≡ q, if and only if p ↔ q is a tautology — equivalently, if they have identical truth tables.
concepts.detail: The symbol ≡ is not the equals sign: it asserts a fact about truth values, and it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. A very useful test: p ≡ q iff p ↔ q is a tautology.

concepts.statement: **¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q** and **¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q**: the negation of a conjunction is the disjunction of the negations, and the negation of a disjunction is the conjunction of the negations.
concepts.detail: Negation flips ∧ into ∨ and vice versa. These are the most-used laws in the chapter — “not (p and q)” means “not p or not q,” not “not p and not q.”

concepts.statement: Identity: p ∧ T ≡ p, p ∨ F ≡ p. Domination: p ∨ T ≡ T, p ∧ F ≡ F. Idempotent: p ∨ p ≡ p, p ∧ p ≡ p. Double negation: ¬¬p ≡ p. Commutative: p ∨ q ≡ q ∨ p, p ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p. Associative: (p ∨ q) ∨ r ≡ p ∨ (q ∨ r), and likewise for ∧. Distributive: p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r), p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r). Absorption: p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p, p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p. Negation: p ∨ ¬p ≡ T, p ∧ ¬p ≡ F.
concepts.detail: These mirror the laws of arithmetic (commutative, associative, distributive) plus logic-specific ones (domination, absorption, negation). Memorize them — every algebraic proof is a chain of these steps.

concepts.statement: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q ≡ ¬q → ¬p. Also p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p (contrapositive) and (p ∧ ¬q) → F is the “proof by contradiction” form. For the biconditional: p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q) ≡ ¬(p ⊕ q).
concepts.detail: The single most useful identity in the book: an implication is an or in disguise. It converts every conditional into ∧/∨/¬ territory, where the algebraic laws operate.

concepts.statement: Every substitution instance of a tautology is a tautology: replacing the variables p, q, r in an equivalence by arbitrary compound propositions yields a new equivalence.
concepts.detail: From De Morgan's law we immediately get ¬((p → r) ∧ (q ∨ s)) ≡ ¬(p → r) ∨ ¬(q ∨ s) without any new truth table. This is why a short list of laws generates endless valid reasoning.

concepts.statement: A compound proposition is **satisfiable** if there is an assignment of truth values to its variables that makes it true. A compound proposition is a tautology if and only if its negation is not satisfiable.
concepts.detail: Satisfiability (SAT) is computationally hard in general but enormously useful: Sudoku, n-queens and circuit verification all reduce to finding a satisfying assignment of a giant compound proposition built from the puzzle's constraints.

concepts.statement: **(1) Truth tables**: build the 2ⁿ rows for each side and compare columns — always works, but doubles with each variable. **(2) Algebraic derivation**: transform one side into the other with the known laws, citing each step.
concepts.detail: Prefer algebra once you have three or more variables. A hybrid strategy is also legitimate: show each side is equivalent to some common third proposition.

concepts.statement: Every compound proposition can be rewritten using only ∧, ∨ and ¬ (conditionals eliminated via p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q), and even using a single connective such as NAND (¬(p ∧ q)), which is functionally complete.
concepts.detail: This is why hardware can be built from one type of gate, and why mastering ∧, ∨, ¬ manipulations is enough in principle — every other connective is an abbreviation.

examples.title: An algebraic equivalence proof
examples.problem: Show that ¬(p ∨ (¬p ∧ q)) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q using the laws of logic.

steps.label: Step 1: Apply De Morgan's second law to the outer negation
Step 2: Apply De Morgan's first law and double negation
steps.text: ¬(¬p ∧ q) ≡ ¬(¬p) ∨ ¬q ≡ p ∨ ¬q, so the whole expression is ¬p ∧ (p ∨ ¬q).

steps.label: Step 4: Negation and identity laws
steps.text: (¬p ∧ p) ≡ F, and F ∨ X ≡ X, leaving ¬p ∧ ¬q.

examples.result: ¬(p ∨ (¬p ∧ q)) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q, proved in four law-cited steps with no truth table.

examples.title: Proving a tautology without a truth table
examples.problem: Show that (p ∧ q) → (p ∨ q) is a tautology.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply De Morgan's law
steps.text: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q, giving (¬p ∨ ¬q) ∨ (p ∨ q).

steps.label: Step 3: Reassociate and pair opposites
steps.text: By commutativity and associativity: (¬p ∨ p) ∨ (¬q ∨ q).

steps.label: Step 4: Apply the negation law, then domination
steps.text: (¬p ∨ p) ≡ T and (¬q ∨ q) ≡ T, so the expression is T ∨ T ≡ T.

examples.result: The proposition is true under every assignment — a tautology.

examples.title: Testing satisfiability
examples.problem: Determine whether (p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (¬p ∨ q) ∧ (¬p ∨ ¬q) is satisfiable.

steps.label: Step 1: Try p = T, q = T
steps.text: The third clause ¬p ∨ ¬q is F — fails.

steps.label: Step 2: Try p = T, q = F
steps.text: The second clause ¬p ∨ q is F — fails.

steps.label: Step 3: Try p = F, q = T
steps.text: The first clause p ∨ ¬q is F — fails.

steps.label: Step 4: Try p = F, q = F
steps.text: All three clauses evaluate to T — the assignment works.

examples.result: The proposition is satisfiable (only at p = F, q = F). Searching the four rows of the truth table was enough here; SAT solvers do exactly this search, but smarter, for millions of variables.

keyTakeaways: p ≡ q iff p ↔ q is a tautology — equivalently, the two truth tables match row for row.
De Morgan's laws: negation swaps ∧ with ∨ — the most frequently used equivalences in the course.
p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q ≡ ¬q → ¬p — one proposition in three shapes.
Algebraic derivation beats truth tables as soon as the variable count grows.
Satisfiable means some assignment makes the proposition true; a tautology's negation is unsatisfiable.
The identity, domination, idempotent, double-negation, commutative, associative, distributive, absorption and negation laws form your complete proof toolkit.

quiz.q: ¬(p ∧ q) is logically equivalent to:
quiz.explanation: By De Morgan's law the negation of a conjunction is the disjunction of the negations: ¬p ∨ ¬q. (p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q is not equivalent: at p = F, q = F we get ¬(F) = T but ¬p ∨ q = F.)

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT equivalent to p → q?
quiz.explanation: ¬p → ¬q is the inverse of the conditional, not equivalent to it. The others are the disjunctive form, the contrapositive, and an absorption-style rewrite — all equivalent to p → q.

quiz.q: The compound proposition (p ∨ ¬p) → q simplifies to:
quiz.explanation: p ∨ ¬p ≡ T, and T → q ≡ ¬T ∨ q ≡ q. The whole proposition says exactly as much as q itself.

quiz.q: The proposition (p ∨ q) ∧ (¬p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (¬p ∨ ¬q) is:
options: a tautology — it is true at p = q = T
satisfiable only at p = T, q = F
not satisfiable — every assignment falsifies at least one clause
quiz.explanation: Check the four assignments: T,T fails clause 4; T,F fails clause 2; F,T fails clause 3; F,F fails clause 1. No assignment satisfies all four clauses, so the proposition is a contradiction (unsatisfiable).

depth.title: Tarskian semantics, definability, and prenex forms

blocks.body: Tarski's 1933 move makes “meaning” precise. A **structure** $\mathcal{A} = (A;\, R^{\mathcal{A}}_1, f^{\mathcal{A}}_1, c^{\mathcal{A}}_1, \dots)$ is a nonempty set $A$ — the **universe** — together with interpretations: a concrete relation for each predicate symbol, a concrete function for each function symbol, a concrete element for each constant. A **variable assignment** is a function $s$ from variables to $A$. Satisfaction $\mathcal{A} \models \varphi[s]$ is then defined by **recursion on formulas**: atoms hold when the interpreted tuple belongs to the interpreted relation; connectives follow the truth tables; and $\mathcal{A} \models \forall x\, \varphi[s]$ exactly when $\mathcal{A} \models \varphi[s(x|a)]$ for **every** $a \in A$, where $s(x|a)$ reassigns $x$ to $a$. A sentence's truth depends on $\mathcal{A}$ alone, and this clause-by-clause definition is what makes every later metatheorem — substitution, prenexing, completeness — provable by induction.

blocks.heading: Prenex normal form
blocks.body: Every first-order formula $\varphi$ is logically equivalent to one of the shape $Q_1 x_1 \cdots Q_k x_k\, \psi$ — all quantifiers in front, the **matrix** $\psi$ quantifier-free — with $k$ at most the number of quantifier occurrences in $\varphi$. The rewriting uses the quantifier dualities $\lnot \forall x\, \varphi \equiv \exists x\, \lnot \varphi$ and $\lnot \exists x\, \varphi \equiv \forall x\, \lnot \varphi$, together with the commutations $(Q x\, \varphi) \circ \chi \equiv Q x (\varphi \circ \chi)$ for a binary connective $\circ$, valid whenever $x$ is not free in $\chi$; renaming bound variables keeps that proviso true. The theorem is the engine behind clausification and Skolemization in every automated prover.

The algorithm: push negations inward with the dualities until they sit on atoms (the propositional De Morgan laws handle the connectives), then pull quantifiers outward past the binary connectives, renaming bound variables whenever the proviso fails. Correctness rests on two lemmas. First, the dualities are semantic facts: by Tarski's recursion, $\mathcal{A} \models \lnot \forall x\, \varphi[s]$ iff not every $a \in A$ yields $\mathcal{A} \models \varphi[s(x|a)]$ iff some $a$ fails iff $\mathcal{A} \models \exists x\, \lnot \varphi[s]$. Second, the **coincidence lemma**: satisfaction of $\chi$ under $s$ depends only on the values of the free variables of $\chi$ (structural induction on $\chi$); so when $x$ is not free in $\chi$, the assignments $s(x|a)$ all agree with $s$ on $\chi$, and the commutation preserves truth at every assignment. Renaming bound variables — alpha-conversion — is sound for the same reason, and fresh names always exist. Each pulling step strictly decreases the number of quantifiers buried under a connective, so the algorithm terminates with all quantifiers in prefix position and the matrix quantifier-free, equivalence preserved at every step.

blocks.heading: What a structure can and cannot define
blocks.body: Work in the structure $\mathcal{Z} = (\mathbb{Z}; +, 0)$. The even integers **are definable**: the formula $\exists y\,(y + y = x)$ holds exactly of the even elements. The order relation is **not definable**, and the proof is the **automorphism method**. The map $\pi(x) = -x$ is an automorphism of $\mathcal{Z}$ — a bijection with $\pi(x + y) = \pi(x) + \pi(y)$ and $\pi(0) = 0$ — and a structural induction shows definable relations are preserved by every automorphism: atomic formulas transfer because $\pi$ respects the interpreted operations, and the quantifier step transfers because $\pi$ is onto. So if some formula $\theta(x, y)$ defined the order, then from $\mathcal{Z} \models \theta(0, 1)$ — true, since $0 < 1$ — preservation would give $\mathcal{Z} \models \theta(\pi(0), \pi(1))$, that is $\mathcal{Z} \models \theta(0, -1)$, forcing $0 < -1$ — false. The method generalizes: to prove undefinability, find a symmetry of the structure that the would-be definition fails to respect, and the same idea scales to Ehrenfeucht–Fraïssé games at Level III of the nested-quantifiers section.

Two classical theorems show first-order logic cannot control cardinality. **Downward Löwenheim–Skolem**: a structure in a countable language has a countable **elementary submodel** — close the interpretations under the functions definable in the language, and a Tarski test shows the closure satisfies the same sentences. **Upward Löwenheim–Skolem**: a theory with an infinite model has models of every larger cardinality — add $\kappa$ fresh constants with axioms making them pairwise distinct; every finite subset is satisfiable in the infinite model, so compactness (proved at Level II of the inference section) supplies a model of the whole. The punchline is the **Skolem paradox**: if Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory is consistent, it has a countable model — a universe internally certifying uncountable sets, itself countable from outside. The escape is instructive: the witnessing bijection is not an element of the model, because countability is not first-order definable within it. First-order expressive power has a hard ceiling; the Level III notes below measure it.

The empty domain is excluded by convention: on it $\forall x\, \varphi$ would be vacuously true and $\exists x\, \varphi$ vacuously false, breaking the duality $\lnot \forall \equiv \exists \lnot$ that the whole apparatus leans on — Tarski's choice, made to keep De Morgan's laws for quantifiers intact. Substitution must also respect binding: substituting a term $t$ containing $y$ into $\varphi(x)$ under a $\forall y$ **captures** the variable, and the result is meaningless. Alpha-conversion — renaming bound variables to fresh ones — is the repair, and capture-avoiding substitution is exactly the hygiene condition every proof assistant, from Prolog to Lean, enforces mechanically before it will accept a rewrite.

depth.title: The expressive ceiling of first-order logic

blocks.body: Church's theorem (1936; Turing's route was independent): **validity in first-order logic is undecidable** — no algorithm decides whether an arbitrary sentence holds in all structures. The reduction encodes a Turing machine's halting problem into a sentence of a small signature, true exactly of encoding structures in which the machine halts. Validity is nevertheless **semidecidable**: Gödel's completeness theorem turns proof search into a sound and complete semi-decision procedure, so valid sentences are eventually proved while invalid ones may run forever — the first great undecidability result, and the reason automated provers must be smarter than enumeration. On finite structures the picture inverts: by Trakhtenbrot's theorem (1950), the set of sentences with **finite** models is not semidecidable either, so finite and classical model theory are genuinely different subjects — a fact that shapes every theorem in this tier, since all of them concern finite structures.

blocks.heading: The zero–one law
blocks.body: Endow the graphs on vertex set $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with the distribution $G(n, 1/2)$ — every labeled graph equally likely. For every first-order sentence $\varphi$ of the language of graphs, the limiting probability $\mu(\varphi) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \Pr\bigl[G(n,1/2) \models \varphi\bigr]$ exists and equals $0$ or $1$. The consequence: any graph property whose asymptotic probability fails to converge, or converges to a value strictly between 0 and 1, is not first-order — parity of the number of edges is the standard casualty, oscillating near one-half forever. There are no asymptotically delicate first-order graph properties (Fagin, 1976).

The engine is the family of **extension axioms**: for all disjoint tuples $\bar a, \bar b$ of distinct vertices, there is a vertex adjacent to every member of $\bar a$ and to none of $\bar b$. In $G(n, 1/2)$ a fixed vertex fails to serve with probability $1 - 2^{-(|\bar a| + |\bar b|)}$, so the probability that no vertex serves is at most $\left(1 - 2^{-(|\bar a| + |\bar b|)}\right)^{n}$, which tends to $0$: each single axiom holds asymptotically almost surely. Let $T$ collect all extension axioms. A back-and-forth argument shows any two models of $T$ satisfy the same first-order sentences — $T$ is complete; its unique countable model is the **Rado graph**, the countable random graph. Now fix $\varphi$. If $T \models \varphi$, compactness yields a finite $T_0 \subseteq T$ entailing $\varphi$, and $\Pr[G \models T_0] \to 1$ by a union bound over finitely many axioms, so $\mu(\varphi) = 1$. Otherwise $T \models \lnot \varphi$, and the same argument gives $\mu(\varphi) = 0$. There is no third outcome, and every first-order sentence is decided by the extension axioms alone.

blocks.heading: Fagin's theorem
blocks.body: A class of finite structures is decidable in **NP** if and only if it is definable by an **existential second-order** sentence — first-order logic augmented with relation variables $R_1, \dots, R_k$ that are existentially quantified, with the body itself first-order. The certificate a nondeterministic machine guesses is nothing but the interpretation of the second-order variables: three-colorability is $\exists R, G, B$ (“the three color classes cover the graph”), and admitting a Hamiltonian path is $\exists L$ (“$L$ linearly orders the vertices with consecutive ones adjacent”). Complexity classes thereby **become logics** — the program of **descriptive complexity** (Fagin, 1974): the polynomial hierarchy is exactly full second-order logic (Stockmeyer), and PSPACE and the exponent-time classes correspond to suitable fixpoint and second-order fragments on ordered structures. The one class that refuses every natural logical characterization is the most important one — the open problem below.

blocks.heading: A logic for polynomial time
blocks.body: Is there a “reasonable” logic whose sentences define exactly the polynomial-time properties of finite structures? Fagin's theorem captures NP elegantly, but P has resisted every candidate: the natural fixpoint logics capture P only on **ordered** structures, and Gurevich conjectured that no logic captures P on unordered structures at all — a conjecture which, if proved, would separate P from NP. Abiteboul and Vianu's reductions show the unordered question collapses onto deep separations between database query languages, one of the rare places where logic, database theory and complexity are provably the same question. After fifty years, the polynomial-time properties of finite structures still have no logic to call home.

intro: Propositions are too coarse to say “every prime larger than 2 is odd” — that sentence talks about objects and needs variables. Predicates are propositions with holes in them, and quantifiers ∀ and ∃ are the tools that plug the holes by sweeping over whole domains. Nearly every theorem in mathematics is a quantified predicate statement.
objectives: Evaluate predicates and propositional functions on concrete domains
Translate between quantified statements and English in both directions
Negate statements with ∀ and ∃ correctly
Understand exactly when universal and existential statements are true or false
Recognize and expand the uniqueness quantifier ∃!

concepts.statement: A **predicate** P(x) is a sentence containing a variable that becomes a proposition when the variable is assigned a value from its domain. P(x) itself is a **propositional function**; P(5) is a proposition.
concepts.detail: “x is greater than 3” is a predicate: substituting x = 5 gives the true proposition “5 > 3,” while x = 2 gives a false one. Predicates can take several variables: P(x, y): “x + y = 0.”

concepts.statement: The **domain** of a predicate is the set of values its variables may take; the truth of a quantified statement is always relative to this domain.
concepts.detail: The statement ∀x (x² ≥ x) is true over the positive integers but false over the real numbers (x = ½ fails). Always ask: quantified over what?

concepts.statement: The **universal quantification** ∀x P(x) is the proposition “P(x) is true for all values of x in the domain.” It is true exactly when P(x) holds for every element, and a single counterexample makes it false.
concepts.detail: English cues: “for all,” “for every,” “all,” “each.” Over the empty domain it is vacuously true. To disprove a universal, exhibit one counterexample; to prove it, you must handle every element.

concepts.statement: The **existential quantification** ∃x P(x) is the proposition “there exists an x in the domain such that P(x).” It is true exactly when at least one **witness** exists, and false when P(x) fails for every element.
concepts.detail: English cues: “there exists,” “some,” “at least one.” To prove an existential, exhibit one witness; to disprove it, you must show every element fails.

concepts.statement: **¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x)** and **¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x)**: negation flips the quantifier and negates the predicate.
concepts.detail: “Not everyone passed the exam” means “someone failed the exam”; “no student failed” means “every student passed.” Getting this backwards is a classic exam error — think through the English, not just the symbols.

concepts.statement: ∀x > 0 (x² ≥ x) abbreviates ∀x (x > 0 → x² ≥ x), while ∃x > 0 (x² = 25) abbreviates ∃x (x > 0 ∧ x² = 25): restricting a **universal** uses a conditional, restricting an **existential** uses a conjunction.
concepts.detail: This asymmetry is the same one as in “all lions are fierce” (∀ with →) versus “some lion is fierce” (∃ with ∧), and mixing them up changes the meaning entirely.

concepts.statement: **∃!x P(x)** means exactly one element of the domain satisfies P(x). It expands as ∃x (P(x) ∧ ∀y (P(y) → y = x)).
concepts.detail: Example: ∃!x (x is an even prime) is true — the witness is 2. Uniqueness assertions appear everywhere in mathematics (“the” inverse, “the” limit), and this is their formal shape.

concepts.statement: A quantifier's **scope** is the statement it directly precedes; a variable is **bound** if it lies in the scope of a quantifier naming it and **free** otherwise. Quantifiers bind tightly: ∀x P(x) ∨ Q(x) means (∀x P(x)) ∨ Q(x).
concepts.detail: Write ∀x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)) if the disjunction belongs inside the quantifier. In a well-formed statement every variable is bound — a formula with free variables is a predicate, not a proposition.

concepts.statement: “All A are B” translates as ∀x (A(x) → B(x)), while “some A is (not) B” translates as ∃x (A(x) ∧ ¬B(x)). Using ∧ with ∀ (or → with ∃) is a meaning-changing error.
concepts.detail: ∀x (Lion(x) ∧ Fierce(x)) absurdly claims that everything in the universe is a fierce lion. The conditional form is weak enough to be true of non-lions — exactly what “all” requires.

examples.title: Truth values over the integers
examples.problem: Over the domain of all integers, determine the truth value of: (a) ∀x (x² ≥ x); (b) ∃x (x² = 2); (c) ∀x (x² > x); (d) ∃x (x³ = −1).

steps.label: Step 1: Analyze (a)
steps.text: For negative x, x² is positive and beats x; at x = 0, 0 ≥ 0; at x = 1, 1 ≥ 1; and for x ≥ 2, x² ≥ 2x > x. Every integer passes — true.

steps.label: Step 2: Analyze (b)
steps.text: x² = 2 requires x = ±√2, which are not integers. No witness exists — false.

steps.label: Step 3: Analyze (c)
steps.text: A single counterexample suffices: x = 0 gives 0 > 0, false. (x = 1 also works.) So the universal is false.

steps.label: Step 4: Analyze (d)
steps.text: The witness is x = −1: (−1)³ = −1. True.

examples.result: (a) true, (b) false, (c) false (counterexamples 0 and 1), (d) true (witness −1).

examples.title: The lion translations
examples.problem: Let L(x) = “x is a lion,” F(x) = “x is fierce,” C(x) = “x drinks coffee,” over the domain of all animals. Translate: (a) All lions are fierce. (b) Some lions do not drink coffee. (c) Then negate (b).

steps.label: Step 1: Universal with conditional
steps.text: (a) ∀x (L(x) → F(x)) — every animal, if a lion, is fierce.

steps.label: Step 2: Existential with conjunction
steps.text: (b) ∃x (L(x) ∧ ¬C(x)) — some animal is a lion and does not drink coffee.

steps.label: Step 3: Negate and push inward
steps.text: ¬∃x (L(x) ∧ ¬C(x)) ≡ ∀x ¬(L(x) ∧ ¬C(x)) by De Morgan for quantifiers.

examples.result: The negation of (b) is ∀x (L(x) → C(x)): “every lion drinks coffee.” Notice how the quantifier flipped and the connective changed from ∧ to →.

examples.title: Expressing uniqueness
examples.problem: Express “there is exactly one even prime number” with quantifiers, using E(x) = “x is even” and P(x) = “x is prime” over the positive integers.

steps.label: Step 2: Expand ∃! as existence plus uniqueness
Step 3: Identify the witness
steps.text: x = 2 satisfies E ∧ P, and any other even prime would have to equal 2 — the uniqueness clause is true.

examples.result: ∃!x (E(x) ∧ P(x)) is true with witness 2: the expansion separates “there is at least one” from “there is at most one.”

keyTakeaways: A predicate becomes a proposition only when its variables are bound — by substitution or by quantifiers.
∀x P(x) is true iff P holds for every element; one counterexample kills it. ∃x P(x) is true iff some witness exists.
Negation flips quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x).
“All A are B” is ∀ with →; “some A is B” is ∃ with ∧ — never mix these pairings.
Quantifiers bind tightly; use parentheses to make scope explicit.
∃!x P(x) means exactly one witness: existence plus ∀y (P(y) → y = x).

quiz.q: ¬∀x P(x) is logically equivalent to:
quiz.explanation: By De Morgan's law for quantifiers, the failure of a universal statement means some element fails: ∃x ¬P(x). The other options are the negation of an existential, a universal negation, or an unchanged predicate.

quiz.q: Over the domain of positive integers, the statement ∀x (x² ≥ x) is:
options: true — the smallest positive integer is 1, and x² ≥ x for every x ≥ 1
true only when x is prime
quiz.explanation: For x ≥ 1, multiplying x ≥ 1 by x gives x² ≥ x, so the universal holds. The proposed counterexamples are outside the domain (0 and 1/2 are not positive integers), so they are irrelevant.

quiz.q: With D(x) = “x is a dog” and F(x) = “x can fly,” the statement “No dog can fly” is:
quiz.explanation: “No dog can fly” is a claim about every animal: if a dog, then it cannot fly. The ∧ version falsely claims everything is a non-flying dog; the ∃ versions merely assert one non-flying dog exists (far weaker).

quiz.q: The statement ∃!x P(x) asserts that:
options: at least one x satisfies P
at most one x satisfies P
quiz.explanation: The uniqueness quantifier demands both existence of a witness and that any other witness equals it — exactly one. “At least one” is plain ∃; “at most one” is the second half alone.

depth.title: Duality, Skolem functions, and generalized quantifiers

blocks.heading: Duality laws for nested quantifiers
blocks.body: For every structure, formula and assignment: $\lnot \forall x\, \varphi$ is equivalent to $\exists x\, \lnot \varphi$, and $\lnot \exists x\, \varphi$ to $\forall x\, \lnot \varphi$; the implication $\exists y\, \forall x\, \varphi \models \forall x\, \exists y\, \varphi$ always holds; and the converse fails in general. These are the precise forms of the section's rule — move the negation inward, flipping every quantifier it passes, and never swap an existential past a universal without a proof.

All three claims are direct consequences of Tarski's recursive satisfaction definition (Level II of the predicates section). For the negation laws: $\mathcal{A} \models \lnot \forall x\, \varphi[s]$ iff not every $a \in A$ satisfies $\mathcal{A} \models \varphi[s(x|a)]$, iff some $a$ fails it, iff some $a$ satisfies $\mathcal{A} \models \lnot \varphi[s(x|a)]$, iff $\mathcal{A} \models \exists x\, \lnot \varphi[s]$ — and dually for the second law. For the order claim, suppose $\mathcal{A} \models \exists y\, \forall x\, \varphi[s]$, witnessed by $b$: for every $a$, the assignment reassigning $y$ to $b$ and $x$ to $a$ satisfies $\varphi$, so choosing the same $b$ for each $x$ witnesses $\mathcal{A} \models \forall x\, \exists y\, \varphi[s]$. The converse fails over the integers with order: let $\varphi(x, y)$ be $y > x$. Each integer has a larger one, so $\forall x\, \exists y\, \varphi$ holds; but no single $b$ exceeds every $x$, so $\exists y\, \forall x\, \varphi$ fails. The witness $y$ may depend on $x$ exactly when its quantifier sits inside — that is the entire content of order sensitivity.

The dependency structure has a name. Given $\forall x\, \exists y\, P(x, y)$, the semantics supplies some witness for each $x$, and the axiom of choice assembles a **Skolem function** $f$ with $\forall x\, P(x, f(x))$; conversely any such $f$ witnesses the quantified statement. Skolemization — replacing existentials that sit under universals by function symbols — is the standard normal form behind automated reasoning, and it makes the game reading vivid: read $\forall x$ as the **falsifier's move** (“choose any $x$”) and $\exists y$ as the **verifier's** (“respond with $y$”), and $\mathcal{A} \models \forall x\, \exists y\, P(x,y)$ says exactly that the verifier has a winning strategy — a function telling her what to answer. Two adjacent universals commute because two falsifier moves can be exchanged; a universal and an existential cannot, because a response must come after its challenge. Alternation count thereby measures a statement's inherent interactivity, and its second-order content: one new function symbol per $\forall\exists$ block.

blocks.heading: Generalized and many-sorted quantification
blocks.body: Two extensions earn their keep in both theory and practice. **Many-sorted logic** partitions each structure into sorts — students, courses, grades — with every variable, quantifier, function and predicate assigned a sort, so that ill-typed formulas are not merely false but ungrammatical. The one-sorted theory is recovered by predicate symbols for the sorts, and the translation preserves validity, but the sorted presentation is the native language of databases, specification languages and SMT solvers, where types guard against meaningless queries. **Generalized quantifiers** then calibrate what $\exists$ and $\forall$ miss. “There are at least $k$” is genuinely first-order, though it needs $k$ variables: $$\exists x_1 \cdots \exists x_k \; \bigwedge_{i < j} \; x_i \ne x_j.$$ But “there are infinitely many” is not first-order — the theorem proved next — and neither is “most $x$ satisfy $P$”. Each proposed quantifier spawns a logic with its own completeness theorem and its own complexity, and choosing quantifiers is how a theory declares exactly how much expressive power it intends to use.

blocks.heading: Finiteness is not first-order expressible
blocks.body: No sentence of first-order logic defines the finite structures; indeed no set of sentences does. The class of infinite structures, by contrast, is defined by the infinite theory $\{\tau_k : k \ge 1\}$ of “at least $k$ elements” sentences, but by no single sentence — an asymmetry between the finite and the infinite that compactness forces on the logic. Second-order quantification repairs the omission instantly: “every injective self-map is surjective” pins finiteness with one quantifier over functions, the first hint of how much stronger second-order logic is (Level III below).
