Suppose a set $\Phi$ defined finiteness, and consider $T = \Phi \cup \{\tau_k : k \ge 1\}$, where $\tau_k$ is the displayed formula of the previous block. Every finite subset of $T$ is satisfiable: it mentions only finitely many of the $\tau_k$, and a finite structure with more elements than the largest mentioned $k$ satisfies those; and it satisfies every member of the finite part of $\Phi$ because it is finite, so $\Phi$ in its entirety holds of it. By the compactness theorem — proved at Level II of the rules-of-inference section — $T$ has a model $M$. $M$ satisfies every $\tau_k$, so $M$ is infinite; but $M \models \Phi$ says $M$ is finite — contradiction. For single sentences the infinitude side falls as well: were $\psi$ true exactly in the infinite structures, its negation would be a single sentence defining finiteness, which the first part rules out. So finiteness cannot be expressed even approximately, while infinitude needs the whole infinite theory $\{\tau_k\}$ — and second-order logic, quantifying over the bijections directly, says it in one stroke.

depth.title: Inexpressibility, Lindström, and finite structures

blocks.heading: Why reachability escapes first-order logic
blocks.body: Connectivity — the transitive closure of the edge relation — is the paradigm of a property expressible with nested quantifiers of unbounded depth but by no finite formula. Suppose a formula $\varphi(x, y)$ defined reachability in every graph. Add constants $a, b$ and, for each $j$, let the sentence $\rho_j$ block paths of length exactly $j$: $$\rho_j \;=\; \lnot\, \exists x_1 \cdots \exists x_j \; \bigl( E(a, x_1) \land \cdots \land E(x_j, b) \bigr).$$ Let $\sigma_k$ conjoin $\rho_1, \dots, \rho_k$, and consider $T = \{\varphi(a,b)\} \cup \{\sigma_k : k \ge 1\}$. Any finite subset of $T$ mentions paths only up to some maximum length $K$; a simple directed path of length $K + 1$ from $a$ to $b$ satisfies $\varphi(a,b)$ — the endpoints are joined — while blocking every path of length at most $K$. So every finite subset of $T$ has a model, and by compactness $T$ itself has a model $M$. In $M$, the interpretation of $\varphi$ says that $a$ reaches $b$; but every finite path from $a$ to $b$ is blocked, so no path exists and $\varphi$ fails — contradiction. The same technique kills acyclicity and well-foundedness; no first-order sentence computes a transitive closure, which is why database languages add recursion by hand.

The method behind all such results is the **Ehrenfeucht–Fraïssé game**. Two players — the **spoiler** and the **duplicator** — alternate pebbling elements of two structures, the spoiler choosing in either structure, the duplicator responding in the other; the duplicator wins $k$ rounds if the pebbled tuples always form a partial isomorphism. The fundamental theorem: the duplicator has a $k$-round winning strategy on $\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B}$ exactly when $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ satisfy the same sentences of quantifier rank at most $k$. Inexpressibility thereby becomes a strategy: to show that no depth-$k$ sentence defines a property, exhibit two structures differing in the property on which the duplicator survives $k$ rounds — two long paths of different lengths do this for connectivity. **Locality** explains the phenomenon wholesale: Gaifman's theorem shows every first-order formula is equivalent to one whose truth at a tuple depends only on bounded-radius neighborhoods around it, so global, recursive properties lie beyond any fixed quantifier depth. Pebbling with a bounded stock of reusable tokens characterizes the finite-variable logics of the open problem below.

blocks.heading: Lindström's theorem
blocks.body: Fix a reasonable abstract notion of “logic” extending first-order logic (Lindström's regular logics: syntax effectively presented, semantic consequence closed under the standard operations). If such a logic satisfies both the **compactness theorem** and the **downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem** — every satisfiable sentence has a countable model — then it is no stronger than first-order logic: every sentence of the logic is equivalent to a first-order sentence. First-order logic is therefore the **strongest** logic with compactness and countable models: the two theorems of Level II are not incidental features but a complete characterization of the logic itself (Lindström, 1969) — the first and most influential of the characterization theorems that treat logics as mathematical objects.

This is a sketch; the full argument is Ebbinghaus–Flum–Thomas's Chapter VIII. The two properties are used in tandem against a putative sentence $\varphi$ of the stronger logic that no first-order sentence matches. Compactness alone yields the finite-basis property: if a first-order theory entails $\varphi$ in the stronger consequence relation, a finite part already does, so any separation between the logics must occur between elementarily equivalent structures. Downward Löwenheim–Skolem then brings all structures down to a countable universe, where an elementary-chain construction powered by compactness — building a chain of partial isomorphisms that the two structures must alternately extend and refute — forces two elementarily equivalent countable structures to disagree about $\varphi$. But the elementary diagram argument shows such a pair cannot exist: one of the two logic properties fails first, and the contradiction lands. Every strengthening of first-order logic must therefore give up compactness or countable models: second-order logic, which defines finiteness, gives up both; the logics $\mathrm{L}_{\omega_1\omega}$ keep countable models and surrender compactness — the theorem's predictions are exact.

blocks.heading: The finite-variable hierarchy
blocks.body: Restrict first-order syntax to $k$ variables in the entire formula ($\mathrm{L}^k$), reusing each as often as needed. Over arbitrary structures the hierarchy is known to be strict — each level expresses something the previous ones cannot. Over **finite** structures, where each level is decidable in principle, strictness is a long-standing open problem: whether every level adds genuinely new expressive power on finite structures has resisted decades of pebble-game technology. The variant with counting quantifiers ($\mathrm{C}^k$) is strict on finite structures — the Cai–Fürer–Immerman construction — and is the exact combinatorial core of the **Weisfeiler–Leman** algorithm for graph isomorphism, so the open question is entangled with the complexity of isomorphism testing itself: how many variables, with counting, does it take to tell two finite graphs apart? No one knows.

intro: Real mathematical statements stack quantifiers: “every positive real has a square root” is ∀ followed by ∃. Nested quantifiers express the deepest facts of mathematics — limits, continuity, surjectivity — but they also hide traps, because swapping a ∀ and an ∃ changes the meaning entirely. This section teaches you to read, write and negate them with confidence.
objectives: Translate statements with two or more quantifiers in both directions
Understand precisely why the order of ∀ and ∃ matters
Express mathematical facts (inverses, roots, sums) with nested quantifiers
Negate nested quantified statements one layer at a time

concepts.statement: Quantifiers are **nested** when one appears inside the scope of another, as in ∀x ∃y P(x, y). Read them left to right: for every x, there exists a y (possibly depending on x) such that P(x, y) holds.
concepts.detail: Predicates with two variables, P(x, y), take pairs of values, and quantifying each variable turns them into genuine propositions — the final truth value depends on the domain and the order of the quantifiers.

concepts.statement: ∀x ∃y P(x, y) and ∃y ∀x P(x, y) are **not** equivalent. In the first, y may be chosen *after* seeing x (y depends on x); in the second, one single y must work for every x. The second implies the first, but not conversely.
concepts.detail: With L(x, y) = “x loves y”: ∀x ∃y L(x, y) says everyone loves someone, while ∃y ∀x L(x, y) says some one person is loved by everybody. Over the reals, ∀x ∃y (x + y = 0) is true (pick y = −x) but ∃y ∀x (x + y = 0) is false (no fixed number is the inverse of everything).

concepts.statement: ∀x ∀y P(x, y) ≡ ∀y ∀x P(x, y) and ∃x ∃y P(x, y) ≡ ∃y ∃x P(x, y): swapping two adjacent universals (or two adjacent existentials) never changes meaning; swapping a universal with an existential usually does.
concepts.detail: Order only becomes critical at the boundary between a ∀ and an ∃ — that is where dependence of choices enters.

concepts.statement: ∀x ∀y P is true when P holds for **every pair**; ∃x ∃y P when **some pair** works; ∀x ∃y P when **each x has its own** y; ∃x ∀y P when **one x works against all** y.
concepts.detail: To falsify ∀x ∀y P, exhibit one bad pair. To falsify ∀x ∃y P, exhibit one x for which no y works. To falsify ∃x ∀y P, show every x fails against some y. Knowing the failure mode tells you what a counterexample must look like.

concepts.statement: Standard translations: “every real has an additive inverse” is ∀x ∃y (x + y = 0); “every nonzero real has a multiplicative inverse” is ∀x (x ≠ 0 → ∃y (xy = 1)); “the product of two negative reals is positive” is ∀x ∀y ((x < 0 ∧ y < 0) → xy > 0).
concepts.detail: The pattern is always the same: decide for each variable whether the claim is universal or existential, then let the inner quantifiers depend on the outer ones. The restricted-domain conditional (x ≠ 0 → …) handles exceptions.

concepts.statement: Move the negation inward one quantifier at a time, flipping each quantifier it passes, and negate the predicate at the end: ¬∀x ∃y P(x, y) ≡ ∃x ¬∃y P(x, y) ≡ ∃x ∀y ¬P(x, y).
concepts.detail: Every quantifier crossed flips: ∀ becomes ∃ and ∃ becomes ∀. Apply De Morgan's law for quantifiers repeatedly — never negate only the innermost piece and leave the quantifiers untouched.

examples.title: Additive inverses: order makes the difference
examples.problem: Over the real numbers, compare the truth values of ∀x ∃y (x + y = 0) and ∃y ∀x (x + y = 0).

steps.label: Step 1: Read the first statement
steps.text: For every real x there is a real y with x + y = 0 — each x gets to choose its own partner y = −x.

steps.label: Step 2: Verify it
steps.text: Given any x, set y = −x: then x + (−x) = 0. True.

steps.label: Step 3: Read the second statement
steps.text: There is a single real y that sums with every real x to 0 — one y must serve all x at once.

steps.label: Step 4: Refute it
steps.text: Fix any candidate y₀ and choose x = 1 − y₀: then x + y₀ = 1 ≠ 0. No y₀ survives, so the statement is false.

examples.result: ∀x ∃y (x + y = 0) is true; ∃y ∀x (x + y = 0) is false. The one-directional implication ∃y∀x … ⟹ ∀x∃y … holds, but not the reverse.

examples.title: Translate, then negate
examples.problem: Express “every positive real number has a multiplicative inverse” over the reals, then negate your expression and read the negation in English.

steps.label: Step 1: Choose quantifiers per variable
steps.text: “Every” is universal; the inverse is a witness that may depend on the number, so it is existential.

examples.result: The negation reads: “there is a positive real number whose product with every real number differs from 1” — a false statement over ℝ, as expected, since the original is true.

examples.title: Who loves whom
examples.problem: With L(x, y) meaning “x loves y” over the domain of all people, express: (a) everybody loves somebody; (b) somebody is loved by everybody; (c) nobody loves everybody.

steps.label: Step 1: Part (a)
steps.text: For each person there exists a person they love: ∀x ∃y L(x, y).

steps.label: Step 2: Part (b)
steps.text: There is one person y such that every x loves them: ∃y ∀x L(x, y).

steps.label: Step 3: Part (c) as a negation
steps.text: “Nobody loves everybody” negates ∃x ∀y L(x, y): ¬∃x ∀y L(x, y).

steps.label: Step 4: Push the negation inward
steps.text: ¬∃x ∀y L(x, y) ≡ ∀x ¬∀y L(x, y) ≡ ∀x ∃y ¬L(x, y): everyone fails to love at least one person.

examples.result: (a) ∀x ∃y L(x, y); (b) ∃y ∀x L(x, y); (c) ∀x ∃y ¬L(x, y) — note how (a) and (b) use the same predicate with the quantifiers swapped and mean different things.

keyTakeaways: Read nested quantifiers left to right: inner choices may depend on outer variables.
∀x ∃y and ∃y ∀x are different statements; the ∀-then-∃ order is the weaker (more often true) one.
Swapping two universals or two existentials is safe; swapping a ∀ past an ∃ is not.
Negation passes through quantifiers by flipping each one, ending with the negated predicate: ¬∀x∃y P ≡ ∃x∀y ¬P.
Mathematical facts are nested quantifications: inverses, roots, boundedness and continuity all have this shape.
To refute ∀x ∃y P you must produce an x that defeats every y — one specific x, not just any bad pair.

quiz.q: The negation of ∀x ∃y P(x, y) is:
quiz.explanation: Each quantifier the negation passes flips: ¬(∀x ∃y P) = ∃x ¬(∃y P) = ∃x ∀y ¬P. Stopping early leaves quantifiers un-flipped and changes the meaning.

quiz.q: Over the real numbers, ∃y ∀x (x + y = 0) is:
options: false — for any fixed y, choosing x = 1 − y gives x + y = 1 ≠ 0
quiz.explanation: The ∀ is outside, so no single y can adapt to x; every candidate y is defeated by x = 1 − y. Note “take y = −x” is illegal here because y may not depend on x, and the two quantifier orders are not equivalent.

quiz.q: “Every nonzero real number has a multiplicative inverse” is:
quiz.explanation: The exception “nonzero” must be a conditional hypothesis, not a conjunct: with ∧ the statement would claim every real is nonzero. The ∃y∀x version demands one universal inverse, which is false.

quiz.q: With L(x, y) meaning “x loves y” over all people, the statement ∃y ∀x L(x, y) says:
quiz.explanation: The ∃y is outermost, so it picks one person y; then ∀x L(x, y) says every x loves that y. “Everybody loves somebody” is the reversed order ∀x ∃y L(x, y).

depth.title: Soundness, completeness, compactness, resolution

blocks.heading: Soundness of the inference rules
blocks.body: Write $\Sigma \vdash \varphi$ when the formula $\varphi$ is derivable from premises $\Sigma$ by finitely many applications of the section's rules — modus ponens and modus tollens, the two syllogisms, addition, simplification, conjunction, resolution, and the four quantifier rules — and $\Sigma \models \varphi$ when every truth assignment, or in the quantified case every structure, satisfying all of $\Sigma$ also satisfies $\varphi$. **Soundness** is the theorem that $\Sigma \vdash \varphi$ implies $\Sigma \models \varphi$: the rules never manufacture truth. The section's definition of a valid argument form — premises-to-conclusion a tautology — is exactly the case of empty $\Sigma$, and the classic fallacies are precisely the candidate rules that fail the property: $q,\; p \to q \vdash p$ breaks at the row where $p$ is false and $q$ is true, the counterexample assignment that convicted affirming the conclusion.

Induct on the length of the derivation. A one-line derivation consists of a premise, which every satisfying assignment satisfies by definition. For the inductive step, the final line follows from earlier lines — already semantic consequences of $\Sigma$ — by one rule; check each rule against the truth tables. Modus ponens: an assignment satisfying $p$ and $p \to q$ must satisfy $q$, because the only row in which $p \to q$ is false has $p$ true and $q$ false. Modus tollens: an assignment satisfying $\lnot q$ and $p \to q$ cannot satisfy $p$, for then it would satisfy $q$ alongside $\lnot q$. Resolution: if $p \lor q$ and $\lnot p \lor r$ hold, whichever truth value $p$ takes forces one disjunct of $q \lor r$. The quantifier rules need their side conditions: universal generalization is sound only when the element instantiated was chosen arbitrarily, with no special assumption about it — exactly the bookkeeping separating a general proof from a special one. Every rule preserves consequence, so every finite chain of rules does too.

blocks.heading: Gödel's completeness theorem
blocks.body: Gödel proved in 1929 that the quantified calculus is adequate to its semantics: if $\Sigma \models \varphi$ then $\Sigma \vdash \varphi$, for any set $\Sigma$ of first-order sentences and any sentence $\varphi$. Two reformulations display the force. Contrapositive, model-existence form: every syntactically consistent set — one from which no pair $\psi, \lnot \psi$ is derivable — has a model. Bolted to the finitude of derivations: if every finite subset of $\Sigma$ is satisfiable, then $\Sigma$ itself is satisfiable — the **compactness theorem**, the corollary on which the next block builds an impossibility argument. Together with soundness, completeness seals a perfect match: $\vdash$ and $\models$ define the same consequence relation, one by grammar and finitude, the other by truth in structures — the calculus neither cheats nor misses. Gödel's own evaluation was sober: completeness shows this calculus is exactly right; his 1931 incompleteness theorems show arithmetic deserves no such luck.

The construction manufactures a model out of syntax in four moves. First, **Henkin constants**: for each sentence $\exists x\, \varphi(x)$ of the expanded language add a fresh constant $c$ and the axiom $\exists x\, \varphi(x) \to \varphi(c)$; an induction over the enumeration shows consistency survives, and every existence claim now has a named witness. Second, **Lindenbaum's lemma**: enumerate all sentences and walk the list, adding each sentence that keeps the set consistent; the union $\Delta$ is maximal consistent, containing exactly one of $\varphi$ and $\lnot \varphi$ for every sentence. Third, the **term model**: take the constant symbols themselves as the domain, interpreting each relation symbol by what $\Delta$ asserts about tuples of constants. Fourth, the **truth lemma**, proved by induction on formula structure: the term model satisfies precisely the sentences of $\Delta$. Hence every consistent set has a model — in particular a consistent $\Sigma \cup \{\lnot \varphi\}$, which exists when $\Sigma \nvdash \varphi$, would have a model satisfying $\Sigma$ but falsifying $\varphi$, contradicting $\Sigma \models \varphi$. So the derivation must exist after all.

blocks.heading: Compactness: reachability is not first-order
blocks.body: Compactness proves that some natural notions are not expressible in first-order logic by any sentence or axiom set. In a graph with edge relation $E$, call $b$ reachable from $a$ when a finite path of edges joins them. Suppose some formula $\theta(x, y)$ defined reachability. Add constants $a, b$ with the sentence $\theta(a, b)$ and, for each $k \ge 1$, an axiom blocking paths of length $k$: $$\lnot\, \exists x_1 \cdots \exists x_{k-1}\, \bigl( E(a, x_1) \land \cdots \land E(x_{k-1}, b) \bigr).$$ Every finite fragment is satisfiable — take a single path graph of length $N$, with $N$ larger than any $k$ mentioned: $a$ reaches $b$, and no shorter path exists. Compactness then supplies one model of all the axioms at once: a graph in which $\theta(a, b)$ holds yet no finite path joins $a$ to $b$, contradicting the defining property of $\theta$. The transitive closure of $E$ is therefore not first-order definable, and no finitary proof system, however clever, repairs this — which is why practical query languages bolt on an explicit recursion operator, Datalog or recursive CTEs in SQL, to compute reachability.

blocks.heading: Resolution: the single sufficient rule
blocks.body: Resolution earns its self-sufficiency through one lemma and one induction. **Lemma**: an assignment satisfying the clauses $A \lor x$ and $B \lor \lnot x$ satisfies the resolvent $A \lor B$ — if $x$ is true, $B \lor \lnot x$ forces $B$; if false, $A \lor x$ forces $A$. Deriving resolvents is therefore sound. **Refutation completeness**: if a finite clause set $S$ is unsatisfiable, resolution alone derives the empty clause $\Box$. Induct on the number of variables. With none, unsatisfiability means $\Box$ already lies in $S$. Otherwise fix a variable $x$ and let $S^{\prime}$ collect the clauses of $S$ not mentioning $x$, plus every resolvent $A \lor B$ of a pair $A \lor x$, $B \lor \lnot x$ from $S$. Any assignment satisfying $S^{\prime}$ extends to one satisfying $S$: choose the truth value of $x$; if both choices left some clause of $S$ unsatisfied, clauses $C \lor \lnot x$ and $D \lor x$ would both be violated, so the resolvent $C \lor D$ — a member of $S^{\prime}$ — would be violated too, impossible. So $S^{\prime}$ is unsatisfiable with one variable fewer, and the induction produces $\Box$. Refuting the negated goal by resolution therefore proves the goal — the engine inside Prolog and the CDCL SAT solvers of the first section's research level.

depth.title: Automated reasoning and the price of proofs

blocks.heading: Superposition: resolution at research scale
blocks.body: First-order resolution is the engine of the research provers **Vampire**, **E** and **SPASS**. Naive resolution drowns in its own consequences, so modern systems run the **superposition calculus** of Bachmair and Ganzinger: a saturation loop in which inference is restricted to maximal literals under a simplification ordering, a selection function suppresses inferable-but-redundant clauses, and equality is built in through paramodulation, the disciplined substitution of equals for equals. A conjecture is proved by saturating the negated goal until the empty clause surfaces. These provers dominate the CADE ATP System Competition and settle tens of thousands of problems from the TPTP library, from pure first-order logic through algebra to software analysis. The industrial continuation is SMT: solvers such as **Z3** couple a resolution-descended reasoning core with dedicated decision procedures for arithmetic and data structures, and now verify cloud access policies and cryptographic protocols at scale. The section's one-line rule — resolve complementary literals, carry on — run with proof-theoretic discipline, became a verification industry.

blocks.heading: Haken's pigeonhole lower bound
blocks.body: The pigeonhole principle — $n + 1$ pigeons cannot be placed in $n$ holes with at most one pigeon per hole — is an obvious truth, yet its natural clause encoding, $\mathrm{PHP}_n$, hides an exponential secret. **Haken's theorem (1985)**: every resolution refutation of $\mathrm{PHP}_n$ contains at least $2^{\Omega(n)}$ clauses. The proof introduces bottleneck counting: at some point in any refutation a large set of pigeons must simultaneously be blocked from a large set of holes, and covering all those pigeon-hole combinations requires exponentially many distinct clauses; the empty clause can only be reached through such a block. Chvátal and Szemerédi (1988) strengthened the bound through random restrictions to essentially tight form. The meaning is twofold. Practically, resolution-based SAT solvers cannot certify the pigeonhole principle in polynomial time — encodings of it are a standard way to make solvers visibly choke. Structurally, it is one of the few unconditional exponential lower bounds for a natural proof system on natural tautologies: a measured fence at the far edge of what efficient proof can reach.

blocks.heading: Polynomially bounded proof systems
blocks.body: Cook and Reckhow (1979) organized the field around one question: does every tautology have a proof of polynomial length, in some proof system? A **polynomially bounded proof system** for tautologies exists if and only if $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{coNP}$ — a collapse widely disbelieved, and a slightly more approachable face of the P versus NP question from the research level of the first section. The known answers are negative and hard-won: resolution, cutting planes, the polynomial calculus and bounded-depth Frege systems are all not polynomially bounded, each by its own combinatorial method. For full **Frege systems** — the textbook axioms-and-modus-ponens calculi — no super-polynomial lower bound is known at all, and **extended Frege**, which lets a proof introduce abbreviating variables, is believed stronger still; separating the two would require circuit lower bounds that current techniques provably cannot supply, the Razborov–Rudich natural-proofs barrier transplanted to provability. Whether polynomial-size proofs of all tautologies exist — and whether, existing, they could be found as readily as checked — is the open heart of proof complexity.

intro: A proof is a chain of small, valid steps — and this section names those steps. The rules of inference are the atomic moves of all mathematical reasoning, from modus ponens (the very shape of “apply the theorem”) to resolution (the engine of automated provers). Learning them individually is what lets you construct and audit longer arguments without gaps.
objectives: Determine whether an argument form is valid
Apply the rules of inference for propositions: modus ponens, modus tollens, the syllogisms, addition, simplification, conjunction, resolution
Use the rules of inference for quantifiers
Recognize the classic fallacies of affirming the conclusion and denying the hypothesis
Combine several rules into one valid multi-step argument

concepts.statement: An **argument** is a sequence of propositions p₁, p₂, …, pₙ (the **premises**) ending in a conclusion q. The argument is **valid** if (p₁ ∧ p₂ ∧ … ∧ pₙ) → q is a tautology; an argument form is valid exactly when every substitution instance is valid.
concepts.detail: Validity is about form, not truth: a valid argument with false premises can conclude something false, and true conclusions can come from invalid forms. What validity guarantees is that *if* the premises hold, the conclusion must hold.

concepts.statement: **Modus ponens**: p, p → q ⊢ q — from a conditional and its hypothesis, infer the conclusion.
concepts.detail: This is the workhorse of mathematics: every time you verify a theorem's hypotheses and then use its conclusion, you are running modus ponens. Its quantified form, universal modus ponens, is ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)) together with P(a), giving Q(a).

concepts.statement: **Modus tollens**: ¬q, p → q ⊢ ¬p — if the conclusion of a conditional fails, the hypothesis must fail too.
concepts.detail: “If the switch were on, the lamp would be lit. The lamp is dark. So the switch is not on.” Together with modus ponens this underlies contraposition-style reasoning in proofs.

concepts.statement: **Hypothetical syllogism**: p → q, q → r ⊢ p → r — conditionals chain transitively.
concepts.detail: This is how lemmas compose into theorems: if A implies B and B implies C, then A implies C.

concepts.statement: **Disjunctive syllogism**: p ∨ q, ¬p ⊢ q — with a disjunction on the table and one option eliminated, the other follows.
concepts.detail: The pattern behind case-elimination and detective work: either the butler or the gardener did it; the gardener has an alibi; so the butler did it.

concepts.statement: **Addition**: p ⊢ p ∨ q (weaken by adding a disjunct). **Simplification**: p ∧ q ⊢ p (extract one conjunct). **Conjunction**: p, q ⊢ p ∧ q (merge two established facts).
concepts.detail: These look trivial but are essential plumbing: addition lets you feed a fact into a disjunctive-syllogism step, simplification pulls out what you need from a compound fact, and conjunction assembles the compound premises that later rules consume.

concepts.statement: **Resolution**: p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ r ⊢ q ∨ r — from two clauses containing a complementary pair (p and ¬p), infer the resolvent with that pair removed.
concepts.detail: Resolution is the single rule powering automated theorem provers and the logic behind Prolog: every propositional theorem can, in principle, be proved by resolution plus refutation (assume the negation of the goal, derive a contradiction).

concepts.statement: **Universal instantiation**: ∀x P(x) ⊢ P(c) for any element c. **Universal generalization**: P(c) for an *arbitrary* c ⊢ ∀x P(x). **Existential instantiation**: ∃x P(x) ⊢ P(c) for some witness c (a new name). **Existential generalization**: P(c) ⊢ ∃x P(x).
concepts.detail: Universal instantiation + modus ponens = “everyone in the class passed; Maria is in the class; so Maria passed.” The arbitrary-element requirement in universal generalization is exactly what a general proof must honor: the c in universal generalization may have no special properties.

concepts.statement: **Affirming the conclusion**: q, p → q ⊢ p — INVALID. **Denying the hypothesis**: ¬p, p → q ⊢ ¬q — equally INVALID. Both err by treating a conditional as a biconditional.
concepts.detail: Check with p = F, q = T: the premises (p → q) and q are both true while p is false, so affirming the conclusion has a counterexample; likewise ¬p true with q true refutes denying the hypothesis. These two fallacies account for an enormous share of bad everyday reasoning.

examples.title: A multi-rule argument
examples.problem: Premises: (1) It is not sunny this afternoon and it is colder than yesterday. (2) We will go swimming only if it is sunny. (3) If we do not go swimming, then we will take a canoe trip. (4) If we take a canoe trip, then we will be home by sunset. Show that these imply: we will be home by sunset.

steps.label: Step 1: Symbolize
steps.text: p: sunny this afternoon; q: colder than yesterday; r: we go swimming; s: we take a canoe trip; t: home by sunset. Premises: ¬p ∧ q; r → p; ¬r → s; s → t.

steps.label: Step 2: Simplification
steps.text: From ¬p ∧ q infer ¬p (simplification).

steps.label: Step 3: Modus tollens
steps.text: From ¬p and r → p infer ¬r — we do not go swimming.

steps.label: Step 4: Modus ponens on premise 3
steps.text: From ¬r and ¬r → s infer s — we take a canoe trip.

steps.label: Step 5: Modus ponens on premise 4
steps.text: From s and s → t infer t.

examples.result: We will be home by sunset — a five-step chain using simplification, modus tollens and modus ponens twice.

examples.title: Catching a fallacy
examples.problem: Is this argument valid? “If the butler committed the crime, then the maid lied. The maid lied. Therefore, the butler committed the crime.”

steps.label: Step 1: Symbolize
steps.text: Premises: p → q and q; conclusion: p, where p = “the butler committed the crime,” q = “the maid lied.”

steps.label: Step 2: Name the form
steps.text: This is affirming the conclusion (q, p → q ⊢ p).

steps.label: Step 3: Hunt for a counterexample assignment
steps.text: Take p = F, q = T: the maid lied, but someone else did it. Then p → q is T (F → T) and q is T, yet the conclusion p is F.

steps.label: Step 4: Conclude
steps.text: Since the premises can be true while the conclusion is false, (premises) → conclusion is not a tautology.

examples.result: The argument is invalid — the maid's lie is consistent with any culprit (or with an innocent explanation), so it cannot single out the butler.

examples.title: Quantifier rules in action
examples.problem: Premises: All lions are fierce. Some lions do not drink coffee. Prove: some fierce creatures do not drink coffee.

steps.label: Step 1: Symbolize
steps.text: ∀x (L(x) → F(x)) and ∃x (L(x) ∧ ¬C(x)); goal ∃x (F(x) ∧ ¬C(x)).

steps.label: Step 2: Existential instantiation
steps.text: From ∃x (L(x) ∧ ¬C(x)) introduce a witness c with L(c) ∧ ¬C(c).

steps.label: Step 3: Simplification
steps.text: From L(c) ∧ ¬C(c) obtain L(c) and ¬C(c) separately.

steps.label: Step 4: Universal instantiation + modus ponens
steps.text: From ∀x (L(x) → F(x)) obtain L(c) → F(c); with L(c), modus ponens gives F(c).

steps.label: Step 5: Conjunction + existential generalization
steps.text: Combine F(c) ∧ ¬C(c), then generalize to ∃x (F(x) ∧ ¬C(x)).

examples.result: The conclusion follows — and the proof shows the standard pipeline: strip the quantifiers with instantiation, reason propositionally, then restore a quantifier with generalization.

keyTakeaways: An argument is valid iff premises-to-conclusion is a tautology — validity is about form, not the actual facts.
Modus ponens and modus tollens are the two shapes of applying a theorem; the syllogisms chain and eliminate options.
Resolution (p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ r ⊢ q ∨ r) alone suffices for automated propositional theorem proving.
Quantified arguments run by instantiating, reasoning propositionally, then generalizing — with an arbitrary witness for ∀ and a fixed new witness for ∃.
Affirming the conclusion and denying the hypothesis are invalid: a conditional does not run backwards.
When auditing an argument, hunt for a truth assignment that makes all premises true and the conclusion false — finding one proves invalidity.

quiz.q: From the premises p → q and ¬q, a valid argument concludes:
quiz.explanation: This is modus tollens: the failure of the conclusion forces the failure of the hypothesis, so ¬p follows. Concluding p (or q) from ¬q would be fallacious.

quiz.q: Which of these argument forms is INVALID?
options: affirming the conclusion: q, p → q ⊢ p
hypothetical syllogism: p → q, q → r ⊢ p → r
quiz.explanation: Affirming the conclusion treats a conditional as reversible: q might hold for reasons unrelated to p. The counterexample p = F, q = T makes the premises true and the conclusion false.

quiz.q: By resolution, from p ∨ q and ¬p ∨ r one may infer:
quiz.explanation: Resolution cancels the complementary pair p, ¬p and merges what is left: q ∨ r. This tiny rule is the complete inference engine of resolution-based provers.

quiz.q: “All CS students know Python. Maria is a CS student. Therefore Maria knows Python.” The proof combines:
options: universal instantiation followed by modus ponens
existential instantiation followed by modus tollens
quiz.explanation: Instantiate ∀x (CS(x) → Knows(x)) at Maria to get CS(Maria) → Knows(Maria), then apply modus ponens with the premise CS(Maria). This pattern — universal modus ponens — is the shape of applying any general theorem to a specific case.

depth.title: The logical anatomy of the standard proof shapes

blocks.heading: Contraposition is the contrapositive
blocks.body: A proof by contraposition of the conditional $P \to Q$ — assume $\lnot Q$, derive $\lnot P$ — is nothing but a direct proof of the sentence $\lnot Q \to \lnot P$. The license is the equivalence $$P \to Q \;\equiv\; \lnot Q \to \lnot P,$$ which holds assignment by assignment: both formulas are false on exactly the one row where $P$ is true and $Q$ is false, so each is a theorem precisely when the other is. The natural-deduction refinement adds a subtlety that matters for strategy. The direction $(P \to Q) \to (\lnot Q \to \lnot P)$ is constructively provable — from $P$, $P \to Q$ and $\lnot Q$ one lands in an immediate contradiction, which is exactly how $\lnot P$ is proved. But the converse direction, the one contraposition actually invokes, needs the classical principle of the next theorem: double-negation elimination. The advice “use contraposition when the negated hypothesis is friendlier” therefore describes a controlled, exactly measurable use of classical strength — more than the direct method demands, less than full proof by contradiction.

Semantic check: with letters $P$ and $Q$ there are four assignments. $P \to Q$ is false only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false; $\lnot Q \to \lnot P$ is false only when $\lnot Q$ is true and $\lnot P$ is false — that is, $Q$ false and $P$ true: the very same single row. Formulas falsified on identical rows are equivalent. Syntactically, from a derivation of $\lnot P$ under the assumption $\lnot Q$, build a derivation of $P \to Q$ as follows: assume $P$; for reductio suppose $\lnot Q$; the given derivation yields $\lnot P$; together with $P$ this is $\bot$; discharge the supposition to obtain $\lnot\lnot Q$; apply double-negation elimination to reach $Q$; finally discharge $P$. The double-negation step is exactly where classical logic enters — constructively the construction stops at $P \to \lnot\lnot Q$, which is why the equivalence itself is classical even though each direction short of it is not.

blocks.heading: Contradiction is double-negation elimination
blocks.body: Proof by contradiction of a proposition $P$ is the inference $$(\lnot P \to \bot) \;\to\; P:$$ if assuming the negation of $P$ lands in absurdity, conclude $P$. Classically this is **double-negation elimination** verbatim, since $\lnot P \to \bot$ is the definition of $\lnot\lnot P$, and $\lnot\lnot P \to P$ is the most conspicuous nonconstructive axiom of classical logic. Intuitionistic reasoning keeps ex falso quodlibet — from $\bot$, anything — and the contraposition-style passage from $P \to Q$ to $\lnot Q \to \lnot P$, but rejects $(\lnot P \to \bot) \to P$ for general $P$, accepting it only where $P$ is decidable. The refinement explains which of this section's proofs are secretly constructive: the irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$ is, because its conclusion is negative — the statement has the shape $\lnot P$, with $P$ the claim $\sqrt{2} \in \mathbb{Q}$ — and deriving $\bot$ from $P$ is precisely how $\lnot P$ is proved directly. Only positive, existential conclusions make contradiction genuinely nonconstructive; those are the province of the next block.

Derive the method from double negation in a calculus with introduction and elimination rules for each connective, the absurdity constant $\bot$, and ex falso. Assume $\lnot P$; suppose it yields both $r$ and $\lnot r$; their conjunction gives $\bot$; the subderivation shows $\lnot P \to \bot$, that is, $\lnot\lnot P$; apply $\lnot\lnot P \to P$ and conclude $P$. Conversely, derive double negation from the method: to show $\lnot\lnot P \to P$, assume $\lnot\lnot P$ and $\lnot P$; these two contradict, so the assumption $\lnot P$ leads to $\bot$, and the contradiction rule converts that into $P$. The two principles are interderivable — each is the other in different dress — so a logic keeps or loses them together: dropping both leaves exactly the intuitionistic fragment, inside which $P \to \lnot\lnot P$ still holds but its converse does not. That is the precise sense in which proof by contradiction is “stronger” than the direct and contrapositive methods: not a proof shape among shapes, but an additional axiom wearing one.

blocks.heading: A witness versus a bare existence
blocks.body: Compare two existence arguments of the same species. First the section's gem: either $\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$ is rational, or $x = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$ and $y = \sqrt{2}$ are both irrational while $x^{y} = \sqrt{2}^{2} = 2$ is rational — either way an irrational pair with rational power exists, though the proof never reveals which case holds. Second, a count argument in the style of the weak (odd) Goldbach conjecture: Vinogradov proved in 1937, by the circle method, that the number of representations of a large odd $n$ as an ordered sum of three primes is on the order of $n^{2}/(\log n)^{3}$ — in particular positive, so a representation exists — yet the original proof was ineffective: it guaranteed a threshold beyond which the count is positive without revealing where the threshold is, and it exhibits no triple for any given $n$. Helfgott completed the conjecture for every odd $n > 5$ in 2013; for $n = 7$ the witness is simply $2 + 2 + 3$. The count proves existence from abundance; the witness exhibits it; only the second is an algorithm — or acceptable to a constructivist.

blocks.heading: Induction and minimal counterexamples
blocks.body: Fix a set $W$ carrying a binary relation that is **well-founded**: every nonempty subset has a minimal element, equivalently there is no infinite descending chain ($\mathbb{N}$ with its usual order is the prototype). Three principles are then equivalent: **well-founded induction** — if $P(x)$ holds whenever $P$ holds at every predecessor of $x$, then $P$ holds on all of $W$; the **least-counterexample principle** — if $\lnot P$ holds somewhere, it holds at a minimal point, so a smallest counterexample exists; and well-foundedness itself. The equivalence is what licenses the working strategy “let $m$ be a minimal counterexample and dismantle it into a smaller one” — the workhorse of finite combinatorics, from extremal graph theory to the classical attacks on the four-color problem — because it converts an obligation to verify infinitely many cases into one local argument: no counterexample can be smallest, so none exists. Ordinary mathematical induction on $n$ is the special case $W = \mathbb{N}$, and strong induction is the version that reads “predecessors” literally.

Induction gives least counterexamples: let $F = \{x \in W : \lnot P(x)\}$. If $F$ is nonempty, well-foundedness supplies a minimal $m \in F$; every predecessor of $m$ lies outside $F$, that is, satisfies $P$ — precisely the hypothesis of the induction principle, which therefore forces $P(m)$, contradicting $m \in F$. So $F$ is empty: no counterexamples at all. Conversely, induction needs minimal elements: suppose some nonempty $S \subseteq W$ had none, and define $Q(x)$ to be “$x \notin S$”. If all predecessors of $x$ satisfy $Q$, then no predecessor of $x$ lies in $S$; if $x$ itself lay in $S$, then $x$ would not be minimal in $S$ — there are no minimal elements — so some member of $S$ would precede $x$, a contradiction. So the implication from predecessors to $Q(x)$ holds for every $x$, and induction concludes $Q$ everywhere: $S$ is empty, contradicting its choice. Hence the two principles stand or fall together — and with them, the tactic of killing conjectures by shrinking their counterexamples.

depth.title: Calibrating, mining, and formalizing proofs

blocks.body: **Reverse mathematics** — Friedman's program, developed with Simpson — calibrates the axioms a theorem needs by proving it from a weak base and then, remarkably, back again: deriving the axioms from the theorem. The base theory $\mathsf{RCA}_0$, recursive comprehension with $\Sigma^{0}_{1}$ induction, captures computable mathematics. Over it, weak König's lemma ($\mathsf{WKL}_0$) turns out equivalent to the completeness theorem for countable first-order logic, to Heine–Borel compactness, and to the prime ideal theorem for countable commutative rings; arithmetical comprehension ($\mathsf{ACA}_0$) is equivalent to Bolzano–Weierstrass and to the infinite Ramsey theorem for triples; and the hierarchy continues through $\Pi^{1}_{1}$ comprehension toward full second-order arithmetic. The calibration has teeth: Seetapun showed in 1995 that Ramsey's theorem for pairs does not imply $\mathsf{ACA}_0$, and the later work of Liu and others separated it from $\mathsf{WKL}_0$ as well, charting exactly which strength the base theory cannot reach. For this chapter the message is sharp: even a single theorem's proof carries a measurable logical price, and reverse mathematics is the invoice.

blocks.heading: Proof mining: unwinding the ineffective
blocks.body: Kreisel asked: when a proof guarantees an object or a bound, can the proof itself be made to yield it? Kohlenbach's **proof mining** is the systematic answer: run a nonconstructive proof through a **proof interpretation** — Gödel's Dialectica interpretation, the no-counterexample interpretation, modified realizability — and extract the uniform quantitative information hidden inside, with fully explicit complexity. The reason this works at all is the fact this level exposed above: a proof can use its principles only in logically controlled ways, and the interpretation replaces each nonconstructive step — choice, comprehension, a compactness appeal — with a finite approximation to its effect. The flagship results sit in nonlinear analysis and ergodic theory: from abstract proofs that merely assert convergence, mining extracts explicit rates — or, when convergence is genuinely too slow to have one, explicit **metastable** bounds in Tao's sense, as in Kohlenbach and Leuştean's quantitative analysis of the mean ergodic theorem. It is the modern continuation of the witness-versus-count dichotomy: circle-method ineffectivity of the Vinogradov kind is exactly the darkness these interpretations are built to unwind, and the extracted bounds routinely beat the classical ones.

blocks.heading: The Liquid Tensor Experiment
blocks.body: On 5 December 2020, Peter Scholze challenged the formalization community: verify, in the Lean proof assistant, Theorem 9.4 of the Clausen–Scholze notes on condensed mathematics — the foundation of the theory of liquid vector spaces — admitting he was not at all certain the proof, on which the theory rests, was actually correct. The **Liquid Tensor Experiment**, led by Johan Commelin and Adam Topaz, proved the heart of the theorem in about six months, and the full statement with its dependencies over the following year; the effort contributed tens of thousands of lines to **mathlib**, the communal library of formalized mathematics, including functional-analytic infrastructure no proof assistant had. Scholze's verdict was striking: the experiment gave him more confidence in the problematic part of the proof than he had ever had, and it taught him where his own understanding was thin. For the strategy of this section the lesson is radical: “reduce the proof to small verifiable steps and check every one” — the exhaustive method of the next section, run at the scale of research mathematics — is now a viable proof method at the frontier, with mathematics and computation sharing the argument.

intro: This is where mathematics becomes a verb: writing proofs. A proof is nothing more than a valid argument whose conclusion is the claim — but constructing one takes craft. You will learn the standard shapes (direct, contraposition, contradiction), the essential definitions (even, odd, rational), and how a single counterexample can settle a universal claim.
objectives: Use the terminology: theorem, lemma, corollary, conjecture
Write direct proofs of conditional statements about integers
Use contraposition and contradiction when the direct route stalls
Give constructive and nonconstructive existence proofs
Disprove universal statements with counterexamples

concepts.statement: A **theorem** is a statement that can be shown true (less important ones are often called **propositions**). A **lemma** is a helper theorem proved as a step toward a bigger result; a **corollary** follows directly from an existing theorem; a **conjecture** is a statement believed true but not yet proved.
concepts.detail: The labeling reflects social convention, not logical difference: Fermat's Last Theorem was a conjecture for 350 years until Wiles proved it. A proof is, formally, a valid argument from premises to the statement.

concepts.statement: The integer n is **even** iff n = 2k for some integer k; **odd** iff n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. The real r is **rational** iff r = p/q for integers p and q with q ≠ 0; otherwise r is irrational.
concepts.detail: These definitions are the atoms of hundreds of textbook proofs: every parity or rationality proof begins by writing the definition's equation and ends by producing the required form. Every integer is exactly one of even or odd (n = 2⌊n/2⌋ or 2⌈n/2⌉ − 1).

concepts.statement: To prove p → q directly: assume p, derive consequences step by step using definitions, known facts and algebra, and arrive at q.
concepts.detail: Template: “Assume n is odd. Then n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. … Therefore n² is odd.” The chain must be unbroken — every step follows from the previous ones by definition, computation or a cited theorem.

concepts.statement: To prove p → q, prove its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p instead: assume ¬q and derive ¬p. Since a conditional and its contrapositive are equivalent, this proves the original.
concepts.detail: Choose contraposition when the negation of the hypothesis gives you better algebra to work with: to prove “if 3n + 2 is odd then n is odd,” assuming n is even is far more tractable than assuming 3n + 2 is odd. Contraposition and contradiction are both called *indirect* proofs.

concepts.statement: To prove p, assume ¬p and derive a contradiction of the form r ∧ ¬r. Since ¬p is impossible, p must be true. Equivalently, prove p → q by showing (p ∧ ¬q) leads to absurdity.
concepts.detail: The classic: √2 is irrational — assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms and deduce that a and b are both even, contradicting lowest terms. Contradiction is the strongest hammer: it works for any statement, not just conditionals, but should be saved for when direct and contrapositive approaches fail.

concepts.statement: A conditional p → q is **vacuously** proved by showing p is always false, and **trivially** proved by showing q is always true — no hypothesis work is needed because F → anything is T and anything → T is T.
concepts.detail: “If x is a real number with x² < 0, then x⁷ = 3” is (vacuously) true. These are legitimate proofs, not cheating — they arise constantly as edge cases inside bigger case analyses.

concepts.statement: To prove ∃x P(x): a **constructive** proof exhibits a specific witness; a **nonconstructive** proof argues that some witness must exist without producing one.
concepts.detail: Famous nonconstructive gem: there exist irrational x and y with $x^{y}$ rational — either $\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$ is rational (done), or $x = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$ and y = √2 give $x^{y} = (\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}})^{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}^{2} = 2$. Both branches conclude existence, yet the proof never reveals which pair works.

concepts.statement: A **counterexample** to a statement ∀x P(x) is a single element a with ¬P(a); it disproves the universal claim outright.
concepts.detail: “Every prime is odd” dies at 2. Because a single witness settles the matter, hunting for counterexamples is the cheapest first move when facing a suspicious conjecture.

concepts.statement: The standard errors: proving the converse instead of the statement; assuming what must be proved (**circular reasoning** / begging the question); treating “not (for all)” as “for all not”; and concluding a universal from a few examples.
concepts.detail: Examples prove ∃-statements but never ∀-statements. Writing the statement in formal logic before proving it (hypothesis, conclusion, quantifiers) is the best defense against these traps.

examples.title: A direct proof about parity
examples.problem: Prove: if n is an odd integer, then n² is odd.

steps.label: Step 1: Unfold the hypothesis's definition
steps.text: n odd means n = 2k + 1 for some integer k.

steps.label: Step 3: Force the target form
steps.text: 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which is 2·(integer) + 1.

steps.label: Step 4: Fold in the conclusion's definition
steps.text: 2(2k² + 2k) + 1 has the shape 2j + 1 with j = 2k² + 2k an integer, so n² is odd.

examples.result: The square of every odd integer is odd — proved directly, with the two definitions of “odd” as the bookends.

examples.title: Contraposition when direct is awkward
examples.problem: Prove: if 3n + 2 is odd, then n is odd (n an integer).

steps.label: Step 1: Consider the direct route
steps.text: Assuming 3n + 2 odd means 3n + 2 = 2k + 1; extracting information about n is messy. Try the contrapositive.

steps.label: Step 2: State the contrapositive
steps.text: If n is even, then 3n + 2 is even.

steps.label: Step 3: Prove it directly
steps.text: n even gives n = 2k; then 3n + 2 = 6k + 2 = 2(3k + 1), an even integer.

steps.label: Step 4: Conclude by equivalence
steps.text: The contrapositive holds, and a conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive.

examples.result: 3n + 2 odd forces n odd — proved by contraposition, the tool of choice when one side of the implication is much easier to reason from.

examples.title: Contradiction: √2 is irrational
examples.problem: Prove that √2 is irrational.

steps.label: Step 1: Assume the negation
steps.text: Suppose √2 were rational: √2 = a/b with integers a, b, in lowest terms (gcd(a, b) = 1).

steps.label: Step 2: Clear denominators and square
steps.text: a = b√2 gives a² = 2b², so a² is even.

steps.label: Step 3: Descend to a
steps.text: a² even forces a even (an odd a would give odd a²), so a = 2c for some integer c.

steps.label: Step 4: Descend to b
steps.text: Substituting: 4c² = 2b², so b² = 2c² is even, and the same reasoning makes b even.

steps.label: Step 5: Unfold the contradiction
steps.text: Both a and b even contradicts the fraction being in lowest terms.

examples.result: The assumption that √2 is rational is impossible, so √2 is irrational — the 2,300-year-old prototype of proof by contradiction.

keyTakeaways: A proof is a valid argument; lemmas, theorems and corollaries differ in role, not in logic.
Direct proof: assume the hypothesis, then chain definitions and algebra to the conclusion.
Contraposition proves p → q by proving ¬q → ¬p — pick it when the negated hypothesis is friendlier.
Contradiction assumes the negation and detonates it against any known fact; it proves any kind of statement, not just conditionals.
Existence proofs are constructive (show a witness) or nonconstructive (show one must exist).
A single counterexample demolishes a universal statement — search for one before attempting a proof.

quiz.q: In a direct proof that the square of an odd integer is odd, after writing n = 2k + 1 we compute n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 and then:
options: factor it as 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which has the form 2·(integer) + 1
note it is positive, hence odd
divide by 2 and check the remainder is 1 only when k is even
quiz.explanation: The definition of odd is “2j + 1 for some integer j,” so the proof must exhibit that form — here j = 2k² + 2k. Positivity and the parity of k are irrelevant.

quiz.q: The contrapositive of “if n² is even, then n is even” is:
options: if n is odd, then n² is odd
if n is even, then n² is even
if n² is odd, then n is odd
n² is odd whenever n is even
quiz.explanation: With p = “n² even” and q = “n even,” the contrapositive is ¬q → ¬p: if n is odd, n² is odd. Option 2 is the converse; option 3 is the inverse — neither is equivalent to the original.

quiz.q: Assuming √2 = a/b in lowest terms and deriving that a and b are both even is:
options: a direct proof that √2 is rational
a proof by contradiction — “both even” contradicts “lowest terms”
a proof by cases on the parity of a
quiz.explanation: The derivation produces an explicit contradiction with a standing assumption, which is exactly proof by contradiction. The negated hypothesis (rationality of √2) is thereby impossible.

quiz.q: The argument “either $\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$ is rational, or $(\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}})^{\sqrt{2}} = 2$ is rational — either way some irrational number raised to an irrational power is rational, though we never learn which” is:
quiz.explanation: The proof establishes that a witness exists in each case without identifying which case actually occurs, so it never exhibits a specific pair — the defining feature of a nonconstructive existence proof.

depth.title: Strategy as proof search and compression

blocks.body: The section's advice — reason forward from hypotheses, backward from the goal — becomes exact in the theory of **proof search**. Gentzen's **sequent calculus** represents a proof state as $\Gamma \Rightarrow \Delta$: working assumptions on the left, goals on the right. Each logical constant then comes with two rules, one per side, that decompose it: to establish $\Gamma \Rightarrow A \land B$ it suffices — this is the right rule for conjunction — to establish $\Gamma \Rightarrow A$ and $\Gamma \Rightarrow B$; to use an assumption $C \lor D$ on the left, it suffices to continue both from $C, \Gamma \Rightarrow \Delta$ and from $D, \Gamma \Rightarrow \Delta$. Many sequent rules are **invertible** — premise and conclusion are interderivable — so applying them backward provably loses nothing, and the strategic reading is immediate: do the invertible decompositions first, and postpone the genuinely committing choices, such as which disjunct to prove on the right or which witness to exhibit for an existential, until the deterministic work has shrunk the problem. Backward chaining is this discipline arranged as search from the goal; resolution refutation — backward chaining on clauses — is its industrial form.

blocks.heading: Case analysis decides propositional logic
blocks.body: Let $\varphi$ be a formula whose variables are among $p_1, \dots, p_n$. Then the exhaustive case analysis over all $2^{n}$ truth assignments is a **complete decision procedure** for propositional logic: $\varphi$ is a tautology if and only if every one of the $2^{n}$ cases verifies it, and if some case fails, that case is a counterexample — a certificate of falsity exactly as checkable as the proof of validity. The method is an exhaustive proof by cases whose splitting principle is the law of excluded middle applied once per atom, $p_i \lor \lnot p_i$, and nothing about $\varphi$ is used beyond truth-functional evaluation inside each case. Consequently propositional logic is **decidable**: an algorithm halts on every input formula, correctly answering “tautology” or presenting a falsifying assignment, in time $O(2^{n} \cdot \lvert \varphi \rvert)$. The exponential is the price of completeness-by-cases — and it is apparently unavoidable, since tautology-testing is coNP-complete, so a polynomial case-analysis procedure would collapse $\mathrm{P}$ and $\mathrm{NP}$.

Soundness of the procedure is the exhaustiveness of the cases. Splitting on $p_1$ via excluded middle divides the problem into two subproblems, $p_1$ true and $p_1$ false, whose cases are disjoint and jointly exhaustive; iterating for $p_2, \dots, p_n$ refines the space into exactly $2^{n}$ cells, each fixing every variable, together covering every possible assignment exactly once. Inside one cell every subformula of $\varphi$ evaluates deterministically, by the recursive clause of its connective, and the evaluation is itself a derivation of $\varphi$ or of $\lnot \varphi$ from the case's atomic assumptions — a miniature direct proof local to the case. If all $2^{n}$ cells derive $\varphi$, then the disjunction of all the cases, a tautology by construction, delivers $\varphi$ unconditionally: a proof by $2^{n}$ exhaustive cases, with the bookkeeping automated. For the running time, each cell costs one evaluation of $\varphi$, linear in $\lvert \varphi \rvert$, giving the $O(2^{n} \cdot \lvert \varphi \rvert)$ bound — decidability honestly earned, with the exponential cost of enumeration paid in full.

blocks.heading: Small cases, large exceptions
blocks.body: Why does “look at small cases” work so often? Because many logics enjoy a **small-model property**: any counterexample can be taken small. For a propositional claim over $n$ atoms the counterexample is a single assignment of $n$ bits, so the truth table is a perfect oracle; modal and description logics, and the guarded fragments, enjoy the **finite model property** — satisfiability, when it holds, is always witnessed by a bounded finite model — which is what justifies small-case inspection algorithmically. But the heuristic stays a heuristic, and the warning is historical: **Pólya's 1919 conjecture**, that for every $n$ the majority of integers up to $n$ have an odd number of prime factors, was confirmed by every computation available, then disproved by Haselgrove in 1958 by a nonconstructive argument — an existence proof for a counterexample, in exactly the style the previous section's Level II dissected — with the first explicit failure appearing at $n = 906{,}150{,}257$. Small cases are evidence; evidence is not proof.

blocks.heading: Lemmas are cuts: Gentzen's Hauptsatz
blocks.body: Every use of a lemma is an instance of Gentzen's **cut rule**: from the derivation $\Gamma \Rightarrow \varphi$ (the lemma's own proof) and the derivation $\varphi, \Gamma \Rightarrow \psi$ (the main argument invoking it), conclude $\Gamma \Rightarrow \psi$ directly. **Gentzen's Hauptsatz** (1934–35) — the cut elimination theorem — states that every sequent-calculus proof can be effectively transformed into a **cut-free** one: lemmas are, in principle, always dispensable. The structural payoff is the **subformula property**: a cut-free proof of $\Gamma \Rightarrow \psi$ mentions only subformulas of the formulas occurring in $\Gamma$ and $\psi$ — every intermediate assertion is a piece of the statement itself. This is the precise theorem behind the strategist's instinct to stay close to the statement: cut-free search has only finitely many possible sentences to consider, which is what makes goal-directed proof search terminate on propositional inputs. It is also why direct proofs feel clean: nothing external can enter a cut-free derivation.

The transformation is a double induction: on the size of the cut formula and, within that, on the heights of the derivations being joined. A cut on an atomic formula can be permuted upward until it meets an axiom, where it disappears. A cut on $A \land B$ is pushed against the proof of $A \land B$, which must end by introducing the conjunction from proofs of $A$ and $B$; the two halves are then spliced into the argument that consumed the conjunction, leaving cuts on the strictly smaller formulas $A$ and $B$ in place of the original. Iterating, every cut dissolves. The cost is fierce: each splice can duplicate an entire subproof, and Orevkov (1982) and Statman (1979) showed the blowup is not bounded by any fixed tower of exponentials — cut elimination is nonelementary in the worst case. Lemmas are therefore exponential compression: the cut-free proof exists, but may be too large to inhabit the universe, and “adapting known proofs” is not laziness but the only way finite mathematicians can write finite mathematics.

Pólya's **How to Solve It** (1945) catalogued the heuristics this section teaches informally: understand, plan, execute, review; draw on known results; work backward; decompose and recombine; exploit symmetry; examine special cases; generalize the problem to make it easier. The limits of the catalog are as instructive as its contents. No heuristic is complete: by the Church–Turing undecidability of first-order validity — the 1936 answer to the Entscheidungsproblem — there is no algorithm, and therefore no mechanically followable strategy, guaranteed to find a proof or refutation of every statement, so creative choice is not a removable overhead but the essence of the craft. Heuristics can also misfire: symmetry invites “without loss of generality” claims that a hidden asymmetry quietly refutes. What strategy adds, formally, is ordering and compression of a search that completeness renders enumerable but undecidability keeps from being automatic — and whether machines can do better is the subject of the research level.

depth.title: Machine mathematics and the shape of proofs

blocks.heading: Neural provers: GPT-f to AlphaProof
blocks.body: The proof-search picture of Level II is now run by learning systems. **GPT-f** (Polu and Sutskever, 2020) coupled a transformer language model with tree search over Metamath derivations and became the first neural prover to contribute new, human-verified proofs to a formal library — machine-found proofs checked line by line. **AlphaGeometry** (Trinh and colleagues, Nature 2024) solved 25 of 30 Olympiad geometry problems in a formal language of its own construction, combining a symbolic deduction engine with a learned generator of auxiliary constructions. **AlphaProof** (Google DeepMind, 2024) fine-tunes a language model to propose steps of Lean proofs, verifies them in a deterministic environment, and trains on the outcome with AlphaZero-style reinforcement learning; combined with AlphaGeometry 2 it reached silver-medal standard at the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad, solving four of the six problems. The persistent bottleneck is the **formal-to-informal gap**: models reason inside verified languages whose statements must still be supplied by humans, and **autoformalization** — translating textbook mathematics into those languages — remains the least automated step of the entire pipeline.

blocks.heading: Can elegance be formalized?
blocks.body: Erdős pictured **the BOOK**: God's volume holding the perfect proof of every theorem, of which human proofs are smudged photocopies; Aigner and Ziegler's **Proofs from THE BOOK** collects candidate pages. Whether book-ness is a formal property is a genuine research question with quantitative proxies: proof length, the canonical measure of proof complexity; economy of concepts, captured exactly by the subformula property of Level II — a cut-free proof reuses only the statement's own material; symmetry, measurable as invariance of the derivation under the statement's automorphisms; and surprise, approximated by Kolmogorov-style compression relative to the statement. Each proxy overshoots or undershoots: a shortest derivation can still feel like mud, and a luminous one-line argument can conceal exponential formal content. Gowers's “two cultures” essay observes that theory-builders and problem-solvers hold genuinely different aesthetics, suggesting elegance is at least partly social. Whether the shadows converge — whether human-judged beauty correlates with formal brevity or locality, and could even be predicted from them — is an open empirical question, one the machine provers of this level are beginning to generate data for.

blocks.heading: Finding proofs versus checking them
blocks.body: Checking a formal proof is cheap: each rule application is a local, mechanical verification, and the whole audit runs in time polynomial in the proof's length. Finding one is another universe. Propositionally, the gap is exactly the P versus NP phenomenon of the first section's research level — certificates are short, discovery apparently is not — and proof complexity quantifies it system by system, with Haken-style lower bounds marking where efficient certification stops. In first-order logic, finding is not even in principle bounded: validity is recursively enumerable but undecidable, so any complete search must sometimes run forever, and strategy can shorten the wait without abolishing it. At research scale the gap turns qualitative: the four-color theorem was settled in 1976 by machine enumeration over 1,936 reducible configurations and formally verified by Gonthier in 2005 — correctness achieved, comprehension deferred. The open problems: is there an algorithm that finds human-readable proofs when they exist; can readability itself be defined well enough to be engineered; and is the hardness of finding versus checking a mathematical fact about proof systems, or a limitation of the ones invented so far? Current provers deliver correctness without comprehension; closing that gap is the open frontier.

intro: Knowing the proof methods is half the craft; the other half is strategy — choosing the right method, splitting the problem into cases, proving things are unique, and adapting proofs you already know. This section assembles the full strategic toolkit, with famous illustrations from checkerboard tilings to unsolved conjectures.
objectives: Structure proofs by cases and use “without loss of generality” correctly
Prove uniqueness statements with the two-part template
Reason forward and backward to find a proof path
Adapt known proofs to new statements
Understand how conjectures are explored, proved or refuted

concepts.statement: An **exhaustive proof** is a proof by cases where the cases are checked literally one by one — feasible only when there are finitely many (and few) possibilities.
concepts.detail: Example: “if n is a positive integer with n ≤ 4, then n² ≤ 16” is proved by checking 1, 2, 3, 4. Computers now make exhaustive proofs respectable for millions of cases (the four-color theorem was settled this way), but the logic is the same.

concepts.statement: To prove ∀x P(x) by cases: split the domain into two or more **exhaustive** (every possibility covered) cases, prove the statement separately in each case, then combine.
concepts.detail: Typical splits: x < 0 / x = 0 / x > 0, or n even / n odd. Each case may use a different argument — that is the whole point. The cases must not overlap the conclusion differently: they must all conclude the same goal.

concepts.statement: **WLOG**: when a symmetric argument lets you prove one case and get the others by merely renaming or swapping variables, you may say “without loss of generality, assume case 1.”
concepts.detail: In proving |xy| = |x||y| you may assume WLOG that x ≥ 0 — the negative case is the mirror argument with x replaced by −x. The phrase is a promise: if you cannot honestly deliver the other cases by symmetry, you have a gap, not a proof.

concepts.statement: To prove ∃!x P(x): **(1)** existence — exhibit or argue for at least one x with P(x); **(2)** uniqueness — assume x₁ and x₂ both satisfy P and derive x₁ = x₂.
concepts.detail: Example shape: the inverse of a group element, the solution of a linear equation, the empty set's subset property. Uniqueness never means “there is at most one” alone — it means exactly one, so both halves are required.

concepts.statement: **Forward reasoning** starts from the hypotheses and derives consequences; **backward reasoning** starts from the goal q and asks what statement would *suffice* to prove it — working back toward something the hypotheses can deliver.
concepts.detail: To prove ∀a≠0 ∃b (ab = 1) backward: it would suffice that b = 1/a; that requires 1/a to exist, which holds for reals a ≠ 0. Backward reasoning is a discovery tool — the final written proof is usually presented forward.

concepts.statement: When a new statement resembles a proved one, try the same proof structure: the same definition-unfolding, the same auxiliary construction, the same contradiction target — adjusting where the objects differ.
concepts.detail: The proof that √2 is irrational adapts to √3 (both descend to “a and b both divisible by 3”); the domino coloring argument adapts from one board shape to another. The idea also runs in reverse: seeing *why* a proof breaks on a new statement often reveals a counterexample.

concepts.statement: **Circular reasoning (begging the question)** uses the statement being proved (or an equivalent) as one of its own premises. Other traps: skipping a case, using a “theorem” that is actually a conjecture, and proving a weaker statement than claimed.
concepts.detail: “The Bible is true because it says so” is the paradigm. In coursework the subtle version appears when a lemma quietly assumes what the main theorem needs to establish. The remedy is to display every premise and check none smuggles in the conclusion.

concepts.statement: A **conjecture** is a proposed statement awaiting proof or refutation. Famous examples: Goldbach's conjecture (every even integer greater than 2 is a sum of two primes) and the 3x + 1 (Collatz) problem — iterate n ↦ n/2 (n even) or n ↦ 3n + 1 (n odd); every start seems to reach 1, but no one can prove it.
concepts.detail: The workflow of discovery: compute examples, spot a pattern, formulate the conjecture, hunt for counterexamples, then attempt a proof. Counterexample hunting kills most conjectures early — which is a success, not a failure.

concepts.statement: A selection heuristic: conditional statement with usable hypothesis → direct proof; hypothesis hard to use, conclusion easy to negate → contraposition; statement mentions “not,” “irrational,” or a maximum/minimum → contradiction; statement splits naturally (parity, sign, ranges) → cases; statement demands a witness → constructive existence; statement demands impossibility → contradiction.
concepts.detail: Keep a fallback hierarchy: try direct, then contraposition, then contradiction. If stuck after all three, look for a counterexample — maybe the statement is false.

examples.title: Proof by cases
examples.problem: Prove that n² ≥ n for every integer n.

steps.label: Step 1: Choose exhaustive cases
steps.text: Every integer falls into exactly one of: n ≤ −1, n = 0, n ≥ 1.

steps.label: Step 2: Case n ≤ −1
steps.text: Then n² ≥ 1 > 0 > n? Carefully: n² ≥ 1 and n < 1, so n² > n — in particular n² ≥ n.

steps.label: Step 3: Case n = 0
steps.text: n² = 0 = n, so n² ≥ n holds with equality.

steps.label: Step 4: Case n ≥ 1
steps.text: n² − n = n(n − 1) is a product of two nonnegative integers, hence ≥ 0.

examples.result: Since every integer belongs to one of the cases and the statement holds in each, n² ≥ n for all integers n.

examples.title: A uniqueness proof
examples.problem: Prove that every nonzero real number has a unique multiplicative inverse: ∃!y (xy = 1) for each x ≠ 0.

steps.label: Step 1: Existence
steps.text: Since x ≠ 0, the real number 1/x exists, and x · (1/x) = 1.

steps.label: Step 2: Set up uniqueness
steps.text: Suppose y and z are both inverses of x: xy = 1 and xz = 1.

steps.label: Step 3: Chain them together
steps.text: y = y · 1 = y(xz) = (yx)z = 1 · z = z, using associativity and the two inverse equations.

steps.label: Step 4: Conclude
steps.text: Any two inverses coincide, so the inverse is unique.

examples.result: Existence (witness 1/x) plus uniqueness (any two inverses are equal) give ∃!y (xy = 1) — the two-part template every uniqueness proof follows.

examples.title: The mutilated checkerboard
examples.problem: Can an 8 × 8 checkerboard with two diagonally opposite corners removed be tiled by 1 × 2 dominoes?

steps.label: Step 1: Find the invariant
steps.text: Color the board in the usual alternating pattern; each domino, wherever placed, covers exactly one black and one white square.

steps.label: Step 2: Count the colors of the full board
steps.text: An intact 8 × 8 board has 32 black and 32 white squares.

steps.label: Step 3: Account for the removals
steps.text: Diagonally opposite corners of a square board share the same color, so removing them leaves 30 of one color and 32 of the other.

steps.label: Step 4: Derive the obstruction
steps.text: Any domino tiling would cover equal numbers of black and white squares — impossible with 30 versus 32.

examples.result: No tiling exists — and the coloring-argument technique transfers to countless other tiling problems, a showcase of adapting proofs rather than brute force.

keyTakeaways: Proof by cases must cover every possibility; each case proves the same conclusion, possibly by different arguments.
“WLOG” is legitimate only when the remaining cases follow by an honest symmetry or renaming.
Uniqueness proofs have two obligatory parts: existence of a witness, and any two witnesses are equal.
Reason backward to discover a path, then write the proof forward.
Adapting a known proof is the mathematician's chief move — and noticing where it breaks finds counterexamples.
Conjectures drive the field: test with examples, hunt counterexamples, then attempt a proof — Goldbach and 3x + 1 remain open.

quiz.q: A valid proof by cases requires that:
options: the cases cover every possibility for the objects under discussion
all cases end with different conclusions
quiz.explanation: Exhaustiveness is the non-negotiable requirement — a single uncovered possibility is a gap in the proof. The cases may be many or few, and every case must conclude the statement being proved.

quiz.q: In a proof you write “without loss of generality, assume x ≤ y.” This is justified when:
options: the argument for x > y is identical to the one given, with x and y interchanged
x and y are always equal
the hypothesis already guarantees x ≤ y
the statement is symmetric in every variable, not just x and y
quiz.explanation: WLOG is a symmetry claim about the proof: the excluded cases must follow from the treated case by swapping names. If the hypothesis guaranteed x ≤ y there would be no need for WLOG at all.

quiz.q: The uniqueness part of proving ∃!x P(x) proceeds by:
options: assuming two witnesses x₁ and x₂ satisfy P and deriving x₁ = x₂
verifying P for every element of the domain
quiz.explanation: Uniqueness means “at most one”: any two objects satisfying P must be the same. Exhibiting a witness is the *existence* half — both halves together give “exactly one.”

quiz.q: An 8 × 8 checkerboard with two diagonally opposite corners removed cannot be tiled by 1 × 2 dominoes because:
options: the two removed squares have the same color, leaving 30 of one color and 32 of the other, while every domino covers one square of each color
the two removed squares are adjacent to each other
quiz.explanation: The coloring invariant settles it: 62 squares remain but the colors are unbalanced 30–32, and each domino consumes exactly one of each. The parity/counting mismatch makes a tiling impossible.

quiz.q: To establish that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational by contradiction, which opening move launches a valid argument?
options: Declare that the decimal expansion of $\sqrt{2}$ never repeats, so it is irrational
Suppose $\sqrt{2} = \frac{p}{q}$ where $p$ and $q$ are positive integers with $\gcd(p,q) = 1$
Suppose every positive real number can be written as a quotient of integers
Suppose $\sqrt{2} = \frac{m}{n}$ where $m$ and $n$ are both even
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate the goal as **negation of rationality** — assume the opposite of what must be shown, namely $\sqrt{2} \in \mathbb{Q}$. Step 2: Recall the key characterization that every rational has a lowest-terms form $\frac{p}{q}$ with $\gcd(p,q) = 1$. Step 3: Square to get $2q^{2} = p^{2}$, hence $p^{2}$ is even and therefore $p$ is even, say $p = 2k$. Step 4: Substitute back to get $2q^{2} = 4k^{2}$, so $q^{2} = 2k^{2}$ and $q$ is even as well — contradicting $\gcd(p,q) = 1$. Step 5: The distractors fail since decimal non-repetition assumes the conclusion, universal rationality is far stronger than needed, and starting with both even concedes the contradiction at once. Step 6: Therefore the initial supposition is impossible and $\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$.

quiz.q: For integers, consider the claim that whenever $n^{2}$ is even then $n$ is even. A contrapositive argument starts by supposing:
options: $n$ is even and deducing that $n^{2}$ is even
$n^{2}$ is odd and deducing that $n$ is odd
$n^{2}$ is even and $n$ is odd simultaneously
$n$ is odd and deducing that $n^{2}$ is odd
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate the implication $P \to Q$ with $P$ as $n^{2}$ is even and $Q$ as $n$ is even. Step 2: Recall the key logical identity $(P \to Q) \equiv (\lnot Q \to \lnot P)$, so proving the contrapositive suffices. Step 3: Negate $Q$ to get $n$ odd, hence $n = 2k+1$ for some integer $k$. Step 4: Compute $n^{2} = 4k^{2} + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^{2} + 2k) + 1$, which has the form $2t+1$ and is therefore odd. Step 5: The distractors confuse direction since starting from $n$ even proves the converse, starting from $n^{2}$ odd targets the inverse, and the joint assumption belongs to contradiction setup rather than contrapositive. Step 6: Thus $\lnot Q \to \lnot P$ holds, and the original claim follows.

depth.title: Naive sets are not enough: Russell's paradox and the ZFC repair

blocks.body: Rosen's definition — a set is an unordered collection of distinct objects, decided element by element — is **naive set theory**: any property you can state carves out a set. Frege's Grundgesetze (1893) made this the **unrestricted comprehension axiom**: for every predicate $P(x)$ there is a set $\{x : P(x)\}$. In June 1902 Russell wrote to Frege with a single question: what happens for $P(x) \equiv x \notin x$? Frege conceded that his foundations were destroyed — one of the most dramatic moments in the history of mathematics, and the reason every modern treatment, including the one you are reading, stands on axiomatic ground.
