Given closed $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, iterate the deletion of isolated points transfinitely: $F^{(\alpha+1)}$ removes the isolated points of $F^{(\alpha)}$, with unions taken at limit stages. A point deleted at stage $\alpha$ has a rational open interval meeting $F^{(\alpha)}$ only in that point; since later stages only shrink the set, that interval continues to separate the point from everything deleted later, and distinct deleted points receive distinct rational intervals — so only countably many points are ever deleted, and the process stabilizes. The remainder is the **perfect kernel** $P$, and $F = P \cup S$ with $S$ countable: the Cantor–Bendixson decomposition. A nonempty perfect set is enormous — split it recursively into two disjoint closed pieces of shrinking diameter, obtaining a binary tree of nested pieces whose branches inject $2^{\mathbb{N}}$ into $P$ — so an uncountable closed set has exactly continuum many points. For analytic $A$: analytic sets are projections of trees on $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and Souslin's dichotomy for such a tree either exhibits a splitting subtree whose projection is a perfect subset of $A$, or — via the **Lusin–Sierpiński boundedness theorem**, which confines the associated ranks below $\omega_1$ — forces $A$ countable. The boundedness step is the deep input; every graduate text in the subject builds it before this theorem.

Games put these sets to work. Players I and II alternately play natural numbers, jointly producing a real $x$; a payoff set $A$ decides who wins, and $A$ is **determined** if one player has a winning strategy. **Gale–Stewart (1953)**: open sets are determined — the proof ranks positions by the stage at which the outcome is settled and observes that the player facing a loss can always step down the rank. **Martin (1975)**: **Borel determinacy** — every Borel set is determined. This is one of the deepest theorems provable in ZFC: Martin's argument assigns to each countable ordinal a layer of unraveling machinery, and Harvey Friedman proved the cost is intrinsic — Borel determinacy at level $\alpha$ requires $\alpha$-many iterations of the power set operation, so Zermelo set theory (ZFC without Replacement) cannot prove it at all: a theorem whose proof-theoretic price tag is exactly known. Determinacy is a regularity engine: under the **axiom of determinacy** of Mycielski and Steinhaus — all sets of reals determined — every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable, has the Baire property, and has the perfect set property, though AD contradicts the axiom of choice. Martin, Steel and Woodin then proved that AD holds in $L(\mathbb{R})$ if there are infinitely many Woodin cardinals: the regularity of sets of reals is bought with large cardinals.

blocks.heading: The inner model problem
blocks.body: How far does the large-cardinal ladder reach inside the universe? The **inner model program** seeks canonical miniatures of $V$ — Gödel's constructible $L$, but rich enough to host large cardinals; Mitchell and Steel reached the Woodin level, but no canonical inner model containing a **supercompact** cardinal is known. This is the inner model problem, arguably the central open problem of set theory: its solution would calibrate the consistency strength of every natural statement about sets of reals, and settle whether the determinacy hierarchy is continuous from below. Woodin's **Ω-conjecture** asserts that Ω-logic — truth invariant under all forcing extensions — admits a complete proof calculus, which would give questions like the size of the continuum a forcing-invariant meaning. Which value the calculus would then dictate is itself unsettled: Woodin's $P_{\max}$ program once pointed to a canonical universe with continuum $\aleph_2$, while his ultimate-$L$ program now points to $\aleph_1$. Whether the conjecture holds, and which — if either — is the right completion of ZFC, is where the fate of the continuum currently rests.

intro: How big is infinity? This section answers it precisely: a set is countable if its elements can be listed one after another. The positive integers, the integers and even the rationals are countable — but Cantor's diagonalization shows the real numbers are strictly bigger, and the power set construction climbs to infinities without end.
objectives: Define equal cardinality via bijections
Prove sets countable by explicit enumeration or bijection
Understand why Z and Q are countable
Run Cantor's diagonalization argument for R
Compare infinite cardinalities, including |P(S)| > |S|

concepts.statement: Sets A and B have the **same cardinality**, |A| = |B|, iff there is a bijection f : A → B. For finite sets this means “same number of elements”; for infinite sets it defines what “same size” means.
concepts.detail: Bijections pair elements perfectly — no leftovers, no collisions. If A and B are finite with |A| = |B| = n, every injection is automatically a bijection (the pigeonhole principle, Chapter 6); for infinite sets an injection can miss, so the bijection requirement has teeth.

concepts.statement: A set is **countable** if it is finite or has the same cardinality as the set Z⁺ of positive integers — equivalently, if its elements can be written as an infinite list a₁, a₂, a₃, … with every element appearing exactly once.
concepts.detail: “Countable” literally means “you can count them”: the list position is the count. An infinite countable set is called **countably infinite** (or denumerable), and all countably infinite sets have cardinality ℵ₀ (“aleph-null”).

concepts.term: Every infinite subset of a countable set is countable
concepts.statement: If S is an infinite subset of a countable set, then S is countably infinite: list the big set and cross off elements not in S — the survivors enumerate S in order.
concepts.detail: Corollaries: the squares, the primes, the multiples of 17 — all countable, however “thin” they seem. This theorem is the standard shortcut for proving countability of natural subcollections.

concepts.statement: A fully occupied hotel with countably many rooms 1, 2, 3, … can still accept a new guest (move each guest from room n to room n + 1) or even infinitely many new guests (move each to room 2n, freeing all odd rooms).
concepts.detail: The paradox resolves once you see it as the bijection n ↦ n + 1 (or n ↦ 2n): the positive integers are in one-to-one correspondence with the even positive integers — a proper subset of the same size. This is the defining pathology of infinite sets (Dedekind's criterion).

concepts.statement: The set Q of rational numbers is countable: arrange positive rationals p/q in a two-dimensional grid and traverse it diagonally (p + q = 2, then 3, then 4, …), skipping duplicates like 2/2; interleave negatives and zero as for Z.
concepts.detail: The diagonal traversal is the crucial trick — a row-by-row scan would never finish the first row. The same technique shows Z × Z is countable, hence Q × Q, hence (by induction) any finite Cartesian power. Countable sets are remarkably robust.

concepts.statement: The real numbers in (0, 1) are uncountable. Given any list r₁, r₂, r₃, … of reals in (0, 1), build x by choosing its nth digit to differ from the nth digit of rₙ (say, 4 if that digit is not 4, else 5). Then x differs from every rₙ in the nth digit, so x is in (0, 1) but not on the list — no list exhausts the interval.
concepts.detail: Avoiding the digits 0 and 9 sidesteps the 0.4999… = 0.5 ambiguity. The theorem's consequence: |R| > |Z⁺| — a genuinely bigger infinity. Diagonalization reappears in logic (the halting problem, Section 3.1) and computability (Chapter 13).

concepts.term: The power set is strictly bigger
concepts.statement: **Cantor's theorem**: |S| < |P(S)| for every set S. In particular the power set of Z⁺ — essentially the set of infinite bit strings — is uncountable, and its cardinality equals that of R.
concepts.detail: The diagonal idea works again: for any function f : S → P(S), the set D = {x ∈ S | x ∉ f(x)} differs from every f(x) at the element x, so f is never onto. Iterating P gives an endless tower of ever-larger infinities.

concepts.statement: If there is an injection f : A → B and an injection g : B → A, then |A| = |B|: a bijection between A and B exists.
concepts.detail: This spares you from constructing an explicit bijection — two one-way embeddings suffice. Standard use: |(0, 1)| = |R| via injections in both directions.

examples.title: The integers are countable
examples.problem: Show that the set Z of all integers is countable.

steps.label: Step 1: Try to list
steps.text: Naively: 0, 1, 2, … never reaches the negatives. A one-direction list fails.

steps.label: Step 2: Zig-zag instead
steps.text: List 0, 1, −1, 2, −2, 3, −3, … — every integer appears at a definite finite position: n ≥ 0 sits at position 2n + 1, and n < 0 at position 2|n|.

steps.label: Step 4: Conclude
steps.text: A bijection with Z⁺ exists, so Z is countably infinite.

examples.result: The zig-zag listing is itself the proof: position in the list = value of the inverse bijection. The same interleave handles Q's signs later.

examples.title: Enumerating the rationals
examples.problem: Explain the diagonal enumeration showing Q⁺ (positive rationals) is countable.

steps.label: Step 1: Grid the fractions
steps.text: Put p/q in row p, column q — every positive rational sits somewhere in the infinite grid.

steps.label: Step 2: Traverse anti-diagonals
steps.text: Read diagonals of constant p + q: 1/1; then 1/2, 2/1; then 1/3, 2/2, 3/1; then 1/4, 2/3, 3/2, 4/1; … Each diagonal is finite, so every cell is reached in finite time.

steps.label: Step 3: Skip duplicates
steps.text: When a fraction reduces to one already listed (2/2 = 1, 2/4 = 1/2), skip it — this keeps the list repetition-free.

steps.label: Step 4: Absorb signs and zero
steps.text: Interleave with the negated list and 0 as for Z; countability is preserved by finite interleavings.

examples.result: Every positive rational is reached at some finite stage, so Q⁺ is countable — and so is Q. No row-by-row scan could do this: only the diagonal order visits every finite cell.

examples.title: Running the diagonal argument
examples.problem: A colleague claims to have listed all reals in (0, 1): r₁ = 0.5000…, r₂ = 0.3333…, r₃ = 0.1414…, r₄ = 0.7071…, …. Build a real the list misses.

steps.label: Step 1: Read off the diagonal digits
steps.text: First digit of r₁ is 5; second of r₂ is 3; third of r₃ is 1; fourth of r₄ is 7; …

steps.label: Step 2: Change each one
steps.text: Use the rule “4 unless the diagonal digit is 4, else 5”: x = 0.4444… for the digits shown (5→4, 3→4, 1→4, 7→4, …).

steps.label: Step 3: Continue the rule forever
steps.text: The nth digit of x is defined against the nth digit of rₙ for every n, so the construction never terminates early.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify x is missed
steps.text: x differs from r₁ in digit 1, from r₂ in digit 2, from rₙ in digit n — so x is not on the list, though x ∈ (0, 1).

examples.result: Every attempted list misses some real in (0, 1), so (0, 1) — and hence R — is uncountable. No cleverer listing can escape: the argument defeats any list by construction.

keyTakeaways: |A| = |B| is defined by bijections, not by counting — this makes infinite sizes comparable.
Countable = finite or listable like Z⁺; every infinite subset of a countable set is countable.
Z and Q are countable (zig-zag and diagonal-traversal listings); countability survives finite products and interleavings.
Cantor diagonalization: any list of reals misses a real built digit-by-digit — so R is uncountable.
Hilbert's hotel shows a set can have the same size as a proper subset — the signature of infinity.
Cantor's theorem: |P(S)| > |S| always, so there is no biggest infinity.

quiz.q: A set is countable when:
options: it is finite or there is a one-to-one correspondence with Z⁺
it can be put in one-to-one correspondence with R
quiz.explanation: Countable means listable: either already finite, or enumerable as a₁, a₂, … exhausting the set — exactly a bijection with the positive integers. The reals are uncountable, integer-ness is irrelevant (Q contains non-integers yet is countable), and finite power sets only come from finite base sets.

quiz.q: Cantor's diagonalization proves R is uncountable by:
options: listing all reals and counting them
building a real whose nth digit differs from the nth listed real, so it appears nowhere on any list
quiz.explanation: Given any proposed complete list, the constructed number disagrees with the nth entry at digit n, defeating every entry simultaneously — so no list is complete. The argument is constructive and applies to every candidate list.

quiz.q: The set of positive even integers 2Z⁺ satisfies:
options: |2Z⁺| < |Z⁺|, since it is a proper subset
quiz.explanation: The map n ↦ 2n pairs every positive integer with exactly one even one — a bijection. This is Hilbert's hotel phenomenon: infinite sets can match their proper subsets, so “subset” does not mean “smaller cardinality.”

quiz.q: To prove that two infinite sets A and B have the same cardinality, one must:
options: exhibit a bijection from A onto B
count the elements of A and B and compare
list the elements of A but not B
quiz.explanation: Same cardinality is *defined* by the existence of a one-to-one correspondence. Counting is meaningless for infinite sets, and (by Schröder–Bernstein) even a pair of injections suffices — but a plain listing or inequality does not.

depth.title: Relations as matrices: Boolean products, paths, and semiring algebra

blocks.heading: Composition of relations
blocks.body: Let $R \subseteq X \times Y$ and $S \subseteq Y \times Z$ be relations, encoded by zero-one matrices $M_R$ and $M_S$. Then the composite relation $S \circ R = \{(x, z) : \exists y \in Y\ (x R y \wedge y S z)\}$ has matrix $$M_{S \circ R} = M_S \odot M_R.$$ Likewise $M_{R \cup S} = M_R \vee M_S$ and $M_{R \cap S} = M_R \wedge M_S$ wherever the shapes agree: the entire calculus of relations is matrix algebra over the Boolean semiring, and this section's Boolean product is not an analogy but the composition operation itself.

Index $X = \{x_1, x_2, \ldots\}$, $Y = \{y_1, y_2, \ldots\}$, $Z = \{z_1, z_2, \ldots\}$. Entry $(i, j)$ of $M_S \odot M_R$ is, by the definition of Boolean product, $$\bigvee_{k} \big( (M_R)_{ik} \wedge (M_S)_{kj} \big),$$ which reads: *some* $k$ with $x_i R y_k$ and $y_k S z_j$ — precisely the definition of $(x_i, z_j) \in S \circ R$, quantifier for quantifier. The join and meet rules are immediate, since membership in a union or intersection is the disjunction or conjunction of memberships. Two remarks ride along. First, the index reversal — $M_S \odot M_R$, not $M_R \odot M_S$ — matches function composition $g \circ f$ and mirrors $(AB)^t = B^t A^t$: whatever acts first sits rightmost. Second, ordinary matrix multiplication over $\mathbb{N}$ computes the **number** of intermediate witnesses $y$ connecting $x$ to $z$, and the Boolean product merely thresholds that count at one — detecting paths and counting paths are the same computation with a different arithmetic.

blocks.heading: Boolean powers and reachability
blocks.body: Let $A$ be the zero-one adjacency matrix of a finite directed graph on $n$ vertices, and let $A^{[k]}$ denote its $k$-fold Boolean product with $A^{[0]} = I_n$. Then the $(i, j)$ entry of $A^{[k]}$ is 1 if and only if there is a directed walk of exactly $k$ edges from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$. Consequently the reachability relation — the reflexive-transitive closure of the edge relation — has matrix $$I \vee A \vee A^{[2]} \vee \cdots \vee A^{[n-1]},$$ and powers beyond $n - 1$ add nothing.

Induction on $k$. For $k = 0$: $A^{[0]} = I$ records exactly the trivial walks, each vertex to itself using no edges. For the inductive step: a walk of length $k + 1$ from $i$ to $j$ is a walk of length $k$ from $i$ to some vertex $v$ followed by an edge $v \to j$; conversely, any such pair concatenates. So length-$(k+1)$ walks from $i$ to $j$ exist if and only if some $v$ admits a length-$k$ walk from $i$ and an edge to $j$ — exactly the $(i, j)$ entry of $A^{[k]} \odot A = A^{[k+1]}$, by the composition theorem just proved. For the closure: any walk from $i$ to $j$ whose length reaches $n$ must revisit some vertex; deleting the portion of the walk between the two visits shortens it while preserving the endpoints. Hence if any walk exists then a *simple* walk exists, and a simple walk visits at most $n$ vertices, so uses at most $n - 1$ edges — the join stabilizes by the $(n-1)$-st power, and its entries say exactly: reachable or not. Warshall's algorithm computes this same closure in $O(n^3)$ steps by admitting one intermediate vertex at a time — dynamic programming over the semiring.

blocks.heading: Invertibility over rings and fields
blocks.body: The determinant decides invertibility, and the reason is a polynomial identity valid over **any commutative ring**. Define the **adjugate** of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ by $\operatorname{adj}(A)_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} \det A^{(j,i)}$, where $A^{(j,i)}$ is $A$ with row $j$ and column $i$ deleted. Then $$A \cdot \operatorname{adj}(A) = \operatorname{adj}(A) \cdot A = \det(A) \cdot I_n.$$ The diagonal entries of the product are the Laplace expansions of $\det A$ along each row; the off-diagonal entries are expansions of matrices with two equal rows, hence zero. Reading consequences off the identity: over a commutative ring $R$, the matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $\det A$ is a **unit** — if $\det A$ divides 1, then $(\det A)^{-1} \operatorname{adj}(A)$ is a genuine inverse with entries in $R$; conversely $1 = \det(A A^{-1}) = \det A \cdot \det A^{-1}$ exhibits an inverse of $\det A$. Over a **field** every nonzero element is a unit, so invertible collapses to $\det A \ne 0$ — the familiar criterion is the field-special case of the ring theorem. Over $\mathbb{Z}$: the diagonal matrix with 2s on the diagonal has determinant 4, not a unit, so it is invertible over $\mathbb{Q}$ but not over $\mathbb{Z}$. And for *square* matrices over a field, a one-sided inverse is two-sided: $AB = I$ makes the linear map $x \mapsto Ax$ surjective, since every $y$ is $A(By)$; a surjective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional space is bijective, so $A^{-1}$ exists and $B = A^{-1}(AB) = A^{-1}$. The finite dimension is essential: on infinite sequences the shift $S(x_1, x_2, \ldots) = (0, x_1, x_2, \ldots)$ satisfies $TS = I$ but $ST \ne I$.

Nothing in the path-counting theorem used subtraction. The entire construction — join, meet, Boolean product, powers, the reachability closure — lives in a **semiring** $(S, \oplus, \otimes, 0, 1)$: two monoids tied together by distributivity. Instantiate $(\oplus, \otimes) = (\vee, \wedge)$ and you get this section's Boolean algebra of relations; $(+, \times)$ over $\mathbb{N}$ counts walks of each length; $(\min, +)$ makes the very same matrix equations compute **shortest paths** — Floyd–Warshall is Gaussian elimination over the min-plus semiring; $(\max, +)$ yields the tropical algebra of the research tier. One theorem, many algebras: choose the semiring, and the matrix machinery answers a different combinatorial question.

depth.title: Tropical algebra, random matrices, and the field with one element

blocks.body: **Tropical algebra** works over the semiring $(\mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty\}, \oplus, \otimes)$ with $a \oplus b = \max(a, b)$ and $a \otimes b = a + b$. As $q \to 0^{+}$, the map $x \mapsto q^x$ dequantizes ordinary algebra into tropical — $q^x + q^y \approx q^{\max(x, y)}$ turns sums into maxima (Maslov dequantization) — so tropical geometry is the logarithmic limit of classical algebra, piecewise-linear in the limit. A tropical linear map $x \mapsto A \otimes x$ is a finite maximum of affine functions; tropical matrix multiplication iterates longest-path computations; and the **tropical eigenvalue** of a matrix is the maximum **cycle mean** $$\lambda = \max_{\text{cycles } C} \frac{w(C)}{|C|}$$ of the weighted digraph — the steady-state throughput of a factory or rail network in the discrete-event systems of Baccelli, Cohen, Olsder and Quadrat. The **tropical determinant** $\bigoplus_\sigma \bigotimes_i a_{i\sigma(i)}$ is the **assignment problem**: the best perfect matching is a determinant computation, and tropical Cramer rules are an active field. Tropical geometry proper — the piecewise-linear shadows of algebraic varieties — rewrote parts of enumerative geometry after Mikhalkin used tropicalization to count curves.

blocks.heading: The billion-dollar eigenvector
blocks.body: Rank the web by its dominant eigenvector. Model browsing as a random walk on the link graph: from each page follow a random outgoing link with probability $\alpha$, or teleport to a uniformly random page with probability $1 - \alpha$. The stationary distribution of this walk is the **PageRank** (Brin and Page, 1998). The mathematics is **Perron–Frobenius**: a matrix with strictly positive entries has a unique eigenvalue of maximal modulus, real and positive, with a strictly positive eigenvector; more generally an irreducible aperiodic nonnegative matrix has a unique nonnegative stationary vector up to scale. The teleportation term is not a user-experience nicety — it makes the Google matrix **positive**, hence primitive, which is exactly what Perron–Frobenius needs to guarantee a *unique* ranking. Computation is the **power method**, $v \leftarrow Gv$, converging geometrically at the rate set by the two largest eigenvalues; because $G$ is sparse, an iteration costs one sweep of the link structure, and a few dozen iterations ranked the web of a billion pages on 1998 hardware. Linear algebra decides which pages you see first: this section's matrix multiplication, iterated until the eigenvector emerges.

blocks.heading: Random matrices: compressed sensing
blocks.body: Randomness makes underdetermined systems solvable. **Johnson–Lindenstrauss (1984)**: any $n$ points in Euclidean space can be mapped by a random linear map into $O(\log n)$ dimensions with all pairwise distances preserved within a factor $1 \pm \varepsilon$ — random projection is the workhorse of dimensionality reduction, sketching, and approximate nearest-neighbor search. **Compressed sensing** (Candès, Romberg and Tao; Donoho; 2006): a signal that is $k$-sparse in a known basis — $k$ nonzero coefficients out of $n$ — can be recovered from merely $m \approx k \log(n/k)$ random linear measurements by $\ell_1$-minimization, because a random $m \times n$ matrix satisfies the **restricted isometry property** with high probability: it approximately preserves the geometry of all sparse vectors at once. The practical wins are enormous: MRI reconstructs from fewer measurements, so scans shorten; single-pixel cameras sample directly in the compressed domain; radar and tomography pipelines restructured around sparsity. In machine learning the same random-matrix calculus prices neural networks: random initialization preserves separation in the Johnson–Lindenstrauss sense, and the Marchenko–Pastur law describes the bulk spectrum of random weight matrices. The random matrix is at once the sensor and the model.

blocks.heading: The field with one element
blocks.body: There is no field with one element — the field axioms demand $0 \ne 1$ — yet large parts of mathematics behave as if $\mathbb{F}_1$ existed, and the quest to define it is a live program. Tits (1957) observed that the Weyl group of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ is what remains of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$ as $q \to 1$: the group 'over the field with one element' should satisfy $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_1) = S_n$. The counting evidence is seductive: $|\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)| = q^{n(n-1)/2} \prod_{i=1}^{n} (q^i - 1)$, and dividing out the diagonal torus $(q - 1)^n$ before letting $q \to 1$ leaves exactly $n!$. Since then Soule has built varieties over $\mathbb{F}_1$, Connes and Consani have pursued topos-theoretic and arithmetic-geometric routes linking it to the Riemann hypothesis through absolute zeta functions, and Lorscheid's blueprints axiomatize the common structure — while matroids behave like vector spaces over $\mathbb{F}_1$, a vector space over it being nothing but a pointed set. Open in earnest: is there a *canonical* $\mathbb{F}_1$-geometry under which the deep analogies — Weil conjectures, Riemann hypothesis, motives — become theorems? The field that does not exist remains one of the most productive fictions in modern mathematics.

intro: Matrices package tables of numbers into a single algebraic object: they represent linear transformations, graphs (Chapter 9), networks, and — in the zero-one case — relations and connectivity. This section covers matrix arithmetic, transposes and the Boolean product that powers reachability computations.
objectives: Perform matrix addition, scalar multiplication and matrix multiplication
Use identity and symmetric matrices correctly
Compute transposes and apply (AB)ᵗ = BᵗAᵗ
Compute the join, meet and Boolean product of zero-one matrices

concepts.statement: An **m × n matrix** is a rectangular array with m rows and n columns; the entry in row i, column j is aᵢⱼ. A matrix with equal numbers of rows and columns is **square**. Two matrices are equal iff they have the same dimensions and identical entries.
concepts.detail: Matrices index by (row, column) in that order — aᵢⱼ lives at the crossing of row i and column j. They will represent relations (Chapter 9), graph adjacency (Chapter 10) and linear systems; here you learn their arithmetic.

concepts.statement: For matrices A, B of the **same** m × n shape: (A + B)ᵢⱼ = aᵢⱼ + bᵢⱼ (add entrywise). For a scalar c: (cA)ᵢⱼ = c·aᵢⱼ. The m × n zero matrix (all entries 0) is the additive identity.
concepts.detail: Addition is commutative and associative, but only defined for matching shapes — a 2 × 3 matrix cannot be added to a 3 × 2 one. Entrywise operations are the easy ones; the interesting one comes next.

concepts.statement: For A of size m × n and B of size n × r, the product AB is the m × r matrix with (AB)ᵢⱼ = ∑ₖ aᵢₖ bₖⱼ — row i of A dotted with column j of B. The inner dimensions must agree; multiplication is associative and distributive but **not commutative**.
concepts.detail: Row-times-column is the chant: the (i, j) entry pairs the kth entry of row i with the kth entry of column j and sums. AB requires “columns of A = rows of B”: a 2 × 3 times a 3 × 4 gives a 2 × 4. Even when both AB and BA exist they usually differ.

concepts.statement: **Iₙ** is the n × n matrix with 1's on the diagonal and 0's elsewhere: (Iₙ)ᵢⱼ = 1 if i = j, else 0. For any m × n matrix A: A·Iₙ = A = Iₘ·A.
concepts.detail: Iₙ is the multiplicative identity for matrices — it corresponds to the “do nothing” transformation. It is the matrix analogue of the number 1.

concepts.statement: The **transpose** Aᵗ is the matrix with rows and columns swapped: (Aᵗ)ᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ. If A is m × n then Aᵗ is n × m. Key identities: (Aᵗ)ᵗ = A, (A + B)ᵗ = Aᵗ + Bᵗ and **(AB)ᵗ = BᵗAᵗ** — note the reversal.
concepts.detail: Transposing reflects entries across the main diagonal. The reversal in (AB)ᵗ = BᵗAᵗ is the algebraic shadow of “row i of A meets column j of B”: after transposing, the roles and order swap.

concepts.statement: A square matrix A is **symmetric** when A = Aᵗ, i.e., aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ for all i, j. The sum of two symmetric matrices (of the same size) is symmetric, and (A + Aᵗ) is always symmetric.
concepts.detail: Caution: the product of two symmetric matrices need not be symmetric — (AB)ᵗ = BᵗAᵗ = BA, which differs from AB in general. Symmetric zero-one matrices encode undirected relations and graphs in later chapters.

concepts.statement: A **zero-one matrix** has every entry 0 or 1. They encode discrete structures: membership grids, adjacency, connectivity. Two special entrywise operations: the **join** A ∨ B (entrywise max/OR) and the **meet** A ∧ B (entrywise min/AND).
concepts.detail: Join and meet parallel ∪ and ∩ for sets and ∨ and ∧ for propositions: (A ∨ B)ᵢⱼ = aᵢⱼ ∨ bᵢⱼ, (A ∧ B)ᵢⱼ = aᵢⱼ ∧ bᵢⱼ. This is Boolean arithmetic on tables — one of the three worlds (sets, logic, matrices) that mirror each other.

concepts.statement: The **Boolean product** of zero-one matrices is matrix multiplication with OR in place of + and AND in place of ×: (A ⊙ B)ᵢⱼ = 1 iff ∃k (aᵢₖ = 1 ∧ bₖⱼ = 1). The **Boolean power** $A^{[n]} = A \odot A \odot \cdots \odot A$ (n factors).
concepts.detail: Computing one entry: scan row i of A and column j of B in parallel; the entry is 1 the moment a pair of 1's aligns, else 0. When A is the adjacency matrix of a graph, $A^{[n]}$'s (i, j) entry records whether a path of length n exists from i to j — the bridge to Chapters 9 and 10.

examples.title: Matrix multiplication is not commutative
examples.problem: With A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[0, 1], [1, 0]], compute AB and BA.

steps.label: Step 1: Compute AB row by row
Step 3: Compare
steps.text: AB ≠ BA — the (1,1) entries alone (2 vs 3) differ.

examples.result: Both products exist yet disagree: matrix multiplication is order-sensitive, so “AB” and “BA” must never be casually interchanged.

examples.title: Transposes and symmetry
examples.problem: For A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], compute Aᵗ and A + Aᵗ, and verify that the result is symmetric.

steps.label: Step 1: Swap rows and columns
steps.text: Aᵗ = [[1, 3], [2, 4]] — entry (1,2) of A (which is 2) moves to (2,1).

steps.label: Step 3: Check symmetry
steps.text: The off-diagonal entries agree (5 = 5), so (A + Aᵗ)ᵗ = A + Aᵗ.

steps.label: Step 4: Note the general fact
steps.text: This always works: ((A + Aᵗ)ᵗ) = Aᵗ + (Aᵗ)ᵗ = Aᵗ + A = A + Aᵗ.

examples.result: A + Aᵗ is always symmetric — a standard trick for symmetrizing a matrix; note that A itself is not symmetric (2 ≠ 3 off-diagonal).

examples.title: Boolean product of zero-one matrices
examples.problem: Compute the Boolean product A ⊙ B for A = [[1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1]] and B = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]].

steps.label: Step 1: Entry (1,1)
steps.text: Row 1 of A is (1,1,0), column 1 of B is (1,0,1): aligned pairs (1,1), (1,0), (0,1) — the first pair is (1,1), so OR of ANDs = 1.

steps.label: Step 2: Entry (1,2)
steps.text: Column 2 of B is (0,1,1): pairs (1,0), (1,1), (0,1) — the pair (1,1) appears, so entry = 1.

steps.label: Step 3: Entries (2,1) and (2,2)
steps.text: Row 2 of A is (0,1,1): against column 1 the pair (1,1) at k = 2 gives 1; against column 2 the pair (1,1) at k = 2 gives 1.

examples.result: The Boolean product is all 1's: every row of A has at least one aligned 1 with every column of B. Contrast ordinary multiplication of the same matrices, which would produce a different, larger-valued matrix.

keyTakeaways: Matrix addition requires equal shapes and is entrywise; multiplication requires matching inner dimensions and is row-times-column.
(AB)ᵢⱼ = ∑ₖ aᵢₖbₖⱼ; a 2×3 times a 3×4 yields a 2×4.
Multiplication is associative but not commutative; the identity Iₙ has 1's on the diagonal.
(AB)ᵗ = BᵗAᵗ — the order reverses; A is symmetric iff A = Aᵗ.
Zero-one matrices use join ∨ (OR) and meet ∧ (AND) entrywise.
Boolean product A ⊙ B replaces × by ∧ and + by ∨; its powers count paths in graphs — the gateway to Chapters 9 and 10.

quiz.q: (AB)ᵗ equals:
quiz.explanation: Transposing a product reverses the order: (AB)ᵗ = BᵗAᵗ. Computing AᵗBᵗ instead generally gives a different (and often differently-shaped) matrix.

quiz.q: If A is a 2 × 3 matrix and B is a 3 × 4 matrix, then AB is:
quiz.explanation: The shared inner dimension 3 cancels; the product takes the outer dimensions: 2 × 4. (BA would be undefined, since 4 ≠ 2.)

quiz.q: In the Boolean product A ⊙ B, the entry (i, j) is 1 exactly when:
options: at least one k has aᵢₖ = 1 and bₖⱼ = 1
the rows of A equal the columns of B
quiz.explanation: Boolean product is OR-of-ANDs: entry (i, j) is 1 iff some position k has 1's aligned in row i of A and column j of B — exactly one matching pair suffices.

quiz.q: A square matrix A is symmetric when:
quiz.explanation: Symmetry means the matrix mirrors across its main diagonal: aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ for all i, j. Zero-one entries define a different (Boolean) world, and A² = I is a separate involutive property.

quiz.q: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ be zero-one matrices. The Boolean product $A \odot B$ equals:
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate the task as computing the **Boolean product** $C = A \odot B$ where $c_{ij} = \bigvee_{k}(a_{ik} \land b_{kj})$. Step 2: Recall the key rule that each entry is $1$ exactly when some position $k$ has $1$ in both row $i$ of $A$ and column $j$ of $B$. Step 3: Compute row $1$: with column $1$ we get $(1 \land 1) \lor (0 \land 0) \lor (1 \land 1) = 1$, and with column $2$ we get $(1 \land 0) \lor (0 \land 1) \lor (1 \land 0) = 0$. Step 4: Compute row $2$: with column $1$ we get $(0 \land 1) \lor (1 \land 0) \lor (0 \land 1) = 0$, and with column $2$ we get $(0 \land 0) \lor (1 \land 1) \lor (0 \land 0) = 1$. Step 5: The all-ones option confuses Boolean product with join, the anti-diagonal option swaps the columns, and the zero option forgets that matching $1$ pairs already exist. Step 6: Hence $C$ is the $2 \times 2$ identity matrix.

quiz.q: How many symmetric $3 \times 3$ zero-one matrices are there?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate the task as counting binary choices subject to the symmetry constraint $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$. Step 2: Recall the key structural fact that a symmetric matrix is fixed by its diagonal plus its strictly upper triangle. Step 3: Count free positions as $3$ diagonal entries plus $\frac{3 \times 2}{2} = 3$ upper-triangular entries, giving $6$ independent bits. Step 4: Each independent bit has $2$ choices, so the total is $2^{6} = 64$. Step 5: The distractor $512 = 2^{9}$ counts all $3 \times 3$ zero-one matrices ignoring symmetry, $8 = 2^{3}$ counts only diagonal freedom, and $6$ counts positions rather than assignments. Step 6: Therefore the symmetric family has $64$ members.

intro: An algorithm is a finite list of unambiguous instructions that turns inputs into outputs — the formal heart of computer science. This section defines what makes a procedure an algorithm, develops the search, sort and greedy classics in pseudocode, and closes with the first great impossibility theorem: the halting problem.
objectives: State the properties every algorithm must have
Read and write pseudocode using Rosen's conventions
Trace linear search, binary search, bubble sort and insertion sort on concrete inputs
Execute the greedy change-making algorithm and recognize when it fails to be optimal
Understand the undecidability proof of the halting problem

concepts.statement: An **algorithm** is a finite sequence of precise, unambiguous instructions for solving a problem. Every algorithm must have: **input** (values from a specified set), **output** (at least one value), **definiteness** (each step precisely defined), **correctness** (produces the correct output for every input), **finiteness** (terminates after finitely many steps), **effectiveness** (each step is basic enough to be carried out), and **generality** (applies to the whole class of problems it claims to).
concepts.detail: The word traces to al-Khowarizmi, a 9th-century Persian mathematician; the modern meaning — effective procedure — is the object computer science studies. An algorithm is an abstract artifact, independent of programming language or hardware.

concepts.statement: Rosen's pseudocode uses: **procedure** *name*(inputs) to begin, **:=** for assignment, blocks delimited by **indentation**, **while** *condition* … **end while**, **for** *var* := *a* to *b* … **end for**, **if** *condition* **then** … **else** … **end if**, **return** to exit with a value, and braces { } for comments.
concepts.detail: Pseudocode is for humans: it strips away language syntax while keeping step-by-step precision. Reading trace: follow the variable values line by line on small inputs — the single best way to understand (or debug) any algorithm.

concepts.statement: **Linear search** scans a list left to right comparing each element with the target x, returning the position of the first match (or 0 / “not found”). It works on any list, sorted or not.
concepts.detail: Worst case: the target is last or absent — n comparisons for a list of n elements (Section 3.3 computes the details). Linear search is the baseline every smarter search must beat, and for unsorted data it is the only option that is still trivially correct.

concepts.statement: **Binary search** on a *sorted* list compares x with the middle element: if equal, stop; if x is smaller, search the left half; if larger, search the right half — halving the remaining interval every step until found or the interval is empty.
concepts.detail: After each comparison at most half the candidates remain, so the number of comparisons is about 2log₂ n. The correctness proof (find the invariant: “if x is present, it lies within the current interval [i, j]”) is a classic use of loop invariants. Binary search is why sorted data is worth maintaining.

concepts.statement: **Bubble sort** makes passes through the list, comparing each adjacent pair and swapping if out of order; larger values “bubble” toward the end. After pass i, the i largest elements occupy their final positions, so pass i need only reach position n − i.
concepts.detail: Rosen's version runs the fixed double loop (n − 1 passes with shrinking inner loops), always performing n(n − 1)/2 comparisons regardless of input — Θ(n²) always (Section 3.3). It is a teaching algorithm: simple, stable, and rarely the practical choice.

concepts.statement: **Insertion sort** builds a sorted prefix one element at a time: take the next unsorted element and slide it left into its correct place among the already-sorted elements by repeated swaps.
concepts.detail: On an already-sorted list each new element compares once and swaps zero times — Θ(n) best case, the reason insertion sort is the standard choice for small or nearly-sorted inputs. Worst case remains Θ(n²) (each element travels past the whole prefix).

concepts.statement: A **greedy algorithm** makes the locally optimal choice at each step. The **greedy change-making algorithm**: repeatedly take the largest coin denomination ≤ the remaining amount. With the US system (25, 10, 5, 1) it always minimizes the number of coins; with arbitrary denominations it can fail.
concepts.detail: Failure example: denominations 25, 10, 1 for the amount 30 — greedy gives 25 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 (six coins) while 10 + 10 + 10 uses three. Greedy is a *strategy*, not a guarantee: each problem needs its own proof that greedy choices compose into a global optimum (Chapter 6 re-encounters this in counting, and algorithm design courses return to it in depth).

concepts.statement: An algorithm is **correct** when it produces the correct output for every valid input — not merely the inputs you tested. For iterative algorithms the standard tool is a **loop invariant**: a statement that holds before and after every iteration and, together with termination, implies correctness.
concepts.detail: For binary search the invariant is “if x is in the list, it lies between positions i and j.” Each iteration preserves it while shrinking the interval; when the loop ends, the invariant pins down the answer. Chapter 5 (induction) makes this reasoning airtight.

concepts.statement: **There is no procedure that decides, for every program P and input I, whether P eventually halts on I.** The problem is *undecidable*: no algorithm solving it can exist.
concepts.detail: Proof by contradiction (diagonalization, Section 2.5): suppose H(P, I) decides halting. Build K(P) which runs H(P, P) and then does the opposite — halting iff H says P(P) loops, looping iff H says it halts. Feeding K to itself, K(K) halts iff it doesn't — contradiction. This shows computation has hard limits, decades before P vs NP asked about *efficient* computation.

examples.title: Tracing binary search
examples.problem: Trace binary search for x = 8 in the sorted list L = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13] (positions 1–7).

steps.label: Step 1: First probe — the middle
steps.text: Interval [1, 7], middle position 4: L(4) = 7. Since 8 > 7, discard positions 1–4; the target can only lie in [5, 7].

steps.label: Step 2: Second probe
steps.text: Interval [5, 7], middle position 6: L(6) = 11. Since 8 < 11, discard position 6 and beyond: now [5, 5].

steps.label: Step 3: Third probe
steps.text: Interval [5, 5], middle position 5: L(5) = 9. Since 8 < 9, the interval shrinks to [5, 4] — empty.

steps.label: Step 4: Termination
steps.text: The interval is empty (start > end), so 8 is not in the list: report not found.

examples.result: Not found — in three comparisons, against seven for linear search. Each probe halves the candidates: 7 → 3 → 1 → 0.

examples.title: Greedy change-making, worked and stress-tested
examples.problem: Apply greedy change-making to 67 cents with denominations 25, 10, 5, 1. Then try the same algorithm with denominations 25, 10, 1 for 30 cents.

steps.label: Step 1: 67 cents, standard coins
steps.text: Largest ≤ 67 is 25 (twice): 67 → 42 → 17. Largest ≤ 17 is 10: 17 → 7. Then 5: 7 → 2. Then 1 + 1: 2 → 0.

steps.label: Step 2: Count the coins
steps.text: 25 + 25 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1 — six coins, which is optimal for the US system.

steps.label: Step 3: Now the awkward denominations
steps.text: 30 cents with {25, 10, 1}: greedy takes 25, leaving 5 — five pennies: 25 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1, six coins.

steps.label: Step 4: Compare with the true optimum
steps.text: Three dimes = 30 exactly: three coins. Greedy's first “locally best” choice (the quarter) blocked the global optimum.

examples.result: Greedy is optimal for the US coin system but not for arbitrary denominations — a concrete demonstration that greedy strategy requires a per-problem optimality proof.

examples.title: The halting problem is unsolvable
examples.problem: Show that no procedure H(P, I) can decide for every program P and input I whether P halts on I.

steps.label: Step 1: Suppose H exists
steps.text: Assume H(P, I) always correctly answers “halts” or “never halts.”

steps.label: Step 2: Build the diagonal program
steps.text: Define K(P): run H(P, P); if the answer is “halts,” loop forever; if “never halts,” stop immediately.

steps.label: Step 3: Feed K to itself — case 1
steps.text: If K(K) halts, then H(K, K) answered “halts”; but by its definition K(K) then loops forever. Contradiction.

steps.label: Step 4: Feed K to itself — case 2
steps.text: If K(K) loops forever, then H(K, K) answered “never halts”; but by its definition K(K) then stops. Contradiction.

steps.label: Step 5: Conclude
steps.text: Both possible behaviors of K(K) contradict the assumption, so H cannot exist.

examples.result: The halting problem is undecidable — no algorithm, however clever or fast, can decide halting for all programs. This is Cantor's diagonalization reborn in computation.

keyTakeaways: An algorithm needs input, output, definiteness, correctness, finiteness, effectiveness and generality — miss one and it is not an algorithm.
Binary search requires sorted input and wins by halving: about 2log₂ n comparisons against linear search's n.
Bubble sort is Θ(n²) always; insertion sort is Θ(n) on nearly-sorted input — matching the algorithm to the data matters.
Greedy = locally best choice each step; prove global optimality per problem (US coins yes, {25,10,1} at 30 cents no).
Correctness demands all inputs, not just tested ones — loop invariants are the standard verification tool.
The halting problem is undecidable: diagonalization proves no decision procedure can exist.

quiz.q: Binary search may be applied when:
options: the list has an even number of elements
quiz.explanation: Halving the interval only makes sense when comparisons split the candidates, which requires order. Distinctness, parity of length, and size are irrelevant — an unsorted list defeats binary search no matter what.

quiz.q: Greedy change-making with denominations 25, 10, 1 applied to 30 cents produces:
options: 6 coins — one quarter and five pennies
quiz.explanation: Greedy takes the quarter first (25 ≤ 30), leaving 5, which only pennies can cover: 25 + 1·5 = six coins. The optimum is three dimes — greedy is not always optimal.

quiz.q: The halting problem asks whether an algorithm can decide, for every program and input:
options: whether the program produces the correct output
whether the program eventually stops running
how much memory the program uses
whether the program is written correctly
quiz.explanation: Halting = eventual termination. The theorem is that no such decision procedure exists — establishing a fundamental limit of computation, separate from questions of speed or memory.

quiz.q: After the first complete pass of bubble sort on the list 5, 1, 4, 2, 8:
options: the largest element, 8, is guaranteed to be in its final position
the smallest element is guaranteed to be first
quiz.explanation: Sweeping adjacent swaps carries the largest-so-far value to the end of the list: 5,1,4,2,8 → 1,5,4,2,8 → 1,4,5,2,8 → 1,4,2,5,8 → 1,4,2,5,8. The list is not yet sorted, but 8 can never move again.

intro: How do you say “this algorithm's work grows no faster than that one” precisely? Big-O, big-Omega and big-Theta notation turn vague fastness claims into inequalities between functions with explicit witnesses. This section builds the definitions, the polynomial and combination theorems, and the growth ladder — log, polynomial, exponential, factorial — that orders the entire zoo of algorithm behaviors.
objectives: Use the definitions of big-O, big-Omega and big-Theta with explicit witnesses
Prove polynomial bounds using the degree theorem
Combine known bounds with the sum and product rules
Order the standard complexity classes by growth rate

concepts.statement: f(x) is **O(g(x))** iff there are constants C > 0 and k (the **witnesses**) such that |f(x)| ≤ C|g(x)| for all x > k. Informally: f grows no faster than a constant multiple of g, eventually.
concepts.detail: The witness pair (C, k) makes the claim checkable: for f(x) = x² + 4x + 17, choosing C = 22, k = 1 works since x² + 4x + 17 ≤ 22x² for x ≥ 1. Big-O is an *upper bound*: “7n³ is O(n³)” and also (loosely) “7n³ is O(n⁴).”

concepts.statement: f(x) is **Ω(g(x))** iff there are witnesses C > 0, k with |f(x)| ≥ C|g(x)| for all x > k — f grows at least as fast as a constant multiple of g. Equivalently: f is Ω(g) iff g is O(f).
concepts.detail: Where big-O bounds from above, Ω bounds from below: “the algorithm takes at least this long in the worst case.” For a positive-leading polynomial, dropping to a constant times the leading term eventually underestimates it: x² + 4x + 17 ≥ x² for x ≥ 1, so it is Ω(x²).

concepts.statement: f(x) is **Θ(g(x))** iff it is both O(g(x)) and Ω(g(x)): there are C₁, C₂ > 0 and k with C₁|g(x)| ≤ |f(x)| ≤ C₂|g(x)| for all x > k. This says f and g have the **same growth rate** up to constant factors.
concepts.detail: Θ is the tight, two-sided classification people mean by “the complexity is …”: x² + 4x + 17 is Θ(x²). Big-Θ is an equivalence-relation-like grouping (reflexive, symmetric, transitive up to the relation's intent) — functions partition into growth classes.

concepts.statement: If f(x) = aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + ⋯ + a₁x + a₀ with aₙ > 0 and degree n, then f(x) is Θ(xⁿ) — every polynomial is big-Theta of its leading term.
concepts.detail: Upper: for x ≥ 1, each |aᵢ|xⁱ ≤ |aᵢ|xⁿ, so |f(x)| ≤ (∑|aᵢ|)xⁿ. Lower: for x ≥ 1, f(x) ≥ (aₙ/2)xⁿ (the tail cannot cancel more than half the leading term — or more simply, aₙxⁿ/2 for x large enough). Consequence: 7x³ + 3x + 100 is Θ(x³), and lower-degree terms never matter.

concepts.statement: If f₁ is O(g₁) and f₂ is O(g₂), then f₁ + f₂ is O(max(|g₁|, |g₂|)) and f₁·f₂ is O(g₁g₂). Also: c·f is O(g) when f is; and big-O is transitive (f O g, g O h ⟹ f O h).
concepts.detail: Sum rule: sequential work adds the dominating term — that is why a program's overall complexity is the max of its parts. Product rule: nested work multiplies — a loop of n iterations each doing n work is n². These two rules alone compute the complexity of most simple code.

concepts.statement: In order of eventual dominance: **O(1) ≺ O(log n) ≺ O(√n) ≺ O(n) ≺ O(n log n) ≺ O(n²) ≺ O(n³) ≺ O(2ⁿ) ≺ O(n!)**. Each class eventually exceeds any constant multiple of the previous one.
concepts.detail: Key comparisons: log grows slower than any positive power of n; every exponential c·dˣ with d > 1 eventually beats every polynomial; and n! eventually beats every exponential. Stirling's formula n! ≈ √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ shows factorial growth towering over 2ⁿ. Practical meaning: an n! algorithm is hopeless beyond n ≈ 12, a 2ⁿ algorithm beyond n ≈ 40.

concepts.statement: To prove f is *not* O(g), show that the ratio |f|/|g| grows beyond every constant: for every C > 0 there is an x with |f(x)| > C|g(x)|. A single row of the ratio table often suffices for exponentials vs polynomials.
concepts.detail: Example shape: 2ˣ/x² → ∞ — doubling x squares the exponential factor (2²ˣ = (2ˣ)²) while the denominator only quadruples, so the ratio grows without bound and no witness C survives. Such impossibility proofs separate classes on the ladder (n² is not O(n log n), 2ⁿ is not O(n¹⁰⁰⁰), n! is not O(2ⁿ)).

concepts.term: Witnesses and the art of the bound
concepts.statement: To prove f is O(g), produce and verify witnesses (C, k). A robust recipe: bound each term of f by a multiple of the corresponding power of g's dominant term on x > k (usually k = 1), then add the multiples.
concepts.detail: For f(x) = x² + 4x + 17 with g(x) = x²: for x > 1, x² ≤ x², 4x ≤ 4x², 17 ≤ 17x², so f ≤ 22x². Witnesses are never unique — smaller ones are elegant but any valid pair certifies the bound.

concepts.statement: The reference functions of algorithm analysis: **1** (constant), **log n** (halving/searching), **n** (scanning), **n log n** (good sorting), **n²** (all-pairs), **n³** (all triples), **cⁿ** (exhaustive subsets), **n!** (all permutations).
concepts.detail: Log bases are interchangeable up to a constant (log₂ n = log n / log 2), so big-O ignores the base. The same ladder prices algorithms in Section 3.3, where worst/average/best case distinctions get attached to these classes.

examples.title: Proving a big-O bound with witnesses
examples.problem: Show that f(x) = x² + 4x + 17 is O(x²), and then show it is actually Θ(x²).

steps.label: Step 1: Set up the target inequality
steps.text: We need C and k with x² + 4x + 17 ≤ C·x² for x > k. Try k = 1: then x ≥ 1 forces x ≤ x² and 1 ≤ x².

steps.label: Step 2: Dominate each term
steps.text: For x ≥ 1: x² ≤ x², 4x ≤ 4x², 17 ≤ 17x². Adding: f(x) ≤ (1 + 4 + 17)x² = 22x².

steps.label: Step 3: State the witnesses
steps.text: C = 22, k = 1 certify f is O(x²). (Tighter pairs exist; any valid pair suffices.)

steps.label: Step 4: Prove the lower bound for Θ
steps.text: For x ≥ 1, f(x) = x² + 4x + 17 ≥ x², so f is Ω(x²) with C = 1, k = 1.

steps.label: Step 5: Combine
steps.text: Upper and lower bounds together: 1·x² ≤ f(x) ≤ 22·x² for x ≥ 1, so f is Θ(x²).

examples.result: f(x) = x² + 4x + 17 is Θ(x²) — consistent with the polynomial theorem: only the leading term matters.

examples.title: A two-sided bound for a cubic
examples.problem: Show that x³ + 3x is Θ(x³) with explicit witnesses.

steps.label: Step 1: Upper bound for x ≥ 1
steps.text: Since x ≤ x³ for x ≥ 1: x³ + 3x ≤ x³ + 3x³ = 4x³. So C₂ = 4 works.

steps.label: Step 2: Lower bound for x ≥ 1
steps.text: Dropping the positive term: x³ + 3x ≥ x³. So C₁ = 1 works.

steps.label: Step 3: Assemble the sandwich
steps.text: 1·x³ ≤ x³ + 3x ≤ 4·x³ for all x ≥ 1.

examples.result: Witnesses C₁ = 1, C₂ = 4, k = 1 prove x³ + 3x is Θ(x³) — the same sandwich pattern proves the general polynomial theorem.

examples.title: Climbing the growth ladder
examples.problem: Order these functions by eventual growth from slowest to fastest: log₂ n, √n, n, n log₂ n, n², 2ⁿ, n!.

steps.label: Step 1: Logarithm first
steps.text: log₂ n grows slower than any positive power: for any ε > 0, log₂ n is $O(n^{\varepsilon})$ (prove by taking ε-th powers: (log₂ n)ᵉ ≤ n eventually).

steps.label: Step 2: Powers of n line up
steps.text: $\sqrt{n} = n^{0.5} \prec n \prec n^{2}$ — compare exponents.

steps.label: Step 3: n log n wedges between n and n²
steps.text: log₂ n ≤ n eventually, so n log₂ n is O(n²) but not O(n) (log₂ n outgrows every constant).

steps.label: Step 4: Exponentials beat all polynomials
steps.text: Compare 2ⁿ with n²: moving from n to n + 1 multiplies the exponential's advantage — 2ⁿ⁺¹/2ⁿ = 2, while (n + 1)²/n² → 1. Repeated doubling wins against any fixed power, so 2ⁿ/n² → ∞.

steps.label: Step 5: Factorial beats exponential
steps.text: For n ≥ 2, every factor of n! = n(n−1)⋯2·1 is at least 2, so n! ≥ 2ⁿ⁻¹ — and the surplus of factors above 2 makes n!/2ⁿ grow beyond every constant.

examples.result: log₂ n ≺ √n ≺ n ≺ n log₂ n ≺ n² ≺ 2ⁿ ≺ n! — the master ordering used throughout Section 3.3 and all of algorithm design.

keyTakeaways: f is O(g) iff witnesses C, k give |f(x)| ≤ C|g(x)| for all x > k — an eventual upper bound.
Ω is the dual lower bound; Θ means both, i.e., f and g grow at the same rate up to constants.
Every polynomial is Θ of its leading term — lower-order terms and constants never matter.
Sums take max (sequential code), products multiply (nested code): the two rules that price most programs.
The ladder: 1 ≺ log n ≺ √n ≺ n ≺ n log n ≺ n² ≺ n³ ≺ 2ⁿ ≺ n! — each rung eventually dominates the previous.
Proving f is NOT O(g) requires the ratio to exceed every constant — a single column of large-x values won't do alone, a limiting argument will.

quiz.q: f(x) = 7x³ + 20x + 9 is:
quiz.explanation: By the polynomial theorem, a degree-3 polynomial with positive leading coefficient is Θ(x³): the linear term and constant are eventually negligible. It is certainly not bounded above by a constant, and no polynomial grows as fast as an exponential.

quiz.q: To prove that f(x) is O(g(x)) you must produce:
options: witnesses C > 0 and k such that |f(x)| ≤ C|g(x)| for all x > k
a single value x₀ with f(x₀) ≤ g(x₀)
a proof that f(x) = C·g(x) for all x
the exact maximum value of f
quiz.explanation: The definition is a witnessed, eventual inequality. One lucky data point proves nothing, exact proportionality is far too strong (and rare), and big-O never requires knowing exact maxima.

quiz.q: Which function grows fastest as n → ∞?
quiz.explanation: Factorial growth dominates: by Stirling's formula n! ≈ √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ, which eventually exceeds any exponential c·dⁿ, and exponentials in turn beat every fixed power n¹⁰⁰⁰.

quiz.q: Which statement is TRUE?
quiz.explanation: Since log n ≤ n for n ≥ 2, n log n ≤ n². The rest fail: n²/(n log n) = n/log n → ∞, exponentials eventually exceed every polynomial, and log n is unbounded so no constant bounds it.

intro: Complexity theory attaches numbers to algorithms: how many operations, how much memory, in the worst case, on average, at best. This section computes the complexity of the Chapter 3 classics — searching, sorting, Euclid's algorithm — and draws the practical dividing line between tractable (polynomial) and intractable (exponential) problems.
objectives: Compute worst-case and average-case complexity of linear and binary search
Count the comparisons made by bubble and insertion sort
Analyze time complexity of Euclid's algorithm
Distinguish time from space complexity
Classify algorithms as tractable or intractable

concepts.statement: The **time complexity** of an algorithm is the amount of computer time it uses as a function of the input size n — in practice, the count of basic operations (comparisons, additions, swaps), each charged a constant cost. By Section 3.2, the count is expressed with big-O, Ω, Θ.
concepts.detail: The convention “every basic operation costs one unit” is coarse but robust: on any real machine the constants shift, the growth classes do not. When comparing two algorithms of the same Θ class, constants and lower-order terms matter again.

concepts.statement: The **space complexity** of an algorithm is the memory it uses as a function of input size, measured in the same asymptotic style. Auxiliary space = memory beyond the input itself.
concepts.detail: Binary search uses O(1) auxiliary space (a few index variables) — in-place. Merge sort (Chapter 5) uses O(n) auxiliary space. Time–space trade-offs are a recurring design theme: caching saves time by spending memory.

concepts.statement: The **worst-case** time complexity is the maximum number of operations over all inputs of size n — the guarantee the algorithm always meets. It is the standard reported measure.
concepts.detail: For linear search: the target is last or absent, giving exactly n comparisons — Θ(n). Worst case is the right number when deadlines matter (real-time systems) and it is usually the easiest to compute: adversarially place the target.

concepts.statement: The **average-case** complexity is the expected number of operations over a probability distribution of inputs (usually uniform). For linear search with the target present and equally likely at each position: (1 + 2 + ⋯ + n)/n = (n + 1)/2 — still Θ(n).
concepts.detail: Average case needs a model of the inputs, which may or may not match reality. Insertion sort is Θ(n²) on average but Θ(n) on (nearly) sorted inputs — for data that is “almost sorted in practice,” the best case is the typical case.

concepts.term: Complexity of linear and binary search
concepts.statement: Linear search: Θ(n) worst case, (n + 1)/2 average (target present, uniform position). Binary search: Θ(log n) worst case — at most about 2log₂ n + 1 element comparisons on a sorted list of n elements.
concepts.detail: Why 2log₂ n + 1: each iteration does at most two comparisons (less-than and greater-than) and there are at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 halvings before the interval empties. Scale: n = 10⁶ — linear does a million comparisons, binary about forty.

concepts.statement: Bubble sort (Rosen's version) always performs exactly n(n − 1)/2 comparisons — Θ(n²) worst, average and best. Insertion sort performs at most n(n −  1)/2 comparisons (Θ(n²) worst), about half that on average, and exactly n − 1 comparisons (Θ(n)) on an already-sorted list.
concepts.detail: The count (n − 1) + (n − 2) + ⋯ + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 is the triangular sum from Section 2.4. Faster general sorts — merge sort at Θ(n log n) — arrive in Chapter 5, and no comparison sort can beat Θ(n log n) (Chapter 6's counting ideas sketch why).

concepts.statement: The number of divisions used by the Euclidean algorithm to compute gcd(a, b) with a ≥ b > 0 is **O(log b)** — the inputs shrink at least geometrically because two consecutive Fibonacci numbers are the worst case (Lamé's theorem).
concepts.detail: Lamé's theorem: if the algorithm takes n division steps with a ≥ b, then b ≥ fₙ₊₁ (Fibonacci), so the step count is at most about log_φ(b) ≈ 1.44 log₂ b. Euclid is thus logarithmic — astonishingly efficient for a 2,300-year-old algorithm.

concepts.statement: A problem is **tractable** if an algorithm solving it runs in polynomial time (nᵏ for some constant k); the class of problems solvable in polynomial time is called **P**. Problems requiring super-polynomial (typically exponential) time in the input size are **intractable** in practice.
concepts.detail: The polynomial/exponential boundary is the practical cliff: on a computer doing 10⁹ operations/second, n = 30 needs 0.03s at n³ but 10⁴ years at 2ⁿ. The class **NP** (solutions *verifiable* in polynomial time) contains P, and whether P = NP is the most famous open problem in mathematics — a million-dollar Millennium Prize.

concepts.statement: Rules of thumb: a Θ(log n) algorithm is effectively instant at any realistic scale; Θ(n) scans are cheap; Θ(n log n) is the price of general comparison sorting; Θ(n²) works to a few tens of thousands of items; Θ(2ⁿ) and Θ(n!) only for tiny n. Hardware speedups shift constants, never classes.
concepts.detail: A 1000× faster computer moves the 2ⁿ-feasible frontier from n ≈ 30 to n ≈ 40 — a logarithmic gain. A better algorithm (say Θ(n log n) instead of Θ(n²)) turns overnight jobs into seconds. This is why complexity classes, not benchmarks, are the theory of computing.

examples.title: Linear vs binary search at scale
examples.problem: Compare worst-case comparisons for linear and binary search on n = 64 and n = 1,000,000.

steps.label: Step 1: Linear search at n = 64
steps.text: Worst case (target absent or last): 64 comparisons — one per element.

steps.label: Step 2: Binary search at n = 64
steps.text: The interval halves 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1: six rounds (log₂ 64 = 6), at most about 2·6 + 1 = 13 comparisons.

steps.label: Step 3: Linear search at a million
steps.text: One million comparisons.

steps.label: Step 4: Binary search at a million
steps.text: log₂(10⁶) ≈ 19.93, so about 2·20 + 1 = 41 comparisons.

examples.result: 64 vs 13, then 10⁶ vs about 41: the gap between Θ(n) and Θ(log n) explodes with scale — doubling n adds just one more binary-search round.

examples.title: Counting bubble sort's comparisons
examples.problem: Derive the exact number of comparisons bubble sort performs on a list of n elements, and evaluate it for n = 100.

steps.label: Step 1: Count the inner loop
steps.text: Pass i compares adjacent pairs in the first n − i + 1 positions — that is n − i comparisons (i = 1, …, n − 1).

steps.label: Step 2: Sum over passes
steps.text: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + ⋯ + 2 + 1 = n(n − 1)/2, the triangular number (Section 2.4).

steps.label: Step 3: Note the input-independence
steps.text: Rosen's loops run a fixed number of times regardless of the data — even a sorted list pays full price.

steps.label: Step 4: Evaluate at n = 100
steps.text: 100 · 99/2 = 4,950 comparisons; at n = 1,000,000 it would be ≈ 5 × 10¹¹ — hours of machine time.

examples.result: Bubble sort always performs n(n − 1)/2 comparisons: Θ(n²), with no best-case discount.

examples.title: Best case earns its keep
examples.problem: How many comparisons does insertion sort perform on the already-sorted list 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and why does bubble sort get no such discount?

steps.label: Step 1: Trace insertion sort
steps.text: Element 2 compares once with 1 (no swap); 3 compares once with 2; 4 once with 3; 5 once with 4. Each new element stops at the first comparison.

steps.label: Step 2: Count
steps.text: n − 1 = 4 comparisons, 0 swaps — Θ(n) best case, because nothing travels.

steps.label: Step 3: Contrast bubble sort
steps.text: Bubble sort's pass structure is fixed: it still runs all n(n − 1)/2 comparisons on sorted input (in Rosen's formulation), because the loops never check whether work remains.

steps.label: Step 4: Draw the practical conclusion
steps.text: For nearly-sorted data, insertion sort behaves near-linearly — the classic reason it survives inside real-world sorting libraries for small runs.

examples.result: Insertion sort: 4 comparisons (Θ(n)); bubble sort: 10 comparisons (Θ(n²)). Best-case analysis is not an academic nicety — it decides which algorithm ships.

keyTakeaways: Time complexity counts basic operations as a function of input size; space complexity counts memory.
Worst case is the universal guarantee; average case needs an input model (uniform-position linear search: (n + 1)/2).
Linear search: Θ(n). Binary search: Θ(log n) — about 2log₂ n + 1 comparisons on sorted input.
Bubble sort always does n(n − 1)/2 comparisons; insertion sort does n − 1 on sorted input but Θ(n²) worst case.
Euclid's algorithm is O(log b) — Fibonacci inputs are the worst case (Lamé's theorem).
Tractable = polynomial time (class P); exponential algorithms are hopeless beyond small n, and P vs NP remains open.

quiz.q: Worst case, linear search on n elements performs:
quiz.explanation: The adversary hides the target last (or omits it), forcing a full scan: n comparisons. The (n + 1)/2 figure is the average case under a uniform-position model, not the worst case.

quiz.q: A binary search on 1,024 sorted elements uses at most about:
quiz.explanation: log₂ 1024 = 10 halvings, at about two comparisons each plus one final check: ≈ 2·10 + 1 = 21. Each comparison eliminates half the remaining candidates.

quiz.q: Bubble sort (Rosen's version) performs:
options: exactly n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, so it is Θ(n²) on every input
Θ(n log n) comparisons on average
fewer comparisons when the input is already sorted
quiz.explanation: The loop bounds are fixed by n, not by the data: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + ⋯ + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 always. Insertion sort — not bubble sort — is the one with a Θ(n) sorted-input best case.

quiz.q: An algorithm is considered tractable when it:
options: runs in polynomial time in the input size
quiz.explanation: Tractability is the polynomial/exponential dividing line: nᵏ for some fixed k scales to large inputs, while 2ⁿ does not, whatever the hardware. Implementation and testing say nothing about asymptotic behavior.

quiz.q: Linear search is applied to a list of $n$ distinct elements, with the target always present and equally likely to occupy any of the $n$ positions. The average number of comparisons equals:
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate the task as the **uniform-position average** of the comparison count $1, 2, \ldots, n$. Step 2: Recall the key formula that average-case cost is the arithmetic mean $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} i$ under the uniform model. Step 3: Sum the series to get $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. Step 4: Divide by $n$ to obtain $\frac{n+1}{2}$, which is $\Theta(n)$ but with a precise constant. Step 5: The distractors confuse models since $n$ is the worst case, $\log_{2} n$ belongs to binary search on sorted input, and $n^{2}$ belongs to sorting. Step 6: Hence the average is $\frac{n+1}{2}$ comparisons.

quiz.q: Insertion sort is run on an already sorted list of $n$ distinct elements. The number of element comparisons performed equals:
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate the run as insertion of each new element into an already ordered prefix. Step 2: Recall the key behavior that on sorted input each element compares once with its predecessor and stops. Step 3: The second element needs $1$ comparison, the third needs $1$, and so on through the $n$th element. Step 4: Total the comparisons as $(n-1) \times 1 = n-1$, giving $\Theta(n)$ best-case time. Step 5: The distractor $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ is the worst case when every element travels the full prefix, $n \log_{2} n$ belongs to merge sort, and $1$ forgets that all $n-1$ insertions must still be verified. Step 6: Therefore sorted input costs exactly $n-1$ comparisons.

intro: Every interesting question about integers eventually runs into remainders. This section formalizes divisibility, proves the division algorithm (every division leaves a unique quotient and remainder), and builds modular arithmetic — the mathematics of clocks, hash tables, and cryptography that powers the rest of the chapter.
objectives: State the definition of divisibility and prove its basic consequences (transitivity, linearity)
Apply the division algorithm to write a = dq + r with 0 ≤ r < d, for negative a as well as positive
Compute a div d and a mod d correctly, including negative dividends
Translate between m | (a − b) and the congruence a ≡ b (mod m)
Add and multiply congruences to compute in $\mathbb{Z}_m$ without ever forming huge numbers

concepts.statement: If a and b are integers with a ≠ 0, then **a divides b**, written **a | b**, when there is an integer c with b = ac. Then a is a factor (divisor) of b and b is a multiple of a. If no such c exists we write a ∤ b.
concepts.detail: 3 | 12 because 12 = 3·4, but 3 ∤ 7 since no integer c gives 3c = 7. Every nonzero integer divides 0 (0 = a·0); 1 divides everything; 0 divides nothing (we require a ≠ 0).

concepts.statement: For integers a, b, c: (1) if a | b and b | c, then a | c (transitivity); (2) if a | b and a | c, then a | (b + c) and a | (b − c); (3) if a | b, then a | bc for every integer c.
concepts.detail: The proofs are one line each: write b = ax and c = ay, then b + c = a(x + y). Example: 5 | 10 and 10 | 40 give 5 | 40; since 3 | 9 and 3 | 15, we get 3 | 24.

concepts.statement: Let d be a positive integer and a any integer. Then there exist **unique** integers q (the quotient) and r (the remainder) with **a = dq + r and 0 ≤ r < d**.
concepts.detail: Despite its name, this is a theorem about existence and uniqueness of remainders — the guarantee that division works the way you learned in school. Example: 101 = 13·7 + 10 with 0 ≤ 10 < 13, so 101 div 13 = 7 and 101 mod 13 = 10.

concepts.statement: For integers a and d with d > 0: **a div d = q** and **a mod d = r** where a = dq + r and 0 ≤ r < d. The mod operation returns the non-negative remainder.
concepts.detail: Watch negatives: −133 = 12·(−12) + 11, so −133 div 12 = −12 and −133 mod 12 = 11. Many programming languages return −1 here because they truncate toward zero — mathematics demands 0 ≤ r < d.

concepts.statement: If a, b are integers and m ≥ 1, then **a is congruent to b modulo m**, written **a ≡ b (mod m)**, when m divides a − b. Congruence mod m is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive — an equivalence relation.
concepts.detail: 17 ≡ 5 (mod 6) because 17 − 5 = 12 is divisible by 6. Two integers are congruent mod m exactly when they leave the same remainder mod m, so the integers split into exactly m congruence classes.

concepts.statement: If a ≡ b (mod m) and c ≡ d (mod m), then a + c ≡ b + d (mod m), a − c ≡ b − d (mod m), and **ac ≡ bd (mod m)**. Consequently $a^k \equiv b^k \pmod{m}$ for every positive integer k.
concepts.detail: You may swap any quantity for a congruent one at any point of a computation — replace 457 by 2 mod 13, or $2^{100}$ by 1 mod 5. The one operation NOT preserved is division: that is section 4.4's business.

concepts.statement: The set $\mathbb{Z}_m = \{0, 1, 2, \dots, m - 1\}$ of remainders is closed under addition and multiplication mod m: compute normally, then reduce mod m. Every integer is congruent to exactly one element of $\mathbb{Z}_m$.
concepts.detail: Example: in $\mathbb{Z}_9$, $7 \cdot 8 = 56 \equiv 2 \pmod{9}$. Working mod m means all arithmetic can be done inside these m small values.

concepts.term: Compute big powers mod m by reducing early
concepts.statement: To evaluate an expression mod m, reduce every factor mod m first and reduce after every operation — never form the huge number and reduce at the end.
concepts.detail: $2^{100} \bmod 5$: the powers of 2 mod 5 cycle 2, 4, 3, 1 with period 4, and 100 ≡ 0 (mod 4), so $2^{100} \equiv 1 \pmod{5}$. Cycles and congruence arithmetic replace billion-digit arithmetic.

examples.title: div and mod with a negative dividend
examples.problem: Find 133 div 12, 133 mod 12, −133 div 12, and −133 mod 12.

steps.label: Set up the negative case
steps.text: For −133 = 12q + r the remainder must still satisfy 0 ≤ r < 12, so the quotient rounds down: −133 = 12·(−12) + 11.

examples.result: 133 = 12·11 + 1 and −133 = 12·(−12) + 11. A remainder from the division algorithm is never negative.

examples.title: Squaring a big number mod 13
examples.problem: Compute 457² mod 13 without ever squaring 457.

steps.label: Square the congruence
steps.text: Congruences multiply: 457² ≡ 2² = 4 (mod 13).

examples.title: Clock arithmetic
examples.problem: If it is 5 o'clock now, what time will the clock show exactly 100 hours later?

steps.label: Model with congruences
steps.text: Clock arithmetic is mod 12: we need 5 + 100 (mod 12).

examples.result: 9 o'clock — 100 hours after 5 o'clock the clock reads 9.

keyTakeaways: a | b means b = ac for some integer c; divisibility is transitive and linear over sums and differences of multiples
Division algorithm: a = dq + r with 0 ≤ r < d, and the pair (q, r) is unique
a div d and a mod d extract q and r — the remainder is always in {0, …, d − 1}, even for negative a
a ≡ b (mod m) exactly when a and b differ by a multiple of m — think same remainder
Congruences can be added, subtracted, and multiplied; reduce early, reduce often

quiz.q: What is −17 mod 5?
quiz.explanation: −17 = 5·(−4) + 3 with 0 ≤ 3 < 5, so the remainder is 3. The division algorithm always produces a non-negative remainder.

quiz.q: Which pair of integers is congruent modulo 6?
quiz.explanation: 17 − 5 = 12 = 6·2, so 17 ≡ 5 (mod 6). For the others: 24 − 4 = 20, 25 − 4 = 21, and 18 − 5 = 13 — none is divisible by 6.

quiz.q: If a ≡ 3 (mod 7) and b ≡ 2 (mod 7), then ab mod 7 equals:
quiz.explanation: Congruences multiply: ab ≡ 3·2 = 6 (mod 7).

quiz.q: Dividing 101 by 13, the division algorithm gives 101 = 13q + r with 0 ≤ r < 13. What are q and r?

intro: Computers think in binary, engineers shorthand in hexadecimal, and RSA lives on fast modular exponentiation. This section builds the conversion machinery between number bases, the algorithms for integer arithmetic, and the repeated-squaring trick that makes encrypting with huge exponents instantaneous.
objectives: Write any integer in base b as n = ∑ aᵢbⁱ and explain why the representation is unique
Convert fluently between decimal, binary, octal, and hexadecimal
Explain why binary converts to octal and hex by grouping 3 or 4 bits
Trace addition and multiplication of integers in binary
Compute $b^n \bmod m$ with fast modular exponentiation in $O(\log n)$ multiplications

concepts.statement: If b ≥ 2 and n is a positive integer, then n has a **unique** representation $n = a_{k-1}b^{k-1} + a_{k-2}b^{k-2} + \cdots + a_1 b + a_0$ with digits $0 \le a_i < b$. It is written $(a_{k-1}\cdots a_1 a_0)_b$.
concepts.detail: Uniqueness is the division algorithm applied repeatedly — each division by b peels off one digit. Example: $(2AE9)_{16} = 2\cdot 16^3 + 10\cdot 16^2 + 14\cdot 16 + 9 = 10{,}985$.

concepts.statement: Base 2: the digits (bits) are 0 and 1, and bit i is worth $2^i$. Example: $(101011111)_2 = 256 + 64 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 351$.
concepts.detail: Binary is the native language of digital hardware: two stable states per digit map to bits, and two's-complement arithmetic is built on it.

concepts.statement: Base 8 uses digits 0–7; base 16 uses 0–9 and A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14, F = 15. Because 8 = 2³ and 16 = 2⁴, each octal digit equals a group of 3 bits and each hex digit equals a group of 4 bits.
concepts.detail: $(11100101)_2 = (345)_8 = (E5)_{16} = 229$ — group the bits from the right in 3s or 4s and read the digits off directly.

concepts.statement: To convert n to base b: divide n by b and record the remainder; divide the quotient by b again; repeat until the quotient is 0. The remainders, read from last to first, are the base-b digits.
Evaluate the digit polynomial: start at the leftmost digit and repeatedly multiply by b and add the next digit (Horner's rule). Example: $(E5)_{16} = 14\cdot 16 + 5 = 229$.
concepts.detail: Horner's rule costs one multiply and one add per digit — the fastest way to convert into decimal by hand or in hardware.

concepts.statement: Grade-school addition and multiplication work in any base. Binary addition carries when 1 + 1 = 10; binary multiplication is a sequence of shifts (doublings) and adds. Adding n-bit integers costs O(n) bit operations; the standard multiplication algorithm costs O(n²).
concepts.detail: Example: 1011 + 110 = 10001, i.e., 11 + 6 = 17. Faster multiplication algorithms (Karatsuba, FFT-based) beat O(n²) for very long numbers.

concepts.statement: To compute $b^n \bmod m$: write n in binary; compute b, b², b⁴, b⁸, … mod m by **repeated squaring** (about log₂ n squarings); multiply together the squares corresponding to the 1-bits of n, reducing mod m after each multiplication. Total: **O(log n) modular multiplications** instead of n − 1.
concepts.detail: Computing $3^{644} \bmod 645$ needs roughly 19 multiplications on numbers below 645 rather than 643 multiplications of ever-growing numbers.

concepts.statement: RSA routinely raises 2048-bit messages to 2048-bit exponents: only the O(log n) repeated-squaring method makes this feasible on everyday hardware.
concepts.detail: The same idea underlies many algorithms: any recurrence $a^{2k} = (a^k)^2$ halves the exponent at one multiplication's cost.

examples.title: Converting 241 to binary
examples.problem: Convert the decimal number 241 to base 2.

steps.label: Read remainders bottom to top
steps.text: The remainders, from the last division to the first, are 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1.

examples.title: Hex and octal at a glance
examples.problem: Convert $(11100101)_2$ to hexadecimal and to octal; convert $(2AE9)_{16}$ to decimal.

examples.title: Fast modular exponentiation: 3⁶⁴⁴ mod 645
examples.problem: Compute $3^{644} \bmod 645$ using repeated squaring.

steps.label: Multiply the needed squares
steps.text: $3^{644} \equiv 3^{512} \cdot 3^{128} \cdot 3^4 \equiv 111 \cdot 396 \equiv 96 \pmod{645}$, then $96 \cdot 81 \equiv 36 \pmod{645}$.

examples.result: $3^{644} \equiv 36 \pmod{645}$, using about 19 multiplications on small numbers.

keyTakeaways: Every positive integer has a unique base-b expansion with digits 0, …, b − 1
Decimal → base b: successive division; base b → decimal: multiply-and-add
Hex and octal are binary with the bits grouped by 4 and 3 — conversions are instant
Binary addition costs O(n) bit operations, standard multiplication O(n²)
Fast modular exponentiation (repeated squaring) needs only O(log n) multiplications — the engine of RSA

quiz.q: The bit string 11110000 is which hexadecimal number?
quiz.explanation: Group into 4-bit chunks: 1111 = F and 0000 = 0, giving $(F0)_{16}$.

quiz.q: What is $(2FB)_{16}$ in decimal?
Roughly how many modular multiplications does repeated-squaring exponentiation need to compute $b^{644} \bmod m$?
quiz.explanation: 644 needs 10 bits; each bit costs one squaring plus possibly one multiplication, giving about 20 modular multiplications — O(log n) versus O(n) naive.

quiz.q: Which binary string represents the decimal number 75?

intro: Primes are the atoms of multiplication: every integer above 1 factors into them in exactly one way. This section proves that, meets the 2300-year-old Euclidean algorithm for greatest common divisors, and derives Bézout's theorem — the fact that gcd(a, b) can be written as a combination sa + tb that later unlocks solving congruences.
objectives: Define primes and composites, and test primality by trial division up to √n
State and apply the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
Compute gcd and lcm from prime factorizations, using gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b) = ab
Run the Euclidean algorithm and find Bézout coefficients by back-substitution
Distinguish relatively prime from pairwise relatively prime

concepts.statement: An integer p > 1 is **prime** if its only positive divisors are 1 and p. An integer n > 1 that is not prime is **composite**. The integer 1 is neither prime nor composite.
concepts.detail: 2 is the only even prime. A composite n has a factorization n = ab with 1 < a ≤ b < n.

concepts.statement: An integer n > 1 is prime if and only if it has no prime divisor p ≤ √n. Reason: if n = ab with both a, b > √n, then ab > n, which is impossible.
concepts.detail: Is 91 prime? √91 ≈ 9.5, so test 2, 3, 5, 7: 91 = 7·13 — composite. Trial division is O(√n), fine for small numbers, hopeless for cryptographic sizes (hundreds of digits).

concepts.statement: To list all primes ≤ n: write down 2, …, n; repeatedly take the smallest uncrossed number p (which is prime) and cross out its multiples p², p² + p, p² + 2p, …. The survivors are exactly the primes.
