quiz.explanation: The pair (c,c) is missing, so R is not reflexive. Symmetry holds (every pair has its reverse) and transitivity holds ((a,b) with (b,a) forces (a,a) and (b,b), both present). Reflexivity does not follow from the other two properties.

quiz.q: The relation a divides b on the positive integers is:
quiz.explanation: a|a always (reflexive); a|b and b|a force a = b (antisymmetric); a|b and b|c force a|c (transitive). It is far from symmetric: 3|6 but 6 does not divide 3.

quiz.q: If R = {(1,2),(2,3)} is a relation on {1,2,3}, what is R ∪ R⁻¹?
quiz.explanation: R⁻¹ = {(2,1),(3,2)}, so the union collects all four ordered pairs — this is exactly the symmetric closure of R.

quiz.q: How many binary relations are there on a set with 3 elements?
quiz.explanation: A relation is any subset of the 3² = 9 ordered pairs, so there are 2⁹ = 512 possible relations.

intro: Databases are the most valuable application of relations on the planet. An n-ary relation is just a table — a set of tuples — and the database operations of projection and join are mathematics performed at industrial scale by every SQL query ever run.
objectives: Define n-ary relations and their degree
Identify primary and composite keys in a database table
Compute projections of relations
Join two relations on specified fields

concepts.statement: An **n-ary relation** on sets A₁, ..., Aₙ is a subset of A₁ × A₂ × ... × Aₙ; its elements are n-tuples (a₁, ..., aₙ), and n is the **degree** of the relation.
concepts.detail: A course-enrollment table of triples (student, course, term) is a 3-ary (ternary) relation; binary relations are the n = 2 special case.

concepts.statement: A **relational database** is a collection of n-ary relations (tables) whose columns are **attributes**, each attribute having a domain of allowed values.
concepts.detail: A table Students(ID, Name, Major, GPA) is a 4-ary relation; rows are tuples and columns are attributes. The name is literal: Codd modeled database tables exactly as mathematical relations.

concepts.statement: An attribute (or set of attributes) is a **primary key** for a database relation if no two distinct tuples agree on all of its values — it uniquely determines the tuple.
concepts.detail: Student ID works as a primary key; Name does not, since two students can share a name. Surrogate ID numbers exist purely to guarantee uniqueness.

concepts.statement: A **composite key** is a set of two or more attributes whose combined values are unique even though no single one is.
concepts.detail: In an Enrollments(StudentID, CourseID, Term) table, the pair (StudentID, CourseID) may repeat across terms, so the triple (StudentID, CourseID, Term) is needed as the key.

concepts.statement: The **projection** $P_{i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_m}(R)$ keeps only components i₁, ..., iₘ of each tuple (in that order) and discards duplicate tuples that result — it selects columns.
concepts.detail: Projecting (Name, Major) from a Students table yields every (name, major) combination that occurs, with duplicates removed — like SQL's SELECT DISTINCT.

concepts.statement: The **join** Jₚ(R, S) of an m-ary relation R and an n-ary relation S (with p ≤ m and p ≤ n) is the (m + n − p)-ary relation of all tuples of R × S that agree on their first p components.
concepts.detail: Joining Flights(Flight#, Gate, Dest) with Gates(Gate, Time) on the shared gate field pairs each flight with its departure time — tuples are glued only when the gate matches.

concepts.statement: Relational algebra is what SQL implements: WHERE is selection, SELECT is projection, and JOIN is the join operation — set operations running at industrial scale.
concepts.detail: Indices built on keys make these operations fast; the mathematics guarantees they are well-defined constructions on relations.

examples.title: Projecting a Table
examples.problem: Let R = {(302, Ha, CS), (210, Li, CS), (101, Ha, MA), (415, Li, CS)} with attributes (ID, Name, Dept). Compute P₂,₃(R).

steps.label: Keep columns 2 and 3
steps.text: Extract (Name, Dept) from each tuple: (Ha, CS), (Li, CS), (Ha, MA), (Li, CS).

steps.label: Delete duplicates
steps.text: (Li, CS) arises twice, and a relation is a set.

examples.result: P₂,₃(R) = {(Ha, CS), (Li, CS), (Ha, MA)}.

examples.title: Joining Flights to Gates
examples.problem: Let R = {(302, A, Detroit), (210, B, Chicago)} with attributes (Flight#, Gate, Dest), and S = {(A, 8:15), (B, 8:30)} with attributes (Gate, Departure). Compute J₁(R, S).

steps.label: Shared component
steps.text: Both relations lead with Gate, so p = 1.

steps.label: Match tuples
steps.text: Flight 302 uses gate A, matching (A, 8:15); flight 210 uses gate B, matching (B, 8:30).

steps.label: Merge
steps.text: Glue the tuples at the shared field, dropping the duplicated copy of it: (302, A, Detroit, 8:15) and (210, B, Chicago, 8:30).

examples.result: J₁(R,S) = {(302, A, Detroit, 8:15), (210, B, Chicago, 8:30)} — every flight with its departure time.

examples.title: Finding Keys
examples.problem: Consider Enrollments = {(1001, CS101, Fall), (1001, MA201, Fall), (1002, CS101, Fall), (1002, CS101, Spring)} with attributes (StudentID, CourseID, Term). Which subsets of attributes form a key?

steps.label: Test StudentID alone
steps.text: Student 1001 appears in two tuples — not a key.

steps.label: Test CourseID alone
steps.text: CS101 appears in three tuples — not a key.

steps.label: Test (StudentID, CourseID)
steps.text: The pair (1002, CS101) occurs twice (Fall and Spring) — not a key.

steps.label: Test all three attributes
steps.text: All four triples are distinct — the full attribute set is a composite key.

examples.result: Only (StudentID, CourseID, Term) is a key; no proper subset works.

keyTakeaways: An n-ary relation is a set of n-tuples — a database table; its degree is the number of attributes.
A primary key uniquely determines tuples; composite keys combine attributes to achieve uniqueness.
Projection selects columns (and collapses duplicates); join glues tables together on shared fields.
SQL's SELECT and JOIN are relational algebra — projection and join — in production.

quiz.q: A relation is a subset of A₁ × A₂ × A₃ × A₄. What is its degree?
options: Depends on the number of tuples
quiz.explanation: The degree of an n-ary relation is n, the number of components (attributes) in each tuple — here 4, regardless of how many tuples it contains.

quiz.q: Which attribute is most likely to serve as a primary key for a Students table?
quiz.explanation: A primary key must be unique across tuples; names, majors and GPAs repeat, while ID numbers are designed to be unique.

quiz.q: In a table with attributes (Student, Course, Grade), the pair (Student, Course) fails as a key because one student took the same course in two different terms. What is the natural fix?
options: Use (Student, Course, Term) as a composite key
Keys are impossible in such tables
quiz.explanation: Extending the composite key with the discriminating attribute Term restores uniqueness — composite keys can be as long as needed.

quiz.q: The projection $P_{i_1,\ldots,i_m}(R)$ is best described as:
options: selecting rows that satisfy a condition
selecting columns and removing duplicate tuples
quiz.explanation: Projection keeps only the listed components of each tuple and, since relations are sets, collapses any duplicates that result.

intro: Computers cannot store ordered pairs directly — but they store matrices and graphs beautifully. This section shows how a zero-one matrix encodes any relation, how Boolean algebra on those matrices mirrors composition, and how digraphs make relational properties visible at a glance.
objectives: Represent relations with zero-one matrices
Read reflexivity, symmetry and antisymmetry off the matrix
Compute Boolean products and relate them to composition
Draw and interpret digraphs of relations

concepts.statement: If A = {a₁, ..., aₘ} and B = {b₁, ..., bₙ}, the **zero-one matrix of R ⊆ A × B** is the m×n matrix $M_R$ with **mᵢⱼ = 1 if (aᵢ, bⱼ) ∈ R** and 0 otherwise.
concepts.detail: Row i is the membership list of everything aᵢ relates to. A relation on an n-element set gets an n×n matrix.

concepts.statement: R on A is **reflexive** iff the main diagonal of $M_R$ is all 1s; **symmetric** iff $M_R = M_R^{t}$ (the matrix equals its transpose); **antisymmetric** iff mᵢⱼmⱼᵢ = 0 for all i ≠ j (no mirrored pair of 1s off the diagonal).
concepts.detail: Transitivity has no simple one-matrix test — it needs powers of the matrix, which is the subject of the next section.

concepts.statement: The **join** M₁ ∨ M₂ and **meet** M₁ ∧ M₂ of zero-one matrices are their entrywise OR and AND.
concepts.detail: Union of relations corresponds to the join of their matrices, intersection to the meet — the Boolean arithmetic that supports composition.

concepts.statement: The **Boolean product** M₁ ⊙ M₂ has (i,j)-entry **⋁ₖ(mᵢₖ ∧ mₖⱼ)** — ordinary matrix multiplication with AND replacing multiplication and OR replacing addition.
concepts.detail: Like arithmetic matrix multiplication, ⊙ is associative, which is exactly what makes matrix powers (and hence relation powers) meaningful.

concepts.statement: The matrix of the composite satisfies $M_{S \circ R} = M_R \odot M_S$ — the order reverses: the matrix of the first-applied relation sits on the left.
concepts.detail: This mirrors the familiar reversal in function composition notation: to apply S∘R, apply R first, so its matrix is written first in the product.

concepts.statement: The matrix of Rⁿ is the n-fold Boolean product $M_R \odot M_R \odot \cdots \odot M_R$; its (i,j)-entry records whether a path of length n leads from aᵢ to aⱼ.
concepts.detail: Boolean squaring of the matrix is the computational route to reachability and the transitive closure in the next section.

concepts.statement: The **directed graph** of a relation R on A has vertex set A and a directed edge a → b for each (a,b) ∈ R; a self-loop marks (a,a).
concepts.detail: Reflexivity = a loop at every vertex; symmetry = every edge paired with its reverse; transitivity = every length-2 path already has its shortcut edge.

concepts.statement: Matrices suit computation (bit operations, fixed-size storage); digraphs suit human insight (paths, components, structure).
concepts.detail: Databases store tables; graph algorithms use adjacency (zero-one) matrices — both are this same mathematics of relations.

examples.title: Matrix to Properties
examples.problem: Write the matrix of R = {(1,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,1)} on {1,2,3} and read off its properties.

steps.label: Build the matrix
steps.text: Rows and columns ordered 1, 2, 3: entries 1 at (1,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,1): $M = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.

steps.label: Reflexive?
steps.text: The diagonal entries are 1, 0, 0 — a diagonal zero kills reflexivity.

steps.label: Symmetric?
steps.text: m₁₂ = 1 but m₂₁ = 0 — not symmetric.

steps.label: Antisymmetric?
steps.text: Check mirrored pairs: (1,2)/(2,1): 1,0; (1,3)/(3,1): 0,1; (2,3)/(3,2): 1,0 — never both 1, so antisymmetric.

steps.label: Transitive?
steps.text: (3,1) and (1,2) force (3,2), which is absent — not transitive.

examples.result: R is antisymmetric only.

examples.title: Boolean Product and Composition

steps.label: Matrices
steps.text: $M_R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $M_S = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

examples.result: Both agree: $M_{S \circ R} = M_R \odot M_S$ is the all-ones matrix — the composite is the universal relation.

examples.title: A Digraph Sketch
examples.problem: Describe the digraph of the divisibility relation on A = {1,2,3,6}.

steps.label: Edges
steps.text: A loop on every vertex (a|a), plus 1→2, 1→3, 1→6, 2→6, 3→6.

steps.label: What you see
steps.text: Vertex 1 points at everything; 6 receives from everything; 2 and 3 are mutually unreachable from each other.

steps.label: Structure
steps.text: The transitive edge 1→6 (which factors through 2 or 3) is exactly what a Hasse diagram will later delete.

examples.result: A looped digraph whose edge pattern mirrors the factor lattice of 6.

keyTakeaways: The zero-one matrix $M_R$ has mᵢⱼ = 1 exactly when (aᵢ, bⱼ) ∈ R.
Reflexivity = 1s on the diagonal; symmetry = M = Mᵗ; antisymmetry = no mirrored 1s off the diagonal.
Boolean product replaces multiplication with ∧ and addition with ∨; $M_{S \circ R} = M_R \odot M_S$ (order reverses).
Digraphs make properties visible: loops for reflexivity, paired edges for symmetry, shortcut edges for transitivity.

quiz.q: A relation R on {1, ..., n} is reflexive exactly when its zero-one matrix satisfies:
options: each row contains at least one 1
quiz.explanation: Reflexivity requires (aᵢ, aᵢ) ∈ R for every i — precisely the diagonal entries mᵢᵢ.

quiz.q: R on a finite set is symmetric exactly when $M_R$ equals:
quiz.explanation: Symmetry means mᵢⱼ = mⱼᵢ for all i, j — exactly the statement that the matrix equals its transpose (reflection across the main diagonal).

quiz.q: The Boolean product M₁ ⊙ M₂ has (i,j)-entry:
quiz.explanation: Boolean product is matrix multiplication with arithmetic replaced by Boolean algebra: multiply with AND, add with OR.

quiz.q: For relations R (from A to B) and S (from B to C), the matrix of the composite satisfies:
quiz.explanation: The first-applied relation goes on the left: $M_{S \circ R} = M_R \odot M_S$ — the same reversal seen in function composition notation.

intro: A relation almost has the property you want — it just misses a few pairs. The closure of R is the smallest relation containing R that truly has the property: add loops to make it reflexive, reversed pairs to make it symmetric, and all shortcut paths to make it transitive — the last task needing Warshall's classic algorithm.
objectives: Define closures as minimal extensions of a relation
Form reflexive and symmetric closures directly
Compute transitive closures via matrix powers and paths
Trace Warshall's algorithm and its Wₖ recurrence

concepts.statement: Given a property P, the **P-closure** of a relation R is the smallest relation S containing R that has property P.
concepts.detail: Closure = add exactly the pairs required and nothing more. Different properties give different closures, and a relation that already has P equals its own P-closure.

concepts.statement: The reflexive closure of R on A is **R ∪ Δ**, where Δ = {(a,a) : a ∈ A} is the diagonal (identity) relation.
concepts.detail: Add the missing loops — nothing else is needed, and any extra non-loop pair would violate minimality.

concepts.statement: The symmetric closure of R is **R ∪ R⁻¹** — add each missing reversed pair.
concepts.detail: If both (a,b) and (b,a) are already in R nothing changes; the union simply guarantees every edge comes with its mirror.

concepts.statement: There is a **path of length n** from a to b in the digraph of R if and only if **(a,b) ∈ Rⁿ** (n-fold composition); a path of some length ≥ 1 exists iff (a,b) ∈ R⁺ = R ∪ R² ∪ R³ ∪ ..., the **connectivity relation**.
concepts.detail: Paths of length 1 are the edges themselves; length-2 paths correspond to R², and so on. A circuit is a path that begins and ends at the same vertex.

concepts.statement: The transitive closure of R on an n-element set is **R⁺ = R ∪ R² ∪ ... ∪ Rⁿ** — every path longer than n repeats a vertex and can be shortened.
concepts.detail: Membership (a,b) ∈ R⁺ means a can reach b. Example: R = {(1,2),(2,3),(3,1)} on a 3-set has R² = {(1,3),(2,1),(3,2)}, R³ = {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)}, and R⁺ = A × A — everything is reachable around the cycle.

concepts.term: Computing the Closure with Matrix Powers
concepts.statement: Form the zero-one matrix M of R; compute the Boolean powers M, M², ..., Mⁿ; the closure matrix is their **join (entrywise OR)**. Naively this costs about n⁴ bit operations, improvable to O(n³ log n) by repeated squaring.
concepts.detail: The Boolean product is associative, so squaring yields M, M², M⁴, ... quickly — still not the best possible.

concepts.statement: Set W₀ = M and iterate for k = 1..n: **Wₖ[i,j] = Wₖ₋₁[i,j] ∨ (Wₖ₋₁[i,k] ∧ Wₖ₋₁[k,j])**. Then Wₙ is the matrix of the transitive closure, computed in Θ(n³).
concepts.detail: A 1 in Wₖ[i,j] means a path from vᵢ to vⱼ using only intermediate vertices from {v₁, ..., vₖ}: either the path avoids vₖ (first term) or passes through it (second term) — a dynamic-programming dichotomy.

concepts.statement: The update can be done in place — row k is OR-ed into exactly those rows having a 1 in column k — because Wₖ and Wₖ₋₁ differ only in entries that never revert.
concepts.detail: The same structural trick powers the Floyd–Warshall all-pairs shortest-path algorithm, with add/min replacing AND/OR.

examples.title: Reflexive and Symmetric Closures
examples.problem: For R = {(1,2),(2,3)} on A = {1,2,3}, find the reflexive closure and the symmetric closure.

steps.label: Verify minimality
steps.text: Removing any added pair would destroy the property, and no other pairs are needed.

examples.result: The reflexive closure adds the 3 diagonal pairs; the symmetric closure adds the 2 reversed pairs.

examples.title: Transitive Closure by Powers
examples.problem: Find the transitive closure of R = {(1,2),(2,3)} on {1,2,3}.

steps.label: Compute R²
steps.text: (1,2) followed by (2,3) gives (1,3): R² = {(1,3)}.

steps.label: Compute R³
steps.text: No path of length 3 exists: R³ = ∅ (and all higher powers are empty too).

steps.label: Check transitivity
steps.text: The only composability was (1,2) then (2,3), and its shortcut (1,3) is present.

examples.result: R⁺ = {(1,2),(2,3),(1,3)} — the shortcut (1,3) was the only missing pair.

examples.title: Warshall's Algorithm on a 3-Cycle
examples.problem: Trace Warshall's algorithm on M = [[0,1,0],[0,0,1],[1,0,0]] (the directed 3-cycle 1→2→3→1).

steps.label: k = 1 (allow vertex 1 as intermediate)
steps.text: Only row 3 has a 1 in column 1, so row 3 gains row 1: W₁ = [[0,1,0],[0,0,1],[1,1,0]] — new edge 3→2.

steps.label: k = 2 (allow vertex 2)
steps.text: Rows 1 and 3 have a 1 in column 2, so both gain row 2 = (0,0,1): W₂ = [[0,1,1],[0,0,1],[1,1,1]] — new edge 1→3.

steps.label: k = 3 (allow vertex 3)
steps.text: Every row has a 1 in column 3, so every row gains row 3 = (1,1,1): W₃ = [[1,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,1,1]].

examples.result: W₃ is all 1s: from any vertex you can reach any other around the cycle.

keyTakeaways: The P-closure of R is the smallest relation with property P that contains R.
Reflexive closure: R ∪ Δ. Symmetric closure: R ∪ R⁻¹.
Transitive closure: R⁺ = R ∪ R² ∪ ... ∪ Rⁿ — the reachability relation.
(a,b) ∈ Rⁿ iff there is a path of length n from a to b in the digraph of R.
Warshall's algorithm computes the transitive closure in Θ(n³) by allowing one new intermediate vertex per stage.

quiz.q: The reflexive closure of a relation R on A is:
options: R ∪ Δ where Δ is the diagonal relation
quiz.explanation: Adding exactly the diagonal pairs (a,a) supplies every missing self-loop, and nothing else is required.

quiz.q: The symmetric closure of R is:
quiz.explanation: Each pair's reverse is added; the intersection R ∩ R⁻¹ would instead keep only the pairs that already have their reverse.

quiz.q: What does (a,b) ∈ Rⁿ mean in the digraph of R?
options: there is a path of length n from a to b
there are n distinct paths from a to b
quiz.explanation: Rⁿ is the n-fold composition; membership records an n-edge walk from a to b.

quiz.q: In Warshall's algorithm, Wₖ[i,j] = 1 means there is a path from vᵢ to vⱼ using:
options: intermediate vertices only from {v₁, ..., vₖ} (plus the endpoints)
at most k vertices in total
quiz.explanation: The index k is the allowed set of intermediate vertices — the dynamic-programming state. After stage n all vertices are allowed, and Wₙ is the transitive closure.

intro: When is it legitimate to treat two different objects as the same? Equivalence relations — reflexive, symmetric and transitive — are the rigorous answer, and their magic is that they cut any set into disjoint classes: fractions, residue classes, isomorphism types and compressed data all live here.
objectives: Verify equivalence relations and compute equivalence classes
Prove the two defining theorems about classes (equal or disjoint)
Establish the bijection between equivalence relations and partitions
Analyze congruence modulo m and its residue classes

concepts.statement: A relation R on A is an **equivalence relation** if it is **reflexive, symmetric and transitive**; when aRb we call a and b equivalent.
concepts.detail: Congruence mod m, equal checksums, same birthday, same chemical valence, graph isomorphism — all are sameness tests.

concepts.statement: For a ∈ A, the **equivalence class of a** is **[a]ᵣ = {s ∈ A : sRa}** — the set of all elements related to a (equal to {s : aRs} by symmetry).
concepts.detail: Every element belongs to its own class by reflexivity, so classes are automatically nonempty and together cover A.

concepts.statement: For any a, b ∈ A: either **[a] = [b] or [a] ∩ [b] = ∅**; moreover **aRb if and only if [a] = [b]**.
concepts.detail: Two classes that share a single element coincide entirely: symmetry and transitivity propagate the overlap to every member.

concepts.statement: A **partition** of A is a collection of nonempty, pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is A; the subsets are the **blocks** (cells) of the partition.
concepts.detail: {{1,2},{3,5},{4}} partitions {1,2,3,4,5}. A partition answers one question of every element: which block do you belong to?

concepts.statement: If R is an equivalence relation on A, its distinct equivalence classes **form a partition of A**; conversely, every partition P of A defines an equivalence relation by aRb iff a and b lie in the same block — and the two constructions are inverse to each other.
concepts.detail: Equivalence relations on A ↔ partitions of A: a genuine bijection. The number of equivalence relations on an n-element set is the Bell number Bₙ.

concepts.statement: **a ≡ b (mod m)** iff m | (a − b); this is an equivalence relation on Z for every m ≥ 1.
concepts.detail: Reflexive: m divides a − a = 0. Symmetric: divisors of a − b divide b − a. Transitive: m | (a−b) and m | (b−c) give m | (a−c).

concepts.statement: The equivalence classes of congruence mod m are **[0], [1], ..., [m−1]** where [r] = {r + km : k ∈ Z}; every integer lies in exactly one residue class, and [a] = [b] iff a ≡ b (mod m).
concepts.detail: For m = 4: [0] = {..., −8, −4, 0, 4, 8, ...} and [1] = {..., −7, −3, 1, 5, ...}. Arithmetic on Z mod m is arithmetic on these m classes.

concepts.statement: Any function f : A → B defines the equivalence relation a ~ b iff f(a) = f(b); conversely every equivalence relation arises this way from its classes map.
concepts.detail: Same birthday = same value of the birthday function; same remainder = same value of the mod-m function. Sameness is always sameness of output.

examples.title: Congruence Classes mod 4
examples.problem: Describe the equivalence classes of a ≡ b (mod 4) on the integers.

steps.label: Verify equivalence
steps.text: m = 4 divides a − a = 0 (reflexive); a − b swaps sign (symmetric); differences add (transitive).

steps.label: Observe the partition
steps.text: Every integer lands in exactly one class according to its remainder on division by 4.

examples.result: Four residue classes partitioning Z exactly like the remainders 0–3.

examples.title: From Partition to Relation
examples.problem: The partition P = {{1,2},{3,5},{4}} of A = {1,2,3,4,5} defines a relation R: aRb iff a and b are in the same block. List R.

steps.label: Block {1,2}
steps.text: All ordered pairs among {1,2}: (1,1),(1,2),(2,1),(2,2).

examples.result: R is the union of the three blocks mini-universal relations: 9 pairs, an equivalence relation whose classes are exactly the blocks.

examples.title: A Textbook Verification
examples.problem: On {1,2,3,4} let R = {(a,b) : a − b is even}. Verify that R is an equivalence relation and find its classes.

steps.label: Reflexive
steps.text: a − a = 0 is even, so (a,a) ∈ R for every a.

steps.label: Symmetric
steps.text: If a − b is even, then b − a = −(a − b) is even.

steps.label: Transitive
steps.text: a − b even and b − c even imply a − c = (a−b) + (b−c) is even.

examples.result: An equivalence relation with two classes: the odds {1,3} and the evens {2,4} — parity.

keyTakeaways: Equivalence relations (reflexive + symmetric + transitive) are rigorous sameness.
Every element lives in exactly one class [a]; classes are equal or disjoint.
Equivalence relations and partitions determine each other — a genuine bijection.
Congruence mod m partitions Z into exactly m residue classes [0], ..., [m−1].
Any function f defines the relation same f-value; every equivalence relation arises this way.

quiz.q: Which property is NOT required of an equivalence relation?
quiz.explanation: Equivalence relations are reflexive, symmetric and transitive; antisymmetry belongs to partial orderings. Congruence mod 5 is symmetric but not antisymmetric: 1 ≡ 6 and 6 ≡ 1 with 1 ≠ 6.

quiz.q: How many distinct equivalence classes does congruence modulo 5 have on the integers?
quiz.explanation: The classes are [0], [1], [2], [3], [4] — one per remainder; for example [5] = [0] and [7] = [2].

quiz.q: If [a] ∩ [b] ≠ ∅ for equivalence classes of R, then:
options: a and b are related to nothing
quiz.explanation: Sharing one element s forces aRs and bRs, hence aRb by symmetry and transitivity, so the classes coincide — classes are equal or disjoint.

quiz.q: The number of different equivalence relations on a 3-element set equals the number of partitions of the set. How many are there?
quiz.explanation: The partitions are {{1,2,3}}, {{1,2},{3}}, {{1,3},{2}}, {{2,3},{1}} and {{1},{2},{3}} — five of them (the Bell number B₃ = 5).

intro: Schedules, hierarchies and subset containment all share one abstract skeleton: the partial order. This section draws Hasse diagrams — the clean pictures of order — separates total from partial, tells maximal elements from greatest ones, and ends with the topological sort theorem that schedules any partial order into a linear plan.
objectives: Verify partial orderings and identify comparable elements
Draw and read Hasse diagrams via the covering relation
Distinguish total orders, well-orders, maximal and greatest elements
Recognize lattices (lub and glb) in divisibility and subset posets
Produce topological sorts of finite posets

concepts.statement: A relation ⪯ on S is a **partial ordering** if it is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; the pair **(S, ⪯) is a poset** (partially ordered set). Elements a and b are **comparable** if a ⪯ b or b ⪯ a.
concepts.detail: Benchmark posets: (Z⁺, |) divisibility, (P(S), ⊆) containment, (Z, ≤) the integers, strings under lexicographic order. Partial because some pairs may be incomparable.

concepts.statement: A poset in which every pair of elements is comparable is a **total order** (linear order); a totally ordered set is called a chain.
concepts.detail: (Z, ≤) is total; (P({a,b,c}), ⊆) is not — {a} and {b,c} are incomparable subsets.

concepts.statement: A total order is **well-ordered** if every nonempty subset has a least element.
concepts.detail: (Z⁺, ≤) is well-ordered; (Z, ≤) is not, since Z itself has no least element. Well-ordering is the engine behind mathematical induction.

concepts.statement: a is **covered by** b, written a ≺ b, if a < b and there is no c with a < c < b — an immediate step in the order.
concepts.detail: In divisibility on divisors of 24, 4 is covered by 12 (nothing strictly between them in the set), but 1 is not covered by 24 because 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 intervene.

concepts.statement: The **Hasse diagram** of a poset has one vertex per element, an edge only between covers, and every edge drawn upward from smaller to larger; loops, arrowheads and transitive edges are omitted.
concepts.detail: To build one from the digraph: delete loops, delete every edge implied by transitivity, delete arrowheads, and orient the drawing so smaller elements sit lower. The order is read as upward reachability.

concepts.statement: Given posets (A₁, ⪯₁) and (A₂, ⪯₂), the **lexicographic order** on A₁ × A₂ sets (a₁,a₂) ⪯ (b₁,b₂) if a₁ ≺₁ b₁, or a₁ = b₁ and a₂ ⪯₂ b₂; iterating gives dictionary order on strings.
concepts.detail: Dictionary order assumes a fixed alphabet and places shorter prefixes first: aardvark before ab. It is a standard way to build total orders on products.

concepts.statement: a is **maximal** if no b ≠ a has a ≺ b, and **minimal** if no b ≠ a has b ≺ a; a is the **greatest** element if b ⪯ a for every b, and the **least** if a ⪯ b for every b.
concepts.detail: A greatest element is unique when it exists (antisymmetry), and every greatest element is maximal — but maximal elements can be many. In divisibility on {2,3,4}, both 3 and 4 are maximal, yet neither is greatest.

concepts.statement: A poset is a **lattice** if every pair {a,b} has a **least upper bound lub(a,b)** (the join) and a **greatest lower bound glb(a,b)** (the meet).
concepts.detail: (Z⁺, |) is a lattice: lub = lcm and glb = gcd. (P(S), ⊆) is a lattice: lub = ∪ and glb = ∩. But divisibility on {2,3,4,6} is not: glb(2,3) would have to be 1, which is not in the set.

concepts.statement: Every finite poset has a **compatible total order** — a topological sort — produced by repeatedly deleting (and listing) a minimal element among those remaining.
concepts.detail: Scheduling with prerequisites: elements are tasks, the order gives constraints, and the algorithm outputs a valid linear plan. It never gets stuck, because every finite nonempty poset has a minimal element.

examples.title: Divisibility Hasse Diagram
examples.problem: Draw the Hasse diagram of the poset (A, |) with A = {1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24}.

steps.label: Place by levels
steps.text: 1 at the bottom; then 2 and 3; then 4 and 6; then 8 and 12; then 24 at the top.

steps.label: Delete transitive edges
steps.text: Edges like 1–24, 2–24, 1–4 and 1–6 vanish — they follow by climbing.

steps.label: Read the order
steps.text: a | b exactly when b is reachable from a by climbing upward.

examples.result: A pyramid with 24 greatest and 1 least; note lub(4,6) = 12 and glb(8,12) = 4 — this poset is a lattice.

examples.title: Is It a Lattice?
examples.problem: Determine whether the divisibility poset on A = {1,2,3,6} and on B = {2,3,4,6} are lattices.

steps.label: Poset A
steps.text: lub(2,3) = lcm(2,3) = 6 ∈ A and glb(2,3) = gcd(2,3) = 1 ∈ A; every pair has both bounds — a lattice.

steps.label: Poset B
steps.text: lub(2,3) = 6 ∈ B is fine, but glb(2,3) = 1 ∉ B.

steps.label: Conclusion for B
steps.text: The pair {2,3} has no greatest lower bound — not a lattice.

examples.result: A is the classic diamond lattice; B is not a lattice — lattice-ness depends on the ground set, not just the relation.

examples.title: Topological Sort
examples.problem: A project has tasks with prerequisites: B requires A; C requires A; D requires B and C; E requires D. Produce a valid schedule.

steps.label: Model
steps.text: Poset on {A,B,C,D,E} with A ≺ B, A ≺ C, B ≺ D, C ≺ D, D ≺ E.

steps.label: First minimal element
steps.text: Only A is minimal — schedule A first.

steps.label: Continue
steps.text: With A gone, B and C are minimal — pick B (a choice!).

steps.label: Finish
steps.text: Then C, then D, then E.

examples.result: A → B → C → D → E is a compatible total order; A → C → B → D → E is equally valid — topological sorts need not be unique.

keyTakeaways: A poset is reflexive + antisymmetric + transitive; incomparable pairs are what make the order partial.
Hasse diagrams draw only covering relations, upward: loops, arrowheads and transitive edges are deleted.
Total orders compare every pair; well-orders add that every nonempty subset has a least element.
Greatest/least elements are unique when they exist; maximal/minimal elements need not be.
Lattices: every pair has a lub and a glb — divisibility gives lcm/gcd, subsets give ∪/∩.
Every finite poset extends to a compatible total order — a topological sort.

quiz.q: Which relation on Z⁺ is a partial ordering?
quiz.explanation: Divides is reflexive (a|a), antisymmetric (a|b and b|a force a = b) and transitive. Congruence mod 5 fails antisymmetry; the others fail reflexivity or more.

quiz.q: In the Hasse diagram of divisibility on {1,2,3,6}, which pair of elements is incomparable?
quiz.explanation: 2 does not divide 3 and 3 does not divide 2 — the incomparable pairs are exactly those with no upward path between them.

quiz.q: A poset can have several maximal elements. How many greatest elements can it have?
options: Exactly as many as maximal elements
None, unless it is a lattice
quiz.explanation: If g₁ and g₂ are both greatest, then g₁ ⪯ g₂ and g₂ ⪯ g₁, so antisymmetry forces g₁ = g₂. Maximal elements need not be comparable; a greatest element dominates everything.

quiz.q: Topological sorting of a finite poset produces:
options: a total order compatible with the partial order
quiz.explanation: The sort linearizes the poset: whenever a ≺ b, a comes before b in the output list — exactly what scheduling with prerequisites requires.

quiz.q: In the poset $(\{2, 3, 4, 6, 12\}, \mid)$ under divisibility, the maximal and minimal elements are:
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate maximal as nothing strictly above it in the set and minimal as nothing strictly below it. Step 2: Recall the key test $a \prec b$ exactly when $a \mid b$ with $a \neq b$. Step 3: Check tops as $2 \mid 12$, $3 \mid 12$, $4 \mid 12$ and $6 \mid 12$, so every element divides $12$ and $12$ is the unique maximal element. Step 4: Check bottoms as no listed element strictly divides $2$ or $3$, while $2 \mid 4$ and $2 \mid 6$, so $2$ and $3$ are minimal and $4, 6$ are not. Step 5: The distractors swap the two notions, promote $4, 6$ which sit below $12$, or claim a singleton can be both maximal and minimal here. Step 6: Hence the maximal element is $12$ and the minimal elements are $2$ and $3$.

intro: Graphs are the mathematics of connection: who knows whom, which wires link which machines, which tasks must precede which. A graph strips away everything except objects and a relation between them, which is exactly why the same tiny theory powers social networks, chip design, ecology and the web.
objectives: Define graphs precisely as G = (V, E) and distinguish simple graphs, directed graphs, multigraphs and pseudographs
Translate real situations into vertex-and-edge models and justify your modeling choices
Recognize the classic graph models: acquaintanceship, influence, collaboration, the Hollywood graph, telephone networks, the web graph, precedence graphs and niche overlap graphs
Explain why modeling decisions (directed vs. undirected, simple vs. multi) are forced by the nature of the underlying relation

concepts.statement: A **graph** G = (V, E) consists of a nonempty finite set V of **vertices** (nodes) and a finite set E of **edges**, where each edge is an unordered pair {u, v} of distinct vertices. In a **simple graph**, at most one edge joins any pair of vertices and no edge joins a vertex to itself.
concepts.detail: Nothing about the drawing matters — only which vertices are paired with which. Two graphs with the same incidence structure are the same graph, no matter how differently they are drawn.

concepts.statement: Vertices u and v are **adjacent** (neighbors) when {u, v} ∈ E. The edge e = {u, v} is **incident** with u and with v, and u, v are the **endpoints** of e. The set of neighbors of v is its neighborhood N(v).
concepts.detail: Adjacent describes vertices; incident pairs a vertex with an edge. Keeping the two words straight prevents most early confusion in graph theory.

concepts.statement: A **directed graph** (digraph) G = (V, E) has each edge an ordered pair (u, v) — an edge from u (the **initial endpoint**) to v (the **terminal endpoint**), drawn with an arrowhead at v.
concepts.detail: Use digraphs when the relation is asymmetric: u influences v without v influencing u, or task u must finish before task v starts.

concepts.statement: A **multigraph** permits **multiple edges** (parallel edges) joining the same pair of distinct vertices. A **pseudograph** also permits **loops** — edges of the form {v, v} that begin and end at the same vertex.
concepts.detail: A telephone network needs multiple edges because several calls can connect the same two phones; the web graph is a directed pseudograph because a page may link to another page and to itself.

concepts.statement: To model a situation as a graph, answer two questions: (1) **what are the vertices?** — the objects of interest; (2) **what relation do edges encode?** Then choose undirected edges if the relation is symmetric (mutual), directed if not, multiple edges if parallel instances matter, and loops if self-relations matter.
concepts.detail: Getting this mapping right is the whole skill of applying graphs: the mathematics that follows only sees vertices, edges and directions.

concepts.statement: The **acquaintanceship graph** (vertices = people, edges between people who know each other) is undirected and enormous. The **influence graph** is directed: u → v means u influences v. The **collaboration graph** connects researchers who co-authored a paper — path length to Erdős defines the famous Erdős number.
concepts.detail: The conjecture that every two people on earth are linked by a chain of at most six acquaintances is purely a statement about distances in this graph.

concepts.statement: The **telephone network** is a multigraph (parallel lines, loops for calls within an exchange). The **web graph** is a directed pseudograph whose trillion-plus edges are hyperlinks. The **Hollywood graph** joins two actors when they have appeared in a film together; the **round-robin tournament graph** has one directed edge between every pair of contestants, from winner to loser.
concepts.detail: In the Hollywood graph an edge between two actors is exactly the Kevin Bacon idea — path length to Bacon is the Bacon number, a second instance of the same distance machinery as Erdős numbers.

concepts.statement: A **precedence graph** is a directed acyclic graph whose vertices are tasks (or circuit components) with an edge u → v when u must be completed before v — used to schedule jobs and lay out circuits. A **niche overlap graph** is undirected: vertices are species, and an edge joins two species that share a food source in their diets.
concepts.detail: Precedence graphs can never contain directed circuits, since a circular chain of prerequisites is impossible to carry out — this foreshadows topological sorting in Chapter 9 and job scheduling later in this chapter.

examples.title: Reading a social model
examples.problem: In the acquaintanceship graph of the world, what does a path of length 3 from Alice to Ben mean, and what claim is made by the saying that everyone is at most six degrees of separation from everyone else?

steps.label: Identify vertices and edges
steps.text: Vertices are people; an undirected edge joins two people who know each other, because knowing is mutual.

steps.label: Interpret a path
steps.text: A path of length 3 is a chain Alice — p₁ — p₂ — Ben of three edges: Alice knows p₁, p₁ knows p₂, and p₂ knows Ben.

steps.label: Translate the slogan
steps.text: Six degrees of separation claims the distance between any two vertices is at most 6 — every pair of people is joined by a path of at most six edges.

examples.result: Social questions like small-world phenomena become quantitative questions about path lengths and distances in a graph.

examples.title: Building a precedence graph
examples.problem: A computer build has tasks: A install power supply, B install motherboard, C install CPU (after B), D install RAM (after C), E mount GPU (after B), F close case (after A, D, E). Build the precedence graph and explain why it has no directed circuits.

steps.label: Place a vertex per task
steps.text: Vertices = {A, B, C, D, E, F} — each task is a vertex.

steps.label: Draw a directed edge per prerequisite
steps.text: B → C and B → E; C → D; A → F, D → F, E → F. Arrows point from prerequisite to dependent task.

steps.label: Check for circuits
steps.text: Following any chain of prerequisites strictly increases order of installation (A/B come first, F comes last), so no directed circuit can exist.

examples.result: A directed acyclic graph whose topological order — for instance A, B, C, D, E, F — is any valid installation schedule.

examples.title: Ecology with edges
examples.problem: Species: hawk, owl, fox, snake, rabbit, mouse. Diets: hawk eats rabbit and mouse; owl eats mouse; fox eats rabbit; snake eats mouse; rabbit and mouse eat grass. Build the niche overlap graph and interpret the neighborhoods.

steps.label: List shared food sources
steps.text: Hawk and owl share mouse; hawk and fox share rabbit; hawk and snake share mouse; owl and snake share mouse; fox and snake share nothing (rabbit vs. mouse); rabbit and mouse share grass.

steps.label: Draw undirected edges
steps.text: Edges: hawk–owl, hawk–fox, hawk–snake, owl–snake, rabbit–mouse. No loops or directions — sharing food is a symmetric relation.

steps.label: Read the structure
steps.text: N(hawk) = {owl, fox, snake} — the hawk competes most broadly. Fox and snake are not adjacent: they exploit different resources and do not compete directly.

examples.result: Ecological competition becomes adjacency: two species interact through exactly the food sources they share.

keyTakeaways: A graph G = (V, E) is pure incidence structure — drawing, distance and edge shape carry no information
Choose directed edges for asymmetric relations (influence, prerequisites, hyperlinks) and undirected edges for symmetric ones (acquaintance, co-authorship, shared food)
Multiple edges model parallel connections such as separate phone calls or cables; loops model self-relations such as a page linking to itself
Vertices do not have to be people: tasks, species, web pages, molecules and bit strings all make fine vertices
The same analysis tool — path and distance — powers Erdős numbers, Bacon numbers and six degrees of separation
A precedence graph must be acyclic; a round-robin tournament digraph must have an edge between every pair of vertices

quiz.q: Which situation should be modeled with a directed graph rather than a simple undirected graph?
options: Two people being acquaintances of each other
A web page placing a hyperlink to another web page
Two actors appearing in the same film
Two species sharing a common food source
quiz.explanation: A hyperlink runs from one page to another without the reverse link necessarily existing, so the relation is asymmetric and needs ordered pairs. Acquaintance, co-appearance and shared food are all symmetric relations.

quiz.q: In the niche overlap graph of an ecosystem, an edge joins two species exactly when they do what?
options: They share a food source in their diets
They live in the same habitat
quiz.explanation: The niche overlap graph is undirected precisely because sharing food sources is symmetric: predator–prey relations would instead require a directed graph.

quiz.q: A round-robin tournament is represented by a digraph in which every pair of distinct vertices is joined by exactly one directed edge. What does the underlying undirected graph look like?
options: A complete graph Kₙ with one orientation chosen for each edge
A bipartite graph between winners and losers
A cycle Cₙ with alternating directions
A wheel Wₙ centered on the champion
quiz.explanation: Every pair plays, so if arrowheads are dropped the graph becomes Kₙ; the digraph is exactly an orientation of a complete graph, sometimes called a tournament.

quiz.q: In the collaboration graph of mathematicians, your Erdős number is 3. What does this say?
options: You wrote 3 papers with Paul Erdős
A chain of 3 co-authorship edges joins you to Erdős, and no shorter chain exists
You have 3 co-authors who each wrote with Erdős
You are 3 citations away from Erdős
quiz.explanation: The Erdős number is the graph distance to Erdős in the collaboration graph: the length of the shortest path of co-authorship edges, so 3 means a 3-edge chain exists and none shorter.

intro: This section arms you with the working vocabulary of graph theory — degrees, neighborhoods, and the celebrity families Kₙ, Cₙ, Wₙ, Qₙ and Kₘ,ₙ — plus two results you will use for the rest of the book: the Handshaking Theorem (∑ deg v = 2|E|) and the odd-cycle characterization of bipartite graphs.
objectives: Compute vertex degrees and apply the Handshaking Theorem ∑deg(v) = 2|E|
Know the vertex and edge counts of complete graphs Kₙ, cycles Cₙ, wheels Wₙ, n-cubes Qₙ and complete bipartite graphs Kₘ,ₙ
Define bipartite graphs and test bipartiteness using the odd-cycle theorem or a 2-coloring
Construct new graphs from old: subgraphs, unions and regular graphs

concepts.statement: The **degree** of vertex v, written deg(v), is the number of edges incident with v, with each loop counting twice. The neighborhood N(v) is the set of vertices adjacent to v, so in a simple graph deg(v) = |N(v)|. A vertex of degree 0 is **isolated**; degree 1 is a **pendant** vertex.
concepts.detail: A loop contributes 2 to the degree because both of its endpoints are the same vertex — this convention is chosen exactly so the Handshaking Theorem stays true for pseudographs.

concepts.statement: If G = (V, E) is an undirected graph (or multigraph) with m = |E| edges, then **∑ᵥ deg(v) = 2m** — the sum of the degrees of all vertices equals twice the number of edges.
concepts.detail: Each edge contributes exactly 1 to the degree of each of its two endpoints, so it contributes 2 to the total sum. At a party, the total number of handshakes counted from each person’s side is twice the number of handshakes.

concepts.statement: An undirected graph has an **even number of vertices of odd degree**.
concepts.detail: Since ∑deg(v) = 2|E| is even, the sum of the degrees of the odd-degree vertices must itself be even, which is only possible when there is an even number of them. This is the classic parity argument: it is why you cannot design a network with exactly one vertex of odd degree.

concepts.statement: The **complete graph** Kₙ on n vertices has an edge between every pair of distinct vertices. It has **n(n − 1)/2 edges** and is (n − 1)-regular.
concepts.detail: The edge count is the number of 2-element subsets of an n-element set — C(n, 2). Kₙ is the densest simple graph on n vertices, so it is the standard worst-case test case.

concepts.statement: The **cycle** Cₙ (n ≥ 3) consists of n vertices v₁, …, vₙ with edges {v₁,v₂}, …, {vₙ₋₁,vₙ}, {vₙ,v₁}: n vertices, n edges, every degree 2. The **wheel** Wₙ is obtained from Cₙ by adding one new vertex adjacent to all n cycle vertices: n + 1 vertices and **2n edges**.
concepts.detail: The extra hub vertex of Wₙ has degree n while the rim vertices have degree 3, so wheels show that a single high-degree vertex coexists with a rigid cycle structure.

concepts.statement: The **n-cube** (hypercube) Qₙ has as vertices all 2ⁿ bit strings of length n, with an edge between two strings exactly when they differ in one bit. Qₙ has **2ⁿ vertices**, **n·2ⁿ⁻¹ edges**, and is n-regular and bipartite.
concepts.detail: Qₙ is built from two copies of Qₙ₋₁ joined by matching corresponding vertices — the architecture of parallel computers. Degrees are all n because each bit position can be flipped once.

concepts.statement: A graph G = (V, E) is **bipartite** if V = V₁ ∪ V₂ (disjoint nonempty parts) and every edge has one endpoint in V₁ and one in V₂; the pair V₁, V₂ is a **bipartition**. The **complete bipartite graph** Kₘ,ₙ has all m·n possible cross edges between parts of sizes m and n.
concepts.detail: Bipartite graphs model two-type matching situations: jobs and workers, students and courses, brides and grooms. Kₘ,ₙ has m + n vertices, mn edges and is the bipartite analogue of a complete graph.

concepts.statement: A graph is bipartite **if and only if it has no circuit of odd length** (in particular, no triangle). Equivalently, a graph is bipartite iff its vertices can be 2-colored so that every edge joins different colors.
concepts.detail: To test bipartiteness, run a 2-coloring from any vertex of each component: color levels alternately. If an edge ever joins same-colored vertices, you have found an odd circuit and the graph is not bipartite — C₅ fails, C₆ passes.

concepts.statement: A graph is **regular of degree k** if every vertex has degree k. A **subgraph** of G = (V, E) is a graph (V′, E′) with V′ ⊆ V and E′ ⊆ E (edges keeping their endpoints). The **union** G₁ ∪ G₂ has vertex set V₁ ∪ V₂ and edge set E₁ ∪ E₂.
concepts.detail: Every cycle is 2-regular, Kₙ is (n−1)-regular, Qₙ is n-regular. Bipartite k-regular graphs with parts of size m must satisfy m = n because counting edges from each side gives km = kn — a one-line argument worth remembering.

examples.title: Counting edges from degrees
examples.problem: A graph has degree sequence (4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2). How many edges does it have, and how many vertices of odd degree?

steps.label: Apply the Handshaking Theorem
steps.text: Since ∑deg(v) = 2|E|, we get |E| = 24/2 = 12 edges.

steps.label: Count odd-degree vertices
steps.text: Four vertices have degree 3 — an even count, exactly as the parity theorem guarantees.

examples.result: The graph has 12 edges and 4 odd-degree vertices; any degree sequence with an odd sum (like four 3s and a 5) would be impossible.

examples.title: Edge counts of the famous families
examples.problem: Compute the number of edges of K₁₀, W₇, Q₄ and K₄,₃ without drawing anything.

steps.label: Complete graph
steps.text: K₁₀ has one edge per pair of vertices: C(10, 2) = 10·9/2 = 45 edges.

steps.label: Wheel
steps.text: W₇ is C₇ plus a hub adjacent to all 7 rim vertices: 7 + 7 = 14 edges (in general Wₙ has 2n edges).

steps.label: Hypercube
steps.text: Q₄ has 16 vertices (all 4-bit strings) and each of the 16 vertices has degree 4, so ∑deg = 64 and |E| = 64/2 = 32 edges — matching n·2ⁿ⁻¹ = 4·8 = 32.

steps.label: Complete bipartite graph
steps.text: K₄,₃ has every one of its 4 left vertices adjacent to every one of its 3 right vertices: 4·3 = 12 edges.

examples.result: K₁₀: 45 edges, W₇: 14 edges, Q₄: 32 edges, K₄,₃: 12 edges — all from formulas, no pictures needed.

examples.title: The odd-cycle test in action
examples.problem: Determine whether C₆ and C₅ are bipartite, and give a bipartition for whichever one is.

steps.label: Try to 2-color C₆
steps.text: Label the cycle v₁…v₆ and color v₁ red; then v₂ blue, v₃ red, v₄ blue, v₅ red, v₆ blue. The closing edge {v₆, v₁} joins blue to red — a valid 2-coloring.

steps.label: Write the bipartition
steps.text: V₁ = {v₁, v₃, v₅} (red), V₂ = {v₂, v₄, v₆} (blue): every edge runs across the two parts, so C₆ is bipartite (in fact it is K₂,₂,₂? No — it is the 6-cycle, a bipartite graph whose parts have size 3).

steps.label: Try to 2-color C₅
steps.text: Color v₁ red, v₂ blue, v₃ red, v₄ blue, v₅ red — but now the closing edge {v₅, v₁} joins red to red. Every alternating attempt fails the same way.

steps.label: Conclude via the theorem
steps.text: C₅ is a circuit of odd length 5, so by the characterization it is not bipartite. Any cycle Cₙ is bipartite exactly when n is even.

examples.result: C₆ is bipartite; C₅ is not — parity of the cycle length decides, and even cycles are always bipartite.

keyTakeaways: ∑deg(v) = 2|E| — the single most used counting identity in graph theory; edges are counted twice, once per endpoint
Every graph has an even number of odd-degree vertices: a parity constraint that instantly rules out many degree sequences
Edge counts to memorize: Kₙ has n(n−1)/2, Wₙ has 2n, Qₙ has n·2ⁿ⁻¹, Kₘ,ₙ has mn
Bipartite ⇔ no odd circuit ⇔ 2-colorable — three interchangeable tests of the same property
Qₙ is the graph of bit strings differing in one bit; it is n-regular, bipartite and built recursively from two Qₙ₋₁
Subgraphs and unions let you assemble and dissect graphs; a k-regular bipartite graph with parts V₁, V₂ forces |V₁| = |V₂|

quiz.q: A graph has 9 vertices and the sum of all degrees is 36. How many edges does it have?
options: Cannot be determined from the sum alone
quiz.explanation: By the Handshaking Theorem ∑deg(v) = 2|E|, so |E| = 36/2 = 18. The theorem converts a degree sum into an edge count with one division.

quiz.q: Which of the following degree sequences is impossible for a simple graph, purely by parity?
quiz.explanation: (3, 3, 3, 3, 3) has five odd degrees — an odd number of odd-degree vertices, which the Handshaking Theorem forbids. The other sequences have 2, 2 and 4 odd entries respectively.

quiz.q: Why must every graph have an even number of vertices of odd degree?
options: Because odd-degree vertices always come in adjacent pairs
Because ∑deg(v) = 2|E| is even, and an odd number of odd summands would make the total odd
Because every graph contains an Euler circuit
Because degrees are bounded by the number of vertices
quiz.explanation: The full degree sum equals 2|E|, which is even. The even-degree vertices contribute an even amount, so the odd-degree vertices must also contribute an even total — possible only if there is an even number of them.

quiz.q: Which graph is bipartite?
quiz.explanation: Q₄ is bipartite: partition its vertices by the parity of the number of 1s in each bit string; flipping one bit always changes parity. C₇ has odd length, K₅ contains triangles, and W₆ contains triangles formed by the hub and adjacent rim vertices.

intro: Computers cannot store drawings, so graphs live in memory as adjacency lists, adjacency matrices or incidence matrices. The same representations power the deepest theoretical question of the section: when are two seemingly different graphs secretly the same object? That question — isomorphism — is answered with invariants.
objectives: Represent graphs with adjacency lists, adjacency matrices and incidence matrices, and know when each is preferred
Read graph properties directly from these matrix representations
Define graph isomorphism as an adjacency-preserving bijection between vertex sets
Use invariants — vertex count, edge count, degree sequence, cycle structure — to prove graphs non-isomorphic, and construct explicit isomorphisms when they exist

concepts.statement: An **adjacency list** stores, for each vertex, the list of vertices adjacent to it. A simple undirected graph needs 2|E| list entries total; a directed graph stores, for each vertex, the terminals of edges leaving it (|E| entries).
concepts.detail: Adjacency lists are the representation of choice for sparse graphs (few edges), since space is proportional to |V| + 2|E| rather than |V|².

concepts.statement: With vertices ordered v₁, …, vₙ, the **adjacency matrix** A is the n × n zero–one matrix with aᵢⱼ = 1 when {vᵢ, vⱼ} (or (vᵢ, vⱼ) for digraphs) is an edge, and 0 otherwise. For an undirected graph A is **symmetric** (aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ); a simple graph has all zeros on the diagonal.
concepts.detail: Row i of A is the adjacency list of vᵢ in matrix clothing: the degree of vᵢ is the sum of row i (in a simple graph). Multigraphs use entry counts instead of 1s for parallel edges; loops appear as diagonal entries.

concepts.statement: An adjacency matrix uses |V|² space and answers is-there-an-edge in O(1) time; adjacency lists use Θ(|V| + |E|) space but need a search through a list to test an edge. **Sparse graphs → lists; dense graphs or constant-time edge queries → matrices.**
concepts.detail: This trade-off mirrors the big-array-versus-linked-list decision in data structures: the right answer depends on how dense the graph is and which operations dominate.

concepts.statement: The **incidence matrix** M of G with vertices v₁, …, vₙ and edges e₁, …, eₘ is the n × m zero–one matrix with mᵢⱼ = 1 when vertex vᵢ is an endpoint of edge eⱼ (a loop at vᵢ makes that entry 2). Each column of a simple graph contains exactly two 1s — one per endpoint.
concepts.detail: Where the adjacency matrix relates vertices to vertices, the incidence matrix relates vertices to edges — useful whenever the edges themselves carry meaning, as in network flow or circuit problems.

concepts.statement: Simple graphs G₁ = (V₁, E₁) and G₂ = (V₂, E₂) are **isomorphic**, written G₁ ≅ G₂, when there is a bijection f: V₁ → V₂ such that {u, v} ∈ E₁ **if and only if** {f(u), f(v)} ∈ E₂. The function f is an **isomorphism**.
concepts.detail: An isomorphism is a relabeling: it must preserve adjacency AND non-adjacency. A useful viewpoint: G₁ and G₂ are isomorphic exactly when their adjacency matrices become equal after the same reordering of rows and columns.

concepts.statement: A property is an **isomorphism invariant** if isomorphic graphs necessarily share it: the number of vertices, the number of edges, the degree sequence (sorted), the number of circuits of each length, being bipartite, connected, regular or planar. **If any invariant differs, the graphs are not isomorphic.**
concepts.detail: Invariants prove non-isomorphism only. Matching invariants never proves isomorphism — you must still exhibit the bijection f, which is the hard part.

concepts.term: Isomorphism testing is hard in general
concepts.statement: No efficient (polynomial-time) algorithm is known for deciding graph isomorphism in general, yet the problem is also not believed to be NP-complete — it sits in a rare complexity class of its own. Practical solvers use invariants plus backtracking refinement.
concepts.detail: This is why textbook problems stay small: you rule candidates out with invariants, then either find the bijection by pattern-matching vertices of distinctive degrees or show one cannot exist.

examples.title: Writing the adjacency matrix
examples.problem: Vertices in order a, b, c, d; edges {a,b}, {a,c}, {b,c}, {c,d}. Write the adjacency matrix A, verify symmetry, and read off all degrees.

steps.label: Fill in entries row by row
steps.text: Row a: adjacent to b and c → 0 1 1 0. Row b: adjacent to a and c → 1 0 1 0. Row c: adjacent to a, b, d → 1 1 0 1. Row d: adjacent to c → 0 0 1 0.

steps.label: Assemble and check symmetry
steps.text: A = [[0,1,1,0],[1,0,1,0],[1,1,0,1],[0,0,1,0]]. Every entry equals its mirror image across the diagonal — as required for any undirected graph.

steps.label: Read degrees from row sums
steps.text: deg(a) = 2, deg(b) = 2, deg(c) = 3, deg(d) = 1 — each row sum counts that vertex’s incident edges.

examples.result: A is symmetric with zero diagonal (no loops), and row sums give the degree sequence (3, 2, 2, 1) up to sorting.

examples.title: Invariants versus proof: C₆ and K₃ ∪ K₃
examples.problem: Show that C₆ and the disjoint union K₃ ∪ K₃ are NOT isomorphic, even though they agree on vertices, edges and degrees.

steps.label: Compare the easy invariants
steps.text: Both graphs have 6 vertices and 6 edges, and every vertex has degree 2 in both — degree sequences match perfectly, so degree arguments are useless here.

steps.label: Examine circuits of length 3
steps.text: K₃ ∪ K₃ contains two triangles (3-cycles). C₆ is a single circuit of length 6 and contains no triangle at all.

steps.label: Apply the invariant
steps.text: The number of circuits of length 3 is an isomorphism invariant; since 2 ≠ 0, no bijection can preserve adjacency.

steps.label: Alternative: connectivity
steps.text: C₆ is connected while K₃ ∪ K₃ has two connected components — connectedness is itself an invariant, so the graphs cannot be isomorphic either way.

examples.result: Non-isomorphic — connectivity (or triangle count) separates them where vertices, edges and degrees could not.

examples.title: Exhibiting an isomorphism
examples.problem: Graph G has vertices {1, 2, 3, 4} and edges {1,2}, {2,3}, {3,4}, {1,4}, {1,3}; graph H has vertices {a, b, c, d} and edges {a,b}, {b,c}, {c,d}, {a,d}, {b,d}. Prove G ≅ H by constructing an isomorphism.

steps.label: Match the distinctive vertex
steps.text: In G, vertex 1 has degree 3 (adjacent to 2, 3, 4) and the other vertices have degree 2. In H, vertex b is the unique degree-3 vertex (adjacent to a, c, d). Any isomorphism must send 1 ↦ b.

steps.label: Check every edge of G
steps.text: {1,2} ↦ {b,a} ✓ is an edge of H; {2,3} ↦ {a,d}? — a is adjacent to b and d? H’s edges are ab, bc, cd, ad, bd: yes {a,d} ✓; {3,4} ↦ {d,c} ✓; {1,4} ↦ {b,c} ✓; {1,3} ↦ {b,d} ✓.

steps.label: Check non-edges and conclude
steps.text: The remaining pair {2,4} ↦ {a,c}, which is a non-edge of H, matching the fact that {2,4} is a non-edge of G. Since G and H have 5 of 6 possible edges, preserving edges automatically preserves the single non-edge.

examples.result: f = (1→b, 2→a, 3→d, 4→c) is an isomorphism, so G ≅ H — both are K₄ minus one edge.

keyTakeaways: Adjacency matrix: n × n, symmetric for undirected graphs, aᵢⱼ = 1 iff {vᵢ, vⱼ} is an edge; row sums give degrees
Incidence matrix: n × m, one column per edge with exactly two 1s in a simple graph (a loop gives a 2)
Sparse graphs prefer adjacency lists (Θ(|V| + |E|) space); dense graphs and constant-time edge tests prefer matrices
Isomorphism = bijection preserving adjacency and non-adjacency; equivalently, identical adjacency matrices up to simultaneous row/column reordering
Invariants (degree sequence, cycle counts, connectivity, bipartiteness) prove graphs NON-isomorphic but never prove them isomorphic
Graph isomorphism has no known polynomial-time algorithm and is not believed NP-complete — a genuinely mysterious complexity class

quiz.q: Why is the adjacency matrix of every undirected graph symmetric?
options: Because undirected graphs must be regular
Because {u, v} ∈ E exactly when {v, u} ∈ E, so aᵢⱼ and aⱼᵢ record the same edge
Because every undirected graph has an even number of edges
Because loops appear on the diagonal
quiz.explanation: An undirected edge is a single unordered pair {u, v}; it forces both aᵢⱼ = 1 and aⱼᵢ = 1 simultaneously. Asymmetry of A is a dead giveaway that the graph is directed.

quiz.q: In the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph, what does the sum of the entries in row i equal?
options: The number of edges of the graph
The number of circuits through vᵢ
Twice the degree of vertex vᵢ
quiz.explanation: Row i has a 1 in column j exactly when vᵢ is adjacent to vⱼ, so the row sum counts vᵢ’s neighbors — which is deg(vᵢ) in a simple graph.

quiz.q: Two graphs both have 8 vertices, 10 edges and degree sequence (4, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1). What can you conclude?
options: They are isomorphic because all invariants match
They are not isomorphic because the degree sequences are equal
Nothing — matching these invariants does not settle isomorphism; you must either find an adjacency-preserving bijection or find an invariant on which they differ
quiz.explanation: Vertex count, edge count and degree sequence are invariants: equal values are necessary for isomorphism but not sufficient. Only a differing invariant or a constructed isomorphism settles the question.

quiz.q: In the incidence matrix of a simple graph, each column contains exactly two 1s. Why?
options: Because every vertex has even degree
Because each edge has exactly two endpoints, and it is incident with precisely those two vertices
Because every edge joins two connected components
quiz.explanation: Columns correspond to edges: the two 1s mark the edge’s two distinct endpoints. A loop would break the pattern — which is why pseudographs use the entry 2 for loops.

intro: How hard is it to get from here to there? Connectivity makes that question precise: paths, circuits, and their directed counterparts. The payoffs are practical — counting routes with adjacency-matrix powers, finding single points of failure (cut vertices and bridges), and Menger’s remarkable theorem linking redundancy to disjoint paths.
objectives: Distinguish paths, simple paths and circuits, and bound simple path lengths
Determine connectedness and find connected components
Identify cut vertices and bridges — the single points of failure in a network
Count paths of length r between two vertices using powers of the adjacency matrix
Classify directed graphs as strongly or weakly connected and appreciate Menger’s theorem

concepts.statement: A **path of length n** from u to v is a sequence of n edges starting at u and ending at v; the path is **simple** if it does not repeat any vertex, and **closed** if it starts and ends at the same vertex. A **circuit** is a path that begins and ends at the same vertex with no other repeated edges; a **simple circuit** repeats no vertex except that start = end.
concepts.detail: Rosen calls an edge sequence with no repeated edge a path, and a path with no repeated vertices simple. A simple path in a graph with n vertices has length at most n − 1, and a simple circuit at most n — the pigeonhole principle forces a repeat otherwise.

concepts.statement: An undirected graph is **connected** when every pair of vertices is joined by a path. A **connected component** is a maximal connected subgraph — connected, and not contained in any larger connected subgraph. The **connectedness** relation (existence of a path) is an equivalence relation whose classes are the components.
concepts.detail: Isolated vertices form singleton components. Every graph decomposes uniquely into components, which is why connectivity questions reduce component by component.

concepts.statement: A **cut vertex** (articulation point) is a vertex whose removal increases the number of components; a **bridge** (cut edge) is an edge with the same property. A graph with no cut vertices is **nonseparable**.
concepts.detail: Cut vertices and bridges are the single points of failure of a network: communication networks and the internet backbone are deliberately designed with redundancy to eliminate them. In any connected graph, a pendant vertex’s single incident edge is always a bridge.

concepts.statement: Let A be the adjacency matrix of a graph (or digraph) with ordered vertices v₁, …, vₙ. The (i, j) entry of **Aʳ** equals the **number of paths of length r from vᵢ to vⱼ** (edge sequences of length r, vertices allowed to repeat).
concepts.detail: Proof by induction: paths of length r + 1 from i to j end with an edge (vₖ, vⱼ) preceded by a length-r path from i to vₖ, giving the matrix multiplication (Aʳ⁺¹)ᵢⱼ = ∑ₖ (Aʳ)ᵢₖ·aₖⱼ. Each product counts paths through a specific penultimate vertex k.

concepts.statement: A **directed path** follows edges only in their arrow directions: a sequence (v₀, v₁), (v₁, v₂), … of directed edges. Vertex u **reaches** v when a directed path from u to v exists; reachability is reflexive and transitive but generally not symmetric.
concepts.detail: The reachability relation is the directed analogue of connectedness — but one-way streets make it asymmetric, which is why directed graphs need their own definitions of connectivity.

concepts.statement: A directed graph is **strongly connected** when every pair of vertices is mutually reachable by directed paths (u reaches v AND v reaches u). It is **weakly connected** when the **underlying undirected graph** (all arrowheads deleted) is connected. Every strongly connected digraph is weakly connected, never conversely.
concepts.detail: A one-way traffic system is strongly connected if you can drive from anywhere to anywhere following the arrows. The **strong components** — maximal strongly connected subgraphs — partition the vertices of any digraph.

concepts.statement: For nonadjacent vertices u and v: the **minimum number of vertices whose removal disconnects u from v equals the maximum number of pairwise internally vertex-disjoint u–v paths**. The edge version holds identically: minimum size of an edge cut = maximum number of edge-disjoint u–v paths.
concepts.detail: Destruction and redundancy are two sides of one quantity: to separate u from v you must break every disjoint path. This is the ancestor of the max-flow/min-cut theorem and the theory of network reliability.

examples.title: Counting paths with A²
examples.problem: A directed graph has vertices a, b, c, d and edges (a,b), (b,a), (b,c), (c,d), (d,b). How many paths of length 2 go from a to c? From a to a? From a to d?

steps.label: Write the adjacency matrix
steps.text: Ordering (a, b, c, d): A has a row of out-neighbors — row a: 0 1 0 0; row b: 1 0 1 0; row c: 0 0 0 1; row d: 0 1 0 0.

steps.label: Compute A²
steps.text: Multiplying: (A²)ₐc = ∑ₖ aₐk·aₖc = aₐb·a_bc = 1·1 = 1; (A²)ₐa = aₐb·a_ba = 1; (A²)ₐd = aₐb·a_bd + aₐc·a_cd = 0 + 0 = 0.

steps.label: Interpret each entry
steps.text: One path of length 2 from a to c (a → b → c); one closed path a → b → a; none of length 2 from a to d (the trip a → b → c → d needs length 3).

steps.label: Verify by inspection
steps.text: The graph is a single 4-cycle a → b → c → d → b with the return edge b → a; enumerating two-step walks confirms exactly the three counts above.

examples.result: Matrix powers count routes: (A²)ₐc = 1, (A²)ₐa = 1, (A²)ₐd = 0 — no drawing or searching required.

examples.title: Hunting cut vertices and bridges
examples.problem: Find all cut vertices and bridges in the graph formed by two triangles sharing exactly one vertex w, with a pendant path w – x – y attached to w.

steps.label: Test the shared vertex
steps.text: Removing w separates the surviving four triangle vertices (two in each triangle) plus x and y into three pieces: two edges and the piece x – y. The component count rises, so w is a cut vertex.

steps.label: Test the path vertices
steps.text: Removing x isolates y but leaves the two triangles joined through w — component count goes from 1 to 2, so x is also a cut vertex. Removing y (a pendant) changes nothing structurally: y is not a cut vertex.

steps.label: Test triangle edges
steps.text: Deleting any edge of either triangle leaves the triangle as a path — still connected through w. So no triangle edge is a bridge.

steps.label: Test the path edges
steps.text: Deleting {w, x} isolates the piece x – y, and deleting {x, y} isolates y: both {w, x} and {x, y} are bridges — as expected, the edges of a pendant path.

examples.result: Cut vertices: w and x. Bridges: {w, x} and {x, y}. Vertices inside cycles are protected; attachments to trees create fragility.

examples.title: Strongly versus weakly connected
examples.problem: A city’s one-way street digraph has vertices N, E, S, W and edges N→E, E→S, S→W, W→N, plus a one-way bypass S→N. Is it strongly connected, weakly connected, or both/neither?

steps.label: Check strong connectivity
steps.text: From any vertex, following the cycle returns home (e.g., N→E→S→W→N), and S can also reach N via the bypass. Every pair is mutually reachable: strongly connected.

steps.label: Check weak connectivity as a sanity check
steps.text: Ignoring all arrows leaves the 4-cycle plus chord S–N: connected. This is automatic here — strong implies weak.

steps.label: Feel the contrast
steps.text: Had the bypass been N→S instead, then W could not reach E... in fact every vertex still reaches E via the cycle and E reaches everyone via E→S→W→N — still strongly connected. Replace the cycle edge E→S by S→E, however, and E can reach no one: strongly connected fails while weak connectivity survives.

examples.result: The digraph is strongly connected (hence also weakly). The moral: deleting or reversing one arrow can destroy strong but never weak connectivity.

keyTakeaways: Simple paths have length at most n − 1 in an n-vertex graph — pigeonhole forces repeats beyond that
Connectivity is an equivalence-like relation on vertices; its classes are exactly the connected components
Cut vertices and bridges are the single points of failure; cycles provide redundancy that protects against them
The (i, j) entry of Aʳ counts the paths of length r from vᵢ to vⱼ — linear algebra answers a routing question
Strongly connected requires mutual reachability in the directed sense; weakly connected only requires connectivity after deleting arrowheads
Menger’s theorem: the fewest vertices (or edges) needed to separate u from v equals the most pairwise disjoint u–v paths you can build

quiz.q: A simple graph has 7 vertices. What is the maximum possible length of a simple path in it?
quiz.explanation: A simple path repeats no vertex, so it can use at most all 7 vertices — that is 7 − 1 = 6 edges. A seventh edge would have to revisit a vertex, by the pigeonhole principle.

quiz.q: In a directed graph, the (2, 5) entry of A³ is 4. What does that tell you?
options: Vertex 5 has 4 paths of length 2 to vertex 2
There are exactly 4 directed paths of length 3 from vertex 2 to vertex 5
The shortest path from 2 to 5 has length 4
Vertices 2 and 5 are in the same strong component
quiz.explanation: By the matrix-power theorem, (A³)₂₅ counts exactly the directed edge-sequences of length 3 beginning at v₂ and ending at v₅ — four of them.

quiz.q: A directed graph is weakly connected but NOT strongly connected. Which statement must be true?
options: Every pair of vertices is mutually reachable
The underlying undirected graph is connected, but some pair of vertices has no directed path in at least one direction
The graph has no directed circuits
The graph has exactly one strong component
quiz.explanation: Weak connectivity is defined by the underlying undirected graph being connected. The failure of strong connectivity means some pair lacks a directed path (at least one way), even though they would be connected if directions were ignored.

quiz.q: Which edge is guaranteed to be a bridge in any connected graph that has one?
options: Any edge lying on a cycle
The edge incident to a pendant (degree-1) vertex
Any edge whose endpoints both have degree at least 2
quiz.explanation: A pendant vertex v with sole neighbor u is reachable only via edge {u, v}; deleting it isolates v. By contrast, an edge on a cycle always has an alternate route around the cycle, so it can never be a bridge.

intro: Two mathematicians, two tours, two very different destinies. Euler circuits — use every edge exactly once — are completely characterized by degrees. Hamilton circuits — visit every vertex exactly once — resist every such characterization, and their optimization version is the traveling salesperson problem, one of the hardest in all of computing.
objectives: State and apply the exact degree conditions for Euler circuits and Euler paths
Understand why those conditions work (the in/out pairing argument at each vertex)
Define Hamilton paths and circuits, and apply Dirac’s and Ore’s sufficient conditions
Explain why the traveling salesperson problem is computationally hard and what that means in practice

concepts.statement: An **Euler circuit** in a graph (or multigraph) G is a **simple circuit containing every edge of G exactly once**; an **Euler path** is a simple path containing every edge exactly once. A graph that has an Euler circuit is called **traversable** — one continuous trip covers every edge.
concepts.detail: Vertices may be (and must be) revisited in an Euler tour; the scarce resource being spent is edges, not vertices. The 1736 Königsberg bridges problem of exactly this form founded graph theory.

concepts.statement: A connected multigraph has an **Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree**.
concepts.detail: Why even: each time a tour passes through a vertex it consumes two incident edges (in and out), so every vertex entered must be leavable — pairing entries with exits forces even degree. The converse builds the circuit by splicing closed sub-tours together. For disconnected graphs every edge must live in one component containing all non-isolated vertices.

concepts.statement: A connected multigraph has an **Euler path but no Euler circuit if and only if exactly two vertices have odd degree** — and every Euler path must begin at one of them and end at the other.
concepts.detail: Start and end vertices are the only ones where an edge is used once without a partner, producing odd degree exactly there. Any other parity pattern (0 odd → circuit; 2 odd → open path; 4, 6, … odd → neither) makes the tour impossible.

concepts.statement: A **Hamilton path** in a graph G is a simple path that passes through **every vertex exactly once**; a **Hamilton circuit** is a simple circuit through every vertex exactly once. (By convention, the start vertex is not counted twice.)
concepts.detail: Now vertices are the scarce resource and edges may be skipped. The duality with Euler is the great trap of the topic: for Euler the criterion is degrees and it is exact; for Hamilton no comparable exact condition exists.

concepts.statement: If G is a simple graph with n ≥ 3 vertices and **every vertex has degree at least n/2**, then G has a Hamilton circuit.
concepts.detail: A density guarantee: with that many edges available everywhere, a longest path can be closed and then converted into a spanning cycle by a rotation argument. Sufficient, not necessary — C₅ has all degrees 2 < 5/2 yet is itself a Hamilton circuit.

concepts.statement: If G is a simple graph with n ≥ 3 vertices and **deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n for every pair of nonadjacent vertices u, v**, then G has a Hamilton circuit.
concepts.detail: Ore generalizes Dirac: instead of every degree individually ≥ n/2, only the sums across missing edges must be large. Dirac’s condition implies Ore’s, so Ore’s conclusion holds for strictly more graphs.

concepts.statement: No known simple necessary-and-sufficient condition characterizes Hamiltonian graphs, and deciding whether a Hamilton circuit exists is NP-complete. Even-degree gives Euler circuits but guarantees nothing here: bipartite graphs Kₘ,ₙ with m ≠ n have no Hamilton circuit regardless of degrees, while the Petersen graph fails despite being 3-regular.
concepts.detail: A useful necessary fact: in a bipartite graph any circuit alternates between the parts, so a Hamilton circuit can exist only when the two parts have equal size — one-line proof, frequently exam-tested.

concepts.statement: The **TSP** asks for a Hamilton circuit of minimum total weight in a complete weighted graph. Brute force inspects (n − 1)!/2 distinct circuits — astronomically many for n beyond ~20 — and TSP is NP-hard, so exact large instances are out of reach. Heuristics such as nearest-neighbor or 2-opt tours trade optimality for speed.
concepts.detail: n = 15 already gives roughly 43.6 billion directed orderings (about 21.8 billion circuits after symmetry). Real logistics, chip layout and DNA sequencing live here — Hamilton’s icosian game of 1857 was the puzzle’s playful origin.

examples.title: The bridges of Königsberg
examples.problem: The city had four land masses A, B, C, D joined by seven bridges; the resulting multigraph has degrees deg(A) = 5, deg(B) = 3, deg(C) = 3, deg(D) = 3. Can a walker cross every bridge exactly once?

steps.label: Model as a multigraph
steps.text: Vertices = land masses, edges = bridges (multiple edges because several bridges join the same pair — this is a multigraph, not a simple graph).

steps.label: Count odd degrees
steps.text: A has degree 5 and B, C, D each have degree 3: four vertices of odd degree (even in number, as the parity theorem demands).

steps.label: Apply the Euler theorems
steps.text: An Euler circuit needs all degrees even — fails. An Euler path needs exactly two odd vertices — fails with four.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.text: No walk crosses every bridge exactly once, whether or not the walker must return to the start. Euler’s 1736 negative answer created graph theory.

examples.result: Impossible — four odd-degree vertices block both an Euler circuit and an Euler path.

examples.title: One missing edge changes everything
