examples.problem: Take K₅ (five vertices, all ten edges) and delete one edge {a, b}. Does the resulting graph have an Euler circuit, an Euler path, or neither? What about a Hamilton circuit?

steps.label: Recompute degrees
steps.text: In K₅ every degree is 4. Deleting {a, b} leaves deg(a) = deg(b) = 3 while the other three vertices keep degree 4.

steps.label: Classify the Euler situation
steps.text: Exactly two vertices have odd degree (a and b), all edges are in one connected component, so there is an Euler path — it must start at a and end at b — but no Euler circuit.

steps.label: Check Hamiltonicity
steps.text: Deleting one edge from K₅ still leaves deg(v) ≥ 3 > 5/2 = n/2 for every vertex, so Dirac’s theorem guarantees a Hamilton circuit (indeed a → c → d → e → b → a works, avoiding only the missing edge).

examples.result: Euler path yes (from a to b), Euler circuit no; Hamilton circuit yes — Euler and Hamilton answer to different masters.

examples.title: Bipartite roadblock to Hamilton circuits
examples.problem: Does K₃,₅ have a Hamilton circuit? Does K₄,₄? Does K₃,₅ at least have a Hamilton path?

steps.label: Set up the alternation argument
steps.text: Every circuit in a bipartite graph alternates between the two parts V₁, V₂, returning to its start: visits to V₁ and V₂ must alternate and balance exactly.

steps.label: Analyze K₃,₅
steps.text: Parts have sizes 3 and 5. A circuit must alternate, so the numbers of V₁-visits and V₂-visits must be equal — impossible when the tour must cover all 8 vertices (3 ≠ 5). No Hamilton circuit.

steps.label: Analyze K₄,₄
steps.text: Parts are balanced (4 = 4), so alternation around an 8-cycle is possible: e.g. v₁w₁v₂w₂v₃w₃v₄w₄v₁ — a Hamilton circuit exists.

steps.label: Recover a Hamilton path for K₃,₅
steps.text: A path does not need to return, so sizes may differ by one: starting in the larger part, alternate v₁w₁v₂w₂v₃w₃w₄? — no: alternate as w₁v₁w₂v₂w₃v₃w₄w₅ fails at the end; the correct chain is v₁w₁v₂w₂v₃w₃w₄w₅ only if consecutive w’s were adjacent, which they are not. In fact the best possible is a path of 7 vertices: w₁v₁w₂v₂w₃v₃w₄ — K₃,₅ has no Hamilton path either, since |5 − 3| = 2 > 1.

examples.result: K₄,₄ has a Hamilton circuit; K₃,₅ has neither a Hamilton circuit nor a Hamilton path — unbalanced bipartition is a structural obstruction no degree condition can override.

keyTakeaways: Euler circuit ⇔ connected (on non-isolated vertices) + all degrees even; Euler path ⇔ connected + exactly two odd degrees
The parity pairing of entries and exits at each vertex is the whole idea behind the Euler theorems
Hamilton circuits trade the edge constraint for a vertex constraint — and lose the clean characterization
Dirac: all degrees ≥ n/2 ⇒ Hamilton circuit; Ore: deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n across nonadjacent pairs ⇒ Hamilton circuit (Ore generalizes Dirac)
Bipartite graphs admit Hamilton circuits only with equal parts (|V₁| = |V₂|), and Hamilton paths only when parts differ by at most one
TSP = minimum-weight Hamilton circuit: brute force is factorial, the problem is NP-hard, and heuristics are the practical answer

quiz.q: A connected multigraph has vertices with degrees 4, 4, 2, 4, 2, 4. Which statement is true?
options: It has an Euler circuit and an Euler path
It has an Euler circuit but no open Euler path is needed to cover all edges
It has an Euler path between the two degree-2 vertices but no Euler circuit
It has neither an Euler path nor an Euler circuit
quiz.explanation: All degrees are even, so the graph has an Euler circuit. (Every graph with an Euler circuit can be traversed edge-by-edge; a special open Euler path adds nothing new here — the even-degree condition is exactly the circuit condition.)

quiz.q: A connected graph has exactly two vertices of odd degree, p and q. Which tour is possible?
options: An Euler path that must start at p and end at q (or vice versa)
An Euler path that may start at any vertex
quiz.explanation: Each interior vertex of the walk pairs entries with exits; only the endpoints of the walk get an unpaired edge. Hence the walk must begin and end at the two odd-degree vertices p and q.

quiz.q: A simple graph has 10 vertices, and every vertex has degree at least 5. What can you conclude?
options: It has a Hamilton circuit, by Dirac’s theorem
It has a Hamilton circuit, by Ore’s theorem only
It must be the complete graph K₁₀
quiz.explanation: deg(v) ≥ 5 = n/2 for every vertex is exactly Dirac’s condition, which guarantees a Hamilton circuit. Euler requires even degrees, which are not given; the graph need not be complete.

quiz.q: Which is the best reason that K₃,₅ has no Hamilton circuit?
options: Every circuit in a bipartite graph alternates between the parts, so a circuit covering all vertices needs |V₁| = |V₂|, but 3 ≠ 5
It violates Euler’s condition for even degrees
quiz.explanation: Alternation forces a bipartite circuit to spend visits to both parts equally; with parts of sizes 3 and 5 no closed tour can include all eight vertices. (Degree parity governs Euler tours, not Hamilton ones.)

intro: Give every edge a length and suddenly the question changes from can I get there? to what is the cheapest way? Dijkstra’s 1959 algorithm answers it with one of the most elegant greedy arguments in computer science — and at O(n²) cost it is fast enough to route packets and plan your road trip.
objectives: Model transportation, communication and dependency problems as weighted graphs
Execute Dijkstra’s algorithm by hand on small graphs, maintaining tentative distances correctly
Explain why once a vertex is added to the found set its distance is provably final
State the O(n²) complexity of Dijkstra’s algorithm and what drives it

concepts.statement: A **weighted graph** assigns each edge e a positive number w(e), its **weight** (length, cost, time). The **length of a path** is the sum of the weights of its edges, and the **distance** between two vertices is the minimum length of any path joining them.
concepts.detail: Weights let one graph encode geography (miles), money (tolls), latency (milliseconds) or risk. Distances respect the triangle-type inequality automatically because they are minima over paths.

concepts.statement: Find shortest paths from a start a to all vertices: maintain a tentative distance d(v) (initially d(a) = 0, all others ∞) and a set S of solved vertices (initially {a}). **Repeat n − 1 times: add to S the vertex u ∉ S of smallest d(u), then relax every edge {u, v}: set d(v) = min(d(v), d(u) + w(u, v)).** Recording the second-to-last vertex on each path lets you recover the actual routes.
concepts.detail: Each pass finalizes one vertex — the closest unsolved one — and pushes its knowledge outward through edge relaxations. Think of a wave of certainty expanding from the start.

concepts.term: Why the greedy choice is safe
concepts.statement: When u enters S it has the smallest tentative distance among unsolved vertices. Any alternative path to u must leave S through some other unsolved vertex x, whose tentative distance is already ≥ d(u) — and with **nonnegative weights** the path can only grow afterward. So no route can beat d(u): the value is final.
concepts.detail: This proof is exactly why Dijkstra **requires nonnegative weights**: with a negative edge, the path through x could later shrink below d(u) and invalidate the finality. (Negative weights call for the Bellman–Ford algorithm instead.)

concepts.statement: With n vertices, Dijkstra’s algorithm performs n − 1 selection passes and relaxes each edge once overall in the straightforward implementation, giving **O(n²)** time with an adjacency matrix — quadratic and fully adequate for dense graphs.
concepts.detail: With binary heaps and adjacency lists the bound improves to O(|E| log |V|); comparing the two shows the classical data-structures lesson of matching the representation to the graph density.

concepts.statement: Shortest path from a to b (Dijkstra) and the shortest tour visiting every vertex (TSP) sound alike but differ utterly: Dijkstra is polynomial — O(n²) — while TSP is NP-hard with factorial brute force. Requiring the trip to be a single closed tour visiting each vertex once is what makes TSP intractable.
concepts.detail: The moral of the chapter: tiny changes in a graph problem’s phrasing can move the answer from centuries-fast to (probably) forever-slow.

concepts.term: Where shortest paths run the world
concepts.statement: Dijkstra-style computation is the engine of GPS navigation, OSPF routing inside the internet (routers exchange link weights and compute shortest-path trees), network latency optimization, robot motion planning and currency/payment routing.
concepts.detail: In OSPF every router runs Dijkstra with itself as the source — the algorithm’s result is a shortest-path tree, which is precisely the forwarding table.

examples.title: Dijkstra’s algorithm, full trace
examples.problem: Directed graph: vertices a, b, c, d, e, f with edges a→b (4), a→c (2), c→b (1), b→d (5), c→d (8), c→e (10), d→e (2), d→f (6), e→f (3). Find the shortest distance from a to every vertex and a shortest route from a to f.

steps.label: Round 2 — add b (d = 3)
steps.text: Relax b → d: d(d) = min(10, 3 + 5) = 8. Nothing else touches.

steps.label: Round 3 — add d (d = 8)
steps.text: Relax d’s out-edges: d(e) = min(12, 8 + 2) = 10; d(f) = 8 + 6 = 14.

steps.label: Round 4 — add e (d = 10)
steps.text: Relax e → f: d(f) = min(14, 10 + 3) = 13.

steps.label: Round 5 — add f (d = 13)
steps.text: All vertices solved. Recover the route to f by tracing back through the relaxing vertex: f ← e ← d ← b ← c ← a.

examples.result: Distances: a 0, c 2, b 3, d 8, e 10, f 13. Shortest route to f: a → c → b → d → e → f with total 2 + 1 + 5 + 2 + 3 = 13.

examples.title: Greedy means global, not local
examples.problem: Undirected edges: a–b with weight 7, a–c with weight 3, c–b with weight 2. Show that Dijkstra correctly prefers the two-hop route a → c → b over the direct edge, and explain the failure mode of a naive nearest-neighbor tour builder.

steps.label: Run the algorithm
steps.text: d(a) = 0; smallest tentative is c with d = 3, so c is solved first; relaxing c–b gives d(b) = min(7, 3 + 2) = 5; then b is solved with 5.

steps.label: Compare routes
steps.text: The direct edge a–b costs 7, but the detour through c costs only 5 — the algorithm keeps the cheaper, longer-hop-count route.

steps.label: Note the contrast
steps.text: Dijkstra is greedy only about which vertex to finalize, never about which edge to take; that is why it finds true minima while nearest-neighbor heuristics (always drive to the closest unvisited city) can be led badly astray on the TSP.

examples.result: Shortest a-to-b distance is 5 via c. Greedy per-vertex selection = optimal paths; greedy per-edge selection = merely approximate tours.

keyTakeaways: Path length in a weighted graph = sum of edge weights; distance = minimum over all paths
Dijkstra: repeatedly finalize the closest unsolved vertex, then relax its incident edges — d(v) = min(d(v), d(u) + w(u, v))
Once a vertex joins S its distance never changes; the argument uses nonnegative weights essentially
Straightforward Dijkstra is O(n²); with heaps and adjacency lists it becomes O(|E| log |V|)
Negative weights break Dijkstra’s finality argument — use Bellman–Ford in that setting
Shortest paths are polynomial; shortest Hamilton tours (TSP) are NP-hard — do not confuse the two problems

quiz.q: In Dijkstra’s algorithm, why is the tentative distance d(u) of the newly added vertex u guaranteed to be its true shortest distance?
options: Because d(u) was computed using every edge of the graph
Because any other path to u must leave the solved set through an unsolved vertex whose tentative distance is already ≥ d(u), and nonnegative weights cannot shrink it below d(u)
Because the algorithm tries all permutations of vertices
Because u is adjacent to the start vertex
quiz.explanation: Every alternative route must exit S at some unsolved vertex x with d(x) ≥ d(u); from there, nonnegative edge weights can only add cost. This is the greedy-exchange heart of the correctness proof.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of the standard implementation of Dijkstra’s algorithm on a graph with n vertices?
quiz.explanation: The textbook implementation scans all n vertices at each of the n − 1 iterations to find the minimum tentative distance, plus linear relaxation work, giving O(n²). (Heap-based variants reach O(|E| log |V|).)

quiz.q: Edges: a–b weight 7, a–c weight 3, b–c weight 2. After the first relaxation round of Dijkstra from a, what is d(b)?
quiz.explanation: From a, tentative distances are d(b) = 7 via the direct edge and d(c) = 3. Vertex c is solved first (smallest d), and relaxing c–b updates d(b) = 3 + 2 = 5 < 7.

quiz.q: Which assumption about edge weights is essential for Dijkstra’s algorithm to be correct?
quiz.explanation: The finality argument needs weights that never reduce a path’s cost after leaving the solved set. A negative edge could make a later route cheaper, invalidating a vertex already finalized — integer or distinct weights are irrelevant.

intro: Can a graph be drawn on paper with no crossing edges? Planarity is the question that makes graph theory feel like geometry: Euler’s formula r = e − v + 2 ties vertices, edges and regions into one equation, and from it flow the impossibility results — K₅ and K₃,₃ cannot be drawn flat, and Kuratowski says they are the only obstacles.
objectives: Define planar graphs and planar representations, and count regions in a planar drawing
Prove and apply Euler’s formula r = e − v + 2 for connected planar graphs
Derive the corollaries e ≤ 3v − 6 and (for triangle-free graphs) e ≤ 2v − 4, and use them to prove K₅ and K₃,₃ nonplanar
State Kuratowski’s theorem and recognize subdivisions of K₅ and K₃,₃

concepts.statement: A graph is **planar** if it can be drawn in the plane with no two edges crossing; such a drawing is a **planar representation**. A drawing partitions the plane into **regions** (faces) — one bounded region per enclosed area, plus the unbounded exterior region.
concepts.detail: Crossing at a point is a property of a drawing, not of the graph: planarity asserts that SOME crossing-free drawing exists. Circuit boards and road maps must be planar — or need layers/overpasses.

concepts.statement: If G is a connected planar graph with v vertices, e edges and r regions, then **r = e − v + 2** (equivalently v − e + r = 2).
concepts.detail: Proof sketch: take a spanning tree of G (v vertices, v − 1 edges, r = 1 region) and add the remaining e − (v − 1) edges one at a time — each added edge splits an existing region in two, raising r by exactly 1. The tetrahedron K₄ checks out: 4 − 6 + 4 = 2.

concepts.statement: If G is a connected simple planar graph with v ≥ 3 vertices and e edges, then **e ≤ 3v − 6**.
concepts.detail: In a simple planar graph each region is bounded by at least 3 edge-sides, so 2e ≥ 3r; substituting r = e − v + 2 gives 2e ≥ 3(e − v + 2), i.e. e ≤ 3v − 6. Edge-sides count double because each edge borders at most two regions.

concepts.statement: If G is a connected simple planar graph with v ≥ 3 vertices that is **bipartite** (equivalently, triangle-free), then **e ≤ 2v − 4**.
concepts.detail: With no 3-cycles every region needs at least 4 edge-sides: 2e ≥ 4r, and Euler’s formula yields e ≤ 2v − 4. This stronger bound is exactly what kills K₃,₃.

concepts.statement: The complete graph **K₅ is not planar**: it has v = 5, e = 10, and 10 > 3·5 − 6 = 9 violates the corollary.
concepts.detail: One edge too many: the densest possible planar graph on five vertices (a triangulation) has 9 edges. No amount of redrawing can rescue the tenth — the obstruction is combinatorial, not artistic.

concepts.statement: The complete bipartite graph **K₃,₃ is not planar**: it is triangle-free with v = 6, e = 9, and 9 > 2·6 − 4 = 8 violates the bipartite corollary.
concepts.detail: The utilities puzzle — three houses each connected to gas, water and electricity without pipe crossings — is exactly K₃,₃ and is unsolvable for this reason.

concepts.statement: A graph is planar **if and only if it contains no subgraph homeomorphic to K₅ or K₃,₃** — that is, no subgraph obtainable from K₅ or K₃,₃ by inserting vertices of degree 2 into edges (subdividing edges) and taking subgraphs.
concepts.detail: Two obstructions generate all nonplanarity: the density obstruction (K₅ — too many edges) and the bipartite obstruction (K₃,₃ — a cyclic-crossing pattern). Kuratowski (1930) says nothing else can go wrong. The equivalent minor version is Wagner’s theorem.

concepts.term: Every planar graph has a small-degree vertex
concepts.statement: Every planar simple graph with v ≥ 2 vertices has a **vertex of degree at most 5**.
concepts.detail: If all degrees were ≥ 6 then 2e = ∑deg ≥ 6v, so e ≥ 3v, contradicting e ≤ 3v − 6. This lemma is the engine of the 6-color and 5-color theorems — and hence of the four color saga in the next section.

examples.title: Verifying Euler’s formula on polyhedra
examples.problem: Check Euler’s formula for the graph of the cube (v = 8, e = 12) and for K₄ (v = 4, e = 6).

steps.label: Cube as a planar graph
steps.text: Flatten the wireframe of a cube: vertices project to 8 points, edges to 12 non-crossing curves, and the plane is divided into 6 regions — 5 squares visible plus the unbounded exterior.

steps.label: K₄ as the tetrahedron
steps.text: Draw K₄ with one vertex inside a triangle: r = 6 − 4 + 2 = 4 regions — three bounded triangles plus the outside.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Polyhedra give the formula its original home: for convex polyhedra, v − e + f = 2 is Euler’s polyhedron formula — the cube has 8 − 12 + 6 = 2.

examples.result: Cube: 6 = 12 − 8 + 2 ✓; K₄: 4 = 6 − 4 + 2 ✓ — planar drawings always balance the books.

examples.title: Impossibility proof by edge counting
examples.problem: Use the corollaries of Euler’s formula to prove that K₅ and K₃,₃ are both nonplanar.

steps.label: Set up K₅
steps.text: K₅ is simple and connected with v = 5 vertices and e = 10 edges.

steps.label: Apply e ≤ 3v − 6
steps.text: If K₅ were planar, the general corollary would force 10 ≤ 3·5 − 6 = 9 — false. So K₅ is nonplanar.

steps.label: Set up K₃,₃
steps.text: K₃,₃ is simple, connected and bipartite with v = 6, e = 9 — but the general bound gives only 9 ≤ 12, which does not yet contradict.

steps.label: Apply the stronger bound
steps.text: Bipartite graphs have no triangles, so each region needs ≥ 4 edge-sides: e ≤ 2v − 4 = 8. But e = 9 > 8 — contradiction. K₃,₃ is nonplanar.

examples.result: K₅ fails the general bound (10 > 9); K₃,₃ fails the triangle-free bound (9 > 8). Two one-line impossibility proofs, no drawing required.

examples.title: Petersen graph via girth counting
examples.problem: The Petersen graph has v = 10, e = 15 and shortest cycle length (girth) 5. Prove it is nonplanar using Euler’s formula with a region-bound argument.

steps.label: Bound region sizes by girth
steps.text: Since there are no 3- or 4-cycles, every region in any planar drawing would be bounded by at least 5 edge-sides: 2e ≥ 5r.

steps.label: Insert Euler’s formula
steps.text: r = e − v + 2, so 2e ≥ 5(e − v + 2), which rearranges to 3e ≤ 5v − 10.

steps.label: Plug in the numbers
steps.text: 3·15 = 45 ≤ 5·10 − 10 = 40 is false — the inequality fails by 5.

steps.label: Conclude and connect to Kuratowski
steps.text: No planar representation exists; in fact the Petersen graph contains a subgraph homeomorphic to K₃,₃, which is Kuratowski’s structural explanation of the same fact.

examples.result: Nonplanar by a sharpened edge count — the general e ≤ 3v − 6 = 24 is far too weak here, but the girth-5 refinement pins it down.

keyTakeaways: Planar = admits SOME crossing-free drawing; region count r includes the unbounded outside region
Euler’s formula: v − e + r = 2 for every connected planar graph — verifiable on any polyhedron
Corollaries: e ≤ 3v − 6 for simple planar graphs; e ≤ 2v − 4 when the graph is triangle-free/bipartite
K₅ (10 > 9) and K₃,₃ (9 > 8) are nonplanar by edge counting alone
Kuratowski: planar ⇔ no subgraph homeomorphic to K₅ or K₃,₃ — subdivisions preserve the obstruction
Every planar graph has a vertex of degree ≤ 5, the key step toward the 5- and 4-color theorems

quiz.q: A connected planar graph has 6 vertices and 12 edges. How many regions does a planar drawing have?
quiz.explanation: Euler’s formula: r = e − v + 2 = 12 − 6 + 2 = 8 regions, counting the unbounded one. (Such a graph is a triangulation — it meets the bound e = 3v − 6 exactly.)

quiz.q: Which is the cleanest proof that K₅ is nonplanar?
options: K₅ has vertices of even degree
K₅ would need 10 edges but e ≤ 3v − 6 = 9 for any simple planar graph on 5 vertices
quiz.explanation: The corollary of Euler’s formula caps simple planar graphs at 3v − 6 edges; K₅ exceeds the cap by exactly one edge, so no crossing-free drawing exists.

quiz.q: A graph contains a vertex of degree 2 in the middle of an edge of a K₅ — i.e., a subdivided K₅. Is the graph planar?
options: No — subdivisions of K₅ remain nonplanar by Kuratowski’s theorem
Only if the degree-2 vertex is removed again
It depends on where the vertex is placed in the drawing
quiz.explanation: Smoothing out degree-2 vertices recovers K₅, and planarity is preserved by subdivision (and its reverse), so any graph containing a subdivided K₅ is nonplanar.

quiz.q: Why does the bound e ≤ 2v − 4 apply to K₃,₃ but not to all planar graphs?
options: Because bipartite graphs have no triangles, so every region in a planar drawing needs at least 4 edge-sides rather than 3
Because K₃,₃ has an Euler path
quiz.explanation: Region-bound counting gives 2e ≥ 3r in general (each region has ≥ 3 sides) but improves to 2e ≥ 4r when no triangles exist — bipartiteness is exactly the no-triangle condition, and 9 > 2·6 − 4 = 8 condemns K₃,₃.

intro: Coloring is the art of conflict-free separation: assign colors to vertices so no edge joins equals, and use as few colors as possible. From final-exam schedules to radio frequencies to register allocation, the chromatic number measures how irreconcilable a conflict structure really is — and for planar graphs the answer is at most four, the most famous theorem in the history of the subject.
objectives: Define proper colorings and the chromatic number χ(G)
Compute chromatic numbers of the standard families: Kₙ, Cₙ, bipartite graphs, wheels
State the four color theorem and the elementary 6- and 5-color results
Model scheduling, frequency assignment and resource allocation problems as graph coloring

concepts.statement: A **proper k-coloring** of a graph is an assignment of one of k colors to each vertex such that **no edge joins two vertices of the same color**. A graph is k-colorable when such a coloring exists; its **chromatic number χ(G)** is the least such k.
concepts.detail: A proper coloring partitions the vertices into k **independent sets** (sets with no internal edges). Since a k-clique needs k distinct colors, χ(G) ≥ clique number; and choosing distinct colors for all n vertices shows χ(G) ≤ |V| always.

concepts.statement: **χ(Kₙ) = n** (every pair conflicts). **χ(Cₙ) = 2 if n is even, 3 if n is odd.** A nonempty bipartite graph has **χ = 2**; a graph with at least one edge needs χ ≥ 2; trees have χ = 2 (or 1 if edgeless); Kₘ,ₙ has χ = 2.
concepts.detail: Even cycles alternate two colors; odd cycles alternate successfully all the way around until the closing edge forces a third. The odd cycle is the unique obstruction to 2-colorability — this is precisely the bipartite characterization of Section 10.2 returning in new clothes.

concepts.statement: **Every planar graph is 4-colorable**: the regions of any map (equivalently, the vertices of any planar graph) can be colored with four colors so that adjacent regions receive different colors.
concepts.detail: Conjectured by Guthrie in 1852, attacked by Kempe’s flawed 1879 proof (whose chain ideas survived), finally proved by Appel and Haken in 1976 with over 1900 computer-checked configurations — the first major computer-assisted proof, still philosophically debated. Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas simplified it in 1997, and Gonthier formalized it in a proof assistant in 2005.

concepts.term: The five and six color theorems
concepts.statement: Every planar graph is **6-colorable** (easy induction using the degree-≤ 5 vertex lemma) and **5-colorable** (Heawood’s 1890 argument using Kempe chain switching). Both are stepping stones toward the 4-color theorem.
concepts.detail: The 6-color proof: remove a vertex of degree ≤ 5, color the rest by induction, reinsert and pick a spare color. The 5-color proof adds the observation that among 5 neighbors two can be recolored by swapping two alternating color classes (Kempe chains). The jump to 4 colors is where everything breaks and computers enter.

concepts.statement: To solve a separation problem: make each item a vertex, add an edge between every pair of items that conflict, then a proper coloring with k colors = a partition into **k conflict-free groups**. The chromatic number is the minimum number of groups — time slots, frequencies or registers needed.
concepts.detail: The modeling step is the whole skill: exams that share students must not share a slot; transmitters within range must not share a channel; variables live at the same time must not share a register.

concepts.statement: Final-exam scheduling (edge = shared student), frequency assignment for cell towers and broadcast stations, register allocation in compilers, timetable construction, and the original map-coloring problem are all chromatic number computations — mostly on graphs whose structure keeps χ small.
concepts.detail: Computing χ(G) exactly is NP-hard in general, but real conflict graphs are often planar, interval-based or near-bipartite, which is why practical systems can color them well — and why the four color theorem matters far beyond cartography.

examples.title: Scheduling final exams
examples.problem: Seven courses must be scheduled in the fewest possible exam slots. Courses share students exactly for these pairs: (1,2), (1,3), (1,4), (2,3), (2,4), (3,4), (3,5), (4,6), (5,6), (5,7), (6,7). Find the chromatic number and exhibit a schedule.

steps.label: Find the clique lower bound
steps.text: Courses 1, 2, 3, 4 are pairwise adjacent — a K₄ — so at least 4 colors (slots) are necessary.

steps.label: Color greedily
steps.text: Course 1 → color A; 2 → B; 3 → C; 4 → D (each conflicts with all previously colored); 5 conflicts only with 3 → A; 6 conflicts with 4 and 5 → B works (4 is D, 5 is A); 7 conflicts with 5 (A) and 6 (B) → C.

steps.label: Verify the coloring
steps.text: Slots: A = {1, 5}, B = {2, 6}, C = {3, 7}, D = {4}. Checking every conflict pair shows no slot contains a clashing pair.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.text: Four slots suffice and three are impossible (the K₄ forces four), so the chromatic number is exactly 4.

examples.result: χ = 4: exam slots A = {1, 5}, B = {2, 6}, C = {3, 7}, D = {4} — the clique number and the coloring meet exactly.

examples.title: Chromatic number of cycles
examples.problem: Determine χ(Cₙ) for every n ≥ 3, with the reasoning.

steps.label: Even n: alternate
steps.text: Walk around the cycle coloring vertices alternately red, blue, red, blue. With an even number of vertices, the sequence closes consistently — the closing edge joins blue to red.

steps.label: Even n: cannot use one color
steps.text: A cycle has edges, so χ ≥ 2; hence χ(C_even) = 2.

steps.label: Odd n: the closing edge breaks
steps.text: Alternating around an odd cycle returns to the start with the same color as the first vertex, so 2 colors fail on the closing edge — χ ≥ 3. Coloring the vertices around the cycle as 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, … uses 3 colors properly.

steps.label: Unify
steps.text: χ(Cₙ) = 2 when n is even and 3 when n is odd — the smallest graphs showing that chromatic number does not require density.

examples.result: Even cycles are bipartite (χ = 2); odd cycles are the minimal 3-chromatic graphs.

examples.title: Map coloring as graph coloring
examples.problem: Explain how coloring a map of countries becomes graph coloring, and why four colors always suffice.

steps.label: Dualize the map
steps.text: Place one vertex in each country; join two vertices when their countries share a border segment (not merely a point). Edges = adjacency of regions.

steps.label: Recognize planarity
steps.text: Draw each vertex inside its country and route each edge across the shared border: the resulting graph is planar by construction.

steps.label: Apply the four color theorem
steps.text: Every planar graph is 4-colorable, so four colors distinguish all neighboring countries — no fifth color is ever needed, however intricate the map.

steps.label: Note the fine print
steps.text: Countries must be contiguous (no exclave split into pieces), and meeting at a single point does not count as adjacency — otherwise more colors may be required.

examples.result: Map coloring = coloring the planar dual graph; the four color theorem guarantees 4 colors always suffice.

keyTakeaways: A proper coloring assigns colors so that every edge joins different colors — a partition into independent sets
χ(Kₙ) = n, χ(Cₙ) = 2 (even n) or 3 (odd n), and bipartite graphs with edges have χ = 2
A k-clique forces χ ≥ k, giving the standard lower bound; greedy coloring gives practical upper bounds
Four color theorem: every planar graph is 4-colorable — proved in 1976 by computer-assisted case analysis
The 6- and 5-color theorems have short elementary proofs using the degree-≤ 5 vertex lemma
Exam scheduling, frequency assignment and register allocation are all chromatic number problems in disguise

quiz.q: What is χ(C₇), the chromatic number of the 7-cycle?
quiz.explanation: Two colors alternate 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1 — but the seventh vertex is color 1, and the closing edge then joins two color-1 vertices, so 2 fails; 3 colors work as 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1. Odd cycles always need exactly 3.

quiz.q: Which graph has chromatic number exactly 5?
quiz.explanation: K₅ needs five colors (a 5-clique forces five distinct colors) and five always suffice — χ(Kₙ) = n. The Petersen graph has χ = 3, K₅,₅ is bipartite with χ = 2, and Q₃ is bipartite with χ = 2.

quiz.q: The four color theorem states that every planar graph can be colored with 4 colors. Why does K₅ not contradict it?
options: K₅ is not planar, so the theorem does not apply to it
The theorem applies only to bipartite graphs
K₅ has no proper coloring at all
quiz.explanation: K₅ is nonplanar (it violates e ≤ 3v − 6), so the four color theorem makes no claim about it — and indeed χ(K₅) = 5. The tension is resolved by planarity, exactly as in Section 10.7.

quiz.q: A university builds a graph whose vertices are courses, with an edge between two courses sharing at least one student. What do the colors in a proper coloring represent?
options: Exam time slots — every pair in the same slot has no shared students
The number of students in each course
quiz.explanation: A proper coloring makes each color class an independent set — no conflicts inside a slot — so each color is exactly one conflict-free exam period. The minimum number of colors is the minimum number of slots.

quiz.q: What is the chromatic number $\chi(C_{5})$ of the cycle on $5$ vertices?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate $\chi(C_{5})$ as the smallest $k$ admitting a proper coloring with $k$ colors. Step 2: Recall the key theorem that a cycle is bipartite exactly when its length is even, so $C_{5}$ needs more than $2$ colors. Step 3: Exhibit a $3$-coloring by coloring consecutive vertices $1, 2, 1, 2, 3$ around the ring, with adjacent vertices always differing. Step 4: Argue $2$ colors fail since alternating $1, 2, 1, 2$ forces the fifth vertex to touch both $1$ and $2$. Step 5: The distractors fail since $5$ counts vertices rather than colors, $4$ invokes a bound that is not tight here, and $2$ ignores oddness. Step 6: Hence $\chi(C_{5}) = 3$.

intro: Delete edges from a connected graph until every last cycle is gone and what remains is a tree — the leanest structure that still holds everything together. Trees are the shape of hierarchy, of recursive computation, and of every efficient index from file systems to databases; this section builds their vocabulary and proves their central identities.
objectives: Define trees and forests, and prove the equivalence: connected acyclic ⇔ unique simple paths
Master rooted-tree terminology: root, parent, child, sibling, ancestor, descendant, leaf, internal vertex, subtree
Classify m-ary, full m-ary and complete m-ary trees, and define level and height
Apply the counting identities n = i + l, n = mi + 1, l = (m − 1)i + 1 and the logarithmic height bounds

concepts.statement: A **tree** is a connected undirected graph with **no simple circuits** (acyclic). A **forest** is an undirected acyclic graph — a disjoint union of trees.
concepts.detail: Equivalences worth internalizing: a tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges; every edge of a tree is a bridge (removing any one disconnects it); adding any new edge between two nonadjacent vertices creates exactly one circuit.

concepts.statement: An undirected graph is a tree **if and only if there is a unique simple path between every two vertices**.
concepts.detail: If two different simple paths joined u and v, splicing them would yield a circuit — contradiction. Conversely, in a graph with cycles, the two arcs around any cycle give two different simple paths between its vertices. This theorem is often the fastest way to prove something is (or is not) a tree.

concepts.statement: A **rooted tree** is a tree in which one vertex is designated the **root**. The choice of root induces a natural orientation of every edge away from the root, turning the tree into a directed graph of ancestry.
concepts.detail: The same unrooted tree can be rooted at different vertices, producing different hierarchies — organization charts, file systems, and parsed programs are rooted trees where the root choice carries meaning.

concepts.statement: In a rooted tree, the **parent** of v is the vertex adjacent to v on the path to the root; v is the parent’s **child**. Vertices with the same parent are **siblings**. The **ancestors** of v are all vertices on the path from v to the root (excluding v); its **descendants** are all vertices having v as an ancestor. A **leaf** has no children; an **internal vertex** has at least one child. The **subtree rooted at v** is the tree induced by v and all its descendants.
concepts.detail: The root is the only vertex with no parent; every other vertex has exactly one parent — the structural fingerprint of hierarchy. Genealogy, HTML/XML nesting and class inheritance all speak this exact language.

concepts.term: m-ary, full and complete m-ary trees
concepts.statement: A rooted tree is **m-ary** when every internal vertex has **at most m** children, and **full m-ary** when every internal vertex has **exactly m** children. m = 2 gives (full) **binary trees**; m = 3 gives ternary trees. A **complete** m-ary tree is balanced: all leaves at levels h or h − 1.
concepts.detail: The phrase full binary tree means every internal vertex branches exactly twice — the workhorse shape of binary search trees, Huffman coding and expression trees in the next sections.

concepts.statement: The **level** of a vertex is the length of the unique simple path from the root to it (root at level 0). The **height** h of the tree is the maximum level of any vertex — equivalently the length of the longest path from root to leaf.
concepts.detail: Height is the tree’s depth of nesting and directly measures worst-case search cost: searching a balanced binary tree costs O(height) = O(log n) comparisons.

concepts.term: Counting identities for full m-ary trees
concepts.statement: A full m-ary tree with n vertices, i internal vertices and l leaves satisfies **n = i + l**, **n = mi + 1** and **l = (m − 1)i + 1**. Every non-root vertex is a child, and children point from the mi slots provided by the i internal vertices.
concepts.detail: For full binary trees: n = 2i + 1 (always odd!) and l = i + 1 (leaves = internal + 1). These instantly answer questions like: 100 leaves ⇒ i = 99 ⇒ n = 199 vertices.

concepts.statement: An m-ary tree of height h has **at most mᵏ vertices at level k** and at most **(mʰ⁺¹ − 1)/(m − 1) vertices in total** (m + m² + … + mʰ for the non-root levels). Consequently an m-ary tree with **l leaves** has **height ≥** $\lceil \log_m l \rceil$, and one with n vertices has height ≥ $\lceil \log_m(n(m-1)+1) \rceil - 1$ — in either case height is forced to grow logarithmically with size.
concepts.detail: A binary tree with l leaves cannot be shorter than log₂ l — exponential branching is the reason binary search halves the problem at every step. A balanced tree attains the bound: height ⌈log₂ l⌉, so searching a balanced binary tree costs O(log n) comparisons.

concepts.statement: Trees are simultaneously the minimal connected structure (n − 1 edges), the maximal acyclic structure (add any edge, make a cycle), the shape of hierarchy (rooted), and the shape of divide-and-conquer (recursion trees, decision trees).
concepts.detail: Whenever an optimization forces connectivity with fewest edges — or acyclicity with most edges — the answer is a tree, and spanning trees in Sections 11.4–11.5 make this a working algorithmic principle.

examples.title: Is this graph a tree?
examples.problem: A graph has vertices {a, b, c, d, e, f, g} and edges {a,b}, {a,c}, {b,d}, {b,e}, {c,f}, {c,g} — 7 vertices, 6 edges. Verify it is a tree in two different ways.

steps.label: Count check
steps.text: It is connected (start at a and reach d, e, f, g through b or c) and has 6 = 7 − 1 edges — consistent with being a tree.

steps.label: Acyclicity check
steps.text: Any circuit would need to reuse a vertex, but from any vertex the path back toward a is forced and unique; no cycle can close.

steps.label: Unique paths
steps.text: By the characterization theorem, verify: the path from d to g is d — b — a — c — g, and it is unique — no alternative route exists because there is exactly one path from any vertex to the root a.

steps.label: Read it as a rooted tree
steps.text: Rooted at a: a has children b, c; b has children d, e; c has children f, g. Leaves {d, e, f, g}, internal vertices {a, b, c}; it is a full binary tree of height 2.

examples.result: Yes — connected and acyclic, with unique simple paths; rooted at a it is a full binary tree with i = 3 internal vertices and l = 4 leaves.

examples.title: Counting vertices, internal vertices and leaves
examples.problem: A full binary tree has 1001 vertices. How many internal vertices and how many leaves does it have? Can a full binary tree have exactly 1000 vertices?

steps.label: Pick the right identity
steps.text: For a full binary (full 2-ary) tree, n = 2i + 1 — solve for i: i = (n − 1)/2.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: i = (1001 − 1)/2 = 500 internal vertices; then l = n − i = 1001 − 500 = 501 leaves (check: l = i + 1 ✓).

steps.label: Test the even case
steps.text: For n = 1000, i = (1000 − 1)/2 = 499.5 is not an integer — no full binary tree with an even number of vertices can exist.

steps.label: Explain the parity
steps.text: Each internal vertex contributes exactly 2 children plus the root contributes itself: n = 2i + 1 is always odd, so even n is impossible by the identity itself.

examples.result: 1001 vertices ⇒ 500 internal, 501 leaves; 1000 vertices is impossible since n = 2i + 1 is always odd.

examples.title: Height lower bounds
examples.problem: A 3-ary tree has 100 leaves. Prove its height is at least 5, and show a tree that achieves it.

steps.label: Apply the level bound
steps.text: A 3-ary tree of height h has at most 3ʰ leaves, so h ≥ ⌈log₃ 100⌉.

steps.label: Evaluate the logarithm
steps.text: 3⁴ = 81 < 100 ≤ 243 = 3⁵, so log₃ 100 is between 4 and 5, and the ceiling is 5.

steps.label: Construct a witness
steps.text: A height-5 tree exists: start from the full 3-ary tree of height 4 (81 leaves) and extend 9 of its leaves with 3 children each (+18 leaves net) plus 1 more leaf with 2 children (+1 net), giving 81 + 18 + 1 = 100 leaves at height exactly 5 — m-ary trees allow any number of children up to m.

steps.label: Conclude the bound
steps.text: No 3-ary tree of height 4 can hold 100 leaves (max 81), so every 3-ary tree with 100 leaves has height ≥ 5 — and 5 is attainable.

examples.result: h ≥ ⌈log₃ 100⌉ = 5 — exponential branching caps the leaves at 3ʰ, forcing logarithmic height.

keyTakeaways: Tree = connected + acyclic; forest = acyclic (each component a tree)
G is a tree ⇔ unique simple path between any two vertices ⇔ connected with n − 1 edges
Rooted trees speak ancestry: parent, child, sibling, ancestor, descendant, leaf, internal vertex, subtree
Full m-ary tree: n = mi + 1 = i + l, and l = (m − 1)i + 1; full binary trees always have an odd number of vertices and leaves = internal + 1
Level k holds ≤ mᵏ vertices; l leaves force height ≥ $\lceil \log_m l \rceil$ — exponential branching is why balanced search is logarithmic
Balanced trees achieve the logarithmic bound — the structural reason binary search runs in O(log n)

quiz.q: Which statement about trees is FALSE?
options: A tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges
Between any two vertices of a tree there is a unique simple path
Every vertex of a tree with n ≥ 2 vertices has degree at least 2
Removing any edge from a tree disconnects it
quiz.explanation: Every tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves — vertices of degree 1 — so degree ≥ 2 everywhere is impossible. The other three statements are standard characterizations of trees.

quiz.q: A full 3-ary tree has 10 internal vertices. How many leaves does it have?
quiz.explanation: l = (m − 1)i + 1 = 2·10 + 1 = 21 leaves. Check with n = mi + 1 = 31 vertices: 31 = 10 + 21 ✓.

quiz.q: Why can no full binary tree have exactly 1000 vertices?
options: Because 1000 is too large for a binary tree
Because n = 2i + 1 forces n to be odd
Because binary trees must be complete
Because full binary trees must have a power-of-two number of vertices
quiz.explanation: Counting children: each of the i internal vertices supplies exactly 2 children, and the root is the only vertex that is nobody’s child, so n = 2i + 1 — an odd number, never 1000.

quiz.q: A 3-ary tree has 100 leaves. What is the minimum possible height it can have?
options: 4, because the tree can be complete
5, because a 3-ary tree of height h has at most 3ʰ leaves and 3⁴ = 81 < 100 ≤ 243 = 3⁵
7, because every level triples and the root is at level 0
No bound exists — a 3-ary tree with 100 leaves can have any height
quiz.explanation: Level h holds at most 3ʰ leaves, so a height-4 tree accommodates at most 3⁴ = 81 leaves — too few. Height 5 can hold up to 243 leaves, and a tree with exactly 100 leaves and height 5 exists, so the minimum possible height is exactly 5.

intro: Trees earn their keep by organizing decisions: binary search trees locate items by asking one yes/no question per level, decision trees prove that some puzzles cannot be solved faster than logarithmically, and Huffman trees turn symbol frequencies into the shortest possible prefix-free codes. One data structure, three industries.
objectives: Build and search binary search trees and analyze their complexity from height
Model yes/no or multi-outcome decision processes as trees and derive information-theoretic lower bounds
Define prefix codes and explain why they decode unambiguously
Run the Huffman coding algorithm by hand and compute the resulting bit count
Understand game trees and minimax evaluation of two-player games

concepts.statement: A **binary search tree (BST)** for a set of keys is a binary tree in which each vertex v with key k(v) satisfies: every key in v’s **left subtree is < k(v)**, every key in the **right subtree is > k(v)** — and this holds recursively at every vertex.
concepts.detail: The BST property is local but its effect is global: from any vertex, the search space halves at each comparison — every vertex discards the entire subtree on the side the target cannot be in.

concepts.statement: **Insert** keys one at a time: start at the root and compare; go left if smaller, right if larger, and attach the new key as a leaf where no child exists. **Search** follows the identical walk and succeeds iff it lands on the key.
concepts.detail: Insertion order shapes the tree: sorted input builds a degenerate path (height n − 1), random input builds a tree with expected height Θ(log n). Balanced insertion/rebalancing (AVL, red-black) guarantees O(log n) worst case — the standard dictionary structure of every major library.

concepts.statement: A **decision tree** models a procedure of successive tests: internal vertices are tests, each branch is one possible outcome, and each **leaf is a final conclusion**. The **complexity of the procedure is the height of the tree** — the number of tests in the worst case.
concepts.detail: Lower-bound principle: a tree with height h and branching factor b (b outcomes per test) has at most bʰ leaves, so distinguishing N conclusions needs **h ≥** $\lceil \log_b N \rceil$ tests. This single observation proves logarithmic lower bounds for sorting, searching and coin-weighing puzzles all at once.

concepts.statement: A comparison-based sort of n items has at most **n!** possible input orders, so its decision tree has ≥ n! leaves and height ≥ **⌈log₂ n!⌉ = Ω(n log n)** — no comparison sort can beat n log n comparisons in the worst case.
concepts.detail: Stirling’s formula gives log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n − 1.44n, so merge sort’s O(n log n) is asymptotically optimal among comparison sorts. Non-comparison sorts (radix, counting) escape the bound by not using binary-outcome comparisons.

concepts.statement: A **prefix code** for an alphabet is a set of binary codewords in which **no codeword is the prefix of another** — equivalently, the codewords are the labels of the leaves of a binary tree. Encoding replaces each symbol by its codeword; decoding reads left to right, cutting off at each complete codeword.
concepts.detail: The prefix property is exactly what makes decoding instantaneous and unambiguous: as soon as the bits read so far match a leaf, that symbol is certain — no lookahead or backtracking is ever needed. Fixed-length codes (like ASCII) are trivially prefix codes; Huffman’s variable-length codes are the optimal ones.

concepts.statement: Given symbol frequencies w₁, …, wₙ: repeatedly take the two trees of **smallest total weight** and merge them under a new root (weight = sum), until one tree remains. Label left edges 0 and right edges 1; the codeword of a symbol is its path from the root. The total encoded length is **∑ (frequency × depth of symbol’s leaf)** — provably minimal among prefix codes.
concepts.detail: Greedy logic: the two least frequent symbols should sit deepest (they cost the least to lengthen) — hence merge first what you will pay for last. Huffman is optimal among all prefix codes for the given frequencies, though not necessarily among all uniquely decodable codes.

concepts.statement: A **game tree** for a two-player game has positions as vertices and legal moves as edges, alternating levels for the two players. **Minimax** assigns each leaf a value (win/lose or numeric payoff) and backs values up the tree: your levels take the max, the opponent’s take the min.
concepts.detail: Game trees explain strategy: tic-tac-toe has fewer than 9! ≈ 362,880 leaves and is a draw with perfect play; chess is far too deep to exhaust, so programs search to a depth cutoff and score leaves heuristically — with alpha–beta pruning discarding provably irrelevant branches.

examples.title: Building a binary search tree
examples.problem: Insert the keys 14, 12, 3, 21, 17, 25, 8, 6, 15 into an empty BST in this order, then trace the search for 15.

steps.label: Insert 14, 12, 3
steps.text: 14 becomes the root. 12 < 14 → left child. 3 < 14 → left; 3 < 12 → left child of 12.

steps.label: Insert 21, 17, 25
steps.text: 21 > 14 → right child of 14. 17 > 14 → right, 17 < 21 → left child of 21. 25 > 14 → right, 25 > 21 → right child of 21.

steps.label: Search for 15
steps.text: Start at 14: 15 > 14 go right; at 21: 15 < 21 go left; at 17: 15 < 17 go left; at 15: found — 3 comparisons, one per level of descent.

examples.result: A height-4 BST with 9 nodes; searching 15 costs 3 comparisons — roughly log₂ 9 ≈ 3.2, the balanced-tree promise.

examples.title: The eight-coin puzzle and its bound
examples.problem: You have 8 coins, one of which is counterfeit and slightly heavier. A balance scale compares two subsets per weighing. Show that 2 weighings suffice and prove 1 cannot.

steps.label: Count the conclusions
steps.text: The answer must name which of the 8 coins is heavy: 8 possible conclusions, so a decision tree needs at least 8 leaves.

steps.label: Apply the branching bound
steps.text: Each weighing has 3 outcomes (left heavy, right heavy, balance), so w weighings distinguish at most 3ʷ conclusions. With w = 1: 3 < 8 — impossible.

steps.label: Check w = 2
steps.text: 3² = 9 ≥ 8, so the counting bound permits two weighings — and a concrete scheme exists (weigh 1,2,3 vs 4,5,6; the outcome narrows to ≤ 3 suspects, then weigh one against one to finish).

steps.label: Read off the general law
steps.text: Coins known only to be heavier-or-lighter: distinguishing n suspects needs ⌈log₃ n⌉ weighings — 12 coins (24 possibilities heavy/light) famously need 3 since 3² = 9 < 24 ≤ 27 = 3³.

examples.result: Two weighings suffice and one is impossible: the information-theoretic bound ⌈log₃ 8⌉ = 2 is tight here.

examples.title: Huffman coding step by step
examples.problem: Symbols a, b, c, d, e occur with frequencies 45, 16, 12, 9, 5. Build the Huffman code and compute the total encoded length.

steps.label: Merge the two smallest (d, e)
steps.text: d(5) + e(9) → node of weight 14. Remaining trees: a45, b16, c12, de14.

steps.label: Merge c with de
steps.text: Smallest two are c(12) and de(14) → node of weight 26. Remaining: a45, b16, cde26.

steps.label: Merge b with cde
steps.text: Smallest two are b(16) and cde(26) → node of weight 42. Remaining: a45, bcde42.

steps.label: Final merge
steps.text: a(45) + bcde(42) → root 87. Label every left edge 0, right edge 1, with a as the right child.

steps.label: Read the codewords
steps.text: a = 1 (depth 1); b = 00 (depth 2); c = 010 (depth 3); d = 0110 (depth 4); e = 0111 (depth 4). No codeword prefixes another — prefix property holds.

steps.label: Total bits
steps.text: 45·1 + 16·2 + 12·3 + 9·4 + 5·4 = 45 + 32 + 36 + 36 + 20 = 169 bits for 87 symbols ≈ 1.94 bits per symbol — versus 261 bits with a fixed 3-bit code for the 5 symbols, a saving of 92 bits.

examples.result: Codes: a→1, b→00, c→010, d→0110, e→0111, total 169 bits — the most frequent symbol got the shortest codeword, as optimality demands.

keyTakeaways: BST property: left subtree < vertex < right subtree, recursively — one comparison per level discards half the candidates
Search/insert cost = height: Θ(log n) balanced, Θ(n) degenerate; random insertion order gives Θ(log n) expected height
Decision tree bound: b-way tests distinguishing N outcomes need height ≥ $\lceil \log_b N \rceil$ — the master lower-bound template that yields the Ω(n log n) comparison-sort bound from n! leaves
Prefix codes = leaf labels of a binary tree: no codeword is a prefix of another, so decoding is instantaneous
Huffman: repeatedly merge the two least-frequent trees; total bits = ∑ frequency × depth, optimal among prefix codes
Game trees + minimax: take max on your moves, min on the opponent’s; alpha–beta prunes without changing the result

quiz.q: Keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are inserted into an empty BST in sorted order. What is the resulting height (root at level 0), and what is the worst-case search cost?
options: Height 4, worst search 5 comparisons — the tree degenerates into a path
quiz.explanation: Each new key is larger than all previous, so every insertion goes right, producing a chain 1→2→3→4→5 of height 4. Searching for the deepest key (or a missing key near it) touches all 5 vertices. Sorted input is the BST’s worst enemy.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a prefix (prefix-free) code?
quiz.explanation: In {0, 10, 110, 111} no codeword starts another one: 0 is not a prefix of 10, and 110, 111 differ in the last bit. The other sets each contain a codeword that begins another (e.g. 0 prefixes 01), making decoding ambiguous.

quiz.q: In Huffman coding, which two symbols are merged into one subtree first?
options: The two symbols with the longest desired codewords
quiz.explanation: Huffman always merges the two trees of smallest total weight first — the rarest symbols are pushed deepest, where extra depth costs the fewest total bits.

quiz.q: A balance scale has 3 outcomes per weighing. What is the minimum number of weighings guaranteed by the counting bound to determine which of 27 coins is heavy (heavy known in advance)?
quiz.explanation: There are 27 possible conclusions and at most 3ʷ distinguishable outcomes after w weighings; 3² = 9 < 27 ≤ 81 = 3³, so ⌈log₃ 27⌉ = 3 weighings are necessary — and a divide-into-threes strategy achieves exactly 3.

intro: A tree stores a hierarchy — but algorithms need a linear order. The three systematic traversals (preorder, inorder, postorder) each convert a tree into a list, and each matches a classic notation: Polish, infix and reverse Polish. Compilers, calculators and tree-sort all live off this one idea.
objectives: Execute preorder, inorder and postorder traversals on any rooted tree, including forests
Build and read expression trees, converting between infix, prefix (Polish) and postfix (reverse Polish) notations
Explain why infix notation needs parentheses while pre/postfix do not
Use inorder traversal of a binary search tree to produce sorted output
Work with universal address systems and lexicographic order

concepts.statement: **Preorder**: visit the root, then traverse each subtree left to right (recursively). For a forest, preorder each tree in turn. It produces the **prefix (Polish) notation** of an expression tree.
concepts.detail: Preorder lists each parent before all of its descendants — the natural order for copying a tree, serializing a file system, or numbering a table of contents (1, 1.1, 1.1.1, …).

concepts.statement: **Inorder** (for binary trees): traverse the left subtree, visit the root, traverse the right subtree. On an expression tree it produces the familiar **infix notation** — which needs parentheses to be unambiguous.
concepts.detail: Inorder is only defined naturally for binary (ordered, two-child) trees. Its celebrity role: inorder of a binary search tree emits the keys in **sorted order** — tree-sort in one traversal.

concepts.statement: **Postorder**: traverse each subtree left to right, then visit the root last. On an expression tree it yields **postfix (reverse Polish) notation**, which evaluates with a plain stack and needs no parentheses.
concepts.detail: Children before parents: postorder is the order of dependency — evaluate operands before operators, free memory after children, compute subtree sizes bottom-up. Compilers generate postfix-style intermediate code for exactly this reason.

concepts.statement: An **expression tree** represents a compound expression: **leaves hold operands (numbers, variables), internal vertices hold operators**; an internal vertex with k children is a k-ary operation on its subtrees. The three traversals produce the infix, prefix and postfix forms of the expression.
concepts.detail: The tree makes precedence and associativity visible as geometry: in ((a + b) · c) − d the − sits at the root, · below it, + at the lowest internal level — structure replaces punctuation.

concepts.term: Inorder of a BST gives sorted output
concepts.statement: The **inorder traversal of a binary search tree lists its keys in increasing order**.
concepts.detail: Proof by the BST property: when we visit a vertex, its entire left subtree (all smaller keys) has already been listed, and its right subtree (all larger) is listed after. This is the tree-sort algorithm: build a BST (O(n log n) average), traverse inorder (O(n)), receive sorted output.

concepts.statement: In the **universal address system**, the root is 1, and the children of the vertex labeled v are v.1, v.2, v.3, … in order. The **lexicographic order** of the labels lists an ancestor before its descendants and equals the **preorder traversal** sequence.
concepts.detail: Book chapters use exactly this system (Section 11.3 is 3.1.3): sorting the addresses as strings reproduces the preorder walk — sorting a hierarchy and traversing it are the same thing.

concepts.statement: Infix notation inherits ambiguity from flattening a tree: a + b · c could come from (a + b) · c or a + (b · c). Conventional precedence/associativity rules — or explicit parentheses — restore the missing structure. Prefix and postfix are prefix-free/suffix-free enough that **no parentheses are ever needed**.
concepts.detail: Depth-first traversal encodes the tree shape into symbol order itself: in + a b, the operator claims the next two sub-expressions; there is exactly one way to parse, so the linear form is unambiguous by construction.

examples.title: Three traversals of one expression tree
examples.problem: Build the expression tree for the fully parenthesized expression ((a + b) · c) − d and write its preorder, inorder and postorder listings.

steps.label: Construct the tree
steps.text: The outermost operation is −: root = − with left child the · subtree and right child the leaf d. The · has left child + (leaves a, b) and right child the leaf c.

steps.label: Preorder (root first)
steps.text: Visit −, then preorder(·): visit ·, preorder(+): visit +, a, b, then c; finally d. Result: − · + a b c d — prefix notation.

steps.label: Inorder (root middle)
steps.text: Inorder(·) first: a + b · c; then root, then d. Result: a + b · c − d — infix, which is ambiguous without parentheses (the true reading is ((a + b) · c) − d).

steps.label: Postorder (root last)
steps.text: Postorder of ·’s children first: a b + c ·, then d, then the root. Result: a b + c · d − — reverse Polish notation.

examples.result: Preorder: − · + a b c d; Inorder: a + b · c − d (needs parentheses); Postorder: a b + c · d − (paren-free).

examples.title: Evaluating postfix with a stack
examples.problem: Evaluate the postfix expression a b + c · d − for a = 2, b = 3, c = 4, d = 1, showing the stack after each symbol.

steps.label: Push operands
steps.text: Read a = 2 → stack [2]. Read b = 3 → stack [2, 3].

steps.label: Apply +
steps.text: Pop 3 and 2, push 2 + 3 = 5 → stack [5].

steps.label: Push c
steps.text: Read c = 4 → stack [5, 4].

steps.label: Apply ·
steps.text: Pop 4 and 5, push 5 · 4 = 20 → stack [20].

steps.label: Push d, apply −
steps.text: Read d = 1 → stack [20, 1]. Read −: pop 1 and 20, push 20 − 1 = 19 → stack [19]. End of input.

examples.result: The value is 19 = ((2 + 3) · 4) − 1 — one left-to-right pass, no parentheses, no precedence rules.

examples.title: Tree-sort via inorder
examples.problem: Insert 14, 12, 3, 21, 17, 25, 8, 6, 15 into a BST and produce the sorted list by inorder traversal.

steps.label: Build the BST
steps.text: Insert in the given order: root 14; 12 left of 14; 3 left of 12; 21 right of 14; 17 left of 21; 25 right of 21; 8 right of 3; 6 left of 8; 15 left of 17.

steps.label: Run inorder
steps.text: Left of 14 first: inorder at 12 → its left is 3 → 3’s left is empty, visit 3; 3’s right is 8 → 8’s left is 6 → visit 6, visit 8; back up: visit 12; right of 12 empty. Now visit 14. Then the right subtree: 15, 17, 21, 25.

steps.label: Assemble the output
steps.text: 3, 6, 8, 12, 14, 15, 17, 21, 25 — the nine keys in increasing order.

examples.result: Inorder emits exactly the sorted sequence — tree-sort costs n insertions (O(n log n) average) plus one O(n) traversal.

keyTakeaways: Preorder = root, then subtrees left to right → prefix (Polish) notation; the order of table-of-contents numbering and serialization
Inorder = left, root, right → infix notation; on a BST it emits keys in sorted order (tree-sort)
Postorder = subtrees, then root → postfix (reverse Polish); children before parents, ideal for evaluation and teardown
Expression trees: leaves = operands, internal vertices = operators — one tree, three notations
Infix needs parentheses (or precedence rules); prefix and postfix encode the structure in symbol order alone
Postfix evaluates with one left-to-right stack pass — operands push, operators pop-apply-push

quiz.q: An expression tree has root +, left child · (leaves a, b), right child leaf c. What is its postorder traversal?
quiz.explanation: Postorder = children first, root last: left subtree yields a b ·, then the right leaf c, then the root +, giving a b · c + — the reverse Polish form of a · b + c.

quiz.q: Which of the three standard traversals of a binary search tree produces the keys in ascending sorted order?
quiz.explanation: Inorder visits the left (smaller) subtree, then the vertex, then the right (larger) subtree — the BST property turns this local rule into a global sorted listing.

quiz.q: Why can the infix form a + b · c not be read unambiguously without precedence rules or parentheses?
options: Because infix traversal is not well defined on binary trees
Because both ((a + b) · c) and (a + (b · c)) flatten to the same infix string a + b · c
Because · is not a valid operator in an expression tree
Because operands must be visited before operators
quiz.explanation: Two different trees — (+ (· a b) c) and (· a (+ b c)) — share the same inorder sequence a + b · c; parentheses or precedence conventions select the intended tree. Prefix (+ · a b c vs · a + b c) and postfix (a b · c + vs a b c + ·) differ and need no help.

quiz.q: In the universal address system, vertices receive labels like 1, 1.1, 1.2, 1.2.1. Sorting these labels lexicographically produces which traversal?
quiz.explanation: Every ancestor’s label is a prefix of its descendants’ labels and sorts before them, and older siblings sort before younger ones — exactly the visit rule of preorder traversal.

intro: Take any connected graph and delete edges — carefully, never breaking connectivity — until no circuit survives: what is left is a spanning tree, a skeleton that reaches every vertex with the minimum possible skeleton of n − 1 edges. Two classic searches, depth-first and breadth-first, build such skeletons automatically and power everything from maze exploration to web crawling.
objectives: Define spanning trees and prove that every connected graph has one
Construct spanning trees by deleting circuit edges, and count how many edges must go
Execute depth-first search (DFS) and breadth-first search (BFS) to build spanning trees
Understand backtracking as DFS with undo, and state Cayley’s count nⁿ⁻² of spanning trees of Kₙ

concepts.statement: A **spanning tree** of a simple graph G is a subgraph of G that is a tree and **contains every vertex of G**. A spanning forest plays the same role for a disconnected graph — one spanning tree per component.
concepts.detail: Spanning = touches all vertices; tree = acyclic and connected. With n vertices it has exactly n − 1 edges, the least any connected subgraph on all of G can have.

concepts.statement: A graph is **connected if and only if it has a spanning tree**. Constructively: as long as the graph contains a circuit, delete one edge of that circuit; deleting a circuit edge never disconnects a graph, so the process terminates at a connected, acyclic spanning subgraph.
concepts.detail: The algorithm implicit in the proof also counts the deletions: a connected graph with n vertices and m edges must lose exactly m − n + 1 edges — the dimension of its cycle space.

concepts.statement: **DFS**: start at a root, follow edges to unvisited vertices as far as possible, and **backtrack** only when stuck; the edges used to first reach each vertex form a **depth-first spanning tree**. With vertices ordered alphabetically, always try the smallest unvisited neighbor next.
concepts.detail: DFS dives deep before widening — a last-in-first-out (stack/LIFO) discipline. Applications: maze solving, detecting circuits and cut vertices, topological sorting, and backtracking search (graph coloring, n-queens, sudoku) where exploring one branch fully before the next is the whole point.

concepts.statement: **BFS**: visit the root, then all vertices at distance 1, then all at distance 2, and so on — a **first-in-first-out (queue)** discipline. The tree edges used to first reach each vertex form a **breadth-first spanning tree whose paths from the root are shortest possible in edge count**.
concepts.detail: BFS is level-by-level exploration — the unweighted ancestor of Dijkstra’s algorithm. It gives the fewest-edges route from the root to every vertex, which is exactly what makes it the core of shortest paths in unweighted networks and of web crawlers.

concepts.statement: **Backtracking** solves constraint problems by DFS over a space of partial solutions: extend the partial solution as far as possible; when it violates a constraint, **undo the last choice and try the next alternative**. The DFS tree of choices is searched systematically, with pruning cutting hopeless branches.
concepts.detail: Graph coloring, sum-of-subsets, the n-queens puzzle and Hamilton-circuit search are all backtracking: build a tree of choices depth-first, retreat when a branch dies. Spanning trees are literally the infrastructure of this search strategy.

concepts.statement: The complete graph **Kₙ has exactly nⁿ⁻² spanning trees** (Cayley’s formula). For example K₃ has 3, K₄ has 16, K₅ has 125, K₆ has 1296.
concepts.detail: nⁿ⁻² grows explosively: an 8-city network has 8⁶ = 262,144 spanning trees — far too many to enumerate, which is why the MST algorithms of the next section find the best one without listing any. (Kirchhoff’s matrix-tree theorem generalizes the count to arbitrary graphs.)

examples.title: Spanning tree by circuit breaking
examples.problem: A connected graph has n = 8 vertices and m = 12 edges. How many edges must be removed to reach a spanning tree, and why is it safe to remove them?

steps.label: Target edge count
steps.text: A spanning tree on 8 vertices has n − 1 = 7 edges.

steps.label: Count the deletions
steps.text: Remove m − (n − 1) = 12 − 7 = 5 edges — always exactly five, no matter which spanning tree you reach.

steps.label: Justify safety
steps.text: Remove only edges lying on circuits: deleting a circuit edge leaves every vertex still reachable (go around the circuit the other way), so connectivity never breaks.

steps.label: Know when to stop
steps.text: Once no circuits remain, the graph is acyclic and still connected — a spanning tree; deleting anything more would disconnect it.

examples.result: Exactly 5 edges removed; each chosen from a circuit, leaving a 7-edge spanning tree.

examples.title: DFS versus BFS on the same graph
examples.problem: Graph G: vertices a, b, c, d, e, f; edges {a,b}, {a,c}, {b,d}, {c,e}, {d,e}, {d,f}. Build the depth-first and breadth-first spanning trees rooted at a (alphabetical tie-breaking), and compare their shapes.

steps.label: Run DFS from a
steps.text: Visit a → smallest unvisited neighbor b → from b, neighbor d (a visited) → from d, smallest unvisited neighbor e → from e, neighbor c (d visited) → c’s neighbors a, e are visited, backtrack to d → visit f. Tree edges: a–b, b–d, d–e, e–c, d–f.

steps.label: Read the DFS tree
steps.text: The DFS tree is one deep path a–b–d–e–c with side branch d–f — depth before breadth; edge a–c exists in G but is not a tree edge.

steps.label: Run BFS from a
steps.text: Queue = [a]; visit a, enqueue b, c (tree edges a–b, a–c). Pop b: enqueue d (edge b–d). Pop c: enqueue e (edge c–e). Pop d: enqueue f (edge d–f). Pop e: nothing new. Tree edges: a–b, a–c, b–d, c–e, d–f.

steps.label: Read the BFS tree and compare
steps.text: Levels: a alone; then b, c; then d, e; then f. The BFS tree is shallow and records shortest edge-count routes (e.g., a → c → e is a 2-edge path); the DFS tree reaches e only on the fourth level via its long path.

examples.result: DFS tree: {a–b, b–d, d–e, e–c, d–f} (deep); BFS tree: {a–b, a–c, b–d, c–e, d–f} (level-by-level, shortest paths from a).

examples.title: Counting what you cannot list
examples.problem: How many edges must be removed from K₅ to obtain a spanning tree, and how many different spanning trees does K₅ have?

steps.label: Edge budget
steps.text: K₅ has C(5, 2) = 10 edges; a spanning tree on 5 vertices needs 4 edges, so exactly 10 − 4 = 6 edges are deleted — every deletion coming off some circuit.

steps.label: Apply Cayley’s formula
steps.text: The number of spanning trees of K₅ is $5^{5-2} = 5^{3} = 125$.

steps.label: Sanity-check a small case
steps.text: For K₃: three edges, spanning tree uses 2, and exactly 3 choices exist — matching $3^{3-2} = 3^{1} = 3$.

steps.label: Appreciate the growth
steps.text: K₈ has 8⁶ = 262,144 spanning trees — enumeration is hopeless, so finding a best one requires the greedy algorithms of the next section.

examples.result: Remove exactly 6 edges from K₅; there are 125 = 5³ distinct spanning trees to choose among.

keyTakeaways: Spanning tree = tree subgraph containing every vertex; exactly n − 1 edges in an n-vertex graph
G is connected ⇔ G has a spanning tree — proved by repeatedly deleting circuit edges
A connected graph with m edges and n vertices needs exactly m − n + 1 deletions to reach any spanning tree
DFS builds a deep spanning tree using backtracking (stack discipline); BFS builds a shallow one via a queue, giving fewest-edge paths from the root
Backtracking = DFS over the tree of partial solutions, pruning branches that violate constraints
Cayley: Kₙ has nⁿ⁻² spanning trees — too many to enumerate, motivating the greedy MST algorithms

quiz.q: A connected graph has 8 vertices and 12 edges. How many edges must you delete to obtain a spanning tree?
quiz.explanation: A spanning tree on 8 vertices has 8 − 1 = 7 edges, so 12 − 7 = 5 edges must go — each one taken from a circuit so connectivity survives.

quiz.q: What property do the root-to-vertex paths of a breadth-first spanning tree have?
options: They are the shortest possible paths in the whole graph in terms of total edge weight
They use the fewest edges among all paths from the root in the unweighted sense
They are always the longest paths found by DFS
They always pass through every vertex
quiz.explanation: BFS visits vertices level by level, so each vertex enters the tree via a path with the minimum number of edges from the root. (Minimum total weight is Dijkstra’s job, not BFS.)

quiz.q: Which data-structure discipline matches each search?
options: DFS: stack (LIFO, backtrack); BFS: queue (FIFO, level order)
quiz.explanation: DFS pushes choices on a stack and pops (backtracks) when stuck — LIFO. BFS processes vertices in arrival order — FIFO — which is what makes it level-by-level.

quiz.q: By Cayley’s theorem, how many spanning trees does the complete graph K₆ have?
quiz.explanation: Kₙ has $n^{n-2}$ spanning trees, so K₆ has 6⁴ = 1296. (Confusing nⁿ⁻² with n! or nⁿ is the classic slip — check with K₃: 3¹ = 3, not 3! = 6.)

intro: Now make every edge cost money. A spanning tree is the cheapest way to connect everything with no redundancy — but which of the astronomically many spanning trees is cheapest? Two greedy algorithms, Prim’s and Kruskal’s, find it in polynomial time, and a single exchange argument explains why greed works at all.
objectives: Define the minimum spanning tree problem on connected weighted graphs
Execute Prim’s algorithm (grow one tree) and Kruskal’s algorithm (merge a forest) by hand
Explain the cut/exchange argument that certifies both algorithms’ correctness
Recognize MST applications in network design and know when the MST is unique

concepts.statement: A **minimum spanning tree (MST)** of a connected weighted graph is a spanning tree whose **total edge weight is minimum** among all spanning trees. It always exists, since a connected finite graph has finitely many spanning trees.
concepts.detail: The MST connects everything at least cost — n − 1 links chosen from possibly thousands. If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique; with ties, several minimum trees may coexist (the set of chosen weights is still the same).

concepts.statement: **Prim**: start with a single vertex (and an empty tree); repeatedly **add the cheapest edge with one endpoint inside the tree and the other outside**; stop when all vertices are included. The growing structure is always one tree.
concepts.detail: Growth by nearest neighbor of the whole tree. A straightforward implementation rescans all edges incident to the tree each round, giving O(n²)-style behavior — the same profile as Dijkstra, and in fact the two algorithms are structural twins.

concepts.statement: **Kruskal**: sort all edges by weight; scan in increasing order and **add each edge unless it forms a circuit with the edges already chosen**; stop after n − 1 edges. The growing structure is a forest whose components repeatedly merge.
concepts.detail: Globally cheapest edges first, circuits vetoed. Circuit detection is maintained efficiently with a disjoint-set (union–find) structure, and the sort dominates: O(e log e) overall — excellent for sparse graphs.

concepts.statement: **Cut argument**: for any partition of the vertices, the cheapest edge crossing the cut belongs to some MST — if an MST T omitted it, adding the edge would create a cycle that crosses the cut a second time, and swapping in the cheap edge cannot raise the total. Prim applies this to the cut around its tree at every step; Kruskal applies it to the cut between the components its edge would join.
concepts.detail: This exchange (swap heavier for lighter, keep a spanning tree) is the certificate of optimality: neither algorithm ever makes a choice that some MST could not contain, so both terminate with a genuine MST. It also proves uniqueness: with distinct weights, every cut has a single cheapest crossing edge, so every MST is forced to make the same choices.

concepts.statement: MSTs design least-cost networks — electrical grids, pipelines, telecommunication backbones, road and sewer systems — and underlie **single-linkage clustering** (stop Kruskal early and read off the components) and approximation algorithms for harder problems like the TSP.
concepts.detail: Any situation of the form connect everything, pay per link, no redundancy needed is an MST. Where redundancy matters (survivability), Steiner trees and survivable-network design take over — the MST is the polynomial baseline they build upon.

examples.title: Prim’s algorithm, full trace
examples.problem: Weighted graph on vertices a, b, c, d, e, f with edges: a–b (1), b–c (2), a–c (5), b–e (3), c–d (4), c–e (6), d–e (3), d–f (8), e–f (4), b–d (7). Run Prim’s algorithm from a and total the result.

steps.label: Start the tree at a
steps.text: Tree = {a}. Crossing edges: a–b (1) and a–c (5) — cheapest is a–b.

steps.label: Grow to b, then c
steps.text: Add a–b (1). Tree = {a, b}: cheapest crossing edge is b–c (2) (beating b–e (3), b–d (7), a–c (5)). Add b–c.

steps.label: Grow to e
steps.text: Tree = {a, b, c}: crossing candidates include b–e (3), c–d (4), c–e (6), a–c now internal — cheapest is b–e (3). Add b–e.

steps.label: Grow to d
steps.text: Tree = {a, b, c, e}: cheapest crossing edge is d–e (3) (vs c–d (4), e–f (4)). Add d–e.

steps.label: Finish with f
steps.text: Tree = {a, b, c, d, e}: cheapest crossing edge to f is e–f (4) (vs d–f (8)). Add e–f — all six vertices are in.

steps.label: Total and verify
steps.text: Edges: a–b (1), b–c (2), b–e (3), d–e (3), e–f (4): five edges = n − 1, total weight 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 13.

examples.result: Prim’s MST: {a–b, b–c, b–e, d–e, e–f} with total weight 13 — one tree growing by its cheapest boundary edge at each step.

examples.title: Kruskal’s algorithm, with a cycle rejection
examples.problem: Run Kruskal’s algorithm on the same weighted graph and show which edge is rejected for creating a circuit.

steps.label: Sort the edges
steps.text: Increasing order: a–b (1), b–c (2), b–e (3), d–e (3), c–d (4), e–f (4), a–c (5), c–e (6), b–d (7), d–f (8).

steps.label: Take the first three
steps.text: a–b (1) ✓, b–c (2) ✓, b–e (3) ✓ — none creates a circuit; forest = {a,b,c} ∪ {e} merged stepwise.

steps.label: Continue and hit the veto
steps.text: d–e (3) ✓ joins d. Next c–d (4): c and d are already connected (c–b–e–d), so c–d would close the circuit c–b–e–d–c — REJECT. Take e–f (4) instead ✓.

steps.label: Stop at n − 1 edges
steps.text: Five accepted edges {a–b, b–c, b–e, d–e, e–f} connect all six vertices — the algorithm stops.

steps.label: Compare with Prim
steps.text: Total weight 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 13 — identical tree to Prim’s, reached from the opposite philosophy (global cheapest edges vs local tree growth).

examples.result: Kruskal’s MST: {a–b, b–c, b–e, d–e, e–f}, weight 13; c–d (4) was rejected for creating the circuit c–b–e–d–c.

examples.title: The exchange argument on one edge
examples.problem: Prove: the cheapest edge e crossing any cut (a partition of the vertices into S and V − S) belongs to some minimum spanning tree.

steps.label: Suppose an MST omits e
steps.text: Let T be an MST with e = {u, v} not in T, where u ∈ S and v ∉ S.

steps.label: Force a cycle
steps.text: T is a tree, so a path from u to v exists inside T; adding e to T creates a unique circuit containing e.

steps.label: Find a second crossing edge
steps.text: That circuit starts at u ∈ S, crosses to v ∉ S via e, and must return to u — so it uses another edge f ≠ e crossing the cut.

steps.label: Exchange
steps.text: Build T′ = T − f + e: still a spanning tree (the cycle is broken, connectivity preserved), with weight w(T′) = w(T) − w(f) + w(e) ≤ w(T) because w(e) ≤ w(f).

steps.label: Conclude
steps.text: T′ is an MST containing e — so the cheapest crossing edge is always safe. Prim and Kruskal never paint themselves into a corner.

examples.result: Every cheapest cut-crossing edge lies in some MST — the one-sentence correctness proof of both greedy algorithms.

keyTakeaways: MST = spanning tree of minimum total weight; exists for every connected weighted graph, unique when all weights are distinct
Prim: grow one tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge leaving it — a Dijkstra-shaped O(n²)-style greedy
Kruskal: sort all edges, take cheapest-first unless it forms a circuit — O(e log e) with union–find for cycle checks
Correctness: cheapest edge across any cut is exchange-safe — add it, swap out a heavier crossing edge, never lose minimality
Both are greedy, both provably optimal, and on the same graph they can return the same MST from opposite strategies
Applications: least-cost utility/communication networks, clustering (early-stopped Kruskal), TSP approximations

quiz.q: Prim’s algorithm is growing the tree on vertices {a, b, c}. Crossing edges available: c–d (4), b–e (3), a–d (6), b–d (5). Which edge does Prim add?
quiz.explanation: Prim adds the cheapest edge with exactly one endpoint in the tree — that is b–e (3), regardless of which tree vertex it touches. Cost matters, not which vertex extends.

quiz.q: During Kruskal’s algorithm, when is an edge rejected?
options: When its weight is larger than the average edge weight
