Counting: only countably many machines, uncountably many functions — uncomputability is the norm, not the exception.

quiz.q: For a Turing machine, δ(s, i) = (s′, i′, d) means:
options: In state s reading symbol i: write i′, move the head one cell in direction d, and enter state s′
Swap the states s and s′ and halt
Erase symbol i from the tape and stop
quiz.explanation: One transition packages all three actions — write, move (L or R), change state — and it fires whenever the machine is in state s scanning symbol i.

quiz.q: The Church–Turing thesis claims that:
options: Turing machines can compute all functions from ℕ to ℕ
Any computation realizable as an effective mechanical procedure can be carried out by a Turing machine
Every Turing machine halts on every input
Finite-state machines are as powerful as Turing machines
quiz.explanation: The thesis identifies informal effective computability with Turing computability; it is not provable, and option 1 is false — uncomputable functions exist.

quiz.q: Turing proved that:
options: The halting problem can be solved given enough tape
No Turing machine decides, for every machine T and input x, whether T halts on x
All computable functions are polynomial-time computable
The tape can always be replaced by finite memory
quiz.explanation: The halting problem is undecidable — Turing's 1936 diagonal argument shows any proposed decider contradicts itself.

quiz.q: The counting argument for uncomputability says:
options: There are more Turing machines than functions
Turing machines form a countable set while functions from ℕ to ℕ form an uncountable set, so most functions are uncomputable
Every function is computable by some Turing machine with enough states
Uncomputable functions cannot be described in any way
quiz.explanation: Machine descriptions are finite strings over a finite alphabet (countable); functions ℕ → ℕ correspond to infinite bit sequences (uncountable) — computation misses almost all of them.

quiz.q: Which of the following problems is undecidable?
options: Given a Turing machine $M$ and input $x$, decide whether $M$ halts on $x$
Given a deterministic finite automaton $D$ and string $w$, decide whether $D$ accepts $w$
Given a deterministic finite automaton $D$, decide whether its language is empty
Given a deterministic finite automaton $D$, decide whether it has exactly $5$ states
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate decidability as existence of a Turing machine that always halts with the correct yes-or-no verdict. Step 2: Recall the key theorem that the **halting problem** $HALT = \{\langle M, x\rangle : M$ halts on $x\}$ admits no decider. Step 3: Sketch the diagonal clash where a hypothetical halting decider yields a machine that halts exactly when the decider says it loops. Step 4: Contrast with finite-automaton questions, all decided by graph reachability on finitely many states in time $O(|Q| + |\delta|)$. Step 5: The distractors fail since simulating a DFA on $w$, searching its reachable accept states, or counting its states are all routine finite procedures. Step 6: Hence only the halting question is undecidable.

depth.title: The kernel boundary as a contract

blocks.body: The two system views deserve to be stated precisely enough to reason about. As a **resource manager**, the kernel is a function from competing requests to a schedule of grants: it multiplexes each physical resource either in **time** — the CPU among processes — or in **space** — memory pages, disk blocks, and device access — subject to fairness and efficiency constraints. As an **extended machine**, the kernel implements a family of virtual machines: files instead of disk blocks, address spaces instead of raw DRAM, sockets instead of packet buffers, each with semantics deliberately cleaner than the hardware beneath. The views are duals rather than rivals. Every abstraction the extended machine sells is paid for by an allocation the manager performs, and every allocation policy is observable only through the abstractions it serves. A well-designed kernel keeps the correspondence tight — the abstraction hides the arbitration, and the arbitration is what makes the abstraction implementable.

Treat the **system-call interface** as a legal document and the whole boundary becomes analyzable. It is an **application binary interface**: a fixed table of entry points — `read`, `write`, `fork`, `mmap` — with binary-stable calling conventions, argument encodings, error numbers and specified semantics; POSIX is its canonical written form. Everything beneath the boundary may change freely — kernel version, scheduler, file-system implementation, hardware — so long as the contract holds; Linux's famous rule that an upgrade must never break user space is exactly this discipline. The boundary is simultaneously a **protection domain**: the kernel's address space and privileged mode form a domain in which all code is necessarily trusted, while each process's user-mode address space is a domain in which code is presumed hostile. The narrowness of the interface is the point. A few hundred entry points can be specified, audited and even formalized; the billions of instructions behind them cannot.

The book defines a process as a program in execution; the graduate definition unpacks into four components. A **process** is, first, an **address space** — the set of virtual addresses the program may reference, together with the mapping that gives them meaning. Second, one or more **threads of control**, each an execution context: a saved program counter, a register set, and a stack. Third, a set of **resources** acquired from the kernel — open file descriptors, sockets, memory mappings. Fourth, **credentials** — user and group identity that gate every future request to the manager. The decomposition matters because the parts evolve independently: the address space, resources and credentials belong to the process, while the thread is the unit the scheduler dispatches; systems that allow many threads per process simply share the first, third and fourth components among several instances of the second. Notice also what the definition accomplishes for the kernel itself — the process is the abstraction through which the resource manager sees all of its customers.

blocks.heading: Trap-and-emulate in one paragraph
blocks.body: A hypervisor turns the extended-machine idea on the machine itself. A virtual machine monitor (VMM) boots a guest kernel in **user mode**, letting it believe it owns privilege the monitor has kept for itself. The guest runs, sets up its page tables, and executes a privileged instruction to install the page-table base register. The hardware refuses — the instruction is privileged at the guest's actual privilege level — and the CPU traps into the trap vector the VMM registered at boot. The monitor inspects the trapped instruction, updates its shadow copy of the guest's page tables to produce the mapping the guest intended, emulates the effect the guest expected to see, and resumes the guest at the following instruction. The guest kernel never learns that it is a tenant: every touch of the hardware it believes it owns is intercepted and re-implemented by the layer beneath. Virtualization is thus the extended-machine principle applied recursively — one level lower than the textbook draws it.

The chapter's deepest engineering rule is the separation of **mechanism** from **policy**. A mechanism answers *how*: the timer that preempts a process, the page-table hardware that translates an address, the signal mechanism that delivers an event. A policy answers *which* and *when*: which process runs next, which page is evicted, which events matter to whom. The kernel should supply mechanisms powerful enough to enforce any reasonable policy while keeping the policy itself replaceable — one timer mechanism supports batch, interactive, and real-time behavior by changing only the decision procedure above it. Conflating the two hardens today's choice into tomorrow's bottleneck, and the architecture of pluggable schedulers, mountable file systems, and loadable modules is this single separation, applied repeatedly.

depth.title: When the definition itself dissolves

blocks.body: This section admits that no completely adequate definition of an operating system exists — and research has spent three decades stress-testing that admission. Under virtualization, the **resource allocator** role migrates upward: the hypervisor decides which guest receives which cores, memory, and devices, while each guest kernel merely allocates what the hypervisor granted it. The operating system becomes firmware for a virtual machine, and cloud platforms complete the demotion by treating operating systems as disposable appliance images, booted by the thousand and discarded on release. Meanwhile the **extended machine** role leaks sideways: a browser or a JVM supplies files, threads, synchronization and networking so completely that applications target it rather than the OS beneath it. The kernel remains the always-running core of its own machine — but both of its classical job descriptions now have competitors on other layers, which is why the 1998 Microsoft boundary dispute keeps recurring with new defendants.

The **exokernel** (MIT, Engler and Kaashoek, 1995) is the sharpest research response to the dual view: **separate protection from management**. The exokernel implements no files, no processes, no virtual memory. It securely multiplexes raw hardware — physical pages, disk blocks, network packets — exposing each resource with minimal interpretation and enforcing only ownership: an application may touch only the pages, blocks, and packet slots it has obtained. All abstraction moves into **library operating systems** linked into each application, so a database can implement a buffer cache tuned to its own access pattern while a web server implements its own thread package. Measurements on the Aegis exokernel showed application-specific abstractions beating the fixed kernel ones by wide margins precisely on the workloads those fixed abstractions served poorly. The design never conquered the mainstream, but it keeps resurfacing, muted, each time a kernel grows a mechanism for applications to install their own policies — `eBPF`, `io_uring`.

blocks.heading: Does the kernel survive as a unit?
blocks.body: Two current research lines attack the definition from opposite directions. **Unikernels** — MirageOS is the exemplar — compile the application, its libraries, and a minimal operating system into a single special-purpose image that runs directly on a hypervisor: there is no kernel at all, system calls become ordinary function calls, the image is tens of kilobytes, boots in milliseconds, and exposes thousands of lines of attack surface instead of millions — but any application bug can corrupt the whole machine, because nothing beneath the application exists to catch it. **WASI**, the WebAssembly System Interface, proposes the opposite move: a portable, capability-checked system-call interface through which any WebAssembly binary runs on any host, from a browser to a cloud runtime — the first operating-system interface designed after kernels stopped being the only programs running at all times. The open question: does 'operating system' remain a meaningful unit of system software, or does it dissolve into a stack of independently evolving contracts?

intro: An operating system is the software that manages a computer’s hardware and acts as the intermediary between the user and that hardware. Before studying how an OS works internally, we need to fix what we mean by ‘operating system’ at all — the answer changes dramatically depending on whose viewpoint you take.
objectives: Describe the four components of a computer system and the OS’s intermediary role
Contrast the user view of an OS across PCs, shared mainframes and handheld devices
Explain the two system-view roles: resource allocator and control program
Distinguish kernel, system programs, middleware and application programs
Use the bare-machine vs extended-machine (virtual machine) framing

concepts.term: Four components of a computer system
concepts.statement: A computer system divides roughly into four components: the **hardware** (CPU, memory and I/O devices — the basic computing resources), the **operating system** (the intermediary that controls and coordinates the hardware’s use), the **application programs** (compilers, word processors, web browsers — the tools that define how resources are used to solve user problems) and the **user**.
concepts.detail: An equivalent cut is hardware, software and data. The book’s simile: an operating system is like a **government** — it performs no useful function by itself, but it creates the environment in which other programs can do useful work.

concepts.statement: The **user view** depends on the interface being used. For a PC or laptop, one user **monopolizes the resources**, so the OS is designed mostly for **ease of use**, with some attention to performance and security and *none* to resource utilization — how hardware and software resources are shared.
concepts.detail: Mainframes and servers with many terminals reverse the priorities: with many users sharing one machine, **resource utilization and fairness** dominate, because every idle second is wasted capacity that several people are paying for. Handheld devices optimize for individual usability plus battery life, featuring touch screens and voice interfaces (Apple’s Siri); embedded computers in cars and home appliances may have little or **no user view at all**, running without user intervention.

concepts.statement: From the computer’s point of view, the OS is the program **most intimately involved with the hardware**, and its first system-view role is **resource allocator**: it manages CPU time, memory space, storage space and I/O devices, deciding among **numerous and possibly conflicting requests** so the system operates **efficiently and fairly**.
concepts.detail: The kernel must answer allocation questions constantly — which process gets the CPU next, which pages live in memory, which job owns the printer — and the quality of those arbitration decisions is what ‘efficiently and fairly’ measures.

concepts.statement: The second system-view role is the **control program**: it **manages the execution of user programs to prevent errors and improper use** of the computer — it is especially concerned with the operation and control of **I/O devices**.
concepts.detail: The two roles are complementary: the allocator decides *who gets what*, the control program polices *what may be done at all*. Every protection mechanism in this book — mode bits, the timer, memory isolation, file permissions — descends from this single idea.

concepts.statement: There is **no completely adequate definition** of an operating system. One view includes **everything the vendor ships** when you order ‘the operating system’ — but shipped systems range from under a megabyte (lacking even a full-screen editor) to multi-gigabyte graphical systems.
concepts.detail: The book’s working definition: the OS is **the one program running at all times — the kernel**. Around it sit **system programs** (associated with the OS but not part of the kernel) and **application programs** (everything not tied to system operation). Mobile systems complicate the boundary by adding **middleware** — frameworks providing extra services to application developers: Apple’s iOS and Google’s Android each ship a kernel plus middleware for databases, multimedia and graphics. The 1998 US Department of Justice suit against Microsoft — essentially a dispute over how much functionality belongs in the OS — shows the boundary is commercially explosive, not merely academic.

concepts.statement: Hardware alone — the **bare machine** — is not particularly easy to use, and applications share common needs such as controlling I/O devices. Gathering those common control-and-allocation functions into one piece of software yields the OS, which turns raw hardware into a cleaner, easier **extended machine** — the core of the **virtual machine** idea.
concepts.detail: The fundamental goal of a computer system is to execute user programs and make solving user problems easier; the OS exists because it is a reasonable way to reach that goal. Everything in this course — files, processes, memory abstractions — is some layer of extension built on bare hardware.

examples.title: Sorting a phone into the OS stack
examples.problem: Classify the software of an Android phone into kernel, system programs, middleware and applications.

steps.label: Step 1: Kernel
steps.text: The modified Linux kernel — the one program running at all times, managing CPU, memory, power and the Binder IPC facility.

steps.label: Step 2: Middleware
steps.text: The Android frameworks above the kernel — database (SQLite), multimedia and graphics support — services provided to application developers rather than to end users directly.

steps.label: Step 3: System programs
steps.text: Programs associated with the OS but not part of the kernel: settings utilities, the window manager, background daemons started at boot.

steps.label: Step 4: Applications
steps.text: Everything the user installs from the app store — each is an application program using the layers beneath, not part of the operating system proper.

examples.result: The ‘vendor ships’ definition would swallow the whole stack; the kernel definition draws the line at the always-running core, with middleware and system programs as scaffolding in between.

examples.title: Two programs, one printer — the resource allocator at work
examples.problem: Two users submit print jobs and compute-intensive programs to a shared mainframe. Show how the OS’s two system-view roles interact.

steps.label: Step 1: Conflicting requests appear
steps.text: Both processes need the single printer and both want CPU time. The requests conflict — the hardware alone cannot arbitrate.

steps.label: Step 2: The allocator decides
steps.text: The OS serializes printer access — one job finishes (or is spooled) before the other starts — so the resource is used efficiently and neither user is starved.

steps.label: Step 3: The control program polices
steps.text: Neither process may program the printer’s device controller directly; all access goes through the OS, preventing errors and improper use of the device.

steps.label: Step 4: Utilization is protected
steps.text: While one process waits for its printout, the CPU is switched to the other user’s computation — the machine never idles while work exists.

examples.result: Allocator (fair, efficient division of resources) plus control program (a gatekeeper over dangerous operations) together describe the OS from the system’s point of view.

keyTakeaways: A computer system = hardware + operating system + application programs + user; the OS is the intermediary between user and hardware.
User view: single-user machines optimize ease of use; shared machines optimize resource utilization; handhelds add power constraints; embedded systems may have no user view.
System view: the OS is both a resource allocator (efficient, fair arbitration) and a control program (prevent errors and improper use, especially of I/O).
The kernel is the one program running at all times; system programs, middleware and applications surround it — and ‘the OS’ as shipped is far bigger than the kernel.
Mobile OSes (iOS, Android) blur the boundary by bundling middleware frameworks into the platform.
The OS as extended machine: common, awkward hardware functions are wrapped into one convenient software layer — the seed of the virtual machine idea.

quiz.q: According to the book’s working definition, the operating system proper is:
options: everything the vendor ships when you order ‘the operating system’
the kernel — the one program running at all times
the collection of all system daemons
the graphical user interface and its applications
quiz.explanation: The ‘everything shipped’ view is acknowledged but rejected as too broad; the text follows the definition of the OS as the always-running kernel, with system programs and applications outside it.

quiz.q: From the user view, an OS for a single-user PC is designed mostly for:
options: ease of use, with some attention to performance and security
fair sharing among many simultaneous users
quiz.explanation: One user monopolizes a PC’s resources, so utilization is nearly irrelevant to that user — the design centers on usability; utilization dominates only when multiple users share one machine, as on mainframes.

quiz.q: In the system view, the control program’s chief concern is:
options: allocating CPU time fairly among processes
managing the execution of user programs to prevent errors and improper use, especially of I/O devices
providing a command interpreter to users
quiz.explanation: The control program role is policing: user programs must not cause errors or misuse the machine, and device control is where the risk concentrates. Fair allocation is the separate resource-allocator role.

quiz.q: Which statement about middleware in mobile operating systems is correct?
options: it runs below the kernel in firmware
it is a set of software frameworks providing additional services to application developers
it exists only on mainframe systems
quiz.explanation: iOS and Android each pair a core kernel with middleware frameworks — databases, multimedia, graphics support — sitting between kernel and applications, which is exactly why ‘what is the OS’ is ambiguous for phones.

depth.title: Interrupts, buses and the price of I/O

blocks.body: The textbook mechanism scales up by adding tables and ranks. On x86, every interrupt source carries a **vector number**, and the CPU dispatches by indexing the **interrupt descriptor table** — 256 entries, each a gate holding the handler's address, its privilege requirements, and the stack to switch to — so dispatch costs one table lookup rather than a poll of every device. Modern hardware abandons the shared wire entirely: a **message-signaled interrupt** is a memory write from the device, carrying its own vector, which lets a PCI Express system deliver thousands of distinct interrupts as discrete messages. The controller assigns each vector an **interrupt priority level**; a handler can itself be preempted by a higher-priority arrival, and the kernel can forbid that during critical processing by raising the CPU's interrupt-priority mask — the hardware ancestor of the software lock. The three requirements the book lists — deferral, efficient dispatch, and multilevel priorities — are therefore not aspirations but table and mask entries.

Electrical semantics decide whether interrupt lines can be shared. A **level-triggered** line stays asserted until the handler services the device and the device deasserts: the CPU samples the level, so a device serviced late simply keeps asking, and several devices can share one line because it stays high while any one of them needs service. The hazard is the **interrupt storm** — a handler that fails to clear the condition re-enters itself forever. An **edge-triggered** line signals only the transition: the controller must latch the edge, and a handler that services devices too slowly can miss one that asserted and deasserted while interrupts were masked — which is why edge-triggered handlers must not dawdle on shared lines. The classic PCI interrupt pins were level-triggered precisely to permit sharing, and message-signaled interrupts dissolve the question entirely by making every interrupt a private, addressed message rather than a level on a common wire.

blocks.heading: What I/O costs the CPU
blocks.body: Compare the two structures by the bytes per second each can sustain. In **programmed I/O** the CPU moves every word itself, so throughput is bounded by processor cycles: $$R_{\text{PIO}} = \frac{f \cdot w}{c},$$ for clock $f$, word size $w$, and $c$ cycles per word — with $f = 3$ GHz, $w = 8$ bytes, and $c = 10$ cycles, a ceiling of $2.4$ GB/s. Now impose the textbook's interrupt discipline of one interrupt per unit transferred, each costing $C_{I}$ of CPU time: at $C_{I} = 1\,\mu\text{s}$ per byte, the CPU can field at most $$R_{\text{int}} = \frac{1}{C_{I}} = 1\,\text{MB/s},$$ while a modern drive delivers a hundred times more. **DMA** inverts the accounting: the CPU spends one setup and one completion interrupt per block of $B$ bytes — roughly $1.2$ nanoseconds of CPU per byte for $B = 8192$ at $10\,\mu\text{s}$ of total attention — and the transfer rate is then bounded by the bus and the device rather than the CPU. The feasibility condition for per-unit interrupts falls out directly: they survive only while $C_{I} \le 1/R$ for device rate $R$ — at $R = 100$ MB/s that demands a 10-nanosecond interrupt, and no machine has ever fielded one.

**Memory-mapped I/O** makes device registers appear as ordinary physical addresses: a store to the controller's command word *is* the command, and a driver is ordinary code performing loads and stores to special addresses — in C, through pointers to `volatile` locations, since neither the compiler nor the CPU may cache or reorder access to device state. The alternative — dedicated I/O instructions, x86's `in` and `out` reaching a separate port space — survives for legacy reasons; mapping devices into the memory address space lets one bus and one instruction set reach both, and lets DMA target device buffers directly. The **device-driver contract** then has a crisp shape. The driver is the one module that knows the controller's register map and command encoding; implements the kernel's uniform interface — open, read, write, control, poll — on top of it; claims its interrupt vectors and handles completions; and prepares the DMA buffers the controller will read and write behind the CPU's back. Everything the rest of the operating system knows about a device is this interface — which is why drivers remain the kernel's largest and least reliable code base.

Because a handler runs with its interrupt line — and often others — masked, an interrupt handler that takes milliseconds silently disables the machine: every device on a masked line loses events while it runs. Real kernels therefore split the work. The **top half**, the registered handler, only acknowledges the device, captures minimal state, and enqueues a request. The **bottom half** — Linux softirqs and tasklets, Windows deferred procedure calls — runs later with interrupts enabled, doing the expensive protocol and buffer work. The section's interrupt architecture is thus an account of where the doorbell rings, not of where the work happens: correctness demands only that the door be answered quickly, and performance demands that everything else be answered elsewhere.

depth.title: The I/O path at machine speed

blocks.body: When gigabit networks arrived, interrupt-driven I/O met a failure mode the textbook picture cannot express: **receive livelock**. Mogul and Ramakrishna, measuring a busy web server at DEC's Western Research Laboratory in the mid-1990s, watched useful throughput collapse to zero while the CPU stayed 100% busy — entirely in interrupt context. The mechanism: every arriving packet raises an interrupt, interrupt handlers run above every process priority, and under overload the arrivals never stop — so the CPU fields interrupts forever and never executes the protocol code that drains the receive queues. The queues overflow, packets drop, and transport-layer retransmissions manufacture still more arrivals: a self-sustaining state in which the machine works hard at accomplishing nothing. The fix, now standard, is hybrid interrupt-polling — Linux's NAPI switches a busy device from interrupts to polling, converting the priority inversion back into ordinary schedulable work.

blocks.heading: Kernel bypass in the data center
blocks.body: The radical conclusion of the livelock studies was that for the fastest devices the kernel should exit the data path entirely. **Kernel-bypass frameworks** — DPDK for packet processing, netmap for high-speed networking, RDMA for remote memory — map device queues and DMA buffers directly into user memory, so an application, or a userspace network stack, polls the hardware itself: no trap, no handler, no copy. Packet forwarding at ten million packets per second on a single core, and remote-memory latencies of a few microseconds, are now routine in production data centers, and RDMA carries the collectives that train modern AI clusters. The price is architectural. Every bypassing application re-implements the buffer management, scheduling, and security the kernel used to provide uniformly, and the machine's protection boundary no longer covers its fastest traffic. The operating system becomes the control plane — configuration, setup, slow paths — while the data plane it once owned runs beside it at user privilege.

blocks.heading: Is the syscall still the right I/O door?
blocks.body: The newest chapter questions the boundary this whole book stands on. `io_uring` — Linux, 2019 — replaces the synchronous system call with shared submission and completion queues between user and kernel: an application enqueues many requests with ordinary memory writes and collects completions asynchronously, amortizing each trap across a batch and enabling zero-copy pipelines; fused with NVMe poll queues, the kernel can be absent from the steady-state fast path without being bypassed at all. The open question is what survives of the classic model in which every I/O operation is a trap, a handler, and a mode switch. If the fastest interface is a shared queue with no trap, the system-call boundary is no longer the operating system's defining edge but one door among several — traps, queues, mapped rings — each with its own performance contract and its own security story, and no existing theory says which combination an operating system should offer.

intro: A modern computer is a CPU and a crowd of device controllers sharing a common bus and memory. Everything the OS does rests on three hardware mechanisms this section makes precise: interrupts, which let devices demand attention; the storage hierarchy, which trades speed against capacity; and DMA, which moves bulk data without drowning the CPU in interrupts.
objectives: Describe von Neumann organization and the fetch–decode–execute cycle, including the interrupt check before each instruction
Explain the roles of device controllers, device drivers and the memory controller on a common bus
Walk the storage hierarchy with representative sizes and access times, and convert storage units
Trace the full interrupt-driven I/O cycle, including vectored dispatch, state save/restore and priority handling
Explain why DMA exists and how it replaces per-byte interrupts with one interrupt per block

concepts.term: Von Neumann architecture and the instruction cycle
concepts.statement: A **von Neumann architecture** keeps instructions and data in one read-write memory. The **instruction cycle**: fetch the instruction from memory into the **instruction register**, **decode** it, optionally fetch operands, **execute**, then store results back to memory. Before executing each instruction the CPU senses the **interrupt-request line**, so hardware can redirect the machine at any instruction boundary.
concepts.detail: The memory unit sees only a stream of addresses — it neither knows nor cares whether an address holds instruction or data, or how the address was generated (program counter, indexing, indirection, literal). The **program counter** supplies the fetch address; a **load** moves a byte or word from memory into a CPU register, a **store** writes a register back to memory. Main memory is built from DRAM, and the CPU can execute only what has been loaded into it.

concepts.term: Device controllers, drivers and the common bus
concepts.statement: A general-purpose computer system is **one or more CPUs and a number of device controllers connected through a common bus** that provides access to shared memory. Each **device controller** is in charge of a specific device type, maintains **local buffer storage** and a set of **special-purpose registers**, and moves data between the peripheral devices it controls and that buffer. The OS side of this interface is the **device driver** — one per controller — which understands the controller and presents a uniform interface to the rest of the OS.
concepts.detail: Depending on the controller, several devices may attach through it — one USB port can feed a hub with many devices. The CPU and the controllers execute **in parallel, competing for memory cycles**, so a **memory controller** synchronizes access to memory. A typical PC bus hosts a disk controller, a USB controller, and a graphics adapter alongside the keyboard, mouse and monitor.

concepts.statement: Storage systems form a **hierarchy** ordered by speed, cost and capacity: **registers → cache → main memory → nonvolatile memory (NVM/flash, SSD) → hard-disk drives (HDD) → optical disk and magnetic tape** (tertiary storage). The rule: **smaller and faster sits closer to the CPU**; volatile levels sit above the line, nonvolatile levels below it.
concepts.detail: Representative values (book Figure 1.14): registers hold under 1 KB and respond in about $0.25$–$0.5$ ns; cache under 16 MB at 0.5–25 ns; main memory under 64 GB at 80–250 ns; solid-state storage up to about 1 TB at 25,000–50,000 ns; magnetic disk to 10 TB at roughly 5,000,000 ns — about **seven orders of magnitude** slower than registers. Unit bookkeeping: a kilobyte is $2^{10}$ bytes, a megabyte $2^{20}$, a gigabyte $2^{30}$, a terabyte $2^{40}$ and a petabyte $2^{50}$ (manufacturers round to powers of ten, and networking counts **bits**, not bytes). Mechanical storage (HDD, optical, tape) is generally larger and cheaper per byte; electrical storage (flash, SSD) is faster but costlier. RAM is **volatile**, so the bootstrap program lives in nonvolatile firmware such as EEPROM — the iPhone, for instance, keeps serial numbers and hardware info there.

concepts.statement: Hardware may trigger an interrupt at any time by signaling on the **interrupt-request line** — the CPU senses that line after executing every instruction. A controller **raises** an interrupt by asserting the line; the CPU **catches** the interrupt and **dispatches** it to a handler; the handler **clears** it by servicing the device. Dispatch is fast because the interrupt number **indexes an interrupt vector** — a table of pointers (typically in low memory) to interrupt service routines.
concepts.detail: Without vectors, a generic routine would have to poll every possible source to find who needs service — far too slow for something that occurs constantly. Indirection through the table means the fixed location the CPU jumps to simply contains the starting address of the right routine. Windows and UNIX dispatch interrupts in exactly this manner.

concepts.statement: On catching an interrupt the CPU reads the interrupt number, uses it as an index into the interrupt vector, and jumps to the handler. The handler **saves any state it will change**, determines the cause of the interrupt, performs the necessary processing, **restores the saved state**, and executes a **return from interrupt** — the interrupted computation resumes as though nothing had happened.
concepts.detail: The interrupt architecture must preserve state because the interruption arrives asynchronously — the running program’s registers and program counter belong to it, not to the device. The book lists three modern requirements beyond the basic mechanism: the ability to **defer** handling during critical processing, an **efficient dispatch** to the proper handler (the vector), and **multilevel priorities** so urgent work preempts routine work.

concepts.term: Maskable vs nonmaskable interrupts, priorities and chaining
concepts.statement: Most CPUs have two interrupt-request lines. The **nonmaskable** interrupt is reserved for events such as unrecoverable memory errors and cannot be turned off; the **maskable** line serves device controllers and can be disabled during critical instruction sequences. **Interrupt priority levels** let high-priority interrupts preempt low-priority ones, and **interrupt chaining** hangs a list of handlers off each vector entry, tried one by one.
concepts.detail: On Intel processors, vector numbers **0–31 are nonmaskable** events signaling error conditions (divide error at 0, page fault at 14, and so on) while **32–255 are maskable**, used for device-generated interrupts. Chaining exists because computers have more devices than the vector has elements — each element points to the head of a handler list, a compromise between a huge table and a single polling handler.

concepts.statement: **Direct memory access** serves bulk data movement: after the device driver sets up **buffers, pointers and counters** for the device, the device controller transfers an entire block **directly between the device and main memory with no intervention by the CPU**, generating **one interrupt per block** on completion instead of one interrupt per byte.
concepts.detail: While the controller works, the CPU is free for other tasks — though controller and CPU still **compete for memory cycles**, the classic cost of DMA known as cycle stealing. On high-end **switch-based** systems, where multiple components converse concurrently instead of arbitrating for a shared bus, DMA is even more effective.

concepts.statement: Interrupt-driven I/O cycle (Figure 1.4): (1) the **device driver initiates I/O** by loading the controller’s registers; (2) the controller starts the transfer into its **local buffer**; (3) on completion the controller **generates an interrupt**; (4) the CPU (checking between instructions) receives it and **transfers control to the interrupt handler**; (5) the handler **processes the data** and returns from interrupt; (6) the CPU **resumes the interrupted task**. With DMA, steps 3–6 collapse: the controller moves the whole block to memory itself and interrupts once, at the end.
concepts.detail: For small transfers (a keystroke, a character to a terminal) interrupt-driven I/O is fine; for large NVS transfers it would bury the CPU in per-byte interrupts. DMA trades a little memory-bus contention for thousands of avoided interrupts — the book’s motivating example for why both I/O structures exist.

examples.title: Anatomy of a keystroke
examples.problem: A user presses a key while the CPU is busy running a compiler. Trace the complete interrupt-driven path from press to delivered character.

steps.label: Step 1: Driver initiates
steps.text: Earlier, the keyboard’s device driver loaded the controller’s registers requesting ‘read a character from the keyboard’ — the controller examines these registers to determine the action to take.

steps.label: Step 2: Controller buffers the data
steps.text: The controller moves the keystroke from the device into its local buffer storage.

steps.label: Step 3: Interrupt is raised and caught
steps.text: On completion the controller asserts the interrupt-request line; at the next instruction boundary the CPU senses it, reads the interrupt number, and indexes the interrupt vector to find the handler’s address.

steps.label: Step 4: Handler saves state and services
steps.text: The handler saves the registers it will modify, determines that a keyboard event caused the interrupt, and hands the character (or a pointer to it) to the driver.

steps.label: Step 5: Restore and resume
steps.text: The handler restores the saved state and executes return from interrupt — the compiler continues exactly where it was, unaware anything happened.

examples.result: One keystroke exercised the full loop: initiate → buffer → raise → catch → dispatch → save → service → restore. The entire sequence is invisible to the interrupted program.

examples.title: Counting interrupts: why DMA exists
examples.problem: A program reads an $8\,\text{KB}$ block from a solid-state drive. Compare the interrupt load with per-byte interrupt-driven I/O versus DMA.

steps.label: Step 2: Per-byte interrupts
steps.text: If the controller interrupted once per byte — as low-speed devices effectively do — the CPU would field $8192$ separate interrupts for this one read, each paying save/dispatch/restore costs.

steps.label: Step 3: Set up DMA
steps.text: The driver instead writes a command block: source device, memory address for the block, and a counter of $8192$ bytes to move.

steps.label: Step 4: Block transfer
steps.text: The DMA controller moves the whole block directly to main memory, cycle by cycle competing with the CPU for memory but never interrupting it.

steps.label: Step 5: One completion interrupt
steps.text: When the block lands, the controller raises a single interrupt telling the driver the operation has completed — a load of $8192$ reduced to $1$.

examples.result: The interrupt count falls by a factor of $2^{13}$: that is the entire argument for DMA whenever transfers are bulk — the CPU spends the saved time doing useful work instead of fielding interrupts.

keyTakeaways: Von Neumann machines interleave instruction and data access in one memory; the CPU checks for interrupts after every instruction, making the system event-driven.
Device controllers own local buffers and registers; drivers give the OS a uniform interface to them; a memory controller serializes shared-memory access.
The storage hierarchy trades speed for capacity at every level — registers ($0.25$–$0.5$ ns) to magnetic disk (about 5,000,000 ns) — with volatility splitting volatile from nonvolatile levels.
Storage units are powers of two: $2^{10}$ bytes = 1 KB up through $2^{40}$ = 1 TB; networking alone counts bits.
Vectored interrupts dispatch directly by number; handlers must save and restore state; maskable vs nonmaskable lines plus priority levels and chaining complete the modern mechanism.
DMA converts one interrupt per byte into one interrupt per block by giving controllers direct access to main memory — at the cost of some memory-cycle contention.

quiz.q: When does the CPU check for pending interrupts?
options: only when a process blocks for I/O
only when the OS issues a poll request
quiz.explanation: The hardware senses the interrupt-request line after every instruction — that is what lets a device seize the CPU’s attention at any instruction boundary, the property that makes the whole system interrupt-driven.

quiz.q: The interrupt vector exists mainly to:
options: let the interrupt number index a table of service-routine addresses for fast dispatch
mask low-priority interrupts during critical sections
translate virtual addresses to physical addresses
quiz.explanation: A table of pointers indexed by a unique number dispatches straight to the right handler with no polling — essential because interrupts occur very frequently and must be handled quickly.

quiz.q: A nonmaskable interrupt is best described as:
options: an interrupt a device can defer until the CPU is idle
an interrupt reserved for events such as unrecoverable memory errors, which cannot be turned off
any interrupt raised by a disk controller
an interrupt whose handler runs in user mode
quiz.explanation: The two hardware lines split duties: the maskable line serves ordinary devices and can be disabled during critical sequences; the nonmaskable line carries hardware-fault events that must never be ignored.

quiz.q: With DMA, interrupts are generated:
options: one per block transferred, when the operation completes
one per memory cycle, as the controller steals cycles
quiz.explanation: The controller moves the entire block between device and memory on its own and interrupts once at completion — replacing the per-byte interrupt storm that makes interrupt-driven I/O unusable for bulk transfers.

quiz.q: Which ordering lists storage from fastest to slowest?
options: main memory → cache → registers → SSD → HDD
registers → cache → main memory → NVM/SSD → hard-disk drives → optical and tape
cache → registers → main memory → HDD → NVM/SSD → tape
registers → main memory → cache → HDD → NVM/SSD → optical
quiz.explanation: Smaller-and-faster lives closer to the CPU: registers, then cache, then DRAM main memory, then electrical nonvolatile memory, then mechanical disks, with optical and tape as tertiary storage at the bottom.

quiz.q: Under per-byte interrupt-driven I/O each byte raises one interrupt, while DMA raises one interrupt per block. A controller must move an $8\,\text{KB}$ block ($8192$ bytes). How many CPU interrupts occur in each case?
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** block size $8\,\text{KB} = 2^{13} = 8192$ bytes. Per-byte rule: one interrupt per byte. DMA rule: one completion interrupt per block after driver setup.
**Step 2 — Rule:** `per-byte count = number of bytes`, `DMA count = number of blocks`.
**Step 3 — Computation:** per-byte $= 8192$, DMA $= 1$. Setup work (`buffers, pointers, counters`) costs CPU time but raises no interrupt.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** ratio is $\frac{8192}{1} = 8192$, i.e. a factor of $2^{13}$. While the DMA controller moves data, the CPU is free except for memory-cycle contention.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** `$1$ and $1$` ignores per-byte cost; `$1$ and $8192$` swaps the two; `$1024$ and $8$` assumes $1$-KB sub-blocks, which the statement never defines.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** per-byte $8192$ versus DMA $1$ — the entire argument for DMA on bulk transfers.

quiz.q: On a machine with $256$ interrupt vectors, a disk controller raises vector $76$ while user code runs. When is the request sensed, and how is the handler located?
options: Only at timer ticks, by polling every device in turn
Only when the running process blocks, via the process table
After the current instruction, by indexing the vector table with $76$
Before the next fetch, by scanning main memory for the controller address
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** vector number $76$, CPU in user mode, $256$-entry table of handler addresses.
**Step 2 — Rule:** hardware senses the request line after each instruction; the vector number indexes the table directly, so dispatch costs one lookup.
**Step 3 — Trace:** CPU finishes the current instruction, reads $76$, jumps to `table[76]`. The handler saves state it will clobber, services the device, restores state, and executes return-from-interrupt.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** requirements met are deferral during critical sections, efficient dispatch via the table, and multilevel priorities letting urgent vectors preempt routine ones.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** polling contradicts vectoring; process-table lookup confuses interrupts with scheduling; memory scanning describes polling, not vectored dispatch.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** sense after each instruction, dispatch by `table[76]`.

depth.title: Coherence, Amdahl and the cost of sharing

blocks.body: Symmetric multiprocessing works only because the caches cooperate. Each core's private cache holds a copy of lines whose home is main memory, so a write in one cache must become visible to all the others — the **cache-coherence problem**, solved in hardware by a protocol. The workhorse is **MESI**, which labels every cached line with one of four states: **Modified** — this cache holds the only copy and memory's is stale; **Exclusive** — sole copy, memory fresh, writable without telling anyone; **Shared** — read-only replicas may exist elsewhere; **Invalid** — no right to use the line. A core wanting to write a Shared line must first broadcast an invalidation that forces every other copy to Invalid, and a read miss consults the other caches (by snooping a shared bus, or by a directory on larger machines) and may fetch fresh data from a peer's Modified copy. Coherence traffic is a concrete reason the book's speed-up is strictly below $N$: the protocol itself consumes interconnect bandwidth — the very resource the extra cores were bought to provide.

blocks.heading: Amdahl's law, derived
blocks.body: Take a workload whose one-processor execution time is $T$, and suppose a fraction $p$ of that work runs in parallel on $n$ processors while the fraction $1 - p$ is inherently serial — coordination, lock contention, sequential phases. On $n$ processors the parallel part shrinks by $n$ and the serial part does not: $$T_n = (1 - p)T + \frac{pT}{n}.$$ Speed-up is the ratio of the times, $$S(n) = \frac{T}{T_n} = \frac{1}{(1 - p) + p/n},$$ and this single fraction governs everything. Two limits: at $n = 1$ the formula consistently returns $S = 1$, and as processors grow without bound, $$\lim_{n \to \infty} S(n) = \frac{1}{1 - p},$$ so the serial fraction alone caps the machine. Worked numbers: with $p = 0.9$, one hundred processors yields $S = 1/(0.1 + 0.009) \approx 9.2$ — nine percent efficiency — and even infinitely many processors never exceed $10$. One serial tenth outweighs a hundred cores; this is the quantitative form of the section's warning that speed-up with $N$ processors is strictly less than $N$.

Two threads write disjoint variables, yet the caches fight as if they shared them: when the variables land in the **same 64-byte cache line**, each write flips the line to Modified in one cache and Invalid in the other, and the line ping-pongs across the interconnect on nearly every store. This is **false sharing** — no data race exists, the program is logically correct, and performance collapses anyway, sometimes by an order of magnitude, for a reason invisible in the source: it depends on the allocator's byte-level placement. The cures — padding structures to line boundaries, per-CPU counters — are the same locality discipline that NUMA demands on a larger scale, and the diagnosis is always the same: the unit of hardware sharing is the line, not the variable.

NUMA turns a hardware asymmetry into an operating-system obligation. In a cache-coherent NUMA machine every processor can address all memory, but at different costs: **local** memory answers over a fast local bus in roughly a hundred nanoseconds, while **remote** memory crosses the interconnect at a multiple of that, and a line held Modified on another node must be fetched from that node, not from memory. The hardware guarantees correctness — only performance differs — so the operating system must supply the discipline. Its tools are **first-touch placement**, allocating a page on the node whose thread first faults it in; **scheduler affinity**, keeping a thread and its memory together at the cost of load-balancing freedom; and, in extremis, **page migration**, moving hot pages toward their users. A scheduling decision and an allocation decision that were independent on a desktop become one decision on a server — and the NUMA penalty is the fee for getting it wrong.

The architecture menu of this section is a latency-versus-failure trade. Inside one chip, cores communicate through shared memory at cache speed — tens of nanoseconds — with hardware coherence keeping them consistent; but the whole machine shares one fate, since a single power fault, memory error, or kernel panic stops every core at once. Across a cluster, nodes share nothing physically; communication is an explicit message over Ethernet or InfiniBand costing microseconds — a hundred to a thousand times a cache hit — but a node's failure is an event the survivors can absorb, which is precisely the high-availability argument for clustering, and the reason a parallel database needs a distributed lock manager where a shared-memory machine would need a mutex. Coherence makes sharing cheap and failure fatal; message passing makes failure survivable and sharing expensive. The industry accordingly built its largest systems as clusters of multicore NUMA machines, and left the operating system to manage every layer of the compromise at once.

depth.title: Scaling the kernel itself

blocks.body: When processors numbered in the tens, kernels stopped scaling before applications did, and the research response was a definitional insight. Clements and colleagues (SOSP 2013) formulated the **commutativity rule**: when the results of a set of operations do not depend on their order — when the operations **commute** — the operating system can implement them so that concurrent executions do not interfere, do not contend on shared cache lines, and therefore scale on any number of cores. The rule is powerful in contrapositive use: compute which system calls commute under which conditions, and you have identified exactly the interface changes that make the kernel a bottleneck. Applying it to Linux — scalable statistics, PID allocation, file-system timestamp handling — produced a modified kernel that scaled nearly linearly on 80 cores where the stock kernel saturated. The deeper point belongs to this chapter: the resource manager must itself scale, and scalability turns out to be a property of the interface, not only of the implementation beneath it.

blocks.heading: RCU: reads that scale without limit
blocks.body: Linux's most consequential scalability mechanism rarely appears in architecture textbooks, yet it is a large part of why the kernel survives machines with thousands of cores. **Read-copy-update** lets readers traverse shared structures — routing tables, file-descriptor tables, security policies — with no locks, no atomic instructions, and no writes to shared memory: a reader announces itself, follows pointers, and is guaranteed that everything it saw stays valid for the duration. Writers make a private copy, modify it, and swing a single pointer to publish; the old version is reclaimed only after a **grace period** proves that every pre-existing reader has finished. Read-mostly workloads therefore scale without bound, and most kernel traffic on a large server is read-mostly. The costs are subtle — writers queue, reclamation is deferred, the API demands strict read-side discipline — but RCU demonstrates that the contention predicted by naive sharing arguments is a property of the implementation, not a law of hardware.

blocks.heading: Can kernels be fully non-blocking?
blocks.body: The endgame of this research line is a kernel with no locks. **Lock-free** data structures guarantee that some thread makes progress in a bounded number of steps even if every other thread is suspended mid-operation; **wait-free** structures guarantee it of every thread. Both are immune to priority inversion, deadlock, and preemption-induced stalls — which is exactly why they matter in kernels, the one place a stalled thread cannot simply be paged out or killed. Lock-free lists, queues and hash tables have accumulated since the 1990s, but the whole-system problem remains open: allocators, garbage collectors, and the scheduler itself resist the lock-free treatment, and non-blocking algorithms often lose their advantage under precisely the high-contention conditions that motivate them, flooding the coherence fabric with invalidations. Whether a complete operating system can be non-blocking, or whether some kernel structures are irreducibly serial — and which definition of progress a kernel should even promise — remain unsettled questions.

intro: Organizing many processors into one computer — or many computers into one system — is the architect’s response to the end of easy single-CPU speedups. This section tours the taxonomy: multiprocessors and multicore chips, NUMA machines, blades, clusters and fully distributed systems, each trading coupling against scalability.
objectives: Define single-processor systems and explain why special-purpose processors do not make one multiprocessor
Compare SMP, multicore and NUMA organizations, including their memory-access properties
Explain why the industry pivoted from faster single cores to more cores (power and memory walls)
Distinguish asymmetric, symmetric and parallel clustering, and the role of SANs
Characterize distributed systems and their LAN/WAN networking substrate

concepts.statement: A **single-processor system** has one general-purpose CPU with a single processing **core** — the component that executes instructions and holds local registers. Such systems may still contain **special-purpose processors** (disk, keyboard, graphics controllers) that run limited instruction sets and do **not** run processes.
concepts.detail: Some special-purpose processors are managed by the OS — a disk-controller microprocessor keeps its own disk queue and scheduling algorithm — while others are autonomous hardware components the OS cannot even address. By the book’s definition, special-purpose processors do not turn a single-processor system into a multiprocessor; and by that same definition, very few contemporary systems are single-processor systems at all.

concepts.statement: A **multiprocessor system** has two or more processors sharing the computer **bus** and sometimes the **clock, memory and peripheral devices** — a uniform memory access (UMA) design. Its primary advantage is **increased throughput**: more work done in less time. The most common form is **symmetric multiprocessing (SMP)**, where each peer CPU performs all tasks, including operating-system functions and user processes; asymmetric designs instead assign each processor a fixed role under a master.
concepts.detail: In an SMP machine every CPU has its own register set and a private (local) cache, but all share physical memory over the system bus — $N$ CPUs can run $N$ processes without significant deterioration. The speed-up ratio with $N$ cooperating processors is **less than $N$**: keeping the parts working correctly plus contention for shared resources eats into the gain. Processors should share certain data structures so the OS can dynamically balance workload among them — carefully written, as Chapters 5 and 6 demand.

concepts.statement: **Multicore** means multiple computing cores reside on a single chip. It is more efficient than multiple single-core chips because **on-chip communication is faster than between-chip communication**, and one multicore chip **uses significantly less power** — vital for mobile devices and laptops. A typical dual-core design gives each core its own registers and local **level-1 (L1) cache** while sharing an on-chip **level-2 (L2) cache**; a multicore processor with $N$ cores appears to the OS as **$N$ standard CPUs**.
concepts.detail: Vocabulary the book fixes: the **CPU** is the hardware that executes instructions, a **processor** is a physical chip containing one or more CPUs, a **core** is the basic computation unit of the CPU, **multicore** puts multiple cores on the same CPU and **multiprocessor** means multiple processors. All modern operating systems — Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS — support multicore SMP.

concepts.term: Why not a faster single core?
concepts.statement: The industry stopped chasing single-core clock speed because dynamic power scales as $P \approx C V^{2} f$: raising frequency $f$ forces voltage $V$ up too, so power grows super-linearly and the chip overheats — the **power wall**. Since the mid-2000s, transistor budgets (still doubling per Moore’s Law) have gone instead into multiple modestly-clocked cores.
concepts.detail: A second wall is **memory latency**: a lone fast core stalls on DRAM accesses that have barely improved, while several cores with on-chip caches can overlap compute and memory waits. This is why the historical pivot — associated with Intel abandoning its push toward ever-higher clock rates in favor of dual- and quad-core designs — happened: parallelism delivers performance that frequency no longer can.

concepts.statement: In a **NUMA** system each CPU (or group) gets **local memory accessed via a small, fast local bus**, while the CPUs share one physical address space through a **shared system interconnect**. Local access is fast and free of contention; **remote access** — CPU 0 reaching into CPU 3’s local memory — suffers increased latency across the interconnect.
concepts.detail: The benefit is scalability: adding CPUs no longer bottlenecks on a single shared bus, which is why NUMA dominates servers and high-performance computing. The drawback — the NUMA penalty — is mitigated by careful **CPU scheduling and memory management** that keep a process and its data close together on one node (revisited in the scheduling and virtual-memory chapters).

concepts.statement: A **blade server** places multiple **processor boards, I/O boards and networking boards in the same chassis**. The difference from a traditional multiprocessor is that **each blade-processor board boots independently and runs its own operating system** — in essence, multiple independent multiprocessor systems in one box.
concepts.detail: Some blade boards are themselves multiprocessors, blurring the taxonomy further: the blade chassis consolidates power, cooling and networking for what are logically separate computers.

concepts.statement: A **cluster** gathers two or more individual systems (**nodes**, each typically multicore) joined by a LAN or a faster interconnect such as **InfiniBand** and **sharing storage** — a **loosely coupled** multiprocessor. Clustering mainly provides **high-availability service**: redundancy lets the system survive a node failure. In **asymmetric clustering** one machine is a **hot-standby** monitoring the active server; in **symmetric clustering** two or more hosts run applications and monitor each other.
concepts.detail: A monitoring node that sees its peer fail can **take ownership of its storage and restart its applications** — users see only a brief interruption. Systems that keep providing service proportional to surviving hardware **degrade gracefully**; fault-tolerant systems go further and survive any single component failure. **Parallel clusters** let multiple hosts access the same data on shared storage, requiring a **distributed lock manager (DLM)** to prevent conflicting operations — Oracle Real Application Cluster is the book’s example. **Storage-area networks (SANs)** allow many systems to attach to a pool of storage, so any host can take over an application whose data lives on the SAN.

concepts.statement: A **distributed system** is a collection of **physically separate, possibly heterogeneous computer systems networked** to give users access to the resources the system maintains — increasing computation speed, functionality, data availability and reliability. Nodes have **no shared memory or clock**: they communicate by messages over the network.
concepts.detail: Networks are characterized by distance: a **LAN** connects computers within a room, building or campus; a **WAN** links buildings, cities or countries; metropolitan-area networks (MAN) and personal-area networks (PAN — Bluetooth, 802.11) fill the gaps. **TCP/IP** is the dominant protocol and the foundation of the Internet. A **network operating system** leaves nodes autonomous (aware of the network, exchanging messages and files); a **distributed operating system** communicates closely enough to create the illusion of a single OS controlling the network.

examples.title: Choosing an architecture for four workloads
examples.problem: Match each requirement to the most appropriate architecture: (a) an office desktop, (b) a large database server needing dozens of CPUs, (c) a web service that must survive machine failure, (d) a chassis of independent multiprocessor boards.

steps.label: Step 1: The desktop
steps.text: A single multicore chip suffices — one processor, several cores, private L1 plus shared L2 caches; the OS sees the cores as standard CPUs and schedules across them.

steps.label: Step 2: The big database server
steps.text: A shared bus saturates as CPUs multiply, so choose NUMA: each processor group gets fast local memory over a local bus, one shared interconnect preserves a single address space, and the OS scheduler keeps work near its data.

steps.label: Step 3: The fault-tolerant web service
steps.text: Cluster several nodes over InfiniBand with storage on a SAN — any surviving host can take ownership of the storage and restart the application if one node dies.

steps.label: Step 4: The dense chassis
steps.text: Blade servers: each board boots its own OS independently, so one chassis hosts many separate multiprocessor systems sharing only power, cooling and the network.

examples.result: Each design answers a different scaling question — more cores per chip, more CPUs per machine, more machines per service — and each changes what the operating system must manage.

examples.title: Failover in an asymmetric cluster
examples.problem: A two-node cluster runs a database. Walk through what happens when the active node fails.

steps.label: Step 1: Normal operation
steps.text: Node A runs the database serving clients; node B is in hot-standby mode, doing nothing but monitoring A over the network.

steps.label: Step 2: Failure detection
steps.text: A crashes. B’s monitoring detects that A has stopped responding — this is the trigger for high-availability logic.

steps.label: Step 3: Take ownership
steps.text: B takes ownership of A’s storage (held on a SAN visible to both nodes) and restarts the database application there.

steps.label: Step 4: Service continues
steps.text: Clients reconnect and see only a brief interruption of service — redundancy converted a machine failure into a hiccup instead of an outage.

examples.result: Asymmetric clustering trades an idle machine for availability; symmetric clustering would instead have both nodes serving traffic and monitoring each other — more efficient, but it requires that more than one application be available to run.

keyTakeaways: Only general-purpose CPUs count toward ‘multiprocessor’; device-specific processors do not run processes.
Multiprocessing buys throughput, but speed-up with $N$ processors is strictly less than $N$ — coordination overhead and shared-resource contention take their cut.
Multicore puts cores on one chip: on-chip communication is faster and power use far lower than multiple single-core chips; the OS simply sees $N$ CPUs.
The single-core era ended at the power wall ($P \approx C V^{2} f$) and the memory wall; Moore’s-Law transistors now fund cores, not clocks.
NUMA scales by giving each CPU local memory on a local bus — remote access pays a latency penalty that scheduling and placement must minimize.
Clusters are loosely coupled nodes sharing storage (often via SANs) for high availability: hot-standby (asymmetric) or mutual (symmetric) monitoring; parallel clusters add a distributed lock manager.
Distributed systems join autonomous, heterogeneous machines by network (LAN/WAN) with no shared memory or clock — messaging is the only glue.

quiz.q: With $N$ processors cooperating on a workload, the expected speed-up is:
options: less than $N$ because of coordination overhead and contention for shared resources
independent of the number of processors
quiz.explanation: Keeping cooperating parts correct plus contention for shared resources lowers the gain below the processor count — the book’s caution against naive linear-scaling expectations.

quiz.q: In a NUMA system, a CPU accessing memory local to a different CPU:
options: is impossible — address spaces are private
pays higher latency because the access crosses the system interconnect
is faster than local access due to caching
causes the OS to migrate the process immediately
quiz.explanation: NUMA keeps one shared physical address space, but remote accesses must traverse the system interconnect — the NUMA penalty the OS fights with careful scheduling and memory placement.

quiz.q: Asymmetric clustering is characterized by:
options: all nodes running applications and monitoring each other
one machine in hot-standby mode while another runs the applications
each node running its own operating system on its own board
nodes sharing a single physical memory bus
quiz.explanation: The hot-standby host does nothing but monitor the active server and takes over when it fails; when both hosts run applications and watch each other, that is symmetric clustering.

quiz.q: Which statement about blade servers is correct?
options: all blades share one operating system
each blade-processor board boots independently and runs its own operating system
blades are another name for NUMA nodes
blades cannot be multiprocessor systems themselves
quiz.explanation: A blade chassis holds multiple processor, I/O and networking boards that are independent computers — and some blades are themselves multiprocessors, blurring the categories.

quiz.q: A system where nodes keep separate memories and clocks and communicate only by network messages is:
quiz.explanation: Distributed systems are physically separate, possibly heterogeneous computers joined by a network — no shared memory or clock, only message passing; SMP, multicore and blades all share hardware within one machine or chassis.

depth.title: Protection and the timer lease

blocks.body: Dual-mode operation deserves a more precise statement than a pair of names. The hardware partitions its instruction set into **unprivileged instructions**, whose effects are confined to the executing program's own registers and memory, and **privileged instructions** — I/O, timer programming, interrupt control, halt, and mode switching itself — whose effects reach beyond one program. The **mode bit** is the single hardware state that gates the class. Together they define the kernel as a **protection domain**: a body of code and data whose integrity does not depend on the good behavior of anything outside it, and they define the **trusted computing base** as everything that must be correct for the domain to hold. The design test is sharp in both directions. Any instruction that can affect another program must be privileged, or protection fails outright; and every privilege the kernel genuinely needs must correspond to some instruction, or the kernel cannot do its work. Interrupts and traps are then the only doors into the domain — and the hardware, not the kernel, is the gatekeeper.

Walk one system call in full detail, because the details are where the security lives. On x86-64, the user library places the call number and arguments in registers and executes `syscall`. The hardware — not software — then does several things atomically: it saves the return address and flags into scratch registers, raises the privilege level to kernel mode, loads the instruction pointer from a model-specific register the kernel configured at boot, and switches the stack pointer to a per-CPU kernel stack, because the user stack is neither trusted nor safely accessible at this point. Execution resumes at the kernel's entry code, which saves the remaining registers and validates the request: the call number must be in range, and every user-supplied pointer must be checked against the user portion of the address space — the kernel cannot simply dereference a user pointer, because a hostile caller would then hand it kernel addresses to read or write. Only then does it dispatch through the system-call table. The return path mirrors the entry: registers restored, `sysret` drops the mode bit, and the instruction after the call continues as if nothing had happened.

Why does cooperative multitasking — programs calling a `yield` function when they are feeling polite — fail? The starvation argument: system correctness then rests on the assumption that **every** program yields within bounded time, and that assumption is unfalsifiable for binary code you did not write. One infinite loop — a bug, not even an act of malice — freezes every other program, the scheduler, and the operating system itself, because the OS never executes again; no priority scheme, however sophisticated, can act on a machine that never runs it. The timer changes the grammar of CPU ownership from gift to **lease**. Before entering user mode, the kernel loads the timer with the quantum; if the lease expires, the hardware interrupts at the next instruction boundary, custody reverts to the kernel, and it either extends the lease or evicts the tenant. Timesharing, and every interactive system since, exists because of this one asymmetry: the hardware will always interrupt a program that never yields.

The control question returns one level up: can the **kernel itself** be preempted while executing a system call? In a **non-preemptive kernel**, a system call runs to completion, so a slow disk operation, a page fault, or a thousand-element copy inside the kernel blocks every higher-priority thread on that CPU — interrupts may still fire, but they cannot cause a context switch inside kernel mode. A **preemptive kernel** allows exactly that: it maintains reentrant data structures, guards them with explicit locks, and becomes preemptible at nearly every instruction boundary. Linux's long migration from voluntary preemption to `PREEMPT` and then `PREEMPT_RT` — where even spinlocks become sleeping locks — is decades of converting the kernel's implicit non-preemption assumptions into explicit, audited locking discipline. And for the systems that cannot trust even that, the **watchdog timer** — hardware that resets the machine unless software periodically proves liveness by patting it — assumes the kernel itself may hang, and converts total software failure into a reboot.

blocks.heading: Scheduling latency, by the numbers
blocks.body: An audio thread wakes when each packet arrives every $10$ ms and must begin running within $3$ ms, or the listener hears a gap. Is the machine safe? On a non-preemptive kernel it depends on luck: the thread can be dispatched only when the CPU returns from kernel mode, and a colleague's uncached disk read can spend $8$ ms executing inside a system call on another process's behalf — the deadline expires before the scheduler ever gets a vote, and no priority assignment fixes this, because the stuck component is the kernel itself. On a preemptive kernel the same wake-up preempts in-kernel execution: the worst case shrinks to the longest interval with preemption disabled — a critical section of tens of microseconds — plus context-switch cost, comfortably inside the $3$ ms budget. The lesson generalizes: real-time behavior is never about the average case, it is about the worst thing the kernel can be doing at the moment the deadline arrives.

depth.title: Scheduling theory and its limits

blocks.heading: Optimality of EDF
blocks.body: Consider a single processor and a finite collection of independent, preemptable jobs, each with a release time, an execution requirement, and a deadline. **Earliest-deadline-first** (EDF) — at every instant, execute the released unfinished job with the earliest deadline — is **optimal** for this model: if any algorithm produces a schedule in which every job meets its deadline, then EDF does too. The guarantee concerns feasibility only; EDF says nothing about response time, fairness, or any other quality measure, and optimality can fail silently outside the model — with nonpreemptable jobs, shared resources, or multiple processors.

Suppose a feasible schedule $A$ exists, and compare it with the EDF schedule $E$. Take the earliest time $t$ at which $A$ runs a job $J_L$ whose deadline is **later** than that of some available unfinished job $J_E$ — the only way $A$ can disagree with EDF's choice. Feasibility of $A$ means $J_E$ executes at some later point $u$, and since $J_L$'s deadline is no earlier than $J_E$'s, running $J_L$ at time $u$ instead still meets $J_L$'s deadline. Exchange the two executions: run $J_E$ during $t$ and $J_L$ during $u$, leaving every job's total execution unchanged. Both jobs still meet their deadlines — $J_E$ completes no later than before, and $J_L$ completes within a deadline at least as late as the one $J_E$ satisfied. Each such exchange strictly reduces the number of instants at which the schedule disagrees with EDF, and a finite schedule admits only finitely many disagreements, so iterating produces a schedule that follows EDF at every instant and misses no deadline.

blocks.heading: Liu–Layland utilization bound
blocks.body: For $n$ independent periodic tasks on one preemptive processor, where task $i$ has worst-case execution time $C_i$, period $T_i$, and relative deadline equal to its period, let the utilization be $$U = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{C_i}{T_i}.$$ If $$U \le n\left(2^{1/n} - 1\right),$$ then the **rate-monotonic** priority assignment — static priorities ordered inversely to period — meets every deadline of every task. The constant is the best possible for fixed priorities: task sets with utilization just above the bound exist that no fixed-priority scheduler can schedule, whereas **earliest-deadline-first** remains feasible all the way to its exact bound $U \le 1$ when deadlines equal periods. The bound decreases in $n$ toward $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$: hard real-time analysis deliberately idles roughly a third of a uniprocessor.

The argument rests on the **critical instant** theorem of Liu and Layland: a task's response time is maximized when it is released simultaneously with every higher-priority task, because any delay in interference can only push work later, never earlier. It therefore suffices to analyze the fully synchronous release. Fix the lowest-priority task and count the demand its first job competes with over one of its periods; the system is schedulable exactly when every such window's demand fits inside it. The extremal case makes every inequality tight — each higher-priority task's work finishes precisely at the release of the next — which forces the task parameters into a geometric progression whose common ratio is $2^{1/n}$; summing that construction's utilization yields exactly $U = n(2^{1/n} - 1)$, and a matching infeasible instance exists just above the bound, so no fixed-priority scheme can guarantee more. EDF's stronger bound follows from optimality plus the observation that, with deadlines equal to periods, no interval's demand can exceed its length when total utilization is at most one — and by optimality, if EDF misses a deadline, every algorithm does.

blocks.heading: Where scheduling theory runs out
blocks.body: The theorems above form a complete uniprocessor story — and little of it survives contact with what real systems actually face. First, the **online** problem: release times and execution requirements are rarely known in advance, and competitive analysis is unforgiving — for total flow time, no online scheduler achieves any bounded competitive ratio on a standard-speed processor, while a modest speedup (the $(1 + \epsilon)$-speed resource-augmentation results of Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs) restores $O(1/\epsilon)$-competitive algorithms built on shortest-remaining-processing-time. Theory here is elegant, yet still far from a scheduler anyone would ship. Second, the **multiprocessor** problem: global EDF exhibits the **Dhall effect**, in which task sets of arbitrarily low total utilization miss deadlines under any list scheduler that greedily runs earliest-deadline jobs; partitioning tasks onto cores is itself bin-packing and NP-hard; and the strongest utilization bounds known for identical multiprocessors are dramatically weaker than the uniprocessor ones. Whether one clean, practical, optimal real-time scheduler for many cores exists — global, federated, or something not yet invented — remains a genuinely open question.

intro: An operating system is interrupt-driven: after boot it does nothing but wait for events.
