Making that safe for untrusted user programs requires hardware support — a mode bit that separates user from kernel, privileged instructions, and a timer that guarantees the OS always regains control. Multiprogramming and timesharing are what the machinery is for.
objectives: Describe the bootstrap sequence and the event-driven (interrupt/trap) nature of OS operation
Explain multiprogramming, the job pool, degree of multiprogramming and CPU utilization
Distinguish timesharing/multitasking from multiprogramming, including time slices and interactive response
Trace dual-mode transitions with the mode bit, and list which instructions are privileged
Compute timer interrupt intervals from clock rate and counter size

concepts.statement: At power-up or reboot the computer runs an initial **bootstrap program** stored in firmware (EEPROM) — it initializes all aspects of the system, locates the **operating-system kernel, and loads it into memory**. Once the kernel runs, it starts system programs as **system daemons** (on Linux the first is **systemd**) and then **sits quietly waiting for something to happen** — events are almost always signaled by an **interrupt**.
concepts.detail: A **trap** (or exception) is a software-generated interrupt, caused either by an **error** (division by zero, invalid memory access) or by a specific user request for an OS service — the **system call**. With no processes to run, no devices to service and no users waiting, the kernel simply idles until hardware or software raises an event.

concepts.statement: **Multiprogramming** increases CPU utilization by keeping **several processes in memory simultaneously** and switching the CPU to another process whenever the current one must wait (for I/O, say). As long as at least one process needs to execute, **the CPU is never idle**.
concepts.detail: The OS picks from a **job pool** of waiting programs when deciding what to load into memory; the number of processes resident in memory is the **degree of multiprogramming**. Motivation: a single program cannot in general keep the CPU or its devices busy — the book’s analogy is a lawyer who, with enough clients, is never idle while one case waits for trial. Memory management, CPU scheduling, synchronization and file systems all become mandatory once multiprogramming begins.

concepts.statement: **Timesharing** is the logical extension of multiprogramming in which switches occur **frequently**, giving each user or process a **time slice** of the CPU and producing fast **interactive response**. Interactive I/O runs at ‘people speeds’ — seven characters per second is fast typing for humans but glacial for a CPU — so the OS switches rather than idles.
concepts.detail: A common method for ensuring reasonable response time is **virtual memory**, letting processes execute even when not fully resident and abstracting memory into a large, uniform array (Chapters 9–10). The book uses the term *multitasking* for this design; the mechanism demands CPU scheduling (Chapter 5), and every chapter afterward on files, protection, synchronization and deadlock services this basic organization.

concepts.statement: To ensure an incorrect or malicious program cannot harm other programs or the OS, hardware distinguishes **user mode** from **kernel mode** (also called supervisor, system or privileged mode). A **mode bit** — **kernel = 0, user = 1** — records the current mode. The system boots in kernel mode, switches to user mode before passing control to a user program, and flips to kernel mode on **every trap or interrupt**.
concepts.detail: The mode transitions: user process executing → system call → trap (bit set to 0, kernel executes the call) → return (bit set to 1, user resumes). At boot the hardware starts in kernel mode and the OS starts user applications in user mode, so the OS always gains control in kernel mode. CPUs extend the idea beyond two modes: Intel processors have four **protection rings** (ring 0 kernel, ring 3 user, rings 1–2 rarely used), ARMv8 systems have seven modes, and virtualization-capable CPUs add a **VMM mode** with privileges between user and kernel.

concepts.statement: Instructions that may cause harm are designated **privileged** and execute **only in kernel mode** — if attempted in user mode, the hardware does not execute them but treats them as **illegal and traps them to the operating system**. The canonical examples: switching to kernel mode, **I/O control**, **timer management**, and **interrupt management** (turning interrupts off).
concepts.detail: This is the enforcement half of dual-mode operation: the kernel can touch devices, halt the CPU and reprogram the timer; a user program cannot. Errors that violate modes — illegal instructions, accesses outside the user’s address space — trap to the OS, which may terminate the program abnormally with an error message and possibly a dump of the program’s memory to a file for later analysis.

concepts.term: The system call as a mode switch
concepts.statement: A **system call** is the method a process uses to request action by the OS: usually a **trap to a specific location in the interrupt vector**, executed by a generic trap instruction or a dedicated **syscall** instruction. The hardware treats it as a **software interrupt** — control passes through the vector to a service routine, the mode bit is set to kernel, the kernel examines the call and parameters, verifies they are legal, executes the request, and returns to the instruction following the call.
concepts.detail: Note carefully: the **process itself** makes the transition — a system call is a **mode switch within the calling process**, not a separate process. Parameters travel in registers, on the stack, or in a memory block whose address is passed in registers. Windows, UNIX and Linux all take advantage of dual-mode protection this way.

concepts.statement: The OS must never lose the CPU to a user program stuck in an infinite loop, so hardware provides a **timer** that can be set to interrupt after a specified period — fixed (for example, $1/60$ second) or variable. A variable timer is implemented by a **fixed-rate clock and a counter** the OS loads; each tick decrements the counter, and when it **reaches 0 an interrupt occurs**. Setting the timer is a **privileged instruction**.
concepts.detail: A 10-bit counter driven by a 1-millisecond clock allows interrupts at intervals from 1 ms to $2^{10} = 1024$ ms, in steps of 1 ms. Before turning control over to a user program, the OS ensures the timer is set — if it fires, control transfers automatically back to the OS, which may grant more time or treat the program as stuck. On Linux the kernel parameter **HZ** sets the interrupt frequency (HZ = 250 means 250 interrupts per second, one every 4 ms), and the variable **jiffies** counts timer interrupts since boot.

examples.title: A system call from user to kernel and back
examples.problem: A C program calls read(fd, buf, 4096). Trace the complete mode transition.

steps.label: Step 1: User mode
steps.text: The process executes in user mode (mode bit = 1) when the run-time library routine places the arguments in registers and issues the trap instruction carrying read’s system-call number.

steps.label: Step 2: The trap
steps.text: The hardware treats the trap as a software interrupt: the mode bit flips to 0 and control passes through the interrupt vector to the system-call service routine.

steps.label: Step 3: Kernel-side validation
steps.text: The kernel examines the interrupting instruction to determine which call occurred, then verifies the parameters — is fd a valid open file? Is buf a legal address in this process’s space? Is the length sane?

steps.label: Step 4: Execution
steps.text: The kernel performs the I/O — the request may block the process until data arrives, in which case the scheduler runs another process meanwhile.

steps.label: Step 5: Return
steps.text: Results and status return to the caller, the mode bit is set back to 1, and execution resumes at the instruction following the system call — same process throughout.

examples.result: One trap, two mode transitions, zero process switches: the system call is the controlled doorway from user code into kernel code.

examples.title: Programming the timer
examples.problem: A system needs timer interrupts every 250 ms, and a second configuration needs intervals up to 2 seconds. The hardware is a 1-millisecond clock with a 10-bit counter. What counter values work, and what are the limits?

steps.label: Step 1: The mechanism
steps.text: A fixed-rate clock ticks every 1 ms; each tick decrements the counter; zero triggers the interrupt. So the interval equals the initial counter value in milliseconds.

steps.label: Step 2: The 250 ms requirement
steps.text: Load the counter with 250 — it reaches 0 after 250 ticks, i.e., 250 ms.

steps.label: Step 3: The range of the 10-bit counter
steps.text: Ten bits hold values from 1 to $2^{10} = 1024$, so intervals run from 1 ms to 1024 ms in 1-ms steps — 250 ms fits comfortably.

steps.label: Step 4: The 2-second requirement
steps.text: 2000 ms exceeds $2^{10}$, so a 10-bit counter cannot produce it directly: the OS needs a larger counter (more bits) or chains two timer interrupts to reach 2 seconds.

examples.result: The 10-bit, 1-ms timer spans exactly 1–1024 ms; anything longer requires wider hardware or software assistance — and only the kernel, via the privileged instruction, may load the counter at all.

keyTakeaways: After bootstrap loads the kernel and starts daemons (systemd on Linux), the OS is purely event-driven — interrupts and traps are the only things that wake it.
Multiprogramming keeps several processes resident so the CPU never idles; the job pool feeds memory and the degree of multiprogramming sets how many run.
Timesharing switches so frequently that interaction feels instant; virtual memory extends usable memory to keep response reasonable.
The mode bit (kernel = 0, user = 1) plus privileged instructions (I/O, timer, interrupt control, mode switch) are the hardware foundation of protection.
A system call is a trap — a mode switch inside the calling process, not a new process: parameters in registers, stack, or a memory block.
The timer guarantees control returns: with a 1-ms clock, a 10-bit counter yields intervals from 1 ms to $2^{10} = 1024$ ms; loading it is privileged.

quiz.q: The mode bit reads 0 while code executes. Which mode and privilege apply?
options: kernel mode — privileged instructions may execute
user mode — no instructions are restricted
quiz.explanation: The convention assigns 0 to kernel (supervisor) mode: there the hardware permits privileged instructions; in user mode (bit = 1) attempting one traps to the OS.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a privileged instruction?
options: set the value of the timer
switch from user to kernel mode
quiz.explanation: Reading the clock harms nothing, so it stays unprivileged; setting the timer, disabling interrupts and performing the mode switch all let a program seize or blind the machine, so only the kernel may issue them.

quiz.q: The best description of a system call is:
options: a new process created by the kernel to service the request
a trap that switches the calling process from user mode to kernel mode
a hardware interrupt raised by a device controller
a message sent from one process to a daemon
quiz.explanation: The system call runs inside the calling process: the trap instruction flips the mode bit, dispatches through the interrupt vector to the OS’s service routine, and returns to the very next instruction — no second process exists.

quiz.q: The timer’s central purpose is to:
options: guarantee the OS regains control of the CPU from user programs
quiz.explanation: Without a timer a program stuck in an infinite loop would never return control; the timer interrupt fires and hands the CPU back, which is also exactly what makes timesharing possible.

quiz.q: Multiprogramming exists primarily to:
options: let several users share one keyboard
increase CPU utilization by switching to another process when one waits
protect memory with the mode bit
quiz.explanation: A single program cannot keep CPU and devices busy; by keeping several processes in memory and switching on waits, the CPU is never idle while runnable work exists.

depth.title: Kernel architectures and virtualization

blocks.body: The chapter gestures at kernel structure; here are the architectures by name. A **monolithic kernel** — Linux and the traditional UNIX design — keeps the whole system in one privileged address space: scheduler, file systems, networking, and drivers cooperating through ordinary function calls. The design is fast, because no boundary is ever crossed, and structurally undisciplined, because any subsystem can corrupt any other. A **microkernel** — Mach, QNX, MINIX 3, seL4 — demotes everything but inter-process communication, basic scheduling, and memory mapping to **user-space servers**: a file access becomes a message to a server process, so a buggy or malicious driver crashes only itself and can be restarted like any failed process. The cost is the boundary itself — what was a function call becomes a trap, two context switches, and a message copy. **Hybrid kernels** — Windows NT, Apple's XNU — adopt the microkernel's organization and the monolith's performance: NT's executive and XNU's BSD layer run in kernel mode atop a Mach-derived core, giving most of the call speed of a monolith with some of the layering of a microkernel.

blocks.heading: The price of a message
blocks.body: Quantify the microkernel penalty. A local procedure call costs a handful of instructions — a few nanoseconds. A cross-address-space message on the same machine costs, at minimum, a trap into the kernel, a thread switch to the server, and the same pair for the reply: $$C_{\text{IPC}} \;\ge\; 2\,C_{\text{trap}} + 2\,C_{\text{switch}} + 2\,C_{\text{copy}}.$$ With 1990s measurements — a trap near $1\,\mu\text{s}$ with its cache-cold register traffic, a thread switch of the same order, two message copies — one message costs tens of microseconds against a call's nanoseconds: a gap of four orders of magnitude, multiplied again for every additional server an operation must traverse. This arithmetic is why first-generation microkernels such as Mach were abandoned as slow, and it defines the research program that answered them. The L4 family attacked each term — copies eliminated by mapping message pages instead of copying them, the fast path reduced to a few hundred instructions, switching folded into the trap — until a message cost a small multiple of a system call. The general lesson: boundary crossings, not abstractions, are the tax; measure the crossing, then attack every term.

Two further architectures calibrate the extremes. The **layered** approach — THE operating system of Dijkstra (1968), the founding artifact of structured system design — orders the kernel into strict levels where level $n$ may call only level $n - 1$, so that each layer can be verified against the services of the layer beneath. It is beloved of provers and avoided by builders, for the same reason: real kernels admit no clean total order — the file system needs memory and I/O; I/O needs memory; memory's page faults need the file system — and every boundary crossed on the way down pays the message tax again. The **modular** approach — Solaris, and Linux's **loadable kernel modules** — keeps the monolithic address space but late-binds the components: `insmod` links object code into the running kernel, resolving its symbols at load time, so a driver or file system can be added to a live machine without a reboot. It buys microkernel flexibility at function-call cost, with the honest trade that a loaded module runs at full kernel privilege — protection deferred to code review rather than enforced by hardware.

Architecture choice is, at bottom, a decision about the **trusted computing base** — the set of all components on whose correct behavior the system's guarantees depend. In a monolithic kernel the TCB is the entire kernel image, drivers included, and empirical studies of Windows and Linux crashes have repeatedly attributed a majority of kernel failures to third-party drivers. A microkernel shrinks the TCB toward its IPC core — seL4's is roughly ten thousand lines of C — at the price of running services as swappable, killable, slower user processes. Virtualization complicates the accounting further: in a hosted, type-2 arrangement the host operating system lies inside the TCB of every guest, while a bare-metal, type-1 hypervisor such as ESX or Xen replaces it with a far smaller dedicated core. The TCB is thus the quantity that monolithic speed, microkernel isolation, and hypervisor design are all trading against one another. The question an architect asks is never only whether a design is fast, but what must be *correct* — hardware, kernel, drivers, hypervisor, compiler — for the design's guarantees to hold.

blocks.heading: Popek–Goldberg
blocks.body: A computer can support an effective **virtual machine monitor** exactly when its set of **sensitive instructions** — the instructions whose behavior depends on, or alters, the processor's mode of operation or its machine configuration — is a subset of its set of **privileged instructions**, those that trap when executed in unprivileged mode. An effective VMM is one delivering the three defining properties: **equivalence**, meaning any program under the VMM behaves, apart from timing, as it would on the bare machine; **resource control**, meaning the VMM has complete authority over the hardware's resources and no guest can affect them against its will; and **efficiency**, meaning a statistically dominant fraction of guest instructions execute directly on the hardware, without traps or emulation.

Run the guest kernel with its privilege reduced: the VMM keeps true kernel mode for itself and arranges to receive every trap. When the guest executes a sensitive instruction, its unprivileged execution traps, and the monitor — which owns the trap vector — reads the offending instruction and the state it meant to change, then **emulates** it: the VMM updates its shadow of the machine, the page tables, interrupt masks and device models, so the guest observes exactly the effect its instruction would have had on bare hardware. Equivalence holds because the guest can reach real machine state only through sensitive instructions, and every sensitive instruction traps — every divergence is funneled through the monitor, which corrects it. Resource control holds for the same reason: no real state changes without passing through the monitor. Efficiency holds because ordinary instructions — arithmetic, loads, stores, branches — are neither sensitive nor privileged and need no intervention at all. Conversely, if some sensitive instruction is unprivileged — x86's `sgdt`, which revealed a privileged table's address without trapping, was the canonical offender — then a guest can observe or alter machine state invisibly, equivalence fails, and trap-and-emulate cannot work; such architectures need hardware virtualization assistance — Intel VT-x, AMD SVM — to force those instructions into the monitor.

depth.title: Verified kernels and the leaky contract

blocks.body: Formal verification entered operating systems through the smallest possible target. Klein and colleagues (SOSP 2009) presented **seL4**, a microkernel with a machine-checked **functional correctness** proof: an Isabelle/HOL theorem that the kernel's C implementation refines its abstract specification — that the code does exactly what the high-level design says, for every input and every interleaving. The proof dwarfed the artifact: on the order of ten thousand lemmas across a couple of hundred thousand lines of script, produced by a team that spent years proving what a few engineers had written in months. Stating the guarantee's edges is the interesting part. Proven: functional correctness, and later properties layered on it, such as integrity and authority confinement. Not proven: timing — no execution-time guarantees follow from correctness — and the trusted computing base did not shrink to the kernel alone, because the theorem is conditional on the C semantics, the compiler, the hardware, and the proof checker itself. A verified kernel is a verified link, not a verified chain.

blocks.heading: CompCert: trusting the compiler
blocks.body: The largest hole the seL4 proof left open was the compiler. **CompCert** — Xavier Leroy's verified C compiler, developed in Coq since 2005 — carries a machine-checked theorem of **semantic preservation**: the generated assembly computes exactly what the source language's formal semantics prescribe, for every execution those semantics define. It was the first realistic optimizing compiler — it schedules instructions, allocates registers, rewrites loops — to carry such a proof, overturning the folk belief that verified compilation at that scale was impossible. For operating systems the consequence is a shorter chain of trust: seL4's follow-up work pushed verification down to the binary, showing the compiled machine code refines the kernel specification — the compiler leaves the trusted computing base for verified builds — and CompCert supplies the same guarantee for applications. The template generalizes. Verification composes: the kernel is verified against the language semantics, the compiler against the same semantics, and each proof makes its neighbors' assumptions true — which is precisely how a trustworthy stack is assembled in practice.

Meltdown and Spectre (2018) are filed under security, but they are operating-system-theory results: they show that the user/kernel contract itself leaks. The hardware kept its promise at the instruction-set level — user mode could not read kernel memory — but speculative execution transiently loaded kernel lines into the cache before checking privilege, then rolled back the architectural state while leaving the **microarchitectural** state behind: which lines are cached, and therefore how fast a later access answers. A user program with a timer is a machine that reads the cache, so a transient, supposedly invisible privilege violation became a durable channel into kernel secrets, and Spectre went further, poisoning branch predictors to manufacture the transient window at will. The response — kernel page-table isolation on every context switch, at a measurable cost in cache performance — concedes the deep point: the protection boundary is defined by microarchitecture, not only by the instruction set, and any account of kernel isolation that ignores timing side channels is incomplete. The dual-mode model of this chapter is an approximation that hardware can violate beneath the proofs.

blocks.heading: Capabilities in silicon
blocks.body: Access-control lists ask who may touch this object; **capability systems** invert the question. A capability is an unforgeable token naming an object and a set of rights, and possession is permission — no ambient authority, no global namespace to police. Operating systems have always carried the idea in file descriptors: a descriptor is a capability for exactly one file. **Capsicum** (Watson and colleagues, FreeBSD) built a full capability mode on that insight, letting a program voluntarily shed the ambient authority of the UNIX environment and run sandboxed with only the descriptors it was handed — the design behind Chromium's and macOS's sandboxing layers. The research endgame is **CHERI**: 128-bit pointers that carry bounds and permissions in hardware, making every pointer a capability and giving spatial memory safety to C at near-native speed, with enforcement in silicon rather than in checks the optimizer can elide. Arm's Morello prototype and the pure-capability CHERI UNIX port run real software with the memory-corruption bug class substantially narrowed — the nearest thing to an answer to the question this chapter's protection discussion begs: what if hardware offered granularity finer than two modes?

The third frontier puts a vault inside the attacker's own machine. **Intel SGX** creates **enclaves** — memory regions encrypted on the fly and inaccessible to everything else on the chip, including the operating system, the hypervisor, and even physical probing of DRAM. The OS still schedules and services the enclave, but it cannot read it; and through cryptographic **attestation**, a remote party can verify exactly which code runs inside before sending secrets. **ARM TrustZone** takes the coarser, earlier route: the processor splits into a **secure world** and a **normal world**, each with its own operating system — a small trusted OS beside the main kernel — and hardware gates every world's access to memory and peripherals; the fingerprint matcher and DRM keys in a phone live in the secure world while everything user-facing runs normally. The research lesson cuts both ways. SGX demonstrates that the operating system can itself be the adversary a defense must survive — a complete inversion of this chapter's trust model — and the long catalog of enclave attacks, from cache side channels to voltage glitching to transient-execution leaks, demonstrates again that the boundary lives in microarchitecture as much as in architecture.

intro: The chapter closes with the OS seen as a manager of four resource classes, a defender (protection and security), a multiplicand of hardware (virtualization), and — under the hood — a heavy user of plain data structures: lists, queues, trees, hash maps and bitmaps. Finally it surveys the environments operating systems actually live in, and the free and open-source movement that makes their source code studyable.
objectives: Enumerate the OS’s responsibilities for process, memory, file, storage and I/O management
Distinguish protection from security, and explain user IDs, groups and privilege escalation
Define virtualization and contrast it with emulation
Pick the right kernel data structure — list, stack, queue, tree, hash map or bitmap — with correct complexity
Characterize client–server, peer-to-peer, cloud, embedded, real-time and mobile environments, and differentiate free software from open source (GPL vs BSD licensing)

concepts.term: Resource management: process, memory, file and I/O
concepts.statement: As a **resource manager** the OS manages four big classes. **Process management** (a **process** is a program in execution — the *active* unit of work, where a program is passive): create and delete user and system processes, schedule processes and threads, suspend and resume, and provide synchronization and communication mechanisms. **Memory management**: track which parts of memory are used and by whom, allocate and deallocate, and decide what moves in and out of memory. **File-system management**: create/delete files and directories, map files onto mass storage, back up to stable media. **I/O and mass-storage management**: mount and unmount, free-space management, storage allocation, disk scheduling, partitioning and protection — with the **I/O subsystem** (buffering, caching, spooling, a general device-driver interface) hiding device peculiarities from users.
concepts.detail: For the CPU to touch disk data, those data must first reach main memory through CPU-generated I/O calls; instructions must be in memory to execute. **Caching** is the recurring principle throughout: information is copied to a faster level on the assumption it will soon be needed again, so one datum can exist simultaneously on disk, in memory, in cache and in a register — and in multiprocessors, **cache coherency** problems arise when each CPU holds its own copy and an update in one must reach them all (in distributed systems, file replicas raise the same issue).

concepts.statement: **Protection** is any mechanism for **controlling the access of processes or users to the resources** defined by a computer system — it must supply means both to specify and to enforce controls. **Security** defends the system from **external and internal attacks**: viruses and worms, denial-of-service, identity theft, theft of service. The system distinguishes users by unique **user identifiers (user IDs** — Windows calls them security IDs, SIDs) attached to every one of the user’s processes and threads, and by **group IDs** for sets of users.
concepts.detail: Sometimes a user must **escalate privileges** to gain extra permission for an activity — on UNIX the **setuid** attribute makes a program run with the file owner’s user ID rather than the caller’s: the process keeps this effective UID until it gives up the privileges or terminates. Adequate protection does not imply security: a user whose authentication is stolen can be impersonated even while file and memory protection work perfectly — a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

concepts.statement: **Virtualization** abstracts the hardware of a single computer — CPU, memory, disks, network cards — into **several different execution environments**, creating the illusion that each environment runs on its own **private computer**; a user can switch among guest operating systems the way one switches among processes. A **virtual machine manager (VMM)** runs the guests, manages their resource use and protects each guest from the others.
concepts.detail: Contrast **emulation**, which simulates a *different* CPU type in software — Apple’s Rosetta let PowerPC applications run on Intel x86 — at a heavy price: every source instruction translates into several target instructions, so emulated code runs much slower when source and target have similar performance. Virtualization instead runs OSes natively compiled for the host CPU. It began on IBM mainframes and reached x86 through VMware; in modern data centers, VMMs like VMware ESX and Citrix XenServer no longer run *on* a host OS — they **are** the host OS. Cloud computing builds directly on this foundation.

concepts.statement: After arrays, **lists** are the kernel’s workhorse: a **singly linked list** points each item to its successor, a **doubly linked** list also to its predecessor, and a **circularly linked** list wraps the last item back to the first. Lists accommodate varying-size items and cheap insertion/deletion, but retrieving a specified item is **linear — $O(n)$**. A **stack** (LIFO: **push/pop**) frames kernel function calls — parameters, local variables and return addresses; a **queue** (FIFO) orders waiting work, like printer jobs or tasks waiting for an available CPU.
concepts.detail: Linux implements list primitives in **<linux/list.h>**, used throughout the kernel source, and provides its queue as **kfifo** (in kfifo.c). Arrays still serve where direct indexing matters — main memory itself is an array of bytes addressed as ‘item number $\times$ item size’.

concepts.statement: A **tree** represents hierarchy through parent–child links; in a **binary search tree** each parent has at most two children with the ordering $\text{left} \leq \text{parent} \leq \text{right}$. An unbalanced BST can degenerate toward a chain — worst case $O(n)$ — but a **balanced** tree of $n$ items has at most $\lg n$ levels, guaranteeing $O(\lg n)$ search.
concepts.detail: Linux uses a balanced **red-black tree** as part of its CPU-scheduling algorithm (the Completely Fair Scheduler, Section 5.7.1), with the implementation living in **<linux/rbtree.h>** — a rare, concrete case of a data-structure choice being visible in scheduling behavior.

concepts.statement: A **hash function** takes data as input, performs a numeric operation, and returns a value used as an index into a table — retrieval can be as good as **$O(1)$** versus $O(n)$ for scanning a list. A **hash map** associates **[key:value] pairs**: hash the key, fetch the value. When two distinct inputs hash to the same slot — a **collision** — a linked list of colliding items hangs off that location, and the more collisions, the less efficient the hash.
concepts.detail: The book’s example: a user name maps to a password; at login the entered user name is hashed, the stored password is retrieved from that hash-map slot, and the two passwords are compared. Hash functions are used extensively throughout operating systems precisely because of the constant-time promise.

concepts.statement: A **bitmap** is a string of $n$ binary digits representing the status of $n$ items: the value of the $i$-th bit tracks the $i$-th resource — 0 might mean available, 1 unavailable. In the book’s example bitmap **001011101**, resources 2, 4, 5, 6 and 8 are unavailable while 0, 1, 3 and 7 remain available.
concepts.detail: Bitmaps shine on space efficiency: one bit per resource is $8\times$ smaller than an eight-bit Boolean per resource, which matters when tracking, say, every block on a multi-terabyte disk. Disk drives — a medium-sized drive divided into several thousand blocks — are the canonical use: the bitmap records the availability of each block.

concepts.statement: The major environments: **traditional** (desktop time-sharing, now rare as such), **client–server** (**compute servers** execute actions and return results; **file servers** provide a file-system interface for create/update/read/delete), **peer-to-peer** (all nodes are peers acting as client or server; services located via a centralized lookup service or by broadcasting a discovery request), **cloud** (computing, storage and applications delivered as a service across a network — **public, private or hybrid**; **SaaS** = applications via the Internet, **PaaS** = a software stack ready for application use, **IaaS** = servers or storage over the Internet), **embedded** (dedicated tasks; some run standard OSes, some special-purpose OSes, some are ASICs with no OS at all), **real-time** (rigid time constraints; the correct result delivered late is a failure) and **mobile** (touch-first, battery-bound handhelds dominated by Apple’s iOS and Google’s Android).
concepts.detail: P2P history: Napster used a centralized index of peers’ files (shut down in 2001 for copyright infringement) while Gnutella broadcast discovery requests; Skype hybridizes both with VoIP. Cloud example: Amazon EC2 — thousands of servers, millions of virtual machines, petabytes of storage, pay-per-use. A real-time system functions correctly **only if it returns the correct result within its time constraints** — a robot arm told to halt after smashing the car is a failed system. Mobile devices trade power for capability: a smartphone may top out at 256 GB of storage where a desktop offers 8 TB.

concepts.statement: **Free software** is licensed to allow no-cost use, redistribution and modification; **open-source software** makes source available but does not necessarily grant those licensing freedoms — so **all free software is open source, but some open-source software is not free**. The **GNU GPL** is a **copyleft** license: source must be distributed with any binaries, and all copies — including modified versions — must carry the same license; the permissive **BSD license** instead allows binary-only redistribution of derivatives.
concepts.detail: History: Stallman began **GNU** (‘GNU’s Not Unix’) in 1984, published the GNU Manifesto and founded the Free Software Foundation in 1985; GNU tools were ready but the kernel was not — until Linus Torvalds released a UNIX-like kernel in 1991 and relicensed it under the GPL in 1992, yielding **GNU/Linux** with hundreds of distributions (Red Hat, SUSE, Fedora, Debian, Slackware, Ubuntu). **BSD UNIX** descends from 1978 AT&T UNIX; after a lawsuit slowed it, the fully open 4.4BSD-lite (1994) spawned FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD and DragonflyBSD — and **Darwin**, the open-source core kernel component of macOS, is BSD-based. Economics: open-source firms earn revenue through **support contracts and hardware** (Red Hat), and the ‘many eyes’ argument holds that bugs are found and fixed faster when everyone can read the code.

examples.title: Sizing a disk-block bitmap
examples.problem: A $1\,\text{TB}$ disk drive is managed in $4\,\text{KB}$ blocks. How much memory does an availability bitmap need, and how does it compare with a byte-per-block table?

steps.label: Step 1: Count the blocks
steps.text: Block count is $\frac{2^{40}}{2^{12}} = 2^{28}$ — about 268 million blocks.

steps.label: Step 2: One bit per block
steps.text: The bitmap needs $2^{28}$ bits, one per block: 1 for unavailable, 0 for available.

steps.label: Step 3: Convert to bytes
steps.text: $2^{28}$ bits is $\frac{2^{28}}{8} = 2^{25}$ bytes $= 32\,\text{MB}$ — the bitmap’s memory cost.

steps.label: Step 4: Compare with a byte table
steps.text: An eight-bit Boolean per block would take $2^{28}$ bytes $= 256\,\text{MB}$ — $8\times$ the bitmap’s size.

steps.label: Step 5: The takeaway
steps.text: Checking availability is also fast: bit $i$ of the bitmap directly answers ‘is block $i$ free?’ — constant-time per block.

examples.result: A 32 MB bitmap tracks 268 million blocks — the space efficiency that makes bitmaps the default structure for disk free-space and resource-availability tracking.

examples.title: One datum, four copies: migration and coherency
examples.problem: An integer A is stored in file B on hard disk and must be incremented. Trace the data’s journey, and identify where coherency trouble begins.

steps.label: Step 1: Disk to memory
steps.text: An I/O operation copies the disk block containing A into main memory — copy 2 now exists.

steps.label: Step 2: Memory to cache
steps.text: The value is copied into cache — copy 3.

steps.label: Step 3: Cache to register
steps.text: A load brings A into an internal CPU register — copy 4 — where the increment actually executes.

steps.label: Step 4: Temporary divergence
steps.text: Until the register value is written back down the chain, the copies of A disagree across levels — correct within one process, dangerous if several processes (or, in a multiprocessor, several CPUs’ caches) hold copies simultaneously.

steps.label: Step 5: Coherency
steps.text: In multiprocessor systems every CPU has a local cache; an update to A in one cache must be reflected in all others — the **cache coherency** problem, usually handled in hardware below the OS.

examples.result: Caching multiplies data; the OS (and hardware) must keep the copies consistent — the same problem reappears for file replicas in distributed systems.

examples.title: A setuid privilege escalation
examples.problem: An ordinary user needs to change her password, which requires writing to the system password file owned by root. How does setuid make this safe-ish?

steps.label: Step 1: The obstacle
steps.text: The password file is protected — the user’s processes run with her user ID and cannot write it directly, and giving everyone write access would be catastrophic.

steps.label: Step 2: The setuid attribute
steps.text: The password-changing program is owned by root and carries the setuid attribute; the OS attaches the file owner’s user ID to processes running it.

steps.label: Step 3: Elevated execution
steps.text: The process runs with root’s effective UID — enough privilege to update the password file — but only within the logic of that audited program.

steps.label: Step 4: Relinquishing
steps.text: The extra privileges vanish when the process turns them off or terminates; nothing else the user runs gains them.

examples.result: setuid is the classic privilege-escalation tool: narrowly-scoped, owner-borrowed rights instead of blanket permissions — and a favorite target of attackers when setuid programs contain bugs.

keyTakeaways: The OS manages processes (the active units), memory, files and mass storage, and I/O — each class with a crisp list of responsibilities, from scheduling to free-space management to spooling.
Caching runs through everything: one datum lives at several hierarchy levels at once, so coherency — per-CPU cache and, in distributed systems, file replicas — is a standing problem.
Protection controls internal resource access; security defends against attacks; users are identified by user IDs and groups, with setuid as the standard escalation mechanism.
Virtualization multiplies one machine into many guests under a VMM — distinct from emulation, which translates between CPU architectures.
Kernel data-structure economics: lists $O(n)$, balanced trees (Linux’s red-black CFS scheduler) $O(\lg n)$, hash maps $O(1)$, bitmaps one bit per resource ($8\times$ smaller than bytes).

Environments: client–server splits compute from file servers; P2P locates services by lookup or discovery; cloud tiers into SaaS, PaaS and IaaS; real-time systems fail when deadlines slip; iOS and Android own mobile.

Free software ≠ open source necessarily: GPL copyleft forces source and license inheritance; BSD permits binary-only derivatives — GNU/Linux (Torvalds 1991, GPL 1992) and the BSD family are the landmark systems.

quiz.q: Which statement about free and open-source software is correct?
options: open-source software is always free software
all free software is open source, but some open-source software is not free
the BSD license is a copyleft license
free software means zero-price software only
quiz.explanation: Free software licenses grant no-cost use, redistribution and modification — open source only guarantees source availability, so the free set sits inside the open-source set; BSD is the permissive counter-example to GPL copyleft.

quiz.q: A balanced binary search tree holding $n$ items has at most how many levels?
quiz.explanation: Balance is what bounds the height: at most $\lg n$ levels, which is exactly why search, insert and delete stay $O(\lg n)$ instead of degrading toward the chain-like $O(n)$ worst case.

quiz.q: The setuid attribute on a UNIX program causes it to:
options: run with the caller’s group ID only
run with the user ID of the file’s owner rather than the caller’s
immediately escalate the entire login session
quiz.explanation: setuid borrows the owner’s identity — root for the password utility — until the process terminates or relinquishes the privilege; it is targeted escalation, not a blanket grant to the user.

quiz.q: In cloud terminology, ‘a software stack ready for application use via the Internet, such as a database server’ is:
quiz.explanation: PaaS delivers a ready platform on which applications are deployed; SaaS delivers the applications themselves and IaaS delivers raw servers and storage — public/private/hybrid is a separate, orthogonal axis.

quiz.q: A real-time system is distinguished by the fact that it:
options: runs faster than a general-purpose system
must return correct results within well-defined time constraints or it fails
quiz.explanation: The correctness criterion includes the deadline: processing must be done within the defined constraints — speed is merely desirable on a desktop, mandatory here.

intro: An operating system provides the environment within which programs are executed. This section inventories what ‘providing an environment’ concretely means: one user-facing interface plus a set of services — some existing to help the user, others existing to keep the system itself efficient, correct and safe.
objectives: Separate the services that help the user from those that ensure efficient system operation
List and explain the five user-facing services: program execution, I/O, file-system manipulation, communications and error detection
Explain the system-facing services: resource allocation, logging and protection/security
Identify which services a given user action exercises

concepts.term: Two views of the service set
concepts.statement: Operating-system services divide into two groups. One set provides functions **helpful to the user** — the interface plus program execution, I/O, file-system manipulation, communications and error detection. A second set exists **not to help the user but to ensure the efficient operation of the system itself** — resource allocation, logging, protection and security.
concepts.detail: The services also make the programming task easier for the programmer: every service in the list is one less thing each application must implement for itself. The user interface, however visible, is substantially removed from the actual system structure — a useful and intuitive UI is not a direct function of the OS proper.

concepts.statement: Almost every OS offers a **user interface (UI)** in one of three forms: a **graphical user interface (GUI)** — a window system with a mouse as pointing device and a keyboard for text; a **touch-screen interface** for phones and tablets, where users slide fingers or press on-screen buttons; or a **command-line interface (CLI)** using text commands typed in a specific format with specific options. Some systems provide two or all three.
concepts.detail: The interface is catalogued here as just another service — the OS’s first job toward its users — and Section 2.2 examines each form in depth.

concepts.statement: The system must be able to **load a program into memory and run it**; the program must be able to **end its execution, either normally or abnormally** (indicating error).
concepts.detail: Everything else in the chapter — loading, linking, scheduling — exists in service of this most basic requirement: turn a stored binary into a running, and eventually finished, computation.

concepts.statement: A running program may require I/O involving **a file or an I/O device**, sometimes with special functions (reading from a network interface, writing to a file system). For **efficiency and protection, users usually cannot control I/O devices directly** — the OS must provide the means to do I/O.
concepts.detail: Raw device control is exactly what privileged instructions (Section 1.4) wall off; the service layer replaces it with safe, shareable, uniform access — hiding the peculiarities of specific hardware devices from the user.

concepts.statement: Programs need to **read and write files and directories**, to **create and delete them by name**, to **search** for a given file and **list file information**; many operating systems add **permissions management** that allows or denies access based on **file ownership**.
concepts.detail: File systems vary widely — many OSes provide several, sometimes for personal choice, sometimes for specific features or performance characteristics — but the service catalogue (create, delete, read, write, search, permissions) is remarkably stable across systems.

concepts.statement: One process often needs to exchange information with another — on the same computer or across a network. Two implementation models: **shared memory**, where two or more processes read and write a common section of memory, and **message passing**, where **packets of information in predefined formats are moved between processes by the operating system**.
concepts.detail: The same OS must usually serve both: processes may exchange smaller messages without conflicts to avoid, while other pairings need the speed of memory-transfer-rate communication. Chapter 3 and Chapter 6 develop both models fully.

concepts.statement: The OS must **constantly detect and respond to errors** in the CPU and memory hardware (memory error, power failure), in I/O devices (parity error on disk, connection failure, printer out of paper) and in the user program (**arithmetic overflow, illegal memory access**). Appropriate action ranges from halting the system, to terminating the offending process, to returning an error code for the process to handle itself.
concepts.detail: A correct and consistent computing environment requires that no error pass silently. Error detection also feeds the debugging services of Section 2.5 — logs, core dumps and traces all begin here.

concepts.statement: When multiple processes run at once, resources must be allocated among them. Some resources (CPU cycles, main memory, file storage) get **special allocation code** — CPU-scheduling routines weigh CPU speed, the processes to run and the number of cores — while others use **general request-and-release code**. **Logging** records which programs use how much and what kinds of resources, for **accounting** (billing users) or for **usage statistics** that guide administrators reconfiguring the system.
concepts.detail: The book calls this record keeping ‘logging’; it is also known as accounting. Usage statistics become a valuable tool for improving computing services — the raw data behind the performance tools of Section 2.5.

concepts.statement: Owners of information in a multiuser or networked system want to control its use; concurrent processes must not interfere with one another or with the OS. **Protection** ensures all access to system resources is controlled; **security** starts with **authenticating each user** (usually by password), extends to **defending external I/O devices, including network adapters, from invalid access**, and records connections so break-ins can be detected.
concepts.detail: If a system is to be protected and secure, precautions must be instituted **throughout** it — the book’s warning that a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Protection is the internal mechanism; security is the defense against outsiders, and Chapters 16 and 17 treat them in depth.

examples.title: Saving a document, service by service
examples.problem: A user types a report in a word processor and clicks Save. Which operating-system services does this one action exercise?

steps.label: Step 1: Program execution
steps.text: The word processor itself is running because the OS loaded it into memory and started it — and it will end normally when the user quits it.

steps.label: Step 2: File-system manipulation
steps.text: The Save command resolves the document’s name, checks the directory for an existing entry, and creates or updates the file — through file-system services, not raw device writes.

steps.label: Step 3: I/O operations
steps.text: The bytes stream to the SSD through OS-provided I/O — the program cannot touch the disk controller directly, for efficiency and protection.

steps.label: Step 4: Error detection
steps.text: If the disk is full or a device fault occurs, the OS detects it and returns an error code instead of letting the failure pass silently.

steps.label: Step 5: The system-side services
steps.text: Meanwhile the OS allocated CPU and memory to the word processor among all running processes, logged its resource usage, and enforced that only the authenticated owner can reach the file at all.

examples.result: A single user click ran the full gamut: program execution, file-system manipulation, I/O, error detection, resource allocation, logging, and protection and security — the complete service catalogue in one action.

examples.title: Choosing an IPC mechanism
examples.problem: Two processes must cooperate: one renders video frames, the other displays them. When should the designer choose shared memory, and when message passing?

steps.label: Step 1: Assess the data rate
steps.text: Video frames are large and continuous — memory-transfer speed matters, pointing toward shared memory: the processes agree to lift the OS’s normal isolation and share a region.

steps.label: Step 2: Assess the coupling
steps.text: Shared memory leaves the form of the data and synchronization — who writes, who reads, when — to the processes themselves; that freedom costs coordination discipline.

steps.label: Step 3: Consider the alternative
steps.text: Message passing moves predefined-format packets through the OS: smaller transfers with no conflicts to avoid, and far easier to implement across computers — but each frame pays a kernel round-trip.

steps.label: Step 4: Decide
steps.text: Same-machine, high-bandwidth, latency-sensitive: shared memory. Cross-machine or small control messages: message passing. The OS service layer supports both.

examples.result: The communications service is a two-model menu, and the choice follows the data’s size, the parties’ location, and how much synchronization the designers want the kernel to own.

keyTakeaways: Services split by beneficiary: user-helpful (program execution, I/O, file systems, communications, error detection) versus system-directed (resource allocation, logging, protection and security).
The UI comes in three forms — GUI, touch screen, CLI — and is itself just another service, largely decoupled from the system core.
Users cannot control I/O devices directly: the OS intermediates every device access for efficiency and protection.
IPC has exactly two models — shared memory and message passing — differing in speed, protection and who owns synchronization.
Error detection is continuous and multi-layer (hardware, devices, programs); responses range from halting the system to returning an error code.
Protection (controlled internal access) and security (defense against outsiders, starting with authentication) must be instituted throughout the system — no weak links.

quiz.q: Which group belongs to the services provided to help the *user*?
options: program execution, I/O operations, file-system manipulation, communications, error detection
CPU scheduling, memory allocation and device release
quiz.explanation: The user-facing five are execution, I/O, files, communications and error detection; resource allocation and logging exist for the system’s own efficiency, and protection/security straddles the boundary by serving both.

quiz.q: The two models for interprocess communication are:
quiz.explanation: Processes either agree to read and write a common memory region, or exchange packets in predefined formats that the operating system moves between them — every other IPC facility is built on one of these two.

quiz.q: Why do operating systems forbid user programs from controlling I/O devices directly?
options: to force users to buy more hardware
because device controllers cannot be programmed
because user programs have no buffers
quiz.explanation: Raw device access would let a buggy or malicious program corrupt shared devices and other processes; channeling all I/O through the OS keeps it safe, uniform and efficiently shareable.

quiz.q: The book’s warning that ‘a chain is only as strong as its weakest link’ applies to:
options: instituting protection and security precautions throughout the system
quiz.explanation: One unprotected component undoes the security of the whole: precautions — authentication, controlled access, defended network adapters — must extend across the entire system.

intro: Users meet the OS through a shell, a desktop or a touch screen; programmers meet it through an API whose functions quietly become system calls — traps that flip the mode bit and enter the kernel. This section connects those two worlds and catalogs the six categories of system calls every operating system provides.
objectives: Compare CLI, GUI and touch interfaces, and the two implementation models for command interpreters
Distinguish system calls from APIs (Win32, POSIX, Java) and explain the run-time environment’s role
Describe the system-call interface mechanism and the three parameter-passing methods
Give concrete examples of calls in all six categories, including fork/exec/wait/exit
Contrast the Arduino’s single-tasking execution with FreeBSD’s multitasking shell flow

concepts.statement: Most systems treat the **command interpreter** as a special program that runs when a process is initiated or when a user first logs on; when several are offered they are known as **shells** — on UNIX and Linux, the C shell, Bourne-Again shell (**bash**) and Korn shell among them. Its main function: **get and execute the next user-specified command**.
concepts.detail: Two implementation models for commands. (1) The interpreter **itself contains the code** for each command — deleting a file jumps to a section of interpreter code that sets parameters and makes the system call; the number of commands determines the interpreter’s size. (2) The UNIX model: the interpreter merely uses the command to **identify a file to load into memory and execute** — `rm file.txt` searches for a program named rm and runs it with the argument file.txt, so programmers add commands by creating new files without touching the shell. Repetitive command sequences can be recorded into **shell scripts** that the interpreter runs like programs.

concepts.statement: A **graphical user interface** is a mouse-based window-and-menu system on a **desktop metaphor**: icons represent programs, files, directories and system functions; clicking invokes, selects or opens menus. **Touch-screen interfaces** replace mouse and keyboard with **gestures** — pressing and swiping fingers across the screen.
concepts.detail: GUIs were born in early-1970s Xerox PARC research (first on the Xerox Alto, 1973), spread with the Apple Macintosh in the 1980s, and matured as Apple’s **Aqua** (macOS) and Microsoft Windows (Version 1.0 layered a GUI onto MS-DOS); open-source desktops include **KDE** and **GNOME** on Linux. The iPhone and iPad use the **Springboard** touch interface. Choice of interface is mostly personal preference — administrators and power users favor the CLI for efficiency and its programmability, and macOS, built partly on a UNIX kernel, offers both Aqua and a command line.

concepts.statement: **System calls** provide the interface to OS services — but application programmers design against an **application programming interface (API)** specifying functions, their parameters and return values. The three most common: the **Windows API**, the **POSIX API** (UNIX, Linux, macOS) and the **Java API**. API functions typically invoke the actual system calls behind the scenes — Windows’ CreateProcess() invokes the kernel’s NTCreateProcess().
concepts.detail: Why program to an API rather than raw system calls? **Portability** — a program can compile and run on any system supporting the same API — and convenience, since actual system calls are often more detailed and difficult. Programmers access the API through a library provided by the OS: **libc** for C on UNIX/Linux, so a `printf()` call is intercepted by the standard C library, which invokes the `write()` system call and returns its result to the user program.

concepts.statement: The **run-time environment (RTE)** — compilers or interpreters plus libraries and loaders — supplies the **system-call interface** that links applications to the kernel. It **intercepts API function calls, maps each to an associated system-call number, indexes a table by that number**, and invokes the intended system call in the kernel, returning its status. The caller knows nothing about the implementation, only the API contract.
concepts.detail: Systems execute thousands of system calls per second — even the simplest programs make heavy use of the OS. Beneath the interface, a call is a **trap**: control passes through the interrupt vector to a service routine, the mode bit is set to kernel, and (as Chapter 1 established) the same process continues in kernel mode — the system-call routine is part of the operating system, not a separate program.

concepts.statement: Three general methods pass parameters to the OS: (1) **in registers** — the simplest, when they fit; (2) in a **block, or table, in memory**, with the block’s **address passed in a register**; (3) **pushed onto the stack** by the program and popped by the OS. Block and stack methods do not limit the number or length of parameters.
concepts.detail: **Linux combines the approaches: five or fewer parameters travel in registers; more than five use the block method.** The block approach is what lets a single register smuggle an arbitrarily large argument structure across the kernel boundary.

concepts.statement: The **process control** category covers: end and abort; **load and execute**; **create and terminate process**; get and set process attributes (priority, maximum execution time); **wait for time or event, signal event**; and allocate/free memory. The UNIX trio: **fork()** creates a copy of the calling process, **exec()** replaces its image with a new program, **exit()** terminates returning a status code (0 or an error code) — with **wait()** for a child’s completion. Windows counterparts: CreateProcess(), ExitProcess(), WaitForSingleObject().
concepts.detail: The book’s contrast: the **Arduino** is a single-tasking system — a boot loader loads one *sketch* into flash that then runs alone (loading another replaces it), with no OS and no user interface beyond sensors. **FreeBSD** is multitasking: the shell fork()s, the child exec()s the command, the parent either wait()s or leaves the child running in the background — background jobs take input through files or the GUI, not the keyboard — and on completion the child exit()s, making its status available to the shell.

concepts.statement: File calls mirror the file life cycle: **create() and delete()** by name with attributes; **open() and close()** around use; **read(), write() and reposition()** (rewind or skip to end); plus **get file attributes() and set file attributes()** for name, type, protection codes and accounting — the same operations applying to directories when a directory structure exists. On the device side, a process needing exclusive access first **request()s a device and later release()s it** — the device analog of open() and close() — after which it can read, write and reposition the device much as with files; unmanaged access risks **device contention and perhaps deadlock** (Chapter 8).
concepts.detail: UNIX’s open(), read(), write() and close() are the canonical examples — the Windows set is CreateFile(), ReadFile(), WriteFile(), CloseHandle(). The similarity between devices and files is so great that UNIX merges them into a **combined file–device structure**: one set of system calls serves both, with devices identified by special file names, directory placement or file attributes — a recurring design decision the user interface mirrors.

concepts.statement: **Information maintenance** transfers data between user program and OS: **time() and date()**, free memory and disk space, OS version, plus debugging support — **dump()** of memory, and on Linux **strace**, which lists each system call as it executes. **Communications** implements both IPC models: **message passing** (get hostid()/get processid() translate names to identifiers; open connection, accept connection, wait for connection; read message() and write message(); close connection) and **shared memory** (shared memory create and attach).
concepts.detail: Receivers of connections are usually special-purpose **daemons**. Message passing suits smaller data and intercomputer communication — no conflicts to avoid and easier to implement; shared memory runs at memory-transfer speed but leaves protection and synchronization to the processes (Chapter 6). Time profiling — recording the program counter at every timer interrupt — builds a statistical picture of where a program spends its time.

concepts.statement: Protection system calls manipulate access controls on resources such as files and disks: **set permission() and get permission()**, plus **allow user() and deny user()** for whether particular users may access particular resources. UNIX: **chmod()** changes permission bits, **umask()** sets defaults for new files, **chown()** changes ownership; Windows: SetFileSecurity() and its security-descriptor colleagues.
concepts.detail: Historically protection mattered only on multiprogrammed, multiuser systems; with networking and the Internet, every system — servers to handhelds — must enforce it, which is why this category rounds out the six (Chapter 17 covers the mechanisms, Chapter 16 the larger security picture).

examples.title: The system calls behind cp in.txt out.txt
examples.problem: Trace the system-call sequence of a program that copies one file to another, following the book’s example (Figure 2.5).

steps.label: Step 1: Acquire the file names
steps.text: The names may arrive as command arguments (cp in.txt out.txt) or interactively — prompting and reading each name already costs write() and read() system calls.

steps.label: Step 2: Open the input file
steps.text: open() on in.txt — which may fail: no such file, or protected against access. Then the program must output an error message (more system calls) and terminate abnormally (a system call).

steps.label: Step 3: Create the output file
steps.text: create()/open() for out.txt — an existing file of that name forces a choice: abort, delete and recreate, or ask the user; each path is more system calls.

steps.label: Step 4: The copy loop
steps.text: read() from the input, write() to the output, repeat — each call returning status for errors such as end-of-file, parity failure or ‘no more disk space’.

steps.label: Step 5: Shut down cleanly
steps.text: close() both files, write() a completion message to the screen, and terminate normally — the final system call.

examples.result: A program that looks like one line of shell work is a long chain of system calls with error handling at every link — and systems execute thousands of such calls per second.

examples.title: How a shell runs a command
examples.problem: On FreeBSD, a user types ./main at the bash prompt. Trace the process-control system calls from keystroke to next prompt.

steps.label: Step 1: The shell forks
steps.text: bash executes fork(), duplicating itself into a child process — same image, separate PID.

steps.label: Step 2: The child execs
steps.text: The child invokes exec() with the name of the executable; the loader replaces the child’s image with main and the new program begins executing (Section 2.3 covers the loader’s part).

steps.label: Step 3: The parent chooses
steps.text: Depending on how the command was issued, bash either wait()s for the child or leaves it running in the background — in the background case the shell immediately prompts for the next command, and the child’s keyboard input must route through files or the GUI instead.

steps.label: Step 4: The child exits
steps.text: The program terminates with exit(0) (or a nonzero error code); the status becomes available to the waiting parent.

steps.label: Step 5: Loop
steps.text: bash reads the next command — the cycle that makes the shell the visible face of process control.

examples.result: fork() + exec() + wait() + exit() is the universal UNIX recipe for running anything — the command interpreter is nothing but a loop around these four system calls.

keyTakeaways: A command interpreter either contains each command’s code (size grows with command count) or — the UNIX way — just loads and executes the named program file, keeping the shell small and extensible.
GUIs descend from Xerox PARC’s Alto (1973) through the Macintosh to Aqua, KDE and GNOME; touch (Springboard on iOS) is the third interface family; admins favor the programmable CLI.
Programmers write to APIs (Windows, POSIX, Java) for portability and convenience; run-time support (libc) maps each API function to the underlying system call — printf() becomes write().

The system-call interface intercepts API calls, indexes a table by call number, and traps into the kernel; parameters pass in registers, in a memory block whose address rides in a register, or on the stack — Linux switches to the block method beyond five parameters.

Six categories: process control (fork/exec/wait/exit), file management (open/read/write/close), device management (request/release), information maintenance (time/date), communications (send/receive, shared memory) and protection (chmod).
Single-tasking (Arduino: one sketch, no OS) and multitasking (FreeBSD: fork-exec-wait shells) bracket the process-control spectrum.

quiz.q: Why do application programmers prefer programming to an API rather than invoking system calls directly?
options: APIs bypass the kernel for faster execution
APIs offer portability across systems and hide the more detailed, difficult raw system calls
API calls run in kernel mode without a trap
quiz.explanation: A program written to the POSIX or Windows API can compile and run on any system supporting that API, while the API’s library functions absorb the messier details — but the kernel is still reached only through system calls, never bypassed.

quiz.q: On Linux, how are the parameters of a system call with more than five arguments passed?
options: in the first five registers only — extra arguments are dropped
in a block or table in memory, whose address is passed in a register
as entries appended to the interrupt vector
they cannot be passed at all
quiz.explanation: Linux uses registers for five or fewer parameters and switches to the block method beyond that — the block approach imposes no limit on the number or length of parameters.

quiz.q: On a UNIX system, when the user types rm file.txt, the shell:
options: executes its own built-in code that deletes the file
jumps to a section of interpreter code with the parameters
loads and executes a program file named rm with the argument file.txt
asks the kernel to interpret the rm command directly
quiz.explanation: UNIX implements most commands as separate system programs: the shell merely uses the command name to find, load and run the file rm — which is why anyone can add a new command by adding a new program file.

quiz.q: Which pairing of system calls correctly follows from a FreeBSD shell running a foreground command?
options: exec() by the shell, then fork() by the kernel
fork() by the shell, exec() by the child, wait() by the parent, exit() by the child
create() by the shell, join() by the child, signal() by the parent
load() by the shell, execute() by the kernel, sleep() by the parent
quiz.explanation: The shell duplicates itself with fork(), the child replaces its image using exec(), the parent blocks in wait() for a foreground job, and the child’s exit() returns status — the canonical UNIX process-control sequence.

quiz.q: Which set of system calls belongs to the communications category?
options: open connection, read message, write message, close connection
set permission, get permission, allow user, deny user
quiz.explanation: Message-passing communication opens a connection, exchanges messages in both directions, and closes the connection — the other sets are file management, process control and protection respectively.

quiz.q: Which system-call sequence correctly copies `in.txt` to `out.txt`, with error handling at every stage?
options: `delete()` the input, then `open()` the output only
`open()` both files once and return without any `read()` or `write()`
`write()` the output before `read()` the input, with no `open()` calls
`open()` the input, `create()` the output, loop `read()` then `write()` checking each status, then `close()` both files
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** two named files, copy loop, every call can fail (missing file, protection, full disk).
**Step 2 — Rule:** file life cycle is `open()`/`create()`, then `read()`/`write()`/`reposition()`, then `close()`; each call returns status that must be checked.
**Step 3 — Sequence:** `open()` input (fail → report and abort); `create()` output (existing name forces abort, delete-recreate, or prompt); loop `read()` chunk then `write()` chunk; `close()` both; `write()` completion message and terminate normally.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** even prompting for names already costs `read()`/`write()` on the terminal; systems execute thousands of such calls per second.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** skipping the loop copies nothing; reversed order reads unwritten data; deleting the source destroys the work.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** the first sequence is the only complete, checked copy.

quiz.q: On Linux a system call takes seven parameters. How are they conveyed into the kernel?
options: All seven ride in registers, extras are dropped
They are appended to the interrupt vector
In a memory block whose address rides in a register
They cannot be passed at all
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** seven parameters, more than fits the register-only path.
**Step 2 — Rule:** three methods exist: registers when they fit, a memory block whose address is passed in a register, or the stack. Linux uses registers for five or fewer and the block method beyond that.
**Step 3 — Apply:** seven exceeds five, so the block method applies: pack the seven into a table, pass its address.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** block and stack methods impose no limit on count or length, unlike pure registers.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** dropping extras corrupts the call; the vector holds handler addresses, not arguments; refusal contradicts the documented fallback.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** a block in memory addressed by one register carries all seven.

intro: Between a programmer’s source files and a running process stand the system services — compilers, editors, daemons — and two crucial translators: the linker, which stitches object files into one executable, and the loader, which brings that executable to life in memory. Understanding that pipeline also explains a stubborn fact: why binaries written for one operating system refuse to run on another.
objectives: List the categories of system services and give daemon examples such as cron
Walk the build pipeline: source → relocatable object file → executable → loaded program
Explain relocation, dynamic linking and the role of shared libraries/DLLs
Identify the major binary formats (ELF, PE, Mach-O) and what an entry point is
Explain why applications are OS-specific: ISA, binary format, system calls and the ABI

concepts.statement: **System services** (system utilities) provide a convenient environment for program development and execution. Categories: **file management** (create, delete, copy, rename, print, list files and directories); **status information** (date, time, available memory or disk, user counts — some systems a **registry** for storing and retrieving configuration); **file modification** (editors, search and transformation commands); **programming-language support** (compilers, assemblers, debuggers, interpreters for C, C++, Java, Python); **program loading and execution** (absolute loaders, relocatable loaders, linkage editors, overlay loaders); **communications** (remote login, message sending, e-mail, web browsing, file transfer); and **background services**.
concepts.detail: Constantly running system-program processes are known as **services, subsystems or daemons**: a network daemon listening for connections, process schedulers that start processes on a specified schedule — cron is the classic UNIX example — error-monitoring services and print servers; typical systems have dozens. The view of the OS seen by most users is defined by these applications and system programs, not by the system calls beneath them.

concepts.statement: From source to running process: **source files → compiler → relocatable object file → linker → binary executable file → loader → program in memory**. In commands: `gcc -c main.c` produces the relocatable object main.o; `gcc -o main main.o -lm` links main.o with other object files and libraries (the math library, -lm) into the executable main; typing **./main** invokes the loader.
concepts.detail: When a program name is entered on the command line, the shell first creates a new process to run the program via fork(), then invokes the loader with exec(), passing the executable’s name; the loader places the program into the new process’s address space. A GUI double-click on the icon triggers the loader through a similar mechanism.

concepts.term: Relocatable object files and the linker
concepts.statement: A **relocatable object file** is compiled to be loaded into **any physical memory location** — its addresses are not final. The **linker** combines the relocatable object files into a **single binary executable file**, pulling in other object files or libraries as needed, such as the standard C or math library.
concepts.detail: Each object file may reference functions and variables defined in the others; linking is what makes those symbols resolve to one program. Executables and objects carry a **symbol table** with metadata about the functions and variables the program references.

concepts.statement: The **loader** brings the binary executable into memory, where it becomes eligible to run on an available CPU core. An activity associated with linking and loading is **relocation**: it **assigns final addresses to the program parts and adjusts code and data to match those addresses**, so that code can call library functions and access its variables as it executes.
concepts.detail: The executable’s format records the program’s **entry point** — the address of the first instruction to execute when the program runs. The loader’s work is why one binary can sit anywhere in memory: nothing in it assumed a fixed address.

concepts.statement: Instead of linking every library into the executable, **dynamic linking** resolves libraries when the program is loaded — or even later, during run time. The linker inserts **relocation information** that lets the library be linked and loaded **if it is required**; Windows calls these **dynamically linked libraries (DLLs)**. Multiple processes can then share a single in-memory copy of a library, saving significant memory.
concepts.detail: The benefit is avoiding the linking and loading of libraries that may never be used — the book’s Figure 2.11 leaves the math library out of main precisely so it can join at load time. The cost is the notorious **versioning** problem — ‘DLL hell’: an updated library can break applications built against an older one, so modern systems version their shared libraries and keep multiple versions available side by side.

concepts.statement: Object and executable files follow standard formats containing the compiled machine code and a **symbol table** of metadata. UNIX and Linux use **ELF** (Executable and Linkable Format) — with separate relocatable and executable variants; Windows uses **PE** (Portable Executable); macOS uses **Mach-O**.
concepts.detail: Linux tooling: `file main.o` reports an ELF relocatable file, `file main` an ELF executable, and **readelf** examines the sections of an ELF file. Important caveat: ELF is not tied to any specific computer architecture — a common format across UNIX systems does not make an ELF binary portable across CPUs.

concepts.statement: A binary compiled on one OS will not run on another because of layered mismatches: the **binary format** (the layout of header, instructions and variables must match what the loader parses), the **instruction set** (only binaries containing the CPU’s ISA execute correctly), and the **system calls** (identity, numbering, operands, invocation and results differ). Above them, **system libraries** expose different APIs — an application written against iOS APIs will not work on Android.
concepts.detail: At the architecture level the contract is the **ABI** — the application binary interface: address width, how parameters are passed to system calls, the organization of the run-time stack, the binary format of system libraries, the size of data types. A binary compiled and linked for a given ABI (say, ARMv8’s) runs on systems honoring that ABI — but since ABIs are defined per OS-and-architecture, they do little for cross-platform compatibility. Firefox running on Windows, macOS, many Linux releases, iOS and Android shows how much porting work these layers create.
