concepts.statement: Three routes to running one application on several OSes: (1) an **interpreted language** (Python, Ruby) — the interpreter, available per OS, reads source and calls the native system calls, at a performance cost and with only a subset of each OS’s features; (2) a **language with a virtual-machine RTE** — Java compiles once to bytecode that runs wherever the JVM (with its loader and byte-code verifier) has been ported; (3) **porting** the source using a standard API such as **POSIX**, recompiling for each target — time-consuming, and repeated for every new version.
concepts.detail: A **cross-compiler** assists route (3): it runs on one platform but generates binaries for another OS or instruction set. In sum, unless an interpreter, RTE or binary is built for the specific OS **and** CPU type, the application will simply fail to run.

examples.title: From main.c to ./main
examples.problem: Follow a C program through the complete build pipeline, naming the artifact and tool at each stage.

steps.label: Step 1: Compile
steps.text: `gcc -c main.c` translates the source into **main.o** — a relocatable object file (ELF relocatable) designed to load at any memory address, carrying a symbol table of its references.

steps.label: Step 2: Link
steps.text: `gcc -o main main.o -lm` invokes the linker: main.o joins any other object files, and needed libraries are attached — statically, or as dynamic-linking information for later.

steps.label: Step 3: Inspect the executable
steps.text: The result **main** is an ELF executable whose header records the **entry point** — the address of the first instruction to execute; `file main` confirms the type.

steps.label: Step 4: Invoke the loader
steps.text: Typing **./main** makes the shell fork() a new process and pass the executable’s name via exec() — the loader places the program into the new process’s address space.

steps.label: Step 5: Relocate and run
steps.text: Relocation assigns final addresses and adjusts code and data to match; execution begins at the entry point. The math library, if the dynamic path was taken, links and loads now — only if actually required.

examples.result: Five stages, one running process — and a pipeline in which every artifact (relocatable object, executable, loaded image) has a defined format and role.

examples.title: Why main.exe will not run on Linux
examples.problem: A Windows executable is copied onto a Linux machine with the same x86-64 CPU. Explain each reason it still fails.

steps.label: Step 1: Binary format mismatch
steps.text: The file is a PE (Portable Executable); the Linux loader parses ELF — it cannot even find the header layout, instructions and variables where it expects them.

steps.label: Step 2: ABI mismatch
steps.text: Even ignoring the container, the two systems disagree on address width usage, parameter passing to system calls, run-time stack organization and the binary format of system libraries — the ABI is per-OS-per-architecture.

steps.label: Step 3: System-call mismatch
steps.text: The binary asks for Windows calls (CreateFile, WaitForSingleObject) by number and calling convention; Linux offers a different set with different numbering and semantics.

steps.label: Step 4: Library mismatch
steps.text: It links against Windows system libraries whose APIs (Win32) do not exist on Linux — POSIX’s open() family is the native interface there.

examples.result: The same instruction set is not enough: format, ABI, calls and libraries all bind a binary to its OS. Porting means recompiling from source; the alternative is an interpreter, a JVM-style runtime — or a subsystem like WSL (Section 2.5).

keyTakeaways: System services span file management, status information, file modification, language support, program loading, communications and background daemons — cron scheduling, network listeners, print servers.

The pipeline is fixed: compiler produces relocatable object files; the linker merges them (plus libraries) into one executable; the loader places that executable into a forked process’s memory and jumps to the entry point.
Relocation assigns final addresses and adjusts code and data accordingly — it is why object files can be ‘relocatable’ at all.
Dynamic linking defers library resolution to load time or run time; shared libraries (DLLs) let many processes share one copy — at the risk of versioning conflicts.
ELF (UNIX/Linux), PE (Windows) and Mach-O (macOS) are the executable formats; ELF is ISA-agnostic, so a common format still does not buy cross-CPU portability.
OS-specificity is structural: instruction set, binary format, system calls and system libraries — pinned down per-platform by the ABI.
Cross-platform escapes: interpreted languages, virtual-machine runtimes (Java), or POSIX-style porting — each with a price in performance, features or effort.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the build pipeline?
quiz.explanation: Compilation yields relocatable object files, the linker merges them into one executable, and only at run time does the loader bring the executable into memory — each stage consumes the previous one’s output.

quiz.q: A relocatable object file is one that:
options: must be loaded at one fixed physical memory address
is designed to be loaded into any physical memory location
quiz.explanation: Relocatable means free of final addresses — the object can land anywhere, because relocation (during linking/loading) will assign final addresses and adjust the code and data to match.

quiz.q: The main benefit of dynamic linking with shared libraries is that:
options: programs run with no system calls
libraries that end up unused are never linked and loaded into the executable, and processes can share one in-memory copy
the linker runs faster at compile time
quiz.explanation: The linker inserts relocation information instead of the library itself; the library loads only if required — and once in memory it can be shared by multiple processes, saving significant memory.

quiz.q: Which item is part of an application binary interface (ABI)?
options: the user’s license terms for the software
methods of passing parameters to system calls, run-time stack organization and data-type sizes
the GUI widget set used by the application
quiz.explanation: The ABI defines how binary components interface for a given OS on a given architecture — address width, parameter passing, stack layout, system-library binary format and data sizes are its clauses.

quiz.q: A Windows .exe file placed on an x86-64 Linux machine fails to run primarily because:
options: the CPU cannot decode x86-64 instructions on Linux
the binary format, ABI, system calls and system libraries all differ between the two operating systems
Linux forbids foreign files by law
the file lacks a symbol table
quiz.explanation: The instruction set is identical — but PE vs ELF formats, per-platform ABIs, different system-call interfaces and different libraries (Win32 vs POSIX) all bind the binary to its home OS.

intro: How should a program the size of an operating system be organized? This section gives the designer’s toolkit: separate mechanisms from policies, then choose a structure — monolithic, layered, microkernel, modular — or, as every successful modern system does, mix them into a hybrid like macOS, iOS or Android.
objectives: State user goals versus system goals in OS design, and the mechanisms/policies separation
Explain why modern kernels are written in C/C++ with minimal assembly
Compare monolithic, layered, microkernel and modular structures on coupling and performance
Describe Darwin’s hybrid structure: Mach + BSD + I/O Kit in one address space
Describe Android’s stack: Linux kernel, HAL, native libraries, ART and frameworks

concepts.statement: The first problem in designing an OS is defining goals and specifications **before** design begins — the hardware and the system type (traditional desktop, mobile, distributed, real-time) shape everything above. **User goals**: the system should be convenient to use, easy to learn, reliable, safe and fast. **System goals**: easy to design, implement and maintain; flexible, reliable, error-free and efficient.
concepts.detail: Both lists are vague — there is no general agreement on how to achieve them — and no unique solution exists: the requirements for Wind River VxWorks (a real-time embedded OS) must differ wildly from those for Windows Server (a large multiaccess enterprise system). Different requirements yield the large variety of solutions in the wild.

concepts.statement: The classic separation principle: **mechanisms determine *how* to do something; policies determine *what* will be done**. The timer construct is a mechanism for ensuring CPU protection; deciding how long the timer should be set for a particular user is a policy decision.
concepts.detail: Separation buys flexibility — policies change across places and over time, and a general mechanism working across a range of policies means a policy change requires only redefining parameters, not rebuilding the mechanism. A priority mechanism, properly separated, can enforce I/O-intensive-over-CPU-intensive priority **or the opposite**. **Microkernels take the separation to the extreme** with nearly policy-free primitives; Microsoft and Apple closely encode both mechanism and policy to enforce a global look and feel; Linux ships a standard scheduling mechanism whose policy anyone may replace. Whenever the question is *how*, determine a mechanism; whenever *what*, a policy.

concepts.statement: Early operating systems were written in assembly language; modern ones are written in **higher-level languages — C or C++ with a small amount of assembly for the lowest levels**. Higher-level implementation means code written faster, more compact, easier to understand and debug, free gains from compiler improvements, and far easier porting to other hardware.
concepts.detail: Android is the book’s example: kernel mostly C with some assembly; system libraries in C or C++; application frameworks mostly Java. The residual disadvantages — reduced speed, increased storage — are minor: for large programs, modern compilers with deep pipelining and multiple functional units beat expert assembly programmers. Major performance improvements come from **better data structures and algorithms**, not from excellent assembly — and only a small fraction of kernel code is performance-critical anyway (interrupt handlers, I/O manager, memory manager, CPU scheduler).

concepts.statement: The simplest organization is **no structure at all**: all kernel functionality in a **single, static binary file running in a single address space** — the **monolithic** structure. The original UNIX consisted of the kernel plus system programs, with everything between the system-call interface and the physical hardware — file system, CPU scheduling, memory management, device drivers — combined in one enormous kernel; Linux runs monolithically (applications reach it through the glibc standard C library) while adding a modular twist.
concepts.detail: Monolithic kernels are difficult to implement and extend — tightly coupled, with wide-ranging ripple effects from any change — but they hold a distinct performance advantage: **very little overhead in the system-call interface and fast communication within the kernel**. That speed is why UNIX, Linux and Windows all still show monolithic structure at their core.

concepts.statement: A **layered** OS divides the system into levels: layer 0 is the hardware, layer $N$ the user interface, and each layer $M$ is an **implementation of an abstract object — data plus the operations that manipulate them**. Layer $M$ offers functions to higher layers and **invokes operations only on lower-level layers**, hiding its data, operations and hardware from above.
concepts.detail: The main advantage is **simplicity of construction and debugging**: layer 1 is debugged against only the (assumed-correct) hardware, then its correctness is assumed while layer 2 is debugged, and so on — an error found must lie in the current layer. The costs: appropriately defining each layer’s functionality is hard, and performance suffers as requests **traverse multiple layers**. Dijkstra’s THE system is the classic early layered design; pure layering is rare in OSes (though TCP/IP and web stacks thrive on it), but modern systems layer partially — fewer layers, more functionality per layer.

concepts.statement: The **microkernel** approach removes **all nonessential components from the kernel** and runs them as **user-level programs in separate address spaces**, leaving a smaller kernel that typically provides minimal **process and memory management plus a communication facility**. Clients and services never interact directly — they **exchange messages through the microkernel**.
concepts.detail: Benefits: easier extension (new services are user programs), easier porting, more security and reliability — a failed service does not touch the kernel. The cost is performance: messages must be **copied between separate address spaces** and the system may have to switch processes to exchange them. Mach (Carnegie Mellon, mid-1980s) is the landmark research microkernel — and Darwin, the kernel component of macOS and iOS, contains one. QNX Neutrino keeps only message passing, process scheduling, low-level network communication and interrupt handling in kernel, all else in user mode. Cautionary tale: Windows NT began with a layered microkernel organization, performed poorly against Windows 95, and by Windows NT 4.0 and XP had moved layers into kernel space — becoming largely monolithic.

concepts.statement: The **modules** design — the best current methodology, per the book — gives the kernel **core components** and links additional services via **loadable kernel modules (LKMs)**, at boot time or during run time. It resembles a layered system in having defined, protected interfaces — but is **more flexible because any module can call any other module** — and resembles a microkernel in having a core with minimal fixed function — but is **more efficient because no message passing is needed**. Solaris, Linux, macOS and Windows all use it.
concepts.detail: Linux uses LKMs primarily for **device drivers and file systems**: a module can be inserted as the system boots or on demand — for example, when a USB device is plugged into a running machine whose kernel lacks the needed driver — and removed at run time. The result is a dynamic, modular kernel that keeps monolithic performance.

concepts.statement: In practice few systems adopt one pure structure; they combine them into **hybrid systems**. Apple’s macOS and iOS stack four layers: **user experience** (macOS’s mouse-and-trackpad **Aqua**; iOS’s touch-first **Springboard**), **application frameworks** (**Cocoa** for macOS, **Cocoa Touch** for iOS — APIs for Objective-C and Swift), **core frameworks** (graphics and media, including QuickTime and OpenGL) and the **kernel environment, Darwin** — which itself combines the **Mach microkernel and the BSD UNIX kernel**.
concepts.detail: Darwin offers **two system-call interfaces** — Mach traps and BSD POSIX calls — beneath a rich library interface. Mach provides memory management, CPU scheduling and IPC (message passing, remote procedure calls) through kernel abstractions: **tasks** (a Mach process), threads, memory objects and ports — a POSIX fork() becomes a Mach task. To dodge microkernel copying costs, Darwin folds Mach, BSD, the **I/O Kit** (device-driver development) and kernel extensions (**kexts**) into **a single address space**, so messages pass without copying data between spaces. Differences: macOS targets Intel architectures, iOS targets ARM with mobile-tuned power and aggressive memory management, **more stringent security** (each iOS app runs sandboxed, with developer access to POSIX and BSD APIs restricted), and Cocoa Touch exists to serve touch-first hardware.

concepts.statement: Android — designed by the Google-led Open Handset Alliance, open-source, running on countless hardware platforms — is a layered stack built on a **modified Linux kernel** (changes for power management, memory management and allocation, and a new IPC facility, **Binder**). Above it: the **HAL (hardware abstraction layer)** presenting a consistent view of cameras, GPS and sensors; **native libraries** including **Bionic**, Google’s smaller-footprint C library (in place of glibc), plus SQLite, webkit and SSL; the **ART runtime**; and the **application frameworks** with Google’s own Java API.
concepts.detail: Apps are written in Java, but compiled to .class bytecode and then translated to **.dex** files for ART. Where many Java virtual machines use **just-in-time (JIT)** compilation, ART performs **ahead-of-time (AOT)** compilation — .dex files compile to native machine code when installed — buying efficient execution and reduced power consumption on limited mobile hardware. The **JNI** escape hatch lets Java code call native libraries directly for specific hardware features, at the cost of portability. Each Android release extends the platform’s versioned **API levels**, against which apps declare the minimum they support.

examples.title: Mechanism or policy?
examples.problem: Classify each design decision as mechanism or policy, and say why the distinction matters: (a) the hardware timer; (b) the timer’s value for user U; (c) a priority-boosting facility; (d) the choice to boost I/O-bound over CPU-bound programs.

steps.label: Step 1: The timer
steps.text: (a) is a **mechanism** — how the OS guarantees regaining the CPU from any user program, independent of who runs.

steps.label: Step 2: The timer value
steps.text: (b) is a **policy** — how long a particular user may run is a *what/who* decision layered on the mechanism.

steps.label: Step 3: The priority facility
steps.text: (c) is a mechanism: a general-purpose way to raise some programs’ priority, able to serve either policy direction.

steps.label: Step 4: The boost choice
steps.text: (d) is a policy — and because (c) was separated from (d), flipping the decision (CPU-bound over I/O-bound) requires redefining parameters, not rebuilding the kernel.

examples.result: The separation principle in action: mechanisms are general tools; policies are the adjustable decisions on top. Microkernels institutionalize the split; Windows and macOS encode both together for uniformity.

examples.title: fork() through Darwin
examples.problem: An application on macOS calls the POSIX fork() system call. Trace what happens inside Darwin’s hybrid kernel.

steps.label: Step 1: Two doors
steps.text: Darwin exposes two system-call interfaces: Mach traps and BSD POSIX calls. fork() enters through the BSD side — one of the two doors into the same kernel.

steps.label: Step 2: BSD handles the POSIX semantics
steps.text: The BSD component implements the POSIX behavior the caller expects, coordinating with process bookkeeping.

steps.label: Step 3: Mach provides the abstraction
steps.text: Underneath, Mach represents the new process with its own kernel abstraction — a **task** — via Mach’s process management (alongside its memory management, scheduling and IPC).

steps.label: Step 4: One address space pays off
steps.text: Because Darwin runs Mach, BSD, the I/O Kit and kexts in a single address space, the internal hand-offs need no message copying between separate spaces — the microkernel performance trap, avoided.

examples.result: One POSIX call, two kernel cultures cooperating: BSD for the interface, Mach for the machinery — the hybrid that lets macOS be a UNIX *and* a Mach descendant at once.

examples.title: An Android app from source to screen
examples.problem: Follow a Java Android application from the developer’s editor to executing on the device’s hardware.

steps.label: Step 1: Write against the Android API
steps.text: The developer writes Java — but against Google’s Android API, not the standard Java API.

steps.label: Step 2: Compile to bytecode
steps.text: The Java compiler produces ordinary .class bytecode files.

steps.label: Step 3: Translate to .dex
steps.text: The build translates those .class files into the compact .dex format that the Android runtime consumes.

steps.label: Step 4: Install with AOT compilation
steps.text: At install time ART **ahead-of-time** compiles the .dex files into native machine code for the device — unlike JVMs that JIT-compile during execution — so runtime work is smaller and power draw lower.

steps.label: Step 5: Run through the stack
steps.text: The app executes through the application frameworks, native libraries (SQLite for data, SSL for security), and the HAL’s consistent view of the camera, GPS or sensors — with Binder, not ordinary pipes, carrying IPC down in the modified Linux kernel.

examples.result: Java source in, native code out, with each layer — ART, frameworks, HAL, kernel — isolating the app from the dizzying variety of Android hardware.

keyTakeaways: Design begins with goals: users want convenience, ease, reliability, safety and speed; system-builders want easy design, implementation and maintenance plus flexibility and efficiency — both sets deliberately vague.
**Mechanisms answer *how*; policies answer *what*.** Separating them lets policies change without rebuilding mechanisms — the timer is the canonical example.

Modern kernels are C/C++ plus a little assembly; performance now comes from data structures and algorithms, with only interrupt handlers, I/O, memory management and CPU scheduling being latency-critical.
Monolithic: everything in one address space — fastest system-call path, hardest to evolve (the Linux and original-UNIX shape).

Layered: each layer uses only lower layers — debuggable and verifiable by construction, but slow (traversal) and hard to divide; microkernel: minimal kernel + user-space services via messages — robust and extensible but pays copying and switch costs.
Loadable kernel modules combine the strengths: any module may call any other, no message passing — Linux’s device drivers and file systems load and unload at run time.
Hybrids dominate: Darwin = Mach microkernel + BSD in one address space (two system-call interfaces); Android = Linux kernel + HAL + Bionic + ART (AOT, .dex) + Java frameworks.

quiz.q: Which pairing correctly separates mechanism from policy?
options: the timer is the policy; its value per user is the mechanism
the timer construct is the mechanism; how long to set it for a particular user is the policy
both the timer and its value are mechanisms
both the timer and its value are policies
quiz.explanation: Mechanisms determine how (the timer hardware construct that guarantees CPU protection); policies determine what (how long a given user’s quantum lasts) — and a policy change should never force a mechanism rewrite.

quiz.q: The main performance problem of pure microkernels is:
options: the kernel cannot load modules at run time
messages must be copied between separate address spaces and processes must switch to exchange them
every system call must traverse many layers
quiz.explanation: With services running as user processes in separate spaces, inter-service communication pays message copying plus process switches — the overhead that derailed Windows NT’s original microkernel organization and that Darwin avoids by merging its components into one address space.

quiz.q: In the layered approach, layer $M$ may:
options: invoke operations only on lower-level layers
call any layer above or below
invoke operations only on higher-level layers
bypass layers and address the hardware directly
quiz.explanation: Strict layering means each layer builds solely on the layers beneath it — which is what makes bottom-up debugging and verification possible, and what makes cross-layer calls too slow to bear in practice.

quiz.q: Darwin combines Mach, BSD, the I/O Kit and kernel extensions into a single address space in order to:
options: avoid the cost of copying messages between separate address spaces
quiz.explanation: A pure microkernel pays message-copying between user-space services; Darwin keeps the Mach structure but shares one address space, so messages pass without data copying — the book’s answer to microkernel overhead.

quiz.q: A key difference between the Android runtime (ART) and typical Java virtual machines is that ART:
options: compiles .dex files to native code ahead-of-time at installation
runs Java bytecode directly on the hardware
quiz.explanation: ART’s ahead-of-time compilation turns .dex files into native machine code when an app is installed — more efficient execution and lower power draw, crucial for devices with limited memory and CPU.

intro: Turning source into a bootable kernel, shepherding the machine from power-on to login, and finding out why it broke when it does — this final section covers the OS lifecycle after the code is written: SYSGEN and boot, dual-boot and WSL, core and crash dumps, counters and tracing, and the eBPF-based tooling that makes a running Linux kernel observable.
objectives: List the SYSGEN steps and the three levels of tailoring, from full system build to run-time modules
Trace the boot process: firmware (BIOS/UEFI), boot block, GRUB, initramfs, systemd, login
Explain dual-boot/multi-boot and how WSL runs native Linux binaries on Windows
Distinguish core dumps, crash dumps and the counter/tracing approaches to performance
Describe BCC/eBPF tracing and formal verification with SAT solvers and model checkers

concepts.statement: Building an OS from scratch: (1) write or obtain the source code, (2) **configure** the system for the machine it will run on, (3) compile, (4) install, (5) boot. Configuration lives in a **configuration file**, and tailoring spans a spectrum: the file can drive **modification of the OS source followed by a complete compile** (a system build); or the **selection of precompiled object modules** from a library, linked together (faster, but possibly overly general); or a **fully modular system** where selection happens at **execution time** — SYSGEN just sets the parameters describing the configuration.
concepts.detail: Building Linux from scratch concretely: download the source from kernel.org; `make menuconfig` generates the **.config** file; `make` compiles the kernel into the **vmlinuz** image; `make modules` compiles and `make modules_install` installs the modules; `make install` installs the new kernel. Embedded systems commonly use the full-build extreme for a static hardware configuration; desktop and mobile systems typically use the second approach with loadable modules for dynamic support.

concepts.term: System boot: firmware and boot stages
concepts.statement: **Booting** is the process of starting a computer by loading the kernel: (1) a small **bootstrap program** (boot loader) in nonvolatile firmware **locates the kernel**; (2) the kernel is **loaded into memory and started**; (3) the kernel **initializes hardware**; (4) the **root file system is mounted**. Classic systems stage this: firmware **BIOS** runs a small first loader that loads a second loader from a fixed disk location called the **boot block** — while modern **UEFI** (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) is a **single, complete boot manager**, faster than the multistage BIOS dance and with better support for 64-bit systems and larger disks.
concepts.detail: The bootstrap also **runs diagnostics** — inspecting memory and the CPU, discovering devices — and initializes everything from CPU registers to device controllers to memory contents. The firmware must match the loader: specific GRUB variants exist for BIOS and UEFI.

concepts.statement: **GRUB** is the open-source bootstrap program for Linux and UNIX: its configuration file loads at startup, and it allows **changing kernel parameters and selecting among different kernels** at boot time. The kernel image is **compressed** (decompressing after loading into memory, to save space and boot time), and the loader typically creates **initramfs** — a temporary RAM file system holding the **drivers and kernel modules needed to reach the real root file system**. Once the kernel switches to the real root, Linux creates **systemd**, the initial process, which starts other services (a web server, a database) before presenting the login prompt.
concepts.detail: Book example from /proc/cmdline: `BOOT_IMAGE=/boot/vmlinuz-4.4.0-59-generic root=UUID=5f2e2232-...` — the kernel image name and the root file system’s unique identifier. Android, though Linux-based, skips GRUB: vendors supply boot loaders, most commonly **LK** (‘little kernel’), and the device **keeps initramfs as its root file system** rather than discarding it. Boot loaders on most systems also offer **recovery or single-user mode** for diagnosing hardware and repairing corrupt file systems.

concepts.statement: One machine can host several operating systems at once — the book’s example is a user **dual-booting from macOS into Windows**: the same user on the same hardware then faces **two entirely different interfaces and application sets** using the same physical resources, sequentially. Multi-boot generalizes this to several OSes on separate partitions or disks, chosen by the boot loader’s menu.
concepts.detail: GRUB’s ability to select among different kernels at boot time is exactly what makes dual- and multi-boot practical on Linux machines — the loader, not the firmware, is the switch. The two systems never run concurrently; only their stored images share the hardware.

concepts.statement: Windows uses a hybrid architecture with user-mode **subsystems** that emulate different OS environments, and Windows 10 adds the **Windows Subsystem for Linux**: native Linux applications (ELF binaries) run on Windows. Typing `bash.exe` presents a bash shell running Linux — internally, WSL creates a Linux instance of the **init process**, which creates **/bin/bash**, with each process running in a Windows **Pico process** that loads the native Linux binary into its own address space.
concepts.detail: Pico processes communicate with the kernel services **LXCore and LXSS**, which translate Linux system calls: when a call has a **one-to-one Windows equivalent**, LXSS forwards it directly; when a call is **similar but not identical**, LXSS does part of the work and invokes the similar Windows call for the rest — Linux fork() is handled by LXSS performing the initial work and then calling **CreateProcess()**; and when there is **no equivalent**, LXSS must implement the functionality itself.

concepts.term: Failure analysis: core dumps and crash dumps
concepts.statement: If a process fails, the OS writes error information to a **log file** and can capture the process’s memory in a **core dump** — the name survives from the early days when main memory was literally called ‘core’ — stored in a file for a debugger to explore code and memory at the time of failure. A kernel failure is a **crash**: error information goes to a log, and memory state goes to a **crash dump**.
concepts.detail: A kernel crash in file-system code makes saving state *through that file system* risky, so the kernel writes its memory image to a **section of disk set aside with no file system on it**; after reboot, a process gathers the data from that area into a proper crash-dump file for analysis — Linux’s implementation of this scheme is **kdump**. Kernel debugging is harder than process debugging: size, complexity, hardware control, and the lack of user-level tools.

concepts.statement: Performance-monitoring tools come in two kinds. **Counter** tools read statistics the kernel already maintains — per-process (**ps** reports process information, **top** real-time statistics) or system-wide (**vmstat** memory, **netstat** network interfaces, **iostat** disk I/O). **Tracing** tools collect data for a **specific event** as it happens — per-process (**strace** traces system calls invoked by a process; **gdb** is the source-level debugger) or system-wide (**perf**, a collection of performance tools; **tcpdump** collects network packets).
concepts.detail: Most Linux counter tools read the **/proc pseudo file system** — a directory hierarchy existing only in kernel memory, with each process’s ID as a subdirectory (e.g., **/proc/2155** holds statistics for process 2155) plus entries for kernel statistics. Windows provides the Task Manager with applications, processes, CPU and memory usage, and networking statistics. Performance tuning means removing the bottlenecks these tools expose.

concepts.statement: **BCC (BPF Compiler Collection)** is a Python front-end to **eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter)** — technology descended from the packet filters of the early 1990s. A BCC tool embeds a subset-of-C program, compiles it to eBPF instructions and inserts it into the **running kernel** using **probes or tracepoints** to capture events such as a specific system call or disk-I/O latency. Before insertion, a **verifier checks that the instructions cannot harm system performance or security** — which is why BCC tools can run on live production systems.
concepts.detail: BCC ships many ready tools: **disksnoop** traces disk I/O with timestamps, byte counts and latency; `opensnoop -p 1225` traces open() calls of a single process; **funccount** counts function invocations; **stacksnoop** traces stack usage. The lineage includes **DTrace** — Solaris’s dynamic tracing framework organized around probes, providers and functions — which pioneered safe, dynamic kernel instrumentation.

concepts.statement: Beyond testing: **formal verification proves properties of a design rather than sampling behaviors**. Applied to OS algorithms and protocols, the tools include **SAT solvers** — engines for boolean satisfiability that search for (or prove the absence of) counterexamples — and **model checkers** such as **Spin**, which exhaustively explores a finite-state model of, say, a locking protocol to prove freedom from deadlock.
concepts.detail: Kernighan’s Law sets the debugging stakes: ‘Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place. Therefore, if you write the code as cleverly as possible, you are, by definition, not smart enough to debug it.’ Modern practice layers the approaches: counters to spot anomalies, BCC/eBPF tracing to find bottlenecks dynamically, and formal methods targeted at the most concurrency-critical pieces.

examples.title: Booting Linux: power button to login prompt
examples.problem: Trace a modern Linux machine’s boot from cold power to the login screen.

steps.label: Step 1: Firmware runs
steps.text: Power-on starts the bootstrap in nonvolatile firmware — UEFI on modern machines (a single, complete boot manager; older BIOS machines stage through the boot block on disk). It runs diagnostics: inspecting memory and the CPU, discovering devices.

steps.label: Step 2: Boot loader loads
steps.text: The firmware hands off to the boot loader — GRUB in the standard Linux flow — whose configuration file loads at startup.

steps.label: Step 3: Kernel selection and load
steps.text: GRUB selects a kernel (by default or from its menu), loads the compressed image into memory, and passes parameters such as BOOT_IMAGE and root=UUID.

steps.label: Step 4: Decompress and mount
steps.text: The kernel decompresses, initializes hardware, and mounts **initramfs** — the temporary RAM file system carrying the drivers needed to reach the real root file system — then switches root to the real one.

steps.label: Step 5: systemd
steps.text: Linux creates the **systemd** process as the first system program, which starts daemons — a web server, a database, the login service.

steps.label: Step 6: Login
steps.text: The user sees the login prompt; only at this point is the system said to be fully booted and running.

examples.result: Firmware diagnostics → GRUB → kernel decompress + initramfs → real root → systemd services → login: every Linux boot replays this chain in seconds.

examples.title: fork() under WSL
examples.problem: A native Linux application running in the Windows Subsystem for Linux calls fork(). What happens?

steps.label: Step 1: The call arrives in a Pico process
steps.text: The Linux binary runs inside a Windows Pico process with its own address space — bash.exe created a Linux instance whose init process spawned /bin/bash, which spawned the application.

steps.label: Step 2: LXSS/LXCore intercept
steps.text: The system call reaches the WSL kernel services, which must translate it — Linux fork() has no exact one-to-one Windows counterpart.

steps.label: Step 3: Partial handling
steps.text: Because the calls are similar but not identical, LXSS performs the initial work of the fork itself.

steps.label: Step 4: CreateProcess finishes
steps.text: LXSS then invokes the similar Windows system call — CreateProcess() — to complete the job, and success returns to the Linux application as if the kernel had natively forked.

examples.result: Near-miss system calls are split between LXSS’s own work and the closest Windows call — the price and the cleverness of running ELF binaries under an alien kernel.

keyTakeaways: SYSGEN = write/obtain, configure, compile, install, boot — with tailoring from full source rebuilds through precompiled-module linking to run-time module selection; on Linux: menuconfig → .config → make → vmlinuz → make modules_install → make install.

Boot: firmware (BIOS-staged or the single-boot-manager UEFI) locates and loads the kernel; the kernel initializes hardware and mounts root; initramfs bridges the driver gap; systemd starts services and yields the login prompt.
GRUB selects among kernels and takes parameters — the machinery that also enables dual- and multi-boot; Android instead vendors LK and keeps initramfs as its root.
WSL runs native Linux ELF binaries in Windows Pico processes; LXSS/LXCore translate system calls — one-to-one when possible, partially implemented (fork() + CreateProcess()) when not.
Failures leave evidence: process core dumps and kernel crash dumps (saved to raw, file-system-free disk and collected by kdump after reboot).

Counters (ps, top, vmstat, netstat, iostat — mostly reading /proc) measure state; tracing (strace, gdb, perf, tcpdump, BCC/eBPF) records events; the eBPF verifier is what makes live-production tracing safe.
When testing is not enough: SAT solvers and model checkers such as Spin prove properties of OS protocols exhaustively.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four steps of booting as the book lists them?
options: the boot loader locates the kernel
the kernel is loaded into memory and started
the window manager draws the desktop
quiz.explanation: The canonical sequence ends with mounting the root file system; desktop drawing comes much later, after systemd has started services and a user has logged in.

quiz.q: The purpose of initramfs during Linux boot is to:
options: serve as the permanent root file system on servers
hold the drivers and kernel modules needed to access the real root file system before it can be mounted
quiz.explanation: The real root often needs drivers the bare kernel lacks; initramfs is a temporary RAM file system carrying exactly those, discarded after the switch to the true root — Android is the exception that keeps it as root.

quiz.q: Under WSL, the Linux fork() system call is handled by:
options: forwarding directly to an identical Windows call
LXSS performing the initial work and then invoking the similar Windows CreateProcess() call to finish
emulating an entire Linux kernel in user space
quiz.explanation: fork() and CreateProcess() are similar but not identical, so LXSS does part of the work itself and delegates the remainder to the near-match Windows call — the hybrid translation strategy WSL uses for near-miss system calls.

quiz.q: The role of the eBPF verifier is to:
options: compress eBPF instructions to save memory
check that inserted instructions cannot harm system performance or security before they run in the kernel
prevent BCC tools from attaching to any process
quiz.explanation: eBPF programs are dynamically inserted into a running kernel; the verifier’s pre-insertion check is what makes that safe — and what allows BCC tools (disksnoop, funccount, stacksnoop) to run on live production systems.

quiz.q: The essential difference between counter-based and tracing tools is:
options: counters are only available on Windows; tracing only on Linux
counters read statistics the kernel already maintains, while tracing collects data for specific events as they occur
counters work per-process only; tracing is always system-wide
tracing tools cannot be used on production systems
quiz.explanation: vmstat or ps ask ‘what is the current value of a maintained statistic?’, while strace or perf ask ‘show me every occurrence of this event’ — the difference between state inspection and event recording.

intro: A process is a program in execution — the active entity that gives a passive executable file its life. This section defines the process, walks the memory layout of a C program from the text section up to the arguments, names the five process states and every transition between them, and opens up the process control block, the data structure the kernel uses to represent each process.
objectives: Distinguish a program from a process, and explain why one program can back many processes
Sketch the memory layout of a C program and place variables in the correct section
Name the five process states and trace every transition in the state diagram
List the contents of a process control block (PCB) and explain why each field exists

concepts.statement: A **process** is a **program in execution**. A **program** is a **passive** entity — a file containing instructions stored on disk (an executable file) — whereas a process is an **active** entity, with a **program counter** specifying the next instruction to execute and a set of associated resources. A program becomes a process when its executable file is loaded into memory.
concepts.detail: Several processes can be associated with the same program: many users running copies of the mail program, or one user opening many browser tabs. Each is a separate process — the text sections are equivalent, but the data, heap and stack sections differ. A process can itself be an execution environment for other code: the JVM runs as an ordinary process that interprets the loaded Java program on the program’s behalf.

concepts.statement: A process in memory is laid out, from low addresses to high addresses, as: the **text** section (the compiled program code), **initialized data** (globals such as $y = 15$), **uninitialized data** (the BSS block, such as a bare $x$), the **heap** (memory allocated dynamically at run time, growing toward higher addresses), and the **stack** (growing down from high addresses), with **arguments and environment** ($argc$, $argv$) at the very top.
concepts.detail: The sizes of the text and data sections are fixed for the whole run; the stack and heap shrink and grow dynamically and grow toward one another, so the operating system must ensure they never overlap. The GNU size command reports the section sizes of an executable: a sample program shows text 1158, data 284 and bss 8 bytes (bss = “block started by symbol”, the uninitialized data).

concepts.statement: The **stack** holds temporary data for function calls: each call pushes an **activation record** containing function parameters, local variables and the return address; returning pops the record. The **heap** holds memory allocated dynamically at run time (C’s malloc(), Java’s new) — it grows as memory is allocated and shrinks as memory is returned to the system.
concepts.detail: Rule of thumb: local variables and call frames live on the stack; everything whose lifetime the programmer controls explicitly lives on the heap. In the book’s example, values = malloc(5 ints) lives in the heap while the loop counter i lives on the stack.

concepts.statement: As a process executes it changes **state**: **new** (being created), **running** (instructions are being executed), **waiting** (halted until some event occurs, such as an I/O completion or a signal), **ready** (waiting to be assigned to a processor), and **terminated** (finished execution). At any instant, only one process can be running on each processor core — but many processes may be ready and waiting.
concepts.detail: The names are arbitrary and vary across operating systems; the states themselves are found on all systems, and some kernels delineate them more finely (Linux adds zombie, stopped and others).

concepts.statement: The state diagram arrows: new → ready (**admitted**); ready → running (**scheduler dispatch**); running → ready (**interrupt** or expired time slice — preemption); running → waiting (**I/O or event wait**); waiting → ready (**I/O or event completion**); running → terminated (**exit**).
concepts.detail: Two arrows are commonly missed: a process is preempted from running back to ready when an interrupt occurs or its time slice expires, and a waiting process never jumps straight to running — it must first re-enter the ready queue.

concepts.statement: Each process is represented in the operating system by a **process control block** (also called a task control block) — one PCB per process. It contains: **process state**; the **program counter** (address of the next instruction to execute); **CPU registers** (accumulators, index registers, stack pointers, general-purpose registers, condition codes); **CPU-scheduling information** (process priority, pointers to scheduling queues, other scheduling parameters); **memory-management information** (base and limit registers, page or segment tables); **accounting information** (CPU and real time used, time limits, account numbers); and **I/O status information** (list of I/O devices allocated, list of open files).
concepts.detail: In brief, the PCB is the repository for all the data needed to start — or restart — a process, along with some accounting data. In Linux the PCB is the task_struct structure in include/linux/sched.h: it holds state, scheduling info, the list of open files, the address space, and pointers to the process’s parent, children and siblings. All active processes are linked in a doubly linked list of task_structs, with a kernel pointer current marking the executing process.

concepts.statement: The program counter and CPU registers together capture a process’s exact position of execution. They must be **saved when an interrupt occurs** so that the process can be continued correctly afterward when it is rescheduled — this is exactly the snapshot the PCB stores.
concepts.detail: This is why context switching (Section 3.2) is possible at all: because the complete CPU state of a suspended process lives in its PCB, the kernel can stop any process at (almost) any instant and later resume it as if nothing had happened.

concepts.statement: The process model so far assumes a process performs a **single thread of execution** — one program counter, one register set, one stack. A single-threaded word processor cannot simultaneously accept keystrokes and run the spell checker. Modern systems extend the process concept to allow **multiple threads of execution** per process, and the PCB is expanded to include information for each thread.
concepts.detail: Chapter 4 develops threads in full: each thread gets its own program counter, registers and stack while sharing the process’s code, data, heap and open files.

examples.title: Placing variables in the memory layout
examples.problem: A C program declares int x; int y = 15; then in main() declares int *values; int i; and calls values = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int) * 5). Locate each item in the process’s memory layout, from the text section to the top.

steps.label: Step 1: The code itself
steps.text: The compiled machine instructions of main() occupy the **text** section at the lowest addresses — fixed in size, read-only in practice.

steps.label: Step 2: The initialized global
steps.text: $y = 15$ is an initialized global, so it lives in the **initialized data** section; the uninitialized global $x$ goes into the **uninitialized data (BSS)** section just above it.

steps.label: Step 3: The dynamic allocation
steps.text: The five integers returned by malloc() live in the **heap**, which grows upward from the data sections as the program allocates.

steps.label: Step 4: The locals and the call frame
steps.text: $values$, $i$, the saved return address and main()’s parameters occupy an **activation record on the stack**, near the top of memory, growing downward. The $argc$ and $argv$ values sit above the stack, at the highest addresses.

steps.label: Step 5: Verify with the tools
steps.text: Compiling and running size on the executable prints text = 1158, data = 284, bss = 8 bytes — the fixed sections are measurable, while the stack and heap heights only exist at run time.

examples.result: text (code) → initialized data ($y$) → uninitialized data/BSS ($x$) → heap (malloc array, growing up) → stack (locals, call frames, growing down) → $argc$/$argv$ and environment at the top.

examples.title: Tracing the states of one command
examples.problem: A shell runs grep, which reads a large file from disk, computes for a while, and exits. Trace the process through all five states and the transitions it takes, including one preemption.

steps.label: Step 1: Creation
steps.text: The shell calls fork() and exec(): the new grep process is in the **new** state while being created, then is **admitted** and enters the **ready** state, joining the ready queue.

steps.label: Step 2: First dispatch
steps.text: The CPU scheduler dispatches it: **ready → running**. It begins reading the file and immediately blocks on the disk: **running → waiting** (I/O wait).

steps.label: Step 3: I/O completes and preemption
steps.text: The disk interrupt fires and the process moves **waiting → ready**. It is dispatched again, and while computing, its time slice expires: **running → ready** (an interrupt, not a wait — it did not block).

steps.label: Step 4: Second dispatch and exit
steps.text: It runs again to completion and calls exit(): **running → terminated**. The kernel removes it from all queues and deallocates its PCB and resources.

examples.result: new → ready → running → waiting → ready → running → ready → running → terminated — every state visited, and both ways of leaving running (wait and preemption) exercised.

keyTakeaways: A program is passive (an executable file on disk); a process is the active, executing entity with a program counter and resources.
Memory layout, low to high: text, initialized data, uninitialized data (BSS), heap (grows up), stack (grows down), arguments and environment.
Stack = activation records (parameters, locals, return addresses); heap = dynamically allocated memory.
Five states — new, ready, running, waiting, terminated — with running → ready (preemption) and waiting → ready (event completion) as the two commonly forgotten arrows.
The PCB stores state, program counter, registers, scheduling info, memory-management info, accounting and I/O status — everything needed to restart the process.
Each process has its own PCB (Linux: task_struct, one per process, linked into a doubly linked list).

quiz.q: The essential difference between a program and a process is that:
options: a program is a passive entity (an executable file), while a process is a program in execution — an active entity
a program runs in user mode, while a process runs in kernel mode
a program is written in C, while a process is written in assembly
a program is loaded in memory, while a process stays on disk
quiz.explanation: A program is the passive set of instructions stored on disk; it becomes a process — an active entity with a program counter and associated resources — when it is loaded into memory and executed.

quiz.q: In the memory layout of a C program, the section that grows toward LOWER addresses and holds function parameters and local variables is the:
quiz.explanation: The stack sits near the top of memory and grows downward; each function call pushes an activation record holding parameters, local variables and the return address. The heap grows in the opposite direction (upward), and text and data have fixed sizes.

quiz.q: Which state transition is NOT possible in the five-state process model?
quiz.explanation: A waiting process must first re-enter the ready queue when its event completes; only the scheduler can then dispatch it. Waiting → running does not exist. Running → ready is the preemption arrow (interrupt or expired time slice).

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT typically stored in a process control block?
options: the program counter and CPU registers of the process
memory-management information such as base and limit registers
accounting information such as CPU and real time used
quiz.explanation: The PCB holds execution state (PC, registers), scheduling, memory-management, accounting and I/O status data. The source code is never kept — the process runs from the compiled text section.

quiz.q: Two processes created from the same program (say, two copies of a mail client) typically:
options: share the same text section but have separate data, heap and stack sections
share the same stack but separate text sections
cannot exist at the same time
quiz.explanation: Each invocation is a separate process with its own PCB, program counter, data, heap and stack; only the (read-only) text — the program’s code — is equivalent between them.

intro: Multiprogramming wants a process running at all times; time sharing wants every interactive process to feel alive. The process scheduler pursues both goals by moving processes among queues — one ready queue, many device queues — while long-, medium- and short-term schedulers decide who gets in, who stays in memory, and who gets the CPU next. Every handoff costs a context switch: pure overhead that no user code benefits from.
objectives: Distinguish the job queue, ready queue and device queues
Follow a process through the queueing diagram and its possible branches
Compare the long-term, short-term (CPU) and medium-term schedulers
Explain what a context switch saves and restores, and why it is pure overhead

concepts.statement: The objective of **multiprogramming** is to have some process running at all times, maximizing **CPU utilization**; the objective of **time sharing** is to switch the CPU among processes so frequently that users can interact with each program while it runs. The number of processes currently in memory is the **degree of multiprogramming**.
concepts.detail: Processes divide into I/O-bound ones (more time doing I/O than computing) and CPU-bound ones (infrequent I/O, long computations). A scheduler that balances both kinds keeps every device and every core busy — long-term schedulers explicitly aim for a good process mix.

concepts.statement: Processes wait in three kinds of queues. The **job queue** consists of all processes in the system. The **ready queue** contains all processes residing in main memory that are ready and waiting to execute — it lives in the kernel as a linked list of PCBs, with a ready-queue header holding pointers to the first and last PCBs (head and tail), and each PCB holding a pointer to the next PCB in the queue. Each **device queue** holds the processes waiting for that particular I/O device.
concepts.detail: A new process enters the ready queue; once running it may terminate, be interrupted, or wait — landing in a device (or event) queue before flowing back to ready. The queues link PCBs, not processes directly: queuing a process means linking its PCB.

concepts.statement: The flow: a new process is placed in the **ready queue**; when dispatched it executes on the **CPU**; then one of four things happens — (1) it issues an **I/O request** and moves to an **I/O wait queue**, returning to ready when the I/O completes; (2) it **creates a child process** and waits in the wait queue for the child’s termination; (3) it is **interrupted or its time slice expires** and is put back in the ready queue; (4) it **terminates** and leaves the system, its PCB and resources deallocated.
concepts.detail: Circles in the diagram represent the resources that serve the queues (the CPU, the devices); arrows show the flow of processes. Interrupt-wait queues are a third wait-queue family: a process waiting for an interrupt re-enters the ready queue when it arrives.

concepts.statement: The **long-term scheduler** (job scheduler) selects processes from the **job pool** — the processes kept in mass-storage waiting to be brought into memory — and loads them into the ready queue. It **controls the degree of multiprogramming** (the number of processes in memory) and is invoked **infrequently**: seconds or minutes may separate its decisions, so it can afford to spend time choosing well.
concepts.detail: It should select a good process mix of I/O-bound and CPU-bound processes: all I/O-bound work leaves the CPU idle; all CPU-bound work leaves devices idle and degrades interactive response.

concepts.statement: The **short-term scheduler**, or **CPU scheduler**, selects one of the processes in the ready queue and allocates a CPU core to it. It executes frequently — at least once every 100 milliseconds, and typically much more often — so its dispatch decisions must be **fast**: an I/O-bound process may execute for only a few milliseconds before waiting again.
concepts.detail: The book’s rule of thumb: if the scheduler takes 1 ms to pick a process that runs for 10 ms, roughly 10% of the CPU is spent purely on scheduling — which is why short-term scheduling algorithms trade sophistication for speed (Chapter 5).

concepts.statement: The **medium-term scheduler** removes processes from memory to reduce the degree of multiprogramming; later the process can be reintroduced into memory and its execution continued where it left off. This scheme is called **swapping**: the process is **swapped out** to disk with its status saved, then **swapped in** back to memory where its status is restored.
concepts.detail: Swapping is typically necessary only when memory has been overcommitted and must be freed up — the classic intermediary between the long-term and short-term schedulers (Chapters 9 and 10 develop the memory-management mechanics).

concepts.statement: Switching the CPU to another process requires a **state save** of the current process and a **state restore** of a different process: the kernel saves the context of the old process **in its PCB** (CPU registers, process state, memory-management information) and loads the saved context of the newly scheduled process. This **context switch** is triggered by an interrupt or a system call.
concepts.detail: The context is exactly the PCB contents: register values plus the process state. When the dispatch cycle repeats, P0 is suspended with its state saved into PCB₀, P1 is reloaded from PCB₁ and runs — and the mirror image switches back.

concepts.term: The cost of a context switch
concepts.statement: Context-switch time is **pure overhead**: the system does no useful work while switching. Switching speed varies with memory speed, the number of registers that must be copied, and the existence of special hardware — a typical figure is a few microseconds, with complex systems taking up to milliseconds.
concepts.detail: Hardware support helps: processors with multiple register sets switch by changing the pointer to the current register set, falling back to copying only when active processes outnumber register sets. Advanced memory management adds work too — the address space of the current process must be preserved while the next one is prepared (Chapter 10).

examples.title: One process, all the queues
examples.problem: An I/O-bound text editor autosaves a document, types a burst of characters, and is preempted by a timer interrupt. List every queue it visits in order, and identify which scheduler moved it each time.

steps.label: Step 1: Entering the system
steps.text: The editor is created and **admitted** from the job pool into memory by the **long-term scheduler** — this is the only time the long-term scheduler touches it.

steps.label: Step 2: Autosave I/O
steps.text: Dispatched from the **ready queue** by the **short-term scheduler**, it issues a write to disk and moves to the **device queue** for that disk. The disk interrupt later returns it to the ready queue.

steps.label: Step 3: Preemption
steps.text: While processing keystrokes its time slice expires — an interrupt moves it **running → ready** with no device queue involved; its PCB is simply relinked at the ready queue’s tail.

steps.label: Step 4: Memory pressure
steps.text: Suppose many other processes launch and memory grows scarce: the **medium-term scheduler (swapper)** swaps the editor out to disk to lower the degree of multiprogramming, and swaps it back in later, restoring its saved status.

examples.result: job pool → (long-term) → ready queue → CPU → disk device queue → ready queue → CPU → preempted to ready queue → swapped out and back in by the medium-term scheduler — all three schedulers appear in one lifetime.

examples.title: Anatomy of a context switch
examples.problem: Process P₀ has been running when a timer interrupt arrives and the kernel decides to run P₁. Walk through the switch, and compute the overhead fraction if the switch costs 10 µs and P₁ will run for 1 ms.

steps.label: Step 1: Save the outgoing context
steps.text: On the interrupt, the kernel saves P₀’s program counter, CPU registers and state **into PCB₀** — the CPU is now executing the kernel, and P₀ is idle in memory with its execution frozen at the interrupted instruction.

steps.label: Step 2: Restore the incoming context
steps.text: The kernel loads P₁’s saved register values, program counter and state **from PCB₁** and jumps into P₁’s code — P₁ resumes exactly where it was last suspended.

steps.label: Step 3: Note what the CPU did meanwhile
steps.text: During save and restore, the CPU executed only kernel bookkeeping — no user instruction of either process advanced. This is the definition of overhead.

steps.label: Step 4: Price it
steps.text: Overhead fraction = $\frac{10\ \mu s}{1000\ \mu s} = 1\%$. Had the switch cost 1 ms, half the CPU would be lost to switching — the reason switch time must stay microscopic.

examples.result: save PCB₀ → reload PCB₁ → P₁ runs. The 10 µs switch against a 1 ms time slice costs about 1% of the CPU — small, but pure loss on every one of the thousands of switches per second.

keyTakeaways: Job queue = all processes; ready queue = in-memory processes waiting for a CPU (a linked list of PCBs with head and tail pointers); device queues = processes waiting on a specific device.
A running process leaves the CPU four ways: I/O request, creating a child and waiting, preemption (interrupt or time slice), or termination.
Long-term scheduler: selects from the job pool, controls the degree of multiprogramming, runs infrequently, wants a good I/O-bound/CPU-bound mix.
Short-term (CPU) scheduler: selects from the ready queue, runs at least every 100 ms and typically far more often — must be fast.
Medium-term scheduler: the swapper — removes and later reintroduces processes to adjust the degree of multiprogramming.
A context switch = save the old process’s context into its PCB, restore the new one from its PCB — pure overhead, typically a few microseconds, sped up by extra hardware register sets.

quiz.q: The ready queue in most kernels is implemented as:
options: a linked list of PCBs with head and tail pointers in a queue header
a sorted array of program counters
a copy of the job queue
quiz.explanation: The ready queue lives in kernel space as a linked list of process control blocks; the header points to the first and last PCB, and each PCB links to the next — queuing a process is relinking its PCB.

quiz.q: Which scheduler directly controls the degree of multiprogramming and is invoked only infrequently?
quiz.explanation: The long-term scheduler selects processes from the job pool into memory, so it alone decides how many processes are in memory (the degree of multiprogramming). Its decisions are separated by seconds or minutes, letting it choose carefully — including balancing I/O-bound against CPU-bound processes.

quiz.q: During a context switch between processes P0 and P1, the kernel:
options: runs user code of both processes simultaneously
saves P0’s state into its PCB and loads P1’s saved state from its PCB
copies P1’s heap into P0’s address space
terminates P0 so P1 can run
quiz.explanation: The switch is a state save of the outgoing process into its PCB followed by a state restore of the incoming process from its PCB. No useful user work happens during the switch — it is pure overhead.

quiz.q: A process whose time slice expires moves:
quiz.explanation: An expired time slice (or any interrupt) preempts the process back to the ready queue — it was not blocked, so it must stay eligible for immediate re-dispatch. Waiting is reserved for blocked processes awaiting an event.

intro: Processes are born from other processes: every system boots a root ancestor — systemd on Linux, running as PID 1 — and grows a tree of children identified by unique pids. UNIX builds that tree with fork() and exec(), Windows with one heavyweight CreateProcess(), and Android ranks the resulting processes by importance so a memory-starved phone knows exactly what to kill first. This section follows a process from creation through termination, zombies included.
objectives: Describe process creation: pids, the parent–child tree, and the resource- and execution-sharing options
Trace fork(), exec() and wait() — and explain why fork() returns twice
Explain zombies, orphans and cascading termination
Compare UNIX fork() with Windows CreateProcess()
Describe Android’s process importance hierarchy and systemd’s role as PID 1

concepts.term: Process creation and the process tree
concepts.statement: During execution a process may create new processes: the creating process is the **parent**, the new ones its **children**, and together they form a **tree of processes**. Each process is identified by a unique integer **process identifier (pid)**, usable as an index into kernel process tables. On Linux the **systemd** process — always pid 1 — is the root parent of all user processes, created first at boot; it spawns service processes such as logind and sshd.
concepts.detail: ps -el lists all active processes on UNIX/Linux; pstree draws the whole tree. Recursively tracing parents from any process leads back to systemd.

concepts.term: Resource and execution options at creation
concepts.statement: A child may obtain resources either **directly from the operating system** or **constrained to a subset of the parent’s resources** (which prevents any process from overloading the system by forking too many children). For execution there are two options: the parent **continues to execute concurrently** with its children, or it **waits** until some or all children terminate. For the address space there are also two: the child is a **duplicate of the parent**, or a **new program is loaded** into it.
concepts.detail: The parent may also pass initialization data — e.g., the name of a file to display — and the restriction-to-subset design is what makes resource quotas enforceable.

concepts.statement: The UNIX **fork()** system call creates a new process consisting of a **copy of the address space of the original** — both processes then continue execution at the instruction after fork(), with one difference: **fork() returns 0 in the child** and the **(nonzero) pid of the child in the parent**. The child inherits the parent’s privileges, scheduling attributes and open files.
concepts.detail: Modern systems implement the copy lazily as copy-on-write (Chapter 10): parent and child initially share the same physical pages, and each is copied only when one of them writes — making fork() cheap even for huge address spaces.

concepts.statement: After a fork(), a process typically calls **exec()** to replace its memory space with a new program: exec() loads a binary file into memory — destroying the memory image of the program containing the exec() call — and starts its execution, returning control **only if an error occurs**. The parent can issue **wait()** to move itself off the ready queue until a child terminates; wait() returns the terminated child’s pid and (via a pointer parameter) its exit status.
concepts.detail: execlp("/bin/ls", "ls", NULL) is one member of the exec() family. A child that skips exec() simply keeps running the parent’s code as an independent copy with its own data.

concepts.statement: A process terminates when it finishes and invokes **exit()** (possibly returning a status value to its waiting parent); all of its resources — memory, open files, I/O buffers — are deallocated. A terminated process whose parent has not yet called wait() is a **zombie**: its entry must remain in the process table because it holds the exit status. If the parent terminates first, the children are **orphans**, traditionally adopted by init/systemd, which periodically calls wait() to collect their statuses.
concepts.detail: All processes pass briefly through the zombie state. A parent can also terminate a child via a system call (TerminateProcess() on Windows) — usually allowed only for one’s own children — and some systems apply cascading termination: when a process terminates, all of its children are terminated with it.

concepts.statement: Some systems do not allow a child to exist if its parent has terminated. In such systems, if a process terminates — normally or abnormally — all of its children must also be terminated, a phenomenon called **cascading termination**, normally initiated by the operating system and propagating from parent down through all descendants.
concepts.detail: UNIX/Linux do not cascade automatically: orphaned children are re-parented to init/systemd instead, and left running.

concepts.statement: Windows processes are created with **CreateProcess()**: unlike fork(), which duplicates the caller’s address space, CreateProcess() **loads a specified program into the child at creation time**. Whereas fork() takes no parameters, CreateProcess() expects **no fewer than ten** — including STARTUPINFO (window properties, standard I/O handles) and PROCESS_INFORMATION (handles and identifiers of the new process and its thread) structures. The parent waits via **WaitForSingleObject(pi.hProcess, INFINITE)**.
concepts.detail: Example: CreateProcess(NULL, "...mspaint.exe", ...) launches Paint as a child, and the parent’s WaitForSingleObject() returns when the child exits — the Windows counterpart of wait().

concepts.statement: Because mobile memory is limited, Android may terminate processes to reclaim resources, choosing victims **in order of increasing importance**. From most to least important: **foreground** (the process on screen, currently interacted with), **visible** (not foreground but performing an activity the foreground refers to), **service** (background work apparent to the user, like streaming music), **background** (activity not apparent to the user), **empty** (holds no active components). Android assigns each process the highest ranking it qualifies for and reclaims empty processes first.
concepts.detail: Following the process life-cycle guidelines, Android saves a process’s state before termination and resumes from the saved state if the user navigates back — so a killed background app reappears where you left it.

concepts.term: systemd, Mach and Android IPC groundwork
concepts.statement: Linux replaced System V **init** with **systemd** as PID 1 — a more flexible root process that starts services described as **units** (services, sockets, targets) and tracks them in **cgroups** (control groups). **Mach** (the kernel beneath macOS/iOS) performs all inter-task communication by messages sent to **ports**. Android exposes cross-process RPC through its **binder** framework and the **AIDL** interface language (Section 3.5).
concepts.detail: Mach ports are finite, unidirectional mailboxes with one receiver but possibly many senders; port rights (like MACH_PORT_RIGHT_RECEIVE) control who may send or receive — an object-oriented, capability-style design.

examples.title: fork() returns twice
examples.problem: A program forks a child and each branch prints one line. Trace the two return values and the output, assuming the parent’s pid is 8415 and the child receives pid 8416.

steps.label: Step 1: The call
steps.text: The parent (pid 8415) executes pid = fork(). The kernel creates a child as a copy of the parent’s address space; both are now runnable at the instruction immediately after the call.

steps.label: Step 2: The parent’s view
steps.text: In the parent, fork() returns the child’s pid — the value 8416 — so the branch (pid == 0) is false and the parent executes its else-path: wait(NULL), then printing its message.

steps.label: Step 3: The child’s view
steps.text: In the child, fork() returns 0, so the branch (pid == 0) is true and the child executes the child-path code — the very same statement, experienced with a different return value.

steps.label: Step 4: What the user sees
steps.text: Two lines of output appear (one from each process, in either order — the scheduler decides): the child’s line first is just as likely as the parent’s. No line prints twice.

examples.result: One fork(), two return values: 0 in the child (pid 8416) and 8416 in the parent (pid 8415) — the call site executes once per process, which is how the same if/else separates parent from child behavior.

examples.title: How a shell runs a command: fork, exec, wait
examples.problem: The book’s Figure 3.8 program forks, the child runs execlp("/bin/ls", "ls", NULL), and the parent runs wait(NULL) followed by printf("Child Complete"). Trace the system-call sequence.

steps.label: Step 1: fork()
steps.text: The shell/parent calls fork(); the child gets a copy of the address space and both continue after the fork. The parent’s copy of pid is the child’s pid; the child’s copy is 0.

steps.label: Step 2: exec() in the child
steps.text: The child takes the (pid == 0) branch and calls execlp(): the ls binary is loaded into the child’s memory, destroying the old image — text, data, heap and stack are replaced. Execution never returns to the C code after execlp() (unless loading fails).

steps.label: Step 3: The parent waits
steps.text: The parent calls wait(NULL), blocking itself off the ready queue until the child terminates; meanwhile the child (now ls) lists the directory.

steps.label: Step 4: Exit and reap
steps.text: ls finishes and invokes exit(); the kernel wakes the parent, whose wait() returns the child’s pid and exit status. The parent prints Child Complete and proceeds to its own exit().

examples.result: fork() → child: exec() → child: exit(); in parallel parent: wait() → prints Child Complete. Every shell command you type follows this exact dance — fork, then the child becomes the command while the shell waits.

examples.title: Reading a Linux process tree
examples.problem: Figure 3.7 of the book shows systemd (pid 1) with children logind (8415), python (2808) and sshd (3028); logind’s child bash (8416) has children ps (9298) and vim (9204). Describe how this tree forms at boot and during a login session.

steps.label: Step 1: Boot
steps.text: The kernel starts systemd as the first user process (pid 1). systemd creates daemons that provide additional services — here logind for local logins and sshd for remote ones (plus python for a running service).

steps.label: Step 2: Login
steps.text: A user logs in at the console: logind creates the bash shell (pid 8416) for the session.

steps.label: Step 3: Working
steps.text: From bash the user runs ps (9298) and opens vim (9204) — each a child of bash, created by fork() (plus exec() to load the actual program).

steps.label: Step 4: Inspecting
steps.text: ps -el lists every process with its pid and parent; recursively following parents from vim leads bash → logind → systemd — the pstree command draws exactly this tree.

examples.result: One root (systemd, pid 1), service daemons in the middle, interactive tools at the leaves — every process on a Linux system has a place in this single genealogy.

keyTakeaways: Every process has a unique integer pid; on Linux, systemd (pid 1) is the root of the process tree — ps -el lists processes, pstree draws the tree.

At creation a child gets resources from the OS or a subset of the parent’s; the parent either runs concurrently with children or waits for them; the child is either a duplicate of the parent or loads a new program.
fork() returns twice: 0 in the child, the child’s pid in the parent; the child is a copy of the address space (made cheap by copy-on-write).
exec() replaces text and data with a new program and never returns on success; wait() blocks the parent and collects a child’s pid and exit status.
A terminated-but-unwaited child is a zombie; orphans are adopted by init/systemd; some systems cascade-terminate whole subtrees.
Windows CreateProcess() loads the new program at creation and takes ten-plus parameters (STARTUPINFO, PROCESS_INFORMATION); WaitForSingleObject() replaces wait().
Android kills processes in order of increasing importance: empty, then background, service, visible, foreground last.

quiz.q: Immediately after a successful fork() system call:
options: the child returns 0 from fork(), while the parent receives the child’s pid
the parent returns 0, and the child receives the parent’s pid
both processes receive the child’s pid
the child begins executing a new program
quiz.explanation: fork() duplicates the address space and both processes continue at the instruction after the call — but the return value differs: 0 in the new (child) process, the child’s nonzero pid in the parent. Loading a new program is exec()’s job, not fork()’s.

quiz.q: A zombie process is one that:
options: has terminated but whose parent has not yet called wait()
is stuck in an infinite loop
has been swapped out to disk
is waiting for I/O to complete
quiz.explanation: On termination the OS reclaims the process’s memory and files, but its process-table entry must survive until the parent calls wait() to collect the exit status — that lingering entry is the zombie. Waiting-for-I/O is the ordinary waiting state, not a zombie.

quiz.q: Which statement about Windows CreateProcess() is correct?
options: it takes no parameters, like fork()
it loads a specified program into the child’s address space at creation time and expects no fewer than ten parameters
it duplicates the parent’s address space, like fork()
it creates a thread pool for the child
quiz.explanation: Unlike fork()’s duplicate-then-exec pattern, CreateProcess() loads the target program immediately and is configured through ten-plus parameters, including the STARTUPINFO and PROCESS_INFORMATION structures.

quiz.q: Under memory pressure, Android reclaims processes in which order (first killed to last killed)?
quiz.explanation: Android ranks processes by importance — foreground (on screen) most important down to empty (no active components) least — and terminates them in increasing order of importance, reclaiming empty and background processes first and touching the foreground process only as a last resort.

quiz.q: On a Linux system, the root of the user-process tree is:
