examples.title: Two threads, two mutexes
examples.problem: pthread_mutex_t first_mutex and second_mutex are initialized unlocked. thread one runs pthread_mutex_lock(&first_mutex); pthread_mutex_lock(&second_mutex); … work …; unlock both; thread two locks second_mutex then first_mutex. Exhibit a deadlocked schedule.

steps.label: Step 1: Both threads start
steps.text: The scheduler runs thread one first: pthread_mutex_lock(&first_mutex) succeeds — thread one now owns first_mutex.

steps.label: Step 2: The second thread takes the other lock
steps.text: Before thread one proceeds, the scheduler switches: thread two executes pthread_mutex_lock(&second_mutex) and succeeds — thread two owns second_mutex.

steps.label: Step 3: The fatal second requests
steps.text: thread one calls pthread_mutex_lock(&second_mutex) — held by thread two — and blocks. thread two calls pthread_mutex_lock(&first_mutex) — held by thread one — and blocks.

steps.label: Step 4: The cycle is closed
steps.text: thread one waits for an event (the unlock of second_mutex) that only thread two can cause, while thread two waits for the unlock of first_mutex, which only thread one can cause. Neither ever reaches its unlock statements.

steps.label: Step 5: The scheduling dependence
steps.text: Had thread one instead acquired and released both locks before thread two requested any, the program would run flawlessly — the deadlock needs the interleaving of Step 1–2. That is why deadlock bugs survive casual testing.

examples.result: Deadlock: each thread holds one mutex and waits for the other’s — circular wait between exactly two threads. The fix previewed in Section 8.5: make both threads acquire the locks in the same order.

examples.title: A graph walk: from safe to deadlocked
examples.problem: A resource-allocation graph has $T = \{T_1, T_2, T_3\}$ and $R = \{R_1, R_2, R_3, R_4\}$ with instances: $R_1$ has one, $R_2$ has two, $R_3$ has one, $R_4$ has three. Edges: $E = \{T_1 \to R_1, T_2 \to R_3, R_1 \to T_2, R_2 \to T_2, R_2 \to T_1, R_3 \to T_3\}$. Is the system deadlocked? What if $T_3$ now requests an instance of $R_2$?

steps.label: Step 1: Translate the edges into state
steps.text: Assignment edges: $R_1$ is held by $T_2$; one instance of $R_2$ by $T_2$ and the other by $T_1$; $R_3$ by $T_3$; no instance of $R_4$ is allocated. Request edges: $T_1$ wants $R_1$; $T_2$ wants $R_3$. So $T_3$ is running freely, holding $R_3$, waiting for nothing.

steps.label: Step 2: Cycle check on the original graph
steps.text: Follow $T_1 \to R_1 \to T_2 \to R_3 \to T_3$: the path dies at $T_3$, which waits for nothing. No cycle exists — by the theorem, the system is definitely not deadlocked, even with $T_1$ and $T_2$ both blocked.

steps.label: Step 3: $T_3$ requests an instance of $R_2$
steps.text: Both instances of $R_2$ are held (by $T_1$ and $T_2$), so the request edge $T_3 \to R_2$ is added and stays — the grant cannot be made.

steps.label: Step 4: Two minimal cycles appear
steps.text: $T_1 \to R_1 \to T_2 \to R_3 \to T_3 \to R_2 \to T_1$ and $T_2 \to R_3 \to T_3 \to R_2 \to T_2$.

steps.label: Step 5: Every thread in the cycles is stuck
steps.text: $T_2$ waits for $R_3$, held by $T_3$; $T_3$ waits for $R_2$, held by $T_1$ and $T_2$; $T_1$ waits for $R_1$, held by $T_2$. Because $R_1$ and $R_3$ are single-instance types, each cycle member is provably deadlocked.

steps.label: Step 6: The idle instances save no one
steps.text: All three instances of $R_4$ sit unused — the waiting threads want the wrong resource type, and spare capacity of the wrong kind breaks nothing.

examples.result: Originally: no cycle, no deadlock (just ordinary waiting). After $T_3$’s request: two cycles through single-instance types — $T_1$, $T_2$ and $T_3$ are deadlocked.

examples.title: A cycle that lies
examples.problem: A graph contains threads $T_1$–$T_4$ and types $R_1$ (single instance) and $R_2$ (multiple instances). $T_1$ holds an instance of $R_2$ and requests $R_1$; $T_3$ holds $R_1$ and requests $R_2$; $T_4$ — otherwise uninvolved — holds another instance of $R_2$. Deadlocked?

steps.label: Step 1: Find the cycle
steps.text: $T_1 \to R_1 \to T_3 \to R_2 \to T_1$ — a genuine cycle through the graph.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply the theorem carefully
steps.text: $R_2$ has multiple instances, so a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock. The cycle alone proves only “one possibility.”

steps.label: Step 3: Look outside the cycle
steps.text: $T_4$ holds an instance of $R_2$ and is not blocked — it may finish and release it at any moment.

steps.label: Step 4: Break the would-be deadlock
steps.text: If $T_4$ releases its instance of $R_2$, that instance can be allocated to $T_3$; $T_3$ then completes, releases $R_1$, and $T_1$ proceeds. The cycle dissolves without any recovery action.

steps.label: Step 5: Conclusion
steps.text: The threads are entangled but not deadlocked — this schedule-dependent tangle is why multi-instance systems need the detection algorithm of Section 8.7 rather than a graph glance.

examples.result: A cycle with multi-instance resource types is a warning, not a verdict: the system may or may not be deadlocked, and only deeper analysis — or waiting — settles it.

keyTakeaways: Resources come in types $R_i$ with $W_i$ identical instances; locks and semaphores are resources and get their own classes.
The lifecycle is request, use, release — and the kernel’s tables plus wait queues are the bookkeeping behind it.
Deadlock = every thread in a set waits for an event only another thread in the set can cause.
The two-mutex pattern (one thread locking A then B, the other B then A) deadlocks only on unlucky schedules — the reason such bugs evade testing.
Four conditions must ALL hold: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait — and circular wait implies hold and wait.
Resource-allocation graphs: request edge $T_i \to R_j$, assignment edge $R_j \to T_i$; no cycle means no deadlock.
A cycle in a single-instance system is a proven deadlock; with multiple instances it is only a possibility — one warning that matrix algorithms must resolve.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock?
quiz.explanation: The four are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Bounded waiting is a correctness requirement for critical-section solutions — a liveness guarantee, not a deadlock ingredient.

quiz.q: If a resource-allocation graph contains no cycle, then:
options: the system is definitely not deadlocked
a deadlock may still exist among waiting threads
quiz.explanation: Acyclicity is the strong direction of the theorem: deadlock requires a cycle, so no cycle rules deadlock out entirely — blocked threads in an acyclic graph are merely waiting for threads that can still run.

quiz.q: A cycle appears in a resource-allocation graph in which one involved resource type has two instances. What can be concluded?
options: A deadlock may or may not exist — the cycle is necessary but not sufficient
The system is definitely not deadlocked
quiz.explanation: With multiple instances, another thread outside the cycle can free an instance and dissolve the tangle — as in the book’s Figure 8.6, where T4 can release R2 and unblock the whole cycle. Single-instance cycles alone are conclusive.

quiz.q: In the two-mutex Pthreads example, deadlock occurs exactly when:
options: each thread acquires its first lock before either acquires its second
both threads request the same single lock
one thread runs to completion first
the mutexes are initialized to different values
quiz.explanation: The deadlock needs the interleaving where thread one holds first_mutex and thread two holds second_mutex, so each then blocks on the other. If either thread completes both acquisitions first, the other simply waits momentarily — no cycle ever forms.

quiz.q: The circular-wait condition implies which other necessary condition?
quiz.explanation: To be part of a circular wait, a thread must be holding one resource while waiting for the next — that is hold and wait by definition. The conditions are therefore not completely independent, though each is still a separately attackable target for prevention.

intro: If deadlock is four conditions holding at once, the first defense is to make one of them impossible — prevention — and the second is to stay out of trouble by knowing the future: avoidance, where each request is granted only if the system provably remains safe. The Banker’s algorithm is the classic avoidance machinery, and its matrices are among the most worked exercises in all of operating systems.
objectives: Name the three global strategies for deadlock and what each costs
Break each of the four necessary conditions and judge the practicality of each scheme
Prove that total ordering of resource types prevents circular wait
Define safe states and distinguish safe, unsafe and deadlocked states
Execute the safety algorithm and the resource-request algorithm on the book’s five-thread example

concepts.statement: A system can **ignore** deadlocks and pretend they never occur — the choice of most operating systems, including Linux and Windows, since deadlocks are rare and prevention is expensive; it falls to developers to write deadlock-free programs. It can **prevent or avoid** deadlocks so the system never enters a deadlocked state. Or it can let deadlocks happen, **detect** them and **recover** — the database approach.
concepts.detail: Undetected deadlock lets performance rot: resources are held by threads that cannot run, more threads sink into the deadlock as they request, and the system eventually stops functioning and needs a manual restart. Databases can afford detection and recovery because they already keep transaction logs.

concepts.statement: A deadlock requires at least one nonsharable resource, so **sharable resources cannot be part of a deadlock**: read-only files can be opened simultaneously by many threads, and no thread ever waits for one. Spooling printer output makes the printer logically sharable — every thread writes to the spool and one daemon owns the device.
concepts.detail: The limit is fundamental: some resources are intrinsically nonsharable — a mutex lock cannot be simultaneously held by several threads — so mutual exclusion cannot be denied in general, only engineered away per resource.

concepts.statement: Two protocols guarantee a thread never holds while waiting. **Request everything up front**: each thread requests and is allocated all its resources before execution begins. **Release then request**: a thread may request resources only when it currently holds none — before asking for anything more it must release what it has.
concepts.detail: Both suffer two disadvantages: **low utilization** (a mutex held for an entire run though needed for a moment) and **starvation** — a thread needing several popular resources may wait indefinitely because one of them is always allocated to somebody else.

concepts.statement: If a thread holding resources requests another and must wait, **all its current resources are preempted** — implicitly released, added to the list it is waiting for; the thread restarts only when it can regain the old resources plus the new. The refined variant: if a request cannot be granted, check whether the wanted resources are held by other **waiting** threads and preempt them from those.
concepts.detail: This works only where state is cheaply saveable and restorable — CPU registers, memory pages, database transactions. It cannot generally be applied to mutex locks and semaphores, precisely the resources where deadlocks most commonly occur.

concepts.statement: Impose a total ordering on resource types via a one-to-one function $F: R \to \mathbb{N}$, and require each thread to request resources only in **increasing order**: it may request $R_j$ only if $F(R_j) > F(R_i)$ for every $R_i$ it holds (equivalently, it must first release any $R_i$ with $F(R_i) \ge F(R_j)$); several instances of one type must be requested together.
concepts.detail: Proof by contradiction: suppose a circular wait $\{T_0, \ldots, T_n\}$ exists, $T_i$ waiting for $R_i$ held by $T_{i+1}$ (indices modulo). Since $T_{i+1}$ holds $R_i$ while requesting $R_{i+1}$, the protocol forces $F(R_i) < F(R_{i+1})$ for all i — so $F(R_0) < F(R_1) < \cdots < F(R_n) < F(R_0)$, impossible by transitivity. Hence no circular wait. In practice: ordering hundreds of locks is hard, Java developers fall back on System.identityHashCode() for the function F — and dynamic lock acquisition (an account-transfer function locking two accounts in whatever order they arrive) can still deadlock despite a global ordering.

concepts.statement: A state is **safe** if the system can allocate resources to each thread up to its maximum and still avoid deadlock — formally, if there exists a **safe sequence** $\langle T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_n \rangle$ such that, for each $T_i$, the requests $T_i$ can still make are satisfied by the currently available resources plus the resources held by all $T_j$ with $j < i$. If no such sequence exists, the state is **unsafe**.
concepts.detail: The containments: every deadlock is an unsafe state, but an unsafe state is not necessarily deadlocked — it merely *may* lead to deadlock depending on how threads behave. A safe state is never a deadlocked state. Avoidance = never leave the safe region: a request is granted only if the resulting state is still safe, so a thread may wait even when resources are available.

concepts.statement: For $n$ threads and $m$ resource types, maintain: **Available** — a length-m vector, $\text{Available}[j] = k$ means $k$ instances of $R_j$ are free; **Max** — an $n \times m$ matrix of maximum demands; **Allocation** — an $n \times m$ matrix of current holdings; **Need** — an $n \times m$ matrix of remaining requirements, with $\text{Need}_{ij} = \text{Max}_{ij} - \text{Allocation}_{ij}$. For vectors, $X \le Y$ iff $X[i] \le Y[i]$ for all i; rows are written $\text{Allocation}_i$, $\text{Need}_i$.
concepts.detail: A thread entering the system must declare its maximum — which may not exceed the system totals — and from then on every request can be checked against Need. The name comes from banking: never loan out cash in a way that leaves the bank unable to satisfy all its customers.

concepts.statement: 1. Initialize Work = Available and Finish[i] = false for all i. 2. Find an index i with Finish[i] == false and $\text{Need}_i \le \text{Work}$; if none exists, go to step 4. 3. Set Work = Work + $\text{Allocation}_i$ and Finish[i] = true; go to step 2. 4. The state is safe **iff** Finish[i] == true for all i.
concepts.detail: The intuition: a thread whose remaining need fits in Work could run to completion even if everything else froze, then return everything it holds — so its allocation can be folded into Work and the next thread examined. The order in which eligible threads are picked does not matter for the yes/no answer. Cost: $O(m \times n^2)$ operations.

concepts.statement: When $T_i$ requests a vector $\text{Request}_i$: **1.** If $\text{Request}_i \le \text{Need}_i$, continue; otherwise raise an error — the thread exceeded its declared maximum. **2.** If $\text{Request}_i \le \text{Available}$, continue; otherwise $T_i$ must wait. **3.** Pretend to grant: $\text{Available} = \text{Available} - \text{Request}_i$; $\text{Allocation}_i = \text{Allocation}_i + \text{Request}_i$; $\text{Need}_i = \text{Need}_i - \text{Request}_i$. Run the safety algorithm: safe — the transaction completes and $T_i$ keeps the resources; unsafe — roll back to the old state and let $T_i$ wait.
concepts.detail: The pretend-and-test structure is the whole of avoidance: each grant is a trial balloon retracted whenever safety would be lost. Note a request can be refused even when the resources are physically available — staying safe is worth more than short-term utilization.

examples.title: Safe today, unsafe tomorrow
examples.problem: A system has 12 instances of one resource type and three threads. Thread $T_0$ requires up to 10 (currently holding 5), $T_1$ up to 4 (holding 2), $T_2$ up to 9 (holding 2); 3 instances are free. Is the state safe? What happens if $T_2$ requests and is granted one more?

steps.label: Step 1: Test safety
steps.text: Try $\langle T_1, T_0, T_2 \rangle$: $T_1$ needs at most $4 - 2 = 2$ more, and $2 \le 3$ available — grant, let it finish, and its 2 held instances return: 5 free.

steps.label: Step 2: Continue the sequence
steps.text: $T_0$ needs $10 - 5 = 5$ more and $5 \le 5$ — it can finish and return its 5, letting the pool reach 10; $T_2$ needs $9 - 2 = 7$ and $7 \le 10$ — all threads can complete. The state is safe.

steps.label: Step 3: $T_2$ is granted one more
steps.text: Holdings become $T_0$: 5, $T_1$: 2, $T_2$: 3 — only 2 remain free.

steps.label: Step 4: Retest safety
steps.text: Only $T_1$ can still be satisfied ($2 \le 2$); once it finishes and returns its 2, only 4 are free. $T_0$ needs 5 and $T_2$ needs 6 — neither fits, and no order of completion helps: no safe sequence exists. The state is unsafe (not yet deadlocked).

steps.label: Step 5: The danger materializes
steps.text: If $T_0$ then requests its 5 and $T_2$ its 6, both block — each waiting for resources that only the other’s completion could free: deadlock.

examples.result: Granting one innocent-looking request flipped the system from safe to unsafe. The avoidance rule: that grant should have been postponed until another thread finished — the decision the Banker’s algorithm automates.

examples.title: The Banker’s safety algorithm, worked
examples.problem: Five threads $T_0$–$T_4$ share three resource types: A has 10 instances, B has 5, C has 7. The snapshot (Allocation | Max) is below with Available = $(3, 3, 2)$: $$\begin{array}{c|ccc|ccc} & A & B & C & A & B & C \\ \hline T_0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 7 & 5 & 3 \\ T_1 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 3 & 2 & 2 \\ T_2 & 3 & 0 & 2 & 9 & 0 & 2 \\ T_3 & 2 & 1 & 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ T_4 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 & 3 & 3 \end{array}$$ Is the system in a safe state?

steps.label: Step 2: First pass over the threads
steps.text: Work = $(3,3,2)$, all Finish false. $T_0$ needs $(7,4,3) \nleq (3,3,2)$ — skip. $T_1$ needs $(1,2,2) \le (3,3,2)$ — eligible.

steps.label: Step 5: Verdict
steps.text: Finish[i] = true for all five threads, so the state is safe. The witness sequence is $\langle T_1, T_3, T_4, T_2, T_0 \rangle$ — the book’s answer; it is not unique (after $T_3$, $T_0$ had also become eligible).

examples.result: The system is safe: $\langle T_1, T_3, T_4, T_2, T_0 \rangle$ is a safe sequence — every thread can run to maximum, in that order, on current resources plus the returns of those before it.

examples.title: Granting a request: $T_1$ asks for $(1, 0, 2)$
examples.problem: From the same snapshot, thread $T_1$ requests one instance of A and two of C: $\text{Request}_1 = (1,0,2)$. Can it be granted immediately? And what about a $(3,3,0)$ request from $T_4$, or a $(0,2,0)$ request from $T_0$?

steps.label: Step 1: Legality check
steps.text: $\text{Request}_1 = (1,0,2) \le \text{Need}_1 = (1,2,2)$ — within the declared maximum. $\text{Request}_1 = (1,0,2) \le \text{Available} = (3,3,2)$ — the resources exist. Proceed to the pretend-allocation.

steps.label: Step 3: Run the safety algorithm on the new state
Step 4: Grant the request
steps.text: All threads finish — the sequence $\langle T_1, T_3, T_4, T_0, T_2 \rangle$ certifies the new state safe, so the transaction completes: $T_1$ keeps the resources.

steps.label: Step 5: The two refusals
steps.text: A $(3,3,0)$ request from $T_4$ fails step 2 outright — with Available now $(2,3,0)$, three instances of A do not exist, so $T_4$ waits. A $(0,2,0)$ request from $T_0$ passes availability — $(0,2,0) \le (2,3,0)$ — but the pretend-state is unsafe: after granting, Work = $(2,1,0)$ and **no** thread’s Need fits ($T_1$ needs two B’s, $T_3$ one C, and so on), so no safe sequence exists. The grant is rolled back and $T_0$ waits.

examples.result: $\text{Request}_1 = (1,0,2)$: granted — the new state is safe. $T_4$’s $(3,3,0)$: refused for lack of resources. $T_0$’s $(0,2,0)$: refused even though the resources are available, because spending them would leave the system in an unsafe state — avoidance in action.

keyTakeaways: Three strategies: ignore (Linux and Windows — deadlocks are rare), prevent or avoid (never deadlock), detect and recover (databases with transaction logs).

Mutual exclusion falls only to sharable resources (spooled printers, read-only files) and preemption only to saveable state (CPU registers, database transactions) — neither negation reaches the mutex locks where deadlocks actually breed.
Hold and wait falls to request-all-up-front or release-then-request, at the price of low utilization and possible starvation.
Total ordering of resource types — always request ascending $F$ values — provably prevents circular wait; dynamic lock acquisition can still defeat it.
Safe state: some completion order $\langle T_1, \ldots, T_n \rangle$ lets every thread reach its maximum on current resources plus earlier returns; unsafe ≠ deadlocked.
Banker’s algorithm: Need = Max − Allocation; the safety algorithm folds finishable threads into Work at $O(m \times n^2)$; the request algorithm pretends, tests safety, and rolls back if unsafe.
Requests can be denied even when resources are free — safety, not availability, is the criterion.

quiz.q: With $\text{Max}_{T_0} = (7,5,3)$ and $\text{Allocation}_{T_0} = (0,1,0)$, the Need row for $T_0$ is:
quiz.explanation: Need is the remaining requirement: $\text{Need}_{ij} = \text{Max}_{ij} - \text{Allocation}_{ij}$, componentwise $(7-0, 5-1, 3-0) = (7,4,3)$. The subtraction is per resource type, never a scalar total.

quiz.q: Requiring every thread to request and be allocated all its resources before it begins execution negates which condition?
quiz.explanation: A thread holding everything it will ever need cannot be waiting for more — hold and wait is impossible. The costs are exactly the two the book lists: resources sit allocated but unused (low utilization), and a thread needing several popular resources may starve.

quiz.q: An unsafe state is one in which:
options: no safe sequence exists — deadlock is possible but not certain
Available exceeds Need for every thread
quiz.explanation: Unsafe means the OS can no longer guarantee a completion order if threads demand their maxima — deadlock becomes possible depending on future requests. Deadlocked states are a subset of unsafe states; the containment is strict.

quiz.q: In the safety algorithm, a thread $T_i$ is selected to “finish” when:
quiz.explanation: Work plays the role of “resources that could be freed for the taking”: a thread whose remaining need fits could run to completion even in the worst case, so its whole allocation is folded into Work and it is marked finished. Selection order does not affect the final verdict.

quiz.q: The book’s example refuses $T_0$’s request $(0,2,0)$ even though the resources are available. Why?
options: Granting it would leave the system in an unsafe state, so the trial allocation is rolled back
Requests of exactly two units are always denied
quiz.explanation: The request passes both legality checks — Need and Available — but the pretend-allocation leaves no thread able to finish: no safe sequence exists. Avoidance rolls the state back and makes $T_0$ wait; physical availability is not the criterion, provable safety is.

**Step 1 — Given data:** compute Need $=$ Max $-$ Allocation: T0 $(7,4,3)$, T1 $(1,2,2)$, T2 $(6,0,0)$, T3 $(0,1,1)$, T4 $(4,3,1)$; Work $= (3,3,2)$.
**Step 2 — Rule:** repeatedly pick unfinished $i$ with Need$_i \le$ Work, then Work $+=$ Allocation$_i$.
**Step 3 — Computation:**
```
Work(3,3,2): T1 fits -> (5,3,2); T3 fits -> (7,4,3);
T4 fits -> (7,4,5); T2 fits -> (10,4,7); T0 fits -> (10,5,7)
```
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** all Finish true, so state is safe; order among eligible threads does not affect the verdict.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** starting with T0 fails since $(7,4,3) \nleq (3,3,2)$; T2-first fails similarly; unsafe verdict contradicts the constructed witness.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** $\langle T_1,T_3,T_4,T_2,T_0 \rangle$ certifies safety.

quiz.q: From the same snapshot (Available $(3,3,2)$), T1 requests $(1,0,2)$. Can it be granted immediately?
options: Yes; the pretend state has safe sequence $\langle T_1,T_3,T_4,T_0,T_2 \rangle$
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** Request$_1 = (1,0,2)$, Need$_1 = (1,2,2)$, Available $= (3,3,2)$.
**Step 2 — Rule:** check Request $\le$ Need, then Request $\le$ Available, then pretend-grant and run safety; roll back if unsafe.
**Step 3 — Computation:** legality holds on both; pretend gives Available $(2,3,0)$, Allocation$_1 = (3,0,2)$, Need$_1 = (0,2,0)$; safety run:
```
(2,3,0): T1 -> (5,3,2); T3 -> (7,4,3); T4 -> (7,4,5); T0 -> (7,5,5); T2 done
```
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** all finish, so the new state is safe and the grant completes. A $(0,2,0)$ ask from T0 with the same Available would instead go unsafe and be rolled back.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** Need and Available both pass, so neither refusal applies; skipping the test abandons avoidance.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** grant now; T1 keeps the resources.

intro: When a system neither prevents nor avoids deadlock, it must catch it in the act and clean up afterward. Detection ranges from cycle-hunting in wait-for graphs to the matrix algorithm for multiple instances; recovery means terminating or preempting with rollback — and both must beware starving the victim they keep choosing. Livelock closes the chapter’s liveness story: threads that never block and never progress.
objectives: Build wait-for graphs and detect deadlock in single-instance systems
Run the multiple-instance detection algorithm and interpret the Finish vector
Choose a detection frequency — per-request, periodic interval, or CPU-utilization threshold
Recover by termination or by preemption with rollback, and prevent victim starvation
Recognize livelock and use lockdep, BCC and Java thread dumps as detection tools

concepts.statement: When every resource type has a **single instance**, the resource-allocation graph collapses into a **wait-for graph**: remove the resource nodes and merge each pair $T_i \to R_q$, $R_q \to T_j$ into one edge $T_i \to T_j$ meaning “$T_i$ is waiting for $T_j$.” A deadlock exists **if and only if** the wait-for graph contains a cycle, so the system maintains it and periodically runs a cycle-detection search — $O(n^2)$ over n threads.
concepts.detail: The biconditional is what makes single-instance systems pleasant: a cycle is a complete verdict, not a warning. The same graph, built live from lock operations, is what the BCC and Java tools automate.

concepts.statement: With several instances per type, maintain **Available** (length m), **Allocation** ($n \times m$) and **Request** ($n \times m$ — what each thread is asking for **right now**). 1. Work = Available; Finish[i] = false for every thread with $\text{Allocation}_i \ne 0$, and Finish[i] = true for any thread holding nothing. 2. Find i with Finish[i] == false and $\text{Request}_i \le \text{Work}$. 3. Work = Work + $\text{Allocation}_i$; Finish[i] = true; repeat step 2. 4. The system is deadlocked iff Finish[i] == false for some i — and exactly those threads are the deadlocked ones.
concepts.detail: The structure mirrors the safety algorithm with Request in place of Need — the future is unknown here, only current demands. Step 3’s optimism: a thread whose request can be met is assumed to need nothing further and to soon return everything; if that assumption is wrong, any resulting deadlock is simply caught on the next invocation. Cost: $O(m \times n^2)$.

concepts.statement: Two factors set the frequency: how often deadlocks are likely, and how many threads are affected when one strikes. The extremes: invoke the algorithm **every time a request cannot be granted immediately** — maximal information (the deadlocked set and the request that closed the cycle) at maximal overhead — or invoke it on a **schedule**: once per hour, or whenever CPU utilization drops below a threshold such as 40 percent, since a deadlock eventually cripples throughput and drags utilization down.
concepts.detail: The middle ground accepts a coarse clock: detection at arbitrary intervals may find many cycles whose triggering request can no longer be identified — all the deadlocked threads jointly caused it, and the “culprit” is a scheduling artifact.

concepts.statement: Break a deadlock by aborting processes: **abort all deadlocked processes** — guaranteed to break the cycle, at the cost of discarding all their partial computations — or **abort one at a time until the cycle dissolves**, re-running the detection algorithm after each termination. Partial termination demands a victim: a policy decision weighing priority, time already computed and time remaining, the number and type of resources used, how many more resources are needed, and how many processes must be terminated.
concepts.detail: Aborting is not clean: a process mid-update leaves files in an incorrect state, and terminating a mutex holder leaves shared data with no integrity guarantees even though the lock itself is marked available. Databases embrace this path — a victim transaction is aborted and rolled back, its locks released, the remaining transactions resume, and the aborted transaction is reissued; MySQL picks victims that minimize the number of rows inserted, updated or deleted.

concepts.statement: Successively **preempt resources** from deadlocked processes and hand them to others until the cycle breaks. Three problems must be addressed: **selecting a victim** — which resources and processes to preempt, minimizing cost (resources held, time consumed); **rollback** — the preempted process must be returned to some safe state, and since identifying one is hard, the simplest policy is a **total rollback** (abort and restart), while rolling back only as far as necessary requires the system to retain much more state, typically via transaction logs; and **starvation**.
concepts.detail: Cost-based victim selection is the mirror of the termination policy: the cheapest casualty is chosen — which is exactly how the same process gets chosen again and again.

concepts.statement: If victim selection is driven by cost factors alone, the same unfortunate process may be picked every time — preempted, rolled back, preempted again — and never complete its task: starvation. The practical fix: ensure a process can be a victim only a small, finite number of times, most commonly by **including the number of rollbacks (its age) in the cost factor**, so a repeatedly victimized process eventually becomes too expensive to choose again.
concepts.detail: Recovery, like every resource policy in this chapter, is really two questions: break the cycle now, and keep the cure from becoming a chronic disease.

concepts.statement: **Livelock** is a liveness failure kin to deadlock: threads are unable to proceed, but for a different reason — a thread continuously attempts an action that keeps failing, changing state all the while. It is the two-people-in-a-corridor shuffle: he steps right, she steps left, still blocking each other; he steps left, she steps right; and so on — nobody is blocked, nobody makes progress.
concepts.detail: The code shape: rewriting the two-mutex deadlock with pthread_mutex_trylock() — each thread acquires its first lock, fails trylock on the second, releases everything, and immediately retries; if both retry in lockstep, both spin forever. The general cure is to retry failing operations at random times — precisely the Ethernet approach to packet collisions, where hosts back off a random interval before retransmitting. Livelock is less common than deadlock but equally scheduling-dependent.

concepts.term: Tools: lockdep, BCC and thread dumps
concepts.statement: **Linux lockdep** verifies locking order in a (running development) kernel: it dynamically tracks the order in which locks are acquired and reports a possible deadlock when locks are grabbed out of order; it also reports when kernel code acquires a spinlock that is also used in an interrupt handler while interrupts are enabled — a spin-forever scenario. The **BCC deadlock detector** traces a user process’s calls to pthread_mutex_lock()/pthread_mutex_unlock(), builds the wait-for graph of its mutexes and reports a possible deadlock when it detects a cycle. **Java thread dumps** (jstack, Ctrl-\ on UNIX/macOS, Ctrl-Break on Windows) snapshot every thread and the locks it waits for; the JVM searches the wait-for graph and reports deadlocked threads.
concepts.detail: lockdep is a development tool — too slow for production systems — but its designers reported deadlock reports reduced by an order of magnitude within a few years of its 2006 introduction, and recent revisions extend it to user applications with Pthreads mutexes. Together these tools are deadlock detection made practical: cycle-hunting, outsourced.

examples.title: Running the detection algorithm
examples.problem: Five threads $T_0$–$T_4$ share three types: A has 7 instances, B has 2, C has 6. The snapshot (Allocation | Request) with Available = $(0,0,0)$: $$\begin{array}{c|ccc|ccc} & A & B & C & A & B & C \\ \hline T_0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ T_1 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 & 2 \\ T_2 & 3 & 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ T_3 & 2 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ T_4 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 2 \end{array}$$ Is the system deadlocked? What if $T_2$ requests one more instance of C?

steps.label: Step 1: Initialize
steps.text: Work = $(0,0,0)$. Every thread has a nonzero Allocation, so Finish[i] = false for all five — including $T_0$, whose Request row is $(0,0,0)$: the book’s zero-request row.

steps.label: Step 2: $T_0$ finishes on an empty request
steps.text: Finish[0] == false and $\text{Request}_0 = (0,0,0) \le (0,0,0)$ — a request for nothing is always satisfiable. Work = $(0,0,0) + (0,1,0) = (0,1,0)$; Finish[0] = true.

steps.label: Step 4: Verdict on the original state
steps.text: Finish[i] = true for every thread — the system is **not** deadlocked; the completion order $\langle T_0, T_2, T_3, T_1, T_4 \rangle$ demonstrates it.

steps.label: Step 5: $T_2$ asks for one more C
steps.text: $\text{Request}_2$ becomes $(0,0,1)$. Re-run: $T_0$ still finishes, Work = $(0,1,0)$ — and now $T_1$ needs $(2,0,2)$, $T_2$ needs $(0,0,1)$, $T_3$ needs $(1,0,0)$, $T_4$ needs $(0,0,2)$: not one of them fits $(0,1,0)$.

steps.label: Step 6: Verdict on the new state
steps.text: Finish stays false for $T_1$, $T_2$, $T_3$ and $T_4$: those four threads are deadlocked — the resources they would return upon completion are exactly what the others are waiting for.

examples.result: Original state: no deadlock — a zero request lets $T_0$ drain its allocation into Work and unlock the whole cascade. After $T_2$’s single extra request for C: deadlock among $T_1$, $T_2$, $T_3$ and $T_4$, with only $T_0$ able to complete.

examples.title: From deadlock to livelock with trylock()
examples.problem: Rewrite the two-mutex deadlock so each thread uses pthread_mutex_trylock() for its second lock and releases both on failure. What behavior emerges?

steps.label: Step 1: The new shape
steps.text: thread one: lock(first_mutex); if (trylock(second_mutex) succeeds) { work; unlock both; done } else unlock(first_mutex); and loop while not done. thread two mirrors it starting from second_mutex.

steps.label: Step 2: The colliding moment
steps.text: thread one acquires first_mutex; thread two acquires second_mutex; each trylock on the other’s mutex fails — the same configuration that deadlocked the original program.

steps.label: Step 3: But nobody blocks
steps.text: On failure each thread releases the lock it holds and loops — the states keep changing: acquire, try, fail, release, acquire, try, fail, release…

steps.label: Step 4: Lockstep doom
steps.text: If both threads retry at the same rate, they keep meeting in the fatal configuration: both are runnable, both are executing instructions — and neither ever holds both locks. No thread is blocked, and no progress occurs: livelock.

steps.label: Step 5: The cure
steps.text: Have each thread retry after a random delay. The two retry streams decorrelate — the Ethernet collision-backoff strategy — and one of them soon finds the other’s lock released, completing its work.

examples.result: Livelock: continuous activity, zero progress — distinct from deadlock’s frozen waiting, and curable by randomness where order creates the pathology.

keyTakeaways: Single-instance systems: collapse the resource-allocation graph into a wait-for graph — deadlock iff a cycle; maintain it and scan periodically at $O(n^2)$.

Multiple-instance detection mirrors the safety algorithm with Request in place of Need — threads holding nothing start with Finish = true, the algorithm optimistically assumes a satisfiable thread will need nothing more, and exactly the threads left with Finish = false are deadlocked.
Run detection per ungrantable request (precise, expensive) or on a schedule — hourly, or when CPU utilization drops below a threshold like 40 percent.
Recovery by termination: all deadlocked processes at once, or one victim at a time chosen by priority, time invested and remaining, resources held and needed, and how many terminations it takes.

Recovery by preemption: select a victim, roll it back (total rollback is simplest; partial needs transaction-log state), and fold rollback counts into victim cost to avoid starving the same process forever.
Livelock: threads retry failing actions in lockstep — never blocked, never progressing; random backoff (Ethernet-style) breaks the symmetry.
Tooling is cycle-hunting at scale: Linux lockdep (lock-order verification in the kernel), the BCC deadlock detector (wait-for graphs from traced mutex calls) and Java thread dumps via jstack.

quiz.q: In the deadlock-detection algorithm, threads whose Allocation row is all zeros are initialized with Finish[i] = true because:
options: they hold nothing, so they cannot be part of a deadlock and their completion adds nothing
their requests are always granted immediately
quiz.explanation: A thread holding no resources cannot be trapped in a hold-and-wait cycle, and there is nothing to reclaim from it — marking it finished at the start simply removes it from consideration while leaving Work unchanged.

quiz.q: The detection algorithm differs from the Banker’s safety algorithm chiefly in that it:
options: uses the current Request matrix instead of the future-oriented Need matrix
does not use an Available vector
requires threads to declare their maximum demands
runs only when the system is safe
quiz.explanation: Detection knows nothing about the future — it sees only what threads are asking for now. Avoidance needs the declared maxima to compute Need; detection deliberately trades that knowledge for applicability to any system.

quiz.q: Including the number of rollbacks in a victim-selection cost function is designed to prevent:
options: starvation — the same process being victimized over and over
quiz.explanation: A purely cost-based choice can pick the same cheapest victim every cycle, so it never finishes. Aging the victim by counting its rollbacks raises its cost until the policy eventually chooses somebody else — a finite number of victimizations per process.

quiz.q: Livelock differs from deadlock in that livelocked threads:
options: keep executing — repeatedly attempting actions that fail — without being blocked
are blocked in the kernel waiting for I/O
quiz.explanation: Deadlock freezes threads in a wait; livelock sets them marching in place: lock, try, fail, release, repeat. The corridor-politeness image captures it — two people sidestepping each other forever, never stopped, never past.

quiz.q: Linux lockdep reports a possible deadlock when:
options: it observes locks being acquired out of the established order, or interrupt-unsafe spinlock use
a thread waits more than two context switches
quiz.explanation: lockdep dynamically tracks lock-acquisition order and flags inversions — the circular-wait pattern forming — along with spinlocks acquired with interrupts enabled when the same lock is used in an interrupt handler, which would make the handler spin on a lock the preempted holder still owns.

intro: Before an instruction can execute, the CPU generates an address — and something must decide which physical byte that address names. This section traces the journey of an address, symbolic in source code, relocatable after compilation, absolute after loading, and introduces the hardware (the MMU) that lets a process live anywhere in memory and even move while it runs.
objectives: Distinguish compile-time, load-time and execution-time address binding, and say when each is possible
Define logical (virtual) and physical addresses and explain why they diverge under execution-time binding
Explain how base/relocation and limit registers implement dynamic relocation and protection
Contrast dynamic loading with dynamic linking, and describe the role of DLLs and shared libraries

concepts.statement: **Address binding** — deciding which physical memory location each symbolic address names — can happen at three moments. At **compile time**, if the process’s future memory location is known, the compiler emits **absolute code** with fixed physical addresses; moving the process later means recompiling. At **load time**, the compiler emits **relocatable code** and the loader patches addresses when the program is placed; a new placement means a reload, not a recompile. At **execution time**, binding is deferred until each reference is made, so the process can move while it runs.
concepts.detail: Execution-time binding is the only scheme compatible with swapping and compaction; it requires special hardware — the memory-management unit — and is what most operating systems use. The classic compile-time binding is the MS-DOS .COM-format program, handed a fixed location with no possibility of relocation.

concepts.statement: A **logical address** (also called a **virtual address**) is generated by the CPU; a **physical address** is the one seen by the memory unit — the address loaded into the memory-address register. Compile-time and load-time binding produce identical logical and physical addresses; execution-time binding makes them differ, and mapping one to the other at run time is the job of the MMU.
concepts.detail: The set of all logical addresses a program generates is its **logical address space**; the corresponding physical addresses form the **physical address space**. The user program creates, stores and compares pointers as pure logical numbers — the memory-mapping hardware translates them only at the moment they are used as addresses.

concepts.statement: The **MMU** is the hardware device that maps virtual to physical addresses at run time. The simplest scheme is a **relocation (base) register**: every logical address a process emits has the base value added to it before it reaches memory, so the physical address is $\text{base} + \text{logical}$.
concepts.detail: With base $= 14000$, a reference to location 0 is dynamically relocated to 14000 and a reference to 346 to 14346. The program itself never sees a physical address — it manipulates 346 as an ordinary integer until the hardware translates it, making this a generalization of the base-register scheme for dynamic relocation.

concepts.statement: Protection comes from pairing the relocation register with a **limit register** holding the size of the process’s logical address space. Each generated address is first compared against the limit (a trap to the operating system if the logical address is not smaller) and then relocated by adding the base. The dispatcher loads both registers as part of every context switch.
concepts.detail: The book’s example values: relocation $= 100040$ and limit $= 74600$, so the process legally spans physical addresses 100040 through 174639. Because every CPU-generated address is checked, both the operating system and other processes are protected; the scheme also lets the OS itself grow and shrink dynamically, loading device-driver code only when needed.

concepts.statement: With **dynamic loading**, a **routine is loaded only when it is called**. All routines sit on disk in a relocatable load format; a calling routine first checks whether its target is in memory and, if not, invokes the relocatable linking loader, updates the program’s address tables to reflect the change, and passes control to the newly loaded routine.
concepts.detail: The payoff is memory saved on rarely used code — error-handling routines are the canonical example, since a large program may execute a much smaller portion of itself. Crucially, dynamic loading requires **no special operating-system support**: designing programs to take advantage of it is the application’s responsibility, though the OS may supply library routines to help.

concepts.statement: **Dynamic linking** postpones the linking of system libraries until run time. A **stub** marks each call to a library routine; when first executed, the stub checks whether the routine is in memory (loading it if not), adjusts addresses to the routine’s location, and replaces itself with the routine’s address. **Dynamically linked libraries (DLLs)** — also called **shared libraries** — let many processes share one in-memory copy.
concepts.detail: Unlike dynamic loading, dynamic linking **does** require operating-system help: only the OS can check whether a routine lives in another process’s memory or let several processes access the same memory addresses. Version information in both program and library prevents incompatible updates from breaking binaries — versions with minor changes keep the number, major changes increment it — and iOS takes the idea further with a shared, prelinked cache of system libraries.

concepts.statement: **Static linking** treats system libraries like any other object module, copying the library code into every executable image. The result is bigger images and duplicated library code in memory — exactly the waste DLLs were invented to remove.
concepts.detail: The trade is real, though: statically linked images are self-contained, with no missing-library failures or version conflicts (the “DLL hell” dynamic linking invites). Dynamic linking pays a small per-call indirection and a runtime dependency in exchange for shared memory and drop-in library updates.

examples.title: Relocating an address with base and limit
examples.problem: A process runs with relocation (base) register $= 14000$ and limit register $= 74600$. What happens when the CPU generates the logical addresses 346 and 75000?

steps.label: Step 1: Check against the limit
steps.text: The MMU first compares the logical address with the limit register. For 346: is $346 < 74600$? Yes — the reference is legal. For 75000: $75000 \geq 74600$, so the hardware traps to the operating system with an addressing error.

steps.label: Step 2: Add the base
steps.text: For the legal address, the MMU computes the physical address $14000 + 346 = 14346$ and sends that to memory.

steps.label: Step 3: What the program sees
steps.text: The program itself dealt only with the number 346 — as a pointer it could be stored, compared and passed around — never knowing it would land at physical 14346.

steps.label: Step 4: Context switch
steps.text: When the dispatcher later switches to another process, both registers are reloaded with that process’s values; the same logical 346 would then map somewhere else entirely.

examples.result: Logical 346 → physical 14346; logical 75000 → protection trap. Two registers buy dynamic relocation and protection at the cost of one comparison and one addition per memory reference.

examples.title: Choosing the binding time
examples.problem: A compiler, a loader and an MMU each claim to fix addresses. Which binding time does each enable, and what happens when the process must move?

steps.label: Step 1: Compile time
steps.text: If the process’s memory location is known when compiling, absolute code can be generated — but moving the process later means recompiling it. This is the classic MS-DOS .COM model.

steps.label: Step 2: Load time
steps.text: If the location is unknown at compile time, the compiler emits relocatable code and the loader patches addresses at placement; a new placement just means a reload, not a recompile.

steps.label: Step 3: Execution time
steps.text: If the process may move while running, final binding must wait until each reference is made — which requires MMU hardware, and is the scheme every modern operating system uses.

steps.label: Step 4: The test
steps.text: Ask: can this process move after its addresses are fixed? Compile-time code: no. Load-time code: only by reloading. Execution-time code: yes, freely.

examples.result: The later the binding, the more freedom — swapping, compaction and paging all depend on execution-time binding.

keyTakeaways: Addresses bind at compile time (absolute code), load time (relocatable code) or execution time (MMU relocation) — only execution-time binding lets a process move while it runs.
Logical = CPU-generated, physical = memory-unit-seen; under execution-time binding the two spaces differ and the MMU maps between them on every reference.
Base + limit registers give dynamic relocation ($\text{physical} = \text{base} + \text{logical}$) and protection ($\text{logical} < \text{limit}$), reloaded by the dispatcher at each context switch.
Dynamic loading is an application-level technique needing no OS support; dynamic linking needs OS help to share one library copy among processes.
DLLs save memory and enable drop-in updates, at the price of version management and a per-call indirection.

quiz.q: A process must be able to move to a different memory region while it is executing. Which binding scheme is required?
options: Any of the above, if the program is small enough
quiz.explanation: Only execution-time binding defers address resolution until each reference is made — and that requires special hardware (the MMU) to translate addresses on the fly. Compile-time code is frozen in absolute addresses; load-time code can move only by being reloaded.

quiz.q: A process runs with base register 14000 and limit register 74600. The logical address 346 maps to physical address:
quiz.explanation: The MMU checks $346 < 74600$ (legal) and then adds the base: $14000 + 346 = 14346$. The program never sees 14346 — it manipulates logical 346 until the hardware translates it.

quiz.q: Which statement about dynamic loading is correct?
options: It requires the operating system to load libraries into the kernel
It is the application’s responsibility and needs no special OS support
It postpones linking until a library routine is first called
It eliminates the need for a loader
quiz.explanation: Dynamic loading loads a routine only when it is called, and the program itself checks and triggers the load — no special OS support is required, though the OS may offer helper libraries. Postponing linking until first call is dynamic linking, a different mechanism.

quiz.q: The main memory saving of shared libraries (DLLs) comes from:
options: several processes sharing one in-memory copy of the library
loading libraries only into kernel space
quiz.explanation: Because DLLs are linked at run time and are shareable, one physical copy serves every process that maps it — otherwise each executable would carry, and load, its own library image. Version information in program and library manages updates.

quiz.q: An address generated by the CPU is called a ____ address; the address seen by the memory unit is a ____ address.
quiz.explanation: The CPU generates logical (virtual) addresses; the memory unit sees physical addresses. The two coincide only under compile-time or load-time binding — execution-time binding makes them differ, with the MMU bridging the gap.

intro: The simplest way to place several processes is to give each one a contiguous chunk of memory and to swap whole processes out when room runs short. This section examines how contiguous allocation works, why it fragments so badly, how first fit, best fit and worst fit compete for the holes it leaves behind, and what modern systems do instead.
objectives: Explain variable-partition allocation and the dynamic storage-allocation problem
Apply first fit, best fit and worst fit to a set of holes and compare them
Distinguish external from internal fragmentation and quantify the 50-percent rule
Describe compaction and why it demands execution-time binding
Compare standard swapping, swapping with paging, and the no-swap strategy of mobile systems

concepts.statement: In **contiguous memory allocation**, each process occupies a single section of memory, contiguous with the section holding the next process. Main memory is usually divided into two partitions: one for the resident **operating system** and one for the **user processes** — the OS may sit in low or high memory (Linux and Windows place it high; the location of the interrupt vector is one deciding factor) — with base-and-limit registers providing protection.
concepts.detail: The OS must decide how to allocate available memory among the processes waiting to be brought in; if memory cannot satisfy an arriving process, it can be rejected or queued until memory frees up.

concepts.statement: Under the **variable-partition** scheme, the operating system keeps a table of which parts of memory are available and which are occupied. Initially all user memory is one large block — a **hole**; as processes arrive and depart, memory becomes a set of holes of various sizes scattered throughout. Allocating splits a hole (the leftover returns to the set); terminating a process returns its block, which merges with adjacent holes.
concepts.detail: Choosing a hole for a request of size $n$ from a list of free holes is an instance of the general **dynamic storage-allocation problem** — the home of first fit, best fit and worst fit.

concepts.term: First fit, best fit, worst fit
concepts.statement: **First fit** allocates the first hole that is big enough (searching can resume where the previous search ended). **Best fit** allocates the smallest hole that is big enough — it must search the entire list unless it is size-ordered, and produces the smallest leftover hole. **Worst fit** allocates the largest hole, producing the largest leftover, which may be more useful than a tiny one.
concepts.detail: Simulations show that first fit and best fit are both better than worst fit in time and storage utilization; neither is clearly better than the other on utilization, but **first fit is generally faster** — which is why it usually wins.

concepts.statement: **External fragmentation** exists when there is enough total memory space to satisfy a request but the available spaces are not contiguous — storage is broken into small, scattered holes. Statistical analysis of first fit reveals that, even with some optimization, given $N$ allocated blocks another $0.5N$ blocks will be lost to fragmentation: as much as **one-third of memory unusable**.
concepts.detail: In the worst case there is a free block between every two processes. Severity depends on total memory and average process size; the choice of first versus best fit, and even which end of a free block gets allocated, can shift the numbers — but no contiguous scheme escapes external fragmentation.

concepts.statement: **Internal fragmentation** is memory allocated to a process but unused — waste inside a partition rather than between partitions. The book’s example: a hole of 18,464 bytes faced with a request of 18,462 bytes — allocating the exact amount would leave a 2-byte hole whose bookkeeping costs more than the hole is worth, so allocators round up and strand the difference.
concepts.detail: This is the argument for breaking physical memory into fixed-sized allocation units (the approach paging takes): fragmentation turns internal, bounded by less than one unit per allocation, instead of accumulating scattered external holes.

concepts.statement: **Compaction** shuffles memory contents so as to place all free memory together in one large block. It is possible **only if relocation is dynamic and done at execution time** — static assembly- or load-time relocation makes compaction impossible, since there is no register to adjust. The simplest algorithm moves all processes toward one end of memory, pushing all holes to the other; the cost is the time spent moving every process.
concepts.detail: One line of history: the 10th edition folds the old segmentation chapter away, because the winning fix for fragmentation was not compaction but noncontiguous allocation — **paging**, the subject of the next section.

concepts.statement: **Standard swapping** moves an **entire process** between main memory and a **backing store** — fast secondary storage large enough to hold copies of all memory images, providing direct access to them. A swap-out writes the process (and, for a multithreaded process, all per-thread data structures) to the store; a swap-in brings it back. The total memory of all processes may exceed physical memory, raising the degree of multiprogramming.
concepts.detail: Traditional UNIX systems used standard swapping; contemporary systems generally do not, because copying entire processes is too slow — Solaris retains it only for dire, extremely-low-memory circumstances. The OS must keep metadata for swapped-out processes so they can be restored.

concepts.statement: Modern systems — including Linux and Windows — swap **pages**, not processes: a **page out** moves one page of a process to the backing store, a **page in** brings one back. Memory is still oversubscribed, but only the small number of pages actually involved pay the cost.
concepts.detail: Terminology today: “swapping” refers to standard whole-process swapping, while “paging” refers to swapping with paging — the form that pairs naturally with the virtual memory of Chapter 10.

concepts.statement: Mobile operating systems typically support **no** swapping in any form: flash storage is space-constrained, tolerates a limited number of writes, and offers poor throughput between main memory and flash. iOS instead asks applications to voluntarily relinquish allocated memory when free memory runs low — read-only data is removed (and reloaded from flash if needed) while modified data such as the stack is never reclaimed — and apps that free too little are terminated. Android similarly terminates processes, but first writes the application state to flash for a quick restart.
concepts.detail: macOS, by contrast, keeps a full swap facility but reaches for **memory compression** first (Section 10.2 of this book’s next chapter). The practical rule for mobile developers: allocate and release memory carefully, because leaks are fatal.

examples.title: First, best and worst fit on one hole list
examples.problem: The set of free holes, in memory order, contains blocks of 100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB and 600 KB. A process requests 212 KB. Where does each strategy place it?

steps.label: Step 1: First fit
steps.text: Scan from the beginning: 100 KB is too small; 500 KB fits — allocate there and stop. The leftover hole is $500 - 212 = 288$ KB.

steps.label: Step 2: Best fit
steps.text: The candidates at least 212 KB are 500, 300 and 600; the smallest is 300 KB, so best fit allocates there, leaving $300 - 212 = 88$ KB.

steps.label: Step 3: Worst fit
steps.text: The largest hole is 600 KB, so worst fit allocates there, leaving $600 - 212 = 388$ KB.

steps.label: Step 4: Compare
steps.text: All three succeed here. Best fit leaves the tiniest residue (88 KB) but scanned the entire list; first fit stopped after two probes; worst fit left the largest remainder — helpful only if a large request is coming.

examples.result: First fit → 500-KB hole (288 left); best fit → 300-KB hole (88 left); worst fit → 600-KB hole (388 left). Simulations favor first fit and best fit over worst fit on both speed and utilization — and first fit is generally faster.

examples.title: The 50-percent rule in numbers
examples.problem: A system runs long enough for first-fit statistics to settle with $N = 120$ allocated blocks. How much memory does the 50-percent rule predict is lost, and what fraction of memory is unusable?

steps.label: Step 1: Apply the rule
steps.text: Given $N$ allocated blocks, about $0.5N$ blocks’ worth of memory is lost to fragmentation holes: $0.5 \times 120 = 60$ block-equivalents stranded.

steps.label: Step 2: Count the total
steps.text: Memory is effectively tied up in $N + 0.5N = 1.5N = 180$ block-equivalents — 120 in use, 60 in holes.

steps.label: Step 3: The unusable fraction
steps.text: Fraction unusable $= 0.5N / 1.5N = 1/3$ — one-third of all memory, in the worst case, serves no process.

examples.result: About 60 block-equivalents are stranded in holes — one-third of memory. This is the number that pushed operating systems from contiguous allocation to paging.

keyTakeaways: Memory divides into OS and user partitions; variable partitions create, split and merge holes as processes arrive and leave.
First fit is generally the fastest and matches best fit on storage utilization; worst fit loses on both counts.
External fragmentation = enough total memory but no contiguous piece; the 50-percent rule says $0.5N$ blocks are lost — up to one-third of memory unusable.
Internal fragmentation = rounding an allocation up past the request (an 18,464-byte hole serving an 18,462-byte request).
Compaction is possible only with execution-time binding, and its cost is moving every process in memory.
Standard swapping (whole processes, classic UNIX) is essentially obsolete; swapping with paging is what modern systems do.
Mobile systems do not swap at all — iOS asks apps to give memory back and terminates those that refuse; Android saves state to flash and restarts.

quiz.q: Which allocation strategy is generally the fastest while matching the others on storage utilization?
options: Next fit after sorting holes by size
quiz.explanation: Simulations show first fit and best fit are both better than worst fit in time and storage utilization, and neither dominates the other on utilization — but first fit stops searching as soon as it finds a big-enough hole, making it generally faster.

quiz.q: The 50-percent rule for first fit predicts that, given $N$ allocated blocks:
options: another $0.5N$ blocks are lost to fragmentation — one-third of memory
half of all processes must wait
quiz.explanation: Statistical analysis of first fit shows about $0.5N$ blocks lost to fragmentation: of the $1.5N$ block-equivalents tied up, only $N$ serve processes — one-third unusable.

quiz.q: Compaction of memory is possible only when:
options: relocation is dynamic, at execution time
quiz.explanation: Compaction moves processes in memory and must then fix their addresses — only execution-time binding can do that (move the program, change the base register). Static relocation leaves the addresses baked into the code.

quiz.q: Standard swapping differs from the paging-based swapping of modern systems because it moves:
options: entire processes between memory and the backing store
quiz.explanation: Standard swapping moves whole processes — its cost is why traditional UNIX-style swapping was abandoned for paging individual pages in and out (retained by Solaris only in extreme low-memory situations).

quiz.q: Why do mobile operating systems such as iOS avoid swapping?
options: Flash tolerates a limited number of writes
quiz.explanation: All three reasons apply — cramped flash, limited write endurance and poor throughput. iOS instead asks apps to relinquish memory voluntarily, removes read-only data, never reclaims modified data, and terminates apps that free too little.

prerequisites: Logical vs. physical address spaces and runtime memory relocation
Binary address dissection: page number $p$ and frame offset $d$
Cache memory fundamentals: hit ratio $h$, associative registers, and miss penalties
intro: Paging drops the requirement that a process occupy contiguous memory: physical memory is chopped into equal-sized frames, logical memory into same-sized pages, and any page can live in any free frame. The cost is one indirection — the per-process page table — and this section works through the address arithmetic, the TLB that rescues its performance, and the page-size tradeoffs that follow.
objectives: Translate a logical address into page number and offset, and compute the physical address
Explain the per-process page table and the MMU’s translation steps
Compute page-table sizes for given address spaces and page sizes
Model TLB performance with the effective-access-time formula
Reason about page-size tradeoffs and the role of ASIDs

concepts.statement: Paging breaks **physical memory into fixed-sized blocks called frames** and **logical memory into blocks of the same size called pages**. When a process executes, its pages are loaded into any available memory frames from their source (a file system or the backing store, itself divided into frame-sized blocks or clusters of frames). Because any free frame can hold any page, a process’s physical address space may be noncontiguous — and **external fragmentation vanishes**.
concepts.detail: A side effect: the logical address space is now totally separate from physical — a process can have a logical 64-bit address space on a machine with far less physical memory, the foundation of virtual memory in Chapter 10.

concepts.statement: Every address generated by the CPU splits into a **page number** $p$ and a **page offset** $d$. The page number is an index into a **per-process page table**, which yields the base address of the frame holding that page; the frame base combined with the offset defines the physical address. The operating system builds and maintains the tables; the MMU hardware performs the translation on every reference.
concepts.detail: Frames are allocated from a free-frame list as a process arrives: each page the process needs gets one frame, and the frame number is recorded in the page table — so the table is the process’s private map of its scattered pages.

concepts.statement: If the logical address space is $2^{m}$ bytes and the page size is $2^{n}$ bytes, then the high-order $m - n$ bits of a logical address form the page number and the low-order $n$ bits the offset. The MMU takes three steps: (1) extract $p$ and use it as an index into the page table; (2) extract the corresponding frame base; (3) **replace the page number with the frame number — the offset bits pass through untouched**.
concepts.detail: Choosing a power-of-two page size makes the split pure bit manipulation — no division hardware. Conceptually, paging is dynamic relocation performed per page: a table of base registers, one per frame, with the offset added to whichever base the table names.

concepts.term: Internal fragmentation, half a page per process
concepts.statement: Frames are allocated as units, so a process whose needs do not fall on page boundaries wastes the tail of its last frame. With 2,048-byte pages, a 72,766-byte process needs 35 pages plus 1,086 bytes and receives 36 frames — wasting $2048 - 1086 = 962$ bytes. In the worst case a process needing $n$ pages plus 1 byte wastes almost an entire frame; averaged over process sizes, expect **one-half page of internal fragmentation per process**.
concepts.detail: This consideration argues for small pages; bigger pages win on table size and I/O efficiency — the tug-of-war settled by the page-size concept below.

concepts.statement: Smaller pages mean less internal fragmentation and finer locality resolution, but more page-table entries and more overhead per transfer; larger pages shrink tables and amortize disk I/O but waste tail space. Page sizes are powers of 2, typically varying **between 4 KB and 1 GB**; today’s systems commonly use 4 or 8 KB, with **huge pages** as a deliberate large-page option (x86-64 supports 4 KB and 2 MB in Windows 10; Linux offers a default size plus architecture-dependent huge pages).
concepts.detail: The page size is an **architectural parameter** fixed by hardware — often with several options the OS may configure. On Linux, getconf PAGESIZE or the getpagesize() system call reports it.

concepts.statement: A **TLB** is an associative, high-speed hardware cache of recent page-number → frame-number mappings, searched **before** the page table. A **TLB hit** costs one memory access; a **TLB miss** costs two — read the page table, then access the data. The percentage of translations found in the TLB is the **hit ratio**. When the TLB fills, entries are replaced by LRU, round-robin or random policies, and key kernel entries can be **wired down** so they are never evicted.
concepts.detail: The TLB is why paging is affordable: without it every memory reference would become two. The percentage of times the desired page number is found in the TLB determines whether the machine feels fast or not.

concepts.statement: With memory-access time $t$ and TLB hit ratio $h$, the book’s model (TLB search time folded away) gives $$\text{EAT} = h \cdot t + (1 - h) \cdot 2t.$$ A fuller model that counts a TLB search time of $\varepsilon$ adds it to every term: $\text{EAT} = \varepsilon + h \cdot t + (1 - h) \cdot 2t$.
concepts.detail: Book numbers, with $t = 10$ ns: an 80-percent hit ratio gives $0.80 \times 10 + 0.20 \times 20 = 12$ ns — a 20-percent slowdown — while a realistic 99 percent gives $0.99 \times 10 + 0.01 \times 20 = 10.1$ ns, only 1 percent. Real CPUs stack TLBs: the Intel Core i7 has a 128-entry L1 instruction TLB and a 64-entry L1 data TLB; an L1 miss costs six cycles to check the 512-entry L2 TLB, and an L2 miss triggers a hardware page-table walk of hundreds of cycles.

concepts.statement: Some TLBs store an **ASID** — a unique process identifier — with each entry. The hardware matches the current process’s ASID against the entry’s; a mismatch is treated as a TLB miss. ASIDs let one TLB hold entries for **several processes simultaneously**, so a context switch does not flush the cache.
concepts.detail: Without ASID support, every switch to a new page table (every context switch) forces the TLB to be flushed, so the next process cannot inherit stale translations — and hit ratios start from cold on every switch.

concepts.statement: The page size, the MMU design and the TLB organization are hardware decisions — but an operating system must implement paging to match the platform’s TLB design, and a hardware change (a new CPU generation) can force an OS redesign.
concepts.detail: That is why a systems programmer needs to understand TLBs even though they are pure hardware: paging policy and hardware features shape each other in both directions.

figures.caption: Paging hardware with TLB: the logical address (p, d) is generated by the CPU. The page number p is checked first in the TLB cache; on a hit, the frame number f is supplied immediately. On a miss, the page table in memory is queried. The offset d passes through unchanged to form the physical address (f, d).

derivations.title: Effective Memory Access Time (EAT) under Paging with TLB and Hierarchical Page Tables
derivations.statement: For a paging system with memory cycle time $t_{\text{mem}}$, TLB search latency $\varepsilon$, and TLB hit ratio $h$, the effective access time is $\text{EAT} = \varepsilon + t_{\text{mem}} + (1 - h) \cdot k \cdot t_{\text{mem}}$, where $k$ is the number of page-table levels.
prerequisites: Associative hardware cache lookup: parallel comparison across all TLB slots
Discrete probability expectation: $\mathbb{E}[T] = P(\text{Hit}) \cdot T_{\text{hit}} + P(\text{Miss}) \cdot T_{\text{miss}}$
Hierarchical page table traversal ($k$-level page walk)

steps.label: Step 1: Quantifying the TLB Hit trajectory
steps.explanation: Every CPU memory reference begins by dispatching the logical page number $p$ to the associative TLB hardware. Searching the TLB registers takes $\varepsilon$ nanoseconds. On a hit (occurring with probability $h$), the matching frame number $f$ is immediately concatenated with offset $d$ to form the physical address. Exactly one physical DRAM access is then executed to read or write the operand.

steps.label: Step 2: Quantifying the TLB Miss penalty in single-level paging
steps.explanation: On a TLB miss (probability $1 - h$), the frame mapping is absent from fast associative cache. The MMU must first access main memory to read the page-table entry at address $(\text{PTBR} + p \times \text{entry\_size})$, consuming $t_{\text{mem}}$. Once frame $f$ is retrieved, a second main memory access fetches the actual data byte, taking another $t_{\text{mem}}$. Total miss latency is $\varepsilon + 2t_{\text{mem}}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Calculating mathematical expectation for single-level paging
steps.explanation: Factoring out $\varepsilon + t_{\text{mem}}$ shows that the average memory latency is base access time plus the miss penalty $(1 - h)t_{\text{mem}}$. When $\varepsilon \ll t_{\text{mem}}$ and folded away, the equation simplifies to the textbook form $\text{EAT} = (2 - h)t_{\text{mem}}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Generalizing to $k$-level hierarchical page tables
steps.explanation: Modern 64-bit architectures cannot store a single flat page table because it would require petabytes of memory. Instead, they use multi-level paging (e.g. two-level in 32-bit x86, four-level PML4 in x86-64, or five-level paging). On a TLB miss, the MMU must walk through $k$ successive levels of page tables stored in DRAM (Outer Page Directory $\to$ Page Middle Directory $\to \dots \to$ Leaf Page Table) before fetching the operand.

steps.label: Step 5: Composite Multi-Level EAT formulation
steps.formula: $$ \text{EAT}_{k} = h(\varepsilon + t_{\text{mem}}) + (1 - h)(\varepsilon + (k + 1)t_{\text{mem}}) = \varepsilon + t_{\text{mem}} + (1 - h) \cdot k \cdot t_{\text{mem}} $$
steps.explanation: Every additional page table level adds exactly $(1 - h)t_{\text{mem}}$ to the expected access time. For a 4-level x86-64 system with $t_{\text{mem}} = 100$ ns and no TLB ($h = 0$), every memory read would cost $500$ ns — an unacceptable 5× performance degradation.

derivations.result: The derived equation $\text{EAT} = \varepsilon + t_{\text{mem}} + (1 - h) \cdot k \cdot t_{\text{mem}}$ reveals the mathematical necessity of the TLB: with a 98\% hit ratio ($h = 0.98$) on a 4-level system, the miss penalty shrinks from $400$ ns to $(0.02)(4)(100) = 8$ ns, keeping effective access time within 8\% of raw unpaged hardware speed. This derivation proves why multi-level virtual memory architectures are only feasible when paired with high-hit-rate associative caches.

examples.title: Translating a virtual address, step by step
examples.problem: A system uses 1-KB ($2^{10}$-byte) pages, and the page table maps page 5 to frame 9. Translate the logical address 5496.

steps.label: Step 1: Split the address
steps.text: With 1-KB pages the offset is 10 bits. Divide: $5496 = 5 \times 1024 + 456$, so the page number is $p = \lfloor 5496 / 1024 \rfloor = 5$ and the offset is $d = 456$.

steps.label: Step 2: Index the page table
steps.text: Entry 5 of the page table says the page lives in frame 9, whose base address is $9 \times 1024 = 9216$.

steps.label: Step 3: Recombine
steps.text: Physical address $= 9216 + 456 = 9672$. The offset 456 was never touched — translation only swaps the page number for a frame number.

steps.label: Step 4: Sanity-check on the book’s tiny machine
steps.text: A 32-byte memory with 4-byte pages ($n = 2$, $m = 4$): logical address 13 is page 3, offset 1; the table maps page 3 to frame 2, so physical $= 2 \times 4 + 1 = 9$ — exactly the book’s Figure 9.10 computation.

examples.result: Logical 5496 → page 5, offset 456 → physical 9672. The same 456-byte displacement lands in whichever frame the page table names — relocation is per page.

examples.title: TLB effective access time
examples.problem: A memory access takes 10 ns. Compute the effective access time for TLB hit ratios of 80 percent and 99 percent.

steps.label: Step 1: Price the hit path
steps.text: TLB hit: the associative lookup supplies the frame number and the data access follows — one memory access, $t = 10$ ns.

steps.label: Step 2: Price the miss path
steps.text: TLB miss: access memory for the page table to get the frame number (10 ns), then access the desired byte (10 ns) — $2t = 20$ ns, assuming the page-table lookup itself takes a single memory access.

steps.label: Step 3: Weight at 80 percent
steps.text: $\text{EAT} = 0.80 \times 10 + 0.20 \times 20 = 12$ ns — a 20-percent slowdown over unpaged memory.

steps.label: Step 4: Weight at 99 percent
steps.text: $\text{EAT} = 0.99 \times 10 + 0.01 \times 20 = 10.1$ ns — only a 1-percent slowdown; this is the hit ratio real systems chase.

steps.label: Step 5: Generalize
steps.text: Counting a TLB search time of $\varepsilon$ adds it to both paths: $\text{EAT} = \varepsilon + h \cdot t + (1 - h) \cdot 2t$; multi-level TLBs and hardware walks complicate the accounting further.

examples.result: 12 ns at an 80-percent hit ratio; 10.1 ns at 99 percent. Paging is cheap only when the TLB hit ratio is very high — the design pressure behind TLBs, ASIDs and huge pages.

examples.title: How big is a page table?
examples.problem: A 32-bit logical address space uses 4-KB pages with 4-byte page-table entries. How large is each process’s page table — and what changes with 8-byte entries?

steps.label: Step 1: Count the pages
steps.text: Number of pages $= 2^{32} / 2^{12} = 2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$ — over one million entries.

steps.label: Step 2: Multiply by entry size
steps.text: At 4 bytes per entry: $2^{20} \times 4$ bytes $= 4$ MB. With 8-byte entries the table doubles to 8 MB.

steps.label: Step 3: Per process!
steps.text: Each process carries its own page table — one hundred processes would hold hundreds of megabytes of page tables, mostly for pages they never touch.

steps.label: Step 4: Note the entry reach
steps.text: A 32-bit entry can point to one of $2^{32}$ physical frames; with 4-KB ($2^{12}$) frames that addresses $2^{44}$ bytes — 16 TB of physical memory.

examples.result: 4 MB per process (8 MB with 8-byte PTEs) — far too big to allocate contiguously. Section 9.4 pages the page table itself.

keyTakeaways: Frames (physical) and pages (logical) are the same size; any page fits any free frame, so external fragmentation disappears entirely.
An address splits into page number + offset; translation replaces only the page number — the offset passes through untouched.
A $2^{m}$-byte space with $2^{n}$-byte pages has $m - n$ page-number bits and $n$ offset bits; a 32-bit space with 4-KB pages has $2^{20}$ pages.
Paging’s internal fragmentation averages one-half page per process (72,766-byte process, 2,048-byte pages → 962 bytes wasted).
TLB hit = one memory access, miss = two; with 10-ns memory, an 80-percent hit ratio yields 12-ns EAT and a 99-percent ratio 10.1 ns.
ASIDs let the TLB hold several processes’ entries at once; without them every context switch flushes the TLB cold.
Page size trades table size and I/O efficiency against fragmentation and locality — an architectural parameter, typically 4–8 KB with huge-page options.

quiz.q: Logical address 5496 in a system with 1-KB pages is page ____ with offset ____.
