quiz.explanation: To place addresses and move data the DMA controller must own the memory bus; whenever it does, the CPU cannot reach memory — but it keeps executing out of its caches. The stolen cycles are far cheaper than the CPU performing the transfer itself.

quiz.q: A DMA command block contains:
options: the interrupt vector and handler address
the device’s major and minor numbers
a list of all pending processes
a pointer to the source, a pointer to the destination, and a count of bytes to transfer
quiz.explanation: Those three fields drive the whole transfer; richer blocks (scatter-gather) add lists of non-contiguous source/destination pairs so one DMA command executes multiple transfers. The CPU writes the block, tells the controller where it is, and gets interrupted once at the end.

quiz.q: A device streams at $50$ MB/s (one byte per $20$ ns) while each per-byte interrupt costs $1$ microsecond of CPU. Can per-byte interrupts keep up, and what is the right structure?
options: No; the bus must be widened
Yes, with a larger vector table
No; at most about $1$ MB/s, so DMA with one interrupt per block is needed
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** rate $R = 50$ MB/s, cost $C_I = 1$ microsecond per byte.
**Step 2 — Rule:** feasible only while $C_I \le 1/R$; max interrupt-sustainable rate is $1/C_I$.
**Step 3 — Computation:** $1/C_I = 1$ MB/s, far below $50$ MB/s; needed $C_I \le 20$ ns, impossible for a full save-dispatch-restore.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** DMA inverts the math: one setup plus one completion per $B$-byte block costs microseconds per block, i.e. nanoseconds per byte for large $B$.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** polling still pays per byte; a larger table speeds dispatch but not the per-byte cost; bus width does not remove interrupts.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** per-byte handling tops near $1$ MB/s; bulk needs DMA.

quiz.q: Which register set and handshake lets a CPU reliably hand a command to a device controller without loss?
options: Control, status, data-in, data-out with busy-bit and command-ready protocol
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** controller with local buffers, CPU and device run concurrently.
**Step 2 — Rule:** CPU writes control, polls status busy-bit until clear, then issues; command-ready strobe latches the command; data registers carry words each way.
**Step 3 — Trace:** set command word, raise ready, controller sees ready, sets busy, moves data, clears busy and raises completion interrupt.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** without status the CPU cannot know when the controller is free; without control it cannot say what to do.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** single registers omit direction or handshaking; interrupts alone do not transfer commands.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** four registers plus busy/command-ready is the minimal reliable contract.

intro: Devices differ wildly — character-stream or block, sequential or random, sharable or dedicated, fast or slow — yet applications must open a file, read it, and close it without knowing anything about the hardware. The operating system achieves this with abstraction and layering: a few standard device classes in the application I/O interface, kernel modules (device drivers) that encapsulate the oddities, and kernel I/O services — scheduling, buffering, caching, spooling — that sit above them all.
objectives: Describe the kernel I/O structure: device drivers under a uniform interface, and the major device classes (block, character, network, clock)
Compare blocking, nonblocking and asynchronous I/O, and explain vectored (scatter-gather) I/O and the ioctl escape hatch
Explain the services of the kernel I/O subsystem: scheduling, buffering, caching, spooling, device reservation, error handling and protection
Explain copy semantics and double buffering
Trace how a file name becomes a device command (mount tables, major/minor numbers, dispatch tables)

concepts.term: Device drivers and the kernel I/O structure
concepts.statement: The kernel’s **I/O subsystem** hides device differences behind **device-driver** modules: each driver is custom-tailored to a device but exports one of the standard interfaces, exactly as system calls standardize the application–kernel boundary. Above the drivers, the kernel I/O subsystem provides services; below them, device controllers do the hardware’s side of a protocol.
concepts.detail: Drivers are OS-specific — one device ships separate drivers for Windows, Linux, AIX and macOS — but the classes above them are standard, which is why new devices can appear without rewriting the OS. The ioctl() system call is the escape hatch: it passes arbitrary commands from an application straight to a driver (device identifier, integer command selector, pointer to a data structure), avoiding a new syscall per device feature.

concepts.statement: A **block device** transfers a block of bytes as a unit, understands read(), write() and (if random-access) seek(), and is normally reached through a file system; a **character-stream device** transfers bytes one by one through get()/put()-style calls — keyboards, mice, modems, printers, audio. Applications see block devices through file systems; a database or the OS itself may prefer **raw I/O** — the device as a simple linear array of blocks, with no OS buffering or locking — or the middle path of **direct I/O** (a file mode that disables OS buffering).
concepts.detail: Memory-mapped file access layers on block drivers: the file is mapped into memory and touched through the virtual-memory machinery — the same demand-paging path — which is why the OS itself uses mapping to load executables and reach swap space. Character devices fit producers that deliver data spontaneously and consumers that want a linear stream. Device naming differs by OS: MS-DOS puts the device in the file name (C:), while UNIX embeds devices in the regular file-system name space, with a mount table mapping path-name prefixes to devices.

concepts.statement: Network I/O differs enough from disk I/O to earn its own interface — the **socket**: an application creates a socket, binds it, connects it to a remote address, listens for remote connections, accepts them, and sends and receives packets; select() manages a *set* of sockets, reporting which have packets waiting or room to send (eliminating per-socket polling). Hardware **clocks and timers** provide three functions — current time, elapsed time, and “trigger operation X at time T” — built on a **programmable interval timer** that interrupts once or periodically.
concepts.detail: The scheduler uses the interval timer to preempt at time-slice end; disk caching uses it to flush dirty buffers periodically; networking uses it to time out stalled operations. Because hardware timer channels are few, the kernel simulates **virtual clocks**: one sorted (earliest-first) list of wanted interrupts, arming the hardware only for the earliest. PCs carry a high-performance event timer (HPET) running in the 10-megahertz range with several comparators; time-of-day drift is corrected by NTP. Block and raw access also imply protection: all I/O instructions are privileged, and memory-mapped I/O regions are guarded by the memory-protection system (with controlled exceptions for graphics).

concepts.statement: A **blocking** system call suspends the calling thread (run queue → wait queue) until the I/O completes — the default, because blocking code is easier to write. A **nonblocking** call returns immediately with whatever is available (full count, fewer bytes, or none). An **asynchronous** call returns immediately and the *entire* transfer completes later, with completion signaled by a variable, a signal or software interrupt, or a call-back outside the thread’s linear control flow.
concepts.detail: The distinction in one line: nonblocking read() gives you *some now*; asynchronous read() gives you *all later*. Multithreading is the other route to overlap (some threads block while others compute). By default even “synchronous” storage and network writes are absorbed by the kernel and completed later — UNIX kernels flush secondary-storage buffers roughly every 30 seconds, and applications can request an immediate flush. Asynchronous completion is delivered via signals or call-back routines.

concepts.statement: **Vectored I/O** lets one system call move data to or from *multiple* buffers: the UNIX readv()/writev() calls take a vector of buffers, scattering an incoming stream across them or gathering the outgoing stream from them. The alternative — copying separate buffers into one big buffer and issuing one call, or issuing several calls — pays extra copies or extra context switches.
concepts.detail: Benefits: fewer system calls and context switches (the kernel is entered once), no pre-staging copy, and — in some implementations — atomicity: the whole gather-scatter happens without interruption, so concurrent threads cannot interleave with those buffers. When available, programmers use scatter-gather to increase throughput and decrease overhead.

concepts.statement: The order applications issue I/O is rarely the best order to execute it. The kernel keeps a **wait queue per device**; the **I/O scheduler** reorders that queue to improve overall efficiency and average response time — serving requests 2, 3, 1 when the disk arm sits near the beginning of the disk — while remaining fair, or prioritizing delay-sensitive work (virtual-memory requests may outrank application requests).
concepts.detail: To track many concurrent requests the kernel maintains a **device-status table** with an entry per device: type, address and state (idle, busy, not functioning), plus the pending request parameters. Disk-scheduling algorithms (Chapter 11) are the flagship instance: reorder to minimize head movement, merge adjacent requests.

concepts.statement: A **buffer** is a memory area holding data in transit between devices or between a device and an application. Buffering exists for three reasons: (1) **speed mismatch** — a network a thousand times slower than an SSD is decoupled by **double buffering** (fill one while draining the other); (2) **transfer-size adaptation** — networking fragments large messages into packets and reassembles them in buffers; (3) **copy semantics** — the version of data written is frozen at the time of the call.
concepts.detail: Copy semantics concretely: after write(fd, buf, n) returns, the application may immediately overwrite buf — the OS guarantees the disk receives the version at call time, by copying the application data into a kernel buffer before returning (or by virtual-memory remapping with copy-on-write). The same kernel buffer often doubles as a **buffer cache**.

concepts.statement: A **cache** holds, on fast storage, a *copy* of data that lives elsewhere; a **buffer** may hold the only existing copy — that is the distinction. A **spool** is a buffer that holds output for a device, like a printer, that cannot accept interleaved streams: each application’s output is spooled to a separate file, and a spooling daemon (or in-kernel thread) copies the queued files to the device one job at a time. For devices that cannot usefully multiplex concurrent access, OS facilities provide **exclusive device reservation** (VMS-style allocate/deallocate, or one-open-handle limits, or Windows’ wait-for-device-object calls).
concepts.detail: Kernel buffer caches serve both purposes: a read first checks the cache (avoiding or deferring disk I/O), and writes accumulate for several seconds so large, efficiently scheduled transfers can be gathered. Spool systems expose a control interface — display the queue, remove jobs, suspend printing. Reservation avoids the opposite failure: two processes interleaving writes to one non-sharable device.

concepts.term: Error handling and kernel data structures
concepts.statement: I/O calls return one success/failure bit; UNIX adds the integer **errno** (about a hundred values — argument out of range, bad pointer, file not open). Transient failures are retried (a disk read, a network resend); permanent ones are reported up. Underneath, hardware can be richer — SCSI reports failures in three levels (sense key → additional sense code → qualifier) plus error-log pages. The kernel tracks all of I/O in structures: **open-file tables** (per-process and system-wide), **device-status tables**, and per-file **dispatch tables** of function pointers.
concepts.detail: The UNIX open-file record contains pointers to read/write, select, ioctl and close routines — one uniform object with dispatch-table-selected behavior for regular files, raw devices or sockets. Devices are named by **major and minor numbers**: major selects the driver, minor the instance (ls -l /dev/sda* shows 8, 0; 8, 1; 8, 2 …). Windows implements I/O as message passing through an I/O manager instead — messages flow to the driver, which may transform them.

examples.title: Copy semantics: why write() copies your buffer
examples.problem: An application calls write(fd, buf, 4096) and immediately overwrites buf with new data before the disk transfer finishes. What does the disk receive — and what did the kernel do to guarantee it?

steps.label: Step 1: The call arrives
steps.text: The kernel validates the arguments and prepares the write. The disk is slow, so the physical transfer cannot complete within the call.

steps.label: Step 2: The kernel copies
steps.text: write() copies the 4,096 bytes from the application’s buffer into a kernel buffer *before returning control* — one extra copy, deliberately.

steps.label: Step 3: The application races ahead
steps.text: Back in user mode the application scribbles new data over buf. The kernel buffer is untouched — a separate memory area.

steps.label: Step 4: The I/O completes
steps.text: The disk write proceeds from the kernel buffer, gathering with other writes for efficient scheduling, and lands the bytes captured at call time.

examples.result: The disk receives the version from the instant of the system call, independent of later buffer changes — that guarantee is copy semantics. The same effect can be had more cheaply with virtual-memory mapping and copy-on-write, which is why both exist.

examples.title: Double buffering a slow download
examples.problem: A file arrives over a network interface about a thousand times slower than the SSD storing it. Show how two buffers keep the producer and consumer decoupled so neither ever waits for the other.

steps.label: Step 1: Fill buffer A
steps.text: Network bytes accumulate in buffer A while the SSD sits idle — the producer races ahead of the consumer with nowhere to put data yet.

steps.label: Step 2: Flip to B
steps.text: When A is full, the kernel requests the SSD write of A — and immediately starts filling buffer B with arriving bytes.

steps.label: Step 3: Overlap
steps.text: The drive drains A while the network fills B. The two timelines no longer meet: by the time B fills, A should be empty.

steps.label: Step 4: Keep alternating
steps.text: The network switches back to A while the drive takes B — a steady seesaw in which each party always has a free buffer.

examples.result: Double buffering decouples producer from consumer, relaxing the timing requirements between them — the canonical first use of buffering, and the reason device-speed tables (from keyboards to networks to drives) can coexist.

keyTakeaways: The application I/O interface reduces all devices to a few classes — block (read/write/seek), character stream (get/put), network sockets, clocks/timers — with ioctl() as the escape hatch and drivers encapsulating the differences.
UNIX names devices inside the file-system name space: a mount table maps path prefixes to devices, and a <major, minor> pair selects the driver and instance (8,0 vs 8,1).

Blocking I/O suspends the thread; nonblocking returns immediately with whatever is available; asynchronous requests the full transfer and completes later via signal or call-back. select() multiplexes sockets without busy-waiting.
Vectored (scatter-gather) I/O moves multiple buffers in one system call: fewer context switches, no staging copies, sometimes atomicity.

The kernel I/O subsystem schedules requests per device (reorder, merge, prioritize — the device-status table tracks them) and buffers, caches, spools and reserves devices; a buffer may hold the only copy while a cache holds a faster copy of data that lives elsewhere.
Spooling serializes output for non-sharable devices — every print job is a queued file; device reservation grants exclusive access when interleaving makes no sense.

Error handling runs from a success bit plus errno to SCSI’s three-level sense data; the kernel keeps open-file tables, device-status tables and per-file dispatch tables of function pointers to route it all.

quiz.q: A nonblocking read() differs from an asynchronous read() in that:
options: asynchronous read() always fails on disks
nonblocking returns immediately with whatever data are available now (possibly none), while asynchronous requests the full transfer and completes it later via a signal or call-back
there is no difference — the terms are synonyms
quiz.explanation: Nonblocking answers “what do you have right now?” — the full count, fewer bytes, or nothing. Asynchronous answers “do it all, tell me when you’re done” — the entire transfer completes later, with completion delivered through a variable, a signal, a software interrupt, or a call-back outside the thread’s linear flow.

quiz.q: The precise difference between a buffer and a cache is:
options: a buffer may hold the only existing copy of a data item; a cache holds a copy of data that resides elsewhere
buffers are only in the kernel; caches are only in hardware
caches are always smaller than buffers
quiz.explanation: A buffer holds data in transit between producer and consumer — it can be the only copy (copy semantics). A cache exists to make reuse faster and holds a copy of something that permanently lives elsewhere. One memory region can serve both jobs — hence the buffer cache.

quiz.q: Copy semantics for write() mean:
options: the data written to disk are guaranteed to be the version in the buffer at the time of the call, regardless of later changes to that buffer
quiz.explanation: The kernel copies the application data into a kernel buffer before write() returns, so the disk write happens from that snapshot. Virtual-memory mapping with copy-on-write achieves the same guarantee without the copy.

quiz.q: Spooling exists because:
options: some devices, like printers, cannot accept interleaved data streams from concurrent applications
spool files are faster than memory
network cards require it for packets
quiz.explanation: Only one job can print at a time, yet many applications print concurrently: the OS intercepts all output, spools each application’s output to a separate file, and a spooling daemon or in-kernel thread queues those files to the printer one at a time — with a control interface to view, remove and suspend jobs.

quiz.q: In UNIX, a device’s major and minor numbers identify:
options: the bus speed and lane count
the file system type and mount point
the driver to route the request to, and the specific instance of the device within that driver
quiz.explanation: Looking up a device name in the file system yields a <major, minor> pair: the OS uses the major number to dispatch to the right driver, and the minor number lets the driver index to the exact device instance — 8,0 and 8,1 are two partitions of one SSD served by driver 8.

intro: I/O is a major factor in system performance: it forces context switches as processes block and unblock, loads the memory bus with data copies, and exposes every weakness of the interrupt machinery. This section follows one blocking read through all ten steps of its life, collects the book’s principles for making I/O fast, and closes with the other side of the coin — power management, from data-center cores to Android’s deepest sleep states.
objectives: Trace the full life cycle of a blocking read() from system call to data return
Explain where the major I/O costs are: context switches, data copies and interrupt handling
List the design principles for improving I/O performance and the device-functionality progression
Describe the STREAMS framework for modular driver and protocol stacks
Explain power management: component states, wake events, power collapse, wakelocks and CPU scaling strategies

concepts.term: The life cycle of an I/O request
concepts.statement: A blocking read() travels: the process issues the call → the kernel checks parameters and the **buffer cache** (hit: return immediately) → on a miss, the process moves to the device’s **wait queue** and the request is scheduled and handed to the **device driver** → the driver allocates kernel buffers and writes commands to the **device controller**’s registers → the controller operates the device → a **DMA transfer** moves the data into kernel memory and raises an interrupt → the **interrupt handler** (via the vector table) stores data and signals the driver → the driver signals the kernel I/O subsystem → the kernel moves the data (and return codes) to the process’s address space and shifts the process from the wait queue to the **ready queue** → the scheduler runs it and the system call completes.
concepts.detail: Before any of this, name translation connects the file name to hardware: the file system maps name → inode (UNIX) or FAT entry (MS-DOS); the UNIX mount table resolves the longest matching path prefix to a device; the device’s <major, minor> numbers select the driver; the driver’s device table holds the controller’s port or memory-mapped address. Drivers can even be loaded on demand for devices detected after boot.

concepts.statement: Each I/O operation crosses protection boundaries (context switches to enter the kernel and back), copies data (controller to kernel buffer, kernel buffer to application), and handles interrupts (state save, dispatch, state restore — a completion typically unblocks a process, paying a full context switch). Network traffic multiplies this: remote login sends **every typed character** through both machines’ full I/O stacks — and the echo doubles the work.
concepts.detail: Interrupt handling is relatively expensive: a quiet macOS desktop absorbed almost 23,000 interrupts in ten seconds — about $ rac{23{,}000}{10} approx 2{,}300$ per second — and servers see hundreds of thousands per second. Programmed I/O can actually beat interrupt-driven I/O when busy-waiting cycles are few — which is why hybrid drivers poll when the I/O rate is high and interrupt when it is low. Mainframes offload the problem entirely to **I/O channels**: dedicated special-purpose CPUs that keep data flowing while the main CPU computes, fed by terminal concentrators multiplexing hundreds of devices onto one port.

concepts.statement: The book’s design rules: **reduce context switches**; **reduce data copies** between device and application; **reduce interrupt frequency** (larger transfers, smart controllers, polling when busy-wait is bounded); **increase concurrency** with DMA-capable controllers or channels offloading simple copying; **move processing primitives into hardware** so they overlap with CPU and bus operation; and **balance CPU, memory, bus and I/O performance** — an overload in one area idles the others.
concepts.detail: Modern additions to the same spirit: interrupt coalescing (one interrupt for a batch of completions), zero-copy paths that DMA directly into user buffers, and memory-mapped files that skip the copy entirely. Where functionality should live is its own trade-off — the **device functionality progression** — starting at the application level (flexible, slow, safe: FUSE file systems in user mode), moving to the kernel (faster, riskier), then the driver, the controller, and finally the device itself (fastest, least flexible, months not days to change: hardware RAID controllers that ignore kernel hints about workload).

concepts.statement: UNIX System V’s **STREAMS** mechanism lets an application assemble pipelines of driver code dynamically. A **stream** is a full-duplex connection between a device driver and a user process, made of a **stream head** (interfaces the process), a **driver end** (controls the device), and zero or more **modules** pushed between them via ioctl(). Each component holds a **read queue and write queue**, and data moves as **messages** between adjacent queues; queues may implement **flow control** (buffering and refusing messages until there is room).
concepts.detail: The process writes with write() (raw data) or putmsg() (messages) and reads with read() or getmsg(); the stream head copies data into messages hand over hand until it reaches the driver end. STREAMS I/O is asynchronous except at the stream head, and modules are reusable across streams (one networking module serving Ethernet and 802.11 cards) — Solaris even implemented sockets on STREAMS. Linux never adopted STREAMS; its socket layer and character-device framework fill the same role, so STREAMS survives mainly as history and as the model for thinking about layered drivers.

concepts.statement: Power management is device management: firmware builds a **device tree** of the hardware topology at boot, and the OS tracks each component’s use (a driver knows if I/O is pending to the flash or the audio device is open). The ACPI standard provides firmware routines the kernel calls through the driver for device-state discovery, error management and power transitions; devices expose power states (PCI defines **D0**, fully on, through **D3**, off) and **wake events** that can re-enable them.
concepts.detail: Data centers feel the same pressure at scale: cooling a modern data center may use twice the electricity of powering the equipment, so management tools evacuate user processes from machines, idle them, and power them off until load returns; CPU cores are suspended (state saved) and resumed on demand. Windows exposes this to laptops as **modern standby** (formerly connected standby) — a low-power idle from which network events can wake the system.

concepts.statement: Android maximizes battery life with three cooperating mechanisms. **Power collapse** puts the device into a very deep sleep — barely more power than fully off, yet able to wake instantly on a button press — by powering off individual components (screen, speakers, I/O subsystem) and parking the CPU in its lowest state: a modern ARM core draws hundreds of milliwatts under load but only a handful of milliwatts in deepest sleep, and can still take an interrupt and resume. **Component-level power management** walks the device tree: an unused component is turned off; if all components on a bus are unused, the bus goes off; if everything is unused, the system enters power collapse. **Wakelocks** let applications temporarily prevent collapse — while an application holds a wakelock, the kernel will not enter power collapse.
concepts.detail: Wakelocks are the safety valve that keeps aggressive power-down from breaking correctness: a game, a video player or an app updater (holding a lock until its download finishes) keeps the device awake exactly as long as needed, then releases it. The pattern generalizes across mobile operating systems, and it composes with component-level management because the kernel consults both usage tracking and outstanding wakelocks before dropping to the next state.

concepts.term: CPU frequency strategies: race to idle
concepts.statement: Beyond powering components off, CPUs can run slower: **dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)** lowers voltage and frequency together — and since dynamic power scales roughly as $P \propto V^2 f$, the savings are superlinear. The competing policy is **race to idle**: finish the work at full speed, then drop straight into the deepest sleep state, exploiting that idle power is tiny. On hardware with fast, efficient deep sleep, racing to idle often wins; workloads with long idle gaps favor slow-and-steady. Linux exposes the trade-off through CPU-frequency **governors** (performance, powersave, and utilization-driven ondemand/schedutil) that choose target frequencies.
concepts.detail: Deep idle states (C-states) have wake-up latency, so the OS balances sleep depth against how soon work arrives — the same per-component reasoning Android applies to its device tree. For I/O-bound systems the strongest lever is avoiding work entirely: fewer context switches and data copies mean fewer wake-ups, so the performance principles of this section are power principles too.

examples.title: The life of a blocking read
examples.problem: A process calls read() on a previously opened file. Follow the request through the kernel to the device and back, and identify every context switch, copy and interrupt along the way.

steps.label: Step 1: System call and cache check
steps.text: The process issues a blocking read(); kernel system-call code checks the parameters and probes the buffer cache — a hit returns the data immediately and the story ends here with no physical I/O at all.

steps.label: Step 2: Sleep and schedule
steps.text: On a miss, the process leaves the run queue for the device’s wait queue (context switch 1), and the I/O subsystem schedules the request and passes it to the device driver — by subroutine call or in-kernel message.

steps.label: Step 3: Driver programs the controller
steps.text: The driver allocates kernel buffer space for the incoming data, schedules the I/O, and writes commands into the device controller’s control registers; the controller operates the device hardware to perform the transfer.

steps.label: Step 4: Data moves by DMA, interrupt fires
steps.text: A DMA controller moves the block into kernel memory without CPU help (cycle stealing for the bus) and raises one interrupt on completion (data copy 1).

steps.label: Step 5: Interrupt path up the stack
steps.text: The vector table dispatches the interrupt to the correct handler, which stores necessary data and signals the driver; the driver identifies the completed request, checks its status, and signals the kernel I/O subsystem.

steps.label: Step 6: Deliver and wake
steps.text: The kernel copies the data into the process’s address space (copy 2), moves the process from the wait queue back to the ready queue, and when the scheduler runs it, the process resumes exactly at the completion of the system call (context switch 2).

examples.result: One logical read cost two context switches, two data copies and one interrupt at minimum — and that is the *optimized* path with DMA. Every performance principle in this section exists to shave items off this list.

examples.title: Remote login: the price of one keystroke
examples.problem: A user types a single character into a remote shell session. Count the journey of that character, and show why the book calls network I/O a driver of context-switch and interrupt load.

steps.label: Step 1: Local machine, input side
steps.text: The keypress raises a keyboard interrupt; the character passes through the interrupt handler to the device driver, into the kernel, and up to the user process (state switches all the way).

steps.label: Step 2: Local machine, output side
steps.text: The process issues a network-I/O system call to send the character: back into the kernel, through the network layers that build a packet, into the network device driver, which hands the packet to the network controller — which raises an interrupt that propagates back up to complete the call.

steps.label: Step 3: Remote machine
steps.text: The packet arrives; the network hardware generates an interrupt; the character is unpacked from the protocol stack and handed to the network daemon, which finds the right login session and passes it to that session’s subdaemon — several more context switches.

steps.label: Step 4: The echo doubles it
steps.text: The remote system echoes the character back for local display, so the same trip — in reverse, with the same interrupt, driver, kernel and process crossings — happens a second time.

steps.label: Step 5: What design can do
steps.text: Line-buffering batches many characters into one packet; large transfers amortize per-byte costs; DMA removes per-word interrupts; front-end processors and terminal concentrators move the multiplexing off the main CPU entirely — mainframes formalized this as dedicated I/O channels.

examples.result: One typed character, two machines, roughly a dozen crossings of the hardware–driver–kernel–process stack — doubled by the echo. That is why interrupt frequency, context-switch count and data-copy count are the levers of I/O performance.

keyTakeaways: A blocking read passes through parameter checks and the buffer cache, a wait queue, the I/O scheduler, the device driver, the controller registers, the device, a DMA transfer, an interrupt, the interrupt handler, and back up the stack to wake the process — ten steps, two context switches, two copies, one interrupt.
Name translation sits in front of it all: mount tables map path prefixes to devices, and major/minor numbers route to the right driver instance.

I/O overhead is context switches (protection crossings), data copies (controller→kernel→application) and interrupts (state save, dispatch, restore); remote login multiplies all three per character — and the echo doubles it.

Efficiency principles: fewer context switches, fewer copies, fewer interrupts (larger transfers, smart controllers, polling where bounded — plus modern interrupt coalescing), more concurrency (DMA, channels), processing in hardware, and balanced CPU/memory/bus/I/O.

Functionality migrates application → kernel → driver → controller → device hardware as it matures, trading flexibility and development speed for efficiency (FUSE at the flexible end; hardware RAID controllers at the rigid end).

STREAMS let System V UNIX stack modules of driver code dynamically — full-duplex streams with per-module read/write queues, message passing and flow control; Linux never adopted it, its socket and character-device layers serving the same needs.

Power management is device management — ACPI firmware routines under driver control, component states D0–D3 with wake events, Android’s power collapse and wakelocks — while DVFS trades voltage and frequency ($P \propto V^2 f$) and race to idle finishes fast then sleeps deep (Linux governors choose).

quiz.q: In the life cycle of a blocking read, what happens if the requested data are already in the buffer cache?
options: the data are returned to the process immediately and no physical I/O is performed
the process is moved to the device wait queue anyway
the request is rejected with an error
quiz.explanation: Step 2 of the life cycle: after parameter checking, the kernel probes the buffer cache first — a hit ends the request right there. Only a miss leads to the wait queue, the driver, the controller and the DMA transfer.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the book’s principles for improving I/O efficiency?
options: reduce the number of times data must be copied in memory
increase the number of context switches so the kernel runs more often
reduce the frequency of interrupts by using large transfers
balance CPU, memory, bus and I/O performance
quiz.explanation: Context switches are pure overhead — every protection crossing costs state save/restore and cache disruption. The real principles: fewer context switches, fewer copies, fewer interrupts (large transfers, smart controllers, polling when bounded), more DMA concurrency, processing moved into hardware, and balanced subsystems.

quiz.q: A wakelock on Android is:
options: a hold an application takes to prevent the system from entering power collapse until the application releases it
a hardware interlock on the power button
a kernel spinlock used by interrupt handlers
a lock on the device tree
quiz.explanation: Power collapse would otherwise be triggered whenever all components are idle; a game, video player or app updater needs the device to stay awake, so it acquires a wakelock — while held, the kernel will not enter power collapse. The updater releases it when its download completes.

quiz.q: Under race to idle, a CPU-bound burst of work is best handled by:
options: running at the lowest possible frequency for as long as possible
running at full speed, then dropping into the deepest sleep state as soon as the work is done
quiz.explanation: Deep idle states consume almost nothing, so finishing fast and sleeping deeply often beats slow-and-steady DVFS — the decision depends on how quickly more work arrives (and how costly the wake-up is). Linux governors encode this policy choice.

quiz.q: In STREAMS, modules are added to a stream by:
options: the ioctl() system call, which pushes a module between the stream head and the driver end
quiz.explanation: A stream is a full-duplex stack — stream head, zero or more modules, driver end — with a read and a write queue in each component, message passing between adjacent queues, and optional flow control. ioctl() pushes modules (e.g. an input-editing module onto a keyboard stream) without touching the rest of the stack.

intro: To most users the file system is the most visible part of an operating system: the mechanism for on-line storage of and access to both data and programs. This section defines the file — a named collection of related information recorded on secondary storage — surveys its attributes and the seven basic operations every file system must support, and explains the open()/close() protocol that makes all the other operations fast. It closes with file typing, internal structure, and the small tax every block-oriented device levies on every file.
objectives: Define a file and list the attributes an operating system typically records for one
Trace the seven basic file operations and what the OS must do for each
Explain why open() and close() exist and what the open-file table stores
Compare file-type mechanisms: extensions, magic numbers, and the macOS type and creator attributes
Relate logical records to physical blocks and quantify internal fragmentation

concepts.statement: A **file** is a named collection of related information that is recorded on secondary storage. From the user’s perspective, a file is the smallest allotment of logical secondary storage — data cannot be written to secondary storage except within a file. Files represent programs (source and object forms) and data (numeric, alphabetic, alphanumeric or binary), free-form like text or rigidly formatted.
concepts.detail: The operating system abstracts away the physical properties of NVM devices, HDDs, tape and optical media to present this one uniform logical storage unit, and because the media are nonvolatile, contents persist across reboots. The abstraction is so general that UNIX exposes kernel state — process details in /proc — through file-system interfaces.

concepts.statement: The information about a file, varying by system but typically: **name** (the only item kept in human-readable form), **identifier** (a unique tag, usually a number, that identifies the file within the file system — the non-human-readable name), **type**, **location** (a pointer to the device and to the file’s position on it), **size** (current, and possibly the maximum allowed), **protection** (access-control information), and **timestamps and user identification** (creation, last modification and last use).
concepts.detail: A directory entry typically holds just the name and the identifier; the identifier — an inode number in UNIX — locates the rest. Recording all attributes can take over a kilobyte per file, so a large system’s directories themselves grow to megabytes or gigabytes and are brought into memory piecemeal, like the files they describe.

concepts.statement: The minimal set every file system must provide: **create** (find space for the file, then make a directory entry), **write** (handle plus data; the system keeps a write pointer for where the next write lands), **read** (handle plus a memory destination; a read pointer advances), **reposition within a file** (reset the current-file-position pointer — a file seek), **delete** (release all file space and erase the directory entry), and **truncate** (erase the contents but keep the attributes, resetting the length to zero).
concepts.detail: Reading and writing usually share one per-process current-file-position pointer, saving space and complexity. Everything else composes from these primitives — copying a file is create plus a read-write loop, and renaming is a directory edit.

concepts.term: open(), close() and the open-file table
concepts.statement: Rather than resolving a file name, searching the directory and re-checking permissions on every operation, all operations except create and delete require an **open()** first. open() resolves the name once, verifies the requested mode (read-only, read–write, append-only) against the file’s permissions, copies the entry into an **open-file table**, and returns a handle — an index into that table — used by every subsequent call. **close()** removes the entry and releases any locks.
concepts.detail: Four things are associated with each open file: the **file pointer** (current position, unique to each process), the **file-open count** (the entry can be reclaimed only when the last close brings it to zero), the **location of the file** (kept in memory so the directory need not be consulted per operation), and the **access rights** of the mode the process opened in. Systems use two levels of tables — a per-process table and a system-wide table — which Chapter 14 traces in detail.

concepts.statement: Writing need not be append-only: a **seek** (reposition) moves the current-file-position pointer anywhere in the file before the next write, so the same write() primitive can overwrite the middle of a file, append at the end, or fill a hole. An append-only open mode simply pins every write to the end of the file.
concepts.detail: Because a seek only updates a pointer in memory, it involves no actual I/O — it is free. The single shared offset is also why two processes reading the same open file without coordination interleave unpredictably; file locking adds the missing coordination.

concepts.term: File types: extensions, magic numbers, type and creator
concepts.statement: Operating systems recognize file types in three ways. **Name extensions** (exe, com, bat, sh, c, java, docx, zip, mp3…) split the name at a period; in UNIX they are hints for users and applications — neither enforced nor depended on by the OS. **Magic numbers** — distinctive values stored at the beginning of some files (the format of an image, the shell language of a script) — identify content from the header alone. **macOS** stores a type (.app for application) plus a **creator** attribute naming the program that created the file, set by the OS during create() and enforced: double-clicking a file launches its creator with the file loaded.
concepts.detail: Type support is a trade-off: an OS that defines five file structures must carry the code for all five, and a user who needs a structure it does not know — an encrypted file is neither ASCII text nor an executable — is stranded. UNIX and Windows choose the minimal approach: every file is a sequence of 8-bit bytes, interpreted by each application itself — maximum flexibility, minimum support.

concepts.term: Internal file structure and internal fragmentation
concepts.statement: All disk I/O is performed in units of fixed-size **physical blocks** (one or more sectors, typically 512 or 4,096 bytes), while a file is a sequence of **logical records** — bytes, lines, or more complex structured items — that rarely match the block size. The OS or the application **packs** logical records into physical blocks; UNIX defines all files as unstructured byte streams (logical record size 1) and packs bytes into blocks automatically. The slack in each file’s last block is **internal fragmentation**, and every file system suffers it.
concepts.detail: Book example: with 512-byte blocks a 1,949-byte file occupies $\lceil 1949/512 \rceil = 4$ blocks — $4 \times 512 = 2048$ bytes of device space — wasting $2048 - 1949 = 99$ bytes. The larger the block (or cluster) size, the greater the internal fragmentation.

examples.title: Packing a file into blocks
examples.problem: A text file holds 1,949 bytes and the device transfers data in 512-byte blocks. How many blocks are allocated, how much space is wasted, and what share of the file’s storage is slack?

steps.label: Step 1: Count the blocks
steps.text: Three full blocks hold $3 \times 512 = 1536$ bytes; the remaining $1949 - 1536 = 413$ bytes require a fourth. Total: $\lceil 1949/512 \rceil = 4$ blocks.

steps.label: Step 2: Space allocated
steps.text: $4 \times 512 = 2048$ bytes of device space now back the file.

steps.label: Step 3: The waste
steps.text: $2048 - 1949 = 99$ bytes are internal fragmentation — the fourth block is only $413/512 \approx 81\%$ full.

steps.label: Step 4: The general rule
steps.text: The slack grows with the block size: a 100-byte file wastes 412 bytes inside a 512-byte block but 3,996 bytes inside a 4,096-byte block. Trade block size against this tax — Chapter 14 returns to it as the cluster-size dilemma.

examples.result: Four blocks, 2,048 bytes allocated, 99 bytes (about 4.8 percent) of internal fragmentation — unavoidable in any block-oriented file system, and the reason administrators do not simply crank the block size to maximum.

examples.title: Why open() exists
examples.problem: A process will read the same file 500 times. Contrast what happens on every read with and without an open-file table.

steps.label: Step 1: Without open()
steps.text: All 500 reads repeat the full ritual: parse the path name, walk each directory, find the entry, re-check access permissions, and only then locate the data. The directory search dominates every operation.

steps.label: Step 2: With open()
steps.text: The ritual happens once: open() resolves the name, checks the requested mode against the file’s permissions, and installs an entry in the open-file table holding the file’s location and access rights.

steps.label: Step 3: Every read after that
steps.text: Each of the 500 reads carries only a small integer handle that indexes the table directly — no searching, no repeated permission checks, no directory I/O.

steps.label: Step 4: close()
steps.text: The final close() decrements the open count and, at zero, removes the entry and releases any locks — reclaiming the table slot for the next file.

examples.result: open() amortizes name resolution and permission checking over all of a file’s operations — the same caching-of-context idea behind every handle, descriptor and session abstraction in systems design.

keyTakeaways: A file is a named collection of related information on secondary storage — the smallest unit of logical storage a user can write to.
Attributes: name, identifier, type, location, size, protection, timestamps and user IDs; the directory stores the name plus the identifier that locates the rest.
The seven basic operations — create, write, read, reposition (seek), delete, truncate — compose into every higher-level file operation.
open() moves name resolution and permission checking out of the per-operation path; later calls use a handle into the open-file table, and close() reclaims the slot when the open count hits zero.
File typing is weakest as a name extension (a hint), stronger as a header magic number, strongest as an OS-enforced type and creator pair (macOS).

Logical records are packed into fixed-size physical blocks; the slack in the last block — internal fragmentation — is unavoidable and grows with block size: a 1,949-byte file occupies $4 \times 512 = 2048$ bytes.

quiz.q: Which file attribute is the only one kept in human-readable form?
quiz.explanation: The name is the human-readable symbol; the identifier (an inode number in UNIX) is the non-human-readable tag, and location, size and protection are all binary metadata.

quiz.q: Most systems require open() before read() because:
options: it locks the file against other users
it loads the entire file into memory
it avoids resolving the file name and checking permissions on every operation
quiz.explanation: open() resolves the name and verifies permissions once, installing an entry in the open-file table; every later operation uses the returned handle to index that table instead of repeating the directory search.

quiz.q: Which operation erases a file’s contents but keeps its attributes and directory entry?
quiz.explanation: Truncate resets the file to length zero and releases its space while leaving the attributes — and the directory entry — intact; delete removes the entry as well.

quiz.q: How does UNIX identify the type of a binary file such as an image?
options: By a magic number stored at the beginning of the file
By the file name extension, which the kernel enforces
By a creator attribute set at create time
By scanning the whole file for patterns
quiz.explanation: UNIX stores magic numbers at the start of some binary and text files to indicate content format; extensions exist only as hints for users and applications, neither enforced nor depended on by the operating system.

quiz.q: With 512-byte blocks, how much device space does a 1,949-byte file occupy, and how much is wasted?
quiz.explanation: The file needs four blocks — three full ones plus 413 bytes in a fourth: 4 × 512 = 2,048 bytes allocated, of which 2,048 − 1,949 = 99 bytes are internal fragmentation.

intro: Once a file exists, how do programs get at its contents? The three classic answers — sequential, direct (relative) and indexed access — span the gap between the tape-era model of read next and the random reads that databases demand. This section defines each method, derives the arithmetic that turns a record number into a block number, and shows how a small index turns a large random-access file into a couple of direct reads.
objectives: Distinguish sequential, direct and indexed access, and name the device model behind the first two
Compute the block and offset of a fixed-length record using the floor and modulo formulas
Explain how an index over a direct-access file accelerates point lookups, and how ISAM generalizes it
Judge which access method fits a workload: batch reads versus random point queries

concepts.statement: **Sequential access** processes a file’s information in order, one record after another: **read next** reads the next portion and automatically advances the file pointer, and **write next** appends to the end and advances to the new end of file. The file can be reset (rewound) to the beginning, and some systems allow skipping forward or backward n records — perhaps only $n = 1$.
concepts.detail: It is based on a **tape model** of a file and works as well on random-access devices as on sequential ones. It is by far the most common access pattern — editors and compilers read files this way — and it suits batch processing that touches every record exactly once.

concepts.statement: **Direct or relative access** views a file as a numbered sequence of fixed-length logical records on a **disk model**: read block 14, then block 53, then write block 7 — any order is allowed. Operations become read(n) and write(n), or equivalently position file(n) followed by read next.
concepts.detail: Essential when large amounts of information must be reached immediately — databases are often of this type. An airline-reservation system might store everything about flight 713 in block 713 of the reservation file. The block number supplied is a **relative block number** — an index relative to the beginning of the file (first block 0 or 1, depending on the system) — so the OS is free to place the file anywhere (the allocation problem) and the user cannot reach blocks outside it, even though the absolute disk address of the first block might be 14,703.

concepts.statement: For a file of fixed-length logical records, a request for record $r$ (0-based) becomes an I/O request for $L \cdot r$ bytes into the file, where $L$ is the record length in bytes. With $B$ records packed per block, record $r$ lives in block $k = \lfloor r / B \rfloor$ at offset $r \bmod B$ within that block.
concepts.detail: Fixed-length records are what make direct access cheap: the address of record $r$ is computed, never searched for. Variable-length records would force a scan from the start of the file to find where record $r$ begins — sequential access by necessity.

concepts.statement: Built on top of direct access: maintain an **index** for the file which, like the index in the back of a book, contains **pointers to the various blocks**. A lookup first searches the index, then uses the pointer to read the one data block that can hold the answer.
concepts.detail: Book example: a retail-price file of 16-byte records (a 10-digit UPC plus a 6-digit price) holds 64 records per 1,024-byte block. Keeping the file sorted by UPC and indexing the first UPC in each block yields about 1,875 entries of 10 digits — roughly 20,000 bytes — small enough to live in memory, so a price lookup costs a binary search of the index plus one block read.

concepts.statement: When the index itself grows too large for memory, **index the index**: a small master index points to disk blocks of a secondary index, which point to the actual data blocks. IBM’s **indexed sequential-access method (ISAM)** works exactly this way — binary-search the master index, read one secondary index block, binary search it, read the data block — locating any record by key in at most two direct-access reads.
concepts.detail: The file is kept sorted on a key, with overflow chains absorbing inserts that no longer fit in place. OpenVMS index and relative files build on the same idea, and relational databases inherit it wholesale: a table is a direct-access file of fixed-length records, and the DBMS builds and maintains its own B-tree indexes on top rather than trusting the file system to do it.

concepts.term: Simulating one method on the other
concepts.statement: Sequential access simulates trivially on a direct-access file: keep a variable cp as the current position — read next becomes read cp followed by $cp := cp + 1$, and reset is $cp := 0$. The converse — direct access on a purely sequential-access medium — is extremely inefficient and clumsy.
concepts.detail: This asymmetry is why direct-access capability is the valuable primitive: it subsumes sequential access, but not the other way around. Systems that support only one method per file (declared at creation) exploit exactly this.

concepts.statement: **Read-everything workloads** favor sequential access: the tape model matches, every block is visited once in order, and buffering is trivial (batch jobs, backups, media streaming). **Point queries** — find one record among millions by key — need direct or indexed access; a sequential scan would read the whole file for one answer.
concepts.detail: Databases sit on direct access plus their own index trees; compilers and log analyzers sit on sequential streams. Mainframe operating systems historically offered many access methods precisely because choosing one was a major application design decision.

examples.title: Locating a record in a direct-access file
examples.problem: A direct-access file stores fixed 16-byte records, 64 records per 1,024-byte block. Record 5,000 is requested. Which block is read, at what offset, and where does the record sit in the file’s byte stream?

steps.label: Step 1: Records per block
steps.text: With record length $L = 16$ bytes and 1,024-byte blocks, $B = 1024/16 = 64$ records are packed per block.

steps.label: Step 2: The block
steps.text: $k = \lfloor 5000/64 \rfloor = \lfloor 78.125 \rfloor = 78$ — the file’s 79th block (block 78, counting from zero) holds the record.

steps.label: Step 3: The offset
steps.text: $5000 \bmod 64 = 8$ — it is the 9th record inside that block, beginning at byte $8 \times 16 = 128$ within the block.

steps.label: Step 4: The file byte offset
steps.text: Equivalently the request is an I/O for $L \cdot r = 16 \times 5000 = 80{,}000$ bytes into the file: the OS can translate it either way in constant time.

examples.result: Record 5,000 → block $\lfloor 5000/64 \rfloor = 78$, offset $5000 \bmod 64 = 8$ (byte 128 within the block, file byte 80,000). Fixed record length turns lookup into address arithmetic — O(1), no searching.

examples.title: Indexing a 120,000-record price file
examples.problem: A sorted retail-price file has 120,000 records of 16 bytes each (10-digit UPC, 6-digit price) on 1,024-byte blocks. A lookup for one UPC arrives. Design the index and count the I/O.

steps.label: Step 1: Size the file
steps.text: Records per block: $B = 1024/16 = 64$. Total blocks: $\lceil 120{,}000 / 64 \rceil = 1875$ — about 2,000 blocks and roughly two million bytes.

steps.label: Step 2: Build the index
steps.text: Keep the file sorted by UPC and record the first UPC of every block: 1,875 entries of 10 digits, about $1875 \times 10 = 18{,}750$ bytes — comfortably resident in memory.

steps.label: Step 3: Search the index
steps.text: Binary-search the in-memory index for the greatest first-UPC not exceeding the query — about $\log_2 1875 \approx 11$ comparisons — identifying the one block that can contain the item.

steps.label: Step 4: One direct read
steps.text: Read that block directly and scan its 64 records for the exact UPC.

examples.result: One direct block read answers a point query over 1.92 MB of data. The index converts a full-file scan into index arithmetic plus one I/O — precisely why databases build their own indexes atop direct access.

keyTakeaways: Sequential access (read next / write next, rewind) is the tape model — the most common pattern and the right one for batch workloads.
Direct access treats the file as numbered fixed-length records; record $r$ sits in block $\lfloor r / B \rfloor$ at offset $r \bmod B$ — computed, never searched.
Relative block numbers free the OS to place the file anywhere and confine user reads to the file itself.
Indexed access adds a pointer structure over direct access: binary-search a small in-memory index, then read one block; ISAM’s multilevel scheme does it in at most two direct reads.
Sequential access simulates trivially on a direct-access file (a cp counter); the converse is hopeless — direct access is the stronger primitive.

quiz.q: Sequential access is said to be based on which device model?
quiz.explanation: Sequential access was designed for the tape: information flows in order, one record after another, with rewind to restart. It still works perfectly on random-access devices, which are strictly more capable.

quiz.q: A direct-access file packs 100 fixed-length records per block. Record 4,517 lives in block:
quiz.explanation: k = floor(4517/100) = 45, and the offset within that block is 4517 mod 100 = 17. The floor-and-modulo pair turns a record number into a block and offset in constant time.

quiz.q: Which workload is the worst fit for pure sequential access?
options: A nightly backup of every file
A compiler reading a source file start to finish
A database looking up one customer by account number
A log analyzer scanning every line
quiz.explanation: A point query needs direct or indexed access: reading one record out of millions should cost one block read, not a full-file scan. Backups, compilers and log analysis naturally read everything in order.

quiz.q: When the index of a large file is itself too large for memory, the classic remedy is:
options: Store the index at the front of the file
Build a multilevel index — an index of the index, as in ISAM
quiz.explanation: A small master index points to secondary index blocks that point to the data, keeping only the top level resident — any record is still found in at most two direct reads.

intro: Directories are the symbol table of the file system: they translate the names humans use into the control blocks the machine uses. This section climbs the ladder of directory organizations — single-level, two-level, tree, acyclic graph, general graph — and shows how each fixes the naming problems of the previous rung while creating new ones. It ends with the two mechanisms that make modern name spaces what they are: links and mounting.
objectives: View a directory as a symbol table and list the operations it must support
Explain the naming-collision and sharing problems that drive the evolution from single-level to graph directories
Distinguish absolute and relative paths, the working directory, and the entries . and ..
Contrast hard links and symbolic links, including dangling links and reference counts
Walk a path name through the directory tree, and describe mounting and cycle management

concepts.statement: A **directory** can be viewed as a symbol table that translates file names into their **file control blocks** (the inode, in UNIX). It must support inserting entries, deleting entries, searching for a named entry and listing all entries. The standard operation set: **search for a file** (including pattern matching over names), **create a file**, **delete a file** (a delete leaves a hole the file system may later defragment away), **list a directory**, **rename a file** (which may also move its position in the structure), and **traverse the file system** — visiting every directory and file, the basis of backups.
concepts.detail: Because the directory must match the volatility of the files, it lives on the same device as they do and is itself brought into memory piecemeal, as needed.

concepts.statement: All files live in one directory. It is easy to support and understand, but **every file name must be unique across the whole system** — a rule that collapses at scale: in one programming class the book recounts, 23 students called their second assignment prog2.c and another 11 called it assign2.c. Even a single user loses track of hundreds of files in one flat list.
concepts.detail: Longer names help — most systems allow up to 255 characters, making unique names possible — but forcing global uniqueness is the wrong invariant once there is more than one user.

concepts.statement: Each user gets a **user file directory (UFD)** listing only their files; a **master file directory (MFD)**, indexed by user name or account number, points to each UFD. Name collisions between users vanish — different users may own files with the same name as long as each UFD is internally unique. Naming a file uniquely now requires both parts: the path /userb/test.txt.
concepts.detail: The cost is isolation: cooperating users cannot easily reach one another’s files, and system files (compilers, libraries) must be found another way — the standard trick is a **search path**, an ordered list of directories consulted when a name is not found locally, as UNIX and Windows both do. A two-level directory is a tree of height 2: the MFD is the root, UFDs its children, files the leaves.

concepts.statement: The natural generalization: a **tree of arbitrary height** with a root directory, so every file has a unique path name. Each process has a **current (working) directory** containing most files of current interest. **Absolute paths** begin at the root (/spell/mail/prt/first); **relative paths** begin at the current directory (prt/first, from /spell/mail). A directory is just a file with a special format — one bit in each entry marks file (0) versus subdirectory (1).
concepts.detail: The entries . (the directory itself) and .. (its parent) anchor relative movement upward. Renaming a file inside a tree is nothing more than moving directory pointers. Deleting a non-empty directory is a policy choice: refuse until it is empty, or recursively delete as UNIX rm does — convenient, and dangerous when the command was a mistake. Kernel caches of directory entries (**dentry caches**) make repeated path resolution cheap by remembering components already resolved.

concepts.statement: A tree prohibits sharing: an **acyclic graph** — a graph with no cycles — allows the same file or subdirectory to exist in two (or more) places at once. Sharing is not the same as copying: with two copies, one programmer’s edits never appear in the other’s; with one shared file, changes are immediately visible through every path to it — crucial for teams, and for a file that legitimately belongs in two projects at once.
concepts.detail: A shared subdirectory is even more valuable: a file added by one team member appears in the shared directory of every member. The price is multiple absolute path names for one file (the aliasing problem — traversals must not visit shared structures twice) and harder deletion: when may the file’s space be reclaimed?

concepts.statement: Two implementations of sharing. A **hard link** is a duplicate directory entry pointing at the same file control block: every link is an equal citizen, the inode keeps a **reference (link) count**, and the file’s space is released only when the last link is deleted. Hard links cannot span file systems (the identifier is meaningful only within one) and are not permitted to directories — which is exactly what keeps file cycles impossible. A **soft or symbolic link** is an indirect pointer: a small file containing the **path name** of the target, resolved at use. Symbolic links can span file systems (Windows shortcuts work this way) but they can **dangle**: deleting the target leaves the link pointing at nothing.
concepts.detail: Deletion under symbolic links is gentler: removing a link never touches the target, and a dangling link simply fails to resolve, treated like any other illegal file name. Hard links demand the reference count; soft links demand tolerance of dangling references — the UNIX approach for files is hard links, with soft links as the flexible cross-filesystem escape hatch.

concepts.statement: If links create cycles — a directory reachable from itself — the structure becomes a **general graph**. Then a **reference count of zero no longer proves a file is unreachable**: a self-referencing directory never drains its count even when nothing outside can reach it. Reclaiming space then needs **garbage collection**: traverse everything reachable, **mark** it, then a second pass collects everything unmarked onto the free list.
concepts.detail: Garbage collection of a disk-based file system is so time-consuming it is seldom attempted; the practical alternative is to **bypass links during directory traversal**, which preserves acyclic behavior at zero cost. A related marking procedure also guarantees a search visits every component exactly once.

concepts.statement: Just as a file must be opened before use, a file system must be **mounted** before its files are available. The operating system is given the name of the device and the **mount point** — the location in the existing file structure where the new file system attaches. Some systems also require a file-system type; others inspect the device’s structures — reading the superblock — to verify that it actually contains a **valid file system** before proceeding. The mount is recorded in the **mount table**, and the files of the newly attached volume appear under the mount point, **hiding whatever directory contents were there before** until it is unmounted.
concepts.detail: Windows marks volumes with a drive letter plus colon (C:\userb\test), while UNIX and Linux fold the device into the name space — the mount table maps directory positions to devices, which is how the OS knows which device serves a given path.

examples.title: Resolving /home/user/file.txt step by step
examples.problem: A UNIX-like system uses tree-structured directories with a dentry cache that is initially empty. Trace the resolution of the absolute path /home/user/file.txt and count the directory reads.

steps.label: Step 1: Start at the root
steps.text: The resolver begins at the root directory — conventionally inode 2, always resident — reading its directory blocks from disk: read 1.

steps.label: Step 2: Look up home
steps.text: The entry home yields home’s inode number; the resolver reads home’s directory blocks — read 2 — and checks the process may traverse it (the x permission on directories).

steps.label: Step 3: Look up user
steps.text: The entry user in /home gives user’s inode number; reading /home/user’s directory blocks is read 3.

steps.label: Step 4: Look up file.txt
steps.text: The entry file.txt yields its inode (say inode 4711). The full resolution read three directories — root, home, user — and an open() would read inode 4711 itself next.

steps.label: Step 5: Warm caches
steps.text: The kernel caches each component (the dentry cache), so a later open of /home/user/other.txt reuses root, home and user and reads only /home/user once — already-resolved prefixes cost nothing.

examples.result: Path resolution costs about one directory read per component on a cold cache — the deeper the tree, the more expensive absolute paths. The working directory and the dentry cache exist precisely to amortize this cost.

examples.title: The life and death of a hard link
examples.problem: A user creates report.tex, makes a hard link notes.tex to it, then deletes report.tex. Repeat the experiment with a symbolic link instead, and compare.

steps.label: Step 1: Create
steps.text: report.tex allocates an inode (say 4711) with its data blocks; the directory entry maps report.tex → 4711 and the inode’s link count is set to 1.

steps.label: Step 2: Hard link
steps.text: ln report.tex notes.tex adds a second directory entry, notes.tex → 4711, and the link count becomes 2. Both names are now equal citizens — there is no original and no copy.

steps.label: Step 3: Delete report.tex
steps.text: The directory entry is removed and the count drops to 1 — the inode and its blocks survive, fully reachable through notes.tex.

steps.label: Step 4: Delete notes.tex too
steps.text: Only when the count reaches 0 does the file system actually free the inode and the data blocks.

steps.label: Step 5: Symbolic contrast
steps.text: ln -s report.tex pointer.txt stores the string report.tex. Deleting report.tex leaves pointer.txt dangling — resolving it fails like any missing name — and the target’s link count never knew the link existed. The symbolic link could equally have pointed into another mounted file system; the hard link could not.

examples.result: Hard links: multiple directory entries, one inode, reference-counted lifetime, filesystem-local. Symbolic links: path-name indirection, count-free, cross-filesystem — and prone to dangling.

examples.title: Scaling a single-level directory
examples.problem: A shared lab computer keeps every user’s files in one flat directory. What breaks as enrollment grows to 50 students, and what does the two-level structure fix?

steps.label: Step 1: The collision
steps.text: 23 students submit prog2.c and 11 submit assign2.c; the second arrival of each name either overwrites the first or is rejected — the unique-name rule fails at trivial scale.

steps.label: Step 2: The workaround
steps.text: Users start encoding identity into names — prog2-maria.c, prog2-chen.c — a manual, error-prone, single-level directory rebuilt by hand.

steps.label: Step 3: Two levels
steps.text: Give each student a UFD: prog2.c can now exist 50 times, once per UFD, with the MFD mapping student → UFD. Deleting a file searches only the local UFD, so no student can accidentally delete another’s same-named file.

steps.label: Step 4: The new problems
steps.text: Isolation bites: sharing course materials needs explicit paths like /instructor/handout.pdf, and system binaries need a search path — motivating the tree, the acyclic graph and everything above.

examples.result: Each rung of the ladder fixes the previous rung’s naming crisis and creates the next one: single-level collides, two-level isolates, trees demand path resolution, graphs demand cycle management.

keyTakeaways: A directory is a symbol table from names to control blocks; it must support search, create, delete, list, rename and traverse.
Single-level directories force globally unique names; two-level (per-user UFDs under an MFD) removes collisions but isolates users; trees add structure, subdirectories and paths.
Relative paths start at the current directory, absolute paths at the root; . and .. anchor upward movement, and dentry caches make repeated resolution cheap.
Acyclic graphs add sharing: one file, many paths — edits are visible everywhere at once, unlike copies.
Hard links duplicate directory entries onto one inode with a reference count — filesystem-local and cycle-free for files; symbolic links store a path, span file systems, and can dangle.
Cycles break reference counting: only garbage collection (mark and sweep) can prove unreachability, and on disk that is too slow — so systems bypass links during traversal instead.
Mounting verifies the device’s structures (the superblock), records the pair in the mount table, and attaches the volume at the mount point — hiding whatever lived beneath it.

quiz.q: In one class, 23 students named their assignment prog2.c. Which directory structure makes this harmless?
options: A two-level directory with a per-user UFD for each student
quiz.explanation: With a separate UFD per user, the same name can exist once in each directory; the MFD maps user to UFD, and prog2.c can legitimately exist 50 times.

quiz.q: Which statement about hard links is true?
options: A hard link stores the target’s path name
A hard link can dangle if the target is deleted
A hard link is a second directory entry pointing at the same inode and cannot cross file systems
A hard link increments the target file’s byte count
quiz.explanation: A hard link duplicates the directory entry onto the same inode, raising its reference count; inode numbers are per-file-system, so hard links cannot span them. Dangling references and path-name storage belong to symbolic links.

quiz.q: A symbolic link can dangle because:
options: it keeps the inode number of the target
it stores only a path name that may stop resolving
quiz.explanation: A symbolic link is just a stored path. If the target is deleted — or replaced — the link still holds the string, and resolution fails at use time like any other illegal file name.

quiz.q: Why do general graph directories need garbage collection while acyclic graphs do not?
options: Graphs hold more files than trees
In a cyclic graph, a nonzero reference count does not prove the file is reachable
Garbage collection is faster than reference counting
quiz.explanation: A cycle can keep every member’s reference count above zero even after nothing outside the cycle points in. Only mark-and-sweep traversal can prove unreachability — which is why systems prefer to bypass links and stay effectively acyclic.

quiz.q: Mounting a file system at /mnt:
options: verifies the device contains a valid file system and attaches it there, hiding what was beneath
quiz.explanation: The OS is given device and mount point, inspects the volume’s structures (the superblock) to confirm a valid file system, records the mount in the mount table, and covers whatever lived at that point until unmount.

intro: Protection answers two different questions: keeping data safe from physical damage — reliability, solved with duplicate copies and backups — and keeping it safe from improper access — protection, solved with access control. This section covers the UNIX owner/group/other permission bits and their octal arithmetic, access-control lists and their Windows incarnation, the memory-mapped file as the fourth way to do file I/O, and file locking for processes that share.
objectives: List the types of file access that protection mechanisms control
Encode and decode the nine UNIX permission bits, including octal mode math and umask
Explain ACLs, their evaluation order, and how they extend owner/group/other
Describe memory mapping and contrast MAP_SHARED, MAP_PRIVATE and read()/write()
Distinguish shared and exclusive file locks, and mandatory from advisory locking

concepts.statement: Keeping information safe means two different things: **reliability** — guarding against physical damage from hardware errors, power failures, head crashes, dirt, temperature, vandalism, bugs and accidental deletion — generally provided by duplicate copies and regular backups; and **protection** — guarding against improper **access**, solved with controlled access rather than prohibition (too restrictive) or free access (too dangerous).
concepts.detail: The types of access that may be controlled: **read**, **write**, **execute**, **append**, **delete**, **list** (the name and attributes) and **attribute change**. Higher-level operations reduce to these: a user with read access can copy and print a file, because copying is just repeated reads.

concepts.term: Owner, group, other and the nine permission bits
concepts.statement: The condensed UNIX scheme classifies users as **owner** (the file’s creator), **group** (a set of users sharing the file, needing similar access) and **other** (everyone else), granting each class the bits **r** (read), **w** (write) and **x** (execute) — nine bits per file. Directory protection uses the same fields with a twist: x on a directory means permission to traverse and search it, r means list its contents.
concepts.detail: A listing like drwxr-xr-x decodes as directory, owner rwx, group r-x, other r-x. Nine bits are compact — fixed-size directory entries — but coarse: they cannot express “Jim and Dawn, but not the whole group, may write.”

concepts.statement: Each class’s rwx triple encodes as one octal digit $d = 4r + 2w + 1x$ (each letter 0 or 1), so a whole mode is three digits: rwxr-xr-x is $755$ and rw-rw-r-- is $664$. New files start from the defaults 0666 (files) and 0777 (directories), with the **umask**’s bits removed: with umask 022 a new file receives $0666 \mathbin{\&} \mathord{\sim} 022 = 0644$ — rw-r--r--.
concepts.detail: The umask is a per-process mask of bits to refuse, not a grant: no file gains rights from a umask, it can only lose the defaults it would otherwise have had.

concepts.statement: The most general identity-dependent scheme associates with each file and directory an **access-control list (ACL)** naming users and the access allowed each. Fully expanded ACLs are unwieldy — enumerating every user with read permission is tedious, and the entry becomes variable-length — so systems **combine** the condensed owner/group/other scheme with ACLs for exceptions: Solaris appends a **+** to the mode when an ACL is present, managed with setfacl and getfacl. Windows NTFS is built entirely on ACLs: a list of **ACEs** (access-control entries) attached to files and **inherited** by the children of a directory, evaluated in order with an explicit deny overriding later allows.
concepts.detail: When modes and ACLs conflict, the more specific mechanism wins — Solaris gives ACL entries precedence, following the general rule that specificity has priority. In the book’s example, Sara grants her helper group read–write on book.tex and everyone else read; a visitor needing chapter-one-only access gets a single ACL entry on chapter 1, because a file can belong to only one group.

concepts.term: Passwords on files and capability lists
