concepts.statement: Instead of writing separate directory and file routines for every file-system type, modern operating systems insert a **VFS layer** between the system-call interface (open, read, write, close and file descriptors) and the implementations. It serves two functions: it separates file-system-generic operations from their implementation by defining a clean **VFS interface** that many implementations satisfy at once, and it provides a file-representation structure — the **vnode** — with a designator that is unique **throughout a network**, because UNIX inode numbers are unique only within a single file system.
concepts.detail: Three layers result: the file-system interface on top, the VFS in the middle, and the file-system implementations at the bottom — local file systems of each type plus remote protocols such as the NFS client. The VFS distinguishes local from remote files, and local files further by type.

concepts.statement: The Linux VFS defines four main object types: the **superblock object**, representing an entire mounted file system; the **inode object**, representing an individual file; the **dentry object**, representing an individual directory entry (path component), cached in the directory-entry cache; and the **file object**, representing an open file — it holds the current file-position offset.
concepts.detail: Two opens of the same file share the inode but each creates its own file object with its own offset. The dentry cache is what makes path resolution fast: /usr/local/dir1 is resolved component by component, but each component’s dentry — and the inode it references — is remembered.

concepts.term: Function tables: dispatch without knowing the type
concepts.statement: Every VFS object contains a pointer to a **function table** — the addresses of the routines implementing that object’s operations for its concrete type (for the file object: open, close, read, write, mmap, defined in the kernel’s fs.h). The VFS invokes a fixed slot in the table without knowing or caring whether the file is a disk file, a directory or a remote file: the right implementation is always in the same place.
concepts.detail: This is object orientation in the kernel: the interface is fixed, the implementation is chosen per object. A read() flows system-call layer → VFS → the type-specific read routine → (for disk file systems) the page cache, with missing blocks fetched by the file-system driver.

concepts.statement: Because the VFS only requires objects with function tables, a file system need not have a disk at all. **procfs** (/proc) exposes process and kernel information as files; **sysfs** (/sys) exposes device and driver state. A read() of such a file calls a kernel routine that generates the contents on demand.
concepts.detail: This generalizes the Solaris menagerie — tmpfs, objfs, ctfs, mntfs are all interfaces to kernel state dressed as file systems. The VFS is what makes them indistinguishable from real storage at the system-call level; a mount -t ext4 and a mount of procfs differ only in the driver behind the objects.

examples.title: mount -t ext4: what the kernel actually does
examples.problem: The administrator runs: mount -t ext4 /dev/sdb1 /data. Walk through the kernel-side steps.

steps.label: Step 1: Identify the type and driver
steps.text: The -t ext4 argument names the file-system type; the kernel checks that the ext4 implementation is available, loading the module if necessary.

steps.label: Step 2: Read and validate the superblock
steps.text: The block device is opened and the ext4 driver reads the superblock from /dev/sdb1, checking its magic numbers and expected format. An invalid structure means refusal — and that a consistency check is needed before mounting can succeed.

steps.label: Step 3: Build the VFS objects
steps.text: The driver fills in a superblock object and reads the root inode; a dentry for the root of the mounted tree is created and attached at the mount point /data.

steps.label: Step 4: Record and publish
steps.text: The mount table gains an entry — device, type, superblock, options — and the in-memory inode of /data is flagged as a mount point. From now on, any lookup reaching /data descends into the ext4 tree.

examples.result: One command turns a block device into a navigable subtree — validated, typed and recorded, so that directory traversal crosses file-system boundaries invisibly.

examples.title: A read() through the VFS — disk file versus /proc file
examples.problem: Compare what happens inside read(fd, buf, 4096) when fd refers to /data/report.tex on ext4 versus /proc/cpuinfo on procfs.

steps.label: Step 1: The common path
steps.text: Both start identically: the system-call layer uses the descriptor to find the file object, whose state includes the current offset.

steps.label: Step 2: Dispatch through the function table
steps.text: The VFS calls the read slot of the file object’s function table. For the ext4 file, that slot points at the ext4 driver’s read routine; for /proc/cpuinfo, at a procfs routine.

steps.label: Step 3: The ext4 side
steps.text: The driver checks the page cache; on a hit, bytes are copied straight from memory. On a miss, the file system computes the needed block(s), asks the block layer to fetch them, and caches the result for next time.

steps.label: Step 4: The procfs side
steps.text: The procfs routine runs kernel code that formats the processor’s live state into text on demand. No disk block is ever read, and nothing persistent is cached.

steps.label: Step 5: The offset advances
steps.text: In both cases the file object’s offset advances by the count and the result returns to the application — which never learns which machinery answered.

examples.result: Identical application code, completely different implementations: that substitution is the entire point of the VFS.

keyTakeaways: Local sharing is mediated by owner/group/other attributes checked on every operation; media that move between machines can silently re-map who the owner is.
Remote sharing follows the client–server model: servers export volumes or directories, clients mount them — and authenticating the client is the hard part.
The VFS separates generic file operations from their implementations, letting dissimilar file systems — local and remote — coexist behind one interface.
vnodes give files network-wide unique identities; raw inode numbers are unique only within a single file system.
Linux’s four VFS objects: superblock (per mounted file system), inode (per file), dentry (per path component, cached), file (per open — it holds the offset).
Function tables dispatch VFS calls to type-specific code, which is why /proc and sysfs can be pure kernel state — file systems without disks.

quiz.q: A process opens the same file twice. Which VFS object is duplicated?
options: The file object — one per open, each with its own offset
quiz.explanation: The inode (one per file) and the dentry (one per path component) are shared; each open() creates a new file object carrying its own current-position offset. Two descriptors into one file therefore read independently.

quiz.q: The two functions of the VFS layer are:
options: defining a clean interface for multiple file-system implementations, and representing files uniquely across a network
quiz.explanation: The VFS separates file-system-generic operations from implementation details — so many types can coexist — and introduces vnodes so a file has a single network-wide identity, which raw inode numbers cannot provide.

quiz.q: In Linux’s VFS, the object representing an entire mounted file system is the:
quiz.explanation: One superblock object per mounted file system; one inode per file; one dentry per directory entry (path component); one file object per open descriptor.

quiz.q: How does the VFS layer execute a read() without knowing the file’s concrete type?
options: It funnels all data through one fixed kernel buffer
It calls the read function in the object’s function table — the right implementation sits in the same slot for every type
It asks the hardware to route the request
It converts every file to a character stream first
quiz.explanation: Each VFS object carries a pointer to a function table listing its type’s implementations. The VFS invokes a fixed slot; whether ext4, NFS or procfs code answers is invisible to the layer above.

quiz.q: File systems such as procfs and sysfs demonstrate that:
options: the VFS interface can back “files” with kernel-generated data instead of disk blocks
dentry objects are optional in Linux
mount points must always be empty
quiz.explanation: A file system in the VFS world is whatever supplies the right objects and function tables. procfs and sysfs generate their contents on demand from live kernel state — no storage device involved.

intro: Remote file systems carry the familiar open/read/write interface across the network. NFS is the canonical example: servers export directories, clients mount them, and remote files become indistinguishable from local ones — a transparency purchased with RPCs, statelessness, idempotent operations and carefully tuned caches.
objectives: Describe the NFS architecture: exports, remote mounts, cascading mounts and transparency
Explain the mount protocol, file handles, and the stateless protocol’s idempotent operations
Detail the client’s attribute and block caches, close-to-open consistency, and the synchronous-write penalty
Summarize how NFS version 4 departs from version 3
Distinguish location transparency from location independence, and describe the GFS and HDFS architectures

concepts.statement: NFS views interconnected machines as independent systems with independent file systems, joined on explicit request. The **server exports** chosen directories (listed with allowed machines and access rights in its export table); a **client mounts** a remote directory over one of its own local directories, after which the remote subtree looks like an integral part of the client’s name space — **transparency**. Only the mount operation itself names the server; every later access is ordinary path resolution.
concepts.detail: Machines are typically both client and server. **Cascading mounts** — mounting a file system on top of an already remotely mounted one — are permitted in some implementations, but mounts are not transitive: a client is affected only by mounts it invoked, and mounting a remote file system does not expose other file systems the server happens to have mounted.

concepts.term: The mount protocol and file handles
concepts.statement: The **mount protocol** establishes the initial logical connection: a mount request names the remote directory and the server machine; the request becomes an RPC to that server’s mount process, which checks it against the **export list**. If the request conforms, the server returns a **file handle** — in UNIX terms a file-system identifier plus an inode number, plus a generation counter that defeats stale reuse — which is the key for all further accesses to files under the mounted directory.
concepts.detail: The server also keeps a list of client machines and their current mounts, but only as an administrative hint — it is not essential for correct operation and is discarded on a crash. The mount protocol also provides unmount and return-export-list procedures; systems usually pre-configure static mounts at boot (such as /etc/vfstab on Solaris).

concepts.statement: The NFS protocol is a set of RPCs supporting: searching for a file within a directory, reading a set of directory entries, manipulating links and directories, accessing file attributes, and reading and writing files. There are deliberately **no open and close operations**: the server is **stateless**, keeping no information about clients from one access to the next. Each request must therefore carry its full arguments — a unique file identifier and an absolute offset inside the file.
concepts.detail: Statelessness makes the design robust — a restarted server simply answers the next request — but also unsecure, since forged requests are hard to detect. The specification is media-independent via RPC and an external data representation (XDR), so heterogeneous machines and file systems interoperate. A single write RPC is atomic and not intermixed with other writes to the same file, but one write() call may decompose into several RPCs — each carries at most $8\,\text{KB}$, and UDP packets are limited to about 1,500 bytes — so two users writing the same remote file may see their data intermixed.

concepts.statement: An operation is **idempotent** when performing it multiple times has the same effect as performing it once. NFS requires this of its file operations so that a request lost to a crash or a timeout can simply be re-executed — retransmission is the recovery story, and no special server-side measures are needed after a crash.
concepts.detail: For durability, modified data (including indirection and status blocks) must be committed to the server’s disk before results return to the client: clients may cache write blocks, but once flushed, they assume the data has reached the server’s stable storage. The performance penalty is large because the caching advantage is lost; battery-backed controller caches are the classic mitigation — the controller acknowledges from nonvolatile memory, and the blocks reach disk later.

concepts.term: Client caches: attributes, blocks and close-to-open consistency
concepts.statement: NFS clients keep two caches: the **file-attribute cache** (inode information) and the **file-blocks cache**. When a file is opened, the kernel checks with the server to fetch or revalidate the cached attributes; cached blocks are used only while the corresponding cached attributes are current (by default they are discarded after $60\,\text{s}$). Read-ahead and delayed-write are both used between client and server, producing **close-to-open consistency**: changes are flushed when the file is closed and validated when it is opened — a newly opening session sees the flushed state, while readers who keep the file open may not.
concepts.detail: Delayed writes are retained even when the file is concurrently open in conflicting modes, so strict UNIX semantics do not hold; newly created files may not be visible elsewhere for about $30\,\text{s}$. The book’s verdict: NFS provides neither strict UNIX semantics nor Andrew’s session semantics — a practical middle with good performance that made it the most widely used multi-vendor distributed system.

concepts.statement: NFSv4 turns the protocol **stateful** to improve security, performance and functionality: opens and locks are tracked with **stateids**; multiple operations travel as one **compound** request (a single round trip); authentication moves to **Kerberos**, fixing the trust-the-client-UID weakness of earlier versions; **delegations** let the server hand a client temporary control so it can cache aggressively; and **referrals** let one server point clients to another, building a federated name space.
concepts.detail: Statefulness is what makes locks and delegations possible — the server now remembers who holds what, at the cost of a recovery story (lease expiration) instead of v3’s crash-and-carry-on simplicity.

concepts.term: DFS naming: location transparency versus independence
concepts.statement: A distributed file system hides where files live, with two escalating guarantees. **Location transparency**: the name reveals nothing about the file’s physical storage — the name-to-location mapping is hidden from users. **Location independence**: the name **survives migration** — the file can move to another server without changing its name, so the mapping is dynamic.
concepts.detail: Static remote mounts (classic NFS) achieve transparency but not independence: the mount itself names the server, so moving the data rewrites the mount. Fully distributed systems maintain a name service that resolves each name to a current location.

concepts.term: Cluster-scale file systems: GFS and HDFS
concepts.statement: At data-center scale, general-purpose network file systems give way to dedicated designs. The **Google File System (GFS)** runs one **metadata server** (the master) plus many **chunk servers**, stores files in large $64\,\text{MB}$ chunks with replication, and favors huge streaming reads and appends — the access pattern of **MapReduce**. **Hadoop HDFS** follows the same shape: a **NameNode** holds the metadata, **DataNodes** store replicated blocks, files are written once and read many times, and replica placement is rack-aware. **GPFS** and **Lustre** serve the same role in high-performance computing.
concepts.detail: The remote-access strategy differs too: **AFS-style whole-file caching** fetches the entire file once and works locally for the session, while **NFS-style block caching** fetches and caches individual blocks on demand. Consistency enforcement differs as well: **validation** has clients re-check with the server (NFS attribute checks), while **callbacks** let the server notify clients when cached data is invalidated (AFS).

examples.title: Life of a remote READ
examples.problem: Machine U has mounted S1:/usr/shared at its local /usr/local. Trace what happens when a program on U opens and reads /usr/local/dir1/notes.txt.

steps.label: Step 1: The path meets the mount point
steps.text: open() resolves /usr/local in the local name space; the mount flag on that directory hands resolution to the NFS client, and the remaining components — dir1 and notes.txt — must be resolved on S1.

steps.label: Step 2: A LOOKUP for every component
steps.text: Path-name translation breaks the remaining path into components and performs a separate NFS lookup for each component-name plus directory-file-handle pair. The server checks access and returns the next file handle; a directory-name-lookup cache on the client (vnodes keyed by path prefix) spares repeated RPCs, and its entries are discarded when server attributes stop matching.

steps.label: Step 3: The open revalidates attributes
steps.text: With the final file handle in hand, the client kernel checks the file’s cached attributes against the server — fetching or revalidating them — and then creates the local file object with offset 0. Close-to-open consistency starts here.

steps.label: Step 4: The READ RPCs
steps.text: read(fd, buf, n) becomes one or more NFS READ requests carrying the file handle, the absolute offset and the count; each returns at most $8\,\text{KB}$ of data. The returned blocks are cached in the file-blocks cache for future reads.

steps.label: Step 5: The server side
steps.text: Each RPC lands in S1’s NFS service layer, is reinjected into S1’s VFS — which sees an ordinary local file — and executes the local file-system read. The result retraces the path back to U.

steps.label: Step 6: The application never knew
steps.text: The file object’s offset advances and read() returns exactly as it would for a local file. Only the RPCs, the caches and the per-component lookups reveal the distance.

examples.result: A remote read is a chain of mount protocol, per-component LOOKUPs, attribute validation and READ RPCs — orchestrated so the system-call interface stays identical to local I/O.

examples.title: Crash in the middle: stateless recovery
examples.problem: A client holds an open NFS file with cached dirty blocks when the server crashes and reboots in 30 seconds. No open state existed on the server. Walk through what the client does and what, if anything, is lost.

steps.label: Step 1: Nothing to rebuild
steps.text: Because the protocol is stateless, the rebooted server holds no per-client open tables to reconstruct — there is simply nothing to lose on the server side. The client’s file handle (file-system id, inode, generation) is still valid.

steps.label: Step 2: Retransmit
steps.text: The client’s RPC layer times out and retransmits the pending requests. Idempotency guarantees the retry is safe: a READ repeated returns the same bytes, and a re-issued WRITE with the same offset overwrites identically.

steps.label: Step 3: Revalidate
steps.text: Cached attributes may have expired during the outage, so the client revalidates them against the server before serving further reads — close-to-open consistency re-establishes itself automatically.

steps.label: Step 4: What can be lost
steps.text: Only data the client had not yet flushed: dirty blocks still in the client cache at crash time were never acknowledged. Applications that need durability must commit (fsync) before proceeding — the price of the simple recovery story.

examples.result: Statelessness makes the crash a non-event for open files: retransmit, revalidate, continue. Only unflushed client-side writes are at risk — durability still requires an explicit commit.

keyTakeaways: Servers export directories; clients mount them; after the mount, remote files are addressed exactly like local ones — transparency.
The mount protocol hands back a file handle — file-system identifier plus inode number plus generation — that keys every later operation.
Statelessness (no open or close on the wire) plus idempotent requests makes crash recovery trivial and security harder; v4 adds stateids, compound operations, Kerberos and delegations.
Clients cache attributes ($60\,\text{s}$ default) and blocks: close-to-open means new opens see flushed changes, while long-open readers may not.
Server writes are synchronous before acknowledgment; battery-backed caches claw back the performance cost.
Location transparency hides where a file is; location independence lets it move without changing its name.
GFS and HDFS — metadata server plus chunk/DataNodes, $64\,\text{MB}$-class chunks or blocks, write-once workloads — trade generality for cluster throughput.

quiz.q: NFS version 3 servers keep no per-client state. What does every request therefore carry?
options: Its complete arguments: file handle, offset and count
quiz.explanation: Statelessness means the server remembers nothing between requests, so each RPC is self-contained: the file handle identifies the file and the absolute offset locates the data. The protocol has no open or close at all.

quiz.q: An idempotent operation is one that:
options: has the same effect whether executed once or many times
cannot be cached by the client
quiz.explanation: Re-execution safety is what lets an NFS client retry a request after a timeout or a server restart without corrupting anything — the effect is the same as if the operation had happened once.

quiz.q: Under close-to-open consistency:
options: changes are flushed at close and validated at open — a reader that stays open may keep stale data
files become immutable after the first write
the server pushes updates to clients eagerly
quiz.explanation: The writer flushes its changes when it closes the file; a reader that opens afterward revalidates its cache and sees them. A reader that stays open across the write is not notified and may continue with old contents.

quiz.q: Location independence differs from location transparency because it:
options: allows a file to move without changing its name
means the client always knows the server’s address
quiz.explanation: Transparency hides the location behind the name. Independence goes further — the name-to-location mapping is dynamic, so the file can be migrated and the same name keeps resolving correctly.

quiz.q: In GFS and HDFS, the metadata/master node:
options: stores metadata only — the data lives in large chunks or blocks on chunk/DataNodes
quiz.explanation: A single metadata authority — the GFS master or the HDFS NameNode — maps files to their $64\,\text{MB}$-class chunks or blocks spread across many storage nodes, streamlining the huge sequential reads and appends that MapReduce-style workloads issue.

quiz.q: Why can an NFS server crash and reboot without losing client file-system state, and what must its operations satisfy?
options: It keeps all state on clients; operations are idempotent so replays are safe
It logs every block to tape
Clients poll until the server returns
It uses strict locking for all writes
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** NFS server exports directories; clients mount them; operations travel as RPCs.
**Step 2 — Rule:** stateless design keeps no per-client open state on the server; every operation carries full arguments and is idempotent (repeatable with the same effect).
**Step 3 — Apply:** after a crash the server restarts empty; a client simply replays the last RPC and gets the same result; no recovery protocol is needed.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** caching (attribute and data caches with close-to-open flushing) preserves performance without breaking the stateless contract.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** tape logging is recovery, not statelessness; polling does not make replays safe; strict locking is stateful.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** stateless plus idempotent gives crash transparency.

quiz.q: Two clients share one file. Client A writes and closes; client B then opens and reads. What does B see under close-to-open, and how does it differ from session semantics?
options: B may see stale data; session would show the write
B sees A’s changes because close flushes and open refreshes; session publishes whole images only at close
B always sees strict single-image order
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** write-then-close followed by open-then-read.
**Step 2 — Rule:** close-to-open flushes dirty data on close and revalidates on open; session semantics publishes each session’s whole image at close with last-close-wins.
**Step 3 — Apply:** A’s close pushes changes; B’s open fetches them, so B reads fresh data. Under pure session rules concurrent images would clash with a lost update.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** neither equals strict single-image order; NFS sits between local discipline and whole-file sessions.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** stale-read contradicts the flush; reboot is irrelevant; strict order needs one kernel image.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** close-to-open makes this pattern fresh; sessions resolve by last close.

intro: Consistency semantics answer a deceptively simple question: when two users have the same file open, when does one see the other’s writes? The answer defines the file system’s character — from the strict single-image model of UNIX, through the relaxed session semantics of Andrew, to immutable files that refuse the question entirely.
objectives: Define consistency semantics and the file session
State UNIX semantics and their implementation consequences
State session semantics and the last-close-wins conflict rule
Explain immutable shared files and why they eliminate sharing races
Map these models onto local UNIX file systems, NFS and AFS

concepts.statement: **Consistency semantics** specify how multiple users simultaneously accessing a shared file observe one another’s modifications — in particular, when a write by one user becomes observable by another. The unit of discussion is a **file session**: the series of accesses (reads and writes) between one open() and the matching close().
concepts.detail: The topic is Chapter 6 synchronization reborn at file scale, but the tools differ. Performing an atomic transaction against a remote disk can involve several network communications, several disk reads and writes, or both — systems that insist on a full set of fine-grained sharing semantics tend to perform poorly. The Andrew file system is the classic successful middle ground.

concepts.statement: Writes to an open file by a user are visible **immediately** to other users who have that file open. One mode of sharing even shares the pointer of the current location into the file, so one user’s advancing the pointer affects everyone. A file is associated with a **single physical image** that interleaves all accesses into one total order, and it is accessed as an exclusive resource — contention for the single image causes delays in user processes.
concepts.detail: This is the strongest common model: a read after a write returns the written value, because there is only one copy and one order of operations on it. The price is serialization — every access contends for the same image.

concepts.statement: Writes to an open file by a user are **not** immediately visible to other users who have the same file open. Once the file is closed, the changes become visible — but only in sessions starting later; already-open instances of the file never reflect them. A file may therefore be associated temporarily with **several images at once**, and users perform reads and writes concurrently on their own images, almost without scheduling constraints.
concepts.detail: This is the Andrew file system (OpenAFS) model. It pairs naturally with whole-file caching: each session works on a private image and publishes it at close.

concepts.statement: Under session semantics, two writers each acquire a private image at open — a **fork** of the file’s state — and each publishes their image at close, where the **join** rule is simply that the **last close wins**. Whoever closes later replaces the published state with their image, and the earlier writer’s changes are a lost update unless applications layer their own coordination.
concepts.detail: The merge is cheap — replace, not reconcile — which is exactly why races are prevented only by convention (or by application protocols that take turns).

concepts.statement: Once a file is declared shared by its creator, it **cannot be modified**: an immutable file’s name may not be reused, and its contents may not be altered. The name therefore certifies fixed contents. New versions are new files — typically created under a temporary name and published with an atomic rename.
concepts.detail: Because sharing is disciplined read-only access, the distributed implementation is simple and all the write-race questions vanish: consistency is trivially achieved. Versioned data sets and published artifacts are natural fits.

concepts.term: Which semantics does my system have?
concepts.statement: A local UNIX file system provides UNIX semantics — one kernel, one image, one order of accesses. NFS v3 approximates but guarantees neither model: close-to-open flushing plus delayed writes mean new opens see recent changes while long-open readers may not. AFS implements session semantics, and immutable-content stores sit at the strict end.
concepts.detail: The book’s caution: NFS’s tunable caches make its effective semantics hard to characterize — visibility delays of tens of seconds are normal and acceptable for most workloads.

examples.title: UNIX semantics: one image, immediate visibility
examples.problem: Users A and B both have a shared file open. A writes the characters “OS” at offset 0, and B reads two bytes at offset 0 immediately afterward. What does B get?

steps.label: Step 1: One image
steps.text: Both descriptors refer to the same physical file — the kernel serializes all accesses into a single interleaving, giving one total order.

steps.label: Step 2: A’s write
steps.text: “OS” lands in the single image; any kernel buffering is transparent because reads consult the same image.

steps.label: Step 3: B’s read
steps.text: B’s read is ordered after A’s write in the total order, so it returns “OS” — the most recent write.

steps.label: Step 4: The cost
steps.text: Because the image is an exclusive resource, A’s and B’s operations contend: a writer can delay readers and vice versa.

examples.result: B reads exactly what A wrote. Correctness is absolute — every read sees the most recent write — but concurrency is throttled by the single image.

examples.title: Session semantics: private images, last close wins
examples.problem: Same starting point, but now each user opens the file as a private session image (as in AFS). A appends “A” and closes; B, unaware, appends “B” to its own image and closes later. What ends up in the file?

steps.label: Step 1: Each session forks an image
steps.text: At open, A and B each acquire a private copy of the file (for AFS, a whole-file cache) to work on for the session.

steps.label: Step 2: A’s session
steps.text: A appends “A” to its image. B, in a separate session, still sees the original contents — writes are invisible to other open sessions.

steps.label: Step 3: A closes first
steps.text: A’s image is written back and published; the file now holds the original contents plus “A”.

steps.label: Step 4: B closes last
steps.text: B’s image — built from the original, plus “B” but not “A” — is written back after A’s and replaces the published state.

steps.label: Step 5: The join
steps.text: Last close wins: A’s append is a lost update. Any session that opens the file now sees the original contents plus “B” only.

examples.result: Final contents: original + “B”. Session semantics bought concurrent access without delay, at the price of silently dropping the earlier writer’s changes.

keyTakeaways: Consistency semantics define when one user’s writes become visible to another’s reads; the unit is the file session — open() to close().
UNIX semantics: a single physical image, one total order, immediate visibility — reads always see the most recent write, and contention delays processes.
Session semantics (Andrew/AFS): private images per session; changes publish at close, and only to sessions starting later.
Under session semantics, concurrent writers resolve by last close wins — the earlier writer’s updates can be lost.
Immutable shared files remove modification entirely — new versions are new files, published by atomic rename.
Real systems: a local file system gives UNIX semantics, AFS gives session semantics, and NFS’s close-to-open approximation guarantees neither.
Fine-grained locking across disk and network latencies performs poorly — every practical model relaxes Chapter 6 rigor somewhere.

quiz.q: Under UNIX semantics, a user who reads a shared file immediately after another user’s write to it:
options: sees the old contents until the file is closed
is returned the newly written value
sees whichever copy their session cached
quiz.explanation: The file is a single physical image whose accesses are interleaved into one total order; a read ordered after a write returns the written value. Visibility is immediate — at the price of exclusive-resource contention.

quiz.q: Under session semantics, changes made to an open file become visible to other users:
options: only after the writer closes the file, and only to sessions that open it afterward
when the server pushes an update
quiz.explanation: Sessions work on private images; at close the changes are published, and only newly starting sessions observe them. Instances already open keep the old contents — the Andrew file system model.

quiz.q: Two writers work on the same file under session semantics; B closes after A. The final file reflects:
options: both A’s and B’s changes merged
only B’s image — the last close wins
whichever writer was first to open the file
quiz.explanation: Each session publishes its whole image at close, and publication order follows close order. B’s close is last, so B’s image replaces A’s — A’s changes are a lost update.

quiz.q: An immutable shared file:
options: can be modified only by its owner
can never have its contents altered or its name reused — new versions are new files
is cached permanently on all clients
may be written once per session
quiz.explanation: Immutability forbids both modification and name reuse. Updates become new files, typically installed with an atomic rename — so sharing is disciplined read-only access and consistency races cannot arise.

quiz.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: AFS implements session semantics; a local UNIX file system implements UNIX semantics
Local file systems implement session semantics
Immutable semantics require a stateful server
quiz.explanation: A single-kernel local file system maintains one image and one order — UNIX semantics. AFS works per session on whole-file caches — session semantics. NFS sits between: close-to-open flushing means new opens see recent changes, but neither guarantee strictly holds.

depth.title: Dimensions, energy chains and Carnot’s bound

blocks.body: Coherence is more than bookkeeping convenience — it is the statement that every physical law is **dimensionally homogeneous**. Any correct equation reduces, on substituting units, to an identity: $P = M\omega$ works because a newton metre times a radian per second is a watt, the radian being dimensionless ($\text{rad} = \text{m}/\text{m}$). The **Buckingham π theorem** makes the idea rigorous: a relation among $n$ quantities built from $k$ independent dimensions collapses into a relation among $n - k$ dimensionless groups. That is why $P = 2\pi N_r M / 60$ needs its peculiar 60 — converting minutes to seconds — and nothing else, and why torque (newton metre) and energy (joule) share dimensions while meaning different things. The working engineer’s check is exactly this: if the units do not balance, no amount of algebra will repair the physics.

blocks.heading: The Carnot bound
blocks.body: Hughes’s station returns $\eta = 0.288$, and the fair question is how much of the missing 71 per cent is engineering carelessness. The **second law** answers. Run an ideal engine reversibly between a hot reservoir at $T_h$ and a cold one at $T_c$: for the reversible cycle, global entropy is conserved, so $Q_c/Q_h = T_c/T_h$, and $$\eta_{max} = \frac{W}{Q_h} = 1 - \frac{Q_c}{Q_h} = 1 - \frac{T_c}{T_h}.$$ Superheated steam near $810\ \text{K}$ rejecting heat to a condenser near $300\ \text{K}$ therefore caps any plant at $\eta_{max} \approx 0.63$; the Rankine cycle’s boilers, turbines and feed heaters then spend half that ideal, and $0.63/2$ brackets Hughes’s figure. Efficiency is bought by raising $T_h$ (supercritical boilers) or by stacking a gas turbine’s exhaust under the steam cycle — **combined cycle** plants reach $\eta \approx 0.62$ — never by polishing the alternator.

Real systems convert energy in stages, and stage efficiencies **multiply**: $\eta = \eta_1\eta_2\cdots\eta_m$, each stage’s output being the next one’s input. Take logarithms and differentiate to get $\frac{d\eta}{\eta} = \sum_j \frac{d\eta_j}{\eta_j}$: a ten per cent relative gain in any single stage yields exactly ten per cent in the chain, so engineering effort flows to whichever stage is cheapest to improve, usually the worst one. Hughes’s $0.288$ decomposes plausibly into boiler and combustion losses of $\approx 0.88$, a thermodynamic-cycle-plus-turbine factor of $\approx 0.36$, and generator plus auxiliaries of $\approx 0.91$, whose product is $0.288$. The same multiplicative logic orders every design decision in an energy chain, and **Sankey diagrams** — arrows whose width is power — remain the engineer’s first audit tool for finding where the biggest slice is lost.

blocks.heading: Auditing a power station
blocks.body: Return to Hughes’s Example 1.6 with the stage view. An output of $280\ \text{MW h}$ per day from $3.5 \times 10^{12}\ \text{J}$ of coal gives $\eta = 0.288$. Suppose the audit finds combustion and boiler at $0.88$ and the generator at $0.97$: the chain then requires $\eta_{cycle} = 0.288/(0.88 \times 0.97) \approx 0.34$, a plausible Rankine figure, so the audit closes. Now replace the cycle with a combined-cycle unit at $0.60$ fed by the boiler’s exhaust: the product becomes $0.88 \times 0.60 \times 0.97 \approx 0.51$, and the same coal delivers about $1.8 \times 10^{12}\ \text{J}$ per day. The moral is structural rather than electrical: because efficiencies multiply, the thermodynamic cycle — not the wiring, not the alternator — decides the fate of half the world’s fuel budget.

depth.title: Metrology rebuilt on the constants

blocks.heading: The 2019 SI redefinition
blocks.body: On 20 May 2019 the SI was quietly rebuilt: every base unit is now defined by fixing the numerical value of a fundamental constant — $c$, $h$, $e$, $k_B$, $N_A$ and $K_{cd}$ — and the platinum–iridium cylinder this section met as the kilogram became a museum piece. The new kilogram is realized with the **Kibble balance**, which equates the electrical power $VI$ of a coil moving in a magnetic field with the mechanical power $mgv$ of the mass it lifts — this chapter’s energy bookkeeping made into an instrument, volts and amperes on one pan, newtons and metres on the other. The **ampere** is now simply the current of $1/(1.602176634 \times 10^{-19})$ elementary charges per second; the force-between-conductors definition quoted in Section 1.3 is retired, and $\mu_0$ stops being an exact number and becomes an experiment.

The deepest consistency check in electrical metrology is the **quantum metrology triangle**. Realize a voltage with the Josephson effect, $V = f/K_J$ where $K_J = 2e/h \approx 483.6\ \text{GHz V}^{-1}$; realize a resistance with the quantum Hall effect, $R_K = h/e^{2} \approx 25.8\ \text{k}\Omega$; realize a current with a single-electron pump that counts charges one at a time. Ohm’s law, $V = RI$, then relates three independently realized quantum standards, and any discrepancy bounds drift — or new physics — in $e$ and $h$ themselves. Pumps presently reach parts in $10^{7}$, and closing the triangle at the $10^{8}$ level is an active metrology goal: one of the few live experiments capable of revealing the fine-structure constant moving underneath the constants the SI is built on.

blocks.heading: Will the second fall next?
blocks.body: The 2019 reform left one unit still defined by a single physical embodiment: the second, tied to the caesium-133 hyperfine transition at $9\,192\,631\,770$ Hz. **Optical clocks** — single trapped ions and optical lattices — now reach fractional uncertainties near $10^{-18}$, two orders of magnitude beyond caesium, so a redefinition is being engineered rather than merely debated. The hard part is comparability: linking clocks across continents by optical fibre or satellite without losing the last digit, and surveying **geopotential** heights to centimetre level, because general relativity makes clocks at different altitudes tick differently — by about $10^{-18}$ per centimetre of height. The open questions are curiously close to electrical engineering: distributing optical frequencies, managing the relativistic bookkeeping of a network, and deciding what synchronized time means when no two clocks sit at the same gravitational potential.

intro: Electrical technology sits on top of mechanics, heat, light and sound: we drive cranes with motors, warm rooms with heaters, and the underlying interest in electricity is always the delivery of energy from a source to a point of application. Before any circuit can be analysed, the quantities involved — force, torque, work, energy, power, efficiency and temperature — need agreed units. This section merges Hughes’s opening chapter on the International System with Nilsson’s compact tables of SI base and derived units.
objectives: Explain what makes the SI a coherent system and list its base quantities
Compute force, torque, work, energy and power in SI units
Relate rotational speed, torque and mechanical power with $P = 2\pi N_r M / 60$
Define efficiency and account for input versus output energy
Convert freely between joules and kilowatt hours

concepts.statement: The **International System of Units**, known as SI in every language, was formally introduced in 1960 and has been accepted by most countries as their only legal system of measurement.
concepts.detail: Its greatest advantage over its predecessors is **coherence**: a system is coherent if the product or quotient of any two unit quantities is the unit of the resultant quantity — unit area results when unit length multiplies unit length, and unit velocity when unit length is divided by unit time. Hughes bases the system on six physical quantities (mass, length, time, electric current, absolute temperature, luminous intensity); the modern SI table Nilsson reproduces adds a seventh, the mole (amount of substance), and lists the ampere among the base units alongside the metre, kilogram, second, kelvin and candela.

concepts.statement: The kilogram is the mass of a **platinum–iridium cylinder preserved at Sèvres** near Paris; the metre is $1\,650\,763.73$ wavelengths of the orange line of a specified krypton discharge lamp; the second is $9\,192\,631\,770$ cycles of the caesium-133 transition; the kelvin is $1/273.16$ of the thermodynamic temperature of the triple point of water.
concepts.detail: On the Celsius scale the triple point of water sits at 0.01 °C, so $0\,^\circ\text{C} = 273.15$ K — and a temperature interval of 1 °C is identical to an interval of 1 K; only the reference zero differs. Standard submultiples of the second are used, but multiples are usually replaced by minutes, hours, days and years. Nilsson adds the engineer’s prefix discipline: use prefixes for powers divisible by 3 (pico $10^{-12}$, nano, micro, milli, kilo, mega, giga, tera) and pick the prefix that puts the base number between 1 and 1000 — a $10^{-5}$ s result is naturally written as 10 µs.

concepts.statement: Each quantity carries a symbol ($W$ for energy, $P$ for power) and each unit an abbreviation (J, W) used **only after numbers** — one writes 16 J but “a few joules of energy”.
concepts.detail: Capital letters normally represent constant quantities; if a quantity varies, the lower-case symbol is used — $W$ indicates constant energy whereas $w$ indicates a time-varying value. Hughes highlights each new quantity in the form: Energy, Symbol: $W$, Unit: joule (J). This lowercase-for-varying convention is exactly the one Nilsson uses for $v$, $i$ and $p$ in circuit analysis.

concepts.statement: The unit of force, the newton, gives a one-kilogram mass an acceleration of one metre per second squared: $$F = ma.$$ The **weight** of a body is the gravitational force exerted by the Earth on it — approximately $9.81m$ newtons at sea level, varying slightly with latitude.
concepts.detail: In Hughes’s Example 1.1 a force of 50 N applied to a 200 kg mass produces $a = 50/200 = 0.25$ m/s². Weight follows from $F = ma$ with $g = 9.81$ m/s²: an 80 kg steel block weighs $80 \times 9.81 = 785$ N (three significant figures — writing 784.8 N would be false accuracy, since the inputs were only given to two or three figures). Hughes’s Fig. 1.1 shows the weight of 1 kg at sea level ranging from about 9.78 N to 9.84 N across latitudes.

concepts.statement: If a force $F$ acts at right angles to a radius $r$ from a point, the turning moment or **torque** about that point is $$T = Fr$$ in newton metres (N m).
concepts.detail: The symbol $M$ is reserved for the torque of a rotating electrical machine, so $T$ and $M$ both mean torque but $M$ specifically flags machine shafts. Torque is the rotational analogue of force: applied to a body, it causes rotational acceleration, just as force causes linear acceleration.

concepts.statement: The joule is the work done when a force of 1 N acts through 1 m in its own direction: $W = Fl$. A body of mass $m$ moving at velocity $u$ carries kinetic energy $W = \tfrac{1}{2}mu^{2}$, and a mass lifted through height $h$ gains potential energy $W \approx 9.81mh$.
concepts.detail: Energy is the capacity for doing work, so both are measured in the same unit. Hughes’s Example 1.3 drops a 30 kg body from 50 m: its potential energy is $294.3 \times 50 = 14\,700$ J, its landing speed is $u = \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 50} = 31.32$ m/s, and its kinetic energy is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 31.32^{2} = 14\,700$ J — the whole of the potential energy converts to kinetic energy, then to heat on impact.

concepts.statement: Power is the rate of doing work, so the SI unit is the joule per second, or **watt**: for linear motion $P = Fu$, and for a rotating machine $$P = M\omega = \frac{2\pi N_r M}{60},$$ where $N_r$ is the rotational speed in revolutions per minute. The commercial unit of energy is the **kilowatt hour** — the work done at 1 kW for one hour, exactly $3.6 	imes 10^{6}$ J.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Example 1.5 finds the shaft torque of a motor developing 10 kW at 900 r/min: the speed is $900/60 = 15$ r/s, so $10\,000 = T \times 2\pi \times 15$ and $T = 106$ N m. The watt is often inconveniently small, hence the kilowatt. Once known as the Board of Trade Unit, the kilowatt hour is what electricity suppliers still call simply “the unit”: a heater drawing 1.84 kW for 12 h consumes about 22 kW h, which is 79 MJ in SI units — the number on every electricity bill.

concepts.statement: When a device converts or transforms energy, some input energy is consumed to make the device operate. The **efficiency** is $$\eta = \frac{\text{energy output in a given time}}{\text{energy input in the same time}} = \frac{W_o}{W_{in}} = \frac{P_o}{P_{in}},$$ a dimensionless ratio always less than one.
concepts.detail: The difference between output and input is usually wastage as heat. In Hughes’s Example 1.6 a generating station outputs 280 MW h per day while burning 500 t of coal at 7 MJ/kg — an input of $3.5 \times 10^{12}$ J against an output of $1.01 \times 10^{12}$ J — giving an overall efficiency of $\eta = 0.288$, a figure typical of thermal generation.

concepts.statement: Absolute temperature is measured in kelvin, but for most introductory electrical purposes **degrees Celsius** suffice; both degrees represent the same change in temperature, the difference being only the reference zero.
concepts.detail: A useful constant: it takes 4185 J to raise the temperature of 1 litre of water through 1 °C. Hughes’s Example 1.8 supplies 2.5 kW h ($9 \times 10^{6}$ J) to 40 litres of water initially at 15 °C; the rise is $9 \times 10^{6} / (40 \times 4185) = 53.8$ °C, giving a final temperature of 68.8 °C. Temperature matters to electrical work because resistance varies with it — the subject of Section 2.5.

examples.title: From force to power: hauling a stone block
examples.problem: A stone block of mass 120 kg is hauled 100 m along a horizontal floor in 2 min; the coefficient of friction is 0.3. Find the horizontal force, the work done and the power. (Hughes Example 1.4)

steps.label: Step 1: Weight of the block
steps.text: The weight is the gravitational force: $F_w \approx 120 \times 9.81 = 1177.2$ N.

steps.label: Step 2: Friction force
steps.text: The horizontal force must overcome friction: $F = 0.3 \times 1177.2 = 353.16$ N, reported as 353 N to match the input’s significant figures.

steps.label: Step 3: Work done
steps.text: Work equals force times distance in the direction of the force: $W = 353.16 \times 100 = 35\,316$ J, i.e. 35.3 kJ.

steps.label: Step 4: Power
steps.text: Power is work per time, and 2 min is 120 s: $P = 35\,316 / 120 = 294$ W.

examples.result: Force 353 N, work 35.3 kJ, power 294 W — a chain of unit bookkeeping that runs from $F = ma$ through $W = Fl$ to $P = W/t$.

examples.title: Torque and efficiency at the shaft
examples.problem: An electric motor develops 10 kW at 900 r/min; find the shaft torque. Separately, a lift of 250 kg is raised at 5 m/s by a motor of efficiency 85 per cent; find the motor input power. (Hughes Examples 1.5 and 1.7)

steps.label: Step 1: Convert the speed
steps.text: Rotational speed $N_r = 900$ r/min is $900/60 = 15$ r/s.

steps.label: Step 2: Solve for torque
steps.text: From $P = 2\pi N_r M$: $10\,000 = T \times 2\pi \times 15$, so $T = 10\,000 / 94.25 \approx 106$ N m.

steps.label: Step 3: Lift output power
steps.text: The lift needs force equal to its weight, $F = mg = 250 \times 9.81 = 2452$ N, moved at $u = 5$ m/s, so $P_o = Fu = 2452 \times 5 = 12\,260$ W.

steps.label: Step 4: Account for efficiency
steps.text: The motor must be fed more than it delivers: $P_{in} = P_o / \eta = 12\,260 / 0.85 \approx 14.5$ kW — the missing 15 per cent leaves as heat inside the motor.

examples.result: Torque 106 N m; lift motor input about 14.5 kW. Efficiency always runs the “wrong way”: divide by $\eta$ to size the input, multiply to predict the output.

examples.title: Energy accounting: a power station and a water heater
examples.problem: A generating station has a daily output of 280 MW h and uses 500 tonnes of coal releasing 7 MJ/kg; find the overall efficiency. Then, an electric heater with 40 litres of water at a mean 15 °C receives 2.5 kW h; find the final water temperature assuming no losses. (Hughes Examples 1.6 and 1.8)

steps.label: Step 1: Energy input from coal
steps.text: $W_{in} = 7 \times 10^{6} \times 500 \times 1000 = 3.5 \times 10^{12}$ J per day (500 t is 500 000 kg).

steps.label: Step 2: Energy output in joules
steps.text: The electrical output is $280\ \text{MW h} = 280 \times 10^{6} \times 3.6 \times 10^{3} \approx 1.01 \times 10^{12}$ J.

steps.label: Step 3: Overall efficiency
steps.text: $\eta = W_o / W_{in} = 1.01 \times 10^{12} / 3.5 \times 10^{12} = 0.288$ — barely 29 per cent of the coal’s chemical energy becomes electricity.

steps.label: Step 4: Heater energy in joules
steps.text: The water receives $2.5\ \text{kW h} = 2.5 \times 3.6 \times 10^{6} = 9 \times 10^{6}$ J.

steps.label: Step 5: Temperature rise
steps.text: Heating 40 litres by 1 °C takes $40 \times 4185$ J, so $\Delta\theta = 9 \times 10^{6} / 167\,400 = 53.8$ °C and $\theta_2 = 15 + 53.8 = 68.8$ °C.

examples.result: Station efficiency 0.288; final water temperature 68.8 °C. Two faces of the same bookkeeping — large-scale conversion losses and controlled beneficial heating.

keyTakeaways: The SI is coherent: products and quotients of unit quantities give unit results, so derived units never need stray numerical factors.
Force follows $F = ma$ (newton), torque $T = Fr$ (newton metre) and work $W = Fl$ (joule); power is $P = Fu$, or $P = 2\pi N_r M / 60$ for a machine shaft with $N_r$ in r/min.
The kilowatt hour is the commercial energy unit: $1\ \text{kW h} = 3.6$ MJ exactly.
Efficiency $\eta = P_o / P_{in}$ is always below unity; the difference is almost always heat, whether wasted in a station (0.288) or wanted in a heater.
Degrees Celsius and kelvin share the same interval size; it takes 4185 J to warm one litre of water by 1 °C.
Respect significant figures: Hughes rounds 784.8 N to 785 N because the 80 kg input carried only two or three figures.

quiz.q: A system of units is called “coherent” when:
options: Every unit is defined from a physical artefact such as the Sèvres cylinder
The product or quotient of any two unit quantities is the unit of the resultant quantity
All units are decimal multiples of each other
Every derived unit has its own special name
quiz.explanation: Coherence means unit length × unit length = unit area, and unit length ÷ unit time = unit velocity — no conversion constants appear in the defining equations. This is the SI’s key advantage over its predecessors.

quiz.q: A motor develops 10 kW at 900 r/min. Using $P = 2\pi N_r M / 60$, the shaft torque is approximately:
quiz.explanation: With $N_r = 900$ r/min, $M = 60 \times 10\,000 / (2\pi \times 900) \approx 106$ N m — Hughes’s Example 1.5, done by converting to 15 r/s and dividing $10\,000$ by $2\pi \times 15$.

quiz.q: One kilowatt hour equals:
quiz.explanation: A kilowatt hour is 1000 W sustained for 3600 s: $1000 \times 3600 = 3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J = 3.6 MJ. Electricity suppliers call it simply “the unit”.

quiz.q: A station burns 500 t of coal (7 MJ/kg) to deliver 280 MW h in a day. Its efficiency is about:
quiz.explanation: Input $3.5 \times 10^{12}$ J, output $\approx 1.01 \times 10^{12}$ J, so $\eta \approx 0.288$. More than two-thirds of the chemical energy is lost before it leaves the station.

quiz.q: An 80 kg block’s weight is computed as 784.8 N, but Hughes reports 785 N. Why?
options: Gravitational acceleration is only known to three figures
The answer should carry no more significant figures than the given data — reporting 784.8 N is false accuracy
The SI forbids decimals in force values
Rounding up is required by the SI convention
quiz.explanation: The input (80 kg, $g = 9.81$ m/s²) carries only two or three significant figures, so the answer must be rounded to a reasonable compromise — 785 N. Hughes repeatedly warns against false accuracy.

quiz.q: A hoist lifts a 400 kg load vertically at a steady 2 m/s. The gearbox efficiency is 0.92 and the motor efficiency is 0.88. The electrical input power drawn by the motor is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: mass $m = 400$ kg, steady velocity $u = 2$ m per s, $g = 9.81$ m per s squared, stage efficiencies $\eta_{g} = 0.92$ and $\eta_{m} = 0.88$. Step 2 — Governing relations: lifting force $F = mg$, mechanical output $P_{o} = Fu$, and stage efficiencies multiply so that $P_{in} = \frac{P_{o}}{\eta_{g}\eta_{m}}$. Step 3 — Algebra: $F = 400 \times 9.81 = 3924$ N, hence $P_{o} = 3924 \times 2 = 7848$ W; the chain product is $0.92 \times 0.88 = 0.8096$, so $P_{in} = \frac{7848}{0.8096} \approx 9694$ W, about 9.7 kW. Step 4 — Sanity check: input exceeds output by roughly 23 per cent of overhead, the kilowatt scale suits a hoist, and units reduce to watts throughout. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 7.8 kW applies only one stage, 6.4 kW multiplies by the efficiencies instead of dividing, and 12.1 kW rounds $g$ upward and adds a spurious margin. Step 6 — Conclude: the draw is about 9.7 kW.

depth.title: Conduction as a field phenomenon

blocks.heading: The Drude model: Newton with drag
blocks.body: Model the conduction electrons as a gas of particles of mass $m$ and charge $-e$, number density $n$, that scatter off the ion lattice on average every $\tau$ seconds — a linear drag term $m\mathbf{v}/\tau$. Between collisions the field $\mathbf{E}$ accelerates them, so the equation of motion is $$m\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt} = -e\mathbf{E} - \frac{m}{\tau}\mathbf{v}.$$ The velocity relaxes to a steady drift within a few $\tau$, leaving $$\mathbf{v}_d = -\frac{e\tau}{m}\mathbf{E}, \qquad \mathbf{J} = -ne\mathbf{v}_d = \frac{ne^{2}\tau}{m}\mathbf{E}.$$ The coefficient of $\mathbf{E}$ is the **conductivity**, $\sigma = \frac{ne^{2}\tau}{m}$ — charge and mass from nature, density and collision time from the material. For copper, $n = 8.5 \times 10^{28}\ \text{m}^{-3}$ and $\tau \approx 2.4 \times 10^{-14}\ \text{s}$ give $\sigma \approx 5.8 \times 10^{7}\ \text{S m}^{-1}$, within a few per cent of the measured value — a startling return for three lines of Newtonian mechanics.

blocks.heading: How fast does drift actually go?
blocks.body: Take 1 A through a copper wire of $1\ \text{mm}^{2}$ cross-section, so $J = 10^{6}\ \text{A m}^{-2}$. The drift velocity is $$v_d = \frac{J}{ne} = \frac{10^{6}}{8.5 \times 10^{28} \times 1.602 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 7.3 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$ — under a tenth of a millimetre per second, slower than a snail. Yet those same electrons move at the **Fermi velocity**, about $1.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so the drift is a bias of order one part in $10^{10}$ imposed on violent thermal motion. The lamp nevertheless lights the instant the switch closes, because what propagates is the **field**, at nearly the speed of light, while the carriers themselves crawl — which is the quiet picture underneath every circuit diagram this book draws.

One formula explains why metals and semiconductors disagree about temperature. In $\sigma = ne^{2}\tau/m$, a metal’s $n$ is fixed by its chemistry: heating only intensifies lattice vibration, phonons scatter electrons more frequently, $\tau$ falls roughly like $1/T$ above the Debye temperature, and **conductivity drops** — resistance climbs almost linearly, which is why a coil of copper doubles as a thermometer. In an intrinsic semiconductor $n$ is not fixed: generation across the band gap makes $n$ grow roughly like $e^{-E_g/2k_BT}$, and that exponential overwhelms the mild decline of $\tau$, so **conductivity rises** with temperature. A platinum resistance thermometer and a thermistor are the same equation wearing opposite signs — the engineer’s first reminder that materials, not circuits, carry the temperature coefficient.

Ohm’s law is not a law of nature but a **constitutive relation** — a statement about materials, valid only where the response is linear. Its local form is $\mathbf{J} = \sigma\mathbf{E}$: field in, current density out, with $\sigma$ the slope of the material’s response. Defining $\rho = 1/\sigma$ and integrating the field along a uniform bar of length $\ell$ and area $A$ returns $R = \rho\ell/A$ — resistance is geometry times material and nothing more. It is often cleaner to bundle the Drude factors into the **mobility** $\mu = e\tau/m$, so that $\sigma = ne\mu$: how many carriers, times how easily each one moves. In a semiconductor both carriers count, $\sigma = q(n\mu_n + p\mu_p)$. The relation fails when the field is so strong that velocity saturates, or when the device is shorter than a mean free path — the research tier below.

blocks.heading: KCL is charge conservation
blocks.body: Kirchhoff’s current law is charge conservation in the lumped limit. In the continuum, applying Gauss’s theorem to the fact that any charge leaving a volume must cross its surface gives the **continuity equation**, $$\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J} = -\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}.$$ Now integrate over the volume of a node — a junction together with the wires meeting there. The left side becomes $\oint\mathbf{J}\cdot d\mathbf{S}$, the net current leaving through the branches: $$\sum_{k} i_k = -\frac{dQ_{node}}{dt}.$$ Circuit theory’s second assumption — no net charge on any component — sets $dQ_{node}/dt = 0$, and KCL falls out: the currents entering a node sum, algebraically, to zero. The law is exact whenever lumping holds, and it fails exactly where charge does pile up — on the plates of a capacitor, which is where the leftover $dQ/dt$ term went to live.

blocks.heading: KVL is Faraday’s law in disguise
blocks.body: Kirchhoff’s voltage law descends from Faraday. Around any closed contour $C$ bounding a surface $S$, $$\oint_{C}\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{l} = -\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}.$$ When no time-varying magnetic flux links the loop — circuit theory’s third assumption, no magnetic coupling — the right side vanishes, the field is conservative, and the terminal voltages around any mesh sum to zero: KVL. The **quasi-static criterion** makes the approximation quantitative. A signal of frequency $f$ has wavelength $\lambda = c/f$; a circuit whose largest dimension $L$ satisfies $$L \ll \lambda = \frac{c}{f}$$ sees essentially one phase of the signal everywhere, the residual phase spread being of order $2\pi L/\lambda$. Nilsson’s one-tenth rule, $L \le \lambda/10$, caps that error near half a radian — the conventional edge of the lumped world, and the reason a 3 cm trace at $10^{9}$ Hz is a transmission line, not a wire.

depth.title: Quantum transport: when Ohm’s law fails

blocks.heading: Landauer formula
blocks.body: Consider a two-terminal conductor so short and so clean that carriers cross it without scattering, connected to reservoirs that fix the electrochemical potentials $\mu_1 > \mu_2$. Its conductance is $$G = \frac{2e^{2}}{h}\,M,$$ where $M$ is the number of occupied transverse modes (subbands) of the constriction and the factor 2 is spin degeneracy. Each mode contributes $2e^{2}/h \approx 77.5\ \mu\text{S}$, a resistance of $h/2e^{2} \approx 12.9\ \text{k}\Omega$ — resistance without any dissipation inside the conductor: the **quantum of resistance**, $h/e^{2} \approx 25.8\ \text{k}\Omega$, is a contact effect, the irreducible price of asking a wave to enter and leave a channel.

blocks.heading: Conductance steps you can see
blocks.body: In 1988 two independent groups — van Wees and co-workers, and Wharam and co-workers — defined a **quantum point contact** in a GaAs/AlGaAs two-dimensional electron gas: gate electrodes pinch the electron gas into a constriction a few hundred nanometres wide. Sweeping the gate voltage admits transverse modes one at a time, and the two-terminal conductance climbs a staircase whose steps are exactly $2e^{2}/h$ — conductance quantization, visible on an oscilloscope. Drude has nothing to say here: the mean free path, tens of micrometres, dwarfs the device, there is nothing to scatter from, and $R = \rho\ell/A$ gives way to waveguide counting. The quantum Hall effect is the same physics with the modes reorganized by a strong perpendicular magnetic field; its plateau value $R_K = h/e^{2}$ now anchors the SI ohm worldwide.

The boundary between Ohm and Landauer is the **mean free path** $\ell_{mfp}$ measured against device length $L$. When $L \gg \ell_{mfp}$, collisions randomize the motion and Drude’s resistivity, proportional to length, holds. When $L \lesssim \ell_{mfp}$, transport is **ballistic**: resistance stops growing with length and is pinned by the contacts at $h/2e^{2}$ per occupied mode. The full statement, $G = \frac{2e^{2}}{h}MT$, assigns each mode a transmission probability $T$ between zero and one; the disordered limit $T \approx \ell_{mfp}/L$ recovers Drude, so Ohm’s law emerges as the diffuse average over Landauer channels. Nor is this exotic: a 20 nm transistor channel, a carbon nanotube and a chain of gold atoms all operate in or near the ballistic regime, and their designers count modes rather than scattering events.

intro: Electricity can be considered from two points of view: the scientist asks what happens inside the phenomenon, while the engineer accepts that it is there and uses its properties. What makes it indispensable is that an electrical system transmits energy easily from a source to a remote point of application — a lamp fed by a generator kilometres away. This section assembles the vocabulary behind every later chapter: charge, the electron, conventional current, the closed circuit, and the ideal circuit element with which we shall model everything.
objectives: Describe the four functional parts of an electrical system and the engineer’s four categories of electrical engineering
State the three assumptions that let circuit theory replace electromagnetic field theory
Apply the rule of one-tenth to decide whether a system is lumped
Relate charge, current and time through $i = dq/dt$ and $Q = It$
Explain conventional current versus electron flow, and the attributes of an ideal basic circuit element

concepts.statement: Electrical engineering falls into four categories — the **production, transmission, application and control** of electrical energy — and the most significant property of electricity for the engineer is that it permits the source of energy to be remote from the point of application.
concepts.detail: Nilsson classifies the resulting systems five ways: communication systems (telephone networks, radar, satellites), computer systems (from calculators to supercomputers), control systems (refinery temperatures, autopilots, canal locks), power systems (generation and the continental grid) and signal-processing systems (weather-satellite imagery, MRI scans). The categories interlock — a commercial aircraft carries all five at once.

concepts.term: The electrical system and its four parts
concepts.statement: A basic electrical system has four constituent parts: the **source** (battery or generator, providing the energy), the **load** (lamps, heaters — absorbing the energy), the **transmission system** (insulated wire) and the **control apparatus** (at minimum a switch).
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Fig. 2.2 sketch of a generator, switch and lamp is hard to read, so circuit diagrams replace sketches with symbols published as IEC 617 (BS EN 60617 in the UK). Diagrams are drawn so that energy reads from **left to right**: source on the left, load on the right, control in between. Most symbols are self-explanatory and are picked up as each diagram is introduced.

concepts.statement: An **electric circuit is a mathematical model** that approximates the behaviour of an actual electrical system; the design loop runs need → design specifications → concept → circuit model → circuit analysis → physical prototype, with refinements fed back from both analysis and measurement.
concepts.detail: Nilsson stresses that we always mean the model unless otherwise stated, and that the ideal circuit components in a model should represent the actual components to an acceptable degree of accuracy. The reward of modelling is enormous: interconnections of ideal elements are described by mathematical equations in measurable quantities — voltage and current — with 40-year-old mature models meeting specifications on the first iteration.

concepts.term: The three assumptions of circuit theory
concepts.statement: Circuit theory replaces electromagnetic field theory by assuming: (1) electrical effects happen **instantaneously** throughout the system (lumped-parameter); (2) the **net charge on every component is always zero**; and (3) there is **no magnetic coupling** between components.
concepts.detail: Assumption (1) works because signals travel at or near the speed of light: if the system is physically small, every point responds simultaneously. Assumptions (2) and (3) become meaningful once the basic elements and interconnection rules are introduced. Nothing else is assumed — these three buy simple solutions to problems that field theory would render hopelessly complicated.

concepts.statement: A system qualifies as lumped when its physical dimension is less than **one-tenth of the signal wavelength** $\lambda = c/f$: at 60 Hz the wavelength is $5 \times 10^{6}$ m, so any power system smaller than about $5 \times 10^{5}$ m (≈ 310 miles) is lumped; a $10^{9}$ Hz radio system must be smaller than 3 cm.
concepts.detail: Whenever a pertinent dimension approaches the wavelength of its signals, electromagnetic field theory must take over. Nilsson’s Example 1.1 gives a related engineering feel for scale: a signal at 80 per cent of the speed of light covers $2.4 \times 10^{8} \times 10^{-9}$ m, i.e. **9.45 inches of cable per nanosecond** — the number that rules high-speed digital design.

concepts.statement: Electricity appears in one of two forms, negative and positive; **electric charge is the excess** of one or the other on a body or in space. Charge is bipolar and exists in discrete quantities that are integer multiples of $1.6022 \times 10^{-19}$ C.
concepts.detail: The electron is an elementary particle carrying a small constant negative charge; the proton carries equal positive charge and the neutron none. The proton count fixes which element an atom belongs to, but electrons can be added or removed without changing that classification — only disturbing the electrical balance. A charged atom is an **ion**, and a body of ionized atoms is electrically charged. Oppositely charged bodies attract; like charges repel.

concepts.statement: Current is conventionally said to flow from a point of **high potential (positive) to low potential (negative)** — but electrons, being negative, physically move in the opposite direction. The word “current” in this text always means conventional current.
concepts.detail: The convention predates the discovery of the electron’s sign and is now universal. The transfer of electrons proceeds readily in media whose atoms release them easily — copper, aluminium, silver — which are called conductors; materials that do not permit electron flow (porcelain, nylon, rubber) are insulators; semiconductors belong to neither family. Nilsson adds the algebraic equivalence: positive charge flowing one way is identical, in every circuit equation, to negative charge flowing the other way.

concepts.term: Current flow needs a closed circuit and an e.m.f.
concepts.statement: Continuous current requires: (1) a **complete circuit** around which electrons may move — if they cannot return to the starting point they will congregate and flow ceases; and (2) a driving influence from the source, the **electromotive force**, giving each charge the energy to go round once more.
concepts.detail: The current is the rate of flow of charge through a section of the circuit. Nilsson formalizes this with the definition of current as $$i = \frac{dq}{dt}.$$ Although current is made of enormous numbers of discrete electrons, we treat it as a smoothly flowing continuous variable — one smoothly flowing entity rather than individuals. Language note: “current” is used both for the flow itself and for its rate; the ambiguity is universal and rarely causes trouble.

concepts.statement: An ideal basic circuit element has three attributes: it has **only two terminals**, it is **described mathematically in terms of current and/or voltage**, and it **cannot be subdivided** into other elements.
concepts.detail: “Ideal” means it does not exist as a realizable physical component — ideal elements are connected to model actual devices; “basic” means it is a building block that cannot itself be modelled by anything simpler. Nilsson draws it as a blank box with a voltage polarity (+/−) and a current reference arrow. Assigning the reference polarity and direction is entirely arbitrary, but once chosen, every subsequent equation must agree with the references.

examples.title: Accumulating charge at a terminal
examples.problem: No charge exists at the left terminal of an element for $t < 0$; at $t = 0$ a 5 A current begins to flow into that terminal. Derive the accumulated charge and evaluate it at 10 s. (Nilsson Example 1.2)

steps.label: Step 1: Start from the definition
steps.text: Current is the rate of charge flow, so charge is its integral: $q(t) = \int_0^t i(x)\,dx$.

steps.label: Step 2: Insert the constant current
steps.text: With $i = 5$ A: $q(t) = \int_0^t 5\,dx = 5x \big|_0^t = 5t$ coulombs for $t > 0$.

steps.label: Step 3: Evaluate at 10 s
steps.text: $q(10) = 5 \times 10 = 50$ C has accumulated at the left terminal.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret
steps.text: Five amperes means five coulombs per second — the definition of the ampere as a base unit in action, and the reason a coulomb is simply an ampere second.

examples.result: Charge grows linearly, $q(t) = 5t$ C, reaching 50 C at $t = 10$ s.

examples.title: Counting electrons in a microampere current
examples.problem: In electronic circuits it is not unusual to encounter currents in the microampere range. Assume a 75 µA current due to the flow of electrons: what is the average number of electrons per second that flow past a fixed reference cross section perpendicular to the direction of flow? (Nilsson Assessment Problem 1.4)

steps.label: Step 1: Current as charge per second
steps.text: A current of 75 µA is a flow of $75 \times 10^{-6}$ coulombs per second.

steps.label: Step 2: The indivisible unit
steps.text: Each electron carries $1.6022 \times 10^{-19}$ C — charge exists only in integer multiples of this quantum.

steps.label: Step 3: Divide
steps.text: $75 \times 10^{-6} / (1.6022 \times 10^{-19}) \approx 4.681 \times 10^{14}$ electrons per second.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret the crowd
steps.text: Even a microamp is an astronomical procession — which is exactly why $i$ can be treated as a continuous variable in every circuit equation that follows.

examples.result: About $4.681 \times 10^{14}$ electrons per second: charge is quantized in principle, continuous in practice.

examples.title: Is it a lumped-parameter system?
examples.problem: United States power systems operate at 60 Hz. Over what physical size may circuit theory be used? Repeat for a communication system whose radio signals propagate at about $10^{9}$ Hz. (Nilsson Section 1.1)

steps.label: Step 1: Wavelength of the power signal
steps.text: Signals propagate as waves with $\lambda = c/f = (3 \times 10^{8})/60 = 5 \times 10^{6}$ m.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply the rule of one-tenth
steps.text: A system is lumped if its largest dimension is below $\lambda/10 = 5 \times 10^{5}$ m — roughly 310 miles, which covers any regional power grid comfortably.

steps.label: Step 3: The radio case
steps.text: At $10^{9}$ Hz the wavelength shrinks to $0.3$ m, so the one-tenth rule demands a system smaller than 3 cm.

steps.label: Step 4: Conclusion
steps.text: A phone-sized radio circuit is marginal and a 30 cm antenna is emphatically not lumped — field theory takes over whenever dimensions approach a wavelength.

examples.result: Power systems are lumped up to about $5 \times 10^{5}$ m; a $10^{9}$ Hz communication system only up to 3 cm — a factor of $10^{7}$ difference in permissible size from a factor of $1.7 \times 10^{7}$ in frequency.

keyTakeaways: An electrical system has four parts — source, transmission system, control apparatus and load — and its diagrams (IEC 617 symbols) read left to right in the direction of energy flow.
Circuit theory rests on three assumptions: instantaneous (lumped) effects, zero net charge on every component, and no magnetic coupling between components.
The rule of one-tenth bounds the lumped approximation: system dimension below $\lambda/10$, with $\lambda = c/f$.
Charge is bipolar, quantized in units of $1.6022 \times 10^{-19}$ C, and carried between conductors by freely moving electrons.
Conventional current flows positive to negative; electrons move the opposite way, and the two descriptions are algebraically equivalent.
Sustained current demands a closed conducting loop and a source e.m.f.; current itself is $i = dq/dt$, the rate of charge flow.
The ideal basic circuit element has two terminals, is described by its terminal voltage and current, and cannot be subdivided.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three assumptions that permit circuit theory to replace electromagnetic field theory?
options: Electrical effects happen instantaneously throughout the system
The net charge on every component is always zero
There is no magnetic coupling between components
quiz.explanation: The three assumptions are lumped behaviour, zero net component charge and no inter-component magnetic coupling. Ohm’s law is a property of one particular element (the resistor, Section 2.1), not a foundation of circuit theory.

quiz.q: A system carries 60 Hz power signals. Using the rule of one-tenth, its largest physical dimension should stay below about:
quiz.explanation: At 60 Hz, $\lambda = 3 \times 10^{8}/60 = 5 \times 10^{6}$ m, so one-tenth of a wavelength is $5 \times 10^{5}$ m — approximately 310 miles, comfortably larger than any practical power system.

quiz.q: Electrons move through a copper wire from terminal B to terminal A. The conventional current is said to flow:
options: From B to A, with the electrons
From A to B, opposite to the electrons
In whichever direction the arrow on the diagram points, regardless of physics
There is no current, only electron flow
quiz.explanation: Conventional current was defined from positive to negative long before the electron’s sign was known. Negative electrons drifting from B to A is algebraically identical to positive current flowing from A to B, so all circuit equations work unchanged.

quiz.q: Which set lists the four constituent parts of Hughes’s basic electrical system?
options: Source, transmission system, control apparatus and load
quiz.explanation: Every electrical system Hughes draws contains a source providing energy, a load absorbing it, a transmission system conducting it, and control apparatus — at its simplest a switch — governing the flow.

quiz.q: An ideal basic circuit element is one that:
options: Exists physically and can be purchased with tolerance ratings
Has two terminals, is described mathematically by voltage and/or current, and cannot be subdivided
Dissipates no power under any circumstance
Works at any frequency including optical wavelengths
