quiz.explanation: Nilsson’s three attributes exactly. “Ideal” means not realizable as a physical component; “basic” means it cannot be reduced to other elements — ideal elements are the building blocks from which circuit models of real devices are constructed.

depth.title: Real sources: fields, Thévenin and matching

blocks.heading: E.m.f. from the field view
blocks.body: Inside a battery, charge is not moved by the electrostatic field but against it; the work is done by chemistry, modelled as a non-electrostatic force per unit charge $\mathbf{E}_s$ concentrated in the electrolyte. Write the total force field on a charge as $\mathbf{E}_{es} + \mathbf{E}_s$. Open-circuited, separated charge builds $\mathbf{E}_{es}$ until it cancels $\mathbf{E}_s$ everywhere inside the cell: no current flows, and the terminal voltage equals the integral of $\mathbf{E}_{es}$ from terminal to terminal, which equals $$E = \oint \mathbf{E}_s \cdot d\mathbf{l},$$ the e.m.f. — this section’s energy-converted-per-unit-charge definition, now backed by a field integral. Close the loop, and the same circulation must also push current through the electrolyte’s own resistance, which is why the terminal voltage sags to $V = E - IR_s$. The e.m.f. belongs to the chemistry; the sag is the lumped summary of fields inside the cell.

A real source reveals itself only at its terminals, and under linear operation every terminal characteristic is a straight line, $v = V_{oc} - R_T i$. The intercept is the **open-circuit voltage**; the slope is the **internal resistance**, obtainable as $R_T = V_{oc}/I_{sc}$ from a deliberate short circuit or from the sag under a known load. That line is the **Thévenin equivalent** — an ideal source $V_{oc}$ in series with $R_T$ — and rewriting it as $i = V_{oc}/R_T - v/R_T$ exhibits the **Norton equivalent**, an ideal current source $I_{sc} = V_{oc}/R_T$ in parallel with the same resistance. Thévenin’s theorem in full — that any linear one-port reduces to this form — waits for the network theorems of later chapters, but the terminal view is already complete engineering practice: a data sheet quotes $V_{oc}$ and $R_T$ and is silent about the electrochemistry inside.

blocks.heading: Where internal resistance lives
blocks.body: A lead–acid car battery must crank several hundred amperes into a starter motor. Measuring the terminal voltage during cranking: $12.6\ \text{V}$ at rest, $9.5\ \text{V}$ at $450\ \text{A}$, so $$R_s = \frac{12.6 - 9.5}{450} \approx 6.9\ \text{m}\Omega.$$ Where does it live? Conduction in the electrolyte is ionic, with carrier densities and mobilities orders of magnitude below copper’s — Drude’s $\sigma = ne\mu$ again — so a few millimetres of sulphuric acid contribute milliohms in series with interfacial reactions and grid metal. Plate area appears in parallel: doubling the plates halves $R_s$, which is why cranking batteries have many thin plates, and why a half-discharged or cold battery (sluggish ions, higher resistivity) sags so far that the starter barely turns over on a winter morning.

blocks.heading: Maximum power transfer
blocks.body: Let a source $E$ with internal resistance $R_s$ feed a load $R_L$: $$P_L = I^{2}R_L = \frac{E^{2}R_L}{(R_s + R_L)^{2}}.$$ Differentiate with respect to the load: $$\frac{dP_L}{dR_L} = \frac{E^{2}(R_s - R_L)}{(R_s + R_L)^{3}},$$ which vanishes at $R_L = R_s$ — the **matched** load — and there delivers $$P_{max} = \frac{E^{2}}{4R_s}.$$ But the efficiency at the match is $\eta = R_L/(R_s+R_L) = 1/2$: half of the source’s production is dissipated inside the source itself. Matching is therefore a **signal-transfer** doctrine — maximum power into the load, at any cost — and never a power-engineering one: the grid delivers at $R_L \gg R_s$ precisely because its business is energy, and an efficiently-run generator is a cool one.

blocks.heading: Match for signal, mismatch for efficiency
blocks.body: A 12 V source with $R_s = 0.5\ \Omega$ (a tired battery) illustrates both doctrines. Matched, $R_L = 0.5\ \Omega$ draws $I = 12\ \text{A}$ and receives $P = I^{2}R_L = 72\ \text{W}$ — with another 72 W dissipated inside the battery, which will not tolerate it for long, and 12 A through every wire. Choose instead $R_L = 11.5\ \Omega$: the current falls to $1\ \text{A}$, the load receives $11.5\ \text{W}$ at $\eta = 11.5/12 \approx 96$ per cent, and the battery loses only $0.5\ \text{W}$ internally. Six times less power is delivered, over a hundred times less is wasted — the right choice depends on whether the load wants energy, or information. A radio antenna and a microphone want every available fraction of a microwatt, and the research tier below shows why matching then pays.

depth.title: Noise: the fluctuation side of dissipation

blocks.heading: Johnson–Nyquist thermal noise
blocks.body: Johnson measured in 1927 that any resistor generates a fluctuating voltage; Nyquist derived it in 1928 by thermodynamics. Connect two equal resistors $R$ by a lossless, matched transmission line: its standing-wave modes are spaced $v/2\ell$ in frequency, and classical equipartition gives each mode energy $k_BT$, half electric and half magnetic. Matched terminations reflect nothing, so in equilibrium the power a resistor emits into the line per mode must equal what it absorbs — which pins the **available noise power** at $k_BT$ per hertz, independent of $R$. Delivering $k_BT\,\Delta f$ into a matched load from an open-circuit source then requires $$\langle v_n^{2}\rangle = 4k_BTR\,\Delta f.$$ This is the classical limit of the **fluctuation–dissipation theorem**: whatever dissipates, fluctuates — the same $\tau$ that gave Drude’s $\sigma = ne^{2}\tau/m$ also agitates the electrons. The quantum correction replaces $k_BT$ per mode by $hf/(e^{hf/k_BT} - 1)$, negligible below terahertz at room temperature.

Section 1.2 counted a 75 µA current as $4.7 \times 10^{14}$ electrons per second; that discreteness returns as **shot noise**. Charges crossing a barrier arrive as independent Poisson events, so the count variance equals the mean, and converting that into current fluctuations gives Schottky’s 1918 formula, $$\langle i_n^{2}\rangle = 2qI\,\Delta f.$$ It grows with bandwidth, and it appears whenever current is forced across a junction — a diode, a vacuum tube, a photodiode counting photons one by one. In an ordinary metal resistor the arrivals are strongly anticorrelated (the long-range Coulomb field forbids pile-ups) and shot noise is suppressed, leaving thermal noise in command. Telling a $2qI$ signature from the $4k_BTg$ of thermal noise remains a standard diagnostic for identifying the conduction channel in modern devices.

blocks.heading: How close are ADCs to the floor?
blocks.body: A 1 kΩ source at room temperature presents $\sqrt{4k_BTR} \approx 4\ \text{nV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$, which integrates over a 20 kHz audio band to about $0.6\ \mu\text{V}$ rms of irreducible signal. Sampled systems pay a second toll, **kT/C noise**: a capacitor $C$ charged through any resistance whatever ends with rms voltage $\sqrt{k_BT/C}$, so a 1 pF sampling capacitor already carries $64\ \mu\text{V}$ before the amplifier says a word. The best 24-bit delta-sigma converters now specify input-referred noise within a few dB of the thermal floor of their source impedances; the designer’s remaining levers are lower source resistance, narrower bandwidth, or cryogenics — and below the classical floor live only quantum-limited sensors such as SQUIDs and photon counters. Thermal noise is where circuit theory meets statistical mechanics: the ideal noiseless resistor of Chapter 2 is not merely ideal, it is thermodynamically impossible.

intro: Two quantities govern every circuit: the electromotive force that pushes charge round a loop and the potential difference that appears wherever energy is handed over. They are measured in the same unit — the volt — yet they play entirely different roles, and confusing them is the classic beginner’s error. This section pins down both, together with the ampere, the coulomb and the energy a battery actually delivers.
objectives: Distinguish electromotive force from potential difference
Read the arrow and polarity conventions on circuit diagrams
Define the volt, the ampere and the coulomb, and relate them through $V = P/I = W/Q$
List the principal sources of e.m.f.
Compute the energy delivered by a source from voltage, current and time

concepts.statement: The **e.m.f.** is the driving influence that causes a current to flow; it is not a force, but the **energy converted during the passing of a unit charge through the source**. Symbol $E$, unit volt. An e.m.f. is always active — it tends to produce current in a circuit.
concepts.detail: Each time charge passes through the source, more energy is provided to permit it to continue round once more; since the current flow is continuous, so is the process. Crucially, e.m.f. is always connected with energy **conversion** — chemical to electrical in a battery, mechanical to electrical in a generator.

concepts.statement: The **potential difference** is the energy transferred due to the passage of unit charge **between two points in a circuit**; across the load it is the change in energy level between the terminals, measured in volts — hence the name **volt drop**.
concepts.detail: If the transmission system is ideal (transmits all energy without loss), the p.d. across the load equals the source e.m.f. Unlike the e.m.f., a p.d. may be passive — with no tendency to create a current — or active. The term “voltage” now serves as a synonym for p.d. irrespective of the unit actually used, from 400 kV on transmission lines down to 5 µV between two points in an electronic circuit.

concepts.statement: An e.m.f. or p.d. is indicated by an arrow whose **head points towards the point of high (or assumed higher) potential** — never an arrowhead at each end as on a dimension line.
concepts.detail: Current flow leaves the source at the positive terminal, moving in the same direction as the source e.m.f. arrow; it enters the load at the positive terminal, so it runs **against** the load p.d. arrow. A separate arrowhead on the transmission system indicates the direction of conventional current. A battery symbol signals direct current; a circle is the general symbol for any d.c. source.

concepts.statement: The volt is the potential difference between two points of a conducting wire carrying 1 A when the power dissipated between those points is 1 W. Hence $$V = \frac{P}{I} \quad \text{and} \quad V = \frac{W}{Q}$$ — the p.d. equals energy per unit charge.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s differential form is $v = dw/dq$ — the formal statement of the volt as a joule per coulomb. In Hughes’s Example 2.2, a circuit delivering 20 W at 10 A has $V = 20/10 = 2$ V, so each coulomb carries $W = VQ = 2$ J.

concepts.term: Charge separation and the electric force
concepts.statement: In circuit theory, **the separation of charge creates an electric force (voltage)**, and the motion of charge creates an electric fluid (current). Whenever positive and negative charges are separated, energy is expended — voltage is the energy per unit charge created by that separation.
concepts.detail: This is why two terminal variables are enough: every electrical effect a circuit model needs is attributed either to separated charge (voltage) or to charge in motion (current). The bipolar nature of charge is what forces the polarity references of Section 1.2 onto both variables before any equation can be written.

concepts.statement: The **ampere** is that current which, maintained in two straight parallel conductors of infinite length and negligible circular cross-section placed 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force of $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N per metre of length — conductors attracting when the currents run the same way, repelling when opposite.
concepts.detail: Hughes remarks that the definition is “outstanding for its complexity” but buys conveniently sized units; the force can be measured with an elaborately constructed balance in which the force between fixed and moving coils is weighed against gravity. The **coulomb** then follows: the quantity of electricity passing a point when 1 A flows for 1 s, so $Q = It$ and $1$ ampere hour $= 3600$ coulombs — the unit in which batteries hold charge.

concepts.statement: The principal sources are: (1) electrodes of dissimilar materials immersed in an electrolyte — **primary and secondary cells**, i.e. batteries; (2) relative movement of a conductor and magnetic flux — **electric generators**; and (3) a difference of temperature between junctions of dissimilar metals — **thermo-junctions**.
concepts.detail: Each converts a different primary energy into electrical energy: chemical, mechanical and thermal respectively. The generator variant can equally be expressed as the variation of magnetic flux linked with a coil, a view developed later for machines.

concepts.statement: A source delivering **direct current** supplies current that flows in one direction only; the battery symbol in Hughes’s Fig. 2.6 and the circle symbol of Fig. 2.7 both denote d.c. sources.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s history of the abbreviation: “dc” literally stands for direct current, but because a direct current was defined as one produced by a constant voltage, a constant voltage became known as a dc voltage. The use of dc for “constant” stuck, and dc current and dc voltage now universally mean constant current and constant voltage — the assumption behind every circuit in Chapter 2.

examples.title: From charge to the energy of a coulomb
examples.problem: If a charge of 25 C passes a given point in 125 ms, determine the current. Then, in a circuit delivering energy at 20 W with a current of 10 A, determine the voltage and the energy carried by each coulomb. (Hughes Examples 2.1 and 2.2)

steps.label: Step 1: Current from charge and time
Step 2: Voltage from power and current
Step 3: Energy per coulomb
steps.text: From $V = W/Q$: each coulomb carries $W = VQ = 2 \times 1 = 2$ J.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret the pair
steps.text: The 200 A pulse and the 2 V delivery are the same bookkeeping seen from two directions: current counts charge per second, voltage counts joules per coulomb, and their product is power.

examples.result: The current is 200 A; the circuit runs at 2 V and each coulomb delivers 2 J to the load.

examples.title: How much energy is in a flashlight battery?
examples.problem: The manufacturer of a 6 V dry-cell battery says it will deliver 15 mA for 60 continuous hours, during which the voltage falls linearly from 6 V to 4 V. How much energy does the battery deliver? (Nilsson Assessment Problem 1.6)

steps.label: Step 1: Model the falling voltage
steps.text: A linear fall from 6 V to 4 V gives an average terminal voltage of $(6 + 4)/2 = 5$ V over the interval.

steps.label: Step 2: Fix the time
steps.text: The discharge lasts $60 \times 3600 = 216\,000$ s at a constant $I = 15$ mA.

steps.label: Step 3: Integrate power over time
steps.text: With constant current, $W = V_{avg}\,I\,t = 5 \times 0.015 \times 216\,000 = 16\,200$ J.

steps.label: Step 4: Sanity-check the size
steps.text: 16.2 kJ from a handheld cell is modest — about 4.5 milliwatt-hours per gram of convenience, which is why primary cells are an expensive way to buy energy but a cheap way to buy portability.

examples.result: The battery delivers 16.2 kJ over its 60 h life.

examples.title: Charge and energy bookkeeping in a resistive load
examples.problem: A p.d. of 12 V is applied to a 7.5 Ω resistor for a period of 5 s. Calculate the electric charge transferred in this time and the energy dissipated. (Hughes Exercise 2.16)

steps.label: Step 1: Current from Ohm’s law
steps.text: $I = V/R = 12/7.5 = 1.6$ A flows for the full 5 s.

steps.label: Step 2: Charge transferred
steps.text: $Q = It = 1.6 \times 5 = 8$ C passes through the resistor.

steps.label: Step 3: Energy via the volt
steps.text: Since each coulomb carries 12 J at 12 V: $W = VQ = 12 \times 8 = 96$ J.

steps.label: Step 4: Cross-check via power
steps.text: $P = VI = 12 \times 1.6 = 19.2$ W, so $W = Pt = 19.2 \times 5 = 96$ J — the same 96 J arrives by either bookkeeping route.

examples.result: 8 C and 96 J: the identities $Q = It$ and $W = VQ$ chain a resistor’s behaviour from current to charge to energy.

keyTakeaways: An e.m.f. converts energy into the circuit per unit charge passing through the source; a p.d. transfers that energy to the rest of the circuit per unit charge between two points.
Both are measured in volts; an e.m.f. is always active, while a p.d. can be passive or active.
Diagram arrows for e.m.f. and p.d. point to the high-potential end; the current arrow on the wiring shows the direction of conventional flow, which leaves the source’s positive terminal.
The volt is defined through $V = P/I$ and equals energy per unit charge, $V = W/Q$ — Nilsson’s $v = dw/dq$.
The ampere is an SI base unit defined by the $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N/m force between parallel conductors; the coulomb is an ampere second and $Q = It$.
Batteries are rated in ampere hours: $1$ A h $= 3600$ C.
Batteries, generators and thermo-junctions are the three principal sources of e.m.f., converting chemical, mechanical and thermal energy respectively.

quiz.q: The essential distinction between an e.m.f. and a potential difference is that:
options: An e.m.f. is measured in volts but a p.d. is measured in watts
An e.m.f. is associated with energy conversion in the source, while a p.d. is the energy transferred per unit charge between two points of the circuit
A p.d. can drive current but an e.m.f. cannot
They are two names for exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: The e.m.f. represents the energy expended passing a unit charge through the source and is always active; the p.d. is the energy handed over per unit charge between any two points and may be passive. With an ideal transmission system, the load p.d. equals the source e.m.f.

quiz.q: On a circuit diagram, the arrow representing an e.m.f. or p.d. is drawn:
options: With arrowheads at both ends, like a dimension line
Pointing towards the point of high (or assumed higher) potential
Pointing in the direction of electron flow
quiz.explanation: The single arrowhead points towards the high-potential end. The current leaves the source at its positive terminal — along the e.m.f. arrow — and enters the load at its positive terminal, against the load’s p.d. arrow.

quiz.q: A circuit delivers 20 W while carrying 10 A. The energy transferred by each coulomb of charge is:
options: Depends on how long the circuit runs
quiz.explanation: $V = P/I = 20/10 = 2$ V, and since a volt is a joule per coulomb, each coulomb carries $W = VQ = 2 \times 1 = 2$ J — Hughes’s Example 2.2.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Hughes’s principal sources of e.m.f.?
options: Dissimilar electrodes immersed in an electrolyte
Relative movement of a conductor and magnetic flux
Difference of temperature between junctions of dissimilar metals
A charged capacitor discharging through a resistor
quiz.explanation: Batteries (chemical), generators (mechanical) and thermo-junctions (thermal) are the three principal sources. A discharging capacitor stores separated charge but converts no primary energy, so it is not counted among the principal sources of e.m.f.

depth.title: Power in the field and Tellegen’s bookkeeping

blocks.heading: Power density in the field view
blocks.body: Take the uniform conducting bar behind the Drude discussion — length $\ell$, cross-section $A$, carrying current density $\mathbf{J}$ in a field $\mathbf{E}$. Its terminal quantities are $V = E\ell$ and $I = JA$, so the absorbed power is $$P = VI = (E\ell)(JA) = (\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E})\,\ell A,$$ and dividing by the volume $\ell A$ leaves the **local power density** $$p = \mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E},$$ in watts per cubic metre. This is Joule heating as a field quantity — the honest microscopic statement of what a resistor does: the field does work on the charges at rate $\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}$, and collisions instantly randomize that work into heat. Design follows the formula directly: a fuse opens where $\mathbf{J}$ concentrates in its necked section, machine windings are sized by the heat they can reject, and $R = \rho\ell/A$ is this very integral evaluated for a uniform bar.

blocks.heading: Tellegen’s theorem
blocks.body: In any lumped network — whatever its branches contain, linear or nonlinear, active or passive, time-varying or not — let the branch voltages $v_1, \ldots, v_b$ satisfy KVL and the branch currents $i_1, \ldots, i_b$ satisfy KCL, all with passive-sign references. Then at every instant $$\sum_{k=1}^{b} v_k i_k = 0,$$ the algebraic sum of branch powers vanishes. The remarkable clause is what the hypothesis omits: no element law, no linearity, no mention of what the branches are made of — only topology and the two Kirchhoff laws enter. A network of sealed black boxes obeys it as exactly as a network of resistors. It is the deepest theorem of pure circuit theory, and the power-balance checksum of this section is its everyday face.

Number the nodes $1, \ldots, n$ and branches $1, \ldots, b$ of the network’s connected graph, and form the reduced incidence matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{(n-1)\times b}$ with $A_{rk} = +1$ if branch $k$ leaves node $r$, $-1$ if it enters, and $0$ otherwise. **KCL** is precisely the row-wise statement $A\mathbf{i} = \mathbf{0}$: each row of $A$ sums the signed currents at one node. **KVL** is the statement that branch voltages are differences of node potentials — there exists a vector $\mathbf{e}$ with $\mathbf{v} = A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e}$. Then $$\sum_{k} v_k i_k = \mathbf{v}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{i} = \left(A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{i} = \mathbf{e}^{\mathsf{T}}\left(A\mathbf{i}\right) = \mathbf{e}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{0} = 0,$$ using nothing deeper than $(XY)^{\mathsf{T}} = Y^{\mathsf{T}}X^{\mathsf{T}}$. Kirchhoff supplies the algebra; the transpose does the physics.

Three consequences reward the generality. First, Tellegen holds for **nonlinear and time-varying** elements — diode networks, switching power converters — because no hypothesis touches the branch relations; the power-balance checksum therefore works even where Ohm’s law does not. Second, since only the incidence matrix entered the proof, the voltages and currents may come from **two different networks sharing the same graph**: $\sum_k v_k i_k^{\prime} = 0$ still holds, the basis of adjoint sensitivity analysis, which tells a designer how every output responds to every element’s drift for the cost of one extra simulation. Third, it is the natural oracle for **SPICE**: a transient solution whose branch powers fail to sum to zero is reporting numerical error, not new physics — which is exactly how this section localized the 20 W bookkeeping error to a single reversed current.

Does a solved circuit have one solution or many? The two-resistor case gives the paradigm: a source line $v = E - R_s i$ and a load characteristic $i = v/R_L$ are both monotone, so they cross exactly once — one operating point. The general linear resistive network packages the same argument: nodal analysis assembles $G\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{i}_s$ with $G = A^{\mathsf{T}}\operatorname{diag}(g)A$, **symmetric positive definite** whenever every conductance is positive, so the solution exists, is unique, and is $\mathbf{e} = G^{-1}\mathbf{i}_s$. Nonlinear elements with strictly increasing characteristics inherit uniqueness — a monotone curve meets any load line exactly once (Duffin’s theorem). But let the characteristic turn back — a tunnel diode’s N-shaped curve, a gas-discharge lamp’s negative resistance — and **multiple operating points** appear. Analysis then needs fixed-point iteration, which may cycle, or damped Newton methods: the daily convergence business of every circuit simulator.

depth.title: Simulation, memory and the single electron

blocks.body: This chapter’s flashlight — seven unknowns awaiting Kirchhoff and Ohm — is **modified nodal analysis** in miniature: write node potentials as unknowns, and for elements that do not fit nodal form (voltage sources, later inductors) append their branch currents as extra unknowns. A million-branch integrated circuit yields a matrix that is overwhelmingly zeros, so **sparse LU** factorization with Markowitz pivoting is the production engine — matrix-ordering heuristics decide runtimes as much as physics does. The research pain is dynamics: transient analysis integrates a **differential–algebraic equation**, and certain topologies — loops of voltage sources and inductors, cutsets of current sources and capacitors — raise its **differential index** to two. Hidden algebraic constraints then force numerical differentiation, the trapezoidal rule rings on fast switching edges, and opening an inductive circuit can stall convergence entirely. Circuit simulation stays an active numerical-analysis field precisely because the DAE index moves underneath the simulator when the circuit is redesigned.

blocks.heading: The missing fourth element
blocks.body: Chua observed in 1971 that circuit theory rests on four fundamental variables — $v$, $i$, charge $q$ with $i = dq/dt$, and flux $\phi$ with $v = d\phi/dt$ — and that of the six pairwise relations, five were already spoken for: the resistor ties $v$ to $i$, the capacitor $q$ to $v$, the inductor $\phi$ to $i$. The remaining $\phi$–$q$ relation defined the **memristor**, a resistor that remembers. In 2008 HP Labs reported one in titanium dioxide: oxygen vacancies drift under bias, so resistance follows the charge history — pinched hysteresis loops, conductance graded one pulse at a time, an almost literal synapse. The open questions are live: whether a strictly ideal 1971 memristor is physically realizable or only its memristive-system approximations; whether crossbar arrays of them can carry **neuromorphic** computing past the memory-bandwidth wall of von Neumann machines; and what the 2008 device truly was — the debate over that paper is itself a running literature.

blocks.heading: One electron at a time
blocks.body: Shrink a device until its total capacitance $C$ is so small that one extra electron costs $E_C = e^{2}/2C$ — more than thermal agitation can pay — and current no longer flows smoothly. The **Coulomb blockade** holds the island charge fixed until a gate or bias supplies the entrance fee, so electrons cross a quantum dot strictly one at a time: the **single-electron transistor**. Room-temperature operation demands $E_C \gg k_BT$, i.e. $C$ below a few attofarads — an island of a few atoms, beyond reliable lithography. The neighbouring route is **molecular electronics**: since Aviram and Ratner’s 1974 single-molecule rectifier proposal, individual molecules have been wired as switches and diodes; a single atomic channel bottoms out near the quantum resistance $h/2e^{2} \approx 12.9\ \text{k}\Omega$ met in Section 1.2’s research tier, and the unsolved problem is variability — how to fabricate $10^{12}$ chemically identical wires, contacts and all, when chemistry itself sets the tolerances.

intro: Voltage and current describe a circuit; power and energy decide whether it survives. Every practical device has a power limit, every source a capacity, and the fastest way to check a circuit calculation is to verify that the power balances — total delivered equals total absorbed. This section develops $p = vi$ with its sign convention, the ideal sources that feed circuits, the efficiency of energy conversion, and the art of building a circuit model of a physical system, using Nilsson’s flashlight and home-power examples.
objectives: Derive power from energy and charge: $p = vi$, with the sign fixed by the passive sign convention
Interpret positive and negative power as absorbing and delivering
Check a solved circuit by balancing supplied power against absorbed power
State the defining constraint of ideal independent and dependent sources
Construct a circuit model from a physical device and name the modelling guidelines

concepts.term: Power as the product of voltage and current
concepts.statement: Power is the time rate of expending or absorbing energy, $p = dw/dt$. Chaining the definitions of voltage and current gives the **power equation** $$p = vi,$$ the power in watts associated with a basic circuit element.
concepts.detail: The derivation is a one-line chain rule: $p = \frac{dw}{dt} = \frac{dw}{dq}\cdot\frac{dq}{dt} = vi$. A water pump rated 75 kW delivers more litres per second than one rated 7.5 kW; similarly, the useful output of an electrical system — sound from a speaker, light from a lamp — is naturally quoted in power even though the analysis variables are $v$ and $i$.

concepts.statement: Whenever the reference direction for the current in an element is in the direction of the reference **voltage drop** across the element, use a positive sign in any expression relating voltage to current ($p = vi$); otherwise use a negative sign ($p = -vi$).
concepts.detail: The convention is a bookkeeping rule applied after the arbitrary references are chosen — not a physical law, and not a function of the element type. Algebraically, positive charge flowing one way equals negative charge flowing the other, so any consistent reference set yields the same physical answer, as Nilsson’s Example 1.3 demonstrates with two classmates computing the same 40 W from different reference choices.

concepts.term: Interpreting the algebraic sign of power
concepts.statement: If $p > 0$, power is being **delivered to** the circuit element (absorbed by it); if $p < 0$, power is being **extracted from** the element (supplied by it). Positive charges lose energy moving through a voltage drop and gain it moving through a rise.
concepts.detail: The four reference combinations of Nilsson’s Fig. 1.6 give $p = vi$ twice and $p = -vi$ twice; the computed sign, not the formula, decides the direction of energy flow. In Hughes’s Example 2.4 a motor outputs 20 kW at 80 per cent efficiency from a 200 V supply: the input is $P_{in} = 20\,000/0.8 = 25\,000$ W, so the motor draws $I = 25\,000/200 = 125$ A.

concepts.statement: Energy is the time integral of power, $$w(t) = \int_0^t p(x)\,dx.$$ For constant $V$, $I$ and $P$: $W = Pt = VIt$, measured in joules (1 J = 1 W s).
concepts.detail: In Nilsson’s Example 1.4 an element carries $v = 10e^{-5000t}$ kV and $i = 20e^{-5000t}$ A: the power is $p = 200\,000e^{-10\,000t}$ W, which evaluates to 9.08 W at $t = 1$ ms, and integrates over all time to exactly 20 J — the element’s total energy absorption.

concepts.statement: The linear circuits studied in this library have **no net power**: the algebraic sum of the power associated with all circuit components must be zero. If the total is not zero, there is an error in the calculation.
concepts.detail: This is the standard self-check of circuit analysis — compute the power of every element with the passive sign convention, add, and expect zero. Nilsson’s Practical Perspective (“Balancing Power”) uses a home distribution circuit of eight components in which the sum comes to −20 W, and the error is localized by dividing by two: exactly one component’s current sign is wrong.

concepts.statement: An ideal **voltage source** maintains its prescribed terminal voltage regardless of the current through it; an ideal **current source** maintains its current regardless of the voltage across it. **Dependent** sources repeat that behaviour with a value controlled by another circuit voltage or current: $v_s = \mu v_x$ (V/V), $v_s = \rho i_x$ (V/A), $i_s = \alpha v_x$ (A/V), $i_s = \beta i_x$ (A/A).
concepts.detail: Sources are **active elements** — models of devices capable of generating electric energy — while resistors, inductors and capacitors are passive. Interconnection rules follow from the constraints: two ideal voltage sources in parallel must agree in voltage and polarity (10 V and 10 V is permitted; 10 V and 5 V is not), two current sources in series must agree in current and direction. Constant sources are called dc sources, the historical abbreviation for “direct current” that now simply means constant.

concepts.statement: The efficiency of a converting device is $$\eta = \frac{P_o}{P_{in}},$$ the ratio of output to input power; the input energy consumed to make the device operate appears as loss.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Example 2.5 makes the accounting concrete for a 200 t train resisting 62.5 N/t over 1 km with motor efficiency 0.87: the tractive work is $W_o = 200 \times 62.5 \times 1000 = 12.5 \times 10^{6}$ J, the electrical input is $W_{in} = 12.5 \times 10^{6}/0.87 = 14.4 \times 10^{6}$ J = 4.0 kW h, costing 32 p at 8 p per kW h; travelling at 80 km/h from a 1.5 kV supply then demands $I = 320 \times 10^{3}/1500 \approx 214$ A.

concepts.term: Constructing a circuit model: the flashlight
concepts.statement: Nilsson models a flashlight with an **ideal voltage source** $v_s$ (the two dry cells in series), a **lamp resistor** $R_l$, a **connector resistor** $R_1$ (the springy coil), a **case resistor** $R_c$, and a switch that toggles between short circuit (on) and open circuit (off).
concepts.detail: Three modelling guidelines emerge: (1) the electrical behaviour of each physical component is what matters — three very different parts (lamp, coiled wire, metal case) all become resistors; (2) models must include **parasitic** effects such as the unwanted case and coil resistance that drain the cells without useful output; (3) modelling requires approximation — an ideal switch, negligible contact resistance and no internal battery dissipation are all assumptions the model does not check. With $v_s = 3$ V the model has seven unknowns — $i_s, i_1, i_c, i_l, v_1, v_c, v_l$ — which Kirchhoff’s laws and Ohm’s law will pin down in Chapter 2.

examples.title: Two reference choices, one physical answer
examples.problem: A student selects the polarity references of Nilsson’s Fig. 1.6(b) and computes $i = 4$ A and $v = -10$ V. Her classmate selects Fig. 1.6(c) and computes $i = -4$ A and $v = 10$ V. What power does each calculate, and is the element absorbing or supplying? (Nilsson Example 1.3)

steps.label: Step 1: Choose the right expression
steps.text: References (b) and (c) both place the current reference against the voltage drop, so each student must use $p = -vi$.

steps.label: Step 2: First student
steps.text: $p = -(-10)(4) = +40$ W — power is delivered to the element, which is absorbing 40 W.

steps.label: Step 3: Second student
steps.text: $p = -(10)(-4) = +40$ W — the identical conclusion from the mirrored references.

steps.label: Step 4: Moral
steps.text: Any of the four reference systems of Fig. 1.6 yields the same result: the passive sign convention generates the correct sign of power regardless of the polarity and direction initially chosen.

examples.result: Both compute $p = +40$ W: the element absorbs 40 W under either reference set.

examples.title: Power and energy of an exponential transient
examples.problem: The voltage and current at an element’s terminals are $v = 10e^{-5000t}$ kV and $i = 20e^{-5000t}$ A for $t \ge 0$ (both zero before). Calculate the power at 1 ms and the total energy delivered. (Nilsson Example 1.4)

steps.label: Step 1: Form the power
steps.text: The current enters the positive terminal, so $p = vi = (10\,000e^{-5000t})(20e^{-5000t}) = 200\,000e^{-10\,000t}$ W.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret
steps.text: The transient delivers a brief kilowatt-scale burst that decays with a 0.1 ms time constant, yet the bookkeeping integrates to a modest 20 J of energy.

examples.result: Power at 1 ms is about 9.08 W; the total energy delivered over all time is 20 J.

examples.title: Balancing power in a home distribution circuit
examples.problem: Nilsson’s model of home power distribution has eight components with the values of Table 1.5: $v_a = 120$ V with $i_a = -10$ A; $v_b = 120$ V, $i_b = 9$ A; $v_c = 10$ V, $i_c = 10$ A; $v_d = 10$ V, $i_d = 1$ A; $v_e = -10$ V, $i_e = -9$ A; $v_f = -100$ V, $i_f = 5$ A; $v_g = 120$ V, $i_g = 4$ A; $v_h = -220$ V, $i_h = -5$ A. Verify the power balance and locate the data error. (Nilsson Practical Perspective)

steps.label: Step 2: Sum the suppliers
steps.text: Components a, b and d show negative power — they supply: $p_{supplied} = -1200 - 1080 - 10 = -2290$ W.

steps.label: Step 3: Sum the absorbers
steps.text: Components c, e, f, g and h absorb: $p_{absorbed} = 100 + 90 + 500 + 480 + 1100 = 2270$ W.

steps.label: Step 4: Check the balance
steps.text: $-2290 + 2270 = -20$ W — not zero, so something is wrong with the data.

steps.label: Step 5: Localize the error
steps.text: Divide the imbalance by two: $-20/2 = -10$ W, exactly the power computed for component d. If $p_d$ were $+10$ W the total would be zero — the current through d should be $-1$ A, not the $+1$ A tabulated.

examples.result: The 20 W discrepancy points straight at component d: reversing its current to −1 A balances the circuit exactly.

keyTakeaways: Power follows from the chain of definitions: $p = dw/dt = (dw/dq)(dq/dt) = vi$, in watts.
The passive sign convention: current reference along the voltage drop means $p = vi$; against it, $p = -vi$. The choice is arbitrary; the bookkeeping must then be consistent.
Positive power means the element absorbs; negative power means it supplies.
Energy is $w = \int p\,dt$; for constant conditions $W = VIt$ (joules = volt · ampere · seconds).
Linear circuits have no net power: if $\sum p \ne 0$, the analysis contains an error — halving the imbalance localizes a single sign error, as in the 20 W home-circuit check.
Ideal sources are active elements; dependent sources carry the dimensions of their gain (V/V, V/A, A/V, A/A), and parallel voltage sources or series current sources must agree in value.
Modelling guidelines: capture the electrical behaviour, include parasitic effects, and accept approximation — the flashlight is a source, three resistors and a switch.

quiz.q: The current reference arrow for an element points against the reference voltage drop (from − to +). Under the passive sign convention the element’s power is:
options: $p = vi$, and the element must be absorbing
$p = -vi$, with the sign of the result deciding absorb versus supply
$p = vi$, with the sign of the result deciding absorb versus supply
Undefined — references must be redrawn before computing power
quiz.explanation: Current against the voltage drop calls for the negative sign, $p = -vi$. If the computed $p$ is then positive the element absorbs; negative means it supplies. Reference direction along the drop instead gives $p = vi$.

quiz.q: A solved circuit’s powers sum to −20 W instead of zero. Following Nilsson’s reasoning, the most likely single cause is:
options: One component’s current or voltage sign is wrong — dividing −20 by 2 gives the power of the offending element
The circuit contains a dependent source
Energy has been stored in a magnetic field
quiz.explanation: A single sign error flips one element’s power $p$ to $-p$, leaving a residual of $\pm 2p$. Halving the imbalance, $-20/2 = -10$ W, identifies the mis-signed component — in the book’s example, component d, whose current should be −1 A.

quiz.q: In the flashlight circuit model, the coiled connector and the metal case appear as:
options: A second voltage source and a switch
Ideal resistors $R_1$ and $R_c$ — parasitic resistances that drain the cells without useful output
A short circuit and an open circuit
Dependent sources controlled by the lamp current
quiz.explanation: Modelling guideline (2): circuit models must account for undesired as well as desired electrical effects. The heat from the lamp’s resistance produces the light; the heat from the case and coil is parasitic and simply wastes battery energy.

quiz.q: A motor outputs 20 kW with 80 per cent efficiency from a constant 200 V supply. The supply current is:
quiz.explanation: $P_{in} = P_o/\eta = 20\,000/0.8 = 25\,000$ W, so $I = P/V = 25\,000/200 = 125$ A — Hughes’s Example 2.4. Efficiency always inflates the current you must supply.

quiz.q: Which interconnection of ideal sources is permitted?
options: A 10 V source in parallel with a 5 V source, same polarity
A 5 A source in series with a 2 A source, same direction
A 10 V voltage source in parallel with a 5 A current source
Two voltage sources in parallel whose voltages have opposite polarities
quiz.explanation: An ideal voltage source fixes the voltage regardless of current and an ideal current source fixes the current regardless of voltage, so one of each in parallel is always consistent. Two ideal voltage sources in parallel must match voltages (and polarities); two current sources in series must match currents (and directions).

quiz.q: In a circuit, one labelled element carries 3 A entering its positive terminal, across which the voltage is 8 V. A second load absorbs 40 W. If a single source supplies the whole circuit, the source power and the role of the first element are:
options: First element delivers 24 W; source supplies 16 W
First element absorbs 24 W; source supplies 64 W
First element absorbs 11 W; source supplies 51 W
First element delivers 24 W; source supplies 64 W
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $v = 8$ V with the reference positive where $i = 3$ A enters, plus a second load taking 40 W. Step 2 — Governing rule: with the passive sign convention $p = vi$ is absorbed when current enters the positive terminal, and absorbed powers must equal delivered powers. Step 3 — Computation: $p_{1} = 8 \times 3 = 24$ W absorbed by the first element, so the source must deliver $24 + 40 = 64$ W. Step 4 — Sanity check: all terms are positive watts, delivered equals absorbed, and the source value exceeds each single load as required. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: options claiming the first element delivers confuse entering with leaving current, 16 W subtracts instead of adding, and 11 W has no algebraic origin. Step 6 — Conclude: the first element absorbs 24 W and the source supplies 64 W.

intro: Georg Ohm found that the potential difference across the ends of many conductors is directly proportional to the current flowing between them — provided the temperature stays constant. From that single proportionality flows the entire vocabulary of resistance: the ohm, the resistor, conductance, the colour code stamped on every physical component, and the reason a cable can pass a large current or a small one. This section merges Hughes’s treatment of resistors and their coding with Nilsson’s sign-aware statement of Ohm’s law.
objectives: State Ohm’s law precisely, including the condition on which it rests
Compute voltage, current, power and energy in a resistor from any two of $V$, $I$, $R$
Convert between resistance and conductance
Read a four-band resistor colour code including tolerance
Distinguish conductors from insulators, and short circuits from open circuits

concepts.statement: The p.d. across the ends of many conductors is **directly proportional to the current flowing between them**, provided the temperature remains constant: $V \propto I$. The constant ratio defines the **ohm** — the resistance between two points of a conductor when a p.d. of 1 V produces a current of 1 A, the conductor not being a source of any e.m.f.
concepts.detail: Hughes is careful: the relation $V = IR$ is **derived from** Ohm’s law rather than being the law itself — the law only notes the constancy of p.d. to current while other physical factors are unchanged; equivalently, the ohm is the resistance in which 1 A generates heat at 1 W. Few conduction processes are exactly proportional, but the relationship is almost constant for many circuits, and we assume it throughout. Nilsson adds the sign discipline: $v = iR$ when the current reference runs along the voltage drop, $v = -iR$ when it runs against it.

concepts.statement: The reciprocal of resistance is the **conductance** $G$, measured in siemens (S): $$G = \frac{1}{R}.$$ An 8 Ω resistor has a conductance of 0.125 S.
concepts.detail: Nilsson uses conductance where it simplifies the algebra — a resistor carrying current in the direction of the voltage drop has $i = vG$, and the power equations rewrite as $p = i^{2}/G = v^{2}G$. In Example 2.3 a 0.2 S conductance with 50 V across it passes $i = (50)(0.2) = 10$ A and dissipates $p = (50)^{2}(0.2) = 500$ W. Parallel networks (Section 2.2) also collapse to a simple conductance sum.

concepts.term: Power dissipation, ratings and the heating effect
concepts.statement: A resistor passing current $I$ receives energy at the rate $I^{2}R$ and must run warmer than its surroundings until it can release that heat as fast as it arrives. Every resistor therefore carries a **power rating** — the maximum it can dissipate without damage.
concepts.detail: A 1 W resistor of 100 Ω can pass $\sqrt{1/100} = 100$ mA, whereas a ¼ W resistor of the same value stands only 50 mA. Common electronic ratings are ¼, ½, 1 and 2 W: a resistor that must dissipate 1.1 W is specified as a 2 W part, since the rating must exceed the operational value. Wires and cables are rated the same way — by the temperature their insulation can withstand. The working trio behind every such calculation is $$V = IR, \qquad I = \frac{V}{R}, \qquad P = IV = I^{2}R = \frac{V^{2}}{R},$$ with energy $W = Pt = I^{2}Rt = IVt$. Power engineers avoid resistors where possible, because every watt burned in one is energy thrown away.

concepts.statement: A resistor is **linear** if the current through it is proportional to the p.d. across its terminals; if the resistance varies with the magnitude of voltage or current, it is **non-linear**.
concepts.detail: Resistors made from semiconductor materials are the classic non-linear examples. Throughout this book resistors are assumed linear — constant resistance while the temperature is held constant — which is exactly the assumption hiding inside Ohm’s law.

concepts.statement: Small fixed resistors are carbon mouldings or metal-oxide film; above about 1 W the construction becomes a thin **nichrome wire wound on a ceramic former**, coated in cement or vitreous enamel (10–20 W); at the top end, resistors are lumps of cast iron or metal bars in ventilated cages.
concepts.detail: Variable resistors come in two flavours. A **potentiometer** uses all three connections — both ends of the coil plus a wiper arm — so the resistance between wiper and end varies with rotation. A **rheostat** makes fixed connections to intermediate points along the wire; such intermediate connections are called **tappings**. The thinner and the longer the wire, the greater its resistance — a fact Section 2.5 turns into the resistivity law.

concepts.statement: Carbon resistors state their value in painted bands: the **first two bands are digits** (black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9), the **third band is the number of zeros**, and the **fourth is the tolerance** — gold ±5 per cent, silver ±10 per cent, no band ±20 per cent.
concepts.detail: A fifth band, where present, is a **reliability factor**: the percentage failure per 1000 h of use (brown 1, red 0.1, orange 0.01, yellow 0.001 per cent). Reading starts from the band placed nearest the end of the resistor. Example readings from Hughes: orange–blue–green gives 3, 6 and five zeros — 3 600 000 Ω; yellow–violet–red gives 4700 Ω; orange–black–gold gives 3.0 Ω (the gold band as multiplier shifts the decimal point).

concepts.statement: Metal-oxide resistors too small for bands use a **letter code** in which the letter marks the decimal point: R47 = 0.47 Ω, 4R7 = 4.7 Ω, 47R = 47 Ω, 470R = 470 Ω, 4K7 = 4.7 kΩ, 47K = 47 kΩ, 4M7 = 4.7 MΩ.
concepts.detail: Readily available standard values run 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.5, 1.6, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 2.4, 2.7, 3.0, 3.3, 3.6, 3.9, 4.3, 4.7, 5.1, 5.6, 6.2, 6.8, 7.5, 8.2, 9.1 and their decade multiples. All exist with 5 per cent tolerance, and the bold-face subset with 10 per cent. The wide tolerance bands exist because manufacturing resistors to an exact value is hard — fortunately, circuits tolerate the spread.

concepts.statement: Connect identical rods of different materials to a constant-e.m.f. battery and measure the current: **metals permit reasonable currents; non-metals permit virtually none.** Conductors include copper, aluminium, silver, platinum, bronze and gold; insulators include glass, rubber, plastic, air, varnish, paper, wood, mica, ceramic and certain oils.
concepts.detail: The classification is a simplification — no material completely stops current, and none passes charge without opposition. The physics: materials with no energy gap readily supply free electrons and make up the circuit; materials with sizeable gaps between valence and conduction bands insulate it and contain the current within the conductors. That is why a cut-open wire shows copper strands in the middle surrounded by plastic, not the reverse.

concepts.term: The circuit in practice: cells, short and open circuits
concepts.statement: Two circuit conditions matter at the extremes: with $R = 0$ there is no limit to the current and the volt drop is zero — a **short circuit**; with $R = \infty$ no current can flow — an **open circuit**.
concepts.detail: Electricity arrives from generating stations (steam- or water-turbine driven, the latter hydroelectric), transmitted by overhead power lines or buried cables — and possibly 20 per cent of UK generation comes from private sources. For portable devices, **primary cells** (torches, radios, watches) buy convenience at a high price per unit of energy and are discarded; **secondary cells** (cars) deliver and accept recharge of much larger energies at the cost of weight. A broken wire open-circuits a circuit; a 240 V supply shorted through 8.5 mΩ would drive 28 kA — which is why protection exists.

examples.title: Reading the colour code
examples.problem: A resistor carries four bands: orange, blue, green, silver. What is its resistance and between what limits does it lie? Then read a resistor with bands brown, black, orange and no fourth band. (Hughes Section 2.10 and Example 2.6)

steps.label: Step 1: Decode the digits
steps.text: Orange = 3 and blue = 6, so the numerical value starts 36.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply the multiplier
steps.text: The green third band calls for five zeros: $36$ followed by $00000$ = 3 600 000 Ω = 3.6 MΩ.

steps.label: Step 3: Apply the tolerance
steps.text: Silver is ±10 per cent, and 10 per cent of 3 600 000 is 360 000, so the resistance lies between 3 240 000 Ω and 3 960 000 Ω.

steps.label: Step 4: Second resistor
steps.text: Brown = 1, black = 0, orange = three zeros: $10\,000\ \Omega = 10$ kΩ. With no tolerance band the spread is ±20 per cent, i.e. between 8 kΩ and 12 kΩ.

steps.label: Step 5: Perspective
steps.text: The apparently huge 8–12 kΩ spread reflects manufacturing reality; circuit designs are made tolerant enough that it rarely matters.

examples.result: 3.6 MΩ ± 10 per cent (3.24–3.96 MΩ); and 10 kΩ ± 20 per cent (8–12 kΩ).

examples.title: Signs and conductance: four resistor snapshots
examples.problem: In each circuit of Nilsson’s Fig. 2.8 either $v$ or $i$ is unknown: a 1 A current into an 8 Ω resistor; 50 V across a 0.2 S conductance; a 1 A current with the voltage a rise in the current direction across 20 Ω; and 50 V with the current directed against the drop through 25 Ω. Find the unknowns and the power dissipated. (Nilsson Example 2.3)

steps.label: Step 1: First resistor
steps.text: Current along the voltage drop: $v_a = (1)(8) = 8$ V.

steps.label: Step 2: Conductance branch
steps.text: Current along the drop through $G = 0.2$ S: $i_b = (50)(0.2) = 10$ A.

steps.label: Step 3: Rise in the current direction
steps.text: With the voltage a rise along the current, $v_c = -(1)(20) = -20$ V.

steps.label: Step 4: Current against the drop
steps.text: $i_d = -50/25 = -2$ A — the minus sign simply reports that the reference was drawn opposite to the actual flow.

examples.result: $v_a = 8$ V, $i_b = 10$ A, $v_c = -20$ V, $i_d = -2$ A; the four resistors dissipate 8 W, 500 W, 20 W and 100 W respectively — sign conventions affect the reported direction, never the absorbed power.

examples.title: Heating effect of a current
examples.problem: A current of 5 A flows in a resistor of resistance 8 Ω. Determine the rate of heat dissipation and the heat dissipated in 30 s. (Hughes Example 2.3)

steps.label: Step 1: Power from current and resistance
Step 2: Energy over the interval
steps.text: $W = Pt = 200 \times 30 = 6000$ J of heat leaves the resistor in 30 s.

steps.label: Step 3: Choose a rating
steps.text: A physical part here must be rated above 200 W — on Hughes’s standard scale that means a wire-wound or caged power resistor, not a 2 W electronic part.

examples.result: The resistor dissipates 200 W and releases 6000 J in 30 s; the rating of the physical part must exceed 200 W.

keyTakeaways: Ohm’s law: $V \propto I$ at constant temperature; the constant ratio $R = V/I$ is the resistance, and $V = IR$ is its working consequence.
The ohm is 1 V per ampere, with no e.m.f. in the conductor; power in a resistor follows $P = IV = I^{2}R = V^{2}/R$ and energy $W = I^{2}Rt$.
Conductance is $G = 1/R$ in siemens; an 8 Ω resistor conducts 0.125 S, and $p = i^{2}/G = v^{2}G$.
Colour code: two digit bands, a zeros band, a tolerance band (gold 5, silver 10, none 20 per cent) and an optional reliability band.
Ratings must exceed operating dissipation — a 1.1 W application takes a 2 W resistor; 100 mA is the limit for a 1 W 100 Ω part and 50 mA for a ¼ W one.
Metals conduct (copper best of the common ones), non-metals insulate; the energy-gap picture explains why copper sits inside the plastic.
A short circuit is $R = 0$ with unbounded current and zero volt drop; an open circuit is $R = \infty$ with none — and portability is why primary cells exist despite their cost per unit of energy.

quiz.q: A resistor’s bands read yellow, violet, red, gold. Its nominal resistance and tolerance are:
quiz.explanation: Yellow = 4, violet = 7, red = two zeros: 4700 Ω. Gold is the ±5 per cent tolerance band. Hughes gives exactly this example: yellow–violet–red means 4700 Ω (a gold band would only change the tolerance, not the digits).

quiz.q: Which statement about Ohm’s law is the careful one Hughes insists on?
options: Ohm’s law states the constancy of the ratio of p.d. to current while other physical factors remain unchanged
Ohm’s law holds for every conductor at every temperature
quiz.explanation: The proportionality $V \propto I$ at constant temperature is the law; $V = IR$ is derived from it. Few conduction processes are exactly proportional, but the assumption is nearly constant for many circuits and is adopted throughout.

quiz.q: A current of 3 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. The power developed is:
quiz.explanation: $P = I^{2}R = 3^{2} \times 10 = 90$ W — Hughes’s Example 3.18, whose energy bookkeeping ($W = Pt$) follows directly.

quiz.q: The conductance of an 8 Ω resistor is:
quiz.explanation: $G = 1/R = 1/8 = 0.125$ S. Conductance measured in siemens is Nilsson’s preferred currency whenever parallel connections dominate.

quiz.q: Two points are connected by a conductor of zero resistance. The circuit condition is called:
options: An open circuit — no current flows
A short circuit — the volt drop between the points is zero
quiz.explanation: With $R = 0$, $V = IR = 0$ regardless of current, so nothing limits the flow — a short circuit. The opposite extreme, $R = \infty$, is the open circuit where $I = V/\infty = 0$.

intro: One lamp on a supply glows normally; wire a second lamp in series with it and both glow feebly, because the current must fight twice the resistance. Wire the second lamp in parallel instead and both shine at full brilliance, because each receives the full supply voltage. Series and parallel connection are the two ways circuits grow, and this section builds their algebra — equivalent resistance, voltage and current sharing — before Kirchhoff’s laws generalize it.
objectives: Derive the series and parallel equivalent-resistance laws from current and voltage behaviour
Compute current and voltage in series ladders and parallel networks
Apply the product-over-sum rule and the current-sharing formula for two resistors
Reduce series–parallel networks step by step and back-substitute for branch currents
Choose between series and parallel connection on practical grounds

concepts.statement: Load units are **series-connected** when the same current passes through each of them — where else can the current go having passed the first but on to the second, there being no other conduction path? Nilsson’s formal version: two elements connected at a single node (and nowhere else) are in series.
concepts.detail: Ammeters placed in each part of a series circuit read identically, whatever the applied voltage. In Hughes’s Fig. 3.5, KVL around the loop gives $V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3 = IR_1 + IR_2 + IR_3$, and comparing with $V = IR$ yields the series law — the same conclusion Nilsson reaches for seven resistors via $-v_s + i_s R_1 + \cdots + i_s R_7 = 0$.

concepts.statement: The total resistance of resistors in series is the sum of the separate resistances: $$R = R_1 + R_2 + R_3.$$ The equivalent is always **greater than the greatest** resistance in the circuit — a ready-made check on the arithmetic.
concepts.detail: In Hughes’s Example 3.1, a 220 V supply drives 73 mA through one 3 kΩ resistor; adding a second 3 kΩ in series doubles the resistance to 6 kΩ and halves the current to 37 mA — exactly the dimming of the two series lamps. In Example 3.3, resistors of 40 Ω, 50 Ω and 70 Ω in series present 160 Ω to a 100 V supply, so $I = 100/160 = 0.625$ A.

concepts.statement: Loads are **parallel-connected** when the same potential difference is applied to each — the current may pass by several side-by-side paths called branches. With more than one circuit present the arrangement is a **network**: two or more circuits.
concepts.detail: Ammeters show that the branch currents always sum to the supply current, $I = I_1 + I_2 + I_3$, and voltmeters show every branch voltage equals the supply voltage. Nilsson warns against geometry as a guide: two elements are parallel because they share terminal voltage, not because they look parallel — in his Fig. 3.6, $R_1$ and $R_3$ are **not** parallel because another resistor dissipates part of the voltage between their terminals.

concepts.statement: The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance equals the sum of the branch reciprocals: $$\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3},$$ or in conductance form $G_{eq} = G_1 + G_2 + \cdots + G_k$. The equivalent is always **less than the smallest** branch resistance.
concepts.detail: The “less than smallest” check catches the classic error of forgetting to invert the final $1/R$. Hughes’s Example 3.6 combines 6.8 Ω, 4.7 Ω and 2.2 Ω: $1/R = 0.147 + 0.213 + 0.455 = 0.815$, so $R = 1/0.815 = 1.23$ Ω — indeed below 2.2 Ω — and a 12 V supply then delivers $I = 12/1.23 = 9.76$ A.

concepts.term: Product over sum for two resistors
concepts.statement: For exactly two resistors in parallel, $$R = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$ — the product of the resistances divided by their sum. The shortcut applies **only** to the two-resistor case.
concepts.detail: It follows from $1/R = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 = (R_1 + R_2)/(R_1 R_2)$. Nilsson uses it constantly in ladder reduction — in his Example 3.1, 20 kΩ in parallel with 5 kΩ gives $(20\,000 \times 5000)/25\,000 = 4$ kΩ — and the same expression reappears as the input resistance of loaded dividers.

concepts.term: Voltage division in a series pair
concepts.statement: Given two resistors in series across a supply $V$, the volt drop across $R_1$ is $$\frac{V_1}{V} = \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2},$$ so the ratio of voltages depends on the ratio of resistances — the **voltage divider**.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Example 3.4 designs one: an output of 10 V from a 30 V input with $R_2 = 100$ Ω requires $10/30 = 100/(R_1 + 100)$, so $R_1 + 100 = 300$ and $R_1 = 200$ Ω. Nilsson generalizes the result to $n$ series resistors in Section 3.4 — the voltage-division equation developed in Section 2.4 of this library.

concepts.term: Current sharing in a parallel pair
concepts.statement: Two parallel resistors share a supply current as $$I_1 = I \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$ — the current in one resistor is the total multiplied by the **other** resistance over the sum.
concepts.detail: Equal resistances share equally; the lesser resistance takes the greater part. Hughes’s Example 3.7: an 8 A supply current divides between a 2 Ω resistor and a 2 Ω resistor as 4.0 A each; replace the first by 4 Ω and the 2 Ω branch takes $8 \times 4/6 = 5.3$ A. The upside-down appearance of the resistances — the *other* resistor on top — is the detail to memorize.

concepts.statement: The electron test: if an electron has **no choice** but to pass through every load unit, they are in series; if it has a **choice**, they are in parallel. Table 3.1 of Hughes gathers the dual relations — series shares current and adds voltages; parallel shares voltage and adds currents.
concepts.detail: Reliability drives the practical preference: with parallel lamps, one failed filament interrupts only its own branch; with series lamps, one failure extinguishes all (the Christmas-tree-light problem). Series connection’s one advantage — sharing the supply voltage so cheap low-voltage lamps can be used — is outweighed for most lighting, so the parallel arrangement is highly preferable.

concepts.statement: Networks mixing both connections are reduced by **starting at the end farthest from the source and working towards it**: combine the innermost series or parallel pair, redraw, and repeat until one equivalent resistance remains; then expand backwards for branch currents.
concepts.detail: In Hughes’s Fig. 3.28, $R_4 \parallel R_5$ and $R_6 \parallel R_7$ are in series with each other, while $R_2$ is parallel with the *network* containing $R_4$–$R_7$ — but $R_2$ is not parallel with $R_6$, because $I_6$ is not derived immediately from $I_1$. Nilsson’s Example 3.2 works a full reduction: right of the terminals, 3 Ω + 6 Ω = 9 Ω; that in parallel with 18 Ω gives 6 Ω; the source sees $4 + 6 = 10$ Ω, so $i_s = 120/10 = 12$ A; then $v_1 = (12)(6) = 72$ V splits as $i_1 = 72/18 = 4$ A and $i_2 = 72/9 = 8$ A.

examples.title: Voltage drops in a series ladder
examples.problem: A current of 1.5 A flows through three series resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 8 Ω. Calculate the voltage across each and the supply voltage. (Hughes Example 3.2)

steps.label: Step 1: Same current everywhere
steps.text: Series connection forces the full 1.5 A through each resistor.

steps.label: Step 4: Check the proportions
steps.text: Each drop takes its share of the supply in the ratio $2{:}3{:}8$ — the voltage-division principle in action before we formalize it.

examples.result: Drops of 3.0 V, 4.5 V and 12.0 V add to a 19.5 V supply — series circuits divide voltage in the ratio of resistances.

examples.title: Parallel reduction, current sharing and power
examples.problem: First reduce a parallel network of 6.8 Ω, 4.7 Ω and 2.2 Ω across a 12 V supply and find the supply current. Then examine how 8 A divides between a 2 Ω resistor and (a) another 2 Ω, (b) a 4 Ω resistor, and the powers that result when 9 A divides between 8 Ω and 4 Ω branches. (Hughes Examples 3.6, 3.7, 3.20)

steps.label: Step 3: Equal sharing
steps.text: With $R_1 = R_2 = 2$ Ω, the second branch takes $I_2 = 8 \times 2/(2+2) = 4.0$ A — equal resistances share equally.

steps.label: Step 4: Unequal sharing
steps.text: With $R_1 = 4$ Ω and $R_2 = 2$ Ω, $I_2 = 8 \times 4/(4+2) = 5.3$ A — the lesser resistance takes the greater current.

steps.label: Step 5: Power split
steps.text: When 9 A divides between 8 Ω and 4 Ω, $I_1 = 9 \times 4/12 = 3$ A and $I_2 = 6$ A, so $P_1 = 3^{2} \times 8 = 72$ W and $P_2 = 6^{2} \times 4 = 144$ W — which Hughes rounds to 140 W, honouring the one-significant-figure inputs.

examples.result: Equivalent 1.23 Ω drawing 9.76 A; current shares 4.0/4.0 A or 5.3/2.7 A as the resistances dictate; power follows the current split, 72 W and about 140 W.

examples.title: Network reduction with back-substitution
examples.problem: Find $i_s$, $i_1$ and $i_2$ for a 120 V source feeding a 4 Ω resistor in series with a network whose remainder is an 18 Ω resistor in parallel with a (3 Ω + 6 Ω) branch. (Nilsson Example 3.2)

steps.label: Step 1: Innermost series
steps.text: Right of the terminals, the 3 Ω and 6 Ω resistors are in series: $3 + 6 = 9$ Ω.

steps.label: Step 2: Parallel pair
steps.text: The 18 Ω resistor parallels the 9 Ω: $R_{eq} = (18 \times 9)/(18 + 9) = 6$ Ω.

steps.label: Step 3: Source current
steps.text: The source now sees $4 + 6 = 10$ Ω, so $i_s = 120/10 = 12$ A.

steps.label: Step 4: Voltage across the parallel section
steps.text: $v_1 = (12)(6) = 72$ V appears across both the 18 Ω and 9 Ω paths.

steps.label: Step 5: Branch currents
steps.text: $i_1 = 72/18 = 4$ A and $i_2 = 72/9 = 8$ A — summing back to 12 A, and the solution satisfies KCL at every node and KVL around all three closed paths.

examples.result: $i_s = 12$ A, splitting as $i_1 = 4$ A and $i_2 = 8$ A — reduce, then unfold: the whole method in two sentences.

keyTakeaways: Series elements carry one current; their voltages and resistances add: $V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$ and $R = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$.
Parallel branches share one voltage; their currents add, and $1/R = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3$ (or $G_{eq} = \sum G_i$).
Series equivalents exceed the largest resistor; parallel equivalents undercut the smallest — use both as arithmetic checks.
Two resistors in parallel: $R = R_1R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$, valid for exactly two.
Voltage divides as $V_1/V = R_1/(R_1 + R_2)$; current divides “the other way”, $I_1 = I \cdot R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$.
Parallel connection wins on reliability — one failed branch leaves the rest alive; series connection saves voltage rating at the cost of total failure.
Reduce from the far end toward the source, then back-substitute: 9 Ω → 6 Ω → 10 Ω → 12 A → 72 V → 4 A and 8 A.

quiz.q: A 100 V supply feeds three series resistors of 40 Ω, 50 Ω and 70 Ω. The circuit current is:
Resistors of 6.8 Ω, 4.7 Ω and 2.2 Ω are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is approximately:
quiz.explanation: $1/R = 0.147 + 0.213 + 0.455 = 0.815$, so $R = 1/0.815 = 1.23$ Ω. Choosing 0.815 Ω is the classic forgotten inversion; 13.7 Ω is the equally classic addition.

quiz.q: An 8 A supply current divides between a 4 Ω resistor and a 2 Ω resistor. The current in the 2 Ω resistor is:
quiz.explanation: The 2 Ω branch takes $I_2 = 8 \times R_1/(R_1 + R_2) = 8 \times 4/6 = 5.3$ A — the lesser resistance takes the greater share, and the multiplying fraction uses the *other* resistor.

quiz.q: You must deliver 10 V from a 30 V source with a divider whose lower resistor $R_2 = 100$ Ω. The upper resistor $R_1$ should be:
Why does Hughes prefer parallel connection for lamps in practice?
options: A failed filament interrupts only its own branch, leaving the others lit
Series circuits cannot share a supply voltage
Parallel connection raises the total resistance
quiz.explanation: In a parallel network each branch is independent; a broken filament open-circuits one branch only. Series lamps share the supply voltage (their one advantage) but one failure blackens the whole string — the Christmas-tree problem.

quiz.q: A 12 V supply feeds a 6 Ω resistor in series with the parallel combination of 3 Ω and 6 Ω. The current through the 3 Ω resistor is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $V_{s} = 12$ V, series arm $6$ Ω, parallel pair $3$ Ω with $6$ Ω. Step 2 — Governing laws: parallel pair combines by $\frac{1}{R_{p}} = \frac{1}{R_{1}} + \frac{1}{R_{2}}$, series arms add, and branch currents share inversely with resistance. Step 3 — Algebra: $R_{p} = \frac{3 \times 6}{3 + 6} = 2$ Ω, total $R = 6 + 2 = 8$ Ω, total current $I = \frac{12}{8} = 1.5$ A, voltage on the pair $V_{p} = 1.5 \times 2 = 3$ V, so $I_{3} = \frac{3}{3} = 1.0$ A. Step 4 — Sanity check: the smaller branch takes the larger share ($1.0$ A versus $0.5$ A), the shares sum to $1.5$ A, and $R_{p} = 2$ Ω sits below the smallest branch as required. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 0.5 A is the companion branch, 1.5 A is the total before sharing, and 2.0 A ignores the series drop. Step 6 — Conclude: the 3 Ω resistor carries about 1.0 A.

intro: The series and parallel rules are shadows of two deeper statements. Gustav Kirchhoff observed that the addition of currents at a junction and the addition of voltages round a loop are particular cases of two general conditions fundamental to every network. Nine times out of ten his laws handle just two currents or two voltages at a time — but applied jointly, with Ohm’s law, they solve networks of arbitrary complexity, including circuits powered by several sources and by sources whose value depends on another branch.
objectives: State Kirchhoff’s current and voltage laws in both Hughes’s and Nilsson’s formulations
Apply KCL at junctions and to whole sections of a network, interpreting negative answers
Apply KVL to any closed loop, including loops with no source and imaginary loops
Solve a two-source network with simultaneous equations and verify it by power balance
Analyse circuits containing dependent sources

concepts.statement: **First (current) law:** at any instant the algebraic sum of the currents at a junction in a network is zero — currents held to flow towards the junction are given one sign, those away from it the other. Nilsson’s version: the algebraic sum of all the currents at any node equals zero.
concepts.detail: Choose a convention — Hughes marks currents flowing towards the junction positive (Fig. 3.23: $I_1 - I_2 + I_3 - I_4 + I_5 = 0$); Nilsson marks currents **leaving** a node positive. Either works; multiplying the equation by −1 converts one to the other. The law is simply conservation: where else can the branch currents come from but the source, there being no other conduction path?

concepts.statement: Kirchhoff’s first law need not be applied only to a junction — it applies equally to a **section of a network** enclosed by any closed surface.
concepts.detail: In Hughes’s Example 3.9, applying KCL at junctions a and b of a two-loop network and eliminating $I_3$ produces $I_1 - I_2 + I_4 + I_5 = 0$ — the balance for the dotted box enclosing part of the network. The practical payoff: quite a complicated network’s internals can be ignored when only input and output quantities are wanted, as in Example 3.10 where $I_3 = -I_1 - I_2 = -1.0$ A for a box with $I_1 = 2.5$ A and $I_2 = -1.5$ A entering.

concepts.statement: **Second (voltage) law:** at any instant in a closed loop, the algebraic sum of the e.m.f.s acting round the loop equals the algebraic sum of the p.d.s round the loop. Nilsson’s version: the algebraic sum of all the voltages around any closed path in a circuit equals zero.
concepts.detail: A loop (closed path) starts at an arbitrarily selected node, traces through selected basic circuit elements, and returns to the start without passing any intermediate node more than once. Tracing clockwise, take p.d.s acting clockwise as negative (Hughes) or, equivalently, assign voltage drops the positive sign (Nilsson) — the two are the same rule with opposite bookkeeping. Hughes’s simple series circuit of Fig. 3.30 says $E = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$; a three-branch parallel network already contains three loops.

concepts.term: Loops without sources and imaginary loops
concepts.statement: A loop need not contain an e.m.f. — applying KVL to the source-free loop B of Hughes’s Fig. 3.31 gives $0 = -V_2 + V_3 + V_4$ — and KVL can even be applied to a **partly imaginary** loop to derive the p.d. across series elements: $0 = -V + V_1 + V_2 + V_3$ yields $V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$.
concepts.detail: In Hughes’s Example 3.13, loop A gives $V_1 = E - V_2 = 12 - 8 = 4$ V and loop B gives $V_3 = V_2 - V_4 = 8 - 2 = 6$ V; loop C then confirms both, since $E = V_1 + V_3 + V_4 = 4 + 6 + 2 = 12$ V. In Example 3.15 the left loop gives $V_1 = 10 - 6 = 4$ V, the right loop gives $E_2 = 6 + 8 = 14$ V, and the outer loop checks it: $10 - 14 = 4 - 8$.

concepts.statement: A **node** is a point where two or more circuit elements meet (terminal dots are the start and end points of individual elements). In a circuit with $n$ nodes, Kirchhoff’s current law provides $n - 1$ independent equations.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s flashlight model has four nodes a–d and four KCL equations, but any one follows from the other three, so only three count. Watch also for wires that cross **without** a connection dot — no node there. When only two elements connect at a node, the elements carry the same current and are in series; recognizing this collapses unknowns before any equation is written.

concepts.statement: Two analysis details cut the algebra: (1) knowing a resistor’s current reveals its voltage through Ohm’s law, so associate **one** unknown with each resistor; (2) when only two elements meet at a node, KCL makes their currents equal, so define **one** unknown for both.
concepts.detail: In Nilsson’s flashlight, applying both disciplines reduces seven unknowns ($i_s, i_1, i_c, i_l, v_1, v_c, v_l$) to just one: KCL at nodes a, b, c gives $i_s = i_1 = -i_c = i_l$, and the single loop equation $v_l - v_c + v_1 - v_s = 0$ with Ohm’s law finishes the job. A circuit is solved when every element voltage and current is known.

concepts.statement: With two unknown currents, write **one KCL equation at a node and one KVL equation around a loop**, express the resistor voltages via Ohm’s law, and solve simultaneously; then verify that total power developed equals total power dissipated.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s Example 2.8 does exactly this for a 120 V source feeding a 10 Ω resistor, a node pair, a 50 Ω resistor and a 6 A source: KCL at node b gives $i_1 - i_o - 6 = 0$; KVL clockwise gives $-120 + 10i_o + 50i_1 = 0$; solving yields $i_o = -3$ A and $i_1 = 3$ A. The power check: the 6 A source delivers 900 W, and the three absorbing elements take exactly 450 + 90 + 360 = 900 W.

concepts.statement: A **dependent (controlled) source** has its value fixed by a voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit: $v_s = \mu v_x$ (V/V), $v_s = \rho i_x$ (V/A), $i_s = \alpha v_x$ (A/V), $i_s = \beta i_x$ (dimensionless). The constants carry the dimensions; the diamond symbol distinguishes them from the circle of independent sources.
concepts.detail: The permissible-interconnection rules extend to them: an independent and a dependent voltage source in parallel must still agree — 5 V versus $3v_x = 15$ V is not permitted. Dependent sources make electronics possible: transistor amplifiers are modelled with a current source $\beta i_B$ (Nilsson’s Example 2.12 derives $i_B = [V_{CC}R_2/(R_1+R_2) - V_0] / [R_1R_2/(R_1+R_2) + (1+\beta)R_E]$), and the node-voltage and mesh-current machinery of Chapter 3 leans on them heavily.

concepts.statement: Not every closed path yields a useful KVL equation and not every node a useful KCL equation: a loop containing a dependent **current** source has an unknown voltage across it and should be avoided in KVL.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s Example 2.10 (a 500 V source, 5 Ω, 20 Ω and a $5i_\Delta$ source) picks the one loop avoiding the dependent source: $-500 + 5i_\Delta + 20i_o = 0$, then KCL at node b: $-i_\Delta + i_o - 5i_\Delta = 0$, so $i_o = 6i_\Delta$ and $500 = 125i_\Delta$, giving $i_\Delta = 4$ A, $i_o = 24$ A and $v_o = 480$ V. Think before writing — select the path and node that reduce the number and complexity of equations.

examples.title: Junction currents — including a negative answer
examples.problem: In Hughes’s Fig. 3.27, a current $I_1 = 3$ A enters junction a, $I_3 = 1$ A runs from a to c, and $I_6 = 1$ A leaves junction b. Write the current relationships for junctions a, b and c and determine $I_2$, $I_4$ and $I_5$. (Hughes Example 3.11)

steps.label: Step 3: Read the negative sign
steps.text: A negative $I_4$ means the current actually flows from b towards c — the drawn reference arrow simply assumed the wrong direction, which is always permissible.

examples.result: $I_2 = 2$ A, $I_4 = -1$ A (upwards, against its reference) and $I_5 = 2$ A — three junction equations, one direction reversal, zero drama.

examples.title: A two-source network by simultaneous equations
examples.problem: In Nilsson’s circuit a 120 V source drives current $i_o$ through a 10 Ω resistor into node b, from which a 6 A source pulls current while a 50 Ω resistor returns current $i_1$ to node c. Find $i_o$, then verify that total power generated equals total power dissipated. (Nilsson Example 2.8)

steps.label: Step 1: Count the unknowns
steps.text: Two unknown currents, $i_o$ and $i_1$, so two independent equations are needed.

steps.label: Step 2: KCL at node b
steps.text: Summing currents leaving the node: $i_1 - i_o - 6 = 0$.

steps.label: Step 3: KVL around the left loop
steps.text: With Ohm’s law $v_o = 10i_o$ and $v_1 = 50i_1$, tracing clockwise: $-120 + 10i_o + 50i_1 = 0$.

steps.label: Step 4: Solve simultaneously
steps.text: Substituting $i_1 = i_o + 6$: $-120 + 10i_o + 50(i_o + 6) = 0$ gives $60i_o = -180$, so $i_o = -3$ A and $i_1 = 3$ A.

steps.label: Step 6: Balance the sources
steps.text: The 120 V source absorbs $p_{120} = -120 \times (-3) = 360$ W; the 50 Ω drops $v_1 = 150$ V, so the 6 A source supplies $p_{6A} = -150 \times 6 = -900$ W. Delivered 900 W = absorbed $450 + 90 + 360 = 900$ W.

examples.result: $i_o = -3$ A, $i_1 = 3$ A, and the power check closes exactly: one 900 W supplier feeding three absorbers.

examples.title: A dependent source: strategy before equations
examples.problem: Find $v_o$ in a circuit where a 500 V source drives a 5 Ω resistor (current $i_\Delta$) into node b of a 20 Ω resistor (current $i_o$), with a dependent current source $5i_\Delta$ also entering node b. (Nilsson Example 2.10)

steps.label: Step 1: Survey before writing
steps.text: Once $i_o$ is known, Ohm’s law gives $v_o = 20i_o$; once $i_\Delta$ is known, the dependent source’s value $5i_\Delta$ is known. Two unknowns, two equations.

steps.label: Step 2: Pick the usable loop
steps.text: KVL cannot use the loop through the dependent current source (its voltage is unknown), so take the loop through the 500 V source and both resistors: $-500 + 5i_\Delta + 20i_o = 0$.

steps.label: Step 3: KCL at node b
steps.text: Summing currents leaving: $-i_\Delta + i_o - 5i_\Delta = 0$, hence $i_o = 6i_\Delta$.

steps.label: Step 4: Substitute and solve
steps.text: $500 = 5i_\Delta + 20(6i_\Delta) = 125i_\Delta$, so $i_\Delta = 4$ A and $i_o = 6 \times 4 = 24$ A.

examples.result: The dependent source multiplies the outcome: a 500 V input produces 480 V across the 20 Ω resistor because $i_o = 6i_\Delta$ — the seed of amplifier action.

keyTakeaways: KCL: the algebraic sum of currents at any junction (or any closed section of a network) is zero.
KVL: the algebraic sum of e.m.f.s round a loop equals the algebraic sum of p.d.s — equivalently, all voltages around any closed path sum to zero.
Sign conventions are free choices fixed in advance: towards-junction positive or leaving-node positive; clockwise drops positive — any consistent set works.
A circuit with $n$ nodes contributes only $n - 1$ independent KCL equations; two-element nodes identify series elements and collapse unknowns.
Negative answers are informative: the assumed reference direction was simply reversed.
