concepts.statement: Lines of magnetic flux are assumed to have these properties: (1) their direction is that of a compass’s north-seeking pole; (2) **each line forms a closed loop**, passing through the magnet itself; (3) lines **never intersect** — a compass needle can point in only one direction; (4) lines behave like **stretched elastic cords always trying to shorten themselves**; (5) lines that are **parallel and in the same direction repel one another**.
concepts.detail: Property (4) explains why **unlike poles attract**: the flux lines running between two suspended magnets A and B behave as if in tension, pulling the magnets together. Property (5) explains why **like poles repel**: between two N poles (or two S poles) the lines are practically parallel and in the same direction, exerting lateral pressure that pushes the magnets apart. Keep these two mechanical pictures — tension along the line, pressure sideways — and most of machine behaviour follows.

concepts.term: Field due to an electric current (Oersted)
concepts.statement: **When a conductor carries an electric current, a magnetic field is produced around that conductor** — the discovery Hans Christian Oersted made in Copenhagen in 1820; viewed along a conductor carrying current away from us, the field is **clockwise** and the flux lines are concentric circles about the wire.
concepts.detail: Oersted placed a wire above a magnetic needle, in line with the needle’s normal direction: the needle deflected clockwise or anticlockwise depending on the current direction. The field shape is beautifully symmetric — circles centred on the wire — and its magnitude grows with current and falls with distance, a fact we make quantitative in Section 5.3 through the field strength $H$.

concepts.statement: A current flowing **towards** the observer is drawn as a **dot** (the approaching point of an arrow); a current flowing **away** is drawn as a **cross** (the departing tail feathers).
concepts.detail: This end-on convention is indispensable for three-dimensional geometry — conductors entering a page, coils seen along their axis, the rotor conductors of a machine. Combined with the screw rule it fixes the field sense instantly: a cross (departing current) seen from the observer’s side gives a clockwise field.

concepts.statement: Place a **corkscrew alongside the conductor**: in order that the screw may travel in the same direction as the current, it must be turned clockwise (viewed from behind the direction of travel); the magnetic field then circulates in that same **clockwise sense** around the conductor.
concepts.detail: The rule is a mechanical memory of the cross product hidden in the geometry — rotate the screw from the current direction into the field circulation. It works for any element of wire, straight or curved, because the local field is always a circle about the local current direction.

concepts.statement: **Grip the conductor with the right hand, thumb outstretched parallel to the conductor and pointing in the direction of the current; the fingers then point in the direction of the magnetic flux** around the conductor.
concepts.detail: The grip rule is the same physics as the screw rule with a hand instead of a tool. Its great value is the dual reading: applied to a coil, the fingers take the role of the current and the thumb that of the field — which is exactly what we need for the solenoid.

concepts.statement: A **solenoid** — a coil wound on a core — behaves like a magnet: wound on a steel rod and connected to a battery, the steel becomes magnetised and the assembly is an **electromagnet** whose field, inside the coil, is directed along the axis.
concepts.detail: Direction by screw rule: place the screw along the solenoid axis and turn it in the direction of the current — it travels in the direction of the field inside the solenoid. Direction by grip rule: grip the solenoid with the right hand, **fingers pointing in the (conventional) current direction; the thumb points along the internal field** — out of the end that is effectively the N pole. Reversing the winding sense, or the current, reverses the polarity; this is the actuator principle behind relays and contactors.

examples.title: Mapping a field with filings and compasses
examples.problem: A bar magnet rests on a table. Describe how steel filings and four compass needles reveal the shape and the direction of its field, and state what the experiment proves.

steps.label: Step 1: Lay out the apparatus
steps.text: Cover the magnet with a sheet of smooth cardboard and sprinkle steel filings uniformly over the sheet, then tap it gently. Each filing becomes a tiny induced magnet and turns along the local field.

steps.label: Step 2: Read the chains
steps.text: The filings set themselves in curved chains running between the poles — the classic picture of lines of magnetic flux. The chains are densest where the field is strongest, near the poles, and permeate the whole space above the magnet.

steps.label: Step 3: Place the compasses
steps.text: With four compass needles set where the chains run, each needle takes up a position with its axis coinciding with the corresponding chain of filings, N pole pointing along the dotted line from the magnet’s N pole towards its S pole, outside the magnet.

steps.label: Step 4: Close the loop mentally
steps.text: The lines are assumed to continue through the body of the magnet from S back to N, so every line forms a closed loop — characteristic (2) of lines of flux. The needles never point two ways at once, confirming that flux lines never intersect.

examples.result: The experiment yields a mental map — curved closed chains from N to S outside the magnet — but the lines themselves are an aid to thought introduced by Faraday, not physical objects.

examples.title: Polarity of a solenoid
examples.problem: A coil is wound on a steel rod and connected to a battery so that, viewed from the left-hand end, the current circulates clockwise at the top of each turn. Which end of the solenoid is the north-seeking end, and what happens if the battery connections are reversed?

steps.label: Step 1: Choose a rule
steps.text: Apply the right-hand grip rule to the coil: the fingers wrap in the direction of the (conventional) current and the outstretched thumb gives the direction of the internal field.

steps.label: Step 2: Wrap the hand
steps.text: With the current circulating clockwise as seen from the left, the fingers of the right hand curl clockwise when the thumb points to the right — so the internal field points to the right, towards the right-hand end.

steps.label: Step 3: Identify the poles
steps.text: The end from which the internal field emerges is the effective N pole: the right-hand end is the north-seeking end, the left-hand end the south-seeking end. The steel core, once magnetised by this field, reinforces the pattern — an electromagnet.

steps.label: Step 4: Reverse the battery
steps.text: Reversing the current reverses the internal field direction, so the ends swap polarity. This immediate electrical control of magnetism is precisely what a relay or a contactor exploits, and it distinguishes the electromagnet from the permanent magnet of Example 1 above.

examples.result: Right-hand end = N pole for the stated winding; reversing the battery swaps N and S. The screw rule gives the same verdict: a screw turned with the current travels along the internal field.

keyTakeaways: A magnetic field surrounds both permanent magnets and current-carrying conductors; the compass needle defines its direction at every point.
Lines of magnetic flux are imaginary (Faraday), form closed loops, never intersect, behave like stretched cords in tension, and repel when parallel and same-directed.
Tension along the lines explains attraction of unlike poles; lateral pressure between same-directed lines explains repulsion of like poles.
A current produces a circulating field (Oersted, 1820): clockwise when viewed along a departing current — dot means towards you, cross means away.
The right-hand screw rule and the grip rule convert any current direction into a field direction, and vice versa.
A solenoid concentrates its field along the axis; grip it with the right hand, fingers in the current sense, and the thumb points to the effective N pole.

quiz.q: Lines of magnetic flux are drawn through the body of a bar magnet. Which characteristic forbids two of these lines from crossing each other?
options: They are under tension, like stretched elastic cords
Each line forms a closed loop
A compass needle at any point can point in only one direction
Lines only exist in non-magnetic media such as air
quiz.explanation: If two lines intersected, a compass placed at the crossing point would need two directions at once — impossible, since the needle points along the local flux direction only. The tension and closed-loop properties are real too, but they are not the reason.

quiz.q: Viewed end-on, a conductor shows a cross (the tail feathers of an arrow). Looking along the conductor in the direction of the current, the magnetic field circulates:
quiz.explanation: A cross means the current departs from the observer. Looking along a departing current, the field is clockwise — exactly what the right-hand screw rule gives when the screw travels away from you.

quiz.q: Two identical suspended magnets are arranged so that their flux lines between them are parallel and point the same way. What happens, and which flux property explains it?
options: They attract — the lines are in tension
Nothing — parallel lines do not interact
They repel — same-directed parallel lines exert lateral pressure
quiz.explanation: Parallel, same-directed lines of flux behave as if they exert lateral pressure on one another, so the magnets are pushed apart. Between like poles this is what we observe; the tension picture belongs to unlike poles, where the lines run from one magnet to the other.

quiz.q: In the grip rule for a single straight conductor, which pairing is correct?
options: Thumb gives the field; fingers give the current
Fingers curl in the field direction; thumb points along the current
Thumb and fingers both give the current direction
Fingers point along the field lines; thumb gives the force on the wire
quiz.explanation: Grip the conductor with the right hand, thumb along the conventional current; the curled fingers show the direction of the magnetic flux circles. For a solenoid the roles swap: fingers follow the winding current, thumb gives the internal axial field.

quiz.q: A solenoid is gripped with the right hand so the fingers follow the current as seen from one end, and the thumb points away from that end. The end you are looking from is:
options: Undefined — the rule gives no polarity
quiz.explanation: The thumb points along the internal field, which emerges from the effective N pole at the far end. The end you are looking from is the one the field enters — the south-seeking end. Reversing the winding or the current would swap the two.

intro: Put a current-carrying wire into someone else’s magnetic field and Newton’s third law demands a force — the force every motor exploits. Move the wire instead, and the field fights back with an induced e.m.f. — the principle of every generator. This section quantifies both effects: $F = BIl$ for the force, Faraday’s law and Lenz’s law for the induced e.m.f., all with Hughes’s own worked numbers.
objectives: Compute the force on a current-carrying conductor with $F = BIl$ and find flux and flux density from $\Phi = BA$
Determine force directions with Fleming’s left-hand rule
Explain electromagnetic induction qualitatively from Faraday’s 1831 experiments
Derive and apply the flux-cutting e.m.f. $E = Blu$ and the rate-of-change forms $e = d\Phi/dt$ and $e = -N\,d\Phi/dt$
Use Fleming’s right-hand rule and Lenz’s law to fix the direction of an induced e.m.f.

concepts.statement: A conductor carrying a current at right angles to a magnetic field experiences a mechanical force **perpendicular to the plane of the conductor and the field**; by Newton’s third law the magnet feels an equal and opposite force.
concepts.detail: Hughes demonstrates it with a copper wire about 2 mm in diameter bent into a rectangular loop BC, its tapered ends dipping into mercury-filled cups so the loop is free to rotate. Passing about 5 A through the loop and bringing the N pole of a magnet near B makes the loop turn anticlockwise viewed from above; reversing the magnet (or the current) reverses the turn; reversing both leaves it unchanged. The one-piece-of-steel design proves the action belongs to the current, not to two magnets.

concepts.term: Magnetic flux density and the tesla
concepts.statement: The **magnetic flux density** $B$ is defined through the force law: a field in which a conductor carrying $1\ \text{A}$ at right angles experiences $1\ \text{N}$ per metre of length has $B = 1$ **tesla** (T). Equivalently, $1\ \text{T} = 1\ \text{Wb/m}^{2}$.
concepts.detail: With the force found to be proportional to current, flux density and the length at right angles to the field, the unit is fixed by this definition. Nikola Tesla (1857–1943), the Yugoslav-born inventor who emigrated to the USA in 1884 and patented two- and three-phase synchronous machines in 1888, gave the unit its name.

concepts.term: Force law F = BIl and flux Φ = BA
concepts.statement: For a conductor of length $l$ at right angles to a uniform field of density $B$, carrying current $I$:
concepts.detail: The full set of book relations is $$F = BIl\quad\text{(newtons)},$$ $$\Phi = BA\quad\text{(webers)},$$ $$B = \frac{\Phi}{A}\quad\text{(teslas)}.$$ The **weber** is the unit of magnetic flux, symbol $\Phi$ (Greek capital phi); flux permeates area $A$ measured in square metres. If the conductor is not perpendicular to the field, only the perpendicular component counts — Hughes’s Example 6.2 multiplies $\Phi$ by $\sin\theta$ when the coil plane is tilted. The symbol convention summary: $B$ in teslas, $\Phi$ in webers, $H$ (field strength, Section 5.3) in amperes per metre.

concepts.statement: Hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of the **left** hand mutually at right angles: point the **First** finger in the **Field** direction, the **seCond** finger in the **Current** direction, and the **thuMb** gives the direction of the **Mechanical force** on the conductor.
concepts.detail: The capital letters embedded in the words are the mnemonic: Field–First, Current–seCond, Motion–thuMb. Reverse either current or field alone and the force reverses; reverse both together and the force direction is unchanged — a check the book makes explicitly and one worth performing by hand.

concepts.statement: **When the magnetic flux linked with a circuit is varied, an e.m.f. is induced in that circuit**; its magnitude is proportional to the rate at which the flux through the circuit changes — Faraday’s great discovery of 1831.
concepts.detail: Two experiments anchor the idea. First, two coils A and C wound on a steel ring R: closing switch S in coil A’s battery circuit deflects galvanometer G one way, opening it deflects G the other way — nothing happens while the current is steady. Weeks later, a permanent magnet NS moved towards a coil C deflects G one way and, withdrawn, the other: relative motion of flux and coil is what matters. Either **flux cutting** a conductor or **flux linking** a coil induces an e.m.f. — the generator principle that supplies most of the electric current used in practice.

concepts.statement: For the **right** hand, again with thumb and two fingers mutually perpendicular: **First** finger in the direction of the **Flux**, thuMb in the direction of **Motion** of the conductor relative to the field, and the **sEcond** finger gives the direction of the induced **e.m.f.**
concepts.detail: The mnemonic is Field–First, Motion–thuMb, e.m.f.–sEcond. Hughes warns that the manipulation presents difficulty to many students and that fluency comes only with practice; if any two of the three are correctly applied, the third follows automatically. Left hand for motor (force from current), right hand for generator (e.m.f. from motion).

concepts.statement: The direction of an induced e.m.f. is always such that it tends to set up a current **opposing the motion or the change of flux** responsible for inducing that e.m.f.
concepts.detail: Enunciated in 1834 by the German physicist Heinrich Lenz, the law is energy conservation in disguise: motion can only be opposed if mechanical work is being done against the opposition, which is exactly the energy the induced current carries away. In Faraday’s ring experiment, when S is closed with the battery polarity shown, the ring flux grows clockwise; the current induced in C must circulate so as to try to produce an anticlockwise flux — from terminal X to Y through the coil — and that is also the direction of the induced e.m.f.

concepts.statement: A conductor of length $l$ moving at velocity $u$ at right angles across a field of density $B$ generates $E = Blu$ volts.
concepts.detail: The derivation is pure energy bookkeeping. Moving a length $l$ of conductor a distance $d$ through the gap requires work $B I l \cdot d$ joules against the electromagnetic force (from $F = BIl$). If the movement takes $t$ seconds at constant speed, the electrical energy generated is $EIt$ joules, so $EIt = B I l d$ and $$E = \frac{B l d}{t} = Blu.$$ But $Bld$ is the total flux $\Phi$ swept, so $E = \Phi/t$: **the e.m.f. equals the rate (Wb/s) at which the conductor cuts flux**. In differential form $e = d\Phi/dt$, which defines the weber: the flux which, cut at a uniform rate by a conductor in one second, generates an e.m.f. of one volt.

concepts.term: Flux linkages and the coil e.m.f.
concepts.statement: For a coil of $N$ turns whose flux changes, the average induced e.m.f. is the rate of change of **flux linkages**: $e = N\,d\Phi/dt$, with the flux linkage $\Psi = N\Phi$ measured in weber-turns.
concepts.detail: Flux linkage $\Psi = N\Phi$ is the product of flux (Wb) and linked turns — Hughes’s example: a coil of 20 turns with 0.1 Wb through it has linkages $0.1 \times 20 = 2$ weber-turns. Since each turn is cut by the changing flux, the instantaneous e.m.f. is $$e = \frac{d(N\Phi)}{dt} = -N\,\frac{d\Phi}{dt}.$$ The minus sign is Lenz’s law made algebraic (Hughes writes magnitudes with the direction rule separate, a convention we honour in worked examples). The weber, again: the flux which, linking a circuit of one turn, induces 1 V when reduced to zero at a uniform rate in 1 s.

examples.title: Force per metre on a heavy conductor (Hughes Example 6.1)
examples.problem: A conductor carries a current of 800 A at right angles to a magnetic field having a density of 0.5 T. Calculate the force on the conductor in newtons per metre length.

steps.label: Step 1: Select the law
steps.text: The force on a straight conductor perpendicular to a uniform field is $F = BIl$, with $B$ in teslas, $l$ in metres and $I$ in amperes.

steps.label: Step 2: Insert the numbers
steps.text: Take $l = 1$ m so the answer is force per metre: $F = 0.5\ [\text{T}] \times 1\ [\text{m}] \times 800\ [\text{A}]$.

steps.label: Step 3: Multiply
steps.text: $F = 400$ N per metre of conductor — about the weight of 40 kg on every metre, which is why heavy current-carrying busbars must be firmly clamped.

steps.label: Step 4: Sanity-check with the left hand
steps.text: Point the first finger of the left hand along the field and the second finger along the (given) current; the thumb confirms the force pushes the conductor sideways, perpendicular to both.

examples.result: The conductor experiences 400 N per metre length — the book’s exact figure from expression $F = BIl$.

examples.title: Flux through a tilted coil (Hughes Example 6.2)
examples.problem: A rectangular coil measuring 200 mm by 100 mm is mounted so it can rotate about the midpoints of its 100 mm sides, the axis of rotation being at right angles to a uniform field of flux density 0.05 T. Find (a) the maximum flux through the coil and its position, and (b) the flux when the 100 mm sides are inclined at 45 degrees to the flux direction.

steps.label: Step 1: Maximum-flux position
steps.text: Flux passes most copiously when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the flux — the coil face fully faces the field.

steps.label: Step 2: Compute the maximum
steps.text: With $A = 200 \times 10^{-3} \times 100 \times 10^{-3} = 0.02\ \text{m}^{2}$, $\Phi = BA = 0.05 \times 0.02 = 1 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{Wb}$ — one milliveber.

steps.label: Step 3: Tilt to 45 degrees
steps.text: Rotating the coil so the 100 mm sides are at $45^{\circ}$ reduces the effective area by $\sin 45^{\circ}$: $\Phi = BA\sin\theta = (1 \times 10^{-3})(0.7071)$.

steps.label: Step 4: State both answers
steps.text: (a) $\Phi_{\max} = 1$ mWb with the coil plane at right angles to the flux; (b) $\Phi = 0.71 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb $= 0.71$ mWb — Hughes’s rounded value.

examples.result: Maximum flux 1 mWb; at 45 degrees the linkage has fallen to about 0.71 mWb — the sine factor that makes a rotating machine generate alternating e.m.f.

examples.title: E.m.f. induced by reversing flux (Hughes Example 6.4)
examples.problem: A magnetic flux of 400 mWb passing through a coil of 1200 turns is reversed in 0.1 s. Calculate the average value of the e.m.f. induced in the coil.

steps.label: Step 1: Find the flux change
steps.text: Reversal means the flux must fall from 400 mWb to zero and then grow to 400 mWb the other way: the total change in the original direction is $2 \times 400 = 800$ mWb.

steps.label: Step 2: Write the average-e.m.f. relation
steps.text: From the flux-linkage law, the average e.m.f. is $E = N\Phi/t$ where $\Phi$ is the total change of flux — here 800 mWb in $t = 0.1$ s through $N = 1200$ turns.

steps.label: Step 3: Substitute and compute
steps.text: $E = \dfrac{1200 \times 800 \times 10^{-6}}{0.1} = \dfrac{0.96}{0.1}$; the division gives $9.6$ V.

steps.label: Step 4: Check the direction
steps.text: While the original flux decays, Lenz’s law makes the induced e.m.f. drive current that would sustain the old flux; through the reversal it then opposes the new direction — the e.m.f. keeps one sense throughout the 0.1 s.

examples.result: The average induced e.m.f. is 9.6 V — Hughes’s answer. (For scale: a car axle 2 m long at 80 km/h in the Earth’s 40-microtesla vertical field cuts $40\times10^{-6} \times 2 \times 22.2 \approx 1776\times10^{-6}$ Wb per second, generating only about 1.78 mV.)

keyTakeaways: A current at right angles to a field feels a force $F = BIl$ perpendicular to both; the tesla is defined by this law (1 N per metre on 1 A).
Flux and flux density are related by $\Phi = BA$; one tesla is one weber per square metre.
Fleming’s left-hand rule (Field–First, Current–seCond, Motion–thuMb) gives the force direction; left hand for motors.
Faraday (1831): varying the flux linked with a circuit induces an e.m.f. proportional to the rate of change — by flux cutting or flux linking.
Fleming’s right-hand rule gives the induced-e.m.f. direction from flux and motion; right hand for generators.
Lenz’s law: the induced current opposes the change producing it — the minus sign in $e = -N\,d\Phi/dt$.
Flux-cutting gives $E = Blu$; in general $e = d\Phi/dt$ for one turn and $e = N\,d\Phi/dt$ for a coil, with flux linkage $\Psi = N\Phi$ in weber-turns.

quiz.q: A conductor carries 200 A at right angles to a uniform field of 0.3 T (Hughes Exercise 6.1). The force per metre of conductor is:
quiz.explanation: $F = BIl = 0.3 \times 1 \times 200 = 60$ N per metre. The same law gives the 400 N of Example 6.1 (0.5 T, 800 A).

quiz.q: In Fleming’s left-hand rule, the first finger points along which quantity?
quiz.explanation: First finger — Field; seCond finger — Current; thuMb — Mechanical force. The right-hand version replaces the force with the induced e.m.f.: First — Flux, thuMb — Motion, sEcond — e.m.f.

quiz.q: A magnet is pushed towards a coil and the coil’s galvanometer deflects. By Lenz’s law, the current circulates so as to:
options: Reinforce the increasing flux through the coil
Follow the direction of the magnet’s motion
Produce a flux opposing the increase
quiz.explanation: The induced current always sets up a flux opposing the change that caused it — here opposing the growth of flux through the coil. The reaction pushes the coil away from the approaching magnet, consistent with Newton’s third law, and guarantees the mechanical work done appears as electrical energy.

quiz.q: A conductor of active length 0.5 m moves at 4 m/s perpendicular to a field of 0.25 T. The generated e.m.f. is:
quiz.explanation: $E = Blu = 0.25 \times 0.5 \times 4 = 0.5$ V. The same product $Bld/t$ came from equating mechanical work $BlId$ to electrical energy $EIt$ in Hughes’s derivation.

quiz.q: A coil of 1500 turns carries a flux of 2.5 mWb which is reversed in 0.2 s (Hughes Exercise 6.12). The average induced e.m.f. is:
quiz.explanation: Reversal changes the flux by $2 \times 2.5 = 5$ mWb, so $E = N\,\Delta\Phi/t = 1500 \times 5 \times 10^{-3}/0.2 = 37.5$ V — the doubling from reversal is the trap, exactly as in Example 6.4 (800 mWb, 1200 turns, 0.1 s, 9.6 V).

quiz.q: A straight conductor of active length 0.40 m carries 50 A at right angles to a uniform field of density 0.80 T. The mechanical force on the conductor is:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $B = 0.80$ T, $I = 50$ A, active length $l = 0.40$ m, right-angle orientation. Step 2 — Governing law: $F = BIl$ for the perpendicular case, directed normal to both field and current. Step 3 — Algebra: $F = 0.80 \times 50 \times 0.40 = 16$ N. Step 4 — Sanity check: force per metre is $40$ N, scaling by $0.40$ m gives newtons, and reversing either field or current reverses the push. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 8 N halves the length, 32 N doubles the field, and 64 N compounds both errors. Step 6 — Conclude: the conductor feels 16 N.

intro: Because every flux line closes on itself, a magnetic field can be guided the way an electric circuit guides current: give the flux a steel loop to travel in and you have a magnetic circuit. This section builds the complete analogy — magnetomotive force drives flux through reluctance, exactly as e.m.f. drives current through resistance — and then shows where the analogy honestly breaks down. Every number comes from Hughes’s wooden-ring, mild-steel-ring and three-part-series examples.
objectives: Define magnetomotive force $F = IN$ and magnetic field strength $H = IN/l$ with their units
Derive the permeability of free space $\mu_0$ from the definition of the ampere and use $B = \mu_0\mu_r H$
Compute reluctance $S = l/\mu A$ and combine series reluctances
Apply the magnetic ‘Ohm’s law’ $\Phi = F/S = IN/S$ to ring cores with and without airgaps
State the respects in which the magnetic–electric analogy fails

concepts.statement: The complete closed path followed by any group of magnetic flux lines is a **magnetic circuit**; the simplest practical form is a steel ring of circular cross-section, called a **toroid**, wound uniformly with $N$ turns.
concepts.detail: Because each flux line forms a closed loop (Section 5.1), a toroid traps nearly all the flux in its steel — flux that leaves the steel and returns through air is *leakage*, the magnetic analogue of a short-circuited detour and one of the reasons the electric analogy is imperfect.

concepts.statement: The **magnetomotive force** of a coil of $N$ turns carrying current $I$ is the total current linked with the magnetic circuit, $F = IN$, expressed in amperes (descriptively, ampere-turns).
concepts.detail: $$F = IN \quad \text{(amperes, or ampere-turns)}.$$ The descriptive unit is the ampere-turn (At), and since the turn is dimensionless the SI unit of m.m.f. is simply the ampere. Just as e.m.f. (volts) drives current around an electric circuit, m.m.f. drives flux around a magnetic circuit — the first pillar of the analogy.

concepts.statement: For a homogeneous magnetic circuit of uniform cross-section and mean length $l$, the m.m.f. per metre of path is the **magnetic field strength** $H = IN/l$, measured in amperes per metre.
concepts.detail: $$H = \frac{IN}{l} = \frac{F}{l} \quad \text{(amperes per metre, A/m)}.$$ Field strength is m.m.f. gradient — the magnetic counterpart of electric field strength $E$ in volts per metre. Note carefully: $H$ measures the *cause* set up by the current; how much flux density $B$ that cause produces depends entirely on the material, through the permeability.

concepts.statement: The ratio $B/H$ in a vacuum (or, to very high accuracy, in air, water, oil, wood, copper or any non-magnetic material) is the **permeability of free space**:
concepts.detail: $$\mu_0 = \frac{B}{H} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{H/m}.$$ Hughes derives the value from the definition of the ampere (Chapter 2): a long straight conductor carrying 1 A produces, on a concentric path of radius 1 m (length $2\pi$ m), $H = 1/(2\pi)$ A/m, while a parallel conductor there feels $B = 2 \times 10^{-7}$ T — hence $\mu_0 = B/H = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ H/m. The unit (henry per metre) is justified in Chapter 6, where $L = \mu N^{2}A/l$.

concepts.term: Maxwell’s link to the speed of light
concepts.statement: Combining the electric and magnetic constants of free space gives
concepts.detail: $$c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}} \approx 2.998 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s},$$ the measured velocity of light. James Clerk Maxwell found this relation in 1865 and predicted radio waves from it some twenty years before Heinrich Hertz demonstrated them — the moment electromagnetism and optics merged into one theory. $\varepsilon_0$, the permittivity of free space, is the electrostatic twin we met in Chapter 4.

concepts.statement: The **relative permeability** $\mu_r$ of a material is the ratio of the flux density it produces to the flux density a vacuum would produce under the same $H$; the **absolute permeability** is $\mu = \mu_0\mu_r$, so that
concepts.detail: $$B = \mu_0 \mu_r H = \mu H.$$ For air $\mu_r = 1$; inserting a steel core in a coil makes the flux hundreds of times larger. Ferromagnetic materials — those containing iron, cobalt, nickel or gadolinium — can reach enormous values: some nickel–iron alloys show relative permeabilities up to about 100,000. Crucially, $\mu_r$ is **not constant**: it varies with $H$, which is why Section 5.4 needs graphs rather than formulas for real materials.

concepts.statement: The **reluctance** $S$ of a uniform magnetic circuit of length $l$, cross-section $A$ and permeability $\mu = \mu_0\mu_r$ is $S = l/(\mu_0\mu_r A)$, measured in amperes per weber.
concepts.detail: $$S = \frac{F}{\Phi} = \frac{l}{\mu_0 \mu_r A} \quad \text{(amperes per weber, A/Wb)}.$$ Compare Chapter 2’s resistivity law $R = l/\sigma A$ written with conductivity: length up means more opposition, area up means less, and permeability plays exactly the role of conductivity. Dividing $\Phi = BA$ by $F = Hl$ produces $S$ in one line — the derivation Hughes performs on his expressions [7.9] and [7.10].

concepts.statement: Magnetomotive force equals flux times reluctance: $F = \Phi S$, or equivalently $NI = \Phi S$.
concepts.detail: $$F = \Phi S \quad\text{or}\quad NI = \Phi S.$$ The dictionary runs: m.m.f. $F$ (A) ↔ e.m.f. $E$ (V); flux $\Phi$ (Wb) ↔ current $I$ (A); permeability ↔ conductivity; reluctance $S$ (A/Wb) ↔ resistance $R$ (Ω); field strength $H$ (A/m) ↔ electric field strength $E$ (V/m); flux density $B$ (T) ↔ current density $J$. Series and parallel laws of resistors carry over to reluctances — Hughes’s three-part Example 7.4 simply adds them.

concepts.statement: Three differences spoil the magnetic Ohm’s law: **reluctance dissipates no energy** (whereas resistance loses power at $I^{2}R$), **flux leaks** through air where current normally does not, and **permeability is not constant**.
concepts.detail: Because $\mu_r$ falls with saturation, doubling the m.m.f. does not double the flux — in an electric circuit, by contrast, $\sigma$ stays constant over a wide range of current density until the conductor grows hot. There is a magnetic counterpart of potential difference (the magnetic potential difference across a section, $F = \Phi S$), which lets Kirchhoff’s laws be applied to magnetic circuits: around a closed loop the sum of m.m.f.s equals the sum of $\Phi S$ drops, and at a junction flux in equals flux out — the basis of Example 7.4.

examples.title: Wooden ring: H, B and Φ (Hughes Example 7.1)
examples.problem: A coil of 200 turns is wound uniformly over a wooden ring having a mean circumference of 600 mm and a uniform cross-sectional area of 500 mm squared. If the current through the coil is 4.0 A, calculate (a) the magnetic field strength, (b) the flux density, and (c) the total flux.

steps.label: Step 1: Field strength
steps.text: The mean circumference is the path length, $l = 0.6$ m: $H = IN/l = (4.0 \times 200)/0.6 = 1333$ A/m (Hughes rounds to 1330 A/m). Wood is non-magnetic, so this is the whole story for the cause.

steps.label: Step 2: Flux density
steps.text: For a non-magnetic circuit $B = \mu_0 H = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1333 = 0.001675$ T, i.e. about 1.68 mT — barely a few times the Earth’s field, despite 800 ampere-turns.

steps.label: Step 3: Total flux
steps.text: With $A = 500 \times 10^{-6}$ m squared, $\Phi = BA = 0.001675 \times 500 \times 10^{-6} = 0.838 \times 10^{-6}$ Wb, i.e. roughly 0.84 microweber.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret
steps.text: A wooden (or air) core is honest but feeble: $\mu_r = 1$ caps the flux. The very same 200 turns on a mild-steel ring (Example 7.3 below) multiply the flux density a thousandfold.

examples.result: $H \approx 1330$ A/m, $B \approx 1.675$ mT, $\Phi \approx 0.84\ \mu\text{Wb}$ — the wooden-ring benchmark against which every steel result is judged.

examples.title: Mild-steel ring: reluctance and magnetising current (Hughes Example 7.3)
examples.problem: A mild-steel ring having a cross-sectional area of 500 mm squared and a mean circumference of 400 mm has a coil of 200 turns wound uniformly around it. Calculate (a) the reluctance of the ring and (b) the current required to produce a flux of 800 microwebers in the ring.

steps.label: Step 1: Find the working flux density
steps.text: $B = \Phi/A = 800 \times 10^{-6} / 500 \times 10^{-6} = 1.6$ T — deep in the region where the steel’s $B$–$H$ curve (Section 5.4) is bending over.

steps.label: Step 2: Read the permeability from the curve
steps.text: From the $\mu_r$-versus-$B$ characteristic for mild steel, $\mu_r \approx 380$ at 1.6 T.

steps.label: Step 3: Compute the reluctance
steps.text: $S = \dfrac{l}{\mu_0 \mu_r A} = \dfrac{0.4}{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(380)(500\times10^{-6})} \approx 1.68 \times 10^{6}$ A/Wb.

steps.label: Step 4: Find the m.m.f. and current
steps.text: $F = \Phi S = 800 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.68 \times 10^{6} \approx 1342$ A, so $I = F/N = 1342/200 \approx 6.7$ A.

steps.label: Step 5: Cross-check the short way
steps.text: Alternatively $H = B/(\mu_0\mu_r) = 1.6/(4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 380) \approx 3350$ A/m, m.m.f. $= Hl = 3350 \times 0.4 \approx 1340$ A — same current, 6.7 A.

examples.result: $S \approx 1.68 \times 10^{6}$ A/Wb and the coil needs about 6.7 A. Compare Example 7.1: the same geometry in wood would have needed an astronomical m.m.f. — steel’s $\mu_r \approx 380$ does the work of 380 turns in every one.

examples.title: Three parts in series, one of them air (Hughes Example 7.4)
examples.problem: A magnetic circuit comprises three parts in series, each of uniform cross-sectional area: (a) 80 mm long, 50 mm squared; (b) 60 mm long, 90 mm squared; (c) an airgap 0.5 mm long, 150 mm squared. A coil of 4000 turns is wound on part (b), and the flux density in the airgap is 0.30 T. Assuming all the flux passes through the given circuit and $\mu_r = 1300$, estimate the coil current.

steps.label: Step 1: Common flux
steps.text: Series means one flux everywhere: $\Phi = B_c A_c = 0.3 \times 150 \times 10^{-6} = 0.45 \times 10^{-4}$ Wb.

steps.label: Step 2: m.m.f. for part (a)
steps.text: $F_a = \Phi S_a = \Phi \cdot l_a/(\mu_0\mu_r A_a) = \dfrac{0.45\times10^{-4} \times 80\times10^{-3}}{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(1300)(50\times10^{-6})} \approx 44.1$ ampere-turns.

steps.label: Step 3: m.m.f. for part (b)
steps.text: Same flux through 60 mm of 90 mm squared steel: $F_b = \dfrac{0.45\times10^{-4} \times 60\times10^{-3}}{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(1300)(90\times10^{-6})} \approx 18.4$ ampere-turns.

steps.label: Step 4: m.m.f. for the airgap
steps.text: Air has $\mu_r = 1$, so even half a millimetre dominates: $F_c = \dfrac{0.45\times10^{-4} \times 0.5\times10^{-3}}{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(1)(150\times10^{-6})} \approx 119.3$ ampere-turns.

steps.label: Step 5: Kirchhoff for magnetic circuits
steps.text: The total m.m.f. is the sum of the drops: $F = 44.1 + 18.4 + 119.3 = 181.8$ At, and the current is $I = F/N = 181.8/4000 \approx 45.4$ mA.

examples.result: Roughly 45.4 mA of coil current — and nearly two-thirds of every ampere-turn is spent on the 0.5 mm airgap, the design fact that makes airgaps both useful (they linearise a choke) and expensive.

keyTakeaways: M.m.f. $F = IN$ (amperes, or ampere-turns); field strength $H = IN/l$ is the m.m.f. per metre of path, and the closed flux loop it drives is the magnetic circuit (toroid: the cleanest case).
$\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H/m follows from the definition of the ampere, and $1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} = c$ (Maxwell, 1865).
Materials enter through $B = \mu_0 \mu_r H$; ferromagnetics reach $\mu_r$ of thousands (up to about 100,000 for some nickel–iron alloys), but $\mu_r$ varies with $H$.
Reluctance $S = l/(\mu_0\mu_r A)$ in A/Wb behaves like resistance $l/\sigma A$; series and parallel combinations carry over.
Magnetic Ohm’s law $F = \Phi S$ maps m.m.f.→e.m.f., flux→current, and lets Kirchhoff’s laws analyse multi-part cores.
The analogy fails in three ways: reluctance is lossless, flux leaks, and permeability is not constant — saturation makes flux grow sub-proportionally with m.m.f.
Airgaps dominate series magnetic circuits: 0.5 mm of air in Example 7.4 demanded 119.3 of the total 181.8 ampere-turns.

quiz.q: A coil of 500 turns carries 2 A. The magnetomotive force is:
quiz.explanation: $F = IN = 500 \times 2 = 1000$ A (ampere-turns). The SI unit is the ampere because the turn is dimensionless, but At is a helpful descriptive unit.

quiz.q: Hughes derives $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H/m from which experimental fact?
options: The force of $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N per metre between parallel 1 A conductors 1 m apart
Oersted’s deflection of a compass needle
quiz.explanation: From the definition of the ampere, a 1 A conductor produces $B = 2\times10^{-7}$ T at 1 m radius, where $H = 1/(2\pi)$ A/m; the ratio $B/H$ is $4\pi\times10^{-7}$ H/m. Maxwell’s speed-of-light relation is a consequence, not the source.

quiz.q: Doubling the mean circumference of a toroidal core, keeping material, area, turns and current the same, does what to the reluctance?
quiz.explanation: $S = l/(\mu_0\mu_r A)$ is proportional to path length, so doubling $l$ doubles $S$ — and halves the flux, since $\Phi = IN/S$. Area and permeability act in the opposite sense.

quiz.q: In the dictionary between electric and magnetic circuits, reluctance $S$ corresponds to which electrical quantity?
quiz.explanation: M.m.f. ↔ e.m.f., flux ↔ current, reluctance ↔ resistance (with $\mu$ playing conductivity’s role). But remember the honest caveats: reluctance dissipates no power, and it is not constant once the core saturates.

quiz.q: A steel magnetic circuit has 5 cm squared cross-section and 25 cm length, wound with 120 turns (Hughes Exercise 7.2). With 1.5 A the flux is 0.3 mWb. The magnetic field strength is:
quiz.explanation: $H = IN/l = 120 \times 1.5/0.25 = 720$ A/m. (The same exercise’s 5 A case gives $H = 2400$ A/m with $B = 1.2$ T — the two points already show $\mu_r$ falling from about 660 to about 400 as the steel hardens towards saturation.)

quiz.q: A toroidal core has mean length 0.50 m and cross-section 400 mm squared, wound with 300 turns carrying 2.0 A. The relative permeability is 800. The core flux is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $l = 0.50$ m, $A = 400 \times 10^{-6}$ m squared, $N = 300$, $I = 2.0$ A, $\mu_{r} = 800$. Step 2 — Governing chain: field strength $H = \frac{NI}{l}$, density $B = \mu_{0}\mu_{r}H$, flux $\Phi = BA$. Step 3 — Algebra: $H = \frac{600}{0.50} = 1200$ A per m; $B = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 800 \times 1200 \approx 1.206$ T; $\Phi = 1.206 \times 400 \times 10^{-6} \approx 482 \times 10^{-6}$ Wb. Step 4 — Sanity check: $1.2$ T sits below deep saturation, steel multiplies the air flux by about $800$, and the microweber scale suits the small area. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 0.12 mWb drops the permeability, 1.20 mWb mistakes area by a decade, and 4.80 mWb compounds both. Step 6 — Conclude: the flux is about 0.48 mWb.

intro: Because relative permeability refuses to stay constant, the magnetic-circuit designer lives off graphs: the $B$–$H$ magnetisation curve, its saturation knee, and the loop it traces when magnetisation cycles — hysteresis. Hughes measures the curve two classical ways (fluxmeter and ballistic galvanometer) and closes the chapter with a dictionary between the electromagnetic and electrostatic quantities you met in Chapter 4.
objectives: Describe the shape of the $B$–$H$ magnetisation curve and the physical meaning of saturation
Explain the fluxmeter and ballistic-galvanometer methods for measuring the $B$–$H$ characteristic of a ring specimen
Define the hysteresis loop, residual flux density and coercive force
Relate the area of the hysteresis loop to the energy dissipated per cycle
Map electromagnetic quantities onto their electrostatic counterparts

concepts.statement: The **magnetisation characteristic** of a material is the graph of flux density $B$ against field strength $H$; for soft magnetic materials it rises steeply at first, then bends over into **saturation** as $H$ grows.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Fig. 7.3 plots the curves for silicon steel, mild steel, cast iron, Mumetal and ferrite over the range $H \approx 1000$ to $10{,}000$ A/m: silicon steel reaches about 2.0 T at the top end, mild steel about 1.75 T, cast iron and Mumetal flatten earlier near 0.5–0.75 T. The corresponding $\mu_r$-versus-$H$ and $\mu_r$-versus-$B$ curves (Figs 7.4 and 7.5) show that permeability peaks at intermediate magnetisation — Mumetal approaching values near 120,000 at low $B$ — and falls on both sides.

concepts.statement: Saturation is the flattening of the $B$–$H$ curve at high $H$: beyond the knee, large increases of m.m.f. buy only small increases of flux density, because the material’s domains are already essentially aligned.
concepts.detail: A saturated core is the magnetic equivalent of a used-up amplifier: Hughes’s mild-steel ring of Example 7.3 needed only modest excitation to reach 1.6 T, yet pushing to 1.63 T in his Chapter 8 example required five times the field strength. Saturation is why real machine cores are kept near or below the knee, and why an airgap — which cannot saturate — can actually raise a coil’s effective inductance over a wide current swing.

concepts.term: Measuring the curve with a fluxmeter
concepts.statement: A steel ring of uniform cross-section is uniformly wound with a magnetising coil P (eliminating leakage) and a search coil S feeds a **fluxmeter**; reversing the current in P and reading the deflection $\theta$ gives $B$ at that $H$.
concepts.detail: The fluxmeter is a special permanent-magnet moving-coil instrument whose coil is suspended by ligaments exerting negligible control, so its deflection is proportional to the change of flux-linkages. The magnetising current is set with resistor $R_1$, and the reversing switch RS is thrown several times to bring the steel into a *cyclic* condition before measuring. If the flux reverses from $\Phi$ to $-\Phi$, the change of linkages with coil S (turns $N_S$) is $2\Phi N_S = c\theta$ with $c$ the fluxmeter constant, so $$B = \frac{c\theta}{2 A N_S}.$$ Repeating for a range of currents plots the whole $B$–$H$ curve point by point.

concepts.statement: A **ballistic galvanometer** has its coil wound on a non-metallic former with a high series resistance, so the first deflection or ‘throw’ is proportional to the charge passed when the discharge time is short compared with one oscillation.
concepts.detail: With galvanometer constant $k$ (coulombs per division) and total secondary-circuit resistance $R$, the average induced current $2\Phi N_S/(tR)$ flowing for time $t$ passes charge $2\Phi N_S/R$, so $k\theta = 2\Phi N_S/R$ and $$\Phi = \frac{k\theta R}{2N_S}.$$ The same ring geometry and reversal trick serve; only the detector differs. Exercise 7.15 gives a real calibration: a 2000-turn coil on a non-magnetic toroid, 1 m mean circumference, 500 mm squared area, and a 100-turn search coil in a 5.1 kΩ circuit — reversing 2.5 A gives 100 divisions.

concepts.statement: **Hysteresis** — from the Greek for ‘lagging’ — is the property that $B$ does not follow $H$ back down the magnetisation curve: when $H$ is reduced to zero, the specimen retains a **residual (remanent) flux density**, and an m.m.f. of opposite sign — the **coercive force** — is needed to bring $B$ to zero.
concepts.detail: Cycling $H$ between equal positive and negative limits traces a closed **hysteresis loop** whose shape is set by the material. Hughes meets the phenomenon through the ferromagnetic-cored inductor: reducing the current from OC to OA (his Fig. 8.7) lets the flux fall only from CD to AE, so the effective inductance is reduced compared with the initial magnetisation curve — the same lag, seen from the circuit side. Hard magnetic materials (wide loop, large coercivity) make permanent magnets; soft materials (narrow loop) make efficient cores.

concepts.statement: The energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle of magnetisation equals the **area of the hysteresis loop** in a $B$–$H$ plot.
concepts.detail: Work done per unit volume over one excursion is $\int H\,dB$ — geometrically the area swept. Over a complete cycle the two legs do not cancel, and the loop area is left as heat in the iron. A core cycled at frequency $f$ therefore dissipates roughly (loop area) $\times$ (volume) $\times$ $f$ of hysteresis power, one reason transformers (Chapter 8’s alternating flux, cycle after cycle) use narrow-loop silicon steel and thin laminations.

concepts.statement: Hughes’s Table 7.2 pairs the two field theories: electric flux $Q$ ↔ magnetic flux $\Phi$; electric flux density $D$ ↔ magnetic flux density $B$; electric field strength $E$ ↔ magnetic field strength $H$; e.m.f. ↔ m.m.f.; $\varepsilon_0$ ↔ $\mu_0$; $\varepsilon_r$ ↔ $\mu_r$.
concepts.detail: The structural relation $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r = D/E$ of Chapter 4 stands exactly beside $\mu = \mu_0\mu_r = B/H$ of this chapter — two parallel stories about how a medium modifies a field. One asymmetry is worth savouring: free magnetic charge does not exist, so flux lines always close on themselves, whereas electric flux lines begin and end on charges.

concepts.statement: Because $\mu_r$ is field-dependent, engineering calculations read $\mu_r$ from the $\mu_r$–$B$ (or $\mu_r$–$H$) characteristic at the working point, then apply the magnetic-circuit algebra of Section 5.3.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Example 7.3 reads $\mu_r \approx 380$ for mild steel at $B = 1.6$ T; his Chapter 8 examples read $B = 1.13$ T at $H = 1000$ A/m and $B = 1.63$ T at $H = 5000$ A/m from the same Fig. 7.3 — implying $\mu_r ≈ 900$ and $\mu_r \approx 260$ respectively, a three-and-a-half-fold drop across the knee. Always quote the working point with any value of $\mu_r$.

examples.title: Reading the B–H curve (after Hughes Example 8.3)
examples.problem: A ring of mild-steel stampings has a mean circumference of 400 mm and a cross-sectional area of 500 mm squared wound with 200 turns. Using Hughes’s Fig. 7.3, find the flux density and the implied relative permeability for magnetising currents of (a) 2 A and (b) 10 A.

steps.label: Step 1: Convert current to field strength
steps.text: (a) $H = IN/l = 200 \times 2/0.4 = 1000$ A/m. (b) $H = 200 \times 10/0.4 = 5000$ A/m — five times the excitation.

steps.label: Step 2: Read B from the mild-steel curve
steps.text: From Fig. 7.3: at $H = 1000$ A/m, $B \approx 1.13$ T; at $H = 5000$ A/m, $B \approx 1.63$ T. The curve is visibly flattening — saturation has begun.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret the fivefold error
steps.text: Five times the m.m.f. bought only 1.63/1.13 ≈ 1.44 times the flux density, and $\mu_r$ fell by a factor of about 3.5. Any $L = \mu N^2A/l$ computed at low current (Chapter 6) overestimates the inductance at high current.

examples.result: 1.13 T at 1000 A/m ($\mu_r \approx 900$); 1.63 T at 5000 A/m ($\mu_r \approx 260$) — the numbers Hughes himself uses for this same ring in his Chapter 8 inductance example.

examples.title: A fluxmeter determination (Hughes Exercise 7.12)
examples.problem: A coil P of 300 turns is uniformly wound on a ferromagnetic ring of cross-sectional area 500 mm squared and mean diameter 400 mm. Another coil S of 30 turns is connected to a fluxmeter of constant 200 microweber-turns per division. When a current of 1.5 A through P is reversed, the fluxmeter deflects 96 divisions. Calculate the flux density in the ring and the magnetic field strength.

steps.label: Step 1: Apply the reversal relation
steps.text: Reversal swings the flux from $\Phi$ to $-\Phi$, so the change of linkages with coil S is $2\Phi N_S$. The fluxmeter reads the same change as $c\theta$.

steps.label: Step 2: Solve for the flux
steps.text: $\Phi = \dfrac{c\theta}{2N_S} = \dfrac{200 \times 10^{-6} \times 96}{2 \times 30} = 320\ \mu\text{Wb}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Compute the field strength
steps.text: Mean circumference $l = \pi \times 0.4 = 1.257$ m, so $H = IN/l = 300 \times 1.5/1.257 \approx 358$ A/m — one point of the ring’s $B$–$H$ curve, obtained without ever measuring flux directly.

examples.result: $B = 0.64$ T at $H \approx 358$ A/m; repeating the reversal at other currents traces the whole magnetisation curve.

keyTakeaways: The $B$–$H$ curve of a soft magnetic material rises steeply, bends at the knee, and saturates: past the knee, m.m.f. buys little extra $B$.
Permeability is a working-point property: mild steel shows $\mu_r \approx 900$ at 1.13 T but only about 260 at 1.63 T.
The fluxmeter method measures $B$ by reversing the magnetising current: $B = c\theta/(2AN_S)$; the ballistic galvanometer variant uses the charge throw, $\Phi = k\theta R/(2N_S)$.
Specimens are ‘cycled’ by repeated reversals before measurement so the readings are repeatable.
Hysteresis makes $B$ lag $H$: residual flux density survives zero $H$, and coercive force is needed to erase it; the loop area is the energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle.
Hard materials (wide loops) are permanent magnets; soft materials (narrow loops) are transformer and machine cores.
The electrostatic dictionary of Chapter 4 pairs $Q, D, E, \varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_r$ with $\Phi, B, H, \mu_0, \mu_r$ — but magnetic flux lines always close, having no charge to start from.

quiz.q: In the fluxmeter method, why is the magnetising current reversed rather than merely switched off?
options: To protect the fluxmeter from overload
Because the change of linkages $2\Phi N_S$ gives a readable deflection proportional to the flux
To keep the ring cool during the measurement
Because a unidirectional current cannot produce flux in steel
quiz.explanation: The fluxmeter responds to change of flux-linkages. Swinging the flux from $\Phi$ to $-\Phi$ doubles the available signal and, by cycling the specimen first, ensures the reading corresponds to the symmetric (cyclic) magnetisation state.

quiz.q: A specimen retains flux density when the magnetising field is reduced to zero. This flux density is called the:
quiz.explanation: Residual flux density is what is left of $B$ at $H = 0$ on the falling branch of the hysteresis loop. The coercive force is the reverse $H$ needed to bring $B$ back to zero.

quiz.q: The energy dissipated per unit volume in cycling a magnetic material once around its hysteresis loop equals:
options: The slope of the B–H curve at the origin
The area enclosed by the loop
Half the product $BH$ at the tip
The permeability times the loop height
quiz.explanation: Work per unit volume is $\int H\,dB$; around a full cycle the rising and falling legs differ by exactly the enclosed area, which is dissipated as heat. Cycling at frequency $f$ multiplies the loss by $f$.

quiz.q: In Hughes’s electromagnetic–electrostatic comparison, the counterpart of the magnetic field strength $H$ is:
quiz.explanation: The pairing is $\Phi \leftrightarrow Q$, $B \leftrightarrow D$, $H \leftrightarrow E$, m.m.f. ↔ e.m.f., with $B/H = \mu_0\mu_r$ standing beside $D/E = \varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r$ from Chapter 4.

quiz.q: A mild-steel core operates at $B = 1.6$ T, where its curve gives $\mu_r \approx 380$. If the excitation is increased until $B = 1.75$ T, the relative permeability will most likely:
quiz.explanation: Approaching saturation, each extra ampere-turn yields less extra $B$, so $B/H$ — and hence $\mu_r$ — keeps falling. Hughes’s curve family shows mild steel’s permeability well past its peak by 1.6 T (the same behaviour as the 900 → 260 drop computed from Fig. 7.3).

intro: Having built magnetic circuits in Chapter 5, we now ask how good a job a coil does at storing magnetic energy — and the answer is a single number called inductance, measured in henrys. Hughes defines it two equivalent ways (volts per ampere-per-second, and flux-linkages per ampere), Nilsson turns the coil into a circuit element with $v = L\,di/dt$, and the section closes with two coils on one core: mutual inductance, the dot convention and the series-aiding/opposing arithmetic.
objectives: Define the henry and apply $e = L\,di/dt$ to compute induced e.m.f.s
Express inductance as flux-linkages per ampere, $L = N\Phi/I$, and as $L = \mu_0\mu_r N^2 A/l$
Explain why the inductance of a ferromagnetic-cored coil varies with current, and define incremental inductance
State the terminal behaviour of an ideal inductor: short circuit for dc, continuous current, stored energy $\tfrac{1}{2}LI^2$
Determine mutual-inductance voltages with the dot convention and combine coupled coils in series

concepts.statement: A circuit in which a change of current is accompanied by a change of flux, and therefore by an induced e.m.f., is **inductive**; a circuit arranged so that its conductor’s magnetising effects cancel is practically **non-inductive**.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s demonstration: a coil $L$ (many turns on a steel core) and a resistor $R$ in parallel, switched across a battery. The resistor current $I_2$ rises almost instantly; the coil current $i_1$ takes an appreciable time, eventually reaching $I_1 = V/(	ext{coil resistance})$. On opening the switch, the coil current keeps flowing — through $R$, in the reverse direction — decaying slowly; without $R$ there is considerable **arcing at the switch**, which is why suddenly breaking the full excitation of an electromagnet (the field winding of a d.c. machine) is dangerous. To make a non-inductive resistor — as in resistance boxes — the wire is **bent back on itself** so the magnetising effect of one conductor is neutralised by its neighbour; the doubled wire can then be coiled without raising the inductance.

concepts.term: The henry and the inductor voltage law
concepts.statement: A circuit has an inductance of **1 henry (H)** if an e.m.f. of 1 volt is induced when the current varies uniformly at the rate of 1 ampere per second; with passive sign convention the inductor’s terminal voltage is $v = L\,di/dt$.
concepts.detail: $$v = L\,\frac{di}{dt}.$$ Joseph Henry (1797–1878), the American physicist, discovered electromagnetic induction independently within a year of Faraday’s 1831 discovery in Britain. Two schools of thought exist about the sign: Hughes writes the induced e.m.f. as a positive volt drop $v_L = +L\,di/dt$, whereas the International Electrotechnical Commission prefers $e = -L\,di/dt$ so that Lenz’s law is built into the algebra; both give $v = Ri + L\,di/dt$ for the series circuit. Nilsson’s convention (used throughout the rest of this chapter) is $v = L\,di/dt$ with the current reference in the direction of the voltage drop.

concepts.statement: Equating $e = L\,di/dt$ with Faraday’s $e = N\,d\Phi/dt$ for a constant-reluctance circuit gives $L = N\Phi/I$ henrys — flux-linkages per ampere.
concepts.detail: $$L = \frac{N\Phi}{I} \quad \text{(henrys)}.$$ The alternative definition of the unit follows immediately: a coil has 1 H of inductance if a current of 1 A through it produces a flux-linkage of 1 weber-turn. Example 8.2 makes the link concrete: 300 turns on a non-magnetic core with $L = 10$ mH carry 5 A, so $\Phi = LI/N = 10\times10^{-3} \times 5/300 = 167\ \mu\text{Wb}$.

concepts.term: Factors determining the inductance of a coil
concepts.statement: For a coil of $N$ turns on a uniform ring of length $l$, area $A$ and permeability $\mu$, the inductance is $L = \mu_0\mu_rAN^{2}/l$ henrys.
concepts.detail: $$L = \frac{\mu_0 \mu_r A N^{2}}{l}.$$ Inductance is proportional to the **square of the turns**, proportional to the cross-sectional area, and inversely proportional to the length of the magnetic circuit — four turns where two grew doubles it fourfold. The $N^2$ also fixes the units of permeability: since $L$ is henrys, $\mu_0$ must be henrys per metre, matching the $4\pi\times10^{-7}$ H/m we met in Chapter 5.

concepts.statement: Because $\mu_r$ of a closed ferromagnetic circuit is not constant, the inductance of a steel-cored coil **varies with the current**, rising to a maximum and then falling as the core saturates; over a small current swing the effective value is the **incremental inductance** $L_d = N\,d\Phi/di$.
concepts.detail: $$L_d = N\,\frac{d\Phi}{di}.$$ Hughes’s Example 8.5: a laminated steel ring with 200 turns whose flux moves between 760 and 800 microwebers as the current swings 5 to 7 A has $L_d = 200\times(40\times10^{-6})/2 = 0.004$ H. Two practical fixes follow: a **short radial airgap** (unsaturable) can actually *increase* the effective inductance over a wide current range, and **compressed magnetic dust cores** (ferrite or nickel–iron particles in shellac) keep the flux-linkages-per-ampere nearly constant — the technique used for loading coils on telephone lines.

concepts.term: The inductor as a circuit element and its energy
concepts.statement: Ideal inductor terminal behaviour: with constant current the voltage is zero (**short circuit for dc**); the current **cannot change instantaneously** (a finite change in zero time would require an infinite voltage); and the stored magnetic energy is $w = \tfrac{1}{2}Li^{2}$ joules.
concepts.detail: When someone opens the switch on a real inductive circuit the current initially continues — across the air gap, a phenomenon called **arcing**, exactly as Hughes’s switch experiment showed. The inverse relation integrates the voltage: $$i(t) = \frac{1}{L}\int_{t_0}^{t} v\,d\tau + i(t_0),$$ so the current remembers its entire voltage history — it is the state variable of the inductor, just as charge (voltage) is the state variable of the capacitor of Chapter 4. With $p = vi = Li\,di/dt$, integrating $Li\,di$ fills the energy bank: $$w = \tfrac{1}{2}Li^{2} \quad \text{(joules)}.$$ Nilsson’s Example 6.3 traces the bookkeeping with $i = 10te^{-5t}$ in a 100 mH coil: 27.07 mJ goes in up to the current peak at $t = 0.2$ s, and the same 27.07 mJ comes back out afterwards — a lossless, passive element. Note the dual truth: inductor **voltage** can jump instantaneously even though the current cannot (Example 6.1 has $v$ stepping at $t=0$ while $i$ stays continuous). When the circuit is broken, this energy must go somewhere: heat in a parallel resistor, or the arc at the switch.

concepts.term: Mutual inductance and the dot convention
concepts.statement: Two coils have a **mutual inductance of 1 henry** if a current in one varying at 1 A/s induces 1 V in the other; the induced voltage is $M\,di_1/dt$, and with the dot convention: **when the reference current enters the dotted terminal of one coil, the voltage it induces in the other is positive at that coil’s dotted terminal**.
concepts.detail: In circuit terms each coil carries two voltages: the self-induced $L_1\,di_1/dt$ plus (or minus) the mutually induced $M\,di_2/dt$. Hughes’s form of the convention: dots at ends 1 and 3 mean the m.m.f.s are **additive** (mutual inductance positive) when *both* currents enter — or both leave — the dotted ends, and in opposition when one enters and one leaves. Dots are determined physically by the right-hand rule applied to both windings, or experimentally with a battery, switch and centre-zero voltmeter: an upscale kick when the switch closes marks the voltmeter’s positive terminal as dotted.

concepts.term: Coupling coefficient and energy of coupled coils
concepts.statement: Because energy storage cannot be negative, mutual inductance obeys $M = k\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ with $0 \le k \le 1$.
concepts.detail: $$M = k\sqrt{L_1 L_2}, \quad 0 \le k \le 1,$$ where $k$ is the **coupling coefficient**: $k = 0$ for no common flux, $k \approx 1$ when essentially all flux links both coils (high-permeance magnetic materials). The total stored energy is $$w = \tfrac{1}{2}L_1i_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}L_2i_2^2 \pm Mi_1i_2,$$ plus when both currents enter dotted terminals. For a non-magnetic core the reciprocity $M_{12} = M_{21} = M$ follows because the stored energy cannot depend on the order in which the currents were established — Hughes shows it by equating the two energies, Nilsson by the equality of permeances.

concepts.term: Coupled coils in series: aiding and opposing
concepts.statement: Two series coils with cumulative (series-aiding) flux have $L_1 = L_A + L_B + 2M$; differentially coupled (series-opposing), $L_2 = L_A + L_B - 2M$; hence
concepts.detail: $$M = \frac{L_1 - L_2}{4}.$$ The $\pm 2M$ appears because each coil carries its own induced e.m.f. plus a mutual term from the other — and the mutual terms reinforce in the cumulative connection and cancel partially in the differential one. This one-quarter-of-the-difference relation is the standard laboratory measurement of $M$. (Nilsson’s mesh-current form of the same physics: a coupled pair contributes $L_1\,di_1/dt \pm M\,di_2/dt$ in each loop equation.)

examples.title: Flux, e.m.f. and reversal (Hughes Example 8.2)
examples.problem: A coil of 300 turns, wound on a core of non-magnetic material, has an inductance of 10 mH. Calculate (a) the flux produced by a current of 5 A, and (b) the average value of the e.m.f. induced when a current of 5 A is reversed in 8 ms.

steps.label: Step 1: Flux from the linkage definition
Step 2: What reversal does to the flux
steps.text: The flux falls from 167 microwebers to zero and then grows to 167 microwebers in the reverse direction: the total change is $\Delta\Phi = 334\ \mu$Wb.

steps.label: Step 3: Average e.m.f. from flux change
steps.text: Rate of change of flux $= 334\times10^{-6}/8\times10^{-3} = 0.04175$ Wb/s, so $E = N\,d\Phi/dt = 300 \times 0.04175 = 12.5$ V.

steps.label: Step 4: Cross-check via the current
steps.text: The current swings from 5 A to −5 A in 8 ms: $di/dt = 10/0.008 = 1250$ A/s, and $e = L\,di/dt = 0.01 \times 1250 = 12.5$ V — identical, as the two definitions of $L$ promise.

examples.result: $\Phi = 167\ \mu$Wb and the average induced e.m.f. is 12.5 V — Hughes’s two answers, agreeing by both routes.

examples.title: Steel core versus air core (Hughes Examples 8.3 and 8.4)
examples.problem: A ring of mild-steel stampings has a mean circumference of 400 mm, a cross-sectional area of 500 mm squared and 200 turns. Using the $B$–$H$ curve of Chapter 5, find the inductance for a reversal of magnetising current of (a) 2 A and (b) 10 A. Then (c) compute the inductance of the same winding on a non-magnetic core.

steps.label: Step 1: Field strength at 2 A
steps.text: $H = IN/l = 200 \times 2/0.4 = 1000$ A/m; the mild-steel curve of Fig. 7.3 gives $B = 1.13$ T.

steps.label: Step 3: Field strength at 10 A
steps.text: $H = 200 \times 10/0.4 = 5000$ A/m; the curve is saturating and gives only $B = 1.63$ T.

steps.label: Step 4: Inductance at 10 A
steps.text: $\Phi = 1.63 \times 0.0005 = 0.000815$ Wb, so $L = (0.000815 \times 200)/10 = 16.3$ mH — five times the current, less than a third of the inductance.

steps.label: Step 5: The air-core comparison
steps.text: With $\mu_r = 1$: $L = \mu_0N^2A/l = 4\pi\times10^{-7} \times 200^{2} \times 0.0005/0.4 = 62.8\ \mu$H — three orders of magnitude below the steel-core value at modest current.

examples.result: Steel core: 56.6 mH at 2 A, 16.3 mH at 10 A; air core: 62.8 microhenrys — the comparison that shows why a large inductance demands a ferromagnetic core, and why its value must be quoted with the current.

examples.title: Series-aiding versus series-opposing (Hughes Example 8.13)
examples.problem: When two coils are connected in series, their effective inductance is found to be 10.0 H. When the connections to one coil are reversed, the effective inductance is 6.0 H. If the coefficient of coupling is 0.6, calculate the self-inductance of each coil and the mutual inductance.

steps.label: Step 1: Add and subtract the measurements
steps.text: Cumulative: $L_A + L_B + 2M = 10.0$ H; differential: $L_A + L_B - 2M = 6.0$ H. Adding: $L_A + L_B = 8.0$ H; subtracting: $2M = 4.0$ H so $M = 1.0$ H.

steps.label: Step 2: Bring in the coupling
steps.text: With $k = 0.6$: $2k\sqrt{L_AL_B} = 2M = 4.0$, so $\sqrt{L_AL_B} = 4.0/1.2 = 3.333$ and $L_AL_B = 11.11$ H squared. Hughes’s quadratic form: $0 = L_B^2 - 8L_B + 2.78$.

steps.label: Step 3: Solve the quadratic
steps.text: $L_B = [8 \pm \sqrt{64 - 11.12}]/2 = 7.63$ H or 0.37 H; correspondingly $L_A = 0.37$ H or 7.63 H.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify with the original data
steps.text: Check: $L_A + L_B + 2k\sqrt{L_AL_B} = 8.0 + 2(0.6)(3.333) = 8.0 + 4.0 = 10.0$ H, and the differential connection gives $8.0 - 4.0 = 6.0$ H. Both measurements are reproduced exactly.

examples.result: The coils are 7.63 H and 0.37 H with $M = 1.0$ H — Hughes’s figures, obtained from nothing but the two series measurements and $k$.

keyTakeaways: One henry: 1 V induced per ampere-per-second of current change; $v = L\,di/dt$ with the passive sign convention.
Equivalently $L = N\Phi/I$: flux-linkages per ampere, one weber-turn per ampere.
For a uniform core $L = \mu_0\mu_r N^2A/l$ — turns-squared, area, inverse length.

Ferromagnetic cores multiply $L$ enormously (56.6 mH versus 62.8 microhenrys in Hughes’s paired examples) but make it current-dependent; incremental inductance $L_d = N\,d\Phi/di$ covers small swings, and an airgap or dust core linearises the coil.
An ideal inductor is a dc short with a continuous current and continuous energy bookkeeping $w = \tfrac{1}{2}Li^2$; its voltage can jump, its current cannot — hence switch arcing.

Mutual inductance $M$ (henrys) couples coils through shared flux; the dot convention fixes the sign of the $M\,di/dt$ terms, and reciprocity plus energy give $M_{12} = M_{21} = M$, $M = k\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ with $0 \le k \le 1$, and $w = \tfrac{1}{2}L_1i_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}L_2i_2^2 \pm Mi_1i_2$.
Series coils: $L = L_A + L_B \pm 2M$, so measuring both connections yields $M = (L_\text{aiding} - L_\text{opposing})/4$.

quiz.q: A 0.5 H coil’s current falls from 5 A to 2 A in 0.05 s (Hughes Example 8.1). The mean induced e.m.f. is:
quiz.explanation: Average $di/dt = (2-5)/0.05 = -60$ A/s, so $e = 0.5 \times (-60) = -30$ V — negative because it acts against the decrease, in the direction of the original current.

quiz.q: Doubling only the number of turns on an air-cored ring (same geometry) multiplies its inductance by:
quiz.explanation: $L = \mu_0N^2A/l$ is proportional to $N^2$, so twice the turns gives four times the inductance — doubling turns ‘double-counts’, once as extra flux and once as extra linkage.

quiz.q: A coil wound on a closed ferromagnetic ring carries a slowly increasing current. As the core passes from the linear region towards saturation, the inductance:
options: Rises to a maximum and then falls
quiz.explanation: Because $\mu_r$ itself rises then falls with $H$, Hughes’s Fig. 8.6 shows the steel-cored coil’s inductance peaking and declining as the current grows — exactly the 56.6 mH to 16.3 mH drop across 2 A to 10 A in Example 8.3.

quiz.q: Two identical coils share a core with $k = 1$ (no leakage). If $L_1 = 0.283$ H and $L_2 = 0.552$ H (Hughes Example 8.12’s ring), the mutual inductance is about:
quiz.explanation: $M = k\sqrt{L_1L_2} = \sqrt{0.283 \times 0.552} = 0.395$ H. Hughes’s ring: mean radius 170 mm, 800 mm squared cross-section, $\mu_r = 1200$, reluctance $8.85\times10^{5}$ A/Wb, giving exactly these numbers from $L = N^2/S$ and $M = N_1N_2/S$.

quiz.q: Nilsson’s coupled coils have $M = 40$ mH, $L_1 = 25$ mH, $L_2 = 100$ mH (Example 6.9). The coupling coefficient is:
quiz.explanation: $k = M/\sqrt{L_1L_2} = 0.04/\sqrt{0.025 \times 0.1} = 0.04/0.05 = 0.8$. The same example shows that with $k$ raised to 1 ($M = 50$ mH), a current of $i_2 = -5$ A against $i_1 = 10$ A leaves zero net stored energy.

quiz.q: Two coupled coils have self-inductances 0.40 H and 0.60 H with mutual inductance 0.30 H. Connected in series aiding, the equivalent inductance is:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $L_{1} = 0.40$ H, $L_{2} = 0.60$ H, $M = 0.30$ H, fluxes aiding. Step 2 — Governing relation: series aiding adds both mutual terms so $L_{aid} = L_{1} + L_{2} + 2M$, while opposing subtracts them. Step 3 — Algebra: $L_{aid} = 0.40 + 0.60 + 2 \times 0.30 = 1.60$ H; the opposing value would be $0.40$ H. Step 4 — Sanity check: aiding must exceed the plain sum $1.00$ H, opposing must fall below it, and $M \le \sqrt{L_{1}L_{2}} \approx 0.49$ H confirms tight but legal coupling. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 1.00 H omits coupling, 0.70 H adds only one $M$, and 0.40 H is the opposing result. Step 6 — Conclude: aiding gives 1.60 H.

intro: Switch a resistive circuit and the current answers instantly; switch an inductive one and it answers on its own clock. The clock is the time constant $T = L/R$, and the answer is always a rising or falling exponential — the Helmholtz equation. Hughes derives growth and decay separately, then runs two-position switch examples in which the second transient starts before the first has finished; Nilsson’s natural-response treatment adds the energy accounting.
objectives: Set up and solve the growth equation $V = Ri + L\,di/dt$ to obtain $i = I(1 - e^{-t/T})$
Define the time constant $T = L/R$ and interpret its 63.2 per cent and initial-slope meanings
Derive the decay form $i = Ie^{-t/T}$ for a short-circuited LR circuit
Analyse transients in LR networks, including switching faster than five time constants
Compute energy dissipated during natural response from $w = \tfrac{1}{2}LI_0^2$

concepts.term: Growth of current: the graphical picture
concepts.statement: In the growth curve $i(t)$, the tangent drawn at any point reaches the final current $I$ in exactly $T = L/R$ seconds; the initial-tangent construction builds the whole curve step by step.
concepts.detail: At any instant during growth, $V = Ri + L\,di/dt$ and $V = RI$, so the rate of rise is $(I-i)R/L$: if the current kept growing at its present rate it would reach $I$ in $L/R$ seconds. Hughes’s graphical construction (Example 8.6): draw the final-current line, mark off $MN = T$, join the origin to $N$; from any point on that line repeat, and the envelope of the construction lines is the growth curve.

concepts.statement: The **time constant** of an LR circuit is $T = L/R$ seconds.
concepts.detail: $$T = \frac{L}{R}\ \text{(seconds)}.$$ The greater the inductance and the smaller the resistance, the longer the current takes to settle. Two readings of $T$: after one time constant the current has reached $1 - e^{-1} = 0.632$ of its final value (63.2 per cent); and $T$ is the time the *initial* rate of rise $V/L$ would need to reach $I = V/R$ — since $I/T = V/L$. The decay of a released LR circuit obeys the same $T$, its initial rate of fall being $-I/T = -RI/L$.

concepts.term: Analysis of growth: the Helmholtz equation
concepts.statement: Integrating $V = Ri + L\,di/dt$ from zero initial current gives the **Helmholtz equation** $i = I(1 - e^{-t/T})$.
concepts.detail: $$i = I\left(1 - e^{-Rt/L}\right) = I\left(1 - e^{-t/T}\right),$$ the **Helmholtz equation**. The derivation separates variables: $R\,dt/L = di/(I-i)$, integrates to $Rt/L = -\ln(I-i) + \ln I$, and exponentiates. Immediately after switch-on, $i = 0$ and the full supply voltage appears across $L$ — the initial rate of change of current is simply $V/L$, with the resistance as yet uninvolved.

concepts.statement: Short-circuiting an LR circuit that carries steady current $I$ (the external voltage now zero) gives $i = Ie^{-t/T}$.
concepts.detail: $$i = Ie^{-Rt/L} = Ie^{-t/T}.$$ With $0 = Ri + L\,di/dt$ the induced e.m.f. now acts *in the direction of the current*, opposing its decrease — Hughes’s Figure 8.12 arrangement, where a resistor $r$ protects the battery and the switch S shorts the coil onto itself. After one time constant the current has fallen to 36.8 per cent of $I$; after about five, it is within 1 per cent of zero.

concepts.term: Natural response of an RL circuit (Nilsson)
concepts.statement: Released from initial current $I_0$ through resistance $R$, the inductor current is $i(t) = I_0e^{-t/\tau}$ with $\tau = L/R$.
concepts.detail: $$i(t) = I_0e^{-t/\tau}, \quad \tau = L/R,$$ derived from $L\,di/dt + Ri = 0$. The continuity of inductor current, $i(0^-) = i(0^+) = I_0$, is what fixes the initial condition — analyse the circuit *before* switching with the inductor as a short circuit, and everything after follows. Nilsson’s four-step method: find $I_0$ from the pre-switch circuit; find $R$ seen by the inductor after switching; write $i(t)$; then derive any other current or voltage by resistive circuit analysis.

concepts.term: Energy accounting in the natural response
concepts.statement: All the energy initially stored in the inductor, $\tfrac{1}{2}LI_0^2$, is eventually dissipated as heat in the resistances of the decay circuit — distributed between them in a way computable by integrating $i^2R$.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s Example 7.1: a 2 H inductor released at 20 A into a network whose equivalent resistance is 10 ohms dissipates 256 J of its 400 J in one particular 10-ohm branch — exactly 64 per cent — the rest going to the other resistors. The exponential integral $\int_0^\infty I_0^2e^{-2t/\tau}R\,dt = \tfrac{1}{2}LI_0^2$ closed-forms the bookkeeping.

concepts.statement: When switching actions follow one another, compare their spacing with **five time constants**: if the interval between switchings exceeds $5T$ the first transient may be considered finished; if not, the second transient starts from the still-moving current.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Example 8.8 vs 8.9: the same circuit switched to its decay position at $t = 100$ ms (ten time constants of the growth phase, current fully settled at 1 A) behaves completely differently from the switch moved at $t = 10$ ms (one time constant in, current only 0.632 A). Pulse-driven networks — digital drivers, chopper circuits — live in precisely this regime.

concepts.statement: Moving a switch mid-transient changes the resistance the inductor sees, so the time constant changes and a **new exponential starts from the current at that instant** — the current itself is continuous.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Example 8.10 wraps the inductor’s supply network in a Norton equivalent (resistance 7.5 ohms, current 0.33 A) before applying the growth formula, then on the second switch position recomputes $T$ from the new resistance. The recipe — Thévenise what the inductor sees, per interval — is exactly the general method that Section 6.3 formalises.

examples.title: Growth numbers for a switched coil (Hughes Examples 8.6 and 8.7)
examples.problem: A coil having a resistance of 4 ohms and a constant inductance of 2 H is switched across a 20 V d.c. supply. Determine (a) the time constant, (b) the final value of the current, and (c) the value of the current 1.0 s after the switch is closed.

steps.label: Step 1: Time constant
steps.text: $T = L/R = 2/4 = 0.5$ s — the growth curve’s tangent construction uses exactly this interval, marked off repeatedly from the origin in Hughes’s Fig. 8.10.

steps.label: Step 2: Final current
steps.text: The inductor is a short circuit once steady: $I = V/R = 20/4 = 5.0$ A.

steps.label: Step 3: Current at 1.0 s
steps.text: Two time constants have passed: $i = I(1 - e^{-t/T}) = 5(1 - e^{-2})$.

steps.label: Step 4: Evaluate
steps.text: With $e^{-2} = 0.1353$, $i = 5(0.8647) = 4.32$ A — 86.5 per cent of the way to 5 A, with 1.35 per cent of a further gap closing every fraction of a time constant.

examples.result: $T = 0.5$ s, $I = 5$ A, $i(1\,\text{s}) = 4.32$ A — Hughes’s figures, with 63.2 per cent (3.16 A) reached at $t = 0.5$ s.

examples.title: Two switchings, two time constants (Hughes Examples 8.8 and 8.9)
examples.problem: A 10 V supply feeds a 10-ohm resistor $r$ and a 0.1 H inductor $L$ through a two-position switch: in position 1 the source drives the inductor through $r$ alone, and position 2 reconnects the inductor into a loop with a 15-ohm resistor $R$ so that the decay path is $r$ in series with $R$ (Hughes’s Fig. 8.14 network). Find the inductor-current expressions and the voltage across $R$ if the switch moves to position 2 (a) at $t = 100$ ms and (b) at $t = 10$ ms.

steps.label: Step 1: Growth phase (both cases)
steps.text: Position 1: $T_1 = L/R_1 = 0.1/10 = 10$ ms and the final current is $10/10 = 1$ A, so $i_1 = 1(1 - e^{-t/10\times10^{-3}})$ A.

steps.label: Step 2: Switching at 100 ms
steps.text: Ten time constants have elapsed — the transient is long finished and $i = 1$ A when the switch moves. Position 2: $T_2 = L/(R_1 + R_2) = 0.1/25 = 4$ ms, so $i_2 = e^{-t/4\times10^{-3}}$ A.

steps.label: Step 3: Voltage across R in the decay
steps.text: The current keeps flowing the same way through $R$, so the volt drop is negative relative to the marked arrow: $v_R = -15e^{-t/4\times10^{-3}}$ V — a 15 V kick that decays.

steps.label: Step 4: Switching at 10 ms instead
steps.text: Now the switch moves after one time constant: $i = 1 - e^{-1} = 0.632$ A. The decay starts from there: $i_2 = 0.632e^{-t/4\times10^{-3}}$ A — a visibly smaller, equally fast transient, because the inductor’s current is continuous even when the switch is not.

examples.result: Early switch: $i_2 = 0.632\,e^{-t/4\ \text{ms}}$ A; late switch: $i_2 = e^{-t/4\ \text{ms}}$ A — identical decay law, different starting height, exactly Hughes’s Example 8.9 versus 8.8.

examples.title: Natural response with an energy audit (Nilsson Example 7.1)
examples.problem: In Nilsson’s Fig. 7.6 circuit the switch opens at $t = 0$ after being closed a long time. The 2 H inductor carries 20 A at switching, and for $t \ge 0$ it discharges through an equivalent resistance of 10 ohms (a 2-ohm resistor in series with 40 ohms in parallel with 10 ohms). Find $i_L(t)$, the current and voltage in the 40-ohm branch, and the percentage of the stored energy dissipated in the 10-ohm resistor.

steps.label: Step 1: Initial current
