The capacitor must furnish $$Q_{C} = P\left(\tan\phi_{\mathrm{old}} - \tan\phi_{\mathrm{new}}\right) \quad \text{vars},$$ and since $Q_{C} = -\omega C V_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}$, the required capacitance follows directly.
concepts.detail: The active power is unchanged by correction — only the var balance moves. Hughes’s Example 13.7 shows both targets: for a load drawing 400 var inductive from 100 V at 50 Hz, unity needs $X_{C} = 100^{2}/400 = 25\ \Omega$ ($C = 127\ \mu\mathrm{F}$), while correcting only to 0.96 lagging needs $Q_{C} = 400 - 800\tan 16.3^\circ = 166\ \mathrm{var}$, a mere $C = 53\ \mu\mathrm{F}$. Correction is rarely taken to unity in practice because the cost of correction equipment must be balanced against the savings in electricity charges.

concepts.statement: In Hughes’s Example 13.6, a generator supplying 300 kW at 0.6 lagging is delivering $300/0.6 = 500\ \mathrm{kVA}$. Raise the power factor to unity and the same kilovolt-ampere loading delivers 500 kW — an extra **200 kW** of salable power from the same machine, the same conductors and the same fuel.
concepts.detail: This is the entire economic argument for correction. The generator winding, the transformer and the supply cable are all heated by the current they carry; the customer is billed only for watts. Everything a utility does with capacitors, synchronous condensers and pf-penalizing tariffs exists to close that gap.

examples.title: From power triangle to load impedance (Nilsson Example 10.4)
examples.problem: An electrical load operates at 240 V(rms) and absorbs an average power of 8 kW at a lagging power factor of 0.8. Calculate (a) the complex power of the load and (b) the impedance of the load.

steps.label: Step 1: Apparent power
steps.text: Because the power factor is lagging the load is inductive and $Q$ is positive. From $P = S\cos\theta$: $S = 8000/0.8 = 10{,}000 = 10\ \mathrm{kVA}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Reactive power
steps.text: Since $\cos\theta = 0.8$, $\sin\theta = 0.6$, so $Q = S\sin\theta = 10{,}000 \times 0.6 = 6\ \mathrm{kvar}$ and $S = 8 + j6\ \mathrm{kVA}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Line current
steps.text: From $P = V I_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos\theta$: $I_{\mathrm{rms}} = 8000/(240 \times 0.8) = 41.67\ \mathrm{A}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Load impedance
steps.text: The impedance angle equals the power factor angle, $\theta = \cos^{-1}(0.8) = 36.87^\circ$, and $|Z| = V/I = 240/41.67 = 5.76\ \Omega$, so $Z = 5.76\angle 36.87^\circ = 4.608 + j3.456\ \Omega$.

examples.result: Two numbers — 8 kW and 0.8 lagging at 240 V — fully determine the load: 41.67 A(rms) through $4.608 + j3.456\ \Omega$, absorbing $8 + j6$ kVA.

examples.title: Correcting a motor with a 127 μF capacitor (Hughes Examples 13.4 and 13.5)
examples.problem: A single-phase motor operating off a 400 V, 50 Hz supply develops 10 kW at an efficiency of 84 per cent and a power factor of 0.7 lagging. First find the input apparent power, the line current and its active and reactive components; then find the capacitance that must be connected in parallel to raise the supply power factor to 0.9 lagging.

steps.label: Step 1: Input volt-amperes
steps.text: Efficiency $=$ output$/({VI\cos\phi})$, so $0.84 = 10\,000/(V I \times 0.7)$ gives $VI = 17\,000\ \mathrm{VA} = 17\ \mathrm{kVA}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Motor current and its components
steps.text: $I = 17\,000/400 = 42.5\ \mathrm{A}$. Active component $42.5 \times 0.7 = 29.75\ \mathrm{A}$; with $\sin\phi = \sqrt{1 - 0.7^{2}} = 0.714$, reactive component $42.5 \times 0.714 = 30.4\ \mathrm{A}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Reactive power
steps.text: $Q = 400 \times 30.35/1000 = 12.1\ \mathrm{kvar}$ inductive.

steps.label: Step 4: Target supply current
steps.text: The capacitor does not change the motor’s 29.75 A active component, so the new supply current is $I = 29.75/0.9 = 33.06\ \mathrm{A}$, whose reactive component is $33.06\sqrt{1 - 0.9^{2}} = 33.06 \times 0.436 = 14.4\ \mathrm{A}$.

examples.result: A 127 μF capacitor in parallel drops the supply current from 42.5 A to 33.1 A without altering either the current or the power taken by the motor — an economy in the size of generating plant and in the cross-sectional area of the supply cable.

examples.title: Two loads, one line, and a 424 μF capacitor (Nilsson Example 10.7)
examples.problem: Two loads are fed from a 250 V(rms) source through a line whose resistance is 0.05 Ω. Load 1 absorbs 8 kW at a leading power factor of 0.8; Load 2 absorbs 20 kVA at a lagging power factor of 0.6. Find the combined power factor, the line current and the line loss; then compute the capacitor that corrects the power factor to 1 and the new line loss.

steps.label: Step 1: Complex power of each load
steps.text: $S_{1} = 8000 - j6000\ \mathrm{VA}$ (leading: $8000 \times 0.6$ vars, capacitive) and $S_{2} = 12{,}000 + j16{,}000\ \mathrm{VA}$ (lagging: $20\,\mathrm{kVA} \times 0.8$ vars, inductive).

steps.label: Step 2: Combine and find the line current
steps.text: $S = 20{,}000 + j10{,}000\ \mathrm{VA}$, so $I_{s}^{*} = S/V = 80 + j40$ and $I_{s} = 80 - j40 = 89.44\angle -26.57^\circ\ \mathrm{A}$; the combined power factor is $\cos 26.57^\circ = 0.8944$ lagging.

steps.label: Step 3: Line loss at 0.8944 power factor
steps.text: $P_{\mathrm{line}} = (89.44)^{2}(0.05) = 400\ \mathrm{W}$ — the source must supply 20,400 W even though the loads use only 20,000 W.

steps.label: Step 4: Size the capacitor
steps.text: Correcting to unity requires the capacitor to furnish the net 10 kvar: $X = V^{2}/Q = 250^{2}/(-10{,}000) = -6.25\ \Omega$. The source operates at 60 Hz, so $\omega = 2\pi(60) = 376.99\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ and $C = -1/(\omega X) = 1/(376.99 \times 6.25) = 424.4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$.

steps.label: Step 5: Line loss after correction
steps.text: Now $I_{s} = 20{,}000/250 = 80\ \mathrm{A}$ and $P_{\mathrm{line}} = (80)^{2}(0.05) = 320\ \mathrm{W}$ — the loss falls by 20 percent, and the power supplied totals 20,320 W.

examples.result: One 424.4 μF capacitor converts a 0.8944-lagging pair of loads into a unity-power-factor load: current falls from 89.44 A to 80 A and the line loss from 400 W to 320 W with the loads none the wiser.

keyTakeaways: Complex power $S = P + jQ$ in volt-amperes; from rms phasors, $S = V_{\mathrm{rms}} I_{\mathrm{rms}}^{*}$, or $\frac{1}{2}VI^{*}$ with amplitude phasors.
The power triangle sides and angle satisfy $|S|^{2} = P^{2} + Q^{2}$ and $\tan\theta = Q/P$; any two of the four quantities determine the rest.
Impedance shortcuts: $P = I_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}R$, $Q = I_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}X$, $P = V_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}/R$, $Q = V_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}/X$ — reactance signs and all.
Parallel loads: watts and vars add algebraically; volt-amperes add as phasors, never arithmetically.
A lagging load is corrected by a parallel capacitor that furnishes $P(\tan\phi_{\mathrm{old}} - \tan\phi_{\mathrm{new}})$ vars; the active power is untouched.
Correction rarely goes to unity: the cost of capacitors is balanced against tariff savings, as Hughes’s 53 μF versus 127 μF comparison makes concrete.
Line loss scales with $I^{2}$, so raising a power factor pays twice — in released kilovolt-amperes and in reduced conductor heating.

quiz.q: A load absorbs 8 kW at 0.8 lagging from a 240 V(rms) supply. Its complex power is:
quiz.explanation: Lagging means $Q$ is positive. $|S| = P/\cos\theta = 8/0.8 = 10\ \mathrm{kVA}$ and $Q = 10 \times 0.6 = 6\ \mathrm{kvar}$, so $S = 8 + j6\ \mathrm{kVA}$.

quiz.q: Two loads operate in parallel. Which statement about combining them is correct?
options: Both the total watts and the total volt-amperes are the sums of the individual values
Watts add algebraically, vars add algebraically, but volt-amperes do not add arithmetically
Only the reactive powers can simply be added, since they share the same axis
None of the three quantities can be summed directly
quiz.explanation: Watts and vars are resolved along the common real and imaginary axes, so they add algebraically (vars with sign: inductive positive, capacitive negative). Each load’s volt-amperes point at its own power factor angle, so they add as phasors — which is why the resultant triangle must be constructed before $|S|$ is known.

quiz.q: In Hughes’s motor example, the 42.5 A motor current at 0.7 lagging contains an active component of:
options: 42.5 A, because the whole current does work
12.1 A, the part that produces 12.1 kvar
quiz.explanation: The active component is $I\cos\phi = 42.5 \times 0.7 = 29.75\ \mathrm{A}$; the quadrature component $I\sin\phi = 42.5 \times 0.714 = 30.4\ \mathrm{A}$ produces the 12.1 kvar of reactive power and no watts.

quiz.q: Why is power-factor correction in practice rarely taken all the way to unity?
options: A unity power factor would overload the correction capacitor
Because the supply authority forbids unity operation
Because the cost of the correction equipment must be balanced against the resulting savings in electricity charges
Because a capacitor that corrects the power factor also reduces the active power delivered
quiz.explanation: Correction equipment is bought by the microfarad. Hughes’s Example 13.7 needs 53 μF to reach 0.96 lagging but 127 μF to reach unity — the last few hundredths of power factor are the most expensive, and the active power is completely unaffected by the capacitor.

quiz.q: In Nilsson Example 10.7, correcting the combined load to unity reduced the line current from 89.44 A to 80 A. The line-loss reduction was:
options: Exactly 10 percent, because the current fell by 10 percent
20 percent, from 400 W to 320 W, because loss scales with the square of the current
50 percent, because the reactive power was eliminated
Negligible, because the line resistance is only 0.05 Ω
quiz.explanation: $P_{\mathrm{line}} = I^{2}R$: before, $(89.44)^{2}(0.05) = 400\ \mathrm{W}$; after, $(80)^{2}(0.05) = 320\ \mathrm{W}$. The current fell by about 10.6 percent, and the loss — which goes as the square — fell by 20 percent.

quiz.q: A 5 kW load at 0.70 lagging power factor, fed at 230 V and 50 Hz, is to be corrected to 0.95 lagging with a parallel capacitor. The required capacitance is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $P = 5000$ W, $\cos\phi_{1} = 0.70$, target $\cos\phi_{2} = 0.95$, $V = 230$ V RMS, $f = 50$ Hz. Step 2 — Governing bookkeeping: $Q_{1} = P\tan\phi_{1}$, $Q_{2} = P\tan\phi_{2}$, capacitor supplies $Q_{c} = Q_{1} - Q_{2} = V^{2}\omega C$. Step 3 — Algebra: $\phi_{1} \approx 45.57$ degrees with $\tan \approx 1.020$ so $Q_{1} \approx 5100$ var; $\phi_{2} \approx 18.19$ degrees with $\tan \approx 0.3287$ so $Q_{2} \approx 1643$ var; $Q_{c} \approx 3457$ var; $C = \frac{3457}{230^{2} \times 314.16} \approx 208 \times 10^{-6}$ F. Step 4 — Sanity check: capacitor vars are positive-supplied, hundreds of microfarads suit kilowatt mains correction, and the corrected current falls while real power is untouched. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 98 μF corrects only toward $0.85$, 142 μF mis-rounds the angles, and 330 μF over-corrects toward unity and beyond. Step 6 — Conclude: about 208 μF.

intro: Resonance is what happens when the inductive and capacitive reactances of an AC circuit are equal in magnitude. It may be achieved by varying the frequency or by varying a component — usually the capacitance — and it makes the circuit respond in a markedly different manner at the resonant frequency than at any other. A series resonant circuit magnifies a chosen signal and separates it from signals of other frequencies; the tuning of a radio is the canonical example. This section follows Hughes Chapter 14 from the dynamic curves of a series RLC circuit through Q, bandwidth and selectivity to the practical parallel resonant rejector.
objectives: Derive the resonant frequency of series and parallel RLC circuits from the reactance equality
Compute the Q factor, the voltage or current magnification and the bandwidth of resonant circuits
Explain the oscillation of energy at resonance and the general definition of Q as a power ratio
Analyse the practical two-branch parallel circuit, its dynamic resistance and its exact resonant frequency

concepts.term: Frequency variation in a series RLC circuit
concepts.statement: The inductive reactance $X_{L} = 2\pi f L$ increases linearly with frequency while the capacitive reactance $X_{C} = 1/(2\pi f C)$ falls hyperbolically, so the impedance $$Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + \left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^{2}}$$ passes through a minimum: below $f_{r}$ the circuit is capacitive, above $f_{r}$ it is inductive, and at $f_{r}$ it is purely resistive.
concepts.detail: The phase angle $\phi = \tan^{-1}[(X_{L} - X_{C})/R]$ swings from $-90^\circ$ through zero to $+90^\circ$ as the frequency sweeps upward, and the current mirrors the impedance: smallest at the extremes, largest at resonance. These dynamic curves — reactance, impedance, current and phase against frequency — are the complete portrait of the resonant circuit.

concepts.statement: Setting $X_{L} = X_{C}$ gives the **resonant frequency** $$f_{r} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} \qquad \left(\omega_{r} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\right).$$ At this frequency $Z = R$ and $I = V/R$: the impedance is a pure minimum, the current a maximum, and the circuit is an **acceptor**.
concepts.detail: The equality $\omega_{r} L = 1/(\omega_{r} C)$ is the only condition; R does not shift the resonant frequency at all — it only limits how large the current peak can become. At $f_{r}$ the phasor diagram collapses onto the resistance axis: $V_{L}$ and $V_{C}$ are equal and opposite and cancel exactly.

concepts.statement: At resonance the voltages across L and C can greatly exceed the applied voltage: $V_{C} = V_{L} = QV$, where $$Q = \frac{\omega_{r} L}{R} = \frac{1}{\omega_{r} C R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}.$$ Q is called the **voltage magnification** because the capacitor and inductor voltages equal $Q$ times the source voltage.
concepts.detail: In communications receivers Q values of tens to hundreds are routine, which is why series-resonant components can suffer damage from voltages many times the supply if the magnification is not anticipated in the design. The definition is symmetric: using $X_{L} = X_{C}$ at resonance, either reactance divided by R gives the same Q.

concepts.statement: At the resonant frequency the maximum magnetic energy $\frac{1}{2} L I_{m}^{2}$ equals the maximum electrostatic energy $\frac{1}{2} C V_{m}^{2}$, and energy oscillates between the two storage elements — electrostatic in the capacitor one quarter-cycle, magnetic in the inductor the next. This yields the general definition $$Q = \frac{\mathrm{reactive\ power}}{\mathrm{average\ power}}$$ evaluated at resonance.
concepts.detail: The resistor is the only sink: as energy shuttles back and forth, $I^{2}R$ losses bleed away what the source must continually replace. The lower the R, the less power is dissipated per cycle of exchange, the higher the Q and the sharper the resonance peak. Hughes offers a mechanical analogy — a mass on a spring, each small downward tap timed to the natural oscillation building large amplitude from small forces, exactly as a watch escapement feeds a balance wheel.

concepts.statement: The **bandwidth** is the frequency range between the half-power points, where $I = I_{\max}/\sqrt{2}$ and the impedance satisfies $Z = R(1 \pm j)$. The defining results are $$\mathrm{BW} = \omega_{2} - \omega_{1} = \frac{\omega_{r}}{Q}, \qquad \omega_{1}\omega_{2} = \omega_{r}^{2}.$$
concepts.detail: At the half-power frequencies the phase angle of the current is exactly $\pm 45^\circ$ — below resonance the circuit is capacitive and $Z = R(1 - j)$, above it inductive with $Z = R(1 + j)$ — and the power dissipated is half of $P_{\max} = V^{2}/R$. The resonance curve is not perfectly symmetrical about $\omega_{r}$, but the product relation shows $\omega_{r}$ is the geometric mean of the half-power points, and for high Q the curve looks symmetrical.

concepts.statement: A circuit is **selective** if its response has a sharp peak and narrow bandwidth; since $\mathrm{BW} = f_{r}/Q$, selectivity is bought with Q, and Q is bought with small R. A series tuned circuit must therefore be driven by a voltage source of low internal resistance if it is to exhibit a pronounced resonance peak.
concepts.detail: Series resonant circuits designed to select a small band of frequencies are the basis of bandpass (passband) filters, treated in the filters chapters. The trade-off is fundamental: narrowing the bandwidth of acceptance means rejecting more of everything else, but it also makes the circuit slower to respond to changes in the signal.

concepts.statement: For the three-branch circuit of R, L and C in parallel, the admittance is $$Y = G + j\left(\omega C - \frac{1}{\omega L}\right),$$ and resonance again occurs when $\omega C = 1/(\omega L)$ — the same $\omega_{r} = 1/\sqrt{LC}$. At resonance $Y = G$ and $V = I/G$: the impedance is a maximum and the total line current a minimum.
concepts.detail: The parallel equations are exact duals of the series ones — $V$ for $I$, $Y$ for $Z$, $G$ for $R$ — so every series result translates. The line current divides between the branches; because the branch currents exceed the supply current, this is the **current magnification** case: $|I_{L}| = Q I$ where $Q = \omega_{r} C/G = B/G$, the susceptance-to-conductance ratio.

concepts.term: The two-branch circuit and dynamic resistance
concepts.statement: A practical inductor has resistance, giving the two-branch circuit of R$_{S}$ + j$\omega$L in parallel with C. Converting the coil to its parallel equivalent gives $R_{P} = Q^{2} R_{S}$ for $Q \gg 1$, and the impedance at resonance is the **dynamic resistance** $$Z_{r} = \frac{L}{C R_{S}}.$$
concepts.detail: The exact resonant frequency of the two-branch circuit is $f_{r} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{1}{LC} - \frac{R_{S}^{2}}{L^{2}}}$, which reduces to the series-circuit value whenever $R_{S} \ll \omega_{r} L$, as in communications coils. The lower the coil resistance, the larger the dynamic resistance — exactly what good selectivity demands of a **rejector**, the parallel resonant stopband element whose impedance peaks and whose line current bottoms at resonance.

examples.title: A 50 Hz resonant circuit with 39× voltage magnification (Hughes Example 14.1)
examples.problem: A circuit having a resistance of 4.0 Ω, an inductance of 0.50 H and a variable capacitance in series is connected across a 100 V, 50 Hz supply. Calculate (a) the capacitance to give resonance, (b) the voltages across the inductance and the capacitance and (c) the Q factor of the circuit.

steps.label: Step 1: Capacitance for resonance
steps.text: Set $2\pi f_{r} L = 1/(2\pi f_{r} C)$ with $f_{r} = 50\ \mathrm{Hz}$: $C = 1/[(2\pi \times 50)^{2} \times 0.5] = 20.3\ \mu\mathrm{F}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Resonant current
steps.text: At resonance $Z = R$, so $I = V/R = 100/4 = 25\ \mathrm{A}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Component voltages
steps.text: $V_{L} = I \cdot 2\pi f L = 25 \times 2\pi \times 50 \times 0.5 = 3930\ \mathrm{V}$, and $V_{C} = 3930\ \mathrm{V}$ as well — each nearly 40 times the supply voltage, though they cancel in the loop equation.

steps.label: Step 4: Q factor
steps.text: $Q = 2\pi f_{r} L/R = (2\pi \times 50 \times 0.5)/4 = 39.3$, confirming $V_{L} = QV = 39.3 \times 100 \approx 3930\ \mathrm{V}$.

examples.result: With C = 20.3 μF the circuit resonates at 50 Hz: 25 A flows, and 3930 V appears across both L and C from a 100 V source — the voltage magnification that makes series resonance powerful and, unmanaged, destructive.

examples.title: Half-power points of a 6 kHz resonant circuit (Hughes Example 14.4)
examples.problem: A series resonant circuit has $R = 4\ \Omega$ and, at resonance, $X_{L} = j20\ \Omega$ and $X_{C} = -j20\ \Omega$, driven by $V = 20\angle 0^\circ$ V with $f_{r} = 6000\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Calculate the current and component voltages at resonance, the Q factor, the bandwidth, the half-power frequencies and the power dissipated at those frequencies.

steps.label: Step 1: Resonant current and voltages
steps.text: $I_{\max} = 20\angle 0^\circ/4 = 5\angle 0^\circ\ \mathrm{A}$; $V_{R} = 20\angle 0^\circ\ \mathrm{V}$; $V_{L} = (5\angle 0^\circ)(20\angle 90^\circ) = 100\angle 90^\circ\ \mathrm{V}$; $V_{C} = 100\angle -90^\circ\ \mathrm{V}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Bandwidth
steps.text: $\mathrm{BW} = f_{r}/Q = 6000/5 = 1200\ \mathrm{Hz}$, so the half-power frequencies sit 600 Hz either side: $f_{1} = 6000 - 600 = 5400\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{2} = 6000 + 600 = 6600\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Power at the half-power points
steps.text: $P_{\max} = I_{\max}^{2} R = 5^{2} \times 4 = 100\ \mathrm{W}$ at resonance; at $f_{1}$ and $f_{2}$ the power is $\frac{1}{2} P_{\max} = 50\ \mathrm{W}$, where $|I| = 5/\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{A}$ and $Z = 4(1 \pm j)\ \Omega$.

examples.result: Q = 5 gives a 1200 Hz bandwidth centred on 6 kHz; power halves at 5400 Hz and 6600 Hz, where the current phase is ±45°.

examples.title: A parallel resonant rejector at 10 kHz (Hughes Example 14.5)
examples.problem: A coil of 1 kΩ resistance and 0.15 H inductance is connected in parallel with a variable capacitor across a 2.0 V, 10 kHz AC supply. Calculate (a) the capacitance when the supply current is a minimum, (b) the effective impedance of the network at resonance and (c) the supply current.

steps.label: Step 1: Capacitance at minimum current
steps.text: The supply current is minimum at resonance, so set $f_{r} = 10\ \mathrm{kHz}$: $C = 1/(4\pi^{2} L f_{r}^{2}) = 1/(4\pi^{2} \times 0.15 \times 10^{8}) = 1.69\ \mathrm{nF}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Dynamic resistance
steps.text: $Z_{r} = L/(C R_{S}) = 0.15/(1.69 \times 10^{-9} \times 1000) = 89\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ — enormously larger than either branch impedance.

steps.label: Step 3: Supply current
steps.text: $I_{S} = V/Z_{r} = 2/(89 \times 10^{3}) = 22.5\ \mu\mathrm{A}$, while the circulating branch currents are milliamperes.

examples.result: With C = 1.69 nF the network is a rejector at 10 kHz: 89 kΩ of dynamic resistance drawn from a 2 V source yields only 22.5 μA of line current.

keyTakeaways: Resonance is the condition $X_{L} = X_{C}$, giving $f_{r} = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ for both series and parallel (ideal) RLC circuits — independent of R.
A series circuit at resonance is a pure resistance R: minimum impedance, maximum current $V/R$, zero phase angle; it is an acceptor.
Voltage magnification: $V_{L} = V_{C} = QV$ with $Q = \omega_{r} L/R = 1/(\omega_{r} C R)$ — component ratings must anticipate it.
Q has a physical definition independent of topology: reactive power divided by average power at resonance, equivalently $2\pi$ times stored energy over energy lost per cycle.
Bandwidth between half-power points is $\mathrm{BW} = f_{r}/Q$, with $\omega_{1}\omega_{2} = \omega_{r}^{2}$ and ±45° current phase at the band edges.
A parallel resonant circuit is a rejector: maximum impedance, minimum line current, and current magnification $|I_{L}| = QI$ in the branches.

The practical two-branch circuit resonates at $\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{1/(LC) - R_{S}^{2}/L^{2}}$ and presents a dynamic resistance $L/(C R_{S})$ at resonance — small coil resistance means high dynamic resistance and good selectivity.

quiz.q: At the resonant frequency of a series RLC circuit, the impedance is:
options: Purely capacitive because $X_{C}$ dominates at low frequency
Exactly $R$, purely resistive and a minimum
Zero, which is why the current becomes infinite
quiz.explanation: At $f_{r}$ the equal and opposite reactances cancel, $Z = R$ and $I = V/R$. Nothing blows up because R limits the current — but the individual voltages $V_{L}$ and $V_{C}$ can be $Q$ times the supply.

quiz.q: In Hughes Example 14.1, a 100 V supply drives a series circuit with Q = 39.3. The voltage across the capacitor at resonance is approximately:
options: 2.5 V, since the current is limited by R
Zero, because the capacitor and inductor cancel
quiz.explanation: Voltage magnification gives $V_{C} = QV = 39.3 \times 100 = 3930\ \mathrm{V}$. The inductor and capacitor voltages cancel in the loop sum, but each one alone is very real and can destroy an under-rated component.

quiz.q: The half-power points of a series resonant circuit are characterized by:
options: Current zero and purely reactive impedance
quiz.explanation: Half the maximum power means $I^{2}$ has halved, so $I = I_{\max}/\sqrt{2}$ and $|Z| = R\sqrt{2}$, written $Z = R(1 \pm j)$ — the current phase is $\mp 45^\circ$ there, capacitive below resonance and inductive above.

quiz.q: A series resonant circuit has $f_{r} = 6000\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $Q = 5$. Its bandwidth and half-power frequencies are:
quiz.explanation: $\mathrm{BW} = f_{r}/Q = 6000/5 = 1200\ \mathrm{Hz}$; the band edges sit $\mathrm{BW}/2 = 600\ \mathrm{Hz}$ either side of 6 kHz, at 5400 Hz and 6600 Hz.

quiz.q: A parallel resonant (rejector) circuit, compared with its series counterpart at resonance, has:
options: Minimum impedance and maximum line current
Maximum impedance and minimum line current, with branch currents of magnitude $QI$
The same impedance as the series circuit, namely $R$
Zero impedance because the susceptances cancel
quiz.explanation: The susceptances cancel, leaving $Y = G$: impedance is maximum and line current minimum. The energy still circulates, so the branch currents are magnified — $|I_{L}| = QI$ — which is current magnification, the dual of the series circuit’s voltage magnification.

quiz.q: A series RLC circuit uses R = 10 Ω, L = 50 mH and C = 20 μF. Its resonant frequency is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $R = 10$ Ω, $L = 50$ mH, $C = 20$ μF. Step 2 — Governing condition: reactances cancel so $\omega_{0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$ and $f_{0} = \frac{\omega_{0}}{2\pi}$, with $Q = \frac{\omega_{0}L}{R}$. Step 3 — Algebra: $LC = 10^{-6}$, $\sqrt{LC} = 10^{-3}$, $\omega_{0} = 1000$ rad per s, $f_{0} = \frac{1000}{2\pi} \approx 159.15$ Hz; $Q = \frac{1000 \times 0.05}{10} = 5$. Step 4 — Sanity check: at resonance impedance is minimum $10$ Ω and purely resistive, $Q$ of $5$ gives a bandwidth near $32$ Hz, and units resolve correctly. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 79 Hz halves by misplacing $2\pi$, 318 Hz doubles, and 1592 Hz drops a decade. Step 6 — Conclude: resonance sits near 159 Hz.

intro: The greater the power supplied at a given voltage, the greater the current — and single-phase supply handles large currents badly: its motors are not self-starting, and its instantaneous power pulsates. Three-phase systems dominate electricity supply because they transmit high powers efficiently, deliver constant instantaneous power (hence smooth motor torque) and provide powerful self-starting motor drives. This section merges Hughes Chapter 28 and Nilsson Chapter 11: star and delta connections, the $\sqrt{3}$ relations between line and phase quantities, the single-phase equivalent circuit, and power measurement by the two-wattmeter method.
objectives: Explain the advantages of three-phase generation and show that the total instantaneous power of a balanced system is constant
Derive and apply the line–phase voltage and current relations for star and delta connections
Analyse a balanced Y-Y circuit with the single-phase equivalent and the $\Delta$-to-Y transformation
Compute total, per-phase and line-loss power in balanced three-phase circuits
Measure power with two wattmeters and extract the power factor from their readings

concepts.statement: A single-phase induction motor is not self-starting without an auxiliary winding; with three windings carrying currents differing in phase by a third of a cycle, the motor is self-starting with better efficiency and power factor. The total instantaneous power of a balanced three-phase system is constant, $$p_{T} = 1.5 V_{m} I_{m} \cos\theta_{\phi},$$ so the torque at the shaft of a three-phase motor never pulsates.
concepts.detail: Three separate loops fixed at 120° to one another on one shaft generate three equal e.m.f.s displaced by a third of a cycle: $e_{R} = E_{m}\sin\theta$, $e_{Y} = E_{m}\sin(\theta - 120^\circ)$, $e_{B} = E_{m}\sin(\theta - 240^\circ)$. Their instantaneous sum is zero at every instant — the fact that lets the three return conductors of six-wire single-phase supply collapse into one (or none). Less vibration in machinery and smaller conductors for the same power complete the argument.

concepts.term: Balanced three-phase voltages and phase sequence
concepts.statement: A set of balanced three-phase voltages has identical amplitudes and frequencies and phase separations of exactly 120°. For the **abc (positive) sequence** $V_{a} = V_{m}\angle 0^\circ$, $V_{b} = V_{m}\angle -120^\circ$, $V_{c} = V_{m}\angle +120^\circ$; for the **acb (negative) sequence** b and c swap. In either case $V_{a} + V_{b} + V_{c} = 0$.
concepts.detail: The sum is zero as phasors and therefore at every instant of time as well. The phase sequence is the clockwise order of the subscripts around the phasor diagram starting from $V_{a}$. Knowing the sequence plus one voltage gives the entire set — the first of the analytical shortcuts that make balanced three-phase analysis a one-phase job.

concepts.statement: Joining the three winding starts at a neutral point N gives the star connection, for which $$V_{L} = \sqrt{3}\, V_{P}, \qquad I_{L} = I_{P}.$$ The line voltages form a balanced set displaced by 30° from the phase voltages (leading for positive sequence).
concepts.detail: The derivation is one phasor subtraction: $V_{AB} = V_{AN} - V_{BN} = \sqrt{3} V_{\phi}\angle 30^\circ$. In the four-wire system, lamps and heaters connect between line and neutral while motors connect across lines; with an exactly balanced load the neutral carries $(i_{R} + i_{Y} + i_{B}) = 0$ at every instant, so the neutral can be omitted, giving the three-wire star system. Hughes illustrates with a 10 A peak set: at one instant 5 A flows out in R and 5 A out in B while 10 A returns in Y; at another, 8.66 A out in R returns in B — the division shifts continuously while the algebraic sum stays zero.

concepts.statement: Connecting the finish of each winding to the start of the next gives the delta or mesh connection, for which $$V_{L} = V_{P}, \qquad I_{L} = \sqrt{3}\, I_{P},$$ the line currents lagging the phase currents by 30° for a positive sequence.
concepts.detail: The mesh can be closed with no circulating current because the three e.m.f.s sum to zero at every instant — Hughes verifies this both algebraically and instant by instant on the waveform diagram. Like the star case, the $\sqrt{3}$ comes from a 30°-half-angle phasor subtraction, here of the branch currents: $I_{R} = I_{1} - I_{3} = \sqrt{3} I_{\phi}\angle -30^\circ$.

concepts.term: Balanced circuits and the single-phase equivalent
concepts.statement: A three-phase circuit is balanced when (1) the sources form a balanced set, (2) each phase of the source has the same impedance, (3) each line has the same impedance and (4) each phase of the load has the same impedance. Then $V_{N} = 0$ and $I_{0} = 0$, and the a-phase can be solved alone as $$I_{aA} = \frac{V_{a^{\prime}n}}{Z_{\phi}}$$ with the b- and c-phases following by $\mp 120^\circ$ shifts.
concepts.detail: The neutral may be removed or replaced by a short circuit — both are valid models since it carries no current. A balanced delta load reduces to wye by the $\Delta$-to-Y transformation of Chapter 3 with $Z_{Y} = Z_{\Delta}/3$ per phase (the impedance angle is unchanged). All ratings in three-phase practice are rms line values: a 345 kV transmission line is 345,000 V(rms) line-to-line.

concepts.statement: Active power per phase is $P_{\phi} = V_{\phi} I_{\phi}\cos\theta_{\phi}$, so the total is $$P_{T} = 3 V_{\phi} I_{\phi}\cos\theta_{\phi} = \sqrt{3}\, V_{L} I_{L} \cos\theta_{\phi},$$ and identically $Q_{T} = \sqrt{3} V_{L} I_{L}\sin\theta_{\phi}$ and $S_{T} = \sqrt{3} V_{L} I_{L}$. The formula is the same for star and delta — only the meaning of $V_{\phi}$, $I_{\phi}$ changes.
concepts.detail: The angle $\theta_{\phi}$ is between the phase voltage and phase current of one phase, not between line quantities. For a Y load, $V_{\phi} = V_{L}/\sqrt{3}$ and $I_{\phi} = I_{L}$; for a $\Delta$ load, $V_{\phi} = V_{L}$ and $I_{\phi} = I_{L}/\sqrt{3}$ — substituting either pair into $3V_{\phi} I_{\phi}\cos\theta_{\phi}$ produces the same $\sqrt{3} V_{L} I_{L}\cos\theta_{\phi}$.

concepts.statement: The current coils of two wattmeters go in any two lines, their potential coils connecting to the third line. The sum of the readings gives the total active power **under all conditions** — balanced or unbalanced, sinusoidal or not. For a balanced load with positive sequence, $$W_{1} = V_{L} I_{L}\cos(\theta_{\phi} + 30^\circ), \qquad W_{2} = V_{L} I_{L}\cos(\theta_{\phi} - 30^\circ).$$
concepts.detail: The proof writes the instantaneous powers as $i_{R}(v_{RN} - v_{YN}) + i_{B}(v_{BN} - v_{YN})$ and collapses it with Kirchhoff’s current law at the neutral, $i_{R} + i_{B} = -i_{Y}$ — no assumption of balance or sinusoidal shape enters. The three readings rules follow from the cosine shifts: if the power factor exceeds 0.5 both meters read positive; at exactly 0.5 one reads zero; below 0.5 one reads negative (reverse its coil connections and record the value as negative). Reversing the phase sequence interchanges the two readings.

concepts.term: Power factor from two wattmeter readings
concepts.statement: Taking the difference over the sum of the readings eliminates the load: $$\tan\theta_{\phi} = \sqrt{3}\,\frac{W_{2} - W_{1}}{W_{2} + W_{1}},$$ from which the power factor follows as $\cos\theta_{\phi}$.
concepts.detail: The derivation adds and subtracts the two cosine expressions — their sum returns $\sqrt{3} V_{L} I_{L}\cos\theta_{\phi}$ (the total power) and their difference returns $V_{L} I_{L}\sin\theta_{\phi}$. Hughes notes the alternative of reading the ratio $W_{1}/W_{2}$ off a plotted calibration curve, and that the sign of $\theta_{\phi}$ — lagging or leading — cannot be recovered from wattmeter data alone.

examples.title: A balanced Y-Y system, start to finish (Nilsson Examples 11.1 and 11.3)
examples.problem: A balanced Y-connected generator with per-phase impedance $0.2 + j0.5\ \Omega$ and internal voltage 120 V/φ feeds a balanced Y load of $39 + j28\ \Omega$/φ through a line of $0.8 + j1.5\ \Omega$/φ. Find the line currents, the load phase voltages and the load line voltages; then compute the power delivered to the load and lost in the line.

steps.label: Step 1: Single-phase equivalent
steps.text: The a-phase total impedance is $(0.2 + 0.8 + 39) + j(0.5 + 1.5 + 28) = 40 + j30\ \Omega$, so $I_{aA} = 120\angle 0^\circ/(40 + j30) = 2.4\angle -36.87^\circ\ \mathrm{A}$; by the positive sequence, $I_{bB} = 2.4\angle -156.87^\circ$ and $I_{cC} = 2.4\angle 83.13^\circ\ \mathrm{A}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Load phase voltages
steps.text: $V_{AN} = (39 + j28)(2.4\angle -36.87^\circ) = 115.22\angle -1.19^\circ\ \mathrm{V}$, with $V_{BN}$ and $V_{CN}$ at $\mp 120^\circ$ from it.

steps.label: Step 3: Load line voltages
steps.text: Line voltages are $\sqrt{3}$ larger and lead by 30°: $V_{AB} = (\sqrt{3}\angle 30^\circ) V_{AN} = 199.58\angle 28.81^\circ\ \mathrm{V}$, with $V_{BC}$ and $V_{CA}$ at $-120^\circ$ spacings.

steps.label: Step 4: Power per phase and total
Step 5: Losses and reactive power
steps.text: Line loss $= 3(2.4)^{2}(0.8) = 13.824\ \mathrm{W}$; generator internal loss $= 3(2.4)^{2}(0.2) = 3.456\ \mathrm{W}$; the load absorbs $Q_{T} = \sqrt{3}(199.58)(2.4)\sin 35.68^\circ = 483.84\ \mathrm{VAR}$.

examples.result: 2.4 A in each line, 115.22 V/φ and 199.58 V line-to-line at the load; 673.92 W delivered, 13.824 W lost in the line, 483.84 VAR magnetizing — the whole three-phase problem solved as one single-phase circuit.

examples.title: A 400 V motor, star or delta (Hughes Example 28.3)
examples.problem: A three-phase motor operating off a 400 V system develops 20 kW at an efficiency of 0.87 per unit and a power factor of 0.82. Calculate (a) the line current and (b) the phase current if the windings are delta-connected.

steps.label: Step 1: Set up the efficiency equation
steps.text: Efficiency is output over input power, and the input to a three-phase motor is $\sqrt{3} V_{L} I_{L}\cos\phi$: $0.87 = 20\,000/(1.73 \times I_{L} \times 400 \times 0.82)$.

steps.label: Step 2: Line current
steps.text: Solving gives $I_{L} = 20\,000/(0.87 \times 1.73 \times 400 \times 0.82) = 40.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Phase current in delta
steps.text: In a delta connection the phase current is the line current divided by $\sqrt{3}$: $I_{P} = 40.0/1.73 = 23.1\ \mathrm{A}$ flowing in each winding.

examples.result: Forty amperes in each line and 23.1 A in each delta winding — the same formula $P = \sqrt{3} V_{L} I_{L} \cos\phi$ serves both star and delta machines.

examples.title: Two wattmeters on a motor (Hughes Example 28.4)
examples.problem: The input power to a three-phase motor is measured by the two-wattmeter method. The readings are 5.2 kW and −1.7 kW, and the line voltage is 400 V. Calculate (a) the total active power, (b) the power factor and (c) the line current.

steps.label: Step 1: Total power
steps.text: $P = W_{1} + W_{2} = 5.2 - 1.7 = 3.5\ \mathrm{kW}$ — valid whatever the sign of the individual readings.

steps.label: Step 2: Power factor from the readings
steps.text: The ratio of the readings is $-1.7/5.2 = -0.327$; using the tangent formula, $\tan\phi = 1.73\,[5.2 - (-1.7)]/[5.2 + (-1.7)] = 1.73 \times 6.9/3.5 = 3.41$, so $\phi = 73^\circ 39^{\prime}$ and $\cos\phi = 0.281$.

steps.label: Step 3: Line current
steps.text: From $P = \sqrt{3} V_{L} I_{L} \cos\phi$: $I_{L} = 3500/(1.73 \times 400 \times 0.281) = 18.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Note the limitation
steps.text: One wattmeter reading negative already tells us the power factor is below 0.5; but from wattmeter data alone it is impossible to state whether the power factor is lagging or leading.

examples.result: P = 3.5 kW at a power factor of 0.281, drawing 18.0 A per line — one meter reading negative is not an error, it is the measurement speaking.

keyTakeaways: Three windings at 120° generate a balanced set of e.m.f.s whose sum is zero at every instant; three-phase motors are self-starting, and the total instantaneous power $1.5 V_{m} I_{m}\cos\theta_{\phi}$ is constant.
Star: $V_{L} = \sqrt{3} V_{P}$ and $I_{L} = I_{P}$, line voltages leading phase voltages by 30° (positive sequence); delta: $V_{L} = V_{P}$ and $I_{L} = \sqrt{3} I_{P}$.
A balanced load carries no neutral current, so the neutral may be removed; the whole system then solves as one single-phase equivalent with $Z_{Y} = Z_{\Delta}/3$ converting delta loads.
Total power, reactive power and apparent power in any balanced three-phase circuit: $\sqrt{3} V_{L} I_{L}$ times $\cos\theta_{\phi}$, $\sin\theta_{\phi}$ or 1 respectively.
Two wattmeters suffice for total power in any three-wire three-phase system — balanced or not; their readings are $V_{L} I_{L}\cos(\theta_{\phi} \pm 30^\circ)$.
Power factor from two wattmeter readings: $\tan\theta_{\phi} = \sqrt{3}(W_{2} - W_{1})/(W_{2} + W_{1})$; one reading goes negative below 0.5 power factor.
Ratings are rms line values throughout three-phase practice — a 400 V system means 400 V line-to-line, with $400/\sqrt{3} = 230\ \mathrm{V}$ to neutral.

quiz.q: In a star-connected three-phase system with balanced load:
options: Both line quantities are $\sqrt{3}$ times their phase counterparts
The neutral current equals the vector sum of the line currents and is large
quiz.explanation: Star: the line current flows through the phase so they are equal, while the line voltage is the phasor difference of two phase voltages, $2 V_{P}\cos 30^\circ = \sqrt{3} V_{P}$. The neutral current of a balanced load is zero — the phasor (and instantaneous) sum of three equal 120°-displaced currents.

quiz.q: The total power formula $P = \sqrt{3} V_{L} I_{L}\cos\theta_{\phi}$ applies:
options: To any balanced load, star or delta, with $\theta_{\phi}$ the phase-voltage-to-phase-current angle
To unbalanced loads whenever the two-wattmeter method is used
quiz.explanation: Substituting the star relations ($V_{\phi} = V_{L}/\sqrt{3}$, $I_{\phi} = I_{L}$) or the delta relations ($V_{\phi} = V_{L}$, $I_{\phi} = I_{L}/\sqrt{3}$) into $3 V_{\phi} I_{\phi}\cos\theta_{\phi}$ produces the same expression — which is exactly why equipment is specified in line quantities.

quiz.q: In Nilsson Example 11.1, the load phase voltage is $V_{AN} = 115.22\angle -1.19^\circ$ V with positive sequence. The line voltage $V_{AB}$ is:
options: $115.22\angle -1.19^\circ$ V — line equals phase in star
quiz.explanation: $V_{AB} = (\sqrt{3}\angle 30^\circ) V_{AN} = 199.58\angle 28.81^\circ\ \mathrm{V}$: multiply the magnitude by $\sqrt{3}$ and advance the angle by 30° for a positive sequence (the line set would lag by 30° for a negative sequence).

quiz.q: A two-wattmeter measurement on a balanced load gives $W_{1} = 0$ with $W_{2}$ positive. The power factor of the load is:
quiz.explanation: With $W_{1} = V_{L} I_{L}\cos(\theta_{\phi} + 30^\circ) = 0$, the angle $\theta_{\phi} = 60^\circ$ and the power factor is $\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$. Below 0.5, $W_{1}$ would go negative; above it, both meters read positive.

quiz.q: Hughes’s motor test gave wattmeter readings of 5.2 kW and −1.7 kW at 400 V. The total power and the line current were:
options: 3.5 kW and 18.0 A at a power factor of 0.281
3.5 kW and 40 A at a power factor of 0.82
1.7 kW, discarding the negative reading as instrument error
quiz.explanation: The total is simply $5.2 - 1.7 = 3.5\ \mathrm{kW}$; then $\tan\phi = \sqrt{3} \times 6.9/3.5 = 3.41$ gives $\cos\phi = 0.281$, and $I_{L} = 3500/(\sqrt{3} \times 400 \times 0.281) = 18.0\ \mathrm{A}$. The negative reading is meaningful data, not an error.

intro: Chapter 4 introduced the great network theorems for dc circuits; the phasor machinery of Chapter 8 turned AC steady-state analysis into complex arithmetic. Put the two together and every theorem — superposition, Thévenin, Norton, source transformation, star–delta and maximum power transfer — carries over to AC networks with impedances simply replacing resistances. Hughes demonstrates each one on worked AC networks in Chapter 15, and Nilsson Section 9.7 supplies the frequency-domain proofs: substitute Z for R and the derivations of Chapter 4 go through unchanged.
objectives: Apply Kirchhoff’s laws, nodal analysis and network reduction to AC networks in complex form
Use the superposition theorem with phasor sources and state its same-frequency limitation
Find Thévenin and Norton equivalents of AC networks, including by the test-source method
Transform between voltage and current sources in the frequency domain
State and apply the conjugate-match condition for maximum average power transfer

concepts.statement: Provided complex notation is applied to all AC quantities, the network theorems are used **in almost the same ways as for dc circuits**, with impedance replacing resistance. The practical choice of method is the same as in Chapter 4: when the data describe component voltages and currents, attack directly with Kirchhoff’s laws; when they describe the supply, use network reduction.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Example 15.1 shows the direct route: guessing $I_{3} = (3 + j0)\ \mathrm{A}$ in the 8 Ω resistor, the 16 Ω capacitive branch and series $8 + j6\ \Omega$ then fix every current and voltage back to the source, $E = (39 + j30)\ \mathrm{V} = 49.2\ \mathrm{V}$. Example 15.4 shows the reduction route: replacing the parallel $R$–$X_{C}$ pair by $Z_{e} = 6.4 - j3.2\ \Omega$ collapses the network to $14.7\ \Omega$ and the same supply current.

concepts.term: Nodal analysis in the frequency domain
concepts.statement: Write KCL at each essential node with **admittances**: $\sum V_{\mathrm{node}}/Z_{k} = \sum$ source currents. The node equation is now a single complex equation per unknown node voltage.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Example 15.7: with sources $(6 + j0)\ \mathrm{V}$ and $(4 + j3)\ \mathrm{V}$ feeding a node through $(2 + j3)\ \Omega$ and $(2 + j1)\ \Omega$, and a 10 Ω load to the reference node, KCL gives $(V_{o} - 6 - j0)/(2 + j3) + (V_{o} - 4 - j3)/(2 + j1) + V_{o}/10 = 0$, which reduces to $V_{o} = (11 + j24)/(4.1 + j4.8) = 4.18\angle 15.9^\circ\ \mathrm{V}$.

concepts.statement: In a linear network with multiple sources, the total current or voltage anywhere is the **phasor sum** of the component responses to each source acting alone, with every other ideal voltage source replaced by a short circuit and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Example 15.8 works a two-source network both ways: the component currents from the $(10 + j0)\ \mathrm{V}$ source alone and the $(6 + j8)\ \mathrm{V}$ source alone sum to $I_{1} = (1.65 - j2.76)\ \mathrm{A} = 3.22\ \mathrm{A}$ and $I_{2} = (-1.18 + j2.58)\ \mathrm{A} = 2.84\ \mathrm{A}$. The theorem assumes all sources operate at the same frequency — at different frequencies the component responses cannot be added as phasors, and one must move to the transform methods of the sections that follow.

concepts.statement: Any two-terminal AC network can be replaced by an equivalent consisting of **a voltage source equal to the open-circuit voltage at the terminals in series with the internal impedance seen from the terminals**, with all independent sources deactivated.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s Example 9.12 shows the subtlety when the network contains a dependent source: preserve the controlling variable, find $V_{\mathrm{Th}}$ from the simplified circuit ($V_{\mathrm{Th}} = 784 - j288\ \mathrm{V}$ there), and obtain $Z_{\mathrm{Th}} = 91.2 - j38.4\ \Omega$ by the **test-source method** — deactivate the independent sources, apply a test source at the terminals, and take the ratio of its voltage to its current.

concepts.statement: Any two-terminal AC network can be replaced by **a current source equal to the short-circuit current at the terminals in parallel with the internal impedance** seen from the terminals. The Norton current is $I_{s/c} = V_{o/c}/Z_{\mathrm{in}}$.
concepts.detail: Norton’s equivalent is the natural partner of Thévenin’s — one is the source transformation of the other. Hughes pairs Examples 15.9 and 15.13 on the same network: where the Thévenin form gives $V_{o/c} = -(24.6 + j29.5)\ \mathrm{V}$ in series with $(0.89 - j3.74)\ \Omega$, the Norton form gives $I_{s/c} = (6 - j8)\ \mathrm{A}$ in parallel with the same impedance. Norton equivalents are associated with light-current, semiconductor applications.

concepts.term: Source transformation in the frequency domain
concepts.statement: A voltage source $V_{s}$ in series with an impedance $Z_{s}$ is equivalent to a current source $$I_{s} = \frac{V_{s}}{Z_{s}}$$ in parallel with $Z_{s}$, and conversely $V_{s} = Z_{s} I_{s}$ — with phasors and complex impedances throughout.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s Example 9.11 chains transformations to reduce a four-branch circuit to a single loop: a $40\angle 0^\circ$ V source with $1 + j3\ \Omega$ becomes $40/(1 + j3) = 4 - j12\ \mathrm{A}$ in parallel with it; parallel impedances merge into $1.8 + j2.4\ \Omega$; the source reconverts to $36 - j12\ \mathrm{V}$; finally $V_{0} = (1.56 + j1.08)(10 - j19) = 36.12 - j18.84\ \mathrm{V}$.

concepts.statement: The dc resistor formulas carry over with impedances. Star to delta: $$Z_{1} = Z_{b} + Z_{c} + \frac{Z_{b} Z_{c}}{Z_{a}},$$ and delta to star: $$Z_{a} = \frac{Z_{2} Z_{3}}{Z_{1} + Z_{2} + Z_{3}}.$$
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Example 15.17 cracks a bridge network by spotting the delta hidden in it: two $2 + j0\ \Omega$ arms and a $3 + j4\ \Omega$ branch convert to a star with $Z_{a} = 0.43 - j0.25\ \Omega$ and $Z_{b} = Z_{c} = 0.78 - j0.12\ \Omega$, after which the network collapses and the load current follows as $I = 5.88\ \mathrm{A}$. Not every delta is drawn as one — the skill is recognizing it.

concepts.term: Maximum power transfer in AC networks
concepts.statement: Maximum average power is transferred when the load impedance is the **conjugate** of the internal source impedance, $$Z_{L} = Z_{\mathrm{Th}}^{*},$$ that is, equal resistance parts and equal-but-opposite reactance parts. If only the magnitude of $Z_{L}$ can be varied, the optimum is $|Z_{L}| = |Z_{\mathrm{Th}}|$.
concepts.detail: The conjugate match makes the total reactance zero, so the current is in phase with the voltage — the observation from Chapter 4 that maximum current comes with unity power factor. Nilsson’s Example 10.9 works a full case: after two source transformations, $V_{\mathrm{Th}} = 19.2\angle -53.13^\circ\ \mathrm{V}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{Th}} = 5.76 - j1.68\ \Omega$, so the matching load is $Z_{L} = 5.76 + j1.68\ \Omega$ and the delivered maximum is $P = V_{\mathrm{Th}}^{2}/(4 R_{L}) = 8\ \mathrm{W}$.

examples.title: Thévenin and Norton of the same network (Hughes Examples 15.9 and 15.13)
examples.problem: A 100 V source feeds a 6 Ω resistor in series with an 8 Ω inductive reactance; a capacitive reactance of 3 Ω is connected across the output terminals, in parallel with the load. Determine the Thévenin and Norton equivalent circuits supplying the load.

steps.label: Step 1: Open-circuit voltage
steps.text: With the load removed, the output voltage is divided between $6 + j8\ \Omega$ and $-j3\ \Omega$: $V_{o/c} = 100 \times (-j3)/(6 + j8 - j3) = 100(-j3)/(6 + j5)$, which evaluates to $-(24.6 + j29.5)\ \mathrm{V}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Internal impedance
steps.text: Short-circuit the source and look into the terminals: $Z_{\mathrm{in}} = (-j3)(6 + j8)/(6 + j8 - j3) = (24 - j18)/(6 + j5) = (0.89 - j3.74)\ \Omega$.

steps.label: Step 3: Thévenin equivalent
steps.text: A source $-(24.6 + j29.5)\ \mathrm{V}$ in series with $(0.89 - j3.74)\ \Omega$ — any load attached sees exactly this.

steps.label: Step 4: Norton short-circuit current
steps.text: Shorting the output puts the whole terminal voltage across $6 + j8\ \Omega$: $I_{s/c} = 100/(6 + j8) = (6 - j8)\ \mathrm{A}$.

steps.label: Step 5: Norton equivalent
steps.text: A source $(6 - j8)\ \mathrm{A}$ in parallel with the same $(0.89 - j3.74)\ \Omega$ — and indeed $V_{o/c}/Z_{\mathrm{in}} = (6 - j8)\ \mathrm{A}$, as the transformation $I_{s} = V_{s}/Z_{s}$ requires.

examples.result: Thévenin: −(24.6 + j29.5) V in series with (0.89 − j3.74) Ω. Norton: (6 − j8) A in parallel with the same impedance. Two pictures, one network.

examples.title: A Thévenin equivalent drives a 10 Ω load (Hughes Examples 15.7 and 15.10)
examples.problem: A network with sources $(6 + j0)\ \mathrm{V}$ (through $2 + j3\ \Omega$) and $(4 + j3)\ \mathrm{V}$ (through $2 + j1\ \Omega$) presents terminals A–B to a 10 Ω load. Use Thévenin’s theorem to find the load current, and compare with the nodal solution.

steps.label: Step 1: Open-circuit voltage
steps.text: With the load removed, one current circulates: $I = [(6 + j0) - (4 + j3)]/[(2 + j3) + (2 + j1)] = (2 - j3)/(4 + j4) = -0.125 - j0.625\ \mathrm{A}$; then $V_{o/c} = (6 + j0) - I(2 + j3) = 4.375 + j1.625 = 4.66\angle 20.4^\circ\ \mathrm{V}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Internal impedance
steps.text: Both sources shorted, the two branches are in parallel across A–B: $Z_{\mathrm{in}} = (2 + j3)(2 + j1)/(4 + j4) = (1 + j8)/(4 + j4) = (1.125 + j0.875)\ \Omega$.

steps.label: Step 3: Load current
steps.text: $I = V_{o/c}/(Z_{\mathrm{in}} + 10 + j0) = 4.66\angle 20.4^\circ/11.16\angle 4.5^\circ = 0.418\angle 15.9^\circ\ \mathrm{A}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Cross-check by nodal analysis
steps.text: The nodal attack of Example 15.7 gives $V_{o} = 4.18\angle 15.9^\circ\ \mathrm{V}$ across the 10 Ω load — that is, $I = 4.18\angle 15.9^\circ/10 = 0.418\angle 15.9^\circ\ \mathrm{A}$. Identical.

examples.result: The load takes 0.418∠15.9° A. Two independent routes — Thévenin and nodal — agree exactly, which is the best available insurance against algebra slips in complex networks.

examples.title: Conjugate matching for maximum power (Hughes Example 15.18)
examples.problem: A network consists of a 12 V source feeding an impedance $(6 + j8)\ \Omega$ in parallel with a capacitive reactance of $-j6\ \Omega$; the load connects across the parallel pair. Determine the load impedance that dissipates maximum power, and find that power.

steps.label: Step 1: Internal impedance
steps.text: Shorting the source puts the two in parallel: $Z_{\mathrm{in}} = (6 + j8)(-j6)/(6 + j8 - j6) = (48 - j36)/(6 + j2) = (5.4 - j7.8)\ \Omega$.

steps.label: Step 3: The matching condition
steps.text: For maximum power the load must be the conjugate of the internal impedance: $Z_{L} = (5.4 + j7.8)\ \Omega$ — the equal resistance parts dissipate equally, and the reactances cancel.

steps.label: Step 4: Current and power
steps.text: The total impedance is purely resistive, $Z = (5.4 - j7.8) + (5.4 + j7.8) = (10.8 + j0)\ \Omega$, so $I = (3.6 + j10.8)/10.8 = 1.05\ \mathrm{A}$ and $P_{L} = I^{2} R_{L} = (1.05)^{2} \times 5.4 = 6.0\ \mathrm{W}$.

examples.result: Matching with $Z_{L} = 5.4 + j7.8\ \Omega$ delivers 6.0 W — half of what the source generates, the unavoidable toll of conjugate matching.

keyTakeaways: Every dc network theorem survives into AC analysis unchanged once resistances become complex impedances and quantities become phasors.
Superposition sums phasor responses source-by-source; it presumes a common frequency, and different frequencies demand the transform methods ahead.
Thévenin: open-circuit voltage in series with the impedance seen from the terminals; Norton: short-circuit current in parallel with the same impedance.
When dependent sources are present, find $Z_{\mathrm{Th}}$ with the test-source method — never by simply deactivating the dependent source.
Source transformation in the frequency domain: $V_{s} = Z_{s} I_{s}$, valid with phasors exactly as in Chapter 4.
Star–delta conversions with impedances: $Z_{1} = Z_{b} + Z_{c} + Z_{b}Z_{c}/Z_{a}$ and $Z_{a} = Z_{2}Z_{3}/(Z_{1} + Z_{2} + Z_{3})$.
Maximum average power transfer requires the conjugate match $Z_{L} = Z_{\mathrm{Th}}^{*}$; with only the magnitude adjustable, set $|Z_{L}| = |Z_{\mathrm{Th}}|$.

quiz.q: When applying superposition to an AC network, each ideal voltage source not under consideration is replaced by:
options: A current source of the same phase
quiz.explanation: An ideal voltage source is replaced by a short circuit (its zero internal impedance), and an ideal current source by an open circuit. The component responses are then summed as phasors — which is why all sources must share one frequency.

quiz.q: A network contains a dependent source. The correct way to find the Thévenin impedance is:
options: Deactivate the dependent source along with the independent ones and combine impedances
Apply a test source at the terminals with only the independent sources deactivated and take the ratio of voltage to current
Divide the open-circuit voltage by the short-circuit current of the dependent source alone
It cannot be found; the theorem does not apply with dependent sources
quiz.explanation: The dependent source must stay alive. In Nilsson Example 9.12 the test-source method yields $Z_{\mathrm{Th}} = 91.2 - j38.4\ \Omega$ for a network whose Thévenin voltage is $784 - j288\ \mathrm{V}$. (Dividing $V_{o/c}$ by $I_{s/c}$ also works but is usually messier.)

quiz.q: For maximum average power transfer from a source whose internal impedance is $Z_{\mathrm{Th}} = 5.4 - j7.8\ \Omega$, the load should be:
options: $5.4 - j7.8\ \Omega$, equal to the source impedance
As large as possible to minimize losses
quiz.explanation: The conjugate $Z_{L} = Z_{\mathrm{Th}}^{*}$ makes the loop purely resistive at $10.8\ \Omega$ in Hughes Example 15.18, so the current is in phase with the voltage and $I^{2}R$ is maximal: 1.05 A and 6.0 W in that example.

quiz.q: Two sources of different frequencies drive a linear network. Superposition:
options: Works as usual — just add the phasor responses
Fails because phasors require a common frequency; the responses must be added in the time domain
Works if the sources are both voltage sources
Works if one source is first converted to its Norton equivalent
quiz.explanation: A phasor is meaningful only against a single shared frequency. Hughes notes that component currents from different-frequency sources can still be found, but not added as phasors — exactly the limitation that the Laplace transform removes in the next section.

quiz.q: The Norton equivalent of a network with open-circuit voltage $V_{o/c}$ and internal impedance $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ has a current source of value:
options: Equal to the open-circuit current, which is zero
quiz.explanation: The source transformation $I_{s} = V_{s}/Z_{s}$ connects the two equivalents. In Hughes Examples 15.9 and 15.13, dividing $-(24.6 + j29.5)\ \mathrm{V}$ by $(0.89 - j3.74)\ \Omega$ gives the Norton current $(6 - j8)\ \mathrm{A}$ directly.

quiz.q: A network presents $V_{Th} = 10 \angle 0°$ V RMS in series with $Z_{Th} = 4 + j3$ Ω. The maximum average power a load can receive, and the matching load, are closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: RMS phasor magnitude $10$ V, $Z_{Th} = 4 + j3$ Ω so $R_{Th} = 4$ Ω. Step 2 — Governing theorem: conjugate match $Z_{L} = Z_{Th}^{∗}$ maximizes transfer, giving $P_{max} = \frac{|V_{Th}|^{2}}{4R_{Th}}$. Step 3 — Algebra: match is $4 - j3$ Ω; $P_{max} = \frac{100}{16} = 6.25$ W. Step 4 — Sanity check: only resistances absorb average power, the reactances cancel at the match, and efficiency at match is one half as theory demands. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: $4 + j3$ Ω doubles reactance instead of cancelling, resistive-only $4$ Ω leaves vars circulating, and $5$ Ω mismatches magnitude. Step 6 — Conclude: 6.25 W with $4 - j3$ Ω.

intro: The phasor transform of Chapter 8 bought algebraic ease but only for the sinusoidal steady state — transients were left behind. The Laplace transform closes that gap: it converts the integrodifferential equations of a circuit with switches, steps, impulses and arbitrary sources into pure algebra in a new variable $s$, solves them, and converts back. Nilsson builds the machine in Chapter 12: the defining integral, the step and impulse functions, tables of functional and operational transforms, partial-fraction inversion, and the poles-and-zeros picture of the s plane that preview’s every circuit’s natural behaviour.
objectives: State the defining integral of the one-sided Laplace transform and explain the choice of the 0⁻ lower limit
Use step and impulse functions to represent switching operations and discontinuities
Build transforms of new functions from the functional and operational transform tables
Invert proper rational functions by partial-fraction expansion, for real and complex roots
Locate poles and zeros on the s plane and apply the initial- and final-value theorems

concepts.statement: The (one-sided) Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is $$\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = \int_{0^{-}}^{\infty} f(t) e^{-st}\, dt = F(s),$$ where $s$ has the dimension of frequency. The transform turns a set of integrodifferential equations in the time domain into a set of **algebraic** equations in the frequency domain.
concepts.detail: The lower limit $0^{-}$ is chosen so that an impulse or discontinuity at the origin is included; the integral from $0^{-}$ to $0^{+}$ is then zero except when the discontinuity is an impulse. Like the phasor, the Laplace transform creates a friendlier domain, solves there, and inverse-transforms back. Functions without transforms — $t^{t}$, $e^{t^{2}}$ — never appear as excitations of linear circuits anyway.

concepts.statement: The **step function** $Ku(t)$ is zero for $t < 0$ and $K$ for $t > 0$; a step at $t = a$ is $Ku(t - a)$. Step functions turn linear segments on and off, so any piecewise-linear waveform can be written as one expression — for example a pulse of height $K$ from $t = 1$ to $t = 3$ is $K[u(t - 1) - u(t - 3)]$.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s Example 12.1 assembles a triangular zigzag this way: $f(t) = 2t[u(t) - u(t-1)] + (-2t + 4)[u(t-1) - u(t-3)] + (2t - 8)[u(t-3) - u(t-4)]$ — one line replacing a five-case piecewise definition. When a finite transition must be specified, the convention is the linear one, $Ku(0) = 0.5K$.

concepts.statement: The **impulse** $K\delta(t)$ is the limit of a variable-parameter function whose amplitude grows without bound, whose duration shrinks to zero and whose area stays constant at $K$: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} K\delta(t)\, dt = K$ and $\delta(t) = 0$ for $t \neq 0$. Its **sifting property** reads $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t)\delta(t - a)\, dt = f(a)$.
concepts.detail: Two consequences matter for circuits: the derivative of a step is an impulse, and the transform of the unit impulse is $\mathcal{L}\{\delta(t)\} = 1$. Impulses model switching operations that transfer finite charge instantaneously — the capacitor switching circuit of Chapter 13 — and the transform of the nth derivative of an impulse is $s^{n}$.

concepts.statement: A **functional transform** is the transform of a specific function. The core table: $\delta(t) \to 1$; $u(t) \to 1/s$; $t \to 1/s^{2}$; $e^{-at} \to 1/(s + a)$; $\sin\omega t \to \omega/(s^{2} + \omega^{2})$; $\cos\omega t \to s/(s^{2} + \omega^{2})$; plus the damped family $te^{-at}$, $e^{-at}\sin\omega t$, $e^{-at}\cos\omega t$.
concepts.detail: Each entry is a direct evaluation of the defining integral — for instance $\mathcal{L}\{\sin\omega t\} = \int_{0}^{\infty}(\sin\omega t)e^{-st} dt = \omega/(s^{2} + \omega^{2})$ via the exponential form of the sine. Linearity then stretches the table: multiplication by a constant and addition of functions carry straight through, so $\sin(\omega t + \theta)$ and shifted sinusoids need no new integrals.

concepts.statement: Differentiation and integration in time become algebraic operations in $s$: $$\mathcal{L}\left\{\frac{df}{dt}\right\} = sF(s) - f(0^{-}), \qquad \mathcal{L}\left\{\int_{0^{-}}^{t} f(x)\, dx\right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.$$ For higher derivatives, $\mathcal{L}\{d^{2}f/dt^{2}\} = s^{2}F(s) - sf(0^{-}) - df(0^{-})/dt$.
concepts.detail: This single pair of properties is the whole reason the method works: an integrodifferential KCL equation such as $v/R + (1/L)\int_{0}^{t} v\, dx + C\, dv/dt = I_{\mathrm{dc}} u(t)$ becomes $V/R + V/(Ls) + C[sV - v(0^{-})] = I_{\mathrm{dc}}/s$ — one algebraic equation in $V(s)$. The initial conditions ride along inside the $f(0^{-})$ terms, which is why the $0^{-}$ limit was chosen.

concepts.statement: A shift in time multiplies the transform by an exponential; a multiplication by an exponential shifts the transform: $$\mathcal{L}\{f(t - a)u(t - a)\} = e^{-as} F(s) \quad (a > 0), \qquad \mathcal{L}\{e^{-at} f(t)\} = F(s + a).$$
concepts.detail: The second rule manufactures the damped-cosine pair from the cosine pair: knowing $\mathcal{L}\{\cos\omega t\} = s/(s^{2} + \omega^{2})$ gives $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-at}\cos\omega t\} = (s + a)/[(s + a)^{2} + \omega^{2}]$ with no integration. Scale changing completes the toolkit: $\mathcal{L}\{f(at)\} = (1/a)F(s/a)$ for $a > 0$.

concepts.statement: Every s-domain response of a lumped linear circuit is a rational function $F(s) = N(s)/D(s)$; if it is proper ($m > n$), expand in partial fractions — one term per distinct root of $D(s)$, $r$ terms for a root of multiplicity $r$ — and invert term by term using the tables: $$F(s) = \sum_{k}\frac{K_{k}}{s + p_{k}} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad f(t) = \sum_{k} K_{k} e^{-p_{k} t} u(t).$$
concepts.detail: Each coefficient is isolated by multiplying through by its own denominator factor and evaluating at that root. Complex roots come in conjugate pairs and their coefficients are conjugates too, so they recombine into damped sinusoids. Always test the finished expansion at a root of the numerator — both sides must vanish there — and remember that an improper rational function must be divided out before expanding.

concepts.statement: Writing $F(s) = K(s + z_{1})(s + z_{2})\cdots/(s + p_{1})(s + p_{2})\cdots$, the roots $-p_{k}$ of the denominator are the **poles** (where $F$ blows up) and the roots $-z_{k}$ of the numerator are the **zeros** (where $F$ vanishes). They are plotted on the complex s plane with X marks and O marks respectively.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s Example 12.8 factorizes $F_{1}(s) = 10(s+5)(s+3+j4)(s+3-j4)/[s(s+10)(s+6+j8)(s+6-j8)]$: poles at $0, -10, -6 \pm j8$; zeros at $-5, -3 \pm j4$. A rational function can also have poles or zeros at infinity; the interesting ones for circuits are the finite ones.

concepts.statement: The endpoint behaviour of $f(t)$ can be read from $F(s)$ before any inversion: $$\lim_{t \to 0^{+}} f(t) = \lim_{s \to \infty} sF(s), \qquad \lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) = \lim_{s \to 0} sF(s).$$ The final-value theorem holds only if all poles of $F(s)$ except a first-order pole at the origin lie in the left half plane.
concepts.detail: These are the built-in sanity checks of the Laplace method: after solving an s-domain circuit equation, test the predicted initial and final values against what the circuit obviously does before and after the transient. A pair of poles on the imaginary axis — a sustained oscillation — voids the final-value test, as Nilsson notes for the sinusoidally driven circuit whose current has poles at $\pm j40{,}000$.

examples.title: A parallel RLC switched at t = 0 (Nilsson Example 12.2)
examples.problem: A current source $I_{\mathrm{dc}} = 24\ \mathrm{mA}$, a resistor $R = 400\ \Omega$, an inductor $L = 25\ \mathrm{mH}$ and a capacitor $C = 25\ \mathrm{nF}$ are in parallel; no energy is stored when the switch opens at $t = 0$. Find the Laplace transform of the voltage $v(t)$ and predict the functional form of $v(t)$.

steps.label: Step 1: Transform the KCL equation
steps.text: The time-domain node equation $v/R + (1/L)\int_{0}^{t} v\, dx + C\, dv/dt = I_{\mathrm{dc}} u(t)$ becomes $V/R + V/(Ls) + C s V = I_{\mathrm{dc}}/s$ with $v(0^{-}) = 0$.

steps.label: Step 4: Predict the response form
steps.text: Writing $V(s) = K_{1}/(s + 20{,}000) + K_{2}/(s + 80{,}000)$, each term is the transform of an exponential, so $v(t)$ is the sum of a decaying $e^{-20{,}000t}$ term and a faster-decaying $e^{-80{,}000t}$ term.

examples.result: The response is overdamped: two real poles at −20,000 and −80,000 rad/s, so $v(t) = K_{1}e^{-20{,}000t} + K_{2}e^{-80{,}000t}$ — the coefficients fall out of the partial fractions of the next example’s technique.

examples.title: Partial fractions with distinct real roots (Nilsson Example 12.3)
examples.problem: Find the inverse Laplace transform of $$F(s) = \frac{96(s + 5)(s + 12)}{s(s + 8)(s + 6)}.$$

steps.label: Step 1: Set up the expansion
steps.text: $F(s) = K_{1}/s + K_{2}/(s + 8) + K_{3}/(s + 6)$ — one term per distinct root $0, -8, -6$.

steps.label: Step 2: Coefficient at s = 0
steps.text: Multiply by $s$ and evaluate at $s = 0$: $K_{1} = 96(5)(12)/[(8)(6)] = 120$.

steps.label: Step 3: Coefficients at s = −8 and s = −6
Step 4: Verify with a numerator root
steps.text: Testing the finished identity at $s = -5$ (a root of the numerator): $-24 - 24 + 48 = 0$ — both sides vanish, as they must.

examples.result: f(t) = (120 − 72e⁻⁸ᵗ + 48e⁻⁶ᵗ)u(t) — the algebraic skeleton of every distinct-real-root inversion.

examples.title: Mapping poles and zeros onto the s plane (Nilsson Example 12.8)

steps.label: Step 1: Extract the constants
steps.text: Factor 40 from the numerator and 4 from the denominator, leaving $10(s^{3} + 11s^{2} + 55s + 125)/[s(s^{3} + 22s^{2} + 220s + 1000)]$.

steps.label: Step 3: Read off poles and zeros
Step 4: Plot
steps.text: Mark X at each pole and O at each zero on the complex s plane — real axis horizontal, imaginary axis vertical. The conjugate pairs sit symmetrically about the real axis.

examples.result: Three zeros and four poles located; such pole–zero maps preview behaviour at a glance — poles on the real axis give pure exponentials, conjugate pairs give damped sinusoids, and imaginary-axis poles mean sustained oscillation.

keyTakeaways: The one-sided transform $F(s) = \int_{0^{-}}^{\infty} f(t)e^{-st} dt$ converts circuit integrodifferential equations into algebraic ones, with initial conditions built in through the $0^{-}$ limit.
Steps model switching; impulses model instant charge or flux transfer; $\mathcal{L}\{u(t)\} = 1/s$ and $\mathcal{L}\{\delta(t)\} = 1$ anchor the tables.
Differentiation multiplies by $s$ and subtracts $f(0^{-})$; integration divides by $s$ — the pair that linearizes dynamic circuit equations.
Time translation multiplies by $e^{-as}$; multiplying by $e^{-at}$ shifts $s$ to $s + a$ — the table doubles in size for free.
Inversion of proper rational functions is mechanical partial fractions, one term per root; verify by testing at a numerator root.
Poles (denominator roots) and zeros (numerator roots) plotted on the s plane summarize the entire natural behaviour of a response.
Check every solution with $\lim sF(s)$ as $s \to \infty$ (initial value) and $s \to 0$ (final value, valid only for left-half-plane poles).

quiz.q: The Laplace transform is called one-sided (unilateral) because:
options: It applies only to single-source circuits
Its integral runs from $0^{-}$ to $\infty$, ignoring $f(t)$ for negative time
Only one initial condition can be accommodated
It transforms only one equation at a time
quiz.explanation: The lower limit $0^{-}$ means $F(s)$ is determined by the behaviour of $f(t)$ for positive time only; whatever happened before $0^{-}$ enters through the initial conditions in the derivative theorem.

quiz.q: If $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then $\mathcal{L}\{df/dt\}$ equals:
quiz.explanation: One integration by parts on the defining integral gives $sF(s) - f(0^{-})$. The last option is the second derivative — which itself follows by applying the first-derivative rule twice.

quiz.q: The Laplace transform of the decaying exponential $e^{-at}$ is:
quiz.explanation: Direct integration: $\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-(a+s)t} dt = 1/(s + a)$. Combined with frequency translation, this single pair generates the entire damped family in Table 12.1.

quiz.q: The rational function $96(s+5)(s+12)/[s(s+8)(s+6)]$ of Nilsson Example 12.3 inverts to:
quiz.explanation: The residues are $K_{1} = 120$ at $s = 0$, $K_{2} = -72$ at $s = -8$ and $K_{3} = 48$ at $s = -6$; each term $K/(s + p)$ inverts to $Ke^{-pt}$.

quiz.q: The final-value theorem $\lim_{t\to\infty} f(t) = \lim_{s\to 0} sF(s)$ may be applied when:
options: Only when all poles of $F(s)$ except a first-order pole at the origin lie in the left half plane
Only when $f(t)$ contains an impulse at the origin
quiz.explanation: A right-half-plane pole means $f(t)$ grows without bound, and imaginary-axis poles mean sustained oscillation — neither has a final value. The initial-value theorem instead requires only that $f(t)$ contain no impulse at the origin.

intro: With the transform machinery built, Nilsson Chapter 13 turns it loose on circuits. Each element — resistor, inductor, capacitor — acquires an s-domain equivalent circuit whose initial stored energy appears as an extra source, and then everything from Chapter 2 through Chapter 4 revives: Ohm’s law, KCL, KVL, voltage division, Thévenin. The chapter culminates in the transfer function $H(s)$, the single rational expression that characterizes a circuit independent of its input, whose poles generate the transient response and whose evaluation at $s = j\omega$ delivers the sinusoidal steady state of Chapter 8 in one line.
objectives: Construct the series and parallel s-domain equivalent circuits for inductors and capacitors carrying initial energy
Apply the seven-step Laplace circuit-analysis method to RC, RLC and multi-mesh circuits
Derive transfer functions and interpret their poles and zeros
Separate the complete response into transient and steady-state parts via the poles of $H(s)$ and of $X(s)$
Compute the sinusoidal steady-state response directly from $H(j\omega)$

concepts.term: Circuit elements in the s domain
concepts.statement: Transforming each element’s defining equation gives: resistor $V = RI$; inductor $$V = sLI - LI_{0}$$ (impedance $sL$ in series with a source $LI_{0}$, or equivalently $sL$ in parallel with $I_{0}/s$); capacitor $$I = sCV - CV_{0}$$ (admittance $sC$ in parallel with a source $CV_{0}$, or impedance $1/sC$ in series with $V_{0}/s$).
concepts.detail: The three-step recipe for each element: write the time-domain terminal equation, Laplace-transform it, and build a circuit that satisfies the algebraic result. The initial-condition sources carry their own algebraic signs — $I_{0}$ is negative if the initial current opposes the reference direction, $V_{0}$ likewise. With zero initial energy both inductor and capacitor reduce to bare impedances $sL$ and $1/sC$.

concepts.term: Ohm’s law and Kirchhoff’s laws in the s domain
concepts.statement: With no initial energy, every passive element obeys $V = ZI$ where the s-domain impedances are $R$, $sL$ and $1/sC$ — **Ohm’s law in the s domain**. Because the transform of a sum is the sum of transforms, KCL and KVL hold unchanged for s-domain currents and voltages: $\sum I = 0$ at every node, $\sum V = 0$ around every loop.
concepts.detail: The consequence is total continuity of technique: series–parallel reduction, voltage and current division, node-voltage and mesh-current methods, source transformations and Thévenin–Norton equivalents — all of Chapters 2 through 4 — apply verbatim to s-domain circuits. The admittances are $1/R$, $1/sL$ and $sC$ siemens.

concepts.statement: Analysis Method 13.1: (1) determine the initial conditions from the $t < 0$ circuit; (2) transform the independent sources with Tables 12.1–12.2; (3) replace time-domain symbols by s-domain symbols; (4) transform the remaining elements with Table 13.1, representing initial conditions as sources; (5) analyse the s-domain circuit with resistive-circuit techniques; (6) check initial and final values with the theorems; (7) inverse-transform by partial fractions.
concepts.detail: The method yields the **complete** response — transient plus steady state — to any circuit whose sources have transforms. That is its decisive advantage over the phasor method of Chapter 8, which returns only the steady state. Step 6 is not optional bookkeeping: in Nilsson’s Example 13.2 the initial-value theorem correctly predicts $v_{o}(0^{+}) = 60\ \mathrm{V}$ and the final-value theorem gives zero, exactly as the physical circuit dictates.

concepts.statement: The **transfer function** is the s-domain ratio of output to input with **all initial conditions zero**: $$H(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{X(s)}.$$ A single circuit yields as many transfer functions as there are choices of input and output: for a series RLC driven by $V_{g}$, $I/V_{g} = sC/(s^{2}LC + RCs + 1)$ but $V/V_{g} = 1/(s^{2}LC + RCs + 1)$.
concepts.detail: The transfer function characterizes the circuit without revealing its components or their interconnection. With multiple sources, find the transfer function of each and superpose. And the impulse input unmasks it completely: $x(t) = \delta(t)$ gives $X(s) = 1$, hence $Y(s) = H(s)$ — the inverse transform of the transfer function is the unit-impulse response, which is also the circuit’s natural response.

concepts.term: Poles of H(s) versus poles of X(s)
concepts.statement: Since $Y(s) = H(s)X(s)$, the partial fraction expansion of the response contains one group of terms generated by the **poles of $H(s)$** — the transient, or natural, components — and one group generated by the **poles of $X(s)$** — the steady-state components that persist after the transients die.
concepts.detail: For a bounded output the poles of $H(s)$ must lie in the left half plane; zeros may lie in either half. Nilsson’s Example 13.10 makes the split visible: driving the Chapter 13.9 circuit with a ramp produces $v_{o} = [10\sqrt{5} \times 10^{-4} e^{-3000t}\cos(4000t + 79.70^\circ) + 10t - 4 \times 10^{-4}]u(t)\ \mathrm{V}$ — a decaying oscillation from the complex pole pair $-3000 \pm j4000$ of $H(s)$, and a ramp from the double pole at the origin of the input.

concepts.statement: If the input is delayed by $a$ seconds, $x(t - a)u(t - a)$ has transform $e^{-as}X(s)$, so the output becomes $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\{H(s)X(s)e^{-as}\} = y(t - a)u(t - a)$: **delaying the input delays the output by the same amount**. A circuit with this property is time invariant.
concepts.detail: Every lumped, linear, constant-parameter circuit — everything in this book — is time invariant. Together with the impulse-response result, this observation sets up the convolution integral: the impulse response $h(t)$ contains enough information to compute the response to any input whatsoever.

concepts.statement: For a sinusoidal input $x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$, the steady-state response is $$y_{ss}(t) = A|H(j\omega)|\cos[\omega t + \phi + \theta(\omega)],$$ where $|H(j\omega)|$ and $\theta(\omega)$ are the magnitude and angle of the transfer function evaluated at $s = j\omega$.
concepts.detail: The derivation needs only the two input poles at $\pm j\omega$; the left-half-plane poles of $H(s)$ contribute terms that decay to zero. Evaluating $H(s)$ on the imaginary axis therefore recovers the entire phasor analysis of Chapter 8 from a single rational function — the bridge between the transform method and frequency-response thinking, developed further in the filter chapters.

examples.title: Natural response of an RC circuit by Laplace (Nilsson Example 13.2)
examples.problem: A 100 V source has charged a 0.5 μF capacitor through 10 kΩ (switch at x). At $t = 0$ the switch moves to y, connecting the capacitor to a 240 kΩ resistor in parallel with a 60 kΩ resistor. Use the Laplace transform method to find $v_{o}(t)$ for $t \geq 0^{+}$.

steps.label: Step 1: Initial condition
steps.text: After a long time in position x the capacitor is an open circuit charged to $V_{0} = 100\ \mathrm{V}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Build the s-domain circuit
steps.text: The capacitor impedance is $1/sC = 2 \times 10^{6}/s\ \Omega$ in series with a source $V_{0}/s = 100/s\ \mathrm{V\text{-}s}$; the two load resistors combine to $240\,\mathrm{k}\Omega \parallel 60\,\mathrm{k}\Omega = 48\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Check with the limit theorems
steps.text: $\lim_{s \to \infty} sV_{o} = 60 = v_{o}(0^{+})$ and $\lim_{s \to 0} sV_{o} = 0 = v_{o}(\infty)$ — both match the physical circuit.

steps.label: Step 5: Invert
steps.text: $v_{o}(t) = \mathcal{L}^{-1}\{60/(s + 25)\} = 60e^{-25t}u(t)\ \mathrm{V}$, matching the first-order methods of Chapter 7.

examples.result: A single pole at −25 rad/s: the capacitor discharges through 48 kΩ with time constant 48 kΩ × 0.5 μF = 24 ms, exactly as Chapter 7 predicts.

examples.title: A two-mesh RL circuit solved as algebra (Nilsson Example 13.5)
examples.problem: A 336 V dc source closes through a switch at $t = 0$ into a network of $42\ \Omega$ in series with $8.4\ \mathrm{H}$, then $48\ \Omega$ in series with $10\ \mathrm{H}$ as the second mesh. No energy is stored initially. Find $i_{1}(t)$ and $i_{2}(t)$ for $t \geq 0$.

steps.label: Step 1: Transform the circuit
steps.text: The source becomes $336/s\ \mathrm{V\text{-}s}$; the inductors become $8.4s\ \Omega$ and $10s\ \Omega$ with no initial-condition sources.

steps.label: Step 2: Write the two mesh equations
Step 4: Verify the endpoints
steps.text: Initial-value theorem: both $sI_{1}$ and $sI_{2}$ vanish as $s \to \infty$, so both currents start at zero. Final-value theorem: $sI_{1} \to 40(9)/(2 \times 12) = 15\ \mathrm{A}$ and $sI_{2} \to 168/24 = 7\ \mathrm{A}$ — matching a dc circuit with both inductors shorted.
