With S positive and T negative across a p-type bar, holes drift through the crystal in the conventional current direction — from the positive electrode toward the negative — being created at S (as electrons leave into S) at exactly the rate they are neutralized at T.

concepts.statement: The carriers supplied by doping vastly outnumber those generated thermally: in **n-type** material electrons are the **majority carriers** and holes the **minority carriers**; in **p-type** material the roles reverse — holes majority, electrons minority.
concepts.detail: The thermally liberated pairs exist in both materials regardless of doping, but at room temperature their numbers are minute beside the doping density. Minority carriers are not a curiosity: they carry the whole reverse current of a diode (next section) and set the leakage that doubles with every few degrees of temperature rise.

concepts.statement: Carriers move by **diffusion** whenever there is a difference in concentration between adjacent regions, and by **drift** whenever there is a difference of potential between two regions — the distinction that governs everything the p–n junction does next.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s sentence is worth memorizing because the junction diode is built on it: diffusion is driven by concentration gradients, drift by electric fields. In the doped crystal under bias, both majority-carrier flows are drift; at the junction of the next section, diffusion initiates the barrier that drift then balances.

examples.title: How many majority carriers per minority carrier?
examples.problem: Silicon has about $5 \times 10^{28}$ atoms per cubic metre. Hughes’s typical doping is one donor atom in $10^8$. With $n_i \approx 1.5 \times 10^{16}$ per cubic metre at 300 K, compare the electron and hole densities in the doped n-type crystal.

steps.label: Step 1: Donor density
steps.text: One donor per $10^8$ silicon atoms gives $n \approx 5 \times 10^{28}/10^8 = 5 \times 10^{20}$ free electrons per cubic metre.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply mass action
steps.text: The hole density follows from $np = n_i^{2}$: $p = n_i^{2}/n = (1.5 \times 10^{16})^{2}/(5 \times 10^{20})$.

steps.label: Step 3: Evaluate
steps.text: $p = 2.25 \times 10^{32}/5 \times 10^{20} = 4.5 \times 10^{11}$ holes per cubic metre.

steps.label: Step 4: The ratio
steps.text: Majority to minority: $n/p = 5 \times 10^{20}/4.5 \times 10^{11} \approx 1.1 \times 10^{9}$ — electrons outnumber holes by more than a billion to one.

examples.result: A doping of one part in $10^8$ leaves holes at only $4.5 \times 10^{11}$ per cubic metre against $5 \times 10^{20}$ electrons: the minority population is about one in a billion, yet those few holes will carry the entire reverse current of the junction diode.

examples.title: Thermal doubling of minority-carrier current
examples.problem: Hughes notes that the reverse current of a silicon junction practically doubles for every 8 °C rise in temperature. A diode’s reverse current is 10 nA at 25 °C. Estimate its value at 85 °C.

steps.label: Step 1: Count the doublings
steps.text: The temperature rise is $85 - 25 = 60$ °C, which is $60/8 = 7.5$ doubling intervals.

steps.label: Step 2: Scale the current
steps.text: Each doubling multiplies the current by two, so $I(85\,^\circ\mathrm{C}) = 10\ \mathrm{nA} \times 2^{7.5}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Evaluate
steps.text: $2^{7.5} = 2^7 \times \sqrt{2} = 128 \times 1.41 \approx 181$, so the reverse current grows to about $1.8\ \mu\mathrm{A}$.

examples.result: A mere 60 °C of warming multiplies leakage by a factor of about 180 — from 10 nA to 1.8 μA. This is why silicon devices are specified to only 150–200 °C, and why the reverse current of the germanium diode, already a hundred times larger, doubles every 10 °C.

keyTakeaways: Silicon and germanium are tetravalent: four valence electrons per atom, crystallizing in the diamond lattice with cube sides near $2.7 \times 10^{-10}$ m (Si) and $2.8 \times 10^{-10}$ m (Ge).
Covalent bonds share electron pairs — eight electrons around each ion — and at absolute zero pure silicon or germanium is a perfect insulator; "pure" means impurities below one part in $10^{10}$.
Thermal agitation generates electron–hole pairs continuously, and mass action fixes their product: $np = n_i^{2}$, with $n_i \approx 1.5 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ for silicon at 300 K.

Pentavalent donors (P, As, Sb) at one part in $10^8$ give n-type material — fixed positive ions plus free electrons; trivalent acceptors (In, Ga, B, Al) give p-type material — fixed negative ions plus mobile holes.
Majority carriers come from doping; minority carriers from thermal pair generation — outnumbered a billion to one in typical n-type silicon, yet responsible for all reverse conduction.
Diffusion is driven by concentration differences, drift by potential differences — the two mechanisms that will build the p–n junction’s barrier.

quiz.q: Silicon is doped with a trace of antimony. The majority carriers are:
options: Electrons donated by the antimony’s fifth valence electron
quiz.explanation: Antimony is pentavalent: four of its five valence electrons complete the covalent bonds and the fifth is donated as a free electron, leaving a fixed positive ion — an n-type (negative-type) semiconductor.

quiz.q: A trivalent acceptor atom embedded in the silicon lattice carries, once its bonds are completed, a net charge of:
quiz.explanation: With all four covalent bonds completed the trivalent atom holds four valence electrons against its $3e$ nuclear charge of valence — a fixed negative ion of $-e$, balanced by the mobile positive hole it released into the crystal.

quiz.q: At absolute zero (−273 °C), pure silicon is:
options: A perfect insulator — no covalent bonds are broken
A semiconductor with resistance depending on doping
quiz.explanation: All valence electrons remain locked in covalent bonds at absolute zero, so there are no free carriers of either sign: perfect insulation. Conduction appears only as thermal energy begins breaking bonds.

quiz.q: In p-type silicon, the minority carriers are:
quiz.explanation: Doping with acceptors makes holes the majority carriers; the thermally generated electron–hole pairs still exist, so electrons remain as a small minority population — the carriers that will conduct under reverse bias.

quiz.q: An n-type crystal has electron density $n = 5 \times 10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. With $n_i = 1.5 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, the hole density is:
quiz.explanation: Mass action: $p = n_i^{2}/n = (1.5 \times 10^{16})^{2}/(5 \times 10^{20}) = 4.5 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ — a billion times fewer holes than electrons.

intro: Join a p-type crystal to an n-type crystal and something remarkable happens at the seam: carriers diffuse across, uncover fixed ions, and the junction charges itself into a barrier that current can pass in only one direction. Hughes builds the depletion layer and its barrier potential first with pictures, then with the Shockley equation — the exponential diode law that everything from rectifiers to transistor biasing rests on. This section adds the practical models that The Art of Electronics recommends for everyday design.
objectives: Explain how diffusion and drift create the depletion layer and the potential barrier at a p–n junction
Describe forward and reverse bias in terms of carrier motion, and define the saturation current
Apply the Shockley diode equation, including its 38.6 per volt exponent at room temperature
Use ideal, offset and piecewise-linear diode models for circuit work
Compare silicon and germanium static characteristics and their temperature behaviour

concepts.statement: When p-type and n-type regions share one crystal, holes **diffuse** from p into n and electrons from n into p — diffusion being the response to a concentration difference — leaving behind a thin region stripped of mobile carriers: the **depletion layer**, whose uncovered fixed ions (negative on the p side, positive on the n side) form a **potential barrier** that halts further migration.
concepts.detail: Both regions start neutral: mobile holes balanced by fixed negative ions on the p side, mobile electrons balanced by fixed positive ions on the n side. As carriers cross, region A (n-side edge of the junction) acquires excess negative charge and region B (p-side edge) excess positive charge; these repel further crossing. Hughes’s dictum from the previous section does the work: diffusion responds to concentration differences, drift to potential differences — at equilibrium the barrier’s drift exactly cancels the diffusion.

concepts.statement: The depletion layer’s barrier must be overcome before meaningful forward current flows: a silicon junction conducts appreciably at about **0.7 V** of forward bias — roughly **double** the corresponding germanium value, per Hughes’s comparison of the two static characteristics.
concepts.detail: This 0.6–0.7 V knee is visible in Hughes’s silicon characteristic curves as the voltage at which current turns steeply upward; germanium turns on near 0.3 V. The offset model of a diode — a 0.7 V battery in series with a small resistance — is the everyday engineering shorthand that this physics justifies.

concepts.statement: With the p side made positive (S positive relative to T), the field drives **holes toward the junction in the p-region and electrons toward the junction in the n-region**; the carriers combine at the junction while the external circuit supplies an electron at T and accepts one at S, sustaining hole flow on one side and electron flow on the other.
concepts.detail: For each recombination, an electron is liberated from a covalent bond near the positive plate S and enters that plate, creating a new hole that travels through the p-material to the junction; simultaneously an electron from the negative plate T enters the n-region and moves to the junction. The diode current is thus hole flow in the p-region, electron flow in the n-region, and a combination of both in the vicinity of the junction — the barrier is flattened, not removed.

concepts.term: Reverse bias and the saturation current
concepts.statement: With the polarity reversed, holes are drawn to the negative electrode and electrons to the positive one, widening the **depletion layer** until it contains virtually no carriers: the junction behaves as an insulator, and only the thermally generated **minority carriers** sustain a small, nearly bias-independent **saturation current** $I_s$.
concepts.detail: Between about 0.1 V of reverse bias and the breakdown voltage, the reverse current of a silicon diode stays close to $I_s$ — a few microamperes at most. In practice the current rises somewhat with bias, mostly through surface leakage; in a diode with negligible leakage it follows the ideal equation below. Raise the reverse voltage far enough and breakdown arrives — constructively, in the Zener diode of Section 12.4.

concepts.statement: The static characteristic of a junction diode with negligible surface leakage is $$i = I_s\left(e^{qv/kT} - 1\right),$$ where $q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C is the electronic charge, $k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K is Boltzmann’s constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature; at 300 K the exponent is $38.6v$, so $$i \approx 10\left(e^{38.6v} - 1\right)\ \mathrm{nA}$$ for $I_s = 10$ nA.
concepts.detail: The numbers are worth feeling in the fingers: at $v = +0.3$ V the current is about 1.1 mA; at +0.4 V, about 51 mA; and at $-0.1$ V, $e^{-3.86} \approx 0.021$, so $i \approx -9.8$ nA — within 2 per cent of $-I_s$: saturation is essentially complete at a tenth of a volt of reverse bias. Because the exponent is 38.6 per volt, every 60 mV of extra forward bias multiplies the current by ten ($38.6 \times 0.06 \times \log_{10} e \approx 1$). At 0.7 V the equation alone predicts absurd currents — real devices there are limited by bulk series resistance, which is why the practical knee sits near 0.7 V rather than anywhere the pure exponential would suggest.

concepts.statement: For circuit work the diode is layered into models: the **ideal switch** (zero forward drop, infinite reverse resistance); the **offset model** — a 0.7 V source in series with a small forward resistance; and the **piecewise-linear model**, such as Hughes’s exercise diode that conducts nothing below 600 mV and then behaves as a constant 20 Ω.
concepts.detail: The Art of Electronics counsels exactly this hierarchy: use the ideal switch for rough reasoning, the 0.6–0.7 V offset for most hand analysis, and refine with resistance when currents are large. For small-signal work the diode’s incremental (dynamic) resistance follows from differentiating the Shockley equation: $r_d = kT/qI \approx 26\ \Omega$ at 1 mA — halving with every doubling of current, a fact the tuned amplifiers of Chapter 13 exploit.

concepts.statement: Comparing the static characteristics: the silicon diode’s **forward voltage drop is roughly double** germanium’s; its reverse current is about **a hundredth** of germanium’s at the same temperature and voltage — and shows little saturation, growing roughly as the square root of reverse voltage until breakdown; silicon withstands higher reverse voltages and junction temperatures of 150–200 °C against germanium’s 75–90 °C.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s germanium rectifier withstood a peak inverse voltage of about 100 V at 20 °C ambient, and its reverse current roughly doubles every 10 °C rise — silicon’s doubles every 8 °C but from a far smaller base. These comparisons are why silicon conquered the industry: less leakage, more voltage, more heat tolerance.

concepts.statement: One classic construction: a thin **n-type wafer** — its area proportional to the current rating — soldered to a copper plate, with an **indium bead** alloyed onto its upper face by heat treatment to form the p-region; a copper electrode is soldered to the bead during the same treatment, and the element is hermetically sealed in an opaque container against light and moisture.
concepts.detail: The opaque canister matters doubly: light generates electron–hole pairs exactly as heat does (the photodiode of Section 12.4 makes a virtue of this), and moisture corrodes the junction. Modern silicon diodes use planar diffusion for the same geometry, but the alloy-junction picture explains the diode symbol’s arrow-and-bar: easy flow toward the bar, blocked flow away from it.

examples.title: Working the diode equation — Hughes’s $I_s = 10$ nA silicon junction
examples.problem: A silicon junction diode with negligible surface leakage has a saturation current of 10 nA. Using the Shockley equation at 300 K, evaluate the current at forward biases of 0.3 V and 0.4 V, and at a reverse bias of 0.1 V.

steps.label: Step 2: Forward 0.3 V
steps.text: The exponent is $38.6 \times 0.3 = 11.58$, and $e^{11.58} \approx 1.07 \times 10^{5}$, so $i \approx 10\ \mathrm{nA} \times 1.07 \times 10^{5} \approx 1.1\ \mathrm{mA}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Forward 0.4 V
steps.text: Now the exponent is 15.44, $e^{15.44} \approx 5.1 \times 10^{6}$, so $i \approx 51\ \mathrm{mA}$ — ten times more current for 100 mV more bias: the 60 mV per decade rule in action (and 0.3 V plus two of those decades is 0.42 V).

steps.label: Step 4: Reverse 0.1 V
steps.text: The exponent is $-3.86$, $e^{-3.86} \approx 0.021$, so $i = 10\,(0.021 - 1) = -9.8$ nA — within 2 per cent of $-I_s$: reverse saturation is effectively reached at just a tenth of a volt.

examples.result: About 1.1 mA at 0.3 V, 51 mA at 0.4 V and $-9.8$ nA at $-0.1$ V: a billion-fold change of current over seven tenths of a volt — the exponential that makes the diode both a rectifier and (differentially) a 26 Ω-at-1 mA resistor.

examples.title: A piecewise-linear diode — Hughes’s Exercise 19.10 device
examples.problem: A silicon diode has effectively infinite reverse resistance. In the forward direction no current flows until the voltage exceeds 600 mV, whereupon the junction behaves as a constant resistance of 20 Ω. Determine the current and the dissipation at a forward voltage of 0.72 V, and at 1.0 V.

steps.label: Step 1: State the model
steps.text: Below 0.6 V: open circuit. Above 0.6 V: the terminal voltage is the 0.6 V knee plus the drop on 20 Ω, so $i = (v - 0.6)/20$ in amperes when $v$ is in volts.

steps.label: Step 3: Dissipation at 0.72 V
steps.text: $P = vi = 0.72 \times 6 \times 10^{-3} = 4.3\ \mathrm{mW}$ — of which $i^{2} \times 20 = 0.72$ mW is in the resistance and 3.6 mW at the knee.

steps.label: Step 4: Current at 1.0 V
steps.text: $i = (1.0 - 0.6)/20 = 0.4/20 = 20\ \mathrm{mA}$, with $P = 20\ \mathrm{mW}$ — the piecewise model’s knee plus slope is doing the work the full exponential did in the previous example, at a fraction of the effort.

examples.result: 6 mA at 0.72 V (4.3 mW) and 20 mA at 1.0 V (20 mW). The piecewise-linear model is the engineer’s daily tool: it captures the 0.6 V threshold and the internal resistance without exponentials.

keyTakeaways: Diffusion across the junction uncovers fixed ions and creates the depletion layer — a potential barrier that equilibrates the tendency of carriers to diffuse.

Forward bias flattens the barrier: holes flow in the p-region, electrons in the n-region, recombining at the junction; reverse bias widens the depletion layer until only minority carriers remain, giving the tiny saturation current $I_s$.

The Shockley equation $i = I_s(e^{qv/kT} - 1)$ governs the static characteristic; at 300 K the exponent is $38.6v$, so current scales tenfold per 60 mV and saturates within 2 per cent of $-I_s$ by $-0.1$ V.
Practical models ladder from ideal switch to 0.7 V offset to piecewise knee-plus-resistance; the small-signal resistance is $r_d \approx 26$ mV divided by the current.

Silicon beats germanium on every axis that matters: half the forward drop next door, one-hundredth the reverse current, higher reverse voltage ratings and 150–200 °C against 75–90 °C of temperature tolerance.
Reverse current roughly doubles every 8 °C for silicon (every 10 °C for germanium) — leakage is a thermal design constraint, not a footnote.

quiz.q: The forward "knee" voltage of a silicon junction diode is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Silicon turns on near 0.7 V — roughly double germanium’s 0.3 V, which is Hughes’s own way of stating the comparison between the two static characteristics.

quiz.q: In the Shockley equation at room temperature, each additional 60 mV of forward bias multiplies the current by about:
quiz.explanation: The exponent $qv/kT = 38.6v$ grows by $38.6 \times 0.06 \approx 2.3 = \ln 10$ for every 60 mV, so the current climbs one decade per 60 mV — the steepest fact of diode life.

quiz.q: Under reverse bias, the current that flows through a p–n junction is carried by:
options: The few thermally generated minority carriers on each side
Holes tunnelling from the metal contact
quiz.explanation: Reverse bias widens the depletion layer until it is empty of majority carriers; only the thermally generated minority carriers — electrons in p-material, holes in n-material — drift across, giving the small saturation current $I_s$.

quiz.q: Compared with a germanium diode at the same temperature and voltage, a silicon diode’s reverse current is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Hughes’s comparison: silicon’s reverse current is roughly one-hundredth of germanium’s — though it shows less saturation, growing about as the square root of reverse voltage until breakdown approaches.

quiz.q: A diode’s incremental (dynamic) resistance at 1 mA forward current, near room temperature, is about:
quiz.explanation: Differentiating the Shockley equation gives $r_d = kT/qI \approx 26\ \mathrm{mV}/I$: at 1 mA that is 26 Ω, halving for every doubling of current.

quiz.q: A silicon junction at room temperature has reverse saturation current 10 pA and thermal voltage 25.85 mV. With 0.60 V forward bias and ideality factor unity, the forward current is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $I_{s} = 10$ pA, $V_{D} = 0.60$ V, $V_{T} = 25.85$ mV, $η = 1$. Step 2 — Governing law: $I_{D} = I_{s}(e^{\frac{V_{D}}{η V_{T}}} - 1)$, exponential because the barrier falls linearly with applied volts. Step 3 — Algebra: exponent $\frac{0.60}{0.02585} \approx 23.21$; $e^{23.21} \approx 1.20 \times 10^{10}$; $I_{D} \approx 10^{-11} \times 1.20 \times 10^{10} = 0.12$ A, that is $120$ mA. Step 4 — Sanity check: hundreds of millivolts giving hundreds of milliamperes matches power-junction scales, a $60$ mV rise would decade the current, and reverse bias would collapse it to $-I_{s}$. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 12 mA and 1.2 mA each miss a decade of the exponent, while 1.2 A adds one decade too many. Step 6 — Conclude: about 120 mA flows.

intro: A diode passes current in one direction only, so an alternating voltage forces it to conduct on just one half-cycle — or, with more diodes, on both. Hughes’s rectifier chapter turns that single fact into d.c. supplies: half-wave and full-wave circuits with their average and r.m.s. values, the bridge that gets the transformer working full time, and the smoothing capacitor that converts pulsating d.c. into something usable. The Art of Electronics then adds the supply-builder’s reality checks — ripple arithmetic, peak currents and worst-case design — that turn textbook rectifiers into working power supplies.
objectives: Derive the mean and r.m.s. load current and voltage for half-wave and full-wave rectifiers
Explain the bridge rectifier’s advantages over the centre-tapped full-wave circuit, and compare their peak inverse voltages
Analyse the capacitor-input smoothing filter: conduction angle, exponential discharge and the CR criterion
Compute ripple factors and size a smoothing capacitor for a specified ripple
Apply worst-case supply design wisdom from The Art of Electronics

concepts.statement: **Rectification** is the process of obtaining unidirectional current or voltage from an alternating supply; the ideal diode has zero forward voltage drop and infinite reverse resistance, so the loop equation of the half-wave circuit is $v = v_d + iR$, with the whole supply voltage appearing across the load while conducting and across the diode while blocked.
concepts.detail: A single diode in series with the load passes current on alternate half-cycles only: half-wave rectification. The load current and load voltage are unidirectional — "direct", though the term is usually reserved for steady quantities. Real diode characteristics (Section 12.2) add a small forward drop during conduction; the idealized characteristic sets the analysis pattern that all the averages below build on.

concepts.statement: For a half-wave rectifier supplying $v = V_m \sin\omega t$ to a resistive load, $$I_{\mathrm{dc}} = \frac{I_m}{\pi} = 0.318\,I_m, \qquad I_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{I_m}{2},$$ with matching voltage relations $V_{\mathrm{dc}} = V_m/\pi$ and $V_{\mathrm{rms}} = V_m/2$; the maximum efficiency is $4/\pi^{2} = 0.405$.
concepts.detail: The mean is taken over the full period (the diode conducts only from 0 to $\pi$); the efficiency compares the d.c. power in the load with the total power $I_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}(r_d + R)$, so any forward diode resistance drags 40.5 per cent downward. The **peak inverse voltage (PIV)** — the largest reverse voltage across the diode, which must stay below breakdown — equals approximately the peak supply voltage $V_m$, since the reverse resistance is much greater than the load resistance.

concepts.statement: A transformer with a **centre tap** feeds two diodes that conduct on alternate half-cycles, delivering both halves of the wave to the load: $$I_{\mathrm{dc}} = \frac{2I_m}{\pi} = 0.637\,I_m, \qquad I_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{I_m}{\sqrt{2}},$$ with efficiency $8/\pi^{2} = 0.81$ — but each diode must withstand a **PIV of $2V_m$**.
concepts.detail: When A is positive with respect to the centre tap C, so is C positive with respect to B: diode $D_1$ conducts while $D_2$ blocks, and the roles reverse on the next half-cycle, the load current keeping one direction throughout. The ripple now repeats at twice the supply frequency — a fact the smoothing capacitor will exploit. The cost: the centre-tapped secondary uses each half of its winding only half of the time.

concepts.statement: Four diodes in a bridge conduct in diagonal pairs — $D_1$ and $D_3$ on one half-cycle, $D_2$ and $D_4$ on the other — giving full-wave output with the same averages and 81 per cent efficiency, but with **PIV of only $V_m$**, and either half the secondary turns for a given output or twice the output for a given diode rating.
concepts.detail: At any instant two diodes conduct, so two forward drops appear in the path — the bridge’s only tax. The current drawn from the supply is purely alternating while the load current is unidirectional: the bridge separates the two halves of the transformer winding’s duty, using the winding all of the time and dispensing with the centre tap altogether.

concepts.statement: A capacitor across the load charges to nearly the supply peak and then discharges exponentially through the load, $$v_R = V\,e^{-(t - t_2)/CR},$$ with the diode conducting only in a short interval around each voltage peak — requiring a time constant $CR$ much longer than the supply period to keep the ripple small.
concepts.detail: The diode conducts while the supply voltage exceeds the load voltage; its current must supply both the load and the capacitor ($i_C = C\,dv/dt$), and analysis of the cut-off gives $\omega t_2 = \pi - \phi$ with $\tan\phi = \omega CR$ — so for $\omega CR \gg 1$ the diode stops conducting almost exactly at the peak. The warning that travels with the formula: the peak diode current increases with $C$, and the maximum allowable diode peak current must not be exceeded. Full-wave circuits halve the discharge interval, roughly halving the ripple for the same capacitor.

concepts.statement: The ripple factor measures the a.c. content of the rectified output, $$\gamma = \sqrt{\left(\frac{I_{\mathrm{rms}}}{I_{\mathrm{dc}}}\right)^{2} - 1},$$ giving $\gamma = 1.21$ for half-wave and $\gamma = 0.482$ for full-wave rectification of a sine wave; with a smoothing capacitor the peak-to-peak ripple is estimated as $\Delta V \approx I_{\mathrm{dc}}/f_r C$, with $f_r$ the ripple frequency (once the supply frequency for half-wave, twice for full-wave).
concepts.detail: Half-wave: $\sqrt{(0.5/0.318)^2 - 1} = \sqrt{1.467} = 1.21$ — more a.c. than d.c. Full-wave: $\sqrt{(0.707/0.637)^2 - 1} = 0.482$. The capacitor estimate follows from charge conservation: the capacitor loses $I_{\mathrm{dc}}$ amps for about $1/f_r$ seconds between charging pulses, so $C\,\Delta V \approx I_{\mathrm{dc}}/f_r$. It is the formula The Art of Electronics wants you to carry in your head.

concepts.statement: Beyond the single shunt capacitor, practical smoothing uses a **series inductor** (high impedance at ripple frequency, low resistance to d.c.), an **LC filter**, the **$\pi$ filter** (capacitor–inductor–capacitor), and the **resistive filter** where a resistor replaces the inductor in low-current applications.
concepts.detail: The design principle Hughes states: put a low impedance at the ripple frequency that presents high resistance to direct current (a capacitor) in parallel with the load, and a high impedance at the ripple frequency with low d.c. resistance (an inductor) in series with the load. The resistive filter trades some d.c. voltage for economy — the resistor drops direct voltage too — but a resistor is far cheaper than a ferromagnetic-cored inductor when currents are small.

concepts.statement: The Art of Electronics’ supply-building lore: size the ripple for the **worst case** — lowest a.c. line, maximum load — and verify that the trough of the ripple still leaves headroom for any regulator; expect the transformer secondary to read well above its rated voltage when lightly loaded; and remember that the rectifier current flows in short, tall pulses near the peaks.
concepts.detail: The peak charging current is far larger than the d.c. output — the capacitor’s entire lost charge must be replaced in the brief conduction interval (Hughes’s $i_C = Cv$ observation in disguise) — so diodes are chosen by surge rating as well as average current, and transformer heating follows the r.m.s. of the spiky current, not its average. Mains tolerance of ±10 per cent on both sides of the line compounds with load variation: a supply that works only at nominal line and half load is not a supply, it is a demo.

examples.title: Bridge rectifier from the mains — Hughes’s Example 20.1
examples.problem: The four diodes in a bridge rectifier have negligible forward resistances and infinite reverse resistances. The alternating supply is 230 V r.m.s. and the resistive load is 46.0 Ω. Calculate (a) the mean load current, (b) the rectifier efficiency.

steps.label: Step 1: Peak current
steps.text: The peak supply voltage is $\sqrt{2} \times 230$ V, so $I_m = \sqrt{2} \times 230/46.0 = 7.07\ \mathrm{A}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Mean load current
steps.text: Full-wave averaging: $I_{\mathrm{dc}} = 2I_m/\pi = 2 \times 7.07/\pi = 4.5\ \mathrm{A}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Efficiency
steps.text: $\eta = I_{\mathrm{dc}}^{2}R/I_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}R = 4.5^{2}/5.0^{2} = 20.25/25 = 0.81$ — the full-wave maximum, 81 per cent, because the diode forward resistances are nil.

examples.result: A mean load current of 4.5 A at 81 per cent efficiency from a 230 V, 46 Ω bridge. Each diode needs a PIV rating of at least the peak supply, $\sqrt{2} \times 230 \approx 325$ V.

examples.title: Battery-charging rectifier — Hughes’s Example 20.2
examples.problem: In a battery-charging circuit, a diode with negligible forward resistance and infinite reverse resistance feeds a 100 V battery in series with a variable resistance R from a supply $v = 200\sin\omega t$ V. Find the value of R that gives a mean charging current of 1.0 A.

steps.label: Step 1: Find the conduction interval
steps.text: The diode conducts only while the supply exceeds the battery: $200\sin\omega t > 100$, i.e. $\sin\omega t > 0.5$, so conduction runs from $\omega t = \pi/6$ to $5\pi/6$.

steps.label: Step 2: Instantaneous current during conduction
steps.text: $i = (200\sin\omega t - 100)/R$, and zero outside the interval.

steps.label: Step 3: Set up the mean
steps.text: Averaging over the full period: $1.0 = \frac{1}{2\pi R}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}(200\sin\omega t - 100)\,d(\omega t)$.

steps.label: Step 4: Evaluate the integral
steps.text: The sine term contributes $200[\,-\cos\omega t\,]$ between the limits $= 200\sqrt{3}$; the constant term removes $100 \times 2\pi/3$. So the numerator is $200\sqrt{3} - 200\pi/3 \approx 346.4 - 209.4 = 137.0$.

examples.result: $R = 21.8$ Ω. The diode conducts for only a third of each cycle, so the peak charging current is far above the 1 A mean — exactly the pulse-shaped rectifier current that diode surge ratings exist for.

examples.title: Sizing the smoothing capacitor
examples.problem: A full-wave bridge runs from 50 Hz mains and must deliver about 12 V d.c. at 100 mA with no more than 1.2 V of peak-to-peak ripple. Size the smoothing capacitor, and check Hughes’s time-constant criterion.

steps.label: Step 1: Ripple frequency
steps.text: Full-wave rectification doubles the ripple frequency: $f_r = 2 \times 50 = 100$ Hz, so the capacitor is recharged every 10 ms.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply the ripple estimate
steps.text: $\Delta V \approx I_{\mathrm{dc}}/f_r C$, so the required capacitance is $C \ge I_{\mathrm{dc}}/(f_r\,\Delta V) = 0.1/(100 \times 1.2) = 833\ \mu\mathrm{F}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Choose the standard value
steps.text: The next standard value up is 1000 μF, which yields $\Delta V = 0.1/(100 \times 1000 \times 10^{-6}) = 1.0\ \mathrm{V}$ of ripple — inside the specification.

steps.label: Step 4: Check the time constant
steps.text: The load resistance is $R = 12/0.1 = 120\ \Omega$, so $CR = 1000 \times 10^{-6} \times 120 = 0.12$ s — twelve times the 10 ms between charging pulses, comfortably satisfying Hughes’s $CR \gg$ period criterion.

steps.label: Step 5: Mind the peak current
steps.text: The 100 mA removed between peaks is restored in a short pulse near each voltage maximum — the peak diode current is several times the mean, so the diodes’ surge rating, not their average rating, chooses the parts.

examples.result: A 1000 μF capacitor holds the ripple to about 1 V peak-to-peak at full load — with the discharge so nearly linear that the exponential sag differs from the estimate by only a few per cent. Design at worst case: minimum line, maximum load.

keyTakeaways: Half-wave rectification delivers $I_{\mathrm{dc}} = I_m/\pi = 0.318\,I_m$ at up to 40.5 per cent efficiency, with the diode seeing a PIV of about $V_m$.
Full-wave rectification doubles the harvest: $I_{\mathrm{dc}} = 2I_m/\pi = 0.637\,I_m$ at up to 81 per cent efficiency — but the centre-tapped circuit demands a PIV of $2V_m$ from each diode.
The bridge gets the same averages with PIV of only $V_m$, half the secondary turns and no centre tap — at the price of two forward drops in series with the load.

Ripple factors are 1.21 (half-wave) and 0.482 (full-wave) before smoothing; the capacitor-input filter then obeys $\Delta V \approx I_{\mathrm{dc}}/f_r C$ with $f_r$ at twice line frequency for full-wave circuits.
The smoothing capacitor needs $CR$ far longer than the period, and its charging current flows in short tall pulses — the peak diode current grows with $C$.
Worst-case supply design: lowest line, heaviest load sets the ripple trough; highest line, lightest load sets the peak voltage the filter and any regulator must survive.
Series inductors, LC, $\pi$ and RC sections extend smoothing when one capacitor is not enough — low impedance across the load, high impedance in series with it.

quiz.q: A half-wave rectifier delivers a peak load current $I_m$. Its mean load current is:
quiz.explanation: Averaging the sine over the full period while the diode conducts only half of it: $I_{\mathrm{dc}} = I_m/\pi = 0.318\,I_m$. The doubled value belongs to full-wave circuits, and $I_m/2$ is the half-wave r.m.s.

quiz.q: For the same transformer secondary voltage, compare the peak inverse voltage faced by the diodes of the centre-tapped full-wave circuit and the bridge:
quiz.explanation: In the centre-tapped circuit the non-conducting diode sees the whole secondary — both halves — so $2V_m$; in the bridge each blocking diode sees only the supply peak $V_m$, one of several reasons bridges won.

quiz.q: The maximum theoretical rectification efficiency of a full-wave rectifier with ideal diodes is:
quiz.explanation: $\eta = (2/\pi)^{2} \times 2 = 8/\pi^{2} = 0.81$: the d.c. power $I_{\mathrm{dc}}^{2}R$ divided by the total $I_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}R$. Any diode forward resistance reduces it, which is why the half-wave ceiling is only $4/\pi^{2} = 0.405$.

quiz.q: Increasing the smoothing capacitance in a capacitor-input filter:
options: Reduces the ripple but increases the peak diode current
Reduces both ripple and peak diode current
Increases ripple while protecting the diode
Has no effect until the load changes
quiz.explanation: More capacitance holds the load voltage up longer — less ripple — but the charge lost between peaks must be replaced in an even shorter conduction interval near the peak, so the diode current pulses grow taller and narrower. Hughes’s warning: the maximum allowable diode peak current must not be exceeded.

quiz.q: A full-wave supply delivers 0.5 A at 100 Hz ripple with a 2200 μF capacitor. The approximate peak-to-peak ripple is:
quiz.explanation: $\Delta V \approx I/(f_r C) = 0.5/(100 \times 2200 \times 10^{-6}) = 0.5/0.22 = 2.3$ V — charge divided by capacitance, per ripple period.

quiz.q: A full-wave bridge fed from a 12 V RMS 50 Hz secondary drives a 100 Ω load through a 2200 μF reservoir capacitor. Allowing about 0.7 V per diode, the peak-to-peak ripple is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: secondary $12$ V RMS, $f = 50$ Hz full-wave so $100$ Hz ripple rate, $R = 100$ Ω, $C = 2200$ μF. Step 2 — Governing estimate: peak output $V_{p} \approx \sqrt{2}V_{rms} - 2V_{D}$ and ripple $V_{r} \approx \frac{I_{dc}}{2fC}$ with $I_{dc} \approx \frac{V_{p}}{R}$. Step 3 — Algebra: $V_{p} \approx 16.97 - 1.4 = 15.57$ V; $I_{dc} \approx 0.156$ A; $V_{r} \approx \frac{0.156}{100 \times 2200 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 0.709$ V. Step 4 — Sanity check: ripple is a few per cent of the rail, doubling $C$ would halve it, and half-wave would double it. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 1.42 V is the half-wave value, 0.36 V doubles the capacitance, and 0.18 V quadruples it. Step 6 — Conclude: ripple is about 0.71 V peak-to-peak.

intro: Breakdown in a diode is normally a failure — unless you design for it. Run a junction into reverse avalanche at a controlled voltage and it becomes a voltage reference; forward-bias a compound semiconductor and it emits light; reverse-bias it in the dark and it measures light instead. Hughes closes his diode chapter with the Zener voltage stabilizer, and The Art of Electronics supplies the catalogue of special-purpose devices — varactors, Schottkys, fast-recovery rectifiers — that fill a practising engineer’s drawer.
objectives: Explain avalanche breakdown and why a Zener diode holds a nearly constant reference voltage
Design a Zener shunt regulator, including its worst-case current and power checks
Describe LED emission and photodiode detection, and size an LED’s current-limiting resistor
Explain the varactor’s voltage-controlled capacitance and its tuning role
State the advantages of Schottky and fast-recovery diodes for high-frequency and switching service

concepts.term: Avalanche breakdown and the Zener diode
concepts.statement: Raise the reverse voltage across a p–n junction far enough and the accelerating carriers dislodge further carriers, which dislodge more in turn — **avalanche breakdown**, a rapid increase of current at a sharply defined voltage; **Zener (voltage regulator) diodes** are built to break down reversely at a chosen voltage between about 4 V and 75 V and to hold that **reference voltage** practically constant over a wide current range.
concepts.detail: The power of a large reverse current, sustained, would ruin an ordinary diode — the regulator diode instead dissipates it steadily, provided the maximum permissible junction temperature is respected. Forward biased, the Zener diode behaves as an ordinary diode; with small reverse bias it shows only the usual microampere leakage until, at the breakdown voltage, ionization by collision multiplies the carriers and the current rises abruptly.

concepts.statement: A Zener diode in parallel with the load, fed through a series resistor R from a variable source, holds the output at $V_z$: the resistor is sized so that at the **worst-case low input and full load** the Zener still draws its knee current, $$R = \frac{V_{\mathrm{in(min)}} - V_z}{I_{z(\mathrm{min})} + I_{L(\mathrm{max})}},$$ and the Zener must survive the opposite extreme of **high input and no load**, when it carries $$I_z = \frac{V_{\mathrm{in}} - V_z}{R}$$ alone.
concepts.detail: This is Hughes’s stabilizer of Fig. 20.12 — variable voltage in, constant voltage out — with the two worst cases made explicit. The Zener absorbs whatever current the load does not: load current up, Zener current down, and the resistor’s drop stays fixed so the output stays put. The price is standing dissipation in R and in the diode, which is why shunt regulation suits references and light loads rather than power supplies.

concepts.statement: The Art of Electronics’ Zener lore: the temperature coefficient of the breakdown voltage crosses zero near **5.6 V** — below that, true Zener (tunnelling) breakdown has a negative coefficient, above it, avalanche breakdown a positive one — so 5.6 V parts make the best references; and the diode’s **dynamic resistance** (a few ohms to tens of ohms) sets how stiff the regulation really is.
concepts.detail: A high-voltage Zener can be temperature-compensated by stacking a forward diode in series with it. For precision work the Zener has been superseded by band-gap references, but for a quick, robust, one-component reference it remains unbeatable — provided you respect the dissipation limits computed in the worst-case design.

concepts.statement: An **LED** is a forward-biased junction of a III–V compound semiconductor (GaAs, GaAsP, GaN families) in which recombination across the band gap releases energy as photons: the forward voltage is set by the material — roughly 1.6–2 V for red, up to 3–4 V for blue and white — and the light output follows the forward current, set by a **series resistor** $R = (V_s - V_f)/I_f$.
concepts.detail: A 5 V supply driving a red LED of 1.8 V at 10 mA needs $R = 3.2/0.01 = 320$ Ω — choose the standard 330 Ω, which gives 9.7 mA. Hughes’s fibre chapter meets LEDs again as light sources: cheaper and longer-lived than diode lasers, able to feed larger cores, but unable to operate as quickly, and coupling about two orders of magnitude less power into a single-mode fibre with two orders wider spectral width.

concepts.statement: A **photodiode** is a junction operated in **reverse bias**: photons with enough energy generate electron–hole pairs in and near the depletion layer, and the resulting photocurrent — proportional to the incident light over a wide range — flows as increased reverse current.
concepts.detail: The material fixes the spectral window: silicon responds near 0.8 μm, germanium near 1.2 μm — Hughes’s fibre-receiver pairing. Run the diode into a high impedance and it acts photovoltaically; the reverse-biased photoconductive mode is faster and linear. The complete optical receiver is a photodetector plus amplifier: the photodetector’s electrical output is weak, so the amplifier (and, for digital signals, signal clean-up) completes the receiver of Fig. 27.10.

concepts.statement: A **varactor** uses the depletion layer of a reverse-biased junction as a capacitor whose plate separation — the layer width — grows with reverse voltage: the junction capacitance falls as the bias rises, giving a voltage-controlled capacitance for electronic tuning.
concepts.detail: Because the reverse current is negligible, the varactor wastes no power and adds no noise worth mentioning — virtues that make it the tuning element of radio and television receivers, where a tuning voltage sweeps the resonant frequency of the LC circuits of Chapter 9. It also serves as a signal multiplier and in parametric amplification.

concepts.statement: A **Schottky diode** is a metal–semiconductor junction: conduction is by majority carriers alone, so there is no minority-carrier storage to discharge — it switches essentially instantly, with a forward drop of only about 0.3–0.4 V; **fast-recovery** junction diodes trade lifetime control (gold doping) for shortened recovery at the cost of higher leakage.
concepts.detail: The Schottky’s speed and low drop make it the rectifier of switching supplies and high-frequency detectors, and it powered Schottky TTL logic; its taxes are higher reverse leakage and lower reverse-voltage ratings. Where a p–n structure must be kept (for voltage rating), fast- and ultrafast-recovery parts with recovery times from hundreds of nanoseconds down to tens of nanoseconds do the switching-supply work.

examples.title: Designing a Zener shunt regulator
examples.problem: A rectified and smoothed source varies between 12 V and 15 V. Design a shunt regulator using a 9 V Zener to supply a load that draws up to 10 mA, assuming the Zener needs at least 5 mA to stay past its knee.

steps.label: Step 1: Size the resistor at the low-line, full-load extreme
steps.text: The resistor must pass the load plus the knee current when the input is at its minimum: $R = (V_{\mathrm{in(min)}} - V_z)/(I_{z(\mathrm{min})} + I_{L(\mathrm{max})}) = (12 - 9)/(5 + 10)\ \mathrm{mA} = 3/0.015 = 200\ \Omega$.

steps.label: Step 2: Check the Zener at the opposite extreme
steps.text: At 15 V input with the load disconnected, the Zener carries everything: $I_z = (15 - 9)/200 = 30\ \mathrm{mA}$, dissipating $P_z = 9 \times 0.03 = 270$ mW — a 0.5 W device is comfortable.

steps.label: Step 3: Check the series resistor
steps.text: Worst case for R is also 15 V at no load: $P_R = (15 - 9)^{2}/200 = 36/200 = 0.18$ W — again comfortably inside a 0.5 W rating.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify regulation at the design point
steps.text: At 12 V input and full 10 mA load the resistor passes $(12-9)/200 = 15$ mA: exactly 10 mA to the load and 5 mA to the Zener — the knee condition, just met.

examples.result: A 200 Ω series resistor with a 9 V, 0.5 W Zener regulates 12–15 V down to a steady 9 V for loads up to 10 mA. Remove the load at 15 V input and the Zener alone absorbs 30 mA — precisely the case that destroys undersized regulators.

examples.title: Choosing an LED series resistor
examples.problem: A red LED with a forward voltage of about 1.8 V is to run at 10 mA from a 5 V logic supply. Choose the series resistor and verify its dissipation.

steps.label: Step 2: Choose the standard value
steps.text: The nearest E12 value above 320 Ω is 330 Ω, giving $I = (5 - 1.8)/330 = 9.7\ \mathrm{mA}$ — within 3 per cent of target.

steps.label: Step 3: Dissipation
steps.text: The resistor drops 3.2 V at 9.7 mA: $P_R = 3.2 \times 9.7\ \mathrm{mA} \approx 31$ mW, and the LED dissipates $1.8 \times 9.7\ \mathrm{mA} \approx 17$ mW — both trivial for standard parts.

steps.label: Step 4: Sanity check the margin
steps.text: If the supply rises to 5.2 V, the current grows only to $(5.2 - 1.8)/330 = 10.3$ mA: the LED’s steep exponential is isolated from the supply by the resistor, which is exactly its job.

examples.result: A 330 Ω resistor runs the red LED at about 9.7 mA from 5 V — bright, safe and self-stabilizing, since the resistor absorbs all supply variation.

keyTakeaways: Avalanche breakdown multiplies carriers by collision; Zener (voltage regulator) diodes exploit it, holding a reference voltage of 4–75 V essentially constant over a wide current range below the maximum junction temperature.
Shunt regulation trades power for simplicity: $R = (V_{\mathrm{in(min)}} - V_z)/(I_{z(\mathrm{min})} + I_{L(\mathrm{max})})$, then verify the Zener at maximum input with no load.
The Zener temperature coefficient crosses zero near 5.6 V — tunnelling below, avalanche above — making 5.6 V the classic reference choice.
LEDs emit on forward recombination with material-set voltages (1.6–2 V red, 3–4 V blue and white); always feed them through a series resistor.
Photodiodes detect in reverse bias with photocurrent proportional to illumination — silicon for 0.8 μm, germanium for 1.2 μm — and form the front end of every optical receiver.

Varactors turn the depletion layer into a voltage-controlled capacitance for tuning; Schottky diodes add majority-carrier speed and a 0.3–0.4 V drop for high-frequency service, with fast-recovery p–n parts covering the high-voltage switching needs.

quiz.q: In normal operation, a Zener voltage regulator diode spends its working life:
options: Reverse biased, in controlled breakdown at its reference voltage
Alternating between forward and reverse bias each cycle
quiz.explanation: The regulator diode is deliberately run into reverse breakdown, where ionization by collision makes the current rise steeply while the voltage barely moves — a constant reference. Forward biased, it is just an ordinary diode.

quiz.q: The worst case for Zener dissipation in a shunt regulator is:
options: Minimum input voltage with maximum load
Maximum input voltage with no load
Any input, since dissipation is constant
quiz.explanation: With the load removed, the current the load would have taken all diverts into the Zener, while a high input pushes the resistor current to its maximum: $I_z = (V_{\mathrm{in}} - V_z)/R$ then flows entirely through the diode. Size the Zener for this corner, and the resistor for its own worst case.

quiz.q: A 12 V supply is to feed a 2 V, 20 mA LED. The series resistor should be approximately:
quiz.explanation: $R = (12 - 2)/0.02 = 500\ \Omega$: the resistor takes the 10 V the LED cannot, setting the current and absorbing all the supply variation.

quiz.q: A photodiode used as a light detector is normally operated:
options: Reverse biased, its photocurrent proportional to illumination
At zero bias with maximum current drawn
quiz.explanation: Reverse bias sweeps photogenerated pairs out of the depletion layer as a photocurrent that tracks light intensity — fast and linear. (Avalanche operation exists, as the APD, but as a deliberately multiplied special case.)

quiz.q: The chief advantage of a Schottky diode over a p–n junction diode is:
options: No stored minority charge — essentially instant turn-off and a 0.3–0.4 V forward drop
quiz.explanation: The metal–semiconductor barrier conducts with majority carriers only, so there is no minority-carrier storage to sweep out at turn-off, and the barrier height is low — fast and efficient, at the cost of higher leakage and lower voltage ratings.

intro: The semiconductor diode of Chapter 12 becomes enormously more powerful when two junctions share one very thin middle layer. That sandwich is the bipolar junction transistor — the device that made electronic amplification cheap, and the ancestor of every amplifier and switch we meet in the rest of this book. Hughes builds it as “a combination of two junction diodes”, then follows the electrons through the base to explain why a tiny base current commands a large collector current.
objectives: Describe the n–p–n and p–n–p layer structures, name the three terminals and state their doping roles
Explain carrier action in normal operation — injection at the emitter junction, diffusion across the base, collection at the collector junction
Apply Kirchhoff’s first law to the terminal currents and compute base current from a given collection fraction
Distinguish the common-base, common-emitter and common-collector connections and explain why the common-emitter stage dominates

concepts.statement: A **bipolar junction transistor (BJT)** is a combination of two junction diodes: either a thin layer of p-type semiconductor sandwiched between two n-type layers (an n–p–n transistor) or a thin layer of n-type sandwiched between two p-type layers (p–n–p). The thin central layer is the **base**; the outer layers are the **emitter** and the **collector**.
concepts.detail: The thickness of the base is of the order of $25\,\mu\text{m}$ ($25\times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}$) — a thousand times thinner than the transistor itself. The word “bipolar” records that both electrons and holes take part in the action, in contrast to the field-effect transistor of Chapter 14, whose current is carried by majority carriers alone. The junction between emitter and base is deliberately forward biased in normal operation; the junction between base and collector is reverse biased.

concepts.statement: In an n–p–n transistor the junction formed by $n_1$–p is forward biased by battery $B_1$, urging free electrons from $n_1$ towards p — hence $n_1$ is the **emitter**. The junction formed by $n_2$–p is reverse biased by $B_2$, and the electrons that diffuse through the base come within the influence of the positive terminal of $B_2$ and are swept into $n_2$ — hence $n_2$ is the **collector**.
concepts.detail: If $B_1$ were disconnected, zero emitter current would leave only the tiny thermally generated minority-carrier current of Chapter 12 flowing between $n_2$ and the base. With $B_1$ connected, electrons from the emitter enter the base and diffuse through it; those that reach $n_2$ are gathered by the metal electrode attached to it. The p–n–p transistor works exactly the same way with the movement of electrons replaced by the movement of holes — all voltages and currents simply reverse sign.

concepts.statement: By making the **base very thin** and the **impurity concentration in the base much less than in the emitter and collector**, the electrons emerging from the emitter have little opportunity of combining with holes — with the result that about **98 per cent** of them reach the collector.
concepts.detail: Some electrons, in passing through the base, combine with holes; others reach the base terminal. The electrons that do not reach the collector are exactly the current at the base terminal — this is the physical origin of $I_B$. The construction therefore sets the current gain: a thinner, lighter-doped base gives less recombination, a larger fraction collected, and a smaller base current for the same output.

concepts.term: Kirchhoff’s first law at the transistor
concepts.statement: The terminal currents satisfy $$I_E = I_B + I_C,$$ so if $I_C = 0.98\,I_E$ then $I_B = 0.02\,I_E$. When $I_E = 1\,\text{mA}$, $I_C = 0.98\,\text{mA}$ and $I_B = 0.02\,\text{mA}$.
concepts.detail: This is the node equation of Fig. 20.15 in Hughes: conventional currents $I_E$, $I_B$ and $I_C$ are drawn with arrows in their true directions for an n–p–n device. The same relation holds for signal changes, $\Delta I_E = \Delta I_C + \Delta I_B$, and it is the hinge on which the α–β relation of Section 13.2 turns.

concepts.statement: A p–n–p germanium transistor is built by purifying the semiconductor to better than **1 part in $10^{10}$**, doping the base slice n-type with about **1 part in $10^{8}$** of antimony, slicing it to about **0.1 mm** thick, and alloying a pellet of p-type indium into each side — the collector pellet about **three times the size** of the emitter pellet.
concepts.detail: The assembly is heated in a hydrogen atmosphere until the pellets melt and dissolve some of the germanium, forming p-type alloy regions on either side of the n-type base. Leads soldered to the surplus pellet material make non-rectifying emitter and collector contacts; a nickel tab solders to the base. Finally the transistor is hermetically sealed in a metal or glass container, the glass being coated with opaque paint, protecting it from moisture and light.

concepts.term: Why the collector bead is larger
concepts.statement: The collector pellet is made about three times the emitter size for two reasons: the current carriers from the emitter **spread outwards** as they cross the base, so a larger area collects them more effectively, and the **larger area assists in dissipating the greater power loss** at the collector–base junction.
concepts.detail: The dissipation is greater at the collector because the potential difference between collector and base is much larger than that between emitter and base — the reverse-biased junction carries almost the whole supply voltage. The emitter and collector are physically and electrically different, which is why a transistor is not a symmetric device despite its two-junction appearance.

concepts.statement: In the **common-base** circuit the base is connected directly to both the emitter (input) and collector (output) circuits. The arrowhead on the line joining the emitter terminal to the base indicates the conventional direction of the current in that part of the circuit.
concepts.detail: The arrow is the circuit-diagram signature of the device: it points in the direction of conventional emitter current — from base to emitter region for the n–p–n symbol, from emitter to base for p–n–p. The common-base connection gives near-unity current gain (Section 13.2) and is used where its low input impedance suits a current source.

concepts.statement: In the **common-emitter** circuit the emitter is connected directly to both the base (input) and collector (output) circuits. This method is more commonly used than the common-base circuit owing to its **higher input resistance** and its **higher current and power gains**.
concepts.detail: The common-collector circuit is used only in special cases and is not treated further by Hughes. Almost every amplifier stage in Sections 13.3–13.4 — the load line, the quiescent point, the h-parameter equivalent circuit — is drawn in the common-emitter form for exactly these reasons. It is the workhorse configuration of analog electronics.

examples.title: Currents in emitter, collector and base circuits
examples.problem: An n–p–n transistor operates with $I_C = 0.98\,I_E$. If the emitter current is $1\,\text{mA}$, find the collector and base currents, and verify the node equation (Hughes, Fig. 20.15).

steps.label: Step 1: State the current law
steps.text: By Kirchhoff’s first law the three terminal currents satisfy $I_E = I_B + I_C$, so the base current is whatever the emitter injects and the collector fails to gather.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply the collection fraction
steps.text: With $I_C = 0.98\,I_E$ and $I_E = 1\,\text{mA}$, the collector current is $I_C = 0.98\,\text{mA}$ — the 98 per cent of injected electrons that survive the crossing of the base.

steps.label: Step 3: Find the base current
steps.text: The remainder returns through the base terminal: $I_B = I_E - I_C = 1\,\text{mA} - 0.98\,\text{mA} = 0.02\,\text{mA}$, that is $20\,\mu\text{A}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret the result
steps.text: The ratio $I_C/I_B = 0.98/0.02 = 49$ is already the essence of transistor action: a $20\,\mu\text{A}$ base current controls a $0.98\,\text{mA}$ collector current. Section 13.2 names this ratio $\beta$.

examples.result: $I_C = 0.98\,\text{mA}$, $I_B = 0.02\,\text{mA}$, and $I_E = I_B + I_C = 1\,\text{mA}$ exactly — one milliampere in, a 49-fold larger current out than the control current.

examples.title: Building an alloy-junction p–n–p transistor
examples.problem: Summarize the constructional numbers Hughes gives for an alloy-junction germanium transistor — purity, doping, geometry and packaging.

steps.label: Step 1: Purify
steps.text: The silicon or germanium is purified until any impurity does not exceed about 1 part in $10^{10}$ — the exceptional degree of purity that Chapter 12 demanded of diode material.

steps.label: Step 2: Form the base slice
steps.text: While molten, an n-type impurity (antimony, for germanium) is added in the proportion of about 1 part in $10^{8}$; the solidified crystal is sawn into slices about $0.1\,\text{mm}$ thick, each forming the base region of a transistor.

steps.label: Step 3: Alloy the junctions
steps.text: A pellet of p-type indium is placed on each side — the collector pellet about three times the size of the emitter pellet — and the assembly is heated in a hydrogen atmosphere until the pellets melt and dissolve some of the germanium, forming the p-type alloy regions.

steps.label: Step 4: Make the contacts and seal
steps.text: Leads are soldered to the surplus pellet material for emitter and collector (non-rectifying contacts), a nickel tab solders to the base, and the assembly is hermetically sealed in metal or glass — the glass coated with opaque paint against moisture and light.

examples.result: A completed junction transistor: emitter and collector of p-type alloy, an n-type base about $0.1\,\text{mm}$ thick, and a collector junction three times the emitter area to catch the spreading carriers and dissipate the larger collector-junction power.

keyTakeaways: A BJT is two junction diodes sharing one thin ($\sim 25\,\mu\text{m}$), lightly doped base — n–p–n or p–n–p.
Normal operation forward biases the emitter junction and reverse biases the collector junction; electrons (or holes) are injected, diffuse across the base and are collected.
Because the base is thin and lightly doped, about 98 per cent of the carriers reach the collector; the remainder is the base current.
The terminal currents obey $I_E = I_B + I_C$ — at $1\,\text{mA}$ emitter current, $I_C = 0.98\,\text{mA}$ and $I_B = 0.02\,\text{mA}$.
The common-emitter connection is preferred for its higher input resistance and higher current and power gains; common-base and common-collector serve special cases.

Alloy-junction construction dopes the base 1 part in $10^{8}$ into $10^{10}$-pure material and makes the collector pellet three times the emitter — asymmetry is deliberate, for collection efficiency and heat dissipation.

quiz.q: In normal operation of an n–p–n transistor, the two junctions are biased as follows:
options: Emitter junction forward, collector junction reverse
Emitter junction reverse, collector junction forward
quiz.explanation: The emitter–base diode is forward biased by $B_1$ so electrons are urged towards the base; the collector–base diode is reverse biased by $B_2$ so its junction field sweeps up the diffusing electrons. Both-forward is saturation and both-reverse is cut-off — the switch states of Section 13.5.

quiz.q: The base region of a bipolar transistor is made very thin and lightly doped so that:
options: The base current is large and stable
Most injected carriers diffuse across to the collector instead of recombining
The collector junction can be forward biased
The device works equally well with emitter and collector interchanged
quiz.explanation: A thin, lightly doped base gives the injected electrons little opportunity to combine with holes, so about 98 per cent reach the collector. That is what makes the base current — and therefore the control current — small.

quiz.q: A transistor has $I_C = 0.98\,I_E$. If $I_E = 1\,\text{mA}$, the base current is:
quiz.explanation: Kirchhoff’s first law gives $I_B = I_E - I_C = 1\,\text{mA} - 0.98\,\text{mA} = 0.02\,\text{mA}$. The collector takes 98 per cent of the emitter current; the base returns the missing 2 per cent.

quiz.q: Why is the collector pellet made about three times the size of the emitter pellet in alloy-junction construction?
options: To increase the emitter doping level
To collect carriers that spread outwards through the base and to dissipate the greater power loss at the collector junction
To make the transistor symmetric so either lead can serve as emitter
quiz.explanation: Carriers from the emitter spread as they cross the base, so a larger collector area gathers them more effectively; and because the collector–base p.d. exceeds the emitter–base p.d., the larger area also helps dissipate the greater junction power.

quiz.q: The common-emitter connection is preferred over common-base because it offers:
options: Lower input resistance but more gain
Higher input resistance together with higher current and power gains
Near-unity current gain and the highest input impedance of the three connections
quiz.explanation: Hughes states it plainly: the common-emitter method is more commonly used owing to its higher input resistance and the higher current and power gains. The common-base stage keeps near-unity current gain; the common-collector (emitter follower) appears only in special cases.

intro: Before a transistor can be biased or amplified into, its terminal behaviour must be measured. Hughes measures it twice — once holding the emitter current fixed (common-base) and once holding the base current fixed (common-emitter) — and the two experiments deliver two current amplification factors, α and β. One algebraic step links them, and one leakage current, I_CBO, sets the stability problem that Section 13.5 has to solve.
objectives: Describe the measurement and shape of common-base and common-emitter static characteristics
Define α and β as ratios of current changes taken at constant output voltage
Derive the relation between α and β and convert between them
Account for the leakage current I_CBO and explain its effect on collector current and bias stability

concepts.statement: To measure the **common-base characteristics**, the emitter current is held constant (say $1\,\text{mA}$) by a slider, and the collector current is noted for various collector–base voltages; repeating for several emitter currents gives a family of curves $I_C$ versus $V_{CB}$.
concepts.detail: For positive $V_{CB}$ the collector current remains almost constant — nearly all the electrons entering the base of an n–p–n transistor are attracted to the collector — and for a given collector–base voltage the collector current is practically proportional to the emitter current. The family (Hughes Fig. 20.20, $I_E$ from 1 to 5 mA) is almost flat: the collector behaves as a current source, not a resistor.

concepts.statement: In accordance with **BS 3363**, a current is positive when its direction is from the external circuit towards the transistor terminal, and $V_{CB}$ is positive when the collector is positive relative to the base. For an n–p–n transistor $I_C$ and $V_{CB}$ are positive but $I_E$ is negative; for p–n–p, all signs reverse.
concepts.detail: The convention is what makes published characteristic sheets mutually consistent: the flat common-base curves of Fig. 20.20 are plotted with the emitter current shown negative (drawn downwards from zero) because the emitter current flows out of the terminal into the external circuit. Data-sheet readers must check which convention a manufacturer uses before comparing devices.

concepts.statement: The ratio of the change $\Delta I_C$ in collector current to the change $\Delta I_E$ in emitter current, for a given collector–base voltage, is the **current amplification factor for a common-base circuit**: $$\alpha = \frac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta I_E} \quad \text{for a given } V_{CB}.$$
concepts.detail: It is the slope (neglecting signs) of the $I_C$–$I_E$ graph of Fig. 20.21, drawn at $V_{CB} = 4\,\text{V}$: an almost straight line through the origin. Because about 98 per cent of the emitter current is collected, α is just under unity — typically 0.95 to 0.998.

concepts.statement: For the **common-emitter characteristics** the base current is held constant (say $25\,\mu\text{A}$) through a microammeter, and the collector current is noted for various collector–emitter voltages $V_{CE}$; the family is completed for several base currents.
concepts.detail: Hughes plots $I_B = 0, 25, 50, 75\,\mu\text{A}$ (Fig. 20.23), the curves rising steeply near the origin and flattening above a volt or so — the familiar “fan” that reappears around every load line in Section 13.3. For a given voltage between collector and emitter, e.g. $V_{CE} = 4\,\text{V}$, the relationship between collector and base currents is practically linear (Fig. 20.24).

concepts.statement: The ratio of the change $\Delta I_C$ in collector current to the change $\Delta I_B$ in base current, for a given collector–emitter voltage, is the **current amplification factor for a common-emitter circuit**: $$\beta = \frac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta I_B} \quad \text{for a given } V_{CE}.$$
concepts.detail: It is the slope of the $I_C$–$I_B$ graph of Fig. 20.24 at $V_{CE} = 4\,\text{V}$ — a straight line, which is why the common-emitter stage is a natural current amplifier. Because $I_B$ is the small residue of $I_E$, values of β from 20 to several hundred are routine; the same transistor measured in common-base gives α just below 1.

concepts.statement: Since $I_E = I_C + I_B$, we have $\Delta I_E = \Delta I_C + \Delta I_B$. Dividing through by $\Delta I_C$ gives $1/\alpha = 1 + 1/\beta$, hence $$\alpha = \frac{\beta}{1 + \beta} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \beta = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}.$$
concepts.detail: Thus if $\alpha = 0.98$ then $\beta = 0.98/0.02 = 49$, and if $\alpha = 0.99$ then $\beta = 0.99/0.01 = 99$: a small variation in α corresponds to a large variation in β. It is therefore better to determine β experimentally and calculate from it the corresponding value of α — the sensitive number is measured directly, the insensitive one derived.

concepts.statement: If the emitter is not connected ($I_E = 0$) a small collector current still flows — the **leakage current** crossing the reverse-biased collector–base junction. It is given the symbol $I_{CBO}$: the collector–base current with zero emitter current.
concepts.detail: This is the saturation current of the reverse-biased junction of Chapter 12, plus surface leakage — only microamperes, but it never disappears. When the emitter is reconnected the leakage is still present, so the total collector current is $I_C = \alpha I_E + I_{CBO}$, and substituting $I_E = I_B + I_C$ collects it into the base-current form below.

concepts.statement: Substituting $I_E = I_B + I_C$ into $I_C = \alpha I_E + I_{CBO}$ gives $I_C(1 - \alpha) = \alpha I_B + I_{CBO}$, so $$I_C = \beta I_B + \frac{I_{CBO}}{1 - \alpha}.$$ If $I_{CBO}$ is very small the last term can be neglected and the relation reduces to $I_C = \beta I_B$.
concepts.detail: The factor $1/(1-\alpha)$ multiplying the leakage is large — 50 when α is 0.98 — so the leakage is amplified into the output along with the signal. Worse, the leakage current is temperature dependent: an increase in temperature causes it to rise, which increases the collector current and changes the bias conditions. Stabilizing the bias against this drift is the business of Section 13.5.

examples.title: From α to β and back
examples.problem: A datasheet quotes common-base current amplification factors α = 0.98 and α = 0.99. Find the corresponding β values, and comment on the sensitivity (Hughes, §20.12).

steps.label: Step 1: Write the relation
steps.text: From $I_E = I_C + I_B$ we have $\Delta I_E = \Delta I_C + \Delta I_B$, so $1/\alpha = 1 + 1/\beta$ and therefore $\beta = \alpha/(1 - \alpha)$.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret
steps.text: A 1 per cent change in α — from 0.98 to 0.99 — doubled β from 49 to 99. A small variation in α therefore corresponds to a large variation in β, which is why β is the experimentally quoted parameter and α the derived one ($\alpha = \beta/(1+\beta)$).

examples.result: $\alpha = 0.98 \Rightarrow \beta = 49$; $\alpha = 0.99 \Rightarrow \beta = 99$. Measure β, calculate α — never the reverse.

examples.title: Verifying β from the terminal currents
examples.problem: Using the current distribution of Fig. 20.15 ($I_E = 1\,\text{mA}$, $I_C = 0.98\,\text{mA}$, $I_B = 0.02\,\text{mA}$), compute α and β directly and check that they satisfy the α–β relation.

steps.label: Step 1: Compute α from the currents
steps.text: Treating the (almost) proportional relation between $I_C$ and $I_E$ as the slope of Fig. 20.21, $\alpha = I_C/I_E = 0.98/1 = 0.98$.

steps.label: Step 2: Compute β from the currents
steps.text: Similarly from the common-emitter slope of Fig. 20.24, $\beta = I_C/I_B = 0.98\,\text{mA}/0.02\,\text{mA} = 49$.

steps.label: Step 3: Check the relation
steps.text: Convert back: $\alpha = \beta/(1+\beta) = 49/50 = 0.98$ — exactly the value from Step 1.

steps.label: Step 4: Note the leakage caveat
steps.text: These quotients ignore $I_{CBO}$; with leakage included the collector current is $I_C = \beta I_B + I_{CBO}/(1-\alpha)$, and the true $\Delta$-ratio definitions of α and β apply only at constant $V_{CB}$ or $V_{CE}$ respectively.

examples.result: α = 0.98 and β = 49 — consistent, because a device that collects 98 per cent of a $1\,\text{mA}$ emitter current delivers a 49-fold base-to-collector current gain.

keyTakeaways: Common-base curves are nearly flat: $I_C$ is almost independent of $V_{CB}$ and practically proportional to $I_E$.
Common-emitter curves fan out from the origin: $I_C$ versus $I_B$ is practically linear at constant $V_{CE}$.
α = ΔI_C/ΔI_E at constant $V_{CB}$ (just under 1); β = ΔI_C/ΔI_B at constant $V_{CE}$ (typically 20–300).
The α–β relation $\alpha = \beta/(1+\beta)$, $\beta = \alpha/(1-\alpha)$: α = 0.98 gives β = 49, α = 0.99 gives β = 99 — measure β, derive α.
With the emitter open a leakage current $I_{CBO}$ still flows; the full collector current is $I_C = \beta I_B + I_{CBO}/(1-\alpha)$.
Leakage rises with temperature, dragging $I_C$ and the bias point with it — the instability that bias networks must suppress.

quiz.q: The current amplification factor α for a common-base circuit is defined as:
quiz.explanation: α is the ratio of the change in collector current to the change in emitter current, taken for a given value of $V_{CB}$ — the slope of the $I_C$–$I_E$ graph. The $\Delta I_C/\Delta I_B$ ratio at constant $V_{CE}$ is β, the common-emitter factor.

quiz.q: A transistor has α = 0.99. Its β is:
quiz.explanation: $\beta = \alpha/(1-\alpha) = 0.99/0.01 = 99$. The tiny uncollected fraction 1 − α is the base current, so β blows up as α approaches unity.

quiz.q: The leakage current $I_{CBO}$ is measured with:
options: The base and emitter terminals shorted
quiz.explanation: $I_{CBO}$ is the collector–base current with zero emitter current — the emitter disconnected. It is the reverse-biased junction’s leakage, and it flows whether or not the transistor is amplifying.

quiz.q: Including leakage, the collector current of a common-emitter stage is:
quiz.explanation: Substituting $I_E = I_B + I_C$ into $I_C = \alpha I_E + I_{CBO}$ gives $I_C = \beta I_B + I_{CBO}/(1-\alpha)$. The leakage is amplified by the large factor $1/(1-\alpha)$, which is why it matters even though it is only microamperes.

quiz.q: Why is β, rather than α, the parameter usually measured and quoted?
options: Because α cannot be measured at all
Because a small variation in α corresponds to a large variation in β, so α is best derived from β
Because β is dimensionless while α is not
Because α depends on temperature but β does not
quiz.explanation: Between α = 0.98 and α = 0.99, β doubles from 49 to 99. The sensitive quantity is β; Hughes accordingly recommends determining β experimentally and calculating α from $\alpha = \beta/(1+\beta)$. Both are dimensionless ratios.

quiz.q: A bipolar transistor has common-base current gain $α = 0.985$ and emitter current 5.0 mA. Its base current is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $α = 0.985$, $I_{E} = 5.0$ mA. Step 2 — Governing links: $β = \frac{α}{1 - α}$, $I_{C} = α I_{E}$ and $I_{B} = \frac{I_{C}}{β} = (1 - α)I_{E}$. Step 3 — Algebra: $β = \frac{0.985}{0.015} \approx 65.67$; $I_{C} = 0.985 \times 5.0 = 4.925$ mA; $I_{B} = 0.015 \times 5.0 = 0.075$ mA, that is $75$ μA. Step 4 — Sanity check: $I_{C} + I_{B} = 5.0$ mA closes KCL, $β$ in the tens suits a small-signal device, and base current is a small fraction of emitter current. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 25 μA uses $1 - α = 0.005$, 250 μA slips a decade, and 750 μA compounds both slips. Step 6 — Conclude: the base draws about 75 μA.

intro: Characteristics describe the device; the load line describes the circuit around it. Supply voltage, collector resistance and the transistor family meet on one straight line, and where the bias current places the operating point on that line decides whether the stage amplifies cleanly or distorts. Hughes carries one common-emitter stage through the whole story — load line, quiescent point, gains, and finally the choice of every component value.
objectives: Draw the d.c. load line on a set of output characteristics from the supply voltage and load resistance
Locate a quiescent point that allows symmetric, linear signal swing and read current and voltage excursions from it
Compute current, voltage and power gains from graphical data, distinguishing the a.c. and d.c. load lines
Select bias resistor, collector resistor and coupling capacitors for a given transistor family

concepts.statement: The **load line** is the locus of the variation of the collector current for any variation in the emitter (or base) current; it is a straight line drawn between the quiescent operating point and the point where the whole supply appears across the load.
concepts.detail: In Hughes’s common-base example the collector–base voltage is to be $3\,\text{V}$ with no signal, and an emitter current of $3\,\text{mA}$ gives a collector current of $2.9\,\text{mA}$ — point D of Fig. 20.27. With a load of $R = 1000\,\Omega$ the p.d. across R is $0.0029 \times 1000 = 2.9\,\text{V}$, so the total collector bias must be $3 + 2.9 = 5.9\,\text{V}$ — point P. The straight line PD is the load line, and the inverse of its slope is the resistance of the load: $HP/DH = 2.9/0.0029 = 1000\,\Omega$.

concepts.statement: Each value of emitter (or base) current intersects the load line at one point, so a sinusoidal input sweep maps directly into a sinusoidal collector current: if $I_E$ varies between 1 and 5 mA, the operating point slides along the line and the collector current follows.
concepts.detail: The output curve will be sinusoidal if the characteristics are linear and equally spaced over the working range. The function of the output capacitor C is to eliminate the d.c. component of the voltage across the load from the output. Hughes’s notation: a lower-case subscript indicates an r.m.s. value compared with a capital for the d.c. value — $I_c R$ is the r.m.s. alternating output voltage and $I_c^2 R$ the output power. The larger the load resistance, the greater the voltage and power gains, the maximum R for a given supply being limited by the maximum permissible distortion.

concepts.statement: The transistor must operate in a **unidirectional mode**: without bias, the negative parts of an alternating input would reverse-bias the emitter–base junction and prevent normal transistor action. A practical stage therefore adds $R_B$ to provide the base bias current and $R_C$ to couple the collector to the positive supply.
concepts.detail: Coupling capacitors separate the direct currents of the transistor arrangement from the alternating signal entering and leaving the amplifier: $C_1$ prevents the signal source from affecting the steady component of base current, and $C_2$ prevents the load from affecting the steady conditions of the collector. Their capacitances are chosen so that the reactances are negligible at the operating frequencies — the amplifier of Chapter 11 reduced to four components and a transistor.

concepts.term: Bias resistor and the load-line equation
concepts.statement: Writing $V_S = I_B R_B + V_{BE}$ for the quiescent base loop gives $$R_B = \frac{V_S - V_{BE}}{I_B},$$ often approximated by $R_B \approx V_S/I_B$ since $V_{BE}$ is small. On the output side, at any instant $v_{ce} = V_S - i_c R_C$, so $$i_c = -\frac{1}{R_C}v_{ce} + \frac{V_S}{R_C}$$ — the load line in equation form.
concepts.detail: These are Hughes relations [20.19]–[20.21]. The intercepts fall out immediately: if $i_c = 0$ then $v_{ce} = V_S$ (the whole supply across the transistor), and if $v_{ce} = 0$ then $i_c = V_S/R_C$ (the whole supply across the resistor). Every graphical construction of this section starts by plotting those two points on the output characteristics.

concepts.statement: For a linear response the stage must operate on that part of the load line which meets the family of characteristics at **regular intervals**; B is the lowest acceptable point, and **Q is more or less halfway between A and B** — the nearer exactly halfway, the better the linear amplification.
concepts.detail: Points A, Q and B correspond to the maximum, mean and minimum values of the base current, $I_B + I_{bm}$, $I_B$ and $I_B - I_{bm}$, with collector currents $I_{CA}$, $I_C$, $I_{CB}$ and collector–emitter voltages $V_{CEA}$, $V_{CE}$, $V_{CEB}$. A quiescent value above A would compress the spacing and distort the top of the waveform; below B the bottom is clipped. The total signal swing is read off as $I_{CA} - I_{CB}$ and $V_{CEB} - V_{CEA}$.

concepts.statement: The **current gain** is $G_i = \Delta I_o/\Delta I_i = (I_{CA} - I_{CB})/2I_{bm}$, the **voltage gain** is $G_v = \Delta V_o/\Delta V_i$, and the **power gain** is $G_p = P_o/P_i$, with $$G_p = G_v G_i.$$
concepts.detail: Care is needed with relation [20.24]: the powers $P_i$ and $P_o$ are those related to the signal frequency and exclude the quiescent powers — the signal power in the load is the product of the r.m.s. signal load voltage and the r.m.s. signal load current.
