The voltage gain needs the change in input voltage that produced the change in base current; little error results from assuming the collector–emitter voltage constant when finding the base–emitter voltage that produces a given base current.

concepts.statement: The **dynamic characteristic** is the relation between $i_c$ and $i_b$ derived from the load line for the given values of $R_C$ and $V_S$; provided it is linear over the operating range, the waveform of $i_c$ will be identical to that of $i_b$.
concepts.detail: A linear dynamic characteristic is usually a good indicator that the transistor amplifier will cause little distortion — but the input characteristics of the transistor are not themselves linear, so the signal base current is not an exact replica of the applied signal. The consequent distortion is generally small provided the source resistance is considerably larger than the input resistance of the transistor.

concepts.statement: When a load $R_L$ is coupled through $C_2$, the effective (a.c.) load on the transistor is $R_C$ and $R_L$ in parallel, $$R_p = \frac{R_C R_L}{R_C + R_L},$$ and the **a.c. load line** of slope $-1/R_p$ is drawn through the same quiescent point Q. The line of slope $-1/R_C$ is the **d.c. load line**.
concepts.detail: The quiescent point is the same for both lines because it refers to the zero-signal condition, when no signal current flows through the coupling capacitor and $R_L$ carries nothing. Signal excursions then follow the steeper a.c. line — the swing available at the output is smaller than the d.c. line alone suggests, which is why the a.c. line must be the one used to read $I_{CA}$ and $I_{CB}$.

concepts.statement: Given the transistor characteristics, select a quiescent point **somewhere in the middle of the family** (Hughes picks the $i_b = 60\,\mu\text{A}$ curve), take $R_B \approx V_S/I_B$, set the quiescent $V_{CE}$ to about **half the supply voltage**, and choose $R_C = (V_S/2)/I_C$ for the resulting collector current.
concepts.detail: With $V_S = 12\,\text{V}$ and $I_B = 60\,\mu\text{A}$: $R_B = 12/60\times 10^{-6} = 200\,\text{k}\Omega$ (about $183\,\text{k}\Omega$ if a base–emitter drop of order $1\,\text{V}$ is allowed for). A quiescent $V_{CE}$ of $6\,\text{V}$ corresponds to $I_C = 2.9\,\text{mA}$ from the curves, giving $R_C = 6/2.9\times 10^{-3} \approx 2\,\text{k}\Omega$. The approximations are acceptable because circuit components are manufactured to tolerances of $\pm 10$ per cent — the $1.8\,\text{k}\Omega$ and $2.2\,\text{k}\Omega$ actually used in Example 20.3 are equally valid. Finally $C_1$ is chosen so that its reactance $1/2\pi f C_1$ is about 10 per cent of the input resistance at the operating frequency; alternative bias schemes include a potential divider across the supply or a resistor between emitter and the 0 V line (Section 13.5).

examples.title: Example 20.3 — gains of a common-emitter stage
examples.problem: A bipolar transistor amplifier stage has $V_S = 12\,\text{V}$, $R_B = 200\,\text{k}\Omega$ and $R_C = 1.8\,\text{k}\Omega$; the transistor characteristics are linear over the working range. A $2.2\,\text{k}\Omega$ load is connected across the output, and a sinusoidal source of $0.6\,\text{V}$ peak and internal resistance $10\,\text{k}\Omega$ drives the input, whose input resistance is effectively constant at $2.7\,\text{k}\Omega$. Determine the current, voltage and power gains of the stage.

steps.label: Step 1: d.c. load line extremities
steps.text: If $i_c = 0$ then $v_{ce} = V_S = 12\,\text{V}$. If $v_{ce} = 0$ then $i_c = V_S/R_C = 12/(1.8\times 10^{3}) \approx 6.7\,\text{mA}$. These two points fix the d.c. load line on Fig. 20.33.

steps.label: Step 2: a.c. load line through the quiescent point
steps.text: The a.c. load is $R_p = (1.8 \times 2.2)/(1.8 + 2.2) \approx 1.0\,\text{k}\Omega$, so the a.c. load line has slope $-1/1\,\text{k}\Omega \approx -1.0\,\text{mA/V}$. The quiescent base current is $I_{B0} = 12/(200\times 10^{3}) \approx 60\,\mu\text{A}$, and the a.c. line is drawn through the intersection Q of the $60\,\mu\text{A}$ characteristic with the d.c. line.

steps.label: Step 3: input circuit and base-current swing
steps.text: The $200\,\text{k}\Omega$ bias resistor shunts the $2.7\,\text{k}\Omega$ transistor input negligibly, so the signal sees $10\,\text{k}\Omega + 2.7\,\text{k}\Omega$. The peak signal base current is $0.6/((10 + 2.7)\times 10^{3}) \approx 47\,\mu\text{A}$, so the base current swings between $60 + 47 = 107\,\mu\text{A}$ and $60 - 47 = 13\,\mu\text{A}$.

steps.label: Step 4: collector-current swing and current gain
steps.text: From the a.c. load line, the swing between the 13 and 107 $\mu\text{A}$ characteristics is $\Delta i_c = 5.1 - 0.9 = 4.2\,\text{mA}$. The change in output current delivered to the $2.2\,\text{k}\Omega$ load is $\Delta i_o = 4.2\times 10^{-3} \times 1.8\times 10^{3}/((1.8 + 2.2)\times 10^{3}) = 1.9\,\text{mA}$, while $\Delta i_i = 107 - 13 = 94\,\mu\text{A}$. The stage current gain is therefore $G_i = 1.9\times 10^{-3}/94\times 10^{-6} = 20$ (the transistor alone gives $4.2\times 10^{-3}/94\times 10^{-6} \approx 45$).

steps.label: Step 5: voltage and power gains
steps.text: From the a.c. load line, $\Delta v_o = v_{ce} = 8.5 - 4.3 = 4.2\,\text{V}$ peak-to-peak. The input swing is $\Delta v_i = \Delta i_i \times R_i = 94\times 10^{-6} \times 2.7\times 10^{3} = 0.25\,\text{V}$ peak-to-peak. Hence $G_v = 4.2/0.25 \approx 17$ and $G_p = G_v G_i = 17 \times 20 = 340$.

steps.label: Step 6: check through r.m.s. powers
steps.text: R.m.s. output voltage $= 4.2/(2\sqrt{2}) = 1.5\,\text{V}$; r.m.s. output current $= 1.5/(2.2\times 10^{3}) = 0.68\,\text{mA}$; $P_o = (0.68\times 10^{-3})^2 \times 2.2\times 10^{3} \approx 1.0\,\text{mW}$. R.m.s. input voltage $= 0.25/(2\sqrt{2}) \approx 88\,\text{mV}$, r.m.s. input current $\approx 33\,\mu\text{A}$, so $P_i \approx 2.9\,\mu\text{W}$ and $G_p = 1.0\times 10^{-3}/2.9\times 10^{-6} \approx 340$, as before.

examples.result: Stage gains: $G_i = 20$, $G_v \approx 17$, $G_p = 340$. The transistor itself would give $G_i \approx 45$ — the difference is the current shared between $R_C$ and the $2.2\,\text{k}\Omega$ load.

examples.title: Selecting the circuit components
examples.problem: Using the characteristics of Fig. 20.33 ($V_S = 12\,\text{V}$), choose the quiescent point and calculate $R_B$ and $R_C$ for a single-stage amplifier (Hughes, §20.15).

steps.label: Step 1: Choose the quiescent base current
steps.text: It is the practice first to select a quiescent point in the middle of the family of characteristics — here the curve for $i_b = 60\,\mu\text{A}$ suggests itself immediately.

steps.label: Step 2: Bias resistor
steps.text: Neglecting the base–emitter voltage, $R_B = V_S/I_B = 12/(60\times 10^{-6}) = 200\,\text{k}\Omega$. The neglect is optimistic — $V_{BE}$ is of the order of $1\,\text{V}$ — leaving $11\,\text{V}$ across the resistor and $R_B \approx 183\,\text{k}\Omega$.

steps.label: Step 3: Collector resistor
steps.text: The quiescent point normally takes a value of about half the supply, $V_{CE} \approx 6\,\text{V}$. From the characteristics the corresponding collector current is $2.9\,\text{mA}$, so with $6\,\text{V}$ across $R_C$: $R_C = 6/(2.9\times 10^{-3}) \approx 2\,\text{k}\Omega$.

steps.label: Step 4: Accept the tolerance
steps.text: Example 20.3 actually used $R_C = 1.8\,\text{k}\Omega$, and $2.2\,\text{k}\Omega$ would be equally acceptable — circuit components are manufactured to $\pm 10$ per cent tolerances, so all three values lie within the same practical band.

steps.label: Step 5: Coupling capacitor
steps.text: Choose $C_1$ so that its reactance $1/2\pi f C_1$ is about 10 per cent of the transistor input resistance at the operating frequency — negligible to the signal, but a complete block to the bias current that must not be diverted through the source.

examples.result: $I_B = 60\,\mu\text{A}$, $R_B \approx 200\,\text{k}\Omega$ ($183\,\text{k}\Omega$ allowing for $V_{BE}$), $R_C \approx 2\,\text{k}\Omega$ with $V_{CE} \approx 6\,\text{V}$ — a design that centers the swing on the load line using the curves alone.

keyTakeaways: The load line joins $v_{ce} = V_S$ at $i_c = 0$ to $i_c = V_S/R_C$ at $v_{ce} = 0$; its inverse slope is the load resistance ($2.9/0.0029 = 1000\,\Omega$ in Hughes’s construction).
The quiescent point belongs halfway between the extreme usable points A and B on the load line; symmetric placement is what makes the amplification linear.
Stage gains read graphically: $G_i = (I_{CA} - I_{CB})/2I_{bm}$, $G_v = \Delta V_o/\Delta V_i$, and $G_p = G_v G_i$ with signal powers only.

Example 20.3: with $V_S = 12\,\text{V}$, $R_C = 1.8\,\text{k}\Omega$, $R_L = 2.2\,\text{k}\Omega$ and a $2.7\,\text{k}\Omega$ input driven at $0.6\,\text{V}$ peak, the stage delivers $G_i = 20$, $G_v \approx 17$, $G_p = 340$.
An external load folds the load line: the a.c. line of slope $-1/R_p$ (with $R_p = R_C R_L/(R_C + R_L) \approx 1.0\,\text{k}\Omega$ here) passes through the same Q.

Component selection is approximate by design: mid-family Q ($60\,\mu\text{A}$), $R_B \approx V_S/I_B = 200\,\text{k}\Omega$, $R_C \approx (V_S/2)/I_C \approx 2\,\text{k}\Omega$, within $\pm 10$ per cent component tolerances.

quiz.q: A common-emitter stage runs from $V_S = 12\,\text{V}$ with $R_C = 1.8\,\text{k}\Omega$. The d.c. load line runs between which two points?
quiz.explanation: Setting $i_c = 0$ in $v_{ce} = V_S - i_c R_C$ leaves the whole supply across the transistor ($12\,\text{V}$); setting $v_{ce} = 0$ leaves it all across $R_C$, giving $i_c = 12/(1.8\times 10^{3}) \approx 6.7\,\text{mA}$. These are the two intercepts the load line joins.

quiz.q: Why is the quiescent point placed roughly halfway between points A and B on the load line?
options: To minimize the supply current drawn by the stage
So the signal can swing almost equally in both directions before hitting cut-off or saturation, keeping amplification linear
Because the transistor dissipates exactly half the supply power there
To make the d.c. and a.c. load lines coincide
quiz.explanation: A is the top of the usable region, B the lowest acceptable point; operating between them at the middle lets $I_B \pm I_{bm}$ produce nearly equal positive and negative excursions. The nearer Q is to exactly halfway, the better the linear amplification.

quiz.q: In Example 20.3 the stage current gain (20) is smaller than the transistor current gain (about 45) because:
options: The transistor’s β falls at low frequency
Part of the collector signal current is shared between $R_C$ and the $2.2\,\text{k}\Omega$ external load
The bias resistor shunts the input signal
The coupling capacitors attenuate the signal
quiz.explanation: Of the $\Delta i_c = 4.2\,\text{mA}$ delivered by the transistor, only the fraction $1.8/(1.8 + 2.2) = 0.45$ flows into the external load — $\Delta i_o = 1.9\,\text{mA}$. The rest flows through $R_C$, which is inside the transistor’s loop but outside the load’s.

quiz.q: A load $R_L = 2.2\,\text{k}\Omega$ is capacitor-coupled to a stage with $R_C = 1.8\,\text{k}\Omega$. The a.c. load the transistor actually drives is:
quiz.explanation: To the signal, $R_C$ and $R_L$ are in parallel: $R_p = (1.8 \times 2.2)/(1.8 + 2.2) \approx 1.0\,\text{k}\Omega$. The capacitor blocks d.c. (so Q is set by $R_C$ alone) but passes the signal (so the swing follows the steeper a.c. line of slope $-1.0\,\text{mA/V}$).

quiz.q: In Example 20.3 the r.m.s. output voltage is $1.5\,\text{V}$ and the r.m.s. output current $0.68\,\text{mA}$ into $2.2\,\text{k}\Omega$. The signal power in the load is about:
quiz.explanation: $P_o = I^2 R = (0.68\times 10^{-3})^2 \times 2.2\times 10^{3} \approx 1.0\,\text{mW}$ (equivalently $1.5\,\text{V} \times 0.68\,\text{mA}$). With $P_i \approx 2.9\,\mu\text{W}$, the power gain is $1.0\times 10^{-3}/2.9\times 10^{-6} \approx 340$ — the same figure as $G_v G_i$.

quiz.q: A common-emitter stage uses $V_{CC} = 12$ V, $R_{C} = 2.0$ kΩ and $R_{E} = 0.50$ kΩ, biased so $I_{C} = 3.0$ mA. The quiescent collector-emitter voltage is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $V_{CC} = 12$ V, $R_{C} = 2.0$ kΩ, $R_{E} = 0.50$ kΩ, $I_{C} \approx I_{E} = 3.0$ mA. Step 2 — Governing load line: $V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_{C}R_{C} - I_{E}R_{E}$, the supply minus both resistive drops. Step 3 — Algebra: drops are $3.0 \times 2.0 = 6.0$ V and $3.0 \times 0.50 = 1.5$ V, so $V_{CE} = 12 - 6.0 - 1.5 = 4.5$ V. Step 4 — Sanity check: the point sits mid-supply with room for symmetric swing, saturation ($0.2$ V) and cutoff ($12$ V) are both distant, and units are consistent. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 2.5 V doubles the emitter drop, 6.0 V omits it, and 7.5 V mistakes the collector drop. Step 6 — Conclude: the stage rests near 4.5 V.

intro: Graphical load lines become clumsy once several stages and source impedances interact, so the transistor is replaced by a small-signal equivalent circuit — a box whose h-parameters are measured once and then reused for every circuit. Hughes derives the current and voltage gains of the common-emitter stage in this language, shows why h_fe is just β wearing a new name, and then multiplies stages together in cascade. The section ends with the observation that pushes electronics toward the FET: the BJT’s input resistance is simply too low.
objectives: Replace a biased transistor by its small-signal h-parameter equivalent circuit and explain what each parameter represents
Derive the current and voltage gains of a loaded common-emitter stage, including the $180\degree$ phase shift
State the full two-port h-parameter equations and justify neglecting the feedback parameter h_re
Compute the overall gain of cascaded stages and quantify the input-resistance limitation of the BJT

concepts.statement: So long as a transistor is operated over the **linear portions of its characteristics**, the actual values of the bias voltages are of no consequence — an equivalent circuit used to calculate gains carries only the **r.m.s. values of the alternating components** of the voltages and currents.
concepts.detail: The transistor is essentially a **current-operated device**: its action depends on the input current, so its equivalent circuit (in the form of Fig. 18.8, the amplifier equivalent networks of the systems chapters) uses a current generator at the output. In converting a real amplifier stage to the equivalent circuit, the capacitors are omitted (their reactances assumed negligible), the bias resistor is seen to shunt the transistor input, and the load becomes the collector resistor in parallel with the external load.

concepts.statement: To indicate that the circuit components and gain ratios apply specifically to the transistor, the general amplifier parameters are renamed **h-parameters**: $h_i$ is the input resistance, $h_o$ the output conductance (in siemens, not ohms), and $h_f$ the current gain, with a second subscript letter indicating the connection mode — $h_{ie}$ for common-emitter, $h_{ib}$ for common-base.
concepts.detail: The basic model of Fig. 20.35 has $h_i$ in series with the input terminals, a current generator $h_f I_i$ in the output, and $h_o$ across the output. Typical magnitudes for a small-signal BJT in common-emitter: $h_{ie}$ of order $1\,\text{k}\Omega$, $h_{fe}$ between 50 and several hundred, $h_{oe}$ of a few tens of microsiemens. The mode subscripts matter because the same physical device presents very different parameters in common-base versus common-emitter connection.

concepts.term: Current gain of transistor and stage
concepts.statement: With the load $R_p = R_C R_L/(R_C + R_L)$, the transistor’s current gain is $$G_i = \frac{h_{fe}}{1 + h_{oe}R_p},$$ and the gain of the whole stage multiplies this by the current divider $R_C/(R_C + R_L)$.
concepts.detail: The output current generator $h_{fe}I_b$ drives $1/h_{oe}$ in parallel with $R_p$: $I_c = (1/h_{oe})/((1/h_{oe}) + R_p) \times h_{fe}I_b$, which rearranges to relation [20.26]. Only the fraction $R_C/(R_C + R_L)$ of $I_c$ reaches the external load, giving the stage gain [20.27]. The distinction matters — Example 20.3 found 45 for the transistor but 20 for the stage.

concepts.term: Voltage gain and the 180° phase shift
concepts.statement: The voltage gain for the transistor is $G_v = V_{ce}/V_{be} = -I_c R_p/(I_b h_{ie})$, hence $$G_v = \frac{-h_{fe}R_p}{h_{ie}\left(1 + h_{oe}R_p\right)}.$$ The minus sign records the $180\degree$ phase shift between input and output of the common-emitter stage.
concepts.detail: Because the voltage across the transistor’s collector–emitter terminals is the same as that across the load, the expression applies both to the transistor and to the amplifier stage. The inversion is visible on an oscilloscope as the output sine dipping whenever the input rises — the property that makes the common-emitter stage an inverting amplifier (and the reason feedback loops must count their inversions, as Chapter 15 will exploit).

concepts.statement: A common-emitter transistor has four signal quantities ($v_{be}$, $i_b$, $v_{ce}$, $i_c$) related by $$v_{be} = h_{ie}I_b + h_{re}V_{ce}, \qquad i_c = h_{fe}I_b + h_{oe}V_{ce}.$$ Here $h_{ie}$ is the **short-circuit input resistance**, $h_{re}$ the **open-circuit reverse voltage ratio**, $h_{fe}$ the **short-circuit forward current ratio** and $h_{oe}$ the **open-circuit output conductance**.
concepts.detail: Six variables ($i_b$, $i_c$, $i_e$, $v_{be}$, $v_{ce}$, $v_{cb}$) reduce to four independent ones because $i_b + i_c = i_e$ and $v_{cb} + v_{be} = v_{ce}$. The voltage generator $h_{re}V_{ce}$ represents a feedback effect — the output signal voltage controlling, to a very limited extent, the input signal current. But $h_{re}$ is always very small (less than $1\times 10^{-3}$), so the feedback generator can be omitted without introducing any important error, and the analyses of the simpler model stand.

concepts.term: h_fe and h_fb: β and α in disguise
concepts.statement: The short-circuit forward current ratio of the common-emitter model is exactly the current amplification factor of Section 13.2: $$h_{fe} = \beta.$$ For the common-base model, $h_{fb}$ has a value just under unity and is negative — it is $-\alpha$ in Hughes’s sign convention.
concepts.detail: The common-base gain expressions are identical in form to the common-emitter ones with the appropriate parameters substituted: $G_i = h_{fb}/(1 + h_{ob}R_p)$ and $G_v = -h_{fb}R_p/(h_{ib}(1 + h_{ob}R_p))$. Because $h_{fb} \approx -1$, there is a $180\degree$ phase shift between $I_e$ and $I_c$ but **no** phase shift between $V_{eb}$ and $V_{cb}$ — the common-base stage does not invert.

concepts.statement: For most bipolar transistors the input resistance $h_{ie}$ tends to be about $1\,\text{k}\Omega$ — a rather small value for electronic circuits. There is always a significant input current, which both limits the achievable gain and increases the size and rating of the input-circuit components.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s illustration: an amplifier of gain 40 and input resistance $1\,\text{k}\Omega$ driven by a $100\,\text{mV}$ source of $50\,\text{k}\Omega$ internal resistance delivers only $V_i \approx 2\,\text{mV}$ to the input, so $V_o = 40 \times 2 = 80\,\text{mV}$ — **less than the source e.m.f.**. Had the input resistance been $1\,\text{M}\Omega$, then $V_i = 95.2\,\text{mV}$ and $V_o = 3.8\,\text{V}$ — an improvement of more than 47 times, with much-reduced input current. In order to obtain that increase in input resistance we have to look for another type of transistor — the field effect transistor of Chapter 14.

concepts.statement: **Cascaded amplifiers** are connected so that the output of one stage is the input to a second, thus providing further gain; the coupling capacitor “conducts” the a.c. signal but “blocks” the d.c. component of the supply.
concepts.detail: The advantage of cascading is the increase of gain, offset by increased distortion due to the non-linearity of each stage. The analysis reuses the single-stage equivalent circuit twice, with current-divider factors threading the stages together (Example 20.9). Component counts quickly reach a hundred or more — the pressure that produced the integrated circuit (Section 14.4).

examples.title: Example 20.4 — h-parameter gains of a stage
examples.problem: A transistor amplifier stage has $h_{ie} = 800\,\Omega$, $h_{fe} = 50$ and $h_{oe} = 20\,\mu\text{S}$, with bias components and coupling capacitors of negligible effect. The input signal is an e.m.f. of $60\,\text{mV}$ from a source of internal resistance $2.2\,\text{k}\Omega$, and the total load on the stage output is $4\,\text{k}\Omega$. Determine the current, voltage and power gains.

steps.label: Step 1: Draw the equivalent circuit
steps.text: The source ($60\,\text{mV}$, $2.2\,\text{k}\Omega$) drives $h_{ie} = 800\,\Omega$; the output is the current generator $h_{fe}I_b = 50I_b$ feeding $1/h_{oe}$ in parallel with the $4\,\text{k}\Omega$ load.

steps.label: Step 2: Base current
steps.text: The input loop is a simple divider: $I_b = 60\times 10^{-3}/(2200 + 800) = 20\times 10^{-6}\,\text{A}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Collector current
steps.text: The output resistance of the model is $1/h_{oe} = 1/(20\times 10^{-6}) \approx 50\,\text{k}\Omega$. The generated current $50 \times 20\,\mu\text{A} = 1000\,\mu\text{A}$ splits between $50\,\text{k}\Omega$ and $4\,\text{k}\Omega$: $I_c = 50/(50+4) \times 1000\,\mu\text{A} = 926\,\mu\text{A}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Current gain
steps.text: $G_i = I_c/I_b = 926\times 10^{-6}/20\times 10^{-6} = 46.3$ — slightly less than $h_{fe} = 50$ because the finite $h_{oe}$ robs part of the generator current.

steps.label: Step 5: Voltage gain
steps.text: $G_v = -I_c R_L/(I_b h_{ie}) = -(926\times 10^{-6} \times 4\times 10^{3})/(20\times 10^{-6} \times 800) = -231.5$. The gain is negative — the stage inverts.

steps.label: Step 6: Power gain
steps.text: $G_p = G_i \times |G_v| = 46.3 \times 231.5 = 10\,720$ — five decades of power gain from one transistor.

examples.title: Example 20.9 — overall gain of a two-stage cascade
examples.problem: A two-stage amplifier has two identical transistors, each with input resistance $1\,\text{k}\Omega$, short-circuit current gain 60 and output conductance $20\,\mu\text{S}$. The source feeds the first stage through $100\,\text{k}\Omega$; the first collector circuit presents $10\,\text{k}\Omega$, $100\,\text{k}\Omega$ (bias) and $25\,\text{k}\Omega$ in parallel to the second stage; the second collector circuit presents $5\,\text{k}\Omega$ and $100\,\text{k}\Omega$; the final load is $2\,\text{k}\Omega$. Determine the overall current and power gains.

steps.label: Step 1: Internal output resistance of each transistor
steps.text: Each transistor’s model has $1/h_{oe} = 1/(20\times 10^{-6}) \approx 50\,\text{k}\Omega$ in parallel with its collector components.

steps.label: Step 2: Combine the first-stage output resistances
steps.text: The $50\,\text{k}\Omega$, $10\,\text{k}\Omega$, $100\,\text{k}\Omega$ and $25\,\text{k}\Omega$ combine as $1/R^{\prime} = 1/50 + 1/10 + 1/100 + 1/25 = 17/100$, so $R^{\prime} = 100/17 = 5.88\,\text{k}\Omega$ — the effective interstage load on the first transistor.

steps.label: Step 3: Combine the second-stage output resistances
steps.text: Similarly $1/R^{\prime\prime} = 1/50 + 1/5 = 11/50$, so $R^{\prime\prime} = 50/11 = 4.55\,\text{k}\Omega$ — the effective load on the second transistor in parallel with the $2\,\text{k}\Omega$ output load.

steps.label: Step 4: Thread the current dividers
steps.text: The first transistor receives $i_1 = (100/101)\,i_i$ of the input current; its generator produces $i_2 = 60\,i_1$. The fraction reaching the second transistor is $5.88/(5.88 + 1) = 5.88/6.88$, so $i_3 = (5.88/6.88) \times 60 \times (100/101)\,i_i$. The second generator gives $i_4 = 60\,i_3$, and the fraction delivered to the load is $4.55/(4.55 + 2) = 4.55/6.55$.

steps.label: Step 6: Power gain
steps.text: The amplifier input resistance is $R_i = (100 \times 1)/(100 + 1) \approx 990\,\Omega$ while the output load is $2\,\text{k}\Omega$, so $A_p = A_i^2 \times R_o/R_i = 2120^2 \times 2000/990 = 9\,080\,000$.

examples.result: $A_i = 2120$ and $A_p = 9\,080\,000$ — cascading squares the current gain and nearly a million-fold power gain through two transistors.

keyTakeaways: Over the linear part of its characteristics a transistor is replaced by an equivalent circuit carrying only r.m.s. signal quantities — the transistor is a current-operated device.
h-parameters: $h_{ie}$ input resistance ($\sim 1\,\text{k}\Omega$), $h_{fe}$ current gain ($= \beta$), $h_{oe}$ output conductance, $h_{re}$ reverse voltage ratio ($< 10^{-3}$, usually omitted).
Loaded stage gains: $G_i = h_{fe}/(1 + h_{oe}R_p)$ (transistor) times $R_C/(R_C + R_L)$ (stage), and $G_v = -h_{fe}R_p/(h_{ie}(1 + h_{oe}R_p))$ with $R_p = R_C R_L/(R_C + R_L)$.
The common-emitter stage inverts: the minus sign in $G_v$ is a real $180\degree$ phase shift; the common-base stage ($h_{fb} \approx -\alpha$) does not invert voltages.
Cascade gains multiply through current-divider chains — Example 20.9: $A_i = 2120$, $A_p = 9\,080\,000$ for two identical stages.
The BJT’s $\sim 1\,\text{k}\Omega$ input resistance loses signal against realistic sources (80 mV out of a 100 mV source with $50\,\text{k}\Omega$ source resistance) — the motivation for the FET.

quiz.q: In the h-parameter naming convention, the subscript letters indicate:
options: The connection mode — e.g. $h_{ie}$ is common-emitter input resistance, $h_{ib}$ common-base
quiz.explanation: The first subscript gives the parameter (input, reverse, forward, output) and the second the connection mode: e = common-emitter, b = common-base. The same transistor presents quite different h-parameters in the two connections.

quiz.q: A transistor has $h_{fe} = 50$ and $h_{oe} = 20\,\mu\text{S}$, driving an effective load $R_p = 4\,\text{k}\Omega$. The transistor current gain is closest to:
quiz.explanation: $G_i = h_{fe}/(1 + h_{oe}R_p) = 50/(1 + 20\times 10^{-6} \times 4000) = 50/1.08 = 46.3$ — the finite output conductance diverts part of the generated current through the model’s own $1/h_{oe} = 50\,\text{k}\Omega$.

quiz.q: Why can the feedback generator $h_{re}V_{ce}$ usually be omitted from the hybrid equivalent circuit?
options: Because $V_{ce}$ is always zero in small-signal operation
Because $h_{re}$ is always very small — less than $1 \times 10^{-3}$ — so the feedback voltage is negligible
Because it only matters in common-base connection
Because it is cancelled exactly by $h_{oe}$
quiz.explanation: Although a transistor’s voltage gain is large (which might suggest appreciable feedback), $h_{re}$ itself is always below $10^{-3}$, so the induced input voltage is negligible — and the omission lies well within component tolerances anyway.

quiz.q: A two-stage cascade of identical stages each with current gain 60 and interstage divider factors of about $5.88/6.88$ and $4.55/6.55$ has an overall current gain nearest to:
quiz.explanation: Example 20.9 threads the dividers: $A_i = (4.55/6.55) \times 60 \times (5.88/6.88) \times 60 \times (100/101) = 2120$. Two stages give roughly the product of their gains minus divider losses.

quiz.q: An amplifier of gain 40 and input resistance $1\,\text{k}\Omega$ is driven by a $100\,\text{mV}$ source with $50\,\text{k}\Omega$ internal resistance. The output voltage is approximately:
quiz.explanation: The input divider leaves only $V_i = (1\times 10^{3}/51\times 10^{3}) \times 100\,\text{mV} \approx 2\,\text{mV}$ across the amplifier, so $V_o = 40 \times 2 = 80\,\text{mV}$. With a $1\,\text{M}\Omega$ input the same source would deliver $95.2\,\text{mV}$ and the output would be $3.8\,\text{V}$ — more than 47 times better.

intro: A transistor left with fixed bias will not stay where it was put: leakage current grows with temperature and drags the quiescent point along with it. Hughes answers with stabilized bias networks — potential divider, emitter resistor, and at the system level the Zener and series transistor regulators — and then embraces the drift by driving the transistor deliberately to the two ends of its load line, where it becomes a switch. The Ebers–Moll view closes the chapter by trading the current picture for a voltage one: the collector current is commanded by V_BE, and transconductance is simply IC over the thermal voltage.
objectives: Explain why leakage current and $V_{BE}$ drift make fixed bias unstable and how potential-divider bias with an emitter resistor stabilizes the operating point
Analyze stabilized supplies using the stability factor S and the internal resistance of the supply
Describe cut-off and saturation as the two states of the transistor switch and assess its quality
Quantify BJT transconductance with the Ebers–Moll relation $g_m = I_C/V_T$

concepts.term: Thermal drift of the operating point
concepts.statement: The leakage current $I_{CBO}$ is temperature dependent: an increase in temperature causes it to rise, which increases the collector current (amplified by $1/(1-\alpha)$) and **changes the bias conditions** of the stage.
concepts.detail: The collector current is $I_C = \beta I_B + I_{CBO}/(1-\alpha)$, so a doubling of leakage moves the quiescent point along the load line even with the signal at zero. The Art of Electronics adds the second, subtler drift: at constant collector current the base–emitter voltage falls by roughly $2\,\text{mV}$ per $\degree\text{C}$ of junction warming — a fixed $V_{BE}$ bias therefore also misbehaves with temperature. Between them, the two effects destroy an unstabilized stage’s operating point as it warms up.

concepts.statement: The change in bias conditions is stabilized by using a **potential divider**, which holds the base voltage almost constant, together with a **resistor in the emitter connection**.
concepts.detail: The divider fixes $V_B$; if the collector current then rises with temperature, the emitter current raises the voltage across the emitter resistor, which reduces the forward bias $V_{BE} = V_B - V_E$ and so cuts the base current back down — negative feedback on the quiescent point. This is the same self-correcting geometry Hughes uses for the base of the series regulator transistor below, and the same trick the MOSFET source resistor performs in Chapter 14.

concepts.statement: The performance of a stabilization circuit is measured by the **stability factor** — the ratio of the change in stabilized voltage across the load to the change in unstabilized supply voltage: $$S = \frac{\text{change in stabilized voltage}}{\text{change in unstabilized voltage}}.$$ For satisfactory stabilization, S should be small — effectively, the smaller the better.
concepts.detail: The stabilization circuit sits between the rectifier (with its smoothing circuits, Chapter 12) and the load, and must hold its output constant when the supply voltage varies, when the load current changes, or both. Example 20.6: an unstabilized supply that swings between 110 V and 80 V with constant load current, stabilized by a circuit of stability factor 0.06, sees its output change by only $0.06 \times 30 = 1.8\,\text{V}$.

concepts.statement: One of the simplest stabilization circuits consists of a **resistor in series with the load and a Zener diode in parallel with the load**; the Zener holds the voltage nearly constant provided the load current and the unstabilized voltage each remain between set limits.
concepts.detail: This is the voltage-regulator diode of Chapter 12 doing its duty: its reverse breakdown voltage is nearly independent of the current through it, so the load sees that voltage whatever the raw supply does within limits. Such a simple circuit cannot handle wide variations of either variable — the set limits may not be acceptably far apart — which is why the series transistor regulator follows.

concepts.term: Internal resistance of a stabilized supply
concepts.statement: The effectiveness of a stabilization circuit when the **load current** changes (with the unstabilized voltage held constant) is indicated by its effective internal resistance: $$R_o = \frac{\Delta V_s}{\Delta I_L},$$ the change in output voltage divided by the change in output current over the range between the set limits.
concepts.detail: Example: a stabilization circuit whose load current ranges from 0 to 40 mA while the voltage applied to the load falls by 0.25 V has $R_o = 0.25/0.04 = 6.25\,\Omega$. As with the stability factor, the internal resistance should be as small as possible — it is the supply’s Thévenin impedance (Chapter 4) seen from the load.

concepts.statement: A better stabilizer places a **transistor in series with the load**, its current controlled by the base voltage; a **comparator network** compares a potentiometer fraction $V_2$ of the output against a Zener reference $V_Z$, amplifies the difference, and applies it to the base until $V_2 = V_Z$.
concepts.detail: If the comparison shows the voltages equal there is no amplifier output and the collector current stays put; any difference is amplified and changes the bias condition of the transistor, causing its emitter current to increase or decrease, changing the output voltage until $V_2$ equals $V_Z$ again. This arrangement can produce very low stability factors as well as low internal resistances — it is the discrete-transistor ancestor of the three-terminal regulator and, with the error amplifier opened out, of the feedback loops of Chapter 15.

concepts.term: The saturated transistor as a switch
concepts.statement: The two extreme conditions of the load line are: both junctions reverse biased — the **cut-off** condition (point A); and both junctions forward biased — the **saturation** condition (point B). In these extremes the transistor operates like a switch in which either the supply voltage appears at the output or it does not.
concepts.detail: The switch is not perfect: not all of the supply voltage is available to the load when switched on, and equally the load is not isolated in the OFF condition. For all its imperfections the transistor switch is useful because it operates effectively in the transmission of digital signals and has a quick switching time, responding to very high bit rates. The bipolar’s imperfections — significant input current when on, and a collector–emitter **offset voltage** — are precisely what the FET switch of Chapter 14 removes.

concepts.statement: The Art of Electronics models the transistor not as a current amplifier but as a **transconductance device**: the collector current is set by the base–emitter voltage, $$I_C = I_S\left(e^{V_{BE}/V_T} - 1\right), \qquad V_T = \frac{kT}{q} \approx 25\,\text{mV},$$ and differentiating gives the transconductance $$g_m = \frac{I_C}{V_T}.$$
concepts.detail: At room temperature $V_T = kT/q \approx 25\,\text{mV}$, so a transistor running at $I_C = 1\,\text{mA}$ has $g_m = 1\,\text{mA}/25\,\text{mV} = 40\,\text{mS}$, and the intrinsic emitter resistance seen from the emitter terminal is $r_e = 1/g_m = V_T/I_E = 25\,\Omega$. Doubling the collector current doubles the transconductance — gain in the Ebers–Moll picture is bought with current, not with β. The model also predicts the $2\,\text{mV}/\degree\text{C}$ drift of $V_{BE}$ and underlies the differential-pair and current-mirror circuits inside every op-amp of Chapter 15.

examples.title: Example 20.6 — a stabilized supply’s range
examples.problem: Without stabilization a supply voltage can change from 110 V to 80 V even though the load current remains constant. With stabilization by a circuit of stability factor 0.06, determine the change in the stabilized voltage.

steps.label: Step 1: State the definition
steps.text: The stability factor is $S = \Delta V_s/\Delta V_u$ — the change in stabilized voltage divided by the change in unstabilized voltage, assuming constant load current.

steps.label: Step 2: Compute the unstabilized swing
steps.text: The raw supply moves by $110 - 80 = 30\,\text{V}$ while the load takes the same current throughout.

steps.label: Step 3: Apply the factor
steps.text: $\Delta V_s = S \times \Delta V_u = 0.06 \times 30 = 1.8\,\text{V}$ — a decrease from the maximum value.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret
steps.text: The stabilization circuit has compressed a 30 V supply sag into a 1.8 V output change — a 50:1 improvement, achieved without any moving parts.

examples.result: The stabilized voltage changes by only $1.8\,\text{V}$ despite the $30\,\text{V}$ swing in the unstabilized input.

examples.title: Example 20.7 — worst-case load voltage
examples.problem: A stabilization circuit has a stability factor of 0.04 and an internal resistance of $5\,\Omega$. The unstabilized voltage can vary between 75 and 100 V, and the load current from 40 to 80 mA. Determine the maximum and minimum stabilized load voltages.

steps.label: Step 1: Identify the extreme conditions
steps.text: The worst cases are low unstabilized voltage with high load current, and high unstabilized voltage with low load current.

steps.label: Step 2: Low input, high current
steps.text: The load voltage is the lower limit of the unstabilized voltage minus the internal-resistance drop: $75 - (80\times 10^{-3} \times 5) = 75 - 0.4 = 74.6\,\text{V}$.

steps.label: Step 3: High input — the allowed rise
steps.text: The unstabilized voltage rises to 100 V, but the circuit allows only $S \times (100 - 75) = 0.04 \times 25 = 1.0\,\text{V}$ of increase in the stabilized output.

steps.label: Step 4: High input, low current
steps.text: The internal-resistance drop with $40\,\text{mA}$ of load is $40\times 10^{-3} \times 5 = 0.2\,\text{V}$, so the load voltage is $75 + 1.0 - 0.2 = 75.8\,\text{V}$.

steps.label: Step 5: State the range
steps.text: The stabilized voltage therefore varies only between 74.6 V and 75.8 V — a $1.2\,\text{V}$ band around 75 V while the raw supply moves through 25 V and the load current through a factor of two.

examples.result: The load voltage stays within $74.6\,\text{V}$ to $75.8\,\text{V}$ — regulation held by S and $R_o$ acting together.

examples.title: Transconductance from Ebers–Moll
examples.problem: Use the Ebers–Moll view to find the transconductance and intrinsic emitter resistance of a transistor biased at $I_C = 1\,\text{mA}$ at room temperature, and compare with a FET of the same current.

steps.label: Step 1: Thermal voltage
steps.text: At room temperature $V_T = kT/q \approx 25\,\text{mV}$ — the voltage across which the exponential collector-current law operates.

steps.label: Step 3: Intrinsic emitter resistance
steps.text: Looking back into the emitter: $r_e = 1/g_m = V_T/I_E = 25\,\Omega$ at $1\,\text{mA}$ — the resistance the input signal effectively drives.

steps.label: Step 4: Compare with the FET
steps.text: A junction FET of the same $1\,\text{mA}$ drain current offers $g_m$ of only 1–10 mS (Chapter 14), so the BJT is the transconductance champion: its gain per milliamp of supply current is several times higher, while the FET repays with its insulated gate.

examples.result: $g_m = 40\,\text{mS}$ and $r_e = 25\,\Omega$ at $1\,\text{mA}$ — both simply and inversely proportional to the collector current.

keyTakeaways: Leakage $I_{CBO}$ rises with temperature and is amplified by $1/(1-\alpha)$ into the collector current; $V_{BE}$ also drifts about $2\,\text{mV}/\degree\text{C}$ — fixed bias wanders.
Potential-divider bias holds the base voltage nearly constant, and an emitter resistor feeds the drift back against itself — the standard stabilized bias.

Stability factor $S = \Delta V_{\text{stabilized}}/\Delta V_{\text{unstabilized}}$ (smaller is better) and internal resistance $R_o = \Delta V_s/\Delta I_L$ (e.g. $0.25\,\text{V}/40\,\text{mA} = 6.25\,\Omega$) quantify a regulator.
A Zener shunt stabilizer needs both supply and load within set limits; the series transistor with comparator and Zener reference achieves very low S and $R_o$.
Both junctions reverse biased = cut-off; both forward biased = saturation: the transistor as an imperfect but very fast switch for digital signals and high bit rates.
Ebers–Moll: $I_C = I_S(e^{V_{BE}/V_T} - 1)$ with $V_T \approx 25\,\text{mV}$, so $g_m = I_C/V_T$ — $40\,\text{mS}$ at $1\,\text{mA}$, with $r_e = 25\,\Omega$.

quiz.q: Why does an increase in temperature shift the bias point of a common-emitter stage?
options: Because β falls with temperature, reducing the collector current
Because the leakage current rises with temperature, increasing the collector current through the amplified term $I_{CBO}/(1-\alpha)$
Because the collector resistor warms and changes value
quiz.explanation: The leakage current crossing the reverse-biased collector–base junction is temperature dependent; its effect on the collector current is multiplied by $1/(1-\alpha)$ — fifty-fold for α = 0.98. The rising current drags the quiescent point along the load line.

quiz.q: A stabilization circuit holds the base voltage of the series transistor nearly constant by comparing it with a Zener reference. The load voltage changes when the unstabilized input swings from 75 V to 100 V by:
options: Nothing at all — the output is perfectly constant
quiz.explanation: The stability factor is the ratio of the change in stabilized output to the change in unstabilized input: $\Delta V_s = S\,\Delta V_u = 0.04 \times 25 = 1.0\,\text{V}$, as in Example 20.7. Regulation is good but never perfect.

quiz.q: A stabilized supply delivers 0 to 40 mA over its allowed load range while its output falls 0.25 V. Its internal resistance is:
quiz.explanation: $R_o = \Delta V_s/\Delta I_L = 0.25/0.04 = 6.25\,\Omega$. Like the stability factor, the internal resistance should be as small as possible — it is the output impedance of the Thévenin source the load actually sees.

quiz.q: In the transistor switch, the cut-off condition corresponds to:
options: The emitter junction forward biased and the collector junction reverse biased
Both junctions reverse biased — point A on the load line
The operating point at the middle of the load line
quiz.explanation: Cut-off is both junctions reverse biased (point A — no output current); saturation is both forward biased (point B — output voltage nearly zero). Between them lies the amplifier region, whose middle the quiescent point of Section 13.3 occupies.

quiz.q: A transistor operates at $I_C = 1\,\text{mA}$ at room temperature. According to the Ebers–Moll view its transconductance is:
options: It equals β and depends only on construction
quiz.explanation: $g_m = I_C/V_T = 1\,\text{mA}/25\,\text{mV} = 40\,\text{mS}$, independent of β. The corresponding intrinsic emitter resistance is $r_e = 1/g_m = 25\,\Omega$.

intro: The bipolar transistor of Chapter 13 paid for its gain with a low input resistance and a current that must constantly be fed into the base. The field-effect transistor removes both costs at a stroke: its conducting channel is controlled by a voltage, and in the most important family that voltage acts on an insulated gate that draws no current at all. Hughes calls the two branches JUGFET and IGFET; the second is better known today as the MOSFET — the device that built the digital world.
objectives: Classify the FET family — JUGFET and IGFET, p- and n-channel, depletion and enhancement modes
Describe the construction of the n-channel JUGFET and the roles of source, gate and drain
Explain depletion-layer control of the channel and the pinch-off condition that limits the drain current to I_DSS
Describe the IGFET/MOSFET structure and distinguish enhancement from depletion operation

concepts.statement: Unlike bipolar junction transistors, which are all basically similar, the **field effect transistor (FET)** is a collective term for a family of devices with two principal groups: the **junction-type FET (JUGFET)** and the **insulated-type FET (IGFET)**. The JUGFET comes in p-channel and n-channel forms; the IGFET has two distinct modes of operation — **depletion** and **enhancement** — each subdividing into p-channel and n-channel.
concepts.detail: Like the BJT, all FETs are three-electrode devices: the **source**, **gate** and **drain**, which can be taken as corresponding to the emitter, base and collector respectively. Where the BJT controls a large current with a small current, every FET controls a current with a voltage — and in the IGFET that voltage is applied to a gate separated from the channel by an insulator, so the control electrode draws no current whatsoever.

concepts.statement: The more common variety of JUGFET is the n-channel type: a piece of **n-type silicon effectively within a tube of p-type silicon** — the shroud — the interface being the same intimate junction as in the bipolar transistor. Non-rectifying contacts connect to each end of the n-type piece (the **source S** and **drain D**) and to the p-type tube (the **gate G**).
concepts.detail: The gate–channel junction is a genuine p–n junction, deliberately reverse biased in normal operation. The p-channel JUGFET is the exact converse, with all polarities and current directions reversed. The contrast to remember against Chapter 13: the BJT’s controlling junction is forward biased and draws current; the JUGFET’s is reverse biased and blocks it.

concepts.statement: With the gate disconnected and a d.c. supply making the **drain positive with respect to the source**, a conventional current flows from drain to source: electrons — the majority carriers in the n-channel — move from source to drain. Because it is semiconductor material, the voltage/current relationship is almost linear and the n-channel more or less behaves as a **resistor**.
concepts.detail: This ohmic region of the output characteristic is the FET’s signature difference from the BJT: with the control electrode open, the device is simply a piece of doped silicon. It is also what makes a fully enhanced FET such a good closed switch (Section 14.4) — the “on” channel really is a small resistance, not a saturated junction with an offset voltage.

concepts.statement: With the gate connected to the source while drain current flows, the channel voltage becomes greater towards the drain, so the reverse bias on the gate–channel p–n junction is **greater nearer the drain** than the source. This produces a **depletion layer** — which acts as an insulator — thicker at the drain end, reducing the effective cross-section of the channel and restricting the flow of electrons: the FET is said to operate in the **depletion mode**.
concepts.detail: The depletion region is the same space-charge layer of Chapter 12, here used as a voltage-controlled squeeze on the channel. Because the layer grows where the channel voltage is highest, its wedge shape is deepest at the drain end — the physical reason the curves of the output characteristic bunch and flatten there.

concepts.statement: If the drain–source voltage is increased, the depletion layer grows until it **completely absorbs the n-channel**; the drain–source current $I_D$ then reaches a limiting value called the **saturation current $I_{DSS}$**, and the point at which this occurs is the **pinch-off point**.
concepts.detail: Beyond pinch-off the current hardly changes with further drain voltage, so the device behaves as a current source commanded by the gate — the flat region in which FET amplifiers operate. Applying a separate bias voltage to the gate sets up an even depletion layer in the channel: pinch-off then occurs at a lower drain voltage and the currents, including the saturation current, are all smaller.

concepts.term: The gate has the stronger grip
concepts.statement: The combined effect of drain–source voltage and gate bias is that **the more negative the gate voltage, the smaller the saturation current**; the gate voltage could stop the flow of drain current altogether if made sufficiently negative. Most importantly, the gate voltage has a **more significant effect on the drain current than the drain voltage** — the essence of voltage control.
concepts.detail: The resulting output characteristics of an n-channel JUGFET — a family for $V_{GS} = 0$, −1 V, −2 V, flat beyond pinch-off and tightly stacked in gate-voltage steps — compare in form with the common-emitter family of Fig. 20.23, and amplifier action is obtained in the same way as in Fig. 20.29. The gate–source junctions present very high resistance (megohms) since they consist of reverse-biased junctions; gate currents are very small, though they vary with temperature as minority-carrier numbers grow.

concepts.statement: As its name indicates, the IGFET has its **gate insulated from the channel**: the bulk of the device is a low-conductivity silicon **substrate** (p-type for an n-channel device) into which a thin n-channel is introduced, terminated in the drain and source electrodes. The gate is separated from the channel by a **layer of silicon dioxide** — an insulator isolating the gate from both source and drain.
concepts.detail: The silicon dioxide can be thought of as the dielectric in a capacitor whose two plates are the gate metallization and the channel. This gate–oxide capacitor is the seat of all MOSFET action: charge the gate positively and it induces negative charge — extra electrons — in the channel beneath it. There is no p–n junction between channel and gate as in the JUGFET; instead the pinch-off effect stems from the p–n junction between channel and substrate, and the substrate is often connected to the source, which conveniently completes the gate–source bias loop.

concepts.statement: If the **gate is made positive** with respect to the source and hence the channel, the drain–source current is increased — the FET is said to be **enhanced**. If the gate is made negative, the current is decreased — the FET is **depleted**. In the **enhancement-mode IGFET** the channel is omitted altogether: conduction can only take place when the gate is positive with respect to the substrate, inducing a conduction channel — so the device is normally OFF.
concepts.detail: The cause of the variation lies in the capacitive effect between gate and channel: a positively charged gate leaves the channel negatively charged, an increase in charge carriers; reverse the bias and there is a depletion of carriers. The enhancement-mode device — conducting only when actively induced — is the form in which the MOSFET conquered digital electronics, because with zero gate voltage it is simply off (Section 14.3).

concepts.statement: The IGFET is sometimes termed a **MOSFET** (metal, oxide, silicon — or MOST for short). IGFETs can easily be **destroyed by the build-up of charge across the dielectric** separating gate and substrate; to avoid this, protective links are often fitted at manufacture and removed only when the devices are installed.
concepts.detail: The gate oxide is so thin that ordinary static electricity — thousands of volts, however tiny in charge — punctures it. Production parts accordingly ship with gate leads shorted together (or with internal protection diodes clamping the gate), and assembly lines take earthed precautions. The vulnerability is the price of the insulated gate’s enormous input resistance — typically $10^{12}\,\Omega$ or more.

examples.title: Tracing an n-channel JUGFET to pinch-off
examples.problem: Describe, step by step, how the drain characteristic of an n-channel JUGFET arises from the gate–channel junction, following Hughes §20.22 (Figs 20.50–20.53).

steps.label: Step 1: Gate open — the ohmic region
steps.text: With the gate disconnected and the drain positive with respect to the source, electrons flow source-to-drain and the channel behaves as a simple resistor: current rises almost linearly with drain–source voltage.

steps.label: Step 2: Gate tied to source — the depletion wedge
steps.text: Connecting the gate to the source reverse biases the gate–channel junction, most strongly at the drain end where the channel voltage is highest. The depletion layer — an insulator — wedges into the channel, reducing its cross-section and flattening the current rise.

steps.label: Step 3: Raise the drain voltage — pinch-off
steps.text: As the drain–source voltage increases further, the depletion layer eventually completely absorbs the channel; the drain current reaches its limiting saturation value $I_{DSS}$ and stays nearly constant — the pinch-off point.

steps.label: Step 4: Add gate bias — level control
steps.text: A fixed negative gate–source voltage sets up an even depletion layer, so pinch-off occurs at a lower drain voltage and with smaller currents throughout; sufficiently negative, the gate stops the drain current altogether. Each gate voltage thus buys its own flat curve in the family of Fig. 20.54 ($V_{GS} = 0$, −1 V, −2 V).

examples.result: The drain characteristic starts ohmic (channel as resistor), bends over at pinch-off where the depletion layer absorbs the channel, and saturates at $I_{DSS}$ — a level the gate voltage, not the drain voltage, controls.

examples.title: Choosing the gate polarity for each FET family
examples.problem: From the transfer characteristics of Figs 20.62–20.63, state the gate voltage required for OFF and for ON in each of the three n-channel switch families.

steps.label: Step 1: n-channel JUGFET
steps.text: The gate voltage must be sufficiently **negative** to ensure that no drain current flows in the OFF condition; any suitable voltage between that value and zero switches the device ON. The BJT’s analogue — forward versus reverse bias of the base–emitter junction — sits on the same axes for comparison.

steps.label: Step 2: n-channel IGFET, depletion mode
steps.text: Same shape of rule: the gate must be sufficiently negative for OFF, and is made positive to switch ON — but note the device also conducts at zero gate voltage (its built-in channel gives a finite $I_{DSS}$).

steps.label: Step 3: n-channel IGFET, enhancement mode
steps.text: OFF is the normal condition: with no gate signal the channel simply does not exist, so no negative voltage is ever needed to guarantee OFF. A positive gate voltage induces the channel and switches the device ON.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret for circuit design
steps.text: The enhancement-mode device is the natural digital switch: output of one gate (near zero or near $V_{DD}$) directly drives the input of the next, with no level shifting — the property that Section 14.3 exploits in the CMOS inverter.

examples.result: JUGFET: negative for OFF, zero-ish for ON. Depletion IGFET: negative for OFF, positive for ON (conducts at zero). Enhancement IGFET: zero is OFF, positive is ON — the digital-friendly one.

keyTakeaways: The FET family splits into junction devices (JUGFET, p- or n-channel) and insulated-gate devices (IGFET/MOSFET, each in depletion and enhancement forms, p- or n-channel).
Electrodes: source, gate, drain — the FET’s answer to emitter, base, collector.
With the gate open the channel is simply a resistor; reverse-biasing the gate junction wedges a depletion layer into it, pinching the channel off at $I_{DSS}$.
The gate voltage controls the drain current more significantly than the drain voltage does — voltage control, with megohms of input resistance in the JUGFET and effectively infinite in the IGFET.
The IGFET gate sits on a silicon-dioxide insulator — a capacitor plate over the channel: positive gate enhances conduction, negative gate depletes it.
The enhancement-mode IGFET has no built-in channel: it conducts only when a positive gate induces one, making it a normally-OFF device.
The MOSFET’s thin gate oxide is easily punctured by static — protective links are fitted at manufacture and removed on installation.

quiz.q: The three electrodes of a FET — source, gate and drain — correspond to which BJT terminals?
quiz.explanation: The source emits the majority carriers into the channel (like the emitter), the drain collects them (like the collector), and the gate controls the flow (like the base) — but by voltage, not current.

quiz.q: In an n-channel JUGFET with the gate connected to the source, the depletion layer is thickest:
options: Near the drain, where the channel voltage — and hence the reverse bias — is highest
Only when the drain voltage is zero
quiz.explanation: Electrons flowing from source to drain raise the channel potential towards the drain, so the gate–channel junction is most reverse biased there and the depletion wedge is deepest at the drain end — the geometry that produces pinch-off.

quiz.q: The symbol $I_{DSS}$ denotes:
options: The drain current at zero gate–source voltage, i.e. the saturation (pinch-off) current
The drain current when the gate is most negative
quiz.explanation: $I_{DSS}$ is the limiting saturation drain current reached at pinch-off — the current with the gate tied to the source. Gate bias reduces the saturation current below this value, and a sufficiently negative gate stops it entirely.

quiz.q: In an n-channel IGFET, making the gate positive with respect to the source:
options: Reverse biases the gate–channel junction and decreases the current
Induces extra charge carriers in the channel and increases the current — enhancement
Has no effect until the substrate is disconnected
quiz.explanation: The gate–oxide–channel system is a capacitor: a positive gate induces negative charge — additional electrons — in the channel, enhancing conduction. A negative gate depletes it. The oxide only punctures when the field is far beyond normal operation (static discharge).

quiz.q: Why is the enhancement-mode IGFET the natural choice for digital switching?
options: It conducts maximally at zero gate voltage
It is normally OFF — with no gate signal there is no channel, so no level-shifting is needed between logic stages
It requires a negative supply as well as a positive one
Its gate draws a large current when ON
quiz.explanation: With the channel omitted in manufacture, zero gate voltage guarantees OFF; a positive gate induces a channel and turns it ON. Logic levels therefore drive gates directly — the arrangement the CMOS inverter of Section 14.3 perfects.

intro: Measured properly, a FET is described by three numbers — drain resistance, mutual conductance and their product — and, on the transfer side, by one elegant parabola: Shockley’s equation. Hughes assembles the small-signal equivalent circuit (input simply open, so no input loading at all), derives the common-source gain, and then shows the device doing the job the BJT found hardest of all: switching analog signals with no offset and no drive current.
objectives: Define drain resistance, mutual conductance and the amplification factor of a FET
Apply the Shockley equation to compute drain current and transconductance of a JFET
Draw the Y-parameter equivalent circuit and derive the common-source voltage gain
Explain why the FET outperforms the BJT as an analog switch

concepts.statement: The ratio of the change $\Delta V_{DS}$ in drain–source voltage to the change $\Delta I_D$ in drain current, for a given gate–source voltage, is the **drain resistance**: $$r_d = \frac{\Delta V_{DS}}{\Delta I_D} \quad \text{for a given } V_{GS}.$$ Its value is large in most FETs — of the order of $10$–$500\,\text{k}\Omega$.
concepts.detail: This is the slope resistance of the flat pinch-off region of the output characteristic: the flatter the curves, the better the FET approximates an ideal current source. In the equivalent circuit $r_d$ appears across the output, exactly as $1/h_{oe}$ did for the BJT in Section 13.4.

concepts.statement: The ratio of the change $\Delta I_D$ in drain current to the change $\Delta V_{GS}$ in gate–source voltage, for a given drain–source voltage, is the **mutual conductance**: $$g_m = \frac{\Delta I_D}{\Delta V_{GS}} \quad \text{for a given } V_{DS}.$$ It is usually measured in milliamperes per volt.
concepts.detail: The transconductance is the FET’s gain currency — the same quantity the Ebers–Moll view gave for the BJT ($g_m = I_C/V_T$, Section 13.5), but set by geometry and bias rather than by the thermal voltage. FET values of 1–10 mA/V are routine, against the BJT’s 40 mS at 1 mA: the FET trades gain for input impedance.

concepts.statement: The product of drain resistance and mutual conductance gives the **amplification factor**: $$\mu = r_d g_m.$$ It is dimensionless — the maximum voltage gain available before output loading is considered.
concepts.detail: Hughes relation [20.40]. The same triple ($r_d$, $g_m$, $\mu$) was used for thermionic valves, and the identity $\mu = r_d g_m$ is why a FET stage loaded by $r_d$ itself would achieve exactly $\mu$ of gain.

concepts.statement: The transfer characteristic of a JFET is parabolic: $$I_D = I_{DSS}\left(1 - \frac{V_{GS}}{V_p}\right)^2,$$ where $I_{DSS}$ is the saturation current at $V_{GS} = 0$ and $V_p$ the pinch-off (cut-off) gate voltage at which the channel closes.
concepts.detail: The curve passes through $I_{DSS}$ at zero gate bias and reaches zero at $V_{GS} = V_p$; halfway in voltage gives a quarter of the current (the square). Differentiating gives the transconductance at any bias: $g_m = -2 I_{DSS}(1 - V_{GS}/V_p)/V_p$, which is maximal at $V_{GS} = 0$ with $g_{m0} = 2I_{DSS}/|V_p|$. The square law also makes the FET a natural mixer and multiplier — the property that made it beloved of receiver designers.

concepts.statement: The FET small-signal equivalent circuit is like the junction transistor’s **except that the input resistance is so high that it can be considered infinite** — equivalent to an open circuit. The parameters are **Y-parameters**: $Y_{fs}$, the forward transconductance (s = common-source mode), and $Y_{os}$, the output conductance.
concepts.detail: Both are ratios of a current to a voltage — amperes per volt, i.e. siemens: $Y_{fs}$ is the small-signal $I_D/V_{GS}$ (it is simply $g_m$ in admittance clothing) and $Y_{os}$ the output admittance ($1/r_d$). The equivalent circuit is drawn with the gate branch open, a current generator $Y_{fs}V_{GS}$ from source to drain, and $Y_{os}$ across the output.

concepts.statement: From the equivalent circuit with load $R_L$: $I = I_D + V_o Y_{os}$, $I_D = V_{GS}Y_{fs}/(1 + R_L Y_{os})$ and $V_o = I_D R_L$, giving Hughes relation [20.41]: $$A_v = \frac{Y_{fs}R_L}{1 + R_LY_{os}}.$$ When $R_LY_{os} \ll 1$ this reduces to $A_v \approx g_m R_L$.
concepts.detail: The output current generator drives $R_L$ in parallel with the model’s own output admittance — the same current-divider that trimmed the BJT stage by $1 + h_{oe}R_p$ in Section 13.4, but with admittances instead of resistances. Unlike the common-emitter stage, the common-source stage driven from the gate takes **no input current**, so the source e.m.f. arrives at the gate undiminished.

concepts.term: The FET as an analog switch
concepts.statement: The bipolar switch is imperfect because there is a **significant input current** when the base–emitter junction is forward biased, and it exhibits a collector–emitter **offset voltage** when on. The FET is better on every count: the insulated gate ensures **no gate current whether ON or OFF**; in the OFF condition effectively **no current flows between drain and source** (an open circuit); when ON, the resistance introduced by the FET is **negligible**.
concepts.detail: A JUGFET switch needs the gate sufficiently negative to guarantee OFF, any voltage between that and zero giving ON; a depletion-mode IGFET behaves the same way but also conducts at zero bias, while the enhancement-mode device is OFF by default and needs only a positive gate to conduct. This near-ideal behavior — bidirectional current, no offset, voltage drive — makes the FET the standard analog gate for chopping, sampling and multiplexing signals.

concepts.statement: Plotted side by side (Hughes Fig. 20.62–20.63), the BJT’s collector current switches as the base–emitter junction moves from reverse to forward bias, the n-channel JUGFET’s drain current switches as the gate goes negative, and the enhancement IGFET switches from its natural OFF state as the gate goes positive.
concepts.detail: The BJT needs a current through its forward-biased junction to stay on; every FET needs only a voltage on a reverse-biased or insulated gate. That single difference — current-controlled versus voltage-controlled switching — is why digital electronics standardized on MOS technology rather than on the bipolar logic families that preceded it.

examples.title: Example 20.8 — FET stage voltage gain
examples.problem: A transistor amplifier stage comprises a FET with $Y_{fs} = 2.2\,\text{mA/V}$ and $Y_{os} = 20\,\mu\text{S}$, with bias components and coupling capacitors of negligible effect. The total load on the output is $2\,\text{k}\Omega$. Determine the voltage gain.

steps.label: Step 1: State the gain relation
steps.text: From the Y-parameter equivalent circuit, $A_v = Y_{fs}R_L/(1 + R_LY_{os})$ — the transconductance times the load, discounted by the model’s own output admittance.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret
steps.text: The unloaded product $g_mR_L = 4.4$ is trimmed only 4 per cent by the FET’s own output admittance — the load is far below $1/Y_{os} = 50\,\text{k}\Omega$, so almost all the generated current reaches the load. Note too that the gate drew no current at all from the source.

examples.result: $A_v = 4.23$ — modest next to the BJT stage of Example 20.4 ($-231.5$), the familiar FET trade of gain for an input that loads nothing.

examples.title: Shockley’s equation at work
examples.problem: A typical n-channel JFET has $I_{DSS} = 10\,\text{mA}$ and pinch-off voltage $V_p = -4\,\text{V}$ (typical datasheet values). Compute the drain current and transconductance at $V_{GS} = -1\,\text{V}$, and at $V_{GS} = -3\,\text{V}$.

steps.label: Step 1: Write the transfer law
steps.text: $I_D = I_{DSS}(1 - V_{GS}/V_p)^2$ — the parabola anchored at $I_{DSS}$ for $V_{GS} = 0$ and at zero current for $V_{GS} = V_p = -4\,\text{V}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Current at −1 V
steps.text: The normalized bias is $1 - (-1)/(-4) = 0.75$, so $I_D = 10\times 0.75^2 = 5.6\,\text{mA}$ — a quarter of the way in voltage, over half the current.

steps.label: Step 3: Current at −3 V
steps.text: The normalized bias is $1 - 0.75 = 0.25$, so $I_D = 10\times 0.25^2 = 0.625\,\text{mA}$ — deep cut-off approach: three quarters of the gate range removes 94 per cent of the current.

steps.label: Step 4: Transconductance
steps.text: Differentiating the parabola, $g_m = 2I_{DSS}(1 - V_{GS}/V_p)/|V_p|$: at $V_{GS} = -1\,\text{V}$, $g_m = 2\times 10\times 0.75/4 = 3.75\,\text{mA/V}$, falling to $1.25\,\text{mA/V}$ at $-3\,\text{V}$.

steps.label: Step 5: Interpret for biasing
steps.text: The transconductance — and with it the stage gain — falls linearly along the transfer curve, halving as the bias moves halfway to pinch-off. Biasing near $I_{DSS}$ buys gain; biasing near pinch-off buys current economy.

keyTakeaways: The three FET figures of merit: $r_d = \Delta V_{DS}/\Delta I_D$ (typically $10$–$500\,\text{k}\Omega$), $g_m = \Delta I_D/\Delta V_{GS}$ (mA/V), and $\mu = r_d g_m$.
Shockley’s law $I_D = I_{DSS}(1 - V_{GS}/V_p)^2$ — the parabolic transfer curve; differentiating gives $g_m$ at any bias.
The Y-parameter model: input open (no gate current), generator $Y_{fs}V_{GS}$, output admittance $Y_{os}$; gain $A_v = Y_{fs}R_L/(1 + R_LY_{os})$.
Example 20.8: $Y_{fs} = 2.2\,\text{mA/V}$, $Y_{os} = 20\,\mu\text{S}$, $R_L = 2\,\text{k}\Omega$ gives $A_v = 4.23$ — only 4 per cent below $g_mR_L$.
As a switch the FET beats the BJT: no gate current ON or OFF, no drain–source current when OFF, negligible resistance when ON — no offset voltage.
Enhancement-mode IGFETs are OFF by default (no channel); depletion-mode devices and JUGFETs conduct at zero gate bias and need negative gate voltage for OFF.

quiz.q: The mutual conductance of a FET is defined as:
quiz.explanation: Mutual conductance (transconductance) is the change in drain current per change in gate–source voltage at fixed drain–source voltage, in mA/V. $\Delta V_{DS}/\Delta I_D$ is the drain resistance and $r_d g_m$ is the amplification factor.

quiz.q: A JFET has $I_{DSS} = 10\,\text{mA}$ and $V_p = -4\,\text{V}$. At $V_{GS} = -2\,\text{V}$ the drain current is:
quiz.explanation: Shockley: $I_D = 10(1 - (-2)/(-4))^2 = 10 \times (0.5)^2 = 2.5\,\text{mA}$ — halfway in gate voltage gives a quarter of the current, the signature of the square law.

quiz.q: A FET stage has $Y_{fs} = 2.2\,\text{mA/V}$, $Y_{os} = 20\,\mu\text{S}$ and $R_L = 2\,\text{k}\Omega$. The voltage gain is closest to:
quiz.explanation: $A_v = Y_{fs}R_L/(1 + R_LY_{os}) = 4.4/(1 + 0.04) = 4.23$. The FET’s own output admittance shaves only 4 per cent off the ideal $g_mR_L = 4.4$ here (Example 20.8).

quiz.q: Compared with the bipolar transistor switch, the FET switch:
options: Requires a steady gate current to stay ON
Exhibits a large drain–source offset voltage when ON
Draws no gate current in either state and offers negligible ON resistance with no OFF current
Cannot switch analog signals, only digital ones
quiz.explanation: The insulated gate ensures no gate current whether ON or OFF; OFF, effectively no current flows drain–source (open circuit); ON, the channel resistance is negligible. This is what makes the FET the standard analog gate — no offset, no drive current.

quiz.q: In the Y-parameter equivalent circuit of a FET, the input branch is drawn as:
options: A resistance of about $1\,\text{k}\Omega$, like $h_{ie}$ of the BJT
A short circuit — the gate voltage appears directly across the generator
An open circuit — the input resistance is considered infinite
A capacitor equal to the gate–channel capacitance
quiz.explanation: The FET’s input resistance is so high it can be considered infinite: no input current, so no input loading. Contrast $h_{ie} \approx 1\,\text{k}\Omega$ for the BJT (Section 13.4) — the very limitation that pushed electronics toward the FET.

quiz.q: An n-channel JFET has $I_{DSS} = 10$ mA and pinch-off voltage $-4.0$ V. With $V_{GS} = -1.0$ V in saturation, the drain current is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $I_{DSS} = 10$ mA, $V_{P} = -4.0$ V, $V_{GS} = -1.0$ V, saturation assumed. Step 2 — Governing parabola: $I_{D} = I_{DSS}(1 - \frac{V_{GS}}{V_{P}})^{2}$. Step 3 — Algebra: $\frac{V_{GS}}{V_{P}} = \frac{-1.0}{-4.0} = 0.25$; $I_{D} = 10 \times (0.75)^{2} = 10 \times 0.5625 = 5.625$ mA. Step 4 — Sanity check: current lies below $I_{DSS}$ as negative bias demands, reaches $I_{DSS}$ at zero bias, and pinches toward zero at $-4$ V. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 7.5 mA drops the square, 2.5 mA squares the ratio instead of its complement, and 10 mA ignores bias. Step 6 — Conclude: about 5.6 mA flows.

intro: The enhancement MOSFET of Section 14.1 becomes a practical amplifier once its gate is biased a couple of volts above its threshold, and the design pattern is the one Hughes already taught for the BJT: set the operating point, then read the gain from the transconductance and the load. The real triumph of this device, though, is what happens when two complementary MOSFETs — one n-channel, one p-channel — are wired as one inverter: the CMOS pair that dissipated no static power and went on to build essentially all of digital electronics.
objectives: Bias a common-source MOSFET stage with a gate divider and source resistor
Compute common-source gain with and without a bypassed source resistor
Explain the complementary symmetry of the CMOS inverter and its linear-region use as an amplifier
Justify CMOS’s dominance of digital electronics using its static and dynamic power terms

concepts.statement: A common-source MOSFET stage is biased by a **resistive divider $R_1$–$R_2$** setting the gate voltage, a **source resistor $R_S$** fixing the drain current as $I_D = (V_G - V_{GS})/R_S$, and a **drain resistor $R_D$** completing the d.c. load line from $V_{DD}$.
concepts.detail: Because the gate draws no d.c. current, the divider sets $V_G$ exactly — the divider can use large resistors without error, keeping the input impedance high. The drain resistor is chosen to drop the drain to roughly mid-supply for maximum symmetric swing, exactly the halfway-up-the-load-line rule of Section 13.3. The MOSFET’s $V_{GS}$ (a couple of volts above threshold at the wanted current) is not precisely known device-to-device, which is what the source resistor is for.

concepts.statement: The source resistor stabilizes the drain current against device spread and temperature exactly as the emitter resistor stabilized the BJT bias of Section 13.5: if $I_D$ rises, the source voltage rises, the gate–source voltage falls, and the current is pulled back down.
concepts.detail: The Art of Electronics treats this self-correcting bias as the standard recipe for both BJTs and FETs. Where the BJT version fights leakage current and $V_{BE}$ drift, the FET version mostly fights manufacturing spread of $V_{GS}$ — the resistor converts an uncertain voltage into a well-defined current, at the price of some gain when it is left unbypassed.

concepts.statement: With the source resistor bypassed by a capacitor at signal frequencies, the common-source voltage gain is $$A_v = -g_m R_D,$$ and with $R_S$ unbypassed it becomes $$A_v = -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S}.$$
concepts.detail: The minus sign is the same $180\degree$ output inversion as the common-emitter stage of Section 13.4. The unbypassed form is the FET’s emitter-degeneration counterpart: the input voltage must first overcome the replica it induces across $R_S$, cutting the effective transconductance to $g_m/(1 + g_mR_S)$. In the limit $g_mR_S \gg 1$ the gain approaches $-R_D/R_S$ — a gain set by resistor ratio alone, independent of the device.

concepts.term: Why FET stages have modest gain
concepts.statement: A small-signal MOSFET running at a milliamp or two offers $g_m$ of only about 1–10 mA/V, against the BJT’s $40\,\text{mS}$ at $1\,\text{mA}$ from the Ebers–Moll relation $g_m = I_C/V_T$. A common-source stage therefore delivers single-figure voltage gains where the common-emitter stage delivered hundreds.
concepts.detail: The FET repays the shortfall with the two things the BJT cannot offer: an input that draws no current at all (Section 13.4’s $1\,\text{k}\Omega$ limitation disappears) and a near-ideal switch. In practice designers use the FET where impedance or switching matters, and reach for the BJT — or the op-amps of Chapter 15, whose input stages are often FETs — where raw gain per milliamp matters.

concepts.statement: The **CMOS (complementary MOS) inverter** connects an n-channel enhancement MOSFET from output to ground and a p-channel enhancement MOSFET from output to the positive rail, with **their gates tied together as the input and their drains tied together as the output**. Input high turns the n-channel device ON and the p-channel OFF — output low; input low does the opposite — output high.
concepts.detail: In either logic state one transistor is fully on and the other is fully off, so the output sits essentially at a supply rail — **rail-to-rail** logic levels — and the pair conducts no current from the supply except leakage. The threshold of the switching is set between the rails by the two devices’ threshold voltages, giving a steep, well-defined transfer characteristic (the very property exploited when the inverter is used as an amplifier).

concepts.statement: Biased at the middle of its transition region, the CMOS inverter has both transistors partially conducting, and its small-signal voltage gain is $$A_v = -(g_{m,n} + g_{m,p})\left(r_{o,n} \parallel r_{o,p}\right)$$ — large, because both transconductances act on the same output node.
concepts.detail: This is the linear use of a digital gate: with the input held near the switching threshold, each transistor behaves as a controlled current source feeding the other’s output resistance, and gains of hundreds are available. It is how CMOS operational amplifiers and RF amplifiers are built at essentially zero quiescent current — and a reminder that Chapter 15’s feedback loops can surround either technology.

concepts.statement: Taking the output from the **source** instead of the drain gives the **source follower**: drain tied to the rail, load in the source lead. Its gain is $$A_v = \frac{g_m R_S}{1 + g_m R_S} \approx 1$$ — just under unity, and **without** the $180\degree$ inversion of the common-source stage.
concepts.detail: The stage is the FET’s answer to the common-collector (emitter-follower) connection that Hughes sets aside as a special case in Chapter 13: enormous input impedance, output impedance of order $1/g_m$ (a few hundred ohms), and faithful unity-gain transfer. It costs one transconductance to run — the follower’s gain misses unity by exactly the $1/g_mR_S$ term — and it appears wherever a high-impedance node must drive a low-impedance load without loading it: buffer stages, the output followers inside op-amps of Chapter 15, and the probe front-ends of oscilloscopes.

concepts.statement: CMOS logic dissipates **essentially no static power** (in every state one transistor is off, so only leakage flows) and its gates draw **no d.c. input current** (each driven gate is an insulated capacitor). The remaining — dynamic — power is $$P = C V_{DD}^2 f,$$ proportional to the switched capacitance, the square of the supply voltage and the clock frequency.
concepts.detail: The quadratic dependence on $V_{DD}$ is why successive technology generations chase lower supply voltages, and the linear dependence on $f$ is why clock speed, not gate count, sets the power bill. Add symmetric output drive (either rail can be pulled hard), tolerance of supply and temperature variation, and near-perfect scalability with lithography, and the explanation is complete: no competing technology combines all of these at once.

examples.title: Designing a common-source stage
examples.problem: Design a common-source MOSFET amplifier from $V_{DD} = 12\,\text{V}$ using typical values: the gate divider sets $V_G = 4.0\,\text{V}$, the MOSFET needs $V_{GS} \approx 2\,\text{V}$ at the wanted drain current of $2\,\text{mA}$, and its transconductance there is $g_m = 2\,\text{mA/V}$. Choose $R_S$, then $R_D$ for a mid-supply drain, and evaluate the gain with and without a bypass capacitor.

steps.label: Step 1: Choose the source resistor
steps.text: The source sits at $V_S = V_G - V_{GS} = 4.0 - 2 = 2.0\,\text{V}$, and it must carry $2\,\text{mA}$: $R_S = 2.0/(2\times 10^{-3}) = 1\,\text{k}\Omega$.

steps.label: Step 2: Choose the drain resistor
steps.text: For the drain to rest near mid-supply, $R_D$ should drop about $6\,\text{V}$ at $2\,\text{mA}$: $R_D = 6/(2\times 10^{-3}) = 3\,\text{k}\Omega$ (the mid-supply rule of Section 13.3, transplanted).

steps.label: Step 3: Gain with the source bypassed
steps.text: The bypass capacitor shorts $R_S$ at signal frequencies, so $A_v = -g_mR_D = -(2\times 10^{-3})(3\times 10^{3}) = -6$ — inverting, single-figure, typical of a FET stage.

steps.label: Step 4: Gain unbypassed
steps.text: Without the bypass, $A_v = -g_mR_D/(1 + g_mR_S) = -6/(1 + 2\times 10^{-3} \times 1\times 10^{3}) = -6/3 = -2$ — the degeneration has bought bias stability at the cost of gain, and in the deep-degeneration limit the gain would approach $-R_D/R_S = -3$.

steps.label: Step 5: Note what the gate cost
steps.text: The divider may use resistors of megohms — the gate current is zero, so the signal source is loaded only by the divider itself, something no BJT stage of Chapter 13 could arrange.

examples.result: $R_S = 1\,\text{k}\Omega$, $R_D = 3\,\text{k}\Omega$, drain resting near $6\,\text{V}$; gain $-6$ bypassed, $-2$ unbypassed — and an input that loads nothing.

examples.title: A CMOS gate’s power budget
