Find the differential output and the residual hum if the matched difference stage provides $60\ \text{dB}$ of CMRR.

steps.label: Step 1: The gain formula
steps.text: The differential gain of the classic three-op-amp circuit is $G = 1 + 2R/R_G$ where $R = 25\ \text{k}\Omega$: $G = 1 + 50{,}000/500 = 101$.

steps.label: Step 2: Amplify the signal
steps.text: The two input stages apply the same gain to the differential component: $5\ \text{mV} \times 101 = 505\ \text{mV}$ of differential signal reaches the output difference stage, which passes it at unity.

steps.label: Step 3: Reject the hum
steps.text: The common-mode component passes through the input stages at unity gain; the output difference stage suppresses it by its CMRR. At $60\ \text{dB}$ the rejection factor is $10^{3}$, so $100\ \text{mV}$ of hum leaves $0.1\ \text{mV} = 100\ \mu\text{V}$ at the output.

steps.label: Step 4: Assess
steps.text: The signal-to-hum ratio went from $5\ \text{mV} / 100\ \text{mV} = 1{:}20$ at the input to $505\ \text{mV} / 0.1\ \text{mV} \approx 5000{:}1$ at the output — the entire point of the topology, and the reason it fronts every bridge sensor and biopotential electrode.

examples.result: $G = 101$; differential output $505\ \text{mV}$ against only $100\ \mu\text{V}$ of residual hum.

keyTakeaways: Golden rules: with negative feedback and an unsaturated output, $V_{-} = V_{+}$ and the input currents are zero — every circuit in this chapter is these rules plus two impedances.
The integrator $v_o = -(1/RC)\int v_i\, dt$ converts square waves to triangles at ramp rate $-v_i/RC$; real integrators need a leakage path or reset switch to fight bias-current drift.
The differentiator $v_o = -RC\, dv_i/dt$ amplifies high-frequency noise and is usually tamed with a small series resistor.
Comparators run open loop and snap rail-to-rail; hysteresis (positive feedback) gives two thresholds and noise immunity — comparator ICs have open-collector outputs for logic levels.
Precision rectifiers place the diode inside the feedback loop so its $0.6\ \text{V}$ drop is invisible; the absolute-value circuit gives $v_o = |v_i|$.
The instrumentation amplifier delivers gain $1 + 2R/R_G$ with one resistor, near-infinite input impedance and high CMRR — the universal bridge-sensor front end.
Practical limits — slew rate, gain–bandwidth, offset, decoupling — decide whether a golden-rule design actually works.

quiz.q: An integrator with $R = 10\ \text{k}\Omega$ and $C = 0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ receives a steady $+2\ \text{V}$ input. At what rate does the output move?
quiz.explanation: The ramp rate is $-v_i/RC = -2/(10^{-3}\ \text{s}) = -2000\ \text{V/s} = -2\ \text{V/ms}$: the inverting integrator ramps downward for a positive input.

quiz.q: Why does a practical integrator usually include a very large resistor in parallel with the feedback capacitor?
options: To provide a dc path for the op amp’s bias current, preventing the output from drifting to a rail
To convert it into a differentiator
To protect the input source from short circuits
quiz.explanation: The tiny bias current flowing into the inverting node would otherwise integrate into an ever-growing ramp, saturating the amplifier. The parallel resistor gives that current a dc path, bounding the output at low frequency.

quiz.q: A comparator with hysteresis (a Schmitt trigger) switches at different thresholds for rising and falling inputs. The purpose of the two thresholds is to:
options: Allow the comparator to work without a supply
Prevent multiple output transitions when a noisy signal crosses the threshold
quiz.explanation: Positive feedback moves the threshold away from the signal after each transition, so noise smaller than the hysteresis window cannot re-trigger the output — chatter is eliminated.

quiz.q: The classic three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier has input-stage resistors $R = 25\ \text{k}\Omega$ and gain resistor $R_G = 500\ \Omega$. Its differential gain is:
quiz.explanation: $G = 1 + 2R/R_G = 1 + 2(25{,}000)/500 = 101$, set by the single gain resistor while both inputs see essentially infinite impedance.

quiz.q: A precision active rectifier outperforms a simple diode rectifier because:
options: Its diodes have a smaller forward drop
The op amp absorbs the diode drop inside the feedback loop, so millivolt signals are rectified faithfully
It works without any power supply
It converts ac directly to regulated dc
quiz.explanation: The loop drives the internal node an extra diode-drop high so that the output node obeys the golden rules exactly; the $0.6$–$0.7\ \text{V}$ penalty never appears at the output, so signals far below a diode drop can be rectified.

quiz.q: An ideal integrator with R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF is driven by a symmetric ±5 V square wave at 1.0 kHz. The steady output triangle has peak-to-peak amplitude closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $R = 10$ kΩ, $C = 100$ nF so $RC = 10^{-3}$ s, square levels ±5 V, period $10^{-3}$ s with half-period $0.5 \times 10^{-3}$ s. Step 2 — Governing ramp: virtual earth gives $i = \frac{V_{in}}{R}$ into $C$, so slope $\frac{dv_{o}}{dt} = -\frac{V_{in}}{RC}$. Step 3 — Algebra: slope magnitude $\frac{5}{10^{-3}} = 5000$ V per s; over one half-period the swing is $5000 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-3} = 2.5$ V peak-to-peak. Step 4 — Sanity check: larger $RC$ would flatten the triangle, higher frequency shrinks it proportionally, and $2.5$ V stays clear of saturation. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 5.00 V uses the full period per ramp, 1.25 V halves the half-period, and 10.0 V mistakes peak for swing. Step 6 — Conclude: the triangle spans about 2.50 V peak-to-peak.

intro: A filter changes the amplitude of an ac voltage as frequency changes, and the whole subject rests on one piece of bookkeeping: reactance varies with frequency while resistance does not. Because the interesting action spans six or more decades, engineers compress the axis with logarithms and the vertical axis with decibels, and then the response collapses into straight lines — the Bode plot. Hughes closes the chapter with the two-port description (z, y and ABCD parameters) that lets filter blocks be cascaded on paper before they are ever built.
objectives: Classify the four filter types and define passband, stopband and cut-off frequency
Manipulate logarithms and read semi-log and log-log scales in decades
Convert power and voltage ratios to decibels and back
Construct idealized Bode magnitude and phase asymptotes for first-order sections
Describe the z, y and ABCD two-port parameter sets and their reciprocity conditions

concepts.statement: If the maximum output voltage at any frequency is $V_m$, the **passband** is the range where the response exceeds $V_m/\sqrt{2}$ and the **stopband** (reject band) where it falls below; the boundary frequency is the **cut-off** or half-power frequency. The four categories are low-pass, high-pass, passband (bandpass) and stopband (bandstop).
concepts.detail: For the bandpass case the cut-off frequencies $f_1$ and $f_2$ bracket the bandwidth around the center $f_0$; for the stopband case they bracket the rejected band. The bandpass response is exactly the series-resonant behavior of Chapter 9, so the resonant circuit is itself a filter — one we have already met.

concepts.statement: The **frequency response** of a circuit is the pair of curves — amplitude response and phase response — describing how the output phasor changes with frequency while the input is held constant; it stems directly from $X_L = \omega L$ rising and $X_C = 1/\omega C$ falling.
concepts.detail: Nilsson formalizes this with the transfer function $H(j\omega)$, whose magnitude and phase angle are plotted separately; an ideal filter would also show linear phase in the passband to avoid phase distortion. Because the frequency range is large, frequency is plotted on a logarithmic scale, and amplitude in decibels.

concepts.statement: The logarithm is the **index of a power**: if $X = a^x$ then $x = \log_a X$. Log rules mirror index rules — $\log(xy) = \log x + \log y$, $\log(x/y) = \log x - \log y$, $\log x^n = n \log x$ — and $\log 2 = 0.3010$, $\log 3 = 0.4771$, $\log 4 = 0.6021$.
concepts.detail: On semi-log paper the linear axis is voltage and the log axis is frequency: $2$ appears about $30$% along a decade, $3$ about $48$%, $4$ about $60$%. A **decade** is a tenfold frequency interval (1 kHz to 10 kHz), an **octave** a twofold one; a log scale begins at $1$ (since $\log 1 = 0$), never at zero. Hughes’ Example 17.1 builds confidence: $\log 90 = 2\log 3 + \log 5 + \log 2 = 1.9542$.

concepts.statement: The decibel is a **logarithmic (base-10) unit of power ratio** — one tenth of a bel, named after Alexander Graham Bell: $$G = 10 \log_{10}\frac{P_2}{P_1} \quad \text{and, for equal resistances,} \quad G = 20 \log_{10}\frac{V_2}{V_1}.$$
concepts.detail: The voltage form is exact only when $R_L = R_{in}$, but the condition is relaxed in practice and voltage gain is quoted as $20 \log_{10}(V_2/V_1)$ anyway. The anchor points to memorize: $0.707 \to -3\ \text{dB}$, $2 \to +6\ \text{dB}$, $10 \to 20\ \text{dB}$, $100 \to 40\ \text{dB}$, and a doubling of **power** is $+3\ \text{dB}$ — a conveniently ear-detectable step.

concepts.statement: At the cut-off frequency the load voltage has fallen to $1/\sqrt{2}$ of its maximum, so the average power delivered — proportional to $V_L^2$ — is exactly **half** of $P_{max}$: $P(\omega_c) = P_{max}/2$. Hence “half-power point”, “$-3\ \text{dB}$ point” and “cut-off frequency” are the same frequency.
concepts.detail: Nilsson derives it from $P = \frac{1}{2} V_L^2/R$ with $V_L(j\omega_c) = (1/\sqrt{2}) V_{L,max}$; Hughes derives the same result for the RC low-pass circuit by computing $P = |I|^2 R$ at $\omega_2 = 1/CR$ and finding $E^2/2R = P_{max}/2$. The passband is therefore the region where the output power is at least half of its maximum.

concepts.statement: A **Bode plot** (after Hendrik Bode, Bell Labs) is gain in dB and phase angle versus log frequency; the idealized version replaces the low-pass response by two straight lines — flat at $0\ \text{dB}$ below the breakpoint, then falling at $-20\ \text{dB}$ per **decade** ($-6\ \text{dB}$ per octave) above it.
concepts.detail: The exact low-pass gain is $G = -10 \log_{10}[1 + (\omega CR)^2]$ (Hughes Eq. 17.6), whose high-frequency asymptote is $G = -20 \log_{10}(\omega/\omega_2)$: a decade of frequency costs $20\ \text{dB}$ and an octave costs $6\ \text{dB}$. The true curve sits $3\ \text{dB}$ below the corner at the breakpoint and converges to the asymptote within about $1\ \text{dB}$ beyond a factor of two either way. The high-pass dual is the mirror image: $+20\ \text{dB}$ per decade below the breakpoint, and its phase runs $+90^\circ \to +45^\circ \to 0^\circ$ while the low-pass phase runs $0^\circ \to -45^\circ \to -90^\circ$.

concepts.statement: Nilsson plots $|H(j\omega)|$ in dB on a log-frequency axis over three or four decades, with $A_{dB} = 20 \log_{10}|H(j\omega)|$; the cut-off is read as the frequency $3\ \text{dB}$ **below the passband magnitude**.
concepts.detail: For example, a low-pass filter whose passband sits at $26\ \text{dB}$ is cut off where the magnitude has fallen to $23\ \text{dB}$. When $A_{dB} = 0$ the transfer magnitude is exactly $1$; negative dB means attenuation.

concepts.statement: A **port** is a terminal pair whose entering and leaving currents are equal; a two-port network exposes an input and an output port, described by parameter sets relating $(V_1, I_1)$ to $(V_2, I_2)$ — **z** (open-circuit impedance), **y** (short-circuit admittance), **h** (hybrid) and **ABCD** (transmission).
concepts.detail: For z: $V_1 = z_{11} I_1 + z_{12} I_2$ and $V_2 = z_{21} I_1 + z_{22} I_2$, each $z$ measured with the opposite port open-circuited. A passive reciprocal network (Hughes’ T example) has $z_{12} = z_{21}$, and reciprocity for the ABCD set reads $AD - BC = 1$. The ideal transformer, with $V_1 = nV_2$ and $I_1 = (1/n)(-I_2)$, has the transmission matrix $\begin{bmatrix} n & 0 \\ 0 & 1/n \end{bmatrix}$ and notably has no z or y matrices at all — its self and mutual inductances are infinite.

examples.title: Decibel arithmetic (Hughes Examples 17.3 and 17.4)
examples.problem: (a) A system has a voltage gain of $40\ \text{dB}$; if the output voltage is $7.0\ \text{V}$, find the applied input voltage. (b) A power level of $200\ \text{W}$ is $3\ \text{dB}$ above what other power level?

steps.label: Step 1: Set up the voltage equation (a)
Step 2: Undo the logarithm
steps.text: $7.0/V_1 = 10^{2}$, hence $V_1 = 7.0/100 = 70\ \text{mV}$. A $40\ \text{dB}$ gain is a factor of $100$ in voltage.

steps.label: Step 3: Set up the power equation (b)
Step 4: Solve and interpret
steps.text: $P_1 = 100\ \text{W}$: $+3\ \text{dB}$ is exactly a doubling of power — the smallest step the ear readily detects, which is why loudspeaker ratings move in 3 dB increments.

examples.result: (a) $V_1 = 70\ \text{mV}$; (b) $P_1 = 100\ \text{W}$ — the $3\ \text{dB}$ point is the half-power level.

examples.title: Constructing a low-pass Bode plot (Hughes Example 17.9)
examples.problem: A low-pass RC filter has $R = 1.25\ \text{k}\Omega$ and $C = 4\ \text{nF}$. Construct the idealized Bode magnitude plot and give the true gain at the breakpoint.

steps.label: Step 1: Locate the breakpoint
steps.text: $\omega_2 = 1/(CR) = 1/(4 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.25 \times 10^{3}) = 200\ \text{krad/s}$ — the corner (half-power, $-3\ \text{dB}$) frequency.

steps.label: Step 2: Draw the low-frequency asymptote
steps.text: Below $200\ \text{krad/s}$ the response is flat at $G = -10\log_{10}(1) = 0\ \text{dB}$: the capacitor’s impedance is enormous and the output follows the input.

steps.label: Step 3: Draw the high-frequency asymptote
steps.text: Above the breakpoint the gain falls at $-20\ \text{dB}$ per decade — at $2000\ \text{krad/s}$ (one decade up) the idealized plot reads $-20\ \text{dB}$, at two decades $-40\ \text{dB}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Correct at the corner
steps.text: The exact expression $G = -10\log_{10}[1 + (\omega/\omega_2)^2]$ gives $G = -10 \log_{10}(2) = -3\ \text{dB}$ at $\omega_2$ itself, and within $1\ \text{dB}$ of the asymptotes beyond about $2\omega_2$ and below about $\omega_2/2$.

examples.result: Two straight lines meeting at $\omega_2 = 200\ \text{krad/s}$: $0\ \text{dB}$ below, $-20\ \text{dB/decade}$ above, with the true curve $3\ \text{dB}$ low at the breakpoint.

examples.title: Idealized versus actual high-pass response (Hughes Example 17.10)
examples.problem: A high-pass RC filter has $C = 94\ \text{nF}$ and $R = 169.3\ \Omega$. Compute the half-power frequency and the actual dB level at $f_1/10$, $f_1/2$, $f_1$ and $2f_1$, comparing each with the idealized straight-line plot.

steps.label: Step 1: The cut-off frequency
steps.text: $f_1 = 1/(2\pi CR) = 1/(2\pi \times 94 \times 10^{-9} \times 169.3) = 10{,}000\ \text{Hz}$ — the breakpoint of the idealized plot.

steps.label: Step 2: A decade below
steps.text: At $f_1/10$: $G = -10\log_{10}[1 + 10^{2}] = -20\ \text{dB}$, matching the idealized line exactly (it has already fallen $20\ \text{dB}$ per decade through this point).

steps.label: Step 3: Half an octave region
steps.text: At $f_1/2$: $G = -10\log_{10}[1 + 2^{2}] = -7\ \text{dB}$, while the idealized plot promises only $-6\ \text{dB}$ — a $1\ \text{dB}$ error, the worst the approximation ever makes. At $f_1$ itself: $G = -10\log_{10}(2) = -3\ \text{dB}$ against the idealized $0\ \text{dB}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Above the corner
steps.text: At $2f_1$: $G = -10\log_{10}[1 + (1/2)^{2}] = -1\ \text{dB}$, the last visible deviation from the $0\ \text{dB}$ shelf. The actual and idealized curves merge above and below the transition.

examples.result: $f_1 = 10\ \text{kHz}$; actual levels $-20$, $-7$, $-3$ and $-1\ \text{dB}$ at $f_1/10$, $f_1/2$, $f_1$ and $2f_1$ versus idealized $-20$, $-6$, $0$ and $0\ \text{dB}$.

keyTakeaways: Filters come in four categories — low-pass, high-pass, bandpass, bandstop — with passbands defined by the $V_m/\sqrt{2}$ (half-power, $-3\ \text{dB}$) boundary.
Frequency response exists because $X_L = \omega L$ and $X_C = 1/\omega C$ vary with frequency; both magnitude and phase change together.
Power ratio in dB is $10 \log_{10}(P_2/P_1)$; voltage ratio is $20 \log_{10}(V_2/V_1)$; $0.707 \to -3\ \text{dB}$, $2 \to 6\ \text{dB}$, $10 \to 20\ \text{dB}$.
The cut-off frequency is the half-power point: output power exactly one half of maximum.

A first-order Bode plot is two straight lines meeting at the breakpoint, falling (or rising) $20\ \text{dB}$ per decade $= 6\ \text{dB}$ per octave, with a $3\ \text{dB}$ error at the corner and at most $1\ \text{dB}$ elsewhere.

Two-port z, y and ABCD parameters make filters cascade-analyzable blocks; reciprocity is $z_{12} = z_{21}$ or $AD - BC = 1$, and the ideal transformer is the pathological $\begin{bmatrix} n & 0 \\ 0 & 1/n \end{bmatrix}$ case.

quiz.q: An output voltage equal to $0.707$ times the maximum corresponds to what decibel level, and what fraction of maximum power?
options: $-3\ \text{dB}$ and one half of the maximum power
$-6\ \text{dB}$ and one quarter of the power
quiz.explanation: $20\log_{10} 0.707 = -3.01\ \text{dB}$, and since power scales as voltage squared, $0.707^{2} = 0.5$ — the half-power point that defines every cut-off frequency.

quiz.q: A filter has a voltage gain of $100$. What is its gain in decibels, and what does doubling the gain add?
quiz.explanation: $20\log_{10} 100 = 40\ \text{dB}$, and $20\log_{10} 2 = 6.02\ \text{dB}$: each doubling of voltage is worth $6\ \text{dB}$, each decade $20\ \text{dB}$.

quiz.q: Above its breakpoint, the idealized Bode magnitude of a first-order low-pass filter falls at:
quiz.explanation: The high-frequency asymptote is $G = -20\log_{10}(\omega/\omega_c)$, a slope of $-20\ \text{dB}$ per decade, equivalent to $-6\ \text{dB}$ per octave. The $-40\ \text{dB/decade}$ slope belongs to second-order sections (Section 16.4).

quiz.q: Nilsson plots a low-pass magnitude whose passband sits at $26\ \text{dB}$. At what magnitude is the cut-off frequency read?
quiz.explanation: The cut-off is the half-power point, so the magnitude must have dropped $3\ \text{dB}$ from the passband value: $26 - 3 = 23\ \text{dB}$.

quiz.q: For a passive reciprocal two-port network, which relation always holds?
quiz.explanation: Equality of the open-circuit transfer impedances, $z_{12} = z_{21}$, is the reciprocity condition — satisfied by most passive time-invariant networks. (For the ABCD set the same fact appears as $AD - BC = 1$.)

intro: The simplest filters are one resistor and one reactive element. Taken across the capacitor, the RC pair passes lows and lags; taken across the resistor, it passes highs and leads — and both switch roles when the reactive element is an inductor. Hughes works the two canonical circuits phasor by phasor, deriving the cut-off $\omega_c = 1/CR$, the $-45^\circ$ phase at that frequency and the semicircular locus of the output phasor; Nilsson adds the design view and the sober warning that a passive filter is at the mercy of whatever load you hang on it.
objectives: Derive the low-pass lag and high-pass lead transfer functions in polar form
Compute the cut-off frequency $f_c = 1/2\pi RC$ and design an RC or RL section to a specification
Predict magnitude and phase at the band extremes and at the cut-off frequency
Quantify the effect of source and load resistance on a passive filter
Assemble bandpass and bandstop responses from cascaded and paralleled sections

concepts.statement: For the series RC circuit with output taken across $C$, $$\frac{V_C}{E} = \frac{1}{1 + j\omega CR} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega CR)^2}} \angle{-\tan^{-1}(\omega CR)}.$$ The **passband ends** at $\omega_2 = 1/CR$ where $|V_C| = E/\sqrt{2}$ and the phase is $-45^\circ$.
concepts.detail: At $\omega = 0$ the output equals the input at $0^\circ$; as $\omega \to \infty$ the output falls to zero and lags by $90^\circ$. Hughes’ circle diagram shows the locus of $V_C$ sweeping a semicircle with $E$ as diameter as $\omega$ goes from zero to infinity. In hertz, $f_2 = 1/(2\pi CR)$.

concepts.statement: For the same series RC pair with output taken across $R$, $$\frac{V_R}{E} = \frac{1}{1 + 1/(j\omega CR)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (1/\omega CR)^2}} \angle{\tan^{-1}(1/\omega CR)}.$$ The **passband begins** at $\omega_1 = 1/CR$, again with $|V_R| = E/\sqrt{2}$ at $+45^\circ$.
concepts.detail: Now $\omega = 0$ gives zero output leading $90^\circ$, and $\omega \to \infty$ gives unity output at $0^\circ$. The cut-off formula is the same $1/CR$ — a series RC circuit has one cut-off frequency whether wired as low-pass or high-pass; only the choice of output node changes.

concepts.statement: Both configurations generalize: any circuit with $$H(s) = \frac{\omega_c}{s + \omega_c}$$ is a **low-pass filter** and any circuit with $$H(s) = \frac{s}{s + \omega_c}$$ is a **high-pass filter** — with $\omega_c = R/L$ for the RL forms and $\omega_c = 1/RC$ for the RC forms.
concepts.detail: The series RL circuit is a low-pass when the output is taken across $R$ and a high-pass across $L$; the series RC is a low-pass across $C$ and a high-pass across $R$. Nilsson also notes the time-domain handshake: the time constant of Chapter 6 satisfies $\tau = 1/\omega_c$, so the same $RC$ or $L/R$ that sets the transient speed sets the frequency selectivity.

concepts.statement: Because $R$ and $C$ (or $L$) enter only as a product, **choose the capacitor first** — capacitor values are far fewer on the shelf — then compute the resistor: $R = 1/(\omega_c C)$; convert the specification to rad/s before substituting.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s electrocardiograph design: to reject $60\ \text{Hz}$ mains noise while passing the $1\ \text{Hz}$ heartbeat, a $10\ \text{Hz}$ low-pass was built with $L = 100\ \text{mH}$, requiring $R = \omega_c L = (20\pi)(0.1) = 6.28\ \Omega$; the measured gains were $0.995$ at $1\ \text{Hz}$, $0.707$ at $10\ \text{Hz}$ and $0.164$ at $60\ \text{Hz}$ — noise attenuated sixfold.

concepts.statement: A load resistor across a passive filter’s output **lowers both the passband magnitude and the cut-off frequency**: Nilsson’s RL high-pass with $R_L = R$ drops the passband gain to $K = R_L/(R + R_L) = 1/2$ and the cut-off from $15\ \text{kHz}$ to $7.5\ \text{kHz}$.
concepts.detail: The loaded transfer function keeps the first-order form $H(s) = Ks/(s + K\omega_c)$ but with everything scaled by $K$. Passive filters can never amplify (the series RLC resonant filter of the next section is the lone exception), and their transfer functions change with the load — the two defects that active filters of Section 16.4 exist to cure.

concepts.statement: A **broadband bandpass** filter is a high-pass section (cut-off $\omega_1$) followed by a low-pass section (cut-off $\omega_2$) in series, with components chosen so that $\omega_1 < \omega_2$; the passband between them is the bandwidth.
concepts.detail: Hughes’ Example 17.7: a $2\ \text{nF}$–$2\ \text{k}\Omega$ high-pass gives $\omega_1 = 1/(R_1 C_1) = 250\ \text{krad/s}$ ($39.8\ \text{kHz}$) and a $5\ \text{pF}$–$50\ \text{k}\Omega$ low-pass gives $\omega_2 = 4000\ \text{krad/s}$ ($636.6\ \text{kHz}$). Hughes cautions that $V_o \ne 0.707 V_{in}$ exactly at those frequencies because the two sections load each other — the same loading theme again.

concepts.statement: A **bandstop (bandreject) filter** runs the low-pass and high-pass sections in **parallel** rather than series: frequencies below $\omega_2$ pass through the low-pass branch, frequencies above $\omega_1$ through the high-pass branch, and only the band between them falls in both stopbands.
concepts.detail: The mirror-image construction of the bandpass cascade: for bandstop, the low-pass cut-off $\omega_2$ must lie below the high-pass cut-off $\omega_1$. Both this and the bandpass construction are broadband approximations; sharp, narrow bands need resonance (next section) or active filters (Section 16.4).

concepts.term: Phase behavior of the first-order pair
concepts.statement: The low-pass phase runs $0^\circ \to -45^\circ \to -90^\circ$ as frequency rises (output lags), while the high-pass phase runs $+90^\circ \to +45^\circ \to 0^\circ$ (output leads); the $45^\circ$ crossing always sits **exactly at the cut-off**.
concepts.detail: Hughes’ Example 17.6 tabulates the high-pass: at $\omega = 1\ \text{krad/s}$ (a tenth of $\omega_1$) the gain is $0.1$ at $84^\circ$; at $5$ it is $0.45$ at $63^\circ$; at $\omega_1 = 10\ \text{krad/s}$ it is $0.707$ at $45^\circ$; at $50$ it is $0.98$ at $11^\circ$; at $100$ it is $0.995$ at $6^\circ$. The current always leads $V_C$ by $90^\circ$, which is what draws the circle diagram.

examples.title: Low-pass response table (Hughes Example 17.5)
examples.problem: A low-pass RC filter has $R = 1\ \text{k}\Omega$ and $C = 400\ \text{pF}$, driven from a $12\ \text{V}$ ac source. Find the half-power frequency and the output magnitude at $100\ \text{kHz}$, $398\ \text{kHz}$, $1\ \text{MHz}$, $2.5\ \text{MHz}$ and $10\ \text{MHz}$.

steps.label: Step 1: The cut-off frequency
steps.text: $f_2 = \frac{1}{2\pi CR} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 400 \times 10^{-12} \times 10^{3}} = 398\ \text{kHz}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Well below cut-off
steps.text: At $100\ \text{kHz}$, $\omega CR = 2\pi(10^{5})(4 \times 10^{-8}) = 0.251$, so $|V_C| = 12/\sqrt{1 + 0.251^{2}} = 12/1.031 = 11.64\ \text{V}$ — almost all of the source appears across $C$.

steps.label: Step 3: At the half-power point
steps.text: At $398\ \text{kHz}$ the response is $1/\sqrt{2}$ by construction: $|V_C| = 0.707 \times 12 = 8.5\ \text{V}$, and the phase is $-45^\circ$.

steps.label: Step 4: Into the stopband
steps.text: At $1\ \text{MHz}$ ($\omega CR = 2.51$): $|V_C| = 12/\sqrt{1 + 6.32} = 4.43\ \text{V}$. At $2.5\ \text{MHz}$: $1.89\ \text{V}$. At $10\ \text{MHz}$ ($\omega CR = 25.1$): $12/25.1 = 0.48\ \text{V}$ — the sixfold-per-octave collapse of the Bode asymptote made visible.

examples.title: High-pass response table (Hughes Example 17.6)
examples.problem: A high-pass RC filter has $R = 500\ \Omega$ and $C = 0.2\ \mu\text{F}$. Compute the half-power frequency and the amplitude and phase of the gain at $1$, $5$, $10$, $50$ and $100\ \text{krad/s}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Express the gain compactly
steps.text: Writing the gain as $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega_1/\omega)^{2}}} \angle \tan^{-1}(\omega_1/\omega)$ lets each row be read off from the ratio $\omega_1/\omega$.

steps.label: Step 3: Tabulate
steps.text: At $1\ \text{krad/s}$ ($\omega_1/\omega = 10$): gain $0.1$ at $84^\circ$. At $5$: $0.45$ at $63^\circ$. At $10$: $0.707$ at $45^\circ$ — the $-3\ \text{dB}$ point. At $50$: $0.98$ at $11^\circ$. At $100$: $0.995$ at $6^\circ$.

steps.label: Step 4: Read the trend
steps.text: A decade below cut-off the gain is almost exactly the frequency ratio ($0.1$), a decade above it the circuit is transparent ($0.995$): the stopband obeys $|H| \approx \omega/\omega_1$, the passband is flat.

examples.title: A cascade bandpass filter (Hughes Example 17.7)
examples.problem: A bandpass filter is built from a high-pass section ($R_1 = 2\ \text{k}\Omega$, $C_1 = 2\ \text{nF}$) followed by a low-pass section ($R_2 = 50\ \text{k}\Omega$, $C_2 = 5\ \text{pF}$). Compute the two cut-off frequencies and state the caveat.

steps.label: Step 3: The passband
steps.text: Since $\omega_1 < \omega_2$, the cascade passes roughly $39.8$–$636.6\ \text{kHz}$: frequencies below $\omega_1$ die in the high-pass stopband, above $\omega_2$ in the low-pass stopband.

steps.label: Step 4: The caveat
steps.text: Because the two RC sections load one another, the output is not exactly $0.707 V_{in}$ at these computed frequencies — the numbers are design guides, and the exact cascade response needs the two-port machinery of Section 16.1 or buffer amplifiers between sections.

examples.result: $\omega_1 = 250\ \text{krad/s}$ ($39.8\ \text{kHz}$) and $\omega_2 = 4000\ \text{krad/s}$ ($636.6\ \text{kHz}$); mutual loading shifts the true $-3\ \text{dB}$ points.

keyTakeaways: Low-pass (lag): $H = 1/(1 + j\omega CR)$ with output across $C$; high-pass (lead): $H = 1/(1 + 1/j\omega CR)$ with output across $R$ — same RC pair, different output node.
Both cut off at $\omega_c = 1/CR$ ($f_c = 1/2\pi CR$); the RL versions cut off at $\omega_c = R/L$, and in every case $\tau = 1/\omega_c$ ties the transient of Chapter 6 to the filter.
At the cut-off the magnitude is $1/\sqrt{2}$ and the phase is exactly $\pm 45^\circ$; the extremes are $0^\circ/\pm 90^\circ$.
Design rule: pick the capacitor from stock first, then $R = 1/(\omega_c C)$ — and convert Hz to rad/s before substituting.
Loading a passive filter shrinks its passband gain and cut-off together ($K = R_L/(R + R_L)$ halves both in Nilsson’s example); passive filters never amplify.
Broadband bandpass = high-pass then low-pass in cascade ($\omega_1 < \omega_2$); bandstop = the same two sections in parallel ($\omega_2 < \omega_1$).
Mutual loading between cascaded passive sections shifts the actual $-3\ \text{dB}$ points — buffering or two-port analysis is needed for exact predictions.

quiz.q: A low-pass RC filter has $R = 1\ \text{k}\Omega$ and $C = 400\ \text{pF}$. Its half-power frequency is:
quiz.explanation: $f_2 = 1/(2\pi CR) = 1/(2\pi \times 400 \times 10^{-12} \times 10^{3}) = 398\ \text{kHz}$ — Hughes’ Example 17.5 filter, whose response at that frequency is $8.5\ \text{V}$ from a $12\ \text{V}$ source.

quiz.q: At its cut-off frequency, the output of a first-order low-pass RC section (output across the capacitor) lags the input by:
quiz.explanation: The phase is $-\tan^{-1}(\omega CR)$, which equals $-45^\circ$ precisely when $\omega CR = 1$, the cut-off condition. The lag deepens toward $90^\circ$ only deep in the stopband.

quiz.q: Nilsson loads an RL high-pass filter (designed for $15\ \text{kHz}$ cut-off, passband gain $1$) with $R_L = R$. The loaded filter now has:
quiz.explanation: The loaded transfer function is $Ks/(s + K\omega_c)$ with $K = R_L/(R + R_L) = 1/2$: both the passband magnitude and the cut-off frequency scale by $K$, giving $0.5$ and $7.5\ \text{kHz}$.

quiz.q: Which statement about the time constant $\tau$ and the cut-off frequency $\omega_c$ of the same RC pair is correct?
options: $\tau = 1/\omega_c$, so the transient speed and the filter bandwidth share one constant
quiz.explanation: The same product $RC$ that governs the natural response of Chapter 6 sets the frequency response: $\tau = RC$ and $\omega_c = 1/RC$, hence $\tau = 1/\omega_c$ — the Laplace transform connecting time and frequency domains.

quiz.q: To build a broadband bandpass filter from passive first-order sections, one cascades:
options: A low-pass with cut-off $\omega_2$ after a high-pass with cut-off $\omega_1 < \omega_2$
A low-pass and a high-pass in parallel
A high-pass with cut-off $\omega_2$ after a low-pass with cut-off $\omega_1 < \omega_2$
quiz.explanation: The high-pass removes everything below $\omega_1$ and the low-pass everything above $\omega_2$; with $\omega_1 < \omega_2$ the surviving band between them is the passband. (The parallel construction produces a bandstop, not a bandpass.)

quiz.q: A series RC low-pass filter uses R = 1.6 kΩ and C = 100 nF, output across the capacitor. At its cutoff frequency the magnitude response and phase are closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $R = 1.6$ kΩ, $C = 100$ nF, capacitive output. Step 2 — Governing transfer: $H = \frac{1}{1 + j\omega RC}$ with cutoff $\omega_{c} = \frac{1}{RC}$ where $|H| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and angle $-45$ degrees. Step 3 — Algebra: $RC = 1.6 \times 10^{-4}$ s, $f_{c} = \frac{1}{2\pi RC} \approx 995$ Hz; at $\omega_{c}$, $|H| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707$ and $\angle H = -45$ degrees. Step 4 — Sanity check: zero frequency passes fully, very high frequency blocks, and the semicircle locus crosses $-45$ degrees exactly at cutoff. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 0.500 halves power correctly but not voltage, $+45$ degrees is the high-pass sign, and unity with zero phase is the direct-current point. Step 6 — Conclude: about 0.707 with −45° lag.

intro: When the passband must be narrow, two resistors and a capacitor no longer suffice — the job calls for resonance. Nilsson’s bandpass machinery revolves around three linked parameters (center frequency, bandwidth, quality factor) of which only two can be chosen freely, and around the elegant duality between the series RLC circuit (bandwidth $R/L$) and its parallel twin (bandwidth $1/RC$). Hughes supplies the tuned-circuit perspective with a series-resonant filter of quality factor $50$. Both books agree on the punchline: the resonant frequency is not just where the response peaks — it is the natural frequency of the circuit itself.
objectives: Define center frequency, bandwidth and quality factor and their interrelations
Derive the series RLC bandpass parameters $\omega_o$, $\beta$ and $Q$
State the dual parameter set of the parallel RLC bandpass filter
Design series and parallel RLC filters from two independent specifications
Predict the effect of source resistance and relate frequency response to damping

concepts.statement: A bandpass (or bandreject) filter is characterized by five parameters — cut-offs $\omega_{c1}$, $\omega_{c2}$, center frequency $\omega_o$, bandwidth $\beta$ and quality factor $Q$ — but **only two can be specified independently**: $$\omega_o = \sqrt{\omega_{c1}\, \omega_{c2}}, \qquad \beta = \omega_{c2} - \omega_{c1}, \qquad Q = \frac{\omega_o}{\beta}.$$
concepts.detail: The center (resonant) frequency is the frequency at which the transfer function is purely real — the geometric mean, not the arithmetic mean, of the cut-offs. $Q$ describes the width of the passband independent of where it sits on the frequency axis.

concepts.statement: The **series RLC circuit** with output across $R$ has $$H(s) = \frac{(R/L)\, s}{s^{2} + (R/L)s + 1/LC}$$ with $$\omega_o = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad \beta = \frac{R}{L}, \qquad Q = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}.$$
concepts.detail: At $\omega_o$ the inductor and capacitor impedances cancel exactly — the series LC pair behaves as a short circuit — so $|H| = 1$: the input appears across $R$ untouched. This is the only passive filter in Chapter 14 whose output can actually exceed what voltage division alone would allow (near resonance the capacitor or inductor voltage can exceed the source voltage, the amplification of Chapter 9’s resonant circuits).

concepts.statement: Setting $|H| = (1/\sqrt{2})H_{max}$ yields $$\omega_{c1} = -\frac{\beta}{2} + \sqrt{\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\right)^{2} + \omega_o^{2}}, \qquad \omega_{c2} = \frac{\beta}{2} + \sqrt{\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\right)^{2} + \omega_o^{2}},$$ and their product confirms $\omega_o$ as the **geometric mean** of the cut-offs.
concepts.detail: Equivalent forms use $Q$ directly: $\omega_{c1,c2} = \omega_o\left[\mp \frac{1}{2Q} + \sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{4Q^{2}}}\right]$. The practical design shortcut is to compute $\omega_o$ and $\beta$ from whatever two parameters are specified, then use $\omega_o = 1/\sqrt{LC}$ and $\beta = R/L$ (series) or $\beta = 1/RC$ (parallel) to solve for the components.

concepts.statement: The parallel RLC circuit (with a series source resistance transformed in) has $H(s) = \frac{s/RC}{s^{2} + s/RC + 1/LC}$ with the **same** $\omega_o = 1/\sqrt{LC}$ but dual loss terms: $$\beta = \frac{1}{RC}, \qquad Q = \omega_o RC = R\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}.$$
concepts.detail: The duality is exact: series resistance widens the band through $R/L$, parallel resistance through $1/RC$; series $Q$ falls as $R$ grows, parallel $Q$ falls as $R$ shrinks. A series circuit wants a small $R$ for a high $Q$, a parallel circuit a large one.

concepts.statement: Take the output across the **inductor–capacitor pair** instead of $R$ and the same series circuit becomes a bandreject filter: $$H(s) = \frac{s^{2} + \omega_o^{2}}{s^{2} + \beta s + \omega_o^{2}},$$ with $|H(j\omega_o)| = 0$ — at resonance the LC pair is a short circuit and the output vanishes.
concepts.detail: The cut-off, bandwidth and quality-factor formulas are identical to the bandpass case; only the numerator changes. At $\omega = 0$ and $\omega \to \infty$ the transfer magnitude is $1$, giving the two passbands on either side of the notch. The parallel RLC bandreject is the exact dual, with $\beta = 1/RC$.

concepts.statement: A nonzero source resistance $R_i$ adds to the series resistance: the center frequency is **unchanged**, but $$\beta = \frac{R + R_i}{L}, \qquad H_{max} = \frac{R}{R + R_i}.$$ With $R_i = R$, Nilsson’s example sees the bandwidth double ($9\ \text{kHz}$ to $18\ \text{kHz}$) and the peak halve.
concepts.detail: The same lesson as passive loading in Section 16.2: the filter’s properties belong to the whole system, source included. Active filters (next section) are immune — the op-amp output isolates the filter from its driver.

concepts.term: Frequency response meets the time domain
concepts.statement: The bandwidth and the **neper frequency** of the Chapter 7 natural response are locked together: $\alpha = R/2L$ and $$\beta = 2\alpha,$$ so the transition from overdamped to underdamped ($\alpha = \omega_o$) occurs at exactly $Q = 1/2$.
concepts.detail: A sharp peak (high $Q$, narrow $\beta$) means an underdamped natural response that rings; a broad, low-$Q$ response means an overdamped one. The resonant frequency of the frequency response is the same $\omega_o$ that characterizes the natural response — one circuit, two languages.

concepts.statement: Hughes designs a **series-resonant bandpass** with $L = 2\ \text{mH}$, $C = 2\ \text{nF}$ and total $R = 20\ \Omega$ driven from $20\ \text{V}$: $f_r = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}) = 79{,}577\ \text{Hz}$, $X_L = 2\pi f_r L = 1000\ \Omega$, $Q = 1000/20 = 50$ and bandwidth $= f_r/Q = 1592\ \text{Hz}$.
concepts.detail: The half-power frequencies sit $\pm 796\ \text{Hz}$ around resonance: $f_1 = 78{,}871\ \text{Hz}$ and $f_2 = 80{,}373\ \text{Hz}$, with the output at those frequencies $0.707 \times 15\ \text{V} = 10.6\ \text{V}$ (the resonant output is $15\ \text{V}$ because $R = 15 + 5\ \Omega$ splits the $20\ \text{V}$ source). The $Q = X_L/R$ form is the tuned-amplifier designer’s favorite.

examples.title: Designing a series RLC bandpass filter (Nilsson Example 14.5)
examples.problem: A graphic equalizer needs a bandpass filter selecting the $1$–$10\ \text{kHz}$ band before amplification. Using the series RLC circuit with a $1\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor, find $R$ and $L$, and verify the cut-off frequencies.

steps.label: Step 1: Center frequency
steps.text: The center frequency is the geometric mean of the cut-offs: $f_o = \sqrt{f_{c1} f_{c2}} = \sqrt{(1000)(10{,}000)} = 3162.28\ \text{Hz}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify
steps.text: Substituting into the cut-off formulas returns $\omega_{c1} = 6283.19\ \text{rad/s}$ ($1000\ \text{Hz}$) and $\omega_{c2} = 62{,}831.85\ \text{rad/s}$ ($10{,}000\ \text{Hz}$) — the specification is met exactly.

examples.result: $L = 2.533\ \text{mH}$, $R = 143.24\ \Omega$ with $C = 1\ \mu\text{F}$; the band is $1$–$10\ \text{kHz}$ with $f_o = 3162.28\ \text{Hz}$ and $Q = 3162/9000 \approx 0.35$.

examples.title: Designing a parallel RLC bandpass filter (Nilsson Example 14.6)
examples.problem: Design a parallel RLC bandpass filter with center frequency $5\ \text{kHz}$ and bandwidth $200\ \text{Hz}$, using a $5\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor.

steps.label: Step 1: The resistor
steps.text: For the parallel form $\beta = 1/RC$, so $R = \frac{1}{\beta C} = \frac{1}{[2\pi(200)](5 \times 10^{-6})} = 159.15\ \Omega$.

steps.label: Step 3: Check the quality factor
steps.text: $Q = \omega_o/\beta = 2\pi(5000)/[2\pi(200)] = 25$ — a narrow band, unachievable with the cascaded first-order sections of Section 16.2 (which top out at $Q = 1/2$).

steps.label: Step 4: Note the roles
steps.text: Compare the division of labor: in the series design $R$ set the bandwidth through $R/L$; here the same job is done through $1/RC$ — with $L$ and $C$ still fixing the center frequency via $1/\sqrt{LC}$ in both circuits.

examples.result: $R = 159.15\ \Omega$ and $L = 202.64\ \mu\text{H}$ with $C = 5\ \mu\text{F}$, giving $f_o = 5\ \text{kHz}$, $\beta = 200\ \text{Hz}$, $Q = 25$.

examples.title: Designing a series RLC bandreject filter (Nilsson Example 14.8)
examples.problem: Using the series RLC bandreject circuit, compute components for a bandwidth of $250\ \text{Hz}$ and a center frequency of $750\ \text{Hz}$ with a $100\ \text{nF}$ capacitor, then find $R$, $L$, the cut-offs and $Q$.

steps.label: Step 1: Quality factor
steps.text: Straight from the definitions: $Q = \omega_o/\beta = 750/250 = 3$.

steps.label: Step 3: The resistor
steps.text: The bandreject shares the series formulas: $R = \beta L = [2\pi(250)](0.45) = 707\ \Omega$.

steps.label: Step 4: The cut-offs
steps.text: $\omega_{c1} = -\beta/2 + \sqrt{(\beta/2)^{2} + \omega_o^{2}} = 3992.0\ \text{rad/s}$ and $\omega_{c2} = 5562.8\ \text{rad/s}$, i.e. $635.3$ and $885.3\ \text{Hz}$. Their difference is $250\ \text{Hz}$ and their geometric mean is $\sqrt{(635.3)(885.3)} = 750\ \text{Hz}$ — both specifications confirmed.

examples.result: $L = 450\ \text{mH}$, $R = 707\ \Omega$, $Q = 3$, with cut-offs $635.3\ \text{Hz}$ and $885.3\ \text{Hz}$.

keyTakeaways: Five parameters ($\omega_{c1}$, $\omega_{c2}$, $\omega_o$, $\beta$, $Q$) describe every bandpass or bandreject filter, but only two are independent; $\omega_o$ is the geometric mean of the cut-offs and $Q = \omega_o/\beta$.
Series RLC bandpass: $\omega_o = 1/\sqrt{LC}$, $\beta = R/L$, $Q = (1/R)\sqrt{L/C}$; at $\omega_o$ the LC pair cancels and the whole source voltage appears across $R$.
Parallel RLC bandpass: same $\omega_o$, dual losses $\beta = 1/RC$, $Q = R\sqrt{C/L}$ — series circuits want small $R$, parallel circuits large $R$.
The bandreject filter is the same circuit with output across the LC pair: $H(s) = (s^{2} + \omega_o^{2})/(s^{2} + \beta s + \omega_o^{2})$, zero transmission at resonance.
Source resistance adds to $R$ in the series circuit: unchanged $\omega_o$, wider $\beta = (R + R_i)/L$, lower peak — filters must be designed with their drivers in mind.
The frequency-domain and time-domain views interlock: $\beta = 2\alpha$ and the damping transition lands at $Q = 1/2$.
Hughes’ tuned circuit: $Q = X_L/R$ at resonance; $Q = 50$ gives a bandwidth of $f_r/50 = 1592\ \text{Hz}$ around $79{,}577\ \text{Hz}$.

quiz.q: For a series RLC bandpass filter, which combination correctly gives $\omega_o$, $\beta$ and $Q$?
quiz.explanation: The series formulas pair $\beta = R/L$ with $Q = \omega_o/\beta = (1/R)\sqrt{L/C}$. The second option is the parallel-circuit set — the duality worth memorizing.

quiz.q: In a series RLC bandpass filter, doubling the resistance $R$ will:
options: Double the bandwidth and halve the quality factor
quiz.explanation: $\beta = R/L$ doubles while $\omega_o = 1/\sqrt{LC}$ stays fixed, so $Q = \omega_o/\beta$ halves. Resistance controls the width of the resonance; $L$ and $C$ fix its position.

quiz.q: A bandpass filter has cut-offs $635.3\ \text{Hz}$ and $885.3\ \text{Hz}$ (Nilsson Example 14.8). Its center frequency is:
quiz.explanation: $\omega_o = \sqrt{\omega_{c1}\omega_{c2}}$: in hertz, $\sqrt{(635.3)(885.3)} = 750\ \text{Hz}$ exactly, confirming the specification. The center frequency is the geometric mean, always slightly below the arithmetic mean.

quiz.q: At the center frequency of a series RLC bandreject filter (output across the LC pair), the output voltage is:
options: Zero, because the series LC pair acts as a short circuit
quiz.explanation: At $\omega_o$ the inductor and capacitor impedances cancel, so the LC pair drops no voltage — everything appears across $R$ and the bandreject output is exactly zero. The bandpass (output across $R$) shows the complementary maximum.

quiz.q: Hughes’ series resonant circuit has $f_r = 79{,}577\ \text{Hz}$, $X_L = 1000\ \Omega$ and total resistance $20\ \Omega$. Its bandwidth is:
quiz.explanation: $Q = X_L/R = 1000/20 = 50$, so the bandwidth is $f_r/Q = 79{,}577/50 = 1592\ \text{Hz}$, placing the half-power frequencies $796\ \text{Hz}$ on either side of resonance.

quiz.q: A series RLC bandpass section uses R = 20 Ω, L = 10 mH and C = 2.5 μF. Its 3 dB bandwidth is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: series $R = 20$ Ω, $L = 10$ mH, $C = 2.5$ μF. Step 2 — Governing trio: $\omega_{0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$, $Q = \frac{\omega_{0}L}{R}$, bandwidth $BW = \frac{f_{0}}{Q} = \frac{R}{2\pi L}$. Step 3 — Algebra: $LC = 2.5 \times 10^{-8}$, $\omega_{0} \approx 6324.6$ rad per s, $f_{0} \approx 1006.6$ Hz; $Q = \frac{6324.6 \times 0.01}{20} \approx 3.16$; $BW = \frac{1006.6}{3.16} \approx 318.5$ Hz, also $\frac{20}{2\pi \times 0.01} \approx 318.3$ Hz. Step 4 — Sanity check: larger $R$ widens the passband, $Q$ above unity promises visible selectivity, and both bandwidth routes agree. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 159 Hz halves by dropping $2\pi$, 637 Hz doubles $R$, and 1007 Hz quotes $f_{0}$ itself. Step 6 — Conclude: the bandwidth is about 318 Hz.

intro: Op amps rescue the filter designer three times over: they replace the inductor (large, heavy, costly, magnetic), they provide passband gain instead of guaranteed attenuation, and their low output impedance makes the transfer function immune to the load. Nilsson’s chapter builds the subject as an escalator — first-order active sections, then scaling, then the Butterworth polynomials with their maximally flat passband, and finally the cascade and parallel architectures that turn small bricks into eighth-order walls — while the Art of Electronics supplies the practicing engineer’s catalog of filter families.
objectives: Design first-order active low-pass and high-pass sections with independent gain and cut-off
Apply magnitude and frequency scaling to turn prototype filters into practical designs
Construct Butterworth filters of any order from the polynomial table
Size the order of a Butterworth filter from transition-band specifications
Transform low-pass prototypes into high-pass, bandpass and bandreject designs

concepts.statement: Active filters beat passive ones on three counts: they build bandpass and bandreject responses **without inductors** (large, heavy, costly, electromagnetically dirty); they provide **passband amplification** $K > 1$; and their op-amp outputs make the transfer function **insensitive to the load**.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s Practical Perspective is the bass volume control: one op amp, a few resistors and capacitors, and an adjustable resistor sets the low-frequency boost or cut independently of the treble control. Every circuit in this section assumes an ideal op amp, so the golden rules of Chapter 15 do all the work.

concepts.statement: An inverting amplifier with $R_2 \parallel C$ in the feedback path gives the active **low-pass** section $$H(s) = -\frac{K\omega_c}{s + \omega_c}, \quad K = \frac{R_2}{R_1}, \ \omega_c = \frac{1}{R_2 C};$$ with $C$ in the input path instead, it gives the active **high-pass** $$H(s) = -\frac{K s}{s + \omega_c}, \quad \omega_c = \frac{1}{R_1 C}.$$
concepts.detail: The gain and the cut-off are set by different components and can be specified independently — the advantage over the passive sections of Section 16.2. The low-pass circuit is the Chapter 6 integrating amplifier: integrating in time is low-pass filtering in frequency, the observation that also explains the Chapter 15 integrator.

concepts.statement: A **prototype** designed at $1\ \text{rad/s}$ with $1\ \Omega$ and $1\ \text{F}$ values becomes practical by scaling: $$R^{\prime} = k_m R, \qquad L^{\prime} = \frac{k_m}{k_f} L, \qquad C^{\prime} = \frac{1}{k_m k_f} C,$$ where $k_m$ scales impedance and $k_f$ scales frequency.
concepts.detail: Magnitude scaling multiplies every impedance by $k_m$ at a given frequency (resistors and inductors up, capacitors down); frequency scaling moves the response along the axis, touching only $L$ and $C$. Nilsson’s Example 15.3 shifts a $1\ \text{rad/s}$ series RLC prototype to $500\ \text{Hz}$ with $k_f = 3141.59$ and lands a $2\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor with $k_m = 159.155$, finishing at $R^{\prime} = 159.155\ \Omega$ and $L^{\prime} = 50.66\ \text{mH}$ with $Q$ unchanged.

concepts.statement: Cascading $n$ identical first-order low-pass sections gives a slope of $20n\ \text{dB}$ per decade, but the cut-off of the cascade **shrinks** to $$\omega_{cn} = \sqrt{2^{1/n} - 1}$$ times the single-section value ($0.435\ \text{rad/s}$ for $n = 4$), and the passband droops badly.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s fourth-order cascade of prototype sections has magnitude $-6\ \text{dB}$ already at $1\ \text{rad/s}$ — each section eats the other’s passband. Frequency scaling ($k_f = \omega_c/0.435$) restores the specified cut-off, but the droop remains: the reason the Butterworth design exists.

concepts.statement: The $n$th-order **Butterworth** (maximally flat) low-pass filter obeys $$|H(j\omega)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega/\omega_c)^{2n}}},$$ with cut-off exactly at $\omega_c$ for every $n$, all $2n$ exponents even, and poles equally spaced on the unit circle of the $s$ plane.
concepts.detail: Butterworth (Wireless Engineering, 1930) derived the polynomials by splitting the roots of $1 + (-1)^{n} s^{2n} = 0$ between the left and right half planes: for $n = 2$ this gives $H(s) = 1/(s^{2} + \sqrt{2} s + 1)$ and for $n = 3$, $H(s) = 1/[(s+1)(s^{2} + s + 1)]$. Table 15.1 extends the list to $n = 8$; each polynomial factors into first- and second-order terms, so any order is built by cascading the matching sections.

concepts.statement: Nilsson’s second-order Butterworth brick — **two equal resistors, two capacitors and a unity-gain op-amp buffer** (the Sallen–Key topology of the Art of Electronics) — realizes $$H(s) = \frac{1}{R^{2} C_1 C_2 s^{2} + 2 R C_1 s + 1}.$$ For the prototype ($R = 1\ \Omega$): $b_1 = 2/C_1$ and $C_1 C_2 = 1$, so matching $s^{2} + b_1 s + 1$ needs $$C_1 = \frac{2}{b_1}, \qquad C_2 = \frac{1}{C_1}.$$
concepts.detail: The second-order Butterworth factor $s^{2} + 1.414 s + 1$ therefore needs $C_1 = 1.41\ \text{F}$, $C_2 = 0.707\ \text{F}$ — a capacitor ratio of exactly $2{:}1$. The fourth-order polynomial $(s^{2} + 0.765 s + 1)(s^{2} + 1.848 s + 1)$ cascades two such stages with $(2.61, 0.38)$ and $(1.08, 0.924)$ farad prototype pairs; frequency and magnitude scaling then make the values real.

concepts.statement: Given a passband specification $A_p$ at $\omega_p$ and stopband specification $A_s$ at $\omega_s$ (both in dB, negative), the required Butterworth order is $$n = \frac{\log_{10}(\sigma_s/\sigma_p)}{\log_{10}(\omega_s/\omega_p)} \ \text{with}\ \sigma = \sqrt{10^{-0.1A} - 1},$$ which simplifies to $n = -0.05 A_s/\log_{10}(\omega_s/\omega_p)$ when $\omega_p$ is the cut-off — and $n$ is **rounded up** to the next integer.
concepts.detail: Nilsson’s Example 15.10: a $1000\ \text{Hz}$ cut-off with at most $-50\ \text{dB}$ at $6000\ \text{Hz}$ needs $n = (0.05 \times 50)/\log_{10} 6 = 2.5/0.778 = 3.21$, so a fourth-order filter is built; its actual $6000\ \text{Hz}$ attenuation is $-62.25\ \text{dB}$.

concepts.statement: The high-pass dual of the Sallen–Key section comes from **interchanging resistors and capacitors**, and its transfer function from replacing $s$ by $1/s$ in the low-pass prototype; a **broadband bandpass** is a low-pass cascade followed by a high-pass cascade and a gain stage, and a **broadband bandreject** runs the same sections in parallel into a summing amplifier.
concepts.detail: The Art of Electronics adds the wider catalog: Chebyshev filters trade passband ripple for a steeper wall, Bessel (linear-phase) filters preserve waveform shape, and the state-variable and multiple-feedback topologies give independently tunable $Q$. Nilsson’s Example 15.5 cascades a $10{,}000\ \text{Hz}$ low-pass and a $100\ \text{Hz}$ high-pass with an inverting stage for gain $2$ — the graphic-equalizer band of Section 16.3 rebuilt without an inductor.

concepts.statement: Cascaded first-order sections cannot exceed $Q = 1/2$; higher $Q$ requires **complex conjugate poles**. Nilsson’s high-Q bandpass circuit gives prototype values $$R_1 = \frac{Q}{K}, \quad R_2 = \frac{Q}{2Q^{2} - K}, \quad R_3 = 2Q,$$ and the twin-T notch filter gives $R = 1/\omega_o C$ with $\sigma = 1 - 1/4Q$.
concepts.detail: Example 15.13 builds a $3\ \text{kHz}$, $Q = 10$, gain-$2$ bandpass: prototype $R_1 = 5\ \Omega$, $R_2 = 10/198\ \Omega$, $R_3 = 20\ \Omega$, scaled with $k_f = 6000\pi$ and $k_m = 10^{8}/k_f$ to $26.5\ \text{k}\Omega$, $268.0\ \Omega$ and $106.1\ \text{k}\Omega$ around $0.01\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitors — the transfer function $-3770\,s/(s^{2} + 1885\,s + 355 \times 10^{6})$.

examples.title: Scaling a prototype low-pass filter (Nilsson Example 15.4)
examples.problem: Starting from the unity-gain prototype low-pass filter of Example 15.1 ($R_1 = R_2 = 1\ \Omega$, $C = 1\ \text{F}$, $\omega_c = 1\ \text{rad/s}$), design a filter with passband gain $5$, cut-off $1000\ \text{Hz}$ and a $10\ \text{nF}$ feedback capacitor.

steps.label: Step 1: Frequency scale factor
steps.text: Move the cut-off from $1\ \text{rad/s}$ to $1000\ \text{Hz}$: $k_f = \omega_c^{\prime}/\omega_c = 2\pi(1000)/1 = 6283.185$.

steps.label: Step 2: Magnitude scale factor
steps.text: The capacitor must land on $10\ \text{nF}$: $k_m = \frac{1}{k_f C^{\prime}} = \frac{1}{(6283.185)(10^{-8})} = 15{,}915.5$.

steps.label: Step 3: Scale the resistors
steps.text: Resistors respond to magnitude scaling only: $R_1^{\prime} = R_2^{\prime} = k_m (1\ \Omega) = 15{,}915.5\ \Omega$.

steps.label: Step 4: Set the gain
steps.text: Adjust $R_1^{\prime}$ alone to fix $K = R_2^{\prime}/R_1^{\prime} = 5$ without disturbing the cut-off (which depends on $R_2$ and $C$ only): $R_1^{\prime} = 15{,}915.5/5 = 3183.1\ \Omega$. The transfer function is $H(s) = -31{,}415.93/(s + 6283.185)$.

examples.result: $R_1^{\prime} = 3183.1\ \Omega$, $R_2^{\prime} = 15{,}915.5\ \Omega$, $C^{\prime} = 10\ \text{nF}$: gain $5$, cut-off $1000\ \text{Hz}$.

examples.title: A fourth-order Butterworth filter (Nilsson Example 15.9)
examples.problem: Design a fourth-order Butterworth low-pass filter with cut-off $500\ \text{Hz}$ and passband gain $10$, using as many $1\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistors as possible, and compare it with the identical-cascade design of Example 15.7.

steps.label: Step 1: Factor the polynomial
steps.text: From Table 15.1, the fourth-order Butterworth polynomial is $(s^{2} + 0.765 s + 1)(s^{2} + 1.848 s + 1)$: two cascaded second-order stages plus an inverting amplifier for the gain.

steps.label: Step 4: Scale to real values
steps.text: Frequency scaling $k_f = 3141.6$ moves the cut-off to $500\ \text{Hz}$; magnitude scaling $k_m = 1000$ turns the $1\ \Omega$ resistors into $1\ \text{k}\Omega$. The capacitors scale by $1/(k_m k_f)$: $C_{1a} = 831\ \text{nF}$, $C_{2a} = 121\ \text{nF}$, $C_{1b} = 344\ \text{nF}$, $C_{2b} = 294\ \text{nF}$. The gain stage uses $R_f = 10\ \text{k}\Omega$ with $R_1 = 1\ \text{k}\Omega$.

steps.label: Step 5: Compare the designs
steps.text: Both filters deliver $20\ \text{dB}$ at dc and cut off at $500\ \text{Hz}$, but the Butterworth passband is flat almost to the corner and its roll-off is steeper immediately after it — the identical cascade droops by several dB inside its own passband.

examples.result: $R = 1\ \text{k}\Omega$ everywhere with $C_{1a} = 831\ \text{nF}$, $C_{2a} = 121\ \text{nF}$, $C_{1b} = 344\ \text{nF}$, $C_{2b} = 294\ \text{nF}$ and $R_f = 10\ \text{k}\Omega$: a flatter, sharper filter than the identical cascade.

examples.title: A broadband bandpass filter without inductors (Nilsson Example 15.5)
examples.problem: Design a bandpass filter for a graphic equalizer with amplification $2$ over the band $100$–$10{,}000\ \text{Hz}$, using $0.2\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitors throughout.

steps.label: Step 1: Check the broadband condition
steps.text: The upper cut-off is $100$ times the lower one ($\omega_{c2} = 100\,\omega_{c1}$), comfortably exceeding the broadband requirement $\omega_{c2}/\omega_{c1} \ge 2$, so each subcircuit can be designed independently.

steps.label: Step 4: The gain stage
steps.text: The inverting amplifier must supply $K = 2$: choose $R_i = 1\ \text{k}\Omega$, so $R_f = 2(1000) = 2\ \text{k}\Omega$. At the center frequency the cascade magnitude evaluates to exactly $K$, meeting the amplification specification; the response is down $1/\sqrt{2}$ from it at both $100\ \text{Hz}$ and $10\ \text{kHz}$.

examples.result: Cascade of $80\ \Omega$ low-pass and $7958\ \Omega$ high-pass sections (both with $0.2\ \mu\text{F}$) plus a $1\ \text{k}\Omega$–$2\ \text{k}\Omega$ inverting stage: gain $2$ across $100$–$10{,}000\ \text{Hz}$, no inductors.

keyTakeaways: Active filters eliminate inductors, provide passband gain, and isolate the transfer function from the load — three advantages passive RC/RL networks cannot offer.
First-order active sections: low-pass $H = -K\omega_c/(s + \omega_c)$ with $\omega_c = 1/R_2 C$, high-pass $H = -Ks/(s + \omega_c)$ with $\omega_c = 1/R_1 C$ — gain and cut-off set independently.
Scaling laws: $R^{\prime} = k_m R$, $L^{\prime} = (k_m/k_f) L$, $C^{\prime} = C/(k_m k_f)$ — design at $1\ \text{rad/s}$ with $1\ \Omega$/$1\ \text{F}$ prototypes, then scale.

The Butterworth magnitude $1/\sqrt{1 + (\omega/\omega_c)^{2n}}$ is maximally flat with the cut-off fixed at $\omega_c$ for every order; its polynomials factor into the first- and second-order stages you cascade.
The unity-gain Sallen–Key second-order section matches $s^{2} + b_1 s + 1$ with $C_1 = 2/b_1$ and $C_2 = 1/C_1$ (equal resistors) — the second-order Butterworth needs a $2{:}1$ capacitor ratio.

Order selection: $n = -0.05 A_s/\log_{10}(\omega_s/\omega_p)$ when the cut-off is the passband edge, rounded up — $1000\ \text{Hz}$ cut-off with $-50\ \text{dB}$ at $6000\ \text{Hz}$ demands a fourth-order filter.

High-pass designs come from interchanging R and C (or $s \to 1/s$); broadband bandpass and bandreject filters come from cascading or paralleling the low-pass and high-pass bricks — and for $Q > 1/2$, complex-pole circuits such as the high-Q bandpass stage and the twin-T notch take over.

quiz.q: A Butterworth low-pass filter must have a $1000\ \text{Hz}$ cut-off and at most $-50\ \text{dB}$ gain at $6000\ \text{Hz}$. What order is required (Nilsson Example 15.10)?
options: $n = 3.21$, rounded up to a fourth-order filter
quiz.explanation: $n = -0.05 A_s/\log_{10}(\omega_s/\omega_p) = (0.05 \times 50)/\log_{10} 6 = 3.21$. Orders are integers, so round up: the fourth-order filter actually delivers $-62.25\ \text{dB}$ at $6000\ \text{Hz}$.

quiz.q: At its cut-off frequency $\omega_c$, an $n$th-order Butterworth low-pass filter has magnitude:
quiz.explanation: $|H(j\omega_c)| = 1/\sqrt{1 + 1} = 1/\sqrt{2}$ for every $n$: the defining elegance of the Butterworth form — the cut-off frequency never moves as sections are added, unlike the identical-section cascade.

quiz.q: A prototype has $R = 1\ \Omega$ and $C = 1\ \text{F}$. Applying magnitude scaling $k_m = 1000$ and frequency scaling $k_f = 3141.6$ produces:
quiz.explanation: Resistors scale only with $k_m$; capacitors with $1/(k_m k_f)$. This is exactly Nilsson’s Example 15.9 step that turned the fourth-order Butterworth prototype into $1\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistors with nanofarad capacitors.

quiz.q: In the unity-gain Sallen–Key second-order section with equal resistors ($R = 1\ \Omega$ prototype), realizing the Butterworth factor $s^{2} + \sqrt{2} s + 1$ requires:
quiz.explanation: Matching $b_1 = 2/C_1 = \sqrt{2}$ gives $C_1 = 1.41\ \text{F}$, and the constant term $1/(C_1 C_2) = 1$ forces $C_2 = 1/1.41 = 0.707\ \text{F}$ — the characteristic $2{:}1$ capacitor ratio of the second-order Butterworth.

quiz.q: Which capability is impossible for a cascade of first-order (real-pole) sections but routine for the active high-Q bandpass circuit?
quiz.explanation: Real poles can at best coincide, capping the cascaded-bandpass quality factor at $Q = 1/2$; complex conjugate poles — supplied by the high-Q circuit with its $R_1 = Q/K$ design equations or by resonant sections — unlock any $Q$.

intro: Chapter 15 showed feedback as a servant: negative feedback traded gain for linearity and bandwidth. Turn the sign around and feedback becomes a creator — an amplifier that feeds its own output back to its input, through a network that selects one frequency, will sing at that frequency forever. This section states the one criterion that governs every oscillator ever built, the Barkhausen criterion, and confronts the two problems it leaves open: how oscillation starts, and what stops it from growing without bound.
objectives: Explain how positive feedback converts an amplifier into an oscillator, in contrast with the negative feedback of Chapter 15
State and apply the Barkhausen criterion for sustained sinusoidal oscillation
Quantify the energy exchange in a resonant LC tank and interpret the Q factor as a loss budget (Hughes, Chapter 14)
Describe the amplitude-stabilization problem and the practical mechanisms that solve it
Connect the electrical resonant circuit to Hughes mechanical analogy of a mass on a spring

concepts.statement: An **oscillator** is an amplifier whose output is returned to its input through a **frequency-selective feedback network** so that the loop sustains an output with no input signal.
concepts.detail: Write the amplifier gain as $A$ and the feedback fraction as $\beta$, so the signal returned to the input is $\beta v_{out}$ and the loop gain is the product $A\beta$. Chapter 15 kept this product small and negative (degenerative feedback, which stabilizes gain). Oscillators do the opposite: the network is chosen so that at one frequency the returned signal arrives in phase with the input and large enough to replace it, and the circuit supplies its own input.

concepts.statement: Sustained oscillation at a single frequency requires a loop gain of exactly unity and a loop phase shift of exactly zero (an integer multiple of $360^\circ$):
concepts.detail: The loop gain $A\beta$ is a complex number, a function of frequency. It is only at the frequency where the phase of $A\beta$ passes through $0^\circ$ that regenerative feedback exists, and only there does the loop ring. The Art of Electronics states the design rule directly: to guarantee startup, the loop gain must exceed unity — say by a factor of two or more — at the desired frequency; the circuit then grows its own signal from noise. The frequency of oscillation is set by the phase crossing, and since the passive network is far more stable than the active device, the network — not the amplifier — sets the frequency.

concepts.term: Loop gain above unity: growth from noise
concepts.statement: With $|A\beta| > 1$ at the phase-crossing frequency, any tiny disturbance is amplified around the loop and **grows exponentially** until something limits it; with $|A\beta| < 1$ the oscillation decays.
concepts.detail: Thermal noise in resistors and the amplifier itself contains energy at every frequency, so an oscillator never needs an external seed. The component of noise at the selected frequency is amplified, fed back, re-amplified, and builds up within a few dozen cycles. This is why a working design deliberately over-provides loop gain: component tolerances, temperature and loading would otherwise drag $|A\beta|$ below unity and the circuit would fall silent.

concepts.statement: A loop gain of exactly unity cannot be designed in — it must be **reached dynamically**: start with $|A\beta| > 1$, then let the growing amplitude reduce the effective gain until the loop settles where $|A\beta| = 1$.
concepts.detail: Whatever mechanism performs this reduction also sets the output purity. A crude limiter — back-to-back diodes, or plain amplifier clipping — clamps the peaks and leaves several per cent distortion. An elegant mechanism reduces gain gradually with amplitude: a small lamp or thermistor whose resistance rises as it warms, or an AGC loop with a JFET as a voltage-controlled resistor. Art of Electronics calls this the central oscillator design problem — making the amplitude stable, not making it oscillate.

concepts.term: Resonant energy exchange in the LC tank
concepts.statement: At the resonant frequency $f_r = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal, and energy **oscillates between electrostatic storage in the capacitor and magnetic storage in the inductor**, a quarter of a cycle apart.
concepts.detail: Hughes (section 14.7) describes the exchange precisely: at one instant the energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}CV_m^2$ in the capacitor, a quarter of a cycle later it is $\tfrac{1}{2}LI_m^2$ in the inductor. The sum would be constant if the series resistance did not dissipate $I^2R$ on every pass. An oscillator built around a tank is exactly a resonant circuit plus an amplifier that replenishes those losses in phase — the electronic twin of pushing a swing.

concepts.term: Q factor as the loss budget
concepts.statement: The **Q factor** is the ratio of reactive power to average power dissipated at resonance, equivalently $Q = 2\pi$ times the energy stored divided by the energy lost per cycle.
concepts.detail: Hughes defines both forms (equations [14.7]–[14.9]): for a series circuit $Q = \omega_r L/R = 1/(\omega_r C R)$. The higher the Q, the less energy the amplifier must reinject per cycle and the sharper the resonance peak — section 14.10 derives the bandwidth as $\mathrm{BW} = f_r/Q$. The practical coil of Hughes Example 14.2 ($r = 5.0\,\Omega$, $L = 1.0\,\text{mH}$) manages only $Q = 14.1$; a quartz crystal reaches $10^4$ to $10^6$, which is why section 17.3 exists.

concepts.term: Mechanical analogy of a resonant circuit
concepts.statement: A mass on a spring released from a displaced position **oscillates at its natural frequency with decaying amplitude**; if it is given a small tap each time it moves downward, the oscillation builds to a large steady amplitude.
concepts.detail: This is Hughes section 14.8, and it is the whole theory of oscillators in one picture: mass corresponds to inductance, spring elasticity to capacitance, friction to resistance. The taps are the feedback amplifier, timed to arrive in phase — at the natural frequency, a small repeated force sustains a large oscillation, and the work it does exactly replaces the frictional loss. Hughes points to the escapement of a clock and the balance wheel of a watch as everyday embodiments.

concepts.statement: Oscillator stability is set almost entirely by the **passive frequency-selective network** — its temperature coefficient and its Q — not by the amplifier.
concepts.detail: A simple RC network drifts by fractions of a per cent per kelvin; an LC tank holds a few hundred ppm because copper and dielectrics expand; a crystal holds a few ppm. The amplifier only needs enough loop gain margin to stay running: because the loop locks at the phase crossing, gain variations move the amplitude, not the frequency, to first order. This hierarchy — RC, LC, crystal — organizes section 17.3.

examples.title: A tank as the frequency-setting element (Hughes, Example 14.2)
examples.problem: A coil of resistance $5.0\,\Omega$ and inductance $1.0\,\text{mH}$ is connected in series with a $0.20\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor across a 2.0 V variable-frequency supply. Find the resonant frequency, the current and reactances at resonance, and the Q factor — the numbers an oscillator designer would need before adding the amplifier.

steps.label: Step 1: Resonant frequency
steps.text: At resonance $\omega_r L = 1/(\omega_r C)$, so $f_r = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$. With $L = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{H}$ and $C = 0.20 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{F}$: $f_r = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{2.0 \times 10^{-10}}) = 11.25\,\text{kHz}$, exactly as Hughes computes.

steps.label: Step 2: Current at resonance
steps.text: The reactances cancel and the circuit is purely resistive: $I_r = V/R = 2.0/5.0 = 0.4\,\text{A}$. This is the maximum the circuit can draw, and the current the losses $I^2R = 0.8\,\text{W}$ are built from.

steps.label: Step 3: Reactances and magnification
steps.text: Each reactance at resonance is $X_L = X_C = 2\pi f_r L = 2\pi \times 11\,250 \times 10^{-3} = 70.7\,\Omega$. The capacitor voltage is $V_C = I_r X_C = 0.4 \times 70.7 = 28.3\,\text{V}$ — fourteen times the 2.0 V supply. A resonant feedback network hands the amplifier this same magnification for free.

steps.label: Step 4: Q factor
steps.text: $Q = \omega_r L/r = 70.7/5.0 = 14.1$. In oscillator terms: each cycle, the tank loses a fraction $1/Q$ of its stored energy per radian, so the feedback loop must reinject about 7 per cent of the stored energy per cycle to keep it ringing.

examples.result: $f_r = 11.25\,\text{kHz}$, $I_r = 0.4\,\text{A}$, $X_L = X_C = 70.7\,\Omega$, $V_C = 28.3\,\text{V}$, $Q = 14.1$ — the voltage magnification of about 14 that the book notes.

examples.title: The energy the amplifier must replenish (Hughes, Example 14.1)
examples.problem: A series circuit with $R = 4.0\,\Omega$ and $L = 0.50\,\text{H}$ takes 25 A from a 100 V, 50 Hz supply at resonance ($C = 20.3\,\mu\text{F}$). How much energy circulates, how much is lost per cycle, and what loop of amplifier and tank would sustain it?

steps.label: Step 1: Stored energy at the peaks
steps.text: The current is sinusoidal with rms value 25 A, so its peak is $I_m = 25\sqrt{2} = 35.4\,\text{A}$. At the instant the inductor current peaks, the stored energy is $W = \tfrac{1}{2}LI_m^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.50 \times 1250 = 312.5\,\text{J}$ — the same energy that appears across the capacitor a quarter of a cycle later.

steps.label: Step 2: Energy lost per cycle
steps.text: The resistance dissipates $P = I^2R = 25^2 \times 4.0 = 2500\,\text{W}$. One cycle lasts $T = 1/50 = 20\,\text{ms}$, so the loss per cycle is $\Delta W = 2500 \times 0.020 = 50\,\text{J}$. This is the energy an oscillation-sustaining amplifier would have to reinject on every cycle.

steps.label: Step 3: Check against the Q factor
steps.text: The book computes $Q = 2\pi f_r L/R = 2\pi \times 50 \times 0.5/4.0 = 39.3$ (and indeed $V_L = V_C = QV = 3930\,\text{V}$ at 25 A). The definition $Q = 2\pi W/\Delta W$ gives $2\pi \times 312.5/50 = 39.3$ — the same number from a completely different direction.

steps.label: Step 4: The oscillator view
steps.text: A feedback amplifier that couples energy back into this tank in the right phase, delivering just $50\,\text{J}$ per cycle (2500 W average), keeps the 3930 V ringing across $L$ and $C$ forever. Deliver more and the amplitude grows; deliver less and it decays — the Barkhausen balance in energy terms.

examples.result: Stored energy 312.5 J sloshes between L and C; 50 J per cycle is dissipated; the ratio gives $Q = 39.3$, matching the book — and fixing the power the sustaining amplifier must supply.

keyTakeaways: Oscillation is positive feedback: an amplifier plus a frequency-selective network that returns a phase-aligned fraction $\beta$ of its own output.
The Barkhausen criterion demands loop gain $|A\beta| = 1$ at $0^\circ$ loop phase; design with margin above unity so noise can start the oscillation.

Amplitude stabilization is the real design problem: gain above unity grows the signal, and a nonlinear element — lamp, thermistor, AGC, or clipping — must settle it where the loop gain is exactly one.
At $f_r = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ a tank exchanges energy between $\tfrac{1}{2}CV^2$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}LI^2$ storage a quarter-cycle apart; losses are $I^2R$ per pass.
The Q factor is the loss budget — energy stored over energy lost per radian — and fixes both how much the amplifier must reinject and how sharp the frequency selection is.
Frequency stability belongs to the passive network: RC worst, LC better, crystal best; amplifier gain changes move amplitude, not frequency.

quiz.q: An amplifier has $A = 100$ and its feedback network returns $\beta = 0.012$ in phase at 1 kHz. What happens at 1 kHz?
options: The loop gain is below unity, so any disturbance decays
The loop gain is exactly unity, so a sustained 1 kHz oscillation results
The loop gain is above unity, so an oscillation grows from noise until something limits it
Nothing — the loop gain is negative, as in Chapter 15
quiz.explanation: The loop gain is $A\beta = 100 \times 0.012 = 1.2 > 1$ with zero loop phase, so the Barkhausen magnitude condition is exceeded: the 1 kHz component of noise circulates and grows until a gain-reducing mechanism — a lamp, an AGC loop or plain clipping — settles the loop gain at exactly one. Had the product been 0.8, the loop would be regenerative in phase but too weak, and the circuit would stay quiet.

quiz.q: Which condition is the Barkhausen criterion for sustained oscillation?
options: Loop gain equal to 1 and loop phase of 180 degrees
Loop gain greater than 1 and loop phase of 90 degrees
Loop gain equal to 1 and loop phase of zero degrees (a multiple of 360 degrees)
Open-loop gain equal to the feedback fraction, at any phase
quiz.explanation: The returned signal must arrive in phase with the signal it replaces (a total loop phase of $0^\circ$, that is $360^\circ$) and with exactly the same amplitude. Loop gain above unity only guarantees startup; something must then reduce it to one to hold a stable amplitude.

quiz.q: In the series resonant circuit of Hughes Example 14.1, why is $V_C = 3930\,\text{V}$ when the supply is only 100 V?
options: The capacitor is charged through a step-up transformer action
At resonance the current (25 A) flows through $X_C = 157\,\Omega$, and the product is Q times the supply voltage
The resonance doubles the supply voltage across each element
The Q factor reduces the current until the voltage rises
quiz.explanation: At resonance the impedance is just $R = 4\,\Omega$, so $I = 25\,\text{A}$, and that current develops $I X_C = 25 \times 157 = 3930\,\text{V}$ across the capacitor. Since $X_C = Q R$, the voltage is magnified by $Q = 39.3$ — the same magnification an LC feedback network offers the oscillator loop.

quiz.q: Why do practical oscillator designs deliberately make the loop gain greater than unity at startup?
options: To make the frequency higher than the network alone provides
So that component tolerances and temperature cannot pull the loop gain below unity and silence the circuit
Because unity loop gain is unstable in principle
To keep the output amplitude exactly proportional to the supply
quiz.explanation: Loop gain above unity guarantees growth from noise even after tolerances eat into the margin. The resulting amplitude then grows until a gain-reducing mechanism — a lamp, thermistor, AGC loop or clipping — settles the loop gain at exactly one. Designing for exactly one from the start would leave the circuit unable to start at all once anything drifts.

quiz.q: In the mass-on-spring analogy of a resonant circuit (Hughes section 14.8), what plays the role of the feedback amplifier?
options: The spring, because it returns the mass toward equilibrium
The mass, because it stores kinetic energy
The small taps timed to the natural frequency, which replace the frictional losses
The friction, because it limits the amplitude
quiz.explanation: The escapement of a clock — the regularly timed small impulses from the mainspring — keeps the balance wheel swinging by replacing exactly the energy lost to friction. The feedback amplifier does the same for the LC tank: it injects in-phase energy equal to the $I^2R$ loss of each cycle.

intro: Not every oscillator needs a resonator. A capacitor, a resistor and anything that switches between two thresholds will oscillate — the capacitor charges until the switch flips, the threshold moves, and the cycle repeats. These relaxation oscillators make square waves instead of sine waves, and one integrated circuit, the 555 timer, packages the whole idea into an eight-pin device that has outsold almost every other chip in history.
objectives: Analyze the op-amp or comparator relaxation oscillator with hysteresis and derive its period from the exponential charging law
Compute a relaxation oscillator frequency from component values, including the equal-resistor special case $T = 2RC\ln 3$
Describe the 555 timer internals: two comparators, the flip-flop and the discharge transistor
Design 555 astable and monostable circuits from the formulas $f = 1.44/((R_A + 2R_B)C)$ and $T = 1.1RC$
Explain why both circuits share the same $\ln 3$ mathematics

concepts.statement: A **relaxation oscillator** generates a square or triangular wave by charging a capacitor toward one threshold, switching the state of a comparator or gate when the threshold is crossed, and letting the capacitor then charge toward the other threshold.
concepts.detail: The timing is exponential, set by an $RC$ product, and the output is rich in harmonics rather than sinusoidal — exactly what a clock, a flasher or a tone generator needs. Unlike the resonant oscillators of section 17.1, frequency accuracy depends on resistor, capacitor and threshold ratios, typically good to a few per cent.

concepts.statement: A comparator with **positive feedback** through a divider $R_1$–$R_2$ switches at two thresholds, $+\gamma V_{sat}$ and $-\gamma V_{sat}$, where $\gamma = R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$ and $\pm V_{sat}$ are the saturated output levels.
concepts.detail: The separation between the thresholds — the hysteresis window $2\gamma V_{sat}$ — is what makes the relaxation oscillator work: the capacitor must genuinely travel between them, and the exponential charging time between the two levels sets the period. Without hysteresis a plain comparator would chatter at the crossing instead of oscillating cleanly.

concepts.statement: With thresholds at fractions $\pm\gamma$ of the saturated output, the capacitor moves exponentially between them and the period is
concepts.detail: During each half-cycle the capacitor charges from $-\gamma V_{sat}$ toward $+V_{sat}$, so $v_C(t) = V_{sat} - V_{sat}(1+\gamma)e^{-t/RC}$; reaching $+\gamma V_{sat}$ takes $t = RC\ln\big((1+\gamma)/(1-\gamma)\big)$. Doubling for the two halves gives the boxed result. For the popular equal-resistor case $\gamma = 1/2$ this collapses to $T = 2RC\ln 3 = 2.197RC$, that is $f = 1/(2RC\ln 3) \approx 0.455/RC$. The Art of Electronics stresses the pleasant consequence: because the thresholds are fixed fractions of the output swing, the frequency is independent of the supply voltage — only the $RC$ product and the ratio $R_2/(R_1+R_2)$ matter.

concepts.statement: The frequency of a relaxation oscillator is set by **ratios of the output swing**, so a saturating op-amp or comparator driven from $\pm 15\,\text{V}$, $\pm 12\,\text{V}$ or a single supply gives essentially the same frequency.
concepts.detail: Both the destination ($\pm V_{sat}$) and the thresholds ($\pm\gamma V_{sat}$) scale with the supply, and the logarithm in the period formula depends only on their ratio. What does shift the frequency is threshold asymmetry, comparator propagation delay (which matters above a few hundred kHz), and the capacitance the comparator itself adds.

concepts.statement: The 555 contains **two comparators** — one tripped at $\tfrac{2}{3}V_{CC}$ (the threshold comparator) and one at $\tfrac{1}{3}V_{CC}$ (the trigger comparator) — an **SR flip-flop** driven by them, an open-collector **discharge transistor** on pin 7, and a buffered output stage on pin 3.
concepts.detail: The trip points come from three equal resistors in series across the supply, which is why every 555 timing result is a supply-independent ratio.
