concepts.detail: Hughes sections 21.3–21.4. **Relative accuracy** is the maximum deviation from the ideal output as a percentage of full scale: Example 21.5 works a converter whose full-scale output is $5 + 0.5\times5 + 0.25\times5 + 0.125\times5 = 9.375\,\text{V}$, so $\pm 0.02$ per cent is $\pm 1.875\,\text{mV}$. **Differential linearity** is the maximum deviation of any step from the ideal step size — the same $\pm 1.875$ mV applied to the 625 mV ideal step. **Settling time** is the time to settle within one LSB of the final value. Resolution and accuracy should be matched — Hughes quotes about 0.2 per cent as the working figure — since a 16-bit resolution behind 1 per cent accuracy is wasted silicon.

concepts.statement: The **R/2R ladder** produces the same binary-weighted outputs using **only two resistor values**: each bit drives a 2R rung onto a rail of R segments terminated in 2R.
concepts.detail: With every inactive bit grounded, successive parallel-series reductions make the resistance looking into the rail 2R at every node, so each rung source sees a Thévenin halving on its way to the summing node. Input D (code 1000) delivers $5/(2R)$ into the virtual ground, and with $R_f = 2R$ the output magnitude is $(5/2R)\times 2R = 5\,\text{V}$ — the MSB alone (Hughes Fig. 21.9). Input C (0100) first Thévenin-reduces to a 2.5 V source behind R (Figs. 21.10–21.11) and gives 2.5 V; each lower bit halves again — 1.25 V, 0.625 V — so the output is proportional to the binary weight of the input bits, exactly as Hughes concludes. Four different precision resistors have become two, and the ratio 2:1 is the easiest of all to hold matched on a chip.

concepts.statement: A **comparator** decides which of two analogue signals is larger; built from an op-amp in high-gain differential mode, it saturates at one supply rail or the other whenever the difference exceeds the **threshold voltage**.
concepts.detail: With $\pm 10$ V supplies the output saturates at $+10$ V or $-10$ V, and a typical open-loop gain of 10 000 makes the linear region only $\pm 1$ mV wide — the threshold. Hughes Example 21.6: a difference of 2 mV exceeds the threshold and saturates the output at $+10$ V, while 0.5 mV leaves the amplifier linear, giving $G\times\Delta V = 10\,000 \times 0.5\,\text{mV} = +5\,\text{V}$. Because supply rails drift, a Zener diode in series with a resistor fixes the delivered levels. The comparator is the decision element of every converter below — and, wired with positive feedback, it is the Schmitt trigger of Chapter 17.

concepts.statement: The **digital-ramp converter** drives a DAC from a counter: a start pulse resets the count and locks out the clock, then the DAC staircase climbs one LSB per pulse until it exceeds the input by at least the threshold, freezing the count at the answer.
concepts.detail: Hughes Fig. 21.15: the counter, DAC and comparator in a loop, with an AND gate preventing clock pulses from disturbing the counter during reset. The frozen count is the digital representation of $V_A$. Its vice is time — conversion length grows linearly with the input magnitude, worst case near full scale. The **continuous** variant substitutes an up/down counter that tracks the input from its previous value instead of restarting, faster on average but still slow in the worst case. Quantization error is inherent: the staircase can land no closer than one step, and Hughes is careful to separate this from the converter’s accuracy, which is set by components and adds to it.

concepts.statement: The **successive-approximation converter** replaces the counter with a register and the linear search with a binary one: set each bit from MSB to LSB, keep it if the DAC output stays below the input, clear it if not.
concepts.detail: Hughes Fig. 21.12 shows the block diagram — comparator, control unit, clock, register and internal DAC — with the operating sequence: start command, clocked register updates, DAC output to the comparator, comparison against $V_A$, stop when the comparator output falls. An $n$-bit conversion takes $n$ comparison cycles whatever the input value, which is the decisive advantage: the 12-bit converter of Example 21.7 needs twelve clock cycles where its ramp counterpart needs thousands of counts. It remains the general-purpose workhorse between the slow ramp and the fast flash.

concepts.statement: A **flash converter** compares the input against every level at once: a resistor divider strings $2^n$ taps between reference and ground, each tap driving its own comparator, and a priority encoder reads the thermometer-coded results.
concepts.detail: One comparison, done — the fastest architecture there is. The cost is hardware: $2^n - 1$ comparators, meaning 255 for 8 bits and over a thousand for 10, each burning power and loading the input with its capacitance. Flash rules where speed is everything — oscilloscope front ends and video — while half-flash and pipelined designs trade some of that speed back for sanity. Hughes closes the chapter with the engineer’s anthem: no matter how fast the converter, engineers will seek better speeds.

examples.title: Weights and accuracy of a weighted DAC (Hughes, Examples 21.4 and 21.5)
examples.problem: A 4-bit weighted DAC has $R_f = 1\,\text{k}\Omega$ with input resistors of 2, 4, 8 and 16 k$\Omega$ for inputs D, C, B, A; bit inputs are 5 V. Find each bit’s weight. A second converter, with input resistors of $R$, $2R$, $4R$, $8R$, has full-scale output 9.375 V and relative accuracy $\pm 0.02$ per cent — find the maximum output deviation.

steps.label: Step 1: Weight of the MSB
steps.text: The summing-amplifier gain for input D is the feedback-to-input resistance ratio, $1\,\text{k}\Omega/2\,\text{k}\Omega = 0.5$, so $V_D = 0.5 \times 5 = 2.5\,\text{V}$.

steps.label: Step 2: The remaining weights
steps.text: Halving down the input ladder: $V_C = 1.25\,\text{V}$, $V_B = 0.625\,\text{V}$ and $V_A = 0.3125\,\text{V}$ — the LSB weight, hence the step size, is 0.3125 V (Hughes prints 0.313 V).

steps.label: Step 3: Full-scale of this unit
steps.text: Input 1111 sums all four weights: $2.5 + 1.25 + 0.625 + 0.3125 = 4.6875\,\text{V}$, in steps of 0.3125 V.

steps.label: Step 4: The accuracy question
steps.text: For the second converter the weights are the doubled set (1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 into 5 V), so full scale is $5 + 0.5\times5 + 0.25\times5 + 0.125\times5 = 9.375\,\text{V}$, as Hughes computes for Example 21.5.

steps.label: Step 5: Maximum deviation
steps.text: Relative accuracy is a percentage of full scale: $0.02 \times 9.375/100 = 1.875\,\text{mV}$. No output may deviate from its ideal value by more than $\pm 1.875$ mV, and the differential-linearity specification applies the same figure to the 625 mV ideal step.

examples.result: Weights 2.5 / 1.25 / 0.625 / 0.3125 V; full-scale 4.6875 V on the first unit, 9.375 V on the second, whose outputs are held within $\pm 1.875$ mV.

examples.title: The R/2R ladder halves at every rung (Hughes, section 21.5)
examples.problem: In the 4-bit R/2R ladder of Hughes Fig. 21.8 ($R_f = 2R$, 5 V bit inputs), compute the output for inputs 1000 and 0100, deduce the other two weights, and evaluate the full-scale input 1111.

steps.label: Step 1: Collapse the ladder for input 1000
steps.text: With A, B and C grounded, successive parallel-series reduction of their rungs leaves an equivalent resistance of 2R looking into the rail from the summing node. Since that node is a virtual ground, no current flows in the equivalent, and the D-bit current is simply $5/(2R)$.

steps.label: Step 2: Output for 1000
steps.text: That current flows on through the feedback resistor: $|V_{\text{out}}| = (5/2R)\times 2R = 5\,\text{V}$ — the MSB alone, matching Hughes Fig. 21.9.

steps.label: Step 3: Output for 0100
steps.text: For input C, Thévenize at the rail junction: the 5 V behind its 2R rung faces the collapsed 2R of the left-hand ladder, halving to a 2.5 V source behind R (Fig. 21.11). Its current flows through the rail into the virtual-ground node and the feedback, giving $|V_{\text{out}}| = 2.5\,\text{V}$ — half the MSB.

steps.label: Step 4: Deduce and sum the rest
steps.text: Each lower rung adds one more Thévenin halving: input B gives 1.25 V and input A gives 0.625 V. For 1111, superposition adds the four: $5 + 2.5 + 1.25 + 0.625 = 9.375\,\text{V}$ — fifteen 0.625 V steps from 0000 to 1111.

examples.result: Outputs 5 V, 2.5 V, 1.25 V and 0.625 V for bits D, C, B, A; full-scale 1111 gives 9.375 V, all with only two resistor values in the network.

examples.title: A 12-bit conversion, ramp versus successive approximation (Hughes, Example 21.7)
examples.problem: A digital-ramp A/D converter has a 1 MHz clock, a 12-bit DAC with 8.190 V full-scale output, and a comparator of 1 mV threshold. For an input $V_A = 4.528$ V find the step size, the counter result and the conversion time; then outline how the successive-approximation version handles the same input.

steps.label: Step 1: Step size
steps.text: A 12-bit converter has $2^{12} - 1 = 4095$ steps, so the internal DAC advances $8190\,\text{mV}/4095 = 2\,\text{mV}$ per count.

steps.label: Step 2: Where the ramp stops
steps.text: The comparator falls only when $V_{DA}$ exceeds $V_A$ by at least the 1 mV threshold. The staircase levels are even millivolts, so 4.529 V is skipped and the count stops at 4.530 V — count $4530/2 = 2265$.

steps.label: Step 3: Read the counter and the clock cost
steps.text: The counter holds $2265 = 100011011001_2$, reached after 2265 clock pulses at one per microsecond — about 2.27 ms. (Hughes prints 4.53 ms for this part, a figure consistent with 1 mV steps rather than the 2 mV steps the book itself computes; the count, 2265, is the book’s own.)

steps.label: Step 4: Resolution and quantization error
steps.text: The resolution is the 2 mV step — $2/8190 \times 100 = 0.024$ per cent — and the quantization error, the largest error the staircase granularity can impose, is one step. Accuracy is separate: component tolerances add to it, not into it.

steps.label: Step 5: The successive-approximation alternative
steps.text: With a register instead of a counter, the same converter runs a binary search: set the MSB (4096 mV — under 4528, keep), try bit 11 (6144 — over, clear), and so on down the twelve bits. The search homes onto $100011101000_2 = 2264$, whose DAC output is 4528 mV exactly — twelve clock cycles, about 12 microseconds, instead of thousands of counts.

examples.result: Ramp: $2265 = 100011011001_2$ after about 2.27 ms. SAR: $100011101000_2$ in twelve cycles. Resolution 2 mV (0.024 per cent) either way.

keyTakeaways: Convert to digital early, process, convert back late: digital stages correct errors; senses, sensors and actuators stay analogue.
A DAC output is proportional to the binary code; the LSB weight is the step size, and percentage resolution is step over full-scale — 8 bits at 5 mV steps gives 635 mV full scale and 0.79 per cent.

The weighted DAC is a summing amplifier with R, 2R, 4R, 8R inputs (Hughes eq. [21.1]); its accuracy lives in the resistor ratios and in the precision-level amplifiers that clamp each bit to exactly 5 V or 0 V.
The R/2R ladder buys the same weighted outputs with only two resistor values — every rung Thévenin-halves, so bits D, C, B, A give 5, 2.5, 1.25, 0.625 V.
The comparator is a high-gain open-loop op-amp: 1 mV of threshold, $\pm 10$ V of saturated decision — the binary decision element of every ADC.

The digital-ramp ADC is simple but slow, its conversion time growing with the input; the successive-approximation ADC replaces counting with a twelve-step binary search; the flash ADC compares against every level at once and pays with $2^n - 1$ comparators.
Quantization error is one LSB, inherent in any finite staircase, and is distinct from accuracy, which adds component tolerances on top.

quiz.q: An 8-bit D/A converter has a step size of 5 mV (Hughes, Example 21.2). Its maximum output voltage and percentage resolution are:
quiz.explanation: There are $2^8 - 1 = 127$ steps above zero, so the maximum (full-scale) output is $127 \times 5 = 635\,\text{mV}$, and the percentage resolution is $5/635 \times 100 = 0.79$ per cent. Resolution tightens as bits are added.

quiz.q: In the R/2R ladder of Hughes Fig. 21.8, taking input C high with all other inputs low reduces (by Thévenin) to:
options: A 2.5 V source behind R, giving a 2.5 V output
quiz.explanation: The 5 V on C looks through its 2R rung into the collapsed 2R of the left-hand ladder: the divider halves the voltage to 2.5 V and the parallel combination leaves a Thévenin resistance of R. The current then flows through the rail into the virtual ground and the 2R feedback, delivering 2.5 V — half the MSB, exactly as binary weighting demands.

quiz.q: A comparator with gain 10 000 and $\pm 10$ V saturation receives $V_1 = 3.1255$ V and $V_2 = 3.1250$ V (Hughes, Example 21.6). Its output is:
options: $+5$ V, still in the linear region
quiz.explanation: The difference is 0.5 mV — below the 1 mV threshold — so the amplifier has not saturated and the output is the gain times the difference: $10\,000 \times 0.5\,\text{mV} = +5\,\text{V}$. A difference above 1 mV would pin the output at $+10$ V.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the successive-approximation ADC from the digital-ramp ADC?
options: It replaces the counter with a register and converges by binary search in n clock cycles
It can only convert inputs near full scale
quiz.explanation: The SAR sets each bit from the MSB down, keeps it if the internal DAC output remains below the input and clears it otherwise — a binary search that always finishes in $n$ comparisons. The ramp counts up one step at a time, taking up to $2^n - 1$ cycles; spending $2^n - 1$ comparators is the flash architecture instead.

quiz.q: The quantization error of an A/D converter is:
options: The sum of all component tolerances
One LSB — the granularity of the staircase itself
quiz.explanation: With 2 mV steps, as in Example 21.7, no input can be represented better than to within one step of the nearest level. Hughes separates this inherent quantization error from the converter accuracy, which is set by the components and adds to it.

intro: Everything so far treated a gate as an ideal symbol. A real gate is a fistful of transistors with analogue appetites: it needs a supply, its inputs load the stage before it, its output swings between two technology-defined voltage levels, and it burns power while switching. Hughes section 23.18 introduces the two families, TTL and CMOS; this section adds the Art of Electronics view of what the numbers mean — noise margins, fan-out, and the daily business of making logic drive lamps, relays and the analogue world, or survive in it.
objectives: Compare TTL and CMOS technologies: construction, power, speed, supply range and ESD sensitivity
Compute noise margins and fan-out from guaranteed logic levels, and explain the AC fan-out limit of CMOS
Explain why and how TTL and CMOS are interfaced, including pull-ups, HCT families and 3.3 V to 5 V level shifting
Design gate-driven LED and relay circuits with correct current limiting and inductive protection
Describe optocouplers and their role in isolation and level translation

concepts.statement: **TTL** builds gates from bipolar junction transistors on a nominal 5 V supply; the classic 74 series guarantees $V_{OH} \ge 2.4$ V, $V_{OL} \le 0.4$ V, and input thresholds of 2.0 V and 0.8 V.
concepts.detail: Hughes section 23.18 values TTL for development work: it is not sensitive to electrostatic discharge, so it survives breadboard handling that would kill an unprotected CMOS device. Its input stage sources current — a standard TTL input pulls about 1.6 mA when driven low — which limits fan-out to the order of ten, and its resistive pull-ups cost milliwatts per gate whether or not it switches. Though no longer the mainstream, TTL is still met in legacy boards and teaching laboratories, and many CMOS families keep pin compatibility so a TTL prototype can transfer straight to CMOS production.

concepts.statement: **CMOS** builds each gate from a complementary pair of N- and P-channel MOSFETs; with a static input one device is off, so the gate draws virtually no supply current and swings its output close to both rails.
concepts.detail: The output is a driven connection to $V_{DD}$ or to ground through a few hundred ohms or less — Chapter 14’s MOSFET used purely as a switch. Hughes notes the two engineering forces: the supply has fallen from 5 V to 3.3 V and below — cutting power, since charging input capacitance dominates dynamic dissipation at $P \approx C V_{DD}^2 f$ — and switching speeds, once CMOS’s weakness, now rival TTL. The price is fragility: the insulated gates are ESD-sensitive, and every input adds roughly 10 pF of capacitance that the driving stage must charge and discharge at every edge.

concepts.statement: The guaranteed levels define the noise margins $$NM_H = V_{OH}(\min) - V_{IH}(\min), \qquad NM_L = V_{IL}(\max) - V_{OL}(\max)$$ — the voltage a delivered level can lose to noise and still be read correctly.
concepts.detail: For standard TTL at 5 V: $V_{OH} \ge 2.4$ V, $V_{IH} \ge 2.0$ V, $V_{IL} \le 0.8$ V, $V_{OL} \le 0.4$ V — margins of 0.4 V in each state. For 74HC CMOS at 5 V the output swings nearly to the rails (about 4.9 V and 0.1 V) while the thresholds sit at 3.5 V and 1.5 V — 70 and 30 per cent of supply — giving margins of about 1.4 V, three and a half times the TTL figures. That is why CMOS tolerates the noisier industrial environments. Margins are guarantees, not typical values: a system designed on typical levels fails in the field.

concepts.statement: **Fan-out** is the number of identical inputs one output can drive: for standard TTL, $\text{fan-out} = I_{OL}/I_{IL} = 16\,\text{mA}/1.6\,\text{mA} = 10$.
concepts.detail: A standard TTL output is guaranteed to sink 16 mA while holding $V_{OL} \le 0.4$ V, and each TTL input pulls 1.6 mA when low — the unit load. Ten unit loads, ten gates: an eleventh would drag the output above $V_{IL}$. CMOS inputs draw only picoamps to microamps at DC, so the DC fan-out of CMOS driving CMOS runs to hundreds — but each input is about 10 pF, and at speed the driver’s finite output resistance charges that capacitance through every edge. Propagation delay grows roughly linearly with added loads, so the AC fan-out — set by edge-rate and timing budgets — is the binding number, often a mere handful of inputs at high clock rates.

concepts.statement: Mixed technologies must have their logic levels matched: TTL driving 5 V CMOS fails on the high side — 2.4 V delivered against 3.5 V required — and is rescued by a **pull-up resistor** or by the TTL-compatible **74HCT** family.
concepts.detail: The margin arithmetic becomes a compatibility test: TTL’s $V_{OH} = 2.4$ V sits below 74HC’s $V_{IH} = 3.5$ V — a negative noise margin and an invitation to intermittent failure. A pull-up of a few k$\Omega$ to the 5 V rail lets the TTL output rise to nearly 5 V when high; alternatively, 74HCT devices accept TTL output levels while keeping CMOS internals, at the price of a slightly reduced input margin. In the other direction CMOS drives TTL easily as long as the current sinking is respected. Between 3.3 V and 5 V logic the mismatch reappears — 3.3 V outputs against 3.5 V thresholds — and HCT inputs, resistor dividers or dedicated level-shifting ICs bridge the gap: the everyday interface arithmetic of mixed-signal boards.

concepts.statement: A logic output drives an LED through a **current-limiting resistor**: for a 2 V red LED at 15 mA from a 5 V output, $R = (5 - 2)/15\,\text{mA} = 200\,\Omega$.
concepts.detail: The LED of Chapter 12 conducts over a narrow forward-voltage band, so the resistor — not the gate — sets the current, and the current sets the brightness. Standard TTL sinks 16 mA far more happily than it sources, so the LED is usually wired from the supply rail into the output, lighting when the output goes low. Sizing: a 5 V rail, a 2 V red LED and 15 mA give $(5-2)/0.015 = 200\,\Omega$; a 3.3 V CMOS output driving a 3.1 V blue LED has only 200 mV of headroom — not enough, which is where dedicated drivers and constant-current sinks enter. Multiplexed displays time-share the current among many LEDs, one digit at a time, a trick as old as the pocket calculator.

concepts.statement: Relay coils need tens of milliamperes — far beyond a gate — so a **transistor driver** interposes, and a **flyback diode** across the coil absorbs the inductive turn-off spike.
concepts.detail: A small 5 V relay might draw 70 mA through its coil; no logic output can supply that, but one bipolar transistor, run into saturation as the Chapter 13 switch, passes it while the gate supplies only base current — about 1 mA through a 4.3 k$\Omega$ base resistor for a forced current gain of 70. When the transistor turns off, the coil current cannot stop instantly — Chapter 5’s $v = L\,di/dt$ — and would otherwise develop hundreds of volts across the switch; the flyback diode, reverse-biased in normal running, gives the current a recirculating path and clamps the spike to about a diode drop. Motor and solenoid drivers are the same story at higher currents, with power MOSFETs taking over from BJTs.

concepts.statement: An **optocoupler** pairs an LED with a phototransistor in one package, so the signal crosses as light and the input and output circuits share no electrical connection at all.
concepts.detail: The LED side drives current — say 10 mA; the phototransistor side delivers a fraction of it as collector current, the ratio quoted as the current transfer ratio, commonly 20 to 100 per cent. The reward is galvanic isolation rated in kilovolts: a logic signal can cross between grounds that differ by hundreds of volts, between a noisy power domain and a quiet measurement domain, or into a patient-connected instrument in the instrumentation tradition of Chapter 15. Optocoupled solid-state relays extend the idea to switching AC mains. The isolated-side transistor behaves like any transistor — it needs biasing and a load resistor, and the plain LED–phototransistor pair is slow, tens of microseconds, with logic-output parts available for the impatient.

examples.title: Noise margins of TTL against 74HC CMOS
examples.problem: A 5 V system can be built in TTL (guaranteed $V_{OH} \ge 2.4$ V, $V_{OL} \le 0.4$ V, thresholds 2.0 V and 0.8 V) or in 74HC CMOS (outputs within 0.1 V of the rails, thresholds 3.5 V and 1.5 V). Compute the noise margins of each and compare.

steps.label: Step 1: TTL high-state margin
steps.text: $NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH} = 2.4 - 2.0 = 0.4\,\text{V}$. A logic 1 may sag by up to 0.4 V before the receiver misreads it.

steps.label: Step 2: TTL low-state margin
steps.text: $NM_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL} = 0.8 - 0.4 = 0.4\,\text{V}$ — symmetric with the high state, by the family’s design.

steps.label: Step 3: 74HC margins
steps.text: With $V_{OH} \approx 4.9$ V and $V_{OL} \approx 0.1$ V: $NM_H = 4.9 - 3.5 = 1.4\,\text{V}$ and $NM_L = 1.5 - 0.1 = 1.4\,\text{V}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret
steps.text: The CMOS margins are about 3.5 times TTL’s: 1.4 V of noise on a CMOS wire is survivable where 0.4 V on a TTL wire corrupts the bit. One caution: CMOS thresholds are ratiometric to the supply, so at 3.3 V the margins shrink with the rail.

examples.result: TTL: 0.4 V in both states. 74HC at 5 V: about 1.4 V in both states.

examples.title: Fan-out arithmetic, DC and AC
examples.problem: A standard TTL output is guaranteed to sink 16 mA at $V_{OL} \le 0.4$ V, and one TTL input draws 1.6 mA when driven low. What is the DC fan-out? What limits fan-out in a CMOS system clocked at 20 MHz if each input presents about 10 pF?

steps.label: Step 1: The unit load
steps.text: Each driven input, held low, pulls 1.6 mA out of the driving output — one TTL unit load.

steps.label: Step 2: The division
steps.text: $\text{fan-out} = I_{OL}/I_{IL} = 16/1.6 = 10$ identical inputs, with the output still meeting its $V_{OL}$ guarantee.

steps.label: Step 3: Why DC is not the whole story for CMOS
steps.text: A CMOS input draws almost no DC current, so its DC fan-out would read in the hundreds; but ten inputs at 10 pF each add 100 pF to every driven node.

steps.label: Step 4: The AC cost
steps.text: Each edge must charge that capacitance through the driver’s output resistance; delay and edge times stretch roughly in proportion, and the dynamic supply current grows as $P = C V_{DD}^2 f$. At 20 MHz it is the timing budget — not the static current — that sets the real fan-out.

examples.result: TTL DC fan-out = 10; CMOS fan-out is capacitance-limited by speed, not by static input current.

examples.title: Making a gate drive an LED and a relay
examples.problem: A 5 V logic output must (a) illuminate a 2 V, 15 mA red LED and (b) energize a 5 V relay whose coil draws 70 mA. Design both interfaces.

steps.label: Step 1: The LED resistor
steps.text: The resistor must drop $5 - 2 = 3$ V at 15 mA: $R = 3/0.015 = 200\,\Omega$. Wiring the LED from the 5 V rail into the gate output lets the output sink the current — the strong direction for TTL totem-pole stages.

steps.label: Step 2: Why the relay cannot connect directly
steps.text: 70 mA exceeds the 16 mA sink rating; connecting the coil directly would pull $V_{OL}$ out of specification and could damage the output stage. The gate drives a transistor instead.

steps.label: Step 3: The transistor driver
steps.text: An NPN switch with a 4.3 k$\Omega$ base resistor draws about $(5 - 0.7)/4.3\,\text{k}\Omega \approx 1$ mA from the gate; with a current gain of 70 it holds the 70 mA coil in saturation.

steps.label: Step 4: The flyback diode
steps.text: The coil’s stored energy must go somewhere at turn-off; a diode across the coil, cathode to the supply, recirculates the current and clamps the collector spike to about one diode drop above the rail instead of hundreds of volts.

steps.label: Step 5: The optocoupler option
steps.text: If the relay must float free of the logic ground, drive its transistor through an optocoupler: the gate lights the internal LED with the same 200 $\Omega$ arithmetic, and the phototransistor does the switching with kilovolts of isolation.

examples.result: LED: 200 $\Omega$ into a sinking output. Relay: 4.3 k$\Omega$ base resistor, NPN driver and a flyback diode — or an optocoupled equivalent when the grounds must not meet.

keyTakeaways: A real gate is an analogue circuit with guaranteed digital behaviour: the four numbers $V_{OH}$, $V_{OL}$, $V_{IH}$ and $V_{IL}$ fix everything about interfacing it.
Noise margins are the gaps between what is delivered and what is demanded: 0.4 V for TTL, about 1.4 V for 5 V 74HC — design to the guarantees, not the typicals.
Fan-out is current arithmetic for TTL ($16\,\text{mA}/1.6\,\text{mA} = 10$) and capacitance arithmetic for CMOS — speed, not DC current, binds the modern case.
CMOS wins static power (near zero) and supply scaling (5 V down to 3.3 V and below); TTL wins robustness on the bench — and 74HCT parts bridge them.
Interfacing analogue and digital is a design genre: pull-ups for TTL-to-CMOS, level shifters for 3.3 V to 5 V, current limiting for LEDs, transistor drivers with flyback diodes for relays.
Optocouplers move the signal as light and buy kilovolts of galvanic isolation — the cleanest way to let two grounds that must never meet still exchange a bit.

quiz.q: A standard TTL output guarantees sinking 16 mA while holding a valid logic 0, and each TTL input draws 1.6 mA when low. The fan-out is:
quiz.explanation: Fan-out is the sink capability divided by the unit load: $16\,\text{mA}/1.6\,\text{mA} = 10$. An eleventh input would pull more current than the guarantee covers and lift $V_{OL}$ above its 0.4 V limit.

quiz.q: For a gate with $V_{OH}(\min) = 2.4$ V, $V_{IH}(\min) = 2.0$ V, $V_{IL}(\max) = 0.8$ V and $V_{OL}(\max) = 0.4$ V, the noise margins are:
quiz.explanation: $NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH} = 2.4 - 2.0 = 0.4$ V and $NM_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL} = 0.8 - 0.4 = 0.4$ V — the classic TTL figures, against roughly 1.4 V for 5 V CMOS.

quiz.q: A 5 V TTL output must drive a 74HC CMOS input ($V_{IH} = 3.5$ V). What is the standard fix?
options: A pull-up resistor to the 5 V rail, or a 74HCT input instead of the 74HC
A coupling capacitor between the stages
quiz.explanation: TTL delivers only 2.4 V guaranteed on a logic 1 — below the 3.5 V the HC input demands, so the noise margin is negative. A pull-up of a few k$\Omega$ lets the high level rise to nearly 5 V; HCT inputs shift the thresholds down to TTL levels while keeping CMOS internals.

quiz.q: Why does a flyback diode accompany every transistor-driven relay coil?
options: It speeds up the relay turn-off
It recirculates the coil current at switch-off, clamping the inductive spike to about a diode drop
It protects the transistor against electrostatic discharge
quiz.explanation: Inductor current cannot stop instantly; interrupting 70 mA in a coil of even modest inductance develops hundreds of volts — $v = L\,di/dt$ — which would avalanche the transistor. The diode, reverse-biased while running, gives the current a path and holds the spike near one diode drop above the rail.

quiz.q: The current transfer ratio (CTR) of an optocoupler describes:
options: The ratio of LED forward voltage to breakdown voltage
The output collector current as a percentage of the input LED current
The isolation voltage rating in kV per amp
quiz.explanation: Drive 10 mA of LED current and a CTR of 50 per cent yields 5 mA available at the phototransistor collector. CTRs run from about 20 per cent in simple parts to 100 per cent and beyond in darlington-output couplers — and it degrades with age, the design margin to watch.

intro: The transformer is the one electrical machine with no moving parts, and it earns its keep by changing voltage with almost no loss of power — a medium-sized unit runs at 97–98 per cent full-load efficiency. Hughes builds the whole apparatus of power engineering on it: a laminated ferromagnetic core, two coupled windings, an e.m.f. equation you can derive in four lines, and an equivalent circuit that turns out to be the template for every machine in the rest of this chapter.
objectives: Describe transformer construction and explain why cores are laminated at 0.35–0.7 mm
Derive and apply the e.m.f. equation $E = 4.44 f N \Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$
Use the turns ratio to relate primary and secondary voltages and currents
Build the equivalent circuit and refer secondary resistance and leakage reactance to the primary
Compute efficiency, voltage regulation and the condition for maximum efficiency, and predict them all from the open-circuit and short-circuit tests

concepts.statement: A transformer core is built of **laminated steel sheets about 0.35–0.7 mm thick**, insulated from one another; the vertical portions are the **limbs** (carrying the windings) and the horizontal portions are the **yokes**. Laminating slashes the eddy-current loss, and the remaining core loss is the sum of **hysteresis loss** (energy spent re-magnetizing the steel each cycle) and **eddy-current loss**.
concepts.detail: The alternating flux induces e.m.f.s in the core material itself, and the resulting $I^{2}R$ losses are the eddy-current losses. Since flux varies little between no load and full load (within about 2 per cent), the core loss is treated as constant at all loads — the key fact that makes the open-circuit test meaningful. The magnetizing current is only 3–5 per cent of full-load primary current, so the no-load power factor is very low.

concepts.term: Principle of action and the turns ratio
concepts.statement: With the whole of the flux set up by the primary linking the secondary, the e.m.f. induced per turn is the same for both windings, so $$\frac{V_2}{V_1} \simeq \frac{N_2}{N_1} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{I_1}{I_2} \simeq \frac{N_2}{N_1}.$$ The magnetic flux is the connecting link: any secondary current produces (by Lenz’s law) a demagnetizing ampere-turn effect that is neutralized by an increase in primary current, giving $I_1 N_1 \simeq I_2 N_2$.
concepts.detail: The balance of primary and secondary ampere-turns is the fundamental relationship wherever transformer action occurs. In power practice, generation at about 22 kV is stepped up for transmission, then stepped back down for motors, lamps and heaters — the loss at each transformation is small, though Hughes wryly notes that 2 per cent of 100 MW is still not insignificant.

concepts.statement: If the flux swings from $+\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$ to $-\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$ in half a cycle ($1/2f$ seconds), the average rate of change is $4 f \Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$ webers per second, and multiplying by the form factor 1.11 of a sine wave gives the r.m.s. e.m.f. per winding: $$E = 4.44\, f\, N\, \Phi_{\mathrm{m}} \ \text{volts}.$$
concepts.detail: The alternative derivation is instantaneous: with $\phi = \Phi_{\mathrm{m}} \sin 2\pi f t$, the induced e.m.f. per turn is $\mathrm{d}\phi/\mathrm{d}t = 2\pi f \Phi_{\mathrm{m}} \sin(2\pi f t + \pi/2)$ — a quarter-cycle ahead of the flux — and $0.707 \times 2\pi f \Phi_{\mathrm{m}} = 4.44 f \Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$. This single equation fixes the core area, the number of turns and the flux density of every transformer and rotating-machine winding designed for sinusoidal flux.

concepts.statement: The no-load current $I_0$ has two components: a **magnetizing component** $I_{0\mathrm{m}}$ in phase with the flux, and a **power (core-loss) component** $I_{0\mathrm{l}}$ in phase with the applied voltage, so $$I_0 = \sqrt{I_{0\mathrm{l}}^2 + I_{0\mathrm{m}}^2}, \qquad \cos\phi_0 = \frac{I_{0\mathrm{l}}}{I_0}.$$
concepts.detail: Because $I_{0\mathrm{l}} \ll I_{0\mathrm{m}}$, the no-load power factor is very low — Hughes’s worked example (Example 29.2, 480-turn primary, 2200 V, 50 Hz) finds $I_0 = 1.21$ A at a power factor of only 0.168 lagging, with $I_{0\mathrm{m}} = 1.19$ A and $I_{0\mathrm{l}} = 0.203$ A. That example also runs the magnetic circuit in reverse: 400 A/m over a 1.8 m path plus a 0.1 mm effective airgap takes 807.5 ampere-turns, the flux $\Phi_{\mathrm{m}} = 0.0206$ Wb at 1.1 T requires 0.0187 m² of core, and 263 kg of steel at 1.7 W/kg gives a 447 W core loss.

concepts.statement: The **useful flux** links both windings and stays practically constant from no load to full load (within about 2 per cent); the **leakage flux** links only its own winding, its value is proportional to the load current, and its effect is that of an inductive reactance in series with each winding.
concepts.detail: The leakage paths are almost entirely through air, so their reluctance is essentially constant — which is why leakage can be represented by the constant series reactances $X_1$ and $X_2$. Hughes lists the practical countermeasures: make the transformer window long and narrow, wind primary and secondary concentrically, sandwich the windings, or use shell-type construction. An ideal transformer in a box — equal p.d. between terminals A–B and C–D — proves that the useful flux is responsible for no voltage drop at all.

concepts.term: Equivalent circuit referred to the primary
concepts.statement: Represent the transformer as an ideal transformer plus series imperfections: winding resistances $R_1$, $R_2$ and leakage reactances $X_1$, $X_2$, with a magnetizing reactor $X_0$ and core-loss resistor $R_0$ across the ideal primary. Referring the secondary to the primary gives $$R_e = R_1 + R_2 \left( \frac{V_1}{V_2} \right)^{\!2}, \quad X_e = X_1 + X_2 \left( \frac{V_1}{V_2} \right)^{\!2}, \quad Z_e = \sqrt{R_e^2 + X_e^2}.$$
concepts.detail: Because $I_0$ is only 3–5 per cent of full-load current, the magnetizing branch may be dropped for full-load calculations, and the two series impedances merged. Hughes’s Example 29.4 (100 kVA, 400/80 turns, $R_1 = 0.3\,\Omega$, $R_2 = 0.01\,\Omega$, $X_1 = 1.1\,\Omega$, $X_2 = 0.035\,\Omega$, 2200 V supply) finds $R_e = 0.55\,\Omega$, $X_e = 1.975\,\Omega$ and $Z_e = 2.05\,\Omega$ referred to the primary — the machine per-unit resistance 0.0114 and reactance 0.0408.

concepts.statement: Voltage regulation is the change of secondary terminal voltage between no load and full load, per unit of the no-load voltage, with the primary voltage held constant; for a lagging load $$\text{p.u. regulation} = \frac{I_1 \left( R_e \cos\phi_2 + X_e \sin\phi_2 \right)}{V_1},$$ and for a leading load the reactance term carries a minus sign.
concepts.detail: The leading case can invert the sign of the regulation entirely: the same 100 kVA transformer of Example 29.4 has +3.36 per cent regulation at 0.8 lagging (secondary falls from 440 V to 425 V) but −1.54 per cent at 0.8 leading (secondary rises to 447 V). Regulation must always be quoted with its power factor.

concepts.statement: With constant core loss $P_{\mathrm{c}}$ and variable copper loss, $$\eta = \frac{\text{output}}{\text{output} + P_{\mathrm{c}} + I_1^2 R_1 + I_2^2 R_2},$$ and efficiency is a maximum when the variable $I^{2}R$ loss equals the constant core loss: $I_2^2 R_{2e} = P_{\mathrm{c}}$.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s 500 kVA transformer (Example 29.6, $R_1 = 0.42\,\Omega$, $R_2 = 0.0019\,\Omega$, 11000/400 V, core loss 2.9 kW, load p.f. 0.8) runs at 98.3 per cent on full load and 98.1 per cent at half load; maximum efficiency occurs at $n = \sqrt{2.9/3.86} = 0.867$ of full load — 433 kVA — where the copper loss has fallen to match the 2.9 kW core loss and $\eta_{\max} = 98.4$ per cent. The fraction of rated apparent power at which this happens is independent of the power factor.

concepts.statement: **Open-circuit test** at rated voltage gives the turns ratio, the no-load current and the core loss $P_{\mathrm{oc}}$ (the no-load $I^{2}R$ loss is less than 1/400 of its full-load value). **Short-circuit test** at reduced voltage — one-twentieth to one-thirtieth of rated — circulates full-load currents and gives the total $I^{2}R$ loss $P_{\mathrm{sc}}$. Then at any load $n$ times full load, $$\eta = \frac{n S \cos\phi}{n S \cos\phi + P_{\mathrm{oc}} + n^{2} P_{\mathrm{sc}}},$$ and the regulation follows from $V_{\mathrm{sc}}\cos(\phi_e - \phi_2)/V_1$.
concepts.detail: The wattmeter power in the short-circuit test is almost pure copper loss because the flux (and hence the core loss) is only about $(1/25)^{2}$ of rated. These two small-power tests replace loading a machine of many hundreds of kVA — Hughes’s Example 29.8 works a complete 50 kVA unit from 430 W and 525 W of measured loss.

examples.title: Working the e.m.f. equation backwards (Example 29.1)
examples.problem: A 250 kVA, 11000 V/400 V, 50 Hz single-phase transformer has 80 turns on the secondary. Calculate (a) the approximate primary and secondary full-load currents, (b) the number of primary turns, and (c) the maximum value of the flux.

steps.label: Step 1: Full-load currents
steps.text: The rating in volt-amperes is the product of voltage and current, so $I_1 \simeq 250\,000/11\,000 = 22.7$ A and $I_2 = 250\,000/400 = 625$ A.

steps.label: Step 2: Primary turns
steps.text: From the turns ratio $N_1 = 80 \times 11\,000/400 = 2200$ turns — 27.5 times more turns on the high-voltage side, as expected.

steps.label: Step 3: Apply the e.m.f. equation to the secondary
steps.text: The secondary must develop 400 V in 80 turns at 50 Hz: $400 = 4.44 \times 80 \times 50 \times \Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Solve for the flux
steps.text: $\Phi_{\mathrm{m}} = 400/17\,760 = 0.0225$ Wb — a peak flux of 22.5 mWb is carried by the core every cycle.

examples.result: $I_1 \simeq 22.7$ A, $I_2 = 625$ A, $N_1 = 2200$ turns and $\Phi_{\mathrm{m}} = 22.5$ mWb. One equation, three design quantities.

examples.title: Equivalent impedance and regulation, lagging and leading (Example 29.4)
examples.problem: A 100 kVA transformer has 400 primary and 80 secondary turns; $R_1 = 0.3\,\Omega$, $R_2 = 0.01\,\Omega$, $X_1 = 1.1\,\Omega$, $X_2 = 0.035\,\Omega$. The supply is 2200 V. Find the equivalent impedance referred to the primary, and the regulation and secondary terminal voltage at full load, 0.8 power factor (i) lagging, (ii) leading.

steps.label: Step 1: Refer the secondary impedances
steps.text: The voltage ratio is $2200/440 = 5$, so the factors of 25 apply: $R_e = 0.3 + 0.01 \times 25 = 0.55\,\Omega$ and $X_e = 1.1 + 0.035 \times 25 = 1.975\,\Omega$.

steps.label: Step 2: Equivalent impedance
steps.text: $Z_e = \sqrt{0.55^2 + 1.975^2} = 2.05\,\Omega$ referred to the primary.

steps.label: Step 4: Regulation, lagging
steps.text: $\frac{45.45 (0.55 \times 0.8 + 1.975 \times 0.6)}{2200} = \frac{45.45 \times 1.625}{2200} = 0.0336$ per unit — 3.36 per cent. The no-load secondary voltage is $2200 \times 80/400 = 440$ V, which falls by $440 \times 0.0336 = 14.8$ V to **425 V** on full load.

steps.label: Step 5: Regulation, leading
steps.text: The reactance term now subtracts: $\frac{45.45 (0.55 \times 0.8 - 1.975 \times 0.6)}{2200} = -0.0154$ per unit — the terminal voltage **rises** by 6.78 V to **447 V**.

examples.result: The same machine regulates +3.36 per cent into a lagging load and −1.54 per cent into a leading one: leakage reactance is the enemy of lagging loads and the friend of leading ones.

examples.title: The two-test prediction (Example 29.8)
examples.problem: A 50 kVA transformer gives these results. Open-circuit test: primary 3300 V, secondary 400 V, primary power 430 W. Short-circuit test: primary 124 V, primary current 15.3 A, primary power 525 W with full-load secondary current. Find the efficiencies at full load and half load at 0.7 power factor, the regulations at 0.7 lagging and leading, and the corresponding secondary voltages.

steps.label: Step 1: Separate the losses
steps.text: Core loss $P_{\mathrm{oc}} = 430$ W; full-load copper loss $P_{\mathrm{sc}} = 525$ W. Total full-load loss is 955 W = 0.955 kW.

steps.label: Step 2: Efficiencies
steps.text: Full load: $\eta = \frac{50 \times 0.7}{50 \times 0.7 + 0.955} = 1 - \frac{0.955}{35.95} = 0.973$ per unit — 97.3 per cent. Half load: copper loss falls to $525 \times 0.25 = 131$ W, so $\eta = 1 - \frac{0.561}{18.06} = 0.963$ — 96.3 per cent.

steps.label: Step 3: Short-circuit power factor
steps.text: $\cos\phi_e = 525/(124 \times 15.3) = 0.2765$, giving $\phi_e = 73^\circ 57^\prime$; for $\cos\phi_2 = 0.7$, $\phi_2 = 45^\circ 34^\prime$.

steps.label: Step 4: Regulation
steps.text: Lagging: $\frac{124 \cos(73^\circ 57^\prime - 45^\circ 34^\prime)}{3300} = \frac{124 \cos 28^\circ 23^\prime}{3300} = 0.033$ per unit — 3.3 per cent. Leading: $\frac{124 \cos 119^\circ 31^\prime}{3300} = -0.0185$ per unit — −1.85 per cent.

steps.label: Step 5: Secondary voltages
steps.text: From the 400 V no-load value: $400 (1 - 0.033) = 387$ V lagging, and $400 (1 + 0.0185) = 407$ V leading.

examples.result: Two tests totalling under a kilowatt of measured loss predict the full-load behaviour of a 50 kVA machine: 97.3 per cent efficiency and 387 V at 0.7 lagging, 96.3 per cent and 407 V at 0.7 leading.

keyTakeaways: A transformer is two windings coupled by a common alternating flux in a laminated steel core; the useful flux is the link, and it stays essentially constant from no load to full load.
The e.m.f. equation $E = 4.44 f N \Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$ comes from averaging the flux swing $2\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$ over half a cycle and applying the sine-wave form factor 1.11.
Voltage transforms with the turns ratio and current inversely with it, because the primary ampere-turns must balance the demagnetizing secondary ampere-turns.
Leakage flux is proportional to load current and appears as series reactance $X_e$; winding resistance gives $R_e$; both referred to one side scale with the square of the voltage ratio.
Regulation at lagging power factor is $I_1 (R_e \cos\phi_2 + X_e \sin\phi_2)/V_1$, and it changes sign for leading loads.
Efficiency peaks when the variable copper loss equals the constant core loss — which is why large transformers run hottest, not most efficiently, at full load.
The open-circuit test measures the core loss and the short-circuit test the copper loss; together they give efficiency and regulation at any load without ever loading the transformer.

quiz.q: The factor 4.44 in the transformer e.m.f. equation is closest in origin to:
options: $4$ from the flux swing over half a cycle, times $1.11$ — the r.m.s.-to-average ratio of a sine wave
The number of quarter-cycles in one cycle of the supply
The permeability of silicon steel at 1.5 T
The ratio of primary to secondary turns in a standard unit
quiz.explanation: The flux goes from $+\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$ to $-\Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$ in $1/2f$ seconds, so the average rate of change is $4 f \Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$; multiplying by the form factor 1.11 of a sine wave gives $4.44 f \Phi_{\mathrm{m}}$ per turn.

quiz.q: A transformer on no load draws a current that is:
options: Large and at unity power factor
Small (typically 3–5 per cent of full load) and at a very low lagging power factor
Zero for an ideal steel core
Small and at a very low leading power factor
quiz.explanation: The no-load current is dominated by the magnetizing component $I_{0\mathrm{m}}$ in phase with the flux; the core-loss component $I_{0\mathrm{l}}$ that carries the power is tiny by comparison, so $\cos\phi_0 = I_{0\mathrm{l}}/I_0$ is very small — 0.168 in Hughes’s example.

quiz.q: In the short-circuit test on a transformer, the measured power is taken to be almost entirely:
options: Core loss, because the current is at its rated value
Copper loss, because the reduced voltage makes the flux (and hence the core loss) negligible
Windage and friction loss of the cooling fans
Leakage-flux loss in the tank walls
quiz.explanation: The applied voltage is only about one-twentieth to one-thirtieth of rated, so the flux and the core loss (roughly proportional to flux squared) collapse, while full-load currents still flow through the winding resistances — the wattmeter reads the $I^{2}R$ loss.

quiz.q: A 500 kVA transformer has 3.86 kW of full-load copper loss and 2.9 kW of core loss. At what fraction of rated output is its efficiency a maximum?
options: Half load, because losses are smallest there
It is the same at every load
quiz.explanation: Maximum efficiency occurs when the variable $I^{2}R$ loss equals the constant core loss: $n^{2} \times 3.86 = 2.9$, so $n = 0.867$. The result is independent of the power factor of the load.

quiz.q: Why can the terminal voltage of a transformer rise above its no-load value when it carries a leading (capacitive) load?
options: The core loss reverses direction and feeds power back
The leakage-reactance drop now opposes the resistive drop in the regulation expression, making the net regulation negative
The turns ratio changes with load current
The magnetizing current cancels the load current exactly
quiz.explanation: At leading power factor the regulation is $I_1 (R_e \cos\phi_2 - X_e \sin\phi_2)/V_1$; since $X_e$ dominates $R_e$, this is negative. In Example 29.8 the 400 V secondary rose to 407 V at 0.7 leading.

quiz.q: A 400 V, 50 Hz single-phase transformer winding has 200 turns. Assuming sinusoidal flux and negligible drops, the maximum core flux is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: RMS voltage $E = 400$ V, $f = 50$ Hz, $N = 200$ turns, sinusoidal flux. Step 2 — Governing equation: $E = 4.44 f N \Phi_{m}$, the form factor $1.11$ times $4$ from Faraday integration over a half-cycle. Step 3 — Algebra: $\Phi_{m} = \frac{400}{4.44 \times 50 \times 200} = \frac{400}{44400} \approx 9.009 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb, that is $9.01$ mWb. Step 4 — Sanity check: mill Weber flux in a power core gives tesla-scale density over a realistic limb area, doubling turns would halve the flux, and higher frequency likewise reduces it. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: 4.50 mWb doubles the turns, 0.90 mWb slips a decade, and 18.0 mWb halves them. Step 6 — Conclude: peak flux is about 9.01 mWb.

intro: Before meeting any specific machine, Hughes asks what every machine has in common: a magnetic field acting as a two-way energy coupling between an electrical system and a mechanical one. From that single idea — plus the observation that magnetic systems try to maximize their stored field energy — flow the forces of alignment and interaction, the reluctance motor, the doubly excited machines, and the single most useful fact in AC machinery: three phase currents make a magnetic field that rotates.
objectives: Explain the magnetic field as the coupling between electrical and mechanical systems, and compute the force of alignment $F = B^2 A / 2\mu_0$ between magnetized surfaces
State the energy balance and the torque relation $M_E = \mathrm{d}W_f/\mathrm{d}\lambda$
Classify the three families of doubly excited machines by their stator and rotor excitation
Derive the synchronous speed relation $f = np$ and the e.m.f. of a stator winding
Show analytically why three-phase currents produce a rotating field of constant magnitude $1.5 B_{\mathrm{m}}$

concepts.statement: An electromagnetic machine links an electrical energy system to another energy system (usually mechanical) by providing **a reversible means of energy flow in its magnetic field**. A motor converts electrical to mechanical energy, a generator the reverse, and a converter — like the transformer of the previous section — transfers electrical energy between electrical systems; at very low power such devices are called transducers.
concepts.detail: The field is the mutual link: energy transferred from one system is temporarily stored in the field and then released to the other. On the electrical side the reaction of the field appears as an e.m.f., and the product of e.m.f. and current is the rate of electrical energy conversion. Machines develop force in two ways — by alignment of magnetized surfaces, or by the interaction $F = Bli$ of a current and a flux.

concepts.term: Magnetic field energy and energy density
concepts.statement: For a linear (air) region, the stored field energy is $W_f = \tfrac{1}{2} Li^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} N \Phi = \tfrac{1}{2} \mathcal{S} \Phi^2$, and the **energy density** in an airgap is $$w_f = \tfrac{1}{2} B H = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0} \ \text{joules per cubic metre}.$$
concepts.detail: All these forms assume flux and m.m.f. are proportional — true of air, which is the only material that matters in most machine airgaps. The energy picture is the master key: whenever a small displacement $\mathrm{d}x$ would increase the stored field energy, the arrangement experiences a force in that direction. Magnetic systems, like mechanical ones released from constraint, run downhill on reluctance and uphill on stored energy.

concepts.term: Force of alignment between magnetized surfaces
concepts.statement: Separating two parallel magnetized surfaces of area $A$ with uniform flux density $B$ by $\mathrm{d}x$ adds gap volume $A\,\mathrm{d}x$ of stored energy at density $B^2/2\mu_0$, so the attracting force is $$F = \frac{B^2 A}{2\mu_0}.$$ More generally, at constant flux, $F = \mathrm{d}W_f/\mathrm{d}x$.
concepts.detail: Hughes’s Example 30.1 works a horseshoe electromagnet lifting a steel block: a force of 20 N across two gaps of 500 mm² needs $B = \sqrt{20 \mu_0 / (500 \times 10^{-6})} = 0.222$ T; with $\mu_r = 700$ over 0.8 m of steel the m.m.f. is 200 At and a 100-turn coil needs $I = 2.0$ A. Example 30.3 applies the same machinery to a relay: at a 1.5 mm gap the coil gives $B = 84$ mT, $L = 6.56$ H, and the pull is $f_E = \tfrac{1}{2} i^2 \, \mathrm{d}L/\mathrm{d}x = 0.88$ N.

concepts.statement: Taking both electrical and mechanical energies as inputs, the balance between any two states is $$\Delta W_E + \Delta W_M = \Delta W_f + \Delta W_s + \Delta W_1,$$ — field energy, stored mechanical energy and loss. In the idealized machine the balance reduces to $\mathrm{d}W_E + \mathrm{d}W_M = \mathrm{d}W_f$, and for rotation the developed torque is $$M_E = \frac{\mathrm{d}W_f}{\mathrm{d}\lambda}$$ where $\lambda$ is the angle of distortion.
concepts.detail: For the attracted-armature relay the analysis yields $f_E = -\tfrac{1}{2} i^2 \, \mathrm{d}L/\mathrm{d}x$: the mechanical power comes out negative for a motor (an output), and the force acts to reduce the circuit reluctance. The four-phase relay story — current rises, armature moves with rising inductance inducing a back e.m.f., the armature hits its end stop, current settles at a new higher inductance — is the template for every electromechanical transient that follows in this book.

concepts.term: Reluctance motor and the synchronous principle
concepts.statement: A salient rotor in a stator field experiences an alignment torque $M_E = B^2 l r l_g /\mu_0$ that seeks the direct axis. With reluctance varying sinusoidally between $\mathcal{S}_d$ and $\mathcal{S}_q$, the average torque contains a term $$M_{E\,\mathrm{av}} = \tfrac{1}{8} \Phi_{\mathrm{m}}^2 \left( \mathcal{S}_q - \mathcal{S}_d \right) \sin 2\alpha$$ that is non-zero only when the rotor turns at exactly the supply frequency — the machine is of the **synchronous type**: its speed is fixed by the supply frequency.
concepts.detail: This is the singly excited machine: only one winding sets up the field, and the rotor merely tries to align with it. Clock motors are the classic application. The price of the constructional simplicity is a fixed speed and a weak, pulsating torque — which is why most useful machines are doubly excited.

concepts.term: Doubly excited machines and the three families
concepts.statement: Exciting both stator and rotor gives each a well-defined m.m.f. axis, and the torque is created by the axes trying to align; cylindrical rotors become possible because saliency is no longer needed. The three families are: **synchronous machines** (stator AC, rotor DC), **asynchronous (induction) machines** (stator AC, rotor AC), and **commutator machines** (stator DC, rotor DC).
concepts.detail: Synchronous and asynchronous machines usually have cylindrical stators; commutator machines have salient-pole stators; most machines have cylindrical rotors. Cylindrical construction is mechanically ideal for high speed — Hughes notes that 1 kg on the outside of a 1 m rotor at 3000 r/min experiences about 50 kN of centrifugal force, so high-speed rotors are solid forgings with slots, not assemblies of bolted poles.

concepts.statement: The armature is the stationary winding and the field rotates, so for a machine with $p$ pairs of poles running at $n$ revolutions per second the generated frequency is $$f = n p.$$ For 50 Hz: a two-pole machine must run at 3000 r/min, a four-pole at 1500 r/min, and a 375 r/min machine needs 16 poles.
concepts.detail: Why stationary armature? Hughes’s example: a 20 MVA, 11 kV machine would need three slip-rings each carrying 1050 A at 6.35 kV working voltage (plus a fourth for the star point), whereas a rotating field needs only two rings carrying the 375 A, 400 V excitation. The arrangement also permits insulation for up to 33 kV and a higher speed from a given frame size. Salient poles suit large-diameter low-speed machines; the cylindrical (turbo-alternator) rotor gives a better e.m.f. waveform.

concepts.term: Stator windings and the winding e.m.f.
concepts.statement: Three-phase stator windings come in **single-layer** and **double-layer** forms, with slots disposed so that adjacent slots are separated by $180^\circ/(\text{slots per pole})$ electrical degrees. For $Z$ conductors in series per phase and $\Phi$ webers of useful flux per pole, the e.m.f. of a winding concentrated in one slot per pole per phase is $$E = 2.22\, Z f \Phi \ \text{volts per phase}.$$
concepts.detail: Distribution across several slots per pole is universal in practice: it makes the slot insulation manageable, and it smooths the e.m.f. waveform, which would otherwise copy the (non-sinusoidal) flux distribution around the periphery. In Hughes’s four-pole, 24-slot example the spacing between adjacent slots is $180/6 = 30$ electrical degrees, so the yellow-phase start sits four slots (120 electrical degrees) from the red-phase start.

concepts.statement: Three sinusoidal currents displaced by $120^\circ$ in three windings displaced by $120^\circ$ in space produce a resultant flux density that is **constant in magnitude $1.5 B_{\mathrm{m}}$ and rotates at synchronous speed**. At a point $\theta$ electrical radians from the reference axis, $$B_1 + B_2 + B_3 = 1.5 B_{\mathrm{m}} \cos(\omega t - \theta),$$ and the field turns through two pole pitches in one cycle, so $n_1 = f/p$.
concepts.detail: The three snapshots of Hughes’s Fig. 31.10 make it visual: when R is at maximum positive current, Y and B are each at half magnitude negative; a twelfth of a cycle later (R and B at 0.866), the field axis has advanced 30°. Summing the three space-and-time sinusoids collapses to $1.5 B_{\mathrm{m}} \cos(\omega t - \theta)$ — a single sinusoid whose peak rides round the airgap. Reversing any two supply connections reverses the direction of rotation, which is one of the everyday advantages of three-phase motors.

examples.title: Forces and current in a lifting electromagnet (Example 30.1)
examples.problem: A horseshoe electromagnet with a 600 mm core of 500 mm² cross-section holds a steel block; the magnetic circuit through the block is 200 mm long, and both parts have $\mu_r = 700$. A 100-turn coil must develop enough force of alignment that 20 N is needed to free the block. Estimate the coil current.

steps.label: Step 1: Flux density from the force
steps.text: There are two airgaps in series, so the parting force is doubled: $f_M = 2 \times B^2 A / 2\mu_0 = B^2 A/\mu_0 = 20$ N, giving $B = \sqrt{20 \mu_0/(500 \times 10^{-6})} = 0.222$ T.

steps.label: Step 2: Field strength in the steel
Step 3: Total m.m.f. around the circuit
steps.text: The flux path is 600 + 200 = 800 mm of steel: $F = Hl = 250 \times 0.8 = 200$ ampere-turns.

examples.result: A 100-turn coil carrying 2.0 A produces the 0.222 T gap density that holds the block with 20 N — the alignment-force formula working as a design tool.

examples.title: Sizing the slip-rings: why the armature stays still
examples.problem: A 20 MVA, 11 kV three-phase synchronous machine is to be built. Compare the slip-ring requirements of (a) a rotating three-phase armature with stationary poles, and (b) the standard arrangement with stationary armature and rotating field excited at 400 V, 150 kW.

steps.label: Step 1: Line current of the armature
steps.text: From $S = \sqrt{3} I_L V_L$: $I_L = 20 \times 10^{6}/(1.73 \times 11 \times 10^{3}) = 1050$ A.

steps.label: Step 2: What a rotating armature would need
steps.text: Three slip-rings rated 1050 A each, insulated for the phase voltage $11/1.73 = 6.35$ kV — and a fourth ring for the earthed star point.

steps.label: Step 3: The rotating-field alternative
steps.text: The excitation needs only $I = 150\,000/400 = 375$ A at 400 V through two slip-rings.

steps.label: Step 4: The verdict
steps.text: Two rings at 375 A and 400 V beat four rings at 1050 A and 6.35 kV on construction and on slip-ring losses, and the stator gets the room it needs for insulation up to 33 kV.

examples.result: Stationary armature, rotating field: construction considerably simplified. The same arithmetic explains the layout of every large synchronous generator.

examples.title: Synchronous speed of the rotating field
examples.problem: A stator is wound for six poles and fed at 50 Hz; another is fed at 60 Hz and must produce a field rotating at 1800 r/min. Find the synchronous speeds and the required pole counts.

steps.label: Step 1: Six poles at 50 Hz
steps.text: Six poles are $p = 3$ pairs, so $n_1 = f/p = 50/3 = 16.67$ r/s — 1000 r/min.

steps.label: Step 2: The 1800 r/min case
steps.text: Rearranged, $p = f/n_1 = 60/30 = 2$ pairs — a four-pole winding.

steps.label: Step 3: Check the generality
steps.text: The same relation $f = np$ fixes machine speed from frequency: 50 Hz gives 3000 r/min for two poles, 1500 for four, 1000 for six, and 375 r/min demands 16 poles.

examples.result: Field speed and pole count trade off directly: $n_1 = f/p$. This is why slow water-turbine generators are large-diameter many-pole machines and why inverter drives must vary frequency to vary speed.

keyTakeaways: Every rotating machine is an energy balance in action: $\Delta W_E + \Delta W_M = \Delta W_f + \Delta W_s + \Delta W_1$, with the magnetic field as the reversible coupling.
Airgap field energy density $B^2/2\mu_0$ gives the alignment force $F = B^2 A/2\mu_0$; the equivalent inductive statement is $f_E = \tfrac{1}{2} i^2 \mathrm{d}L/\mathrm{d}x$.
Torque is the rate of change of field energy with angle: $M_E = \mathrm{d}W_f/\mathrm{d}\lambda$ — rotate $x$ into $\lambda$ and force into torque.
Reluctance (singly excited) machines are synchronous by nature; their average torque exists only at rotor speed equal to supply frequency.
Doubly excited machines divide into synchronous (AC stator, DC rotor), asynchronous (AC, AC) and commutator (DC, DC) families.
Frequency and speed are locked by $f = np$; the armature is stationary in practice because slip-rings for megavolt-ampere currents would be unmanageable.
Three-phase currents produce a rotating field of constant magnitude $1.5 B_{\mathrm{m}}$ at $n_1 = f/p$; swapping any two phases reverses it.

quiz.q: The force of alignment between two parallel magnetized pole faces of area $A$, gap density $B$, is:
options: $F = B^2 A / 2\mu_0$, attracting the faces together
$F = B A / \mu_0$, repelling the faces apart
$F = 2\mu_0 B^2 A$, independent of the area
$F = B l i$, depending on a winding current
quiz.explanation: Separating the faces by $\mathrm{d}x$ adds gap volume $A\,\mathrm{d}x$ at energy density $B^2/2\mu_0$; the work done against the attraction equals the added stored energy, so $F = B^2 A/2\mu_0$ — a pure attraction.

quiz.q: Which combination identifies the three families of doubly excited rotating machines?
options: Synchronous: AC stator, DC rotor; asynchronous: AC stator, AC rotor; commutator: DC stator, DC rotor
Synchronous: DC stator, AC rotor; asynchronous: AC stator, DC rotor; commutator: AC stator, AC rotor
All three families use DC on both stator and rotor
quiz.explanation: Hughes classifies by the excitation of the two m.m.f. axes. Synchronous machines carry direct current on the rotor; induction machines induce alternating current in the rotor; d.c. machines use direct current on both, with the commutator performing the switching.

quiz.q: A three-phase, 50 Hz stator is wound for eight poles. The speed of the rotating field is:
quiz.explanation: Eight poles are $p = 4$ pairs, so $n_1 = f/p = 50/4 = 12.5$ r/s = 750 r/min. Speed falls linearly with the number of pole pairs at fixed frequency.

quiz.q: The resultant flux of three equal phase m.m.f.s, each producing a peak gap density $B_{\mathrm{m}}$ acting alone, is:
options: A pulsating field of peak $3 B_{\mathrm{m}}$ on the fixed axis of one phase
A rotating field of constant magnitude $1.5 B_{\mathrm{m}}$
A rotating field of constant magnitude $B_{\mathrm{m}}$
Zero, because the three phase fields cancel
quiz.explanation: Summing the three space-and-time sinusoids gives $1.5 B_{\mathrm{m}} \cos(\omega t - \theta)$: the peak stays fixed at 1.5 times one phase maximum and its position rotates through two pole pitches every cycle.

quiz.q: Why does a practical stator winding distribute its conductors over several slots per pole instead of one?
options: To raise the winding resistance and limit fault current
To keep the slot size and insulation thickness manageable and to improve the e.m.f. waveform
Because a single slot cannot hold a full coil side at any voltage
To eliminate the need for laminations
quiz.explanation: A winding concentrated in one slot per pole per phase would overheat its insulation (heat must flow radially outward through many conductors) and would reproduce the non-sinusoidal flux distribution in its e.m.f.; distribution solves both problems at the cost of a small e.m.f. reduction.

intro: Synchronous machines run the power system; induction motors run industry — Hughes remarks that about half of all electric power consumption is due to induction motor loads. This section follows Hughes through armature reaction, synchronous impedance and the 600 MVA generator whose regulation nearly quadruples between unity and 0.8 power factor, then into the induction motor: slip, the transformer-like equivalent circuit, the torque-slip curve, and every practical way of starting a cage rotor that draws four to seven times full-load current if you dare switch it straight onto the line.
objectives: Explain armature reaction and calculate the voltage regulation of a synchronous generator from its synchronous impedance
Define slip and rotor frequency and apply $s = (n_s - n)/n_s$ and $f_r = s f$
Use the induction-motor equivalent circuit to find current, power factor, output power, torque and efficiency
Predict the effect of rotor resistance on the torque-slip curve and the maximum-torque condition
Compare the starting methods for cage motors and the constructions of single-phase motors

concepts.statement: The rotating m.m.f. set up by the stator (armature) currents is the **armature reaction**. At unity power factor it distorts the main flux, skewing it against the direction of rotation so the driving engine must supply more torque; at a current **lagging** the e.m.f. by $90^\circ$ it directly opposes the rotor flux (demagnetizing); at a current **leading** by $90^\circ$ it adds to it (magnetizing).
concepts.detail: The consequences for terminal voltage are immediate: with constant excitation the voltage falls slowly with a unity-power-factor load, much faster at 0.8 lagging (the demagnetizing effect), and actually rises with a capacitive load. This single phenomenon — not winding resistance — dominates the regulation of large alternators, and it is also what lets an over-excited synchronous motor support the voltage of a whole system.

concepts.statement: The armature-reaction e.m.f. lags the current by a quarter cycle and therefore behaves exactly like a reactance — the **synchronous reactance** $X_s$. With the winding resistance $R$, the synchronous impedance per phase is $Z_s = \sqrt{R^2 + X_s^2}$, and $$E^2 = V^2 + (I Z_s)^2 + 2 V \cdot I Z_s \cos(\alpha - \phi),$$ where $E$ is the no-load (open-circuit) e.m.f. and the per-unit regulation is $(E - V)/V$.
concepts.detail: Because $R \ll X_s$ in generator windings, $Z_s \approx X_s$ in rough work. Hughes measures it by the open-circuit/short-circuit ratio: run the generator open-circuit for the e.m.f., then short-circuit through an ammeter at the same excitation — the ratio of phase voltage to short-circuit current is $Z_s$. Saturation and saliency make the numerical value only approximate, but the method survives in practice.

concepts.statement: Two generators paralleled on the same busbars share load according to their **driving torques**: the machine whose rotor falls back by angle $\theta$ receives almost reactive circulating current (since the impedance angle is near $90^\circ$) and is motored by the other. Changing the **excitation** mainly changes the busbar voltage, not the load sharing.
concepts.detail: The circulating current is $I = E_Z / 2 Z_s$ at angle $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(X_s/R)$ to $E_Z$. So the operating rules are: (1) the distribution of kW between generators is set by the engines; (2) the terminal voltage is set by the excitations. Exactly the same mechanics, run in reverse, is the principle of the synchronous motor — the rotor still falls back or advances by a load angle, and power flows whichever way the angle dictates.

concepts.term: The synchronous motor and the synchronous capacitor
concepts.statement: A synchronous motor runs at exactly synchronous speed with its rotor poles locked to the rotating stator field. Its principal advantages are **controllable power factor** — an over-excited machine draws leading current and can correct the lagging current of a whole factory of induction motors — and absolutely constant speed; its disadvantages are higher cost per kW, the need for DC rotor excitation, and starting arrangements.
concepts.detail: Run on no load purely for power-factor correction or line-voltage support, the machine is called a **synchronous capacitor**. The excitation is usually supplied by a small DC shunt generator on an extension of the shaft.

concepts.statement: The rotating stator field induces e.m.f.s in the rotor conductors, whose currents distort the gap flux and drag the rotor around. The rotor can never reach synchronous speed — at synchronism there is no relative motion, no rotor e.m.f., no current and no torque. The **slip** is $$s = \frac{n_s - n}{n_s},$$ and the rotor frequency is $f_r = s f$. Full-load slip is about 6 per cent for small motors and 2 per cent for large ones.
concepts.detail: The cage rotor — uninsulated copper or aluminium bars short-circuited by end rings, cast in one piece below about 50 kW — makes the induction motor the cheapest and most robust machine in existence. Because rotor and stator fields both rotate at synchronous speed relative to the stator ($s n_s + n_r = n_s$), the machine is exactly a transformer with an airgap: magnetizing current (up to 30 per cent of full load) and leakage are correspondingly larger than in a transformer.

concepts.term: Equivalent circuit of the induction motor
concepts.statement: Per phase, the stator contributes $R_1$ and $X_1$; the magnetizing branch $X_m$ with core-loss resistor $R_c$ sits across the airgap; the rotor is a short-circuited secondary with e.m.f. $s E_2$, resistance $R_2$ and reactance $s X_2$. Dividing the rotor loop by $s$ splits the resistance into $R_2$ (rotor copper loss) plus $\left(\frac{1-s}{s}\right) R_2$ — the mechanical output power.
concepts.detail: The rotor current is $I_2 = E_2/\sqrt{(R_2/s)^2 + X_2^2}$, so the rotor power factor $\cos\phi = (R_2/s)/\sqrt{(R_2/s)^2 + X_2^2}$ swings dramatically with slip: in Hughes’s Example 33.2, $\phi = 8^\circ 24^\prime$ at 4 per cent slip but $74^\circ 51^\prime$ at standstill. The final circuit — stator $I^2R$, iron loss, rotor $I^2R$, and the $(1-s)R_2/s$ resistor labelled mechanical power — makes the whole power-flow diagram of the machine read like a circuit analysis.

concepts.term: Torque, mechanical power and the torque-slip curve
concepts.statement: The total three-phase mechanical power is $$P_{\mathrm{m}} = 3\,\frac{1-s}{s}\, R_2^{\prime} \left|I_1\right|^2,$$ and the torque is $M = P_{\mathrm{m}}/\omega_{\mathrm{m}}$. Neglecting the magnetizing current, torque depends on slip as $$M = \frac{K\, s R_2^\prime}{(R_2^\prime)^2 + \left( s X_2^\prime \right)^2}.$$ Maximum torque occurs when $R_2^\prime = s X_2^\prime$, and $M_{\max} = K/2 X_2^\prime$ — **independent of rotor resistance**.
concepts.detail: Increasing rotor resistance therefore pushes the peak of the curve toward higher slip (better starting torque) without changing its height — Hughes illustrates with $X_2^\prime = 8\,\Omega$ and $R_2^\prime$ of 1, 2 and 4 $\Omega$, the last peaking at $s = 0.5$. The named points on the curve: locked-rotor (starting) torque, pull-up torque, pull-out (breakdown) torque, full-load torque. A higher rotor resistance gives higher starting torque but lower running efficiency — the classic design trade.

concepts.statement: Direct-on-line starting draws **four to seven times full-load current**. Reduced-voltage methods: the **star-delta starter** (phase voltage, current and torque each divided by 3 at start); the **auto-transformer starter** (torque and supply current scale with the square of the tapping ratio $n$); and the **solid-state soft starter** (thyristor firing-angle control, jerk-free, current held at a chosen maximum through acceleration).
concepts.detail: A slip-ring rotor attacks the problem at the source: external star-connected resistors in the rotor circuit via the slip-rings, cut out progressively as the motor accelerates, giving maximum torque at standstill if $R_2 = X_2$. The cage rotor answers with cheapness, robustness, slightly better efficiency and power factor, and no sparking (explosion-proof). For braking, reversing two phases makes the slip nearly 2 — plugging — demanding but well tolerated by cage machines.

concepts.statement: A single winding produces **two equal counter-rotating fields**, so the single-phase motor has zero torque at standstill; once moving, the forward-field motor action exceeds the backward braking action and the rotor accelerates. Starting therefore needs a second, phase-shifted winding: **capacitor-run**, **split-phase** (high-resistance auxiliary winding) or **shaded-pole** constructions.
concepts.detail: Split-phase starting torque is about 50 per cent above design load torque; the capacitor-run machine suits fans whose torque rises with speed squared; the shaded-pole motor is the cheapest of all and tops out at small ratings. Most one-phase motors produce outputs up to about 1 kW. Variable-speed operation of three-phase machines — varying the supply frequency so the torque-speed family moves bodily — belongs to the power electronics of the next chapter.

examples.title: Regulation of a 600 MVA generator (Example 32.1)
examples.problem: A three-phase, 600 MVA generator has a rated line voltage of 22 kV; the star-connected stator has $R = 0.014\,\Omega$/phase and synchronous impedance $Z_s = 0.16\,\Omega$/phase. Calculate the voltage regulation at (a) unity and (b) 0.8 lagging power factor.

steps.label: Step 1: Full-load current
steps.text: From $600 \times 10^{6} = 1.73 I_L \times 22 \times 10^{3}$, $I_L = 15.7$ kA, which equals the phase current in star.

steps.label: Step 2: Phase quantities
steps.text: Terminal phase voltage $V = 22\,000/1.73 = 12\,700$ V; synchronous-impedance drop $I Z_s = 15\,700 \times 0.16 = 2540$ V; $\cos\alpha = R/Z_s = 0.014/0.16 = 0.088$.

examples.result: The same 600 MVA machine regulates 3.7 per cent at unity but 14.4 per cent at 0.8 lagging: armature reaction, not resistance, is what alternator regulation is made of.

examples.title: Slip, rotor e.m.f., current and power factor (Examples 33.1 and 33.2)
examples.problem: A four-pole, 50 Hz motor has a delta-connected stator with 240 conductors per phase and a star rotor with 48 conductors per phase; the rotor has $R_2 = 0.013\,\Omega$/ph and standstill leakage reactance $X_2 = 0.048\,\Omega$/ph; the supply is 400 V and the stator impedance is negligible. Find the synchronous speed, the rotor speed at 4 per cent slip, the rotor frequency at 600 r/min, and the rotor e.m.f., current and phase angle at 4 per cent slip.

steps.label: Step 2: Slip quantities
steps.text: At $s = 0.04$ the rotor turns at $1500 (1 - 0.04) = 1440$ r/min. At 600 r/min, $s = (1500 - 600)/1500 = 0.6$ and the rotor frequency is $f_r = s f = 0.6 \times 50 = 30$ Hz.

steps.label: Step 3: Rotor e.m.f. at standstill
steps.text: The turns ratio gives $E_2 = 400 \times 48/240 = 80$ V per phase; at 4 per cent slip the rotor e.m.f. is $s E_2 = 3.2$ V.

steps.label: Step 5: Phase angle
steps.text: $\tan\phi = s X_2/R_2 = 0.00192/0.013 = 0.1477$, so $\phi = 8^\circ 24^\prime$ at 4 per cent slip — but at standstill $\tan\phi = 0.048/0.013 = 3.69$ and $\phi = 74^\circ 51^\prime$.

examples.result: Slip scales everything on the rotor: e.m.f. in proportion, reactance in proportion, and the rotor power factor from near-unity running to a dismal $\cos 74^\circ 51^\prime$ at standstill — the reason starting current is large and starting torque is not.

examples.title: Full performance from the equivalent circuit (Example 33.3)
examples.problem: A 400 V, 33 kW, 60 Hz, three-phase, star-connected, four-pole, 1755 r/min induction motor has per-phase parameters $R_1 = 0.2\,\Omega$, $X_1 = 0.5\,\Omega$, $X_m = 20\,\Omega$, $R_2^\prime = 0.1\,\Omega$, $X_2^\prime = 0.2\,\Omega$, with windage and friction of 650 W and iron loss of 300 W. At full load and rated speed, find the slip, input current and power factor, input power, output torque and efficiency.

steps.label: Step 2: Rotor branch impedance
steps.text: $R_2^\prime/s + j X_2^\prime = (0.1/0.025) + j0.2 = 4 + j0.2\,\Omega$; adding the stator, $Z = 4.2 + j0.7\,\Omega$. Combining with the magnetizing admittance $-j0.05\,\Omega^{-1}$ gives $Z_t = 4.03 \angle 21^\circ\,\Omega$.

steps.label: Step 3: Current and power factor
steps.text: Phase voltage $= 400/\sqrt{3} = 230.9$ V, so $I_1 = 230.9/4.03 = 57.3$ A at $\cos 21^\circ = 0.93$ lagging.

steps.label: Step 4: Power audit
steps.text: Input $P_{\mathrm{in}} = \sqrt{3} \times 400 \times 57.3 \times 0.93 = 36\,918$ W. Stator copper loss $3 \times 57.3^2 \times 0.2 = 1970$ W; iron loss 300 W; airgap power $= 34\,650$ W; rotor copper loss $3 \times 57.3^2 \times 0.1 = 985$ W; windage 650 W. Output $= 36\,918 - 3905 = 33\,010$ W — the nameplate 33 kW.

steps.label: Step 5: Torque and efficiency
steps.text: Rotor speed in rad/s: $\omega_{\mathrm{m}} = 1755 \times 2\pi/60 = 183.78$ rad/s, so $M = 33\,000/183.78 = 179.6$ N m. Efficiency $= 33\,000/36\,918 = 89.4$ per cent.

examples.result: One circuit, the whole machine: 57.3 A at 0.93 lagging in, 33 kW and 179.6 N m out, 89.4 per cent efficient — with every loss located on the diagram (Hughes Example 33.4 runs the same audit on a 415 V motor at 5 per cent slip and finds 80.5 per cent).

keyTakeaways: Armature reaction distorts the flux at unity power factor, demagnetizes at lagging and magnetizes at leading — which is why the synchronous-impedance method lumps it into $X_s$: $E^2 = V^2 + (IZ_s)^2 + 2 V I Z_s \cos(\alpha - \phi)$, with regulation $(E - V)/V$.
In parallel, driving torque shares the kW and excitation sets the busbar voltage; a synchronous machine motoring is simply one whose rotor has fallen back in angle.
An induction motor cannot run at synchronous speed; slip $s = (n_s - n)/n_s$ scales the rotor e.m.f., the rotor reactance and the rotor frequency ($f_r = s f$).
The $(1-s)R_2/s$ resistor in the equivalent circuit is the mechanical output; rotor copper loss is $s$ times the airgap power — which is why high-slip running is hot running.
Maximum torque $M_{\max} = K/2X_2^\prime$ is independent of rotor resistance; rotor resistance only chooses the slip at which it occurs ($R_2^\prime = s X_2^\prime$).
Star-delta divides starting current and torque by three, an auto-transformer by $n^2$; slip-ring rotors buy starting torque with external resistance; soft starters ramp the firing angle.
A single-phase motor is two counter-rotating machines superposed; it needs a capacitor, split-phase or shaded-pole auxiliary to break the symmetry and start.

quiz.q: A generator delivers rated current at 0.8 power factor lagging instead of unity. Its voltage regulation will:
options: Stay roughly the same, since the current magnitude is unchanged
Increase sharply, because the lagging armature reaction demagnetizes the machine
Become negative, because the terminal voltage rises
Depend only on the winding resistance
quiz.explanation: In Hughes’s 600 MVA example the same full-load current gives 3.7 per cent regulation at unity power factor but 14.4 per cent at 0.8 lagging: the quadrature armature reaction directly opposes the rotor flux.

quiz.q: An induction motor with a 4-pole, 50 Hz stator runs at 1440 r/min. The slip and rotor frequency are:
quiz.explanation: Synchronous speed is $1500$ r/min, so $s = (1500 - 1440)/1500 = 0.04$; the rotor conductors see the field slipping by 60 r/min, giving $f_r = s f = 0.04 \times 50 = 2$ Hz.

quiz.q: In the final per-phase equivalent circuit, what does the resistance $\left(\frac{1-s}{s}\right) R_2^\prime$ represent?
options: The mechanical power developed by the machine
