quiz.explanation: Among all bases $a > 0$, exactly one gives tangent slope exactly 1 at the point $(0, 1)$; that base is $e \approx 2.71828$, the natural base whose derivative will be itself.

depth.title: Inverses, honestly: existence, slopes, mirror symmetry

blocks.heading: Inverses of monotone continuous functions
blocks.body: Let $f$ be continuous and strictly increasing on an interval $I$; the strictly decreasing case is analogous. Then the image $f(I)$ is an interval, the map $f : I \to f(I)$ is a bijection, and the inverse $f^{-1} : f(I) \to I$ exists, is strictly increasing, and is continuous. In particular, every strictly monotone continuous function on an interval is invertible on its range — the Horizontal Line Test becomes a theorem rather than an inspection.

Injectivity is immediate from strict monotonicity. That $f(I)$ is an interval needs the supremum argument: let $y$ lie strictly between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ with $a < b$, and say $f(a) < y < f(b)$. The set $S = \{x \in [a, b] : f(x) \le y\}$ contains $a$ and is bounded, so $c = \sup S$ exists. If $f(c) < y$, continuity keeps $f$ below $y$ on a neighborhood of $c$, and since $f(b) > y$ we have $c < b$, so points just right of $c$ still belong to $S$ — contradicting that $c$ is an upper bound. If $f(c) > y$, continuity keeps $f$ above $y$ near $c$, and then some $c - \delta$ is an upper bound of $S$ — contradicting that $c$ is the least upper bound. Hence $f(c) = y$, so every intermediate value is attained. Monotonicity of $f^{-1}$ is forced, and continuity of $f^{-1}$ follows by order: for $y_0 = f(x_0)$ with $x_0$ interior and $\varepsilon > 0$ small, the values $y_\pm = f(x_0 \pm \varepsilon)$ bracket $y_0$, and every $y$ with $y_- < y < y_+$ satisfies $x_0 - \varepsilon < f^{-1}(y) < x_0 + \varepsilon$ by monotonicity — continuity with $\delta = \min(y_0 - y_-,\, y_+ - y_0)$.

blocks.heading: The slope of an inverse
blocks.body: Assume in addition that $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$ with $f'(x_0) \ne 0$, and that $f^{-1}$ is differentiable at $y_0 = f(x_0)$ — the theorem guarantees existence and continuity, never differentiability. Differentiate the cancellation equation $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$ with the Chain Rule: $$1 = \frac{d}{dx} f^{-1}(f(x)) \Big|_{x_0} = (f^{-1})'(y_0)\cdot f'(x_0), \qquad \text{hence} \qquad (f^{-1})'(y_0) = \frac{1}{f'(x_0)} = \frac{1}{f'\big(f^{-1}(y_0)\big)}.$$ Read aloud: the slope of the inverse at the reflected point is the reciprocal of the slope. Sanity check with $f(x) = x^2$ on $x \ge 0$: the inverse is $\sqrt{y}$, and the formula gives slope $\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}$ at $y = x^2$, matching the direct computation $\tfrac{d}{dy}\sqrt{y} = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}$. The steep part of $f$ becomes the flat part of $f^{-1}$, and where $f'(x_0) = 0$ the formula blows up — visible as the vertical tangent of $\sqrt{y}$ at $y = 0$.

The graphical rule — reflect the graph in the line $y = x$ — is a theorem about swapping coordinates, not folklore. The graph of $f^{-1}$ is exactly the set $\{(y, x) : (x, y) \text{ lies on the graph of } f\}$, by the defining equivalence $f^{-1}(y) = x \iff f(x) = y$. The map $R(x, y) = (y, x)$ is a linear involution, $R^2 = \mathrm{id}$, whose fixed points form the line $y = x$; a distance-preserving involution with a line of fixed points is the reflection in that line, so graphs of inverse pairs are mirror images. Two by-products: reflection swaps the Vertical and Horizontal Line Tests — invertibility is vertical-line-tested on the reflected graph — and reflection across $y = x$ preserves “uphill,” which is why $f$ and $f^{-1}$ share the direction of their monotonicity.

blocks.heading: arcsin, built from a bare restriction
blocks.body: Sine is not one-to-one on $\mathbb{R}$, but its restriction to $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ is: there $\sin$ is strictly increasing, running from $-1$ to $1$, so it is a bijection $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \to [-1, 1]$, and the theorem guarantees that the inverse — call it $\arcsin$ — exists, is increasing, and is continuous. The cancellation equations hold **with range clauses**: $\sin(\arcsin x) = x$ for every $x \in [-1, 1]$, but $\arcsin(\sin\theta) = \theta$ only for $\theta \in \left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ — which is exactly why $\arcsin\left(\sin\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\right) = -\tfrac{\pi}{4}$: the angle must first be folded back onto the restricted branch. The slope formula gives $(\arcsin x)' = \tfrac{1}{\cos(\arcsin x)} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$, and the **positive** root is forced because cosine is nonnegative precisely on the chosen branch — the restriction is still doing work, one layer up.

The natural logarithm is an integral wearing an inverse-function costume. Define, for $x > 0$, $$L(x) = \int_1^x \frac{dt}{t}$$ — no exponential is needed to state it. A substitution proves the logarithm’s defining law, $L(xy) = L(x) + L(y)$: since $$L(xy) - L(y) = \int_y^{xy} \frac{dt}{t} = \int_1^{x} \frac{y\,du}{yu} = L(x)$$ using $t = yu$, products of inputs become sums of values, which is the exponential law read backwards. Because the integrand is positive, $L$ is strictly increasing; the functional equation forces $L(1) = 0$ and pushes $L(x) \to \infty$ as $x \to \infty$ and $L(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to 0^+$, so $L$ maps $(0, \infty)$ onto $\mathbb{R}$; by the theorem of this tier $L$ has an inverse, and that inverse is **defined** to be the exponential, with $e$ the number satisfying $L(e) = 1$. This is exactly how Stewart’s own starred treatment proceeds late in the book: the logarithm is built by an integral, and the exponential is recovered as its inverse — the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, waiting to happen.

depth.title: Fractional calculus: derivatives of order half

blocks.body: The inverse theme of this section has a spectacular generalization. Integration is an operator, $(If)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$, and the Fundamental Theorem says $D \circ I = \mathrm{id}$ on nice functions — differentiation is a left inverse of integration. Iterating, $I^2 f(x) = \int_0^x \int_0^u f(t)\,dt\,du$, and swapping the order of integration over the triangle $0 \le t \le u \le x$ collapses it: $I^2 f(x) = \int_0^x (x - t)\,f(t)\,dt$. The pattern continues to $I^n f(x) = \frac{1}{(n-1)!}\int_0^x (x - t)^{n-1} f(t)\,dt$, and Cauchy noticed that the formula survives non-integer $n$ once factorials are replaced by the Gamma function $\Gamma(\alpha)$, with $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!$. The **Riemann–Liouville fractional integral** is born: $I^\alpha f(x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^x (x - t)^{\alpha - 1} f(t)\,dt$ for any $\alpha > 0$, and one verifies the semigroup law $I^\alpha I^\beta = I^{\alpha + \beta}$ — the honest reason this deserves to be called a fraction of an operator.

blocks.heading: A half-derivative, computed
blocks.body: Take the constant function $1$ and $\alpha = \tfrac{1}{2}$. Using $\Gamma\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \sqrt{\pi}$: $$I^{1/2}[1](x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_0^x \frac{dt}{\sqrt{x - t}} = \frac{2\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{\pi}}.$$ To differentiate half as much as one integrates, define $D^{1/2} = \frac{d}{dx} \circ I^{1/2}$, and then $$D^{1/2}[1](x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi x}}.$$ The half-derivative of a constant is **not zero** — fractional operators remember the lower limit $x = 0$ forever, because $I^{1/2}$ averages the whole history of $f$ on $[0, x]$. Checking the monomial $f(x) = x$: $I^{1/2}[x](x) = \frac{4x^{3/2}}{3\sqrt{\pi}}$, and running $D^{1/2}$ on that half-integral returns $\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^2/2\right) = x$, confirming that half and half make a whole.

blocks.heading: Materials with memory
blocks.body: Why would anyone want a derivative of order one-half? Because nature is full of processes caught halfway between storing and dissipating. A perfectly elastic spring obeys $\sigma(t) = E\,\varepsilon(t)$ — stress proportional to strain, a law of order zero; a viscous dashpot obeys $\sigma(t) = \eta\,\frac{d\varepsilon}{dt}$, a law of order one. Real materials — polymers, biological tissue, dampers, electrodes — sit in between: **viscoelasticity** is modeled by constitutive laws of order $\alpha$ with $0 < \alpha < 1$, the exponent a measured material constant. In control engineering, the fractional PID controller adds a tunable integration order $\alpha$ between the classical I and D and outperforms standard PID on plants with long memory. Electrochemistry’s Warburg impedance — the response of a diffusion-limited electrode — carries a characteristic $\sqrt{\omega}$ signature in frequency, the fingerprint of a half-order derivative in the frequency domain.

blocks.heading: Which fractional derivative is real?
blocks.body: There is no single fractional calculus. Riemann–Liouville, Caputo, Grünwald–Letnikov, Hadamard, Riesz — the definitions disagree about constants and initial conditions (the Riemann–Liouville derivative of a constant is nonzero; the Caputo derivative of a constant is zero), and the disagreement changes what an initial-value problem even means: Riemann–Liouville demands fractional-order initial data, while Caputo accepts classical values like $f(0)$ and $f'(0)$. Even the semigroup law is fragile — $D^\alpha D^\beta = D^{\alpha + \beta}$ can pick up boundary terms when $\alpha + \beta$ crosses an integer. Which operator deserves to be **the** derivative of order one-half, and whether some canonical calculus interpolates the integer orders while keeping the semigroup law, a sensible product rule, and physically meaningful initial data, remains genuinely open — rival theories compete on numerical and physical evidence, not on proof.

intro: Many important operations — taking roots, taking logarithms, converting temperatures, decrypting messages — are reversals of other operations, and their mathematical home is the inverse function. Section 1.5 characterizes exactly which functions can be reversed (the one-to-one ones), gives the four-step recipe for finding inverses, and derives the logarithm as the inverse of the exponential. The section ends with the inverse trigonometric functions and the change-of-base formula, completing the catalog of transcendental functions the rest of the book differentiates.
objectives: Test whether a function is one-to-one using the Horizontal Line Test and monotonicity
Find the inverse of a one-to-one function by the four-step procedure and verify it with the cancellation equations
Explain the geometric relationship between the graphs of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ (reflection about $y = x$)
Define logarithms, apply their laws, and convert bases with the change-of-base formula
Use the natural exponential and natural logarithm as the canonical inverse pair, and state the domains and ranges of $\arcsin$, $\arccos$ and $\arctan$

concepts.term: One-to-one functions and the Horizontal Line Test
concepts.statement: A function is **one-to-one** if it never takes the same value twice: $x_1 \ne x_2$ implies $f(x_1) \ne f(x_2)$. Graphically, no horizontal line intersects the graph more than once — the **Horizontal Line Test**.
concepts.detail: Only one-to-one functions are reversible, because an inverse must route each output back to a single input. The solution manual’s examples: the line $f(x) = 2x - 3$ is one-to-one (distinct inputs give distinct outputs), while $f(x) = x^4 - 16$ is not ($f(-1) = f(1) = -15$); $r(t) = t^3 + 4$ is one-to-one, and so is $g(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}$. A shortcut: any function **increasing** (or decreasing) on its whole domain is automatically one-to-one — the manual proves $t^3 + 4$ this way. This is why $x^2$ becomes invertible after restricting its domain to $x \ge 0$.

concepts.statement: If $f$ is one-to-one with domain $A$ and range $B$, its **inverse function** $f^{-1}$ has domain $B$ and range $A$ and is defined by $$f^{-1}(y) = x \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad f(x) = y.$$ The inverse routes each output of $f$ back to the unique input that produced it.
concepts.detail: The inverse swaps the roles of input and output — whatever $f$ does, $f^{-1}$ undoes. Domains swap with ranges: the domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$ and the range of $f^{-1}$ is the domain of $f$. Caution: $f^{-1}$ is a statement about reversing, **not** the reciprocal $1/f(x)$ — the notation is unlucky but standard. The manual’s compact reading: $f^{-1}(y) = x \iff f(x) = y$ for $y$ in $B$.

concepts.statement: For $x$ in the domain of $f$ and $y$ in the domain of $f^{-1}$: $$f^{-1}(f(x)) = x \qquad \text{and} \qquad f(f^{-1}(y)) = y.$$ Each function undoes the other, in either order.
concepts.detail: These two identities are both the definition-check and the sanity-check for inverses. Example from the manual: given a one-to-one $f$ with $f^{-1}(3) = 2$, we immediately have $f(2) = 3$; and knowing $f(1) = 3$ for an increasing $f$ gives $f^{-1}(3) = 1$, after which $f(f^{-1}(2)) = 2$ holds automatically. The cancellation equations are what make inverse pairs like $e^x$ and $\ln x$ so useful in solving equations.

concepts.term: How to find an inverse: the four steps
concepts.statement: To find $f^{-1}$: (1) write $y = f(x)$; (2) solve this equation for $x$ in terms of $y$; (3) interchange $x$ and $y$; (4) the result is $y = f^{-1}(x)$, with domain equal to the range of $f$. Graphically, the graph of $f^{-1}$ is the **reflection** of the graph of $f$ about the line $y = x$.
concepts.detail: Solving for $x$ is the hard step and is exactly where domain restrictions earn their keep: for $f(x) = 1 - x^2$ with $x \ge 0$, the equation $y = 1 - x^2$ gives $x = \sqrt{1 - y}$ (choosing the nonnegative root because the original domain was $x \ge 0$), so $f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{1 - x}$. Reflection about $y = x$ is why the graph of $\arcsin$ is the mirror image of the sine curve on its restricted domain — the manual draws exactly this.

concepts.statement: The **logarithmic function** with base $b$ ($b > 0$, $b \ne 1$) is the inverse of $b^x$: $$\log_b x = y \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad b^y = x.$$ Its domain is $(0, \infty)$, its range is $\mathbb{R}$, and its graph passes through $(1, 0)$.
concepts.detail: The logarithm answers the question “$b$ raised to **what** gives $x$?” — it is the exponent-finder for base $b$. Because it inverts an increasing function, $\log_b$ is increasing for $b > 1$; its graph is the reflection of $y = b^x$ about $y = x$, with a vertical asymptote at $x = 0$. Only positive inputs are allowed: no real power of a positive base is negative or zero.

concepts.statement: For positive $x$ and $y$: $$\log_b (xy) = \log_b x + \log_b y, \qquad \log_b \frac{x}{y} = \log_b x - \log_b y, \qquad \log_b \left(x^r\right) = r \log_b x.$$
concepts.detail: Each law is the exponential law $b^{x + y} = b^x b^y$ read through the inverse: because logarithms ARE exponents, products of inputs become sums of logs. The classic warning: there is **no** law for $\log_b(x + y)$, and $\log_b x + \log_b y \ne \log_b(x + y)$ — conflating these is the most common algebra error in the course. The power law $\log_b(x^r) = r \log_b x$ is the workhorse for solving exponential equations.

concepts.term: Natural logarithm and change of base
concepts.statement: The **natural logarithm** is $\ln x = \log_e x$, the inverse of $e^x$. Any logarithm converts to natural logs: $$\log_b x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b}.$$
concepts.detail: Since $e$ is the base of calculus (Section 1.4), $\ln$ is the logarithm of calculus. The change-of-base formula lets a calculator with only $\ln$ (or $\log_{10}$) evaluate any $\log_b$: the solution manual uses it to solve the doubling-time problem $n = 100 \cdot 2^{t/3}$ by writing $t = 3 \log_2(n/100) = 3\, \frac{\ln(n/100)}{\ln 2}$.

concepts.statement: $y = e^x$ (domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $(0, \infty)$) and $y = \ln x$ (domain $(0, \infty)$, range $\mathbb{R}$) are inverses: $$\ln(e^x) = x \ \text{ for all } x, \qquad e^{\ln x} = x \ \text{ for } x > 0,$$ and their graphs are reflections about $y = x$.
concepts.detail: This is the cancellation equations incarnate, and the reason “$e$ to the” and “el-en” cancel in equations: $e^{1 - x} = 7$ becomes $1 - x = \ln 7$ so $x = 1 - \ln 7 \approx -0.95$ (the manual’s Exercise 27), and $3 \ln(x - 2) = y$ becomes $x = 2 + e^{y/3}$ (its Exercise 28). Derivative-wise this pair is perfect: the slope of $\ln x$ at $x = e^a$ is $e^{-a}$ — the mirror of $e^x$’s slope — making $\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}$ in Section 3.6.

concepts.statement: Restricting sine to $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$ makes it one-to-one, and its inverse is $y = \arcsin x = \sin^{-1} x$ with domain $[-1, 1]$ and range $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$. Similarly $\arccos$ has range $[0, \pi]$ and $\arctan$ has domain $\mathbb{R}$ and range $(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2})$.
concepts.detail: The trig functions are periodic, hence wildly non-one-to-one; restricting to a monotone branch fixes this — the same trick as restricting $x^2$ to $x \ge 0$. The solution manual’s evaluations set the standard: $\arcsin(0.5) = \tfrac{\pi}{6}$ because $\sin \tfrac{\pi}{6} = 0.5$ **and** $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ lies in the range $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$; likewise $\arcsin(-\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) = -\tfrac{\pi}{4}$. The range clause is essential: $\arcsin(\sin \tfrac{5\pi}{4}) = -\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, not $\tfrac{5\pi}{4}$.

examples.title: Finding an inverse with a domain restriction (Exercise 23 style)
examples.problem: Find the inverse of $f(x) = 1 - x^2$ on the restricted domain $x \ge 0$, and verify with the cancellation equations.

steps.label: Step 1: Confirm one-to-one
steps.text: On $x \ge 0$ the function is decreasing (as $x$ grows, $-x^2$ falls), so $f$ is one-to-one and the inverse exists. The range is $(-\infty, 1]$ — outputs never exceed 1.

steps.label: Step 2: Write and solve for $x$
steps.text: Set $y = 1 - x^2$ with $x \ge 0$. Then $x^2 = 1 - y$, and because $x \ge 0$ we must take the nonnegative root: $x = \sqrt{1 - y}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Interchange variables
steps.text: Swap names: $y = \sqrt{1 - x}$, so the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{1 - x}$ with domain $x \le 1$ — exactly the range of $f$.

examples.result: $f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{1 - x}$ on $(-\infty, 1]$. The restriction $x \ge 0$ chose the square-root branch; without it the parabola fails the Horizontal Line Test and has no inverse at all.

examples.title: Working the $e^x$ / $\ln x$ pair (Exercises 27–28 style)
examples.problem: Solve each equation for $x$: (a) $e^{1 - x} = 7$; (b) $3 \ln(x - 2) = 6$. Then evaluate $\ln(e^3)$ and $e^{\ln 4}$.

steps.label: Step 1: Kill the exponential with $\ln$
steps.text: (a) Apply $\ln$ to both sides: $\ln(e^{1 - x}) = \ln 7$. The cancellation equation $\ln(e^u) = u$ collapses the left side to $1 - x = \ln 7$.

steps.label: Step 3: Kill the logarithm with $e^x$
steps.text: (b) Divide by 3: $\ln(x - 2) = 2$. Exponentiate: $e^{\ln(x - 2)} = e^2$, and the cancellation $e^{\ln u} = u$ gives $x - 2 = e^2$, so $x = 2 + e^2 \approx 9.39$.

steps.label: Step 4: Evaluate the pure cancellations
steps.text: $\ln(e^3) = 3$ (the exponent-finder question: $e$ to what power gives $e^3$?) and $e^{\ln 4} = 4$. In both directions the pair is transparent.

examples.result: (a) $x = 1 - \ln 7 \approx -0.95$; (b) $x = 2 + e^2 \approx 9.39$; and $\ln(e^3) = 3$, $e^{\ln 4} = 4$. The exponential and logarithm are the same operation read in opposite directions.

examples.title: Doubling time and change of base (Exercise 67 style)
examples.problem: A bacteria count follows $n(t) = 100 \cdot 2^{t/3}$, with $t$ in hours. Express $t$ as a function of $n$, and find when the count reaches 50,000.

steps.label: Step 1: Isolate the exponential
steps.text: From $n = 100 \cdot 2^{t/3}$ divide by 100: $\frac{n}{100} = 2^{t/3}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Take $\log_2$ of both sides
steps.text: The definition of the logarithm converts the exponential statement: $\log_2\!\left(\frac{n}{100}\right) = \frac{t}{3}$, so $t = 3 \log_2\!\left(\frac{n}{100}\right)$.

steps.label: Step 3: Change the base to compute
steps.text: For a calculator with only natural logs, use change of base: $t = 3 \cdot \frac{\ln(n/100)}{\ln 2}$ — the manual’s exact move.

steps.label: Step 4: Insert the target
steps.text: At $n = 50{,}000$: $t = 3 \log_2(500) = 3 \cdot \frac{\ln 500}{\ln 2} \approx 3 \cdot \frac{6.215}{0.693} \approx 3 \cdot 8.966 \approx 26.9$ hours.

examples.result: $t(n) = 3 \log_2(n/100) = \frac{3 \ln(n/100)}{\ln 2}$; the culture reaches 50,000 at about $t \approx 26.9$ hours. Logarithms turn “when?” questions about exponential growth into single subtractions of logs.

keyTakeaways: Only one-to-one functions have inverses; test with the Horizontal Line Test or by monotonicity (increasing or decreasing on the domain suffices).
The inverse satisfies $f^{-1}(y) = x \iff f(x) = y$, and swaps domain with range: $D_{f^{-1}} = R_f$.
The cancellation equations $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$ and $f(f^{-1}(y)) = y$ are the definition-check and the equation-solving tool.
To find an inverse: write $y = f(x)$, solve for $x$, interchange the variables — the domain restriction chooses the branch when solving.
The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ about the line $y = x$.
$\log_b x = y \iff b^y = x$; the laws of logs mirror the laws of exponents (products become sums), and $\log_b x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b}$ converts any base.

$e^x$ and $\ln x$ are the canonical inverse pair; $\arcsin$, $\arccos$ and $\arctan$ invert restricted trig branches with domains $[-1, 1]$, $[-1, 1]$ and $\mathbb{R}$, and ranges $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$, $[0, \pi]$ and $(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2})$.

quiz.q: Why does $f(x) = x^4 - 16$ fail to have an inverse on $\mathbb{R}$?
options: It fails the Vertical Line Test
quiz.explanation: The function is even, so distinct inputs share outputs and no horizontal line test passes — the solution manual’s own example. Restricting to $x \ge 0$ restores invertibility.

quiz.q: A one-to-one function satisfies $f(6) = 17$. What is $f^{-1}(17)$?
options: It cannot be determined from the information given
quiz.explanation: The definition $f^{-1}(y) = x \iff f(x) = y$ runs the arrow backward: since $f(6) = 17$, the inverse sends 17 back to 6. Note this is function reversal, not the reciprocal $1/17$.

quiz.q: Which equation is the correct “cancellation” for the natural exponential pair?
quiz.explanation: The exponential undoes the logarithm on the logarithm’s domain: $e^{\ln x} = x$ for $x > 0$. Symmetrically $\ln(e^x) = x$ for every real $x$.

quiz.q: Simplify $\log_b (x^2 y^3)$ for positive $x$ and $y$.
quiz.explanation: Products inside a log become sums of logs, and exponents come out in front: $\log_b(x^2) + \log_b(y^3) = 2\log_b x + 3\log_b y$.

quiz.q: Evaluate $\arcsin(0.5)$, respecting the range of the inverse sine.
quiz.explanation: $\sin(\tfrac{\pi}{6}) = 0.5$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ lies in the range $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$ — both conditions are required, which is why $\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$ (also with sine 0.5) is rejected.

quiz.q: If $f(x) = 3x - 7$, then $f^{-1}(5)$ equals:
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate the inverse value as the unique $x$ with $f(x) = 5$. Step 2: Recall the key definition $f^{-1}(y) = x \iff f(x) = y$. Step 3: Set $3x - 7 = 5$ to get $3x = 12$. Step 4: Divide to obtain $x = 4$. Step 5: The distractors fail since $8$ adds instead of solving, $\frac{22}{3}$ mis-reads the equation as $3 \times 5 - 7$ over a wrong denominator, and $-4$ flips a sign. Step 6: Hence $f^{-1}(5) = 4$.

quiz.q: Solve $\log_{2} x + \log_{2}(x-2) = 3$ for $x$.
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate the domain first as $x > 0$ and $x - 2 > 0$, so $x > 2$. Step 2: Recall the key law $\log_{2} x + \log_{2}(x-2) = \log_{2}(x(x-2))$. Step 3: Convert to exponential form $x(x-2) = 2^{3} = 8$. Step 4: Solve $x^{2} - 2x - 8 = 0$ to get $(x-4)(x+2) = 0$, so $x = 4$ or $x = -2$. Step 5: Discard $x = -2$ since it violates $x > 2$, and reject $x = 2$ and $x = 8$ which do not satisfy the original equation. Step 6: Therefore the admissible solution is $x = 4$.

prerequisites: Algebraic functions and Cartesian coordinate geometry: points $(x, f(x))$ and curve graphs
Slope of a secant line through two points: $m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$
Polynomial expansion, binomial identities, and factoring of rational expressions
intro: Chapter 2 opens with two ancient problems that elementary algebra cannot solve: finding the tangent line to a curve at a point, and finding the instantaneous velocity of a moving object. Both are answered the same way — compute an easy average quantity over a shrinking window and watch where it settles. That settling behavior is the limit, and this section builds the intuition before the formal definition arrives in Section 2.4.
objectives: Compute slopes of secant lines through a fixed point $P$ and nearby points $Q$
Interpret average velocity as the slope of a secant line of the position curve
Estimate instantaneous velocity and tangent slope from tables of secant values
Set up and simplify the $h$-form difference quotient for a position function

concepts.statement: The **tangent line** to a curve at a point $P$ is the limit of secant lines through $P$ and nearby points $Q$: as $Q$ slides toward $P$ along the curve, the secant lines turn and settle onto the tangent.
concepts.detail: Euclid’s circles have tangents from classical geometry, but an arbitrary curve has no obvious tangent construction. The insight — due to Fermat and systematized by Newton and Leibniz — is to define the tangent slope as a limit of secant slopes rather than construct it directly. Zooming into a smooth curve, it looks more and more like its tangent line — the property of **local linearity** that makes derivatives useful for approximation (Section 3.10).

concepts.statement: For a point $P(a, f(a))$ and a nearby point $Q(x, f(x))$ on the graph, the slope of the **secant line** $PQ$ is $$m_{PQ} = \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}.$$ It is the average rate of change of $f$ between $a$ and $x$.
concepts.detail: The formula is just “rise over run,” but writing it as $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ reveals its role: the change in output divided by the change in input over a window. The solution manual computes such slopes directly from data points — for instance secant slopes near a point $P(15, 250)$ equal to $-44.4$, $-38.8$, $-27.8$, $-22.2$ and $-16.6$, homing in on the tangent slope.

concepts.statement: If $s(t)$ is a **position function**, the average velocity over the time interval $[a, a + h]$ is $$\frac{\text{displacement}}{\text{elapsed time}} = \frac{s(a + h) - s(a)}{h}.$$
concepts.detail: This is the same difference quotient with time as the input: the slope of the secant line of the position curve. The manual’s falling-object example makes the algebra explicit: for $y = 275 - 16t^2$ at $t = 4$, the average velocity over the next $h$ seconds simplifies to $\frac{-128h - 16h^2}{h} = -128 - 16h$ for $h \ne 0$ — a linear function of the window width.

concepts.statement: The **instantaneous velocity** at time $a$ is the value the average velocities approach as the time interval $h$ shrinks to 0: $$v(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{s(a + h) - s(a)}{h}.$$
concepts.detail: No division by zero ever occurs — we observe averages over shorter and shorter windows and identify the trend. In the falling-object example the averages $-129.6$, $-128.8$ and $-128.16$ ft/s (for $h = 0.1$, $0.05$, $0.01$) squeeze down on $-128$ ft/s, which is the instantaneous velocity. The velocity is negative because height is decreasing.

concepts.statement: Writing the second point as $x = a + h$ turns the secant slope into $$m = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h},$$ the form used throughout the rest of the book.
concepts.detail: The two forms are interchangeable — $x = a + h$ with $x \to a$ is the same limit as $h \to 0$ — but the $h$-form is the one that generalizes cleanly to the derivative of a function in Section 2.7. The solution manual works the same tangent problem both ways: with $f(x) = x^2 + 3x$ at $P(-1, -2)$, the $x$-form factors as $\frac{(x + 2)(x + 1)}{x + 1}$, while the $h$-form factors as $\frac{h(h + 1)}{h}$ — both collapse to $h + 1 \to 1$.

concepts.statement: To estimate a tangent slope or instantaneous velocity: compute the secant quantity for points approaching $P$ from **both sides**, and watch for a common settling value; averaging the two nearest secant slopes from either side is a quick graphical estimate.
concepts.detail: The manual does exactly this with a walking-pace example: secant slopes of $106.3$ steps/min just before $t = 20$ and $91.4$ just after average to about $98.85$, and a graph confirms the tangent slope there. Symmetric averaging cancels the curvature error to first order — the idea behind the symmetric difference quotient that calculators use.

figures.caption: Secant lines through $Q_1$, $Q_2$, $Q_3$ swing onto the tangent at $P$ as $Q$ slides toward $P$ along the curve. Each secant slope $\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}$ is an average rate of change over a window of width $h = x - a$; the tangent slope is its limit as $h \to 0$ — here the slopes run $0.6 \to 0.5 \to 0.45 \to 0.4$.

derivations.title: Instantaneous Tangent Slope from the Difference Quotient
derivations.statement: For the parabolic curve $f(x) = x^2$, the slope of the tangent line at any point $x$ is given by the derivative limit: $$ f\prime(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} = 2x $$
prerequisites: Difference quotient definition of secant slope $m_{\text{sec}} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$
Binomial expansion of $(x + h)^2 = x^2 + 2xh + h^2$
Algebraic limit cancellation of indeterminate forms $\left[\frac{0}{0}\right]$

steps.label: Step 1: Difference quotient setup across window h
steps.explanation: We select a fixed anchor point $P(x, x^2)$ on the parabola and a variable secondary point $Q(x + h, (x + h)^2)$ separated by a horizontal displacement $h \ne 0$. The slope of the straight secant line passing through $P$ and $Q$ is the ratio of vertical rise to horizontal run.

steps.label: Step 2: Binomial expansion of the numerator
steps.explanation: Expanding $(x + h)^2$ yields three terms: the original squared term $x^2$, the linear cross-term $2xh$, and the second-order perturbation $h^2$. Subtracting $f(x) = x^2$ cancels the leading term completely, leaving only terms possessing at least one factor of $h$.

steps.label: Step 3: Factoring and cancelling the zero-divisor factor h
steps.explanation: Directly substituting $h = 0$ into the original quotient would produce the undefined arithmetic form $0/0$. However, because secant slopes are evaluated for $Q \ne P$ where $h \ne 0$, dividing through by $h$ is mathematically rigorous, simplifying the difference quotient to the affine linear function $2x + h$.

steps.label: Step 4: Evaluating the limit as window width h shrinks to zero
steps.explanation: As $Q$ slides continuously along the parabola toward $P$, the increment $h$ approaches 0. The second-order term $h$ vanishes, leaving the exact invariant value $2x$.

derivations.result: The tangent slope at any point $(x, x^2)$ on the parabola is identically $2x$. For instance, at $x = 1$, the tangent line has slope $m = 2$; at $x = 3$, $m = 6$; and at the vertex $x = 0$, $m = 0$ (a horizontal tangent). This fundamental derivation overcomes the paradox of instantaneous rate of change that baffled ancient mathematicians, demonstrating that a limit of valid finite averages $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ yields the exact instantaneous velocity.

examples.title: Secant slopes converging to a tangent (Exercise 3 style)
examples.problem: The curve $y = \frac{1}{1 - x}$ passes through $P(2, -1)$. Compute the slopes of secant lines through $P$ and $Q$ for $x = 1.5$, $1.9$, $1.99$ and $2.5$, guess the tangent slope, and write the tangent line.

steps.label: Step 1: Tabulate the nearby points
steps.text: Each $x$ gives $Q\left(x, \frac{1}{1 - x}\right)$: at $x = 1.5$ the point is $(1.5, -2)$; at $x = 1.9$ it is $(1.9, -1.111)$; at $x = 1.99$ it is $(1.99, -1.010)$.

steps.label: Step 3: Guess the tangent slope
steps.text: As $Q$ approaches $P$ from the left the secant slopes run $2 \to 1.111 \to 1.010$, and from the right $0.667 \to$ (values approaching 1). Both sides settle at slope $1$.

steps.label: Step 4: Write the tangent line
steps.text: Through $P(2, -1)$ with slope 1: $y - (-1) = 1(x - 2)$, that is $y = x - 3$.

examples.result: Secant slopes from both sides converge to 1, so the tangent line is $y = x - 3$. The tangent is defined as the limit of the secants, not by any single secant.

examples.title: Falling object: average to instantaneous velocity (Exercise 5 style)
examples.problem: An object falls from height $y = 275 - 16t^2$ feet, $t$ seconds after release. Find the average velocity over $[4, 4 + h]$ for $h = 0.1$, $0.05$, $0.01$, and the instantaneous velocity at $t = 4$.

steps.label: Step 1: Anchor the point
steps.text: At $t = 4$: $y = 275 - 16(16) = 275 - 256 = 19$ feet — the object still has 19 feet to fall.

steps.label: Step 3: Evaluate the shrinking windows
steps.text: $h = 0.1$: $-129.6$ ft/s; $h = 0.05$: $-128.8$ ft/s; $h = 0.01$: $-128.16$ ft/s. The averages march toward $-128$ as the window closes.

steps.label: Step 4: Conclude the instantaneous velocity
steps.text: Letting $h \to 0$ in $-128 - 16h$ gives $-128$ ft/s — about 87 mi/h downward. The negative sign encodes direction: height is decreasing.

examples.result: The instantaneous velocity at $t = 4$ is $-128$ ft/s. The average velocities are honest, computable numbers; the instantaneous velocity is their limit.

examples.title: A rock on Mars (Exercise 6 style)
examples.problem: A rock thrown straight up on Mars has height $s(t) = 10t - 1.86t^2$ meters after $t$ seconds (Mars gravity pulls it down at about $3.72\ \text{m/s}^2$). Estimate and then confirm its velocity at $t = 1$.

steps.label: Step 1: Anchor the position
steps.text: At $t = 1$: $s(1) = 10 - 1.86 = 8.14$ m. The rock is still rising at this moment — its velocity only reaches zero at the peak, $t_{\text{peak}} = 10/3.72 \approx 2.69$ s.

steps.label: Step 2: Average velocities over shrinking windows
Step 3: Read off the limit
steps.text: The averages approach $6.28$ m/s as $h \to 0$: the rock is rising at $6.28$ m/s one second after release.

steps.label: Step 4: Sanity-check with physics
steps.text: Mars surface gravity $g \approx 3.72\ \text{m/s}^2$ strips speed at rate $g$: after one second, $v = 10 - 3.72 = 6.28$ m/s — exactly the value the table converged to. The derivative machinery reproduces the physics formula $v = v_0 - gt$.

examples.result: The rock’s velocity at $t = 1$ is $6.28$ m/s upward. One difference quotient, $6.28 - 1.86h$, contains the whole story — its value at $h = 0$ is the instantaneous velocity, and its rate of change in $h$ is the (constant) gravity.

keyTakeaways: The tangent slope at $P$ is the limiting value of secant slopes $m_{PQ}$ as $Q$ approaches $P$ along the curve.
Average velocity over $[a, a+h]$ is the difference quotient $\frac{s(a+h) - s(a)}{h}$ — the slope of a secant line of the position graph.
Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocities; it is never computed at a single instant, only approached.
Both problems share one algebraic object, the difference quotient, in either the $x$-form $\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$ or the $h$-form $\frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$.
Numerical strategy: approach the point from both sides; if the secant values settle to the same number, that number is the limit — if they settle to different numbers, the limit does not exist.
Zooming in on a smooth curve makes it look straight — the tangent line is the line the curve impersonates up close, which is why derivatives power approximation later in the course.

quiz.q: The slope of the secant line through $P(a, f(a))$ and $Q(x, f(x))$ is:
quiz.explanation: Slope is rise over run: the change in outputs $f(x) - f(a)$ divided by the change in inputs $x - a$ — the average rate of change of $f$ over that window.

quiz.q: Average velocities for $h = 0.1$, $0.05$, $0.01$ come out $-129.6$, $-128.8$, $-128.16$ ft/s. The best estimate of the instantaneous velocity is:
options: The average of the three, about $-128.85$ ft/s
quiz.explanation: The averages converge to $-128$ ft/s (the limit of $-128 - 16h$ as $h \to 0$). The limit is defined by approach, not by plugging in $h = 0$.

quiz.q: For the falling object $y = 275 - 16t^2$ at $t = 4$, the average velocity over $[4, 4+h]$ simplifies to:
quiz.explanation: Expanding: $\frac{(275 - 16(4+h)^2) - 19}{h} = \frac{-128h - 16h^2}{h} = -128 - 16h$ for $h \ne 0$; the division by $h$ is legal because averages only use $h > 0$.

quiz.q: Why does the tangent problem require a limiting process rather than plain algebra?
options: Because two points determine a line but one point does not, and the second point must be allowed to merge with the first
Because tangent lines have irrational slopes
Because secant lines do not exist for curves
quiz.explanation: A line through two points is elementary; the tangent is what that line becomes when the second point collapses onto the first — a limit of secants.

quiz.q: A walking-rate example gives secant slopes $106.3$ steps/min just before $t = 20$ and $91.4$ just after. The symmetric estimate of the tangent slope at $t = 20$ is:
quiz.explanation: Averaging the flanking secant slopes cancels the leading curvature error — the solution manual’s own graphical technique, confirmed against the tangent line.

intro: Section 2.2 makes the word “limit” precise enough to compute with — first intuitively, by reading graphs and tables — and immediately broadens the idea in two directions: one-sided limits (what the function does as you approach from one side only) and infinite limits (what happens near a vertical asymptote). The central lesson is that a limit is about the values a function is heading toward, not the value it happens to attain: a limit can exist where the function does not, and a function value can disagree with its limit.
objectives: Estimate limits from graphs and from tables of values
Compute one-sided limits and use the criterion that a two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree
Distinguish a function’s limit from its value at a point
Recognize infinite limits and identify vertical asymptotes
Understand the language of “arbitrarily close” and “sufficiently close”

concepts.statement: $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means: the values of $f(x)$ can be made as close to $L$ **as we like** by taking $x$ sufficiently close to $a$ — but not equal to $a$.
concepts.detail: The solution manual phrases it exactly this way: “the values of $f(x)$ can be made as close to 5 as we like by taking $x$ sufficiently close to 2 (but $x \ne 2$).” Two clauses matter: the tolerance is ours to choose (any closeness), and the point $x = a$ itself is excluded — $f(a)$ may be wrong, different, or missing entirely without disturbing the limit. Section 2.4 turns this sentence into the ε–δ definition.

concepts.statement: The **left-hand limit** $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)$ restricts $x$ to approach $a$ through values less than $a$; the **right-hand limit** $\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$ uses values greater than $a$.
concepts.detail: One-sided limits are the right tool whenever a function behaves differently on the two sides of a point — piecewise functions and jump behavior. The manual reads them off graphs all section: approaching 2 from the left the values approach 3, from the right they approach 1, so the two one-sided limits are $\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = 3$ and $\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = 1$.

concepts.statement: $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ **exists if and only if** both one-sided limits exist and are equal: $$\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x).$$ If they differ, the two-sided limit does not exist — the graph has a jump.
concepts.detail: The manual applies this instantly: “$\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ does not exist since the left-hand limit does not equal the right-hand limit.” Note that a jump kills the two-sided limit even though each one-sided limit is perfectly respectable — “does not exist” is a precise verdict, not an admission of defeat.

concepts.term: A limit is not a value
concepts.statement: The limit of $f$ at $a$ is about the **neighborhood** of $a$, not the point itself: the graph may have a hole at $(2, 5)$ with $f(2) = 3$, and still $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 5$.
concepts.detail: The solution manual’s opening exercise: “As $x$ approaches 2, $f(x)$ approaches 5 — and yes, the graph could have a hole at $(2, 5)$ and define $f(2) = 3$.” Its Exercise 4 runs the contrast in reverse: $\lim_{x \to 4} f(x) = 4$ even though $f(4)$ does not exist at all. Redefining a single point changes no limit — the fact that makes “removable discontinuities” removable in Section 2.5.

concepts.statement: $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = \infty$ means the values of $f(x)$ can be made **arbitrarily large** by taking $x$ sufficiently close to $a$. Similarly $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = -\infty$ for arbitrarily large negative values. Infinite limits are a way of saying a limit **does not** exist, with extra information about how.
concepts.detail: The manual’s phrasing: “$\lim_{x \to -3} f(x) = \infty$ means the values of $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily large by taking $x$ sufficiently close to $-3$,” and for the one-sided version “$\lim_{x \to 4^+} f(x) = -\infty$ … through values larger than 4.” Infinity is not a number here — the notation describes unbounded growth, and the limit still does not exist.

concepts.statement: The line $x = a$ is a **vertical asymptote** of $f$ if at least one of the one-sided limits at $a$ is $\infty$ or $-\infty$. The graph climbs or dives without bound near the line without ever touching it.
concepts.detail: The classic producer is division by shrinking denominators: for $f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2}$, the values explode to $+\infty$ from both sides of 0, so $x = 0$ is a vertical asymptote. For $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ the one-sided limits disagree in sign: $\infty$ from the right, $-\infty$ from the left. Graph-reading exercises in the manual identify vertical asymptotes at $x = 1$ and $x = 3$ (with horizontal asymptotes $y = -2$ and $y = 2$) from the picture alone.

concepts.statement: To guess $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$, evaluate $f$ at a sequence of inputs marching toward $a$ from both sides and watch the outputs settle; verify the guess with algebra (Section 2.3) before trusting it.
concepts.detail: The book’s own example, $f(x) = \frac{x - 1}{x^2 - 1}$ near $x = 1$, gives values $0, 0.333, 0.392, 0.399, 0.3999$ from the left and $0.6, 0.426, 0.402, 0.4002$ from the right — both sides converge to $\tfrac{1}{2}$. A calculator table can mislead when the function oscillates or the values underflow, which is why numerical guessing is a heuristic and the limit laws of Section 2.3 are the proof.

examples.title: Reading limits off a graph (Exercise 4 style)
examples.problem: From the graph of $f$: as $x \to 2^-$ the values approach 3; as $x \to 2^+$ the values approach 1; the point $(2, 3)$ is on the graph; as $x \to 4$ the values approach 4 but $f(4)$ is undefined. Determine $\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x)$, $\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x)$, $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$, $f(2)$, $\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)$ and $f(4)$.

steps.label: Step 1: Record the one-sided limits at 2
steps.text: From the graph: $\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = 3$ and $\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = 1$ — the heights the graph is heading toward on each side.

steps.label: Step 2: Rule on the two-sided limit
steps.text: Because $3 \ne 1$, the one-sided limits disagree, so $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ **does not exist** — the graph jumps at $x = 2$.

steps.label: Step 3: Separate the value from the limit
steps.text: The solid dot at $(2, 3)$ says $f(2) = 3$. Note the coincidence with the left-hand limit is an accident of the drawing: at $x = 4$ the limit is 4 while $f(4)$ does not exist — the open circle contributes nothing.

steps.label: Step 4: Summarize the taxonomy
steps.text: Limits: $3$, $1$, DNE, then $4$. Values: $f(2) = 3$, $f(4)$ undefined. Every combination of “limit exists / value exists / they agree” occurs somewhere on this graph — which is exactly why continuity (Section 2.5) is defined as agreement.

examples.result: $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ does not exist (jump); $\lim_{x \to 4} f(x) = 4$ even though $f(4)$ is undefined. Limits read the trend; values read the dot.

examples.title: Guessing a limit from a table (book Example 2 style)
examples.problem: Guess $\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x - 1}{x^2 - 1}$ from a table of values, then confirm the guess with algebra.

steps.label: Step 1: March in from the left
Step 2: March in from the right
steps.text: At $x = 1.5$: $f = 0.4$; at $x = 1.1$: $0.4762$; at $x = 1.01$: $0.4975$; at $x = 1.001$: $0.4998$ — converging to the same value from below. Both sides agree: the guess is $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Confirm with algebra
steps.text: For $x \ne 1$, factor the denominator: $\frac{x - 1}{x^2 - 1} = \frac{x - 1}{(x - 1)(x + 1)} = \frac{1}{x + 1}$. The hole in the domain at $x = 1$ is gone from the simplified form.

steps.label: Step 4: Evaluate the clean form
steps.text: As $x \to 1$, $\frac{1}{x + 1} \to \frac{1}{1 + 1} = \frac{1}{2}$ — confirming the table. This cancellation move is the first limit technique of Section 2.3.

examples.result: $\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x - 1}{x^2 - 1} = \frac{1}{2}$: guessed numerically, proved algebraically. The function is undefined at $x = 1$, and the limit does not care.

examples.title: Infinite limits and the vertical asymptote of $\frac{1}{x}$
examples.problem: Analyze the behavior of $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ as $x \to 0$ from the left and from the right, and identify the vertical asymptote.

steps.label: Step 1: Approach 0 from the right
steps.text: For small positive $x$ — take $x = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001$ — the reciprocals are $10, 100, 1000$: growing without bound. So $\lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1}{x} = \infty$.

steps.label: Step 2: Approach 0 from the left
steps.text: For small negative $x$ — $-0.1, -0.01, -0.001$ — the reciprocals are $-10, -100, -1000$: plunging without bound. So $\lim_{x \to 0^-} \frac{1}{x} = -\infty$.

steps.label: Step 3: Rule on the two-sided limit
steps.text: The one-sided limits are infinite (and of opposite sign), so $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{x}$ does not exist. Dividing 1 by numbers arbitrarily close to 0 has no limiting value — the magnitudes explode.

steps.label: Step 4: Name the asymptote
steps.text: Because at least one one-sided limit at 0 is infinite, the line $x = 0$ (the $y$-axis) is a vertical asymptote of $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$; the hyperbola clings to it without crossing.

examples.result: $\lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1}{x} = \infty$, $\lim_{x \to 0^-} \frac{1}{x} = -\infty$, the two-sided limit does not exist, and $x = 0$ is a vertical asymptote. Shrinking denominators are the standard engine of infinite limits.

keyTakeaways: $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$: values of $f$ get as close to $L$ as desired whenever $x$ is close enough to $a$ (with $x \ne a$) — the behavior near a point, not at it.
The two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree; a jump is a failed limit.
A limit can exist where the function is undefined, and a defined value can disagree with the limit — holes and open circles do not affect limits.
$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = \infty$ (or $-\infty$) describes unbounded growth near $a$; it is a refined way for a limit not to exist.
A vertical asymptote occurs at $x = a$ whenever a one-sided limit there is infinite; division by vanishing denominators is the usual cause.
Numerical tables suggest limits; algebraic laws and techniques prove them.

quiz.q: If $\lim_{x \to 3^-} f(x) = 1$ and $\lim_{x \to 3^+} f(x) = 4$, what is $\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)$?
quiz.explanation: The two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal. Here they disagree, so the limit does not exist — the graph jumps from height 1 to height 4.

quiz.q: A graph has a hole at $(2, 5)$ but a solid dot at $(2, 3)$. What is $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$?
quiz.explanation: The limit reads the trend of nearby values, which head to the hole’s height 5; the redefined value $f(2) = 3$ at the single point is invisible to the limit.

quiz.q: The statement $\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = -\infty$ means:
options: The limit exists and equals a large negative number
The values of $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily large negative by taking $x$ sufficiently close to $a$ through values larger than $a$
The function has a horizontal asymptote
quiz.explanation: Infinite one-sided limits describe unbounded behavior from that side — negative without bound here. Infinity is a description, not a number the limit equals.

quiz.q: For $f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2}$ near $x = 0$, the one-sided limits are:
options: $\infty$ from the left, $-\infty$ from the right
$-\infty$ from the left, $\infty$ from the right
quiz.explanation: Squaring makes every nearby value positive, so the reciprocals blow up to $+\infty$ from both sides — the two-sided limit is still “infinite,” meaning it does not exist as a number, and $x = 0$ is a vertical asymptote.

quiz.q: Which statement about limits is FALSE?
options: A limit can exist even when $f(a)$ is undefined
If $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ exists, then $f(a) = L$
The value $f(a)$ has no bearing on whether $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists
quiz.explanation: Nothing forces $f(a)$ to match the limit — that agreement is precisely the definition of continuity, a special condition studied in Section 2.5, not a consequence of limits.

intro: Graph-reading is a fine way to guess a limit, but calculus needs limits that are computed and proved. Section 2.3 supplies the eleven limit laws — algebra for limits that mirrors algebra for numbers — plus the direct substitution property that makes polynomials and rational functions effortless. When direct substitution fails (the famous 0/0 form), the section teaches the three algebraic repairs: factor and cancel, rationalize with a conjugate, combine over a common denominator. It closes with the Squeeze Theorem, the tool that will pin down the most important limit in trigonometry: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$.
objectives: State and apply the limit laws for sums, differences, products, quotients, powers and roots
Use direct substitution for polynomials and rational functions (where the denominator limit is nonzero)
Resolve 0/0 forms by factoring, rationalizing or finding a common denominator
Apply the Squeeze Theorem to functions trapped between two functions with a common limit
Present the geometric squeeze argument for $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$

concepts.statement: If $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M$ both exist, then: $$\lim [f \pm g] = L \pm M, \quad \lim [c f] = cL, \quad \lim [f g] = LM, \quad \lim \frac{f}{g} = \frac{L}{M} \ (M \ne 0),$$ and $\lim [f(x)]^n = L^n$ and $\lim \sqrt[n]{f(x)} = \sqrt[n]{L}$ (for even $n$, $L > 0$).
concepts.detail: Limits pass through sums, products, constant multiples, quotients (when the denominator limit is nonzero), powers and roots. The solution manual annotates every step of a calculation with the law used, e.g. $\lim_{x \to 2} [f(x) + 5g(x)] = \lim f(x) + 5\lim g(x) = 4 + 5(-2) = -6$, citing Laws 1 and 3. The fine print matters: the quotient law needs $M \ne 0$; the root law for even roots needs a nonnegative limit; and each law presupposes that the constituent limits exist.

concepts.statement: Polynomials and rational functions are **continuous** wherever they are defined, so their limits can be evaluated by **direct substitution**: $\lim_{x \to a} P(x) = P(a)$, and $\lim_{x \to a} \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = \frac{P(a)}{Q(a)}$ whenever $Q(a) \ne 0$.
concepts.detail: The manual computes $\lim_{x \to 5} (4x^2 - 5x) = 75$ and $\lim_{x \to -3} (2x^3 + 6x^2 - 9) = -9$ line by line with the laws, then observes the shortcut: if the function is a polynomial, just plug in. The word “continuous” is formally defined in Section 2.5 — direct substitution is its practical reward.

concepts.statement: If blind substitution produces $\frac{0}{0}$, the limit is **indeterminate** — it may exist and equal anything, or not exist. The value is hidden by a factor of $(x - a)$ that must be canceled or exposed before the limit can be read.
concepts.detail: The quotient law does not apply when the denominator tends to 0, but that does not mean the limit fails — it means algebra must intervene first. The manual’s warning example: if $\lim g(x) = 0$ while the numerator tends to a nonzero number, then $\frac{f}{g}$ genuinely has no limit (one-sided limits become infinite); but if both tend to 0, anything can happen and the factor causing the vanishing must be found.

concepts.statement: For a rational function in a 0/0 situation at $x = a$: factor numerator and denominator, cancel the common factor $(x - a)$, and then substitute. Example: $$\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3} = \lim_{x \to 3} \frac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{x - 3} = \lim_{x \to 3} (x + 3) = 6.$$
concepts.detail: The cancellation is legal for every $x \ne 3$ — and limits never look at $x = a$ itself, so the simplified function has the same limit. This single move resolves every 0/0 problem with polynomial structure: the goal is to expose the surviving factor and evaluate it at $a$.

concepts.statement: When radicals cause the 0/0, multiply numerator and denominator by the **conjugate**: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x^2 + 9} - 3}{x} = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x^2}{x\left(\sqrt{x^2 + 9} + 3\right)} = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 9} + 3} = \frac{0}{6} = 0.$$
concepts.detail: The conjugate $\sqrt{x^2 + 9} + 3$ turns the numerator into $(x^2 + 9) - 9 = x^2$ via the difference of squares $(a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2$. The factor of $x$ that must be canceled now appears in the numerator. The technique is the same game as factoring — manufacture and cancel the vanishing factor — just with radicals.

concepts.term: Common denominators for differences of fractions
concepts.statement: For limits of the form $\lim_{x \to a} \left[\frac{f}{g} - \frac{h}{k}\right]$ that produce $\frac{c}{0}$ or $\frac{0}{0}$: combine over a common denominator first, then factor and cancel as usual.
concepts.detail: The difference of two fractions each defined at $a$ may combine into an expression whose numerator vanishes there; rewriting as one fraction exposes the $(x - a)$ factor. This is the standard opening for limits like $\lim_{x \to 4} \left(\frac{1}{x - 4} - \frac{5}{x^2 - 16}\right)$ and it foreshadows the derivative computations of Section 2.7, where difference quotients $\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$ are exactly this shape.

concepts.statement: If $f(x) \le g(x) \le h(x)$ near $a$ (except possibly at $a$), and $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a} h(x) = L$, then $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = L$ — the trapped function is squeezed to the same limit.
concepts.detail: The manual’s applications: since $-1 \le \sin(\pi/x) \le 1$, multiplying by $x^2$ gives $-x^3 + x^2 \le x^3 + x^2 \sin(\pi/x) \le x^3 + x^2$, and both bounds tend to 0, so $\lim_{x \to 0} \left[x^3 + x^2 \sin(\pi/x)\right] = 0$. The bounded-but-oscillating factor contributes nothing because it is crushed between functions whose limits are forced.

concepts.statement: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1,$$ where $x$ is measured in **radians**. Geometrically, the sector of the unit circle is squeezed between two triangles whose areas both approach $\tfrac{1}{2}x$.
concepts.detail: The squeeze proof (worked in the example below) compares three areas on the unit circle for $0 < x < \pi/2$: the small triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}\sin x$, the sector of area $\tfrac{1}{2}x$, and the large triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}\tan x$. Dividing through by $\tfrac{1}{2}\sin x$ and taking reciprocals yields $\cos x \le \frac{\sin x}{x} \le \frac{1}{\cos x}$, and both bounds squeeze to 1 as $x \to 0^+$ (the left-hand limit follows by symmetry since both $\sin x$ and $x$ are odd). Radians are essential — the sector formula $\tfrac{1}{2}x$ is what ties the angle to the arc length. This limit is the engine of every trigonometric derivative in Section 3.3.

examples.title: Evaluating limits with the laws (Exercises 3–6 style)
examples.problem: Evaluate (a) $\lim_{x \to 5} (4x^2 - 5x)$ and (b) $\lim_{t \to 7} \frac{3t^2 + 1}{t^2 - 5t + 2}$, citing the laws used.

steps.label: Step 1: Split the polynomial
steps.text: (a) By the difference law and constant multiple law: $\lim_{x \to 5} (4x^2 - 5x) = 4\lim_{x \to 5} x^2 - 5\lim_{x \to 5} x = 4(25) - 5(5) = 75$ — the manual’s own line-by-line computation, each step tagged with its law.

steps.label: Step 2: Recognize the shortcut
steps.text: The function is a polynomial, so direct substitution gives the same answer instantly: $4(5)^2 - 5(5) = 75$. The laws justify the shortcut.

steps.label: Step 3: Check the quotient’s denominator first
steps.text: (b) At $t = 7$ the denominator is $49 - 35 + 2 = 16 \ne 0$, so the quotient law applies: $\lim_{t \to 7} \frac{3t^2 + 1}{t^2 - 5t + 2} = \frac{3(49) + 1}{16} = \frac{148}{16} = \frac{37}{4}$.

steps.label: Step 4: State the general principle
steps.text: If substitution gives a number over a nonzero number, that number is the limit. If it gives $\frac{0}{0}$, algebra must intervene — and if it gives nonzero over 0, the limit does not exist (one-sided limits are infinite).

examples.result: (a) $75$; (b) $\frac{37}{4}$. The limit laws reduce polynomial and rational limits to arithmetic — with the 0/0 exception that launches the next example.

examples.title: Escaping 0/0: factoring and rationalizing
examples.problem: Evaluate (a) $\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$ and (b) $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x^2 + 9} - 3}{x}$.

steps.label: Step 1: Diagnose (a) as 0/0
steps.text: Substituting $x = 3$: numerator $9 - 9 = 0$, denominator $3 - 3 = 0$. Indeterminate — the factor $(x - 3)$ is hiding in the numerator.

steps.label: Step 2: Factor and cancel
steps.text: $\frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3} = \frac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{x - 3} = x + 3$ for $x \ne 3$, so the limit is $\lim_{x \to 3} (x + 3) = 6$.

steps.label: Step 3: Diagnose (b) as 0/0
steps.text: Substituting $x = 0$: $\sqrt{9} - 3 = 0$ over 0. The vanishing factor is entangled with the radical, so multiply by the conjugate $\sqrt{x^2 + 9} + 3$.

steps.label: Step 4: Rationalize and simplify
steps.text: $\frac{\sqrt{x^2 + 9} - 3}{x} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x^2 + 9} + 3}{\sqrt{x^2 + 9} + 3} = \frac{x^2 + 9 - 9}{x\left(\sqrt{x^2 + 9} + 3\right)} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 9} + 3}$ for $x \ne 0$.

steps.label: Step 5: Substitute into the clean form
steps.text: Now direct substitution works: $\frac{0}{\sqrt{9} + 3} = \frac{0}{6} = 0$. The limit exists and equals 0 despite the original 0/0 appearance.

examples.result: (a) $6$ by factoring; (b) $0$ by rationalizing. Every 0/0 rescue is the same plot: manufacture the vanishing factor, cancel it, substitute.

examples.title: The squeeze proof that $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$
examples.problem: Show that $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$ by squeezing, using areas on the unit circle.

steps.label: Step 1: Set up the geometry
steps.text: On the unit circle, let $x$ be the angle (in radians) at the center, $0 < x < \tfrac{\pi}{2}$. Three regions share the vertex: the small triangle with base 1 and height $\sin x$; the circular sector of angle $x$; and the large triangle with base 1 and height $\tan x$.

steps.label: Step 2: Write the three areas
steps.text: Small triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \sin x$ (area $\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 \cdot \sin x$). Sector: $\tfrac{1}{2} x$ (a fraction $\frac{x}{2\pi}$ of the circle’s area $\pi$). Large triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \tan x$. Nesting gives $$\tfrac{1}{2}\sin x \; \le \; \tfrac{1}{2} x \; \le \; \tfrac{1}{2}\tan x.$$

steps.label: Step 3: Rearrange into a squeeze on $\frac{\sin x}{x}$
steps.text: Multiply through by $\frac{2}{\sin x}$: $1 \le \frac{x}{\sin x} \le \frac{1}{\cos x}$. Taking reciprocals (all positive, so inequalities flip): $$\cos x \; \le \; \frac{\sin x}{x} \; \le \; \frac{1}{\cos x}.$$

steps.label: Step 4: Take the limit of the bounds
steps.text: As $x \to 0^+$, both $\cos x \to 1$ and $\frac{1}{\cos x} \to 1$. The Squeeze Theorem forces $\lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$.

steps.label: Step 5: Handle the left side and conclude
steps.text: Both $\sin x$ and $x$ are odd, so $\frac{\sin(-x)}{-x} = \frac{\sin x}{x}$: the function is even and the left-hand limit equals the right-hand limit. Hence $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$ — the derivative of every trig function in Section 3.3 flows from this one squeeze.

examples.result: Triangles below and above the sector squeeze $\cos x \le \frac{\sin x}{x} \le \frac{1}{\cos x}$, and both bounds tend to 1. The ratio of arc to chord vanishes — the sine and its argument become indistinguishable near 0.

keyTakeaways: The limit laws let limits pass through sums, differences, products, constant multiples, powers, roots and quotients (nonzero denominator) — provided each constituent limit exists.
Polynomials and rational functions (where defined) submit to direct substitution: plug in and read.
A 0/0 result is a signal, not an answer: factor and cancel, rationalize with a conjugate, or combine over a common denominator to expose the vanishing factor.
If the numerator tends to a nonzero number while the denominator tends to 0, the limit does not exist — the one-sided limits are infinite.
The Squeeze Theorem: a function trapped between two functions with a common limit $L$ has limit $L$ — the tool for taming bounded oscillators like $x^2 \sin(\pi/x)$ near 0.
$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$ (radians!) — proved by squeezing the unit-circle sector between two triangles; it powers every trigonometric derivative.

quiz.q: Which law justifies $\lim_{x \to 2} [f(x) \cdot g(x)] = \left(\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)\right)\left(\lim_{x \to 2} g(x)\right)$?
quiz.explanation: The product law says the limit of a product is the product of the limits — provided both limits on the right exist. The manual cites it step by step in its Law 4 annotations.

quiz.q: Evaluating $\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$ by direct substitution gives $\frac{0}{0}$. The correct next move is to:
options: Factor and cancel the common factor $(x - 3)$, then substitute
Conclude the limit does not exist
quiz.explanation: 0/0 is indeterminate: canceling $\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3}$ to $x + 3$ gives the limit 6. Only if the numerator stayed nonzero while the denominator vanished would the limit fail to exist.

quiz.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0} x^2 \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{x}\right)$.
options: It does not exist because $\sin(\pi/x)$ oscillates
quiz.explanation: Since $-1 \le \sin(\pi/x) \le 1$, we get $-x^2 \le x^2 \sin(\pi/x) \le x^2$, and both bounds tend to 0. The oscillation is crushed between two vanishing functions — exactly the manual’s Exercise-39 reasoning.

quiz.q: The value of $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}$ is:
quiz.explanation: The geometric squeeze gives $\cos x \le \frac{\sin x}{x} \le \frac{1}{\cos x}$ and both bounds tend to 1. Radians are load-bearing: the sector area $\tfrac{1}{2}x$ is what ties angle to arc.

quiz.q: If $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = 5$ and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = 0$, what can be said about $\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$?
options: It does not exist (the one-sided limits are infinite)
The quotient law gives $\frac{5}{0}$, which is fine
quiz.explanation: A nonzero numerator over a vanishing denominator grows without bound — the quotient law explicitly requires a nonzero denominator limit, and the manual flags this exact case as “does not exist.”

intro: The intuitive limit of Section 2.2 says “as close as we like,” and this section converts that phrase into a two-quantifier challenge the whole world can play: for every tolerance ε, there must exist a response window δ. The ε–δ definition is what makes limits provable rather than plausible, and this section teaches both directions — reading δ off graphs for a given ε, and writing complete proofs for linear and quadratic limits, including the bounding trick that makes quadratics tractable.
objectives: State the precise (ε–δ) definition of a limit and explain the role and order of its quantifiers
Read a δ off a graph for a given ε as the more restrictive of the two side-distances
Prove limits of linear functions with the choice $\delta = \varepsilon/|m|$
Prove a quadratic limit by first bounding the variable factor (the $\min(1, \varepsilon/M)$ technique)
Interpret ε–δ as a tolerance game: error tolerance ε on the output, control window δ on the input

concepts.term: The ε–δ definition of a limit
concepts.statement: $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means: for **every** $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that $$0 < |x - a| < \delta \quad \Longrightarrow \quad |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon.$$
concepts.detail: Read it as a challenge–response protocol: an adversary names an output tolerance ε (how close $f(x)$ must stay to $L$); you must answer with an input window δ (how close $x$ must stay to $a$) that guarantees it. The definition quantifies “as close as we like” with the universal quantifier on ε and “sufficiently close” with the existential quantifier on δ — and the order of the quantifiers is what makes δ allowed to depend on ε. The punctured condition $0 < |x - a|$ excludes $x = a$ itself, honoring the principle that limits ignore the point.

concepts.statement: For a given ε, draw the band $L - \varepsilon < y < L + \varepsilon$; project the part of the graph inside the band down to the $x$-axis; the resulting interval around $a$ has endpoints $a - \delta_1$ and $a + \delta_2$, and any $\delta \le \min(\delta_1, \delta_2)$ works.
concepts.detail: The solution manual’s Exercise 1: if $|f(x) - 1| < 0.2$ holds for $0.7 < x < 1.1$ near $a = 1$, then $\delta = \min\{1 - 0.7,\ 1.1 - 1\} = \min\{0.3, 0.1\} = 0.1$ — “or any smaller positive number.” Taking the minimum is the rule because the window must work on both sides simultaneously, and asymmetric graphs (like $y = x^2$ at $x = 2$, where the manual finds $\delta = 1.44$ from an asymmetric band) make the asymmetry visible.

concepts.statement: The quantifier order — **for all ε, there exists δ** — means δ is a function of ε. Shrinking the demanded accuracy typically shrinks the usable window; but no single δ must work for every ε.
concepts.detail: Reversing the quantifiers (“there exists a δ that works for every ε”) would force $f$ to be constant near $a$. The manual’s linear examples make the dependence explicit and linear: for $\lim_{x \to 2}(5x - 7) = 3$ the winning choice is $\delta = \varepsilon/5$, so ε = 0.1 demands δ = 0.02, ε = 0.01 demands δ = 0.002 — halving the tolerance halves the window.

concepts.statement: A manufacturing reading of the definition: the machinist must hit a target output $L$ (area 1000 cm²) within tolerance ε (5 cm²); the ε–δ statement guarantees this is achievable by controlling the input (radius) within some window δ of the target input.
concepts.detail: The manual’s disk-area example: a disk of radius $r$ has area $A = \pi r^2$; the target $A = 1000$ cm² requires $r = \sqrt{1000/\pi} \approx 17.8412$ cm; the tolerance $|A - 1000| \le 5$ is achieved exactly when $17.7966 \le r \le 17.8858$, i.e. within about 0.0445 cm of the target radius. Here $x$ is the radius, $f(x)$ the area, $a$ the target radius, $L$ the target area, ε the area tolerance and δ the radius tolerance — the definition as a quality-control contract.

concepts.statement: To prove $\lim_{x \to a} (mx + b) = L$: work backward from the target inequality. Factor $|(mx + b) - L| = |m| \cdot |x - a|$; then $|(mx+b) - L| < \varepsilon$ is guaranteed by $|x - a| < \frac{\varepsilon}{|m|}$, so choose $\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{|m|}$ and verify.
concepts.detail: The manual proves exactly this shape three times: $\lim_{x \to 1} (4x + 3) = 7$ with $\delta = \varepsilon/4$; $\lim_{x \to 2} (5x - 7) = 3$ with $\delta = \varepsilon/5$; and $\lim_{x \to 2} (2 - 3x) = -4$ with $\delta = \varepsilon/3$. The scratch work (discovering δ) and the proof (verifying it) are separate activities — the proof only needs the verification direction, run forward.

concepts.term: The bounding trick for nonlinear functions
concepts.statement: When the factor multiplying $|x - a|$ is itself variable, **bound it first**: restrict $\delta \le 1$ to confine $x$ to a known interval, bound the variable factor by a constant $M$ there, then choose $\delta = \min\{1, \varepsilon/M\}$.
concepts.detail: The classic target is $\lim_{x \to 3} x^2 = 9$: $|x^2 - 9| = |x + 3|\,|x - 3|$. If $\delta \le 1$ then $|x - 3| < 1$ forces $2 < x < 4$, so $|x + 3| < 7$; hence $|x^2 - 9| < 7\,|x - 3| < 7\delta$, and $\delta = \min\{1, \varepsilon/7\}$ makes the product less than ε. The trick trades precision (a slightly smaller δ) for the luxury of a constant coefficient.

figures.caption: The $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ picture: given the output tolerance band $L-\varepsilon < y < L+\varepsilon$ (amber), the definition demands an input window $a-\delta < x < a+\delta$ (teal) whose image stays inside the band — the darker lens where the bands overlap is exactly what the definition guarantees, and the usable $\delta$ is the smaller of the two side-distances.

examples.title: Reading a δ off a graph (Exercise 1 style)
examples.problem: From the graph of $f$ near $a = 1$ with $L = 1$: the inequality $|f(x) - 1| < 0.2$ holds exactly when $0.7 < x < 1.1$. Find a valid δ.

steps.label: Step 1: Translate ε into an output band
steps.text: $|f(x) - 1| < 0.2$ means $-0.2 < f(x) - 1 < 0.2$, i.e. the band $0.8 < f(x) < 1.2$ — ε measures how far the output may wander from $L$.

steps.label: Step 2: Project the band onto the $x$-axis
steps.text: Reading the graph, the curve stays inside the band precisely for $0.7 < x < 1.1$ — an asymmetric window around $a = 1$ (note $x = 1$ excluded, per $0 < |x - a|$).

steps.label: Step 3: Take the more restrictive side
steps.text: Left distance: $1 - 0.7 = 0.3$; right distance: $1.1 - 1 = 0.1$. The window must fit both sides, so $\delta = \min\{0.3, 0.1\} = 0.1$.

steps.label: Step 4: State the conclusion in ε–δ language
steps.text: If $0 < |x - 1| < 0.1$, then $|f(x) - 1| < 0.2$ — and any smaller positive δ works too, since shrinking the window never expels points that were already inside.

examples.result: $\delta = 0.1$ (or any smaller positive number). The minimum of the two side-distances is always the safe choice — the graph, not the formula, sets the geometry here.

examples.title: A full ε–δ proof for a linear limit (Exercise 14 style)
examples.problem: Prove that $\lim_{x \to 2} (5x - 7) = 3$ using the ε–δ definition. Then write down the δ that works for ε = 0.1.

steps.label: Step 1: Set up the target inequality
steps.text: We must show: for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 with $0 < |x - 2| < \delta \Rightarrow |(5x - 7) - 3| < \varepsilon$.

steps.label: Step 2: Do the backward scratch work
steps.text: Simplify the target quantity: $|(5x - 7) - 3| = |5x - 10| = |5(x - 2)| = 5\,|x - 2|$. The error in the output is exactly five times the error in the input.

steps.label: Step 3: Solve the inequality for the window
steps.text: We need $5|x - 2| < \varepsilon$, which is the same as $|x - 2| < \frac{\varepsilon}{5}$. So the choice $\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{5}$ suggests itself.

steps.label: Step 4: Run the proof forward
steps.text: Given any ε > 0, choose δ = ε/5 > 0. If $0 < |x - 2| < \delta$, then $|(5x - 7) - 3| = 5|x - 2| < 5\delta = 5 \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{5} = \varepsilon$. This proves $\lim_{x \to 2}(5x - 7) = 3$. ∎

steps.label: Step 5: Read off specific tolerances
steps.text: For ε = 0.1: δ = 0.02; for ε = 0.05: δ = 0.01; for ε = 0.01: δ = 0.002 — the manual’s own table. The same pattern proves $\lim_{x \to 2}(3x - 5) = 1$ with $\delta = \varepsilon/3$, and in general linear maps rescale tolerances by the slope.

examples.result: The proof succeeds with $\delta = \varepsilon/5$. Linear functions are ε–δ-transparent: the input window is the output tolerance divided by the absolute slope.

examples.title: A quadratic limit: $\lim_{x \to 3} x^2 = 9$
examples.problem: Prove that $\lim_{x \to 3} x^2 = 9$ with the ε–δ definition.

steps.label: Step 1: Factor the error
steps.text: The target quantity is $|x^2 - 9| = |x + 3|\, |x - 3|$. Unlike the linear case, the coefficient $|x + 3|$ varies with $x$ — it cannot simply be divided out.

steps.label: Step 2: Bound the variable factor
steps.text: Insist on δ ≤ 1 for starters. Then $|x - 3| < 1$ implies $2 < x < 4$, so $5 < x + 3 < 7$ and in particular $|x + 3| < 7$. On this restricted window, $|x^2 - 9| < 7\,|x - 3|$.

steps.label: Step 3: Choose δ as a minimum
steps.text: Now demand $|x - 3| < \frac{\varepsilon}{7}$ as well: taking $\delta = \min\{1, \frac{\varepsilon}{7}\}$ enforces both $|x - 3| < 1$ (so the bound 7 is valid) and $|x - 3| < \frac{\varepsilon}{7}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify forward
steps.text: If $0 < |x - 3| < \delta$, then $|x^2 - 9| = |x + 3|\,|x - 3| < 7 \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{7} = \varepsilon$. Hence for every ε > 0 this δ works, proving $\lim_{x \to 3} x^2 = 9$. ∎

examples.result: The quadratic limit holds with $\delta = \min\{1, \varepsilon/7\}$ — the bounding trick converts the variable slope of a curve into a constant the linear machinery can handle.

keyTakeaways: $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$: for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that $0 < |x - a| < \delta$ implies $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ — a challenge (ε) and a response (δ).
The order of quantifiers is the content: δ may depend on ε, and the game must be winnable for every ε, however small.
The condition $0 < |x - a|$ excludes the point itself: the limit is a statement about the punctured neighborhood of $a$.
Graphically, δ is the smaller of the two side-distances that keep the graph inside the ε-band about $L$.
Linear proofs: factor $|(mx + b) - L| = |m|\,|x - a|$ and choose $\delta = \varepsilon/|m|$; the manual’s pattern for $4x + 3$, $5x - 7$ and $2 - 3x$.
Nonlinear proofs: restrict δ ≤ 1 to bound the variable factor by a constant $M$, then take $\delta = \min\{1, \varepsilon/M\}$ — the technique that tamed $x^2 \to 9$.
The definition doubles as engineering: output tolerance ε is met by controlling the input within δ — the machinist’s disk and the power-temperature examples from the manual.

quiz.q: In the ε–δ definition, why must δ be chosen after ε?
options: Alphabetical order in the Greek alphabet
Because δ is allowed to depend on ε: each output tolerance may need a different input window
Because ε must be an integer
Because δ is always larger than ε
quiz.explanation: The quantifiers read “for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0”: the responder sees the challenge before answering. If one fixed δ had to serve all ε, only constant functions could pass.

quiz.q: For $\lim_{x \to 2}(5x - 7) = 3$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$, the proof’s choice of δ is:
quiz.explanation: The scratch work gives $|(5x - 7) - 3| = 5|x - 2| < \varepsilon$ exactly when $|x - 2| < \varepsilon/5 = 0.02$ — the input tolerance is the output tolerance divided by the slope.

quiz.q: The condition $0 < |x - a|$ in the definition exists to:
options: Prevent division by zero in the proof
Exclude the point $a$ itself, since a limit describes behavior near — not at — $a$
quiz.explanation: Limits are punctured-neighborhood statements: $f(a)$ may be wrong, different or missing. Even a function with a hole at $(a, L)$ satisfies the definition.

quiz.q: A graph stays within the band $0.8 < f(x) < 1.2$ exactly for $0.7 < x < 1.1$. For $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 1$ with ε = 0.2, a valid δ is:
quiz.explanation: The window must fit inside $(0.7, 1.1)$ on both sides of 1: the left slack is 0.3 and the right slack is 0.1, and δ must respect the smaller: δ = 0.1 (or less).

quiz.q: In proving $\lim_{x \to 3} x^2 = 9$, why does one assume δ ≤ 1 at the start?
options: Because ε is always at least 1
To confine $x$ near 3 so that the variable factor $|x + 3|$ can be bounded by the constant 7
quiz.explanation: The error factors as $|x + 3|\,|x - 3|$, and $|x + 3|$ varies with $x$. Restricting δ ≤ 1 forces $2 < x < 4$, so $|x + 3| < 7$ — a constant the linear argument can use, with δ = min{1, ε/7}.

intro: Continuity is the formal name for what most people intuitively mean by an unbroken graph: at every point, the value the function is heading toward and the value it assigns must agree. Section 2.5 turns that agreement into three checkable conditions, classifies the ways it can fail (removable, jump and infinite discontinuities), certifies that all the familiar function families are continuous on their domains, and then cashes the whole account in for a theorem with real computational teeth: the Intermediate Value Theorem, which locates roots of equations that algebra cannot solve.
objectives: State the three conditions for continuity at a point and check them for specific functions
Define continuity on an interval, including one-sided continuity at endpoints
Classify discontinuities as removable, jump or infinite
Use the continuity theorems: combinations, compositions, and the standard families on their domains
Apply the Intermediate Value Theorem to prove roots exist, and locate them by bisection

concepts.statement: A function $f$ is **continuous** at a number $a$ if $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a).$$ Unpacked, three conditions must all hold: (1) $f(a)$ is defined; (2) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists; (3) the two agree.
concepts.detail: The definition is the limit machinery of Sections 2.2–2.4 pointed at one specific question: does the graph pass through where it is heading? The solution manual proves continuity by computing: for $f(x) = 3x^2 + (x + 2)^5$ at $a = -1$, the limit laws give $\lim_{x \to -1} f(x) = 3(-1)^2 + 1 = 4 = f(-1)$, so $f$ is continuous there. Each of the three conditions can fail independently — and each failure mode gets its own name below.

concepts.term: Continuity on an interval; one-sided at endpoints
concepts.statement: A function is **continuous on an interval** if it is continuous at every interior point; at an endpoint of a closed interval, the one-sided limits are used: continuous from the right at the left endpoint, from the left at the right endpoint.
concepts.detail: For instance, $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ is continuous on $[0, \infty)$ — at 0 it is continuous from the right because $\lim_{x \to 0^+} \sqrt{x} = 0 = f(0)$. The manual works this pattern for $f(x) = x + \sqrt{x - 4}$, continuous on $[4, \infty)$ via right-continuity at 4.

concepts.statement: A discontinuity at $a$ is **removable** if $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists but fails to equal $f(a)$ (or $f(a)$ does not exist) — a hole. Redefining (or defining) $f(a) := \lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ repairs it.
concepts.detail: The manual’s example: $f(x) = \frac{x^4 - 1}{x - 1} = (x^2 + 1)(x + 1)$ for $x \ne 1$ has a removable discontinuity at 1; the function $g(x) = x^3 + x^2 + x + 1$ (the same formula with the hole filled in) is continuous on all of $\mathbb{R}$. Removable discontinuities are “clerical errors” — the limit exists and merely needs to be assigned.

concepts.statement: A **jump discontinuity** occurs when both one-sided limits exist but differ; an **infinite discontinuity** occurs when a one-sided limit is $\pm\infty$ (typically a vertical asymptote). Neither can be repaired by redefining one point.
concepts.detail: The manual’s toll-road example is the canonical jump: a $5 toll outside rush hours and $7 between 7–10 am and 4–7 pm has jumps at $t = 7, 10, 16, 19$ — the price never passes through intermediate values, so drivers time their crossings. For an infinite case, $f(x) = \frac{1}{x + 2}$ has an infinite discontinuity at $x = -2$ where $f(-2)$ is undefined and the one-sided limits are $\mp\infty$.
