examples.title: Computing a cross product and checking orthogonality
examples.problem: Find $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ for $\mathbf{a} = \langle 2,\ 3,\ 0\rangle$ and $\mathbf{b} = \langle 1,\ -2,\ 4\rangle$, and verify the result is perpendicular to both factors.

steps.label: Set up the determinant
steps.text: Write $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 4 \end{vmatrix}.$$ Covering the $\mathbf{i}$ column leaves the minor $3 \cdot 4 - 0 \cdot (-2)$.

steps.label: Expand along the first row
steps.text: The three cofactors give $\mathbf{i}\,(3 \cdot 4 - 0 \cdot (-2)) - \mathbf{j}\,(2 \cdot 4 - 0 \cdot 1) + \mathbf{k}\,(2 \cdot (-2) - 3 \cdot 1) = 12\,\mathbf{i} - 8\,\mathbf{j} - 7\,\mathbf{k}$.

steps.label: Check against a
steps.text: Dot with the first factor: $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) = 2(12) + 3(-8) + 0(-7) = 24 - 24 + 0 = 0$. Perpendicular ✓

steps.label: Check against b
steps.text: Dot with the second factor: $\mathbf{b} \cdot (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) = 1(12) + (-2)(-8) + 4(-7) = 12 + 16 - 28 = 0$. Perpendicular ✓

examples.result: $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \langle 12,\ -8,\ -7\rangle$, orthogonal to both $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ — the two dot-product checks vanish identically.

examples.title: Area of a triangle in space
examples.problem: Find the area of the triangle with vertices $P(1,\ 0,\ -1)$, $Q(2,\ 4,\ 5)$ and $R(3,\ 1,\ 7)$.

steps.label: Form edge vectors
steps.text: Take $P$ as the base point: $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \langle 1,\ 4,\ 6\rangle$ and $\overrightarrow{PR} = \langle 2,\ 1,\ 8\rangle$.

steps.label: Cross the edges
steps.text: $\overrightarrow{PQ} \times \overrightarrow{PR} = \langle 4 \cdot 8 - 6 \cdot 1,\ 6 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 8,\ 1 \cdot 1 - 4 \cdot 2\rangle = \langle 26,\ 4,\ -7\rangle$.

steps.label: Parallelogram area
steps.text: The magnitude is $|\langle 26, 4, -7\rangle| = \sqrt{676 + 16 + 49} = \sqrt{741}$.

steps.label: Halve for the triangle
steps.text: The triangle is half the parallelogram its edge vectors span, so its area is $\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{741} \approx 13.6$.

examples.result: Area $= \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{741} \approx 13.6$ square units — no sketching, no base-times-height gymnastics: two subtractions, one determinant, one square root.

examples.title: Torque about the origin
examples.problem: A force $\mathbf{F} = \langle 2,\ 0,\ -3\rangle$ newtons is applied at the point with position vector $\mathbf{r} = \langle 0.5,\ 0.8,\ 0\rangle$ meters. Find the torque about the origin.

steps.label: Apply the definition
steps.text: The torque is $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}$, the position vector crossed with the force.

steps.label: Compute the components
steps.text: $\tau_x = 0.8(-3) - 0 \cdot 0 = -2.4$; $\tau_y = 0 \cdot 2 - 0.5(-3) = 1.5$; $\tau_z = 0.5 \cdot 0 - 0.8 \cdot 2 = -1.6$, all in newton-meters.

steps.label: Interpret the magnitude
steps.text: $|\boldsymbol{\tau}| = \sqrt{2.4^2 + 1.5^2 + 1.6^2} = \sqrt{10.57} \approx 3.25$ N·m, equal to the lever arm times the component of force perpendicular to it.

examples.result: $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \langle -2.4,\ 1.5,\ -1.6\rangle$ N·m, with $|\boldsymbol{\tau}| \approx 3.25$ N·m along the axis the right-hand rule picks out.

examples.title: Volume of a parallelepiped
examples.problem: Find the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\mathbf{a} = \langle 1,\ 2,\ -1\rangle$, $\mathbf{b} = \langle 2,\ 1,\ 3\rangle$ and $\mathbf{c} = \langle 1,\ 0,\ 2\rangle$.

steps.label: Cross the base vectors
steps.text: $\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} = \langle 1 \cdot 2 - 3 \cdot 0,\ 3 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 2,\ 2 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1\rangle = \langle 2,\ -1,\ -1\rangle$.

steps.label: Dot with the third vector
steps.text: $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = 1(2) + 2(-1) + (-1)(-1) = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1$.

steps.label: Take the absolute value
steps.text: The signed volume is $1$; since it is positive, the triple $(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c})$ is right-handed, and the volume is $|1| = 1$.

examples.result: Volume $= 1$ cubic unit — a single $3 \times 3$ determinant in disguise: expand along the $\mathbf{a}$ row and the same three minors appear.

keyTakeaways: The cross product $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \langle a_2b_3 - a_3b_2,\ a_3b_1 - a_1b_3,\ a_1b_2 - a_2b_1\rangle$ is a vector perpendicular to both factors, directed by the right-hand rule, with length $|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta$.
It is anticommutative ($\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a} = -\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$) and NOT associative — parentheses are mandatory, and the Jacobi identity stands in for associativity.

Lagrange's identity $|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|^2 = |\mathbf{a}|^2|\mathbf{b}|^2 - (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b})^2$ is the algebraic engine behind the geometric length formula, reducing it to $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$.

Areas and volumes become one-liners: parallelogram $|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|$, triangle half that, parallelepiped $|\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})|$ — with coplanarity detected by a vanishing triple product.

Physics leans on it constantly: torque $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}$, angular momentum $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p}$, magnetic force $q\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}$ — always a vector result from two vector causes.
A vanishing cross product ($\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$, with neither factor zero) means the vectors are parallel — the standard parallelism test in space.

quiz.q: Compute $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ for $\mathbf{a} = \langle 3,\ -1,\ 2\rangle$ and $\mathbf{b} = \langle 2,\ 0,\ 1\rangle$.
quiz.explanation: Minors: $(-1)(1) - 2 \cdot 0 = -1$; $2 \cdot 2 - 3 \cdot 1 = 1$; $3 \cdot 0 - (-1)(2) = 2$. So $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \langle -1, 1, 2\rangle$. Quick check: $\mathbf{a} \cdot \langle -1,1,2\rangle = -3 - 1 + 4 = 0$ ✓

quiz.q: Which vector is perpendicular to both $\langle 3,\ -1,\ 2\rangle$ and $\langle 2,\ 0,\ 1\rangle$?
quiz.explanation: Only $\langle -1, 1, 2\rangle$ gives dot product $0$ with both: $3(-1) + (-1)(1) + 2(2) = 0$ and $2(-1) + 0 + 1 \cdot 2 = 0$. It is exactly $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$.

quiz.q: Evaluate $\mathbf{i} \times (\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{j})$ and $(\mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{j}) \times \mathbf{j}$, respectively.
quiz.explanation: $\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{j} = \mathbf{0}$, so the first product is $\mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$. But $\mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{j} = \mathbf{k}$, and $\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{j} = -\mathbf{i}$. Different answers — the cross product is not associative.

quiz.q: The area of the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf{a} = \langle 1,\ 1,\ 0\rangle$ and $\mathbf{b} = \langle 0,\ 1,\ 1\rangle$ is:
quiz.explanation: $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \langle 1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 1,\ 0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1,\ 1 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot 0\rangle = \langle 1, -1, 1\rangle$, whose length is $\sqrt{1 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{3}$.

quiz.q: A triangle has vertices $(0,0,0)$, $(2,0,0)$ and $(1,3,0)$. Its area is:
quiz.explanation: Edge vectors $\langle 2,0,0\rangle$ and $\langle 1,3,0\rangle$ cross to $\langle 0, 0, 6\rangle$ (all area along $z$). Parallelogram area $6$, triangle area $\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 6 = 3$.

quiz.q: If $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = 0$ with all three vectors nonzero, the vectors must be:
quiz.explanation: A zero scalar triple product means the parallelepiped has zero volume — the height of $\mathbf{a}$ above the plane spanned by $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ is $0$, so all three vectors lie in one common plane (some two of them may even be parallel).

quiz.q: For nonzero vectors, $|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|$ is largest when the angle $\theta$ between them is:
quiz.explanation: $|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}| = |\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta$, and $\sin\theta$ peaks at $1$ when $\theta = \pi/2$ — perpendicular vectors span the biggest parallelogram, while parallel ones span none at all.

quiz.q: A force $\mathbf{F} = \langle 0,\ 10,\ 0\rangle$ N acts at the point $\langle 0.3,\ 0.4,\ 0\rangle$ m. The magnitude of the torque about the origin is:
quiz.explanation: $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F} = \langle 0.4 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 10,\ 0 \cdot 0 - 0.3 \cdot 0,\ 0.3 \cdot 10 - 0.4 \cdot 0\rangle = \langle 0, 0, 3\rangle$, so $|\boldsymbol{\tau}| = 3$ N·m — lever arm $0.5$ m times the perpendicular force component $6$ N.

quiz.q: Simplify $(2\mathbf{a}) \times \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$.
quiz.explanation: Scalars slide through the cross product: $(2\mathbf{a}) \times \mathbf{b} = 2(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})$, and the two terms share the vector $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$, so they add to $3(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})$.

quiz.q: The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\langle 1, 2, -1\rangle$, $\langle 2, 1, 3\rangle$ and $\langle 1, 0, 2\rangle$ is:
quiz.explanation: $\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} = \langle 2, -1, -1\rangle$ and $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1$: a sliver of a box with volume exactly $1$.

depth.title: The algebra behind the product

blocks.heading: Deriving the component formula from the geometry
blocks.body: Suppose we insist only on the geometry: a product $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ that is perpendicular to both factors, has length $|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta$, and points by the right-hand rule. Writing $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \langle x, y, z\rangle$, perpendicularity gives two linear equations: $a_1x + a_2y + a_3z = 0$ and $b_1x + b_2y + b_3z = 0$. The solution space of this pair is a line, and one reads off a direction vector for it as the formal determinant $\langle a_2b_3 - a_3b_2,\ a_3b_1 - a_1b_3,\ a_1b_2 - a_2b_1\rangle$. The length requirement then fixes the scale, which Lagrange's identity confirms is exactly $|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta$, and the right-hand rule fixes the sign. The determinant formula is not a convention — it is the only possible answer.

blocks.heading: BAC-CAB identity
blocks.body: For all vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$, $$\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}).$$ The double cross product lands back in the plane of $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ — the identity shows this by writing the result as a linear combination of exactly those two vectors.

blocks.heading: BAC-CAB by components
blocks.body: Take $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{j}$ first: $\mathbf{i} \times (\mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{j})$? Better to verify the identity on a basis: both sides are trilinear (linear in each vector separately — the left by the linearity of $\times$ in each slot, the right because the dot product is bilinear), so it suffices to check the $3^3 = 27$ combinations of basis vectors. For $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{i}$: left $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$; right $\mathbf{i}(a_1) - \mathbf{i}(a_1) = \mathbf{0}$ ✓. For $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{j}$: left $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{k} = \langle a_2, -a_1, 0\rangle$; right $\mathbf{i} a_2 - \mathbf{j} a_1$ ✓ — and the remaining cases follow by cyclic symmetry of $\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}$. By trilinearity, the identity holds for all vectors.

blocks.heading: Angular momentum
blocks.body: Newton's second law for rotation is a cross product statement. Define the **angular momentum** of a mass $m$ at position $\mathbf{r}$ with velocity $\mathbf{v}$ as $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r} \times m\mathbf{v}$. Differentiating, $\frac{d\mathbf{L}}{dt} = \mathbf{v} \times m\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{r} \times m\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt} = \mathbf{0} + \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F} = \boldsymbol{\tau}$, because a vector crossed with itself is zero. For a planet under the sun's gravity — a force parallel to $\mathbf{r}$ at every instant — the torque vanishes, so $\mathbf{L}$ is conserved: the orbit stays in one fixed plane, and the radius vector sweeps equal areas in equal times, which is Kepler's second law recovered from one line of vector algebra.

blocks.heading: The magnetic force
blocks.body: A charge $q$ moving with velocity $\mathbf{v}$ through a magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ feels the Lorentz force $q\,\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}$ — perpendicular to both motion and field. Because the force is always perpendicular to $\mathbf{v}$, it does no work ($\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$), and the speed never changes; only the direction bends. With $\mathbf{v} \perp \mathbf{B}$ the charge runs in a circle of radius $r = mv/(qB)$, the cyclotron orbit, and reversing $q$ or the field direction reverses the sense of circulation — exactly the anticommutativity of $\times$ in the laboratory.

blocks.heading: Rotation is the origin of the algebra
blocks.body: The cross product's strange algebra — anticommutative, non-associative, yet satisfying the Jacobi identity — is not an accident of the formula but a portrait of what it represents. The Jacobi identity is precisely the statement that the operators "rotate about $\mathbf{a}$, then $\mathbf{b}$, then $\mathbf{c}$, and undo all three in reverse order" compose to the identity to first order; the algebra of rotations is a **Lie algebra**, and $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the cross product is its smallest nontrivial example, $\mathfrak{so}(3)$. When rotations compose in different orders and the results genuinely differ, non-associativity is the algebra catching the geometry.

depth.title: Why three dimensions is special

blocks.heading: The wedge product
blocks.body: The coordinate-free object behind the cross product is the **exterior product** (wedge) of linear algebra. For vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$, the wedge $\mathbf{a} \wedge \mathbf{b}$ is an antisymmetric bilinear object that lives not in $\mathbb{R}^n$ but in the second exterior power $\wedge^2 \mathbb{R}^n$, a space of dimension $\binom{n}{2}$. It encodes exactly the oriented parallelogram: its magnitude is the area, its "direction" is the plane the two vectors span. The cross product is what you get by identifying $\wedge^2 \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\mathbb{R}^3$ itself — possible because $\binom{3}{2} = 3$ — using the Hodge star dual and the orientation (volume form). That numerical coincidence is why the cross product exists only in three dimensions.

blocks.heading: Differential forms
blocks.body: Multiplication of differentials in integral calculus is the wedge in disguise. A **2-form** such as $\omega = P\,dy \wedge dz + Q\,dz \wedge dx + R\,dx \wedge dy$ is a field of oriented area elements, and its three coefficients are precisely the components of a vector field through the same Hodge identification. The flux integral $\iint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}\, dS$ is the integral of the 2-form over the surface; the divergence theorem becomes Stokes' theorem for forms, $\int_{\partial M} \omega = \int_M d\omega$; and the identity $\nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) = 0$ is just $d \circ d = 0$ — antisymmetry of the wedge, not a miracle of vector calculus.

blocks.heading: Dimensions three and seven
blocks.body: A theorem of Eckmann (1943) and Whitehead classifies all "vector products": bilinear maps $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying $\mathbf{x} \times \mathbf{y} \perp \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}$ and $|\mathbf{x} \times \mathbf{y}|^2 = |\mathbf{x}|^2|\mathbf{y}|^2 - (\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y})^2$. They exist **only** for $n = 3$ and $n = 7$. The 7-dimensional product is built from the octonions, the largest of the four normed division algebras (real $1$, complex $2$, quaternion $4$, octonion $8$ — Hurwitz's theorem), and its automorphism group is the exceptional Lie group $G_2$. The quaternions themselves supply the 3-dimensional story: $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ is the imaginary part of the quaternion product, which is why rotations compose so cleanly through $q = \cos(\theta/2) + \mathbf{u}\sin(\theta/2)$ — the algebra computer graphics uses to avoid gimbal lock.

blocks.heading: Why the exceptional structures
blocks.body: The exceptional Lie groups ($G_2$, $F_4$, $E_6$–$E_8$) are all anchored to the octonions and their 7-dimensional cross product, and they appear stubbornly in the wild: $G_2$ as the holonomy of 7-dimensional manifolds that feature in M-theory compactifications, $E_8$ in the gauge symmetries of heterotic string theory and in the 2007 ATLAS of Lie group representations. Whether these appearances are deep or coincidental — whether the universe "uses" the exceptional algebra or merely permits it — remains an open philosophical-physical question with real mathematical substance: no known principle selects the octonionic path, yet nothing forbids it either.

intro: A point is located by three numbers; a line is located by a point and a direction; a plane by a point and a normal. Those three data pairs are the whole grammar of flat geometry in space, and this section writes the equations that encode them. The line is the set of all points a fixed step vector can reach from one starting point; the plane is the set of all points whose displacement from a given point is perpendicular to a given vector. Everything else — symmetric equations, scalar equations of planes, angles between planes, distances from points to planes — falls out of these two descriptions by pure vector algebra from Sections 12.2–12.4.
objectives: Write the vector, parametric and symmetric equations of a line in space
Decide whether a point lies on a given line, and parametrize the line through two given points
Recognize skew lines — neither parallel nor intersecting — and reason about them
Find the equation of a plane from a point and a normal, or from three points, or from a point and two spanning vectors
Read off normals, test parallel and orthogonal planes, and compute the angle between planes
Derive and apply the distance from a point to a plane, and the distance between two skew lines

concepts.term: The vector equation of a line
concepts.statement: The line through the point $P_0$ with position vector $\mathbf{r}_0$ and parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$ is the set of tips of $$\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + t\,\mathbf{v}, \qquad t \in \mathbb{R}.$$ The parameter $t$ slides the tip from $\mathbf{r}_0$ (at $t = 0$) in both directions forever; $\mathbf{v}$ is a **direction vector** of the line.
concepts.detail: One point plus one direction is the minimum information a line carries — exactly as in the plane, but now the direction vector has three components. Any nonzero scalar multiple of $\mathbf{v}$ describes the same line (with the parameter rescaled), which is why a line's equations are never unique: the same line has infinitely many valid parameterizations.

concepts.statement: Equating components in $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + t\mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{r}_0 = \langle x_0, y_0, z_0\rangle$ and $\mathbf{v} = \langle a, b, c\rangle$ gives the **parametric equations** $$x = x_0 + at, \qquad y = y_0 + bt, \qquad z = z_0 + ct.$$
concepts.detail: Each coordinate is a linear function of the single parameter $t$. To test whether a point $P$ lies on the line, solve one equation for $t$ and check the other two — all three must agree on the same $t$. To parametrize the line through two points $P_0$ and $P_1$, take $\mathbf{v} = \overrightarrow{P_0P_1}$: one subtraction, then the machinery above.

concepts.statement: Eliminating $t$ from the parametric equations (solve each for $t$ and set them equal) gives the **symmetric form** $$\frac{x - x_0}{a} = \frac{y - y_0}{b} = \frac{z - z_0}{c}.$$ If one component of $\mathbf{v}$ is $0$ — say $c = 0$ — the line lies in the plane $z = z_0$, and the honest equations are the pair $\frac{x - x_0}{a} = \frac{y - y_0}{b}$ together with $z = z_0$.
concepts.detail: The symmetric form makes two things readable at a glance: the direction vector $\langle a, b, c\rangle$ sits in the denominators, and a point $\langle x_0, y_0, z_0\rangle$ sits in the numerators. It is the spatial version of the point-slope form of a line in the plane — and the caveat about zero components is the first place where 3D genuinely differs from 2D: a line can be parallel to a coordinate plane, and the algebra must not divide by zero to say so.

concepts.statement: Two lines in space that are not parallel and do not intersect are **skew**. Two lines are parallel when their direction vectors are scalar multiples; otherwise they meet at most once — and in 3D they may miss each other entirely, something impossible in the plane.
concepts.detail: Detecting skewness: directions not proportional rules out parallel; solving two of the three intersection equations for $s$ and $t$ and checking the third rules out (or confirms) a meeting. Geometrically, two skew lines always admit exactly one common perpendicular — the shortest segment joining them — which leads to the distance formula in this section's final method.

concepts.term: The vector and scalar equations of a plane
concepts.statement: A **plane** through the point $P_0$ with position vector $\mathbf{r}_0$, with (nonzero) **normal vector** $\mathbf{n}$, is the set of all points whose displacement from $P_0$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$: $$\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) = 0.$$ Expanding the dot product with $\mathbf{n} = \langle a, b, c\rangle$ gives the **scalar (linear) equation** $$ax + by + cz = d, \qquad d = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{r}_0 = ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0.$$
concepts.detail: The normal is the plane's DNA: it fixes the orientation completely. Two planes are **parallel** when their normals are proportional ($\mathbf{n}_2 = k\mathbf{n}_1$ with different constants $d$), **identical** when proportional with matching ratio in $d$, and **perpendicular** exactly when $\mathbf{n}_1 \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 = 0$. The angle between two planes is defined as the angle between their normals (or its supplement, whichever is acute).

concepts.term: Every plane is a linear equation, and back
concepts.statement: **Theorem.** (a) Every plane has an equation $ax + by + cz = d$ with $\langle a, b, c\rangle \ne \mathbf{0}$. (b) Conversely, the solution set of any such equation is a plane with normal $\langle a, b, c\rangle$.
concepts.detail: Proof. (a) is the expansion above. For (b), fix any solution $P_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0)$, so $ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0 = d$. Subtracting, every solution $P$ satisfies $a(x - x_0) + b(y - y_0) + c(z - z_0) = 0$, i.e. $\mathbf{n} \cdot \overrightarrow{P_0P} = 0$ with $\mathbf{n} = \langle a, b, c\rangle$: the solution set is exactly the plane through $P_0$ with normal $\mathbf{n}$. This converse is why "graph of a linear equation in three variables" and "plane" are synonyms.

concepts.term: Distance from a point to a plane
concepts.statement: The distance from $P_1 = (x_1, y_1, z_1)$ to the plane $ax + by + cz + d = 0$ is $$D = \frac{|ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}.$$
concepts.detail: Derivation: take any point $P_0$ on the plane and drop the perpendicular from $P_1$. The distance is the absolute value of the **scalar projection** of $\overrightarrow{P_0P_1}$ onto the unit normal $\mathbf{n}/|\mathbf{n}|$: $D = |\operatorname{comp}_{\mathbf{n}} \overrightarrow{P_0P_1}| = |\mathbf{n} \cdot \overrightarrow{P_0P_1}|/|\mathbf{n}|$. Choosing $P_0$ conveniently and expanding the dot product, the numerator becomes $|ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d|$ — the plane's left side evaluated at the point, whose sign even tells you which side of the plane the point is on.

concepts.statement: For skew lines $\mathbf{r}_1 + t\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2 + s\mathbf{v}_2$, the direction perpendicular to both is $\mathbf{v}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_2 \ne \mathbf{0}$ (it exists precisely because the lines are not parallel). With $P_1, P_2$ one point on each line, the distance between them is $$D = \frac{|\overrightarrow{P_1P_2} \cdot (\mathbf{v}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_2)|}{|\mathbf{v}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_2|}.$$
concepts.detail: The numerator is the absolute scalar triple product — the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overrightarrow{P_1P_2}, \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2$ — and dividing by the area $|\mathbf{v}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_2|$ of the base leaves the height: exactly the length of the common perpendicular. Every piece of Sections 12.3 and 12.4 is used at once: the cross product to find the common perpendicular direction, the dot product to measure along it.

figures.caption: The vector equation of a line: from the point $P_0$ with position vector $\mathbf{r}_0$, the direction vector $\mathbf{v}$ carries the tip of $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{r}_0 + t\mathbf{v}$ along the line — backward for $t < 0$, forward for $t > 0$. One point and one direction: the least a line can be known by.

examples.title: Three forms of one line
examples.problem: Find the vector, parametric and symmetric equations of the line through $P_0(1,\ -2,\ 3)$ parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle 4,\ 2,\ -5\rangle$, and decide whether $(9,\ 2,\ -7)$ lies on it.

steps.label: Vector form
steps.text: With $\mathbf{r}_0 = \langle 1, -2, 3\rangle$: $\mathbf{r} = \langle 1, -2, 3\rangle + t\langle 4, 2, -5\rangle$.

steps.label: Parametric form
steps.text: Component by component: $x = 1 + 4t$, $y = -2 + 2t$, $z = 3 - 5t$.

steps.label: Symmetric form
steps.text: Solve each for $t$ and equate: $\frac{x - 1}{4} = \frac{y + 2}{2} = \frac{z - 3}{-5}$ (mind the signs: $y - (-2) = y + 2$).

steps.label: Test the point
steps.text: From $x$: $t = (9 - 1)/4 = 2$. Check $y$: $-2 + 2(2) = 2$ ✓. Check $z$: $3 - 5(2) = -7$ ✓. The same $t = 2$ satisfies all three — the point is on the line.

examples.result: All three descriptions of the same line; $(9, 2, -7)$ is the point at $t = 2$, one full direction-step beyond $2\mathbf{v}$ from $P_0$.

examples.title: A plane through three points
examples.problem: Find the plane through $P(1,\ 3,\ 2)$, $Q(3,\ -1,\ -6)$ and $R(5,\ 2,\ 1)$.

steps.label: Two spanning vectors
steps.text: $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \langle 2, -4, -8\rangle$ and $\overrightarrow{PR} = \langle 4, -1, -1\rangle$ both lie in the plane.

steps.label: Normal by cross product
steps.text: $\overrightarrow{PQ} \times \overrightarrow{PR} = \langle (-4)(-1) - (-8)(-1),\ (-8)(4) - (2)(-1),\ (2)(-1) - (-4)(4)\rangle = \langle -4, -30, 14\rangle$, which simplifies to $\mathbf{n} = \langle 2, 15, -7\rangle$.

steps.label: Verify with the third point
steps.text: Check $R$: $2(5) + 15(2) - 7(1) = 10 + 30 - 7 = 33$ ✓ — and $Q$ gives $6 - 15 + 42 = 33$ ✓. All three points lie on the plane.

examples.result: $2x + 15y - 7z = 33$, with normal $\langle 2, 15, -7\rangle$ — the cross product of any two in-plane edge vectors is the standard way to produce a normal.

examples.title: Distance from a point to a plane
examples.problem: How far is the point $(1,\ 2,\ 3)$ from the plane $2x - 3y + 6z - 1 = 0$, and which side of the plane is it on?

steps.label: Plug into the formula
steps.text: The denominator is the normal's length: $\sqrt{2^2 + (-3)^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{49} = 7$.

steps.label: Read the sign
steps.text: The left side evaluates to $+13 > 0$; the origin evaluates to $-1 < 0$. The point sits on the opposite side of the plane from the origin, at distance $\frac{13}{7} \approx 1.86$.

examples.result: Distance $\frac{13}{7}$, on the far side from the origin — the sign of $ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0 + d$ is a side-detector, and its magnitude over $|\mathbf{n}|$ is the exact distance.

examples.title: Where a line pierces a plane
examples.problem: Find the point where the line $x = 1 + 2t$, $y = 2 - t$, $z = 3 + t$ meets the plane $x + 2y + 3z = 6$.

steps.label: Substitute the line into the plane
steps.text: $(1 + 2t) + 2(2 - t) + 3(3 + t) = 6$ — the line's point travels, and we want the instant it satisfies the plane equation.

examples.result: The line pierces the plane at $\left(-\frac{13}{3},\ \frac{14}{3},\ \frac{1}{3}\right)$ — one linear equation in one unknown; the parameter is the price of reducing geometry to algebra.

keyTakeaways: A line is a point and a direction: $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + t\mathbf{v}$, with parametric forms $x = x_0 + at$, $y = y_0 + bt$, $z = z_0 + ct$ and symmetric form $\frac{x - x_0}{a} = \frac{y - y_0}{b} = \frac{z - z_0}{c}$ (zero components handled separately).

A plane is a point and a normal: $\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) = 0$, equivalently $ax + by + cz = d$ with $\mathbf{n} = \langle a, b, c\rangle$; conversely every linear equation in $x, y, z$ draws a plane.
Planes are parallel when their normals are proportional, perpendicular when their normals are orthogonal; the angle between planes is the angle between normals.
Distance from point to plane: $D = \frac{|ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0 + d|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$ — a scalar projection of any connecting vector onto the unit normal.

Skew lines are a genuinely spatial phenomenon; their common perpendicular has direction $\mathbf{v}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_2$, and the distance between them is a scalar triple product divided by an area.
Lines and planes intersect (or fail to) by pure algebra: substitute the parametric line into the plane equation and solve the single resulting equation in $t$.

quiz.q: The line through $(2,\ 1,\ -3)$ and $(5,\ 1,\ -3)$ has direction vector:
quiz.explanation: Subtract: $\langle 5 - 2,\ 1 - 1,\ -3 - (-3)\rangle = \langle 3, 0, 0\rangle$ — the line runs parallel to the $x$-axis with $y$ and $z$ frozen.

quiz.q: Which point lies on the line $\frac{x - 1}{4} = \frac{y + 2}{2} = \frac{z - 3}{-5}$?
quiz.explanation: At $(9, 2, -7)$: $(9-1)/4 = 2$, $(2+2)/2 = 2$, $(-7-3)/(-5) = 2$ — all three ratios equal $t = 2$, so the point is on the line. (The point $(1, -2, 3)$ also lies on it at $t = 0$, but option 3 says "only", which is false.)

quiz.q: A normal vector to the plane through $(1,3,2)$, $(3,-1,-6)$ and $(5,2,1)$ is:
quiz.explanation: The edge vectors $\langle 2,-4,-8\rangle$ and $\langle 4,-1,-1\rangle$ span the plane; their cross product $\langle -4, -30, 14\rangle$ is the normal, which scales to $\langle 2, 15, -7\rangle$. The edge vectors themselves lie IN the plane, so they cannot be normals.

quiz.q: The plane $x - 2y + 3z = 5$ is parallel to the plane:
quiz.explanation: Normals $\langle 1,-2,3\rangle$ and $\langle 2,-4,6\rangle$ are proportional ($\times 2$), and the constants $5 \ne 10$ differ, so the planes are parallel and distinct. Identical normals with equal constants would be the same plane.

quiz.q: The planes $x + y + z = 1$ and $x + y - 2z = 1$ are:
quiz.explanation: Normals $\langle 1,1,1\rangle$ and $\langle 1,1,-2\rangle$: dot product $1 + 1 - 2 = 0$, so the normals are orthogonal and the planes are perpendicular. Non-proportional normals also guarantee they meet (in a line).

quiz.q: The distance from $(1,\ 2,\ 3)$ to the plane $2x - 3y + 6z - 1 = 0$ is:
quiz.explanation: Numerator $|2 - 6 + 18 - 1| = 13$; denominator $\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$; distance $13/7 \approx 1.86$. Note $\sqrt{49} = 7$, so the last option is just a distractor phrasing of the same thing incorrectly.

quiz.q: The angle between the planes $x + y + z = 1$ and $x - 2y + 3z = 1$ satisfies $\cos\theta = $
quiz.explanation: Normals $\langle 1,1,1\rangle$ and $\langle 1,-2,3\rangle$: $\cos\theta = \frac{|1 - 2 + 3|}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{14}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{42}}$, giving $\theta \approx 72°$.

quiz.q: The lines $x = 1 + t,\ y = 2 - t,\ z = t$ and $x = 2 - s,\ y = 1 + 2s,\ z = 4 + s$ are:
quiz.explanation: Directions $\langle 1,-1,1\rangle$ and $\langle -1,2,1\rangle$ are not proportional (not parallel). Solving $x$ and $z$: $1 + t = 2 - s$ and $t = 4 + s$ give $t = 2.5$, $s = -1.5$; checking $y$: $2 - 2.5 = -0.5$ but $1 + 2(-1.5) = -2$ — no agreement. The lines miss each other: skew.

quiz.q: The line $x = 1 + 2t,\ y = 2 - t,\ z = 3 + t$ meets the plane $x + 2y + 3z = 6$ at:
For skew lines with directions $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$, the direction of their common perpendicular is:
quiz.explanation: The cross product is perpendicular to both direction vectors at once — exactly what a segment meeting both lines at right angles requires. It is nonzero precisely when the lines are not parallel.

depth.title: Lines, planes and their arithmetic

blocks.heading: The point-to-plane distance, honestly
blocks.body: Start from the projection picture. Choose any point $P_0$ on the plane $ax + by + cz + d = 0$ and let $P_1$ be the external point. The sought distance is the component of $\overrightarrow{P_0P_1}$ along the normal direction $\mathbf{n} = \langle a, b, c\rangle$: $D = \left| \frac{\mathbf{n} \cdot \overrightarrow{P_0P_1}}{|\mathbf{n}|} \right| = \left| \frac{a(x_1 - x_0) + b(y_1 - y_0) + c(z_1 - z_0)}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}} \right|$. Since $P_0$ lies on the plane, $ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0 = -d$, and the numerator becomes $|ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d|$: the plane's left-hand side, evaluated at the point. The derivation shows the formula is nothing but Section 12.3's scalar projection wearing plane clothing — and it generalizes verbatim to $n$ dimensions, where it becomes the distance from a point to a hyperplane.

blocks.heading: The distance between skew lines
blocks.body: Let the lines be $P_1 + t\mathbf{v}_1$ and $P_2 + s\mathbf{v}_2$. The squared distance between a generic pair of points is $q(t,s) = |\overrightarrow{P_1P_2} + t\mathbf{v}_1 - s\mathbf{v}_2|^2$; setting both partial derivatives $\partial q/\partial t$ and $\partial q/\partial s$ to zero yields the normal equations $\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot (\overrightarrow{P_1P_2} + t\mathbf{v}_1 - s\mathbf{v}_2) = 0$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 \cdot (\overrightarrow{P_1P_2} + t\mathbf{v}_1 - s\mathbf{v}_2) = 0$ — the closest connecting segment is perpendicular to both lines. Solving and simplifying collapses the minimal distance to $|\overrightarrow{P_1P_2} \cdot (\mathbf{v}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_2)|/|\mathbf{v}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_2|$: the height of the parallelepiped whose base is spanned by the two directions. This is least squares in miniature — the same normal equations Gauss used for orbits.

blocks.heading: Linear equations are planes
blocks.body: The correspondence is exact: the graph of $ax + by + cz = d$ (with $\langle a,b,c\rangle \ne \mathbf{0}$) is the plane through any one of its solutions with normal $\langle a, b, c\rangle$; and every plane arises this way. The same theorem holds in every dimension — the solution set of one linear equation in $n$ unknowns is an $(n-1)$-dimensional hyperplane, and the coefficient vector is its normal. Systems of linear equations then ask where hyperplanes meet: two planes in space meet in a line, three in a point — or in nothing, when the algebra reports inconsistency that geometry calls parallel.

blocks.heading: Normals in computer graphics
blocks.body: Real-time 3D lives on this section's arithmetic. Every triangle of a mesh carries a normal (the cross product of two edges — Example 2's computation run billions of times per second). Lambert's lighting law shades a surface by $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{L}$, the cosine between normal and light direction, which is why faces turn dark as they turn away. **Backface culling** discards a triangle when $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} > 0$ (its normal points away from the camera, so it must be on the far side of the object). And ray tracing intersects a view ray $\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$ with a plane by exactly Example 4's substitution: $t = \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{o})/(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d})$, then checks the hit point against the triangle's edges.

blocks.heading: Robotics and collision axes
blocks.body: A robot arm's rotational joints have axes — lines in space — and the mathematics of screw motion pairs each rotation axis with a sliding along it. Two successive rotations about skew axes compose to a rotation about a third skew axis plus a translation, computed with exactly the common-perpendicular machinery of this section. In robotics this is the theory of screws (Ball, 1900; modern formulations via dual quaternions); in everyday terms it is why your shoulder-then-elbow motion moves your hand in an arc no single joint explains.

blocks.heading: Why skewness needs three dimensions
blocks.body: Count degrees of freedom. A line in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has $2n - 2$ parameters (a point on it up to sliding, plus a direction up to scale); forcing two lines to share a point imposes $n - 1$... in $\mathbb{R}^3$ two generic lines each have 4 parameters and the meeting condition is codimension 2, so generically they miss. In the plane, two non-parallel lines must meet — there is no room to dodge. In $\mathbb{R}^4$ and beyond, skewness is generic even for pairs of lines in "general position". The pattern is worth internalizing: incidence questions in geometry are dimension counts in disguise, a principle that grows into intersection theory.

depth.title: Hyperplanes, duality, and beyond

blocks.heading: Hyperplanes and machine learning
blocks.body: Replace "plane" by **hyperplane** — the set $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} = b$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ — and this section's geometry becomes the geometry of data. A linear classifier labels points by the sign of $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} - b$, i.e. by which side of the hyperplane they fall on: the two sides of a plane, made into a decision. The support vector machine finds the separating hyperplane that maximizes the margin $2/|\mathbf{w}|$ between the classes — the point-to-plane distance formula of this section is literally the objective. The separating hyperplane theorem (two disjoint convex sets can be split by a hyperplane, proved by projecting onto the segment of closest approach — the same projection argument as the distance derivation) is the load-bearing result of convex analysis and optimization duality.

blocks.heading: Affine geometry
blocks.body: This section has quietly been doing **affine geometry**: the study of points, lines and planes with no notion of angle or distance, only incidence and parallelism. The vector equation $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + t\mathbf{v}$ is affine, not linear — it does not pass through the origin unless $\mathbf{r}_0 = \mathbf{0}$. The plane through three points is the set of **barycentric combinations** $\alpha P + \beta Q + \gamma R$ with $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1$ — the weights are the triangle's barycentric coordinates, which is how graphics cards decide which triangle a pixel belongs to (every point of the plane is a unique affine combination of the three vertices, and the weights interpolate color and depth). Barycentric coordinates have themselves become a research field — generalized barycentric coordinates for polygons and meshes power modern mesh deformation and finite elements.

blocks.heading: Duality and incidence
blocks.body: In the projective plane, points and lines are interchangeable: the dual of "two points determine a line" is "two lines determine a point". The duality maps a point to its set of incident lines and back, and it converts hard incidence questions about points into dual questions about hyperplanes. The **Szemerédi–Trotter theorem** bounds how many incidences $n$ points and $n$ lines can share ($O(n^{4/3})$ — the grid-and-lattice construction shows the bound is tight), and its proof, the crossing-number method of Székely, is one of the pillars of discrete geometry. The exact constant remains open, and every hyperplane variant — incidences with hyperplanes in higher dimensions, unit-distance problems, distinct-distances (the Erdős problem Guth and Katz nearly closed) — is an active frontier where this chapter's humble plane meets combinatorics.

intro: Curves were easy to draw and hard to describe; surfaces are the reverse — a single equation in $x$, $y$ and $z$ describes a surface, but seeing which one takes training. This section supplies the training. The two great tools are the **trace** (slice the surface by a plane and read the curve that appears) and the **classification of quadric surfaces** — the complete census of second-degree equations, which turns out to be exactly six shapes plus their rotated and shifted relatives. The parabola, ellipse and hyperbola of single-variable calculus all return, extruded and revolved into the third dimension, joined by two newcomers: the saddle that dips and rises along different directions, and the hyperboloids that curve outward in opposite senses.
objectives: Recognize cylinders — surfaces generated by lines moving parallel to a missing variable — and identify their ruling direction
Use the trace technique: slice a surface by coordinate planes and parallel planes to identify it
Sketch and classify the six quadric surfaces: ellipsoid, elliptic paraboloid, hyperbolic paraboloid, elliptic cone, and the two hyperboloids
Read off axis intercepts and the axis of symmetry from a quadric equation
Complete the square to identify quadrics that are shifted off the origin

concepts.statement: A **cylinder** is a surface generated by a straight line (**ruling**) that moves parallel to a fixed axis while tracing a plane curve. Algebraically, an equation with a missing variable draws a cylinder parallel to that variable's axis: $z = x^2$ is a **parabolic cylinder** (a parabola extruded along the $y$-axis), $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ a circular cylinder along $z$.
concepts.detail: The rule is mechanical: whatever variable does not appear, the surface is constant along — every point $(x_0, z_0)$ on the parabola $z = x^2$ in the $xz$-plane lifts to the entire line of points $(x_0, y, z_0)$, all $y$. Cylinders over ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas inherit their names from the curve. Note that in 3D "cylinder" no longer means circular — any extruded curve qualifies.

concepts.statement: A **trace** of a surface is its intersection with a plane — usually the coordinate planes $x = 0$, $y = 0$, $z = 0$, or parallels like $z = k$. To identify a surface: set each variable to zero (and to convenient constants) in its equation, recognize the resulting plane curves, and assemble the shape from its slices.
concepts.detail: The traces are the diagnostic fingerprints: an elliptic paraboloid has ellipses in horizontal planes and parabolas in vertical ones; a hyperboloid of one sheet has ellipses horizontally and hyperbolas vertically; a cone has ellipses shrinking to a point. Sketching a quadric well is drawing three or four informative traces and letting the reader's eye interpolate between them.

concepts.statement: A **quadric surface** is the graph of a second-degree equation in $x$, $y$, $z$. In standard position it is one of six types: the **ellipsoid** $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} + \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$; the **elliptic paraboloid** $z = \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2}$; the **hyperbolic paraboloid** (saddle) $z = \frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{x^2}{a^2}$; the **elliptic cone** $\frac{z^2}{c^2} = \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2}$; the **hyperboloid of one sheet** $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$; and the **hyperboloid of two sheets** $\frac{z^2}{c^2} - \frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.
concepts.detail: The variable carrying the minus sign (or the squared-away variable of the paraboloids) names the **axis**: the one-sheeted hyperboloid above opens around the $z$-axis; its two-sheeted relative opens along the $z$-axis. Shifting the center away from the origin replaces $x$ by $(x - x_0)$ everywhere, and the standard completing-the-square drill recovers the center.

concepts.statement: The **ellipsoid** has all-positive signs; its traces are all ellipses, with intercepts $(\pm a, 0, 0)$, $(0, \pm b, 0)$, $(0, 0, \pm c)$, and it is bounded. The **elliptic paraboloid** $z = \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2}$ opens along the positive $z$-axis with a minimum at the origin; horizontal traces are ellipses growing with height, vertical traces are parabolas.
concepts.detail: If two semiaxes of an ellipsoid are equal it is a spheroid (revolved); if all three are equal, a sphere. The elliptic paraboloid is the shape of satellite dishes and headlights precisely because of the reflection property in this section's deeper results: rays entering parallel to the axis all reflect through one point — the focus.

concepts.statement: The **hyperbolic paraboloid** $z = \frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{x^2}{a^2}$ curves upward along the $y$-direction and downward along the $x$-direction. The trace $z = k$ is the hyperbola $\frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{x^2}{a^2} = k$ (opening along $y$ for $k > 0$, along $x$ for $k < 0$, degenerating to two lines at $k = 0$); vertical traces are parabolas of opposite concavity.
concepts.detail: At the origin the surface rises in one direction and falls in the perpendicular one — the origin is neither a maximum nor a minimum but a **saddle point**, the 3D avatar of the second-derivative test's failure case $f_{xx}f_{yy} < f_{xy}^2$. The shape is the Pringles chip, and near its center it approximates the minimal surface a soap film stretches to — which is why saddle-shaped roofs and saddle joints appear wherever curvature must fight load.

concepts.statement: The **elliptic cone** $\frac{z^2}{c^2} = \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2}$ has elliptical traces shrinking to the vertex at the origin, with straight lines (the generators) lying wholly on the surface. The **hyperboloid of one sheet** (one minus sign) is connected — a cooling tower — and is also a ruled surface. The **hyperboloid of two sheets** (minus signs on two variables, constant moved) separates into two pieces, one above $z = c$, one below $z = -c$.
concepts.detail: A quick discriminator for $Ax^2 + By^2 + Cz^2 + J = 0$: all signs agreeing after normalization gives an ellipsoid (if the constant has the right sign), one disagreement gives the one-sheeted hyperboloid, two disagreements the two-sheeted, and $J = 0$ with one disagreement gives the cone between them — in fact the cone is the limiting surface the hyperboloids approach as their waist or gap closes.

concepts.statement: A shifted quadric is returned to standard position by completing the square in each variable: $x^2 - 2x = (x-1)^2 - 1$, so an equation like $x^2 + 2y^2 + z^2 - 2x + 8y - 2z = 1$ becomes $$(x - 1)^2 + 2(y + 2)^2 + (z - 1)^2 = 11$$ — an ellipsoid centered at $(1,\ -2,\ 1)$.
concepts.detail: The drill is exactly the 2D one, done three times: gather each variable's linear and quadratic terms, add and subtract the square of half the linear coefficient, and collect the leftover constants on the right. What survives on the left is a sum of shifted squares; comparing signs and constants with the six standard forms finishes the identification. Rotation of axes (when an $xy$-term is present) is a linear-algebra matter — the eigenvalue discussion in the deeper results.

figures.caption: The ellipsoid $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} + \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$ with its traces: every horizontal slice is an ellipse, shrinking from the $z = 0$ waist ellipse to points at the intercepts $(0, 0, \pm c)$. All traces of an ellipsoid are ellipses — that is its fingerprint.

examples.title: Identifying an ellipsoid
examples.problem: Describe and sketch $x^2 + \frac{y^2}{9} + \frac{z^2}{4} = 1$.

steps.label: Compare with the standard form
steps.text: All three variables squared with plus signs and total $1$: an **ellipsoid** with $a = 1$, $b = 3$, $c = 2$.

steps.label: Read the intercepts
steps.text: Setting pairs of variables to zero: $(\pm 1, 0, 0)$, $(0, \pm 3, 0)$, $(0, 0, \pm 2)$ — six axis crossings.

steps.label: Check the traces
steps.text: In the plane $z = k$ (for $|k| \le 2$): $x^2 + \frac{y^2}{9} = 1 - \frac{k^2}{4}$, an ellipse shrinking as $|k|$ grows to $2$; the $z = 0$ waist is the largest, $x^2 + \frac{y^2}{9} = 1$. Vertical traces like $x = 0$ give $\frac{y^2}{9} + \frac{z^2}{4} = 1$, also ellipses.

examples.result: An ellipsoid stretched farthest along $y$ (semi-axis 3), with all traces ellipses — a rugbly ball around the origin.

examples.title: Identifying an elliptic paraboloid
examples.problem: Identify $z = 4x^2 + y^2$ and describe its traces.

steps.label: Shape of the equation
steps.text: One linear variable ($z$) equals a sum of positive squares: an **elliptic paraboloid** opening upward along $+z$, with vertex at the origin.

steps.label: Horizontal trace
steps.text: At $z = 4$: $4x^2 + y^2 = 4$, i.e. $x^2 + \frac{y^2}{4} = 1$ — an ellipse with semi-axes $1$ (along $x$) and $2$ (along $y$). Higher slices give bigger ellipses.

steps.label: Vertical traces
steps.text: At $y = 0$: $z = 4x^2$, a parabola four times as steep as $z = x^2$; at $x = 0$: $z = y^2$, a gentler one. The bowl is steeper across than along.

examples.result: An upward elliptic paraboloid, steeper in the $x$-direction, every horizontal trace an ellipse growing with height.

examples.title: A hyperboloid of one sheet
examples.problem: Identify $\frac{x^2}{4} + y^2 - \frac{z^2}{4} = 1$ and describe its traces.

steps.label: Count the minus signs
steps.text: Two plus signs and one minus, equalling $+1$: a **hyperboloid of one sheet** — a connected surface, a cooling tower.

steps.label: Name the axis
steps.text: The minus sign sits on $z$, so the axis of the surface is the $z$-axis; the smallest horizontal trace is at $z = 0$.

steps.label: Horizontal traces
steps.text: At height $z = k$: $\frac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1 + \frac{k^2}{4}$ — ellipses, smallest at the waist $z = 0$ and growing in both directions.

steps.label: Vertical trace
steps.text: At $x = 0$: $y^2 - \frac{z^2}{4} = 1$, a hyperbola opening along $y$ — the tower's silhouette in profile.

examples.result: One-sheeted hyperboloid about the $z$-axis: elliptical belts growing away from the waist, hyperbolic profiles containing it — and (deeper result) straight lines lying wholly on it.

examples.title: Completing the square three times
examples.problem: Identify $x^2 + 2y^2 + z^2 - 2x + 8y - 2z = 1$.

steps.label: Read off the surface
steps.text: A sum of shifted positive squares equalling a positive constant: an **ellipsoid** centered at $(1,\ -2,\ 1)$, with semiaxes $\sqrt{11}$, $\sqrt{11/2}$, $\sqrt{11}$.

examples.result: A shifted ellipsoid about $(1, -2, 1)$ — the three completing-the-square moves return any shifted quadric to standard position.

keyTakeaways: A missing variable means a cylinder: the surface is the named curve extruded along the missing axis.
The trace technique — slice by coordinate and parallel planes — identifies any surface from its cross-sections.

The six quadrics: ellipsoid (all ellipses), elliptic paraboloid (ellipses + parabolas, bowl), hyperbolic paraboloid (saddle, parabolas both ways, hyperbola traces), cone (ellipses through a point), hyperboloids of one sheet (connected, cooling tower) and two sheets (two pieces).
The variable carrying the minus sign names the axis of a hyperboloid; the linear variable names the opening direction of a paraboloid.
Shifted quadrics are identified by completing the square in each variable — three 2D drills and a read-off.
Hyperboloids of one sheet and cones are ruled surfaces — straight lines lie entirely on them, which is why they are built from straight steel beams.

quiz.q: The equation $z = x^2$ in three-dimensional space draws:
options: a parabolic cylinder with rulings parallel to the $y$-axis
a parabolic cylinder with rulings parallel to the $z$-axis
quiz.explanation: The variable $y$ is missing, so every point of the parabola extends into a full line of constant $x, z$ and varying $y$: a parabolic cylinder ruled along $y$.

quiz.q: The intercepts of the ellipsoid $x^2 + \frac{y^2}{9} + \frac{z^2}{4} = 1$ on the $y$-axis are:
quiz.explanation: Set $x = z = 0$: $\frac{y^2}{9} = 1$ gives $y = \pm 3$. The denominators are squared semi-axes, not the semi-axes' reciprocals.

quiz.q: The surface $z = x^2 + 4y^2$ has traces:
options: ellipses in horizontal planes, parabolas in vertical planes
hyperbolas in horizontal planes, parabolas in vertical planes
parabolas in horizontal planes, lines in vertical planes
quiz.explanation: At $z = k > 0$: $x^2 + 4y^2 = k$, an ellipse; at $x = 0$ or $y = 0$: a parabola in $z$. That signature — ellipses and parabolas — is the elliptic paraboloid.

quiz.q: The trace of $\frac{x^2}{4} + y^2 - \frac{z^2}{4} = 1$ in the plane $z = 2$ is:
quiz.explanation: Substituting $z = 2$: $\frac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1 + 1 = 2$, i.e. $\frac{x^2}{8} + \frac{y^2}{2} = 1$ — an ellipse, as every horizontal trace of a one-sheeted hyperboloid must be.

quiz.q: A cooling-tower shape is best modeled by:
quiz.explanation: The cooling tower has a circular waist and flares outward both up and down while staying connected — the one-sheeted hyperboloid, built from straight steel rulings lying on the surface.

quiz.q: The axis of the hyperboloid $\frac{x^2}{9} - \frac{y^2}{4} + \frac{z^2}{4} = 1$ is:
quiz.explanation: The minus sign sits on $y$: the surface opens around the $y$-axis. Its horizontal $y = k$ traces are ellipses $\frac{x^2}{9} + \frac{z^2}{4} = 1 + \frac{k^2}{4}$, smallest at the waist $y = 0$.

quiz.q: In the saddle $z = x^2 - y^2$, the trace in the plane $x = 0$ is:
quiz.explanation: Setting $x = 0$ leaves $z = -y^2$: a parabola opening downward, while the $y = 0$ trace $z = x^2$ opens upward. Opposite concavities in perpendicular planes are the saddle's defining signature.

quiz.q: Completing the square shows that $x^2 + 2y^2 + z^2 - 2x + 8y - 2z = 1$ is:
options: an ellipsoid centered at the origin
quiz.explanation: The completed form is $(x-1)^2 + 2(y+2)^2 + (z-1)^2 = 11$: a positive-definite sum of shifted squares equal to a positive constant — an ellipsoid about $(1, -2, 1)$. (Mind the sign: $y + 2$ means the center's $y$-coordinate is $-2$.)

quiz.q: The surface $z^2 = \frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{y^2}{9}$ is:
quiz.explanation: A squared variable equals a sum of positive squares: at each height $z = k$ the trace is the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{4k^2} + \frac{y^2}{9k^2} = 1$, shrinking linearly to the vertex — an elliptic (double) cone about the $z$-axis.

quiz.q: Which surface is a ruled surface — containing straight lines lying wholly in it?
quiz.explanation: Both one-sheeted hyperboloids and cones carry families of straight rulings (the hyperboloid two families, doubly ruled); the ellipsoid and paraboloid are strictly curved — no line segment of either lies in its surface.

quiz.q: The surface $x^{2} + y^{2} - z^{2} = -1$ is:
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restate the task as reading the sign pattern of $\frac{x^{2}}{1} + \frac{y^{2}}{1} - \frac{z^{2}}{1} = -1$. Step 2: Recall the key census that one minus sign with constant $-1$ separates into two pieces along the axis of the isolated variable. Step 3: Check horizontal traces as $x^{2} + y^{2} = z^{2} - 1$, empty for $|z| < 1$ and elliptical for $|z| > 1$. Step 4: Note the gap $|z| < 1$ splits the surface into upper and lower sheets about the $z$-axis. Step 5: The distractors fail since the cone needs constant $0$, the one-sheeted form needs constant $+1$, and the ellipsoid needs all plus signs. Step 6: Hence the surface is a hyperboloid of two sheets.

depth.title: Classification, curvature and structure

blocks.heading: Why exactly six quadrics
blocks.body: The general quadric $Ax^2 + By^2 + Cz^2 + Dxy + Ezx + Fyz + Gx + Hy + Iz + J = 0$ looks like it has ten shapes' worth of freedom, but almost all of it is disguise. Step one, eliminate the cross terms $Dxy, Ezx, Fyz$: they form the off-diagonal of a symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix, and the spectral theorem orthogonally diagonalizes it — geometrically, a rotation of axes kills every cross term. Step two, complete the square in whatever variables remain, translating the center to the origin. What survives is $\epsilon_1 \tilde{x}^2 + \epsilon_2 \tilde{y}^2 + \epsilon_3 \tilde{z}^2 = J$ with each $\epsilon_i \in \{+1, -1, 0\}$ — and counting the sign patterns (up to permuting variables and scaling) produces exactly the six nondegenerate shapes, plus cylinders and the degenerate empty set, points and lines. The classification is a theorem about diagonalizing quadratic forms, which is why the same six-family census reappears for conics, and again in relativity for the metric.

blocks.heading: Rulings on the one-sheeted hyperboloid
blocks.body: The hyperboloid $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$ contains two distinct families of straight lines, each line lying wholly in the surface, with exactly one line of each family through every surface point. The identity behind it: for any parameter $\lambda$, the intersection of the two planes $$\frac{x}{a} + \frac{z}{c} = \lambda\left(1 + \frac{y}{b}\right), \qquad \lambda\left(\frac{x}{a} - \frac{z}{c}\right) = 1 - \frac{y}{b}$$ lies on the hyperboloid, because multiplying the two left sides and the two right sides reproduces $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{z^2}{c^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ after cancellation. Varying $\lambda$ sweeps one family; $\lambda \to -1/\lambda$-style exchange gives the second.

blocks.heading: The paraboloid reflection property
blocks.body: Rays entering parallel to the axis of the paraboloid $z = \frac{r^2}{4f}$ all reflect through the focus $(0, 0, f)$. Proof for the 2D profile $z = \frac{x^2}{4f}$ (revolving preserves it): the tangent at $(x_0, z_0)$ has slope $\frac{dz}{dx} = \frac{x_0}{2f}$, so the tangent line makes angle $\alpha = \arctan\frac{x_0}{2f}$ with the horizontal. The focal segment from $(x_0, z_0)$ to $(0, f)$ has slope $\frac{z_0 - f}{x_0} = \frac{x_0^2/4f - f}{x_0} = \frac{x_0^2 - 4f^2}{4fx_0}$; elementary angle-chasing with $\tan 2\alpha = \frac{2(x_0/2f)}{1 - x_0^2/4f^2} = \frac{4fx_0}{4f^2 - x_0^2}$ shows the tangent bisects the angle between the incoming vertical ray and the focal segment (the two slopes are negatives), which is exactly the law of reflection. Hence every dish pointed at the sky concentrates the signal at one point — radio telescopes, satellite dishes and solar furnaces are this proof in steel.

blocks.heading: The saddle in the second-derivative test
blocks.body: For $f(x, y)$ with $f_x = f_y = 0$ at a critical point, the quadratic Taylor remainder is governed by the Hessian $H = \begin{pmatrix} f_{xx} & f_{xy} \\ f_{xy} & f_{yy} \end{pmatrix}$, and the test reads its eigenvalues: both positive — bowl up (minimum); both negative — bowl down; mixed signs — **saddle**, the hyperbolic paraboloid $z \approx \lambda_1 u^2 + \lambda_2 v^2$ with $\lambda_1 \lambda_2 < 0$ in rotated coordinates $u, v$. The discriminant $f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2$ is just $\det H$, the product of the eigenvalues. This section's surface is the local shape of every smooth function of two variables at a critical point: minima are elliptic paraboloids, saddles are hyperbolic paraboloids, and optimization lives or dies by the difference.

blocks.heading: Architecture of straight lines
blocks.body: Because the one-sheeted hyperboloid is ruled, a curved tower can be built from entirely straight beams: rotate each ruling about the axis and the envelope of the family is the hyperboloid. This is literally how cooling towers, Kobe Port Tower, Shukhov towers (Vladimir Shukhov's 1896 gridshell patents — the same mathematics done a century before CAD) and many airport roofs are constructed: steel straight, surface curved. The saddle, for its part, approximates a **minimal surface** near its center — soap films bounded by a square frame pull themselves into exactly that shape, minimizing area, which is why saddle-shaped shells are extraordinarily rigid for their weight (the Pringle).

blocks.heading: The cone as the boundary case
blocks.body: Squeeze the waist of a one-sheeted hyperboloid or close the gap of a two-sheeted one and both limits are the cone — algebraically, sending the constant $J$ to $0$ in $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{z^2}{c^2} = J$ passes through the cone at $J = 0$ and switches sheets at $J < 0$. The cone is the degenerate quadric separating the families, and it is also the asymptote surface of both hyperboloids: each hyperboloid hugs the cone's surface at infinity. This "cone between the hyperboloids" picture generalizes to cones over any curve — and the asymptotic cone of a hyperboloid is the 3D shadow of how hyperbolas carry their asymptote lines.

depth.title: Curvature, minimal surfaces, equivalence

blocks.heading: Gauss curvature sorts the zoo
blocks.body: Gauss curvature $K$ — the product of the two principal curvatures — divides this section's surfaces topologically. The ellipsoid and elliptic paraboloid have $K > 0$ everywhere (dome-like: both curvatures agree); the saddle has $K < 0$ everywhere (curvatures oppose); the cylinder and cone have $K = 0$ (flat in one direction — they can be unrolled to a plane without stretching, which is why cones and cylinders develop for sheet metal and maps). Gauss's **Theorema Egregium** says $K$ is intrinsic — measurable within the surface, unchanged by bending without stretching — so the sign of $K$ is a genuine birthmark, not a viewpoint artifact.

blocks.heading: From the saddle to minimal surfaces
blocks.body: The mean curvature $H$ averages the principal curvatures; surfaces with $H = 0$ everywhere are **minimal surfaces** — locally area-minimizing, and the physical shape of every soap film. The saddle $z = y^2 - x^2$ has $H = 0$ only at the origin, but a genuine minimal surface with boundary a wire square is the closely related saddle-shaped **Scherk-like** graph. The classical minimal surfaces (catenoid, helicoid; Costa's 1982 embedded example with its three-punctured-torus topology) all wear the local shape of this section's hyperbolic paraboloid, and Plateau's problem — prove that every closed wire bounds some minimal surface — was solved (Douglas and Radó, 1930s) by methods that grew into geometric measure theory.

blocks.heading: How many shapes, really
blocks.body: Euclidean classification says: six quadrics. But up to **projective** equivalence, all nondegenerate conics are one curve — the projective plane has no parallel lines, no distances, no circles vs hyperbolas; the ellipse, parabola and hyperbola differ only in how they sit relative to the line at infinity. The classification questions then sharpen: within affine geometry, the signature $(p, q)$ of the quadratic form is the complete invariant (Sylvester's law of inertia); within projective geometry even that collapses. Which classification is "right" depends on what the surface is for — and in the mathematics of general relativity, the level surfaces of the Minkowski metric's quadratic form are exactly hyperboloids: the two-sheeted hyperboloid is the shape of constant proper time from an event, and its asymptotic cone is the light cone. Whether the quadrics' appearance at the foundations of spacetime is bookkeeping or structure remains a matter of interpretation, not theorem.

intro: A plane curve, studied in Chapter 10 as a pair of parametric equations $x = f(t)$, $y = g(t)$, becomes far more powerful in space: a vector function $\mathbf{r}(t)$ bundles three component functions into a single moving arrow whose tip traces a **space curve**. This section defines vector functions, their domains and limits, and trains the eye on the most important example of the chapter — the circular helix — before the calculus machinery arrives in 13.2.
objectives: Write a vector function in component form $\mathbf{r}(t) = f(t)\,\mathbf{i} + g(t)\,\mathbf{j} + h(t)\,\mathbf{k}$ and find its domain
Sketch the space curve traced by a vector function, including the circular helix
Compute the limit of a vector function component by component
Parametrize the curve of intersection of two surfaces, such as a cylinder cut by an oblique plane
Connect space curves to the plane curves of Chapter 10 and the vectors of Chapter 12

concepts.statement: A **vector function** on a domain set $D$ assigns to each $t$ in $D$ a vector $\mathbf{r}(t)$. In component form, $$\mathbf{r}(t) = f(t)\,\mathbf{i} + g(t)\,\mathbf{j} + h(t)\,\mathbf{k} = \langle f(t),\ g(t),\ h(t)\rangle,$$ where $f$, $g$ and $h$ are real-valued component functions of the parameter $t$.
concepts.detail: Vector functions are the natural language of motion: if a particle sits at the point $(x, y, z)$ at time $t$, the arrow from the origin to the particle is exactly $\mathbf{r}(t)$. Everything from Chapter 12 about vectors — addition, dot and cross products, length — applies to these moving vectors at each fixed $t$.

concepts.statement: The **space curve** traced by $\mathbf{r}$ is the set of all points $(f(t), g(t), h(t))$ obtained by pinning the tail of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at the origin and following its tip as $t$ runs through $D$. The equations $x = f(t)$, $y = g(t)$, $z = h(t)$ are its **parametric equations**.
concepts.detail: Every curve in this chapter arises this way, and projecting the curve onto the coordinate planes (setting one coordinate to zero) is the standard trick for visualizing it: the projection shows the shadow, while the remaining coordinate shows how the curve lifts off that plane.

concepts.statement: The prototype space curve is $$\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos t\,\mathbf{i} + \sin t\,\mathbf{j} + t\,\mathbf{k},$$ a **circular helix**: its projection onto the $xy$-plane is the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, while the height $z = t$ rises at a constant rate, so the curve coils around the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 1$.
concepts.detail: Each time $t$ increases by $2\pi$ the point completes one turn and climbs $2\pi$ units — the **pitch** of the helix. DNA’s double helix, a spiral staircase and the thread of a screw all follow this family: $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle a\cos t, a\sin t, bt\rangle$ has radius $a$ and pitch $2\pi b$. In the book’s DNA exercise the radius is 10 angstroms and each turn rises 34 angstroms.

concepts.statement: The **domain** of $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t)\rangle$ is the intersection of the domains of $f$, $g$ and $h$: every component must be defined simultaneously.
concepts.detail: For example, $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \ln(1 - t),\ \sqrt{1 + t},\ 1/t\rangle$ requires $t < 1$ (logarithm), $t \ge -1$ (square root) and $t \ne 0$ (reciprocal), so the domain is $[-1, 0) \cup (0, 1)$ — exactly the same bookkeeping as for single-variable functions in Chapter 1.

concepts.term: Limits and continuity of vector functions
concepts.statement: If $\lim_{t \to a} f(t) = L_1$, $\lim_{t \to a} g(t) = L_2$ and $\lim_{t \to a} h(t) = L_3$, then $$\lim_{t \to a} \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle L_1, L_2, L_3\rangle.$$ The limit exists exactly when all three component limits exist.
concepts.detail: Because everything is componentwise, $\mathbf{r}$ is continuous at $a$ precisely when $f$, $g$ and $h$ are, and the limit laws (sum, product with a scalar, dot and cross product) carry over from Chapter 12 vector algebra unchanged.

concepts.term: Curves of intersection of two surfaces
concepts.statement: To parametrize the **intersection of two surfaces**, parametrize one surface and use the other equation to eliminate a variable: for the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ cut by the plane $y + z = 2$, put $x = \cos t$, $y = \sin t$ (the cylinder) and $z = 2 - \sin t$ (the plane), giving $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, 2 - \sin t\rangle$.
concepts.detail: This is the book’s standard technique (Stewart’s Section 13.1 worked example): one surface supplies a two-parameter description, the other cuts it down to one. Here the result is an ellipse wrapped around the cylinder — squashing that ellipse flat would leave the unit circle as its shadow.

examples.title: Analyzing a circular helix
examples.problem: Sketch the curve traced by $\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos t\,\mathbf{i} + \sin t\,\mathbf{j} + t\,\mathbf{k}$ and describe how it lies relative to the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 1$.

steps.label: Step 1: Read off the parametric equations
steps.text: The components are $x = \cos t$, $y = \sin t$ and $z = t$, so as $t$ flows the point circles in $x$ and $y$ while climbing steadily in $z$.

steps.label: Step 2: Project onto the $xy$-plane
steps.text: Because $x^2 + y^2 = \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$, the shadow of the curve is the unit circle: the curve lies on the cylinder of radius 1 about the $z$-axis, the way a thread lies on a spool.

steps.label: Step 3: Watch the height
steps.text: The height $z = t$ increases at the constant rate of one unit per unit of $t$, so instead of closing up like the circle, the curve spirals upward forever.

steps.label: Step 4: Measure one revolution
steps.text: As $t$ runs from $0$ to $2\pi$ the point starts at $(1, 0, 0)$, makes exactly one full revolution, and ends at $(1, 0, 2\pi)$: the climb per turn (the pitch) is $2\pi$.

examples.result: The curve is a circular helix coiling around the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, rising $2\pi$ units per revolution — the book’s defining picture of a space curve.

examples.title: Finding the domain of a vector function
examples.problem: Find the domain of $\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle \ln(1 - t),\ \sqrt{1 + t},\ \dfrac{1}{t} \right\rangle$.

steps.label: Step 1: First component
steps.text: $\ln(1 - t)$ is defined only when $1 - t > 0$, that is $t < 1$.

steps.label: Step 2: Second component
steps.text: $\sqrt{1 + t}$ requires $1 + t \ge 0$, that is $t \ge -1$.

steps.label: Step 3: Third component
steps.text: $1/t$ requires $t \ne 0$.

steps.label: Step 4: Intersect
steps.text: All three conditions must hold at once: $t \ge -1$ and $t < 1$ give $[-1, 1)$, and removing $t = 0$ splits this into two intervals.

examples.result: The domain is $[-1, 0) \cup (0, 1)$: a union of two intervals, exactly as domains of single-variable functions behaved in Chapter 1.

examples.title: Parametrizing a curve of intersection
examples.problem: The cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ intersects the plane $y + z = 2$ in a curve $C$. Find a vector function that traces $C$.

steps.label: Step 1: Parametrize the cylinder
steps.text: Every point of the cylinder has $x = \cos t$, $y = \sin t$ for some $t$, with $0 \le t \le 2\pi$ covering it once.

steps.label: Step 2: Use the plane
steps.text: Points of $C$ must also satisfy $y + z = 2$, so $z = 2 - y = 2 - \sin t$.

steps.label: Step 3: Assemble and verify
steps.text: Take $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, 2 - \sin t\rangle$. Check: $x^2 + y^2 = \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$ and $y + z = \sin t + 2 - \sin t = 2$, so the curve lies on both surfaces.

steps.label: Step 4: Identify the shape
steps.text: Projected onto the $yz$-plane the curve satisfies $z = 2 - y$ (a segment), so $C$ is an ellipse wrapped around the cylinder — a slanted slice of a circular tube.

examples.result: $\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos t\,\mathbf{i} + \sin t\,\mathbf{j} + (2 - \sin t)\,\mathbf{k}$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, traces the ellipse once.

keyTakeaways: A vector function $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t)\rangle$ packages three parametric equations into one object; its domain is the intersection of the component domains.
Pinning the tail of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at the origin, its tip traces the space curve; projections onto the coordinate planes are the key visualization tool.
The circular helix $\langle \cos t, \sin t, t\rangle$ winds around the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ with pitch $2\pi$.
Limits — and therefore continuity — of vector functions are computed componentwise and exist exactly when all three component limits exist.
To parametrize the intersection of two surfaces, parametrize one surface and eliminate a variable with the other equation.

quiz.q: The curve traced by $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, 3t\rangle$ lies on which surface?
quiz.explanation: The $x$ and $y$ components satisfy $x^2 + y^2 = \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$, so the curve coils around the cylinder of radius 1, climbing $6\pi$ units per revolution.

quiz.q: What is the domain of $\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle \sqrt{4 - t^2},\ \ln(t + 1) \right\rangle$?
quiz.explanation: The square root needs $|t| \le 2$, the logarithm needs $t > -1$; the intersection is $-1 < t \le 2$, written $(-1, 2]$.

quiz.q: Which vector function parametrizes the curve of intersection of the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ and the plane $z = y + 1$?
quiz.explanation: The cylinder of radius 2 forces $x = 2\cos t$, $y = 2\sin t$; the plane then gives $z = y + 1 = 2\sin t + 1$. Only the third option satisfies both equations.

quiz.q: The limit $\lim_{t \to a} \mathbf{r}(t)$ exists precisely when:
options: At least one of the component limits exists
The limit of the length $|\mathbf{r}(t)|$ exists
Each component function is continuous at $a$
quiz.explanation: Limits are computed componentwise: $\mathbf{r}(t) \to \langle L_1, L_2, L_3\rangle$ exactly when each of the three component functions approaches a (finite) limit. Existence of $|\mathbf{r}(t)|$ alone does not pin down a direction.

intro: Differentiating a vector function is done componentwise — but the geometry is new: the derivative is a **tangent vector** pointing in the direction of travel, with length equal to the speed. This section builds the calculus of $\mathbf{r}(t)$: the derivative and its limit definition, the algebra rules (including product rules for the dot and cross products), integrals, and the smoothness condition that makes the geometry well behaved.
objectives: Compute the derivative of a vector function from the limit definition or componentwise
Interpret $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ as a tangent vector and find tangent lines to space curves
Form the unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}(t) = \mathbf{r}'(t)/|\mathbf{r}'(t)|$
Apply the differentiation rules for sums, dot products, cross products and chains
Evaluate definite and indefinite integrals of vector functions and define smooth curves

concepts.statement: The derivative of $\mathbf{r}$ is $$\mathbf{r}'(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\mathbf{r}(t + h) - \mathbf{r}(t)}{h}$$ provided the limit exists; in components, $\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle f'(t), g'(t), h'(t)\rangle$ — differentiate each component.
concepts.detail: The quotient is the displacement $\mathbf{r}(t + h) - \mathbf{r}(t)$ divided by the elapsed time, so it is an average velocity vector; the limit is instantaneous velocity. Geometrically the difference quotient is a secant vector, and its limit points along the tangent — the same picture as the tangent problem of Section 2.1, now in space.

concepts.statement: If a point moves along a curve $C$ with position $\mathbf{r}(t)$, then $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ is a **tangent vector** to $C$ at the point $\mathbf{r}(t)$, pointing in the direction of increasing $t$. The tangent line at $t = t_0$ is the line through the tip of $\mathbf{r}(t_0)$ with direction $\mathbf{r}'(t_0)$: $\mathbf{L}(s) = \mathbf{r}(t_0) + s\,\mathbf{r}'(t_0)$.
concepts.detail: The tangent vector only defines a line through the point when $\mathbf{r}'(t_0) \ne \mathbf{0}$; at points where the derivative vanishes the curve can have a cusp or a corner and the tangent machinery breaks down — this is why smoothness (below) matters.

concepts.statement: The **unit tangent vector** is the direction of motion with the speed divided out: $$\mathbf{T}(t) = \frac{\mathbf{r}'(t)}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|}, \qquad |\mathbf{T}(t)| = 1.$$
concepts.detail: The direction of travel and the rate of travel are separated: $\mathbf{r}'(t) = |\mathbf{r}'(t)|\,\mathbf{T}(t)$, length times direction, exactly as a vector was decomposed in Chapter 12. The unit tangent is the backbone of the curvature theory in Section 13.3.

concepts.statement: If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are differentiable vector functions and $c$ is a scalar, then: $(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v})' = \mathbf{u}' + \mathbf{v}'$, $(c\,\mathbf{u})' = c\,\mathbf{u}'$, $$\frac{d}{dt}\bigl[\mathbf{u}(t) \cdot \mathbf{v}(t)\bigr] = \mathbf{u}'(t) \cdot \mathbf{v}(t) + \mathbf{u}(t) \cdot \mathbf{v}'(t),$$ $$\frac{d}{dt}\bigl[\mathbf{u}(t) \times \mathbf{v}(t)\bigr] = \mathbf{u}'(t) \times \mathbf{v}(t) + \mathbf{u}(t) \times \mathbf{v}'(t),$$ and $\frac{d}{dt}\,\mathbf{u}(f(t)) = f'(t)\,\mathbf{u}'(f(t))$.
concepts.detail: The dot-product rule looks exactly like the scalar product rule of Section 3.2. The cross-product rule also has two terms — but the order of the factors must be preserved, because the cross product is not commutative. Writing $\mathbf{v}' \times \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{u}'$ instead gives a different (wrong) vector.

concepts.statement: Indefinite integral: $\int \mathbf{r}(t)\,dt = \left\langle \int f(t)\,dt,\ \int g(t)\,dt,\ \int h(t)\,dt \right\rangle$ where the three constants of integration combine into one constant vector $\mathbf{C}$. Definite integral: $\int_a^b \mathbf{r}(t)\,dt = \left\langle \int_a^b f,\ \int_a^b g,\ \int_a^b h \right\rangle$.
concepts.detail: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus applies componentwise: if $\mathbf{R}'(t) = \mathbf{r}(t)$ then $\int_a^b \mathbf{r}(t)\,dt = \mathbf{R}(b) - \mathbf{R}(a)$. This is the tool for reconstructing position from acceleration in Section 13.4.

concepts.statement: A curve $C$ traced by $\mathbf{r}$ is **smooth** on an interval if $\mathbf{r}'$ is continuous and $\mathbf{r}'(t) \ne \mathbf{0}$ there. A **piecewise-smooth** curve is a finite union of smooth pieces joined end to end.
concepts.detail: Smooth means the curve has a continuously turning unit tangent — no corners, no cusps. A polygon, for example, is piecewise smooth but not smooth at its vertices; the arc length and curvature machinery is applied to such curves one piece at a time.

examples.title: Derivatives of the helix and its unit tangent
examples.problem: For $\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos t\,\mathbf{i} + \sin t\,\mathbf{j} + t\,\mathbf{k}$, find $\mathbf{r}'(t)$, $\mathbf{r}''(t)$, the speed $|\mathbf{r}'(t)|$, and the unit tangent vector at $t = 0$.

steps.label: Step 1: Differentiate componentwise
steps.text: $\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle -\sin t, \cos t, 1\rangle$ and $\mathbf{r}''(t) = \langle -\cos t, -\sin t, 0\rangle$.

steps.label: Step 2: Compute the speed
steps.text: $|\mathbf{r}'(t)| = \sqrt{\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t + 1} = \sqrt{2}$, constant: the point moves along the helix at constant speed even though it constantly changes direction.

steps.label: Step 3: Evaluate at $t = 0$
steps.text: The point is $\mathbf{r}(0) = \langle 1, 0, 0\rangle$ and the tangent vector is $\mathbf{r}'(0) = \langle 0, 1, 1\rangle$.

steps.label: Step 4: Normalize
steps.text: $\mathbf{T}(0) = \mathbf{r}'(0)/|\mathbf{r}'(0)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\langle 0, 1, 1\rangle$, a unit vector halfway between the $y$- and $z$-directions — up and around at once, as a helix demands.

examples.result: $\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle -\sin t, \cos t, 1\rangle$, $\mathbf{r}''(t) = \langle -\cos t, -\sin t, 0\rangle$, speed $\sqrt{2}$, and $\mathbf{T}(0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\langle 0, 1, 1\rangle$.

examples.title: Tangent line to a helix at a point
examples.problem: Find parametric equations for the tangent line to the helix $x = 2\cos t$, $y = \sin t$, $z = t$ at the point $\left(-\sqrt{3},\ \frac{1}{2},\ \frac{5\pi}{6}\right)$.

steps.label: Step 1: Locate the parameter value
steps.text: The given point must be on the curve: $2\cos t = -\sqrt{3}$ and $\sin t = \frac{1}{2}$ give $t = \frac{5\pi}{6}$, which also matches $z = t$.

steps.label: Step 2: Differentiate the components
steps.text: $x'(t) = -2\sin t$, $y'(t) = \cos t$, $z'(t) = 1$, so $\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle -2\sin t, \cos t, 1\rangle$ is the tangent direction.

steps.label: Step 3: Evaluate at $t_0 = \frac{5\pi}{6}$
steps.text: $\mathbf{r}'\!\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \left\langle -1,\ -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\ 1 \right\rangle$, using $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\cos\frac{5\pi}{6} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

steps.label: Step 4: Write the line
steps.text: The line through $\left(-\sqrt{3}, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{5\pi}{6}\right)$ with that direction: $x = -\sqrt{3} - s$, $y = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s$, $z = \frac{5\pi}{6} + s$.
