quiz.explanation: new creates the object, links it to the class’s prototype (so distance is inherited, not copied), and runs the constructor with this set to the new object; no return is needed — the object itself is the result.

quiz.q: A script containing only the line `console.log(typeof console)` runs unchanged in both a browser tab and a Node process. What does this show about `console`, and where is it defined?
options: `console` is core syntax defined by ECMA-262, so every conforming engine ships an identical copy
`console` is a host-provided API, so the browser and Node each supply their own object behind the same name
`console` is a Node-only module that browsers download at runtime before running any script
`console` is a keyword like `return`, so `typeof console` is a syntax error in both hosts
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is one line with no imports that behaves identically in two hosts. Step 2: The governing rule is the core-versus-host split: ECMA-262 defines a core with deliberately no input or output, and each host attaches its own globals through host hooks plus extra objects, with `console` specified outside ECMA-262. Step 3: Tracing the two runs, the browser resolves `console` to its devtools console object while Node resolves it to its own wrapper over standard output, so `typeof console` reports an object in both without either host consulting the language standard. Step 4: The distractors fail because `console` appears in no ECMA-262 clause, browsers never download a Node module to print, and `console` is an ordinary property name rather than a reserved keyword. Step 5: Therefore the identical behavior comes from a shared host-API convention, not from the core language.

depth.title: What the engine really does with your program

blocks.body: Run the histogram program and you exercise a tiered compiler, not an interpreter in the casual sense. **Ignition** parses the source to an abstract syntax tree, lowers it to register-based bytecode, and interprets it, recording **feedback** into slots of a per-function feedback vector as it runs. Functions that turn hot — measured against an interpreter budget, here the per-character counting loop of `Histogram.add` — tier up: **Sparkplug** (2021) compiles the bytecode to unoptimized machine code quickly and without speculation; **Maglev** (2023) adds cheap type speculation in a mid tier; **TurboFan**, the top tier, builds a sea-of-nodes graph, speculates on the collected feedback — monomorphic shapes, taken branches — inlines small callees, and emits aggressively optimized code guarded by runtime checks. When a guard fails because reality disagrees with the speculation, the function **deoptimizes**: optimized frames are mapped back to interpreter frames mid-execution and execution resumes, correct but slow, while the feedback accumulates again.

Watch `this.totalLetters` inside `add` at the bytecode level. The property load is a single instruction, and its feedback slot starts **uninitialized**. First execution: the runtime resolves the property generically and memoizes the answer — this shape, at this offset — into the slot. From then on, the same instruction hits an **inline cache**: compare the object’s hidden class against the remembered one and, on a match, load the remembered offset directly; the generic lookup is skipped. One remembered shape is **monomorphic**, the fast case. Two to four shapes make the site **polymorphic**: a short case list, still cheap. Beyond four, V8 gives up and marks the site **megamorphic** — every access detours through a global stub cache or the runtime, several times slower, and if TurboFan had specialized on one shape, it deoptimizes and discards the optimized code. The irony at the heart of JavaScript performance: the interpreter teaches the compiler, one feedback slot at a time, and the shape of your data is the lesson plan.

**Hidden classes** — V8 says maps, the research literature says shapes — are what make those caches possible. Every object carries a hidden pointer to its shape, and shapes form a **transition tree**: adding `letterCounts` to a fresh `Histogram` and then `totalLetters` walks two transitions, so every `Histogram` the program constructs shares one path — which is why the counting loop stays monomorphic and its property loads cost one comparison plus one offset. `DefaultMap`’s constructor adds `defaultValue` after `super()`: its own transition, its own stable shape. The moment one access site mixes shapes — a comparator receiving objects built along different paths, property keys computed at runtime, a library returning dictionary-mode objects — the site degrades toward megamorphic and optimized code must fall back. The performance culture of “write monomorphic code” is the folk practice of this mechanism: keep every access site seeing one shape, and the engine compiles your object access into two instructions.

Memory tells the same generational story. V8’s heap is split by the **weak generational hypothesis**: most objects die young. New allocations — the temporary strings from `text.replace()` and `toUpperCase()`, spread-built arrays, fresh closures — go into a young semispace, and a **scavenge** (Cheney’s algorithm) copies the few live objects into the other semispace and reclaims the dead majority by simply flipping the spaces; cost is proportional to survivors, not to garbage. Objects surviving two scavenges are **promoted** to old space, which is managed by **mark-compact**: tri-color marking to find live data, run **incrementally** in slices to bound pause times and concurrently with the program where possible, then sweeping and occasionally compacting pages to fight fragmentation. The histogram’s Map entries accumulate from the first chunk to the last, so they are promoted early and marked at the end; its string temporaries die before their second scavenge. A well-shaped program and a well-shaped heap reward the same design instinct.

blocks.heading: Predicting the allocations of add()
blocks.body: Before profiling, predict. Per input chunk, `Histogram.add` performs: one `text.replace(/\s/g, "")` returning a **new string**, because strings are immutable; one `.toUpperCase()` returning another; then, per character, iteration slicing — and for one-byte strings V8 serves one-character substrings from a 256-entry cache, so `character` usually allocates nothing; per counted letter, one `Map.set` allocating an entry, with small integers up to about $2^{31}$ traveling unboxed as **Smis**, and occasionally, when the load factor trips, a rehash that allocates a larger backing store. Steady state per chunk: two temporary strings plus a handful of table cells, and the two strings become garbage the moment the next statement executes. Prediction: minor scavenges recycle the temporaries nearly for free, scaling with chunk count, while old space grows only with the number of **distinct letters** — a few dozen entries for English text, whatever the corpus size. Verify with `--trace-gc`: scavenges track the chunks; mark-compact events barely register.

depth.title: Speculation: security, verification, analysis at scale

blocks.body: The JIT’s superpower, speculation, turned out to be a security liability. **Spectre** (Kocher and colleagues, 2019) broke the browser sandbox’s core assumption — that script cannot read memory it does not own — without exploiting any implementation bug. A proof of concept in JavaScript trained the branch predictor with in-bounds iterations, then fed an out-of-bounds index; the processor mispredicted speculatively, the transient path touched a secret-dependent cache line, and a high-resolution timer converted the cache state into leaked bytes. The browser response was sweeping: coarsening and reducing timer precision, disabling `SharedArrayBuffer` platform-wide in 2018 because it enabled precise timing, shipping **Site Isolation** so each origin runs in its own process, and later re-enabling `SharedArrayBuffer` only for cross-origin-isolated pages under COOP and COEP. The deep lesson for language implementation: speculative optimization is a **constant-time violation by design** — the security contract became about what can be observed, not just what executes.

**WebAssembly** emerged partly as the safer target the JavaScript JIT could never be. A wasm module is **validated** before execution against a typed, stack-disciplined grammar, so no malformed instruction stream ever reaches code generation; control flow is **structured**, closing off large classes of code-reuse attacks; linear memory is explicit and bounds-checked rather than an ambient graph of objects; and there is no `eval`, no `with`, no prototype chain to make name resolution dynamic. That is why wasm became the compilation substrate for C, Rust and Go on the web — beyond raw speed, the type discipline is something JavaScript’s feedback-driven speculation only approximates. It is not a panacea: wasm shares the same hardware and the same cache side channels, needs its own constant-time hardening for cryptographic code, and its sandboxing story — memory controls, the component model, capabilities across module boundaries — remains an active design surface rather than a settled one.

blocks.heading: Verifying the optimizing JIT
blocks.body: An optimizing JavaScript compiler is a frontier for verification, and the frontier is wide. Verified compilation exists for C — CompCert, with Frama-C supplying verified analyses of C programs — but the analogous result for a JIT would have to prove that the optimizing pipeline **refines the source semantics on every path, deoptimizations included**, through a tiering system that rewrites stack frames mid-execution while concurrent garbage collection moves objects underneath. A modern optimizing tier is hundreds of thousands of lines of C++ that deliberately change every release; tiering, speculation, inline caches and the memory model all interact. What exists today is fragmentary: translation validation that checks one compilation after the fact, verified intermediate representations, verified interpreters, and conformance testing at Test262 scale. The open problem in full: a semantics of the pipeline, not merely the language, strong enough to prove that no optimization, however speculative, can be observed except through its intended results.

blocks.heading: The type-less type checker
blocks.body: This chapter’s closing program has an industrial ancestor: Google’s **Closure Compiler**, which for years compiled the company’s largest JavaScript — Docs, Maps, pages served at planetary scale — by performing **type inference over untyped code**, guided by optional JSDoc annotations. Crucially, its type system existed to **optimize**: types drive inlining, dead-code elimination and property flattening in ADVANCED mode, and a program with no annotations at all is still analyzed and still shrinks. The inversion is the insight — inference for optimization rather than for guarantees — and it anticipated a decade of scholarship on what static reasoning is actually for. Modern descendants run the loop at npm scale: bundlers doing whole-program reachability analysis on every commit, linters with real dataflow engines, and server-side checkers re-deriving facts no one annotated. Soundness was simply not the customer; throughput was, and across tens of millions of lines of untyped code, the customer was right.

blocks.heading: LLMs as program analysts
blocks.body: The newest frontier swaps the solver for a model. Large language models read JavaScript the way they read prose, and npm — the largest package ecosystem ever assembled — is both their training corpus and their workload: learned bug finding, test generation and migration tooling already outperform classical analysis on tasks that resist formalization, like understanding the intent behind a legacy pyramid of callbacks. But the trade inverts everything above: learned inference is unsound, unstated and unrepeatable — no guarantee, no contract, and possibly a different answer after the next retrain. The open question for programming-language research is the hybrid: models proposing, analyses disposing — learned heuristics generating candidate invariants, contracts and summaries that a sound checker then proves, refutes, or feeds back as training signal. What the $\lambda_{JS}$ line achieved by desugaring, the learned line must achieve by hypothesis and test, and whether that loop can ever be made trustworthy is, right now, genuinely open.

intro: The chapter ends with a short but nontrivial program: a Node tool that reads text from standard input, counts how often each letter occurs, and prints a histogram of the most frequent characters. It is real-world JavaScript — a Map subclass, a domain class, a regular expression, array destructuring, sorting, and an async function consuming a stream — and every piece of it is explained in the chapters that follow. Here you read it end to end for shape, then trace one run through it.
objectives: Run the program: `node charfreq.js < charfreq.js` and interpret its output
Explain the two classes: DefaultMap (a Map with a default for missing keys) and Histogram (counts letters)
Follow the data flow: chunk → add(text) → letterCounts Map → sorted entries → formatted lines
Identify the modern features at work: class extends, template literals, destructuring, async/await
Appreciate the program’s shape as a model of readable, commented JavaScript

concepts.statement:
Example 1-1 reads text from **standard input**, computes the frequency of each letter in that text, and displays a histogram of the most frequently used characters. You can run it on its own source:
```js
$ node charfreq.js < charfreq.js
T: ########### 11.22%
E: ########## 10.15%
R: ####### 6.68%
S: ###### 6.44%
A: ###### 6.16%
N: ###### 5.81%
O: ##### 5.45%
I: ##### 4.54%
```
Each line shows a character, a bar of `#` characters, and the percentage of all letters it represents.
concepts.detail: The program requires Node 12 or higher and, in a Unix environment, is invoked as `node charfreq.js < corpus.txt`. Do not expect to understand every line yet — but by the end of the book, every line will be yours.
The trick this enables: `counts.get(c) + 1` needs no "does the key exist yet?" test the first time a letter appears — a missing key reads as 0, not undefined.

Features on display: a regular expression `/\s/g` matching whitespace (Chapter 11), `for/of` over a string character by character (Chapter 5), spread `...` to copy a Map into an array (Chapter 7), `sort` with a comparator (Chapter 7), `map` with a destructuring arrow parameter `([l,n]) =>` (Chapters 3 and 8), and a template literal with `${...}` interpolation (Chapter 3).

The function returns a **Promise** — a placeholder for a value that arrives later (Chapter 13). `for await` loops over the chunks of standard input without blocking; `.then()` registers the code to run when the promised histogram finally exists. All of the input is processed as it streams in, which is the whole point of the asynchronous style.

concepts.term: Reading the program as an architecture
concepts.statement: Beyond syntax, notice the program’s shape: two small classes with clearly separated responsibilities (storage with defaults; counting and formatting), a comment header explaining how to run it, one function that adapts the async input stream to the domain class, and a one-line main. It is a miniature of how well-structured JavaScript of any size is organized.
concepts.detail: When you reach for this program later, notice also what it does not do: no mutation of input text (strings are immutable — a new string is returned), no manual memory management, and no loop indices in the counting loop — iteration is delegated to `for/of`.

examples.title: Trace: the program’s full run on a small input
examples.problem: You run `echo "banana" | node charfreq.js`. What does the engine do, from process start to printed histogram?

steps.label: Step 1: Classes are defined
steps.text: The engine evaluates the two class definitions and the async function declaration, then runs the final line. `histogramFromStdin()` is called immediately — it returns a Promise — and `.then()` registers the printer for later. Then top-level code is done and control returns to the event loop.

steps.label: Step 2: The stream delivers "banana"
steps.text: Inside the async function, `for await` receives one chunk: the string "banana". The loop body calls `histogram.add("banana")`.

steps.label: Step 3: add() normalizes the text
steps.text:
```js
text = text.replace(/\s/g, "").toUpperCase();
```
The regular expression matches every whitespace character and replaces each with "", producing "BANANA".

steps.label: Step 4: Letters are counted in the DefaultMap
steps.text: `for(let character of text)` yields "B", then "A", "N", "A", "N", "A". Each `get` returns the running count (0 for the first "B", thanks to the default) and `set` writes back one more; `totalLetters` reaches 6. Final map: B→1, A→3, N→2.

steps.label: Step 5: The stream ends, the Promise resolves
steps.text: `for await` finishes when input ends, and `return histogram` resolves the Promise. The event loop then calls the `.then` callback, which runs `histogram.toString()`.

steps.label: Step 6: toString() sorts and formats
steps.text: Entries are spread to [["B",1],["A",3],["N",2]], sorted by count descending → A(3), N(2), B(1). Each count becomes a percentage of 6: A → 50, N → 33.33, B → 16.67. The `map` formats each as a template literal with `Math.round(n)` hash marks and `n.toFixed(2)` percentages, and `join("\n")` glues the lines.

examples.result:
```js
A: ################################################## 50.00%
N: ################################# 33.33%
B: ################ 16.67%
```
Streaming in, counting with a defaulted Map, sorting and formatting out — the program’s whole job done in one pass.

examples.title: Trace: why DefaultMap removes the "first time" special case
examples.problem: Rewrite `add()` to use a plain `Map` and count the same text. What extra work appears, and why?

steps.label: Step 1: The plain-Map version
Step 2: Count the branches
steps.text: For every single letter, the engine now evaluates `has()` and then takes one of two different `set()` calls. The reading loop is interrupted by bookkeeping that has nothing to do with counting.

steps.label: Step 3: The DefaultMap version
steps.text:
```js
let count = this.letterCounts.get(character); // 0 if absent
this.letterCounts.set(character, count + 1);
```
One code path. The "is this the first time?" question is answered once, inside `DefaultMap.get`, instead of being re-asked at every letter of every text.

steps.label: Step 4: The general lesson
steps.text: Subclassing a standard class (here `Map`) to move a special case into the data structure is a small, classic piece of object-oriented design — and it is exactly why the program reads so clean.

examples.result: Same histogram output, but the plain-Map version pays an extra has() test and a branch per letter; DefaultMap centralizes the missing-key default so the counting loop is branch-free.

keyTakeaways: The program is run as `node charfreq.js < corpus.txt`; each output line is `letter: #bar percentage`, sorted most frequent first.
DefaultMap subclasses Map (via `extends`, `super()` and `super.get()`) so a missing key reads as a chosen default — eliminating the "first occurrence" special case.

Histogram.add() strips whitespace with a regex, uppercases, and counts with `for/of` over the string’s characters; toString() spreads the Map to an array, sorts by count, converts to percentages, and formats with map + template literals.
Input is consumed asynchronously with `for await` over `process.stdin`; the function returns a Promise, and `.then()` runs the printing when it resolves.
Every feature used — classes, Map, regex, destructuring, spread, sort comparators, template literals, async iteration — gets a full treatment in Chapters 3 through 13.
The program models good structure: small classes with one responsibility each, a comment header with usage, and a one-line main.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the DefaultMap class in the character-frequency program?
options: It returns a caller-chosen default value from get() when a key is not in the map
It stores the histogram’s total letter count
It converts the Map to a sorted array automatically
quiz.explanation: DefaultMap extends Map and overrides get() to return this.defaultValue (0 in this program) for missing keys, so `get(c) + 1` works even the first time a letter is seen.

quiz.q: In `Histogram.add()`, what does the statement `text = text.replace(/\s/g, "").toUpperCase();` accomplish?
options: It replaces every letter with whitespace and then lowercases the result
It removes all whitespace characters and converts the text to upper case
It splits the text into an array of words
It replaces the character class \s with the letter g
quiz.explanation: The regex /\s/g globally matches whitespace characters; replacing each with "" deletes them. toUpperCase() then normalizes case so "a" and "A" count as the same letter.

quiz.q: After processing the text "mom" (3 letters: M once, O once, M again), what does `this.letterCounts` contain?
options: An error, because M is added twice to the Map
quiz.explanation: Each of the three characters is counted: M is set to 1 then 2, O to 1; totalLetters is incremented once per character, so it is 3.

quiz.q: Why is `histogramFromStdin()` declared `async`, and what does `for await` add over a plain `for/of`?
options: It makes the program run faster on multicore CPUs
It lets the function return a Promise and consume the input stream chunk-by-chunk as data arrives, without blocking
It is required syntax whenever a program reads files, enforced by Node
It converts the text to UTF-8 before counting
quiz.explanation: async functions return Promises and enable await; `for await` is asynchronous iteration (Chapter 13) — the loop body runs once per chunk as the stream delivers it, and the event loop stays free between chunks.

quiz.q: The final line of the program is `histogramFromStdin().then(histogram => { console.log(histogram.toString()); });`. What is true of this line?
options: It blocks until all input has been read, then prints synchronously
It calls the function, which starts the reading and returns a Promise, and registers a callback to print the histogram once that Promise resolves
It prints the histogram immediately, before any input is read
It declares a function named histogram that will be called later by Node
quiz.explanation: The call starts the async work and returns a Promise immediately; .then() registers the printing callback that runs when the reading completes and the Promise resolves with the finished histogram.

intro: The lexical structure of a programming language is the set of elementary rules that specify how you write programs in that language — the lowest-level syntax: what counts as one token versus another, what variable names look like, how comments are delimited, and how one statement is separated from the next. This section covers the character-level ground rules: JavaScript is case sensitive, and it is mostly indifferent to your spaces and line breaks.
objectives: State the case-sensitivity rule and predict which identifiers collide
List the characters JavaScript treats as whitespace and as line terminators
Explain why formatting freedom does not extend to line breaks next to certain tokens

concepts.statement: JavaScript is a **case-sensitive** language: keywords, variables, function names and all other identifiers must always be typed with a consistent capitalization of letters. The `while` keyword must be typed "while", not "While" or "WHILE". Similarly, `online`, `Online`, `OnLine` and `ONLINE` are **four distinct variable names**.
concepts.detail: This bites programmers coming from HTML (case-insensitive tag and attribute names) when they move to client-side JavaScript: `getElementById` is not `getElementbyID`. Consistency in capitalization is the cure.

concepts.statement: JavaScript ignores spaces that appear **between tokens** in programs. Beyond the regular space character (\u0020), the whitespace set includes tabs, assorted ASCII control characters, and various Unicode space characters. Because you can use spaces freely, you can format and indent programs in a neat, consistent way that makes code easy to read and understand.
concepts.detail: Whitespace is required only where it separates tokens that would otherwise fuse: `let x` cannot be written `letx`. Otherwise the engine discards it.

concepts.statement: For the most part, JavaScript also ignores line breaks — but with an important exception: the automatic semicolon insertion rules of Section 2.5 mean some line breaks **do** change the meaning of your program. The recognized line terminators are the newline (\n), the carriage return (\r), and the carriage-return/line-feed sequence (\r\n).
concepts.detail: A program may be written as one enormous line or spread elegantly over many; both parse the same, provided no line break splits a token or triggers the ASI rules of Section 2.5.

concepts.statement: The tokenizer splits source into **tokens**: identifiers, keywords, numeric and string literals, and punctuators such as `+`, `++`, `=>`, `(`, `{`. It always takes the **longest valid token** starting at each position, so `a+++b` tokenizes as `a ++ + b`, never as `a + ++ b` by choice.
concepts.detail: Whitespace matters exactly at token boundaries: it prevents two adjacent identifier characters or digits from fusing into one longer token. `let x` is keyword + identifier; `letx` is a single identifier because the space that separated the tokens is gone.

concepts.term: Line breaks that matter: preview of ASI hazards
concepts.statement: Most line breaks are plain whitespace, but three positions turn a break into a terminator: after `return`, `throw`, `break`, `continue` or `yield` before its expression; between a postfix `++`/`--` and its operand; and between an arrow parameter list and `=>`. A line starting with `(` or `[` can also glue itself to the previous line as a call or index.
concepts.detail:
So `return
true` returns `undefined` and `x
++` is two statements, while `let y = x + f
(a+b).toString()` parses as one call `f(a+b)`. Section 2.5 states the full rule; the habit starts here: never break after a jump keyword, and never start a statement with `(` or `[` without a guarding semicolon.

examples.title: Trace: which of these are the same name?
examples.problem: A program declares `let online = 1;`. For each reference below, decide whether it refers to that same binding, or to something new (or an error).

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```js
Online
```
Capital O. Identifiers are compared character by character, and "O" (U+004F) is not "o" (U+006F). This is a **different identifier** — reading it before any declaration of its own throws a ReferenceError.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text:
```js
OnLine
```
A third distinct identifier — the internal capital L differs again. Four spellings, four names.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text:
```js
ONLINE
```
Yet a fourth. Only the exact sequence `online` refers to the declared variable. The lesson: pick one spelling convention (the book uses camelCase) and keep every reference identical.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text:
```js
while (x) {}   // ok
While (x) {}    // While is NOT the while keyword
```
The same rule governs keywords: capitalizing `While` turns the keyword into a plain identifier, which is a syntax error when used where a statement is expected.

examples.result: online, Online, OnLine and ONLINE are four unrelated names; keywords are case sensitive in exactly the same way.

examples.title: Trace: spaces that fuse and breaks that do not
examples.problem:
Predict how the engine tokenizes each fragment:
```js
let x = 2;
letx = 2;
let a
a = 3
return
true
```

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```js
let x = 2;
```
Three tokens before the value: keyword `let`, identifier `x`, punctuator `=`. The spaces separate `let` from `x` so the tokenizer sees two names, not one.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text:
```js
letx = 2;
```
No separator: the tokenizer takes the longest identifier `letx` — one name. In strict mode this is a syntax error (no declaration); in sloppy mode it assigns to an accidental global named `letx`.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text:
```js
let a
a = 3
```
The line break between `a` and `a` cannot continue one statement (`let a a` is unparseable), so it acts as a separator: `let a; a = 3;`. Reformatting the same tokens onto one enormous line without a `;` would fail — breaks help only where a semicolon could go.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text:
```js
return
true
```
The break after `return` always terminates (Section 2.5 exception 1): `return; true;`. The function returns `undefined` and `true` is dead code — the preview of why some breaks matter.

examples.result: Spaces separate tokens that would fuse (`let x` vs `letx`); line breaks separate statements only where parsing needs a boundary — and after `return` the break always ends the statement.

keyTakeaways: Lexical structure = the lowest-level rules of the language: tokens, comments, literals, identifiers, Unicode and semicolons.
JavaScript is case sensitive: `while`, `While` and `WHILE` are different, and `online`/`Online`/`OnLine`/`ONLINE` are four distinct variable names.
Spaces and line breaks between tokens are ignored — you may format and indent freely.
Whitespace includes the regular space, tabs, ASCII control characters and Unicode spaces; line terminators are newline (\n), carriage return (\r) and the \r\n pair.
Line breaks are not always inert: the automatic semicolon insertion rules of Section 2.5 can turn a line break into a statement separator.

quiz.q: How many distinct variables are named by the identifiers `id`, `ID`, `Id` and `iD`?
options: It depends on whether the program is in strict mode
quiz.explanation: JavaScript identifiers are case sensitive and compared character by character, so four spellings that differ in the capitalization of i and d name four different variables.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT treated as a line terminator by JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: Form feed is in the whitespace/control set, not the line-terminator set — the terminators are newline, carriage return, and the CR/LF pair, and only these interact with semicolon insertion.

quiz.q: You delete all spaces from the line `let x = 2;` producing `letx=2;`. What happens?
options: It still works: JavaScript ignores all spaces
It is a syntax error (or creates a variable named letx): whitespace separated the keyword let from the variable name
It assigns 2 to the existing global variable letx, always
Strict mode rejects it but sloppy mode accepts it
quiz.explanation: Spaces are ignored only BETWEEN tokens. Removing the space between let and x fuses them into the single identifier letx, so the statement becomes an assignment to a (possibly undeclared) variable named letx — a syntax error in strict mode, an accidental global otherwise.

intro: Two small topics share this section: comments — the two ways JavaScript lets you embed prose for humans inside code for machines — and literals, the values written directly in the source. Every value a program ever manipulates starts life either as a literal, as input, or as the result of an operator or function.
objectives: Write both comment styles and explain why block comments cannot nest
Define “literal” and identify literals of each type in a line of code
Preview the literal forms detailed in Chapter 3 (numbers, strings) and Chapter 4 (object and array initializers)

concepts.detail: The multi-line style is often written with a decorative star at the start of each line. The single-line style is preferred for short notes because it cannot accidentally swallow code beyond the line.

concepts.statement:
A **literal** is a data value that appears directly in a program. The following are all literals:
```js
12            // The number twelve
1.2           // The number one point two
"hello world" // A string of text
'Hi'          // Another string
true          // A Boolean value
false         // The other Boolean value
null          // Absence of an object
```
concepts.detail: Compare with names: `twelve` is an identifier that might hold 12; `12` is the value itself. Complete details on numeric and string literals appear in Chapter 3; object `{x: 1, y: 2}` and array `[1, 2, 3]` initializers — sometimes called object and array literals, though they are built from subexpressions — are in Chapter 4.

concepts.statement: The book’s example comments frequently begin with an arrow: `// => 42` shows the value produced by the preceding code; `// a == 42` means the variable `a` holds 42 after the code runs; and `// !` marks a line that throws an exception. These double as executable assertions.
concepts.detail: When you copy examples into your own environment, the comments can become real checks — assert the printed value equals the comment, and you have caught your first typo.

concepts.statement: Chapter 3 details the spellings: decimal `12`, hex `0xFF`, binary `0b101`, octal `0o17`, separators `1_000_000`, exponents `1.2e3`; strings in single 'Hi', double "hello world" or backtick `hi ${name}` quotes. The quote choice never changes the value — only what needs escaping inside.
concepts.detail: A leading `0x`, `0b` or `0o` switches base for integer literals; an underscore between digits is ignored (`1_000 === 1000`). Backtick strings are template literals (Chapter 3 and Section 14.4): the only strings that interpolate `${...}`.

concepts.term: Object and array initializers as composite literals
concepts.statement: The expressions `{x: 1, y: 2}` and `[1, 2, 3]` are called **object and array literals** (or initializers): they build a fresh object or array from a comma-separated list of subexpressions. Unlike simple literals they are evaluated — each element expression runs — and trailing commas are allowed.
concepts.detail:
```js
const point = { x: 1 + 1, y: Math.sqrt(4) };  // values computed, then stored
const sparse = [1, , 3];                     // a hole at index 1
```
Full rules appear in Chapter 4; the point here is birthplace: every object and array value starts as one of these two bracketed forms.

examples.title: Trace: a commented, literal-heavy line
examples.problem: Annotate every token of this statement as comment, literal, identifier or keyword, then say what the engine keeps.

steps.label: The code
steps.text:
```js
let speed = 299792.458; // speed of light, km/s
/* old value: 186282 miles per second */
```

steps.label: Step 1: Keywords and identifiers
steps.text: `let` is a keyword introducing a declaration; `speed` is the identifier being declared. Neither is a value.

steps.label: Step 2: The literal
steps.text: `299792.458` is a floating-point numeric literal — a real number written as integral part, decimal point, and fractional part. It is the only data value in the statement.

steps.label: Step 3: What the engine discards
steps.text: The `//` comment to end of line and the `/* ... */` block comment are both stripped after tokenization. The engine never evaluates the number 186282 — comments are not code.

steps.label: Step 4: The result
steps.text: After execution, the binding `speed` refers to the number 299792.458 — the literal is the value’s birthplace.

examples.result: One keyword, one identifier, one literal, two ignored comments: the entire statement reduces to binding speed to the value 299792.458.

examples.title: Why block comments do not nest
examples.problem: A programmer comments out a region that already contains a block comment. What goes wrong?

steps.label: The code
Step 1: The engine scans for the first */
steps.text: A block comment ends at the **first** `*/` it encounters — the one after "initialize x". The engine does not track nesting depth at all.

steps.label: Step 2: What re-enters the program
steps.text: The text `let y = 2;` is now live code again, and the trailing `*/` on the last line is parsed as operators — a syntax error. The region between the two inner stars was never commented out.

steps.label: Step 3: The fix
steps.text: To disable a region containing `/* */`, comment it line by line with `//`, or temporarily delete. Single-line comments are nestable precisely because each ends at its own line end.

examples.result: The first */ closes the whole comment; code after it becomes live and the stray final */ is a syntax error. Use // for commenting-out and /* */ only for prose blocks.

keyTakeaways: Two comment styles: // to end of line, and /* … */ across lines; block comments cannot nest.
A literal is a value written directly in source: numbers, strings, true/false, null (and later object/array initializers and regex literals).
Comments are stripped by the tokenizer — the engine never evaluates their contents.
The book’s // => value comments double as verified assertions of what the code produces.
Use single-line comments to disable code: they nest safely; block comments do not.

quiz.q: Which one of these lines contains a literal?
quiz.explanation: null is one of the literals listed in the chapter (the absence of an object); the other lines contain a keyword/identifier, an operator on a name, and a comment — and the 3 in the comment is stripped before evaluation.

quiz.q:
What is wrong with this attempt to comment out a region?
```js
/* disable this:
let a = 1;  /* note */
let b = 2;
*/
```
options: Nothing — block comments nest in ES6 and later
The comment ends at the first */ (after “note”), so `let b = 2;` becomes live code and the final */ is a syntax error
Block comments must start with more than one asterisk
Comments cannot span more than two lines
quiz.explanation: A /* comment runs only until the very next */, regardless of intent or nesting; everything after that first closer is parsed as code again.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a literal?
quiz.explanation: answer is an identifier — a name for a value, not a value written directly. Numbers, strings, true/false and null are all literals.

intro: Identifiers are simply names: they label constants, variables, properties, functions and classes, and provide labels for loops. JavaScript’s naming rules are permissive — letters, digits, underscores and dollar signs — but a sizeable set of words is reserved for the language itself. Knowing which words are forbidden, and which merely contextual, prevents a whole family of confusing syntax errors.
objectives: State the rules for legal identifiers: first character and subsequent characters
Explain why digits cannot start an identifier
Recognize the reserved words and the future-reserved list
Explain contextual keywords: why `from`, `of`, `get`, `set` and `target` remain safe, and why `let` is complicated

concepts.statement:
An **identifier** is simply a name. A JavaScript identifier must begin with a **letter**, an **underscore** (`_`), or a **dollar sign** (`$`). Subsequent characters can be letters, digits, underscores, or dollar signs. These are all legal:
```js
i
my_variable_name
v13
_dummy
$str
```
concepts.detail: Digits are not allowed as the first character so that JavaScript can easily distinguish identifiers from numbers: seeing a digit at the start of a token tells the tokenizer, unambiguously, that a numeric literal is under way.

concepts.statement:
JavaScript reserves certain identifiers for use by the language itself; these "reserved words" cannot be used as the names of constants, variables, functions, or classes — though they **can** all be used as the names of properties within an object. The reserved list:
```js
as       const     export      get          null      target    void
async    continue  extends     if           of        this      while
await    debugger  false       import       return    throw     with
break    default   finally     in           set       true      yield
case     delete    for        instanceof   static    try
catch    do        from        let          super     typeof
class    else      function   new          switch    var
```
concepts.detail: Two groups deserve extra care. First, `arguments` and `eval` are not allowed as identifiers in certain circumstances and are best avoided entirely. Second, the so-called "soft" words — `get`, `set`, `from`, `of`, `static`, `as`, `target` — are reserved only in limited contexts and are perfectly legal as ordinary identifiers; the book singles out `from`, `set` and `target` as safe and already in common use.

concepts.statement: Some keywords — notably `let` — cannot be fully reserved without breaking older programs that used them as variable names. So there are complex rules governing when `let` can be an identifier and when it cannot: `let` can be a variable name if declared with `var` outside a class, for example, but not when declared inside a class or with `const`. **The simplest course is to avoid using any of these words as identifiers**, except for `from`, `set` and `target`.
concepts.detail: You will never need this knowledge to write good code — treat the whole reserved list as taken, and the three safe words as available.

concepts.statement:
JavaScript also reserves or restricts keywords that are **not currently used** by the language but might be in future versions:
```js
enum    implements   interface   package   private   protected   public
```
concepts.detail: These words (familiar from Java) are mostly restricted only in strict-mode code and class bodies — but as with `let`, the practical advice is simply: never use them as names.

concepts.term: arguments and eval are poison names
concepts.statement: `arguments` and `eval` are not on the reserved list, but they are **restricted as identifiers**: in strict mode neither may name a variable, function, parameter or catch binding, and assigning to `eval` breaks the indirect-eval machinery of Section 3.6. The book rule is blunt: never use either as a name in any mode.
concepts.detail:
```js
let eval = 1;        // SyntaxError in strict mode (modules, classes)
function f(arguments) {}  // SyntaxError in strict mode
```
Even where sloppy mode permits them, shadowing `eval` disables the `eval(x)` function and shadowing `arguments` hides the call arguments object — two silent breakages for one saved name.

concepts.statement: After a dot, any reserved word is legal (`o.class`, `o.for`, `o.while`); inside brackets, any string is legal (`o["my-var"]`, `o["two words"]`). Property position has no reserved list — only variable, function, class and parameter positions do.
concepts.detail:
```js
const o = { class: "CS", for: 4 };  // legal: property names
o.while;                            // legal read
o["my-var"] = 1;                    // dashes need brackets, not dots
```
Quoted keys also allow names no identifier could spell — the reason JSON-style data (`{"first-name": "Ada"}`) always uses brackets or quotes.

examples.title: Trace: legal versus illegal names
examples.problem: Classify each of these proposed variable names as legal or illegal, and explain each verdict.

steps.label: Name 1
steps.text:
```js
let $str = "money";
```
**Legal.** `$` is allowed as a first character and beyond — a legacy of generated code (and jQuery’s famous `$` function).

steps.label: Name 2
steps.text:
```js
let v13 = 13;
```
**Legal.** Digits are fine as long as they are not the first character.

steps.label: Name 3
steps.text:
```js
let 3v = 3;
```
**Illegal.** A leading digit marks the token as a numeric literal, so "3v" is not even tokenizable as a name. The tokenizer must be able to distinguish identifiers from numbers at a glance — this rule is why.

steps.label: Name 4
steps.text:
```js
let my_variable_name = 1;
```
**Legal.** Underscores are permitted anywhere. Snake_case like this is a legal (if un-idiomatic) alternative to camelCase.

steps.label: Name 5
steps.text:
```js
let class = "CS";
```
**Illegal.** `class` is a reserved word. Use it as an object **property** and it is fine: `const o = { class: "CS" };` — reserved words are barred as identifiers, not as property names.

steps.label: Name 6
steps.text:
```js
let _dummy;
```
**Legal.** Leading underscore, common convention for "internal, ignore me" parameters and fields.

examples.result: Legal: `$str`, `v13`, `my_variable_name`, `_dummy`. Illegal: `3v` (leading digit), `class` (reserved). Reserved words remain usable as property names — only identifier roles are barred.

examples.title: Trace: reserved, soft, or property-only?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```js
let from = 1;
```
**Legal.** `from` is a soft/contextual word (import/export syntax only) — the book lists `from`, `set`, `target` as safe. It names a variable with no restriction.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text:
```js
let enum = 1;
```
**Illegal in strict mode.** `enum` is future-reserved: modules, classes and all strict code forbid it as a name. The fix is any other spelling — the reservation exists so a future `enum` declaration cannot silently capture your variable.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text:
```js
const o = { while: 5 };
o.while;   // => 5
```
**Legal.** Property position has no reserved list: `while` as a key and after a dot is an ordinary name. The same word as a variable (`let while`) would be a syntax error.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text:
```js
let eval = 1;
```
**SyntaxError in strict mode; dangerous everywhere.** `eval` is restricted, not reserved: strict mode bans it as a binding, and sloppy-mode use shadows the `eval()` function. Rename to `result` or `value` — no program needs this collision.

examples.result: `from` is safe, `enum` is future-reserved (strict-mode error), `while` is property-only, `eval` is poison in every mode. Identifier rules depend on position: variable slots are strict, property slots are free.

keyTakeaways: An identifier starts with a letter, `_` or `$`; subsequent characters may also be digits.
Digits cannot start an identifier so the tokenizer can tell numbers from names.
Reserved words (`if`, `while`, `class`, `yield`, …) cannot name constants, variables, functions or classes — but all of them can name object properties.
Some words are contextual or soft (`from`, `of`, `get`, `set`, `target`): usable as identifiers; `let` has complicated rules — avoid the entire list when naming.
Future-reserved words to avoid: enum, implements, interface, package, private, protected, public.
Avoid `arguments` and `eval` as identifiers entirely; they are restricted in certain circumstances.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a legal JavaScript identifier?
quiz.explanation: Identifiers cannot begin with a digit — a leading digit signals a numeric literal to the tokenizer. The other three are explicitly listed as legal names in the chapter.

quiz.q: Why does JavaScript forbid digits as the first character of an identifier?
options: It is a leftover from the Java language and has no effect
So that the tokenizer can easily distinguish identifiers from numeric literals
Because identifiers are stored as numbers internally
It is only forbidden in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Seeing a digit first tells the tokenizer unambiguously that a numeric literal has begun, which keeps the two token classes trivially separable.

quiz.q: You write `const o = { for: 4, while: 5 };`. What happens?
options: A syntax error: reserved words cannot appear in object literals
It works: reserved words cannot be identifiers, but they can be property names
It works only in strict mode
The properties are silently renamed to for_ and while_
quiz.explanation: The chapter notes that reserved words can all be used as the names of properties within an object — the restriction applies to naming constants, variables, functions and classes.

quiz.q: Which statement about the word `let` is correct, per the chapter?
options: `let` is fully reserved and can never be used as a variable name in any context
`let` can never be used as a variable name declared with var
Because of backward compatibility, `let` has complicated rules: it can be a var-declared variable name outside a class, but not a const-declared one or one inside a class
`let` is one of the three words (with from and set) explicitly recommended for free use
quiz.explanation: To keep old code working, `let` cannot be fully reserved, so its usability as an identifier depends on declaration form and context — the simplest course is to avoid it (and the rest of the reserved list) entirely.

quiz.q: Which word is on JavaScript’s list of reserved-for-the-future words?
quiz.explanation: enum belongs with implements, interface, package, private, protected and public as words reserved or restricted for possible future use; the others are all active keywords today.

intro: JavaScript programs are written using the Unicode character set, and any Unicode character may appear in strings and comments. Identifiers are more restricted — Unicode letters, digits and ideographs are allowed, but not emojis — and any character can be spelled with an ASCII-only escape sequence. The section closes with the sneakiest hazard in the chapter: two visually identical strings can be encoded two different ways, and JavaScript will not normalize them for you.
objectives: Use non-ASCII characters legally in identifiers, strings and comments
Write Unicode escape sequences in both forms: `\uXXXX` and `\u{XXXXXX}`
Explain when each escape form is needed (pre-ES6 vs codepoints above 16 bits)
Recognize the Unicode normalization hazard and the two encodings of “é”

concepts.statement:
JavaScript programs are written using the **Unicode character set**, and you can use any Unicode characters in strings and comments. For portability and ease of editing, it is common to use only ASCII letters and digits in identifiers — but that is a convention only: the language allows Unicode letters, digits and ideographs (though **not emojis**) in identifiers:
```js
const π = 3.14;   // A Greek letter as a constant name
const sí = true;     // A Spanish word
```
concepts.detail: Programmers can use mathematical symbols and words from non-English languages as constants and variables — a small courtesy of the language’s design that real, international codebases do use.

concepts.statement:
To support systems that cannot display, input, or correctly process the full Unicode set, JavaScript defines **escape sequences** that write Unicode characters using only ASCII. Escapes begin with `\u` and are either followed by **exactly four hexadecimal digits**, or by **one to six hexadecimal digits enclosed in curly braces**:
```js
let café = 1;       // Define a variable using a Unicode character
caf\u00e9            // => 1: access it via a 4-digit escape
caf\u{E9}            // => 1: same escape, curly-brace form
```
concepts.detail: Unicode escapes may appear in string literals, regular expression literals, and identifiers — but **not** in language keywords. In comments they are allowed but never interpreted, since comments are ignored.

concepts.term: The ES6 curly-brace form and emoji
concepts.statement:
Early versions of JavaScript only supported the four-digit escape. The curly-brace version was introduced in ES6 to support Unicode **codepoints that require more than 16 bits**, such as emoji:
```js
console.log("\u{1F600}");   // Prints a smiley face emoji
```
concepts.detail: A codepoint like U+1F600 cannot fit in four hex digits (max U+FFFF), so before ES6 there was no escape for it. The two-form system is also the bridge to Chapter 3’s discussion of UTF-16 code units, where the same emoji occupies a length of 2 in a string.

concepts.statement:
Unicode allows more than one way to encode the same character. The string "é" can be encoded as the single codepoint \u00E9, **or** as a regular ASCII "e" followed by the acute-accent **combining mark** \u0301. The two encodings typically look exactly the same in an editor but have different binary values — so JavaScript considers them different, which can produce two visually indistinguishable constants:
```js
const café = 1;   // This constant is named caf\u{e9}
const café = 2; // This constant is different: cafe\u{301}
café            // => 1: this constant has one value
café            // => 2: this indistinguishable constant has another
```
concepts.detail: The Unicode standard defines a **normalization procedure** that converts text to a canonical form suitable for comparison. JavaScript assumes source code has already been normalized and does no normalization itself. If you use non-ASCII characters in programs, ensure your editor or another tool normalizes the source — the fix is NFC normalization, the same operation the string method `normalize()` performs (Chapter 3).

concepts.statement: JavaScript strings are sequences of 16-bit **UTF-16 code units**, not codepoints: characters at or below U+FFFF occupy one unit, characters above (emoji, historic scripts) occupy two — a **surrogate pair**. So `"\u{1F600}".length` is `2`, indexing splits the pair, and only `codePointAt()` / `for...of` see the character whole.
concepts.detail:
```js
"\u{1F600}".length;                 // => 2: two code units, one character
[..."\u{1F600}"].length;             // => 1: iteration is codepoint-aware
"\u{1F600}".codePointAt(0).toString(16);  // => "1f600"
```
The curly-brace escape exists precisely because four hex digits cannot name these characters — and Chapter 3 shows why `charAt` on emoji returns half a face.

concepts.statement: Two strings that look identical can compare unequal when one uses composed é (U+00E9) and the other uses e + combining accent (U+0301). The fix is to normalize both sides before comparing: `a.normalize() === b.normalize()` (NFC by default), which canonicalizes composed and decomposed forms to one spelling.
concepts.detail:
```js
const a = "caf\u00e9";      // composed é
const b = "cafe\u0301";     // e + combining accent
a === b;                      // => false: different code units
a.normalize() === b.normalize();  // => true: canonical forms match
```
Normalize user input at the boundary (usernames, filenames, search keys) and normalize source files on save — JavaScript never does it for you, in identifiers or in string equality.

examples.title: Trace: three spellings of one variable
examples.problem: A session defines `let café = 1;` using the composed character. Predict the result of reading the variable through each of three spellings.

steps.label: The declaration
steps.text:
```js
let café = 1;  // one codepoint: the é is U+00E9
```
The identifier’s stored name is the 5-codepoint sequence c, a, f, é(composed), exactly as typed.

steps.label: Read 1: identical spelling
steps.text:
```js
café   // => 1
```
Same codepoint sequence → same name → value found.

steps.label: Read 2: 4-digit escape
steps.text:
```js
caf\u00e9   // => 1
```
Escapes are resolved before identifiers are compared, so `caf\u00e9` and `café` are the **same** identifier. Escapes are a way of typing, not a different name.

steps.label: Read 3: the combining-mark twin
steps.text:
```js
café   // Not the same identifier! e + combining accent (U+0301)
```
This name is the 6-codepoint sequence c, a, f, e, ́ — visually identical to café on screen, but a different sequence of values. If no such variable was declared, this is a ReferenceError; if one was, it holds a different value (in the book’s example, 2).

steps.label: The lesson
steps.text: What you see is not what the engine sees. Visual identity of characters does not imply identity of codepoints — and the engine never merges them for you.

examples.result: café, caf\u00e9 and caf\u{E9} all name one variable; cafe + combining accent names another, visually indistinguishable one. Normalize source (NFC) to avoid this trap.

examples.title: Choosing between the two escape forms
examples.problem: You must write, using only ASCII characters, the identifiers `résumé` and the emoji-smuggler string `"hello U0001F600"`. Which escape form works for each, and why?

steps.label: Step 1: Check the codepoints
steps.text: é is U+00E9 — a value below U+10000, expressible in four hex digits. The grinning-face emoji is U+1F600 — beyond four hex digits (U+FFFF is the four-digit ceiling).

steps.label: Step 2: The 4-digit form
steps.text:
```js
let r\u00e9sum\u00e9 = "CV";
```
Works: both é characters fit the classic `\u00XX` form that existed before ES6.

steps.label: Step 3: The curly-brace form
steps.text:
```js
let s = "hello \u{1F600}";
```
The curly-brace form takes 1–6 hex digits, so it covers all of Unicode including emoji. ES6 added it precisely for codepoints like this one — four digits simply cannot express U+1F600.

steps.label: Step 4: Consistency note
steps.text: The curly form also works for small codepoints (`\u{E9}` is é again), so it can be used everywhere ES6 is available; the four-digit form survives for pre-ES6 compatibility.

examples.result: résumé: either form (\u00e9 or \u{E9}); emoji: only \u{1F600}, the curly-brace form, because the codepoint exceeds four hex digits.

keyTakeaways: JavaScript source is Unicode: any character may appear in strings and comments; identifiers may use Unicode letters, digits and ideographs — but not emojis.
Unicode escapes start with \u and come in two forms: exactly 4 hexadecimal digits, or 1–6 hex digits in curly braces (ES6).
Escapes work in string literals, regex literals and identifiers — not in keywords; in comments they are allowed but never interpreted.
The curly-brace form exists for codepoints above 16 bits, such as emoji: `console.log("\u{1F600}")` prints a smiley face.
Unicode normalization is the hidden trap: "é" as U+00E9 and "e" + U+0301 look identical but are different to JavaScript, allowing two visually indistinguishable constants to coexist.
JavaScript does not normalize your source — ensure your editor does (NFC normalization).

quiz.q: Which of these may legally appear in a JavaScript identifier?
options: The Greek letter π, as in `const π = 3.14;`
quiz.explanation: Unicode letters, digits and ideographs are legal in identifiers — the book’s own example uses π and sí. Emojis are explicitly excluded, leading digits make a numeric literal, and const is reserved.

quiz.q: What does `console.log("\u{1F600}")` print, and why does the curly-brace form exist?
options: The literal text \u{1F600}, because escapes never work in strings
A smiley-face emoji; the ES6 curly form expresses codepoints requiring more than 16 bits, which four hex digits cannot
A smiley-face emoji; the curly form is the only escape allowed in ES6
quiz.explanation: The escape prints the grinning-face emoji. Four hex digits top out at U+FFFF, so ES6 added the 1–6 digit curly-brace form to reach codepoints beyond 16 bits — emoji being the flagship example.

quiz.q: Two constants are declared, one named with é as the single codepoint U+00E9 and one with e followed by the combining accent U+0301. What is true?
options: The second declaration is a syntax error
JavaScript automatically normalizes them into the same name, so the declarations conflict
They are different, visually indistinguishable identifiers that can coexist with different values
They are equal under == but not under ===
quiz.explanation: The two encodings have different binary values, and JavaScript performs no normalization of its own — so both declarations are legal and name different constants (the book’s example shows values 1 and 2).

quiz.q: Where can a Unicode escape sequence such as `\u00E9` NOT be used?
quiz.explanation: The chapter lists string literals, regular expression literals and identifiers as escape-capable; keywords are excluded — you cannot spell the while keyword with an escape. In comments escapes are allowed but ignored.

intro: Like many languages, JavaScript uses the semicolon to separate statements — but unlike most, it makes the semicolon optional much of the time. The rule that fills the gap, automatic semicolon insertion (ASI), is simple to state and treacherous in practice: a line break is treated as a semicolon only when the program cannot otherwise be parsed. Three exceptions — return and friends, postfix ++/--, and the arrow — make certain line breaks dangerous, and two punctuation characters at the start of a line can silently glue it to the previous statement.
objectives: State the ASI rule and the three situations that terminate statements regardless of parseability
Predict when a semicolon is required between statements on one line
Recognize the return/throw/yield/break/continue line-break exception and its consequences
Apply the defensive-semicolon technique for lines beginning with ( or [
Choose and follow a personal semicolon style with knowledge of the hazards

concepts.statement: JavaScript uses `;` to separate statements. You can **usually** omit the semicolon between two statements written on separate lines (and always at the end of a program or just before a closing `}`). More precisely: JavaScript treats a line break as a semicolon **only if it cannot parse the code without adding one** — that is, if the next nonspace character cannot be interpreted as a continuation of the current statement. Otherwise the line break is just whitespace.
concepts.detail: Two legitimate styles follow from this: many programmers (and this book) use semicolons to explicitly mark every statement end; others omit them everywhere except the few places where they are required. Whichever you choose, the details below are worth understanding either way.

concepts.term: How the parser decides: the continuation test
concepts.statement:
The engine tries to keep parsing across the line break. This code needs no semicolons at all:
```js
let a
a
=
3
console.log(a)
```
JavaScript interprets it as `let a; a = 3; console.log(a);` — the first line break **does** become a semicolon, because `let a a` cannot be parsed as one statement; but the second line break does **not**, because `a = 3` continues the statement legitimately.
concepts.detail: The engine is always greedy for the longest statement it can parse. A line break becomes a statement terminator only where that greed would otherwise produce a syntax error.

concepts.statement:
Because parentheses can continue an expression as a function call and brackets as an array index, a line beginning with `(` or `[` can be glued to the previous line. This looks like two statements:
```js
let y = x + f
(a+b).toString()
```
but JavaScript parses it as:
```js
let y = x + f(a+b).toString();
```
calling `f` with `(a+b)` — almost certainly not the author’s intent. In general, if a statement begins with `(`, `[`, `/`, `+`, or `-`, there is a chance it will be interpreted as a continuation of the statement before. Statements beginning with `/`, `+` and `-` are rare; `(` and `[` are not.
concepts.detail: This is why semicolon-free codebases are disciplined about never leaving a line ending in a bare expression that could invite continuation, and why the defensive semicolon below exists.

concepts.statement:
Some programmers protect lines that begin with `(` or `[` by **starting** them with a semicolon:
```js
let x = 0                        // Semicolon omitted here
;[x,x+1,x+2].forEach(console.log) // Defensive ; keeps this separate
```
The leading `;` terminates whatever came before, so the statement works even if the line above is later edited and its terminating semicolon removed.
concepts.detail: Whether or not you adopt the style, you will encounter it in the wild — an initial semicolon is not a typo, it is armor.

concepts.term: Exception 1: return, throw, yield, break, continue
concepts.statement:
These five statements are often followed by an identifier or expression. If a **line break appears after any of these words** before any other token, JavaScript **always** interprets that line break as a semicolon. The classic casualty:
```js
return
true;
```
JavaScript assumes you meant `return; true;` — the function returns `undefined` and `true` becomes a dead statement. You almost certainly meant `return true;` (one line). **Never insert a line break between return, break, or continue and the expression that follows.**
concepts.detail: This is the single most dangerous ASI behavior, because it fails silently: no syntax error, just a function that mysteriously returns undefined. The same rule applies to `throw`, and to `yield` in generator functions.

concepts.statement: The second exception involves `++` and `--`: to use either as a **postfix** operator, it must appear on the same line as the expression it applies to — otherwise the line break is read as ending the statement. The third exception involves arrow functions: the `=>` itself must appear on the same line as the parameter list. These exceptions exist so that postfix increments and arrows cannot be severed from their operands.
concepts.detail:
So `x
++` is parsed as `x; ++` (a syntax error, since `++` then has nothing to increment) — the engine will not treat `++` as applying to `x` across the break. Keep postfix operators and arrows attached to their left.

examples.title: Trace: the return-newline bug
examples.problem: A function is written to double a number, but its author broke the line after `return`. What happens at run time?

steps.label: The code
Step 1: ASI fires after return
steps.text: The parser reaches `return` and encounters a line break before any other token. Exception 1 applies: the break becomes a semicolon. The function body is now `return;` followed by the statement `x * 2;`.

steps.label: Step 2: Execution
steps.text: Calling `double(21)` executes `return` with no expression — such a return yields **undefined** to the caller, immediately. The `x * 2;` statement is never executed; it is dead code after an unconditional return.

steps.label: Step 3: No error is raised
steps.text: The program is syntactically legal — `x * 2;` is a valid (pointless) expression statement. The bug is purely semantic, which makes it hard to see and hard to debug.

steps.label: Step 4: The fix

examples.result: double(21) returns undefined, not 42: the line break after return terminates the function per ASI exception 1, and the computed expression becomes unreachable dead code.

examples.title: Trace: when a required semicolon goes missing
examples.problem: Two assignments are written on one line with one semicolon, then on two lines with none. Which forms are legal, and why?

steps.label: Form 1: two lines, no semicolons
steps.text:
```js
a = 3
b = 4
```
**Legal.** After `a = 3`, the next line starts with `b`, which cannot continue the assignment `a = 3` (the statement is complete), so the line break acts as a semicolon.

steps.label: Form 2: one line, no semicolon
steps.text:
```js
a = 3 b = 4
```
**Syntax error.** On a single line there is no line break to convert — the parser needs an explicit `;` (or a comma, with different meaning) to separate the statements.

steps.label: Form 3: one line, correct
steps.text:
```js
a = 3; b = 4;
```
**Legal.** The semicolon does the separating; the trailing one is optional before end-of-program or `}` but harmless and stylistically common.

steps.label: The rule behind all three
steps.text: ASI never "inserts" text into your file — it is a parsing rule about line breaks. Where there is no line break, the rule has nothing to act on, so the semicolon must be explicit.

examples.result: Two lines: no semicolon needed. One line: semicolon required. The engine’s separation rule is about line breaks that cannot be parsed as continuations.

examples.title: Trace: the silent function call
examples.problem: Semicolon-free code ends a line with an expression, and the next line begins with `(`. Predict the parsed program and the run-time consequence.

steps.label: The code
steps.text:
```js
let a = [1, 2]
(function() { console.log("hi"); })()
```

steps.label: Step 1: The parse
steps.text: `[1, 2]` followed by `( ... )` parses as an **indexing expression** — the parenthesized function is used as an array index. No line break helps, because `[1, 2](...)` is grammatically a valid continuation of the initializer expression.

steps.label: Step 2: Execution
steps.text: The engine tries to evaluate the function object as a property key for the array. The function is coerced toward a string; the attempt to call/index misfires and typically throws a TypeError — or worse, performs a silent no-op lookup.

steps.label: Step 3: The defensive fix
steps.text:
```js
let a = [1, 2]
;(function() { console.log("hi"); })()
```
The leading semicolon terminates the previous statement explicitly, so the IIFE (immediately invoked function expression) is parsed standalone, as intended.

examples.result: Without the defensive ;, the ( glues the lines into one accidental indexing expression. With it, two clean statements — the standard defense in semicolon-free style.

keyTakeaways: Semicolons separate statements; you may omit them between statements on separate lines, at end of program, and before a closing }.
ASI rule: a line break is treated as a semicolon only if the next nonspace character cannot be interpreted as a continuation of the current statement.
Statements beginning with (, [, /, + or - risk being glued to the previous line; ( and [ are the common ones — guard them with a leading defensive semicolon.
Exception 1: a line break after return, throw, yield, break or continue always ends the statement — `return\nvalue` returns undefined and is a notorious silent bug.
Exception 2: postfix ++/-- must stay on the same line as its operand. Exception 3: => must stay on the same line as the parameter list.
Pick a style — always-semicolon (the book’s) or semicolon-free — and apply it with knowledge of these hazards, not by accident.

quiz.q: Under automatic semicolon insertion, JavaScript treats a line break as a semicolon when:
options: the line break is followed by a comment
the next nonspace character cannot be interpreted as a continuation of the current statement (plus three special exceptions)
the line ends with a closing brace
the program is in strict mode
quiz.explanation: That is the ASI rule: the engine greedily parses the longest statement it can, and only converts a line break into a terminator when parsing would otherwise fail — plus the return/throw/yield/break/continue, postfix ++/--, and => exceptions.
A line break after return always terminates the statement (exception 1), so the function executes return with no value — undefined — and the 42 statement is dead code.

quiz.q: Why do some programmers begin certain statements with a semicolon, as in `;[x].forEach(f)`?
options: It is a comment marker in older dialects
As a defensive semicolon: it terminates any previous statement so a line beginning with ( or [ cannot be glued to it as a continuation
It is required syntax for array methods
It makes the statement execute in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Statements starting with ( or [ can accidentally continue the previous line (as a call or index); a leading ; explicitly ends whatever came before, keeping the statement separate even if the earlier line is edited.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three ASI exceptions in which a line break always acts as a semicolon?
options: A break after return, throw, yield, break or continue
A break between a postfix ++ or -- and the expression it follows
A break between a function’s parameter list and the => of an arrow function
A break between an if keyword and its parenthesized condition
quiz.explanation: The three exceptions are the jump keywords, postfix ++/--, and the => arrow. A break between if and ( is ordinary whitespace between tokens of one statement — no ASI involved.

quiz.q:
This code fails mysteriously. Why?
```js
let y = x + f
(a+b).toString()
```
options: `f` must be declared before use in strict mode
The two lines parse as one statement — a call `f(a+b)` followed by `.toString()` — instead of two statements
`let` cannot appear at the start of a program
quiz.explanation: Because ( can continue an expression as an argument list, ASI does not fire; the program parses as let y = x + f(a+b).toString(); — an unintended function call, which is why an explicit semicolon after the first line is required here.

Step 1: The code given returns on one line and places an object literal on the next. Step 2: The governing rule is the ASI exception for jump keywords: a line break after `return`, `throw`, `yield`, `break`, or `continue` always ends the statement, so `return` completes with no value and the function yields `undefined`. Step 3: Tracing line by line, the engine executes a bare `return`, exits with `undefined`, then parses `{ ready: true };` as a separate block containing a labeled statement, which produces nothing. Step 4: The distractors fail because the object never becomes the returned value, no boolean is produced, and no undeclared name is read, so no ReferenceError arises. Step 5: Therefore the program prints `undefined`.

intro: Computer programs work by manipulating values, and the kinds of values a language can represent are its types. This section draws the master dividing line of the whole chapter — primitive types versus object types — then surveys what the object side of that line includes, why functions and classes are themselves values, and how JavaScript frees you from ever deallocating memory by hand.
objectives: Partition JavaScript’s types into primitives and objects, naming every primitive
List the special-purpose object types provided by the core language and standard library
Explain why functions and classes count as values in JavaScript
Describe garbage collection and the one responsibility it still leaves the programmer

concepts.statement: JavaScript types divide into two categories: **primitive types** and **object types**. The primitives are **numbers**, **strings**, and **booleans**, plus the special values **null** and **undefined** (each typically considered the sole member of its own type) and **symbols** (ES6). Any value that is not a number, string, boolean, symbol, null or undefined is an **object**: a collection of properties, each with a name and a value (a primitive or another object).
concepts.detail: Numbers, strings and booleans get the largest share of this chapter (Sections 3.2–3.4); symbols and the global object are in 3.5; objects themselves get Chapter 6.

concepts.statement: An ordinary object is an **unordered** collection of named values. The language also defines **arrays** — ordered, numbered collections with special syntax and behavior (Chapter 7) — and the standard library adds more: `Set` (a set of values), `Map` (key-to-value mapping), typed arrays for bytes and binary data, `RegExp` for textual pattern matching, `Date` for dates and times, and `Error` and its subtypes for run-time failures (Chapter 11).
concepts.detail: One very special object, the **global object** (Section 3.5), is worth covering early because its properties are the globally defined identifiers of your program.

concepts.statement: JavaScript differs from more static languages in that **functions and classes are not just syntax — they are values** that programs can manipulate: assigned to variables, stored in arrays, passed as arguments, returned from functions. Like any non-primitive value, functions and classes are a specialized kind of object (Chapters 8 and 9).
concepts.detail: This one design decision — first-class functions — is what makes possible the functional programming style of Chapter 8 and the callbacks and Promise chains of Chapter 13.

concepts.statement: The JavaScript interpreter performs **automatic garbage collection** for memory management: when a value is no longer **reachable** — when no running code has any way to refer to it — the interpreter knows it can never be used again and automatically reclaims its memory. Programmers generally do not worry about destroying or deallocating values.
concepts.detail: The residual responsibility runs the other way: take care that values do not **inadvertently remain reachable** — and therefore non-reclaimable — longer than necessary. A forgotten event handler or lingering array of large objects is JavaScript’s version of a memory leak.

concepts.statement:
JavaScript supports an object-oriented programming style: rather than globally defined functions operating on values, the **types themselves define methods**. To sort array `a`, we do not pass `a` to a `sort()` function — we invoke the `sort()` method of `a`:
```js
a.sort();   // The object-oriented version of sort(a).
```
Technically only objects have methods, but numbers, strings, booleans and symbols **behave as if** they have methods (a wrapper performs the magic, Section 3.7). `null` and `undefined` are the only values methods cannot be invoked on.
concepts.detail: The practical consequence: `s.toUpperCase()` works on a string variable even though the string is a primitive — JavaScript creates a transient String object, runs the method, and discards the wrapper.

examples.title: Trace: classifying values from a line of code
examples.problem: Classify every value in this statement as primitive (which?) or object (which special kind?), and identify the method call.

steps.label: Step 1: The literal
steps.text: `"3.14"` is a **string** — a primitive. It is an immutable ordered sequence of 16-bit values.

steps.label: Step 2: The method call
steps.text: `.slice(0, 1)` looks like a method on a primitive. Since only objects truly have methods, JavaScript transiently wraps the string in a String object, invokes slice, and returns a new primitive string "3". The wrapper is discarded immediately.

steps.label: Step 3: The binding
steps.text: `s` now holds the primitive "3". The variable itself is not typed — it can later hold a number or an object with no ceremony — but the value it currently holds is a string primitive.

steps.label: Step 4: The taxonomy check
steps.text: Nothing here is an object at rest: the literal is primitive, the result is primitive, and the only object ever involved (the wrapper) existed for one method call. Had we written `new String("3.14")` instead, the value would have been a genuine String object — a historical leftover to avoid.

examples.result: One primitive in, one primitive out, one transient wrapper object for the method call — the everyday mechanics of "primitives with methods".

examples.title: Reachability decides collection
examples.problem: Two arrays are created. One is returned from a function and stored; the other is local and dropped. What can be collected, and when?

steps.label: The code
Step 1: During the call
steps.text: Both million-element arrays are reachable — through `keep` and `drop` from the executing function’s scope.

steps.label: Step 2: After the return
steps.text: `drop` and its inner array are no longer referred to by anything: the function’s scope is gone and no other binding points at them. They are unreachable — garbage, no matter how large.

steps.label: Step 3: What survives
steps.text: `keep` (and its million-element contents) remains reachable through the global `kept`. The garbage collector may reclaim `drop`’s memory but must not touch `kept`’s.

steps.label: Step 4: The programmer’s half of the deal
steps.text: Had the function also stored `drop` into a global cache "just in case", both arrays would stay reachable forever — the classic accidental leak that garbage collection cannot fix for you.

examples.result: Unreachable values are collected automatically; the programmer’s only memory duty is not to keep values reachable longer than needed.
