keyTakeaways: JavaScript converts implicitly wherever a type is expected: strings for string contexts, numbers-or-NaN for numeric contexts, truthiness for boolean contexts.
Surprising table rows: null → 0, "" → 0 (but falsy), all objects including [] and new Boolean(false) → true, [] → 0 and [9] → 9 as numbers.
== converts: null == undefined, "0" == 0, 0 == false, "0" == false are all true; === never converts — prefer it (and !==).
Explicit conversions: Number(), String(), Boolean(); the idioms +x, x-0, x+"", !!x do the same jobs.

Objects convert via prefer-string (toString then valueOf), prefer-number (valueOf then toString), or no-preference (Date → string, everything else → number); first primitive result wins, else TypeError.
Number([]) === 0 because arrays’ default valueOf() returns the object itself, so toString() runs: "" → 0; Number([9]) === 9 via "9" → 9.
+ prefers strings (concatenate if either operand is string-like after object conversion); * - / % prefer numbers; + is left-associative, so 1+2+"m" ≠ 1+(2+"m").

quiz.q: Which one of these == comparisons is FALSE?
quiz.explanation: == has a special rule making null and undefined equal, converts "0"→0 and false→0; but it NEVER converts its operands to booleans — so undefined == false is false, despite both being falsy. Convertibility does not imply equality.

quiz.q: What is `Number([9])` and why?
options: 9 — the prefer-number algorithm finds valueOf() returns the object itself, so toString() runs, producing "9", which converts to the number 9
quiz.explanation: The default valueOf() is not a primitive, so the algorithm falls back to toString(): a one-element array stringifies to its element’s string "9", which parses to 9. The same cascade with [] gives "" → 0.

quiz.q: Which of these values is TRUTHY?
quiz.explanation: Object-to-boolean conversion is trivial: ALL objects convert to true — including empty arrays and even the wrapper object wrapping false. Only undefined, null, 0, -0, NaN and "" are falsy.

quiz.q: What are the values of `1 + 2 + " mice"` and `1 + (2 + " mice")`?
quiz.explanation: + is left-associative: 1+2 is numeric addition (3), then 3 concatenates with the string. With parentheses, 2 concatenates first ("2 mice"), and 1 then joins the text — "12 mice". Order matters when strings are mixed with +.

quiz.q: When an object must convert to a number, which method does JavaScript try FIRST (for ordinary, non-Date objects)?
quiz.explanation: Number contexts use the prefer-number algorithm: valueOf() first, falling back to toString() only if valueOf() is missing or returns an object. String contexts reverse the order (prefer-string), and + and == use the no-preference variant.

intro: Before you can use a name, you must declare it. Modern JavaScript gives you let and const — block-scoped, with a temporal dead zone that makes use-before-declaration an actual error — while legacy var hoists declarations to the top of the function and quietly yields undefined. This section covers all three keywords, their scoping rules, the hoisting hazards, and then the jewel of ES6 declarations: destructuring assignment, which unpacks arrays and objects into variables with defaults, rest, skipping and nesting.
objectives: Declare variables and constants with let and const, with initialization best practices
Explain block scope versus var’s function scope, and read a nested-scope example correctly
Define hoisting and the temporal dead zone, and predict each one’s error behavior
Describe how undeclared assignments become (deletable) globals outside strict mode
Destructure arrays and objects: defaults, rest (...), skipping commas, renaming with colon, and nesting

concepts.detail: Two schools of thought on when to use const: only for fundamentally unchanging values (physical constants, version numbers) — the author’s preference — or for *any* value that does not happen to change, switching to let only when needed. Note: const prevents **reassignment**, not mutation of object contents.
In Node and in client-side modules, a "global" is scoped to its file. In traditional client-side script, a global declared in one <script> is visible in every script that runs after the declaration.

concepts.statement:
Using the same name in **two let/const declarations of the same scope is a syntax error**. Declaring a new variable with the same name in a **nested** scope is legal (though best avoided) — the inner declaration **shadows** the outer:
```js
const x = 1;        // Declare x as a global constant
if (x === 1) {
    let x = 2;      // Inside a block, x can refer to a different value
    console.log(x); // Prints 2
}
console.log(x);     // Prints 1: back in the global scope
let x = 3;          // ! Syntax error: re-declaring x in the same scope
```
concepts.detail: Also note: JavaScript variable declarations carry no type — a variable may hold a number now and a string later (`let i = 10; i = "ten";` is legal if poor style). TypeScript and Flow (Chapter 17) add optional type annotations.
In modern JavaScript there is really no reason to use var instead of let — except reading old code, where var’s hoisting explains otherwise mysterious undefineds.

concepts.statement:
let and const are hoisted too — the name is known to the engine from the start of the block — but they live in a **temporal dead zone (TDZ)** until the declaration statement executes. Referencing the variable in that window does not yield undefined: it **throws a ReferenceError**. This is let’s correction of var’s silent-undefined misfeature: use-before-declaration becomes an actual error instead of a quiet bug:
```js
{
    console.log(x);   // !ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x'
    let x = 1;        // …before initialization
}
```
concepts.detail: The error message engines give ("Cannot access ‘x’ before initialization") is the TDZ made visible. The practical rule it enforces: declare before you use — the same discipline every reader of the code already assumed.

The moral: always declare. A typo in an assignment (`conts = 3;`) silently becomes a global under sloppy mode and corrupts unrelated code; strict mode turns it into an immediate error at the exact line.

concepts.statement:
ES6 destructuring unpacks structured values into variables. The left side mimics array and object literal syntax:
```js
let [x,y] = [1,2];   // Same as let x=1, y=2
[x,y] = [x+1,y+1];   // Same as x = x + 1, y = y + 1
[x,y] = [y,x];       // Swap the values of the two variables
[x,y]                // => [3,2]: incremented and swapped
```
It shines with functions returning arrays:
```js
function toPolar(x, y) {          // Convert [x,y] to [r,theta]
    return [Math.sqrt(x*x+y*y), Math.atan2(y,x)];
}
function toCartesian(r, theta) {   // Polar to Cartesian
    return [r*Math.cos(theta), r*Math.sin(theta)];
}
let [r,theta] = toPolar(1.0, 1.0);   // r == Math.sqrt(2); theta == Math.PI/4
let [x,y] = toCartesian(r,theta);    // back to [1.0, 1.0]
```
concepts.detail: Destructuring works in let/const/var declarations, in plain assignments to already-declared variables, and — from Chapter 8 — in function parameter lists.

concepts.term: Destructuring extras: skip, rest, nested, objects, defaults
concepts.statement:
The full toolkit, each rule shown in one line:
```js
let [x,y] = [1];        // x == 1; y == undefined: extras get undefined
[x,y] = [1,2,3];        // x == 1; y == 2: extra values ignored
[,x,,y] = [1,2,3,4];    // x == 2; y == 4: commas skip values
let [x, ...y] = [1,2,3,4];  // y == [2,3,4]: rest collects the remainder
let [a, [b, c]] = [1, [2,2.5], 3];  // a==1; b==2; c==2.5: nesting
let [first, ...rest] = "Hello";  // first=="H"; rest==["e","l","l","o"]
```
Arrays destructure any **iterable** (that is why the string works). Object destructuring uses braces, matching property names; `name: local` renames, and the left side ignores unmatched properties:
```js
let transparent = {r: 0.0, g: 0.0, b: 0.0, a: 1.0};
let {r, g, b} = transparent;         // r == g == b == 0.0
const {sin, cos, tan} = Math;       // same as three separate consts
const { cos: cosine, tan: tangent } = Math;  // renamed copies
let [{x: x1, y: y1}, {x: x2, y: y2}] = [{x: 1, y: 2}, {x: 3, y: 4}];
// a mix of nested arrays/objects works too — see the chapter’s points example
```
In `for` loops and with `Object.entries()`:
```js
let o = { x: 1, y: 2 };
for(const [name, value] of Object.entries(o)) {
    console.log(name, value);   // "x 1" then "y 2"
}
```
concepts.detail: Object destructuring may include **defaults**: `let { timeout = 1000 } = options;` assigns 1000 when the property is undefined — the idiom behind default options objects. To check a complex destructuring, flip it: after `let [{x: x1}, {x: x2}] = points;`, the left side `[{x: x1}, {x: x2}]` should work as a valid literal reproducing the structure.

examples.title: Trace: the temporal dead zone
examples.problem: Contrast var’s silent undefined with let’s loud ReferenceError for the same use-before-declaration.

steps.label: The var version
The let version
Why the TDZ is a feature
steps.text: The var version hides the bug: undefined flows onward and fails somewhere far away. The let version fails **at the offending line**, with a message naming the variable — the difference between debugging for an hour and reading one error message.

steps.label: A subtle companion case

examples.result: var: undefined, bug deferred. let: ReferenceError at the exact line. The TDZ converts a silent hazard into an immediate, located error.

examples.title: Trace: destructuring with skip, rest and swap
examples.problem: Evaluate each destructuring statement, giving the final values of all variables.

steps.label: Statement 1: basics and mismatch
Statement 2: skipping with commas
Statement 3: rest
Statement 4: the swap
Statement 5: string as iterable

examples.result: x and y from [1]: 1 and undefined. After all statements: skipping selects positions, rest gathers arrays, and the swap pattern [x,y]=[y,x] exchanges values in one line.

examples.title: Trace: object destructuring into renamed and nested targets
examples.problem: Starting from `let points = { p1: [1, 2], p2: [3, 4] };`, write one destructuring that yields x1, y1, x2, y2 — then verify it by flipping the assignment.

steps.label: Step 1: Read the shape
steps.text: The value is an object with two properties (p1, p2), each an array of two numbers. The destructuring must mirror that: braces at the top, brackets inside.

steps.label: Step 2: The destructuring
steps.text:
```js
let { p1: [x1, y1], p2: [x2, y2] } = points;
```
`p1: [x1, y1]` means: take the property named p1, then destructure its value as an array into x1 and y1. Property names always sit on the left of the colon — exactly as in an object literal.

steps.label: Step 3: The results
steps.text: x1 == 1, y1 == 2, x2 == 3, y2 == 4 — four scalars unpacked from nested data in one statement.

steps.label: Step 4: The flip check
Step 5: The style warning
steps.text: Complex destructuring is hard to write and hard to read. Four plain assignments — `let x1 = points.p1[0];` and so on — are always legal and often kinder to the next reader.

examples.result: Nested object-array destructuring unpacks all four coordinates; the flip-the-assignment test confirms the pattern; prefer plain assignments when the pattern stops being obvious.

keyTakeaways: let declares variables, const constants (must be initialized; assignment throws TypeError). Initialize at declaration whenever possible.
let/const are block-scoped; loop headers scope the loop variable to the body — and const is legal there if the body never reassigns.
Redeclaring in the same scope is a SyntaxError; shadowing in a nested block is legal but risky.
var is function-scoped, hoisted (usable anywhere in the function, undefined before initialization), legal to redeclare, and its globals become global-object properties.
let/const have a temporal dead zone: referencing before the declaration runs throws ReferenceError instead of yielding undefined — an error at the bug, not far from it.
Outside strict mode, assignment to an undeclared name creates a global (deletable, unlike var globals); strict mode makes it a ReferenceError.
Destructuring unpacks arrays and objects: defaults, commas to skip, ...rest to collect the remainder, colon to rename (property name on the left), and arbitrary nesting — and works on any iterable.

options: undefined — the var declaration is hoisted, so x exists from the top of the function but is uninitialized
quiz.explanation: var declarations are hoisted to the top of the enclosing function: x exists before the log runs, holding undefined until its initialization line executes. let, in contrast, would throw a ReferenceError from the temporal dead zone.

quiz.q: Which statement about const is TRUE?
options: A const declaration must be initialized at declaration time, and its binding can never be reassigned
The value held by a const object is frozen: its properties cannot change
const cannot be used in a for/of loop header
const variables are function-scoped like var
quiz.explanation: const requires an initializer and forbids reassignment — but it does not freeze object contents (const o = {}; o.x = 1; is legal; o = {} is not). for(const x of data) is legal and idiomatic when the body never reassigns, and const is block-scoped like let.

quiz.q: After `let [x, ...y] = [1, 2, 3, 4];`, what are the values of x and y?
quiz.explanation: The first target takes the first element; the rest parameter (...) collects all remaining values into a new array. Skipping, defaults and rest are the three positional tools of array destructuring.

quiz.q: In the object destructuring `const { cos: cosine } = Math;`, which name is the property and which is the variable?
options: cos is the variable; cosine is the property
cos is the property name (on Math); cosine is the variable being assigned
Both are variables declared by the statement
Both are property names; nothing is declared
quiz.explanation: Property names always appear on the left of the colon — in both object literals and destructuring. The statement reads Math.cos into a new constant named cosine (equivalent to const cosine = Math.cos).

quiz.q: Outside strict mode, what does `function f() { oops = 42; } f();` do?
options: It creates a new local variable oops inside f
It creates a new global variable oops — a property of the global object, deletable with the delete operator
quiz.explanation: Assignment to an undeclared name creates a global, no matter how deeply nested the code — one of the best arguments for strict mode, where the same line throws. Unlike proper var globals, these accidental globals can be deleted.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a difference between var and let?
options: var is function-scoped while let is block-scoped
var declarations are hoisted (usable as undefined before initialization) while let bindings live in a temporal dead zone
var globals become properties of the global object while let globals do not
var requires an initializer while let does not
quiz.explanation: Neither requires an initializer (only const does). The real differences are scope (function vs block), hoisting behavior (silent undefined vs TDZ ReferenceError), global-object property status, and redeclaration legality (var allows it, let does not).

Step 1: The code given reads `status` before its `let` declaration executes, catches whatever happens, then reads it again after. Step 2: The governing rule is the temporal dead zone: a `let` binding exists from block entry but stays uninitialized until the declaration runs, and any read in that window throws a ReferenceError instead of yielding `undefined`. Step 3: Tracing line by line, the `try` block reads an uninitialized binding and throws, the `catch` prints `ReferenceError`, the declaration then initializes `status` to `'ready'`, and the final log prints `ready`. Step 4: The distractors fail because `undefined` is the legacy `var` hoisting behavior rather than the `let` behavior, and the second read occurs after initialization so it cannot throw. Step 5: Therefore the output is `ReferenceError` followed by `ready`.

intro: Expressions are the phrases of a JavaScript program — the pieces that evaluate to values — and statements are the sentences that make things happen (Chapter 5). This section starts at the bottom of the expression tower with the **primary expressions** that contain no smaller expression: literals, reserved words and bare identifiers. It then covers the two initializers that look like literals but are not: the object and array initializers, which happily embed arbitrary subexpressions, computed names, methods and the spread operator.
objectives: Distinguish expressions from statements, and classify the three kinds of primary expression
Read and write object initializer syntax: shorthand, computed keys, methods, accessors and spread
Read and write array initializer syntax, including elisions that create sparse arrays
Explain when and how initializers are evaluated, and why spread copies only one level deep

concepts.statement: An **expression** is a phrase of JavaScript that can be **evaluated** to produce a value. Expressions nest: the operands of an operator are themselves expressions, so `x + y * z` is one expression built from three variable references and two operators. Chapter 4 covers every way to write an expression; Chapter 5 covers statements, which *do* things rather than compute values.
concepts.detail: The test that separates the chapters: an expression answers "what value?", a statement answers "what happens next?". Statements contain expressions; expressions never contain statements (except function bodies, which live in their own scope).

concepts.statement: The simplest expressions — the atoms — are **primary expressions**: they are self-contained and require no smaller expression inside them. They are the constant **literals**, certain **reserved words** (`true`, `false`, `null`, `this`), and **variable references** — bare identifiers that evaluate to the value of the variable or constant they name (`undefined` behaves this way too: it is a predefined global property, not a keyword). Everything else in this chapter is built up from these.
concepts.detail: One "literal" is more than it looks: the template literal interpolates arbitrary expressions, and the object and array initializers below are compound expressions rather than true literals.

concepts.statement:
A **literal** is a data value that appears directly in the source, its meaning fixed by the way it is written. JavaScript has literals for strings, numbers in several bases, booleans, null, BigInt, and regular expressions:
```js
"hello"            // string literal
`hello ${name}`     // template literal (ES6): a literal CONTAINING a subexpression
12  1.2  .5        // numeric literals
0xff  0b101  0o17  // hex, binary, octal (Section 3.2)
1_000_000n          // BigInt literal
true  false  null  // boolean and null literals
/ab+c/gi            // regular-expression literal
```
The template literal is the odd one out: its `${...}` interpolates any expression at evaluation time, which is why it behaves more like an initializer than a pure literal.
concepts.detail: A regex literal may not be empty — `/` on its own is division — and a slash inside the pattern must be escaped. Regexes get a full chapter later (Section 11.3).

concepts.statement: A bare **identifier** on its own is an expression: it evaluates to the value of the variable, constant, or global property it names — `x`, `total`, `Math`, `console`. The interpreter consults the enclosing scopes from innermost outward to find the binding; Section 3.8 explains how `var` hoisting and the `let` temporal dead zone decide what the identifier means before this expression ever runs.
concepts.detail: An identifier that names no binding at all throws a `ReferenceError` at runtime — unless you probe it with `typeof` (Section 4.7), which is exactly why feature detection has a special form.
Section 6.6 catalogs the remaining literal extensions (getters/setters, symbol keys, spread on setters). What matters here: the initializer is evaluated, not merely read.
Spread into an object is ES2018; computed keys and shorthand are ES6. Spread never copies inherited properties, and a later explicit key overrides the spread-in value.

concepts.statement:
The **array initializer** is a comma-separated list of values in brackets — the commas carry the structure:
```js
const primes = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11];
const pairs = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];     // nesting is fine
const more = [...primes, 13];       // ES6 spread: 2,3,5,7,11,13
const sparse = [1, , 3];            // ELISION: a hole at index 1!
const two = [1, 2, ];                // trailing comma: length is 2
```
Omitting a value between commas creates a **hole** — a sparse array — rather than an `undefined` element. Spread copies an array’s indexed elements into a brand-new array (one level deep).
concepts.detail: Section 7.2 shows why holes matter: they are absent properties, so `length` counts them but iteration methods skip them. Trailing commas are free in both initializers.

concepts.statement: An initializer is not a compile-time constant: each time execution reaches it, every property value is evaluated **from scratch, left to right**. `let stamps = [Date.now(), Date.now()]` records two (possibly different) timestamps, and a `f()` inside a literal runs on every evaluation. Spread likewise runs on the spot — and copies only **one level deep**: `{ ...o }` shares nested objects rather than cloning them (Section 6.2).
concepts.detail: Fresh evaluation is exactly what makes initializers safe to place inside loops and function bodies: each pass builds a new container with new values — never a shared one.

examples.title: Trace: one object literal, evaluated
examples.problem: Given `const method = "GET"; const tag = "route";`, evaluate `make("list", "/api")` step by step and describe the resulting object.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: the return statement is reached
steps.text: Evaluation of the object initializer begins. No object exists yet — nothing is allocated until the braces close.

steps.label: Step 2: shorthand properties resolve
steps.text: Left to right: `action` is shorthand for `action: action` — the property name "action" gets the parameter value "list". Then `method` is shorthand for `method: method` — the name on the left is fixed, the value on the right reads the **outer variable** `method`, yielding "GET". Shorthand never invents properties; it reads what is in scope.

steps.label: Step 3: computed keys run as expressions
steps.text: `[tag]` evaluates the variable to the string "route", which becomes the property name holding "/api". `["h" + "its"]` concatenates to "hits" and stores 1. The bracket contents are ordinary expressions — function calls would run here too.

steps.label: Step 4: the method lands and the object is done
steps.text: Method shorthand creates a function value stored under "log". The finished object has five own properties — action: "list", method: "GET", route: "/api", hits: 1, log: the function — plus the inherited Object.prototype methods. If make is called again, every step reruns and a fresh object appears.

examples.result: req is { action: "list", method: "GET", route: "/api", hits: 1, log: f }. Shorthand reads outer-scope values, computed keys evaluate expressions, and each evaluation builds a new object.

examples.title: Trace: holes are not undefined
examples.problem: Compare `[1, , 3]` with `[1, undefined, 3]` — same length, same reads. What is actually stored, and what proves the difference?

steps.label: The code
steps.text:
```js
const a = [1, , 3];           // sparse: hole at index 1
const b = [1, undefined, 3];  // dense: real undefined at index 1
a.length === b.length          // => true (3)
a[1] === b[1]                 // => true (undefined)
1 in a                        // => false — NO property "1" at all
1 in b                        // => true — a property holding undefined
Object.keys(a)                // => ["0", "2"]
Object.keys(b)                // => ["0", "1", "2"]
```

steps.label: Step 1: the elision skips a property
steps.text: In `a`, the comma pair is an **elision**: the initializer simply does not create index 1. Reading `a[1]` yields undefined only because reading any absent property yields undefined — nothing was stored there.

steps.label: Step 2: the explicit value exists
steps.text: In `b`, index 1 exists and holds the value undefined. Both arrays agree on length and on every element read, so ordinary code cannot tell them apart.

steps.label: Step 3: existence tests can
steps.text: The `in` operator (Section 4.5) tests property existence, not value: `1 in b` is true, `1 in a` is false. `Object.keys` shows the same split: two keys versus three.

steps.label: Step 4: iteration can too
steps.text: Chapter 7’s array methods skip holes but still call their callbacks for explicit undefined elements — so `forEach` runs three times on `b` and twice on `a`. When you mean undefined, write undefined; when you mean absent, write the elision — and expect sparse arrays to surprise readers either way.

examples.result: A hole is an absent property; an explicit undefined is a stored value. The arrays agree on length and reads but differ under in, Object.keys and the iteration methods.

keyTakeaways: Primary expressions — literals, certain reserved words (true, false, null, this) and bare identifiers — are the atoms every other expression is built from.
Object and array initializers look like literals but are compound expressions: subexpressions inside them are evaluated each time execution reaches them.
Object initializer toolbox: property: value pairs, ES6 shorthand, computed keys [expr], method shorthand, accessor properties, and spread ...obj (later keys win).
Array literals nest, spread, and can contain elisions — commas that create holes (absent properties) rather than undefined elements; trailing commas change nothing.
Initializers evaluate fresh on every pass — safe in loops and function bodies — and spread copies only one level deep, sharing nested objects.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a primary expression?
options: A bare identifier such as total
A property access such as o.x
quiz.explanation: Property access builds a larger expression from a primary one — it needs an object expression and a name. Literals, certain reserved words and variable references are the primary atoms.

quiz.q: When `x` and `y` are in scope, what does the shorthand `{ x, y }` stand for?
options: A declaration of two new variables
quiz.explanation: ES6 shorthand uses each identifier once as the property name and once as the value: the property "x" gets the value of the variable x, and likewise for y.

quiz.q: After `const a = [1, , 3];`, what is the value of `1 in a`?
options: false — there is no property "1" at all
quiz.explanation: The comma pair is an elision: a hole. Index 1 never becomes a property, so the existence test is false even though a[1] reads as undefined.

quiz.q: Given `const defaults = { color: "teal", size: 1 };`, what is `{ ...defaults, color: "rose" }`?
options: { color: "rose", size: 1 } — the later explicit key overrides the spread-in value
{ color: "rose" } — only later keys are kept
A SyntaxError — spread cannot be followed by other properties
quiz.explanation: Spread copies properties in order; a property written after it (with the same key) overwrites the copied value. Reverse the order and the spread-in teal would win instead.

quiz.q: An object initializer containing `Date.now()` sits inside a loop body that runs three times. How many times does Date.now() execute?
options: Once — literals are folded at parse time
Three times — initializers are evaluated fresh each time execution reaches them
Zero — function calls are not allowed in literals
Once per property in the whole program
quiz.explanation: Initializers are live expressions: every property value is evaluated on every pass, left to right. That is what makes them safe to reuse in loops — each pass gets fresh values and a fresh object.

intro: Between the atoms of Section 4.1 and the operators of Section 4.3 sit the expressions that make objects usable: **function definition expressions** (values that are also behavior), **property access expressions** (the two syntaxes for reading a property) and **invocation expressions** (calling the function). Together they introduce this — the keyword whose value is decided not by where a function is defined but by how it is invoked, a distinction that will echo through Chapters 8 and 9.
objectives: Write anonymous, named and arrow function definition expressions and know when each is appropriate
Choose between expression.identifier and expression[expression] for property access
Invoke functions and methods, including with spread arguments and the conditional ?.( ) form
Predict the value of this for method calls versus plain function calls
Explain how ?. short-circuits a property access that would otherwise throw

concepts.detail: A function definition becomes a *declaration statement* (Chapter 5) only when the `function` keyword is the very first token of the statement — otherwise it is this expression.

concepts.statement:
A property is read (or assigned) with either **dot notation** `expression.identifier` or **bracket notation** `expression[expression]`:
```js
o.x          // dot: fixed name, valid identifier only
o["x"]       // bracket: same read, string key
o[0]         // key becomes the string "0"
let k = "color";
o[k]         // reads the property the variable names
o["main color"]  // spaces, dashes, any string: brackets only
```
The dot requires the property name to be a literal identifier; the bracket form evaluates its own subscript expression and converts it to a **string** key. Use dot whenever you can, brackets whenever you must.
concepts.detail: Note that `o.m` never consults a variable m — the identifier after the dot is the property name, literally. `o[m]` never ignores the variable m — the subscript is always evaluated.

concepts.statement: The dot accepts only identifiers: letters, digits, `$` and `_`, not starting with a digit, no spaces or punctuation. So numeric keys (`a[0]`), keys with spaces or hyphens (`o["data-id"]`), keys stored in variables, and keys computed at runtime all require brackets — brackets are **mandatory** for every one of those cases. Since ES5, reserved words are legal after the dot (`o.class`, `o.new`), but they are the one case linters still squint at. Mixed chains are the norm: `data.rows[i].cells[j]`.
concepts.detail: The classic bug is writing `routes.m` when a variable m holds the key — the dot reads the literal property "m" (usually undefined) instead. Section 4.2’s second worked example is exactly this trap.

concepts.statement:
ES2020 adds a **conditional access** form. `a?.b` reads `a.b` when `a` is not null or undefined; when it is, the access yields `undefined` instead of throwing `TypeError`:
```js
o?.x          // undefined when o is null/undefined; else o.x
o?.[k]        // conditional bracket form
f?.(arg)      // conditional invocation, below
```
The short circuit covers the whole chain: in `a?.b.c.d`, a null `a` skips the entire remainder — `.c` is never even evaluated.
concepts.detail: Section 4.6 pairs ?. with ?? to rebuild values that would otherwise be errors: `settings.user?.profile?.name ?? "guest"`. One caveat: the result undefined cannot distinguish "the property is missing" from "the property holds undefined".

concepts.statement: An **invocation expression** is `f(args)`: JavaScript evaluates `f` (if the result is not callable it throws `TypeError`), then evaluates each argument **left to right**, then runs the function body with parameters bound to those values. `f(...a)` **spreads** an array’s elements as the arguments. The value of the invocation expression is the function’s return value — or `undefined` if it falls off the end.
concepts.detail: Argument evaluation order is why `f(i++, i++)` passes two different values (Section 4.4 traces it). Spread in calls is ES6, the mirror image of spread in array literals.

concepts.statement: When the property access that yields the function is part of the invocation itself, it is a **method invocation** and `this` is bound to the object: `o.m(x)` runs `m` with `this === o`. A plain invocation — `let g = o.m; g(x)` — loses that association: in strict mode `this` is `undefined`, in sloppy mode the global object. **The value of this depends on how the function is invoked, not on where it is defined.**
concepts.detail: Chapters 8 and 9 complete the story: arrows inherit this lexically, call/apply/bind set it explicitly, and classes have their own rules. The call-form distinction — o.m() versus g() — is the part to master now.

concepts.statement: The pieces of an access or invocation are evaluated strictly **left to right**: in `a[i++] = a[i++]` the first postfix increment happens first, so the two accesses can see different indices. Method chains read the same way — `o.m().n()` calls `m` first, then accesses `.n` on its *result*. Relying on evaluation order across side effects is legal but a readability hazard; sequence such effects with separate statements.
concepts.detail: This left-to-right rule is a JavaScript constant: it governs operators (Section 4.3), arguments, and the pieces of property access alike. Other languages leave some of it unspecified — JavaScript never does.

examples.title: Trace: dot, bracket and a dynamic key
examples.problem: A routes object is indexed by HTTP method read from a request. Which access forms work, and which one silently reads the wrong property?

steps.label: The code
Step 1: dot reads the literal name
steps.text: (1) `routes.GET` is dot notation: the identifier GET names the property "GET" — object keys are strings and `GET` converts to exactly that key. Result "/list".

steps.label: Step 2: bracket reads through the variable
steps.text: (2) `routes[m]` evaluates the variable m first (the string "GET"), converts it to the key, and reads the same property: "/list". Whenever the name comes from data, brackets are the form.

steps.label: Step 3: non-identifier keys need brackets
steps.text: (3) `routes["POST /save"]` cannot be written with a dot — spaces make "POST /save" an invalid identifier — but bracket keys accept any string. Result "/save".

steps.label: Step 4: the classic bug
steps.text: (4) `routes.m` does NOT read through the variable — the dot wants a property literally named "m", which does not exist, so the result is `undefined` with no error. If you want the variable, it must sit inside brackets.

examples.result: Dot is fixed-name, bracket is computed-name. `routes.m` versus `routes[m]` is the classic lookup bug: same letter, opposite meanings.

examples.title: Trace: this follows the call form
examples.problem: An object’s method that uses this is called three ways: as a method, as a plain function, and through an arrow wrapper. Predict all three outcomes in strict mode.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: method invocation
steps.text: (1) The access `counter.bump` is part of the call, so this is counter: `++this.count` increments the object’s own property and returns 1.

steps.label: Step 2: plain invocation
steps.text: (2) The expression before the parentheses is just a variable — not an access on counter — so this is undefined in strict mode. `++this.count` throws `TypeError: Cannot set properties of undefined`. The function was not broken; the call form was.

steps.label: Step 3: the arrow re-establishes the method call
steps.text: (3) The arrow ignores its own call form entirely (arrows have no this of their own) and its body performs `counter.bump()` — a genuine method invocation. count becomes 2.

steps.label: Step 4: the lesson generalized
steps.text: Detach a method from its object (assign it, pass it as a callback) and you change this unless you re-attach it. Chapter 8 adds the tools — bind, arrows, class fields — that make the re-attachment routine.

examples.result: Same function, three answers: 1, a TypeError, then 2. this is a property of the invocation, not of the function.

keyTakeaways: Function definition expressions (function or arrow) create function values; the name in a named expression is a recursion-only local binding.
Dot for literal identifier names, brackets for computed or non-identifier keys — and o.m never consults a variable named m.
?. conditional access short-circuits the whole chain to undefined when its base is null/undefined; f?.(x) is its call form.
Invocation evaluates f and the arguments left to right, then runs the body; f(...a) spreads an array into the argument list.
this is decided by the call form: method call o.m() binds o, plain call binds undefined (strict) or the global object (sloppy); arrows inherit this from their enclosing scope.

quiz.q: `o.x` is equivalent to which bracket-form expression?
options: None — dot and bracket read different properties
quiz.explanation: The dot reads the literal identifier x as a string key, exactly like o["x"]. o[x] would instead evaluate the variable x — a different read whenever x holds anything but the string "x".

quiz.q: Which property CANNOT be accessed with dot notation?
quiz.explanation: Identifiers may contain letters, digits, `$` and `_` but not hyphens — "data-id" is not an identifier, so brackets `o["data-id"]` are mandatory. `$total` and `Save2` are perfectly legal identifier names.

quiz.q: After `const f = o.m; f();` in strict mode, what is this inside m?
quiz.explanation: The call form is plain — the expression before ( ) is a variable, not an access on o — so strict mode binds this to undefined. In sloppy code it would be the global object instead.

quiz.q: When a is null, what does `a?.b.c` evaluate to?
options: undefined, and the rest of the chain is not evaluated
A TypeError from reading .b of null
undefined only if c is also missing
quiz.explanation: The ?. short-circuits the entire chain: once a is known nullish, neither .b nor .c is evaluated and the whole expression is undefined — no exception, no further work.

quiz.q: In the call `f(a, b)`, when are the two arguments evaluated?
options: Left to right, before the function body starts running
Right to left, before the body runs
Lazily, inside the body, at first use
In undefined order — the specification leaves it open
quiz.explanation: JavaScript always evaluates subexpressions left to right: a first, then b, then the invocation. Lazy argument evaluation is a feature of some other languages, never JavaScript.

intro: The new operator creates the objects that constructor functions and classes work on; after that one addition, this section steps back and organizes the whole chapter. Operators are classified by arity, by the operand types they convert, and by their side effects — and then the two rules that decide how a long unparenthesized expression is grouped before anything runs: **precedence** and **associativity**, with the surprise that evaluation order is a separate, simpler rule of its own.
objectives: Describe what a new expression does: fresh object, prototype link, constructor call
Classify operators by arity, operand types, side effects and result types
Apply the precedence and associativity table to parse complex expressions
Explain why evaluation order is always left to right, independent of precedence

concepts.statement:
An **object creation expression** creates a new object and invokes a function as its **constructor**:
```js
const now = new Date();       // no-argument form
const p = new Point(2, 3);     // constructor with arguments
```
Evaluation: create a new empty object whose prototype is the constructor’s `.prototype` property; invoke the constructor with `this` bound to the new object; the value of the `new` expression is that new object — unless the constructor explicitly returns an object of its own, in which case that object wins.
concepts.detail: Chapter 9 builds classes on exactly this mechanism: class constructors run with new-like semantics, and the class syntax is largely a cleaner wrapper around prototype objects.

concepts.statement: An **operator** combines one or more operand expressions into a larger one. By **arity**: unary (`-x`, `typeof x`), binary (`x + y`) and ternary — JavaScript has exactly one ternary operator, the conditional `?:`. One symbol can serve several operators: `-` is both unary negation and binary subtraction, `++` exists in postfix and prefix forms with different values, and `*` is multiplication while `*=` is assignment. Operators are written with punctuation or with keywords (`typeof`, `void`, `delete`, `in`, `instanceof`, `await`).
concepts.detail: A few operators change program state (assignment, delete, ++/--): these have **side effects**, flagged in the reference table. Everything else merely computes a value.

concepts.statement: Most operators expect primitive operands and **convert** whatever they receive: `*`, `/`, `%`, `-` and unary `-` convert with `Number()`, so `"2" * 3` is 6 and `"" - 1` is -1. When conversion fails the answer is `NaN`, never an exception. The comparisons and `+` behave differently depending on operand types (Section 4.5, Section 4.4), and object operands are first reduced via `valueOf`/`toString` (Section 3.7). Bitwise operators are the strict ones: they truncate to 32-bit integers.
concepts.detail: Assignment operators require an lvalue on the left — a variable, object property or array element — and throw a ReferenceError otherwise. The result of an assignment expression is the assigned value.

Two consequences worth memorizing: unary operators bind looser than postfix but tighter than `**`, and `&` binds tighter than `^` which binds tighter than `|` — all tighter than `&&` and `||`, which surprises people coming from other languages.

concepts.statement: **Associativity** decides grouping when several operators of the SAME precedence compete for an operand. Most operators group **left to right** (L): `a - b - c` is `(a - b) - c`. The right-to-left (R) exceptions matter in practice: unary operators (`!~-x` is `!(~(-x))`), exponentiation (`2**3**2` is `2**(3**2)` = 512), assignment (`a = b = c` pushes c into b then a), the conditional `?:`, and `??`. Postfix `++`/`--` attach to the single expression on their left, so no question arises.
concepts.detail: `2 ** 3 ** 2` and `a = b = c` are the two chains you will actually type. Assignment returns the assigned value — that is what makes the chain work: b = c evaluates to c, and a = (that value) evaluates to c as well. If a mixed expression needs more than a second of thought, parenthesize it — clarity beats cleverness in review.

concepts.term: Evaluation order is left to right
concepts.detail: This is the same left-to-right discipline seen in arguments and property access (Section 4.2) — it is a property of the whole language, not of any one operator.

concepts.statement: Parentheses are not an operator: they are **grouping syntax** that forces the parse you mean, overriding both precedence and associativity. `(2 + 3) * 4` is 20 where `2 + 3 * 4` is 14; `(a || b) ?? c` is legal where `a || b ?? c` is a SyntaxError (Section 4.6). Parentheses do not force evaluation order — that is already fixed — but they do change which value flows where.
concepts.detail: When in doubt in code that others will read, parenthesize. The linters of Chapter 17 agree: they flag precedence-sensitive mixtures like a & b == c even when the parse is technically correct.

examples.title: Trace: new, step by step
examples.problem: Show exactly what `new Point(2, 3)` does — and what would change if the constructor returned an object of its own.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: allocate and link
steps.text: new creates a new empty object and sets its prototype to Point.prototype — the object that gives every Point its shared methods.

steps.label: Step 2: run the constructor with this
steps.text: The constructor body executes with this bound to the fresh object. The two assignments create own properties x and y on it — nothing is returned, which means "return this" by default.

steps.label: Step 3: the return rule
steps.text: The new expression evaluates to the fresh object — unless the constructor executes `return someObject`, in which case that object replaces it (returning a primitive is ignored). Had Point returned { z: 0 }, every new Point would be that empty-ish object and p.x would be undefined.

steps.label: Step 4: identity and instanceof
steps.text: Each new expression manufactures a fresh object: p and q are distinct references (Section 3.6), so p === q is false — while both inherit through Point.prototype, so p instanceof Point is true (Section 4.5).

examples.result: new = allocate a fresh object, prototype-link it, invoke the constructor with this bound to it, and yield that object unless the constructor returns its own object.

examples.title: Trace: parsing without parentheses
examples.problem: Group and evaluate three expressions using only the precedence and associativity rules.

steps.label: Step 1: (A) three levels at once
steps.text: ** (level 5) beats * (level 6), which beats + (level 7): the grouping is x + (3 * (4 ** 2)). So 4 ** 2 = 16, then 3 * 16 = 48, then 2 + 48 = 50.

steps.label: Step 2: (B) right associativity
steps.text: Two ** operators compete for the middle 3; ** is right-associative so the right pair groups first: 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512. Left-associative grouping would have given (2 ** 3) ** 2 = 64 — not what JavaScript does.

steps.label: Step 3: (C) assignment chains flow right to left
steps.text: Assignment is also right-associative: b = 3 runs first, and the value it yields (3) flows left into a = 3. Both variables now hold 3, and the expression’s value is 3.

steps.label: Step 4: override when the parse is not the intent
steps.text: Parentheses change the grouping, not the order discipline: (x + 3 * 4) ** 2 is (2 + 12) ** 2 = 196. When code reviewers would reach for the table, write the parentheses instead.

examples.result: (A) 50, (B) 512, (C) both variables 3 with expression value 3 — precedence groups, associativity breaks ties, and neither changes left-to-right execution.

keyTakeaways: new allocates a fresh object, links it to the constructor’s prototype, invokes the constructor with this, and returns the object — unless the constructor returns an object of its own.
Operators are unary, binary or (exactly one) ternary; some symbols encode several operators, and a few have side effects.
Most operators convert their operands — NaN is the failure answer, never an exception; bitwise operators truncate to 32 bits; assignment needs an lvalue.
Precedence groups, associativity breaks same-precedence ties: only unary operators, **, ?:, ?? and assignment (plus new and =>) associate right to left.
Evaluation order is always left to right at every level — independent of precedence and associativity.
Parentheses override grouping (and are required to mix ?? with && / ||); they do not change evaluation order.

quiz.q: Which list contains ONLY right-associative operators?
quiz.explanation: The right-to-left exceptions are unary operators, **, ?:, ?? and assignment (with new and =>). Everything else — arithmetic, equality, logical, relational, shifts and comma — groups left to right.

quiz.q: In `x + y * z`, if x, y and z are function calls, which runs first?
options: x, because evaluation order is always left to right
z, because the rightmost is evaluated first
quiz.explanation: Precedence decides grouping (y * z first), but execution is left to right regardless: x is evaluated before either of the others. Grouping and order are independent rules.

quiz.q: What does `2 ** 3 ** 2` evaluate to?
quiz.explanation: ** is right-associative: the grouping is 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512. The would-be left grouping (2 ** 3) ** 2 = 64 is not what the language does.

quiz.q: What happens when a constructor function invoked with new executes `return { z: 0 };`?
options: The new expression evaluates to that returned object instead of the fresh one
A TypeError — constructors cannot return values
The returned object is ignored and the fresh object is used
The fresh object gains a z property
quiz.explanation: new yields whatever object the constructor explicitly returns; only when it returns nothing (or a primitive, which is ignored) does the freshly allocated this become the value of the expression.

quiz.q: Which of these binds its operand TIGHTEST?
quiz.explanation: Postfix ++/-- sit above the unary operators, which sit above multiplication, which sits far above &&: the table’s top three levels are member access/call, new, then postfix increment and decrement.

intro: Arithmetic in JavaScript is generous to a fault: every operator accepts every operand, converting as needed and preferring NaN over an error. This section covers the arithmetic operators proper — **, *, /, % and the two-faced + — then the unary forms including prefix and postfix ++/-- with their famous evaluation trap, NaN propagation, and the bitwise family that quietly truncates everything to 32 bits and unlocks flag masks, bit sets, and the two’s complement arithmetic behind signed and unsigned shifts.
objectives: Predict results of **, *, /, %, + and - across all string/number operand combinations
Distinguish prefix from postfix ++ and --, tracing both their values and their side effects
Explain NaN propagation through arithmetic and its two ** exceptions
Evaluate `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>` and `>>>` on 32-bit two’s complement operands
Use bit masks to set, test, clear and toggle flag bits

concepts.statement: The ** operator (ES2016) raises its left operand to the power of its right: `2 ** 10` is 1024, `x ** 0.5` is a square root. It is **right-associative** (Section 4.3) and has a deliberate grammar surprise: `-3 ** 2` is a **SyntaxError** — unary minus binds too loosely for the parser to guess your intent, so you must write `(-3) ** 2` (9) or `-(3 ** 2)` (-9). The `**=` form assigns the result.
concepts.detail: ** works for BigInt operands too (Chapter 3); it does not accept a negative base with a fractional exponent (that returns NaN). Math.pow is the identical function form.

concepts.statement: All three convert their operands with `Number()`: `"2" * 3` is 6, `"x" * 3` is NaN. **Division always produces a floating-point result** — there is no integer division: `7 / 2` is 3.5 (use `Math.floor` or `Math.trunc` to integerize). Division by zero yields Infinity, -Infinity or NaN (Section 3.2). The remainder `%` takes the **sign of the dividend**: `-5 % 2` is -1 and `5 % -2` is 1 — like Java, unlike Python. For a true mathematical modulo: `((n % m) + m) % m`.
concepts.detail: Practical uses of %: parity tests (n % 2), cycling through indexes ((i + 1) % len), and splitting a quantity into units. Remember the sign rule when the dividend can be negative.

concepts.statement:
Binary `+` adds numbers or concatenates strings — and it decides which after converting objects to primitives. **If either operand is (or converts to) a string, + concatenates**, converting the other side to a string; otherwise both go through Number():
```js
1 + 2          // 3 — both numbers
"1" + 2        // "12" — a string on either side wins
1 + 2 + "3"    // "33" — (1 + 2) first, then 3 + "3"
"3" + 1 + 2    // "312" — string first, all concat after
true + true    // 2 — booleans numberify
null + 1       // 1 — null converts to 0
undefined + 1  // NaN — undefined converts to NaN
1 + {}         // "1[object Object]"
1 + []         // "1" — empty array converts to ""
"6" - 1        // 5 — minus has ONE behavior
"6" * "7"      // 42
```
Every other arithmetic operator coerces to number; only + consults the types this way.
concepts.detail: This is the operator behind accidental "12" results from numeric-looking input. When summing, convert explicitly with Number() or unary + — Section 3.7 has the full conversion rules.

concepts.statement:
The unary operators convert to a number and act: unary **minus negates** after ToNumber; unary **plus converts and does nothing else** — it is the idiomatic shorthand for `Number()`, commonly written without a space:
```js
+"3"        // 3
+"3.14"     // 3.14
+""         // 0
+"x"        // NaN
-"3"        // -3
- -x        // double negation — x, converted, twice
```
Objects consult `valueOf` first, then `toString` — which is why `+new Date()` yields the millisecond timestamp (the Date’s numeric heart, Section 3.2).
concepts.detail: Prefer Number(x) when the conversion is the point and unary + when it is incidental (like the Date idiom). Unary operators bind tighter than * — `-x * y` is (-x) * y.

concepts.statement:
`++` and `--` add or subtract 1 from an lvalue (variable, property or element) and always work numerically — even `"5"++` becomes 6, no concatenation. The difference is what the **expression itself yields**: the **postfix** form (`i++`) returns the value *before* adjusting; the **prefix** form (`++i`) returns the value *after*:
```js
let i = 1;
let a = i++;   // a = 1, i = 2 — old value out, then bump
let b = ++i;   // b = 3, i = 3 — bump first, new value out
```
Both forms have the same side effect; only the yielded value differs.
concepts.detail: Because arguments evaluate left to right (Section 4.2), `f(i++, i++)` passes two different values — the worked example traces it. When the value is unused, prefer prefix: it reads as one idea.

concepts.statement: NaN is sticky: any arithmetic operation with a NaN operand produces NaN — `NaN + 1`, `NaN * 0` are all NaN — and every comparison involving NaN is false (Section 4.5). The single exception is IEEE-faithful: `NaN ** 0` is 1. NaN is JavaScript’s failure sentinel for numeric work — `parseInt("x")`, `Number("x")`, `undefined + 1` all land there rather than throwing.
concepts.detail: Detect it with `Number.isNaN(x)` or the self-inequality idiom `x != x` (Chapter 3). Because it propagates silently, validate at the boundary — one NaN in a running sum poisons the whole result.

concepts.statement:
The bitwise operators convert their operands to **32-bit signed integers** (two’s complement), combine them bit by bit, and return a number:
```js
0x0F & 0x3D   // => 0x0D (13): AND — 1 only where BOTH are 1
0x0F | 0x3D   // => 0x3F (63): OR — 1 where EITHER is 1
0x0F ^ 0x3D   // => 0x32 (50): XOR — 1 where EXACTLY ONE is 1
~0x0F         // => -16 (0xFFFFFFF0): NOT — flip every bit
```
These are precisely the AND, OR and XOR gates of Mano’s Digital Logic (Chapters 1–2) — the truth tables Rosen’s Boolean algebra chapter (Ch 12) formalizes — evaluated here on numbers instead of wires. Values outside the 32-bit range wrap: -1 is all ones, so `-1 & 0xFF` is 255.
concepts.detail: Bitwise operands beyond $\pm 2^{31}$ wrap modulo $2^{32}$, and NaN/Infinity convert to 0. BigInt has its own bitwise operators with no width limit (Chapter 3).

concepts.statement:
The three **shift operators** move the 32-bit pattern left or right, with a sign difference on the right:
```js
5 << 3          // => 40: left shift = multiply by 2^3
1 << 31         // => -2147483648: overflow into the sign bit
-12 >> 2        // => -3: >> keeps the sign bit (arithmetic shift)
-12 >>> 2       // => 1073741821: >>> fills with zeros (unsigned)
-1 >>> 0        // => 4294967295: the same bits, read as unsigned
```
`>>` treats the value as signed and sign-extends; `>>>` treats the same 32 bits as an unsigned integer and pushes in zeros — the tool for reading a bit pattern without its sign, used heavily with the typed arrays of Chapter 11.
concepts.detail: A left shift is multiplication by $2^{n}$ with wraparound; a right `>>` by $n$ is floor division by $2^{n}$ for both signs (-12 >> 2 is floor(-3) = -3). Beyond 31, shift counts wrap modulo 32: 1 << 32 is 1.

examples.title: Trace: postfix versus prefix
examples.problem: Evaluate each line, then predict a two-argument call that increments the same variable twice.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: (1) postfix — old value out
steps.text: i++ yields the value before the increment: a is 1. The side effect still happens — i is 2 after the statement.

steps.label: Step 2: (2) prefix — new value out
steps.text: ++i bumps first: i goes 2 to 3, and b receives the new value 3. Same operator family, same side effect, different yielded value.

steps.label: Step 3: (3) both forms in one expression
steps.text: Left to right: i++ yields 3 (i becomes 4), then ++i bumps to 5 and yields 5. c = 3 - 5 = -2, with i left at 5. Mixing forms like this is legal and unwise — this line exists so the trace can prove you understand it, not as a style model.

steps.label: Step 4: (4) the argument-order trap
steps.text: Arguments evaluate left to right: n++ yields 0 (n becomes 1), then ++n bumps to 2 and yields 2. show returns [0, 2] — two different values from the "same" variable. In languages with unspecified argument order this line would be unanswerable; in JavaScript it is merely a bad idea.

examples.result: a = 1, b = 3, c = -2 (i ends 5), and show(n++, ++n) returns [0, 2]. Postfix hands out the old value, prefix the new one — and left-to-right order fixes every question.

examples.title: Worked: a permission mask
examples.problem: Implement a Unix-style permission word with bits for READ, WRITE and EXEC: grant, test, clear and toggle permissions using only bitwise operators.

steps.label: Step 1: define the bits
steps.text:
```js
const READ = 0b001;   // 1
const WRITE = 0b010;  // 2
const EXEC = 0b100;  // 4
let perms = 0;        // no permissions
```
Each constant is one bit position; any combination is their union — a set encoded as a number.

steps.label: Step 2: grant a bit
steps.text:
```js
perms = READ | WRITE;   // 0b011 = 3
perms |= EXEC;          // 0b111 = 7 — add a bit without disturbing others
```
OR sets bits: a 0 becomes 1 where the mask has a 1, and existing 1s stay. This is set union, gate for gate the OR of Chapter 2 in Mano’s Digital Logic.

steps.label: Step 3: test for a bit (never with truthiness alone)
steps.text:
```js
(perms & READ) !== 0    // true — READ is set
(perms & EXEC) !== 0    // false — EXEC is not
perms & (READ | EXEC)   // 0b101 = 5 — which of several bits are set
```
AND masks out everything but the bit(s) of interest. Compare with `!== 0` as a discipline: `&` yields a NUMBER (here 1 or 5), and when you test several bits at once the nonzero result cannot tell you which ones — only the comparison can.

steps.label: Step 4: clear and toggle
steps.text:
```js
perms &= ~READ;   // 0b110 — READ cleared, others untouched
perms ^= WRITE;   // 0b100 — WRITE toggled off
perms |= READ;    // 0b101 — and back on
```
`~READ` is all ones except the READ bit, so AND-ing with it erases exactly that bit. XOR flips the masked bits in place — 1 to 0, 0 to 1.

examples.result: A number behaves as a bit set: `|` grants, `&` tests, `& ~` clears, `^` toggles — four idioms that cover essentially every flag-manipulation need.

examples.title: Trace: >>, >>> and two’s complement
examples.problem: Explain the three different results of shifting the same negative number, starting from its 32-bit representation.

steps.label: Step 1: write the bits
steps.text: 12 is 0b1100. In 32-bit two’s complement, -12 is the bitwise complement of 11 plus 1: 0xFFFFFFF4 — every high bit set, the low four bits 0100.

steps.label: Step 2: the arithmetic shift >>
steps.text:
```js
-12 >> 2    // => -3
```
>> shifts right two places, copying the sign bit in from the left — the value stays negative. It is floor division by 4: floor(-12 / 4) = -3 exactly.

steps.label: Step 3: the zero-fill shift >>>
steps.text:
```js
-12 >>> 2   // => 1073741821
```
>>> pushes in zeros instead, so the same bit pattern 0xFFFFFFF4 becomes 0x3FFFFFFD — read as an unsigned integer, 1073741821. The bits did not change; the interpretation did.

steps.label: Step 4: the unsigned-view idiom
steps.text:
```js
-1 >>> 0    // => 4294967295 (2^32 - 1)
```
Shifting by zero converts nothing yet re-reads the pattern unsigned: -1 is all 32 ones, so as an unsigned value it is $2^{32} - 1$. This is the standard trick for inspecting what a negative number looks like to the bitwise operators — and for the unsigned reads in Chapter 11’s typed arrays.

examples.result: Same bits, three answers: -3 (sign-extended), 1073741821 (zero-filled), 4294967295 (unsigned re-read). >> preserves sign, >>> does not, and x >>> 0 displays the raw 32-bit pattern.

keyTakeaways: ** is right-associative and -3 ** 2 is a SyntaxError — parenthesize (-3) ** 2 or -(3 ** 2).
Division is always floating point; % takes the sign of the dividend (-5 % 2 is -1); use ((n % m) + m) % m for true modulo.
+ concatenates when either operand converts to a string — the only arithmetic operator that consults types this way; every other one numberifies (and yields NaN on failure).
Postfix i++ yields the old value, prefix ++i the new one; both bump the same way, and argument lists evaluate left to right so f(i++, i++) passes two different values.
NaN poisons arithmetic (NaN ** 0 being the lone 1 exception) and makes every comparison false — validate at input boundaries.
Bitwise operators work on 32-bit two’s complement integers: `&` masks, `|` sets, `^` toggles, `~` inverts; `<<` multiplies by $2^{n}$, `>>` floor-divides preserving sign, `>>>` re-reads unsigned.
The flag idioms: grant with `|=`, test with `(flags & bit) !== 0`, clear with `&= ~bit`, toggle with `^=`.

quiz.q: What are the values of `"7" - 1` and `"7" + 1`?
quiz.explanation: Minus has one behavior — numeric coercion — so "7" becomes 7 and the result is 6. Plus sees a string operand and concatenates, giving "71". The two operators are not symmetric.

quiz.q: What does the expression `-3 ** 2` do?
options: Throws a SyntaxError at parse time
quiz.explanation: The grammar forbids an unparenthesized unary operand directly left of ** — the designers chose a hard error over silent ambiguity. Write (-3) ** 2 for 9 or -(3 ** 2) for -9.

quiz.q: After `let i = 2; const r = [i++, i++];`, what are r and i?
quiz.explanation: Array elements evaluate left to right: the first postfix yields 2 (i becomes 3), the second yields 3 (i becomes 4). Both entries reflect the old value at the moment each was evaluated.

quiz.q: Which expression tests whether n is odd?
quiz.explanation: AND with 1 masks everything but the low bit, which is 1 exactly for odd numbers. `n && 1` is a truthiness test of n, `n | 1` forces the bit on, and `n ^ 1` flips it.

quiz.q: What is the value of `-1 >>> 0`?
quiz.explanation: -1 is thirty-two 1-bits in two’s complement; >>> re-reads the same pattern as unsigned — $2^{32} - 1$ = 4294967295. Shifting by zero leaves every bit in place.

intro: Relational expressions ask how two values stand to each other — equal, identical, ordered, contained. JavaScript makes the chapter’s sharpest split here: **===** compares values with no conversion at all, **==** compares after a well-defined conversion dance, and the six comparison operators consult strings or numbers depending on both sides. Add in — which tests property existence, and instanceof, which walks prototype chains — and you have every "is this related to that" question the language can ask.
objectives: Apply the strict equality rules: primitives by value, objects by identity, NaN and +0/-0 corner cases
Apply the == conversion algorithm, including the special null/undefined pairing
Predict < <= > >= for string, mixed and NaN operands, and for Dates
Use the in operator and distinguish own from inherited properties
Use instanceof to test prototype chains, including its primitive exception

concepts.statement: **Strict equality** compares two values with no conversion whatsoever. Two numbers are equal when they have the same value — with the two famous exceptions: `NaN === NaN` is false, and `+0 === -0` is true. Two strings are equal when they have exactly the same length and the same 16-bit values in the same order. Two booleans when identical. Two objects (including arrays and functions) only when they are **the same object** — `[]` and `[]` are never equal. And values of different types are never strictly equal: `1 === "1"` is false, `true !== 1`.
concepts.detail: This is the equality to use by default — it never surprises. The only coercion it performs is none at all, which is exactly why linters (Chapter 17) enforce it.

concepts.statement:
**Loose equality** first normalizes its operands, then compares. The algorithm: (1) `null` and `undefined` are equal to each other and to nothing else — no conversion applies to them; (2) same type → the === rules; (3) number vs string → the string converts to a number; (4) boolean vs anything → the boolean converts to a number first, then retry; (5) object vs primitive → the object converts to a primitive (`valueOf`, then `toString`, Section 3.7), then retry. Everything else — genuinely different non-nullish types — is false:
```js
1 == "1"          // true: "1" converts to 1
0 == false        // true: false converts to 0
"" == 0           // true: "" converts to 0
null == undefined // true — the special pairing
null == 0         // false: null converts to nothing
NaN == NaN        // false: NaN is unequal to everything
[1] == 1          // true: [1] converts to "1" then 1
[] == ""          // true: [] converts to ""
```
concepts.detail: The one idiom that earns its keep: `x == null` matches both null and undefined — a concise "is absent" test. Beyond it, == mostly produces bugs; prefer === everywhere else.

concepts.statement: The **inequality operators** `!=` and `!==` are the exact negations: `a != b` is precisely `!(a == b)`, and `a !== b` is `!(a === b)`. No extra conversion rules of their own. The strict forms inherit all the advice: use `!==` by default, and reach for `!=` only in the `x != null` absence test.
concepts.detail: Because equality questions are binary, negation never changes the conversion story — only the answer. The full decision procedure lives in the two operators above.

concepts.statement:
The four comparisons follow one rule: **if both operands are strings, compare code units; otherwise convert both to numbers** (objects via `valueOf`/`toString` with the numeric hint). If either conversion yields NaN, **every comparison is false** — including `x >= NaN` and `x < NaN` both:
```js
1 + 1 < 3          // true — numbers
"11" < "3"        // true! — STRING compare: "1" < "3"
"11" < 3          // false — numeric: 11 < 3 is false
"one" < 3         // false — "one" converts to NaN
new Date(2020, 0) < new Date(2021, 0)   // true — timestamps
```
Dates work because their `valueOf` is the millisecond timestamp (Section 3.2) — the one object comparison people write on purpose.
concepts.detail: The all-strings rule is character-by-character on UTF-16 code units, so uppercase letters sort before lowercase ("Z" < "a") — Chapter 3’s localeCompare exists for human ordering.

concepts.statement: The **in operator** asks whether an object has a named property — own or inherited: `"x" in o`. It expects a string or something that converts to one on the left and an object on the right. On arrays, indices are property names: `0 in [10, 20]` is true, `2 in [10, 20]` is false. Inherited properties count: `"toString" in {}` is true — it lives on Object.prototype. To test only own properties, use `Object.hasOwn(o, "x")` or the older `o.hasOwnProperty("x")` (Section 6.4).
concepts.detail: in tests existence, not value — the exact tool that distinguished array holes from stored undefined in Section 4.1. The for/in statement of Chapter 5 is built on the same property-name enumeration.

concepts.statement:
The **instanceof operator** — `object instanceof Constructor` — asks whether the constructor’s `.prototype` appears anywhere on the object’s prototype chain. It walks the chain of the left operand (after confirming it is an object) looking for that exact prototype object:
```js
function Point(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
const p = new Point(1, 2);
p instanceof Point     // true — chain starts at Point.prototype
p instanceof Object   // true — chain continues to Object.prototype
[] instanceof Array    // true
[] instanceof Object  // true — arrays are objects
"s" instanceof String  // false! — a primitive has no chain
new String("s") instanceof String   // true — this one does
```
Primitives always answer false: instanceof tests objects, and a string primitive is not a String object (Section 3.6).
concepts.detail: Cross-realm objects (from another window or frame) can answer false unexpectedly — the classic iframe gotcha. Chapter 9 leans on instanceof for classes; Chapter 11’s Array.isArray is the robust array test that avoids both pitfalls.

concepts.statement:
A short museum of **comparison surprises**, all of which follow from the rules above:
```js
NaN === NaN              // false — unequal to everything, itself included
[1, 2] == [1, 2]         // false — two distinct array objects
let a = [1, 2];
a == a                   // true — the SAME object
"1" == true              // true — true converts to 1, "1" to 1
({}) == "[object Object]" // true — object converts to that string
null == 0                // false — null pairs only with undefined
```
None of these is a language bug; each is the algorithm doing exactly what it says.
concepts.detail: The practical defense is a house rule: === always, == null when you mean "absent", and deep comparison libraries when you mean contents — Chapter 7 covers why arrays need them.

examples.title: Worked: the == versus === comparison table
examples.problem: Predict every result below before reading the explanation column — each row exercises one clause of the == algorithm or one === rule.

steps.label: Step 1: (a) versus (b) — the string clause
steps.text: (a) Different types under ===: false, immediately, no questions asked. (b) == with number vs string converts the string: 1 == 1 → true.

steps.label: Step 2: (c) and (d) — the boolean clause
steps.text: (c) false converts to 0, then 0 == 0 → true. (d) both sides convert — false to 0, "" to 0 — so true as well. This is why empty strings and false look identical to ==, which is rarely what anyone wants.

steps.label: Step 3: (e) and (f) — the nullish pairing
steps.text: (e) null and undefined are equal to each other and nothing else: true. (f) null does NOT convert to 0 for == — false. The pairing is the single special case in the whole algorithm.

steps.label: Step 4: (g) — NaN exclusion
steps.text: NaN fails even self-equality: false under both operators. The only values for which x == x is false are NaN (and NaN === NaN likewise false).

steps.label: Step 5: (h) and (i) — the object clause
steps.text: (h) [1] converts to the primitive "1" (valueOf hands back the array, toString produces "1"), then the string clause finishes the job: true. (i) [] converts to "" and the empty string equals the empty string: true.

steps.label: Step 6: (j) and (k) — object identity
steps.text: Two fresh empty objects are distinct references: (j) false — == never deep-compares contents. The same object on both sides: (k) true. For objects, both equality operators answer "same object?", never "same contents?".

examples.result: (a) F (b) T (c) T (d) T (e) T (f) F (g) F (h) T (i) T (j) F (k) T — one algorithm, six clauses, zero magic.

examples.title: Trace: in and instanceof
examples.problem: Given a constructor, an instance and a primitive, walk both tests: which properties exist (where?), and which prototype chains contain which prototypes?

steps.label: The code
steps.text:
```js
function Point(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
const p = new Point(1, 2);
"x" in p               // (1)
"toString" in p        // (2)
"z" in p               // (3)
p instanceof Point      // (4)
p instanceof Object     // (5)
[] instanceof Array     // (6)
"s" instanceof String  // (7)
```

steps.label: Step 1: own properties answer first
steps.text: (1) true — x is an own property, created by the constructor’s assignment. (3) false — z was never created, and nothing defines it up the chain either.

steps.label: Step 2: inheritance counts for in
steps.text: (2) true — p has no own toString, but the walk continues to Point.prototype, then Object.prototype, where toString lives. in answers "does it exist anywhere on this object?" — use Object.hasOwn(p, "toString") to get false here.

steps.label: Step 3: instanceof walks the same chain
steps.text: (4) p’s chain is p → Point.prototype → Object.prototype → null. Point.prototype is the first link: true. (5) Object.prototype appears further along: true. Every plain object answers true to instanceof Object.

steps.label: Step 4: arrays and the primitive exception
steps.text: (6) An array’s chain includes Array.prototype: true. (7) A string primitive is not an object — there is no chain to walk — so instanceof evaluates to false without consulting String at all. Only new String("s"), a wrapper object, would say true.

examples.result: in searches properties (own then inherited); instanceof searches prototype chains for one specific prototype object; primitives sit outside both games.

keyTakeaways: === never converts: numbers by value (NaN unequal, +0 equals -0), strings by exact 16-bit sequence, objects by identity, different types always false.
== normalizes first: null pairs only with undefined; strings convert to numbers; booleans convert to numbers; objects convert to primitives — then compare.
Use === everywhere except the deliberate absence test x == null; != and !== are exact negations of their partners.
Comparisons are string-vs-string only when BOTH are strings; otherwise numeric — and any NaN operand makes all four comparisons false.
in tests property existence including inherited properties; own-only tests need Object.hasOwn (or hasOwnProperty).
instanceof walks the prototype chain for Constructor.prototype; primitives always answer false.

quiz.q: Which of these is TRUE?
quiz.explanation: Positive and negative zero are strictly equal (distinguishable only as divisors, Chapter 3). NaN equals nothing including itself, two array literals are distinct objects, and null and undefined are different types under ===.

quiz.q: Under ==, which pair converts the string operand to a number?
quiz.explanation: The mixed number/string case converts the string to a number and compares numerically. null never converts for ==, the nullish pairing needs no conversion, and two strings compare as strings.

quiz.q: What is the value of `"11" < "3"`?
options: true — string comparison of code units
false — comparing a string with a number is an error
quiz.explanation: When both operands are strings the comparison is lexicographic on code units: "1" < "3" at the first character decides it. "11" < 3 would be the numeric case (false), but this pair is two strings.

quiz.q: What does `"toString" in {}` evaluate to?
options: true — inherited properties count for in
A TypeError — the left operand must be an identifier
quiz.explanation: in walks the whole property chain, and Object.prototype contributes toString. To restrict the test to own properties, use Object.hasOwn or hasOwnProperty.

quiz.q: Which expression is false?
quiz.explanation: A string primitive is not an object and has no prototype chain, so instanceof answers false — only the wrapper new String("s") would pass. The others walk real chains that contain the named prototype.

intro: JavaScript’s logical operators are liars in the best sense: && and || do not really compute booleans at all — they **return one of their operands**, chosen with short-circuit evaluation, which makes them the language’s guard and default-value idioms rather than its logic. This section covers that truth, the ! and ?? refinements, the assignment operators (including destructuring with defaults and rest), and the one operator the language has spent twenty years regretting: eval.
objectives: Explain why && and || return operand values, and use them as guards and defaults
Apply ! and the truthiness rules; convert any value to a real boolean with !!
Distinguish ?? from || and know when each is correct
Read and write assignment operators, chains, and destructuring with defaults and rest
State the dangers of eval and name the safe alternatives

concepts.statement:
The **logical AND** evaluates its first operand and tests it for truthiness. If it is falsy, the expression **is** that first value — the second operand is never evaluated at all. If it is truthy, the expression is the value of the second operand. The result: `a && b` is "a if a is falsy, else b" — booleans only if you feed it booleans:
```js
0 && "x"            // 0 — falsy first operand returned as-is
"left" && "right"   // "right"
null && anything    // null — anything never runs
if (a === b) start();   // is equivalent to the guard
(a === b) && start();   // ...but write the if — the guard is famous
```
The classic use is the **guard**: `a && a.b` — evaluate a.b only when a exists (ES2020’s ?. is the modern replacement for that exact pattern).
concepts.detail: Because the second operand can be skipped, && is one of the operators no function can imitate (Section 4.3). Its other idiom — "poor man’s if" — is legal, terse and widely discouraged.

concepts.statement:
The **logical OR** mirrors it: `a || b` is "a if a is truthy, else b". One operand always survives, and the first truthy one ends the search:
```js
let max = maxWidth || 500;          // default when maxWidth is falsy
let o = {};
o.counter = o.counter || 1;         // initialize-if-absent
"fallback" || "unused"              // "fallback" — second never evaluated
```
This is the default-value idiom — powerful, and subtly wrong whenever **0, an empty string, or false is a legitimate value**, because those are falsy and get replaced. That flaw is exactly what motivated ??.
concepts.detail: Note the two readings of ||: "logical OR" when you care about truthiness, "default selector" when you care about values. Same mechanics — the difference is what you do with the result.

concepts.statement:
The **logical NOT** applies ToBoolean and negates — it is the one logical operator that always returns a boolean. Two applications of it give the canonical **booleanize** idiom:
```js
!null          // true
!0             // true
!""            // true
!NaN           // true
!undefined     // true
!false         // true
!!"0"          // true! — nonempty strings are truthy
!!value        // the value as a real boolean
```
The six falsy values (false, undefined, null, 0, -0, NaN, "" — seven tokens, six values, Section 3.4) define everything else as truthy — including "0", "false", [] and {}.
concepts.detail: !!x is the honest way to answer "is this truthy?" with a boolean — Boolean(x) says the same thing more explicitly and just as fast.

concepts.statement:
ES2020’s **??** is || with better manners: it falls back only when the left operand is **null or undefined** — never for the other falsy values:
```js
0 ?? 100        // 0 — zero survives
0 || 100        // 100 — zero is replaced
"" ?? "none"    // ""
false ?? true   // false
null ?? 10      // 10
undefined ?? 10 // 10
```
Use || when "any truthy value or a fallback" is the intent; use ?? when "absent means default, but 0/false/empty-string are real answers". ?? is right-associative and **cannot be mixed with && or || without parentheses** — `a ?? b || c` is a SyntaxError; write `a ?? (b || c)`.
concepts.detail: The prefix "nullish" names the two values it cares about: null and undefined. It pairs naturally with ?. (Section 4.2): `settings.user?.name ?? "guest"`.

concepts.statement:
