Section 4.2 introduced the access forms; the **full optional-chaining family** is:
```js
o?.x            // property: undefined if o is nullish
o?.[k]          // bracket property
f?.(x)          // conditional invocation — call only if f is not
                // null/undefined (else the expression is undefined)
a?.b.c?.d       // chains: each ?. guards everything to its right
```
Like &&, the short circuit is total: nothing after the ?. evaluates. And like every short-circuit, the undefined result cannot say WHY — missing property and explicit undefined look identical.
concepts.detail: f?.(x) answers "call this callback if it was provided": `onDone?.(result)` replaces the old `if (onDone) onDone(result)`. The call form still requires f to be callable when present — ?. checks nullish, not callability.

concepts.statement:
Assignment expects an **lvalue** on the left — a variable, object property or array element — and yields the assigned value as its own, so chains work right to left: `a = b = c = 0`. The compound forms combine an operation with the assignment: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `**=`, `<<=`, `>>=`, `>>>=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`:
```js
total += 5;       // total = total + 5
flags |= EXEC;    // the bit-set idiom of Section 4.4
word <<= 2;       // shift-and-assign
```
In the property form `o[f()] += 1`, the reference is evaluated **once** — the function does not run twice. Assignment does not declare anything: the binding must already exist (or you create an accidental global, Section 3.8).
concepts.detail: Section 3.8 covered the declaration side (let/const/var and what each may assign). Here assignment is purely an operator — which is why it can appear inside initializers, arguments and return values.

concepts.statement:
A **destructuring assignment** puts a pattern where a value normally goes, and assigns into its variables. Section 3.8 met it in declarations; as a pure assignment it also swaps and rebinds:
```js
let x = 1, y = 2;
[x, y] = [y, x];            // swap — no temp
const [first, , third] = [1, 2, 3];       // skip by elision: 1, 3
const { a, b: renamed, c = 9 } = { a: 1, b: 2 };  // rename + default
const [head, ...rest] = [1, 2, 3, 4];      // rest collects: 1, [2,3,4]
let [min, max] = [3, 1];    // any iterable fits the array pattern
```
Defaults apply when the source property/element is undefined; **rest** (...) collects what remains; object patterns read by property name, array patterns by position. A statement whose first token is `{` is parsed as a block — so an object destructuring at statement level must be parenthesized: `({ a } = o);`.
concepts.detail: The idioms it powers: multiple return values (return an array, destructure at the call site), configuration objects with defaults, and swapping. Nested patterns work too, but readability sets the practical limit.

concepts.statement:
`eval(code)` parses and executes a string of JavaScript **at runtime, in the calling scope**, and returns the value of the last expression. Three prices, one per word: it is **slow** (the code crosses the interpreter boundary and defeats optimization), **scope-corrupting** (evaluated code sees and mutates local variables), and — the killer — a **security hole** when any part of the string comes from outside:
```js
const total = eval(input.value);      // NEVER: user input becomes code
const area = eval("w * h");          // avoid: string-built code
```
If input.value can be influenced by anyone, they can execute anything the page can. Alternatives: JSON.parse for data, plain expressions for computation, and the Function constructor for the rare sanctioned case (indirect eval runs globally, but is still a red flag).
concepts.detail: Chapter 17’s linters reject eval by default, and Section 10.3 notes that ES6 modules forbid it from leaking declarations into scope. Legitimate uses are so rare that the working rule is: it is always a bug until proven otherwise.

examples.title: Trace: the || default, the zero trap, and the ?? fix
examples.problem: A drawing function defaults width and padding. The caller passes zeros — legal values both. Which defaults behave?

steps.label: The code
Step 1: (A) || tests truthiness, and 0 is falsy
steps.text: options.width is 0 — a perfectly legitimate "thinnest line" — but || only asks "truthy?". The answer is no, so the fallback 300 wins. width is now wrong: the caller asked for 0 and got 300.

steps.label: Step 2: (B) ?? tests nullishness, and 0 is not nullish
steps.text: options.padding is 0 — also falsy, but ?? checks only for null and undefined. Neither applies, so the value 0 survives. pad is right for the wrong-feeling reason: not because 0 is meaningful to ??, but because 0 is not null or undefined.

steps.label: Step 3: the result and the fix
steps.text: The call returns [300, 0] — one default honored, one overridden. Changing (A) to `options.width ?? 300` gives [0, 0]: both zeros respected, and the defaults now fire only when the properties are absent (or explicitly null/undefined).

steps.label: Step 4: choosing the operator
steps.text: Ask one question about the missing-value domain: can a falsy non-nullish value ever be legitimate? If yes (widths, offsets, counts, flags, empty strings), only ?? is correct. If "anything truthy counts, or default" is genuinely the rule — a label, a mode string — || is the right tool.

examples.result: draw returned [300, 0] under the mixed operators; with ?? throughout it returns [0, 0]. || replaces falsy values; ?? replaces only absence.

examples.title: Worked: destructuring with defaults and rest
examples.problem: Unpack a configuration object with defaults, a rename, and a rest collect — then pull three elements from an array, skipping the middle.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: present properties bind directly
steps.text: host finds "db" on options and binds it. No default is consulted — defaults apply only when the source property is undefined.

steps.label: Step 2: missing properties fall back
steps.text: port is absent from the object, so the default 8080 binds. Note the default lives on the target side — it is about the pattern’s variable, not the source object.

steps.label: Step 3: rename and default together
steps.text: `retries: attempts = 3` reads the source property "retries" (absent here) into a variable named attempts, defaulting to 3. The colon syntax is the same as in object literals: source name on the left, target on the right — here with a default riding along.

steps.label: Step 4: rest collects what the pattern did not take
steps.text: After host, port and retries are matched, `...rest` gathers every remaining own enumerable property: { tags: ["a"] }. This is the spread of Section 4.1 in reverse — gathering instead of distributing.

steps.label: Step 5: positional patterns skip with elisions
steps.text: The array pattern [first, , third] binds 1 and 3 and skips index 1 — the same elision syntax as sparse array literals. Result: ["db", 8080, 3, { tags: ["a"] }, 1, 3].

examples.result: host "db", port 8080 (defaulted), attempts 3 (renamed + defaulted), rest { tags: ["a"] }, first 1, third 3 — defaults fire only on undefined, rest swallows the rest, elisions skip.

examples.title: eval: one caution
examples.problem: A comment-count feature receives an expression string from a URL parameter and "just evals it". Show the failure modes and the repair.

steps.label: The code under review
Step 1: what the first line actually does
steps.text: The string is compiled and executed with the privileges of the page. A crafted expression can read cookies, make requests, and call any API — there is no sandbox, no allowlist, nothing. This is a textbook XSS injection point.

steps.label: Step 2: why the second line is also wrong
steps.text: Even with no attacker, "w * h" crosses into the interpreter at runtime: the surrounding function becomes hard to optimize, the code is invisible to static tools (typos surface only when the path runs), and the scope rule means the string can see and change w and h. It is also simply unnecessary — the expression is known at write time.

steps.label: Step 3: the repair
steps.text:
```js
const area = w * h;                   // it was just arithmetic
const count = Number(input.expression); // data is data
```
If the requirement is "parse a number", parse a number. If code must be generated dynamically, generate it with the Function constructor in a locked-down environment — and treat that as a design smell to justify in review.

steps.label: Step 4: the standing rule
steps.text: Never eval anything influenced by outside input; prefer evaling nothing at all. Chapter 17’s linters encode this as a default error, which matches the industry’s conclusion about the operator.

examples.result: The eval lines are a security hole, a performance hazard and an obscurity — replaced by direct arithmetic and Number(). The rule: data is parsed, never executed.

keyTakeaways: && returns its first operand if falsy (skipping the second), else its second operand; || returns the first truthy operand — value selectors, not boolean computers.
The guard (a && a.b) and default (x || fallback) idioms are the operators’ daily jobs; the "poor man’s if" form is legal but frowned on.
! always yields a boolean; !!x (or Boolean(x)) is the honest truthiness conversion. Six falsy values; everything else — including "0" and [] — is truthy.
?? falls back only on null/undefined, so 0, "" and false survive; it cannot be mixed with && / || without parentheses.
?. guards a whole chain (.x, [k], and the f?.(x) call form) and pairs with ?? for safe navigation with defaults.

Assignment is an expression yielding the assigned value; compound forms include all arithmetic and bitwise operators; destructuring adds patterns, defaults, renames, elisions and rest — parenthesize object destructuring at statement start.
eval executes strings in the calling scope: slow, opaque, and a security hole on any outside input. Parse data instead.

quiz.q: What is the value of `0 || "fallback"`?
quiz.explanation: || returns the first operand if it is truthy, else the second. 0 is falsy, so the expression is "fallback" — exactly the behavior that makes || wrong when 0 is a legitimate value.

quiz.q: What is the value of `false && "x"`?
quiz.explanation: The first operand is falsy, so && IS that operand and the second never evaluates. The operator returns operand values — here the boolean false, not a computed conjunction.

quiz.q: With `const pad = opts.padding ?? 8;`, which padding value still results in 8?
quiz.explanation: ?? falls back only for null and undefined. 0, "" and false are falsy but not nullish, so they survive — that is precisely the difference from ||.

quiz.q: After `const [a, ...b] = [1, 2, 3];`, what are a and b?
quiz.explanation: The first pattern position takes the first element; the rest parameter collects the remaining elements into a new array. The same ... syntax spreads in literals and gathers in patterns.

quiz.q: Why is `let count = eval(userText);` flagged as a security hole?
options: Because eval is slower than a function call
Because the string is executed with the page’s full privileges — attacker-supplied code runs as your code
Because eval cannot see local variables
quiz.explanation: The performance cost and scope visibility are real but secondary: the fatal issue is executing untrusted strings with everything the running program can do. Parse input as data instead.

quiz.q:
What is the value of `result`?
```js
let result = 0 || 'hi' && null || 5;
```
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is one expression mixing `||` and `&&` over non-boolean operands. Step 2: The governing rules are that `&&` binds tighter than `||`, that `&&` yields its first falsy operand or its last operand, and that `||` yields its first truthy operand or its last operand. Step 3: Tracing stepwise, `'hi' && null` evaluates first and yields `null`, reducing the expression to `0 || null || 5`; `0 || null` yields `null` since both are falsy; `null || 5` yields `5`. Step 4: The distractors fail because `0` is falsy and never survives `||`, `'hi'` is consumed inside the `&&`, and `null` is falsy so the final `||` moves past it. Step 5: Therefore `result` holds `5`.

intro: The last operators are the miscellany that round out the chapter: the conditional ?: that packs an if/else into a single expression, typeof for probing types without exceptions, delete for removing properties, void for discarding a value on purpose, and the comma operator that sequences two expressions into one. It closes with a first meeting of await — the operator that will dominate Chapter 13.
objectives: Use the conditional operator, including nested chains and its lazy evaluation
List every string typeof can return and apply its quirks safely
Apply delete: what it removes, what it returns, and strict mode’s hard errors
Use void and the comma operator, and distinguish the comma operator from comma separators
Recognize await as the (Chapter 13) bridge from expressions to asynchronous values

concepts.detail: One condition, two values — when you need statements or side effects per branch, write the if/else instead. Nested deeper than two levels, the ladder stops being readable.

concepts.statement:
The **typeof operator** returns one of exactly eight strings: `"undefined"`, `"object"`, `"boolean"`, `"number"`, `"string"`, `"function"`, `"bigint"`, `"symbol"`. The quirks that matter:
```js
typeof null           // "object" — the famous JS1 bug, permanent for compatibility
typeof NaN            // "number" — NaN is a number value
typeof function () {} // "function" — callables get their own answer
typeof []             // "object" — arrays need Array.isArray
typeof undeclaredName // "undefined" — NO ReferenceError, uniquely
```
The last quirk is a feature: `if (typeof fetch === "function")` probes for an API that may not exist without throwing — the standard feature-detection pattern.
concepts.detail: typeof answers "what kind of VALUE is this", not "what constructor made it" — for the latter use instanceof (Section 4.5) or the class-specific predicates like Array.isArray (Chapter 7). Parentheses around the operand are legal and never change the answer.

concepts.statement:
The unary **delete** removes a property from an object (or an element from an array, leaving a hole). It returns true when the property is gone afterward — which includes properties that never existed — and false when the deletion failed (sloppy mode):
```js
const o = { x: 1, y: 2 };
delete o.x          // true
"x" in o            // false
delete o.z          // true — nothing named z, but "z" in o is false either way
const a = [1, 2, 3];
delete a[1];        // true — but a is now [1, <hole>, 3], length 3
```
What it cannot do: remove declared variables or function bindings. **Strict mode is stricter twice**: `delete x` on a bare identifier is a SyntaxError at parse time, and deleting a nonconfigurable property (a frozen object’s, or Object.prototype) throws a TypeError instead of returning false.
concepts.detail: One historical wrinkle from Section 3.8: accidental sloppy-mode globals ARE properties of the global object, so `oops = 42; delete oops;` works there — a party trick, not a technique. Section 6.3 covers property configuration in depth.

concepts.statement: The unary **void** evaluates its operand and then yields `undefined`, discarding whatever the operand produced: `void 0` is undefined, `void (1 + 1)` is undefined (the 2 vanishes). Its honest uses are narrow: making a value explicitly undefined (`void 0` predates a time when undefined was writable), the legacy `javascript: void doThing()` URL idiom that suppresses link navigation, and — the modern one — marking a promise as deliberately fire-and-forget: `void prefetch()` says "I know this returns a promise and I am choosing not to await it".
concepts.detail: void does not prevent side effects — the operand runs! It discards only the value. Code that needs void to be readable usually wants a comment instead.

Do not confuse the operator with the comma *separators* in array literals [1, 2], argument lists f(a, b) and declarations let x = 1, y = 2 — those delimit items; the operator evaluates left to right and keeps only the last value.

The one-line summary for now: await converts "value later" into "value here", for this function only, without freezing anything else. The full event-loop story is Chapter 13 (and Operating System Concepts Chapter 4 tells the kernel-side counterpart).

examples.title: Worked: typeof — every answer, every quirk
examples.problem: Evaluate typeof against one value of every kind, then use it to write a safe feature check for an API that may not exist.

steps.label: The battery
steps.text:
```js
typeof 42            // "number"
typeof NaN           // "number" (!)
typeof "x"           // "string"
typeof true          // "boolean"
typeof undefined     // "undefined"
typeof null          // "object" (!)
typeof 1n            // "bigint"
typeof Symbol()      // "symbol"
typeof function () {} // "function"
typeof []            // "object"
typeof {}            // "object"
typeof undeclaredName // "undefined" (!)
```

steps.label: Step 1: the primitive reports
steps.text: Numbers (NaN included — it is a numeric value), strings, booleans, undefined, BigInt and symbol each report their type. This is the happy path: typeof on a primitive tells the truth.

steps.label: Step 2: the two famous lies
steps.text: `typeof null` is "object" — a bug from the first JavaScript implementation, kept because "fixing" it would break the web. And `typeof []` is "object" — arrays are a kind of object, so Array.isArray (Chapter 7) is the real array test.

steps.label: Step 3: functions stand alone
steps.text: Callables report "function" — the one object subtype typeof distinguishes. Classes also answer "function" (they are constructors, Chapter 9), which is a hint, not a rule.

steps.label: Step 4: the undeclared case — the feature check

examples.result: Eight possible answers, two documented lies (null, arrays), one unique exemption (undeclared names) — and the safest feature check in the language.

examples.title: Trace: ?: as an expression, delete as an operation
examples.problem: Use the conditional operator to pick a stylesheet, then delete properties from a plain object and a frozen one — in both strict and sloppy mode.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: the conditional picks one arm
steps.text: (1) The comparison is true, so only "#111" is evaluated — the light value is skipped, and any side effects it might have carried would not run. The whole thing is an expression, so it initializes the const directly.

steps.label: Step 2: delete removes an own configurable property
steps.text: (2) x was created by an ordinary literal, so it is configurable: delete removes it (true), and the existence test confirms. The object still holds y.

steps.label: Step 3: deleting what is not there is still true
steps.text: (3) delete answers "is the property absent afterward?" — so a no-op deletion returns true. The return value is about the outcome, not about whether anything was removed.

steps.label: Step 4: nonconfigurable is a wall — and strict mode makes it loud
steps.text: (4) Object.freeze made keep nonconfigurable. In sloppy code delete would return false and move on; in strict code it throws `TypeError: Cannot delete property 'keep'`. The same throw-on-failure rule applies to assignments that fail (Section 5.5).

examples.result: bg is "#111"; o loses x; and the frozen object’s delete escalates from silent failure to a TypeError — strict mode converts property mistakes from no-ops into errors.

keyTakeaways: ?: evaluates only the chosen arm and is an expression — usable in initializers, arguments and returns; right-associativity makes chains read as else-if ladders.

typeof returns one of eight strings; null lies ("object"), arrays report "object", functions get "function" — and undeclared identifiers answer "undefined" instead of throwing, enabling safe feature checks.

delete removes own configurable properties (leaving holes in arrays), returns true when the property is absent afterward, and is doubled-barred in strict mode: bare identifiers are a SyntaxError, nonconfigurable targets throw.
void evaluates and discards a value, yielding undefined — its modern job is marking fire-and-forget promises; the comma operator keeps the last value and lives mainly in for headers.
await (Chapter 13) pauses its async function until a promise settles and yields the value — the operator-shaped preview of asynchronous JavaScript.

quiz.q: What is `typeof null`?
quiz.explanation: A bug in the earliest JavaScript implementation, kept for backward compatibility: null reports "object" and always has. Test for null with x === null, not typeof.

quiz.q: Why does `if (typeof someLibrary !== "undefined")` not throw, even when someLibrary was never declared?
options: Because typeof returns a string even for errors
Because typeof is specified to evaluate its operand’s type without requiring a binding — undeclared names yield "undefined"
Because undeclared variables are automatically created as undefined
quiz.explanation: typeof is the one operator exempt from the ReferenceError on unbound identifiers — it reports their absence as "undefined", which makes it the standard feature-detection tool.

quiz.q: In `dark ? loadDark() : loadLight()`, how many of the two calls run?
options: Exactly one — only the chosen arm is evaluated
quiz.explanation: The conditional operator is lazy: it evaluates the condition, then only the selected arm. Side effects in the unselected branch never happen — the same short-circuit property && and || have.

quiz.q: In strict mode, what does `let x = 1; delete x;` do?
options: Is a SyntaxError before the code ever runs
quiz.explanation: delete with a bare (unqualified) identifier is an early error in strict mode — the parser rejects it. Variables are not deletable properties; only an object property can be a delete target.

quiz.q: What is the value of `void (2 + 2)`?
quiz.explanation: void evaluates its operand (the addition happens) and then discards the result, yielding undefined. The operator hides values, not side effects.

intro: A JavaScript program is a list of **statements**: the sentences that give orders — declare a variable, call a function, run a loop, branch on a condition, throw an error. This opening section separates expressions (which compute values) from statements (which perform actions), introduces the expression statements that blur the line, the declaration statements, the compound statement (block) that groups statements as one, and the empty statement — occasionally exactly what you mean, and occasionally a bug that eats a loop body.
objectives: Distinguish expression statements from declaration statements, and identify which expressions earn their semicolon
Use blocks to group statements, and state when a block does and does not need a trailing semicolon
Predict block scoping for var versus let/const
Recognize the empty statement, its legitimate uses and its hazard

concepts.statement: JavaScript statements come in a handful of kinds, and Chapter 5 covers them all: **expression statements** and **declaration statements** (this section), **conditionals** (`if/else`, `switch`), **loops** (`while`, `do/while`, `for`, `for/of`, `for/in`), **jumps** (`break`, `continue`, `return`, `yield`, `throw`, `try/catch/finally`) and the miscellany (`with`, `debugger`, `"use strict"`). A program executes its statements top to bottom unless a jump redirects it.
concepts.detail: Statements are separated by semicolons — usually optional at the end of a line, thanks to the automatic semicolon insertion rules of Section 2.5, which is exactly why the return pitfall of Section 5.4 exists.

concepts.statement: Any expression can stand alone as a statement: evaluate it, discard the value, continue. In practice the ones worth writing have **side effects** — assignment (`count = 0;`), increment (`count++;`), deletion (`delete o.x;`) and, above all, function calls (`console.log("hi");`), the most common statement in the language. A pure expression like `1 + 2;` is legal but useless, and linters (Chapter 17) flag it as a probable mistake.
concepts.detail: Two expressions that look statement-worthy are not: `function f() {}` at the start of a line is a declaration, not an expression statement, and a class declaration likewise. That distinction decides where the semicolon goes — and what can appear on the right side of an =.

concepts.statement: The declaration statements introduce bindings: `let`, `const` (and legacy `var`) declare variables — several at once with declarators: `let x = 1, y = 2;` — and destructuring patterns from Section 3.8; `function` and `class` declare callable and constructable bindings. **Function declarations are fully hoisted** — defined before the statement is reached, so they can be called earlier in the same scope — while `class` bindings live in the temporal dead zone like `let`.
concepts.detail: Section 3.8 has the var/let/const story: var hoists to the function, initializes undefined, and becomes a global-object property; let and const are block-scoped and TDZ-guarded. Here they simply count as statements.
A standalone block is legal and occasionally useful for grouping or restricting let-scoped temporaries — most blocks you write will belong to a control structure.

concepts.statement:
A lone semicolon is the **empty statement**: it does nothing, and it is a real statement — able to serve as a loop body that has no work. Flanagan’s canonical example zeroes an array with no body at all:
```js
for (let i = 0; i < a.length; a[i++] = 0) /* empty */ ;
```
The increment clause does the work, so the body has nothing left to do. The hazard is the accidental one — a stray semicolon after `if (...)` or `for (...)` becomes the *entire* body, and the indented statement after it runs unconditionally (or once, after the loop). Mark intentional emptiness with a comment; delete unintentional semicolons.
concepts.detail: The empty statement is also the grammar’s way of making semicolons optional-but-meaningful: `{}` and `;` are both valid bodies, and Section 5.3’s for(;;) relies on clauses being optional rather than statements being non-empty.

examples.title: Trace: classify every line
examples.problem: A six-line program mixes declaration, expression, and compound statements. Classify each, and justify each semicolon decision.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: the directive
steps.text: (1) is the "use strict" directive prologue — a string expression statement with a special meaning to the interpreter (Section 5.5), semicolon customary.

steps.label: Step 2: declarations do not need semicolons
steps.text: (2) is a declaration statement — the semicolon terminates the declarator list and is required. (3) is a function declaration: the body’s closing brace ends it, so no semicolon — and its body happens to be a single return expression statement.

steps.label: Step 3: the workhorse expression statements
steps.text: (4) is an invocation expression statement; (5) is an increment expression statement; (7) is an assignment expression statement inside the block. All three exist for their side effects — the classic expression statements.

steps.label: Step 4: the compound body
steps.text: (6) is an if statement whose test is an expression; its body is the block (6)–(8). The closing brace at (8) needs no semicolon — and the fact that `total = 0;` inside DOES need one is the contrast worth remembering: blocks end bare, statements end punctuated.

examples.result: Two declarations, three side-effecting expression statements, one directive, one compound if: a complete statement taxonomy in eight lines.

examples.title: Trace: the stray semicolon
examples.problem: A loop was meant to total the numbers 0 through 4. With the semicolon as written, what does total end up being — and why?

steps.label: The code
steps.text:
```js
let total = 0;
for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++);   // <-- the bug: this ; is the loop body
total += i;                     // intended body — actually runs AFTER
```

steps.label: Step 1: parse the for statement
steps.text: The for header is followed by a `;` — which parses as the empty statement, the complete body of the loop. The indented `total += i` is a separate statement that the loop does not own. Indentation is decoration; the grammar already decided.

steps.label: Step 2: run the loop — five empty iterations
steps.text: i takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; each pass executes the empty statement and the increment; the test finally fails when i is 5. Nothing was added; total is still 0.

steps.label: Step 3: the orphaned statement runs once
steps.text: After the loop, execution continues with `total += i` — exactly once, with i left at its final value 5. total becomes 5, not the intended 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

steps.label: Step 4: the fix and the habit
steps.text: Delete the semicolon — and write braces for any body longer than one line, so an accidental semicolon becomes a visible `{ ; }` anomaly instead of a silent five-fold error. Linters catch this pattern specifically (no-unexpected-multiline, Chapter 17).

examples.result: total is 5 — the loop iterated five times doing nothing, then the intended body executed once with i === 5. One semicolon redirected the entire program.

keyTakeaways: Expressions compute values; statements perform actions — and every statement in Chapter 5 is one of: expression, declaration, compound, conditional, loop, jump, or miscellany.
Expression statements earn their keep through side effects: assignments, increments, deletes and function calls; pure expression statements are lint bait.
let/const/var, function and class declarations are statements; function declarations hoist fully while class bindings obey the temporal dead zone.
Blocks group statements as one and need no trailing semicolon; with let/const a block is a new scope (var leaks through to function scope).
A lone semicolon is the empty statement — a legitimate no-op body, and a classic bug when it accidentally swallows an if or for body.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT useful as an expression statement?
quiz.explanation: 1 + 2 evaluates to 3 and the value is discarded — no side effect, no result kept. The other three are the classic side-effecting expression statements: assignment, call, deletion.

quiz.q: Which statement requires NO semicolon after it?
options: A function declaration ending with its closing brace
A const declaration with an initializer
quiz.explanation: The body’s closing brace terminates a function declaration. Declarations of variables, and expression statements generally, need their semicolons (inserted by ASI at line ends, but required on one line).

quiz.q: Inside a standalone block, `let blockScoped = 1; var fnScoped = 2;` is declared. After the block, what is visible?
options: blockScoped is gone (ReferenceError); fnScoped is still visible
blockScoped is visible; fnScoped is gone
quiz.explanation: Blocks are scopes for let and const but not for var: the let binding dies with the block, while var hoists to the enclosing function (or global) and survives — Chapter 3’s scoping rules in statement clothing.

quiz.q: What does the semicolon in `for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++);` (followed by a total += i line) actually do?
options: It becomes the entire loop body — the empty statement — leaving the next line outside the loop
It separates the loop from the next statement with no other effect
It terminates the for statement early, skipping all iterations
quiz.explanation: The empty statement is a valid body, so the loop runs five no-op iterations and total += i executes exactly once afterward with i === 5 — the classic stray-semicolon bug.

intro: Conditionals choose. JavaScript has exactly two forms: the if statement for one- and two-way decisions (and else-if ladders for more), and the switch statement for dispatching on the value of a single expression — with semantics that surprise the unwary: matching uses strict equality, there is no implicit break, and a missing break means the cases deliberately run together. This section covers both forms, the dangling-else ambiguity, the fallthrough discipline, and the switch-on-true idiom.
objectives: Write if, else and else-if chains, evaluating tests by truthiness
Resolve the dangling-else ambiguity and defend against it with braces
Trace switch matching (strict ===, default, runtime case expressions) and fallthrough
Apply break discipline and the grouped-cases sharing pattern
Recognize and evaluate the switch(true) dispatch idiom

concepts.statement: `if (expression) statement1` evaluates the expression and converts it with the truthiness rules (the six falsy values of Section 3.4), running statement1 when the result is truthy. The optional `else statement2` covers the other case. Any statement can be the body — a single statement directly, or a block for several. The test must be wrapped in parentheses; assignments work as tests (`if (x = next())`), which is usually a typo worth a lint rule.
concepts.detail: Style guidance used across the book: braces around every multi-statement body, and around single-statement bodies too when a reader might mis-attach an else — which is precisely the dangling-else problem below.
A final bare else is the catch-all: without it, a value that matches nothing silently falls through the whole ladder.

The indentation above happens to tell the truth; the danger is code where it does not. This is the single most-cited reason style guides mandate braces: the grammar has an opinion, and the layout cannot override it.
The switch expression is evaluated once, then compared left to right. Because matching is ===, NaN can never match a case, and string/number lookalikes fail exactly as === says they must.
The discipline: every case ends in break, return or throw unless a comment says /* fall through */. Chapter 17’s lint rules (no-fallthrough) enforce exactly this, comments included.
Remember the === rule: the case expression must actually evaluate to the boolean true — a truthy non-boolean (like 1 or "yes") does NOT match. That subtlety is the idiom’s main trap.

examples.title: Trace: the dangling else
examples.problem: With a === 1 and b === 2, what does this unbraced nest print — and what did the author intend?

steps.label: The code
Step 1: the grammar pairs the else inward
steps.text: An else clause attaches to the nearest if that can accept one — here the inner `if (b === 1)`, regardless of indentation. The parse is: if (a === 1) { if (b === 1) log("both"); else log("a is not 1"); }.

steps.label: Step 2: evaluate with a = 1, b = 2
steps.text: The outer test passes (a is 1). The inner test fails (b is not 1). The inner else — which the layout labeled as the outer catch-all — fires: the message "a is not 1" prints even though a IS 1.

steps.label: Step 3: the case that reveals the bug
steps.text: Call check(2, 1): the outer test fails, the entire inner statement (including its else) is skipped, and nothing prints at all. The author’s intended "a is not 1" message never runs in the one case it was written for.

steps.label: Step 4: the brace fix
steps.text: Wrap the outer body: `if (a === 1) { if (b === 1) log("both"); } else log("a is not 1");`. Now the else can only pair with the outer if, and both calls behave as intended — check(1, 2) prints nothing, check(2, 1) prints the message.

examples.result: The original printed "a is not 1" for a === 1 — the else belonged to the inner if. Braces make the pairing visible and the code honest.

examples.title: Worked: a switch with grouped cases and one missing break
examples.problem: A shipping-cost switch groups adjacent weight tiers and forgets one break. Predict the outputs for 2 kg and 5 kg, then fix it.

steps.label: The buggy code
Step 1: (1) a 2 kg parcel finds its case
steps.text: kg <= 1 is false; kg <= 5 is true, so execution jumps there and sets cost = 8. But the case body has no break — execution falls through into kg <= 20, overwriting cost to 12, and only then hits break. The answer is 12: the customer is charged for a large parcel.

steps.label: Step 2: (2) a 5 kg parcel does the same
steps.text: kg <= 5 is true (boundary included), then the same fallthrough sets 12. Both inputs return 12 — the 8 tier is unreachable as written, a strong signal that something structural is wrong.

steps.label: Step 3: the fix
Step 4: when fallthrough is the tool
steps.text: Contrast with deliberate grouping: `case kg <= 1: case kg <= 2: cost = 6; break;` — two labels, one body, no orphaned statements between them. Grouping shares a body; falling through runs two bodies by accident. The comment rule (write /* fall through */ when you mean it) exists so the reader can tell them apart at a glance.

examples.result: Before: both calls returned 12 — one missing break erased a whole pricing tier. After: 8 for both, and each case ends in break unless a comment declares an intentional group.

examples.title: Trace: strict matching in switch
examples.problem: A dispatch table keys on user input. Show why `switch ("1")` and `case 1` fail to meet — and two ways to repair the dispatch.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: (1) the number finds its case
steps.text: The switch value 1 compares with === against each label in order: 1 === 1 is true — "number route".

steps.label: Step 2: (2) the string never matches the number label
steps.text: "1" === 1 is false — switch never converts. The comparison continues to "1" === "1", which is true: "string route". The two cases are genuinely different arms, and reversing their order changes nothing.

steps.label: Step 3: (3) everything else lands in default
steps.text: "one" matches neither label, so the default clause answers "no route". Without default the switch would simply do nothing and route would return undefined.

steps.label: Step 4: repairing a genuine mismatch
steps.text: If input arrives as a string but the labels are numbers, normalize first — `switch (Number(cmd))` — or make every label a string. Silent type juggling is not an option: the === rule is the switch’s contract, and it is the same contract === itself uses in Section 4.5.

examples.result: "number route", "string route", "no route" — switch matches with strict equality, so string "1" and number 1 are different destinations, and normalization must happen before the switch.

keyTakeaways: if converts its test with the truthiness rules (six falsy values); else-if ladders are nested else statements with the first truthy test winning.
A dangling else pairs with the nearest if that can accept it — braces make the pairing explicit and refactor-safe.
switch evaluates its expression once and compares with strict ===: string "1" never matches case 1, and NaN matches nothing.
default is the no-match clause (placeable anywhere); case labels are expressions evaluated when the switch is reached.
Execution falls through every case without a break — group cases deliberately (case a: case b: shared body), end the rest with break/return/throw, and comment any intentional fallthrough.
switch (true) with boolean case expressions is the ladder alternative — but only real booleans match (true === 1 is false).

quiz.q: In nested unbraced if statements, an else clause pairs with:
options: The if whose indentation aligns with it
The nearest enclosing if that can accept it
Whichever if has no other else — chosen at random
quiz.explanation: The grammar binds an else to the nearest if lacking one — layout is irrelevant. This is why style guides demand braces around nested if bodies.

quiz.q: What does `switch (2)` do when the matching case body contains statements but no break, and another case follows?
options: It stops at the end of the matching case body
It keeps executing into the following case’s statements until a break, return, throw, or the closing brace
It throws a SyntaxError — every case needs a break
It re-tests the value against the next case label first
quiz.explanation: Cases are labels, not fences: execution falls through to the next case body without re-testing. The missing-break fallthrough is the classic switch bug.

quiz.q: Which comparison does switch use to match a case label?
quiz.explanation: Matching is strict: switch(1) does not match case "1". Normalize the switched value before the switch when the inputs might arrive in the wrong type.

quiz.q: In `switch (true) { case x > 5: ... }`, which case expression MATCHES?
quiz.explanation: The comparison is true === case-expression, strict: only the actual boolean true matches. Truthy values like 6, "yes" or objects do not — the idiom’s little trap.

quiz.q: What is the legitimate fallthrough pattern?
options: Omitting breaks on every case for compactness
Grouping several case labels to share one body: case 12: case 1: case 2: return "winter"
Using continue instead of break inside a switch
Placing default first so it runs before the cases
quiz.explanation: Adjacent labels with no statements between them share the body that follows — deliberate, readable grouping. Stray missing breaks elsewhere are bugs; continue does not apply to switch (it is not a loop).

intro: JavaScript has five loops: while and do/while (condition-tested), the three-clause for (counting and indexing), for/of (iterating the VALUES of anything iterable) and for/in (enumerating the property NAMES of any object). The two for variants are the chapter’s best-known trap: on an array they produce different things — index strings versus element values — and for/in includes inherited properties, which is why the Object.keys filter idiom exists. Along the way: the exact timing of the for clauses, the do/while post-check, and how await fits inside a loop body.
objectives: Write while and do/while loops, applying the pre-test versus post-check difference
Trace the for loop’s init/test/increment timing, including fully omitted clauses
Iterate arrays, strings, Maps and Sets with for/of, including destructured entries
Explain await-in-a-loop sequencing, and distinguish it from for await...of
Contrast for/in with for/of on arrays, and filter with Object.keys or Object.hasOwn

concepts.statement: `while (expression) statement` is the plain loop: evaluate the expression (truthiness rules), run the statement if truthy, repeat. The test comes FIRST, so the body may run **zero times**. The programmer owns progress toward termination — a variable the body never advances is an infinite loop. Braces around multi-statement bodies are the same recommendation as for if.
concepts.detail: while is the loop of choice when the iteration count is unknown in advance — polling a queue, consuming input — and when the natural structure is "check, then do".
Any do/while can be rewritten as a while with the body duplicated ahead of the loop; the do form exists to say "at least once" in one readable place.

concepts.statement:
The for statement packs loop bookkeeping into a header: `for (initialize; test; increment) statement`. The timing is exact: **initialize runs once** before anything; **test runs before every iteration** (including the first — a false test means zero iterations); **increment runs after the body**, before the next test. All three clauses are optional — an omitted test is true forever:
```js
for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { ... }   // canonical
for (;;) { ... }                             // infinite: no test
let i = 0;
for (; i < 3;) { i++; }                       // work split out
```
The initialize clause may declare (let/const — a fresh binding per loop, scoped to the loop) or assign (var — function-scoped), and the comma operator (Section 4.7) lets one clause juggle two variables: `for (let i = 0, j = 9; i <= j; i++, j--)`.
concepts.detail: Use let in the header unless the index must survive the loop — a var counter is still visible afterward at its final (failed-test) value, which the stray-semicolon example exploited.

concepts.statement:
ES6’s **for/of** iterates the VALUES of any **iterable** — an object that knows how to produce a sequence (Chapter 12): arrays (elements, in index order; holes surface as undefined), strings (by code point, so surrogate pairs stay whole), Sets (members), Maps (entry arrays — destructure them), typed arrays, NodeLists, arguments:
```js
for (const v of [10, 20, 30]) use(v);        // values
for (const ch of "hi\uD83D\uDE00") log(ch);   // "h", "i", ONE emoji
for (const [k, v] of aMap) log(k, v);         // destructure entries
for (const el of document.querySelectorAll("p")) el.classList.add("x");
```
A plain object is not iterable — `for (const v of {})` throws `TypeError: {} is not iterable`. Use for/in or Object.entries for plain objects. `const` in the header is idiomatic (a fresh binding per element); assignment to it is a SyntaxError.
concepts.detail: for/of is the modern default for arrays: no off-by-one indexing, no length recomputation, and it visits elements via the array iterator — extra properties (the for/in trap below) are ignored.
One await per element is not automatically slow: it is slow only when the iterations are independent. Decide sequential versus parallel deliberately, never by accident.
for/in predates the iterator protocol and was JavaScript’s only loop-in-object mechanism for years — which is why its quirks (inherited properties, string keys) are baked into so much legacy code.

concepts.term: for/in versus for/of on an array
concepts.statement:
The chapter’s classic trap, side by side:
```js
const arr = ["x", "y", "z"];
arr.tag = "letters";          // arrays are objects: property fits
for (const k in arr) log(k);  // "0", "1", "2", "tag"  (!)
for (const v of arr) log(v);   // "x", "y", "z"
```
for/in hands you property names — including non-index properties and inherited ones — as **strings**, so `arr[k]` is required to reach the value and `k + 1` is "01". for/of hands you the element values via the iterator: no tag, no strings, no surprises. **Rule: for/of for arrays, for/in (filtered) for plain objects.**
concepts.detail: The filter idiom for objects that might inherit: `for (const k in o) if (Object.hasOwn(o, k)) { ... }` — or sidestep entirely with `for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(o))`, which enumerates own properties only.

concepts.statement:
A one-line decision table:
```js
for (const v of array)          // array elements (or string/Map/Set)
for (const [k, v] of aMap)      // Map entries via destructuring
for (const c of "text")          // string code points
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)      // when you need the INDEX
for (const p in object)          // property NAMES (own + inherited)
for (const k of Object.keys(o))  // own property names, safe
while (test)                    // condition-driven, zero-or-more
do body while (test);            // condition-driven, at-least-once
```
Default to for/of for sequences; fall back to the three-clause for when the index itself matters (sparseness, stepping backwards, multiple cursors).
concepts.detail: Chapter 7 adds the array methods — forEach, map, filter — which cover most index-free array loops at a higher level of intent.

examples.title: Trace: do/while runs the body before it asks
examples.problem: A tokenizer loop processes until an END marker. Trace both a normal input and one that begins with END — then compare with the while form.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: (1) normal input
steps.text: The body runs first: t = "a", push "A". Test: "a" !== "END" → true, loop again: "B". Third pass: t = "END", push "END" — the marker is processed — and now the test fails and the loop exits. Result ["A", "B", "END"]. The marker-included behavior is a design decision living in the body, not the loop.

steps.label: Step 2: (2) the immediate END
steps.text: Even with END first, the body executes once BEFORE any test: t = "END", out gets "END", and only then does the condition stop the loop. Result ["END"] — a do/while is incapable of zero iterations.

steps.label: Step 3: the while form needs priming
Step 4: choosing the form
steps.text: Write do/only when "at least once" is the truth of the problem — prompting for input, consuming a first item, executing once before asking. If zero iterations is a meaningful case, the test belongs on top.

examples.result: readTokens(["a","b","END"]) is ["A","B","END"]; readTokens(["END"]) is ["END"] — the body always runs once, and the required trailing semicolon is part of the syntax.

examples.title: Trace: the for anatomy, timed precisely
examples.problem: For `let sum = 0; for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { sum += i; }`, state exactly when each clause runs, and give the final sum. Then read the all-omitted form.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: initialize — once, before everything
steps.text: i is created and set to 1 one time. This clause never runs again, no matter how many iterations follow — and with let, i is scoped to the loop: asking for i afterward is a ReferenceError.

steps.label: Step 2: test — before EACH iteration, including the first
steps.text: The sequence of tests is 1<=5, 2<=5, 3<=5, 4<=5, 5<=5 (all true — five bodies), then 6<=5, which fails. The failed test is the loop’s exit; note that i is 6 at exit, not 5 — the increment ran after the last body.

steps.label: Step 3: increment — after the body, before the next test
steps.text: The per-iteration order is always: test, body, increment, test, body, increment, ... So during the last body i is 5, and the increment to 6 is what lets the final test fail. sum accumulates 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15.

steps.label: Step 4: omitting clauses

examples.result: sum is 15, with the timing test-body-increment repeating five times and the final i === 6. for(;;) is the canonical infinite loop, exited by break.

examples.title: Worked: for/in versus for/of on an array — and the safe object idioms
examples.problem: An array carries a custom property and an object inherits one. Show what each loop sees, then filter for/in to own properties only.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: (1) for/in on the array
steps.text: Output: "0", "1", "2", "tag". Property names as STRINGS — including the custom tag property the iterator never sees. Arithmetic on them misbehaves ("0" + 1 is "01"), and the body needs arr[k] to reach a value at all.

steps.label: Step 2: (2) for/of on the array
steps.text: Output: "x", "y", "z". The iterator hands over element values only — no tag, no string keys, holes surfacing as undefined rather than being skipped. This is the array default.

steps.label: Step 3: (3) for/in on the object — inheritance included
steps.text: Output: "own", "inherited". The loop enumerates every enumerable string property up the prototype chain, not just the object’s own. For library-tainted objects, prototype pollution turns into surprise keys.

steps.label: Step 4: (4) the hasOwn guard
steps.text: Output: "own" only. Object.hasOwn(child, k) (or the older child.hasOwnProperty(k)) filters the loop to own properties — the defensive idiom to use whenever for/in meets objects you do not fully control.

steps.label: Step 5: (5) the keys sidestep
steps.text: Object.keys returns own enumerable property names only, so iterating its array with for/of gives "own" with no guard — and Object.entries(o) goes one better, yielding [name, value] pairs for destructuring. When in doubt, use the object statics (Section 6.4) instead of for/in.

examples.result: Same array, two loops, different worlds: names-with-strings-and-extras versus values-only. Own-property discipline comes from Object.hasOwn or the Object.keys/entries sidestep.

keyTakeaways: while tests first (zero or more iterations); do/while tests last (at least one) and is the one loop whose required semicolon ASI will not supply.
for runs initialize once, test before every iteration (including the first), increment after every body — all clauses optional, an omitted test looping forever.
for/of iterates VALUES of iterables: arrays (holes as undefined), strings (by code point), Sets, Maps (entry arrays — destructure them). Plain objects are not iterable.
await in a for/of body makes the loop sequential — deliberate for dependent work; Chapter 13 has the parallel patterns and the for await...of form for async sequences.
for/in enumerates enumerable string property NAMES, own AND inherited; on arrays that means string indices plus any custom properties.
Default: for/of for arrays; for/in only on plain objects, guarded with Object.hasOwn — or replaced by Object.keys/entries iteration.
Three-clause for earns its keep when the index itself matters; everything else is cleaner as for/of or the array methods of Chapter 7.

quiz.q: How many times is the body of a do/while loop guaranteed to execute?
options: Zero or more — the test runs first
Exactly once — do/while does not loop
At least once — the body precedes the test
quiz.explanation: The do body executes before the condition is ever evaluated, so one iteration is the floor. Zero-iteration behavior requires a while (or for) instead.

quiz.q: In `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)`, when does the increment run?
options: After the body of each iteration, before the next test
Only once, after the loop ends
Before the body of each iteration
quiz.explanation: The cycle is test, body, increment. That is why the loop variable holds the first failing value after exit — the increment runs, then the test fails.

quiz.q: What does `for (const x of someObj)` do when someObj is a plain object like { a: 1 }?
options: Throws TypeError: someObj is not iterable
quiz.explanation: for/of requires the iterable protocol (Chapter 12), and plain objects do not implement it. Use for/in, or iterate Object.keys/values/entries of the object.

quiz.q: For `const arr = ["a", "b"]; arr.extra = "!";`, what does `for (const k in arr)` log?
quiz.explanation: for/in yields property names as strings — the index keys "0" and "1" plus the custom property "extra". for/of is the loop that visits only the elements a, b.

quiz.q: Inside an async function, what does `for (const url of urls) { await fetch(url); }` guarantee?
options: Each fetch completes before the next iteration begins — sequential execution
The loop body is skipped if a fetch is pending
Nothing — await is not allowed in loop bodies
quiz.explanation: await pauses its function until the promise settles, so the next iteration starts only afterward. Parallel fetching is a deliberate Chapter 13 pattern (Promise.all), never an accident of the loop.

intro: Jumps interrupt the top-to-bottom flow: break and continue leave loops early (with labels, out of several at once), return leaves a function, yield pauses a generator, and throw leaves the whole block in search of a handler. The try/catch/finally statement is where thrown exceptions land — with the rule that finally ALWAYS runs, even through a return, and that a finally of its own can override the outcome it interrupts. And one hazard belongs to every JavaScript engineer’s scar tissue: the return keyword followed by a newline.
objectives: Label statements and jump to labels with break and continue from inside nested loops
Explain continue behavior in each loop form
Apply return — and recognize the automatic-semicolon return hazard
Throw any value, following the best practice of Error objects, and rethrow selectively
Trace try/catch/finally including finally’s always-runs and override semantics

concepts.detail: Labels can also mark blocks (`search: { break search; }`) for a mid-block exit — rarer, but legal. Chapter 4’s conditional expression covers choosing values; labels cover escaping structures.
break also ends switch cases (Section 5.2). It cannot jump backward — a break label must enclose the break lexically; a forward goto is not a thing JavaScript has.
Flanagan’s honest observation: continue is one of the less-used statements — a well-placed if around the body often reads better. The labeled form, though, has no cleaner substitute.

The same ASI rule affects ++, -- and arrow-parameter lists in minor ways, but return is the dangerous one because it silently produces undefined instead of erroring. Linters call it no-unexpected-multiline.

yield is an operator-like statement form: like await (Section 4.7) it moves control between caller and callee without unwinding the stack. The full story — yield*, passing values back in, async generators — is Chapter 12’s.

A thrown value that nothing catches propagates out of the function, the event handler or the promise chain it started in — the error surfaces wherever the runtime decides the buck stops. Never throw strings or numbers: catch blocks lose all structure.

The recommended catch discipline: inspect the exception (instanceof the expected types), handle what you recognize, and rethrow the rest — swallowing an unknown error with an empty catch is the classic anti-pattern.

examples.title: Worked: break to a label from a nested loop
examples.problem: Search a grid for a target value: exit both loops the moment it is found, and report the coordinates — then adapt the same structure to continue-to-label.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: label the outer loop
steps.text: The label outer names the whole row loop. Labels are declarations of jump targets — inert until some break or continue names them.

steps.label: Step 2: the hit and the double exit
steps.text: (1) Scanning row 1: grid[1][1] is 5 — found is set to [1, 1] — and `break outer` transfers past the END of the outer loop. Without the label, break would exit only the inner loop and the search would keep scanning row 2.

steps.label: Step 3: the miss
steps.text: (2) No cell matches; the loops complete naturally, found stays null, and the single return after the label handles both outcomes — one exit point for a two-loop search.

steps.label: Step 4: the continue variant

examples.result: find(grid, 5) returns [1, 1] having exited both loops; find(grid, 99) returns null. break label leaves; continue label skips to the next pass of the labeled loop.

examples.title: Trace: the return newline pitfall
examples.problem: A function returns an object literal, formatted onto its own line. What comes back — and why does the fix with parentheses work?

steps.label: The code
Step 1: ASI sees a complete statement
steps.text: return on its own line cannot be continued by anything the parser expects next — the grammar treats a lone return as a complete statement, so a semicolon is inserted. The function has returned.

steps.label: Step 2: the orphaned object is not even an object
steps.text: The next line `{ ok: signedIn };` parses as a BLOCK — braces as a compound statement — containing `ok: signedIn` as a labeled expression statement (the label syntax of this section, in the wild). As a value it is unreachable code after the return: harmless, useless, invisible in the output.

steps.label: Step 3: the result
steps.text: (1) status(true) is **undefined** — no error, no warning from the language itself; the bug type that costs an afternoon. (2) fixed(true) is { ok: true }, because keeping the opening brace (or any opening delimiter) on the return line defeats ASI: the statement is visibly incomplete.

steps.label: Step 4: the habits
steps.text: Three defenses: keep the expression on the return line; start multiline values with an opening delimiter on that line; and run the no-unexpected-multiline lint rule (Chapter 17) that flags exactly this shape. The same newline rule is why ++ and -- should never be split from their operand.

examples.result: The split return yields undefined and a dead block; the same-line brace returns the object. ASI is a convenience at line ends and a hazard at statement continuations.

examples.title: Worked: finally always runs — and can override
examples.problem: Trace three functions: a normal path, a handled-exception path, and a finally that returns of its own — then use the pattern to rethrow only what a catch cannot handle.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: the happy path
steps.text: (1) risky(5) returns 10; the try completes normally with "got 10" pending as the return value. Before the function actually returns, finally runs — "finally: always" logs — and then the pending "got 10" is delivered.

steps.label: Step 2: the handled exception
steps.text: (2) risky(-1) throws; the rest of the try is skipped; catch receives the RangeError, recognizes it with instanceof, and prepares "handled: negative". finally still runs — the log proves it — then the catch’s value returns. Unfamiliar exceptions take the other branch: `throw e` re-raises, and finally runs on the way OUT too, before the exception continues its search for a handler above.

steps.label: Step 3: the override
steps.text: (3) The try computes "from try" — but before returning it, finally executes and returns "from finally" of its own. A finally return replaces the pending outcome; a finally throw would likewise replace a pending exception. The result is "from finally": proof that finally is not just cleanup, it is the last word.

steps.label: Step 4: the design lesson
steps.text: Use finally for cleanup that must happen (closing files, releasing locks, clearing "busy" flags) — work with no control-flow opinions. Never return or throw from finally except in rare, deliberate patterns: an innocent-looking return there silently discards errors and values alike.

examples.result: (1) "got 10" with the log; (2) "handled: negative" with the log; (3) "from finally". finally runs on every exit path and, if it completes the function itself, wins.

keyTakeaways: Labels (identifier: statement) are jump targets for break and continue — the double-exit and skip-to-next-item tools for nested loops.
break leaves the nearest loop or switch (or the labeled statement); continue starts the next iteration — via the re-test in while, the increment in for, the bottom condition in do/while.
return delivers a value and exits — but ASI turns return-plus-newline into return undefined; keep values (or their opening delimiter) on the return line.
yield suspends a generator and hands out a value (Chapter 12); it pauses rather than leaves.
Throw any value — but throw Error objects (or subclasses) so catch blocks get message and stack; rethrow what you cannot handle.
finally ALWAYS runs — normal completion, return, break, continue, or exception — and a return/throw inside finally overrides the pending outcome; keep it to side-effect-free cleanup.

quiz.q: After `outer: for (...) { for (...) { break outer; } }`, where does execution continue?
options: At the next iteration of the outer loop
Immediately after the END of the entire labeled (outer) statement
At the next iteration of the inner loop
It is a syntax error — labels cannot appear on for loops
quiz.explanation: break with a label transfers past the end of the labeled statement itself — both loops end together. Unlabeled break would have continued the outer loop instead.

quiz.q: In a for loop, `continue` transfers control to:
options: The increment expression, then the test
The closing brace, ending the loop
The first statement of the body without testing
quiz.explanation: continue means "start the next iteration": in a for it jumps to the increment, then the test decides whether the body runs again. In a while it jumps straight to the test.
Automatic semicolon insertion completes the return statement at the line break, so the function returns undefined and the 42 is unreachable code. Keep the value on the return line.

quiz.q: A try block ends with `return "A";` and the finally block contains `return "B";`. What does the function return?
options: "B" — the finally return overrides the pending value
quiz.explanation: finally runs before the function actually returns, and a return inside it completes the function with ITS value — the pending "A" is discarded. This is why returns in finally are discouraged.

quiz.q: Which value SHOULD you throw to signal a programming-interface misuse?
options: An Error subclass: throw new TypeError("expected a function");
quiz.explanation: Error objects (and subclasses like TypeError) carry message and stack — everything a catch block or a console needs. Strings and numbers lose that structure, and null throws away even the identity of the failure.

Step 1: The code given nests two loops under the label `outer` and breaks that label when `j` reaches 1. Step 2: The governing rule is that a labeled `break` terminates the labeled statement entirely, exiting both loops at once, whereas a plain `break` would exit only the inner loop. Step 3: Tracing iteration by iteration, `i = 0, j = 0` prints `0:0`, then `j = 1` triggers `break outer`, which abandons the inner and outer loops together, so no further lines print. Step 4: The distractors fail because three lines would need a plain inner `break` per row, `0:1` would need the guard to print instead of break, and the first iteration does print before any break. Step 5: Therefore only `0:0` is printed.

intro: The chapter closes with the odds and ends — one statement the language has since forbidden, one that exists to talk to debuggers — and with strict mode: a five-character string that switches JavaScript into the less forgiving dialect ES5 introduced. Strict mode is where the accidental global, the silent property failure, the octal literal and the lying this of Section 4.2 all become loud errors instead of quiet bugs.
objectives: Read the with statement, and state why strict mode forbids it
Use the debugger statement and know what it does without a debugger
Write "use strict" correctly at file and function level, and know which contexts are strict automatically
List strict mode’s behavioral changes: accidental globals, this coercion, octal literals, arguments.callee, duplicate parameters, failed writes and deletes

concepts.statement:
The legacy **with** statement temporarily made an object’s properties available as bare identifiers:
```js
with (Math) {               // SyntaxError in strict mode
  const r = 2 * sqrt(PI);  // meant Math.sqrt, Math.PI
}
```
It is now forbidden: strict mode makes it a parse-time SyntaxError, and ES6 modules and class bodies never allowed it. The reasons are structural — every identifier inside with becomes ambiguous (property of the object? outer variable? global?), so code is harder to read, refactor and optimize, and the scope chain grows a runtime-dependent link. Nothing of value was lost: write `Math.sqrt(Math.PI)`.
concepts.detail: with is the only ES3-era statement the language has actually removed from the strict dialect — the clearest precedent for why new code never uses it and linters reject it.
No "debug mode" flag exists at runtime: the statement simply cooperates with whatever tooling is listening. It has no effect on production behavior, unlike the bugs it helps you find.
Because it is just a string expression, old interpreters that do not understand it run it harmlessly as a no-op — the design that let ES5 ship a new dialect without breaking the web.

concepts.term: Strict mode: scoping and this changes
concepts.statement:
The changes that bite the most code:
```js
"use strict";
oops = 42;              // ReferenceError — sloppy: creates a global!
function f() { return this; }
f() === undefined;      // true — sloppy: f() === globalThis
let n = 010;            // SyntaxError — legacy octal forbidden
function g(a, a) {}     // SyntaxError — duplicate parameters
function h() { return arguments.callee; }
h();                    // TypeError — callee is off-limits
```
Accidental globals become errors; a plain function call binds **this to undefined** instead of the global object (the call-form rules of Section 4.2, made loud); legacy octal literals (`010` for 8) are rejected — write `0o10`; duplicate parameter names are rejected; and `arguments.callee` (self-reference without naming the function) is banned.
concepts.detail: The this change also means call/apply no longer box primitive receivers: in strict code, this stays the actual primitive (or undefined), which is why `this` can legitimately be a number in a strict function called with one.

concepts.term: Strict mode: property and syntax hardening
concepts.statement:
The changes that turn silent failure into exceptions:
```js
"use strict";
const o = Object.freeze({ x: 1 });
o.x = 2;                // TypeError — sloppy: silently ignored
delete o.x;            // TypeError — sloppy: returns false
delete Object.prototype; // TypeError — a protected property
var y = 1;
delete y;              // SyntaxError — deleting a bare identifier
```
Assigning to a non-writable property, deleting a non-configurable one, deleting an unqualified identifier — all escalate from quiet no-ops (or false) to thrown TypeErrors or SyntaxErrors. With statements are SyntaxErrors (above), function declarations become block-scoped where allowed, and reserved words are enforced as such.
concepts.detail: Every rule here is Section 4.6 and Section 4.7’s delete/assignment semantics in their strict clothing — the same operations, with failure no longer suppressed.

concepts.statement: Migration guidance: strict mode can be adopted **per function** (directive at the top of each function body) or per file — the practical pattern for a legacy codebase is wrapping a file’s contents in an IIFE with the directive inside (Section 8.4), because a top-of-file directive in a concatenated bundle would leak to every other file joined after it. New code needs none of this: **write modules (Section 10.3), which are strict by definition**, and let class bodies (Section 9.3) be strict automatically.
concepts.detail: Linters make the whole question mostly historical: Chapter 17’s ESLint configurations enable strictness rules by default, and the modern bundler pipeline (Chapter 17) works entirely in modules — where "use strict" is simply always true.

examples.title: Trace: the this coercion, sloppy versus strict
examples.problem: A method that increments this.count is called three ways, first in a sloppy script and then in a strict one. Predict all six outcomes.

steps.label: The code
Step 1: the method call is mode-independent
steps.text: (1) The call form c.bump() binds this to c in both modes — the method rule of Section 4.2 has no strict/sloppy split. count becomes 1.

steps.label: Step 2: sloppy — the plain call globalizes this
steps.text: (2) In sloppy code a plain call binds this to the global object. this.count++ reads globalThis.count — undefined — and undefined++ is NaN: the increment writes NaN back as a NEW global property and returns it. No error, one corrupted global, a bug that can run for weeks.

steps.label: Step 3: strict — the plain call fails fast
steps.text: (3) In strict code the same call binds this to undefined, so `this.count` throws `TypeError: Cannot set properties of undefined` at the very first access. The failure is immediate, at the scene, with a stack trace pointing at the exact line.

steps.label: Step 4: reading the difference
steps.text: Same function, same call — different worlds: sloppy mode quietly poisons the global object; strict mode throws. This is the strict-mode philosophy in one example: convert the silent failure modes of Sections 4.6–4.7 and this section into errors you cannot miss.

examples.result: (1) 1 in both modes; (2) sloppy NaN with a new global; (3) strict TypeError. Loose this handling is a bug in both dialects — strict mode merely refuses to hide it.

examples.title: Worked: six strict-mode changes, side by side
examples.problem: Run one statement per behavioral change in both dialects and tabulate the outcomes.

steps.label: The battery
Step 1: the undeclared assignment
steps.text: Sloppy: `undeclared = 42` creates a property of the global object (Section 3.8’s accident). Strict: ReferenceError before anything is written. The typo in a variable name now fails at the typo, not three functions later.

steps.label: Step 2: the syntax-era leftovers
steps.text: Legacy octal `010` (value 8) was a decades-old confusion source — strict mode rejects it in favor of the explicit `0o10`; duplicate parameter names (`a, a`) were legal but parasitic — the second binding shadowed the first — and are now a SyntaxError; `arguments.callee` enabled anonymous recursion but broke engines’ inlining — now a TypeError.

steps.label: Step 3: the property writes
steps.text: On a frozen object, sloppy assignment is a silent no-op (the program continues as if it had succeeded) and sloppy delete merely returns false. Strict mode throws TypeError for both — and for deleting protected properties like Object.prototype. Failed writes stop the program where the failure happened.

steps.label: Step 4: what strict mode is FOR
steps.text: Every row is the same trade: sloppy mode’s answer is to continue with damage; strict mode’s answer is to stop with an explanation. That is why ES6 modules and classes made strict the DEFAULT — the language committee’s recommendation is visible in what new code cannot opt out of.

examples.result: Six behaviors flipped: accidental global, octal literal, duplicate params, arguments.callee, silent write failure, silent delete failure — each a quiet bug in sloppy code, a thrown error in strict.

keyTakeaways: with (object) injected properties as identifiers — ambiguous, slow, and forbidden: a SyntaxError in strict code, never present in modules or classes.
debugger; pauses execution only when a debugger is attached; otherwise it is a harmless no-op.
"use strict" is a directive prologue string — top of file or function; ES6 modules and class bodies are strict automatically.
Strict scoping: undeclared assignment throws ReferenceError; plain-call this is undefined (not globalThis); primitives passed as this stay unboxed.
Strict syntax: legacy octal literals, duplicate parameter names and arguments.callee are all rejected.
Strict properties: writing non-writable, deleting non-configurable or unqualified targets throw instead of silently failing or returning false.
Modern code inherits strictness from modules — the directive itself is mostly a legacy-migration tool, and linters make the question historical.

quiz.q: What does `with (Math) { const r = sqrt(PI); }` do in strict mode?
options: Computes the square root of pi into r
Throws a TypeError at runtime when with runs
Is a SyntaxError — the statement is forbidden in strict code
Creates a new scope that shadows Math’s properties
quiz.explanation: Strict mode removed with at the grammar level: the parser rejects it before the code ever runs. Modules and class bodies — always strict — never allowed it at all.

quiz.q: Where must "use strict" appear to take effect?
options: Anywhere in the file — it is a runtime function call
As the first statement of the script or function body (the directive prologue)
Only at the top of the file
quiz.explanation: Directives are recognized only in the prologue — the leading sequence of string-literal statements. Later in the code, "use strict" is an inert expression with no effect.

quiz.q: In sloppy mode, what does the assignment `oops = 42;` do when oops was never declared?
options: Creates a property on the global object — a new global variable
Creates a local variable in the enclosing function
quiz.explanation: Assignment to an undeclared name writes to the global object — the accidental global of Section 3.8. Strict mode changes the answer to a ReferenceError.

quiz.q: Which failure becomes a TypeError in strict mode but a silent no-op in sloppy mode?
options: Calling a method with the wrong this
Assigning to a property of a frozen (non-writable) object
Declaring two variables with the same let name
quiz.explanation: Sloppy mode continues past the failed write as if it succeeded; strict mode throws at the attempt. Reading undeclared variables throws in both modes, and duplicate let declarations are a SyntaxError in both.

quiz.q: In strict mode, what is `this` inside a function invoked as a plain call — `f()` rather than `o.f()`?
quiz.explanation: Strict mode does not coerce a missing receiver to the global object: a plain call binds this to undefined. Sloppy mode binds it to globalThis — the difference the worked example traced.

intro: A JavaScript **object** is an unordered collection of named values, and it is the single structure out of which nearly everything else in the language is built: arrays, functions, classes, even strings behave like objects. This section defines properties precisely, introduces the attributes a property carries (writable, enumerable, configurable) and the three attributes every object itself carries (prototype, class, extensible). Every code example is traced statement by statement, the way the engine would run it.
objectives: Define an object as a collection of properties and read the name/value distinction
Distinguish data properties from accessor properties
Name the three attributes every object carries: prototype, class and extensible
Trace a property lookup that finds an inherited value through the prototype
Explain why arrays, functions and strings are still, at bottom, objects

concepts.statement: An **object** is an **unordered collection of properties**, each a **name/value pair**: the property name is a **string or a symbol**, and the value is any JavaScript value — primitive, object or function. A value that is a function is called a **method**. Objects are mutable and manipulated **by reference**, never copied as a whole by assignment.

A property name is sometimes called a **key**. Keys are always **strings or symbols** even when they look like numbers: array indices like `a[0]` are the string `"0"` under the hood, which is exactly why ordinary objects can model mappings from strings to values.
concepts.detail: The value can be any type whatsoever — objects nest arbitrarily: `book.publisher.address.city` is three property accesses in a row. The string-to-value association inside one object is why a plain object doubles as a lookup table (a full treatment of the purpose-built `Map` is in Chapter 11).

concepts.statement: A **data property** simply holds a value. An **accessor property** holds no value of its own: reading it invokes a **getter** function and writing it invokes a **setter** function, so it looks like a property but behaves like a pair of hidden methods.
concepts.detail: Accessor properties are written with the `get` and `set` keywords in an object literal (Section 6.6). In Chapter 8 you will see them combined with closures to build genuinely private, validated state.

concepts.statement: Every property, data or accessor, carries three attributes: **writable** (may the value be changed? — data properties only), **enumerable** (does the property show up in `for/in` loops and `Object.keys()`?) and **configurable** (may the property be deleted or its attributes changed?). Accessor properties swap the writable/value pair for `get` and `set` functions.
concepts.detail: These are normally invisible machinery, but Chapter 14 exposes them through `Object.defineProperty()` and friends — the foundation for freezing objects, hiding properties and metaprogramming.

concepts.statement: Every object carries a **prototype** attribute: a reference to a second object from which it **inherits properties**. Setting an object property may be blocked by a read-only inherited property, and reading `o.x` walks up the prototype chain if `x` is not an own property of `o`. The prototype is normally fixed at object creation time.
