concepts.detail: You can inspect it: `Object.getPrototypeOf(o)` returns it, and `o1.isPrototypeOf(o2)` tests whether `o1` sits anywhere in `o2`’s chain. Most objects inherit, directly or transitively, from `Object.prototype`, the root object that supplies `toString`, `hasOwnProperty` and friends.

concepts.statement: An object’s **class attribute** is a string such as `"Object"` or `"Array"` that classifies it — essentially historical, retrievable only indirectly via `Object.prototype.toString.call(o)`. The **extensible attribute** says whether new properties may be added: it can be cleared with `Object.preventExtensions(o)` and friends (Chapter 14), after which the object is frozen against growth.
concepts.detail: Chapter 9 leans on the prototype attribute constantly — classes are nothing but prototypes plus a constructor function. The class attribute, by contrast, is mostly a curiosity you will not use directly.

concepts.statement: Arrays are objects whose properties are numbered and that carry a magical `length`; functions are objects with executable code attached; a **string** is an object-like value with numbered characters and a `length`; `RegExp`, `Date`, `Error` and `Map` instances are objects. It is objects all the way down.
concepts.detail: This is why `typeof` returns `"object"` for arrays and `"function"` for functions — but both still pass every object rule in this chapter. Strings, being primitive, only *borrow* object behavior when you use `s.length` or `s[i]` (a temporary wrapper object is created, used and discarded).

examples.title: Reading a real object literal
examples.problem: For the `book` object below, list every property as a name/value pair, give the type of each value, and identify one property the object inherits but did not declare.

steps.label: Step 1: The literal
Step 2: The own properties
steps.text: Three own properties: `title` (name is the string `"title"`, value is a string), `edition` (value is the number 7) and `authors` (value is an array, itself an object). The names are always strings — `edition` looks like an identifier but the engine stores the key `"edition"`.

steps.label: Step 3: The nested object
steps.text: The value of `book.authors` is itself an object, so `book.authors[0]` performs a property access on the string `"0"` of that inner array object, yielding `"David Flanagan"`.

steps.label: Step 4: The inherited property
steps.text: `book.toString` is not an own property. The engine follows `book`’s prototype up to `Object.prototype`, which owns a `toString` method — so `book.toString()` returns `"[object Object]"` without the literal ever mentioning it.

steps.label: Step 5: Confirm with a test
steps.text: `book.hasOwnProperty("title")` is `true` (own), while `book.hasOwnProperty("toString")` is `false` (inherited) — the existence-testing tools of Section 6.4 in action.

examples.result: Own: `title` → string, `edition` → number, `authors` → array. Inherited: `toString` (plus every other property of `Object.prototype`) — the object literal you write is only the bottom layer of the object you get.

examples.title: Trace the engine: a lookup through the prototype
examples.problem: Given `let p = { x: 1 };` and `let o = Object.create(p); o.y = 2;` — what do `o.x`, `o.y`, `o.z` and `o.toString` evaluate to, and why does `o.z.q` behave differently from `o.z`?

steps.label: Step 1: The two objects
steps.text: `Object.create(p)` makes a new empty object whose prototype is `p`. So the chain is `o` → `p` → `Object.prototype` → `null`. The assignment `o.y = 2` creates an own property on `o`.

steps.label: Step 2: o.x
steps.text: `x` is not an own property of `o`, so the engine looks at the prototype `p`, finds `x: 1`, and returns `1`. Nothing was copied — `o` and `p` share one `x`.

steps.label: Step 3: o.y and o.z
steps.text: `o.y` is an own property → `2`. `o.z` is nowhere in the chain → the expression evaluates to `undefined`, **not an error**: a missing property is a value of `undefined`.

steps.label: Step 4: o.z.q — the error case
steps.text: `o.z.q` tries to read property `q` **of** `undefined`, which throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. The lesson: the missing property itself is safe; it is chaining *through* it that throws.

steps.label: Step 5: o.toString
steps.text: `toString` is not on `o` or `p`, but it is on `Object.prototype` at the top of the chain — so `o.toString` is that inherited function.

examples.result: `o.x` → 1 (inherited from `p`), `o.y` → 2 (own), `o.z` → `undefined` (missing, no error), `o.z.q` → TypeError, `o.toString` → function inherited from `Object.prototype`.

examples.title: Copying an object copies the reference
examples.problem: Trace what happens when a variable holding an object is assigned to a second variable, then one property is changed through the second name.

steps.label: Step 1: One object, two names
steps.text:
```
let a = { n: 1 };
let b = a;   // copies the REFERENCE, not the object
```

steps.label: Step 2: Mutate through b
steps.text:
```
b.n = 2;
console.log(a.n); // 2
```
There is only one object; `a` and `b` are two labels for it, so the change is visible through both.

steps.label: Step 3: A real copy
steps.text:
```
let c = { ...a }; // spread copies own enumerable properties
c.n = 5;
console.log(a.n); // still 2 — a is untouched
```
`c` is a new object with its own properties (a **shallow** copy — nested objects are still shared, as Section 6.5 explains).

examples.result: Assignment aliases objects; `{ ...o }` (or `Object.assign({}, o)`) makes a fresh shallow copy. Comparing distinct objects with `===` is always `false` even with identical contents — identity, not structure, is compared.

keyTakeaways: An object is an unordered collection of properties: string-or-symbol name → any value; a function-valued property is a method.
Data properties hold values; accessor properties run a getter on read and a setter on write.
Every property has writable, enumerable and configurable attributes; every object has prototype, class and extensible attributes.
Reading a missing property yields `undefined`; chaining a further property through that `undefined` throws a TypeError.
Objects are compared and assigned by reference — spreading makes a shallow copy.
Arrays, functions, Dates and Maps are all objects; the prototype supplies shared behavior like `Object.prototype.toString`.

quiz.q: In JavaScript, the name of an object property may be:
quiz.explanation: Property names are always strings or symbols; numbers like array indices are converted to strings, and other primitives are converted before use as keys.

quiz.q: An object’s prototype attribute is:
options: the function that created the object
a second object from which the first inherits properties
a string naming the class of the object
an array of the object’s own property names
quiz.explanation: The prototype is a reference to another object consulted on failed lookups and at creation time; the class is the string, and the creating function is the constructor.

quiz.q: Evaluating the expression `o.z.q` when `o` has no property `z`:
quiz.explanation: `o.z` is safely undefined, but then reading `.q` of that undefined value throws TypeError — you cannot read a property of undefined.

quiz.q: Which statement about data vs accessor properties is true?
options: accessor properties are only available on class instances, never plain objects
an accessor property has get and set functions in place of the value and writable attributes
quiz.explanation: Accessors swap value/writable for getter/setter functions; they exist in ordinary literals too (get/set syntax), and enumerability is an independent attribute.

intro: There are exactly three ways to bring a new ordinary object into the world: write an **object literal**, invoke a **constructor with `new`**, or call **`Object.create()`** with an explicit prototype. This section works all three, then shows the prototype-based creation pattern that powers the Range classes of Chapter 9 — creating objects that share a prototype of default values and inherited methods.
objectives: Create objects with literals, the new operator and Object.create()
Explain what Object.create(null) produces and when you want it
Use a prototype to supply shared default values and shared methods
Predict when a fresh object is created versus when an existing one is reused

concepts.statement: An **object literal** is a comma-separated list of `name: value` pairs between braces: `{ x: 1, y: 2 }`. It is an **expression** — it is evaluated (and creates a brand-new object) every time the statement runs — and it may nest arbitrarily with array and function literals.

`new` creates a new object that inherits from the specified **constructor function**’s `prototype` property, then invokes the constructor with the new object as the value of `this`: `let o = new Object();` creates an empty object just like `{}`. The same mechanism produces `new Array()`, `new Date()`, `new Map()` and — in Chapter 9 — your own classes.
concepts.detail: The full four-step mechanics of `new` are traced in Section 9.2. For now: constructor invocation is the second route to an object, and the built-in constructor `Object()` is almost never worth calling — `{}` is shorter and idiomatic.

concepts.statement: **`Object.create(p)`** creates a new empty object with **`p` as its prototype**, before any properties are assigned — letting you pick the prototype explicitly. `Object.create(Object.prototype)` produces another plain empty `{}`-equivalent; `Object.create(null)` produces an object with **no prototype at all**, inheriting nothing.
concepts.detail:
```
let o1 = Object.create({ x: 1, y: 2 });
o1.x + o1.y // 3 — inherited
let o2 = Object.create(null); // no toString, no nothing
o2.toString // undefined
```
`Object.create()` is also useful defensively: a dictionary built on `Object.create(null)` cannot be tricked by an inherited `toString` when property names are untrusted.

concepts.term: The prototype as a source of defaults
concepts.statement: Because reads fall through to the prototype and writes stay on the object itself, a shared prototype doubles as a store of **default values**: instances list only their differences, and setting a property **shadows** the inherited one rather than changing it for everyone.
concepts.detail:
```
let defaults = { theme: "light", volume: 5, muted: false };
let options = Object.create(defaults);
options.theme = "dark";     // own property, shadows the default
console.log(options.volume); // 5 — still from the prototype
```
This one-inherit-per-lookup scheme is memory-friendly too: the default values exist once, not once per options object.

concepts.statement: A literal inside a loop body or function body runs again on each iteration or call, so a factory function returning `{ x, y }` hands out a **fresh object on every call**. The confusion case is the opposite: storing a literal in a `const` variable creates one object that is simply shared by everyone holding that variable.

examples.title: Trace the engine: three empty objects and a fourth with no past
examples.problem: Create an empty object each of the three ways, plus one via `Object.create(null)`. For each, say what `o.toString` is and why.

steps.label: Step 1: The three routes
steps.text:
```
let a = {};                        // literal
let b = new Object();              // constructor
let c = Object.create(Object.prototype);
```
All three are empty ordinary objects whose prototype is `Object.prototype` — functionally identical.

steps.label: Step 2: The inherited method
steps.text: For `a`, `b` and `c`, `o.toString` is the function on `Object.prototype`, so `String(o)` gives `"[object Object]"` for each.

steps.label: Step 3: The null-prototype object
steps.text:
```
let d = Object.create(null);
d.toString // undefined
```
`d`’s prototype is `null`, the end-of-chain marker — it has no inherited properties at all, not even `toString` or `hasOwnProperty`.

steps.label: Step 4: Where the null prototype shines
steps.text: Converting `d` to a primitive (`String(d)`, `` `${d}` ``) throws `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` — but as a pure dictionary keyed by untrusted names it is the safest object in the language: no inherited property can collide with a stored key.

examples.result: `{}`, `new Object()` and `Object.create(Object.prototype)` all yield a standard empty object inheriting from `Object.prototype`; `Object.create(null)` yields a bare dictionary with no inherited members.

examples.title: A prototype ladder of settings
examples.problem: Build a chain `defaults` → `options` and trace every read and write, including what happens after `delete`.

steps.label: Step 1: Set up the chain
Step 2: Reads
steps.text: `options.theme` → `"dark"` (own property found first, lookup stops). `options.volume` → `5` (falls through to `defaults`). `options.muted` → `undefined` (nowhere in the chain).

steps.label: Step 3: The write never leaks upward
steps.text: `options.volume = 0` creates an own `volume` on `options`; `defaults.volume` still reads `5`. Shadowing is per-object: the shared default is intact for other objects created from it.

steps.label: Step 4: Delete restores the inherited view
steps.text: `delete options.theme` removes the own property, so `options.theme` is `"light"` again — the inherited value shows through (the delete operator is traced fully in the next section).

examples.result: Reads fall down the chain, writes stay on the top object, deletes un-shadow: `theme` goes `"light"` → `"dark"` → (delete) → `"light"`, while `defaults` never changed.

examples.title: How many objects does this loop create?
examples.problem: How many distinct objects exist after running the code below, and which variables see which ones?

steps.label: Step 1: The code
Step 2: Count the literals
steps.text: The loop body runs three times and the literal `{ x: i, y: 0 }` is evaluated each time — three distinct points with `x` of 0, 1 and 2. Plus `origin` and the array itself: five objects.

steps.label: Step 3: They do not share state
steps.text: `points[0].x = 99` changes only the first point; `origin` and the other points are untouched because each literal evaluation made a fresh object.

steps.label: Step 4: The trap that does not apply here
steps.text: Had the loop pushed `origin` instead of a literal, all three slots would alias one object and the mutation would be visible three times. Literal-per-iteration is what saves you.

examples.result: Five objects: `origin`, the array, and three loop-fresh points. Each literal evaluation is a new object; only explicit sharing of a variable re-uses one.

keyTakeaways: Three creation routes: the literal `{}` (idiomatic), `new Constructor()`, and `Object.create(proto)` with an explicit prototype.
An object literal is an expression evaluated on every run — fresh object each time it executes.
`Object.create(p)` links the new object to `p`; reads inherit and writes shadow.
`Object.create(null)` produces a prototype-less dictionary: no inherited `toString`, immune to name collisions, unsafe to convert to a primitive.
A shared prototype is an efficient store of defaults: instances hold only their overrides.
`{}`, `new Object()` and `Object.create(Object.prototype)` are the same object shape.

quiz.q: The expression `Object.create(null)` yields an object that:
options: has no inherited properties at all, not even toString
cannot have properties added to it
inherits from Object.prototype like every object
quiz.explanation: `null` is the end of every prototype chain, so the new object inherits nothing; it is still extensible and perfectly usable as a dictionary.

quiz.q: After `let p = { x: 1 }; let o = Object.create(p); o.x = 2; delete o.x;` the expression `o.x` is:
quiz.explanation: The write created an own property that shadowed the inherited one; deleting the own property re-exposes the inherited `x: 1`.

quiz.q: A function body contains the statement `return { seed: 1 };` and is called five times. How many seed objects exist?
options: one — the literal was compiled once
five — the literal is evaluated at each call
quiz.explanation: Object literals are expressions: every evaluation creates and returns a new object, so five calls produce five independent `{ seed: 1 }` objects.

quiz.q: `new Date()` creates an object whose prototype is:
options: Date.prototype, which itself inherits from Object.prototype
quiz.explanation: Constructor invocation links the new object to the constructor’s prototype property; Date.prototype’s own prototype is Object.prototype, forming the chain.

intro: Property access looks trivial until you ask what `o.x` really does — and then square brackets, dynamic keys, prototypes, null bases and deletion all matter. This section covers the two access forms, when each is required, exactly which operations throw, and the `delete` operator that removes own properties while leaving inherited ones alone.
objectives: Choose between dot and square-bracket property access and convert between them
Use bracket notation for computed and arbitrary property names
Predict the TypeErrors that come from null and undefined base objects
Trace how assignment creates or overwrites own properties — never inherited ones
Delete own properties and explain what happens to inherited ones

concepts.statement: **Dot notation** `o.x` names a property with an identifier: simple, preferred when the name is known ahead of time and is a legal identifier. The identifier after the dot is used literally as the string key — `o.x` and `o["x"]` are the same access.
concepts.detail: Reserved words are actually allowed after the dot in modern JavaScript (`o.class`, `o.for`), but the safe style treats anything identifier-like as dot territory and everything else as bracket territory.

concepts.statement: **Bracket notation** `o[expr]` evaluates the bracketed expression and **converts the result to a string** to use as the key. It is required when the name is not a legal identifier (`o["main title"]`), when it contains punctuation, or when it is **computed at run time** (`o[name]`).
concepts.detail: Because the index becomes a string, `a[2]` and `a["2"]` on an array are the same element — arrays are objects with string keys that merely look numeric.

concepts.statement: Bracket notation turns an object into a **string-to-value map** whose keys are data. The classic pattern — increment a counter for each word, where the words come from input rather than from your source code — is a loop over bracket accesses: `counts[word] = (counts[word] || 0) + 1`.
concepts.detail: This is the pre-`Map` idiom from every edition of the book. Its modern caveats: inherited keys can collide, keys are limited to strings, and it needs `Object.create(null)` or careful `hasOwnProperty` checks — reasons the `Map` of Chapter 11 exists.

concepts.term: TypeErrors on null and undefined bases
concepts.statement: Reading a property of `null` or `undefined` throws `TypeError` — but **reading a missing property of a valid object never throws**; it yields `undefined`. The same rule applies to writes: `o.x = 1` is fine, `null.x = 1` throws. Guard chains with `&&` or the optional chaining operator `?.`.
concepts.detail:
```
let book = null;
book.title            // TypeError: Cannot read properties of null
book && book.title    // null — the && short-circuits
let shelf = {};
shelf.book && shelf.book.title // undefined — safe chain
```

concepts.statement: Property assignment **creates an own property** if the name is absent and **overwrites the own property** if present. It never modifies a prototype: assigning `o.x = 1` when `x` is inherited shadows it with an own copy. A write throws only in strict mode when the property (own or inherited) is non-writable, or when the object is frozen.
concepts.detail: Reads consult the chain; writes stay local. That asymmetry is exactly why the shared-defaults pattern of Section 6.2 works and why classes can share methods safely (Chapter 9).

concepts.statement: `delete o.x` removes an **own, configurable** property — it operates on a property access expression, not a bare variable. It returns `true` when the deletion succeeded **or when nothing needed deleting**, and `false` (sloppy mode) or a TypeError (strict mode) for non-configurable properties such as array `length` or properties of the global object created with `var`.
concepts.detail:
```
let o = { x: 1 };
delete o.x; // true — now gone
"x" in o;    // false
delete o.x; // true again — deleting a missing property is a no-op success
```
Deleting does not touch the prototype: if `x` is inherited, `delete o.x` returns true but the inherited `x` remains — and is what you get from then on.

concepts.statement: Setting `o.x = undefined` hides the value but keeps the key — property name in the object, `"x" in o` still true, `Object.keys` still lists it. `delete o.x` removes the property itself. The distinction matters for existence tests, enumeration and JSON output.
concepts.detail: On arrays the distinction is sharper: `a[i] = undefined` keeps a dense array with an undefined element; `delete a[i]` punches a **hole** (a sparse array) — Section 7.2 traces the difference.

examples.title: Trace the engine: word counts with computed keys
examples.problem: Given `let words = ["red", "blue", "red"];` build a count table using bracket notation, tracing every read and write.

steps.label: Step 1: The loop
Step 2: First iteration, w is red
steps.text: `counts["red"]` is `undefined` (fresh object); `undefined || 0` is `0`; `0 + 1` is `1`; write creates the own property `red: 1`.

steps.label: Step 3: Second iteration, w is blue
steps.text: Same dance: `blue` was absent → `blue: 1` is created. The two keys are unrelated data — the object is being used as a map.

steps.label: Step 4: Third iteration, w is red again
steps.text: Now `counts["red"]` is `1`, so `1 + 1` gives `2` and the own property is overwritten: `red: 2`.

steps.label: Step 5: Read back
steps.text: `counts` is `{ red: 2, blue: 1 }`; `Object.keys(counts)` is `["red", "blue"]` in insertion order. Note that `counts[w]` — with the loop variable — is exactly what dot notation cannot express: the key arrives as a string at run time.

examples.result: The `|| 0` default plus an overwrite-on-write gives a tally in three iterations: `{ red: 2, blue: 1 }` — computed keys are the entire trick.

examples.title: The delete trace: shadow, delete, inherit
examples.problem: Start from `let p = { x: 1 };` and `let o = Object.create(p);`. Set `o.x = 2`, delete it twice, and explain every value read along the way.

steps.label: Step 1: The shadowing write
steps.text: `o.x = 2` creates an **own** property `x` on `o`. `o.x` reads `2` (own found first, prototype never consulted); `p.x` still reads `1`.

steps.label: Step 2: The first delete
steps.text: `delete o.x` returns `true` and removes the own property. The next read `o.x` falls through to `p` and returns `1` — the inherited value was never touched, merely hidden.

steps.label: Step 3: The second delete
steps.text: `delete o.x` again — there is no own `x` on `o`, so the operator has nothing to remove. It returns `true` (a no-op success) and **the inherited `x` survives**: `o.x` is still `1`.

steps.label: Step 4: The moral
steps.text: `delete` operates on the object in the expression `o.x` — the base `o` — never on the prototype chain behind it. Deleting your own shadow is the only way to re-expose an inherited value.

examples.result: `o.x` reads: 2 (own) → 1 (after delete re-exposes the inherited value) → 1 (second delete is a no-op; inherited properties are out of its reach).

examples.title: Guarding a chained access
examples.problem: Why does the book write `book && book.author && book.author.name` instead of just `book.author.name`, and how does optional chaining shorten it?

steps.label: Step 1: The failure
steps.text: If `book` is `null` or `book.author` is `undefined`, then `book.author.name` throws TypeError for reading `.name` of that null/undefined — one missing layer kills the whole chain.

steps.label: Step 2: The && ladder
steps.text:
```
let name = book && book.author && book.author.name;
```
Each `&&` evaluates to its left side when that side is falsy — `null` or `undefined` — stopping the chain before the fatal read. The result is `undefined` instead of an exception.

steps.label: Step 3: Optional chaining
steps.text:
```
let name = book?.author?.name;
```
The `?.` operator does the same test automatically: if the base is null/undefined the whole expression is `undefined`; otherwise evaluation proceeds to the right. `?.` is an ES2020 operator covered with the operators in Chapter 4.

steps.label: Step 4: Writes need the long form
steps.text: `book?.author = ...` is illegal — optional chaining is for reads. To assign safely you must first ensure each layer exists, which is what constructor functions and classes (Chapter 9) do.

examples.result: Missing mid-chain data should produce `undefined`, not a TypeError — the `&&` ladder and `?.` both deliver that, at the cost of one construct per link.

keyTakeaways: `o.x` requires an identifier; `o[expr]` converts any expression to a string key and is the only form for computed or exotic names.
Reading a missing property yields `undefined`; reading any property of `null`/`undefined` throws TypeError — guard with `&&` or `?.`.
Assignment creates or overwrites an own property; it never writes to the prototype — inherited values are shadowed, not changed.
`delete o.x` removes the own configurable property and returns true; deleting a missing or inherited property changes nothing.
Delete removes the property; assigning `undefined` keeps the key with a dead value — different `in`/enumeration/JSON consequences.
Arrays are objects with string keys: `a[2]` is `a["2"]`.

quiz.q: Which expression is the correct way to read the property whose name is held in the variable `key`?
quiz.explanation: Bracket notation evaluates its contents, converting the result to the string key; `o.key` would look up the literal name "key".

quiz.q: After `let o = { a: 1 };` the expression `delete o.b` returns:
options: false, because b does not exist
true — deleting a nonexistent property is a successful no-op
quiz.explanation: delete returns true when the property is gone or was never there; it only fails (false or TypeError in strict mode) for non-configurable properties.

quiz.q: If `o` inherits property `x` from its prototype, then after `o.x = 5` executes:
options: o gains an own property x equal to 5, shadowing the inherited one
a TypeError is thrown because x already exists
quiz.explanation: Writes never reach the prototype: assignment creates an own property on the base object of the access expression, hiding the inherited value for this object only.

quiz.q: Which single expression throws a TypeError?
quiz.explanation: A missing property safely evaluates to undefined — but reading .deeper of that undefined throws; the other three read properties of a valid object.

quiz.q: The main reason bracket notation exists alongside dot notation is:
options: brackets are faster at run time
brackets accept computed names, so keys can be data rather than identifiers
dot notation only works on class instances
brackets copy the property value instead of referencing it
quiz.explanation: Dot form needs a literal identifier known at write-time; brackets evaluate an expression to a string key, enabling the map-like uses of objects.

Step 1: The code given links `child` to `base`, shadows `x`, deletes the shadow, then reads `x`. Step 2: The governing rules are that assignment always creates or updates an own property without touching the prototype, that `delete` removes only own properties and never prototype members, and that a read walks from the object up the prototype chain. Step 3: Tracing line by line, `child.x = 2` creates an own `x` hiding the prototype's `1`, `delete child.x` removes exactly that own property, and the final read finds no own `x` so it continues to `base` and yields `1`. Step 4: The distractors fail because `2` describes the state before the deletion, `undefined` would need the prototype link gone, and `delete` on a configurable own property never throws. Step 5: Therefore the program prints `1`.

intro: Does this object have that property — and do you mean have it *itself*, or merely *reach* it through the prototype? JavaScript answers those questions with three different tools (`in`, `hasOwnProperty` and comparing against `undefined`) and enumerates properties with `for/in` plus the `Object.keys` family. This section works every tool and traces the exact differences in a side-by-side example.
objectives: Test property existence with in, hasOwnProperty and the !== undefined idiom
Explain when each test gives a different answer
Enumerate properties with for/in and with Object.keys, Object.values and Object.entries
State and trace the modern property enumeration order rule
Explain why built-in properties do not clutter for/in loops

concepts.statement: **`"x" in o`** tests whether the property `x` exists **anywhere** in `o`’s prototype chain — own or inherited. It is about **existence of the key**, not the value: `"x" in { x: undefined }` is `true`.
concepts.detail:
```
"toString" in {} // true — inherited from Object.prototype
"x" in { x: undefined } // true — the key exists
```
`in` on the right-hand of `for/in` is not this operator — the loop form is its own statement (below).

concepts.statement: **`o.hasOwnProperty("x")`** tests whether `x` is an **own property** of `o`, ignoring the prototype chain entirely. It is the stricter of the two existence tests and the one that matters for data you actually stored on the object.
concepts.detail: Because the method itself is inherited from `Object.prototype`, a null-prototype object must borrow it explicitly: `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(o, "x")`. The related `o.propertyIsEnumerable("x")` additionally requires the enumerable attribute to be set.

concepts.statement: The quick test `o.x !== undefined` conflates **existence with value**: it returns false for a property that exists but holds `undefined`, and true only when some key along the chain maps to a defined value. Use it when undefined is not a legal value in your data model.
concepts.detail:
```
let o = { x: undefined };
"x" in o                 // true
o.hasOwnProperty("x")   // true
o.x !== undefined        // false — the value IS undefined
```
Three tests, three answers: this object is the worked example of why the distinction survives.

concepts.statement: **`for (let p in o)`** iterates the **string** property names of `o` — own and inherited **enumerable** names alike, walking the prototype chain. It does not enumerate symbol-keyed properties, and it skips non-enumerable ones.

The three functions return arrays built from the **own, enumerable, string-keyed** properties of the argument: `Object.keys(o)` the names, `Object.values(o)` the values, `Object.entries(o)` an array of `[key, value]` pairs. Inherited properties are excluded — the key behavioral difference from `for/in`.
concepts.detail:
```
let o = { a: 1, b: 2 };
Object.keys(o)       // ["a", "b"]
Object.values(o)     // [1, 2]
Object.entries(o)    // [["a", 1], ["b", 2]]
```
Being arrays, the results are iterable with `for/of`, mappable with `.map`, and generally the modern answer to walking an object — the array methods of Chapter 7 apply directly.

concepts.statement: Modern JavaScript guarantees enumeration order for own properties: **integer-like string keys in ascending numeric order first**, then remaining string keys **in insertion order**, then symbol keys in insertion order. `Object.keys` follows this rule, and `for/in` enumerates own properties in the same order before moving up the prototype chain.
concepts.detail:
```
let o = { b: 1, 2: "two", 1: "one", a: 3 };
Object.keys(o) // ["1", "2", "b", "a"]
```
The two integer-like keys jump to the front sorted numerically even though `b` was written first; `b` then `a` follow insertion order. Note that only non-negative integers up to the array-index limit count as integer-like.

concepts.statement: The built-in properties of `Object.prototype` — `toString`, `valueOf`, `hasOwnProperty` and friends — are **non-enumerable**, which is why a `for/in` over a plain object does not spew them. The mechanism that keeps the loop clean is the enumerability attribute, and it is also exactly what prototype-patching code must respect (Section 9.4).
concepts.detail: This is the design insight of the chapter: inheritance from a shared prototype is only tolerable in everyday code because the inherited built-ins carry `enumerable: false`. You inherit their behavior without inheriting their noise.

examples.title: Trace the engine: three existence tests, three answers
examples.problem: Given `let o = { x: undefined };` determine the value of every expression below before running it, and explain each.

steps.label: Step 1: The setup
steps.text: The object has exactly one own property: the key `x`, whose value is `undefined`. Its chain then runs to `Object.prototype`.

steps.label: Step 2: "x" in o
steps.text: The `in` operator checks the key — own first, found → `true`. The value being undefined is irrelevant to `in`.

steps.label: Step 3: o.hasOwnProperty("x")
steps.text: Own test — `x` is an own property → `true`. Same answer as `in` here because the property is own rather than inherited.

steps.label: Step 4: o.x !== undefined
steps.text: Reads the value → `undefined`, so the comparison is `false`. The key exists; the idiom says it does not.

steps.label: Step 5: "toString" in o and o.hasOwnProperty("toString")
steps.text: `in` walks the chain → `true` (inherited from `Object.prototype`). `hasOwnProperty` → `false` — the strict test denies it. Four expressions, and every one of the three tools was needed to describe this one object.

examples.result: `"x" in o` → true, `o.hasOwnProperty("x")` → true, `o.x !== undefined` → false, `"toString" in o` → true, `o.hasOwnProperty("toString")` → false — existence, ownness and value are three separate questions.

examples.title: The worked diff: for/in versus the Object.keys family
examples.problem: Build an object with one inherited enumerable property and one own property, then run `for/in`, `Object.keys`, `Object.values` and `Object.entries` over it and account for every difference in output.

steps.label: Step 1: The setup
Step 2: for/in
steps.text: The loop enumerates own enumerable names first, then walks up the chain — output `own` and then `inherited`. It sees **two** properties.

steps.label: Step 3: Object.keys
steps.text: `Object.keys(o)` → `["own"]`. The chain is not consulted: only own, enumerable, string-keyed names appear.

steps.label: Step 4: Object.values and Object.entries
steps.text: `Object.values(o)` → `[20]`; `Object.entries(o)` → `[["own", 20]]`. Same own-only rule, and the pairs format pairs perfectly with destructuring: `for (let [k, v] of Object.entries(o))`.

steps.label: Step 5: The rule to remember
steps.text: Inherited properties are visible to `in` and to `for/in`, invisible to the `Object.keys` family. When enumerating data you stored, the trio is the safer tool — no prototype surprises can reach it.

examples.result: `for/in` yields `own`, `inherited`; `Object.keys` yields `["own"]`; values `[20]`; entries `[["own", 20]]` — the diff is exactly the prototype chain.

examples.title: Enumeration order, traced
examples.problem: Predict the output of `Object.keys` on `let o = { b: 1, 2: "two", 1: "one", a: 3 };` and of the `for/in` loop over the same object.

steps.label: Step 1: Classify the keys
steps.text: String keys: `"b"`, `"2"`, `"1"`, `"a"`. Of these, `"1"` and `"2"` are **integer-like**; `"b"` and `"a"` are not.

steps.label: Step 2: Integer-like keys first, numerically
steps.text: The rule sorts integer-like keys ascending: `"1"` then `"2"` — regardless of the fact that `b` was written first and `2` before `1`.

steps.label: Step 3: Then strings in insertion order
steps.text: Among the rest, insertion order governs: `"b"` (written first) then `"a"`. Symbols would come last in their own insertion order — there are none here.

steps.label: Step 4: The result
steps.text: `Object.keys(o)` → `["1", "2", "b", "a"]`, and `for (let p in o) console.log(p)` prints the same four names in the same order (nothing is inherited).

steps.label: Step 5: Why this rule exists
steps.text: The integer-first clause keeps array-like keys (and arrays themselves) visiting indices 0, 1, 2… in a sane order, while insertion order for named keys matches programmer intuition about "the order I added them".

examples.result: `["1", "2", "b", "a"]` — integers sorted numerically lead; named keys follow in written order.

keyTakeaways: `"x" in o` tests existence anywhere in the prototype chain; `o.hasOwnProperty("x")` tests own-ness only.
`o.x !== undefined` conflates existence with value — false for a property that exists with value undefined.
`for/in` enumerates own and inherited enumerable string keys; `Object.keys/values/entries` enumerate own enumerable string keys only.
Guaranteed order: integer-like keys ascending, then strings in insertion order, then symbols.
Built-ins stay out of loops because they are non-enumerable — enumerability, not existence, is what keeps `for/in` clean.
Prefer the `Object.entries` + `for/of` combination for walking data objects: array methods apply immediately.

quiz.q: For `let o = { x: undefined };` which expression is false?
quiz.explanation: The property exists with the value undefined, so only the value comparison fails — the key tests all pass.

quiz.q: The key behavioral difference between a `for/in` loop and `Object.keys` is that:
options: for/in includes inherited enumerable properties; Object.keys reports only own enumerable string keys
for/in visits values instead of keys
quiz.explanation: Both enumerate string keys, but the loop walks the prototype chain while Object.keys stops at own properties — and neither enumerates symbols.

quiz.q: Given `let o = { b: 1, 2: "two", 1: "one", a: 3 };` what does `Object.keys(o)` return?
quiz.explanation: Integer-like keys sort first in ascending numeric order ("1", "2"), then the remaining string keys follow insertion order ("b" before "a").

quiz.q: Why does a `for/in` loop over a plain object not list `toString`?
options: because toString is inherited rather than own, and for/in skips all inherited properties
because toString lives on the constructor, not the prototype
quiz.explanation: for/in actually does include inherited enumerable properties — it skips toString because that built-in carries the enumerable: false attribute.

intro: Objects grow and travel: `Object.assign` and the spread operator copy properties from one object into another, and `JSON.stringify` with `JSON.parse` turns objects into text and back. Both operations have sharp edges — shallow copies, last-write-wins merging, dropped functions, `undefined` and symbols — and both are traced below statement by statement, including the `toJSON` escape hatch that makes serialization customizable.
objectives: Extend objects with Object.assign and the object spread operator, knowing exactly what each copies
Predict the winner when multiple sources define the same property
Trace what JSON.stringify keeps, drops and transforms
Round-trip an object through JSON.parse and know what cannot survive the trip
Customize serialization with toJSON

concepts.statement: **`Object.assign(target, ...sources)`** copies the **own enumerable** properties (string and symbol keyed) of each source object into `target` — reading each value from its source and **writing** it into the target — then returns the (mutated) target. If several sources define the same key, **the last one wins**.

The **object spread operator** `{ ...source }` inside a literal copies the own enumerable properties of `source` into the new object being built. `let copy = { ...o }` is the idiomatic shallow copy, and `{ ...defaults, ...options }` the idiomatic merge — same semantics as the `Object.assign({}, ...)` idiom, fresh object guaranteed.

Both `Object.assign` and spread copy **one level** of properties. If a property value is a nested object, the copy gets a reference to the *same* nested object — mutating it through either parent is visible through both. Deep copies need a recursive walk or `structuredClone()`.

**`JSON.stringify(o)`** serializes the own enumerable string-keyed properties of `o` into JSON text. It drops functions, `undefined` values and symbol-keyed properties; converts `NaN` and `Infinity` to `null`; serializes `Date` objects as ISO strings (via their `toJSON`); and throws `TypeError` on circular (cyclically nested) structures.
concepts.detail:
```
JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: [true, null] })
// '{"a":1,"b":[true,null]}'
JSON.stringify({ f: () => 1, g: undefined, h: NaN })
// '{"h":null}'
```
Optional second and third arguments filter keys and pretty-print: `JSON.stringify(o, null, 2)` indents with two spaces. Arrays serialize element by element, with holes and undefined elements both becoming `null` (Chapter 7).

concepts.statement: **`JSON.parse(text)`** parses JSON text into new objects, arrays and primitive values. The result is made of **plain objects and arrays**: no classes, no methods, no prototypes beyond the ordinary ones — functions that were dropped by stringify cannot come back.
concepts.detail: A second reviver argument can transform values during parsing — the mirror image of `toJSON`, treated with the whole JSON API in Chapter 11. For now: round-tripping state through JSON yields data-shaped objects, and rebuilding a class instance is your job (`Object.assign(new Range(0, 0), parsed)` is a serviceable start).

concepts.statement: If an object has a method named **`toJSON`**, `JSON.stringify` calls it and serializes **its return value** instead of the object itself. This is how `Date` produces its ISO string, and how you teach your own classes to serialize: return the plain data that should represent the object.

examples.title: Trace the engine: a three-way merge
examples.problem: Given defaults for a chart and two override objects, trace `Object.assign({}, defaults, options)` and its spread twin, and say exactly which object gets mutated.

steps.label: Step 1: The inputs
Step 2: Assign into a fresh target
steps.text:
```
let chart = Object.assign({}, defaults, options);
```
First the empty `{}` receives `width: 100`, `height: 100`, `color: "red"` from `defaults` — then `options` overwrites `width` to `200`. Result: `{ width: 200, height: 100, color: "red" }`.

steps.label: Step 3: Last write wins
steps.text: The overwrite rule is purely sequential: each later source rewrites any key an earlier source set. Reordering the arguments reorders the winners — `Object.assign({}, options, defaults)` would end with `width: 100`.

steps.label: Step 4: The originals are intact
steps.text: `defaults.width` still reads `100` and `options` still has only `width` — only the fresh literal was written into. Omit it (`Object.assign(defaults, options)`) and defaults itself would be mutated — a classic bug.

steps.label: Step 5: The spread twin
steps.text:
```
let chart2 = { ...defaults, ...options };
```
Identical result, guaranteed-fresh target by construction. Note both are **shallow**: a nested `axis: { min: 0 }` would be shared, not copied.

examples.result: `{ width: 200, height: 100, color: "red" }` — a new object; `defaults` and `options` untouched; last-mentioned source owns every collision.

examples.title: Trace the engine: what survives a JSON round trip
examples.problem: Serialize the `lecture` object below and account for every property that is kept, transformed or dropped; then parse the text back and compare.

steps.label: Step 1: The object
Step 2: Walk the own enumerable string keys in order
steps.text: `title` → string, kept. `room` → `null` is legal JSON, kept. `when` → a Date: stringify consults `toJSON`, which yields the ISO string `"2027-03-14T00:00:00.000Z"`. `canceled` → `undefined`, **dropped from the object entirely**. `describe` → a function, dropped.

steps.label: Step 3: The text
Step 4: Parse it back
steps.text: `let copy = JSON.parse(s);` yields `{ title: "Closures", room: null, when: "2027-03-14T00:00:00.000Z" }` — note `when` is now a **string**, not a Date; parsing is literal, so reviving typed values needs code (or a reviver).

steps.label: Step 5: The audit
steps.text: Survived: title, room. Transformed: when (Date → string). Lost: canceled (undefined), describe (function), the original’s prototype identity — `copy.describe` is undefined and `copy instanceof` anything interesting is false.

examples.result: JSON keeps plain data, converts Dates to ISO strings via toJSON, and silently discards functions, undefined and symbols — parse gives back data-shaped plain objects, never class instances.

examples.title: toJSON to the rescue: serializing a Set
examples.problem: A `Set` serializes to `{}` — explain why, then fix it with `toJSON` on a subclass and trace the output.

steps.label: Step 1: The failure
steps.text:
```
JSON.stringify(new Set([1, 2, 3])) // "{}"
```
A Set stores its members in internal slots, not in own enumerable string-keyed properties — so the property-walking serializer sees nothing.

steps.label: Step 2: The fix
Step 3: Trace the serialization
steps.text: `JSON.stringify(new SerializableSet(["a", "b"]))` — stringify finds `toJSON`, calls it, gets `["a", "b"]`, and serializes that array: `'["a","b"]'`.

steps.label: Step 4: Round trip
steps.text: `JSON.parse` yields the array `["a", "b"]`; turning it back into a Set is one constructor call: `new SerializableSet(parsed)` — the pair of directions is symmetric only because we wrote both ends.

steps.label: Step 5: Generalize the lesson
steps.text: `toJSON` is the single sanctioned hook for making any class or built-in serializable: return the plain value (primitive, array, plain object) that *represents* the object, and stringify handles the rest recursively.

examples.result: From `"{}"` to `'["a","b"]'` — one method, called before enumeration, that swaps the object for its serializable stand-in.

keyTakeaways: `Object.assign(target, ...sources)` mutates and returns the target, copying own enumerable properties; later sources win collisions.
`{ ...o }` spreads the same own enumerable properties into a fresh object — the safe-copy and safe-merge idiom.
Both copies are shallow: nested objects are shared between original and copy.
`JSON.stringify` keeps own enumerable string-keyed data, converts NaN/Infinity to null, stringifies Dates via toJSON, and drops functions, undefined and symbol keys.
`JSON.parse` returns plain data — no methods, no classes; circular structures make stringify throw.
A `toJSON` method swaps an object for its serializable representation before anything else happens.

quiz.q: After `Object.assign(target, s1, s2)` where both sources define property `x`, the value of `target.x` comes from:
quiz.explanation: Properties are copied source by source in argument order, so the last source to write a key owns the final value.

quiz.q: Which value is NOT silently dropped by `JSON.stringify` when serializing `{ f: fn, n: NaN }`?
quiz.explanation: Functions and undefined are dropped from objects, but NaN is converted to the JSON value null — it survives as a value, not as a number.

quiz.q: The expression `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` is best described as:
options: a deep copy of the JSON-representable part of obj
a no-op that returns obj itself
a shallow copy that preserves methods
quiz.explanation: Serialization recurses through nested objects, so the copy is deep — but functions, undefined, symbols and Dates-as-Dates do not survive, and cycles throw.

quiz.q: During `JSON.stringify(o)`, if `o` has a method named `toJSON`, stringify:
options: ignores it because it is a function
calls it and serializes its return value instead of o
calls it only if o is a Date
quiz.explanation: toJSON is the earliest hook in the pipeline: its return value — not the object itself — is what gets serialized, which is exactly how Date becomes an ISO string.

quiz.q: `let a = { deep: { v: 1 } }; let b = { ...a }; b.deep.v = 2;` — now `a.deep.v` is:
quiz.explanation: The spread copied the reference to the one nested deep object, so both parents see the mutation — shallow copies share second-level state.

intro: Object methods are just function-valued properties — but the `this` keyword that runs through them, the `toString`/`valueOf` conversion protocol, and the extended literal syntax of ES6 (shorthand properties, computed keys, symbols, shorthand methods, getters and setters) give them real power. This section closes the chapter with the full literal toolbox and a worked accessor that validates its writes.
objectives: Define methods and explain what this is in a method invocation
Customize string and number conversion with toString and valueOf
Use every ES6 literal extension: shorthand properties, computed keys, symbols, shorthand methods, spread
Define getter and setter accessor properties in an object literal
Build a validated accessor pair that protects its state

concepts.statement: A **method** is a function stored as a property, invoked through its object: `o.m()`. Inside the call, the keyword **`this`** holds the object of invocation — so `this.x` in a method reads or writes the receiving object’s own state. `this` is determined **by how the function is called**, not where it is defined (the full invocation table is Section 8.2).

Every object inherits **`toString()`** (a string representation — the default is `"[object Object]"`) and **`valueOf()`** (a primitive stand-in for number contexts — by default the object itself). Overriding `toString` customizes template literals and `String(o)`; overriding `valueOf` customizes arithmetic and comparison conversions.

Inside an object literal, a bare name stands for the variable of that name: `{ x, y }` is exactly `{ x: x, y: y }`. The shorthand is why factory functions returning state can be so compact, and it pairs with destructuring throughout the book’s later code.

Inside a literal, square brackets around an **expression** compute the property name at object-creation time: `{ [prop + "Name"]: value }`. Everything the bracket accessor can do to a name, the computed key can do while the object is being built.

A **symbol** (Chapter 3) is a primitive guaranteed unique even against an identical description, so symbol-keyed properties cannot collide with anyone else’s string keys. They are invisible to `for/in` and `Object.keys`, ignored by `JSON.stringify`, and are the mechanism for both pseudo-private object state and the well-known protocol hooks like `Symbol.iterator` (Chapters 12 and 14).

A literal method drops the colon and the `function` keyword: `{ area() { return this.r * this.r * Math.PI; } }`. It is the same function expression with the name recorded properly for stack traces — and the syntax also hosts generator (`*m()`) and async (`async m()`) shorthand.

An **accessor property** defined in a literal pairs `get name()` and/or `set name(v)` functions with one property name. Reading `o.name` runs the getter; assigning runs the setter. Accessors hold no value attribute — compute or guard the value in the pair — and they are the natural home of validation and derived properties.

concepts.term: Accessor properties are enumerable and configurable
concepts.statement: Accessors created with literal syntax have `enumerable: true` and `configurable: true` — they show up in `Object.keys` like any data property. The writable attribute does not exist for them: it is replaced by the presence or absence of the setter (get-only = read-only).
concepts.detail: A getter without a setter makes a property assignment fail silently in sloppy mode or throw TypeError in strict mode — the same read-only behavior a non-writable data property shows.

examples.title: The worked accessor: a validating thermometer
examples.problem: Build a thermometer object whose celsius property validates writes (numbers only, never below absolute zero) and whose fahrenheit property is computed, then trace four operations including one that throws.

steps.label: Step 1: The object
Step 2: The first read
steps.text: `thermometer.celsius` runs the getter → `0`. No function call syntax is written or needed — the property read *is* the call.

steps.label: Step 3: A legal write
steps.text: `thermometer.celsius = 25;` runs the setter; the argument is a finite number above −273.15, so the guard passes and `_celsius` becomes 25. Then `thermometer.fahrenheit` → `25 * 1.8 + 32` = `77` — computed on demand, stored nowhere.

steps.label: Step 4: The illegal writes
steps.text: `thermometer.celsius = "warm"` throws `RangeError` — `typeof` check fails. `thermometer.celsius = -300` throws — below absolute zero. The stored value is untouched: **validation happens before the assignment**, so bad data never lands.

steps.label: Step 5: What the outside world sees
steps.text: `Object.keys(thermometer)` lists `"_celsius"`, `"celsius"` and `"fahrenheit"` — the accessors are ordinary enumerable properties; only their behavior differs. And `JSON.stringify(thermometer)` serializes the backing store, not the computed fahrenheit.

examples.result: Reads compute, writes validate, and the fahrenheit property is derived fresh on every access — with `RangeError: invalid celsius value: -300` guarding the bottom of the scale.

examples.title: Trace the engine: conversion protocol on a point
examples.problem: For the `point` object with custom `toString` and `valueOf` below, trace `String(point)`, `` `${point}` ``, `point * 2` and `+point`.

steps.label: Step 1: The object
Step 2: String contexts
steps.text: `String(point)` calls the custom `toString` → `"(3, 4)"`. A template literal is a string context too — `` `${point}` `` produces the same `"(3, 4)"` (the default would have been `"[object Object]"`).

steps.label: Step 3: Number contexts
steps.text: `point * 2` needs a number, so `valueOf` runs → `Math.hypot(3, 4)` = `5`, and `5 * 2` = `10`. Unary `+point` → `5`, and `Number(point)` → `5`.

steps.label: Step 4: The + ambiguity
steps.text: `"" + point` prefers string conversion (the left operand is a string), so it concatenates with `toString` → `"(3, 4)"` — the one operator whose choice of conversion is historical rather than numeric.

steps.label: Step 5: Why both hooks
steps.text: Two conversion methods exist because objects live in both textual and numeric contexts. Overriding one and not the other gives half the story — the defaults are `"[object Object]"` and the object itself, respectively.

examples.result: `String(point)` and template literals give "(3, 4)"; arithmetic goes through `valueOf` (5) — so `point * 2` is 10 and `+point` is 5.

examples.title: Symbols as keys: hiding state in plain sight
examples.problem: Use a symbol to hold a stack’s size where neither `Object.keys` nor `JSON.stringify` nor a `for/in` loop will report it, and verify the hiding with all three.

steps.label: Step 1: The setup
Step 2: The key was computed
steps.text: The literal computed `[SIZE]` at creation time — the only literal syntax that can — making an own symbol-keyed property with value 2 after the two pushes.

steps.label: Step 3: The enumeration tests
steps.text: `Object.keys(stack)` → `["push", "size"]` — the method and the accessor are ordinary string keys, so they are listed. But `SIZE` appears in neither `Object.keys` nor a `for/in` loop: symbol keys are skipped by both.

steps.label: Step 4: JSON agrees
steps.text: `JSON.stringify(stack)` → `{}`. Symbol keys are invisible to the serializer, so the counter and nothing else travels — string-keyed methods are dropped anyway because they are functions.

steps.label: Step 5: The access rule
steps.text: Anyone who can name the symbol can read the state: `stack[SIZE]` → `2` works fine, because a symbol is a key, not a lock. Real privacy comes from the closure techniques of Section 8.5 or the `#` fields of Chapter 9 — symbols are about collision-proof *convention*.

examples.result: The size lives at a key no string can name by accident: invisible to enumeration and serialization, visible to code holding the symbol — pseudo-private by uniqueness, not by secrecy.

keyTakeaways: A method is a function-valued property; inside `o.m()`, `this` is `o` — decided by the invocation, not the definition.
Overriding `toString` customizes string conversion; overriding `valueOf` customizes numeric conversion; both defaults are nearly useless.
Literal shorthand: `{ x, y }` for existing variables, `{ [expr]: v }` for computed names, `{ m() {} }` for methods.
Symbol keys cannot collide, are skipped by for/in, Object.keys and JSON.stringify, and require computed-key syntax in literals.
Getters and setters create accessor properties: reads and writes run functions, enabling validation and derived values.
A get-only accessor is read-only — assignment throws in strict mode; the backing underscore property is convention, not privacy.

quiz.q: In `let o = { m() { return this; } };` what does `o.m()` return?
quiz.explanation: A method invocation binds this to its receiving object — the object before the dot — which is o here.

quiz.q: Which syntax creates a property whose name is the value of the variable `key`?
quiz.explanation: Computed property names evaluate the bracketed expression at literal-creation time and use the result (string or symbol) as the key.

quiz.q: A property created with `get` and no `set` is best described as:
options: read-only — assignment throws in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Accessor properties with only a getter cannot be assigned: sloppy mode ignores the write and strict mode throws a TypeError, like any read-only property.

quiz.q: Why does `JSON.stringify(o)` ignore a property keyed by a symbol?
options: JSON serialization only covers own enumerable string-keyed properties
quiz.explanation: The JSON format has only string keys, so the serializer walks string-keyed properties only — symbol-keyed data (and functions, undefined) never appear.

quiz.q: Inside a template literal, an object is converted to a string using its:
quiz.explanation: String contexts — template literals, String(), concatenation with a string — convert objects through toString; valueOf serves numeric contexts and toJSON exists only for JSON.stringify.

options: A TypeError is thrown on the second call
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The code given calls the same function once as a method and once detached, logging both results. Step 2: The governing rule is that `this` is fixed by the call form: a method call `meter.read()` sets `this` to `meter`, while a plain call `detached()` sets `this` to the global object in sloppy mode, which carries no `v` property. Step 3: Tracing call by call, the method form reads `meter.v` and yields `7`, and the detached form reads `globalThis.v`, which is absent, yielding `undefined`. Step 4: The distractors fail because the binding does not travel with the function reference, a TypeError would need strict-mode `undefined` dereferenced further, and the first call clearly resolves through `meter`. Step 5: Therefore the output is `7` followed by `undefined`.

intro: An array is an ordered collection of numbered values — and in JavaScript it is a specialized object: indices are string keys that merely look numeric, and the automatic `length` property is what makes those keys behave like positions. This section covers the four creation routes, the read/write rules for elements, and the precise law that ties `length` to the highest index.
objectives: Create arrays with literals, the spread operator, Array.of and Array.from
Read and write elements with bracket index expressions
State the rule that defines length as one more than the highest index
Predict when writes grow the array, create holes, or truncate it

concepts.statement: An **array** is an **ordered collection of values**, each called an **element** and numbered by a non-negative integer **index** starting at 0. An array is really a specialized object: the index is the string key `"0"`, `"1"`, `"2"` and so on, plus one special own property, `length`.
concepts.detail:
```
let primes = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11];
primes[0]     // 2 — bracket access with the numeric index
primes.length // 5
```
Any JavaScript value may be an element — including `undefined`, objects, and other arrays.

concepts.statement: The **array literal** is a comma-separated list of expressions between square brackets: `[1, 2, 3]`. It is an expression, evaluated fresh each time it runs (a loop pushing `[0, 0]` creates a new pair per iteration); an empty literal `[]` is the idiomatic empty array, and a trailing comma is allowed.

The **spread operator** `...` inside a literal expands an **iterable** (another array, a string, a Set) into elements: `let copy = [...original]` makes a new array with the same elements in order. Spread at the top level is the idiomatic copy, concat and combine.
concepts.detail:
```
let a = [1, 2, 3];
let b = [...a];       // [1, 2, 3] — a new array, same elements
let c = [0, ...a, 4]; // [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
[..."abc"]            // ["a", "b", "c"] — strings are iterable
```
Spread copies elements (shallow), never the array object itself — `b.push(4)` leaves `a` untouched.

concepts.statement: **`Array.of(...values)`** creates an array from its arguments, always treating them as elements. It exists to fix the notorious single-number behavior of the `Array()` constructor: `Array.of(3)` is `[3]`, while `new Array(3)` is a length-3 array with three holes and no elements.
concepts.detail:
```
Array.of()        // []
Array.of(3)       // [3]
new Array(3)      // length 3, zero elements present (Section 7.2)
Array.of(1, 2, 3) // [1, 2, 3]
```
`Array.of` is one of two **static array functions** — the other being `Array.from` — and the reason to prefer it over `new Array(...)` is entirely the one-argument case.

concepts.statement: **`Array.from(iterableOrArrayLike, mapFn?)`** builds a true array from anything iterable or array-like, optionally passing each element through `mapFn` first. It is the bridge between the array world and everything that merely resembles arrays — strings, Sets, `arguments`, NodeLists (Section 7.5).
concepts.detail:
```
Array.from([1, 2, 3], x => x * x)    // [1, 4, 9]
Array.from("abc")                     // ["a", "b", "c"]
Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i) // [0, 1, 2]
```
The mapping function runs during the copy — one pass instead of copy-then-map — and receives `(element, index)` like every array callback.

concepts.statement: Element access is bracket notation: `a[i]` converts `i` to a string and looks it up. **Out-of-bounds reads never throw** — they return `undefined`. **Writes to a non-negative integer index below `2**32 - 2` always work**: a write beyond the current end grows the array, and a write to a negative or non-integer key does not touch the array as an array at all — it just adds a property that happens to live on the object.
concepts.detail:
```
let a = ["a", "b", "c"];
a[0]          // "a"
a[3]          // undefined — out of bounds, no error
a[-1]         // undefined — negative keys are not indices
a["0"]       // "a" — same element: the index is the string "0"
a[10000] = 1; // length becomes 10001
```

concepts.statement: `length` is always **one more than the highest index present** (for dense arrays, simply the element count). It is writable in both directions: a **smaller** value instantly **truncates** the array, discarding the tail; a larger value grows the array with holes and loses nothing.
concepts.detail:
```
let a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
a.length = 3;    // a is [1, 2, 3] — 4 and 5 are gone
a.length = 5;    // [1, 2, 3, , , ] — holes where 4, 5 were
a[a.length] = 6; // append — the idiomatic pre-push form
```
Truncation via `length` is destructive and permanent: there is no undo for the discarded elements.

examples.title: Trace the engine: four creation routes, one resulting array
examples.problem: Produce the array `[1, 2, 3]` each of the four ways, and state what each route is uniquely good at.

steps.label: Step 1: Literal
steps.text:
```
let a1 = [1, 2, 3];
```
Best when you can see the elements in the source — a fresh array per evaluation.

steps.label: Step 2: Spread of another array
Step 3: Array.of
steps.text:
```
let a3 = Array.of(1, 2, 3);
```
Best when the elements arrive as an argument list — and the only safe choice when a single number might be the sole element, where `new Array(3)` would build three holes.

steps.label: Step 4: Array.from with a map function
steps.text:
```
let a4 = Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i + 1);
```
Best for generated and transformed arrays — the second argument transforms during the copy, so `a4` is `[1, 2, 3]` without a separate `.map` pass.

steps.label: Step 5: The common guarantee
steps.text: All four produce genuine arrays: `Array.isArray` is `true` for each, each has the full method set of Section 7.4, and each starts dense (no holes).

examples.result: Four routes to `[1, 2, 3]`: write it down, spread an existing one, list it with `Array.of`, or generate it with `Array.from` — the choice is about where the elements come from.

examples.title: Trace the engine: Array.from with a mapping function
examples.problem: Trace `Array.from({ length: 4 }, (_, i) => i * i)` element by element, then the string-mapping form `Array.from("cat", c => c.toUpperCase())`.

steps.label: Step 1: The array-like first argument
steps.text: `{ length: 4 }` is not an array — it is an **array-like** object with a length and no elements (reads yield `undefined`). `Array.from` treats it as four slots.

steps.label: Step 2: The callback runs per slot
steps.text: Slot 0: the element is `undefined`, the index is `0`, so `(_, 0) => 0 * 0` produces `0`. Slot 1: `1 * 1` = `1`. Slot 2: `2 * 2` = `4`. Slot 3: `3 * 3` = `9`.

steps.label: Step 3: The result
steps.text: `[0, 1, 4, 9]` — a generated array, built and transformed in a single pass. The conventional `_` names the ignored element argument.

steps.label: Step 4: The string form
steps.text: `"cat"` is iterable, so `Array.from("cat", c => c.toUpperCase())` iterates its three characters — `"c"`, `"a"`, `"t"` — mapping each to its uppercase form: `["C", "A", "T"]`.

steps.label: Step 5: Why not copy then map
steps.text: `Array.from(x).map(f)` gives the same answer in two passes; the map-function argument is the built-in single-pass version — the pattern `map` and `flatMap` make idiomatic in Section 7.4.

examples.result: `[0, 1, 4, 9]` and `["C", "A", "T"]` — Array.from turns array-likes, iterables and strings into real arrays, transforming along the way.

examples.title: Trace the engine: length obeys the highest index
examples.problem: Starting from `let a = [];` trace `a[5] = true`, then `a.length = 2`, then `a[1] = 7`, then `a[a.length] = 9`, and report the array and its length after each step.

steps.label: Step 1: The far write
steps.text: `a[5] = true` sets index 5; `length` jumps from 0 to **6** — one more than the highest index. Indices 0 through 4 do not exist (holes), which Section 7.2 examines closely.

steps.label: Step 2: The truncating write
steps.text: `a.length = 2` shrinks the array: index 5 (and 2 through 4) are discarded. The array is now length 2 with both slots holes — `1 in a` is still false, and `a[5]` now reads `undefined` because it is out of bounds.

steps.label: Step 3: Refill
steps.text: `a[1] = 7` fills the second slot: length stays 2 (index 1 < length), and now `a` is `[hole, 7]` — `a[0]` still undefined-by-absence and `a[1]` equal to 7.

steps.label: Step 4: The append idiom
steps.text: `a[a.length] = 9` writes index 2, the first position past the end — length becomes 3. This grows-by-one is exactly what `push` does for you (Section 7.3).

steps.label: Step 5: The rule check
steps.text: After every step, length was exactly one more than the highest present index — the invariant the engine maintains for you and that a manual `length` write can bend or snap.

examples.result: After the sequence: `a[5] = true` gives length 6; truncation to 2 discards indices 2 through 5; `a[1] = 7` fills in place; `a[a.length] = 9` appends — length tracks the top index plus one at every moment.

keyTakeaways: An array is a specialized object whose indices are string keys plus the special `length` property.
Four creation routes: literal, spread `[...a]`, `Array.of(...)` (fixes the `new Array(3)` hole trap), `Array.from(x, mapFn)` for array-likes and iterables.
Out-of-bounds reads return `undefined`; writes to valid indices always succeed and may grow the array.
`length` is one more than the highest index; writing a smaller value truncates permanently, writing a larger one creates holes.
Spread copies elements into a new array — shallowly, like every copy in this language.
`a[a.length] = x` appends by hand; `Array.from` with a map function builds generated arrays in one pass.

quiz.q: What is the result of `Array.of(3)` versus `new Array(3)`?
options: [3] versus an empty array of length 3
quiz.explanation: Array.of treats its arguments as elements; the Array constructor treats a single number as a length, producing three holes and no elements.

quiz.q: After `let a = [1, 2, 3]; a[10] = 4;` what is `a.length`?
quiz.explanation: The highest index is now 10, and length is defined as one more than the highest index — indices 3 through 9 become holes.

quiz.q: The expression `a["2"]` where `a = [10, 20, 30]` evaluates to:
options: undefined, because the key is a string
30, because the key is the same string the array stores for index 2
quiz.explanation: Bracket notation converts its expression to a string key, and the key stored for the third element is the string "2" — so the lookup succeeds.

quiz.q: Setting `a.length = 0` on a dense array of five elements:
options: leaves the elements accessible but reports length 0
removes every element — the array is empty
quiz.explanation: Writing a smaller length truncates the array permanently: every element at or beyond the new length is discarded, making length 0 the classic clear-the-array move.

intro: Most JavaScript arrays are **dense** — every index from 0 to length − 1 holds a real element. But nothing enforces that: `delete`, sparse literals, a growing `length`, or `new Array(n)` all create **holes** — missing indices that read as `undefined` yet are not elements at all. This section makes the hole/`undefined` distinction precise and traces the differences through existence tests, iteration and JSON.
objectives: Define sparse arrays and list the four ways holes are created
Distinguish a hole from an element whose value is undefined
Trace how forEach and for/of treat holes differently
Explain why dense arrays are the recommended default

concepts.statement: An array is **sparse** when some indices in its range hold no element — a **hole**. Then `length` overstates the element count: an array can have length 100 and contain three elements. Sparse arrays arise from deleting elements, skipping in a literal, growing `length`, or creating with `new Array(n)`.
concepts.detail:
```
let a = new Array(5); // length 5, five holes
let b = [1, , 3];     // hole at index 1
let c = [1, 2, 3];
delete c[1];          // hole at index 1
let d = [];
d.length = 3;         // three holes
```

concepts.statement: `[1, undefined, 3]` and `[1, , 3]` both read `a[1]` as `undefined` — but the first **has** an element at index 1 (the value happens to be undefined) while the second **does not**. The existence test `1 in a` is the discriminator: `true` for the dense array, `false` for the sparse one.
concepts.detail:
```
let dense = [1, undefined, 3];
let sparse = [1, , 3];
dense[1]     // undefined
sparse[1]    // undefined — same read
1 in dense   // true — an element exists
1 in sparse  // false — a hole, not an element
```

concepts.statement: The array **methods** (`forEach`, `map`’s callback, `filter`, `reduce` — every callback-driven method) **skip holes entirely**: the callback is never invoked for them. The `for/of` loop, driven by the array iterator instead, **yields `undefined` for each hole** — one value per index.
concepts.detail:
```
let sparse = [1, , 3];
sparse.forEach(v => console.log(v)); // logs 1, then 3 — no call for the hole
for (let v of sparse) console.log(v); // logs 1, undefined, 3 — one per index
```
`map` preserves hole positions in its output without calling the callback there; `filter` simply drops them.

concepts.statement: The JSON serializer converts every hole to `null` in arrays — and so does an `undefined` element. Round-tripping a sparse array through JSON therefore **densifies** it: the holes come back as explicit `null` values.
concepts.detail:
```
JSON.stringify([1, , 3])         // '[1,null,3]'
JSON.stringify([1, undefined, 3]) // '[1,null,3]' — identical text
```
Existence and position survive; the hole/undefined distinction does not — one more reason not to rely on it.

concepts.statement: The book’s advice is blunt: sparse arrays are legal, quirky and best avoided. When you need an empty slot, storing `undefined` or `null` explicitly keeps every test, loop and serialization consistent — and engines store and optimize dense layouts far better.
concepts.detail: The historical use for sparse arrays — a lookup keyed by huge numbers with mostly-missing entries — is properly served by a `Map` (Chapter 11), which does not pretend the keys between stored ones exist.

concepts.statement: Two `length` operations bookend the section: writing a **smaller** length truncates (elements are gone, no holes created), and writing a **larger** one creates trailing holes. `a.length = 0` empties an array completely — the fastest clear there is.
concepts.detail:
```
let a = [1, 2, 3];
a.length = 1; // [1] — 2 and 3 truncated away
a.length = 4; // [1, , , ] — holes after index 0
```

examples.title: The worked diff: hole versus undefined element
examples.problem: Given `let sparse = [1, , 3];` and `let dense = [1, undefined, 3];` run the read test, the existence test, `Object.keys`, `forEach` and `JSON.stringify` on both and account for every difference.

steps.label: Step 1: The read test agrees
steps.text: `sparse[1]` is `undefined` and `dense[1]` is `undefined` — from the reading side the two arrays are indistinguishable.

steps.label: Step 2: The existence test disagrees
steps.text: `1 in sparse` → `false` (no element). `1 in dense` → `true` (an element whose value is undefined). This is the definitive probe.

steps.label: Step 3: Object.keys agrees with existence
steps.text: `Object.keys(sparse)` → `["0", "2"]`; `Object.keys(dense)` → `["0", "1", "2"]` — the hole contributes no key, the undefined element does.

steps.label: Step 4: forEach disagrees
steps.text: `sparse.forEach(cb)` invokes the callback twice (values 1 and 3); `dense.forEach(cb)` invokes it three times (values 1, undefined and 3). The loop bodies you write really can observe the difference.

steps.label: Step 5: JSON erases the difference
steps.text: Both serialize to `'[1,null,3]'` — holes and undefined elements both become `null`, so after a round trip through `JSON.parse` you hold a dense array with a `null` element in both cases.

examples.result: Same reads, different existence (`in`, keys, forEach) — and JSON papers over the whole distinction with `null`.

examples.title: Trace the engine: delete makes a hole, splice does not
examples.problem: Starting from `let a = ["a", "b", "c", "d"];` compare `delete a[1]` with `splice(1, 1)` on a fresh copy — array, length and `1 in a` after each.

steps.label: Step 1: The delete
steps.text: `delete a[1]` removes the property `"1"` from the array object. The result is `["a", , "c", "d"]`: `length` is still 4 and `a[1]` reads `undefined` because nothing is there.

steps.label: Step 2: The hole’s ripple
steps.text: `1 in a` → false; a `forEach` over `a` now processes only `"a"`, `"c"`, `"d"`; iterating with `for/of` yields `"a"`, `undefined`, `"c"`, `"d"`.

steps.label: Step 3: The splice on a fresh copy
Step 4: Why splice is the array way
steps.text: `delete` is an object operation that happens to work on arrays, leaving a hole; `splice` is the array operation that renumbers the elements after the cut — Section 7.3 dissects it fully.

examples.result: delete leaves length 4 with a hole; splice leaves length 3, dense and renumbered — for removing elements, splice (or filter for copies) is the tool.

keyTakeaways: A sparse array has holes: indices within its length that hold no element.
Holes are created by `delete`, by missing values in a literal, by a larger `length` write, and by `new Array(n)`.
A hole and an undefined element read identically; `i in a` and `Object.keys` distinguish them.
Callback methods skip holes; `for/of` yields undefined for them; JSON writes null for both.
Prefer dense arrays — store explicit `undefined` or `null`, or use a `Map` for genuinely sparse numeric keys.
`splice` removes elements and renumbers; `delete` removes a key and leaves a hole.

quiz.q: Given `let a = [1, , 3];` which expression is false?
quiz.explanation: The middle slot is a hole: it reads as undefined, but no element exists there, so the in-operator returns false.

quiz.q: A forEach callback passed over `[10, , 30]` is invoked:
options: twice — once for 10 and once for 30
once — forEach stops at the hole
quiz.explanation: The array methods skip holes entirely: the callback sees the elements that exist, never learning the hole was there.

quiz.q: The best way to remove the element at index 2 of a five-element array and keep the array dense is:
quiz.explanation: splice removes the element and shifts the tail down, keeping every remaining index occupied; delete leaves a hole and assignment leaves a dead value, and truncating the length would discard elements 3 and 4.

quiz.q: After `let a = [1, 2, 3]; a.length = 5;` the array is:
options: of length 5 with holes at indices 3 and 4
of length 5 with undefined elements at 3 and 4
quiz.explanation: Growing length adds nothing — it creates holes; a[3] and a[4] read undefined but fail the in-test, unlike explicit undefined elements.

intro: Arrays are built to change at the ends and in the middle: `push`/`pop` work the back, `shift`/`unshift` work the front, and `splice` does anything anywhere — insert, delete or replace. For walking the result there are three idioms — `for/of`, `forEach` and the classic `for` — each with a precise reason to be chosen. This section works the full toolkit with the loop-unrolling traces.
objectives: Implement stack and queue behavior with push/pop and push/shift
Predict every splice argument’s effect: start, deleteCount and inserted items
Choose between for/of, forEach and the classic for loop
Explain why delete is the wrong removal tool and splice is the right one

concepts.statement: **`push(...values)`** appends one or more values at the **end** of the array and returns the new length; **`pop()`** removes and returns the **last** element (`undefined` on an empty array). Both mutate the array. Together they are the **stack** (LIFO: last in, first out).
concepts.detail:
```
let stack = [];
stack.push(1, 2); // returns 2 — new length
stack.pop();      // returns 2 — the last value pushed
```

concepts.statement: **`unshift(...values)`** prepends values at the **front** (returning the new length); **`shift()`** removes and returns the **first** element.
