options: they copy each value at definition time
they hold references to the bindings, so later mutations are visible through them
variables cannot be captured at all
values are copied at invocation time
quiz.explanation: The capture is of the binding itself — which is exactly why counter’s count and reset share one n, and why the loop pitfall produces shared final values.

options: Nothing, because the callbacks never run
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The code given registers three timer callbacks inside a `var` loop and finishes the loop first. Step 2: The governing rules are that `var` creates one function-scoped binding shared by all iterations, that each arrow function closes over that single binding rather than over a snapshot value, and that timers run only after the synchronous loop completes. Step 3: Tracing phase by phase, the loop advances the shared `i` from 0 to 3 while queueing three callbacks, then each callback reads the same binding, now holding `3`, so all three print `3`. Step 4: The distractors fail because per-iteration values would need the block-scoped `let` form, and queued timers do run once the call stack clears. Step 5: Therefore the output is `3` three times.

intro: Functions are objects, so they have properties (`name`, `length`, `prototype`) and methods (`call`, `apply`, `bind`, `toString`) and even a constructor — the `Function()` constructor that compiles a function from strings and that you should almost never use. This section works the properties and the invocation-choosing trio, with `bind` doing double duty as the partial-application engine.
objectives: Read the name and length properties and their rules
Invoke with an explicit receiver via call and apply
Build bound and partially applied functions with bind
Explain why the Function() constructor is avoided
Borrow methods from unrelated objects

concepts.statement: **`f.length`** is the function’s **arity**: the number of parameters declared **before the first default value or rest parameter** — the count of arguments the function *requires*. It powers arity dispatch checks and API introspection; it does not include optional or collected parameters.

**`f.name`** is the function’s name string, used in stack traces and debuggers. It is usually the declared name — but the specification also **infers** names for anonymous assignments: `let square = function () {};` yields the name `"square"`, and the same inference applies to arrow functions bound to variables and to object shorthand methods.

Every non-arrow function has a **`prototype`** property: an object whose purpose is to become the prototype of instances created when the function runs as a **constructor** with `new`. This single property links Chapter 8 to Chapter 9 — classes are constructor functions whose methods live on `this.prototype`.

**`f.call(receiver, ...args)`** invokes `f` with `this` set to `receiver` and the listed arguments; **`f.apply(receiver, argsArray)`** does the same with the arguments supplied as an array. Historically `apply` was how a variadic array of arguments reached a fixed-arity function — since ES6, **spread at the call site** (`f.call(o, ...args)`, or just `f(...args)`) has erased most of that need.
concepts.detail:
```
function greet(name) { return `${this.honorific} ${name}`; }
let knight = { honorific: "Ser" };
greet.call(knight, "Gregor");     // "Ser Gregor"
greet.apply(knight, ["Gregor"]); // "Ser Gregor"
```
A classic use: `Object.prototype.toString.call([])` → `"[object Array]"` — borrowing the type-revealing toString from the root prototype (Section 9.4 leans on the same idea).

concepts.statement: **`f.bind(receiver, ...preset)`** returns a **new function** that, when called, runs `f` with `this` fixed to `receiver` and the `preset` arguments placed **before** whatever arguments the new call supplies — **partial application**. The binding is permanent: a later `call`, `apply` or even `bind` cannot retarget `this`.
concepts.detail:
```
function f(y, z) { return this.x + y + z; }
let g = f.bind({ x: 1 });
let h = g.bind({ x: 2 }); // this cannot be re-bound
g(2, 3); // 6
h(2, 3); // 6 — still x: 1
let p = f.bind({ x: 1 }, 2); // y is pre-filled
p(3);    // 6
```
`bind` is the standard cure for the detached-method bug of Section 8.2 — the receiver travels with the function forever.

concepts.statement: **`new Function(args..., body)`** builds a function at run time from **string** arguments (`new Function("x", "y", "return x + y")`). Two reasons to avoid it: the compiled function runs in **global scope only** — it closes over nothing, so it cannot see your local variables (even though it is literally created inside your code) — and building code from strings is a standing invitation for injection and the death of tooling.

**`f.toString()`** returns the function’s source text (implementation-defined in format but required to be a valid function definition). Useful for logging and inspection — and for metaprogramming trickery (Chapter 14 uses it in memoization caches keyed by function identity in some libraries).
concepts.detail:
```
(() => 1).toString(); // "() => 1"
```
Built-ins may return a placeholder like `"function toString() { [native code] }"` — the native-code marker.

examples.title: Trace the engine: bind — receiver first, then arguments
examples.problem: Given `function f(y, z) { return this.x + y + z; }` trace `f.bind({x: 1})`, a second bind on the result, and `f.bind({x: 1}, 2)` — every call and every value.

steps.label: Step 1: The base function
steps.text: `f` reads `this.x` and two parameters. Called bare it is a function-form invocation (Section 8.2) — undefined receiver, and `this.x` throws in strict mode. Everything below fixes that by construction.

steps.label: Step 3: The unbreakable binding
steps.text:
```
let h = g.bind({ x: 2 });
h(2, 3); // 6 — NOT 7
```
`this` was already bound when `g` was created; a second `bind` (or a `call`) cannot overwrite it. Only the **first** receiver sticks — `h` still sees `x: 1`.

steps.label: Step 4: Partial application
steps.text:
```
let p = f.bind({ x: 1 }, 2);
p(3); // 6
```
Now `y` is pre-filled with 2: the new call needs only the remaining argument, which arrives as `z` = 3 → `1 + 2 + 3` = 6. Preset arguments queue ahead of call-time arguments, however many of each.

steps.label: Step 5: Where the pattern pays
steps.text: Partial application is how a general function becomes a specialized one: from `pow(base, exp)` you can pre-bake `square = pow.bind(null, 2)`-style helpers (with `this` irrelevant here) — the functional toolkit of Section 8.7 is built on exactly such transformations.

examples.result: 6, 6 (the second bind could not retarget this), and 6 via the partially applied `p` — bind fixes the receiver first and presets arguments ahead of the caller’s.

examples.title: Trace the engine: borrowing a method with call
examples.problem: Use `Object.prototype.toString.call` to reveal the real class of an array and of `null`, and explain why `call` is needed rather than a plain method call.

steps.label: Step 1: The wrong tool fails quietly
steps.text: `[1, 2].toString()` → `"1,2"` — arrays override `toString` with a join, so the generic type-tagging version on `Object.prototype` never runs. The override hides exactly the information we want.

steps.label: Step 2: Call it directly
steps.text:
```
Object.prototype.toString.call([1, 2]); // "[object Array]"
Object.prototype.toString.call(null);    // "[object Null]"
Object.prototype.toString.call(/x/);     // "[object RegExp]"
```
The receiver we want is the array — but we want to run the *base* method, not the override. `call` executes `Object.prototype`’s function with `this` bound to our value, sidestepping the override entirely.

steps.label: Step 3: Why this works
steps.text: `Object.prototype.toString` reads `this`’s internal class tag and builds the `"[object X]"` string. Method-form invocation on the array would dispatch to `Array.prototype.toString`; `call` chooses **which function object** runs, and separately **what receiver** it sees — two decisions the dot notation bundles into one.

steps.label: Step 4: apply, the array form
steps.text: `f.apply(o, [1, 2])` ≡ `f.call(o, 1, 2)`: with arguments already in an array (say, accumulated in a loop), `apply` delivers them in one piece. Since spread, `f.call(o, ...args)` reads the same and needs no separate form.

steps.label: Step 5: The idiom in the wild
steps.text: Borrowing shows up everywhere: `Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments)` (the old array-like converter), `Math.max.apply(null, values)` before spread (`Math.max(...values)` now) — the general shape is "run function F with receiver R and args A", which is precisely rows of the Section 8.2 table.

examples.result: `"[object Array]"` and `"[object Null]"` — `call` decouples which function runs from who receives it, letting you borrow base implementations over derived overrides.

examples.title: Trace the engine: introspecting name and length
examples.problem: Predict `f.length`, `g.name`, `h.length` and `k.name` for the four definitions below, and one call through the `Function()` constructor to show what it cannot see.

steps.label: Step 1: The definitions
Step 2: f.length — the arity rule
steps.text: `f` declares three parameters, but `length` counts only those **before** the first default or rest: `f.length` is 1. The signature’s required-argument count is the number that matters to callers.

steps.label: Step 3: g.name and h — inference
steps.text: `g.name` is `"g"` — the anonymous function expression picked up the variable name. `h.length` is 2 (two plain parameters) and `h.name` is `"h"` — the same inference for arrows.

steps.label: Step 4: k — the bound twin
steps.text: `k.name` is `"bound f"` — bound functions advertise their origin — and `k.length` is 0 or less the preset count (binding no arguments here, it still reflects `f`’s 1). The metadata chain survives the transformation.

steps.label: Step 5: The constructor that sees nothing

examples.result: `f.length` 1; `g.name` "g"; `h.length` 2; `k.name` "bound f" — and the `Function()` constructor throws the ReferenceError that proves it runs scope-blind.

keyTakeaways: `f.length` counts parameters before the first default or rest — the required-argument count.
`f.name` is the declared name, or inferred from the binding for anonymous functions and arrows.
Every non-arrow function has a `prototype` property used by `new` — the bridge into Chapter 9.
`call(receiver, ...args)` and `apply(receiver, array)` invoke with an explicit receiver; spread has absorbed most of apply’s old job.
`bind(receiver, ...preset)` returns a permanently bound, partially applied function — and cannot be re-bound.
Avoid `new Function(...)`: global scope only (no closures), string-based code, injection risk.
`toString()` on a function returns (approximate) source text; built-ins show a native-code placeholder.

quiz.q: For `function f(a, b = 1, ...rest) {}` what is `f.length`?
quiz.explanation: Arity counts only the parameters before the first default value or rest parameter — here just a.

quiz.q: `let p = f.bind(obj, 1);` — calling `p(2, 3)` invokes `f` as:
options: f(1, 2, 3) with this = obj — preset arguments come first
quiz.explanation: bind presets arguments ahead of the call-time ones and fixes the receiver: the invocation becomes f with this = obj and arguments 1, 2, 3.

quiz.q: Which statement about `g = f.bind(obj)` is true?
options: this in g is permanently obj — further bind or call cannot change it
g is the same function object as f
quiz.explanation: The receiver is baked in at bind time; the first binding wins over every later attempt to retarget, which is exactly why bind fixes the detached-method bug.

quiz.q: The `Function()` constructor is discouraged chiefly because its products:
options: run in global scope with no closure over local variables, and are built from strings
quiz.explanation: A Function-constructed function closes over nothing but global scope — invisible to your locals — and string-assembled code defeats tools and invites injection.

intro: Treating functions as the primary unit of composition changes how you process data: instead of loops that mutate accumulators, you build **pipelines** — `map` to transform, `filter` to select, `reduce` to collapse — over arrays of records. This section works the book’s canonical data analysis (mean and standard deviation), pure functions and why they are worth writing, and composition as the assembly language of pipelines.
objectives: Process arrays declaratively with forEach, map, filter and reduce
Compute statistics with a reduce/map pipeline, step by step
Define pure functions and state their practical advantages
Compose functions into new functions and understand data flow direction
Recognize when the functional style is a poor fit

concepts.statement: The chapter’s array-processing trio, in pipeline order: **`forEach`** runs a function for side effects over each element; **`map`** transforms elements into a new array; **`filter`** selects a subarray; **`reduce`** collapses to a single value. Each takes a function and applies it — the data stays passive, the *behavior* is the argument.
concepts.detail:
```
let data = [1, -2, 3, -4, 5];
data.forEach(x => console.log(x));       // side effects
data.filter(x => x > 0);                 // [1, 3, 5]
data.map(x => x * x);                    // [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
data.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);         // 3
```
The full method catalog, worked example by worked example, is Section 7.4 — this section is about the *style* those methods enable.

concepts.statement: A **pure function** has no side effects and depends on nothing but its arguments: same inputs, same output, every time — `x => x * x` is pure; anything that logs, mutates outside state, reads the clock or network, or throws nondeterministically is not. Purity is what makes a function testable, cacheable (Section 8.5’s memoize), safely reorderable and trivially parallelizable.
concepts.detail:
```
const pureArea = r => Math.PI * r * r;      // same r, same answer
let calls = 0;
const loudArea = r => { calls++; return pureArea(r); }; // impure
```
`Math.random()` and `Date.now()` are pure *impurity* — the standard library’s own reminder that not everything can be a pure function.

concepts.statement: Beyond sums, `reduce` expresses any "array in, one value out" computation: maxima, averages, flattening, grouping into a Map, reversing (with `unshift`), building trees. The two things to decide are the **initial accumulator** (whose type is the result type) and the **combining step** — everything else is bookkeeping the method does for you.

**Composition** builds a new function from two: `(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x))`, or in code `const compose = (f, g) => (x) => f(g(x))`. Composed pipelines read **right to left** (innermost first); many codebases define the flipped `pipe = (f, g) => (x) => g(f(x))` so the stages read in execution order. Either way, composition is function-as-value doing its most structured work.

Real functional style in this book runs over **arrays of records**: filter to a subset, map to a projection, reduce to an aggregate — each stage a pure function, the original data untouched, each intermediate array inspectable in a debugger or test.
concepts.detail:
```
let records = [
  { name: "a", value: 1 },
  { name: "b", value: 2 },
  { name: "c", value: 3 }
];
records.filter(r => r.value > 1)
       .map(r => r.value * 10)
       .reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // 50
```
Compare with the same computation as one loop: identical result, but the pipeline names its stages, and each stage is reusable and testable in isolation.

concepts.statement: The style has costs: every `map`/`filter` stage allocates an intermediate array (hot inner loops may want the single classic `for`), and deeply chained pipelines can obscure as easily as they clarify. The book’s own advice is pragmatic — use the functional forms wherever clarity wins, drop to a loop when profiling or plain readability says otherwise.
concepts.detail: One rule keeps you out of most trouble: keep the **stages** pure even when the program is not — a pipeline whose links are pure functions can be reordered, cached and tested; one that mutates shared state mid-chain has none of those properties.

examples.title: Trace the engine: mean and standard deviation as a pipeline
examples.problem: Given `data = [1, 1, 3, 5, 5]`, compute the mean and the sample standard deviation entirely with `reduce` and `map` — and lay out every intermediate array.

steps.label: Step 1: The sum and the mean
steps.text:
```
let data = [1, 1, 3, 5, 5];
let sum = (x, y) => x + y;
let total = data.reduce(sum);  // 15 — first element seeds, fold the rest
let mean = total / data.length; // 3
```
`reduce(sum)` folds 1+1+3+5+5 = 15; dividing by the count of 5 gives the mean 3.

steps.label: Step 2: The deviations
steps.text:
```
let deviations = data.map(x => x - mean); // [-2, -2, 0, 2, 2]
```
`map` produces one new array — same length, each element the distance from the mean. The original `data` is untouched throughout this example.

steps.label: Step 3: Squares and variance
steps.text:
```
let squares = deviations.map(x => x * x); // [4, 4, 0, 4, 4]
let variance = squares.reduce(sum) / (data.length - 1); // 16 / 4 = 4
```
Note the classic statistics detail: the sample variance divides by n − 1, not n — the pipeline encodes the formula, so the formula’s details are on display.

steps.label: Step 4: The standard deviation
steps.text:
```
let stddev = Math.sqrt(variance); // 2
```
For this textbook data the answer is exactly 2 — a tidy check that the whole pipeline ran correctly.

steps.label: Step 5: One expression, all stages

examples.result: total 15 → mean 3 → deviations [-2,-2,0,2,2] → squares [4,4,0,4,4] → variance 4 → **stddev = 2**, with no loop counters and no mutated inputs.

examples.title: Trace the engine: composition, right to left
examples.problem: Build `halfOfSquare = compose(halve, square)` and `squareOfHalf = compose(square, halve)`, call both on 6, and show exactly which stage runs first.

steps.label: Step 1: The combinator
steps.text:
```
const compose = (f, g) => (x) => f(g(x));
```
`compose` is a higher-order function returning a closure over its two function arguments — Section 8.4’s "functions as return values" doing structural work.

steps.label: Step 2: The stages
Step 3: halfOfSquare(6)
steps.text: `compose(halve, square)` — the returned function computes `halve(square(6))`: the **rightmost** stage runs first. `square(6)` = 36, then `halve(36)` = 18.

steps.label: Step 4: squareOfHalf(6)
steps.text: `compose(square, halve)` computes `square(halve(6))`: `halve(6)` = 3, then `square(3)` = 9. Same two functions, same input, different assembly order — 18 versus 9, entirely from the argument order.

steps.label: Step 5: Reading direction and pipes
steps.text: Because composition applies right-to-left, pipeline-style codebases often flip it: `const pipe = (f, g) => (x) => g(f(x));` then `pipe(square, halve)(6)` = 18 reads "square, then halve" — execution order on the page. Both are the same idea: naming the **assembly** of functions separately from the functions themselves.

examples.result: `halfOfSquare(6)` = 18 (square first), `squareOfHalf(6)` = 9 (halve first) — the argument order of compose is the execution order, read right to left (or left to right with a pipe).

examples.title: Trace the engine: pure versus impure under memoize
examples.problem: Wrap a pure and an impure area function in the Section 8.5 `memoize` and show which one memoizes correctly — and exactly what the impure one loses.

steps.label: Step 1: The two candidates
Step 2: Memoize the pure one
steps.text:
```
const mArea = memoize(pureArea);
mArea(2); // computes, caches "[2]"
mArea(2); // cache hit — same value, instantly
```
Both calls return the identical number, and nothing in the world changed between them — the cache is invisible, exactly as intended.

steps.label: Step 3: Memoize the impure one
steps.text:
```
const mLoud = memoize(loudArea);
mLoud(2); // calls becomes 1
mLoud(2); // cache hit — calls stays 1!
```
The second call never reaches `loudArea`, so the counter does not advance: memoization silently **deleted the side effect**. The returned number is right; the world is wrong.

steps.label: Step 4: The boundary
steps.text: The failure generalizes: any result that depends on global state, randomness, the clock or mutable inputs becomes stale or skipped when cached. Purity is not aesthetic — it is the precondition for every "same input, same behavior" optimization (memoize, React render caching, test doubles).

steps.label: Step 5: The pragmatic split
steps.text: Real programs are impure at the edges (I/O, UI, network) and pure in the middle (transforms, selections, folds). Push the pure core outward and the functional toolkit of this section applies to everything it touches.

examples.result: The pure memoizes perfectly; the impure one loses its side effect on the second call — `calls` counts 1 instead of 2 — because memoize assumes what purity promises.

keyTakeaways: The pipeline toolkit: `forEach` for side effects, `map` to transform, `filter` to select, `reduce` to collapse.
Pure functions (same inputs → same outputs, no side effects) are testable, reorderable and cacheable.
`reduce` generalizes to any array-to-value computation — the accumulator type is the result type.
Composition `(f, g) => x => f(g(x))` assembles new functions; arguments read right to left (pipes read left to right).
Statistics pipelines make formulas inspectable: mean 3, deviations, squares, variance 4, stddev 2 on the book’s data.
Keep stages pure even when the program is not — and drop to a loop when allocation or clarity demands it.

quiz.q: For `data = [1, 1, 3, 5, 5]`, the pipeline `data.map(x => x - 3).map(x => x * x).reduce((a, b) => a + b)` yields:
quiz.explanation: Deviations are [-2,-2,0,2,2]; squares are [4,4,0,4,4]; their sum is 16 — the numerator of the sample variance computed in two maps and a reduce.

quiz.q: `compose(halve, square)(6)` evaluates to:
quiz.explanation: compose applies its arguments right to left: square(6) = 36, then halve(36) = 18.

quiz.q: A pure function is one that:
options: returns the same output for the same inputs and causes no side effects
quiz.explanation: Purity is determinism plus side-effect freedom — the two properties that make testing, reordering and memoization safe.

quiz.q: Why does memoizing an impure function change program behavior?
options: the cache converts functions to strings
cache hits skip the call — and with it any side effect the function would have performed
quiz.explanation: A memoized wrapper returns the stored result without invoking the wrapped function, so logging, counters or state changes that would have run are silently skipped on hits.

intro: Long before ES6 introduced the `class` keyword, JavaScript had classes — assembled from two ordinary ingredients: a function that **initializes** each new object, and a **prototype** object whose properties every instance shares. The `class` keyword of Section 9.3 is pure shorthand for this machinery, so understanding it by hand is not history: it is the mental model that makes `instanceof`, `extends` and every "method not found" question decidable. The core mechanism is **delegation** — a property read that misses an object continues along its prototype link.
objectives: Define a class the pre-ES6 way: a factory function plus a shared prototype object
Trace a property lookup across a multi-link prototype chain to its end
Explain why a failed read yields undefined instead of an error
Distinguish own properties from inherited ones with Object.hasOwn
Predict what assignment does when a property exists only on the prototype

concepts.term: A class is a factory plus a prototype
concepts.statement: A JavaScript **class** is a set of objects that share behavior by delegating to one common **prototype object**. The class exists because every instance points at that one object — nothing in the language marks it as special. The pre-`class` recipe: a factory function creates and initializes each instance, and the prototype object holds the methods.

Every object carries one internal **prototype link** (`[[Prototype]]`, readable as `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`) to another object or to `null`. Reading `obj.x` looks at `obj` first; on a miss, the lookup **continues at the prototype**, then the prototype’s prototype, and so on — returning the first hit found.
concepts.detail: The link is read with `Object.getPrototypeOf(r)`; the historical `r.__proto__` accessor is standardized but the method forms (`Object.getPrototypeOf`, `Object.create`) are the clean interface. Section 6.1 introduced this for plain objects — a class is the same single link, used systematically: instances hold data, the prototype holds behavior.

concepts.statement: For ordinary objects the chain is `obj` → `Object.prototype` → `null`. `Object.prototype` supplies `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf` and friends to every object in the language, and **its** prototype is `null` — the sentinel that stops the walk. A read that falls off the end is therefore not an error: `r.nonesuch` evaluates to `undefined`.
concepts.detail: Walking the chain one link at a time is a **linear search** — long chains cost a little on every miss, which is why classes keep their chains short. `Object.create(null)` produces a prototype-less object with no inherited methods at all, occasionally used for bare lookup tables (though Section 11.1’s `Map` is the modern answer).

concepts.term: Reads walk the chain; writes never do
concepts.statement: Assignment `r.x = 99` does **not** search the chain. If `x` is not an own property, it is created **on the object itself** — the prototype is never touched — and the new property **shadows** any same-named property further up. (The one exception: a setter along the chain intercepts the write, Section 9.3.)
concepts.detail: This asymmetry is what makes shared behavior safe to share: one range writing `r.name = "renamed"` can never clobber a `name` property for the other instances, because the write never climbs.

concepts.statement: A property stored directly on the object is **own**; anything found along the chain is **inherited**. `Object.hasOwn(r, "from")` is true for the factory-built range while `Object.hasOwn(r, "includes")` is false — the method lives on `range.methods`, and `r` merely reaches it through the link.
concepts.detail: for/in (Section 5.3) enumerates own enumerable properties **and** inherited ones — which is exactly why careless additions to shared prototypes leak into every loop, the hazard Section 9.4 documents.

examples.title: Trace the engine: one lookup, three links
examples.problem:
Given the `range` factory above, trace each expression to its verdict:
```js
const r = range(1, 3);

r.from;                      // ?
r.includes(2);               // ?
r.hasOwnProperty("from");    // ?
r.nonesuch;                  // ?

r.nonesuch = 99;
r.nonesuch;                  // ?
range.methods.nonesuch;      // ?
```

steps.label: Step 1: Own data hit at link zero
steps.text: The lookup for `r.from` never leaves the instance: the factory assigned `from` and `to` directly onto r, so they are own properties — `1` returns immediately.

steps.label: Step 2: Method hit at link one
steps.text: `r.includes` is not an own property, so the engine follows r’s `[[Prototype]]` link to `range.methods` — where `includes` lives. The function is retrieved and invoked with `this` bound to r, reading `this.from` and `this.to` back on the instance.

steps.label: Step 3: Hit at link two
steps.text: `r.hasOwnProperty` misses on r, misses on `range.methods`, and arrives at `Object.prototype` — the shared ancestor of (nearly) every object — where `hasOwnProperty` is defined. The chain so far: `r` → `range.methods` → `Object.prototype` → `null`.

steps.label: Step 4: The total miss
steps.text: `r.nonesuch` walks all three nodes, reaches `null`, and stops. A failed **read** is not an error: the expression evaluates to `undefined`. (Contrast a failed **call** — `r.nonesuch()` would throw a TypeError, because calling undefined does throw.)

steps.label: Step 5: The write never climbs
steps.text: `r.nonesuch = 99` creates a new own property on r. Proof: `range.methods.nonesuch` is still `undefined` afterward, and every other range built from the same prototype is untouched. The chain is a read path, not a write path.

examples.result: `r.from` → 1; `r.includes(2)` → true (method at link one); `r.hasOwnProperty("from")` → true (method at link two); `r.nonesuch` → undefined (fell off the chain at null); after assignment `r.nonesuch` → 99 as an own property while the prototype stays clean.

examples.title: Making the prototype-class iterable

steps.label: Step 1: Symbols as property names
steps.text: `Symbol.iterator` (Section 3.5) is the protocol key the language looks up — computed property names like `[Symbol.iterator]` attach methods without any chance of collision with ordinary string-keyed properties.

steps.label: Step 2: A generator as the method
steps.text: The `function*` form (Section 12.3) makes the method return an iterator directly — no separate iterator class needed. Because it sits on `range.methods`, every range — including ones created before this line ran — is iterable retroactively, the same live-prototype upgrade Section 9.4 formalizes.

steps.label: Step 3: Consumers are duck-typed
steps.text: The spread operator and `for/of` never ask what a range **is** — they only look up `Symbol.iterator` and call it. Delegation supplies the method; the protocol machinery does the rest, which is how a hand-built class slots into the language’s built-in syntax.

examples.result: `[...range(1, 4)]` → `[1, 2, 3, 4]`; the for/of loop logs 3, then 4, then 5 — a pre-class class fully participating in modern iteration.

keyTakeaways: A class is a factory (or constructor) plus a shared prototype object — instances hold data, the prototype holds behavior.
Property reads walk the prototype link on every miss: `obj` → prototype → prototype’s prototype → … → `null`.
The chain for ordinary objects ends `Object.prototype` → `null`; `Object.prototype` supplies `toString` and friends to everything.
A read that falls off the chain is `undefined`, not an error; only calling or otherwise operating on that undefined throws.
Assignment never walks the chain — it creates an own property that shadows any inherited one, leaving shared prototypes untouched.
`Object.hasOwn(obj, k)` separates own properties from inherited ones; for/in sees both, which is why prototype hygiene matters.

quiz.q: Reading `r.nonesuch` where `r` is a factory-built range and no property named nonesuch exists anywhere on its chain evaluates to:
options: undefined — the lookup walks to the end of the chain (null) and quietly fails
null — the value of the last prototype link
quiz.explanation: Failed property reads are not errors: the walk ends at null and the expression evaluates to undefined. Only calling the result (`r.nonesuch()`) throws.

quiz.q: For a plain object literal `{}`, what is the full prototype chain?
quiz.explanation: Object literals delegate to Object.prototype, whose own prototype is null — two links, and the reason every object has toString and hasOwnProperty.

quiz.q: A property `name` exists on an object’s prototype. Executing `obj.name = "new"` —
options: rewrites the property on the prototype for all instances
creates an own property on obj that shadows the inherited one
throws, because the property is inherited
deletes the prototype property and adds it to obj
quiz.explanation: Writes never climb the chain: a same-named own property is created on the object itself, and subsequent reads stop at the shadow before reaching the prototype.

quiz.q: For a range built by the `range` factory, `Object.hasOwn(r, "includes")` returns:
options: true — the instance can call the method
false — the method is inherited from range.methods, not stored on r
true only after includes has been called once
quiz.explanation: hasOwn tests for own properties only; includes resolves through the prototype link at call time but never lives on the instance.

intro: A **constructor function** is the classic way to mass-produce instances: write an ordinary function, invoke it with `new`, and the language performs four well-defined steps that manufacture the object, wire its prototype link and run the initializer. Those four steps explain everything downstream — why `instanceof` works, where the `constructor` property comes from, and the one famous way a constructor can betray its caller: by returning an object of its own.
objectives: Write a constructor function and invoke it with new
Recite and apply the four steps new performs, in order
Explain what instanceof tests and how it uses the prototype chain
Use isPrototypeOf for the object-side equivalent check
Predict the result when a constructor explicitly returns an object or a primitive

concepts.statement: A **constructor** is an ordinary function invoked with the `new` operator: it initializes a freshly manufactured object through `this`. The convention is a capitalized name. The pairing with `new` is what turns a function into a class factory.

Evaluating `new C(args)` performs, in order: **(1)** create a brand-new empty object; **(2)** set its prototype link to `C.prototype`; **(3)** call `C` with `this` bound to the new object; **(4)** return that object — **unless** the constructor explicitly returned a non-null object, which wins instead.

Every function automatically receives a `prototype` property when it is defined — an object whose single property, `constructor`, points back to the function. With `new`, that object becomes the prototype of the instances. **Mutating** it upgrades every instance; **replacing** it wholesale severs the `constructor` back-reference.
concepts.detail: After `Range.prototype = { includes…, toString… }`, an instance can no longer find `Range` via `r.constructor` — the lookup falls through the literal’s own prototype to `Object.prototype.constructor`, which is the `Object` function. Add `constructor: Range` into the replacement literal, or extend the existing prototype with `Object.assign` (Section 9.4), to keep the back-reference honest.

concepts.statement: `obj instanceof C` asks exactly one question: **does the object `C.prototype` appear anywhere on obj’s prototype chain?** It never looks at the function body, the name, or how the object was made — only the link.
concepts.detail:
```js
const r = new Range(1, 3);
r instanceof Range;              // true: chain is r → Range.prototype → …
r instanceof Object;              // true: Object.prototype is also on the chain
[] instanceof Range;               // false: Array.prototype chain never meets it
```
It answers "does this object delegate to that prototype", which makes it the standard runtime class test.

concepts.statement: The object-side converse of instanceof: `p.isPrototypeOf(obj)` asks whether **p** appears on obj’s prototype chain. `Range.prototype.isPrototypeOf(r)` and `r instanceof Range` are the same question from two directions — and isPrototypeOf needs no constructor reference at all.
concepts.detail: `Object.prototype.isPrototypeOf({})` is true for any ordinary object — the reason instanceof Object always succeeds. This form shines when you hold a prototype object but not the class that made it.

concepts.statement: A constructor’s `return` obeys the rule in step 4: returning an **object** (or function or array) hands that object to the caller instead of the constructed `this`; returning a **primitive** (number, string, boolean…) is silently ignored and `this` is delivered as usual.
concepts.detail:
```js
function Ghost() { return { spooky: true }; }
new Ghost() instanceof Ghost;   // false! the plain object delegates to Object.prototype

function Wand(size) { this.size = size; return 42; }
new Wand(9).size;                // 9 — the primitive return was ignored
```
The object-return rule is not a curiosity: it is how built-in constructors hand back their exotic objects, and how `extends Array` (Section 9.5) produces real arrays.

examples.title: Trace the engine: what new Range(1, 3) actually does
examples.problem:
Using the constructor version of Range above, verify each of the four steps with code:
```js
const r = new Range(1, 3);

Object.getPrototypeOf(r) === Range.prototype;   // ?
Object.hasOwn(r, "from") && Object.hasOwn(r, "to");   // ?
r instanceof Range;                              // ?
Range.prototype.isPrototypeOf(r);                // ?
r.constructor;                                   // ?
```

steps.label: Step 1+2: Create and link
steps.text: new manufactures an empty object and points its `[[Prototype]]` at `Range.prototype` — the object literal holding `includes` and `toString`. The probe `Object.getPrototypeOf(r) === Range.prototype` confirms the wiring is identity, not a copy.

steps.label: Step 3: Initialize through this
steps.text: Range runs with `this` bound to the new object; the two assignments create the own properties `from` = 1 and `to` = 3. The method object is never copied — every instance stays two fields plus one link.

steps.label: Step 4: Return this
steps.text: Range finishes without a return statement, so new delivers the initialized object. Both class tests pass: `r instanceof Range` walks the chain and meets `Range.prototype`; `Range.prototype.isPrototypeOf(r)` asks the same from the other side.

steps.label: Step 5: The lost constructor
steps.text: Because the class definition **replaced** `Range.prototype` with a fresh literal, the default prototype object (the one carrying the `constructor` back-reference) was discarded. `r.constructor` therefore resolves through the literal’s own prototype: it is the built-in `Object` function, not Range. Add `constructor: Range` to the literal — or better, use the class keyword (9.3), which maintains it for you.

steps.label: Step 6: The upgrade property
steps.text: Note what did **not** happen: no per-instance copies of methods. Swap `includes` for a fixed version on `Range.prototype` right now, and `r.includes(2)` picks it up on the next call — the lookup happens at call time, every time.

examples.result: All four wiring probes return true; `r.constructor` is `Object` — the one casualty of replacing the prototype wholesale. The instance itself is exactly `{ from: 1, to: 3 }` plus one prototype link.

examples.title: The return-value game

steps.label: Step 1: Wizard — the normal case
steps.text: No return statement means step 4 sees `undefined`, a primitive, and delivers `this`: `{ power: 10 }` linked to `Wizard.prototype`. This is the behavior every constructor in Section 9.1 and 9.3 relies on.

steps.label: Step 2: Ghost — the object return wins
steps.text: Ghost explicitly returns an object literal, so **that object** is the value of `new Ghost()` — the half-built `this` is thrown away. The literal’s prototype is `Object.prototype`, so `new Ghost() instanceof Ghost` is **false**: no link to Ghost survives the hijack.

steps.label: Step 3: Wand — the primitive return is ignored
steps.text: `return 42` is a primitive, so step 4 ignores it entirely and hands back `this`. `new Wand(9).size` is 9, and the instance is a perfectly ordinary Wand. The rule is binary: objects override, primitives evaporate.

steps.label: Step 4: Why the rule exists
steps.text: Built-in constructors **must** return exotic objects — a real Array carries internal length machinery no plain `this` could fake. ES6 subclassing leans on exactly this: when `class EZArray extends Array` calls `super()`, the Array constructor returns a genuine array object, and that becomes the subclass instance (Section 9.5). The quirk you just traced is the mechanism modern inheritance is built on.

examples.result: `new Wizard(10)` → the constructed instance; `new Ghost()` → `{ spooky: true }`, **not** instanceof Ghost; `new Wand(9).size` → 9 — object returns win, primitive returns are ignored.

keyTakeaways: A constructor is an ordinary function plus the `new` operator; the capitalization is convention, the behavior is the four steps.
new: **create** an empty object, **link** it to `C.prototype`, **call** C with this = the object, **return** it — unless C returned an object of its own.
`obj instanceof C` tests only whether `C.prototype` is on obj’s prototype chain; `p.isPrototypeOf(obj)` is the same question asked from the prototype side.
Replacing `C.prototype` wholesale drops the `constructor` back-reference (it then resolves to Object); mutating it in place keeps every link intact.
Constructor object-returns hijack the instance (and defeat instanceof); primitive returns are silently ignored.
Calling a constructor without new runs its body against the global object — the classic era bug that classes fix by throwing.

quiz.q: What, precisely, does `r instanceof Range` test?
options: Whether r was created by the Range function
Whether the object `Range.prototype` appears anywhere on r’s prototype chain
Whether r has a constructor property equal to Range
Whether r has all the methods Range defines
quiz.explanation: instanceof never inspects provenance or shape — only the chain: it walks from r looking for the specific object Range.prototype.

quiz.q: Which lists the four steps of `new C()` in the correct order?
options: Run the constructor, create the object, set the prototype, return
Create an empty object, set its prototype to C.prototype, call C with this bound to it, return the object (unless C returned an object)
Set the prototype, create the object, return, run the constructor
Create the object, run the constructor, set the prototype, validate the return
quiz.explanation: Create → link → initialize → return: the link exists before the body runs, which is why this-bound code can already call inherited methods.

quiz.q: `function F() { return { x: 1 }; }` — what does `new F() instanceof F` evaluate to?
options: true — the object came from F
false — the explicit object return wins, and it delegates to Object.prototype, not F.prototype
true — instanceof checks the constructor property
quiz.explanation: An explicit object return replaces the constructed this; the returned literal has no link to F.prototype, so the chain walk fails.

quiz.q: After `Range.prototype = { ...methods... }` (a wholesale replacement), `r.constructor` for instances resolves to:
options: The Object function — the replacement literal lost the constructor property, so the lookup falls through to Object.prototype.constructor
quiz.explanation: Only the auto-created default prototype carries the constructor back-reference; a replacement literal must add `constructor: Range` itself or the lookup lands on Object.

intro: The `class` keyword is a cleaner surface over the exact machinery of Sections 9.1–9.2: a constructor function, a prototype object with non-enumerable methods, and stricter defaults. Declarations are **not hoisted**, methods live on the prototype, `static` methods live on the class itself, and modern field syntax adds per-instance **public fields**, language-enforced **private `#fields`**, getters and setters, and one-time **static blocks**. This section reads the full syntax and proves the sugar equivalence with live probes.
objectives: Write class declarations and expressions and explain why they are not hoisted
Locate every class member: instance methods, statics, accessors, fields
Prove that class syntax desugars to the constructor+prototype pattern
Use getters and setters to build validated computed properties
Use #private fields and static blocks for real encapsulation

concepts.statement: A **class declaration** `class Range { ... }` defines a constructor plus its prototype in one block; a **class expression** `const R = class { ... }` does the same inline. Unlike function declarations, class declarations are **not hoisted**: the binding is in the temporal dead zone until the definition is evaluated — using the class one line early throws a ReferenceError.

The body’s `constructor(...)` method is the initialization function that `new` calls (step 3 of Section 9.2). At most one is allowed; omitting it entirely is legal and inserts a default — an empty constructor for base classes, or `constructor(...args) { super(...args); }` for derived ones (Section 9.5).
concepts.detail: The constructor is for initializing `this`, not for heavy work: by convention it makes the object valid and returns nothing.

concepts.statement: Inside a class body, a method definition is a **non-enumerable property of the class’s prototype** — the identical slot Section 9.2 wired by hand. `typeof Range` is still `"function"`: the keyword creates a constructor function object, not a new kind of entity.

A method marked `static` becomes a property **of the class itself**, not of the prototype: it is called as `Range.parse(...)` and does not exist on instances. Inside a static method, `this` is the class — making statics the natural home for factories, comparators and class-wide helpers.

concepts.term: Getters and setters in class bodies
concepts.statement: Accessor syntax from object literals (Section 6.6) works in class bodies: `get name() { ... }` intercepts reads of `name`, `set name(v) { ... }` intercepts writes. The pair becomes a single accessor property on the prototype, inherited by all instances — computed and validated properties without storing anything.

A class body may declare **instance fields** with initializers: `count = 0;` creates a public own property on every instance, initialized **before the constructor body runs**, in declaration order. `static` fields (`static origin = ...`) attach to the class once.
concepts.detail:
```js
class Counter {
  count = 0;              // public instance field — one per instance
  static origin = "counter";   // static field — one per class
}
```
Fields are assignment spelled declaratively: they make per-instance state visible at the top of the class instead of buried in constructor lines.

concepts.statement: A field named with a leading `#` — `#count = 0;` — is **private**: the name is meaningful only inside the class body that declares it. Outside, the token is not even valid syntax (a SyntaxError at parse time); from a different class, access throws a TypeError. Privacy is enforced by the language, not by convention.

A `static { ... }` block runs **once**, when the class is defined, after static field initializers — the place for static initialization too complex for one expression: try/catch parsing, loops, conditional setup. It may read and write the class’s private statics.

examples.title: The same class twice: proving the sugar

steps.label: Step 1: A class is a function
steps.text: `typeof Range` is `"function"`. The class keyword creates an ordinary constructor function object — the very thing `new` operates on — plus a prototype. There is no separate "class instance" machinery in the language.

steps.label: Step 2: The methods land on the prototype
steps.text: `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Range.prototype)` lists `["constructor", "includes", "toString"]` — the identical set the manual pattern builds, including the `constructor` method standing where Section 9.2’s lost back-reference used to live. Instance storage (`from`, `to`) is still created per-object by the constructor, exactly as before.

steps.label: Step 3: Instances are indistinguishable
steps.text: Both `new Range(1, 3)` and `new RangeFn(1, 3)` are `{ from: 1, to: 3 }` plus one prototype link; `instanceof` passes for both; both inherit methods through the same one-link lookup of Section 9.1. Any code consuming the objects behaves identically.

steps.label: Step 4: The three genuine differences
steps.text: Class methods are **non-enumerable** (invisible to for/in, Section 5.3); the class body runs in **strict mode** always; and the class name binding is **not hoisted** — plus calling without `new` throws. Everything else — including `constructor`, `typeof`, the prototype wiring — is the pattern of 9.2 wearing syntax.

steps.label: Step 5: Why keep both readings
steps.text: Older codebases, error stacks and metaprogramming (Section 14.2) all present the desugared form; reading `Range.prototype.includes` in the wild should map instantly to "a method in the class body". The equivalence is the load-bearing fact for Sections 9.4 and 9.5.

examples.result: `typeof Range` → "function"; prototype names → `["constructor", "includes", "toString"]`; instanceof → true. The class is the constructor+prototype pattern with stricter defaults — sugar, verified.

examples.title: Validated data with a getter/setter pair

steps.label: Step 1: The read computes
steps.text: `t.fahrenheit` finds no stored property — the accessor pair on the prototype intercepts the read and computes `0 * 9 / 5 + 32` = **32**. No fahrenheit value is ever stored, so it can never go stale when celsius changes.

steps.label: Step 2: The write routes through the setter
steps.text: `t.fahrenheit = 212` does not create a property: the setter runs, converts to `(212 - 32) * 5 / 9` = 100, and stores **one** number — `t.celsius` is now 100. Assignment syntax, method semantics: the API reads like data, behaves like validation.

steps.label: Step 3: Validation guards the write
steps.text: `t.fahrenheit = -500` throws `RangeError: below absolute zero` **before** any mutation — the object is never corrupted. Reads of the stored field remain unvalidated; the choke point is the derived write path.

steps.label: Step 4: The static factory
steps.text: `Temperature.fromFahrenheit(98.6)` constructs via the class-level method — `this` in a static method is the class itself. The instance API and the class API stay separate: `t.fromFahrenheit` is undefined.

steps.label: Step 5: One pair, all instances
steps.text: The get/set pair is a single property on `Temperature.prototype`, so every instance — past and future — shares it. Nothing per-instance exists except the celsius field: minimal storage, maximal invariant.

examples.result: 32, then after the assignment 100, and `fromFahrenheit(98.6)` gives celsius ≈ 37. One stored field, one computed view with validation — the accessor pattern in five lines.

examples.title: A counter with #count

steps.label: Step 1: Declaration is mandatory
steps.text: The body declares `#count;` with no initializer; the constructor then assigns `this.#count = start`. Unlike ordinary properties, a private field **must** be declared in the body first — `this.#x = 1` inside a class that never declared `#x` is a SyntaxError, so private state is always visible in the class source.

steps.label: Step 2: Privacy is name-scope, not per-object
steps.text: Inside any method, constructor or getter of Counter, `this.#count` reads and writes normally. Outside the class body the token does not parse at all — the third probe fails before the program even runs. A second class with its own `#count` is a **different** private name: no collisions, no cross-access.

steps.label: Step 3: Every instance gets its own copy
steps.text: `#count` is an instance field — each Counter has its own slot, initialized to 10 here. The methods `increment` and the `value` getter are shared on the prototype (Section 9.1), but the state they guard is strictly per-instance.

steps.label: Step 4: The private static counts the class
steps.text: `static #created` belongs to the class itself, and only class code can touch it. The constructor increments it on every construction; the static getter `Counter.instances` exposes the census. After one construction the answer is **1** — try a second `new Counter()` and it reads 2.

steps.label: Step 5: Chaining via returned this
steps.text: `increment` returns `this`, so `c.increment(5).increment()` is one expression: 10 + 5 = 15, then +1 = **16**. `c.value` is 16; `c.count` is undefined — no public twin of the private field was ever created, so there is nothing to corrupt.

examples.result: `c.value` → 16; `c.count` → undefined (no public property exists); `c.#count` from outside → SyntaxError (will not even parse); `Counter.instances` → 1. Encapsulation enforced by the grammar itself.

keyTakeaways: A class is a function: `typeof Range` is "function", and methods become non-enumerable properties of `Range.prototype` — the 9.1–9.2 pattern with stricter defaults.
Class declarations are not hoisted (TDZ), their bodies are strict mode, and calling without new throws a TypeError.
`static` members live on the class, instance members on the prototype, fields on the instances — three addresses, one syntax.
Get/set pairs in class bodies give computed properties with write-side validation, shared through the prototype.
Public instance fields (`x = 0`) initialize before the constructor body; omitting the constructor inserts a default.
`#private` fields are declared in the body, checked at parse time, invisible outside — real encapsulation, unlike the `_name` convention.
`static { ... }` blocks run once at class definition and may initialize private statics — the escape hatch for complex static setup.

quiz.q: Where do methods defined in a class body live?
options: On each instance, copied at construction
On the class’s prototype object, as non-enumerable properties
In a hidden per-class method table
quiz.explanation: Class methods are prototype properties — exactly the manual wiring of Section 9.2, plus non-enumerable so for/in never sees them.

quiz.q: What happens if code references a class by name one line above its declaration?
options: It works — class declarations hoist like function declarations
ReferenceError — class bindings live in the temporal dead zone until the definition is evaluated
undefined — the class exists but is empty
TypeError — classes cannot be referenced before construction
quiz.explanation: Classes behave like let/const: not hoisted for use. The definition must execute before any reference resolves.

quiz.q: Outside the class body, what does the expression `new Counter().#count` do?
options: Returns undefined — the field is private
Fails with a SyntaxError — the parser rejects the private name outside its declaring class
Returns the field’s value because # is only a convention
quiz.explanation: Private names are lexically scoped to the class body: code outside it cannot even mention them, so the program fails to parse — stronger than any runtime check.

quiz.q: For `class T { get fahrenheit() {...} set fahrenheit(f) {...} }`, what does `t.fahrenheit = 212` do?
options: Creates an own property fahrenheit = 212 on the instance
Runs the setter function with 212 — assignment syntax, method semantics
quiz.explanation: The setter intercepts the assignment: writes never climb the prototype chain (Section 9.1) because the accessor pair catches them first.

quiz.q: A public instance field `count = 0;` in a class body is initialized:
options: Once, on the prototype, for all instances
On each new instance, before the constructor body runs
quiz.explanation: Fields are per-instance initializers that run at construction time before the constructor body — every instance gets its own copy.

intro: A prototype is a live object, so a class is **retroactively upgradeable**: add a method to the prototype today and every instance — including ones created yesterday — can call it tomorrow. For classes you own, `Object.assign` makes that a one-line batch operation. For the language’s built-in prototypes, the same move is a famous hazard: it poisons `for/in` loops everywhere and collides with the entire future of the standard library — this section shows exactly why, and the subclassing alternative that replaced it.
objectives: Add methods to an existing class with Object.assign on its prototype
Explain why every instance, past and future, picks up the addition
Demonstrate the for/in poisoning that built-in patching causes
Use Object.defineProperty to make a patch non-enumerable — and still say no
Choose subclassing (Section 9.5) as the safe way to extend built-ins

concepts.term: Prototype patching for your own classes
concepts.statement: `Object.assign(SomeClass.prototype, { method1() {...}, method2() {...} })` copies any number of methods onto the existing prototype **in place** — the `constructor` back-reference and all prior methods survive, and because lookups happen at call time (Section 9.1), every existing instance immediately understands the new names.

Adding properties to `Array.prototype`, `Object.prototype`, `String.prototype` and friends is known as **monkey patching** and is rejected by every style guide for three compounding reasons: the additions are **global** (every script on the page sees them), they **collide** with other scripts and with future standards, and — because assignment creates **enumerable** properties — they surface inside every `for/in` loop in the program.
concepts.detail: The standards process itself has been bitten: a widely-used library that pre-defined `Array.prototype.flatten` forced the committee to rename the language feature to `flat`. Your clever helper is tomorrow’s compatibility report.

concepts.statement: `Object.defineProperty(Array.prototype, "last", { value, writable: true, configurable: true, enumerable: false })` installs a method that `for/in` cannot see — non-enumerability is exactly how the built-in methods avoid polluting loops. It fixes the loop symptom, not the collision disease.

The modern route to "an Array with extra methods" is `class EZArray extends Array { ... }` — your names live in **your** namespace, instances are still real arrays, and nobody else’s code changes behavior. Section 9.5 builds the full machinery; the rule of thumb lands here: **extend what you own, never edit what you share**.
concepts.detail: If you do not control the class, wrap it or subclass it; if you need a utility function, a plain function (`last(a)`) is always safe. Prototype patching of built-ins is the one JavaScript habit with no defenders left.

concepts.statement: A **polyfill** backports a standard method missing on old engines — and it is the only built-in patch the book tolerates, under three rules: feature-check first (`if (!Array.prototype.flat)`), match the specification exactly, and install with `Object.defineProperty` as non-enumerable. Anything else is monkey patching by another name.

Patching `Object.prototype` poisons **every** object — arrays, functions, dates, null-prototype dictionaries excepted — because every ordinary chain ends there (Section 9.1). One enumerable addition appears in every `for/in` in the program, breaks every `in` check for that name, and collides with every future standard key at once.
concepts.detail: The `flatten` → `flat` rename was an `Array.prototype` collision affecting arrays only; an `Object.prototype` collision affects the language itself. Dictionary objects (`{}` as maps) are the first casualty: `"myKey" in dict` can no longer distinguish data from inheritance — the reason Section 14.2 prefers `Object.create(null)` and Chapter 11 prefers `Map`.

examples.title: Upgrade every instance at once

steps.label: Step 1: The instances exist first
steps.text: r1 and r2 were created **before** any `equals` method existed — at that moment, `r1.equals` would have walked the chain and returned undefined (a total miss, Section 9.1).

steps.label: Step 2: Object.assign mutates in place
steps.text: The call copies `equals` onto the **existing** prototype object — no replacement, no new object. The prototype’s identity is unchanged, which is why the `constructor` back-reference and every earlier method survive untouched.

steps.label: Step 3: Old instances learn instantly
steps.text: Lookup is per-call: `r1.equals(new Range(1, 3))` now walks r1 → `Range.prototype`, finds the new method, and returns **true**; `r1.equals(r2)` compares 1 vs 2 and returns false. No instance was rebuilt, migrated or notified — the chain simply has one more property.

steps.label: Step 4: Nothing else changed
steps.text: `r1.constructor` still resolves to Range, and `r1.includes(2)` still works — both probes confirm the in-place edit. Contrast Section 9.2’s wholesale replacement, which would have orphaned `constructor` and forced every instance onto a new (identical-looking) prototype.

steps.label: Step 5: When this is legitimate
steps.text: Patching **your own** class is a real technique: split a large class across files, upgrade a library class you maintain for all its users, or attach cross-cutting behavior as mixins (next section). The line this section draws is ownership — built-ins are shared by every program in the page.

examples.result: true, false, Range (constructor intact), true — one `Object.assign` upgraded every existing and future instance, with zero side effects on the prototype’s existing residents.

examples.title: The for/in poison
examples.problem:
A teammate "improves" arrays for everyone. Predict the loop before running it:
```js
Array.prototype.last = function () { return this[this.length - 1]; };

const a = [10, 20, 30];
a.last();                        // ?
for (const i in a) console.log(i);   // what logs?
```

steps.label: Step 1: The patch seems to work
steps.text: `a.last()` returns 30 — the method is found by the normal prototype walk, and nothing about the call site looks wrong. This is what makes the hazard seductive: the first hundred uses are fine.

steps.label: Step 2: The loop betrays it
steps.text: The for/in logs `"0"`, `"1"`, `"2"` — and then `"last"`. for/in enumerates every enumerable property on the **entire prototype chain** (Section 5.3), and assignment-created properties are enumerable by default. The loop that iterated three elements now iterates four, the fourth being the string key "last" (its value: the function).

steps.label: Step 3: Why built-ins never do this
steps.text: Every method the language itself installs — `map`, `push`, `toString` — is defined with `enumerable: false`, which for/in skips. That is the entire reason ordinary loops over arrays and objects have always been clean: the built-ins are politely invisible.

steps.label: Step 4: The half-fix
steps.text: Reinstalling the method via `Object.defineProperty` with `enumerable: false` removes the loop symptom. But the collision disease remains: any other script that defines `last` differently now conflicts, page-wide, and a future standard could claim the name (the `flatten` → `flat` episode).

steps.label: Step 5: The real fixes
steps.text: A plain function `const last = (a) => a[a.length - 1]` needs no shared object. Or subclass — `class EZArray extends Array { get last() { return this[this.length - 1]; } }` — your method in your namespace, on instances that are still real arrays. Both routes keep the shared prototypes pristine.

examples.result: `a.last()` → 30, but the loop logs 0, 1, 2 and **"last"** — an enumerable inherited property leaking into every for/in on the page. Non-enumerable defineProperty hides it; a function or subclass avoids it entirely.

keyTakeaways: Prototypes are live: `Object.assign(C.prototype, {...})` upgrades every instance — existing ones included — because method lookup happens at call time.
Object.assign mutates the prototype in place, preserving `constructor` and prior methods, unlike wholesale replacement.
Never patch built-in prototypes: the change is global, collides with other scripts and future standards, and assignment-created properties are enumerable.
for/in walks the whole prototype chain, so enumerable additions to `Array.prototype` (or worse, `Object.prototype`) appear in every loop in the program.
`Object.defineProperty` with `enumerable: false` is how built-ins stay invisible to for/in — an explanation, not a license.
The safe extensions of shared types are plain functions or subclasses (`class EZArray extends Array`), never edits to the shared prototype.

quiz.q: Why do instances created **before** `Object.assign(SomeClass.prototype, { go() {} })` still get the `go` method?
options: They are rebuilt when the prototype changes
Method lookup walks the prototype chain at call time, and the mutated prototype is on that chain
go is copied to each instance lazily
They do not — only future instances see it
quiz.explanation: Instances hold only a link, not a copy: every property read re-walks the chain, so a prototype mutation is visible to old and new instances alike.

quiz.q: After `Array.prototype.last = function () {...}`, `for (const i in [1, 2])` logs:
options: 0, 1 — and "last", because assignment-created properties are enumerable and for/in walks the chain
quiz.explanation: for/in visits enumerable properties on the whole prototype chain; the patched-in method is enumerable by default, so its key shows up after the array indexes.

quiz.q: What does `enumerable: false` in an `Object.defineProperty` patch accomplish?
options: Hides the property from for/in loops — the same trick every built-in method uses
Deletes the property from the prototype
Makes the method available only to arrays
quiz.explanation: Non-enumerability keeps loops clean, which is how built-ins avoid poisoning for/in — though collisions with other scripts remain possible.

quiz.q: The recommended way to give arrays a custom `last` behavior today is:
options: Assign it to Array.prototype with a distinctive name
Define it on Object.prototype so everything benefits
Subclass (`class MyArray extends Array`) or write a plain function — never edit the shared prototype
quiz.explanation: Extend what you own: a subclass keeps your names in your namespace while instances stay real arrays; a plain function is even simpler when no state is needed.

intro: **Inheritance** with `extends` chains prototypes on two levels at once — instance prototypes behind instance prototypes, and the classes themselves behind one another for statics. The derived constructor must call `super()` before touching `this`, because in a derived class it is the **base** constructor that performs Section 9.2’s create-and-link steps. Overridden methods can borrow their parent versions through `super.method()`, built-ins like `Array` and `Error` subclass cleanly, and for everything else there are two lighter tools: abstract base classes and mixins.
objectives: Draw the two prototype links that extends establishes
Apply the super()-before-this rule and its ReferenceError
Override a method and delegate back with super.method()
Subclass built-ins: Array, Error, Map
Use new.target guards for abstract classes and Object.assign mixins for composition

concepts.statement: `class Sub extends Super` wires **two** links: `Sub.prototype` → `Super.prototype` (so instances inherit through both — a Sub instance is also a Super instance for instanceof), and `Sub` → `Super` itself (so **statics are inherited**: `Sub.parse` works if Super defines one).

In a **derived** class constructor, `this` does not exist until `super()` has been called — the base constructor performs the create-and-link steps (Section 9.2) and returns the object that becomes `this`. Reading or writing `this` first throws a ReferenceError; omitting the constructor entirely inserts `constructor(...args) { super(...args); }` automatically.

A derived class can redefine an inherited method — its version, being closer on the chain, **shadows** the parent’s (Section 9.1’s rule again). Inside the override, `super.method(...)` invokes the parent’s implementation, so a subclass can **extend** behavior instead of copying it.

Subclassing `Array`, `Error`, `Map`, `Set` and the rest is reliable in ES6: the built-in constructor returns its exotic object through `super()`, the instance carries the full built-in method set, `instanceof` works across the chain, and statics like `Array.of` produce **subclass** instances.

JavaScript has no abstract keyword, but the idiom is three lines: a base class whose constructor throws when **directly** instantiated. `new.target` is the constructor `new` was actually invoked with — the base class itself for a direct `new Abstract()`, but the **subclass** when reached through `super()` — so the guard trips only on direct construction.

Inheritance answers "is-a" and is limited to one parent; **composition** answers "has-this-behavior" and is unlimited. A **mixin** is a plain object of methods stamped onto any number of classes with `Object.assign(Class.prototype, mixin)` — Section 9.4’s tool, used to share behavior sideways instead of down.

examples.title: TypedMap: validate, then super, then this

steps.label: Step 1: Enter the derived constructor — this does not exist yet
steps.text: Unlike a base class, `new TypedMap(...)` creates nothing up front: the derived constructor starts with `this` uninitialized, because the object will be whatever `Map`’s constructor returns (Section 9.2’s object-return rule). The validation loop runs **before** super because it needs no `this` — it only touches its parameters.

steps.label: Step 2: super(entries) builds the real object
steps.text: Calling `super` invokes `Map` with the entries; Map performs the create-and-link steps, installs its internal hash storage, and returns a genuine Map object. That returned object becomes `this` inside TypedMap’s constructor — one shared object, half built by each class.

steps.label: Step 3: Private state after super
steps.text: Only now can `this.#valueType = valueType` run — a line earlier it would throw `ReferenceError: Must call super constructor in derived class before accessing this`. The `#valueType` declaration in the class body is what makes the field assignable at all (Section 9.3’s declaration rule).

steps.label: Step 4: Override and delegate
steps.text: The `set` override adds the type check, then calls `super.set(key, value)` — the parent’s storage logic, unchanged — and **returns its result**, preserving Map’s chainable API. Extend, then delegate: the shape of almost every good override.

steps.label: Step 5: The two failure paths
steps.text: Construction with a bad entry throws at the validation loop — nothing was ever stored. The later `m.set("d", "x")` throws from the override — and note that `super.set` was never reached, so the bad pair is not half-inserted: the check happens before the delegation, so the parent’s invariants (and its return value) are never compromised.

examples.result: `m.set("c", 3)` succeeds; `m.set("d", "x")` throws TypeError (checked before super.set runs); the bad-entry construction throws during validation. Order inside a derived constructor is a rule, not a style choice: no-super code first, super, then this.

examples.title: EZArray: extends Array in action

steps.label: Step 1: The inherited static builds a subclass instance
steps.text: `EZArray.of(10, 20, 30)` — `of` is inherited through the Sub → Super class-side link — constructs via the subclass, so `a` is a genuine EZArray: real array storage, real length, plus `first` and `last` one link above `Array.prototype`.

steps.label: Step 2: instanceof crosses the whole chain
steps.text: `a instanceof Array` is **true**: the walk `a` → `EZArray.prototype` → `Array.prototype` meets `Array.prototype`, so every array method from Section 7.4 — push, slice, reduce — is inherited. The extras sit closer to the instance and shadow nothing, so both layers cooperate.

steps.label: Step 3: Derived methods construct the subclass
steps.text: `a.map(x => x * 2)` returns an **EZArray**, so `doubled.last` is **60** — one expression chaining a built-in transform with a custom accessor. By default, built-in producers use the subclass (the `Symbol.species` hook of Section 14.3 exists precisely to tune or disable this).

steps.label: Step 4: Why ES6 made this possible
steps.text: Pre-ES6, faking array subclasses broke because hand-rolled constructors returned plain objects that lacked the array’s internal machinery. ES6’s fix is exactly Section 9.2’s return rule plus super: `super()` hands back the real exotic object, and the subclass decorates it. The same recipe subclasses `Error` — `class NotFound extends Error {}` — giving instanceof-able custom errors (Section 11.4).

examples.result: true, 30, and 60: the subclass instance passes instanceof Array, reads its own accessors, and even `map` returns an EZArray — built-ins and user classes in one chain.

examples.title: A mixin by Object.assign

steps.label: Step 1: Mixins are plain objects of methods
steps.text: No class, no extends: each mixin is a behavior package — event registration and emission in one, timestamping in another. They express **has-a-capability**, not is-a-kind-of, and any class can adopt them without spending its single inheritance slot.

steps.label: Step 2: Stamping with Object.assign
steps.text: The one-line stamp copies both method sets onto `Note.prototype` (Section 9.4’s tool — in place, constructor preserved). Method resolution is the ordinary chain walk of Section 9.1: `n.on` resolves through the class prototype, which is why `Object.hasOwn(n, "on")` is false while `Object.hasOwn(Note.prototype, "on")` is true.

steps.label: Step 3: Compose any number of them
steps.text: Note now behaves as Evented **and** Timestamped — the chained `n.on(...).touch()` is one expression across both mixins. Inheritance chains like this need a diamond of classes; mixins are stamped sideways, one Object.assign per concern, and a class can adopt ten without hierarchy gymnastics.

steps.label: Step 4: The getter caveat
steps.text: Object.assign copies **values**: had Evented used `get handlers()` accessors, assign would have invoked them once and copied the resulting data (Section 6.6). Accessor-preserving mixins use `Object.defineProperties(Note.prototype, Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors(Evented))` — or keep mixins to plain methods, the common discipline.

steps.label: Step 5: Choosing inheritance vs composition
steps.text: Use extends when a real is-a substitution applies (a TypedMap **is a** Map) and the chain stays short; use mixins for orthogonal capabilities shared across unrelated classes; use plain functions when neither state nor polymorphism is needed. Deep hierarchies are the code smell both patterns exist to prevent.

examples.result: The emit fires the listener ("changed" logs); `Object.hasOwn(n, "on")` → false; `Object.hasOwn(Note.prototype, "on")` → true. Two capabilities, one line each, zero inheritance spent.

keyTakeaways: `extends` chains both levels: `Sub.prototype` → `Super.prototype` for instances, and `Sub` → `Super` for inherited statics — instanceof holds across the whole chain.
A derived constructor must call `super()` before touching `this`; the base constructor is what actually creates the object (and may return an exotic one, like a real Array).
Omitting a derived constructor inserts `constructor(...args) { super(...args); }`; overriding a method shadows it, and `super.method()` borrows the parent version.
ES6 subclassing of built-ins works: `EZArray.of(...)` and `map` produce subclass instances, and `class NotFound extends Error` gives instanceof-able errors.
Abstract-class idiom: throw in the base constructor when `new.target === BaseClass` — the guard sees the subclass (not the base) when reached through super().
Mixins share behavior sideways: plain method objects stamped with `Object.assign(Class.prototype, mixin)` — remember assign copies values, so accessor mixins need defineProperties.
Prefer composition when capabilities are orthogonal; reserve extends for true is-a relationships, and keep chains short.

quiz.q: In a derived-class constructor, what happens if you read `this` before calling `super()`?
options: ReferenceError — the base constructor has not yet created the object that this will refer to
It works, but methods are missing
quiz.explanation: Derived classes do not create their own this: super() runs the base constructor, whose returned object becomes this. Touching it early is a hard error.

quiz.q: What two links does `class Sub extends Super` establish?
options: Instances of Sub copy both classes’ methods
quiz.explanation: Instance inheritance runs through the prototype chain; the classes themselves are also chained, which is why Sub.of or Sub.parse resolves to the parent’s statics.

quiz.q: An omitted constructor in a class that `extends` another is equivalent to:
options: Nothing — the class cannot be instantiated
quiz.explanation: The default derived constructor forwards all arguments to super — the forwarding form is what "no constructor" means for a subclass.

quiz.q: Inside an override, `super.method()`:
options: Invokes the parent class’s implementation of that method, so the override can extend rather than replace it
Creates a new instance of the parent
Is only valid inside the constructor
quiz.explanation: super starts the property lookup one level above the prototype the method is defined on — borrow the inherited behavior, then add yours around it.

quiz.q: What does `Object.assign(Note.prototype, Evented)` do if Evented contains `get handlers()`?
options: Copies the getter onto the prototype
Invokes the getter once and copies its resulting **value** — accessor-preserving mixins need Object.defineProperties with getOwnPropertyDescriptors
quiz.explanation: Object.assign reads property values from the source, which runs getters; the destination receives plain data. defineProperties is the descriptor-level alternative.

options: A ReferenceError, because `super()` must run before `this` is touched
A TypeError, because `A` is not a constructor
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The code given builds a derived constructor that writes `this.extra` before calling `super()`. Step 2: The governing rule is that in a derived class the `this` binding stays uninitialized until `super()` runs, since the base constructor performs the create-and-link steps, and touching `this` earlier throws a ReferenceError. Step 3: Tracing construction, `new B` enters the derived constructor with no usable `this`, the assignment to `this.extra` executes first, and the engine throws before `super()` is ever reached. Step 4: The distractors fail because no instance survives to carry properties, nothing about `A` being callable is at fault, and reordering the two lines would be required for success. Step 5: Therefore construction throws a ReferenceError.

intro: A module is a self-contained unit of code that hides its implementation behind a public API. Before ES6 the language had no module system at all — no `import` and no `export` — so JavaScript programmers built modules out of the tools they had: **objects**, **classes** and **closures**. This section is the prehistory of modules, and it still explains exactly what every later module system is trying to achieve: private state behind a narrow public interface, and no name collisions in the global namespace.
objectives: Explain the two problems modules solve: managing the global namespace and enabling code reuse
Use objects and classes with static methods as namespaces for related functions
Implement the closure-based module pattern with an immediately invoked function expression (IIFE)
Trace how private variables survive the return of the IIFE and remain reachable only through the exported API
Distinguish module-level (shared) state from per-instance state

concepts.statement: In a classic script, every top-level `const`, `function` and `class` declaration becomes a property of the global object (`globalThis`), so unrelated scripts can silently overwrite one another’s functions and variables. Flanagan frames modules with two goals: keep details that are not part of the API **private**, and ensure that code does not **leak names** into the global namespace.
