concepts.statement: Subtract two Date objects directly — the `-` operator coerces via `valueOf()` — to get milliseconds; divide by 86,400,000 for days. Add a duration by constructing `new Date(date.getTime() + ms)` or using the component setters, which handle month lengths and leap years for you.
concepts.detail: Two cautions: across a daylight-saving transition, “local midnight to local midnight” can be 23 or 25 hours — round day counts (`Math.round(ms / 86400000)`) or compute in UTC; and for month arithmetic use `setMonth`, because months have no fixed millisecond length.

concepts.statement: The default `toString()` family (`toString`, `toDateString`, `toTimeString`) produce locale-dependent, machine-inconsistent text; `toISOString()` is always UTC ISO format — ideal for logs and APIs; `toUTCString()` and `toLocaleString()` fill the rest. Rolling your own format means remembering the three traps: **months are 0-based**, `getDay` is the weekday while `getDate` is the day of month, and manual padding of `3` to `"03"`.

`new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, options).format(date)` produces locale-correct dates: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "long" })` gives `"March 3, 2026"`, while the German locale gives `"3. März 2026"`. Options choose the parts (`weekday`, `year`, `month`, `day`, `hour`, `minute`, `timeZone`) and their style (`"long"`, `"short"`, `"numeric"`).
concepts.detail: Formatting objects are comparatively expensive to build — create one per locale/options pair and reuse it, rather than constructing one per date. The same object can format many dates; Section 11.6 generalizes the pattern to numbers and collation.

concepts.statement: `new Error(message)` creates an exception object with two useful properties: `message` and `name` (default `"Error"`), plus the nonstandard-but-universal `stack` — a string trace of where the error was created. The standard subclasses — `TypeError`, `RangeError`, `ReferenceError`, `SyntaxError`, `URIError` — signal specific failure classes, and all can be caught, inspected and re-thrown with `instanceof`.
concepts.detail: Technically `throw` accepts any value (`throw "oops"` works) — but thrown non-Errors lose the message/stack contract and break `instanceof Error` handlers, so always throw Error objects.

concepts.statement: Extend `Error`, call `super(message)`, and set `this.name` to the subclass name — otherwise caught instances still report `"Error"`. Extra properties carry context (`status`, `url`, `code`), and because `class` extends wires the prototype chain, `instanceof` works for both the subclass and `Error`.

examples.title: Trace the engine: days between two dates

steps.label: Step 1: Build local midnights
steps.text: The three-argument constructor takes (year, month, day) in **local** time — and the month argument is 0-based, so `0` is January and `2` is March. Both Dates internally store a UTC millisecond count for each local midnight.

steps.label: Step 2: Subtracting Dates subtracts numbers
steps.text: The `-` operator has no Date arithmetic — it calls `valueOf()` on both, producing `getTime()` values, and subtracts those: `ms = end.getTime() - start.getTime()`.

steps.label: Step 3: Convert to days
steps.text: One day is 86,400,000 ms. Counting calendar-wise: Jan 15 → Feb 15 is 31 days, Feb 15 → Mar 3 is 16 days (2026 is not a leap year, February has 28) — 47 days total, so `ms` is 47 × 86,400,000 = **4,060,800,000** and `days` is **47**.

steps.label: Step 4: Adding a duration
steps.text: `start.getTime() + 7 * 86400000` shifts the raw count by one week and wraps it in a new Date: January 22, 2026 — constructing fresh rather than mutating `start`, which other code may still hold.

steps.label: Step 5: The DST caveat
steps.text: If the interval crosses a spring-forward or fall-back night, local midnight to local midnight is 23 or 25 hours and the division yields 46.958... — `Math.round(ms / 86400000)` recovers the calendar answer; or build both dates with `Date.UTC(...)` and count purely in UTC where days are always exact.

examples.result: `ms` = 4,060,800,000; `days` = 47; adding 7 × 86,400,000 ms lands on January 22 — arithmetic on the raw millisecond count is the whole secret.

examples.title: Formatting without the off-by-one disasters
examples.problem:
Display March 3, 2026 as a long human-readable date — first with naive getters, then with `Intl.DateTimeFormat`:
```js
const d = new Date(2026, 2, 3);
d.getMonth();            // ?
d.getDay();              // ?
d.getDate();             // ?
new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "long" }).format(d);
```

steps.label: Step 1: The month trap
steps.text: `d.getMonth()` returns **2** — March, because months are 0-based. Every hand-rolled format needs `getMonth() + 1` or a name table, and forgetting the `+ 1` is the most common Date bug in the language.

steps.label: Step 2: The day traps
steps.text: `d.getDate()` is 3 — day of **month** — while `d.getDay()` is 2 — **Tuesday**, day of week with 0 = Sunday. Swapping these two produces dates like “March Tuesday, 2026” or silently wrong weekdays.

steps.label: Step 3: A correct manual format
steps.text: `` `${d.getMonth() + 1}/${d.getDate()}/${d.getFullYear()}` `` yields `"3/3/2026"` — right, but it hardcodes an American shape and does no zero-padding. (`toISOString()` is not the answer here: it always renders UTC, which can shift the calendar day itself.)

steps.label: Step 4: Delegate to Intl
steps.text: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "long" }).format(d)` returns `"March 3, 2026"` — correct names, punctuation and order for the locale, with zero manual bookkeeping. The German locale gives `"3. März 2026"` from the same Date object.

steps.label: Step 5: Reuse the formatter
steps.text: Formatting objects carry setup cost; hoist `const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "long" })` and call `fmt.format(...)` per date — one object, many dates.

examples.result: `getMonth()` → 2, `getDate()` → 3, `getDay()` → 2; the Intl formatter yields `"March 3, 2026"` — the library does the names, the padding and the locale.

examples.title: A custom HTTPError subclass

steps.label: Step 1: Extend and call super
steps.text: `class HTTPError extends Error` puts Error on the prototype chain, so `e instanceof Error` remains true for every instance — existing catch blocks keep working. `super(message)` runs the Error constructor, which sets `message` and captures a `stack` trace at construction.

steps.label: Step 2: Fix the name
steps.text: Without `this.name = "HTTPError"`, a caught instance still reports `e.name === "Error"`. Setting it costs one line and makes logs readable: `HTTPError: Not Found`.

steps.label: Step 3: Carry the context
steps.text: `this.status = 404` attaches the domain data — the caller can branch on `e.status` (`if (e.status === 404) showEmptyPage()`) instead of parsing strings out of a message.

steps.label: Step 4: Throw and catch
steps.text: When the fetch fails, `throw new HTTPError(404, "Not Found")` unwinds to the nearest catch. There, `e instanceof HTTPError` is true, `e instanceof Error` is true, `e.message` is `"Not Found"`, `e.status` is `404`, and `e.stack` points at the construction site — five usable facts from one object.

steps.label: Step 5: Compose with cause (ES2022)
steps.text: To wrap a network failure: `throw new HTTPError(503, "upstream down", { cause: err })` — the third argument’s `cause` preserves the original error object for the handler that needs it, without flattening it into a message string.

examples.result: A catch block sees `instanceof HTTPError` true, `name` `"HTTPError"`, `status` 404, a working `stack` — custom errors are just Error subclasses with context bolted on.

keyTakeaways: A Date is one number: milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC; `-` between Dates works because of `valueOf()` coercion.
Component constructors use **local** time and 0-based months: `new Date(2026, 2, 3)` is March 3.
`getMonth()` is 0-based; `getDate()` is day of month; `getDay()` is weekday — and `getYear()` is deprecated.
Day arithmetic divides by 86,400,000 ms — round, or work in UTC, to survive daylight-saving transitions.
`toISOString()` is always UTC; `Intl.DateTimeFormat` gives correct, reusable, locale-aware human formatting.
Throw Error objects, not strings: they carry `message`, `name` and `stack`, and they satisfy `instanceof`.
Custom subclasses: `extends Error`, `super(message)`, set `this.name`, add context fields such as `status`; ES2022 `cause` preserves wrapped errors.

quiz.q: What does `new Date(2026, 2, 3).getMonth()` return?
options: 0 — only January can be constructed that way
quiz.explanation: Date months run 0 (January) through 11 (December): the constructor field 2 selects March, and getMonth reads back that same 0-based value.

quiz.q: What does the expression `d2 - d1` evaluate to for two Date objects?
options: A new Date representing the difference
The difference in milliseconds — a number, via valueOf() coercion
quiz.explanation: The subtraction operator converts both operands to primitives with valueOf(), which for Dates is the epoch-millisecond count — so the result is a plain number of milliseconds.

quiz.q: Which Date method always renders the timestamp in UTC?
quiz.explanation: toISOString always produces the ISO 8601 form in UTC (with a Z suffix); the toString family is locale-and-engine dependent and toLocaleString follows the local zone.

quiz.q: Why must a custom error subclass assign `this.name`?
options: Because name is a required constructor parameter
Otherwise instances inherit the default "Error" name and log misleadingly
quiz.explanation: super(message) leaves name at "Error"; overriding it makes the exception identify itself — instanceof correctness comes from the prototype chain, not from name.

quiz.q: Which pair correctly distinguishes “day of month” from “day of week”?
options: Both return the day of month
Both return the day of week
quiz.explanation: getDate() is 1–31 within the month; getDay() is 0–6 with 0 = Sunday — the naming is historical and backwards from every intuition, so memorize the pair.

intro: JSON is the lingua franca of APIs — and JavaScript ships its own compiler for it: `JSON.stringify` turns values into text and `JSON.parse` turns text back into values. Both take a second argument that changes everything: a **replacer** that filters or transforms on the way out, and a **reviver** that rebuilds on the way in. The format’s limits — no `undefined`, no functions, no cycles, and `NaN` quietly becoming `null` — are exactly what those second arguments exist to work around.
objectives: Serialize values with `JSON.stringify`, including indentation with the space argument
Use array replacers as whitelists and function replacers to transform or omit values
Parse with `JSON.parse` and a reviver that reconstructs Dates and other types
Predict the format’s failures: circular structures, NaN, functions, undefined and Maps
Design `toJSON` methods as per-class escape hatches

concepts.statement: `JSON.stringify(value, replacer?, space?)` serializes a value to JSON text: objects become `{...}`, arrays `[...]`, strings are quoted and escaped, numbers use their `toString()` form (with `null` for the non-finite). The **space** argument — a number of spaces or a string — pretty-prints with newlines and indentation.

The second argument filters what gets serialized. An **array** is a whitelist of property names, applied recursively at every nesting level. A **function** `(key, value) => value` runs for every property of every object (and once for the root with key `""`) — return the value to keep it, a different value to transform it, or `undefined` to **omit the property entirely**.
concepts.detail: The array form cannot express “hide passwords” — only “show these names” — so anything rule-based needs the function form: `JSON.stringify(user, (k, v) => k === "password" ? undefined : v)`.

concepts.statement: Before serializing any object, `stringify` checks for a `toJSON()` method and uses its return value instead. `Date` implements it — returning `toISOString()` — which is why Dates serialize as ISO strings automatically; user classes can do the same to define their own wire form.

`JSON.parse(text, reviver?)` builds plain objects, arrays and primitives from text, then calls the **reviver** function `(key, value) => value` on every property **from the deepest level up, root last**. The returned value replaces the parsed one — return a `new Date(value)` for stored date strings and Dates come back to life.

The format has **no** representation for: `undefined`, functions, symbols, `NaN`/`Infinity` (all become `null`), `Map`, `Set`, `Date` (saved only as its ISO string via `toJSON`), or object identity. **Circular structures throw `TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON`.** In objects, `undefined`/function/symbol properties are dropped; in **arrays** they become `null`, so positions survive.

To round-trip class instances, have `toJSON` add a type tag plus raw data, and have the reviver read the tag and rebuild: `toJSON() { return { _class: "Point", x: this.x, y: this.y }; }` — the reviver sees `_class` and constructs a real instance. This is the pattern behind every JSON-persisted object store.
concepts.detail: It restores the constructor information JSON deliberately discards — the text says what it *was*, the reviver decides what it *becomes*. For plain deep copies, prefer `structuredClone` (which understands Map, Set, Date and typed arrays); JSON round-trips only what JSON can say.

examples.title: Trace the engine: selective serialization

steps.label: Step 1: The array replacer as whitelist
steps.text: `JSON.stringify(user, ["name", "email"], 2)` walks the object keeping only properties named in the array — recursively, so a nested `{ name, email }` object would also be filtered to the same fields. `password`, `attempts` and `createdAt` never make the output.

steps.label: Step 2: The output
steps.text: The result is the two-line pretty-printed object `{ "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" }` — the `2` indents every level two spaces, which is what makes audit logs diffable.

steps.label: Step 3: The function replacer as rule
steps.text: `JSON.stringify(user, (key, value) => key === "password" ? undefined : value)` is called first for the root (`key === ""`, value = the whole `user`), then once per property. Returning `undefined` for `"password"` **omits** that key; everything else passes through untouched.

steps.label: Step 4: Watch the automatic Date handling
steps.text: The function version keeps `createdAt` — and it appears in the output as `"2026-01-15T00:00:00.000Z"`, because `stringify` consults Date’s built-in `toJSON()` method before the replacer even sees the value.

steps.label: Step 5: Choose deliberately
steps.text: Whitelist when the safe set is small and known (public API payloads); rule-based when the structure is deep or the condition is comparative (hide any key matching `/token/i`). Both beat deleting properties from the source object — which mutates data other code may still need.

examples.result: The whitelist gives `{"name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com"}` indented; the function gives the full record with only the password gone — two replacer styles, two intents.

examples.title: Reviving Dates on the way in

steps.label: Step 1: Parse builds plain data first
steps.text: Without a reviver, `JSON.parse` would produce `back.createdAt` as the *string* `"2026-01-15T00:00:00.000Z"` — JSON has no date type, so every date arrives as text.

steps.label: Step 2: The reviver walks depth-first
steps.text: The reviver is invoked **post-order** — deepest properties first, the root object last (its key is the empty string). For our record: `name`, `email`, `password`, `attempts`, `createdAt`, then `""`.

steps.label: Step 3: Transform on sight
steps.text: At `key === "createdAt"` the reviver returns `new Date(value)`: the string is parsed by the Date constructor (ISO strings parse as UTC — the exact form `toJSON` produced), and the parsed value becomes the property value.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify the revival
steps.text: `back.createdAt instanceof Date` is `true` and `back.createdAt.getFullYear()` returns `2026` — calendar arithmetic is available again. A more general reviver tests the value’s shape (`/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T/`) instead of one key name, reviving every ISO date anywhere in the structure.

examples.result: Dates live in JSON only as strings — but the reviver converts them back to Date objects on every parse, restoring the type system JSON refuses to carry.

examples.title: The four ways stringify drops your data

steps.label: Step 1: Non-finite numbers become null
steps.text: JSON numbers have no `NaN` or `Infinity`, so both are serialized as `null`: the first call returns `{"n":null,"i":null}` — a silent type change that readers of the log must simply know about.

steps.label: Step 2: Unserializable properties vanish from objects
steps.text: Functions, `undefined` and symbols are simply **omitted** from object output: the second call returns `{}` — no `f`, no `u`, no `s`, and no error. Empty is not a bug report; it is the format speaking.

steps.label: Step 3: But arrays preserve positions
steps.text: Removing a middle array element would corrupt every later index, so `undefined` and friends become `null` placeholders instead: the third call returns `"[1,null,2]"` — note the *different* rule for arrays versus objects.

steps.label: Step 4: Cycles throw
steps.text: The fourth call throws `TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON` — the serializer, having no reference syntax, refuses to loop forever. The fixes: a `toJSON()` that returns a safe, acyclic view; or a replacer that detects and skips the back-reference.

steps.label: Step 5: Read the rules as a design tool
steps.text: Knowing exactly what drops is how JSON is used for *public shapes*: put only data in the objects you serialize. When types must survive — Maps, Sets, class identity — either add tag-and-revive logic (the `toJSON` pattern above) or use `structuredClone`, which understands them.

examples.result: `{"n":null,"i":null}`, then `{}`, then `"[1,null,2]"`, then a `TypeError` — four data-loss behaviors, each with its own rationale and workaround.

keyTakeaways: `JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space)`: the replacer filters (array = whitelist, function = transform or omit via `undefined`), the space pretty-prints.
A function replacer runs for every key at every depth, root first with key `""`; returning `undefined` deletes the property from the output.
`toJSON()` defines a class’s own wire format — Date uses it to emit ISO strings; stringify consults it before anything else.
`JSON.parse(text, reviver)` invokes the reviver post-order — deepest properties first, root last — letting each value be replaced or rebuilt.
JSON cannot say `undefined`, functions, symbols, `Map`/`Set`, or non-finite numbers: `NaN`/`Infinity` become `null`, objects drop the properties, arrays keep positions with `null`.
Circular structures throw `TypeError` — break the cycle with `toJSON` or a replacer; use the `_class` tag-and-revive pattern to round-trip instances.

quiz.q: What does `JSON.stringify({ a: NaN })` produce?
options: `{"a":null}` — NaN is not representable and becomes null
quiz.explanation: JSON numbers exclude NaN and Infinity, so both serialize as null — the value survives as a placeholder, unlike undefined/function values in objects, which vanish entirely.

quiz.q: How do `undefined` values behave differently in objects versus arrays during stringification?
options: They are dropped from objects but replaced with null in arrays, preserving positions
They throw in arrays but not objects
quiz.explanation: Object properties that cannot be serialized are omitted; array elements become null, because deleting a middle element would silently renumber the rest.

quiz.q: What does `JSON.stringify(user, ["name", "email"])` do?
options: Serializes only the properties named in the array, at every nesting level
Renames the properties to name and email
Sorts all properties and keeps the first two
Throws if user has more than two properties
quiz.explanation: The array replacer is a recursive whitelist: only listed keys appear in the output, at every depth — the quick way to build a public projection of an object.

quiz.q: A function replacer returns `undefined` for a key. What happens?
options: The property is serialized with the string "undefined"
The property is omitted from the JSON output entirely
The value is replaced with null
quiz.explanation: Returning undefined from the replacer deletes the key from the output — the mechanism behind hiding passwords and other secrets.

quiz.q: In what order is a reviver called by `JSON.parse`?
options: Root first, then top-down through the levels
Deepest properties first, with the root object last (key "")
In the order the keys appear in the text, depth irrelevant
quiz.explanation: Revivers run post-order: children are revived before their parents, so by the time an object is processed its transformed children are already in place — and the root is the final call with an empty-string key.

options: A TypeError, because functions are not serializable
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The code given stringifies an object mixing a number, `undefined`, a function, and an array containing `undefined`. Step 2: The governing rules are that `JSON.stringify` drops object properties whose values are `undefined`, functions, or symbols, while it converts those same values to `null` when they appear as array elements. Step 3: Tracing key by key, `a` serializes normally, `b` and `c` are dropped entirely, and `d` serializes with its middle hole rendered as `null`, giving `{"a":1,"d":[1,null,2]}`. Step 4: The distractors fail because no error is raised for unserializable values, `null` placeholders never appear for dropped object keys, and the array survives with its hole nulled. Step 5: Therefore the printed string keeps `a` and `d` only.

intro: JavaScript ships an internationalization engine: under the `Intl` namespace, **Collator** compares strings the way humans do, **NumberFormat** formats numbers and currency per locale, and **DateTimeFormat** (Section 11.4) does the same for dates. Alongside them, the **console** API goes far beyond `log` with tables, timers and stack traces, and the **URL** class parses and edits web addresses whose query strings are managed by `URLSearchParams` — the last piece being the difference between guessing at query parameters and reading them.
objectives: Sort strings locale-correctly with Intl.Collator, including natural numeric ordering
Format numbers and currency with Intl.NumberFormat
Use the console surface: format strings, tables, timers, trace, assert
Parse URLs with the URL class and read their structural parts
Read, test and mutate query strings with URLSearchParams

concepts.statement: The `Intl` object is the namespace for locale-aware behavior, parameterized by **BCP 47 language tags**: `"en"`, `"en-US"`, `"fr-CA"`, `"de-DE"`. The same data formats differently per locale — 12345.6 is `"12,345.6"` in en-US but `"12.345,6"` in de-DE — and every Intl constructor takes the tag (or `undefined` for the runtime default) plus an options object.
concepts.detail: Construct a formatter once and reuse it: building an `Intl` object is comparatively expensive, formatting through it is cheap — hoist formatters the way you would hoist compiled regexes.

concepts.statement: `new Intl.Collator(locale, options)` builds a comparator whose `compare(a, b)` sorts strings by locale rules: accented letters fold toward their base letter, and the `numeric: true` option sorts embedded numbers **by value** ("Response2" before "Response10"). Options include `sensitivity` (`"base"`, `"accent"`, `"case"`, `"variant"`) and `ignorePunctuation`.

`new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, options).format(n)` formats numbers: grouping separators and decimal marks per locale; `style: "currency"` with `currency: "EUR"` adds symbols and placement; `style: "percent"` multiplies by 100 and appends the sign; further options fix `minimumFractionDigits` or `notation: "compact"` (12k).

Beyond `console.log` and `console.error`/`warn`/`info` (each with its own severity styling), the console understands **printf-style placeholders** — `%s` string, `%d`/`%i` integer, `%f` float, `%o`/`%O` object, `%c` CSS — plus `console.table(data)` for aligned grids, `console.time(label)` / `console.timeEnd(label)` pairs for millisecond timings, `console.trace()` to print the current stack, `console.count(label)` to tally calls, and `console.assert(cond, msg)` which prints only on failure.

`new URL(absoluteUrl)` — or `new URL(relativeUrl, baseUrl)` — parses an address into structural parts exposed as properties: `protocol`, `hostname`, `port`, `host`, `pathname`, `search` (with its leading `?`), `hash` (with its `#`), the read-only `origin`, and the whole `href`. The parts are **live**: assign `url.pathname = "/x"` and `url.href` updates; the constructor also normalizes and validates, throwing on hopeless input.
concepts.detail:
```js
const u = new URL("https://api.example.com:8443/search?q=js#top");
u.hostname;   // "api.example.com"
u.port;       // "8443"
u.search;     // "?q=js"
u.hash;       // "#top"
u.origin;     // "https://api.example.com:8443"
```

concepts.statement: `url.searchParams` is a **URLSearchParams** object — also constructible alone from `"q=js&page=2"` — that manages a query string as ordered key/value pairs: `get(key)` (first value, as a **string**), `getAll(key)` (every value for repeated keys), `has`, `set(key, value)` (replaces *all* values of the key), `append` (adds another), `delete`, `sort`, and iteration as `[key, value]` pairs. Mutations write straight through to `url.search` and `url.href`, with percent-encoding handled automatically.
concepts.detail: The two classic bugs this class kills: comparing `params.get("page")` to the *number* 2 (it is the string `"2"`), and hand-concatenating query strings without encoding — `URLSearchParams.toString()` always emits correct `&`-joined, percent-encoded output.

examples.title: Sorting like a human: Collator and currency formatting

steps.label: Step 1: Default sort is by code units
steps.text: `[...names].sort()` compares UTF-16 code units: every uppercase letter sorts before every lowercase one, and accented characters sort near the end. The result is `["Répillion", "apple", "zebra", "èclair"]` — `"Répillion"` first because `R` (82) is less than `a` (97) — alphabetical only by accident.

steps.label: Step 2: The collator knows the alphabet
steps.text: With `new Intl.Collator("fr").compare`, `é` folds toward `e` and case is handled by the locale’s rules: the result is `["apple", "èclair", "Répillion", "zebra"]` — what a French reader calls alphabetical order. The comparator is a real function object, so it drops into `sort` directly.

steps.label: Step 3: Natural numeric ordering
steps.text: Plain comparison says `"Response10" < "Response2"` because it compares character by character (`"1" < "2"`). With `numeric: true`, embedded digit runs compare **as numbers**: `["Response2", "Response9", "Response10"]` — the ordering file lists, invoices and version numbers actually need.

steps.label: Step 4: Currency per locale
steps.text: The German formatter returns `"12.345,60 €"` — dot as thousands separator, comma as decimal mark, symbol after the number. The American formatter returns `"$12,345.60"` — the same number, two conventions, zero manual string surgery.

steps.label: Step 5: Hoist the objects
steps.text: Collators and formatters are built once and reused: construct them at module scope (Section 10.1) and call `compare`/`format` per item — the expensive locale data is consulted at construction.

examples.result: French order `["apple", "èclair", "Répillion", "zebra"]`, natural order `["Response2", "Response9", "Response10"]`, and `"12.345,60 €"` / `"$12,345.60"` — locale-aware output with no hand-rolled rules.

examples.title: Trace the engine: query strings with URLSearchParams

steps.label: Step 1: The URL constructor does the parsing
steps.text: `new URL(...)` validates and splits the address — no regex required (Section 11.3 is for fun; this is for production). The query string lives at `url.search` as `"?q=js&page=2&tags=modules&tags=es6"`.

steps.label: Step 2: Single and repeated values
steps.text: `p.get("q")` returns `"js"` — and `p.get("page")` returns `"2"`, **a string**: comparing it with `=== 2` is false, the single most common query-string bug. `p.getAll("tags")` returns `["modules", "es6"]` — the two values of the repeated key, in order.

steps.label: Step 3: Test before trusting
steps.text: `p.has("sort")` returns `false` here, and `p.get("missing")` returns `null` — distinguish absence (`null`) from present-but-empty (`""`) in validation code.

steps.label: Step 4: Mutations replace or append
steps.text: `p.set("page", "3")` first **removes every existing value of the key**, then adds one — `page` is now 3, and it would have collapsed multiple `page` values had there been any. `p.append("sort", "stars")` adds a second value if `sort` already existed, or creates the key.

steps.label: Step 5: The URL updates itself
steps.text: The searchParams object is a live view: after the mutations, `url.search` is `"?q=js&page=3&tags=modules&tags=es6&sort=stars"` and `url.href` carries the full updated address — encoding, separators and all, ready for `fetch(url)`.

examples.result: `"js"`, the string `"2"`, `["modules", "es6"]` — then a rewritten URL with `page=3` and `sort=stars`, all through the live view: never build a query string by concatenation again.

examples.title: The console beyond log

steps.label: Step 1: Format strings keep logs tidy
steps.text: `console.log("loaded %d users", 2)` substitutes the placeholder — `%s`, `%d`, `%f`, `%o` are the useful set — so the log statement reads like a sentence instead of an object dump.

steps.label: Step 2: Tables align objects
steps.text: `console.table(users)` renders the array as a grid with columns for the index and each property — the fastest way to eyeball a list of homogeneous records in a browser console or Node terminal.

steps.label: Step 3: Timers bracket the work
steps.text: `console.time("sort")` starts a labeled millisecond clock; `console.timeEnd("sort")` stops it and prints something like `"sort: 0.4ms"` — a zero-setup benchmark, precise enough to compare before/after a rewrite.

steps.label: Step 4: Traces answer "how did I get here?"
steps.text: `console.trace(...)` logs the message **plus the call stack** that reached it — the poor developer’s stack trace, inserted at exactly the suspicious line.

steps.label: Step 5: Assertions fail loudly
steps.text: `console.assert(cond, msg)` prints the message (with a stack, in Node) **only when the condition is false** — here `users.length > 0` is true, so nothing prints. It documents invariants without polluting successful runs.

examples.result: One line, one table, one measured timing, an on-demand stack trace and a silent invariant check — the console is a lightweight instrumentation suite, not just a print function.

keyTakeaways: Intl objects are locale-parameterized: construct once, reuse — comparison and formatting are cheap after construction is paid for.
Intl.Collator sorts the way readers expect: accent folding per locale, and `numeric: true` for natural number ordering.
Intl.NumberFormat handles grouping separators, decimal marks, currency symbols and placement per locale — never hand-place a thousands separator again.
The console supports `%s`/`%d`/`%o` placeholders, `table`, `time`/`timeEnd`, `trace`, `count` and `assert`.
`new URL(str, base?)` parses an address into live structural parts; `origin` is read-only, everything else is assignable.

`url.searchParams` is a live URLSearchParams view: `get` returns strings (first value), `getAll` returns repeats, `set` replaces all values of a key, `append` adds — and mutations rewrite `url.href` with correct encoding.

quiz.q: Why does `["Response10", "Response2"].sort()` put "Response10" first?
options: Because the default sort compares UTF-16 code units character by character, and "1" < "2"
Because sort is stable and preserves input order
It does not — Response2 comes first by default
quiz.explanation: Default sort is lexicographic by code units: at the first differing character, "1" (49) precedes "2" (50). Use `new Intl.Collator("en", { numeric: true }).compare` to compare digit runs by value.

quiz.q: What type does `url.searchParams.get("page")` return for `?page=2`?
quiz.explanation: Query values are always strings — `params.get("page") === 2` is false; convert explicitly (`Number(params.get("page"))`) when numbers are needed.

quiz.q: What is the difference between `params.set("tag", "a")` and `params.append("tag", "b")` when `tag` already has values?
options: set adds another value; append replaces all values
set replaces ALL existing values of the key with one new value; append adds a value alongside existing ones
set throws if the key exists
quiz.explanation: set removes every prior value of the key first, then installs one; append always adds — which is how repeated keys like tags accumulate.

quiz.q: Which console pair measures elapsed milliseconds?
quiz.explanation: time starts a labeled clock and timeEnd stops it, printing the elapsed duration — labels let multiple measurements interleave.

quiz.q: What does `new Intl.NumberFormat("de-DE", { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" }).format(12345.6)` return?
quiz.explanation: German formatting uses dots for grouping and a comma decimal mark, and places the euro symbol after the number — all handled by the locale data, not by your code.

intro: The `for/of` loop looks like a language feature baked in for arrays, but it is really a **protocol**: any object that can produce an iterator can be looped over, spread into an array, or destructured. The protocol is two small ideas — an **iterator** is an object with a `next()` method, and an **iterable** is an object with a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method that produces iterators — and they quietly power half the language surface you use every day.
objectives: State the iterator protocol: next() returns {value, done}
Distinguish an iterator from an iterable and connect them via Symbol.iterator
Trace how for/of consumes an iterable, one next() call at a time
List the built-in iterables and the language features that consume the protocol
Explain why iterators are one-shot cursors while iterables can produce fresh ones

concepts.statement: An **iterator** is any object with a `next()` method that takes no arguments and returns `{ value, done }`: `value` is the current item and `done` is `false` while more remain. The final call returns `{ value: undefined, done: true }` — and every later call returns that same exhausted result.
concepts.detail: The returned object is a plain record each time — a fresh `{value, done}` per call. Iterators may also implement optional `return()` and `throw()` methods (Section 12.4), but `next()` is the whole contract.

concepts.statement: An **iterable** is any object with a method named by the **well-known symbol** `Symbol.iterator` that takes no arguments and returns an iterator. The method is how the object *answers the question* “loop over me” — and because it is called fresh for each loop, a well-behaved iterable can be iterated again and again.
concepts.detail: Classes declare it with computed method names: `[Symbol.iterator]() { ... }`. A bare iterator that also has `[Symbol.iterator]() { return this }` is both iterator and iterable — exactly what generator objects do (Section 12.3).

The `while` form shows why an iterator’s `done` handling matters: the loop checks `done` *before* using `value`, so the return value carried by the final `{value, done: true}` is skipped by for/of — it is only visible to manual `next()` callers (Section 12.3).

concepts.statement: These types implement `Symbol.iterator` out of the box: **Array** (elements), **String** (code points, not UTF-16 code units), **Map** (entries `[key, value]`), **Set** (values), `arguments`, DOM **NodeList** and friends, and the **typed arrays** of Section 11.2. Note the absent: plain objects are **not** iterable — `for/of` over `{a: 1}` throws.
concepts.detail: String iteration walks code points, so `"héllo"` iterates 5 characters even though one of them occupies two UTF-16 code units — `"héllo".length` is still 5, but emoji-heavy strings can differ between `length` and iteration count.

concepts.statement: It is not just `for/of`: the **spread operator** (`[...set]`), **array destructuring** (`const [first, ...rest] = iterable`), `Array.from(iterable)`, `Promise.all(iterable)`, `Map`/`Set` constructors, `yield*` (Section 12.3) and `for await` (Section 13.4) all obtain their items through `Symbol.iterator`. Implement the protocol once and the whole language starts working with your type.
concepts.detail: Flanagan’s framing: iteration is the mechanism that **decouples** producers of sequences from consumers of sequences — the same way function interfaces decouple callers from implementations.

concepts.statement: An iterator is a **cursor with state**: once it reports `done: true` it is exhausted forever, and two loops that share one iterator each get only part of the data. The fix is structural — iterate `Symbol.iterator()` results, never a shared iterator; each call to for/of on an iterable requests a **fresh** iterator.
concepts.detail: This is also the feature: a one-pass iterator can represent a stream that cannot be rewound — lines arriving from a network, rows from a cursor — where “start over” has no meaning.

examples.title: Trace the engine: a hand-built iterator

steps.label: Step 1: The closure holds the cursor
steps.text: Calling `makeIterator` creates a scope with `i = 0` and returns an object whose `next` closes over both `i` and `items` — the position lives in the closure, not in a field someone could poke.

steps.label: Step 2: First next()
steps.text: With `i = 0` and three items, `0 < 3` holds, so the ternary returns `{ value: "a", done: false }` — and the post-increment advances `i` to 1 **as a side effect of producing the value**. Every next() both reports and advances.

steps.label: Step 3: The middle calls
steps.text: The second call returns `{ value: "b", done: false }` with `i` now 2; the third returns `{ value: "c", done: false }` with `i` now 3 — the last productive call, though `done` still reads `false` on delivery.

steps.label: Step 4: Exhaustion is permanent
steps.text: The fourth call finds `3 < 3` false and returns `{ value: undefined, done: true }` — note `value: undefined` explicitly, because `value` is part of the contract even when empty. Calls five, six, ten: the same exhausted object forever; nothing resets `i`.

steps.label: Step 5: Fresh iterators, fresh cursors
steps.text: `const it2 = makeIterator(["a", "b", "c"])` starts over at `i = 0` — independent state, same factory. Iterability comes from being able to call the factory; exhaustion comes from calling next too many times on one cursor.

examples.result: Four `next()` calls yield `{value: "a", done: false}`, `{value: "b", done: false}`, `{value: "c", done: false}`, `{value: undefined, done: true}` — the entire protocol in eleven lines.

examples.title: Making the iterator self-iterable

steps.label: Step 1: The trick
steps.text: Adding `[Symbol.iterator]() { return this }` makes the iterator its own iterable — the exact design generator objects use. When for/of asks “may I iterate you?”, the object answers “use me directly”.

steps.label: Step 2: for/of calls the protocol
steps.text: The loop executes `it[Symbol.iterator]()` (returning `it` itself), then calls `it.next()` — logging `"x"`, then `"y"` as the cursor advances through the loop’s internal while.

steps.label: Step 3: Exhaustion in a loop
steps.text: The third `next()` inside the loop’s check returns `done: true`, so the loop exits **after two iterations** — the loop never sees an undefined value, it only checks `done`.

steps.label: Step 4: The one-shot lesson
steps.text: A second `for (const v of it)` now runs **zero times**: `Symbol.iterator` returned the same exhausted cursor. Arrays work repeatedly because their `Symbol.iterator` builds a *new* iterator each call — the design decision Section 12.2 formalizes.

examples.result: One added method turns an iterator into a for/of-compatible iterable — at the cost of one-shot semantics, the same trade generators make.

keyTakeaways: An iterator is an object whose `next()` returns `{value, done}`; exhaustion is permanent and reports `value: undefined`.
An iterable is an object whose `[Symbol.iterator]()` **method** returns an iterator — fresh per call, which is what makes re-iteration possible.
for/of desugars to `Symbol.iterator()` + a `while (!done)` loop of `next()` calls; non-iterables throw TypeError immediately.
Built-in iterables: Array, String (code points), Map (entries), Set, `arguments`, NodeList, typed arrays — but **not** plain objects.
Spread, destructuring, `Array.from`, `Promise.all`, Map/Set constructors and `yield*` all consume the same protocol — implement it once, use it everywhere.
Iterators are stateful one-shot cursors: never share one between two loops; ask the iterable for a fresh one instead.

quiz.q: What must a method named `next()` on an iterator return?
options: The next value directly, or null when finished
An object like { value, done } — with done true on the final call
A Promise of the next value
quiz.explanation: The protocol is `{value, done}` per call: value carries the item and done reports whether iteration has finished — the pair, not the value alone.

quiz.q: What makes an object *iterable*?
options: Having a method named [Symbol.iterator] that returns an iterator
Being an array or a string
quiz.explanation: Iterability is the presence of the Symbol.iterator method — it is the capability for/of, spread and destructuring test for; next() alone only makes an iterator.

quiz.q: What does `for (const x of {}) { }` do?
quiz.explanation: Plain objects do not implement Symbol.iterator — object iteration requires Object.keys/values/entries (or a custom protocol), and for/of refuses before the body executes.

quiz.q: After an iterator returns `{value: undefined, done: true}`, what does its next call return?
options: The first value again — iterators restart
The same exhausted result {value: undefined, done: true}
quiz.explanation: Exhaustion is permanent by contract: once done is true, the iterator keeps reporting done — rewindable sequences come from re-invoking Symbol.iterator on the iterable, not from the cursor.

quiz.q: Which language feature does NOT consume the iteration protocol?
quiz.explanation: Object destructuring is property access by name — it never asks Symbol.iterator; spread in arrays, destructuring of arrays, and for/of over strings all go through the protocol.

intro: Making your own class iterable is one method: `[Symbol.iterator]()` returning an iterator. Do that and `for/of`, spread, destructuring and `Array.from` all accept your objects as first-class citizens. This section builds the canonical example — a `Range` class that iterates `[from, to]` inclusive — and then the detail that separates toy iterators from production ones: the optional `return()` method that runs when a loop quits early.
objectives: Implement [Symbol.iterator]() in a class with a computed method name
Trace iteration over a Range class and prove its re-iterability
Keep cursor state in the iterator, not the iterable, and explain why
Implement return() for cleanup when a loop exits early via break or throw

concepts.statement: A class or object literal defines the protocol method with **bracket syntax**: `[Symbol.iterator]() { ... }`. The brackets are not decoration — they evaluate the expression between them to compute the property name, which is how a symbol becomes a method name.
concepts.detail: Writing `symbolIterator()` would create a normal property named that — the engine would never find it. The brackets are required precisely because `Symbol.iterator` is a value, not an identifier.
The class may also define ordinary methods (`includes(x)`, `toString()`) — being iterable is a capability it acquires, not the whole identity.

concepts.statement: The cursor variables (`next`, `last`) are declared **inside** `[Symbol.iterator]()` — so each loop call creates them fresh. If the class instead kept `this.next` as an instance field, the second `for/of` over the same Range would resume at the exhausted position and iterate nothing.
concepts.detail: Design rule: the **iterable** describes what can be traversed; the **iterator** tracks how far one particular traversal has gone. Conflating the two is the classic first bug in custom iteration.

concepts.statement: An iterator may implement `return()`, called by the engine when a loop exits **before** exhaustion — via `break`, `return`, `continue` to an outer label, or a thrown exception. Its job is cleanup (closing files, releasing locks); it must return an iterator result, conventionally `{ done: true }`. Without it, early exits simply skip the cleanup.
concepts.detail: `return()` is not called when the loop finishes normally — exhaustion is already clean. Generators implement it automatically from their code structure (Section 12.4), which is one more reason to prefer them.

concepts.statement:
Because a Map’s default iteration yields `[key, value]` entries, the destructuring loop is the idiomatic dictionary walk:
```js
for (const [name, role] of team) {  // team is a Map
  console.log(name, "->", role);
}
```
And `Object.entries(obj)` bridges the non-iterable plain object into the same shape.
concepts.detail: That bridge is worth internalizing: `[...Object.entries(config)]`, `new Map(Object.entries(config))` — plain data flows into iterable structures through the entries view.

examples.title: Trace the engine: iterating a Range

steps.label: Step 1: The loop asks for an iterator
steps.text: The first for/of evaluates `r[Symbol.iterator]()`. That call runs the method body: `next = this.from` (1) and `last = this.to` (4) become closure variables, and the fresh iterator object is handed to the loop.

steps.label: Step 2: Four productive next() calls
steps.text: The internal while calls `next()` four times — values 1, 2, 3, 4 with `done: false` each time, the cursor advancing from 1 to 5. The fifth call finds `5 <= 4` false and returns `{ done: true }`, ending the loop after logging 1, 2, 3, 4.

steps.label: Step 3: Spread asks again
steps.text: `[...r]` invokes `r[Symbol.iterator]()` **a second time** — a second closure with `next = 1` — and drives it to exhaustion, collecting `[1, 2, 3, 4]`. The spread never reuses the loop’s old cursor; it cannot even see it.

steps.label: Step 4: The second loop, from scratch
steps.text: The second for/of likewise gets a third fresh iterator and logs 1, 2, 3, 4 again — **re-iterability**, the payoff of keeping the cursor in the iterator: `r` itself has no position to run down.

steps.label: Step 5: Ranges are values
steps.text: Because nothing is consumed, a Range composes like data: `[...new Range(1, 10)].filter(n => n % 3 === 0)` yields `[3, 6, 9]` — the range behaves as a value that can be viewed, not a resource that can be drained.

examples.result: Both loops and the spread each produce 1, 2, 3, 4 — three independent iterators from one iterable, because cursor state is created per iteration, never stored on the Range.

examples.title: Cleanup with return(): breaking out early

steps.label: Step 1: Iteration proceeds normally
steps.text: The loop obtains an iterator and calls `next()` twice, logging `"INFO start"` then `"INFO ok"` — the cursor `i` sits at 2.

steps.label: Step 2: The break fires mid-loop
steps.text: The third `next()` delivers `"ERROR crash"`; the body executes `break` — an **abrupt exit** with two items still unconsumed and the file handle still open.

steps.label: Step 3: The engine calls return()
steps.text: Because the loop exits before `done: true`, the for/of machinery calls `it.return()` — the iterator’s chance to tidy up. Our implementation closes the handle (`"closed app.log"` prints) and returns `{ done: true }` to acknowledge the shutdown.

steps.label: Step 4: What happens without return()
steps.text: A bare iterator with no `return()` method simply gets abandoned — the handle stays open until garbage collection notices it. The optional method exists so iteration can participate in deterministic resource management.

steps.label: Step 5: Normal exhaustion skips it
steps.text: Had the loop run to the end (no ERROR line), `done: true` would end it and `return()` would **not** be called — a completed traversal has nothing left to clean. Only abrupt exits — break, return, throw — trigger the callback.

examples.result: The loop logs two INFO lines, breaks on the error, and the `return()` method closes the file on the way out — early exit with cleanup, the contract production iterators honor.

keyTakeaways: Define `[Symbol.iterator]()` with bracket syntax — computed method names are how symbols become method names.
Keep cursor state in local variables of the iterator: each `Symbol.iterator()` call creates fresh state, making the iterable re-iterable.
The Range class is the canonical teaching example: `[from, to]` inclusive, one fresh cursor per loop, spread and destructuring work immediately.
The optional `return()` method runs on abrupt exits (break, return, throw) for cleanup — never on natural exhaustion.
Map iteration yields `[key, value]` pairs; `Object.entries()` bridges plain objects into the same shape.
A generator function (Section 12.3) writes this whole pattern in two lines — but the manual form is what the generator compiles down to conceptually.

quiz.q: Inside a class, the correct way to declare the iteration protocol method is:
quiz.explanation: The bracketed form computes the property name from the Symbol value; the plain identifier forms create ordinary properties the engine will never consult.

quiz.q: A Range class keeps its cursor `next` as an instance field `this.next` instead of a local in [Symbol.iterator](). What breaks?
options: The first for/of loop over a Range fails
The second loop over the same Range instance starts where the last ended — and iterates nothing if exhausted
Nothing — it is an equivalent design
quiz.explanation: Shared cursor state makes the iterable one-shot: the second traversal resumes at the abandoned position; fresh-local state per Symbol.iterator() call is what restores re-iterability.

quiz.q: When is an iterator’s `return()` method called?
options: When the loop exits early — break, return or a thrown error
When the iterator is garbage collected
quiz.explanation: return() is the abrupt-exit hook: for/of invokes it so the iterator can close files or release locks; natural exhaustion ends cleanly without it.

quiz.q: For `new Range(1, 3)` implemented as in this section, what is `[...range]`?
options: `[1, 2, 3]` — the range is inclusive of both ends
It throws — Ranges must be iterated with for/of only
quiz.explanation: The condition `next <= last` includes the upper bound: 1, 2, 3 — and spread consumes the same protocol for/of uses, so both produce the inclusive sequence.

quiz.q: Which loop shape is the idiomatic way to walk a `Map` named `team`?
options: `for (const entry of team)` then index `entry[0]` and `entry[1]`
quiz.explanation: Map iteration yields [key, value] arrays, so destructuring in the loop head names both parts at once — `for...in` is the property-name loop for plain objects and the wrong tool entirely.

intro: Writing iterators by hand is ceremony: the object, the closure, the `{value, done}` bookkeeping. **Generators** make it trivial: a function declared with `function*` whose body can **pause itself** at each `yield`. Calling a generator does not run its body — it returns a generator object that runs the body one segment at a time as you call `next()`. The result is iterable, reusable for exactly one pass, and powerful enough to express infinite sequences and recursive traversals in a few lines.
objectives: Define generators with function* and read yield as "pause and produce"
Trace stepped execution: where the body pauses, what next() returns, what resumes
Use the value passed to next(x) as the result of the paused yield expression
Delegate with yield* and explain its return value
Write lazy infinite sequences and consume them safely

concepts.statement: A function declared `function* g() { ... }` (or a method `*g() { ... }` in a class, or an expression) is a **generator function**. Calling it does **not** execute the body — it returns a **generator object**, paused at the very start. Nothing inside runs until the first `next()`.
concepts.detail: The asterisk is part of the function, not the name: `function* gen()` and `function *gen()` are the same, and the convention is `function* gen()`. `typeof` still reports `"function"` for the declaration itself.

concepts.statement: `yield value` **pauses** the generator: the enclosing `next()` call returns `{ value, done: false }` with the yielded operand. The next `next()` **resumes** execution exactly at that yield — local variables, loops and try blocks intact — and runs to the next yield or the end of the body.
concepts.detail: This is cooperative multitasking in miniature: the function chooses where to pause (`yield`) and the consumer chooses when to continue (`next()`). No callback, no closure juggling — the compiler saves your place.

concepts.statement: Because execution pauses *at* the yield, the value of the whole `yield x` expression is whatever the **next** `next(v)` call passes as its argument: `const got = yield x;` first produces `x`, then — on resume — `got` becomes `v`. Generators are two-way channels, not one-way taps.
concepts.detail: The first `next()` has nothing to resume, so its argument is ignored — a protocol quirk that generator-based coroutines must account for (Section 12.4 uses it for pumping pipelines).

concepts.statement: A `return x` inside a generator body (or falling off the end) produces the **final** result: `{ value: x, done: true }` — visible only to a manual `next()`. `for/of`, spread and `yield*` treat `done: true` as “stop” and **discard that value** — except `yield*`, which evaluates to it.
concepts.detail: After the final result, the generator is exhausted: further `next()` calls return `{ value: undefined, done: true }` forever — the one-shot cursor of Section 12.1.

concepts.statement: The object returned by a generator call implements the full iterator protocol — `next()`, `return()`, `throw()` (Section 12.4) — **and** `[Symbol.iterator]() { return this }`. So `for/of`, spread, destructuring and `Array.from` all consume generators directly; destructuring takes items from the front: `const [first] = fibGen()`.
concepts.detail: Being its own iterable is what makes a generator one-shot: two loops over the same generator object share one cursor. To re-iterate, call the generator function again — a fresh paused body each time.

concepts.statement: `yield* iterable` delegates: it pulls every item from the inner iterable and re-yields each one **as if written inline**, then evaluates to the inner iteration’s **return value** — the `{value, done: true}` value that for/of would have discarded. Recursion plus `yield*` flattens nested structures in two lines.

A generator only computes values **on demand**, so it can define a sequence with no end at all — `fibonacci()` can yield forever. Safety comes from the consumer side: take a bounded number of items, and the remaining mathematics simply never happens.
concepts.detail: This laziness is what pipes unbounded streams through `filter`/`map`-style generator stages (Section 12.4) — each stage processes one item at a time, memory stays flat, and early exit skips the rest of the sequence entirely.

examples.title: Trace the engine: stepping through a generator

steps.label: Step 1: Calling the function runs nothing
steps.text: `conversation()` evaluates and returns a generator object — the body has not executed a single statement; it is paused at the top. That is the fundamental difference from ordinary functions.

steps.label: Step 2: First next() runs to the first yield
steps.text: `g.next()` starts the body, which runs `yield "hello"` — producing `{ value: "hello", done: false }` — and pauses **at** the yield, the first statement only half-executed.

steps.label: Step 3: Second next() — still nothing resumes into a variable
steps.text: The second `g.next()` (no argument) resumes: the `yield "hello"` expression evaluates to `undefined` (nothing was passed), the body proceeds to `yield "what is your name?"` and pauses there, returning that value with `done: false`.

steps.label: Step 4: Third next("ada") — the argument becomes the yield’s value
steps.text: The call resumes the paused `const got = yield "what is your name?"` — and this time the argument flows in: `got` binds to `"ada"`. The body runs to `yield "nice to meet you, ada"` and pauses, returning it.

steps.label: Step 5: Fourth next() reaches the return
steps.text: Resuming, the body executes `return "goodbye"` — the generator finishes and the call returns `{ value: "goodbye", done: true }`. The return value exists **only** here; `for/of` would have stopped one call earlier and never seen it.

steps.label: Step 6: Fifth next() — exhausted
steps.text: The body is over; the call returns `{ value: undefined, done: true }`, as will every future call. Re-running the conversation requires a fresh `conversation()` — the body, its variables and its position die with the generator.

examples.result: The five calls return: `{value: "hello"}`, `{value: "what is your name?"}`, `{value: "nice to meet you, ada"}`, `{value: "goodbye", done: true}`, `{value: undefined, done: true}` — pause, resume, channel-in, return, exhaust.

examples.title: Flattening nested arrays with yield*

steps.label: Step 1: The outer generator walks the top level
steps.text: The spread drives `flatten([1, [2, [3, 4]], 5])`: item 1 is not an array, so `yield 1` produces it directly. Item 2 **is** an array, so the generator hits `yield* flatten([2, [3, 4]])` — creating a second, nested paused body.

steps.label: Step 2: Delegation is re-yielding
steps.text: The `yield*` loop is invisible from outside: each item the inner generator yields (first `2`) passes through the outer generator **as if it had been yielded there**. The consumer’s next() pulls through both levels; there is no nested iterator for it to manage.

steps.label: Step 3: Recursion bottoms out
steps.text: Inside, item `[3, 4]` triggers `yield* flatten([3, 4])` — a third level — which yields 3, then 4. Each value transits every enclosing `yield*` on its way out: 3 and 4 surface through two delegations.

steps.label: Step 4: The tail completes
steps.text: Back at the top, item 5 yields plainly. The spread collects, in order: `1`, `2`, `3`, `4`, `5` — a **depth-first** walk produced by recursion that reads like the data structure it traverses.

steps.label: Step 5: Why this beats the loop version
steps.text: An iterative flattener needs an explicit stack and a while loop pushing and popping; the recursive generator lets the **call stack** be the data stack, with `yield*` doing the wiring — the same structure, a third of the code, and lazy: each value is produced only when the consumer asks.

examples.result: `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` — depth-first flattening where `yield*` transparently forwards every nested yield to the top.

examples.title: An infinite fibonacci generator

steps.label: Step 1: A loop with no exit
steps.text: The `for (;;)` never ends by design: the generator defines the *entire* sequence 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8... without computing any of it. Called alone, `fibonacci()` just returns a paused body — no infinite loop runs yet.

steps.label: Step 2: take() is a bounded lens
steps.text: `take(6, seq)` loops over the sequence (the protocol of Section 12.1) and re-yields six items, then `return`s on the seventh pull — a generator wrapping a generator, both lazy.

steps.label: Step 3: The pull chain
steps.text: The spread pulls from `take`; `take` pulls from `fibonacci`; the fibonacci body executes exactly **seven** segments — six yields producing 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 plus the partial run that hits the `return`. The remaining infinite mathematics never happens.

steps.label: Step 4: The result
steps.text: `[...take(6, fibonacci())]` is `[0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5]` — bounded consumption of an unbounded definition, with memory flat: only `a`, `b`, `n` and the current item ever exist.

steps.label: Step 5: Composability
steps.text: Because every consumer uses the same protocol, `take` works on **any** iterable — arrays, Ranges, other generators — and new stages (skip, map, filter as generators) compose the same way. This is the pipeline pattern Section 12.4 develops into a full toolkit.

examples.result: Six Fibonacci numbers from an endless generator: laziness means the definition can be infinite because evaluation is finite — demand-driven computation.

keyTakeaways: A `function*` call does not run the body; it returns a generator object paused at the start.
`yield x` pauses the body and returns `x` from the current `next()`; the next call resumes exactly there with all local state intact.
The value passed to `next(v)` becomes the value of the paused `yield` expression — a two-way channel (the first call’s argument is ignored).
A `return x` in the body produces the final `{value: x, done: true}` — for/of discards it; `yield*` evaluates to it.
Generator objects implement next/return/throw and `[Symbol.iterator]() { return this }` — iterable, but one-shot: re-iterate by calling the function again.
`yield* iterable` re-yields every inner item inline; recursion plus `yield*` flattens or walks nested structures in a few lines.
Generators are lazy: infinite sequences are safe when consumers bound them — the uncomputed tail never runs.

quiz.q: What does `const g = gen();` do for `function* gen() { console.log("ran"); yield 1; }`?
options: Returns a generator object — the body has not started, so nothing logs
Throws, because generators must be invoked with next()
quiz.explanation: Calling a generator function never executes its body; it returns a paused generator object — the first line runs only when the first next() is called.

quiz.q: Inside a generator, `const got = yield x;` — what is `got` bound to?
options: Whatever argument is passed to the NEXT next() call that resumes this yield
quiz.explanation: Execution pauses at the yield; when the consumer calls next(v), v becomes the value of the yield expression and thus of got — the mechanism that makes generators two-way.

quiz.q: A generator body ends with `return "end"`. Which consumer can ever see the string "end"?
options: `for (const v of gen())` — it logs "end" last
A manual `next()` call, which receives { value: "end", done: true }
None — the value is discarded by every consumer
quiz.explanation: Return values ride only the final {value, done: true} result, which loop constructs treat purely as "stop" — only a hand-driven next() (or yield*) reads the value.

quiz.q: What does `yield* inner` do inside a generator?
options: Yields the inner generator object itself as one value
Delegates: re-yields every value the inner iterable produces, then evaluates to its return value
Runs the inner generator to completion immediately, discarding values
quiz.explanation: yield* is delegation — every inner item surfaces as if yielded locally, and the whole expression’s value is the inner iteration’s final return value.

quiz.q: Why is an infinite generator like `function* fibonacci() { for (;;) { yield a; ... } }` safe?
options: The engine stops it after 1000 values
Nothing runs until a consumer pulls values — bounded consumption computes only what is demanded
It is not safe — it will hang the program on call
The for(;;) is special-cased by generators
quiz.explanation: Generators are lazy: calling fibonacci() runs nothing, and each next() executes only to the next yield — the infinite tail beyond the consumer’s interest is never evaluated.

options: `{ value: 1, done: false }`, `{ value: 2, done: false }`, then `{ value: undefined, done: true }`
`{ value: 1, done: true }` on the first call
A TypeError, because generators need a `for/of` loop
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The code given creates a two-yield generator and pulls it three times. Step 2: The governing rules are that a generator body stays paused until `next()` is called, that each `next()` runs to the following `yield` and returns a `{ value, done }` record, and that running past the last `yield` returns `done: true`. Step 3: Tracing pull by pull, the first call runs to `yield 1` and reports `{ value: 1, done: false }`, the second runs to `yield 2` and reports `{ value: 2, done: false }`, and the third finishes the body reporting `{ value: undefined, done: true }`. Step 4: The distractors fail because `next()` always wraps values in result records, the first call pauses rather than completes, and manual `next()` calls are fully supported. Step 5: Therefore the three result records print in that order.

intro: The advanced half of generators makes them a general-purpose control-flow tool: `next(x)` pushes values **in**, `throw(e)` injects an exception **at the paused yield**, `return(x)` terminates with `finally` cleanup — and generators that consume other generators become **lazy pipelines**. Then the finale: `async function*` marries generators with `await`, producing asynchronous sequences that `for await...of` drains — the pattern for reading paginated APIs and streaming data (Section 13.4 continues the story).
objectives: Drive generators with next(x), return(x) and throw(e) — and catch injected exceptions inside
Build lazy pipelines by chaining generator functions that consume iterables
Declare async generators with async function* and consume them with for await...of
Trace an async generator walking a paginated HTTP API end to end

concepts.statement: The argument of `it.next(x)` becomes the value of the currently paused `yield` expression. A pipeline consumer uses this to pump data **into** a generator mid-flight — each `yield` becomes a request for the next input: `const input = yield output;` produces `output` and, on resume, receives the caller’s next value.
concepts.detail: The asymmetry to remember: the **first** `next()` argument is ignored (nothing is paused yet), so a pump loop usually discards the first result or primes the generator with `next()` before feeding it.

concepts.statement: `it.return(value)` acts as if a `return` statement were inserted at the paused yield: the generator body unwinds — any `finally` blocks **run** — and the call returns `{ value, done: true }`. Afterwards the generator is exhausted.
concepts.detail: This is the manual form of the for/of early-exit cleanup from Section 12.2: the loop’s break calls `return()`; you can call it yourself to shut a generator down deterministically — closing a pipeline stage you no longer need.

concepts.statement: `it.throw(error)` makes the currently paused `yield` **throw** the given error, as if the expression itself raised it. The generator can catch it with a `try/catch` around that yield — turning the generator into a coroutine with external signaling; an uncaught injected error propagates back out of the `throw()` call itself.
concepts.detail: Between `next`, `throw` and `return`, the caller holds all three controls of a paused generator: advance, alarm and abort — the vocabulary of cooperative coroutines.

concepts.statement: A generator function that takes an **iterable** and yields transformed items composes with others: `[...pipeline3(pipeline2(pipeline1(source)))]` — each stage pulls one item at a time from the stage above. Nothing is buffered: map and filter stages stay $O(1)$ in memory, and stages run interleaved per item, not per stage.

`async function* gen() { ... }` allows `await` inside the body, and each `yield` still pauses — but now `next()` returns a **Promise** of `{value, done}`, resolving when the awaited operation completes and the next item is ready. Async generators are consumed with `for await (const x of gen())`, never with plain `for/of`.
concepts.detail: The rule of thumb: `yield` produces a value to the consumer; `await` consumes a value from a promise. In `const data = yield await fetchJson(url)`, the fetch finishes first, then its result is yielded.

concepts.statement: `for await (const item of asyncIterable)` awaits each `next()` promise before running the body with the resolved value — sequential asynchronous iteration, one item at a time, in order. It also accepts **sync** iterables (awaiting each yielded value if it is a promise), and it rejects the whole loop if any awaited step rejects.
concepts.detail: Where `Promise.all` (Section 13.2) fetches a **fixed** array of things in parallel, `for await` drains a **sequence of unknown length** — pages, lines, events — the async counterpart of Section 12.1’s one-shot iterators.

examples.title: Trace the engine: return() and throw() into a guarded generator

steps.label: Step 1: The try is live across the yields
steps.text: Both yields sit inside `try`. While the generator is paused at `yield 1`, that try block is *active* — so both an injected throw and an early return interact with it.

steps.label: Step 2: return() unwinds through finally
steps.text: `g.next()` yields 1 and pauses. `g.return("stop")` now behaves as if `return "stop"` replaced the paused `yield 1`: the `finally` block runs — `"cleanup"` logs — and the call returns `{ value: "stop", done: true }`. The catch block is skipped (no error), and `g` is finished.

steps.label: Step 3: throw() makes the yield raise
steps.text: For `h`: after the first `next()`, `h.throw(new Error("inject"))` turns the paused `yield 1` expression into a throwing expression — control jumps to the `catch`.

steps.label: Step 4: The generator catches and recovers
steps.text: Inside, `e` is the injected Error; the catch logs `"caught Error: inject"` and runs `yield "recovered"` — so the `throw()` call itself returns `{ value: "recovered", done: false }`. The generator survived the injection and can continue.

steps.label: Step 5: The control picture
steps.text: The caller of a paused generator can advance it (`next`), raise into it (`throw`) or end it (`return`) — and the generator’s own `try/catch/finally` decides what those mean. This is exactly the control surface `for/of` uses invisibly on every `break` and every body exception.

examples.result: Path one logs `"cleanup"` and ends with `{value: "stop", done: true}`; path two logs `"caught Error: inject"` and returns `{value: "recovered", done: false}` — shutdown and injection, both catchable.

examples.title: A lazy pipeline of generator stages

steps.label: Step 1: Three paused bodies, zero work
steps.text: The expression evaluates `map(source, ...)`, wraps it in `filter`, wraps that in `take` — each call returns a fresh, paused generator. The source array is untouched; no squares exist yet.

steps.label: Step 2: The spread pulls item by item
steps.text: The spread drives `take.next()`, which pulls `filter.next()`, which pulls `map.next()`, which pulls one item from the array (1), squares it (1) and yields; filter tests `1 % 2 === 0` — false — and pulls again (2 → 4, passes). One value has crossed all three stages.

steps.label: Step 3: Interleaving, not staging
steps.text: The stages do NOT run “map everything, then filter everything”: 1 is mapped, tested and rejected *before* 2 is mapped. Work happens per item, across all stages — each stage holds at most one value in flight, so memory stays $O(1)$ regardless of source size.

steps.label: Step 4: take() stops the chain early
steps.text: After delivering 4, 16, 36 — three even squares — the next pull finds `n` at 0 and `return`s. The remaining seven items (7 through 10 and their squares) are **never computed**: take’s return unwinds, and the abandoned generators become garbage.

steps.label: Step 5: Compare the array version
steps.text: `source.map(x => x * x).filter(...).slice(0, 3)` builds two full intermediate arrays of ten squares — and computes all ten — before slicing. The generator chain computes exactly four inputs (1, 2, 4, 6) and produces three outputs. On infinite sources, only the pipeline version terminates at all.

examples.result: `[4, 16, 36]` — squares of 2, 4 and 6 — computed lazily, interleaved across stages, with early exit skipping the rest of the source entirely.

examples.title: Trace the engine: an async generator over a paginated API

steps.label: Step 1: Nothing runs at call time
steps.text: `searchPages(...)` returns an async generator object immediately — no fetch has been issued. The `for await` loop then calls `next()` and awaits the returned promise: iteration pauses the *loop*, not the thread (Section 13.3).

steps.label: Step 2: The first page
steps.text: The body starts: `await fetch(url)` suspends until the response arrives; `await response.json()` suspends again for the body. Then `yield* page.results` — and here async meets delegation: each item is re-yielded as its own asynchronous step.

steps.label: Step 3: The loop receives items one at a time
steps.text: For a page of `[item1, item2]`, the loop body runs twice (logging two ids), each iteration awaiting one more `next()` — which resumes inside `yield*` to produce the next item without refetching.

steps.label: Step 4: The cursor advances
steps.text: When the page is exhausted, the delegation ends and `url = page.next` either points at the next page — the `while` loops and a **new** fetch begins — or is `null`, ending the loop with `done: true` after the last item.

steps.label: Step 5: Errors reject the whole loop
steps.text: A failed fetch throws inside the body; because `next()` returned a promise, that promise **rejects**; because the loop `await`s it, the rejection surfaces at the `for await` — where an ordinary `try/catch` (Section 13.3) handles it. Meanwhile only two items ever sit in memory: the current one and the page in hand.

examples.result: The loop logs every id across every page — sequential, lazy, constant-memory — with pagination, backpressure and error propagation handled by three keywords: `async`, `yield*`, `await`.

keyTakeaways: `next(x)` feeds a value into the paused yield — generators are two-way channels; the first call’s argument is ignored.
`return(x)` terminates as if `return` sat at the paused yield — `finally` blocks run; `throw(e)` makes the paused yield raise, catchable inside the body.
Generator stages (map, filter, take over an iterable) compose into lazy pipelines: $O(1)$ memory per stage, work interleaved per item, early exit skips computation.
`async function*` permits `await` inside the body; each `next()` returns a Promise of `{value, done}`.
`for await (const x of asyncIterable)` drains async sequences in order, one item at a time — and rejects the loop if any step rejects.
Async generators fit unknown-length sources: paginated APIs, streams, message queues — where `Promise.all` fits only fixed known arrays.

quiz.q: A generator is paused at `yield` inside a try block. What does `it.return(v)` do?
options: Resumes as if the yield returned v as its value
Unwinds the body from the paused yield — running finally blocks — and returns {value: v, done: true}
quiz.explanation: return() behaves like a return statement inserted at the pause point: the finally chain executes, the catch is bypassed (no error occurred), and the generator finishes with the given value.

quiz.q: What happens when `it.throw(new Error("x"))` is called on a generator paused at a yield inside a try/catch?
options: The error propagates out of throw() immediately
The paused yield expression throws; if a surrounding catch exists it runs — otherwise the error escapes the throw() call
The generator restarts from the beginning
quiz.explanation: throw() converts the paused yield into a raising expression: an enclosing catch can recover (and even yield again); without one, the exception propagates back to the throw() caller.

quiz.q: In a pipeline `take(3, filter(map(src, f), p))`, when is the square of the 7th element computed?
options: Immediately — every stage buffers its input
Never — take(3) ends the pipeline after three outputs, so items beyond the needed ones are never mapped
After the loop completes, as cleanup
quiz.explanation: Stages pull one item at a time; once take has yielded three values it returns, and the abandoned upstream generators never advance — the 7th element is never squared.

quiz.q: What does calling `next()` on an **async** generator return?
options: A Promise that resolves to {value, done}
quiz.explanation: async function* makes every next() asynchronous: it returns a promise that resolves with the usual iterator result once the awaited operations complete — which is why for await is required to consume it.

quiz.q: Which source is the BEST fit for an async generator with for await?
options: A fixed array of five URLs to fetch in parallel
A paginated API whose next URL arrives with each response, and whose total length is unknown
A single file read into memory
quiz.explanation: for await drains sequential, unknown-length asynchronous sequences — pages, lines, events; a fixed known set of parallel work is the job of Promise.all (Section 13.2).

intro: Network requests, disk reads and timers take milliseconds to seconds — a geological age compared with nanosecond CPU work — so a single-threaded language must never sit and wait. JavaScript’s answer is **asynchronous, event-driven programming**: functions register interest in the future, return immediately, and the **event loop** calls them back when the world has an answer. This section covers the callback style that started it all, the error-first convention that disciplined it, and the “pyramid of doom” that motivated promises.
objectives: Explain why single-threaded JavaScript must use asynchronous I/O
Describe the event loop and the run-to-completion rule that governs callbacks
Read and write event-driven handlers with addEventListener and timers
Apply Node’s error-first callback convention
Recognize callback hell and flatten it with named continuations

concepts.statement: A JavaScript program has **one call stack** and one thread of execution: any operation that blocks it — waiting on a disk, a network, a user — freezes every click, animation and other tab served by that thread. So long-latency operations are structured as requests plus **callbacks**: the code registers a function and returns; the engine keeps working meanwhile. (Operating System Concepts Chapter 4 gives the kernel-side view — threads and scheduling; JavaScript deliberately avoids shared-memory threads and lets the OS do the waiting. Chapter 12 of that book covers the I/O subsystem — interrupts and DMA — that actually delivers the data while JavaScript looks away.)
concepts.detail: The contrast with threads: a thread-per-request server (the OSC Ch 4 model) interleaves work by preempting stacks; a JavaScript runtime interleaves work by returning to one loop between callbacks — cooperative instead of preemptive, with no locks because nothing is ever mid-statement.
