concepts.statement: The runtime keeps a queue of pending callbacks. The **event loop** takes one, runs it **to the end** — every statement, synchronously — then takes the next. No callback ever starts while another is half-finished: there is no preemption inside JavaScript, so no callback needs a lock to protect shared state.
concepts.detail: This is the run-to-completion rule, and it is why a slow `while` loop freezes the page while ten timers pile up behind it. The microtask refinement — promises jumping the queue — arrives in Section 13.2.

concepts.statement: Programs are organized as **registrations**: `element.addEventListener("click", handler)`, `fs.readFile(path, callback)`, `setTimeout(fn, ms)` — each parks a function for the future and returns at once. The program’s shape becomes: set up, return quickly, and exist only inside handlers thereafter.

Node standardized the shape of asynchronous failure: the callback’s **first parameter is reserved for an error** — `null`/`undefined` on success — and results follow it. The first thing a correct handler does is check that parameter: `if (err) { handleIt; return; }`. Throwing from an async operation is useless because no stack is there to catch it.

concepts.term: Callback hell — the pyramid of doom
concepts.statement: When step two needs step one’s result, callbacks nest: each successive operation is indented inside the previous callback, and the code drifts rightward into a **pyramid**. The costs: unreadable flow, duplicated error handling at every level, and **inversion of control** — your continuation lives inside a function you handed to someone else’s API.
concepts.detail: The classic mitigations before promises: named functions instead of anonymous ones (each step calls the next by name, keeping the source flat), and module-level state to carry results across steps. Promises (13.2) and async/await (13.3) solve it structurally instead of stylistically.

examples.title: Trace the engine: three clocks on one event loop

steps.label: Step 1: The synchronous prefix
steps.text: The script itself is the first unit of run-to-completion work. `"start"` logs; both timers are **scheduled** — their callbacks parked with due times — and the `setTimeout` calls return instantly without waiting.

steps.label: Step 2: The spin occupies the one thread
steps.text: The `while` loop burns 100 ms **on the only thread there is**. The 0 ms timer is already due — but “due” only means eligible; a queued callback cannot interrupt running code. It waits.

steps.label: Step 3: The script finishes
steps.text: `"sync done"` logs and the initial unit of work ends. Only now does the event loop look at the queue: the 0 ms callback is eligible and runs — `"0ms timer"` — a full 100 ms *after* its nominal time.

steps.label: Step 4: The queue drains as things become due
steps.text: The loop idles (the host may render, other tabs may run) until the 200 ms timer matures around t = 200 — measured from scheduling, and unaffected by the spin since both started at t ≈ 0 — and `"200ms timer"` logs.

steps.label: Step 5: The lessons
steps.text: One: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` means “as soon as the loop is free”, never “immediately” — the minimum-delay caveat of Section 11.6’s timers. Two: a busy loop delays everything behind it, because run-to-completion gives callbacks no way to preempt. The whole model — including the microtask refinement coming in 13.2 — is about *when the loop is free*.

examples.result: Output order: `"start"`, `"sync done"`, `"0ms timer"` (about 100 ms late), `"200ms timer"` — timers fire when the single thread gets around to them.

examples.title: The pyramid of doom, then the flattened refactor

steps.label: Step 1: Read the shape of the pyramid
steps.text: Each step’s logic lives **inside** the previous step’s callback, indented one level deeper — three operations, three levels, and the final `"done"` log is indented as far right as the screen allows. Sequential logic has become spatially nested.

steps.label: Step 2: Count the error handling
steps.text: Three anonymous callbacks, three `err` checks, three `console.error` calls — and every future step duplicates the same guard. One missed check and an error silently becomes `undefined` data in the next step.

steps.label: Step 3: The inversion of control
steps.text: The continuation of each step is now a function owned by `fs.readFile` — if the API calls it twice, or never, or on the wrong turn of the loop, your program simply misbehaves. You have handed over *when and whether your own code runs*.

steps.label: Step 4: Flatten with named continuations
Step 5: The real fix is structural
steps.text: Promises (Section 13.2) make each step **return** a value instead of accepting a continuation — chaining replaces nesting; async/await (13.3) then restores the original top-to-bottom shape entirely. Know the pyramid to appreciate why both exist.

examples.result: The nested version works but reads inside-out with triplicated error handling; named functions flatten the source yet keep the same hazards — the structural cure is promises.

keyTakeaways: One thread, one call stack: blocking I/O would freeze everything, so long operations are requests plus callbacks and the code returns immediately.
The event loop runs each queued callback to completion before starting the next — no callback preempts another, so no locks are needed (contrast OSC Ch 4 threads).
The OS does the actual waiting — interrupts and DMA deliver the data (OSC Ch 12); JavaScript just gets a callback on a future loop turn.
Node’s error-first convention — `(err, result) => ...` with the err check first — is the discipline that made async failures explicit.
Sequencing with callbacks nests rightward into the pyramid of doom: duplicated error handling and inversion of control.
Named continuations flatten the pyramid stylistically; promises and async/await fix it structurally.

quiz.q: What is the Node.js error-first convention?
options: The callback’s first parameter is reserved for an error value — null/undefined on success — and results come after it
Errors are passed as the second argument, after the result
Callbacks must be wrapped in try/catch
quiz.explanation: Node reserves the callback’s first parameter for the error so failure is impossible to overlook: every correct handler checks err before touching the results that follow it.

quiz.q: A `while` loop spins for 200 ms, and a timer with a 0 ms delay was scheduled before it started. When does the timer callback run?
options: After roughly 200 ms — once the current unit of work completes, since callbacks cannot preempt running code
quiz.explanation: Run-to-completion: the event loop only picks up eligible callbacks between units of work, so a 0 ms timer fires as soon as the busy loop yields — about 200 ms late.

quiz.q: Why does throwing an exception inside an async operation fail to inform the caller?
options: Exceptions are disabled after the first await
By the time the error occurs, the original call stack has long since returned — there is no catcher left to unwind into
The event loop catches all exceptions silently
quiz.explanation: The request function already returned; its stack is gone — which is exactly why async APIs deliver errors through the callback (or, later, promise rejections) instead of exceptions.

quiz.q: What is “inversion of control” in callback-based code?
options: Callbacks always run on the main thread
Your continuation is a function you hand to another API, which decides if, when and how many times your code runs
Control flow inverted into a loop
Errors control the flow of the program
quiz.explanation: Passing a callback transfers authority over your program’s next step to the callee — the trust problem promises address with guaranteed, one-time settlement semantics.

quiz.q: Which refactoring flattens the pyramid of doom WITHOUT changing the underlying callback mechanism?
options: Replacing anonymous callbacks with named step functions
quiz.explanation: Named continuations turn nested arrows into a flat sequence of top-level functions — better readability, though duplication and inversion of control persist until promises arrive.

intro: A **Promise** is an object that represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation: a placeholder for a value that is not here yet but whose arrival — or failure — you can plan around. Promises turn callbacks inside out: instead of handing your continuation to the operation, the operation hands **you** a value-like object you can call `.then()` on. Chains replace nesting, errors propagate automatically, and the microtask queue gives promise callbacks a guaranteed — and surprising — place in the event loop order.
objectives: State the three promise states and the semantics of settling
Build chains with then, catch and finally, tracing value and error flow through them
Create promises with executors and with Promise.resolve/reject
Explain and use all, race, allSettled and any
Predict execution order across the script, microtask and timer queues — including the classic interview question

concepts.statement: A promise is an object in one of three states: **pending** (the operation has not finished), **fulfilled** (it succeeded — carrying a **value**), or **rejected** (it failed — carrying a **reason**, conventionally an Error). Fulfilled and rejected together are **settled**, and settling is **final**: a promise’s state and payload never change again.
concepts.detail: Immutability of settlement is what makes promises composable: any number of `.then()` callbacks can be attached at any time, before or after the result arrives, and they all see the same answer.

concepts.statement: `p.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)` registers the success path (and optionally the failure path); `p.catch(fn)` is shorthand for `then(null, fn)`; `p.finally(fn)` runs cleanup on **both** paths, passing value or reason through untouched. All three return a **new** promise — the basis of chaining.
concepts.detail: The second then argument is rare in practice — a catch later in the chain reads more naturally and catches the onFulfilled handler’s own errors too.

concepts.statement: Because each `then` returns a new promise, calls stack left-to-right, not inside-out: a callback’s **return value** fulfills the next link; a **thrown error** rejects it. Rejections skip every success callback until the nearest `catch`, which can recover — its return value resumes the success chain below it.
concepts.detail: This is the inversion of the pyramid: the steps of Section 13.1’s file pipeline become `readConfig().then(readData).then(writeSummary).catch(logError)` — one indentation level, one error handler at the end.

concepts.statement: `new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })` invokes its **executor** function immediately, on the current stack — the async part is not the executor but the **callbacks**: resolve/reject only record the outcome and schedule already-registered handlers on the **microtask queue**. A promise can therefore settle before any `.then()` was ever attached.

`Promise.resolve(v)` returns a promise fulfilled with `v` — or, if `v` is already a promise, that very promise unchanged (flattening, so chains never nest promises inside promises). `Promise.reject(e)` returns a rejected promise. Both are the idiomatic ways to enter a chain from a plain value.
concepts.detail: A non-promise object with a `.then()` method is a **thenable** — Promise.resolve adopts it, which is how promise-like libraries interoperate with native chains.

concepts.statement: Static methods run arrays of promises together: **`Promise.all(ps)`** fulfills with an array of all values **in input order** (not completion order) once every promise fulfills — or rejects immediately with the first rejection (fail-fast). **`race(ps)`** settles with the first promise to settle at all — value or reason. **`allSettled(ps)`** never rejects: it fulfills with `{status, value}`/`{status, reason}` records for every input. **`any(ps)`** fulfills with the first fulfillment, rejecting with an `AggregateError` only if they all fail.
concepts.detail: Use all for “need everything, together”; race for timeouts and first-wins; allSettled for batch reports where partial failure is normal; any for mirrors and fallbacks — “the first that works”.

concepts.term: Microtasks: then callbacks jump the queue
concepts.statement: Promise callbacks run as **microtasks**: when the current unit of work finishes, the engine drains the entire microtask queue — **all** of it — before taking the next timer or I/O event from the macrotask queue. So `p.then(f)` beats `setTimeout(g, 0)` even though both are “later”: script first, then microtasks, then timers.
concepts.detail: This scheduling is where JavaScript meets the scheduler theory of OSC Chapter 4: the event loop is a scheduler with two priority classes, and microtasks are the higher-priority queue — one callback deep, but with a strict, examinable ordering.

concepts.statement: Node’s `util.promisify(fs.readFile)` wraps an error-first callback function into one returning a promise; the modern `fs/promises` module and `fetch` are promise-native from the start — returning to the file pipeline of 13.1 as `await fsPromises.readFile(...)`.
concepts.detail: This is the migration path from callback-era code: wrap the old API at the boundary, then consume it with modern chains and async/await (13.3).

examples.title: Trace the engine: values and errors through a chain
examples.problem:
Predict the logged output of this chain, including which callbacks never run:
```js
Promise.resolve(2)
  .then(x => x * 3)
  .then(x => { throw new Error("boom"); })
  .then(x => { console.log("skipped:", x); return x + 1; })
  .catch(e => { console.log("caught:", e.message); return 99; })
  .then(x => console.log("final:", x));
```

steps.label: Step 1: The first link passes 2 through arithmetic
steps.text: `Promise.resolve(2)` enters the chain; the first callback maps it to `6`, and because it returns a plain number, the next link’s promise fulfills with `6`.

steps.label: Step 2: The throw becomes a rejection
steps.text: The second callback throws `"boom"` — the throw is caught by the machinery and converted into the **rejection** of the next promise in the chain. No value propagates past a throw.

steps.label: Step 3: Success callbacks are skipped, not crashed
steps.text: The third `.then` never executes its callback — its input is rejected, so it passes the rejection along intact. Skipping is the rule: a rejection slides past every onFulfilled until a handler for rejections exists.

steps.label: Step 4: The catch recovers
steps.text: `.catch` receives the Error — `e.message` is `"boom"`, which logs `"caught: boom"` — and **returns `99`**, a normal value. That return fulfills the next link: recovery means the chain is back on the success track.

steps.label: Step 5: The final link sees the recovered value
steps.text: The last `.then` runs with `99` and logs `"final: 99"`. Total picture: one multiplication, one conversion of throw to rejection, one skip, one recovery, one resumed value — the entire state machine of chaining in five links.

examples.result: Exactly two lines log: `"caught: boom"` and `"final: 99"` — the middle success callback is skipped by the rejection, and the catch’s return value restarts the success path.

examples.title: Trace the engine: all versus race, with a clock

steps.label: Step 1: Read the clock
steps.text: `fast` fulfills at t = 100 ms, `slow` at t = 300 ms, and `fail` is rejected **at construction** — t = 0, before the race even attaches its handlers.

steps.label: Step 2: Promise.all waits for everyone
steps.text: At t = 100, `fast` resolves but `all` stays pending — it needs every input. At t = 300, `slow` resolves and `all` fulfills **now**: it logs `all: ["slow", "fast"]` — the values appear in **input order** (`[slow, fast]`), not completion order (`fast` finished first).

steps.label: Step 3: The fail-fast rule
steps.text: Had `fail` been in the `all` array, the aggregate would have rejected at t = 0 with `Error("no")`, discarding `fast` and `slow` entirely — `all` reports the first **rejection** immediately, not the last result. Partial results are not delivered.

steps.label: Step 4: race takes the first settler of any kind
steps.text: In `Promise.race([fast, fail])`, `fail` settled first (t = 0), so the race **rejects** with that same error: the catch logs `"race err: no"` at t = 0. `fast` still resolves later at t = 100 — the race has already ended; later settlers are ignored, not errors.

steps.label: Step 5: Choosing the combinator
steps.text: all for all-or-nothing parallel work; race when the fastest answer wins — including the timeout pattern `Promise.race([fetchIt, timeoutPromise])`; allSettled when you want a full report including failures; any when any single success is enough and you only fail if every option fails.

examples.result: `all: ["slow", "fast"]` at t = 300 (input order preserved); `race err: no` at t = 0 (the early rejection wins the race).

examples.title: The famous question: 1, 4, 3, 2

steps.label: Step 1: The synchronous run
steps.text: The script is one unit of work. `console.log(1)` runs; `setTimeout(..., 0)` **schedules** the timer callback on the timer (macrotask) queue and returns; `Promise.resolve().then(...)` schedules the microtask and returns; `console.log(4)` runs. Two logs are printed: **1, 4**.

steps.label: Step 2: The script ends — drain microtasks first
steps.text: The unit completes. Before the engine looks at timers or I/O, it drains the **microtask queue completely**: the `.then` callback runs now, printing **3** — even though it was scheduled after the timer and the timer has 0 ms of delay.

steps.label: Step 3: Then the macrotask
steps.text: Only when microtasks are empty does the loop fetch the next event: the expired timer runs its callback, printing **2**. The zero delay bought it nothing but a place at the back of the *later* queue.

steps.label: Step 4: The general order
steps.text: Final output: **1, 4, 3, 2** — synchronous code first, then every pending microtask, then the first timer callback. Each timer callback itself ends with another microtask drain, so long chains of `.then` calls interleave between timer events but always finish before the next timer fires.

steps.label: Step 5: Why the rule exists
steps.text: Microtasks are promise-resolution work: they are kept short and given priority so that chained promises reach their answers without waiting on unrelated I/O. It is a two-class scheduler — exactly the kind of queue-priority design OSC Chapter 4 discusses for CPU scheduling, here applied to a single-threaded event loop (Section 13.1’s run-to-completion model).

examples.result: Logs print in the order 1, 4, 3, 2: sync code, then the microtask (promise callback), then the timer — the single most-asked ordering question in JavaScript interviews, fully explained by queue priority.

keyTakeaways: A promise is pending until it fulfills with a value or rejects with a reason — settlement is immutable; there is no third callback after done.
then/catch/finally each return a **new** promise: return values fulfill the next link, throws reject it, and rejections skip ahead to the nearest catch, whose return value recovers the chain.
The executor passed to `new Promise` runs **synchronously**; only the handlers are deferred — as microtasks.
`Promise.resolve(v)` flattens promises and thenables; use it to enter chains from plain values.
`all` waits for every value (input order, fail-fast); `race` takes the first settlement of either kind; `allSettled` never rejects; `any` takes the first fulfillment.
Microtask discipline: when the current work ends, ALL pending microtasks run before ANY timer — hence the classic order 1, 4, 3, 2 (script, microtask, timer).
In Node, `util.promisify` and the `fs/promises` module convert error-first callback APIs into promise-returning ones.

quiz.q: Once a promise has been fulfilled with a value, what can change its state?
options: A later resolve call with a different value
Nothing — settlement (fulfilled or rejected) is final and the value is fixed
quiz.explanation: Settling is immutable: extra resolve calls are ignored and every subsequent then — attached whenever — observes the same one-time outcome.

quiz.q: A `.then()` callback throws an Error. What happens to the next `.then()` in the chain?
options: It runs with undefined as input
Its success callback is skipped; the rejection passes along until a catch (or an unhandled rejection)
The whole chain crashes the program
quiz.explanation: A thrown error rejects the promise that then returned; success callbacks along the way are bypassed until a catch handles the reason and can recover by returning a value.

quiz.q: Two promises: A fulfills in 100 ms, B fulfills in 300 ms. What does `Promise.all([B, A])` resolve to, and when?
options: ["B’s value", "A’s value"] at 300 ms — the input array’s order, after the slowest settles
quiz.explanation: all waits for every input and delivers values in the order of the input array — B first here — at the time of the slowest promise (300 ms), regardless of completion order.

quiz.q: In `Promise.race([slowFetch, fastReject])`, `fastReject` rejects after 10 ms and `slowFetch` would have fulfilled after 2 s. What does the race do?
options: Waits for slowFetch and fulfills, ignoring the rejection
Rejects after 10 ms with fastReject’s reason — the first settlement of either kind wins
quiz.explanation: race settles the moment any input settles: a fast rejection wins just as a fast fulfillment would — the property behind the timeout pattern.

quiz.q: What does this print: `console.log("a"); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("b")); setTimeout(() => console.log("c"), 0); console.log("d");`?
quiz.explanation: Synchronous logs first (a, d), then the microtask queue drains before any timer (b), then the macrotask timer (c) — the 1, 4, 3, 2 pattern in new letters.

Step 1: The code given logs synchronously, queues a fulfilled-promise callback, then logs synchronously again. Step 2: The governing rule is the two-queue discipline: synchronous code runs to completion first, promise callbacks wait as microtasks, and microtasks drain before the engine moves to the next macrotask. Step 3: Tracing execution, `first` prints immediately, the `.then` callback waits in the microtask queue, `third` prints synchronously, and only then does the queued callback print `second`. Step 4: The distractors fail because the promise callback can never run before the synchronous lines finish, and it always runs before any timer or I/O macrotask. Step 5: Therefore the order is `first`, `third`, `second`.

intro: **async and await** are promises with the awkward parts removed: an async function writes like synchronous code, `await` marks exactly where it pauses, and `try/catch` handles rejections like ordinary exceptions. Underneath, nothing new exists — `await` compiles to the `then` chains of Section 13.2 — but the translation makes async code readable for the first time. This section is the translation manual, plus the one performance trap everyone hits: awaiting sequentially what should run in parallel.
objectives: Explain why an async function always returns a promise
Translate between await-based code and then-chains mechanically
Handle rejections with try/catch/finally around awaits
Distinguish sequential awaits from parallel Promise.all — with a timed comparison
Recognize the forEach-with-async bug and the correct loop forms

concepts.statement: Marking a function `async` changes its return contract: `return 42` comes back as a promise **fulfilled with 42**; `throw e` comes back as a **rejected** promise with reason e. The caller can never see a bare value from an async function — only its eventual result.

`await expression` suspends the async function until the expression’s promise settles, then evaluates to its **value** — or, if it rejected, **throws** its reason at this exact line. The thread does not block: only this one function pauses, and the event loop (Section 13.1) keeps running everything else.
concepts.detail: Awaiting a non-promise value is legal — `await 5` is `5` on the next microtask — which lets code be promisified opportunistically. In ES2022 modules, top-level `await` is allowed outside any function.

concepts.statement: Every async/await function has a mechanical then-chain translation: each `await` splits the function at that line, the code below becomes the next link’s callback, and the value below the await is the callback’s parameter. Reading and writing both forms fluently is the skill.

A rejection arriving at an `await` throws at that line — so ordinary `try { ... } catch { ... } finally { ... }` covers async failures, with the usual semantics: catch recovers by returning a value, finally runs cleanup on both paths, and an uncaught error rejects the async function’s own promise.
concepts.detail: The rule of placement: wrap exactly the region from which you can meaningfully recover — a try around three sequential awaits that catches and falls back treats any of the three failing the same way; per-step recovery needs per-step try blocks.

concepts.statement: Two awaits in sequence **serialize**: the second operation does not start until the first settles — total time is the **sum**. Starting both promises first and awaiting them together — `const [a, b] = await Promise.all([f(), g()])` — runs them concurrently: total time is the **maximum**. Await is where the pause happens, and promises start when created, not when awaited.
concepts.detail: This is the single most common async/await performance bug: `const user = await getUser(); const posts = await getPosts();` pays user + posts when the two calls never needed each other’s results. (And it is precisely the latency-hiding idea OSC Chapter 12 develops for I/O: overlapping waits instead of queueing them.)

concepts.statement: Inside a plain `for` or `for/of` loop, `await` works as read: each iteration waits for the previous — sequential by design, which is correct when steps depend on each other, and a bug when they do not. But `array.forEach(async ...)` **does not wait at all**: forEach invokes the callbacks, ignores the returned promises, and the loop finishes long before any await resolves.

examples.title: Trace the engine: the then-chain translation

steps.label: Step 1: The call starts real work immediately
steps.text: `fetchPrice("ACME")` runs synchronously up to the first `await` — the fetch is **issued** before any suspension — and returns a pending promise to the caller. The async function’s body is now parked at the first await.

steps.label: Step 2: First await = first chain link
steps.text: The translation is: `fetch(...).then(next)`, where `next(response)` is “everything below the await”. When the response arrives, the microtask queue (Section 13.2) runs `next` — if `response.ok` is false, it throws, which rejects the link; otherwise it calls `response.json()` and returns **that promise**, which the chain adopts.

steps.label: Step 3: Second await = second link
steps.text: Because `next` returned a promise, the chain flattens it (the promise-resolution rule): `quote` binds to the parsed body when it arrives — `await` of an await, invisible in the chain shape.

steps.label: Step 4: The return fulfills the outer promise
steps.text: `return quote.price` resolves the promise that `fetchPrice` originally returned — the caller’s `const p = await fetchPrice("ACME")` (or `.then(...)`) now resumes with the number.

steps.label: Step 5: The error path, both dialects
steps.text: A rejection at either link — the fetch itself, the thrown HTTPError, or json() failing — skips every success callback and surfaces at the caller as a rejected promise: exactly `p.catch(e => ...)`. In the async dialect, the caller writes `try { await fetchPrice(...) } catch (e) { ... }` — same machinery, different clothes. One dialect, mechanical translation — that is the whole concept.

examples.result: Line-for-line: each await splits the body into the next then callback; the try/catch of the caller is the catch link; the returned value is the final fulfillment — prove it by translating any await code this way.

examples.title: Sequential versus parallel: a timed comparison

steps.label: Step 1: The sequential timeline
steps.text: t = 0: `getUser()` is called and awaited — the function suspends. t = 200: the user arrives; **only now** is `getPosts()` called. t = 500: the posts arrive. Total: 200 + 300 = **500 ms**, because the second request never overlapped the first.

steps.label: Step 2: The await placement is the pause, not the start
steps.text: The bug is thinking `await` “wraps” the operation. Promises begin when the function that creates them is **called** — `await` merely parks the current function at that line. Sequencing two awaits is sequencing two calls.

steps.label: Step 3: The parallel timeline
steps.text: t = 0: inside the array literal, `getUser()` and `getPosts()` are **both invoked immediately** — two pending promises, two requests in flight. `Promise.all` combines them into one; the single `await` suspends once. t = 200: user arrives (all stays pending). t = 300: posts arrive — all fulfills **now**.

steps.label: Step 4: The arithmetic
steps.text: Total: max(200, 300) = **300 ms** — a 40% saving for one line of restructuring. The results land in the destructured `[user, posts]` in input order (the all guarantee from 13.2), so downstream code does not change at all.

steps.label: Step 5: When sequential IS correct
steps.text: If the second call needs the first’s result — `const id = (await getUser()).id; const posts = await getPostsFor(id)` — the dependency forces order, and all would be meaningless. The rule: no data dependency → start together and combine; data dependency → await in order.

examples.result: Sequential ≈ 500 ms, parallel ≈ 300 ms — same requests, same results object; only the start times differ. Overlap independent waits, order dependent ones.

examples.title: The forEach trap and its two correct forms

steps.label: Step 1: What forEach actually does with the callback
steps.text: forEach calls the arrow for each item and **discards its return value** — which is a promise, because the arrow is async. forEach has no concept of awaiting anything; it finishes its synchronous loop instantly.

steps.label: Step 2: The observable symptom
steps.text: `"done"` logs first, then the saves complete in whatever order they resolve — and if `saveItem` rejects, the rejection is unhandled: no catch anywhere is attached to those discarded promises.

steps.label: Step 3: Fix one — parallel
Step 4: Fix two — sequential
Step 5: Choosing the fix
steps.text: If the items are independent, the parallel form is usually right (total time = slowest save); if order matters — batch writes, dependent records, rate limits — the sequential form is the tool. What is never right is forEach: it cannot wait, by design.

examples.result: The bug: forEach discards the async callbacks’ promises, so it never waits. Fixes: `await Promise.all(items.map(fn))` for parallel, `for...of` with await for sequential — forEach cannot be repaired into waiting.

keyTakeaways: An async function always returns a promise: `return 42` fulfills it, `throw` rejects it — callers never see a bare value.
`await p` suspends only the current async function until p settles, yielding the value or throwing the reason; the thread keeps running other work.
The translation is mechanical: code below an await is the next then callback; a try/catch around awaits is a catch link.
Sequential awaits serialize independent work (time = sum); `await Promise.all([...])` overlaps it (time = max) — promises start when called, not when awaited.
Wrap awaits in try/catch/finally where recovery is possible; uncaught errors reject the async function’s promise.
`forEach(async ...)` never waits — use `Promise.all(items.map(asyncFn))` for parallel or a for/of with await for sequential iteration.

quiz.q: What does `async function f() { return 42; }` give its caller?
options: A promise fulfilled with the value 42
A promise that resolves to another promise
quiz.explanation: Async functions wrap every return in a promise — 42 arrives via .then or await; the caller can never receive the raw value synchronously.

quiz.q: Requests A (200 ms) and B (300 ms) are independent. What is the approximate total time of `const a = await A(); const b = await B();`?
options: About 500 ms — the second starts only after the first completes
It depends on the microtask queue
quiz.explanation: Await serializes: B is not even called until A settles, so the times add — 500 ms. Moving both calls into Promise.all runs them concurrently for ~300 ms.

quiz.q: How does a promise rejection surface inside an async function?
options: It throws at the awaiting line — catchable by an ordinary try/catch around the await
quiz.explanation: await converts rejection into a throw at that exact line — which is why standard try/catch/finally handles async errors with no special machinery.

quiz.q: What is wrong with `items.forEach(async (item) => { await save(item); }); console.log("done");`?
options: forEach discards the promises the async callbacks return, so it never waits and "done" logs first
quiz.explanation: forEach has no promise awareness: the async callbacks all start, their promises are dropped, and the loop completes synchronously — replace it with Promise.all + map, or a for/of with await.

quiz.q: Which form runs its per-item async work strictly one item at a time?
quiz.explanation: Inside a for/of, each await suspends the function before the next iteration begins — true sequencing; the map/all forms run items concurrently, and forEach runs them detached and unawaited.

Step 1: The code given calls an async function that logs, awaits, and logs again, with one more log after the call. Step 2: The governing rules are that an async function body runs synchronously up to its first `await`, that the `await` suspends the function and schedules its remainder as a microtask, and that the caller continues synchronously. Step 3: Tracing stepwise, `work()` starts and prints `1`, suspends at `await null`, the caller prints `3`, and the microtask queue then resumes the function to print `2`. Step 4: The distractors fail because `2` cannot print before the suspension lifts, and `3` cannot precede `1` since the function starts synchronously. Step 5: Therefore the order is `1`, `3`, `2`.

intro: Some asynchronous things are not “one value later” but “many values, over time”: lines arriving from a log file, pages from an API, messages from a queue. For those, the **asynchronous iteration protocol** combines Section 12.1’s iterators with Section 13.2’s promises: `next()` returns a promise of `{value, done}`, and the `for await...of` loop drains the sequence one awaited item at a time. Node streams implement it natively — making “read a file line by line” read exactly like a plain loop.
objectives: State the async iteration protocol: Symbol.asyncIterator and promise-valued next()
Consume async iterables with for await...of
Read Node streams chunk by chunk, handling records split across chunk boundaries
Convert callback- or event-based sources into async iteration

concepts.statement: An **asynchronous iterable** is an object with a `[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` method returning an iterator whose `next()` returns a **Promise of `{value, done}`** — the ordinary protocol of Section 12.1 with each step wrapped in a promise. A distinct well-known symbol keeps sync and async iteration from ever colliding on the same object.
concepts.detail: The naming is mnemonic: **yield** produces a value (Section 12.3); **await** consumes a promise (Section 13.3); async generators get to do both, and consumers get to `for await` the result.

concepts.statement: `for await (const item of asyncIterable) { ... }` awaits each `next()` promise before running the body with the resolved value — a loop that pauses per item while the thread stays free (Section 13.3’s await semantics, in loop form). It also accepts ordinary **sync** iterables, awaiting each value; and if any step’s promise rejects, the whole loop throws.
concepts.detail: Where `Promise.all` (13.2) handles a fixed, known set of async results **in parallel**, `for await` handles a **sequential stream of unknown length** — the two tools answer different questions and compose naturally: `for await` a stream whose items are themselves processed in parallel.

Chunks arrive in buffer-sized pieces (typically 64 KB), not in logical records — the line-splitting pattern below is the standard remedy. Backpressure is handled by the protocol itself: while the loop body awaits, the stream waits.

concepts.statement: When a file is read in chunks, a logical record (a line) can be split across two chunks. The standard pattern buffers a **leftover** tail: concatenate, split on the separator, pop the final (possibly partial) piece back into the buffer, process only the complete records — and flush the last leftover after EOF.

An `async function*` (Section 12.4) is the shortest path to a custom async iterable — the paginated-API example there is this section’s general pattern: `await` to fetch the next batch, `yield*` to emit its items, loop until exhausted. Any callback-based source can be wrapped the same way.
concepts.detail: The composition rule: **await inside the producer** (fetches), **for await at the consumer** (drains). Between them, the promise-valued `next()` carries each item across the boundary — the same decoupling Section 12.1 gave sync iteration, made asynchronous.

examples.title: Trace the engine: reading a stream with for await

steps.label: Step 1: The stream opens, nothing is read yet
steps.text: `createReadStream` returns a Readable stream — an async iterable wrapping a file descriptor. The for await calls `[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` once and then `next()` — a promise that resolves when the **first chunk** of data has actually arrived from the OS.

steps.label: Step 2: Each iteration is one completed read
steps.text: The body receives a Buffer (`chunk` — a Uint8Array view, Section 11.2) holding up to 64 KB, adds `chunk.length` to `total`, and loops — which calls `next()` again and **awaits the next arrival**. While waiting, the thread is free: the event loop (13.1) runs other work; the kernel delivers the data on its own schedule (OSC Ch 12’s I/O subsystem doing the actual transfer).

steps.label: Step 3: Backpressure for free
steps.text: Because the loop does not ask for chunk N+1 until the body of chunk N finished, a slow consumer automatically slows the reading — the file is never read faster than it is processed, and memory holds one chunk at a time, whatever the file’s size.

steps.label: Step 4: EOF ends the loop
steps.text: When the final read returns fewer bytes and the next `next()` resolves with `{value: undefined, done: true}` — the async form of Section 12.1’s exhaustion — the loop exits, `total` is the byte count, and the stream is closed by the loop machinery (the early-exit `return()` analog of Section 12.2 exists here too: `break` cleans up).

examples.result: One number, constant memory, natural pacing: `for await` over a Node stream is file reading that reads exactly as fast as it is consumed.

examples.title: Line splitting across chunk boundaries

steps.label: Step 1: Chunk one arrives
steps.text: Leftover starts empty; `"INFO a\nINFO b"` splits into `["INFO a", "INFO b"]`. The **pop** removes `"INFO b"` into `leftover` — it cannot be known complete (the next chunk might continue it). Only `["INFO a"]` is counted: `count` = 1.

steps.label: Step 2: Chunk two stitches the boundary
steps.text:
The next chunk is `"c
INFO d
"`. The concatenation `leftover + chunk` is `"INFO bc
INFO d
"` — the boundary heals invisibly — splitting into `["INFO bc", "INFO d", ""]`. The pop stores `""` (the file ended with a newline), and both complete lines count: `count` = 3.

steps.label: Step 3: EOF flushes any true remainder
steps.text: After the loop, a non-empty `leftover` is a final line that lacked a trailing newline — the `+ (leftover ? 1 : 0)` accounts for it. Here `leftover` is empty, so the answer is **3**; had the file ended mid-line, the tail would count once.

steps.label: Step 4: Why pop and not slice
steps.text: The invariant: the buffer always holds at most one **possibly-partial** tail; every string before it is a complete record. Without the leftover (say, processing `chunk.split("\n")` directly), the boundary would emit the fake lines `"INFO b"` and `"c"`, silently corrupting every record that happens to straddle a 64 KB edge — a bug that appears on large files only.

steps.label: Step 5: The general shape
steps.text: Replace `"\n"` with any separator — `\r\n`, commas, JSON per line — and the pattern is the standard adapter from **byte streams** to **record streams**: for await provides the chunks; the leftover buffer provides the framing; `TextDecoder`’s `{ stream: true }` mode does the same stitching for multi-byte characters (Section 11.2).

examples.result: Three lines from two chunks — `"INFO a"`, `"INFO bc"`, `"INFO d"` — with the boundary-crossing line reassembled exactly once by the leftover buffer.

examples.title: Wrapping a countdown: an async generator consumed by for await

steps.label: Step 1: The generator sleeps before each item
steps.text: Inside the async generator (Section 12.4), each iteration awaits a 100 ms timer — so `next()` cannot resolve its `{value, done}` promise until the sleep completes. The timer callback resolves the promise; the promise resolution resumes the generator; the yield delivers the value — three layers of later, each doing one job.

steps.label: Step 2: The loop drains, one item at a time
steps.text: The for await awaits `next()`, gets `3`, runs the body (logs 3), awaits `next()` again — which starts a fresh 100 ms sleep. Sequential by construction: no item is fetched before the previous body finished.

steps.label: Step 3: Completion flows through the protocol
steps.text: When `i` reaches 0, the loop for the generator ends and its `next()` resolves `{value: undefined, done: true}` — the for await exits and `"liftoff"` logs, roughly 300 ms after the start, with the thread free the entire time (the sleeps awaited; nothing blocked).

steps.label: Step 4: The consumer controls pacing implicitly
steps.text: Had the body been slow — say each log took 50 ms of work — the generator’s next sleep would simply overlap the consumer’s work: the pattern degrades gracefully in either direction, which is why it also fits pages-from-an-API (Section 12.4) and events-from-a-queue: one item, one await, whenever both sides are ready.

examples.result: 3, 2, 1 at ~100 ms intervals, then `"liftoff"` — a custom async iterable built with async generator syntax and drained by for await, with the thread never blocked.

keyTakeaways: Async iterables implement `[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` whose `next()` returns a **Promise of `{value, done}`** — the sync protocol with promised steps.
`for await...of` awaits each step before running the body; it accepts sync iterables too, and any step rejection throws out of the loop.
`Promise.all` is for a **fixed known set** in parallel; `for await` is for an **unknown-length sequence** in order — different questions, both essential.
Node streams are async iterables: `for await (const chunk of createReadStream(p))` reads in ~64 KB chunks with backpressure and constant memory.
Logical records can straddle chunk boundaries: keep a leftover tail, split, pop the partial piece back, and flush after EOF.
Async generators (`async function*`) are the standard adapter from any async source — APIs, queues, timers — into the async iteration protocol.

quiz.q: What distinguishes an async iterator from a sync one (Section 12.1)?
options: It uses Symbol.iterator with a different return type
Its next() returns a Promise that resolves to {value, done}
It can only be consumed by while loops
quiz.explanation: The async protocol is the same {value, done} contract, one promise deep — each step resolves when the data is ready; Symbol.asyncIterator keeps it separate from sync iteration.

quiz.q: What does each iteration of `for await (const chunk of createReadStream(path))` wait for?
options: The entire file to be read into memory
The next chunk to arrive from the OS — one read completion per iteration
quiz.explanation: Each next() resolves when a chunk has actually arrived: the loop advances at the pace of the producer, holding one chunk at a time instead of the whole file.

quiz.q: Why does the line-splitting pattern `lines.pop()` the last element of each split?
options: Because the final piece may be a partial line whose remainder arrives in the next chunk — it is buffered, not counted
Because pop is faster than slice
quiz.explanation: Records can straddle chunk boundaries: the popped tail is concatenated with the next chunk, so boundary-crossing lines are reassembled exactly once — counting it early would split one record into two fragments.

quiz.q: Which tool fits “process an unbounded sequence of messages arriving over time, in arrival order”?
options: `for await...of` over an async iterable that yields each message
A single await of the last message
quiz.explanation: Unknown length and sequential arrival define async iteration; Promise.all needs a complete, finite array up front — the wrong shape for a stream.

quiz.q: Inside `async function* g()`, what may the body do that a normal generator’s cannot?
quiz.explanation: async generators allow await in the body — each next() becomes a promise that resolves once the awaited operation and the following yield both complete (Section 12.4).

intro: Every property you create in JavaScript carries hidden configuration: three attributes that decide whether its value can be changed, whether loops can see it, and whether it can be deleted or reconfigured. This section reads that configuration with `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor()`, rewrites it with `Object.defineProperty()`, and then climbs a ladder of object-level locks — `preventExtensions()`, `seal()` and `freeze()` — that can forbid new properties, deletions and writes outright. Everything here is the API the rest of the chapter builds on: proxies intercept exactly these operations.
objectives: Read and interpret the property descriptor returned by `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor()`
Create read-only, hidden and locked properties with `Object.defineProperty()`, and explain the silent-versus-strict failure modes
Distinguish extensibility, sealedness and frozenness, and test each with the matching `Object.is*` predicate
Explain why `Object.freeze()` is shallow, and write a `deepFreeze()` that reaches nested objects and arrays

concepts.statement: Every property has a **name**, a **value** and three **attributes**: **writable** (may the value be changed?), **enumerable** (does the property appear in `for/in` loops and `Object.keys()`?) and **configurable** (may the property be deleted or its attributes changed again?). Properties created by assignment or object literals get `true` for all three attributes.
concepts.detail: Accessor properties replace the `value`/`writable` pair with a **get** and/or **set** function, but keep `enumerable` and `configurable`. Arrays are a good illustration of non-default attributes: the `length` property is writable but neither enumerable nor configurable, which is why `Object.keys([1])` returns `['0']` and not `['0', 'length']`.

concepts.statement: A **property descriptor** is the object that describes attributes: a complete data-property descriptor is `{ value, writable, enumerable, configurable }`, and a complete accessor descriptor is `{ get, set, enumerable, configurable }`.

`Object.defineProperty(o, name, descriptor)` creates a new property or edits the attributes of an existing one, and returns the (modified) object `o`. For a **new** property, any attribute you leave out of the descriptor defaults to `false`; when **redefining** an existing property, omitted attributes keep their current values.
concepts.detail:
Redefinition is only allowed when the existing property is **configurable** — with a single exception: a configurable property may always be flipped from `writable: true` to `writable: false`, never the reverse.
```js
const settings = { retries: 3 };
Object.defineProperty(settings, 'retries', { writable: false });
settings.retries = 5;   // silently ignored in sloppy mode
settings.retries;        // 3 — and in strict mode the assignment throws TypeError
```

concepts.statement: An object is **extensible** when new properties may be added to it. `Object.preventExtensions(o)` makes `o` permanently non-extensible — there is no undo — and `Object.isExtensible(o)` tests it. A non-extensible object can still modify and delete the properties it already has.
concepts.detail: The silent/strict split applies here too: assigning a new property to a non-extensible object does nothing in sloppy mode and throws `TypeError` in strict mode (modules and class bodies are always strict).

concepts.statement: `Object.seal(o)` is `Object.preventExtensions(o)` plus `Object.defineProperty(o, name, { configurable: false })` for every own property. A sealed object can neither gain nor lose properties, but the values of its existing data properties remain writable. Test with `Object.isSealed(o)`.
concepts.detail: Sealing is the right tool for objects whose **set** of properties must stay fixed (a record shape, a set of API endpoints) while their values keep updating.

concepts.statement: `Object.freeze(o)` is `Object.seal(o)` plus `writable: false` on every own data property: nothing about the object’s own data properties can change again. Accessor properties keep working — their getters can still compute fresh values. Test with `Object.isFrozen(o)`. A frozen object is always sealed, and a sealed object is always non-extensible.
concepts.detail: Freeze is a cheap way to ship constant configuration tables: `const API = Object.freeze({ base: 'https://api.example.com', retries: 3 });`. Because arrays are objects, freezing one makes `push` and `pop` throw `TypeError` in strict mode.

concepts.statement: `Object.freeze()` is **shallow**: it locks the object’s own properties, but any property value that is itself an object — a nested record, an array — remains fully mutable, and `Object.isFrozen()` reports `false` for it until you freeze it explicitly.
concepts.detail: Deep immutability must be written by hand: walk the own properties, freeze every value that `typeof v === 'object'`, and recurse. Cycles are safe if you skip already-frozen values, because `Object.isFrozen()` becomes your visited-set.

examples.title: Reading a descriptor and locking a property
examples.problem: The object `const config = { host: 'api.example.com', retries: 3 };` is used everywhere in a large codebase. You have been asked to turn `retries` into a fixed constant that cannot be overwritten, enumerated or deleted, while leaving `host` an ordinary property.

steps.label: Step 1: Inspect before changing
steps.text: `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(config, 'retries')` returns `{ value: 3, writable: true, enumerable: true, configurable: true }` — an ordinary, fully permissive data property.

steps.label: Step 2: Redefine with defineProperty
Step 3: Observe the write failure
steps.text: `config.retries = 5;` leaves `config.retries` equal to `3`. In a module or class body (always strict mode) the same line throws `TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'retries'` — sloppy mode is silent, strict mode is loud.

steps.label: Step 4: Confirm invisibility
steps.text: `Object.keys(config)` now returns `['host']`: the non-enumerable `retries` is skipped by `Object.keys()`, `for/in` and `JSON.stringify()`, yet direct reads like `config.retries` still return `3`.

steps.label: Step 5: Confirm permanence
steps.text: `delete config.retries` is a no-op that evaluates to `false` (strict mode throws), and because `configurable` is `false`, not even `Object.defineProperty()` can re-open the property — the attribute set is now final.

examples.result: `retries` is a constant: readable everywhere, invisible to loops and serializers, immune to deletion and redefinition — while `host` remains a normal mutable property on the same object.

examples.title: Climbing the ladder: preventExtensions → seal → freeze
examples.problem: Demonstrate on a single object exactly which operations each level of locking forbids, and verify each level with its matching `Object.is*` predicate.

steps.label: Step 1: Start permissive
steps.text: `const o = { a: 1 };` — `Object.isExtensible(o)` is `true`, `Object.isSealed(o)` is `false`, `Object.isFrozen(o)` is `false`.

steps.label: Step 2: preventExtensions
steps.text: After `Object.preventExtensions(o)`: `o.b = 2` fails (no new properties), but `o.a = 10` works and `delete o.a` still works — existing properties remain fully live.

steps.label: Step 3: seal
steps.text: Re-add `a` and call `Object.seal(o)`: now `delete o.a` fails too, because every own property became non-configurable, while `o.a = 20` continues to work — values are still writable.

steps.label: Step 4: freeze
steps.text: `Object.freeze(o)` is the final rung: `o.a = 30` fails as well, because every own data property is now non-writable.

steps.label: Step 5: Read the predicates
steps.text: At the end, `Object.isExtensible(o) === false`, `Object.isSealed(o) === true` and `Object.isFrozen(o) === true` — each predicate accepts everything at or above its own level.

examples.result: Each rung forbids strictly more: `preventExtensions` blocks **addition**, `seal` blocks addition **and deletion**, `freeze` blocks addition, deletion **and mutation** of own data properties.

examples.title: The depth of freeze — and a deepFreeze()
examples.problem: `const config = { api: { host: 'api.example.com', retries: 3 }, tags: ['prod', 'eu'] };` was frozen with `Object.freeze(config)`, yet a colleague reports that the API host changed at runtime. Explain why, then fix it.

steps.label: Step 1: Freeze and check
steps.text: `Object.isFrozen(config)` returns `true` — but `Object.isFrozen(config.api)` and `Object.isFrozen(config.tags)` both return `false`. Freeze never descends into property values.

steps.label: Step 2: Reproduce the bug
steps.text: `config.api.host = 'evil.example.net'` succeeds and so does `config.tags.push('staging')` — both mutate **nested** objects that the top-level freeze never touched.

steps.label: Step 3: Write deepFreeze
Step 4: Apply it
steps.text: `deepFreeze(config)` freezes `config`, then `config.api` and `config.tags` — the `!Object.isFrozen(v)` test doubles as a cycle guard, since a frozen object is skipped on revisit.

steps.label: Step 5: Verify
steps.text: After the deep freeze, `config.api.host = 'evil.example.net'` throws `TypeError` in strict mode, and `config.tags.push('staging')` throws because frozen arrays reject new indices (`TypeError: Cannot add property 2, object is not extensible`).

examples.result: `Object.freeze()` is shallow by design — it cannot guess which nested objects you want immutable, and recursion costs time on every call. True immutability for a configuration tree is the four-line `deepFreeze()` above, applied once at startup.

keyTakeaways: Three attributes — `writable`, `enumerable`, `configurable` — govern change, visibility and deletion; assignment- and literal-created properties get all three as `true`.
For **new** properties, attributes omitted from an `Object.defineProperty()` descriptor default to `false`; when **redefining** an existing property, omitted attributes keep their current values.
`getOwnPropertyDescriptor()` reads one descriptor; `defineProperty()` writes one — together they are the complete metaprogramming surface for individual properties.
The locking ladder: `preventExtensions` < `seal` < `freeze`, tested by `isExtensible` / `isSealed` / `isFrozen`; each frozen object is also sealed and non-extensible.
Violations are silent in sloppy mode and throw `TypeError` in strict mode — and modules, classes and ES2022 class fields are always strict.
`Object.freeze()` is shallow: nested objects and arrays stay mutable until a `deepFreeze()` recursion reaches them; frozen arrays throw on `push`.

quiz.q: What does `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor({ id: 42 }, 'id')` return?
options: `{ value: 42, writable: true, enumerable: true, configurable: true }`
`{ value: 42, writable: false, enumerable: false, configurable: false }`
`{ get: undefined, set: undefined, enumerable: true }`
`undefined`, because descriptors are only available on frozen objects
quiz.explanation: Properties created by object literals get `true` for all three attributes, and the descriptor of a data property carries value/writable/enumerable/configurable.

quiz.q: On a fresh empty object, `Object.defineProperty(o, 'x', { value: 1 })` has just run. Which statement is TRUE?
options: `o.x` is enumerable but cannot be deleted
`o.x` cannot be read with the dot operator
quiz.explanation: When defineProperty creates a **new** property, any attribute omitted from the descriptor defaults to `false` — only explicit `true` values count.

quiz.q: An object is sealed but NOT frozen. Which operation still succeeds?
options: Adding a new property to it
Deleting one of its existing properties
Assigning a new value to an existing data property
Changing a property’s attributes back to configurable
quiz.explanation: `seal()` makes every own property non-configurable (no adds, no deletes, no reconfiguration) but leaves them writable, so value assignment still works.

quiz.q: `const cfg = { api: { host: 'x' } }; Object.freeze(cfg);` — which operation still SUCCEEDS afterwards?
quiz.explanation: Freeze is shallow: it locks `cfg`’s own properties, but the nested object `cfg.api` was never frozen, so writes to its properties still go through.

quiz.q: `Object.isFrozen(o)` returns `true` when:
options: the object was merely passed to `Object.preventExtensions()`
the object is non-extensible, all own properties are non-configurable, and all own data properties are non-writable
the object contains no accessor properties
quiz.explanation: Frozen = non-extensible + everything non-configurable + all own data properties non-writable; enumerability and accessor properties are irrelevant to the predicate.

intro: Property lookup in JavaScript is a walk up a chain of objects: every object records its **prototype**, and a missing property name is looked for there next. This section makes that usually-invisible link explicit — reading it with `Object.getPrototypeOf()`, rewiring it with `Object.setPrototypeOf()` and `Object.create()` — and then uses the two links to build class inheritance by hand, exactly the way the `class` keyword of Chapter 9 does it under the hood.
objectives: Trace a property read and a property write through a multi-level prototype chain
Use `Object.getPrototypeOf()`, `Object.setPrototypeOf()` and `Object.create()` to inspect and change an object’s prototype
Explain why `Object.create(null)` yields a prototype-less dictionary object
Wire a constructor-function subclass manually: the prototype link, the constructor reset, and static method inheritance

concepts.statement: Every object carries an internal **prototype** attribute pointing at another object (or `null`). Reading `o.x` finds an **own** property of `o` or, failing that, walks `o`’s prototype, that object’s prototype, and so on — the **prototype chain** — until the name is found or the walk reaches `null` and yields `undefined`. **Writing** `o.x = v` (with no setter involved) instead creates an own property of `o`, shadowing any same-named property further up the chain.
concepts.detail: Delegation is per-lookup and never mutates the prototype: `delete o.x` removes only the own property, and the next read simply falls through to the inherited one again.

concepts.statement: `Object.getPrototypeOf(o)` returns the prototype object; `Object.setPrototypeOf(o, p)` re-points it and returns `o`; `Object.create(p)` returns a brand-new object whose prototype is `p`. The `__proto__` accessor property is the deprecated, legacy spelling of the same operations.

`Object.create(null)` produces an object with **no prototype at all** — no `toString`, no `hasOwnProperty`, nothing inherited. It is the clean base for dictionary objects keyed by arbitrary strings, because inherited names like `'constructor'` or `'toString'` cannot collide with your data.
concepts.detail: A plain `{}` used as a map answers `'constructor' in dict` with `true` — an inherited property, not your data. The null-prototype object answers `false`, which is exactly what a dictionary should say. (Chapter 11’s `Map` solves the same problem more completely.)

concepts.statement: Without the `class` keyword, a subclass `Sub` of `Sup` is wired by hand in two links: set `Sub.prototype = Object.create(Sup.prototype)` so instances inherit the parent’s methods, and reset `Sub.prototype.constructor = Sub`; optionally also `Object.setPrototypeOf(Sub, Sup)` so the subclass inherits the parent’s **static** methods.
concepts.detail: That is precisely what `class Sub extends Sup {}` computes: the chain `instance` → `Sub.prototype` → `Sup.prototype` → `Object.prototype` for methods, plus the constructor-to-constructor link `Sub` → `Sup` for statics — see Chapter 9, Section 9.5.

concepts.statement: `x instanceof C` walks the prototype chain of `x` looking for `C.prototype` (Section 4.5, and §14.3 for how to override it). A hand-wired subclass therefore satisfies `instanceof` for both the subclass and every ancestor class automatically.
concepts.detail: `const tm = new TypedMap(...)` with `TypedMap.prototype` chained to `Map.prototype` makes both `tm instanceof TypedMap` and `tm instanceof Map` return `true` — no registration, no declarations, just the link.

concepts.statement: The “assignment creates an own property” rule has one exception: if the prototype chain contains an **accessor property** with only a `set` function for that name, the assignment calls the setter instead of creating an own property on the receiver.
concepts.detail: This is how exotic objects behave like they have magic properties: the assignment is delegated, the receiver stays untouched, and the setter decides what actually happens.

examples.title: Tracing lookups up a three-object chain
examples.problem: Given `const q = { kind: 'quad' }; const p = Object.create(q); const o = Object.create(p); o.kind = 'own';` — trace what reads and writes on `o` do, and what happens when the own property is later deleted.

steps.label: Step 1: Read an own property first
steps.text: `o.kind` returns `'own'` — the own property shadows `q.kind` without altering it; `q.kind` is still `'quad'`.

steps.label: Step 2: Read an inherited property
steps.text: `p.kind` returns `'quad'` — `p` has no own `kind`, so the lookup climbs the link to `q`. The full chain above `o` is `p` → `q` → `Object.prototype` → `null` (object literals inherit from `Object.prototype`).

steps.label: Step 3: Watch a lookup miss
steps.text: `o.nope` returns `undefined` — the walk visits `o`, `p`, `q` and `Object.prototype`, finds nothing, and stops at `null`.

steps.label: Step 4: Write on the middle object
steps.text: `p.kind = 'parent'` creates an **own** property on `p`; `o.kind` still returns `'own'` (its own shadow wins), but a fresh `Object.create(p).kind` would now return `'parent'`.

steps.label: Step 5: Delete and re-expose
steps.text: `delete o.kind` removes the shadow; the next `o.kind` read falls through to `p.kind` and returns `'parent'`.

examples.result: Reads walk the chain upward with first-match-wins; writes and deletes always act on the receiver itself. Inheritance in JavaScript is delegation for **reads**, isolation for **writes**.

examples.title: A manual subclass of Map, no class keyword
examples.problem: Build `TypedMap` — like `Map`, but `set()` rejects keys and values of the wrong type — using constructor functions and explicit prototype wiring, such that `tm instanceof Map` still returns `true` and all inherited `Map` behavior keeps working.

steps.label: Step 1: The constructor stores types and a real Map
Step 2: Wire the instance chain
Step 3: Override set with type checks
Step 4: Use it
steps.text:
```js
const tm = new TypedMap([['one', 1]], 'string', 'number');
tm.set('two', 2);   // ok — inner map now has 2 entries
tm.set(2, 'two');   // TypeError: 2 is not of type string
```

steps.label: Step 5: Verify both chains
steps.text: `tm instanceof TypedMap` → `true` and `tm instanceof Map` → `true`, because `Map.prototype` sits in `tm`’s prototype chain. Methods you did not override (`get`, `has`, `forEach`) come straight from `Map.prototype`; static methods like `Map.groupBy` would only be inherited after also calling `Object.setPrototypeOf(TypedMap, Map)`.

examples.result: Two `Object.create`/`setPrototypeOf` links reproduce what `extends` does automatically: instances delegate through `TypedMap.prototype` to `Map.prototype`, so every `Map` method keeps working and `instanceof` reports both classes.

keyTakeaways: Property **reads** walk the prototype chain (own properties first, then upward); property **writes** and `delete` act on the receiver alone, shadowing rather than mutating the prototype.
`Object.getPrototypeOf()` reads the link, `Object.setPrototypeOf()` re-points it (with a performance cost if done late), and `Object.create(p)` builds the link at construction time.
`Object.create(null)` gives a prototype-less dictionary: no inherited `toString` or `constructor` can collide with your keys.

Manual subclassing = `Sub.prototype = Object.create(Sup.prototype)` + `Sub.prototype.constructor = Sub`, plus `Object.setPrototypeOf(Sub, Sup)` for statics — exactly what `class Sub extends Sup` computes.
`instanceof` consults the prototype chain, so hand-wired subclasses satisfy it for every ancestor class for free.

quiz.q: If `const o = Object.create(p)`, then `Object.getPrototypeOf(o)` is:
options: `o` itself, because objects are their own prototypes
quiz.explanation: `Object.create(p)` sets the new object’s prototype attribute to `p`, and `Object.getPrototypeOf()` reads exactly that attribute.

quiz.q: `const proto = { n: 1 }; const o = Object.create(proto); o.n = 5;` — after these lines, what are `o.n` and `proto.n`?
options: `o.n` is `1` and `proto.n` is `1` — writes are delegated downward
The assignment `o.n = 5` throws, because `n` belongs to the prototype
quiz.explanation: Assignment creates an own property on the receiver, shadowing the inherited one; the prototype object is never touched by an ordinary write.

quiz.q: Why would a programmer choose `Object.create(null)` for a lookup table?
options: It is faster than `{}` at runtime in all engines
It removes all inherited properties, so keys like `'toString'` cannot collide with inherited names
It automatically converts numeric keys to integers
quiz.explanation: A null prototype severs the link to `Object.prototype`, so `'constructor' in dict` is `false` unless your data put it there — the clean dictionary semantics (with `Map` being the fuller solution).

quiz.q: Which pair of lines wires up inheritance from `Sup` to a constructor function `Sub` for **instance** methods?
quiz.explanation: `Object.create(Sup.prototype)` chains instances through `Sub.prototype` to `Sup.prototype` **without** running `Sup`’s constructor; resetting `constructor` keeps the back-reference truthful.

quiz.q: In the manual `TypedMap` example, why is `tm instanceof Map` true?
options: Because `Map.prototype` is in `tm`’s prototype chain after the wiring
Because `TypedMap` registered itself with `Map` as a subclass
quiz.explanation: `instanceof` walks the prototype chain of the left operand looking for the right operand’s `.prototype`; the `Object.create(Map.prototype)` link puts `Map.prototype` on that walk.

intro: JavaScript exposes its own extension points as **well-known symbols** — a fixed set of built-in symbol values, static properties of the `Symbol` class, that core operators consult before using their default behavior. Assign one of them as a computed property name and you can redefine what `instanceof` tests, what `Object.prototype.toString` prints, whether `concat` spreads an object, and even how your objects convert to primitives under the plus and multiplication operators.
objectives: Explain what well-known symbols are and why they must be symbols rather than strings
Redefine `instanceof` for a type by implementing `Symbol.hasInstance`
Customize `Object.prototype.toString` output with `Symbol.toStringTag`
Control spreading in `concat()` with `Symbol.isConcatSpreadable`
Take full control of object-to-primitive conversion with `Symbol.toPrimitive` and its three hints

concepts.statement: A **well-known symbol** is one of the static properties of the `Symbol` class — `Symbol.hasInstance`, `Symbol.toStringTag`, `Symbol.toPrimitive` and about a dozen more — that the JavaScript runtime itself consults. Because they are symbols, user code can never accidentally shadow them with a string-keyed property, and because they are shared built-ins, every library sees the same values.
concepts.detail: They are unrelated to the global symbol registry of `Symbol.for('name')`/`Symbol.keyFor()`: well-known symbols are not registered, they are simply properties of the `Symbol` object.

concepts.statement: The `instanceof` operator, on seeing `x instanceof C`, first looks for a method named `Symbol.hasInstance` **on `C`** and calls it with `x`; only when that method is absent does it fall back to the default walk of `x`’s prototype chain for `C.prototype`. The method receives the left operand as-is, so it can be a primitive.

`Object.prototype.toString` consults the `Symbol.toStringTag` property (a string, or a getter returning one) to build its result, replacing the generic `'[object Object]'` with `'[object YourTag]'`. The built-ins set it themselves: `Math[Symbol.toStringTag]` is `'Math'` and `JSON[Symbol.toStringTag]` is `'JSON'`.

`Array.prototype.concat` spreads true arrays into the result but appends array-**like** objects as single elements — unless the object’s `Symbol.isConcatSpreadable` property is `true`, which forces spreading; setting it `false` on a true array forces it to be appended as one nested element.

When an object must convert to a primitive value, the runtime calls its `Symbol.toPrimitive` method with a **hint** — `'number'`, `'string'` or `'default'` — and uses whatever primitive comes back. It takes precedence over the older `valueOf()`/`toString()` protocol of Section 3.7, and returning an object from it throws a `TypeError`.
concepts.detail: Which operators give which hint: `+v`, `v * 2` and `Number(v)` pass `'number'`; template literals and `String(v)` pass `'string'`; the ambiguous `+` between two operands and relational comparisons pass `'default'`, letting your method choose a strategy.

concepts.statement: `Symbol.iterator` powers `for/of` and spread (Chapter 12); `Symbol.asyncIterator` powers `for/await/of` (Chapter 13); `Symbol.species` controls which constructor built-ins like `Array` and `Promise` use when they spawn new instances; and `Symbol.match`, `Symbol.replace`, `Symbol.search` and `Symbol.split` let objects plug themselves into `String.prototype`’s regex methods.
concepts.detail: The common pattern: a built-in method checks for the symbol method on its operand first, and only falls back to its default algorithm when the symbol is absent — metaprogramming as an orderly protocol.

examples.title: instanceof that answers a predicate
examples.problem: You want `x instanceof Even` to be a readable test for even integers — without any class, constructor or prototype being involved.

steps.label: Step 1: Define the object with the computed symbol method
Step 2: Evaluate the operator
steps.text: `2 instanceof Even` → the engine finds `Symbol.hasInstance` on `Even`, calls it with `2`, and returns the boolean `true`.

steps.label: Step 3: Check the negative case
steps.text: `3 instanceof Even` → `false`, and `2.5 instanceof Even` → `false` (since `2.5 % 2` is `0.5`). The left operand is passed through raw — no boxing — so primitives work directly.

steps.label: Step 4: Note what was bypassed
steps.text: No prototype-chain walk ever happened: `Even` has no `prototype` property at all. The default `instanceof` algorithm only runs when the `Symbol.hasInstance` method is missing.

examples.result: One computed-method definition turned a plain object into an `instanceof` target — the cleanest way to express predicate-style type tests like `x instanceof NonEmptyString`.

examples.title: A readable tag for Object.prototype.toString
examples.problem: Debug output full of `'[object Object]'` is useless. Give instances of a `Transaction` class a label that `Object.prototype.toString` reports as `'[object Transaction]'`.

steps.label: Step 1: Confirm the default
steps.text:
```js
class Transaction { }
Object.prototype.toString.call(new Transaction());  // '[object Object]'
```

steps.label: Step 2: Add the tag
Step 3: Test it
steps.text: `Object.prototype.toString.call(new Transaction())` now returns `'[object Transaction]'` — on instances and on anything else carrying that tag.

steps.label: Step 4: Note the boundary
steps.text: `String(new Transaction())` still uses the ordinary `toString()` method, and `JSON.stringify` ignores the tag entirely — `toStringTag` customizes exactly one debugging entry point.

examples.result: `'[object Transaction]'` in logs and console dumps, with zero changes to the class’s public API.

examples.title: Controlling + and * with Symbol.toPrimitive
examples.problem: For a `Vector` class, you want arithmetic like `v * 2` and unary `+v` to use the vector’s magnitude, while template literals show the coordinates — and the old `valueOf` fallbacks should never be consulted.

steps.label: Step 1: Define the class with the conversion method
Step 2: Number contexts
steps.text: `+v` (unary plus) → `5`; `v * 2` → `10`; `Number(v)` → `5` — all pass the `'number'` hint, and the method returns the magnitude `Math.hypot(3, 4) = 5`.

steps.label: Step 3: The ambiguous default hint
steps.text: `v + 0` → `5` and `v < 6` → `true`: mixed-operator contexts pass `'default'`, and the method again answers with the magnitude.

steps.label: Step 4: String contexts
steps.text: Interpolating `v` into a template literal, and `String(v)` — both pass the `'string'` hint and return `'<3,4>'`, formatting the coordinates instead.

steps.label: Step 5: Note the failure mode
steps.text: A `Symbol.toPrimitive` that returned another object (say `this`) would throw `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` — the runtime requires a primitive answer.

examples.result: One method now decides every conversion: `5` for arithmetic, `'<3,4>'` for display — old-style `valueOf`/`toString` pairs never run because `Symbol.toPrimitive` outranks them.

keyTakeaways: Well-known symbols are the runtime’s extension points: symbol-keyed methods that core operators consult before their default algorithms.
`Symbol.hasInstance` on the right-hand operand redefines `instanceof`, and it receives the left operand raw — primitives included.
`Symbol.toStringTag` changes only `Object.prototype.toString`’s label, not `String()` or `JSON.stringify`.
`Symbol.isConcatSpreadable` flips `concat`’s spreading decision for array-likes (`true`) and for real arrays (`false`).
`Symbol.toPrimitive` replaces the `valueOf`/`toString` dance, receives the hint `'number'`, `'string'` or `'default'`, and must return a primitive or throw.
Other members of the family: `Symbol.iterator`, `Symbol.asyncIterator`, `Symbol.species` and the four string-method symbols.

quiz.q: Why are well-known symbols implemented as **symbols** rather than special string property names?
options: No string-keyed property — user data or typos — can ever collide with or shadow them
Symbols are stored on the prototype, strings on the instance
Symbols can be compared with `===`, strings cannot
quiz.explanation: Symbol keys live in a separate namespace from string keys, so the runtime’s protocol names can never be accidentally (or maliciously) overwritten by ordinary object properties.

quiz.q: `const Even = { [Symbol.hasInstance](n) { return n % 2 === 0; } };` — what is `2 instanceof Even`?
quiz.explanation: When `Symbol.hasInstance` is present on the right-hand object, `instanceof` simply calls it with the left operand and uses its boolean result — no constructor required.

quiz.q: After adding `get [Symbol.toStringTag]() { return 'Circle'; }` to a class, which output changes?
options: `$` interpolation of `new Circle()` inside a template literal
quiz.explanation: `toStringTag` is consulted only by `Object.prototype.toString`; template literals, `String()` and `JSON.stringify` use other conversion paths.

quiz.q: Which hint does the `Symbol.toPrimitive` method receive for the expression `v + 0`, where `v` is an object?
options: No hint — the method is called with no arguments
quiz.explanation: The binary `+` is ambiguous (could mean string concatenation), so it passes the `'default'` hint and lets the method choose; unary `+v` and arithmetic pass `'number'`, templates pass `'string'`.

quiz.q: You set `obj[Symbol.isConcatSpreadable] = true` on an object with `length: 2` and numeric keys `0` and `1`. What does `[9].concat(obj)` return?
options: `TypeError`, because spreading non-arrays is not allowed
quiz.explanation: With the flag true, `concat` reads the object’s `length` and copies its numbered properties into the result, just as it would for a real array.

intro: A **template tag** turns a template literal from data into a function call: writing a function reference immediately before a template literal invokes that function — the **tag** — with the literal’s text and the values of its expressions, and the tag’s return value becomes the value of the whole expression. Tags are how libraries embed little languages inside JavaScript source, and how the built-in `String.raw` escapes the unescaping. This section builds a production-grade `escapeHtml` tag — the single most useful security idiom in the chapter.
objectives: Explain what a tagged template literal is and when it evaluates (parse time versus runtime)
Write the signature of a tag function: the frozen `strings` array plus one argument per substitution
Use the `raw` property and the built-in `String.raw` tag
Implement `escapeHtml()` as a tag that escapes interpolated values but trusts the literal’s text

concepts.statement: A template literal immediately preceded by a function reference is not a string — it is a **call to that function**. The function is the **tag**; the template’s pieces are its argument list, and whatever the tag returns is the value of the whole expression. The tag is an ordinary function: it can be passed around, curried or returned from another function.

A tag receives one leading **`strings` array** followed by one argument per substitution: `tag(strings, ...values)`. `strings` has exactly `values.length + 1` elements (a template with $n$ substitutions has $n + 1$ text chunks), is **frozen** by the runtime, and carries a `raw` property — an array of the raw, unprocessed source text of each chunk.

`String.raw` is a built-in tag that returns the template’s chunks **without processing escape sequences** — the go-to for regex strings, Windows paths and any text where a backslash must survive literally.
concepts.detail:
