```js
String.raw`C:
ew\docs`;   // 'C:
ew\docs' — two real backslashes
`C:
ew\docs`;            // contains a NEWLINE: 
 was processed
```

concepts.statement: The literal chunks of a template are **part of the program’s source code** — authored, reviewed and frozen at parse time — while the values interpolated through the substitution slots are **runtime data**. Security-sensitive tags therefore treat the two differently: the text flows through untouched, and only the substituted values get validated, escaped or parameterized.
concepts.detail: This is the same trust boundary as SQL’s separation of query text from bound parameters, and it is why tagged templates are the natural basis for safe HTML, safe SQL and safe URL builders.

concepts.term: The strings array is cached per call site
concepts.statement: For each distinct tagged-template literal in source, the runtime creates **one** frozen `strings` array and reuses its identity on every evaluation of that literal: `tag` can use the array object itself as a `Map` or `WeakMap` key to memoize parsed templates. Different literals — even with identical text — get different arrays.

Unlike `escapeHtml`, which returns a string, a safe-SQL tag returns a **parameterized query** `{ text, values }`: the literal chunks become `$1, $2` placeholders and the substitutions travel separately, so the database driver never parses data as SQL. Encoding, not escaping, is the defense.

examples.title: An escapeHtml tag for safe HTML strings
examples.problem: A comment renderer builds HTML with `'' + username + ' says: ' + comment` and assigns the result to `innerHTML`. A user named `` executes in every visitor’s browser. Rewrite the builder as a tagged template so the page’s own markup stays intact while interpolated data is neutralized.

steps.label: Step 1: Write the tag
Step 2: Call it as a tag
Step 3: Inspect what the tag received
steps.text: `strings` is `['', ' says: ', '']` — frozen, three chunks for two substitutions; `values` is `['Ada <3', '']`.

steps.label: Step 4: Read the result
steps.text: `html` is `'Ada <3 says: <script>alert("x")</script>'` — the `` markup passes through untouched, while every character of the data that could open a tag became an entity.

steps.label: Step 5: Assign safely
steps.text: `list.innerHTML = html;` renders `Ada <3 says:` in bold followed by the comment’s text displayed literally — the script markup is now inert text, and there is no way for any value passed through a substitution to close the `<b>` and open a new tag.

examples.result: The tagged call produces display-safe HTML: the literal markup is trusted because it is source code, and the two interpolated values are escaped because they are data. The same pattern gives you safe SQL, safe shell commands and safe URLs — hand the template to a tag whose only job is neutralizing one kind of injection.

examples.title: Seeing the two arrays: cooked versus raw
examples.problem: Write a small `showParts` tag that prints exactly what the runtime passes, to make the `strings` array, the `values` array and `strings.raw` concrete.

steps.label: Step 1: Define the tag
Step 2: Count the chunks
steps.text: The template has one substitution, so `strings.length` is `2` and `values.length` is `1` — the invariant `strings.length === values.length + 1` every tag can rely on.

steps.label: Step 3: Compare cooked and raw
steps.text: `strings[0]` contains a real TAB character because the template’s `\t` was processed; `strings.raw[0]` contains the two characters backslash and `t`, because `raw` preserves the source as typed.

steps.label: Step 4: Note the freeze
steps.text: Attempting `strings.push('z')` throws `TypeError` — the runtime freezes the arrays precisely so tags cannot smuggle state between calls of the same template.

examples.result: A tag sees four things: cooked chunks, raw chunks, values, and the guarantee that the chunk arrays are frozen — enough to implement everything from `String.raw` to full little languages.

keyTakeaways: A tagged template is a call, not a string: the tag function receives the pieces, and its return value is the expression’s value.
Signature: `tag(strings, ...values)` with `strings.length === values.length + 1`; both arrays are frozen.
`strings.raw` holds the unprocessed source text — and the built-in `String.raw` tag returns exactly that.
Template text is trusted source; substitutions are untrusted data — the trust boundary that makes tags a security tool.
`escapeHtml` as a tag escapes every substitution while leaving the surrounding markup byte-for-byte intact.

quiz.q: A template literal with one substitution is tagged with `escapeHtml`. How many arguments does `escapeHtml` receive?
options: It depends on the length of `name`
quiz.explanation: One `strings` array (`['', '']`) plus one value per substitution — two arguments for a template with one substitution.

quiz.q: Which expression yields a string containing a real backslash followed by the letter n, with no newline?
options: A plain template literal whose source text is `C:\new`
`String.raw` applied to a template whose source text is `C:\new`
`escapeHtml` applied to a template whose source text is `C:\new`
quiz.explanation: `String.raw` skips escape processing, so the source characters backslash and n survive literally; a normal template processes `\n` into a newline.

quiz.q: In the `escapeHtml` tag, why is only the **substituted value** passed through the escaping replacements?
options: For performance — literals are usually shorter
Because literals are trusted program source, while substitutions are untrusted runtime data
Because the `strings` array is frozen and cannot be modified after replacement
Because HTML entities are not valid inside literal chunks
quiz.explanation: The literal text was authored and reviewed as part of the program; the substituted values are user data — escaping them (and only them) keeps markup intact while neutralizing injection.

quiz.q: A tag is applied to a template whose first text chunk is typed in source as `x\ty` (x, backslash, t), followed by one substitution and the final chunk `y`. What does `strings.raw[0]` contain?
options: A string containing a TAB character
quiz.explanation: `raw` preserves the unprocessed source text: the cooked chunk has a real tab, the raw chunk has the two source characters backslash and t.

quiz.q: A tag is applied to a template with the single text chunk `hello` and no substitutions, and the tag returns the number `42`. What is the value of the tagged-template expression?
options: `'hello'`, because templates always evaluate to strings
`42` — the tag’s return value is the value of the expression
quiz.explanation: Nothing constrains the return type: a tagged template evaluates to whatever its tag function returns.

intro: The `Reflect` object is not a class and not a constructor — it is a **namespace of 13 static functions**, one for each fundamental object operation the language itself performs. Each is the functional counterpart of an operator or `Object` method: `Reflect.get(o, 'x')` for `o.x`, `Reflect.has(o, 'x')` for `'x' in o`, `Reflect.deleteProperty(o, 'x')` for `delete o.x`. Their superpower is uniformity: same arguments, predictable return values, and a one-to-one correspondence with the proxy traps of the next section.
objectives: List the 13 `Reflect` statics and the operator each one replaces
Invoke functions with `Reflect.apply()` using an array of arguments and an explicit receiver
Explain why the fallible `Reflect` methods return `false` instead of throwing, and where that composes better
Use `Reflect.ownKeys()` and describe its ordering guarantee

concepts.statement: `Reflect` groups one static function per fundamental object operation. Calling `Reflect.get(target, 'x')` performs exactly the operation `target.x` would — same prototype-chain walk, same getters — but as a **function**, so it can be stored in a variable, passed as a callback, or invoked with computed names in higher-order code.
concepts.detail: It also patches historical asymmetries: `Reflect.setPrototypeOf` returns a boolean instead of silently failing on non-extensible objects, and `Reflect.defineProperty` returns `false` instead of throwing.

concepts.statement: The complete set: `apply`, `construct`, `get`, `set`, `has`, `deleteProperty`, `defineProperty`, `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, `ownKeys`, `getPrototypeOf`, `setPrototypeOf`, `isExtensible` and `preventExtensions` — one per proxy trap (§14.6) and one per fallible object operation in the language.
concepts.detail:
```text
Reflect.apply(target, thisArg, args)          f.apply(thisArg, args)
Reflect.construct(target, args)               new target(...args)
Reflect.get(target, prop)                     target[prop]
Reflect.set(target, prop, value)              target[prop] = value
Reflect.has(target, prop)                     prop in target
Reflect.deleteProperty(target, prop)          delete target[prop]
Reflect.defineProperty(target, key, desc)     Object.defineProperty
Reflect.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(target, key)  Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor
Reflect.ownKeys(target)                        Object.keys + symbols
Reflect.getPrototypeOf(target)                Object.getPrototypeOf
Reflect.setPrototypeOf(target, proto)         Object.setPrototypeOf
Reflect.isExtensible(target)                  Object.isExtensible
Reflect.preventExtensions(target)             Object.preventExtensions
```

concepts.statement: The `Reflect` forms of fallible operations return `false` on failure where the operator or `Object` method would throw: `Reflect.defineProperty` returns `false` where `Object.defineProperty` throws a `TypeError`, and `Reflect.deleteProperty` returns `false` where a strict-mode `delete` throws. `Reflect.set` likewise returns whether the assignment stuck.
concepts.detail: Boolean-returning operations compose: you can count, filter and short-circuit without `try/catch` scaffolding — and proxy handlers can forward operations and report the outcome truthfully to the proxy machinery.

concepts.statement: `Reflect.apply(target, thisArg, argumentsList)` invokes `target` with an explicit receiver and an **array** of arguments — the modern, non-throwing replacement for `Function.prototype.apply`. `Reflect.construct(target, args)` is its `new` counterpart: it runs the constructor with `args` and returns the fresh instance.

`Reflect.ownKeys(target)` returns every own property key — string keys **and** symbol keys, enumerable or not — in a fixed order: integer-like keys ascending first, then string keys in insertion order, then symbol keys in insertion order.

Every `Reflect` static is paired one-for-one with a proxy trap, so a handler can forward any intercepted operation with the identically-named `Reflect` function — one vocabulary for intercepting an operation and for performing it.

examples.title: Reflect.apply with receivers and argument arrays
examples.problem: A call-tracking wrapper must call an arbitrary function with an arbitrary `this` value and an argument list that arrives as an array — and it must not depend on `Function.prototype.apply`’s `this` pitfalls.

steps.label: Step 1: Variadic built-ins
steps.text:
```js
const prices = [19.99, 4.5, 250, 89.9];
Reflect.apply(Math.max, null, prices);   // 250
Reflect.apply(Math.min, null, prices);   // 4.5
``` `Math.max` cares nothing about `this`, so `null` is the receiver.

steps.label: Step 2: A method that needs its receiver
Step 3: Methods on primitives
steps.text: `Reflect.apply(String.prototype.toUpperCase, 'hello', [])` returns `'HELLO'` — receiver and arguments both flow through the same three-parameter shape.

steps.label: Step 4: Wrap it

examples.result: `Reflect.apply` gives every dynamic call one uniform shape — function, receiver, argument array — which is exactly what wrappers, dispatch tables and proxy `apply` traps need.

examples.title: Operations that never throw
examples.problem: A migration helper copies a chosen set of properties from a legacy record onto a locked, partially-frozen target. With operators it needs `try/catch` around every step; rebuild it with the boolean-returning `Reflect` operations.

steps.label: Step 1: Create a target that will refuse some writes
Step 2: Redefinition without exceptions
steps.text: `Reflect.defineProperty(locked, 'id', { value: 2 })` returns `false` (the property is non-configurable), where `Object.defineProperty` throws `TypeError` — the caller learns the same fact as a value.

steps.label: Step 3: Count the writes that stuck
Step 4: Observe the totals
steps.text: `safeAssign(locked, { id: 9, note: 'x' }, ['id', 'note'])` returns `1`: the frozen `id` write was refused and counted out, while `note` was created successfully.

examples.result: The fallible object operations become ordinary boolean-returning functions — decision logic replaces exception handling, and the same style feeds straight into proxy traps.

examples.title: ownKeys: the complete, ordered key list
examples.problem: Log every own key of an object that mixes integer-like keys, string keys and a symbol key, and predict the order.

steps.label: Step 1: Build the object
Step 2: Call ownKeys
steps.text: `Reflect.ownKeys(obj)` returns `['2', 'b', 'a', Symbol(flags)]` — integer-like keys first in ascending numeric order, then strings in insertion order (`'b'` before `'a'`), then symbols.

steps.label: Step 3: Compare with Object.keys
steps.text: `Object.keys(obj)` returns `['2', 'b', 'a']`: same string ordering, but the symbol key is invisible — and any non-enumerable string keys would be missing too.

steps.label: Step 4: Use the difference deliberately
steps.text: A property-copy utility that should be lossless iterates `Reflect.ownKeys(src)` and uses `Reflect.get(src, key)`; one that should mimic `JSON.stringify` iterates `Object.keys(src)` instead.

examples.result: `Reflect.ownKeys` is the lossless enumeration — integers ascending, then strings, then symbols — and the only single call that reveals all three categories.

keyTakeaways: `Reflect` is a namespace of 13 statics — one per fundamental object operation — not a constructor; `new Reflect()` is a `TypeError`.
Each static is the functional form of an operator: `get`/`set` for property access, `has` for `in`, `deleteProperty` for `delete`, `apply`/`construct` for calls and instantiation.
Fallible operations return `false` instead of throwing (`defineProperty`, `deleteProperty`, `set`, `setPrototypeOf`), which composes without `try/catch`.
`Reflect.apply(f, thisArg, args)` and `Reflect.construct(C, args)` are the uniform dynamic-call forms.
`Reflect.ownKeys` lists every own key — strings and symbols, enumerable or not — as integers, then strings, then symbols.
The 13 statics pair one-to-one with proxy traps: handlers forward with the same-named `Reflect` function.

quiz.q: Which `Reflect` static is the functional counterpart of the `delete` operator?
quiz.explanation: `Reflect.deleteProperty(target, prop)` performs the same operation as `delete target[prop]`, returning `false` on refusal where strict mode would throw.

quiz.q: How many static functions does the `Reflect` object define, and what do they correspond to?
options: 10, one per array method that `Object` also has
13, one per fundamental object operation / proxy trap
It is open-ended — engines keep adding them
quiz.explanation: Thirteen: apply, construct, get, set, has, deleteProperty, defineProperty, getOwnPropertyDescriptor, ownKeys, getPrototypeOf, setPrototypeOf, isExtensible, preventExtensions.

quiz.q: `Object.defineProperty` throws a `TypeError` when it fails. What does `Reflect.defineProperty` do in the same situation?
options: Also throws — they are identical in every case
Returns a string describing the failure
quiz.explanation: The `Reflect` form reports failure as a boolean return value, which is easier to branch on and is exactly what proxy traps are expected to return.

quiz.q: `Reflect.ownKeys({ 2: 'a', b: 1, 1: 'z', [Symbol('s')]: 0 })` returns keys in which order?
options: `['b', '1', '2']` — symbols and integers are both excluded
quiz.explanation: Integer-like keys come first in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order, then symbol keys — so `1`, `2`, `b`, then the symbol.

quiz.q: Why is `Reflect.apply` sometimes preferred over `f.apply(thisArg, args)`?
options: It is always faster in every engine
It cannot be broken by a function that overwrites its own `apply` property, and it takes the arguments as a real array
It converts the arguments to strings first, avoiding type errors
It calls the function in a new thread
quiz.explanation: `f.apply` is a method read off the function object (and can be missing or shadowed), while `Reflect.apply` dispatches through the runtime with the same three-argument shape every time.

intro: A `Proxy` wraps a target object and lets your code intercept its fundamental operations — property reads, writes, `in` tests, deletion, even calls and construction — by supplying **trap** methods on a handler object. Proxies are the endpoint of this chapter: everything before (descriptors, prototypes, symbols, `Reflect`) is what proxies intercept. Two worked examples build the classics — an access-logging proxy and a private-property-enforcing proxy — and a third hands out a capability you can later revoke.
objectives: Create a proxy with `new Proxy(target, handler)` and explain which operations each of the six core traps intercepts
Forward intercepted operations correctly using the matching `Reflect` functions
Build a logging proxy that records every get/set/has/delete, and a proxy that throws on access to underscore-private properties
Explain proxy invariants and use `Proxy.revocable()` to withdraw a capability permanently

concepts.statement: `new Proxy(target, handler)` returns an object that **forwards every operation to `target`** unless the same operation has a **trap** — a method of that name on `handler` — in which case your method runs instead. Operations not covered by any trap behave exactly as they would on the target, and the target itself is unchanged by being wrapped.
concepts.detail: A proxy is transparent-looking but not identical: `proxy === target` is `false`, and `Object.getPrototypeOf(proxy)` consults the trap, not the target’s actual link.

concepts.statement: The six core traps pair with language operations: `get(target, property, receiver)` intercepts property reads; `set(target, property, value, receiver)` intercepts writes; `has(target, property)` intercepts the `in` operator; `deleteProperty(target, property)` intercepts `delete`; `apply(target, thisArg, args)` intercepts calls (function targets only); and `construct(target, args, newTarget)` intercepts `new`.
concepts.detail: The remaining traps mirror the rest of the `Reflect` API: `ownKeys`, `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, `defineProperty`, `getPrototypeOf`, `setPrototypeOf`, `isExtensible` and `preventExtensions` (§14.5).

concepts.statement: The runtime enforces language semantics even on trapped operations and throws `TypeError` when a trap’s answer would make the target lie: you cannot report a non-configurable target property as missing, return `true` from `set` when the corresponding `Reflect.set` would have failed, or fake a prototype for a non-extensible target.
concepts.detail: Invariants are what keep proxies composable with the rest of the language — a proxy of a frozen object still acts frozen, because violating traps are rejected rather than honored.

concepts.statement: A handler whose `get`, `set`, `has` and `deleteProperty` traps throw `TypeError` for any property name beginning with an underscore turns that naming convention into an enforced rule — the wrapped object’s methods are bound to the target so they can still use the private fields internally.
concepts.detail: This is the pattern behind many library classes: hand out `privacyProxy(this)` instead of `this`, and callers simply cannot reach `_cache`, `_listeners` and friends, while the implementation’s own calls — dispatched on the target — work normally.

concepts.statement: `Proxy.revocable(target, handler)` returns `{ proxy, revoke }`. The proxy behaves normally until `revoke()` is called once; afterwards **every** operation on it throws `TypeError` — a permanent, one-way switch for withdrawing access you previously granted.
concepts.detail: Use it when handing an object reference to untrusted or long-lived code: revoke on logout, on timeout, or on subscription cancellation, and even code still holding the reference is locked out.

concepts.statement: Classic applications: logging and profiling, validation on write, private-name enforcement, negative array indices or virtual properties, remote-object RPC layers, memoization, test doubles — anywhere the **meaning** of a property access needs to change rather than its value.
concepts.detail: Limits to keep in mind: traps fire on property operations, not on internal slots — a proxied `Date` still delegates its data to the target; `==`, `typeof` and a few built-in internal reads bypass traps entirely.

examples.title: A full access-logging proxy
examples.problem: Audit every read, write, membership test and deletion performed on a `user` object over one debugging session, without touching the object or any of its callers.

steps.label: Step 1: Write the handler
Step 2: Wrap and exercise it
steps.text:
```js
const user = makeLoggingProxy({ name: 'Ada', role: 'admin' }, 'user');
user.name;              // a read
user.role = 'editor';    // a write
'name' in user;          // a membership test
delete user.role;        // a deletion
```

steps.label: Step 3: Read the session log
steps.text:
```text
get    user.name -> Ada
set    user.role = editor [true]
has    user.name [true]
delete user.role [true]
```

steps.label: Step 4: Note the forwarding discipline
steps.text: Every trap uses the same-named `Reflect` function rather than touching `t` directly — that keeps receiver semantics (getters, setters, prototype walks) exactly as they would be without the proxy, and satisfies the `set` invariant by returning the truthful outcome.

steps.label: Step 5: Swap the proxy out
steps.text: The original object still exists unchanged; dropping the proxy reference and handing callers `user` again removes the logging with zero code changes at the call sites.

examples.result: Four traps and four `Reflect` calls give a complete, zero-caller-impact audit trail of property traffic — the debugging use case, and the template for validation, memoization and RPC proxies.

examples.title: Enforcing private properties with a proxy
examples.problem: A `Counter` class stores internal state under names beginning with `_`. The convention is not enforced — callers keep poking `counter._value`. Return a proxy from the constructor so underscore properties are unreachable from outside but fully usable from the class’s own methods.

steps.label: Step 1: Write the guarding handler
Step 2: Return the proxy from the constructor
Step 3: The bind makes methods work
steps.text: The `get` trap binds every returned function to the target `t`, so when a caller does `counter.increment()` the method’s `this` is the unguarded target — the class’s own code can use `_value` freely even though callers cannot.

steps.label: Step 4: Test the enforcement
steps.text:
```js
const c = new Counter(10);
c.increment();        // 11 — public method, bound to target
c.n();                // 11 — public method
c._value;             // TypeError: private property _value
c._value = 0;         // TypeError: private property _value
'_value' in c;        // false — hidden from membership tests too
```

steps.label: Step 5: Acknowledge the boundary
steps.text: A determined caller can still reach the target through a bound method’s receiver or by holding the raw object — proxy privacy is strong convention enforcement, not cryptography; true hard privacy needs the `#field` syntax of Chapter 9.

examples.result: The underscore convention became a runtime rule: public methods work, underscore properties throw, `in` lies to no one, and the class implementation itself is unaffected.

examples.title: Handing out access you can take back
examples.problem: A settings service lends a `session` object to third-party plugin code. On logout you need the plugin’s held reference to become useless — even though you cannot reach into the plugin to delete its variables.

steps.label: Step 1: Create a revocable proxy
Step 2: Use it while it lasts
steps.text: `session.user` returns `'ada'`; `session.expires` returns the string — all traps behave like a normal proxy.

steps.label: Step 3: Revoke on logout
Step 4: Observe the aftermath
steps.text: Any later use by the plugin throws: `session.user` → `TypeError: Cannot perform 'get' on a proxy that has been revoked`. The same applies to writes, `in`, `delete`, `apply` and every other operation — there is no trap that can rescue it.

steps.label: Step 5: Note the design pattern
steps.text: This is a capability revocation: the object was never the resource, only a key to it. Pair it with a timer (`setTimeout(revoke, 3600000)`) for expiring grants, or with an event listener to revoke on teardown.

examples.result: One `revoke()` call neutralizes every outstanding reference at once — cheaper and safer than chasing down and nulling each variable yourself.

keyTakeaways: `new Proxy(target, handler)` wraps an object; handler methods named after operations — `get`, `set`, `has`, `deleteProperty`, `apply`, `construct` — intercept them, and absent traps fall through to the target.
Traps should forward with the same-named `Reflect` function, returning its truthful result — that satisfies the proxy invariants that would otherwise throw `TypeError`.
`apply` and `construct` require a callable target and turn the proxy into a wrapped function or class.
A `get` trap that binds returned functions to the target is the key trick for private-property proxies — methods keep private access, callers do not.
`Proxy.revocable(target, handler)` returns `{ proxy, revoke }`; after `revoke()`, every operation on the proxy throws `TypeError` forever.
Proxies change the **meaning** of property operations: logging, validation, virtual properties, privacy, RPC and test doubles — not the target’s own state.

quiz.q: Which handler trap intercepts the expression `'secret' in proxy`?
quiz.explanation: The `in` operator routes through the `has(target, property)` trap; `get` covers property reads and `ownKeys` covers `Object.keys`-style enumeration.

quiz.q: A proxy’s `set` trap runs `Reflect.set(t, prop, value)` which returns `false` on a frozen target property, but the trap returns `true` anyway. What happens?
options: Nothing — trap return values are advisory
The runtime throws a `TypeError`, because the trap violated a proxy invariant
The write is forced through to the frozen property
The proxy is silently unwrapped to the target
quiz.explanation: Invariants forbid reporting success for operations that actually failed — the proxy machinery checks the trap’s answer against the target’s reality and throws.

quiz.q: In the private-property proxy, why does the `get` trap bind returned functions to the target object?
options: So that public methods called through the proxy have `this` set to the unguarded target and can still use `_private` fields
Because proxies cannot return unbound functions
To make `typeof method` return 'function' instead of 'proxy'
quiz.explanation: The class’s own methods must keep unrestricted access to its private fields; binding them to the target sends their `this` around the guard entirely.

quiz.q: After `const { proxy, revoke } = Proxy.revocable(t, h); revoke();` — what does `proxy.anything` do?
options: Forwards to the target one last time, then blocks
Throws `TypeError` — revoked proxies cannot perform any operation
quiz.explanation: Revocation is total and one-way: get, set, has, delete, apply, construct — every operation throws `TypeError` on a revoked proxy.

quiz.q: Which trap only exists when the proxy target is a **function**?
quiz.explanation: `apply(target, thisArg, args)` intercepts calls and (with `construct`) `new` — both only make sense for callable targets; using them with object targets throws at proxy creation.

Step 1: The code given reads the same property once through a doubling proxy and once straight from the target. Step 2: The governing rules are that a `get` trap intercepts only reads performed through the proxy object, that it should forward with the matching `Reflect`-style read `t[prop]`, and that direct reads of the target bypass every trap. Step 3: Tracing read by read, `shop.price` enters the trap, reads `10`, doubles it to `20`, while `target.price` skips the handler and yields the stored `10`. Step 4: The distractors fail because the trap never rewrites the target itself, and direct reads never consult the handler. Step 5: Therefore the output is `20` followed by `10`.

intro: A web browser is a **host environment**: it parses HTML into a live tree of objects, runs your scripts against it, and dispatches **events** when the world changes. Everything in this chapter — documents, styles, graphics, networking, storage — hangs off a handful of globals: `window`, `document`, `location`. Two facts organize it all: scripts are guests of the HTML parser (hence `async` and `defer`), and the whole platform is **single-threaded** per page — the same run-to-completion rule of Section 13.1, with the browser’s renderer waiting on the same thread.
objectives: Embed scripts with script tags and choose between inline, external, async and defer
Name the key browser globals and what each provides
Predict script execution order and DOMContentLoaded timing for each embedding mode
Explain the single-threaded execution model and its consequences for responsiveness
Attach load-phase handlers at the right granularity (DOMContentLoaded vs load)

concepts.statement: JavaScript enters an HTML page through `<script>`: **inline** code between the tags runs immediately where it appears; a `src` attribute fetches an external file. A `<script type="module" src="...">` is an ES6 module (Section 10.3) — its imports and exports make it a separate scope, and it is automatically deferred.
concepts.detail:
```html
<script>
  console.log("runs immediately, right here in the parse");
</script>
<script src="app.js"></script>
<script type="module" src="app.js"></script>   <!-- module: deferred by default -->
```
The position matters for plain scripts: one in `<head>` runs before any body HTML exists, which is why decades of scripts lived at the end of `<body>` — and why `defer` exists.

concepts.statement: Both boolean attributes let the file **download in parallel** while parsing continues; they differ on **when it runs**. `defer`: execution is postponed until the document has been parsed, and deferred scripts run **in document order**. `async`: execution begins **as soon as the download completes** — possibly mid-parse, possibly before other async scripts that started earlier — so order is not guaranteed.
concepts.detail: Rule of thumb: `defer` for scripts that need the DOM (the common case — they still finish before DOMContentLoaded); `async` for fully independent code such as analytics and ad tags that touch no page state.

concepts.statement: The `window` object **is** the global object of browser JavaScript: global variables and `window` properties are the same storage (Section 3.5). It doubles as the browser API surface — `window.location` (the `Location` object wrapping the current URL), `window.history` (15.9), `navigator` (the browser itself), `screen`, and the timers of Section 13.1.
concepts.detail:
```js
window.window === window;        // true — it is a property of itself
globalThis === window;             // true in browsers
location.href;                    // the full URL, live
```
`document` is reachable as `window.document` and is the root of the page itself — the entry point for all of Section 15.3.

concepts.statement: The HTML parser builds the **Document Object Model** — a live tree of objects with `document` at the root, `document.documentElement` (the `<html>` element), its `.head` and `.body` children, and element, text and comment nodes below. "Live" means the tree is the page: script mutations appear on screen, and user edits appear in the tree.
concepts.detail: The DOM is where the language meets the document: `document.getElementById`, `querySelector` and friends (15.3) are queries against this tree, and event handlers (15.2) fire with nodes of it as their targets.

concepts.statement: Browser JavaScript runs on **one thread per page**: one call stack, run-to-completion (Section 13.1), and the user-interface work — parsing, styling, layout, paint — queues behind it. A long-running script blocks **everything**: clicks go unprocessed, animations freeze, the tab may flag the page unresponsive. The host gets the same treatment an OS gives a monopolizing process (Operating System Concepts, Chapter 4) — except there is no preemption, so the fix is cooperative: return quickly, schedule the rest.
concepts.detail: The escape hatches: asynchronous APIs (Section 13.2 — promises and the event loop), and real parallelism via Worker threads (Section 15.12), which give a page additional kernel threads that cannot touch the DOM. Compare OSC Chapter 4’s threading model — JavaScript deliberately exposes none of its shared-memory hazards.

concepts.statement: `document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", fn)` fires once the tree is fully parsed and deferred scripts have run — images and stylesheets may still be downloading. `window.addEventListener("load", fn)` waits for **all** resources (images, stylesheets, subframes). The first is where scripts initialize page logic; the second, where pixel-dependent work belongs.

examples.title: Four script tags, one timeline: the async/defer comparison
examples.problem:
Predict when each script runs and when DOMContentLoaded fires:
```html
<head>
  <script src="a.js"></script>              <!-- 1 -->
  <script src="b.js" defer></script>        <!-- 2 -->
  <script src="c.js" async></script>        <!-- 3 -->
</head>
<body>
  <!-- ...content... -->
  <script src="d.js" defer></script>        <!-- 4 -->
</body>
```

steps.label: Step 1: Script 1 — the parser-blocking default
steps.text: Parsing stops dead at the tag: the browser downloads a.js **synchronously with the parse**, runs it to completion, then resumes parsing. Whatever a.js needs from the document, only content parsed so far exists. This is the behavior `defer` was invented to abolish.

steps.label: Step 2: Scripts 2 and 4 — deferred, in order
steps.text: b.js and d.js download in parallel with parsing but do not run yet. When the parser finishes the document, deferred scripts execute **in document order**: b.js first, then d.js — each seeing the complete tree. Only after the last one does `DOMContentLoaded` fire. Two scripts that share state can rely on that order.

steps.label: Step 3: Script 3 — async, racing
steps.text: c.js also downloads in parallel, but runs the **moment its download completes** — mid-parse if the network was fast, before b.js if b.js was slow. Nothing about relative order is guaranteed, and other async scripts may overtake it. `DOMContentLoaded` does **not** wait for async scripts that are still pending.

steps.label: Step 4: Assemble the timeline
steps.text: Typical fast-network timeline: a.js (blocking, in head) → parsing proceeds, c.js fires whenever ready → parse completes → b.js → d.js → DOMContentLoaded → images finish → load. On a slow CDN for c.js, the same page could run b.js, d.js and DOMContentLoaded **before** c.js — async code must never depend on page state.

steps.label: Step 5: Choose by dependency
steps.text: Needs the DOM or another script → `defer` (or a module, which defers by default). Independent, fire-and-forget → `async`. Needs to run exactly where it sits in the document (e.g., writing content inline) → plain blocking, the rarest and weakest option.

examples.result:
```text
mode     | downloads  | executes                 | order      | blocks parse
---------+------------+--------------------------+------------+-------------
default  | blocks     | immediately, at the tag  | document   | YES
async    | parallel   | on download completion   | arbitrary  | NO
defer    | parallel   | after parse, pre-DCL     | document   | NO
module   | parallel   | deferred                 | document   | NO
```
Deferred scripts run in order before DOMContentLoaded; async scripts race and are not waited for.

examples.title: DOMContentLoaded vs load: where to initialise without freezing

steps.label: Step 1: DOMContentLoaded builds structure
steps.text: The nav needs only elements, so it runs at DOMContentLoaded — tree parsed, deferred scripts done, images possibly still downloading. Querying here is safe; measuring image widths here is not, because layout is not final.

steps.label: Step 2: load measures geometry
steps.text: The gallery layout reads image widths, so it waits for the window load event — every stylesheet, image and subframe done. Section 15.5 geometry measured here is stable; measured earlier it would shift as images arrive.

steps.label: Step 3: The 300 ms freeze
steps.text: Calling sortTitles on the main thread blocks the one page thread: parsing, styling, paint and click handlers queue behind it. During those 300 ms the tab ignores input — the single-threaded rule with the renderer in the same queue.

steps.label: Step 4: The cooperative fix
steps.text: Chunk the sort with async slices or move it to a Worker (Section 15.12): buildNav and layoutGallery stay on DOMContentLoaded and load, and the heavy work yields between chunks so clicks and paint interleave.

examples.result: Nav at DOMContentLoaded, geometry at load, heavy work off the critical path — one thread means initialisation timing and responsiveness are the same decision.

keyTakeaways: Scripts enter via `<script>` — inline runs immediately; `src` fetches a file; `type="module"` is scoped and deferred by default.
`defer` downloads in parallel, runs after parsing in document order, before DOMContentLoaded; `async` runs on arrival in arbitrary order.
Plain scripts block the parser; end-of-body placement was the pre-defer workaround.
`window` is the global object and the browser API surface; `document` roots the live DOM tree; `location` wraps the current URL.
One thread per page: long scripts block rendering and input — the run-to-completion rule of Section 13.1 with the renderer behind it in the queue (contrast OSC Ch 4 threads).
Use DOMContentLoaded for tree-dependent initialization and `load` for resource-complete work such as geometry (15.5).

quiz.q: Two scripts must run in a specific order and both need the parsed document. The right embedding is:
options: Both `defer` — execution follows document order after parsing
One inline in head, one at end of body
quiz.explanation: defer preserves document order and guarantees the full tree; async gives no ordering guarantee, and plain scripts block parsing in head.

quiz.q: When does an `async` script execute?
options: After the document finishes parsing, in order
As soon as its download completes — possibly mid-parse and in arbitrary order relative to other async scripts
quiz.explanation: async decouples execution from the parse entirely: arrival time is the only schedule, which is why async scripts must be self-contained.

quiz.q: Which statement about the browser execution model is TRUE?
options: Each script runs on its own thread
Page JavaScript shares one thread with parsing, layout and paint — a long task freezes all of them
Rendering happens on a second thread, so long scripts never affect it
The OS preempts scripts every 16 ms to keep the page responsive
quiz.explanation: One thread per page, no preemption: the renderer queues behind the script (Section 13.1 run-to-completion; OSC Ch 4 contrasts with preemptive threads). Workers (15.12) are the real parallel escape hatch.

quiz.q: The DOMContentLoaded event fires when —
options: all images and stylesheets have downloaded
the document tree is fully parsed and deferred scripts have run — pending async scripts are not waited for
quiz.explanation: DOMContentLoaded marks the parsed tree plus deferred scripts; resource-complete is the separate load event on window.

intro: The browser is **event-driven**: clicks, keys, submits, network completions and timer expirations all arrive as event objects dispatched to your handlers. `addEventListener` registers interest; the **propagation model** carries each event down and then back up the tree (capture and bubble), which makes **delegation** — one listener for a whole subtree — the platform’s most valuable pattern. Options like `once`, `capture` and `passive` tune registration, and `CustomEvent` lets your own code speak the same language with `detail` payloads.
objectives: Register and remove listeners, including the legacy property form
Use the options object: once, capture and passive
Trace an event through capture, target and bubble phases
Distinguish stopPropagation from preventDefault precisely
Implement event delegation and dispatch custom events with detail payloads

concepts.statement: `target.addEventListener(type, listener)` registers a function (or any object with a `handleEvent` method) for events of the given type; calling it again adds more handlers — the legacy one-handler-per-property form (`element.onclick = fn`) is overwritten by assignment and can hold only one.

The third argument tunes registration: **`once: true`** auto-removes the handler after its first run (one-shot setup); **`capture: true`** listens on the way **down** the tree instead of the way up; **`passive: true`** promises the handler will never call `preventDefault` — the browser may then scroll immediately without waiting for the handler, the standard for touch and wheel listeners.

An event dispatched at a target element travels the tree in **three phases**: **capture** (from `window`/`document` down through ancestors to the target’s parent), **target** (the handlers on the target itself), then **bubble** (back up the same path to document and window). Ordinary listeners fire in the bubble phase; `{ capture: true }` listeners fire in the capture phase — the same event object visits both.
concepts.detail: The path is computed **at dispatch time** from the target’s current position in the tree. Not every event bubbles (focus and mouseenter do not), but click, key, input, submit and most UI events do.

concepts.statement: The two cancellations are orthogonal. **`e.stopPropagation()`** stops the **propagation** — later listeners on the path never run (and `e.stopImmediatePropagation()` also silences later listeners on the **same** element). **`e.preventDefault()`** cancels the **default action** — the navigation of a link, the submission of a form, the checkbox toggle — while propagation continues untouched.
concepts.detail: Four combinations are all meaningful: prevent the action and let handlers run everywhere; stop the propagation and still let the default happen; both; neither. See the worked trace — the pair is the most-confused duo in event programming.

concepts.statement: Because events bubble, **one listener on a common ancestor** can handle events for all its descendants: inspect `e.target`, find the relevant node with `e.target.closest(selector)`, and act. Rows added to the table later are covered with zero new listeners — the ancestor was listening all along.
concepts.detail: The pattern’s economics: 1,000 rows with one listener each means 1,000 closures and 1,000 registrations; delegation means one. It also survives dynamic content — innerHTML rebuilds, template clones, user-added items.

concepts.statement: Application code can speak the platform’s language: `new CustomEvent("note-added", { detail: payload })` creates an event whose `detail` property carries any data, and `target.dispatchEvent(event)` runs it through the full capture-target-bubble machinery — synchronously, with the same propagation rules as a click.

The handler receives one **event object**: `e.type` (the event name), `e.target` (the deepest node where it happened — constant through propagation), `e.currentTarget` (the node the running handler is attached to — changes at each hop), `e.timeStamp`, plus per-type fields like `e.key` or `e.clientX`. In a function handler, `this` equals `currentTarget`.
concepts.detail: The target/currentTarget split is what delegation is made of: the listener sits on the table (`currentTarget`) while `target` points at whatever inside it was actually clicked.

examples.title: Trace the engine: one click, two cancellations

steps.label: Step 1: Capture — the dive from the top
steps.text: The click at the anchor is dispatched through its **path** (computed from its position): window → document → outer → list → link. Capture-phase listeners run top-down: `outer` logs first, then `list` — each seeing `e.target` = link and `e.currentTarget` = itself.

steps.label: Step 2: Target — the handlers on the node itself
steps.text: At the anchor, its own listener runs: `"target link"` is pushed, and `e.preventDefault()` records that the **default action** (following the href) must not happen. Propagation is untouched — the event keeps moving.

steps.label: Step 3: Bubble — the climb back
steps.text: The event reverses up the same path. Only `outer` has a bubble-phase listener here, so the final log is `["capture outer", "capture list", "target link", "bubble outer"]` — four entries, one user action. **No navigation occurs** despite all four handlers running.

steps.label: Step 4: Swap in stopPropagation instead
steps.text: Replace the target handler’s `preventDefault()` with `e.stopPropagation()`: the log ends at `["capture outer", "capture list", "target link"]` — no bubble hop — but the browser **navigates to example.com** anyway. Stopping propagation does not stop the default action; the two switches are on separate circuits.

steps.label: Step 5: The remaining variants
steps.text: A `stopPropagation()` in the **capture** listener on outer strangles the event immediately: the log is just `["capture outer"]`, no target handlers run — and the link still navigates unless something also calls preventDefault. And `stopImmediatePropagation()` would have silenced even sibling listeners on the same node. The complete matrix: propagation and default action are independent axes.

examples.result: `["capture outer", "capture list", "target link", "bubble outer"]` with no navigation — preventDefault cancels the action; with stopPropagation instead, the log is three entries **and the page navigates**. Cancel propagation, cancel the action — or both, but never confuse them.

examples.title: One listener, every row: event delegation

steps.label: Step 1: The listener sits above the action
steps.text: Registration is on the `<tbody>` — an ancestor of every row. Clicks on any delete button **bubble up** to it (Section 15.2’s propagation law), so the handler runs with `e.currentTarget` = tbody and `e.target` = whatever was actually clicked (the button, or a span inside it).

steps.label: Step 2: closest() finds the thing you meant
steps.text: The click may land on the button’s icon or label, not the button element itself. `event.target.closest("button.delete")` walks **up** from the click target to the nearest matching ancestor — the robust way to recover the intended element from an arbitrary inner one. A null means the click was elsewhere: return early.

steps.label: Step 3: The containment guard
steps.text: `contains(button)` verifies the found button really is inside this tbody — with nested tables or document-level listeners, a matching element from some other container could bubble through. One boolean closes the hole; `closest` + `contains` is the standard delegation pair.

steps.label: Step 4: New rows are covered automatically
steps.text: The freshly appended row needs no listener: its clicks bubble along the same path to the same handler. This is why delegation pairs so well with the dynamic content of Section 15.3 — rebuild the tbody wholesale and the single listener keeps working.

steps.label: Step 5: The economics and the limits
steps.text: One closure, one registration, O(1) setup instead of O(rows) — and memory that does not grow with the document. The limits: events that do not bubble (focus, mouseenter) cannot be delegated this way, and `stopPropagation` from a third-party handler between target and ancestor will swallow the event — the platform’s version of the interference problem.

examples.result: One listener handles 1,000 rows, 10,000 rows and rows not yet created — clicks bubble, `closest` recovers the button, `contains` scopes it, `tr.remove()` acts. Delegation is the event model’s payoff for having a bubble phase.

keyTakeaways: addEventListener stacks multiple handlers; the legacy `.onclick =` property holds only one; removal needs the identical function reference.
Options tune registration: `once` for one-shot, `capture` for the downward phase, `passive` to let scrolling proceed (never preventDefault there).
Every event travels capture (top → down), target, bubble (up → top); `e.target` is where it happened, `e.currentTarget` is which handler is running.
`stopPropagation` halts the path (stopImmediatePropagation also halts same-element rivals); `preventDefault` cancels the default action — completely independent switches.
Delegation: one ancestor listener + `e.target.closest(sel)` + `contains` guard handles any number of descendants, including future ones.
`new CustomEvent(type, { detail })` + `dispatchEvent` gives application code the same synchronous machinery with typed payloads; synthetic events have isTrusted false.

quiz.q: In a propagation trace, `e.currentTarget` is —
options: the element whose handler is currently running — it changes hop by hop
quiz.explanation: target stays fixed at the dispatch point; currentTarget walks the path with the handler — the asymmetry that makes delegation inspectable.

quiz.q: A link’s click handler calls only `e.stopPropagation()`. What happens?
options: The navigation is cancelled and other handlers still run
Ancestor handlers are skipped but the browser still navigates to the href
Both propagation and navigation are cancelled
Nothing — stopPropagation must be paired with preventDefault
quiz.explanation: stopPropagation affects only the event path; the default action is a separate circuit — canceling navigation needs preventDefault.

quiz.q: Which listener option tells the browser it may start scrolling without waiting for your wheel handler to finish?
quiz.explanation: passive promises no preventDefault, letting scrolling proceed immediately — mandatory hygiene for scroll, wheel and touch listeners.

quiz.q: Why does event delegation keep working for rows added after registration?
options: The browser re-registers the listener for new rows
Clicks from the new rows bubble to the same ancestor that holds the single listener
New rows inherit listeners through their prototype
Delegation polls the DOM for changes
quiz.explanation: The listener is on the ancestor, and propagation is computed per event from the target’s current position — any descendant, old or new, reaches it.

quiz.q: How does a custom event carry data to its handlers?
options: Through the event’s detail property, set via new CustomEvent(type, { detail: payload })
Through a second argument to the handler
quiz.explanation: The options object’s detail field is the payload slot; dispatchEvent then runs the same capture-target-bubble machinery, synchronously.

intro: The **Document Object Model** is the page as a live tree of objects, and scripting it is the heart of browser programming: select nodes, read and write their attributes, classes and data, then create, insert and remove nodes to reshape the page. Two safety lines run through everything: `querySelector`/`querySelectorAll` give CSS-grade querying, and `textContent` — not `innerHTML` — is the default way to put untrusted text on screen.
objectives: Select elements with querySelector, querySelectorAll and getElementById
Distinguish static NodeLists from live HTMLCollections
Read and write attributes, classes and data-* state
Create, insert, replace and remove nodes — and batch them with DocumentFragment
Explain why innerHTML with untrusted text is an XSS hole and textContent is not

concepts.term: The DOM as a live tree
concepts.statement: The document is a tree of **nodes**: the `Document` root, **Element** nodes for tags, **Text** nodes for character data, **Comment** nodes, each with `parentNode`, `children` (element children) and `childNodes` (all children). The tree is **live** — mutating it changes the rendered page, and the page changing (user typing, scripts) changes the tree.
concepts.detail:
```js
document.documentElement;      // <html>
document.body;                // <body>
document.body.children[0];     // first element child
docEl.parentNode;             // the Document — the top of the tree
```
Traversal properties (`firstElementChild`, `nextElementSibling`) come in element-only and all-node pairs — prefer the element forms.

concepts.statement: `document.querySelector(cssSelector)` returns the **first** element matching any CSS selector, or null; `document.querySelectorAll(sel)` returns **all** matches; both also work on any element, searching its subtree. `document.getElementById(id)` is the classic by-id fast path. Class and tag lookups (`getElementsByClassName`, `getElementsByTagName`) exist too — but return **live** collections.
concepts.detail:
```js
document.querySelector("#main .item.active");   // CSS selector, first match
const items = document.querySelectorAll("li.todo");  // all matches
items.length;                                     // snapshot size
for (const li of items) { /* NodeList is iterable */ }
```
Selector power comes from CSS itself: `input[type="checkbox"]:checked`, `.item:not(.done)`, combinators — the full grammar of stylesheets (15.4) is your query language.

concepts.statement: `querySelectorAll` returns a **static** NodeList — a snapshot that does not change when the document does. The `getElementsBy*` methods return **live** HTMLCollections that grow and shrink with the tree: looping over one while you mutate the document can process nodes twice or skip them. Snapshot semantics are the safer default.
concepts.detail: A live collection is a view, not an array — `HTMLCollection` has no `map`. Convert with `Array.from(collection)` when array methods are needed; a static NodeList supports `forEach` directly and is iterable (Section 12.1’s protocol).

concepts.statement: Attributes are the HTML-serialized face of an element: `el.getAttribute(name)`, `setAttribute(name, value)`, `hasAttribute(name)`, `removeAttribute(name)`. Most common attributes have mirror **properties** (`id`, `title`, `src`, `href`), but attributes and properties can diverge — `value` on an input is the attribute only until the user edits, after which the property holds the truth.

`el.classList` is a live token list for the class attribute: `add`, `remove`, `toggle(name, force?)`, `contains`, `replace` — no string splitting ever again. Custom `data-*` attributes surface as the `el.dataset` object: `data-priority="high"` becomes `el.dataset.priority === "high"` (dashes become camelCase).
concepts.detail:
```js
el.classList.toggle("done", finished);   // force form: add if finished, else remove
el.dataset.lastEditedBy = "ada";         // creates data-last-edited-by="ada"
```
`data-*` attributes are the sanctioned channel for stashing small state in markup — visible in the DOM inspector, trivially read in handlers and delegation (15.2).

concepts.statement: New nodes come from `document.createElement(tag)` and `document.createTextNode(str)`; the modern insertion API puts them relative to any node: `parent.append(...nodes)` (inside, at the end), `prepend` (inside, start), `sibling.before(...)` / `after(...)` (outside), `el.replaceWith(...nodes)`, `el.remove()`. `cloneNode(true)` deep-copies.

A **fragment** is a lightweight container for a batch of nodes: build the batch inside it, then insert the whole fragment **once** — the children move, the fragment itself stays out of the tree. When inserting many nodes, one insert means one reflow calculation instead of one per node.

`el.textContent = s` sets plain text — the string is **data**, never parsed as markup, so nothing inside it can execute. `el.innerHTML = s` parses the string as **HTML**: any script or event-handler markup in it becomes live — with untrusted input, that is **cross-site scripting (XSS)**. Read of `textContent` also flattens children to their concatenated text.
concepts.detail: ```js const comment = ''; div.innerHTML = comment; // XSS: the onerror handler RUNS div.textContent = comment; // SAFE: literal text, angle brackets visible ``` Reserve `innerHTML` for trusted template strings you wrote yourself; for anything a user touched, `textContent` and `createElement` — or a library that escapes — are the rule. `insertAdjacentHTML` has the same trust requirement.

examples.title: Filtering a page: querySelectorAll + dataset

steps.label: Step 1: Select once, outside the handler
steps.text: `querySelectorAll("li.skill")` runs at setup and captures a **static NodeList** — a snapshot of the current matches. Inside the handler we only read it, so static semantics are exactly right; a live `getElementsByClassName` would also work but re-queries on every access.

steps.label: Step 2: The selector carries the query’s meaning
steps.text: CSS syntax does the filtering: `li.skill` means "list items with class skill" — descendant combinators, attribute selectors and pseudo-classes are all available (Section 15.4’s grammar). `document.querySelector("#filter")` grabs the first — and only — element with that id.

steps.label: Step 3: dataset reads the data-level attribute
steps.text: `li.dataset.level` returns the value of `data-level` — the dashes-to-camelCase mapping, applied in reverse for writes. State rides along in markup, so any handler (or delegated one, Section 15.2) can read it without a lookup table.

steps.label: Step 4: The hidden property toggles visibility
steps.text: Setting `li.hidden` reflects to the `hidden` HTML attribute — a no-JS, no-CSS visibility switch every browser honors. The boolean expression folds both cases: matching rows and "all" stay visible, everything else hides.

steps.label: Step 5: Why not rebuild the list instead
steps.text: An `innerHTML` rebuild would also work but costs a full parse of new markup plus the loss of all existing node state (listeners on children, focus, input values). Toggling `hidden` mutates one property per row — the targeted-update habit that scales.

examples.result: Changing the select instantly shows only the matching rows — one static query, per-row `dataset` reads, and `hidden` toggles; no markup is ever re-parsed.

examples.title: Building a list: DocumentFragment and the innerHTML trap

steps.label: Step 1: replaceChildren clears in one step
steps.text: The modern clearing call removes every child of the list at once (the old way: a while-loop of `removeChild(firstChild)`). Starting from an empty list makes the render a pure function of the data — no stale rows survive.

steps.label: Step 2: createElement + textContent for each row
steps.text:
Each `
  • ` is a real element built in detached space; `textContent` assigns the title **as text data** — if a title is ``, the page will literally display those characters, harmlessly. `dataset.done` stamps the completion state into a `data-done` attribute for CSS hooks (15.4).

steps.label: Step 3: The fragment batches the insertion
steps.text: One hundred rows appended one-by-one means one hundred layout invalidations. Appending the **fragment** moves all its children into the list in a single tree operation — the batch enters together, and the browser computes layout once. The fragment itself never appears in the tree.

steps.label: Step 4: The unsafe variant, dissected
steps.text: The `innerHTML` version is shorter and one reflow too — but it **parses** every title as markup. A malicious title like `` becomes a real element with a real event handler: cross-site scripting, in one line. The rule of Section 15.3: `innerHTML` is for template strings **you** wrote; user data goes in via `textContent` or attribute APIs only.

steps.label: Step 5: When innerHTML is legitimate
steps.text: Static, developer-authored markup — a row template with fixed structure and placeholders filled from safe values, ideally via `insertAdjacentHTML` — is a fine use. The dividing line is **trust**: markup that exists in your source is trusted; anything that passed through a user is not. When in doubt, build nodes and set `textContent`.

examples.result: The fragment version renders any array of titles — hostile ones included — as inert text in one reflow. The unsafe version executes markup smuggled into a title: same visual output for honest data, XSS for hostile data.

keyTakeaways: The DOM is a live tree of Document/Element/Text/Comment nodes; script mutations and page state are two views of one thing.
`querySelector`/`querySelectorAll` speak full CSS — first match and static snapshot respectively; `getElementById` is the by-id fast path.
Prefer the static NodeList of querySelectorAll over live HTMLCollections when iterating around mutations; snapshot semantics are predictable.
Attributes are markup (`getAttribute`/`setAttribute`); properties are state — `value` diverges from its attribute after user input.
`classList` manages classes without string surgery; `data-*` attributes mirror onto `dataset` for markup-riding state.
Modern insertion — `append`, `prepend`, `before`, `after`, `replaceWith`, `remove` — plus `replaceChildren` for clearing; `DocumentFragment` batches many nodes into one reflow.
`textContent` is the safe channel for untrusted text; `innerHTML` parses markup and is an XSS hole unless every byte is trusted.

quiz.q: What does `document.querySelectorAll(".item")` return?
options: A live HTMLCollection that updates as the document changes
A static NodeList — a snapshot of the current matches, iterable and forEach-able
quiz.explanation: querySelectorAll snapshots: later document changes do not alter it — the predictable default versus the live getElementsBy* collections.

quiz.q: An input has `value="a"` in its HTML, the user types "b", then the script runs `input.setAttribute("value", "c")`. What does `input.value` read?
options: "b" — the property holds the user’s edit; setting the attribute does not overwrite it
quiz.explanation: The value attribute sets the initial value; the property diverges on first user input and stays authoritative — read state from properties.

quiz.q: Why insert a batch of nodes through a DocumentFragment rather than appending them one by one?
options: The whole batch enters the tree in one operation — one layout pass instead of one per node
Fragments are required for createElement to work
quiz.explanation: The fragment is a detached container: a single append moves all its children at once, so the browser computes layout once — the DOM’s batch-update idiom.

quiz.q: A comment string from a user is placed on the page. Which is the XSS-safe assignment?
options: `div.innerText += comment;` after setting innerHTML to the comment
quiz.explanation: textContent treats the string as data, never markup — angle brackets render as characters. Any innerHTML route parses it, and a smuggled onerror handler executes.

quiz.q: `li.dataset.lastEditedBy` corresponds to which attribute in the HTML?
quiz.explanation: dataset keys map to data-* attributes with camelCase ↔ dash-case conversion: dataset.lastEditedBy ↔ data-last-edited-by.

Step 1: The data given is two collections taken before a matching paragraph is appended, then both lengths logged. Step 2: The governing rules are that `querySelectorAll` returns a static snapshot fixed at call time, while `getElementsByClassName` returns a live view that tracks DOM mutations automatically. Step 3: Tracing mutation by mutation, both collections start with length `2`, the append adds a third matching paragraph, the static list stays at `2`, and the live collection grows to `3`. Step 4: The distractors fail because the static list never follows later mutations, and the live collection always does. Step 5: Therefore the program prints `2 3`.

intro: CSS owns the presentation; JavaScript owns the **decisions** — and the bridge between them is deliberately narrow. Most scripting should flip **classes** and let stylesheets do the work; the `style` property touches a single element’s inline styles; `getComputedStyle` reads what the cascade actually resolved; and flipping a class is exactly how you arm a CSS **transition** so the browser animates the change for you.
objectives: Toggle classes with classList and keep appearance rules in stylesheets
Read and write inline styles via the style property
Explain the difference between el.style and getComputedStyle(el)
Trigger CSS transitions by class flips, in both directions
Know the stylesheet-scripting API exists (insertRule) and why it is rarely used

concepts.statement: The primary script-CSS interface is `el.classList`: `add`, `remove`, `toggle(name, force)` and `contains` manage state classes, and **stylesheets** map those classes to appearance. Behavior ("which state") lives in JS; appearance ("what the state looks like") lives in CSS — the separation that keeps both maintainable.

`el.style` is the element’s **inline** style declaration — reading it sees only inline styles (and what JS previously wrote there), never the cascade; writing it sets inline styles, which outrank stylesheet rules of equal specificity. Property names are camelCase (`backgroundColor`), and dashes work through `setProperty("--gap", "8px")` — also the way to set custom properties.
concepts.detail:
```js
el.style.backgroundColor = "teal";       // writes style="background-color: teal"
el.style.setProperty("--accent", "#0f0");
el.style.transform;                      // "" if the transform comes from CSS
el.style.removeProperty("background-color");
```
Inline styles are the heaviest hammer: they override the cascade and hide the page’s appearance logic inside scripts — reserve them for genuinely dynamic values (computed positions, measured sizes).

concepts.statement: `getComputedStyle(el)` returns a **read-only, live** view of every property **after the full cascade and inheritance** — stylesheet rules, inline styles, browser defaults, all resolved to concrete values. `el.style` is what was written inline; `getComputedStyle(el)` is what the user actually sees.
concepts.detail:
```js
const el = document.querySelector(".card");
el.style.transform;                          // "" — nothing inline
getComputedStyle(el).transform;              // "matrix(1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0)" — real
getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue("--accent");   // custom properties too
```
The returned values are **computed** (percentages become pixels for layout properties), and the object is live — read it mid-transition (15.4 example) and you get the interpolated in-flight value.

concepts.statement: A CSS **transition** animates a property change automatically when the element matches a rule before and after. The JavaScript recipe: declare the `transition` property **on the base state** (so it covers both directions), then flip the state class from a handler — the browser interpolates every transitioned property between the computed values.

Stylesheets themselves are scriptable: `document.styleSheets`, each sheet’s `cssRules` list, and `sheet.insertRule("selector { ... }", index)` / `deleteRule(i)` can add rules at runtime. It is the tool for generated CSS (hundreds of rules) — and overkill for state changes, where a class is clearer and cacheable.
concepts.detail: A `<style>` element’s text can also be rewritten wholesale (`styleEl.textContent = generatedCss`). Most applications never touch either — class flips cover the mainstream, and computed inline styles cover the dynamic remainder.

examples.title: One class flip, two animated properties

steps.label: Step 1: The transition lives on the base state
steps.text: Declaring `transition` on `.card` (not `.card.flipped`) means the rule applies **before and after** every change — flipping in animates, flipping back animates. Put it only on `.flipped` and the reverse change would snap instantly: the most common transition bug, fixed by rule placement.

steps.label: Step 2: The flip is one class toggle
steps.text: The handler contains no transform, no shadow, no timing — only the **decision** `classList.toggle("flipped")`. The stylesheet maps the class to new values; because the property changed while a transition covers it, the browser interpolates 300 ms of intermediate frames at native speed, off the JavaScript thread entirely.

steps.label: Step 3: el.style sees none of it
steps.text: Both probes on `card.style` return empty strings — before, because nothing was written inline; after, because the transform and shadow come from **stylesheet rules**, and `style` only reflects inline declarations. JavaScript that wrote nothing reads nothing.

steps.label: Step 4: getComputedStyle sees everything
steps.text: `getComputedStyle(card).transition` reads back `"transform 300ms ease, box-shadow 300ms ease"` — the cascade-resolved value, visible even though no inline style exists. Read `getComputedStyle(card).transform` **mid-transition** and you get the interpolated matrix of the current frame — proof that the object is live, and the way to measure where an animation is.

steps.label: Step 5: Why not animate in JavaScript
steps.text: The JS alternative — a requestAnimationFrame loop writing `style.transform` each frame — exists (and is right for genuinely dynamic motion), but the class-flip version costs one line, runs on the compositor, and keeps the visual definition in CSS where designers can tune it. Script the state, stylesheet the style.

examples.result: `card.style.transform` → "" both times; `card.style.transition` → ""; `getComputedStyle(card).transition` → the full resolved transition. One class toggle, two properties, 300 ms — with the animation owned by CSS.

examples.title: Theming with custom properties and one generated rule

steps.label: Step 1: Variables are the theme API
steps.text: The stylesheet never names a theme color directly — every rule reads var(--bg), var(--fg) or var(--accent). Changing the value in one place repaints every consumer, which is why variables beat per-element inline colors for theming.

steps.label: Step 2: setProperty writes a dynamic value
steps.text: The accent comes from a color picker at runtime, so no static class can hold it: card.style.setProperty("--accent", picker.value) writes an inline custom property on that card only. Sibling cards keep the old accent — genuinely dynamic state, the legitimate use of inline style.

steps.label: Step 3: getComputedStyle reads the resolved theme
steps.text: To verify, read getComputedStyle(card).getPropertyValue("--accent") — the cascade-resolved value after inheritance from :root and the inline override. Reading card.style.getPropertyValue shows only what script wrote, never the inherited default.

steps.label: Step 4: insertRule is for generated CSS
steps.text: If the app needs one hundred utility classes (.m-0 through .m-99), document.styleSheets[0].insertRule(".m-42 { margin: 42px; }", 0) creates them programmatically. For state changes like dark mode it is overkill — a class flip or two setProperty calls are clearer and cacheable.

examples.result: Two setProperty calls retheme the page, one per-card setProperty tints a single accent, getComputedStyle verifies the resolved values — and insertRule stays reserved for generated rule batches, not state.

keyTakeaways: Flip classes (`classList.toggle`) and let stylesheets decide appearance — behavior in JS, presentation in CSS.
`el.style` reads and writes only **inline** styles; camelCase names; setProperty also sets custom properties like `--accent`.
`getComputedStyle(el)` is the read-only live view of the resolved cascade — computed values, including in-flight transition frames.
Put `transition` on the base rule so both directions animate; flipping a state class is all JavaScript needs to do.
Stylesheet scripting (`insertRule`, editing a `<style>` text) exists for generated CSS; class flips are the mainstream interface.

quiz.q: An element is styled by a stylesheet rule that sets `color: red`. What does `el.style.color` return from a script that never wrote inline styles?
options: An empty string — el.style reflects only inline declarations
quiz.explanation: The style property is the inline declaration only; to learn what the cascade produced, query getComputedStyle(el).color — which is "red".

quiz.q: A transition must animate in BOTH directions (adding the class, and removing it). Where should the `transition` property be declared?
options: On the base state (.card) — so it applies before and after every change
Inline via el.style.transition in the handler
quiz.explanation: A transition animates a change when the property is covered at both endpoints — declaring it on the base rule guarantees coverage for adding and removing the state class.

quiz.q: Which statement about `getComputedStyle(el)` is TRUE?
options: It returns the inline style string
It returns a read-only live object with the cascade-resolved, computed values of every property
It only works for properties set by JavaScript
quiz.explanation: getComputedStyle folds stylesheet rules, inline styles, inheritance and defaults into computed values — live, so reads during a transition return interpolated frames.

quiz.q: The recommended division of labor for "highlight this card when clicked" is:
options: JS writes the full highlight CSS inline on the element
JS toggles a class; the stylesheet defines what the class looks like
JS rewrites the page stylesheet with insertRule
CSS decides which card is clicked
quiz.explanation: JavaScript owns the decision (which state), CSS owns the appearance (what the state means visually) — the separation that keeps both sides greppable.

intro: Geometry in a browser has exactly two coordinate systems: **viewport coordinates**, which move with the page as it scrolls, and **document coordinates**, which are fixed to the content. Every positioning question — is this element visible, which section am I in, where did the user click — reduces to converting between them by adding the scroll offset. Programmatic scrolling (`scrollTo`, `scrollBy`, `scrollIntoView`) completes the toolkit.
objectives: Distinguish viewport from document coordinates and convert between them
Read element geometry with getBoundingClientRect
Relate mouse event coordinates (clientX vs pageX) to the two systems
Scroll windows and elements programmatically, including smooth scrolling
Assemble the pieces into a scroll-spy indicator

concepts.statement: The **viewport** is the visible window; its origin (0, 0) is the top-left of **what is currently visible**, so a point fixed on screen keeps its viewport coordinates as you scroll. **Document** coordinates are fixed to the content: the top-left of the page, wherever it has been scrolled to. The conversion is one addition: `documentY = viewportY + window.scrollY`.
concepts.detail: Zoom and pixel density make the browser’s CSS pixels the unit, not device pixels — `window.scrollY` and all geometry here are in CSS pixels. The page can be larger than the viewport in both axes; only vertical scrolling is common.

concepts.statement: `el.getBoundingClientRect()` returns the element’s box in **viewport coordinates**: `x`/`left`, `y`/`top`, `right`, `bottom`, `width`, `height` — position and size in one call. Because the origin is the viewport, the same element returns different `top` values as the page scrolls; add `window.scrollY` for a scroll-independent position.

Mouse and pointer events carry both systems: `e.clientX`/`clientY` are **viewport** coordinates (compare directly with getBoundingClientRect), `e.pageX`/`pageY` are **document** coordinates (client + scroll offset). The same event, two frames of reference.
concepts.detail: Client coordinates pair naturally with element rectangles; page coordinates suit anything stored across scrolls (annotations, drag targets recorded in content space). `screenX`/`screenY` are a third system — the physical monitor — rarely useful in page logic.

concepts.statement: The window scrolls with `window.scrollTo(x, y)` (absolute) and `window.scrollBy(dx, dy)` (relative); both accept an options object for smoothness: `window.scrollTo({ top: 800, behavior: "smooth" })`. Scrollable elements have the same methods plus `scrollTop`/`scrollLeft` read-writable properties.
concepts.detail:
```js
window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: "smooth" });   // animated back-to-top
container.scrollBy({ top: 60 });                  // one item down
```
Current offsets live at `window.scrollX`/`scrollY` (aliases `pageXOffset`/`pageYOffset`).

concepts.statement: `el.scrollIntoView(options)` scrolls the nearest scrollable ancestors until the element is visible — the one-liner for "bring this into view": `el.scrollIntoView({ behavior: "smooth", block: "center" })`. `block` picks the vertical alignment (`start`, `center`, `end`, `nearest`) and `inline` the horizontal one.
concepts.detail: With no arguments it does `block: "start"` instantly — the classic jump-to-anchor behavior that CSS `scroll-margin` can now pad. Prefer it over hand-computed `scrollTo(el.offsetTop)` — it handles nested scrollers, and it does not fight the layout.

examples.title: A scroll spy in fifteen lines

steps.label: Step 1: Pick a line and express it in document coordinates
steps.text: The "current" section is defined by a **reading line** one-third of the viewport down: `window.scrollY + window.innerHeight / 3` converts a viewport-relative line into the document frame — the one addition that all geometry here reduces to.

steps.label: Step 2: getBoundingClientRect + scrollY = scroll-independent top
steps.text: Each section’s `box.top` is viewport-relative — it changes on every scroll — but `box.top + window.scrollY` is the section’s fixed document position. Compare the reading line against `[top, top + box.height)` and exactly one section contains it.

steps.label: Step 3: Toggle classes, not styles
steps.text: The active link gets its `active` class flipped per Section 15.4 — the stylesheet decides what highlighting means. The toggle’s second argument is the force form: on when the section matches, off otherwise, with no if/else.

steps.label: Step 4: Passive scroll listener
steps.text: The spy runs on every scroll event — dozens of times per second during a flick. `{ passive: true }` promises no `preventDefault`, so the browser scrolls immediately without waiting on the handler (Section 15.2); the handler’s own work is one rect call per section.

steps.label: Step 5: Clicks scroll smoothly
steps.text: The delegated nav handler (one listener — Section 15.2 again) finds the anchor with `closest`, cancels the default hash jump with `preventDefault`, and hands the scroll to `scrollIntoView({ behavior: "smooth" })` — the browser computes the target position across however many nested scrollables exist, and animates it natively.
