examples.result: The nav tracks the section under the one-third line as the user scrolls (one rect + one toggle per section per event, never blocking scrolling), and clicking a link glides to its section instead of jumping.

examples.title: Sticky annotations that survive scrolling: client vs page

steps.label: Step 1: Hit-test in client coordinates
steps.text: The click and the rect share a frame: e.clientX/clientY minus box.left/top gives the position inside the diagram in viewport pixels. Comparing client values against the rect is the only frame where the math lines up without conversion.

steps.label: Step 2: Convert to document coordinates for storage
steps.text: Adding window.scrollY (and scrollX) converts the viewport point into document coordinates — fixed to the content. A pin stored as client coordinates would drift by exactly the scroll delta on the next scroll; stored as page coordinates it is stable.

steps.label: Step 3: Render back through the rect
steps.text: On scroll, position each pin absolutely as left = pin.x and top = pin.y in document space, or recompute its viewport position as pinDoc - window.scrollY. The scroll spy reads rects; the annotation layer writes them — same conversion, opposite direction.

steps.label: Step 4: Why pageX exists
steps.text: e.pageX/pageY are client plus scroll in one property — the stored form for free. Use client values for comparisons against getBoundingClientRect, page values for anything persisted across scrolls.

examples.result: Hit-test with clientX against the rect, store with page coordinates, render in document space — the pin sticks to the diagram through any amount of scrolling.

keyTakeaways: Two systems only: viewport (moves with scroll) and document (fixed to content); `documentY = viewportY + window.scrollY`.
`getBoundingClientRect()` is the geometry primitive — viewport-relative box including borders; add the scroll offset for stable positions.
Mouse events carry both frames: `clientX/Y` pairs with rects, `pageX/Y` pairs with document-anchored logic.
`scrollTo`/`scrollBy` (with `{ behavior: "smooth" }`) and `el.scrollIntoView({ block, behavior })` are the programmatic scrolling tools.
Scroll handlers must be cheap and `passive` — they fire continuously, and the browser must never wait on them to scroll.

quiz.q: An element’s `getBoundingClientRect().top` reads -240. How far down is it, in document coordinates?
options: window.scrollY + (-240) — its document top equals the scroll offset minus 240
It cannot be computed from the rect alone
quiz.explanation: The rect is viewport-relative: a negative top means it is above the viewport top by 240 CSS pixels, so its document position is scrollY - 240 — one addition either way.

quiz.q: Which coordinates from a mouse event compare directly against `getBoundingClientRect()` values?
quiz.explanation: Both the rect and clientX/Y are viewport-relative — the frames match. pageX/Y are document coordinates; screenX/Y are monitor coordinates.

quiz.q: The one-line, nested-scroller-safe way to reveal an off-screen element with animation is:
quiz.explanation: scrollIntoView walks every scrollable ancestor to bring the element into view, with native smooth animation — no manual math, no missed parent scrollers.

quiz.q: Why register scroll handlers with `{ passive: true }`?
options: To run them before capture listeners
To promise they never call preventDefault, so the browser can scroll without waiting for them to finish
To make them fire on the worker thread
quiz.explanation: Scroll events fire continuously; a handler that might preventDefault forces the browser to block scrolling until it returns. Passive promises it will not, keeping scrolling smooth.

intro: **Web components** are the platform’s answer to component libraries: define your own elements with `customElements.define`, encapsulate their internals behind a **shadow DOM**, and stamp out instances from inert `<template>` markup. The heart of the model is the **element lifecycle** — callbacks the platform invokes when your element is connected to the document, disconnected, or has an observed attribute changed — which tells you exactly when it is legal and useful to render.
objectives: Define custom elements with customElements.define and the naming rules
Order and use the lifecycle callbacks: connected, disconnected, attributeChanged
Explain what shadow DOM isolates and how mode open/closed differs
Project light-DOM children into a shadow tree with slots
Instantiate markup from a template element without parsing side effects

concepts.statement: `customElements.define("my-badge", MyBadgeClass)` registers a class (extending `HTMLElement`) under a tag name that **must contain a hyphen** and must not collide with built-ins. Thereafter the parser upgrades `<my-badge>` elements into instances of the class — and `document.createElement("my-badge")` constructs one directly.

The platform calls four optional methods: **`connectedCallback()`** — the element was inserted into the document (render here; it may fire again if the element is moved); **`disconnectedCallback()`** — it was removed (cleanup: timers, listeners, observers); **`attributeChangedCallback(name, oldV, newV)`** — an **observed** attribute changed (declare the list in `static observedAttributes`); **`adoptedCallback()`** — it moved to another document (rare, mainly frames).
concepts.detail: Ordering rule: the constructor runs **first and minimal** (no rendering — children and attributes may not exist yet), attribute callbacks fire as the parser sets attributes, and `connectedCallback` fires once the element is fully in the tree — the correct place to first render. Re-connecting a detached element fires connected again: design rendering to be idempotent.

concepts.statement: `this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" })` inside the constructor gives the element a private **shadow root** — a second, encapsulated tree whose children, ids and styles are invisible to page CSS and queries. Page styles do not leak in; the element’s internals do not leak out: styles and queries (querySelector) stop at the shadow boundary.
concepts.detail: The element’s public face stays the **light DOM** — what page authors write between its tags. With `mode: "closed"`, even `element.shadowRoot` returns null (only code holding the root object can reach in); `"open"` is the practical default, and the one progressive enhancement prefers.

concepts.statement: A shadow tree can contain `<slot>` elements that **project** light-DOM children into designated places: `<slot name="icon">` pulls in the child with `slot="icon"`, and a bare `<slot>` receives all unattributed children. The children themselves stay in the light DOM (inspectable, stylable by the page) — only their rendering position moves.
concepts.detail: ```html Ada ``` Slots make a custom element a container with an internal layout instead of an opaque box — the composition model React popularized, natively.

concepts.statement: Content inside `<template>` is parsed but **inert**: not rendered, not executed, not queryable through the page — a blueprint. Clone it at element-creation time with `template.content.cloneNode(true)` and insert the copy into the shadow root, giving custom elements cheap, pre-parsed markup without string concatenation or innerHTML.
concepts.detail: ```html ``` A `

examples.title: <user-badge>: render on connect, re-render on attribute change

steps.label: Step 1: Constructor is wiring, not rendering
steps.text: The constructor calls `super()` (mandatory for custom elements) and attaches the shadow root — that is all. It must not read attributes or children: the parser may not have supplied them yet, and the element is not in any document. Rendering this early would race the parser.

steps.label: Step 2: attributeChangedCallback fires while parsing
steps.text: Because `static observedAttributes` lists `name` and `role`, the platform notifies the class when either is set — including when the HTML parser sets them from markup. Those calls arrive **before** connection, which is why `render()` is guarded by `this.isConnected`: there is no shadow content to compute meaningfully yet, and connectedCallback will render anyway.

steps.label: Step 3: connectedCallback is the render signal
steps.text: When the element enters the document, `connectedCallback` runs `render()`: attributes are guaranteed parsed, the shadow root exists, and the element is about to be visible. The method will fire again if the element is ever removed and re-inserted — rendering is written idempotently (`replaceChildren` clears first), so reconnection just redraws.

steps.label: Step 4: Live updates through the same path
steps.text: Script-side, `badge.setAttribute("role", "owner")` triggers `attributeChangedCallback` with `("role", "admin", "owner")` — old and new values in hand — and the guard passes (the element is connected), so `render()` rebuilds the shadow content from the new attribute values. One rendering function serves parse, connect and update.

steps.label: Step 5: What the page sees
steps.text: The rendered `Ada admin` lives in the **shadow tree**: page CSS cannot restyle it and `document.querySelector("b")` cannot find it, while `` itself remains a normal element for layout, delegation and inspection. `disconnectedCallback` is the symmetric hook for timers, observers and listeners that would otherwise leak — logged here to show the boundary.

examples.result: The badge renders "Ada admin" on insertion, re-renders on any attribute change (guarded to connected state), cleans up on removal — with its internals invisible to the page and its implementation one class, one render method.

examples.title: A templated card with slots and sealed styles
examples.problem: Build so page authors supply an icon and body, the component supplies layout and style, and page CSS cannot restyle its internals: ```html AdaPioneer of computing. ```

steps.label: Step 1: Clone the blueprint, do not parse strings
steps.text: In the constructor, const tpl = document.getElementById("card-tpl"); this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" }).append(tpl.content.cloneNode(true)) stamps pre-parsed markup — no innerHTML, no per-instance parse cost, and the template itself never renders.

steps.label: Step 2: Slots project, children stay put
steps.text: The span with slot="heading" renders inside the named slot; the text node flows into the default slot. Both remain light-DOM children — inspectable and page-stylable — while their rendered position is inside the shadow tree.

steps.label: Step 3: Styles stop at the boundary
steps.text: The page rule b { color: red } does not reach the shadow .title, and document.querySelector(".title") returns null — encapsulation verified. Only inherited custom properties and ::part cross deliberately.

steps.label: Step 4: Fallback content covers missing slots
steps.text: An <info-card> with no heading child shows Untitled from inside the slot element itself — default content without a conditional in script.

examples.result: One template, two slots, zero leaks: authors compose with plain HTML, the component owns layout and style, and the shadow boundary keeps both sides honest.

keyTakeaways: Custom elements are classes extending HTMLElement registered under a hyphenated name; the parser upgrades matching tags into instances.

Lifecycle: constructor (minimal wiring) → attributeChangedCallback for observed attributes → connectedCallback (first render — may re-fire on moves) → disconnectedCallback (cleanup) → adoptedCallback (new document).
Only attributes listed in `static observedAttributes` generate attributeChangedCallback events.
Shadow DOM isolates the component’s internal tree from page CSS and queries; `mode: "open"` exposes `element.shadowRoot`, `"closed"` hides even that.
Slots project light-DOM children into the shadow tree by name — children stay page-inspectable, rendering position moves inside the component.
`<template>` holds inert, pre-parsed markup; `content.cloneNode(true)` stamps instances; styles inside a shadow root are component-scoped.

quiz.q: Which lifecycle callback is the right place for the FIRST render of a custom element?
options: `connectedCallback` — the element is in the document with attributes parsed
quiz.explanation: In the constructor, attributes and children may not exist and the element is not yet in the tree; connectedCallback guarantees the full element is live — render there (idempotently, since it re-fires on moves).

quiz.q: What does `static observedAttributes = ["name"]` accomplish?
options: Lists the attributes whose changes invoke attributeChangedCallback — unlisted attributes change silently
quiz.explanation: The platform notifies attribute changes only for observed attributes: the static list is the opt-in that keeps callbacks from firing for every irrelevant attribute.

quiz.q: A page stylesheet styles all `b` elements red. Inside a component’s shadow tree, its own `<b>` element will —
options: Also be red — the page cascade crosses the shadow boundary
Keep the component’s own styling: page selectors do not match nodes inside the shadow root
Inherit red only if the component allows it in its HTML
quiz.explanation: The shadow boundary blocks page selectors (and document.querySelector) from matching internal nodes — encapsulation is the point of shadow DOM; custom properties and ::part are the deliberate escape hatches.

quiz.q: Why clone `<template>` content rather than build elements with innerHTML strings?
options: Template content is parsed once and inert — cloneNode stamps pre-parsed markup without string concatenation or XSS exposure of the component’s structure
innerHTML does not work inside shadow roots
Templates are required for custom elements
quiz.explanation: The template is parsed (never rendered or executed) at page load; each clone is cheap and constant — the platform’s answer to markup blueprints for component instances.

intro: Browsers provide two distinct graphics architectures for drawing custom visuals: **Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG)** and the **HTML <canvas> element**. SVG is a retained-mode XML vector graphic language integrated directly into the DOM tree, where every circle, path and rect has identity, styles, and event listeners. The <canvas> element is an immediate-mode pixel raster surface programmed via JavaScript 2D and WebGL contexts. SVG excels at scalable diagrams and interactive UI components; canvas excels at high-frequency animations, games, data visualizations, and image processing where thousands of retained DOM nodes would overwhelm browser layout engines.
objectives: Contrast SVG retained-mode DOM trees with canvas immediate-mode 2D rendering surfaces
Create and manipulate SVG shapes dynamically with document.createElementNS
Draw paths, rectangles, curves and text using the CanvasRenderingContext2D API
Apply coordinate transformations (translate, rotate, scale) with save() and restore()
Manipulate raw pixel data using getImageData and putImageData

concepts.statement: SVG elements are real DOM elements residing in the SVG namespace (`http://www.w3.org/2000/svg`). They scale infinitely without pixelation, support CSS styling and animations, and dispatch standard mouse and touch events.

A `<canvas>` element provides an immediate-mode bitmap surface. Its `width` and `height` HTML attributes set the pixel grid buffer resolution, while `canvas.getContext("2d")` obtains the drawing context.
concepts.detail: The element attributes determine the bitmap drawing buffer size, while CSS width and height set its display size on screen. To prevent blurry rendering on high-DPI (Retina) displays, scale the canvas buffer by `window.devicePixelRatio` while setting CSS dimensions to logical pixels.

concepts.statement: SVG is **retained-mode**: the browser maintains a persistent tree of shape objects and redraws them automatically when styles or attributes change. Canvas is **immediate-mode**: shapes are burned directly into a pixel grid and forgotten — redraws require clearing the canvas with `clearRect` and re-executing drawing commands.
concepts.detail: For 100 interactive icons with hover states, SVG is faster and cleaner. For 10,000 moving particles or 60fps game rendering, Canvas avoids the memory and garbage collection overhead of 10,000 DOM nodes.

concepts.statement: `ctx.save()` pushes the current transformation matrix, clipping path, and style properties onto an internal drawing state stack; `ctx.restore()` pops the previous state back.

Complex vector shapes on canvas are drawn using path subroutines: `ctx.beginPath()`, `moveTo(x, y)`, `lineTo(x, y)`, `arc(x, y, r, startAngle, endAngle)`, and `ctx.closePath()`, followed by `ctx.stroke()` or `ctx.fill()`.
concepts.detail: Calling `beginPath()` is mandatory before drawing a new shape; otherwise, subsequent `stroke()` or `fill()` calls will re-stroke and re-fill all previously defined path segments.

concepts.statement: `ctx.getImageData(sx, sy, sw, sh)` returns an `ImageData` object containing a `Uint8ClampedArray` of raw RGBA pixel bytes (four bytes per pixel: red, green, blue, alpha from 0 to 255).

figures.caption: Canvas 2D coordinate system and transformation stack: the default canvas coordinate space has origin (0,0) at the upper-left, with +X extending rightward and +Y extending downward. Calling ctx.translate(dx, dy) repositions the local origin, while ctx.rotate(θ) rotates subsequent drawing operations around that translated origin.

examples.title: Drawing a Scaled Donut Segment with Canvas
examples.problem: Draw a high-DPI donut slice (arc from 0 to \pi/2) centered at (150, 150) with outer radius 80 and inner radius 50.

steps.label: High-DPI Setup
steps.text: Set canvas.width = 300 * dpr and canvas.height = 300 * dpr, then call ctx.scale(dpr, dpr).

steps.label: Begin Path
steps.text: Call ctx.beginPath() and use arc(150, 150, 80, 0, Math.PI / 2) for the outer contour.

steps.label: Inner Counter-Arc
steps.text: Use arc(150, 150, 50, Math.PI / 2, 0, true) to trace back along the inner radius in reverse.

steps.label: Close and Fill
steps.text: Call ctx.closePath(), set ctx.fillStyle = "#10b981", and call ctx.fill().

examples.result: A crisp, anti-aliased green quadrant ring rendered on the canvas.

examples.title: Clickable dots with SVG: retained-mode events

steps.label: Step 1: createElementNS, not createElement
steps.text: SVG elements live in the SVG namespace — createElement would make an unknown HTML element that never renders. The NS constant plus setAttribute for cx, cy, r and fill is the whole construction API.

steps.label: Step 2: Interaction without a loop
steps.text: Each circle is a DOM node: CSS circle:hover { r: 14 } enlarges it and the click listener fires per shape. No hit-testing, no clearRect, no frame loop — the browser retains the tree and dispatches events itself.

steps.label: Step 3: Update by attribute
steps.text: Moving a point is c.setAttribute("cx", next) — the browser repaints that shape alone. The canvas twin would clear the bitmap and replay every arc each frame.

steps.label: Step 4: Know the crossover
steps.text: Five dots favor SVG; five thousand animating particles favor canvas immediate-mode. Retained nodes cost memory per shape — the Section 15.7 rule of thumb in one example.

examples.result: Five circles, five listeners, no redraw loop — hover and click work because SVG shapes are elements, the canvas complement to the donut immediate-mode draw.

keyTakeaways: SVG elements are live DOM nodes supporting CSS styles, media queries, and click handlers.
Canvas 2D is an immediate-mode pixel buffer with no retained shape objects in the DOM.
Always set canvas width and height attributes scaled by window.devicePixelRatio for Retina screens.
Pair ctx.save() and ctx.restore() to contain coordinate translations, rotations, and style settings.

quiz.q: Which function must be used to create SVG elements programmatically in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: SVG elements belong to the W3C SVG namespace; creating them with document.createElementNS using the SVG namespace URL ensures the browser constructs true SVG DOM objects rather than unrecognized HTMLUnknownElement instances.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of ctx.save() and ctx.restore() in canvas scripting?
options: To commit and rollback database transactions
To push and pop canvas drawing styles and transformation matrices onto an internal stack
To save canvas pixels to localStorage
To pause and resume requestAnimationFrame loops
quiz.explanation: save() preserves the current state (transforms, stroke/fill styles, clip paths) onto a stack, and restore() returns to that state, preventing local transforms from leaking.

quiz.q: Why can drawing text or shapes on a canvas look blurry on a high-density (Retina) display?
options: Canvas does not support vector rendering
The canvas buffer dimensions (width/height attributes) are 1x logical pixels while the display has multiple device pixels per CSS pixel
Antialiasing is turned off by default
Canvas fonts must be loaded as SVG fonts
quiz.explanation: If the canvas width/height attributes match CSS dimensions on a 2x display, the browser stretches a 1x raster image over 2x physical pixels. Multiplying buffer dimensions by devicePixelRatio and calling ctx.scale(dpr, dpr) fixes it.

quiz.q: What data structure is returned by ctx.getImageData().data?
options: A two-dimensional Array of hex color strings
A Uint8ClampedArray with sequential [R, G, B, A] values between 0 and 255
A Float32Array of normalized [0..1] color coordinates
quiz.explanation: ImageData.data is a contiguous 1D Uint8ClampedArray where each pixel occupies 4 bytes: Red, Green, Blue, and Alpha in the range 0..255.

intro: Modern browser audio spans two complementary layers: the high-level declarative **HTMLAudioElement** (<audio> and new Audio(url)) for stream playback and podcast controls, and the modular **Web Audio API** for procedural sound synthesis, multi-track mixing, sound effects in games, and frequency visualization. Centralized around an AudioContext, the Web Audio API routes audio through a directed graph of connected AudioNode instances — oscillators, buffers, biquad filters, gain controls, and spatial panners — terminating at the speaker output.
objectives: Use HTMLAudioElement for basic audio playback, track loading, and volume control
Create an AudioContext and construct a directed audio processing graph
Generate procedural sound using OscillatorNode with standard waveforms
Automate smooth audio transitions using AudioParam scheduling methods
Comply with browser user-gesture autoplay policies by resuming suspended contexts

concepts.statement: The `<audio>` element and `const audio = new Audio("track.mp3")` provide media player controls for streaming and playing encoded audio files (MP3, AAC, Ogg, WAV).
concepts.detail: Methods include `play()`, `pause()`, and setting `currentTime` or `volume`. It fires events such as `loadedmetadata`, `canplay`, `timeupdate`, and `ended`. It is ideal for continuous media streaming but lacks sample-accurate timing for games.

concepts.statement: The **Web Audio API** operates as a directed graph rooted in an `AudioContext`. Audio streams flow from source nodes through processing nodes and exit at `audioCtx.destination` (the physical audio output).
An `OscillatorNode` synthesizes periodic waveforms without external audio files. Supported types include `"sine"`, `"square"`, `"sawtooth"`, and `"triangle"`.
concepts.detail: The pitch is controlled via `osc.frequency.value` (in Hertz). An oscillator can only be started once with `osc.start()` and stopped with `osc.stop()`; to play another tone, instantiate a new oscillator node.

concepts.statement: Audio parameters (such as frequency, gain, filter cutoff) are `AudioParam` objects that support sample-accurate scheduled changes on the audio rendering thread without main-thread jitter.
concepts.detail: Methods include `setValueAtTime(value, time)`, `linearRampToValueAtTime(value, time)`, and `exponentialRampToValueAtTime(value, time)`. Times are expressed in seconds relative to `ctx.currentTime`, eliminating audible clicks when changing volume.

concepts.statement: Modern browsers block sound from playing until the user has interacted with the page. An `AudioContext` created prior to user interaction starts in the `"suspended"` state.
concepts.detail: When the user taps, clicks, or presses a key, call `audioCtx.resume()`. `audio.play()` on an HTMLAudioElement returns a Promise that rejects with `NotAllowedError` if autoplay restrictions are violated.

examples.title: Synthesizing an Exponential Decay Tone
examples.problem: Play a 440 Hz (A4) sine wave tone that decays exponentially over 0.5 seconds upon user click.

steps.label: Create Context
steps.text: const ctx = new AudioContext(); if (ctx.state === "suspended") ctx.resume();

steps.label: Create Nodes
steps.text: const osc = ctx.createOscillator(); const gain = ctx.createGain(); osc.type = "sine"; osc.frequency.value = 440;

steps.label: Schedule Envelope
steps.text: const now = ctx.currentTime; gain.gain.setValueAtTime(0.3, now); gain.gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(0.001, now + 0.5);

steps.label: Connect and Run
steps.text: osc.connect(gain); gain.connect(ctx.destination); osc.start(now); osc.stop(now + 0.5);

examples.result: A pleasant chime tone that smoothly fades out without audio clipping.

examples.title: A podcast player with HTMLAudioElement and the autoplay guard

steps.label: Step 1: play() inside the gesture
steps.text: The play call sits in the click handler — a user gesture — so the autoplay policy allows it. Called on load it would reject with NotAllowedError; the try/catch turns that rejection into a tap-again hint instead of an unhandled rejection.

steps.label: Step 2: Volume and seek are properties
steps.text: audio.volume (0 to 1) and audio.currentTime (seconds) are plain read-write properties — no graph, no AudioParam scheduling. Ideal for long streaming media where sample accuracy does not matter.

steps.label: Step 3: Events report progress
steps.text: timeupdate fires during playback for the progress readout; ended fires at the finish for an auto-next episode. loadedmetadata gives duration once headers arrive — the declarative counterpart to the Web Audio graph events.

steps.label: Step 4: When not to use it
steps.text: Gapless game effects or synthesized tones need the AudioContext graph of the first example — HTMLAudioElement cannot schedule sample-accurate envelopes. Streaming talk favors audio tags; synthesis favors oscillators.

examples.result: One Audio object, one play promise, two properties and two events — streaming playback with the autoplay guard handled, the high-level complement to the oscillator graph.

keyTakeaways: HTMLAudioElement manages streaming tracks and audio player controls.
Web Audio API builds modular processing graphs for synthesis, effects, and games.
AudioParams automate volume and frequency changes on the audio thread with sample accuracy.
AudioContext must be resumed inside a user interaction handler to satisfy browser autoplay policies.

quiz.q: What is audioCtx.destination in the Web Audio API?
options: A URL pointing to an MP3 file
The special AudioNode representing the computer speakers or headphone output
A callback invoked when audio decoding finishes
The folder where recorded audio is stored
quiz.explanation: audioCtx.destination is the terminal node of the audio graph, representing the physical audio hardware (speakers, headphones).

quiz.q: Why should you use linearRampToValueAtTime or exponentialRampToValueAtTime instead of changing gain.gain.value directly in a setTimeout loop?
options: Because JavaScript setTimeout cannot change audio node values
Direct changes cause audible clicks and pops; AudioParam ramps calculate smooth per-sample curves on the audio thread
Ramping converts mono audio to stereo
Ramping saves power on mobile devices
quiz.explanation: Sudden instantaneous amplitude changes cause audible waveform discontinuities (clicks). AudioParam ramp methods interpolate smoothly on the audio thread.

quiz.q: If an AudioContext is created on page load before any user interaction, what is its initial state?
quiz.explanation: Browsers initialize AudioContext in the "suspended" state until a user gesture (click, keypress) permits audio playback via audioCtx.resume().

quiz.q: Can an OscillatorNode be started again after calling osc.stop()?
options: No, OscillatorNodes are single-use source nodes; create a new OscillatorNode for subsequent tones
Only if osc.loop is set to true
quiz.explanation: In the Web Audio API, source nodes like OscillatorNode and AudioBufferSourceNode are lightweight and single-use: once stopped, they cannot be restarted.

intro: The browser URL bar is both the entry point of a web application and its most visible state store. JavaScript inspects and changes the active URL through **window.location**, while the **HTML5 History API** (history.pushState and history.replaceState) enables client-side Single-Page Applications (SPAs) to update the address bar without triggering full server document reloads. Working together with URLSearchParams and the popstate event, client applications achieve responsive routing and bookmarkable URLs with native Back and Forward button support.
objectives: Deconstruct and inspect URL properties with the window.location interface
Parse, modify, and serialize query strings using URLSearchParams
Contrast location.assign(), location.replace(), and location.href assignments
Update browser URLs and history state without page reloads using history.pushState and replaceState
Handle user Back and Forward navigation by listening to the window popstate event

concepts.statement: `window.location` reflects the document’s active URL, exposing components: `protocol`, `hostname`, `port`, `pathname`, `search`, and `hash`.
concepts.detail: Assigning to `location.href` or individual properties (like `location.pathname`) triggers an immediate browser navigation. The only exception is modifying `location.hash`, which scrolls to the matching element anchor without reloading the page.

concepts.statement: The `URLSearchParams` API provides a clean interface for query string manipulation: `params.get(key)`, `params.set(key, val)`, `params.append(key, val)`, and `params.toString()`.
`location.assign(url)` loads a new document and records the current page in session history. `location.replace(url)` loads a new document and replaces the current history entry.
concepts.detail: Use `location.replace()` for redirection logic (such as unauthorized redirects to a login page). This prevents the user from being trapped in an infinite redirect loop when clicking the browser Back button.

concepts.statement: `history.pushState(state, unused, url)` pushes a new entry to the browser session history and changes the address bar URL **without reloading the document**.
concepts.detail: `state` is an arbitrary serializable object stored with the history entry. `history.replaceState(state, unused, url)` updates the current entry in place without creating a new history step.

concepts.statement: The `window.onpopstate` event fires whenever the active history entry changes due to user navigation (clicking Back or Forward, or calling `history.back()`).
concepts.detail: The event object exposes `event.state`, containing the state object originally passed to `pushState` or `replaceState`. Note: calling `pushState()` or `replaceState()` programmatically does NOT fire `popstate`.

examples.title: Implementing Client-Side Routing with State
examples.problem: Update the page view to "chapter-2" on click, update the URL to /chapter/2, and support the browser Back button.

steps.label: Push State on Click
steps.text: history.pushState({ view: "chapter", id: 2 }, "", "/chapter/2"); renderView("chapter", 2);

steps.label: Listen to popstate
steps.text: window.addEventListener("popstate", (e) => { const state = e.state || { view: "home" }; renderView(state.view, state.id); });

steps.label: Initial State
steps.text: history.replaceState({ view: "home" }, "", window.location.pathname);

examples.result: Seamless SPA navigation where browser Back and Forward restore the correct view instantly.

examples.title: A shareable filter view with URLSearchParams and replaceState

steps.label: Step 1: Read the URL on load
steps.text: URLSearchParams parses ?q=ada&sort=price — get returns the value, percent-decoding automatically. The input is seeded from the URL so a pasted link reproduces the view.

steps.label: Step 2: replaceState while typing
steps.text: Each keystroke rewrites the current entry in place: the address bar stays shareable but Back does not step through every letter. This is the filter rule — replace for ephemeral edits, push for milestones.

steps.label: Step 3: pushState to save
steps.text: Save view pushes one entry, so Back returns to the pre-save filter. The state object carries { q } so popstate can re-render without re-parsing in the common case.

steps.label: Step 4: Contrast with location.assign
steps.text: Assigning location.search = params would reload the document and lose scroll and component state; pushState/replaceState change the bar without a navigation — the SPA distinction of the first example, applied to query state.

examples.result: Typing rewrites the query string silently, Save pushes one history step, links carry the filter — query state in the URL without reloads or history spam.

keyTakeaways: window.location exposes URL parts; modifying href or pathname navigates to a new page.
URLSearchParams simplifies reading and writing query parameters with automatic encoding.
Use location.replace() for redirects to avoid trapping users in back-button loops.
history.pushState() updates the URL bar without a page reload; popstate handles Back/Forward.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between location.assign(url) and location.replace(url)?
options: assign() only accepts relative URLs while replace() requires absolute URLs
assign() adds a new entry to the browser history; replace() overwrites the current entry so Back skips it
replace() reloads the page while assign() performs client-side routing
assign() is asynchronous while replace() is synchronous
quiz.explanation: location.replace() deletes the current page from session history, making it ideal for redirects so the user does not get stuck in a loop when clicking Back.

quiz.q: Does calling history.pushState() directly trigger the window popstate event?
options: Yes, immediately on the next tick
No, popstate only fires when user navigation changes the active history entry (e.g. Back/Forward buttons)
Only if the URL points to a different domain
Yes, if the state argument is not null
quiz.explanation: history.pushState() and replaceState() do not dispatch popstate; the event is exclusively for user-initiated history traversals like clicking Back or Forward.

quiz.q: Which URL property change on window.location will NOT cause a full document reload?
quiz.explanation: Changing location.hash only scrolls to the matching fragment identifier or dispatches the hashchange event without reloading the page.

quiz.q: Can history.pushState() specify a URL belonging to a different origin (e.g. google.com from myapp.com)?
options: Yes, any valid URL is allowed
No, the browser throws a SecurityError to prevent origin spoofing
Only if CORS headers allow it
Yes, but only in HTTPS mode
quiz.explanation: Browsers strictly forbid pushState() across origins to prevent malicious sites from disguising their address bar as a trusted third-party bank or login page.

intro: Client-server communication in modern web applications centers on the **fetch() API**, the Promise-based standard that superseded XMLHttpRequest. Beyond basic JSON retrieval, modern networking encompasses streaming response bodies, request cancellation with **AbortController**, bidirectional full-duplex communication with **WebSockets**, and unidirectional real-time push updates with **Server-Sent Events (EventSource)**. Mastering status validation, header configuration, and streaming transfers is fundamental to building resilient web software.
objectives: Execute HTTP requests with fetch() and inspect response status, headers, and body formats
Distinguish network errors from HTTP error status codes (4xx and 5xx)
Cancel in-flight requests and set request timeouts using AbortController and AbortSignal
Stream chunked responses using the ReadableStream API on response.body
Establish real-time full-duplex connections with WebSockets and event streams with EventSource

concepts.statement: `fetch(resource, options)` initiates an asynchronous HTTP request and returns a Promise that resolves to a `Response` object as soon as server headers arrive.
`response.ok` is a boolean getter returning `true` if and only if `response.status` is in the 200–299 range. Robust code must always inspect `response.ok` before reading the body.
concepts.detail: Because server error pages (404, 500) may return HTML instead of JSON, attempting to call `res.json()` without checking `res.ok` frequently causes unexpected SyntaxError parse crashes.

concepts.statement: An `AbortController` provides an `AbortSignal` that can be linked to `fetch({ signal })`. Calling `controller.abort()` halts network transmission and rejects the fetch Promise with an `AbortError`.
concepts.detail: Modern browsers also provide `AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`, generating an auto-aborting signal in a single line without manual timer tracking.

concepts.statement: The body of a `Response` can only be read once. Built-in body consumers include `.json()`, `.text()`, `.blob()`, and `.arrayBuffer()`.
concepts.detail: For streaming progress or LLM generation, `response.body.getReader()` exposes a `ReadableStreamDefaultReader` returning `{ value: Uint8Array, done: boolean }` chunks as they travel across the wire.

concepts.statement: `new WebSocket("wss://...")` establishes a persistent, bidirectional, full-duplex TCP socket connection over a single connection.
concepts.detail: Events include `open`, `message`, `error`, and `close`. Messages are sent via `socket.send(data)`. WebSockets avoid HTTP polling overhead, making them ideal for multiplayer gaming, trading desks, and live chat.

concepts.statement: `new EventSource(url)` opens an HTTP stream where the server pushes text events formatted as `text/event-stream`.
concepts.detail: EventSource is unidirectional (server to client) and includes built-in auto-reconnection and event ID tracking. It is simpler than WebSockets when the client only needs to receive live notifications.

examples.title: Fetch with Automatic 5-Second Timeout and JSON Parsing
examples.problem: Fetch /api/status, aborting if the server does not respond within 5000ms, and parse JSON if successful.

steps.label: Create Signal
steps.text: const signal = AbortSignal.timeout(5000);

steps.label: Send Fetch
steps.text: const res = await fetch("/api/status", { signal });

steps.label: Validate Status
steps.text: if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP Error " + res.status);

steps.label: Parse JSON
steps.text: const data = await res.json();

examples.result: Guaranteed termination within 5 seconds with structured error handling.

examples.title: A live echo chat over WebSocket with clean close

steps.label: Step 1: Full-duplex after open
steps.text: Unlike fetch, the socket stays open: either side can send at any time with send(). Waiting for open before the first send avoids the INVALID_STATE_ERR that an immediate send would throw.

steps.label: Step 2: Messages are events, not responses
steps.text: Each server frame arrives as a message event — no polling, no second request. Text arrives as string data; binary arrives as Blob or ArrayBuffer per binaryType. The fetch example waits once; the socket listens indefinitely.

steps.label: Step 3: Close codes explain the ending
steps.text: close carries a code (1000 normal, 1006 abnormal) and a reason. Closing with 1000 on pagehide tells the server the departure was clean; an abnormal close signals a reconnect attempt.

steps.label: Step 4: WebSocket vs EventSource
steps.text: Chat needs client-to-server messages, so EventSource (server-push only) cannot do it — full-duplex picks WebSocket. A news ticker would pick EventSource for its auto-reconnect and last-event-ID tracking.

examples.result: Hello sent on open, messages appended live, 1000 close on leave — bidirectional realtime beside the fetch timeout pattern, with EventSource reserved for server-only pushes.

keyTakeaways: fetch() Promise resolves on HTTP 404/500 errors; always check response.ok.
Response bodies are single-use streams; call .json() or .text() once per response.
Use AbortSignal.timeout(ms) to prevent hanging network requests.
WebSockets offer full-duplex low-latency communication; EventSource offers simple server-push.

quiz.q: Under what condition does the Promise returned by fetch() reject?
options: When the server responds with a 404 Not Found status
When the server responds with a 500 Internal Server Error status
Only when a network error occurs (DNS failure, offline) or when the request is aborted
Whenever the response Content-Type is not application/json
quiz.explanation: fetch() only rejects on network failures or abort signal triggers; HTTP status codes like 404 or 500 resolve successfully with response.ok set to false.

quiz.q: What happens if you call response.json() twice on the same Response object?
options: It re-parses the cached JSON object
It returns null on the second call
It throws a TypeError because the response body has already been consumed (stream locked/disturbed)
It triggers a second network request automatically
quiz.explanation: Response bodies are readable streams that can only be consumed once. To read a body multiple times, call response.clone() before reading.

quiz.q: Which API provides automatic reconnection and last-event-ID tracking out of the box for server push?
quiz.explanation: EventSource natively handles auto-reconnect and sends the Last-Event-ID header upon reconnecting, unlike WebSockets which require manual reconnection logic.

quiz.q: How do you cancel an active fetch request in modern JavaScript?
options: Pass an AbortSignal from an AbortController in the fetch options and invoke controller.abort()
quiz.explanation: AbortController is the standard web cancellation mechanism; passing controller.signal to fetch lets controller.abort() terminate the request.

intro: Web applications rely on client-side storage for offline access, session caching, and user customization. Browsers provide a hierarchy of storage options: **localStorage** and **sessionStorage** for synchronous string key-value pairs, **cookies** for small credentials shared with HTTP requests, and **IndexedDB** for asynchronous, transactional storage of large structured datasets. Understanding their capacity boundaries, performance trade-offs, and security boundaries (such as XSS vulnerability vs HttpOnly protection) is critical for client application architecture.
objectives: Compare the lifetime, quota, and storage semantics of localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies, and IndexedDB
Store and retrieve structured data in Web Storage using JSON serialization
Configure cookie attributes including Max-Age, Path, SameSite, Secure, and HttpOnly
Perform transactional CRUD operations in an IndexedDB object store
Synchronize cross-tab application state using the window storage event

concepts.statement: Both provide synchronous key-value storage of strings (`getItem`, `setItem`, `removeItem`, `clear`). `localStorage` persists indefinitely across sessions; `sessionStorage` is cleared when the browser tab is closed.
concepts.detail: Capacity is approximately 5MB per origin. Because all methods are synchronous, reading or writing large payloads can block the UI thread during disk I/O.

concepts.statement: When `localStorage` is modified in one document, a `storage` event fires in **all other same-origin tabs and windows**, passing `key`, `oldValue`, `newValue`, and `url`.
concepts.detail: The window that made the change does not receive the event. This mechanism enables live multi-tab synchronization (e.g. logging out in one tab immediately updates all other open tabs).

concepts.statement: Cookies are small text strings (max ~4KB each) attached automatically to HTTP headers on matching requests. Created in JavaScript with `document.cookie = "key=val; SameSite=Lax; Secure"`.
concepts.detail: Server-set cookies with the `HttpOnly` flag cannot be accessed or read by JavaScript, providing strong protection against session token theft via Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).

concepts.statement: **IndexedDB** is an asynchronous, transactional, object-oriented database in the browser capable of storing hundreds of megabytes of structured JavaScript objects, binary blobs, and files.
concepts.detail: Unlike Web Storage, IndexedDB operates asynchronously without blocking the main thread, uses structured cloning (storing complex objects, arrays, and typed buffers directly without JSON stringify), and supports index-based queries.

concepts.statement: Every IndexedDB read and write occurs within a transaction: `db.transaction(["books"], "readwrite")`. Transactions auto-commit as soon as the microtask/event queue becomes idle.
concepts.detail: If an error occurs or `transaction.abort()` is called, all changes inside the transaction roll back atomically, guaranteeing database consistency.

examples.title: Storing and Retrieving Structured Objects with localStorage
examples.problem: Store a user preferences object in localStorage with fallback defaults and JSON parse safety.

steps.label: Save Object
steps.text: localStorage.setItem("user_prefs", JSON.stringify({ theme: "dark", fontSize: 16 }));

steps.label: Load Raw
steps.text: const raw = localStorage.getItem("user_prefs");

steps.label: Parse with Fallback
steps.text: const prefs = raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : { theme: "light", fontSize: 14 };

examples.result: Safely persisted and retrieved user configuration object.

examples.title: Offline notes in IndexedDB with an atomic batch

steps.label: Step 1: Versioned schema setup
steps.text: onupgradeneeded runs once per version bump: it creates the notes store with autoIncrement ids and a by-updated index for newest-first queries. Later versions add stores without touching existing data.

steps.label: Step 2: Atomic batch write
steps.text: const tx = db.transaction(["notes"], "readwrite"); tx.objectStore("notes").add({ title, body, updated: Date.now() }); — two adds in one transaction commit together; tx.abort() or any error rolls both back, unlike two localStorage.setItem calls.

steps.label: Step 3: Indexed read without blocking
steps.text: db.transaction(["notes"]).objectStore("notes").index("by-updated").getAll(null, 20) returns the newest twenty asynchronously — no main-thread disk block, and structured cloning preserves Dates without JSON.

steps.label: Step 4: When localStorage still wins
steps.text: A theme string or auth flag stays in localStorage — synchronous, tiny, cross-tab via the storage event. Hundreds of notes with queries and atomicity need IndexedDB; the first example and this one are the two ends of the capacity ladder.

examples.result: Versioned store plus index, atomic multi-add, async newest-first read — offline data with transactions, beside the synchronous localStorage preferences pattern.

keyTakeaways: localStorage persists across browser restarts; sessionStorage expires when the tab closes.
Web Storage APIs are synchronous and limited to ~5MB of string data per origin.
Cookies marked HttpOnly protect authentication tokens from XSS script theft.
IndexedDB is an asynchronous transactional database designed for large structured offline datasets.

quiz.q: Why should you NOT store large datasets (e.g. 5MB) in localStorage?
options: localStorage automatically deletes data after 24 hours
localStorage API is synchronous and reading/writing large strings blocks the main thread UI rendering
localStorage only supports numbers, not strings
Data in localStorage is sent to the server on every HTTP request
quiz.explanation: localStorage operations run synchronously on the main thread; disk reads and writes of large strings block user interaction and frame rendering.

quiz.q: What is the primary security benefit of the HttpOnly cookie attribute?
options: It encrypts the cookie on the user’s hard drive
It prevents JavaScript from accessing document.cookie, protecting session tokens from XSS extraction
It ensures cookies are only transmitted over HTTPS
It expires the cookie immediately when the browser closes
quiz.explanation: HttpOnly tells the browser that the cookie must not be exposed through document.cookie, preventing malicious scripts injected via XSS from reading session tokens.

quiz.q: When does the window "storage" event fire?
options: In the same tab that invoked localStorage.setItem()
In all other same-origin tabs and windows when localStorage is modified
Only when the browser disk space runs low
quiz.explanation: The storage event fires exclusively in other open windows/tabs of the same origin to facilitate cross-tab coordination without infinite self-notification loops.

quiz.q: How does IndexedDB handle data serialization compared to localStorage?
options: IndexedDB uses the structured clone algorithm, storing Maps, Sets, Blobs, and Objects natively without string serialization
IndexedDB only stores plain text strings
IndexedDB stores data in CSV format
quiz.explanation: IndexedDB natively supports the structured clone algorithm, storing typed arrays, Blobs, Dates, and nested objects without manual JSON conversion.

intro: Because browser JavaScript executes on a single event-driven UI thread, CPU-intensive computations — cryptographic hashing, physics engines, image filters, and statistical models — can freeze the user interface. **Web Workers** introduce true operating-system-level multithreading to the browser without the race conditions of shared-memory threading (compare Operating System Concepts, Chapter 4). Dedicated Workers run in isolated execution contexts, communicating with the main thread exclusively through asynchronous message passing.
objectives: Instantiate dedicated Web Workers using new Worker() and handle message exchange
Pass complex data safely across thread boundaries using structured cloning
Transfer zero-copy binary buffers using Transferable Objects (ArrayBuffer)
Identify execution capabilities and restrictions inside WorkerGlobalScope (no DOM, yes fetch)
Terminate worker threads cleanly using worker.terminate() and self.close()

concepts.statement: A dedicated worker is an independent background thread created via `const worker = new Worker("worker.js")`. It runs on a separate operating system thread with its own event loop.
concepts.detail: Workers prevent CPU-intensive tasks from degrading UI responsiveness or causing frame drops on the main thread.

concepts.statement: Inside a worker, the global object is a `DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope` (accessible via `self` or `globalThis`). Workers have **no access** to `window`, `document`, or DOM elements.
concepts.detail: Workers **do** have access to `navigator`, `location`, timers (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`), `fetch()`, `IndexedDB`, `WebSockets`, and the `crypto` API.

concepts.statement: Threads communicate strictly through message passing: `worker.postMessage(data)` dispatches a message, received via `onmessage = (event) => { ... event.data ... }`.
concepts.detail: By default, data passed to `postMessage` is copied using the **Structured Clone algorithm**, allowing complex graphs with cyclic references, Dates, RegExps, Maps, and Sets to be passed without shared-memory hazards.

concepts.statement: For large binary datasets, `ArrayBuffer` instances can be transferred rather than copied by passing them in the transfer list: `worker.postMessage({ buffer }, [buffer])`.
concepts.detail: Ownership of the memory buffer transfers instantly in $O(1)$ time with zero memory allocation. Once transferred, the buffer in the sending thread becomes **detached** with `byteLength === 0`, preventing concurrent modification.

concepts.statement: The main thread terminates a worker immediately using `worker.terminate()`. Inside the worker, the thread can shut itself down using `self.close()`.
concepts.detail: Workers consume memory and OS thread resources. Always terminate workers when long-running computations conclude.

examples.title: Offloading Heavy Array Sorting to a Worker with Transferable Buffers
examples.problem: Send a Float64Array of 1,000,000 random numbers to a worker for sorting with zero-copy overhead.

steps.label: Create Buffer
steps.text: const data = new Float64Array(1_000_000); // fill with random numbers

steps.label: Transfer to Worker
steps.text: worker.postMessage({ buffer: data.buffer }, [data.buffer]); // data is now detached

steps.label: Worker Sorts and Returns
steps.text: // Inside worker: const arr = new Float64Array(e.data.buffer); arr.sort(); self.postMessage({ buffer: arr.buffer }, [arr.buffer]);

steps.label: Main Thread Receives
steps.text: worker.onmessage = (e) => { const sorted = new Float64Array(e.data.buffer); };

examples.result: One million numbers sorted on a background thread with zero main-thread UI stutter.

examples.title: A cancellable prime sieve with progress and self-close

steps.label: Step 1: Structured clone carries the job
steps.text: postMessage({ limit }) copies a small object via structured cloning — no transfer list needed for plain data. Large binary input would add the transfer list of the first example; control messages travel by copy.

steps.label: Step 2: Progress without the DOM
steps.text: The worker posts { progress: 42 } between sieve passes; it never touches document or window — WorkerGlobalScope has fetch, IndexedDB and timers, but DOM access throws. All rendering stays on the main-thread onmessage handler.

steps.label: Step 3: Cancel from outside, finish from inside
steps.text: Cancel calls worker.terminate() — immediate, no cleanup inside. Success calls self.close() at the end of the worker — the thread frees itself. Both paths release the OS thread; forgetting both leaks it.

steps.label: Step 4: Two examples, two payloads
steps.text: Sorting a Float64Array favored zero-copy transfer; sieving favors progress messages plus self-close. Same postMessage machinery, opposite bottleneck — bulk bytes versus long compute.

examples.result: Progress bar fills from worker messages, Cancel terminates instantly, completion self-closes — responsive compute with explicit lifecycle, the control-plane twin to the transferable-buffer data plane.

keyTakeaways: Web Workers execute on separate OS threads, keeping the main thread responsive.
Workers cannot access the DOM or window object; communication occurs strictly through postMessage.
postMessage copies data via structured cloning; use Transferable Objects for zero-copy memory transfer.
Call worker.terminate() or self.close() to free thread resources when work completes.

quiz.q: Which of the following can be accessed directly from inside a Web Worker script?
quiz.explanation: Web Workers have no access to window, document, or DOM elements; however, they have access to networking APIs (fetch, WebSocket) and client storage (IndexedDB).

quiz.q: What happens to an ArrayBuffer on the main thread after sending it as a Transferable Object via postMessage(data, [data.buffer])?
options: It remains readable and writable by both threads simultaneously
Its memory is duplicated, consuming twice as much RAM
It becomes detached (neutered) on the sending thread, and its byteLength becomes 0
It is converted to a JSON string
quiz.explanation: Transferring an ArrayBuffer transfers memory ownership without copying; the sending thread’s buffer becomes detached with byteLength 0 to prevent data races.

quiz.q: How does postMessage() serialize standard JavaScript objects by default?
options: Using the Structured Clone algorithm, which supports circular references, Dates, and Maps
quiz.explanation: The structured clone algorithm copies complex object graphs, Maps, Sets, TypedArrays, and cyclic references without JSON string limitations.

quiz.q: How can the main thread immediately stop an active Web Worker?
quiz.explanation: worker.terminate() immediately destroys the worker thread without waiting for its operations to finish.

intro: The same V8 engine that runs in your browser also runs in data centers: **Node.js** wraps V8 in a host environment built for programs rather than pages — files, processes, sockets and HTTP instead of documents, windows and events. Everything in this chapter rests on Chapter 13: Node keeps JavaScript **single-threaded and event-driven**, but makes the whole operating system reachable through **non-blocking APIs**. This is JavaScript meeting the machine of Operating System Concepts Chapters 4 and 5 — except that where a kernel preempts threads, Node schedules callbacks cooperatively, one run-to-completion unit at a time.
objectives: Describe Node’s architecture — V8, libuv and the standard library — and how the host differs from a browser
Run code interactively in the REPL and as scripts, and manage projects with node, npm and npx
Read command-line arguments from process.argv and configuration from process.env
Write a robust command-line argument parser from scratch
Consume standard input line by line with the readline module

concepts.term: Node’s architecture: V8 plus a host
concepts.statement: Node is **V8** (the JavaScript compiler and runtime) plus a **host environment**: a standard library of server-oriented APIs, and **libuv**, the C library that provides the event loop, non-blocking file and socket I/O, and a small pool of OS threads. Node runs scripts from files instead of web pages, and has no DOM, no window and no browser sandbox.
concepts.detail: The JavaScript side of Node is **one thread** with one call stack — the run-to-completion rule of Section 13.1 holds unchanged. The waiting is done elsewhere: when JavaScript asks for a file, libuv hands the blocking system call to a pool thread or the OS kernel, and the completion becomes a queued callback. In Operating System Concepts terms (Chapters 4 and 5), the event loop is a scheduler — but a cooperative one: JavaScript code is never preempted mid-statement, which is why Node code needs no locks (and why one slow callback stalls everything).

concepts.statement: Typing `node` with no arguments starts an interactive **REPL** — a read-eval-print loop where each expression is evaluated and its value printed; typing `node script.js` runs a file; `node -e "code"` runs a string. The REPL supports multi-line functions, tab completion, and dot-commands like `.exit` and `.help`.

Node speaks both module dialects of Chapter 10: the original **CommonJS** (`const fs = require("node:fs")`, `module.exports = value`) and, when `package.json` declares `"type": "module"` (or the file ends in `.mjs`), the **ES6** form (`import fs from "node:fs"`, `export default value`). The `node:` prefix marks a built-in module and resolves slightly faster.
concepts.detail: Rule of thumb for new code: use ES6 `import`/`export` (Section 10.3) — it is the standard, it is statically analyzable (which is what makes bundler tree-shaking possible, Section 17.3), and top-level `await` works in ES modules. Section 16.5 and this chapter’s examples use whichever dialect reads best for the point being made.

concepts.statement: `process` is a global that **is the running program**: `process.argv` is the command-line arguments array, `process.env` the environment variables object, `process.cwd()` the current working directory, `process.exit(code)` ends the program immediately, and `process.stdin`/`stdout`/`stderr` are its standard streams.
concepts.detail:
```js
process.argv
// ["/usr/local/bin/node", "/app/greet.js", "--name", "Ada"]
process.env.HOME        // environment variables: all strings
process.env.NODE_ENV    // conventions like "production"
process.exit(1)         // stop NOW with exit code 1
process.stdout.write("no automatic newline\n")
```
Arguments are always **strings** — parse numbers yourself (`Number(arg)`).

concepts.term: Exit codes: talking to the shell
concepts.statement: A Node program is usually one command in a larger shell pipeline, and shells communicate success through **exit codes**: 0 means success, anything else means failure. `console.log` writes to stdout (data); `console.error` writes to stderr (diagnostics) — keeping them separate lets `node tool.js > out.txt` capture output while errors still reach the terminal.
concepts.detail: Prefer setting `process.exitCode = 1` and letting the program end naturally: `process.exit()` kills the event loop instantly, and `console.error` output still sitting in a buffer can be lost. A thrown, uncaught exception already exits with code 1 — the idiomatic way for a CLI to fail.

concepts.statement: `process.stdin` is a **Readable stream** (Section 16.3), so a Node script can join shell pipelines: `node count.js < notes.txt`. The `readline` module wraps the byte stream and emits **lines**, applying exactly the record-splitting pattern of Section 13.4 internally.

examples.title: A command-line argument parser, from process.argv up

steps.label: Step 1: Inspect the raw argv
steps.text: For `node greet.js --name Ada --times 3`, `process.argv` is `["…/bin/node", "…/greet.js", "--name", "Ada", "--times", "3"]`. Element 0 is the Node executable and element 1 the script path — **real arguments start at index 2**, which is why the loop begins there.

steps.label: Step 2: Pair flags with values
steps.text: Each iteration expects a `--key` at `argv[i]` and its value at `argv[i + 1]`. Copying the value and then doing `i++` moves the index past the pair, so the loop always lands on the next flag — `--name Ada --times 3` takes two iterations, not four.

steps.label: Step 3: Fail loudly on malformed input
steps.text: A bare word (`greet.js hello`) hits the `!startsWith("--")` branch; `--name` at the end of the line finds `undefined`, and `--name --times` finds another flag — both throw with a message naming the offender. Because nothing catches the error, the uncaught exception prints a stack trace and exits with code 1: the shell sees failure (exit codes, above).

steps.label: Step 4: Defaults make the tool forgiving
steps.text: The seed object `{ name: "world", times: 1 }` means `node greet.js` with no arguments still does something sensible — arguments override, absence inherits. Values are stored as **strings** (`"3"`), so `Number(args.times)` converts at the point of use, and a non-numeric value becomes `NaN` — zero loops, a visible symptom rather than a crash.

steps.label: Step 5: Run it

examples.result: `node greet.js --name Ada --times 3` prints three greetings; `node greet.js` prints one `Hello, world!`; `node greet.js --name` exits with a missing-value error and code 1.

examples.title: A word-count filter over stdin

steps.label: Step 1: The pipeline provides the input
steps.text: Run as `node count.js < notes.txt` or `cat report.md | node count.js`. The shell wires the file (or upstream command) to the script’s `process.stdin`; Node opens nothing itself. This composition — small programs joined by pipes — is why CLIs read stdin instead of filenames by default.

steps.label: Step 2: readline converts bytes to lines
steps.text: `process.stdin` delivers raw **Buffers** in arbitrary chunks (Section 16.3). The readline interface does the Section 13.4 job underneath: it decodes UTF-8 across chunk boundaries, splits on newlines, and holds back any partial final line until EOF confirms it is complete. The `for await` loop (Section 13.4) suspends until each next line is ready — the thread stays free between lines.

steps.label: Step 3: Count per line
steps.text: `line.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean)` splits on runs of whitespace and drops the empty strings that leading/trailing whitespace would produce. `chars` counts the string’s `.length` — code units, not UTF-8 bytes (`Buffer.byteLength(line)` would give bytes; see the encoding example in Section 16.3).

steps.label: Step 4: EOF ends the loop, the report prints once
steps.text: When the input ends, the last `next()` resolves `{done: true}`, the loop exits, and the single summary line goes to stdout — where redirection like `node count.js < a.txt > stats.txt` captures it. Errors (a closed pipe, for example) reject the iteration, land in `main().catch`, and set `process.exitCode` so the shell can detect failure without losing buffered stderr.

examples.result: For a 3-line, 12-word, 74-character input, `node count.js < notes.txt` prints `3 12 74` — a program that combines with any Unix pipeline, never blocking the thread while it waits for data.

keyTakeaways: Node = V8 + libuv + a server API library: one JavaScript thread with an event loop, plus OS-level waiters — the cooperative counterpart of the preemptive schedulers in OSC Chapters 4 and 5.
Run code three ways: `node` (REPL), `node script.js` (files), `node -e` (one-liners); `.exit` leaves the REPL.
`process.argv` holds node, script path and arguments — real arguments start at index 2, and every one of them is a string.
Exit codes are the CLI contract: 0 success, non-zero failure; `process.exitCode` is safer than `process.exit()`, which kills pending output.
stdout is data, stderr is diagnostics; keeping them separate is what makes shell redirection work.
process.stdin is a Readable stream — readline turns it into lines, making Node scripts full citizens of shell pipelines.

quiz.q: For `node greet.js --name Ada`, what are `process.argv[0]` and `process.argv[1]`?
options: The first flag and its value
The Node executable path and the script path — arguments begin at index 2
The script path and the first argument
Undefined — argv only holds the arguments
quiz.explanation: argv[0] is the interpreter and argv[1] the script being run; user arguments occupy index 2 onward, which is why argument loops start at `i = 2`.

quiz.q: Which statement about Node’s threading model is TRUE?
options: Node runs one OS thread per pending I/O operation
JavaScript callbacks can preempt each other mid-statement
There is one JavaScript thread; blocking system calls are performed off-thread by libuv’s pool or the OS kernel
V8 compiles every callback onto its own thread
quiz.explanation: The JavaScript side is single-threaded with run-to-completion (Section 13.1); the actual waiting happens in the OS or libuv’s small thread pool, whose completions become queued callbacks.

quiz.q: Why is `process.exitCode = 1` generally preferred over `process.exit(1)`?
options: It allows the event loop to drain naturally, so buffered stdout/stderr writes are not lost
It sets the code for the parent shell instead of the current process
process.exit(1) only works in the REPL
quiz.explanation: process.exit() kills the loop immediately — writes still sitting in kernel buffers can vanish. Setting exitCode and returning lets pending output flush before the natural exit.

quiz.q: In the stdin loop `for await (const line of rl)`, what does each iteration wait for?
options: The whole file to be read into memory first
The next complete line, after readline has stitched chunks and split on newlines
quiz.explanation: readline applies the record-splitting pattern of Section 13.4 under the hood, so each iteration receives one full line the moment it is assembled — constant memory, whatever the input size.

quiz.q: What does an uncaught exception do to a Node command-line program?
options: Prints a stack trace and exits with code 1 — the idiomatic CLI failure path
It is ignored; the program continues with the next statement
It restarts the script from the top
quiz.explanation: No catcher means Node prints the error and exits non-zero — exactly what a shell pipeline expects from a failed stage, no explicit exit call needed.

intro: In the browser, synchronous I/O was an accident you could have; in Node it is a design decision you almost always decline. **Every Node I/O API is asynchronous by default** — a request returns immediately, the single thread keeps running, and the result arrives later as a callback or a settled promise. Node exposes the same operations in **two dialects**: the error-first callback style of Section 13.1, and the promise style of Section 13.2 that `await` was built for. This section reads both fluently and translates between them.
objectives: Explain why Node made async the default and what the single thread does while I/O is in flight
Recognize the two dialects of every Node API: error-first callbacks and promise-returning modules
Translate nested callback code into flat async/await with fs/promises
Choose deliberately between sequential and parallel I/O with await and Promise.all

concepts.statement: There is no synchronous XMLHttpRequest-style divide in Node: the primary file, socket, DNS and crypto APIs **never block the JavaScript thread**, and synchronous variants (`fs.readFileSync`, `crypto.pbkdf2Sync`) exist only for one-off startup work. A blocked thread is a stalled server — run-to-completion means nothing else runs until the block ends.
concepts.detail: The scale gap is the reason: a disk read is milliseconds, a network hop tens to hundreds — millions of instructions of JavaScript could run meanwhile. Node’s bet is that one thread that never waits, plus an event loop dispatching completions, serves more concurrent clients than a thread per connection — and it removes shared-memory races entirely (contrast OSC Chapter 4 thread-per-request servers).

concepts.statement: Node’s history spans both halves of Chapter 13, so most APIs ship in **two forms**: `fs.readFile(path, (err, data) => ...)` takes an error-first callback (Section 13.1), while the `node:fs/promises` module returns promises (Section 13.2): `fsPromises.readFile(path)` — `await`able, chainable, and it **throws** on failure inside an async function.
concepts.detail:
```js
const fs = require("node:fs");            // callback dialect
const fsp = require("node:fs/promises");  // promise dialect

fs.readFile("a.txt", "utf8", (err, text) => { /* error-first */ });
const text = await fsp.readFile("a.txt", "utf8");  // throws on error
```
The promise dialect is the modern default for application code — `util.promisify` (Section 13.2) wraps any remaining error-first function when you need it.

concepts.term: What the thread does while you await
concepts.statement: While `await fsp.readFile(...)` is pending, the JavaScript thread is **not blocked** — it is back in the event loop, running other callbacks, timers and requests. The OS or a libuv pool thread performs the actual read; its completion is queued and the awaiting function resumes as a microtask-adjacent continuation.
concepts.detail: This is the OSC Chapter 5 picture redrawn cooperatively: the event loop is a scheduler with a ready queue, and I/O completions are the interrupt-driven arrivals (OSC Chapter 12’s I/O subsystem does the transfer). The practical consequence: a Node server overlaps thousands of in-flight operations on one thread, and the only way to ruin it is a long synchronous computation — Section 16.7 shows the worker-thread escape hatch.

concepts.statement: With `await`, operations run **in order, one after the next** — the reading order of the source is the execution order. Parallelism is the thing you now opt into: start several promises together, then `await Promise.all([p1, p2])` (Section 13.2) for all of them at once.

concepts.term: Errors: three checks versus one catch
concepts.statement: The callback dialect forces an error check at **every step** (`if (err) return ...` — Section 13.1), because that is the only place failure can be seen. The promise dialect centralizes it: any rejection in the whole sequence propagates to a **single** `try/catch` (or `.catch`) around the awaited calls — the failure model of exceptions restored on top of async I/O.
concepts.detail: Centralized handling is not just less typing: it is more reliable. Every hand-written `if (err)` is a chance to forget one; the single catch covers the steps you add next month, too.

examples.title: The same three-step pipeline, in both dialects

steps.label: Step 1: The same three operations
steps.text: Both versions do exactly the same I/O in the same order: read config, read data, write report. The bytes read and written are identical, and so is the wall-clock behavior — nothing blocks in either version.

steps.label: Step 2: Shape — nesting versus reading order
steps.text: The callback version indents one level per step because **step N’s logic lives inside step N−1’s callback** — Section 13.1’s pyramid of doom. The await version reads top-to-bottom in source order; the mental compiler work (“which runs first?”) is gone.

steps.label: Step 3: Error handling — three gates versus one net
steps.text: The callback version checks `err`/`err2`/`err3` separately, each with an early return — and a forgotten check feeds `undefined` into the next step. The await version has **one** `.catch` at the boundary: a missing config.json, a missing data file or a failed write all land there as rejections (Section 13.2’s propagation), each skipping the remaining steps.

steps.label: Step 4: Values flow through variables again
steps.text: In the callback version, `config` is in scope for the inner callbacks by closure — adding a step between the reads means threading it deeper. In the await version, `config` and `data` are ordinary `const` locals in one function scope: refactoring, logging and type-checking all get easier.

steps.label: Step 5: `main().catch(...)` — the boundary idiom
steps.text: Top-level `await` is only legal in ES modules; the CommonJS idiom is an async `main()` with one `.catch` attached — the single place the program reports an unhandled failure and (via `process.exitCode = 1`) tells the shell. Note what did not change: JSON.parse still throws synchronously on bad JSON, and its throw is caught by the same catch — sync and async errors meet in one handler.

examples.result: Both versions write the identical report and log `"done"`; the await version is four lines shorter, has one error path instead of three, and reads in execution order — the same reason Section 13.3 exists.

examples.title: Sequential versus parallel — a timing trace

steps.label: Step 1: The loop serializes by construction
steps.text: Each iteration awaits before the next `readFile` call is even made, so the reads cannot overlap: 100 + 100 + 100 ≈ **300 ms**. The order is guaranteed — useful when step N needs step N−1’s result, wasteful when they are independent.

steps.label: Step 2: `map` starts all three at once
steps.text: `files.map(f => fsp.readFile(...))` calls `readFile` three times synchronously, before any await — three requests in flight together, one promise each. The thread then waits at the `Promise.all`, free to do anything else in between.

steps.label: Step 3: all waits for the slowest, not the sum
steps.text: The reads overlap, so the total is roughly **100 ms** — the max, not the sum. `Promise.all` still fulfills with results **in input order** (Section 13.2), so `par[0]` is `a.json` even if `c.json` finished first.

steps.label: Step 4: The decision rule
steps.text: Sequential `await` when each step **consumes** the previous result (config → data → report). `Promise.all` when steps are **independent** (fetch 3 files, then aggregate). Mixing them up costs either latency (unneeded order) or correctness (unawaited dependencies) — and `Promise.all` still fails fast if any read rejects.

examples.result: Sequential ≈ 300 ms, parallel ≈ 100 ms on 100 ms-per-file disks — overlap bought with one `map` and a `Promise.all`, no threads touched.

keyTakeaways: Node I/O APIs are async by default: requests return immediately and the single thread keeps the event loop turning — blocking variants are for startup only.
Every API has two dialects: error-first callbacks (Section 13.1) and the promise-returning `node:fs/promises` style that `await` (Section 13.3) consumes.
While you await, the thread serves other work — the OS or libuv’s pool does the waiting (OSC Chapters 4–5 scheduling, cooperatively redrawn).
Await is sequential by default; `Promise.all` over an array of started promises is the opt-in to parallel — max latency, not the sum.
The promise dialect restores exception-style error flow: one catch covers every step, versus one `if (err)` per callback.
The CommonJS idiom: `async function main() { ... }` plus `main().catch(...)` — a single failure boundary for the whole pipeline.

quiz.q: What does the JavaScript thread do while `await fsp.readFile(...)` is pending?
options: Blocks in a read() system call
Returns to the event loop and runs other queued callbacks — the OS/libuv does the waiting
Spawns a worker thread for the read
quiz.explanation: The await suspends only the current async function; the thread goes back to the loop and serves other events, which is how one thread overlaps thousands of operations.

quiz.q: Three independent file reads each take ~100 ms. Roughly how long does `await Promise.all(files.map(f => fsp.readFile(f)))` take?
options: About 100 ms — the reads overlap, so the total is the slowest, not the sum
About 300 ms — they are still executed one at a time
About 33 ms — the work is split across cores
It depends on how many callbacks are queued
quiz.explanation: map calls readFile for all files immediately, putting every request in flight together; Promise.all then waits for the last completion — max latency ≈ 100 ms.

quiz.q: Which is the error-first signature for reading a file with the callback dialect?
quiz.explanation: Node reserves the callback’s first parameter for the error and passes results after it (Section 13.1) — check `err` before touching `data`.

quiz.q: In the async rewrite of the config → data → report pipeline, where does a missing config.json surface?
options: As an err parameter checked in each nested callback
As a rejection that propagates to the single .catch around the sequence
It crashes the process with no chance to log
It is silently ignored and data becomes undefined
quiz.explanation: The first readFile rejects, the await throws, remaining steps are skipped, and the one catch sees the error — centralized failure handling across the whole pipeline.

intro: Files, sockets and pipes move **bytes**, not strings — and real data can be terabytes that no single string should hold. Node’s answer is a trio of abstractions: **Buffer** (a fixed-length byte container), **EventEmitter** (the observer pattern that decouples producers from consumers), and **streams** (processing pipelines that hold one chunk at a time). The three compose: streams emit Buffers through events, `pipe()` wires them into pipelines, and transforms let you rewrite data as it flows.
objectives: Create and inspect Buffers; convert text through utf8, hex and base64 encodings
Explain Buffer length versus string length for multi-byte characters
Decouple producers from consumers with EventEmitter: on, once, emit, removeListener
Read, write and transform streams, and chain them with pipe() and pipeline()
Explain backpressure and why pipeline() is preferred over pipe()
