concepts.statement: A **Buffer** is a fixed-length array of bytes (0–255) — a subclass of `Uint8Array` (Section 11.2) — and the currency of all Node I/O. `Buffer.from(string, encoding)` encodes text into bytes; `buf.toString(encoding)` decodes back. `Buffer.alloc(n)` creates zero-filled storage; `Buffer.allocUnsafe(n)` skips the zeroing for speed.
concepts.detail:
```js
const buf = Buffer.from("Node", "utf8");
buf.length      // 4
buf[0]          // 78 — a byte, not "N"
buf.toString("utf8")    // "Node"
```
Use `Buffer.from`/`Buffer.alloc` — the old `new Buffer()` constructor is deprecated because it could leak uninitialized memory.

concepts.statement: An **encoding** names the bytes-to-text mapping at a conversion boundary: `utf8` is the default (variable width — 1 to 4 bytes per character); `hex` maps each byte to two characters (`6e6f6465`); `base64` packs 3 bytes into 4 characters for safe text transport (data URLs, email); `latin1`/`binary` is one byte per character.
concepts.detail:
```js
const raw = Buffer.from("café", "utf8");
raw.length                    // 5 — é is TWO bytes (0xc3 0xa9)
raw.toString("hex")           // "636166c3a9"
raw.toString("base64")        // "Y2Fmw6k="
Buffer.from("636166c3a9", "hex").toString("utf8")  // "café" — round trip
```
`Buffer.byteLength("café")` gives 5 while `"café".length` gives 4 — the byte/string distinction that Content-Length headers depend on.

concepts.term: Slicing is a view, not a copy
concepts.statement: `buf.subarray(start, end)` returns a **new Buffer that shares the same memory** — a window on the original bytes. Mutating the slice mutates the parent, and vice versa. Use `Buffer.concat([a, b])` to copy pieces into fresh storage, or `buf.copy(target, ...)` for explicit copies.
concepts.detail:
```js
const req = Buffer.from("GET /index.html HTTP/1.1");
const method = req.subarray(0, 3);   // "GET" — zero-copy view
method[0] = 0x50;                    // also changes req[0] — "PET /index.html"
```
A cheap view is exactly what protocol parsing wants (find the header boundary, look at pieces) — just remember you are looking **into**, not **at a copy of**, the bytes.

concepts.statement: **EventEmitter** is Node’s built-in pub/sub class: `emitter.on(event, listener)` subscribes, `emitter.emit(event, ...args)` invokes every listener **synchronously, in registration order**, and `emitter.once`/`emitter.off` (alias `removeListener`) manage membership. `emit` returns true if any listener ran. Streams, servers and sockets are all EventEmitters.
concepts.detail: Because emit runs listeners immediately on the same thread (Section 13.1’s run-to-completion), listeners need no locks — but a slow listener delays everything after it. A same-named event with more than 10 listeners logs a warning (a leak detector — raise it with `emitter.setMaxListeners(n)` if the count is intentional, as in a room of sockets).

concepts.statement: A **stream** is an EventEmitter that moves data incrementally: a **Readable** produces chunks (`fs.createReadStream`), a **Writable** consumes them (`fs.createWriteStream`, `process.stdout`, HTTP responses), a **Duplex** does both (a TCP socket), and a **Transform** reads chunks and writes transformed ones (compression, encryption — the example below). Chunks are Buffers, typically ≤ 64 KB (`highWaterMark`).
concepts.detail: Two consumption styles for Readables: the event style (`on("data")`, `on("end")` — push mode) and — usually better — the async-iteration style `for await (const chunk of stream)` (Section 13.4), which applies backpressure automatically by requesting the next chunk only after the body finishes with the current one.

concepts.statement: `readable.pipe(writable)` pumps data across streams as it arrives and returns the destination (so `.pipe().pipe()` chains). `stream.pipeline(src, ...streams, callback)` (or `stream/promises`’ promise-returning `pipeline`) does the same **and** propagates errors and destroys every stream in the chain when any one fails — which bare `pipe()` does not.

concepts.term: Backpressure: the flow control of streams
concepts.statement: When a Writable cannot keep up, its `write()` returns **false** — the signal for the Readable to **pause** reading until `"drain"` fires. This is **backpressure**: memory stays bounded (a few chunks in flight) no matter how big the file or how slow the consumer. `pipe()`/`pipeline()` and `for await` honor it automatically.
concepts.detail: Without backpressure, reading a 10 GB file into a slow socket would buffer all 10 GB in RAM — the Node version of an unbounded queue (compare OSC Chapter 3’s bounded buffer). The readable-vs-writable handshake is Node’s application-level copy of TCP’s own window flow control: the consumer signals capacity, the producer respects it.

examples.title: Hex and base64 round trips — and the multi-byte trap

steps.label: Step 1: Encode, and count bytes not characters
steps.text: UTF-8 encodes ASCII as one byte — `c` = `0x63`, `a` = `0x61`, `f` = `0x66` — but `é` (U+00E9) needs **two**: `0xc3 0xa9`. So `buf.length` is 5 while `s.length` is 4: `Buffer.byteLength(s)` is the number that belongs in a `Content-Length` header.

steps.label: Step 2: hex and base64 are byte-to-text alphabets
steps.text: `toString("hex")` prints each byte as two hex digits — `636166c3a9` — a lossless, human-readable rendering. `toString("base64")` packs the 5 bytes into `Y2Fmw6k=`: 4 output characters per 3 input bytes, padded with `=` — the transport-safe alphabet of data URLs and MIME.

steps.label: Step 3: Round trips are exact
steps.text: `Buffer.from(hexString, "hex").toString("utf8")` rebuilds the same 5 bytes, and decoding yields `"café"` — encode/decode through any single encoding is lossless. This is the standard trick for hex dumps, checksums and tests that must show binary data in text.

steps.label: Step 4: Cutting between the bytes of one character
steps.text: `subarray(0, 4)` keeps `63 61 66 c3` — ending **inside** é’s two-byte sequence. Decoding finds a dangling `0xc3`, replaces what it cannot decode with U+FFFD (the replacement character `\ufffd`), and `"caf\ufffd"` is the silent corruption: no exception, just wrong data. This is exactly why Section 13.4’s line-splitting and `TextDecoder`’s streaming mode exist — always cut on **record or code-point** boundaries, never blindly by byte.

examples.result: 5 bytes; hex `636166c3a9`; base64 `Y2Fmw6k=`; the hex round trip reproduces `"café"` exactly — and slicing at byte 4 corrupts the final character into a replacement character.

examples.title: A publish/subscribe temperature monitor with EventEmitter

steps.label: Step 1: emit is a synchronous fan-out
steps.text: Each tick, `thermo.emit("reading", temp)` calls every listener immediately, in the order they registered — logger first, alarm second — and only then returns. Same thread, run-to-completion (Section 13.1): no queue, no microtasks, no interleaving. The event name plus the argument list is the whole contract.

steps.label: Step 2: Subscribers are independent
steps.text: The logger does pure observation; the alarm holds state (its threshold) and decides for itself when its job is done. Neither knows the other exists — adding a third consumer (a CSV writer, an MQTT forwarder) is one more `on("reading", fn)` with zero changes to the sensor.

steps.label: Step 3: removeListener changes the future, not the present
steps.text: When the alarm removes itself, the **current** emit has already captured the listener list — it still finishes its own run — but the next `emit` finds only the logger. The alarm retires exactly once, however many further spikes occur. (Symmetrically: `removeAllListeners("reading")` would unsubscribe everyone.)

steps.label: Step 4: once for lifecycle events
steps.text: `once("shutdown", ...)` registers a listener that un-registers itself the first time it runs — the idiom for “on the way down, do this one time,” immune to double-shutdown calls. It is exactly `on` plus automatic `removeListener` after the first invocation.

steps.label: Step 5: Why pub/sub here
steps.text: The sensor source is a `setInterval` now; later it is a hardware device or an HTTP feed — the publisher and the consumers are coupled only by the `"reading"` contract. That decoupling is the EventEmitter’s whole point, and it is the pattern every long-lived Node object reuses: streams emit `"data"`/`"end"`, servers emit `"request"`, sockets emit `"connect"` (next sections).

examples.result: Log lines every 250 ms; when the random walk first crosses 30 °C, one `ALARM:` line prints and the alarm never fires again — the logger keeps logging, and a `shutdown` emit would print its message exactly once.

examples.title: An uppercase Transform, and copying a file with backpressure

steps.label: Step 1: Three stages, one flowing pipeline
steps.text: The Readable pulls chunks of at most ~64 KB from the disk; the **Transform** sits between the two ends — it implements both the read side and the write side, converting each chunk it receives; the Writable pushes them to the output file. At any instant the whole pipeline holds a handful of chunks, whether `in.txt` is 6 KB or 6 GB.

steps.label: Step 2: The transform contract
steps.text: For every incoming `chunk`, `transform(chunk, encoding, callback)` runs: do the work (here — decode as UTF-8, uppercase, pass the string along), then call `callback(null, output)` to push the result downstream. Calling `callback(err)` instead rejects the pipeline; passing nothing (`callback()` with no second argument) drops the chunk — that is how a filter stream works.

steps.label: Step 3: pipeline, not pipe, for production
steps.text: `await pipeline(read, transform, write)` resolves when every stream has ended cleanly — and if **any** stage errors (disk full, permissions), it destroys all three and rejects the promise. The bare `pipe()` equivalent would leak the open file descriptors and hang forever on a mid-copy error (the reason the promise-returning `pipeline` exists).

steps.label: Step 4: Backpressure keeps memory flat
steps.text: If the disk writing `out.txt` falls behind, the Writable’s `write()` returns false, the Transform pauses, and the Readable stops pulling from the source until the `"drain"` event — the consumer’s pace throttles the producer automatically. Without this handshake, a fast SSD feeding a slow network sink would buffer the entire file in memory; with it, the copy runs at exactly the sink’s speed in constant memory.

steps.label: Step 5: A caveat worth knowing
steps.text: `chunk.toString("utf8")` assumes no character straddles a chunk boundary — true for pure ASCII (the uppercase example), not for arbitrary text: a 2-byte `é` split across chunks would corrupt exactly like the hex example above. The general fix is the leftover-tail pattern of Section 13.4 (or `new StringDecoder`); in real code, `zlib.createGzip()`-style binary Transforms are safe by construction because they never decode to text.

examples.result: A copy whose output is the input uppercased, executed in ~64 KB chunks with constant memory, correct cleanup on failure, and automatic throttling by the slowest stage.

keyTakeaways: Buffer is Node’s byte container — a Uint8Array (Section 11.2) — created with `Buffer.from(...)`/`Buffer.alloc(n)`, never the deprecated `new Buffer()`.
UTF-8 is variable width: `Buffer.byteLength("café")` is 5, `"café".length` is 4 — byte counts and character counts are different numbers (Content-Length wants bytes).
`subarray` shares memory — a view, not a copy; `Buffer.concat` is the copying combine; slicing mid-code-point corrupts text silently.
EventEmitter is built-in pub/sub: synchronous, in-order listener invocation via `emit`; `once` self-removes; `removeListener` affects future emits only; >10 listeners warns.
Four stream kinds — Readable, Writable, Duplex, Transform — and two consumption styles: events (`on("data")`) or `for await` (Section 13.4), which backpressures for you.
`pipeline()` over `pipe()`: it propagates errors and destroys every stream in the chain; bare pipe leaks on mid-stream failure.
Backpressure (write() → false, pause until drain) bounds memory to a few chunks whatever the file size — the consumer throttles the producer.

quiz.q: What is `Buffer.byteLength("café")` and why does it differ from `"café".length`?
options: 4, because the string has four characters
5 — é takes two UTF-8 bytes, and byteLength counts bytes, not characters
5, because Buffer adds a null terminator
It throws — café contains a non-ASCII character
quiz.explanation: Strings count UTF-16 code units; Buffers count bytes. UTF-8 encodes é as 0xc3 0xa9, so the byte count is 5 while the string length is 4 — the number a Content-Length header needs.

quiz.q: After `const b = buf.subarray(1, 3); b[0] = 0xff;` — what is in `buf`?
options: buf[1] is now 0xff — the slice is a view sharing the parent’s memory
quiz.explanation: subarray is a zero-copy window: writes through the slice are writes into the parent — handy for protocol parsing, surprising if you expected a copy (use Buffer.concat or copy for that).

quiz.q: When does `emitter.emit("x", arg)` invoke the listeners registered with `on("x", ...)`?
options: On the next turn of the event loop, as microtasks
Synchronously, immediately, in registration order — before emit returns
Only once, then they are removed
quiz.explanation: emit is a synchronous fan-out on the caller’s stack: listeners run in the order registered and finish before emit returns — run-to-completion (Section 13.1), no locks needed.

quiz.q: A Transform stream is best described as…
options: A Readable that is also an EventEmitter
A stream that both reads and writes, converting input chunks to output chunks
A buffer that grows without limit
A writable stream that never ends
quiz.explanation: Transform implements both ends: each incoming chunk goes through transform(chunk, encoding, callback), and what you pass to callback flows downstream — compression and the uppercase example both work this way.

quiz.q: Why is `pipeline()` preferred over `pipe()` in production code?
options: It is faster because it skips the event loop
It propagates errors and destroys every stream in the chain when one fails; pipe leaks descriptors and hangs
It reads the whole file into memory first
It disables backpressure for more throughput
quiz.explanation: pipe wires flows but is silent on failure — an error mid-copy leaves the destination open and the program hanging; pipeline cleans up all stages and reports the error through a callback or a rejected promise.

quiz.q: A Writable’s write() has returned false. What should the Readable feeding it do?
options: Keep reading — the data will buffer somewhere safe
Pause producing until the Writable emits "drain"
Double the chunk size to catch up
quiz.explanation: false means the sink is full: stop, let it flush, resume on drain. That handshake is backpressure — the reason a pipeline of streams runs in constant memory.

intro: Between its APIs, Node lets a program look at **itself and its machine**: which directory it runs in, how much CPU and memory the host has, what the load average says, and precisely how long a piece of code took. These are the `process` details and the `os` module — small APIs, but they are how CLIs find their context, how dashboards report health, and how benchmarks avoid the classic wall-clock trap.
objectives: Query the working directory, process identity and environment with process
Measure elapsed time correctly with process.hrtime.bigint() — and explain why Date.now() is the wrong clock for durations
Read process.memoryUsage() and the os module (cpus, totalmem, loadavg) to report host health
Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM to shut servers down gracefully

concepts.term: Where am I: cwd, pid, argv-adjacent facts
concepts.statement: `process.cwd()` returns the current working directory (where the shell started you — not where your script lives) and `process.chdir(dir)` changes it; `process.pid` is the process id; `__dirname`/`import.meta.url` (Chapter 10) locate your own module instead.
concepts.detail:
```js
process.cwd()    // "/home/ada/project" — from the shell
process.chdir("/tmp");
process.pid       // 4711
```
The cwd/pid pair is process identity in the OSC Chapter 3 sense: your program is one address space among many, and these are its coordinates.

concepts.term: hrtime: a stopwatch, not a clock
concepts.statement: `process.hrtime.bigint()` returns a **monotonic** nanosecond count as a BigInt — it never goes backwards and is immune to NTP adjustments, leap seconds or manual clock changes. Take it twice and subtract: the difference is elapsed time. `Date.now()` is a **wall clock** — fine for timestamps, wrong for durations.

`process.memoryUsage()` reports four numbers in bytes: **heapUsed** (JavaScript objects currently live), **heapTotal** (the V8 heap including free space), **rss** (resident set size — all OS pages, including the interpreter and code), and **external** (memory outside the V8 heap, notably Buffers).
concepts.detail: rss is what `ps` and container limits see; heapUsed is what GC pressure is about. A server holding many large Buffers can be near its rss limit with a modest heapUsed — the split tells you which side to tune. Numbers move with garbage collection timing, so treat them as a snapshot, not an accounting ledger (compare OSC Chapter 9’s view of what a process’s memory actually is).

concepts.term: The os module: the machine’s dashboard
concepts.statement: `os.cpus()` lists cores (and per-core load), `os.totalmem()`/`os.freemem()` report RAM, `os.loadavg()` the 1/5/15-minute load averages, `os.uptime()` the machine’s, `os.hostname()`, `os.platform()`, `os.arch()`, and `os.EOL` the platform newline.
concepts.detail:
```js
const os = require("node:os");
os.cpus().length      // 8 — also the default libuv thread-pool size
os.loadavg()         // [1.24, 0.98, 0.87] — Linux/macOS; [0,0,0] on Windows
os.totalmem()        // 17179869184
```
Load average is OSC Chapter 5 in one number — the run-queue length smoothed over time; sustained values above `cpus().length` mean more runnable work than cores.

concepts.statement: The OS can send a process **signals**: SIGINT (Ctrl-C) and SIGTERM (the default kill) both terminate Node by default, but `process.on("SIGINT", handler)` intercepts them — the hook for closing servers, flushing logs and disconnecting cleanly before exiting.

examples.title: Timing a function the right way

steps.label: Step 1: Two BigInt snapshots, one subtraction
steps.text: `hrtime.bigint()` returns an opaque BigInt count of nanoseconds since an arbitrary origin. Subtracting the two snapshots is **exact** integer arithmetic — no floating-point rounding over long spans — and `Number(...)` converts only the (small) difference, once, to milliseconds.

steps.label: Step 2: Why not Date.now()
steps.text: `Date.now()` reads the wall clock, which the OS or an NTP daemon may step **backward or forward** between the two calls — durations come out wrong or even negative. The monotonic stopwatch ticks only forward, tied to no calendar at all. (For the same reason, monotonic clocks are what kernels use for scheduling decisions — OSC Chapter 5.)

steps.label: Step 3: What the measurement includes
steps.text: Because JavaScript runs to completion (Section 13.1), nothing interleaves with `work()` — the stopwatch covers the whole sort, not fragments of it. What it cannot cover is the first-run effect: V8 compiles and optimizes as it warms up, so a second measurement is typically faster. Report the **minimum of several runs** for stable numbers.

steps.label: Step 4: Pair timing with memory
steps.text: The second line snapshots `heapUsed` after the sort — 300k boxed doubles plus the array is on the order of a few MB, visible in the delta. Seeing time **and** memory together is the profiling habit: an O(n log n) sort and an accidental O(n²) both run; the heap is often what distinguishes them.

examples.result: A trustworthy line like `sorted 300000 numbers in 48.3 ms` plus a heap reading — measured on a clock that cannot lie about direction, exact to the nanosecond.

examples.title: A one-screen host status command

steps.label: Step 1: Identity and capacity
steps.text: Hostname, platform and architecture identify the box; `cpus().length` is how much parallelism exists — and, usefully, also the **default size of libuv’s thread pool**, so it gates how many simultaneous blocking file/crypto operations one process can have in flight.

steps.label: Step 2: Read the load with the scheduler in mind
steps.text: Load average counts runnable + uninterruptible tasks averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Dividing by cores gives utilization-per-core: a load of 6.4 on 8 cores is busy-but-healthy; on 2 cores it means a run queue (OSC Chapter 5) four deep — requests are waiting. On Windows it is always `[0, 0, 0]`; use `cpus()` times there instead.

steps.label: Step 3: Separate free memory from process memory
steps.text: `os.freemem()/totalmem()` describe the **machine** — is swapping near? `memoryUsage()` describes **this process** — is our heap the problem? A leak shows up as heapUsed and rss climbing together across restarts; a big external means Buffers, not objects. One number answers where; the other answers who.

steps.label: Step 4: Where such a command lives
steps.text: This is the body of every `/health` endpoint, `docker inspect`-style probe and ops dashboard tile: run it in-process (a periodic report or an HTTP route) rather than a shell alias, and the same calls stream into monitoring — the concepts transfer directly to Kubernetes readiness probes (OSC Chapter 3’s services view).

examples.result: Eight readable lines — machine identity, cores, load, free memory, and the process’s own pid/heap/rss — the minimum viable health report, with no dependency beyond Node built-ins.

keyTakeaways: `process.cwd()` is where the shell started you (chdir changes it); `process.pid` is your process id; `import.meta.url`/`__dirname` locate your module file.
Use `hrtime.bigint()` for durations — monotonic and nanosecond-exact; `Date.now()` is a wall clock that can step, making durations wrong or negative.
Measure the difference of two BigInts, convert to ms once; report the min of several runs — V8 warms up.
`memoryUsage()`: heapUsed = live JS objects, rss = total OS pages, external = Buffers off-heap — rss is what container limits enforce.
The os module gives the host: `cpus().length` (also libuv’s default pool size), totalmem/freemem, loadavg (run-queue depth — OSC Ch 5), platform, EOL.
SIGINT/SIGTERM are catchable with `process.on(...)` — the graceful-shutdown hook; SIGKILL is not.

quiz.q: Why is Date.now() the wrong tool for measuring how long an operation took?
options: It reads the wall clock, which can be stepped forward or back by the OS — durations can be wrong or negative
It is disabled inside async functions
quiz.explanation: Durations need a monotonic source: process.hrtime.bigint() only ever moves forward, making the subtraction trustworthy — the same property kernels rely on for scheduling (OSC Ch 5).

quiz.q: A dashboard shows heapUsed holding steady but rss climbing steadily. What is a likely cause?
options: Growing off-heap memory — e.g. Buffers — counted in rss and external, not the V8 heap
The process is swapping in its own code pages
heapUsed is always smaller than rss, so nothing is wrong
quiz.explanation: rss includes everything the OS maps for the process; external (Buffers, typed arrays) growing shows exactly this signature — steady heap, climbing rss — and points the fix away from GC.

quiz.q: On an 8-core machine, which 1-minute load average most suggests a run queue is forming?
quiz.explanation: Load above the core count means more runnable work than processors — roughly 1.5 tasks waiting per core at 9.50, the classic queueing delay of OSC Chapter 5 (and why CPU scheduling exists).

quiz.q: What does `process.on("SIGTERM", handler)` enable?
options: Intercepting the termination signal to close servers and flush state before exiting
quiz.explanation: SIGTERM (and Ctrl-C’s SIGINT) are catchable: the handler runs, so the process can finish in-flight work and exit cleanly — SIGKILL, by contrast, cannot be caught.

intro: The `fs` module is Node’s workhorse: it reads, writes, appends, stats, creates, removes and **walks** files and directories — in all three dialects of Section 16.2 (sync, callback, promise). Its APIs are a perfect laboratory for everything this chapter has built: streams for large files, Buffers for bytes, and `await` for readable sequencing. This section works the daily driver operations and finishes with the recursive directory walk that ties them together.
objectives: Choose among the three fs dialects — sync, callback, promise — and know when each is appropriate
Inspect files with stat: size, mtime, file-type predicates
Create, write and append files, understanding overwrite semantics and recursive mkdir
Build a recursive directory walk with readdir and Dirent
Watch files for changes with fs.watch

concepts.term: Three dialects of every fs operation
concepts.statement: Each file operation exists in three spellings: `fs.readFileSync(path)` (blocks the event loop until done), `fs.readFile(path, cb)` (error-first callback), and `fsPromises.readFile(path)` (awaitable promise). All three read the same bytes — the choice is about **when** and **how failure arrives**.
concepts.detail:
```js
const fs = require("node:fs");
const fsp = require("node:fs/promises");

const a = fs.readFileSync("cfg.json", "utf8");            // startup only
fs.readFile("cfg.json", "utf8", (err, t) => { /* ... */ }); // legacy
const c = await fsp.readFile("cfg.json", "utf8");          // modern default
```
The sync form is acceptable exactly where blocking is harmless: loading config once at boot, or a one-shot build script. In a server, it stalls every other request (Section 16.1’s scheduler, starved).

concepts.statement: `fsPromises.stat(path)` returns a **Stats** object describing the filesystem entry: `size` in bytes, `mtime` (modification time), and type predicates `isFile()`, `isDirectory()`, `isSymbolicLink()`. It reads **metadata**, not content — no bytes of the file are read.
concepts.detail:
```js
const st = await fsp.stat("report.pdf");
console.log(st.size);                 // 2841103 — bytes
console.log(st.mtime.toISOString());   // "2025-10-09T12:00:42.000Z"
console.log(st.isFile());              // true
```
stat ENOENTs (throws) for missing paths — the idiom for existence checks (never “open and look for an error” unless you are about to use the file anyway: TOCTOU — time-of-check-to-time-of-use — says just open it).

concepts.statement: `readFile` waits for and returns the **entire file** as one Buffer (or string with an encoding) — fine for configs and templates, wrong for gigabytes. `createReadStream` returns a **Readable stream** (Section 16.3) that delivers ~64 KB chunks with backpressure — the way to copy, hash or upload any file regardless of size.
concepts.detail: The rule of thumb from Section 16.3: if you would not want the whole thing in a string in memory, it is a stream. `for await (const chunk of createReadStream(p))` (Section 13.4) is the readable consumption form; `pipeline()` is the copy form.

concepts.statement: `writeFile(path, data)` **creates or truncates** — it replaces the file’s entire content, so a stray write can erase it. `appendFile(path, data)` only ever adds to the end (creating if absent). `mkdir(path, { recursive: true })` creates intermediate directories like `mkdir -p`; `rm(path, { recursive: true, force: true })` removes files or whole trees.
concepts.detail:
```js
await fsp.writeFile("app.log", "session start\n");   // overwrite!
await fsp.appendFile("app.log", `tick ${Date.now()}\n`);
await fsp.mkdir("data/2025/10", { recursive: true }); // all levels as needed
await fsp.rm("data/2024", { recursive: true, force: true });
```
All accept string **or** Buffer data — a Buffer writes exactly those bytes with no encoding surprises (Section 16.3).

concepts.term: readdir and Dirent: listing without stat-ing
concepts.statement: `fsPromises.readdir(dir)` returns names as strings; `readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true })` returns **Dirent** objects that already know their type — `entry.isDirectory()`, `entry.isFile()` — from the single directory read, avoiding one extra `stat` system call per entry.

`fs.watch(dir)` returns an EventEmitter that fires `"change"` events when files in the directory change (`eventType` of `"change"` or `"rename"`, plus the filename). Under the hood it uses the OS’s own notification — inotify on Linux, FSEvents on macOS, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows.
concepts.detail: Events can coalesce or arrive slightly out of order, and editors firing several events per save — so watchers usually debounce before reacting. This is exactly the mechanism under dev-server hot reload (Section 17.3’s HMR): save a file, watch fires, the server recompiles just that module.

examples.title: An append-only log with a stat report

steps.label: Step 1: writeFile truncates — say it out loud
steps.text: Because `writeFile` replaces the whole file, `"session start\n"` here is a deliberate reset: if `app.log` existed with history, this line erases it. Writing a log line you **must keep** is `appendFile` — that is the next call. The pair is the difference between “make the file contain X” and “add X to the file”.

steps.label: Step 2: appendFile creates-if-absent
steps.text: Each append opens, seeks to the end, writes and closes — so the two `tick`/`tock` lines land after `"session start"`. Template-literal timestamps make the content self-describing (and they are the values you would correlate with the mtime in step 3).

steps.label: Step 3: stat reads the label, not the contents
steps.text: `stat` returns metadata the filesystem already keeps: `st.size` is 53 bytes here (count the characters, newlines included), `st.mtime` updates on the last write. No file content crosses into memory — the right tool when a dashboard needs “how big, how stale”, and the only tool that answers for a file too big to read.

steps.label: Step 4: Confirm, then generalize
steps.text: The final `readFile` (with `"utf8"`, so a string not a Buffer) is proof the file holds what we intended. The operational shape — append on events, stat on reports, read only when the content itself is needed — scales to real logging; for high-volume logging, wrap the destination in `createWriteStream` with `{ flags: "a" }` so the descriptor stays open instead of reopening per line.

examples.result: Three lines in `app.log`, then: `…/app.log: 53 bytes, modified 2025-10-09T12:00:42.011Z` — and the content echoes back, appended in order, timestamps intact.

examples.title: A recursive directory walk

steps.label: Step 1: One readdir per directory, type included
steps.text: Each call reads one directory’s entries and their types in a single syscall — `{ withFileTypes: true }` is what makes the walk cheap. Without it, deciding whether `full` is a directory costs an extra `stat` **per entry**, doubling system calls for big trees.

steps.label: Step 2: path.join, never string concatenation
steps.text: `path.join("src", "lib", "util.js")` inserts the right separator for the platform (`\` on Windows) and normalizes `.`/`..` segments. Hand-built `dir + "/" + name` produces mixed-separator paths that break on Windows and defeat deduplication — the bug class `path` exists to erase.

steps.label: Step 3: Recursion is depth-first
steps.text: A subdirectory is fully walked (awaited!) before the next sibling is listed — so directory bookkeeping happens in stack order. The `await` inside the loop keeps one directory read in flight at a time; for wide trees, `Promise.all(entries.filter(isDir).map(walk))` walks subdirectories concurrently — the same sequential-versus-parallel choice as Section 16.2, applied to syscalls.

steps.label: Step 4: Filter deliberately
steps.text: The walk collects only `isFile()` and recurses only `isDirectory()` — symlinks, sockets and devices are neither, so they are skipped (a symlinked cycle cannot loop the walk). Real tools add filters: skip `node_modules`, match extensions, respect `.gitignore` — each is one predicate on `entry.name` or `full`.

steps.label: Step 5: Sort last, at the top
steps.text: Sorting inside recursion would sort each directory’s fragment; sorting the final array gives the whole tree in one lexicographic order — deterministic output, which is what tests and diffs want. The `.then(files => ..., console.error)` shape is the CLI boundary idiom from Section 16.1: errors (permission denied on a subdirectory) print and the process exits non-zero.

examples.result: For a `src` containing `main.js`, `lib/a.js`, `lib/b.js`, `lib/util/c.js`: four sorted paths and `4 files` — the skeleton of every file-processing tool, ~15 lines with no dependencies.

keyTakeaways: fs operations come in three dialects — sync (startup only), callback (legacy), `fs/promises` (modern default) — reading the same bytes differently.
`stat` gives metadata without content: size in bytes, mtime, and isFile()/isDirectory() predicates; a missing path throws ENOENT.
`readFile` is whole-file; `createReadStream` is chunks — if you would not hold it in a string, stream it (Section 16.3).
`writeFile` truncates — “make the file contain X”; `appendFile` only adds — “add X to the file”; mkdir recursive is `mkdir -p`; rm recursive+force is `rm -rf`.
readdir with `{ withFileTypes: true }` returns Dirents — type arrives with the listing, one syscall per directory instead of two per entry.
path.join builds platform-correct paths; never concatenate separators by hand.
fs.watch rides the OS’s change notification — the mechanism beneath dev-server hot reload (Section 17.3).

quiz.q: What does `await fsp.writeFile("data.txt", "hello")` do if data.txt already exists with 2 MB of content?
options: Truncates the file to exactly "hello" — the previous content is gone
quiz.explanation: writeFile is create-or-truncate: the file afterwards contains exactly the bytes written. Preserving history is appendFile’s job — knowing which one you are calling is the whole game.

quiz.q: Why pass `{ withFileTypes: true }` to readdir when walking a tree?
options: The returned Dirents carry isDirectory()/isFile() from the listing itself — avoiding an extra stat syscall per entry
It returns file contents as well as names
quiz.explanation: Plain readdir returns names only, and classifying each would cost one stat per entry; Dirents arrive with the type embedded, halving the system calls a walk makes.

quiz.q: Which mkdir call creates data/2025/10 in one step, even if data does not exist yet?
quiz.explanation: recursive: true creates every missing level — the mkdir -p semantics; the plain form ENOENTs as soon as any parent is missing.

quiz.q: You need to know a 4 GB file’s size and last-modified time. What is the right call?
options: await fsp.readFile(path) and check the result’s .length
await fsp.stat(path) — metadata only, no content read
quiz.explanation: stat answers from the directory entry: size and mtime without moving a byte of the file — reading 4 GB to learn two numbers is the anti-pattern the API split exists to prevent.

options: P, because synchronous reads use less memory
Both behave identically, because V8 compiles them the same way
Q, because it returns to the event loop while the system reads, while P blocks the only thread until the whole file arrives
P, because callbacks cannot report read errors
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is one blocking file read and one callback-driven file read on a single-threaded server. Step 2: The governing rule is the event-driven design: JavaScript runs on one thread, blocking calls freeze every connection until they return, and non-blocking calls delegate waiting to the system while the loop serves other events. Step 3: Tracing both paths, P holds the thread from call to full delivery so no request handler runs meanwhile, while Q registers interest, yields the thread immediately, and resumes only through its callback with `err` reporting failures. Step 4: The distractors fail because memory use is not the issue, the two forms schedule entirely differently, and the callback's first parameter exists exactly to report errors. Step 5: Therefore the callback form is the matching choice for a live server.

intro: The `http` module turns Node into a web server with one function call: **every request is an event**, and the request and response objects are **streams** — so everything from Chapter 13 and Section 16.3 composes directly. On the client side, Node ships the same global `fetch` the browser has (Section 15.10), promise-native and awaitable. This section builds a complete, framework-free JSON server — routing, body reading, status codes — and then the client that talks to it.
objectives: Write an HTTP server with http.createServer and route on method and pathname
Read request bodies by treating req as a readable stream
Send correct status codes, headers and JSON bodies
Use global fetch as a client: res.ok, res.json(), POST with headers and bodies
Add timeouts and aborts to client requests

concepts.statement: `http.createServer(handler)` returns a server that emits the handler for every incoming request; the handler receives `(req, res)`. `req` (an IncomingMessage) is a **Readable stream** already parsed into `req.method`, `req.url` and `req.headers`; `res` (a ServerResponse) is a **Writable stream** with `writeHead`, `setHeader`, `write` and `end`. `server.listen(port)` starts accepting.

concepts.term: Routing: a table keyed by method and path
concepts.statement: A router is a dispatch on `(req.method, pathname)` — parse `req.url` with `new URL(req.url, "http://x")` to separate `pathname` from `search` (query string), then match. Full frameworks (Express, Fastify) are this table plus middleware and path patterns — nothing more magical.

concepts.term: Reading a request body: req is a stream
concepts.statement: A POST body arrives as **chunks on the req stream** — never assume one chunk, never assume a size. Collect them into a Buffer with the data/end events (or `for await`), then parse. The Section 13.4 leftovers matter if you parse incrementally; for whole-body JSON, collect **then** parse once.

`res.writeHead(status, headersObject)` sets status and headers **once, before any write**; `res.end(body)` sends the final chunk and finishes the response. `res.statusCode = 404` plus `res.setHeader(...)` are the incremental alternative. Setting `Content-Type: application/json` before sending `JSON.stringify(...)` is the whole JSON contract.
concepts.detail: Because `res` is a Writable, it accepts streams directly — `pipeline(createReadStream(file), res)` serves a file in chunks with backpressure (Section 16.3), which is how a static file server fits in five lines. Common statuses: 200 OK, 201 Created, 400 bad input, 404 no route, 500 you failed.

concepts.term: fetch: the same client as the browser
concepts.statement: Node 18+ exposes the WHATWG `fetch` (Section 15.10) as a global: `const res = await fetch(url, init)` sends the request; `res.ok` is true for 2xx, `res.status` the code; `await res.json()` (or `.text()`, `.arrayBuffer()`) returns a promise because **the body streams in separately** from the headers.

concepts.term: Timeouts: race the request against a clock
concepts.statement: A hung server must not hang your client: create an `AbortController`, wire its `signal` into `fetch`, and a `setTimeout` that calls `controller.abort()` — fetch then rejects with an AbortError. This is Section 13.2’s **race** pattern, installed as a safety net under every network call.

examples.title: A complete tiny JSON server

steps.label: Step 1: One handler, two stream objects
steps.text: Each request invokes the async handler with the two streams: read facts off `req` (`method`, `url` — already parsed by Node, no socket work), write the answer through `res`. Because the handler is `async`, awaits inside it suspend **only this request** — the event loop keeps serving others (Section 16.2’s model at HTTP scale).

steps.label: Step 2: Routing is method + pathname
steps.text: Each route is a guard on the `(method, pathname)` pair, with `return` after each response so exactly one branch ever writes. `new URL(req.url, "http://localhost")` splits the URL — the second argument is a base for a relative request-target, and buys query access (`searchParams`) for free. Unmatched pairs fall to the 404 tail — the default case of the routing table.

steps.label: Step 3: Read the body before parsing it
steps.text: A POST body is not an argument — it is **a stream of chunks** arriving after the headers. `readBody` wraps the data/end/error events into a promise (Chapter 13.2’s pattern), concatenates the Buffer chunks, and decodes once. Then, and only then, `JSON.parse` — parsing per-chunk would split records across boundaries (Section 13.4’s lesson, binary edition).

steps.label: Step 4: Respond with intent
steps.text: Success is 200 with `Content-Type: application/json` and a `JSON.stringify`ed body; malformed input is a 400 with a JSON error — **machine-readable failure**, the contract that makes APIs debuggable. Note `Buffer.byteLength(text)` for the byte count: the byte/string distinction of Section 16.3, exactly where a Content-Length would need it. `writeHead` comes before any body write — headers lead, always.

steps.label: Step 5: Exercise it with curl

examples.result: A ~45-line server serving correct JSON with proper statuses: time on GET, echo + byte count on POST, 400 for bad JSON, 404 for unknown routes — and curl transcripts prove every branch.

examples.title: The client side: a fetch wrapper with errors and a timeout

steps.label: Step 1: fetch resolves on headers, not on the body
steps.text: The first `await` completes when **status and headers** have arrived — the body is still streaming. That is why `res.json()` is itself a promise, and why reading `res.status` is safe before it: checking `res.ok` right after the first await is the pattern that gives clients real error semantics (404 is not an exception to fetch — it is a successful HTTP conversation reporting a failure).

steps.label: Step 2: Turn statuses into exceptions at the wrapper boundary
steps.text: Raw `fetch` resolves happily for 404 and 500 — a deliberate API decision. A project wrapper is the place to convert: `if (!res.ok) throw` — so every caller downstream can `try/catch` or `await`-throw uniformly instead of re-checking statuses everywhere. One boundary, one policy (the same centralize-errors lesson as Section 16.2).

steps.label: Step 3: POST is options plus a stringified body
steps.text: The `init` object carries the method, the header that says what the bytes are, and the body — which is a **string**: `JSON.stringify` is the serialization step, the Content-Type the promise of what those bytes mean. The server from the previous example reads exactly this shape off its req stream — the two examples are one conversation.

steps.label: Step 4: The abort races the network
steps.text: Section 13.2’s race, embodied: the timer fires at 5 s and aborts, fetch rejects with an AbortError, the `finally` clears the timer on every path. Without it, a wedged server wedges your program — client-side timeouts are not pessimism, they are the difference between a degraded feature and a hung one.

steps.label: Step 5: await or return — both are correct
steps.text: `return res.json()` returns the promise directly (no extra await needed — the caller awaits the same settlement), while `getUser` awaits to finish its error mapping first. Both styles are idiomatic inside async functions; the rule is just: never **ignore** the promise.

examples.result: `getUser(7)` resolves to the parsed user or throws with a status-bearing message; `postScore` POSTs JSON; both survive a dead server for at most 5 seconds — a wrapper that behaves like a library function rather than a raw socket.

keyTakeaways: `http.createServer(handler)`: each request is an event; req is a Readable stream with parsed method/url/headers, res is a Writable stream with writeHead/setHeader/end.
Routing is a dispatch on (method, pathname) — parse req.url with `new URL(...)` and let an unguarded tail return the 404.
Request bodies arrive as Buffer chunks: collect with data/end events (wrap in a promise) or `for await`, then parse once — and cap the size you are willing to buffer.
Headers lead: writeHead before any body write; `Content-Type: application/json` plus JSON.stringify is the whole JSON contract; 400 for bad input, 404 for no route.
Global fetch (Node 18+, Section 15.10) is promise-based: first await = headers/status, `res.json()` = the streaming body — and `res.ok` is where non-2xx becomes a throw.
Wrap fetch at a project boundary: status-to-exception mapping plus an AbortController timeout — Section 13.2’s race as a safety net.

quiz.q: Inside `http.createServer(async (req, res) => ...)`, what are req and res?
options: Two plain objects with strings only
req is a Readable stream (with parsed method/url/headers); res is a Writable stream (with writeHead/end)
req is a Writable stream; res is a Readable stream
Both are EventEmitters with no stream methods
quiz.explanation: The handler receives the two halves of the conversation as streams: you read the request body off req chunk by chunk, and write the response into res — every Section 16.3 tool applies.

quiz.q: Why must the POST body be collected before JSON.parse, rather than parsing chunk by chunk?
options: A JSON document can straddle chunk boundaries — only the concatenated whole is parseable
It is faster to parse once per chunk
quiz.explanation: Chunk boundaries are byte-accidents of transport, not record boundaries (Section 13.4): the end of one chunk may cut a JSON value in half — collect, concat, then parse once.

quiz.q: Right after `const res = await fetch(url)`, what has actually arrived?
options: Nothing — fetch has only sent the request
Status and headers; the body is still streaming and res.json() returns a promise for it
quiz.explanation: fetch settles on headers (so status/ok are readable immediately) and exposes the body as a separate streamed promise — the two-await rhythm of fetch clients.

quiz.q: Why does a robust client check `res.ok` rather than waiting for fetch to throw on a 404?
options: It does not — fetch rejects on 404
Because fetch resolves for any received HTTP response — non-2xx is a successful transport reporting an application failure, so the wrapper converts it
Because exceptions are disabled in async functions
quiz.explanation: fetch models HTTP faithfully: the request succeeded at the protocol level, so the response object resolves — mapping 4xx/5xx into thrown Errors is the client wrapper’s policy (and Section 17.2 will mock exactly this shape).

intro: When JavaScript alone is not enough — when you need a raw TCP service, a program from another process, or more CPU than one thread can give — Node reaches outside itself with three escalating tools: the **net** module (TCP servers, socket as duplex stream), **child processes** (`exec`, `spawn`, `fork` — new OS processes, with an IPC channel for fork), and **worker threads** (real threads in the same process, for CPU-bound work). Each has a clear job, and each maps onto an Operating System Concepts counterpart: Chapters 3 and 4 made concrete from JavaScript.
objectives: Build a TCP echo server with the net module, treating sockets as duplex streams
Choose among exec, spawn and fork for child processes — buffering, streaming and IPC
Exchange structured messages with a forked child over the built-in IPC channel
Offload CPU-bound work to worker threads with postMessage and stay responsive
Use Atomics on a SharedArrayBuffer for race-free shared counters

concepts.statement: `net.createServer(conn => ...)` listens on a port and hands you each connection as a **Duplex stream** (Section 16.3): read incoming bytes with `on("data")` or `for await`, write the reply with `conn.write(...)`. HTTP is a protocol on top of exactly this — `net` is the layer under it, and also the layer for databases, Redis clients and anything that speaks TCP.

`child_process.exec(command, callback)` runs a command **through a shell**, buffers all its stdout and stderr (default cap 1 MB), and delivers both to the callback along with the exit status. Convenient for one-shot commands with small output — and unsafe with user input, because every shell metacharacter is live.

`child_process.spawn(file, args)` starts a process **without a shell**, so arguments are passed verbatim (injection-safe), and its stdout/stderr are **Readable streams** you consume as the child produces them — the right tool for long-running or large-output commands. `execFile` is spawn-with-buffering.

`child_process.fork(script)` spawns **a new Node process** running `script` and opens a **built-in message channel**: `child.send(value)` and `child.on("message", ...)` in both directions, values passing via structured clone (serializable data only). fork is how Node multiplies itself — worker farms, the cluster module, and crash isolation for risky work.
concepts.detail: Messages, not shared memory: a forked child is a separate process (OSC Chapter 3) with its own V8 heap and its own event loop — the isolation that makes a crash in child.js survivable. Compare POSIX `fork()`, which duplicates the address space: Node’s fork never shares; it communicates. `child.kill()` sends SIGTERM; `child.on("exit")` reports the code.

concepts.term: Worker threads: real threads for real CPU work
concepts.statement: `new Worker(filename, { workerData })` (from `node:worker_threads`) starts a **real OS thread** in the same process, with its own V8 isolate and its own event loop. The main thread and the worker exchange messages via `postMessage`/`on("message")` — **copies**, like fork — or share memory through a `SharedArrayBuffer`. Same API shape as the browser’s Web Workers (Section 15.12).
concepts.detail: The use case is **CPU-bound work**: while I/O already overlaps on one thread (Section 16.2), a three-second computation blocks it outright — run-to-completion has no preemption (Section 13.1). Workers exist for compression, image processing, parsing and crypto at scale: OSC Chapter 4’s parallelism, finally available, minus the data races — unless you opt into shared memory.

concepts.term: Atomics: indivisible operations on shared memory
concepts.statement: `Atomics.add(typedArray, index, value)` performs a read-modify-write on a typed-array cell backed by a `SharedArrayBuffer` as **one indivisible step** — no other thread can interleave between its read and its write. `Atomics.load/store` are the matching non-tearing reads and writes; `Atomics.compareExchange` is compare-and-swap.

examples.title: A TCP echo server (and how to talk to it)

steps.label: Step 1: Each connection is one duplex stream
steps.text: For every client that connects, the callback receives `conn` — readable and writable on the same object: the incoming bytes are the read side, `conn.write(...)` the write side (Section 16.3’s Duplex). One socket, two directions, no request/response grammar unless you invent one — that is what “raw TCP” means.

steps.label: Step 2: data events are byte accidents
steps.text: A client sending `"hello"` may deliver it as one 5-byte chunk or as `"he"` + `"llo"` — chunks are transport artifacts, not messages (Section 13.4’s framing lesson at the byte level). For an echo server it does not matter; a line protocol would need the leftover-buffer pattern, and a length-prefixed protocol would need a header parser.

steps.label: Step 3: The echo is one line
steps.text: The handler writes the same bytes back — `conn.write(chunk)` returns immediately (it is async underneath, backpressure and all). The order of bytes is preserved by TCP, so the client reads back exactly what it sent, eventually.

steps.label: Step 4: Conversation end and errors are events
steps.text: `end` fires when the client half-closes; `error` fires on abrupt failure (a reset). Neither handler is required, but sockets are resources — a real server tracks its connections (a Set), removes them on end/error, and closes the server itself on SIGTERM (Section 16.4) so in-flight writes finish.

steps.label: Step 5: Test from the shell

examples.result: Everything a client sends comes back verbatim: a complete TCP service in ~10 lines, with chunk-boundary and error handling understood rather than assumed.

examples.title: fork with IPC: parent and child exchanging messages

steps.label: Step 1: fork = a Node process plus a pipe
steps.text: Internally fork is `spawn(process.execPath, [script])` with an extra message channel wired to the child’s stdin/stdout — so the two Node processes exchange JavaScript values without inventing a wire format. `child.pid` is a real OS process id (Section 16.4): check it with `ps` while the example runs.

steps.label: Step 2: Messages are cloned, not shared
steps.text: Each `send` serializes the value (structured clone) and each side receives its own copy — strings, numbers, arrays, plain objects travel; functions, sockets and live handles do not. After the child mutates `m.numbers`, the parent’s array is unaffected: message passing buys **isolation by construction**, the opposite of shared memory.

steps.label: Step 3: The protocol is yours
steps.text: Node transports the messages; the `{type: "sum"}` / `{type: "result"}` grammar is a convention this pair of files agrees on — the same discriminated-message pattern a protocol or a reducer uses. Scale it by routing on `type` in both files: `"sum"`, `"avg"`, `"shutdown"`…

steps.label: Step 4: Lifecycle: kill, exit, exit codes
steps.text: `child.kill()` sends SIGTERM; the child (no handler) terminates, and its `"exit"` event delivers the code — 0 or otherwise — to the parent, which can decide to restart it. That supervision loop (fork, watch, restart on crash) is process management in the OSC Chapter 3 sense, implemented in a dozen lines — and it is why risky work goes in a fork: a segfault in the child is a restart, not an outage.

steps.label: Step 5: When fork is the wrong tool
steps.text: If the goal is CPU parallelism (not isolation), workers are cheaper: same-process threads instead of a whole new V8 heap — the next example. And if the goal is just running `ls`, exec/spawn never needed a second Node at all. fork earns its keep when the child must **stay alive**, hold its own state, and survive independently.

examples.result: The parent logs the child’s pid, receives `sum = 15` over IPC, terminates the child and reports its exit — two cooperating Node processes, no shared memory, one agreed message protocol.

examples.title: Worker threads: keep serving while the CPU grinds

steps.label: Step 1: Why this needs a thread at all
steps.text: fib(40) is ~1.5 billion recursive calls — seconds of pure CPU. On the main thread that is seconds of **every** request stalled (run-to-completion, Section 13.1) — I/O async does not help because this work is not I/O. A Worker is a real OS thread (OSC Chapter 4): it computes on another core while the main loop keeps turning.

steps.label: Step 2: workerData in, postMessage out
steps.text: The `{ n: 40 }` option is **copied** to the worker before it starts (its `workerData`), and `parentPort.postMessage(result)` copies the answer back — the same message-passing discipline as fork, but between threads of one process: no serialization to a pipe, no second interpreter startup, cheaper by an order of magnitude. Errors in the worker surface on `worker.on("error")` instead of crashing the process.

steps.label: Step 3: The heartbeat proves the concurrency
steps.text: Every 500 ms the main thread logs that it is alive — and during the whole computation those lines keep printing at a steady rhythm, because the worker owns the busy stack, not the loop. In a server, the same property reads as “health checks keep answering during heavy work.” Stop the interval when the result arrives (a leftover timer keeps the process alive — Section 16.1’s exit rule).

steps.label: Step 4: postMessage copies — until you share deliberately
steps.text: The default is no shared state: races are impossible because there is nothing to race on. The escape hatch is `SharedArrayBuffer`: pass one to the worker, wrap it in a typed array on both sides, and now the same bytes have two writers — which is exactly when `Atomics` becomes mandatory.

steps.label: Step 5: The Atomics one-liner
steps.text: `Atomics.add(shared, 0, 1)` looks like `shared[0]++`, but the ++ is three instructions — load, add, store — and two threads can interleave them so both increments read the same old value and one is lost: the lost-update race that opens OSC Chapter 6. `Atomics.add` performs the read-modify-write **indivisibly** (the software meaning of the hardware test-and-set/compare-and-swap instructions that chapter teaches). One line, one guarantee — and message passing remains the first choice when a counter is not genuinely shared.

examples.result: “main thread alive” lines print at an even 500 ms cadence while fib(40) computes on another core, then `fib(40) = 102334155` — and the shared counter, if used, increments without a lost update in sight.

keyTakeaways: net.createServer hands you each TCP connection as a Duplex stream: `on("data")` reads, `conn.write` writes — HTTP is a protocol layered on exactly this.
exec runs a shell command and buffers output (1 MB cap; shell-injection risk with user input); spawn streams stdout live with verbatim args (safe); execFile is spawn+buffering.
fork = spawn of a Node script + a built-in IPC channel: `send`/`on("message")` both directions, structured-clone values only — messages, never shared memory.
A forked child is a separate process with its own event loop: crash isolation and supervision (kill/exit codes) — OSC Chapter 3 from JavaScript.
Worker threads are real threads in one process with their own V8 isolate and loop — the fix for CPU-bound work that would starve the event loop; same shape as browser Web Workers (Section 15.12).
postMessage copies (races impossible by construction); SharedArrayBuffer shares (races possible) — and then Atomics.add/load/store/compareExchange are the indivisible operations (OSC Chapter 6).
Decision order: I/O → stay single-threaded (async); CPU-bound → Worker; risky/isolated long-lived work → fork; quick command → exec/spawn.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between exec and spawn?
options: exec is faster because it skips the filesystem
exec runs the command through a shell and buffers all output; spawn takes an argument array (no shell) and streams stdout/stderr live
exec returns a promise; spawn uses callbacks
quiz.explanation: exec = convenience + shell metacharacters (injection risk with user input) + a 1 MB buffer; spawn = verbatim args (safe) + Readable-stream output (unbounded) — pick per output size and input trust.

quiz.q: Why choose fork() rather than spawn() to run another Node script?
options: fork is the only one that can start Node
fork additionally opens a built-in IPC channel — send/on("message") — and targets the same Node executable automatically
fork shares memory with the parent
fork does not create a new process
quiz.explanation: fork = spawn(process.execPath, [script]) plus the message pipe: structured-clone messages both directions with zero wire-format work — spawn would leave you hand-rolling stdin/stdout framing.

quiz.q: A worker thread and the main thread want a shared hit counter. Why `Atomics.add(cell, 0, 1)` instead of `cell[0]++`?
options: ++ is load-add-store and two threads can interleave, losing increments; Atomics.add does the read-modify-write as one indivisible step
cell[0]++ does not work on Int32Array
quiz.explanation: The lost-update race of OSC Chapter 6: non-atomic ++ can have both threads read the same old value; Atomics makes the update indivisible — the JavaScript face of test-and-set/compare-and-swap.

quiz.q: Your HTTP server must run a 4-second image conversion on every upload. What is the right tool?
options: Make the handler async — await makes it concurrent
A worker thread — CPU-bound work off the event loop, leaving the main thread serving requests
Nothing: Node handles CPU work automatically in parallel
quiz.explanation: await only helps I/O (Section 16.2); CPU work blocks the one thread (run-to-completion). A Worker computes on another core while the loop keeps answering requests.

quiz.q: In the net echo server, why can a `"data"` chunk not be treated as one client message?
options: TCP reorders packets, so chunks arrive scrambled
Chunk boundaries reflect transport buffering, not message boundaries — one logical message may straddle several chunks
data events fire only once per connection
Buffers cannot hold a full message
quiz.explanation: TCP preserves byte order but not framing: the 64 KB-ish chunk is an accident of buffering (Section 13.4 at byte level), so protocols add framing — newlines, length prefixes, or JSON per line.

intro: Programs are read far more often than they are written — and read by machines even more than by humans. Two tools close that loop: **ESLint** reads your code without running it and reports the bugs that static analysis can prove (loose equality, assignments in conditions, misspelled variables), while **Prettier** reprints your code in a single canonical style so no human ever debates it again. One finds errors; the other erases bikeshedding. Together they form the floor of every serious JavaScript project.
objectives: Explain what a linter can and cannot detect without executing code
Configure ESLint: rule severities, recommended presets and the flat config file
Recognize the classic violations — loose equality, assignment in conditions, unused and undeclared variables
Justify automatic formatting: why Prettier eliminates an entire class of review noise
Divide the responsibilities: Prettier for layout, ESLint for correctness

concepts.statement: A **linter** parses the source into an AST (the tree of Chapter 14’s metaprogramming world) and walks it looking for **patterns that are always or almost always mistakes** — using an undeclared variable, comparing with `==`, leaving a variable unused, writing code after `return`. It never executes the program, so it finds problems before the first run, in code paths tests never reach.
concepts.detail: The boundary is important: a linter proves things about **all executions** from the text alone, so it cannot catch a wrong algorithm that is syntactically honest — sorting with a broken comparator is invisible to it (that is a job for tests, Section 17.2). Its kills are typos, coercions and dead code: the bugs that hide in plain sight.

concepts.statement: The workhorse rules: **no-undef** (using a variable that was never declared — catches `console.lgo` typos and missing imports), **no-unused-vars** (declared but never read — usually leftover logic), **eqeqeq** (`==` coerces types; `0 == ""` is true), **no-cond-assign** (an `=` typed where `===` was meant in a condition), plus unreachable code, duplicate keys, and suspicious fallthrough.
concepts.detail:
```js
const total = quantity * price;
if (total = 0) { ... }        // no-cond-assign: was === meant?
if (total == "0") { ... }      // eqeqeq: 0 == "" — coercion alert
console.lgo(total);             // no-undef: lgo is not a function of console
```
Each is a program that parses, runs, and quietly misbehaves — which is precisely why a machine should check it.

concepts.statement: ESLint reads a config file — the modern flat config `eslint.config.js` — that lists **rules with severities**: `"off"` (0), `"warn"` (1) and `"error"` (2); errors fail the lint run. You do not write rules from scratch: `js.configs.recommended` is a curated baseline of the rules that catch real bugs, and you override individual rules on top of it.

**Prettier** parses the code (the same AST trick) and reprints it in **one canonical layout** — spacing, line width, quotes, trailing commas, where the line breaks — with almost no options. `prettier --write .` normalizes an entire codebase in one command, and editor-on-save keeps it that way.
concepts.detail: Prettier never interprets: the output is guaranteed semantically identical to the input (same AST modulo formatting), which is why it is safe to run blindly across a repository — and why it deliberately offers only a handful of options (printWidth, semi, singleQuote): the point is to have **no decision left to make**.

concepts.statement: Every hour spent aligning indentation is an hour not spent on the program; every diff polluted with re-indentation hides the one line that actually changed. Formatting is a solved problem with one right answer per project: let the machine apply it, and code review discusses **behavior only** — the entire style category of review comments simply stops existing.
concepts.detail: The diff argument is the underrated one: a file reformatted by hand mixes cosmetic churn with real edits, and human reviewers stop trusting the diff. A canonical format means reformat commits are large, boring, once — and every later diff is semantic.

concepts.statement: Run **Prettier for format, ESLint for correctness**, in that order — and disable ESLint’s stylistic rules entirely (the `eslint-config-prettier` preset does exactly this) so the two tools can never disagree. Wire both into the pipeline: format-on-save in the editor, then `npm run lint` in CI (Section 17.3) so the main branch cannot drift.

examples.title: Three violations that conspire to pay nothing
examples.problem:
This program compiles, runs, and prints `"paid in full"` — while computing a total of zero. Find the three lint-detectable violations and watch them cooperate, then see the exact ESLint report and the minimal fix.
```js
function total(quantity, price) {
  const taxRate = 0.08;              // (2) assigned, never used
  if (quantity = 0) {                // (1) assignment in a condition
    return 0;                        //     ...so this guard is dead
  }
  return quantity * price;           //     and quantity is now 0
}

const paid = total(3, 4);            // 0 — not 12
if (paid == "") {                    // (3) loose equality
  console.log("paid in full");        //     0 == "" is true!
}
```

steps.label: Step 1: Read the intent
steps.text: The author meant: guard against a zero quantity, apply a tax rate, compute the total, and confirm it. Every one of those intentions is present in the text — and every one is broken by a one-character slip that JavaScript happily accepts.

steps.label: Step 2: Violation 1 — `=` where `===` was meant
steps.text: `if (quantity = 0)` **assigns** 0 to quantity and uses the assigned value (0) as the condition — falsy, so the guard never fires. Worse, the side effect stands: `quantity` is 0 from here on, so the return line computes `0 * price`. One character changed control flow **and** data. This is what no-cond-assign exists to flag.

steps.label: Step 3: Violation 2 — the unused taxRate
steps.text: `taxRate` is declared and never read: the calculation below hand-multiplies nothing (the author presumably meant `quantity * price * (1 + taxRate)`). A leftover from a refactor or an unfinished thought, it signals that **this function does not do what its variables claim** — no-unused-vars is a logic smell, not a tidiness one.

steps.label: Step 4: Violation 3 — `==` makes the wrong check pass
steps.text: `paid` is 0, and `0 == ""` is **true**: both operands coerce to the number 0. With the intended `paid === 12`, the check would fail loudly and the bug would surface here. Loose equality did not cause the bug — it **hid** it, which is why eqeqeq is error-severity in most configs.

steps.label: Step 5: The report and the fix

examples.result: ESLint reports all three violations by rule name with file and line; fixing them makes `total(3, 4)` return the taxed total and the confirmation check compare real numbers — a program that was “working” only because two bugs and one coercion cancelled out.

examples.title: Prettier before and after — semantics untouched

steps.label: Step 1: Catalog the mechanical changes
steps.text: Missing semicolons and trailing commas added; spacing normalized around operators and braces; the collapsed `if` exploded to braces and its own lines; the overlong line split at the default 80-character print width; the stray space before the newline removed. Every change is layout — **not one token of meaning moved**.

steps.label: Step 2: Why the output is trustworthy
steps.text: Prettier parses to an AST and **prints** the tree — it never interprets or optimizes, so the output is by construction the same program: same bindings, same expressions, same execution. That guarantee is what makes “format the whole repository” a routine command instead of a code review event.

steps.label: Step 3: What the team gains
steps.text: The next person to touch this file sees the same shapes they see in every other file — curly-brace style, quote style, comma placement are no longer facts about individual authors. Review diffs shrink to semantic changes only, because nobody hand-reformats while editing anymore.

steps.label: Step 4: Where the few knobs are
steps.text: The config is tiny by design — `printWidth`, `tabWidth`, `semi`, `singleQuote`, `trailingComma` — set once in `.prettierrc` and never discussed again. The restriction is the feature: fewer options means fewer arguments, and a single obvious style per codebase. If you find yourself wishing Prettier would indent something differently, that is the moment to let go.

steps.label: Step 5: Wire it into the day
steps.text: Editor format-on-save is the loop that matters — the file is canonical the instant it is written, and nobody runs a formatting command by hand. CI then only needs to check (`prettier --check .`) that nothing bypassed the editor — belt and suspenders, with ESLint handling correctness on the same pipeline stage.

examples.result: Semantically identical code in canonical style — gained in one command, kept by the editor, enforced by CI; the entire topic of “how should this file be formatted” is retired from the project permanently.

keyTakeaways: A linter parses to an AST and reports bug-shaped patterns without executing: it covers all code paths before the first run — but cannot judge algorithms (tests, 17.2).
The money rules: no-undef (typos, missing imports), no-unused-vars (leftover logic), eqeqeq (coercion), no-cond-assign (= vs ===).
Severities are the management model: "off" / "warn" / "error" (0/1/2); start from js.configs.recommended and override deliberately.
Prettier reprints code in one canonical layout with near-zero options — same AST in, same program out, so it is safe to run blindly.
Automatic formatting kills a whole category of review noise and keeps diffs semantic; format-on-save plus a CI check keeps it permanent.
Division of labor: Prettier owns layout, ESLint owns correctness; disable ESLint’s stylistic rules (eslint-config-prettier) so they never fight.

quiz.q: Which bug can a linter NOT detect?
options: A comparison using == where coercion changes the result
A sort comparator that returns the wrong sign, producing wrong order with valid syntax
Using an undeclared variable due to a typo
An assignment typed inside an if condition
quiz.explanation: Linting reasons about the text via the AST; a well-typed, well-formed comparator that implements the wrong ordering is a behavioral bug — the province of unit tests (Section 17.2).

quiz.q: In an ESLint config, what does severity "error" (2) mean?
options: The rule produces a warning that never fails the run
A violation fails the lint command — typically failing CI
quiz.explanation: off/warn/error is the whole policy dial: warnings are visible but survivable; errors make `eslint .` exit non-zero, which is exactly how CI enforces the rules the team agreed on.

quiz.q: Why is `if (paid == "")` worth an eqeqeq error even when it happens to work?
options: == applies type coercion — 0 == "" is true — so the check passes or fails on hidden conversions rather than the values compared
It only works in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Loose equality compares after coercing both sides (Section 3.7): empty string, zero and false collapse together — the comparison’s truth is an accident of conversion rules, not of the data.

quiz.q: What is the correct division of labor between Prettier and ESLint?
options: Prettier owns canonical layout; ESLint owns correctness rules — with stylistic rules disabled so they never conflict
Both must be run manually before every commit
Use either one; they are interchangeable
quiz.explanation: Formatting and correctness are different problems: Prettier prints one canonical style from the AST, ESLint flags bug patterns — keeping each in its lane (eslint-config-prettier) removes the possibility of contradictory rulings.

intro: A test is a tiny program whose job is to fail loudly when your real program is wrong. **Jest** is the de facto standard harness: `describe` groups tests, `it` runs one, `expect(...)` asserts — and its matcher vocabulary plus first-class mocking make asynchronous, dependency-heavy code testable in isolation. This section covers the structure, the one matcher trap everyone hits (`toBe` versus `toEqual`), setup hooks, mocks for network calls, async tests and coverage.
objectives: Structure test suites with describe and it, and assert with expect and matchers
Choose correctly between toBe and toEqual — and explain the object-reference gotcha
Share setup and teardown with beforeEach/afterEach
Replace dependencies with jest.fn() mocks and assert how they were called
Test asynchronous code with awaits and the resolves/rejects matchers, and read coverage output

concepts.term: describe and it: tests as suites
concepts.statement: A test file is a tree of **suites** and **tests**: `describe("cart", () => { it("sums prices", () => { ... }) })`. Each `it` (alias: `test`) is one independently-run unit that passes if every assertion inside holds and fails on the first that does not — and each `it` describes one behavior in its name, so failures read as specifications.

`expect(actual)` wraps a value and hands it to a **matcher** that decides pass/fail and prints the diff when it fails. The core: `toBe` (identity), `toEqual` (deep equality), `toStrictEqual` (deep + type + undefined-keys), plus the specialists:
```js
expect(n).toBeCloseTo(0.3, 5);    // floating point
expect(s).toMatch(/err/);          // regex on strings
expect(arr).toContain("x");        // array membership
expect(arr).toHaveLength(3);       // .length of anything
expect(fn).toThrow("boom");         // sync throw
expect(obj).toHaveProperty("a.b"); // nested path
expect(obj).toMatchObject({ a: 1 });// partial deep match
```
concepts.detail: Choosing the specialist over a hand-rolled check is not pedantry: the matcher’s **failure message** is the product. `toHaveLength(3)` failing prints “expected length 3, received 5” — your `expect(arr.length).toBe(3)` prints nearly the same, but `toCloseTo` on floats replaces an always-wrong `toBe(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)` with an honest tolerance.

concepts.term: toBe versus toEqual: the classic gotcha
concepts.statement: `toBe` is **identity** — the same rule as `===` (via Object.is): two objects with identical contents are **not** the same object, because variables hold references (Sections 3.6 and 6.1). `toEqual` is **deep equality** — it recursively compares contents. Use `toBe` for primitives, `toEqual` for anything made with `{}` or `[]` — the error Jest prints for an equal-looking pair is famously confusing: *“Received: serializes to the same string.”*
concepts.detail:
```js
const a = { x: 1 };
const b = { x: 1 };       // same content, different object
expect(b).toBe(a);        // FAILS — different references
expect(b).toEqual(a);     // passes — deep compare
expect(b === a).toBe(false); // the language agrees
```
And the mirror-image trap: `toEqual` also passes when a function accidentally returns a *fresh copy* — if identity matters (same object, not a clone), reach for toBe or toStrictEqual.

concepts.statement: Hooks run around each test in their suite: **beforeEach** builds a fresh fixture (a new cart, a new temp directory), **afterEach** tears it down; **beforeAll/afterAll** run once per suite for expensive shared setup. The rule: tests must not depend on each other — order should never matter.

`jest.fn()` creates a **mock function**: a callable that records every call (arguments, order, results) and returns whatever you program — `mockReturnValue(v)`, `mockResolvedValue(p)` for promises, or `mockImplementation(fn)` for full behavior. The unit under test uses it in place of a real dependency, and the test then asserts **how it was called**: `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)`, `toHaveBeenCalledWith(args)`.
concepts.detail: Why mock at all: a real network call is slow (milliseconds vs microseconds), flaky (the third-party’s bad day becomes your red build), and ordered (test A’s POST changes what test B sees). A mock makes each test **deterministic and hermetic** — and lets you simulate the failure paths (a 500, a timeout) that a real service would never politely provide on demand.

concepts.statement: Jest waits on whatever a test returns: **return or await the promise**, and the assertion runs after settlement. For failures, the `resolves`/`rejects` matchers await a promise and match its settlement: `await expect(p).resolves.toBe(42)`, `await expect(p).rejects.toThrow("x")` — no try/catch scaffolding, and a promise that never settles fails on timeout rather than silently passing.

concepts.term: Coverage: what ran, not what is right
concepts.statement: `jest --coverage` instruments the source and reports the percentage of **statements, branches, functions and lines** executed by the tests, per file. It is a map of untested territory — a branch never taken is a behavior never checked — but 100% coverage proves only that every line **ran**, not that the outcomes were asserted.
concepts.detail: Read coverage as a floor, not a goal: a test with no assertions executes code all day long. The numbers to care about are the uncovered ones — an uncovered error handler is a bug shipping with no net. And note the asymmetry with linting (17.1): coverage is measured by running; that is exactly why it cannot be checked statically.

examples.title: The toBe/toEqual gotcha, demonstrated and diagnosed

steps.label: Step 1: A JSON round trip builds a genuinely new object
steps.text: `JSON.stringify` walks the object into text; `JSON.parse` walks it back into **fresh objects** — every array and nested object is new storage. Content survives; identity does not (Chapter 11.5’s serialization boundary).

steps.label: Step 2: Assertion (a) — deep equality passes
steps.text: toEqual recursively compares: same keys, same array elements, same primitives — the clone **equals** the cart in the sense a person means. This is the right matcher for “did I build the thing correctly?”

steps.label: Step 3: Assertion (b) — identity fails, with the infamous message
Step 4: Assertions (c) and (d) — state the real intent
steps.text: If the test’s point is “it is a copy, mutations do not leak back”, assert that: `(c)` the language-level `clone === cart` is `false`, and (stronger) `expect(clone.items).not.toBe(cart.items)` — the **nested** arrays are distinct too, so pushing to `clone.items` leaves `cart.items` alone. `(d)` confirms the copy is faithful.
