Identity assertions and equality assertions together say everything: same shape, different storage.

steps.label: Step 5: The rule you keep
steps.text: Primitives (numbers, strings, booleans, symbols): `toBe`. Objects and arrays: `toEqual` (or `toStrictEqual` when `undefined`-valued keys and class mismatches matter). When a toBe fails with “serializes to the same string”, it is this section happening to you — and if identity genuinely matters (caching, memoization), keep it and document why.

examples.result: Test 1 fails on the toBe with “Received: serializes to the same string” while its toEqual passes; test 2 passes both assertions — clone and cart are equal in content and distinct in identity, which is exactly what a deep copy promises.

examples.title: Mocking a fetch wrapper — plus async tests and coverage

steps.label: Step 1: Replace the dependency, not the unit
steps.text: The unit is `getUser` — its URL building, its `res.ok` policy, its parse. The dependency is `fetch`. Assigning `global.fetch = jest.fn()` swaps the dependency for a recording stand-in: every call the wrapper makes is captured (arguments, count, order), and the wrapper itself runs its real code. `beforeEach` re-creates the mock per test, so call counts from one test never leak into the next (fresh fixtures).

steps.label: Step 2: Program the happy path
steps.text: `mockResolvedValue` makes the mock return a promise (Section 13.2 vocabulary) — so `await fetch(...)` inside the wrapper settles with the fake Response `{ok: true, json: ...}`. Note `json` is itself an async function returning a promise: the wrapper’s second await (`return res.json()`) must also be fed. The mock models exactly the shape the real API offers — an object with ok and a json() method — nothing more.

steps.label: Step 3: Assert the call, then the result
steps.text: Two kinds of assertion: **interaction** (`toHaveBeenCalledWith("/api/users/7")` — the wrapper called the dependency with the right argument, once) and **outcome** (`user` deep-equals the parsed object). Both matter: a wrapper that fetches the wrong URL but happens to return a hand-built object passes only the outcome — the interaction assertion is what makes the test mean “this wrapper talks to that API”.

steps.label: Step 4: The failure path, with zero try/catch
steps.text: The second test programs `{ok: false, status: 404}` and awaits `rejects.toThrow("HTTP 404")` — the matcher awaits the promise, expects a rejection, and matches the message (Section 13.2’s rejection, asserted without scaffolding). This is the determinism mocks buy: a 404 on demand, every run, in milliseconds — the real server would offer it only on its own schedule.

steps.label: Step 5: Read the coverage, know its limits

examples.result: Two green tests: the wrapper fetches the right URL once and returns the parsed user; it rejects with a status-bearing message on 4xx — in milliseconds, offline, deterministically — and coverage confirms both branches ran.

keyTakeaways: Suites are describe/it trees; one behavior per it, named as a sentence — failures should read like a broken spec.

toBe is identity (=== via Object.is) — wrong for equal-content objects; toEqual is deep equality (toStrictEqual adds type and undefined-key strictness); the tell “Received: serializes to the same string” means two equal-looking but distinct objects hit a toBe.
Use specialists for better failure messages: toBeCloseTo (floats), toMatch, toContain, toHaveLength, toThrow, toMatchObject, toHaveProperty.
beforeEach builds fresh fixtures so tests are order-independent; jest.fn() replaces dependencies with recording doubles — mockResolvedValue for promises.
Assert interactions AND outcomes: toHaveBeenCalledWith checks the contract, toEqual checks the result.
Async: await the work or return the promise; rejects/resolves match settlement without try/catch — never let a test finish before its promises do.
Coverage maps what ran (statements/branches/functions/lines) — a floor for finding untested code, not proof of correctness.

quiz.q: `const a = {x: 1}; const b = {x: 1};` — which assertion passes?
quiz.explanation: Two object literals are two objects: === (and toBe) compares references and fails; toEqual compares contents recursively and passes — the copy/clone gotcha in one line.

quiz.q: Why does Jest print “Received: serializes to the same string” for a failing toBe?
options: The objects are circular and cannot be printed
The two values print identically but are different objects — an identity comparison failed, so toEqual was probably meant
Jest cannot stringify objects with methods
quiz.explanation: toBe is === for objects: equal-looking content, distinct identity. The message is Jest diagnosing the classic gotcha for you — the values differ only in being two separate allocations.

quiz.q: When does the beforeEach hook run?
options: Before every it() in its describe block — each test gets a fresh fixture
quiz.explanation: Per-test setup is what keeps tests order-independent: every it starts from the same known state, so failures point at behavior, not at which tests happened to run first.

quiz.q: Why replace fetch with jest.fn() in unit tests?
options: To make the tests run in a browser
For determinism and speed: no network latency, no third-party outages, and failure paths (404, 500) programmable on demand — while asserting how the unit called it
Because fetch is not part of JavaScript
quiz.explanation: Mocks make tests hermetic and fast and record the interaction (toHaveBeenCalledWith) — the real dependency’s mood swings stop being your build’s mood swings.

quiz.q: What does 100% branch coverage prove?
options: Every assertion passed and the code is correct
Every branch was executed by the tests — not that every outcome was asserted or is correct
The tests run in under a second
quiz.explanation: Coverage is an execution map: it finds untested territory, but assertions are what decide pass/fail — a test with no expects covers code while proving nothing.

options: S, because the runner verifies comments
T, because printed output fails the build on mismatch
S and T are both equivalent to R
R, because it states an assertion the runner executes and reports
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is one real test case, one prose comment, and one manual print of the same computation. Step 2: The governing rule is that a test is a tiny program that fails loudly: `test()` registers a case, `expect().toBe()` asserts a value, and the runner executes every case and reports passes and failures. Step 3: Tracing each proposal, R runs the function, compares against `10`, and reports the verdict; S is never executed as a check; T displays a number no tool compares. Step 4: The distractors fail because comments assert nothing, console output passes regardless of content, and only the assertion form connects the computation to a verdict. Step 5: Therefore the assertion form is the intended Jest usage.

intro: JavaScript ships as **packages** — units of reusable code identified by name and version — and arrives in browsers as **bundles**. `npm` is the package manager at the center: `package.json` declares what you depend on, **semantic versioning** decides how much change you accept, and the **lockfile** pins exactly what you got. Bundlers then assemble those modules (and tree-shake what you never use) into deployable output. One file, one manifest, one build — this section reads them all.
objectives: Read and write package.json: metadata, scripts and the three dependency kinds
Explain semantic versioning and the meaning of ^, ~ and exact versions
Determine exactly which versions a range such as ^2.3.1 accepts
Use npx to run project tools without global installs, and explain lockfiles
Explain what bundlers do, how tree-shaking works, and what HMR buys the dev loop

concepts.statement: `package.json` is a project’s manifest: identity (`name`, `version`, `type`), the **scripts** that build/test/run it, and the dependency lists that npm installs. Everything npm and the toolchain know about your project starts here — a repo is not “an npm project” until this file exists.

The `scripts` map names shell commands: `npm test`, `npm run lint`, `npm start` (start/test have shortcuts). `npm run <name>` executes the command with `node_modules/.bin` on the PATH, so locally-installed tools run **without global installs or ./node_modules prefixes** — the entire team (and CI) shares one interface to the project.
concepts.detail: Adding a tool later means adding one script line, and every consumer — a teammate, a CI pipeline, a Makefile wrapper — uses the same name. Pre/post conventions (`pretest`) run hooks around them; the discipline is that “how do I run the tests” should always have the same one-word answer.

concepts.statement: **dependencies** are needed **at runtime** (marked renders markdown when your server runs). **devDependencies** are needed to **build and test** (jest, eslint, prettier, typescript). **peerDependencies** are things the **host must provide** — a React component library declares react as a peer, so the app’s single React is used instead of the library smuggling in a second copy.
concepts.detail: The split matters most when you publish: `npm install` on your package pulls its dependencies but **not** its devDependencies — consumers get the runtime needs, never your test tools. For an application (never published) the distinction is bookkeeping; for a library it is a contract. `npm i -D jest` writes to devDependencies.

concepts.statement: A version is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`: **PATCH** for bug fixes, **MINOR** for backward-compatible additions, **MAJOR** for breaking changes. A range says how far you trust: **`^2.3.1`** accepts changes that keep the leftmost nonzero component — `>=2.3.1 <3.0.0`; **`~2.3.1`** allows patch-level only — `>=2.3.1 <2.4.0`; a bare **`2.3.1`** pins exactly.
concepts.detail: The trust model behind ^: “bug fixes and new features, but never a breaking change” — exactly what semver promises within a major. The exception that proves the rule: **`^0.3.1` means `>=0.3.1 <0.4.0`**, because 0.x is the unstable band where the **minor** plays the breaking role. `npm install pkg` writes `^` by default — you opt into trust unless you pin.

concepts.statement: `package-lock.json` records the **exact resolved tree** — every package, every transitive dependency, every checksum — from the last successful install. `npm ci` installs from it verbatim: byte-identical node_modules on your machine, your teammate’s machine and CI. Without it, two installs of `^2.3.1` on different days can silently differ.
concepts.detail: Ranges are declarations of intent; the lockfile is a record of fact. The workflow: range bumps come with dependency updates (a deliberate, reviewable commit that updates the lockfile); automatic upgrades never happen by accident. Commit the lockfile — for applications it is as much source code as anything in src/.

concepts.statement: `npx <command>` finds the named binary: in the project’s `node_modules/.bin` first, or — if it is not there — downloads a temporary copy and runs it, no global install. `npx create-next-app myapp` bootstraps a project with a tool you never meant to keep; `npx jest` runs the project’s exact local version.
concepts.detail: The global-install habit it replaces: `npm install -g some-tool` puts a version on your machine that shadows or clashes with each project’s own. npx prefers the local one — so the same command name runs the version the lockfile says, per project, per machine.

concepts.term: Bundlers: from modules to deployable output
concepts.statement: A **bundler** starts at an entry file, follows every `import` recursively through the module graph (Chapter 10), and emits **one or a few output files** containing the whole program — with transforms applied (Babel, Section 17.4) and unreferenced exports dropped. webpack is the classic; Rollup, Parcel and the fast newcomers (esbuild, Vite) share the model.
concepts.detail: Why bundle at all: fewer requests over HTTP/1.1, one minified artifact to cache and deploy, and — most importantly today — a build step where the whole toolchain (transpilation, JSX, CSS modules) plugs in. The dev server (below) is what makes the bundler feel instant during development.

concepts.statement: Because ES module `import`/`export` are **static** — analyzable from the text without running the code (Section 10.3) — a bundler can compute which exports are reachable from the entry and **omit the rest**. Import one function from a 200-export utility library and the bundle contains that function’s code, not the library’s whole file.
concepts.detail: The reachability walk is mark-and-sweep over the module graph: mark every import and every export those modules actually use; sweep away unmarked declarations. Two things defeat it: **side effects** at module top level (the safest assumption is to keep code that might do something — package.json’s `"sideEffects": false` is the library promising it is pure) and **CommonJS** `require`, which is a runtime function call no static analysis can see — the reason tree-shaking needs ES modules.

concepts.statement: A bundler’s dev server watches source files; on save it rebuilds **only the changed module** and swaps it into the running app — **hot module replacement** — without a full page reload, preserving application state in the process (React Fast Refresh keeps component state across edits). The edit-to-see loop drops from seconds to milliseconds.
concepts.detail: Underneath it is Section 16.5’s `fs.watch`: file changes fire events, the watcher debounces them, and the server pushes an update over a websocket. The production build remains the full optimized bundle — HMR is the development-mode experience, which is precisely what makes iterating in a big bundled codebase feel like editing one small file.

examples.title: What does ^2.3.1 actually accept?
examples.problem:
Your package.json says `"leftpad": "^2.3.1"`. For each candidate release — 2.3.0, 2.3.1, 2.3.7, 2.4.0, 2.9.99, 3.0.0 — decide whether `npm update` would install it, then state the range in inequalities and compare with ~2.3.1.
```js
"leftpad": "^2.3.1"   // resolves to: >=2.3.1 <3.0.0
"leftpad": "~2.3.1"   // resolves to: >=2.3.1 <2.4.0
"leftpad": "2.3.1"    // resolves to: exactly 2.3.1
```

steps.label: Step 1: Expand the caret
steps.text: `^2.3.1` locks the **leftmost nonzero component** — the major, 2 — and lets everything to its right float: the range is `>=2.3.1 <3.0.0`. The floor is the written version (nothing older than you asked for); the ceiling is the next major (nothing semver promises to be compatible with).

steps.label: Step 2: Walk the candidates against the floor
steps.text: **2.3.0** is below the floor — rejected (it is older than the version you named). **2.3.1** and **2.3.7** — patches — accepted: semver says patches are bug fixes only. **2.4.0** and **2.9.99** — minors — accepted: backward-compatible additions, which is the trust `^` expresses. **3.0.0** — rejected: the ceiling is exclusive, and a new major is allowed to break you.

steps.label: Step 3: Compare the tilde
steps.text: `~2.3.1` stops at the minor: `>=2.3.1 <2.4.0`. So 2.3.7 yes, 2.4.0 no — **patch-level trust only**. Choose it when a dependency’s minors have historically brought risk, or for teammates of stability-critical builds; the price is forgoing backward-compatible features until you bump deliberately.

steps.label: Step 4: The zero-band exception
steps.text: Run the same expansion on `^0.3.1` and the leftmost **nonzero** component is the 3, not the 0: the range is `>=0.3.1 <0.4.0`. Zero-major versions declare “unstable — the minor may break,” so the caret conservatively treats it like a major. Same rule, different anchor — and the reason 0.x caret ranges surprise people.

steps.label: Step 5: Where the decision actually lands
steps.text: The range only decides what `npm update` **may** fetch; the lockfile records what it **did** fetch. If the lockfile says 2.7.4, every install is 2.7.4 even after 2.8.0 ships — upgrades happen when you re-resolve and commit the new lockfile. The range is policy; the lockfile is fact; CI runs `npm ci` on the fact.

examples.result: ^2.3.1 accepts 2.3.1, 2.3.7, 2.4.0 and 2.9.99; rejects 2.3.0 (below floor) and 3.0.0 (at ceiling — exclusive) — while ~2.3.1 would additionally reject 2.4.0 and 2.9.99.

examples.title: Tree-shaking, traced through the module graph

steps.label: Step 1: The entry marks its imports
steps.text: The bundler parses `main.js`, finds the static `import { used }`, and marks the export `used` as **reachable**. The word “static” is doing the work: an ES import is a declaration the parser can see (Section 10.3), not a runtime value — no execution is needed to know who wants what.

steps.label: Step 2: Mark-and-sweep decides what survives
steps.text: In `math.js`, `used` is marked; `unused` is not — and nothing else references it either. The sweep drops it: the emitted bundle contains only the arithmetic of `used` (inlined to `x => x + 1` by the minifier). Scale that to a 200-export library and one import costs bytes, not kilobytes.

steps.label: Step 3: Break it with a side effect
steps.text: Add `console.log("math.js loaded")` at the top of math.js and shake again: the log **survives**, and so may anything the bundler cannot prove pure around it. Top-level code runs for its effects — dropping it changes the program. The escape is the library’s declaration `"sideEffects": false` in its package.json: a promise that its modules are pure, restoring the aggressive drop.

steps.label: Step 4: Break it with CommonJS
steps.text: Rewrite math.js as `exports.unused = function (x) { return x * 2; }; exports.used = ...` — a `require`-world module. Now what lands on `exports` is decided by **runtime** code paths (loops, conditionals, dynamic keys); the static walk is blind, and the safe output is the whole module. This is the tree-shaking argument for ES modules (Section 10.3) over CommonJS (10.2) in one example — reachability analysis needs syntax that declares itself.

steps.label: Step 5: Confirm the result empirically
steps.text: The honest check is bundle size: build with the import commented out, build with it present — the delta is the true cost of that one function. Two builds, one subtraction, no trust in anyone’s tree-shaking claims — and if the delta is the whole library, the import is dynamic (`import()`), the module has side effects, or the package ships CommonJS.

examples.result: One import of one function yields a bundle containing exactly that function’s code — until a side effect or a CommonJS export forces the conservative fallback; the mechanism throughout is static reachability over the ES module graph.

keyTakeaways: package.json is the manifest — identity, scripts (npm run/test/start) and dependency lists; scripts put node_modules/.bin on the PATH so tools run without global installs.
dependencies = runtime; devDependencies = build/test (never installed by consumers); peerDependencies = provided by the host (one React, not two).

Semver: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH = breaking / compatible-additions / fixes; ^2.3.1 accepts >=2.3.1 <3.0.0 and ~2.3.1 stops at <2.4.0 — and because the caret locks the leftmost NONZERO component, ^0.3.1 stops at 0.4.0 (the 0.x band treats minors as breaking).
The lockfile records the exact resolved tree; npm ci reproduces it byte-for-byte — ranges are policy, the lockfile is fact, and it belongs in version control.
npx runs local-or-temporary binaries — the project’s locked version, no global installs.
Bundlers follow the static ES import graph from an entry into deployable output; tree-shaking is mark-and-sweep reachability — defeated by side effects and by CommonJS.
HMR (atop fs.watch, Section 16.5) swaps just the changed module, preserving state — the dev-loop payoff that made bundlers universal.

quiz.q: Which release will `npm update` NOT install for the range `^2.3.1`?
quiz.explanation: The caret range is >=2.3.1 <3.0.0 — a new major is the ceiling and it is exclusive: semver allows it to break, which is exactly what the range declines to trust.

quiz.q: Jest appears under which key in package.json for an application you will not publish?
options: devDependencies — it builds and tests the project but is not needed to run it
optionalDependencies — it is nice to have
quiz.explanation: Jest is a tool: needed to develop and verify, not to execute the shipped program — the devDependencies slot, which also keeps it (and its transitive weight) out of consumers’ installs if you ever publish.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of peerDependencies in a React component library?
options: To install two copies of React for redundancy
To declare that the host application must supply React — so the library shares the app’s single instance instead of bundling its own
To mark dependencies that failed to install
quiz.explanation: Two Reacts in one page means two reconcilers fighting over one DOM — peers let the library demand the host’s copy and interoperate with its hooks and context.

quiz.q: Why does tree-shaking work with ES modules but hardly at all with CommonJS?
options: ES import/export are static — analyzable from the source without running it — while CommonJS require/exports are runtime values the analyzer cannot see through
quiz.explanation: Reachability analysis needs to know who-uses-what before execution: the ES import declaration provides that statically; a require call is just a function whose result is decided at runtime (Sections 10.2 vs 10.3).

quiz.q: What does the lockfile guarantee that package.json ranges do not?
options: The exact, checksummed version of every package (including transitive ones) — reproducible installs across machines and CI
That no dependency ever needs updating
quiz.explanation: A range like ^2.3.1 resolves differently on different days; the lockfile freezes what was actually resolved, so npm ci installs the identical tree everywhere until someone deliberately updates it.

intro: Modern JavaScript runs on ancient browsers — because **Babel** rewrites it first. Babel is a **transpiler**: a source-to-source compiler that parses your ES2024-era code and emits equivalent code in an older dialect, driven by a list of target environments. Its companion trick is the **polyfill**: when the missing piece is a runtime method rather than syntax, you cannot rewrite your way out and must install the behavior instead. Knowing which problem you have — syntax or behavior — is the whole skill.
objectives: Distinguish transpilation (syntax, compile-time) from polyfilling (behavior, runtime)
Configure @babel/preset-env with browser targets through browserslist
Predict how modern syntax — optional chaining — compiles to older JavaScript, and why Babel’s real output caches the intermediate value
Know what Babel cannot do (missing built-ins) and what to import instead

concepts.statement: **Transpilation** is compiling one high-level language into another high-level language: Babel parses modern JavaScript into an AST (the same metaprogramming machinery as Chapter 14), transforms the tree — replacing newer syntax with equivalent older syntax — and prints JavaScript back out. Input and output are the same language, just different dialects.
concepts.detail: The direction is always “new syntax → old syntax”: arrow functions become `function` expressions, classes become constructor functions, template literals become concatenation. Output readability is not a goal — nobody edits it; it exists to run where the source cannot.

concepts.term: Syntax versus behavior: transpile versus polyfill
concepts.statement: A language feature is either **syntax** (`?.`, `??`, classes — a form the parser must understand) or **behavior** (`Array.prototype.flat`, `Promise`, `Object.entries` — methods and objects the runtime must provide). Babel fixes the first by rewriting; the second needs a **polyfill** — a library that installs the missing method if it is absent: `if (!Array.prototype.includes) { Array.prototype.includes = function... }`.
concepts.detail:
```js
// syntax — Babel rewrites it at build time:
const street = user?.address?.street;         // ES2020 in
const street = user == null ? void 0 : ...;   // ES5 out

// behavior — only a polyfill can provide it:
[1, 2, 3].includes(2);   // method call: identical syntax in ES5 and ES2020
```
A method call looks the same in every dialect — there is nothing to rewrite; either the method exists at runtime or your program throws. The classification question — “syntax or behavior?” — decides the whole toolchain.

concepts.statement: A **preset** is a curated bundle of plugins; **preset-env** is the meta-preset: given your target environments, it enables **exactly the transforms those targets need** and no more. Modern browsers get (nearly) a no-op build; a legacy-supporting build gets the full translation — one config, two correct outputs.

Targets are written as **browserslist** queries — a shared mini-language used by Babel, Autoprefixer and more: `"> 0.25%, not dead"` (browsers with >0.25% share, excluding unmaintained ones), `"defaults"`, `"last 2 versions"`, `"node 18"`. The same string steers every tool in the chain.
concepts.detail: The query **is** the product decision: every target you add is older syntax in everyone’s bundle. “not dead” excludes browsers that no longer receive security updates; a corporate build may need `ie 11` — which is precisely when preset-env earns its keep, and when bundle sizes climb.

concepts.statement: Babel runs as a build step: `@babel/cli` for direct invocation (`babel src -d lib`), but more commonly as the transform stage inside the bundler (Section 17.3’s loader pipeline), or — for JSX — inside the framework’s own toolchain (Section 17.5). `@babel/core` is the engine; plugins are individual transforms; presets are plugin bundles.
concepts.detail: The division: @babel/core parses and prints; plugins each do one transform; preset-env picks plugins from targets. Fast Rust-based transpilers (esbuild, SWC) increasingly replace Babel for speed while keeping the same conceptual model — targets in, equivalent older syntax out — so the vocabulary here outlives the tool.

examples.title: Optional chaining, compiled by hand

steps.label: Step 1: What the ?. promise is
steps.text: For `a?.b`: if `a` is null or undefined, the **entire chain short-circuits to undefined** — `a.b` is never evaluated, and neither is anything after it. Two semantics in one operator: a null test and a skip. That is what must survive every compile.

steps.label: Step 2: The `== null` idiom — both nulls in one test
steps.text: The hand-compiled test is `user == null` — the one place loose equality remains idiomatic: it is true for **both** `null` and `undefined` (Section 3.7). Note the tension with Section 17.1’s eqeqeq — ESLint configs commonly carve out exactly this pattern (`{ "eqeqeq": ["error", "always", { "null": "ignore" }] }`).

steps.label: Step 3: void 0 — undefined, spelled safely
steps.text: Babel writes `void 0` where the hand version wrote `undefined`: `void 0` evaluates to undefined, is shorter to emit, and — in pre-ES5 code where `undefined` was a writable global — could not be tampered with. Today it is belt-and-suspenders history, but you will meet it constantly in compiled output, so read it as `undefined`.

steps.label: Step 4: Why Babel’s real output uses a temp variable
steps.text: The hand version evaluates `user.address` **twice** — once in the null test, once in the access. If `address` were a getter with side effects (a log line, a counter), the hand compile would run it twice and change the program. Babel instead reads `user.address` once into a temp variable and tests that — output that preserves semantics **including** evaluation counts, which is the entire difference between “looks right” and “is right”.

steps.label: Step 5: preset-env would not even blink here
steps.text: Point the same config at modern Chrome and none of this happens: `?.` is supported natively, so preset-env leaves the line untouched. One target list (`ie 11` present or absent) is the difference between a no-op build and the ternary cascade — targets, not effort, decide the output.

examples.result: The chain compiles to nested null-guarded ternaries that short-circuit to undefined — with Babel’s real output caching each intermediate access in a temp variable so getters never run twice, and modern targets skipping the transform entirely.

examples.title: The polyfill side: what no syntax rewrite can fix

steps.label: Step 1: Classify by “does the parser care?”
steps.text: `items.length ?? 0` is a form the parser must understand — **syntax**: Babel rewrites it (to a ternary testing `== null`, the previous example’s machinery). `[1,2,3].includes(2)` parses identically in ES5 and ES2020 — it is a **behavior** question: does the runtime provide the method? Nothing to rewrite; either it is there or it is not.

steps.label: Step 2: A polyfill is a feature-detecting installer
steps.text: The canonical shape is the `if (!Array.prototype.includes)` guard: check whether the platform already provides it, and only then patch it in. That is why polyfills are safe on modern runtimes — they self-verify and do nothing — and why they must be loaded **before** first use.

steps.label: Step 3: The core-js library is the polyfill catalog
steps.text: You do not hand-write these — **core-js** (with regenerator-runtime for generators) implements the whole standard library for old environments. `useBuiltIns: "usage"` in preset-env scans your code for used features (`includes`, `Promise`, `entries`), and injects `import "core-js/..."` only for the ones your targets actually lack: the include list, computed per build.

steps.label: Step 4: What each mechanism costs
steps.text: Syntax transforms cost **bytes always** (the ternary is larger than the `?.`) and zero runtime — dead weight on modern browsers you chose to support. Polyfills cost **bytes conditionally** (only for the features used and missing) and a load-order discipline. Both costs are your targets list itemized — the browserslist string from the previous concept, priced.

steps.label: Step 5: The modern footnote
steps.text: Today `?.`, `??` and classes run natively for >95% of users, so many projects transpile almost nothing and ship the source — but the syntax/behavior split never retires: every new standard feature (array grouping, temporal) re-asks the question, and the answer is always “transform if syntax, polyfill if behavior, targets decide.”

examples.result: Syntax gets rewritten at build time; behaviors get installed at runtime via feature-detecting polyfills (core-js, auto-injected per usage); the targets list is the single knob that prices both.

keyTakeaways: Babel is a source-to-source compiler: modern syntax in, equivalent older syntax out — driven entirely by the target environment list.
The classification question: syntax (parser must know it — classes, ?, ??) → transpile; behavior (runtime must provide it — includes, Promise, entries) → polyfill.
A polyfill feature-detects and installs missing methods/objects only when absent — safe everywhere, required before first use.
preset-env + browserslist targets select exactly the transforms needed; useBuiltIns: "usage" + core-js injects only the polyfills your code actually uses.
Compiled output idioms: `== null` tests both nulls (the eqeqeq-sanctioned exception), `void 0` is undefined, temp variables cache property reads so getters never run twice.
Targets are the product decision: every browser supported is older syntax and more polyfill in everyone’s bundle.

quiz.q: Which feature can Babel transpile, and which needs a polyfill?
options: Neither — both require a newer browser
quiz.explanation: Nullish coalescing is a form the parser must understand — rewritable into a ternary. flat is a method: the call syntax is identical in every era, so the only fix is installing the method at runtime when it is missing.

quiz.q: Why does Babel’s compiled optional chaining store `user.address` in a temporary variable?
options: To avoid evaluating the property twice — a getter with side effects must run exactly once, as in the source
Because var cannot hold member expressions
It is a legacy artifact with no purpose
quiz.explanation: The naïve rewrite tests and then accesses user.address — two evaluations where the source had one. The temp preserves evaluation counts: the difference between “looks equivalent” and “is equivalent.”

quiz.q: What does `void 0` mean in Babel output?
options: undefined — an expression that evaluates to undefined and cannot be shadowed
A placeholder for a to-be-computed value
quiz.explanation: void always yields undefined; void 0 is the canonical spelling that pre-ES5 code needed when the undefined global was writable — compiled output still uses it as a safe, short undefined.

quiz.q: What does `useBuiltIns: "usage"` do in a preset-env config?
options: Scans the code for used standard-library features and injects core-js polyfill imports only for those the targets lack
quiz.explanation: It automates the polyfill classification: used features, missing on the declared targets, get imported from core-js — nothing unused, nothing redundant, per build.

intro: **JSX** is the most successful JavaScript extension ever shipped: HTML-looking tags that are actually **expressions** — compiled away before the browser ever sees them. A JSX element looks like markup and behaves like a function call that returns a plain object describing UI; React is one consumer of that idea, and the compile step (Babel, Section 17.4) is what dissolves the syntax into ordinary JavaScript. This section hand-compiles JSX until the illusion is fully dispelled: you will see exactly what the tags become.
objectives: Explain what JSX is — a compiled extension, not part of ECMAScript — and why it cannot run unparsed
Hand-compile JSX to React.createElement calls and to the automatic JSX runtime
Apply the rules: single root, JavaScript only inside {}, className for class, capitalized components, closed tags
Treat elements as data: building them in expressions, loops and arrays

concepts.term: JSX: markup that is an expression
concepts.statement:
**JSX** extends the expression grammar with tags: `
hi
` is a single **expression** whose value is an object describing the element — the tag, its props and its children. It is not standard ECMAScript: without a compile step (Babel or TypeScript) that rewrites the tags into function calls, a Node process handed this file is a **SyntaxError** at line one.
concepts.detail: The illusion is the point: UI code is nested and visual, and tags let the source read like the tree it builds. But every construct in JSX maps to something you already know — function calls, objects, arrays — which is what makes hand-compiling it (the worked example) both possible and enlightening.

concepts.statement:
The classic transform maps each tag to `React.createElement(type, props, ...children)`: `
  • {label}
    • ` becomes `React.createElement("li", { key: id }, label)`. The modern **automatic runtime** instead injects `import { jsx } from "react/jsx-runtime"` and emits `jsx("li", { key: id, children: label })` — no React import required in your file.

Four compile-blocking or bug-causing rules: (1) **one root element** — wrap siblings in a fragment `<>...`; (2) **JavaScript goes in braces** `{expr}` — attributes and children both — because bare text is literal text; (3) **close every tag** (``, `
`) — no HTML-style tag omission; (4) the attribute for CSS classes is **className**, because `class` is a reserved word in the expression position.
concepts.detail: Plus the naming law: a lowercase tag means an HTML/host element (the string `"div"` goes to the renderer); a **capitalized** tag means a component — an identifier the compiled call references: `<ItemList/>` compiles to `createElement(ItemList, ...)`, so the variable must be in scope. Rename it to `itemList` and it compiles to a call with the string `"itemList"` — the classic silent break.

concepts.statement: Everything inside `{}` is one **expression** — a value: `{items.map(...)}`, `{count > 0 ? "yes" : "no"}`, `{style}`. There are no `if` statements and no `for` loops inside JSX braces: the tools are the conditional operators and the array methods of Chapters 4 and 7 — `map` to make child lists, ternaries and `&&` to choose between pieces.

A JSX element evaluates to a **plain, immutable object** — a description (`{type: "li", props: {...}}`), not a DOM node. You can store elements in variables and arrays, pass them as props, build them inside loops and functions (Chapter 8’s functions-as-values), and create thousands without touching the document — rendering is a separate act performed by the framework.
concepts.detail: This is the mental unlock of declarative UI: the markup describes **what** should exist; the reconciler diffs that description against the screen and performs the **how**. `key` — the next example’s map prop — is a hint to that diffing algorithm, not a prop your component receives: it identifies which array item is which across reorderings.

examples.title: Hand-compiling a list component

steps.label: Step 1: The outer tag is a call with a props object
Step 2: Children are extra arguments, nested calls
steps.text:
```js
    { className: "item-list" },
    React.createElement("h2", null, "Items"),
    React.createElement("ul", null, /* the mapped lis */)
```
The two child elements (`<h2>` and `<ul>`) become **third and fourth arguments** — and they are themselves `createElement` calls. Nesting tags is nesting calls: the markup tree and the call tree have the same shape. `null` is the empty props of the `<h2>`.

steps.label: Step 3: Braces become the expression, verbatim
steps.text:
The `{items.map(item =>
  • {item.label}
    • )}` compiles to the **same expression** in the children position: ```js items.map((item) => React.createElement("li", { key: item.id }, item.label) ) ``` Nothing happened to the map — JSX compiled its **body** (the `
  • ` became a call), and the resulting array of elements is passed as the `
      `’s child. An array of elements inside children is flattened into the child list — array-in-children is legal and pervasive.

steps.label: Step 4: Where key went — and why it is not a prop
steps.text: In the compiled `<li>` call, `key` sits in the props-object position `{ key: item.id }` — but React **extracts it before props reach your component**: it is metadata for the reconciler. When items reorder, keys tell the diff which `<li>` is which (move this one, do not rebuild all). Keys are for **array items across renders**, not for one-of-a-kind elements — and they come from stable identity (an id), never the array index when the list can reorder.

steps.label: Step 5: The complete compiled function

examples.result: Five createElement calls deep, props objects with className and key in their exact positions, the map untouched but its body compiled — proof that JSX is sugar over function calls that produce plain objects.

examples.title: Spot the rule violations

steps.label: Step 1: One expression, one root
steps.text: The `return (` needs **one** value; two sibling tags are two expressions — a syntax error at the JSX level (and, compiled, two values with nowhere to go). The fix is a fragment — `<> <Nav /> <Feed /> </>` — a wrapper that contributes no DOM node of its own, or an actual containing element when one is wanted.

steps.label: Step 2: Braces or text — never both by accident
steps.text:
`

count: items.length

` renders the literal text `items.length` — bare characters are characters. The fix: `{items.length}`. And the second snippet’s `{if ...}` is illegal in a **different** way: braces hold one expression; `if` is a statement (Section 5.1) with no value. The expression toolkit: ternary `n > 0 ? "some" : "none"`, or short-circuit `n > 0 && "some"` — the compiled call needs a value, so the syntax demands one.

steps.label: Step 3: XML strictness, and the class collision
steps.text: Unclosed `` fails to parse — JSX is XML-strict: every tag closes, self-closing allowed (``). And `class="card"` is not an unknown-attribute warning: in an attribute position, `class` collides with the reserved word — the attribute is **className** (or, for the actual HTML attribute via a framework escape hatch, `htmlFor` for `for`). Habit-breaking, then muscle memory.

steps.label: Step 4: The capitalization law
steps.text: `<itemList .../>` compiles to `createElement("itemList", ...)` — a **host element** named itemList, which no renderer defines: silent no-render (React warns “The tag itemList is unrecognized in this browser”). Capitalize it — `<ItemList .../>` — and it compiles to `createElement(ItemList, ...)`: a **reference to the variable in scope**, your component. One character is the difference between a string and an identifier — the rule exists so that host tags and user components never need namespaces.

steps.label: Step 5: What all four rules share
steps.text: Every rule exists because the tag compiles into an expression with strict shape: one root (one value), braces (one expression), closed tags (a parseable grammar), className/capitals (the rules of the surrounding JavaScript — reserved words and identifiers). JSX never escapes JavaScript — it **is** JavaScript, wearing tags; break a JS rule through JSX and the compiler simply reports it at build time, which is the quiet gift of a compile step (Section 17.4).

examples.result: Fixed: a fragment around the siblings; `{items.length}` and a ternary in the braces; `className` and a self-closed ``; `` capitalized — each violation traced to the expression grammar the tags compile into.

keyTakeaways: JSX tags are expressions that compile to function calls returning plain objects — not part of ECMAScript; unparsed, the file is a SyntaxError.

Classic transform: `
hi
` → `React.createElement("div", {className: "x"}, "hi")`; automatic runtime: `jsx("div", {className: "x", children: "hi"})` with the import injected.
Children are extra arguments; nested tags are nested calls; an array of elements (from map) is flattened into children.
Braces hold exactly one expression — map, ternary, && — never statements (if/for are values-less); bare text outside braces is literal.
Rules: single root (fragments `<>…</>`), close every tag, className not class, capitalized tags are in-scope component references (lowercase means a host-element string).
Elements are immutable data — storable, passable, buildable in loops (Chapter 8) — rendering is a separate act; key is reconciler metadata for array identity, not a component prop.

quiz.q:
What does `
hi
` compile to under the classic transform?
options: A DOM node created with document.createElement
React.createElement("div", { className: "x" }, "hi") — a function call returning an object
Nothing — the browser interprets JSX directly
quiz.explanation: Tag → first argument, attributes → props object, children → further arguments: a call returning a plain description object, which is why elements are storable data.

quiz.q: Why does `<itemList />` silently render nothing while `<ItemList />` works?
options: JSX is case-insensitive but Node is not
A lowercase tag compiles to the host-element string "itemList"; a capitalized tag compiles to a reference to the in-scope component identifier
quiz.explanation: createElement("itemList", ...) asks the renderer for a host element no browser defines; createElement(ItemList, ...) passes your component function — the capitalization is the dispatch, one character deciding string versus identifier.

quiz.q: Which is legal inside JSX braces, `{ ... }`?
options: An if statement choosing between elements
An expression such as items.map(i => <Row key={i.id} />) or cond ? <A /> : <B />
quiz.explanation: Braces become an argument of the compiled call, and arguments are values: map/ternary/&& produce values; if and for are statements with none — the expression toolkit of Chapters 4 and 7 in markup.

quiz.q: What is the `key` prop on a mapped list element for?
options: It is passed to your component like any prop
It identifies which array item is which across renders, so the reconciler can move elements instead of rebuilding — and it is stripped before props arrive
It is the HTML id attribute
quiz.explanation: Keys are diffing metadata: stable identity (an id) lets a reorder become moves rather than rebuilds; React removes key from the props your component receives.

quiz.q: Why must JSX attributes use className instead of class?
options: The attribute position compiles into a JavaScript object literal, where class is a reserved word that cannot be a property key in that expression
HTML forbids class in JSX files
quiz.explanation: Attributes become the props object — and the surrounding JavaScript’s rules apply to it: class is reserved (Section 2.3), so the property is named className (htmlFor similarly for the for attribute).

intro: JavaScript’s types are checked at runtime, at the worst possible moment — in production. **Flow** (Meta) adds a static type checker on top of the language: annotations that describe what values are allowed, checked before the program runs, then stripped away so the shipped code is plain JavaScript. Flow itself ultimately lost the ecosystem war — **TypeScript** won it with the same core ideas — but the ideas (maybe types, refinements, discriminated unions) transfer one-to-one, which makes this section a TypeScript primer by other means.
objectives: Annotate function parameters and return types with Flow syntax
Use maybe types (?T) and refinements to make null an explicit, checked part of the contract
Model alternatives with union types and discriminate them safely
Explain why TypeScript became the ecosystem winner — and why Flow concepts transfer intact

concepts.statement: **Flow** is a static type checker: a tool that reads annotated JavaScript and verifies that every value matches its declared type — before running anything. The `// @flow` pragma at the top of a file opts it in; annotations are erased at build time (a Babel plugin strips them — Section 17.4), so the runtime cost is zero.
concepts.detail: “Gradual” means the annotations are opt-in per file and per binding: unannotated code still type-checks through inference (a parameter used only as a number is inferred as one), and you add types where they earn their keep — the contract surfaces: parameters, returns, exported data.

concepts.statement: The syntax is `name: Type` for parameters and variables, and `function f(): Type` for return types: `(width: number, label: string): string`. Object types are structural — `{ id: number, name: string }` means “any object with at least these members of these types”, and `?` makes a field or parameter a **maybe**: `height: ?number` admits `null` (and `undefined`) as well.

A maybe type `?T` means “T or null or undefined” — the contract **admits** absence, so the checker then **demands** you prove presence before use: using a maybe-typed value without a null check is an error. A check narrows: after `if (x != null)` or `const h = height ?? 1`, the value is known to be T (or the fallback), and the code after it type-checks.

A **union** `A | B` means “either shape”: `type Result = { ok: true, value: string } | { ok: false, error: Error }`. A field with literal types (`ok: true` / `ok: false`) acts as a **discriminant**: testing it narrows the union to that variant, so after `if (result.ok)` only `value` is in scope — accessing `result.error` there is a compile error, not a surprise at 3 a.m.

**TypeScript** (Microsoft) is the same bet as Flow — gradual structural types over JavaScript, erased at compile time — and it won decisively: a dedicated compiler that **is** the build step, generics and utility types, the DefinitelyTyped corpus of library typings, first-class support in every framework and editor (and in the very toolchain of Sections 17.3–17.5). New projects choose it by default; Flow survives mainly inside Meta’s own codebases.
concepts.detail: Why that matters here: nothing in this section is Flow-specific. Maybe types are TypeScript’s `number | null`; refinements are its **narrowing**; discriminated unions are the same pattern with the same syntax shape; even the annotation placement is near-identical (`(width: number) => string`). Learn the concepts once — optional absence, checked unions, typed contracts — and they transfer intact to the tool the industry standardized on.

examples.title: A typed function with a maybe parameter
examples.problem:
Annotate `area(width, height)` where height is optional in a null-explicit way: callers may omit intent with null, but the body must prove it handled absence. Then read the errors the annotations catch.
```js
// @flow

function area(width: number, height: ?number = null): number {
  const h = height ?? 1;          // refinement — h: number from here on
  return width * h;
}

area(3, 4);      // fine — 12
area(3, null);   // fine — null is an explicit maybe — 3
area(3);         // fine — the default supplies null — 3
area("3", 4);   // error: string is not a number
area(3, "4");   // error: string is not a ?number
area(3, 4, 2);  // error: too many arguments
```

steps.label: Step 1: The annotations state the contract
steps.text: `width: number` — required number, no exceptions. `height: ?number = null` — an **explicit maybe**: the parameter admits number, null or undefined, with a default that makes “not provided” mean the same thing as “provided as null”. The return type `: number` promises the caller a number without reading the body.

steps.label: Step 2: The refinement earns the arithmetic
steps.text: Without the `??`, `width * height` is an error: height might be null, and `number * null` is `NaN` waiting to happen (Section 3.4). The `?? 1` does double duty — runtime behavior (null becomes 1) and compile-time refinement (after this line, `h` **is** a number). Every use of a maybe must pass through some such gate: `??`, `if (x != null)`, or `x || default`.

steps.label: Step 3: Read the errors as design review
steps.text: `area("3", 4)` — a string where a number is declared: caught at the call site, in the editor, before any run (the failure mode in untyped JavaScript is silent NaN propagation). `area(3, 4, 2)` — even **arity** is checked: extra arguments are not silently dropped the way untyped JavaScript drops them. Each error is a would-be bug relocated from production to before-commit.

steps.label: Step 4: What the types do NOT say
steps.text: Nothing here validates that 3 is a sensible width, that the caller is not passing a temperature — types constrain **shapes and absence**, not semantics. The maybe discipline is the honest scope: null stops being a runtime landmine and becomes a type-level obligation; meaning itself still needs tests (Section 17.2) and review.

steps.label: Step 5: The erasure payoff
steps.text: The Babel plugin strips every annotation, and the emitted function is exactly `function area(width, height) { const h = height ?? 1; return width * h; }` with the default restored — zero runtime cost, zero new behavior: the checks were free, paid entirely at build time. That is the whole economics of gradual typing.

examples.result: Three legal calls (12, 3, 3 — the default making omission explicit) and three compile-time errors — string-as-number, wrong-maybe, and arity — with null handled by contract, not by luck.

examples.title: A discriminated union for load results

steps.label: Step 1: Two shapes, one tagged with literals
steps.text: Each variant carries the same field name `ok` with a **literal type** — `true` in one, `false` in the other. Literals are types too (`true` is a type with exactly one value), and the shared field makes the union **discriminated**: every value of LoadResult answers “which am I?” unambiguously.

steps.label: Step 2: The discriminant test narrows
steps.text: Inside `if (r.ok)`, the checker reasons: ok is true, and only the first variant allows that — so `r` **is** `{ok: true, value: string}` there. In the else path, `r` is the second variant. Access follows proof: this is the same refinement move as the null check — one test, and the type of everything under it sharpens.

steps.label: Step 3: Attack it — the illegal shapes do not compile
steps.text: `{ok: true, value: 42}`: wrong member type — value must be a string. `{ok: true, error: ...}`: the true-variant has no `error`, and `value` is missing — a malformed hybrid that untyped code would happily construct and then crash on later. `{value: "x"}` with no `ok` at all: not a member of the union, rejected — **absence of the discriminant is itself a type error**, which is the “make illegal states unrepresentable” promise.

steps.label: Step 4: The runtime shape is unchanged
steps.text: These are ordinary object literals at runtime — Flow adds no wrapper, no class, no field. The union exists in the checker; the erasure principle from the previous example holds here too: the program you ship is the program you wrote, only proven narrower at every branch.

steps.label: Step 5: The same pattern in TypeScript — deliberately
steps.text: Spell the identical thing in TS: `type LoadResult = { ok: true; value: string } | { ok: false; error: Error }` — same literals, same narrowing on `if (r.ok)`, same exhaustive checking in switch statements. That near-verbatim portability is the closing point of this chapter: Flow teaches the ideas; TypeScript pays the bills — and both are one Babel/plugin step (Section 17.4) away from the plain JavaScript this book spent sixteen chapters on.

examples.result: render handles both variants with each field access proven by narrowing; the malformed calls — wrong type, hybrid shape, missing discriminant — are all compile errors; and the whole pattern ports to TypeScript by changing the `type` keyword and nothing else.

keyTakeaways: Flow is a gradual static type checker: `// @flow` opts a file in, annotations are checked pre-run and stripped at build — zero runtime cost.
Annotations: `(width: number, height: ?number): number` — structural object types, literals as types, and arity checked too.
A maybe `?T` admits null/undefined explicitly — and then demands proof before use: `??`, `!= null` checks, or defaults refine T out of the maybe.
Null stops being a landmine and becomes an obligation — the compile-time version of ?. and ?? (Sections 3.4, 17.4).
Unions model “one of several shapes”; a literal discriminant (ok: true | ok: false) lets a test narrow the union — wrong-field access becomes a compile error.

TypeScript won the ecosystem with the same concepts — maybe = `T | null`, refinements = narrowing, unions identical — so these skills transfer one-to-one; treat this section as a TS primer with different syntax.

quiz.q: What does the annotation `height: ?number` mean?
options: height must be a number or the function throws
height may be a number, null or undefined — a maybe type that admits absence explicitly
height is optional at runtime only
height can be any type at all
quiz.explanation: ?T is the maybe type: T plus null plus undefined — absence becomes part of the typed contract, and the checker then requires a refinement before the value is used as T.

quiz.q: In Flow, why does `width * height` fail to type-check when height is `?number` — until `const h = height ?? 1` is added?
options: Multiplication is not allowed in Flow files
Because a maybe-typed value must pass a null check first — the ?? refines h to plain number, proving absence was handled
It does not — Flow only checks strings
quiz.explanation: The maybe could be null, and number * null is NaN at runtime; the refinement (??, if != null, || default) proves the value is a number from that line on — absence handled by contract.

quiz.q: Given `type R = { ok: true, value: string } | { ok: false, error: Error }`, what happens inside `if (r.ok)`?
options: Nothing — Flow does not track conditions
r narrows to the first variant, so r.value is legal and r.error there is a compile error
quiz.explanation: The literal discriminant lets one test narrow the union to the matching variant: the fields of the other variant are provably absent — the wrong-field access moves from a runtime surprise to a compile error.

quiz.q: Why does the book close by pointing at TypeScript?
options: TypeScript won the ecosystem — same core ideas (maybes, narrowing, unions) with massive library typings and toolchain adoption — so Flow concepts transfer one-to-one
TypeScript removes the need for tests and linting
quiz.explanation: The ideas here are portable: T | null, narrowing and discriminated unions are spelled nearly identically in TS, which became the default choice — learning Flow’s model is learning TypeScript’s model.

depth.title: From physical switches to mathematical logic

blocks.body: The argument for binary hardware was completed in 1937, in a master’s thesis at MIT. Claude Shannon’s “A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits” observed that George Boole’s algebra of logic (1854) — for eighty years a piece of pure mathematics — describes switching networks exactly: a **series** connection of two contacts conducts only when both are closed, which is the AND of the two switch variables; a **parallel** connection conducts when either is closed, which is OR; and the two states of a contact, open and closed, realize the two truth values. The calculus of propositions thereby became a calculus of circuits: engineers could design, transform, and minimize relay networks by algebra rather than by intuition. Section 1.8’s truth tables and its AND, OR and NOT are not a convenient notation imposed on hardware after the fact — they are the native language of two-state devices. Binary signaling is not a compromise forced by noisy components; it is what makes the hardware a physical model of logic itself.

blocks.heading: Binary versus three-level noise margins
blocks.body: Take a 5 V supply and suppose every driver holds its output within $\pm 0.3\ \text{V}$ of its intended level while every receiver’s decision threshold is uncertain by $\pm 0.2\ \text{V}$; call the combined slop $\Delta = 0.5\ \text{V}$. With **binary** signaling the levels sit at $0$ and $5$, the decision boundary is $2.5\ \text{V}$ from each nominal level, and the guaranteed noise margin per side is $5/2 - \Delta = 2.0\ \text{V}$. With a **three-level** code the levels must be $0$, $2.5$, $5$, so the boundaries move to $1.25$ and $3.75$, and each level sits only $5/4 - \Delta = 0.75\ \text{V}$ from its boundary. For $r$ evenly spaced levels the margin is $V_{DD}/(2(r-1)) - \Delta$, so every doubling of the level count halves the immunity: a ten-level decimal machine would need $5/18 - 0.5$, which is negative — the tolerances already exceed the spacing between levels. The arithmetic explains the industry’s whole history: two levels put each decision at the extremes of the swing, where a transistor is most comfortable, and the exponential loss of margin is why multi-valued logic (this section’s research tier) remains exotic.

Strictly speaking there are no digital signals — only analog signals interpreted digitally. A wire carries a continuous voltage; the **digital abstraction** declares it a 0 or a 1 according to thresholds, and a **restoring** gate re-transmits a clean level no matter how far inside the legal region its input drifted. This is **quantization** applied twice: value is quantized onto the two-symbol alphabet, and time is quantized by the clock of Section 1.7, so that a single instant defines each sample. The payoff is that noise stops accumulating: an analog amplifier chain adds irrecoverable distortion at every stage, but a chain of restoring gates erases input perturbations — provided they stay within the margins of the worked example above. Quantization does charge tuition: the boundary between analog and digital carries a half-symbol error floor (the half-**LSB** of a converter), and information is destroyed at every threshold decision. But a finite alphabet of reliably distinguishable symbols is exactly what the section’s “discrete elements of information” demands; the rest of this chapter is the mathematics of paying that cost once, deliberately, instead of continuously.

The stored-program concept is Turing’s 1936 universal machine built in metal. Because instructions are data — bit patterns in memory — one fixed machine can imitate any other digital system by interpreting its program; fetch, decode and execute is the universal machine’s single loop, and everything else in Mano’s book is engineering arranged around that loop. The same duality explains compilers, loaders, and operating systems as programs that write programs — and, less cheerfully, why self-modifying code and viruses need no special hardware to exist.

depth.title: Beyond two states: signals at the frontier

blocks.heading: Flash memories are multivalued
blocks.body: The margin arithmetic of the master’s tier is a live industrial battlefield. A **QLC flash cell** stores four bits by holding its floating-gate charge at one of sixteen distinguishable threshold-voltage levels — multi-valued logic shipping by the exabyte. Each generation (MLC, 2 bits, 4 levels; TLC, 3 bits, 8 levels; QLC, 4 bits, 16 levels) halves the level spacing in exchange for density, directly spending the noise margin computed above: reads become slow and repeated, sensing needs multiple passes, retention and write endurance fall, and every page is wrapped in **LDPC error correction** (the research tier of Section 1.6) because the raw channel is too unreliable to decode alone. Chip-to-chip links are multivalued too: **PAM-4** serial interfaces put four voltage levels on a wire to double throughput at 56 and 112 gigabaud, accepting an eye one third as tall as binary signaling — about $9.5\ \text{dB}$ of noise tolerance surrendered, since $20 \log 3 \approx 9.5$. The binary-versus-multivalued question is thus not settled dogma but a measured engineering trade: margins against bits per physical state, re-argued at every process node.

blocks.heading: The quantum register
blocks.body: Section 1.7’s register holds one definite word; a quantum register of $n$ **qubits** holds a superposition — a unit vector in a $2^n$-dimensional complex space, one amplitude per classical word. Measuring forces one definite word with probability the squared magnitude of its amplitude, and the rest of the superposition is destroyed: the digital abstraction of this section survives only at measurement time. The divergence runs deeper. **No-cloning** forbids copying an unknown state, so fan-out — free in every circuit of this book — is illegal; useful quantum gates must be reversible (Toffoli gates compute AND while retaining the information needed to undo it); and even erasing a classical bit has a thermodynamic price, $kT \ln 2$ (Landauer). Quantum error correction must therefore protect amplitudes, not bits: parity checks generalize to stabilizer checks on superpositions. What remains open is building fault-tolerant machines whose registers hold their delicate states long enough to compute with. The definite, clonable, two-valued word of this chapter is precisely what quantum research is trying to transcend — and to protect, using codes descended from its own parity bit.

intro: Mano opens the book by taking apart the very idea of a computer. A digital computer is a machine that manipulates discrete elements of information under the direction of a stored program, and the whole apparatus — hardware, codes, number systems, and logic — exists to make that manipulation fast, reliable, and cheap. This section describes the machine as a block diagram of three functional units and explains why every one of them is built from binary signals.
objectives: Define a digital computer and a digital system in terms of discrete information processing
Describe the hardware block diagram — CPU, memory unit, and input/output units — and the role of each
Explain the stored program concept and the fetch–decode–execute behavior it implies
Justify why digital hardware uses binary (two-valued) signals rather than ten-valued decimal signals

concepts.statement: A **digital computer** is a system that accepts discrete elements of information (numbers, letters, symbols), stores and processes them according to a **stored program** of instructions, and delivers the results. Each quantity of information is represented inside the machine by a pattern of binary digits.
concepts.detail: Mano stresses two words: digital (discrete, countable information, as opposed to the continuous signals of an analog computer) and stored program (the instructions live in memory alongside the data and are fetched one at a time). Everything in the rest of the book — codes, Boolean algebra, gates, registers, the whole processor design — is scaffolding for this one machine.

concepts.statement: A computer’s hardware divides into three functional units, whether the machine is a room-sized 1979 mainframe or a modern chip: a **central processing unit (CPU)**, a **memory unit**, and **input/output (I/O) equipment**, all interconnected by buses that carry addresses, data, and control signals.
concepts.detail: In words, the block diagram is: the memory unit holds the program instructions and the data; the CPU fetches instructions from memory, interprets (decodes) them, and executes them. Inside the CPU, a **control unit** directs the operation sequence, an **arithmetic and logic unit (ALU)** performs the microoperations, and a small set of **processor registers** (program counter, instruction register, accumulator, and friends) hold the operands in flight. Input equipment transfers information from the outside world into memory; output equipment reports results back. Chapters 8–11 of Mano build this exact diagram piece by piece.

concepts.statement: Because instructions are stored in memory as binary words, the computer can **fetch, decode, and execute** them one at a time in sequence — and it can even manipulate its own instructions as data, since both are just bit patterns.
concepts.detail: This is the von Neumann organization. The processor keeps a program counter with the address of the next instruction, increments it each fetch (unless a branch instruction changes it), and the cycle repeats. A program is nothing more than a stored list of binary instruction codes; changing the program changes the machine’s behavior without touching the wiring.

concepts.statement: Digital hardware uses **binary** signals because physical devices that must distinguish two states are far easier to build, cheaper, and more reliable than devices that must distinguish ten voltage levels.
concepts.detail: A transistor operating as a switch is either cut off or saturated; its output is meant to be interpreted as one of two clearly separated voltage ranges. With only two ranges to recognize, noise and component drift can be enormous before a 0 is mistaken for a 1. Early machines did try decimal arithmetic with ten-level signals, and they lost to binary machines precisely because the two-level circuits could use the cheapest, most reliable components. The number of states is small — but so is the cost of getting each state right.

concepts.statement: A **digital system** is any system that manipulates discrete elements of information: a digital watch counting seconds, a calculator combining keypresses, a traffic-light controller sequencing lamps. Digital computers are the most general digital systems because they are **programmable** — the same hardware runs different stored programs.
concepts.detail: Mano’s point is one of levels: combinational and sequential circuits (Chapters 3–7) are the elementary digital systems; registers and register transfers (Chapters 8–10) assemble them into a processor; the basic computer of Chapter 11 assembles that into a complete stored-program machine. Each level reuses the binary logic of this chapter.

concepts.statement: Every kind of information a computer handles — numbers, letters, control symbols, even instructions — is encoded as a **binary word**, a finite string of bits $b_{n-1} \ldots b_1 b_0$ whose meaning comes from a code agreement between designer and machine.
concepts.detail: The same eight bits can stand for the number 65, the letter A, or an opcode — the encoding convention decides. Sections 1.2 through 1.6 develop the three great encoding topics: number systems (quantity), binary codes (symbols), and complements (signed arithmetic).

examples.title: Tracing one instruction through the block diagram
examples.problem: In words, follow an “add the contents of memory location to the accumulator” instruction through the CPU, memory, and buses, showing which functional unit is active at each step.

steps.label: Step 1: Fetch
steps.text: The control unit places the contents of the program counter on the address bus; the memory unit responds by placing the instruction word on the data bus, and it is captured into the instruction register inside the CPU.

steps.label: Step 2: Decode
steps.text: The control unit examines the instruction’s opcode bits and determines that an add from memory is required; it generates the control signals (read, register enable, ALU select) for the steps to follow.

steps.label: Step 3: Fetch the operand
steps.text: The address field of the instruction is placed on the address bus; the memory responds with the data word, which is captured into a CPU data register.

steps.label: Step 4: Execute
steps.text: The ALU adds its two inputs — the data register and the accumulator — and the sum is transferred back into the accumulator, while status information (such as a carry) may be recorded.

steps.label: Step 5: Next instruction
steps.text: The program counter was already incremented during the fetch, so the next instruction is ready to be fetched; the cycle repeats until a halt instruction is reached.

examples.result: One instruction has touched every block: memory (twice), the buses (twice), the CPU registers (IR, PC, accumulator, data register), the control unit (decode and sequencing), and the ALU (the add).

examples.title: Why not build a decimal computer?
examples.problem: Argue from circuit reliability why a two-state machine beats a ten-state machine for general-purpose computation.

steps.label: Step 1: Physical state separation
steps.text: Suppose a circuit must resolve a signal into one of $r$ levels. The average gap between adjacent levels shrinks roughly like the reciprocal of $r$; with $r = 2$ the two levels can sit at the extremes of the voltage swing.

steps.label: Step 2: Noise immunity
steps.text: Any noise smaller than the full separation between the two ranges is automatically rejected. With ten levels packed into the same swing, noise a fraction as large already corrupts a digit.

steps.label: Step 3: Device economics
steps.text: A transistor makes a superb two-state switch (fully on or fully off) but a poor ten-level amplifier when mass-produced with 1970s tolerances; the binary design uses the device where it is most reliable.

steps.label: Step 4: The trade accepted
steps.text: The price is verbosity: ten decimal digits need about $\lceil \log_2 10^{10} \rceil = 34$ bits, and binary arithmetic and codes must be developed (Sections 1.2–1.6) to make up for the lost compactness of a ten-symbol digit.

examples.result: Binary wins because reliability per component, not compactness per digit, is what scales: a machine built from parts that never confuse their two states can be made arbitrarily large, and the encoding burden shifts to mathematics instead of hardware.

keyTakeaways: A digital computer stores and processes discrete information under control of a stored program of instructions held in memory.
The hardware block diagram has three units: CPU (control unit + ALU + processor registers), memory, and input/output equipment, tied together by address, data and control buses.
The stored program concept makes instruction fetch, decode and execute the machine’s fundamental cycle, and lets programs be changed without rewiring.
Binary signals are used because two-state devices are cheaper and far more noise-resistant than ten-state devices.
Digital computers are the most general digital systems; watches, calculators and controllers are fixed-program relatives.
Every form of information — numbers, characters, instructions — enters the machine as an encoded binary word.

quiz.q: Which functional unit contains the control unit, the ALU, and the processor registers?
quiz.explanation: The CPU integrates sequencing (control unit), computation (ALU), and the working registers; memory stores, and I/O communicates with the world.

quiz.q: What does the stored program concept directly enable?
options: Changing the computer’s behavior by loading different instructions into memory
Reducing the number of bits needed per number
quiz.explanation: Because instructions are ordinary memory words, a new program changes the machine without touching the wiring — the defining property of a stored-program computer.

quiz.q: The strongest hardware argument for binary rather than decimal internal signals is:
options: Binary numbers are shorter than decimal numbers
Two-state circuits are cheaper and far more noise-resistant than ten-level circuits
Decimal arithmetic cannot be implemented with logic gates
quiz.explanation: With only two voltage ranges to distinguish, each state is maximally protected against noise and component variation; the length penalty of binary is paid in encoding, not reliability.

quiz.q: During the fetch phase of an instruction cycle, the memory unit:
options: Places the instruction word at the addressed location onto the data bus for the CPU to capture
quiz.explanation: Fetch is a memory read at the address held in the program counter: memory drives the instruction word onto the data bus and the CPU latches it into the instruction register. Decode and increment belong to the CPU.

depth.title: Positional notation as algebra

blocks.body: A radix-$r$ numeral is a polynomial in disguise, $N = \sum_i d_i r^i$ with digit coefficients, and everything in this section is polynomial algebra. Reading a numeral is **evaluation**, best organized by Horner’s rule, $$N = \bigl( \cdots \bigl( (d_{n-1} r + d_{n-2}) r + \cdots \bigr) r + d_1 \bigr) r + d_0,$$ which needs only $n-1$ multiplications and additions and never forms a power of $r$ explicitly. Writing a numeral in a new base is the inverse operation: repeated division by $r$ is **synthetic division**, peeling off the constant coefficient first, so the two conversion procedures of the core section are the two classical algorithms of polynomial manipulation. This is why conversions cannot fail: the value is an integer that exists independently of its dress, and base conversion merely re-expresses the same quantity over a different sequence of weights. Carries — the deeper subject of Section 1.3 — are the normalization that keeps digit coefficients inside $\{0, \ldots, r-1\}$.

blocks.heading: Uniqueness of positional notation
blocks.body: For every radix $r \ge 2$, every integer $N$ with $0 \le N \le r^n - 1$ has exactly one representation as a digit string $d_{n-1} \ldots d_0$ with each $d_i$ in $\{0, 1, \ldots, r-1\}$ and $N = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} d_i r^i$. In particular, expansion to radix $r$ is a bijection between the integers in range and the length-$n$ digit strings: no two numerals collide, and no integer is missed. The same uniqueness holds for finite fractional expansions of length $m$, because multiplying by $r^m$ reduces that case to the integer one. The digit produced at each step of the division algorithm is therefore not merely a plausible choice but the only choice there is.

Existence is the repeated-division algorithm itself, and it terminates: by the division algorithm $N = q_1 r + d_0$ with $0 \le d_0 < r$, and since $q_1 = \lfloor N/r \rfloor < N$ whenever $N \ge 1$ and $r \ge 2$, the successive quotients strictly decrease, so after at most $\lceil \log_r (N+1) \rceil$ steps the quotient reaches $0$ and the collected remainders are the digits — the conversion procedure of the core section is a proved algorithm, not a heuristic. Uniqueness: given any representation, reduce $N = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} d_i r^i$ modulo $r$; every term except $d_0$ is a multiple of $r$, so $d_0 \equiv N \pmod{r}$, and since both $d_0$ and $N \bmod r$ lie in $\{0, \ldots, r-1\}$ they are equal — no choice. Subtract $d_0$ and divide by $r$; the same argument forces $d_1$, and induction on position determines every digit from $N$ alone, so the numeral is a canonical name for the integer. For a finite fractional expansion of length $m$, multiply by $r^m$: the scaled value is an integer whose digits are forced exactly as above.

blocks.heading: Terminating expansions
blocks.body: A positive rational $p/q$ in lowest terms has a finite expansion in base $r$ **if and only if** every prime factor of $q$ divides $r$. Which fractions terminate is therefore a property of the base, not the fraction: $1/4$ terminates in both decimal and binary, $1/5$ terminates in decimal but not in binary, and $1/10$ has no finite binary form because $10 = 2 \cdot 5$ while no power of $2$ contains a factor $5$. Dually, every rational terminates in some base (take $r$ divisible by $q$), while an irrational such as $\sqrt{2}$ terminates in none — and, being irrational, repeats in none either: the rationals are exactly the eventually periodic expansions in every base.

Suppose first that every prime factor of $q$ divides $r$. Then $q$ divides some power $r^m$ (each prime’s exponent is eventually met), say $r^m = q \cdot s$, so $p/q = ps/r^m$ — an integer over a power of $r$, which has a finite expansion of at most $m$ fractional digits: write $ps$ in base $r$ and move the radix point $m$ places. Conversely, suppose $p/q = \sum_{i=1}^{m} d_{-i} r^{-i}$ is a finite expansion. Multiply through by $r^m q$: the left side is the integer $r^m p$, the right side is $q \cdot t$ where $t = \sum_{i=1}^{m} d_{-i} r^{m-i}$ is an integer. So $q$ divides $r^m p$, and since $\gcd(p, q) = 1$, Euclid’s lemma forces $q \mid r^m$: every prime factor of $q$ divides $r$. Now apply the criterion to $0.1 = 1/10$: termination in base 2 would force $10 \mid 2^m$, impossible because $5$ divides $10$ but no power of $2$ does. The expansion is necessarily infinite and, being rational, eventually periodic — $(0.0\overline{0011})_2$, exactly the pattern the core section computed by hand. This is why binary floating point stores only a rounded surrogate for one-tenth, and why $0.1 + 0.2 \ne 0.3$ in IEEE arithmetic.

depth.title: Alternative number systems for real hardware

blocks.heading: Logarithmic number systems
blocks.body: A logarithmic number system (LNS) represents a value as a sign bit plus the fixed-point logarithm of its magnitude. Multiplication becomes addition of the logs, division subtraction, square roots a shift — the entire multiplicative structure of arithmetic collapses onto the cheap integer operations of this chapter, and each multiplication rounds only once, so long products do not accumulate rounding error the way repeated mantissa rounding does. The price is addition itself: $\log(a + b) = \log a + \log\bigl(1 + 2^{\,\log b - \log a}\bigr)$, whose correction term is transcendental and was historically supplied by table lookup and interpolation.
