keyTakeaways: A combinational circuit is a memoryless wiring of Boolean functions: $n$ inputs, $m$ outputs, truth table only, no history.
The design procedure is invariant: specification → truth table → simplification (K-maps) → logic diagram, then verify by re-deriving the table.
Don’t-cares for impossible inputs shrink the logic — the BCD-to-Gray $G_2$ fell from a four-literal XOR to $B_3 + B_2$.
The finished BCD-to-Gray converter: $G_3 = B_3$, $G_2 = B_3 + B_2$, $G_1 = B_2′B_1 + B_2B_1′$, $G_0 = B_2B_0′ + B_1B_0′ + B_2′B_1′B_0$ — eight gates.
Gray code adjacency (one bit changes per step) is the same property that orders K-map cells — Chapter 3’s maps are Gray-laid-out tables.
Gate count, literal count and level count are the three cost figures of merit, and they trade against each other.

quiz.q: The first step of the combinational design procedure is:
options: Stating the specification of the circuit precisely
quiz.explanation: Nothing mechanical can begin until the problem is fixed: what the inputs mean, which combinations are possible, and what each output must be — the truth table and the maps are downstream of that decision.

quiz.q: For the BCD-to-Gray converter, the truth table has how many rows and how many are don’t-cares?
quiz.explanation: Four input bits give $2^{4} = 16$ combinations; BCD uses only ten, so rows $1010$ through $1111$ are marked X and are free to be 0 or 1 on the maps.

quiz.q: The simplification $G_2 = B_3 + B_2$ is legal only because:
options: The input combinations $1010$ through $1111$ never occur, so their outputs are don’t-cares
OR is cheaper than XOR in every family
quiz.explanation: On the invalid rows the don’t-cares let the 1s at rows 8–9 group with rows 10–11 and 12–15; forced 0s there would clip those groups and leave $G_2 = B_3′B_2 + B_3B_2′$.

quiz.q: Which property distinguishes a combinational circuit from a sequential one?
options: Its outputs depend only on the present input values, never on past inputs
It must be built from NAND gates
quiz.explanation: No memory, no feedback, no clock: the outputs are pure functions of the present inputs. Sequential circuits (Chapter 6) are exactly the circuits that remember.

intro: Arithmetic is where combinational design earns its keep. Two bits in, a sum and a carry out: the half adder. Add a carry-in and the full adder appears — the single cell from which every integer ALU in existence is built. Cascading four cells gives the ripple-carry adder, whose speed is limited by the carry crawling through every stage; computing the carries in parallel from generate and propagate signals gives the look-ahead carry adder. A mode line and exclusive-OR gates turn the same hardware into a subtractor with overflow detected by one more XOR.
objectives: Derive the half adder and full adder equations from their truth tables
Build a 4-bit ripple-carry adder and compute its worst-case delay in gate delays
Define carry generate and propagate and derive the look-ahead carry equations $C_{i+1} = G_i + P_iC_i$
Compare ripple and look-ahead speeds quantitatively for 4- and 16-bit adders
Explain the mode-controlled adder-subtractor and detect signed overflow with $V = C_n \oplus C_{n-1}$

concepts.statement: A **half adder** adds two bits $A$ and $B$, producing the sum bit $S = A′B + AB′ = A \oplus B$ and the carry $C = AB$. The truth table’s four rows read, in the order $AB = 00, 01, 10, 11$: $S = 0, 1, 1, 0$ and $C = 0, 0, 0, 1$.
concepts.detail: Two gates realize it: one XOR and one AND. It is called half because it cannot accept a carry from a previous stage — that omission is what forces the full adder into existence.

concepts.statement: A **full adder** adds three bits — $A$, $B$ and the carry-in $C_{\text{in}}$ — producing $$S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{\text{in}}, \qquad C_{\text{out}} = AB + (A \oplus B)C_{\text{in}}.$$ The SOP form from the truth table is $S = A′B′C_{\text{in}} + A′BC_{\text{in}}′ + AB′C_{\text{in}}′ + ABC_{\text{in}}$ and $C_{\text{out}} = AB + AC_{\text{in}} + BC_{\text{in}}$.
concepts.detail: The XOR form of $S$ is the reason Section 2.6’s exclusive-OR matters so much: the three-literal minterm version costs four AND gates and an OR, while $A \oplus B \oplus C_{\text{in}}$ costs two XOR gates. The carry in the form $AB + (A \oplus B)C_{\text{in}}$ exposes the structure used next: a carry is either generated here ($AB$) or propagated up from below.

concepts.statement: An **$n$-bit ripple-carry adder** cascades $n$ full adders: stage $i$ computes bit $S_i$ from $A_i$, $B_i$ and $C_i$, and passes $C_{i+1}$ to the next stage. The final carry $C_n$ is the carry out of the whole sum.
concepts.detail: The structure is perfectly regular — which is why it was the first multi-bit adder anyone built — but the carry must travel through every stage: with 2 gate delays from $C_i$ to $C_{i+1}$ (one AND, one OR), the 4-bit carry out $C_4$ appears after 8 gate delays, and an $n$-bit adder needs $2n$. Long words make the ripple adder painfully slow: a 32-bit sum waits 64 gate delays for its top carry.

concepts.statement: For each bit position define the **generate** and **propagate** signals $$G_i = A_iB_i, \qquad P_i = A_i \oplus B_i,$$ from which each carry is computed **in parallel**: $$C_{i+1} = G_i + P_iC_i.$$ Expanded for a 4-bit block, with external carry $C_0$: $$C_1 = G_0 + P_0C_0, \quad C_2 = G_1 + P_1G_0 + P_1P_0C_0,$$ $$C_3 = G_2 + P_2G_1 + P_2P_1G_0 + P_2P_1P_0C_0,$$ $$C_4 = G_3 + P_3G_2 + P_3P_2G_1 + P_3P_2P_1G_0 + P_3P_2P_1P_0C_0.$$
concepts.detail: The reading is the whole idea: stage $i$ generates a carry when both its bits are 1 ($G_i$), and propagates an incoming carry when exactly one bit is 1 ($P_i$). Every carry is then a flat two-level AND-OR function of the $G$s, $P$s and $C_0$ — no carry waits on another carry, so all four carries exist simultaneously.

concepts.statement: A **look-ahead carry adder** computes all carries with the flat equations above: the $G_i$ and $P_i$ appear one gate delay after the inputs, each $C_{i+1}$ is a two-level AND-OR expression two delays later (3 total), and each sum bit $S_i = P_i \oplus C_i$ follows one XOR after that (4 total) — independent of word length.
concepts.detail: For 4 bits the gain is 8 gate delays down to 4; for 16 bits, built as four look-ahead blocks whose own group generate and propagate feed a second look-ahead level, the ripple’s 32 delays fall to roughly 8. The price is hardware: the flat $C_4$ expression alone needs four AND gates of fan-in up to 5 and one wide OR. Real designs (the 74182 look-ahead generator among them) stop at two levels of look-ahead and accept the residual ripple between blocks.

concepts.statement: A single 4-bit adder adds **and** subtracts: each $B_i$ passes through an XOR gate with the mode line $M$ — $B_i \oplus M$ — and $M$ also feeds the carry input $C_0$. With $M = 0$: $S = A + B$. With $M = 1$: $S = A + B′ + 1 = A - B$ in two’s complement, exactly the complement-plus-one rule of Section 1.4.
concepts.detail: The XOR gate doubles as a programmable inverter: $B_i \oplus 0 = B_i$ passes the bit, $B_i \oplus 1 = B_i′$ complements it. Feeding $M$ into $C_0$ adds the required 1 for free. One adder, one set of XOR gates, two operations — the standard arrangement in every two’s-complement processor.

concepts.statement: Adding two’s-complement numbers, **signed overflow** is detected by comparing the carry into and out of the sign stage: $$V = C_n \oplus C_{n-1}.$$ If $V = 1$ the sign of the result is wrong — the true sum lies outside $-2^{n-1}$ to $2^{n-1} - 1$.
concepts.detail: The rule: adding two positives (carry into the sign stage 0) that produces a negative result (carry out 1) is overflow, and so is the symmetric negative case. One XOR gate, already fed by both carries in the look-ahead structure, produces $V$. This is the same $C_8 \oplus C_7$ flag the ALU of Chapter 9 latches alongside every addition.

examples.title: From half adder to full adder by truth table
examples.problem: Derive the full adder’s equations from its truth table and realize the cell with two XOR gates, one AND and one OR gate.

steps.label: Step 1: The half adder table
steps.text: Two inputs give four rows: $A B = 00 \to S = 0, C = 0$; $01 \to S = 1, C = 0$; $10 \to S = 1, C = 0$; $11 \to S = 0, C = 1$. The sum column $0110$ is exclusive-OR; the carry column $0001$ is AND: $S = A \oplus B$, $C = AB$.

steps.label: Step 2: Add the carry-in — the full adder table
steps.text: Three inputs give eight rows; the sum $S$ is 1 for an odd number of 1s among $A, B, C_{\text{in}}$ (rows 001, 010, 100, 111) and the carry $C_{\text{out}}$ is 1 when at least two inputs are 1 (rows 011, 101, 110, 111).

steps.label: Step 3: Read the sum as XOR
steps.text: The odd-parity column gives $S = A′B′C_{\text{in}} + A′BC_{\text{in}}′ + AB′C_{\text{in}}′ + ABC_{\text{in}}$, which factors as $S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{\text{in}}$ — two XOR gates replace four ANDs and an OR.

steps.label: Step 4: Read the carry in generate-propagate form
steps.text: The majority column gives $C_{\text{out}} = AB + AC_{\text{in}} + BC_{\text{in}}$, which regroups as $C_{\text{out}} = AB + (A \oplus B)C_{\text{in}}$: generate the carry if $A = B = 1$, else propagate it if $A \oplus B = 1$ and the carry-in is 1.

steps.label: Step 5: Draw the cell
steps.text: Gate 1: $P = A \oplus B$. Gate 2: $G = AB$. Gate 3: $S = P \oplus C_{\text{in}}$. Gate 4: $C_{\text{out}} = G + PC_{\text{in}}$. Four gates, with $P$ and $G$ brought out as side outputs — exactly the signals the look-ahead structure of the next example consumes.

steps.label: Step 6: One numeric check
steps.text: $A = 1, B = 1, C_{\text{in}} = 1$: $S = 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 = 1$, $C_{\text{out}} = 1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 1 = 1$ — one plus one plus one is eleven ($3 = 11_2$): sum 1, carry 1 ✓.

examples.result: The full adder: $S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{\text{in}}$, $C_{\text{out}} = AB + (A \oplus B)C_{\text{in}}$ — four gates per bit, with $P$ and $G$ exported for carry look-ahead.

examples.title: Ripple versus look-ahead: the speed comparison
examples.problem: Add $A = 0101$ and $B = 0011$ with a 4-bit ripple-carry adder and time the worst-case carry; then build the look-ahead version and compare.

steps.label: Step 1: Trace the ripple addition
steps.text: Stage 0: $1 + 1 + 0 = 10$: $S_0 = 0$, $C_1 = 1$. Stage 1: $0 + 1 + 1 = 10$: $S_1 = 0$, $C_2 = 1$. Stage 2: $1 + 0 + 1 = 10$: $S_2 = 0$, $C_3 = 1$. Stage 3: $0 + 0 + 1 = 01$: $S_3 = 1$, $C_4 = 0$. The result is $1000 = 8 = 5 + 3$, and the carry had to pass through all four stages to prove $C_4 = 0$.

steps.label: Step 2: Time the ripple
steps.text: Each stage costs 2 gate delays from $C_i$ to $C_{i+1}$ (the AND and the OR of $C_{\text{out}} = G + PC_{\text{in}}$): $C_1$ at 2, $C_2$ at 4, $C_3$ at 6, $C_4$ at 8 gate delays, and $S_3 = P_3 \oplus C_3$ one delay after $C_3$, at 7. Worst-case output: $C_4$ at **8 gate delays** — and in general $2n$ for $n$ bits.

steps.label: Step 3: Build the look-ahead signals
steps.text: Compute $G_i = A_iB_i$ and $P_i = A_i \oplus B_i$ for all stages at once (1 gate delay): $G_0 = 1 \cdot 1 = 1$ and every other $G_i = 0$; $P_1 = P_2 = 1$ while $P_0 = P_3 = 0$.

steps.label: Step 4: Evaluate the flat carry equations
Step 5: Time the look-ahead
steps.text: The $G$s and $P$s exist after 1 gate delay; each $C_{i+1}$ is a two-level AND-OR function of them and $C_0$, valid at delay 3; each sum bit $S_i = P_i \oplus C_i$ is valid at delay 4. All four carries and all sums are ready after **4 gate delays**, versus 7–8 for the ripple — a 2× speedup at 4 bits.

steps.label: Step 6: Extrapolate to 16 bits
steps.text: Ripple: $C_{16}$ after $2 \times 16 = 32$ gate delays. Look-ahead in four 4-bit blocks with a second-level of group generate/propagate: the block carries appear after roughly 8 gate delays total. The gap widens linearly with word length — which is why every wide fast adder since the MSI era is a look-ahead (or a cousin of it).

examples.result: Same sums, different physics: ripple delivers $C_4$ at 8 gate delays ($2n$ in general), look-ahead at 4 ($3$ for all carries plus $1$ for the sums) — independent of $n$ at every level of look-ahead.

examples.title: The adder-subtractor and its overflow flag
examples.problem: Use the mode-controlled adder-subtractor to compute $5 - 3$, $3 - 5$, and $7 + 6$ (4-bit two’s complement), tracing every carry and the overflow flag $V = C_4 \oplus C_3$.

steps.label: Step 1: Set up the hardware
steps.text: Mode $M$ feeds $C_0$ and one input of every $B$-side XOR gate. $M = 0$ passes $B$ through: $S = A + B$. $M = 1$ complements $B$ and adds 1: $S = A + B′ + 1 = A - B$.

steps.label: Step 5: Read the flags
steps.text: In Step 4, $V = C_4 \oplus C_3 = 0 \oplus 1 = 1$: overflow — two positives summed to a negative because 13 exceeds $2^{3} - 1 = 7$. In Steps 2 and 3 the carries agreed ($V = 0$) and the signed results were exact. The carry out $C_4$ by itself means unsigned overflow only; $V$ alone speaks for the signed world — the two flags are independent, as Chapter 9’s ALU will re-emphasize.

examples.result: One adder plus four XOR gates and one mode bit perform $5 - 3 = 0010$, $3 - 5 = 1110$ (i.e. $-2$) and $7 + 6 = 1101$ with $V = C_4 \oplus C_3 = 1$ flagging the third case as out of signed range.

keyTakeaways: Half adder: $S = A \oplus B$, $C = AB$. Full adder: $S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{\text{in}}$, $C_{\text{out}} = AB + (A \oplus B)C_{\text{in}}$ — four gates per bit.
The ripple-carry adder is $n$ cascaded full adders; its worst-case delay is $2n$ gate delays because the carry walks every stage.
Look-ahead carry: $G_i = A_iB_i$ (generate), $P_i = A_i \oplus B_i$ (propagate), $C_{i+1} = G_i + P_iC_i$ — flat two-level carry equations, all carries valid 3 gate delays after the inputs.
4-bit comparison: 8 gate delays (ripple) versus 4 (look-ahead); 16-bit: 32 versus roughly 8 with two-level look-ahead — speed bought with extra AND-OR hardware.
Mode line through XOR gates turns the adder into a subtractor: $M = 1$ computes $A + B′ + 1 = A - B$, the two’s-complement rule of Chapter 1 wired into gates.
Signed overflow: $V = C_n \oplus C_{n-1}$ — carry into and out of the sign stage disagree exactly when the signed result is out of range.

quiz.q: Why is a half adder called half?
options: It handles only half the truth table
It adds two bits but cannot accept a carry-in from a previous stage
It works at half the clock speed
quiz.explanation: It has no $C_{\text{in}}$ input, so it cannot be cascaded — the full adder exists precisely to add the third bit that makes multi-bit addition possible.

quiz.q: In the look-ahead adder, the propagate signal of stage $i$ is:
options: $P_i = A_i \oplus B_i$ — the carry passes when exactly one operand bit is 1
quiz.explanation: Generate $G_i = A_iB_i$ creates a carry on the spot; propagate $P_i = A_i \oplus B_i$ lets an incoming carry pass through the stage. (An OR-based $P_i = A_i + B_i$ also propagates correctly, but the XOR form is free — it is the sum bit.)

quiz.q: A 16-bit ripple-carry adder’s final carry is valid after approximately how many gate delays?
quiz.explanation: Each stage adds 2 gate delays to the carry chain ($2n$ in general): $2 \times 16 = 32$ — the linear growth that look-ahead exists to break.

quiz.q: With $A = 0111$, $B = 0110$ and $M = 0$, the 4-bit adder-subtractor produces which flags?
options: $C_4 = 0$ and $V = 1$ — signed overflow, no unsigned carry
quiz.explanation: The sum is $1101$: as unsigned it fits ($13 < 16$, so $C_4 = 0$), but signed it reads $-3$ — the carries into and out of the sign stage disagree, so $V = C_4 \oplus C_3 = 1$.

quiz.q: In the mode-controlled adder-subtractor, the mode bit $M$ does what when $M = 1$?
options: Complements every $B_i$ through the XOR gates and supplies the $+1$ through $C_0$, so the adder computes $A - B$
Shifts the result left by one
quiz.explanation: The XOR gates act as programmable inverters ($B_i \oplus 1 = B_i′$) and $M$ into $C_0$ adds the 1: together $A + B′ + 1 = A - B$ — two’s-complement subtraction with no extra adder.

quiz.q: A full adder has inputs $x$, $y$, $z$ (carry-in). Which pair gives sum $S$ and carry $C$?
options: $S = x \oplus y \oplus z$, $C = xy + xz + yz$
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** three input bits, two outputs.
**Step 2 — Rule:** sum is odd parity (three-way XOR); carry is majority (at least two inputs $1$).
**Step 3 — Check:** $S = x \oplus y \oplus z$ is $1$ on $1,2,4,7$; $C = xy + xz + yz$ is $1$ on $3,5,6,7$.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** half adder is the $z = 0$ case: $S = x \oplus y$, $C = xy$, consistent.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** swap sum and carry roles; OR-sum ignores parity; single minterm covers one row only.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** XOR trio for sum, three ANDs ORed for carry.

quiz.q: Each full-adder stage contributes $2$ circuit delays to the carry chain. After how many delays is the final carry valid in an $8$-bit ripple-carry adder?
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** $n = 8$ stages, $2$ delays per stage.
**Step 2 — Rule:** ripple delay grows linearly as $2n$ since each carry waits for the previous stage.
**Step 3 — Computation:** $2 \times 8 = 16$ delays.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** $4$-bit gives $8$, $16$-bit gives $32$; the $16$-bit figure in the text matches this $2n$ law.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** $8$ counts one per stage; $4$ counts half; $32$ is the $16$-bit figure.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** $16$ delays, the linear cost look-ahead removes.

quiz.q: A $4$-bit mode-controlled adder-subtractor adds with $M = 0$: $A = 0111$ ($7$), $B = 0100$ ($4$). What are result, carry and signed-overflow $V$?
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** $M = 0$ passes $B$ unchanged; add $0111 + 0100$.
**Step 2 — Rule:** $M$ XORs each $B$ bit ($M = 1$ inverts for subtraction); overflow $V = C_{3} \oplus C_{4}$ (carry into sign XOR carry out).
**Step 3 — Computation:** bit-wise $0111 + 0100 = 1011$; carries into sign $1$, out $0$; $V = 1$.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** $7 + 4 = 11$ exceeds $+7$ max, so signed overflow must flag; unsigned $11$ is legal, hence carry $0$.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** $V = 0$ misses the range breach; unchanged ignores addition; zero result is unrelated.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** $1011$ with overflow.

intro: Between adders and NAND conversion sits a family of circuits that are pure translation: code converters, which re-encode the same information for a different consumer, and magnitude comparators, which decide order. Both are the design procedure of Section 4.1 applied again — but each hides an algebraic shortcut. The BCD-to-excess-3 converter is the book’s grand worked design; binary-to-Gray is one exclusive-OR per bit; and the 4-bit comparator shows how a per-bit test snowballs into a cascade expression.
objectives: Design a BCD-to-excess-3 converter completely: truth table, four K-maps with don’t-cares, equations, circuit
Convert between binary and Gray code with the exclusive-OR relation and back with the cumulative exclusive-OR
Derive the 1-bit magnitude comparator’s three outputs
Extend to the 4-bit comparator and its cascade expression
Explain how MSI comparator chips cascade to arbitrary word length

concepts.statement: A **code converter** is a combinational circuit that translates binary information from one encoding to another: $n$ inputs in the source code, $m$ outputs in the target code, one truth-table row per valid symbol. The BCD-to-Gray converter of Section 4.1 was one; the classic worked example of the book is **BCD to excess-3**.
concepts.detail: Excess-3 codes each decimal digit as its value plus three, which makes the code self-complementing — complementing the bits yields the nine’s complement of the digit, a property the subtracting hardware of the era exploited. The converter receives $A\,B\,C\,D$ (BCD, digit value $8A + 4B + 2C + D$) and emits $W\,X\,Y\,Z$ with value $8W + 4X + 2Y + Z = 8A + 4B + 2C + D + 3$.

concepts.statement: Minimizing the four output maps (1s on rows for digits $d$, don’t-cares on rows 10–15) yields $$W = A + BC + BD, \qquad X = B′C + B′D + BC′D′ + AB′,$$ $$Y = C′D′ + CD, \qquad Z = D′.$$
concepts.detail: The last two show the arithmetic underneath: $Y$ and $Z$ are the two low bits of $d + 3$ viewed as functions of the BCD bits, and $Z = D′$ says the excess-3 low bit is simply the complement of the BCD low bit — adding three flips the parity of the low bit for every digit. The $X$ equation is the messiest because the carry structure of $+3$ crosses the middle of the digit range.

concepts.statement: For the **full binary** code (all $2^n$ combinations), Gray bits come from adjacent binary bits: $$G_n = B_n, \qquad G_i = B_{i+1} \oplus B_i \quad (i < n).$$ The inverse recovers binary cumulatively: $B_n = G_n$ and $B_i = B_{i+1} \oplus G_i$.
concepts.detail: Exclusive-OR of neighboring bits measures where the binary code changes step to step, which is exactly the one-bit-at-a-time property of Gray. The BCD-to-Gray converter of Section 4.1 could not use this clean chain on all four outputs only because its don’t-cares bought cheaper sums — restricted to the ten valid rows, the two designs agree.

concepts.statement: Comparing single bits $A$ and $B$ needs three outputs: $$ (A > B) = AB′, \qquad (A = B) = AB + A′B′ = (A \oplus B)′, \qquad (A < B) = A′B, $$ exactly one of which is 1 for any input pair.
concepts.detail: The equality output is the coincidence (XNOR) function of Section 2.6. The three functions are exhaustive and mutually exclusive — the property that lets wider comparators combine the per-bit verdicts with pure AND-OR logic.

concepts.statement: With per-bit equality $x_i = A_iB_i + A_i′B_i′$, the 4-bit verdicts are $$ (A = B) = x_3x_2x_1x_0, $$ $$ (A > B) = A_3B_3′ + x_3A_2B_2′ + x_3x_2A_1B_1′ + x_3x_2x_1A_0B_0′, $$ and symmetrically $$ (A < B) = A_3′B_3 + x_3A_2′B_2 + x_3x_2A_1′B_1 + x_3x_2x_1A_0′B_0. $$
concepts.detail: Read $(A > B)$ aloud: $A$ is bigger iff it wins at the most significant position where the two numbers differ — each term guards the higher equal bits with their $x$ factors and then demands $A_i = 1, B_i = 0$ at the deciding position. The three outputs remain mutually exclusive; hardware can compute the third as the NOR of the other two.

concepts.statement: A 4-bit comparator chip (the MSI 7485 of Chapter 5’s catalog) adds **cascade inputs** — the $(A > B)$, $(A = B)$, $(A < B)$ verdicts of a lower-order block — and reaches its verdict for the pair of 8-bit operands by consulting them only when its own four bits tie.
concepts.detail: The cascade expression above already contains the mechanism: when all $x_i = 1$ (a local tie), the external verdicts must flow through, so a chip wires its cascade inputs into the tail of its $(A > B)$ and $(A < B)$ chains. Word length then grows by a chip per 4 bits with no extra logic — the same packaging trick that made adders and counters one-chip functions in the MSI era that Chapter 5 surveys.

examples.title: The complete BCD-to-excess-3 design
examples.problem: Design the converter from BCD inputs $A\,B\,C\,D$ to excess-3 outputs $W\,X\,Y\,Z$, exploiting the six don’t-care rows.

steps.label: Step 1: Specification and table
steps.text: Each output is the corresponding bit of (digit $+\,3$): digit $0 = 0000 \to 0011$; $1 \to 0100$; $2 \to 0101$; $3 \to 0110$; $4 \to 0111$; $5 \to 1000$; $6 \to 1001$; $7 \to 1010$; $8 \to 1011$; $9 \to 1100$. Rows for $1010$ through $1111$ are X in all four output columns.

steps.label: Step 2: Map $W$ (the top bit)
steps.text: 1s on digits 5–9 (rows 5–9). One quad with the don’t-cares gives $A$ (all of rows 8–15); the remaining 1s at rows 5, 6, 7 pair up as $BC$ (rows 6, 7 + 14, 15) and $BD$ (rows 5, 7 + 13, 15): $W = A + BC + BD$ — 1 exactly when the digit is 5 or more, i.e. when $d + 3 \ge 8$.

steps.label: Step 3: Map $Z$ (the bottom bit)
steps.text: 1s on even digits 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (rows 0, 2, 4, 6, 8): every one of them has $D = 0$, and all don’t-care rows with $D = 0$ make the column quad free: $Z = D′$ — the cleanest possible output, one inverter.

steps.label: Step 4: Map $Y$
steps.text: 1s on digits 0, 3, 4, 7, 8 (rows 0, 3, 4, 7, 8): the column quad $\{0, 4, 8, 12\}$ gives $C′D′$ and the column quad $\{3, 7, 11, 15\}$ gives $CD$: $Y = C′D′ + CD$ — the equivalence function of the two low BCD bits.

steps.label: Step 5: Map $X$ (the hard one)
steps.text: 1s on digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 (rows 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9). Prime groups: the quad $\{1, 3, 9, 11\} = B′D$; the quad $\{2, 3, 10, 11\} = B′C$; the quad $\{8, 9, 10, 11\} = AB′$; and digit 4 can only pair with the don’t-care row 12: $BC′D′$. So $X = B′C + B′D + AB′ + BC′D′$ — 4 terms, 9 literals.

steps.label: Step 6: Verify two rows end to end
Step 7: Draw the diagram
steps.text: Count the gates: $W$ needs two 2-input ANDs and one 3-input OR; $X$ needs three 2-input ANDs, one 3-input AND and a 4-input OR; $Y$ one 2-input AND with an inverter, one AND, one OR; $Z$ one inverter — roughly a dozen gates plus shared complemented literals, exactly the two-level SOP shape the maps produce.

examples.result: BCD-to-excess-3 in four equations: $W = A + BC + BD$, $X = B′C + B′D + AB′ + BC′D′$, $Y = C′D′ + CD$, $Z = D′$ — verified on rows 4 and 9 and the textbook’s showcase of don’t-cares at work.

examples.title: Binary to Gray and back in one line each
examples.problem: Convert $1011_2$ to Gray code and convert the Gray word $1110$ back to binary.

steps.label: Step 1: Write the conversion rule
steps.text: Binary $B_3B_2B_1B_0$ to Gray $G_3G_2G_1G_0$: $G_3 = B_3$, then each lower Gray bit is the XOR of two adjacent binary bits: $G_i = B_{i+1} \oplus B_i$.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply to $1011$
steps.text: $G_3 = 1$; $G_2 = B_3 \oplus B_2 = 1 \oplus 0 = 1$; $G_1 = B_2 \oplus B_1 = 0 \oplus 1 = 1$; $G_0 = B_1 \oplus B_0 = 1 \oplus 1 = 0$. Gray word: $1110$.

steps.label: Step 3: Check the adjacency claim
steps.text: Binary $1011 = 11$: the Gray code of 11 is $1110$, and counting Gray steps from $1010$ (ten) to $1110$ changes exactly one bit at a time — the defining property survives the conversion.

steps.label: Step 4: Invert the map — Gray to binary
steps.text: Recovery runs top-down: $B_3 = G_3$; $B_2 = B_3 \oplus G_2$; $B_1 = B_2 \oplus G_1$; $B_0 = B_1 \oplus G_0$ — each binary bit accumulates the XOR of the Gray bits above it.

steps.label: Step 5: Apply to $1110$
steps.text: $B_3 = 1$; $B_2 = 1 \oplus 1 = 0$; $B_1 = 0 \oplus 1 = 1$; $B_0 = 1 \oplus 0 = 1$ → $1011$ — back to the original word, as the round trip must guarantee.

examples.result: Binary $1011 \to$ Gray $1110$; Gray $1110 \to$ binary $1011$ — conversion is a fan of XOR gates, recovery a cumulative chain of them.

examples.title: A 4-bit comparison, term by term
examples.problem: Evaluate the 4-bit comparator outputs for $A = 1010$ and $B = 1001$ using the cascade expressions.

steps.label: Step 1: Per-bit equality
steps.text: $x_3 = 1 \cdot 1 + 1′ \cdot 1′ = 1$; $x_2 = 1$ (both bits 0); $x_1 = 1 \cdot 0 + 1′ \cdot 0′ = 0$ (bits 1 vs 0); $x_0 = 0 \cdot 1 + 0′ \cdot 1′ = 0$ (bits 0 vs 1). The first difference appears at bit position 1.

steps.label: Step 2: Evaluate $(A = B)$
steps.text: $(A = B) = x_3x_2x_1x_0 = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 0 \cdot 0 = 0$ — the words are unequal, as the differing bits already showed.

steps.label: Step 3: Evaluate $(A > B)$
steps.text: Term by term: $A_3B_3′ = 1 \cdot 0 = 0$; $x_3A_2B_2′ = 1 \cdot 0 \cdot 1 = 0$; $x_3x_2A_1B_1′ = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1$ — hit: the words agree above position 1 and $A_1 = 1 > B_1 = 0$ there; the last term cannot matter once one fires: $(A > B) = 1$.

steps.label: Step 4: Evaluate $(A < B)$
steps.text: Every term dies: $A_3′B_3 = 0$; $x_3A_2′B_2 = 0$; $x_3x_2A_1′B_1 = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 0 \cdot 0 = 0$; the tail likewise: $(A < B) = 0$. Exactly one output is high ✓.

steps.label: Step 5: Interpret the structure
steps.text: The verdict came from the most significant differing position, guarded by the equality bits above it — which is exactly how the decimal comparison $10 > 9$ feels: the first digit that differs decides, everything to its right is irrelevant.

examples.result: $A = 1010 > B = 1001$: $(A{>}B) = 1$, $(A{=}B) = 0$, $(A{<}B) = 0$ — decided at bit 1, the highest position where the words differ.

keyTakeaways: A code converter is the design procedure pointed at a re-encoding: BCD-to-excess-3 gives $W = A + BC + BD$, $X = B′C + B′D + AB′ + BC′D′$, $Y = C′D′ + CD$, $Z = D′$.
The six invalid BCD rows are don’t-cares and routinely halve the logic — $Z$ collapses to a single inverter.
Full binary-to-Gray is one XOR per bit ($G_i = B_{i+1} \oplus B_i$); Gray-to-binary is the cumulative XOR chain.
1-bit comparison: $(A{>}B) = AB′$, $(A{=}B) = (A \oplus B)′$, $(A{<}B) = A′B$ — exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
4-bit comparison decides at the most significant differing bit; the $x_i$ guard terms make the expression a cascade, and MSI chips chain that way (Chapter 5).
The three comparator outputs are one-hot: hardware may compute the third as the NOR of the other two.

quiz.q: Why is excess-3 of the digit $d$ computed as $d + 3$?
options: To make room for a parity bit
The code is self-complementing: complementing the bits yields the nine’s complement of the digit
quiz.explanation: Excess-3 maps $d \to d + 3$ so that $9 - d$ corresponds to the bitwise complement of the code word — the property decimal machines used for nine’s-complement subtraction.

quiz.q: In the BCD-to-excess-3 design, the output $Z$ equals:
options: $D′$ — a single inverter, because adding 3 flips the parity of the low bit
quiz.explanation: Every even digit maps to an odd excess-3 value and vice versa: $Z = D′$ is the whole function — the cleanest demonstration of don’t-cares plus insight beating brute force.

quiz.q: The Gray code of binary $1011$ is:
options: $1110$ — each Gray bit XORs adjacent binary bits
quiz.explanation: $G_3 = 1$, $G_2 = 1 \oplus 0 = 1$, $G_1 = 0 \oplus 1 = 1$, $G_0 = 1 \oplus 1 = 0$: the word $1110$, one bit different from every Gray neighbor.

quiz.q: In the 4-bit comparator, the purpose of the $x_i$ factors in the term $x_3x_2A_1B_1′$ is to:
options: Ensure position 1 decides only when the higher positions are equal
quiz.explanation: The first differing position must decide; each term guards the higher bits with equality factors so it fires only if everything above agrees and $A_i = 1, B_i = 0$ at that position.

intro: The maps hand us sum-of-products expressions, but the physical part catalog hands us NAND and NOR — the natural transistors of TTL and CMOS. Fortunately the two universal gates can realize anything: a two-level AND-OR diagram converts to all-NAND by inspection, multilevel circuits convert by a disciplined bubble game, and the AND-OR-INVERT gate packages the complement of an SOP in one device. This section is the translator between Boolean algebra and the parts you can actually buy.
objectives: Show that NAND and NOR are functionally complete
Convert two-level AND-OR (SOP) circuits to two-level NAND circuits and POS circuits to NOR circuits
Use the alternate graphic symbols and the bubble-pushing transformation on multilevel circuits
Convert an arbitrary AND-OR network to an all-NAND network step by step
Recognize and use the AND-OR-INVERT (AOI) gate

concepts.statement: A gate type is **universal** if any Boolean function can be realized with gates of that type alone. NAND is universal: NOT is NAND with tied inputs ($x′ = (xx)′$), AND is NAND followed by that inverter, OR is NAND of the complemented inputs. By duality, NOR is universal too.
concepts.detail: The proof is three constructions: $x′ = (x \cdot x)′$; $xy = ((xy)′)′$; $x + y = (x′y′)′$ — the last by De Morgan. Since {NOT, AND, OR} generates every function, so does NAND alone. Economically this is why IC families lead with NAND: one mask, every circuit — the point Section 2.7 made about gate families and Chapter 5 will make about programmable logic.

concepts.statement: A two-level **AND-OR** circuit realizing an SOP expression $F = AB + CD$ converts to an all-NAND circuit by replacing both levels with NAND gates: $$F = AB + CD = \big((AB)′ \cdot (CD)′\big)′,$$ the second De Morgan theorem with the complement pushed to the inputs. The diagram: two NANDs feeding a third.
concepts.detail: The rule generalizes: an SOP with any number of product terms becomes NAND of NANDs, one NAND per product term plus one at the output. The two circuits have identical truth tables but different gate inventories — and the NAND version matches what the catalog sells.

concepts.term: Alternate graphic symbols and bubble pushing
concepts.statement: By De Morgan a NAND gate is **also** an OR gate whose inputs are inverted — its alternate symbol is an OR shape with bubbles on the inputs. Likewise NOR is an AND with bubbled inputs. **Bubble pushing** slides these inversion circles through the diagram in pairs: two bubbles on a wire cancel, and any single leftover bubble must be matched by complementing a literal.
concepts.detail: The game is what makes multilevel conversion visual: convert every AND-OR diagram so that gates alternate shapes-and-bubbles until every internal wire carries either two bubbles (which cancel) or zero, leaving NAND and NOR shapes only. One bubble left alone on an input means feeding that input’s complement literal instead.

concepts.statement: To convert an arbitrary AND-OR network to all-NAND: **(1)** express the function with AND and OR so that alternate levels are AND and OR (factor or expand as needed); **(2)** insert complementation pairs so each AND becomes a NAND whose output bubble feeds the next level; **(3)** cancel bubble pairs on internal wires; **(4)** complement any input literals that still meet a lone bubble; a first-level OR keeps its inputs complemented and becomes a NAND.
concepts.detail: Equivalently, by algebra: rewrite every AND as the NAND of the same inputs followed by double negation, and every OR as NAND of complemented inputs — $x + y = (x′y′)′$ — then cancel the double negations that share a wire. What survives is all-NAND by construction.

concepts.statement: An **AND-OR-INVERT (AOI)** gate is a single LSI/TTL device (the 54/7454 pattern) realizing $F = (AB + CD + \ldots)′$ — several ANDs feeding one NOR — i.e. the complement of an SOP in one package, one logic level faster than separate gates.
concepts.detail: Whenever the required function is the complement of a sum of products — comparator outputs like $(A{<}B)$, the $\overline{\text{enable}}$ signals of Chapter 5’s decoders — the AOI realizes it directly. The dual **OR-AND-INVERT** gate realizes the complement of a POS. Recognizing when a spec is naturally an inverted SOP is the mark of a designer who reads part catalogs.

concepts.statement: Everything above dualizes: a two-level **OR-AND** (POS) circuit converts to all-NOR, and a spec that arrives as a product of sums should be built that way. Which family to choose is set by which form the function naturally takes — SOP from the 1s of the map, POS from the 0s (Section 3.4).
concepts.detail: NAND-for-SOP and NOR-for-POS are the two sides of one coin, exactly as duality predicts. Mixing them — NAND here, NOR there — almost always costs extra inverters and levels; the disciplined designer picks one and sticks to it.

examples.title: Two-level conversion: $F = AB + CD$ to all-NAND
examples.problem: Convert the AND-OR realization of $F = AB + CD$ into a circuit using only NAND gates, and prove the equivalence.

steps.label: Step 1: The AND-OR circuit
steps.text: Two 2-input AND gates compute $AB$ and $CD$; one OR gate combines them — the literal wiring of the SOP form, three gates.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply De Morgan to the output
steps.text: $F = AB + CD$. By the second De Morgan theorem, $AB + CD = \big((AB)′ \cdot (CD)′\big)′$: the OR of two terms is the complement of the AND of their complements.

steps.label: Step 3: Recognize the NAND shapes
steps.text: Each inner term $(AB)′$ and $(CD)′$ is exactly a 2-input NAND of the literals; the outer complemented AND is a NAND of those two outputs: three NAND gates total.

steps.label: Step 4: Prove equivalence with the alternate symbols
steps.text: Push the output OR gate’s bubble onto its inputs: the OR-with-bubbles accepts the complemented products. Each input bubble meets an AND gate — an AND followed by a bubble **is** the NAND’s own alternate reading — so every gate is a NAND shape with no stray bubbles. The transformation cancelled itself into the catalog part.

steps.label: Step 5: One truth-table spot check
steps.text: At $ABCD = 1100$: $AB = 1$, $CD = 0$, so $F = 1$; the NAND circuit computes $(AB)′ = 0$, $(CD)′ = 1$, and the output NAND gives $(0 \cdot 1)′ = 1$ ✓. At $ABCD = 0000$: $F = 0$; the NAND circuit computes $(AB)′ = 1$, $(CD)′ = 1$, and the output gives $(1 \cdot 1)′ = 0$ ✓.

examples.result: Three NAND gates replace the AND-OR pair — $F = ((AB)′ \cdot (CD)′)′$ — the same truth table with one gate species instead of two.

examples.title: Multilevel conversion: $F = A(B + CD) + B′C$ to all-NAND
examples.problem: Convert the multilevel AND-OR realization of $F = A(B + CD) + B′C$ into an equivalent circuit using NAND gates only.

steps.label: Step 1: Draw the AND-OR levels
steps.text: Level by level: gate 1 computes $CD$ (AND); gate 2 computes $B + CD$ (OR); gate 3 computes $A \cdot (B + CD)$ (AND); gate 4 computes $B′C$ (AND, with a complemented literal); gate 5 (OR) produces $F$.

steps.label: Step 2: Transform the inner OR
steps.text: The OR gate becomes a NAND whose inputs are complemented: $B + CD = (B′ \cdot (CD)′)′$ — a NAND gate fed by $B′$ and by $(CD)′$.

steps.label: Step 3: Feed the NANDs
steps.text: The term $(CD)′$ is itself a NAND of $C$ and $D$ — so gate 1 turns into that NAND. The literal $B′$ needed by the inner NAND comes from a NAND with its two inputs tied: $B′ = (B \cdot B)′$.

steps.label: Step 4: Transform the upper levels
steps.text: Gate 3, $A \cdot (B + CD)$, becomes a NAND producing $\big(A(B + CD)\big)′$ — i.e. the NAND gate’s own complemented output; likewise gate 4 becomes a NAND of $B′$ and $C$ producing $(B′C)′$.

steps.label: Step 5: Combine at the top
steps.text: The final OR accepts the two complemented products, so it is a NAND of them: $F = \big(\big(A(B+CD)\big)′ \cdot (B′C)′\big)′ = A(B + CD) + B′C$ by De Morgan. Count: six NAND gates, of which one is the tied-input inverter for $B′$.

steps.label: Step 6: Verify one input combination
steps.text: At $ABCD = 1110$: target $F = 1(1 + 1 \cdot 0) + 1′ \cdot 0 = 1$. NAND chain: $(CD)′ = (10)′ = 1$; $B′ = 0$; inner NAND $= (0 \cdot 1)′ = 1$ (this is $B + CD = 1$); upper NAND $= (A \cdot 1)′ = 0$ (i.e. $A(B+CD) = 1$); side NAND $= (0 \cdot 0)′ = 1$; final NAND $= (0 \cdot 1)′ = 1$ ✓.

examples.result: Six NAND gates — including the tied-input NOT — realize the multilevel function with an identical truth table: bubble pushing turned AND-OR into the one-gate-type catalog circuit.

examples.title: One AOI gate for an inverted SOP
examples.problem: The Section 4.1 Gray converter needs $Y = (B_2B_0′ + B_1B_0′)′$ for a later stage. Realize it with a single AND-OR-INVERT gate.

steps.label: Step 1: Recognize the shape
steps.text: The required function is the complement of a two-term SOP — exactly the AOI pattern $F = (AB + CD)′$ with inputs $A = B_2$, $B = B_0′$, $C = B_1$, $D = B_0′$.

steps.label: Step 2: Wire the gate
steps.text: Feed the two AND sections of the AOI with $(B_2, B_0′)$ and $(B_1, B_0′)$; the device internally ORs the products and complements the result — the output is $Y$ with one package and one logic level.

steps.label: Step 3: Check the levels
steps.text: Built from discretes, the same function costs two ANDs, one OR and one inverter — three levels; the AOI does it in its single internal level, roughly halving the propagation delay.

steps.label: Step 4: Read the dual use
steps.text: Dually, if a POS complement were needed — $(x + y)(z + w)$ inverted — the OR-AND-INVERT gate would play the same trick on a product of sums. The lesson: before building the complement of a standard form, check the one-gate versions.

examples.result: One AOI package replaces four gates: $Y = (B_2B_0′ + B_1B_0′)′$ in a single level — inverted SOPs are a part number, not a project.

keyTakeaways: NAND (and dually NOR) is universal: NOT, AND and OR all fall out of one gate type, so one mask can build anything.
Two-level AND-OR ⇄ two-level NAND-NAND by De Morgan: $F = AB + CD = ((AB)′(CD)′)′$; POS ⇄ NOR-NOR dually.
Multilevel conversion is bubble pushing: insert complement pairs, cancel doubles on internal wires, complement literals that meet a lone bubble.
The worked multilevel conversion: $F = A(B + CD) + B′C$ needs exactly six NAND gates, one used as a tied-input inverter.
The AND-OR-INVERT gate realizes $(AB + CD + \ldots)′$ in one package and one level — reach for it whenever the spec is a complemented SOP.
Pick the family by the natural form: NAND with SOP (1s of the map), NOR with POS (0s of the map); mixing families buys inverters.

quiz.q: The inverter built from one NAND gate is:
options: NAND with both inputs tied to the same signal: $x′ = (x \cdot x)′$
quiz.explanation: Tying the inputs makes the AND redundant: $(x \cdot x)′ = x′$ — the first of the three constructions that prove NAND universal.

quiz.q: Converting the SOP circuit for $F = AB + CD$ to all-NAND yields how many gates, and of what kind?
options: Three NANDs — two for the products, one combining them
quiz.explanation: Each product term becomes one NAND (output complemented), and the combining OR becomes a NAND of those complemented products — De Morgan does the swap for free.

quiz.q: During bubble pushing, two inversion bubbles on the same internal wire:
options: Must be removed and replaced with an inverter
Cancel each other — the wire carries the uncomplemented signal
quiz.explanation: Double complementation is identity: $x″ = x$. Cancelling bubble pairs is how the transformation keeps the truth table invariant while reshaping the gates.

quiz.q: An AND-OR-INVERT gate directly realizes:
options: The complement of a sum of products: $(AB + CD + \ldots)′$
quiz.explanation: The AOI is ANDs feeding an internal NOR — one package, one level, the negated SOP — the exact shape of many enable and comparator signals.

intro: Beyond a handful of gates, designing every combinational function from discrete logic is wasteful. The MSI and LSI families package the recurring building blocks of digital design — decoders, encoders, multiplexers — as single integrated circuits, and the designer’s job becomes selecting and interconnecting them. This section shows how each block works internally and how it is used as a universal function implementer.
objectives: Explain what the MSI and LSI integration levels provide over gate-level (SSI) design
Expand decoders with enable inputs into larger decoders and implement Boolean functions as sums of minterms with a decoder plus one OR gate
Analyze and design priority encoders, including the valid-output signal
Use a multiplexer as a general-purpose function generator for any $n$-variable function
Describe the demultiplexer as a decoder operated with its enable as a data input

concepts.statement: Digital integrated circuits are classified by complexity: **SSI** (small scale) provides a few gates per package, **MSI** (medium scale) provides a dozen to a hundred gates wired into a standard function such as a decoder, adder or register, and **LSI** (large scale) provides a thousand or more gates in a single subsystem such as a memory or a microprocessor.
concepts.detail: The MSI/LSI viewpoint inverts the design process: instead of minimizing a Boolean function and drawing gates, the designer picks a catalog part whose internal structure already computes a general class of functions, then customizes the wiring around it. The same MSI part may be a decoder in one application, a demultiplexer in another, and a code converter in a third. This is the theme of the whole chapter: decoders, encoders, multiplexers, ROMs, PLAs and PALs are progressively more general function implementers.

concepts.statement: A **decoder** with $n$ inputs and $2^{n}$ outputs asserts exactly one output line — the one whose index equals the binary value of the inputs. Output $D_i = m_i$, so a decoder is a hardware **minterm generator**: it produces all $2^{n}$ minterms of its $n$ select variables.
concepts.detail: A 3-to-8 decoder with select inputs $x, y, z$ produces $D_0 = x'y'z'$, $D_1 = x'y'z$, up to $D_7 = xyz$. Decoders usually carry one or more **enable** inputs: when the enable is inactive, all outputs are 0 no matter what the selects are; when active, the decoder behaves normally. Enables are what make decoder expansion possible, and they are drawn as gate inputs in the block symbol.

concepts.statement: Two $3 \times 8$ decoders with enables combine into one **$4 \times 16$ decoder**: the three low-order inputs go to both decoders, and the fourth input drives the two enables in complementary polarity, so exactly one half is active at a time.
concepts.detail: For inputs $w, x, y, z$: connect $x, y, z$ to both decoders’ selects, enable decoder 1 with $w'$ (so it produces minterms $D_0$ through $D_7$ when $w = 0$) and decoder 2 with $w$ (minterms $D_8$ through $D_{15}$ when $w = 1$). The same idea scales both dimensions: four $3 \times 8$ decoders plus a $2 \times 4$ decoder on the enables build a $5 \times 32$ decoder.

concepts.term: Implementing functions with a decoder and OR gate
concepts.statement: Because the decoder outputs are the minterms, any Boolean function expressed as a sum of minterms, $F = \sum(\ldots)$, is realized by **OR-ing the decoded minterms** with a single OR gate. A NOR gate on the same outputs yields $F'$ directly.
concepts.detail: An $n$-input decoder plus one wide OR gate implements any function of $n$ variables, with no minimization required — the decoder does not care that most of its minterms are unused. Multiple output functions of the same variables share one decoder, each with its own OR gate. The price is the unused decoding capacity: this is exactly the trade-off the ROM of the next section makes formal.

concepts.statement: An **encoder** performs the inverse of a decoder: $2^{n}$ input lines produce an $n$-bit code. A plain encoder assumes exactly one input is asserted; a **priority encoder** resolves multiple simultaneous assertions by outputting the code of the highest-priority input, and it adds a **valid output $V$** to distinguish “input 0 asserted” from “no input asserted”. Both are false in the plain encoder, which is why $V$ is needed.
concepts.detail: Priority encoders are essential for interrupt systems (chapter 8 returns to them) and for keyboard scanning. The don’t-care entries in the priority truth table — all lower-priority inputs are irrelevant once a higher one is asserted — are what keep the minimized equations small.

concepts.statement: A **multiplexer (MUX)** routes one of $2^{k}$ data inputs to a single output under control of $k$ **select lines**: a $4 \times 1$ MUX with selects $S_1, S_0$ computes $$Y = S_1'S_0'\,I_0 + S_1'S_0\,I_1 + S_1S_0'\,I_2 + S_1S_0\,I_3.$$ Because each product is a minterm of the selects, a MUX is a sum of minterms whose coefficients are the data inputs.
concepts.detail: Inside, a $2^{k} \times 1$ MUX is a decoder whose AND gates are enlarged by the data input, feeding one OR gate — so MUX, decoder and ROM are one family of circuits. MSI examples: the 74153 is a dual $4 \times 1$ MUX and the 74151 is an $8 \times 1$ MUX with an enable (and a complementary output). An enable input also makes a MUX tree possible: two $4 \times 1$ MUXes plus the enable trick build an $8 \times 1$.

concepts.statement: Any Boolean function of $k$ variables can be implemented with **one $2^{k-1} \times 1$ MUX**: put $k-1$ variables on the select lines, and the remaining variable, its complement, 0 or 1 on each data input.
concepts.detail: The construction collapses the truth table in pairs: the two minterms that share a select combination determine one data input — $z$ if both are 1, $z'$ if the first is 1, the constant 1 if both are 1, 0 if both are 0. This works for functions of any size (iterate the halving for a MUX tree), at the cost of wiring density. A $k$-variable function that is genuinely arbitrary costs $2^{k-1}$ data connections; compare this with the $2^{k}$ words of storage a ROM would spend.

concepts.statement: A **demultiplexer** routes a single data input to one of $2^{n}$ destinations — the mirror image of the multiplexer. A decoder with an enable **is** a demultiplexer: the data go into the enable, and the select lines choose which output follows the data.
concepts.detail: When the enable input carries data, every output is 0 except the selected one, which equals the data stream — serial-to-parallel distribution. The dual use of the same part (decoder with enable = demux) is a classic example of MSI parts wearing several hats, and it appears again in chapter 8 where decoders drive the register-select lines of a common bus system.

examples.title: Building a 4×16 decoder from two 3×8 decoders
examples.problem: Using two 3×8 decoders, each with one enable input, construct a 4×16 decoder with inputs $w, x, y, z$, and then use it to implement the function $F(w,x,y,z) = \sum(1, 2, 4, 8)$.

steps.label: Step 1: Assign the low-order inputs
steps.text: Feed $x, y, z$ to the select inputs of both 3×8 decoders. Both decoders therefore decode the same three-bit value into a one-hot line $m_0 \ldots m_7$ of the pair $xyz$.

steps.label: Step 2: Use the fourth input for the enables
steps.text: Feed $w$ through an inverter to decoder 1’s enable and directly to decoder 2’s enable. When $w = 0$ only decoder 1 is enabled, so its outputs are $D_0$ through $D_7$ (the minterms with $w = 0$); when $w = 1$ only decoder 2 is enabled, giving $D_8$ through $D_{15}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Check the coverage
steps.text: Every 4-bit combination now asserts exactly one of the sixteen outputs: input 0110, for instance, has $w = 0$ and $xyz = 110$, so it asserts $D_6$ from decoder 1 while decoder 2 is fully disabled.

steps.label: Step 4: Realize the function
steps.text: For $F = \sum(1, 2, 4, 8)$, OR the outputs $D_1$, $D_2$, $D_4$ and $D_8$ with a 4-input OR gate. No gates other than the OR (and one inverter) are needed — the decoder supplies every minterm ready-made.

steps.label: Step 5: Observe the structure of $F$
steps.text: The minterms 0001, 0010, 0100, 1000 are pairwise non-adjacent on the K-map, so a gate realization needs four 4-input AND terms — the decoder-plus-OR version is not just simpler to design but also uses no more silicon.

examples.result: Two enabled 3×8 decoders plus an inverter form a 4×16 decoder; one 4-input OR gate on minterms 1, 2, 4, 8 completes the “exactly one of four inputs is 1” detector.

examples.title: Designing an 8-to-3 priority encoder
examples.problem: Derive the outputs of an 8-to-3 priority encoder with inputs $D_7$ (highest priority) down to $D_0$ (lowest), outputs $x$, $y$, $z$ and valid bit $V$, where the output code is the binary index of the highest asserted input.

steps.label: Step 1: Tabulate the behavior
steps.text: When $D_7 = 1$ the output is 111 regardless of $D_6 \ldots D_0$; when $D_7 = 0$ and $D_6 = 1$ the output is 110; and so on down to $D_1 = 1$ giving 001 and $D_0 = 1$ giving 000. When all inputs are 0, the outputs are 000 and $V = 0$; otherwise $V = 1$.

steps.label: Step 2: Mark the don’t-cares
steps.text: Each row of the table below the highest asserted input is irrelevant — these don’t-care conditions are what allow two-level minimization to stay small.

steps.label: Step 3: Derive $x$ and $V$
steps.text: The MSB of the code is 1 exactly for inputs 4 through 7: $x = D_4 + D_5 + D_6 + D_7$. The valid bit is the OR of everything: $V = D_0 + D_1 + \cdots + D_7$.

steps.label: Step 4: Derive $y$
steps.text: The middle bit is 1 for codes 2, 3, 6, 7 — that is, whenever $D_6$ or $D_7$ is asserted, or (with all of $D_7, D_6, D_5, D_4$ low) $D_2$ or $D_3$ is asserted: $y = D_6 + D_7 + D_4'D_5'(D_2 + D_3)$.

steps.label: Step 5: Derive $z$
steps.text: The LSB is 1 for the odd indices 1, 3, 5, 7. Gating each with the higher-priority zeros gives $z = D_7 + D_6'D_5 + D_6'D_4'D_3 + D_6'D_4'D_2'D_1$.

steps.label: Step 6: Verify two rows
steps.text: If only $D_5 = 1$: $x = 1$, $y = D_6'D_5 = 1$, $z = D_6'D_5 = 1$ — code 101, the index of $D_5$. If only $D_2 = 1$: $x = 0$, $y = D_4'D_5'(D_2 + D_3) = 1$, $z = 0$ — code 010. Both correct, and $V = 1$ in both.

examples.result: A 4-to-2 priority encoder is the same idea one size smaller; the 8-to-3 version needs 6 gates beyond the $V$ OR, and its equations show the tell-tale pattern of masked lower-priority inputs.

examples.title: Implementing a 3-variable function with a 4×1 multiplexer
examples.problem: Implement $F(x, y, z) = \sum(1, 3, 5, 6)$ using a single $4 \times 1$ multiplexer, and compare the cost with the decoder-plus-OR approach.

steps.label: Step 1: Choose the select variables
steps.text: Put the two most significant variables $x, y$ on the select lines $S_1, S_0$. Each data input $I_i$ then covers the pair of minterms that share that $xy$ combination, with $z$ as the free variable.

steps.label: Step 2: Evaluate each pair
steps.text: For $S_1S_0 = 00$ (minterms 0 and 1): $F = 0$ at 0 and $1$ at 1, so $I_0 = z$. For $01$ (minterms 2 and 3): $F = 1$ only at 3, so $I_1 = z$ as well. For $10$ (minterms 4 and 5): $F = 1$ at 5, so $I_2 = z$. For $11$ (minterms 6 and 7): $F = 1$ at 6 and $0$ at 7, so $I_3 = z'$.

steps.label: Step 3: Write the resulting circuit
steps.text: The multiplexer output is $Y = x'y'z + x'yz + xy'z + xyz'$, which is exactly the given function. Only the wiring of $z$ and $z'$ to the data inputs is needed — no external gates at all.

steps.label: Step 4: Compare with a decoder
steps.text: The same function via a 3×8 decoder needs an OR gate over minterms 1, 3, 5, 6. The MUX version uses fewer packages for a single function, while the decoder version is more economical when many functions of the same variables must be built together — the book makes exactly this comparison when introducing MSI selection criteria.

examples.result: Data inputs $(z, z, z, z')$ on a $4 \times 1$ MUX with $x, y$ on the selects implement $F$ with no auxiliary gates; in general a $k$-variable function needs a $2^{k-1} \times 1$ MUX.

keyTakeaways: An $n$-input decoder asserts exactly one of $2^{n}$ outputs and is therefore a complete minterm generator.
Enable inputs let small decoders compose into large ones: two enabled 3×8 decoders build a 4×16.
A decoder plus one OR gate realizes any sum-of-minterms function of its inputs; a NOR gate realizes the complement.
A priority encoder outputs the index of the highest-priority asserted input, with a valid bit $V$ to flag the all-zeros case.
A $2^{k} \times 1$ multiplexer output is a sum of minterms of its select lines weighted by the data inputs.
Any $k$-variable function fits one $2^{k-1} \times 1$ MUX: selects carry $k-1$ variables, data inputs carry the last variable, its complement, 0 or 1.
A decoder with its enable used as a data input is a demultiplexer — one MSI part, two design roles.

quiz.q: A $4 \times 16$ decoder is built from two $3 \times 8$ decoders. What drives the two enable inputs?
options: The two lowest-order select bits, one to each decoder
The highest-order input bit and its complement, one to each decoder
A common clock signal to both decoders
The valid output $V$ of an encoder
quiz.explanation: The low-order bits feed both decoders; the extra bit $w$ steers the enables so decoder 1 covers words 0–7 ($w = 0$) and decoder 2 covers words 8–15 ($w = 1$).

quiz.q: A Boolean function $F(A,B,C) = \sum(0, 2, 5, 7)$ is to be implemented with a 3×8 decoder and one logic gate. Which gate, connected to which outputs?
options: An XOR gate on outputs 0 and 7
quiz.explanation: Decoder output $D_i$ is minterm $m_i$, so a sum of minterms is just an OR of the listed outputs — one OR gate and no minimization required.

quiz.q: In a priority encoder, the valid output $V$ exists because:
options: The output code must be latched before it changes
The code 000 must be distinguishable from “no input asserted”
Priority encoders can only handle even numbers of inputs
quiz.explanation: When input $D_0$ is asserted the output code is 000 — the same as the idle code. $V$ is the OR of all inputs, so it separates “input 0 asserted” from “nothing asserted”.

quiz.q: To implement an arbitrary Boolean function of 6 variables using a single multiplexer, the MUX size required is:
options: $32 \times 1$ with 5 variables on the select lines
$64 \times 1$ with all 6 variables on the select lines
$16 \times 1$ with 4 variables on the select lines
$8 \times 1$ with 3 variables on the select lines
quiz.explanation: The function-generator construction halves the table: $2^{k-1} = 32$ data inputs, with the sixth variable (or its complement, or a constant) wired to each input.

quiz.q: How is a demultiplexer most economically obtained in an MSI-based design?
options: By connecting two multiplexers back to back
By using a decoder and applying the data to its enable input
By adding OR gates to the outputs of a priority encoder
By disabling the select lines of a MUX
quiz.explanation: With data on the enable, the selected output follows the data and all others stay 0 — routing one source to one of $2^{n}$ destinations.

quiz.q: $F(A,B,C) = \Sigma(0,2,5,7)$ is to be built with a $3$-to-$8$ decoder and one logic unit. Which unit on which outputs does it?
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** three variables, listed $1$-minterms $0,2,5,7$.
**Step 2 — Rule:** decoder output $D_i$ equals minterm $m_i$; a sum of minterms is an OR of those outputs.
**Step 3 — Apply:** wire $D_0, D_2, D_5, D_7$ into a $4$-input OR; output $1$ exactly on the listed rows.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** complement rows $1,3,4,6$ would need NOR/AND forms, not asked here.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** AND of $1$-rows gives $0$ almost everywhere; NOR of complement rows is dual but not the asked wiring; two-input XOR covers two rows only.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** one OR over $0,2,5,7$.

quiz.q: How is $F(A,B,C) = \Sigma(1,2,6,7)$ built with one $8$-to-$1$ multiplexer?
options: It cannot be done with a multiplexer
Select $S_2S_1S_0 = ABC$, data $D_1 = D_2 = D_6 = D_7 = 1$, rest $0$
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** three-variable truth table with four $1$-rows.
**Step 2 — Rule:** an $8$-to-$1$ unit with select $= ABC$ routes exactly one data input per row; tying data to constants programs the table.
**Step 3 — Apply:** set $D_1,D_2,D_6,D_7$ to $1$ and the other four to $0$; the output reproduces $F$ row by row.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** a $4$-to-$1$ version would instead use $AB$ as select and $C$/constants as data — same idea, fewer pins.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** $AB$-only select needs data functions of $C$, not constants alone; two units are unnecessary; impossibility contradicts universality.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** program four data lines to $1$.

intro: A read-only memory is the combinational circuit concept pushed to LSI scale: a fixed decoder feeding a programmable OR plane. Internally it is just a decoder plus OR gates, yet because the stored pattern can be chosen per unit, a ROM replaces whole boards of random logic for multi-output functions. Programming a ROM means writing out its truth table.
objectives: Describe the internal organization of a ROM as decoder plus programmable OR connections
State the size of a ROM as $2^{n}$ words of $m$ bits for $n$ address lines, and compute total bit counts
Program a ROM from a truth table, exploiting don’t-care conditions
Explain the difference between mask-programmed ROMs and user-programmable PROMs
Judge when a ROM is the right implementation medium for a set of functions

concepts.statement: A **read-only memory (ROM)** is an LSI combinational unit with $n$ address inputs and $m$ data outputs: it contains $2^{n}$ fixed words of $m$ bits, and the address word selects which stored **data word** drives the outputs. Internally it is an $n \times 2^{n}$ decoder whose outputs (the word lines) feed $m$ OR gates through connections that are either made or absent.
concepts.detail: The book insists on the combinational view: nothing is stored dynamically and there is no clock — the outputs are a pure function of the address inputs, determined by which fuse connections exist on each word line. A $32 \times 8$ ROM has 5 address lines, 32 words of 8 bits, and internally a 5×32 decoder feeding eight 32-input OR gates.

concepts.statement: A ROM is specified as **$2^{n} \times m$**: $2^{n}$ words of $m$ bits each, so the total storage is $2^{n} \cdot m$ bits and the package exposes $n$ address pins and $m$ data pins.
concepts.detail: A $16 \times 4$ ROM stores $64$ bits; a $1024 \times 8$ ROM stores $8192$ bits. When a ROM is used as a combinational circuit, the $n$ inputs are the address lines, the $m$ outputs are the functions, and the $2^{n}$ stored words are exactly the rows of the truth table.

concepts.statement: To implement a set of $n$-input, $m$-output functions in a ROM: list the full truth table with all $2^{n}$ rows, and make each row a stored word. The ROM then emits row $i$ whenever the inputs equal the binary value $i$ — **the truth table itself is the program**.
concepts.detail: No minimization is required or even useful: the decoder already generates every minterm internally, whether the function uses it or not. Don’t-care rows can be programmed arbitrarily (usually 0) since the corresponding input combinations never occur in the application.

concepts.statement: A **mask-programmed ROM** has its connection pattern fixed at manufacture by a metallization mask — cheap per unit in huge volumes, but a design change means a new mask. A **PROM** (programmable ROM) ships blank and is programmed once by the customer, typically by blowing fusible links with current pulses.
concepts.detail: The blow-a-fuse step is irreversible, so PROM prototyping is done carefully with verified patterns. The book also notes erasable variants (EPROM), which clear the pattern with ultraviolet light so the same silicon can be reprogrammed. The mask-versus-PROM decision is an economic one: mask cost amortizes over volume, PROM flexibility pays for low-volume and development work.

concepts.statement: A ROM is the natural medium when the functions are **complex, multi-output, and dense in minterms** — code converters, arithmetic look-up tables, character generators. When functions are sparse (few minterms used), most of the $2^{n}$ words store nothing useful, and a PLA (next section) does the same job with far less silicon.
concepts.detail: The decision sequence the book builds across this chapter: gates for small functions, MSI decoders/MUXes for a few functions, ROM when the whole truth table is genuinely needed, PLA when product terms can be shared and minimized, PAL as the economical middle ground.

examples.title: A squaring ROM: 3-bit input, 6-bit output
examples.problem: Design a ROM-based combinational circuit that accepts a 3-bit number $A_2A_1A_0$ and outputs its square. Minimize the required ROM size by exploiting structure in the table.

steps.label: Step 1: Compute the squares
steps.text: For inputs 0 through 7 the squares are $0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49$ — six-bit values ranging from $000000$ to $110001$. A naive design stores all six output bits for each of the 8 words: an $8 \times 6$ ROM.

steps.label: Step 3: Examine the least significant bit
steps.text: The LSB column of the squares reads $0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1$ — exactly the input bit $A_0$. Squares inherit the parity of their root, so $B_0 = A_0$ always.

steps.label: Step 4: Remove the redundant column
steps.text: Wire $A_0$ directly to output $B_0$ and store only $B_5B_4B_3B_2B_1$ in the ROM: an $8 \times 5$ ROM with data $00000, 00000, 00010, 00100, 10000, 11000, 10010, 11000$.

steps.label: Step 5: Verify two rows
steps.text: Input $110$ (6): stored word $10010$ plus hard-wired $B_0 = 0$ gives $100100 = 36$. Input $101$ (5): stored $11000$ plus $B_0 = A_0 = 1$ gives $110001 = 25$. Correct.

examples.result: An $8 \times 5$ ROM (40 bits) plus one wire implements the squarer; observing $B_0 = A_0$ saved an entire output column, the book’s standard demonstration of pruning a ROM table.

examples.title: A BCD-to-excess-3 code converter in a 16×4 ROM
examples.problem: Implement the 4-input, 4-output BCD-to-excess-3 converter in a ROM, handling the six unused BDC input combinations sensibly.

steps.label: Step 2: Treat invalid codes as don’t-cares
steps.text: Inputs $1010$ through $1111$ never occur in BCD, so those six words are don’t-cares. In a gate design they would shrink the K-maps; in a ROM they are simply programmed with 0s (or any convenient filler) — the capacity is paid for either way.

steps.label: Step 3: Size the ROM
steps.text: Four address lines require $2^{4} = 16$ words; four outputs require $m = 4$ bits per word: a $16 \times 4$ ROM, 64 bits total.

steps.label: Step 4: Program it
steps.text: Store the ten output codes at addresses 0–9 and zeros at 10–15. The converter is complete — one package, no gates, and if the specification later changes to excess-3 with different entries, only the stored pattern changes.

steps.label: Step 5: Compare with gates
steps.text: The gate-minimized version of this same converter (a chapter 4 design problem) needs several packages of AND/OR logic. The ROM wins on parts count and on design time; it loses on silicon utilization since 6 of 16 words are wasted.

examples.result: A $16 \times 4$ ROM programmed with the ten excess-3 codes implements the converter in a single LSI part — the classic demonstration of a ROM as four functions sharing one truth table.

keyTakeaways: A ROM is an $n \times 2^{n}$ decoder plus $m$ OR gates with fixed (made-or-absent) connections — purely combinational, no clock.
Size notation $2^{n} \times m$ means $2^{n}$ stored words of $m$ bits; total bits $= 2^{n} m$.
Programming a ROM means writing its truth table; minimization is unnecessary because the decoder generates every minterm anyway.
Don’t-care input combinations cost nothing to leave unminimized in a ROM, but their words still occupy capacity.
Mask-programmed ROMs are fixed at manufacture; PROMs are field-programmed once by blowing fuses; EPROMs add erasability.
ROMs shine for dense multi-output functions; sparse functions waste most of the $2^{n}$ words and belong in a PLA.

quiz.q: A ROM has 10 address pins and 8 data pins. How many bits does it store, and how is it specified?
quiz.explanation: Ten address lines address $2^{10} = 1024$ words of 8 bits each: $1024 \times 8$ = 8192 stored bits.

quiz.q: When implementing combinational functions in a ROM, the stored program is best described as:
options: The full truth table, one row per address
The K-map groupings of each output
A list of required product terms
quiz.explanation: Each address word stores the row of the truth table; the decoder selects the row matching the current inputs, so the table itself is the ROM’s content.

quiz.q: A 4-input function uses only 3 of its 16 possible input combinations. Why is a ROM still an acceptable but inefficient choice?
options: ROMs cannot implement functions with unused input combinations
The 13 unused words still occupy address space and silicon, wasting capacity
The ROM would need external gates to suppress the unused words
ROM outputs are only valid for sequential circuits
quiz.explanation: ROM capacity is paid in full regardless of use: for sparse functions most of the $2^{n}$ words are wasted, which is exactly the gap a PLA fills.

quiz.q: The essential difference between a mask-programmed ROM and a PROM is:
options: The PROM is faster because it is smaller
The mask ROM’s pattern is fixed at manufacture; the PROM is field-programmed once, usually by blowing fuses
The PROM can be written and rewritten at run time
The mask ROM stores fewer bits per package
quiz.explanation: Mask programming amortizes a one-time mask cost over volume; PROM programming (fuse blowing) happens at the user’s site and is irreversible. Run-time rewritable behavior belongs to later RAM/EEPROM families, not the ROM of this chapter.

intro: The ROM’s decoder always generates every minterm; the programmable logic array relaxes this by making the AND plane programmable too. Only the product terms a design actually needs are formed, and any output may share them. The PAL then trades some of that flexibility for lower cost. Together with the ROM these three parts span the practical options for two-level combinational design at LSI scale.
objectives: Describe the AND-OR structure of a PLA and its $n \times p \times m$ size specification
Construct a PLA programming table with 1/0/– entries and implement multiple functions sharing product terms
Explain the PAL’s fixed OR plane and its consequences for term sharing
Choose among ROM, PLA and PAL for a given set of functions

concepts.statement: A **PLA** is an LSI combinational unit with a **programmable AND plane feeding a programmable OR plane**: $n$ inputs, $p$ product-term (AND) gates and $m$ sum (OR) gates. Any set of sum-of-products functions with at most $p$ total product terms fits, and one product term can feed several OR gates.
concepts.detail: Each AND gate sees every input and its complement and programmably selects which to include — it can thus form any product term, not only minterms. Each OR gate programmably selects which of the $p$ terms to sum. Because the AND plane is not a full decoder, a PLA of modest size ($p \ll 2^{n}$) implements sparse functions far more economically than a ROM.

concepts.statement: The PLA program is a table with one row per product term: the **inputs columns** carry $1$ (variable in true form), $0$ (complemented) or $–$ (absent), and the **outputs columns** carry $1$ (term connected to that OR gate) or $–$ (not connected).
concepts.detail: For example, a row $(1, –, 1 \,|\, 1, –)$ is the term $A C$ connected to the first output only. The table is the complete fuse map of the device — the designer’s minimization work happens before writing it, because every product term saved is a row (and real silicon) saved.

concepts.statement: When several functions are implemented together, they must be **minimized jointly**: a product term used by more than one output is realized once in the AND plane and simply connected to each OR gate that needs it. Minimizing each function in isolation forfeits this sharing.
concepts.detail: The procedure: simplify each function with K-maps (or Quine–McCluskey from chapter 3), then look for terms common to several functions and re-express the functions to maximize overlap. The total number of distinct product terms is the PLA resource that matters — it can be smaller than the sum of the individual function needs.

concepts.statement: A **PAL** has a **programmable AND plane and a fixed OR plane**: each output OR gate is hard-wired to a dedicated set of AND lines (typically three or four per output in commercial parts). Programmability exists only on the input side.
concepts.detail: The fixed OR plane removes a level of programmable wiring, making a PAL cheaper and faster than a comparable PLA, at the cost of flexibility: a function needing more product terms than its output’s allowance must be restructured (for instance by factoring through another output). PALs with flip-flops on the outputs become the registered PALs used for sequential design.

concepts.term: Choosing among ROM, PLA and PAL
concepts.statement: Use a **ROM** when nearly every minterm of the inputs is needed (dense tables); use a **PLA** when functions are sparse and share many product terms; use a **PAL** when cost dominates and each output fits the fixed term count.
concepts.detail: All three are two-level AND–OR structures; they differ only in which plane is programmable. ROM: fixed AND (full decoder), fixed-at-manufacture OR. PLA: programmable AND, programmable OR. PAL: programmable AND, fixed OR. The PLA is the most flexible and most expensive; the PAL dominates commodity programmable logic for exactly the reason economies of scale predict.

examples.title: Programming a PLA for two functions with a shared product term
examples.problem: Implement $F_1(A,B,C) = \sum(3, 5, 6, 7)$ and $F_2(A,B,C) = \sum(3, 4, 5, 6, 7)$ in a PLA, minimizing the number of product terms by sharing.

steps.label: Step 1: Minimize $F_1$
steps.text: The minterms 011, 101, 110, 111 pair up on the K-map as $AB$, $AC$ and $BC$ — this is the majority function: $F_1 = AB + AC + BC$ (three 2-literal terms, no simpler cover exists).

steps.label: Step 2: Minimize $F_2$
steps.text: Minterms 100, 101, 110, 111 are covered by the single literal $A$; minterm 011 ($A'BC$) is covered by $BC$: $F_2 = A + BC$.

steps.label: Step 3: Identify the sharing
steps.text: The term $BC$ appears in both functions. Total distinct product terms: $AB$, $AC$, $BC$ and $A$ — four rows in the PLA table, versus five if each function were wired independently.

steps.label: Step 4: Write the programming table
steps.text: Row 1 ($AB$): inputs $(1, 1, –)$, outputs $(1, –)$ — feeds $F_1$. Row 2 ($AC$): inputs $(1, –, 1)$, outputs $(1, –)$. Row 3 ($BC$): inputs $(–, 1, 1)$, outputs $(1, 1)$ — feeds both. Row 4 ($A$): inputs $(1, –, –)$, outputs $(–, 1)$.

steps.label: Step 5: Verify with an input
steps.text: At $ABC = 011$: rows 1, 2, 4 evaluate to 0; row 3 ($BC$) is 1, so $F_1 = 1$ and $F_2 = 1$. Checking against the minterm lists: $011 = 3$ appears in both — correct.

examples.result: A PLA of size $3 \times 4 \times 2$ (3 inputs, 4 product terms, 2 outputs) implements both functions; a ROM doing the same job would need all $8$ decoded words.

examples.title: The same functions in a PAL
examples.problem: Repeat the implementation of $F_1 = AB + AC + BC$ and $F_2 = A + BC$ in a PAL whose OR gates each draw from a dedicated set of three AND terms, and compare the resource counts.

steps.label: Step 1: Map $F_1$ to a PAL output
steps.text: $F_1$ needs exactly three product terms ($AB$, $AC$, $BC$), which fits a three-term output. The PAL assigns dedicated AND lines: $AB$, $AC$ and $BC$ all feed $F_1$’s OR gate.

steps.label: Step 2: Map $F_2$ to another output
steps.text: The fixed OR plane means $F_2$ cannot borrow the $BC$ term already formed for $F_1$ — each output owns its AND lines exclusively. $F_2$’s output therefore needs its own copies: $A$ and $BC$, two of its three available terms.

steps.label: Step 3: Count the AND gates
steps.text: The PAL forms $AB$, $AC$, $BC$, $A$ and a second copy of $BC$: five product terms total. The PLA needed only four because it shared $BC$ between outputs.

steps.label: Step 4: Assess the trade
steps.text: The PAL uses one extra AND gate but saves the entire programmable-OR wiring layer — in a commodity part with dozens of outputs, this trade is what makes the PAL cheaper to manufacture and buy.

steps.label: Step 5: Note the design rule
steps.text: If a function ever needs more terms than its output provides, the designer factors it (e.g., routing a partial sum through a spare output) — a constraint that simply never arises in a PLA.

examples.result: PAL: 5 AND terms, no sharing possible; PLA: 4 AND terms with $BC$ shared; ROM: 8 full minterms. The trio cleanly illustrates the flexibility-versus-cost ladder.

keyTakeaways: A PLA is a programmable AND plane into a programmable OR plane, specified as $n \times p \times m$ (inputs × product terms × outputs).
The programming table uses 1/0/– input entries (true/complement/absent) and 1/– output entries (connected or not).
Functions implemented together must be minimized together so that shared product terms are realized once.
A PAL fixes the OR plane: each output gets a dedicated bundle of AND terms, so sharing between outputs is impossible but silicon is cheaper.
Choose ROM for dense truth tables, PLA for sparse shared-term logic, PAL for low-cost moderate logic.
All three devices are two-level AND–OR structures differing only in which plane is programmable — the chapter’s unifying insight.

quiz.q: In a PLA programming table, the input entry “–” in a product-term row means:
options: The variable does not participate in that product term
The term is disconnected from all outputs
The value is a don’t-care to be chosen later
quiz.explanation: 1 = variable in true form, 0 = complemented, – = absent from the term; $–$ entries are what let a PLA form reduced product terms rather than only minterms.

quiz.q: Two functions share the product term $BC$. How does this affect a PLA versus a PAL implementation?
options: Both realize the term once and route it to both outputs
The PLA realizes $BC$ once; the PAL must duplicate it on each output that needs it
Neither device can implement shared terms
The PAL realizes it once because its AND plane is fixed
quiz.explanation: The PLA’s programmable OR plane can connect one AND output to several OR gates; the PAL’s fixed OR wiring dedicates AND lines to a single output, forcing duplication.

quiz.q: Which structure corresponds to a ROM’s internal organization?
options: Programmable AND plane and programmable OR plane
Fixed full decoder (AND plane) with fixed-at-manufacture OR connections
Programmable AND plane with fixed OR plane
A bank of D flip-flops with a common clock
quiz.explanation: A ROM always decodes every input combination (full AND plane) and stores its pattern in the made-or-absent OR connections, fixed by mask or fuse.

quiz.q: A design needs 12 functions of 10 variables, each using only 4 or 5 product terms. Which implementation is most appropriate?
options: A ROM, because the table is $1024 \times 12$
A PLA, because the functions are sparse and may share terms
quiz.explanation: A ROM would store $1024$ words per output and use only a handful; a PLA with roughly $12 \times 5$ product terms (fewer with sharing) exploits the sparsity exactly.

intro: A combinational circuit forgets everything when its inputs change; a sequential circuit remembers. The memory lives in storage elements whose outputs feed back to their own inputs, and the gentlest of them — the latch — is just two cross-coupled gates. This section builds the ladder from the basic SR latch through clocked, edge-triggered flip-flops to the JK and T types that make counters and state machines practical.
objectives: Explain the difference between combinational and sequential circuits, and the role of feedback
Analyze the cross-coupled NAND SR latch in all four input combinations, including the forbidden one
State the characteristic tables and equations of the SR, D, JK and T flip-flops
Describe edge triggering, the master-slave construction and the asynchronous set/reset inputs
Apply setup and hold time constraints to compute a maximum clock frequency

concepts.statement: A **sequential circuit** has outputs that depend not only on the present inputs but on the past history of inputs — its **internal state**, held in storage elements. The state plus the inputs determine both the outputs and the next state, so sequential circuits contain feedback paths from storage outputs back to their inputs.
concepts.detail: Combinational circuits can always be described by a truth table; sequential circuits need a state table or state diagram (Section 6.2). When all state elements change on a common clock signal, the circuit is **synchronous**; without a clock (as in the basic latch or an asynchronous ripple counter) it is **asynchronous**.
