Settling delay is one flip-flop delay plus carry-logic delay — independent of counter length under lookahead carry.
The toggle law $T_i = Q_0Q_1\cdots Q_{i-1}$ generates a binary up-counter of any width.
The synchronous BCD counter wraps 9 → 0 with $J_2 = Q_1Q_8'$ and $K_8 = Q_1$ doing the decade-specific work; carry out is $Q_8Q_1$.
Serial carry chains enable signals through one AND gate per stage; parallel (lookahead) carry computes each enable in one level from the state.
Unused-state analysis must confirm no lockout: every unused code should funnel back into the count sequence.

quiz.q: What primarily limits the maximum clock frequency of a long synchronous binary counter with serial carry?
options: The serial carry chain — each stage adds one gate delay to the next stage’s enable
The number of output decode gates
quiz.explanation: Within a stage the decision is one flip-flop delay, but with ripple carry the $i$-th stage’s enable waits for $i$ chained AND gates — the counter’s speed degrades linearly like a ripple counter’s.

quiz.q: In the synchronous BCD counter, why does $J_2$ include the factor $Q_8'$?
options: So that at count nine, with $Q_1 = 1$ and $Q_8 = 1$, bit 2 stays 0 and the counter wraps to 0000 instead of reaching 1010
quiz.explanation: The binary toggle law would set $Q_2$ at the 9 → next transition; masking it with $Q_8'$ is the decade correction that makes the sequence return to zero.

quiz.q: Parallel (lookahead) carry in a counter is characterized by:
options: Each enable computed directly as the AND of the current enable and all lower blocks’ ready signals — one gate level deep
Using the flip-flops’ direct clear inputs
quiz.explanation: Lookahead trades wide AND gates for depth: every stage’s toggle permission comes straight from the present state, so the total carry delay stays constant as the counter grows.

quiz.q: A synchronous counter powers up in an unused state and never reaches the intended count sequence. This failure is called:
quiz.explanation: Lockout: the unused states form a closed cycle under the synthesized equations. The design check — evaluate the equations on every unused code — prevents it.

intro: Counters do more than count events: sequenced properly, they manufacture time. A control unit needs a repeating ladder of timing signals — $T_0$, $T_1$, …, one per clock — to say “do this now, that next,” and a whole-word interval for serial operations. Ring counters, switch-tail (Johnson) counters and modulo-$N$ counters are the three standard generators, each trading flip-flops against decode gates differently.
objectives: Generate timing signal sequences $T_0, T_1, \ldots$ with a ring counter or a switch-tail counter
Decode Johnson counter states with two-input AND gates
Design a modulo-$N$ counter with T flip-flops for arbitrary $N$, including the unused-state check
Produce a word-time control interval for serial operations and compare implementation costs

concepts.statement: A set of **timing signals** $T_0, T_1, \ldots, T_{k-1}$ is a one-hot sequence recurring every $k$ clocks: exactly one signal is high in each period. The basic computer of chapter 8 gates every microoperation with such signals ($T_0$: fetch address, $T_1$: fetch instruction, $T_2$: decode — and so on).
concepts.detail: Timing signals are the state assignment made visible: any counter plus a decoder produces them, but dedicated shift-register structures produce them with fewer gates or fewer flip-flops depending on the choice below. The period $k$ is chosen to match the longest operation to be sequenced.

concepts.statement: A **ring counter** is a shift register whose last output feeds its serial input, circulating a single 1. With $k$ flip-flops it produces $k$ states — $k$ timing signals — with **no decoding gates at all**: each flip-flop output is directly a $T_i$.
concepts.detail: The circulating one is initialized through the direct set input of stage 0 (and clears of the rest). The cost is flip-flop-inefficiency: $k$ states from $k$ flip-flops versus the $\lceil\log_2 k\rceil$ a binary counter needs. For $k = 8$, the ring uses 8 flip-flops and zero decode gates — maximum simplicity, minimum density.

concepts.statement: A **switch-tail counter** circulates the complement of the last stage: shift register with $Q_{n-1}'$ fed back to the serial input. It passes through $2n$ states (twice a ring counter’s yield), and every state is uniquely decoded by **one two-input AND gate** of an adjacent flip-flop pair.
concepts.detail: The 4-bit sequence is 0000 → 1000 → 1100 → 1110 → 1111 → 0111 → 0011 → 0001 → (repeat). Decodes: the first state is $Q_3'Q_0'$, the second $Q_3Q_2'$, the third $Q_2Q_1'$, the all-ones state $Q_3Q_0$, and so on — every state is a boundary between a run of 1s and a run of 0s, and that boundary is visible in exactly one adjacent pair.

concepts.statement: A **modulo-$N$ counter** counts $0, 1, \ldots, N-1$ and returns to 0, using $n = \lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ flip-flops and $N - 2^{n}$ unused states, which serve as K-map don’t-cares. Timing signals come from an $n$-to-$2^n$ decoder on the state bits.
concepts.detail: This is the general design procedure of Section 6.4 applied to a counting sequence; the interesting engineering is the wrap logic and the lockout check. Cost profile: minimum flip-flops, $n$-wide decode gates — the opposite corner of the ring counter.

concepts.statement: A **word-time** is the interval spanning one full pass of the bit positions of a serial word: $n$ clock periods for an $n$-bit word. It is generated by an $n$-state timing chain (ring, Johnson or mod-$N$) whose first and last timing signals mark the interval boundaries.
concepts.detail: Serial adders, multipliers and the I/O of the basic computer need exactly this envelope signal to know when a word transfer has completed. The OR of all $n$ timing signals gives the word-time waveform directly; alternatively, a mod-$n$ counter with an outer flip-flop toggled at the count reset achieves the same thing for very long words.

examples.title: A mod-6 counter with T flip-flops
examples.problem: Design a synchronous modulo-6 counter (states $Q_2Q_1Q_0$ counting 000 → 101 → 000) using T flip-flops, and verify recovery from the unused codes.

steps.label: Step 1: State table
steps.text: The six transitions: 000→001, 001→010, 010→011, 011→100, 100→101, 101→000. States 110 and 111 are don’t-cares in the excitation maps.

steps.label: Step 2: Excitation requirements
steps.text: Rule: $T = 1$ wherever the bit must change. $Q_0$ changes in every transition: $T_0 = 1$. $Q_1$ changes only at 001→010 (0→1) and 011→100 (1→0): $T_1 = 1$ at states 001 and 011. $Q_2$ changes at 011→100 and 101→000: $T_2 = 1$ at states 011 and 101.

steps.label: Step 3: K-maps with the two don’t-cares
steps.text: For $T_1$ (ones at 001, 011; dcs at 110, 111): the groups give $T_1 = Q_0(Q_1 + Q_2')$. For $T_2$ (ones at 011, 101; dcs at 110, 111): the groups give $T_2 = Q_0(Q_1 + Q_2)$.

steps.label: Step 5: Check lockout
steps.text: From unused state 110: $T_0 = 1$, others 0 → 111. From 111: $T = (1, 1, 1)$ → 000 — inside the cycle. A power-up in either unused code re-enters the count within two clocks: no lockout.

steps.label: Step 6: Derive the timing signals
steps.text: Six 3-input decode gates on the state bits give $T_0 \ldots T_5$; the OR of all six is the 6-clock word-time envelope for 6-bit serial operations.

examples.result: $T_0 = 1$, $T_1 = Q_0(Q_1 + Q_2')$, $T_2 = Q_0(Q_1 + Q_2)$ — three flip-flops, three gates; both unused states funnel back into the cycle.

examples.title: Word-time with a switch-tail counter
examples.problem: Generate eight timing signals $T_0 \ldots T_7$ and the 8-bit word-time envelope for a serial subsystem, using a 4-bit switch-tail counter, and compare the cost with a ring counter and a binary counter.

steps.label: Step 1: Build the switch-tail
steps.text: Four D flip-flops in a shift register with the complement of the last stage fed back: $D_0 = Q_3'$, $D_i = Q_{i-1}$. Initialize to 0000 through the direct inputs.

steps.label: Step 2: Write the state sequence
steps.text: 0000 → 1000 → 1100 → 1110 → 1111 → 0111 → 0011 → 0001 → back to 0000: eight states from four flip-flops — twice the ring counter’s yield.

steps.label: Step 3: Decode with two-input gates
steps.text: Each state is the unique boundary between the leading run of 1s and the trailing run of 0s. $T_0 = Q_3'Q_0'$ (all clear), $T_1 = Q_3Q_2'$, $T_2 = Q_2Q_1'$, $T_3 = Q_1Q_0'$, $T_4 = Q_3Q_0$ (all set), $T_5 = Q_3'Q_2$, $T_6 = Q_2'Q_1$, $T_7 = Q_1'Q_0$ — eight 2-input AND gates, no wider logic.

steps.label: Step 4: Form the word-time envelope
steps.text: The word-time signal is the OR of the eight timing signals (one 8-input gate): high for the full eight-clock span, one period per serial bit position. Its falling edge marks “word complete” for the handshake logic.

steps.label: Step 5: Compare implementations
steps.text: Ring counter: 8 flip-flops, zero decode gates. Switch-tail: 4 flip-flops, eight 2-input gates. Binary mod-8: 3 flip-flops, an 8-output 3×8 decoder (gates of 3 inputs). All three produce the same eight timing signals — the choice is where the hardware budget is spent.

examples.result: A 4-bit switch-tail counter plus eight 2-input AND gates yields $T_0 \ldots T_7$ and the word-time envelope; flip-flop count and gate count can be traded freely among the three structures.

keyTakeaways: Timing signals are one-hot-per-clock sequences $T_0, T_1, \ldots$; chapter 8 gates every microoperation on them.
A ring counter gives $k$ states from $k$ flip-flops with no decoding gates.
A switch-tail (Johnson) counter gives $2n$ states from $n$ flip-flops, each decoded by one two-input AND gate.
A modulo-$N$ counter uses the fewest flip-flops ($\lceil\log_2 N\rceil$) and a decoder for the signals.
Design of mod-$N$ counters follows Section 6.4’s procedure; the lockout check on unused states is mandatory.
The word-time envelope — the OR of all timing signals — spans $n$ clock periods and frames serial word transfers.

quiz.q: How many distinct states does a 5-bit switch-tail (Johnson) counter cycle through, and with what decode gate complexity?
options: 10 states, each decoded with one 2-input AND gate
quiz.explanation: The switch-tail doubles the ring’s yield ($2n = 10$) and every state is a unique 1s/0s boundary visible in one adjacent flip-flop pair — a 2-input AND per state.

quiz.q: A timing subsystem needs $T_0 \ldots T_7$ with absolutely minimal combinational logic and has flip-flops to spare. The best choice is:
options: A mod-8 binary counter with a 3×8 decoder
A ripple counter with decoded outputs
quiz.explanation: The ring counter’s flip-flop outputs are the timing signals directly — zero decode gates — at the cost of 8 flip-flops, exactly the trade stated in the question.

quiz.q: In the mod-6 design, the toggle equations are $T_0 = 1$, $T_1 = Q_0(Q_1 + Q_2')$, $T_2 = Q_0(Q_1 + Q_2)$. Starting from state 101, the next state is:
quiz.explanation: At 101: $T_1 = 1(0 + 0) = 0$ and $T_2 = 1(0 + 1) = 1$, so only $Q_2$ toggles: 101 → 000 — the modulo-6 wrap.

quiz.q: The word-time signal for an 8-bit serial operation:
options: Is a single clock pulse at the end of the word
Spans eight clock periods — one per bit position of the word
Is the clock divided by 8 only
quiz.explanation: The envelope must cover every bit period of the word: high for all eight clocks, typically formed as the OR of the eight timing signals.

quiz.q: How many distinct states does a $4$-bit ring counter cycle through?
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** $4$ stages, single circulating $1$.
**Step 2 — Rule:** ring holds one $1$ rotating through $n$ positions; states $= n$.
**Step 3 — Trace:** $1000 \to 0100 \to 0010 \to 0001 \to 1000$.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** no decoding needed for timing use; each stage directly is one timing pulse $T_i$.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** $16$ is binary-counter states; $8$ is $3$-bit binary; $10$ is $5$-bit Johnson.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** $4$ states.

quiz.q: A $5$-bit switch-tail (Johnson) counter cycles through how many states, each decoded with what complexity?
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** $n = 5$, complemented feedback.
**Step 2 — Rule:** Johnson states $= 2n$; each state is identified by two adjacent stage values, hence $2$-input decoding.
**Step 3 — Count:** $2 \times 5 = 10$ states ($00000, 10000, 11000, \ldots, 00001$).
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** $5$-bit binary would give $32$; ring would give $5$; Johnson doubles the ring by using both phases.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** $32$ is binary; $5$ is ring; $20$ doubles twice.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** $10$ states, $2$-input decodes.

quiz.q: A control unit needs $8$ repeating timing pulses with minimal decoding. Which counter fits, and how many flip-flops does it need?
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** $8$ pulses, minimize decode complexity.
**Step 2 — Rule:** ring needs $n$ stages for $n$ pulses; Johnson needs $n/2$ stages for $n$ pulses ($2n$ states); binary needs $\log_2 n$ stages but multi-input decodes.
**Step 3 — Compare:** ring $8$ stages; Johnson $4$ stages with $2$-input decodes; binary $3$ stages with $3$-input decodes.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** Johnson halves the ring at the cost of $2$-input decodes; binary minimizes flip-flops but maximizes decode width.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** $8$-bit binary wastes stages; $8$-bit ring is the largest; $3$-bit binary is smallest but decode-heavy.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** $4$-bit Johnson balances stages and decoding.

intro: A random-access memory is the register concept industrialized: thousands of storage cells addressed through one decoder, read and written under external control. This section treats the RAM as a system component — its address, select and read/write control lines, its access-time timing, and above all the technique of building large memories from small chips by expanding words, bits, or both at once.
objectives: Describe the RAM block: address lines, bidirectional data, memory select and read/write controls
Explain the internal address decoding that selects one word out of $2^k$
State the read-cycle and write-cycle timing requirements including access time
Expand memory in the word direction using chip selects from the extra address bits
Expand memory in the bit direction with parallel chips and combine both expansions

concepts.statement: A **RAM** is a read/write memory in which any of its $2^k$ words is reached equally fast: a $k$-bit address, decoded internally, selects the word; $m$ bidirectional data lines carry the word; a **memory select (CS)** enables the chip and a **read/write (R/W)** control chooses the direction.
concepts.detail: “Random access” contrasts with sequential media (tapes, shift-register memories) where reach time depends on position. A $16 \times 4$ RAM has 4 address lines, 4 data lines, and 16 words of 4 bits — 64 storage cells. Static RAMs store each bit in a flip-flop-like cell; the RAM of this chapter is the static kind.

concepts.statement: Inside the RAM, a $k \times 2^k$ decoder turns the address into a one-hot **word line** that enables one row of cells; the read/write logic then gates either the cells’ stored bits onto the data lines (read) or the data lines into the cells (write).
concepts.detail: The decoder is exactly the chapter 5 component: word $i$ is selected when the address equals $i$. Because one decoder serves the whole chip, the cost of decoding is amortized across all cells — the same economy of scale that made ROMs attractive. The chip select, in effect an enable on the whole decoder, is what permits the expansion techniques below.

concepts.statement: A **read cycle** holds the address stable, asserts CS with R/W = 1, and the data appear on the outputs after the **access time** $t_A$; a **write cycle** holds the address stable, asserts CS with R/W = 0, and pulses the data in — the address must be established before the write command and held after it, and the data must satisfy setup and hold around it.
concepts.detail: Access time is the RAM’s headline number: the delay from a stable address to valid output data. The address setup margin before the write edge, the write pulse width, and the data hold after the edge complete the specification — the same three-number timing contract ($t_{su}$, width, $t_h$) that governs flip-flops in Section 6.1, now at the system level.

concepts.statement: To build a memory with **more words** from small chips: give every chip the low-order address bits in parallel, and drive each chip’s select from a decoder on the high-order bits — one extra address bit doubles the word count and selects between two chips.
concepts.detail: The extra address lines run to a small decoder whose outputs become the individual CS inputs; at any instant exactly one chip drives the shared data lines. This requires the chips to have disabled (high-impedance or open) outputs when deselected — the tri-state discipline of chapter 8’s bus.

concepts.statement: To build a memory with **wider words**: connect chips in parallel with identical address, select and R/W wiring; each chip contributes its own slice of the data lines. Two $16 \times 4$ chips make a $16 \times 8$ memory with no extra logic whatsoever.
concepts.detail: Every chip sees the same address at the same time and performs the same operation on its slice of the word — the memory equivalent of the carry-parallel structure of an adder. Combining both directions: $c$ chips of $2^k \times m$ build up to $c \cdot 2^k \times m$ words of $c \cdot m$ bits in a $\sqrt{c} \times \sqrt{c}$ arrangement.

examples.title: Word expansion: two 16×4 RAMs into a 32×4 RAM
examples.problem: Build a 32-word by 4-bit memory from $16 \times 4$ RAM chips. Specify all wiring and verify the addressing of location 22.

steps.label: Step 1: Determine the new address width
steps.text: Thirty-two words require $2^5 = 32$ codes: five address bits $A_4A_3A_2A_1A_0$. Each chip itself decodes only four bits, so the fifth bit selects which chip holds the word.

steps.label: Step 2: Wire the low-order address
steps.text: Connect $A_3A_2A_1A_0$ in parallel to the four address pins of both chips — both chips see the same 4-bit offset within their own 16-word space.

steps.label: Step 3: Decode the extra bit into chip selects
steps.text: Use an inverter (a $1 \times 2$ decoder): chip 0’s CS gets $A_4'$ and chip 1’s CS gets $A_4$. When $A_4 = 0$, addresses 0–15 reach chip 0; when $A_4 = 1$, addresses 16–31 reach chip 1. (With active-low CS inputs, the inverter is placed on the appropriate branch.)

steps.label: Step 4: Merge the data lines
steps.text: Connect the two chips’ data outputs to the same four data lines: the deselected chip’s outputs are in the high-impedance state, so only the selected chip drives the bus. For writes, both CS and R/W gating steer the data into the selected chip only.

steps.label: Step 5: Verify location 22
steps.text: $22 = 10110_2$: $A_4 = 1$ selects chip 1, and the offset $0110_2 = 6$ addresses chip 1’s internal word 6 — which is the seventh word of the upper block: global location $16 + 6 = 22$. Reading $A_4A_3A_2A_1A_0 = 10110$ returns exactly the stored word.

examples.result: Five address lines, one inverter, two $16 \times 4$ chips: a $32 \times 4$ memory in which the MSB of the address chooses the chip and the rest choose the word within it.

examples.title: Bit expansion: two 16×4 RAMs into a 16×8 RAM
examples.problem: Build a 16-word by 8-bit memory from $16 \times 4$ RAM chips and state how to extend the technique to $32 \times 8$.

steps.label: Step 1: Wire the shared control
steps.text: Connect the four address lines, the memory select CS and the read/write control identically to both chips — every operation happens to both chips simultaneously.

steps.label: Step 2: Split the data bus
steps.text: Chip 0 supplies data lines $D_3D_2D_1D_0$ (the low nibble) and chip 1 supplies $D_7D_6D_5D_4$ (the high nibble). No decoding logic is needed: the two chips never contend because they drive disjoint lines.

steps.label: Step 3: Verify a write
steps.text: Writing the byte $1011\,0110$ to address $7$: both chips receive address 0111 and R/W = write; chip 0 stores $0110$ in its word 7, chip 1 stores $1011$ in its word 7. A later read of address 7 reassembles the full byte.

steps.label: Step 4: Combine with word expansion
steps.text: For $32 \times 8$: take the bit-expanded pair above and duplicate it, using the $A_4$/$A_4'$ inverter trick from the previous example to select between the two pairs — four chips total: two for word doubling, two for bit doubling, one inverter.

steps.label: Step 5: State the general count
steps.text: Chips needed $= (\text{words desired}/\text{words per chip}) \times (\text{bits desired}/\text{bits per chip})$: here $32/16 \times 8/4 = 4$ chips of $16 \times 4$.

examples.result: Bit expansion is pure parallelism (identical control wiring, disjoint data slices); combined with the chip-select technique it builds any $2^n \times m$ memory from small parts.

keyTakeaways: A RAM exposes $k$ address lines, $m$ bidirectional data lines, a chip select and a read/write control; internally a $k \times 2^k$ decoder selects one word line.
Read: address stable, CS active, R/W = 1, data valid after access time $t_A$. Write: address setup before and hold after the write command, with data setup/hold around it.
Word expansion feeds low address bits to all chips and decodes the extra bits into chip selects.
Bit expansion wires chips in parallel with identical control, each contributing a slice of the data lines.
A $2^a \times m$ memory from $2^k \times m_0$ chips needs $2^{a-k} \times m/m_0$ chips.
Merged output lines require deselected chips to present high impedance — the same tri-state discipline the common bus of chapter 8 relies on.

quiz.q: A $64 \times 8$ RAM has how many address and data lines?
quiz.explanation: $64 = 2^6$ words need 6 address bits; the word width is 8 bits, so 8 data lines.

quiz.q: In word expansion, the extra address bits (beyond each chip’s address pins) are used to:
options: Drive a decoder whose outputs become the individual chip selects
quiz.explanation: The high-order bits select which chip owns the addressed word; the low-order bits select the word within the enabled chip.

quiz.q: Two $16 \times 4$ RAM chips are wired with common address, CS and R/W, chip A on data lines $D_3 \ldots D_0$ and chip B on $D_7 \ldots D_4$. The resulting memory is:
quiz.explanation: Same word count (16), doubled word width (8): classic bit expansion with no extra logic.

quiz.q: During a RAM write cycle, the address must be:
options: Allowed to change freely during the write pulse
Stable before the write command begins and held until after it ends
Latched only after the data are removed
quiz.explanation: If the internal decoder’s selection changes mid-write, the data can be stored into the wrong word — address setup and hold margins are part of the write-cycle contract, like flip-flop timing.

quiz.q: When several RAM outputs share one set of data lines in a word-expanded memory, the mechanism that prevents contention is:
options: Series resistors sized for worst case
Deselected chips drive high impedance (tri-state) outputs, so only the selected chip drives
quiz.explanation: The chip select disables the output drivers of every chip except the one being read — the tri-state discipline formalized in chapter 8’s common-bus systems.

intro: A digital computer is, at bottom, an enormous collection of registers and gates. This chapter opens the register-transfer level of description: a symbolic language in which R1 ← R2 says everything that matters about moving a word, and a control function P says when it may happen. From those two ideas — the transfer and its control — grow the arithmetic, logic and shift microoperations, the common bus, the instruction code and finally the whole fetch–decode–execute rhythm of the basic computer that the rest of this chapter assembles.
objectives: Define the register-transfer language and explain what level of design it occupies
Read and write transfer statements with control functions, including the conditional if (P) then (R1 ← R2) form
Use the basic RTL symbols: letters, parentheses, arrows, commas, colons and subscripts
Execute arithmetic microoperations, including subtraction by both 1’s- and 2’s-complement addition
Apply the logic microoperations AND, OR, XOR and NOT to selective-set, selective-complement, selective-clear, mask, insert and clear
Distinguish logical shifts, circular shifts through E, arithmetic shifts with sign preservation, and serial transfer

concepts.statement: A **register-transfer language** is a symbolic notation for describing the inter-register transfers and elementary operations of a digital system at a level between logic design (gates and flip-flops) and system design (processors and memories).
concepts.detail: Instead of drawing circuits, the designer writes statements. The statement names registers, states what moves where, and states the Boolean condition under which the move happens. Mano uses this language through the rest of the book: the processor of Chapter 9, the control unit of Chapter 10 and the complete basic computer are all specified in it.

concepts.statement: The statement **R1 ← R2** means: replace the content of register R1 with the content of register R2, the transfer occurring at the next clock pulse edge. The arrow points from source to destination; R2 is unchanged.
concepts.detail: A register is always *some* binary string, so the statement really says: copy the n wires driven by R2 into the n flip-flops of R1 at the edge. If the destination can capture data on its own clock, the hardware is nothing but wires plus a load enable — the schematic of Figure 1. Transfers are written per register, never per bit: the whole word moves as one.

concepts.term: Control functions and the conditional form
concepts.statement: A **control function** is a Boolean function of timing and status variables that gates a transfer: **P: R1 ← R2** means “if (P) then (R1 ← R2)” — the transfer occurs at every clock pulse for which P = 1.
concepts.detail: The colon terminates the control function. P may be a timing signal $T_1$, a decoded opcode such as $D_3$, or any product such as $D_3 T_4$. In hardware the control function is an AND gate that enables the destination register’s load input, which is why a transfer never happens “whenever” — only at a clock edge while its control line is asserted. Two microoperations separated by a comma execute in the same clock period; two statements written on separate lines execute in different periods.

concepts.statement: The language uses six conventions: **capital letters** (with digits) denote registers; **parentheses** denote a bit or bit range of a register; the **arrow** ← denotes a transfer; the **comma** separates simultaneous microoperations; the **colon** terminates a control function; **subscripts** name individual flip-flops or bit ranges.
concepts.detail: Examples: AR, PC, DR are registers; DR(0–11) or the subscripted form $\mathrm{DR}_{0\text{–}11}$ names the low-order twelve bits of DR; T: AR ← PC, PC ← PC + 1 says both happen under control function T in one period. Brackets enter the language in Section 8.2, where M[AR] names the memory word whose address sits in AR. Every microoperation of the basic computer is written with no more than these symbols.

concepts.statement: The **arithmetic microoperations** are addition $R_3 \leftarrow R_1 + R_2$, subtraction $R_3 \leftarrow R_1 - R_2$, increment $R \leftarrow R + 1$ and decrement $R \leftarrow R - 1$ — each a single clock-period operation of the adder network.
concepts.detail: Subtraction never needs a subtractor: the 2’s complement converts it to addition, $R_1 - R_2 = R_1 + \bar{R}_2 + 1$, and the carry out of the most significant position is simply discarded. The 1’s-complement variant $R_1 + \bar{R}_2$ omits the +1 and instead adds the **end-around carry**: if the addition produces a carry out, that carry is fed back into the least significant position. Increment and decrement are the special cases of adding 1 and adding $-1$ (the all-ones word).

concepts.statement: The **logic microoperations** manipulate bits of a word independently: $A \leftarrow A \wedge B$ (AND), $A \leftarrow A \vee B$ (OR), $A \leftarrow A \oplus B$ (XOR) and $A \leftarrow \bar{A}$ (NOT). Their five classic applications are selective-set, selective-complement, selective-clear, mask and insert.
concepts.detail: With B selecting bit positions: **selective-set** ($A \vee B$) forces 1s where B has 1s; **selective-complement** ($A \oplus B$) flips exactly the bits where B has 1s; **selective-clear** ($A \wedge \bar{B}$) forces 0s where B has 1s; **mask** ($A \wedge B$) keeps the bits where B has 1s and clears the rest; **insert** replaces a field with new bits by first masking it clear and then OR-ing in the value. Clearing a whole register is $A \leftarrow A \oplus A$ (or $A \wedge 0$), the cheapest constant generator in the machine.

concepts.statement: The **shift microoperations** are shl (shift left), shr (shift right), cil (circular left) and cir (circular right); **arithmetic shifts** ashl and ashr move the magnitude bits while preserving the sign bit, dividing and multiplying by 2.
concepts.detail: Logical shifts enter 0s at the empty end. Circular shifts rotate through the carry flip-flop E, the basic computer’s link between the shifter and the ALU: cir moves AC(0) into E and E into AC(15). An arithmetic shift right replicates the sign bit so that $\text{ashr}(x)$ computes $\lfloor x/2 \rfloor$ for signed x — note $11011$ (−5) shifts to $11101$ (−3), rounding toward minus infinity, not toward zero. **Serial transfer** moves a word between registers one bit per clock over a single wire — the n-bit transfer costs n pulses.

examples.title: Reading and writing RTL statements
examples.problem: Translate between words and symbols. (a) What does T1: AR ← PC, PC ← PC + 1 do, and in how many clock periods? (b) Write symbolically: “if the decoded instruction D3 and timing signal T4 are both 1, store AC into the memory word addressed by AR.” (c) What does the subscripted range IR(0–11) name in a 16-bit instruction register?

steps.label: Step 1: Parse (a)
steps.text: One control function T1 gates two comma-separated microoperations, so both happen in the SAME clock period: AR takes the program counter’s value while PC simultaneously advances — a parallel transfer plus an increment, not a sequence.

steps.label: Step 2: Write (b)
steps.text: The control function is the AND of D3 and T4; the transfer is a memory write: **D3T4: M[AR] ← AC**. This is exactly the execute step of the store instruction STA in Section 8.4.

steps.label: Step 3: Interpret (c)
steps.text: Parentheses (or the subscript form $\mathrm{IR}_{0\text{–}11}$) name the low-order twelve bits of IR — in the basic computer, the address field of an instruction word.

steps.label: Step 4: Count the commas
steps.text: Note the contrast with T: AR ← PC followed on the next line by T: PC ← PC + 1 — written as two statements they claim two periods; the comma is what buys simultaneity.

examples.result: The colon = control, the arrow = transfer, the comma = same period, parentheses = bit selection. With these four conventions plus register names, every microoperation of the basic computer is expressible.

examples.title: Subtraction by complement addition
examples.problem: With 4-bit registers A = 0110 (6) and B = 0011 (3), compute A − B three ways: with a true subtractor, with the 1’s-complement method including the end-around carry, and with the 2’s-complement method. Then repeat with A = 0011 (3) and B = 0110 (6) to see the negative case.

steps.label: Step 1: 2’s complement, positive result
steps.text: Add the complement plus one: $0110 + \bar{B} + 1 = 0110 + 1100 + 1$. The sum $0110 + 1100 = 10010$, and $10010 + 1 = 10011$. The leftmost bit is a carry OUT of the 4-bit word; it is discarded, leaving **0011 = 3**.

steps.label: Step 2: 1’s complement with end-around carry
steps.text: Add without the +1: $0110 + 1100 = 10010$. A carry appeared, so it is NOT discarded here — it is added back to the least significant bit: $0010 + 1 = 0011 = 3$ ✓. The end-around carry is the manual correction for the missing +1.

steps.label: Step 3: The negative case, 1’s complement
steps.text: Now A = 0011, B = 0110: $0011 + 1001 = 1100$. No carry out means the result is negative and needs NO correction: $1100$ reads as −3 in 1’s complement ✓ (check: invert for magnitude, $0011 = 3$).

steps.label: Step 4: The negative case, 2’s complement
steps.text: Same operands with the +1: $0011 + 1001 + 1 = 1101$, which reads as −3 in 2’s complement ✓ — and again no carry to worry about.

examples.result: Carry out + discard means the 2’s-complement result is positive; no carry means negative. The end-around carry of the 1’s-complement method is precisely the bookkeeping the +1 does for free in the 2’s-complement method — the masters depth derives why this always works.

examples.title: The five logic-microoperation applications
examples.problem: Take AC = 1010 and the selector word B = 0110 (it selects bit positions 1 and 2). Show the effect of each application: selective-set, selective-complement, selective-clear, mask, and an insert that replaces the low two bits of AC with 11. Finish by clearing AC entirely.

steps.label: Step 1: Selective-set (OR)
steps.text: AC ← AC ∨ B = $1010 \vee 0110 = 1110$: the selected positions (bits 1, 2) are forced to 1 regardless of their prior value.

steps.label: Step 2: Selective-complement (XOR)
steps.text: AC ← AC ⊕ B = $1010 \oplus 0110 = 1100$: exactly the selected bits flip (bit 1: 1→0, bit 2: 0→1), the others pass through.

steps.label: Step 3: Selective-clear (AND with complement)
steps.text: AC ← AC ∧ B̄ = $1010 \wedge 1001 = 1000$: the selected positions are forced to 0.

steps.label: Step 4: Mask and insert
steps.text: Mask: AC ← AC ∧ 1100 = $1000$ — keep the field where the mask is 1, clear the rest. Insert: first mask the field away, then OR the new value in: $(1010 \wedge 1100) \vee 0011 = 1000 \vee 0011 = 1011$ — the low two bits now read 11.

steps.label: Step 5: Clear
steps.text: AC ← AC ⊕ AC = $0000$: XOR of a word with itself annihilates every bit — no constant inputs needed.

examples.result: One operand word B and three gates (AND, OR, XOR) give the machine surgical control over arbitrary bit fields of AC — the mechanism behind the AND, CMA and CLA instructions of Section 8.3.

examples.title: Shifting a word through E
examples.problem: With the 4-bit accumulator AC = 1010 and the carry flip-flop E = 1, give the result (and the new E) of shr, shl, cil, cir, and of the arithmetic shifts ashr and ashl applied to the signed 5-bit value 11011 (−5). How long does a serial transfer of the word take?

steps.label: Step 1: Logical shifts
steps.text: shr: 0 enters the left, E ← AC(0) = 0: AC = 0101, E = 0. shl: the left bit leaves into E, 0 enters the right: AC = 0100, E = 1.

steps.label: Step 2: Circular shifts through E
steps.text: cir (rotate right): E circulates into the top: AC = 1101 with E ← old AC(0) = 0. cil (rotate left): E enters the bottom: AC = 0101 with E ← old AC(3) = 1. Nothing is lost — the 5 bits AC·E just rotate.

steps.label: Step 3: Arithmetic shifts
steps.text: ashr of 11011 (−5): the sign bit stays and replicates: 11101 = −3 = $\lfloor -5/2 \rfloor$ — note it rounds DOWN, not toward zero. ashl: 10110 = −10 with E ← 1 capturing the shifted-out bit; a true multiply-by-2 only when the sign does not change.

steps.label: Step 4: Serial transfer
steps.text: Moving the 4-bit word from one register to another over a single wire shifts one bit per clock pulse: 4 pulses, each clocking both the source’s shr and the destination’s shl — the cost of saving three wires.

examples.result: Logical shifts drop bits, circular shifts keep them in AC·E, arithmetic shifts preserve the sign and compute multiply/divide by 2 — with the floor-toward-minus-infinity asymmetry that the masters depth examines.

keyTakeaways: RTL describes a system at the register level: **P: R1 ← R2** means “if (P) then (R1 ← R2)” at the next clock edge, with the colon marking the control function.
The comma buys simultaneity: two microoperations in one statement share one clock period.
Subtraction needs no subtractor: $A - B = A + \bar{B} + 1$ (2’s complement, discard the carry) or $A + \bar{B}$ with end-around carry (1’s complement).
The logic microoperations give field surgery on words: OR sets, XOR complements, AND masks, insert = mask then OR, and A ⊕ A clears.
Circular shifts rotate AC·E; arithmetic shifts preserve the sign, and ashr computes $\lfloor x/2 \rfloor$.
Serial transfer moves a word one bit per clock — n pulses for n bits.

quiz.q: R1 holds 1010 and R2 holds 0110. After the microoperation R1 ← R2, what does R1 hold?
quiz.explanation: The destination takes the source’s content: R1 ← 0110. The source R2 is unchanged.

quiz.q: In the statement P: R2 ← R1, what is P and what does it do?
options: A register that is copied along with the transfer
A Boolean control function; the transfer occurs at every clock pulse for which P = 1
The parity of the word being moved
quiz.explanation: The colon terminates the control function — an AND of timing and status variables that gates the destination’s load input.

quiz.q: Which pair of microoperations executes in a single clock period?
options: AR ← PC and PC ← PC + 1 written with a comma between them
AR ← PC written on one line and PC ← PC + 1 written on the next line
No two transfers can ever share a period
quiz.explanation: The comma marks simultaneous microoperations — one statement, one clock period. Separate statements claim separate periods.

quiz.q: With A = 0110 (6) and B = 0011 (3), the 2’s-complement subtraction $A + \bar{B} + 1$ produces 10011 in 5 bits. What is the 4-bit result?
options: 0100 = 4, keeping the carry as a sign bit
quiz.explanation: The carry out has weight $2^4$ beyond the 4-bit word and is discarded; the remaining 0011 is the correct difference $6 - 3 = 3$.

quiz.q: In 1’s-complement subtraction, when is the end-around carry added back?
options: Only when the addition produces a carry out of the most significant position — the positive-result case
Only when the result is negative
quiz.explanation: A carry out means the true difference was positive; adding the carry back to the LSB supplies the missing +1. No carry means the result stands as a negative 1’s-complement value.

quiz.q: AC = 1010. After the selective-complement microoperation AC ← AC ⊕ 0110, AC holds:
quiz.explanation: XOR flips exactly the bits where the operand has 1s: bit 1 (1→0) and bit 2 (0→1), giving $1010 \oplus 0110 = 1100$.

quiz.q: AC = 1010 and the mask word is 1100. After AC ← AC ∧ 1100, AC holds:
quiz.explanation: The mask keeps bits where it has 1s (the high pair) and clears the rest: $1010 \wedge 1100 = 1000$.

quiz.q: To replace the low two bits of AC = 1010 with the new value 11, the insert sequence is:
quiz.explanation: Insert = mask the field clear, then OR in the new bits: $1000 \vee 0011 = 1011$. The direct OR could not force 0-bits to change to the intended pattern.

quiz.q: AC = 1001 and E = 1. After cir (circular shift right through E), what are AC and E?
quiz.explanation: E enters the most significant position and AC(0) circulates into E: AC = 1100 and the old AC(0) = 1 lands in E.

quiz.q: The arithmetic shift right of the signed 4-bit word 1101 (−3) produces:
quiz.explanation: The sign bit replicates: $1101 \to 1110 = -2 = \lfloor -3/2 \rfloor$. Arithmetic shift right floors toward minus infinity, unlike truncating division.

depth.title: Algebra and architecture of the microoperation

blocks.heading: Two’s-complement subtraction as modular arithmetic
blocks.body: Why does discarding the carry make $A + \bar{B} + 1$ equal $A - B$? Work in the ring $\mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$, where the wraparound at $2^n$ is invisible. The bitwise complement satisfies $\bar{B} = 2^n - 1 - B$, because each of the $n$ bits contributes its complement to the sum of all-ones. Therefore $A + \bar{B} + 1 = A + (2^n - 1 - B) + 1 = A - B + 2^n \equiv A - B \pmod{2^n}$. The end carry is literally the $2^n$ term being flushed out of the register; discarding it is not a trick but the definition of modular equality. The 1’s-complement method omits the $+1$: $A + \bar{B} = A - B + 2^n - 1$. If $A > B$, the left side overflows past $2^n$, producing a carry of weight $2^n$ while the register retains $A - B - 1$; feeding that carry back into the least significant bit adds the missing $1$ — hence the name **end-around carry**. If $A \le B$, no carry appears, no correction applies, and the register content $2^n - 1 - (B - A)$ is precisely the 1’s-complement encoding of the negative difference $-(B - A)$, with the $A = B$ case yielding the notorious $111\ldots1$ “minus zero” that motivated the 2’s complement’s dominance.

blocks.heading: Arithmetic shift and the two rounding rules
blocks.body: A 4-bit machine divides $-5$ (1101) by 2 with ashr and gets $1110 = -2$; a 5-bit machine dividing $-5$ (11011) gets $11101 = -3$. Both are “correct” — they are different rounding rules. Sign replication computes $\text{ashr}(x) = \lfloor x/2 \rfloor$: for $x = -5$ in 5 bits, $\lfloor -2.5 \rfloor = -3$. A truncating divider (rounding toward zero) would give $-2$. For non-negative $x$ the two rules coincide, because truncation and floor agree on positives; the asymmetry lives entirely in the odd negatives. The hardware reason is structural: the sign flip-flop drives both the outgoing sign and the incoming replicated bit, so the shifter cannot “round toward zero” without an extra correction step — add 1 to the result when the shifted-out bit is 1 AND the sign is 1, which is precisely the restoring step a truncating division unit must add. Compilers that strength-reduce a division by a constant into shifts must therefore emit the correction sequence for signed operands, a real code-generation decision flowing straight from this section’s timing diagram.

blocks.heading: The multiplexer bus as a router
blocks.body: Viewed abstractly, the multiplexer bus of Section 8.2 is a router: at any instant it connects exactly one of $k$ source registers to the shared word-path. The cost accounting explains why Mano draws it so carefully. With $k$ registers of $n$ bits, the bus needs $n$ multiplexers of $k$ inputs each — $nk$ gate inputs, growing linearly in both registers and width. Each $k$-input multiplexer built from 2:1 stages has depth $\lceil \log_2 k \rceil$, so the source-select delay grows only logarithmically with the register count — the reason a 32-register file can still be routed in a couple of gate delays. The tri-state alternative of Section 8.2 replaces this combinational tree with a shared wire: selection cost drops to driving one enable line, but the wire itself becomes a capacitive node whose delay grows with length and tap count, and exactly one driver must be enabled at a time or the outputs fight. The two implementations are the two poles of a genuine engineering trade — logic depth versus wire RC — that every bus designer still navigates.

blocks.heading: Clock periods per instruction of the basic computer
blocks.body: Mano’s machine spends exactly one clock period per microoperation, so an instruction’s cost is the count of its timing states. Fetch and decode are universal: $T_0$ (AR ← PC), $T_1$ (IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1), $T_2$ (decode, AR ← address field) — three periods. A direct AND or ADD adds two more: $T_4$ reads the operand into DR, $T_5$ computes into AC and clears SC — five periods; an indirect version spends $T_3$ reading the effective address, making six. STA and BUN finish in one execute state ($T_4$): four periods. BSA needs two ($T_4$, $T_5$): five. ISZ is the longest: read, increment, write-back and test occupy $T_4$, $T_5$, $T_6$: six. Register-reference and input-output instructions execute entirely in the $T_3$ slot: four periods. Weighting a plausible mix — 35% ALU-from-memory at 5, 20% store/branch at 4, 5% subroutine call at 5, 5% ISZ at 6, 35% register-reference at 4 — gives $0.35(5) + 0.20(4) + 0.05(5) + 0.05(6) + 0.35(4) = 4.5$ clock periods per instruction, and every additional level of indirection adds one more. The single-period-per-microoperation discipline is what makes this arithmetic exact.

blocks.heading: Wilkes and the stored control word
blocks.body: Maurice Wilkes, building EDSAC at Cambridge, proposed in 1951 that the control signals sequenced by this chapter’s timing states could themselves be stored in a read-only memory: a row per clock period, a column per control line. Each microoperation of this section — a transfer, its control function, the SC ← 0 that ends an instruction — becomes a bit pattern in a **control word**, and each instruction becomes a short routine of such words. This is **microprogramming**, and it reframes the whole chapter: the RTL listing of the instruction cycle is not merely a specification but a program, executable by a very small sequencer reading control memory. Mano’s Chapter 10 develops exactly this: the hardwired gates that realize $D_3 T_4$ become table entries. The idea dominated real machines from the IBM System/360 (whose wide 1958-vintage vertical microcode made a family of compatible models share one architecture) through the CISC era, because it traded a handful of gates for editability — fixing a control bug became rewriting a row of ROM rather than re-cutting a board.

blocks.heading: The logic microoperations are functionally complete
blocks.body: The logic-microoperation repertoire is not an arbitrary menu: {AND, OR, XOR, NOT} is functionally complete — every bitwise function of two operands is expressible in it. Even the pair {AND, NOT} suffices by De Morgan, and Chapter 2 showed NAND alone suffices; what the four-op set buys is *economy of expression* for the field operations of this section. The XOR identities are the workhorses: $A \oplus 0 = A$ (pass), $A \oplus 1 = \bar{A}$ (complement), $A \oplus A = 0$ (clear) — three constants from one gate. Deeper: XOR computes the sum bits of an addition while AND computes the carry bits ($A + B = (A \oplus B) + ((A \wedge B) \ll 1)$ iterated), so the arithmetic and logic microoperations of this section are two views of one adder network — the very ALU that Chapter 9 builds as a single combinational block selectable by an operation code.

depth.title: From RTL notation to research practice

blocks.heading: Register transfer as guarded commands
blocks.body: Formally, Mano’s control function is a guard: the pair “P: R1 ← R2” is exactly Dijkstra’s guarded command **if P then R1 ← R2**, and a whole system of them is a synchronous transition system whose state is the vector of all registers. Because every guarded transfer fires simultaneously at the clock edge, the semantics is the parallel-assignment semantics — what Verilog later standardized as the non-blocking assignment (R1 <= R2 under a clocked always block) as opposed to the sequential blocking assignment, a distinction that generates endless beginner bugs precisely because RTL notation makes the parallel reading look so natural. Ill-formed RTL with circular combinational dependencies (A ← B, B ← A without registers) has no fixpoint semantics and must be rejected by construction tools — the register boundary is what makes the mathematical model deterministic and simulable in two passes per clock: evaluate all next-state functions from current state, then commit.

blocks.heading: Model checking a register-transfer description
blocks.body: Because a clocked RTL system is a finite-state machine (the basic computer has roughly $2^{100}$ reachable states — astronomical, but finite), it is a natural target for temporal-logic model checking. Properties of this chapter’s material become CTL formulas: “the transfer is safe” is $\mathrm{AG}(P \rightarrow \mathrm{AX}\, R_1 = R_2)$ — in every state where P holds, at the next tick R1 equals R2. Bus discipline becomes $\mathrm{AG}(\text{at most one source enable})$; the sequencer becomes $\mathrm{AG}(\mathrm{SC} \le 7)$. Tools from nuSMV to modern SMT-based bounded model checkers verify such properties by symbolic traversal (BDDs) or unrolling to a depth k; industrial sign-off (JasperGold-class apps) routinely discharges exactly these one-hot-enable and no-capture-without-load properties on millions of RTL states. The basic computer is small enough that a full CTL check of its instruction cycle is a semester exercise — and historically, the verification of a real microcode-sequenced machine (the AAMP5, early 1990s) was among the first industrial model-checking successes.

blocks.heading: The synchronous hypothesis and its limits
blocks.body: All of this chapter assumes the **synchronous hypothesis**: gates are ideal (zero delay), wires are ideal, and a single clock edge reaches every flip-flop simultaneously. Real silicon violates all three — each path has a delay that varies with temperature, voltage and process corner, and the clock itself arrives skewed across the chip. RTL reasoning survives because the discipline of clocked design pushes all timing questions into two numbers per path (setup and hold relative to the local clock), and static timing analysis verifies those numbers across corners; the notation of “one microoperation per clock period” is thus an abstraction maintained by tooling, not a physical fact. The hypothesis visibly frays at multi-gigahertz scales: a single cycle can no longer span a whole chip, so clocks are generated per domain (GALS — globally asynchronous, locally synchronous), and a transfer like R1 ← R2 crossing domains needs synchronizers and pays metastability risk — the point where Section 8.2’s three-state buffer and its timing assumptions become a research topic rather than a given.

blocks.heading: Verified compilation from RTL to gates
blocks.body: This chapter writes behavior; Chapters 9 and 10 realize it in hardware; and the implicit promise is that the realization matches the description. Keeping that promise is still an open engineering-science problem. Logic synthesis (from the RTL-to-gates flows of the 1980s to modern high-level synthesis from C or Chisel) is trusted through massive simulation plus structural equivalences between adjacent refinement steps, but a fully verified chain — behavioral RTL proven equivalent to the placed netlist, through all retiming, duplication and clock-gating transformations — exists only in fragments: the Kami framework verified a RISC-V core against its ISA by construction, and individual transformations (retiming, unrolling) have mechanical proofs, yet signoff-grade synthesis remains empirical. The prize is large: a machine like Mano’s, specified in one page of RTL, could be compiled to silicon with a machine-checked proof that every gate array implements every colon and arrow of this chapter exactly.

intro: One destination register is easy: draw n wires. But a computer must move words between many registers, and wiring every pair is hopeless — the wire count explodes quadratically. Mano’s answer is the common bus: one shared word-path that any register can drive and from which any register can load, with multiplexers (or three-state buffers) deciding who drives and a decoder deciding who captures. The same section adds the last transfer primitive: the memory unit, addressed through AR and read or written with the statements DR ← M[AR] and M[AR] ← DR.
objectives: Explain the common-bus concept and why it replaces point-to-point register wiring
Construct a multiplexer bus for four registers, sizing the select lines S1S0 and the number of MUX stages
Write bus transfers in the two-step form BUS ← C, R1 ← BUS and in the simplified one-statement form
Describe the three-state buffer, its high-impedance Z state, and the tri-state bus alternative
State the memory read and write microoperations and the role of AR as the address gate
Account for the one-word-per-period economy that the shared bus forces on every later design

concepts.statement: A **common bus** is a single shared word-path to which every register’s outputs can be connected as a source and every register’s inputs as a destination; it carries exactly one word per clock period, so one source is selected at a time.
concepts.detail: With k registers, point-to-point wiring needs $k(k-1)$ ordered register-pair paths — for eight registers, 56 paths of n wires each. The bus replaces all of them with n shared wires plus selection hardware. The price is serialization: two transfers that would have run in parallel on dedicated wires must now occupy two clock periods. Every timing count in Section 8.4 is a consequence of this one trade.

concepts.statement: A MUX bus for four registers of n bits uses **n multiplexers of four inputs each (4×1)**, all sharing the two select lines $S_1 S_0$: 00 selects A, 01 selects B, 10 selects C, 11 selects D. The construction extends word-by-word — one MUX stage per bit position.
concepts.detail: Each MUX output is one bus line; its four inputs are the corresponding bit of the four registers. Mano’s figure draws two of the stages explicitly, which is enough to make the pattern visible: register bit i of every source fans into the i-th MUX, and the shared $S_1 S_0$ code routes one register’s bit i onto bus line i. For k registers the select needs $\lceil \log_2 k \rceil$ lines; for wider words you simply add more identical MUX stages — the select wiring does not grow at all.

concepts.statement: A transfer through the bus is written in two steps: **BUS ← C, R1 ← BUS** — register C is gated onto the bus and register R1 captures it. When the bus is understood, the statement simplifies to **R1 ← C**.
concepts.detail: The two-step form exposes the bus’s two decisions: the source (chosen by the MUX select) and the destination (chosen by which register’s load input is enabled — a 2×4 decoder can turn a 2-bit destination code into exactly one load enable). The simplified one-line form is what Sections 8.3 and 8.4 use throughout; the bus is implied in every register-to-register transfer of the basic computer.

concepts.term: Three-state buffers and the tri-state bus
concepts.statement: A **three-state buffer** has outputs 0, 1 and **Z** (high impedance). When its enable control is 1 it passes its input; when 0 its output disconnects entirely. A bus built from tri-state drivers needs no multiplexers — the wired-OR of all registers’ outputs is the bus line.
concepts.detail: The Z state is not a logic level: the driver transistor simply releases the wire, leaving it floating (held briefly by its parasitic capacitance). One driver enabled at a time reproduces exactly the MUX bus’s behavior; two enabled simultaneously means two gates fighting — contention, with currents flowing where they should not. Tri-state construction wins when the bus spans physical distance (the wire IS the bus), which is why it became the standard for backplanes and processor buses.

concepts.term: The memory unit and address selection
concepts.statement: The **memory unit** stores $2^k$ words of n bits; a k-bit address in the **address register (AR)** selects the one word accessed. The basic computer’s memory holds $2^{12} = 4096$ words of 16 bits, addressed by a 12-bit AR.
concepts.detail: Inside the memory unit, a k-to-$2^k$ decoder (Chapter 5) turns the binary address into one asserted word-select line — the same selection problem as the bus, at industrial scale. The address must be stable in AR before the read or write strobe, which is exactly why the basic computer spends timing states loading AR before touching memory. Memory and registers share one uniform language: M is treated as an extension of the register file in which the register number itself is a stored number.

concepts.statement: The **memory read** DR ← M[AR] brings the addressed word into the data register; the **memory write** M[AR] ← DR stores the data register into the addressed word. The brackets name a memory word by its address.
concepts.detail: These are the only two memory statements in the language, and every instruction of Section 8.3 reduces to a timed sequence of them plus register transfers. In the basic computer the write path actually sources AC (the STA instruction: M[AR] ← AC) or PC (the subroutine call BSA: M[AR] ← PC), while every read lands in DR or IR — the hardware consequence of a single write port. The register-transfer level makes the whole memory look like one enormous indexed register, an abstraction every later architecture keeps.

concepts.statement: The common bus carries one word per clock period, so every pair of bus-needing microoperations of an instruction must occupy successive timing states — the single most important constraint in the timing design of Section 8.4.
concepts.detail: The exceptions are the transfers with dedicated paths: PC ← PC + 1 rides its own incrementer, which is why it shares timing state T1 with the memory read IR ← M[AR] during fetch. This serialization is not a weakness of the designers but the honest cost of the shared wire; pipelined and superscalar machines of later chapters exist precisely to recover the parallelism the bus budget gave up.

A 16-bit machine simply repeats the 2-MUX pair eight times to make 16 stages.
