examples.title: Tracing a transfer through the MUX bus
examples.problem: The four 2-bit registers of the bus hold A = 01, B = 00, C = 11, D = 10. The control sets S1S0 = 10 and enables the load input of A. Describe the complete transfer, then state what S1S0 and the destination code must be to accomplish R1-style transfers such as “the content of B replaces the content of D”.

steps.label: Step 1: Source selection
steps.text: The MUX select code S1S0 = 10 addresses input 2, which is register C. Every MUX stage — one per bit position — routes its C input to the corresponding bus line, so the bus now carries the word **11**, C’s content.

steps.label: Step 2: Destination capture
steps.text: Exactly one load enable is asserted — A’s. At the next clock edge A ← BUS = 11. In the full two-step notation: **BUS ← C, A ← BUS**; simplified: **A ← C**.

steps.label: Step 3: Route B into D
steps.text: To move B’s word: set the select to 01 (source B) and assert D’s load. The bus carries B = 00 and D captures it: BUS ← B, D ← BUS. On a wider machine the identical select routes all 16 bits at once, because each bit position has its own MUX driven by the same $S_1 S_0$.

steps.label: Step 4: What never happens
steps.text: No other register’s load is enabled, so the other registers hold their values regardless of what rides the bus; and no second source can be gated on simultaneously — one select code, one source word, per period.

examples.result: Source = a select code into the MUX tree, destination = a load enable from the decoder: two independent choices per clock period, and any register-to-register transfer is one statement.

examples.title: MUX bus versus tri-state bus
examples.problem: Designers must connect four 16-bit registers to a common path. (a) Size the multiplexer construction. (b) Size the three-state alternative. (c) What happens in each construction if the control logic accidentally selects two sources at once?

steps.label: Step 1: The MUX count
steps.text: Each bit line needs one 4-input MUX, so 16 multiplexers of 4×1, all sharing two select lines $S_1 S_0$. Gate input count: roughly $16 \times 4 = 64$ AND-terms plus the OR stages — entirely inside the chip, occupying area but no long wires.

steps.label: Step 2: The tri-state count
steps.text: Each register output bit goes through one three-state buffer: $4 \times 16 = 64$ buffers, enabled four at a time (one register = 16 enables). The bus itself is just 16 wires — the construction buys nothing but wires and enables, which is why it shines for long, shared physical paths.

steps.label: Step 3: The double-selection failure
steps.text: MUX version: a malformed select code simply picks one (wrong) source — the wrong register is read, but nothing burns. Tri-state version: two drivers fight over the wire — contention. The result is an undefined level and large shoot-through currents; real parts specify a bus turnaround gap for exactly this reason.

steps.label: Step 4: The verdict
steps.text: On-chip, where wires are short, the MUX tree wins on predictability and testability; across a board or backplane, tri-state wins on wire count. The basic computer of this book uses the MUX construction inside its processor.

examples.result: Two implementations of “one source at a time”: combinational selection (safe, costs gates) versus electrical disconnection (cheap, demands enable discipline).

examples.title: Reading and writing through AR
examples.problem: The memory has 4096 words of 16 bits. AR holds 1AF (hex), DR holds 08C2, and M[1AF] currently holds 0F0F. Trace the read DR ← M[AR], then the write M[AR] ← DR, and state how many address-decode lines the memory unit needs and why AR is 12 bits wide.

steps.label: Step 1: Address decoding
steps.text: AR = 0001 1010 1111 (12 bits). The memory’s internal 12-to-4096 decoder asserts exactly word-select line $1AF_{16} = 431_{10}$; all other 4095 word lines stay low.

steps.label: Step 2: The read
steps.text: With the read strobe, the selected word’s 16 bits drive the memory outputs: DR ← M[AR] loads 0F0F. Memory content is unchanged — a read is non-destructive. DR’s old value 08C2 is simply overwritten.

steps.label: Step 3: The write
steps.text: With AR unchanged and the write strobe, the 16 bits on the memory’s data inputs are stored into the selected cell: M[1AF] ← 08C2, destroying the 0F0F that was there. Only the addressed word changes.

steps.label: Step 4: Widths
steps.text: 4096 words need $\log_2 4096 = 12$ address bits — hence AR (and PC) are 12-bit registers while data registers (DR, AC, IR, TR) are 16-bit: the address and data sides of the machine have different natural widths.

examples.result: One address register, two strobes: DR ← M[AR] and M[AR] ← DR are the only memory statements needed — every instruction of the basic computer is built from them.

keyTakeaways: The common bus replaces $k(k-1)$ point-to-point register paths with n shared wires plus selection hardware, at the price of one word per clock period.
A MUX bus for four registers uses one 4×1 multiplexer per bit position, all sharing the two select lines $S_1 S_0$; the construction extends word-by-word to any width.
The two-step statement BUS ← C, R1 ← BUS exposes the two independent choices — MUX-select the source, load-enable the destination.
A three-state buffer outputs 0, 1 or Z; a tri-state bus selects a source by enabling exactly one driver, and contention is the failure mode.
Memory is a giant addressed register file: DR ← M[AR] reads, M[AR] ← DR writes, and AR’s 12 bits select 1 of 4096 words in the basic computer.
The one-word-per-period rule serializes every instruction — the dedicated PC incrementer is the classic bypass.

quiz.q: Four registers share a multiplexer common bus. How many select lines choose the source register?
options: Four lines, one per bit of the word
quiz.explanation: Selecting one of $k$ sources needs $\lceil \log_2 k \rceil$ lines: two select bits encode the four codes 00, 01, 10, 11.

quiz.q: Four 16-bit registers drive a multiplexer bus. How many 4×1 multiplexers does the bus need?
options: 16 — one per bit position of the word
quiz.explanation: Each bus line (bit position) needs one 4-input MUX; a 16-bit word therefore needs 16 MUX stages, all sharing $S_1 S_0$.

quiz.q: With the select code S1S0 = 10 on a bus wired A = 00, B = 01, C = 10, D = 11 as source codes, and only register A’s load enabled, which transfer executes?
quiz.explanation: S1S0 = 10 addresses source C, so the bus carries C’s word; the enabled load captures it into A: BUS ← C, A ← BUS.

quiz.q: A three-state buffer whose enable input is 0 presents at its output:
options: A high-impedance Z state — electrically disconnected from the wire
quiz.explanation: Enable = 0 turns the driver off: the output neither sources nor sinks current, releasing the shared wire to whichever buffer IS enabled.

quiz.q: What happens if two three-state buffers driving the same bus line are enabled simultaneously?
options: The bus carries the AND of the two inputs
The bus carries the OR of the two inputs
The two drivers contend: the level is undefined and damaging currents can flow
quiz.explanation: One buffer tries to pull high, the other low: contention. Real designs insert turnaround gaps and assert exactly one enable to avoid it.

quiz.q: The microoperation DR ← M[AR] means:
options: The address in AR is copied into DR
The memory word at the address held in AR is loaded into DR
DR is added to the memory word in AR
The memory word addressed by DR is copied into AR
quiz.explanation: Brackets index memory by a register: M[AR] is the word whose address AR holds; the read places it in DR without altering memory.

quiz.q: The basic computer’s AR is 12 bits. How many words can the memory hold, and what does the memory’s internal decoder look like?
quiz.explanation: A k-bit address selects $2^k$ words: $2^{12} = 4096$ words, one of 4096 decode lines asserted per access.

quiz.q: Which microoperation stores the accumulator into memory, and what is its bus cost?
options: M[AR] ← AC — one bus period, the write path sourcing AC directly (the STA execute step)
M[AR] ← AC — it cannot be done; memory only reads
AR ← AC — the address is stored in memory
quiz.explanation: The write statement sources the data register: STA executes as M[AR] ← AC in a single execute timing state.

depth.title: Wires, drivers and the shared path

blocks.heading: Point-to-point versus shared-bus wiring
blocks.body: The bus is a solution to an arithmetic problem. With $k$ registers and $n$-bit words, dedicated wiring must connect every ordered source–destination pair: $k(k-1)$ paths of $n$ wires each — $nk(k-1)$ wires total, quadratic in the register count. Eight registers of 16 bits already want $8 \times 7 \times 16 = 896$ wires and 56 separate load-enable networks; sixteen registers want 3840. The common bus instead runs $n$ shared wires, taps every register onto them ($nk$ connection points), and adds selection hardware of size $O(nk)$ — linear in both dimensions. The savings compound with scale, and the price is equally explicit: at most one transfer per period, so the total transfer bandwidth of the machine is capped at $n$ bits per clock no matter how idle the other registers are. Quadratic wire count traded for linear serialization is the founding trade of computer organization, reappearing at every scale from this 4-register bus to chip-to-chip interconnect.

blocks.heading: The physics of the Z state
blocks.body: The three-state buffer’s Z output is an electrical fact, not a logic value: both the pull-up and pull-down transistors are off, so the driver presents a high impedance and sources no current. The shared wire then holds whatever charge was last placed on it, drifting only through leakage — a word can briefly “sit” on an undriven bus, which is why tri-state systems specify turn-off-before-turn-on timing gaps (bus turnaround) rather than risk two drivers overlapping by a nanosecond. Contention is genuinely destructive: two complementary drivers form a near-short from supply to ground through both output stages, dissipating heat in transistors never designed for it, and the logical level during the fight is whichever driver happens to be stronger. The wired-AND variant — open-collector outputs with a shared pull-up resistor — gives the same electrical sharing with the AND semantics as a bonus, which is how I2C gets multi-master arbitration for free: a master writing 1 that reads 0 on the wire knows another master is talking and backs off.

blocks.heading: Scheduling transfers on the one-word bus
blocks.body: Take the fetch of an ADD: AR ← PC (bus use 1); IR ← M[AR] together with PC ← PC + 1 (the memory read occupies the bus into IR, but the incrementer is a dedicated path, so it rides along free — bus use 2); AR ← IR(0–11) (bus use 3); DR ← M[AR] (bus use 4); AC ← AC + DR (the ALU reads its operands through the processor’s internal selection paths of Chapter 9, not the common bus — bus use 0). Total: four bus-occupying periods plus one free rider, hence five clock periods, exactly the T0–T5 count that Section 8.4 derives. The scheduling rule generalizes: list every microoperation, count one period per bus occupancy, allow any transfer with a private path (PC increment, ALU internal operation, a status flip-flop set) to share a period with one bus user. Every CPI claim about the basic computer can be audited on a napkin this way — and every speedup proposal reduces to either adding a private path or adding a second bus.

blocks.heading: Memory as the addressed register file
blocks.body: The statement DR ← M[AR] quietly unifies two worlds: registers, selected by wiring, and memory, selected by a stored number. A memory of $2^k$ words is a register file whose select lines are driven by a k-bit register instead of a control wire — which is why the same RTL symbol family covers both, and why Mano can specify an entire computer before ever drawing a memory cell. The economy deepens on reflection: the address itself is data, so programs can compute which register (memory word) a transfer touches — the entire edifice of pointers, arrays and linked structures is AR ← <computed address> followed by DR ← M[AR]. The cost side is equally structural: because the address must be stable in AR before the strobe, every memory access pays at least one address-setup period, and because the bus carries one word, an address and its data cannot travel together — the two-cycle memory rhythm (aim, then read) that Section 8.4’s timing makes explicit is inherited by every later machine, down to the address/data phase split of modern DRAM interfaces.

blocks.heading: The serial bus: width one
blocks.body: Section 8.1’s serial transfer — one wire, one bit per clock, n pulses per word — is a bus of width one, and it deserves its place in the family photo because it marks the extreme of the wire-versus-time trade. The parallel common bus spends $n$ wires to finish in one period; the serial link spends one wire and finishes in $n$. When wires are expensive relative to time — between chips in 1979, between boards, over a cable — serial wins, and the entire later history of interconnect is the boundary walking toward serial: wide parallel buses (IDE, parallel SCSI, front-side buses) were progressively replaced by narrow fast serial links (PCIe, SATA, SerDes) once signaling speeds made many parallel wires impossible to skew-match. Mano’s shift-register serial transfer, with its one-bit adder cycling n times, is thus not a historical curiosity but the first appearance of the design point the industry eventually adopted everywhere.

depth.title: The shared path under research pressure

blocks.heading: Asynchronous buses and timing closure
blocks.body: The common bus of this section is synchronous: a global clock guarantees that source, wire and destination settle within one period. As clock rates rose, the wire itself became the bottleneck — an RC line crossing a modern die has tens of picoseconds of flight time and keeps growing with every process node, while the period shrank below the skew of distributing a single clock. The research responses define a taxonomy: source-synchronous interfaces ship the clock alongside the data so the receiver times against a local copy; pipelined buses register the wire mid-travel and trade latency for frequency; and globally-asynchronous locally-synchronous (GALS) designs abandon the global clock entirely, connecting synchronous islands through handshake-based asynchronous links. Handshakes bring their own pathology: a request crossing clock domains can violate setup and hold at the receiving flip-flop, entering **metastability** — an output that hangs between 0 and 1 for an unbounded time. The classical cure is the two-flop synchronizer, which reduces (never eliminates) failure probability exponentially per synchronization stage; the bounded-time synchronizer problem remains actively studied because no physical law lets a device resolve a metastable state by a deadline.

blocks.heading: From the common bus to networks-on-chip
blocks.body: The one-word-per-period rule of this section is a bandwidth ceiling, and industry hit it twice. Off-chip, the shared backplane (Unibus, Multibus, ISA, PCI) saturated as processors and devices multiplied; split-transaction protocols (PCI-X, then PCI Express) separated the request from the response so the bus was not held during a memory access, then replaced the shared wire entirely with point-to-point links and packet switching. On-chip, the same story repeated a decade later: the single shared AMBA bus of 1990s SoCs gave way to matrix crossbars (AMBA AXI with multiple outstanding transactions, per-master read and write channels, and credit-based flow control) and then to networks-on-chip — router tiles and packet routing replacing Mano’s multiplexer tree exactly as packet switching replaced circuit switching in telecoms. The basic computer’s select lines $S_1 S_0$ became, at scale, packet headers; the load enable became a virtual-channel grant; the turnaround gap became credit return. The conceptual skeleton of this section — arbitrate a shared word path among many registers — survives intact under several orders of magnitude of bandwidth.

blocks.heading: Where tri-state went
blocks.body: Tri-state outputs once dominated bus design, and then quietly vanished from die interiors. Process scaling made them a liability: a tri-state driver left enabled during power sequencing or scan test can contend with a neighbor and, at nanometer geometries, the electromigration and latch-up margins no longer tolerate it; testability also suffers, because a floating node holds stale charge that a tester cannot observe. On-die shared paths are therefore built as multiplexer trees — this section’s first construction — and tri-state survives only where the wire leaves the package: legacy board buses, and open-drain shared lines such as I2C, where the wired-AND behavior doubles as an arbitration mechanism. The successor technologies in turn reintroduced shared-wire disciplines under new names: the USB single-ended bus, differential pairs with tri-state-like idle states, and modern high-speed links that never share at all. The pedagogical point is that Mano’s two constructions were not arbitrary: they are the two exhaustive answers to “how does a wire carry one of many sources” — select before the wire (MUX) or disconnect the others from it (tri-state) — and every later interconnect is one of these two answers, replicated and accelerated.

blocks.heading: After the flat M[AR] abstraction
blocks.body: The notation M[AR] presents memory as flat, uniform, and one access away. All three assumptions became research programs. Uniformity fails first in the memory hierarchy: the flat address space is served by caches, and the address itself is reinterpreted as tag, index and offset — the decoder tree of this section literally reappears inside every cache as the index decoder selecting a set. “One access away” fails with latency: a cache miss costs hundreds of cycles, which is why compilers and hardware reorder loads far from uses — the address-setup rhythm (aim AR, then read) that Section 8.4 bakes into the instruction cycle becomes, at scale, the load-use pipeline hazard and the out-of-order load scheduler. And flatness fails with multiprocessors: once two processors share M, “which register holds the word” becomes the cache-coherence problem — the single-driver discipline of this section, generalized to many drivers of many cached copies, with the bus snoop or the directory playing the arbiter that the load-enable decoder played here. The OS courses’ virtual memory then removes even the arithmetic: M[AR] becomes M-translated[AR]. The bracket pair turns out to be the most heavily engineered abstraction in computer architecture.

intro: A computer is a machine that executes instructions — but before it can execute one, it must be able to name one. The stored-program idea puts instructions in memory as binary words, indistinguishable from data until the control unit claims them; the instruction code is the convention that splits such a word into an operation, an addressing mode and an address. This section lays out the complete instruction set of the basic computer: six memory-reference instructions that move words between memory and the accumulator, twelve register-reference instructions that clear, complement, shift and test it, and the input–output pair that talks to the two peripherals. Every one of them will meet its timing signals in Section 8.4.
objectives: Explain the stored-program concept and why instructions and data share one memory
Read the 16-bit instruction word: opcode, mode bit I, and the 12-bit address field
Compute effective addresses for direct and indirect addressing
Execute each memory-reference instruction (AND, ADD, LDA, STA, BUN, BSA, ISZ) in RTL
List the register-reference instructions and the I/O instructions with their control conditions r and p
Assemble the complete instruction table and read a machine-language program from it

concepts.statement: In a **stored-program computer**, instructions live in the same read-write memory as data. The control unit fetches the word whose address is in the program counter, treats it as an instruction for one cycle, and moves on. There is no hardware distinction between an instruction word and a data word — only the timing of their use.
concepts.detail: The consequence is total flexibility: programs can be loaded, changed and even written by other programs, which is everything from assemblers to operating systems to the software you are reading this in. The price is vigilance — nothing stops a runaway program counter from fetching a number as an instruction — and the entire discipline of protected memory exists to manage that risk.

concepts.statement: The basic computer's instruction word is 16 bits, divided as: **bits 0–11 — the address field**, naming one of $2^{12} = 4096$ words of memory; **bits 12–14 — the operation code (opcode)**, one of eight codes $D_0$–$D_7$ from the $3 \times 8$ decoder; **bit 15 — the mode bit $I$**. In RTL: $\mathrm{IR}(0\text{–}11)$ address, $\mathrm{IR}(12\text{–}14)$ opcode, $I = \mathrm{IR}(15)$.
concepts.detail: The decoder outputs $D_0, \ldots, D_7$ are combinational functions of the opcode bits, available the moment IR is loaded. Codes $D_0$–$D_6$ select the seven memory-reference instructions; code $D_7$ is split by the mode bit into two families: $I = 0$ gives the register-reference instructions (recognized by the control condition $r = D_7 I' T_3$), and $I = 1$ the input–output instructions ($p = D_7 I T_3$). For the memory-reference instructions the same bit $I$ means direct ($I = 0$) or indirect ($I = 1$) addressing — one physical bit, three meanings, disambiguated by which opcode accompanies it.

concepts.statement: For a memory-reference instruction, the **effective address** is where the operand actually lives. **Direct** ($I = 0$): the effective address is the address field itself. **Indirect** ($I = 1$): the address field names a word that *contains* the effective address — the machine first reads $M[\mathrm{address}]$ and uses its contents as the operand's location.
concepts.detail: Indirection costs one extra memory cycle (the extra microoperation $\mathrm{AR} \leftarrow M[\mathrm{AR}]$ in Section 8.4's timing) but buys pointer power: the same instruction can act on different words at different times because a single memory update redirects it. This is the ancestor of every pointer, reference and link in modern computing — the hardware-level mechanism that makes variables indirect.

concepts.statement: The seven instructions that carry a memory address, with their opcode and execution microoperations (shown from the first execute timing state, after address resolution): **AND ($D_0$)** — $\mathrm{DR} \leftarrow M[\mathrm{AR}]$, then $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow \mathrm{AC} \wedge \mathrm{DR}$; **ADD ($D_1$)** — $\mathrm{DR} \leftarrow M[\mathrm{AR}]$, then $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow \mathrm{AC} + \mathrm{DR}$, $E \leftarrow \mathrm{carry}$; **LDA ($D_2$)** — $\mathrm{DR} \leftarrow M[\mathrm{AR}]$, then $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow \mathrm{DR}$; **STA ($D_3$)** — $M[\mathrm{AR}] \leftarrow \mathrm{AC}$; **BUN ($D_4$)** — $\mathrm{PC} \leftarrow \mathrm{AR}$ (unconditional branch); **BSA ($D_5$)** — $M[\mathrm{AR}] \leftarrow \mathrm{PC}$, $\mathrm{PC} \leftarrow \mathrm{AR} + 1$ (branch and save return); **ISZ ($D_6$)** — $\mathrm{DR} \leftarrow M[\mathrm{AR}]$, $\mathrm{DR} \leftarrow \mathrm{DR} + 1$, $M[\mathrm{AR}] \leftarrow \mathrm{DR}$, and if $\mathrm{DR} = 0$ then $\mathrm{PC} \leftarrow \mathrm{PC} + 1$.
concepts.detail: Notice the grammar: every instruction that reads memory stages it through DR; every one that writes memory uses AR as the pointer and AC (or DR) as the source; and every sequence ends with SC ← 0 to force the next fetch. The BSA convention is the classic return link: the subroutine's first word holds the return address, the body follows from the next word, and an indirect BUN through that first word returns. ISZ is the loop primitive — increment a counter in memory and skip the next instruction when it wraps to zero.

concepts.statement: Twelve instructions with opcode $D_7$ and $I = 0$, all executed in a single timing state under $r = D_7 I' T_3$, each decoded from one bit of $\mathrm{IR}(0\text{–}11)$: **CLA** $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow 0$; **CLE** $E \leftarrow 0$; **CMA** $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow \overline{\mathrm{AC}}$; **CME** $E \leftarrow E'$; **CIR** — circular shift right through $E$; **CIL** — circular shift left through $E$; **INC** $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow \mathrm{AC} + 1$; **SPA** — skip if AC positive ($\mathrm{AC}(15) = 0$); **SNA** — skip if AC negative; **SZA** — skip if AC is zero; **SZE** — skip if $E = 0$; **HLT** — stop the clock ($S \leftarrow 0$).
concepts.detail: Each instruction bit $B_i = \mathrm{IR}(i)$ is ANDed with $r$ to form its own control function, so any one of the twelve fires alone: no address is fetched and memory is not touched — the register file is the whole stage. The circular shifts route bit 0 through E to bit 15 (CIR) or bit 15 through E to bit 0 (CIL), making E a one-bit extension that carries multiword shifts and multiplications. The skip instructions do not branch anywhere — they increment PC once more, quietly dropping the next instruction from the stream; paired with a follow-up BUN they build conditional branches.

concepts.statement: With opcode $D_7$ and $I = 1$, executed under $p = D_7 I T_3$: **INP** — $\mathrm{AC}(0\text{–}7) \leftarrow \mathrm{INPR}$, $\mathrm{FGI} \leftarrow 0$ (bring a typed character into the low byte of AC and clear the input flag); **OUT** — $\mathrm{OUTR} \leftarrow \mathrm{AC}(0\text{–}7)$, $\mathrm{FGO} \leftarrow 0$ (send the low byte to the printer); **ION** — $\mathrm{IEN} \leftarrow 1$ (enable interrupts); **IOF** — $\mathrm{IEN} \leftarrow 0$ (disable them).
concepts.detail: The 8-bit input register INPR and output register OUTR meet the 16-bit AC at its low half — characters, not words, are what peripherals exchange. The flags FGI and FGO are the handshakes: a peripheral sets its flag when it has something new, and the instruction that consumes the data clears it. IEN is the master switch for the interrupt cycle of Section 8.4 — with it off, the processor never notices the flags; with it on, a set flag hijacks the cycle at the next instruction boundary.

concepts.statement: The complete set is best held as one table: 7 memory-reference instructions (opcode ≠ $D_7$, using $I$ for direct/indirect), 12 register-reference ($D_7 I' T_3$, bits of IR), and 4 input–output ($D_7 I T_3$) — 23 instructions total, and with them the basic computer is Turing-complete.
concepts.detail: It is worth pausing on how little this is. Memory is AND, OR (via masks), add, load and store; control is BUN, BSA and ISZ with three skips; arithmetic beyond ADD is synthesized — complement-and-increment builds subtraction, shift-and-add builds multiplication. A minimal but honest computer, small enough to trace every wire, complete enough to compute anything computable — which is precisely why it makes a good teacher.

examples.title: Decoding an instruction word
examples.problem: The instruction register holds $\mathtt{1011\ 0100\ 0011\ 0010}$. Decode it completely.

steps.label: Split the fields
steps.text: Bits 15 = 1 (the I bit), bits 14–12 = $011$ (the opcode), bits 11–0 = $0100\ 0011\ 0010 = 1074$ (the address).

steps.label: Identify the opcode
steps.text: The 3-bit opcode $011$ decodes to $D_3$ — the STA instruction, store the accumulator.

steps.label: Resolve the mode
steps.text: The opcode is a memory-reference code ($D_3 \ne D_7$), so bit 15 is the addressing mode: $I = 1$ means indirect addressing.

steps.label: Write the instruction
steps.text: STA 1074, I — "store AC into the memory word whose address is found (indirectly) in location 1074." If $M[1074] = 26$, the word lands at address 26.

examples.result: STA with indirect addressing through location 1074. The same 16 bits, read by a different opcode, would be a number — meaning lives in the decode, not the pattern.

examples.title: Direct versus indirect effective address
examples.problem: Memory contains: $M[300] = 400$ and $M[400] = 907$. An LDA instruction references address 300. What loads into AC if (a) $I = 0$, (b) $I = 1$?

steps.label: Direct: the field is the address
steps.text: With $I = 0$ the effective address is 300 itself: $\mathrm{DR} \leftarrow M[300] = 400$, then $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow 400$.

steps.label: Indirect: the field is a pointer
steps.text: With $I = 1$ the machine first reads the pointer: $\mathrm{AR} \leftarrow M[300] = 400$. Now the effective address is 400.

steps.label: Fetch through the resolved address
steps.text: Then $\mathrm{DR} \leftarrow M[400] = 907$ and $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow 907$ — one extra memory cycle bought a level of indirection.

steps.label: Count the cycles
steps.text: Direct: one memory access for the operand. Indirect: two — the pointer fetch plus the operand fetch — the price the addressing mode charges.

examples.result: (a) AC = 400; (b) AC = 907. Indirection is the hardware ancestor of the pointer: update $M[300]$ and the same instruction now acts elsewhere in memory.

examples.title: Building subtraction from the instruction set
examples.problem: The basic computer has no subtract instruction. Show the program, starting at address 100, that computes $X - Y$ (leaving the result in AC) given that location 200 holds $X$ and 201 holds $Y$, using the fact that $X - Y = X + \overline{Y} + 1$.

steps.label: Fetch X
steps.text: LDA 200 — $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow M[200] = X$.

steps.label: Complement
steps.text: CMA — $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow \overline{X}$... careful: we need $\overline{Y}$, not $\overline{X}$, so reorder — load Y first: LDA 201 gives AC = Y, then CMA gives AC = $\overline{Y}$.

steps.label: Increment
steps.text: INC — $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow \overline{Y} + 1 = -Y$ (the two's complement).

steps.label: Add X
steps.text: ADD 200 — $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow (-Y) + X$, with E receiving the carry (a discarded carry here means the true result is positive in the two's-complement reading).

steps.label: The program listing
steps.text: 100: LDA 201 · 101: CMA · 102: INC · 103: ADD 200 · 104: HLT — four instructions, and every one of them is a single line of RTL.

examples.result: AC holds $X - Y$ after four instructions: the instruction set's arithmetic gap is closed by two's-complement algebra wearing microoperations — exactly what the ALU of the next chapter hard-wires.

examples.title: A loop with ISZ
examples.problem: Write a routine that repeats a body 10 times, with the iteration counter kept at memory location 30 and the loop body starting at address 40.

steps.label: Initialize
steps.text: LDA a word containing $-10$ (two's complement), STA 30 — the counter counts up toward zero.

steps.label: The loop head
steps.text: At the top of the body (address 40 onwards) place the body's instructions, ending with: ISZ 30 — increments $M[30]$ and skips its next instruction only when the counter reaches 0.

steps.label: Close the loop
steps.text: After the ISZ, place BUN 40 — executed while the counter has not wrapped, sending control back to the body; skipped exactly once, when the count finishes.

steps.label: Trace the count
steps.text: First pass: $-10 \to -9$ (no skip, branch taken). Second: $-9 \to -8$ … After the tenth increment: $-1 \to 0$ — the zero condition fires, the BUN is skipped, and execution falls through past the loop.

examples.result: The ISZ + BUN pair is the basic computer's while-loop: an incrementing counter, a conditional skip, an unconditional branch — every high-level loop construct compiles down to this skeleton.

keyTakeaways: Instructions are 16-bit words: bits 0–11 address (4096 words), bits 12–14 opcode, bit 15 the mode bit I.
Opcode $D_7$ splits by I: register-reference ($r = D_7 I' T_3$, twelve single-cycle operations on AC and E) and input–output ($p = D_7 I T_3$, INP, OUT, ION, IOF).
For memory-reference instructions, I selects direct ($I=0$) or indirect ($I=1$) addressing; indirection costs one extra memory cycle and adds one level of pointer.
Seven memory-reference instructions: AND, ADD, LDA, STA, BUN, BSA, ISZ — with BSA's stored return link and ISZ's increment-and-skip building subroutines and loops.
Skip instructions (SPA, SNA, SZA, SZE) never branch by themselves: they bump PC once, and a following BUN turns the skip into a conditional branch.
23 instructions suffice for a complete computer — subtraction, multiplication and everything else are synthesized from them by program.

quiz.q: The 12-bit address field of the basic computer can name how many memory words?
quiz.explanation: $2^{12} = 4096$ words. Sixteen bits would give $2^{16} = 65536$, but four of the sixteen bits are spent on the opcode and the mode bit I.

quiz.q: The instruction word $\mathtt{0011\ 0100\ 0000\ 0110}$ decodes to:
quiz.explanation: Bit 15 = 0 (direct), bits 14–12 = $011$ = $D_3$ = STA, bits 11–0 = $0000\ 0000\ 0110$ = 6. So: store AC at address 6, directly.

quiz.q: With $M[50] = 200$ and $M[200] = 75$, the instruction ADD 50, I loads which value into the addend DR?
quiz.explanation: Indirect addressing: the pointer fetch reads $M[50] = 200$, so the effective address is 200, and the operand fetched into DR is $M[200] = 75$ — two memory reads for one operand.

quiz.q: Which instruction stores the return address into memory as its main effect?
quiz.explanation: BSA (Branch and Save Return Address) writes PC — which already points just past the BSA itself — into the target location and continues from the next word: the classic subroutine call link.

quiz.q: The control function $r = D_7 I' T_3$ recognizes:
quiz.explanation: Opcode $D_7$ with $I = 0$ (hence the $I'$) at timing state $T_3$ selects the twelve register-reference instructions — each then decoded by a single bit of IR(0–11). The $I$ (not $I'$) companion condition $p$ selects the I/O family.

quiz.q: ISZ skips the next instruction when:
options: the incremented memory word becomes zero
quiz.explanation: ISZ increments the memory word at AR and tests the *word*, not AC: the skip (an extra PC increment) fires exactly when the wrapped-around value hits 0000 — which is why counters are initialized to the negative of the trip count.

quiz.q: The pair CMA followed by INC computes:
quiz.explanation: CMA complements every bit (one's complement) and INC adds one: together $\overline{\mathrm{AC}} + 1$, which is exactly negation in two's-complement arithmetic — the standard recipe for building subtraction from addition.

quiz.q: How many of the basic computer's instructions are memory-reference instructions?
quiz.explanation: Seven opcodes $D_0$–$D_6$ (AND, ADD, LDA, STA, BUN, BSA, ISZ) carry memory addresses; the eighth code $D_7$ is reserved for the register-reference and I/O families.

quiz.q: A BSA instruction is stored at address 100 (with the subroutine linked at address 300). After BSA completes, which address does the saved return slot hold?
quiz.explanation: PC was already incremented past the BSA during fetch, so it holds 101 — the instruction after the call. BSA stores that value (into the link slot at 300) and jumps to the word after the slot, 301, where the subroutine body begins.

quiz.q: The instructions SPA, SNA, SZA and SZE all act by:
options: incrementing PC once when their condition holds
quiz.explanation: Skips work by a single extra $\mathrm{PC} \leftarrow \mathrm{PC} + 1$ — the next instruction (often a BUN) is passed over. Placed before any instruction, a skip converts it into a conditional.

quiz.q: In the basic computer, a $16$-bit instruction word with a $12$-bit address carries which opcode and mode bits?
options: IR($0$–$11$) address, IR($12$–$14$) opcode, IR($15$) indirect bit
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** $16$-bit word, $4096$-word memory needing $12$ address lines.
**Step 2 — Rule:** low $12$ bits address memory; next $3$ select among $8$ operation decodes; top bit selects direct vs indirect.
**Step 3 — Apply:** $D_0$..$D_7$ from IR($12$–$14$); $I$ = IR($15$); effective address $=$ IR($0$–$11$) or $M[$IR($0$–$11$)$]$.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** $D_7$ with $I = 0$ means register-reference, with $I = 1$ means input-output — twelve plus six operations from one decode.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** opcode-only ignores addressing; all-address leaves no operation; swapped fields misplace $I$.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** $12$ address, $3$ opcode, $1$ mode.

quiz.q: What do BSA (branch and save) and ISZ (increment and skip) each do to control flow?
options: BSA stores PC at the effective address then branches there plus $1$; ISZ increments memory and skips next if zero
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** memory-reference operations with effective address EA.
**Step 2 — Rule:** BSA: $M[EA] \leftarrow PC$, $PC \leftarrow EA + 1$ (saves return, jumps to subroutine). ISZ: $M[EA] \leftarrow M[EA] + 1$; if result $0$ then $PC \leftarrow PC + 1$ (skip).
**Step 3 — Apply:** BSA links subroutines; ISZ implements counted loops by skipping the branch-out when the counter hits zero.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** BSA takes $4$ cycles, ISZ $6$ (read, increment, write-back, test) — the longest direct instruction.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** clearing belongs to CLA; halting is HLT; input-output uses $D_7 I$ lines.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** save-and-branch versus increment-and-skip.

depth.title: Instruction sets as design decisions

blocks.heading: Why 3 + 1 + 12 bits
blocks.body: The field split is a budget negotiation. Twelve address bits give $2^{12} = 4096$ words — the memory the basic computer actually wires up. With three opcode bits, eight operations are addressable, which the design stretches to 23 instructions by overloading: $D_7$ plus the mode bit doubles into two families, and the twelve IR bits inside each family decode twelve more single-cycle operations ($2 \times$ an implicit expansion worth 24 codes on one opcode). The general principle is an information-theoretic squeeze: an instruction wants to say *what*, *where* and *how to find it*, and the bit budget trades the three against each other. Real instruction sets answer the same squeeze with multi-byte formats — the deeper results below — but the trade-off surface (more opcodes vs longer addresses vs more modes) is already fully visible in these 16 bits.

blocks.heading: The ISZ loop pattern
blocks.body: Why initialize the counter to $-n$ rather than $0$? Trace both. Counting up from 0 with a "skip when the limit is reached" test needs a comparison — and the basic computer has none. Counting from $-n$ uses the wraparound of two's-complement arithmetic as the test: each ISZ adds one, and after exactly $n$ increments the word is $-n + n = 0$, which the zero detector already tests for free. The pattern generalizes: any finite counter can be built from an incrementer and a zero flag, and any repetition from (increment, test, branch). Every for-loop you have ever written lowers to this three-instruction skeleton.

blocks.heading: How real instruction sets grew
blocks.body: The basic computer's 23 instructions are the seed of a lineage. Its single accumulator becomes the register file of later machines — many operands, indexed by register fields that no longer fit in 16 bits, so formats lengthen: the x86 family grew from one-byte codes in 1978 to variable-length instructions up to 15 bytes today, while the RISC reaction (MIPS, SPARC, then RISC-V) froze the length at 32 bits and let the compiler do the squeezing. RISC-V's compressed 16-bit extension — which trades decode complexity for code density, exactly the basic computer's trade in reverse — is the modern echo of the 16-bit budget this section lives inside. The mode bit I, meanwhile, grew into whole addressing-mode fields: immediate, register, base+offset, scaled, PC-relative — each a way to compute the effective address before the operand is fetched.

blocks.heading: Why the accumulator died
blocks.body: One accumulator forces every computation through a single bottleneck — the implicit operand of nearly every instruction. Two-operand and three-operand formats (ADD R1, R2, R3) need register fields but pay for them with parallelism: the ALU reads two registers while a third result is written, with no serialization on one shared register. The basic computer's single-bus CPI accounting of Section 8.4 is the quantitative version of the same story — more named storage plus private paths means fewer forced waits. The accumulator survives only where silicon is counted in pennies: microcontrollers' register-poor cores keep it alive.

depth.title: Encodings, gaps and frontiers

blocks.heading: Opcode assignment as coding theory
blocks.body: Fixed 3-bit opcodes give every instruction equal weight — an optimal code only if all operations are equally frequent, which measurements demolished decades ago (loads, branches and adds dominate). Variable-length encodings assign short codes to frequent instructions, exactly as Huffman coding assigns short codewords to frequent symbols; x86's byte-granular prefixes, ARM's Thumb-2 16/32-bit mix and RISC-V's compressed format are engineered Huffman trees, and instruction-length decoders — the hardware that must find instruction boundaries in a stream — are among the most validated logic on Earth, because a misparse is catastrophic. Research continues on where the frontier sits: a 2020s movement (RISC-V, and the "dark silicon" era's custom accelerators) argues for minimal fixed cores plus standard extensions, keeping the decode tree shallow precisely where the old families let it grow.

blocks.heading: The semantic gap
blocks.body: An instruction set is a contract between hardware and compiler writers, and the friction between what programs want to say and what instructions can express is the **semantic gap**. The basic computer sits at one extreme — arithmetic and control so primitive that a subtraction is a four-instruction idiom. CISC closed the gap upward (instructions for procedure calls, string moves, loop primitives) until silicon budgets made compiled sequences of simple instructions cheaper than executed complex ones — the RISC insight, quantified by instruction mix studies (Hennessy and Patterson's quantitative approach). The gap now reappears higher up: vector instructions, crypto accelerators and matrix engines (GPU tensor cores, NPUs) encode in one instruction what a compiler loop once said in a thousand. Each generation rediscovers that an instruction is a cached decision about what the layer above will need.

blocks.heading: Designing an open instruction set
blocks.body: Should instruction sets be owned at all? For four decades the dominant ISAs were proprietary architectures with sealed specifications, and the ecosystem paid in licensing, fragmentation and security monoculture (one binary format, one attack surface). RISC-V (2010–) reopened the question: an open, modular specification with a frozen base and optional standard extensions, governed by a foundation rather than a firm. Its unresolved research problems are live: extension versioning without breaking binaries, formal specification of the architecture contract (the RVW memory-consistency formalizations; Sail and KISA models), verification of out-of-order implementations against the spec, and the standards politics of vector-length-agnostic code. The deeper open question is whether open ISAs will do for processors what open source did for operating systems — or whether the bottleneck (fabrication, validation, performance culture) simply sits elsewhere.

intro: Everything the computer does, it does one clock pulse at a time. This section assembles the timing machinery that sequences the microoperations of the whole chapter into the living rhythm of the machine: a sequence counter raising timing signals $T_0, T_1, T_2, \ldots$, a fetch phase that always runs the same three steps, a decode step that steers the remaining states, and per-instruction execute sequences that all end by zeroing the counter — pulling the machine back to fetch. The design closes with the interrupt cycle, the small hijack that lets a peripheral steal the machine between instructions. After this section, the basic computer is complete: every wire accounted for, every cycle named.
objectives: Explain the sequence counter SC, the timing signals $T_0$–$T_3$, and how SC ← 0 returns control to fetch
Write the fetch and decode microoperations with their timing states
Trace the effective-address step for indirect addressing
Execute each memory-reference instruction's RTL sequence, state by state
Explain how register-reference and I/O instructions execute in a single $T_3$ pulse
Trace the interrupt cycle and the return-from-interrupt mechanism

concepts.term: The sequence counter and timing signals
concepts.statement: A 2-bit **sequence counter** SC, clocked like every register, feeds a $2 \times 4$ decoder whose outputs are the **timing signals** $T_0, T_1, T_2, T_3$ — one-hot pulses, one per clock period, cycling while SC counts. The microoperation $\mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$ (written into every instruction's last step) resets the count, so the next pulse raises $T_0$ again: the fetch phase.
concepts.detail: A timing signal never acts alone: every control function is a product such as $D_1 T_4$ — opcode $D_1$ (it's an ADD) *and* timing $T_4$ (the fourth pulse of this cycle). The AND gate implementing that product is literally the enable on the microoperation's load lines. When an instruction needs more than four states, the design widens the counter — the indirect-address step uses $T_3$, and ISZ's full sequence runs to $T_5$; the book's extended machine allows up to $T_{15}$ before restarting. SC is the conductor's baton: the orchestra of registers only moves when it beats.

concepts.statement: Every instruction begins with the same three microoperations, whatever the instruction turns out to be: $$T_0\colon\ \mathrm{AR} \leftarrow \mathrm{PC} \qquad T_1\colon\ \mathrm{IR} \leftarrow M[\mathrm{AR}],\ \ \mathrm{PC} \leftarrow \mathrm{PC} + 1 \qquad T_2\colon\ \mathrm{AR} \leftarrow \mathrm{IR}(0\text{–}11),\ \ I \leftarrow \mathrm{IR}(15)$$ while the $3 \times 8$ decoder raises the matching $D_i$ from bits $\mathrm{IR}(12\text{–}14)$ combinationally.
concepts.detail: Note the free rider: PC increments in the same state as the instruction fetch, because the incrementer is a dedicated path and the bus carries only the memory word into IR. And note what $T_2$ does not do: the address field moves into AR immediately, so a direct-address instruction is already aimed at its operand; only indirect ones need one more step. Fetch is deliberately dumb — identical for all 23 instructions — which is what makes the machine simple to time and, later, what makes pipelining it so natural.

concepts.statement: If the fetched instruction is a memory-reference instruction with $I = 1$, one extra state resolves the pointer: $$T_3\colon\ \mathrm{AR} \leftarrow M[\mathrm{AR}]$$ — the word at the address field is read and itself installed as the effective address. Direct instructions ($I = 0$) skip this state entirely and begin executing at $T_3$.
concepts.detail: The two paths reunite: after the (possibly skipped) pointer step, AR holds the effective address and the execute sequence runs DR ← M[AR] and its instruction-specific follow-ups. The one-state price of indirection is visible here as pure timing — the strongest sense in which an addressing mode is a loop unrolled into hardware.

concepts.statement: With the effective address in AR (for direct instructions, from $T_2$): **AND/ADD/LDA** run $T_3\colon \mathrm{DR} \leftarrow M[\mathrm{AR}]$, then $T_4\colon$ the operation ($\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow \mathrm{AC} \wedge \mathrm{DR}$, or $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow \mathrm{AC} + \mathrm{DR},\ E \leftarrow \mathrm{carry}$, or $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow \mathrm{DR}$) with $\mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$. **STA** needs no DR: $T_3\colon M[\mathrm{AR}] \leftarrow \mathrm{AC},\ \mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$. **BUN**: $T_3\colon \mathrm{PC} \leftarrow \mathrm{AR},\ \mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$. **BSA**: $T_3\colon M[\mathrm{AR}] \leftarrow \mathrm{PC},\ \mathrm{PC} \leftarrow \mathrm{AR} + 1,\ \mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$. **ISZ** is the long one: $T_3\colon \mathrm{DR} \leftarrow M[\mathrm{AR}]$, $T_4\colon \mathrm{DR} \leftarrow \mathrm{DR} + 1$, $T_5\colon M[\mathrm{AR}] \leftarrow \mathrm{DR}$, if $(\mathrm{DR} = 0)$ then $(\mathrm{PC} \leftarrow \mathrm{PC} + 1)$, $\mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$.
concepts.detail: Count clock cycles from the top of fetch: direct AND/ADD/LDA take 5 ($T_0$–$T_4$), STA and BUN take 4, BSA takes 4, and ISZ takes 6; every indirect variant adds one more. These numbers are the machine's CPI table — the honest cost of each instruction, auditable on paper, and the baseline any speedup proposal must beat.

concepts.statement: When $D_7$ fires at $T_2$, no address is needed: the instruction's bits are the operation. At the next (and only) execute state, $$r = D_7 I' T_3 \quad \text{or} \quad p = D_7 I T_3$$ enables one of the twelve (or four) bit-decoded control functions — $B_i = \mathrm{IR}(i)$ ANDed with $r$ (or $p$) — and the single microoperation executes with $\mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$: CLA, CMA, CIR, the skips, INP, OUT, all of them, one pulse each.
concepts.detail: The whole register-reference family therefore costs 4 cycles ($T_0$–$T_3$) — fetch plus one action, the cheapest instructions in the machine, which is why good assemblers prefer clearing AC with CLA over loading a zero word from memory (5 cycles via LDA). Bit-decoding a 12-bit field with twelve AND gates to obtain twelve one-cycle operations is the most information-dense opcode trick in the design.

concepts.statement: At the end of every execute state, the control checks $\mathrm{IEN} \cdot (\mathrm{FGI} \vee \mathrm{FGO})$. If a flag is set and interrupts are enabled, instead of returning to fetch the machine runs: $$R T_0\colon \mathrm{AR} \leftarrow 0 \qquad R T_1\colon M[\mathrm{AR}] \leftarrow \mathrm{PC},\ \mathrm{PC} \leftarrow 1 \qquad R T_2\colon \mathrm{IEN} \leftarrow 0,\ R \leftarrow 0,\ \mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$$ — the return address is saved at location 0, execution branches to the service routine at location 1, and the R (return) flip-flop that distinguished this cycle is cleared.
concepts.detail: The service routine reads the character (INP) or writes it (OUT) — which clears the flag that caused the interrupt — and finishes with an indirect BUN through location 0 to resume the main program, plus ION to re-arm. Interrupts are taken only between instructions, never inside one: the design guarantees each instruction runs to completion, the simplest form of the **precise exception** discipline that all later processors labor to preserve.

concepts.statement: The whole machine is one loop: **fetch** ($T_0$–$T_1$) → **decode** ($T_2$) → effective address ($T_3$ if indirect) → **execute** (one to three states) → interrupt check → fetch. The state diagram draws exactly this cycle with the indirect and interrupt branches as its two detours.
concepts.detail: Reading the diagram is reading the machine: every arrow carries its timing label, every box its RTL, and the two decision diamonds (I? and flag?) are the only conditionals the control unit itself ever evaluates. Everything else — the 23 instructions — is data steering a fixed loop, which is the sense in which the fetch–decode–execute cycle deserves its name as the heartbeat of every stored-program computer since 1949.

figures.caption: The instruction-cycle state diagram: the fetch phase ($T_0$: AR ← PC; $T_1$: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1) leads to decode ($T_2$), which steers to the indirect-address step ($T_3$, when I = 1), the execute states, and back to fetch — with the interrupt check as the one detour that can hijack the loop between instructions.

examples.title: Tracing one LDA instruction, state by state
examples.problem: PC holds 250, location 250 holds an LDA 500 instruction (direct), and $M[500] = 0111\ 0000\ 0000\ 0001$. Trace every timing state with the register values (SC starts at 0).

steps.label: T0 — aim the memory
steps.text: $\mathrm{AR} \leftarrow \mathrm{PC} = 250$. The bus carries PC into AR; SC advances to 1.

steps.label: T1 — fetch and advance
steps.text: $\mathrm{IR} \leftarrow M[250] = \mathtt{0010\ 0100\ 0000\ 0100}$... the LDA opcode $010$ with address $0100\ 0000\ 0100 = 516$ — say instead the word is LDA 500; then PC takes 251 (the incrementer's free ride).

steps.label: T2 — decode and aim
steps.text: Bits 14–12 = $010$ raise $D_2$ (LDA); $\mathrm{AR} \leftarrow \mathrm{IR}(0\text{–}11) = 500$; $I = \mathrm{IR}(15) = 0$ — direct, so no indirect state.

steps.label: T4 — load and reset
steps.text: $\mathrm{AC} \leftarrow \mathrm{DR}$ and $\mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$: five clock pulses per LDA, and the machine returns to fetch with PC = 251.

examples.result: AC = 28673 (0x7001), after exactly 5 cycles: fetch 3, read 1, load 1 — the CPI table's row for a direct LDA, verified on the bench.

examples.title: The six-cycle ISZ, end to end
examples.problem: Location 300 holds ISZ 350 (direct); $M[350] = 1111\ 1111\ 1111\ 1111$ ($-1$). Trace the complete instruction.

steps.label: Fetch: T0, T1, T2
steps.text: $\mathrm{AR} \leftarrow 300$; $\mathrm{IR} \leftarrow M[300]$, PC: 301; decode $D_6$ (ISZ), $\mathrm{AR} \leftarrow 350$, $I = 0$.

steps.label: T3 — read the counter
steps.text: $\mathrm{DR} \leftarrow M[350] = -1$ (all ones).

steps.label: T4 — increment
steps.text: $\mathrm{DR} \leftarrow \mathrm{DR} + 1 = 0$ — the wraparound the pattern was waiting for.

steps.label: T5 — write back and test
steps.text: $M[350] \leftarrow 0$; since DR = 0, also $\mathrm{PC} \leftarrow \mathrm{PC} + 1$ (the skip fires — the next instruction is bypassed); $\mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$.

steps.label: Count the pulses
steps.text: Six: $T_0, T_1, T_2, T_3, T_4, T_5$ — the longest instruction in the machine, and the workhorse of every loop.

examples.result: The counter wraps to zero, the skip takes effect, and the whole instruction cost 6 cycles — ISZ is why loop overhead, not arithmetic, dominates this machine's profiles.

examples.title: A subtraction program, cycle-counted
examples.problem: The program of Section 8.3's third example (LDA 201; CMA; INC; ADD 200; HLT — all direct, values already in memory) runs from address 100. How many clock cycles does it take in total?

steps.label: LDA, direct
steps.text: Fetch (3) + read (1) + load (1) = 5 cycles.

steps.label: CMA, register-reference
steps.text: Fetch (3) + one execute pulse (1) = 4 cycles.

steps.label: INC, register-reference
steps.text: 4 cycles, same as CMA.

steps.label: ADD, direct
steps.text: Fetch (3) + read (1) + add (1) = 5 cycles.

steps.label: HLT, register-reference
steps.text: Fetch (3) + stop (1) = 4 cycles — and SC freezing is the machine's only rest.

examples.result: $5 + 4 + 4 + 5 + 4 = \mathbf{22}$ cycles for a subtraction — the two's-complement idiom's cost in the machine's own currency, the number every hardware-multiply proposal compares against.

examples.title: An interrupt in flight
examples.problem: During the ADD of that same program, the user presses a key: FGI sets while IEN = 1. Trace what happens at the ADD's final state and after.

steps.label: The ADD completes anyway
steps.text: The check is only made between instructions: the ADD runs to its last state and executes $\mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$ as always — the interrupt never lands mid-instruction.

steps.label: The hijack replaces fetch
steps.text: Instead of $T_0\colon \mathrm{AR} \leftarrow \mathrm{PC}$, the R flip-flop routes the counter's pulses into the interrupt cycle: $RT_0\colon \mathrm{AR} \leftarrow 0$.

steps.label: Save and branch
steps.text: $RT_1\colon M[0] \leftarrow \mathrm{PC}$ (the address of the HLT that never ran yet — the resume point) and $\mathrm{PC} \leftarrow 1$.

steps.label: Disarm and resume fetch
steps.text: $RT_2\colon \mathrm{IEN} \leftarrow 0$, $R \leftarrow 0$, $\mathrm{SC} \leftarrow 0$. The next pulse is an ordinary fetch — of the service routine's first instruction at address 1.

steps.label: The routine's duty
steps.text: It INPs the character (which clears FGI — disarming the cause), does its work, then returns with an indirect BUN through location 0 and re-enables interrupts with ION.

examples.result: The main program resumes at exactly where it was pushed aside, one instruction boundary later — a context switch in five states, with the return address standing in for everything a full OS would save.

keyTakeaways: The sequence counter SC plus a decoder raises one-hot timing signals $T_0, T_1, \ldots$; every control function is a product of a decoded opcode and a timing state, and SC ← 0 is the universal "go to fetch".

Fetch is invariant: $T_0\colon \mathrm{AR} \leftarrow \mathrm{PC}$; $T_1\colon \mathrm{IR} \leftarrow M[\mathrm{AR}],\ \mathrm{PC} \leftarrow \mathrm{PC} + 1$; $T_2\colon$ decode + aim. The PC increment rides free in $T_1$.
Indirect addressing costs exactly one extra state, $T_3\colon \mathrm{AR} \leftarrow M[\mathrm{AR}]$, skipped by direct instructions.
Cycle counts: register-reference and I/O instructions 4; STA, BUN, BSA 4; direct AND/ADD/LDA 5; ISZ 6; every indirect one adds 1 — the machine's CPI table, derivable by hand.
Register-reference and I/O instructions execute entirely in a single $T_3$ pulse via bit decoding under $r = D_7 I' T_3$ or $p = D_7 I T_3$.

The interrupt cycle fires only between instructions, saves PC at location 0, branches to the routine at 1, disables itself (IEN ← 0), and returns via indirect BUN — precise interruption by construction.

quiz.q: During the fetch phase, the program counter increments at timing state:
options: $T_1$, riding free with the instruction read
quiz.explanation: PC ← PC + 1 shares $T_1$ with IR ← M[AR] because the incrementer is a dedicated path that does not occupy the common bus — the classic free rider of the timing design.

quiz.q: The microoperation SC ← 0, written at the end of every execute sequence, causes:
options: the next clock pulse to raise $T_0$ — a new fetch
quiz.explanation: Zeroing the sequence counter makes the decoder raise $T_0$ next, and $T_0$'s only microoperation is AR ← PC — the fetch of the next instruction. SC ← 0 is the machine's single "return to start".

quiz.q: At $T_2$ of a fetch, the control raises $D_5$ and finds $I = 0$. The next microoperation to execute is:
quiz.explanation: $D_5$ is BSA and $I = 0$ means direct — no pointer step, so execute begins immediately: the return address (PC) is stored and execution continues from AR + 1.

quiz.q: Which instruction takes the most clock cycles (direct addressing)?
quiz.explanation: ISZ needs read, increment, write-back and the zero test: $T_0$–$T_5$, six cycles. BUN takes 4, CMA 4, LDA 5.

quiz.q: The register-reference instructions all execute at timing state:
quiz.explanation: With opcode $D_7$ and $I = 0$, no memory operand exists, so one pulse finishes the job: each of the twelve operations is one bit of IR(0–11) ANDed with $r = D_7 I' T_3$.

quiz.q: A direct ADD (opcode $D_1$) executes its addition under the control function:
quiz.explanation: Fetch takes $T_0$–$T_2$; $T_3$ reads the operand into DR; the ALU work happens at $T_4$ (AC ← AC + DR, E ← carry, SC ← 0). For an indirect ADD everything shifts one state later.

quiz.q: The interrupt cycle stores the return address:
options: at the address field of the interrupted instruction
quiz.explanation: RT0 aims AR at 0 and RT1 writes PC there — the interrupted program's resume point — while PC takes 1, the service routine's start. The routine returns with an indirect BUN through location 0.

quiz.q: Interrupts are recognized:
quiz.explanation: The flag test is wired into the end-of-instruction transition: each instruction runs to completion, then the flag condition diverts the cycle. This between-instructions discipline is the ancestor of precise exceptions.

quiz.q: The R flip-flop in the interrupt cycle exists to:
options: route the timing counter's pulses into the interrupt microoperations
remember the result of the last ALU operation
quiz.explanation: R simply renames the timing states: while R = 1, the pulses $T_0, T_1, T_2$ are interpreted as $RT_0, RT_1, RT_2$ — the interrupt sequence instead of a fetch. Clearing R at RT2 hands the baton back.

quiz.q: How many clock cycles does the program LDA 100 · CLE · HLT take (all direct, ignoring the interrupt check)?
quiz.explanation: LDA: fetch 3 + read 1 + load 1 = 5. CLE (register-reference): fetch 3 + execute 1 = 4. HLT: fetch 3 + stop 1 = 4. Total $5 + 4 + 4 = 13$ cycles.

depth.title: Timing, cost and speedups

blocks.heading: The CPI table, derived
blocks.body: Every instruction's cycle count follows from one rule: list the microoperations, and charge one clock period per occupancy of the common bus, letting dedicated paths ride free. Fetch is fixed at three ($T_0, T_1, T_2$: bus, memory, decode-aim). Add one state if indirect. Then per instruction: register-reference and I/O add 1 (one bus-free pulse); STA adds 1 (one memory write); BUN and BSA add 1 (register transfers); AND/ADD/LDA add 2 (memory read plus the ALU state); ISZ adds 3 (read, increment, write-back plus test). The totals — 4, 4, 4, 5, 6 and the indirect +1 — are not a table to memorize but a budget to recompute, and the same audit (bus occupancies, free riders) prices any microarchitecture on paper before it is built.

blocks.heading: Microprogramming the control
blocks.body: Hardwiring every control function $D_i T_j$ (and every $r B_k$, $p B_k$) is a Boolean sum-of-products per control line — correct, fast, and brittle: a design change rewires gates. Wilkes's 1951 alternative stores the control signals themselves in a ROM: each cycle reads one **control word** (one bit per control line — horizontal microcode; or an encoded micro-op field — vertical microcode) and the word's sequencer bits choose the next address. The basic computer's entire control then becomes a 64-ish-word table, one row per (opcode, state) pair, and adding an instruction means adding rows, not gates. Real machines used microcode for exactly this (the VAX and the IBM 360 model 40's writable control store; x86's modern micro-ops are its direct descendant), trading speed for flexibility at the boundary where hardwired timing closure stops scaling.

blocks.heading: Pipelining the cycle away
blocks.body: The fetch–decode–execute loop is sequential by construction: the machine finishes instruction $n$ before touching $n+1$, so the CPI column is also the latency column. The classical speedup overlaps the phases: while instruction $n$ executes, instruction $n+1$ decodes and $n+2$ fetches — the five-stage pipeline, pushing CPI toward 1. The basic computer's own structure predicts the hazards: its single memory port means fetch and a data read contend (the structural hazard a split instruction/data cache later solves), and its BUN overwrites the very PC the fetch is using (the control hazard that branch prediction later hides). Reading this section, one has already met every reason pipelines are hard.

depth.title: Verification and the clock's future

blocks.heading: RTL verification at scale
blocks.body: Because every microoperation and every control function of this machine is written down, its whole behavior is a finite-state system — and finite-state systems yield to model checking: exhaustive or symbolic exploration proving, for instance, that no reachable state ever enables two drivers of the same register in one pulse (the single-writer discipline this design obeys by hand). That property is exactly what industrial RTL verification checks on designs a million times larger, and its failure modes are the famously expensive ones: the 1994 Pentium FDIV bug — a missing table entry in the division microcode, shipped before formal verification was standard — cost Intel $475 million and made formal methods a line item ever since. Modern signoff routinely proves cache-coherence protocols and pipeline invariants with tools (TLA+, Alloy, model checkers, symbolic simulation) that would fit this machine in an afternoon.

blocks.heading: Precise exceptions and out-of-order cores
blocks.body: This machine's interrupts are precise by construction: nothing is ever mid-flight when the flag check happens. Out-of-order processors destroy that comfort — twenty instructions may be partially executed, some past a faulting one — and recovering an exact architectural state (the precise exception) requires the reorder buffer: completed results are held in a completion queue and retired in program order, so the faulting instruction's frontier is always clean. The basic computer's SC ← 0 at a known instruction boundary is, in miniature, the invariant that multi-million-transistor machinery exists to preserve: the interrupted program sees its own execution as sequential, no matter what the silicon did in parallel.

blocks.heading: Life without the clock
blocks.body: Every timing state of this section assumes a global clock beating in lockstep — but clock distribution is now the limiting cost of large chips (skew budgets, power spent toggling synchronously, GHz-limited by the slowest path). The asynchronous alternative removes the clock entirely: modules handshake (request/acknowledge), data validity replaces timing validity, and average-case rather than worst-case speed governs. Delay-insensitive circuits go further, correct under arbitrary gate delays. The open problems are decades old and stubborn: automatic verification of asynchronous correctness (the handshake discipline is a concurrency problem, and the tools of the previous block apply directly), competitive EDA tooling, and the systems question — how much of a clocked ecosystem (memories, buses, software timing assumptions) an asynchronous island must emulate to interoperate. That a complete, understandable computer like this one is the natural testbed for all of it is the strongest argument for having built it at all.

intro: Chapter 8 described registers and microoperations abstractly — statements such as AC ← AC + DR with no commitment to wires. This chapter builds the machinery that makes those statements real: a general processor unit in which a bank of registers feeds two selector multiplexers, an arithmetic logic unit, a shifter and a set of status flags, and in which every microoperation is nothing but a control word applied for one clock period. The design is exactly the one the basic computer of Chapter 11 will use.
objectives: Describe the organization of a general processor unit: registers, selectors, buses, ALU, shifter and flags
Explain how a multiplexer selects the ALU’s two source registers and how a decoder selects the destination
Define the control word and size each of its fields for a given register set
Encode a specific microoperation as a binary control word
Connect this hardware view to the system-level view of Operating System Concepts (OSC Ch 2)

concepts.statement: A **processor unit** is the collection of hardware that executes microoperations: a set of registers, two selector circuits that choose ALU operands, the arithmetic logic unit, a shifter, and status flags, all joined by buses and governed by control words.
concepts.detail: Mano draws this as the canonical block diagram: registers $R_1, R_2, ldots, R_n$ across the top, a MUX A and a MUX B feeding the A and B inputs of the ALU, the shifter after the ALU output, and a destination decoder that enables exactly one register load. Every instruction a computer executes is ultimately a timed sequence of transfers through this one structure.

concepts.statement: The processor’s **register set** mixes general working registers with special-purpose ones: a **program counter (PC)** holding the next instruction address, an **address register (AR)** driving memory, a **data register (DR)** for operands, an **accumulator (AC)** for ALU results, an **instruction register (IR)**, and a **temporary register (TR)**.
concepts.detail: In the basic computer of Chapter 11 this set becomes exactly AC, IR, PC, AR, DR, TR, INPR and OUTR. The special registers exist because the fetch–decode–execute rhythm of Chapter 8 demands fixed places to hold the instruction, its address and its operand.

concepts.statement: Two **multiplexers (MUX A and MUX B)** select which two registers drive the A and B buses into the ALU; their select codes are the SELA and SELB fields of the control word.
concepts.detail: With $k$ registers each selector needs $\lceil \log_2 k \rceil$ select lines. Because the two selections are independent, the ALU can receive any register on the A side and any register on the B side in the same clock period — this is what makes microoperations such as AC ← AC + DR a single control word.

concepts.statement: The **destination decoder** converts the SELD field of the control word into one-hot load enable lines, so that exactly one register captures the ALU/shifter output at the next clock pulse.
concepts.detail: SELD is decoded rather than used literally because a register load is an enable signal, not a multiplexer address: the decoder produces $2^{d}$ enable lines from a $d$-bit field, and the unused codes either idle all registers or perform no transfer at all.

concepts.statement: A **control word** is the concatenation of the selection fields that specifies one microoperation: **SELA | SELB | SELD | OPR**, where OPR selects the ALU operation and the shifter function.
concepts.detail: For a processor with eight registers, SELA, SELB and SELD are three bits each; if the ALU has eight operations (three select lines $s_2 s_1 s_0$) and the shifter has three functions plus no-shift (two select lines), OPR is five bits, giving a 14-bit control word. Chapter 10 is entirely about generating sequences of these words.

concepts.statement: An $n$-bit processor has $n$-bit registers, $n$-bit buses, an $n$-bit ALU and an $n$-bit shifter; the status flags are one bit each and are computed from the $n$-bit result.
concepts.detail: Width is a design constant: the basic computer uses $n = 16$ with a 16-bit AC and 16-bit memory words, while the arithmetic worked examples of this chapter use $n = 4$ purely so every bit can be seen. The logic of the two designs is identical.

concepts.term: Datapath and control: the great division
concepts.statement: A computer divides into a **datapath** (this chapter: registers, buses, ALU, shifter, flags) and a **control unit** (Chapter 10) that emits control words — the same division that operating systems inherit, with the OS seeing only the instruction set the two layers expose.
concepts.detail: Cross-link: OSC Ch 2 describes an operating system as software layered over hardware services; every process context it saves is precisely the register file and flags designed here, and every system call it dispatches is an instruction fetched through the datapath of Section 9.4. Mano Ch 8 defined the microoperations; this chapter realizes them in gates.

examples.title: Sizing and encoding a control word
examples.problem: A processor has registers AR, PC, DR, AC, IR and TR plus the 8-bit input register INPR. The ALU performs eight operations (transfer, add, add-complement, increment, AND, OR, XOR, complement) and the shifter performs no-shift, shift-right or shift-left. Determine the control word length and encode AC ← AC + DR.

steps.label: Step 1: Size the selection fields
steps.text: There are seven registers (INPR counts as one source), so each of SELA, SELB and SELD needs $\lceil \log_2 7 \rceil = 3$ bits — eight codes with one to spare.

steps.label: Step 2: Size the operation field
steps.text: Eight ALU operations require three select lines $s_2 s_1 s_0$, and the shifter needs two more lines (00 no shift, 01 shift right, 10 shift left), so OPR is five bits.

steps.label: Step 3: Concatenate
steps.text: The control word is SELA (3) + SELB (3) + SELD (3) + OPR (5) = **14 bits**, the same size Mano uses for the eight-register processor of his example.

steps.label: Step 4: Assign register codes
steps.text: Choose AR = 000, PC = 001, DR = 010, AC = 011, IR = 100, TR = 101, INPR = 110 (111 spare).

steps.label: Step 5: Encode the microoperation
steps.text: For AC ← AC + DR: SELA = AC = 011, SELB = DR = 010, SELD = AC = 011, OPR = 00100 (add, no shift). The word is 011 010 011 00100.

examples.result: A 14-bit control word, and AC ← AC + DR is the single word 01101001100100. The control unit of Chapter 10 does nothing but emit sequences of such words, one per clock period.

examples.title: Following a microoperation through the datapath
examples.problem: Trace the composite microoperation AC ← sl AC + DR (add, then shift the sum left into AC) through the processor organization, with AC = 0110 and DR = 0011.

steps.label: Step 1: Source selection
steps.text: MUX A places AC = 0110 on the A bus (SELA = 011) and MUX B places DR = 0011 on the B bus (SELB = 010). Both buses carry their words simultaneously.

steps.label: Step 2: ALU operation
steps.text: With OPR selecting addition, the ALU — a combinational network of full adders — forms $0110 + 0011 = 1001$ during this clock period.

steps.label: Step 3: Shifter action
steps.text: The shifter follows the ALU: shift-left moves every bit one position toward the more significant end, so 1001 becomes 0010, with the outgoing most significant bit 1 discarded (a full design can capture it in the carry flag instead).

steps.label: Step 4: Destination load and flags
steps.text: The destination decoder (SELD = 011 for AC) raises AC’s load line; at the next clock pulse AC takes 0010 and the status flags latch the ALU’s condition bits for the addition (carry 1 from $6 + 3 = 9$ in 4 bits, nonzero, positive).

examples.result: The microoperation completes in one clock period through selection, addition, shifting and load — the pipeline structure every instruction of Chapter 11 will reuse.

keyTakeaways: A processor unit is registers + two source multiplexers + ALU + shifter + destination decoder + status flags.
SELA and SELB select the ALU’s two operands; SELD is decoded to enable exactly one destination register load.
The control word SELA | SELB | SELD | OPR completely specifies one microoperation — 14 bits for the eight-register example.
Each selection field needs $\lceil \log_2 k \rceil$ bits for $k$ registers.
The shifter sits after the ALU, so composite microoperations such as AC ← sl AC + DR are single control words.
This chapter is the hardware realization of Chapter 8’s register-transfer language, and the layer an OS (OSC Ch 2) ultimately rides on.

quiz.q: A processor has 16 registers. How many bits do SELA, SELB and SELD each need?
options: 3 bits each, one per operand bus
8 bits each, one per byte of the word
quiz.explanation: Selecting one of $k$ registers requires $\lceil \log_2 k \rceil$ lines; for 16 registers that is 4 bits for each of the three fields.

quiz.q: What does the SELD field of the control word do after decoding?
options: It raises the load-enable line of exactly one destination register
It drives the address bus to memory
quiz.explanation: SELD goes through a decoder whose one-hot output enables a single register load, so the ALU/shifter result lands in exactly the intended register.

quiz.q: Why does the processor organization use two separate source multiplexers (MUX A and MUX B) rather than one?
options: Because the ALU takes two operands, and the two selections must be independent so operations like AC ← AC + DR fit in one control word
Because registers have two outputs each
To provide redundancy against multiplexer failure
quiz.explanation: A two-operand ALU needs two simultaneously selected sources; independent SELA and SELB codes let any register pair meet at the ALU in a single clock period.

quiz.q: In the worked 14-bit control word, what does the OPR field contain?
options: The ALU operation select bits plus the shifter select bits
quiz.explanation: OPR is the operation field: three bits $s_2 s_1 s_0$ for the eight ALU microoperations and two bits for the shifter (no-shift, right, left).

quiz.q: Which statement best connects this chapter’s processor to OSC Ch 2’s operating-system structures?
options: The OS replaces the ALU with software
The register file and flags designed here are exactly the per-process context an OS saves and restores, and the ISA the OS targets is the interface this datapath exposes
The control word is stored in the file system
Multiplexers are managed by the OS scheduler
quiz.explanation: The OS never sees gates — it sees the instruction set. But every process context is the register set of this chapter, and every context switch is a save/restore of these registers driven by the datapath of Section 9.4.

intro: The arithmetic logic unit is where microoperations become arithmetic. Mano’s method is beautiful because it reuses one structure three times: an arithmetic circuit is just a chain of full adders whose per-stage inputs are made functions of the selection lines; a logic circuit is a per-bit selector among AND, OR, XOR and complement; and the combined ALU is both, sharing the selection code so that three lines choose among eight microoperations.
objectives: Design a 4-bit arithmetic circuit from full adders with two selection lines
Derive the per-stage input equations $x_i$, $y_i$ and the initial carry from the desired microoperation table
Verify arithmetic selections with concrete binary numbers
Design the logic circuit for AND, OR, XOR and complement microoperations
Present the combined 8-microoperation ALU table and its selection encoding

concepts.statement: An **arithmetic circuit** is a cascade of full adders whose stage inputs $x_i$ and $y_i$ and initial carry $c_1$ are Boolean functions of the operands $A_i$, $B_i$ and the selection lines, so that one wiring performs several arithmetic microoperations.
concepts.detail: Each stage computes the sum bit $F_i = x_i \oplus y_i \oplus c_i$ and carry $c_{i+1} = x_i y_i + x_i c_i + y_i c_i$ exactly as in Chapter 4’s adders; the design freedom lies entirely in what $x_i$, $y_i$ and $c_1$ are wired to be. The carries ripple between stages exactly as in the ripple-carry adder of Chapter 4.

concepts.statement: To design the arithmetic circuit, first tabulate what each selection must add to $A$: with select $s_1 s_0$ equal to 00, 01, 10 and 11 the circuit performs transfer ($F = A$), addition ($F = A + B$), add-complement ($F = A + \bar{B}$) and increment ($F = A + 1$).
concepts.detail: Reading the table as full-adder inputs: 00 needs $y = 0$ and $c_1 = 0$; 01 needs $y = B$, $c_1 = 0$; 10 needs $y = \bar{B}$, $c_1 = 0$; and 11 needs $y = 0$ with the single 1 injected as the initial carry $c_1 = 1$. Tabulating $y_i$ over the $s_1 s_0$ cells of a Karnaugh map gives the two-product expression below.

concepts.statement: The arithmetic circuit design yields $x_i = A_i$, $y_i = \bar{s}_1 s_0 B_i + s_1 \bar{s}_0 \bar{B}_i$ and initial carry $c_1 = s_1 s_0$.
concepts.detail: Check each selection: 00 gives $y_i = 0$, $c_1 = 0$ (transfer); 01 gives $y_i = B_i$ (add); 10 gives $y_i = \bar{B}_i$ (add the complement); 11 gives $y_i = 0$ but $c_1 = 1$ (increment). Every row of the design table is satisfied by one small gate network per stage.
