concepts.statement: Subtraction reuses the adder because $A - B = A + \bar{B} + 1$: complementing every bit of $B$ and injecting a carry of 1 into the least significant stage forms the two’s complement.
concepts.detail: This is why selection 10 (add-complement) plus an incoming carry of 1 is true subtraction — the trick used by the basic computer and by every two’s-complement machine since. No separate subtractor circuit is ever built.

concepts.statement: The **logic circuit** performs bitwise Boolean microoperations: per stage it selects among $A_i \wedge B_i$ (AND), $A_i \vee B_i$ (OR), $A_i \oplus B_i$ (XOR) and $\bar{A}_i$ (complement) under the same two selection lines.
concepts.detail: Each stage is essentially a small multiplexer over the four functions of $A_i$ and $B_i$. Because the operations are bitwise, there are no carries at all in logic mode — the design simply gates the carry chain off.

concepts.statement: One structure with three selection lines $s_2 s_1 s_0$ performs eight microoperations: $s_2 = 0$ gives the arithmetic set (transfer, add, add-complement, increment) and $s_2 = 1$ gives the logic set (AND, OR, XOR, complement).
concepts.detail: The arithmetic network of full adders handles the $s_2 = 0$ codes; the per-bit logic network handles $s_2 = 1$; the mode bit $s_2$ steers the stage output between them (and disables the carry chain in logic mode). Add the shifter of Section 9.3 after the output and the result is the complete ALU of a processor.

concepts.statement: In a ripple arithmetic circuit the worst-case delay grows with the word length because the carry must propagate through every stage; the remedy is the **carry-lookahead** logic of Chapter 4, which real ALU chips use.
concepts.detail: Mano’s designs keep the ripple cascade for clarity — the per-stage selection logic is the lesson — but the same $x_i$, $y_i$, $c_1$ equations plug directly into a lookahead adder when speed matters.

examples.title: Designing the arithmetic circuit selection with $s_1 s_0$
examples.problem: Design a 4-bit arithmetic circuit that performs transfer, addition, add-complement and increment on inputs $A$ and $B$, and verify every selection with $A = 0110$ and $B = 0011$.

steps.label: Step 1: Write the microoperation table
steps.text: Select $s_1 s_0$: 00 → $F = A$; 01 → $F = A + B$; 10 → $F = A + \bar{B}$; 11 → $F = A + 1$. These cover the register-transfer needs of the processor (move data, add, set up subtraction, count).

steps.label: Step 2: Translate to full-adder inputs
steps.text: Each selection must express $F = A + y + c_1$ for some per-stage bit-pattern $y$ and initial carry $c_1$: 00 → $y = 0$, $c_1 = 0$; 01 → $y = B$, $c_1 = 0$; 10 → $y = \bar{B}$, $c_1 = 0$; 11 → $y = 0$, $c_1 = 1$.

steps.label: Step 3: Simplify with a Karnaugh map
steps.text: Plotting $y_i$ over the four $s_1 s_0$ cells gives $y_i = \bar{s}_1 s_0 B_i + s_1 \bar{s}_0 \bar{B}_i$; the initial carry is $c_1 = s_1 s_0$ because only increment injects a 1 into the least significant stage.

steps.label: Step 4: Wire one stage
steps.text: Stage $i$ receives $x_i = A_i$ directly, one AND–OR network computes $y_i$ from $B_i$, $s_1$, $s_0$, and the stages chain carry to carry exactly like Chapter 4’s adder.

examples.result: One cascade of full adders plus a handful of gates per stage implements four arithmetic microoperations — and feeding an incoming carry of 1 turns selection 10 into true subtraction: $6 + 12 + 1 = 19 = 10011$, so $F = 0011 = 3 = 6 - 3$. ✓

examples.title: The logic circuit: AND, OR, XOR, complement
examples.problem: Design the per-stage logic selection for the four Boolean microoperations and verify them with $A = 1010$ and $B = 0110$.

steps.label: Step 1: Tabulate the bitwise functions
steps.text: Select $s_1 s_0$: 00 → $F = A \wedge B$; 01 → $F = A \vee B$; 10 → $F = A \oplus B$; 11 → $F = \bar{A}$. Each is a function of the two stage bits only — no carries exist in logic mode.

steps.label: Step 2: Build one stage
steps.text: Per stage, small gate networks form $A_i B_i$, $A_i + B_i$, $A_i \oplus B_i$ and $\bar{A}_i$, and a selection network (effectively a 4-to-1 multiplexer on $s_1 s_0$) passes the chosen function to $F_i$.

steps.label: Step 3: Verify AND ($s_1 s_0 = 00$)
steps.text: $1010 \wedge 0110 = 0010$ ✓ — only the bit position where both words carry a 1 survives.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify OR, XOR, complement
steps.text: OR: $1010 \vee 0110 = 1110$ ✓. XOR: $1010 \oplus 0110 = 1100$ ✓ (the bits that differ). Complement: $\bar{A} = 0101$ ✓.

examples.result: Four logic microoperations per bit with two selection lines; chained across all stages they operate on whole words at once, which is why mask and test operations in the basic computer are single instructions.

examples.title: The combined ALU microoperation table
examples.problem: Assemble the arithmetic and logic selections into one ALU with three selection lines $s_2 s_1 s_0$ and run two selections numerically.

steps.label: Step 1: Assign the arithmetic block
steps.text: $s_2 = 0$: 000 → transfer $F = A$; 001 → add $F = A + B$; 010 → add-complement $F = A + \bar{B}$; 011 → increment $F = A + 1$.

steps.label: Step 2: Assign the logic block
steps.text: $s_2 = 1$: 100 → AND $F = A \wedge B$; 101 → OR $F = A \vee B$; 110 → XOR $F = A \oplus B$; 111 → complement $F = \bar{A}$.

steps.label: Step 3: Combine the hardware
steps.text: The mode bit $s_2$ selects between the full-adder path and the logic path per stage and suppresses the carry chain in logic mode — one shared output bus, one set of stage pins.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify one arithmetic and one logic selection

examples.result: Three selection lines, eight microoperations — this table is the OPR field of Section 9.1’s control word, and it is the very instruction repertoire the basic computer applies to AC and DR.

keyTakeaways: An arithmetic circuit is a full-adder cascade whose stage inputs are functions of the selection lines: $x_i = A_i$, $y_i = \bar{s}_1 s_0 B_i + s_1 \bar{s}_0 \bar{B}_i$, $c_1 = s_1 s_0$.
The four arithmetic selections are transfer, add, add-complement and increment; an incoming carry converts add-complement into subtraction via $A - B = A + \bar{B} + 1$.
The logic circuit selects AND, OR, XOR or complement per bit with the same two selection lines and no carries.
The combined ALU uses $s_2$ as a mode bit: eight microoperations under three selection lines $s_2 s_1 s_0$.
The OPR field of the processor control word drives exactly these selection lines.
Ripple carry limits speed; the Chapter 4 lookahead technique applies unchanged.

quiz.q: In the arithmetic circuit design, what does selection $s_1 s_0 = 11$ compute?
options: $F = A + 1$, because $y_i = 0$ and the initial carry $c_1 = 1$
quiz.explanation: With both selection lines high, the per-stage $y$ network output is 0 but $c_1 = s_1 s_0 = 1$, so exactly one 1 is injected at the least significant stage: $F = A + 1$.

quiz.q: How is true subtraction obtained from the add-complement selection?
options: By injecting an incoming carry of 1, giving $A + \bar{B} + 1 = A - B$
quiz.explanation: Two’s complement guarantees $-B = \bar{B} + 1$, so add-complement plus a forced initial carry performs subtraction with no extra hardware.

quiz.q: With $A = 0110$ and $B = 0011$, the add-complement selection produces:
quiz.explanation: Selection 10 forms $A + \bar{B} = 0110 + 1100 = 10010$; the 4-bit result is 0010 with carry out 1. Add the incoming carry and you get 0011, the true difference $6 - 3$.

quiz.q: What distinguishes logic mode from arithmetic mode in the combined ALU?
options: Logic mode is bitwise with the carry chain disabled, while arithmetic mode ripples carries between stages
Logic mode requires two clock periods
quiz.explanation: AND, OR, XOR and complement act independently on each bit, so no carry propagates; the mode bit $s_2$ both steers the stage output and gates off the carry chain.

quiz.q: How many selection lines does the combined ALU of this section need, and what do they choose among?
options: 3 lines among 8 microoperations: four arithmetic and four logic
quiz.explanation: $s_2 s_1 s_0$: with $s_2 = 0$ the full-adder cascade performs transfer, add, add-complement, increment; with $s_2 = 1$ the logic network performs AND, OR, XOR, complement.

quiz.q: With selection $S_2S_1S_0$, how does the arithmetic circuit choose among its eight microoperations?
options: $S$ lines feed the per-stage full adders’ input functions, picking transfer, increment, add, subtract and related forms
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** chain of full adders with per-stage $X_i, Y_i$ made functions of $A_i, B_i$ and $S$.
**Step 2 — Rule:** three lines encode eight operations (e.g. $F = A$, $F = A + 1$, $F = A + B$, $F = A + B′ + 1$ for subtract, plus complements and transfers).
**Step 3 — Apply:** setting $S$ rewires every stage identically, so one code adds across all bits while another subtracts.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** the logic section reuses the same $S$ idea with a per-bit selector among AND, OR, XOR, complement — one code space, two circuits.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** clock, memory choice and halt are control-unit jobs, not ALU data selection.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** $S$ programs the adder inputs.

quiz.q: After an ALU operation yielding all-zero result with a carry out of the MSB, which flags are set?
options: Zero $= 1$, carry $= 1$; overflow depends on signed interpretation
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** $n$-bit result zero, end carry $1$.
**Step 2 — Rule:** zero flag $= 1$ iff every result bit $0$; carry $=$ out of MSB; overflow $= C_{n-1} \oplus C_n$; sign $=$ MSB.
**Step 3 — Apply:** zero $1$, carry $1$; e.g. $1111 + 0001 = 0000$ with carry $1$ sets both.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** overflow here is $0$ for that unsigned wrap (both carries $1$); sign $0$ since result MSB $0$.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** clearing both ignores the observed zero and carry; sign-only misses them; no-change contradicts flag logic.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** zero and carry set.

intro: Two small blocks complete the processor: the shifter, a combinational network that sits between the ALU output and the destination bus, and the status flags — carry, overflow, zero and sign — which remember one bit of information about the last result and are the raw material of every conditional branch a computer ever takes.
objectives: Design a combinational shifter with right/left/none selection
Trace concrete shift microoperations on 4-bit data
Define each status flag C, V, Z, S and state when it is set
Compute overflow with the XOR-of-carries rule $V = C_8 \oplus C_7$ on worked 8-bit additions
Distinguish carry (unsigned overflow) from overflow (signed overflow)

concepts.statement: The **shifter** is a combinational network between the ALU output and the destination bus: with select lines it passes the word unchanged, shifts it one position right, or shifts it one position left — all in the same clock period as the ALU operation.
concepts.detail: Because it is purely gates (no flip-flops), the shifter is drawn inside the processor’s combinational path, after the ALU. Its select bits occupy the last two bits of the OPR field of the control word.

concepts.statement: Shift-right connects each output bit to its left neighbor ($F_i = A_{i+1}$, serial 0 into the most significant position); shift-left connects each output bit to its right neighbor ($F_i = A_{i-1}$, serial 0 into the least significant position); the end bits are simply discarded.
concepts.detail: These are logical shifts — the incoming serial bit is always 0. Shifting left multiplies the unsigned value by 2 (losing the top bit if it was 1), and shifting right divides by 2 — which is why multiply-by-2 loops in the basic computer are written with the CIL circulate instruction instead, so the shifted-out bit survives in E.

concepts.statement: The two shifter select bits encode: **00 no shift, 01 shift right, 10 shift left** (11 unused or no-transfer), appended to the ALU select bits inside the 5-bit OPR field.
concepts.detail: A microoperation such as AC ← sr AC is therefore the control word with SELA = SELD = AC and OPR = transfer + shift-right — proof that shifting is just another transfer through a slightly different combinational path.

concepts.statement: A **barrel shifter** uses per-bit multiplexers to shift by any amount from 0 to $n - 1$ positions in a single pass, instead of one position per microoperation.
concepts.detail: Mano’s processor shifts one bit at a time because each microoperation takes one clock period; LSI microprocessors of Chapter 12 embed barrel shifters so that a single instruction can scale by any power of two. The trade is gates versus time — the classic hardware–software equivalence again.

concepts.statement: The **status flags** are flip-flops latched together with the ALU result: **C** (carry out of the most significant stage), **V** (signed overflow), **Z** (result is all zeros) and **S** (sign — the most significant bit of the result).
concepts.detail: The flags belong to the ALU: whenever a destination register is loaded from the ALU output, the same clock edge stores the four condition bits. Every skip and branch instruction of the basic computer — SPA, SNA, SZA, SZE, and the ISZ loop test — reads exactly these flip-flops.

concepts.statement: **C** signals that the unsigned interpretation went out of range; **V** signals that the signed two’s-complement interpretation went out of range. They are independent: either can be set without the other.
concepts.detail: A carry out of the top stage is normal and expected in two’s-complement arithmetic (for example $-1 + 1$ produces one), whereas V = 1 means the result has the wrong sign and is genuinely wrong as a signed number. Programs that treat data as unsigned test C; programs that treat data as signed test V.

concepts.statement: For an 8-bit ALU, overflow is computed directly from the carry chain: $V = C_8 \oplus C_7$ — the carry **into** the most significant stage XOR the carry **out of** it.
concepts.detail: If the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry leaving it, the sign bit was corrupted by carry propagation — exactly the definition of two’s-complement overflow. Hardware cost: one XOR gate, no matter how wide the ALU.

examples.title: A 4-bit shifter worked in all three modes
examples.problem: Show the shifter’s output for the word $A = 1011$ under no-shift, shift-right and shift-left, and note what happens to the end bits.

steps.label: Step 1: No shift
steps.text: Select 00 passes the word through combinationally: $F = 1011$. This is the ordinary path for non-shift microoperations.

steps.label: Step 2: Shift right
steps.text: Select 01 wires $F_i = A_{i+1}$ with a serial 0 entering the most significant position: $F = 0101$. The original least significant bit 1 falls off the right end and is lost (the basic computer would use CIR instead to keep it in E).

steps.label: Step 3: Shift left
steps.text: Select 10 wires $F_i = A_{i-1}$ with a serial 0 entering the least significant position: $F = 0110$. The most significant bit 1 falls off the left end — unsigned arithmetic would say $11 \times 2 = 22 > 15$ does not fit in 4 bits.

steps.label: Step 4: Read the control word view
steps.text: Each case is one control word: same SELA/SELD, OPR = transfer plus the two shift bits — shifting is a transfer through a rotated wiring pattern, costing no extra clock period.

examples.result: No shift: 1011; sr: 0101 (bit lost on the right); sl: 0110 (bit lost on the left) — the serial input is 0 and the end bits are discarded.

examples.title: Setting every flag, including $V = C_8 \oplus C_7$

steps.label: Step 1: Case (a) — add 1 to 127
steps.text: The carries ripple up through the low seven 1-bits: the carry into the most significant stage is $C_7 = 1$, and the top stage computes $0 + 0 + 1 = 1$ with carry out $C_8 = 0$. Result $10000000$: S = 1, Z = 0.

steps.label: Step 2: Case (a) overflow
steps.text: $V = C_8 \oplus C_7 = 0 \oplus 1 = 1$ — signed overflow, as expected: $127 + 1 = -128$ is out of the signed range $-128$ to $127$. Yet C = 0, because as unsigned arithmetic $127 + 1 = 128$ fits comfortably in 8 bits.

steps.label: Step 4: Case (b) flags
steps.text: $V = 1 \oplus 1 = 0$ — perfectly correct signed arithmetic, $-1 + 1 = 0$. The carry C = 1 is simply the discarded weight $2^8$ and is harmless in two’s complement.

steps.label: Step 5: Case (c) — add −128 to −128
steps.text: $10000000 + 10000000 = 1\,00000000$: the low seven stages see $0 + 0$, so the carry into the top stage is $C_7 = 0$, while the top stage’s $1 + 1$ produces $C_8 = 1$. Result $00000000$, Z = 1, S = 0.

steps.label: Step 6: Case (c) overflow
steps.text: $V = 0 \oplus 1 = 1$ — signed overflow again: $-128 + -128 = -256$ is far outside range, and C = 1 also flags that unsigned $128 + 128 = 256$ does not fit either.

examples.result: The three cases prove the independence of C and V: (a) V without C, (b) C without V, (c) both. One XOR gate comparing $C_7$ and $C_8$ computes V for every addition the ALU will ever perform.

keyTakeaways: The shifter is combinational, sits after the ALU, and offers no-shift, shift-right and shift-left under two select bits inside OPR.
Shift-right reads $F_i = A_{i+1}$, shift-left reads $F_i = A_{i-1}$; the serial input is 0 and end bits are discarded.
Left shift doubles, right shift halves unsigned values; the circulate instructions of Chapter 11 keep the end bit in E.
Flags C, V, Z, S latch with the ALU result and drive every conditional branch.
C means unsigned overflow; V means signed overflow; they are independent of each other.
$V = C_8 \oplus C_7$ (carry into XOR carry out of the sign stage) detects signed overflow with a single gate.

quiz.q: What does the 4-bit shifter produce for $A = 1011$ under shift-right with serial input 0?
options: 0101, with the old least significant bit discarded
quiz.explanation: Shift-right moves every bit toward the less significant end, a 0 enters the most significant position, and the least significant 1 is lost: $1011 \to 0101$.

quiz.q: Why does the ALU compute overflow as $V = C_8 \oplus C_7$ rather than just using the carry C?
options: Because a carry into the sign stage that does not exit (or vice versa) is exactly what corrupts the sign bit in two’s-complement arithmetic
Because C is used for the Z flag
quiz.explanation: If the carry entering the sign bit differs from the one leaving it, the sign bit’s value was determined by a lost carry — the definition of signed overflow. C alone says nothing about sign correctness.

quiz.q: Adding $11111111 + 00000001$ in 8 bits gives result 00000000 with which flags?
options: C = 1, V = 0, Z = 1 — correct signed arithmetic with a harmless carry
quiz.explanation: Both carries are 1, so $V = 1 \oplus 1 = 0$; the sum $-1 + 1 = 0$ sets Z = 1 and the carry out C = 1 is simply the discarded $2^8$ weight.

quiz.q: Which flag would an unsigned comparison loop test after an addition, and why?
options: V, because unsigned numbers are signed in disguise
C, because a carry out of the most significant bit means the unsigned result exceeded the word range
S, because it holds the top bit
Z, because zero is the only interesting result
quiz.explanation: For unsigned interpretation the word is the value; a carry out means the true sum did not fit, so C is the unsigned overflow signal. V plays the same role for signed data.

quiz.q: How do the shifter’s select bits reach the hardware?
options: They are the last two bits of the OPR field of the processor control word
They are stored in memory before each shift
They are generated only by the shifter itself
quiz.explanation: The control word’s OPR field carries the three ALU select bits plus two shifter select bits, so a shifted microoperation is one 5-bit operation code inside the control word.

intro: Now the pieces act together. An instruction is a scripted sequence of control words that walks data through the datapath: the program counter to the address register to memory, the fetched word into the instruction register, the decoder’s output into the address register again, the operand into the data register, and finally the ALU and accumulator. This section traces one instruction through every register and bus.
objectives: State the fetch microoperations that load IR and increment PC
Trace a complete memory-reference instruction through PC, AR, memory, IR, decoder, DR, ALU and AC
Write the control word executed at each timing step of the trace
Extend the trace to indirect addressing, where one extra memory read produces the effective address
Explain why one common bus forces instructions into multiple timing steps

concepts.statement: The **datapath** is the fixed wiring of registers, buses, ALU and shifter through which every instruction’s microoperations flow; only the sequence of control words differs from one instruction to the next.
concepts.detail: This is the central economy of computer design: one datapath, many programs. The fetch hardware is identical for all instructions; execution paths diverge only after the decoder recognizes the opcode and the control unit begins emitting instruction-specific control words.

concepts.statement: Every instruction begins: **T0:** AR ← PC; **T1:** IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1; **T2:** decode the opcode, AR ← IR(address field), I ← IR(indirect bit).
concepts.detail: T0 aims the memory at the instruction; T1 brings the instruction into IR while the dedicated incrementer advances PC so the next fetch is already aimed; T2 extracts the 12-bit address field into AR and the indirect bit into I, leaving the decoder outputs ready to steer execution. (The basic computer of Chapter 11 numbers the states slightly differently to accommodate indirect addressing at T3.)

concepts.statement: A memory-reference execution continues **T3:** DR ← M[AR] (operand fetch), then an ALU step such as AC ← AC + DR with the flags latching alongside; register-reference instructions skip memory entirely and act on AC and E in one step.
concepts.detail: The common rhythm — aim (AR), read (M[AR] onto the bus), load (destination), compute (ALU into AC) — repeats at every level of computer architecture, which is why Mano can design the whole machine around one bus and one ALU.

concepts.statement: Because the single common bus carries one word per clock period, microoperations that need the bus must occupy successive timing steps — this, not any lack of gates, is what makes instructions take several clock periods.
concepts.detail: The exceptions prove the rule: PC ← PC + 1 happens inside T1 alongside the memory read because the incrementer feeds PC directly without the bus. Parallelism in the basic computer appears exactly where a dedicated path bypasses the bus.

concepts.term: Control words as the instruction’s script
concepts.statement: Each timing step of an instruction corresponds to one 14-bit control word — for example, the fetch’s T0 is SELA = PC, SELB = unused, SELD = AR, OPR = transfer: 001 000 000 00000.
concepts.detail: Seen this way, an instruction is a short program of control words and the control unit is a machine for running such programs — the insight that leads directly to microprogramming in Chapter 10.

concepts.statement: The complete path of one memory-reference instruction is: **PC → AR → memory → IR → decode → AR → memory → DR → ALU → AC**, with PC incremented on the way and flags latched at the end.
concepts.detail: Memorize this chain and every computer organization question becomes a question about where in the chain a given design stops, repeats or adds a stage — indirect addressing simply inserts one more memory → AR link before the operand read.

examples.title: Full trace of a direct-address ADD through the datapath
examples.problem: Memory location 3 holds the instruction ADD 5 (opcode 001, direct), location 5 holds the value 9, and AC holds 6. Trace the instruction through every register and bus, writing the control word at each step.

steps.label: Step 1: T0 — aim memory at the instruction
steps.text: Control word 001 000 000 00000 (SELA = PC, SELD = AR, transfer): AR ← PC = 3. The address bus now carries 3 to memory.

steps.label: Step 2: T1 — fetch and advance
steps.text: Memory read places M[3] = the ADD instruction word on the bus and IR ← M[AR]; in the same period the dedicated incrementer performs PC ← PC + 1 = 4, so the next fetch is already aimed.

steps.label: Step 3: T2 — decode and extract
steps.text: The decoder finds opcode 001 (ADD) and raises its control output; AR ← IR(address field) = 5 via control word 100 000 000 00000 (SELA = IR, SELD = AR); I ← 0, so no indirect step is needed.

steps.label: Step 4: T3 — read the operand
steps.text: Memory read with the address bus still driven by AR: the word M[5] = 9 appears on the bus and DR ← M[AR]. One bus, one word, one period.

steps.label: Step 5: T4 — compute and latch
steps.text: Control word 011 010 011 00100 (SELA = AC, SELB = DR, SELD = AC, OPR = add): the ALU forms $6 + 9 = 15 = 1111$; at the clock edge AC ← 1111 and the flags latch C = 0, V = 0, Z = 0, S = 0.

steps.label: Step 6 — next instruction
steps.text: The control returns to T0 with PC = 4: AR ← 4 and the machine fetches whatever the programmer placed after the ADD.

examples.result: PC → AR → memory → IR → decode → AR → memory → DR → ALU → AC: AC finishes with $1111 = 15$ and PC with 4, exactly the chain of the section title — five control words, five clock periods.

examples.title: The same instruction with indirect addressing
examples.problem: Now memory location 3 holds ADD 5 with the indirect bit I = 1; location 5 holds the pointer 7; location 7 holds the operand 9. Show what changes.

steps.label: Step 1: Fetch is identical
steps.text: T0: AR ← 3; T1: IR ← M[3], PC ← 4; T2: AR ← IR(address field) = 5, but now I ← 1 — the control unit sees that the effective address must be fetched from memory.

steps.label: Step 2: The indirect step
steps.text: T3: the memory word M[5] = 7 is read onto the bus and its address field is loaded into AR: AR ← 7. This is the one extra memory → AR link in the chain.

steps.label: Step 3: Operand and execute follow
steps.text: T4: DR ← M[7] = 9; T5: AC ← AC + DR with flags latched — AC ← $6 + 9 = 15$ exactly as before, one timing state later.

steps.label: Step 4: Count the cost
steps.text: Indirect addressing bought pointer flexibility (the operand can move without editing the instruction) at the price of one extra memory read and one extra clock period — the trade the basic computer quantifies with its T3 state in Chapter 11.

examples.result: The chain grows to PC → AR → memory → IR → decode → AR → memory → AR → memory → DR → ALU → AC: the same datapath, one more bus cycle. Chapter 11 gives this pattern its exact basic-computer timing.

keyTakeaways: The fetch is universal: AR ← PC; IR ← M[AR] with PC ← PC + 1; then decode, AR ← address field, I ← indirect bit.
Execution of a memory-reference instruction adds DR ← M[AR] and an ALU step such as AC ← AC + DR with flags latched.
Every timing step is one control word; an instruction is a short program of control words.
The single common bus serializes transfers — instructions take multiple clock periods because of bus contention, not gate shortage.
PC’s dedicated incrementer is the one parallel path that shares a period with the memory read.
Indirect addressing inserts one extra memory → AR step before the operand read.

quiz.q: Which pair of microoperations happens in the same timing period during fetch, and why?
options: AR ← PC and IR ← M[AR], because both use the bus
IR ← M[AR] and PC ← PC + 1, because the incrementer feeds PC directly without using the common bus
AR ← IR and DR ← M[AR], because both are reads
PC ← PC + 1 and AC ← AC + DR, because both are arithmetic
quiz.explanation: The memory read occupies the bus into IR, while PC is advanced by its own dedicated incrementer — the classic exception to the one-bus-per-period rule.

quiz.q: In the traced ADD, what does AR hold immediately after the T2 (decode) step?
options: The operand address 5, copied from IR’s address field
quiz.explanation: T2 extracts the instruction’s 12-bit address field into AR (via SELA = IR, SELD = AR), aiming memory at the operand — 5 in the example.

quiz.q: What exactly does indirect addressing add to the datapath chain?
options: One extra memory read whose result is loaded into AR as the effective address
quiz.explanation: With I = 1, an extra step reads the pointer word M[address field] into AR; the operand is then read from that effective address — one more memory → AR link.

quiz.q: A designer wants fetch, operand read and execute to happen in fewer clock periods. Which change actually helps?
options: Widen the common bus to 32 bits
Add dedicated paths that bypass the single bus (as the PC incrementer already does), or add a second bus so two transfers can proceed at once
Increase the memory size to $2^{16}$ words
quiz.explanation: The bottleneck is bus serialization: only transfers that avoid the common bus can share a period. Additional buses or dedicated paths (as in later pipeline designs) are the real speedups.

intro: Chapter 9 built the datapath — now something must tell it what to do, when. The control unit reads three kinds of input — the decoded instruction, the status flags and the timing signals — and turns them into the control functions that open gates, load registers and select ALU operations. Mano develops two ways to build it: hardwired logic derived from a state table, and a stored program of control words called a microprogram.
objectives: Identify the three classes of control-unit input: instruction decode signals, status flags and timing signals
List the control-unit outputs and relate them to the Chapter 9 control word
Explain the sequence counter and decoder that generate timing signals T0, T1, T2, …
Contrast hardwired and microprogrammed control organizations
Relate the hardware control unit to the OS-level structures of OSC Ch 2

concepts.statement: The **control unit** is the part of the computer that governs the datapath: it initiates every microoperation by raising **control functions** — gate signals that select register sources, enable loads, and command memory reads and writes — in the proper sequence.
concepts.detail: In Mano’s organization the control unit and the processor together exhaust the machine: the processor is what moves and combines data; the control is what decides which transfer happens during which clock period. Everything else in the book is refinement of this split.

concepts.statement: The control unit’s inputs come from three sources: the **instruction decoder** (outputs $D_0, D_1, ldots, D_7$ recognizing the opcode in IR), the **status flags** (C, V, Z, S, the indirect bit I, and the interrupt flags IEN, FGI, FGO), and the **timing signals** $T_0, T_1, T_2, ldots$ from the sequence counter and its decoder.
concepts.detail: A control function is a Boolean product of these, such as $D_1 T_4$ for the operand read of an ADD, or $\text{IEN}(\text{FGI} + \text{FGO})$ for recognizing an interrupt. Design the products and you have designed the machine.

concepts.statement: The control unit’s outputs are the datapath’s command lines: the **control word** (SELA, SELB, SELD, OPR), the register load enables, memory read and write, the PC incrementer enable, the flag and flip-flop set/reset lines, and the sequence counter clear.
concepts.detail: Counting them for the basic computer gives roughly two to three dozen signals — seven register loads, two memory strobes, the ALU selects, the incrementer enable, E/I/S/R/IEN/FGI/FGO set and reset, and SC ← 0. Every one of these is a combinational function of decode, status and timing.

concepts.statement: Timing signals come from a **sequence counter (SC)** driven by the master clock through a decoder: each count value raises one timing signal $T_i$, and the counter is cleared (SC ← 0) when an instruction finishes so the next fetch restarts at $T_0$.
concepts.detail: The register-reference and I/O instructions of the basic computer finish during $T_3$; memory-reference instructions run through $T_4$ and $T_5$; the counter simply keeps advancing while the control logic decides, at each state, whether to clear it. A **start/stop flip-flop S** (set by power-on, cleared by HLT) gates the clock so the machine can be halted.

concepts.statement: **Hardwired control** implements the control functions as fixed logic — gates and flip-flops designed once from the state table; changing the instruction set means changing wires.
concepts.detail: Its virtues are speed (a control function is one or two gate delays after its inputs settle) and low recurring cost in mass production; its vice is that any design change ripples through the whole network. The PLA approach of Section 10.3 tames the wiring without giving up the speed.

concepts.statement: **Microprogrammed control** stores the control words in a read-only **control memory** and sequences through them with a control address register — the control unit becomes a small computer inside the computer.
concepts.detail: Each stored word is a **microinstruction**; each machine instruction corresponds to a **microroutine**. Adding an instruction then means writing new microcode rather than rewiring gates — the flexibility that made microprogramming dominant for complex instruction sets. Section 10.2 designs both organizations for the same two-instruction machine.

concepts.statement: Everything an operating system does rides on this control unit: interrupts and traps are just more inputs (IEN, FGI, FGO) and the halt instruction is just S ← 0 — the hardware side of the system-call and process machinery of OSC Ch 2.
concepts.detail: Cross-link: OSC Ch 2 presents an OS as a layer that multiplexes hardware among processes; here is that hardware. The interrupt cycle designed in Chapter 11 is the exact mechanism through which every OS regains control of the CPU.

examples.title: Deriving the control functions for fetch and one execute step
examples.problem: Write the control functions (Boolean products) that open the gates for the fetch steps and for the execute step AC ← AC + DR of a direct ADD.

steps.label: Step 1: Fetch, timing state $T_0$
steps.text: AR ← PC requires the AR load enable to be a function of $T_0$ alone: control function $T_0$, because every instruction starts this way regardless of opcode.

steps.label: Step 2: Fetch, timing state $T_1$
steps.text: IR ← M[AR] needs memory-read plus the IR load enable, and PC ← PC + 1 needs the incrementer enable — all under the single control function $T_1$.

steps.label: Step 3: Decode, timing state $T_2$
steps.text: AR ← IR(address field) is again universal: control function $T_2$. The decoder outputs $D_k$ become valid during this state and are ANDed with later timing to specialize execution.

steps.label: Step 4: Execute for ADD specifically
steps.text: The operand read DR ← M[AR] is common to several memory-reference instructions, so its function is a sum of products $(D_0 + D_1 + D_2 + D_6) T_4$; the addition AC ← AC + DR is unique to ADD: control function $D_1 T_5$, which simultaneously drives SELA = AC, SELB = DR, OPR = add and the AC load enable, and lets the flags latch.

steps.label: Step 5: End the instruction
steps.text: Whichever execute step finishes last raises SC ← 0, returning the timing to $T_0$ for the next fetch.

examples.result: Six gate expressions — $T_0$, $T_1$, $T_2$, $(D_0 + D_1 + D_2 + D_6)T_4$, $D_1 T_5$ and the counter clear — already sequence an entire ADD; the full basic computer is the same discipline applied to every instruction.

examples.title: Taking inventory of the control outputs
examples.problem: Count the control signals a basic computer’s control unit must generate, as a preview of the logic sizes in Sections 10.2 and 10.3.

steps.label: Step 1: Register loads
steps.text: AR, PC, DR, IR, TR each need a load enable; AC’s load is folded into its attached ALU path — about five signals, each fed by several control functions ORed together.

steps.label: Step 2: Memory and ALU
steps.text: Memory read and memory write strobes (2), the ALU operation selects shared with the AC path (3), and the shifter selects (2).

steps.label: Step 3: Special flip-flops
steps.text: Set/reset lines for E, I, S, R, IEN, FGI, FGO and the SC clear — each is a tiny dedicated control function of decode and timing (or, for FGI/FGO, of the device interfaces).

steps.label: Step 4: Total
steps.text: The count lands in the low twenties of independent signals — far too many for random wiring to stay sane, which is exactly why Mano immediately turns to systematic design: state tables in Section 10.2, PLAs in Section 10.3.

examples.result: About 20–25 output lines, each a Boolean function of perhaps a dozen inputs (7 decode outputs, 6–8 status bits, 4–6 timing states): a problem of pure combinational logic — with a few flip-flops for sequencing — i.e. a synchronous sequential circuit.

keyTakeaways: The control unit sequences microoperations by raising control functions derived from three input classes: decode outputs, status flags and timing signals.
A control function is a Boolean product such as $D_1 T_5$ — decode × timing, sometimes × status.
Timing comes from a sequence counter + decoder producing $T_0, T_1, T_2, ldots$; SC ← 0 ends each instruction and restarts fetch.
The start/stop flip-flop S halts the clock; HLT is simply S ← 0.
Hardwired control is fast but rigid; microprogrammed control stores control words in ROM and trades speed for flexibility.
Interrupts, traps and halts are control-unit inputs/outputs — the hardware layer beneath the OS services of OSC Ch 2.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT an input to the control unit?
options: The status and interrupt flags such as Z and FGI
The timing signals from the sequence counter
The data word on the common bus
quiz.explanation: The bus carries data for the datapath, not decisions for the control. The control unit consumes decode, status and timing — and emits gate signals.

quiz.q: A control function is best described as:
options: A Boolean product of decode, status and timing variables that gates one or more microoperations
The memory address of an operand
quiz.explanation: In the hardwired view, each microoperation is enabled when its control function — e.g. $D_1 T_5$ — is true; the designer’s job is deriving all such functions systematically.

quiz.q: What resets the sequence counter SC to zero?
options: The control logic at the end of each instruction, so the next fetch restarts at $T_0$
quiz.explanation: Instructions have different lengths — register-reference ones finish at $T_3$, memory-reference ones at $T_5$ — so the logic that completes the last microoperation of an instruction also clears SC.

quiz.q: The essential difference between hardwired and microprogrammed control is:
options: Hardwired uses flip-flops, microprogrammed does not
Hardwired realizes control functions in fixed gates, while microprogrammed control stores control words in a control memory and sequences through them
Hardwired control requires a control address register
quiz.explanation: Both end up raising the same output lines; the difference is whether those functions exist as designed gates (fast, rigid) or as entries of a stored program read through a CAR (flexible, slower per step).

intro: This section designs one small control unit twice. First the hardwired way: treat the control as a synchronous sequential circuit, draw its state diagram, build the state and excitation tables, and derive flip-flop input equations — Chapter 6’s method pointed at a real machine. Then the microprogrammed way: store the same behavior as words in a control memory, and let a sequencer with a condition field, a select field and an address field walk through them.
objectives: Model a control unit as a synchronous sequential circuit with states, inputs and control outputs
Design the control for a two-instruction machine by the state-table method: state diagram → state table → excitation table → input and output functions
Define the microinstruction format: condition field, select field, address field
Explain the control address register, its incrementer, the conditional branch logic and the opcode mapping
Write a complete microprogram for the same machine and compare the two implementations

concepts.statement: A control unit is a synchronous sequential circuit whose **states** are the timing conditions, whose **inputs** are the decoded opcode bits and status flags, and whose **outputs** are the control functions.
concepts.detail: This is the decisive abstraction: once the control is seen as a state machine, the entire Chapter 6 repertoire — state diagrams, state tables, excitation tables, flip-flop input equations — applies to it directly. The timing-signal approach of Section 10.1 is the special case where the state register is a counter and the states are decoded one-hot.

concepts.statement: The hardwired design procedure: (1) draw the state diagram, one state per timing condition; (2) assign binary values to states with $n$ flip-flops; (3) derive the state table; (4) choose a flip-flop type and fill in the **excitation table**; (5) simplify the flip-flop input functions and the output functions with Karnaugh maps.
concepts.detail: Mano’s worked design in this chapter is exactly this pipeline for a small computer. The method scales to the basic computer of Chapter 11, where the diagram simply acquires more states (an indirect state, an interrupt cycle) and more input labels.

concepts.statement: The worked machine has two instructions: **LDA** (opcode bit $q = 0$: AC ← M[adr], direct) and **BZ** (opcode bit $q = 1$: if the zero flag $Z = 1$ then PC ← adr). Its five states are the fetch ($T_0, T_1$), decode ($T_2$) and execute ($T_3, T_4$) conditions.
concepts.detail: State flow: $T_0$: AR ← PC; $T_1$: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1; $T_2$: AR ← IR(address field) and decode $q$; then LDA executes in two states ($T_3$: DR ← M[AR]; $T_4$: AC ← DR) while BZ executes in one ($T_3$: branch if Z). The asymmetry — different instructions take different numbers of states — is the whole point of the state diagram’s branch at $T_2$.

concepts.statement: Encoding the five states in three D flip-flops $Q_2 Q_1 Q_0$ ($T_0 = 000$, $T_1 = 001$, $T_2 = 010$, $T_3 = 011$, $T_4 = 100$) and simplifying gives the input functions $D_2 = \bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 \bar{q}$, $D_1 = \bar{Q}_2 (Q_1 \oplus Q_0)$ and $D_0 = \bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_0$.
concepts.detail: Read them as: $D_0$ copies the pattern “state is $T_0$ or $T_2$” (both have $Q_0 = 0$); $D_1$ recognizes $T_1$ or $T_2$ via the XOR of the low bits; $D_2$ fires only from $T_3$ when the instruction is LDA. The flags enter through the outputs, not the state: BZ’s branch signal is $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 q Z$ — status gates a control function without changing the state flow.

concepts.statement: A **microinstruction** packs three fields: a **condition field** (selects which status bit to test), a **select field** (the Chapter 9 control word SELA | SELB | SELD | OPR plus memory read/write), and an **address field** (the branch target in control memory).
concepts.detail: For the worked machine: 2-bit condition, 14-bit select, 4-bit address = a 20-bit microinstruction; a 16-word control memory then holds every routine with room to spare. The condition codes are: 00 = never branch (just increment), 01 = branch if $Z = 1$, 10 = branch always, 11 = **map** (jump to the routine selected by the opcode).

concepts.statement: The **control address register (CAR)** addresses control memory; each step it either increments or loads the microinstruction’s address field, depending on the tested condition, and at the end of fetch a **mapping** operation loads the opcode-derived address of the instruction’s routine.
concepts.detail: The condition field drives a multiplexer over the status bits (with constants 0 and 1 for never/always); the mux output chooses increment-versus-load. Mapping is the microprogram version of the decoder: where hardwired logic ANDs $D_k$ into every relevant control function, the microprogram branches once to the routine that belongs to opcode $k$.

concepts.statement: A microprogram is organized as one shared **fetch routine** (ending in a map) plus one **microroutine per instruction**, each ending with an unconditional branch back to the fetch — precisely mirroring the instruction cycle.
concepts.detail: Sharing the fetch routine across all instructions is why microprogramming shines for large instruction sets: the $k$-th instruction costs one routine, not a redesign of the whole control network. This is the structure of every microcoded processor.

concepts.statement: Hardwired control executes a step at gate-delay speed but must be rewireed to change; microprogrammed control costs one control-memory read per step (tens of nanoseconds in the era’s ROMs) but changes by rewriting ROM contents.
concepts.detail: Mano’s rule of thumb: use hardwired logic for small, stable, speed-critical control (counters, simple machines); use microprogramming when the instruction set is rich or still evolving. Real processors historically used both — hardwired for the simplest operations, microcoded for the rest.

examples.title: State-table design of the two-instruction control
examples.problem: Design the hardwired control for the machine with LDA (q = 0) and BZ (q = 1, branch if Z = 1) using three D flip-flops.

steps.label: Step 1: Draw the state diagram
steps.text: States: $T_0$ (AR ← PC), $T_1$ (IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1), $T_2$ (AR ← IR address, decode $q$), $T_3$, $T_4$. Transitions: $T_0 \to T_1 \to T_2 \to T_3$; from $T_3$, LDA continues to $T_4$ while BZ is finished and returns to $T_0$; $T_4 \to T_0$.

steps.label: Step 2: Assign state codes
steps.text: $T_0 = 000$, $T_1 = 001$, $T_2 = 010$, $T_3 = 011$, $T_4 = 100$ — three D flip-flops $Q_2 Q_1 Q_0$, codes chosen so successive states count naturally upward.

steps.label: Step 3: Build the state table
steps.text: Next states: 000 → 001; 001 → 010; 010 → 011; 011 → 100 if $q = 0$, else 000; 100 → 000. The input $Z$ does not affect next states at all — it only gates BZ’s branch output.

steps.label: Step 4: Fill the excitation table for D flip-flops
steps.text: For D flip-flops the excitation equals the next state, so $D_2, D_1, D_0$ are the next-state bits written as functions of $Q_2 Q_1 Q_0$ and $q$.

steps.label: Step 5: Simplify with Karnaugh maps
steps.text: $D_2 = \bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 \bar{q}$ (fires only from $T_3$ when the instruction is LDA); $D_1 = \bar{Q}_2 (Q_1 \oplus Q_0)$ (recognizes $T_1$ and $T_2$); $D_0 = \bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_0$ (recognizes $T_0$ and $T_2$).

steps.label: Step 7: Derive the output functions
steps.text: Decode the states for the microoperation gates: $T_0 = \bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_1 \bar{Q}_0$ (AR ← PC), $T_1 = \bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_1 Q_0$ (IR ← M, PC ← PC + 1), $T_2 = \bar{Q}_2 Q_1 \bar{Q}_0$ (AR ← IR), $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 \bar{q}$ (DR ← M for LDA), $Q_2 \bar{Q}_1 \bar{Q}_0$ (AC ← DR for LDA), and $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 q Z$ (PC ← AR, taken only when BZ finds Z = 1).

examples.result: Three flip-flops, three input functions and six output functions completely specify the control: the state-table method turned an instruction set into algebra, and the algebra into gates.

examples.title: Microprogramming the same machine
examples.problem: Write the microprogram for the LDA/BZ machine using the 20-bit format condition(2) | select(14) | address(4), with condition codes 00 = increment, 01 = branch if Z = 1, 10 = branch always, 11 = map.

steps.label: Step 1: The shared fetch routine at address 0000
steps.text: 0000: condition 00, select = AR ← PC (SELA = PC, SELD = AR, transfer). 0001: condition 00, select = IR ← M[AR] (memory read) together with PC ← PC + 1. 0010: condition 11 (map), select = AR ← IR(address field).

steps.label: Step 2: The mapping rule
steps.text: The map operation loads CAR with the fixed prefix followed by the opcode bit: $q = 0$ (LDA) maps to address 1000, $q = 1$ (BZ) maps to address 1010 — the two routines begin one map apart.

steps.label: Step 3: The LDA microroutine at 1000
steps.text: 1000: condition 00, select = DR ← M[AR] (memory read). 1001: condition 10 (always), select = AC ← DR (SELA = DR, SELD = AC, transfer), address = 0000 — control returns to the shared fetch.

steps.label: Step 4: The BZ microroutine at 1010
steps.text: 1010: condition 01 (test Z), address = 1100 — if Z = 1 the CAR loads 1100, otherwise it increments to 1011. 1011: condition 10, select = nothing (no microoperation), address = 0000 — the not-taken path simply goes home.

steps.label: Step 5: The taken branch at 1100
steps.text: 1100: condition 10, select = PC ← AR (SELA = AR, SELD = PC, transfer), address = 0000 — the taken branch loads the target and returns to fetch.

steps.label: Step 6: Count the hardware
steps.text: Eight used words of a 16 × 20 control memory (320 bits), a 4-bit CAR with incrementer, a 4-to-1 condition multiplexer and the small mapping logic — no gates rewired if the instruction set changes.

examples.result: The same behavior as the worked state-table design, stored as data: fetch (3 words) + map + LDA (2 words) + BZ branch test and two paths (3 words) = 8 microinstructions.

examples.title: Adding a third instruction: the cost comparison
examples.problem: Suppose a third instruction, STA (M[adr] ← AC, opcode 10), is added. Compare the change to the hardwired and microprogrammed designs.

steps.label: Step 1: Hardwired change
steps.text: The opcode becomes two bits ($q_1 q_0$), so every input function and output function depending on $q$ must be re-derived from new Karnaugh maps; the excitation logic grows; and the wiring of any other instruction that shared terms with the changed ones must be re-checked.

steps.label: Step 2: Microprogrammed change
steps.text: Append a two-word routine (write AC to memory, branch back to 0000) at free addresses, e.g. 1110 and 1111, and widen the map from one opcode bit to two — the CAR, sequencer and fetch routine are untouched.

steps.label: Step 3: Speed comparison
steps.text: Per microoperation, hardwired logic costs a gate delay — a few nanoseconds; a microinstruction costs a control-memory read — several times slower in the era’s ROMs, and it serializes: one microinstruction per clock period.

steps.label: Step 4: Decide
steps.text: A stable, small, fast control (a counter, a fixed protocol) suits hardwired logic; a rich or evolving instruction set suits microcode. This is precisely the trade real processor families made as their instruction sets grew.

examples.result: One instruction added: the hardwired design redoes the excitation algebra; the microprogram writes two words. The speed gap — gate delay versus ROM access — is the price of that flexibility.

keyTakeaways: A control unit is a synchronous sequential circuit: states = timing conditions, inputs = opcode and status, outputs = control functions.
The state-table method runs: state diagram → state assignment → state table → excitation table → simplified input and output functions.
For the worked machine: $D_2 = \bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 \bar{q}$, $D_1 = \bar{Q}_2 (Q_1 \oplus Q_0)$, $D_0 = \bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_0$, with status Z gating outputs only.
A microinstruction = condition field + select field (the processor control word) + address field; 20 bits in the worked format.
The CAR increments by default, branches when the selected condition is true, and maps the opcode to a routine entry at the end of fetch.
Microprograms share one fetch routine plus one routine per instruction — adding instructions costs words, not rewiring.
Hardwired: fast, rigid. Microprogrammed: flexible, slower per step. Choose by stability and richness of the instruction set.

quiz.q: In the worked two-instruction design, why does the zero flag Z not appear in the flip-flop input functions $D_2, D_1, D_0$?
options: Because Z is only sampled by memory
Because Z affects only an output control function — BZ returns to $T_0$ whether or not the branch is taken, so the state flow is the same either way
Because the machine has no flags
Because Z is latched into a flip-flop first
quiz.explanation: The taken and not-taken BZ paths both end the instruction; Z only decides whether the microoperation PC ← AR is issued ($\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 q Z$). Status gates outputs, not states.

quiz.q: What does the condition field value that selects “map” do?
options: It loads the CAR with an address formed from the opcode bits — the entry point of that instruction’s microroutine
It writes the IR into control memory
quiz.explanation: Mapping is the microprogram counterpart of instruction decode: a fixed prefix plus the opcode selects the routine, replacing the hardwired decoder products $D_k$.

quiz.q: Which sequence correctly describes the organization of the microprogram for the two-instruction machine?
options: One routine per instruction, each containing its own fetch code
A shared fetch routine ending in a map, then a short routine per instruction, each ending with an unconditional branch back to the fetch
A single 100-word routine with no branches
Fetch and execute interleaved in the same word
quiz.explanation: Every machine instruction reuses the same fetch microcode; only the mapped routine differs, and each routine ends by branching to address 0000 to fetch the next instruction.

quiz.q: The microinstruction format of the worked design is:
options: condition field | select field (the processor control word) | address field — 2 + 14 + 4 = 20 bits
quiz.explanation: Twenty bits: which status to test, what the datapath should do this period, and where to go next — sequencing and operation in one word.

quiz.q: The main advantage of microprogrammed over hardwired control is:
options: The instruction set can be changed or extended by rewriting control memory instead of redesigning gate networks
It eliminates the need for status flags
quiz.explanation: Flexibility: microroutines are data in a ROM. The cost is one control-memory access per microoperation, which is why pure speed still favors hardwired logic.

quiz.q: A processor’s instruction set is still changing weekly. Which control style fits, and why?
options: Hardwired discrete circuits, fastest per step
Microprogrammed control: changes are edits to control memory, not rewiring
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** weekly ISA edits, correctness plus agility needed.
**Step 2 — Rule:** hardwired control is a sum-of-products per line (fast, brittle); microcode stores one control word per (state, opcode) with sequencer fields.
**Step 3 — Apply:** redesigned instruction $=$ rewritten routine rows; no derivation or rewiring.
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** the worked unit’s shared term survives in both styles; PLA sits between (reprogrammable once, faster than microcode).
**Step 5 — Distractors:** hardwired needs re-derivation weekly; no control cannot sequence; clock alone adds no behavior.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** microprogram for flexibility.

quiz.q: A microprogram holds $64$ control words. How wide is its address field, and what do its sequencer fields do?
options: $6$ bits; condition selects, select and address choose the next word
quiz.explanation:
**Step 1 — Given data:** $64$ words in control memory.
**Step 2 — Rule:** address bits $= \log_2(\text{words})$; sequencer has condition field (which flag to test), select/next-address logic.
**Step 3 — Computation:** $\log_2 64 = 6$ bits ($2^6 = 64$).
**Step 4 — Cross-check:** $32$ words would need $5$; $128$ would need $7$.
**Step 5 — Distractors:** $64$ bits confuses words with width; $8$ over-provisions; $4$ addresses only $16$.
**Step 6 — Conclude:** $6$-bit address plus test/branch fields.

intro: The state-table method ends in a list of sum-of-products equations — and there is a chip for exactly that: the programmable logic array. This section sizes a PLA that replaces the whole gate network of the worked control unit, compares it with a ROM realization, and closes the chapter with the design decision — hardwired gates, one PLA, or a microprogram — that every control designer faces.
objectives: Describe the PLA as an AND–OR structure programmable in both planes (from Chapter 5)
Translate the worked control unit’s equations into a PLA programming table
Compute the required PLA size: inputs, product terms and outputs
Compare the PLA with a ROM realization of the same control
Summarize when to choose hardwired, PLA or microprogrammed implementation

concepts.statement: A **programmable logic array (PLA)** is an AND plane feeding an OR plane: the AND plane generates chosen product terms of the inputs, and the OR plane sums chosen subsets of those terms into each output — any set of two-level (sum-of-products) functions in one chip.
concepts.detail: From Chapter 5: each input appears in both true and complemented form at every AND gate’s disposal, each AND gate output can drive any OR gate, and each output can optionally be inverted. Programming = specifying the connections, whether by mask (factory), by fuses (field-programmable) or by erasable technology.

concepts.statement: A PLA is specified by **inputs × product terms × outputs**; a classic commercial part is **16 × 48 × 8** — 16 inputs, 48 AND terms, 8 outputs.
concepts.detail: The numbers bound the design: the worked control needs no more than 5 of the 16 inputs, 8 of the 48 product terms and exactly 8 outputs — a comfortable fit in one classic part, with headroom for a larger instruction set.

concepts.statement: To realize a control unit in a PLA: finish the state-table design, list every flip-flop input function and output function as sum-of-products, merge the product-term lists (shared terms are programmed once), and enter the result as the PLA’s connection table.
concepts.detail: This keeps the hardwired speed — outputs appear after one AND and one OR delay — while replacing dozens of gates and their interconnections with a single structured, documented chip. The state flip-flops (with the PLA feeding their D inputs and receiving their outputs) close the sequential loop.

concepts.statement: One PLA product term can drive several outputs, which the worked design exploits: the term $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 \bar{q}$ is simultaneously the D input of flip-flop 2 and the DR ← M[AR] control function.
concepts.detail: Sharing is free in a PLA (an AND gate output can feed every OR gate) but expensive in discrete gates, where each fan-out means another package pin and wire. It is the single biggest reason PLA control beats gate control in board area.

concepts.statement: A ROM fully decodes its address inputs — it stores one word for **every** input combination, $2^n$ words for $n$ inputs — while a PLA implements only the product terms the functions actually need.
concepts.detail: For the worked control, a ROM would need $2^5 = 32$ words of 8 bits; the PLA needs only 8 product terms. Control functions are sparse (most input combinations never occur), so PLAs exploit the sparsity and ROMs waste it — though a ROM is simpler to program when the truth table is dense anyway, and the microprogrammed design of Section 10.2 is exactly a control ROM plus sequencer.

concepts.statement: The three realizations of one control unit: **discrete gates** (fastest, most wiring), **PLA** (nearly as fast, one chip, structured), **microprogram** (flexible, one memory read per step).
concepts.detail: Mano’s closing message: the choice is engineering, not doctrine. Small fixed controllers — counters, sequencers, the timing of the basic computer — suit gates or a PLA; rich or evolving instruction sets suit microcode. The basic computer of Chapter 11 is small enough to design completely with hardwired control functions, and that design is carried out in full.

examples.title: Sizing the PLA for the worked control unit
examples.problem: Realize the two-instruction control unit (LDA/BZ, three D flip-flops $Q_2 Q_1 Q_0$, inputs $q$ and $Z$) in a PLA and compute its size.

steps.label: Step 1: Count the inputs
steps.text: Five: $Q_2, Q_1, Q_0$ (state), $q$ (opcode bit), $Z$ (status). Each is available in both polarities inside the AND plane.

steps.label: Step 2: List the functions to realize
steps.text: Flip-flop inputs: $D_2 = \bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 \bar{q}$; $D_1 = \bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_1 Q_0 + \bar{Q}_2 Q_1 \bar{Q}_0$; $D_0 = \bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_0$. Control outputs: $T_0 = \bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_1 \bar{Q}_0$; $T_1 = \bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_1 Q_0$; $T_2 = \bar{Q}_2 Q_1 \bar{Q}_0$; the DR load with memory read $= \bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 \bar{q}$; $T_4 = Q_2 \bar{Q}_1 \bar{Q}_0$; and the branch enable $= \bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 q Z$.

steps.label: Step 3: Expand the XOR
steps.text: The compact form $D_1 = \bar{Q}_2 (Q_1 \oplus Q_0)$ is not two-level; expand it as $\bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_1 Q_0 + \bar{Q}_2 Q_1 \bar{Q}_0$ — two product terms, which the AND plane handles directly.

steps.label: Step 4: Merge and share product terms
steps.text: Distinct terms: $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 \bar{q}$, $\bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_1 Q_0$, $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 \bar{Q}_0$, $\bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_0$, $\bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_1 \bar{Q}_0$, $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0$, $Q_2 \bar{Q}_1 \bar{Q}_0$, $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 q Z$ — eight in all. Note the sharing: $\bar{Q}_2 \bar{Q}_1 Q_0$ feeds both $D_1$ and $T_1$; $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 \bar{Q}_0$ feeds both $D_1$ and $T_2$; $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 \bar{q}$ feeds both $D_2$ and the DR-load output.

steps.label: Step 5: Count the outputs
steps.text: Eight: $D_2$, $D_1$, $D_0$, and the five control signals $T_0$, $T_1$, $T_2$, DR-load (with the $T_4$ and branch-enable signals as the remaining outputs).

steps.label: Step 6: State the size and compare
steps.text: The design needs a PLA of 5 inputs × 8 product terms × 8 outputs — inside a classic 16 × 48 × 8 part with more than half its capacity free for additional instructions and states.

examples.result: One PLA chip plus three D flip-flops replaces the whole control network; with the classic part’s spare terms, several more instructions could be added before a second chip is needed.

examples.title: The same control in a ROM
examples.problem: Compare the PLA realization with storing the same control functions in a ROM addressed by the state and input bits.

steps.label: Step 1: Size the ROM
steps.text: Five address inputs ($Q_2 Q_1 Q_0 q Z$) mean $2^5 = 32$ addressed words, each 8 bits wide for the eight output functions — 256 bits total, versus the PLA’s 8 product terms.

steps.label: Step 2: Fill the truth table sparsely
steps.text: Of the 32 input combinations, only the 10 with valid state codes 000–100 matter for each input pair; the rest are don’t-cares whose stored bits are never used — the ROM decodes every combination anyway.

steps.label: Step 3: Account for the difference
steps.text: The PLA’s AND plane synthesizes just the 8 needed terms; the ROM’s internal full decoder hardwires all 32 minterms whether used or not. Sparse control logic — most functions here have 3–5 literals per term — is the PLA’s natural habitat.

steps.label: Step 4: When the ROM wins
steps.text: If the control is already expressed as a microprogram (Section 10.2), the ROM is not implementing Boolean functions at all — it stores sequenced microinstructions, and the CAR plus condition logic supply the sequencing the PLA design gets from its flip-flops.

examples.result: PLA: 8 product terms, fast two-level logic, best for combinational control. ROM: 32 decoded words, best when behavior is stored and sequenced (microcode). Both fit the same design in about one chip.

keyTakeaways: A PLA is a programmable AND plane into a programmable OR plane — any set of sum-of-products functions on one chip.
PLA sizes are quoted as inputs × product terms × outputs; a classic commercial part is 16 × 48 × 8.
The worked control unit fits in a 5 × 8 × 8 PLA plus three state flip-flops.
Product terms can be shared across outputs — the term $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 \bar{q}$ serves both a flip-flop input and a control signal.
A ROM fully decodes all $2^n$ input combinations; a PLA implements only the needed product terms, exploiting the sparsity of control logic.
Implementation choice: discrete gates (speed, wiring), PLA (speed, structure, one chip), microprogram (flexibility, one memory read per step).

quiz.q: A commercial PLA described as 16 × 48 × 8 provides:
options: 16 inputs, 48 programmable product terms, and 8 outputs
quiz.explanation: The PLA size notation counts inputs, AND-plane product terms and OR-plane outputs: inputs × product terms × outputs.

quiz.q: Why did the PLA realization of the worked control unit need only eight product terms while an equivalent ROM needs 32 words?
options: Because the PLA runs at a lower clock rate
Because control functions are sparse — the PLA’s AND plane synthesizes only the product terms actually used, while the ROM’s full decoder provides all $2^5$ minterms
Because the PLA uses flip-flops instead of memory
quiz.explanation: A ROM internally decodes every input combination; a PLA programs only the terms the functions require. With 5 inputs, that is 8 terms versus 32 decoded minterms.

quiz.q: Which term in the worked design is shared between a flip-flop excitation function and a control output?
options: $\bar{Q}_2 Q_1 Q_0 \bar{q}$, which serves both $D_2$ and the DR ← M[AR] control function
None — each output needs its own terms
quiz.explanation: One AND-gate output can drive many OR gates, so the term recognizing “state $T_3$ with opcode LDA” both advances the state and issues the memory read into DR — free sharing that discrete gates pay for in wiring.

quiz.q: Which control style would you choose for a processor whose instruction set is still being redesigned weekly?
options: A PLA, because it is the fastest possible
Microprogrammed control, because instruction changes are edits to control memory rather than hardware redesigns
quiz.explanation: Microcode stores the control as data: a redesigned instruction is a rewritten routine. PLAs and gates need re-derivation and re-programming of the logic for every change, though they execute each step faster.

prerequisites: Digital logic gates (AND, OR, NOT) and Boolean algebra
Synchronous flip-flops, 4-bit binary counters, and $4 \times 16$ decoders
Register transfer level (RTL) micro-operations and common bus multiplexing
intro: Chapter 11 integrates the datapath components, arithmetic logic unit, and timing generators from previous chapters into a fully operational digital computer. Mano\’s basic computer contains a memory unit of 4,096 words of 16 bits each, nine discrete hardware registers interconnected by a 16-bit common bus system, and a sequence counter decoded into 16 discrete timing signals $T_0 \dots T_{15}$. Understanding this structural organization reveals how hardware control gates choreograph the transfer of binary information between memory and processor registers.
objectives: Diagram the complete register configuration and word sizes of the basic computer
Explain the common bus multiplexer organization and its 3-bit selection lines S2, S1, S0
Describe the memory unit capacity (4096 x 16) and its 12-bit address bus interface
Identify the role of the 4-bit sequence counter (SC) and the timing signals T0 through T15
Trace control gate logic controlling register load and increment operations

concepts.statement: The computer consists of nine working registers: **AR** (12-bit address register), **PC** (12-bit program counter), **DR** (16-bit data register), **AC** (16-bit accumulator), **IR** (16-bit instruction register), **TR** (16-bit temporary register), **INPR** (8-bit input register), **OUTR** (8-bit output register), and **SC** (4-bit sequence counter).
concepts.detail: AR holds memory addresses (0 to 4095); PC tracks the next instruction to fetch; DR holds operands read from memory; AC is the multi-purpose processing register; IR preserves the fetched instruction word while control logic decodes it.

concepts.statement: A common bus with three selection inputs ($S_2, S_1, S_0$) connects the outputs of six registers and memory to the inputs of all registers. Values $1 \dots 7$ select AR, PC, DR, AC, IR, TR, and Memory respectively, while 0 denotes no transfer.
concepts.detail: The bus avoids separate point-to-point wiring between all register pairs. When $S_2 S_1 S_0 = 010_2$, the 12-bit PC output is placed onto the bus (zero-extended to 16 bits) and can be loaded into AR by raising the AR load enable line: $AR \leftarrow PC$.

concepts.statement: The memory unit contains $4096 \times 16$ bits ($2^{12}$ words of 16 bits). It requires a 12-bit address supplied exclusively by the **AR** register, with separate read and write strobe inputs.
concepts.detail: Reading memory puts $M[AR]$ onto the common bus (selected when $S_2 S_1 S_0 = 111_2$). Writing memory transfers the 16-bit bus content into $M[AR]$ when the write input is pulsed.

concepts.term: Timing signals and the sequence counter
concepts.statement: The control unit timing originates from a 4-bit sequence counter (**SC**) decoded by a $4 \times 16$ decoder into sixteen mutually exclusive timing signals $T_0, T_1, \dots, T_{15}$.
concepts.detail: The counter increments on each clock pulse: $SC \leftarrow SC + 1$. When an instruction cycle completes, control logic pulses the synchronous clear line: $SC \leftarrow 0$, resetting the machine to timing state $T_0$ for the next fetch cycle.

concepts.statement: Every register load, clear, and increment signal is driven by a Boolean combination of timing signals ($T_i$), instruction opcode decodes ($D_j$), and status flip-flops.
concepts.detail: For example, AR is loaded during $T_0$ ($AR \leftarrow PC$), during $T_2$ ($AR \leftarrow IR(0-11)$), and during $T_3$ for indirect addressing ($AR \leftarrow M[AR]$). Thus, the load control input for AR is synthesized as $LD(AR) = T_0 + T_2 + D_7\prime I T_3$.
