examples.title: A full MAX-HEAPIFY trace
examples.problem: Run `MAX-HEAPIFY(A, 2)` on $A = \langle 16, 4, 10, 14, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1 \rangle$ ($n = 10$), listing every comparison and swap.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: At $i = 2$: value 4; children $A[4] = 14$ (LEFT) and $A[5] = 7$ (RIGHT). Largest of ${4, 14, 7}$ is 14 at LEFT — swap $A[2] \leftrightarrow A[4]$: $A = \langle 16, 14, 10, 4, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1 \rangle$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Recurse at $i = 4$: value 4; children $A[8] = 2$ and $A[9] = 8$. Largest is 8 at RIGHT — swap $A[4] \leftrightarrow A[9]$: $A = \langle 16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1 \rangle$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Recurse at $i = 9$: $\text{LEFT}(9) = 18 > 10$, so node 9 is a leaf — the recursion stops. Total: 2 swap steps, 4 key comparisons (two per visited node).

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Verify: $14 \ge 8, 7$ at node 2; $8 \ge 2, 4$ at node 4 — every pair on the touched path now satisfies the max-heap property, and untouched pairs were valid before.

examples.result: Final array $\langle 16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1 \rangle$ — a valid max-heap, reached with 2 exchanges along a single root-to-leaf path of the subtree.

examples.title: Where the $2n/3$ comes from
examples.problem: Exhibit a heap of $n$ nodes where MAX-HEAPIFY at the root recurses into a subtree holding as close to $2n/3$ of the nodes as possible.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Take a perfect heap of height $h$ and delete the entire last level of the **right** subtree, leaving the left subtree perfect of height $h-1$ and the right subtree perfect of height $h-2$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Sizes: left $= 2^h - 1$, right $= 2^{h-1} - 1$, root $= 1$, so $n = 3 \cdot 2^{h-1} - 1$ and the recursed (left) side has $2^h - 1$ nodes.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Ratio: $(2^h - 1)/(3 \cdot 2^{h-1} - 1) \approx 2^{h}/(3 \cdot 2^{h-1}) = 2/3$. For $h = 4$: left $= 15$, right $= 7$, $n = 23$, ratio $15/23 \approx 0.65$ and it creeps toward $2/3$ as $h$ grows.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Hence the recurrence charges each level of the descent $\Theta(1)$ work while the problem shrinks by the factor $2/3$ at worst: $T(n) \le T(2n/3) + \Theta(1) = O(\lg n)$.

examples.result: The bottom-heavy complete tree is exactly the shape that makes MAX-HEAPIFY as expensive as its $O(\lg n)$ bound allows.

keyTakeaways: MAX-HEAPIFY fixes a single node in $O(\lg n)$: two comparisons plus at most one recursive call, following one path down the tree.
Its precondition — both subtrees already valid heaps — is what makes the one-path repair sufficient; BUILD-MAX-HEAP manufactures this precondition from the bottom up.
The worst-case recurrence is $T(n) \le T(2n/3) + \Theta(1)$ because the left subtree can absorb the entire last level, not because heaps are left-heavy by rule.

quiz.q: The precondition of `MAX-HEAPIFY(A, i)` is:
options: the whole array is a max-heap
the subtrees rooted at LEFT(i) and RIGHT(i) are max-heaps
quiz.explanation: The procedure repairs only the node i by descending a single path; it can never detect violations off that path, so it needs the subtrees to be heaps already.

quiz.q: The worst-case running time of MAX-HEAPIFY on a subtree of $n$ nodes is:
quiz.explanation: Each step does constant work and descends one level, so the cost is O(height) = O(lg n). Formally T(n) ≤ T(2n/3) + Θ(1), which the master theorem resolves to Θ(lg n).

quiz.q: In the recurrence $T(n) \le T(2n/3) + \Theta(1)$, the fraction $2/3$ arises because:
options: the array is two-thirds full by definition
in the worst case the deepest level is filled entirely inside the left subtree, which then holds up to $2n/3$ nodes
two of every three nodes are leaves
each node has at most three children
quiz.explanation: The tree must stay nearly complete, so the last level can only be lopsided to the left; a perfect left subtree of the same height as the right one minus one holds 2/3 of all nodes in the limit.

quiz.q: On $A = \langle 16, 4, 10, 14, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1 \rangle$, how many element exchanges does `MAX-HEAPIFY(A, 2)` perform?
quiz.explanation: The value 4 swaps with 14, then with 8, and stops at the leaf: two exchanges — the descent length of the node.

quiz.q: MAX-HEAPIFY is called on index $2$ of $A = [16, 4, 10, 14, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1]$ (1-indexed), where both subtrees of node $2$ are already max-heaps. The resulting array is:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $A[2] = 4$ with children $A[4] = 14$ and $A[5] = 7$, heap size $10$. Step 2 — Governing rule: compare the node with both children, swap with the largest if it exceeds the node, then recurse at the swapped position. Step 3 — Trace: largest of ${4, 14, 7}$ is $14$ at index $4$, swap to get $[16, 14, 10, 4, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1]$; at index $4$ the children are $2$ and $8$, largest is $8$ at index $9$, swap to get $[16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1]$; index $9$ is a leaf, halt. Step 4 — Sanity check: every parent now dominates its children, only the path $2 \to 4 \to 9$ moved, and cost is bounded by height $O(\lg n)$. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: the second option stops after one swap leaving $4$ above $8$, the third swaps with the smaller child, and the fourth moves the root illegally. Step 6 — Conclude: $[16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1]$.

intro: Building a heap looks like it should cost $n$ heapifies times $O(\lg n)$ — but that bound is a factor of $\lg n$ too pessimistic. The nodes that are expensive to fix are exponentially rare: half the array never gets a call at all, and only one node has the full height. Charging each node by its height makes the arithmetic collapse to a geometric sum.
objectives: Execute BUILD-MAX-HEAP and justify its ⌊n/2⌋ starting point
Prove the tight $O(n)$ bound via the height-sum $\sum_h \lceil n/2^{h+1} \rceil \cdot O(h)$
Contrast the loose $O(n \lg n)$ argument and see exactly where it overcharges

concepts.statement: **`BUILD-MAX-HEAP(A)`** sets `A.heap-size = n` and runs `MAX-HEAPIFY(A, i)` for $i = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1, \ldots, 1$.
concepts.detail: Running **bottom-up** guarantees the loop invariant: when `MAX-HEAPIFY(A, i)` is called, both subtrees of $i$ have already been heapified (or are leaves), so the precondition of Section 6.2 holds by construction. Positions after $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ are leaves and need no call at all.

concepts.term: The loose bound and why it fails
concepts.statement: Each of the $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ heapify calls costs $O(\lg n)$, giving $O(n \lg n)$ — a correct but **loose** bound, because it charges every node the *maximum* height as if it were the root.
concepts.detail: The root is the only node of height $\lfloor \lg n \rfloor$; half the nodes are leaves with height 0 and cost $O(1)$. An analysis that ignores where nodes live in the tree throws away exactly the structure that makes the algorithm fast.

concepts.statement: A heap of $n$ elements contains **at most $\lceil n/2^{h+1} \rceil$ nodes of height $h$**, for every $h$ from 0 to $\lfloor \lg n \rfloor$.
concepts.detail: Nodes of height $h$ sit at depth at most $\lfloor \lg n \rfloor - h$, and any two of them at the *same* depth root disjoint subtrees; each such subtree contains at least $2^{h+1} - 1$ nodes, which the book rounds conservatively to the usable bound $\lceil n/2^{h+1} \rceil$. Fewer than one in $2^{h+1}$ positions can afford such a tall subtree.

concepts.statement: BUILD-MAX-HEAP runs in $O(n)$: $\sum_{h=0}^{\lfloor \lg n \rfloor} \lceil n/2^{h+1} \rceil \cdot O(h) = O\!\left(n \sum_{h=0}^{\infty} \frac{h}{2^{h+1}}\right) = O(2n) = O(n)$.
concepts.detail: The series $\sum_{h \ge 0} h/2^{h+1} = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum h/2^h = 1$ (since $\sum_{h \ge 0} h x^h = x/(1-x)^2$ at $x = 1/2$ gives 2). Doubling the count of height-$h$ nodes for the ceiling, the total charge is bounded by a constant times $n$ — the heights form a converging geometric weight, so the cheap bottom dominates.

concepts.statement: For $|x| < 1$, $\sum_{h \ge 0} h x^h = x/(1-x)^2$; at $x = 1/2$ the sum is $2$. Hence $\sum_h \lceil n/2^{h+1} \rceil \cdot O(h) = O(n \sum_h h/2^h) = O(n)$: halving of node counts beats linear growth of heights.
concepts.detail: Differentiate $\sum_{h \ge 0} x^h = 1/(1-x)$ term by term and multiply by $x$. The same series bounds BUILD-MAX-HEAP, the linear-time heapify of Exercise 6.3-3 variants, and the $O(n)$ bound for building a heap bottom-up in any $d$-ary heap.

examples.title: Build a heap by hand
examples.problem: Run BUILD-MAX-HEAP on $A = \langle 5, 3, 17, 10, 84, 19, 6, 22, 9 \rangle$ ($n = 9$).

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: $\lfloor 9/2 \rfloor = 4$, so heapify $i = 4, 3, 2, 1$. At $i = 4$: value 10, children $A[8] = 22$, $A[9] = 9$ — 22 wins, swap: $\langle 5, 3, 17, 22, 84, 19, 6, 10, 9 \rangle$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: $i = 3$: value 17, children $A[6] = 19$, $A[7] = 6$ — 19 wins, swap: $\langle 5, 3, 19, 22, 84, 17, 6, 10, 9 \rangle$; node 6 is a leaf, so the recursion stops.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: $i = 2$: value 3, children 22 and 84 — 84 wins, swap: $\langle 5, 84, 19, 22, 3, 17, 6, 10, 9 \rangle$; recursion at node 5 stops (its children $\text{LEFT}(5) = 10 > 9$).

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: $i = 1$: value 5 — 84 wins (swap), then at node 2: 22 wins (swap), then at node 4: 10 wins (swap). Result: $\langle 84, 22, 19, 10, 3, 17, 6, 5, 9 \rangle$.

examples.result: A valid max-heap in 6 exchanges total. Note the calls at $i = 4, 3$ cost one swap each, $i = 2$ cost one, and only the root cascaded three levels deep — the bottom-heavy cost profile the $O(n)$ analysis formalizes.

examples.title: The height census for $n = 16$
examples.problem: For a heap with $n = 16$ elements, tabulate the number of nodes of each height and the total heapify work they represent.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: By the census bound: height 0 (leaves) at most $\lceil 16/2 \rceil = 8$ nodes; height 1: $\lceil 16/4 \rceil = 4$; height 2: $\lceil 16/8 \rceil = 2$; height 3: $\lceil 16/16 \rceil = 1$; height 4 (the root): $\lceil 16/32 \rceil = 1$ — and $\lfloor \lg 16 \rfloor = 4$ exactly, since the tree is perfect.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Check: $8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 16$ nodes — the census is exact for this shape.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Work charged: $\sum \lceil n/2^{h+1} \rceil \cdot h = 8 \cdot 0 + 4 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 4 = 0 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 15$ units.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Compare the loose bound: $16 \cdot \lg 16 = 64$ units — more than four times the honest charge, and the gap widens to a full factor $\lg n$ in general.

examples.result: Total charge 15 units versus the geometric bound $\sum_h h/2^{h+1} \cdot n \cdot O(1) \le 2n = 32$: the linear bound holds with room to spare.

keyTakeaways: BUILD-MAX-HEAP heapifies nodes $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ down to 1 — bottom-up, so every call's precondition (heaped subtrees) is already true.
At most $\lceil n/2^{h+1} \rceil$ nodes have height $h$; since a height-$h$ node costs $O(h)$, the total is $O(n \sum_h h/2^{h+1}) = O(n)$.
The $O(n \lg n)$ bound is correct but loose by a logarithmic factor — a reminder to charge algorithms by what they actually touch, not by the worst node.

quiz.q: BUILD-MAX-HEAP calls MAX-HEAPIFY for which indices (root at 1, size $n$)?
quiz.explanation: Positions ⌊n/2⌋+1..n are leaves — trivially heaps — so the loop starts at the last internal node ⌊n/2⌋ and walks down to the root, ensuring subtrees are heapified before each call.

quiz.q: The tight asymptotic running time of BUILD-MAX-HEAP is:
quiz.explanation: Charging each node by its height: Σ ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉·O(h) ≤ O(n Σ h/2^h) = O(n). The n lg n estimate overcharges every node the root's height.

quiz.q: For $n = 16$, how many nodes have height exactly 1?
quiz.explanation: At most ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉ = ⌈16/4⌉ = 4 nodes of height 1: for a full 16-node heap these are positions 5–8, the nodes whose children are leaves but whose grandchildren do not exist (node 8 has just the one child at position 16).

quiz.q: The geometric series powering the linear bound is $\sum_{h \ge 0} h/2^h$, which equals:
quiz.explanation: From Σ h·x^h = x/(1−x)² at x = 1/2. The halving of node counts per level beats the linear growth of heights, so the series converges to 2 and the build cost is O(n).

intro: With a heap in hand, sorting becomes an exchange routine: the maximum is always parked at $A[1]$, so swap it to the back, shrink the heap by one, and repair the root. Heapsort thereby achieves $\Theta(n \lg n)$ in the worst case using $O(1)$ extra space — the same asymptotic guarantee as merge sort with none of its auxiliary array.
objectives: Execute heapsort on a full example, separating the build phase from the extraction loop
Establish the $O(n \lg n)$ worst-case bound and the in-place property
Compare heapsort's guarantees with merge sort, quicksort and insertion sort

concepts.statement: **`HEAPSORT(A)`**: first `BUILD-MAX-HEAP(A)`; then for $i = n$ down to 2: swap $A[1] \leftrightarrow A[i]$, decrement `A.heap-size`, and call `MAX-HEAPIFY(A, 1)`.
concepts.detail: After the swap, the old maximum sits at position $i$ and is **frozen**: the heap-size has shrunk past it, so no later operation can touch it. Each iteration thus retires one element to its final sorted position, from the end of the array backward.

concepts.statement: At the start of each loop iteration, $A[1 \ldots \text{heap-size}]$ is a max-heap containing the smallest $\text{heap-size}$ values, and $A[\text{heap-size}+1 \ldots n]$ holds the largest $n - \text{heap-size}$ values already in sorted order.
concepts.detail: The invariant holds initially (the build makes $A[1..n]$ a heap) and is preserved: extracting the root removes the largest remaining element, and the MAX-HEAPIFY call restores the heap property for the shortened array. When heap-size reaches 1, the whole array is sorted.

concepts.statement: HEAPSORT runs in $O(n \lg n)$ worst case — $O(n)$ for the build plus $n - 1$ heapify calls at $O(\lg n)$ each — using **$O(1)$ auxiliary space** beyond a constant number of variables.
concepts.detail: The bound holds for *every* input: there is no quicksort-style bad pivot, because the heap shape forces the maximum to the root in $O(\lg n)$ regardless of key order. This is why heapsort is the standard worst-case backstop (and, folded with a depth cap, the fallback of introsort).

concepts.statement: Heapsort is **in-place and $\Theta(n \lg n)$ worst case** — but its memory access pattern (tree jumps of stride $2i$) is far less local than merge sort's sequential sweeps or insertion sort's short shifts, so on real machines it often loses despite better asymptotics than quicksort's $\Theta(n^2)$ corner.
concepts.detail: Insertion sort wins on nearly-sorted inputs ($O(n + \text{inversions})$), merge sort is stable with sequential access but pays $\Theta(n)$ space, quicksort is the fastest in practice but quadratic in the worst case, heapsort is the safe all-rounder. Chapter 8 shows $\Omega(n \lg n)$ is optimal for comparison sorts — so no comparison sort can asymptotically beat these.

concepts.statement: Equal keys can reverse their relative order: the long-distance swap $A[1] \leftrightarrow A[i]$ throws a duplicate maximum past equal keys sitting in the suffix, and no later step remembers which copy came first. Stability must be bought with satellite sequence numbers if it is needed.
concepts.detail: Example: $\langle 2_a, 2_b, 1 \rangle$ builds to $\langle 2_a, 2_b, 1 \rangle$, swaps $2_a$ to the end, and finishes $\langle 1, 2_b, 2_a \rangle$. Merge sort keeps the order; heapsort does not promise it.

examples.title: Heapsort, two phases
examples.problem: Sort $A = \langle 5, 13, 2, 25, 7, 17, 20, 8, 4 \rangle$ ($n = 9$) with heapsort, showing the build and the first two extractions.

steps.label: Step 1 (build)
steps.text: BUILD-MAX-HEAP heapifies $i = 4 \ldots 1$. $i{=}4$: value 25 beats children 8, 4 — no swap. $i{=}3$: value 2, children 17, 20 — 20 wins: $\langle 5,13,20,25,7,17,2,8,4\rangle$. $i{=}2$: value 13, children $A[4] = 25$ and $A[5] = 7$ — 25 wins, swap, then 13 beats children 8, 4 and stops: $\langle 5,25,20,13,7,17,2,8,4\rangle$.

steps.label: Step 2 (build, root)
steps.text: $i{=}1$: value 5, children 25, 20 — 25 wins, swap; recurse at node 2: children 13, 7 — 13 wins, swap; recurse at node 4: children 8, 4 — 8 wins, swap. Built heap: $\langle 25,13,20,8,7,17,2,5,4\rangle$.

steps.label: Step 3 (extract 1)
steps.text: Swap $A[1] \leftrightarrow A[9]$: $\langle 4, 13, 20, 8, 7, 17, 2, 5, \mathbf{25} \rangle$, heap-size 8, heapify root: 4 swaps with 20, then with 17: $\langle 20, 13, 17, 8, 7, 4, 2, 5 \rangle$.

steps.label: Step 4 (extract 2)
steps.text: Swap $A[1] \leftrightarrow A[8]$: the array becomes $\langle 5, 13, 17, 8, 7, 4, 2, 25 \rangle$ with 25 frozen at position 8; heap-size 7, heapify root: 5 loses to 17, swaps down to node 3, then stops since $5 \ge$ children 4, 2: $\langle 17, 13, 5, 8, 7, 4, 2 \rangle$.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Continuing: extract 17, 13, 8, 7, 5, 4, 2 — the sorted output is $\langle 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 13, 17, 20, 25 \rangle$.

examples.result: Build cost ≈ 6 exchanges; the eight extractions cascade progressively shorter paths — total $\Theta(n \lg n)$ with zero auxiliary arrays.

examples.title: Heapsort's final three extractions
examples.problem: Finish heapsort on the heap $A = \langle 4, 3, 2, 1 \rangle$ with heap-size $4$, showing how the frozen suffix grows.

steps.label: Extract 4
steps.text: Swap $A[1] \leftrightarrow A[4]$: $\langle 1, 3, 2, \mathbf{4} \rangle$, heap-size $3$, heapify root: $1$ loses to $\max(3,2) = 3$, swap: $\langle 3, 1, 2 \rangle$; at node $2$, $1$ is a leaf, stop.

steps.label: Extract 3
steps.text: Swap $A[1] \leftrightarrow A[3]$: $\langle 2, 1, \mathbf{3}, \mathbf{4} \rangle$, heap-size $2$, heapify root: $2 \ge 1$, no swap.

steps.label: Extract 2
steps.text: Swap $A[1] \leftrightarrow A[2]$: $\langle 1, \mathbf{2}, \mathbf{3}, \mathbf{4} \rangle$, heap-size $1$, done. Sorted: $\langle 1, 2, 3, 4 \rangle$.

steps.label: Count
steps.text: Three extractions, one exchange in the first, none after: the paths shorten as the heap shrinks, which is why the extraction phase totals $\sum_{i=2}^{n} O(\lg i) = O(n \lg n)$ and not $n$ times the maximum height.

examples.result: Final array $\langle 1, 2, 3, 4 \rangle$; the suffix $\mathbf{2}, \mathbf{3}, \mathbf{4}$ froze in decreasing extraction order, each in its final sorted position.

keyTakeaways: Heapsort = build a max-heap in $O(n)$, then repeatedly swap the root maximum to the shrinking suffix and heapify in $O(\lg n)$.
Its frozen-suffix loop invariant makes correctness a two-line induction; each iteration fixes one final array position.
Worst case $\Theta(n \lg n)$, in-place $O(1)$ extra space, not stable — the same asymptotics as merge sort at a fraction of the memory.

quiz.q: HEAPSORT's worst-case running time on $n$ elements is:
quiz.explanation: The O(n) build plus n−1 root heapifies at O(lg n) each gives Θ(n lg n) — and unlike quicksort there is no input that degrades it.

quiz.q: At the start of each iteration of the extraction loop, where is the largest remaining heap element?
quiz.explanation: The heap property parks the maximum at the root A[1]; the iteration's first move swaps it into its final position at the end of the current array prefix.

quiz.q: How much auxiliary storage does heapsort require beyond the input array?
quiz.explanation: Heapsort rearranges the array itself with a constant number of extra variables; the heapify recursion follows one path and is trivially made iterative, so the book classifies heapsort as in-place.

quiz.q: Immediately after the swap $A[1] \leftrightarrow A[i]$, the algorithm:
options: inserts $A[i]$ into the sorted suffix by shifting
quiz.explanation: The swapped-down value may violate the property only at the root, and only within the shrunken heap — exactly the situation one root heapify repairs.

quiz.q: BUILD-MAX-HEAP on an $n$-element array runs in:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $n$ leaves-to-root heapify calls, node at height $h$ costs $O(h)$. Step 2 — Governing count: at most $\lceil\frac{n}{2^{h+1}}\rceil$ nodes have height $h$, so total cost is bounded by $\sum_{h} \frac{n}{2^{h+1}} O(h)$. Step 3 — Summation: $n\sum_{h \ge 0} \frac{h}{2^{h+1}} = O(n)$ since $\sum_{h} \frac{h}{2^h} = 2$, a convergent geometric-arithmetic series. Step 4 — Sanity check: half the array (leaves) costs nothing, only the root pays full height, and the bound is tight as shown by a full tree. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: $\Theta(n\lg n)$ multiplies worst height by $n$ ignoring rarity, $\Theta(n^2)$ has no basis, and $\Theta(\lg n)$ is one call, not $n$. Step 6 — Conclude: $\Theta(n)$ time.

intro: A heap quietly keeps the maximum available at all times — which is precisely the contract of a priority queue. This section turns the heap into a data structure supporting insert, peek, extract and increase-key, all in logarithmic time, and shows why event-driven simulators, schedulers and shortest-path algorithms are all heap clients underneath.
objectives: Define the priority queue ADT and its four operations on a max-heap
Trace HEAP-EXTRACT-MAX and HEAP-INCREASE-KEY on real numbers
Connect the bubbling-up of INCREASE-KEY to MAX-HEAPIFY's trickling-down symmetry

concepts.statement: A **priority queue** maintains a set $S$ of elements, each with a **key** (priority) plus satellite data, supporting: `INSERT(S, x)`, `MAXIMUM(S)` (peek without removal), `EXTRACT-MAX(S)`, and `INCREASE-KEY(S, x, k)` (raise $x$'s key to $k \ge$ old key).
concepts.detail: It is the 'queue' where service order is by key, not arrival. A max-heap implements it in $O(\lg n)$ per mutating operation and $O(1)$ for MAXIMUM; min-versions (or negated keys) serve symmetric needs — Dijkstra's frontier, for instance, uses a min-priority queue on tentative distances.

concepts.statement: Return $A[1]$; move the last element $A[\text{heap-size}]$ to the root; decrement heap-size; `MAX-HEAPIFY(A, 1)`. Total $O(\lg n)$.
concepts.detail: Deleting the root leaves a hole — the cheapest legal filler is the last leaf, which by position is the least-committed value in the structure. The root then trickles down a single path, exactly the Section 6.2 machinery.

concepts.statement: `MAX-HEAP-INSERT` appends the element with key $-\infty$, increments heap-size, then calls `HEAP-INCREASE-KEY` to raise it to the true key: while $i > 1$ and $A[\text{PARENT}(i)] < A[i]$, swap and continue at the parent. Both run in $O(\lg n)$.
concepts.detail: INCREASE-KEY is MAX-HEAPIFY upside down: the heap property can break only on the *upward* chain of the promoted element, so the fix is a single climb toward the root. The $-\infty$ sentinel append is the trick that lets one procedure handle insertion of any key.

concepts.term: Heaps under the hood of real systems
concepts.statement: Discrete-event simulators store events keyed by time and always need the soonest; operating-system schedulers pick the highest-priority runnable task; Dijkstra's and Prim's algorithms repeatedly extract the minimum-key frontier node — all are priority queues in disguise.
concepts.detail: The book also derives a converse application: given $n$ sorted lists, merging them into one sorted stream is $n$ simultaneous insert/extract operations on a min-queue. When the number of lists is modest, this beats concatenating and re-sorting from scratch.

concepts.statement: `HEAP-MAXIMUM(A)` returns $A[1]$ without modifying the heap: $\Theta(1)$ time, since the max-heap property parks the maximum at the root. Every other priority-queue operation pays $O(\lg n)$ precisely because it must restore what this peek does not disturb.
concepts.detail: The min twin `HEAP-MINIMUM` is symmetric. Peeks never change `heap-size`, so a sequence of $k$ peeks costs $\Theta(k)$ while $k$ extracts cost $\Theta(k \lg n)$.

examples.title: Extract then insert
examples.problem: Start from the heap $A = \langle 16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1 \rangle$ ($n = 10$). Perform HEAP-EXTRACT-MAX, then MAX-HEAP-INSERT a new element with key 15.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: EXTRACT-MAX returns 16. Move the last leaf to the root and shrink: $A = \langle 1, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4 \rangle$, $n = 9$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Heapify the root: 1 loses to $\max(14, 10) = 14$ — swap; then at node 2, 1 loses to $\max(8, 7) = 8$ — swap; then at node 4, 1 loses to $\max(2, 4) = 4$ — swap. Result: $\langle 14, 8, 10, 4, 7, 9, 3, 2, 1 \rangle$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Insert 15: append $-\infty$ at position 10, $n = 10$: $\langle 14, 8, 10, 4, 7, 9, 3, 2, 1, -\infty \rangle$; raise it to 15.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: The climb: parent $A[5] = 7 < 15$ — swap up; parent $A[2] = 8 < 15$ — swap up; parent $A[1] = 14 < 15$ — swap to the root. Final heap: $\langle 15, 14, 10, 4, 8, 9, 3, 2, 1, 7 \rangle$ — verify: $15 \ge 14, 10$; $14 \ge 4, 8$; $10 \ge 9, 3$; $4 \ge 2, 1$.

examples.result: After extraction the max is 14; after inserting 15 the heap is $\langle 15, 14, 10, 4, 8, 9, 3, 2, 1, 7 \rangle$ — both operations touched only one root-to-leaf path each.

examples.title: A priority queue as an event loop
examples.problem: A simulator holds events keyed by time: (7, 'msg'), (3, 'ack'), (9, 'close'), (1, 'open'). Show the heap states as it runs the four events in order.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Insert keys 7, 3, 9 into a min-heap (soonest first): after three inserts, $A = \langle 3, 7, 9 \rangle$ with satellite data riding along.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Insert key 1: append, then climb past 3 to the root: $A = \langle 1, 3, 9, 7 \rangle$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Extract-min → key 1 ('open'). Last leaf 7 moves to the root, sinks below 3: $A = \langle 3, 7, 9 \rangle$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Extract-min → 3 ('ack') — heap $\langle 7, 9 \rangle$; then insert 5 ('ping') → climbs to root: $\langle 5, 9, 7 \rangle$; extract-min → 5, then 7, then 9 ('close').

examples.result: Output order: open(1), ack(3), ping(5), 7, close(9) — every operation $O(\lg 4)$ steps, and the queue never held more than 4 events.

keyTakeaways: A heap implements the priority queue ADT: MAXIMUM in $O(1)$; INSERT, EXTRACT-MAX and INCREASE-KEY in $O(\lg n)$.
EXTRACT-MAX plants the last leaf at the root and trickles down; INCREASE-KEY bubbles a raised key up — the two repairs are vertical mirror images.
Min-heaps serve selection workloads (Dijkstra, event simulation) either by symmetric code or by storing negated keys in a max-heap.

quiz.q: The running time of HEAP-EXTRACT-MAX on a heap of $n$ elements is:
quiz.explanation: One root heapify after the swap: a single path down the tree, O(lg n) — the O(1) return of the root itself is only half the operation.

quiz.q: MAX-HEAP-INSERT places a new element by:
options: appending key $-\infty$ and raising it with INCREASE-KEY, bubbling up while the parent is smaller
quiz.explanation: The −∞ sentinel append keeps the shape valid instantly; INCREASE-KEY then climbs the single parent chain the new key can violate, in O(lg n).

quiz.q: HEAP-INCREASE-KEY raises $A[i]$ from 9 to 15, where the parent holds 12. What happens?
options: nothing — the heap property is intact since $12 \ge 9$
the element swaps with its parent and keeps climbing while the parent is smaller
the element is sifted down by MAX-HEAPIFY
the whole heap is rebuilt in $O(n)$
quiz.explanation: What matters is the *new* key: 15 > 12 violates the property, so the element swaps with its parent and continues upward. The 'does nothing' option applies only when the new key stays at or below the parent — raising 9 to 10 would indeed be free.

quiz.q: Which application is a direct client of a (min-)priority queue?
options: a discrete-event simulation keyed by event time
quiz.explanation: The simulator must repeatedly retrieve the soonest event — extract-min on a time key — exactly the ADT a heap implements; Dijkstra's algorithm is the other canonical client.

intro: Quicksort inverts mergesort's division of labor: all the work happens in the *divide* step, and the *combine* step does nothing. The PARTITION procedure sweeps the subarray once, groups elements around a pivot value, and drops the pivot into its final sorted position — everything else is two recursive calls on whatever remains.
objectives: State the quicksort recurrence structure and the PARTITION procedure line by line
Prove PARTITION's loop invariant and explain why the pivot lands in its final position
Trace a complete partition on real numbers, region by region

concepts.statement: **`QUICKSORT(A, p, r)`**: if $p < r$, then $q = \text{PARTITION}(A, p, r)$, followed by `QUICKSORT(A, p, q-1)` and `QUICKSORT(A, q+1, r)` — with **no combine step at all**.
concepts.detail: Contrast mergesort: there, dividing is trivial and all work is in the $\Theta(n)$ merge; here the partition does the sorting work and the recursive calls merely finish. The initial call is `QUICKSORT(A, 1, n)`. Both pivots of the two recursions are disjoint from the pivot position $q$.

concepts.statement: **`PARTITION(A, p, r)`** chooses the pivot $x = A[r]$, maintains $i = p - 1$, and for $j = p \ldots r-1$: whenever $A[j] \le x$, increments $i$ and swaps $A[i] \leftrightarrow A[j]$. Finally it swaps $A[i+1] \leftrightarrow A[r]$ and returns $i+1$.
concepts.detail: The scan does exactly one comparison per element — $r - p$ comparisons total — plus $O(1)$ bookkeeping, so a partition of an $n$-element subarray costs $\Theta(n)$ and $\Theta(n)$ swaps in the worst case, all inside the input array (no auxiliary storage). The pivot is simply the last element here; Section 7.3 randomizes this choice.

concepts.statement: At the start of each iteration $j$, the subarray satisfies three regions: **$A[p \ldots i] \le x$**, **$A[i+1 \ldots j-1] > x$**, and **$A[j \ldots r-1]$ unexamined**, with $A[r] = x$ untouched.
concepts.detail: Initialization holds vacuously ($i = p-1$, $j = p$); maintenance moves $A[j]$ into the correct region by the conditional swap; at termination $j = r$ the array is split into $\le x$ then $> x$. The final swap places $x$ **between** the regions: every element of the left region is $\le x$ and every element of the right region is $> x$, so $A[q]$ equals its rank — the pivot is in its final sorted position forever.

concepts.statement: Each partition permanently fixes **one** element — the pivot — into its sorted position, and hands back two strictly smaller subproblems whose sizes sum to $n-1$.
concepts.detail: The split can be anything from $0 / n-1$ (disaster, Section 7.2) to $\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor / \lceil (n-1)/2 \rceil$ (ideal). Quicksort's quality is entirely hostage to pivot luck — which is why Section 7.3 randomizes and Section 7.4 analyzes the average.

concepts.statement: CLRS uses Lomuto's partition (pivot at $A[r]$, one-directional scan, $\Theta(n)$ swaps worst case). Hoare's original scheme scans from both ends toward the middle, does fewer swaps on average, and returns a split point that is not the pivot's final home, so the recursion covers $A[p..q]$ and $A[q+1..r]$.
concepts.detail: Both are $\Theta(n)$-time and in-place; Lomuto is chosen for its three-region invariant, which is easier to prove. Production quicksorts often use Hoare or dual-pivot variants for the constant-factor win.

figures.caption: PARTITION on $A = \langle 2, 8, 7, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4 \rangle$ with pivot $x = A[8] = 4$. Row (b) shows the invariant mid-scan at $j = 6$: $A[1..3] \le x$ (shaded), $A[4..5] > x$, $A[6..7]$ unseen, the $i$ and $j$ pointers below. Row (c) is the final state: the pivot 4 has been swapped into position $q = 4$, splitting the array into $\{2,1,3\} \le 4 < \{7,5,6,8\}$ — with 4 in its final sorted position.

examples.title: A complete PARTITION trace
examples.problem: Run `PARTITION(A, 1, 8)` on $A = \langle 2, 8, 7, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4 \rangle$, recording the state after each scan step.

steps.label: Setup
steps.text: Pivot $x = A[8] = 4$; $i = 0$; the scan runs $j = 1 \ldots 7$ with the three-region invariant.

steps.label: j = 1, 2, 3
steps.text: $A[1] = 2 \le 4$: $i{=}1$, swap $A[1]$ with itself — no change. $A[2] = 8 > 4$ and $A[3] = 7 > 4$: nothing happens; the $> x$ region grows: $A[2..3] = \{8, 7\}$.

steps.label: j = 4, 5
steps.text: $A[4] = 1 \le 4$: $i{=}2$, swap $A[2] \leftrightarrow A[4]$: $\langle 2, 1, 7, 8, 3, 5, 6, 4 \rangle$. $A[5] = 3 \le 4$: $i{=}3$, swap $A[3] \leftrightarrow A[5]$: $\langle 2, 1, 3, 8, 7, 5, 6, 4 \rangle$.

steps.label: Final swap
steps.text: Swap $A[i+1] = A[4] \leftrightarrow A[8]$: $\langle 2, 1, 3, 4, 7, 5, 6, 8 \rangle$, and return $q = 4$. Elements $1..3$ are $\le 4$, elements $5..8$ are $> 4$ — and position 4 holds the 4th smallest value, permanently.

examples.result: Seven comparisons (one per scanned element), four swaps, and the pivot's final home is index 4: the left subarray $\langle 2,1,3 \rangle$ and right subarray $\langle 7,5,6,8 \rangle$ remain to be sorted.

examples.title: Partitioning with many equals
examples.problem: Run PARTITION on $A = \langle 4, 2, 4, 1, 4 \rangle$ with pivot $x = A[5] = 4$ and count how the $\le x$ test treats duplicates.

steps.label: Setup
steps.text: Pivot $x = 4$, $i = 0$, scan $j = 1..4$. The test is $A[j] \le 4$, so equal keys join the left region.

steps.label: Scan
steps.text: $j=1$: $4 \le 4$, $i=1$, self-swap. $j=2$: $2 \le 4$, $i=2$, swap $A[2] \leftrightarrow A[2]$. $j=3$: $4 \le 4$, $i=3$, self-swap. $j=4$: $1 \le 4$, $i=4$, self-swap. Array unchanged: $\langle 4, 2, 4, 1, 4 \rangle$ with $i = 4$.

steps.label: Final swap
steps.text: Swap $A[5] \leftrightarrow A[5]$ (self-swap), return $q = 5$. Left region $A[1..4] = \langle 4, 2, 4, 1 \rangle \le 4$, right region empty.

steps.label: Moral
steps.text: With all-equal keys Lomuto still splits $n-1:0$ every time, hence $\Theta(n^2)$ on $n$ equals. Section 7.4's randomized analysis and the three-way partition of Exercise 7.1-2 exist to repair exactly this case.

examples.result: Pivot lands at $q = 5$ after $4$ comparisons and no effective swaps; duplicates all pile left, so equal keys do not save Lomuto from quadratic behavior.

keyTakeaways: Quicksort = partition, then recurse on both sides; there is no combine step — PARTITION has already done the sorting work.
PARTITION's invariant keeps $\le x$ left of $i$, $> x$ between $i+1$ and $j-1$, and unexamined elements from $j$; the final swap seats the pivot in its final sorted position.
One pass, $\Theta(n)$ time, in-place, one comparison per element — but the split quality is entirely up to the pivot's rank.

quiz.q: The last action of PARTITION — swapping $A[i+1]$ with $A[r]$ — accomplishes what?
options: moves the largest element to the end
places the pivot into its final sorted position, between the ≤ x and > x regions
quiz.explanation: After the swap, every element left of position i+1 is ≤ x and every element right of it is > x, so the pivot sits exactly at its sorted rank and is never touched again.

quiz.q: During the scan, the region $A[i+1 \ldots j-1]$ holds exactly the elements that are:
quiz.explanation: The invariant's middle region collects elements that failed the test A[j] ≤ x: they are strictly greater than the pivot and were skipped by the i-pointer.

quiz.q: The running time of PARTITION on a subarray of $n$ elements is:
quiz.explanation: The loop runs j from p to r−1 with one comparison each, plus constant-time swaps: linear, and no element is compared twice.

quiz.q: In this section's version of PARTITION, the pivot value is:
quiz.explanation: The textbook procedure fixes x = A[r]; its predictability is exactly what Section 7.3's RANDOMIZED-PARTITION removes.

quiz.q: Lomuto PARTITION with the last element as pivot runs on $[2, 8, 7, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4]$. The pivot final index (1-indexed) is:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: pivot $x = 4$, scan indices $1$ through $7$ with boundary $i = 0$. Step 2 — Governing invariant: entries up to $i$ are at most $x$, entries $i+1$ through $j-1$ exceed $x$. Step 3 — Trace: $2$ swaps into place ($i = 1$); $1$ swaps with $8$ ($i = 2$); $3$ swaps with $7$ ($i = 3$); $5$ and $6$ are skipped; closing exchange puts $4$ at $i + 1 = 4$, giving $[2, 1, 3, 4, 7, 5, 6, 8]$. Step 4 — Sanity check: three keys not exceeding $4$ precede it, larger keys follow, and each key moved at most once. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: $3$ counts only part of the small keys, $5$ includes the pivot among the large ones, and $8$ is the pivot start position. Step 6 — Conclude: index $4$.

intro: Quicksort's running time is a function of pivot quality, and pivot quality spans a dangerous range. The worst case — every split as unbalanced as possible — is quadratic; the best case is the familiar $n \lg n$. The reassuring result of this section is that the boundary between the two is extremely wide: *any* constant split proportion, even 99-to-1, still lands in $\Theta(n \lg n)$.
objectives: Derive the worst-case $\Theta(n^2)$ recurrence and exhibit a triggering input
Derive the best-case $\Theta(n \lg n)$ recurrence
Show that any constant-proportion split gives depth $\Theta(\lg n)$ — the robustness argument

concepts.statement: If every partition is maximally unbalanced ($0$ and $n-1$ elements), then $T(n) = T(n-1) + T(0) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n^2)$.
concepts.detail: Trigger: the pivot is always the smallest or largest element of its subarray — e.g., an **already-sorted array** with the last-element rule (each pivot is the maximum of its range), or an array of $n$ identical keys under this two-region partition. The recursion degenerates into a single chain of $n$ levels costing $n + (n-1) + \cdots + 1 = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \Theta(n^2)$ comparisons.

concepts.statement: If every pivot lands in the middle, $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$, which solves to $\Theta(n \lg n)$ — quicksort's ideal, matching merge sort.
concepts.detail: The split is at best $\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$ and $\lceil (n-1)/2 \rceil$ because the pivot itself retires from the subproblems; the master theorem (case 2) or a recursion tree of cost $\le cn$ per level over $\lg n$ levels gives the bound.

concepts.statement: A split into fractions $\alpha$ and $1-\alpha$ of the array (any fixed $0 < \alpha < 1$) gives recurrence $T(n) = T(\alpha n) + T((1-\alpha) n) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n \lg n)$ — a 9:1 split only changes the *constant*, by the factor $1 / \lg(10/9) \approx 6.6$.
concepts.detail: Recursion-tree view: every level costs at most $cn$ (the level's subproblems partition disjoint ranges), and shrinking by factor $10/9$ per level needs $\log_{10/9} n \approx 6.6 \lg n$ levels. Even a pathological 99:1 split yields $\log_{100/99} n \approx 69 \lg n$ levels — still logarithmic, still $\Theta(n \lg n)$.

concepts.statement: Bad and good splits alternate — half the splits $0:(n-1)$, half perfectly balanced — quicksort still runs in $\Theta(n \lg n)$, at about twice the best-case constant.
concepts.detail: A worst-case split costs $\Theta(n)$ and leaves one big subproblem; the balanced split that follows costs half that and cuts the problem into quarters. Working the recursion tree, the pair ‘bad then good’ behaves like a single halving step costing $1.5$-times-n work — so the alternation gives $\Theta(n \lg n)$ with about twice the best-case constant. The moral CLRS draws: quicksort's average experience is governed by the mix of splits, and badness must persist to hurt — occasional lopsided splits are amortized by the good ones around them.

concepts.statement: Quicksort's recursion depth equals the longest chain of nested subproblems: $\Theta(n)$ in the worst case ($0:n-1$ splits) and $\Theta(\lg n)$ when every split is a constant proportion. Tail-recursing on the smaller side first caps the stack at $O(\lg n)$ even when the time is $\Theta(n^2)$.
concepts.detail: Depth and total cost are different resources: depth counts the tallest path, total cost sums every level. A 99:1 split is $69\times$ deeper than balanced yet still logarithmic, so both its stack and its time stay $\Theta(\lg n)$ and $\Theta(n \lg n)$.

examples.title: Depth arithmetic for split ratios
examples.problem: For $n = 10^6$ elements, compare recursion depths for (a) perfectly balanced splits, (b) 9:1 splits every time, (c) 99:1 splits every time.

steps.label: Balanced
steps.text: Each level at least halves the largest remaining subproblem: depth $\approx \lg 10^6 = 6 \lg 10 \approx 19.9$ — call it 20 levels, each costing up to $cn$, for about $20cn$ total work.

steps.label: 9:1 split
steps.text: The large side keeps $9/10$ of its elements: depth $\log_{10/9} 10^6 = \frac{6 \ln 10}{\ln(10/9)} = \frac{13.82}{0.1054} \approx 131$ levels — $6.6$ times deeper than balanced.

steps.label: 99:1 split
steps.text: The large side keeps $99/100$: depth $\frac{13.82}{\ln(100/99)} = \frac{13.82}{0.01005} \approx 1374$ levels — 69 times deeper than balanced, but still $\Theta(\lg n)$.

steps.label: The bill
steps.text: Every level does at most $cn$ work regardless of shape (subproblems are disjoint), so totals are $\approx 20cn$, $131cn$ and $1374cn$: the same order $\Theta(n \lg n)$, with constants $1 \times$, $6.6\times$ and $69\times$.

examples.result: All three are $\Theta(n \lg n)$; the split ratio only rescales the constant — $1/\lg(1/(1-\alpha))$ to be precise. Only a split ratio approaching 1:0 with $n$ (like the $n-1 : 0$ worst case) breaks logarithmic depth.

examples.title: Worst-case chain on five sorted elements
examples.problem: Run deterministic QUICKSORT (pivot $A[r]$) on $\langle 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \rangle$ and sum the partition costs.

steps.label: Level 1
steps.text: PARTITION on $1..5$, pivot $5$: $4$ comparisons, split $4:0$, pivot fixed at $5$.

steps.label: Level 2
steps.text: PARTITION on $1..4$, pivot $4$: $3$ comparisons, split $3:0$.

steps.label: Level 3-4
steps.text: Costs $2$ then $1$ comparisons; the recursion is a chain of depth $5$.

steps.label: Total
steps.text: $4+3+2+1 = 10 = 5 \cdot 4/2 = n(n-1)/2$ comparisons: $\Theta(n^2)$, with stack depth $n$.

examples.result: $10$ comparisons on $n = 5$ sorted input; in general $n(n-1)/2 = \Theta(n^2)$ comparisons and $\Theta(n)$ stack depth.

keyTakeaways: Worst case $\Theta(n^2)$: every split $0 : n-1$ — triggered by sorted input with the last-element pivot rule.
Best case $\Theta(n \lg n)$: splits as even as the pivot's removal allows, $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$.

Robustness: any constant split fraction $\alpha : 1-\alpha$ keeps quicksort at $\Theta(n \lg n)$ with constant inflated by $1/\lg \frac{1}{1-\alpha}$ — even 99:1 costs only a $\approx 69\times$ depth constant.

quiz.q: Quicksort's worst-case running time and a natural triggering input are:
options: $\Theta(n^2)$ on an already-sorted array when the pivot is the last element
$\Theta(n^2)$ only when all keys are random
quiz.explanation: With pivot = A[r] and sorted input, each pivot is the maximum of its range: splits are 0 : n−1, the recursion is a chain, and the level costs sum to n(n+1)/2.

quiz.q: The best-case recurrence for quicksort is:
quiz.explanation: Central pivots split each subarray into two halves (the pivot itself retires), giving the mergesort recurrence and Θ(n lg n) by the master theorem.

quiz.q: If every partition splits the current subarray 9-to-1, the recursion depth is approximately:
quiz.explanation: The large subproblem shrinks by the factor 10/9 per level, so depth is log base 10/9 — about 6.6 times the balanced depth, but still Θ(lg n).

quiz.q: Why does every recursion level cost at most $cn$ total, regardless of how lopsided the splits are?
options: because the pivot is always cheap
because the level's subproblems are disjoint slices of the original array, so their sizes sum to at most n
quiz.explanation: Subproblems at one depth partition a subset of the array — sizes add up to ≤ n — and each partition costs linear in its own subarray, giving ≤ cn per level.

quiz.q: Quicksort with the last-element pivot sorts the ascending array $[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]$. The number of key comparisons is:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: sorted ascending input of size $5$, deterministic last-element pivot. Step 2 — Governing recurrence: worst-case split $0$ against $n - 1$ gives $T(n) = T(n-1) + \Theta(n)$. Step 3 — Count: partition sizes compare $4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$ keys, since each pivot meets every remaining key once. Step 4 — Sanity check: $10 = \frac{5 \times 4}{2}$ matches the triangular number, recursion depth is $5$, and random pivots avoid this trap in expectation. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: $7$ undercounts the shrinking scans, $15$ counts all pairs including symmetric ones, and $5$ counts one scan only. Step 6 — Conclude: $10$ comparisons, the quadratic worst case.

intro: The worst case of Section 7.2 comes from an adversary who knows the pivot rule. Randomizing the pivot moves the surprise into the algorithm: no fixed input is systematically bad, because the input cannot know the coin flips. This one-line change converts quicksort from fragile to provably fast in expectation — on every input without exception.
objectives: State RANDOMIZED-PARTITION and its one-line difference from PARTITION
Explain why no single input is bad for randomized quicksort
Classify randomized algorithms: Las Vegas versus Monte Carlo

concepts.statement: **`RANDOMIZED-PARTITION(A, p, r)`**: pick $i$ uniformly at random from ${p, \ldots, r\}$ — `i = RANDOM(p, r)` — swap $A[r] \leftrightarrow A[i]$, then run the ordinary `PARTITION(A, p, r)`.
concepts.detail: The whole algorithm changes by one random swap: the pivot is a uniformly random element of the subarray, so its rank is uniform on $\{1, \ldots, m\}$ for subarray size $m$. RANDOMIZED-QUICKSORT is QUICKSORT with this replacement.

concepts.statement: For **deterministic** quicksort there exists an input that forces $\Theta(n^2)$; for **randomized** quicksort, no fixed input forces anything — the expected running time is $O(n \lg n)$ *for every input*, the average being taken over the algorithm's own random choices.
concepts.detail: The sorted array that destroyed the last-element rule now gets a random pivot like any other array: the probability of drawing an extreme rank is $1/n$ per level, not 1. What disappears is the correlation between *input structure* and *pivot quality* — the input cannot predict the coins.

concepts.statement: A **Las Vegas algorithm** always produces the correct answer; only its running time is a random variable. Randomized quicksort is Las Vegas — Monte Carlo algorithms (e.g., primality tests) instead trade a small error probability for guaranteed speed.
concepts.detail: For Las Vegas algorithms one analyzes $E[T(n)]$ over the internal coin flips. Quicksort never inspects the outcome of its randomness to decide correctness — the randomness only steers the pivot choice.

concepts.term: The two views of the same process
concepts.statement: Averaging a deterministic algorithm over uniformly random inputs and averaging a randomized algorithm over its coins on a fixed input are **the same computation** when the randomization is a uniform pivot: randomized quicksort on any array behaves exactly like deterministic quicksort on a uniformly random permutation.
concepts.detail: This 'random permutation view' is the bridge used in Section 7.4's analysis: we may fix the elements' sorted order $z_1 < \cdots < z_n$ and treat every pivot as a uniform draw, because a uniformly random pivot on a fixed array explores the same split statistics as a fixed pivot on a shuffled array.

concepts.statement: On a subarray of size $m$, RANDOMIZED-PARTITION makes the pivot's rank uniform on $\{1, \ldots, m\}$: $\Pr\{\mathrm{rank} = k\} = 1/m$ for every $k$. The split sizes $(k-1, m-k)$ are therefore equally likely over all $m$ possibilities.
concepts.detail: Uniformity is what the Section 7.4 analysis consumes: the $2/(j-i+1)$ pair probability is exactly the chance that two fixed elements are the first among their interval to be drawn as a uniform pivot.

examples.title: How much damage can luck do?
examples.problem: Randomized quicksort runs on the already-sorted array $\langle 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \rangle$. Compute the probability that it degenerates into the $\Theta(n^2)$ worst case, and the probability of a perfect first split.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: The worst case needs every pivot to be an extreme element (max or min) of its subarray. First call: the pivot is uniform among ranks $\{1, \ldots, 5\}$; extremes have probability $2/5$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Continuing: the subproblems have sizes 4, 3, 2, each needing an extreme pivot again — with probabilities $2/4$, $2/3$, and the size-2 case is automatically extreme ($1$).

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Product: $\frac{2}{5} \cdot \frac{2}{4} \cdot \frac{2}{3} \cdot 1 = \frac{8}{60} = \frac{2}{15} \approx 0.133$ for this particular all-extreme chain — and other worst-case chains give the same order. Deterministic quicksort on this input: probability 1.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: A perfect first split needs the median (rank 3): probability $1/5$ — versus $0$ for the deterministic version on a bad input. Each rank is equally likely: the expected split quality is the average over all of them.

examples.result: The catastrophic behavior that deterministic quicksort suffers with certainty happens only with small probability under random pivots — and its complement, the perfect median split, is now reachable at rate $1/n$ per level instead of never.

examples.title: Split distribution on four elements
examples.problem: For RANDOMIZED-PARTITION on $m = 4$ distinct elements, tabulate the split probabilities and the chance of a 1:1-or-better balance.

steps.label: Ranks
steps.text: Pivot rank $1,2,3,4$ each with probability $1/4$, giving splits $0:3$, $1:2$, $2:1$, $3:0$.

steps.label: Balanced outcomes
steps.text: Ranks $2$ and $3$ are the balanced splits ($1:2$ and $2:1$): total probability $1/2$.

steps.label: Extremes
steps.text: Ranks $1$ and $4$ are maximally unbalanced: probability $1/2$. Randomization does not prevent bad splits; it makes them a fair coin flip per level.

steps.label: Expectation
steps.text: Expected larger side: $(3+2+2+3)/4 = 2.5 = 0.625m$, a constant fraction below $m$, which is why the expected depth stays logarithmic.

examples.result: Balanced with probability $1/2$ per level on $m = 4$; the expected larger side is $2.5$ elements, so progress is geometric in expectation.

keyTakeaways: RANDOMIZED-PARTITION = one uniform random swap of the pivot into the last slot, then ordinary PARTITION.
No input is a guaranteed ambush: the expectation is over the algorithm's coins, and every input enjoys $E[T(n)] = O(n \lg n)$.
Randomized quicksort is Las Vegas — always correct, randomly timed; and on a fixed array it is statistically identical to deterministic quicksort on a random permutation.

quiz.q: RANDOMIZED-PARTITION differs from PARTITION by:
options: choosing the pivot uniformly at random from the subarray and swapping it into the last position
quiz.explanation: i = RANDOM(p, r), swap A[r] with A[i], then the standard partition runs — one line of randomness that makes the pivot's rank uniform.

quiz.q: For randomized quicksort on a *fixed* input, the statement $E[T(n)] = O(n \lg n)$ averages over:
options: the algorithm's own random pivot choices
quiz.explanation: The input is fixed and arbitrary; the expectation is over the internal coins. That is what makes the bound input-independent — no distributional assumption on the data.

quiz.q: Randomized quicksort is an example of a:
options: Monte Carlo algorithm — it may mis-sort with small probability
Las Vegas algorithm — always correct, with randomized running time
quiz.explanation: The output is always the sorted array; only the time is random. Monte Carlo algorithms accept an error probability in exchange for time guarantees.

quiz.q: The 'random permutation view' says randomized quicksort on a fixed array is equivalent to:
options: deterministic quicksort on a uniformly random permutation of that array
insertion sort on the sorted output
quiz.explanation: Uniform pivot ranks on a fixed array reproduce exactly the split statistics of a fixed pivot rule (last element) on a random shuffle — the view that powers Section 7.4's analysis.

intro: The final piece is honest mathematics: proving that the expected running time of randomized quicksort is $\Theta(n \lg n)$. The famous subtlety — flagged by the book itself — is that the two recursive calls are *not* independent, so the tempting recurrence $E[T(n)] = 2E[T(n/2)] + \Theta(n)$ has no legal foundation. The repair is one of the most celebrated arguments in the book: count comparisons pairwise with indicator random variables and let linearity of expectation do all the work.
objectives: Carry out the substitution proof that the worst case is $O(n^2)$
State the expected-comparison theorem and the separation lemma behind it
Compute exact expected comparison counts for small $n$ from the pair-sum formula

concepts.statement: The worst-case running time of quicksort is $O(n^2)$: with $T(n) \le \max_{0 \le q \le n-1}\big(T(q) + T(n-q-1)\big) + \Theta(n)$ and the guess $T(n) \le c n^2$, the inner expression $q^2 + (n-q-1)^2$ is maximized at the endpoints $q = 0$ or $q = n-1$, giving $T(n) \le c(n-1)^2 + \Theta(n) \le c n^2$ for suitable $c$.
concepts.detail: Concretely: $c(n-1)^2 + \Theta(n) = cn^2 - 2cn + c + \Theta(n) \le cn^2$ once $c$ is large enough that the linear term is dominated — the quadratic guess holds because the sum of the children's squares is *most dangerous when one child has everything*, exactly the unbalanced split of Section 7.2. (Section 4.3's warning applies: the guess must also be checked against the boundary conditions and small $n$, which the base case $T(n) = O(1)$ for $n \le n_0$ absorbs.)

concepts.statement: The naive expectation argument — 'each side is a uniformly random subarray, so $E[T(n)] = 2E[T((n-1)/2)] + \Theta(n)$' — is **invalid**: given the pivot's rank, the two subarrays' *element compositions* are complementary, and the running times of the two recursive calls are dependent random variables.
concepts.detail: CLRS is explicit: conditioning on the first pivot fixes both subproblem sizes simultaneously, so their behaviors are coupled — a huge left subtree means a small right one. Linearity of expectation never needs independence, which is precisely why the correct proof routes every quantity through it.

concepts.statement: Randomized quicksort on any fixed input performs $E[X] = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \sum_{j=i+1}^{n} \Pr\{z_i \text{ compared with } z_j\} = \sum_{i<j} \frac{2}{j-i+1} \le 2n H_n = O(n \lg n)$ comparisons in expectation, where $z_1 < z_2 < \cdots < z_n$ are the sorted elements and $H_n$ is the $n$th harmonic number.
concepts.detail: The pair probability is exactly $2/(j-i+1)$ — the separation lemma below — and the sharpened evaluation of the same sum gives the exact count $2(n+1)H_n - 4n \approx 1.39\, n \lg n$ comparisons, worked out in the depth section below.

concepts.statement: Elements $z_i$ and $z_j$ ($i < j$) are compared **if and only if** the first pivot ever selected from the closed set $\{z_i, z_{i+1}, \ldots, z_j\}$ is one of the two endpoints $z_i$ or $z_j$ — whence $\Pr\{z_i \text{ vs } z_j\} = 2/(j-i+1)$.
concepts.detail: Pivots chosen from outside the set keep the whole interval together in one subarray (they are all smaller than $z_i$ or all larger than $z_j$). The first pivot from inside the set either is an endpoint — it is compared against every remaining element of the subarray, including the other endpoint, exactly once — or is an interior $z_k$, which permanently splits the interval so $z_i$ and $z_j$ never meet. Each of the $j-i+1$ members is equally likely to be that first pivot.

concepts.statement: Nearby elements compare often (adjacent pairs with probability $1$), far-apart elements almost never (extremes with probability $2/n$) — and the sum over all $n(n-1)/2$ pairs still lands at $O(n \lg n)$ because far pairs are cheap *and* numerous.
concepts.detail: This is the payoff of linearity: $E[X] = \sum_{i<j} E[X_{ij}]$ where $X_{ij}$ is the comparison indicator — no independence among the $X_{ij}$ is required or used, defusing the trap of the naive analysis. The same lemma, read one-sided, is what gives RANDOMIZED-SELECT its $\Theta(n)$ in Chapter 9.

examples.title: The exact expectation for $n = 8$
examples.problem: Compute the expected number of comparisons $E[X]$ of randomized quicksort on 8 elements, directly from the pair probabilities, and compare with the worst and best possible runs.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Group the $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ pairs by distance $d = j - i + 1$: there are $n - d + 1$ pairs at each $d$, each comparing with probability $2/d$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Total: $E[X] = 7 + 4 + 2.5 + 1.6 + 1 + 0.571 + 0.25 \approx 16.92$ comparisons. The sharp closed form $2(n+1)H_n - 4n = 18 \cdot 2.7179 - 32$ gives the same $16.92$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Context: a perfectly balanced sequence of pivots (ranks 4, then 2, 2, then 1 of the last pair) costs only $7 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 13$ comparisons — the floor, since a run's comparisons equal the sum of depths in its pivot tree. The degenerate chain costs $7 + 6 + \cdots + 1 = 28 = \binom{8}{2}$.

examples.result: Expected $\approx 16.92$, best 13, worst 28 — and the upper bound $2nH_n = 43.5$ used in the book's proof is honest but loose for small $n$.

examples.title: Sanity-checking the separation lemma
examples.problem: For $n = 4$ elements $z_1 < z_2 < z_3 < z_4$, list each pair, its interval, and its comparison probability.

steps.label: Adjacent pairs
steps.text: $(z_1,z_2)$, $(z_2,z_3)$, $(z_3,z_4)$: intervals of size 2 — the first pivot from each interval is an endpoint with probability $2/2 = 1$. Adjacent elements are always compared (whichever becomes pivot first meets the other).

steps.label: Distance 2
steps.text: $(z_1,z_3)$, $(z_2,z_4)$: intervals $\{z_1,z_2,z_3\}$ and $\{z_2,z_3,z_4\}$ of size 3 — probability $2/3$ each. The enemy is $z_2$ (resp. $z_3$) sneaking in as pivot first and separating them forever.

steps.label: Extremes
steps.text: $(z_1,z_4)$: interval of all 4 — probability $2/4 = 1/2$; they meet only if one of them is the very first pivot drawn from the whole array.

steps.label: Total
steps.text: $E[X] = 3 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot \tfrac{2}{3} + 1 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} = 3 + 1.333 + 0.5 = 4.83$ — and the closed form $2(n+1)H_n - 4n = 10 \cdot 2.0833 - 16$ gives $4.83$. Consistent.

examples.result: The probability table $1, 1, 1, 2/3, 2/3, 1/2$ over the six pairs is the entire theorem for $n = 4$ — linearity of expectation simply adds these up.

keyTakeaways: Worst case $O(n^2)$ by substitution: the children's quadratic costs are maximized at extreme splits — the same splits that trigger the disaster.
The naive $2E[T(n/2)]$ analysis is illegal because the two recursive calls are dependent; the indicator-variable proof needs no independence at all.

$z_i$ meets $z_j$ iff an endpoint of their closed interval is the first pivot drawn from it — probability $2/(j-i+1)$ — so $E[X] \le 2nH_n = O(n \lg n)$, sharply $2(n+1)H_n - 4n \approx 1.39 n \lg n$.

quiz.q: In the substitution proof that quicksort's worst case is $O(n^2)$, the expression $q^2 + (n-q-1)^2$ is maximized:
options: at the endpoints $q = 0$ or $q = n-1$, the unbalanced splits
quiz.explanation: The convex sum of squares is largest when one child takes everything: exactly the 0 : n−1 split, confirming that unbalanced partitions are the worst case.

quiz.q: The probability that $z_i$ and $z_j$ (with $i < j$) are compared equals $2/(j-i+1)$ because:
options: every pair is compared with equal probability
they are compared exactly when one of them is the first pivot chosen from the closed set $\{z_i, \ldots, z_j\}$
the pivot is always a median
quiz.explanation: An interior pivot from the set separates them permanently; an endpoint pivot compares them immediately. Each of the j−i+1 members is equally likely to be first.

quiz.q: The indicator-variable analysis is immune to the dependence between recursive calls because:
options: the indicators are independent by construction
linearity of expectation holds for any dependent random variables
the expectation is conditioned on the pivot
quiz.explanation: E[X] = Σ E[X_ij] needs no independence whatsoever — which is exactly why the pair-counting proof succeeds where the naive recurrence-based argument fails.

quiz.q: The bound $E[X] \le 2nH_n$ places randomized quicksort's expected comparisons at:
quiz.explanation: H_n ≈ ln n, so 2nH_n ≈ 2n ln n = (2 ln 2) n lg n ≈ 1.39 n lg n — quicksort's famous average constant.

depth.title: The expected-time theorem in full: linearity of expectation carries the proof

blocks.body: The book's warning deserves to be internalized before the proof: if you find yourself writing $E[T(n)] = 2E[T(n/2)] + \Theta(n)$ for quicksort, you have already made an error. Conditioning on the first pivot's rank $q$ fixes **both** subproblem sizes at once, and the running times of the two recursive calls are dependent — a left call that goes deep forces the right call's input, and vice versa. Worse, within a single recursive call, the subarray is *no longer a uniformly random permutation* of its elements: it is a size-biased survivor of the first partition. The proof that follows succeeds because it never takes a recurrence at all. It counts the only thing quicksort actually does — pairwise comparisons — and lets **linearity of expectation** bypass every dependence question in one stroke.

blocks.heading: Expected comparisons of randomized quicksort
blocks.body: Let $z_1 < z_2 < \cdots < z_n$ be the input elements in sorted order, and let $X$ be the total number of comparisons RANDOMIZED-QUICKSORT performs. Then $$E[X] \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \sum_{j=i+1}^{n} \Pr\{z_i \text{ compared with } z_j\} \;=\; \sum_{i<j} \frac{2}{j-i+1} \;=\; 2(n+1)H_n - 4n \;<\; 2nH_n,$$ where $H_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} 1/k$ is the $n$th harmonic number. In particular $E[X] \approx 2n \ln n \approx 1.386\, n \lg n$, so $E[X] = O(n \lg n)$.

blocks.heading: The separation lemma and the sum
blocks.body: Define $X_{ij} = 1$ if $z_i$ is ever compared with $z_j$, so $X = \sum_{i<j} X_{ij}$ and, by linearity, $E[X] = \sum_{i<j} \Pr\{X_{ij} = 1\}$ — no independence required. **Claim:** $X_{ij} = 1$ iff the first pivot drawn from the closed set $Z_{ij} = \{z_i, z_{i+1}, \ldots, z_j\}$ is $z_i$ or $z_j$. *Why:* a pivot outside $Z_{ij}$ is smaller than every member of $Z_{ij}$ or larger than every member, so the partition keeps the whole set intact inside one child subarray — the interval shrinks around $Z_{ij}$ but never cuts through it. The first pivot $z_k$ taken from $Z_{ij}$ splits it: if $i < k < j$, then $z_i$ goes left and $z_j$ goes right, into subarrays that never interact again — no comparison, ever. But if the first member picked is $z_i$ (or $z_j$), the partition at that instant compares the pivot against **every** other element of the current subarray — which still contains the entire interval — so $z_i$ and $z_j$ are compared exactly once. By symmetry every member of $Z_{ij}$ is equally likely to be that first pivot, so $\Pr\{X_{ij}=1\} = \frac{2}{|Z_{ij}|} = \frac{2}{j-i+1}$. Summing over $d = j-i+1$, with $n-d+1$ pairs at each distance $d$: $E[X] = \sum_{d=2}^{n} \frac{2(n-d+1)}{d} = 2\sum_{d=2}^{n}\left(\frac{n+1}{d} - 1\right) = 2(n+1)(H_n - 1) - 2(n-1) = 2(n+1)H_n - 4n$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.heading: From the exact sum to $O(n \lg n)$
blocks.body: The telescoping in the last step deserves its own line: $\frac{n-d+1}{d} = \frac{n+1}{d} - 1$, so the double sum collapses to harmonic numbers minus a linear term. Now bound it: $H_n = 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n} \le 1 + \int_1^{n} \frac{dx}{x} = 1 + \ln n$, giving $E[X] \le 2(n+1)(\ln n + 1) - 4n = 2n\ln n + O(\ln n)$. Converting bases, $2\ln n = 2 \ln 2 \cdot \lg n \approx 1.386 \lg n$, which is where quicksort's average constant comes from. For the bound CLRS states, loosen before summing: $E[X] \le \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \sum_{j=i+1}^{n} \frac{2}{j-i+1} \le \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{2}{k+1} < 2n \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k} = 2nH_n = O(n \lg n)$ — cruder, but it keeps every step one-line.

Notice what the lemma really says: the *only* comparisons quicksort ever performs are pivot-vs-element, so a pair meets iff one member achieves 'local first' status in its interval. Read it again for Chapter 9: in RANDOMIZED-SELECT the recursion is **one-sided**, so an interior pivot $z_k$ still separates $z_i$ from $z_j$, but only the *side containing the target rank* is explored — the same separation lemma, applied to a process that discards half the tree, is what ultimately yields that algorithm's $\Theta(n)$ expected time. The pair $2/(j-i+1)$ is the atom from which both analyses are built.

blocks.heading: The theorem on $n = 8$, to three decimals
blocks.body: Grouping the 28 pairs by distance $d = j-i+1$: contributions $7(1) + 6(2/3) + 5(1/2) + 4(2/5) + 3(1/3) + 2(2/7) + 1(1/4) = 7 + 4 + 2.5 + 1.6 + 1 + 0.5714 + 0.25 = 16.9214$. The closed form agrees: $2 \cdot 9 \cdot H_8 - 32$ with $H_8 = 2.717857\ldots$ gives $48.9214 - 32 = 16.9214$. The book's looser bound $2nH_n = 43.49$ is off by $2.6\times$ at this size — asymptotic bounds are honest about order, not constants, and this example measures exactly how much room the constants leave at small $n$.

depth.title: Beyond the bound: exact constants, introsort and the partition race

blocks.body: The exact expectation $E[X] = 2(n+1)H_n - 4n$ (Sedgewick's sharpening of the CLRS sum) is worth expanding to see the machine under the hood: with $H_n = \ln n + \gamma + \tfrac{1}{2n} + O(1/n^2)$, one gets $E[X] = 2n\ln n + (2\gamma - 4)n + 2\ln n + o(n) \approx 1.386\, n \lg n - 1.846\, n$. Compare the information-theoretic floor $\lg n! \approx n \lg n - 1.443n$: quicksort pays roughly **39% more comparisons than necessary** in the leading term. It wins anyway because comparisons are not the only cost — partition is a single sequential scan with superb cache behavior and trivial constant per element, while comparison-optimal schemes (merge-insertion sort à la Ford–Johnson, optimal for small $n$) pay heavily in data movement and branch misprediction.

blocks.heading: Introsort: the engineering answer to the worst case
blocks.body: Musser's **introsort** (1997) runs quicksort but tracks recursion depth; if it exceeds $c \cdot \lg n$ (with $c \approx 2$), it switches the current subproblem to heapsort — Chapter 6's $\Theta(n \lg n)$ worst case with $O(1)$ space. The result inherits quicksort's average speed and heapsort's worst-case guarantee simultaneously: $\Theta(n \lg n)$ *always*, with the quicksort constant *usually*. This hybrid is what C++'s `std::sort` has shipped since the SGI STL — the standard mandates $O(n \lg n)$ worst case, which pure quicksort cannot offer. The depth-cap idea is exactly Section 7.2's robustness observation weaponized: unbalanced splits are fine in moderation; only *persistent* degeneration is fatal, and a depth counter detects persistence in $O(1)$ bookkeeping per level.

The partition scheme itself remained open ground: Yaroslavskiy's **dual-pivot** partition (2009) splits the array into three regions around two pivots, and both the analysis and the practice surprised the field — it performs *more* comparisons yet *fewer* writes, winning on real Java workloads, and it replaced the classic scheme in `java.util.Arrays.sort` for primitive types in 2011. Wild, Nebel and Neininger's exact analysis of dual-pivot quicksort showed the comparison count constant rises (to about $1.9\, n\lg n$) while scan costs drop — a trade invisible to any model that counts only comparisons. The general question '**which partition scheme minimizes total work on a real machine?**' is therefore genuinely open in the sense that its answer is architecture-dependent: cache lines, branch predictors and write bandwidth all vote.

blocks.heading: What is the true optimum for in-place sorting?
blocks.body: Three frontiers remain active. (1) **In-place stability**: quicksort's partition is unstable and no in-place stable variant with quicksort's constant is known; the best in-place stable mergesorts (symmerge, Grail) achieve $O(n \lg n)$ time and $O(1)$ space but with large constants — closing the gap to unstable speeds is open. (2) **Optimal adaptive sorting**: the comparison count should ideally degrade to $O(n(1 + \lg(\text{Inv}/n)))$ for inputs with Inv inversions; formal lower bounds (estimating presortedness) meet algorithms only partially. (3) **Comparison-optimal sorting**: the exact minimal worst-case comparison count is known only for small $n$ via Ford–Johnson-style merge-insertion (e.g., 30 comparisons for $n = 12$, one above the $\lceil \lg 12! \rceil = 29$ bound, and provably optimal there), and merge-insertion is known to fall short of optimal at some larger sizes (first at $n = 15$), while whether it stays asymptotically optimal — within $o(n)$ comparisons of the best possible — remains open. Where quicksort sits relative to a comparison-optimal in-place stable algorithm remains unknown: the 1.386 constant is proven for the scheme, but no one has proved a matching lower bound for *partition-based* methods. The gap between 1.386 and the information floor 1.000 is a territory still being mapped.

intro: Merge sort and heapsort run in $O(n \lg n)$ — is there anything faster? This section proves that in the comparison model the answer is no: every comparison sort makes $\Omega(n \lg n)$ comparisons in the worst case. The proof is a counting argument over an abstract object — the decision tree — that captures every comparison sort at once, no matter how clever its control flow.
objectives: Model any comparison sort as a decision tree and argue why correctness demands at least $n!$ leaves
Prove the $\Omega(n \lg n)$ lower bound via $h \ge \lg(n!)$ and Stirling's approximation
Explain why merge sort and heapsort are asymptotically optimal comparison sorts

concepts.statement: A **comparison sort** determines the sorted order **only by comparing elements with each other** — the algorithm's sole view of a key is the outcome of a test $a_i \le a_j$. Insertion sort, merge sort, heapsort and quicksort are all comparison sorts.
concepts.detail: The model is a radical abstraction: values are never inspected, hashed, or used as indices. A comparison sort would run unchanged on encrypted keys, provided the comparison answers stayed consistent. That very abstraction is what the lower bound exploits.

concepts.statement: A sort's execution on a given input is a path down a **decision tree**: each **internal node** is labeled by a comparison $i{:}j$ (compare $a_i$ to $a_j$), the two outcomes label the edges (we assume a two-way $\le$ / $\gt$ test), and each **leaf** holds a permutation — the sorted order output for every input that reaches it.
concepts.detail: Control flow, data movement and loop bookkeeping vanish; only comparisons remain. The **height** of the tree — the longest root-to-leaf path — is the algorithm's worst-case number of comparisons.

concepts.statement: A comparison sort that handles $n$ distinct keys correctly must have a decision tree with **at least $n!$ reachable leaves**.
concepts.detail: Each of the $n!$ orderings of the input must arrive at some leaf, and no leaf can serve two of them: two distinct permutations that follow the same path give identical answers to every comparison on that path, so the algorithm outputs the same permutation for both — wrong for at least one.

concepts.statement: Any comparison sort requires $\Omega(n \lg n)$ comparisons in the worst case. A binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves, so $n! \le 2^h$, giving $h \ge \lg(n!) \ge \lg(n/e)^n = n(\lg n - \lg e) = \Omega(n \lg n)$ by Stirling's approximation.
concepts.detail: Stirling gives $n! \ge (n/e)^n$, i.e. $\lg n! \ge n \lg n - n \lg e$. Since the height lower-bounds the worst-case comparison count, no comparison sort beats $n \lg n$ by more than a constant factor — randomized comparison sorts included, since a random algorithm is just a probability distribution over trees.

concepts.term: Corollary 8.2 — optimality of merge sort and heapsort
concepts.statement: Heapsort and merge sort are **asymptotically optimal** comparison sorts: their $O(n \lg n)$ upper bounds meet the $\Omega(n \lg n)$ lower bound.
concepts.detail: Quicksort is not covered — its worst case is $\Theta(n^2)$, so it is optimal only in expectation. The bound is about *comparisons*: the next three sections escape it by using key values as array indices instead of comparing them.

figures.caption: The decision tree that insertion sort follows on three distinct keys $a_1, a_2, a_3$. Internal nodes labeled $i{:}j$ compare $a_i$ with $a_j$; left edges answer $\le$, right edges $\gt$; each leaf holds the output permutation. The tree owns all $3! = 6$ orderings — one per leaf — and its height 3 is the worst-case comparison count, exactly $\lceil \lg 6 \rceil = \lceil 2.59 \rceil$: insertion sort is optimal for $n = 3$.
