examples.title: Branch-free deletion and a failed search
examples.problem: On the sentinel list $\text{L.nil} \Leftrightarrow 9 \Leftrightarrow 16 \Leftrightarrow 4 \Leftrightarrow 25$, (a) delete the node with key 4 given a pointer $x$ to it; (b) search for key 13.

steps.label: Delete: write 1
steps.text: $x.prev.next = x.next$: node 16's `next` field now points directly at node 25 — 4 is bypassed from the left.

steps.label: Delete: write 2
steps.text: $x.next.prev = x.prev$: node 25's `prev` field now points directly at node 16 — 4 is bypassed from the right. That is the entire deletion: **two pointer writes, no conditionals** — the code never asked whether 4 was first or last.

steps.label: Search for 13
steps.text:
`LIST-SEARCH'` walks from `L.nil.next`: 9 ($
e 13$) $	o$ 16 ($
e 13$) $	o$ 25 ($
e 13$) — after the deletion — and the next step reaches `L.nil` itself: the loop's termination condition fires.

examples.result: The ring now reads $\text{L.nil} \Leftrightarrow 9 \Leftrightarrow 16 \Leftrightarrow 25$; key 13 is reported absent because the walk came home. The same two-line delete works for node 9, node 25, or the last remaining node — uniformity is the sentinel's whole point.

examples.title: Inserting at both ends
examples.problem: On circular doubly linked list with sentinel $nil$, insert $9$ at the head and $1$ at the tail starting from $\langle 5 \rangle$.

steps.label: Start
steps.text: $nil.next = 5$, $5.prev = nil$, $5.next = nil$, $nil.prev = 5$: one element, head and tail coincide.

steps.label: Head insert 9
steps.text: LIST-INSERT puts $9$ before the head: $9.next = 5$, $5.prev = 9$, $9.prev = nil$, $nil.next = 9$: list $\langle 9, 5 \rangle$.

steps.label: Tail insert 1
steps.text: Insert after $nil.prev$: $5$ stays, $1.prev = 5$, $1.next = nil$, $5.next = 1$, $nil.prev = 1$: list $\langle 9, 5, 1 \rangle$.

steps.label: Delete middle
steps.text: LIST-DELETE($5$): $9.next = 1$, $1.prev = 9$ in two writes, no case split for head/tail: $\langle 9, 1 \rangle$.

examples.result: Head and tail inserts are the same four-write splice at different anchors; sentinel deletion never branches on position.

keyTakeaways: Linked lists trade search time ($\Theta(n)$ from the head) for $O(1)$ splicing: doubly linked deletion from a given pointer is two pointer writes; singly linked deletion needs the predecessor and costs a linear scan.
A sentinel node replaces both boundary NILs and closes the list into a ring — empty and one-element lists need no special cases, and delete becomes unconditional.
Sentinels cost one node per list and replace NIL-termination with 'return to L.nil' conditions — worth it whenever branch-light code matters.

quiz.q: Deleting a node $x$ from a doubly linked list, given a pointer to $x$, takes $O(1)$ via:
options: scanning from the head to find $x$'s predecessor
marking $x$'s key as deleted and compacting later
quiz.explanation: The node carries both neighbors, so both bypasses are single writes. (If x is the head, the head pointer is also updated — still O(1), and the sentinel version removes even that case.)

quiz.q: From a singly linked list, deleting a given node $x$ requires:
options: $\Theta(n)$ — the predecessor must be found by walking from the head
$O(\lg n)$ — binary search over the list
the list's length as a parameter
quiz.explanation: Only x.next is stored, so the predecessor — the node whose next must be rewired — is reachable only by traversing the list from the head.

quiz.q: Replacing NIL by a sentinel in a circular doubly linked list primarily buys:
options: smaller memory — the sentinel replaces two null pointers
simpler, branch-free code — no special cases for the ends in SEARCH, INSERT or DELETE
quiz.explanation: Every real node has real neighbors on both sides, so the end-of-list conditionals vanish from the operations — the same code path handles every position, including the empty ring.

quiz.q: In the sentinel version, how does `LIST-SEARCH'` detect that a key is absent?
options: it returns NIL because the loop exits at a null pointer
the walk returns to `L.nil` — the sentinel marks the end of the ring
a boolean flag is set by the last node visited
quiz.explanation: The termination test is x ≠ L.nil rather than x ≠ NIL: the walk chases next pointers around the ring and stops exactly when it arrives back at the sentinel.

intro: What is a pointer, really? This section answers by building objects without them: a linked list can live in three parallel arrays, with ordinary integers playing the role of addresses. Allocation and deallocation become a free list threaded through the unused cells — a two-line allocator that is the ancestor of every object pool.
objectives: Represent a linked list in the multiple-array and single-array forms, with integer indices as pointers
Implement ALLOCATE-OBJECT and FREE-OBJECT on the free list in $O(1)$
Explain the trade-offs between the two packed representations

concepts.statement: Represent a doubly linked list by three parallel arrays — `key`, `next`, `prev` — indexed by object number, plus a variable `L` holding the index of the first object. A 'pointer' to a node **is an integer index**; NIL is 0 (or any reserved non-index).
concepts.detail: Node $i$'s key is `key[i]`, its neighbors `next[i]` and `prev[i]`. Traversal, insertion and deletion run exactly as before with index arithmetic instead of pointer dereference — the structure is identical because the *shape* of a linked list lives in the pointer values, not in memory layout.

concepts.statement: Alternatively pack all objects into **one array**: object $i$'s $k$ fields occupy the consecutive cells $k \cdot i + 1, \ldots, k \cdot i + k$, and a pointer is the base index — field $f$ of object $i$ is found at the computed address $k \cdot i + f$.
concepts.detail: This is how real compilers lay out `struct` arrays — pointer arithmetic on a base plus a stride. The multiple-array version is more flexible (fields of different widths, easy to grow one field); the single-array version is more compact and matches hardware addressing.

concepts.statement: The unused cells are threaded into a **singly linked list** — the free list — using the `next` array itself. **`ALLOCATE-OBJECT()`**: if `free == NIL` report out of space; else $x = $ `free`; `free = next[x]`; return $x$. **`FREE-OBJECT(x)`**: `next[x] = free`; `free = x`. Both $O(1)$.
concepts.detail: The allocator is a stack discipline on free cells (LIFO), implemented in the objects' own storage: an unallocated node's `next` field is exactly where its free-list successor is recorded. No scanning, no heaps, no garbage — just relink.

concepts.statement: Besides supporting languages without pointer types, the array representation makes explicit what abstract pointers hide: **allocation policy**. The free list gives deterministic $O(1)$ allocate/free but cannot defragment or grow; garbage-collected heaps trade that control for safety and convenience.
concepts.detail: This is the machinery inside object pools, arena allocators and the classic technique for packing sparse structures into flat memory — e.g., symbol tables in early compilers. When CLRS later needs to store objects of bounded size it simply reuses this scheme.

concepts.statement: Unused cells form a singly linked free list threaded through their $next$ fields with head $free$: ALLOCATE-OBJECT pops the head in $O(1)$ and signals overflow when $free = \mathrm{NIL}$; FREE-OBJECT pushes the cell back in $O(1)$. Allocated and free cells partition the array.
concepts.detail: Invariant: every array slot is either reachable from the stored list(s) or from $free$, never both, never neither. Compaction is unnecessary because allocation reuses whatever the free list offers first.

examples.title: A list in three arrays, one allocation, one deletion
examples.problem: Arrays `key`, `next`, `prev` of length 8 hold the list $9 \to 16 \to 4 \to 25$ in cells 4, 1, 7, 5 (`L` = 4); the free list chains cells $2 \to 3 \to 6 \to 8$. Insert key 17 at the front, then delete key 4.

steps.label: Initial layout
steps.text: `key = ⟨·, 16, ·, 9, 25, ·, 4, ·⟩`; `next[4]=1, next[1]=7, next[7]=5, next[5]=NIL`; `prev[4]=NIL, prev[1]=4, prev[7]=1, prev[5]=7` — the list reads cells 4 → 1 → 7 → 5.

steps.label: ALLOCATE for 17
steps.text: `free = 2`, so the object goes to cell 2 and `free` advances to `next[2] = 3`. Write `key[2] = 17`; splice: `next[2] = 4`, `prev[4] = 2`, `L = 2` — the list is $17 \to 9 \to 16 \to 4 \to 25$.

steps.label: Delete key 4 (cell 7)
steps.text: Splice: `next[1] = 5`, `prev[5] = 1`. Then `FREE-OBJECT(7)`: `next[7] = 3` (the current free head), `free = 7` — cell 7 rejoins the free list in front of cell 3.

steps.label: Final state
steps.text: List $17 \to 9 \to 16 \to 25$ in cells 2 → 4 → 1 → 5; free list $7 \to 3 \to 6 \to 8$. Every operation: a constant number of array writes.

examples.result: Both operations are $O(1)$; nothing was scanned and no memory moved — the pointer *discipline* survived the loss of real pointers completely.

examples.title: Exhausting the free list
examples.problem: With array size $5$ and free list $1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4 \to 5$, allocate three objects, free the middle one, then allocate twice more.

steps.label: Allocate 3
steps.text: Pop $1,2,3$: $free = 4$. Stored list uses cells $1,2,3$; free list $4 \to 5$.

steps.label: Free cell 2
steps.text: Push $2$: $2.next = 4$, $free = 2$. Stored cells $1,3$; free $2 \to 4 \to 5$.

steps.label: Allocate 2
steps.text: Pop $2$ then $4$: $free = 5$. Stored cells $1,3,2,4$ in allocation order, free $5$.

steps.label: Overflow next
steps.text: One more allocation pops $5$ ($free = \mathrm{NIL}$); the following allocation signals overflow: $5$ cells hold at most $5$ objects.

examples.result: Free-list allocation is $O(1)$ per operation with no search; overflow is exactly $free = \mathrm{NIL}$, i.e. every slot allocated.

keyTakeaways: A linked list needs only parallel arrays plus integer indices — the multiple-array form (key/next/prev) and the packed single-array form (stride arithmetic) are equivalent in power.
The free list threads unused cells through the `next` array, giving $O(1)$ ALLOCATE-OBJECT and FREE-OBJECT — a stack allocator with zero auxiliary storage.
This representation exposes allocation policy explicitly: deterministic relink-based management, at the price of manual free-list discipline that garbage collectors would automate.

quiz.q: In the multiple-array representation of a doubly linked list, a 'pointer' to a node is:
options: a language-level reference to an object
an integer index into the parallel `key`/`next`/`prev` arrays — NIL for 'no object'
a memory address returned by the heap allocator
a pointer to a row of a two-dimensional array
quiz.explanation: Node i exists exactly at the index i across all three arrays; storing, comparing and dereferencing 'pointers' is ordinary integer arithmetic.

quiz.q: ALLOCATE-OBJECT runs in $O(1)$ because:
options: it scans the arrays for a cell with an empty key
the free cells are chained by the `next` array; it pops the free-list head and updates `free` in a couple of writes
a hash table maps keys to cells
allocation is amortized over all insertions
quiz.explanation: The free list is threaded through the very cells it manages, so allocating is: x = free; free = next[x]; return x — three operations, no search.

quiz.q: In the single-array packed representation with $k$ fields per object stored consecutively from index 1, field $f$ of object $i$ lives at:
options: $k \cdot i + f$ — computed by index arithmetic
a location recorded in a separate index array
an arbitrary cell chosen by the free list
quiz.explanation: Objects occupy fixed strides: object i's fields are cells k·i+1 … k·i+k, so any field is base-plus-offset arithmetic — exactly how struct arrays are addressed in real machines.

intro: A binary tree fits in three pointers per node, but what if a node may have any number of children? Storing a list of children per parent works, but CLRS's answer is leaner: give every node a left-child pointer and a right-sibling pointer, and a whole rooted forest — however wide — fits in $O(n)$ fields with $O(1)$ parent, first-child and next-sibling access.
objectives: Represent binary trees with p, left and right pointer fields
Represent arbitrary rooted trees with the left-child, right-sibling scheme
Analyze the costs of traversals and the trade-offs among representations

concepts.statement: Each node of a **binary tree** stores three fields: `p` (parent), `left` (left child) and `right` (right child) — the root's `p` and missing children are NIL. $O(1)$ parent, left-child and right-child access; $3n$ fields total.
concepts.detail: When the tree is complete (like a heap, Chapter 6) even these pointers vanish: the implicit array layout computes children at $2i$ and $2i+1$. The explicit pointer representation is for arbitrary shapes — and for Chapter 12's search trees.

concepts.statement: For a rooted tree with **unbounded branching**, each node stores: `p` (parent), `left-child` (its leftmost child, NIL if a leaf) and `right-sibling` (the next child of the same parent, NIL if last). A parent points at its **first** child only; the remaining children form a singly linked list through sibling pointers.
concepts.detail: Any rooted tree — however many children per node — fits in exactly three fields per node: $O(n)$ space with no dependence on the branching factor. To enumerate all children of node $u$: follow `left-child` once, then `right-sibling` until NIL.

concepts.statement: Enumerating all $k$ children of a node costs $O(k)$ — one hop per child — and finding whether $v$ is a child of $u$ likewise scans the chain. Parent queries remain $O(1)$, and converting a general tree to this form is a single pass.
concepts.detail: Contrast with the alternative — each node storing a variable-length array of children: same asymptotic total space ($O(n)$ pointers overall), $O(1)$ random access to the $j$th child, but heavier per-node objects and no fixed record size. The sibling chain trades indexed access for uniform, pointer-sized records.

concepts.statement: For an **ordered** rooted tree with at most two children per node, the left-child, right-sibling representation coincides with the ordinary binary-tree layout: the first child becomes the left pointer, the second child (a sibling of the first) becomes the right pointer.
concepts.detail: This is the classic 'rotation' that maps any forest onto a binary tree — the engine of the Knuth transform and of the correspondence between general trees and binary trees. Every algorithm for binary trees thereby inherits a meaning for arbitrary trees.

concepts.statement: A free tree is an acyclic connected undirected graph; rooting it at any vertex $r$ orients every edge away from $r$ and defines parent, child, ancestor and descendant. The left-child, right-sibling scheme stores any rooted forest, however wide, in two pointers per node.
concepts.detail: Theorem B.5 in the appendix: $|E| = |V|-1$ characterizes trees, so rooting never changes the edge count, only the vocabulary. Binary trees are the special case where right-sibling chains have length at most $1$.

figures.caption: One rooted tree, two representations. (a) The tree with root A; A has children B, C, D; B has children E, F; D has child G. (b) The same tree in left-child, right-sibling form: A's `left-child` points at B only — its **first** child — and B → C → D is a sibling chain. Likewise B's left-child is E, with F reached as E's right-sibling, and D's left-child is G. Each node also keeps a parent pointer (dashed, shown for a few nodes). Seven nodes cost exactly 21 fields regardless of how wide the tree grows.

examples.title: The seven-node tree as a field table
examples.problem: Write the left-child, right-sibling tables for the figure's tree (A root; A's children B, C, D; B's children E, F; D's child G) and enumerate A's children.

steps.label: The table
steps.text: A: $p = \Lambda$, left-child $= B$, right-sibling $= \Lambda$. B: $p = A$, left-child $= E$, right-sibling $= C$. C: $p = A$, left-child $= \Lambda$, right-sibling $= D$. D: $p = A$, left-child $= G$, right-sibling $= \Lambda$. E: $p = B$, left-child $= \Lambda$, right-sibling $= F$. F: $p = B$, left-child $= \Lambda$, right-sibling $= \Lambda$. G: $p = D$, left-child $= \Lambda$, right-sibling $= \Lambda$.

steps.label: Enumerate A's children
steps.text: $c = A.\text{left-child} = B$ (yield B); $c = c.\text{right-sibling} = C$ (yield C); $c = c.\text{right-sibling} = D$ (yield D); $c = c.\text{right-sibling} = \Lambda$ — stop. Three hops for three children.

steps.label: Space audit
steps.text: Seven nodes × 3 fields = 21 fields, of which 12 hold non-NIL pointers (6 parent, 3 left-child, 3 sibling) — and the count would stay at 21 fields even if A had a thousand children.

examples.result: Children of any node are enumerable in $O(k)$ for $k$ children; parents are $O(1)$; total space is exactly $3n$ fields — independent of the tree's width.

examples.title: Walking sibling chains
examples.problem: Node $a$ has children $b,c,d,e$ in left-child, right-sibling form. Count the steps to reach $e$ from $a$ and to list all children.

steps.label: First child
steps.text: $a.left = b$: $O(1)$ to the first child.

steps.label: Chain
steps.text: $b.right = c$, $c.right = d$, $d.right = e$, $e.right = \mathrm{NIL}$: reaching $e$ costs $4$ right steps, i.e. $O(\mathrm{degree})$.

steps.label: List all
steps.text: Enumerating $k$ children costs $\Theta(k)$ right steps; a binary-tree coincidence would cost $\Theta(1)$ per child via indexed children.

steps.label: Tradeoff
steps.text: Space $O(n)$ regardless of width versus $O(\mathrm{degree})$ access per child: the scheme buys unbounded branching with two fields at the price of linear child scans.

examples.result: First child $O(1)$, $k$th child $O(k)$: sibling chains trade child-access time for fixed $O(1)$ fields per node.

keyTakeaways: Binary trees need only `p`, `left`, `right` per node; complete trees (heaps) even elide the pointers into array arithmetic.
The left-child, right-sibling scheme represents arbitrary rooted trees in $3n$ fields: a parent points at its first child, and the children of each node form a sibling chain.
Sibling chains make child enumeration $O(k)$ for $k$ children — and, for trees with at most two children, the scheme coincides exactly with the standard binary-tree representation.

quiz.q: In the left-child, right-sibling representation, all children of a node are found by:
options: following `left-child` once, then `right-sibling` repeatedly until NIL
scanning the whole array of nodes
quiz.explanation: The parent points only at its leftmost child; each subsequent child is the previous one's right-sibling, so enumeration is one left-child hop then k − 1 sibling hops.

quiz.q: Compared with giving each node a variable-length list of children, the left-child, right-sibling representation uses:
options: $O(n \cdot d)$ fields, where $d$ is the maximum number of children
exactly three fields per node — $O(n)$ total, independent of branching
a fixed number of fields per tree, not per node
quiz.explanation: Every node contributes one parent, one left-child and one right-sibling field; the wide fan-out is absorbed into chains rather than stored per parent.

quiz.q: Enumerating all $k$ children of one node in this representation costs:
quiz.explanation: The children live in a singly linked sibling chain, so visiting them costs one pointer hop each — the standard price of chained versus indexed access.

quiz.q: For an ordered tree with at most two children per node, the left-child, right-sibling scheme:
options: cannot represent it, since binary trees need left/right child pointers
coincides with the usual binary-tree layout — first child = left pointer, second child = right-sibling of the first
requires extra parent pointers to disambiguate
stores the two children in a hash table keyed by position
quiz.explanation: A node's second child is exactly the first child's right-sibling, so the three-field layout maps onto p/left/right — the correspondence that turns general-tree algorithms into binary-tree ones.

intro: A dictionary supports INSERT, SEARCH and DELETE, and the fastest possible dictionary is an array indexed directly by key. When the universe of keys is small this is exactly what CLRS does: one array slot per possible key, each operation touching exactly one slot. The section also explains why this luxury usually fails — and what we will trade away in the rest of the chapter to get the space cost down.
objectives: Define a direct-address table and argue that each dictionary operation costs $\Theta(1)$
Explain the pointer-to-satellite-data design and why deletion stays cheap
Identify exactly when direct addressing becomes impractical

concepts.statement: Let the universe of keys be $U = \{0, 1, \ldots, m-1\}$. A **direct-address table** is an array $T[0 \ldots m-1]$ with **one slot for every possible key**: slot $k$ represents key $k$, and each slot holds either a pointer to the element with key $k$ or **NIL** when no element with that key is stored.
concepts.detail: The table is a perfect simulation of the key space — searching is array indexing, so the hash function is the identity map. Space is $\Theta(|U|)$.

concepts.statement: With satellite data stored in objects pointed to by the slots: **DIRECT-ADDRESS-SEARCH**$(T, k)$ returns $T[k]$; **DIRECT-ADDRESS-INSERT**$(T, x)$ sets $T[x.key] = x$; **DIRECT-ADDRESS-DELETE**$(T, x)$ sets $T[x.key] =$ NIL. Each takes $\Theta(1)$ time.
concepts.detail: Compare a stack or queue, where only privileged positions are accessible — here every key gives immediate access.

concepts.statement: Each slot stores a **pointer to the element**, and the element itself carries its key in the field $x.key$. Deleting then costs $\Theta(1)$: given a pointer to $x$ we read $x.key$ and NIL out the slot, with no searching and no moving of data.
concepts.detail: If objects were stored directly in the slots, deletion would need to know the slot index — the key field inside the object serves exactly that purpose.

concepts.statement: Direct addressing needs $\Theta(|U|)$ space even when the number of keys actually stored, $n$, is tiny. It is hopeless when the universe is astronomical — all 64-bit integers, all character strings — or when $n \ll |U|$ so that almost every slot is wasted.
concepts.detail: A hash table shrinks the array to $m \approx n$ slots and maps keys through a hash function $h : U \to \{0, \ldots, m-1\}$; the price, studied next, is **collisions**.

concepts.statement: Let $|U|$ be the universe of possible keys and $m$ the table slots. Direct addressing sets $m = |U|$: $\Theta(|U|)$ space for $\Theta(1)$ operations. Hashing (Sections 11.2-11.4) keeps $m = \Theta(n)$ for the $n$ keys actually stored, trading worst-case time for space.
concepts.detail: When $|U|$ is $2^{64}$ (all 64-bit integers) direct addressing is impossible; when $|U|$ is employee IDs below $10^4$ it is ideal. The rest of the chapter is the space-time negotiation between these poles.

figures.caption: A direct-address table with $m = |U| = 9$ slots. Slot $k$ either points to the record for key $k$ or is empty — SEARCH, INSERT and DELETE each touch exactly one slot in $\Theta(1)$, but the array itself costs $\Theta(m)$ space regardless of how few keys are stored.

examples.title: A tiny payroll keyed by employee id
examples.problem: Employee ids are the integers 0 through 99 and only keys 2, 5 and 7 are in use. Give the table, the three operations, and the space bill.

steps.label: Step 1: Size the table
steps.text: The universe has $m = 100$ keys, so allocate $T[0 \ldots 99]$ — one slot per id, 100 slots regardless of how many employees exist.

steps.label: Step 2: Run the operations
steps.text: Insert Alice with id 2: set $T[2] \to$ Alice. Search id 5: read $T[5]$ directly — one array access, no comparisons. Delete id 7: given the object, set $T[7] =$ NIL.

steps.label: Step 3: Count the cost
steps.text: Each operation is a single array access: $\Theta(1)$. The array itself is $\Theta(100)$ space even though only 3 keys are live — a 97% waste rate.

steps.label: Step 4: Diagnose
steps.text: Now suppose ids become 9-digit social-security numbers: $|U| = 10^9$ slots for a handful of employees is absurd — this is exactly the failure mode that forces hashing.

examples.result: Direct addressing gives perfect $\Theta(1)$ operations whenever $|U|$ is small, but its space is $\Theta(|U|)$, not $\Theta(n)$.

examples.title: When the universe is huge
examples.problem: Keys are 9-digit Social Security numbers ($|U| = 10^9$) but only $n = 1000$ are stored. Compare direct addressing with chaining.

steps.label: Direct cost
steps.text: Table of $10^9$ slots: gigabytes of pointers for $1000$ keys, $\Theta(|U|) = \Theta(10^9)$ space, $\Theta(1)$ time.

steps.label: Chaining cost
steps.text: Table of $m = 1000$ slots with chains: $\Theta(n+m) = \Theta(2000)$ space, expected $\Theta(1+\alpha) = \Theta(2)$ search with $\alpha = 1$.

steps.label: Verdict
steps.text: Direct addressing wastes $10^6\times$ the space for identical $O(1)$ time: hashing wins whenever $|U| \gg n$.

steps.label: When direct wins
steps.text: If instead $|U| = 2000$ and $n = 1000$, direct addressing costs $2000$ slots versus $2000$ for chaining with no hash computation: direct wins.

examples.result: Direct addressing is $\Theta(|U|)$ space; hashing is $\Theta(n)$ space: choose by the ratio $|U|/n$.

keyTakeaways: A direct-address table dedicates one array slot to every possible key: SEARCH, INSERT and DELETE are all $\Theta(1)$ by array indexing.
Slots hold pointers to elements, and each element stores its own key so that deletion from an object pointer stays $\Theta(1)$.
The scheme needs $\Theta(|U|)$ space — untenable for large or sparsely used universes; hash tables cut space to $\Theta(m)$ with $m \approx n$ at the price of collisions.

quiz.q: A direct-address table uses an array T[0 … m−1]. What must m equal?
options: The number of keys actually stored, n
The size of the key universe, m = |U|
The first prime larger than n
quiz.explanation: One slot per possible key: m = |U|. The number n of stored keys is irrelevant to the array size — that is both the scheme's simplicity and its weakness.

quiz.q: Why does each element x stored in a direct-address table carry its own key in x.key?
options: So SEARCH can verify the key was found
So DELETE can NIL the right slot when handed only a pointer to x
To keep the keys sorted for inorder traversal
To support doubling the table when it gets full
quiz.explanation: Deletion receives a pointer to x; without x.key it would not know which slot to empty. With it, T[x.key] = NIL is O(1).

quiz.q: Which scenario makes direct addressing the WRONG choice?
options: Universe U = {0, …, 999} with 900 keys in use
Universe U = {0, …, 999} with 10 keys in use
Keys are exactly the ASCII codes 0–127
A fixed set of 32 interrupt vectors
quiz.explanation: 10 keys out of 1000 slots wastes 99% of the space — n ≪ |U|. Direct addressing is attractive only when the universe is small and densely used.

quiz.q: In a direct-address table, what is the worst-case cost of an unsuccessful search?
options: Θ(1) — one array read returns NIL
quiz.explanation: Search reads exactly one slot T[k]; if it is NIL the key is absent. Success or failure never costs more than one array access.

intro: Shrinking the array from |U| slots to m slots means many keys share a slot — a collision. Chaining resolves collisions by letting each slot head a linked list of all the elements that hash to it. The section's payoff is a clean average-case analysis: under a mild uniformity assumption, a search costs $\Theta(1 + \alpha)$ where $\alpha = n/m$ is the load factor.
objectives: Describe collision resolution by chaining and implement the three dictionary operations on it
Define the load factor α and its role in the average-case analysis
State and interpret the Θ(1 + α) expected-search bound under simple uniform hashing

concepts.statement: A **hash table** uses $m$ slots indexed $0 \ldots m-1$ and a **hash function** $h : U \to \{0, \ldots, m-1\}$. With **chaining** (also called separate chaining), slot $j$ heads a linked list containing every element whose key hashes to $j$; we say keys with $h(k) = h(k')$ for $k \ne k'$ **collide**.
concepts.detail: CLRS uses doubly linked lists so that deletion, given a pointer to the element, is $\Theta(1)$ without searching the chain.

concepts.statement: For a hash table with $n$ stored elements and $m$ slots, the **load factor** is $\alpha = n/m$ — the average number of elements per chain. With chaining, $\alpha$ may exceed 1 (chains just get longer); under uniform hashing each chain has expected length exactly $\alpha$.
concepts.detail: The load factor, not n or m alone, is what governs average performance: keeping $n = O(m)$ keeps $\alpha = O(1)$.

concepts.statement: **INSERT** splices the new element at the **head** of its chain — $O(1)$ without even comparing keys. **SEARCH** hashes the key, then scans one chain. **DELETE**, given a pointer, unlinks from a doubly linked list in $O(1)$. Worst case (all keys collide) search degenerates to $\Theta(n)$.
concepts.detail: Inserting at the head is what makes insertion O(1): no traversal of the chain is needed to find the splice point.

concepts.statement: The analysis assumes **simple uniform hashing**: each key is equally likely to hash to any of the $m$ slots, **independently** of where every other key hashes. It is an idealization — no practical hash function achieves it — but it is the yardstick against which real hash functions are judged.
concepts.detail: The assumption is about the distribution of keys over slots, not about the keys' own values.

concepts.statement: Under simple uniform hashing, an **unsuccessful** search examines an expected $\alpha$ elements, and a **successful** search an expected $1 + \frac{\alpha}{2} - \frac{\alpha}{2n}$ elements; both are $\Theta(1 + \alpha)$. Thus with $n = O(m)$, average search is $O(1)$ — independent of the number of keys stored.
concepts.detail: For a successful search the target's chain holds it ahead of the keys inserted after it, on average halfway down — hence the α/2 instead of α.

figures.caption: Chaining with $h(k) = k \bmod 9$: inserting $5, 28, 19, 15, 20, 33, 12, 17, 10$ gives $n = m = 9$, so $\alpha = 1$ and the average chain holds one key — but keys $10, 19, 28$ all satisfy $k \equiv 1 \pmod 9$ and pile into slot 1. INSERT splices at the head; SEARCH walks a single chain.

examples.title: Searching, inserting and measuring the table of Figure 11.3
examples.problem: With $m = 9$, $h(k) = k \bmod 9$, and the nine keys $5, 28, 19, 15, 20, 33, 12, 17, 10$ inserted in that order, trace a successful search for 19, an unsuccessful search for 71, and the insertion of 100.

steps.label: Step 1: The chains
steps.text: Hashing each key: $5 \to 5$, $28 \to 1$, $19 \to 1$, $15 \to 6$, $20 \to 2$, $33 \to 6$, $12 \to 3$, $17 \to 8$, $10 \to 1$. Slot 1 holds $\{10, 19, 28\}$ and slot 6 holds $\{33, 15\}$; the other five occupied slots hold one key each.

steps.label: Step 2: Successful search for 19
steps.text: $h(19) = 19 - 2 \cdot 9 = 1$, so scan slot 1's list: compare against the head 10 (miss), then 19 (hit) — **2 elements examined**.

steps.label: Step 3: Unsuccessful search for 71
steps.text: $h(71) = 71 - 7 \cdot 9 = 8$, so scan slot 8's list: one element, 17, which is not 71 — 1 element examined and the search fails.

steps.label: Step 4: Insert 100 and re-measure
steps.text: $h(100) = 100 - 11 \cdot 9 = 1$, so 100 becomes the new head of slot 1's list. Now $n = 10$ and $\alpha = 10/9 \approx 1.11$: the theory predicts about 1.11 examined elements for a future unsuccessful search.

examples.result: Chaining keeps every operation localized to one list; with α held near 1 the average search inspects only a couple of elements.

examples.title: Load factor above one
examples.problem: Insert $n = 12$ keys into $m = 5$ slots with chaining under simple uniform hashing. What is the expected search cost?

steps.label: Load
steps.text: $\alpha = n/m = 12/5 = 2.4$: average chain length $2.4$.

steps.label: Hit
steps.text: Successful search: $\Theta(1+\alpha) = \Theta(3.4)$ expected touches: one hash plus half the chain on average plus the target.

steps.label: Miss
steps.text: Unsuccessful search: $\Theta(\alpha) = \Theta(2.4)$: must scan the whole hashed chain to conclude absence.

steps.label: Fix
steps.text: Rehash to $m = 12$ ($\alpha = 1$): expected cost drops to $\Theta(2)$. Chaining degrades gracefully ($\Theta(1+\alpha)$) rather than failing when $\alpha > 1$.

examples.result: Expected $\approx 3.4$ touches at $\alpha = 2.4$; chaining stays linear in $\alpha$, so doubling the table halves the excess.

keyTakeaways: Chaining puts every element with $h(k) = j$ into a linked list headed at slot $j$; insertion at the head is $O(1)$ and deletion is $O(1)$ given a pointer.
Under simple uniform hashing the expected search cost is $\Theta(1 + \alpha)$ with $\alpha = n/m$ — keeping $n = O(m)$ buys average $O(1)$ regardless of how many keys are stored.
The worst case is still $\Theta(n)$: if every key hashes to one slot, the table degenerates into a single linked list.

quiz.q: A hash table with chaining has n = 1000 keys in m = 100 slots. Assuming simple uniform hashing, roughly how many elements does an unsuccessful search examine?
options: 1000, because every chain must be checked
quiz.explanation: The search hashes once, then scans the one chain for that slot, whose expected length is α = 1000/100 = 10. Expected cost is Θ(1 + α) ≈ 10.

quiz.q: Why does CHAINED-HASH-INSERT splice the new element at the head of its chain?
options: To keep each chain sorted by key
So insertion runs in O(1) without scanning the chain at all
Because the tail pointer is unavailable
quiz.explanation: Head insertion needs only the slot pointer — no traversal, no comparisons. Sorting chains by key would speed searches slightly but would make insertion Θ(α).

quiz.q: What exactly does the simple uniform hashing assumption state?
options: Every slot receives the same number of keys
Each key hashes to any of the m slots with probability 1/m, independently of all other keys
The hash function is chosen randomly at each lookup
quiz.explanation: It is an independence-and-uniformity assumption about where keys land — the idealization that makes E[chain length] = α exact and that real hash functions only approximate.

quiz.q: Under simple uniform hashing with n = 2m (α = 2), the expected number of elements examined in a successful search is closest to:
quiz.explanation: The successful-search expectation is 1 + α/2 − α/(2n) = 1 + 1 − 1/n ≈ 2: on average the target sits halfway down its chain of α ≈ 2 elements.

quiz.q: A hash table with chaining has $m = 10$ slots holding $n = 30$ keys under simple uniform hashing. The average number of keys examined in an unsuccessful search is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $m = 10$, $n = 30$, chaining, simple uniform hashing. Step 2 — Governing quantity: load factor $\alpha = \frac{n}{m}$, and an unsuccessful search scans the whole hashed chain, expected length $\alpha$. Step 3 — Arithmetic: $\alpha = \frac{30}{10} = 3$, so about $3$ keys are examined. Step 4 — Sanity check: $\Theta(1 + \alpha)$ stays constant while $\alpha$ is bounded, doubling the table would halve the cost, and the bound needs no assumption beyond uniformity. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: $1$ suits an empty table, $10$ quotes the slot count, and $30$ scans every key as in a list. Step 6 — Conclude: about $3$ keys examined.

intro: The Θ(1 + α) analysis presumed keys scatter uniformly — this section is about actually achieving that. CLRS first insists on the interpretation of keys as natural numbers, then gives two workhorse methods (division and multiplication), and finally universal hashing: choose the hash function at random from a family, so that no adversary can engineer collisions against you.
objectives: Interpret arbitrary keys as natural numbers and apply the division and multiplication methods by hand
Explain why the modulus in the division method should be prime and far from a power of 2
Define a universal family of hash functions and explain what randomness buys against adversarial inputs

concepts.statement: Every hash-function discussion in CLRS assumes keys are **natural numbers**: any data — a string, a record, an IP address — is first interpreted as an integer, typically by radix conversion. E.g. the string “pt” in ASCII is $112 \cdot 128 + 116 = 14452$ when read base 128.
concepts.detail: The interpretation only has to be injective; any consistent encoding works.

concepts.statement: $h(k) = k \bmod m$. **Choose $m$ to be a prime not too close to a power of 2.** If $m = 2^r$ only the low $r$ bits of the key survive, so key patterns that repeat in the low bits collide catastrophically.
concepts.detail: The method is one division — fast on most hardware — but the quality depends entirely on the modulus, since h(k) is just k's remainder.

concepts.statement: $h(k) = \lfloor m \,(kA \bmod 1) \rfloor$ where $0 < A < 1$ and $kA \bmod 1$ is the fractional part of $kA$. The value of $m$ is **not critical** (powers of 2 work well — extract the high bits of $k \cdot A \cdot 2^w$), and Knuth recommends $A \approx (\sqrt{5} - 1)/2 \approx 0.618$.
concepts.detail: The golden-ratio multiplier spreads consecutive keys: the slot index is essentially the leading bits of the fractional part of kA.

concepts.statement: A family $\mathcal{H}$ of hash functions $U \to \{0, \ldots, m-1\}$ is **universal** if for every pair of distinct keys $k \ne l$, $\Pr_{h \in \mathcal{H}}[h(k) = h(l)] \le 1/m$. At run time we **choose $h$ randomly from the family once**, then use it for all operations.
concepts.detail: Motivation: for any fixed deterministic h there is a bad key set that collides wildly; a random choice means the adversary cannot know which h to aim at, and any n keys get expected chain behavior α.

concepts.statement: Pick a prime $p$ with $p > |U|$ and define $h_{a,b}(k) = ((ak + b) \bmod p) \bmod m$ with $a \in \{1, \ldots, p-1\}$, $b \in \{0, \ldots, p-1\}$. The family $\mathcal{H}_{p,m} = \{h_{a,b}\}$ of $p(p-1)$ functions is **universal**.
concepts.detail:
Proof idea: for fixed $k 
e l$, the values $r = (ak+b)  mod p$ and $s = (al+b)  mod p$ are distinct (as $a 
ot\equiv 0$), and each pair $r 
e s$ arises from exactly one choice of $(a,b)$; at most a $1/m$ fraction of the distinct pairs satisfies $r \equiv s \pmod m$.

examples.title: Division method: why m = 2^r is a trap
examples.problem: Hash the keys $4, 16, 28, 40, 52$ with the division method using $m = 12$ and then $m = 13$. Compare the collision behavior.

steps.label: Step 1: Try m = 12
steps.text: Every key here is $\equiv 4 \pmod{12}$: $4 \bmod 12 = 4$, $16 \bmod 12 = 4$, $28 \bmod 12 = 4$, $40 \bmod 12 = 4$, $52 \bmod 12 = 4$. All five keys land in slot 4 — one chain of length 5.

steps.label: Step 2: Diagnose
steps.text: The keys are multiples of 4 spaced 12 apart; because 12 shares the factor 4 with the key pattern, the residues collide. With $m = 2^r$ the same thing happens whenever keys differ only in bits above the low r.

steps.label: Step 3: Switch to the prime m = 13
steps.text: $4 \bmod 13 = 4$, $16 \bmod 13 = 3$, $28 \bmod 13 = 2$, $40 \bmod 13 = 1$, $52 \bmod 13 = 0$ — five distinct slots, no collisions at all.

steps.label: Step 4: The rule
steps.text: A prime modulus shares no structure with typical key patterns (powers of 2, multiples of common bases), which is exactly why CLRS demands prime $m$ not close to a power of 2.

examples.result: m = 12 piles all five keys into one chain; m = 13 spreads them perfectly. The modulus is the whole game in the division method.

examples.title: Multiplication method with the golden ratio
examples.problem: Using $A = 0.6180339\ldots$ (so that $A = (\sqrt{5}-1)/2$) and $m = 8$, hash the consecutive keys $k = 61, 62, 63$.

steps.label: Step 1: k = 61
steps.text: $61 \times 0.6180339 = 37.7000\ldots$, so $kA \bmod 1 = 0.7000\ldots$ and $h(61) = \lfloor 8 \times 0.7000 \rfloor = \lfloor 5.60 \rfloor = 5$.

steps.label: Step 2: k = 62
steps.text: $62 \times 0.6180339 = 38.3181\ldots$, fractional part $0.3181\ldots$, and $h(62) = \lfloor 8 \times 0.3181 \rfloor = \lfloor 2.54 \rfloor = 2$.

steps.label: Step 3: k = 63
steps.text: $63 \times 0.6180339 = 38.9361\ldots$, fractional part $0.9361\ldots$, and $h(63) = \lfloor 8 \times 0.9361 \rfloor = \lfloor 7.49 \rfloor = 7$.

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret
steps.text: Three keys that differ by 1 map to slots 5, 2 and 7 — nowhere near each other. The fractional parts of multiples of the golden ratio are famously well spread, which is precisely the property Knuth exploited.

examples.result: Consecutive keys scatter across the table — and since only the fractional part matters, m can be any convenient value, including a power of 2.

keyTakeaways: Interpret every key as a natural number first; then the division method $h(k) = k \bmod m$ wants $m$ prime and away from powers of 2, while the multiplication method $h(k) = \lfloor m(kA \bmod 1)\rfloor$ with $A \approx 0.618$ is insensitive to $m$.
Universal hashing randomizes the function itself: drawing $h_{a,b}(k) = ((ak+b) \bmod p) \bmod m$ from the CLRS class guarantees $\Pr[h(k) = h(l)] \le 1/m$ for every distinct pair.
Randomizing the hash function converts adversarial inputs into average-case inputs — the same defensive move as randomizing quicksort's pivot.

quiz.q: In the division method h(k) = k mod m, why is m = 2^r a poor choice?
options: Modulo a power of 2 is too slow to compute
h(k) then depends only on the low r bits of k, so keys sharing those bits collide
Powers of 2 make the load factor exceed 1
It forces the table to have exactly r slots
quiz.explanation: k mod 2^r discards everything but the low r bits. Real keys (addresses, multiples of common bases) often repeat low-bit patterns, which then pile into a few slots.

quiz.q: With A = 0.618 and m = 8, the multiplication method gives h(100) = ⌊8 · frac(61.8)⌋ = ?
quiz.explanation: 100 × 0.618 = 61.8; the fractional part is 0.8, and 8 × 0.8 = 6.4, whose floor is 6.

quiz.q: A family H of hash functions is universal precisely when:
options: Every h in H distributes every key set uniformly
For all k ≠ l, the fraction of functions h in H with h(k) = h(l) is at most 1/m
Each h in H is a bijection from U to the m slots
H contains at least m distinct functions
quiz.explanation: Universality is a pairwise collision guarantee over the random choice of h: any two fixed distinct keys collide with probability at most 1/m — one function chosen from the family once does the whole job.

quiz.q: In the CLRS universal family h_ab(k) = ((ak + b) mod p) mod m, what is required of the parameters?
options: p any integer larger than m
p a prime larger than |U|, with a ≠ 0 mod p and b arbitrary
p a prime smaller than m so the table fits
quiz.explanation: p > |U| keeps distinct keys distinct mod p; a ≠ 0 (mod p) makes the inner map a bijection; b shifts freely. These three facts drive the ≤ 1/m collision probability.

intro: Open addressing abolishes the chains: all elements live in the table itself, so a slot holds a key, not a pointer. Searching for a key now means following a computed probe sequence through the slots until the key or an empty slot turns up. The design question is what those probe sequences look like — and the section ends with the one real weakness: deletion.
objectives: Define open addressing, the probe-sequence requirement, and the α ≤ 1 constraint
Compare linear probing, quadratic probing and double hashing and their clustering pathologies
Apply the expected-probe bounds 1/(1 − α) and (1/α) ln(1/(1 − α)) and explain the deletion problem

concepts.statement: In **open addressing** every element is stored **in a slot of the table itself** — no pointers, no lists — so the table holds at most $m$ elements and the load factor satisfies $\alpha = n/m \le 1$. The hash function is extended to a **probe sequence** $h : U \times \{0, \ldots, m-1\} \to \{0, \ldots, m-1\}$: for key $k$ the algorithm tries $h(k, 0), h(k, 1), h(k, 2), \ldots$ in order.
concepts.detail: HASH-INSERT probes until finding an empty slot and deposits the key there; HASH-SEARCH probes until finding the key or an empty slot; a full m-slot search that never hits an empty slot means the table is full.

concepts.term: Uniform hashing assumption and probe bounds
concepts.statement: Assume **uniform hashing**: each key's probe sequence is equally likely to be any of the $m!$ permutations of the slots. Then with load factor $\alpha < 1$, an **unsuccessful** search takes at most $\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$ expected probes, and a **successful** search at most $\frac{1}{\alpha}\ln\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$.
concepts.detail: Numbers to know: α = 0.5 → 2 and 1.39 probes; α = 0.75 → 4 and 1.85; α = 0.9 → 10 and 2.56. The lesson: keep α well below 1 — doubling the table before α hits a threshold (say 0.75) keeps searches at a handful of probes.

concepts.statement: $h(k, i) = (h'(k) + i) \bmod m$. Trivially fast, but it suffers **primary clustering**: every key with the same initial hash walks the same row of slots, so runs of occupied slots merge into long clusters that every new insertion must walk through.
concepts.detail: Clusters feed on themselves — the longer a run, the more likely the next insertion extends it — which is why linear probing's observed probe counts exceed the uniform-hashing prediction.

concepts.statement: $h(k, i) = (h'(k) + c_1 i + c_2 i^2) \bmod m$. The quadratic stride prevents the long linear runs — but **two keys with the same $h'$ follow the same probe sequence**, the milder defect called **secondary clustering**. The constants must be chosen so the first $m$ probes are distinct.
concepts.detail: It also cannot be relied on to find an empty slot unless the constants and m are chosen so that a full permutation of slots is probed.

concepts.statement: $h(k, i) = (h_1(k) + i \cdot h_2(k)) \bmod m$. With $\Theta(m^2)$ distinct probe pairs $(h_1, h_2)$ this scheme produces $\Theta(m^2)$ different probe sequences — the closest practical approach to uniform hashing. **$h_2(k)$ must be relatively prime to $m$**: for $m = 2^r$ make $h_2$ return odd values; for prime $m$ take $h_2 \in \{1, \ldots, m-1\}$.
concepts.detail: If gcd(h₂(k), m) = d > 1 the probe sequence revisits only m/d slots and can miss empty slots entirely.

figures.caption: Inserting $k = 74$ into a 13-slot table with slots $\{0, 1, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12\}$ occupied ($\alpha = 7/13$). Double hashing with $h_1(k) = k \bmod 13 = 9$ and $h_2(k) = 1 + (k \bmod 11) = 9$ probes $9, 5, 1, 10, 6$ — five probes that leap across the table and land in slot 6. Linear probing with the same $h_1 = 9$ must thread through the wrap-around cluster $9, 10, 11, 12, 0, 1$ before finding slot 2 — seven probes.

examples.title: A deletion that silently breaks the table
examples.problem: In a 13-slot open-addressed table with linear probing, $h'(k) = k \bmod 13$: key 61 was inserted at slot 9 and key 23 ($h' = 10$) at slot 10. Key 9 ($h' = 9$) probed 9, 10, 11 and was stored at slot 11. What goes wrong if we delete 61 by emptying slot 9?

steps.label: Step 1: The state before deletion
steps.text: Slot 9 holds 61, slot 10 holds 23, slot 11 holds 9. Note that key 9 is **not** in its home slot 9 — its probe went past two occupied slots.

steps.label: Step 2: Empty slot 9 naively
steps.text: Setting slot 9 to “empty” removes 61 correctly, but the table now claims slots 9, 10, 11 are: empty, occupied, occupied.

steps.label: Step 3: Search for key 9
steps.text: HASH-SEARCH(9) probes slot 9, finds it **empty**, and concludes the key is absent — yet key 9 sits in slot 11. The empty slot terminated a probe sequence that should have continued.

steps.label: Step 4: The standard repair
steps.text: Deletion must write a **DELETED** tombstone instead of “empty”: searches treat it as occupied and keep probing, while insertions may reuse it. Because tombstones accumulate and push the effective load factor up, a periodically rebuilt table is the standard long-term answer.

examples.result: A NIL-ed slot amputates every probe sequence that passes through it — deletion in open addressing demands tombstones (or rehashing), never simple clearing.

examples.title: Linear probing cluster of three
examples.problem: Table $m = 7$, $h(k) = k \bmod 7$, linear probing. Insert $14, 21, 28$ then search $28$.

steps.label: Insert 14
steps.text: $14 \bmod 7 = 0$: slot $0$ free, store there.

steps.label: Insert 21
steps.text: $21 \bmod 7 = 0$ occupied, probe $1$: free, store at $1$. Cluster $0-1$ forms.

steps.label: Insert 28
steps.text: $28 \bmod 7 = 0$, probe $1$ occupied, probe $2$: free, store at $2$. Cluster $0-2$ length $3$.

steps.label: Search 28
steps.text: Probe $0,1,2$: $3$ probes. Next key hashing to $0-2$ will extend the cluster: primary clustering feeds on itself, the textbook pathology of linear probing.

examples.result: Three keys, one cluster of length $3$, search cost $3$ probes; double hashing would have scattered them with independent second hashes.

keyTakeaways: Open addressing stores keys in the table itself, probing $h(k, 0), h(k, 1), \ldots$ — each key's sequence must be a permutation of the slots, and $\alpha \le 1$.
Expected probes: $\le 1/(1-\alpha)$ unsuccessful, $\le (1/\alpha)\ln(1/(1-\alpha))$ successful — so keep the load factor modest; at $\alpha = 0.9$ an unsuccessful search already averages 10 probes.
Linear probing clusters, quadratic probing clusters mildly, double hashing (with $\gcd(h_2, m) = 1$) approaches uniform hashing; deletion requires tombstones.

quiz.q: An open-addressed table is filled to α = 0.75. Under uniform hashing, the expected number of probes for an unsuccessful search is:
quiz.explanation: Unsuccessful search: 1/(1 − α) = 1/0.25 = 4. The 1.85 figure is the successful-search bound (1/α)ln(1/(1−α)).

quiz.q: Double hashing uses h(k, i) = (h₁(k) + i·h₂(k)) mod m with m = 2¹⁶. What constraint keeps the probe sequence from missing slots?
options: h₂(k) must be relatively prime to m — i.e. odd
h₂(k) must be a multiple of 16
quiz.explanation: The sequence touches exactly m/gcd(h₂, m) distinct slots; with m a power of two only odd strides are coprime to m, guaranteeing all 2¹⁶ slots are reachable.

quiz.q: Primary clustering is the signature defect of which scheme?
quiz.explanation: Linear probing's unit stride makes all keys hashing near a slot walk the same run, and runs merge as they grow. Double hashing's varied strides break exactly this.

quiz.q: Why does open-addressed deletion write a DELETED marker rather than clearing the slot?
options: To remember the key for undo
Because a truly empty slot would terminate probe sequences that pass through it
To keep the load factor α below 1
Because slots cannot be emptied in arrays
quiz.explanation: HASH-SEARCH stops at the first empty slot; clearing would make later keys unreachable. Tombstones keep probes alive at the cost of gradual clutter, eventually cured by rehashing.

quiz.q: Into an empty table of $11$ slots, three keys all hashing to $5$ are inserted by linear probing. The third key lands in slot:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $m = 11$, probe origin $h = 5$ for all three keys, linear probing. Step 2 — Governing sequence: probe $k$ tries $(h + k) \bmod m$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ until an empty slot appears. Step 3 — Trace: first key takes $5$; second probes $5$ (occupied) then $6$; third probes $5$, $6$ (both occupied) then $7$. Step 4 — Sanity check: consecutive occupancy forms a primary cluster, each arrival extends it by one, and wraparound arithmetic is never needed here. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: $5$ ignores occupancy, $6$ stops one probe early, and $8$ skips a slot as quadratic probing would. Step 6 — Conclude: slot $7$.

intro: Every scheme so far had Θ(1) expected time but Θ(n) worst case — a single unlucky chain can spoil a search. Perfect hashing removes the luck: when the set of keys is fixed in advance, a two-level scheme achieves Θ(1) worst-case lookup in O(n) space. The trick is to spend quadratic space on each bucket, because with n_j² secondary slots a collision-free hash function is easy to find.
objectives: Describe the two-level perfect-hashing scheme and why worst-case lookup is exactly 2 probes
Justify the m_j = n_j² secondary table size via the birthday/Markov argument
Explain why the expected total space is O(n) and when the scheme is appropriate

concepts.statement: Perfect hashing assumes the **set S of n keys never changes** after construction — a compiler's reserved-word table, a dictionary on read-only media, a fixed symbol set. With no insertions or deletions, the only cost that matters is lookup, and it can be driven to $O(1)$ **worst case**.
concepts.detail: If keys must be inserted and deleted dynamically, this two-level structure is not the tool — Chapters 12 and 13 take over.

concepts.statement: Level 1 hashes the $n$ keys into $m = n$ slots with a function $h$ drawn from a universal family. Bucket $j$ receives $n_j$ keys and gets its **own secondary table of $m_j = n_j^2$ slots** with its own function $h_j$, again universal, chosen so that **no two of the bucket's keys collide at level 2**.
concepts.detail: A lookup computes h(k) then h_j(k): exactly two hash evaluations and two slot reads, always — the worst case is 2 probes.

concepts.statement: For a bucket with $n_j$ keys and $m_j = n_j^2$ secondary slots, a hash function drawn from a universal family has **no collisions with probability at least 1/2**: the expected number of colliding pairs is at most $\binom{n_j}{2}/m_j < 1/2$, and by Markov's inequality $\Pr[\text{at least one pair collides}] < 1/2$.
concepts.detail: So a handful of random trials per bucket is enough to find a collision-free h_j — the same birthday-paradox counting that makes 23 people likely to share a birthday.

concepts.statement: With the level-1 table of size $m = n$ and universal hashing, $\mathrm{E}\big[\sum_j n_j^2\big] = n + \frac{n(n-1)}{m} < 2n$, so the **expected total space of the whole structure is O(n)**; by Markov, $\Pr[\sum_j n_j^2 \ge 4n] \le 1/2$, so a good pair of levels is found in a few random trials.
concepts.detail: The identity E[n_j²] = E[n_j] + 2·E[# pairs in bucket j] turns the square into a pair-count, and each of the C(n,2) key pairs lands together with probability 1/m.

concepts.statement: With $m = n$ slots and simple uniform hashing, expected collisions total $\binom{n}{2}/n < n/2$, so the expected sum $\sum_j n_j^2 = n + 2 \times$ collisions is $O(n)$. The first level need only be linear for the second level's quadratic tables to total linear space in expectation.
concepts.detail: Markov then bounds the chance the construction retries: with $E[\sum n_j^2] = O(n)$, a fresh universal hash succeeds with constant probability, so expected retries are $O(1)$.

figures.caption: Perfect hashing of $S = \{17, 42, 88, 96, 103, 140\}$ with level 1 $h(k) = k \bmod 5$. Bucket 2 receives $\{17, 42\}$ and bucket 3 receives $\{88, 103\}$; each gets $n_j^2 = 4$ secondary slots and a collision-free function, here $h_2(k) = (3k \bmod 101) \bmod 4$ (17 → 3, 42 → 1) and $h_3(k) = ((2k+1) \bmod 101) \bmod 4$ (88 → 0, 103 → 1). Total secondary slots: $1 + 1 + 4 + 4 = 10 < 2n = 12$.

examples.title: Building the two levels for six keys
examples.problem: Perfectly hash $S = \{17, 42, 88, 96, 103, 140\}$ using level 1 $h(k) = k \bmod 5$ and quadratic secondary tables. Verify the secondary functions are collision-free.

steps.label: Step 2: Size the secondary tables
steps.text: $m_j = n_j^2$: single slots for buckets 0 and 1, four slots each for buckets 2 and 3, and no table at all for the empty bucket 4.

steps.label: Step 3: Test h₂(k) = (3k mod 101) mod 4 on bucket 2
steps.text: $3 \cdot 17 = 51$, and $51 \bmod 4 = 3$; $3 \cdot 42 = 126 \equiv 25 \pmod{101}$, and $25 \bmod 4 = 1$. Slots 3 and 1 — no collision, so this h₂ is accepted.

steps.label: Step 4: Test h₃(k) = ((2k+1) mod 101) mod 4 on bucket 3
steps.text: $2 \cdot 88 + 1 = 177 \equiv 76 \pmod{101}$, and $76 \bmod 4 = 0$; $2 \cdot 103 + 1 = 207 \equiv 5 \pmod{101}$, and $5 \bmod 4 = 1$. Slots 0 and 1 — collision-free again.

steps.label: Step 5: Audit the space
steps.text: Secondary slots: $1 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 0 = 10$, comfortably under the $2n = 12$ that the expectation $\mathrm{E}[\sum n_j^2] < 2n$ promises on average.

examples.result: Any key in S is found by computing two hashes and reading two slots — Θ(1) worst case, no luck involved.

examples.title: Second-level sizes on skewed buckets
examples.problem: With $n = 6$, first-level buckets hold $n_j = 3, 2, 1, 0, 0, 0$. Size the second level and total the space.

steps.label: Quadratic sizing
steps.text: Second tables $m_j = n_j^2$: $9, 4, 1, 0, 0, 0$ slots: total $14$ slots for $6$ keys.

steps.label: Why squares
steps.text: With $n_j^2$ slots a random hash is collision-free with probability $\ge 1/2$ (birthday bound $\binom{n_j}{2}/n_j^2 < 1/2$), so each bucket retries $O(1)$ times expected.

steps.label: Skew cost
steps.text: The $3$-bucket alone costs $9$ slots; had the six keys spread $1$ each, total would be $6$ slots. Skew is paid quadratically, which is why the expectation needs uniform hashing.

steps.label: Lookup
steps.text: Worst case $2$ probes: one to $h(k)$, one to $h_j(k)$ in the $n_j^2$ table: $O(1)$ worst case, not merely expected.

examples.result: $14$ second-level slots for the $3$-$2$-$1$ split; worst-case lookup $2$ probes with $O(n)$ expected space.

keyTakeaways: Perfect hashing handles a fixed key set: level 1 spreads n keys into m = n buckets, and each bucket gets $m_j = n_j^2$ secondary slots with a collision-free universal hash.
The quadratic secondary size makes a collision-free function easy: the expected number of colliding pairs is below 1/2, so each bucket succeeds with probability ≥ 1/2 per trial.
Expected total space is $O(n)$ because $\mathrm{E}[\sum_j n_j^2] < 2n$ — the two-level table is both worst-case fast and asymptotically compact.

quiz.q: In the two-level perfect-hashing scheme, how large is each secondary table?
options: n_j slots, matching the bucket's key count
n_j² slots, the square of the bucket's key count
quiz.explanation: Quadratic secondary tables make a collision-free universal function likely: with n_j² slots the expected number of colliding pairs in a bucket is under 1/2.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case number of hash evaluations and slot reads to look up a key?
quiz.explanation: One level-1 hash lands in a bucket, and one level-2 hash lands in a collision-free secondary slot — exactly two probes, always.

quiz.q: Why is the expected total space of the two-level scheme O(n)?
options: Because each secondary table has exactly n slots
Because E[Σ n_j²] = n + n(n−1)/m < 2n when the level-1 table has m = n slots
Because the level-1 hash never produces collisions
Because empty buckets get large tables
quiz.explanation: E[n_j²] = E[n_j] + 2·E[pairs in j] and each of the C(n,2) key pairs shares a bucket with probability 1/m; summing over m = n buckets gives E[Σ n_j²] = n + n(n−1)/n < 2n.

quiz.q: Which application is the natural habitat for perfect hashing?
options: A database index with constant inserts
A compiler's keyword table fixed before compilation
A web cache with a changing key set
A hash table that must support range queries
quiz.explanation: The scheme requires the key set to be static. Reserved words, error codes, or dictionary contents fixed at build time are ideal; dynamic sets need Chapter 12–13 structures instead.

intro: A binary search tree is a linked structure whose shape is dictated by insertion order but whose content obeys one powerful invariant: everything in the left subtree is smaller, everything in the right subtree is larger. This section defines the invariant, the representation, and the inorder tree walk — the traversal that quietly turns a tree into a sorted list.
objectives: State the binary-search-tree property precisely and test a given tree against it
Implement and analyze the inorder tree walk, including its correctness argument
Distinguish inorder, preorder and postorder walks and their uses

concepts.statement: For every node $x$: the keys in the **left subtree** of $x$ are at most $x.key$, and the keys in the **right subtree** are at least $x.key$. Equivalently, every key in the subtree rooted at $x$ lies between the keys on the path bounding it — the property is inherited down entire subtrees, not just parent–child pairs.
concepts.detail: The property forces the minimum key to the leftmost node and the maximum to the rightmost node of the whole tree.

concepts.statement: Each node $x$ stores its key and satellite data plus three pointers: $x.left$, $x.right$ and $x.p$ (the parent); absent children and the parent of the root are **NIL**. The tree is identified by its root pointer, and if $x.p =$ NIL then $x$ is the root.
concepts.detail: The minimum node is found by following left children from the root until NIL; the maximum symmetrically with right children.

concepts.statement: **INORDER-TREE-WALK**$(x)$: if $x \ne$ NIL, walk $x.left$, print $x.key$, then walk $x.right$. On any binary search tree this prints the keys **in sorted order**, and it costs $\Theta(n)$ for a tree with $n$ nodes — every node is visited once, with constant overhead per visit.
concepts.detail: Correctness is a loop-invariant argument: the walk on a subtree rooted at x prints exactly its keys, left subtree before x before right subtree — which sorted order demands by the BST property.

concepts.statement: **Preorder** prints the node before its subtrees; **postorder** prints it after. The three walks differ only in where the print statement sits relative to the two recursive calls, and each runs in $\Theta(n)$.
concepts.detail: Preorder is the natural order for copying a tree (a node must exist before its children attach); postorder for freeing one (children must be released first).

concepts.statement: Inorder tree walk prints keys in nondecreasing order if and only if the binary-search-tree property holds at every node. The walk is therefore both a correctness test and the definition's operational meaning.
concepts.detail: Theorem 12.1: the walk takes $\Theta(n)$ time for $n$ nodes. Preorder ($root$, left, right) records structure for copying; postorder (left, right, $root$) suits deletion; only inorder is sorted.

figures.caption: A binary search tree on the keys $\{15, 6, 18, 3, 7, 17, 20, 2, 4\}$. The green badges record the inorder walk's visiting order — $2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 15, 17, 18, 20$ — which is exactly the sorted key sequence, whatever the tree's shape.

examples.title: Spotting a fake BST
examples.problem: A tree has root 15 with left child 6; node 6 has left child 3 and right child 20. Every parent–child pair is correctly ordered. Is this a valid binary search tree?

steps.label: Step 1: Check parent–child pairs only
steps.text: Each edge looks fine: $6 < 15$, $3 < 6$, $20 > 6$. A hasty check stops here and says yes.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply the full property
steps.text: The BST property speaks about **subtrees**: every key in 15's left subtree must be at most 15. But 20 sits in 15's left subtree (via 6's right child) and $20 > 15$ — violation.

steps.label: Step 3: Cross-check with the inorder walk
steps.text: An inorder walk prints $3, 6, 20, 15$ — the sequence is not sorted, which is the giveaway: a tree is a BST **if and only if** its inorder walk is sorted.

steps.label: Step 4: Repair
steps.text: Moving 20 into the right subtree of 15 (say as 18's child) restores the invariant: the walk then prints $3, 6, 15, 18, 20$ sorted.

examples.result: Invalid — the BST property constrains whole subtrees, so a node deep on the left must still respect every ancestor above it, not just its parent.

examples.title: Inorder on five keys
examples.problem: Inorder-walk the BST with root $4$, left child $2$ (children $1,3$), right child $5$. List the output and the visit order.

steps.label: Left subtree
steps.text: Walk $2$: walk $1$ (print $1$), print $2$, walk $3$ (print $3$): yields $1,2,3$.

steps.label: Root
steps.text: Print $4$: sequence $1,2,3,4$.

steps.label: Right
steps.text: Walk $5$: print $5$: final $1,2,3,4,5$: sorted, confirming the BST property.

steps.label: Cost
steps.text: Each edge traversed twice (down and up): $2(n-1)$ edge steps plus $n$ prints $= \Theta(n)$.

examples.result: Output $1,2,3,4,5$ in $\Theta(5)$ time; any BST-property violation would surface as an inversion in this list.

keyTakeaways: The BST property orders whole subtrees: left keys ≤ node key ≤ right keys, recursively — a single deep misplaced node breaks it.
The inorder tree walk (left, node, right) prints the keys in sorted order in $\Theta(n)$, and this characterizes BSTs.
Preorder and postorder visit every node too ($\Theta(n)$); their positions relative to the recursive calls suit copying and deleting trees respectively.

quiz.q: Which traversal of a binary search tree outputs keys in sorted order?
quiz.explanation: Inorder (left subtree, node, right subtree) matches sorted order exactly because of the BST property — the left keys are smaller, the right keys larger.

quiz.q: A node with key 8 sits as the right child of a node with key 5, which is the left child of the root 20. Is the tree necessarily invalid?
options: Yes — 8 > 5 but the pair sits in the root's left subtree, so 8 must be ≤ 20, which holds; more information is needed
Yes — right children must have keys larger than the root
No — only the root's direct children matter
quiz.explanation: Being in the left subtree of 20 forces key ≤ 20; 8 ≤ 20 is fine and 8 > 5 satisfies its parent. With only these three keys the tree is valid — the constraint to check was ≤ 20, not ≤ 5.

quiz.q: How much time does INORDER-TREE-WALK take on a tree with n nodes, regardless of its shape?
options: Θ(n lg n) because it sorts
quiz.explanation: Every node is visited exactly once with constant work per visit — Θ(n) whether the tree is balanced or a chain. No sorting machinery is invoked; sorted output is a free consequence of the walk order.

quiz.q: Where is the minimum key of any binary search tree?
options: At the leftmost node, reached by following left children from the root
At whichever leaf was inserted first
quiz.explanation: Following left children strictly decreases keys and must terminate at the leftmost node; every other node has some key ≤ it to its left by the subtree property.

intro: The BST property makes searching feel like binary search, and it makes minima, maxima, successors and predecessors follow simple pointer rules. Every one of these queries runs in time proportional to the tree's height h — which is why h, and everything that controls it, will dominate this entire chapter.
objectives: Implement TREE-SEARCH, MINIMUM and MAXIMUM and argue the O(h) bound
Execute the two cases of TREE-SUCCESSOR by hand, including the ancestor-climb case
Explain why height is the governing resource and how badly it can degrade

concepts.statement: To search for a key $k$: start at the root; if $k <$ node key go left, if $k >$ node key go right, and stop at a match or at NIL. The recursive and iterative forms are equivalent, and the search path traces a single **root-to-node path**, so the cost is $O(h)$.
concepts.detail: Each comparison discards an entire subtree — exactly the binary-search move, but along pointers instead of array halves.

concepts.statement: TREE-MINIMUM$(x)$: while $x.left \ne$ NIL, set $x = x.left$; return $x$. TREE-MAXIMUM symmetrically follows right children. Both walk a single descending path and cost $O(h)$.
concepts.detail: They also form the base case of the successor computation — the successor uses the minimum of a right subtree.

concepts.statement: The successor of node $x$ (the smallest key greater than $x.key$) is found in two mutually exclusive cases: **(a)** if $x$ has a right subtree, the successor is the **minimum of that right subtree**; **(b)** otherwise, it is the **lowest ancestor of $x$ whose left child is also an ancestor of $x$** (walk up while taking right-child edges; the first left turn's parent is it). The successor of the maximum is NIL.
concepts.detail: PREDECESSOR is the mirror image: maximum of the left subtree, else the lowest ancestor approached from the right.

concepts.statement: SEARCH, MINIMUM, MAXIMUM, SUCCESSOR and PREDECESSOR all run in $O(h)$, where $h$ ranges from $\lfloor \lg n \rfloor$ (perfectly balanced) up to $n - 1$ (a chain built by inserting sorted keys). The same tree can therefore support $\Theta(\lg n)$ or $\Theta(n)$ searches depending purely on insertion order.
concepts.detail: Sorting n keys by inserting them into a BST and then walking inorder costs Θ(nh) — Θ(n lg n) only when the tree is balanced; this is exactly the gap Chapter 13's red-black trees close.

concepts.statement: Starting at the root, while $x \ne \mathrm{NIL}$ and $k \ne x.key$, go left if $k < x.key$ else right. Same $O(h)$ bound as recursion with $O(1)$ extra space: the loop follows one root-to-leaf path.
concepts.detail: Recursion depth equals height $h$; iteration removes the call stack. MINIMUM/MAXIMUM are the same loop driven to the extreme child.

examples.title: Both successor cases on one tree
examples.problem: On the BST with keys $\{15, 6, 18, 3, 7, 17, 20, 2, 4\}$ (root 15; 6 has children 3 and 7; 18 has children 17 and 20; 3 has children 2 and 4), find the successor of 7 and of 4.

steps.label: Step 1: Successor of 7 — check the right subtree
steps.text: Node 7 has **no right child**, so case (a) does not apply; the answer is above 7, not below it.

steps.label: Step 2: Climb from 7
steps.text: Walk up: 7 is the **right child** of 6 — keep climbing, it cannot be the answer (6 < 7). Next, 6 is the **left child** of 15 — stop. The successor of 7 is $15$.

steps.label: Step 3: Verify with sorted order
steps.text: Sorted: $2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 15, 17, 18, 20$ — indeed 15 directly follows 7.

steps.label: Step 4: Successor of 4 — again no right child
steps.text: Node 4 is the right child of 3 — climb. Node 3 is the **left child** of 6 — stop: successor of 4 is $6$, which the sorted list confirms.

steps.label: Step 5: Contrast the easy case
steps.text: For 18, which **has** a right subtree, the successor is simply the minimum of that subtree: leftmost from 20 is $20$ itself. Case (a), one descending walk.

examples.result: With a right child: descend to that subtree's minimum. Without: climb until the path takes a left turn — the turn's parent is the successor.

examples.title: Predecessor when left subtree exists
examples.problem: Find TREE-PREDECESSOR of node $15$ whose left child $10$ has right subtree $10 \to 12 \to 14$.

steps.label: Rule
steps.text: With a left subtree, predecessor is MAXIMUM of that subtree: go left once, then right until $\mathrm{NIL}$.

steps.label: Walk
steps.text: $15 \to 10$ (left), $10 \to 12$ (right), $12 \to 14$ (right), $14.right = \mathrm{NIL}$: stop at $14$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: $14$ is the largest key below $15$: inorder neighbours are $\ldots, 14, 15, \ldots$.

steps.label: Other case
steps.text: Without a left subtree the answer would be the lowest ancestor whose right child is also an ancestor: the climb case covered in the section's first example.

examples.result: Predecessor is $14$ after one left step and two right steps: $O(h)$ with $h = 3$ here.

keyTakeaways: All BST queries — SEARCH, MINIMUM, MAXIMUM, SUCCESSOR, PREDECESSOR — follow a single path and cost $O(h)$.
SUCCESSOR has two cases: minimum of the right subtree if it exists, otherwise the lowest ancestor whose left child is also an ancestor.
Height ranges from $\lg n$ to $n-1$ depending on insertion order; unbalanced BSTs degrade to linked lists — the motivation for Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Node x has no right subtree. Its successor is:
options: NIL, because only leaves have successors
The lowest ancestor of x whose left child is also an ancestor of x
The minimum of the left subtree
quiz.explanation: Climb from x while you arrived from a right child; the first ancestor you approach from its left child is the smallest key above x. The parent is the answer only in that special case.

quiz.q: Which statement about the time bounds of the BST queries is correct?
options: SEARCH is O(lg n) always, the others are O(n)
All of SEARCH, MINIMUM, MAXIMUM, SUCCESSOR run in O(h), and h can be n − 1
MINIMUM runs in O(lg n) always because it is a binary search
quiz.explanation: Every query follows one root-to-node or node-to-root path of length at most h. In a chain h = n − 1, so all queries degrade to Θ(n) — no query has an unconditional O(lg n) bound.

quiz.q: In the tree of the worked example, TREE-SUCCESSOR of 3 is:
quiz.explanation: Node 3 has a right subtree (containing 4), so case (a) applies: the successor is its minimum, the leftmost node there — 4 itself.

quiz.q: Keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are inserted in order into an empty BST. What is the cost of a subsequent unsuccessful search?
options: Θ(n) — the tree is a right-leaning chain
quiz.explanation: Sorted insertion builds a chain of height n − 1 = 4; searching for 6 walks all five nodes. Only random or balanced insertion orders keep the tree short.

intro: Insertion is a walk down to a leaf plus one pointer change. Deletion is the intricate half of the chapter: three structurally different cases, unified by a small pointer-surgery helper called TRANSPLANT. Getting the two-children case right — splice the successor — is the classic exam skill this section drills.
objectives: Insert a new key as a leaf with TREE-INSERT and account for its O(h) cost
Explain TRANSPLANT as pure subtree replacement
Execute all three deletion cases, including the deep-successor case

concepts.statement: To insert key $k$: descend from the root as a search would, carrying a trailing parent pointer, until hitting NIL; attach the new node (with key $k$, children NIL) as that parent's left or right child. Cost $O(h)$, and the new node always enters as a **leaf**.
concepts.detail: Insertion never rearranges existing nodes — which is precisely why a bad insertion order produces a lopsided tree.

concepts.statement: **TRANSPLANT**$(T, u, v)$ replaces the **subtree rooted at $u$** by the **subtree rooted at $v$**: it updates $u$'s parent to point at $v$ and sets $v.p = u.p$ (handling root and NIL cases). It is blind to keys — pure pointer surgery, $O(1)$.
concepts.detail: TRANSPLANT never touches the children of u or v; it only rewires the single edge that hangs the subtree.

concepts.statement: Deleting node $z$: **(1) no children** — TRANSPLANT$(z, \mathrm{NIL})$; **(2) one child** — TRANSPLANT$(z, z$'s child$)$, splicing $z$ out; **(3) two children** — find $y = $ TREE-MINIMUM$(z.right)$, the successor; if $y \ne z.right$, first TRANSPLANT$(y, y.right)$ to slide $y$'s right subtree up, then TRANSPLANT$(z, y)$ and give $y$ both of $z$'s old subtrees.
concepts.detail: In case (3) the key that physically moves is z's successor — the smallest key of the right subtree, which by construction has no left child.

concepts.statement: Insertion and deletion both run in $O(h)$ time on a BST of height $h$ — and both can change the tree's height. Deletion in particular can silently make a tree **more** lopsided over time, which is why the balanced-tree machinery of the next chapter exists.
concepts.detail: CLRS's warning: as a rule, the height of a BST over a sequence of operations is the adversary's plaything — an alternating pattern of inserts and deletes can leave the tree much taller than n would suggest.

concepts.statement: Deleting the root uses the same three cases with $parent = \mathrm{NIL}$: TRANSPLANT updates the tree's $root$ pointer instead of a parent's child field. The deep-successor case still splices $y$ out of its old parent before moving it to the root.
concepts.detail: Root deletion is the stress test for TRANSPLANT: no parent exists, so the procedure's first branch ($u.p = \mathrm{NIL}$) is the only one exercised, and the successor's original parent must still be rewired.

figures.caption: The three deletion cases. Case 1: a childless $z$ is replaced by NIL. Case 2: $z$'s single child $c$ is spliced directly into $z$'s place. Case 3: with two children, the successor $y$ = MINIMUM(right($z$)) rises into $z$'s slot while its own right subtree ($x$) slides under $r$; every key remains inorder-sorted.
