examples.title: Deleting three nodes from the running tree
examples.problem: Starting from the BST with keys $\{15, 6, 18, 3, 7, 17, 20, 2, 4\}$ (root 15; 6 has children 3, 7; 18 has children 17, 20; 3 has children 2, 4), delete key 3, then the root 15. Show every pointer change.

steps.label: Step 1: Delete 3 — two children
steps.text: $z = 3$ with left child 2 and right child 4. The successor is $y = $ MINIMUM(right subtree) $= 4$, which happens to be $z$'s own right child. Case: TRANSPLANT$(z, y)$ directly — 4 rises into 3's place keeping left child 2.

steps.label: Step 2: Tree after step 1
steps.text: Node 6 now has left child 4, and 4 has left child 2: subtree $6 (4 (2, \cdot), 7)$ — inorder $2, 4, 6, 7$ still sorted.

steps.label: Step 3: Delete the root 15 — two children again
steps.text: $z = 15$ with left subtree rooted at 6 and right subtree rooted at 18. Successor $y = $ MINIMUM$(18, \ldots) = 17$. Here $y \ne z.right$: 17 is 18's left child.

steps.label: Step 4: Slide y's right subtree up
steps.text: $y = 17$ has no right child, so TRANSPLANT$(y, y.right)=$ TRANSPLANT$(17, \mathrm{NIL})$: 18's left child becomes NIL.

steps.label: Step 5: Move y into z's place
steps.text: TRANSPLANT$(15, 17)$: 17 becomes the root; its left child is set to 6, its right child to 18. Final tree: root 17 with left subtree $6 (4 (2, \cdot), 7)$ and right subtree $18 (\cdot, 20)$.

steps.label: Step 6: Verify
steps.text: Inorder walk of the result: $2, 4, 6, 7, 17, 18, 20$ — exactly the original sorted order minus the deleted keys.

examples.result: Key insight: when the successor is not z's right child, its own right subtree is first lifted out (TRANSPLANT(y, y.right)) and only then does y take z's place.

examples.title: Deleting a node whose successor is deep
examples.problem: Delete $z = 15$ with right child $20$ whose left spine is $20 \to 17 \to 16$. Show the two transplants.

steps.label: Successor
steps.text: $y = 16$ (minimum of right subtree), $y.p = 17 \ne z$: deep case.

steps.label: Splice $y$ out
steps.text: TRANSPLANT($y$, $y.right = \mathrm{NIL}$): $17.left = \mathrm{NIL}$; attach $y.right = 20$'s left? Precisely: $y$ leaves, $20$'s left spine shortens.

steps.label: Replace $z$
steps.text: TRANSPLANT($z$, $y$): $y$ takes $15$'s position with $y.left = 15.left$, $y.right = 15.right = 20$.

steps.label: Verify
steps.text: BST property holds: $y = 16$ exceeds all of $15$'s left subtree and precedes everything else in $15$'s right subtree.

examples.result: Two TRANSPLANTs and $O(h)$ pointer writes; the deep case costs one extra splice versus successor-is-child.

keyTakeaways: TREE-INSERT walks one root-to-leaf path and attaches the new key as a leaf in $O(h)$ — no existing node moves.
TRANSPLANT(T, u, v) is the O(1) primitive that replaces one subtree with another; all deletion cases are combinations of it.
Two-children deletion promotes the successor $y = $ MINIMUM(z.right): if $y \ne$ z.right, first lift $y$'s right subtree, then transplant $y$ into $z$'s position.

quiz.q: Deleting a node z that has two children: which node's key ends up in z's structural position?
options: The successor of z — the minimum of z's right subtree
The largest key of the left subtree
quiz.explanation: The successor is the smallest key above z.key, so it can legally replace z; and because it is the minimum of the right subtree it has no left child, making the splice simple.

quiz.q: What does TRANSPLANT(T, u, v) do?
options: Copies v's key into u and deletes v
Replaces the subtree rooted at u with the subtree rooted at v, updating only the parent pointers involved
Swaps the subtrees of u and v
Rebalances the path from the root to u
quiz.explanation: TRANSPLANT rewires one edge: u's parent comes to point at v, and v.p is set to u.p. Keys, children of u, and children of v are untouched.

quiz.q: In the worked example, after deleting 3 and then the root 15, which key is the new root?
quiz.explanation: 17 is the successor of 15 and moves into the root slot, with 6's subtree on the left and 18's on the right — the inorder sequence stays sorted.

quiz.q: Why does CLRS warn that deletion can make a BST lopsided over time?
options: Deletion always removes nodes near the root
Asymmetry of the case analysis: deleting nodes from one side can leave a tall, thin remainder whose height is no longer governed by n
Deletion doubles the number of NIL leaves
quiz.explanation: Nothing in ordinary BST deletion maintains balance: repeated deletes can strip one side of the tree, raising h. Red-black trees (Chapter 13) add exactly the machinery to prevent this.

quiz.q: Keys $[8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13]$ are inserted into an empty binary search tree in that order. Deleting key $3$ (which has two children) puts which key in its place?
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given insertion order, node $3$ has left child $1$ and right subtree rooted at $6$ holding ${4, 6, 7}$. Step 2 — Governing rule: a two-child deletion splices in the successor, the minimum of the right subtree, via TRANSPLANT pointer surgery. Step 3 — Trace: successor of $3$ is $\min({4, 6, 7}) = 4$; node $4$ (a leaf) lifts into position $3$, keeping $1$ left and $6$ right with $7$ still under $6$. Step 4 — Sanity check: inorder before deletion reads $1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14$ and after reads the same minus $3$, so the property holds. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: $1$ is the predecessor-side minimum, $6$ is the right child but not its minimum, and $8$ is the uninvolved root. Step 6 — Conclude: key $4$ replaces key $3$.

intro: Since a BST's shape depends on insertion order, the honest question is: what shape do we get on average? The answer — a height of O(lg n) in expectation — is the guarantee that plain BSTs actually deliver logarithmic behavior when built from random data, and it foreshadows the worst-case guarantees red-black trees will buy with color discipline.
objectives: Define a randomly built binary search tree and relate it to random insertion permutations
State the expected-height theorem and the exponential-height technique behind its proof
Connect random BSTs to randomized quicksort's analysis

concepts.statement: A **randomly built binary search tree** on $n$ keys is what results from inserting those keys in an order chosen **uniformly at random** — equivalently, each of the $n!$ insertion permutations is equally likely. Equivalently one may randomize the algorithm itself (insert keys after a random shuffle).
concepts.detail: The randomness is over insertion orders, not over the set of keys; the same fixed key set gives many possible trees.

concepts.statement: **Theorem 12.4 (CLRS):** the expected height $\mathrm{E}[X_n]$ of a randomly built BST on $n$ keys is $O(\lg n)$ — even though the worst case (a sorted insertion order) is $n - 1$. Randomization converts an adversarial worst case into an average case.
concepts.detail: E.g. for n = 3 the six permutations give heights 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2 — expectation 5/3, already suggesting the log.

concepts.statement: The proof works on the **exponential height** $Y_n = 2^{X_n}$ instead of $X_n$ itself: one shows $\mathrm{E}[Y_n] = O(n^3)$ by exploiting that a subtree's height sits below the max of two smaller subproblems, and then applies Jensen's inequality to the concave logarithm: $\mathrm{E}[X_n] = \mathrm{E}[\lg Y_n] \le \lg \mathrm{E}[Y_n] = O(\lg n)$.
concepts.detail: Squaring the problem into an exponential random variable is CLRS's signature move here: sums are easier to take expectations of than maxima.

concepts.statement: A randomly built BST is structurally the **recursion tree of randomized quicksort** on the same keys: the first inserted key (the root) plays the pivot, its left and right subtrees are the two partitions. Hence BST search cost relates directly to quicksort comparison counts, and both enjoy $O(n \lg n)$ expected behavior.
concepts.detail: This is why randomizing insertion order is the same defensive trick as randomizing the pivot — it prevents the sorted-input worst case.

concepts.statement: A randomly built BST from distinct keys $k_1 < \cdots < k_n$ has the same distribution as inserting the keys in uniformly random order. The shape depends only on relative rank order of arrival, never on key values themselves.
concepts.detail: Hence the analysis may fix sorted keys $z_1 < \cdots < z_n$ and randomize the permutation: identical to RANDOMIZED-QUICKSORT's random-permutation view, which is why both share the $O(n \lg n)$ expectation and the quicksort correspondence.

examples.title: Every three-key BST and the expected height
examples.problem: Compute the expected height of a randomly built BST on the keys {1, 2, 3}, where height counts edges on the longest root-to-leaf path.

steps.label: Step 2: Build each tree
steps.text: $(1,2,3)$: 1 at root, 2 its right child, 3 below — a right chain, height 2. $(1,3,2)$: root 1, right child 3 with left child 2 — height 2. $(3,2,1)$ and $(3,1,2)$: mirror chains, height 2.

steps.label: Step 3: The balanced orders
steps.text: $(2,1,3)$ and $(2,3,1)$: 2 lands at the root with 1 and 3 as children — a perfect tree of height 1.

steps.label: Step 4: Average
steps.text: $\mathrm{E}[X_3] = \frac{2+2+1+1+2+2}{6} = \frac{10}{6} = \frac{5}{3} \approx 1.67$ — comfortably below the worst case 2 and already close to $\lg 3 \approx 1.58$.

examples.result: E[height] = 5/3 for n = 3: the average tree is nearly balanced even though one third of the orders build chains.

examples.title: Height 3 on four keys is rare
examples.problem: With keys $1,2,3,4$ inserted in random order, what is the probability the BST has height $3$ (a chain)?

steps.label: Chains
steps.text: Height $3$ needs sorted or reverse-sorted arrival: $1,2,3,4$ or $4,3,2,1$: $2$ of $4! = 24$ permutations.

steps.label: Probability
steps.text: $2/24 = 1/12 \approx 0.083$: chains are rare; expected height is $O(\lg n)$ because balanced arrivals dominate.

steps.label: Typical
steps.text: Median-first arrivals (e.g. $2$ or $3$ first) give height $2$: $16/24$ of permutations yield the minimum height.

steps.label: Moral
steps.text: Random order makes degenerate shapes exponentially unlikely, the same mathematics that makes quicksort's worst case unlikely under random pivots.

examples.result: Chain probability $1/12$ on $n = 4$; random BSTs are balanced with high probability, height $O(\lg n)$ in expectation.

keyTakeaways: A randomly built BST comes from a uniformly random insertion order — n! equally likely shapes for a fixed key set.
Expected height is $O(\lg n)$ though the worst case is $n-1$; the proof studies $Y_n = 2^{X_n}$, bounds $\mathrm{E}[Y_n] = O(n^3)$, and applies Jensen's inequality.
Random BSTs are the recursion trees of randomized quicksort — randomization defends against adversarial input in both.

quiz.q: What exactly is “randomly built” in a randomly built binary search tree?
options: Each node is assigned a random key
The insertion order is a uniformly random permutation of the keys
The tree is balanced with random tie-breaking
Each pointer is rewired at random after construction
quiz.explanation: The randomness is the choice among the n! insertion orders; the key set itself is fixed. Each order yields one deterministic tree shape.

quiz.q: For keys {1, 2, 3}, the expected height of a randomly built BST is:
quiz.explanation: Two of the six permutations give the balanced tree of height 1, the other four give chains of height 2: E[X₃] = (2·1 + 4·2)/6 = 10/6 = 5/3.

quiz.q: Why does the CLRS proof analyze Y_n = 2^{X_n} instead of the height X_n directly?
options: Because E[max of subtrees] is unwieldy while E of a sum like 2·(Y_left + Y_right) is tractable, and Jensen then converts back: E[lg Y] ≤ lg E[Y]
Because binary trees store powers of 2
To avoid using the BST property
quiz.explanation: Exponentiating turns the max in the height recurrence into an additive bound (max ≤ sum), giving E[Y_n] = O(n³); concavity of lg then yields E[X_n] ≤ lg E[Y_n] = O(lg n).

quiz.q: The deep connection between randomly built BSTs and randomized quicksort is that:
options: Both were invented by the same authors
The BST root plays the pivot: the tree is quicksort's recursion tree, so insertion order ↔ pivot choice and both analyses share structure
Both run in O(n) expected time
quiz.explanation: First-inserted key = first pivot partitions the remaining keys the same way; the subtrees are the partitions. Randomization defends both against sorted inputs.

intro: A red-black tree is a binary search tree with one extra bit of storage per node — its color — and five simple counting rules that together cap the tree's height at $2\lg(n+1)$. This section defines the invariant, introduces black-height as the counting tool, and establishes the logarithmic height bound that makes every dynamic-set operation run in $O(\lg n)$ worst-case time.
objectives: State all five red-black properties and check a concrete tree against them
Compute the black-height of every node in a red-black tree
Apply the height bound $h \le 2\lg(n+1)$ and explain why it makes searches logarithmic

concepts.statement: A **red-black tree** is a binary search tree in which each node stores a color field $x.color \in \{\text{RED}, \text{BLACK}\}$ and the tree obeys: (1) every node is either red or black; (2) the root is black; (3) every leaf (the NIL sentinel) is black; (4) if a node is red, **both** of its children are black — no two reds in a row on any path; (5) for each node, all simple paths from the node down to descendant leaves contain the **same number of black nodes**.
concepts.detail: Properties 4 and 5 do the balancing: 4 limits how densely reds can crowd a path, while 5 forces equal black depth everywhere in the tree.

concepts.statement: The **black-height** $bh(x)$ of a node $x$ is the number of black nodes on any simple path from, **but not including**, $x$ down to a descendant leaf (NIL included in the count). Property 5 guarantees the number is identical on every such path, so $bh$ is well defined; $bh(\text{NIL}) = 0$.
concepts.detail: A red node and its black children can share the same black-height — red nodes are free riders that never raise the black count of a path.

concepts.statement: A red-black tree with $n$ internal nodes has height at most $2\lg(n+1)$. Consequently SEARCH, MINIMUM, MAXIMUM, SUCCESSOR and PREDECESSOR — all $O(h)$ operations on binary search trees by Chapter 12 — run in $O(\lg n)$ worst-case time, and so (after Sections 13.3 and 13.4) do INSERT and DELETE.
concepts.detail: The proof rests on two facts: the subtree rooted at any node $x$ contains at least $2^{bh(x)} - 1$ internal nodes, and the root's black-height is at least $h/2$. Both are proved in full in the deeper tier below.

concepts.statement: CLRS implements all NILs as **one shared sentinel node** $T.nil$: a black node whose color may be read but never written, playing every NIL leaf and the root's parent simultaneously. All algorithms treat it as an ordinary child pointer.
concepts.detail: The sentinel removes hundreds of NIL tests — for example the uncle in RB-INSERT-FIXUP may be the sentinel, whose color BLACK is exactly what the case analysis needs to see.

concepts.statement: A red-black tree stores no heights and no balance factors. One global counting invariant — equal blacks on every root-to-leaf path, reds never adjacent — is enough to cap the height at twice the ideal. Updates maintain the count with recolorings (cheap, $O(\lg n)$ of them) and a constant number of rotations: at most 2 per insertion and 3 per deletion.
concepts.detail: This makes red-black trees cheaper to update than height-balanced AVL trees, which is why C++ `std::map`, Java's `TreeMap` and the Linux scheduler's rbtree-based run queue are all red-black trees.

figures.caption: A red-black tree on $n = 7$ internal keys with black-heights in green. Red nodes 3 and 10 sit directly under the black root; every root-to-NIL path passes exactly two black nodes besides the root (counting the black NIL). The height is $h = 3$ while $2\lg(n+1) = 2\lg 8 = 6$ — the bound holds with room to spare, because this tree is far more balanced than the worst case CLRS allows.

examples.title: Auditing a red-black tree
examples.problem: Verify that the tree of the figure — root 7 black; red children 3 and 10; black grandchildren 1, 5, 8, 12 — is a legal red-black tree, and check the height bound.

steps.label: Step 1: Properties 1–3
steps.text: Every node carries a color; the root 7 is black; the eight NIL leaves (drawn as small squares) are black. All three structural color rules hold.

steps.label: Step 2: Property 4 — no red-red pairs
steps.text: The only red nodes are 3 and 10, and each has exclusively black children: 3 has 1 and 5; 10 has 8 and 12. No red node sits under another red node.

steps.label: Step 3: Property 5 — equal black depth
steps.text: Each of the four root-to-NIL paths, such as $7 \to 3 \to 1 \to \text{NIL}$ and $7 \to 10 \to 12 \to \text{NIL}$, crosses exactly two black nodes besides the root — the grandchild and the NIL. So every path agrees: $bh(7) = 2$, and the tree is a valid red-black tree.

steps.label: Step 4: The height bound
steps.text: The longest path (say $7 \to 3 \to 1 \to \text{NIL}$) has $h = 3$ edges. Lemma 13.1 allows up to $2\lg(n+1) = 2\lg 8 = 6$: the bound is satisfied with slack, since this tree is better balanced than the worst case.

examples.result: All five properties hold, so the tree is a red-black tree; its height 3 respects the $2\lg(n+1) = 6$ guarantee.

examples.title: Black-height audit on five nodes
examples.problem: Tree: black root $7$, red children $3, 11$, black leaves $1, 5$ under $3$. Verify all five properties and compute $bh$.

steps.label: Properties 1-2
steps.text: Every node red or black ✓; root $7$ black ✓.

steps.label: Properties 3-4
steps.text: Leaves $T.nil$ black ✓; red nodes $3, 11$ have black children ($1,5$ black, $nil$ black) ✓.

steps.label: Property 5
steps.text: Paths from $7$: $7 \to 3 \to 1 \to nil$ has blacks $7,1,nil = 3$; $7 \to 3 \to 5 \to nil$ also $3$; $7 \to 11 \to nil$ has $7,nil = 2$? Violation unless $11$'s missing children count: $11$ is red with black $nil$ children, path $7 \to 11 \to nil$ has blacks $7,nil = 2 \ne 3$: not a valid red-black tree.

steps.label: Repair
steps.text: Recolor $11$ black or restructure: black-height must agree on every root-to-leaf path. Here $bh(7)$ is undefined, which is exactly what Lemma 13.1's hypothesis excludes.

examples.result: Fails property $5$: black counts $3$ vs $2$. A valid tree needs uniform black-height; the audit catches it by counting.

keyTakeaways: Five properties: every node colored, black root, black NILs, red nodes have black children, and all paths from a node down to leaves carry the same number of blacks.
Black-height $bh(x)$ counts the black nodes strictly below $x$ on any path to a leaf; property 5 makes the count path-independent.
$h \le 2\lg(n+1)$ turns every Chapter 12 operation into an $O(\lg n)$ worst-case guarantee — the entire point of the coloring.

quiz.q: A colleague recolors the root of an otherwise valid red-black tree red, leaving all other nodes alone. Which property is necessarily violated?
quiz.explanation: Property 2 demands a black root. Property 4 constrains the children of a red node — if the root's children happen to be black, that property still holds; and no black count changes, so property 5 is safe.

quiz.q: A red-black tree has $n = 100$ internal nodes. Its height is at most:
quiz.explanation: Lemma 13.1: $h \le 2\lg(n+1) = 2\lg 101 \approx 13.3$, so the integer height is at most 13. The tighter $\lg 101$ is what a perfectly balanced tree would achieve — the red-black guarantee pays for itself with a factor of only 2.

quiz.q: The black-height $bh(x)$ of a node $x$ is:
options: the number of black nodes on a path from the root down to $x$
the number of black nodes on any path from $x$, excluding $x$ itself, down to a descendant leaf
the number of black nodes on a path from $x$, including $x$, down to a leaf
the total number of black nodes in the tree
quiz.explanation: The definition excludes $x$ itself and counts every black node below it on the path, NIL included. Property 5 guarantees the same answer on every path.

quiz.q: A subtree is rooted at a node $x$ with $bh(x) = 4$. At minimum, how many internal nodes does that subtree contain?
quiz.explanation: The first half of Lemma 13.1's proof: a subtree of black-height $b$ contains at least $2^b - 1$ internal nodes, here $2^4 - 1 = 15$.

quiz.q: A red-black tree stores $15$ internal nodes. Its height is at most:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: $n = 15$ internal nodes, red-black properties enforced. Step 2 — Governing bound: black-height at least halves the height, giving $h \le 2\lg(n + 1)$. Step 3 — Arithmetic: $n + 1 = 16$, $\lg 16 = 4$, so $h \le 8$. Step 4 — Sanity check: $8$ is logarithmic against $15$ linear, a plain BST could degenerate to $15$ while coloring forbids it, and the bound is tight up to constants. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: $4$ is the black-height alone, $6$ interleaves incorrectly, and $16$ is the degenerate chain the colors prevent. Step 6 — Conclude: height at most $8$.

depth.title: The height bound, proved in full: h ≤ 2 lg(n + 1)

blocks.heading: Lemma 13.1 (CLRS)
blocks.body: A red-black tree with $n$ internal nodes has height at most $2\lg(n+1)$.

blocks.heading: Part 1 — subtree size from black-height
blocks.body: We first show that the subtree rooted at any node $x$ contains at least $2^{bh(x)} - 1$ internal nodes, by induction on the height of $x$. **Base case** ($x = \text{NIL}$, a leaf): $bh(x) = 0$ and the subtree contains exactly $2^0 - 1 = 0$ internal nodes. **Inductive step** ($x$ internal): both children of $x$ have smaller height, so the induction hypothesis applies to them. A child's black-height is either $bh(x)$ — when the child is **red**, since red nodes are never counted — or $bh(x) - 1$ — when the child is **black**. Either way each child's subtree holds at least $2^{bh(x)-1} - 1$ internal nodes, and counting $x$ itself gives $$\text{subtree}(x) \;\ge\; 1 + 2\,\bigl(2^{bh(x)-1} - 1\bigr) \;=\; 2^{bh(x)} - 1,$$ completing the induction.

blocks.heading: Part 2 — the root's black-height is at least half the height
blocks.body: Take a longest root-to-leaf path — it has $h$ edges, the tree's height — and consider the $h$ nodes on it strictly below the root, the black NIL at the bottom included. **Charge every red node on the path to its child on the path.** By property 4 a red node's children are black, so every charge lands on a black node; and since each node on a path has exactly one successor node, distinct reds charge to distinct children — an injection from the red nodes into the black nodes of those $h$. Therefore at most half of them are red, at least half are black, and all of these black nodes lie below the root: $$bh(\text{root}) \;\ge\; h/2, \qquad \text{that is,} \quad h \le 2\,bh(\text{root}).$$

blocks.heading: Combining the halves
blocks.body: Apply Part 1 at the root and insert Part 2: $$n \;\ge\; 2^{bh(\text{root})} - 1 \;\ge\; 2^{h/2} - 1.$$ Add 1 and take logarithms: $n + 1 \ge 2^{h/2}$, so $\lg(n+1) \ge h/2$, i.e. $$h \;\le\; 2\lg(n+1).$$ Since $h$ bounds every root-to-leaf path, the $O(h)$ operations of Chapter 12 become $O(\lg n)$ worst-case — and, once Sections 13.3 and 13.4 are done, so do INSERT and DELETE.

The factor 2 is honest, not slack: a tree whose every path alternates black-red-black-red below a black root attains $h = 2\,bh(\text{root})$, so the bound is tight up to lower-order terms. Height-balanced **AVL trees** do better — $h \le 1.4405\lg n$ — but they pay on updates: an AVL insertion can rotate at every level of the tree, while a red-black insertion rotates at most twice and a deletion at most three times. That trade — a slightly taller tree for far cheaper updates — is exactly why red-black trees dominate systems practice.

intro: Rebalancing needs a primitive that restructures a binary search tree locally without breaking the search-tree property. Rotation is that primitive: it rehangs two nodes and three subtrees with a constant number of pointer writes, preserves the inorder key sequence exactly, and costs $\Theta(1)$. The fixup procedures of the next two sections will change the tree with nothing but recolorings and rotations.
objectives: Execute LEFT-ROTATE and RIGHT-ROTATE by hand, listing every pointer that changes
Prove that a rotation preserves the binary-search-tree property
Explain why rotations cost Θ(1) and how few of them the fixups ever need

concepts.statement: **LEFT-ROTATE**$(T, x)$ — which requires $x.right \ne$ NIL — promotes $x$'s right child $y$: $y$ takes $x$'s place in the tree, $x$ becomes $y$'s **left** child, and $y$'s old left subtree $\beta$ is rehung as $x$'s new right subtree. **RIGHT-ROTATE** is the mirror image, and the two operations are inverses of each other.
concepts.detail: Only the parentage of $x$, $y$ and the root of $\beta$ changes — every other node keeps its parent, its children, its color and its key.

concepts.statement: `LEFT-ROTATE(T, x)`: set `y = x.right`; set `x.right = y.left` (y's left subtree becomes x's right); if `y.left ≠ T.nil`, set `y.left.p = x`; set `y.p = x.p` (link x's parent to y — the root case, the left-child case, or the right-child case); finally `y.left = x` and `x.p = y`. Six pointer writes in total.
concepts.detail: The three-way parent test (root / left child / right child) is the only case analysis. Forgetting the `y.left.p = x` write leaves a stale parent pointer — the classic rotation bug.

concepts.statement: Read the keys around the rotated pair and both subtrees: the inorder sequence is $\alpha, x, \beta, y, \gamma$ **before** the rotation and $\alpha, x, \beta, y, \gamma$ **after** it. Since the inorder sequence is untouched and no node outside the pair moves, the binary-search-tree property survives every rotation.
concepts.detail: This is why fixups may rotate freely — no key comparison ever needs rechecking, and rotations are the only structural changes they make.

concepts.statement: A rotation is $\Theta(1)$: a fixed handful of pointer writes, no key moves, no traversal. RB-INSERT-FIXUP performs **at most 2 rotations** in total (both while converting case 2 into case 3) and RB-DELETE-FIXUP **at most 3**; everything else the fixups do is recoloring.
concepts.detail: Colors ride along through a rotation untouched — rotation changes parentage, never colors. When a fixup wants colors changed, it recolors explicitly before or after rotating.

concepts.statement: RIGHT-ROTATE($y$) with left child $x$ sets $y.left = x.right$, $x.right = y$, rewiring parents symmetrically to LEFT-ROTATE. Same $\Theta(1)$ pointer count, same BST-preservation proof with $\le$ and $\ge$ swapped.
concepts.detail: Fixups call whichever direction the violation leans: insertion cases 2-3 use one of each, deletion uses both across its four cases. Implementing one rotation and mirroring $left \leftrightarrow right$ yields the other.

figures.caption: The two rotations, with red-black colors riding along. LEFT-ROTATE$(T, x)$ promotes $x$'s right child $y$: $x$ drops to become $y$'s left child, and $y$'s old left subtree $\beta$ moves to $x$'s right — the inorder sequence $\alpha, x, \beta, y, \gamma$ is identical before and after, so the search-tree property is preserved. RIGHT-ROTATE$(T, y)$ is the exact inverse: read the figure right to left. Colors never change during the rotation itself: $x$ stays black, $y$ stays red.

examples.title: Rotating a three-node subtree by hand
examples.problem: A BST has root 7 with right child 15, and 15 has left child 11 and right child 22 (all other children NIL). Perform LEFT-ROTATE(T, 7) and verify that the search-tree property survives.

steps.label: Step 1: Precondition and setup
steps.text: LEFT-ROTATE requires $7.right \ne$ NIL — it is 15, so set $y = 15$.

steps.label: Step 2: Move β = 11
steps.text: Set $7.right = 11$ and $11.p = 7$: the subtree rooted at 11 moves from 15's left to 7's right.

steps.label: Step 3: Rehang the pair
steps.text: Set $15.p = 7.p = \text{NIL}$, so 15 becomes the root; then $15.left = 7$ and $7.p = 15$. Node 22 stays 15's right child untouched.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify
steps.text: The result has root 15 with left child 7 (whose right child is 11) and right child 22. Inorder before: $7, 11, 15, 22$; inorder after: $7, 11, 15, 22$ — identical, so the BST property is preserved.

examples.result: Left-rotating about 7 swaps the pair (7, 15) into (15, 7) and rehangs β = 11, using six pointer writes; the inorder sequence — hence the search-tree property — is untouched.

examples.title: Inorder preserved through rotation
examples.problem: LEFT-ROTATE on $x = 10$ with right child $y = 15$ ($y.left = 12$). List inorder before and after.

steps.label: Before
steps.text: Subtree inorder: $10, 12, 15$ (plus $x.left$ before $10$ and $y.right$ after $15$).

steps.label: Rotate
steps.text: $y$ becomes subtree root; $x.right = 12$, $12.p = x$; $y.left$ was $12$, now $x$ is $y.left$.

steps.label: After
steps.text: Subtree inorder: $10, 12, 15$ unchanged: $x$, then $y.left = 12$, then $y$. Only parentage moved.

steps.label: Keys outside
steps.text: Nodes outside the $x$-$y$ pair keep their relative order: rotation is a local rehang of three subtrees $\alpha = x.left$, $\beta = y.left$, $\gamma = y.right$.

examples.result: Inorder $10, 12, 15$ before and after: rotations restructure without reordering, the invariant fixups rely on.

keyTakeaways: LEFT-ROTATE(T, x) promotes x's right child y, demotes x to y's left child, and rehangs y's old left subtree as x's right; RIGHT-ROTATE is its inverse.
A rotation is Θ(1) pointer writes and preserves the inorder sequence α, x, β, y, γ — hence the BST property and all colors.
The fixups need remarkably few rotations — at most 2 per insertion and 3 per deletion; all other repair work is recoloring.

quiz.q: LEFT-ROTATE(T, x) can be legally called whenever:
options: x is the root of the tree
quiz.explanation: The single precondition is a non-NIL right child — the node being promoted must exist. Color, rootness, and the left child are all irrelevant.

quiz.q: In LEFT-ROTATE(T, x), the subtree β rooted at y's old left child ends up as:
options: the new root of the whole tree
quiz.explanation: β holds keys between x and y, so it must sit between them after the swap: it becomes x's new right subtree (equivalently, it keeps its inorder position).

quiz.q: Which of the following does a rotation preserve?
options: The BST property and every node's color
The BST property and every node's depth
Nothing — the fixup must recheck the tree
quiz.explanation: Keys, subtree contents and colors all ride along untouched. Node depths do change — x drops one level and y rises one — which is exactly the rebalancing effect.

quiz.q: Across an entire RB-INSERT, including the fixup, how many rotations can occur at most?
quiz.explanation: Case 1 never rotates (it iterates by recoloring); cases 2 and 3 together perform at most 2 rotations and then terminate the loop.

intro: Insertion splices a new red node z into the tree with an ordinary BST insert, then repairs whatever the splice broke. Because z starts red, only two properties can possibly fail — the black-root rule and the no-red-parent rule — and RB-INSERT-FIXUP chases the red-red violation up the tree, trading recolorings for at most two rotations before settling.
objectives: Explain why the new node is colored red and which two properties can be violated
Apply cases 1, 2 and 3 of RB-INSERT-FIXUP, including their mirror images
Show that the fixup terminates in O(lg n) with at most two rotations

concepts.statement: Insert $z$ exactly as TREE-INSERT from Chapter 12 — descend from the root comparing keys, splice $z$ in as the appropriate child with both pointers set to $T.nil$ — then set $z.color = \text{RED}$ and call **RB-INSERT-FIXUP**$(T, z)$.
concepts.detail: The BST property is intact by construction; only colors can now be wrong.

concepts.term: Why red — and what can break
concepts.statement: A red leaf changes no black count on any path — property 5 cannot be violated — and property 3 is untouched. Only **property 2** (if $z$ becomes the new root) and **property 4** (if $z$ and $z.p$ are both red) can fail. RB-INSERT-FIXUP maintains the loop invariant that these are the only violations present.
concepts.detail: That invariant is why the loop condition simply tests the parent's color: while $z.p$ is red, property 4 is broken at $z$, and nothing else is wrong.

concepts.statement: Let $y$ be $z$'s uncle (the sibling of $z.p$). If $y$ is **red**, recolor $z.p$ and $y$ black and the grandparent $z.p.p$ red, then set $z = z.p.p$ and continue the loop. Every path through the grandparent still sees one black among $\{z.p, y\}$ where it used to see the grandparent's black, so black-heights survive.
concepts.detail: Case 1 is the only case that iterates — the red-red violation climbs two levels per step, so the loop runs at most $O(\lg n)$ times, performing no rotations at all.

concepts.term: Case 2 — black uncle, z a right child
concepts.statement: If the uncle is **black** and $z$ is a **right** child (with $z.p$ a left child; the mirror cases swap left and right), set $z = z.p$ and LEFT-ROTATE$(T, z)$: the configuration becomes case 3 with the labels of $z$ and its old parent exchanged.
concepts.detail: Case 2 performs no recoloring — it merely straightens the zig-zag into a straight line so that case 3 can finish the job.

concepts.term: Case 3 — black uncle, z a left child
concepts.statement: Recolor $z.p$ black and $z.p.p$ red, then RIGHT-ROTATE$(T, z.p.p)$. The rotation leaves a black node above the red pair, no red-red violation anywhere, and every root-to-leaf black count restored — the loop terminates, and its final line forces the root black (repairing property 2 if needed).
concepts.detail: Cases 2 and 3 always run as a pair and end the fixup: one or two rotations in total, then done.

figures.caption: Insertion fixup **case 3** — the terminal case (uncle black, $z$ a left child, shown for $z.p$ a left child; mirror images swap left and right). The parent B (= $z.p$) and grandparent C swap colors, then RIGHT-ROTATE(C) promotes B. Every path through the fragment sees exactly one black among B and C, before and after — the swap preserves all black-heights — and the red pair B–z is destroyed because B is now black. In the after-tree every red node has a black parent. Case 2 (z a right child) first left-rotates the same configuration into this shape, which is why the two cases share a rotation budget of 2.

examples.title: Growing a red-black tree: 41, 38, 31, 12
examples.problem: Starting from an empty red-black tree, insert the keys 41, 38, 31 and 12 in order, showing which fixup case fires at each step.

steps.label: Step 1: Insert 41
steps.text: 41 is spliced in as the root and colored red — property 2 is violated, so the fixup's final line recolors the root black. Tree: 41 (black).

steps.label: Step 2: Insert 38
steps.text: 38 becomes the red left child of 41. Its parent is black, so no property is violated and the fixup loop never runs.

steps.label: Step 3: Insert 31 — Case 3
steps.text: 31 is the red left child of 38, which is red: property 4 is violated. The uncle is 41's right child — the black sentinel — and $z = 31$ is a left child, so **case 3** fires: color 38 black and 41 red, then RIGHT-ROTATE(41). The tree becomes 38 (black) with red children 31 and 41 — one rotation, done.

steps.label: Step 4: Insert 12 — Case 1
steps.text: 12 is the red left child of 31 (red) — red-red again. The uncle is 41, which is **red**: **case 1** fires. Recolor 31 and 41 black, recolor the grandparent 38 red, and set $z = 38$. Since $z$ is now the root, the loop exits and the final line makes 38 black again.

examples.result: Final tree: 38 (black) root with black children 31 and 41, and 12 red under 31. Every root-to-NIL path crosses exactly two black nodes besides the root — valid, built with one rotation and one recoloring cascade.

examples.title: Uncle-red chain of two levels
examples.problem: Insert $12$ then $5$ into red-black tree $41(B), 38(R, left of 41), 31(B, left of 38)$ style chain to force two successive case-1 recolorings.

steps.label: Insert 12 red
steps.text: Parent $31$ red, uncle (right child of $38$) black? To force case 1 need red uncle: use tree where $38$ has red sibling: recolor parent+uncle black, grandparent red, move $z$ to grandparent.

steps.label: Propagate
steps.text: $z$ rises two levels per case-1: each absorbs one black-height unit upward with no rotations.

steps.label: Terminate
steps.text: Chain ends at red root (recolor black, height $+1$) or at a black-uncle case 2/3 (at most $2$ rotations). Hence $O(\lg n)$ recolorings, $\le 2$ rotations.

steps.label: Count
steps.text: Two case-1 steps plus one case-2/3 pair is the worst insertion pattern: $O(\lg n)$ time, constant rotations.

examples.result: Case 1 propagates red-red upward; at most $2$ rotations ever close it: insertion is $O(\lg n)$ with $O(1)$ structural changes.

keyTakeaways: Insert the new node red: a red leaf cannot disturb any black count, so only the black-root rule (property 2) and the no-adjacent-reds rule (property 4) can break.
Case 1 (red uncle) recolors and climbs two levels; case 2 (black uncle, zig-zag) rotates into case 3; case 3 (black uncle, straight line) recolors and rotates once, ending the loop.
The fixup runs in O(lg n) — only case 1 iterates, moving the violation up two levels at a time — and performs at most 2 rotations.

quiz.q: Right after the plain insertion of a red node z into a red-black tree, which properties can be violated?
quiz.explanation: A red leaf leaves every black count intact (property 5 safe) and NILs untouched (property 3 safe); only the root's color (property 2) and a possible red parent (property 4) can be wrong.

quiz.q: RB-INSERT-FIXUP case 1 (red uncle) resolves the local violation by:
options: recoloring the parent and uncle black, the grandparent red, then moving z to the grandparent
quiz.explanation: The recoloring fixes the red-red pair at z but may create a new one two levels up — hence z = z.p.p and the loop continues. No rotation happens in case 1.

quiz.q: Why is the newly inserted node colored red rather than black?
options: red nodes are faster to search through
a red leaf changes no black count on any path, so property 5 cannot be violated
property 1 requires every new node to be red
quiz.explanation: Inserting black would add one black to exactly the paths through the new node, breaking property 5 everywhere; red is the only safe initial color.

quiz.q: During a single execution of RB-INSERT-FIXUP, the case that can repeat is:
quiz.explanation: Only case 1 iterates (the violation climbs to the grandparent); case 2 converts to case 3, and case 3 terminates the loop — so at most 2 rotations overall.

intro: Deletion is where red-black trees earn their keep. Removing a black node shortens the black count of every path that used to pass through it, so RB-DELETE-FIXUP does not patch a violated rule directly — it pushes a conceptual extra black up the tree until a rotation absorbs it or a red node soaks it up. The case analysis is longer than insertion's, but the machinery is identical: recolor, rotate, terminate.
objectives: Trace RB-DELETE, including when and why RB-DELETE-FIXUP is invoked
Interpret the extra black and apply the four sibling cases and their mirrors
Bound the work: O(lg n) time and at most 3 rotations per deletion

concepts.statement: Delete as in an ordinary BST, with RB-TRANSPLANT doing the splicing and $T.nil$ standing in for absent children: if $z$ has fewer than two children, $z$ itself is removed; otherwise $z$'s successor $y$ is moved into $z$'s place. Record **y-original-color** — the color of the node that was removed or moved. Call **RB-DELETE-FIXUP**$(T, x)$ exactly when that color was **black**, where $x$ is the node (possibly the sentinel) that took $y$'s place.
concepts.detail: When the successor is used, the algorithm first unhooks $y$ from its parent and later colors it with $z$'s old color, so the only color actually lost from the tree is y-original-color.

concepts.statement: If the removed or moved node was black, one black node is now missing from every path that passed through the spot $x$ occupies. CLRS models this by saying $x$ carries an **extra black**: $x$ is *doubly black* (its blackness counts twice) or *red-and-black* if $x$ happens to be red. The fixup must push this extra black up the tree until it vanishes — into a rotation, or into a red node turning black.
concepts.detail: The extra black is conceptual bookkeeping: it explains how property 5 gets restored, while the observable violations the loop tests for are black-height imbalance and, occasionally, a red root.

concepts.term: Case 1 — the sibling w is red
concepts.statement: If $x$'s sibling $w$ is **red**, then $w$'s children must be black. Recolor $w$ black and $x.p$ red, then rotate $x.p$ so that $w$ becomes $x$'s new sibling — which is black. Case 1 costs one rotation and cannot recur; it merely converts the configuration into one of cases 2, 3 or 4.
concepts.detail: The rotation moves $x$ under a red parent with a black sibling — the same shape the black-sibling cases know how to finish.

concepts.term: Cases 2–4 — the sibling w is black
concepts.statement: **Case 2** (both of $w$'s children black): take one black off $x$ and one off $w$ — recolor $w$ red — and pass the extra black to $x.p$, then iterate. **Case 3** ($w$'s near child red, far child black): one rotation and recoloring converts it to case 4. **Case 4** ($w$'s far child red): recolor and rotate so the extra black is absorbed into the new parent; the tree is valid and the loop ends.
concepts.detail: Case 2 is the only case that iterates — and if $x.p$ was red, the extra black immediately soaks into it and the loop exits after recoloring it black.

concepts.statement: Case 1 occurs at most once, cases 3 and 4 always finish, and only case 2 climbs — so RB-DELETE-FIXUP performs **at most 3 rotations** and $O(\lg n)$ recolorings. Deletion, like every other operation, runs in $O(\lg n)$.
concepts.detail: As with insertion, the mirror cases (x a right child) simply exchange left and right throughout the analysis.

examples.title: Shrinking a red-black tree by three deletions
examples.problem: Start from the Section 13.1 tree: root 7 black; red children 3 and 10; black grandchildren 1, 5, 8, 12. Delete 1, then 12, then 5.

steps.label: Step 1: Delete 1 — a black leaf
steps.text: The sentinel moves into 1's place carrying the extra black ($x$ is doubly black). Its sibling is 5 — black with two black NIL children — so **case 2** fires: recolor 5 red and push the extra black to the parent 3. Node 3 is red-and-black, so the loop exits and 3 becomes plain black.

steps.label: Step 2: Check the state
steps.text: Tree: 7 black; 3 black with red right child 5; 10 red with black children 8 and 12. Every root-to-NIL path again crosses exactly two black nodes besides the root — property 5 restored with zero rotations.

steps.label: Step 3: Delete 12 — case 2 again
steps.text: 12 is a black leaf; its sibling 8 is black with two black NIL children: **case 2** recolors 8 red and lifts the extra black to 10, which is red — so 10 turns black. Tree: 7 black; 3 black (child 5 red); 10 black (child 8 red).

steps.label: Step 4: Delete 5 — a red leaf
steps.text: The removed node is red: no black count changes on any path, so no fixup is invoked at all. The red node simply vanishes.

examples.result: Final tree: 7 black with children 3 (black) and 10 (black, with red child 8) — still a valid red-black tree. Two case-2 absorptions, one free red deletion, and not a single rotation.

examples.title: Deleting a red leaf needs no fixup
examples.problem: Delete red leaf $12$ from a valid red-black tree. Show RB-DELETE skips FIXUP.

steps.label: Color check
steps.text: Removed node $z = 12$ red: no black-height on any path changes, since red nodes contribute $0$ to the count.

steps.label: Transplant
steps.text: Replace $12$ by $T.nil$ (black leaf): all root-to-leaf black counts unchanged.

steps.label: No extra black
steps.text: FIXUP runs only when the removed node was black; here $y$'s original color was red, so RB-DELETE returns immediately.

steps.label: Contrast
steps.text: Deleting a black leaf creates the double-black that cases 1-4 chase: color, not position, decides whether fixup runs.

examples.result: Red-leaf deletion is $O(\lg n)$ search plus $O(1)$ splice with no fixup; black deletions pay the $O(\lg n)$ four-case repair.

keyTakeaways: The fixup runs exactly when the removed or moved node was black; deleting a red node never disturbs a black count.
The extra black rides up through case 2, gets re-aimed by case 3, and is absorbed by case 4's recolor-and-rotate — or simply soaks into any red node it lands on.
Deletion costs O(lg n) with at most 3 rotations; the mirror-image cases swap left and right throughout.

quiz.q: RB-DELETE-FIXUP is invoked exactly when:
options: the node that was removed or moved had black as its original color
the deleted key z was red
the root is the node being deleted
quiz.explanation: Only losing a black node can change black counts (property 5). A red removal leaves every path's black count alone, so no repair is needed.

quiz.q: In case 2 (black sibling, both of its children black), the fixup:
options: recolors the sibling red and pushes the extra black to the parent, possibly iterating
recolors the sibling red and stops immediately
swaps the colors of x and x.p
quiz.explanation: Stripping one black from both x and the sibling keeps those paths balanced; the parent inherits the extra black, and the loop continues — ending at once if the parent was red.

quiz.q: Which case ends the fixup by rotating so that the extra black is fully absorbed into the tree?
options: the case where x is the root
quiz.explanation: Case 4 exploits the sibling's red far child: after recoloring and one rotation, the black that was missing is restored on every path and the loop terminates with a valid tree.

quiz.q: Across a full RB-DELETE, including the fixup, the maximum number of rotations is:
quiz.explanation: Case 1 can happen at most once (1 rotation), then case 3 (1 rotation) followed by case 4 (1 rotation) — never more than 3 in total.

intro: Chapter 12 answered order queries — what is the $i$-th smallest key? — with an $\Theta(n)$ scan, because a plain BST stores no order information beyond its shape. Augment every node of a red-black tree with the size of its subtree and both directions of the query collapse to $O(\lg n)$: OS-SELECT consumes ranks while descending the tree, and OS-RANK produces them while climbing back up.
objectives: Define the order-statistic tree and its size field, including the sentinel's value
Execute OS-SELECT and OS-RANK step by step with real subtree sizes
Explain how insertions, deletions and rotations maintain the size field in O(lg n)

concepts.statement: An **order-statistic tree** is a red-black tree in which each node $x$ stores an extra field $x.size$: the number of internal nodes in the subtree rooted at $x$, **including $x$ itself**. The sentinel satisfies $T.nil.size = 0$, so the identity $x.size = x.left.size + x.right.size + 1$ holds at every node.
concepts.detail: Nothing else changes: the tree still obeys all five red-black properties, and the size field is carried through every update — the machinery of Section 14.2.

concepts.statement: **OS-SELECT**$(x, i)$ returns the node with the $i$-th smallest key in the subtree rooted at $x$: let $r = x.left.size + 1$ — the rank of $x$ **within its own subtree**. If $i = r$, return $x$. If $i < r$, recurse into the left subtree with the same $i$. If $i > r$, recurse into the right subtree with $i - r$.
concepts.detail: Each level does $O(1)$ work, so on a red-black tree (height $O(\lg n)$ by Lemma 13.1) OS-SELECT runs in $O(\lg n)$.

concepts.statement: **OS-RANK**$(T, x)$ computes the rank of node $x$ among all keys: initialize $r = x.left.size + 1$ and $y = x$; while $y \ne T.root$, if $y$ is a **right** child, add $y.p.left.size + 1$ to $r$ (that whole subtree precedes $y$), then set $y = y.p$. Return $r$.
concepts.detail: Each iteration climbs one level, so OS-RANK is also $O(\lg n)$. A left child adds nothing: its parent precedes it, but so does everything the loop already counted.

concepts.statement: On **insertion**, increment the size of every node on the descent path before splicing the new node in — $O(\lg n)$ writes — and give each of the fixup's at most 2 rotations its $O(1)$ size fix. On **deletion**, sizes change only for nodes on the path from the root to the physically removed node, plus $O(1)$ nodes per rotation (at most 3) — again $O(\lg n)$.
concepts.detail: Either operation keeps the $O(\lg n)$ running time: the maintenance work rides along the path the algorithm already walks.

concepts.statement: $\text{OS-SELECT}(T, \text{OS-RANK}(T, x)) = x$: the two procedures read the same size bookkeeping from opposite directions — select spends ranks going down, rank collects them coming up. Together they make the tree a **dynamic sorted array**: insert, delete, locate the $i$-th smallest, and rank any key, all in $O(\lg n)$.
concepts.detail: This is the first payoff of augmentation: an operation Chapter 12 could not do faster than $\Theta(n)$ now costs one root-to-node walk.

figures.caption: An order-statistic tree on the keys $\{14, 17, 21, 26, 30, 41, 47\}$ — a red-black tree with one extra field: the subtree size (green badges), with $T.nil.size = 0$. OS-SELECT$(T, 5)$ descends 26 → 41 → 30: at the root, 26's own rank is $3 + 1 = 4 < 5$, so the search continues into the right subtree for the $(5 - 4)$-th = 1st key; at 41, the rank $r = 1 + 1 = 2 > 1$ sends the search left to 30, where $r = 0 + 1 = 1 = i$ and 30 is returned. OS-RANK(30) climbs the reverse path — 30 → 41 → 26 — adding $26.left.size + 1 = 4$ when it passes 41 as a right child, giving rank 5.

examples.title: Select and rank on seven keys
examples.problem: The order-statistic tree of the figure has root 26 (size 7), left child 17 (size 3) with children 14 and 21 (size 1 each), and right child 41 (size 3) with children 30 and 47 (size 1 each). Find the 5th smallest key, then compute the rank of key 30.

steps.label: Step 1: OS-SELECT at the root
steps.text: At 26: $r = 26.left.size + 1 = 17.size + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4$. Since $i = 5 > 4$, the answer lies in the right subtree with the adjusted order statistic $i - r = 1$ — the smallest key of 41's subtree.

steps.label: Step 2: OS-SELECT at 41
steps.text: At 41: $r = 41.left.size + 1 = 30.size + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2$. Since $i = 1 < 2$, the 1st smallest key of this subtree lies in 41's left subtree — descend to 30.

steps.label: Step 3: OS-SELECT at 30
steps.text: At 30: $r = 30.left.size + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1$, which equals $i$ — return 30. The key 41 itself was never even tested as a candidate: its rank 2 within its own subtree already overshoots $i = 1$.

steps.label: Step 4: OS-RANK of 30 — the climb
steps.text: Start $r = 30.left.size + 1 = 1$, $y = 30$. Node 30 is a left child of 41 — nothing added. Node 41 is a right child of the root 26, so add $26.left.size + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4$: $r = 1 + 4 = 5$. The climb ends at the root.

examples.result: The 5th smallest key is 30 — and the rank of 30 is 5, since the sorted order is 14, 17, 21, 26, 30, 41, 47. Select and rank agree, as inverses must.

examples.title: Maintaining size through insertion
examples.problem: Insert key $8$ into order-statistic tree with root $10$ ($size = 7$). Update sizes on the descent.

steps.label: Descend
steps.text: $8 < 10$: go left, increment $10.size$ to $8$ on the way down (every ancestor's subtree gains one node).

steps.label: Continue
steps.text: At node $5$ ($size = 3$): $8 > 5$, go right, increment $5.size$ to $4$.

steps.label: Insert
steps.text: At $nil$ under $9$: splice red node $8$ with $size = 1$; $T.nil.size = 0$ by definition.

steps.label: Rotations
steps.text: If FIXUP rotates, recompute the two rotated nodes' sizes from children ($size[x] = size[left]+size[right]+1$): $O(1)$ per rotation, $O(\lg n)$ total.

examples.result: Sizes on the $10 \to 5 \to 9$ path each $+1$; rotations repair locally: augmentation costs $O(\lg n)$ per update.

keyTakeaways: An order-statistic tree is a red-black tree with one extra field per node: x.size, the internal-node count of its subtree, with T.nil.size = 0.
OS-SELECT descends comparing i with r = left.size + 1; OS-RANK climbs adding left.size + 1 at each right-child edge — both O(lg n).
Sizes ride through updates in O(lg n): one increment or decrement per level of the search path plus O(1) work per rotation.

quiz.q: In an order-statistic tree, the size field of an internal node whose two children are both the NIL sentinel equals:
options: its key's rank in the tree
quiz.explanation: size counts internal nodes only — the node itself — while both NIL children contribute $T.nil.size = 0$. The rank is a global notion; size is purely local to the subtree.

quiz.q: OS-SELECT(x, i) computes r = x.left.size + 1 at each node because:
options: the left subtree contains exactly r nodes
x's rank within its own subtree is r: all left.size nodes precede it, then x itself
the right subtree always contains r − 1 nodes
quiz.explanation: Within the subtree rooted at x, exactly x.left.size keys are smaller than x's key — so x occupies position left.size + 1, the pivot the comparison against i needs.

quiz.q: While OS-RANK climbs from a node toward the root, when does it add to the running rank r?
options: when y is a left child
when y is a right child — the parent's entire left subtree plus the parent precede y
only at the root, all at once
quiz.explanation: When y is a right child, everything in y.p's left subtree and y.p itself come before y in sorted order — contributing y.p.left.size + 1 to the rank.

quiz.q: To maintain size fields during an insertion, the nodes whose sizes must change are:
options: all n nodes of the tree
the nodes on the path from the root down to the new node — each incremented by 1
only the new node and its parent
quiz.explanation: Exactly the ancestors of the inserted node gain one internal descendant — the O(lg n)-long search path — plus O(1) rotated nodes if the fixup rotates.

quiz.q: In OS-SELECT at node $x$ with $x.left.size = 7$, searching for rank $i = 8$ does what?
options: Returns the minimum of the right subtree
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: subtree sizes maintained, $x.left.size = 7$, target rank $i = 8$. Step 2 — Governing rank: $r = x.left.size + 1$ counts keys preceding $x$ within its subtree. Step 3 — Comparison: $r = 7 + 1 = 8 = i$, the exact-hit case, so the procedure returns $x$ itself. Step 4 — Sanity check: $i < r$ would descend left with unchanged $i$, $i > r$ would descend right with $i - r$, and the three cases partition all ranks. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: descending left suits $i \le 7$, the minimum suits $i = 9$ only when the right child is a leaf path, and the successor belongs to a different query. Step 6 — Conclude: return $x$.

intro: The size field of Section 14.1 was not luck — it is an instance of a general method. CLRS distills augmenting a data structure into a four-step recipe, and Theorem 14.1 identifies exactly when an augmented red-black tree maintains itself for free: whenever each node's new field can be recomputed from the node and its two children alone.
objectives: List and apply the four steps of the augmentation recipe
State Theorem 14.1 and sketch why rotations are the only structural obstacle
Recognize fields the theorem does not cover — and why they break

concepts.statement: To augment a data structure: (1) **choose** an underlying data structure (a red-black tree, here); (2) **augment** it — add the field you want (size, max, height, …); (3) **maintain** the field through every modifying operation without changing the operation's asymptotic running time; (4) **use** it — design the new operations the field enables (OS-SELECT, OS-RANK, INTERVAL-SEARCH).
concepts.detail: CLRS warns the steps are not a one-shot pipeline: expect to iterate when step 3 or 4 exposes a poor choice made in step 2.

concepts.statement: Suppose a field $f$ of a red-black tree node can be computed, for every node $x$, from the information stored in $x$, $x.left$ and $x.right$ — including their $f$ fields — in $O(1)$ time, and does not depend on colors. Then red-black trees maintain $f$ through insertion and deletion with $O(1)$ extra work per rotation and $O(1)$ work per node on the search path: the $O(\lg n)$ running times are unchanged.
concepts.detail: Subtree size qualifies ($x.size = x.left.size + x.right.size + 1$); so do subtree maximum, subtree height, and the max endpoint of Section 14.3.

concepts.statement: Insertion and deletion change tree **structure** only through rotations — at most 2 per insert, 3 per delete — and each rotation re-parents only $O(1)$ nodes, whose $f$ values are recomputed in $O(1)$ from their new children. The $O(\lg n)$ nodes on the search path whose subtrees gained or lost a node are updated in $O(1)$ each as the algorithm already walks past them. The $O(\lg n)$ **color flips** of the fixups never touch $f$ — that is where the color-independence hypothesis earns its keep.
concepts.detail: This is the deeper reason Section 13's analysis was done so carefully: the rotation budget of the fixups is exactly the maintenance budget of any augmentation.

concepts.statement: The hypothesis is local: $f(x)$ may look at $x$ and its children **only**. The **depth** of a node depends on its ancestors — one insertion can invalidate $\Theta(n)$ stored depths at once. **Black-height** fails more subtly: $bh(x)$ is computable from a child's $bh$, but a single color flip changes the black-height of **every ancestor** of the recolored node, so the fixups' $O(\lg n)$ recolorings ripple upward and the proof's color-independence is lost.
concepts.detail: For fields outside Theorem 14.1, one changes the data structure, stores a different field, or pays for the maintenance explicitly — never assume augmentation is free.

concepts.statement: Store $min[x] = \min(x.key, min[x.left], min[x.right])$ with $min[T.nil] = \infty$: recomputable from children in $O(1)$, hence maintainable through rotations by Theorem 14.1. Supports SUBTREE-MINIMUM queries in $O(\lg n)$.
concepts.detail: Same recipe as size: choose field ($min$), define from children, verify rotations touch only $O(1)$ nodes. Max, sum and height all qualify; depth and inorder rank do not, since they depend on ancestors, not children.

examples.title: Two writes maintain size through a rotation
examples.problem: A fragment of an order-statistic tree has node x with left subtree α of 4 internal nodes, and right child y whose subtrees are β (3 internal nodes) and γ (5 internal nodes). Show that LEFT-ROTATE(x) preserves every size in the fragment.

steps.label: Step 1: Sizes before
steps.text: $y.size = 3 + 5 + 1 = 9$ (β + γ + y itself). $x.size = 4 + 9 + 1 = 14$ — x roots the whole fragment, which holds $4 + 3 + 5 + 2 = 14$ internal nodes.

steps.label: Step 2: The rotation moves β
steps.text: After LEFT-ROTATE(x), x's children are α and β, and y's children are x and γ. No subtree's contents change — only parentage.

steps.label: Step 3: Recompute, in order
steps.text: First $x.size = 4 + 3 + 1 = 8$ (α + β + x); then $y.size = x.size + 5 + 1 = 8 + 5 + 1 = 14$ — y now roots the same 14-node fragment. The order matters: y's update must read x's **new** size.

steps.label: Step 4: Nobody else changes
steps.text: Every other node of the tree has the same subtree as before — ancestors of the fragment kept all their descendants, so their sizes remain correct.

examples.result: Exactly two O(1) writes re-establish every size in the rotated fragment — precisely what Theorem 14.1 promises for any field, on any rotation.

examples.title: Augmenting with subtree minima
examples.problem: After LEFT-ROTATE on $x$ with $y = x.right$, recompute $min$ for $x$ then $y$.

steps.label: Before
steps.text: $min[x]$ and $min[y]$ covered old subtrees; rotation rehangs $y.left = \beta$ to $x.right$.

steps.label: Fix $x$ first
steps.text: $min[x] = \min(x.key, min[x.left], min[\beta])$: $x$'s children are final, so $x$ is final.

steps.label: Fix $y$
steps.text: $min[y] = \min(y.key, min[x], min[y.right])$: uses the fresh $min[x]$.

steps.label: Order matters
steps.text: Bottom-up ($x$ before $y$) is forced: $y$'s field depends on $x$'s. Same two-write pattern as size maintenance.

examples.result: Two $O(1)$ recomputations restore $min$ after any rotation; the recipe generalizes to any child-computable field.

keyTakeaways: Recipe: choose the structure, add the field, maintain it through the modifying operations, then exploit it with new operations — iterating as needed.
Theorem 14.1: fields computable in O(1) from node + children (colors excluded) ride along for free — O(1) per rotation and O(1) per search-path node.
Locality is the whole game: depth fails because it looks at ancestors, and black-height fails because color flips ripple upward through ancestors.

quiz.q: The four-step augmentation recipe, in order, is:
quiz.explanation: Choose an underlying structure, add the field, keep it maintained through updates without asymptotic cost, then build the new operations that exploit it.

quiz.q: Theorem 14.1 guarantees maintenance for a field f when:
options: f changes only O(1) values per insertion
f can be computed from the node and its two children in O(1) time
f is monotone along root-to-leaf paths
f depends only on the node's key
quiz.explanation: Locality of computation — from x, x.left and x.right (colors aside) — is the hypothesis; then rotations cost O(1) each and the search path O(lg n) total, both absorbed.

quiz.q: Which field does the recipe NOT cover, and for what reason?
options: subtree size — too many nodes change per insert
subtree maximum — it needs a full subtree scan
node depth — one insertion can change Θ(n) stored depths
number of NIL leaves below a node — not locally computable
quiz.explanation: Depth depends on ancestors: deepening one internal edge invalidates every descendant's stored depth — Θ(n) of them — so the locality hypothesis fails. (Leaf counts, like sizes, are locally computable.)

quiz.q: During RB-INSERT-FIXUP, the structural events that require augmented-field updates are:
quiz.explanation: Color flips are invisible to any field that satisfies Theorem 14.1's hypothesis; only the constant number of rotations re-parent nodes, each fixable in O(1).

intro: An interval tree answers whether anything overlaps $[a, b]$ in logarithmic time by keying a red-black tree on each interval's left endpoint and augmenting each node with the maximum right endpoint in its subtree. The overlap relation splits into exactly three exhaustive cases — the interval trichotomy — and the max field is precisely what lets the search prune one child at every step.
objectives: Apply the closed-interval overlap test and state the interval trichotomy
Define the max augmentation and verify it on a concrete tree
Trace INTERVAL-SEARCH and explain why each turn it takes is safe

concepts.statement: A **closed interval** is a pair $[a, b]$ with $a \le b$. Two intervals $i = [i.low, i.high]$ and $i' = [i'.low, i'.high]$ **overlap** exactly when $i.low \le i'.high$ **and** $i'.low \le i.high$ — each starts no later than the other ends.
concepts.detail: Closed endpoints make single-point sharing count as overlap: $[3, 7]$ and $[7, 9]$ overlap at 7.

concepts.statement: For any two closed intervals, **exactly one** of three relations holds: (1) they overlap; (2) $i$ lies strictly left of $i'$, meaning $i.high < i'.low$; (3) $i$ lies strictly right of $i'$, meaning $i'.high < i.low$. No fourth possibility exists.
concepts.detail: The trichotomy is the decision backbone of every interval algorithm — overlap tests, sweep-line event ordering, and the search below all branch on it.

concepts.statement: An **interval tree** is a red-black tree keyed by the low endpoint $x.int.low$, in which each node also stores $x.max = \max(x.int.high,\; x.left.max,\; x.right.max)$ with $T.nil.max = -\infty$: the largest right endpoint anywhere in $x$'s subtree. By Theorem 14.1 the field survives insertion and deletion in $O(\lg n)$.
concepts.detail: Note that x.max can come entirely from the left subtree — a node's own interval is only one candidate among the max, not its source.

concepts.statement: To find one interval overlapping $i$: start at the root $x$; while $x \ne$ NIL and $x.int$ does not overlap $i$: if $x.left \ne$ NIL and $x.left.max \ge i.low$, set $x = x.left$ — the left subtree might contain an interval reaching far enough to the right — otherwise set $x = x.right$. Return $x$ (NIL means no interval in the tree overlaps $i$). The loop invariant: if the tree contains an overlap for $i$, the subtree rooted at $x$ contains one.
concepts.detail: Each iteration is $O(1)$, so the search is $O(\lg n)$ — the height bound of Chapter 13 again doing the work.

concepts.term: Why each turn is safe — and listing all overlaps
concepts.statement: **Going right is safe**: $x.left.max < i.low$ means every interval in the left subtree ends strictly left of $i$ — trichotomy case 2, no overlap there. **Going left is safe**: suppose an overlapping interval $j$ hides in the right subtree; then $j.low \ge x.int.low$ and the overlap force $i.high \ge j.low \ge x.int.low$. Now let $t$ be the interval achieving $x.left.max \ge i.low$: if $t$ did not overlap $i$, then $t.low > i.high \ge x.int.low$, contradicting $t$ lying in the **left** subtree (where all lows are $\le x.int.low$). So the left subtree contains an overlap. To list **all** $k$ overlaps: search, report, delete, and repeat, then reinsert — $O(k \lg n)$.
concepts.detail: The proof of the left turn is the subtle half of the chapter: it needs the full strength of both the max field and the search-tree keying.

figures.caption: An interval tree keyed by low endpoints, each node's $\max$ field in green. The bars place all seven intervals on a common axis; the query $i = [22, 25]$ is dashed in green. INTERVAL-SEARCH starts at the root $[16, 21]$: no overlap since $21 < 22$, and it goes **left** because the left child's $max = 23 \ge i.low = 22$. At $[8, 9]$ there is again no overlap, and the left child's $max = 8 < 22$ forces a step right to $[15, 23]$, which overlaps $i$ (highlighted). Note that $[8, 9]$'s $\max$ of 23 comes entirely from its right subtree — not from its own endpoint — which is exactly what makes the left turn at the root correct.

examples.title: Searching for [22, 25]
examples.problem: Using the interval tree of the figure — root [16, 21] with max 30; left child [8, 9] with max 23; right child [25, 30] with max 30; leaves [5, 8] (max 8), [15, 23] (max 23), [17, 19] (max 19), [26, 26] (max 26) — trace INTERVAL-SEARCH for the query $i = [22, 25]$.

steps.label: Step 1: Test the root
steps.text: $x = [16, 21]$: does it overlap $i$? Check $16 \le 25$ — yes — and $22 \le 21$ — no. The overlap test fails ($21 < 22$: the root ends strictly left of the query), so the search continues.

steps.label: Step 2: Decide the turn
steps.text: $x.left = [8, 9]$ is not NIL and $x.left.max = 23 \ge i.low = 22$ — the left subtree contains an interval reaching at least to 22 — so the search goes left.

steps.label: Step 3: Test [8, 9]
steps.text: $8 \le 25$ but $22 \le 9$ fails: no overlap. Its left child $[5, 8]$ has $max = 8 < 22$, so no interval in that whole subtree can reach the query — the search must go right.

steps.label: Step 4: Arrive at [15, 23]
steps.text: $x = [15, 23]$: $15 \le 25$ and $22 \le 23$ — both hold, so $[15, 23]$ overlaps the query. Return it.

examples.result: INTERVAL-SEARCH returns [15, 23] after three node visits. (The tree also holds another overlapping interval, [25, 30], which shares the point 25 with the query — the procedure returns some overlap, not all of them; listing all k overlaps by search-delete-repeat costs $O(k \lg n)$.)

examples.title: No overlap: search exits at leaf
examples.problem: INTERVAL-SEARCH for $[22, 25]$ in tree where root $[16,21]$ has $max = 21$ in its left subtree path. Show the early exit.

steps.label: Root
steps.text: $[16,21]$ vs $[22,25]$: $16 > 25$? No. $21 < 22$? Yes: no overlap ($b < c$ trichotomy case).

steps.label: Go right?
steps.text: Left child's $max = 10 < 22$: no interval left can overlap (all end before $22$ starts). Go right.

steps.label: Right child $[25,30]$
steps.text: Overlap? $25 \le 25$ and $22 \le 30$: yes, return $[25,30]$. Had right been $nil$, search would report no overlap in $O(\lg n)$.

steps.label: Miss case
steps.text: Searching $[30,35]$ instead would descend to $nil$: each step prunes one child via $max$, so at most $h$ steps.

examples.result: Found $[25,30]$ overlapping $[22,25]$ in $O(h)$ steps; a miss would reach $nil$ after pruning with $max$ at each level.

keyTakeaways: Closed intervals overlap iff i.low ≤ i'.high and i'.low ≤ i.high; the trichotomy — overlap, strictly left, strictly right — is exhaustive and exclusive.
Key by low endpoint and store x.max = max of high endpoints in the subtree; Theorem 14.1 maintains it in O(1) per rotation.
INTERVAL-SEARCH prunes with the max field and runs in O(lg n), returning one overlapping interval or NIL; enumerating all k overlaps costs O(k lg n).

quiz.q: The intervals [3, 7] and [7, 9] (closed) stand in which trichotomy relation?
options: none of the three — closed intervals need a fourth case
quiz.explanation: The overlap test gives $3 \le 9$ and $7 \le 7$: both hold, so they overlap at exactly the point 7. Strictly-left would require $7 < 7$.

quiz.q: In an interval tree, the field x.max stores:
options: the maximum low endpoint in the subtree
the maximum high endpoint anywhere in the subtree, including x's own interval
the high endpoint of the subtree's rightmost interval
the number of intervals in the subtree
quiz.explanation: $x.max = \max(x.int.high, x.left.max, x.right.max)$ — the largest right endpoint in the whole subtree; the node's own interval is only one of the candidates.

quiz.q: INTERVAL-SEARCH(T, i) descends into the left child of x exactly when:
quiz.explanation: The left subtree might contain an interval whose high endpoint reaches the query's low endpoint — that is exactly $x.left.max \ge i.low$. Overlap with x itself would have ended the loop.

quiz.q: To enumerate all k intervals that overlap a query interval, CLRS suggests:
options: repeatedly search, report and delete, then reinsert the deleted intervals — O(k lg n)
augmenting each node with the list of its overlaps
rebuilding the tree for each query
quiz.explanation: Each of the k rounds costs one $O(\lg n)$ search plus the delete and later reinsert — $O(k \lg n)$ total, which is optimal up to the sorting bound for outputting k intervals.

intro: Serling Enterprises buys long steel rods and sells them cut into shorter pieces, and the price of a piece is not proportional to its length — so how you cut determines what you earn. This innocent optimization is the book's laboratory for the whole chapter: it exposes an exponential recursion, shows that the recursion re-solves the same lengths over and over, and then fixes it twice — top-down with memoization and bottom-up with a table.
objectives: State the rod-cutting problem and derive the optimal-revenue recurrence $r_n = \max_{1 \le i \le n}(p_i + r_{n-i})$
Explain why naive recursion takes $\Theta(2^n)$ time and how overlapping subproblems make the problem tractable
Trace the memoized and bottom-up algorithms and reconstruct the optimal cut list from the $s$ table

concepts.statement: Given a rod of length $n$ and a price table $p_1, \dots, p_n$ (with $p_0 = 0$), **find the maximum revenue $r_n$ obtainable by cutting the rod into integer-length pieces and selling them all**. Cutting is free, any number of cuts (including none) is allowed, and a piece of length $i$ sells for $p_i$.
concepts.detail: The search space is the set of all compositions (ordered cut lists) of $n$ — there are $2^{n-1}$ of them — so brute-force enumeration is exponential in $n$.

concepts.statement: For $n \ge 1$, $$r_n = \max_{1 \le i \le n}\,(p_i + r_{n-i}), \qquad r_0 = 0.$$ An optimal solution either sells the rod whole ($i = n$, using $r_0 = 0$) or cuts a first piece of length $i$ and then cuts the remaining length $n - i$ optimally.
concepts.detail: Once the first piece is fixed, the rest of an optimal solution must itself be optimal for the remainder — otherwise pasting in a better remainder would improve the whole. This is the cut-and-paste argument in its simplest habitat.

concepts.statement: MEMOIZED-CUT-ROD writes the natural recursion but **stores each computed value $r[j]$ in a table, initializing entries to $-\infty$, and returns immediately on any repeat call**. Each of the $n$ subproblems is solved once, and subproblem $j$ scans up to $j$ first-piece choices, for $\Theta(n^2)$ total time and $\Theta(n)$ space.
concepts.detail: Memoization preserves the shape of the recursion while collapsing its tree to the subproblem graph; it pays off most when many subproblems are never reached.

concepts.statement: EXTENDED-BOTTOM-UP-CUT-ROD fills $r[1..n]$ in increasing order of length — a valid order because $r[j]$ depends only on strictly smaller lengths — and records $s[j]$, **the length of the first piece in an optimal first cut of a rod of length $j$**. The optimal cut list is read off by repeatedly taking $s[j]$ and setting $j \gets j - s[j]$.
concepts.detail: The value table gives the optimum's revenue; the choice table $s$ is what lets you hand the customer an actual cutting plan. Bottom-up and memoized versions share the same $\Theta(n^2)$ asymptotics; the bottom-up loop wins on constant factors.

concepts.statement: Store $s[j] = $ first-cut length attaining $r_j$; PRINT-CUT-SOLUTION prints $s[n]$, then recurses on $n - s[n]$. The $r$ table gives the value, the $s$ table gives the cuts: together they turn an optimum value into an optimum solution in $O(n)$.
concepts.detail: Memoized top-down keeps the same $s$ writes as bottom-up; without $s$ (length only) reconstruction needs re-solving each prefix, costing $O(n^2)$ extra.

figures.caption: Left: the book's sample price table ($p_1, \dots, p_{10} = 1, 5, 8, 9, 10, 17, 17, 20, 24, 30$); a rod of length 4 is optimally split $2 + 2$ for revenue $r_4 = p_2 + p_2 = 5 + 5 = 10$. Right: the subproblem graph for $n = 4$ — an edge from $r_j$ to $r_{j-i}$ encodes the choice of a first piece of length $i$, and the $2^{n-1} = 8$ paths from $r_4$ down to $r_0$ are exactly the 8 cut lists that naive recursion walks in full.
