examples.title: Inserting 13, 16, 17, then 18 into the $t = 3$ tree
examples.problem: Starting from the tree of Figure 1 (root [10, 20, 30], second child [12, 15]), insert 13, 16, 17, and 18 in order, showing where the first split happens.

steps.label: Step 1: Insert 13
steps.text: Descend: $13 \in (10, 20)$, so enter child [12, 15]. It is not full (2 keys < 5), so insert in place: [12, 13, 15]. No split.

steps.label: Step 2: Insert 16
steps.text: Same leaf: [12, 13, 15] → [12, 13, 15, 16]. Still not full — 4 keys < $2t-1 = 5$.

steps.label: Step 3: Insert 17
steps.text: The leaf becomes [12, 13, 15, 16, 17] — exactly 5 keys, **full**, but the insertion itself still fits, so nothing splits yet.

steps.label: Step 4: Insert 18 — the split
steps.text: Before descending into the full child, the root splits it: median $y.key_3 = 15$ (the $t$-th key) is promoted; the left half keeps [12, 13]; the new node $z$ gets [16, 17]. The root becomes [10, 15, 20, 30] with 5 children. Now descend into $z$ (since $18 \in (15, 20)$) and insert: $z$ = [16, 17, 18].

examples.result: Final root [10, 15, 20, 30]; children [2, 5, 8], [12, 13], [16, 17, 18], [22, 25, 28], [32, 35, 38, 40, 44] — a valid $t = 3$ tree, after exactly one split for four insertions.

examples.title: When does the tree grow?
examples.problem: Continue inserting into the root [10, 15, 20, 30] until the height increases, and explain what triggers it.

steps.label: Step 1: Fill the root
steps.text: Inserting keys in (8, 10) splits the first child and promotes, then keys in (10, 15), (15, 20) promote more medians: the root reaches 5 keys = $2t-1$ — full.

steps.label: Step 2: The next insertion
steps.text: With a full root, `B-TREE-INSERT` first splits the root itself: a new root [15] (say) is allocated with the old root as its only child, and height becomes 2. Only then does the descent continue, splitting a full child on the way down.

steps.label: Step 3: Observe the invariant
steps.text: Every leaf is still at depth 2 — the new level appeared above everyone at once, not below a single leaf.

examples.result: Height grows only at the root split; that is why all leaves stay at one common depth without any rebalancing pass.

keyTakeaways: Splitting a full child of $2t-1$ keys promotes the median $y.key_t$ and leaves two nodes of $t-1$ keys each — the parent must be non-full to receive it.
Pre-emptive splitting on the way down means insertion never backtracks: one root-to-leaf pass, $O(t \log_t n)$ CPU, $O(\log_t n)$ page accesses.
The tree grows only when the root splits: height increases at the top, preserving the equal-depth property.

quiz.q: B-TREE-SPLIT-CHILD(x, i) may be invoked only when:
quiz.explanation: The parent must have room ($\le 2t-2$ keys) to absorb the promoted median, and the child must be full ($2t-1$ keys) for a split to be warranted.

quiz.q: After splitting a full child, the two resulting nodes each hold how many keys?
quiz.explanation: Of the $2t-1$ keys, one (the median) leaves upward: $(2t-1-1)/2 = t-1$ remain in each half — the legal minimum occupancy.

quiz.q: The height of a B-tree increases by one exactly when:
options: the root is split during an insertion
quiz.explanation: Only the root split allocates a new root above the old one; leaf and internal splits keep the height fixed.

quiz.q: Pre-emptive splitting (splitting a full child before descending into it) guarantees:
options: nodes are always at least half full
insertion needs only one downward pass with no backtracking
quiz.explanation: Because you never enter a full node, the parent of any node you might split is guaranteed non-full — so the algorithm never has to climb back up to make room.

intro: Deletion is the mirror image of insertion, and CLRS leaves the full pseudocode as an exercise — the interesting content is the design of the cases. The rule of the game: never descend into a node holding only $t-1$ keys, because a deletion there would leave it underfull with no cheap repair from a leaf. So on the way down we top up any minimal node by borrowing from a rich sibling or merging with a poor one, and internal keys are replaced by their predecessor or successor before being discarded.
objectives: Execute the three deletion cases: leaf keys, internal keys, and the descent into minimal nodes
Choose correctly between borrowing from a sibling and merging with one
Explain why height can only decrease at the root and why merges are amortized O(1) per operation

concepts.statement: `B-TREE-DELETE` maintains the invariant that **every node it enters (except the root) holds at least $t$ keys** — one more than the minimum. Repair happens before descending: if the child about to be entered has $t-1$ keys, borrow or merge so it has $t$.
concepts.detail: With this invariant, deleting from the leaf where the key actually lives can never push it below $t-1$ keys, so no underflow repair ever happens at the bottom of the tree.

concepts.term: Case 1: the key is in a leaf
concepts.statement: If the node holds more than $t-1$ keys, simply remove the key. Otherwise — already handled by the descent invariant, which ensured at least $t$ keys on entry — removal still leaves $t-1$, the legal minimum.
concepts.detail: This is the payoff of pre-emptive repairs: the leaf case itself is trivial.

concepts.term: Case 2: the key is in an internal node
concepts.statement: Let the key sit between children $y$ (before) and $z$ (after). If $y$ has $\ge t$ keys, replace the key by its **predecessor** — the maximum key of $y$'s subtree — and recursively delete the predecessor from $y$. Symmetrically use the **successor** (minimum of $z$'s subtree) if $z$ has $\ge t$ keys. If both are minimal ($t-1$ keys), **merge** the key, $y$, and $z$ into one node of $(t-1) + 1 + (t-1) = 2t-1$ keys and recursively delete from that node.
concepts.detail: The merge is legal precisely because $2t-1$ is the maximum occupancy — the merged node is instantly full but valid.

concepts.term: Case 3: repairing a minimal child before descent
concepts.statement: To enter a child with $t-1$ keys, first give it a $t$-th key: if an adjacent **sibling has $\ge t$ keys, rotate** — pull the separating parent key down into the child and push the sibling's nearest key up to replace it (a two-key move that shifts one key sideways). If both siblings are minimal, **merge** the child, the separator, and a sibling into one $2t-1$-key node, which costs the parent one key.
concepts.detail: The merge may leave the parent at $t-1$ keys — harmless, since the invariant applies to the node being *entered*, and by the time we enter the parent's children again it will itself be repaired.

concepts.statement: Height drops only when the **root ends up with 0 keys**: if it has one child, that child becomes the new root; if the tree is empty, the root becomes a childless leaf. Each merge destroys one node and each split creates one, so intermixed sequences of insertions and deletions perform $O(1)$ structural changes per operation amortized.
concepts.detail: A single deletion costs $O(t \log_t n)$ CPU and $O(\log_t n)$ page accesses — the same shape as insertion.

examples.title: Deleting 20, then 16, then 17 from the $t = 3$ tree
examples.problem: Start from root [10, 15, 20, 30] with children [2, 5, 8], [12, 13], [16, 17, 18], [22, 25, 28], [32, 35, 38, 40, 44]. Delete 20, then 16, then 17, naming the case used each time.

steps.label: Step 1: DELETE 20 — internal key, rich child
steps.text: 20 sits in the root. The preceding child [16, 17, 18] has $3 \ge t = 3$ keys, so use its predecessor: the subtree maximum 18. The root becomes [10, 15, 18, 30]; recursively delete 18 from the leaf, leaving [16, 17] — still $\ge t-1 = 2$ ✓.

steps.label: Step 2: DELETE 16 — minimal leaf, rich sibling
steps.text: The leaf [16, 17] has $t - 1 = 2$ keys, so before entering it, repair: the right sibling [22, 25, 28] has $3 > t-1$ keys — **rotate**. The separator 18 comes down into the child ([16, 17, 18]); the sibling's first key 22 goes up to the root. Now the child holds 3 keys; delete 16: [17, 18] ✓.

steps.label: Step 3: DELETE 17 — minimal leaf, minimal siblings
steps.text: The leaf [17, 18] is minimal again. Its left sibling [12, 13] has $t-1 = 2$ keys and the right sibling [25, 28] also has 2 — nobody can lend. **Merge**: left sibling + separator 15 + the node = [12, 13, 15, 17, 18], a full $2t-1$-key node; the root loses key 15: [10, 22, 30] (still $\ge 1$ ✓). Delete 17: [12, 13, 15, 18] ✓.

examples.result: Root [10, 22, 30] with children [2, 5], [12, 13, 15, 18], [25, 28], [32, 35, 38, 40, 44] — one predecessor-replacement, one rotation, and one merge, exactly one per case.

examples.title: A rotation in slow motion, and when the tree shrinks
examples.problem: From root [10, 22, 30] with children [2, 5], [12, 13, 15, 18], [25, 28], [32, 35, 38, 40, 44], delete 5 — a key sitting in a minimal leaf — and then say when the height would ever decrease.

steps.label: Step 1: Spot the minimal leaf
steps.text: 5 sits in child [2, 5], which holds only $t - 1 = 2$ keys. The algorithm may not enter it yet, so it repairs first.

steps.label: Step 2: Rotate through the parent
steps.text: The right sibling [12, 13, 15, 18] has $4 \ge t$ keys — rich. The separator 10 moves down into the minimal child, making [2, 5, 10]; the sibling's nearest key 12 moves up, giving root [12, 22, 30] and sibling [13, 15, 18]. Every range stays consistent: the child now owns keys below 12, the sibling keys in $(12, 22)$.

steps.label: Step 3: Delete
steps.text: Now enter the 3-key child and remove 5, leaving [2, 10] — exactly the legal minimum $t - 1$.

steps.label: Step 4: When does height drop?
steps.text: Only when merges cascade up to the root and leave it with 0 keys: its lone child is then promoted and $h$ decreases by one. Since each merge destroys one node and each split creates one, mixed sequences perform $O(1)$ structural changes per operation amortized.

examples.result: Root [12, 22, 30] with children [2, 10], [13, 15, 18], [25, 28], [32, 35, 38, 40, 44]; the rotation cost two pointer moves and one key swap — no nodes were created or destroyed.

keyTakeaways: Never descend into a node with $t-1$ keys: borrow from a sibling with $\ge t$ keys, or merge with a minimal sibling around the separating key.
An internal key is replaced by its predecessor or successor (recursively deleted), or absorbed into a merge of its two adjacent children.
Merging child + separator + sibling yields exactly $2t-1$ keys; height decreases only when an empty root is discarded.

quiz.q: During B-TREE-DELETE's descent, every node the algorithm enters (other than the root) is guaranteed to hold at least how many keys?
quiz.explanation: The descent invariant keeps one key of slack ($\ge t$ on entry), so the deletion at the leaf cannot push it below the legal minimum of $t-1$.

quiz.q: A node has $t-1$ keys and both adjacent siblings have $t-1$ keys. The repair is:
options: a merge of the node, the separating parent key, and a sibling into one $2t-1$-key node
quiz.explanation: With no rich sibling to lend, the only move is the merge: $(t-1) + 1 + (t-1) = 2t-1$ keys — exactly full, and the parent loses one key.

quiz.q: During a deletion the root ends up with 0 keys and one child. What happens?
options: The root keeps 0 keys until the next insert
Its lone child becomes the new root and the height drops by one
The tree is rebuilt from scratch
quiz.explanation: A merge consumed the root's only key; the child is promoted and the tree gets shallower — the mirror of the insertion-time root split.

quiz.q: Deleting a key found in an internal node when the following child $z$ has $\ge t$ keys is done by:
options: replacing it with the predecessor from the preceding child
replacing it with the successor — the minimum of $z$'s subtree — and recursively deleting that
quiz.explanation: A rich following child can afford to give up its minimum; the symmetric predecessor rule applies when the *preceding* child is the rich one.

intro: Binomial heaps merge two heaps in $O(\lg n)$ but charge every insertion for keeping the trees tidy. Fibonacci heaps (Fredman and Tarjan, 1987) take the opposite bargain: let the collection of trees grow ragged, never tidy up until forced to, and pay for the deferred work out of a banked potential. The admission price is pure bookkeeping — a circular root list and one mark bit per node — and the payoff is $O(1)$ amortized INSERT, UNION and DECREASE-KEY, exactly what Dijkstra needs to run in $O(V \lg V + E)$. This section defines the structure; the next two make the amortized bounds precise.
objectives: Define a Fibonacci heap: a collection of min-heap-ordered trees threaded into a circular, doubly linked root list, with degree and mark fields on every node
State precisely when a node's mark bit is set and cleared, and why roots are never marked
Compute the potential $\Phi(H) = t(H) + 2m(H)$ for a concrete heap and explain why marks are weighted double

concepts.statement: A **Fibonacci heap** is a collection of **min-heap-ordered** trees — every node's key is less than or equal to each of its children's keys — that need not be binomial: the trees may have arbitrary shapes, and several trees may even share a degree. The heap keeps a pointer $H.min$ to the root with the overall minimum key, and the roots of all trees are threaded into a **circular, doubly linked list** called the **root list**.
concepts.detail: Heap order must hold within each tree; across trees there is no order at all, which is why the minimum has to be tracked explicitly in $H.min$ rather than found by walking the root list.

concepts.term: Node fields and the circular lists
concepts.statement: Each node stores its key, a parent pointer $x.p$, a pointer $x.child$ to *one* of its children, and sibling pointers $x.left$, $x.right$, plus two integers: $x.degree$ (number of children) and $x.mark$ (a boolean). The children of any node also form a **circular, doubly linked list**, so any node can be spliced into or out of a sibling list, or into the root list, with $O(1)$ pointer updates.
concepts.detail: This is the structural fact behind every $O(1)$ bound in the chapter: circularity removes end-cases, and double linkage removes the need to search for a predecessor.

concepts.statement: **A node is marked iff, being a non-root, it has lost one child since the last time it was linked to its current parent.** The bit is set when an unmarked node loses a child; it is cleared when the node is linked as a child of another node or when it becomes a root. A **root is never marked**, and a marked node that loses a second child is immediately cut from its parent and sent to the root list (Section 19.3).
concepts.detail: The mark is a promise the heap makes to its own analysis: no non-root node ever loses more than one child — the invariant that the degree bound of Section 19.4 silently relies on.

concepts.statement: For a heap $H$, let $t(H)$ be the number of trees in the root list and $m(H)$ the number of marked nodes. The potential is $$\Phi(H) = t(H) + 2\,m(H),$$ with $\Phi$ of an empty heap $= 0$. Each root-list tree banks **1 unit** (it must eventually be consolidated away) and each marked node banks **2 units** (its mark hides a future cut).
concepts.detail: Since $\Phi \ge 0$ always, any sequence of operations costs at most its total amortized charges — the potential method of Chapter 17, applied to a pointer machine.

concepts.statement: UNION does no tree merging at all — it just splices two root lists together, $O(1)$ actual work. A binomial heap instead must combine equal-degree trees at merge time, costing $\Theta(\lg n)$. The deferred work stays bounded only because the **maximum degree** $D(n)$ of any node in an $n$-node Fibonacci heap is $O(\lg n)$ — the theorem Section 19.4 finally proves — so consolidation is never expensive.
concepts.detail: Laziness is the design principle: every operation does the minimum now and leaves a mess that a bounded, pre-paid cleanup absorbs later.

figures.caption: A Fibonacci heap of $n = 10$ nodes: three min-heap-ordered trees rooted at 7, 38 and 55, joined in a circular, doubly linked root list (double arrows carry both next and prev; the arc shows the wrap-around $55 \to 7$). Node 17 carries the mark ✱ — it has lost a child since 7 linked it, so one further loss sends it to the root list. The potential is $\Phi = t + 2m = 3 + 2 \cdot 1 = 5$.

examples.title: Reading the heap of Figure 1
examples.problem: For the heap in the figure (roots 7, 38, 55; 7 has children 17, 23, 24; 17 has child 30 and is marked; 38 has children 41, 52), verify every structural invariant and compute the potential.

steps.label: Step 1: Heap order
steps.text: Check each tree: $7 \le 17, 23, 24$; $17 \le 30$; $38 \le 41, 52$ ✓. Nothing constrains 7 against 38 or 55 — across trees, only $H.min$ matters, and it correctly points at 7.

steps.label: Step 2: Mark
steps.text: 17 is marked and is a non-root ✓ (roots are never marked). Its mark records a past child loss: 17 once had two children, so its current degree 1 plus one remembered loss is consistent.

steps.label: Step 3: Degrees
steps.text: $\deg(7) = 3$ (children 17, 23, 24), $\deg(38) = 2$, $\deg(55) = 0$, $\deg(17) = 1$. All are at most $D(n)$; for $n = 10$, Section 19.4 gives $D(10) \le \lfloor \log_\varphi 10 \rfloor = \lfloor 4.78 \rfloor = 4$ ✓.

steps.label: Step 4: Potential
steps.text: $t = 3$ trees in the root list, $m = 1$ marked node, so $\Phi = t + 2m = 3 + 2 = 5$.

examples.result: The heap is structurally legal, and its banked potential is $\Phi = 5$ units — 3 for the trees that consolidation must one day merge, 2 for the cut that 17's mark has pre-paid.

examples.title: UNION adds nothing but potential
examples.problem: Union the heap of Figure 1 ($t = 3$, $m = 1$) with a second Fibonacci heap of two singleton roots 100 and 200 ($t = 2$, $m = 0$). Compare with the binomial-heap alternative.

steps.label: Step 1: Splice
steps.text: Concatenate the two circular root lists — 4 pointer updates — and point $H.min$ at 7, the smaller of the two minima. $O(1)$ actual work, no keys touched.

steps.label: Step 2: Potential adds
steps.text: $\Phi$ of the union is $t = 5$ trees and $m = 1$ mark: $\Phi = 5 + 2 = 7 = \Phi(H_1) + \Phi(H_2) = 5 + 2$. Potentials are additive, so the union banks exactly what its inputs banked — the amortized cost is $O(1)$.

steps.label: Step 3: The binomial comparison
steps.text: A binomial heap union must interleave two sorted-by-degree root lists and combine every colliding pair, $\Theta(\lg n)$ work on the spot — it cannot defer, because its invariant (at most one tree per degree) would break.

examples.result: Fibonacci UNION is $O(1)$ amortized precisely because the structure tolerates duplicate degrees; the debt is recorded in $t$ and collected later by CONSOLIDATE.

keyTakeaways: A Fibonacci heap is a loose collection of min-heap-ordered trees with a circular, doubly linked root list and a pointer to the minimum — shape discipline is deliberately absent.
The mark bit guarantees every non-root node has lost at most one child since its last link; roots are never marked.
The potential $\Phi = t + 2m$ prices both kinds of deferred work: root-list trees (1 unit each) and hidden cuts (2 units per mark).

quiz.q: Why is the root list kept as a circular, doubly linked list?
options: So that heap order can be checked in $O(1)$ at the roots
So that UNION can splice two root lists together with $O(1)$ pointer updates
To keep the roots sorted by key for MINIMUM
To bound every node's degree by $D(n)$
quiz.explanation: Splicing two circular doubly linked lists is a constant number of pointer updates — the shape that makes lazy merging free. Heap order is never checked at roots, MINIMUM reads $H.min$, and the degree bound comes from Section 19.4's analysis, not the list shape.

quiz.q: A marked non-root node loses a second child. What must happen?
options: Nothing — the mark is only bookkeeping
The node is cut from its parent, spliced into the root list, and unmarked
The whole tree is rebuilt by CONSOLIDATE
Its parent is marked instead, and the node keeps its mark
quiz.explanation: The mark is a one-strike counter: the second loss triggers a cut of the node itself (Section 19.3's cascading cut), and marks are always cleared when a node becomes a root.

quiz.q: A heap has $t = 6$ trees in its root list and $m = 4$ marked nodes. Its potential is:
quiz.explanation: $\Phi = t + 2m = 6 + 2 \cdot 4 = 14$. The factor 2 on marks is what makes each future cascading cut self-funding.

quiz.q: Why are marked nodes charged 2 potential units in $\Phi = t + 2m$?
options: Because a marked node has at most two children left
So that unmarking during a cascading cut releases 2 units — one pays for the new root, and the profit funds the cut itself
Because marks double the actual cost of DECREASE-KEY
quiz.explanation: Cutting a marked node to the root list adds a tree ($+1$) but clears the mark ($-2$), a net release of 1 unit — exactly the budget an $O(1)$ cut consumes. This is the accounting trick behind decrease-key's $O(1)$ amortized bound.

intro: This section builds the mergeable-heap operations and prices them. MAKE-HEAP, INSERT, MINIMUM and UNION each do a few pointer updates and are $O(1)$ amortized by inspection. EXTRACT-MIN is where the laziness bill comes due: it removes the minimum, splices the minimum's children into the root list, and then — only then — tidies up, running CONSOLIDATE to merge equal-degree roots until at most one root of each degree remains. The potential $\Phi = t + 2m$ pays the bill: every tree that leaves the root list releases one banked unit, so the amortized cost comes out $O(D(n))$, which Section 19.4 shows is $O(\lg n)$.
objectives: Execute INSERT, MINIMUM and UNION and verify their $O(1)$ amortized costs from the potential
Trace EXTRACT-MIN and CONSOLIDATE on a concrete root list, including equal-degree linking
Show why the amortized cost of EXTRACT-MIN is $O(D(n))$ even though the actual work is $O(t + D(n))$

concepts.statement: A mergeable heap supports MAKE-HEAP, INSERT, MINIMUM, EXTRACT-MIN and UNION; with DECREASE-KEY and DELETE it becomes a priority queue. Fibonacci-heap amortized costs versus binary heaps: **INSERT $O(1)$ vs $O(\lg n)$; MINIMUM $O(1)$ vs $O(1)$; UNION $O(1)$ vs $\Theta(n)$; EXTRACT-MIN $O(\lg n)$ vs $O(\lg n)$; DECREASE-KEY $O(1)$ vs $\Theta(\lg n)$; DELETE $O(\lg n)$ vs $\Theta(\lg n)$**.
concepts.detail: The one-row summary: everything a binary heap does in $O(\lg n)$ that does not have to — inserting, merging, decreasing — becomes $O(1)$. That is what drops Dijkstra to $O(V \lg V + E)$.

concepts.term: The O(1) quartet: make-heap, insert, minimum, union
concepts.statement: `FIB-HEAP-INSERT(H, x)` makes $x$ a singleton tree and splices it into the root list, updating $H.min$ if $x$ is smaller — $O(1)$ actual, and $\Delta\Phi = +1$ (one new tree). `FIB-HEAP-MINIMUM(H)` returns $H.min$ — $O(1)$, $\Delta\Phi = 0$. `FIB-HEAP-UNION(H1, H2)` concatenates the root lists and keeps the smaller minimum — $O(1)$ actual, and $\Phi(H) = \Phi(H_1) + \Phi(H_2)$, so the amortized cost is $O(1)$.
concepts.detail: No keys are compared except against the minima, and no tree is ever re-shaped. Laziness in its purest form.

concepts.statement: Save the minimum $z$; splice each child of $z$ into the root list (clearing its mark — roots are never marked); remove $z$; if the root list is now empty set $H.min = \text{NIL}$; otherwise run **CONSOLIDATE** and then set $H.min$ to the smallest remaining root. Actual cost: $O(D(n) + t)$, where $t$ is the number of roots before consolidating and $D(n)$ bounds both the children spliced and the array walk.
concepts.detail: Extracting the minimum is the only operation that is ever *allowed* to be slow — it is the designated cleanup moment for all the laziness that came before.

concepts.statement: Maintain an array $A[0..D(n)]$ with at most one root per degree. Walk the root list; for each root $w$ of degree $d$: while $A[d]$ already holds a root $y$, **link** the two — the smaller-keyed root stays in the list and the other becomes its child (its mark cleared, its degree incremented) — and $d$ increments; finally store $w$ in $A[d]$. At the end, rebuild the root list from $A$, which now has at most one root per degree $0, \dots, D(n)$.
concepts.detail: The result is binomial-like shape *at the roots only* — a snapshot of tidiness that the next O(1) operations immediately begin to soil again.

concepts.statement: **The amortized cost of EXTRACT-MIN is $O(D(n))$.** The actual cost is $O(D(n) + t)$, and the potential change is $\Delta\Phi = t' + 2m' - (t + 2m) \le (D(n) + 1) - t$: at most $D(n)+1$ trees survive consolidation and marks only decrease (new roots are unmarked). Each of the $t$ disappearing trees releases a unit, so the merging work is paid for by the potential drop: amortized $=$ actual $+ \Delta\Phi = O(D(n))$.
concepts.detail: Units are scaled so one potential unit pays one pointer update — the standard license of the potential method. With $D(n) = O(\lg n)$ (Section 19.4), EXTRACT-MIN is $O(\lg n)$ amortized.

examples.title: Consolidating after EXTRACT-MIN
examples.problem: Extract the minimum from the heap of Figure 1 (Section 19.1). The minimum 7 has children 17 (marked), 23, 24, so the root list becomes, in order: 38 (degree 2), 55 (degree 0), 17 (degree 1, now a root and unmarked), 23 (degree 0), 24 (degree 0). Run CONSOLIDATE.

steps.label: Step 1: Roots in place
steps.text: $t = 5$ roots with degrees $[2, 0, 1, 0, 0]$. Array $A$ starts empty ($D(10) \le 4$, so $A[0..4]$).

steps.label: Step 2: 38, 55, 17
steps.text: Store $A[2] = 38$, $A[0] = 55$, $A[1] = 17$ — no collisions yet.

steps.label: Step 3: 23 (degree 0)
steps.text: $A[0] = 55$ collides: $23 < 55$, so 55 becomes 23's child (23 now degree 1). $A[1] = 17$ collides: $17 < 23$, so 23 (with 55 beneath it) becomes 17's child (17 now degree 2). $A[2] = 38$ collides: $17 < 38$, so 38 (with children 41, 52) becomes 17's child — 17 now has degree 3. Store $A[3] = 17$.

steps.label: Step 4: 24 (degree 0)
steps.text: $A[0]$ is empty now, so store $A[0] = 24$.

steps.label: Step 5: Rebuild
steps.text: Root list $= \{17, 24\}$: 17 with children 30, 23, 38 (degrees $3$), and singleton 24. $H.min = 17$ ✓ — heap order held throughout because every link put the smaller key on top.

examples.result: Three links; the root list shrinks from 5 trees to 2, and $\Phi$ falls from $t = 5, m = 0 \Rightarrow 5$ (the mark on 17 was cleared when it became a root) to $t = 2 \Rightarrow \Phi = 2$.

examples.title: The ledger: why the amortized cost is $O(D(n))$
examples.problem: Account for the same EXTRACT-MIN with actual cost versus potential change.

steps.label: Step 1: Actual work
steps.text: Remove 7 (1), splice 3 children (3), walk 5 roots (5), perform 3 links (3), write/rebuild from $A$ (≈4) — roughly 16 pointer-level units, i.e. $\Theta(t + D(n))$ with $t = 5$, $D(10) \le 4$.

steps.label: Step 2: Potential change
steps.text: Before: $\Phi = 3 + 2 \cdot 1 = 5$. After: $\Phi = 2 + 0 = 2$. So $\Delta\Phi = -3$: each of the 3 links dissolved a root-list tree, and the mark on 17 evaporated.

steps.label: Step 3: Amortized
steps.text: Amortized cost $=$ actual $+ \Delta\Phi \approx 16 - 3 = 13$ units. Formally the bound $\Delta\Phi \le (D(n)+1) - t = 5 - 5 = 0$ absorbs the entire per-root traversal: the $t$ term of the actual cost is paid by the trees' own banked units as they leave the list.

steps.label: Step 4: The regime check
steps.text: Whatever $t$ is — it can be as large as $n$ after many lazy inserts — each disappearing root releases one unit, so the amortized cost stays $O(D(n)) = O(\lg n)$, never $O(t)$.

examples.result: A long-suffering extract-min collects exactly the debt the previous cheap operations ran up — no more.

keyTakeaways: INSERT, MINIMUM and UNION are $O(1)$ amortized: pure pointer splicing, with each insert banking exactly one potential unit.
EXTRACT-MIN consolidates equal-degree roots until at most one root per degree remains; linking always makes the smaller key the parent.
The potential drop $\Delta\Phi \le (D(n)+1) - t$ converts the actual $O(t + D(n))$ work into an amortized $O(D(n)) = O(\lg n)$.

quiz.q: Which operation has amortized cost $O(\lg n)$ rather than $O(1)$ in a Fibonacci heap?
quiz.explanation: EXTRACT-MIN (and DELETE, which uses it) pays $O(D(n)) = O(\lg n)$ amortized; insert, union and minimum are $O(1)$ amortized — the entire point of the structure.

quiz.q: After EXTRACT-MIN leaves roots with degrees, in processing order, $[2, 2, 0, 0]$, how many FIB-HEAP-LINK calls does CONSOLIDATE make?
quiz.explanation: First two degree-2 roots collide and link into a degree-3 root; the two degree-0 roots collide and link into a degree-1 root. Two links, and the final list has degrees $[3, 1]$ — one root per degree.

quiz.q: FIB-HEAP-LINK(H, y, x) during consolidation:
options: makes $x$ a child of $y$ whenever their degrees match
makes $y$ a child of $x$ (the smaller-keyed root), clears $y$'s mark, and increments $x.degree$
quiz.explanation: CONSOLIDATE first exchanges the names so that $x$ carries the smaller key; then $y$ leaves the root list to become $x$'s newest child — marks are cleared on linking, which is why newly linked roots start unmarked.

quiz.q: The amortized cost of EXTRACT-MIN is $O(D(n))$ rather than $O(t + D(n))$ because:
options: every root is marked before consolidation begins
each tree that leaves the root list during consolidation releases one potential unit, so the $t$ merging operations are paid by the potential drop
$t$ is always at most $D(n)$ in a Fibonacci heap
quiz.explanation: $\Delta\Phi \le (D(n) + 1) - t$: the surviving roots number at most $D(n)+1$ and marks only fall, so the $t$ roots that vanish each hand back one banked unit — the cleanup is pre-paid by the operations that dirtied the heap.

intro: DECREASE-KEY is the operation that earned Fibonacci heaps their fame, and the one binary heaps cannot cheapen. The plan: if the new key violates heap order with the node's parent, cut the node loose and make it a root — but cutting makes trees thin, and thin trees would break the degree bound that EXTRACT-MIN's cost rests on. The mark bit is the escape: a node that has already lost a child gets cut as well when it loses a second, cascading up the tree. One operation can therefore cascade $\Theta(n)$ cuts, yet the potential $\Phi = t + 2m$ refunds one unit per cascading cut, and the amortized cost is $O(1)$.
objectives: Execute DECREASE-KEY with CUT and CASCADING-CUT, including exactly when marks are set and cleared
Prove the $O(1)$ amortized bound: actual $O(c)$ versus $\Delta\Phi \le 4 - c$
Implement DELETE as decrease-to-$-\infty$ plus EXTRACT-MIN, at $O(\lg n)$ amortized

concepts.statement: `FIB-HEAP-DECREASE-KEY(H, x, k)` errors if $k > x.key$; otherwise it sets $x.key = k$, and if $x$ is not a root and the new key is smaller than $x.p.key$, it cuts $x$ from its parent (`CUT`) and runs `CASCADING-CUT(H, x.p)`. Finally $H.min$ is updated if $x$ is now the smallest root.
concepts.detail: If heap order survives the decrease, nothing structural happens at all — the cheap case is genuinely $O(1)$ actual.

concepts.statement: `CUT(H, x, y)` removes $x$ from the child list of its parent $y$ (decrementing $y.degree$), splices $x$ into the root list, sets $x.p = \text{NIL}$ and $x.mark = \text{FALSE}$. `CASCADING-CUT(H, y)` examines $z = y.p$: if $z$ is NIL, stop; if $y$ is unmarked, set $y.mark = \text{TRUE}$ and stop; if $y$ is marked, `CUT` it and recurse on $z$.
concepts.detail: The cascade walks strictly up the ancestor chain, so its length is bounded by the tree height — but each step unmarks one node, and unmarking is where the refund comes from.

concepts.statement: Cascading cuts enforce the invariant that **every non-root node has lost at most one child since it was linked to its parent**. Without it, a node of degree $d$ could be stripped of $d - 1$ children while keeping a high degree, and the minimum subtree size for degree $d$ could fall below the Fibonacci number $F_{d+2}$ — destroying the $D(n) = O(\lg n)$ bound of Section 19.4 and with it the $O(\lg n)$ extract-min.
concepts.detail: This is the chapter's central trade: DECREASE-KEY pays for its $O(1)$ bound by promising, via marks, that trees stay Fibonacci-fat even under arbitrary cutting.

concepts.statement: **A DECREASE-KEY that performs $c$ cuts costs $O(1)$ amortized.** The actual cost is $O(c)$ — each cut is constant pointer work. If $c$ cuts occur, the root list gains $c$ trees ($+c$); the $c-1$ intermediate ancestors that were cut had their marks cleared ($-2$ each) and at most one new mark is set on the parent where the cascade stops, so $\Delta\Phi \le c + 2(-(c-1) + 1) = 4 - c$. Amortized cost $= O(c) + (4 - c) = O(1)$.
concepts.detail: Read the inequality as an exchange rate: every cascading cut beyond the first arrives with a $-1$ net potential attached, which exactly covers its constant work. The worst single case, $c = \Theta(n)$, is fully pre-paid by $\Theta(n)$ marks banked earlier.

concepts.statement: `FIB-HEAP-DELETE(H, x)` runs DECREASE-KEY with $k = -\infty$ — making $x$ the minimum, cut loose from its parent in $O(1)$ amortized — and then EXTRACT-MIN to remove it. Total amortized cost: $O(1) + O(D(n)) = O(\lg n)$.
concepts.detail: No Fibonacci-heap operation ever finds nodes by key; DELETE assumes the caller already holds a pointer to $x$.

figures.caption: Path compression on a disjoint-set chain — the potential method's other showcase. A FIND-SET on the 9-node chain at left walks 8 parent pointers, then re-points every node on the walked path directly at the root, producing the star at right. The amortized philosophy is identical to this chapter's: an occasionally expensive restructuring ($\Theta(n)$ pointers here, $\Theta(n)$ cuts in a cascade) is paid for by potential banked in the structure — $\Phi = t + 2m$ for Fibonacci heaps, a rank-based potential in Chapter 21.

examples.title: A cascade of four cuts, fully accounted
examples.problem: A Fibonacci heap has roots 7, 38, 55 ($t = 3$) and a chain $7 \to 17 \to 30 \to 42 \to 50$ of marked nodes 17, 30, 42 ($m = 3$; each has previously lost a child). Run DECREASE-KEY(50, 4) and account for it.

steps.label: Step 1: The violation
steps.text: $4 < 42 = $ parent's key, so 50 must be cut. Heap order on the chain held until now: $7 < 17 < 30 < 42 < 50$ ✓.

steps.label: Step 2: The cascade
steps.text: Cut 50 to the root list (unmarked, as all roots are). Its parent 42 is marked — cut it too, unmark. Then 30 is marked — cut it. Then 17 is marked — cut it. Now the walk reaches 7, a root: roots are never marked, so the cascade stops. Total $c = 4$ cuts (nodes 50, 42, 30, 17).

steps.label: Step 3: The heap after
steps.text: Root list: 7, 38, 55, 50, 42, 30, 17 — seven trees, all unmarked. The chain below 7 is gone; $t = 7$, $m = 0$.

steps.label: Step 4: The ledger
steps.text: Actual cost $O(c) = O(4)$ pointer updates. Potential: before $\Phi = 3 + 2 \cdot 3 = 9$; after $\Phi = 7 + 0 = 7$; so $\Delta\Phi = -2$. Check against the bound $\Delta\Phi \le 4 - c = 0$ ✓ (the actual drop beats the bound). Amortized cost $= O(4) - 2 = O(1)$: cuts 2–4 each brought a $-1$ net refund (new root $+1$, unmark $-2$), paying for their own constant work.

examples.result: Four cuts — potentially $\Theta(n)$ in general — priced at $O(1)$ amortized because three banked marks plus the structure of $\Phi$ absorbed the cascade.

examples.title: DELETE via decrease-to-$-\infty$
examples.problem: Delete node 41 from the heap of Figure 1 (Section 19.1): roots 7, 38, 55; 38 has children 41, 52; 17 is marked.

steps.label: Step 1: Decrease 41 to $-\infty$
steps.text: Heap order with parent 38 is violated, so CUT moves 41 to the root list; 38 was unmarked, so it becomes marked and the cascade stops after one cut. Roots: 7, 38, 55, 41 with $-\infty$; $\Phi$ moves from $3 + 2 = 5$ to $4 + 2 \cdot 2 = 8$ — an $O(1)$ amortized step (it banked a mark).

steps.label: Step 2: EXTRACT-MIN
steps.text: The minimum is the $-\infty$ node 41; it has no children. Root list to consolidate: 7 (degree 3), 38 (degree 1 — it just lost 41), 55 (degree 0). No degrees collide, so CONSOLIDATE makes no links: the final root list is exactly $\{7, 38, 55\}$ with $H.min = 7$.

steps.label: Step 3: The result
steps.text: 41 is gone; $\Phi$ ends at $3 + 2 \cdot 2 = 7$. The delete consumed its $O(\lg n)$ amortized budget on the extraction, as designed.

examples.result: DELETE = one $O(1)$ amortized decrease-key plus one $O(\lg n)$ amortized extract-min — $O(\lg n)$ amortized overall, with the node never searched for.

keyTakeaways: DECREASE-KEY cuts the node when heap order with its parent breaks, then lets CASCADING-CUT walk up the ancestor chain, cutting every already-marked ancestor.
The mark discipline guarantees every non-root node has lost at most one child since its last link — the structural invariant behind Section 19.4's degree bound.
$\Delta\Phi \le 4 - c$ against actual cost $O(c)$ gives amortized $O(1)$; DELETE is decrease-to-$-\infty$ plus EXTRACT-MIN, $O(\lg n)$ amortized.

quiz.q: A cascade of cuts triggered by DECREASE-KEY ends when:
options: the heap has no marked nodes left
the walk upward reaches an unmarked ancestor — which gets marked — or reaches a root
the decreased node becomes the minimum
every ancestor has lost two children
quiz.explanation: CASCADING-CUT marks an unmarked ancestor and stops there; if the ancestor was already marked it is cut and the walk continues; roots are never marked, so reaching one also stops the cascade.

quiz.q: A single DECREASE-KEY can cascade $c = \Theta(n)$ cuts, yet its amortized cost is $O(1)$ because:
options: long cascades are so rare they can be ignored
each cascading cut unmarks a node — $-2$ potential against $+1$ for the new root — so every cut after the first releases a unit that pays for its own constant work
cuts cost nothing in the potential method
the mark bits are all cleared by the next EXTRACT-MIN anyway
quiz.explanation: The refund is exact bookkeeping: $\Delta\Phi \le 4 - c$ while the actual cost is $O(c)$, and the two cancel. The marks being cleared later by extract-min is precisely what keeps $\Phi$ from running the refund twice.

quiz.q: The mark discipline guarantees the structural fact that Section 19.4 needs:
options: every non-root node has lost at most one child since it was linked to its parent
marked nodes have degree at least 2
the root list is sorted by degree
quiz.explanation: This one-loss invariant is what forces subtrees to stay Fibonacci-fat: it enters the proof of $y_i.degree \ge i - 2$ and hence the whole $D(n) = O(\lg n)$ bound.

quiz.q: The amortized cost of FIB-HEAP-DELETE is:
options: $O(\lg n)$ — a decrease-key to $-\infty$ plus an extract-min
quiz.explanation: The decrease-key is $O(1)$ amortized and only makes the node the minimum; actually removing it requires EXTRACT-MIN at $O(D(n)) = O(\lg n)$ amortized.

intro: Everything in this chapter has leaned on one unproven quantity: $D(n)$, the maximum degree of any node in an $n$-node Fibonacci heap. EXTRACT-MIN is $O(D(n))$ amortized, so the whole structure is only as good as $D(n)$. The name of the chapter is this section's punchline: the smallest possible subtree rooted at a node of degree $d$ has $F_{d+2}$ nodes — a Fibonacci number — because the mark bit stops trees from getting thin. Since Fibonacci numbers grow like $\varphi^d$ with the golden ratio $\varphi \approx 1.618$, an $n$-node heap caps degrees at $D(n) \le \lfloor \log_\varphi n \rfloor \approx 1.4404 \lg n$.
objectives: State the Fibonacci recurrence and the golden-ratio growth $F_k \ge \varphi^{k-2}$
Prove the linking-order lemma $y_i.degree \ge i - 2$ and the size bound $N(x) \ge F_{degree(x)+2}$
Derive $D(n) \le \lfloor \log_\varphi n \rfloor = 1.4404 \lg n$ and evaluate it for concrete $n$

concepts.detail: Growth is geometric: $F_k = \Theta(\varphi^k)$ — each term is about 1.618 times its predecessor, which is why degrees are only logarithmic in subtree size.

concepts.statement: $\varphi = \frac{1 + \sqrt 5}{2} \approx 1.61803$ satisfies $\varphi^2 = \varphi + 1$, and its conjugate $\hat\psi = \frac{1 - \sqrt 5}{2} = -1/\varphi \approx -0.61803$ satisfies $|\hat\psi| < 1$. Binet's formula: $F_k = \frac{\varphi^k - \hat\psi^k}{\sqrt 5}$, and since the second term is smaller than $1/2$ in absolute value, $F_k = \lfloor \varphi^k / \sqrt 5 + 1/2 \rfloor$.
concepts.detail: The identity $\varphi^2 = \varphi + 1$ is the engine of every induction below; note also $\log_\varphi n = \lg n / \lg \varphi \approx 1.4404 \lg n$.

concepts.statement: Let $x$ be any node of degree $d$ with children $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_d$ in the order in which they were linked to $x$. Then $y_i.degree \ge i - 2$ — the children cannot be too thin, because at linking time $y_i$'s degree matched $x$'s (which was at least $i - 1$), and **the mark bit ensures $y_i$ has lost at most one child since**.
concepts.detail: This lemma is where the mark bit cashes in: delete the one-loss invariant and a stripped node of degree 5 could have children of degrees $0,0,0,0,0$, breaking everything downstream.

concepts.statement: If $N(x)$ is the number of nodes in the subtree rooted at $x$ (including $x$), then $$N(x) \ge F_{x.degree + 2}.$$ A degree-0 node holds $\ge F_2 = 1$ node; degree 3 forces at least $F_5 = 5$ nodes; degree 8 forces at least $F_{10} = 55$.
concepts.detail: The minimal trees are literally built by the Fibonacci recurrence: link a degree-0, a degree-0, then degrees $1, 2, 3, \dots$ beneath a fresh root and the sizes come out $1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, \dots$

concepts.statement: **For any node $x$ in an $n$-node Fibonacci heap, $n \ge N(x) \ge F_{degree(x)+2} \ge \varphi^{degree(x)}$, so $degree(x) \le \log_\varphi n$ and** $$D(n) \le \lfloor \log_\varphi n \rfloor = \frac{\lg n}{\lg \varphi} \approx 1.4404 \lg n = O(\lg n).$$ This closes the loop: EXTRACT-MIN is $O(\lg n)$ amortized after all.
concepts.detail: Numbers: $n = 10 \Rightarrow D \le 4$; $n = 1000 \Rightarrow D \le 14$; $n = 2^{32} \Rightarrow D \le 46$ — versus 32 for a perfectly binomial structure. The 44% slack is the price of laziness.

examples.title: The minimal degree-3 tree is Fibonacci-sized
examples.problem: Construct the smallest subtree that can sit under a node $x$ of degree 3, and verify $N(x) \ge F_5 = 5$.

steps.label: Step 1: Apply the lemma
steps.text: Children in link order $y_1, y_2, y_3$ need degrees $\ge 0, 0, 1$ respectively — so the third child cannot be a leaf.

steps.label: Step 2: Build minimally
steps.text: Give $y_1$ and $y_2$ degree 0 (single nodes), and $y_3$ degree 1 (itself plus one leaf child). Total: $1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 5$ nodes — a root with three children, one of which has a baby.

steps.label: Step 3: Check the bound
steps.text: $F_{3+2} = F_5 = 5$ ✓ — the construction is tight. For degree 4 the same build gives $5 + F_4 = 5 + 3 = 8 = F_6$; for degree 5, $8 + F_5 = 13 = F_7$: the minimal sizes follow the Fibonacci recurrence exactly.

examples.result: Minimal sizes by degree: $1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, \dots$ — the Fibonacci sequence shifted, which is where the heap's name comes from.

examples.title: Capping degrees at $n = 1000$
examples.problem: An $n = 1000$ node Fibonacci heap: what is the largest degree any node can carry?

steps.label: Step 3: Cross-check the closed form
steps.text: $\log_\varphi 1000 = \ln 1000 / \ln \varphi = 6.9078 / 0.4812 = 14.36$, and $\lfloor 14.36 \rfloor = 14$ ✓ — the table and the logarithm agree exactly.

steps.label: Step 4: The extract-min bill
steps.text: CONSOLIDATE needs an array of size $D(n) + 1 = 15$ and does $O(t + 14)$ work — a very small constant in front of the $\lg n$.

examples.result: $D(1000) = 14$; any node claiming degree 15 would need at least $F_{17} = 1597 > 1000$ nodes beneath it.

keyTakeaways: The linking-order lemma ($y_i.degree \ge i - 2$) holds because consolidation links equal-degree roots and the mark bit limits each child to one loss since linking.
A degree-$d$ node anchors at least $F_{d+2}$ nodes — Fibonacci-fat trees are the mark bit's structural dividend.
$D(n) \le \lfloor \log_\varphi n \rfloor \approx 1.4404 \lg n$ completes the analysis: EXTRACT-MIN and DELETE are $O(\lg n)$ amortized.

quiz.q: The smallest possible number of nodes in the subtree rooted at a degree-8 node is:
quiz.explanation: $N(x) \ge F_{8+2} = F_{10} = 55$. The distractors are $F_9 = 34$ (off by one index), the degree bound for $2^{32}$ nodes, and $F_8 = 21$.

quiz.q: The lemma $y_i.degree \ge i - 2$ for the $i$-th-linked child relies on which two facts?
options: that Fibonacci-heap trees are binomial, and keys are distinct
that consolidation links equal-degree roots — so $y_i$ had degree $\ge i-1$ when linked — and the mark bit ensures it lost at most one child since
that the root list is circular, and $H.min$ is always correct
that cascading cuts stop at roots, and marks are cleared by UNION
quiz.explanation: Equal degrees at link time give $y_i$ degree $\ge i - 1$; the one-loss mark invariant shaves at most 1, leaving $\ge i - 2$. Remove either fact and the lemma — and the whole degree bound — collapses.

quiz.q: For $n = 2^{32}$ nodes, the maximum degree is at most:
quiz.explanation: $D(n) \le 1.4404 \lg n = 1.4404 \cdot 32 = 46.09$, so $D \le 46$. The answer 32 is the binomial-heap value — laziness costs 44% more degree.

quiz.q: The structure is called a Fibonacci heap because:
options: the minimum subtree sizes follow the Fibonacci recurrence — a degree-$d$ node needs at least $F_{d+2}$ nodes
the number of trees after consolidation is always $F_n$
the potential function sums Fibonacci numbers
quiz.explanation: The size lemma $N(x) \ge F_{degree(x)+2}$ is the namesake: the laziest legal trees are exactly Fibonacci-sized, which is what keeps degrees logarithmic despite arbitrary cutting.

depth.title: The D(n) = O(lg n) degree bound, proved from the golden ratio

blocks.body: The chapter has promised $D(n) = O(\lg n)$ since Section 19.2, and everything now hangs on delivering it: EXTRACT-MIN is $O(D(n))$ amortized, and CONSOLIDATE allocates an array of size $D(n)+1$. The proof is a chain of four links: **equal-degree linking** (from CONSOLIDATE), **one loss per child** (from the mark bit), **Fibonacci-size subtrees** (by induction), and **golden-ratio growth** (Binet). Here is the whole chain, with nothing borrowed.

blocks.heading: Linking-order lemma
blocks.body: Let $x$ be any node of a Fibonacci heap, and let $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_d$ be the children of $x$ in the order in which they were linked to $x$, from earliest to latest. Then $y_i.degree \ge i - 2$ for all $i$.

blocks.heading: Why the children stay fat
blocks.body: When $y_i$ was linked to $x$, FIB-HEAP-LINK had just merged two roots of equal degree, so at that moment $y_i.degree = x.degree$ exactly. And $x$ already had children $y_1, \dots, y_{i-1}$ — at least $i - 1$ children — so $y_i.degree \ge i - 1$ at link time. Since then, $y_i$ has lost at most one child: a first loss sets $y_i.mark$, and a *second* loss would have cut $y_i$ off $x$ entirely (CASCADING-CUT), contradicting that it is still a child. Hence $y_i.degree \ge (i-1) - 1 = i - 2$. $\square$ — Observe where the mark bit enters: it is the entire content of the second sentence. Without it, an adversary could strip $y_d$ down to degree 0 and the analysis dies; with it, every child carries $i-2$ degrees of obligation.

blocks.heading: Fibonacci size lemma
blocks.body: For every node $x$ in a Fibonacci heap, $N(x) \ge F_{x.degree + 2}$, where $N(x)$ counts the nodes in the subtree rooted at $x$.

blocks.heading: Induction on the degree
blocks.body: For $d = 0, 1, 2$ the claim reads $N \ge F_2, F_3, F_4 = 1, 2, 3$: a degree-$d$ node has $d$ children plus itself, and $1 + d \ge F_{d+2}$ for $d \le 2$ ✓. For $d \ge 3$, write the children in link order. By the lemma $y_i.degree \ge \max(i - 2, 0)$, so by induction $N(y_i) \ge F_{\max(i-2,0) + 2}$: that is $F_2 = 1$ for $i = 1, 2$ and $F_i$ for $i \ge 3$. Summing, $$N(x) \;=\; 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{d} N(y_i) \;\ge\; 1 + F_2 + F_2 + \sum_{i=3}^{d} F_i.$$ Now use the Fibonacci telescoping identity $\sum_{i=1}^{d} F_i = F_{d+2} - 1$, i.e. $\sum_{i=3}^{d} F_i = F_{d+2} - 1 - F_1 - F_2 = F_{d+2} - 3$. Then $N(x) \ge 1 + 1 + 1 + (F_{d+2} - 3) = F_{d+2}$. $\square$

blocks.heading: From Binet to the 1.4404 constant
blocks.body: First, $F_k \ge \varphi^{k-2}$ for $k \ge 2$, by induction: the bases are $F_2 = 1 = \varphi^0$ and $F_3 = 2 > \varphi$, and the step is the golden-ratio identity itself: $F_{k+1} = F_k + F_{k-1} \ge \varphi^{k-2} + \varphi^{k-3} = \varphi^{k-3}(1 + \varphi) = \varphi^{k-3} \cdot \varphi^2 = \varphi^{k-1}$. (The same identity explains Binet's formula $F_k = (\varphi^k - \hat\psi^k)/\sqrt 5$: the sequences $\varphi^k$ and $\hat\psi^k$ both satisfy $s_k = s_{k-1} + s_{k-2}$.) Now let $x$ be any node of an $n$-node heap with $d = x.degree$: $$n \;\ge\; N(x) \;\ge\; F_{d+2} \;\ge\; \varphi^{d} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad d \;\le\; \log_\varphi n.$$ Converting bases, $\log_\varphi n = \lg n / \lg \varphi$ and $\lg \varphi = \ln \varphi / \ln 2 = 0.4812 / 0.6931 = 0.6942$, so $D(n) \le \lfloor \log_\varphi n \rfloor = 1.4404 \lg n$. Spot checks: $n = 10$: $1.4404 \cdot 3.32 = 4.78 \to 4$; $n = 10^3$: $14.36 \to 14$ (matching $F_{16} = 987 \le 1000 < F_{17}$); $n = 2^{32}$: $46.09 \to 46$.

blocks.heading: The minimal trees, degree by degree
blocks.body: The bound is tight in shape: build a root, link children of degrees $0, 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$ beneath it (each new child needs degree $i-2$, and linking it raises the root's degree to $i$). The resulting minimal subtree sizes are exactly $1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55$ for degrees $0$ through $8$ — the Fibonacci sequence with $F_{d+2}$ nodes at degree $d$. Such *Fibonacci trees* are what the mark bit forces every heap to imitate: an adversary may cut, but only once per child, and the recurrence rebuilds itself from the wreckage.

Two historical notes. First, the 1.4404 constant is the visible price of laziness: a binomial heap of $n$ nodes caps degrees at $\lfloor \lg n \rfloor$, while a Fibonacci heap pays a 44% premium for its $O(1)$ decrease-key — a trade overwhelmingly worth making in Dijkstra ($O(V \lg V + E)$ instead of $O(E \lg V)$) and Prim. Second, the structure is Fredman and Tarjan's (1987), and its name records exactly this section: heaps whose worst-case trees are Fibonacci trees. Their practical cousin, the **pairing heap**, achieves similar performance with simpler code, but to this day no $O(1)$ amortized decrease-key bound has been proved for it — Fibonacci heaps remain the canonical structure with the guarantee.

intro: Binary search trees answer dictionary queries in $O(\lg n)$, where $n$ is the number of keys stored — but when the keys come from a small universe $\{0, \dots, u-1\}$, the universe itself can be the data structure: a bit vector answers INSERT and MEMBER in $O(1)$, at the price of $\Theta(u)$ scans for MINIMUM and SUCCESSOR. This section builds the two ideas that shrink that price: superimpose a tree of summary bits over the array, then make the tree short and fat ($\sqrt u$ branching) and apply the trick to itself. The recurrence $T(u) = T(\sqrt u) + O(1)$ emerges, and its solution $O(\lg \lg u)$ is the van Emde Boas idea.
objectives: Analyze the plain bit vector: O(1) INSERT/DELETE/MEMBER versus Θ(u) MIN/MAX/SUCCESSOR/PREDECESSOR
Explain the superimposed binary tree and then the two-level √u structure with its O(√u) successor bound
Derive the recurrence T(u) = T(√u) + O(1) = O(lg lg u) that motivates the whole chapter

concepts.statement: Maintain an array $A[0..u-1]$ of bits with $A[x] = 1$ iff $x$ is in the set $S$. **INSERT, DELETE and MEMBER take $O(1)$** — one array access — but **MINIMUM, MAXIMUM, SUCCESSOR and PREDECESSOR take $\Theta(u)$ in the worst case**, because finding the next set bit after $x$ may require scanning the whole array. Space is $\Theta(u)$.
concepts.detail: The vector is attractive when $u$ is small or dense (a bitmap allocator); it fails exactly when the *ordering* queries matter — order lives in position, and positions must be walked.

concepts.statement: Overlay a binary tree on the array: leaf $i$ is bit $A[i]$, and each internal node stores the **OR of its children's bits** (1 iff some descendant leaf is set). Then MINIMUM, MAXIMUM, SUCCESSOR and PREDECESSOR each walk down or up at most one root-to-leaf path — $O(\lg u)$ — by descending through the leftmost 1-subtree, or climbing from $x$'s leaf to the lowest ancestor whose right side contains a 1. The cost: INSERT and DELETE now update $\lg u$ ancestor bits, and space remains $\Theta(u)$.
concepts.detail: The summary bits convert *position scanning* into *tree walking* — every operation becomes $O(\lg u)$, no better than a balanced BST on $n$ keys, but independent of $n$: the bounds depend on the universe $u$ alone.

concepts.statement: Make the superimposed tree short and fat: a root with $\sqrt u$ children, each covering $\sqrt u$ consecutive bits. The root holds a **summary bit-vector of $\sqrt u$ bits** — bit $i$ set iff group $i$ contains a set bit. SUCCESSOR($x$): scan the remainder of $x$'s group ($\le \sqrt u$ bits); if that fails, scan the summary for the next nonempty group ($\le \sqrt u$), then scan that group from its start ($\le \sqrt u$) — **$O(\sqrt u)$ total**. INSERT, DELETE, MEMBER return to $O(1)$ since only one group bit and the summary bit of that group change.
concepts.detail: Trade height for width: height 2 instead of $\lg u$, at the price of $\sqrt u$-wide scans. The next idea is to recurse the trade.

concepts.term: The recursive leap to lg lg u
concepts.statement: Now treat the summary bit-vector — and each group — as **smaller instances of the same structure**, recursively. Each level of recursion cuts the universe to its square root, and one query makes $O(1)$ work per level, giving $$T(u) = T(\sqrt u) + O(1) = O(\lg \lg u).$$ This double-logarithmic bound is the van Emde Boas idea (van Emde Boas, 1975–77): universe size, not element count, drives the height.
concepts.detail: The chapter assumes $u = 2^{2^k}$ (2, 4, 16, 256, 65536, …) so that $\sqrt u$ is an exact integer power of 2 at every level; general $u$ rounds up to the next such value.

concepts.statement: Full van Emde Boas trees keep $min$ and $max$ outside the recursive structure: MINIMUM/MAXIMUM then cost $O(1)$ and deletions avoid recursing for the extremes. The preliminary structures of this section pay $\Theta(\sqrt u)$ or $O(\lg \lg u)$ for the same queries because they store everything uniformly.
concepts.detail: Foreshadowing: Section 20.3's $min$/$max$ fields also let INSERT skip recursion when the new key is a new extreme, and let SUCCESSOR return $max$ without descending. The idea is born from the preliminary structures' weakness.

examples.title: Three structures, one universe: $u = 2^{32}$
examples.problem: Compare worst-case SUCCESSOR times on the universe ${0, \dots, 2^{32}-1}$ (4,294,967,296 elements) for the three structures of this section.

steps.label: Step 1: The bit vector
steps.text: One scan can visit every bit: $\Theta(u) = \Theta(2^{32}) \approx 4.3$ billion steps in the worst case — although INSERT/MEMBER stay $O(1)$.

steps.label: Step 2: The two-level √u structure
steps.text: $\sqrt{2^{32}} = 2^{16} = 65{,}536$, so SUCCESSOR costs at most about $3\sqrt u \approx 196{,}608$ bit inspections — better by four orders of magnitude, still not logarithmic.

steps.label: Step 3: The recursive structure
steps.text: Each level squares-roots the universe: $2^{32} \to 2^{16} \to 2^8 \to 2^4 \to 2^2 \to 2$. That is $\lg \lg u = \lg 32 = 5$ levels of $O(1)$ work — SUCCESSOR in 5 steps, whatever $n$ is.

steps.label: Step 4: The catch
steps.text: The recursion needs space proportional to $u$ at every level (Section 20.2 counts it) — the price of a universe-indexed structure rather than an element-indexed one.

examples.result: Bit vector $\Theta(u)$, two-level $O(\sqrt u) = 65{,}536$-ish, recursive $O(\lg \lg u) = 5$: each idea buys a double exponent, and the last buys two logs.

examples.title: SUCCESSOR(80) in the two-level structure, counted exactly
examples.problem: Universe $u = 256$ with $\sqrt u = 16$ groups of 16 bits, holding $S = \{3, 70, 200\}$. Count the bit inspections of SUCCESSOR(80).

steps.label: Step 1: Finish x's group
steps.text: 80 lies in group 5 (bits 80–95). Scanning bits 81 through 95 — the group is empty — costs 15 inspections.

steps.label: Step 2: Search the summary
steps.text: Scan summary bits for groups 6, 7, …: groups 6 through 11 are empty, group 12 (bits 192–207) is the next with a set bit — 7 more inspections.

steps.label: Step 3: Enter the new group
steps.text: Scan group 12 from bit 192: 192, …, 200 — the 9th inspection finds the set bit. Answer: SUCCESSOR(80) = 200.

steps.label: Step 4: Compare with the bound
steps.text: Total $15 + 7 + 9 = 31$ inspections, within $3\sqrt u = 48$ and of course far below the bit vector's possible 255. Each of the three scans is capped by $\sqrt u = 16$.

examples.result: 31 bit inspections — $O(\sqrt u)$, and the reason to recurse is visible: the *scans themselves* are the problem the next level of structure will solve.

keyTakeaways: A u-bit array gives O(1) insert/member but Θ(u) order statistics; order queries are the bottleneck.
Superimposed summary bits turn scans into walks: a binary tree gives O(lg u) for everything, a height-2 √u-branching tree gives O(√u) successors with O(1) inserts.
Recursing the √u split yields T(u) = T(√u) + O(1) = O(lg lg u) — the van Emde Boas idea, assuming u = 2^2^k.

quiz.q: In a plain bit vector over a universe of size $u$, the worst-case cost of MINIMUM is:
quiz.explanation: The minimum is the first set bit, which may sit at the very end of the array — a full scan. INSERT and MEMBER are the O(1) operations; the four order queries are the Θ(u) ones.

quiz.q: With the two-level structure (a $\sqrt u$-bit summary plus $\sqrt u$ groups of $\sqrt u$ bits), SUCCESSOR costs:
quiz.explanation: Three capped scans: the rest of x's group, the summary, and the next nonempty group — each at most $\sqrt u$ bit inspections. The $\lg \lg u$ bound needs the fully recursive structure.

quiz.q: The recurrence $T(u) = T(\sqrt u) + O(1)$ solves to:
quiz.explanation: Writing $u = 2^{2^k}$, each level decrements $k$: $2^{2^k} \to 2^{2^{k-1}} \to \dots \to 2$, so there are $lg lg u$ levels of constant work.

quiz.q: Why does superimposing a full binary tree of height $\lg u$ over the bit vector fail to give $O(1)$ operations?
options: INSERT and DELETE must update the $\lg u$ ancestor bits on the leaf's path, and searches still walk $O(\lg u)$ levels
It cannot represent the empty set
quiz.explanation: Every set/unset of a leaf flips a bit on every level up to the root, and each order query descends or climbs a full path — all operations become $O(\lg u)$, the balanced-BST bound. Space stays Θ(u), so nothing is lost there.

intro: The recursive idea deserves a concrete implementation before the final tree, and that implementation — the proto-vEB structure — is the chapter's honest laboratory: it achieves the double logarithm exactly where the two-calls-per-level branching allows, and falls back to $O(\lg u)$ precisely where it does not. MEMBER descends one cluster per level, $O(\lg \lg u)$; but MINIMUM, SUCCESSOR and INSERT must consult *both* a cluster and the summary, the branching doubles at each of the $\lg \lg u$ levels, and $2^{\lg \lg u} = \lg u$ — no better than a binary search tree. Section 20.3 fixes the branching; this section shows why the fix is needed.
objectives: Define the proto-vEB structure recursively, including the base case, and the high/low/index decomposition
Trace MEMBER, MINIMUM, SUCCESSOR and INSERT on a concrete proto-vEB(16), and state their recurrences
Explain why the two-recursive-calls branching gives Θ(lg u) and why proto-vEB uses Θ(u) space

concepts.statement: Assuming $u = 2^{2^k}$, a **proto-vEB$(u)$** structure holds: a **summary** — a pointer to a proto-vEB$(\sqrt u)$ — and an **array cluster$[0..\sqrt u - 1]$** of pointers, each to a proto-vEB$(\sqrt u)$. The **base case** $u = 2$ drops both and stores just a two-bit array $A[0..1]$. The element $x$ lives in **cluster$[\mathrm{high}(x)]$** at position $\mathrm{low}(x)$; cluster $i$ is nonempty iff $i$ is in the summary.
concepts.detail: The figure below draws a full proto-vEB(16): five proto-vEB(4) boxes and fifteen proto-vEB(2) pills — $u - 1$ leaves in all.

concepts.statement: For a proto-vEB$(u)$ structure, split $x$ by its top half bits: $$\mathrm{high}(x) = \lfloor x / \sqrt u \rfloor, \qquad \mathrm{low}(x) = x \bmod \sqrt u, \qquad \mathrm{index}(i, j) = i\sqrt u + j.$$ So $x$'s cluster is $\mathrm{high}(x)$ and its position within that cluster is $\mathrm{low}(x)$ — the same split at every level, with $\sqrt u$ shrinking each time.
concepts.detail: For $u = 16$: high and low are the two nibbles of a 4-bit key ($x = 4 \cdot \mathrm{high} + \mathrm{low}$); one level down, $u = 4$ splits by $\lfloor x/2 \rfloor$ and $x \bmod 2$.

concepts.statement: With one recursive call per level: **MEMBER is $O(\lg \lg u)$** — $T(u) = T(\sqrt u) + O(1)$. With two recursive calls (cluster, then summary): **MINIMUM, MAXIMUM, SUCCESSOR, PREDECESSOR, INSERT and DELETE are all $O(\lg u)$** — $T(u) = 2T(\sqrt u) + O(1)$, and $2^{\lg \lg u} = \lg u$ call instances.
concepts.detail: proto-vEB-INSERT inserts unconditionally into *both* the cluster and the summary; SUCCESSOR tries the cluster first and, on failure, the summary plus a MINIMUM. Every one of them branches.

concepts.statement: Let $S(u)$ be the space of a proto-vEB$(u)$: one summary plus $\sqrt u$ clusters gives $S(u) = (\sqrt u + 1)S(\sqrt u) + O(1)$, which solves to $\Theta(u)$. Concretely, a proto-vEB(16) contains $1 + 5 \cdot 4 = 21$ structures whose $u - 1 = 15$ base-case pills hold $2(u-1) = 30$ bits; a proto-vEB(256) contains $1 + 17 \cdot 21 = 358$ structures with 255 pills (510 bits).
concepts.detail: The recursion tree has exactly $u - 1$ leaves: a full binary split of the universe's bits, which is why the space tracks the universe, not the number of stored keys.

concepts.statement: The branching is the whole story. MEMBER never needs to ask two questions, so it rides the $\lg \lg u$ depth directly; but SUCCESSOR must ask *is there anything above $x$ in x's cluster?* — a question that itself costs a recursive call — and INSERT must maintain two structures. The remedy (Section 20.3): **store the minimum and maximum of every structure**, so the in-cluster question is answered in $O(1)$ by one comparison, leaving at most one recursive call per level.
concepts.detail: The fix must also dodge a subtlety: storing min/max in every node naively doubles the space; the min-outside-the-clusters convention of the real vEB tree is what keeps space at $O(u)$.

figures.caption: The proto-vEB structure over the universe $\{0, \dots, 15\}$ holding $S = \{1, 6, 8, 9, 15\}$. The top structure splits each key with $\mathrm{high}(x) = \lfloor x/4 \rfloor$ and $\mathrm{low}(x) = x \bmod 4$; each box is a proto-vEB(4) with its own summary pill and two cluster pills; each pill is a proto-vEB(2) — two bits, no recursion. The amber path is MEMBER(9): into cluster[2] (since $\mathrm{high}(9) = 2$), then into its cluster[0] (since within that structure $\mathrm{high}(1) = 0$), then read bit $A[1] = 1$ — one recursive call per level, $O(\lg \lg u)$.

examples.title: MEMBER on the figure: a hit and a miss
examples.problem: Run MEMBER(9) and MEMBER(5) on the proto-vEB(16) of the figure ($S = \{1, 6, 8, 9, 15\}$) and count the recursive calls.

steps.label: Step 1: MEMBER(9) — the first split
steps.text: $\mathrm{high}(9) = \lfloor 9/4 \rfloor = 2$, $\mathrm{low}(9) = 1$: recurse into V.cluster[2], asking MEMBER(1) of that proto-vEB(4).

steps.label: Step 2: MEMBER(9) — the second split
steps.text: Inside cluster[2]: $\mathrm{high}(1) = 0$, $\mathrm{low}(1) = 1$: recurse into its cluster[0], a proto-vEB(2), asking for bit $A[1]$.

steps.label: Step 3: MEMBER(9) — the base
steps.text: $A[1] = 1$ (the amber pill, set because both 8 and 9 live in cluster[2]) — return TRUE after exactly $\lg \lg u = 2$ recursive calls.

steps.label: Step 4: MEMBER(5) — the miss
steps.text: $\mathrm{high}(5) = 1$, $\mathrm{low}(5) = 1$: into V.cluster[1] (which holds only low 2, from the element 6); there $\mathrm{high}(1) = 0$, $\mathrm{low}(1) = 1$: its cluster[0] pill reads $A[1] = 0$ — return FALSE, again 2 calls.

examples.result: Both queries take one call per level — $O(\lg \lg u)$ — because MEMBER never needs the summary: the cluster to descend into is read off the key itself.

examples.title: Counting the cost at $u = 256$: MEMBER versus SUCCESSOR
examples.problem: A proto-vEB over $u = 256$. Count worst-case recursive calls for MEMBER and for SUCCESSOR, and count the structures used.

steps.label: Step 1: The levels
steps.text: $256 \to 16 \to 4 \to 2$: three recursive steps to the base case — indeed $\lg \lg 256 = \lg 8 = 3$ levels below the root, so MEMBER makes 3 recursive calls.

steps.label: Step 2: SUCCESSOR branches
steps.text: Each SUCCESSOR invocation can call SUCCESSOR on a cluster *and* on the summary — two children per node of the recursion tree. With depth 3, the tree has up to $2^3 = 8$ call instances — and $\lg u = \lg 256 = 8$: the branching exactly cancels the double logarithm, leaving $O(\lg u)$.

steps.label: Step 3: Space
steps.text: Structure count: $N(256) = 1 + 17 \cdot N(16)$ and $N(16) = 1 + 5 \cdot N(4)$, $N(4) = 1 + 3 \cdot 1 = 4$: so $N(16) = 21$ and $N(256) = 1 + 17 \cdot 21 = 358$ structures — with $u - 1 = 255$ base-case pills holding $2 \cdot 255 = 510 = 2(u-1)$ bits, $\Theta(u)$ overall.

steps.label: Step 4: The verdict
steps.text: MEMBER at $O(\lg \lg u)$ is genuinely double-logarithmic, but every operation that must look at the summary too is $\lg u$ — the proto structure realizes the idea only halfway.

examples.result: MEMBER: 3 calls. SUCCESSOR: up to 8. Space: $\Theta(u)$ — 358 structures for 256 elements of universe.

keyTakeaways: proto-vEB(u) = a summary proto-vEB(√u) + √u cluster proto-vEB(√u)s, with a 2-bit array at u = 2; high/low split each key level by level.
MEMBER is O(lg lg u) — one recursive call per level — but MINIMUM, SUCCESSOR and INSERT are O(lg u), because each branches into both a cluster and the summary: 2^(lg lg u) = lg u.
Space is Θ(u): the recursion tree has exactly u − 1 leaves, one per bit-pair of the universe.

quiz.q: Which proto-vEB operation runs in $O(\lg \lg u)$ time?
quiz.explanation: MEMBER descends into the single cluster named by high(x) at each level — one recursive call per level, $T(u) = T(\sqrt u) + O(1)$. The others must also consult the summary and so branch.

quiz.q: proto-vEB-SUCCESSOR costs $\Theta(\lg u)$ rather than $O(\lg \lg u)$ because:
options: each level scans $\sqrt u$ bits of the array
it can make two recursive calls per level — into the cluster and into the summary — so the call tree doubles at each of the $\lg \lg u$ levels: $2^{\lg \lg u} = \lg u$
the base case reads both bits A[0] and A[1]
quiz.explanation: The doubling per level exactly cancels the halving of depth: $\lg \lg u$ levels of branching give $\lg u$ total call instances — the same order as walking a balanced binary search tree.

quiz.q: The space used by a proto-vEB structure over universe ${0, \dots, u-1}$ is:
quiz.explanation: $S(u) = (\sqrt u + 1)S(\sqrt u) + O(1)$ — one summary plus √u clusters at every level — which solves to Θ(u): the structure indexes the universe, not the stored set. (Θ(n) is the tempting wrong answer for any universe-indexed structure.)

quiz.q: MEMBER(x) on a proto-vEB over $u = 65536$ makes how many recursive calls?
quiz.explanation: $u = 2^{16}$, so $\lg \lg u = \lg 16 = 4$: the chain $65536 \to 256 \to 16 \to 4 \to 2$ has four steps. SUCCESSOR, by contrast, could make up to $2^4 = 16 = \lg u$ calls on the same structure.

intro: The van Emde Boas tree fixes proto-vEB's one flaw with two stored numbers. Every structure keeps its **minimum and maximum** in $V.min$ and $V.max$: the minimum is stored *only* there — never in a cluster — which both saves space and makes every emptiness question an $O(1)$ comparison. Suddenly the branching question 'is there anything above $x$ inside x's cluster?' is answered by comparing $\mathrm{low}(x)$ with the cluster's stored maximum, and each operation makes **at most one recursive call per level**: $T(u) = T(\sqrt u) + O(1) = O(\lg \lg u)$ for the full repertoire — INSERT, MEMBER, MINIMUM, MAXIMUM, SUCCESSOR, PREDECESSOR — over a universe of fixed size $u$.
objectives: Define the vEB tree with its min/max fields, summary, and clusters, including the invariant that V.min is stored outside every cluster
Trace SUCCESSOR and INSERT on a concrete vEB(16), including the min-swap on inserting a new minimum
Prove the O(lg lg u) time bound and the O(u) space bound via the telescoping product identity

concepts.statement: A **vEB tree** $V$ over $\{0, \dots, u-1\}$ with $u = 2^{2^k}$ stores: $V.min$ and $V.max$ (elements, not pointers), a **summary** — a vEB tree over $\{0, \dots, \sqrt u - 1\}$ — and an **array cluster$[0..\sqrt u - 1]$** of vEB trees over $\sqrt u$ elements each. For $u = 2$ only $min$ and $max$ are stored. **Invariant: $V.min = \text{NIL}$ iff the set is empty; the minimum is stored in $V.min$ and in *no* cluster; the maximum is stored in $V.max$ *and* in its cluster.**
concepts.detail: The min-outside-the-clusters convention is the linchpin: it prevents double storage at every level, keeping the space at $O(u)$ instead of $O(u \lg u)$, and it gives every recursion an $O(1)$ early exit.

concepts.statement: Testing whether $V$ holds any element is comparing $V.min$ with NIL; MINIMUM and MAXIMUM read $V.min$ and $V.max$. No recursion at all — the stored endpoints are the answer, for any $u$.
concepts.detail: Contrast proto-vEB, where MINIMUM had to recurse into the summary to find the first nonempty cluster and then into that cluster: two calls per level because nothing was cached.

concepts.statement: `vEB-TREE-SUCCESSOR(V, x)`: if $u = 2$, answer from the two stored values; if $x < V.min$, return $V.min$ (the successor hides below the stored minimum); otherwise compute $\text{max-low} = V.cluster[\mathrm{high}(x)].max$ **in $O(1)$** — if $\mathrm{low}(x) < \text{max-low}$, recurse once into that cluster; else recurse once into the summary to find the next nonempty cluster $j$ and return $\mathrm{index}(j, V.cluster[j].min)$. **One recursive call per level: $T(u) = T(\sqrt u) + O(1) = O(\lg \lg u)$.**
concepts.detail: PREDECESSOR is symmetric, comparing $\mathrm{low}(x)$ with the cluster's stored minimum. MEMBER also enjoys the endpoints: if $x$ equals $V.min$ or $V.max$, answer immediately.

concepts.statement: `vEB-TREE-INSERT(V, x)`: if $V$ is empty, store $x$ in both fields ($O(1)$). Else if $x < V.min$, **exchange $x$ with $V.min$** — the new element becomes the stored minimum and the *old minimum* descends into the clusters (it was never there). If $u > 2$: if cluster$[\mathrm{high}(x)]$ is empty, set it up in $O(1)$ and recurse into the **summary**; otherwise recurse into the **cluster**. Update $V.max$ if $x$ exceeds it. Either way, exactly **one** recursive call per level.
concepts.detail: The swap is what keeps the minimum out of the clusters without losing it — and it can cascade: the displaced minimum provokes an insertion one level down, possibly swapping again.

concepts.term: Space: O(u), not O(u lg u)
concepts.statement: A vEB$(u)$ has one summary plus $\sqrt u$ clusters, each vEB$(\sqrt u)$: $$S(u) = (\sqrt u + 1)\,S(\sqrt u) + O(1) = O(u).$$ Writing $u = 2^{2^k}$, the product of the multiplicative factors telescopes: $\prod_{i=1}^{k}\left(2^{2^{i-1}} + 1\right) \le 2^{2^k - 1} \cdot \prod_{j \ge 0}\left(1 + 2^{-2^j}\right) = \tfrac{u}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - 1/2} = u$, using the identity $\prod_{j \ge 0}(1 + x^{2^j}) = \frac{1}{1-x}$ at $x = 1/2$.
concepts.detail: The naive bound — multiplying out all $(\sqrt u + 1)$ factors as if each were $\sqrt u$-ish — would suggest $O(u \lg u)$; the $+1$s are what the identity harvests. For universes not of the form $2^{2^k}$, round up (at worst squaring the universe, still $O(u)$).

concepts.term: When a vEB tree is the right tool
concepts.statement: All bounds are in $u$, not $n$. The tree wins when the universe is **polynomial in $n$** — say $u \le n^2$, as when keys are pairs or coordinates — because then $\lg \lg u \le \lg \lg n^2 = O(\lg \lg n)$ beats a balanced tree's $O(\lg n)$, and the $O(u)$ space is $O(n^2)$ or better. Applications: priority queues with small integer keys, IP routing tables, and geometric sweeping over grid coordinates.
concepts.detail: For huge universes with sparse keys, hashing ($O(1)$ expected insert/member but no order queries) or trees ($O(\lg n)$ everything) remain the tools of choice.

figures.caption: The van Emde Boas tree over $\{0, \dots, 15\}$ holding $S = \{1, 6, 8, 9, 15\}$: the top structure's fields are its stored minimum 1 (amber — stored *only* here, never in a cluster), its maximum 15 (also present inside cluster[3]), the summary, and four clusters. The numbered amber path is SUCCESSOR($V$, 7): (1) cluster[1] has $\max = 2 < \mathrm{low}(7) = 3$, so no successor there; (2)–(3) the summary ${1,2,3}$ answers 'successor of 1' $= 2$; (4) cluster[2]'s minimum is 0; (5) the answer is $2 \cdot 4 + 0 = 8$. One recursive call per level: $O(\lg \lg u)$.
