examples.title: Five augmentations, one backward edge, one saturated cut
examples.problem: Run the Ford-Fulkerson method by hand on the chapter network (capacities as in Section 26.1) from the zero flow. A poor early path choice gets repaired by a backward edge; then certify the answer with a cut.

steps.label: Augment 1
steps.text: Path $s \to v_2 \to v_1 \to v_3 \to t$; residuals $13, 4, 12, 20$ — bottleneck 4. Value $= 4$. The cross edge $v_2 \to v_1$ is convenient now and awkward later.

steps.label: Augment 2
steps.text: $s \to v_1 \to v_3 \to t$: residuals $16,\ 12 - 4 = 8,\ 20 - 4 = 16$ — bottleneck 8. Value $= 12$; $v_1 \to v_3$ is saturated at 12.

steps.label: Augment 3
steps.text: $s \to v_2 \to v_4 \to t$; residuals $13 - 4 = 9, 14, 4$ — bottleneck 4. Value $= 16$.

steps.label: Augment 4
steps.text: $s \to v_2 \to v_4 \to v_3 \to t$; residuals $9 - 4 = 5, 14 - 4 = 10, 7, 16 - 8 = 8$ — bottleneck 5. Value $= 21$. Both $s \to v_2$ (13/13) and $v_2 \to v_1$ (4/4) are now saturated — this is the state drawn in the residual-network figure.

steps.label: Augment 5 — the repair
steps.text: Exactly one augmenting path remains: $s \to v_1 \to v_2 \to v_4 \to v_3 \to t$. Its second edge is *backward*: $c_f(v_1,v_2) = 0 - f(v_1,v_2) = 0 - (-4) = 4$. Bottleneck $\min(8, 4, 5, 2, 3) = 2$: push 2, canceling $f(v_2,v_1)$ down to 2 and redirecting those units through $v_2 \to v_4 \to v_3 \to t$. Value $= 23$.

steps.label: Stop and certify
steps.text: From $s$ in $G_f$ we reach $v_1$ ($s \to v_1$ has 6 left), $v_2$ (via backward $v_1 \to v_2$, 2 left), and $v_4$ (3 left on $v_2 \to v_4$) — but $v_4$'s exits $v_4 \to v_3$ and $v_4 \to t$ are both saturated, so $t$ is unreachable. Thus $S = \{s, v_1, v_2, v_4\}$ and $c(S,T) = c(v_1,v_3) + c(v_4,v_3) + c(v_4,t) = 12 + 7 + 4 = 23 = |f|$.

examples.result: Maximum flow 23, certified by the minimum cut $(\{s, v_1, v_2, v_4\}, \{v_3, t\})$ of capacity 23 — flow equals cut, so neither can improve (Theorem 26.6). The final flow: $f(s,v_1) = 10$, $f(s,v_2) = 13$, $f(v_2,v_1) = 2$, $f(v_1,v_3) = 12$, $f(v_2,v_4) = 11$, $f(v_4,v_3) = 7$, $f(v_4,t) = 4$, $f(v_3,t) = 19$, $f(v_3,v_2) = 0$.

examples.title: Augmenting through a backward edge
examples.problem: Network $s \to a(3)$, $s \to b(3)$, $a \to t(3)$, $b \to t(3)$, $a \to b(2)$. After pushing $3$ on $s-a-b-t$, show the next augmentation uses $(b,a)$ backward? Actually trace the textbook reroute.

steps.label: First push
steps.text: Path $s \to a \to b \to t$ bottleneck $2$? Capacities $3,2,3$: push $2$: $f(s,a) = 2$, $f(a,b) = 2$, $f(b,t) = 2$.

steps.label: Residual
steps.text: Backward capacities $2$ on $(a,s),(b,a),(t,b)$ appear; forward $s \to a$ remains $1$, $b \to t$ remains $1$.

steps.label: Second push
steps.text: Path $s \to a \to t$ ($1$ left) plus $s \to b \to t$ ($1$ left): push $1+1 = 2$ more: total $4$? Optimal is $6$: further augmentations $s \to a \to t$? Systematically Ford-Fulkerson reaches $6$ by also using $a \to b$ forward then cancelling if needed.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.text: Backward edge $(b,a)$ would carry flow if early pushes oversubscribed $a \to b$: augmenting $s \to b \to a \to t$ cancels $1$ unit of $a \to b$ to rebalance toward the $3+3$ optimum.

examples.result: Residual backward edges make every push revisable; max flow $6$ needs the $a \to b$ capacity plus its backward undo, certified by the $\{s\}$ cut $3+3$.

keyTakeaways: The residual network is the search space: its $s$-$t$ paths are exactly the remaining improvements, and backward edges are how the method repairs earlier routing mistakes.
Lemma 26.4 — $|f| = f(S,T) \le c(S,T)$ for every cut — is weak duality: no flow beats any cut.
Max flow = min cut: when Ford-Fulkerson halts, the set reachable from $s$ in $G_f$ yields a saturated cut, a cheaply checkable certificate that the flow is optimal.

quiz.q: A pair with no edge — $c(u,v) = 0$ — has $f(u,v) = -4$ (4 units net $v \to u$). What is the residual capacity $c_f(u,v)$?
quiz.explanation: $c_f(u,v) = c(u,v) - f(u,v) = 0 - (-4) = 4$: a backward residual edge exists purely to cancel those 4 units. Residual capacity is defined on all pairs, not just edges.

quiz.q: Ford-Fulkerson is called a method rather than an algorithm because:
options: it may fail to terminate on irrational capacities
the choice of augmenting path is left unspecified, and different choices yield different algorithms and running times
it requires integer capacities to be well defined
it only computes an approximate maximum flow
quiz.explanation: The sentence 'while an augmenting path exists, push along it' fixes no path-selection rule; DFS-style paths give $O(E|f^*|)$, BFS gives Edmonds-Karp's $O(VE^2)$. (Irrational capacities can indeed cause non-termination — but that is a consequence of the freedom, not the reason for the name.)

quiz.q: For a flow $f$ and an arbitrary cut $(S,T)$, which identity always holds?
quiz.explanation: Lemma 26.4: the value equals the net flow across every cut and is bounded by that cut's capacity. Equality with $c(S,T)$ holds only when $f$ is maximum and $(S,T)$ is minimum.

quiz.q: The Edmonds-Karp algorithm selects augmenting paths by BFS (fewest edges) and runs in time:
quiz.explanation: Shortest augmenting paths make each pair of vertices' distance labels monotone, so each edge becomes critical only $O(V)$ times — $O(VE)$ augmentations over $O(E)$-length paths: $O(VE^2)$, polynomial independent of capacity magnitudes.

quiz.q: Capacities: $s\to a:10, s\to b:8, a\to b:3, a\to t:7, b\to t:12$. The maximum $s$-$t$ flow value is:
quiz.explanation: Step 1 — Given: five directed capacities, source $s$, sink $t$. Step 2 — Governing duality: flow value is capped by every $s$-$t$ cut and equals the minimum one. Step 3 — Augmentation: push $7$ on $s\to a\to t$, $8$ on $s\to b\to t$, then $3$ on $s\to a\to b\to t$ (using $b\to t$ residual $4$); total $18$; cut $({s,a},{b,t})$ has $8 + 7 + 3 = 18$, certifying optimality. Step 4 — Sanity check: $18$ respects out-of-$s$ ($18$) and into-$t$ ($19$) caps, residuals show no augmenting path left, and backward edges were available throughout. Step 5 — Distractor analysis: $15$ misses the cross edge, $17$ leaves one unit unpushed, and $20$ exceeds the source cap. Step 6 — Conclude: maximum flow $18$.

depth.title: The max-flow min-cut theorem, proved completely

blocks.body: Every duality theorem in combinatorial optimization traces its lineage to this one. The theorem couples three a priori unrelated statements — an optimization claim (some flow is best), an algorithmic claim (a search space is exhausted), and a certificate claim (a cut is tight) — and proves them equivalent. The proof is three implications, and each carries an idea worth stealing: **augmentation** (contrapositive), **reachability** (construction), and **weak duality** (bookkeeping). Throughout, $f$ is a flow in $G = (V, E)$ and $G_f$ its residual network.

blocks.heading: Theorem (CLRS Theorem 26.6)
blocks.body: The following are equivalent: (1) $f$ is a maximum flow; (2) $G_f$ contains no augmenting path; (3) there exists a cut $(S, T)$ with $|f| = c(S, T)$. Moreover, in that case $(S,T)$ is a minimum cut; and for *every* maximum flow $f^*$ and minimum cut $(S^*, T^*)$, $|f^*| = c(S^*, T^*)$.

blocks.heading: (1) ⇒ (2): an augmenting path is a certificate of suboptimality
blocks.body: We prove the contrapositive. Let $p = \langle s = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k = t \rangle$ be a simple path in $G_f$ and $c_f(p) = \min_{0 \le i < k} c_f(v_i, v_{i+1}) > 0$. Define a function on $G_f$'s pairs by $f'(v_i, v_{i+1}) = c_f(p)$ along path edges, $f'(v_{i+1}, v_i) = -c_f(p)$, and $0$ elsewhere. It is a flow in $G_f$: capacity holds because $c_f(p) \le c_f(v_i, v_{i+1})$ on every path edge (and the negative entries sit at or below 0); skew symmetry is built in; and conservation holds at each internal $v_i$ because the simple path gives it exactly one edge in and one out, netting $c_f(p) - c_f(p) = 0$. Its value is $|f'| = c_f(p) > 0$. Now combine: $f \uparrow f'$, defined by $f(u,v) + f'(u,v) - f'(v,u)$, is a flow in $G$ of value $|f| + c_f(p)$ (the combination lemma). So $f$ was not maximum.

blocks.heading: (2) ⇒ (3): the cut hiding in the residual network
blocks.body: Suppose $G_f$ has no $s$-$t$ path. Let $S = \{v : v \text{ reachable from } s \text{ in } G_f\}$ and $T = V - S$, so $s \in S$, $t \in T$. Claim: $c_f(u,v) = 0$ for every $u \in S, v \in T$ — otherwise the residual edge $(u,v)$ would make $v$ reachable. Unpack that as $c(u,v) - f(u,v) = 0$, i.e. $f(u,v) = c(u,v)$ for *every* ordered pair crossing from $S$ to $T$: crossing edges are saturated, and pairs with no edge carry $0 = 0$. Skew symmetry has already folded the backward direction into the same statement — a positive $f(v,u)$ with $v \in T, u \in S$ would give $c_f(u,v) = c(u,v) + f(v,u) > 0$, contradicting the claim. Summing over all crossing pairs and applying the cut identity of Lemma 26.4: $|f| = f(S,T) = \sum_{u \in S, v \in T} f(u,v) = \sum_{u \in S, v \in T} c(u,v) = c(S,T)$.

blocks.heading: Lemma 26.4: every cut sees the same value (weak duality)
blocks.body: For an arbitrary cut $(S,T)$, expand $f(S,V) = \sum_{u \in S}\sum_{v \in V} f(u,v)$ by the second coordinate: $f(S,V) = f(S,S) + f(S,T)$. The internal term vanishes — $f(S,S) = \sum_{u, v \in S} f(u,v) = 0$ — because skew symmetry cancels each ordered pair against its reverse. Evaluate the left side vertex by vertex instead: for each $u \in S - \{s\}$ (note $t \notin S$), conservation gives $\sum_v f(u,v) = 0$, so only $u = s$ survives, contributing $\sum_v f(s,v) = |f|$. Chaining the three displays: $|f| = f(S,T)$ for *every* cut. Finally the capacity constraint gives the termwise bound $f(u,v) \le c(u,v)$, so $|f| = f(S,T) \le c(S,T)$ — every flow's value is at most every cut's capacity. This single inequality is all the geometry the theorem needs.

blocks.heading: (3) ⇒ (1): tightness spreads in both directions
blocks.body: Suppose $|f| = c(S,T)$ for some cut. For any flow $f'$, weak duality gives $|f'| \le c(S,T) = |f|$, so $f$ is a maximum flow. Symmetrically, for any cut $(S', T')$, $c(S',T') \ge |f| = c(S,T)$, so $(S,T)$ is a minimum cut. The three statements now collapse into one: (1) ⇒ (2) ⇒ (3) ⇒ (1). Note also *where* the minimum cut came from in the second implication — the set reachable from $s$ in $G_f$ — which is why any run of Ford-Fulkerson that halts hands you the cut for free (Corollary 26.7).

blocks.heading: Certificates, integrality, and the LP view
blocks.body: Three consequences deserve a flag. **Certificates**: a max flow plus its saturated cut is a pair of efficiently checkable witnesses — 'here is a good flow' and 'here is why nothing better exists' — making maximum flow a rare optimization problem with fully checkable optimality proofs. **Integrality**: if all capacities are integers, every augmentation adds an integer, so Ford-Fulkerson terminates at an *integral* maximum flow; that fact is exactly what makes the bipartite-matching reduction of Section 26.3 sound. **Linear programming**: maximizing $|f|$ subject to the flow constraints is a linear program, and cuts correspond to feasible solutions of its dual — max-flow min-cut is LP strong duality in combinatorial clothing, a special case of the general duality theory CLRS develops in Chapter 29.

intro: Here is the payoff: a purely combinatorial question — pair up as many left vertices with right vertices as possible, no vertex used twice — becomes a maximum-flow instance by directing every edge and giving everything unit capacity. The reduction is the chapter's first showcase of its power, and it comes with a bonus: König's theorem, one of graph theory's classic dualities, falls out of max-flow min-cut for free.
objectives: Define matchings, maximum matchings and perfect matchings in bipartite graphs
Build the unit-capacity flow model and explain the matching-flow correspondence
Derive König's theorem from the minimum cut and bound the running time

concepts.statement: In an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$, a **matching** is a subset $M \subseteq E$ no two of whose edges share an endpoint. A **maximum matching** has the largest cardinality among all matchings; a **perfect matching** covers every vertex of the graph. In a **bipartite graph** $G = (L \cup R, E)$, every edge joins a vertex of $L$ to a vertex of $R$.
concepts.detail: Typical instances: assigning workers to shifts, courses to rooms, or processes to machines — two parties, and each pairing consumes one member of each side.

concepts.term: The flow model of a matching instance
concepts.statement: Given bipartite $G$, direct every edge from $L$ toward $R$, add an edge $s \to l$ for each $l \in L$ and $r \to t$ for each $r \in R$, and give **every edge capacity 1**. Then matchings in $G$ correspond exactly to flows in the model that take only the values 0 and 1, with $|M| = |f|$.
concepts.detail: Why capacity 1 everywhere: $s \to l$ caps how many matches $l$ can hold, $r \to t$ caps $r$, and the middle edge *is* the match. The direction that needs a theorem is the converse — that a maximum flow may be taken integral — which is where integrality does the work.

concepts.statement: Ford-Fulkerson with integer capacities terminates with an integral maximum flow, so applied to the unit-capacity model it outputs a **maximum matching**. Each augmenting path has bottleneck exactly 1 (every path edge has capacity 1) and $|f^*| \le \min(|L|, |R|)$, so the method uses $O(V)$ augmentations of $O(E)$ work each: **maximum bipartite matching in $O(VE)$ time**.
concepts.detail: The $O(VE)$ bound is CLRS's stated result for the reduction with a plain augmenting-path search. Faster dedicated algorithms exist (Hopcroft-Karp at $O(E\sqrt{V})$), but the point here is the reduction's cleanliness.

concepts.statement: In any bipartite graph, the maximum size of a matching equals the minimum size of a **vertex cover** — a set of vertices touching every edge: $\max |M| = \min |C|$.
concepts.detail: Read it off the residual-reachable minimum cut ($S$ = the vertices reachable from $s$ in $G_{f^*}$): $C = (L \cap T) \cup (R \cap S)$ is a minimum vertex cover. No $L \to R$ edge can cross from $S$ to $T$ — an unsaturated one would make its right endpoint reachable in the residual, and a saturated one would demand more than $s \to l$'s single unit of supply through its left endpoint — so $C$ touches every edge, and $|C| = c(S,T) = |f^*| = |M^*|$.

concepts.statement: Maximal means no edge can be added without sharing a vertex (greedy achieves it); maximum means no larger matching exists (needs augmenting paths / flow). Every maximum matching is maximal, but maximal can be half the size of maximum.
concepts.detail: The section's repair example is a maximal-but-not-maximum matching: one alternating path augments it by $1$. Bipartite maximum matching is maximum flow with unit capacities, so Ford-Fulkerson's augmentations are exactly matching augmentations.

examples.title: When greedy needs a repair
examples.problem: Left vertices $l_1, \dots, l_4$; right vertices $r_1, \dots, r_4$; edges $l_1$–$r_1$, $l_1$–$r_2$, $l_2$–$r_1$, $l_3$–$r_2$, $l_3$–$r_3$, $l_4$–$r_3$, $l_4$–$r_4$. Greedy, taking $l_1$–$r_1$ first, gets stuck at a matching of size 3. Run the flow model instead.

steps.label: Step 1: Greedy's dead end
steps.text: Matching $\{l_1\text{-}r_1, l_3\text{-}r_2, l_4\text{-}r_3\}$ blocks $l_2$, whose only neighbor $r_1$ is taken. Size 3 — one short.

steps.label: Step 2: First augmentation
steps.text: Path $s \to l_1 \to r_1 \to t$, bottleneck 1. Flow value 1: matching $\{l_1\text{-}r_1\}$.

steps.label: Step 3: The repair, via a backward edge
steps.text: From $l_2$, the residual path $s \to l_2 \to r_1 \to l_1 \to r_2 \to t$ runs through the *backward* edge $r_1 \to l_1$ (it cancels the match $l_1$–$r_1$). Augmenting by 1 re-matches $l_1$–$r_2$ and frees $r_1$ for $l_2$: matching $\{l_1\text{-}r_2, l_2\text{-}r_1\}$, value 2. Greedy's mistake was repairable, not fatal.

steps.label: Step 4: Finish
steps.text: $s \to l_3 \to r_3 \to t$ and $s \to l_4 \to r_4 \to t$, each bottleneck 1. Value 4: the perfect matching $\{l_1\text{-}r_2,\ l_2\text{-}r_1,\ l_3\text{-}r_3,\ l_4\text{-}r_4\}$.

steps.label: Step 5: König check
steps.text: All four edges into $t$ are saturated, so the residual-reachable set is just $S = \{s\}$, giving the cover $(L \cap T) \cup (R \cap S) = \{l_1, l_2, l_3, l_4\}$ of size 4. No smaller cover can exist, since the four matching edges are pairwise disjoint and each needs its own covering vertex.

examples.result: A maximum (here perfect) matching of size 4, certified by König: a disjoint-edge argument shows no cover is smaller than the matching, and the flow's saturated cut exhibits a cover of exactly that size.

examples.title: Reading a minimum vertex cover off the residual reachability
examples.problem: Bipartite graph with $L = \{l_1, l_2, l_3, l_4\}$, $R = \{r_1, r_2, r_3\}$ and edges $l_1$–$r_1$, $l_2$–$r_1$, $l_2$–$r_2$, $l_3$–$r_2$, $l_3$–$r_3$, $l_4$–$r_3$ — four left vertices but only three right ones. Extract König's minimum vertex cover from the minimum cut.

steps.label: Step 1: A maximum matching and its flow
steps.text: The matching $\{l_1\text{-}r_1,\ l_2\text{-}r_2,\ l_3\text{-}r_3\}$ has size 3, and $l_4$ is left over — it must be, since only three right vertices exist. In the flow model, $s \to l_4$ carries 0 while every $r_j \to t$ is saturated at 1. No augmenting path survives, because any one must exit through some $r_j \to t$ and all are full.

steps.label: Step 2: The reachability cascade
steps.text: Compute $S$ = vertices reachable from $s$ in $G_f$: the leftover capacity on $s \to l_4$ admits $l_4$; the unsaturated $l_4 \to r_3$ admits $r_3$; the saturated match $l_3$–$r_3$ contributes the backward edge $r_3 \to l_3$, admitting $l_3$; then the unsaturated $l_3 \to r_2$ admits $r_2$; its match drags in $l_2$; then $l_2 \to r_1$ admits $r_1$; and finally the match on $l_1$–$r_1$ admits $l_1$. Every vertex except $t$ is reachable: $S = V - \{t\}$.

steps.label: Step 3: The cut and the cover
steps.text: The cut $(S, \{t\})$ has capacity $c(r_1,t) + c(r_2,t) + c(r_3,t) = 3 = |f^*|$ — minimum, exactly as Theorem 26.6 demands. König's cover is $C = (L \cap T) \cup (R \cap S) = \emptyset \cup \{r_1, r_2, r_3\}$: all of $R$.

steps.label: Step 4: Check the cover
steps.text: Every edge has its right endpoint in $C$: $l_1$–$r_1$, $l_2$–$r_1$, $l_2$–$r_2$, $l_3$–$r_2$, $l_3$–$r_3$, $l_4$–$r_3$ — all covered. And no cover can be smaller: the three matching edges are pairwise disjoint, so any cover needs one vertex per edge. Maximum matching = minimum cover = 3.

examples.result: König's theorem made concrete: the alternating cascade of Step 2 — forward along an unsaturated edge, backward along a saturated match — is precisely the alternating-path structure of the classical proof, and it terminates in a cover of size exactly $|M^*|$.

keyTakeaways: Unit capacities turn matching into flow: integral maximum flows are exactly matchings, with $|M| = |f|$, found in $O(VE)$ augmentations of bottleneck 1.
Backward residual edges *are* re-matching: an augmenting path through $r \to l$ un-assigns one pair to create a better one — greedy choices are repairable.
König's theorem (max matching = min vertex cover in bipartite graphs) is max-flow min-cut in disguise: the cover is $(L \cap T) \cup (R \cap S)$.

quiz.q: In the flow model of bipartite matching, an augmenting path that traverses a backward edge $r \to l$ corresponds to:
options: assigning a second partner to some vertex
re-matching: canceling one match to enable a better one
doubling the flow value in one step
quiz.explanation: The backward edge cancels the existing match on $l$–$r$; the path then re-routes $l$ to another right vertex, freeing $r$ for the left vertex where the path started.

quiz.q: Why can Ford-Fulkerson's output on the unit-capacity model be interpreted as a matching?
options: integrality: every augmentation adds an integer, and unit capacities force each flow value to 0 or 1
the residual network of a bipartite graph is bipartite
because the source has unbounded capacity
quiz.explanation: With integer (unit) capacities, augmentations preserve integrality — the flow on each edge stays in $\{0,1\}$ — and such flows are precisely matchings.

quiz.q: The running time CLRS gives for maximum bipartite matching via the Ford-Fulkerson reduction is:
quiz.explanation: Every augmenting path has bottleneck exactly 1, at most $\min(|L|,|R|) \le |V|$ augmentations are needed, and each costs $O(E)$: $O(VE)$ total.

quiz.q: König's theorem — maximum matching equals minimum vertex cover — holds:
options: in bipartite graphs; it can fail on graphs with odd cycles
only when a perfect matching exists
quiz.explanation: The 5-cycle $C_5$ has maximum matching 2 but needs 3 vertices to cover all 5 edges; the min cut of the flow model, which produces the cover, exists only for bipartite instances.

intro: Ford-Fulkerson improves a flow only along whole $s$-$t$ paths — a global detour for every unit of progress. Push-relabel (Goldberg and Tarjan, 1988) works locally instead: flood a preflow through the network, letting vertices hold excess, then let each overflowing vertex push its excess one step downhill or raise its own height when nothing is downhill. The plumbing picture is honest — fill the pipes beyond capacity, then let the surplus drain toward the sink or bubble back to the source.
objectives: Distinguish a preflow from a flow via the excess $e(u)$
Apply PUSH and RELABEL with their exact applicability conditions
Summarize the $O(V^2 E)$ analysis: relabels, saturating pushes, nonsaturating pushes

concepts.statement: A **preflow** satisfies the capacity constraint and skew symmetry but relaxes conservation to $\sum_{v \in V} f(v,u) \ge 0$ for $u \in V - \{s,t\}$. The surplus is the **excess** $e(u) = \sum_{v \in V} f(v,u)$ — flow that entered $u$ and has not yet left. A vertex with $e(u) > 0$ is **overflowing**; a preflow with no overflowing vertex is an ordinary flow.
concepts.detail: Push-relabel floods first and drains later. The initialization itself creates excess: saturate every edge out of $s$, and let the interior vertices hold what they receive until heights route it onward.

concepts.statement: A **labeling** is a function $h : V \to \mathbb{N}$ with $h(s) = |V|$, $h(t) = 0$, and $h(u) \le h(v) + 1$ for every residual edge $(u,v) \in E_f$. Flow moves only *downhill, one step at a time*: a push from $u$ to $v$ requires exactly $h(u) = h(v) + 1$.
concepts.detail: The invariant means each residual edge drops height by at most 1, so $h(u)$ never exceeds the residual distance from $u$ to $t$ while that distance is finite. Once $t$ is unreachable, relabels inflate the label toward $2|V| - 1$ — at which point the height is really measuring the climb back to $s$.

concepts.statement: **PUSH$(u,v)$** applies when $u$ is overflowing, $c_f(u,v) > 0$, and $h(u) = h(v) + 1$; it moves $\delta = \min(e(u), c_f(u,v))$ units from $u$ to $v$, decreasing $e(u)$ by $\delta$ and increasing $e(v)$ by $\delta$. It is **saturating** if $\delta = c_f(u,v)$, **nonsaturating** otherwise. **RELABEL$(u)$** applies when $u$ is overflowing but has no admissible outgoing edge; it sets $h(u) = 1 + \min\{h(v) : (u,v) \in E_f\}$ — the smallest height that creates one.
concepts.detail: Heights only ever increase. Pushes to $t$ absorb the excess into the sink; pushes back to $s$ (possible once $h(u)$ climbs to $h(s)+1$) return it to the source — both are how the algorithm terminates with all excess gone.

concepts.term: The generic algorithm and its $O(V^2 E)$ bound
concepts.statement: **GENERIC-PUSH-RELABEL**: while some vertex overflows, apply any applicable push or relabel. Every execution terminates with a maximum flow in $O(V^2 E)$ time. The three ingredients: each vertex relabels at most $2|V| - 1$ times (heights never exceed $2|V|-1$ — reachable-$t$ vertices are capped by their distance, unreachable ones by the climb back to $s$); each edge endures at most $2|V|$ saturating pushes ($O(VE)$ total); and a potential argument caps nonsaturating pushes at $O(V^2 E)$ — the hard part of the analysis.
concepts.detail: The local moves are the point: no $s$-$t$ path is ever searched for. With practical heuristics (highest-label selection, gap relabeling), push-relabel descendants remain the standard heavy-duty max-flow codes used in vision and scheduling applications.

concepts.statement: Valid labels satisfy $h(s) = |V|$, $h(t) = 0$, $h(u) \le h(v)+1$ for every residual edge $(u,v)$; heights only rise and RELABEL raises $u$ to $1+\min h(v)$ over residual neighbours, so $h(u) \le 2|V|-1$ always (a simple path to $s$ or $t$ has $< |V|$ edges).
concepts.detail: The cap bounds relabels at $O(V^2)$ ($|V|$ vertices $\times$ $2|V|$ heights) and saturating pushes at $O(VE)$: the two easy thirds of the $O(V^2E)$ generic bound. Nonsaturating pushes need the potential argument.

examples.title: Push, relabel, and one trip home to the source
examples.problem: Vertices $\{s, u, v, t\}$; edges $s \to u$ (10), $u \to t$ (8), $u \to v$ (4), $v \to t$ (1). Initialize $h(s) = |V| = 4$, $h = 0$ elsewhere, and saturate the source edge: $f(s,u) = 10$, so $e(u) = 10$. Discharge overflowing vertices as they come.

steps.label: Step 1: Flood
steps.text: After initialization only $u$ overflows: $e(u) = 10$; heights are $h(s) = 4$, everything else 0.

steps.label: Step 2: Discharge $u$ (h: 0 → 1)
steps.text: No edge out of $u$ is admissible at $h(u) = 0$, so RELABEL: $h(u) = 1 + \min\{h(t), h(v), h(s)\} = 1$. Then PUSH $u \to t$: $\delta = \min(10, 8) = 8$ (saturating). PUSH $u \to v$: $\delta = \min(2, 4) = 2$ (nonsaturating). Now $e(u) = 0$, $e(v) = 2$.

steps.label: Step 3: Discharge $v$ (h: 0 → 1 → 2)
steps.text: RELABEL $h(v) = 1$; PUSH $v \to t$: $\delta = \min(2,1) = 1$ (saturating). Stuck — $v \to t$ is full — so RELABEL $h(v) = 2 = h(u)+1$; PUSH $v \to u$ on the *backward* residual edge: $\delta = \min(1, 2) = 1$. This cancels one unit of $f(u,v)$, returning it as excess: $e(v) = 0$, $e(u) = 1$, $f(u,v) = 1$.

steps.label: Step 4: The excess bounces
steps.text: Now a pattern: $u$ relabels up by 2 (to 3, then 5) and pushes its single unit to $v$; $v$ relabels up by 2 (to 4, then 6) and pushes it back. Four relabels and four pushes later: $e(u) = 1$ with $h(u) = 5$, $h(v) = 6$, $f(u,v) = 1$ still. Heights stay below $2|V| - 1 = 7$, as the bound promises.

steps.label: Step 5: Home to the source
steps.text: At $h(u) = 5 = h(s) + 1$, the backward residual edge $u \to s$ finally becomes admissible, with $c_f(u,s) = 0 - f(u,s) = 10$. PUSH $u \to s$: $\delta = 1$ — the last unit of excess returns to the source, $f(s,u) = 9$.

steps.label: Step 6: Read off the answer
steps.text: No vertex overflows, so the preflow is a flow: $f(s,u) = 9$, $f(u,t) = 8$, $f(u,v) = 1$, $f(v,t) = 1$, and $|f| = 9$. The cut $(\{s,u,v\}, \{t\})$ has capacity $8 + 1 = 9$ — maximum, certified.

examples.result: Maximum flow 9, using 10 pushes (one of them the initializing saturating push from $s$) and 7 relabels. The ping-pong of Step 4 — excess climbing two height units per bounce with nothing but local moves — is exactly the behavior the $O(V^2 E)$ analysis must tame.

examples.title: Push then relabel on three vertices
examples.problem: Preflow $s \to a(3)$ saturated, $h(s) = 3$, $h(a) = 0$, $h(t) = 0$, edge $a \to t(2)$. Discharge $a$ with excess $3$.

steps.label: Push $a \to t$
steps.text: Admissible? Needs $h(a) = h(t)+1$: $0 = 1$? No: $a \to t$ not admissible (equal heights). No push.

steps.label: Relabel $a$
steps.text: Residual neighbours $t(0)$, $s(3)$? $(a,s)$ residual $3$ (backward): $\min = 0$: $h(a) = 1$.

steps.label: Push $a \to t$
steps.text: Now $1 = 0+1$ admissible: push $\min(3, 2) = 2$ (saturating): $e(a) = 1$, $e(t) = 2$.

steps.label: Push $a \to s$?
steps.text: $h(a) = 1$, $h(s) = 3$: $1 = 4$? No: must relabel $a$ to $4$ before pushing home: heights ratchet, never fall.

examples.result: One relabel ($0 \to 1$) enabled one saturating push of $2$; excess $1$ waits for the next relabel: heights gate pushes.

keyTakeaways: Preflow = flood now, drain later: conservation is repaired rather than assumed, with $e(u)$ tracking each vertex's debt.
Pushes move excess one downhill step ($h(u) = h(v)+1$); relabels raise the ground when nothing is downhill; heights only rise, bounded by $2|V| - 1$.
$O(V^2 E)$ total: $O(V^2)$ relabels, $O(VE)$ saturating pushes, and the hard-won $O(V^2 E)$ bound on nonsaturating pushes — all without any global path search.

quiz.q: A preflow relaxes flow conservation to:
options: $\sum_{v \in V} f(v,u) \ge 0$ — vertices may hold excess (inflow exceeding outflow)
capacities may be exceeded on edges out of $s$
flow may also leave the sink $t$
quiz.explanation: Only internal vertices' conservation is relaxed, and only in one direction: $e(u) = \sum_v f(v,u) \ge 0$. Capacity and skew symmetry stay in force.

quiz.q: PUSH$(u,v)$ requires $u$ overflowing, $c_f(u,v) > 0$, and:
quiz.explanation: Flow moves exactly one label downhill — the admissibility condition of valid labelings. A mere height advantage is not enough; the drop must be exactly one step.

quiz.q: Why is the source initialized with $h(s) = |V|$?
options: so the source sits above every vertex — excess that cannot reach $t$ can always climb back to $s$ along admissible edges
to bound the number of edges at $s$
purely a convention with no effect on correctness
quiz.explanation: Any simple residual path has fewer than $|V|$ edges, so $h(s) = |V|$ starts the source above the whole network. Vertices whose height climbs to $h(s)+1$ can push excess back home — the algorithm's escape hatch.

quiz.q: The generic push-relabel algorithm terminates in:
quiz.explanation: Relabels contribute $O(V^2)$, saturating pushes $O(VE)$, and nonsaturating pushes $O(V^2 E)$ — the last term dominates. Note the bound is independent of capacity magnitudes, unlike plain Ford-Fulkerson.

intro: The generic push-relabel method leaves the *order* of operations free, and a bad order wastes pushes on vertices that were about to become pushable anyway. Relabel-to-front imposes one: keep the nonsource, nonsink vertices in a list, discharge each vertex completely before moving on, and move any vertex that relabeled to the front. That single scheduling heuristic tightens the running time from $O(V^2 E)$ to $O(V^3)$.
objectives: Define admissible edges and explain why the admissible network is acyclic
Execute DISCHARGE with current pointers and trace a full relabel-to-front run
State the $O(V^3)$ bound and identify which cost it improves

concepts.statement: A residual edge $(u,v)$ is **admissible** if $c_f(u,v) > 0$ and $h(u) = h(v) + 1$. The **admissible network** $G_A = (V, E_A)$ contains exactly the admissible edges, and it is **acyclic**: every admissible edge strictly decreases $h$, so a directed cycle would have to return $h$ to its starting value.
concepts.detail: Pushes travel only on admissible edges, so following them from any vertex must terminate. A relabel of $u$ is precisely the event that creates new admissible edges *out of* $u$ — the moment the schedule should revisit it.

concepts.statement: **DISCHARGE$(u)$** processes all of $u$'s excess at once: scan $u$'s edge list with a persistent **current** pointer; push along each admissible edge until it saturates or the excess runs out; when the list is exhausted, RELABEL $u$ and restart the pointer. Each neighbor is examined at most once between two relabels of $u$.
concepts.detail: The current pointer is the amortization device: between relabels, a discharge sweeps $u$'s edge list once, costing $O(\deg u)$; over the whole run the scanning totals $O(VE)$ since each vertex relabels $O(V)$ times.

concepts.statement: **RELABEL-TO-FRONT** maintains a list $L$ of the vertices $V - \{s, t\}$ (any initial order) and scans it: discharge the vertex under the scan; if its height increased during that discharge, move it to the *front* of $L$; continue with the vertex that follows it in the (possibly just rearranged) list. When the scan runs off the end, the algorithm terminates with a maximum flow.
concepts.detail: The heuristic is greed: a vertex that relabeled is 'hot' — it just gained height, and new admissible edges around it may let its neighbors push back — so it is processed again soon rather than after a full pass.

concepts.statement: **Relabel-to-front runs in $O(V^3)$** — better than the generic $O(V^2 E)$ whenever the graph is dense (since $E \le V^2$). The improvement is entirely in the nonsaturating pushes: CLRS proves at most $4V^3$ of them, exploiting that the admissible network is acyclic and each discharge either empties its vertex or relabels it. All other costs are smaller: $O(V^2)$ relabels, $O(VE)$ saturating pushes, $O(VE)$ current-pointer scanning.
concepts.detail: The FIFO preflow-push variant achieves the same $O(V^3)$; highest-label selection with gap and global relabeling heuristics is what fast practical codes use. The relabel-to-front list is the simplest schedule that gets the bound.

concepts.statement: DISCHARGE scans $u$'s adjacency once via $u.current$: each neighbour is examined until it becomes inadmissible or a saturating push exhausts it, and the pointer only advances (wrapping on relabel). Total neighbour scans are $O(VE)$ across the whole run, not $O(VE)$ per discharge.
concepts.detail: Without the pointer each discharge would rescan all $\deg(u)$ neighbours after every nonsaturating push; with it each $(u,v)$ pair is scanned $O(V)$ times (once per height of $u$), giving the $O(V^3)$ bound's discharge term.

examples.title: The same run, scheduled by a list
examples.problem: Run RELABEL-TO-FRONT on the network of Section 26.4's example — $s \to u$ (10), $u \to t$ (8), $u \to v$ (4), $v \to t$ (1) — with the initial list $L = \langle u, v \rangle$ and both current pointers at the heads of their edge lists.

steps.label: Step 1: Initialize
steps.text: Saturate $s \to u$: $e(u) = 10$, $h(s) = 4$, all other heights 0. The scan starts at the head of $L$.

steps.label: Step 2: Discharge $u$ (h: 0 → 1)
steps.text: Relabel $u$ to 1; push 8 to $t$ (saturating) and 2 to $v$. The height increased, so $u$ moves to the front — a no-op at the front. The scan advances to $v$.

steps.label: Step 3: Discharge $v$ (h: 0 → 1 → 2)
steps.text: Relabel $v$ to 1, push 1 to $t$ (saturating); relabel $v$ to 2, push 1 back to $u$ on the backward edge. Height increased → $v$ moves to the front: $L = \langle v, u \rangle$, and the scan continues with $u$ (now the front's successor).

steps.label: Step 4: Ping-pong under move-to-front
steps.text: The discharges alternate: $u$ relabels 1 → 3 and pushes its unit to $v$ (moves to front, $L = \langle u, v\rangle$); $v$ relabels 2 → 4 and pushes it back ($L = \langle v, u \rangle$); $u$ relabels 3 → 5 and pushes ($L = \langle u, v\rangle$); $v$ relabels 4 → 6 and pushes back ($L = \langle v, u\rangle$). Each move-to-front naturally bounces the scan between the two hot vertices — exactly where the action is.

steps.label: Step 5: Last discharge — no relabel, no move
steps.text: With $h(u) = 5 = h(s) + 1$, discharging $u$ finds the backward edge $u \to s$ admissible immediately and pushes the final unit home ($f(s,u) = 9$, $e(u) = 0$). No relabel occurred, so the move-to-front rule correctly does *not* fire, and the scan proceeds.

steps.label: Step 6: Terminate
steps.text: The scan visits $v$ (no excess — discharge is a no-op) and runs off the end of $L$. No vertex overflows: the preflow is the same maximum flow as before, $|f| = 9$, with $h(u) = 5$, $h(v) = 6$.

examples.result: The same maximum flow of value 9 as the generic run — 10 pushes and 7 relabels — but with a deterministic schedule: the list flip-flops six times, and each flip is the heuristic saying 'this vertex just changed the landscape; look at it first.'

examples.title: Move-to-front on two vertices
examples.problem: List $[a, b]$, both with excess. $a$ discharges cleanly, $b$ relabels. Show the list move.

steps.label: Discharge $a$
steps.text: Push excess downstream, no relabel: $a$ stays, advance to $b$.

steps.label: Discharge $b$
steps.text: Push, then relabel $b$ ($h$ rises): move $b$ to front: list $[b, a]$.

steps.label: Rescan
steps.text: Restart after $b$ (now front): discharge $b$ again (now higher, may push back to $a$), then $a$.

steps.label: Bound
steps.text: Each relabel moves its vertex front ($O(V)$ relabels $\times$ $O(V)$ scans); nonsaturating pushes between relabels are $O(1)$ per discharge: total $O(V^3)$.

examples.result: List $[b,a]$ after $b$'s relabel; move-to-front revisits relabeled vertices first, the scheduling that tightens $O(V^2E)$ to $O(V^3)$.

keyTakeaways: Admissible = residual and exactly one step downhill; the admissible network is acyclic because heights strictly decrease along its edges.
Discharge bundles all of a vertex's work between relabels, and the persistent current pointer amortizes edge scanning down to $O(VE)$.
Move-to-front is the scheduling heuristic that cuts nonsaturating pushes to $O(V^3)$ — the whole content of the $O(V^3)$ theorem, since every other cost is smaller.

quiz.q: An admissible edge is a residual edge $(u,v)$ with:
quiz.explanation: Both conditions: enough residual capacity, and the height drop of exactly one label. Pushes travel only on admissible edges.

quiz.q: The admissible network $G_A$ is guaranteed to be:
quiz.explanation: Every admissible edge drops $h$ by exactly 1, so along any directed cycle the height would have to end strictly below where it started — impossible.

quiz.q: In RELABEL-TO-FRONT, vertex $u$ is moved to the front of the list $L$ whenever:
options: $u$ gains excess during another vertex's discharge
the discharge of $u$ increased $h(u)$ — a relabel occurred
a push from $u$ saturates an edge
the scan reaches the end of $L$
quiz.explanation: The test compares $h(u)$ before and after DISCHARGE$(u)$: only a relabel (new admissible edges out of $u$) justifies immediate reprocessing. Gaining excess alone does not move a vertex.

quiz.q: Relabel-to-front runs in time:
quiz.explanation: The move-to-front schedule bounds nonsaturating pushes by $4V^3$; relabels ($O(V^2)$), saturating pushes and scanning ($O(VE)$) are dominated since $E \le V^2$.

intro: A multithreaded algorithm is written as ordinary pseudocode sprinkled with two keywords — spawn and sync — plus a parallel for loop. This 'dynamic multithreading' model hides schedulers and processors from the programmer, yet supports precise analysis: two measures, work and span, bound the running time on any number of processors before a single machine is chosen.
objectives: Write and trace algorithms using spawn, sync and parallel for
Define work $T_1$, span $T_\infty$ and parallelism, and derive each for a given dag
State and apply the work law, the span law and the greedy scheduler bound
Explain why the greedy scheduler is within a factor of 2 of optimal

concepts.statement: **spawn** $\ \texttt{x = spawn fib(n-1)}$ starts a child subroutine that may run in parallel with its parent; the parent continues immediately. **sync** waits until all strands spawned by the current procedure have finished. A **parallel for** loop (`parfor`) runs all its iterations concurrently and implicitly syncs at the end.
concepts.detail: The keywords express *logical parallelism* only — which computations may proceed together. How they actually overlap is the scheduler's job, so the same algorithm runs unchanged on 1 core or 1000.

concepts.statement: An execution is a directed acyclic graph of **strands** (maximal instruction sequences without spawn/sync), joined by **continuation edges** (parent after spawn), **spawn edges** (parent to child) and **sync edges** (child back to the waiting parent). A legal schedule is any topological order of this dag.
concepts.detail: Every instruction sequence the program can possibly produce is a linearization of one dag — the dag is the complete specification of the computation's structure.

concepts.statement: The **work** $T_1$ is the total time to execute all strands on one processor; the **span** $T_\infty$ is the time on infinitely many processors — the length of the longest (critical) path in the dag.
concepts.detail: $T_P$ denotes the time on $P$ processors. The span is also called the *critical path* or *depth*: no amount of hardware can beat it, because its strands are serially dependent.

concepts.statement: For every $P \ge 1$: the **work law** $T_P \ge T_1 / P$ (a $P$-processor machine does at most $P$ units of work per tick) and the **span law** $T_P \ge T_\infty$. Hence the **parallelism** $T_1 / T_\infty$ is the maximum possible speedup — beyond it, extra processors idle.
concepts.detail: Perfect linear speedup $T_P = T_1/P$ holds only up to $P \approx T_1/T_\infty$; after that the span law dominates and the curve flattens.

concepts.statement: **(Greedy scheduling theorem.)** A greedy scheduler — one that never leaves a processor idle while a ready strand exists — running a computation with work $T_1$ and span $T_\infty$ on $P$ processors achieves $T_P \le \dfrac{T_1 + T_\infty (P-1)}{P} = \dfrac{T_1}{P} + T_\infty \cdot \dfrac{P-1}{P} < \dfrac{T_1}{P} + T_\infty$.
concepts.detail: Combined with the two lower bounds, greedy is never worse than twice optimal whenever $P \le T_1/T_\infty$: since $T_P^* \ge \max(T_1/P,\, T_\infty)$, the bound gives $T_P / T_P^* \le 2$. Any online scheduler without future knowledge suffers this factor.

figures.caption: The computation dag of $\text{P-FIB}(4)$. Solid edges are continuations (the thread keeps going), amber edges are spawns (a child thread begins), teal edges are syncs (the parent waits to join). Nine strands give work $T_1 = 9$; the highlighted critical path $s_1 \to t_1 \to u_1 \to w_1 \to u_2 \to t_2 \to s_3$ of 7 strands gives span $T_\infty = 7$. On $P = 2$ processors the greedy bound promises $T_2 \le (9 + 7)/2 = 8$ ticks, while the span law forbids anything below 7.

examples.title: Work, span and the greedy bound for P-FIB
examples.problem: Analyze the multithreaded Fibonacci program `x = spawn FIB(n-1); y = FIB(n-2); sync; return x+y` and evaluate the greedy bound for the dag of $\text{P-FIB}(4)$ above.

steps.label: Step 1: Count the work
steps.text: Each call does $\Theta(1)$ work plus the work of its two children: $T_1(n) = T_1(n-1) + T_1(n-2) + \Theta(1) = \Theta(\varphi^n)$ where $\varphi \approx 1.618$. For $n = 4$ there are exactly 9 calls, hence 9 strands of $\Theta(1)$ work.

steps.label: Step 2: Measure the span
steps.text: The spawned $\text{FIB}(n-1)$ runs concurrently with $\text{FIB}(n-2)$, so the span follows the *longer* child: $T_\infty(n) = T_\infty(n-1) + \Theta(1) = \Theta(n)$. Concretely, the critical path $4 \to 3 \to 2 \to 1$ threads through 7 strands of the dag.

steps.label: Step 3: Compute parallelism
steps.text: $T_1/T_\infty = \Theta(\varphi^n / n)$ — astronomically large: for $n = 30$ the work is about 1.3 million strand-units against a span of about 30.

steps.label: Step 4: Apply the greedy bound at $P = 2$
steps.text: $T_2 \le (T_1 + T_\infty)/2 = (9+7)/2 = 8$ ticks, and the span law says $T_2 \ge 7$; the dag is so serialized at this tiny size that the second processor helps only marginally — the asymptotic gain needs large $n$.

examples.result: Work $\Theta(\varphi^n)$, span $\Theta(n)$, parallelism $\Theta(\varphi^n/n)$; the scheduler theorem bounds $T_P$ within $T_1/P + T_\infty$ for any $P$.

examples.title: Why parallel for beats spawn-per-iteration
examples.problem: A loop of $n$ iterations is implemented (a) by spawning each iteration, (b) by a `parfor` that recursively halves the range. Compare span when each iteration costs $\Theta(n)$.

steps.label: Step 1: Spawn-per-iteration
steps.text: $n$ children spawn serially from one strand: the spawning alone has span $\Theta(n)$, so $T_\infty \ge \Theta(n)$ even before any iteration runs — plus each child adds its own $\Theta(n)$, giving $T_\infty = \Theta(n)$ from spawn overhead already.

steps.label: Step 2: Recursive parfor
steps.text: The range splits like a balanced binary tree: $\Theta(\lg n)$ spawn levels, then the longest iteration $\Theta(n)$: $T_\infty = \Theta(n) + \Theta(\lg n)$ — the log overhead is negligible.

steps.label: Step 3: The grain-size lesson
steps.text: When iterations are cheap, clumping $k$ iterations per spawned chunk (a *grain size*) trades span for spawn overhead; CLRS fixes the grain when it removes the $\Theta(\lg n)$ term from the span of loops whose body is $O(1)$.

examples.result: Both give $\Theta(n)$ span here, but the recursive `parfor` exposes the $\Theta(\lg n)$-overhead structure that grain-size tuning removes.

keyTakeaways: spawn, sync and parallel for express logical parallelism; the dag of strands, continuation, spawn and sync edges is the complete specification of what can run concurrently.
Work $T_1$ = total strand time, span $T_\infty$ = critical-path time; the laws $T_P \ge T_1/P$ and $T_P \ge T_\infty$ sandwich every schedule.
Parallelism $T_1/T_\infty$ caps the useful processor count; past it, hardware idles on the critical path.
Greedy scheduling guarantees $T_P \le T_1/P + T_\infty$ — never worse than twice optimal for $P \le T_1/T_\infty$.
P-FIB is a toy: its work is exponential. Multithreading an exponential algorithm is still exponential — first fix the algorithm, then parallelize it.

quiz.q: In the dynamic-multithreading model, the keyword sync causes the executing thread to:
options: acquire a lock on shared data
wait until every strand spawned by the current procedure has completed
yield the processor to the scheduler
flush its cache before a memory barrier
quiz.explanation: sync is the join point: control resumes only after all children spawned by this procedure finish. Locks are a separate concern the model deliberately does not expose.

quiz.q: Which inequality is the span law?
quiz.explanation: The span law: even with unbounded processors, the serial chain on the critical path cannot be shortened, so $T_P \ge T_\infty$. The first option is the work law; the third is the greedy upper bound.

quiz.q: A dag has $T_1 = 900$ and $T_\infty = 100$. What does the greedy scheduler bound promise on $P = 10$ processors?
quiz.explanation: $T_{10} \le T_1/P + T_\infty (P-1)/P = 90 + 90 = 180 \le 190$. Only the combined form $(T_1 + T_\infty(P-1))/P$ is exact; with $T_\infty = 100$ the slack makes 190 a valid bound (and the exact greedy bound is 180).

quiz.q: The parallelism $T_1/T_\infty$ of a computation is 500. Buying 2000 processors will:
options: cut the running time by exactly 10× versus 200 processors
not help much beyond 500 — the span law floors the time
quiz.explanation: Past $P \approx T_1/T_\infty$ the span dominates: $T_P \ge T_\infty$ no matter how many cores you add, so the extra 1500 processors mostly idle.

intro: Matrix multiplication is the perfect stress test for the multithreaded model: its natural triple loop parallelizes in three different ways with wildly different parallelism, and the recursive quadrant algorithm hides a subtlety — enormous theoretical parallelism that memory behavior punishes in practice.
objectives: Derive work and span for parallel loops via the parallel-for costs
Analyze MAT-VEC with a parallelized outer loop
Analyze the recursive quadrant matrix multiply: $T_1 = \Theta(n^3)$, $T_\infty = \Theta(\lg n)$
Explain why practical implementations stop recursing early

concepts.term: The span of a parallel loop
concepts.statement: A `parfor` implemented by recursive halving over $n$ iterations has work $\Theta(n)$ and span $\Theta(\lg n)$ (the spawn tree). If each iteration is itself a strand of cost $c$, the loop's span is $\Theta(\lg n) + \max_i c_i$.
concepts.detail: For a body of $\Theta(1)$, this $\Theta(\lg n)$ spawn overhead is *not* negligible relative to the work — the standard fix is a grain size: one spawned chunk handles $n/\lg n$ iterations, restoring $T_\infty = \Theta(1)$ per level of nesting.

concepts.term: MAT-VEC: parallelize the outer loop only
concepts.statement: For $y = A x$ with a parallel outer loop and serial inner loop: $T_1(n) = \Theta(n^2)$, $T_\infty(n) = \Theta(n)$ (the longest iteration is a full dot product). Parallelism is $\Theta(n)$.
concepts.detail: Parallelizing the inner loop too would give span $\Theta(\lg n)$ and parallelism $\Theta(n^2 / \lg n)$ — but the spawn overhead per $\Theta(1)$ inner iteration dwarfs the work. The outer loop alone already exposes $n$-fold parallelism, which suits real matrix libraries that vectorize the inner loop instead.

concepts.statement: `P-MATRIX-MULTIPLY-RECURSIVE(C, A, B)` splits $A, B, C$ into $n/2 \times n/2$ quadrants, **spawns** the 8 recursive products $T_{ij} = A_{ik} B_{kj}$ (2 per quadrant of $C$), syncs, then adds: $C_{ij} = T_{ij}^{(1)} + T_{ij}^{(2)}$ — the 4 additions run concurrently.
concepts.detail: Base case $n = 1$ is a scalar multiply. The additions after the sync are a single parallel step: each $C_{ij}$ gets one add.

concepts.statement: $T_1(n) = 8 T_1(n/2) + \Theta(1) = \Theta(n^3)$; the span follows the *longest single child* plus one combine step: $T_\infty(n) = T_\infty(n/2) + \Theta(1) = \Theta(\lg n)$. Parallelism is $\Theta(n^3 / \lg n)$.
concepts.detail: For $n = 8$: exactly $8^3 = 512$ scalar multiplies and $4 \cdot (8^3 - 1)/7 = 292$ additions, with span $\lg 8 + 1 = 4$ combine/multiply steps — parallelism $\approx 804/4 \approx 201$.

concepts.statement: Quadrant recursion strides through memory: at depth $d$ each submatrix read touches rows $n/2^d$ apart, wrecking spatial locality and TLB behavior. Real libraries (BLAS) recurse only to a large base case and hand the leaves to cache-blocked, vectorized kernels.
concepts.detail: CLRS emphasizes the point: an asymptotically gorgeous $\Theta(n^3/\lg n)$ parallelism is worthless if the memory system serializes you. Strassen's algorithm can additionally cut the work to $\Theta(n^{\lg 7})$ and composes with the parallel analysis.

examples.title: Counting strands in the $8 \times 8$ quadrant multiply
examples.problem: Run the recursive quadrant algorithm on $n = 8$ matrices down to scalars, and account for every operation and the critical path.

steps.label: Step 1: Multiplies
steps.text: The recursion bottoms out at $1 \times 1$ blocks: exactly $n^3 = 512$ scalar multiplications, one per leaf of the 8-ary recursion tree.

steps.label: Step 2: Additions
steps.text: The tree has $(8^3-1)/7 = 73$ internal nodes, each performing 4 concurrent scalar additions to combine its two spawned products: $4 \cdot 73 = 292$ adds.

steps.label: Step 3: Span
steps.text: On the critical path: one leaf multiply plus one add per level — $\lg 8 = 3$ levels of recursion, each contributing $\Theta(1)$: $T_\infty = 4$ strand-steps for $n = 8$, $\Theta(\lg n)$ in general.

steps.label: Step 4: Parallelism
steps.text: Total work $804$ steps against span 4: parallelism $\approx 201$, matching the asymptotic $\Theta(n^3/\lg n) = 512/3 \approx 171$ up to lower-order terms.

examples.result: The theoretical recipe: work $\Theta(n^3)$, span $\Theta(\lg n)$ — but stop the recursion at a tuned base case so the memory system can keep up.

examples.title: Span of nested parallel loops
examples.problem: MAT-VEC $y = Ax$ ($n \times n$) with outer loop parallelized, inner serial: compute work $T_1$ and span $T_\infty$.

steps.label: Work
steps.text: Each of $n$ dot products does $n$ multiply-adds: $T_1 = \Theta(n^2)$ regardless of parallelization.

steps.label: Span
steps.text: Outer parallel-for spawns $n$ strands in $\Theta(\lg n)$ span; each dot product serial $\Theta(n)$: $T_\infty = \Theta(\lg n + n) = \Theta(n)$.

steps.label: Parallelism
steps.text: $T_1/T_\infty = \Theta(n)$: linear parallelism, not quadratic: parallelizing only the outer loop leaves the inner $n$ on the critical path.

steps.label: Quadrant contrast
steps.text: Recursive quadrant multiply parallelizes both dimensions: $T_\infty = \Theta(\lg n)$ with $T_1 = \Theta(n^3)$: $\Theta(n^3/\lg n)$ parallelism, exponentially more.

examples.result: MAT-VEC outer-only: $T_1 = \Theta(n^2)$, $T_\infty = \Theta(n)$, parallelism $\Theta(n)$: inner loop bounds the span.

keyTakeaways: A recursive parallel for costs $\Theta(\lg n)$ span of pure spawn overhead — control it with grain sizes when bodies are cheap.
MAT-VEC with only the outer loop parallel: $T_1 = \Theta(n^2)$, $T_\infty = \Theta(n)$, parallelism $\Theta(n)$ — usually the right trade.
Quadrant matrix multiply: work $\Theta(n^3)$, span $\Theta(\lg n)$, parallelism $\Theta(n^3/\lg n)$ — enormous on paper, but strided access makes large base cases essential in practice.
Parallelism multiplies with algorithmic improvement: Strassen reduces work and composes with the same span analysis.

quiz.q: In MAT-VEC with the outer loop parallelized (serial inner loops of $n$ multiplies each), the span is:
quiz.explanation: The longest strand is one full inner loop of $\Theta(n)$; the outer `parfor` adds only $\Theta(\lg n)$ of spawn overhead, which the $\Theta(n)$ iteration swallows.

quiz.q: The recursive quadrant multiply has span $T_\infty(n) = T_\infty(n/2) + \Theta(1)$ because:
options: the 8 recursive calls run concurrently, so the span is the longest one plus the constant-time combine
quiz.explanation: All 8 spawned subproblems overlap; after the sync, the 4 scalar additions are one $\Theta(1)$ parallel step. Hence $\Theta(\lg n)$ span.

quiz.q: Why do production matrix kernels stop the quadrant recursion at a large base case?
options: to avoid overflowing the spawn stack
to reduce spawn overhead and preserve cache locality on strided submatrix access
because the analysis fails below the base case
quiz.explanation: Spawn overhead per $\Theta(1)$ leaf is ruinous, and submatrices at depth $d$ have rows $n/2^d$ apart — the cache and TLB serialize the beautiful span unless the leaf is big enough for blocked, vectorized kernels.

intro: Merge sort looks embarrassingly parallel, but its merge is a serial bottleneck: recursing on both halves concurrently still leaves a $\Theta(n)$ merge on the critical path. The fix is a divide-and-conquer *merge* — split both arrays by rank, spawn one half — which crushes the span from $\Theta(n)$ to $\Theta(\lg^2 n)$ and the whole sort to $\Theta(\lg^3 n)$.
objectives: Explain why ordinary merging forces span $\Theta(n)$
Describe P-MERGE: median split, binary-search rank, one spawned half
Derive $T_\infty^{\text{merge}} = \Theta(\lg^2 n)$ and $T_\infty^{\text{sort}} = \Theta(\lg^3 n)$
Compare serial merge sort, P-MERGE-SORT and randomized sorting on span

concepts.statement: Parallelizing both recursive calls of merge sort leaves the merge: output element $i$ cannot be chosen until its predecessor's position is known, so a standard two-pointer merge has span $\Theta(n)$ and the sort has $T_\infty(n) = \Theta(n)$.
concepts.detail: An ordinary multithreaded merge sort therefore has parallelism $\Theta(n \lg n / n) = \Theta(\lg n)$ — feeble. The parallelism must come from restructuring the merge itself.

concepts.statement: To merge $A[p_1..r_1]$ (the longer run) with $A[p_2..r_2]$ into $C$: take the **median** $A[q_1]$ of the first run, `BINARY-SEARCH` its **rank** $q_2$ in the second run. Then **spawn** $\text{P-MERGE}(A[p_1..q_1{-}1],\ A[p_2..q_2{-}1])$ into $C$'s front and run the other half ($A[q_1..r_1]$ with $A[q_2..r_2]$) inline; the two output ranges are disjoint, so no sync is needed *inside* the merge.
concepts.detail: Each element's output position is computed arithmetically: the spawn handles elements below the median, the continuation those above — the same total order, two independent subproblems.

concepts.statement: The binary search costs $\Theta(\lg n)$; each level of the merge recursion halves the output size, and the subproblems are *uneven* but their recursion depth is at most $\lg n$ levels each costing a search: $T_\infty^{\text{merge}}(n) = \Theta(\lg^2 n)$, while the work stays linear: $T_1^{\text{merge}}(n) = \Theta(n)$.
concepts.detail: Total work per level is $\Theta(n)$ (the searches are dominated by the elements they place), and there are $\Theta(\lg n)$ levels of span.

concepts.statement: $T_1(n) = 2T_1(n/2) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n \lg n)$; $T_\infty(n) = T_\infty(n/2) + \Theta(\lg^2 n) = \Theta(\lg^3 n)$. Parallelism: $\Theta(n / \lg^2 n)$.
concepts.detail: The span recurrence stacks a merge span on each of the $\lg n$ sort levels. For $n = 2^{20}$: span $\approx 1000$ against work $\approx 2 \times 10^7$ — parallelism about 20,000.

concepts.statement: P-MERGE finds the cross-ranks $k - j$ via binary search on the opposite subarray in $O(\lg n)$: $x_{k}$’s rank in $B$ is $\mathrm{rank} = \mathrm{lower\_bound}(B, x_k)$. The two submerges $(A_1,B_1)$, $(A_2,B_2)$ are then independent and spawned in parallel.
concepts.detail: Rank queries cost $O(\lg n)$ span on the critical path, which is why P-MERGE’s span recurrence is $T_\infty(n) = T_\infty(n/2) + O(\lg n) = \Theta(\lg^2 n)$ and not $\Theta(\lg n)$.

figures.caption: P-MERGE splits by rank. The median 13 of the longer run $A$ splits $A$ after 8; its rank in $B$ (three elements of $B$ are below 13) splits $B$ after 7. The lower halves merge into a **spawned** call (teal) filling the front of $C$, the upper halves merge inline into the back — disjoint output ranges, so the two merges never touch and no inner sync is needed. Result: $T_\infty^{\text{merge}} = \Theta(\lg^2 n)$ from the binary searches stacked on the recursion.

examples.title: One rank split, by hand
examples.problem: Execute the top-level split of `P-MERGE` on $A = [2, 5, 8, 13, 16, 19, 22, 25]$ and $B = [1, 3, 7, 14]$.

steps.label: Step 1: Take the median of the longer run
steps.text: $A$ has 8 elements, $B$ only 4 (P-MERGE exchanges so the first run is longer). The median is the 4th element: $A[q_1] = 13$.

steps.label: Step 2: Binary-search its rank in $B$
steps.text: Elements of $B$ below 13: exactly $1, 3, 7$ — so $\operatorname{rank}(13) = 3$ and $B$ splits into $[1,3,7] \,|\, [14]$.

steps.label: Step 3: Spawn the lower merge
steps.text: $\text{P-MERGE}([2,5,8], [1,3,7])$ is spawned; it produces $[1,2,3,5,7,8]$ into the first 6 slots of $C$ — its output positions are known immediately, no communication needed.

steps.label: Step 4: Continue with the upper merge
steps.text: The parent merges $[13, 16, 19, 22, 25]$ with $[14]$ inline into $[13, 14, 16, 19, 22, 25]$, the last 6 slots. Concatenation: $C = [1,2,3,5,7,8,13,14,16,19,22,25]$ — the correct merge of all 12 keys.

examples.result: Two independent half-size merges whose outputs occupy disjoint ranges: this is the one step that turns merging from a serial scan into a parallel recursion.

examples.title: Span bookkeeping: where $\lg^3$ comes from
examples.problem: Account for the span of P-MERGE-SORT on $n$ elements.

steps.label: Step 1: One merge costs $\lg^2$ on the critical path
steps.text: Each P-MERGE level does a $\Theta(\lg n)$ binary search then recurses on a smaller merge; the recursion depth is at most $\lg n$ levels (output size halves along any root-to-leaf path): $T_\infty^{\text{merge}}(n) = \Theta(\lg^2 n)$.

steps.label: Step 2: Stack the sort levels
steps.text: The sort spawns both halves (parallel) then merges: $T_\infty(n) = T_\infty(n/2) + \Theta(\lg^2 n) = \Theta(\lg^3 n)$.

steps.label: Step 3: Compare the alternatives
steps.text: Serial merge sort: span $\Theta(n)$. Ordinary parallel merge sort with serial merge: span $\Theta(n)$. Randomized multithreaded sorting (padding): $\Theta(\lg n)$ expected span. P-MERGE-SORT's deterministic $\Theta(\lg^3 n)$ sits in between, with linear-log work.

examples.result: Work $\Theta(n \lg n)$, span $\Theta(\lg^3 n)$, parallelism $\Theta(n / \lg^2 n)$: for $n = 10^6$, about $10^6/400 = 2500$-fold.

keyTakeaways: The serial merge is the span killer: naive parallel merge sort tops out at parallelism $\Theta(\lg n)$.
P-MERGE splits both runs by the median-and-rank trick so the two sub-merges write disjoint output ranges and need no synchronization.
P-MERGE: $T_1 = \Theta(n)$, $T_\infty = \Theta(\lg^2 n)$ (binary searches stacked on the recursion); P-MERGE-SORT: $T_1 = \Theta(n \lg n)$, $T_\infty = \Theta(\lg^3 n)$.
Parallelism $\Theta(n/\lg^2 n)$ is thousands-fold for realistic inputs — genuine parallel sorting with deterministic guarantees.

quiz.q: Why does P-MERGE not need a sync between its two recursive sub-merges?
options: both submerges return values instead of writing memory
they write to disjoint ranges of the output array, computed from the split positions
the runtime inserts a lock-free buffer
quiz.explanation: The rank split fixes each half's output positions in advance; the spawned lower merge and the inline upper merge never touch the same cells, so no join is needed inside the merge.

quiz.q: The span of P-MERGE-SORT is:
quiz.explanation: $\Theta(\lg n)$ sort levels, each paying the $\Theta(\lg^2 n)$ merge span: $\Theta(\lg^3 n)$. The merge alone is $\Theta(\lg^2 n)$ and the serial-merge version is $\Theta(n)$.

quiz.q: In P-MERGE, the purpose of the binary search for $\operatorname{rank}(A[q_1])$ in the second run is to:
options: find the element equal to the median
locate where the second run splits so both sub-merges stay sorted and disjoint
quiz.explanation: The rank tells exactly how many elements of $B$ precede the median, fixing both output ranges — that is what makes the two recursive merges independent.

intro: Solving $Ax = b$ by Gaussian elimination is the oldest algorithm on this shelf and still the workhorse of scientific computing. Its modern form — factor once into $LUP$, then solve triangular systems — costs $\Theta(n^3)$ once and $\Theta(n^2)$ per right-hand side, and pivoting makes it work for every nonsingular matrix.
objectives: Perform forward and back substitution on triangular systems
Compute an LU decomposition and explain when it exists
Describe LUP decomposition with pivoting and why it always exists for nonsingular $A$
Analyze the costs: $\Theta(n^3)$ to factor, $\Theta(n^2)$ per solve

concepts.statement: If $L$ is lower triangular, $Ly = b$ solves top-down: $y_i = \big(b_i - \sum_{j<i} \ell_{ij} y_j\big) / \ell_{ii}$. If $U$ is upper triangular, $Ux = y$ solves bottom-up analogously. Each costs $\Theta(n^2)$.
concepts.detail: Substitution is the 'pay per use' part of the pipeline: cheap enough that re-solving with new right-hand sides is nearly free after the factorization.

concepts.statement: $A = LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular and $U$ upper triangular exists **iff all leading principal minors are nonzero** — equivalently, Gaussian elimination on $A$ never hits a zero pivot.
concepts.detail: The multipliers used to kill entries below pivot $k$ become the column $\ell_k$ of $L$; what remains is $U$. For nonsingular $A$ with a zero minor (e.g. $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$), $LU$ fails and rows must be exchanged — which is exactly what $P$ is for.

concepts.statement: For **every** nonsingular $A$ there is a permutation matrix $P$ with $PA = LU$. LUP-DECOMPOSITION pivots: at step $k$ it swaps the row with the largest $|a_{ik}|$ in the active submatrix into the pivot position (partial pivoting), then eliminates below it.
concepts.detail: The factorization is found in place: the strict lower triangle holds $L$ (unit diagonal implicit), the upper triangle $U$, and a single $\pi$ array records the row permutation — $O(n)$ extra space.

concepts.statement: LUP-DECOMPOSITION does $\Theta(n^3)$ arithmetic (the three nested loops of updates $a_{ij} \mathrel{-}= \ell_{ik} u_{kj}$). Each subsequent solve is $2\Theta(n^2)$ substitutions. Solving $n$ systems with the same $A$ (e.g. for inversion) therefore costs $\Theta(n^3) + n \cdot \Theta(n^2) = \Theta(n^3)$ — the same order as one naive Gaussian elimination *without* reuse.
concepts.detail: This 'factor once, solve many' pattern is why numerical libraries never run raw Gaussian elimination on repeated right-hand sides.

concepts.statement: Choosing the largest-magnitude pivot keeps multipliers $|\ell_{ik}| \le 1$, which bounds the growth of round-off error: partial pivoting makes Gaussian elimination backward stable in practice.
concepts.detail: Tiny pivots would divide by near-zero numbers, amplifying rounding error catastrophically even in exact-arithmetic-feasible systems.

figures.caption: The triangularization wavefront in LUP-DECOMPOSITION after two iterations. Shaded left columns below the diagonal hold the already-computed multipliers of $L$; the shaded top rows hold the finished rows of $U$; only the $4 \times 4$ active submatrix (outlined) still needs work. Iteration $k = 3$ picks the largest-magnitude entry in its column of the active submatrix as the next pivot (circled), swaps it into place, fills column $k$ of $L$ with multipliers $\ell_{ik} = a_{ik}/u_{kk}$, and rank-1-updates the trailing submatrix with $a_{ij} \mathrel{-}= \ell_{ik} u_{kj}$.

examples.title: LU, then two substitutions, by hand
examples.problem: Solve $Ax = b$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 7 & 5 \\ 6 & 18 & 22 \end{pmatrix}$, $b = (6, 16, 46)^T$ using the decomposition $A = LU$ with $L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 9 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $U = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -8 \end{pmatrix}$.

steps.label: Step 1: Verify the factorization
steps.text: Row 2 of $LU$: $2 \cdot (2,3,1) + 1 \cdot (0,1,3) = (4, 7, 5)$ ✓. Row 3: $3 \cdot (2,3,1) + 9 \cdot (0,1,3) + 1 \cdot (0,0,-8) = (6, 18, 22)$ ✓. Both pivots 2, 1 were nonzero — no permutation needed.

steps.label: Step 3: Back substitution $Ux = y$
steps.text: $-8 x_3 = -8 \Rightarrow x_3 = 1$; $x_2 + 3 x_3 = 4 \Rightarrow x_2 = 1$; $2 x_1 + 3 x_2 + x_3 = 6 \Rightarrow x_1 = 1$.

examples.result: The pipeline: pay $\Theta(n^3)$ once for the factorization, then any new $b$ costs just the two $\Theta(n^2)$ triangular sweeps.

examples.title: When LU fails and pivoting rescues it
examples.problem: Explain why $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has no $LU$ decomposition, and how LUP handles it.

steps.label: Step 1: Chase the zero pivot
steps.text: With $\ell_{11} = 1$ fixed by the unit-diagonal convention, $u_{11}$ must equal $a_{11} = 0$. The first elimination step then divides by $u_{11} = 0$ — impossible.

steps.label: Step 2: Recognize the invariant
steps.text: $A$ is perfectly nonsingular (det $= -1$); the failure is about *order of rows*, not about $A$.

steps.label: Step 3: Pivot
steps.text: Swap rows: $P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ gives $PA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I \cdot I$: $L = U = I$. Now solve $PAx = Pb$, i.e. $LUx = Pb$.

examples.result: Partial pivoting guarantees a nonzero pivot at every step of any nonsingular matrix — $PA = LU$ always exists.

keyTakeaways: Triangular systems solve by substitution in $\Theta(n^2)$: forward for $L$, backward for $U$.
$A = LU$ exists iff every leading principal minor is nonzero; for any nonsingular $A$, permuting rows first ($PA = LU$) always works.
Partial pivoting — bring the largest-magnitude entry of the active column to the diagonal — keeps multipliers $\le 1$ and the algorithm numerically stable.
Cost split: $\Theta(n^3)$ to factor once, $\Theta(n^2)$ per right-hand side — the economic heart of the chapter.

quiz.q: After computing $PA = LU$ for a fixed $A$, solving a second system $Ax = b'$ costs:
quiz.explanation: Only the two triangular substitutions run again: $Ly = Pb'$ then $Ux = y$, each $\Theta(n^2)$. The $\Theta(n^3)$ factorization is amortized away.

quiz.q: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has no LU decomposition because:
options: its first pivot $a_{11} = 0$ forces division by zero during the first elimination step
L must have a zero diagonal
quiz.explanation: The matrix is nonsingular (det $= -1$); the failure is purely that Gaussian elimination without row exchanges meets a zero pivot — LUP fixes it with one swap.

quiz.q: In LUP-DECOMPOSITION the multipliers stored in column $k$ of $L$ are:
options: $\ell_{ik} = a_{ik} / u_{kk}$ computed from the current, already-updated active submatrix
quiz.explanation: Each multiplier is exactly what Gaussian elimination divides by: the (updated) entry to kill divided by the pivot. Pivoting first ensures $|\ell_{ik}| \le 1$.

quiz.q: Partial pivoting (choosing the largest-magnitude entry of the active column) exists mainly to:
options: minimize the total number of arithmetic operations
keep multipliers at most 1 in magnitude, controlling round-off growth
quiz.explanation: The operation count is unchanged by row order; stability is what pivoting buys — small multipliers stop rounding errors from compounding.

intro: Once LUP decomposition is on the shelf, inverting a matrix is almost boring: $A^{-1}$ is the matrix $X$ whose columns solve $Ax = e_i$ for each standard basis vector $e_i$. One $\Theta(n^3)$ factorization plus $n$ cheap triangular solves inverts any nonsingular matrix in $\Theta(n^3)$ total.
objectives: Derive matrix inversion from n solves of $Ax = e_i$
Verify the correctness identity $X = A^{-1}$ from $PA = LU$
Explain why explicitly inverting is the wrong way to solve systems in practice
Discuss the effect of condition number on computed inverses

concepts.statement: **LUP-INVERSE(A):** compute $PA = LU$; for each $i = 1, \ldots, n$, solve $LUx = P e_i$ by forward then back substitution and store the solution as column $i$ of $X$. Then $AX = I$.
concepts.detail: Why $P e_i$ and not $e_i$: $Ax = e_i \iff PAx = Pe_i \iff LUx = Pe_i$ — the permutation is just a reordering of the right-hand side's entries.

concepts.statement: Let $X$ be the matrix LUP-INVERSE produces. Since column $i$ of $X$ solves $Ax = e_i$, we get $AX = [Ae_1' \ldots] = I$ column by column. As $A$ is nonsingular, its inverse is unique, hence $X = A^{-1}$.
concepts.detail: The proof is a column-by-column verification that $AX = I$ — no matrix products needed beyond the definition of matrix–vector multiplication.

concepts.statement: LUP: $\Theta(n^3)$. The $n$ column solves: $n \cdot \Theta(n^2) = \Theta(n^3)$. Total $\Theta(n^3)$ — the same order as a single Gaussian elimination, and asymptotically optimal for dense inversion by known lower-bound arguments.
concepts.detail: A subtlety: the $n$ right-hand sides $Pe_i$ form a permuted identity matrix, so blocked variants of the algorithm multiply triangular matrices by blocks, improving cache behavior without changing the $\Theta(n^3)$ count.

concepts.statement: To solve $Ax = b$, computing $A^{-1}b$ costs *more* than one LUP + substitution, and in floating point it is less accurate: the inverse is formed and rounded, then multiplied, compounding error at each step.
concepts.detail: The computed $\hat{x}$ from a backward-stable solve satisfies $(A + \Delta A)\hat{x} = b$ with $\|\Delta A\|$ tiny relative to $\kappa(A)\|A\|$ — a guarantee the explicit-inverse route loses.

concepts.statement: The **condition number** $\kappa(A) = \|A\| \cdot \|A^{-1}\| \ge 1$ measures how a relative perturbation of $A$ or $b$ can inflate the relative error of $x$: roughly $\kappa(A)$ is the worst amplification.
concepts.detail: A large-$\kappa$ (ill-conditioned) matrix can be inverted exactly by the algorithm yet yield useless answers: rounding $b$ slightly moves the true solution a lot. Even singular-in-the-limit Vandermonde-like systems teach the same lesson.

examples.title: Inverting a 2×2 matrix through the LUP pipeline
examples.problem: Invert $A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$ via $PA = LU$ and two column solves.

steps.label: Step 1: Factor
steps.text: No pivoting needed ($4$ is the larger column entry anyway): $L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $U = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 0 & 2.5 \end{pmatrix}$ (multiplier $2/4 = 0.5$).

steps.label: Step 4: Assemble and verify
steps.text: $X = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & -0.7 \\ -0.2 & 0.4 \end{pmatrix}$. Multiply: $AX = \begin{pmatrix} 4(0.6)+7(-0.2) & 4(-0.7)+7(0.4) \\ 2(0.6)+6(-0.2) & 2(-0.7)+6(0.4) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ ✓. (Sanity: $\det A = 10$, and $X = \frac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix} 6 & -7 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$.)

examples.result: Two triangular solves per column: the entire inverse for the price of about one elimination.

examples.title: Solving without inverting
examples.problem: Solve $A x = b$ with $A = [[2,1],[1,2]]$, $b = [3,3]$ via LUP (no explicit inverse) and compare with $A^{-1}b$.

steps.label: Versus inverse
steps.text: $A^{-1} = [[2/3,-1/3],[-1/3,2/3]]$: $A^{-1}b = [1,1]$ same, but inversion needed $2$ solves ($e_1,e_2$) plus a multiply: $3\times$ the work for one $b$.

examples.result: $x = [1,1]$ in $\Theta(n^2)$ after one $\Theta(n^3)$ factorization; explicit $A^{-1}$ costs $n$ solves for the same answer.

keyTakeaways: Invert by solving $Ax = e_i$ for every $i$; assembling the solution vectors as columns gives $X = A^{-1}$ with $AX = I$ verified columnwise.
Total cost $\Theta(n^3)$: one LUP decomposition plus $n$ substitutions at $\Theta(n^2)$ each.
The permuted right-hand sides $Pe_i$ reappear because $Ax = e_i \iff LUx = Pe_i$.
In practice, never compute $A^{-1}b$ to solve a system — substitute instead: cheaper and numerically safer.
The condition number $\kappa(A) = \|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|$ bounds how much rounding in $A$ or $b$ can distort $x$.

quiz.q: LUP-INVERSE solves, for column $i$ of the inverse, the system:
quiz.explanation: Multiplying $Ax = e_i$ by $P$ gives $LUx = Pe_i$ — the permutation moves to the right-hand side; the solver sees a permuted unit vector.

quiz.q: The total asymptotic cost of inverting an $n \times n$ matrix via LUP-INVERSE is:
quiz.explanation: $\Theta(n^3)$ for the decomposition plus $n \cdot \Theta(n^2) = \Theta(n^3)$ for the solves — the solve phase does not change the exponent.

quiz.q: Which statement about solving $Ax = b$ by first computing $A^{-1}$ is correct?
options: it is both faster and more accurate
it does more arithmetic than an LUP solve and loses the backward-stability guarantee of substitution
it is required when $b$ changes rarely
it is required when $A$ is symmetric
quiz.explanation: Explicit inversion wastes a factor of $n$ versus substitution and introduces extra rounding: computing and multiplying by a rounded inverse is a strictly worse pipeline.

intro: Symmetric positive-definite matrices — the Hessians of convex functions, the Gram matrices of data — Gaussian elimination can attack without any pivoting: all pivots come out positive. That observation yields the Cholesky factorization $A = LL^T$, and the same normal-equations machinery gives the method of least squares its algebraic backbone.
objectives: Define symmetric positive-definite matrices and recognize common examples
Prove $A^T A$ is SPD exactly when $A$ has full column rank
Derive the normal equations $A^TA\hat{x} = A^Tb$ from orthogonality of the residual
Compute a Cholesky factorization and fit a least-squares line

concepts.statement: $A$ is **SPD** if $A = A^T$ and $x^T A x > 0$ for every $x \ne 0$. Equivalently (for symmetric $A$): all eigenvalues are positive.
concepts.detail: Testable without eigenvalues: a symmetric matrix is SPD iff Gaussian elimination runs without row exchanges and produces all *positive* pivots — which is precisely what makes Cholesky work.

concepts.term: Least squares and the normal equations
concepts.statement: For $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$, the least-squares problem minimizes $\|Ax - b\|_2$. The minimizer $\hat{x}$ satisfies the **normal equations** $A^T A \hat{x} = A^T b$: geometrically, $A\hat{x}$ is the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space of $A$ — the residual $b - A\hat{x}$ is perpendicular to every column of $A$.
concepts.detail: 'Perpendicular to every column of $A$' translates verbatim to $A^T(b - A\hat{x}) = 0$.

concepts.statement: $A^TA$ is always symmetric positive-*semi*definite; it is SPD **iff $A$ has full column rank** (i.e. $Ax = 0$ only at $x = 0$). When $A$ has full column rank the least-squares solution exists and is $\hat{x} = (A^TA)^{-1}A^T b$.
concepts.detail: The one-line proof: $x^T A^T A x = \|Ax\|_2^2 > 0$ unless $Ax = 0$. So the normal equations inherit a unique solution exactly when the columns of $A$ are independent — repeated data columns or collinear regressors destroy uniqueness.

concepts.statement: Every SPD matrix factors as $A = LL^T$ with $L$ lower triangular and **positive diagonal**. The entries follow recursively from symmetry: $\ell_{kk} = \sqrt{a_{kk} - \sum_{j<k} \ell_{kj}^2}$ and $\ell_{ik} = \big(a_{ik} - \sum_{j<k} \ell_{ij}\ell_{kj}\big)/\ell_{kk}$.
concepts.detail: Cost: $\Theta(n^3)$ — but with roughly *half* the arithmetic of LU, because the algorithm exploits symmetry: it computes only the lower triangle and mirrors it. The positive pivots of the SPD elimination are exactly the squares $\ell_{kk}^2$.

concepts.term: Why least squares is the right fallback
concepts.statement: Overdetermined systems ($m > n$) usually have no exact solution; minimizing the 2-norm of the residual is the variational substitute, and the normal equations convert it into a square SPD system solvable by Cholesky in $\Theta(n^3)$.
concepts.detail: This is the computational engine of linear regression: $A$ holds a column of 1s and a column of predictor values, $b$ the responses.

figures.caption: Least squares on data $(1,2), (2,3), (3,5), (4,6), (5,9)$. The normal equations $A^TA\hat{x} = A^Tb$ with $A = [\mathbf{1}, x]$ give slope $1.7$, intercept $-0.1$: the fitted line $\hat{y} = 1.7x - 0.1$. Vertical dashed segments are the residuals $b_i - \hat{y}_i = 0.4, -0.3, 0, -0.7, 0.6$ — they sum to exactly $0$ (perpendicular to the constant column) and their squares total $\mathrm{SSE} = 1.10$, the minimum over all lines.
