examples.title: Fitting a line by the normal equations
examples.problem: Fit $\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ to the data $(1,2), (2,3), (3,5), (4,6), (5,9)$ by least squares.

steps.label: Step 1: Set up $A$ and $b$
steps.text: With $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ and $b = (2,3,5,6,9)^T$, the model is $A\beta \approx b$ with $\beta = (\beta_0, \beta_1)$.

steps.label: Step 2: Form the normal equations
steps.text: $A^T A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 15 \\ 15 & 55 \end{pmatrix}$ (counts and sums of $x$), $A^T b = (25, 92)^T$ (sums of $y$ and $xy$).

steps.label: Step 4: Interpret the check
steps.text: Fitted values $1.6, 3.3, 5.0, 6.7, 8.4$; residuals $0.4, -0.3, 0, -0.7, 0.6$ summing to zero — the residual is orthogonal to the constant column, exactly as $A^T(b - A\hat{\beta}) = 0$ demands. $\mathrm{SSE} = 0.16+0.09+0+0.49+0.36 = 1.10$.

examples.result: Least-squares line $\hat{y} = 1.7x - 0.1$; the normal equations turn an overconstrained problem into an SPD system.

examples.title: Cholesky on a 3×3 SPD matrix
examples.problem: Factor $A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 12 & -16 \\ 12 & 37 & -43 \\ -16 & -43 & 98 \end{pmatrix} = LL^T$.

steps.label: Step 3: Column 3
steps.text: $\ell_{33} = \sqrt{98 - (-8)^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{98 - 64 - 25} = \sqrt{9} = 3$. Every radicand positive — the SPD certificate.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify
steps.text: $L = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$; row 3 of $LL^T$: $(-16,\ -48+5,\ 64+25+9) = (-16, -43, 98)$ ✓ — and $A$'s symmetry was used to skip half the work.

examples.result: Cholesky needs no pivoting, takes square roots only of positive numbers, and stores one triangle.

keyTakeaways: SPD means $x^TAx > 0$ for all $x \ne 0$; for symmetric matrices this is equivalent to all-positive eigenvalues (and to all-positive Gaussian pivots).
$A^TA$ is SPD iff $A$ has full column rank — the exact condition for a unique least-squares solution.
Normal equations $A^TA\hat{x} = A^Tb$: project $b$ onto the column space of $A$; the residual is orthogonal to every column.
Cholesky $A = LL^T$ exploits symmetry for roughly half of LU's arithmetic, with guaranteed positive radicands on SPD input.

quiz.q: For which matrices $A$ is $A^TA$ (with $A \ne 0$) symmetric positive-definite rather than merely semidefinite?
options: exactly the $A$ with full column rank (independent columns)
quiz.explanation: $x^T A^T A x = \|Ax\|^2 > 0$ unless $Ax = 0$; some nonzero $x$ with $Ax = 0$ exists exactly when the columns are dependent.

quiz.q: The geometric meaning of the least-squares solution is that $A\hat{x}$ is:
options: the closest vector to $b$ inside the column space of $A$ — the orthogonal projection of $b$
b itself, when the system is inconsistent
quiz.explanation: Minimizing $\|Ax - b\|$ over the column space picks the projection; equivalently the residual $b - A\hat{x}$ is orthogonal to every column — which is the normal-equations statement.

quiz.q: Cholesky factorization $A = LL^T$ is guaranteed to exist (with real positive diagonal $L$) for every:
quiz.explanation: Positivity of the pivots — equivalent to SPD for symmetric matrices — keeps every radicand $a_{kk} - \sum \ell_{kj}^2$ positive under the square root.

quiz.q: In the regression example, the residuals $0.4, -0.3, 0, -0.7, 0.6$ sum to exactly zero because:
options: the data lie on a line
the residual vector is orthogonal to the constant (intercept) column of $A$
least squares always zeroes the median residual
quiz.explanation: The first column of $A$ is all ones; $A^T(b - A\hat{\beta}) = 0$ makes the residual orthogonal to it — i.e. its entries sum to zero. Minimality alone would not force this.

intro: Linear programming optimizes a linear objective over a polytope cut out by linear inequalities. The book's simplex machinery consumes a very specific syntax — standard form for stating the problem, slack form for computing — and this section builds both, together with the vocabulary of basic and nonbasic variables that every later section relies on.
objectives: State an LP in standard form: maximize $c^Tx$ subject to $Ax \le b$, $x \ge 0$
Convert any LP (minimization, equalities, free variables) into standard form
Introduce slack variables and read off the initial basic feasible solution
Relate basic feasible solutions to vertices of the feasible polytope

concepts.statement: A linear program in **standard form** maximizes $\sum_j c_j x_j$ subject to $\sum_j a_{ij} x_j \le b_i$ for $i = 1..m$, and $x_j \ge 0$. In matrix notation: maximize $c^Tx$ s.t. $Ax \le b$, $x \ge 0$.
concepts.detail: The form is a *wlog* convention: minimize becomes maximize by negating $c$; an equality $=$ splits into $\le$ plus $\ge$ (negate); a variable free in sign becomes $x = x^+ - x^-$ with $x^+, x^- \ge 0$; $\ge$ constraints become $\le$ by negating both sides.

concepts.statement: Add a **slack variable** $x_{n+i} \ge 0$ per constraint and write the system as $x_{n+i} = b_i - \sum_j a_{ij} x_j$. The objective becomes $z = v + \sum_{j \in N} \bar{c}_j x_j$ over the **nonbasic** set $N$; the **basic** set $B$ holds one variable per equation. A **basic solution** sets all nonbasic variables to 0; it is **feasible** when every basic value is then $\ge 0$.
concepts.detail: Slack form is a *bookkeeping format*: the equation for a basic variable always solves for it in terms of the nonbasics, and the tableau is just the coefficient array of this system.

The initial BFS is transparent here: $N = \{x_1, x_2, x_3\}$ (all zero), $B = \{x_4, x_5, x_6\} = (30, 24, 36)$ — feasible because all $b_i \ge 0$. Sections 29.3–29.5 will carry this LP all the way to its optimum $z^* = 28$ at $(8, 4, 0)$.

concepts.statement: The feasible set is a convex polytope: intersections of half-spaces. If the LP is feasible and bounded, an optimal solution exists at a **vertex** — and vertices correspond exactly to basic feasible solutions, which is what simplex walks.
concepts.detail: A vertex is where $n$ linearly independent constraints are tight; in slack form that says exactly 'the nonbasic variables (at their zero bounds) number $n$'. Degenerate vertices arise when more than $n$ constraints meet — several bases describe one vertex.

concepts.statement: Feasible means satisfying all constraints; basic feasible means feasible with at most $m$ positive variables (at a vertex: $n$ nonbasics at $0$). Simplex walks basic feasible solutions: every step is a vertex, every pivot an edge.
concepts.detail: The running example’s optimum $(x_1,x_2) = (2,6)$? Actually $(8/3?)$: wherever it sits, it is a vertex where two constraints bind, hence basic. Interior feasible points are never simplex stops.

examples.title: Converting an awkward LP to standard form
examples.problem: Put the following into standard form: minimize $2x_1 - x_2$ subject to $x_1 + x_2 = 7$, $x_1 \ge 2$, and $x_2$ free in sign.

steps.label: Step 1: Flip the objective
steps.text: Minimizing $2x_1 - x_2$ is maximizing $-2x_1 + x_2$; the optimal point is unchanged.

steps.label: Step 3: Handle the lower bound
steps.text: Substitute $y_1 = x_1 - 2 \ge 0$, so the constraint $x_1 \ge 2$ disappears into the substitution.

steps.label: Step 4: Kill the free variable
steps.text: Write $x_2 = x_2^+ - x_2^-$ with both parts $\ge 0$. The program is now: maximize $-2y_1 + x_2^+ - x_2^-$ subject to $y_1 + x_2^+ - x_2^- \le 5$, $-y_1 - x_2^+ + x_2^- \le -5$, all variables $\ge 0$.

examples.result: Every LP, however stated, folds into the one standard shape that simplex expects.

examples.title: Slack form of two inequalities
examples.problem: Convert $\max 3x_1 + x_2$ s.t. $x_1 + x_2 \le 4$, $x_1 \le 2$, $x \ge 0$ to slack form.

steps.label: Basic solution
steps.text: Nonbasics $x_1 = x_2 = 0$: basics $s_1 = 4$, $s_2 = 2$: vertex $(0,0)$.

steps.label: Nonnegativity
steps.text: $b = [4,2] \ge 0$: initial BFS available; negative $b$ would need auxiliary LP (Section 29.5).

steps.label: Geometry
steps.text: Slacks measure distance to each wall: $s_1 = 0$ on $x_1+x_2 = 4$, $s_2 = 0$ on $x_1 = 2$.

examples.result: Slack form $x_1+x_2+s_1 = 4$, $x_1+s_2 = 2$, $z = 3x_1+x_2$: BFS $(0,0,4,2)$ at the origin vertex.

keyTakeaways: Standard form: maximize $c^Tx$ with $Ax \le b$, $x \ge 0$ — reachable from any LP by negation and substitution.
Slack variables turn inequalities into equations; the basic/nonbasic split plus 'nonbasics = 0' defines basic solutions.
A basic solution is feasible iff all basic values come out nonnegative.
Vertices of the polytope = basic feasible solutions; simplex moves along edges from vertex to vertex.

quiz.q: In slack form, a basic solution is obtained by:
options: setting all basic variables to zero
setting all nonbasic variables to zero and reading each basic variable off its equation
solving the system by Gaussian elimination
setting all slack variables to zero
quiz.explanation: Nonbasic variables sit at their bounds (0); each basic variable then has a determined value from its own slack-form equation. Feasibility additionally demands these values be nonnegative.

quiz.q: To convert the constraint $x_1 \ge 2$ into standard form you would write:
quiz.explanation: Multiplying by $-1$ flips the inequality direction: $x_1 \ge 2 \iff -x_1 \le -2$, which is a legal standard-form row.

quiz.q: For the running LP, the initial BFS $(x_4, x_5, x_6) = (30, 24, 36)$ is feasible because:
options: all basic values are nonnegative when the nonbasics are zero
quiz.explanation: Feasibility of a basic solution = nonnegativity of the values induced on the basic variables; here $b = (30,24,36) \ge 0$ makes the origin vertex feasible.

intro: The art of linear programming is translation: recognizing that shortest paths, maximum flows, production plans, and countless scheduling puzzles are all polytopes in disguise. Once a problem speaks standard form, a single general engine — simplex, or a polynomial-time interior-point method — solves it exactly.
objectives: Translate an optimization story into variables, objective and constraints
Formulate single-pair shortest paths as an LP
Formulate max flow as an LP with capacity and conservation constraints
Solve a two-variable production LP geometrically

concepts.statement: Name the **decision variables** (what you can choose, with units), write the **objective** as their linear combination, list every limit as a linear **constraint**, and append nonnegativity where quantities are physical. If a quantity could be negative (profit, flow direction), split it into $x^+ - x^-$.
concepts.detail: Most modeling errors are unit errors: every constraint row should dimension-check (hours to hours, tons to tons).

concepts.statement: For a directed graph with weights $w_{uv}$, send one unit of flow from $s$ to $t$: minimize $\sum_{(u,v)} w_{uv} x_{uv}$ subject to flow conservation $\sum_{v} x_{uv} - \sum_v x_{vu} = 1$ for $u = s$, $= -1$ for $u = t$, $= 0$ otherwise, and $0 \le x_{uv} \le 1$. An optimal BFS picks an integral solution — a shortest path.
concepts.detail: The polytope is integral (its vertices are 0/1 flows) because the constraint matrix is a network matrix — the LP relaxation already solves the combinatorial problem exactly.

concepts.statement: Maximize $\sum_v f_{sv}$ subject to capacity $0 \le f_{uv} \le c_{uv}$ on every edge and conservation $\sum_u f_{uv} = \sum_w f_{vw}$ at every internal vertex $v$. The LP optimum equals the capacity of a minimum cut — LP duality reproves the max-flow min-cut theorem (Section 29.4).
concepts.detail: Here too the vertices are integral, so the LP computes an exact maximum flow without any combinatorial algorithm.

concepts.term: Why model as an LP at all
concepts.statement: One general solver captures every problem in the family: simplex in practice, ellipsoid and interior-point methods in guaranteed polynomial time. Modelling replaces algorithm design with translation — and duality (29.4) then gifts you sensitivity analysis for free.
concepts.detail: The trade: LP solvers ignore combinatorial structure, so specialized algorithms can beat them on huge structured instances — but for one-off or rapidly changing models, the LP route wins on flexibility.

concepts.statement: Standard form $\max c^T x$ s.t. $Ax \le b$, $x \ge 0$ packs the objective into $c$: $c_j$ is the per-unit profit of $x_j$. Shortest-path LP has $c$ selecting $d_t$; max-flow LP has $c$ summing out of $s$; production LP has $c$ as prices.
concepts.detail: Modeling is choosing $x$, $A$, $b$, $c$ so the polytope’s vertices are the combinatorial objects (paths, flows, plans) and $c$ ranks them: the LP optimum is then the combinatorial optimum.

examples.title: A production plan, solved on the corner points
examples.problem: A workshop makes desks ($x_1$) and chairs ($x_2$). A desk needs 1 hour of assembly and 3 hours of finishing; a chair needs 2 and 2. Assembly has 40 hours, finishing 60. Profit is 20 per desk, 30 per chair. Maximize profit.

steps.label: Step 1: Write the LP
steps.text: Maximize $20x_1 + 30x_2$ subject to $x_1 + 2x_2 \le 40$ (assembly), $3x_1 + 2x_2 \le 60$ (finishing), $x_1, x_2 \ge 0$.

steps.label: Step 2: List the vertices of the polytope
steps.text: Intersections of the binding constraints: $(0,0)$ with $z = 0$; $(20, 0)$ (finishing tight) with $z = 400$; $(0, 20)$ (assembly tight) with $z = 600$; and the intersection of both resource lines.

steps.label: Step 4: Compare objective values
steps.text: $z(10, 15) = 200 + 450 = 650$, beating 600 and 400 — the optimum sits at the vertex where both resources are exhausted simultaneously.

examples.result: Make 10 desks and 15 chairs for profit 650: a preview of how simplex only ever needs the vertices.

examples.title: Two constraints from one conservation law
examples.problem: Formulate the LP relaxation of the single-pair shortest path from $s$ to $t$ on edges $(s,a), (a,t), (s,t)$ with weights 3, 4, 5, and read off its meaning.

steps.label: Step 1: Variables
steps.text: $x_{sa}, x_{at}, x_{st} \in [0, 1]$: how much of the unit of flow uses each edge.

steps.label: Step 2: Conservation
steps.text: At $s$: $x_{sa} + x_{st} = 1$ (one unit leaves). At $a$: $x_{sa} = x_{at}$ (whatever enters leaves). At $t$: $x_{at} + x_{st} = 1$ (one unit arrives).

steps.label: Step 3: Objective
steps.text: Minimize $3x_{sa} + 4x_{at} + 5x_{st}$. Substituting $x_{at} = x_{sa}$: minimize $7x_{sa} + 5x_{st}$ with $x_{sa} + x_{st} = 1$ — the path $s\!-\!a\!-\!t$ costs 7 versus 5 direct.

steps.label: Step 4: Read the optimum
steps.text: The minimum $5$ is attained at $x_{st} = 1$, $x_{sa} = x_{at} = 0$: the LP's optimal vertex *is* the shortest path $s \to t$.

examples.result: Flow conservation plus 0/1 bounds produces a polytope whose vertices are paths — the LP solves the graph problem.

keyTakeaways: Modeling = decision variables, linear objective, linear constraints, nonnegativity; free quantities split as $x^+ - x^-$.
Shortest path: minimize $\sum w_{uv} x_{uv}$ with one unit of flow conserved from $s$ to $t$, $0 \le x \le 1$.
Max flow: maximize total outflow of $s$ under capacities and conservation; duality proves max-flow min-cut.
Network LPs are integral — their vertices are the combinatorial objects, so exact answers fall out of the general solver.

quiz.q: In the shortest-path LP, the constraints $\sum_v x_{uv} - \sum_v x_{vu} = 1$ for $u = s$ (0 at internal nodes, −1 at $t$) express:
options: flow conservation of a single unit traveling from s to t
quiz.explanation: One unit appears at the source, disappears at the sink, and is neither created nor destroyed anywhere else — that is conservation.

quiz.q: The production LP of the example has optimum at the vertex where both resource lines meet because:
options: the objective is parallel to neither constraint
an LP optimum over a bounded polytope is attained at a vertex, and the best vertex here is that intersection
quiz.explanation: Linear objectives on polytopes attain optima at vertices; comparing the four candidate vertices identifies $(10, 15)$ as best.

quiz.q: Which feature lets network LPs return integral (0/1) optima without any rounding step?
options: their constraint matrices are network (totally unimodular) matrices, making every vertex integral
the number of constraints is even
quiz.explanation: Total unimodularity makes every basis inverse integral, so basic solutions — including the optimum — are integral automatically.

intro: Simplex is a local search over vertices: pick a nonbasic variable whose objective coefficient promises improvement, slide along an edge until some basic variable hits zero, and re-express. The tableau is the bookkeeping; the ratio test chooses the leaving variable; Bland's rule keeps the walk from ever cycling back.
objectives: Execute a pivot: entering variable, ratio test, leaving variable, tableau update
Trace simplex on the running LP to its optimum
Define degeneracy and explain how cycling can occur
State Bland's rule and the Klee–Minty caveat on worst-case running time

concepts.statement: In slack form $z = v + \sum_{j \in N} \bar{c}_j x_j$, pick an entering variable $x_e$ with $\bar{c}_e > 0$ (increasing it improves $z$). The **ratio test** finds the tightest limit: $\Delta = \min_{i: a_{ie} > 0} b_i / a_{ie}$ over the equations of basic variables; the argmin **leaves** the basis at value 0. Rewrite the leaving variable's equation to solve for $x_e$ and substitute everywhere — one **pivot**.
concepts.detail: Geometrically: move along one edge of the polytope (only $x_e$ changes among nonbasics) until a constraint blocks further motion; the blocking constraint's slack enters the nonbasic set at zero.

concepts.statement: The tableau stacks the slack-form equations as a grid: one row per basic variable plus the objective row $z - \sum \bar c_j x_j = v$. Entering-column entries are the substitution coefficients; the $b$ column holds the current basic values.
concepts.detail: Each pivot modifies only the rows whose entering coefficient is nonzero — elementary row operations in disguise, exactly like one step of Gaussian elimination.

concepts.statement: A BFS is **degenerate** when some basic variable sits at 0. The ratio test can then give $\Delta = 0$: the pivot changes the basis but not the point. If bases repeat, simplex **cycles** and never terminates.
concepts.detail: Cycling needs degeneracy as a necessary condition; it is rare in practice but real — the fix is a deterministic tie-breaking rule with a termination proof.

concepts.statement: **Bland's rule:** always enter the *lowest-indexed* eligible nonbasic, and break ratio ties by the lowest-indexed leaving variable. With Bland's rule simplex never repeats a basis, hence terminates.
concepts.detail: The proof is a clever minimal-counterexample argument about the set of variables that ever both enter and leave. Other common rules (Dantzig's most-negative coefficient) are faster in practice but not cycle-proof.

concepts.statement: Klee and Minty built deformed cubes on which simplex visits $2^n - 1$ vertices: exponential worst case. Yet average-case and smoothed analyses, plus decades of practice, keep simplex the default — and the ellipsoid and interior-point methods decide LPs in polynomial time if guarantees are needed.
concepts.detail: This is a central lesson of the book: practical dominance and worst-case optimality are different virtues.

figures.caption: The initial tableau of the running LP, mid-decision. The entering column $x_1$ (amber) is chosen for the most negative objective coefficient $-3$; the leaving row is picked by the **ratio test** $b_i / a_{i1}$: $30/1 = 30$, $24/2 = 12$, $36/4 = 9$ — the minimum 9 marks $x_6$ (teal row) as leaving. The pivot element $4$ (ringed) divides the leaving row; the new BFS has $x_1 = 9$, $x_4 = 21$, $x_5 = 6$, $z = 27$. One more pivot (on $x_2$, with $x_5$ leaving at ratio 4) reaches the optimum $z = 28$ at $(8, 4, 0)$.

examples.title: Two pivots from origin to optimum
examples.problem: Run simplex on the running LP (maximize $3x_1 + x_2 + 2x_3$) from the initial tableau of the figure to the optimal vertex.

steps.label: Step 1: First pivot — $x_1$ enters
steps.text: The z-row $z - 3x_1 - x_2 - 2x_3 = 0$ has most negative entry $-3$ on $x_1$. Ratio test on the $x_1$ column: $30/1 = 30$, $24/2 = 12$, $36/4 = 9$ → $x_6$ leaves at $x_1 = 9$.

steps.label: Step 2: Re-express and read the new BFS
steps.text: Substituting $x_1 = 9 - \frac14 x_2 - \frac12 x_3 - \frac14 x_6$ everywhere: $z = 27 + \frac14 x_2 + \frac12 x_3 - \frac34 x_6$, with $x_4 = 21$, $x_5 = 6$. Both coefficients on nonbasics $x_2, x_3$ are positive — more improvement available.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify optimality
steps.text: After pivoting, $z = 28 - \frac16 x_3 - \frac16 x_5 - \frac23 x_6$ — every coefficient nonpositive, so no edge improves: the optimum is $z^* = 28$ at $(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (8, 4, 0)$ with $x_4 = 18$ (30 − 12) still slack in the first constraint.

examples.result: Vertex sequence $(0,0,0) \to (9,0,0) \to (8,4,0)$ with $z$: $0 \to 27 \to 28$ — two edges of the polytope.

examples.title: A degenerate pivot that goes nowhere
examples.problem: Explain how the ratio test can produce a zero-length step even when the entering coefficient is positive.

steps.label: Step 1: Set up
steps.text: Suppose some basic variable $x_B$ has current value $b_B = 0$ (the BFS is degenerate) and a positive coefficient in the entering column.

steps.label: Step 2: Ratio test
steps.text: Its ratio $0 / a = 0$ wins the minimum, so it leaves the basis and the entering variable enters at value $\Delta = 0$: the point does not move.

steps.label: Step 3: The danger
steps.text: The basis changed while $z$ did not; a second degenerate pivot can return to a previously seen basis — cycling. With Bland's rule (lowest-index entering, lowest-index leaving on ties) no basis ever repeats, so termination is guaranteed.

examples.result: Degeneracy is common (it just means $> n$ constraints through one vertex); cycling is the pathology, Bland the cure.

keyTakeaways: A pivot: choose an entering nonbasic with positive objective coefficient, ratio-test for the leaving basic, re-express the slack form.
The tableau is the slack form as a grid; pivoting is Gaussian elimination on it.
Degenerate BFS values of 0 allow zero-length pivots; cycling is possible without a tie-breaking rule — Bland's rule guarantees termination.
Simplex is exponential in the worst case (Klee–Minty cubes) yet fast in practice; interior-point methods give polynomial guarantees.

quiz.q: In the first pivot of the example, $x_6$ leaves because:
options: it has the largest coefficient in the $x_1$ column
its row attains the minimum ratio $b_i / a_{i1} = 36/4 = 9$
it is the last slack variable
quiz.explanation: The ratio test bounds how far the entering variable can grow: the first basic variable to hit 0 is $x_6$, at ratio 9, so it leaves the basis.

quiz.q: A slack form $z = 28 - \frac16 x_3 - \frac16 x_5 - \frac23 x_6$ certifies optimality because:
options: every nonbasic coefficient is nonpositive, so no edge direction improves the objective
quiz.explanation: Raising any nonbasic from 0 only subtracts from $z$; with feasibility intact, the current vertex is a local (hence global) optimum.

quiz.q: Bland's rule prevents cycling by:
options: always taking the largest possible step
a deterministic lowest-index choice of entering and leaving variables, which makes basis repetition impossible
quiz.explanation: The fixed-index tie-break gives a potential argument under which no basis can repeat — simplex then terminates after finitely many pivots.

quiz.q: The Klee–Minty construction shows that simplex can take:
options: polynomially many pivots on some inputs
exponentially many pivots on specially deformed cubes
infinitely many pivots on feasible LPs
fewer pivots than the number of variables
quiz.explanation: On these cubes simplex visits $2^n - 1$ vertices — an exponential lower bound that motivated the polynomial-time ellipsoid and interior-point methods.

intro: Every linear program has a mirror image — its dual — whose feasible solutions bound the primal objective from the other side. Weak duality is a two-line inequality; strong duality says the bounds meet exactly at the optimum, turning any primal-dual feasible pair into a checkable certificate of optimality. The dual variables read as prices: what each constraint is worth per unit.
objectives: Write the dual of a standard-form LP mechanically
Prove weak duality and state strong duality
Verify complementary slackness on the running LP
Interpret dual variables as shadow prices

concepts.statement: Primal: maximize $c^Tx$ s.t. $Ax \le b$, $x \ge 0$. **Dual:** minimize $b^Ty$ s.t. $A^Ty \ge c$, $y \ge 0$. Each primal constraint spawns a dual variable $y_i$; each primal variable $x_j$ spawns a dual constraint; the dual of the dual is the primal.
concepts.detail: Mechanics: transpose the constraint matrix, swap $b$ and $c$, flip maximization to minimization and $\le$ to $\ge$. An equality constraint in the primal makes the corresponding $y_i$ free; a free primal variable makes its dual constraint an equality.

concepts.statement: For any primal-feasible $x$ and dual-feasible $y$: $c^Tx \le y^TAx \le b^Ty$. (First step: $c \le A^Ty$ and $x \ge 0$; second: $Ax \le b$ and $y \ge 0$.) Hence every dual value upper-bounds every primal value.
concepts.detail: Consequences arrive instantly: if the primal is unbounded the dual must be infeasible (and vice versa); a duality gap $b^Ty - c^Tx$ measures how far a candidate pair is from optimal.

concepts.statement: If the primal LP has an optimal solution $x^*$, the dual has an optimal $y^*$ with $b^Ty^* = c^Tx^*$ — the bounds meet exactly. (Conversely, feasibility on both sides with equal objective values certifies optimality of both.)
concepts.detail: The proof (sketched in many texts, including via simplex's final tableau: the z-row coefficients of the slack variables are exactly a dual optimal solution) is constructive — running simplex on the primal hands you the optimal dual for free.

concepts.statement: At an optimal pair $(x^*, y^*)$: for each primal constraint $i$, either it is tight or $y_i^* = 0$; for each primal variable $j$, either its dual constraint is tight or $x_j^* = 0$. Formally: $y_i^* (b_i - a_i^Tx^*) = 0$ and $x_j^* ((A^Ty^*)_j - c_j) = 0$.
concepts.detail: A positive price $y_i$ means the constraint is a scarce resource actually consumed; a zero price means slack. This is the sensitivity readout engineers want from the solver.

concepts.statement: The optimal dual variables are marginal values: $y_i^* \approx \partial z^*/\partial b_i$ — the change in optimum per unit increase of resource $b_i$, valid while the optimal basis does not change.
concepts.detail: Dual of the max-flow LP gives edge prices whose sum is the min cut — duality *is* the max-flow min-cut theorem; similarly, shortest path vs. potentials is another primal-dual pair.

figures.caption: Weak duality sandwiches both problems. Every primal-feasible point gives a value $c^Tx$ (teal markers on the left axis — the simplex walk visits $0 \to 27 \to 28$); every dual-feasible point gives $b^Ty$ (amber markers on the right axis, e.g. 90, 54, 45, 36 from feasible price vectors). No primal value ever exceeds any dual value — the shaded band is the duality gap. At the optimum the band pinches shut: the dual solution $(0, 1/6, 2/3)$ attains exactly $28$, the primal optimum — strong duality.

examples.title: The dual of the running LP, verified
examples.problem: Write the dual of the running LP, guess the optimal dual from complementary slackness, and verify strong duality.

steps.label: Step 1: Transcribe the dual
steps.text: Minimize $30y_1 + 24y_2 + 36y_3$ subject to $y_1 + 2y_2 + 4y_3 \ge 3$, $y_1 + 2y_2 + y_3 \ge 1$, $3y_1 + 5y_2 + 2y_3 \ge 2$, $y \ge 0$ — one dual variable per primal constraint, one dual constraint per primal variable.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply complementary slackness to the primal optimum
steps.text: Optimal $(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (8, 4, 0)$: constraint 1 has slack ($8+4+3\cdot0 = 12 < 30$) → $y_1 = 0$. Variables $x_1, x_2 > 0$ → their dual constraints are tight: $2y_2 + 4y_3 = 3$ and $2y_2 + y_3 = 1$ (using $y_1 = 0$).

steps.label: Step 3: Solve the two tight equations
steps.text: Subtract: $3y_3 = 2 \Rightarrow y_3 = 2/3$, then $2y_2 = 1 - 2/3 \Rightarrow y_2 = 1/6$. Candidate dual: $(0, 1/6, 2/3)$.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify feasibility and value
steps.text: Third dual constraint: $5(1/6) + 2(2/3) = 13/6 \ge 2$ ✓ (slack, consistent with $x_3 = 0$). Objective: $30(0) + 24(1/6) + 36(2/3) = 4 + 24 = 28 = c^Tx^*$ — strong duality holds.

examples.result: The pair $(8,4,0)$ and $(0, 1/6, 2/3)$ is a self-certifying optimum: feasibility on both sides plus equal objective values.

examples.title: Weak duality gap on two variables
examples.problem: Primal $\max x_1 + x_2$ s.t. $x_1 + 2x_2 \le 4$, $4x_1 + 2x_2 \le 12$, $x \ge 0$. Exhibit primal $x$ and dual $y$ with gap $2$, then close it.

steps.label: Feasible pair
steps.text: Primal $(1,1)$: $3 \le 4$, $6 \le 12$ ✓ value $2$. Dual $(0.5,0.5)$: $0.5+2 = 2.5 \ge 1$ ✓ value $4 \cdot 0.5 + 12 \cdot 0.5 = 8$. Gap $8-2 = 6$ (weak duality: primal $\le$ dual ✓).

steps.label: Optima
steps.text: Primal optimum $(2.67,0.67)$? Solve binding: $x_1+2x_2 = 4$, $4x_1+2x_2 = 12$: $x_1 = 8/3$, $x_2 = 2/3$: value $10/3 \approx 3.33$. Dual optimum $(1/6,1/6)$? Check: $1/6+4/6 = 5/6 < 1$ infeasible; true optimum $y = (0,0.5)$? $0+2 = 2 \ge 1$ ✓, $0+1 = 1 \ge 1$ ✓ value $6$: gap $6-3.33$? Still gap: exact optima need simplex; weak duality only bounds.

steps.label: Certificate
steps.text: Any feasible $y$ upper-bounds every feasible $x$: $c^Tx \le y^TAx \le y^Tb = b^Ty$. Strong duality closes the gap at optima.

examples.result: Feasible $(1,1)$ value $2$ vs feasible dual value $8$: gap $6 \ge 0$ (weak duality); optima meet (strong duality).

keyTakeaways: Dual of $\max c^Tx, Ax \le b, x \ge 0$ is $\min b^Ty, A^Ty \ge c, y \ge 0$ — constraints ↔ variables, $b$ ↔ $c$.
Weak duality $c^Tx \le b^Ty$ for all feasible pairs: two lines, and it already rules out simultaneous unboundedness of both.
Strong duality: optimal values coincide; the pair of optimal solutions certifies each other.
Complementary slackness: a positive price sits only on a binding constraint; a positive primal variable has a tight dual constraint.
Dual variables are shadow prices $\partial z^*/\partial b_i$ — the economic reading of the LP.

quiz.q: The dual of a standard-form primal with $m$ constraints and $n$ variables has:
quiz.explanation: Constraints and variables swap roles under dualization: each primal constraint prices a dual variable, each primal variable demands a dual constraint.

quiz.q: If some primal-feasible $x$ and dual-feasible $y$ satisfy $c^Tx = b^Ty$, then:
options: both are optimal for their respective LPs
quiz.explanation: Weak duality forces every primal value below $b^Ty$ and every dual value above $c^Tx$; equality pins both at the common optimum — the standard optimality certificate.

quiz.q: In the running LP, constraint 1 ($x_1 + x_2 + 3x_3 \le 30$) has slack 18 at the optimum. Complementary slackness therefore implies:
quiz.explanation: Slack resources are free: $y_1^* (b_1 - a_1^Tx^*) = 0$ with slack $18 > 0$ forces the price $y_1^* = 0$.

quiz.q: The economic reading of the optimal dual variable $y_i$ is:
options: the cost of the cheapest primal variable
the marginal change in the optimal objective per unit increase of the right-hand side $b_i$
the number of pivots simplex needs
quiz.explanation: Shadow price: relax resource $i$ by one unit and the optimum moves by about $y_i$ — exact while the optimal basis stays put.

intro: Simplex needs a starting vertex, but a slack form is only guaranteed to give one when every $b_i \ge 0$ — and real LPs often don't. The fix is elegant: solve one auxiliary LP whose optimum is either a certificate of infeasibility or a feasible basis for the original problem. This is the two-phase method.
objectives: Recognize why negative slack values block an initial BFS
Construct the auxiliary LP and its trivial initial BFS
Run Phase 1 and pivot the auxiliary variable out of the basis
State what Phase 1's optimal value proves about feasibility

concepts.statement: After converting to slack form, some equation may read $x_B = b_i - \ldots$ with $b_i < 0$: setting nonbasics to 0 makes $x_B < 0$ — not a BFS. A constraint like $x_1 + x_2 \ge 2$ (a minimum production quota) does exactly this.
concepts.detail: The origin is infeasible; simplex cannot start. Geometrically the polytope avoids the positive orthant's corner, so we need a helicopter to a vertex.

concepts.statement: Introduce one extra variable $x_0 \ge 0$ added to the *left* of every violated constraint: minimize $x_0$ subject to the relaxed system. Setting $x_0 = -\min_i b_i \ge 0$ (with all other nonbasics zero) is trivially feasible — an instant initial BFS.
concepts.detail: Intuition: $x_0$ is a slack *budget* that absorbs how badly the constraints are violated; the auxiliary optimum measures the minimum total violation that cannot be squeezed away.

concepts.statement: **Phase 1:** run simplex on the auxiliary LP. If its optimal value is $> 0$, the original LP is **infeasible**. If it is $0$: if $x_0$ left the basis, what remains is a feasible basis of the original LP; if $x_0$ sits at 0 in the basis, one degenerate pivot removes it. **Phase 2:** run simplex on the original objective from that basis.
concepts.detail: Why infeasibility: any feasible $x$ of the original LP extends to $(x, x_0 = 0)$ of the auxiliary one, so a positive auxiliary minimum means no such $x$ exists — and the final Phase-1 tableau hands you the separating witnesses.

concepts.statement: Phase 2 can still discover an unbounded edge: an entering column with *no positive entries* lets the entering variable grow forever. No ratio test candidate exists, and the LP has no finite optimum.
concepts.detail: So the full simplex lifecycle is: Phase 1 settles feasibility (or proves infeasibility), Phase 2 terminates at optimality or unboundedness — every LP ends in exactly one of three verdicts.

concepts.statement: Phase 1 answers feasibility ($\bar b$ sign pattern); Phase 2 answers optimality-or-unboundedness (reduced costs and ratio test). Infeasible means no vertex satisfies $Ax \le b$; unbounded means the feasible polytope has a ray improving $c$ forever; otherwise an optimal vertex exists.
concepts.detail: Auxiliary optimum $x_0 = 0$ certifies feasibility with a basis; $x_0 > 0$ certifies infeasibility with a Farkas proof. Unboundedness is detected in Phase 2 when an entering variable has no leaving constraint.

examples.title: Two-phase on a quota-constrained LP
examples.problem: Solve: maximize $2x_1 + 3x_2$ subject to $x_1 + x_2 \ge 2$, $x_1 + 4x_2 \le 12$, $x_1 \le 3$, $x \ge 0$.

steps.label: Step 1: Slack form exposes the problem
steps.text: The quota becomes $x_1 + x_2 - s_1 = 2$, i.e. $s_1 = -2 + x_1 + x_2$: the naive origin BFS has $s_1 = -2 < 0$ — infeasible start.

steps.label: Step 2: Build the auxiliary LP
steps.text: Minimize $x_0$ subject to $x_1 + x_2 - s_1 + x_0 = 2$, $x_1 + 4x_2 + s_2 = 12$, $x_1 + s_3 = 3$. Initial BFS: nonbasics $x_1 = x_2 = s_1 = 0$ give $x_0 = 2$, $s_2 = 12$, $s_3 = 3$ — all nonnegative.

steps.label: Step 3: Phase 1 pivot
steps.text: From $x_0 = 2 - x_1 - x_2 + s_1$, the entering variable $x_2$ (any variable with a negative coefficient) reduces $x_0$. Ratio test: $x_0$ hits 0 at $x_2 = 2$; $s_2$ allows $12/4 = 3$; $s_3$ has no $x_2$. Minimum 2 → $x_0$ leaves the basis, $x_2 = 2$, $x_0 = 0$: feasible in one pivot.

steps.label: Step 4: Drop $x_0$, run Phase 2
steps.text: The basis $\{x_2, s_2, s_3\} = (2, 4, 3)$ is feasible for the original LP (point $(0, 2)$, $z = 6$). Successive pivots: $s_1$ enters ($z = 9$ at $(0,3)$), then $x_1$ enters with $s_3$ leaving at $x_1 = 3$ → $(3, 9/4)$ with $z = 2\cdot3 + 3\cdot(9/4) = 51/4 = 12.75$.

steps.label: Step 5: Verify
steps.text: $x_1 + x_2 = 5.25 \ge 2$ ✓ (slack), $x_1 + 4x_2 = 3 + 9 = 12$ ✓ (tight), $x_1 = 3$ ✓ (tight). No edge improves: optimal.

examples.result: Phase 1 buys a starting vertex in one pivot; Phase 2 walks $z$: $6 \to 9 \to 12.75$.

examples.title: Auxiliary objective $x_0$
examples.problem: LP with $x_1 + x_2 \le -1$, $x \ge 0$ (infeasible: left $\ge 0$). Form the auxiliary LP and read $x_0$.

steps.label: Auxiliary
steps.text: $\max -x_0$ s.t. $x_1 + x_2 + x_0 \le? $ Standard: $x_1 + x_2 - s + x_0 = -1$? With $x_0$ added to each violated constraint: $x_1 + x_2 + x_0 \ge? $ Precisely: subtract surplus, add $x_0$ to infeasible rows.

steps.label: Initial BFS
steps.text: $x_0 = 1$, $x_1 = x_2 = 0$ satisfies $0+0+1 \ge? $: feasible start for auxiliary.

steps.label: Optimum
steps.text: Minimize $x_0$: best is $x_0 = 1 > 0$ (need $x_1+x_2 \ge? $ can’t reach $-1$ with nonnegatives): $x_0^* > 0$ proves original infeasible.

steps.label: Versus feasible
steps.text: Had optimum been $x_0^* = 0$, dropping $x_0$ would leave a feasible basis for Phase 2.

examples.result: Auxiliary optimum $x_0^* = 1 > 0$: certificate of infeasibility; $x_0^* = 0$ would have handed Phase 2 its starting vertex.

keyTakeaways: Negative $b_i$ in slack form means the origin is not feasible — simplex has no starting BFS.
The auxiliary LP adds one variable $x_0$ absorbing violations; its origin BFS is free to construct.
Auxiliary optimum $> 0$ proves infeasibility; $= 0$ hands Phase 2 a genuine feasible basis (degenerate pivot out if $x_0$ lingers at zero).
An entering column with no positive entries certifies unboundedness — the third and final verdict simplex can return.

quiz.q: The auxiliary variable $x_0$ is added to the left side of each violated constraint so that:
options: setting nonbasics to zero yields a feasible basis, with $x_0$ absorbing all violations
quiz.explanation: With $x_0$ basic at $-\min b_i \ge 0$, every basic value is nonnegative: an instant legal BFS for Phase 1 to start from.

quiz.q: Phase 1 terminates with optimal value $x_0 = 3 > 0$. Conclusion:
options: the original LP is infeasible — no x satisfies all constraints
Phase 2 must be rerun with a different pivot rule
quiz.explanation: Any original-feasible point would give auxiliary value 0; a positive minimum proves no such point exists.

quiz.q: Phase 2 is about to pivot on an entering variable whose column contains only negative or zero coefficients. This means:
options: the LP is unbounded — the entering variable can grow without limit
quiz.explanation: No basic variable decreases as the entering one grows, so the ratio test finds no blocking constraint: an infinite improving edge exists.

intro: A polynomial can live in two worlds: as a list of coefficients, or as its values at chosen points. Addition is cheap in coefficients, multiplication is cheap in point-value form — and a degree-bound $n$ polynomial is pinned down by its values at any $n$ distinct points. The whole FFT story is about shuttling between the two representations fast enough to make multiplication cheap everywhere.
objectives: Convert between coefficient and point-value representations (evaluation, interpolation)
State the uniqueness of the degree-bound-n representation through n points
Tabulate the costs of each operation in each representation
Set up the three-step pipeline for fast multiplication

concepts.statement: A polynomial of **degree bound $n$** is the coefficient vector $a = (a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1})$ standing for $A(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} a_j x^j$. Evaluation of $A$ at one point takes $\Theta(n)$ by Horner's rule; adding two such polynomials costs $\Theta(n)$; multiplying them costs $\Theta(n^2)$ (each $a_i$ meets each $b_j$).
concepts.detail: The coefficient world is the schoolbook world: the $\Theta(n^2)$ convolution of coefficients is the bottleneck this chapter demolishes.

concepts.statement: Choose $n$ distinct points $x_0, \ldots, x_{n-1}$ and store $\{(x_k, y_k) : y_k = A(x_k)\}$. Addition and multiplication of polynomials are **pointwise** — $\Theta(n)$ each: the product $C = AB$ (degree bound $2n$) is represented by its values at $2n$ points.
concepts.detail: Caveat: to multiply two degree-bound-$n$ polynomials you need $2n$ points, so both inputs must first be *padded* — zero-extended to degree bound $2n$ (adding zero coefficients changes nothing).

concepts.statement: **(Uniqueness of degree-bound-$n$ polynomials.)** A degree-bound-$n$ polynomial is uniquely determined by its values at any $n$ distinct points: the linear map from coefficients to values is given by the Vandermonde matrix $(x_k^j)$, which is invertible when the $x_k$ are distinct. Recovering the coefficients (**interpolation**) costs $\Theta(n^2)$ by Lagrange's formula or Gaussian elimination.
concepts.detail: Lagrange: $A(x) = \sum_k y_k \prod_{j \ne k} \frac{x - x_j}{x_k - x_j}$ — each basis polynomial is 1 at $x_k$ and 0 at the other points, so the sum visibly matches the data.

concepts.term: The cost ledger and the strategy
concepts.statement: Evaluate at $n$ points: $\Theta(n^2)$ naively (or $\Theta(n \lg n)$ by FFT at the roots of unity). Pointwise multiply: $\Theta(n)$. Interpolate: $\Theta(n^2)$ (or $\Theta(n \lg n)$ by inverse FFT). Pipeline for $C = AB$: evaluate both, multiply pointwise, interpolate — $\Theta(n^2) + \Theta(n) + \Theta(n^2)$ naively, or $\Theta(n \lg n)$ with FFTs.
concepts.detail: The chapter's punchline: naive evaluation and interpolation are the *only* obstacles between us and near-linear multiplication; choosing the evaluation points to be roots of unity removes both at once (Section 30.2).

concepts.statement: Evaluate $A(x) = a_0 + a_1x + \cdots + a_{n-1}x^{n-1}$ as $a_0 + x(a_1 + x(a_2 + \cdots + x a_{n-1}))$: $n-1$ multiplies and adds, $\Theta(n)$ per point, $\Theta(n^2)$ for $n$ points. Point-value multiplication needs this $n$ times, hence $\Theta(n^2)$ naive conversion.
concepts.detail: Horner is optimal for single-point evaluation (no method uses fewer operations on general coefficients), but evaluating at $n$ arbitrary points is still $\Theta(n^2)$: the FFT beats it by choosing the points to be roots of unity.

examples.title: Multiplication through point-value form
examples.problem: Multiply $A(x) = x^2 + 1$ and $B(x) = x + 2$ (degree bounds 3 and 3 after padding) using the values at $x = 0, 1, 2$.

steps.label: Step 1: Evaluate both at the points
Step 2: Multiply pointwise
steps.text: Product values: $(0, 1 \cdot 2), (1, 2 \cdot 3), (2, 5 \cdot 4) = (0, 2), (1, 6), (2, 20)$ — three $\Theta(1)$ multiplications.

steps.label: Step 3: Interpolate
steps.text: The product $C(x) = (x^2+1)(x+2) = x^3 + 2x^2 + x + 2$ is a cubic, so *these three points underdetermine it* — the honest pipeline needs $2n = 4$ points (padding the inputs to degree bound 4). Adding the value at $x = 3$: $A(3) = 10$, $B(3) = 5$, $C(3) = 50$; and indeed $27 + 18 + 3 + 2 = 50$ ✓.

steps.label: Step 4: Recover coefficients
steps.text: With 4 points $(2, 6, 20, 50)$ at $x = 0..3$, solving the Vandermonde system returns $C = (2, 1, 2, 1)$: $C(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 + x + 2$ ✓ — check at $x = 2$: $8 + 8 + 2 + 2 = 20$ ✓.

examples.result: Pointwise multiplication is trivial; the cost lives entirely in evaluation and interpolation — exactly what the FFT accelerates.

examples.title: Evaluating $1+2x+3x^2$ at three points
examples.problem: Evaluate $A(x) = 1+2x+3x^2$ at $x = 0,1,2$ by Horner and count operations.

steps.label: Horner form
steps.text: $A(x) = 1 + x(2 + 3x)$: $2$ operations per point.

steps.label: $x = 2$
steps.text: $1 + 2 \cdot (2+6) = 17$. Three points $\times 2$ ops $= 6$: $\Theta(n^2)$ for $n = 3$; FFT does $n$ special points in $\Theta(n \lg n)$.

examples.result: Values $[1,6,17]$ in $6$ operations; $n$ arbitrary points cost $\Theta(n^2)$, motivating the roots-of-unity shortcut.

keyTakeaways: Coefficient form: $\Theta(n)$ evaluation (Horner) and addition, $\Theta(n^2)$ multiplication.
Point-value form: $\Theta(n)$ addition and multiplication — but the product of degree-bound-$n$ polynomials needs $2n$ points.
Uniqueness: values at $n$ distinct points determine a degree-bound-$n$ polynomial (invertible Vandermonde).
Pipeline evaluate → multiply pointwise → interpolate; FFT makes both ends $\Theta(n \lg n)$ instead of $\Theta(n^2)$.

quiz.q: Multiplying two degree-bound-$n$ polynomials purely in point-value form requires:
options: 2n distinct points, with inputs zero-padded to degree bound 2n
quiz.explanation: The product has degree bound $2n-1$ (degree ≤ 2n−2), so 2n values are needed to pin it down; padding the operands with zero coefficients keeps their values unchanged.

quiz.q: The map from coefficients to values at $n$ fixed distinct points is invertible because:
options: the Vandermonde matrix $(x_k^j)$ has nonzero determinant when the points are distinct
evaluation is linear in the points
quiz.explanation: det = product of pairwise differences $\prod_{k<j}(x_j - x_k) \ne 0$ — this is the uniqueness theorem that makes interpolation possible.

quiz.q: In the multiplication pipeline with FFTs, the $\Theta(n \lg n)$ terms are:
options: evaluation and interpolation (two FFTs of size 2n and one inverse FFT)
quiz.explanation: Pointwise multiplication stays $\Theta(n)$; the two transforms and the inverse transform carry the $\Theta(n \lg n)$ cost — still far below $\Theta(n^2)$.

intro: Evaluate at special points — the complex roots of unity — and evaluation collapses into a divide-and-conquer recursion: the even and odd coefficients form half-size polynomials evaluated at the *squared* points, which by the halving lemma are again roots of unity, half as many. That single geometric fact is the entire engine of the $\Theta(n \lg n)$ FFT.
objectives: Define roots of unity and primitive roots; compute with them
State the DFT as evaluation at the $n$th roots of unity
Derive the FFT recurrence from the even/odd split of $A(x)$
Invert the DFT by conjugating the roots and scaling by $1/n$

concepts.statement: A **complex $n$th root of unity** satisfies $\omega^n = 1$. There are exactly $n$ of them: $\omega_n^0, \omega_n^1, \ldots, \omega_n^{n-1}$ for the **primitive** root $\omega_n = e^{2\pi i/n}$ — equally spaced points on the unit circle. Key identities: $\omega_n^n = 1$, $\omega_n^{n/2} = -1$, $\omega_n^{k + n/2} = -\omega_n^k$.
concepts.detail: For $n = 8$: $\omega_8 = \frac{1+i}{\sqrt 2}$; for $n = 4$: $\omega_4 = i$. Powers repeat with period $n$ — exponents are understood modulo $n$.

concepts.statement: The **discrete Fourier transform** of $a = (a_0, \ldots, a_{n-1})$ is $y = \mathrm{DFT}_n(a)$ with $y_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} a_j \omega_n^{jk} = A(\omega_n^k)$ — the values of $A$ at *all $n$ roots of unity*.
concepts.detail: Matrix form: $y = V a$ with the Vandermonde matrix $V_{kj} = \omega_n^{jk}$. The DFT is nothing but evaluation at these particular $n$ points — chosen so that evaluation has a fast algorithm.

concepts.statement:
Split $A(x) = A^{[0]}(x^2) + x A^{[1]}(x^2)$, where $A^{[0]}$ collects the even-position coefficients and $A^{[1]}$ the odd ones (degree bound $n/2$ each). Then for $k = 0, \ldots, n/2 - 1$:
$$y_k = A(\omega_n^k) = A^{[0]}(\omega_n^{2k}) + \omega_n^k A^{[1]}(\omega_n^{2k}), \qquad y_{k+n/2} = A^{[0]}(\omega_n^{2k}) - \omega_n^k A^{[1]}(\omega_n^{2k}).$$
The two half-size problems are DFTs of length $n/2$ (since $(\omega_n^k)^2 = \omega_{n/2}^k$), so $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n \lg n)$.
concepts.detail: The second line is the first with $\omega_n^{k+n/2} = -\omega_n^k$ — one complex multiplication $\omega_n^k \cdot A^{[1]}(\ldots)$ feeds both outputs: the *butterfly*. RECURSIVE-FFT: split, recurse on $y^{[0]} = \mathrm{FFT}(a^{[0]})$ and $y^{[1]} = \mathrm{FFT}(a^{[1]})$, combine with the two-line loop.

concepts.statement: $a = \mathrm{DFT}_n^{-1}(y)$ is computed by $a_j = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} y_k \omega_n^{-jk}$: run the same FFT algorithm with $\omega_n$ replaced by $\omega_n^{-1}$ and divide every result by $n$.
concepts.detail: The proof is a Vandermonde inverse computation: $V^{-1} = \frac{1}{n}$ times the matrix with entries $\omega_n^{-jk}$ — the conjugate roots. Interpolation is thus the *same algorithm* as evaluation.

concepts.term: Why roots of unity and not, say, 1..n
concepts.statement: The recursion needs the squared evaluation points of the children to form *one* half-size set, not two overlapping ones. Squaring the $n$ roots of unity yields exactly the $n/2$ roots of unity of order $n/2$, each hit exactly twice (halving lemma) — any other choice of points scatters into $2n$ distinct values and the recursion never shrinks.
concepts.detail: This is the design decision that makes the whole chapter work — the masters tier below proves it carefully.

figures.caption: The halving lemma on the unit circle ($n = 8$): the eight 8th roots $\omega_8^k$ (dots) square onto the four 4th roots — the ringed points $\omega_8^{2j} = \omega_4^j$ — each hit exactly twice: $(\omega_8^{k+4})^2 = \omega_8^{2k}$ since $\omega_8^{2k+8} = \omega_8^{2k}$. Amber arcs show $\omega_8^5 \mapsto \omega_8^{10} = \omega_8^2$, $\omega_8^3 \mapsto \omega_8^6$, $\omega_8^1 \mapsto \omega_8^2$… squaring doubles the angle. The right circle is the induced half-size problem: $A^{[0]}$ and $A^{[1]}$ are evaluated at just the 4th roots, exactly as a length-4 DFT requires.

examples.title: A 4-point DFT by hand, via the even/odd split
examples.problem: Compute $y = \mathrm{DFT}_4(1, 2, 3, 4)$ — the values of $A(x) = 1 + 2x + 3x^2 + 4x^3$ at $\omega_4^k = 1, i, -1, -i$ — using the FFT recurrence.

steps.label: Step 1: Split into even and odd
Step 2: Two base-case DFTs of length 2

examples.result: $y = (10,\ -2-2i,\ -2,\ -2+2i)$ — five complex multiplies at this size, $\frac{n}{2}\lg n$ in general.

examples.title: Inverse FFT scaling by $1/n$
examples.problem: DFT of $[1,1,1,1]$ is $[4,0,0,0]$. Invert with $\omega^{-1}$ and $1/4$ scaling.

steps.label: Inverse roots
steps.text: Use $\omega^{-1} = \bar\omega$: same butterfly with conjugated twiddles: FFT$([4,0,0,0])$ with $\omega^{-1}$ gives $[4,4,4,4]$.

steps.label: Scale
steps.text: Divide by $n = 4$: $[1,1,1,1]$ recovered. Forgetting $1/n$ returns $nA$, the classic inverse-FFT bug.

steps.label: Cost
steps.text: Forward $\Theta(n \lg n)$ + inverse $\Theta(n \lg n)$ + pointwise $\Theta(n)$: multiplication in $\Theta(n \lg n)$ total.

examples.result: Inverse yields $[4,4,4,4]/4 = [1,1,1,1]$; $1/n$ scaling is what makes FFT$^{-1}$(FFT($A$)) $= A$.

keyTakeaways: The primitive root $\omega_n = e^{2\pi i/n}$ generates $n$ equally spaced roots of unity on the unit circle; $\omega_n^{n/2} = -1$.
DFT = evaluation at all $n$ roots of unity: $y_k = \sum_j a_j \omega_n^{jk}$ — a Vandermonde product.
FFT splits even/odd coefficients, evaluates them at the *squared* roots (a half-size DFT by the halving lemma), and combines with one butterfly per output pair: $\Theta(n \lg n)$.
The inverse DFT is the same algorithm on $\omega_n^{-1}$ with a final division by $n$.

quiz.q: The DFT of a coefficient vector $a$ equals the values of $A(x)$ at the points:
quiz.explanation: $y_k = A(\omega_n^k)$ — evaluation at $\omega_n^0, \ldots, \omega_n^{n-1}$, the choice that makes the halving recursion collapse.

quiz.q: In the FFT combine step, $y_{k+n/2}$ differs from $y_k$ by:
options: the sign of the odd-polynomial term: $y_{k+n/2} = A^{[0]}((\omega_n^k)^2) - \omega_n^k A^{[1]}((\omega_n^k)^2)$
quiz.explanation: Since $\omega_n^{k+n/2} = -\omega_n^k$ while the squared arguments coincide, the two outputs share $A^{[0]}$ and the $\omega A^{[1]}$ term flips sign — the butterfly.

quiz.q: To compute the inverse DFT with the same FFT code, you:
options: run it with $\omega_n^{-1}$ in place of $\omega_n$ and divide all outputs by $n$
quiz.explanation: The inverse Vandermonde is the conjugate root matrix scaled by $1/n$: interpolation becomes evaluation at conjugate points plus one scalar division.

quiz.q: Why must the FFT's recursion depth be exactly $\lg n$ (power-of-two sizes)?
options: each level halves the number of evaluation points, and the halving lemma produces exactly $n/2$ squared roots only for even $n$ — the book assumes $n$ a power of 2 (padding otherwise)
quiz.explanation: Squaring the $n$th roots yields $n/2$ points only when $n$ is even; halving repeatedly forces $n$ to be a power of two — smaller problems pad with zeros.

depth.title: FFT correctness via the halving lemma

blocks.body: The FFT's correctness is often taken on faith because the algebra looks like bookkeeping. It is worth proving once, cleanly, because the entire $\Theta(n \lg n)$ edifice — multiplication of polynomials, convolution of signals — rests on one lemma about the geometry of roots of unity. We prove that the recursive combine step of RECURSIVE-FFT computes exactly $\mathrm{DFT}_n(a)$.

blocks.heading: Halving lemma
blocks.body: If $n \ge 1$ is even, the squares of the $n$ complex $n$th roots of unity are the $n/2$ complex $(n/2)$th roots of unity, each occurring exactly twice: $\{ (\omega_n^k)^2 : k = 0, \ldots, n-1 \} = \{ \omega_{n/2}^j : j = 0, \ldots, n/2 - 1 \}$ with $k$ and $k + n/2$ yielding the same square.

Fix $k$. First, $(\omega_n^k)^2 = \omega_n^{2k}$, and using $\omega_n = e^{2\pi i/n}$, $\omega_n^{2k} = e^{4 \pi i k / n} = e^{2 \pi i k / (n/2)} = \omega_{n/2}^k$ (the *cancellation lemma*: $\omega_{dn}^{dk} = \omega_n^k$). Second, $k$ and $k + n/2$ collide: $(\omega_n^{k+n/2})^2 = \omega_n^{2k} \cdot \omega_n^n = \omega_n^{2k} \cdot 1 = (\omega_n^k)^2$. So the squaring map sends the $n$ roots onto at most $n/2$ values, and the values $\omega_{n/2}^k$ for $k = 0, \ldots, n/2-1$ are all distinct (they are powers of a primitive $(n/2)$th root) — each is hit exactly twice. $\blacksquare$

blocks.heading: FFT correctness
blocks.body: For even $n$, let $a^{[0]}$ and $a^{[1]}$ be the even- and odd-indexed halves of $a$, and let $y^{[0]} = \mathrm{DFT}_{n/2}(a^{[0]})$, $y^{[1]} = \mathrm{DFT}_{n/2}(a^{[1]})$. Then for $k = 0, \ldots, n/2 - 1$ the combine step produces $$y_k = y^{[0]}_k + \omega_n^k y^{[1]}_k, \qquad y_{k+n/2} = y^{[0]}_k - \omega_n^k y^{[1]}_k,$$ and this vector equals $\mathrm{DFT}_n(a)$.

Factor $A(x) = \sum_j a_j x^j = \sum_j a_{2j} x^{2j} + x \sum_j a_{2j+1} x^{2j} = A^{[0]}(x^2) + x A^{[1]}(x^2)$ — splitting by the parity of $j$; both $A^{[0]}$ and $A^{[1]}$ have degree bound $n/2$. Evaluate at $x = \omega_n^k$ for $0 \le k < n/2$. By the halving lemma $(\omega_n^k)^2 = \omega_{n/2}^k$, so
$$A(\omega_n^k) = A^{[0]}\big(\omega_{n/2}^k\big) + \omega_n^k\, A^{[1]}\big(\omega_{n/2}^k\big) = y^{[0]}_k + \omega_n^k\, y^{[1]}_k,$$
exactly the definition of the length-$n/2$ DFT outputs at index $k$. For the upper half, $\omega_n^{k+n/2} = \omega_n^k \cdot \omega_n^{n/2} = -\omega_n^k$ while the squared argument is unchanged — the *same* halving-lemma collapse $(\omega_n^{k+n/2})^2 = (\omega_n^k)^2 = \omega_{n/2}^k$ — giving
$$A(\omega_n^{k+n/2}) = A^{[0]}\big(\omega_{n/2}^k\big) - \omega_n^k\, A^{[1]}\big(\omega_{n/2}^k\big) = y^{[0]}_k - \omega_n^k\, y^{[1]}_k.$$
No other values of $A$ are needed: the $n$ evaluation points split into two groups whose squares coincide in pairs, so the two length-$(n/2)$ DFTs supply every required value. Induction on $n$ (base: $\mathrm{DFT}_1(a) = a$) completes the proof. $\blacksquare$

Notice what the lemma bought twice. First, well-foundedness: the children need evaluation at only $n/2$ points, because the parents' $n$ points square down onto them — a different choice of evaluation points would generally produce $2n$ distinct squares and the recursion would *grow*. Second, the butterfly: the two outputs $y_k, y_{k+n/2}$ share both child values, so one complex multiplication $\omega_n^k y^{[1]}_k$ serves both — this pairing is exactly where the factor-of-two savings per level lives, giving $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n \lg n)$.

blocks.heading: Consequences that follow for free
blocks.body: With correctness in hand: (1) the inverse DFT is the same recursion with $\omega_n^{-1}$, because the proof only ever used $\omega_n^{2k} = \omega_{n/2}^k$ and $\omega_n^{n/2} = -1$, both of which hold for the conjugate root $\omega_n^{-1}$ as well; (2) polynomial multiplication follows by the pipeline of Section 30.1 — evaluate at the $2n$ roots of unity, multiply pointwise, interpolate — all three stages $\Theta(n \lg n)$; (3) the same identity powers the convolution theorem of Section 30.3 and every FFT-based signal-processing pipeline built on it.

intro: The recursive FFT hides a beautiful pattern: the leaves of the recursion arrive in *bit-reversed* index order. Unrolling the recursion into loops over stages of butterflies yields the iterative, in-place FFT — the version that actually runs on hardware, with no recursion overhead and no extra memory.
objectives: Compute the bit-reversal permutation and explain why the recursion produces it
Trace ITERATIVE-FFT: stages, blocks, butterflies
Invert the FFT and state the convolution theorem
Explain why the iterative version is the implementation of choice

concepts.statement: For $n = 2^{\lg n}$ a power of two, $\mathrm{REV}_n(k)$ reverses the $\lg n$ bits of $k$: e.g. for $n = 8$ (3 bits) $\mathrm{REV}(001) = 100$, giving the order $0, 4, 2, 6, 1, 5, 3, 7$.
concepts.detail: Where it comes from: each recursion level splits by the *low* bit of the index (even/odd) but keeps halves by the high bit. After $\lg n$ levels, the element at input position $k$ sits in the leaf labeled by $k$'s bits read backwards. The book's BIT-REVERSE-COPY scatters the input into this order first.

concepts.statement: ITERATIVE-FFT: after the bit-reversal copy, loop $s = 1$ to $\lg n$ with block size $m = 2^s$ and root $\omega_m = \omega_n^{n/m}$; within each block, each butterfly at offset $k$ computes $t = \omega_m^k \cdot x[k + m/2]$, then $x[k] \mathrel{+}= t$, $x[k+m/2] \mathrel{-}= t$ — all in place, arrays only.
concepts.detail: Stage $s$ performs exactly the butterflies the recursion's combine step would do at height $s$: the same $\Theta(n \lg n)$ arithmetic with zero function-call overhead and perfect locality within a block.

concepts.statement: The 2-in/2-out gadget $\begin{pmatrix} u' \\ v' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \omega \\ 1 & -\omega \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix}$ — one complex multiply, one add, one subtract. The full FFT is $\frac{n}{2} \lg n$ butterflies arranged in $\lg n$ stages.
concepts.detail: The factor $\omega$ is a *twiddle factor*: at stage $s$, butterfly $k$ of a block uses $\omega_m^k$ — a power of $\omega_8$ for the last stage of an 8-point transform, and so on down.

concepts.term: The inverse FFT and the convolution theorem
concepts.statement: Replacing $\omega$ by $\omega^{-1}$ in every butterfly and dividing the final array by $n$ inverts the transform. **Convolution theorem:** for vectors $a, b$ padded to length $n \ge$ sum of degrees + 1: $a \otimes b = \mathrm{DFT}^{-1}(\mathrm{DFT}(a) \cdot \mathrm{DFT}(b))$ — polynomial multiplication, big-integer multiplication, and signal filtering all in $\Theta(n \lg n)$.
concepts.detail: The pointwise product of transforms is the transform of the coefficient convolution — the identity that Section 30.1's pipeline operationalizes.

concepts.statement: The iterative FFT needs no stack, touches memory in progressively larger strides, and admits vectorization and parallelization (each stage's butterflies are independent — the multithreaded FFT of Chapter 27 is a natural sequel).
concepts.detail: Real implementations precompute twiddle-factor tables once per $n$ and reuse them across transforms — the trig evaluation is more expensive than the butterfly arithmetic itself.

figures.caption: The 8-point iterative FFT as three stages of butterflies ($\lg 8 = 3$). Inputs enter in **bit-reversed order** — $a_0, a_4, a_2, a_6, a_1, a_5, a_3, a_7$ — because each recursion level splits on the low bit while the halves are indexed by the high bit. Straight wires carry the sum output, amber crossings carry the $\omega$-weighted path: each butterfly computes $x_k + \omega_m^k x_{k+m/2}$ and $x_k - \omega_m^k x_{k+m/2}$. Stage 1 uses $\omega_2^0$ (plain subtraction), stage 2 the fourth roots ($\omega_4^0 = 1$, $\omega_4^1 = i$), stage 3 the eighth roots $\omega_8^0 \ldots \omega_8^3$. Outputs emerge in natural order $y_0 \ldots y_7$.

examples.title: Bit-reversal, by hand
examples.problem: Compute the bit-reversal permutation for $n = 8$ and verify where $a_3$ lands.

steps.label: Step 3: Track $a_3$ through the recursion
steps.text: $3 = 011$ is odd, so the first split sends $a_3$ right; its half index $1 = 01$ is odd again — right; then $0$ — left. Path R-R-L: the leaf position is $100_2 = 4$… read the path bits as they accumulate high-to-low: odd, odd, even = $110 = 6$? Careful: each level contributes the *current low bit* of the index — 1, then 1, then 0 — which assemble into the leaf label read as (first-split bit = most significant) $110_2 = 6$.

steps.label: Step 4: Confirm
steps.text: REV(3): $011 \to 110 = 6$ ✓. So $a_3$ is copied to array slot 6 — matching the input column of the figure.

examples.result: BIT-REVERSE-COPY puts $a_k$ into slot $\mathrm{REV}(k)$; the butterfly stages then overwrite the array in place into natural order.

examples.title: Multiplying polynomials with the convolution theorem
examples.problem: Use the pipeline to multiply $A = (1, 2, 3, 4)$ (i.e. $1 + 2x + 3x^2 + 4x^3$) by $B = (0, 1, 0, 0)$ (i.e. $x$).

steps.label: Step 1: Pad
steps.text: The product has degree bound $8 - 1 = 7$? Degrees: $3 + 1 = 4$, so degree bound $5$ suffices — round up to a power of two: 8. Both padded to length 8.

steps.label: Step 2: Transform
steps.text: $y = \mathrm{DFT}_8(a)$: the values of $A$ at all 8th roots of unity; $y' = \mathrm{DFT}_8(b)$: the values of $x$, i.e. $\omega_8^k$ themselves.

steps.label: Step 3: Pointwise multiply
steps.text: $y''_k = y_k \cdot \omega_8^k$ — the values of $A(x) \cdot x$ at the 8th roots (since $(A \cdot B)(\omega_8^k) = A(\omega_8^k) \cdot \omega_8^k$).

steps.label: Step 4: Inverse transform
steps.text: $\mathrm{IDFT}_8(y'')$ returns the coefficients of $x + 2x^2 + 3x^3 + 4x^4$ — the shift by one that multiplication by $x$ performs. Total: three $\Theta(n \lg n)$ transforms and $n$ multiplies.

examples.result: The convolution theorem turns coefficient multiplication into pointwise multiplication — the reason the FFT ends up inside every signal processor and bignum library.

keyTakeaways: Unrolling the recursion: inputs enter in bit-reversed order because levels split on the low bit while halves are indexed by the high bit.
ITERATIVE-FFT: bit-reversal copy, then $\lg n$ stages of $n/2$ butterflies each, twiddle factors $\omega_m^k$ per stage — in place, no recursion.
Inverse FFT: swap $\omega \leftrightarrow \omega^{-1}$, divide by $n$; the same code serves both directions.
Convolution theorem: $\mathrm{DFT}^{-1}(\mathrm{DFT}(a) \cdot \mathrm{DFT}(b))$ multiplies polynomials in $\Theta(n \lg n)$.
$\frac{n}{2} \lg n$ butterflies = the entire arithmetic of an FFT — engineering effort goes to twiddle tables and memory layout.

quiz.q: In the iterative 8-point FFT, the element $a_1$ (binary 001) is first copied to the array slot:
quiz.explanation: REV reverses the 3 bits: 001 becomes 100 = 4 — bit-reversal copy places $a_1$ in slot 4, next to $a_0$.

quiz.q: Stage $s$ of ITERATIVE-FFT uses butterflies of width $m = 2^s$ with twiddle factor for offset $k$:
quiz.explanation: Each stage's butterflies need only the $m$th roots; $\omega_m = \omega_n^{n/m}$, and butterfly $k$ of a block uses $\omega_m^k$ — the smaller roots come for free as powers of the big one.

quiz.q: The convolution theorem states that polynomial multiplication equals:
options: the inverse DFT of the pointwise product of the two DFTs (after padding)
the pointwise product of the two coefficient vectors
the sum of the two transforms
quiz.explanation: Values of the product = products of values: transform both, multiply pointwise, transform back — $\Theta(n \lg n)$ end to end.

quiz.q: The advantage of the iterative FFT over the recursive one is:
options: in-place operation with no recursion overhead — same $\Theta(n \lg n)$ count, but practical speed and locality
it does not need powers of two
quiz.explanation: The butterfly arithmetic is identical; eliminating the call stack, enabling bit-reversal preprocessing and stage-local memory access is what implementations actually gain.

intro: Number theory enters algorithms through one question: what can be computed about the integers when the integers involved are hundreds of digits long? This section assembles the primitive vocabulary — divisibility, the division theorem, common divisors, gcd and lcm — including the single most heavily used fact of the chapter: dividing by $n$ leaves a canonical remainder between $0$ and $n - 1$.
objectives: Apply the definition of divisibility and its closure under integer linear combinations
State the division theorem with its uniqueness clause, including for negative dividends
Compute gcd and lcm from divisor lists and verify the identity $\gcd(a,b) \cdot \mathrm{lcm}(a,b) = ab$

concepts.statement: For integers $d$ and $a$ with $d \ne 0$, we write **$d \mid a$** ($d$ divides $a$) if there is an integer $k$ with $a = kd$; $d$ is then a **divisor** of $a$. Every integer divides $0$, and if $d \mid a$ with $a \ne 0$ then $|d| \le |a|$.
concepts.detail: Divisibility is closed under integer linear combinations: if $d \mid a$ and $d \mid b$, then $d \mid (ax + by)$ for all integers $x$ and $y$ — every common divisor of $a$ and $b$ divides every combination of them. This innocuous-looking fact powers the correctness of Euclid's algorithm (31.2) and the solvability theory of modular equations (31.4).

concepts.statement: For any integer $a$ and any positive integer $n$, there exist **unique** integers $q$ and $r$ such that $$a = qn + r \quad \text{and} \quad 0 \le r < n.$$ The values are $q = \lfloor a/n \rfloor$ (the quotient) and $r = a \bmod n$ (the remainder).
concepts.detail: Uniqueness: if $a = qn + r = q'n + r'$ with both remainders in range, then $n \mid (r - r')$ while $|r - r'| < n$, forcing $r = r'$ (and $q = q'$). Beware negative dividends — $-11 = (-3) \cdot 5 + 4$, so $-11 \bmod 5 = 4$, not $-1$.

concepts.statement: For integers $a$ and $b$ not both zero, **$\gcd(a, b)$** is the largest of their common divisors; for positive $a$ and $b$, **$\mathrm{lcm}(a, b)$** is the smallest positive common multiple. The two are locked together by $$\gcd(a,b) \cdot \mathrm{lcm}(a,b) = ab.$$
concepts.detail: The fundamental theorem of arithmetic — every integer above 1 factors uniquely into primes — makes gcd and lcm look computable by comparing factorizations. The point of this chapter is that gcds can be computed far faster than factorizations: Euclid's algorithm (31.2) never factors anything, which matters because factoring (31.9) is believed intractable.

concepts.statement: Every integer $a > 1$ factors uniquely as a product of primes (up to order): $a = p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_k^{e_k}$. Existence by strong induction on $a$, uniqueness by Euclid's lemma ($p \mid ab$ implies $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$).
concepts.detail: Uniqueness is what makes gcd-by-factorization well defined, but the chapter never factors: EUCLID computes gcds in $O(\beta)$ operations while factoring is believed exponential, which is why RSA is safe.

concepts.statement: The class $[a]_n = \{a + kn : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ collects all integers with remainder $a \bmod n$. There are exactly $n$ classes $[0]_n, \ldots, [n-1]_n$, partitioning $\mathbb{Z}$; Section 31.3 turns them into the ring $\mathbb{Z}_n$.
concepts.detail: The division theorem guarantees each integer lands in exactly one class (its remainder): $[a]_n = [b]_n$ iff $a \equiv b \pmod n$, the vocabulary modular arithmetic runs on.

examples.title: Divisors, gcd, lcm, and a negative division
examples.problem: List the divisors of 30 and 21, read off $\gcd(30, 21)$ and $\mathrm{lcm}(30, 21)$, verify the product identity, and express $a = -11$ under the division theorem with $n = 5$.

steps.label: Divisors of 30
steps.text: Since $30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$, the divisors are $\{1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30\}$ — one per subset of the prime factors.

steps.label: Divisors of 21
steps.text: $21 = 3 \cdot 7$, so the divisors are $\{1, 3, 7, 21\}$.

steps.label: Common divisors
steps.text: The common divisors are $\{1, 3\}$, so $\gcd(30, 21) = 3$. Note $3 = 30 \cdot (-2) + 21 \cdot 3 = -60 + 63$ — the gcd is itself an integer combination, and both common divisors 1 and 3 divide it.

steps.label: lcm and the identity
steps.text: Multiples of 30 first hit a multiple of 21 at $210 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$, so $\mathrm{lcm}(30, 21) = 210$. Check: $\gcd \cdot \mathrm{lcm} = 3 \cdot 210 = 630 = 30 \cdot 21$ ✓.

steps.label: Negative dividend
steps.text: With $a = -11$ and $n = 5$: $q = \lfloor -11/5 \rfloor = -3$ and $r = -11 - (-3)(5) = 4$, so $-11 = (-3) \cdot 5 + 4$ with $0 \le 4 < 5$ — the remainder is 4, never $-1$.

examples.result: $\gcd(30, 21) = 3$ and $\mathrm{lcm}(30, 21) = 210$ with $3 \cdot 210 = 630 = 30 \cdot 21$; and $-11 \bmod 5 = 4$ because the division theorem always lands the remainder in $[0, n)$.

examples.title: Residues mod 6
examples.problem: List the $6$ residue classes mod $6$, place $-11, 30, 21$ in theirs, and verify $\gcd(30,21) = 3$ divides every combination.

steps.label: Combinations
steps.text: $30x+21y$ is always a multiple of $3$: e.g. $30(-2)+21(3) = 3$: common divisors divide every combination, so $\gcd$ does too.

keyTakeaways: The division theorem pins every integer to a unique quotient and remainder $0 \le r < n$ — the foundation on which $\bmod$ is built.
Common divisors are closed under integer combinations, which is why gcds can be computed without ever factoring.
$\gcd(a,b) \cdot \mathrm{lcm}(a,b) = ab$ ties the two central functions of the section together for positive $a, b$.

quiz.q: By the division theorem, what is $-11 \bmod 5$?
quiz.explanation: $-11 = (-3) \cdot 5 + 4$ with $0 \le 4 < 5$; the remainder must always land in the canonical range, even for negative dividends.

quiz.q: If $d \mid a$ and $d \mid b$, which statement is guaranteed?
options: $d$ divides every integer linear combination $ax + by$
quiz.explanation: Closure under combinations: $ax + by$ is a multiple of $d$ whenever $a$ and $b$ are. The others fail (signs are irrelevant, $d$ divides both by assumption, and $a + 1$ need not be a multiple of $d$).

quiz.q: What is $\gcd(30, 21) \cdot \mathrm{lcm}(30, 21)$?
quiz.explanation: The product always equals $ab = 30 \cdot 21 = 630$; here it is $3 \cdot 210$.

intro: Euclid's algorithm is the oldest algorithm still in standard use — about 2,300 years old — and it computes gcds of 1000-digit numbers in microseconds without ever factoring anything. Its correctness rests on one line of algebra, and its running time is governed by the Fibonacci numbers, making it a classic case study in algorithm analysis. The extended version additionally returns the Bézout coefficients that make modular inverses computable.
objectives: Run EUCLID by hand and prove that the common-divisor set never changes
Run EXTENDED-EUCLID and produce Bézout coefficients satisfying $ax + by = \gcd(a, b)$
Use Lamé's theorem to bound the number of recursive calls

concepts.statement: **`EUCLID(a, b)`** computes $\gcd(a,b)$ by recursion: if $b = 0$ return $a$; otherwise return `EUCLID(b, a mod b)`. On $(30, 21)$ it runs $\gcd(30,21) = \gcd(21,9) = \gcd(9,3) = \gcd(3,0) = 3$.
concepts.detail: Each call replaces the pair $(a, b)$ with $(b, a \bmod b)$, and since $0 \le a \bmod b < b$ the second argument strictly shrinks, so the recursion terminates. The total cost is $O(\beta)$ arithmetic operations on $\beta$-bit inputs — exponential speedup over factoring both arguments.

concepts.statement: $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b)$: the pairs $(a, b)$ and $(b, a \bmod b)$ have exactly the same set of common divisors, so the gcd rides the recursion unchanged down to $\gcd(d, 0) = d$.
concepts.detail: Write $a = qb + r$ with $r = a \bmod b$. Any common divisor of $a$ and $b$ divides $r = a - qb$ (a combination); any common divisor of $b$ and $r$ divides $a = qb + r$. The same linear-combination argument shows $\gcd(a,b)$ is the smallest positive value of $ax + by$ — Bézout coefficients always exist.

concepts.statement: If $a > b \ge 1$ and `EUCLID(a, b)` performs $k \ge 1$ recursive calls, then $a \ge F_{k+2}$ and $b \ge F_{k+1}$, where $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ is the Fibonacci sequence. Consequently the number of recursive calls is $O(\lg b)$, and EUCLID costs $O(\beta)$ arithmetic operations (or $O(\beta^3)$ bit operations) on $\beta$-bit inputs.
concepts.detail: The worst case is consecutive Fibonacci numbers: every quotient is 1 and the arguments shrink as slowly as the recursion permits (two steps of EUCLID cost at least one Fibonacci step of size). Since $F_k \approx \varphi^k / \sqrt{5}$, inverting gives $k = O(\lg b)$ — EUCLID(5, 3), on the tightest small input, already needs 3 calls.

concepts.statement: EXTENDED-EUCLID($a,b$) returns $(d,x,y)$ with $d = \gcd(a,b) = ax+by$: if $b = 0$ return $(a,1,0)$; else recurse on $(b, a \bmod b)$ to get $(d,x',y')$ and return $(d, y', x'-\lfloor a/b \rfloor y')$. Same $O(\lg b)$ calls as EUCLID.
concepts.detail: The unwinding uses $a = qb+r$: $d = x'b+y'r = y'a+(x'-qy')b$. Section 31.4 reads $x \bmod n$ as the modular inverse when $d = 1$.

concepts.statement: For any $a,b$ not both zero there exist integers $x,y$ with $ax+by = \gcd(a,b)$, and $\gcd(a,b)$ is the smallest positive such combination. EXTENDED-EUCLID constructs the coefficients; the remainder invariant proves no smaller positive combination exists.
concepts.detail: Corollary: $\gcd(a,n) = 1$ iff $a$ has an inverse mod $n$ (take $ax+ny = 1$: $ax \equiv 1$). RSA's $d = e^{-1} \bmod \varphi(n)$ is a Bézout coefficient.
