examples.title: A complete toy RSA run: $n = 143$, $e = 7$, $d = 103$
examples.problem: With $p = 11$, $q = 13$: generate the keys, encrypt $M = 9$, and decrypt the ciphertext using the CRT decomposition a real implementation would use.

steps.label: Key generation
steps.text: $n = 11 \cdot 13 = 143$; $\varphi(n) = 10 \cdot 12 = 120$. Pick $e = 7$ ($\gcd(7, 120) = 1$). Since $7 \cdot 103 = 721 = 6 \cdot 120 + 1$, extended Euclid gives $d = 103$. Public: $(7, 143)$; secret: $103$.

steps.label: Encrypt $M = 9$
steps.text: By repeated squaring: $9^2 = 81$; $9^4 = 6561 \equiv 126$; then $9^7 = 9^4 \cdot 9^2 \cdot 9 \equiv 126 \cdot 81 = 10206 \equiv 53$, and $53 \cdot 9 = 477 \equiv 48 \pmod{143}$. The ciphertext is $C = 48$.

steps.label: Decrypt — split by the CRT
steps.text: Work modulo each prime: $48 \equiv 4 \pmod{11}$ and $48 \equiv 9 \pmod{13}$. Exponents reduce modulo $p - 1$ and $q - 1$ (Fermat): $103 \equiv 3 \pmod{10}$ and $103 \equiv 7 \pmod{12}$.

steps.label: Exponentiate per prime
steps.text: Mod 11: $4^3 = 64 \equiv 9$. Mod 13: $9^7 = 9^4 \cdot 9^2 \cdot 9$, and $9^2 = 81 \equiv 3$, $9^4 \equiv 9$, so $9^7 \equiv 9 \cdot 3 \cdot 9 = 243 \equiv 9 \pmod{13}$.

steps.label: Recombine
steps.text: We need $x \equiv 9 \pmod{11}$ and $x \equiv 9 \pmod{13}$; the CRT (coprime moduli) says the unique solution modulo 143 is exactly $x = 9$ — the original message.

examples.result: Ciphertext $C = 48$; decryption returns $M = 9$ ✓. Note the decrypt step never computed $48^{103}$ directly — it worked modulo 11 and 13 with reduced exponents, precisely how production RSA decryption is organized.

examples.title: Decrypting $C = 48$ with CRT speedup
examples.problem: With $p = 11, q = 13, e = 7, d = 103$, decrypt $C = 48$ via $M = C^d \bmod 143$ using CRT (mod $p$ and mod $q$ separately).

steps.label: Mod $11$
steps.text: $48 \equiv 4$: $4^3 = 64 \equiv 9 \pmod{11}$ (since $55$): $M \equiv 9$.

steps.label: Mod $13$
steps.text: $48 \equiv 9$: $9^2 = 81 \equiv 3$, $9^4 \equiv 9$, $9^7 = 9^4\cdot 9^2\cdot 9 \equiv 9\cdot 3\cdot 9 = 243 \equiv 9 \pmod{13}$: $M \equiv 9$.

steps.label: Combine
steps.text: $M \equiv 9$ both sides: CRT gives $M = 9$ mod $143$ (numbers $\equiv 9$ mod $11$ and $13$ are $9, \ldots$; $9 < 143$ so $M = 9$). Two small exponentiations beat one $103$rd power.

examples.result: $M = 9$: CRT decryption does $O(\lg d_p)+O(\lg d_q)$ work on half-size moduli, $\approx 4\times$ faster than direct $C^d$.

keyTakeaways: Key generation is: two primes, $n = pq$, $\varphi(n) = (p-1)(q-1)$, a coprime $e$, and $d = e^{-1} \bmod \varphi(n)$ from extended Euclid.
Encryption and decryption are both single MODULAR-EXPONENTIATION calls; correctness for all messages needs Euler plus the CRT (depth tier).
Recovering $d$ from $(e, n)$ requires $\varphi(n)$, and knowing $\varphi(n)$ is equivalent to factoring $n$ — RSA's security transfers to a 2000-year-old problem.

quiz.q: For $n = 143 = 11 \cdot 13$, what is $\varphi(n)$?
quiz.explanation: $\varphi(pq) = (p-1)(q-1) = 10 \cdot 12 = 120$ — both primes minus one, multiplied.

quiz.q: The secret exponent $d$ is chosen so that:
options: $d$ is arbitrary, since it is never published
quiz.explanation: $d$ is the inverse of $e$ modulo $\varphi(n) = (p-1)(q-1)$, computed by extended Euclid: in the toy run $7 \cdot 103 = 6 \cdot 120 + 1$.

quiz.q: Why can an attacker not simply compute $d$ from the public $(e, n)$?
options: $d$ is transmitted only over secure channels, so it is never computable
Computing $d$ requires $\varphi(n)$, and knowing $\varphi(n)$ is equivalent to factoring $n$
$d$ is protected by a collision-resistant hash of $e$
$n$ is too large for modular exponentiation to finish
quiz.explanation: From $\varphi(n)$ one gets $p + q = n - \varphi(n) + 1$, and $p, q$ are the roots of $x^2 - (p+q)x + n$ — so $\varphi(n)$ and the factorization are interchangeable secrets.

depth.title: Why RSA is correct: Euler's theorem plus the Chinese remainder theorem

blocks.heading: What must be proved
blocks.body: RSA must decrypt **every** message, not just the convenient ones. We need $M^{ed} \equiv M \pmod{n}$ for all $M \in \mathbb{Z}_n$, where $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\varphi(n)}$, say $ed = 1 + k\varphi(n)$. The easy route — Euler's theorem — only applies when $\gcd(M, n) = 1$, yet messages divisible by $p$ or by $q$ are legal inputs a correct cryptosystem cannot ignore. The full proof uses Euler for the coprime case and then the CRT (with Fermat) to extend to every message without exception.

blocks.heading: Euler's theorem
blocks.body: If $n \ge 1$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, then $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$.

blocks.heading: Euler's theorem via the group $\mathbb{Z}_n^*$
blocks.body: The residues coprime to $n$ form the multiplicative group $\mathbb{Z}_n^*$ of order $\varphi(n)$; list its elements $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{\varphi(n)}$. Multiplication by the unit $a$ **permutes** the group: if $ax_i \equiv ax_j \pmod n$, then canceling the invertible $a$ (extended Euclid supplies $a^{-1}$) gives $x_i \equiv x_j$. Multiplying out the two listings of the same elements, $$\prod_i x_i \equiv \prod_i (a x_i) \equiv a^{\varphi(n)} \prod_i x_i \pmod{n},$$ and since $\prod_i x_i$ is itself a unit it may be canceled from both sides, leaving $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n$. For $n = p$ prime, $\varphi(p) = p - 1$ and this is exactly Fermat's little theorem.

blocks.heading: The coprime case
blocks.body: Assume $\gcd(M, n) = 1$ with $n = pq$. Then $$M^{ed} = M^{1 + k\varphi(n)} = M \cdot \left(M^{\varphi(n)}\right)^{k} \equiv M \cdot 1^{k} = M \pmod{n},$$ exactly as Euler promises. This covers every message except the $p + q - 1$ residue classes with $p \mid M$ or $q \mid M$ — a vanishing fraction of $\mathbb{Z}_n$, but a real one.

blocks.heading: All messages, via the CRT
blocks.body: Work one prime at a time. Modulo $p$: if $p \mid M$ then $M^{ed}$ and $M$ are both $\equiv 0$, so the claim holds trivially. Otherwise Fermat gives $M^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$, and since $\varphi(n) = (p-1)(q-1)$ is a multiple of $p - 1$, $$M^{ed} = M^{1 + k\varphi(n)} = M \cdot \left(M^{p-1}\right)^{k(q-1)} \equiv M \pmod p.$$ The same argument modulo $q$ gives $M^{ed} \equiv M \pmod q$. Now the CRT applies to the pair of congruences $x \equiv M \pmod p$, $x \equiv M \pmod q$: because $\gcd(p,q) = 1$, the common solution is unique modulo $pq = n$, and $x = M$ is visibly a solution — hence $M^{ed} \equiv M \pmod{n}$ for **every** message, coprime or not.

blocks.heading: CRT-based decryption in practice
blocks.body: Real implementations run decryption exactly along these lines — one prime at a time. They precompute $d_p = d \bmod (p-1)$ and $d_q = d \bmod (q-1)$, exponentiate the ciphertext modulo $p$ and modulo $q$ separately with these half-size exponents and moduli, and recombine the two residues with the CRT. The toy run did precisely that: $48^{103} \equiv 4^{3} \equiv 9 \pmod{11}$ and $48^{103} \equiv 9^{7} \equiv 9 \pmod{13}$ recombine to $M = 9$ modulo 143. Halving the modulus quarters each multiplication's cost — an overall speedup of about a factor of 4, which is why every production RSA decryption is CRT-based.

blocks.heading: Why the two-branch proof matters
blocks.body: A tempting one-line proof — '$M^{ed} = M \cdot (M^{\varphi(n)})^k \equiv M$ by Euler' — silently assumes $\gcd(M, n) = 1$. For random 1024-bit messages the probability of hitting a multiple of $p$ or $q$ is about $2^{-510}$: vanishingly unlikely, but never zero. A cryptosystem that returns garbage on a measure-zero set of inputs is simply buggy; this is precisely why CLRS carries the CRT into the RSA section, and the same mod-$p$-and-mod-$q$ discipline is what lets implementations certify correctness for every ciphertext they will ever see.

intro: RSA needs primes, and it needs them fast. Trial division is hopeless at cryptographic sizes, and the obvious shortcut — Fermat's little theorem — has systematic impostors: Carmichael numbers such as 561. Miller-Rabin repairs the flaw by hunting nontrivial square roots of 1, yielding a randomized test that errs with probability at most $2^{-s}$ and never errs when it says 'composite'.
objectives: Define pseudoprimes and Carmichael numbers and explain why Fermat testing must fail
Trace WITNESS and MILLER-RABIN, including the nontrivial-square-root test
Analyze the error probability and the cost of generating a random $\beta$-bit prime

concepts.statement: A composite $n$ that satisfies $a^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ is a **pseudoprime to base $a$**. A **Carmichael number** is a composite that passes this Fermat test for *every* base coprime to it — the smallest is $561 = 3 \cdot 11 \cdot 17$, and infinitely many exist.
concepts.detail: The Fermat-based test PSEUDOPRIME picks a base $a$ and answers 'composite' if $a^{n-1} \not\equiv 1$ (a certain verdict — the violated congruence is a certificate) and 'prime' otherwise (possibly wrong). Carmichael numbers make the error systematic: no amount of base selection repairs a Fermat test.

concepts.statement: Write $n - 1 = 2^t u$ with $u$ odd. `WITNESS(a, n)` computes the chain $x_0 = a^u \bmod n$, $x_i = x_{i-1}^2 \bmod n$ for $i = 1, \ldots, t$, and proves compositeness if (i) some $x_i = 1$ while $x_{i-1} \notin \{1, n-1\}$ — a **nontrivial square root of 1**, impossible when $n$ is prime — or (ii) $x_t \ne 1$ (a Fermat violation). `MILLER-RABIN(n, s)` tests $s$ independent random bases, answering 'composite' on the first witness and 'prime' otherwise.
concepts.detail: Why (i) is decisive: $x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod p$ for prime $p$ means $p \mid (x-1)(x+1)$, and a prime dividing a product divides a factor, so $x \equiv \pm 1 \pmod p$. Each round detects any given composite with probability at least $1/2$, so $s$ rounds err with probability at most $2^{-s}$ — a one-sided error: 'composite' verdicts are always correct (the witness certifies it); only 'prime' can ever be wrong.

concepts.statement: To build a random $\beta$-bit prime: draw a random $\beta$-bit odd integer, run `MILLER-RABIN(n, s)` with $s$ large enough (50 makes the error $2^{-50}$), and retry on failure. By the prime number theorem the density of primes near $2^{\beta}$ is about $1/(\beta \ln 2)$, so an odd candidate succeeds with probability $\approx 2/(\beta \ln 2)$ — an expected $(\ln 2^{\beta})/2$ trials, about 177 for $\beta = 512$.
concepts.detail: Key generation is randomized but fast: roughly 177 Miller-Rabin runs for a 512-bit prime, each polynomial. 'Probably prime' is good enough — an error probability of $2^{-50}$ per key sits far below hardware failure rates.

concepts.statement: Modulo prime $p$, $x^2 \equiv 1$ forces $x \equiv \pm 1$ (field: $(x-1)(x+1) \equiv 0$ implies a factor is $0$). A solution $x \not\equiv \pm 1$ mod $n$ is a nontrivial square root of $1$ and witnesses compositeness: primes have none, so finding one proves $n$ composite.
concepts.detail: WITNESS squares $x_0 = a^d$ through $x_{i} = x_{i-1}^2$ toward $a^{n-1}$; hitting $1$ from $x \ne \pm 1$ is the nontrivial root that Fermat's test misses on Carmichael numbers like $561$.

concepts.statement: MILLER-RABIN with $s$ random bases errs (says prime on composite) with probability at most $2^{-s}$: at most $1/4$ of bases are non-witnesses for any composite $n$ (at most $1/2$ for most), so $s$ independent trials drive error exponentially low while never erring on prime or on composite-with-witness.
concepts.detail: One-sided error (composites may slip, primes never miscalled) plus $O(s\beta^3)$ cost: $s = 50$ gives $2^{-50}$ error, negligible beside hardware failure, which is why crypto libraries test with dozens of bases.

examples.title: WITNESS(7, 561): catching the smallest Carmichael number
examples.problem: Run the Miller-Rabin witness test with base $a = 7$ on $n = 561 = 3 \cdot 11 \cdot 17$, which Section 31.6 showed satisfies $7^{560} \equiv 1 \pmod{561}$.

steps.label: Start of the chain
steps.text: $x_0 = 7^{35} \bmod 561$. From 31.6's square table, $7^{35} = 7^{32} \cdot 7^2 \cdot 7 \equiv 511 \cdot 49 \cdot 7 \equiv 355 \cdot 7 = 2485 \equiv 241 \pmod{561}$.

steps.label: The verdict
steps.text: $x_4 = 1$ with predecessor $x_3 = 67 \notin \{1, 560\}$: 67 is a nontrivial square root of 1 modulo 561 — impossible for a prime. WITNESS returns TRUE: 561 is composite.

steps.label: What Fermat alone saw
steps.text: The chain ends at 1, so the Fermat test $7^{560} \bmod 561 = 1$ reports 'prime'. The intermediate structure — the square root of 1 at position 3 — is exactly the extra evidence Miller-Rabin extracts.

examples.result: The chain $241 \to 298 \to 166 \to 67 \to 1$ exposes $67^2 \equiv 1$ with $67 \not\equiv \pm 1$, proving 561 composite despite its perfect Fermat behavior toward base 7.

examples.title: Bases that spare $561$ and bases that catch it
examples.problem: Fermat base $2$ spares Carmichael $561$ ($2^{560} \equiv 1$); show Miller-Rabin base $7$ catches it via a nontrivial root.

steps.label: Chain
steps.text: $7^{35} \equiv 263$? Computed by repeated squaring: $263^2 = 69169 \equiv 166$, $166^2 \equiv 67$, $67^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{561}$: hits $1$ from $67 \ne \pm 1$ ($\pm 1 = 1,560$).

steps.label: Witness
steps.text: $67^2 \equiv 1$ with $67 \not\equiv \pm 1$: nontrivial square root of $1$ mod $561$: WITNESS returns TRUE (composite).

steps.label: Versus Fermat
steps.text: Final $7^{560} \equiv 1$ would pass Fermat; Miller-Rabin inspects the chain, not just the endpoint, so Carmichael numbers cannot hide.

examples.result: Base $7$ witnesses $561$ via $67^2 \equiv 1$, $67 \ne \pm 1$: Miller-Rabin catches what Fermat misses.

keyTakeaways: Fermat's $a^{n-1} \equiv 1$ is necessary but not sufficient for primality; Carmichael numbers such as $561 = 3 \cdot 11 \cdot 17$ defeat it for every coprime base.
Miller-Rabin adds the nontrivial-square-root-of-1 test: each round catches any composite with probability $\ge 1/2$, and a 'composite' verdict is always correct.
$s$ rounds give error $\le 2^{-s}$; with about $\ln 2^{\beta}/2$ odd candidates per $\beta$-bit prime, key generation is randomized but fast.

quiz.q: The Fermat test with base 7 is run on $n = 561$. What does it report?
options: prime, since $7^{560} \equiv 1 \pmod{561}$ — 561 is a pseudoprime to base 7
quiz.explanation: $7^{560} \bmod 561 = 1$ was computed in 31.6, so the Fermat test is fooled: 561 is composite ($3 \cdot 11 \cdot 17$) yet passes — indeed it passes for every coprime base, being Carmichael.

quiz.q: In the trace of WITNESS(7, 561) the chain is $x_0 \ldots x_4 = 241, 298, 166, 67, 1$. Why does this prove 561 composite?
options: $67$ squares to 1 but is neither 1 nor 560 — a nontrivial square root of 1, impossible modulo a prime
quiz.explanation: $x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod p$ forces $x \equiv \pm 1$ for prime $p$ (since $p \mid (x-1)(x+1)$); 67 is neither, so the modulus cannot be prime.

quiz.q: MILLER-RABIN(n, s) declares $n$ prime after $s$ independent rounds find no witness. The probability that a composite $n$ survives is at most:
quiz.explanation: Each random round catches a composite with probability at least $1/2$, so $s$ rounds leave an escape probability of at most $2^{-s}$ — one-sided: a 'composite' verdict is always correct.

intro: The final pillar: given a composite $n$, find a nontrivial factor. The assumed intractability of this problem — not of primality, not of gcd — is what stands between RSA's public keys and its secrets. Pollard's rho heuristic factors medium-size numbers in about $n^{1/4}$ operations by walking a rho-shaped path through the residues and waiting for a birthday collision.
objectives: Explain why trial division is exponential in the bit length of $n$
Trace POLLARD-RHO, including the role of Floyd-style cycle detection
State the factorization difficulty assumption and its role in RSA's security

concepts.statement: Testing $n$ for divisibility by $2, 3, \ldots, \lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor$ finds any factor, but costs $\Theta(\sqrt{n}) = \Theta(2^{\beta/2})$ divisions on a $\beta$-bit input — exponential in the input length. Finding factors is a different game from recognizing primes.
concepts.detail: Primality, remarkably, is provably in P — the deterministic AKS algorithm (2002) — and practically fast via Miller-Rabin, which is why generating RSA keys takes milliseconds. Factoring the resulting modulus is the part believed intractable; that asymmetry is the whole of public-key cryptography.

concepts.statement: **`POLLARD-RHO(n)`** iterates $x_{i+1} = (x_i^2 - 1) \bmod n$ from a random seed, keeping a saved value $y$ that is re-anchored to $x_k$ whenever $i$ reaches a power of 2 (Floyd-style cycle detection). At each step it computes $d = \gcd(y - x_i, n)$; if $1 < d < n$, a nontrivial factor is found. The iteration walks a **rho-shaped** trajectory — a tail into a cycle — modulo any prime factor $p$.
concepts.detail: Once two iterates collide modulo $p$ (their difference is divisible by $p$) without colliding modulo $n$, the gcd splits off exactly $p$. The birthday paradox governs the wait: collisions among $p$ residues appear after about $\sqrt{p}$ steps, so the expected cost is $O(\sqrt{p}) \le O(n^{1/4})$ arithmetic operations for the smallest factor $p$ — a heuristic analysis (the iteration is not truly random) that matches practice superbly.

concepts.statement: No polynomial-time classical algorithm for factoring is known, despite centuries of work; the best known methods are subexponential but superpolynomial in the bit length. RSA's practical security rests on this difficulty assumption — and a large-scale quantum computer would shatter it, since **Shor's algorithm** factors in polynomial time.
concepts.detail: The chain of custody for RSA's security: recovering messages at scale seems to require $d$; $d$ requires $\varphi(n)$; $\varphi(n)$ is equivalent to factoring $n$. The assumption is therefore about a 2000-year-old number-theory problem rather than about the cipher's design — which is exactly why the assumption is respected.

concepts.statement: For prime divisor $p$ of $n$, a random walk modulo $p$ repeats with constant probability after $\Theta(\sqrt p)$ steps (birthday paradox: $k$ samples from $p$ collide with probability $\approx k^2/2p$). POLLARD-RHO's iterates mod $n$ project to such a walk mod $p$, so $\gcd(|x_i-x_j|, n)$ reveals $p$ in $O(\sqrt p) = O(n^{1/4})$ expected steps for balanced $n$.
concepts.detail: Heuristic: $f(x) = x^2+c$ behaves pseudorandomly mod $p$; Floyd detects the repeat with $O(1)$ memory. Worst case $p \approx n$ (prime input) costs $O(\sqrt n)$, which is why rho is a factoring heuristic, not a primality test.

concepts.statement: Tortoise $x_{i+1} = f(x_i)$ and hare $y_{i+1} = f(f(y_i))$ meet iff the sequence cycles; POLLARD-RHO checks $d = \gcd(|x_i-y_i|, n)$ each step: $d = 1$ continue, $1 < d < n$ factor found, $d = n$ restart with new $c$. $O(1)$ memory versus $O(\sqrt p)$ stored pairs.
concepts.detail: Same trick as linked-list cycle detection (Exercise in Chapter 10): two pointers at speeds $1,2$ meet in $O(\mu+\lambda)$ steps ($\mu$ tail, $\lambda$ cycle), here applied to residues mod $p$ hidden inside residues mod $n$.

examples.title: POLLARD-RHO factors $1387 = 19 \cdot 73$
examples.problem: Run POLLARD-RHO on $n = 1387$ with seed $x_1 = 2$ and iteration $x_{i+1} = (x_i^2 - 1) \bmod n$, listing the sequence and the gcd test at each step.

steps.label: Initialize
steps.text: $x_1 = y = 2$ and $k = 2$ (the saved value re-anchors at every power-of-two index). Hidden from the algorithm: $1387 = 19 \cdot 73$.

steps.label: The hit
steps.text: $i=7$: $\gcd(63 - 177, 1387) = \gcd(114, 1387) = 19$ — since $114 = 6 \cdot 19$ and 73 divides neither. A nontrivial factor.

examples.result: After seven iterations POLLARD-RHO returns 19, and $1387 = 19 \cdot 73$. The saved value and the current iterate collided modulo 19 — $63 \equiv 177 \equiv 6 \pmod{19}$ — without being congruent modulo $n$ itself, so $\gcd(63 - 177, 1387) = \gcd(114, 1387)$ split off exactly the factor 19.

examples.title: Rho walk on $n = 91$
examples.problem: POLLARD-RHO on $n = 91 = 7\cdot 13$ with $f(x) = x^2+1$, $x_0 = 2$. Show the first $\gcd > 1$.

steps.label: Hare
steps.text: Hare moves twice: $y_1 = x_2 = 26$, $y_2 = x_4 = 54$.

steps.label: GCDs
steps.text: $|x_1-y_1| = |5-26| = 21$: $\gcd(21,91) = 7$ ✓ factor found at step $1$ (lucky: $5 \equiv 26 \pmod 7$ birthday collision mod $7$).

steps.label: Split
steps.text: $91/7 = 13$: both prime, done. Had $d = 1$ we would continue; $d = 91$ would restart with new $c$.

examples.result: Factor $7$ at the first check ($|5-26| = 21$, $\gcd = 7$); cofactor $13$: rho needs $O(\sqrt 7)$ steps here, not $O(91)$ trial divisions.

keyTakeaways: Trial division costs $\Theta(2^{\beta/2})$ on $\beta$-bit inputs — exponential; primality is in P but factoring is believed not to be.
Pollard's rho walks a tail-plus-cycle ('ρ') path and factors via $\gcd(y - x_i, n)$ once a collision occurs modulo a prime factor — expected $O(\sqrt{p})$ steps.
RSA's security chain — message to $d$ to $\varphi(n)$ to factorization — rests entirely on the factorization difficulty assumption; Shor's quantum algorithm is the known exception.

quiz.q: Trial division on a $\beta$-bit integer $n$ costs on the order of:
quiz.explanation: It tests divisors up to $\sqrt{n}$, and $\sqrt{n} = \sqrt{2^{\beta}} = 2^{\beta/2}$ — exponential in the input length, unlike primality testing.

quiz.q: In POLLARD-RHO, a nontrivial factor of $n$ is announced when:
options: $x_i$ equals the saved value $y$ exactly, modulo $n$
$\gcd(y - x_i, n)$ comes out strictly between 1 and $n$
quiz.explanation: The gcd is divisible by $p$ (a collision occurred modulo the factor $p$) but not by all of $n$, so it splits $n$. An exact collision modulo $n$ gives $\gcd = n$ — the failure case that triggers a restart.

quiz.q: The expected number of POLLARD-RHO iterations to find the smallest prime factor $p$ of $n$ is:
quiz.explanation: The birthday paradox: among $p$ residues a collision appears after about $\sqrt{p}$ steps — at most $n^{1/4}$ when $p \approx \sqrt{n}$.

intro: Given a pattern $P[1..m]$ and a text $T[1..n]$, string matching asks for every shift at which the pattern occurs in the text. The naive algorithm simply tries all $n - m + 1$ shifts, comparing character by character — a $\Theta((n-m+1)m)$ brute force in the worst case. This section fixes the notation the whole chapter uses, analyzes the brute force exactly, and names the wasted work that Rabin–Karp, finite automata and KMP each eliminate in a different way.
objectives: Define valid shifts and count them: exactly $n - m + 1$ candidate positions
Analyze NAIVE-STRING-MATCHER and exhibit inputs that attain the $\Theta((n-m+1)m)$ worst case
Explain what partial-match information the brute force throws away at every failed shift

concepts.statement: Given a text $T[1..n]$ and a pattern $P[1..m]$ with $m \le n$, both strings over a common finite alphabet $\Sigma$ of size $d$, find **all valid shifts**: the values $s \in \{0, 1, \ldots, n-m\}$ such that $$T[s+1..s+m] = P[1..m],$$ i.e. the pattern equals the length-$m$ substring of the text starting at position $s+1$. Each valid shift is an **occurrence** of $P$ in $T$. There are exactly $n - m + 1$ possible shifts, from $0$ to $n - m$.
concepts.detail: The chapter measures algorithms by preprocessing time (before seeing the text) plus matching time; an algorithm that reports overlapping occurrences must not restart after each hit.

concepts.statement: For each shift $s = 0, 1, \ldots, n-m$ in turn, compare $T[s+1], T[s+2], \ldots$ against $P[1], P[2], \ldots$ left to right, stopping at the first mismatch; if all $m$ characters agree, report the occurrence at shift $s$ and move to $s+1$. No preprocessing is needed, and every shift is examined independently of every other.
concepts.detail: The inner comparison loop costs between 1 and $m$ character comparisons per shift, depending on where (or whether) the first mismatch appears.

concepts.statement: The naive string matcher takes $\Theta((n-m+1)m)$ time in the worst case. **Upper bound:** each of the $n-m+1$ shifts performs at most $m$ comparisons. **Tightness:** with $P = a^m$ and $T = a^n$ over $\Sigma = \{a, b\}$, every one of the $n-m+1$ shifts matches all $m$ characters, so the bound is attained exactly. When $m = \Theta(n)$ — say $m = n/2$ — this is quadratic.
concepts.detail: Even patterns that never occur can force the worst case: $P = a^{m-1}b$ inside $T = a^n$ fails at the last character of every shift, costing $m$ comparisons each and finding nothing.

concepts.statement: When a shift fails after $j$ matched characters, the matcher has just **learned** the text block $T[s+1..s+j]$ — it equals $P[1..j]$ — yet the next shift re-compares $T[s+2..s+j]$ against $P[1..j-1]$ from scratch, as if nothing had been discovered. The brute force remembers nothing between shifts.
concepts.detail: Every algorithm in the rest of this chapter is a different answer to one question: how much of this discarded partial-match information can be carried forward, and at what cost?

concepts.statement: With $|T| = n$, $|P| = m$, shifts $s = 0..n-m$ number $n-m+1$: $s$ is valid iff $T[s+1..s+m] = P[1..m]$. The naive matcher tries all $n-m+1$ shifts with up to $m$ comparisons each, hence $\Theta((n-m+1)m)$ worst case.
concepts.detail: Edge cases: $m > n$ gives zero shifts (no match); $m = 0$ matches everywhere by convention. Counting shifts first prevents the off-by-one that drops the last alignment.

examples.title: Counting the brute force's comparisons
examples.problem: Run the naive matcher twice with $m = 4$: (a) $P = aaab$ in $T = aaaaaaa$ ($n = 7$); (b) $P = abab$ in $T = abababab$ ($n = 8$). Count the character comparisons and the occurrences.

steps.label: Step 1: The worst case (a)
steps.text: Each shift compares a, a, a successfully and then fails on the fourth character ($b$ vs $a$), so every shift costs exactly 4 comparisons. There are $n - m + 1 = 7 - 4 + 1 = 4$ shifts, giving $4 \cdot 4 = 16$ comparisons — the maximum $(n-m+1)m$ — and zero occurrences.

steps.label: Step 2: A luckier instance (b)
steps.text: The shifts $s = 0, 2, 4$ match fully (4 comparisons each), while $s = 1, 3$ fail on the very first character ($b$ vs $a$), costing 1 each. Total: $4 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 4 = 14$ comparisons against the worst-case ceiling of $5 \cdot 4 = 20$.

steps.label: Step 3: Where the waste sits
steps.text: In (a) the three matched $a$ characters at shift $s$ are re-matched as a prefix at shift $s+1$ and re-matched again at $s+2$ — the same text characters are compared $m$ times each. In (b) the mismatch appears early, so little is wasted; the cost of the brute force is wildly instance-dependent.

steps.label: Step 4: The takeaway
steps.text: Both searches use the same algorithm, yet 16 of 16 possible comparisons are wasted work in (a) while (b) runs near the $n + m$ information-theoretic floor. Worst-case analysis protects us against (a); the next three sections design it away.

examples.result: (a) 16 comparisons, no occurrences — the worst case $(n-m+1)m$ is attained. (b) 14 comparisons, occurrences at shifts $s = 0, 2, 4$.

examples.title: Worst case $a^{n-1}b$ versus $a^m$
examples.problem: Text $T = a^{10}$ ($10$ a's), pattern $P = a^4b$ ($m = 5$). Count NAIVE-STRING-MATCHER comparisons.

steps.label: Per shift
steps.text: Each shift matches $4$ a's then fails on $b$ vs $a$: $5$ comparisons per shift.

steps.label: Total
steps.text: $6 \times 5 = 30 = (n-m+1)m$: worst case attained because every shift nearly matches.

steps.label: Versus KMP
steps.text: KMP scans once ($\Theta(n) = 10$ steps) via $\pi$: the $24$ wasted re-comparisons of $a$'s are what $\pi$ and $\delta$ memoize.

examples.result: $30$ comparisons, $\Theta((n-m+1)m)$: near-misses on every shift realize the brute-force worst case.

keyTakeaways: String matching = finding all valid shifts $s \in \{0, \ldots, n-m\}$; there are exactly $n - m + 1$ candidates.
The brute force is $\Theta((n-m+1)m)$ worst case — quadratic when $m$ is a constant fraction of $n$.
Every failed shift reveals $m$ text characters that the next shift re-reads from scratch; carrying that information forward is the entire subject of 32.2–32.4.

quiz.q: A pattern of length 5 is sought in a text of length 100. How many shifts does any correct matcher have to consider?
quiz.explanation: The valid shifts range over $0 \le s \le n - m$, which is $100 - 5 + 1 = 96$ candidate positions — one more than the naive difference $n - m$.

quiz.q: The worst-case running time of the naive matcher is:
quiz.explanation: Shifts times per-shift cost: $(n-m+1)$ shifts at up to $m$ comparisons each. $\Theta(nm)$ overstates the truth when $m$ is close to $n$: with $m = n$ there is a single shift costing $m = n$, not $n^2$.

quiz.q: Which input attains the worst-case number of comparisons (with the pattern never necessarily occurring)?
quiz.explanation: All-$a$ inputs make every shift match all $m$ characters. A pattern starting with $b$ fails at the first character (1 comparison per shift); $ab$ against all $a$ text fails immediately; the alternating case mismatches by the second character.

quiz.q: The inefficiency of the naive matcher is best described as:
options: it uses $O(m)$ extra memory per shift
it re-examines text characters that earlier shifts have already matched
it must sort the pattern before searching
it tries shifts in right-to-left order
quiz.explanation: A failed shift has already identified $T[s+1..s+j] = P[1..j]$, but the next shift re-compares those same text characters against the pattern prefix as if nothing were known — the information is discarded.

intro: Rabin–Karp attacks the per-shift cost with arithmetic. It hashes each $m$-character window of the text to a single number modulo a prime $q$ and compares characters only when two hashes agree. The key is a rolling update that computes the next window's hash from the current one in $O(1)$, so all $n - m + 1$ fingerprints cost only $\Theta(n)$. The price of working modulo $q$ is the spurious hit — a hash collision that must be verified character by character.
objectives: Compute the rolling-hash update and the multiplier $h = d^{m-1} \bmod q$
Define spurious hits and apply the verify-on-hit discipline
Derive the expected running time and explain the choice of the prime $q$

concepts.statement: View a length-$m$ string over an alphabet of size $d = |\Sigma|$ as the digits of a base-$d$ integer read left to right. The pattern's **fingerprint** is that number reduced modulo a prime $q$: $$p = \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{m} P[i]\, d^{m-i}\Bigr) \bmod q,$$ and similarly $t_s$ is the value of the window $T[s+1..s+m]$ mod $q$. Preprocessing computes $p$ and the initial window value $t_0$ in $\Theta(m)$ by Horner-style evaluation.
concepts.detail: Comparing the full integers would cost $\Theta(m)$ per window — no better than the naive matcher. Reducing mod $q$ keeps every value in one machine word, so comparisons and arithmetic are $O(1)$.

concepts.statement: Let $h = d^{m-1} \bmod q$, the place value of the window's leading digit. Then for $s = 0, 1, \ldots, n-m-1$: $$t_{s+1} = \bigl(d\,(t_s - T[s+1]\,h) + T[s+m+1]\bigr) \bmod q.$$ Subtract the leading digit times its place value, multiply by $d$ (shifting all remaining digits left), and add the new trailing digit. Each update is a constant number of word operations, so all $n - m + 1$ window hashes are computed in $\Theta(n - m + 1)$ total.
concepts.detail: Because $t_s - T[s+1]h$ can be negative, implementations add a multiple of $q$ before reducing to stay nonnegative — the congruence is unaffected.

concepts.statement: A shift $s$ is a **hit** when $t_s \equiv p \pmod q$. A hit is **valid** if $T[s+1..s+m] = P$ and **spurious** otherwise: distinct strings can share a residue mod $q$. Therefore the algorithm verifies every hit character by character in $O(m)$ before reporting it; the hash test is a filter, never a proof.
concepts.detail: If verification were skipped, Rabin–Karp would report false occurrences whenever two different windows collided mod $q$ — which happens for any fixed $q$ on adversarial inputs.

concepts.statement: Treating the window values as roughly uniform in $\{0, \ldots, q-1\}$, each window hits with probability about $1/q$, so the expected number of (true plus spurious) hits is $v + (n-m+1)/q$, where $v$ is the number of true occurrences. Expected time is then $O(n) + O(m(v + (n-m+1)/q))$: choosing a word-sized prime $q$ comfortably above $n$ makes the expected total $O(n + mv)$. The **worst case remains** $\Theta((n-m+1)m)$ — an adversary can make every window a hit.
concepts.detail: Rabin–Karp also generalizes gracefully: one pass can test several patterns of the same length, and the same fingerprint idea gives expected linear-time two-dimensional matching.

concepts.statement: With alphabet size $d = |\Sigma|$ and prime $q$, the high-order multiplier $h = d^{m-1} \bmod q$ strips the leading digit in the rolling update $t_{s+1} = (d(t_s - T[s+1]h) + T[s+m+1]) \bmod q$. Precompute $h$ once in $\Theta(m)$ by repeated $\times d \bmod q$.
concepts.detail: Without $h$ each window would cost $\Theta(m)$; with $h$ each costs $O(1)$. Choosing $q$ with $dq$ fitting a machine word keeps the arithmetic single-precision (text's $d = 10$, $q = 13$ toy uses one digit).

examples.title: Rabin–Karp on decimal digits
examples.problem: Search for $P = 26$ in the text $T = 3141592653589793$ using base $d = 10$ and prime $q = 13$. Find all occurrences and all spurious hits.

steps.label: Step 1: Preprocessing
steps.text: The fingerprint is $p = 26 \bmod 13 = 0$. The place value is $h = 10^{2-1} \bmod 13 = 10$. The first window is $T[1..2] = 31$, so $t_0 = 31 \bmod 13 = 5$.

steps.label: Step 2: Roll the hash
steps.text: For the next window, $t_1 = (10\,(t_0 - T[1]\,h) + T[3]) \bmod 13 = (10(5 - 3 \cdot 10) + 4) \bmod 13 = -246 \bmod 13$. Since $-246 = 13 \cdot (-19) + 1$, we get $t_1 = 1$ — and indeed the window is 14 and $14 \bmod 13 = 1$.

steps.label: Step 3: The full sweep
steps.text: Rolling through all fifteen windows gives $t_0, t_1, \ldots, t_{14} = 5, 1, 2, 2, 7, 1, 0, 0, 1, 9, 6, 11, 6, 1, 2$. The hits ($t_s = p = 0$) are at $s = 6$ and $s = 7$ only.

steps.label: Step 4: Verify the hits
steps.text: At $s = 6$ the window is $T[7..8] = 26 = P$: a valid occurrence. At $s = 7$ the window is $T[8..9] = 65 \ne 26$: a spurious hit, rejected after two comparisons. Check the roll into $s = 7$: $t_7 = (10(0 - 2\cdot10) + 5) \bmod 13 = -195 \bmod 13 = 0$, exactly the collision $65 \equiv 26 \equiv 0 \pmod{13}$.

steps.label: Step 5: The cost
steps.text: Fifteen $O(1)$ hash updates, plus two verifications of $m = 2$ comparisons each — one productive, one wasted on the collision. With a larger $q$ such collisions would be rarer still.

examples.result: Exactly one occurrence, at shift $s = 6$; one spurious hit at $s = 7$ (window 65), detected by verification.

examples.title: Spurious hit, then verified miss
examples.problem: Alphabet $d = 10$, $q = 11$, $P = 26$ ($p = 4$? $26 \bmod 11 = 4$), text $31415$: find a spurious hit.

steps.label: Hit
steps.text: Window $15$ hashes $4 = p$: hash hit at shift $3$; verify characters $15 \ne 26$: spurious hit (collision mod $11$).

steps.label: Cost
steps.text: One $m = 2$-character verification on the spurious hit; other windows cost $O(1)$ hash only.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: With $q$ prime $\approx m$, spurious rate $\approx 1/q$ per shift: $\Theta(n)$ expected plus $O(m)$ per true/spurious verification.

examples.result: Shift $3$ hash-hits but character-misses: spurious hit verified in $O(m)$, all other shifts $O(1)$.

keyTakeaways: Fingerprint every window mod a word-sized prime; roll with $t_{s+1} = (d(t_s - T[s+1]h) + T[s+m+1]) \bmod q$ where $h = d^{m-1} \bmod q$.
A hit is only a suspicion: verify each in $O(m)$, because different strings share residues mod $q$.
Expected time $O(n + mv)$; worst case $\Theta((n-m+1)m)$ — Rabin–Karp trades the worst-case guarantee for speed, simplicity, and easy generalization.

quiz.q: In the worked example, why did the window 65 trigger character verification?
options: because 65 and 26 share their last digit
because the digit sums of 65 and 26 agree
quiz.explanation: The test is congruence mod $q$: $65 \equiv 0 \pmod{13}$ and $p = 26 \equiv 0 \pmod{13}$, so the window hits. Verification then exposes it as spurious.

quiz.q: The purpose of the rolling update is to:
options: avoid reading the text more than once per window boundary
compute $t_{s+1}$ from $t_s$ with $O(1)$ arithmetic instead of $\Theta(m)$
reduce the number of valid shifts
quiz.explanation: Re-fingerprinting each window from scratch costs $\Theta(m)$; the recurrence subtracts the departing digit and adds the arriving digit in constant time, for $\Theta(n)$ over all windows.

quiz.q: What must the algorithm do whenever $t_s \equiv p \pmod q$?
options: verify the window against the pattern character by character
choose a new prime and restart
quiz.explanation: Congruence is necessary but not sufficient for equality — spurious hits exist for every $q$. The $O(m)$ check on each hit is what makes the algorithm correct rather than merely fast.

quiz.q: To keep the expected total verification cost at $O(n)$ (for few true occurrences), the prime $q$ should be chosen:
options: large — comfortably above $n$ yet still fitting in one machine word
quiz.explanation: The expected number of spurious hits is about $(n-m+1)/q$: the larger the prime, the rarer the collisions. It must still fit in a word so that arithmetic mod $q$ stays $O(1)$.

intro: A string-matching automaton compiles the pattern into a finite state machine. The machine scans the text once, making exactly one table-driven transition per character, and reports a match whenever it enters its single accepting state $m$. All the intelligence lives in the transition function $\delta$, precomputed from the pattern alone: it encodes exactly how much of a partial match survives each incoming character. The correctness rests on one invariant: the current state is always the length of the longest prefix of $P$ that is a suffix of the text read so far.
objectives: Build the state machine for a pattern and trace it on a text
State and prove the invariant linking the current state to the longest matched prefix-suffix
Explain the $O(m\,|\Sigma|)$ construction of $\delta$ and the resulting $\Theta(n)$ matching time

concepts.statement: For a pattern $P[1..m]$ over alphabet $\Sigma$, the automaton has state set $Q = \{0, 1, \ldots, m\}$, start state $0$, and the **single** accepting state $m$. State $q$ means: the last $q$ characters read form $P[1..q]$. The transition function $\delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q$ is built from the pattern before the text is seen; matching = feed $T$ through the machine with one $O(1)$ table lookup per character and report an occurrence ending at position $i$ whenever the machine enters state $m$ (shift $i - m$).
concepts.detail: The machine never moves backward in the text: this is what makes the matching phase exactly $\Theta(n)$ — one transition per text character, with no per-step dependence on $m$.

concepts.statement: $\delta(q, a)$ is the length of the **longest prefix of $P$ that is also a suffix of the string $P_q a$**, where $P_q$ denotes $P[1..q]$: $$\delta(q, a) = \max\{k \le \min(q+1, m) : P[1..k] \text{ is a suffix of } P[1..q] \cdot a\}.$$ Micro-example for $P = \text{ababaca}$: $\delta(4, a) = 5$ because $\text{abab} \cdot a$ ends with $\text{ababa}$; $\delta(5, b) = 4$ because $\text{ababab}$ ends with $\text{abab}$ but not with $\text{ababa}$.
concepts.detail: After reaching the accepting state $m$ the machine keeps going — $\delta(m, a)$ is defined the same way — so overlapping occurrences are all reported.

concepts.statement: After the automaton has read $T[1..i]$, its state equals the length of the longest prefix of $P$ that is a suffix of $T[1..i]$. **Proof (induction on $i$):** before any input the state is 0 and the empty prefix is the suffix of the empty text. If the invariant holds at $i$ with state $q$, then appending character $T[i+1]$ leaves exactly the suffix structure of $P_q \cdot T[i+1]$ to analyze — which is precisely the definition of $\delta(q, T[i+1])$, so the invariant holds at $i+1$. Consequently the machine is in state $m$ after reading $T[1..i]$ **iff** an occurrence of $P$ ends at position $i$.
concepts.detail: This invariant is the entire correctness proof: it identifies each state with a fact about the text already read, and the definition of $\delta$ is exactly what preserves that fact.

concepts.statement: Computing $\delta$ naively — for each of the $m \cdot |\Sigma|$ entries testing candidate suffixes — costs $O(m^3\,|\Sigma|)$. The efficient route uses the prefix function $\pi$ of Section 32.4: if $q < m$ and $P[q+1] = a$, then $\delta(q,a) = q+1$; otherwise $\delta(q,a) = \delta(\pi(q), a)$, anchored at $\delta(0, a) = 1$ if $P[1] = a$ and $0$ otherwise. Filling the table with this recurrence (memoized, in order of decreasing $q$) costs $O(m\,|\Sigma|)$.
concepts.detail: For a constant-size alphabet this is linear preprocessing; the matcher then runs in $\Theta(n)$ regardless of $m$ — a total of $O(n + m\,|\Sigma|)$.

concepts.statement: State $q$ means the longest prefix of $P$ that is a suffix of text read so far has length $q$; $q = m$ means $P$ itself just matched, so FINITE-AUTOMATON-MATCHER reports shift $i-m$. The automaton stays in $m$'s transitions (via $\delta(m, a)$) to find overlapping matches.
concepts.detail: Overlaps need $\delta(m,\cdot)$: pattern $aaa$ in text $aaaa$ matches at shifts $0$ and $1$ because $\delta(3,a) = 3$, not $0$. Resetting to $0$ would miss the second.

examples.title: The machine for P = ababaca
examples.problem: Build the transition table of the string-matching automaton for $P = \text{ababaca}$ over $\Sigma = \{a, b, c\}$ and run it on $T = \text{abababacaba}$.

steps.label: Step 1: The transition table
steps.text: States 0 through 7; rows list $\delta(q, a), \delta(q, b), \delta(q, c)$. State 0: 1, 0, 0. State 1: 1, 2, 0. State 2: 3, 0, 0. State 3: 1, 4, 0. State 4: 5, 0, 0. State 5: 1, 4, 6. State 6: 1, 0, 7. State 7: 1, 2, 0.

steps.label: Step 2: Spot-check two entries
steps.text: $\delta(5, b) = 4$: reading $b$ in state 5 (matched $\text{ababa}$) gives the string $\text{ababab}$, whose longest $P$-prefix suffix is $\text{abab}$ — length 4. And $\delta(6, c) = 7$ completes the pattern, while $\delta(7, b) = 2$ because $\text{ababaca} \cdot b$ ends with $ab$.

steps.label: Step 3: Run the text
steps.text: Feeding $T = \text{abababacaba}$ one character per transition produces the state sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 5, 6, 7, 2, 3. The descent from 5 to 4 at the sixth character is exactly the $\delta(5,b) = 4$ fallback — the mismatch is absorbed by the table, with no backtracking.

steps.label: Step 4: Read off the occurrences
steps.text: The machine hits state 7 (accepting) after reading $T[9]$, so an occurrence ends at position 9: shift $9 - 7 = 2$, and indeed $T[3..9] = \text{ababaca}$. After accepting, it falls to state 2 (via $\delta(7, b) = 2$ on the next character) and continues hunting.

steps.label: Step 5: Cost
steps.text: Eleven text characters, eleven table lookups, zero re-reads. The price was building the $8 \times 3$ table once.

examples.result: Transition table as listed; the text drives the machine through states 1,2,3,4,5,4,5,6,7,2,3, finding the single occurrence at shift 2 in $\Theta(n)$.

examples.title: Overlapping matches via $\delta(m,a)$
examples.problem: Pattern $P = aa$ ($m = 2$) on text $T = aaa$ ($n = 3$). Trace the automaton and list shifts.

steps.label: Transitions
steps.text: $\delta(0,a) = 1$, $\delta(1,a) = 2$, $\delta(2,a) = 2$ (longest prefix of $aa$ suffixing $aaa$ is $aa$ itself).

steps.label: Shifts
steps.text: Valid shifts $0,1$: $n-m+1 = 2$ windows, both $aa$ ✓.

steps.label: Naive contrast
steps.text: Naive rechecks each window ($2\times 2 = 4$ comparisons); automaton uses $n = 3$ transitions, $\Theta(n)$.

examples.result: Shifts $0,1$ both match; $\delta(2,a) = 2$ (not $0$) is what captures the overlap.

keyTakeaways: States are matched-prefix lengths $0..m$ with only $m$ accepting; $\delta(q,a)$ = length of the longest prefix of $P$ that is a suffix of $P_q a$.
The invariant — state = longest prefix of $P$ that is a suffix of the text so far — is the whole correctness proof, and matching is one transition per character: $\Theta(n)$.
Preprocessing costs $O(m\,|\Sigma|)$ via the prefix-function recurrence (Section 32.4); the automaton is the pattern in compiled form.

quiz.q: For $P = \text{ababaca}$, the machine sits in state 5 and reads $b$. What is the next state?
quiz.explanation: State 5 means $\text{ababa}$ is matched; appending $b$ gives $\text{ababab}$, whose longest prefix of $P$ that is a suffix is $\text{abab}$ — length 4, so $\delta(5,b) = 4$.

quiz.q: A pattern of length $m$ yields a matching automaton with how many states, and which are accepting?
quiz.explanation: States record the matched-prefix length, which ranges from 0 to $m$; only the full match $m$ is an occurrence, so it alone is accepting.

quiz.q: The matching phase runs in $\Theta(n)$ because:
options: each character of the text is re-examined at most $m$ times
the automaton performs exactly one $O(1)$ table transition per text character and never rereads the text
the text is preprocessed down to its distinct characters
the pattern is at most half the text length
quiz.explanation: The text pointer only advances: state changes are table lookups whose cost is independent of $m$. No backtracking ever occurs — unlike the naive matcher.

quiz.q: $\delta(q, a)$ is defined as:
options: the length of the longest prefix of $P$ that is a suffix of $P_q a$
the number of occurrences of $a$ in $P_q$
the longest common subsequence of $P_q$ and $a$
quiz.explanation: After reading $a$ in state $q$, the machine must sit at the longest prefix of $P$ matching a suffix of everything read — that is, a suffix of the string $P_q a$.

intro: Knuth–Morris–Pratt is the automaton matcher with the table built lazily. The prefix function $\pi$ records, for each position $q$ of the pattern, the length of the longest proper prefix of $P[1..q]$ that is also its suffix — exactly the state to fall back to on a mismatch. The matcher never moves the text pointer backward: on a mismatch it consults $\pi$ and continues, achieving $\Theta(m)$ preprocessing and $\Theta(n)$ matching. That linearity is an amortized fact, not a per-step one — the complete proof is the depth tier below.
objectives: Compute $\pi$ for a pattern by hand, position by position
Trace KMP on a text, using $\pi$ to recover from mismatches without rereading the text
Justify the $\Theta(m) + \Theta(n)$ running time with the two-counter amortized argument

concepts.statement: $\pi[q]$ is the length of the **longest proper prefix of $P[1..q]$ that is also a suffix of $P[1..q]$** (proper: strictly shorter than $q$; so $\pi[1] = 0$): $$\pi[q] = \max\{k < q : P[1..k] \text{ is a suffix of } P[1..q]\}.$$ Such a prefix-suffix is called a **border**. For $P = \text{ababaca}$: $\pi = 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1$ — e.g. $\pi[5] = 3$ because $\text{aba}$ is the longest border of $\text{ababa}$, and $\pi[6] = 0$ because $\text{ababac}$ ends in $c$ while no nonempty prefix does.
concepts.detail: The figure below draws $\pi$ as fallback arcs and shows the slide they induce on a real mismatch.

concepts.statement: Iterating $\pi$ from $q$ enumerates **all** borders of $P[1..q]$ in strictly decreasing order: $q, \pi[q], \pi[\pi[q]], \ldots, 0$. Consequently, when a mismatch occurs after $q$ matched characters, the longest prefix of $P$ that can still be aligned against the text ending at the current position has length exactly $\pi[q]$ — the fallback $q \leftarrow \pi[q]$ loses no candidate. This is why KMP is correct and why the automaton's $\delta$ of 32.3 can be computed from $\pi$: $\delta(q,a) = q+1$ if $P[q+1] = a$, else $\delta(q,a) = \delta(\pi(q), a)$.
concepts.detail: The enumeration claim follows by induction: any border of $P_q$ shorter than $\pi[q]$ is a prefix of $P_{\pi[q]}$ and a suffix of it, hence a border of $P_{\pi[q]}$.

concepts.statement: Preprocess $P$ into $\pi$ in $\Theta(m)$. Then scan with state $q = 0$ for $i = 1$ to $n$: **while** $q > 0$ and $P[q+1] \ne T[i]$: set $q \leftarrow \pi[q]$; **if** $P[q+1] = T[i]$: set $q \leftarrow q + 1$; **if** $q = m$: report the occurrence at shift $i - m$ and set $q \leftarrow \pi[q]$ to continue (which is what finds overlapping occurrences). The text index $i$ never decreases.
concepts.detail: The matcher is the 32.3 automaton with $\delta$ evaluated on the fly: the while loop is the multi-step fallback compressed into a chain of $\pi$-jumps.

concepts.statement: The matcher runs in $\Theta(n)$ and performs at most $2n$ character comparisons; preprocessing is $\Theta(m)$. The proof is a two-counter (aggregate) argument: the state $q$ increases at most once per text character — at most $n$ total increases from 0 — while every while-loop iteration strictly decreases $q$, and $q$ never goes below 0, so the number of fallback jumps is at most $n$ as well.
concepts.detail: The bound is amortized: a single text character can trigger $\Theta(m)$ consecutive fallbacks, provided earlier characters built the state up. The masters tier below proves both linearity and the exhaustive-ness of the fallback chain in full.

concepts.statement: Compute $\pi[1..m]$ in $\Theta(m)$: keep $k = \pi[q-1]$, while $k > 0$ and $P[k+1] \ne P[q]$ fall back $k = \pi[k]$, then $\pi[q] = k + (P[k+1] == P[q])$. Same amortized $k$-only-rises argument as KMP-MATCHER, with $P$ playing both pattern and text.
concepts.detail: Figure 32.10: $k$ rises at most $m$ times total, so fallbacks total $O(m)$. $\pi$ is the automaton restricted to pattern-on-pattern, which is why KMP needs no $\delta$ table.

figures.caption: Top: the prefix function $\pi$ for $P = \text{ababaca}$ — each arc falls back from position $q$ to $\pi[q]$, so a mismatch slides the pattern right by $q - \pi[q]$ positions. Bottom: matching against $T = \text{abababacaba}$: after five green matches the comparison at $i = 6$ fails ($b$ vs $c$), the matcher jumps $q \leftarrow \pi[5] = 3$, and the slid pattern's first three characters are already known to match — the amber box resumes at $T[6]$ and the text pointer never moves left.
