examples.title: KMP on one mismatch
examples.problem: Search for $P = \text{ababaca}$ ($\pi = 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1$) in $T = \text{abababacaba}$, tracking the state $q$ at every character.

steps.label: Step 1: Climb
steps.text: Reading $T[1..5] = \text{ababa}$, every character extends the match: the state rises $q = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ with one comparison each.

steps.label: Step 2: The mismatch at i = 6
steps.text: $T[6] = b$ but $P[6] = c$: with $q = 5$ matched, the while loop fires once, $q \leftarrow \pi[5] = 3$. No other fallback is needed: $P[4] = b$ equals $T[6]$, so the if raises $q$ to 4. The text position $i = 6$ is compared twice in total — never moved backward.

steps.label: Step 3: Why 3 characters carry over
steps.text: The five matched characters were $\text{ababa}$; its longest border is $\text{aba}$ of length $\pi[5] = 3$. The slid pattern (shift 2) therefore has $P[1..3] = \text{aba}$ already aligned with $T[3..5]$ — exactly the green overlap in the figure.

steps.label: Step 4: To the occurrence
steps.text: Continuing: $i = 7$ ($a$) gives $q = 5$, $i = 8$ ($c$) gives $q = 6$, $i = 9$ ($a$) gives $q = 7 = m$: an occurrence ends at position 9, shift $9 - 7 = 2$ — and $T[3..9] = \text{ababaca}$ checks out. The matcher sets $q \leftarrow \pi[7] = 1$ and keeps scanning.

steps.label: Step 5: The tail and the count
steps.text: The last two characters give $q = 2, 3$ and no further occurrence. Grand total: eleven characters read, twelve comparisons ($11$ if-tests plus one re-test after the single fallback) — against the naive matcher's potential $5 \cdot 7 = 35$.

examples.result: One occurrence, at shift 2; a single mismatch resolved by one $\pi$-jump ($5 \to 3$); state sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 5, 6, 7, 2, 3.

examples.title: Amortized credit on $ababaca$
examples.problem: KMP-MATCHER for $P = ababaca$ ($m = 7$) scans $T$ of length $10$ with $3$ mismatches. Bound the fallback steps.

steps.label: $\pi$
steps.text: $\pi = [0,0,1,2,3,0,1]$ for $a,b,a,b,a,c,a$: each fallback follows $\pi$ down.

steps.label: Potential
steps.text: $\Phi = q$ (current state): matches raise $q$ by $1$ ($\le n$ rises); each fallback lowers $q$ ($\le n$ falls): total fallbacks $O(n)$.

steps.label: Count
steps.text: $10$ character steps + $\le 10$ fallbacks $= O(n)$: per-step cost amortized $O(1)$, worst single step $O(m)$ (long fallback chain).

steps.label: Versus automaton
steps.text: Automaton pays $O(1)$ worst per character via $\delta$ table ($O(m|\Sigma|)$ space); KMP pays $O(1)$ amortized with $O(m)$ space ($\pi$ only).

examples.result: $\le 20$ state moves on $n = 10$: KMP is linear amortized, $\pi$ compresses $\delta$.

keyTakeaways: $\pi[q]$ = the longest border of $P[1..q]$; iterating $\pi$ enumerates every border in decreasing length, so no candidate alignment is ever skipped.
On a mismatch: $q \leftarrow \pi[q]$ with the text index $i$ unchanged — the text pointer never moves left, and overlapping occurrences are still found.
$\Theta(m)$ preprocessing plus $\Theta(n)$ matching with at most $2n$ comparisons — an aggregate amortized bound, proved in full below.

quiz.q: The prefix function of the pattern aaaa is:
quiz.explanation: $P[1..q] = a^q$ has the proper prefix $a^{q-1}$ as its longest suffix, so $\pi[q] = q - 1$: the values $0, 1, 2, 3$. ($1, 2, 3, 4$ is impossible since a border must be proper — shorter than $q$.)

quiz.q: In KMP, after a mismatch at text position $i$ with $q$ characters matched, the matcher:
options: moves the text pointer back to $i - q + 1$ and restarts
skips the text ahead by $m$ positions
quiz.explanation: The fallback re-aligns the pattern using the border of the matched prefix; the text character that failed is simply re-tested against the new $P[q+1]$. This is why matching is $\Theta(n)$.

quiz.q: $\pi[q]$ is precisely:
options: the length of the longest proper prefix of $P[1..q]$ that is also a suffix of $P[1..q]$
the length of the longest prefix of $P$ that occurs anywhere in $T$
the number of distinct characters in $P[1..q]$
the position in $P$ where the previous mismatch occurred
quiz.explanation: It is a purely pattern-internal quantity — a border of the first $q$ pattern characters — computable before the text is ever seen.

quiz.q: Across an entire run on $n$ text characters, the total number of $\pi$-fallback jumps (while-loop iterations) is at most:
quiz.explanation: Each jump strictly decreases $q$, and $q$ increases at most once per text character (at most $n$ increases from 0) — decreases can never outnumber increases.

depth.title: The amortized linearity of KMP — a complete proof

blocks.heading: The claim
blocks.body: COMPUTE-PREFIX-FUNCTION runs in $\Theta(m)$, and KMP-MATCHER processes the text in $\Theta(n)$ after $\Theta(m)$ preprocessing, performing at most $2n$ character comparisons. No $O(1)$ per-character bound holds — the guarantee is **amortized**, and it is tight.

blocks.heading: Two counters for COMPUTE-PREFIX-FUNCTION
blocks.body: The procedure maintains $k$ with $\pi[q] = k$, executing: $\pi[1] = 0$; $k = 0$; for $q = 2$ to $m$: while $k > 0$ and $P[k+1] \ne P[q]$: $k \leftarrow \pi[k]$; if $P[k+1] = P[q]$: $k \leftarrow k+1$; $\pi[q] = k$. Track the total movement of $k$. The increase step $k \leftarrow k + 1$ executes at most once per outer iteration — at most $m - 1$ increases in the whole run, starting from $k = 0$. Every while-loop iteration executes $k \leftarrow \pi[k]$, and $\pi[k] < k$ always holds (a border is proper), so each iteration **strictly decreases** $k$, which is never allowed below 0. A variable that starts at 0, increases at most $m - 1$ times in steps of 1, and never goes negative can be decremented at most $m - 1$ times: the while loop runs at most $m - 1$ times in total. All remaining work is $O(1)$ per outer iteration, so the whole procedure is $\Theta(m)$.

blocks.heading: The same budget for the matcher
blocks.body: KMP-MATCHER's loop over $i = 1$ to $n$ has the identical shape with $q$ in place of $k$. The step $q \leftarrow q + 1$ executes at most once per text character, so $q$ increases at most $n$ times from its start at 0. Each while-loop iteration performs $q \leftarrow \pi[q]$, a strict decrease, and $q \ge 0$ always. Hence the total number of fallback jumps over the entire scan is at most $n$. Character comparisons: each of the $n$ loop iterations performs one comparison in its if-test, plus one per while-iteration — at most $n + n = 2n$ in total, and the running time is $\Theta(n)$.

blocks.heading: The potential-function view
blocks.body: The same argument dressed as the potential method: let $\Phi = q$ before each loop iteration ($\Phi = k$ in preprocessing). For an ascent step (the if succeeds), the actual cost is 1 comparison and $\Delta\Phi = +1$, for an amortized cost of 2. For each fallback jump, the actual cost is 1 comparison and $\Delta\Phi \le -1$ (a strict decrease), for an amortized cost of at most 0. Since $\Phi \ge 0$ throughout, the total actual cost never exceeds the total amortized cost, which is at most $2n$. The aggregate and potential versions are the same economy: descents are financed by prior ascents.

blocks.heading: A single step can be expensive
blocks.body: Take $P = a^m$ and a text built from blocks $a^{m-1}b$. After $m - 1$ letters $a$, the state is $q = m - 1$; the following $b$ fails against $P[m] = a$, so $q \leftarrow \pi[m-1] = m - 2$, which fails again, and so on: the state descends $m-1, m-2, \ldots, 1, 0$ — $m - 1$ fallback jumps caused by **one** text character, and then $P[1] = a$ fails against $b$ as well. That single character costs $\Theta(m)$. Yet the total over the whole text stays at $2n$, because rebuilding $q = m - 1$ before the next $b$ consumes $m - 1$ further characters. Amortized $O(1)$ per character coexists with unbounded single-character cost.

blocks.heading: What the counting argument does not show
blocks.body: Linearity says the fallback budget balances; it does not by itself justify that falling back only to $\pi[q]$ (rather than further) is **exhaustive**. That is the border-closure property: if $w$ is any border of $P_q$ with $|w| < \pi(q)$, then $w$ is a prefix of $P_{\pi(q)}$ (it is shorter) and also a suffix of it (it is a suffix of $P_q$, and $P_{\pi(q)}$ is itself a suffix of $P_q$) — so $w$ is a border of $P_{\pi(q)}$. By induction, the iterates $\pi(q), \pi^2(q), \ldots, 0$ list every border exactly once, in decreasing order. The while loop therefore never skips a candidate state, which is the correctness half; the counting above is the efficiency half.

blocks.heading: Where the machinery lands
blocks.body: KMP is the single-pattern special case of the Aho–Corasick dictionary matcher, which builds a failure function over a set of patterns and finds all occurrences of any of them in $O(n + z + M)$, where $M$ is the total pattern length and $z$ the number of hits — the engine behind virus scanners and intrusion-detection filters. The $\pi$ table also exposes periodicity: $m - \pi[m]$ is the shortest period of $P$ (for $\text{abababa}$, $\pi[7] = 5$ gives period 2), the seed from which the classical Fine–Wilf periodicity lemmas and many string-reconstruction results grow.

intro: Computational geometry replaces geometric intuition with exact integer arithmetic. The central tool is the cross product: two subtractions and two multiplications decide whether a directed turn goes left, right, or straight — no angles, no slopes, no division, and therefore no numerical fragility. This section builds the orientation test and assembles it into the constant-time decision problem of whether two line segments intersect.
objectives: Compute cross products and interpret their sign as counterclockwise, clockwise, or collinear
Decide segment intersection with four orientation tests plus the on-segment check
Explain why cross-product tests are exact on integer inputs, unlike slope- and angle-based tests

concepts.statement: For points $p_1 = (x_1, y_1)$ and $p_2 = (x_2, y_2)$, viewed as vectors from the origin, the **cross product** is the scalar $$p_1 \times p_2 = x_1 y_2 - x_2 y_1.$$ If $p_1 \times p_2 > 0$ then $p_2$ is counterclockwise from $p_1$ about the origin; if $< 0$, clockwise; if $= 0$, the two vectors are collinear with the origin. Its magnitude $|p_1 \times p_2|$ is the area of the parallelogram they span — that is, twice the area of the triangle $(0,0), p_1, p_2$.
concepts.detail: Anchor example: $(1,0) \times (0,1) = 1 > 0$ — the positive $y$-axis is a counterclockwise quarter turn from the positive $x$-axis, which fixes the sign convention.

concepts.statement: The direction test $$\text{Direction}(p_0, p_1, p_2) = (p_1 - p_0) \times (p_2 - p_0)$$ classifies the turn $p_0 \to p_1 \to p_2$: **positive** means counterclockwise ($p_2$ lies to the left of the directed line $p_0 p_1$), **negative** means clockwise ($p_2$ to the right), and **zero** means the three points are collinear. Subtracting $p_0$ translates both vectors without changing their cross product, so orientation is translation-invariant; and $|\text{Direction}|$ is twice the signed area of triangle $p_0 p_1 p_2$.
concepts.detail: For example, $\text{Direction}((0,0), (4,0), (2,3)) = 4 \cdot 3 - 0 \cdot 2 = 12 > 0$: $(2,3)$ sits to the left of the eastward ray, and the triangle has area $6$.

concepts.statement: A zero direction only says that $p_2$ lies on the **infinite line** through $p_0$ and $p_1$ — it may lie far outside the segment. ON-SEGMENT($p_0, p_1, p_2$), called only when the three points are collinear, checks the bounding box: $$\min(x_0, x_1) \le x_2 \le \max(x_0, x_1) \quad\text{and}\quad \min(y_0, y_1) \le y_2 \le \max(y_0, y_1).$$ Both inequalities must hold for $p_2$ to lie on the closed segment $p_0 p_1$.
concepts.detail: This is the branch of the decision procedure that catches touching endpoints and collinear overlaps — the degenerate cases the sign test alone cannot distinguish.

concepts.statement: To decide whether the segment $p_1 p_2$ intersects the segment $p_3 p_4$, compute four orientations: $d_1 = \text{Direction}(p_3, p_4, p_1)$, $d_2 = \text{Direction}(p_3, p_4, p_2)$, $d_3 = \text{Direction}(p_1, p_2, p_3)$, $d_4 = \text{Direction}(p_1, p_2, p_4)$. **Proper crossing:** $d_1 d_2 < 0$ and $d_3 d_4 < 0$ (each segment strictly straddles the other's line). **Touching:** if any $d_i = 0$, the corresponding point is collinear with the other segment — test it with ON-SEGMENT (e.g. $d_1 = 0$ and $p_1$ on segment $p_3 p_4$ means they intersect at $p_1$). **Otherwise** the segments are disjoint. Four cross products — eight multiplications, exact on integers.
concepts.detail: Slope-based tests need case analysis for vertical segments and introduce rounding error under floating point; the cross product formulation has neither defect, which is why every algorithm in this chapter is phrased with it.

concepts.term: Area as half the cross product
concepts.statement: For vectors $u,v$, $|u \times v|/2$ is the area of the triangle they span; sign is orientation (positive: counterclockwise turn). SEGMENTS-INTERSECT needs only signs and the on-segment bounding check, never the area value, which is why integer arithmetic stays exact.
concepts.detail: Robustness: slopes need division ($\Delta y/\Delta x$) and angles need trigonometry, both rounding on integers; cross products use $2$ multiplies and a subtract, exact in $O(\log C)$ bits for coordinates bounded by $C$.

examples.title: Two segment-intersection decisions
examples.problem: (a) Do the segments $p_1 p_2$ from $(0,0)$ to $(4,4)$ and $p_3 p_4$ from $(0,4)$ to $(4,0)$ intersect? (b) What if instead $p_3 = (5,1)$ and $p_4 = (7,3)$?

steps.label: Step 2: The verdict for (a)
steps.text: $d_1 d_2 = (-16)(16) < 0$ and $d_3 d_4 = (16)(-16) < 0$: each pair of endpoints straddles the other segment, so the segments properly intersect. Indeed the lines $y = x$ and $y = 4 - x$ meet at $(2,2)$, which lies on both segments — a pure crossing, no endpoint touching.

steps.label: Step 3: Four orientations for (b)
steps.text: With $p_3 = (5,1)$, $p_4 = (7,3)$: $d_1 = (2,2) \times (-5,-1) = 2(-1) - 2(-5) = 8$ and $d_2 = (2,2) \times (-1,3) = 2 \cdot 3 - 2(-1) = 8$. Both positive: $p_1$ and $p_2$ lie on the same (left) side of the line through $p_3 p_4$.

steps.label: Step 4: The verdict for (b)
steps.text: $d_1 d_2 = 64 > 0$ already fails the straddle condition — and symmetrically $d_3 = \text{Direction}(p_1,p_2,p_3) = (4,4) \times (5,1) = -16$, $d_4 = (4,4) \times (7,3) = -16$, so $d_3 d_4 = 256 > 0$. No product of opposite signs, no zero directions, no endpoint on the other segment: the segments are disjoint, with $p_3 p_4$ passing above the diagonal.

steps.label: Step 5: The cost
steps.text: Each decision used exactly four cross products — eight multiplications and a handful of additions and subtractions on the integer inputs, exact in every digit.

examples.result: (a) Yes — a proper crossing at $(2,2)$. (b) No — both endpoints of each segment lie strictly on the same side of the other's line.

examples.title: Collinear overlap versus touch
examples.problem: Segments $p_1p_2 = (0,0)-(4,0)$, $p_3p_4 = (2,0)-(6,0)$ (overlap) versus $p_3p_4 = (4,0)-(6,0)$ (touch). Decide with cross products.

steps.label: Directions
steps.text: All cross products $0$ (collinear): $d_1 = (p_4-p_3)\times(p_1-p_3) = 0$, similarly $d_2 = d_3 = d_4 = 0$.

steps.label: On-segment (overlap)
steps.text: $p_3 = (2,0)$ on $p_1p_2$ ($0 \le 2 \le 4$ both axes) ✓: INTERSECT true (proper overlap $2..4$).

steps.label: On-segment (touch)
steps.text: $p_3 = (4,0)$ on $p_1p_2$ at the endpoint ✓: INTERSECT true (endpoint touch counts). Shift to $(5,0)-(6,0)$: no endpoint on the other: false.

steps.label: Straddle case
steps.text: Non-collinear needs $d_1,d_2$ opposite signs and $d_3,d_4$ opposite: straddling replaces on-segment.

examples.result: Overlap and endpoint touch both intersect (on-segment ✓); disjoint collinear $(5,0)-(6,0)$ does not.

keyTakeaways: $u \times v = u_x v_y - u_y v_x$: positive = left/counterclockwise turn, negative = right/clockwise, zero = collinear; the magnitude is twice the triangle area.
Segments intersect properly iff each endpoint pair straddles the other segment ($d_1 d_2 < 0$ and $d_3 d_4 < 0$); zero directions route to the bounding-box on-segment check.
Four cross products = eight integer multiplications, division-free and exact — the primitive every algorithm in this chapter is built on.

quiz.q: For $p_1 = (3,1)$ and $p_2 = (2,5)$, the cross product $p_1 \times p_2$ equals 13. What does the sign say?
quiz.explanation: $p_1 \times p_2 = 3 \cdot 5 - 2 \cdot 1 = 13 > 0$, and a positive cross product means $p_2$ lies counterclockwise from $p_1$ about the origin.

quiz.q: $\text{Direction}(p_0, p_1, p_2)$ returns 0. It follows that:
options: the three points are collinear and $p_2$ lies between $p_0$ and $p_1$
the three points are collinear, but $p_2$ may still lie outside the segment $p_0 p_1$
the segments $p_0 p_1$ and $p_1 p_2$ intersect
the triangle $p_0 p_1 p_2$ has area 2
quiz.explanation: Zero cross product only pins $p_2$ to the infinite line through $p_0$ and $p_1$; deciding whether it lies on the segment requires the bounding-box ON-SEGMENT check.

quiz.q: Two segments properly cross (no endpoint touching the other segment) exactly when:
options: at least one of $d_1, d_2, d_3, d_4$ is zero
quiz.explanation: Each segment must strictly straddle the line of the other — both products strictly negative. Weak inequalities admit the touching cases handled by ON-SEGMENT, and a single product is one-sided evidence only.

quiz.q: The triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$, $(2,3)$ has a direction cross product of magnitude 12. Its area is:
quiz.explanation: The cross product magnitude is the parallelogram area — twice the triangle area — so the triangle covers $12/2 = 6$ (indeed $\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 6$).

intro: Deciding whether ANY pair among $n$ segments intersects looks inherently quadratic — until the sweep line arrives. Sort all $2n$ endpoints and sweep left to right, maintaining the segments currently crossed by the line in a red-black tree ordered top to bottom. Between events, non-intersecting segments never swap vertical order, so the only pairs that can matter are those adjacent in this order — and the algorithm tests exactly those, at $O(\lg n)$ cost per event, for $O(n \lg n)$ total.
objectives: Describe the sweep-line total order and why it can only change at an intersection
Apply the insertion and deletion neighbor tests that drive ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT
Prove the adjacency invariant and derive the $O(n \lg n)$ running time

concepts.term: The sweep and its total order
concepts.statement: Sort the $2n$ endpoints lexicographically — by $x$, breaking ties by $y$ — and process them as events. At any position between events, the segments crossed by the (vertical) sweep line are totally ordered by the $y$-coordinate of their intersection with it: one segment is **below** another. If no two segments intersect, this order is fixed between events, because a change of vertical order at some $x$ would itself be an intersection point. The sweep visits each endpoint once, in $O(n \lg n)$ for the sort.
concepts.detail: Ties at equal $x$ are exactly why the sort key is the pair $(x, y)$: they fix a deterministic order for segments starting or ending on the same vertical line, including vertical segments.

concepts.term: The red-black tree of active segments
concepts.statement: ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT maintains the active segments in a red-black tree keyed by the sweep order. At a **left endpoint**: insert the segment and test it against its new tree-predecessor and tree-successor. At a **right endpoint**: the deleted segment's predecessor and successor become adjacent — test that pair — then delete. Return TRUE at the first positive test; if the sweep finishes, return FALSE. Each test is the $O(1)$ cross-product decision of 33.1.
concepts.detail: The tree gives INSERT, DELETE, and neighbor queries in $O(\lg n)$ each; a sorted array would force $\Theta(n)$ shifts per event and lose the bound.

concepts.statement: If any two of the segments intersect, then some pair of segments adjacent in the sweep order at some event intersects — and the algorithm tests exactly those pairs. **Proof sketch (general position):** among all intersecting pairs, take the one whose leftmost intersection point $p$ is leftmost, breaking ties by lowest $y$; say segments $s$ and $s'$ cross at $p$. Just to the left of $p$, both are active. If a third active segment $t$ lay between them in the order, then since $s$ and $s'$ meet at $p$ while $t$ avoids $p$ (general position), $t$ must cross $s$ or $s'$ strictly left of $p$ — contradicting the choice of $p$. So $s$ and $s'$ are adjacent just left of $p$. They became adjacent at some earlier event — either when the later one was inserted (tested against its neighbor) or when a segment between them was deleted (its two new neighbors were tested) — and both tests would have found them.
concepts.detail: Degenerate cases (shared endpoints, three segments through one point) are absorbed by the endpoint-sort conventions; the book's argument extends with the same skeleton.

concepts.statement: ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT runs in $O(n \lg n)$ time: the endpoint sort is $O(n \lg n)$, there are $2n$ events, each performing $O(1)$ red-black tree operations at $O(\lg n)$ apiece and $O(1)$ constant-time segment tests — $O(1)$ tests per event, not per pair. It is correct: TRUE iff some pair of closed segments intersects, including endpoint touching.
concepts.detail: The same sweep with a small extension reports ALL $k$ intersections in $O((n + k) \lg n)$ — the basis of the Bentley–Ottmann algorithm.

concepts.statement: Events are the $2n$ endpoints sorted by $x$ (ties by $y$, left before right): $O(n \lg n)$ sort dominates. The sweep processes left to right; insertions/deletions at events cost $O(\lg n)$ in the red-black active order, giving $O(n \lg n)$ total.
concepts.detail: No two events share $x$ is the textbook simplification (perturb or tie-break); without it vertical segments need the $y$-tie rule. Intersections themselves are not events here (unlike full arrangement sweep): the algorithm stops at the first one found.

examples.title: A sweep that finds the crossing before it happens
examples.problem: Run ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT on three segments: $s_1$ from $(0,0)$ to $(8,8)$, $s_2$ from $(2,6)$ to $(6,2)$, and $m$ from $(2,5)$ to $(3,4)$.

steps.label: Event (0,0): insert s1
steps.text: The left endpoint of $s_1$ (the line $y = x$). The tree is empty, so $s_1$ has no predecessor or successor: no test is made.

steps.label: Event (2,5): insert m
steps.text: At $x = 2$ the sweep crosses $s_1$ at $y = 2$ and the new segment $m$ (on $y = 7 - x$) at $y = 5$, so the order is $s_1$ below $m$. Insert $m$; its predecessor is $s_1$: test $m \times s_1$ — their lines would meet at $x = 3.5$, outside $m$'s span $[2,3]$, so no intersection.

steps.label: Event (2,6): insert s2
steps.text: The tie at $x = 2$ is broken by $y$: $(2,5)$ was processed before $(2,6)$. Now the sweep order is $s_1$ (at $y = 2$), $m$ (at $y = 5$), $s_2$ (at $y = 6$). $s_2$'s predecessor is $m$: test $s_2 \times m$ — the lines $y = 8 - x$ and $y = 7 - x$ are parallel, never meeting. No successor yet.

steps.label: Event (3,4): delete m
steps.text: The right endpoint of $m$. Before deleting, test the two neighbors that are about to become adjacent: $s_1 \times s_2$. Their lines $y = x$ and $y = 8 - x$ meet at $(4,4)$, and $x = 4$ lies inside both spans $[0,8]$ and $[2,6]$: they intersect — return TRUE.

steps.label: The punchline
steps.text: The crossing itself sits at $x = 4$, but the algorithm answered TRUE at the event $x = 3$ — one unit BEFORE the crossing exists geometrically. The order structure (a segment between them vanished) exposed the intersection; no intersection point is ever an event.

examples.result: TRUE, detected at the fourth event: deleting $m$ makes $s_1$ and $s_2$ adjacent, and their test finds the crossing at $(4,4)$.

examples.title: Neighbour test that catches nothing
examples.problem: Segments $a: (0,0)-(4,4)$, $b: (0,4)-(4,0)$ cross at $(2,2)$; $c: (5,0)-(5,4)$ far right. Show which neighbour test fires.

steps.label: Insert $a$
steps.text: Active $[a]$: no neighbours.

steps.label: Insert $b$
steps.text: Active $[a,b]$ or $[b,a]$ by $y$ at $x = 0^+$: neighbours $(a,b)$ tested: SEGMENTS-INTERSECT true: return TRUE before $c$ is ever inserted.

steps.label: Had no crossing
steps.text: Without $a$-$b$ crossing, each insertion/deletion would test at most $2$ neighbours ($O(1)$ segment tests) for $2n$ events: $O(n \lg n)$ with no false negatives by the adjacency invariant.

examples.result: Neighbour pair $(a,b)$ tested at $b$'s insertion, crossing found: sweep tests $O(n)$ neighbour pairs, not $\binom{n}{2}$.

keyTakeaways: Sweep the $2n$ sorted endpoints; the red-black tree of active segments keeps the top-to-bottom order with $O(\lg n)$ updates.
Only neighbors are ever tested — on insertion (new segment vs predecessor and successor) and on deletion (the two segments that become adjacent).
Adjacency invariant: the leftmost intersecting pair is adjacent just before it crosses, so it cannot escape a neighbor test — total $O(n \lg n)$.

quiz.q: In the worked example, the crossing point $(4,4)$ is geometrically at $x = 4$. The algorithm reported TRUE at:
options: the event $x = 3$, strictly before the crossing
$x = 6$, when the first right endpoint of the pair is processed
it cannot report until the sweep ends
quiz.explanation: Deleting $m$ at its right endpoint $(3,4)$ makes $s_1$ and $s_2$ adjacent in the order, and the deletion's neighbor test finds their intersection — one unit before the segments actually meet.

quiz.q: Which pairs of segments does ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT actually test?
options: all $\Theta(n^2)$ pairs, but each with the fast cross-product test
each newly inserted segment against its current predecessor and successor, plus the two neighbors of each deleted segment
only pairs that share an endpoint
quiz.explanation: The adjacency invariant limits attention to neighbors in the sweep order: $O(1)$ tests per event, $2n$ events — never the quadratic pair set.

quiz.q: Between two consecutive events, the vertical order of the active segments cannot change because:
options: the red-black tree rebalances and restores it
two segments that swapped vertical order would have to intersect — an event in itself
the segments are sorted by length at preprocessing time
quiz.explanation: A swap of order at some $x$ means the two segments pass through a common point: an intersection. If none exists, the order is stable between events, which is exactly why the event set (endpoints) suffices.

quiz.q: The total running time of ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT on $n$ segments is:
quiz.explanation: Sorting the $2n$ endpoints plus $2n$ events, each with $O(1)$ tree operations at $O(\lg n)$ and constant-time tests, gives $O(n \lg n)$.

intro: The convex hull is the tightest rubber band around a point set — the smallest convex polygon containing it. Graham scan finds it in $O(n \lg n)$: anchor at the lowest point (guaranteed to be a hull vertex), sort the rest by polar angle, then walk the angular order once, popping every point that makes a nonleft turn. The stack always holds the hull of the points processed so far, and although the pop loop can fire repeatedly, each point is pushed once and popped at most once — the same amortized economy that made KMP linear.
objectives: Define CH(Q) as the intersection of convex sets and identify which points are hull vertices
Run Graham scan by hand, including the pops and the collinear case
Compare $O(n \lg n)$ Graham scan with the output-sensitive $O(nh)$ Jarvis march

concepts.statement: The **convex hull** $\text{CH}(Q)$ of a set $Q$ of points is the intersection of all convex sets containing $Q$ — itself convex, and the smallest such set. For finite $Q$ it is a convex polygon whose vertices, the **extreme points**, belong to $Q$; every other point of $Q$ lies inside or on the boundary. A point of $Q$ is a hull vertex exactly when it is not a convex combination of the other points.
concepts.detail: Hulls serve as bounding containers in collision detection, graphics culling, and statistics (outlier detection via peeling); most such pipelines need only the hull, not the whole cloud.

concepts.statement: Step 1 — pick $p_0$: the point of $Q$ with the lowest $y$-coordinate, ties broken by lowest $x$; it is certainly a hull vertex, and every other point lies at polar angle in $[0°, 180°)$ from it, making the sort well defined. Step 2 — sort the remaining points by polar angle about $p_0$ (ties by distance: keep the farthest). Step 3 — scan: push $p_0$, then the first two sorted points; for each later point $p_i$: **while** the turn from NEXT-TO-TOP($S$) to TOP($S$) to $p_i$ is a nonleft turn — clockwise or collinear — pop the stack; then push $p_i$. At the end the stack holds the hull vertices in counterclockwise order.
concepts.detail: The pop test is exactly the 33.1 orientation: a positive cross product is a left turn (keep); zero or negative pops.

concepts.statement: At the start of each loop iteration, the stack $S$ contains exactly the vertices of $\text{CH}(\{p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_{i-1}\})$ in counterclockwise order. Hence at termination $S$ is the hull of the whole set. **Running time:** $O(n \lg n)$, dominated by the sort. The scan itself is $O(n)$ amortized: each point is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so the while loop executes at most $n$ pops over the entire run — the same two-counter argument as KMP's fallback chain.
concepts.detail: The invariant is maintained because popping removes exactly the points that lie inside the hull of the prefix enlarged by $p_i$: a nonleft turn certifies the top of the stack is not extreme anymore.

concepts.statement: Start at any hull vertex ($p_0$ again works). Repeatedly **wrap**: from the current hull vertex with the current direction, the next hull vertex is the point of $Q$ that is most clockwise (equivalently, the winner of the orientation test against all candidates). Each wrap is a linear scan over the $n$ points and produces one hull edge, so the total is $O(nh)$ for a hull with $h$ vertices.
concepts.detail: Output sensitivity: $O(nh)$ beats $O(n \lg n)$ precisely when $h = o(\lg n)$ — a cloud of points inside a triangle has $h = 3$ and Jarvis runs in $\Theta(n)$. When points lie on a circle ($h \approx n$), Graham scan wins.

concepts.statement: Pick $p_0$ as lowest $y$ (then lowest $x$ on ties): $p_0$ is always a hull vertex, and every other point lies strictly above the horizontal through $p_0$ (or right on it), so polar-angle sort around $p_0$ is well defined in $(-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ with no $\pi$ wrap.
concepts.detail: Ties on the ray from $p_0$ keep only the farthest (closer points cannot be hull vertices unless all are collinear, when the two extremes survive). $p_0$ needs no stack test: it is pushed unconditionally.

figures.caption: Graham scan on nine points. Left: with the anchor $p_0 = (0,0)$ (lowest $y$, then lowest $x$), the other eight points are visited in polar-angle order 0°, 18.4°, 21.8°, 33.7°, 36.9°, 45°, 63.4°, 90°. Right: the moment the scan processes $(6,4)$ with stack $\langle (0,0), (6,0), (5,2) \rangle$: the turn at $(5,2)$ is clockwise — the cross product is $-4$ — so $(5,2)$ is popped and $(6,4)$ pushed; later $(4,3)$ and $(2,2)$ pop as well, and the surviving stack is the hull $(0,0), (6,0), (6,4), (3,6), (0,4)$.

examples.title: Graham scan on nine points, four pops
examples.problem: Run Graham scan on $Q = \{(0,0), (6,0), (3,1), (5,2), (6,4), (4,3), (2,2), (3,6), (0,4)\}$, tracking the stack through every push and pop.

steps.label: Step 1: Anchor and sort
steps.text: $p_0 = (0,0)$ (lowest $y$, and it also has the lowest $x$ among the bottom row, ahead of $(6,0)$). The polar-angle order of the rest: $(6,0)$ at 0°, $(3,1)$ at $\arctan(1/3) \approx 18.4°$, $(5,2)$ at $\arctan(2/5) \approx 21.8°$, $(6,4)$ at $\arctan(2/3) \approx 33.7°$, $(4,3)$ at $\arctan(3/4) \approx 36.9°$, $(2,2)$ at 45°, $(3,6)$ at $\arctan(2) \approx 63.4°$, $(0,4)$ at 90°.

steps.label: Step 2: First pop — (3,1)
steps.text: Push $p_0, (6,0), (3,1)$. Processing $(5,2)$: the turn $(6,0) \to (3,1) \to (5,2)$ has cross product $(-3,1) \times (-1,2) = -6 + 1 = -5 < 0$ — clockwise, so pop $(3,1)$. Now the turn $(0,0) \to (6,0) \to (5,2)$ has cross $6 \cdot 2 - 0 \cdot 5 = 12 > 0$: push $(5,2)$. Stack: $(0,0), (6,0), (5,2)$.

steps.label: Step 3: Second pop — (5,2)
steps.text: Processing $(6,4)$: the turn $(6,0) \to (5,2) \to (6,4)$ has cross $(-1,2) \times (0,4) = -4 < 0$ — the step drawn in the figure — so pop $(5,2)$; the turn $(0,0) \to (6,0) \to (6,4)$ has cross $24 > 0$, push $(6,4)$. Stack: $(0,0), (6,0), (6,4)$.

steps.label: Step 4: A collinear pop — (4,3)
steps.text: Processing $(4,3)$: left turn (cross $= 8$), push. Processing $(2,2)$: the turn $(6,4) \to (4,3) \to (2,2)$ has cross $(-2,-1) \times (-4,-2) = 4 - 4 = 0$ — the three points are collinear (all on $y = x/2 + 1$), and collinear counts as a nonleft turn, so pop $(4,3)$; then $(0,0) \to (6,0) \to (2,2)$ is a left turn (cross 16) and $(2,2)$ is pushed.

steps.label: Step 5: Third pop — (2,2), then the finish
steps.text: Processing $(3,6)$: the turn $(6,4) \to (2,2) \to (3,6)$ has cross $(-4,-2) \times (-3,2) = -8 - 6 = -14 < 0$, pop $(2,2)$; push $(3,6)$. Finally $(0,4)$ makes a left turn at $(3,6)$ (cross $12 > 0$) and is pushed. Stack: $(0,0), (6,0), (6,4), (3,6), (0,4)$.

steps.label: Step 6: Audit
steps.text: Nine pushes, four pops — the four interior points $(3,1), (5,2), (4,3), (2,2)$ each spent exactly one pop, the defining amortized economy. The five survivors, in counterclockwise order, are the hull; every popped point fails the convex-combination test (e.g. $(2,2) = \tfrac{1}{2}(0,0) + \tfrac{1}{2}(4,4)$-style mixtures of hull points).

examples.result: CH(Q) = the polygon $(0,0), (6,0), (6,4), (3,6), (0,4)$ — five vertices found with 9 pushes and at most 4 pops after an $O(n \lg n)$ angular sort.

examples.title: Collinear points on the hull edge
examples.problem: Points $(0,0) = p_0$, $(1,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(1,1)$. Run GRAHAM-SCAN's sort and pop rule.

steps.label: Sort
steps.text: Angles from $p_0$: $(1,0),(2,0)$ angle $0$ (tie: farther $(2,0)$ kept, $(1,0)$ discarded); $(1,1)$ angle $45^\circ$. Order: $p_0,(2,0),(1,1)$.

steps.label: Walk
steps.text: Push $p_0,(2,0)$; consider $(1,1)$: turn $p_0 \to (2,0) \to (1,1)$ is left ($cross = 2 > 0$): push: stack $p_0,(2,0),(1,1)$.

steps.label: Close
steps.text: Hull $p_0,(2,0),(1,1)$: $(1,0)$ correctly absent (interior to edge $p_0-(2,0)$). Had all four been collinear, scan would keep only $p_0$ and $(2,0)$.

steps.label: Jarvis contrast
steps.text: Jarvis march from $p_0$ would also step to $(2,0)$ (most counterclockwise among collinear), then wrap in $h = 2$ steps if collinear: output-sensitive $O(nh)$.

examples.result: Hull $(0,0),(2,0),(1,1)$: collinear $(1,0)$ discarded by the farthest-wins tie rule; left-turn test keeps the stack convex.

keyTakeaways: CH(Q) is the intersection of all convex sets containing Q — a polygon whose extreme-point vertices all come from Q.
Graham scan: anchor at the lowest point, sort by polar angle, pop every nonleft turn; the stack is always the hull of the points so far, and the scan is O(n) amortized.
The $O(n \lg n)$ total is dominated by the sort; Jarvis march trades it for $O(nh)$, which wins exactly when the hull has few vertices ($h = o(\lg n)$).

quiz.q: Graham scan anchors at the point with the lowest $y$-coordinate (ties by lowest $x$) because:
options: it minimizes the total sort time
it is guaranteed to be a hull vertex, and all other points then lie at polar angles in a half-plane $[0°, 180°)$, so the angular order is well defined
it makes the hull come out clockwise
it guarantees all angular gaps are equal
quiz.explanation: The bottommost point is extreme, and from it every other point of Q sits in the closed upper half-plane — no angle exceeds 180°, so sorting by angle needs no wraparound case analysis.

quiz.q: In the worked example, why was $(4,3)$ popped when $(2,2)$ arrived?
options: its turn was clockwise — the cross product was negative
its turn was collinear — cross product zero, and collinear counts as a nonleft turn
it had the largest polar angle so far
it was the closest point to the anchor
quiz.explanation: $(6,4), (4,3), (2,2)$ all lie on one line: the cross product is exactly 0. Graham scan pops on nonleft turns — clockwise OR collinear — so middle points of collinear runs are removed and only the extremes survive.

quiz.q: The total running time of Graham scan is $O(n \lg n)$ because:
options: the scan loop may execute $\Theta(n^2)$ times in the worst case
each point is pushed once and popped at most once, so the scan is $O(n)$ and the angular sort dominates
the polar angles can be computed in $O(\lg n)$ each
the hull has at most $\lg n$ vertices
quiz.explanation: The two-counter argument caps total pops by total pushes; the sort is the bottleneck. (Sorting by angle via arctangent needs care with precision — CLRS compares with cross products instead.)

quiz.q: Jarvis march is preferable to Graham scan exactly when:
options: all points lie on the hull
the points are already sorted by $x$
the hull has few vertices — $h = o(\lg n)$ so $O(nh) < O(n \lg n)$
quiz.explanation: Jarvis costs one linear scan per hull edge: $O(nh)$. That beats $O(n \lg n)$ only for small hulls; when $h \approx n$ (points on a circle) it degrades to $O(n^2)$.

intro: The closest pair of points seems to demand $\Theta(n^2)$ comparisons — every pair against every pair. Divide and conquer cuts it to $O(n \lg n)$: split the points at the median $x$, recurse on both halves, and only the pairs straddling the dividing line can still beat the half-minimum $\delta$; those points lie in a strip of width $2\delta$. A packing argument then shows each strip point must be compared with at most its 7 successors in $y$-order, making the combine step linear.
objectives: Set up the divide, the recursion, and the minimum $\delta$ of the two halves
Prove the strip's width and the 7-neighbor bound via the packing argument
Solve the recurrence and explain why $O(n \lg n)$ is optimal in the algebraic decision-tree model

concepts.statement: Presort the points by $x$-coordinate once, $O(n \lg n)$. Each recursive step splits at the median $x$ into a left half $Q_L$ and a right half $Q_R$ of $n/2$ points, recurses to obtain $\delta_L$ and $\delta_R$, and sets $\delta = \min(\delta_L, \delta_R)$. Any pair with both points in the same half already has distance $\ge \delta$, so only cross pairs remain. To keep the combine step $O(n)$, the recursion also maintains the points of each half sorted by $y$, obtained by **merging** the two children's $y$-lists rather than re-sorting.
concepts.detail: Re-sorting by $y$ at every level would give $O(n \lg^2 n)$; the merge keeps every level linear, which is what the master theorem needs.

concepts.statement: The **strip** is the set of input points within distance $\delta$ of the dividing vertical line: $|x - x_{\text{mid}}| < \delta$, a band of total width $2\delta$. Any pair achieving distance below $\delta$ must have both points in the strip — one on each side, since a same-side pair is at distance $\ge \delta$. The combine step scans the strip points in $y$-order and, for each point $p$, compares $p$ with the following strip points only while their $y$-coordinate is within $\delta$.
concepts.detail: The strip typically contains far fewer than $n$ points; its size is data-dependent, but the argument below never needs it to be small — only the local packing matters.

concepts.statement: Fix a strip point $p$. Every strip point $q$ with $d(p, q) < \delta$ lies in the $2\delta \times \delta$ rectangle whose vertical sides are the strip boundaries and whose height is $\delta$ centered on $p$. That rectangle splits into two $\delta \times \delta$ squares, one per side of the line; within each square all points come from the same half, where pairwise distances are $\ge \delta$. A $\delta \times \delta$ square contains **at most 4** such points — 5 points would force two into the same $\delta/2 \times \delta/2$ quadrant at distance $\le \delta/\sqrt{2} < \delta$ (pigeonhole). So the rectangle holds at most 8 points including $p$: all candidates are among the **next 7 points in $y$-order**, and the whole strip scan is $O(n)$.
concepts.detail: The number 7 is not tight — 5 suffices with a finer cut — but 7 is the clean bound the rectangle argument yields, and constant is all that matters.

concepts.statement: The running time satisfies $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$ — two recursive calls plus a linear combine (strip scan and $y$-merge) — which the master theorem (case 2: $a = 2$, $b = 2$, $f(n) = \Theta(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 2})$) resolves to $T(n) = \Theta(n \lg n)$. This is optimal in the algebraic decision-tree model: the element-uniqueness problem (do any two of $n$ reals coincide?) reduces to closest pair by placing the reals on the $x$-axis — the minimum distance is 0 iff some element repeats — and element uniqueness has an $\Omega(n \lg n)$ lower bound there.
concepts.detail: So no exact algorithm that compares coordinates algebraically can beat $n \lg n$ in general; linear expected time is possible only against random distributions (grid hashing), outside the worst-case model.

concepts.statement: Sort once by $x$ (divide) and once by $y$ (strip order): recursion passes the $y$-sorted subarray filtered in $O(n)$ per level (merge-style), so total presort $O(n \lg n)$ plus $O(n \lg n)$ divide-and-conquer gives $O(n \lg n)$ overall with no $O(n \lg^2 n)$ log factor.
concepts.detail: Naive per-level $y$-sort would cost $O(n \lg n)$ per level ($O(n \lg^2 n)$ total); the linear filter (stable partition of $Y$ by midline) is what keeps the combine linear and the recurrence $T(n) = 2T(n/2)+O(n)$.

examples.title: Closest pair across the dividing line
examples.problem: Find the closest pair among $P = \{(0,0), (0,4), (2,2), (3,3), (5,0), (5,4)\}$ by the divide-and-conquer method.

steps.label: Step 1: Split at the median x
steps.text: The $x$-sorted points split evenly between $(2,2)$ and $(3,3)$: the dividing line is $x = 2.5$. Left half $Q_L = \{(0,0), (0,4), (2,2)\}$, right half $Q_R = \{(3,3), (5,0), (5,4)\}$.

steps.label: Step 2: Recurse
steps.text: In $Q_L$ the distances are $d((0,0),(0,4)) = 4$, $d((0,0),(2,2)) = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$, $d((0,4),(2,2)) = \sqrt{8}$, so $\delta_L = 2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.83$. In $Q_R$: $d((3,3),(5,0)) = \sqrt{13} \approx 3.61$, $d((3,3),(5,4)) = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.24$, $d((5,0),(5,4)) = 4$, so $\delta_R = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.24$. Hence $\delta = \min(\delta_L, \delta_R) = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.236$.

steps.label: Step 3: Build the strip
steps.text: Points with $|x - 2.5| < 2.236$, i.e. $0.264 < x < 4.736$: only $(2,2)$ and $(3,3)$ qualify — the pairs $(0,0)/(0,4)$ and $(5,0)/(5,4)$ sit outside the band on their sides.

steps.label: Step 4: Scan the strip in y-order
steps.text: The strip in increasing $y$: $(2,2)$, then $(3,3)$. Their distance is $\sqrt{(3-2)^2 + (3-2)^2} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 < \delta$ — a new champion. Since only two strip points exist, the 7-neighbor cap is far from binding; the packing lemma guarantees it never could be exceeded by genuine candidates.

steps.label: Step 5: Verify against the brute force
steps.text: Checking all 15 pairs confirms: the minimum is $\sqrt{2}$, achieved uniquely by $\{(2,2), (3,3)\}$. Note the winner straddles the dividing line — a same-side scan would never have found it; the strip exists precisely for this case.

examples.result: The closest pair is $(2,2)$ and $(3,3)$ at distance $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$, found by the strip scan with $\delta = \sqrt{5}$ descending from the two recursive halves.

examples.title: Seven neighbours suffice on the strip
examples.problem: Strip with $\delta = 1$ (half-minimum), points $y$-sorted $0, 0.5, 1.0, \ldots$. Why check only $7$ ahead from $y = 0$?

steps.label: Packing
steps.text: Halves left/right each have min distance $\delta = 1$: $1 \times 1$ squares hold at most $4$ points each? Precisely $\delta/2 \times \delta/2$ sub-squares hold $1$ point: $2\delta \times \delta$ strip window holds $\le 8$, so $7$ successors suffice.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: From $y = 0$, compare $y = 0.5, 1.0$ ($\le \delta$ in $y$? $1.0$ is boundary): farther points differ in $y$ by $> \delta$, hence distance $> \delta$ regardless of $x$.

steps.label: Linear combine
steps.text: Each strip point does $\le 7$ distance tests: $O(n)$ combine, recurrence $T(n) = 2T(n/2)+O(n) = O(n \lg n)$.

steps.label: Optimality
steps.text: Algebraic-decision-tree $\Omega(n \lg n)$ lower bound ( sorting reduces to closest pair) makes this optimal up to constants.

examples.result: $7$ successors per point, $O(n)$ strip scan: packing lemma turns quadratic strip into linear combine.

keyTakeaways: Split at the median $x$, recurse, take $\delta = \min(\delta_L, \delta_R)$; only strip pairs can beat $\delta$, and maintaining $y$-lists by merging keeps the combine linear.
Each strip point needs comparison with at most its 7 successors in $y$-order: the $2\delta \times \delta$ rectangle packs at most 8 points, four per $\delta \times \delta$ half.
$T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = \Theta(n \lg n)$ — and element uniqueness reduces to closest pair, so this is optimal among algebraic decision-tree algorithms.

quiz.q: The strip extends only $\delta$ to each side of the dividing line because:
options: wider strips would exceed the recursion depth

any pair closer than $\delta$ with both points on one side is impossible — same-side pairs are at distance $\ge \delta$ — so a beating pair must straddle, putting both points within $\delta$ of the line
the $y$-sorted list would otherwise be too long
points farther than $\delta$ from the line cannot be compared in constant time
quiz.explanation: Within each half the recursive minimum is already $\ge \delta$, so a sub-$\delta$ pair needs one point per half — and each point of such a pair lies within $\delta$ of the boundary.

quiz.q: Each point of the strip is compared only against the next 7 points in $y$-order because:
options: 7 is an empirical constant that works well
the $2\delta \times \delta$ rectangle around it holds at most 8 points: each $\delta \times \delta$ half contains at most 4 points that are pairwise $\ge \delta$ apart
the strip never contains more than 8 points in total
the $y$-sort puts candidates in blocks of 8
quiz.explanation: Pigeonhole on the four $\delta/2 \times \delta/2$ quadrants of a half-square: 5 points would force two within $\delta/\sqrt{2} < \delta$, contradicting the half's minimum. Two half-squares give at most 8 points, so 7 possible partners.

quiz.q: The recurrence $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$ solves to $O(n \lg n)$. What goes wrong if each level re-sorts the strip by $y$ instead of merging pre-sorted lists?
options: the algorithm becomes incorrect for even $n$
the combine cost rises to $O(n \lg n)$ per level, giving $O(n \lg^2 n)$ overall
the recursion no longer splits evenly
nothing — sorting and merging cost the same
quiz.explanation: An extra $\lg n$ factor inside each of the $\lg n$ levels: $2T(n/2) + O(n \lg n)$ solves to $O(n \lg^2 n)$. Merging the children's $y$-lists restores a linear combine.

quiz.q: Why is $\Omega(n \lg n)$ a barrier for closest pair in the algebraic decision-tree model?
options: because the median must be found by sorting
because element uniqueness reduces to it: put the reals on the x-axis and the minimum distance is 0 iff a duplicate exists
because the strip scan is inherently linear
it is not — an $O(n)$ worst-case algorithm exists
quiz.explanation: Element uniqueness carries an $\Omega(n \lg n)$ decision-tree lower bound, and the reduction preserves it — so worst-case exact closest-pair cannot be done in $o(n \lg n)$ with algebraic comparisons.

intro: Before we can say a problem is hard, we must say what an instance weighs and what an algorithm costs. This section fixes the vocabulary: abstract problems become bit strings through encodings, algorithms become language deciders, and polynomial time becomes the official border of tractability — a border that turns out to be astonishingly robust.
objectives: Explain why polynomial time is the definition of tractability and how it survives changes of machine model
Distinguish abstract problems from concrete ones via encodings, and predict when the encoding choice matters
Use the formal-language framework: alphabet, language, accepting versus deciding, and the class P

concepts.statement: An **abstract problem** $Q$ is a binary relation on a set $I$ of **problem instances** and a set $S$ of **problem solutions**: $Q \subseteq I \times S$. A **decision problem** restricts the solution set to $S = \{0, 1\}$ — every instance is a yes-instance or a no-instance — and it is the decision versions that the theory of this chapter classifies.
concepts.detail: Optimization problems convert to decision problems by adding a threshold: SHORTEST-PATH asks for a minimum-weight path, while PATH asks whether a path of weight at most $k$ exists. The versions are polynomially interrelated — you can binary-search the optimum with a decision oracle — so classifying the decision version classifies the problem.

concepts.statement: An **encoding** $e : I \to \{0,1\}^*$ maps abstract instances to binary strings; an abstract problem plus an encoding is a **concrete problem**, whose input size is the length $|e(x)|$. Complexity classes such as P are properties of concrete problems.
concepts.detail: Encodings that differ polynomially never change tractability: adjacency lists ($\Theta(V + E)$ bits) and adjacency matrices ($\Theta(V^2)$ bits) are polynomially related, so a polynomial algorithm for one yields a polynomial algorithm for the other. But binary and unary integer encodings are exponentially related: SUBSET-SUM becomes polynomial-time solvable under unary encoding — the pseudo-polynomial phenomenon that Chapter 35 turns into an approximation scheme.

concepts.statement: Let $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$ be the binary alphabet, $\Sigma^*$ the set of all finite binary strings (the **Kleene star**), and $\epsilon$ the empty string. A **language** is any subset $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$. An algorithm $A$ **accepts** a string $x$ when $A(x) = 1$ and **rejects** it when $A(x) = 0$.
concepts.detail: Acceptance is weaker than decision: $A$ **accepts the language** $L$ when $x \in L$ implies $A(x) = 1$, even if it runs forever on strings outside $L$; $A$ **decides** $L$ only if it also halts with 0 on every $x \notin L$. Decision — halting on every input — is what complexity classes demand.

concepts.statement: $$P = \{\, L \subseteq \{0,1\}^* : \text{some algorithm decides } L \text{ in } O(n^k) \text{ time for some constant } k \,\}$$ — the languages decidable in **polynomial time** in the input length $n$.
concepts.detail: Membership in P is a property of a language, not of one algorithm: a single clever polynomial-time decider promotes the language forever, however slow earlier attempts were.

concepts.term: Why polynomial time is the dividing line
concepts.statement: **Polynomial time is robust.** Reasonable machine models — random-access machines, Turing machines, actual computers — simulate one another with at most polynomial overhead, so the class of polynomial-time problems is model-independent. Polynomials are also **closed under composition**: a polynomial number of calls to polynomial-time subroutines is polynomial, which is exactly what lets reductions combine solvers later in this chapter.
concepts.detail: Empirically, natural problems in P come with low-degree algorithms, while problems outside P have resisted decades of attack. The degree still matters enormously in practice — $n^2$ beats $n^3$ — but as a coarse theory of tractability, polynomial time draws the only line that survives every reasonable formalization of computation.

examples.title: PATH: a decision problem, decided in polynomial time
examples.problem: A directed weighted graph has vertices s, a, b, t and arcs s→a (weight 2), a→t (3), s→b (1), b→t (6). Decide the PATH instances ⟨G, s, t, k⟩ for k = 5 and for k = 4.

steps.label: Step 1 — model
steps.text: PATH = the set of triples ⟨G, u, v, k⟩ such that G contains a path from u to v of total weight at most k. It is a decision problem: the answer is 0 or 1.

steps.label: Step 3 — compare with k
steps.text: For k = 5: $d(t) = 5 \leq 5$ — accept. For k = 4: $5 > 4$ — reject. Both answers followed from one shortest-path computation.

steps.label: Step 4 — cost
steps.text: Dijkstra with a binary heap runs in $O(E \lg V)$ — polynomial in the encoded instance length, so PATH ∈ P.

examples.result: PATH ∈ P; the same computation decides every threshold k by one comparison.

examples.title: When the encoding changes everything
examples.problem: The SUBSET-SUM instance ⟨{27, 38, 52}, 90⟩ is encoded (a) in binary and (b) in unary. Which encoding keeps the input small, and what does the classic O(n·t) dynamic program become?

steps.label: Binary
steps.text: Each number costs $\Theta(\lg t)$ bits: the whole instance has length $\Theta(n \lg t)$ — for this instance, about 6 bits per number plus 7 for t.

steps.label: Unary
steps.text: The target alone costs $t = 90$ bits; the instance length is $\Theta(n t)$ — exponentially larger than the binary encoding.

steps.label: Consequence
steps.text: The $O(n t)$ table-filling algorithm is polynomial in the unary length but exponential in the binary length — pseudo-polynomial time.

examples.result: SUBSET-SUM is only weakly intractable under binary encoding — the slack that Chapter 35’s FPTAS will exploit.

keyTakeaways: Tractability = polynomial time in the length of the encoding; P is a class of languages over {0,1}*.
Accepting a language is weaker than deciding it — a decider must halt on every input.
Polynomially related encodings (lists vs matrices) never move a problem across the P border; exponentially related ones (binary vs unary) can.

quiz.q: A polynomial-time algorithm written for a random-access machine is ported to a Turing machine. What is guaranteed?
options: It remains polynomial-time, possibly with a larger degree
It becomes exponential, since Turing machines are slower
Nothing can be said without knowing the algorithm
It stays within the same O-notation
quiz.explanation: Reasonable models simulate each other with polynomial overhead — that model-independence is precisely why P is defined by polynomials.

quiz.q: Algorithm A halts with output 1 exactly on the strings of language L and may loop forever elsewhere. Then A…
options: accepts L but does not decide it
quiz.explanation: A decider must halt with 0 on every non-member; A only guarantees correct 1s on members — it accepts but does not decide.

quiz.q: Adjacency lists use Θ(V + E) bits and the adjacency matrix Θ(V²). Why does the choice not affect membership in P?
options: The two lengths are polynomially related, so a polynomial algorithm for one encoding gives one for the other
P is defined only for list encodings
The matrix encoding is exponentially larger
quiz.explanation: Polynomially related encodings preserve polynomial solvability in both directions; only exponentially different encodings can separate.

quiz.q: Which of these is a decision problem in CLRS’s sense?
options: Find a shortest path from u to v
Is there a path from u to v of weight at most k?
Find the maximum clique in G
quiz.explanation: The threshold parameter k makes it a yes/no question — the other three ask for a witness object, not a bit.

intro: Finding a Hamiltonian cycle looks hopeless; certifying one is trivial. This asymmetry — hard to search, easy to check — defines the class NP. This section formalizes verification, states NP exactly, and maps the border country where P, NP and co-NP meet but whose walls nobody has been able to climb.
objectives: Define verification algorithms and certificates, and verify a HAM-CYCLE instance by hand
State the formal definition of NP via polynomially bounded, polynomially checkable certificates
Situate co-NP, NP ∩ co-NP and P relative to one another, separating known facts from open questions

concepts.statement: A **verification algorithm** $A$ takes two inputs: an instance $x$ and a **certificate** $y$. It **verifies** $x$ if there exists a $y$ with $A(x, y) = 1$ — the certificate is evidence that $x$ is a yes-instance. The running time is measured in $|x|$, the instance length alone.
concepts.detail: The certificate is supplied by a hypothetical prover; the verifier only checks. For PATH, a certificate is the path itself and the checker sums its weights; for HAM-CYCLE, the purported cycle; for 3-CNF-SAT, the satisfying assignment.

concepts.statement: A **certificate** for a yes-instance is any string that convinces the verifier. Crucially, certificates are quantified existentially: the problem ‘has’ one iff some string of polynomial length works — nobody needs to produce it efficiently for membership in NP.
concepts.detail: What a certificate is NOT: a hint. It must carry complete, checkable proof of the yes-answer. For COMPOSITES the certificate is a nontrivial factor; for (the complement language) primality, Pratt certificates prove primality — both directions are checkable, which is why COMPOSITES sits in NP ∩ co-NP.

concepts.statement: A language $L$ belongs to **NP** if there is a two-input polynomial-time algorithm $A$ and a constant $c$ such that $$L = \{\, x : \exists\, y \in \{0,1\}^*,\ |y| \leq |x|^c \text{ and } A(x, y) = 1 \,\}.$$ Equivalently: NP is the class of languages whose yes-instances have polynomial-size, polynomially checkable certificates.
concepts.detail: The initials stand for **nondeterministic polynomial time** — a nondeterministic machine guesses a certificate and verifies it in polynomial time. Since a decider may ignore its certificate, $P \subseteq NP$; whether the inclusion is strict is the P versus NP question.

concepts.statement: No polynomial-time algorithm is known for HAM-CYCLE — brute force inspects up to $(n-1)!/2$ candidate cycles — yet verification is easy: check that the proposed sequence visits every vertex exactly once and that each of the $n$ consecutive pairs (including the wraparound) is an edge of the graph. NP collects exactly the problems with this search/check asymmetry.
concepts.detail: The lesson generalizes: a verification algorithm is a weak form of algorithm, because it gets help. The entire chapter’s drama is that for NP-complete problems, no amount of cleverness has converted this weak help back into a real algorithm.

concepts.term: co-NP and the border with P
concepts.statement: **co-NP** is the class of languages whose complements lie in NP: $L \in \text{co-NP}$ iff $\bar{L} \in NP$. COMPOSITES lies in NP ∩ co-NP — a factor certifies compositeness, a Pratt certificate certifies primality — while no such dual certificates are known for SAT.
concepts.detail: Whether NP = co-NP is open, exactly like P versus NP, and P ⊆ NP ∩ co-NP is known (decide the problem, ignore the certificate). Since the AKS algorithm (2002), PRIMES is known to lie in P outright — a rare wall that did fall.

figures.caption: The landscape of classes, after CLRS Figure 34.3. P sits inside the lens NP ∩ co-NP; NP-complete problems live in NP but (conjecturally) outside co-NP. Whether any region properly contains another beyond P ⊆ NP ∩ co-NP is open.

examples.title: Verifying a Hamiltonian cycle
examples.problem: Let G have vertex set {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and edge set {12, 23, 34, 45, 51, 13}. Verify the certificate y = ⟨1, 2, 3, 4, 5⟩, then the certificate y′ = ⟨1, 3, 2, 4, 5⟩.

steps.label: Step 1 — format
steps.text: A certificate lists 5 vertices claiming the Hamiltonian cycle $v_1 \to v_2 \to v_3 \to v_4 \to v_5 \to v_1$.

steps.label: Step 2 — distinctness
steps.text: For y: the entries 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are all distinct ✓. For y′: 1, 3, 2, 4, 5 — also distinct ✓.

steps.label: Step 3 — edges
steps.text: y: 12 ∈ E ✓, 23 ∈ E ✓, 34 ∈ E ✓, 45 ∈ E ✓, 51 ∈ E ✓ — verified, G is Hamiltonian. y′: 13 ∈ E ✓, 32 = 23 ∈ E ✓, but 24 ∉ E ✗ — reject.

steps.label: Step 4 — cost
steps.text: Five lookups plus a duplicate scan: $O(V + E)$ work, polynomial in the instance — HAM-CYCLE ∈ NP.

examples.result: y verifies; y′ dies on the missing edge 24. Checking never searched the 12 possible cycles.

examples.title: Verifying VERTEX-COVER
examples.problem: Graph path $1-2-3-4$, certificate $C = \{2,3\}$, $k = 2$. Verify in polynomial time.

steps.label: Edges
steps.text: Check each edge has an endpoint in $C$: $1-2$ ($2$ ✓), $2-3$ ($2$ ✓), $3-4$ ($3$ ✓): $O(|E|)$ scans.

steps.label: Certificate length
steps.text: $|C| \le |V|$: polynomially bounded in input size ✓.

steps.label: NP membership
steps.text: Verifier $O(V+E)$: VERTEX-COVER $\in$ NP (finding $C$ is hard, checking is easy: the asymmetry defining NP).

examples.result: $C = \{2,3\}$ verified in $O(V+E)$: certificates are short and checkable, search is not.

keyTakeaways: NP means polynomially verifiable, not polynomially solvable — certificates plus checkers.
The certificate bound |y| ≤ |x|^c is what keeps verification polynomial in the instance alone.
P ⊆ NP ∩ co-NP is known; NP versus co-NP, like P versus NP, is open.

quiz.q: HAM-CYCLE belongs to NP because…
options: a polynomial-time algorithm finds a Hamiltonian cycle in any graph
a proposed cycle of n vertices can be checked against E in polynomial time
every graph has a Hamiltonian cycle
the complement of HAM-CYCLE is in P
quiz.explanation: Membership in NP needs only a checker: the cycle itself is the certificate, verified by n edge lookups and a distinctness scan.

quiz.q: Why does the definition of NP bound the certificate by |x|^c?
options: To keep the verifier’s runtime polynomial in |x|, since it must at least read y
To make NP a subset of P
Because certificates are always short in practice
quiz.explanation: An exponentially long certificate would make even a linear scan of it exponential in |x|; the polynomial bound is part of what ‘verification’ means.

quiz.q: If a problem is in NP, what follows about its complement?
options: Nothing — whether NP = co-NP is open
quiz.explanation: By definition the complement is in co-NP; whether it is also in NP would follow from NP = co-NP, a famous open question.

quiz.q: Which containment is actually known (not open)?
quiz.explanation: A polynomial-time decider serves as its own verifier with an empty certificate; every other displayed relation is unresolved.

intro: Reducibility is the chapter’s engine: one problem translated into another so that a solver for the second solves the first. With it come the definitions of NP-hard and NP-complete, the collapse theorem tying them all to P versus NP, and the seed of the entire theory — the circuit-satisfiability problem, whose NP-completeness is proved straight from the definition of NP.
objectives: Define polynomial-time reducibility and use its transitivity and P-closure, including the output-length lemma
State NP-hard and NP-complete, and prove the collapse theorem: one NP-complete problem in P implies P = NP
Reproduce the proof that CIRCUIT-SAT is NP-complete — the seed reduction

concepts.statement: A language $L_1$ is **polynomial-time reducible** to $L_2$, written $L_1 \leq_p L_2$, if a polynomial-time computable function $f : \{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}^*$ satisfies $$x \in L_1 \iff f(x) \in L_2 \quad \text{for every } x.$$ Intuition: $L_2$ is **at least as hard** as $L_1$ — compose $f$ with a solver for $L_2$ to solve $L_1$.
concepts.detail: The direction is the classic trap: the reduction flows FROM the hard-known problem TO the target. Writing $L_1 \leq_p L_2$ reads ‘$L_1$ is no harder than $L_2$’, like an inequality between difficulties.

concepts.statement: **Transitivity.** $L_1 \leq_p L_2$ and $L_2 \leq_p L_3$ imply $L_1 \leq_p L_3$: compose the functions; running times and degrees multiply. **P-closure.** If $L_1 \leq_p L_2$ and $L_2 \in P$, then $L_1 \in P$. The hidden lemma making both work: a reduction running $O(n^k)$ steps **outputs at most $O(n^k)$ bits** — a machine cannot write more bits than steps — so the downstream solver’s input is polynomially long.
concepts.detail: Skip the output-length lemma and the closure proof is subtly broken: the second algorithm’s running time must be polynomial in $n$, not in an unbounded $|f(x)|$.

concepts.statement: A language $L$ is **NP-hard** if every language $L' \in NP$ satisfies $L' \leq_p L$ — everything in NP reduces to it. $L$ is **NP-complete** if it is NP-hard **and** $L \in NP$. NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP; thousands are now known.
concepts.detail: NP-hard alone does not require membership in NP — a problem can sit above the class entirely. NP-completeness is the conjunction: hard for all of NP, and inside it.

concepts.statement: **If any NP-complete problem lies in P, then P = NP.** Dually, if any single problem in NP lies outside P, then no NP-complete problem lies in P. The reason: if the NP-complete $L$ is decidable in polynomial time, so is every $L' \in NP$, because $L' \leq_p L$ and P is closed under reductions.
concepts.detail: This is why one efficient SAT solver would settle every open problem in the catalog at once — and why, conversely, decades of failure on SAT are evidence (though not proof) that P ≠ NP.

concepts.statement: **CIRCUIT-SAT is NP-complete.** *In NP:* the certificate assigns 0/1 to each input wire; evaluating gates in topological order verifies the output is 1 in time linear in the circuit size. *NP-hard:* for any $L \in NP$ with verifier $A(x, y)$ and bound $|y| \leq |x|^c$, fix $x$ and construct a combinational circuit whose input variables are the bits of $y$ and whose gates compute $A(x, y)$ — the verifier’s execution, unrolled computation-step by computation-step with $x$ hard-wired as constants. The circuit outputs 1 for some $y$ iff $x \in L$.
concepts.detail: Every layer of the unrolled computation has polynomial size because $A$ runs in polynomial time — that is precisely where ‘polynomial verification’ becomes ‘polynomial circuitry’. The construction is the theoretical ancestor of the practical observation that any computation is a circuit.

figures.caption: A satisfiable combinational circuit computing $y = (x_1 \land \neg x_2) \lor x_3$. The annotated assignment $(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (1, 0, 0)$ propagates to $y = 1$; checking it gate by gate is exactly the certificate verification in CIRCUIT-SAT ∈ NP.
