examples.title: The ultracentrifuge
examples.problem: An ultracentrifuge spins a sample at 75 000 revolutions per minute, at a point 4.00 cm from the rotation axis. Find the speed there and the centripetal acceleration, in m/s² and in units of $g$.

steps.label: Rate to frequency
steps.text: 75 000 rev/min $= 1250$ rev/s, so each revolution takes $T = 1/1250 = 8.0 \times 10^{-4}$ s.

steps.label: Speed
steps.text: $v = 2\pi r f = 2\pi(0.0400)(1250) = 314$ m/s — faster than most aircraft.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: This is why ultracentrifuges can sort viruses by mass — and why their rotors are forged from titanium.

examples.title: Uniform Circular Motion: centripetal numbers
examples.problem: A car rounds a curve of radius $25\ \text{m}$ at $15\ \text{m/s}$. Find the centripetal acceleration.

steps.label: Formula
steps.text: $a = v^2/r$ toward the center.

examples.result: $a \approx 9\ \text{m/s}^2$ inward.

keyTakeaways: Uniform circular motion is accelerated motion: the direction of $\vec v$ turns continuously.
$a = v^2/r$ centripetal, perpendicular to $\vec v$ — constant speed by construction.
$v = 2\pi r/T$ links speed, radius and period; the two routes to $a$ agree: $v^2/r = 4\pi^2r/T^2$.

quiz.q: A particle moves at constant speed on a circle. Its acceleration points
quiz.explanation: Only the velocity's direction changes, and turning toward the next tangent means steering toward the center — centripetal, always.

quiz.q: Doubling the speed at fixed radius changes the centripetal acceleration by a factor of
quiz.explanation: $a = v^2/r$ is quadratic in the speed: $2v$ gives $4a$.

quiz.q: On a circular track of radius 50 m a cyclist rides at 10 m/s. The acceleration is
quiz.explanation: $a = v^2/r = 100/50 = 2.0$ m/s², directed toward the center of the track.

quiz.q: The period and speed of uniform circular motion are related by
quiz.explanation: One period covers one circumference: speed = distance over time = $2\pi r/T$.

intro: What is physics? The passenger was walking at 2 m/s — measured by whom? Every velocity is a statement about two things: the object moving and the frame doing the measuring. This section builds the one-dimensional bookkeeping that connects them — two subscripts and one addition — and shows why a strolling passenger can be breaking the speed limit relative to the ground.
objectives: Use the two-subscript notation $x_{PA}$ and identify what each subscript names
Apply $x_{PA} = x_{PB} + x_{BA}$ and its differentiated consequences for velocities
Translate one-dimensional motion between frames moving at constant relative velocity

concepts.statement: **A reference frame is the body from which a measurement is made — the track, the train, the riverbank.** The subscript pattern $x_{PA}$ reads: the position of P as measured in frame A — first subscript the object, second the frame.
concepts.detail: Reversing the subscripts negates: $x_{AB} = -x_{BA}$. The pattern of inner cancellation is exactly like fractions.

concepts.statement: **$x_{PA} = x_{PB} + x_{BA}$**: the position of P relative to A equals its position relative to B plus the position of B relative to A.
concepts.detail: The chain generalizes over any number of frames — Zurich time plus Zurich–Paris offset plus Paris–Rome offset gives Rome time.

concepts.statement: **Differentiating gives $v_{PA} = v_{PB} + v_{BA}$, and once more $a_{PA} = a_{PB} + a_{BA}$ — which collapses to $a_{PA} = a_{PB}$ whenever the frames move at constant relative velocity.**
concepts.detail: All constant-velocity observers measure the same acceleration — the fact that makes inertial frames special in Chapter 5.

concepts.statement: **In 1D the whole machinery is signed addition: pick the positive direction once, then add the velocities with their signs.**
concepts.detail: Most relative-motion errors are sign errors born of switching the convention mid-problem.

concepts.term: Relative Motion in One Dimension: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Relative Motion in One Dimension problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is decoupling 2D motion into independent 1D motions sharing the clock $t$; the working equation is $\vec r = x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$, $\vec v = d\vec r/dt$, $R = v_0^2\sin 2\theta_0/g$, $a = v^2/r$, $\vec v_{PA} = \vec v_{PB}+\vec v_{BA}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{m/s}$, $\text{m/s}^2$ and vector direction) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against ranges $10$--$100\ \text{m}$ for $v_0\sim 20\ \text{m/s}$; centrifuge $a_c$ to $10^5g$; no air, uniform $g$, $v\ll c$; frames must be inertial for $\vec a$ agreement.

examples.title: Walking the aisle
examples.problem: A train moves at 20 m/s in the $+x$ direction. A passenger walks at 1.5 m/s relative to the train, (a) toward the front and (b) toward the rear. Find her velocity relative to the ground in each case. (c) Two cyclists then approach one another at 5.0 m/s and 3.0 m/s in this same frame; find the velocity of the first relative to the second.

steps.label: Identify frames
steps.text: P = passenger, B = train, A = ground. Given $v_{BA} = +20$ m/s and $v_{PB} = \pm 1.5$ m/s.

steps.label: (b) Toward the rear
steps.text: $v_{PA} = -1.5 + 20 = +18.5$ m/s — still forward, just slower.

steps.label: (c) Cyclists
steps.text: $v_{12} = v_{1A} - v_{2A} = 5.0 - (-3.0) = +8.0$ m/s: each measures the other closing at 8.0 m/s.

examples.result: (a) +21.5 m/s, (b) +18.5 m/s, both forward; (c) the cyclists close at 8.0 m/s.

examples.title: Relative Motion in One Dimension: frame addition check
examples.problem: A train moves at $20\ \text{m/s}$ and a passenger walks at $1.5\ \text{m/s}$ relative to the train toward the front. What is the passenger speed over the ground?

steps.label: Add
steps.text: $v_{PA} = 1.5+20 = 21.5\ \text{m/s}$ forward.

steps.label: Rear check
steps.text: Walking rearward gives $-1.5+20 = 18.5\ \text{m/s}$ — still forward.

examples.result: $21.5\ \text{m/s}$ forward ($18.5$ rearward).

keyTakeaways: $x_{PA} = x_{PB} + x_{BA}$; differentiate twice for velocities and accelerations.
Subscripts cancel like fractions; reversing the order negates the quantity.
Constant-velocity frames always agree on acceleration.

quiz.q: In the notation $v_{PA}$, the second subscript names
options: the frame from which the velocity is measured
quiz.explanation: First subscript = object, second = observer's frame: $v_{PA}$ is the velocity of P as A measures it.

quiz.q: Two cars approach each other, one at +12 m/s and one at −15 m/s in the ground frame. The velocity of the first car relative to the second is
quiz.explanation: $v_{12} = v_{1G} - v_{2G} = 12 - (-15) = +27$ m/s: head-on approach at 27 m/s in the first car's frame.

quiz.q: You walk at 1.5 m/s toward the rear of a train moving forward at 20 m/s. Relative to the ground you move
quiz.explanation: $v_{PG} = -1.5 + 20 = +18.5$ m/s — walking backward on a forward train still means moving forward over the ground.

quiz.q: If frame B moves at constant velocity relative to frame A, observers in A and B disagree about an object's
quiz.explanation: Velocities transform by adding $v_{BA}$; the time derivative of a constant is zero, so accelerations agree.

intro: What is physics? A plane in a crosswind, a boat crossing a river, raindrops seen through a bus window — in two dimensions the frame connection is no longer signed addition but vector addition, and geometry returns with a vengeance. One diagram, two known arrows, one unknown: this section teaches the recipe that navigators and pilots run before every leg.
objectives: Apply the vector relation $\vec v_{PA} = \vec v_{PB} + \vec v_{BA}$ with head-to-tail geometry
Solve for drift, and for the heading that cancels it (the wind-correction angle)
Explain why accelerations agree across constant-velocity frames

concepts.statement: **$\vec v_{PA} = \vec v_{PB} + \vec v_{BA}$ — the same two-subscript addition as in one dimension, now with arrows.** Attach the vectors head to tail and read off the resultant.
concepts.detail: Given any two of the three velocities, the third follows from vector addition or subtraction; sketching the triangle first prevents most sign catastrophes.

concepts.statement: **A vehicle pointed one way in a cross flow travels another way over the ground: the current's velocity simply adds to the vehicle's heading velocity.** The ground track is the diagonal of the parallelogram.
concepts.detail: Drift is why light aircraft hang crooked in a crosswind — nose crabbed into the wind, ground track straight.

concepts.statement: **To travel straight across a flow, aim upstream by the angle whose sine is $v_{\text{flow}}/v_{\text{craft}}$; the ground speed drops to $\sqrt{v_{\text{craft}}^2 - v_{\text{flow}}^2}$.**
concepts.detail: Pilots call it the wind-correction angle; the arithmetic is one right triangle.

concepts.statement: **When B moves at constant velocity relative to A, $\vec a_{PA} = \vec a_{PB}$: all constant-velocity observers agree on accelerations.** This invariance is the seed of relativity — Galileo's, and later Einstein's.
concepts.detail: It is also why Chapter 5's laws can be stated once, without appending a list of preferred observers.

concepts.term: Relative Motion in Two Dimensions: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Relative Motion in Two Dimensions problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is decoupling 2D motion into independent 1D motions sharing the clock $t$; the working equation is $\vec r = x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$, $\vec v = d\vec r/dt$, $R = v_0^2\sin 2\theta_0/g$, $a = v^2/r$, $\vec v_{PA} = \vec v_{PB}+\vec v_{BA}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{m/s}$, $\text{m/s}^2$ and vector direction) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against ranges $10$--$100\ \text{m}$ for $v_0\sim 20\ \text{m/s}$; centrifuge $a_c$ to $10^5g$; no air, uniform $g$, $v\ll c$; frames must be inertial for $\vec a$ agreement.

examples.title: A light aircraft in a crosswind
examples.problem: A light aircraft has airspeed (speed relative to the air) 215 km/h, pointed due north. The wind blows at 65 km/h toward the east. (a) Find the plane's velocity relative to the ground. (b) To actually travel due north, at what angle must the pilot head, and what is the ground speed then?

steps.label: (a) Add the vectors
steps.text: $\vec v_{PG} = \vec v_{PA} + \vec v_{AG}$: 215 north plus 65 east gives $|\vec v_{PG}| = \sqrt{215^2 + 65^2} = \sqrt{50\,450} = 225$ km/h.

steps.label: Direction of drift
steps.text: The drift angle east of north is $\tan^{-1}(65/215) = 16.8°$ — the nose points north but the track runs 17° east of it.

steps.label: (b) Cancel the wind
steps.text: Head west of north by $\alpha$ with $215\sin\alpha = 65$, so $\alpha = \sin^{-1}(65/215) = 17.6°$.

steps.label: Ground speed
steps.text: $v_{PG} = 215\cos 17.6° = 205$ km/h — straight north, but slower than the airspeed: the wind's toll.

examples.result: (a) 225 km/h at 16.8° east of north; (b) head 17.6° west of north at 205 km/h.

examples.title: Relative Motion in Two Dimensions: frame addition check
examples.problem: A train moves at $20\ \text{m/s}$ and a passenger walks at $1.5\ \text{m/s}$ relative to the train toward the front. What is the passenger speed over the ground?

steps.label: Add
steps.text: $v_{PA} = 1.5+20 = 21.5\ \text{m/s}$ forward.

steps.label: Rear check
steps.text: Walking rearward gives $-1.5+20 = 18.5\ \text{m/s}$ — still forward.

examples.result: $21.5\ \text{m/s}$ forward ($18.5$ rearward).

keyTakeaways: $\vec v_{PA} = \vec v_{PB} + \vec v_{BA}$ as vector addition — draw the triangle before computing.
Crosswinds and currents cause drift; cancel them by aiming upstream, at the price of ground speed.
All constant-velocity observers measure the same acceleration — Galileo's invariance.

quiz.q: A boat that can travel 4.0 km/h in still water aims straight north across a river flowing at 3.0 km/h east. Its ground velocity is
quiz.explanation: The vectors 4.0 north and 3.0 east add to $\sqrt{16 + 9} = 5.0$ km/h at $\tan^{-1}(3/4) = 37°$ east of north.

quiz.q: To reach the point directly opposite on that river, the boater must aim
options: due north anyway and accept the drift
quiz.explanation: The upstream aim satisfies $\sin\alpha = 3.0/4.0$, giving $\alpha = 48.6°$ west of north, with the crossing speed dropping to $\sqrt{16 - 9} = 2.6$ km/h.

quiz.q: A bus moves east at 10 m/s while rain falls vertically at 8.0 m/s relative to the ground. To a passenger, the rain's velocity is
options: 12.8 m/s, tilted toward the front of the bus
12.8 m/s, tilted toward the rear of the bus
quiz.explanation: Chain the frames: $\vec v_{RB} = \vec v_{RG} + \vec v_{GB}$ with $\vec v_{GB} = -\vec v_{BG}$ pointing west at 10 m/s. The rain thus gains a 10 m/s westward component in the bus frame: 12.8 m/s at $\tan^{-1}(10/8) = 51°$ from vertical, slanting toward the rear of the bus.

quiz.q: Observers in two frames moving at constant relative velocity will agree on the value of
options: all three: position, velocity and acceleration
quiz.explanation: Position and velocity pick up frame-dependent offsets; the acceleration is untouched because the relative velocity is constant.

intro: Chapters 2–4 were kinematics: they described motion without asking what changes it. This chapter opens dynamics, where force is the agent of change. Newton's first law tells us when velocity stays put; his second law says exactly how much acceleration a given net force produces in a given mass.
objectives: State Newton's first law and explain how it singles out inertial reference frames as the arenas where Newtonian mechanics holds
Apply Newton's second law, $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$, component by component, to find a body's acceleration from the forces acting on it
Treat mass as the measure of inertia and use the newton, a derived unit equal to 1 kg·m/s²

concepts.statement: **A force is a push or a pull, and it is the agent of change in mechanics.** Force is a vector: every force has a magnitude, a direction, and a line of action, and several forces combine into their vector sum, the net force $\vec{F}_{net} = \sum \vec{F}$. Dynamics is the study of how forces change motion.
concepts.detail: Forces arise from interactions — a rope's tug, a floor's push, air's drag, Earth's pull — and are measured in newtons, with the spring scale as the everyday instrument.

concepts.statement: **If no net force acts on a body, the body's velocity cannot change.** A body at rest stays at rest; a moving body keeps its speed and direction. Uniform motion needs no cause and no sustaining agent.
concepts.detail: The first law defines an inertial reference frame: a frame in which the law holds. Frames accelerating relative to an inertial frame are not inertial, and Newton's laws as stated fail there. The ground is inertial only to good approximation — its acceleration from Earth's rotation is small for laboratory purposes.

concepts.statement: **Mass is the measure of inertia: the resistance of a body to a change in its velocity.** Apply the same net force to two bodies: the one that accelerates less has the larger mass. Mass is a scalar, measured in kilograms.
concepts.detail: HRW operationalizes the comparison: put each body in turn on a frictionless surface, apply the same force, and compare accelerations. Doubling the mass halves the acceleration produced by the same force.

concepts.statement: **The net force on a body equals the product of its mass and its acceleration: $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$.** The acceleration points along the net force, and the vector equation is three scalar equations at once: $F_{net,x} = ma_x$, $F_{net,y} = ma_y$, $F_{net,z} = ma_z$.
concepts.detail: Read it carefully: $m\vec{a}$ is not a force — it is what the vector sum of the real forces equals. The law holds in inertial frames for bodies of constant mass, and it is the working equation for the rest of this book.

concepts.term: Newton's First and Second Laws: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Newton's First and Second Laws problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Newton's laws with $\vec F_{\text{net}} = m\vec a$; the working equation is $\vec F_{\text{net}} = m\vec a$, $W = mg$, $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (newtons and free-body arrows) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $1\ \text{N}$ (apple) to $10^4\ \text{N}$ (braking car); inertial frames only; $m$ constant and $v\ll c$.

examples.title: Two forces at right angles
examples.problem: A 2.0 kg puck on frictionless ice is pushed simultaneously by a 3.0 N force aimed east and a 4.0 N force aimed north. Find the puck's acceleration (magnitude and direction).

steps.label: Add first
steps.text: The second law uses the net force, so the two pushes must be added as vectors before dividing by the mass. East and north are perpendicular.

steps.label: Magnitude
steps.text: The forces form a 3–4–5 right triangle: $F_{net} = \sqrt{(3.0)^2 + (4.0)^2} = 5.0$ N.

steps.label: Direction
steps.text: $\tan\theta = 4.0/3.0$ gives $\theta = 53^{\circ}$ north of east.

steps.label: Second law
steps.text: $a = F_{net}/m = 5.0/2.0 = 2.5$ m/s² at $53^{\circ}$ north of east.

examples.result: $\vec{a} = 2.5$ m/s² at $53^{\circ}$ north of east (components $a_x = 1.5$, $a_y = 2.0$ m/s²).

examples.title: An emergency stop
examples.problem: The driver of a 1200 kg car brakes hard; the road's frictional force on the tires is a constant 6.0 kN opposite the motion. The car enters the braking at 25 m/s. How long, and how far, does it take to stop?

steps.label: Acceleration
steps.text: $a = F/m = 6000/1200 = 5.0$ m/s², directed opposite the motion.

examples.result: The car stops in 5.0 s after 62.5 m — about two football fields of warning that speed costs distance.

keyTakeaways: Only the net force matters: forces are vectors and must be added before Newton's second law is applied.
The first law defines inertial frames — uniform motion is the natural state that needs no cause.
The second law $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$ is a vector equation; the newton is the derived unit 1 kg·m/s².

quiz.q: Which statement is Newton's first law?
options: A body on which no net force acts keeps its velocity constant in both magnitude and direction
A body at rest remains at rest unless a force starts it moving
Any moving body must be pushed along by a force in the direction of motion
In the absence of forces all bodies eventually come to rest
quiz.explanation: Constant velocity — which includes rest — is the force-free state. Only changes of velocity need a cause, which is exactly the opposite of the old idea that motion needs a sustaining push.

quiz.q: The same net force is applied in turn to body A and to body B, which has four times A's mass. The acceleration of B is:
quiz.explanation: Since $a = F/m$, quadrupling the mass at fixed force divides the acceleration by four.

quiz.q: A puck on frictionless ice is pushed by two perpendicular forces, 6.0 N and 8.0 N. The direction of the acceleration is:
options: impossible to determine without the puck's mass
along the diagonal — a 10 N resultant at 53° from the 6 N force
quiz.explanation: The acceleration points along the net force, which for perpendicular 6 N and 8 N pushes is the 10 N diagonal. The mass sets the size of $a$, not its direction.

intro: Four particular forces account for almost every everyday situation: the gravitational pull we call weight, the perpendicular push of a surface (the normal force), the pull of a taut cord (tension), and the parallel push of a surface (friction). Their exact behavior holds surprises — the normal force is not always $mg$, and an ideal cord pulls equally at both ends — and learning those surprises is what makes Newton's laws usable.
objectives: Compute a body's weight from its mass, and keep weight (a force) separate from mass (a scalar property)
Find the normal force from Newton's second law, and explain why it equals $mg$ only in special cases
Describe tension in an ideal cord and name the static/kinetic split within the friction family

concepts.statement: **The weight $\vec{F}_g$ of a body is the force on it due to gravity. Near Earth's surface it is a vector of magnitude $W = mg$ pointing straight down**, with $g = 9.8$ m/s².
concepts.detail: Mass and weight are different things. Mass (kg) measures inertia and belongs to the body; weight (N) is a force that depends on the local gravitational field. On the Moon ($g = 1.7$ m/s²) a 70 kg astronaut still has mass 70 kg but weighs about 120 N — a sixth of the 686 N weighed on Earth.

concepts.statement: **The normal force is the component, perpendicular to the surface, of the force a surface exerts on a body in contact with it.** Its magnitude is NOT fixed at $mg$: the surface pushes exactly as hard as Newton's laws require — no more, no less.
concepts.detail: Microscopically, the surface's atoms act like little springs. Press down on a book and the table's normal force grows by the same amount; the equation that fixes its value is $\sum F_y = ma_y$ applied to the body.

concepts.statement: **Tension is the force a taut cord exerts on whatever it is attached to — directed along the cord, pulling away from the body.** For an ideal cord (massless, inextensible) passing over a frictionless pulley, the magnitude $T$ is the same everywhere.
concepts.detail: A rope can only pull, never push. Real ropes stretch slightly and carry mass, but the idealization is superb for the problems of this chapter.

concepts.statement: **Friction is the component of a surface's force parallel to the surface.** When the surfaces grip without sliding it is static friction, self-adjusting up to a maximum $f_{s,max} = \mu_s N$; once sliding occurs it is kinetic friction, fixed at $f_k = \mu_k N$ and opposing the sliding.
concepts.detail: Chapter 6 develops friction fully. The point to carry out of this section is the split: static friction adjusts to what equilibrium demands (up to its limit), while kinetic friction has one fixed value set by $\mu_k$ and $N$.

concepts.statement: **Solve Some Particular Forces problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Newton's laws with $\vec F_{\text{net}} = m\vec a$; the working equation is $\vec F_{\text{net}} = m\vec a$, $W = mg$, $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (newtons and free-body arrows) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $1\ \text{N}$ (apple) to $10^4\ \text{N}$ (braking car); inertial frames only; $m$ constant and $v\ll c$.

examples.title: The bathroom scale in an elevator
examples.problem: A 72 kg passenger stands on a scale in an elevator that accelerates (a) upward at 3.2 m/s² and (b) downward at 3.2 m/s². What does the scale read in each case, and at rest?

steps.label: FBD
steps.text: The passenger touches only the scale. Forces: weight $mg$ down and the normal force $N$ up — and the scale reads $N$, the apparent weight.

steps.label: Upward case
steps.text: With +y up: $N - mg = ma$, so $N = m(g + a) = 72 \times (9.8 + 3.2) = 72 \times 13.0 = 936$ N.

steps.label: At rest
steps.text: $a = 0$, so $N = mg = 706$ N — the reading you know from your bathroom.

examples.result: 936 N accelerating up, 475 N accelerating down, 706 N at rest: apparent weight tracks $m(g \pm a)$.

examples.title: A chandelier on two wires
examples.problem: A 5.0 kg chandelier hangs from a knot where two wires meet: wire 2 runs up and to the right at 40° above the horizontal to the ceiling, and wire 1 runs horizontally to a wall. Find the tension in each wire.

steps.label: Equilibrium
steps.text: The chandelier pulls the knot down with $mg = 49$ N, and nothing accelerates, so $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$ at the knot.

examples.result: $T_2 \approx 76$ N along the angled wire, $T_1 \approx 58$ N along the horizontal wire — the angled wire carries more because it also holds the weight.

keyTakeaways: Weight is a force of magnitude $mg$ directed down; mass is inertia in kilograms and never changes with location.
The normal force is whatever a surface must push with to satisfy Newton's second law — it equals $mg$ only when nothing else pushes vertically and there is no vertical acceleration.
An ideal cord transmits one tension magnitude along its length and past a frictionless pulley; friction splits into self-adjusting static and fixed kinetic.

quiz.q: A 10 kg crate sits on the floor while you push down on it with an extra 20 N. The normal force of the floor on the crate is:
quiz.explanation: Equilibrium in the vertical direction requires $N = mg + 20 = 98 + 20 = 118$ N. The normal force adjusts to the total demand.

quiz.q: An astronaut stands on Mars, where $g = 3.7$ m/s². Compared with Earth, the astronaut's mass and weight are:
options: mass the same, weight about 0.38 times
mass about 0.38 times, weight the same
quiz.explanation: Mass is intrinsic to the body; weight $= mg$ scales with the local field: $3.7/9.8 \approx 0.38$.

quiz.q: You pull horizontally on a heavy trunk and it does not budge. The friction on it:
options: matches your pull, whatever it is, up to the limit $\mu_s N$
quiz.explanation: Static friction self-adjusts to balance the applied force until the impending-motion maximum $\mu_s N$ is reached; $\mu_s N$ is only the ceiling, not the value.

intro: Newton's third law ties every force to a partner of equal magnitude and opposite direction acting on the other body involved. Combined with free-body diagrams — one body isolated at a time, only the forces acting on it drawn — the third law turns the second law from a slogan into a problem-solving machine for pulleys, inclines and connected bodies.
objectives: State Newton's third law and identify the partner of any force, including why partners never cancel on a single free-body diagram
Draw a correct free-body diagram and run the five-step recipe to a numerical answer
Analyze connected bodies: one tension along an ideal cord, one acceleration magnitude along the constraint

concepts.statement: **When two bodies interact, the force $\vec{F}_{AB}$ that body A exerts on body B equals, in magnitude and direction-reversed, the force $\vec{F}_{BA}$ that B exerts on A: $\vec{F}_{AB} = -\vec{F}_{BA}$.** The two forces act on different bodies, are of the same type, and appear and vanish together.
concepts.detail: The third-law partner of Earth's pull on you is your pull on Earth. The partner of the normal force on a crate is the crate's push on the floor — which is why weight and normal force are NOT a third-law pair: they act on the same body.

concepts.statement: **A free-body diagram isolates one body, shrinks it to a dot, and draws one arrow for each force acting ON that body — nothing else.** No forces the body exerts on others, no internal forces, no net-force or $m\vec{a}$ arrows mixed in.
concepts.detail: This is where mistakes are made and caught: forget a force and the algebra cannot be saved; add a phantom force and the equations will lie.

concepts.statement: **(1)** Draw a free-body diagram for each body. **(2)** Choose axes — tilt them along an incline or the expected acceleration. **(3)** Resolve every force into components. **(4)** Write $\sum F_x = ma_x$ and $\sum F_y = ma_y$ for each body. **(5)** Solve, then check the result against limiting cases.
concepts.detail: Limiting-case checks — let an angle go to zero, a mass grow huge — are the cheapest error filter in physics.

concepts.statement: **An ideal cord ties connected bodies together: the tension magnitude is the same throughout, and the bodies' speeds and acceleration magnitudes are equal**, because the cord's length cannot change.
concepts.detail: Choose one positive direction along the motion — say the hanging block's downward direction — and keep that sign convention in both bodies' equations.

concepts.statement: **Solve Applying Newton's Laws problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Newton's laws with $\vec F_{\text{net}} = m\vec a$; the working equation is $\vec F_{\text{net}} = m\vec a$, $W = mg$, $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (newtons and free-body arrows) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $1\ \text{N}$ (apple) to $10^4\ \text{N}$ (braking car); inertial frames only; $m$ constant and $v\ll c$.

The dashed line and the marked angle $\theta$ show how the tension will be resolved once axes are chosen.

examples.title: Two blocks, one cord, one pulley
examples.problem: A 2.0 kg block lies on a frictionless horizontal table, connected by a light cord over a frictionless pulley to a hanging 3.0 kg block. Find the acceleration and the cord tension.

steps.label: FBDs
steps.text: Table block: weight and normal force (which cancel vertically) plus tension $T$ toward the pulley. Hanging block: weight $3.0g$ down, tension $T$ up.

steps.label: Equations
steps.text: Table block, $x$ along the cord: $T = m_1 a$. Hanging block, down positive: $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$.

steps.label: Add
steps.text: Adding eliminates $T$: $m_2 g = (m_1 + m_2)a$, so $a = (3.0 \times 9.8)/5.0 = 5.9$ m/s².

examples.result: $a = 5.9$ m/s² toward the pulley; $T \approx 12$ N — less than the hanging block's 29 N weight, which is exactly why that block accelerates downward.

examples.title: Crate on a frictionless ramp
examples.problem: An 8.0 kg crate slides down a frictionless 30° incline. Find its acceleration and the normal force.

steps.label: Tilt the axes
steps.text: Take +x down the slope and +y perpendicular to it. The weight resolves into $mg\sin\theta$ along the slope and $mg\cos\theta$ into it.

steps.label: Perpendicular
steps.text: No acceleration perpendicular to the slope: $N - mg\cos\theta = 0$, so $N = 8.0 \times 9.8 \times 0.866 = 68$ N.

steps.label: Along the slope
steps.text: $mg\sin\theta = ma$, so $a = g\sin 30^{\circ} = 4.9$ m/s² — independent of the mass.

examples.result: $a = 4.9$ m/s² down the slope; $N = 68$ N. On a 90° 'incline' the same recipe returns $a = g$: free fall, as it must.

keyTakeaways: Third-law partners are equal, opposite and on different bodies — they can never cancel each other on one free-body diagram.
One body per free-body diagram, only the forces acting on it, with axes bent to fit the geometry.
Connected bodies share one tension and one acceleration magnitude along the cord: write the second law for each body and combine.

quiz.q: A book rests on a table. The third-law partner of the table's normal force on the book is:
options: the book's downward force on the table
Earth's gravitational pull on the table
quiz.explanation: Partner forces act on the other participant of the interaction: the surface's push on the book pairs with the book's push on the surface. Weight's partner is the book's pull on Earth.

quiz.q: Why can't third-law partner forces cancel each other?
options: Because they are the same type
Because they act on different bodies
They do cancel — that is why nothing moves
quiz.explanation: Cancellation requires both forces to act on the same body. Third-law partners always act on different bodies, so each appears on a different free-body diagram.

quiz.q: In the two-block pulley system (2.0 kg on a frictionless table, 3.0 kg hanging), the hanging mass is made much larger. The acceleration:
options: decreases, because more mass is harder to move
increases, approaching $g$ when the hanging mass greatly exceeds the table mass
becomes exactly $g$ for any hanging mass
quiz.explanation: $a = m_2 g/(m_1 + m_2)$ grows with $m_2$ and approaches $g$ as $m_2 \gg m_1$ — the table mass becomes negligible baggage.

quiz.q: A free-body diagram should show:
options: every force in the problem, on all bodies
the forces acting on the chosen body plus its acceleration arrow
only the forces acting on the chosen body, one arrow each
the forces the chosen body exerts on other bodies
quiz.explanation: The diagram is a per-body ledger of forces acting ON the body. Acceleration is what those forces produce, not a force; forces the body exerts on others belong on those bodies' diagrams.

intro: Friction is the force we love to hate and cannot live without: it stops cars, walks us forward, holds every nail and knot — and wastes energy as heat. Microscopically it is a story of atoms: surfaces so rough at the atomic scale that they weld together at scattered spots. That story carries two empirical rules, and this section turns them into problem-solving machinery.
objectives: Distinguish static from kinetic friction and compute each from the normal force and the correct coefficient
Decide whether a body slides: compare the friction the situation demands with the maximum $\mu_s N$
Solve inclined-plane problems with friction, including the angle of repose

concepts.statement: **Pressed-together surfaces touch only at scattered high spots, which cold-weld; sliding must rip these welds apart.** The true contact area is microscopic — which is why friction depends on how hard the surfaces are pressed (through $N$) but not on the apparent contact area.
concepts.detail: Kinetic friction is usually smaller than static because a moving surface has less time to settle into and weld with the other. Like the normal force, friction is ultimately electromagnetic.

concepts.statement: **Static friction is self-adjusting: it takes whatever value equilibrium requires, up to a ceiling $f_{s,max} = \mu_s N$.** In symbols, $f_s \le \mu_s N$, with $\mu_s$ the coefficient of static friction for the surface pair.
concepts.detail: Push a crate gently and friction pushes back gently; push harder and it matches you — until at $f_{s,max}$ the crate breaks loose. The maximum is the useful number: it is the breakaway threshold.

concepts.statement: **Once sliding occurs, friction has one fixed magnitude: $f_k = \mu_k N$, directed opposite the relative sliding.** Coefficients are properties of the pair: rubber on dry concrete ($\mu_s \approx 1.0$, $\mu_k \approx 0.80$) grips hard; waxed wood on wet snow ($0.14$, $0.10$) barely; Teflon's $\mu_k \approx 0.04$ is why nothing sticks to it.
concepts.detail: The empirical content of the law is that the ratio $f_k/N$ stays roughly constant — independent of speed over a wide range and of apparent contact area.

concepts.statement: **First decide whether the body slides.** Test the static case (with $a = 0$ if the body is at rest): compute the friction the situation demands. If its magnitude is at most $\mu_s N$, the body holds and that is the friction. If not, it slides — switch to $f_k = \mu_k N$ opposite the motion and solve with Newton's second law.
concepts.detail: The classic error is writing $f_s = \mu_s N$ for a body not on the verge of slipping — that formula is only the maximum, not the value.

concepts.statement: **Solve Friction problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is friction, drag and centripetal dynamics; the working equation is $f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$, $f_k = \mu_k N$, $D = \tfrac12\rho CAv^2$, $F = mv^2/r$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (dimensionless $\mu$ and $\text{m/s}$ terminal speed) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\mu_s\sim 0.1$--$1.0$; skydiver terminal $\sim 60\ \text{m/s}$ closed, $\sim 5\ \text{m/s}$ open; Coulomb friction and $D\propto v^2$ are empirical; $mv^2/r$ needs the real inward agent.

examples.title: The angle of repose
examples.problem: A crate rests on a ramp whose tilt is slowly increased. The crate first slips when the ramp reaches 22°. What is the coefficient of static friction between crate and ramp?

steps.label: On the verge
steps.text: At the breakaway angle, the driving component $mg\sin\theta$ just equals the maximum static friction $\mu_s N$, with $N = mg\cos\theta$ from the perpendicular balance.

steps.label: Set equal
steps.text: $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$ — the weight cancels, so the angle of repose does not depend on mass.

steps.label: Solve
steps.text: $\mu_s = \tan\theta = \tan 22^{\circ} = 0.40$.

examples.result: $\mu_s = 0.40$; any ramp steeper than the angle of repose $\tan^{-1}\mu_s = 22^{\circ}$ sheds the crate.

examples.title: Sliding down the rough ramp
examples.problem: A 5.0 kg crate slides down a 30° ramp with $\mu_k = 0.30$ between crate and ramp. Starting from rest, how fast is it moving after 4.0 m?

steps.label: Forces along the slope
steps.text: Driving component $mg\sin\theta$ down the slope; friction $f_k = \mu_k N$ up the slope, with $N = mg\cos\theta$ perpendicular.

steps.label: Kinematics
steps.text: From rest, $v = \sqrt{2ad} = \sqrt{2 \times 2.35 \times 4.0} = 4.3$ m/s.

examples.result: $a = 2.4$ m/s²; after 4.0 m the crate is moving at 4.3 m/s. (Without friction, $a = g\sin 30^{\circ} = 4.9$ m/s².)

keyTakeaways: Static friction adjusts to demand, up to $\mu_s N$; kinetic friction is fixed at $\mu_k N$ once sliding starts, directed against the sliding.
Whether a body slides is a comparison: friction demanded versus $\mu_s N$ — do the static test first.
The angle of repose is $\tan^{-1}\mu_s$: tilt past it and the body breaks loose; mass cancels.

quiz.q: A 20 kg sled is pulled across snow ($\mu_k = 0.10$) at constant speed by a horizontal rope. The rope tension is:
quiz.explanation: Constant speed means zero net force: $T = f_k = \mu_k mg = 0.10 \times 20 \times 9.8 = 19.6 \approx 20$ N.

quiz.q: You push a couch horizontally with 150 N and it stays put. The static friction on it is:
quiz.explanation: With no motion and no acceleration, friction must exactly balance the applied force. $\mu_s N$ is only the ceiling it could reach.

quiz.q: Anti-lock brakes are better than locked, skidding brakes because:
options: kinetic friction is larger than static friction
the tires keep gripping in the static regime, where friction can reach $\mu_s N > \mu_k N$
quiz.explanation: A rolling, unskidding tire works through static friction, whose maximum exceeds the kinetic value that applies during a skid.

quiz.q: A coin rests on a book that is pushed horizontally, and the coin accelerates along with it. The static friction on the coin points:
options: forward — friction opposes relative sliding, not motion
quiz.explanation: Without forward static friction the coin would slide backward relative to the accelerating book. Friction opposes relative slip between surfaces, which is not the same as opposing motion.

intro: Friction with air — drag — grows with the square of the speed, and that fact has a striking consequence: a falling body cannot keep accelerating forever. When drag grows to match gravity, the acceleration vanishes and the body falls at its terminal speed, the number that decides whether a raindrop stings and a skydiver survives.
objectives: Compute the drag force $D = \frac{1}{2}C\rho A v^2$ and say what each factor means
Derive and evaluate the terminal speed $v_t = \sqrt{2mg/(C\rho A)}$
Describe how speed approaches $v_t$ in time, for both quadratic and linear drag

concepts.statement: **Air drag on a blunt body moving at speed $v$ through air of density $\rho$ is $D = \frac{1}{2}C\rho A v^{2}$, directed opposite the motion relative to the air.** $A$ is the effective cross-sectional area and $C$ the drag coefficient — a number near 0.5 for blunt shapes that encodes streamlining.
concepts.detail: The quadratic law holds for everyday sizes and speeds. Doubling the speed quadruples the drag, which is why highway fuel bills climb steeply with speed.

concepts.statement: **Terminal speed is the speed at which drag balances weight: $\frac{1}{2}C\rho A v_t^{2} = mg$, so $v_t = \sqrt{2mg/(C\rho A)}$.** At that speed the net force — and the acceleration — is zero, and the body keeps falling at constant velocity.
concepts.detail: Mass sits in the numerator (heavy skydivers fall faster) and area in the denominator (spread out and slow down): the physics of the parachute.

concepts.statement: **The approach is asymptotic: for quadratic drag, $v(t) = v_t\tanh(gt/v_t)$ starting from rest.** The falling body reaches 76% of $v_t$ at $t = v_t/g$, 96% at $2v_t/g$, and is at $v_t$ for all practical purposes a few of those time units later.
concepts.detail: It is a feedback loop: as $v$ grows, $D$ grows, shrinking the net force $mg - D$ toward zero — the acceleration dies out gradually rather than switching off.

concepts.statement: **For very small or very slow bodies — mist droplets, pollen, the oil drops of Millikan's experiment — drag is linear: $D = bv$, and the terminal speed is $v_t = mg/b$.**
concepts.detail: The dividing line is fluid dynamics' Reynolds number: 'blunt and fast' is quadratic, 'tiny and slow' is the viscous (Stokes) regime.

concepts.term: The Drag Force and Terminal Speed: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve The Drag Force and Terminal Speed problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is friction, drag and centripetal dynamics; the working equation is $f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$, $f_k = \mu_k N$, $D = \tfrac12\rho CAv^2$, $F = mv^2/r$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (dimensionless $\mu$ and $\text{m/s}$ terminal speed) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\mu_s\sim 0.1$--$1.0$; skydiver terminal $\sim 60\ \text{m/s}$ closed, $\sim 5\ \text{m/s}$ open; Coulomb friction and $D\propto v^2$ are empirical; $mv^2/r$ needs the real inward agent.

examples.title: Terminal speed of a skydiver
examples.problem: A 75 kg skydiver falls spread-eagle, with effective cross-sectional area $A = 0.70$ m², drag coefficient $C = 0.50$, and air density $\rho = 1.21$ kg/m³. Find the terminal speed.

steps.label: Condition
steps.text: At terminal speed, drag equals weight: $\frac{1}{2}C\rho A v_t^2 = mg$.

steps.label: Solve
steps.text: $v_t = \sqrt{2mg/(C\rho A)} = \sqrt{2 \times 75 \times 9.8/(0.50 \times 1.21 \times 0.70)}$.

examples.result: $v_t \approx 59$ m/s (about 210 km/h) — the classic belly-first terminal speed.

examples.title: How the speed builds up
examples.problem: For the same skydiver ($v_t = 59$ m/s), estimate the falling speed at $t = 6$, $12$ and $30$ s after the jump, starting from rest.

steps.label: Time unit
steps.text: $\tau = v_t/g = 59/9.8 = 6.0$ s is the natural clock of the fall.

steps.label: Formula
steps.text: $v(t) = v_t \tanh(t/\tau)$.

examples.result: 45 m/s at 6 s, 57 m/s at 12 s, and effectively the terminal 59 m/s after that — 96% of terminal within two time units.

keyTakeaways: Quadratic drag $D = \frac{1}{2}C\rho Av^2$ opposes the motion; terminal speed comes from $D = mg$ and is set by mass, area, shape and air density — not by how the fall started.
Speed approaches $v_t$ asymptotically: 76% at $v_t/g$, 96% at $2v_t/g$.
Tiny, slow bodies feel linear drag $D = bv$ instead, with terminal speed $mg/b$.

quiz.q: If a skydiver pulls in her arms and legs, cutting her effective area to a quarter, her terminal speed:
quiz.explanation: $v_t \propto 1/\sqrt{A}$: quarter the area and $v_t$ grows by $\sqrt{4} = 2$.

quiz.q: A raindrop and a hailstone of the same shape and drag coefficient fall from the same cloud. The heavier hailstone has:
quiz.explanation: More mass raises the gravity side of $\frac{1}{2}C\rho A v_t^2 = mg$, so a larger $v_t$ is needed to balance it.

quiz.q: For very small droplets the drag law becomes $D = bv$ because:
options: air density is smaller around them
at tiny sizes and speeds the viscous, linear law dominates the quadratic one
quiz.explanation: At low Reynolds number — small length and slow speed — viscosity, not inertia, sets the resistance, and drag becomes proportional to $v$.

intro: A body moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating — toward the center, at $a = v^2/R$ — so Newton's second law demands a real net force pointing inward. This section collects the suppliers of that inward force: friction on a flat curve, tension on a string, the normal force on a banked road, gravity on the Moon.
objectives: State the centripetal requirement $F_{net} = mv^2/R$ and explain why 'centripetal force' is not a new force
Solve flat-curve problems with friction, and vertical-circle problems at the top and bottom of the loop
Derive the banked-curve relation $\tan\theta = v^2/(gR)$ and use it at the design speed

concepts.statement: **Uniform circular motion at speed $v$ on radius $R$ requires a net radial force of magnitude $mv^2/R$, pointed at the center.** The acceleration is inward (chapter 4), and the second law fixes what the force must supply.
concepts.detail: This is a requirement, not a force. Something real — friction, tension, gravity, a normal force — must add up to it, or the motion will not be a circle.

concepts.statement: **'Centripetal force' names the inward sum that real forces must produce — it is not itself a force.** Never draw it on a free-body diagram; draw the real forces and verify that their inward components total $mv^2/R$.
concepts.detail: On a flat curve the supplier is static friction; on a banked curve, the normal force's horizontal component; for the Moon, Earth's gravity. Same requirement, different employees.

concepts.statement: **At the top of a vertical loop, gravity and the track both point toward the center: $N + mg = mv^2/R$.** The slowest possible passage has $N = 0$, giving $v_{min} = \sqrt{gR}$. At the bottom the track pushes harder than gravity: $N - mg = mv^2/R$.
concepts.detail: That is why roller-coaster riders feel squashed in the valley and light at the crest: the sensation of weight tracks $N$, not $mg$.

concepts.statement: **A curve banked at angle $\theta$ needs no friction at its design speed, given by $\tan\theta = v^2/(gR)$.** The horizontal component of the normal force supplies the centripetal requirement while the vertical component holds up the car.
concepts.detail: Below the design speed a car tends to slide down the banking, above it, up the banking — friction must make up the difference in both cases.

concepts.statement: **Solve Uniform Circular Motion problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is friction, drag and centripetal dynamics; the working equation is $f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$, $f_k = \mu_k N$, $D = \tfrac12\rho CAv^2$, $F = mv^2/r$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (dimensionless $\mu$ and $\text{m/s}$ terminal speed) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\mu_s\sim 0.1$--$1.0$; skydiver terminal $\sim 60\ \text{m/s}$ closed, $\sim 5\ \text{m/s}$ open; Coulomb friction and $D\propto v^2$ are empirical; $mv^2/r$ needs the real inward agent.

examples.title: How fast around the flat curve?
examples.problem: A 1200 kg car rounds an unbanked curve of radius 50 m. The tires' static friction coefficient on the dry pavement is 0.70. What is the fastest possible speed?

steps.label: FBD
steps.text: Vertically, $N = mg$. Horizontally, the only force is static friction pointing at the center — it is the centripetal supplier.

steps.label: Grip limit
steps.text: $f_{s,max} = \mu_s N = 0.70 \times 1200 \times 9.8 = 8232$ N.

steps.label: Requirement
steps.text: $mv^2/R \le f_{s,max}$, with equality at the fastest speed: $v = \sqrt{\mu_s g R} = \sqrt{0.70 \times 9.8 \times 50}$.

examples.result: $v_{max} = 18.5$ m/s (67 km/h). The mass cancels: grip per unit weight is the same for a loaded van.

examples.title: Loop-the-loop
examples.problem: A roller-coaster car passes the top of a vertical loop of radius 8.0 m. (a) What is the minimum speed at the top? (b) At 12 m/s, what force does a 60 kg rider's seat exert on them there?

steps.label: Top of the loop
steps.text: Both gravity and the seat push toward the center (downward there): $N + mg = mv^2/R$.

steps.label: Minimum speed
steps.text: The seat force cannot go below zero, so the floor of possibility is $mg = mv^2/R$: $v_{min} = \sqrt{gR} = \sqrt{9.8 \times 8.0} = 8.9$ m/s.

examples.result: $v_{min} = 8.9$ m/s; at 12 m/s the seat pushes 492 N — the rider (weight 588 N) feels light at the crest.

keyTakeaways: Circular motion at speed $v$ and radius $R$ demands an inward net force $mv^2/R$, supplied by real forces such as friction, tension, gravity or a normal force.
Top of a vertical loop: $N + mg = mv^2/R$, so the minimum speed is $\sqrt{gR}$; flat curve: $v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g R}$.
Banked without friction: $\tan\theta = v^2/(gR)$ — the design speed where the road alone does all the steering.

quiz.q: A car rounds a flat curve at the maximum frictional speed and then hits a patch of ice ($\mu \approx 0$). The car:
options: moves off along a straight line tangent to the curve
continues around the curve at the same speed
quiz.explanation: With no inward force the velocity cannot keep turning; Newton's first law gives straight-line, tangential motion.

quiz.q: A 0.50 kg ball is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 1.0 m at 2.0 m/s on a string. The tension is:
quiz.explanation: $T = mv^2/R = 0.50 \times (2.0)^2/1.0 = 2.0$ N — the string is the entire centripetal supplier.

quiz.q: A frictionless curve has radius 100 m and is banked at 20°. Its design speed is:
quiz.explanation: $v = \sqrt{gR\tan\theta} = \sqrt{9.8 \times 100 \times 0.364} = 18.9$ m/s.

intro: Energy enters physics in its simplest form here: the energy of motion. Kinetic energy grows with mass and with the square of speed — a quadratic dependence whose consequences run from braking distances to why 'speed kills' is physics rather than rhetoric. This short section defines the quantity and its unit; the next gives it a job.
objectives: Compute kinetic energy $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and state its SI unit, the joule
Explain the physical meaning of the quadratic speed dependence and its everyday consequences
Compare kinetic energies by ratio, and explain why $K$ depends on the reference frame

concepts.statement: **A body of mass $m$ moving at speed $v$ carries kinetic energy $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$.** It is a scalar — no direction — and never negative, being built from a square. Its unit is the joule (J).
concepts.detail: Only the speed matters, not the direction of motion: a 1500 kg car at 25 m/s has the same $K$ whether heading north or east.

concepts.statement: **Kinetic energy grows as the square of speed: double the speed and the energy quadruples.** Stopping distance inherits this — with roughly constant braking force it too grows as the square, which is why 90 km/h is not 'a bit' worse than 60 km/h.
concepts.detail: Leibniz called the quantity vis viva, 'living force', and insisted $mv^2$ was the true measure of motion; the argument with the $mv$ camp ended only when work (next section) showed the two sides measuring different things.

concepts.statement: **1 joule $= 1$ kg·m²/s²: the kinetic energy of a 2 kg mass moving at 1 m/s.** Everyday scale: an apple of 0.1 kg falling 1 m arrives with about 1 J; a car at highway speed carries hundreds of kilojoules.
concepts.detail: The joule is the shared unit of work and every form of energy — the first of many accounts that will exchange into it.

concepts.statement: **$K$ depends on the reference frame.** To a trackside observer, the train's dining cart has enormous kinetic energy; to a passenger, none at all.
concepts.detail: The work–kinetic-energy theorem will hold in both frames, but the bookkeeping is per-frame: there is no frame-free value of kinetic energy.

concepts.statement: **Solve Kinetic Energy problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is kinetic energy and the work--kinetic-energy theorem; the working equation is $K = \tfrac12mv^2$, $W = \vec F\cdot\vec d$, $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$, $P = \vec F\cdot\vec v$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (joules and watts) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $K\sim 10^2\ \text{J}$ (sprinter) to $10^6\ \text{J}$ (car at highway speed); $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$ is general; $P_{\text{avg}} \ne P_{\text{inst}}$.

examples.title: A baseball and a car
examples.problem: Compute the kinetic energy of (a) a 145 g baseball pitched at 40 m/s and (b) a 1500 kg car at 25 m/s (90 km/h).

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: The car carries about $4000$ times the baseball's energy — mass matters linearly, speed quadratically.

examples.result: $K_{ball} = 116$ J; $K_{car} = 4.7 \times 10^{5}$ J — a factor of $4.0 \times 10^{3}$.

examples.title: Kinetic Energy: kinetic energy numbers
examples.problem: A $1250\ \text{kg}$ car moves at $30\ \text{m/s}$. Compute its kinetic energy and the work needed to stop it.

steps.label: Formula
steps.text: $K = \tfrac12mv^2$; $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$.

steps.label: Stopping
steps.text: Stopping work is $-K$: the brakes must absorb 5.63\times 10^{+5}\ \text{J}$.

examples.result: $K \approx 5.63\times 10^{+5}\ \text{J}$.

keyTakeaways: Kinetic energy is the scalar $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, measured in joules, and never negative.
The quadratic speed law means doubling speed quadruples energy — and, at fixed braking force, the stopping distance.
Kinetic energy is frame-dependent: every observer tallies it relative to their own rest frame.

quiz.q: If a body's speed triples, its kinetic energy grows by a factor of:
quiz.explanation: $K \propto v^2$: tripling $v$ multiplies $K$ by $3^2 = 9$.

quiz.q: Kinetic energy can be:
options: positive or negative depending on the direction of motion
negative when the body moves backward
quiz.explanation: $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is built from a square: it vanishes at rest and is otherwise positive, whatever the direction of travel.

quiz.q: A passenger holds a 1.0 kg book still on a smoothly moving train. The book's kinetic energy:
options: is the same in the passenger's frame and the ground frame
is zero in the passenger's frame but large in the ground frame
is large in the passenger's frame
quiz.explanation: In the passenger's frame the book's speed is zero; for a trackside observer the book shares the train's speed, so $K$ is large.

intro: Work is the bridge between force and energy: it measures how much kinetic energy a force delivers. For a constant force, work is the dot product of force and displacement — force times distance times the cosine of the angle between them — and the total over all forces equals the change in kinetic energy. That statement is the work–kinetic-energy theorem, the first of physics' great bookkeeping rules.
objectives: Compute the work done by a constant force, $W = Fd\cos\phi$, with the correct sign
Apply the work–kinetic-energy theorem $W_{net} = \Delta K$ to find speeds without kinematics
Recognize when a force does positive, negative or zero work

concepts.statement: **If a body undergoes a displacement of magnitude $d$ while a constant force $\vec{F}$ acts at angle $\phi$ to the displacement, the force does work $W = Fd\cos\phi$.** Work is a scalar in joules; only the force component along the displacement counts.
concepts.detail: The same statement reads as a dot product: $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d}$.

concepts.statement: **Work is positive when the force has a component along the displacement, negative when against it, and zero when perpendicular.** Friction on a sliding box does negative work; the normal force on a box sliding along a floor does none; gravity does negative work on a rising ball.
concepts.detail: Zero work is not 'no force': carrying a bag at constant speed, you exert a sizable upward force but do zero work on the bag, because the force is perpendicular to the motion.

concepts.statement: **The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: $W_{net} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i$.** Positive net work speeds the body up; negative slows it; zero leaves the speed unchanged.
concepts.detail: For a constant net force along a straight line, multiply $v_f^2 - v_i^2 = 2ad$ by $m/2$ and use $F = ma$: $Fd = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2$. The theorem survives curved paths and variable forces (section 7-5) and becomes the base of the whole energy ledger.

concepts.statement: **Only the net work changes kinetic energy.** Individual forces' works can be large and cancel: lifting a book slowly, your hand does $+mgh$ while gravity does $-mgh$ — net zero, so the book's kinetic energy is unchanged.
concepts.detail: When solving, tally the work of every force acting, add with signs, and set the total equal to $K_f - K_i$.

concepts.term: Work and Kinetic Energy: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Work and Kinetic Energy problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is kinetic energy and the work--kinetic-energy theorem; the working equation is $K = \tfrac12mv^2$, $W = \vec F\cdot\vec d$, $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$, $P = \vec F\cdot\vec v$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (joules and watts) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $K\sim 10^2\ \text{J}$ (sprinter) to $10^6\ \text{J}$ (car at highway speed); $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$ is general; $P_{\text{avg}} \ne P_{\text{inst}}$.

examples.title: A push starts a sled
examples.problem: A 10 kg sled on frictionless ice is pushed by the only horizontal force, 20 N, through 4.0 m starting from rest. How fast is it moving at the end?

steps.label: Work
steps.text: $W = Fd = 20 \times 4.0 = 80$ J, all of it net work (the vertical forces do none).

steps.label: Theorem
steps.text: $W_{net} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - 0$.

steps.label: Cross-check
steps.text: Kinematics agrees: $a = F/m = 2.0$ m/s², so $v^2 = 2ad = 2 \times 2.0 \times 4.0 = 16$.

examples.title: Friction reads out the coefficient
examples.problem: A 2.0 kg block sliding at 3.0 m/s coasts 1.5 m across a rough floor before stopping. Find the friction force and the coefficient of kinetic friction.

steps.label: Net work
steps.text: Only friction has a component along the motion, so $W = 0 - \frac{1}{2} \times 2.0 \times 3.0^2 = -9.0$ J.

examples.result: $f_k = 6.0$ N and $\mu_k = 0.31$ — the work–energy theorem converts a stopping distance into a friction measurement.

keyTakeaways: Work by a constant force is $W = Fd\cos\phi$: positive, negative or zero according to the angle.
The net work on a body equals its change in kinetic energy — the work–kinetic-energy theorem.
A force perpendicular to the displacement does no work, however large it is.

quiz.q: A 5.0 N force acts on a box that moves 2.0 m while the angle between force and displacement is 60°. The work done is:
quiz.explanation: $W = Fd\cos\phi = 5.0 \times 2.0 \times 0.50 = 5.0$ J.

quiz.q: You carry a 10 kg bag horizontally at constant speed across a room. The work you do on the bag is:
options: zero, since your upward force is perpendicular to the displacement
negative, because the bag is heavy
quiz.explanation: $\cos 90^{\circ} = 0$: the supporting force does no work during horizontal travel.

quiz.q: The net work done on a body is negative. Its speed:
options: could do any of these — sign alone does not decide
quiz.explanation: Negative net work means $\Delta K < 0$: the kinetic energy, and with it the speed, drops.

quiz.q: A net work of 24 J is done on a 3.0 kg body initially at rest. Its final speed is:

intro: Gravity does work in a particularly simple way: it cares only how far you fall, not how you get there. Drop a coin, slide it down a ramp, or throw it in an arc — if the endpoints are at the same heights, gravity's work is identical. This path independence is the seed of potential energy in chapter 8.
objectives: Compute gravity's work $W_g = mg(y_i - y_f)$ for any change of height
Explain why gravity's work is path-independent, and contrast it with friction
Relate the work done by a hand that lifts slowly to the negative work gravity does

concepts.statement: **When a body of mass $m$ moves from height $y_i$ to height $y_f$, gravity does $W_g = mg(y_i - y_f) = mgh$, where $h$ is the drop.** Downward motion brings positive work; upward motion, negative.
concepts.detail: On an incline of angle $\theta$, a displacement $d$ along the slope changes height by $d\sin\theta$, and the same formula gives $mgd\sin\theta$.

concepts.statement: **The work done by gravity depends only on the endpoints' heights — not on the route between them.** Straight drop, zigzag path, frictionless slide, projectile arc: all give the same $mg(y_i - y_f)$.
concepts.detail: Forces with this property are called conservative. Friction is the canonical non-conservative force: its work depends on the path length — drag a crate around any loop and friction bills you for every centimeter.

concepts.statement: **To lift a body at essentially constant speed, your hand does $+mgh$ while gravity does $-mgh$: the net work is zero, so the kinetic energy is unchanged.** Equal and opposite works — not equal and opposite forces.
concepts.detail: The hand's upward force equals $mg$ only in the slow limit; any excess accelerates the body and shows up as kinetic energy.

concepts.term: Work Done by the Gravitational Force: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Work Done by the Gravitational Force problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is kinetic energy and the work--kinetic-energy theorem; the working equation is $K = \tfrac12mv^2$, $W = \vec F\cdot\vec d$, $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$, $P = \vec F\cdot\vec v$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (joules and watts) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $K\sim 10^2\ \text{J}$ (sprinter) to $10^6\ \text{J}$ (car at highway speed); $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$ is general; $P_{\text{avg}} \ne P_{\text{inst}}$.

concepts.term: Work Done by the Gravitational Force: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Work Done by the Gravitational Force lives at $K\sim 10^2\ \text{J}$ (sprinter) to $10^6\ \text{J}$ (car at highway speed) and the textbook model holds while $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$ is general; $P_{\text{avg}} \ne P_{\text{inst}}$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Work Done by the Gravitational Force calculation gives seconds when joules and watts demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $K\sim 10^2\ \text{J}$ (sprinter) to $10^6\ \text{J}$ (car at highway speed), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Three routes down
examples.problem: A 5.0 kg package descends 2.0 m: (a) dropped, (b) slid down a frictionless 30° ramp ($d = 4.0$ m along the slope), (c) carried down a spiral staircase. Compare gravity's work on the three routes.

steps.label: Drop
steps.text: $W = mgd\cos 0^{\circ} = 5.0 \times 9.8 \times 2.0 = 98$ J.

steps.label: Ramp
steps.text: Force and displacement differ by $\phi = 60^{\circ}$ here: $W = mgd\cos 60^{\circ} = 5.0 \times 9.8 \times 4.0 \times 0.50 = 98$ J.

steps.label: Spiral
steps.text: The path length is unknown — and irrelevant: $W = mgh = 98$ J again.

examples.result: 98 J by every route. Dragging the package 2.0 m horizontally afterward adds nothing: gravity's work for zero height change is zero.

examples.title: Throwing up
examples.problem: A 2.0 kg ball is thrown straight up and rises 3.0 m before stopping momentarily. (a) How much work does gravity do during the rise? (b) How much kinetic energy did the ball have at release?

steps.label: Gravity's work
steps.text: $W_g = -mgh = -2.0 \times 9.8 \times 3.0 = -59$ J.

steps.label: Energy at the top
steps.text: The ball is momentarily at rest there, so $K_{top} = 0$ and the theorem reads $-59 = 0 - K_{launch}$.

steps.label: At release
steps.text: $K_{launch} = 59$ J — which is also the work the thrower's hand did during the release, over a negligible height change.

examples.result: $W_g = -59$ J on the way up; the hand put in 59 J, and gravity takes it all back.

keyTakeaways: Gravity's work is $mg(y_i - y_f)$: only the height change matters, and the sign follows the direction of vertical motion.
Gravity is conservative (path-independent); friction is not.
A slow lift involves equal and opposite works by hand and gravity, so the book's kinetic energy never changes.

quiz.q: A 1.0 kg ball is thrown 5.0 m up and falls back to its launch height. The total work done by gravity over the round trip is:
quiz.explanation: The up leg gives $-49$ J and the down leg $+49$ J; the endpoint heights are the same, so the total is zero.

quiz.q: Which of these forces is NOT conservative (its work depends on the path)?
quiz.explanation: Friction's work grows with the path length; gravity and spring work depend only on endpoints.

quiz.q: A 60 kg hiker descends 500 m along a winding trail. The work gravity does on the hiker is about:
options: zero, because the trail is not vertical
impossible to compute without the trail length
quiz.explanation: $W = mgh = 60 \times 9.8 \times 500 = 2.9 \times 10^{5}$ J — the winding route is irrelevant to gravity.

intro: A stretched spring pulls back with a force proportional to the stretch — Hooke's law — and the constant $k$ measures stiffness. Work accumulated against such a force is a triangle of area on a force–displacement graph, and the $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ that results is the second great energy storehouse, alongside $mgh$.
objectives: State Hooke's law and interpret the spring constant $k$
Compute the work done by a spring between two positions: $W_s = \frac{1}{2}kx_i^2 - \frac{1}{2}kx_f^2$
Evaluate work as the area under an F–x curve, and combine spring work with the work–kinetic-energy theorem

concepts.statement: **An ideal spring pulls (or pushes) back along its axis with $F = -kx$, where $x$ is the displacement of its end from the relaxed position and $k$ is the spring constant, in N/m.** The minus sign says the force opposes the displacement — a restoring force.
concepts.detail: Stiff springs have large $k$: a 200 N/m spring stretches 5 cm under a 10 N pull. Spring scales and force meters are just calibrated springs.

concepts.statement: **A spring moves a body from $x_i$ to $x_f$ doing $W_s = \frac{1}{2}kx_i^{2} - \frac{1}{2}kx_f^{2}$.** Stretching further from relaxed, the spring does negative work; relaxing back, positive work.
concepts.detail: Like gravity, spring work depends only on the endpoints — another conservative force, and chapter 8 will bank its work as $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ of potential energy.

concepts.statement: **On a graph of force versus position, work is the signed area under the curve.** For a slowly stretched spring the pulling force grows along $F = kx$, and the area is a triangle of base $x$ and height $kx$: $W = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}$.
concepts.detail: The spring's own force is $-kx$ — below the axis while stretching — so its work is the negative of the hand's. The same area rule holds for any force shape: chop into thin strips and add them up, which is the integral of section 7-5.

concepts.statement: **Release a compressed spring against a block and the work–kinetic-energy theorem converts spring work into speed: $\frac{1}{2}kx_i^{2} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ when the block leaves at the relaxed length.**
concepts.detail: This is the popgun and pinball-launcher calculation, and the seed of every 'spring energy' problem in chapter 8.

concepts.term: Work Done by a Spring Force: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Work Done by a Spring Force problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is kinetic energy and the work--kinetic-energy theorem; the working equation is $K = \tfrac12mv^2$, $W = \vec F\cdot\vec d$, $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$, $P = \vec F\cdot\vec v$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (joules and watts) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $K\sim 10^2\ \text{J}$ (sprinter) to $10^6\ \text{J}$ (car at highway speed); $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$ is general; $P_{\text{avg}} \ne P_{\text{inst}}$.

figures.caption: Work as area: stretching a spring from $0$ to $x_1$, the pulling force grows along the line $F = kx$, and the work done is the shaded triangle's area, $W = \frac{1}{2}(kx_1)(x_1) = \frac{1}{2}kx_1^2$. The inset shows the physical setup — pull slowly, and the hand's force matches the spring's at every instant.
