examples.title: A golf ball leaves the tee
examples.problem: A club exerts the half-sine force pulse of the figure on a 45 g golf ball initially at rest: peak force 9.9 kN, contact time 0.50 ms. Find the impulse and the launch speed.

steps.label: Model the pulse
steps.text: For a half-sine $F(t) = F_{max}\sin(\pi t/\Delta t)$ on $0 \le t \le \Delta t$, the area is $J = \int_0^{\Delta t} F_{max}\sin(\pi t/\Delta t)\,dt = \frac{2}{\pi}F_{max}\Delta t$.

steps.label: Compute the impulse
steps.text: $J = (0.637)(9900\ \text{N})(5.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}) = 3.15\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s}$, directed along the drive.

steps.label: Convert to speed
steps.text: The ball starts at rest, so $J = \Delta p = mv$: $v = 3.15/0.045 = 70$ m/s $= 252$ km/h — a professional-grade drive.

steps.label: Sanity check the average force
steps.text: $F_{avg} = J/\Delta t = 3.15/5.0\times10^{-4} = 6.3$ kN, about 14,000 times the ball's 0.44 N weight: gravity was indeed negligible during contact.

examples.result: $J = 3.15\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s}$ and $v = 70$ m/s. The same arithmetic run in reverse tells you the impulse the ball delivered back to the club: $-3.15$ N·s, exactly.

examples.title: Bend your knees
examples.problem: A 70 kg person drops from a 2.0 m ledge and lands at 6.3 m/s. Compare the average force on the legs when landing stiff-legged (stopping in 0.020 s) versus with bent knees (0.50 s).

steps.label: Impulse required
steps.text: The momentum change is $J = \Delta p = (70)(6.3) = 441\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s}$ upward, no matter how it is delivered.

steps.label: Stiff-legged
steps.text: $F_{avg} = J/\Delta t = 441/0.020 \approx 2.2\times10^{4}$ N — about 32 times body weight (686 N), enough to fracture a heel.

steps.label: Knees bent
steps.text: $F_{avg} = 441/0.50 \approx 880$ N, only 1.3 times body weight: a comfortable stop. (Strictly the ground must also support the weight; the point stands — lengthening $\Delta t$ by a factor of 25 cut the force by 25.)

examples.result: Identical impulse, forces 22 kN versus 0.88 kN. The whole job of an airbag or a crumple zone is to buy collision time.

keyTakeaways: Impulse is the area under the $F(t)$ curve, and $\vec J = \Delta\vec p$ always — no matter how complicated the force's time profile.
A half-sine pulse of peak $F_{max}$ and width $\Delta t$ carries $J = \frac{2}{\pi}F_{max}\Delta t \approx 0.64 F_{max}\Delta t$; the average force is $F_{avg} = J/\Delta t$.
For fixed $\Delta p$, stretching the contact time $\Delta t$ shrinks the force in inverse proportion — the design principle behind every safety device that deforms.

quiz.q: During a collision the force on a ball varies as a complicated spike. Which quantity is guaranteed to equal the ball's change in momentum?
options: the peak force times the collision time
the area under the force-time curve
the average force divided by the collision time
the peak force divided by the mass of the ball
quiz.explanation: $\vec J = \int \vec F\,dt$ is exactly $\Delta\vec p$. Peak times duration would overestimate a spike (it only matches a flat pulse), and dividing by time has the wrong units.

quiz.q: Two identical eggs fall onto different surfaces and stop from the same speed. Egg A stops on concrete ($\Delta t \approx 1$ ms); egg B sinks into a 25-mm foam pad ($\Delta t \approx 25$ ms). The average force on egg B is roughly:
options: 25 times larger than on egg A
the same as on egg A
1/25 of the force on egg A
zero, because the foam does not push back
quiz.explanation: Both eggs need the same impulse $\Delta p$. Since $F_{avg} = \Delta p / \Delta t$, stretching the stopping time by a factor of 25 divides the average force by 25 — the whole reason packaging foam exists.

quiz.q: A 0.15 kg baseball arrives at 40 m/s and leaves in the opposite direction at 50 m/s after 2.0 ms of contact. The impulse the bat delivered has magnitude:
quiz.explanation: Take the outgoing direction as positive: $\Delta p = m(v_f - v_i) = 0.15\,(50 - (-40)) = 0.15 \times 90 = 13.5$ N·s. The reversal makes the impulse larger than either momentum alone; the average force is $13.5/0.0020 = 6.8$ kN.

quiz.q: For a half-sine force pulse with peak $F_{max}$ lasting $\Delta t$, the impulse equals:
quiz.explanation: The integral of a half sine over its half-period is $2/\pi \approx 0.637$ of the bounding rectangle $F_{max}\Delta t$. A triangular pulse would give $\frac12 F_{max}\Delta t$; a flat pulse the full rectangle — always read the area for what it is.

intro: If no impulse comes from outside — nothing pushes on the system from beyond its boundary — the total momentum cannot change. Conservation of linear momentum is the workhorse of collision physics: it holds even when energy is devoured by crumpling metal, and it even works one axis at a time. Recoil, rocketry and radioactive decay all surrender to the same bookkeeping.
objectives: Define closed and isolated systems, the two conditions behind momentum conservation
Apply $\vec P_i = \vec P_f$ to recoil, explosion and decay problems, including component-by-component
Recognize when only one component of momentum is conserved, and exploit it

concepts.statement: A system is **closed** if no matter crosses its boundary, and **isolated** if no net external force acts on it. For such a system the total momentum is conserved. During a brief collision, colliding bodies are effectively isolated even when ordinary forces act, because the impulsive contact forces dwarf them.
concepts.detail: The definition is a modeling choice: the boundary is wherever you draw it. The plus-and-minus bookkeeping of internal forces (Newton's third law) is what makes the total of a closed system insensitive to everything happening inside.

concepts.statement: If the system is closed and isolated, $$\vec P = \text{constant}: \qquad \vec P_i = \vec P_f.$$ Components work independently: if the net external force has no $x$-component, then $P_x$ alone is conserved — gravity acting vertically does not disturb horizontal momentum.
concepts.detail: This follows from $\vec F_{net,ext} = d\vec P/dt$: zero force means constant $\vec P$. It survives relativity (with the corrected momentum) and quantum mechanics — conservation of momentum is anchored in the deep symmetry that the laws of physics are the same everywhere in space.

concepts.statement: Explosions, decays and launches are collisions run backward: a system at rest tears itself into pieces whose momenta must still total zero. A cannon that fires a shell forward recoils; a nucleus that decays recoils; a rocket is a continuous version of the same trick.
concepts.detail: In one dimension the recoil speed of the rest of the system is automatic: $m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = 0$ means the light fragment moves fast, the heavy fragment slowly, in inverse proportion to their masses.

concepts.term: Conservation of Linear Momentum: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Conservation of Linear Momentum problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is center of mass, momentum and impulse; the working equation is $\vec p = m\vec v$, $\vec J = \Delta\vec p = \int\vec F\,dt$, $M\vec a_{\text{com}} = \vec F_{\text{net}}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ and $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $p\sim 10^2\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ (running person); closed plus isolated for strict conservation; impulse is vector area under $F(t)$.

concepts.term: Conservation of Linear Momentum: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Conservation of Linear Momentum lives at $p\sim 10^2\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ (running person) and the textbook model holds while closed plus isolated for strict conservation; impulse is vector area under $F(t)$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Conservation of Linear Momentum calculation gives seconds when $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ and $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $p\sim 10^2\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ (running person), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Throwing a ball on frictionless ice
examples.problem: A 45 kg skater at rest on frictionless ice throws a 5.0 kg medicine ball horizontally at 8.0 m/s (relative to the ice). What is her recoil speed?

steps.label: Set up conservation
steps.text: Skater-plus-ball is closed; the ice is frictionless and the throw is brief, so horizontal external impulse is negligible: $P_x$ is conserved.

steps.label: Initial momentum
steps.text: $P_{x,i} = 0$ (everything at rest).

steps.label: Energy note
steps.text: Her muscles supplied the energy — 160 J for the ball plus her 17.8 J share — none of which momentum conservation tracks. The two laws answer different questions.

examples.result: Recoil speed 0.89 m/s backward. If she had thrown a 1.0 kg dumbbell at the same speed, her recoil would drop to 0.18 m/s — light projectiles move the thrower least.

examples.title: Recoil of a radium decay
examples.problem: A radium-226 nucleus at rest decays into radon-222 plus an alpha particle (helium nucleus, 4 u) emitted at $1.5\times10^7$ m/s. Find the recoil speed of the radon-222.

steps.label: Isolated system
steps.text: Nothing external pushes on the nucleus during the decay: total momentum after must equal the zero before.

steps.label: Check the scale
steps.text: The heavy daughter moves at $1/55.5$ of the alpha's speed — momentum splits inversely with mass, kinetic energy (which favors the light particle, $\propto 1/m$) does not.

examples.result: The radon nucleus recoils at $2.7\times10^5$ m/s. Nuclear physicists reconstruct decays exactly this way: unseen particles are inferred from missing momentum.

keyTakeaways: Momentum is conserved for a closed, isolated system — and component-by-component whenever the net external force has no component along that axis.
During brief collisions ordinary external forces are negligible, so colliding bodies may always be treated as isolated for the contact duration.
Recoil, explosions and radioactive decays are 'reverse collisions': from rest, fragments separate with momenta summing to zero, speeds inversely proportional to masses.

quiz.q: A shell at the top of its arc explodes into three fragments. Which quantity of the fragment system is conserved during the explosion (neglecting air drag)?
options: total momentum, but not kinetic energy
kinetic energy, but not total momentum
neither, since the com accelerates downward
quiz.explanation: The explosion is internal, so total momentum is conserved — but chemical energy converts to kinetic energy, so K increases. Gravity acts throughout, yet it does not spoil momentum conservation at any instant; it simply accelerates the com of the system along the parabola.

quiz.q: Two skaters, initially at rest, push off each other. Skater A (60 kg) moves off at 2.0 m/s. The 40 kg skater B moves:
options: at 2.0 m/s in the same direction
at 3.0 m/s in the opposite direction
at 1.33 m/s in the opposite direction
not at all, since she did not push
quiz.explanation: Total momentum stays zero: $(60)(2.0) + (40)v_B = 0$ gives $v_B = -3.0$ m/s. The lighter skater always takes the larger speed — action-reaction forces are equal, but $a = F/m$ is not.

quiz.q: A projectile fired at an angle explodes mid-flight (fragments stay airborne, drag negligible). Which component(s) of the fragments' total momentum are conserved?
quiz.explanation: The external force is gravity, which is purely vertical. $P_x$ has no external influence and is conserved exactly; $P_y$ changes at the rate $-Mg$. Conservation works axis by axis — use the clean axis and let the messy one go.

quiz.q: Which system is NOT isolated for the purposes of momentum conservation?
options: two railway cars coupling on a level frictionless track
a rifle and bullet during the few ms the bullet travels up the barrel
a car braking hard to a stop on a dry road
a radioactive nucleus during its decay
quiz.explanation: The braking car's collision is with the road/Earth — external to the car system, delivering a large impulse. The other three involve only internal interactions during their brief events (rail friction and air drag on the cars are negligible over the coupling moment).

intro: Every collision conserves momentum; not every collision conserves kinetic energy. That single sentence sorts all collisions into three families — elastic, inelastic, and completely inelastic — and tells you which equations you may write down. The classification is worth internalizing before the algebra of the next two sections.
objectives: Classify collisions as elastic, inelastic or completely inelastic based on kinetic-energy bookkeeping
Explain why momentum is conserved in every collision but kinetic energy generally is not, and where the 'lost' energy goes
Compute velocities and kinetic-energy losses in completely inelastic collisions

concepts.statement: A collision is **elastic** if the system's total kinetic energy is the same before and after: $K_i = K_f$ (in addition to $\vec P_i = \vec P_f$). Collisions between hard steel balls, billiard balls, or atoms and molecules at ordinary energies are close to elastic.
concepts.detail: During contact the bodies briefly store energy in elastic deformation and then pay it all back. On the atomic scale, gas molecules collide essentially elastically — which is why the ideal-gas model of Chapter 19 works at all.

concepts.statement: A collision is **inelastic** if some kinetic energy converts to internal energy — deformation, heat, sound, rotation of the fragments' own parts. An inelastic collision in which the bodies **stick together** is called **completely inelastic**: the bodies share a common final velocity, and the kinetic-energy loss is the largest allowed by momentum conservation.
concepts.detail: 'Completely' does not mean all kinetic energy is lost: the com must keep moving (momentum is conserved), so even two lumps of putty retain the energy $\frac12 M v_{com}^2$. The bookkeeping: $\Delta E_{int} = K_i - K_f \ge 0$ for every real collision.

concepts.statement: In **every** collision — elastic or not — the total momentum of the colliding system is conserved (contact forces are internal and dwarf external forces during the brief contact). Kinetic energy is conserved **only** in the elastic case: in all others, $K_f < K_i$ with the difference deposited as internal energy.
concepts.detail: Total energy is always conserved; kinetic energy is only one of its costumes. When a 10 g bullet buries itself in a block and everything ends up warmer, momentum arithmetic is untouched — which is what makes inelastic problems solvable at all.

Check the answer against $p\sim 10^2\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ (running person); closed plus isolated for strict conservation; impulse is vector area under $F(t)$.

figures.caption: Momentum versus kinetic energy, side by side. Top: an **elastic** collision — 2 kg at 4 m/s meets 6 kg at rest; the bodies separate with velocities $-2$ m/s and $+2$ m/s and $K$ is unchanged (16 J $\to$ 16 J). Bottom: the **completely inelastic** version — the bodies stick and coast at 1 m/s; momentum is still 8 kg·m/s but $K$ drops from 16 J to 4 J, with 12 J (75%) converted to deformation and heating of the lumps.

examples.title: Bullet into a block
examples.problem: A 10 g bullet moving horizontally at 400 m/s buries itself in a 2.0 kg block resting on a frictionless surface. Find the final speed and the fraction of kinetic energy converted to internal energy.

steps.label: Type the collision
steps.text: The bullet stays embedded: completely inelastic — momentum conserved, kinetic energy not.

steps.label: The verdict
steps.text: 796 J — 99.5% of the bullet's kinetic energy — became heat and deformation in block and bullet. This is why embedded bullets are hot.

examples.result: Final speed 1.99 m/s; 99.5% of the kinetic energy went to internal energy. Momentum marched through untouched.

examples.title: The equal-mass swap
examples.problem: A 2.0 kg glider at 4.0 m/s on an air track elastically strikes an identical 2.0 kg glider at rest. What are the final velocities?

steps.label: Write both laws
steps.text: Elastic means two equations: momentum $2.0(4.0) = 2.0v_{1f} + 2.0v_{2f}$ and kinetic energy $\frac12(2)(16) = \frac12(2)v_{1f}^2 + \frac12(2)v_{2f}^2$.

steps.label: Solve
steps.text: Dividing through by the common mass: $4 = v_{1f} + v_{2f}$ and $16 = v_{1f}^2 + v_{2f}^2$. The only solution with distinct speeds is $v_{1f} = 0$, $v_{2f} = 4.0$ m/s (the other root restores the initial state).

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Identical masses **swap velocities** in a 1D elastic collision — the incoming glider stops dead and the target takes over its velocity, momentum 8 kg·m/s and energy 16 J both intact.

examples.result: $v_{1f} = 0$, $v_{2f} = 4.0$ m/s. Newton's cradle is this example wearing a suit.

keyTakeaways: Momentum is conserved in every collision; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic ones.
Completely inelastic collisions (bodies stick) lose the maximum kinetic energy allowed by momentum conservation — but never all of it, since the com keeps moving.
'Lost' kinetic energy becomes internal energy — deformation, heat, sound — tracked by $\Delta E_{int} = K_i - K_f \ge 0$.

quiz.q: Two lumps of putty collide head-on and stick. The collision is:
options: completely inelastic — the kinetic-energy loss is maximal
impossible to classify without the speeds
quiz.explanation: Sticking defines the completely inelastic case. Momentum is still conserved, but no other outcome loses more kinetic energy while respecting that conservation.

quiz.q: In which collision is kinetic energy conserved?
options: a car crumpling into a wall
a meteorite burying itself in the ground
two billiard balls colliding at moderate speed
quiz.explanation: Hard, elastic bodies with little permanent deformation return their stored contact energy — billiard balls (and gas molecules) are the textbook elastic cases. The others convert the bulk of their kinetic energy to internal energy.

quiz.q: A completely inelastic collision between a moving body and a stationary one always leaves the system with:
options: final kinetic energy equal to the initial value
the kinetic energy of the center-of-mass motion, $P^2/2M$
more kinetic energy than it started with
quiz.explanation: With all mass moving at $v_{com}$, the surviving kinetic energy is $\frac12 M v_{com}^2 = P^2/2M$ — the minimum compatible with the conserved momentum. Everything in excess of that com motion is internal energy.

quiz.q: A 1200 kg car at 20 m/s rear-ends a stationary 2400 kg truck and the two lock bumpers (completely inelastic). Their common speed is:
quiz.explanation: $(1200)(20) = (3600)v$ gives $v = 6.7$ m/s. The kinetic energy drops from 240 kJ to 80 kJ — the missing 160 kJ folded the metal.

intro: One-dimensional elastic collisions are the rare problem you can solve in your head — once you know the trick. Momentum conservation plus kinetic-energy conservation collapse into a single statement about relative velocity: the speed of approach equals the speed of separation. From it come the general final-velocity formulas and the three iconic special cases every physicist carries around.
objectives: Derive and use the relative-speed relation $v_{1i} - v_{2i} = -(v_{1f} - v_{2f})$ for 1D elastic collisions
Apply the general final-velocity formulas for arbitrary masses
Predict the three special cases: equal masses, a massive target, a massive projectile

concepts.statement: A 1D elastic collision obeys two equations: momentum, $$m_1 v_{1i} + m_2 v_{2i} = m_1 v_{1f} + m_2 v_{2f},$$ and kinetic energy, $$m_1 v_{1i}^2 + m_2 v_{2i}^2 = m_1 v_{1f}^2 + m_2 v_{2f}^2.$$ In the center-of-mass frame their solution is trivial: each velocity simply reverses.
concepts.detail: The quadratic energy equation makes direct substitution messy. The professional move is to subtract the two equations in a way that factors the difference of squares, which is exactly the relative-speed trick of the next concept — turn the algebra into a linear relation first, then solve.

concepts.statement: For any 1D elastic collision, $$v_{1i} - v_{2i} = -(v_{1f} - v_{2f}):$$ the speed of approach before the collision equals the speed of separation after it. In the center-of-mass frame the collision just flips both velocities.
concepts.detail: Proof sketch: divide the energy equation by 2, write each as $\frac{m}{2}(v_i^2 - v_f^2) = \frac{m}{2}(v_i - v_f)(v_i + v_f)$, and use the momentum difference $m_1(v_{1i} - v_{1f}) = -m_2(v_{2i} - v_{2f})$ to cancel the common factor. The relative velocity reverses — a statement true only for elastic collisions, and the fastest route to answers.

concepts.statement: Solving momentum plus the reversed relative velocity gives $$v_{1f} = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i} + \frac{2m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_{2i}, \qquad v_{2f} = \frac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i} + \frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_{2i}.$$ (With a stationary target, set $v_{2i} = 0$.)
concepts.detail: Check the limits: these formulas reduce to the velocity swap for $m_1 = m_2$, to reflection for a wall ($m_2 \to \infty$), and they conserve both momentum and energy identically — substitute and watch each check pass.

concepts.statement: With target 2 initially at rest: (a) $m_1 = m_2$: the bodies **swap velocities** ($v_{1f} = 0$, $v_{2f} = v_{1i}$); (b) $m_2 \gg m_1$: the light projectile **rebounds** ($v_{1f} \approx -v_{1i}$) while the wall barely stirs ($v_{2f} \approx 0$); (c) $m_1 \gg m_2$: the heavy projectile **plows on** ($v_{1f} \approx v_{1i}$) and the light target shoots ahead at $2v_{1i}$.
concepts.detail: This is why a tennis ball fired at a bowling ball comes straight back, and why a slow heavy truck that nudges a ping-pong ball launches it at twice the truck's speed. It is also why neutron moderators are made of light nuclei: a neutron loses the most energy per collision when the target mass matches its own.

concepts.statement: **Solve Elastic Collisions in One Dimension problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is center of mass, momentum and impulse; the working equation is $\vec p = m\vec v$, $\vec J = \Delta\vec p = \int\vec F\,dt$, $M\vec a_{\text{com}} = \vec F_{\text{net}}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ and $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$) emerges naturally.

Check the answer against $p\sim 10^2\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ (running person); closed plus isolated for strict conservation; impulse is vector area under $F(t)$.

examples.title: Light projectile, heavy target
examples.problem: A 2.0 kg glider moving at 4.0 m/s elastically strikes a 6.0 kg glider at rest on an air track. Find both final velocities and verify the energy.

steps.label: Relative-speed check
steps.text: Approach speed $v_{1i} - v_{2i} = 4.0$; separation speed $v_{1f} - v_{2f} = -2.0 - 2.0 = -4.0$. Reversed exactly — elastic confirmed.

steps.label: Energy check
steps.text: Before: $\frac12(2)(16) = 16$ J; after: $\frac12(2)(4) + \frac12(6)(4) = 4 + 12 = 16$ J. Conserved to the joule.

examples.result: $v_{1f} = -2.0$ m/s (bounces back), $v_{2f} = +2.0$ m/s. The light glider gave up three-quarters of its energy to the heavy one.

examples.title: Why moderators are made of light atoms
examples.problem: A neutron (mass 1 u) at speed $v$ elastically collides head-on with a stationary nucleus of mass $A$ u. Show that the fraction of its kinetic energy transferred is $4A/(1+A)^2$, and evaluate it for hydrogen and for lead.

steps.label: Neutron after speed
steps.text: With $m_1 = 1$, $m_2 = A$ (in u) and $v_{2i} = 0$: $v_{1f} = \frac{1-A}{1+A}v$. The nucleus takes $v_{2f} = \frac{2}{1+A}v$.

steps.label: Energy fraction lost by neutron
steps.text: The neutron keeps $\left(\frac{1-A}{1+A}\right)^2$ of its energy, so the fraction transferred is $1 - \left(\frac{1-A}{1+A}\right)^2 = \frac{(1+A)^2 - (1-A)^2}{(1+A)^2} = \frac{4A}{(1+A)^2}$.

steps.label: Hydrogen
steps.text: $A = 1$: fraction $= 4/4 = 1.00$ — a head-on hit on a proton hands over **all** the neutron's kinetic energy (it can stop dead).

steps.label: Lead
steps.text: $A = 207$: fraction $= 828/208^2 \approx 0.019$ — about 2%. Firing neutrons at lead is a terrible way to slow them; water works because its protons match the neutron mass.

examples.result: Fraction transferred $= 4A/(1+A)^2$: 100% on hydrogen, 2% on lead. Nuclear reactor moderators are water or graphite — light nuclei — by this exact arithmetic.

keyTakeaways: A 1D elastic collision satisfies both momentum conservation and relative-speed reversal: $v_{1i} - v_{2i} = -(v_{1f} - v_{2f})$ — approach speed equals separation speed.
The general formulas: $v_{1f} = \frac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}v_{1i} + \frac{2m_2}{m_1+m_2}v_{2i}$ and its partner; memorize the three special cases instead.
Equal masses swap velocities; a heavy target reflects a light projectile; a heavy projectile plows through and flings the light target ahead at $2v_{1i}$.

quiz.q: A 4.0 kg ball at 5.0 m/s elastically strikes a 12 kg ball at rest (head-on, 1D). The final velocities are:
In a one-dimensional elastic collision, the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation. This statement:
options: holds for all collisions, elastic or not
is equivalent to kinetic-energy conservation combined with momentum conservation
is a separate empirical rule discovered after Newton
holds only when one body is initially at rest
quiz.explanation: It is derived by factoring the energy equation and canceling with the momentum difference — it packs the two conservation laws into one linear statement, valid for any masses and any initial velocities along the line of centers.

quiz.q: A golf ball is fired head-on at a massive bowling ball at rest. To excellent approximation the golf ball:
options: stops dead and the bowling ball rolls away at the golf ball's speed
bounces back with nearly its incoming speed
continues at half its incoming speed
quiz.explanation: The $m_2 \gg m_1$ limit of the elastic formulas: $v_{1f} \to -v_{1i}$ and $v_{2f} \to 0$. The wall-like target returns all the energy because it takes essentially none — momentum transfer $2m_1 v_{1i}$ with negligible velocity.

quiz.q: A heavy truck moving at 10 m/s elastically bumps a stationary ping-pong ball head-on. The ball leaves at approximately:
quiz.explanation: The $m_1 \gg m_2$ case: the projectile's speed barely changes, $v_{2f} \to 2v_{1i} = 20$ m/s. In the truck's frame the ball simply bounces off an approaching wall — doubling the ground-frame speed.

intro: Most real collisions are glancing: billiard balls kiss at an angle and head off in different directions. Momentum is still a vector equation — which now means two scalar equations, one per axis — and if the collision is also elastic, energy supplies the third. The beautiful special case: identical bodies, one at rest, elastic — they always separate at right angles.
objectives: Set up the two component momentum equations for a glancing collision and know when to add the energy equation
Prove and apply the 90-degree rule for equal-mass elastic collisions with a stationary target
Describe glancing collisions in the center-of-mass frame and transform back to the lab frame

concepts.statement: For a collision in the $xy$ plane, momentum conservation is two equations: $$P_x: \quad m_1 v_{1ix} + m_2 v_{2ix} = m_1 v_{1fx}\cos\theta_1 + m_2 v_{2fx}\cos\theta_2,$$ and similarly for $P_y$ with $\sin\theta$ factors. If the collision is elastic, add $K_i = K_f$; if completely inelastic, set the final velocities equal instead.
concepts.detail: Count your unknowns before diving in: two outgoing speeds and two outgoing angles are four unknowns; the two momentum equations plus energy (elastic) close the problem only if one unknown is given or measured. Real collision analysis — nuclear or vehicular — always combines conservation laws with measured data.

concepts.statement: In an **elastic** collision between identical masses in which one is initially at rest, the two bodies depart along **perpendicular** directions: $\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90^\circ$. One of them may take all the speed (head-on limit, $90^\circ \to 0^\circ + 90^\circ$ counts too).
concepts.detail: Proof: momentum $\vec v_i = \vec v_1 + \vec v_2$ (masses cancel) means the three velocity vectors form a triangle; energy $v_i^2 = v_1^2 + v_2^2$ makes it a right triangle with $\vec v_i$ as hypotenuse — so $\vec v_1 \perp \vec v_2$. Watch two billiard balls collide: the cue ball's post-collision path and the object ball's path meet at a right angle.

concepts.statement: In the com frame a two-body collision is always head-on: the momenta are equal and opposite before and after, so elastic scattering simply **rotates** the common velocity magnitude. Lab-frame results follow by adding $\vec v_{com}$ back to every velocity.
concepts.detail: This is why high-energy physicists live in the com frame: the physics is cleanest there, and the messy lab frame is recovered by one vector addition. Even for inelastic collisions the com frame splits the kinetic energy cleanly into com motion (untouchable, $\frac12 M v_{com}^2$) and internal motion (the only part a collision can spend).

concepts.term: Collisions in Two Dimensions: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Collisions in Two Dimensions problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is center of mass, momentum and impulse; the working equation is $\vec p = m\vec v$, $\vec J = \Delta\vec p = \int\vec F\,dt$, $M\vec a_{\text{com}} = \vec F_{\text{net}}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ and $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $p\sim 10^2\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ (running person); closed plus isolated for strict conservation; impulse is vector area under $F(t)$.

concepts.term: Collisions in Two Dimensions: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Collisions in Two Dimensions lives at $p\sim 10^2\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ (running person) and the textbook model holds while closed plus isolated for strict conservation; impulse is vector area under $F(t)$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Collisions in Two Dimensions calculation gives seconds when $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ and $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $p\sim 10^2\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ (running person), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: A glancing elastic collision of identical pucks
examples.problem: On frictionless ice, puck A (2.0 kg) moves east at 3.0 m/s and strikes identical puck B at rest. After the elastic glancing collision A moves at $53.1^\circ$ north of east with speed 1.8 m/s. Find B's final velocity, and confirm the 90-degree rule.

steps.label: Assemble B
steps.text: $\vec v_B = (1.92, -1.44)$ m/s: speed $= \sqrt{3.69 + 2.07} = 2.4$ m/s at $\arctan(1.44/1.92) = 36.9^\circ$ south of east.

steps.label: Checks
steps.text: Angles: $53.1^\circ + 36.9^\circ = 90.0^\circ$ — the rule holds. Energy: $\frac12(2)(9.0) = 9.0$ J versus $\frac12(2)(3.24) + \frac12(2)(5.76) = 3.24 + 5.76 = 9.0$ J. Both laws satisfied.

examples.result: Puck B moves at 2.4 m/s, $36.9^\circ$ south of east; A and B separate at exactly right angles — the elastic equal-mass signature.

examples.title: Collisions in Two Dimensions: momentum numbers
examples.problem: A ball of mass $0.25\ \text{kg}$ moves at $30\ \text{m/s}$. Find its momentum and the impulse needed to stop it.

steps.label: Momentum
steps.text: $p = mv = 0.25\times 30 = 7.5\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.

steps.label: Impulse
steps.text: $J = \Delta p = 0-7.5 = -7.5\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s}$.

steps.label: Time sense
steps.text: A $-0.15\ \text{s}$ stop at $50\ \text{N}$ average force gives the same $J$.

examples.result: $p \approx 7.5\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.

keyTakeaways: In 2D, momentum conservation is two scalar equations (one per axis); elasticity adds the energy equation — count unknowns before solving.
Identical masses, elastic, target at rest: the outgoing velocities are perpendicular — the billiard player's 90-degree rule, provable by the velocity right-triangle.
In the com frame every two-body collision is head-on and elastic scattering just rotates velocities; return to the lab by adding $\vec v_{com}$ back.

quiz.q: Two identical billiard balls collide elastically; one was at rest. After the collision the struck ball moves at 30° north of east. The cue ball must move:
quiz.explanation: The 90-degree rule: the two outgoing paths are perpendicular, so the cue ball's direction is $90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$ on the other side of the original line of motion — 60° south of east.

quiz.q: Why do you need the kinetic-energy equation when analyzing an elastic glancing collision?
options: momentum alone is not a vector equation
there are more unknowns (two speeds and two angles) than the two momentum component equations
energy is conserved in all collisions anyway
quiz.explanation: Momentum gives two scalar equations for four unknowns. The energy equation supplies the third relation; a measurement of one angle or speed must supply the fourth.

quiz.q: In the center-of-mass frame, an elastic collision between two bodies looks like:
options: both bodies stop after the collision
the bodies exchange their speeds and reverse direction, always head-on
the velocities keep their magnitudes but rotate to new directions
one body takes all the kinetic energy
quiz.explanation: Momentum conservation pins the momenta to be equal and opposite, and energy conservation pins their magnitudes — so elastic scattering in the com frame can only re-aim the velocities. The lab frame adds $\vec v_{com}$ back.

quiz.q: Puck A (2.0 kg) at 4.0 m/s east hits stationary puck B (2.0 kg); they stick together (completely inelastic, 2D). The combined puck moves:
options: in a direction that depends on where they stick
quiz.explanation: Sticking means a single final velocity: $\vec v_f = \vec P/M = (2.0 \times 4.0)/4.0 = 2.0$ m/s east. The impact parameter is irrelevant to the final velocity — only the impulse (zero here, they stick) matters.

intro: A spinning rigid body cannot be tracked by following every point — but it does not need to be. One number, the angular position, tells you where every point is; its derivatives describe every point's motion. This section defines the angular variables θ, ω and α that describe rotation, and fixes the sign conventions and the radian conversions that everything later depends on.
objectives: Define angular position in radians and angular displacement with its sign convention
Define angular velocity and angular acceleration as time derivatives, and convert between rad/s, rev and degrees
Explain why every point of a rigid body shares the same ω and α but not the same linear speed

concepts.statement: For a body rotating about a fixed axis, pick a reference line fixed in the body and a fixed reference direction. The **angular position** $\theta$ is the angle between them: $$\theta = \frac{s}{r}$$ where $s$ is the arc length traced by a point at radius $r$. The radian is the natural unit: $1\ \text{rev} = 2\pi\ \text{rad} = 360^\circ$, and radians are dimensionless.
concepts.detail: Convention: looking along the axis toward the body, counterclockwise rotation corresponds to increasing $\theta$. Because it is a ratio of lengths, the radian carries no units — which is exactly why it slips silently through the linear-angular relations of Section 10.3.

concepts.statement: The **angular velocity** is the rate of change of angular position: $$\omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt},$$ in rad/s (positive for counterclockwise). Practical rotations are quoted in rev/min: $1\ \text{rev/min} = \frac{2\pi}{60}\ \text{rad/s} \approx 0.1047\ \text{rad/s}$.
concepts.detail: A ceiling fan at 300 rev/min spins at $31.4$ rad/s; the minute hand of a clock at $-1.05\times10^{-3}$ rad/s (negative: clockwise). Every point of the body shares the same $\omega$, whatever its distance from the axis — the defining feature of rigid rotation.

concepts.statement: The **angular acceleration** is $$\alpha = \frac{d\omega}{dt},$$ in rad/s². A rigid body speeding up from rest to $\omega = 12$ rad/s in 4.0 s has $\alpha = 3.0\ \text{rad/s}^2$ — every point, rim or hub, shares this value.
concepts.detail: The vector character of $\vec\omega$ and $\vec\alpha$ (directions along the axis by the right-hand rule) becomes essential in Chapter 11; for a fixed axis, signs carry all the needed information, with counterclockwise positive.

concepts.term: One body, one set of angular variables
concepts.statement: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, $\theta$, $\omega$ and $\alpha$ describe the **whole body**: a point 5 cm from the axis and a point 50 cm from it have identical angular variables — but linear speeds and accelerations that differ, in proportion to radius.
concepts.detail: This division of labor is why rotation is worth its own calculus: three numbers $\theta(t), \omega(t), \alpha(t)$ encode the trajectories of every point of an arbitrarily complicated object.

concepts.statement: **Solve Rotational Variables problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rotation about a fixed axis; the working equation is $\omega = d\theta/dt$, $v = \omega r$, $a_c = \omega^2r$, $K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12I\omega^2$, $\tau = rF\sin\phi = I\alpha$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere); rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.

examples.title: From revolutions to radians to arc length
examples.problem: A wheel of radius 0.30 m rotates through 2.5 revolutions. Through what angle does it turn, and how far does a point on the rim travel?

steps.label: Convert the angle
steps.text: $\theta = 2.5\ \text{rev} \times 2\pi\ \text{rad/rev} = 5\pi = 15.7$ rad.

steps.label: Arc length
steps.text: $s = \theta r = (15.7)(0.30) = 4.7$ m along the rim.

steps.label: Note the structure
steps.text: A point at half the radius traces half the arc, but the same 15.7 rad — angle belongs to the body, arc length to the point.

examples.result: $\theta = 15.7$ rad; rim point travels 4.7 m.

examples.title: Converting a spin rate
examples.problem: A laboratory centrifuge specification reads 1200 rev/min. Express the angular velocity in rad/s, and find the period of one rotation.

steps.label: Convert
steps.text: $\omega = 1200\ \frac{\text{rev}}{\text{min}} \times \frac{2\pi\ \text{rad}}{1\ \text{rev}} \times \frac{1\ \text{min}}{60\ \text{s}} = 125.7\ \text{rad/s}$.

steps.label: Period
steps.text: $T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{125.7} = 0.050$ s — twenty revolutions per second.

steps.label: Check by counting
steps.text: $1200\ \text{rev}/60\ \text{s} = 20$ rev/s and $20 \times 2\pi = 125.7$ rad/s. Consistent.

examples.result: $\omega = 1.26\times10^{2}$ rad/s, $T = 50$ ms.

keyTakeaways: Angular position $\theta = s/r$ in radians; counterclockwise is positive when viewed along the axis toward the body.
Angular velocity $\omega = d\theta/dt$ and angular acceleration $\alpha = d\omega/dt$; convert rev/min to rad/s with $2\pi/60$.
All points of a rigid body share the same $\theta$, $\omega$ and $\alpha$; their linear speeds and accelerations differ in proportion to radius.

quiz.q: A wheel turns through 3.0 revolutions. In radians this is:
quiz.explanation: Each revolution is $2\pi$ radians, so $3.0 \times 2\pi = 6\pi \approx 18.8$ rad. (Option 4 is nonsense phrasing — 540 degrees equals $3\pi$ rad, not the required 3 revolutions.)

quiz.q: Which quantity is NOT shared by all points of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis?
quiz.explanation: Linear speed grows with radius ($v = \omega r$), so a rim point outruns a hub point even though both sweep the same angle per second.

quiz.q: A wheel spins clockwise (as viewed by you) and is slowing down. Taking counterclockwise as positive, its angular acceleration is:
options: negative, because the rotation is clockwise
positive, because the wheel is slowing
zero, since it is still spinning
impossible to sign without knowing the radius
quiz.explanation: Clockwise means $\omega < 0$; slowing down means $\omega$ is becoming less negative, so $\alpha = d\omega/dt > 0$. Angular acceleration points opposite to angular velocity whenever a spin is dying.

quiz.q: A DVD spins at 7.5 rad/s. Its period of rotation is about:
quiz.explanation: $T = 2\pi/\omega = 6.28/7.5 = 0.84$ s — about 1.2 revolutions per second, a slow-motion DVD but a fine quiz question.

intro: Constant angular acceleration is the rotational twin of Chapter 2's constant-acceleration kinematics — the same four equations, every symbol translated. Learn the dictionary once (x → θ, v → ω, a → α) and every straight-line kinematic technique you own transfers to spinning machinery.
objectives: Write the four constant-angular-acceleration equations and the condition for their validity
Solve spin-up and spin-down problems with consistent units of radians and seconds
Convert angular results into revolutions for practical reporting

concepts.statement: For constant angular acceleration $\alpha$ (and only then), $$\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t, \qquad \theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac12 \alpha t^2,$$ $$\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta, \qquad \theta = \tfrac12(\omega_0 + \omega)t.$$ Each is the term-by-term translation of its linear counterpart.
concepts.detail: Derivation is identical to Chapter 2: integrate $d\omega = \alpha\,dt$ and $d\theta = \omega\,dt$ with $\alpha$ constant. Units discipline: $\omega$ in rad/s, $\alpha$ in rad/s², $t$ in s — radians cancel, so $\theta$ may be reported in rev only after the calculation is done.

concepts.statement: | linear | rotational | | --- | --- | | $x$ | $\theta$ | | $v$ | $\omega$ | | $a$ | $\alpha$ | | $v = v_0 + at$ | $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$ | Every kinematics trick — stacking equations, eliminating variables, graph reading — translates.
concepts.detail: The dictionary is safe because the angular variables obey the same calculus. It will grow through the whole chapter: force → torque, mass → rotational inertia, momentum → angular momentum. Physics repeats its structure at each level.

concepts.statement: In a uniform spin-down to rest, $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$ links the stopping angle to the initial spin — doubling the initial speed **quadruples** the rotations needed to stop, exactly as stopping distance quadruples with speed on a highway.
concepts.detail: This is why flywheels and grindstones are treated with respect: a wheel twice as fast carries four times the angle (and four times the kinetic energy, Section 10.4) before friction can still it.

concepts.term: Rotation with Constant Angular Acceleration: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Rotation with Constant Angular Acceleration problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rotation about a fixed axis; the working equation is $\omega = d\theta/dt$, $v = \omega r$, $a_c = \omega^2r$, $K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12I\omega^2$, $\tau = rF\sin\phi = I\alpha$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere); rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.

concepts.term: Rotation with Constant Angular Acceleration: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Rotation with Constant Angular Acceleration lives at $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere) and the textbook model holds while rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Rotation with Constant Angular Acceleration calculation gives seconds when $\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: A fan spins down
examples.problem: An electric fan blade spinning at 22.0 rad/s is switched off and coasts uniformly to rest in 6.0 s. Find the angular acceleration, the angle turned, and the number of revolutions.

steps.label: Acceleration
steps.text: $\alpha = \frac{\omega - \omega_0}{t} = \frac{0 - 22.0}{6.0} = -3.67\ \text{rad/s}^2$ — negative: it opposes the spin.

steps.label: Angle — time form
steps.text: $\theta = \tfrac12(\omega_0 + \omega)t = \tfrac12(22.0 + 0)(6.0) = 66$ rad.

steps.label: Angle — cross-check
steps.text: $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$: $0 = 484 + 2(-3.67)\theta$ gives $\theta = 484/7.33 = 66$ rad. Same answer, independent route.

steps.label: Report in revolutions
steps.text: $66\ \text{rad} \div 2\pi = 10.5$ revolutions during the coast.

examples.result: $\alpha = -3.67\ \text{rad/s}^2$, $\theta = 66$ rad $= 10.5$ rev. The average spin during the coast was half the initial, which is what the third equation says.

examples.title: Spin-up of a grinding wheel
examples.problem: A grinding wheel accelerates uniformly from rest at $\alpha = 3.0\ \text{rad/s}^2$ for 4.0 s. Find the final angular velocity and the total angle.

steps.label: Velocity
steps.text: $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t = 0 + (3.0)(4.0) = 12\ \text{rad/s}$.

steps.label: Angle
steps.text: $\theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac12\alpha t^2 = 0 + \tfrac12(3.0)(16) = 24$ rad.

steps.label: Consistency check
steps.text: $\omega^2 = 2\alpha\theta$: $144 = (2)(3.0)(24) = 144$. The three equations agree — a quick way to catch arithmetic slips.

examples.result: $\omega = 12$ rad/s, $\theta = 24$ rad $= 3.8$ rev.

keyTakeaways: For constant α only: $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$, $\theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac12\alpha t^2$, $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$, $\theta = \tfrac12(\omega_0+\omega)t$.
Work in rad and s throughout; convert to revolutions only at the end ($1\ \text{rev} = 2\pi$ rad).
The equations are exact translations of Chapter 2 — any linear-kinematics strategy is a valid rotational strategy.

quiz.q: A wheel starts at 8.0 rad/s and accelerates uniformly at 2.0 rad/s² for 3.0 s. Its final angular velocity is:
quiz.explanation: $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t = 8.0 + (2.0)(3.0) = 14$ rad/s. The angle would be $\theta = \omega_0 t + \frac12\alpha t^2 = 24 + 9 = 33$ rad.

quiz.q: A rotor decelerates uniformly from 60 rad/s to rest, turning 120 rad in the process. Its angular acceleration was:
quiz.explanation: $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$: $0 = 3600 + 2\alpha(120)$, so $\alpha = -3600/240 = -15\ \text{rad/s}^2$. The stopping time is $60/15 = 4.0$ s.

quiz.q: Doubling a wheel's initial angular speed (same constant braking α) multiplies the number of revolutions needed to stop by:
quiz.explanation: From $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$ with final zero: $\theta \propto \omega_0^2$. Double the speed, quadruple the angle — the rotational twin of highway braking distances.

intro: A point on a spinning body moves in a circle, so its linear motion — speed, tangential acceleration, centripetal acceleration — is completely determined by the angular variables of the body and its distance from the axis. This section builds the three bridge equations s = θr, v = ωr, a = αr (plus the centripetal term ω²r) that let you translate freely between the two descriptions.
objectives: Use s = θr, v = ωr and the two acceleration relations to convert between angular and linear quantities
Compute the tangential and radial (centripetal) components of a point's acceleration and combine them
Explain why these relations demand radians and why the radial component never vanishes at constant ω

concepts.term: Position and speed on a rotating body
concepts.statement: For a point at distance $r$ from a fixed rotation axis, $$s = \theta r \quad \text{and} \quad v = \omega r$$ with $\theta$ in **radians** and $\omega$ in rad/s. All points share $\theta$ and $\omega$; the linear quantities scale linearly with $r$.
concepts.detail: The derivation is one differentiation: $s = \theta r$ with fixed $r$ gives $ds/dt = r\,d\theta/dt$. The rim of a 0.30 m wheel at 125.7 rad/s moves at $v = 37.7$ m/s while a point halfway in moves at 18.8 m/s.

concepts.statement: The acceleration of a point on a rotating body splits into a **tangential** component (changing the speed) and a **radial** (centripetal) component (changing the direction): $$a_t = \alpha r, \qquad a_r = \omega^2 r,$$ with total magnitude $a = \sqrt{a_t^2 + a_r^2}$, directed at angle $\arctan(a_t/a_r)$ from the radius toward the direction of motion.
concepts.detail: At constant $\omega$ the tangential part vanishes but $a_r = \omega^2 r$ never does — uniform circular motion is still acceleration. These are the same components met in uniform circular motion (Chapter 4), now generated by the body's angular variables.

concepts.statement: The bridge equations hold **only** when angles are measured in radians. With $\omega$ in rad/s, $v = \omega r$ is dimensionally clean (rad cancels); plug in rev/s and you must insert $2\pi$ by hand — a classic exam error.
concepts.detail: The radian is defined as the ratio $s/r$ precisely so that the calculus of circular motion works without conversion constants. Every derived formula of this chapter silently assumes it.

concepts.term: Relating the Linear and Angular Variables: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Relating the Linear and Angular Variables problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rotation about a fixed axis; the working equation is $\omega = d\theta/dt$, $v = \omega r$, $a_c = \omega^2r$, $K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12I\omega^2$, $\tau = rF\sin\phi = I\alpha$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere); rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.

concepts.term: Relating the Linear and Angular Variables: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Relating the Linear and Angular Variables lives at $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere) and the textbook model holds while rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Relating the Linear and Angular Variables calculation gives seconds when $\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: A laboratory centrifuge
examples.problem: A centrifuge rotor of radius 0.20 m spins at 1200 rev/min. Find the linear speed of the rim and the centripetal acceleration, in units of g.

steps.label: Angular velocity in rad/s
steps.text: $\omega = 1200(2\pi/60) = 125.7\ \text{rad/s}$ (Section 10.1's conversion).

steps.label: Rim speed
steps.text: $v = \omega r = (125.7)(0.20) = 25$ m/s — freeway speed, in a circle, 20 times a second.

steps.label: In g units
steps.text: $a_r/g = 3160/9.8 = 322$ — a sample in this rotor weighs 322 times its normal weight, which is how centrifuges separate cells and sediment.

examples.result: $v = 25$ m/s and $a_r = 3.2\times10^{3}\ \text{m/s}^2 \approx 320g$ at the rim.

examples.title: Both acceleration components
examples.problem: A disk starts from rest with angular acceleration 2.5 rad/s². At t = 4.0 s, find the acceleration components of a point at r = 0.20 m, and the total acceleration.

steps.label: Angular velocity by then
steps.text: $\omega = \alpha t = (2.5)(4.0) = 10\ \text{rad/s}$.

steps.label: Tangential component
steps.text: $a_t = \alpha r = (2.5)(0.20) = 0.50\ \text{m/s}^2$ — the part that is speeding the point up.

steps.label: Radial component
steps.text: $a_r = \omega^2 r = (100)(0.20) = 20\ \text{m/s}^2$ — already 40 times the tangential part.

steps.label: Total
steps.text: $a = \sqrt{0.50^2 + 20^2} \approx 20.0\ \text{m/s}^2$, tilted only $1.4^\circ$ ahead of the radius. In spinning machinery the centripetal term quickly dominates.

examples.result: $a_t = 0.50\ \text{m/s}^2$, $a_r = 20\ \text{m/s}^2$, total $\approx 20\ \text{m/s}^2$ nearly radial.

keyTakeaways: Bridge equations (radians mandatory): $s = \theta r$, $v = \omega r$, $a_t = \alpha r$, $a_r = \omega^2 r$.
Tangential acceleration changes a point's speed; radial acceleration $\omega^2 r$ changes its direction and persists even at constant ω.
The radial term grows as $\omega^2 r$ and dominates machine-scale rotation: 1200 rpm at 20 cm radius already means ~320g at the rim.

quiz.q: Two points sit on the same rotating disk, one at 5.0 cm and one at 15.0 cm from the axis. At any instant their linear speeds are in the ratio:
quiz.explanation: Both share the same $\omega$, and $v = \omega r$, so speed scales with radius: 1:3. The ratio is set by geometry, not by how fast the disk spins.

quiz.q: A point on a wheel rotating at constant ω has:
quiz.explanation: Constant $\omega$ means $\alpha = 0$, killing the tangential part. But the direction of motion still changes, so the centripetal $a_r = \omega^2 r$ persists — uniform circular motion is accelerated motion.

quiz.q: At 1200 rev/min, a point 0.20 m from the axis has centripetal acceleration of about 3.2×10³ m/s². Doubling the spin rate to 2400 rev/min makes it about:
quiz.explanation: $a_r = \omega^2 r$ grows with the square of the angular velocity: doubling $\omega$ quadruples $a_r$ to $\approx 1.28\times10^{4}$ m/s², roughly 1300g — why rotor bursts are catastrophic.

quiz.q: The relation v = ωr gives the speed in m/s only if ω is expressed in:
quiz.explanation: Only radians — defined as arc over radius — make $\omega r$ dimensionally and numerically correct without a $2\pi$ or $\pi/180$ correction factor.

intro: Rotating bodies store energy — sometimes enormously. The kinetic energy of rotation is ½Iω², where the rotational inertia I measures how the body's mass is distributed about the axis. Mass far from the axis is expensive, squared; this single fact explains flywheels, engine balance, and why a rolling hoop loses races to a rolling sphere in Chapter 11.
objectives: Define rotational inertia I = Σmᵢrᵢ² about an axis and explain its dependence on axis choice
Compute rotational kinetic energy K = ½Iω² and solve flywheel energy problems
Compare rotational and translational kinetic energy for the same body

concepts.statement: The **rotational inertia** (moment of inertia) of a system of particles about a fixed axis is $$I = \sum_i m_i r_i^2,$$ where $r_i$ is each particle's perpendicular distance from the axis. Units: kg·m². It depends on the mass, the axis, and — crucially — how far the mass sits from the axis.
concepts.detail: Distance enters squared: 1 kg at 2 m from the axis costs as much inertia as 4 kg at 1 m. This is why a barbell spun about its grip is sluggish, and why moving mass to the center is the universal strategy for spinning things up quickly — the figure skater of Section 11.8.

concepts.statement: A rigid body rotating about a fixed axis at angular speed $\omega$ has $$K = \tfrac12 I\omega^2.$$ The derivation is term-by-term: each particle moves at $v_i = \omega r_i$, so $\sum \frac12 m_i v_i^2 = \frac12(\sum m_i r_i^2)\omega^2 = \frac12 I\omega^2$.
concepts.detail: The formula is the rotational twin of $\frac12 mv^2$ with $I$ playing the role of mass and $\omega$ the role of speed. Combined with translation it gives the rolling energy of Section 11.1: $K = \frac12 Mv_{com}^2 + \frac12 I\omega^2$.

concepts.statement: Because $K \propto \omega^2$, a flywheel stores four times the energy when it spins twice as fast — and delivers it back as mechanical work when the load demands. Engine flywheels smooth the pulses between combustion events; regenerative braking systems store braking energy as spin.
concepts.detail: The same $\omega^2$ law is a safety liability: the stress in a spinning rim also grows as $\omega^2$, so burst speed, not energy capacity, sets the engineering limit. Energy per kilogram of advanced flywheels rivals batteries.

concepts.term: Kinetic Energy of Rotation: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Kinetic Energy of Rotation problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rotation about a fixed axis; the working equation is $\omega = d\theta/dt$, $v = \omega r$, $a_c = \omega^2r$, $K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12I\omega^2$, $\tau = rF\sin\phi = I\alpha$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere); rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.

concepts.term: Kinetic Energy of Rotation: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Kinetic Energy of Rotation lives at $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere) and the textbook model holds while rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Kinetic Energy of Rotation calculation gives seconds when $\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Energy in a flywheel
examples.problem: A solid uniform disk flywheel of mass 24 kg and radius 0.30 m spins at 900 rev/min. Find its rotational inertia and kinetic energy.

steps.label: Rotational inertia of a disk
steps.text: For a solid disk about its central axis, $I = \frac12 MR^2 = \frac12(24)(0.30)^2 = 1.08\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ (from the table of Section 10.5).

steps.label: Compare with translation
steps.text: The rim moves at $v = \omega R = 28.3$ m/s; translating the same 24 kg at rim speed would carry $\frac12(24)(28.3)^2 = 9.6$ kJ — twice as much. The factor 2 is the disk's inertia being $\frac12 MR^2$: its mass sits, on average, at less than the rim radius.

examples.result: $I = 1.08\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ and $K = 4.8$ kJ — enough to lift the flywheel itself 20 m.

examples.title: A dumbbell's rotation
examples.problem: Two 3.0 kg masses are welded to the ends of a light rod and rotate about the rod's midpoint, each 0.50 m from the axis, at ω = 8.0 rad/s. Find I and K.

steps.label: Role of the rod
steps.text: A light rod contributes almost nothing — its mass sits near the axis where $r^2$ is small. Sliding the same masses out to 0.80 m would raise $I$ to $3.8\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$, more than doubling it.

examples.result: $I = 1.5\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$, $K = 48$ J. Rotational inertia is bought with radius squared.

keyTakeaways: Rotational inertia $I = \sum m_i r_i^2$ (kg·m²) depends on the mass distribution and on which axis you choose — always name the axis.
Rotational kinetic energy is $K = \frac12 I\omega^2$; since $K \propto \omega^2$, energy and rim stress both quadruple when spin doubles.
Mass far from the axis is penalized as $r^2$ — hence light rims, hollow-frame bicycles, and tucked-in skaters.

quiz.q: Two wheels have the same mass and radius; one is a hoop with all mass at the rim, the other a uniform disk. About their central axes:
options: they have the same rotational inertia
the hoop has twice the inertia of the disk
the disk has twice the inertia of the hoop
the disk has four times the inertia of the hoop
quiz.explanation: Hoop: $I = MR^2$. Disk: $I = \frac12 MR^2$, because the disk's mass sits on average at only $R/\sqrt{2}$ from the axis. The factor of 2 decides rolling races.

quiz.q: If a flywheel's angular speed doubles, its rotational kinetic energy:
quiz.explanation: $K = \frac12 I\omega^2$ with $I$ fixed — $K$ scales as $\omega^2$. This is also why flywheel stresses, which scale with rim speed squared, set the burst limit.

quiz.q: The SI units of rotational inertia are:
quiz.explanation: $I = \sum m r^2$ sums mass times distance squared: kg·m². (N·m is torque; kg·m²/s² is energy — all three appear in this chapter; do not mix them.)

quiz.q: A 2.0 kg hoop and a 2.0 kg disk, each of radius 0.10 m, spin at 10 rad/s. The ratio of kinetic energies (hoop:disk) is:
quiz.explanation: $K_{hoop} = \frac12(MR^2)\omega^2$ versus $K_{disk} = \frac12(\frac12 MR^2)\omega^2$ — the hoop stores exactly twice the energy, here 0.10 J versus 0.050 J.

intro: Rotational inertia is not a single number per body — it is a function of the axis. This section shows how to compute it: directly by integration for simple shapes, by look-up for standard ones, and — the professional's move — by the parallel-axis theorem, which converts any known inertia about the center of mass into the inertia about any parallel axis in one line.
objectives: Compute rotational inertia by integrating $I = \int r^2\,dm$ for a rod and other simple bodies
Use the table of standard inertias (rod, hoop, disk, sphere, shell)
Apply the parallel-axis theorem $I = I_{com} + Mh^2$ and verify it numerically

concepts.statement: For a continuous body, replace the sum by an integral over mass elements: $$I = \int r^2\,dm.$$ For a uniform rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ about a perpendicular axis through one end, write $dm = (M/L)\,dx$ and integrate $x$ from 0 to $L$: $$I = \frac{M}{L}\int_0^L x^2 dx = \frac{1}{3}ML^2.$$
concepts.detail: About the rod's center the same integral, from $-L/2$ to $+L/2$, gives $\frac{1}{12}ML^2$ — four times less, because the mass sits closer to the axis. The distance-squared penalty is why axis placement matters so much.

concepts.statement: About the symmetry axis through the center of mass: hoop $I = MR^2$; **disk** $I = \frac12 MR^2$; **rod** (perpendicular, at center) $\frac{1}{12}ML^2$; **solid sphere** $\frac{2}{5}MR^2$; **spherical shell** $\frac{2}{3}MR^2$; **slab** (through center, in-plane) $\frac{1}{12}M(a^2+b^2)$.
concepts.detail: Two patterns are worth noticing: only the hoop puts all its mass at one radius, so it is the maximum $MR^2$ for a given $M$ and outer radius; and pushing mass into shells away from the axis (shell vs solid sphere, 2/3 vs 2/5) always raises $I$.

concepts.statement: If $I_{com}$ is the rotational inertia about an axis through the center of mass, then about any **parallel** axis a perpendicular distance $h$ away, $$I = I_{com} + Mh^2.$$ The shift always **adds** $Mh^2 \ge 0$: the com axis is the cheapest parallel axis.
concepts.detail: Proof idea: write each point's position as com-plus-offset. The cross terms vanish exactly because the origin sits at the center of mass — $\sum m_i \vec r'_i = 0$ — leaving $\sum m_i r_i'^2 + Mh^2$. This theorem turns one table entry into every off-center axis you will ever need.

concepts.statement: For a composite body, inertias about a **common axis** simply add: $I_{total} = I_1 + I_2 + \cdots$. Holes are negative mass. The trick is choosing the common axis so that each part's inertia is easy (often via the parallel-axis theorem).
concepts.detail: Example: a hoop of mass $M_h$ welded to a disk of mass $M_d$, same radius $R$, spins about their common central axis: $I = M_hR^2 + \frac12 M_dR^2$ — a bicycle wheel with a heavy rim and a light hub, close to $MR^2$ overall.

concepts.term: Calculating the Rotational Inertia: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Calculating the Rotational Inertia problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rotation about a fixed axis; the working equation is $\omega = d\theta/dt$, $v = \omega r$, $a_c = \omega^2r$, $K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12I\omega^2$, $\tau = rF\sin\phi = I\alpha$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere); rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.

figures.caption: The parallel-axis theorem. A uniform rod ($M = 2.4$ kg, $L = 1.0$ m) has $I_{com} = \frac{1}{12}ML^2 = 0.20\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ about the central axis. About the parallel axis at its end, $h = L/2 = 0.50$ m away, $$I_{end} = I_{com} + Mh^2 = 0.20 + (2.4)(0.25) = 0.80\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2 = \tfrac13 ML^2$$ — exactly what the direct integration gives. Moving the axis away from the center of mass is always expensive.

examples.title: A rod about its end, two ways
examples.problem: A uniform rod of mass 2.4 kg and length 1.0 m. Find its rotational inertia about a perpendicular axis through one end, (a) by integration, (b) by the parallel-axis theorem.

steps.label: Integration
steps.text: With $dm = (M/L)dx$ measured from the end: $I = \frac{M}{L}\int_0^L x^2\,dx = \frac{M}{L}\cdot\frac{L^3}{3} = \frac13 ML^2 = (2.4)(1.0)/3 = 0.80\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$.

steps.label: Start from the center
steps.text: The table gives $I_{com} = \frac{1}{12}ML^2 = 0.20\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ about the midpoint axis.

steps.label: Shift the axis
steps.text: The end axis is $h = L/2 = 0.50$ m from the com: $I = I_{com} + Mh^2 = 0.20 + (2.4)(0.50)^2 = 0.20 + 0.60 = 0.80\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$.

steps.label: Agreement
steps.text: Both routes agree exactly — the theorem is an identity, not an approximation. Note the shift term $Mh^2 = 0.60$ dwarfed the original 0.20: end-mounted rods are expensive to spin.

examples.result: $I = 0.80\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2 = \frac13 ML^2$ about the end, confirmed by two independent methods.

examples.title: Checking the theorem's direction
examples.problem: For the same rod, is there any parallel axis about which the inertia is smaller than 0.20 kg·m²?

steps.label: Write the general shift
steps.text: $I = I_{com} + Mh^2$ with $Mh^2 = 2.4h^2 \ge 0$ for every $h$.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.text: No: the minimum over all parallel axes occurs at $h = 0$ — the com axis. Any other placement, by any distance, adds a non-negative $Mh^2$.

steps.label: A quick number
steps.text: Shifting to $h = 0.30$ m: $I = 0.20 + (2.4)(0.09) = 0.42\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ — more than double, from a modest offset.

examples.result: The center-of-mass axis is always the minimum-inertia axis in its direction. Machinery that must spin up fast is designed so the axis passes through the com.

keyTakeaways: Compute $I = \int r^2 dm$ for simple bodies; a uniform rod gives $\frac13 ML^2$ about its end but only $\frac{1}{12}ML^2$ about its center.
Parallel-axis theorem: $I = I_{com} + Mh^2$ — the com axis is always the cheapest parallel axis, and inertias about a common axis add for composite bodies.
Standard results to memorize: hoop $MR^2$, disk $\frac12 MR^2$, solid sphere $\frac25 MR^2$, spherical shell $\frac23 MR^2$.

quiz.q: A uniform rod (M = 1.2 kg, L = 0.80 m) rotates about a perpendicular axis through one end. Its rotational inertia is:
A disk has rotational inertia 0.090 kg·m² about its central axis. Shifted to a parallel axis 0.30 m from the center, with the disk's mass 2.0 kg, the new inertia is:
quiz.explanation: $I = I_{com} + Mh^2 = 0.090 + (2.0)(0.30)^2 = 0.090 + 0.18 = 0.27\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$. The offset often contributes more than the body itself.

quiz.q: Of two bodies with equal mass and equal outer radius, the one with the LARGEST rotational inertia about its central axis is:
quiz.explanation: The shell keeps all its mass at radius $R$ ($\frac23 MR^2$), beating the solid sphere ($\frac25 MR^2$) whose mass crowds the center. Only the hoop among planar shapes does better relative to its radius.

quiz.q: The parallel-axis theorem $I = I_{com} + Mh^2$ requires that the two axes be:
options: any two axes through the body
parallel, with one through the center of mass
both through the center of mass
quiz.explanation: The derivation splits each particle's position into com-plus-offset, which only works for parallel axes, and uses $\sum m_i \vec r_i' = 0$, which is the definition of the com axis. Drop either hypothesis and the theorem fails.

intro: Torque is the turning effectiveness of a force — and effectiveness, not effort, is what matters: the same push can be useless at a hinge and decisive at a handle. This section defines torque about an axis, introduces the lever arm picture that makes computations visual, and fixes the sign convention (counterclockwise positive) that the next section's law of motion will inherit.
objectives: Compute torque about an axis from $\tau = rF\sin\phi$ and from the lever arm $\tau = Fr_\perp$
Determine the sign of a torque about a chosen axis
Explain why torque depends on the choice of axis and differs from work despite sharing units of N·m

concepts.statement: The **torque** of a force $\vec F$ applied at point $P$ about a fixed axis through origin $O$ is $$\tau = r F \sin\phi,$$ where $\vec r$ points from $O$ to $P$ and $\phi$ is the angle between $\vec r$ and $\vec F$. Unit: N·m, positive for counterclockwise turning about the axis.
concepts.detail: Torque depends on three things: the force, where it is applied, and the axis you chose — change the axis and every torque changes. A force applied along a line through the axis ($\phi = 0$) produces zero torque however large it is: you cannot turn a door by pushing on its hinges.

concepts.statement: The **lever arm** (moment arm) $r_\perp$ is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of the force: $$r_\perp = r\sin\phi, \qquad \tau = F r_\perp.$$ The line of action is the infinite line along $\vec F$ through the application point.
concepts.detail: The lever arm picture is the fast way to compute torques in equilibrium problems: drop a perpendicular from the pivot to each force's line of action, measure, multiply. It also makes the geometry memorable — a force is most effective when its line of action passes far from the axis and perpendicular to the radius.

concepts.statement: Torque and work share the unit N·m but describe different things: work $W = Fd\cos\theta$ is energy transferred along a displacement; torque depends on force and lever arm with **no** displacement required. A stalled motor delivering 50 N·m at a standstill does no work while exerting full torque.
concepts.detail: The distinction sharpens in Section 10.8, where a torque acting through an angular displacement $d\theta$ does work $dW = \tau\,d\theta$ — there the joule really appears. For now, treat N·m of torque as a static measure of turning push.

concepts.statement: **Solve Torque problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rotation about a fixed axis; the working equation is $\omega = d\theta/dt$, $v = \omega r$, $a_c = \omega^2r$, $K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12I\omega^2$, $\tau = rF\sin\phi = I\alpha$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere); rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.

concepts.statement: **Torque lives at $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere) and the textbook model holds while rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Torque calculation gives seconds when $\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

figures.caption: Torque and the lever arm. A force $F = 80$ N applied at the end of a 2.40 m rod, at angle $\phi = 37^\circ$ to the rod, about a pivot at the left end. The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action: $r_\perp = r\sin\phi = (2.40)(0.60) = 1.44$ m, giving $\tau = Fr_\perp = (80)(1.44) \approx 115$ N·m, clockwise (negative). Had the force acted at 90° to the rod, the lever arm would be the full 2.40 m and the torque 192 N·m — geometry, not muscle, sets the turning power.
