examples.title: Wrench mathematics
examples.problem: A mechanic pulls on a 0.30 m wrench with 80 N. (a) Perpendicular to the handle; (b) at 37° to it; (c) along the handle. Find the torque about the bolt in each case.

steps.label: Perpendicular
steps.text: $\phi = 90^\circ$: $\tau = rF = (0.30)(80) = 24$ N·m — the maximum this force can deliver at this radius.

steps.label: At 37°
steps.text: $\tau = rF\sin 37^\circ = (0.30)(80)(0.60) = 14$ N·m — the lever arm has shrunk to $0.30\sin 37^\circ = 0.18$ m.

steps.label: Along the handle
steps.text: $\phi = 0$: $\tau = 0$. Pulling along the wrench's own axis turns nothing — the line of action passes through the bolt.

steps.label: The lesson
steps.text: The mechanic's instinct — pull at right angles to the tool, and use a longer tool — is exactly $\tau = Fr_\perp$.

examples.result: 24 N·m, 14 N·m, 0 — same 80 N pull, three different turning powers, set entirely by geometry.

examples.title: Why you push a door at the far edge
examples.problem: A door is 0.90 m wide, hinged on the left. You push with 20 N at the handle, (a) perpendicular to the door face; (b) perpendicular but at 0.10 m from the hinge. Compare torques about the hinge.

steps.label: At the handle
steps.text: $\tau = (0.90)(20) = 18$ N·m (counterclockwise if you push the door's opening direction — sign aside, magnitude 18).

steps.label: Near the hinge
steps.text: $\tau = (0.10)(20) = 2.0$ N·m — one-ninth of the turning power for the same push.

steps.label: Recovering it
steps.text: To get 18 N·m from near the hinge you would need 180 N. Physics formalizes the everyday rule: push the door where the lever arm is largest.

examples.result: 18 N·m versus 2.0 N·m. Torque, not force, opens doors.

keyTakeaways: Torque about an axis: $\tau = rF\sin\phi = F r_\perp$, in N·m, with counterclockwise positive; it depends on the axis chosen.
The lever arm $r_\perp$ is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the force's line of action — the fastest route to torques in statics problems.
Torque is not work: no displacement is needed for torque, and a force whose line passes through the axis contributes zero.

quiz.q: A 100 N force is applied to a door 1.2 m from the hinge, at 30° to the door's surface (i.e., 60° to the plane of the door's swing, so the angle between r and F is 60°). The torque about the hinge is:
quiz.explanation: $\tau = rF\sin\phi = (1.2)(100)\sin 60^\circ = 120(0.866) \approx 104$ N·m. Only the component perpendicular to the radius, times the radius, turns the door.

quiz.q: A force produces zero torque about an axis whenever:
options: its line of action passes through the axis
it is applied at a large radius
quiz.explanation: If the line of action crosses the axis, $r_\perp = 0$ and $\tau = Fr_\perp = 0$ however large $F$ is. Magnitude and direction both matter only through the lever arm.

quiz.q: A stalled motor holds its shaft at rest while exerting 50 N·m. The work it does on the shaft is:
options: zero, because there is no angular displacement
quiz.explanation: Torque does work $W = \int \tau\,d\theta$; with $d\theta = 0$ nothing is transferred. Torque's N·m only become joules after rotation — Section 10.8 makes this precise.

quiz.q: The same force is applied to the same point of a body, but you recompute the torque about a different axis. The torque:
options: stays the same; torque is a property of the force alone
generally changes, because r and the lever arm change
becomes zero for any axis not through the application point
quiz.explanation: Torque is defined relative to an axis: the vector $\vec r$ from axis to application point, and hence $\tau = rF\sin\phi$, changes when the axis moves. Always state what you are taking torques about.

intro: Net torque causes angular acceleration, and the constant of proportionality is the rotational inertia: τ_net = Iα, the exact rotational twin of F = ma. The law closes the loop this chapter opened — kinematics, energy and now dynamics all hang off the same three quantities θ, ω, α and their inertial partner I. Pulleys stop being decoration and start having mass that matters.
objectives: State Newton's second law for rotation and the conditions on the axis for its validity
Solve single-torque and Atwood-machine problems with massive pulleys
Use the linear-rotational dictionary to translate between the two second laws

concepts.statement: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, $$\tau_{net} = I\alpha,$$ where $\tau_{net}$ is the sum of all **external** torques about that axis and $I$ is the rotational inertia about the **same** axis. Internal torques cancel in pairs, exactly as internal forces did in Chapter 9.
concepts.detail: Requirements: the axis must be fixed in an inertial frame (the shortcuts for accelerating axes come with Chapter 11's full vector treatment). Note the honesty of the formula: a light pulley ($I \approx 0$) needs $\tau_{net} \approx 0$, which is why string tensions on either side of an ideal pulley are equal — and unequal the moment the pulley has mass.

concepts.statement: | translation | rotation | | --- | --- | | $\sum F = ma$ | $\sum \tau = I\alpha$ | | $m$ | $I$ | | $F$ | $\tau$ | | $a$ | $\alpha$ | | $p = mv$ | $L = I\omega$ (Ch. 11) | | $\frac12 mv^2$ | $\frac12 I\omega^2$ |
concepts.detail: The analogy is structural, not accidental — both columns are the same mechanics written about different variables. It extends to work ($Fs \to \tau\theta$) and to momentum conservation in the next chapter. But do not push it blindly: $I$ depends on the axis while $m$ never does.

concepts.statement: When a pulley has rotational inertia $I$, the tensions on its two sides **differ**: the difference supplies the torque $\tau = (T_2 - T_1)R = I\alpha$. An ideal (massless, frictionless) pulley has $I \to 0$, forcing $T_1 = T_2$.
concepts.detail: In a belt or chain drive, unequal tension is the whole point — the tension difference times the pulley radius is what spins up the machinery. Watch for it also in yo-yos (Section 11.3), where the string tension both accelerates the center of mass and torques the spin.

concepts.term: Newton's Second Law for Rotation: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Newton's Second Law for Rotation problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rotation about a fixed axis; the working equation is $\omega = d\theta/dt$, $v = \omega r$, $a_c = \omega^2r$, $K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12I\omega^2$, $\tau = rF\sin\phi = I\alpha$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere); rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.

concepts.term: Newton's Second Law for Rotation: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Newton's Second Law for Rotation lives at $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere) and the textbook model holds while rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Newton's Second Law for Rotation calculation gives seconds when $\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Spin-up of a heavy disk
examples.problem: A uniform disk (M = 3.0 kg, R = 0.10 m) on a frictionless bearing has a string wrapped around its rim. Pulling the string with a constant tangential 24 N, find the angular acceleration and the state after 2.0 s.

steps.label: Torque
steps.text: The pull is tangential, so $\tau = TR = (24)(0.10) = 2.4$ N·m.

steps.label: After 2.0 s from rest
steps.text: $\omega = \alpha t = 320$ rad/s and $\theta = \frac12\alpha t^2 = 320$ rad. The energy check comes in Section 10.8: the string's work $T(R\theta) = 768$ J should equal $\frac12 I\omega^2 = \frac12(0.015)(320)^2 = 768$ J. It does.

examples.result: $\alpha = 160\ \text{rad/s}^2$; after 2.0 s, $\omega = 320$ rad/s. A modest 2.4 N·m on a small inertia gives ferocious spin-up.

examples.title: Atwood machine with a massive pulley
examples.problem: A 2.0 kg and a 3.0 kg mass hang from a string over a solid disk pulley (M = 2.0 kg, R = 0.10 m, $I = \frac12 MR^2 = 0.010$). Find the acceleration and both tensions.

steps.label: Three unknowns, three laws
steps.text: Newton for each hanging mass (down positive for the 3.0 kg side): $3.0g - T_2 = 3.0a$ and $T_1 - 2.0g = 2.0a$; rotation for the pulley: $(T_2 - T_1)R = I\alpha = I a/R$.

steps.label: Solve
steps.text: Eliminating tensions: $(T_2 - T_1) = Ia/R^2 = 1.0a$; substituting, $3.0g - 2.0g - 1.0a = 5.0a$, so $a = g/6 = 1.63\ \text{m/s}^2$.

steps.label: Ideal-pulley check
steps.text: With $I = 0$ the formula gives $a = g/5 = 1.96$ m/s² and $T_1 = T_2$ — the Chapter 5 result. The pulley's inertia brakes the system.

examples.result: $a = 1.63\ \text{m/s}^2$, $T_1 = 22.9$ N, $T_2 = 24.5$ N. Unequal tensions are the signature of a pulley that really spins.

keyTakeaways: $\tau_{net} = I\alpha$ about a fixed axis: external torques only, with $I$ computed about that same axis.
A massive pulley forces unequal string tensions — the difference $(T_2 - T_1)R$ is exactly the torque spinning it up.
The translation ↔ rotation dictionary ($F \to \tau$, $m \to I$, $a \to \alpha$) organizes the whole chapter and extends into Chapter 11.

quiz.q: A disk with I = 0.020 kg·m² experiences a net torque of 3.0 N·m about its fixed central axis. Its angular acceleration is:
quiz.explanation: $\alpha = \tau/I = 3.0/0.020 = 150\ \text{rad/s}^2$. Small inertias spin up hard — the lever-and-flywheel world in one division.

quiz.q: The string tensions on the two sides of an ideal (massless) pulley must be equal because:
options: with $I \to 0$, $\tau_{net} = I\alpha$ forces the net torque, hence the tension difference, to zero
quiz.explanation: $(T_2 - T_1)R = I\alpha$ with $I = 0$: any tension difference would demand infinite $\alpha$. Masslessness is exactly the license to treat both sides as having one tension.

quiz.q: In an Atwood machine, replacing the light pulley with a heavy one (same radii, string does not slip):
options: the acceleration is unchanged; only the tensions change
quiz.explanation: The pulley's inertia joins the resistance to motion: $a = (m_2 - m_1)g/(m_1 + m_2 + I/R^2)$. Extra denominator, smaller acceleration — and the tensions now differ.

quiz.q: Which torque must be summed in $\tau_{net} = I\alpha$?
options: only external torques about the chosen fixed axis
only torques perpendicular to the axis of rotation of the body itself
quiz.explanation: Internal torques cancel in pairs (Newton's third law along joining lines), so only external ones survive the sum — the rotational rerun of the Chapter 9 argument for $\vec F_{net,ext}$.

intro: A torque acting while a body rotates does work — the rotational work-energy theorem completes the chapter's dynamics. The work is τ dθ per small turn, the kinetic energy is ½Iω², and their bookkeeping closes exactly as F ds did for ½mv². Power, the rate of delivering work, becomes the product τω — the equation printed on every motor's nameplate.
objectives: Compute rotational work $W = \int \tau\,d\theta$ (and $W = \tau\theta$ for constant torque) and rotational power $P = \tau\omega$
Apply the rotational work-energy theorem $W_{net} = \Delta(\frac12 I\omega^2)$
Solve combined problems where a torque spins a body up from rest and verify the energy ledger

concepts.statement: A torque $\tau$ acting while a body turns through $d\theta$ does $$dW = \tau\,d\theta, \qquad W = \int_{\theta_i}^{\theta_f} \tau\,d\theta,$$ which reduces to $W = \tau\theta$ for constant torque. The formula is $W = F\,ds$ in rotational dress: the 'displacement' is angular.
concepts.detail: Check the units: N·m times rad = J, with radians canceling silently. Only the component of any force along the motion works, and only torque about the actual rotation axis does rotational work.

concepts.statement: $$W_{net} = \int \tau_{net}\,d\theta = \tfrac12 I\omega_f^2 - \tfrac12 I\omega_i^2.$$ The net work done by torques about the fixed axis equals the change in rotational kinetic energy — with variable inertia, sum the changes interval by interval.
concepts.detail: Proof for constant $I$: $\tau = I\alpha = I\frac{d\omega}{dt} = I\omega\frac{d\omega}{d\theta}$ (chain rule with $\omega = d\theta/dt$), so $\tau\,d\theta = I\omega\,d\omega = d(\frac12 I\omega^2)$. One integration gives the theorem — the same trick that proved the linear version.

concepts.statement: $$P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \tau\omega.$$ An engine delivering 200 N·m at 3000 rpm ($\omega = 314$ rad/s) outputs $P = 6.3\times10^{4}$ W — about 84 hp. Motor nameplates quote torque and speed; their product is the power.
concepts.detail: This is why the same engine feels strong at low rpm (high torque available) yet delivers its peak power higher in the rev range, and why gears trade torque for speed at constant power: $\tau\omega$ is what the engine can supply, and the gearbox only repackages it.

concepts.term: Work and Rotational Kinetic Energy: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Work and Rotational Kinetic Energy problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rotation about a fixed axis; the working equation is $\omega = d\theta/dt$, $v = \omega r$, $a_c = \omega^2r$, $K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12I\omega^2$, $\tau = rF\sin\phi = I\alpha$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere); rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.

concepts.term: Work and Rotational Kinetic Energy: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Work and Rotational Kinetic Energy lives at $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere) and the textbook model holds while rigid body with fixed axis for $\tau = I\alpha$; $\theta$ in radians.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Work and Rotational Kinetic Energy calculation gives seconds when $\text{rad}$, $\text{rad/s}$, $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $I\sim \tfrac12MR^2$ (disk) to $\tfrac25MR^2$ (sphere), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Energy audit of the spun-up disk
examples.problem: Section 10.7's disk ($I = 0.015\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) was pulled by a tangential 24 N at radius 0.10 m (torque 2.4 N·m) through θ = 320 rad from rest. Verify the work-energy ledger.

steps.label: Kinetic energy gained
steps.text: From rest to $\omega = 320$ rad/s: $K_f = \frac12 I\omega^2 = \frac12(0.015)(320)^2 = 768$ J.

steps.label: Ledger closes
steps.text: Work in, energy stored: $768 = 768$. Every joule the string delivered — equivalently $T \times (R\theta) = 24 \times 32$ m of string pull — sits in the disk's rotation.

examples.result: Work 768 J = energy stored 768 J. The work-energy theorem is an audit tool: compute both sides when a dynamics problem looks tangled.

examples.title: Motor power and torque
examples.problem: A motor turns a shaft at 1000 rev/min while delivering a constant 25 N·m. Find the power in watts and horsepower.

steps.label: Power
steps.text: $P = \tau\omega = (25)(104.7) = 2618\ \text{W} \approx 2.6$ kW.

steps.label: Horsepower
steps.text: Dividing by 746 W/hp: about 3.5 hp — a serious shop motor.

steps.label: Torque-speed trade
steps.text: Geared down to 100 rev/min with the same power available, the shaft could deliver $\tau = P/\omega = 2618/10.5 = 250$ N·m — ten times the torque. Gears buy torque with speed.

examples.result: $P \approx 2.6$ kW $\approx 3.5$ hp, and $P = \tau\omega$ shows how a gearbox converts speed into torque at fixed power.

keyTakeaways: Rotational work: $dW = \tau\,d\theta$; constant torque does $W = \tau\theta$ (joules, with radians canceling).
Work-energy theorem: $W_{net} = \frac12 I\omega_f^2 - \frac12 I\omega_i^2$ — the rotational twin of $\frac12 mv^2$ bookkeeping.
Power is $P = \tau\omega$: motor nameplate torque times speed, and the reason gearboxes trade torque for angular speed at constant power.

quiz.q: A constant 5.0 N·m torque turns a flywheel through 12 revolutions. The work done is about:
quiz.explanation: Convert first: $12\ \text{rev} = 24\pi = 75.4$ rad, so $W = \tau\theta = (5.0)(75.4) = 377$ J. Skipping the radian conversion is the classic error (option A).

quiz.q: A wheel with I = 2.0 kg·m² spins at 15 rad/s. The net work needed to bring it to rest is:
quiz.explanation: $W_{net} = \Delta K = 0 - \frac12(2.0)(15)^2 = -225$ J: the friction torque must remove 225 J, doing negative work.

quiz.q: An engine delivers 150 N·m at 2000 rpm. Its output power is closest to:
quiz.explanation: $\omega = 2000(2\pi/60) = 209$ rad/s, so $P = \tau\omega = (150)(209) \approx 3.1\times10^{4}$ W — about 42 hp.

quiz.q: The rotational work-energy theorem is derived from $\tau = I\alpha$ by:
options: integrating both sides over time only
using the chain rule to write $\alpha = \omega\,d\omega/d\theta$ so that $\tau\,d\theta = I\omega\,d\omega$
assuming the torque is always constant
quiz.explanation: With $\omega = d\theta/dt$, one has $\alpha = d\omega/dt = (d\omega/d\theta)(d\theta/dt) = \omega\,d\omega/d\theta$; then $\tau\,d\theta = I\omega\,d\omega = d(\frac12 I\omega^2)$ — integrate to finish, no constancy of $\tau$ required.

intro: A rolling wheel is doing two jobs at once: its center translates while every spoke rotates about that center. Remarkably, the two motions are welded together by one simple equation, v = ωR, and the wheel's contact with the road is — for an instant — perfectly still. Rolling is the first place where the linear and rotational halves of mechanics must be used simultaneously.
objectives: Describe rolling as translation of the center of mass plus rotation about the center of mass
Derive and apply the rolling-without-slipping constraint $v_{com} = \omega R$ and its differentiated form $a_{com} = \alpha R$
Show that rolling is instantaneously a pure rotation about the contact point, with the top of the wheel moving at twice the com speed

concepts.statement: A rolling body's motion is the superposition of (i) **pure translation** — every point moves with $\vec v_{com}$ — and (ii) **pure rotation** about an axis through the center of mass. The velocity of any point is the vector sum of the two contributions.
concepts.detail: This decomposition is exact, not an approximation, and it is the bookkeeping device for everything in this chapter: kinetic energy splits the same way ($\frac12 Mv_{com}^2 + \frac12 I_{com}\omega^2$), and each point's velocity comes from adding the two vector pieces.

concepts.statement: For rolling **without slipping**, the translational and angular motions are locked: $$v_{com} = \omega R, \qquad a_{com} = \alpha R$$ (the second by differentiation). The arc length laid on the road equals the distance traveled: $s = R\theta$.
concepts.detail: The proof is one sentence: the contact point must have zero velocity relative to the ground, and the contact point's velocity is $v_{com}$ (translation) minus $\omega R$ (rotation moving backward), forcing the equality. Skidding — a locked wheel on ice — is exactly the failure of this constraint.

concepts.term: Instantaneous axis at the contact point
concepts.statement: Because the contact point is momentarily at rest, the rolling wheel is instantaneously in **pure rotation about that point**: the top of the wheel moves at $2v_{com}$, the center at $v_{com}$, the contact at zero. The wheel pivots about its own footprint, over and over.
concepts.detail: This is why the top of a moving bicycle wheel is a blur while the valve stem near the hub is trackable — and why a mud flap placed high on a truck catches flung debris: the top of the tire swings forward at twice the truck's speed. The full trajectory of a rim point is a cycloid.

concepts.statement: **Solve Rolling problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rolling and angular momentum; the working equation is $v_{\text{com}} = \omega R$ (no slip), $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$, $L = I\omega$, $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = d\vec L/dt$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit); no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.

concepts.statement: **Rolling lives at $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit) and the textbook model holds while no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Rolling calculation gives seconds when $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

figures.caption: Rolling without slipping. The wheel translates at $v_{com}$ while rotating at $\omega$, and the two are locked by $v_{com} = \omega R$: the bottom point's backward rotational speed $\omega R$ exactly cancels the forward translation, so the contact point is **instantaneously at rest**. Point speeds stack: zero at contact, $v_{com}$ at the hub, $2v_{com} = 2\omega R$ at the top. The wheel may be viewed as pure rotation about the contact point at each instant.

examples.title: A bicycle's wheel speed
examples.problem: A bicycle rolls at 6.2 m/s on wheels of radius 0.33 m. Find the wheels' angular velocity and the speed of the topmost point of a wheel.

steps.label: Angular velocity
steps.text: From $v_{com} = \omega R$: $\omega = 6.2/0.33 = 18.8\ \text{rad/s}$, or $\omega/2\pi = 3.0$ rev/s.

steps.label: Top point
steps.text: Translation gives $+6.2$ m/s; rotation about the hub adds $\omega R = 6.2$ m/s in the same direction at the top: total $12.4$ m/s forward.

steps.label: Contact point
steps.text: The two contributions cancel there: the point on the tire touching the road is momentarily at rest relative to the road — rolling is a sequence of pivots about the footprint.

examples.result: $\omega = 18.8$ rad/s (3.0 rev/s); the tire's crown races ahead at 12.4 m/s while its footprint stands still.

examples.title: How far per revolution
examples.problem: A car moves at 20 m/s on tires of radius 0.33 m. Find the tire's angular velocity in rev/s, and the distance the car travels per wheel revolution.

steps.label: Distance per turn
steps.text: $s = R\theta$ for one turn: $s = 2\pi R = (2\pi)(0.33) = 2.07$ m — the tire's circumference, as it must be.

steps.label: Cross-check
steps.text: At 9.65 turns per second times 2.07 m per turn: $9.65 \times 2.07 = 20$ m/s. Consistent — the constraint stitches the two descriptions together.

examples.result: $\omega = 60.6$ rad/s $= 9.65$ rev/s; each revolution carries the car 2.07 m, one full circumference.

keyTakeaways: Rolling = translation of the com + rotation about the com; without slipping the two are locked by $v_{com} = \omega R$ and $a_{com} = \alpha R$.
The contact point is instantaneously at rest, so rolling is pure rotation about the contact point: point speeds run from 0 (contact) to $2v_{com}$ (top).
Distance traveled equals arc laid down: $s = R\theta$, one circumference per revolution.

quiz.q: A wheel of radius 0.40 m rolls without slipping at 6.0 m/s. Its angular velocity is:
quiz.explanation: $\omega = v_{com}/R = 6.0/0.40 = 15$ rad/s — about 2.4 rev/s only in the separate sense that $15/2\pi \approx 2.39$; the clean answer in the requested unit is 15 rad/s.

quiz.q: For a wheel rolling without slipping, which point is instantaneously at rest?
options: the point in contact with the ground
no point; rolling motion never rests
quiz.explanation: At the contact point the backward rotational speed $\omega R$ cancels the forward translation $v_{com} = \omega R$ — the footprint is momentarily stationary, which is precisely why static friction can grip it.

quiz.q: A car travels at 15 m/s. The top of a tire moves forward, relative to the road, at:
quiz.explanation: Translation ($v_{com}$) and rotation ($\omega R = v_{com}$) add at the top: $2v_{com} = 30$ m/s. This is why high tire flings debris so far — and why the speedometer's cable is safe inside the hub.

intro: Why does a can of soup beat a hoop down a ramp? Because rolling energy splits between translation and spin, and how much goes to spin is set by the body's shape through the single ratio I_com/MR². One derivation gives the acceleration of any round body on an incline, and the famous race result: sphere first, disk next, hoop last — independent of mass and radius.
objectives: Write the kinetic energy of a rolling body as $K = \frac12 Mv_{com}^2 + \frac12 I_{com}\omega^2$ and combine it with the rolling constraint
Derive $a_{com} = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I_{com}/MR^2}$ for rolling down an incline, using force/torque analysis
Predict and verify the rolling race: sphere beats disk beats hoop, independent of M and R

concepts.statement: A body rolling at $v_{com}$ with spin $\omega$ has $$K = \tfrac12 M v_{com}^2 + \tfrac12 I_{com}\omega^2 = \tfrac12 M v_{com}^2\left(1 + \frac{I_{com}}{MR^2}\right),$$ where the second form uses the rolling constraint $\omega = v_{com}/R$.
concepts.detail: The dimensionless shape factor $k = I_{com}/MR^2$ is all that matters: hoop $k = 1$, disk $k = \frac12$, solid sphere $k = \frac25$. A hoop devotes half its rolling energy to spin; a sphere only 2/7 of the total. Note mass and radius have cancelled — shape alone decides.

concepts.statement: Newton's second law along the incline plus the torque equation about the com gives, for rolling without slipping, $$a_{com} = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I_{com}/MR^2}.$$ Derivation: $Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma_{com}$ and $fR = I_{com}\alpha = I_{com}a_{com}/R$; eliminate $f$.
concepts.detail: The friction $f$ is **static** — the contact point does not slide — so it does no work and wastes no energy; it merely redistributes energy from translation into spin. On a frictionless ramp the body would slide at $g\sin\theta$ and never rotate at all.

concepts.statement: Ranking by shape factor $k$: sphere ($\frac25$) > disk ($\frac12$) > hoop ($1$) in acceleration, whatever their masses and radii. At the bottom of a drop of height $h$, $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+k}}:$$ sphere $\sqrt{10gh/7}$, disk $\sqrt{4gh/3}$, hoop $\sqrt{gh}$.
concepts.detail: The finish order is a pure geometry statement — a marble beats a coin beats a hula hoop on any ramp, every time. Cans of soup race by their contents: liquid soup barely rotates ($k \approx 0$) and outruns a solid can, a classic lecture demo.

concepts.term: Forces and Kinetic Energy of Rolling: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Forces and Kinetic Energy of Rolling problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rolling and angular momentum; the working equation is $v_{\text{com}} = \omega R$ (no slip), $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$, $L = I\omega$, $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = d\vec L/dt$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit); no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.

concepts.term: Forces and Kinetic Energy of Rolling: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Forces and Kinetic Energy of Rolling lives at $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit) and the textbook model holds while no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Forces and Kinetic Energy of Rolling calculation gives seconds when $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: The ramp race, numerically
examples.problem: A solid sphere, a solid disk and a hoop, each of the same mass 1.0 kg and radius 0.10 m, are released together on a 30° incline of height 1.2 m. Find each acceleration and each speed at the bottom.

steps.label: Energy audit for the sphere
steps.text: $Mgh = (1.0)(9.8)(1.2) = 11.8$ J; at the bottom $K_{trans} = \frac12(1)(16.8) = 8.4$ J and $K_{rot} = \frac12 (\frac25 MR^2)(v/R)^2 = \frac15 v^2 = 3.4$ J. Total $11.8$ J — the gravitational payment is split 5:2 between translation and spin, exactly the sphere's $1 + \frac25$.

steps.label: Mass and radius
steps.text: Cancel everywhere: a 5 g marble and a 5 kg bowling ball tie, and so would a coin and a manhole cover of the same shape.

examples.result: Accelerations 3.5 / 3.3 / 2.5 m/s² and bottom speeds 4.10 / 3.96 / 3.43 m/s for sphere, disk, hoop — shape alone sets the podium.

examples.title: How much friction does rolling need?
examples.problem: For the sphere of the previous example on the 30° ramp, find the static friction force and the minimum coefficient of friction.

steps.label: Torque equation
steps.text: $fR = I_{com}\alpha$ with $I = \frac25 MR^2$ and $\alpha = a/R$: $f = \frac25 Ma = (0.4)(1.0)(3.5) = 1.4$ N.

steps.label: Minimum μ
steps.text: $\mu_{min} = f/N = 1.4/8.5 = 0.16$. Any grippier surface and the sphere rolls; any slicker and it slips, and then both the acceleration and the analysis change.

steps.label: Note who does the work
steps.text: Static friction acts at a point of zero velocity, so it does no work: it levies no energy tax, it only redirects energy into spin.

examples.result: $f = 1.4$ N and $\mu_{min} \approx 0.16$: just enough grip to enforce $v_{com} = \omega R$.

keyTakeaways: Rolling energy splits as $K = \frac12 Mv^2(1 + k)$ with shape factor $k = I_{com}/MR^2$ — mass and radius cancel, shape alone matters.
Down an incline, $a_{com} = g\sin\theta/(1 + k)$; the required friction is static and does no work.
Race order: sphere ($k = 2/5$) before disk ($1/2$) before hoop ($1$), with bottom speeds $\sqrt{10gh/7}$, $\sqrt{4gh/3}$, $\sqrt{gh}$.

quiz.q: A solid sphere and a hoop roll from rest down the same incline. At the bottom:
options: both have the same speed; the hoop spins faster
the sphere is faster, because less of its energy is tied up in rotation
the hoop is faster, because it stores more rotational energy
the winner depends on their masses
quiz.explanation: $v = \sqrt{2gh/(1+k)}$ is larger for smaller $k$: the sphere's $\frac25$ beats the hoop's $1$. Energy is conserved either way; the sphere just spends less of it spinning.

quiz.q: A solid disk rolls down a 30° incline without slipping. Its acceleration is:
quiz.explanation: $a = g\sin\theta/(1 + \frac12) = (9.8)(0.5)/1.5 = 3.27\ \text{m/s}^2$. The sliding disk (no friction) would accelerate at 4.9 — rolling always brakes relative to sliding.

quiz.q: The friction acting on a body rolling without slipping down an incline:
options: does negative work, dissipating energy as heat
does no work, because it acts on an instantaneously stationary contact point
does positive work, driving the rotation
is kinetic friction and depends on the sliding speed
quiz.explanation: The contact patch is momentarily at rest, so $P = \vec f \cdot \vec v = 0$ there: static friction transfers energy between translation and spin without taxing it. That is why the bottom speeds obey energy conservation exactly.

quiz.q: A soup can (liquid center, barely rotates) races a solid can of the same size down a ramp. The winner is:
options: the liquid can, because almost none of its energy goes to spin
the solid can, because it is heavier
a tie, since both have the same mass and radius
the solid can, because solid cans have lower centers of mass
quiz.explanation: The liquid mostly translates ($k \to 0$ effectively for the soup), so $a \to g\sin\theta$: nearly the full gravitational payment goes into forward motion. The demo works precisely because the soup refuses to spin with the can.

intro: A yo-yo is a rolling body whose ramp is its own string: it falls, translating and spinning, with the string tension torquing the spin. The analysis is one force equation plus one torque equation, and the result — that a solid-disk yo-yo falls at two-thirds of g — showcases the clean division of labor between Newton's two laws.
objectives: Model the yo-yo as a body rolling down its string and derive its acceleration and tension
Verify the solution by energy bookkeeping
Explain why a yo-yo's axle radius and body inertia, not its mass, set the behavior

concepts.statement: A yo-yo is a spool of radius $R$ and rotational inertia $I$ hanging from a string wound around its axle. As it falls a distance $d$, the com translates downward while the string unwinds without slipping: the 'rolling constraint' is $v_{com} = \omega R$ with the string's exit point playing the road's contact point.
concepts.detail: The string is vertical and (ideally) massless; the tension $T$ acts at the rim of the axle, tangent to it, so it delivers torque $TR$ about the center of mass. Real yo-yos have a thin axle, but the textbook model treats the string radius as $R$ — the inertia $I$ absorbs the difference in shape.

concepts.statement: Newton's second law for the fall plus the torque equation about the com: $$Mg - T = Ma_{com}, \qquad TR = I\alpha = I\frac{a_{com}}{R}.$$ Eliminating $T$: $$a_{com} = \frac{g}{1 + I/MR^2}, \qquad T = \frac{Mg}{1 + MR^2/I}.$$ For a solid-disk yo-yo ($I = \frac12 MR^2$): $a = \frac23 g$ and $T = \frac13 Mg$.
concepts.detail: The yo-yo is a ramp-less rerun of Section 11.2: gravity pulls, the string tension both brakes the fall and drives the spin, and the shape factor $I/MR^2$ fixes the split. A massive-rim yo-yo ($I \to MR^2$) would fall at $g/2$; the string would be doing half the work of holding it.

concepts.statement: Energy descent: $Mgh = \frac12 Mv^2 + \frac12 I\omega^2 = \frac12 Mv^2(1 + I/MR^2)$, so $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1 + I/MR^2}}$$ — identical to the rolling-down-a-ramp result with $h$ the distance unwound. For the solid-disk yo-yo, $v = \sqrt{4gh/3}$.
concepts.detail: That the force analysis and the energy analysis agree is a nontrivial consistency check on the tension's role: tension does no net work (the string's contact point with the axle is instantaneously at rest relative to the string), so gravity's energy splits cleanly between the two kinetic forms.

concepts.statement: **Solve The Yo-Yo problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rolling and angular momentum; the working equation is $v_{\text{com}} = \omega R$ (no slip), $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$, $L = I\omega$, $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = d\vec L/dt$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit); no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.

concepts.statement: **The Yo-Yo lives at $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit) and the textbook model holds while no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a The Yo-Yo calculation gives seconds when $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: A falling yo-yo
examples.problem: A yo-yo modeled as a solid disk of mass 0.20 kg and string radius 2.0 cm falls from rest. Find its acceleration, the string tension, and its speed after unwinding 1.0 m.

steps.label: Acceleration
steps.text: With $I = \frac12 MR^2$: $a = g/(1 + \frac12) = \frac23(9.8) = 6.5\ \text{m/s}^2$ — a yo-yo is a lazy faller.

steps.label: Tension
steps.text: $T = Mg - Ma = M(g - \frac23 g) = \frac13 Mg = \frac13(0.20)(9.8) = 0.65$ N. The string holds only a third of the weight while the yo-yo is descending.

steps.label: Speed after 1.0 m
steps.text: Kinematics: $v = \sqrt{2as} = \sqrt{2(6.53)(1.0)} = 3.6$ m/s. Energy: $Mgh = \frac12 Mv^2(1.5)$ gives the same $v^2 = 2gh/1.5 = 13.1$.

steps.label: Spin
steps.text: $\omega = v/R = 3.6/0.020 = 180$ rad/s — about 29 rev/s. Most of the energy is spin: $\frac12 I\omega^2 = \frac12 M v^2$ equals the translational share for a disk.

examples.result: $a = 6.5\ \text{m/s}^2$, $T = 0.65$ N, $v = 3.6$ m/s and $\omega = 180$ rad/s after 1.0 m of fall.

examples.title: The Yo-Yo: angular-momentum numbers
examples.problem: A solid disk ($M \approx 4\ \text{kg}$, $R = 0.30\ \text{m}$, $I = \tfrac12MR^2$) spins at $14\ \text{rad/s}$. Compute $L = I\omega$.

steps.label: Inertia
steps.text: $I = 0.5\times 4\times 0.09 = 0.18\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$.

steps.label: Momentum
steps.text: $L = I\omega = 0.18\times 14 = 2.52\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$.

steps.label: Conservation
steps.text: With $\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$ this $L$ is frozen — halving $I$ doubles $\omega$.

examples.result: $L \approx 2.52\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$.

keyTakeaways: A yo-yo rolls down its string: $a_{com} = g/(1 + I/MR^2)$ and $T = Mg - Ma_{com}$ — for a solid disk, $a = \frac23 g$ and $T = \frac13 Mg$.
The string tension simultaneously brakes the fall and torques the spin; it does no work, so energy splits cleanly between $\frac12 Mv^2$ and $\frac12 I\omega^2$.
The yo-yo's mass is irrelevant; the inertia ratio $I/MR^2$ (its shape) fixes everything.

quiz.q: A yo-yo modeled as a uniform disk falls, unwinding its string. Its downward acceleration is:
quiz.explanation: $a = g/(1 + \frac12) = \frac23 g \approx 6.5\ \text{m/s}^2$. The spinning takes a share of gravity's driving, braking the fall below free fall.

quiz.q: While the solid-disk yo-yo of the example descends, the string tension is:
options: zero, since the yo-yo is falling
quiz.explanation: $T = M(g - a) = M(g - \frac23 g) = \frac13 Mg$. A hand holding the string feels only a third of the yo-yo's weight during the descent — and more than its weight at the sharp yank at the bottom.

quiz.q: Two yo-yos have identical mass and radius, but one has most of its mass at the rim. Descending, the rim-weighted yo-yo has:
options: larger acceleration than the disk-like one
the same acceleration; only the tension differs
quiz.explanation: A rim-weighted body has larger $I/MR^2$, so both $a = g/(1+k)$ drops and $T = Mg\,k/(1+k)$ rises: more of the string's force goes into fighting the fall, because it is busy spinning up a flywheel.

intro: Until now torque lived in a plane, with a sign telling clockwise from counterclockwise. The full three-dimensional theory makes torque a vector — the cross product of the position vector with the force — whose direction is along the rotation axis by the right-hand rule. This vector is what makes gyroscopes, angular momentum and the whole second half of the chapter possible.
objectives: Compute the torque vector $\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F$, its magnitude and its direction
Use the right-hand rule and component (determinant) cross products
Explain the role of the choice of origin, and sum torques as vectors

concepts.statement: The torque about origin $O$ of a force $\vec F$ applied at point $P$ is $$\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F,$$ with $\vec r$ from $O$ to $P$. Magnitude $\tau = rF\sin\phi$ (Section 10.6's scalar), direction perpendicular to the plane of $\vec r$ and $\vec F$, set by the right-hand rule.
concepts.detail: Right-hand rule: point the fingers of your right hand along $\vec r$, curl them toward $\vec F$; your thumb gives $\vec\tau$. The same rule fixes the positive sense of rotations: curl the fingers the way the body turns, and the thumb is the rotation axis' positive direction.

concepts.statement: With $\vec r = (r_x, r_y, r_z)$ and $\vec F = (F_x, F_y, F_z)$: $$\vec\tau = (r_y F_z - r_z F_y,\; r_z F_x - r_x F_z,\; r_x F_y - r_y F_x),$$ the determinant expansion $$\vec\tau = \begin{vmatrix} \hat x & \hat y & \hat z \\ r_x & r_y & r_z \\ F_x & F_y & F_z \end{vmatrix}.$$
concepts.detail: The component recipe is the safe route whenever the geometry is not obviously planar. A torque perpendicular to the page's plane appears as a pure $\hat z$-component; torques about different points add as vectors only after each is computed about the same origin.

concepts.statement: $\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F$ changes when you move the origin, because $\vec r$ changes. The net torque on a system about different origins differs by $\vec R \times \vec F_{net}$ — so if the net force vanishes, the net torque is origin-independent, a fact Chapter 12 exploits in equilibrium.
concepts.detail: For a single force, shifting the origin along the force's own line of action leaves $\vec\tau$ unchanged (the lever arm does not move). Zero-force systems — couples — carry the same torque about every origin, which is why a pure twist is a genuinely origin-free object.

concepts.statement: **Solve Torque Revisited problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rolling and angular momentum; the working equation is $v_{\text{com}} = \omega R$ (no slip), $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$, $L = I\omega$, $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = d\vec L/dt$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit); no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.

concepts.statement: **Torque Revisited lives at $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit) and the textbook model holds while no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Torque Revisited calculation gives seconds when $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: A torque out of the page
examples.problem: A force $\vec F = 40\hat y$ N acts at $\vec r = 0.30\hat x$ m from the origin. Find $\vec\tau$. Then find the torque if the same force is redirected to $\vec F = 40(\cos 60^\circ\,\hat x + \sin 60^\circ\,\hat y)$ N.

steps.label: Cross product
steps.text: $\vec\tau = (0.30\hat x) \times (40\hat y) = (0.30)(40)(\hat x \times \hat y) = 12\hat z$ N·m — 12 N·m pointing out of the page (counterclockwise turn).

steps.label: Tilted force
steps.text: Only the $\hat y$-component (perpendicular to $\vec r$) torques: $\tau = r F \sin 60^\circ = (0.30)(40)(0.866) = 10.4$ N·m, still $+\hat z$.

steps.label: The x-component
steps.text: The $\hat x$-part of $\vec F$ is parallel to $\vec r$ and contributes nothing — the vector statement of 'you cannot push a door into its hinges'.

examples.result: $\vec\tau = 12\hat z$ N·m; tilted to 60°, $10.4\hat z$ N·m. Direction out of the page both times.

examples.title: Torque in three dimensions
examples.problem: A force $\vec F = (6.0, 0, 0)$ N acts at the point $\vec r = (0, 0.50, 0)$ m. Find the torque vector.

steps.label: Apply the formula
steps.text: $\vec\tau = (r_y F_z - r_z F_y,\; r_z F_x - r_x F_z,\; r_x F_y - r_y F_x)$.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: A $-3.0\hat z$ torque: it would drive a clockwise rotation in the $xy$-plane — check with the right-hand rule: fingers along $+\hat y$, curling toward $+\hat x$, thumb points $-\hat z$.

examples.result: $\vec\tau = -3.0\hat z$ N·m. Component arithmetic and the right hand agree.

keyTakeaways: $\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F$: magnitude $rF\sin\phi$, direction along the rotation axis by the right-hand rule.
The component formula (or determinant) handles all geometry; forces along $\vec r$ itself contribute zero torque.
Torque vectors depend on the origin; for zero net force the net torque is the same about every origin — the lever arm becomes a free choice.

quiz.q: A force points in the +x direction and is applied at a point on the +y axis. The torque about the origin points:
quiz.explanation: $\vec\tau = (r\hat y) \times (F\hat x) = rF(\hat y \times \hat x) = -rF\hat z$. Fingers along $+y$, curl toward $+x$: thumb points into the page, $-\hat z$.

quiz.q: When is the torque $\vec r \times \vec F$ zero?
options: when $\vec r$ and $\vec F$ are parallel or antiparallel
when $\vec r$ and $\vec F$ are perpendicular
only when the force acts at the origin
quiz.explanation: $\tau = rF\sin\phi$ vanishes for $\phi = 0$ or $180^\circ$ — a force aimed through the origin has no lever arm about it. Perpendicular forces give the maximum torque $rF$.

quiz.q: You compute the torque of a single force about origin A, then about origin B displaced by a vector $\vec d$ from A. The two torques differ by:
quiz.explanation: With $\vec r_B = \vec r_A - \vec d$, $\vec\tau_B = (\vec r_A - \vec d)\times\vec F = \vec\tau_A - \vec d \times \vec F$: shifting the origin subtracts the cross product of the shift with the force.

intro: Angular momentum is the rotational twin of linear momentum: for a single particle it is the cross product of position with momentum. It measures the 'quantity of rotational motion' about a chosen point, and — like torque — it depends on where you put the origin. For a particle in a circular orbit it collapses to the friendly product mvr.
objectives: Define the angular momentum of a particle, $\vec l = \vec r \times \vec p$, and compute magnitude and direction
Specialize to circular motion: $l = mr^2\omega$
Explain the origin dependence of angular momentum and its vector direction

concepts.statement: A particle of momentum $\vec p = m\vec v$ at position $\vec r$ (from origin $O$) has angular momentum about $O$: $$\vec l = \vec r \times \vec p,$$ magnitude $\ell = rmv\sin\phi = m v r_\perp$, direction by the right-hand rule. Units: kg·m²/s.
concepts.detail: A particle moving in a straight line generally has nonzero angular momentum about off-line origins — it 'would sweep by' that point. Only motion aimed exactly through the origin gives $\ell = 0$. Like torque, $\vec l$ depends on the choice of origin and must be recomputed if you move it.

concepts.statement: For a particle in a circle of radius $r$ about the origin, $\vec r \perp \vec p$ at every instant, so $$\ell = rmv = mr^2\omega,$$ directed along the rotation axis with the sense of the circulation.
concepts.detail: The formula splits physics from geometry: doubling the orbital radius at fixed $\omega$ quadruples $\ell$. When a circling particle is pulled inward with no torque about the center, $mr^2\omega$ must hold — radius down, angular speed up — which is exactly the ice-skater effect one particle at a time.

concepts.term: Angular momentum is a bookkeeping about a point
concepts.statement: Angular momentum is not a new substance: it is linear momentum's moment, weighted by lever arm. A system's total is the vector sum $\vec L = \sum \vec l_i$; different particles may contribute angular momenta that reinforce or cancel.
concepts.detail: Two identical particles on opposite sides of a circling pair contribute equal, parallel $\vec l$'s — they add. In Chapter 10's language, summing $m r_i^2 \omega$ over a rigid body is precisely how $L = I\omega$ will be built in Section 11.7.

concepts.statement: **Solve Angular Momentum problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rolling and angular momentum; the working equation is $v_{\text{com}} = \omega R$ (no slip), $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$, $L = I\omega$, $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = d\vec L/dt$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit); no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.

concepts.statement: **Angular Momentum lives at $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit) and the textbook model holds while no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Angular Momentum calculation gives seconds when $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: The angular momentum of Earth's orbit
examples.problem: Treat Earth's orbit as a circle of radius $1.50\times10^{11}$ m. With $M = 5.98\times10^{24}$ kg and period $T = 3.16\times10^{7}$ s, find the orbital angular momentum.

steps.label: Direction
steps.text: The orbit circulates counterclockwise seen from north ecliptic pole, so $\vec l$ points toward that pole (along $+\hat z$ in ecliptic coordinates) — the axis every planet's orbit shares to within a few degrees.

examples.result: $\ell = 2.7\times10^{40}$ kg·m²/s, along the north ecliptic pole — 10⁷ times Earth's spin angular momentum, computed in Section 11.7.

examples.title: A puck on a string, pulled in
examples.problem: A 0.50 kg puck circles at 3.0 m/s on a frictionless table at the end of a 1.2 m string through a hole at the origin. You pull the string to shorten the radius to 0.60 m. Find $\ell$ before and after, and the new speed.

steps.label: The physics of pulling
steps.text: The string's tension points along $\vec r$ — toward the origin — so its torque about the origin is zero and $\ell$ cannot change.

steps.label: After
steps.text: $1.8 = (0.50)v(0.60)$ gives $v = 6.0$ m/s: halving the radius doubled the speed.

steps.label: Energy ledger
steps.text: Kinetic energy rose from 2.25 J to 4.5 J — the extra 2.25 J is the work your hand did pulling against the puck's tendency to fly outward. Angular momentum is free; energy is not.

examples.result: $\ell = 1.8\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ throughout; speed doubles to 6.0 m/s as the radius halves, paid for by the puller's work.

keyTakeaways: $\vec l = \vec r \times \vec p$ with $\ell = mv r_\perp$; circular motion gives the clean $\ell = mr^2\omega$ along the axis.
Angular momentum depends on the chosen origin, like torque; motion aimed at the origin carries none about it.
A central force (aimed at the origin) exerts zero torque, so it cannot change $\ell$ — the seed of both Kepler's second law and the skater's spin-up.

quiz.q: A 2.0 kg particle moves at 4.0 m/s along a line that passes 0.50 m from the origin. Its angular momentum about the origin has magnitude:
quiz.explanation: $\ell = m v r_\perp = (2.0)(4.0)(0.50) = 4.0\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ — the perpendicular offset (the 'impact parameter') is the lever arm that matters, not the instantaneous distance.

quiz.q: A particle moves in a straight line directly toward the origin. Its angular momentum about that origin is:
options: zero only at the instant of closest approach
quiz.explanation: $\vec r$ is antiparallel to $\vec v$ the whole way, so $\vec r \times \vec p = 0$ throughout. Motion on a 'collision course' with the origin carries no angular momentum about it.

quiz.q: A puck on frictionless ice is pulled toward the center of its circle by a string. About the center, its angular momentum:
options: stays constant, so the speed grows as 1/r
stays constant, so the speed stays constant
quiz.explanation: The tension is a central force: zero torque about the center, so $\ell = mvr$ is fixed and $v \propto 1/r$. The kinetic energy grows only because the puller does work.

intro: Newton's second law has an angular form: net torque equals the rate of change of angular momentum. The proof is a one-line differentiation that shows why force-free moments of momentum simply persist — and buried in it is Kepler's second law of planetary motion, which stops being a mystery and becomes a cross product.
objectives: Derive $\vec\tau_{net} = d\vec l/dt$ for a particle from $\vec F = d\vec p/dt$
Write the system form $\vec\tau_{net,ext} = d\vec L/dt$ and explain why internal torques cancel
Apply the central-force result: zero torque means constant angular momentum — Kepler's second law

concepts.term: Newton's second law in angular form
concepts.statement: For a single particle, $$\vec\tau_{net} = \frac{d\vec l}{dt}.$$ Proof: $\frac{d}{dt}(\vec r \times \vec p) = \vec v \times m\vec v + \vec r \times \frac{d\vec p}{dt} = 0 + \vec r \times \vec F_{net}$, since $\vec v \times \vec v = 0$ identically.
concepts.detail: Every statement of Chapter 2's law has an angular shadow: torque is what changes angular momentum, and the cross product's antisymmetry does the bookkeeping. Zero net torque about a point does not mean zero force — it means the existing angular momentum about that point is frozen.

concepts.statement: For a system of particles, $$\vec\tau_{net,ext} = \frac{d\vec L}{dt}, \qquad \vec L = \sum \vec l_i.$$ Internal torques cancel in pairs — by Newton's third law, the forces between two particles give $\vec r_{12} \times \vec F_{12}$ plus $\vec r_{21} \times \vec F_{21} = (\vec r_{12}) \times (\vec F_{12} + \vec F_{21}) = 0$ for forces along the line joining them.
concepts.detail: The cancellation requires only that internal forces act **along the line joining the particles** — true for gravity, springs, electrostatics. This is the angular rerun of Section 9.2's argument that internal forces cannot move the center of mass.

concepts.statement: A central force (gravity, aimed at the Sun) exerts zero torque about the force center, so each planet's $\vec l$ about the Sun is constant — therefore $\tfrac12 |\vec r \times \vec v|$ is constant: the **areal velocity** $dA/dt = \ell/2m$ is fixed, and the radius vector sweeps equal areas in equal times.
concepts.detail: Kepler found the law in Tycho Brahe's data (1609); Newton's cross product explains it in one line. A planet moves fastest at perihelion not by whimsy but because it must sweep the same area rate at small radius as at large — angular momentum is the invisible contract.

examples.title: Torque changes angular momentum, quantitatively
examples.problem: A particle at rest is acted on for 3.0 s by a constant net torque of 2.0 N·m about the origin. Find the angular momentum after 3.0 s.

steps.label: Integrate the law
steps.text: $\vec\tau = d\vec l/dt$ with constant $\vec\tau$ integrates to $\Delta \vec l = \vec\tau t$ — the angular impulse-momentum theorem.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $\Delta \vec l = (2.0)(3.0) = 6.0\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ along the torque's direction, starting from zero.

steps.label: Note the structure
steps.text: Exactly as impulse $\vec J = \vec F\Delta t$ changes linear momentum, an angular impulse $\vec\tau\Delta t$ changes angular momentum — same theorem, rotated.

examples.result: $\ell = 6.0\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ after 3.0 s of 2.0 N·m.

examples.title: Earth's areal velocity
examples.problem: Using Earth's orbital angular momentum ($\ell = 2.7\times10^{40}$ kg·m²/s), verify Kepler's second law numerically: compute the areal velocity and check it against the total orbital area over one year.

steps.label: Area per year
steps.text: $(2.3\times10^{15})(3.16\times10^{7}) = 7.1\times10^{22}\ \text{m}^2$ swept per orbit.

steps.label: Independent check
steps.text: The ellipse's area $\pi a b$ with $a = 1.496\times10^{11}$ m and $b = a\sqrt{1-e^2} \approx 1.4959\times10^{11}$ m (e = 0.0167): $\pi (1.496)(1.4959)\times10^{22} \approx 7.0\times10^{22}$ m². Agreement to the precision carried.

examples.result: Areal velocity $2.3\times10^{15}$ m²/s, constant by the central-force theorem — Kepler's law, audited and passed.

keyTakeaways: $\vec\tau_{net} = d\vec l/dt$ for a particle; $\vec\tau_{net,ext} = d\vec L/dt$ for a system, with internal torques cancelling pairwise.
Zero net torque about a point freezes the angular momentum about that point — no force is required for this, only no torque.
Central forces give zero torque, so planetary $\vec l$ is constant and equal areas are swept in equal times: Kepler's second law is a cross product identity.

quiz.q: The net torque on a particle about a point is zero. We may conclude:
options: no force acts on the particle
its angular momentum about that point is constant
it moves in a straight line
quiz.explanation: $\vec\tau = d\vec l/dt = 0$ freezes $\vec l$ about that point. Forces may still act — gravity does, on every orbiting planet — as long as none delivers torque about the chosen point.

quiz.q: Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times) follows from:
options: the central nature of gravity: zero torque about the Sun means constant angular momentum
the inverse-square form of the force law specifically
the small eccentricity of planetary orbits
quiz.explanation: Any central force — inverse-square or not — gives constant $\ell$ about the center, hence constant areal velocity $dA/dt = \ell/2m$. The area law predates Newton's specific force and is more general than it.

quiz.q: A 3.0 N·m constant torque acts on a particle for 4.0 s. The change in the particle's angular momentum is:
quiz.explanation: $\Delta \ell = \tau t = (3.0)(4.0) = 12\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ — the angular twin of impulse $F\Delta t$.

intro: For a rigid body spinning about a fixed axis, all the individual angular momenta of its particles point along the axis and add to one product: L = Iω. This is the rotational twin of P = Mv, and with it the torque law becomes τ = dL/dt = Iα — Chapter 10's law reborn as a statement about momentum. It also quantifies the vast spin stored in planets and flywheels.
objectives: Derive $L = I\omega$ for a rigid body about a fixed axis by summing particle angular momenta
Use $\tau_{net} = dL/dt = I\alpha$ and compute angular momenta of real spinning bodies
Distinguish spin angular momentum from orbital angular momentum

concepts.term: Angular momentum of a rigid body
concepts.statement: A rigid body rotating about a fixed axis at angular velocity $\omega$ has angular momentum along that axis: $$L = I\omega$$ where $I$ is the rotational inertia about the same axis. Derivation: each particle contributes $\ell_{i,z} = m_i r_i^2 \omega$, and $\sum m_i r_i^2 = I$.
concepts.detail: The direction comes from the right-hand rule along the rotation axis. With $L = I\omega$, the whole angular-momentum machinery of the chapter applies to flywheels, planets and figure skaters alike — and the vector form survives even when the axis moves, as the gyroscope will show.

concepts.term: Torque law for a rigid body
concepts.statement: For rotation about a fixed axis with constant $I$: $$\tau_{net} = \frac{dL}{dt} = I\alpha.$$ It is the same law as Chapter 10's $\tau_{net} = I\alpha$, now recognized as the angular-momentum form $\vec\tau = d\vec L/dt$ — and when $I$ changes with time (a skater pulling in her arms), only $L = I\omega$ with $\tau = dL/dt$ is the safe statement.
concepts.detail: The rigid-body law inherits the system theorem's conditions: external torques only, about a fixed axis in an inertial frame. Its great power is conservation: if the net external torque vanishes, $L$ stays fixed even while $\omega$ runs wild — the next section's engine.

concepts.statement: The angular momentum of a body's own rotation about its com is its **spin**; the angular momentum of the com orbiting some external point is its **orbital** part. Earth carries both: spin ($5.8\times10^{33}$ kg·m²/s) and solar orbit ($2.7\times10^{40}$ kg·m²/s), seven million times larger.
concepts.detail: The split is exactly the rolling decomposition of Section 11.1 applied to momentum: a rolling wheel's angular momentum about a point on the floor is the sum of its spin $I_{com}\omega$ and the orbital $M v_{com} R$. Physicists meet the same split in quantum mechanics, where spin and orbital angular momentum belong to different operators — but the classical bookkeeping came first.

examples.title: Earth's spin angular momentum
examples.problem: Model Earth as a uniform sphere of mass $5.98\times10^{24}$ kg and radius $6.37\times10^{6}$ m, rotating once per day. Find its spin angular momentum.

steps.label: Inertia
steps.text: $I = \frac25 MR^2 = (0.4)(5.98\times10^{24})(6.37\times10^{6})^2 = 9.7\times10^{37}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ (a uniform sphere; Earth's real, centrally-condensed value is smaller, $\approx 0.33MR^2 = 8.0\times10^{37}$).

steps.label: Angular velocity
steps.text: One rotation per sidereal day: $\omega = 2\pi/86{,}164 = 7.29\times10^{-5}$ rad/s.

steps.label: Spin
steps.text: With the realistic $I = 8.0\times10^{37}$: $L = I\omega = 5.8\times10^{33}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$, pointing along Earth's rotation axis (out the North pole).

steps.label: Scale
steps.text: Compare the orbital $2.7\times10^{40}$: the orbital part is $4.7\times10^{6}$ times larger — Earth's motion is overwhelmingly its journey around the Sun.

examples.result: $L_{spin} \approx 5.8\times10^{33}$ kg·m²/s along the North polar axis — the vast reservoir that gyrocompasses and Foucault pendulums tap.

examples.title: Braking a flywheel
examples.problem: The flywheel of Section 10.4 ($I = 1.08\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) spins at 94.2 rad/s. A constant friction torque brings it to rest in 30 s. Find the torque.

steps.label: Initial angular momentum
steps.text: $L_i = I\omega = (1.08)(94.2) = 102\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$.

steps.label: Torque from the law
steps.text: $\tau = dL/dt = \Delta L/\Delta t = (0 - 102)/30 = -3.4$ N·m — negative: it opposes the spin.

steps.label: Consistency with Chapter 10
steps.text: $\alpha = \tau/I = -3.4/1.08 = -3.1\ \text{rad/s}^2$, and $\omega_f = \omega_i + \alpha t = 94.2 - 94 = 0$. The two chapters agree.

examples.result: A friction torque of $-3.4$ N·m drains 102 kg·m²/s of angular momentum in half a minute.

keyTakeaways: A rigid body spinning about a fixed axis carries $L = I\omega$ along the axis — the rotational twin of $P = Mv$.
$\tau_{net} = dL/dt = I\alpha$ for fixed $I$; the angular-momentum form is the safe one when $I$ changes.
Spin (about the com) and orbital (com about a point) angular momentum add; Earth's orbital part dwarfs its spin by a factor of millions.

quiz.q: A solid sphere and a hollow sphere of equal mass and radius spin at the same angular speed. Their angular momenta compare as:
quiz.explanation: $L = I\omega$ with $I_{solid} = \frac25 MR^2$ and $I_{hollow} = \frac23 MR^2$: the ratio is $2/5 : 2/3 = 3 : 2$. The hollow sphere's far-flung mass carries more angular momentum per unit spin.

quiz.q: A flywheel with I = 2.5 kg·m² spins at 40 rad/s. Its angular momentum is:
quiz.explanation: $L = I\omega = (2.5)(40) = 100\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$. A 5.0 N·m friction torque would take 20 s to remove it.

quiz.q: For a body with fixed rotational inertia, $\tau_{net} = dL/dt$ reduces to:
quiz.explanation: With $I$ constant, $dL/dt = d(I\omega)/dt = I\alpha$ — Chapter 10's rotational Newton's second law is this chapter's momentum law in disguise.

intro: When no external torque acts, angular momentum is locked — even if the body changes shape. Pull mass inward and the spin must rise to keep Iω constant; a diver tucks and whirls; a collapsing star spins up from once a month to hundreds of times a second. Conservation of angular momentum is the third great conservation law of mechanics, and the only one that lets kinetic energy grow while nothing external acts.
objectives: State the conservation law for angular momentum and its per-axis validity
Apply $I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f$ to skaters, divers and collapsing stars, including the energy bookkeeping
Explain why the kinetic energy can increase under angular-momentum conservation, and identify the energy source

concepts.statement: If the net external torque on a system about a point (or a fixed axis) is zero, then $$\vec L = \text{constant}: \qquad I_i \omega_i = I_f \omega_f$$ even as $I$ changes by internal rearrangement. Component form: if $\tau_{ext,z} = 0$, then $L_z$ alone is conserved.
concepts.detail: The hypothesis is zero torque, not zero force — gravity can rain down on a system all day and still deliver no torque about the right point. And because the conserved object is $I\omega$ rather than $\omega$ itself, the angular speed is free to change dramatically: mass toward the axis, spin up; mass away, spin down.

concepts.term: The skater and the energy surprise
concepts.statement: A skater pulling her arms in decreases $I$, so $\omega$ rises as $I$ falls — and her kinetic energy $K = \frac12 I\omega^2 = \frac{L^2}{2I}$ **increases**. Angular-momentum conservation does not conserve energy; the muscles do work $W = \frac{L^2}{2}\left(\frac{1}{I_f} - \frac{1}{I_i}\right)$ to pull the mass inward.
concepts.detail: This is the one conservation law whose exercise can create kinetic energy from internal sources — pushing mass toward the rotation axis costs work against the 'centrifugal' tendency to fly outward. Reverse it: letting the arms out does work on the skater and the spin dies.

concepts.statement: A spinning body with large $L$ resists changes to its axis direction — to re-aim $\vec L$ requires a torque sustained for time. This is why rifling stabilizes bullets, why gyroscopes hold attitude in spacecraft navigation, and why a passed football spirals instead of tumbling.
concepts.detail: The quantitative statement is the vector law $\vec\tau = d\vec L/dt$: with $\vec L$ huge, a given torque changes the axis only slowly (the precession of Section 11.9). Falling cats exploit the same law in reverse — twisting internal parts one way to rotate the rest the other, with total $L \approx 0$ throughout.
