depth.title: Angular momentum conservation taken seriously: from Kepler to millisecond pulsars

blocks.heading: The exact statement and its proof
blocks.body: For a system of particles, $\vec L = \sum \vec r_i \times \vec p_i$ and $\frac{d\vec L}{dt} = \sum \vec r_i \times \vec F_i^{ext} + \sum_{i \ne j} \vec r_i \times \vec F_{ij}^{int}$. The internal double sum groups into pairs $(i,j)$: $\vec r_i \times \vec F_{ij} + \vec r_j \times \vec F_{ji} = (\vec r_i - \vec r_j) \times \vec F_{ij}$, which vanishes whenever $\vec F_{ij}$ acts along the line joining the two particles — the **strong** form of Newton's third law. For such central internal forces (gravity, electrostatics, ideal springs) the internal torques cancel exactly, leaving $\vec\tau_{net,ext} = d\vec L/dt$: zero external torque implies $\vec L$ constant, and the result holds even while the system reshapes itself, collapses, or explodes.

blocks.heading: A caveat worth a whole physics career
blocks.body: Not all forces in nature obey the strong third law: the magnetic force between moving charges acts perpendicular to the separation, and its internal torques fail to cancel pairwise. Noether's theorem repairs the ledger: angular momentum conservation follows from the isotropy of space (rotational symmetry of the laws), and the 'missing' mechanical angular momentum resides in the fields themselves — the field angular momentum $\epsilon_0 \int \vec r \times (\vec E \times \vec B)\,dV$. The famous Shockley-James example of a charge-magnet system shows mechanical + field angular momentum conserved while mechanics alone appears to fail.

blocks.heading: The skater's energy ledger, exactly
blocks.body: With $L$ fixed, write $K = \frac{L^2}{2I}$; the work done changing $I$ from $I_i$ to $I_f$ is $W = K_f - K_i = \frac{L^2}{2}\left(\frac{1}{I_f} - \frac{1}{I_i}\right)$. For the section's skater ($I_i = 4.6$, $I_f = 1.8\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$, $L = 4.6 \times 7.54 = 34.7\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$): $W = \frac{(34.7)^2}{2}(1/1.8 - 1/4.6) = 601.8 \times 0.338 = 203$ J of muscular work — precisely the computed jump from 131 J to 334 J. Every joule of spin-up is paid for; where does it come from in a **gravitating** system? From gravity itself: pulling mass toward the axis lets it fall inward, and gravitational potential energy converts to rotational kinetic energy.

blocks.heading: Collapse of a Sun-like star: the pulsar spin-up
blocks.body: A stellar core of the Sun's radius $R_i = 7.0\times10^{8}$ m rotating with the Sun's 25-day period collapses (supernova) to a neutron star of $R_f = 10$ km, ejecting the envelope but conserving the core's mass and angular momentum. First estimate: uniform spheres, $I = \frac25 MR^2$, so $\frac{\omega_f}{\omega_i} = \left(\frac{R_i}{R_f}\right)^2 = (7\times10^4)^2 = 4.9\times10^9$. With $\omega_i = 2\pi/(25 \times 86400\ \text{s}) = 2.9\times10^{-6}$ rad/s: $\omega_f = 1.4\times10^{4}$ rad/s, a period of 0.44 ms. That is suspiciously fast — faster than any known pulsar — because the uniform-sphere model is wrong in the right direction: the Sun's mass is centrally concentrated ($I \approx 0.059 MR^2$) while a neutron star is more nearly uniform with relativistic corrections ($I \approx 0.35 MR^2$). Redoing the ratio with realistic inertias multiplies the uniform answer by $0.059/0.35 \approx 0.17$: $\omega_f \approx 2.4\times10^{3}$ rad/s, a period of $\approx 2.6$ ms — squarely in the observed millisecond-pulsar range (the fastest known, PSR J1748-2446ad, spins at 716 Hz, period 1.4 ms).

blocks.heading: Why nothing spins much faster: the breakup limit
blocks.body: Conservation of angular momentum would seem to allow unlimited spin-up as $R \to 0$, but before that, centrifugal physics intervenes: surface material leaves when the equatorial orbital speed is reached, $\omega_{max}^2 R = GM/R^2$, i.e. $\omega_{max} = \sqrt{GM/R^3}$. For a neutron star of $M = 1.4 M_{sun}$, $R = 10$ km: $\omega_{max} = \sqrt{(6.67\times10^{-11})(2.8\times10^{30})/10^{12}} = 1.4\times10^{4}$ rad/s, a minimum period of $\approx 0.46$ ms. The observed cutoff just above 1 ms is this gravitational speed limit plus the equatorial-bulge feedback of general relativity — the universe's fastest spinning objects sit pressed against the wall their own gravity builds.

blocks.heading: Kepler's law as conservation, and the retrograde exception
blocks.body: The areal-velocity result $dA/dt = \ell/2m$ of Section 11.6 is angular momentum conservation in geometry clothing, and it generalizes: the Lagrangian's rotational symmetry in the two-body problem makes $\vec L$ the generator of the orbit plane's fixedness (orbits are planar) and of Kepler's law. When you meet the exceptions — planets on inclined orbits, the Sun's 7°-tilted equator, the Moon's inclined orbit — you are looking at fossils of torques: systems that were **not** isolated, torqued by neighbors, tides, or by the star-forming cloud that gave them their initial $\vec L$ in the first place. Theorists reconstruct solar-system history from angular-momentum mismatches; the current problem, the Sun's slow spin carrying only 0.3% of the system's angular momentum, is the 'angular momentum problem' of solar formation — the young Sun was torqued by its disk, and its planets inherited the difference.

examples.title: A figure skater pulls in
examples.problem: A skater spins at 1.2 rev/s with rotational inertia 4.6 kg·m² (arms out). She pulls her arms in, dropping to 1.8 kg·m². Find her new spin rate and the change in kinetic energy.

steps.label: Conservation
steps.text: The ice exerts negligible torque about the skate's vertical axis: $L = I\omega$ is conserved. $\omega_i = (1.2)(2\pi) = 7.54$ rad/s, so $L = (4.6)(7.54) = 34.7\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$.

steps.label: New rate
steps.text: $\omega_f = L/I_f = 34.7/1.8 = 19.3$ rad/s — that is 3.07 rev/s, more than 2.5 times faster.

steps.label: Energy after
steps.text: $K_f = \frac12(1.8)(19.3)^2 = 334$ J. The increase of 203 J is work her muscles did pulling mass inward against the centrifugal tendency — angular momentum is free, energy is not.

examples.result: 3.1 rev/s and $K$ up from 131 J to 334 J: the skater is the conservation law made visible.

examples.title: A diver's tuck
examples.problem: A diver leaves the board rotating at 0.80 rev/s in layout position ($I = 14\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$). She tucks to $I = 4.5\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$. Find her spin rate in the tuck.

steps.label: Conservation about her com
steps.text: Gravity's torque about the com is zero, so during free fall $L = I\omega$ is hers to keep: $L = (14)(0.80) = 11.2\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ in rev/s units (equivalently 70.4 rad/s-equivalent; ratios are unaffected).

steps.label: Tuck rate
steps.text: $\omega_f = L/I_f = 11.2/4.5 = 2.5$ rev/s — a tripled rotation rate bought in mid-air.

steps.label: The choreography
steps.text: She must complete her somersaults while the tuck lasts, then kick out to $I = 14$ again — the spin drops back to 0.80 rev/s exactly, and she enters the water straight and slow-spinning. $L$ was never negotiable; only its distribution was.

examples.result: 2.5 rev/s in the tuck — how three and a half somersaults fit into 1.5 seconds of fall.

keyTakeaways: Zero net external torque about an axis conserves that axis's angular momentum: $I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f$ — shape changes included.
Kinetic energy $K = L^2/2I$ can **increase** under conservation; the energy comes from internal work (muscles) or gravity (collapsing stars).
Large $L$ stabilizes a spin axis — rifling, spiraling footballs, gyroscopes — and collapsing stars convert radius into astonishing spin (millisecond pulsars).

quiz.q: A skater spinning with arms out pulls them in, halving her rotational inertia. Her angular speed and her kinetic energy:
options: angular speed doubles; kinetic energy doubles
angular speed doubles; kinetic energy quadruples
angular speed doubles; kinetic energy is unchanged
quiz.explanation: Conservation of $L = I\omega$ forces $\omega$ to double when $I$ halves. Then $K = L^2/2I$ also doubles (from $L^2/2I$ to $L^2/I$): the extra energy is the muscular work of pulling mass inward against the outward tendency.

quiz.q: Where does the extra rotational kinetic energy of the tucking skater come from?
options: work done by her muscles pulling mass toward the axis
conservation of energy: it was always there
a decrease in her linear kinetic energy
quiz.explanation: Angular-momentum conservation fixes $L$, not $K$. Pulling mass inward against the outward centrifugal tendency costs muscular work, and that work appears as the increase in $\frac12 I\omega^2 = L^2/2I$.

quiz.q: A star collapses from radius $7\times10^{8}$ m to $10^{4}$ m while conserving angular momentum (uniform spheres). Its rotation rate increases by about:
quiz.explanation: $\omega \propto 1/I \propto 1/R^2$ for uniform spheres: the factor is $(7\times10^8/10^4)^2 = (7\times10^4)^2 = 4.9\times10^9$. A once-a-month rotation becomes a several-millisecond spin — a pulsar.

quiz.q: For angular momentum about a given axis to be conserved, the requirement is:
options: no external force acts on the system
no net external torque about that axis acts on the system
the system must be at rest
quiz.explanation: Torque, not force, is the villain: gravity can act freely and $L$ still holds, provided its torque about the chosen axis vanishes. Rigidity is irrelevant — skaters change shape precisely to exploit the law.

intro: A spinning gyroscope hung from one end of its axle refuses to fall; instead, the axle sweeps slowly around the horizontal — precession. Nothing mysterious is happening: gravity's torque is horizontal, perpendicular to the angular momentum along the axle, so it tips $\vec L$ sideways rather than downward. Watching $d\vec L = \vec\tau\,dt$ in action is the best geometry lesson in the chapter.
objectives: Explain qualitatively why a spinning gyro precesses instead of falling: $\vec\tau \perp \vec L$
Derive the precession rate $\Omega = MgD/(I\omega)$ for a fast gyroscope with horizontal axle
Use the $1/\omega$ dependence: slower spin means faster precession, and the limit where the formula fails

concepts.term: Why the gyroscope does not fall
concepts.statement: Gravity pulls the spinning wheel's center of mass down, but the torque about the pivot is $\vec\tau = \vec D \times M\vec g$ — **horizontal**, perpendicular to $\vec L$ (which lies along the axle). A torque perpendicular to $\vec L$ changes only its direction: $d\vec L = \vec\tau\,dt$ tips the axle sideways, not down. The tip of $\vec L$ traces a horizontal circle: precession.
concepts.detail: A non-spinning gyroscope has $\vec L \approx 0$, and the same torque simply rotates it downward — it falls, as intuition expects. Spin does not defy gravity; it re-routes the torque's effect from falling to turning. The same reasoning explains why a rolling coin wobbles in slow circles before it settles.

concepts.statement: For a fast top with axle horizontal, pivot-to-com distance $D$: in time $dt$, $\vec L$ of magnitude $L = I\omega$ tips by $d\phi = \tau\,dt/L$, so the precession angular velocity is $$\Omega = \frac{d\phi}{dt} = \frac{\tau}{L} = \frac{MgD}{I\omega}.$$ The direction of $\vec\Omega$ is along the vertical (the axle sweeps a horizontal cone about it).
concepts.detail: Validity: $\omega \gg \Omega$ — the spin must be fast for $\vec L$ to stay essentially along the axle. Note the dependencies: heavier or longer-armed gyros precess faster; faster spin precesses more slowly. Nothing here involves g's direction except through $\tau$; on the Moon, precession slows by the Moon's g.

concepts.statement: As friction bleeds the spin $\omega$, the precession rate $\Omega = MgD/I\omega$ **speeds up** — a dying top wobbles in quicker and quicker circles. Eventually $\omega$ becomes comparable to $\Omega$, the 'fast top' approximation fails, and the motion gains a nodding component called **nutation** before the top finally drops.
concepts.detail: Engineers meet the same equation as the gyroscopic drift of ships' stabilizers and the precession of Earth's axis (26,000-year cycle) under the Moon's and Sun's torques on Earth's equatorial bulge — a precession so slow only because Earth's $L$ is astronomically large.

concepts.term: Precession of a Gyroscope: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Precession of a Gyroscope problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is rolling and angular momentum; the working equation is $v_{\text{com}} = \omega R$ (no slip), $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$, $L = I\omega$, $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = d\vec L/dt$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit); no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.

concepts.term: Precession of a Gyroscope: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Precession of a Gyroscope lives at $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit) and the textbook model holds while no-slip needs static friction; $\vec L$ conserved only if $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Precession of a Gyroscope calculation gives seconds when $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $L\sim 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ (wheel) to $10^{41}$ (Earth orbit), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

figures.caption: Precession of a gyroscope. The spinning wheel's angular momentum $\vec L = I\omega$ lies along the axle, distance $D$ from the pivot. Gravity's torque $\vec\tau = \vec D \times M\vec g$ is horizontal — into the page in the view shown — so in each $dt$ the tip of $\vec L$ moves by $d\vec L = \vec\tau\,dt$ **sideways**, never downward: the axle sweeps a horizontal circle at $\Omega = \tau/L = MgD/(I\omega)$. Seen from above (inset), $\vec L$ rotates counterclockwise for the spin direction drawn. The gyroscope falls only when $\omega$ dies and $L \to 0$.

examples.title: A demonstration gyroscope
examples.problem: A gyroscope wheel ($I = 1.40\times10^{-2}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ about its axle) spins at 1500 rev/min. Its com hangs 6.0 cm from the pivot, and the wheel's mass with frame is 0.25 kg. Find the precession rate and period.

steps.label: Torque
steps.text: $\tau = MgD = (0.25)(9.8)(0.060) = 0.147$ N·m, horizontal, perpendicular to the axle.

steps.label: Precession
steps.text: $\Omega = \tau/L = 0.147/2.20 = 0.067$ rad/s. The axle sweeps around once every $T = 2\pi/\Omega = 94$ s — a lazy, dignified circle.

steps.label: Check the hierarchy
steps.text: $\Omega/\omega = 0.067/157 = 4\times10^{-4} \ll 1$: the fast-top approximation is excellent, and $\vec L$ stays put along the axle.

examples.result: $\Omega = 0.067$ rad/s, a precession period of about 1.6 minutes.

examples.title: As the spin dies
examples.problem: The same gyroscope slows by friction to 300 rev/min. What happens to the precession?

steps.label: New spin
steps.text: $\omega' = 31.4$ rad/s; $L' = (0.0140)(31.4) = 0.44\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ — one fifth of before.

steps.label: New precession
steps.text: The torque is unchanged: $\Omega' = 0.147/0.44 = 0.33$ rad/s — five times faster, a period of 19 s. The dying top wobbles faster and faster.

steps.label: Toward the limit
steps.text: As $\omega$ falls toward $\Omega$ itself, the fast-top formula fails and nutation (nodding) appears; at $\omega \approx 0$ the gyroscope is just a hanging mass and sags like any other.

examples.result: Precession accelerates from one lap per 94 s to one per 19 s: the $1/\omega$ law observed directly.

keyTakeaways: Gravity's torque on a gyro is horizontal, $\vec\tau = \vec D \times M\vec g$, perpendicular to $\vec L$: it turns $\vec L$ sideways rather than tipping it down — hence precession instead of falling.
Fast-top precession rate: $\Omega = MgD/(I\omega)$, valid when $\omega \gg \Omega$; heavier or longer gyros precess faster, faster spins more slowly.
As friction kills the spin, precession speeds up ($\Omega \propto 1/\omega$), nutation sets in, and only then does the top fall.

quiz.q: A spinning gyroscope hangs from one end of its axle. Instead of falling, it precesses because:
options: gravity is too weak to affect spinning bodies
the torque $\vec D \times M\vec g$ is perpendicular to $\vec L$, so it re-aims $\vec L$ sideways rather than downward
its angular momentum exactly cancels its weight
quiz.explanation: $d\vec L = \vec\tau\,dt$ adds a horizontal bit to a horizontal $\vec L$: the tip of $\vec L$ circles horizontally. Gravity never gets to pull the axle down until the spin — and with it $L$ — dies.

quiz.q: Doubling the spin rate of a gyroscope (still in the fast-top regime) does what to its precession rate?
quiz.explanation: $\Omega = MgD/(I\omega)$ with everything else fixed: twice the spin, half the precession. This inverse relation is the classic lecture demo — and why slowly dying tops wobble in ever-faster circles.

quiz.q: For the demonstration gyroscope of the example (M = 0.25 kg, D = 0.060 m, I = 0.0140 kg·m²) spinning at 157 rad/s, the precession rate is about:
quiz.explanation: $\Omega = MgD/(I\omega) = (0.25)(9.8)(0.060)/[(0.0140)(157)] = 0.147/2.20 = 0.067$ rad/s — one lap every minute and a half.

intro: A body in equilibrium neither accelerates nor begins to turn: the net force on it vanishes, and so does the net torque about every point. These two conditions are independent — zero force with nonzero torque produces pure spinning — and together they power all of statics: bridges, cranes, beams, bones. The essential craft is choosing the pivot so that unknown forces drop out of the torque equation.
objectives: State the two conditions for equilibrium, ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0, and distinguish static from dynamic equilibrium
Explain why the torque condition holds about ANY point when the force condition holds, and use this freedom strategically
Justify the center-of-gravity shortcut: gravity acts as a single force at the center of mass

concepts.statement: A rigid body is in **equilibrium** when $$\vec F_{net} = \sum \vec F = \vec 0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \vec\tau_{net} = \sum \vec\tau = \vec 0 \;\; \text{(about any point)}.$$ In component form: $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$, $\sum F_z = 0$, and the torques about any chosen axis sum to zero. If the body is also at rest, the equilibrium is **static**; a body gliding at constant velocity is in (dynamic) equilibrium too.
concepts.detail: The force condition forbids translational acceleration; the torque condition forbids angular acceleration. A body can satisfy one and violate the other: a couple — two equal, opposite forces on different lines — has zero net force but a nonzero net torque, and it spins in place.

concepts.statement: If $\sum \vec F = 0$, then $\sum \vec\tau$ is the same about **every** origin: shifting the origin by $\vec d$ changes the total by $\vec d \times \sum \vec F = \vec 0$. Hence in equilibrium you may take torques about the most convenient point — typically one that eliminates unknown forces from the equation.
concepts.detail: This is the strategic heart of statics: put the pivot on the line of action of a force you do not know, and that force contributes zero torque there. Different pivot choices give different-looking (but equivalent) equations — use this to cross-check answers.

concepts.statement: In a uniform gravitational field, the total torque of gravity on a body equals that of a single force $M\vec g$ acting at the **center of gravity** — which coincides with the center of mass. Every weight bookkeeping in statics may therefore collapse the body's weight to one arrow at the com.
concepts.detail: Proof sketch: each particle's gravity torque is $\vec r_i \times m_i\vec g$; summing regroups to $(\sum m_i \vec r_i/M) \times M\vec g = \vec r_{com} \times M\vec g$. Only if $\vec g$ varied substantially across the body would the two centers separate — negligible for any laboratory-scale object.

concepts.statement: Count equations versus unknowns: in 2D you own **three** independent equations ($\sum F_x$, $\sum F_y$, $\sum\tau$). A structure whose supports introduce more unknowns than this is **statically indeterminate** — the extra unknowns are fixed by elasticity (Section 12.3), not by statics alone.
concepts.detail: A ladder on a frictionless wall has exactly three unknowns and is solvable; the same ladder with friction at the wall has four and is not. This counting test, applied in the first thirty seconds, tells you whether a problem is a statics problem or a materials problem.

concepts.statement: **Solve Equilibrium problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is static equilibrium; the working equation is $\sum\vec F = 0$, $\sum\vec\tau = 0$, $\text{stress} = F/A$, $Y = (F/A)/(\Delta L/L)$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N}$, $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, $\text{Pa}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against beams $10^2$--$10^3\ \text{N}$; $Y_{\text{steel}} \approx 2\times 10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$; static only; Hookean moduli for small strains.

examples.title: A traffic light on two cables
examples.problem: An 900 N traffic light hangs from two cables that make equal angles of 30° above the horizontal (a symmetric Y). Find the tension in each cable.

steps.label: Set up equilibrium
steps.text: The joint where the three cables meet: vertical equilibrium requires $2T\sin 30^\circ = W$, since the two tensions pull symmetrically upward and outward.

steps.label: Solve
steps.text: $T = W/(2 \sin 30^\circ) = 900/(2 \times 0.50) = 900$ N — each cable carries the **full** weight, a hallmark of shallow cable angles.

steps.label: Horizontal check
steps.text: The horizontal components $T\cos 30^\circ$ cancel by symmetry: $\sum F_x = 0$ holds automatically.

steps.label: The shallow-cable warning
steps.text: Had the cables drooped to 10°, each tension would be $900/(2\sin 10^\circ) = 2600$ N. Shallow cables are high-tension cables — the physics of tightrope walking.

examples.result: $T = 900$ N in each cable, three times what each would carry if vertical: symmetric 30° geometry doubles the demand.

examples.title: Zero force, nonzero torque: the couple
examples.problem: Two 50 N forces act on a rod: one up at the left end, one down at the right end, separated by 0.40 m. Show that the net force vanishes but the net torque does not.

steps.label: Net force
steps.text: $\vec F_{net} = (+50\hat y) + (-50\hat y) = \vec 0$: the force condition is satisfied — the com will not accelerate.

steps.label: Net torque about the center
steps.text: Each force has lever arm 0.20 m: $\tau = (50)(0.20) + (50)(0.20) = 20$ N·m, same sense — the rod spins up.

steps.label: Moral
steps.text: Equilibrium needs BOTH conditions. A body can be force-balanced yet torque-rich — the situation every doorknob illustrates when you twist it with two fingers.

examples.result: $\sum F = 0$ but $\sum \tau = 20$ N·m: pure rotation, no translation. The two equilibrium conditions are genuinely independent.

keyTakeaways: Equilibrium demands both $\sum \vec F = 0$ and $\sum \vec\tau = 0$; the conditions are independent (couples satisfy one, violate the other).
When $\sum\vec F = 0$, the net torque is the same about every point — choose the pivot to eliminate unknown forces.
In uniform gravity, the body's weight may be treated as a single force $Mg$ at the center of mass; in 2D you have exactly three independent equations.

quiz.q: A body has zero net force acting on it but a nonzero net torque. The body will:
options: accelerate in the direction of the larger force
rotate with its center of mass fixed
move in a circle at constant speed
quiz.explanation: Zero net force pins the center of mass; the nonzero torque spins the body about it — a 'couple' in action. Both conditions must hold for equilibrium.

quiz.q: In a statics problem you may compute torques about any convenient point because:
options: torques are the same about every point in every situation
when the net force vanishes, the net torque is independent of the pivot choice
the pivot must always be the center of mass
torques about off-center points are automatically zero
quiz.explanation: Shifting the origin by $\vec d$ changes the torque sum by $\vec d \times \vec F_{net}$, which is zero in equilibrium. Strategically, pick the pivot on the line of action of an unknown force to delete it from the equation.

quiz.q: In two dimensions, the number of independent equilibrium equations available for one rigid body is:
quiz.explanation: $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$, and one torque equation — three. More unknowns than this means the structure is statically indeterminate.

quiz.q: The center of gravity of a body coincides with its center of mass:
options: never; the two are different points
quiz.explanation: The identification follows from summing gravity torques and regrouping: $\sum \vec r_i \times m_i\vec g = \vec r_{com} \times M\vec g$ requires $\vec g$ to be the same for every particle. Symmetry is not needed — only uniformity of the field.

intro: Static equilibrium problems are solved by ritual, not brilliance: draw the free-body diagram, choose a clever pivot, write the three equations, and solve. This section runs the ritual on the two classic cases — a beam on two supports and a ladder against a frictionless wall — and then meets the boundary of the method: structures with too many unknowns, where statics gives way to elasticity.
objectives: Execute the four-step statics recipe on beam and ladder problems
Solve the ladder-with-frictionless-wall problem and find the minimum coefficient of friction
Recognize statically indeterminate structures and explain why elasticity must decide them

concepts.statement: **Step 1:** isolate the body and draw every external force (weights at coms; normal forces perpendicular to surfaces; friction along surfaces; tensions along cables). **Step 2:** choose a pivot through which unknown forces pass. **Step 3:** write $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$. **Step 4:** write $\sum\tau = 0$ about the pivot, with consistent signs (counterclockwise positive).
concepts.detail: The ritual's power is its audit trail: every force appears exactly once in each equation, so missing or invented forces are caught. When a problem asks for 'the minimum coefficient of friction', solve first for the friction force, then divide by the normal force.

concepts.statement: A uniform ladder against a **frictionless wall** has exactly three unknowns — the wall's normal force $N_w$ (horizontal), the floor's normal force $N_g$ (vertical), and the floor's friction $f$ (horizontal) — matching the three equations. Torque about the ladder's base eliminates both floor forces at once, giving $N_w$; then $f = N_w$ and $N_g = (M+m)g$.
concepts.detail: The frictionless-wall idealization is the physics of a freshly painted wall; a rough wall makes the system indeterminate. The answer always pairs: the friction the floor must supply is the wall's push, and the safety question reduces to $\mu_{min} = N_w/N_g$.

concepts.statement: A beam on three supports has four unknown force components but only three equations: no arrangement of statics can find them. The actual distribution depends on **how the beam deforms** — the elastic analysis of Section 12.3. Nature solves the simultaneous equations of stress and strain; statics alone merely bounds them.
concepts.detail: Engineers deliberately design into indeterminacy: redundant supports mean that if one fails, the others share the load. Modern codes compute the elastic distribution by finite-element methods — but the counting test that flags the situation is exactly this section's three-equation budget.

concepts.term: Some Examples of Static Equilibrium: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Some Examples of Static Equilibrium problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is static equilibrium; the working equation is $\sum\vec F = 0$, $\sum\vec\tau = 0$, $\text{stress} = F/A$, $Y = (F/A)/(\Delta L/L)$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N}$, $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, $\text{Pa}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against beams $10^2$--$10^3\ \text{N}$; $Y_{\text{steel}} \approx 2\times 10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$; static only; Hookean moduli for small strains.

concepts.term: Some Examples of Static Equilibrium: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Some Examples of Static Equilibrium lives at beams $10^2$--$10^3\ \text{N}$; $Y_{\text{steel}} \approx 2\times 10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$ and the textbook model holds while static only; Hookean moduli for small strains.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Some Examples of Static Equilibrium calculation gives seconds when $\text{N}$, $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, $\text{Pa}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond beams $10^2$--$10^3\ \text{N}$; $Y_{\text{steel}} \approx 2\times 10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

figures.caption: Free-body diagram for a ladder against a frictionless wall. A uniform 5.0 m ladder (20 kg) leans at $\theta = 50^\circ$; a 70 kg painter stands 4.0 m up the ladder. Torques about the base kill $N_g$ and $f$: $$N_w = \frac{(196)(2.5\cos 50^\circ) + (686)(4.0\cos 50^\circ)}{5.0\sin 50^\circ} = 543\ \text{N}.$$ Then $f = N_w = 543$ N and $N_g = 882$ N, so the floor must supply $\mu_{min} = 543/882 = 0.62$. Note how each painter step upward increases the base-pivot torques but not the balancing wall torque — climbing a ladder gets more dangerous, not less, as you ascend.

examples.title: A beam on two bathroom scales
examples.problem: A uniform 6.0 m beam of weight 200 N rests on scales at its two ends. A 600 N person stands 2.0 m from the left end. Find each scale reading.

steps.label: Free-body diagram
steps.text: Three vertical forces: $N_L$, $N_R$ up at the ends; weights 600 N at 2.0 m and 200 N at the 3.0 m midpoint, all down.

steps.label: Sanity check
steps.text: The person stands left of center, and the left scale indeed reads more. Torque about the right end: $N_L(6.0) = (600)(4.0) + (200)(3.0) = 3000$ — gives $N_L = 500$ N again. Consistent.

examples.result: Left scale 500 N, right scale 300 N. Move the person toward the right end and watch the readings trade places — the seesaw's arithmetic.

examples.title: A painter on a ladder
examples.problem: A uniform 5.0 m ladder of mass 20 kg leans against a frictionless wall at 50° to the ground. A 70 kg painter stands 4.0 m along the ladder. Find the wall force, the floor forces, and the minimum coefficient of static friction.

steps.label: Unknowns
steps.text: $N_w$ (wall, horizontal), $N_g$ (floor, vertical), $f$ (floor, horizontal) — three unknowns, three equations: solvable.

steps.label: Torque about the base
steps.text: Both floor forces pass through the base: $N_w(5.0\sin 50^\circ) = (196)(2.5\cos 50^\circ) + (686)(4.0\cos 50^\circ)$. Numerically: $N_w(3.83) = 314.7 + 1764.4 = 2079$, so $N_w = 543$ N.

steps.label: Force balance
steps.text: Horizontal: $f = N_w = 543$ N. Vertical: $N_g = 196 + 686 = 882$ N.

steps.label: Minimum friction
steps.text: $\mu_{min} = f/N_g = 543/882 = 0.62$. A dry concrete floor ($\mu \approx 0.8$) holds; wet tile ($\mu \approx 0.2$) does not — and note that climbing higher only increases $N_w$, so the danger grows with altitude.

examples.result: $N_w = 543$ N, $f = 543$ N, $N_g = 882$ N, $\mu_{min} = 0.62$ — the ladder lives on the floor's friction alone.

keyTakeaways: The recipe — free-body diagram, clever pivot, $\sum F_x = \sum F_y = 0$, $\sum\tau = 0$ — solves every determinate statics problem.
Ladder against a frictionless wall: torque about the base gives the wall force directly; then $f = N_w$ and $N_g = $ total weight, so $\mu_{min} = N_w/N_g$.
More unknowns than the three 2D equations means a statically indeterminate structure: elasticity, not statics, distributes the load.

quiz.q: In the beam example, the 600 N person walks from 2.0 m to 4.0 m from the left end of the 6.0 m beam (beam weight 200 N). The right scale now reads:
quiz.explanation: Torque about the left end: $N_R(6.0) = (600)(4.0) + (200)(3.0) = 3000$, so $N_R = 500$... careful — recompute: $N_R = 3000/6.0 = 500$ N? The person at 4.0 m: $600 \times 4 = 2400$, plus $200 \times 3 = 600$, total 3000, $N_R = 500$ N — so the correct answer is 500 N (option C).

quiz.q: Why take torques about the base of the ladder?
options: the torque of gravity is largest there
the unknown floor forces pass through the base and drop out of the equation
the base is the center of mass of the system
torques are always computed about the lowest point
quiz.explanation: Choosing the pivot on the lines of action of $N_g$ and $f$ deletes both unknowns at once, leaving one equation with one unknown ($N_w$). Any other pivot works too — but with more algebra.

quiz.q: For the painter's ladder (Nw = 543 N, total weight 882 N), the minimum static friction coefficient is:
quiz.explanation: $\mu_{min} = f/N_g = 543/882 = 0.616 \approx 0.62$. Below this, the floor cannot supply the friction the wall's push demands, and the base slides out.

quiz.q: A horizontal beam rests on three supports. Statics alone:
options: determines two of them and leaves the third arbitrary
cannot determine the three support forces; the elastic deformation of the beam decides
shows the middle support carries everything
quiz.explanation: Four unknown force components (two end supports with vertical + possibly horizontal components, or three vertical reactions plus geometry) against three equations: the system is statically indeterminate. How much each support carries depends on the beam's stiffness distribution — Section 12.3's physics.

intro: Rigid bodies were a fiction; real materials stretch, shear and squeeze. Elasticity replaces 'rigid' with a linear law — stress is proportional to strain — and assigns each material its moduli. The numbers are small: a steel cable holding a car stretches by millimeters. But those millimeters are exactly what resolves the indeterminate structures of the previous section, and what lets engineers prove that a bridge will come back.
objectives: Define stress and strain, and compute them for tension, shear and hydraulic compression
Apply the three moduli — Young's, shear and bulk — through $\Delta L = FL/(YA)$ and its analogs
Explain the elastic limit and the meaning of engineering safety factors

concepts.statement: **Stress** is force per area (units N/m² = Pa); **strain** is the resulting fractional deformation (dimensionless). Three standard loadings: **tension/compression** (pull or push along a bar's length), **shear** (forces parallel to a face, sliding layers), and **hydraulic compression** (pressure on all faces of a volume).
concepts.detail: Stress is the cause, strain the effect, and the proportionality between them is a property of the material alone — which is the whole point of separating the two: a thick and a thin steel wire strain identically under the same stress, though their forces differ.

concepts.term: Hooke's law for materials: the moduli
concepts.statement: Within the elastic limit, $$\text{stress} = \text{modulus} \times \text{strain}.$$ Tension/compression: $\frac{F}{A} = Y\frac{\Delta L}{L}$ (Young's modulus $Y$); shear: $\frac{F}{A} = G\frac{x}{L}$ (shear modulus $G$, with $x$ the sideways shift across thickness $L$); hydraulic: $p = B\frac{\Delta V}{V}$ (bulk modulus $B$). Solving the first: $$\Delta L = \frac{FL}{YA}.$$
concepts.detail: Representative values: steel $Y \approx 200$ GPa, $G \approx 80$ GPa, $B \approx 160$ GPa; aluminum $Y \approx 70$ GPa; water $B \approx 2.2$ GPa and effectively zero shear rigidity. The moduli are huge because strain is tiny: steel at 250 MPa stress strains only $1.25\times10^{-3}$.

concepts.statement: Hooke's proportionality holds only up to the **proportional limit**; beyond it lies the **elastic limit** (the last stress that fully recovers), then plastic deformation, then fracture. Engineers work at a fraction of the elastic limit — the safety factor — because real materials carry cracks, and stress concentrates at them.
concepts.detail: A structural steel's yield stress near 250 MPa against an ultimate strength of 400–550 MPa, combined with working stresses of perhaps 100 MPa, embodies a safety factor of roughly 2.5. The field that computes where cracks become fatal — fracture mechanics — is the modern descendant of this section's bookkeeping.

concepts.statement: **Solve Elasticity problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is static equilibrium; the working equation is $\sum\vec F = 0$, $\sum\vec\tau = 0$, $\text{stress} = F/A$, $Y = (F/A)/(\Delta L/L)$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N}$, $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, $\text{Pa}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against beams $10^2$--$10^3\ \text{N}$; $Y_{\text{steel}} \approx 2\times 10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$; static only; Hookean moduli for small strains.

concepts.statement: **Elasticity lives at beams $10^2$--$10^3\ \text{N}$; $Y_{\text{steel}} \approx 2\times 10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$ and the textbook model holds while static only; Hookean moduli for small strains.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Elasticity calculation gives seconds when $\text{N}$, $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, $\text{Pa}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond beams $10^2$--$10^3\ \text{N}$; $Y_{\text{steel}} \approx 2\times 10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Stretching a steel cable
examples.problem: A steel cable of cross-section 2.0 mm × 1.0 mm... take $A = 2.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2$ — length 5.0 m, Young's modulus $Y = 2.0\times10^{11}$ Pa — hangs vertically holding a 500 N load. Find the stretch, the stress, and the strain.

steps.label: Stress
steps.text: $\sigma = F/A = 500/2.0\times10^{-6} = 2.5\times10^{8}$ Pa = 250 MPa — comparable to structural steel's working limit, so this cable is appropriately beefy for 500 N.

steps.label: Strain
steps.text: $\epsilon = \sigma/Y = 2.5\times10^{8}/2.0\times10^{11} = 1.25\times10^{-3}$ — about 0.1%, invisible to the eye but perfectly real.

steps.label: Perspective
steps.text: Doubling the length would double the stretch; doubling the area would halve it. Long thin cables are rubber bands in disguise.

examples.result: Stress 250 MPa, strain $1.25\times10^{-3}$, stretch 6.3 mm — steel's stiffness in one arithmetic line.

examples.title: Squeezing water hydraulically
examples.problem: A sample of water is subjected to a pressure of 100 atm ($1.01\times10^{7}$ Pa). With bulk modulus $B = 2.2\times10^{9}$ Pa, find the fractional volume change, and the pressure needed to compress water by 1%.

steps.label: Fractional compression
steps.text: $\Delta V/V = p/B = 1.01\times10^{7}/2.2\times10^{9} = 4.6\times10^{-3}$ — 0.46% at 100 atmospheres.

steps.label: One percent
steps.text: For $\Delta V/V = 0.010$ you would need $p = B(0.010) = 2.2\times10^{7}$ Pa $\approx 220$ atm.

steps.label: Moral
steps.text: 'Incompressible' is a 99.5%-true approximation for water at ordinary pressures — but sound propagates through water precisely because of that stubborn 0.5%, at $v = \sqrt{B/\rho} \approx 1500$ m/s (Chapter 17's business).

examples.result: 0.46% at 100 atm; about 220 atm for a 1% squeeze. The ocean floor presses water only a percent or two smaller.

keyTakeaways: Stress (Pa) = force/area; strain = fractional deformation; within the elastic limit, stress = modulus × strain for tension ($Y$), shear ($G$) and hydraulic ($B$) loading.
$\Delta L = FL/(YA)$: stretch grows with length and load, shrinks with area and stiffness — 6 mm for a heavily loaded 5 m steel cable.
Beyond the elastic limit lies plastic deformation and fracture; engineers hold working stresses well below it (safety factors), because stress concentrates at flaws.

quiz.q: A steel wire (Y = 2.0×10¹¹ Pa) of length 4.0 m and cross-section 1.0×10⁻⁶ m² carries a 100 N load. Its stretch is:
Which modulus governs the deformation when a book is pushed sideways along its top cover, its spine held fixed?
options: no modulus; the book is rigid
quiz.explanation: Forces parallel to a surface, sliding layers past each other, with thickness as the length scale: that is shear, $F/A = G(x/L)$. Young's is for along-length pulls; bulk for all-around pressure.

quiz.q: Two steel wires have the same length and load, but wire A has twice the cross-sectional area of wire B. Compared to B, wire A stretches:
quiz.explanation: $\Delta L = FL/(YA)$ is inversely proportional to area: doubling $A$ halves the stretch. Stress halves too — which is why fat cables carry big loads.

quiz.q: The elastic limit of a material is the:
options: maximum stress from which it recovers its original dimensions when unloaded
stress at which Hooke's law is exactly obeyed
strain at which the modulus doubles
quiz.explanation: Recoverability defines the elastic limit; Hooke's linearity ends slightly earlier (proportional limit), and fracture comes later still (ultimate strength). Between the elastic limit and fracture, the material deforms permanently.

intro: Newton's masterstroke in the Principia (1687) was to claim that the force pulling an apple to the ground and the force holding the Moon in its orbit are one and the same. The law he proposed is breathtakingly simple — every pair of masses attracts along the line joining them — and it turned the heavens into a machine that calculus could predict. This section states the law, meets its constant $G$, and gets a feel for the size of the force.
objectives: State Newton's law of gravitation with the correct direction, proportionality, and constant
Evaluate gravitational forces between real astronomical bodies
Explain why the weakest fundamental force nevertheless rules the cosmos

concepts.statement: **Every particle attracts every other particle with a force along the line joining them, proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation:** $$F = G\,\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}.$$ The force is always attractive, never repulsive.
concepts.detail: For extended spherical bodies (Earth, Sun, a uniform ball), $r$ is measured center to center — a shortcut justified by the shell theorem of Section 13-4. The law is universal: the same $G$ works for apples, moons, and galaxies.

concepts.statement: $$G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$$ is the gravitational constant, measured by Henry Cavendish in 1798 with a torsion balance — 111 years after the law was published.
concepts.detail: Because $G$ is tiny, gravity between laboratory objects is almost immeasurably small. Cavendish's measurement of $G$ instantly gave the mass of the Earth, $M_E = gR^2/G$ — which is why his experiment is remembered as weighing the Earth.

concepts.statement: Tripling the separation cuts the force to $1/9$; halving it multiplies the force by 4. The $1/r^2$ dependence is the signature of a force that spreads out over spheres of area $4\pi r^2$.
concepts.detail: Because the same total flux of influence threads ever-larger spheres, its intensity per unit area dies as $r^{-2}$. Newton tested this against the Moon: the Moon is 60 Earth radii away, and $9.8/60^2 = 2.7\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ — exactly the Moon's orbital centripetal acceleration.

concepts.statement: Gravitation is by far the **weakest** of the fundamental interactions (about $10^{38}$ times weaker than the strong force between two protons), yet it structures the universe because it is **always attractive and has infinite range**.
concepts.detail: Electric charge comes in two signs and cancels; mass only comes in one sign, so gravity accumulates relentlessly over astronomical amounts of matter. In ordinary life gravity matters only because the Earth beneath you is enormously massive.

concepts.term: Newton's Law of Gravitation: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Newton's Law of Gravitation problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Newton gravitation with superposition and the shell theorem; the working equation is $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$, $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, $U = -GMm/r$, $T^2 = 4\pi^2r^3/GM$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N}$, $\text{J}$, years for $T$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $v_{\text{esc}} = 11.2\ \text{km/s}$; $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ at the surface; point masses or spherical symmetry (shell theorem); outside or $r\gg$ size.

examples.title: The Sun–Earth pull
examples.problem: The Sun ($M = 1.99\times10^{30}$ kg) and Earth ($m = 5.97\times10^{24}$ kg) are separated by $r = 1.496\times10^{11}$ m, center to center. (a) What gravitational force does the Sun exert on Earth? (b) Compare with the Moon's pull on Earth ($m_{Moon} = 7.35\times10^{22}$ kg at $r_{Moon} = 3.84\times10^{8}$ m).

steps.label: Write the law
steps.text: $F = Gm_1 m_2/r^2$ with $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$.

examples.result: $F_{Sun} \approx 3.5\times10^{22}$ N — about 178 times the Moon's $2.0\times10^{20}$ N. Gravity governs the planets because the masses are astronomical, not because the force is strong between everyday objects.

examples.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation: orbit weight check
examples.problem: A $1500\ \text{kg}$ satellite orbits $400\ \text{km}$ above Earth ($r \approx 6.77\times 10^6\ \text{m}$). What gravitational force holds it?

steps.label: Formula
steps.text: $F = GMm/r^2$ with $GM = 3.98\times 10^{14}\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $F \approx 13000\ \text{N}$ ($8.69\ \text{m/s}^2$, about $0.89g$).

examples.result: $F \approx 13000\ \text{N}$.

keyTakeaways: $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$ along the line joining the two masses, always attractive.
$G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$ was measured by Cavendish and lets us compute the Earth's mass.
Gravity is the weakest interaction but never cancels, so it dominates astronomy.

quiz.q: If the separation between two point masses is tripled, the gravitational force between them becomes:
quiz.explanation: The force is proportional to $1/r^2$; tripling $r$ divides $F$ by $3^2 = 9$.

quiz.q: Cavendish's 1798 measurement of G is called weighing the Earth because it first allowed computation of:
options: the distance from Earth to the Moon
the Sun's mass from Kepler's third law
a standard value of g in any laboratory
quiz.explanation: With $G$, $g$, and $R$ measured, $M_E = gR^2/G$ follows immediately — a mass no scale could ever weigh directly.

quiz.q: Both masses in a pair are doubled and the center-to-center separation is also doubled. The gravitational force is:
quiz.explanation: The mass factor gives $2\times2 = 4$ in the numerator; the distance factor gives $2^2 = 4$ in the denominator. They cancel.

quiz.q: Gravity structures the universe despite being the weakest interaction because it:
options: is always attractive and has infinite range, so it accumulates over huge masses
quiz.explanation: There is no negative mass to cancel the attraction, so over astronomical amounts of matter gravity always wins in the end.

intro: Newton's law gives the force between two particles. Real situations have three or more bodies: a planet tugged by a star and its sibling planets, a spacecraft feeling Earth and Moon at once. Gravitation obeys a principle of superposition: each pair interacts as if the others were not there, and the net force is the plain vector sum. All of multi-body gravitation is bookkeeping on top of that one rule.
objectives: Compute net gravitational forces by componentwise vector addition
Exploit symmetry to predict when forces cancel
Explain when an extended body may be treated as a point mass

concepts.statement: **Gravitational forces add as vectors.** The net force on particle 1 is $$\vec F_{1,net} = \sum_{j=2}^{N} \vec F_{1j},$$ where each $\vec F_{1j} = -Gm_1m_j\,\hat r_{1j}/r_{1j}^2$ is computed as if the other particles were absent.
concepts.detail: Gravity is linear in its sources. Nature does not let one planet shield or modify another planet’s pull — you simply keep adding arrows, one per pair, with signs and components carrying all the geometry.

concepts.statement: For each source body $j$: compute $F_{1j} = Gm_1m_j/r_{1j}^2$, resolve it into components along your axes with the geometry of the layout, then sum the $x$-components and $y$-components separately before recombining into magnitude and direction.
concepts.detail: A sketch with all force arrows drawn away from the target particle is the essential first step. Errors in these problems are almost always sign errors, not arithmetic errors.

concepts.statement: When identical masses sit symmetrically about the target, the net force can vanish: at the midpoint between two equal masses the pulls cancel exactly, and three equal masses at the corners of an equilateral triangle each feel a resultant aimed at the centroid.
concepts.detail: Lagrange exploited such cancellations: there exist points (L1–L5) in the Sun–Earth system where gravitational pulls and orbital motion balance, and modern telescopes park there.

concepts.statement: A uniform sphere (or any spherically symmetric mass distribution) attracts an external particle **as if all its mass were concentrated at its center**.
concepts.detail: This is half of the shell theorem proved in Section 13-4. It is why the $r$ in the law of gravitation may be taken center-to-center for planets and stars, and why Newton could apply his law to the Moon even though Earth is not a point.

concepts.term: Gravitation and the Principle of Superposition: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Gravitation and the Principle of Superposition problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Newton gravitation with superposition and the shell theorem; the working equation is $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$, $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, $U = -GMm/r$, $T^2 = 4\pi^2r^3/GM$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N}$, $\text{J}$, years for $T$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $v_{\text{esc}} = 11.2\ \text{km/s}$; $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ at the surface; point masses or spherical symmetry (shell theorem); outside or $r\gg$ size.

examples.title: Net force from two nearby masses
examples.problem: A $m_3 = 20$ kg sphere sits at the origin. A $m_1 = 500$ kg sphere is at $(-0.30, 0)$ m and a $m_2 = 300$ kg sphere is at $(0, +0.40)$ m. Find the net gravitational force on $m_3$.

steps.label: Geometry
steps.text: Distances: $r_1 = 0.30$ m (along $-x$), $r_2 = 0.40$ m (along $+y$). Pulls point from $m_3$ toward each source.

examples.result: A net force of $7.8\times10^{-6}$ N — a whisper, even though half a tonne of matter is within half a meter. Gravity is genuinely weak.

examples.title: Gravitation and the Principle of Superposition: orbit weight check
examples.problem: A $2000\ \text{kg}$ satellite orbits $400\ \text{km}$ above Earth ($r \approx 6.77\times 10^6\ \text{m}$). What gravitational force holds it?

steps.label: Formula
steps.text: $F = GMm/r^2$ with $GM = 3.98\times 10^{14}\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $F \approx 17400\ \text{N}$ ($8.69\ \text{m/s}^2$, about $0.89g$).

examples.result: $F \approx 17400\ \text{N}$.

keyTakeaways: Net gravitational force = vector sum of the individual pair forces.
Sum components separately; geometry errors live in the signs.
Symmetry can kill whole force terms before any arithmetic begins.

quiz.q: A particle sits exactly at the midpoint between two identical masses. The net gravitational force on it is:
options: twice the force from one mass
quiz.explanation: The two equal-magnitude pulls point in opposite directions along the same line, so they cancel exactly.

quiz.q: Three equal masses sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle. The net force on any one of them due to the other two points:
options: along a side, toward either neighbor
toward the centroid of the triangle
quiz.explanation: The two equal pulls add along the angle bisector by symmetry — which is the line from that vertex to the centroid.

quiz.q: To find the net gravitational force on body 1 from bodies 2 and 3, you should:
options: add the magnitudes and keep the sign of the larger
add the force vectors component by component
quiz.explanation: Superposition is vector addition; magnitudes alone would be correct only if the forces happened to be collinear.

quiz.q: A uniform sphere attracts an external particle as if:
options: its mass were spread along the line joining it to the particle
all its mass were concentrated at its center
only the half of the sphere facing the particle acted
quiz.explanation: This is the shell theorem (Section 13-4), and it licenses center-to-center $r$ in the law of gravitation for planets and stars.

intro: Near Earth's surface the free-fall acceleration $g$ is the gravitational pull of the planet divided by your mass — which means the same law that moves the Moon fixes how fast an apple falls. Applied at the surface, the law predicts $g$ from Earth's mass and radius. It also predicts precisely how $g$ weakens with altitude, and — comparing with measurement — reveals that the real Earth is lumpy, spinning, and inhomogeneous.
objectives: Derive $g = GM/R^2$ from the law of gravitation and check it against $9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$
Compute $g$ at a given altitude above the surface
Explain the observed variation of $g$ over Earth’s surface

concepts.term: g from the law of gravitation
concepts.statement: Setting the gravitational force on a mass $m$ equal to $mg$ at Earth's surface gives $$g = \frac{GM_E}{R^2} = \frac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(5.98\times10^{24})}{(6.37\times10^{6})^2} \approx 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ The mass of the falling body cancels — all bodies fall alike.
concepts.detail: That $m$ cancels is the equality of gravitational and inertial mass, an experimental fact Newton took as given and Einstein would later elevate to a founding principle (Section 13-8).

concepts.statement: At height $h$ above the surface, $$g(h) = \frac{GM_E}{(R_E+h)^2}.$$ At the space shuttle's $h = 300$ km this still gives $g \approx 9.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ — 91% of the surface value.
concepts.detail: Astronauts float not because gravity is absent up there but because they and their spacecraft are in perpetual free fall around the Earth. Weightlessness is free fall, not zero-$g$.

concepts.statement: Measured $g$ runs from $9.780\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ at the equator to $9.832\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ at the poles, because the spinning Earth bulges at the equator (surface farther from the center) and because rotation must supply centripetal acceleration there.
concepts.detail: Both effects make the equatorial $g$ about 0.052 m/s² smaller. Mountains, ocean trenches, and density contrasts in the crust add finer ripples of order $10^{-5}$ m/s².

concepts.statement: A gravimeter trekking across countryside measures tiny local changes in $g$ that map density contrasts below: heavy ore bodies pull slightly harder, salt domes and oil traps pull slightly weaker.
concepts.detail: This is superposition in the field: the local value of $g$ is the vector sum of the contribution of the whole Earth plus the anomaly of the buried body.

concepts.term: Gravitation Near Earth's Surface: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Gravitation Near Earth's Surface problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Newton gravitation with superposition and the shell theorem; the working equation is $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$, $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, $U = -GMm/r$, $T^2 = 4\pi^2r^3/GM$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N}$, $\text{J}$, years for $T$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $v_{\text{esc}} = 11.2\ \text{km/s}$; $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ at the surface; point masses or spherical symmetry (shell theorem); outside or $r\gg$ size.

examples.title: g at shuttle altitude
examples.problem: What is the free-fall acceleration at the altitude of a satellite orbiting $h = 300$ km above Earth's surface ($M_E = 5.98\times10^{24}$ kg, $R_E = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m)?

steps.label: Compare with surface
steps.text: $g \approx 8.96\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, which is $8.96/9.82 \approx 91\%$ of the sea-level value.

examples.result: $g \approx 8.96\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ at 300 km. Orbiting astronauts feel nothing not because gravity has faded but because they fall with their ship.

examples.title: Gravitation Near Earth's Surface: orbit weight check
examples.problem: A $2500\ \text{kg}$ satellite orbits $400\ \text{km}$ above Earth ($r \approx 6.77\times 10^6\ \text{m}$). What gravitational force holds it?

steps.label: Formula
steps.text: $F = GMm/r^2$ with $GM = 3.98\times 10^{14}\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $F \approx 21700\ \text{N}$ ($8.69\ \text{m/s}^2$, about $0.89g$).

examples.result: $F \approx 21700\ \text{N}$.

keyTakeaways: $g = GM_E/R_E^2$ at the surface; the falling mass cancels.
$g$ falls off as $1/r^2$ from Earth's center: only 9% weaker at 300 km.
Latitude and density variations make $g$ a measurably local quantity.

quiz.q: At an altitude of one Earth radius above the surface (distance $2R_E$ from the center), the free-fall acceleration is:
quiz.explanation: Doubling the distance from the center divides $g$ by $2^2 = 4$.

quiz.q: g is smaller at the equator than at the poles mainly because:
options: the equatorial surface is farther from the center and rotation supplies part of the needed centripetal acceleration
the oceans are deeper at the equator
air pressure is lower at the poles
quiz.explanation: The bulge (larger $R$) and the centrifugal requirement (rotation) both reduce the measured $g$ at the equator by a combined 0.052 m/s².

quiz.q: A planet has the same mass as Earth but twice the radius. Its surface gravitational acceleration is:
quiz.explanation: $g = GM/R^2$; doubling $R$ with $M$ fixed divides $g$ by four.

quiz.q: Gravimeters can detect buried ore bodies because:
options: ore changes the local value of $G$
a dense body adds a small extra pull to the local $g$, while a low-density body subtracts from it
$g$ depends on the time of day
quiz.explanation: Superposition: the buried anomaly adds its own inverse-square contribution to the background field of the Earth.

intro: What does Earth weigh when you are inside it? Newton proved a result so elegant it deserves its own name: a uniform spherical shell of matter exerts no net gravitational force on a particle inside it, while outside the shell pulls as if all its mass sat at the center. Together these two statements — the shell theorem — turn gravitation inside a planet into a one-line computation, and they even make the fantasy of a gravity train through the Earth a solvable physics problem.
objectives: State both halves of the shell theorem and their consequence for computing forces
Compute $g$ inside a uniform Earth as a function of $r$
Treat the through-Earth tunnel as simple harmonic motion

concepts.statement: A uniform shell of matter attracts a particle **outside** it as if the entire shell’s mass were concentrated at its center. Any spherically symmetric body is a nest of such shells, so planets and stars may be treated as point masses for external bodies.
concepts.detail: The proof integrates the vector contributions of shell elements over the sphere; the transverse components cancel pairwise and the radial pieces assemble exactly into $GmM_{shell}/r^2$.

concepts.statement: A uniform shell of matter exerts **no net force** on a particle located anywhere inside it. Every pull from the near wall is exactly canceled by the combined pull of the more distant, but more extensive, far wall.
concepts.detail: The cancellation is a geometric miracle of the inverse-square law: it fails for any other force law. Inside a hollow planet you would float in permanent free fall at the center of a bottomless well.

concepts.statement: At radius $r < R$ only the mass interior to you pulls (the outer shells cancel), and that interior mass is $M(r) = M_E\,(r/R)^3$. So $$g(r) = \frac{GM(r)}{r^2} = \frac{GM_E}{R^3}\,r = g_{surface}\frac{r}{R}:$$ **linear in $r$, zero at the center.**
concepts.detail: Down you go, more mass is left behind you and less lies beneath: $g$ decreases smoothly from 9.8 m/s² at the surface to zero at the center — for a uniform planet.

concepts.statement: The real Earth is not uniform: the iron core is about twice as dense as the mantle, so $g$ actually **increases** as you descend, peaking near $10.7\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ at the core–mantle boundary before falling to zero at the center.
concepts.detail: Seismology reads this density profile from earthquake waves; gravitation fixes its consequences. Uniform-density modeling is the idealization to be refined, not the truth.

concepts.statement: **Solve Gravitation Inside Earth problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Newton gravitation with superposition and the shell theorem; the working equation is $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$, $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, $U = -GMm/r$, $T^2 = 4\pi^2r^3/GM$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N}$, $\text{J}$, years for $T$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $v_{\text{esc}} = 11.2\ \text{km/s}$; $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ at the surface; point masses or spherical symmetry (shell theorem); outside or $r\gg$ size.

figures.caption: Free-fall acceleration $g$ versus distance $r$ from the center for an idealized uniform Earth: $g = GMr/R^3$ rises linearly from zero at the center to $GM/R^2$ at the surface, then joins the inverse-square $1/r^2$ falloff outside. For the real (denser-cored) Earth the interior curve bulges above this line, peaking near $10.7\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ at the core–mantle boundary.

examples.title: The through-Earth gravity train
examples.problem: A straight tunnel is bored through the center of a uniform-density Earth ($R_E = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m). A package is dropped in. Show that its motion is simple harmonic and find the one-way travel time to the antipodes.

steps.label: Force inside
steps.text: By the shell theorem only the mass interior to the package pulls, so $g(r) = (GM_E/R_E^3)\,r$ — proportional to the displacement $s$ from the center and pointing back toward it.

steps.label: Recognize SHM
steps.text: $a = -(GM_E/R_E^3)s$ matches $a = -\omega^2 s$ with $\omega = \sqrt{GM_E/R_E^3} = \sqrt{g/R_E}$.

steps.label: Period
steps.text: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{R_E/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{6.37\times10^{6}/9.8} = 5.06\times10^{3}$ s $\approx 84$ min.

steps.label: One-way trip
steps.text: The antipodes are reached at half a period: about 42 min. At the center the speed is $\omega R_E = \sqrt{gR_E} = 7.9$ km/s — exactly the surface orbital speed.

examples.result: A 42-minute ride to the far side of the planet, independent of the tunnel length through the center — the same physics Chapter 15 develops as simple harmonic motion.

examples.title: Gravitation Inside Earth: orbit weight check
examples.problem: A $1000\ \text{kg}$ satellite orbits $400\ \text{km}$ above Earth ($r \approx 6.77\times 10^6\ \text{m}$). What gravitational force holds it?

steps.label: Formula
steps.text: $F = GMm/r^2$ with $GM = 3.98\times 10^{14}\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $F \approx 8690\ \text{N}$ ($8.69\ \text{m/s}^2$, about $0.89g$).

examples.result: $F \approx 8690\ \text{N}$.

keyTakeaways: Shell theorem: outside, a shell acts as a point mass; inside, it exerts no net force at all.
Only the mass interior to your radius pulls you inward.
Uniform Earth: $g = g_s r/R$ linear inside; the real Earth’s dense core raises the interior curve.

quiz.q: Inside a uniform spherical shell of matter, the net gravitational force on a particle placed anywhere inside the shell is:
options: proportional to the distance from the center
quiz.explanation: Near-wall pulls are weaker but the far wall has more of them; for an inverse-square force the cancellation is exact.

quiz.q: For a uniform-density Earth, the value of $g$ at $r = R/2$ from the center is:
quiz.explanation: Inside a uniform sphere $g$ is linear in $r$: at half the radius it is half the surface value.

quiz.q: A package dropped into a frictionless tunnel through the center of a uniform Earth will:
options: fall with constant acceleration 9.8 m/s² until it reaches the center
oscillate in simple harmonic motion with a period of about 84 min
come permanently to rest at the center
fly out the far side and escape
quiz.explanation: The restoring force is proportional to displacement from the center — the definition of SHM — with $T = 2\pi\sqrt{R/g} \approx 84$ min.

quiz.q: In the real Earth, $g$ increases slightly as you descend from the surface because:
options: the shell theorem fails for nonuniform bodies
the dense iron core means the mass interior to you shrinks more slowly than $r^2$
quiz.explanation: $g = GM(r)/r^2$ grows when $M(r)$ falls more slowly than $r^2$ — which is what a dense core guarantees until near the center.

intro: Near Earth's surface we wrote $U = mgy$, but that linear formula is a local approximation to something deeper: the exact potential energy of gravitation falls off as $-1/r$ and is defined to be zero only at infinite separation. The negative sign is not decoration — it is what makes orbits, escape speeds, and the very notion of a bound system quantitative. This section builds that exact energy function and puts it to work.
objectives: Use $U = -Gm_1m_2/r$ with its zero at infinite separation
Derive and compute escape speeds
Apply energy conservation to motion in a gravitational field

concepts.statement: For two masses separated by $r$, $$U = -\,\frac{Gm_1 m_2}{r},$$ with the arbitrary zero chosen at $r = \infty$ (where $U = 0$).
concepts.detail: Because $U$ approaches zero from below as $r$ grows, any finite separation stores negative energy. Pulling masses apart requires positive work — gravity is attractive, so separation costs energy.

concepts.statement: The negative sign encodes binding: a system with **total** energy $E = K + U < 0$ cannot separate to infinity (where $K \ge 0 = U$), and is therefore bound. Escape is exactly the condition $E = 0$.
concepts.detail: The choice $U(\infty) = 0$ is what makes this bookkeeping universal — every bound system in the universe, atom to galaxy cluster, is negative-total-energy by this convention.

concepts.statement: The work done by gravity moving a mass from $r_2$ to $r_1$ is $$W = Gm_1m_2\!\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right),$$ independent of the path taken — gravitation is a **conservative** force.
concepts.detail: Only the endpoints appear, so $U$ is a genuine state function and $W = -\Delta U$ for any route, curved or straight, thrown or lowered.

concepts.statement: Setting $K = -U$ at the surface: $$v_{esc} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = 11.2\ \mathrm{km/s}$$ for Earth — independent of the projectile's mass and launch direction.
concepts.detail: The Moon’s smaller $M/R$ gives 2.4 km/s, which is why gas molecules escaping lunar gravity stripped its atmosphere, while Earth’s 11.2 km/s retains most gases.

concepts.statement: **Solve Gravitational Potential Energy problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Newton gravitation with superposition and the shell theorem; the working equation is $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$, $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, $U = -GMm/r$, $T^2 = 4\pi^2r^3/GM$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N}$, $\text{J}$, years for $T$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $v_{\text{esc}} = 11.2\ \text{km/s}$; $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ at the surface; point masses or spherical symmetry (shell theorem); outside or $r\gg$ size.

examples.title: Escape from Earth — and a partial climb
examples.problem: (a) What launch speed escapes Earth's gravity from the surface? (b) A projectile is instead launched straight up at 5.0 km/s. How high does it coast before falling back? ($GM_E = 3.99\times10^{14}$, $R_E = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m.)

steps.label: Escape condition
steps.text: Escape means arriving at infinity with zero speed: $\tfrac12 mv^2 - GM_Em/R_E = 0$, so $v = \sqrt{2GM_E/R_E}$.

steps.label: Part (b): conserve energy
steps.text: $\tfrac12 v_0^2 - GM_E/R_E = -GM_E/r_{max}$, so $r_{max} = 1/\left(\frac{1}{R_E} - \frac{v_0^2}{2GM_E}\right)$.

examples.result: 11.2 km/s to escape forever; at 5.0 km/s the projectile peaks only 1600 km up and falls back. Energy bookkeeping decides everything.

examples.title: Gravitational Potential Energy: orbit weight check
examples.problem: A $1500\ \text{kg}$ satellite orbits $400\ \text{km}$ above Earth ($r \approx 6.77\times 10^6\ \text{m}$). What gravitational force holds it?

steps.label: Formula
steps.text: $F = GMm/r^2$ with $GM = 3.98\times 10^{14}\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $F \approx 13000\ \text{N}$ ($8.69\ \text{m/s}^2$, about $0.89g$).

examples.result: $F \approx 13000\ \text{N}$.

keyTakeaways: $U = -Gm_1m_2/r$ with $U(\infty) = 0$; gravitation is conservative.
$E < 0$ means bound; $E = 0$ is the escape boundary.
Escape speed from Earth is 11.2 km/s, independent of mass or direction.

quiz.q: The gravitational potential energy of a two-body system is negative because:
options: the zero is chosen at infinite separation and bound systems have $E < 0$ by that convention
the masses carry negative gravitational charge
quiz.explanation: Convention plus binding: it takes positive work to raise $U$ to zero at infinity, so every finite-separation state sits below zero.

quiz.q: The escape speed from a planet depends on:
options: the mass of the escaping projectile
the planet’s mass and radius only
the speed the projectile has at infinity
quiz.explanation: $v = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ — energy conservation cancels the projectile mass, and any direction works because escape depends on energy alone.

quiz.q: A probe's gravitational potential energy at $r = 2R$ from a planet's center is $-40$ MJ. Moving it to $r = 4R$ changes $U$ to:
quiz.explanation: $U \propto -1/r$: doubling $r$ halves the magnitude, from $-40$ MJ to $-20$ MJ.

quiz.q: With $U_{surface} = -6.3\times10^{9}$ J for a 100 kg object at Earth's surface, the work an external agent must supply to move it to infinity is:
quiz.explanation: To end at $U = 0$ from $U = -6.3\times10^{9}$ J the agent adds exactly $+6.3\times10^{9}$ J (gravity does $-6.3\times10^{9}$ J).

intro: Tycho Brahe's naked-eye data and Kepler's twenty years of curve-fitting produced three laws of planetary motion a full generation before Newton explained them. Newton's triumph was to show that all three laws are not separate empirical facts but corollaries of the inverse-square law plus conservation of angular momentum. This section states the three laws and derives them from gravitation — the masters tier carries the complete derivation.
objectives: State Kepler’s three laws precisely
Explain the second law as angular momentum conservation
Use the law of periods to weigh a central body

concepts.term: First law: the law of orbits
concepts.statement: **Each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.** The orbit is a closed curve with the Sun off-center, not a circle.
concepts.detail: The eccentricity $e = c/a$ (focus offset over semi-major axis) measures the departure from circularity: Earth’s $e = 0.017$ is nearly round; Halley’s comet has $e = 0.967$.

concepts.term: Second law: the law of areas
concepts.statement: The line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out **equal areas in equal times**: the planet speeds up near perihelion and slows near aphelion.
concepts.detail: This is conservation of angular momentum in disguise: since the gravitational force is central (zero torque about the Sun), $L = mrv_\perp$ is constant, and the areal velocity $dA/dt = L/2m$ is constant with it.

concepts.term: Third law: the law of periods
concepts.statement: For all bodies orbiting the same central mass, $$\frac{T^2}{a^3} = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}$$ is the same constant, where $a$ is the semi-major axis.
concepts.detail: In solar units ($T$ in years, $a$ in AU) the constant is 1 for everything orbiting the Sun — a planet, an asteroid, a comet. The law measures the central mass: $M = 4\pi^2a^3/GT^2$.

concepts.statement: An ellipse has semi-major axis $a$, semi-minor axis $b$, and focal offset $c = \sqrt{a^2 - b^2}$; the Sun sits at a focus. Closest approach is **perihelion** ($r_p = a - c$), farthest is **aphelion** ($r_a = a + c$).
concepts.detail: The mean of $r_p$ and $r_a$ is exactly $a$ — which is why the semi-major axis, not the average distance in time, appears in the third law.

concepts.term: Planets and Satellites: Kepler's Laws: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Planets and Satellites: Kepler's Laws problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Newton gravitation with superposition and the shell theorem; the working equation is $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$, $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, $U = -GMm/r$, $T^2 = 4\pi^2r^3/GM$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N}$, $\text{J}$, years for $T$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $v_{\text{esc}} = 11.2\ \text{km/s}$; $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ at the surface; point masses or spherical symmetry (shell theorem); outside or $r\gg$ size.

figures.caption: Kepler's first two laws: the orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at a focus, and the radius vector sweeps equal areas in equal times. The fat wedge near perihelion and the needle-thin wedge near aphelion contain the same area — so the planet races through the near-Sun end of its orbit and crawls through the far end.
