Check the answer against $60\ \text{dB}$ conversation at $10^{-6}\ \text{W/m}^2$; $10\%$ Doppler shift at $30\ \text{m/s}$; $v_S,v_D < v$; $I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^2$ reference.

examples.title: Clarinet versus flute
examples.problem: Both instruments have a 0.60 m sounding length (take $v = 343$ m/s). Compare the lowest three frequencies each can sound.

steps.label: Flute (open–open)
steps.text: $f_n = nv/2L = n(343/1.20) = n(286)$ Hz: 286, 572, 857 Hz — all harmonics present.

steps.label: Clarinet (closed–open)
steps.text: $f_n = nv/4L = n(343/2.40)$ Hz: $n = 1$ gives 143 Hz, $n = 3$ gives 429 Hz, $n = 5$ gives 715 Hz — odd integers only.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: The clarinet’s fundamental is an octave below the flute’s (143 vs 286 Hz), and its next usable mode jumps by a factor of 3 — a twelfth, not an octave.

steps.label: Why
steps.text: Two antinodes fit half-wavelengths ($L = n\lambda/2$); a node plus an antinode fit quarter-wavelengths ($L = n\lambda/4$, $n$ odd) — hence the factor-of-2 offset and the odd-only ladder.

examples.result: Flute: 286, 572, 857 Hz. Clarinet: 143, 429, 715 Hz — missing every even harmonic.

examples.title: Sources of Musical Sound: decibel check
examples.problem: A source radiates $1.0\ \text{mW}$ uniformly. Find $I$ at $r = 10\ \text{m}$ and the sound level.
examples.result: $I \approx 7.96\times 10^{-7}\ \text{W/m}^2$ ($59\ \text{dB}$).

keyTakeaways: Closed pipe end = displacement node and pressure antinode; open end = displacement antinode and pressure node.
Open–open: $f_n = nv/2L$, all harmonics. Closed–open: $f_n = nv/4L$, odd $n$ only.
Pitch comes from the surviving modes ($L$ and $v$); timbre comes from which harmonics the instrument sustains.

quiz.q: A pipe closed at one end supports which harmonics?
options: all integer multiples of the fundamental
quiz.explanation: Node at one end, antinode at the other: $L = n\lambda/4$ can be satisfied only with odd $n$.

quiz.q: The lowest frequency of a pipe open at both ends is $v/2L$. Doubling the length:
quiz.explanation: $f_1 = v/2L$ is inversely proportional to length: twice the pipe, half the pitch.

quiz.q: At the closed end of a pipe, the pressure variation is:
quiz.explanation: The wall blocks the displacement, so the air there compresses and decompresses fully: maximum $\Delta p$.

quiz.q: Opening tone holes along a flute effectively:
options: shortens the sounding length, raising the pitch
quiz.explanation: The first open hole pins a pressure node there, so the standing wave occupies only the shorter remaining column.

intro: Tune a guitar by ear and you listen for the throb: strike the string against a reference and you hear not two notes but one note pulsing — loud, soft, loud, soft. The pulsing is the interference of two waves of nearly equal frequency, and its rate measures the frequency mismatch exactly. Beats turn frequency measurement into rhythm measurement, which is how every orchestra in the world gets tuned.
objectives: Superpose two equal-amplitude waves of slightly different frequencies and describe the beat pattern
Apply $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_2 - f_1|$ and explain why loudness maxima occur at this rate
Use beats to tune: interpret slowing beats as convergence on the target frequency

concepts.statement: **When two waves of slightly different frequencies $f_1$ and $f_2$ (equal amplitude $A$) superpose, the resultant alternates between large amplitude $2A$ and zero: a fast oscillation at the average frequency whose envelope — the loudness — swells and fades.** The slow pulsing is the beat.

**The sum is** $$y = 2A\cos\!\left(2\pi\,\frac{f_1 - f_2}{2}\,t\right)\sin\!\left(2\pi\,\frac{f_1 + f_2}{2}\,t\right),$$ a carrier at the average frequency inside an envelope $2A|\cos(\pi(f_1 - f_2)t)|$. **The loudness peaks recur at the beat frequency** $$f_{\text{beat}} = |f_2 - f_1|.$$
concepts.detail: The envelope returns to full strength once per $1/|f_2-f_1|$ seconds: four beats over 4 s means the frequencies differ by 4 Hz.

concepts.statement: **Beats are audible only while $|f_2 - f_1|$ is roughly 10 Hz or less.** Beyond that the throbbing blurs into roughness, and further still the ear simply resolves two separate tones. Tuners work inside the beat zone deliberately.
concepts.detail: Piano tuners also exploit beats between harmonics of different strings — a string’s second harmonic against a reference’s fundamental — to check intervals by ear.

concepts.statement: **Solve Beats problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is sound: intensity, sources, beats and Doppler; the working equation is $I = P/4\pi r^2$, $\beta = 10\log(I/I_0)$, $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_1-f_2|$, $f' = f(v\pm v_D)/(v\mp v_S)$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (decibels and hertz) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $60\ \text{dB}$ conversation at $10^{-6}\ \text{W/m}^2$; $10\%$ Doppler shift at $30\ \text{m/s}$; $v_S,v_D < v$; $I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^2$ reference.

concepts.statement: **Beats lives at $60\ \text{dB}$ conversation at $10^{-6}\ \text{W/m}^2$; $10\%$ Doppler shift at $30\ \text{m/s}$ and the textbook model holds while $v_S,v_D < v$; $I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^2$ reference.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Beats calculation gives seconds when decibels and hertz demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $60\ \text{dB}$ conversation at $10^{-6}\ \text{W/m}^2$; $10\%$ Doppler shift at $30\ \text{m/s}$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

figures.caption: Beats from $f_1 = 6.0$ Hz and $f_2 = 7.0$ Hz (equal amplitudes $A$). Top: the two component sinusoids; bottom: their sum — a carrier at the average frequency 6.5 Hz inside the dashed envelope $\pm 2A\cos(\pi t)$. Loudness peaks at $t = 0, 1, 2$ s and dies at $t = 0.5, 1.5$ s: one beat per second, exactly $|7.0 - 6.0|$ Hz. At the silent instants the two waves are in fully destructive opposition; at the loud instants, fully constructive.

examples.title: Which way was it flat?
examples.problem: A tuning fork sounds 440 Hz. A guitar string played with it beats 4 times per second. Tightening the string very slightly makes the beats slow down. What was the string’s original frequency?

steps.label: Two candidates
steps.text: Beats of 4 Hz mean $f_{\text{string}} = 440 \pm 4$: either 444 Hz or 436 Hz — the beat count alone cannot tell sharp from flat.

steps.label: The tightening test
steps.text: Tightening raises $v = \sqrt{\tau/\mu}$ and hence raises the string’s frequency.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: The beats slowed, so the string moved toward 440 Hz — it was below and is rising: originally 436 Hz.

steps.label: Finish
steps.text: Keep tightening until the beats vanish entirely; at that point the string is exactly 440 Hz.

examples.result: The string was flat at 436 Hz; the slowing beats under tightening expose the sign that the beat count alone hides.

examples.title: Beats: decibel check
examples.problem: A source radiates $1.0\ \text{mW}$ uniformly. Find $I$ at $r = 15\ \text{m}$ and the sound level.
examples.result: $I \approx 3.54\times 10^{-7}\ \text{W/m}^2$ ($55.5\ \text{dB}$).

keyTakeaways: Nearly equal frequencies superpose into a carrier at the average frequency inside the envelope $2A|\cos(\pi(f_1-f_2)t)|$.
Loudness maxima — beats — recur at $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_2 - f_1|$.
Beats slower than roughly 10 Hz are heard as throbbing; tuning means driving the beat frequency to zero.

quiz.q: Two tones at 505 Hz and 510 Hz produce beats at:
As two nearly matched strings are brought closer in frequency, the beats:
quiz.explanation: The beat frequency is the frequency difference; perfect tuning makes it vanish.

quiz.q: Two tones at 500 Hz and 600 Hz are played together. You hear:
options: two separate tones — the difference is far beyond the beat zone
quiz.explanation: A 100 Hz difference is far beyond the roughly 10 Hz beat zone: the ear resolves two tones instead of throbbing.

quiz.q: The envelope of two beating equal-amplitude waves peaks at:
quiz.explanation: At each loud instant the two waves are momentarily in phase, doubling the amplitude to $2A$.

intro: Stand on a sidewalk as the ambulance wails past: the tone is high, high, high — then drops the instant the truck passes. Nothing about the siren changed; what changed is the motion of the source relative to the air carrying the sound, and the wavefronts it leaves behind tell the whole story. Getting the sign conventions right in the Doppler formulas is a perennial exam exercise, and the wavefront picture is the way never to get them wrong.
objectives: Explain the Doppler effect with wavefront bunching ahead of a moving source and stretching behind
Apply $f' = f(v \pm v_D)/v$ for a moving detector and $f' = fv/(v \mp v_S)$ for a moving source
Combine motions with the general formula and choose signs so that approach raises the detected frequency

concepts.statement: **When the source or the detector moves relative to the medium, the detected frequency differs from the emitted frequency.** Motion toward — by either party — raises the detected frequency; motion away lowers it.

**A detector moving at $v_D$ through still air meets wavefronts at the combined rate** $$f' = f\,\frac{v \pm v_D}{v},$$ plus for motion toward the source, minus for away. The wavelength in the air is untouched — the detector simply runs through the crests faster or slower.

**A source moving at $v_S$ crowds its wavefronts ahead and stretches them behind: the wavelength becomes $\lambda' = (v \mp v_S)/f$, and** $$f' = \frac{fv}{v \mp v_S}$$ — minus sign in the denominator when the source approaches the detector, plus when it recedes. Here the wavelength itself changes; the wave speed in the medium is still $v$.
concepts.detail: Ahead of the source each new crest starts from a nearer position, so crests stack closer together: shorter $\lambda'$, higher $f'$. Behind, they spread: longer $\lambda'$, lower $f'$.

concepts.statement: **The general formula $f' = f\,(v \pm v_D)/(v \mp v_S)$ never fails if you (i) choose signs so that approach gives $f' > f$, and (ii) measure all speeds relative to the medium — in a wind, that means the moving air’s frame.** For light the same physical idea survives, but the medium-free relativistic formula replaces it — the recession redshift of galaxies is its cosmic application.
concepts.detail: Radar speed guns, weather Doppler radar and blood-flow ultrasound all time the echoes of waves bouncing off moving targets.

concepts.statement: **Solve The Doppler Effect problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is sound: intensity, sources, beats and Doppler; the working equation is $I = P/4\pi r^2$, $\beta = 10\log(I/I_0)$, $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_1-f_2|$, $f' = f(v\pm v_D)/(v\mp v_S)$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (decibels and hertz) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $60\ \text{dB}$ conversation at $10^{-6}\ \text{W/m}^2$; $10\%$ Doppler shift at $30\ \text{m/s}$; $v_S,v_D < v$; $I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^2$ reference.

figures.caption: The Doppler effect for a source moving right at $v_S = 0.6v$. Each circle is a wavefront emitted 1 s apart, centered on the source’s position at emission (labeled 0 s, 1 s, 2 s; the source is at the labeled later position now). Ahead of the source the circles bunch — shorter wavelength $\lambda' = (v - v_S)/f$, higher detected frequency $f' = fv/(v - v_S)$; behind they stretch — $\lambda' = (v + v_S)/f$, lower frequency.
