intro: Compress a gas quickly — no time for heat — and it warms; let it expand against a piston without heat input and it cools. Adiabatic processes power diesel engines and shape the temperature profile of the atmosphere. Their governing curve, $pV^\gamma = $ constant, is derived from the first law in the masters tier below.
objectives: Apply the adiabatic relations $pV^\gamma = $ const and $TV^{\gamma-1} = $ const
Compute temperature and pressure changes for adiabatic compression or expansion
Explain why adiabats are steeper than isotherms, and why free expansion is different

concepts.statement: **A quasi-static adiabatic process has $Q = 0$, so the first law reads $$\Delta E_\text{int} = -W.$$** Compress the gas (work done on it, $W < 0$) and the internal energy — the temperature — rises; let it expand doing work and it cools.
concepts.detail: Speed or insulation buys adiabaticity: sound waves, pump strokes and rising air parcels are all effectively adiabatic because heat conduction is far slower than the process.

concepts.statement: **Along a quasi-static adiabat of an ideal gas with constant $\gamma$, $$pV^{\gamma} = \text{const},\qquad TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{const}.$$** Work done by the gas: $$W = \frac{p_iV_i - p_fV_f}{\gamma - 1} = nC_V(T_i - T_f).$$
concepts.detail: The masters tier derives $pV^\gamma$ from $nC_V\,dT = -p\,dV$ in three lines of calculus — the cleanest example in the book of a thermodynamic law emerging from the first law.

concepts.statement: **An adiabat through any point falls $\gamma$ times steeper than the isotherm through that point** (slopes $-\gamma p/V$ versus $-p/V$), because expansion along an adiabat loses both pressure and temperature. **Free expansion into a vacuum is adiabatic but not quasi-static: no piston, no work, and the ideal gas does not cool — $pV^\gamma$ does not apply.**
concepts.detail: The two processes look similar in a diagram (gas rushes into a bigger volume) but are thermodynamically different worlds: one is a controlled curve of equilibrium states, the other an irreversible jump between two equilibrium states with no quasi-static path between them.

depth.title: Deriving $pV^\gamma = $ constant — the adiabatic laws from the first law

blocks.heading: The adiabatic laws
blocks.body: Let an ideal gas with constant heat capacities undergo a **quasi-static adiabatic** process (infinitesimally slow, zero heat exchange). Then along the process curve, $$pV^{\gamma} = \text{const},\qquad TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{const},\qquad T^{\gamma}p^{1-\gamma} = \text{const},$$ where $\gamma = C_P/C_V$. Hypotheses matter: the gas must be ideal, the path quasi-static (a curve of equilibrium states), and $\gamma$ constant over the temperature range.

blocks.heading: First law with the heat tap closed
blocks.body: Write the first law for an infinitesimal step: $dE_\text{int} = dQ - p\,dV$. Adiabatic means $dQ = 0$, and since ideal-gas internal energy depends only on temperature, $dE_\text{int} = nC_V\,dT$. Therefore $$nC_V\,dT = -p\,dV.$$ The pressure is not free — the gas stays on its equation of state $pV = nRT$ throughout the quasi-static process. Substituting $p = nRT/V$: $$nC_V\,dT = -\frac{nRT}{V}\,dV.$$

blocks.heading: Separate, integrate, identify γ − 1
blocks.body: Separating variables: $$\frac{dT}{T} = -\frac{R}{C_V}\frac{dV}{V}.$$ Now $R = C_P - C_V$ (Section 19-7), so $R/C_V = C_P/C_V - 1 = \gamma - 1$. Integrating from state $i$ to state $f$: $$\ln\frac{T_f}{T_i} = -(\gamma-1)\ln\frac{V_f}{V_i},$$ that is, $$T_fV_f^{\gamma-1} = T_iV_i^{\gamma-1}.$$ To reach the pressure form, insert $T = pV/nR$ from the equation of state: $$pV^{\gamma} = (nR)\,T\,V^{\gamma-1} = \text{const},$$ since the right-hand side is a product of constants.

blocks.heading: The work formula, two ways
blocks.body: Work done by the gas is $W = \int p\,dV$ with $p = K/V^{\gamma}$ (K constant along the adiabat): $$W = K\int_{V_i}^{V_f}V^{-\gamma}\,dV = \frac{K\,V_i^{1-\gamma} - K\,V_f^{1-\gamma}}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{p_iV_i - p_fV_f}{\gamma - 1}.$$ The first law demands the same answer as $W = -\Delta E_\text{int} = nC_V(T_i - T_f)$; the two agree because $p_iV_i - p_fV_f = nR(T_i - T_f)$ and $C_V = R/(\gamma-1)$ — an exact identity following from $\gamma = C_P/C_V$ and $C_P = C_V + R$.

blocks.heading: A diesel stroke
blocks.body: Diesel engines ignite fuel without a spark by brute compression. Air ($\gamma = 1.40$) enters at $T_i = 300$ K and is squeezed to $1/16$ of its volume. Then $T_f = T_i(V_i/V_f)^{\gamma-1} = 300\times16^{0.4} = 300\times3.03 = 909$ K, and $p_f = p_i(V_i/V_f)^{\gamma} = 16^{1.4}\,p_i = 48.5\,p_i$ — near fifty atmospheres. The spray injected into 909 K (636 °C) air self-ignites; the Otto engine can match that temperature only with a spark and timed flame.

blocks.heading: Why free expansion escapes the law
blocks.body: Every step above used quasi-staticness: $W = \int p\,dV$ only makes sense when the gas has a single well-defined pressure at each instant. In free expansion the gas rushes into a vacuum — no piston, no defined intermediate pressure, $W = 0$ exactly. Yet heat is also zero, so $\Delta E_\text{int} = 0$ and the ideal gas lands at its original temperature. Same $Q = 0$, wildly different outcome: the adiabatic *curve* describes controlled equilibrium steps, while free expansion is an irreversible jump between two equilibrium points. The distinction is invisible to the first law and central to the second — it is precisely free expansion whose entropy increase (Chapter 20) cannot be undone.

intro: The first law says energy is conserved — but it smiles equally on a cup of coffee warming up or cooling down, and only one of those ever happens. Entropy is the bookkeeping that breaks the tie: a state function that isolated systems can only increase, making the second law of thermodynamics the only fundamental law of physics with a direction of time built in.
objectives: Compute entropy changes with $\Delta S = \int dQ/T$ along a reversible path
Apply the second law, $\Delta S \ge 0$ for isolated systems, to real (irreversible) processes
Evaluate $\Delta S$ for phase changes, temperature changes and heat exchange with reservoirs

concepts.statement: **When a system absorbs heat $dQ$ reversibly at Kelvin temperature $T$, its entropy changes by $$dS = \frac{dQ}{T},\qquad \Delta S = \int_i^f \frac{dQ}{T}.$$** The unit is J/K. For a reservoir — a body so large its temperature never budges — $\Delta S = Q/T$ exactly, whatever the sign of $Q$.
concepts.detail: The division by $T$ is the whole idea: a jouole of heat is more "surprising" (more entropy) when delivered to a cold body than to a hot one.

concepts.statement: **$S$ depends only on the state of the system, not on how it got there.** To compute $\Delta S$ for a messy real process, replace it in your imagination by any reversible path connecting the same endpoints and integrate $dQ/T$ along that instead.
concepts.detail: This is the same privilege internal energy enjoys in the first law — and it is why entropy can be tabulated in tables while heat and work cannot.

concepts.statement: **Isothermal phase change: $\Delta S = Lm/T$. Temperature change at constant heat capacity: $\Delta S = cm\ln(T_f/T_i)$. Heat $Q$ into a reservoir at $T$: $\Delta S = Q/T$.**
concepts.detail: Melting 1 kg of ice at 273.15 K: $\Delta S = (3.33\times10^{5})/273.15 = 1.22$ kJ/K — the latent heat enters the ledger divided by the melting temperature.

concepts.statement: **If a process occurs in a closed (isolated) system, the entropy of the system increases: $$\Delta S > 0$$ for irreversible processes, $$\Delta S = 0$$ for reversible ones. Entropy never decreases in an isolated system.**
concepts.detail: Real processes are irreversible — friction, mixing, free expansion, heat flow across a finite temperature difference — so the total entropy of the universe grows with every event that happens in it. That asymmetry, not energy conservation, is why time has a direction.

concepts.statement: **Solve Entropy problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is entropy and the Carnot bound; the working equation is $\Delta S = \int dQ_{\text{rev}}/T$, $e_{\text{Carnot}} = 1-T_L/T_H$, $S = k\ln W$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{J/K}$ and dimensionless $e$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $e_{\text{Carnot}}\sim 0.3$--$0.5$ for $T_H\sim 500\ \text{K}$; reversible for the Carnot bound; $\Delta S \ge 0$ for isolated systems.

examples.title: The entropy of melting ice
examples.problem: One kilogram of ice melts reversibly at 0 °C. What is its entropy change?

steps.label: Reversible isothermal path
steps.text: Melting at exactly 273.15 K with the surroundings at the same temperature is the reversible version of the process, so $\Delta S = Q/T$ applies directly.

steps.label: Heat absorbed
steps.text: $Q = L_F m = (333\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J/kg})(1.00\ \mathrm{kg}) = 3.33\times10^{5}$ J.

examples.result: Melting a kilogram of ice raises its entropy by about $1.22$ kJ/K — disorder gained by freeing the molecules from the crystal.

examples.title: Hot water dumped on a cold reservoir
examples.problem: One kilogram of water at 100 °C is poured into a very large 0 °C reservoir. Show that the total entropy change is positive even though the water's own entropy decreases.
examples.result: The water loses entropy while the reservoir gains more — the total rises by $+227$ J/K, so the process is allowed and, being spontaneous, irreversible.

keyTakeaways: $\Delta S = \int dQ/T$ along any reversible path between the endpoints; for reservoirs $\Delta S = Q/T$.
Second law: $\Delta S \ge 0$ for isolated systems, with equality only for reversible processes.
One system's entropy may fall — as long as some other system's rises by more.

quiz.q: A system absorbs 100 J of heat reversibly while held at a constant 200 K. Its entropy change is

increases, because it absorbs latent heat at constant T

quiz.explanation: $\Delta S = L_F m/T > 0$: heat in at fixed temperature always raises entropy.

quiz.q: In the water-and-cold-reservoir example, the water's entropy fell by 1306 J/K. Why does this not violate the second law?

The reservoir gained 1533 J/K, so the total change is +227 J/K
The internal energy also decreased, which compensates
quiz.explanation: The second law governs the isolated total: the reservoir gains more than the water loses.

quiz.q: For any process taking place in an isolated system,
options: $\Delta S \ge 0$, with equality only for a reversible process
$\Delta S < 0$ if the process is fast
$\Delta S$ can have either sign depending on the path
quiz.explanation: That is the entropy statement of the second law — the direction-finder that the first law lacks.

intro: A heat engine is any device that siphons energy from a hot reservoir, converts part of it to work, and dumps the rest into a cold reservoir — steam plants, car engines, jet turbines all share this skeleton. The second law caps how good any of them can be, and the cap belongs to Carnot's idealized reversible cycle, the efficiency yardstick no real engine beats.
objectives: Define engine efficiency $e = |W|/Q_H = 1 - |Q_C|/Q_H$ and apply the energy ledger
Describe the four strokes of the Carnot cycle and why it is reversible
Use the Carnot efficiency $e_C = 1 - T_C/T_H$ and state Carnot's theorem

concepts.statement: **A heat engine operates in a cycle: over each cycle it absorbs heat $Q_H$ from a hot reservoir, does work $W$, and ejects heat $|Q_C|$ to a cold reservoir. Energy conservation over a cycle ($\Delta E_\text{int} = 0$) gives $$Q_H = W + |Q_C|,$$ and the efficiency is $$e = \frac{W}{Q_H} = 1 - \frac{|Q_C|}{Q_H}.$$**
concepts.detail: The ejection is not an engineering flaw — it is the price the second law charges. A cycle that turned all of $Q_H$ into work would return the working gas to its start while destroying entropy, which the universe forbids.

concepts.statement: **Carnot's ideal engine runs a gas through four reversible strokes between reservoirs at $T_H$ and $T_C$: (1) isothermal expansion at $T_H$, absorbing $Q_H$; (2) adiabatic expansion, cooling to $T_C$; (3) isothermal compression at $T_C$, ejecting $|Q_C|$; (4) adiabatic compression, heating back to $T_H$.**
concepts.detail: Every step is run so gently that the gas is never more than infinitesimally out of equilibrium — which is what makes the cycle reversible: run it backward and it is a perfect refrigerator. On a $pV$ diagram it is a closed loop of two isotherms joined by two (steeper) adiabats.

concepts.statement: **For any reversible engine operating between Kelvin temperatures $T_H$ and $T_C$, $$e_C = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H}.$$** Nothing else about the engine — working substance, size, design — enters.
concepts.detail: The proof is one line of entropy bookkeeping: reversibility forces $Q_H/T_H = |Q_C|/T_C$, and substituting into $e = 1 - |Q_C|/Q_H$ gives the result. Raising the steam temperature is the whole game of power-plant engineering.

concepts.statement: **No real engine operating between two given reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same two reservoirs; all reversible engines between them are equally (Carnot) efficient.**
concepts.detail: If a better engine existed, pairing it with a Carnot refrigerator would run a composite machine that transferred heat from cold to hot with no other effect — the Clausius violation of the second law.

concepts.statement: **Solve Entropy in the Real World: Engines problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is entropy and the Carnot bound; the working equation is $\Delta S = \int dQ_{\text{rev}}/T$, $e_{\text{Carnot}} = 1-T_L/T_H$, $S = k\ln W$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{J/K}$ and dimensionless $e$) emerges naturally.

Check the answer against $e_{\text{Carnot}}\sim 0.3$--$0.5$ for $T_H\sim 500\ \text{K}$; reversible for the Carnot bound; $\Delta S \ge 0$ for isolated systems.

examples.title: A steam plant between 800 K and 300 K
examples.problem: An ideal (Carnot) engine runs between a boiler at $T_H = 800$ K and a condenser at $T_C = 300$ K. What is its efficiency, and how much work does it deliver per 1000 J of absorbed heat?

steps.label: Rejected heat
steps.text: $|Q_C| = Q_H - W = 375$ J — the unavoidable toll of the second law.

examples.result: $62.5\%$ of the heat becomes work at best; real steam plants reach about $40\%$, paying extra for irreversibility.

examples.title: From efficiency to power
examples.problem: A real engine absorbs $Q_H = 1000$ J per cycle with efficiency $e = 0.40$ and completes 50 cycles per second. What is its power output?

steps.label: Rate
steps.text: $P = W \times (\text{cycles/s}) = 400 \times 50 = 2.0\times10^{4}$ W.

steps.label: Reject rate
steps.text: It must also eject $600\times50 = 3.0\times10^{4}$ J/s — the radiator and exhaust exist to satisfy the second law.

examples.result: The engine delivers $20$ kW while dumping $30$ kW as waste heat.

keyTakeaways: Engine ledger: $Q_H = W + |Q_C|$ over each cycle, $e = W/Q_H = 1 - |Q_C|/Q_H$.
Carnot cycle = two isotherms + two adiabats, fully reversible; its area on a pV diagram is the work per cycle.
$e_C = 1 - T_C/T_H$ is the ceiling for any engine between those reservoirs (Carnot's theorem); use kelvin.

quiz.q: An engine absorbs 800 J per cycle and ejects 600 J. Its efficiency is
A Carnot engine runs between reservoirs at 500 K and 300 K. Its efficiency is
Carnot's theorem says no engine between two given reservoirs can beat the Carnot efficiency, because a better one would
options: violate the second law of thermodynamics
have to run slower than a Carnot engine
quiz.explanation: Paired with a Carnot refrigerator it would move heat cold-to-hot with no other effect — a Clausius violation. Energy conservation would survive fine.

quiz.q: Over one complete Carnot cycle, the total entropy change of gas plus reservoirs is
options: zero, because every step is reversible
positive, since the engine does work
quiz.explanation: Reversible means no net entropy production: the gas returns to its state ($\Delta S = 0$) and the two reservoirs exactly cancel.

intro: Run a heat engine backward and it becomes a refrigerator: work in, heat pumped out of a cold space into a warm one. The same second law that caps engines caps refrigerators in reverse — no refrigerator can be perfect, but surprisingly their performance figures can far exceed 100%.
objectives: Define the coefficient of performance $K = |Q_C|/W$ for refrigerators and $K_\text{hp} = |Q_H|/W$ for heat pumps
Apply the Carnot limits $K_C = T_C/(T_H - T_C)$ and $K_\text{hp} = T_H/(T_H - T_C)$
State the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius forms of the second law and their equivalence

concepts.term: A refrigerator is a reversed engine
concepts.statement: **A refrigerator extracts heat $|Q_C|$ from the cold interior by doing work $W$ on the working fluid, ejecting $|Q_H| = |Q_C| + W$ to the room. Its figure of merit is the coefficient of performance $$K = \frac{|Q_C|}{W},$$** and $K$ can be — and usually is — larger than 1.
concepts.detail: $K > 1$ is not perpetual motion: the machine does not create energy, it only relocates it. What the second law forbids is $W = 0$, i.e. heat flowing cold-to-hot unassisted.

concepts.statement: **A heat pump is the same machine judged by what it delivers indoors: $|Q_H|$ per unit of work. Since $|Q_H| = |Q_C| + W$, $$K_\text{hp} = \frac{|Q_H|}{W} = K + 1.$$**
concepts.detail: Winter economics: a heat pump with $K_\text{hp} = 4$ delivers four joules of heat per joule of electricity — three of them imported free (from the viewpoint of your bill) from the outside air.

concepts.statement: **A perfectly reversible (Carnot) refrigerator between Kelvin temperatures $T_C$ and $T_H$ achieves $$K_C = \frac{T_C}{T_H - T_C},$$** the maximum possible. Real refrigerators fall below it, badly when the temperature gap is large.
concepts.detail: A kitchen fridge ($T_C \approx 277$ K, $T_C \approx$ room 300 K) could in principle reach $K_C = 277/23 \approx 12$; a laboratory cryostat pumping from 1 K to 300 K manages at best $K_C = 1/299$, which is why liquid helium is expensive.

concepts.statement: **Kelvin–Planck: no cyclic device converts heat entirely into work — some $|Q_C|$ must always be ejected. Clausius: no process has as its sole result the transfer of heat from a colder to a hotter body.** The two statements are equivalent: violate either and, with a suitable engine or refrigerator, you can violate the other.
concepts.detail: Both are negative laws — they rule machines out. The entropy statement ($\Delta S \ge 0$) is their quantitative unification: it says exactly how much ejection is mandatory and how much pumping work is irreducible.

concepts.term: Refrigerators and Real Engines: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Refrigerators and Real Engines problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is entropy and the Carnot bound; the working equation is $\Delta S = \int dQ_{\text{rev}}/T$, $e_{\text{Carnot}} = 1-T_L/T_H$, $S = k\ln W$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{J/K}$ and dimensionless $e$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $e_{\text{Carnot}}\sim 0.3$--$0.5$ for $T_H\sim 500\ \text{K}$; reversible for the Carnot bound; $\Delta S \ge 0$ for isolated systems.

examples.title: The minimum work to freeze a tray of ice
examples.problem: How much work must a perfectly reversible refrigerator, freezing water at 273.15 K in a kitchen at 300 K, do to remove the heat of fusion from 1.00 kg of water?
examples.result: At least $32.7$ kJ of work must be bought (and $366$ kJ delivered to the kitchen) — a real ice maker needs several times more.

examples.title: A heat pump in winter
examples.problem: An ideal heat pump maintains a house at 293 K while the outdoors sits at 273 K. If it draws 1.00 kW of electrical power, how much heat does it deliver?

steps.label: Heat delivered
steps.text: $|Q_H|/t = K_\text{hp} \times P = 14.7$ kW of heating from 1.00 kW of electricity.

steps.label: Perspective
steps.text: A resistive heater would give exactly 1.00 kW; the pump wins because it imports an extra 13.7 kW from the cold — but cold — outside air.

examples.result: Up to $14.7$ kW delivered; the advantage shrinks fast on bitter days, since $K_\text{hp} \propto 1/(T_H - T_C)$.

keyTakeaways: Refrigerator: $K = |Q_C|/W$; heat pump: $K_\text{hp} = |Q_H|/W = K + 1$ — both may exceed 1.
Carnot ceilings: $K_C = T_C/(T_H - T_C)$, and $K_\text{hp} = T_H/(T_H - T_C)$; small temperature gaps are cheap to bridge.
Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements are equivalent faces of the second law.

quiz.q: The coefficient of performance $K$ of a refrigerator is defined as
quiz.explanation: Benefit over cost: cold extracted per joule of work purchased. It routinely exceeds 1.

quiz.q: An ideal refrigerator keeps its interior at 277 K in a 300 K room. Its Carnot coefficient of performance is about
The Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law forbids
options: heat flowing from hot to cold
a cyclic engine that converts absorbed heat entirely into work
quiz.explanation: The "single-reservoir engine" is forbidden; perfect heat-to-work conversion would shrink the entropy of the universe.

quiz.q: For the same machine running as a heat pump, $K_\text{hp} = K + 1$ because
options: the numerator changes from $|Q_C|$ to $|Q_H| = |Q_C| + W$ while the cost $W$ is the same
the work doubles in heating mode
the COP is defined with Fahrenheit temperatures
quiz.explanation: Same ledger, different output side: adding the purchased work $W$ to the heat moved raises the numerator by exactly one $W$.

intro: Why does entropy always grow? Boltzmann's answer: because the overwhelming majority of the microscopic arrangements consistent with the macroscopic facts are arrangements we would call disordered. Entropy is then just a count — and the second law becomes a statement of probability, near-certainty only because molecules come in moles.
objectives: Define microstates, macrostates and multiplicity $\Omega$
Compute entropy from Boltzmann's formula $S = k_B\ln\Omega$ and changes from $\Delta S = k_B\ln(\Omega_f/\Omega_i)$
Explain why macroscopic violations of the second law are effectively impossible

concepts.statement: **A microstate is one complete specification of the system at the molecular level (which molecule is where, with which velocity). A macrostate is the coarse description we actually observe. The multiplicity $\Omega$ is the number of microstates consistent with a given macrostate.**
concepts.detail: Six atoms split between two chambers of a box: "3 on the left, 3 on the right" is one macrostate with $\Omega = \binom{6}{3} = 20$ microstates; "all on the left" has $\Omega = 1$. Spread-out macrostates win the census by astronomical margins once $N \sim N_A$.

concepts.statement: **The entropy of a macrostate is $$S = k_B\ln\Omega,$$ with $k_B$ the Boltzmann constant.** The logarithm makes entropies additive for independent systems (multiplicities multiply) and ties the microscopic count to the macroscopic $dQ/T$ definition of Section 20-1 — they are the same entropy.
concepts.detail: The formula is carved on Boltzmann's tombstone in Vienna. It converts the second law from a mystery into an audit: isolated systems evolve toward the macrostates with the most microstates because those are the ones you almost always find when you re-examine the dice.

concepts.statement: **For any process, $$\Delta S = k_B\ln\frac{\Omega_f}{\Omega_i}.$$** Doubling the accessible volume of an ideal gas doubles each molecule's options, so $\Omega_f/\Omega_i = 2^N$ and $\Delta S = Nk_B\ln 2 = nR\ln 2$ — the free-expansion result, recovered by pure counting.
concepts.detail: This is the bridge formula: it evaluates the entropy of irreversible endpoints (like free expansion) that no reversible intuition easily reaches.

concepts.statement: **Nothing forbids a macroscopic system from sliding toward lower entropy — it is just mind-bendingly improbable.** For a mole of gas to spontaneously compress into half its volume, every one of $\sim10^{23}$ molecules must choose the same half: probability $2^{-N_A} \sim 10^{-180,000,000,000,000,000,000,000}$.
concepts.detail: Randomness never "wants" anything; it merely visits macrostates in proportion to their multiplicity, and the even-spread macrostates outnumber the ordered ones so overwhelmingly that the visit is for all practical purposes permanent. Irreversibility is big-number certainty, not mechanical law.

concepts.term: A Statistical View of Entropy: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve A Statistical View of Entropy problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is entropy and the Carnot bound; the working equation is $\Delta S = \int dQ_{\text{rev}}/T$, $e_{\text{Carnot}} = 1-T_L/T_H$, $S = k\ln W$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{J/K}$ and dimensionless $e$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $e_{\text{Carnot}}\sim 0.3$--$0.5$ for $T_H\sim 500\ \text{K}$; reversible for the Carnot bound; $\Delta S \ge 0$ for isolated systems.

figures.caption: Multiplicity $\Omega$ of each macrostate for six atoms split between two chambers of a box ($2^6 = 64$ microstates total). The even 3–3 split owns 20 of them — 31% — while the fully ordered 6–0 split owns exactly 1. As $N$ grows toward $N_A$, the central bin dwarfs all others and the second law becomes a statistical certainty.

examples.title: Free expansion by counting
examples.problem: One mole of ideal gas doubles its volume freely (into an evacuated, insulated chamber). What is $\Delta S$, and what is the probability that all the molecules spontaneously crowd back into the original half?

steps.label: Multiplicity ratio
steps.text: Each molecule gains a factor of 2 in accessible positions, so $\Omega_f/\Omega_i = 2^N = 2^{N_A}$.

steps.label: The return probability
steps.text: $P = 2^{-N_A} = 10^{-N_A\log 2} = 10^{-1.8\times10^{23}}$ — a decimal point followed by $1.8\times10^{23}$ zeros.

examples.result: $\Delta S = +5.76$ J/K — exactly what $dQ/T$ bookkeeping gives for the reversible path — and the un-expansion, though not impossible, is the most impossible number in physics.

examples.title: How impossible is "all heads"?
examples.problem: A fair coin is flipped 100 times. Compare the all-heads outcome with the roughly-even outcomes, and decide whether you would ever expect to see it.

steps.label: Probability
steps.text: One specific sequence in $2^{100}$ equally likely ones: $P = 2^{-100} = 7.9\times10^{-31}$.

steps.label: Time scale
steps.text: Flipping a billion times per second for the age of the universe ($4.4\times10^{17}$ s) executes $4.4\times10^{26}$ flips — giving a cumulative chance of $4.4\times10^{26}\times7.9\times10^{-31} \approx 3\times10^{-4}$.

steps.label: Scale to molecules
steps.text: Now replace 100 coins with $10^{23}$ molecules: the exponent grows by 21 orders of magnitude, and the probability becomes the $10^{-1.8\times10^{23}}$ of the previous example.

examples.result: You would need roughly 3000 universe-lifetimes of billion-per-second flipping to see 100 heads once — and a mole of coins would never, ever show all heads.

keyTakeaways: Microstate vs macrostate: $\Omega$ counts the microstates behind one macrostate; $S = k_B\ln\Omega$.
$\Delta S = k_B\ln(\Omega_f/\Omega_i)$; free expansion gives $nR\ln 2$ by pure counting.
The second law is statistics: violations have probabilities like $2^{-N_A}$ — not forbidden, just unseeable.

quiz.q: If the multiplicity of a system doubles, $\Omega_f/\Omega_i = 2$, the entropy change is
quiz.explanation: $\Delta S = k_B\ln(\Omega_f/\Omega_i) = k_B\ln2$.

quiz.q: In the free expansion of an ideal gas, $Q = 0$ yet $\Delta S > 0$. This is consistent because
options: entropy is determined by the multiplicity of the endpoints, and $dQ/T$ only computes it along reversible paths
quiz.explanation: Doubling the volume doubles each molecule's options: $\Delta S = nR\ln2$ by counting, no heat required.

quiz.q: The equilibrium macrostate of an isolated collection of atoms is the one
quiz.explanation: Random reshuffling visits macrostates in proportion to their multiplicity, so the widest bin wins — and $S = k_B\ln\Omega$ is maximal.

quiz.q: Macroscopic violations of the second law (entropy decreasing in an isolated system) are never observed because
options: they are mechanically forbidden by Newton's laws
their probabilities scale like $2^{-N_A}$, which is indistinguishable from zero
the universe is not actually isolated
quiz.explanation: Every molecular trajectory exists; it is the counting — $10^{23}$ coins — that makes the ordered outcome unseeable in any lifetime of the universe.

intro: In 1785 Charles-Augustin de Coulomb, with the torsion balance he had invented for measuring feeble forces, established the law that turned electrostatics from a parlor of rubbed amber and pith balls into a quantitative science: the electric force between two charged particles is proportional to each charge and falls off as the square of their separation. It is the same inverse-square form Newton had postulated for gravity a century earlier. This section states the law precisely, writes it as a vector equation, checks its size against gravity, and uses superposition to handle more than two charges.
objectives: State Coulomb's law in scalar and vector form and evaluate forces with $k = 1/4\pi\varepsilon_0 = 8.99\times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2/C^2}$
Apply superposition to find the net electric force on one charge due to several others
Explain why charged spherical conductors act on external charges as point charges, and compare electric and gravitational forces

concepts.statement: **The electric force between two charged particles is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.** For point charges (or uniformly charged spheres) a distance $r$ apart, center to center, $$F = k\,\frac{|q_1||q_2|}{r^2},\qquad k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 8.99\times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2/C^2},$$ with charge measured in coulombs. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
concepts.detail: The law holds for charged particles at rest (electrostatics). HRW writes the vector form on particle 1 from particle 2 as $\vec F_{21} = k\,q_2 q_1\,\hat r_{21}/r^2$, where the unit vector $\hat r_{21}$ points along the line joining the two charges, from the charge that acts toward the charge acted upon; the sign of the product $q_2 q_1$ then automatically gives the correct sense (push for like, pull for unlike).

concepts.statement: **The two charges exert equal and opposite forces on each other, no matter how unequal the charges are.** $\vec F_{21} = -\vec F_{12}$: a tiny charge and a huge charge pull on each other with exactly the same magnitude $k|q_1||q_2|/r^2$.
concepts.detail: This is the electrical twin of the third law you used for gravity and contact forces, and it is the reason a system of charges cannot accelerate its own center of mass.

concepts.statement: **A charged spherical conductor (or a uniform spherical shell of charge) acts on external charges exactly as if all its charge were concentrated at its center.** Coulomb measured this with his balance and it is proved in Chapter 23 with Gauss’ law — the electric shell theorem.
concepts.detail: For non-spherical or non-uniform bodies the law still holds for each tiny charge element, and the total force follows by vector superposition.

concepts.statement: **Both fundamental forces are inverse-square, but their strengths differ by almost forty orders of magnitude.** For the proton–electron pair in hydrogen, $F_e/F_g \approx 2.3\times 10^{39}$. Charge comes in two signs (so matter can be neutral); mass comes in one sign (so gravity always attracts and never cancels).

**Solve Coulomb's Law problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Coulomb's law with quantized, conserved charge; the working equation is $F = k|q_1q_2|/r^2$, $k = 8.99\times 10^9\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$, $e = 1.60\times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (coulombs and newtons) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $F\sim 1\ \text{N}$ for $\mu\text{C}$ at cm; $1\ \text{C} \approx 6\times 10^{18}e$; point charges at rest; $q = ne$.

figures.caption: Coulomb's law as a vector pair. Here the charges have unlike signs, so each particle is pulled toward the other along the line joining them, with equal magnitudes $F = k|q_1||q_2|/r^2$. Reverse either sign and both arrows flip outward — repulsion.

examples.title: Electron and proton in hydrogen: electric vs gravitational force
examples.problem: In the Bohr model the electron orbits the proton at radius $r = 5.29\times 10^{-11}$ m. Compare the electric attraction $F_e$ with the gravitational attraction $F_g$ between the two particles ($m_e = 9.11\times 10^{-31}$ kg, $m_p = 1.673\times 10^{-27}$ kg).

steps.label: Charges
steps.text: Each carries magnitude $e = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ C, so $|q_1||q_2| = e^2 = 2.566\times 10^{-38}\ \mathrm{C^2}$.

examples.result: The electric force is about $8.2\times 10^{-8}$ N, some $10^{39}$ times gravity — in atoms, gravity is utterly negligible.

examples.title: Superposition: three charges on a line
examples.problem: Charge $q_A = +3.0\ \mu$C sits at $x = 0$, $q_B = +5.0\ \mu$C at $x = 0.40$ m, and $q_C = -2.0\ \mu$C at $x = 0.80$ m. Find the net force on $q_C$.

steps.label: Force from A
steps.text: The charges have opposite signs, so $q_C$ is pulled toward A (leftward): $F_{CA} = k|q_C||q_A|/r^2 = (8.99\times 10^{9})(2.0\times 10^{-6})(3.0\times 10^{-6})/(0.80)^2 = 8.4\times 10^{-2}$ N.

steps.label: Force from B
steps.text: Opposite signs again, pull toward B (leftward): $F_{CB} = (8.99\times 10^{9})(2.0\times 10^{-6})(5.0\times 10^{-6})/(0.40)^2 = 0.56$ N.

steps.label: Vector sum
steps.text: Both forces point in the $-x$ direction, so they add: $F_\text{net} = 0.084 + 0.56 = 0.65$ N directed toward $-x$.

examples.result: The net force on $q_C$ is about 0.65 N toward the two positive charges — superposition means compute each pairwise force separately, then add vectors.

keyTakeaways: $F = k|q_1||q_2|/r^2$ with $k = 1/4\pi\varepsilon_0 = 8.99\times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2/C^2}$; the forces on the two charges are equal, opposite, and directed along the line joining them.
The sign of the product $q_1q_2$ encodes the physics: positive means repulsion, negative means attraction.
Charged spheres behave as point charges for external points, and the electric force between elementary charges outruns gravity by a factor of about $10^{39}$.

quiz.q: Two point charges exert a force of magnitude $F$ on each other at separation $d$. If the separation grows to $3d$, the new magnitude is:
quiz.explanation: The force scales as $1/r^2$; tripling $r$ divides the force by $3^2 = 9$.

quiz.q: Charges $+q$ and $-3q$ sit a distance $d$ apart. Compare the magnitudes of the two forces:
options: The force on $-3q$ is three times larger
The force on $+q$ is three times larger
It depends on the masses of the charges
quiz.explanation: Coulomb's law is symmetric in the two charges, and the pair obeys Newton's third law: each feels the same magnitude $3kq^2/d^2$.

quiz.q: In SI units the Coulomb constant $k$ equals:
quiz.explanation: By convention $k = 1/4\pi\varepsilon_0 = 8.99\times 10^{9}$ N·m²/C².

quiz.q: A negative charge sits to the right of a positive charge. The direction of the force on the negative charge is:
options: Perpendicular to the line joining them
quiz.explanation: Unlike charges attract: the force on each points along the line toward the other charge.

intro: Millikan's oil-drop experiment (1909–1913) weighed tiny charges one by one and found something remarkable: every charge he measured, however produced, was an integer multiple of one elementary unit. Charge is not a continuous fluid that can be shaved arbitrarily fine; it comes in identical packets. This section states quantization, counts electrons in macroscopic charges, and asks what quarks do to the story.
objectives: State the quantization of charge, $q = ne$ with $n$ an integer and $e = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ C
Convert between a net charge and a number of excess or missing electrons
Explain what Millikan measured and why free quarks do not violate quantization in units of $e$

concepts.statement: **Electric charge is quantized: every observable free charge is an integer multiple of the elementary charge** $$e = 1.602176634\times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C},$$ an exact value since the 2019 SI revision fixed the coulomb through it. A body with $n$ excess electrons carries $q = -ne$.

**Every droplet’s charge was an integer multiple of one smallest charge.** Balancing electric force against gravity for thousands of drops, Millikan found charges like $4.8\times 10^{-19}$ C, $6.4\times 10^{-19}$ C, $1.6\times 10^{-19}$ C — never $2.1\times 10^{-19}$ C — the fingerprint of a smallest unit.

**Quarks carry $\pm e/3$ or $\pm 2e/3$, yet they are never seen free.** Confinement binds quarks into protons, neutrons and mesons whose net charges are integer multiples of $e$, so all isolated particles still obey $q = ne$.
concepts.detail: Fractional charge is real inside hadrons — it just cannot be brought to your lab bench as a separate object.

concepts.statement: **To convert charge to particles, divide by $e$.** A net charge $q$ corresponds to $n = |q|/e$ excess electrons (negative $q$) or missing electrons (positive $q$); $1.00\ \mathrm{C} = 6.24\times 10^{18}$ elementary charges.

**Solve Charge Is Quantized problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Coulomb's law with quantized, conserved charge; the working equation is $F = k|q_1q_2|/r^2$, $k = 8.99\times 10^9\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$, $e = 1.60\times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (coulombs and newtons) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $F\sim 1\ \text{N}$ for $\mu\text{C}$ at cm; $1\ \text{C} \approx 6\times 10^{18}e$; point charges at rest; $q = ne$.

examples.title: How many electrons are missing?
examples.problem: A metal sphere carries a net charge of $+6.4\ \mu$C. How many electrons are missing, and what fraction of the sphere's electrons is that?

steps.label: Count the units
steps.text: Positive net charge means electrons were removed: $n = q/e = (6.4\times 10^{-6})/(1.602\times 10^{-19}) = 4.0\times 10^{13}$ missing electrons.

steps.label: Compare with the supply
steps.text: A 1 g copper sphere holds about $2.6\times 10^{24}$ electrons (about $9\times 10^{21}$ atoms times 29 electrons each).

steps.label: Fraction
steps.text: The deficit is $4.0\times 10^{13}/2.6\times 10^{24} \approx 1.5\times 10^{-11}$ — about one electron missing per hundred billion.

examples.result: $4.0\times 10^{13}$ electrons are missing — an utterly negligible fraction of the total, which is why matter stays essentially neutral even when charged enough to shock you.

examples.title: Charge Is Quantized: Coulomb numbers
examples.problem: Two $3\ \mu\text{C}$ charges sit $10\ \text{cm}$ apart. Find the repulsion.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $F \approx 8.09\ \text{N}$.

examples.result: $F \approx 8.09\ \text{N}$ repulsive.

keyTakeaways: Charge is quantized: $q = \pm ne$ with $e = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ C, now an exact SI value.
Macroscopic charges involve enormous numbers of elementary charges; $-1.0\ \mu$C is $6.2\times 10^{12}$ excess electrons.
Quarks have fractional charge but are confined, so every isolated particle still has a charge that is an integer multiple of $e$.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an impossible net charge for an isolated particle?
quiz.explanation: Divide by $e = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ C: the first, second and fourth give $n = 1, -2, 3$, but $2.5/1.602 \approx 1.56$ is not an integer.

quiz.q: A charge of $-1.0\ \mu$C corresponds to how many excess electrons?
Free quarks would carry charges like $e/3$, yet no free particle has ever shown a charge smaller than $e$ in magnitude. Why?
options: Quarks are too small to measure
Confinement — quarks are never observed in isolation
Quarks neutralize each other by exchanging photons
The value of $e$ is defined only for leptons
quiz.explanation: The strong force confines quarks into hadrons; every hadron that can be isolated has a net charge of $ne$ with $n$ an integer.

intro: If charge is quantized, it is also conserved: no process anywhere in physics — chemical, nuclear, or particle-level — has ever changed the net charge of an isolated system. Rubbing, touching and inducing merely move packets of charge around. This section states the conservation law, tracks charge through pair production and electron transfer, and applies it to two conductors that share charge.
objectives: State conservation of charge and apply it to isolated systems
Track charge transfer in rubbing, contact and induction processes
Use charge conservation together with the equal-sharing rule for identical conductors

concepts.statement: **The net charge of an isolated system never changes.** Charge can be transferred from one part of the system to another, or created/destroyed in particle–antiparticle pairs whose total is zero, but the algebraic sum $(+\text{s}) + (-\text{s})$ stays exactly constant in every known process.

**A gamma ray can turn into an electron and a positron ($\gamma \to e^- + e^+$), and matter can vanish into light — but the charge books stay balanced.** The pair carries net charge $-e + e = 0$, exactly the photon’s charge.
concepts.detail: Conservation of charge is more restrictive than conservation of mass or energy bookkeeping alone: it forbids reactions like $\gamma \to e^- + e^-$ even though energy could be arranged.

concepts.statement: **Rubbing or touching does not create charge — it moves electrons.** Glass rubbed with silk becomes positive because electrons leave the glass for the silk; the two bodies acquire equal and opposite charges whose sum is zero.
concepts.detail: Only the electrons migrate; the far heavier positive ions stay put. That asymmetry is why "positive charge flowing" is always a bookkeeping fiction for missing electrons.

concepts.statement: **Two identical conducting spheres that touch end up with equal charges**: each carries half the algebraic total of the pair. This follows from symmetry — nothing distinguishes one sphere from the other.

**Solve Charge Is Conserved problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Coulomb's law with quantized, conserved charge; the working equation is $F = k|q_1q_2|/r^2$, $k = 8.99\times 10^9\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$, $e = 1.60\times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (coulombs and newtons) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $F\sim 1\ \text{N}$ for $\mu\text{C}$ at cm; $1\ \text{C} \approx 6\times 10^{18}e$; point charges at rest; $q = ne$.

examples.title: Two identical spheres share charge
examples.problem: Identical conducting spheres carry $q_A = +8.0\ \mu$C and $q_B = -2.0\ \mu$C. They are touched together and then separated to a distance of $r = 10$ cm. What force does each now exert on the other?

steps.label: Conserve, then share
steps.text: The total charge is $+8.0\ \mu\mathrm{C} + (-2.0\ \mu\mathrm{C}) = +6.0\ \mu$C; after contact each identical sphere keeps half: $+3.0\ \mu$C.

examples.result: Each sphere feels a repulsive force of about 8.1 N — same sign now, so they push apart; the force has flipped from attractive to repulsive through the sharing.

examples.title: Charge Is Conserved: Coulomb numbers
examples.problem: Two $1\ \mu\text{C}$ charges sit $12.5\ \text{cm}$ apart. Find the repulsion.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $F \approx 0.575\ \text{N}$.

examples.result: $F \approx 0.575\ \text{N}$ repulsive.

keyTakeaways: The net charge of an isolated system is exactly conserved, in classical physics and in all particle reactions.
Charging processes transfer whole electrons; the donor and receiver acquire equal and opposite charges.
Identical conductors in contact share the total algebraic charge equally — use that, then reapply Coulomb’s law.

quiz.q: A rubber balloon rubbed on wool acquires a negative charge. What happened?
options: Protons moved from wool to balloon
Electrons moved from wool to balloon
Electrons moved from balloon to wool
Negative charge was created on the balloon
quiz.explanation: Only electrons are mobile; wool loses electrons (becoming positive) as the balloon gains them — the pair’s net charge stays zero.

quiz.q: A single gamma-ray photon turns into an electron and a positron ($\gamma \to e^- + e^+$). Conservation of charge says:
options: This is forbidden — charge would be created
It is allowed: the net charge is zero before and after
It requires the photon to carry charge $-e$
It only happens near a nucleus because charge is not conserved there
quiz.explanation: The photon has charge 0 and the pair has $-e + e = 0$; the books balance. (A nearby nucleus takes momentum, not charge.)

quiz.q: Two neutral, isolated, identical conductors are connected long enough for $2.0\times 10^{13}$ electrons to move from A to B. The final charges are:
quiz.explanation: A loses $2.0\times 10^{13}$ electrons, so $q_A = +ne = +(2.0\times 10^{13})(1.602\times 10^{-19}) = +3.2\ \mu$C, and B gains the same electrons with the opposite sign; the total remains zero.

intro: Action at a distance troubled Faraday, and his answer was one of the great ideas of physics: a charge does not tug on distant charges directly — it fills the surrounding space with an electric field, and that field pushes whatever charge happens to be there. The field is defined operationally by the force on a small positive test charge, it can be mapped with field lines, and it is the object Chapter 23 and all of electromagnetism are built on.
objectives: Define the electric field as force per unit test charge, $\vec E = \vec F/q_0$, with units N/C
State the four rules for electric field lines and read both direction and relative magnitude from a field-line picture
Explain why the test charge must be small, and why superposition applies to fields

concepts.statement: **The electric field at a point is the electric force per unit positive charge placed there:** $$\vec E = \frac{\vec F}{q_0},$$ measured in N/C. The test charge $q_0$ must be tiny so it does not disturb the charges that create the field; in the limit $q_0 \to 0$ the field is a property of the point in space, with or without any charge present.

**A field line is a curve whose tangent at every point gives the direction of $\vec E$ there.** Four rules: (1) lines start on positive charge and end on negative charge (or run off to infinity); (2) the tangent to a line gives the direction of $\vec E$; (3) lines never cross (a point has one field direction); (4) the density of lines is proportional to the magnitude of $\vec E$ — where lines crowd, the field is strong.

**The field is the physical intermediary, not a bookkeeping device.** Charge $q_1$ modifies the state of space around it; charge $q_2$ responds to the field at its own location. This localization of cause and effect becomes indispensable once charges move and waves propagate.

**Fields add vectorially.** If several charges are present, each contributes its own $\vec E$ at every point as if the others were absent, and the net field is the vector sum. Field-line pictures respect this automatically: lines of the total field never cross.

**Solve The Electric Field problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is the electric field and dipoles; the working equation is $\vec E = \vec F/q_0$, $E = kq/r^2$, $\vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E$, $U = -\vec p\cdot\vec E$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N/C}$ ($\text{V/m}$)) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $E\sim 10^3$--$10^6\ \text{N/C}$ in textbook setups; small test charge; far-field dipole $1/r^3$ only for $z\gg d$.

examples.title: Reading a field specification
examples.problem: At a certain point the electric field is uniform with magnitude $E = 100$ N/C directed east. Find the force on (a) a $+3.0\ \mu$C charge and (b) an electron placed at that point.

steps.label: Positive charge
steps.text: $\vec F = q\vec E$: magnitude $F = (3.0\times 10^{-6})(100) = 3.0\times 10^{-4}$ N, directed east (parallel to $\vec E$).

steps.label: Direction
steps.text: The electron is negative, so the force is antiparallel to the field: $1.6\times 10^{-17}$ N west.

examples.result: $3.0\times 10^{-4}$ N east for the positive charge; $1.6\times 10^{-17}$ N west for the electron — same field, opposite forces.

examples.title: The Electric Field: point-charge field check
examples.problem: Find $E = kq/r^2$ at $15\ \text{cm}$ from a $4\ \mu\text{C}$ point charge.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $E \approx 1.60\times 10^{+6}\ \text{N/C}$ radially outward.

examples.result: $E \approx 1.60\times 10^{+6}\ \text{N/C}$.

keyTakeaways: $\vec E = \vec F/q_0$ defines the field at a point independently of whether a charge is actually there; units are N/C.
Field-line tangents give directions, line density gives magnitude, and the lines begin/end on charges.
Net field = vector sum of the fields of all charges present.

quiz.q: The direction of $\vec E$ at a point is defined as the direction of the force on:
quiz.explanation: By convention the field direction is that of the force on a positive test charge; negative charges feel the opposite force.

quiz.q: Field lines can never cross because:
options: the field has a unique direction at each point
crossing lines would mean infinite charge
quiz.explanation: At an intersection the tangent — and hence $\vec E$ — would have two directions at once, which is impossible.

quiz.q: Where field lines are drawn more densely:
quiz.explanation: Rule 4 of field-line pictures: density is proportional to field magnitude.

quiz.q: A charge placed at a point where $\vec E = 0$ must have:
options: zero force and zero potential energy
zero force; its potential energy depends on $V$ there
zero force only if it is positive
a nonzero force along the field line
quiz.explanation: Force needs $\vec E$, but potential energy depends on the scalar potential $V$ — a point of zero field can sit at nonzero potential.

intro: A single charged particle is the simplest possible source of field, and its field — radial, inverse-square, pointing outward for positive charge — is the building block from which every other field in this book is assembled by superposition. This section writes the point-charge field, fixes the direction conventions for both signs of source charge, and finds the points where two fields cancel.
objectives: Write and evaluate the field of a point charge, $E = kq/r^2$ radially
Combine two or more point-charge fields as vectors, including locating null points
Recognize that the field of a source charge exists independently of any test charge

concepts.statement: **A particle of charge $q$ produces at distance $r$ the field** $$\vec E = k\,\frac{q}{r^2}\,\hat r,$$ where $\hat r$ points radially away from the charge. For $q > 0$ the field points outward; for $q < 0$ the same formula holds and the minus sign pulls the field inward.
concepts.detail: Dividing Coulomb’s law $\vec F = q_0\vec E$ by the test charge gives this immediately — the field is the force per unit charge, computed once for all future probes.

concepts.statement: **Doubling the distance from a point charge cuts the field to one quarter.** The field spreads over spheres of area $4\pi r^2$, and the same flux divides over ever-larger shells — the geometric root of the inverse-square law.

**The net field of several point charges is the vector sum of the individual fields.** Compute each $\vec E_i$ with its own distance and direction, then add components — never add magnitudes blindly, because fields in opposite directions cancel.
**A charge’s field permeates all space whether or not anything is there to feel it.** The test charge is a measuring device, not a participant: remove it and the field at the point remains.

concepts.term: The Electric Field Due to a Charged Particle: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve The Electric Field Due to a Charged Particle problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is the electric field and dipoles; the working equation is $\vec E = \vec F/q_0$, $E = kq/r^2$, $\vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E$, $U = -\vec p\cdot\vec E$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N/C}$ ($\text{V/m}$)) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $E\sim 10^3$--$10^6\ \text{N/C}$ in textbook setups; small test charge; far-field dipole $1/r^3$ only for $z\gg d$.

examples.title: The field inside the hydrogen atom
examples.problem: Find the magnitude of the electric field produced by the proton at the orbit radius of the electron, $r = 5.29\times 10^{-11}$ m.
examples.result: $E = 5.1\times 10^{11}$ N/C, directed radially away from the proton — an enormous field by laboratory standards, produced by a single elementary charge at atomic distance.

examples.title: Where the field cancels
examples.problem: Charges $q_1 = +2.0\ \mu$C sit at $x = 0$ and $q_2 = +8.0\ \mu$C at $x = 6.0$ m. Where on the $x$ axis is the net electric field zero?

steps.label: Locate the region
steps.text: Between the charges the two fields are oppositely directed (away from each positive charge), so cancellation is possible there; outside the segment both point the same way.

examples.result: The null point is $x = 2.0$ m from the smaller charge — always closer to the weaker source.

keyTakeaways: $\vec E = kq\hat r/r^2$; one sign rule covers both charges: the field points away from positive sources and toward negative ones.
Multiple-charge fields add as vectors; null points lie between like charges, nearer the smaller charge.
The proton in hydrogen creates a field of $5.1\times 10^{11}$ N/C at the electron’s orbit.

quiz.q: The field of a negative point charge at distance $r$ is:
options: of magnitude $kq/r^2$, pointing away from the charge
of magnitude $kq/r^2$, pointing toward the charge
quiz.explanation: The magnitude formula uses $|q|$; for negative sources the field points radially inward.

quiz.q: At twice the distance from a positive point charge, the field magnitude is:
quiz.explanation: The field spreads over $4\pi r^2$: doubling $r$ multiplies the area by 4 and divides $E$ by 4.

quiz.q: With $+2.0\ \mu$C at $x = 0$ and $+8.0\ \mu$C at $x = 6.0$ m, the net field is zero at:
quiz.explanation: Equal magnitudes require $2/x^2 = 8/(6-x)^2$, giving $x = 2.0$ m, nearer the smaller charge.

quiz.q: A point charge produces a field at a point in empty space. The field at that point:
options: exists only when a test charge is placed there
exists whether or not a test charge is present
exists only if the source charge is positive
is always canceled by the test charge’s own field
quiz.explanation: The test charge merely samples the field; the field itself is a property of the point due to the source charge.

intro: Two equal and opposite charges separated by a fixed distance form the electric dipole — the simplest electrically neutral object, and the workhorse model for molecules. Because the two charges nearly cancel, the dipole’s far field falls off one power of $r$ faster than a point charge’s. HRW derives the field on the dipole axis and states the result on the perpendicular bisector; both are inverse-cube in $p/r^3$.
objectives: Define the electric dipole and its moment $\vec p = q\vec d$ (directed from $-$ to $+$)
Derive and use the far-field results on the axis, $E = 2kp/r^3$, and on the bisector, $E = kp/r^3$ antiparallel to $\vec p$
Explain why neutral systems produce fields that fall faster than $1/r^2$

concepts.statement: **An electric dipole is a pair of charges $+q$ and $-q$ separated by distance $d$.** Its **dipole moment** is $$\vec p = q\vec d,$$ a vector of magnitude $qd$ pointing from the negative charge to the positive one. Water ($p = 6.2\times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\cdot m}$) and HCl are permanent dipoles.

concepts.term: Field on the dipole axis (far away)
concepts.statement: **At a point on the dipole axis a distance $r \gg d$ from the center, the field points along $\vec p$ with magnitude** $$E = \frac{1}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{p}{r^3} = \frac{2kp}{r^3}.$$ The far charge is subtracted from the near one and the difference is of order $d/r$ times either field.
concepts.detail: Exact derivation: the point is $r - d/2$ from $+q$ and $r + d/2$ from $-q$; subtracting the two inverse-squares and expanding to first order in $d/r$ gives $2kqd/r^3$.

concepts.statement: **At a point on the bisector of the dipole, far from it, the field is opposite to $\vec p$ with half the axial magnitude:** $$\vec E = -\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\vec p}{r^3}.$$ On the bisector both charges push/pull at the same distance, and their components along $\vec p$ add while the perpendicular ones cancel.

**Neutral systems cancel their leading $1/r^2$ fields.** What survives at large distance is the dipole $1/r^3$ term — this is why distant neutral matter (your heart’s electric signals, molecules) communicates so feebly, and why higher multipoles matter only nearby.

concepts.term: The Electric Field Due to a Dipole: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve The Electric Field Due to a Dipole problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is the electric field and dipoles; the working equation is $\vec E = \vec F/q_0$, $E = kq/r^2$, $\vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E$, $U = -\vec p\cdot\vec E$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{N/C}$ ($\text{V/m}$)) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $E\sim 10^3$--$10^6\ \text{N/C}$ in textbook setups; small test charge; far-field dipole $1/r^3$ only for $z\gg d$.

figures.caption: Field lines of an electric dipole. Every line leaves the positive charge and ends on the negative one, so the pattern is symmetric about both the dipole axis and the perpendicular bisector. On the axis (between the charges) $\vec E$ points from $+$ to $-$, along $\vec p$; on the bisector it points opposite $\vec p$ — both far-field results of this section.
