examples.title: Field of a ring, differentiated
examples.problem: A ring of radius $R = 3.0$ cm carries $q = +2.0\ \mu$C. Use the ring potential to find $E_z$ on the axis at $z = 4.0$ cm.

steps.label: Differentiate
steps.text: $E_z = -dV/dz = kq z\,(z^2+R^2)^{-3/2}$ — the Chapter 22 ring-field formula, for free.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.text: $E_z = 5.8\times 10^{6}$ N/C, pointing away from the ring.

examples.result: $E_z = 5.8\times 10^{6}$ N/C — one derivative replaces the vector integration of Chapter 22.

examples.title: Calculating the Field from the Potential: volt check
examples.problem: Find $V = kq/r$ at $1\ \text{m}$ from $1\ \mu\text{C}$ (zero at infinity).

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $V \approx 8990\ \text{V}$.

examples.result: $V \approx 8990\ \text{V}$.

keyTakeaways: $E_s = -\partial V/\partial s$ in every direction; the full statement is $\vec E = -\nabla V$.
On symmetry axes a single derivative $E_z = -dV/dz$ recovers the whole axial field.
Constant $V$ region means $\vec E = 0$; the minus sign sends fields from high to low potential.

quiz.q: The electric field at any point points:
quiz.explanation: $\vec E = -\nabla V$: the field is the downhill direction of the potential landscape.

quiz.q: In a region the potential is $V = 5x^2$ (volts, with $x$ in meters). At $x = 2.0$ m, $E_x$ equals:
If $V$ is constant throughout a region of space, then there:
options: is no electric field in that region
quiz.explanation: Zero slope everywhere means $\vec E = -\nabla V = 0$; charges may still sit outside the region.

quiz.q: V/m and N/C are:
options: units of potential and flux respectively
quiz.explanation: From $W = q\Delta V$ and $E_s = -\partial V/\partial s$, both reduce to force per charge.

depth.title: The gradient, fully worked: the dipole field from its potential

blocks.heading: Why one scalar beats three components
blocks.body: A vector field demands three numbers per point; the electrostatic potential promises just one, yet loses nothing. The reason is the conservative character of the field: its work around any closed loop is zero, so $V$ is a well-defined function of position, and all three components of $\vec E$ are partial derivatives of it. Whatever tool produced $V$ — direct integration, symmetry, a Laplace solver, or a voltmeter sweeping a tank of electrolyte — differentiation returns the complete field. The price is that differentiation must be done in the coordinates the symmetry hands you, which is where the spherical-coordinate gradient enters.

blocks.heading: E = −∇V in spherical coordinates
blocks.body: For a potential with no φ-dependence (any axisymmetric distribution — point charge, ring, disk, dipole), the gradient has two components: $$E_r = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial r},\qquad E_\theta = -\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial V}{\partial \theta}.$$ The factor $1/r$ on the θ-term is the metric of spherical coordinates — a small angular step covers a distance $r\,d\theta$, and slope must be change-in-$V$ per unit actual distance. The φ term drops out by symmetry, and each component carries its own minus sign.

blocks.heading: The dipole field, component by component
blocks.body: Start from the far-field potential of Section 24-4, $V = kp\cos\theta/r^{2}$. The radial derivative gives $$E_r = -\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^{2}}\right) = \frac{2kp\cos\theta}{r^{3}},$$ and the angular derivative gives $$E_\theta = -\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left(\frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^{2}}\right) = \frac{kp\sin\theta}{r^{3}}.$$ The full dipole field is therefore $$\vec E = \frac{kp}{r^{3}}\left(2\cos\theta\,\hat r + \sin\theta\,\hat\theta\right),$$ with every $1/r^{3}$ power and every trigonometric factor inherited from differentiating the $1/r^{2}$ scalar — no vector sums, no law of cosines, no component bookkeeping.

blocks.heading: The two special directions, checked
blocks.body: On the dipole axis ($\theta = 0$): $\hat\theta$ contributes nothing and $\vec E = (2kp/r^{3})\hat r$ — exactly the axial result $2kp/r^{3}$ of Section 22-3, along $\vec p$. On the perpendicular bisector ($\theta = 90^\circ$): $\cos\theta = 0$ kills $E_r$, leaving $\vec E = (kp/r^{3})\hat\theta$; at the equator $\hat\theta$ points opposite to $\vec p$, recovering the bisector result $kp/r^{3}$ antiparallel to the dipole moment. Numerically for water ($p = 6.2\times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\cdot m}$) at $r = 10$ nm and $\theta = 30^\circ$: $E_r = 2kp\cos 30^\circ/r^{3} = 97$ N/C and $E_\theta = kp\sin 30^\circ/r^{3} = 28$ N/C, combining to $|\vec E| = 100$ N/C at $17^\circ$ from the radial direction.

blocks.heading: What the gradient formalism proves about the field
blocks.body:
Any field of the form $\vec E = -
abla V$ has identically zero curl — $
abla	imes
abla V = \vec 0$ is a vector identity — which is precisely the statement that the electrostatic work $\oint \vec E\cdot d\vec s$ vanishes around closed loops. The converse holds too: every curl-free field on a simply connected region is a gradient. Potential theory is thus not a convenience layered on electrostatics but equivalent to it, and it is this structure that Laplace’s equation $
abla^{2}V = 0$ exploits in charge-free regions. The day fields become time-dependent, Faraday’s law breaks the zero-curl property, $\vec E$ acquires a $-\partial\vec A/\partial t$ part, and the scalar potential alone no longer suffices — the first hint of the vector potential that carries light.

blocks.heading: Conductors, corona and lightning rods
blocks.body: The gradient viewpoint makes conductor physics immediate. Inside the metal $\vec E = 0$, so $V$ is constant — a conductor is an equipotential volume, and its surface is an equipotential that the external field meets at right angles. Near a sharp point of radius of curvature $r$, the equipotential surfaces crowd together to stay perpendicular to the surface, so $|\vec E| \approx \Delta V/\Delta d$ grows large where $\Delta d$ shrinks; when it exceeds about $3\times 10^{6}$ V/m, air itself breaks down and corona discharge leaks charge away. A lightning rod is nothing more than a device for concentrating gradient: it raises itself to the cloud’s potential neighborhood while presenting a tiny radius on which $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ exceeds breakdown — and bleeds the storm quietly rather than explosively.

intro: A single charge brings no energy cost from infinity — but bring a second charge nearby and you must push against the first, and a third against both. The total work to assemble a system of charges, brought in from infinity one at a time, is stored as the system’s electric potential energy: one $kq_iq_j/r$ term for every pair, counted once. Because the force is conservative, the answer cannot depend on the order or the paths — only on the final arrangement.
objectives: Write the potential energy of a system of charges as $U = \Sigma_{\text{pairs}} kq_iq_j/r_{ij}$
Compute assembly work charge by charge, and verify order-independence
Interpret the sign of $U$: positive for like-charge repulsion, negative for bound unlike pairs

concepts.statement: **The electric potential energy of a system of point charges is the sum over all distinct pairs:** $$U = \sum_{i<j} \frac{k q_i q_j}{r_{ij}}.$$ It equals the total external work needed to assemble the system from infinity, one charge at a time — in any order, along any paths.

**Bring the charges in one at a time and add the work of each step.** The $n$-th charge costs $W_n = q_n\Sigma_{i<n} kq_i/r_{in}$ — the potential of everything already in place, times the newcomer. Summing all steps reproduces the pair formula with each pair once.

**Like pairs cost positive work (pushed together under repulsion); unlike pairs release energy (bound).** Positive total $U$ means the system flies apart if released; negative total $U$ — like the electron’s $-27$ eV in hydrogen — means it holds together.

**The assembly result is a function of the final configuration only.** Reorder the assembly, take wild curved paths, pause midway — the conservative field keeps the books and the same $U$ drops out, because each pair’s energy depends only on its separation.

concepts.term: Electric Potential Energy of a System of Charged Particles: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Electric Potential Energy of a System of Charged Particles problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is electric potential from work per charge; the working equation is $V = U/q_0$, $V = kq/r$, $E = -dV/dx$ (1D), $U = kq_1q_2/r$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (volts ($\text{J/C}$)) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $V\sim 10^2$--$10^4\ \text{V}$ for $\mu\text{C}$ at cm--m; $V = 0$ at infinity convention; $E = -\nabla V$ always.

figures.caption: Assembling a triangle of three like charges: $q_1$ is free, $q_2$ costs $kq_1q_2/r$, and $q_3$ costs $kq_3(q_1+q_2)/r$ — two pair terms. The total $U = 3kq^2/r$ for equal charges counts every edge of the triangle exactly once, whichever order the charges arrive.

examples.title: Assembling an equilateral triangle
examples.problem: Three charges $q = +5.0\ \mu$C are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side $a = 3.0$ cm. How much work does the assembly take?

steps.label: One pair
steps.text: A single pair stores $kq^2/a = (8.99\times 10^{9})(5.0\times 10^{-6})^2/0.030 = 7.5$ J.

steps.label: Count pairs
steps.text: Three charges give $\binom{3}{2} = 3$ pairs: three edges of the triangle.

examples.result: The assembly stores 22.5 J — release the clamps and the like charges spend exactly that much kinetic energy flying apart.

examples.title: Electric Potential Energy of a System of Charged Particles: volt check
examples.problem: Find $V = kq/r$ at $1.25\ \text{m}$ from $2\ \mu\text{C}$ (zero at infinity).

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $V \approx 14400\ \text{V}$.

examples.result: $V \approx 14400\ \text{V}$.

keyTakeaways: System energy: $U = \Sigma_{\text{pairs}} kq_iq_j/r_{ij}$, each pair counted once.
Assembly work is order- and path-independent — conservatism guarantees it.
Positive $U$ means stored repulsion (explodes); negative $U$ means binding.

quiz.q: A system of three charges has how many pair terms in its potential energy?
quiz.explanation: Each unordered pair contributes once: $\binom{3}{2} = 3$ terms.

quiz.q: The potential energy of an electron–proton pair at separation $r$ is:
options: zero, since the charges are equal in magnitude
quiz.explanation: The product $q_1q_2 < 0$, so $U < 0$: work is released as they come together — the hydrogen ground state’s $-13.6$ eV structure.

quiz.q: For three equal charges at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side $a$, the total assembly work is:
quiz.explanation: Three identical pairs, each $kq^2/a$.

quiz.q: Assembling the same final configuration in a different order:
options: doubles the number of pair terms
quiz.explanation: The electrostatic force is conservative: $U$ depends only on the final pair separations, never on the assembly sequence.

intro: A conductor already knows it is an equipotential — now that becomes quantitative. An isolated charged sphere of radius $R$ sits entirely at $V = kq/R$, the same formula as a point charge evaluated at the surface. Connect two distant spheres by a thin wire and they become one conductor: charge flows until both share the same potential, piling more charge (and more surface density) onto the bigger sphere — the physics of the lightning rod, the Van de Graaff generator’s belt-to-dome handoff, and every sharp edge that hisses in the rain.
objectives: Show that a charged isolated conductor is at a single potential, $V = kq/R$ for a sphere
Analyze connected conductors: charge splits so that $V_1 = V_2$
Explain why sharp points (small $R$, large $\sigma$) reach breakdown first — corona discharge

concepts.statement: **A charged isolated conductor is at one potential throughout — surface and interior alike.** For a sphere of radius $R$ carrying charge $q$: $$V = \frac{kq}{R}$$ at and inside the surface, while outside $V = kq/r$ as if all charge sat at the center.

**Charges joined by a wire flow until the whole assembly is one equipotential.** Two distant spheres ($R_1, R_2$, total charge $Q$) reach $V = kQ/(R_1+R_2)$, carrying $q_1 = Q R_1/(R_1+R_2)$ and $q_2 = Q R_2/(R_1+R_2)$: charge goes to the larger sphere, surface density $\sigma = q/4\pi R^2$ goes to the smaller one.

**Equal potentials mean $\sigma \propto 1/R$.** The smaller sphere ends with the larger surface charge density and the stronger surface field $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0$ — curvature is where field concentrates.

**When the surface field of a conductor exceeds about $3\times 10^{6}$ V/m, air ionizes and corona discharge leaks charge away.** Because sharp points have tiny local $R$, they reach this limit first — the reason lightning rods are pointed, high-voltage hardware is rounded, and Saint Elmo’s fire glows on mast tips in storms.

concepts.term: Potential of a Charged Isolated Conductor: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Potential of a Charged Isolated Conductor problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is electric potential from work per charge; the working equation is $V = U/q_0$, $V = kq/r$, $E = -dV/dx$ (1D), $U = kq_1q_2/r$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (volts ($\text{J/C}$)) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $V\sim 10^2$--$10^4\ \text{V}$ for $\mu\text{C}$ at cm--m; $V = 0$ at infinity convention; $E = -\nabla V$ always.

examples.title: Two spheres on a wire
examples.problem: Spheres of radii $R_1 = 1.0$ cm and $R_2 = 2.0$ cm, far apart, are connected by a thin wire, and the pair carries total charge $Q = +3.0$ nC. Find the common potential and the charge on each sphere.

steps.label: Equal potentials
steps.text: $q_1/R_1 = q_2/R_2$ with $q_1 + q_2 = Q$ — one conductor, one potential.

steps.label: Densities
steps.text: $\sigma_1 = q_1/4\pi R_1^2 = 0.80\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$ versus $\sigma_2 = 0.40\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$: the small sphere carries twice the density and twice the surface field.

examples.result: Common potential 900 V; charges 1.0 nC and 2.0 nC — the bigger sphere hoards the charge, the smaller one the field.

examples.title: Potential of a Charged Isolated Conductor: volt check
examples.problem: Find $V = kq/r$ at $0.5\ \text{m}$ from $3\ \mu\text{C}$ (zero at infinity).

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $V \approx 53900\ \text{V}$.

examples.result: $V \approx 53900\ \text{V}$.

keyTakeaways: An isolated charged sphere sits entirely at $V = kq/R$; outside, $V = kq/r$ like a point charge.
Connected conductors reach a single potential; charge divides in proportion to radius, density as $1/R$.
Sharp points mean large $\sigma$ and $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0$, reaching air’s breakdown field first — corona.

quiz.q: A conducting sphere of radius $R$ carries charge $q$. The potential at its center (inside the metal) is:
options: $kq/R$ — the same as at the surface
quiz.explanation: The conductor is a single equipotential: $V = kq/R$ on the surface and everywhere inside.

quiz.q: Two distant spheres connected by a thin wire share their total charge. After equilibrium, compared with the smaller sphere, the larger sphere has:
quiz.explanation: Equal potentials force $q \propto R$ but $\sigma = q/4\pi R^2 \propto 1/R$.

quiz.q: A Van de Graaff dome is made smoothly round rather than knobby because:
options: round domes hold more total charge
knobs have small local radii, hence large $\sigma$ and fields that trigger corona at lower voltage
the potential of a knob is higher than that of the dome
quiz.explanation: The whole conductor is at one potential; local surface field $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ blows up at small radii of curvature, and air breaks down near $3\times 10^{6}$ V/m.

intro: In 1746 the Leyden jar showed Europe that electric charge could be bottled and released in one violent spark; three centuries later the same idea, miniaturized, stores the 1's and 0's in every DRAM cell and the jolt of a defibrillator. A capacitor is any pair of conductors separated by an insulator, and this section introduces the one number — capacitance — that measures how much charge the pair hoards per volt applied.
objectives: Define capacitance and use $C = Q/V$ to relate charge, potential difference and capacitance
Explain why the capacitance of a given pair of conductors depends only on geometry, never on $Q$ or $V$
Work with the farad and its practical submultiples (mF, μF, pF)

concepts.statement: **A capacitor is a pair of conductors separated by an insulator (air, paper, ceramic, oxide…).** When the pair is connected to a potential difference, charge $+Q$ accumulates on one conductor and $-Q$ on the other; the device as a whole remains electrically neutral.
concepts.detail: The simplest and most important case is two parallel metal plates, but any two isolated conductors form a capacitor — including the gate and channel of a transistor or two neighboring traces on a circuit board (stray capacitance).

concepts.statement: **Capacitance is the ratio of the magnitude of the charge on either conductor to the potential difference between them:** $$C = \frac{Q}{V},$$ where $V = V_+ - V_-$. The SI unit is the **farad**: $1\ \mathrm{F} = 1\ \mathrm{C/V}$.
concepts.detail: One farad is enormous; everyday capacitors run from picofarads (radio circuits) through microfarads (power supplies) to farad-scale supercapacitors. Because $1.0\ \mathrm{C}$ is a huge amount of charge, even $V = 1$ V with $C = 1$ F is a large storage.

concepts.statement: **For a given, isolated pair of conductors, $C$ depends only on the size, shape and separation of the conductors — not on $Q$ or $V$.** Doubling $V$ doubles $Q$, leaving the ratio $Q/V$ untouched: the $Q$-vs-$V$ relation of an empty capacitor is a straight line through the origin.
concepts.detail: The linear relation $Q \propto V$ is a consequence of superposition: doubling all the charge doubles the field everywhere between the conductors and hence doubles the potential difference. Nearby objects (a hand, a shield) do perturb $C$, which is why real components are measured in place when precision matters.

concepts.statement: **A battery is a charge pump: it moves charge through the wires until the potential difference of the capacitor equals the battery's terminal voltage.** Then $Q = CV$ and the flow stops.
concepts.detail: Only conduction electrons actually move in a metal-wired circuit; the net charge of each plate is set by an extremely thin surface layer of added or missing electrons, while the field between the plates spans the whole gap.

concepts.statement: **Solve Capacitance problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is capacitance and field energy; the working equation is $C = q/V$, $C = \varepsilon_0A/d$ (parallel plate), $U = \tfrac12CV^2$, $u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (farads and joules) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $C\sim \text{pF}$--$\mu\text{F}$; $U\sim \text{mJ}$ for $\mu\text{F}$ at $100\ \text{V}$; fixed $q$ versus fixed $V$ when a dielectric is inserted.

examples.title: Charging a 4.0 μF capacitor
examples.problem: A $4.0\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is connected to the terminals of a $12\ \mathrm{V}$ battery. (a) How much charge accumulates on each plate? (b) How many electrons were transferred through the battery from one plate to the other?

steps.label: Charge
steps.text: $Q = CV = (4.0\times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{F})(12\ \mathrm{V}) = 4.8\times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C} = 48\ \mu\mathrm{C}$, with $+48\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ on one plate and $-48\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ on the other.

steps.label: Electrons moved
steps.text: Each electron carries $e = 1.602\times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, so $n = Q/e = 4.8\times 10^{-5}/1.602\times 10^{-19} = 3.0\times 10^{14}$ electrons.

steps.label: Scale check
steps.text: That is a mere $5\times 10^{-10}$ mol of electrons — a film far thinner than one atomic layer — yet it is enough to hold $12\ \mathrm{V}$ across the gap.

examples.result: Each plate carries $48\ \mu\mathrm{C}$, corresponding to $3.0\times 10^{14}$ electrons pumped through the battery.

examples.title: Capacitance: parallel-plate numbers
examples.problem: A parallel-plate capacitor has $A = 200\ \text{cm}^2$ and $d = 1.0\ \text{mm}$. Find $C = \varepsilon_0A/d$ and $U$ at $100\ \text{V}$.

steps.label: Energy
steps.text: $U = \tfrac12CV^2 = 0.5\times 1.77\times 10^{-10}\times 10^4 = 8.85\times 10^{-7}\ \text{J}$.

examples.result: $C \approx 177\ \text{pF}$; $U \approx 8.85\times 10^{-7}\ \text{J}$.

keyTakeaways: Capacitance is $C = Q/V$: charge stored per volt, measured in farads ($1\ \mathrm{F} = 1\ \mathrm{C/V}$).
A capacitor stays overall neutral: the two conductors carry equal and opposite charges $\pm Q$.
For fixed geometry $C$ is a constant — $Q$ and $V$ rise and fall together in strict proportion.

quiz.q: A capacitor connected to a battery acquires charge $Q$ at potential difference $V$. If the battery is swapped for one that maintains $2V$, the new charge and capacitance are:
quiz.explanation: The same geometry fixes $C$; with $C$ unchanged, doubling $V$ doubles $Q = CV$.

quiz.q: One farad is equal to one:
quiz.explanation: From $C = Q/V$, the farad is a coulomb divided by a volt. A joule per coulomb is a volt, not a farad.

quiz.q: A 200 pF capacitor is charged to 9.0 V. The charge on either plate is about:
quiz.explanation: $Q = CV = (200\times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F})(9.0\ \mathrm{V}) = 1.8\times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C} = 1.8$ nC.

quiz.q: The capacitance of a given, isolated pair of conductors depends on:
quiz.explanation: Capacitance is fixed by geometry alone; $Q$ and $V$ always adjust to keep $Q/V = C$ constant.

intro: Capacitance can be computed from first principles for any geometry: put charge $Q$ on the conductors, find the field with Gauss' law, integrate it to get the potential difference, and divide. Here the recipe is run on the three canonical shapes — parallel plates, coaxial cylinders and concentric spheres — giving the formulas every circuit designer carries in their head.
objectives: Execute the standard recipe: assume $\pm Q$, find $E$ from Gauss’ law, integrate for $V$, then divide
Compute $C = \varepsilon_0 A/d$ for parallel plates, $C = 2\pi\varepsilon_0 L/\ln(b/a)$ for coaxial cylinders and $C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 ab/(b-a)$ for concentric spheres
Use the isolated-sphere limit $C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$ and appreciate the size of the farad

concepts.statement: **To compute a capacitance: (1) put charge $\pm Q$ on the conductors; (2) use Gauss' law to find $E$ in the gap; (3) integrate $V = -\int \vec E\cdot d\vec s$ from the negative to the positive conductor; (4) divide: $C = Q/V$.** The $Q$ you assumed cancels out.
concepts.detail: Every step relies only on tools from Chapters 22–23, which is why capacitance is the first great application of Gauss’ law to device design.

concepts.statement: **For two plates of area $A$ separated by distance $d$ (edge effects neglected):** $$C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}.$$ Inside, the field is uniform, $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0 = Q/(\varepsilon_0 A)$, and $V = Ed$.
concepts.detail: Capacitance grows with plate area and shrinks with separation — make the gap atomic-scale and even $1\ \mathrm{mm^2}$ of plates can hold microfarads, the principle of the electrolytic and super capacitors.

concepts.statement: **For coaxial conductors of radii $a$ (inner) and $b$ (outer) and length $L$, with $L \gg b$:** $$C = \frac{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L}{\ln(b/a)}.$$ The field between them is $E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)$, largest at the inner conductor.
concepts.detail: This is the capacitance per unit length of coaxial cable, the workhorse of instrumentation and RF systems — typically tens of picofarads per meter.

concepts.statement: **For concentric spheres of radii $a$ and $b$:** $$C = \frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0 ab}{b - a},$$ which tends to the **isolated-sphere value** $C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$ as $b \to \infty$.
concepts.detail: Even a body as large as the Earth ($R = 6.37\times 10^{6}$ m) has a capacitance of only $4\pi\varepsilon_0 R \approx 0.71$ mF — a vivid reminder of how big a unit the farad is.

concepts.statement: **Solve Calculating the Capacitance problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is capacitance and field energy; the working equation is $C = q/V$, $C = \varepsilon_0A/d$ (parallel plate), $U = \tfrac12CV^2$, $u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (farads and joules) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $C\sim \text{pF}$--$\mu\text{F}$; $U\sim \text{mJ}$ for $\mu\text{F}$ at $100\ \text{V}$; fixed $q$ versus fixed $V$ when a dielectric is inserted.

figures.caption: A parallel-plate capacitor. The battery pumps charge until the plates hold $\pm Q$ and the potential difference equals the battery voltage. Between the plates the field is uniform, $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0$, so $V = Ed$ and $C = Q/V = \varepsilon_0 A/d$. The stored energy sits in the field, with density $\tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$.
