examples.title: Wire bent into a semicircle
examples.problem: A 2.0 A current runs in from the left along a horizontal line, bends counterclockwise through a semicircle of radius $R = 4.0$ cm, and continues out to the right. Find the magnetic field at the center of the semicircle.

steps.label: Straight sections
steps.text: Each straight piece runs along a line through the center, so $d\vec s \parallel \hat r$ and $\sin\theta = 0$: they contribute exactly zero at the center.

steps.label: Semicircle
steps.text: Only the arc contributes, with $\phi = \pi$: $B = \mu_0 i\phi/4\pi R = \mu_0 i/4R$.

steps.label: Direction
steps.text: The current traverses the semicircle counterclockwise as drawn, so by the right-hand rule $\vec B$ points out of the page.

examples.result: The center sits in a field of about $1.6\times10^{-5}$ T directed out of the page — produced entirely by the arc, none by the radial leads.

examples.title: Magnetic Field Due to a Current: wire-field check
examples.problem: Find $B = \mu_0I/2\pi r$ at $2.0\ \text{cm}$ from a long wire carrying $10\ \text{A}$.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: $B = 4\pi\times 10^{-7}\times 10/(2\pi\times 0.020)$.

examples.result: $B \approx 1.00\times 10^{-4}\ \text{T}$ circling the wire.

keyTakeaways: $d\vec B = (\mu_0/4\pi)\,i\,d\vec s\times\hat r/r^2$; superpose (integrate) over the whole circuit to get $\vec B$.
Long wire: $B = \mu_0 i/2\pi R$; circular arc at its center: $B = \mu_0 i\phi/4\pi R$; full loop: $B = \mu_0 i/2R$.
The right-hand rule fixes directions; elements parallel to the line toward the field point contribute nothing.

quiz.q: A long vertical wire carries current straight up. Directly to the west of the wire, the field $\vec B$ points:
quiz.explanation: Thumb up: the field circles the wire counterclockwise as seen from above, and on the west side the tangent points south.

quiz.q: Doubling the perpendicular distance from a long straight wire changes the field magnitude from $B$ to:
quiz.explanation: The field of a line source falls off as $1/R$.

quiz.q: At the center of a single full circular loop of radius $R$ carrying current $i$, the field magnitude is:
quiz.explanation: Set $\phi = 2\pi$ in the arc formula: $B = \mu_0 i\phi/4\pi R = \mu_0 i/2R$.

quiz.q: A current element happens to point exactly toward the point where you want the field. Its contribution there is:
options: The largest any element can give
quiz.explanation: The cross product of parallel (or antiparallel) vectors is zero, and $\sin\theta = 0$.

intro: A current makes a field, and a field pushes on a current — so two currents must push on each other. The force between parallel wires is tiny per meter but exactly measurable, and for most of the SI's history it defined the ampere itself. The surprise for students fresh from electrostatics: parallel currents attract.
objectives: Derive $F/L = \mu_0 i_1 i_2/2\pi d$ from the field of a long wire and the force law $F = iLB$
Determine attraction versus repulsion for parallel and antiparallel currents
Explain how the ampere was defined and why that definition fixed the value of $\mu_0$

concepts.statement: **Two long parallel wires a distance $d$ apart, carrying currents $i_1$ and $i_2$, exert on each other a force per unit length** $$\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 i_1 i_2}{2\pi d}.$$ Wire 2 sits in the field $B_1 = \mu_0 i_1/2\pi d$ made by wire 1, and a length $L$ of it feels $F = i_2 L B_1$ — Chapter 28's force law applied to currents.
concepts.detail: The derivation is two lines: substitute the wire's field into $\vec F = i\vec L\times\vec B$ with $\vec L$ perpendicular to $\vec B$ for parallel wires.

concepts.statement: **Currents in the same direction attract each other; antiparallel currents repel.** Reversing either current reverses the force — the sign comes from $\vec F = i\vec L\times\vec B$ with the right-hand rule.
concepts.detail: Contrast with like electric charges, which repel: the magnetic interaction between neutral current-carrying wires has the opposite sign pattern.

concepts.statement: **One ampere is the constant current that, maintained in two straight parallel conductors of infinite length and negligible cross-section, 1 meter apart in vacuum, produces a force of exactly $2\times10^{-7}$ newton per meter of length.** With $i_1 = i_2 = 1$ A and $d = 1.00$ m, the force law gives $F/L = \mu_0/2\pi = 2\times10^{-7}$ N/m.
concepts.detail: Because the definition fixed $\mu_0/2\pi$, it fixed $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\cdot m/A}$ exactly — until the 2019 SI revision defined the ampere through the elementary charge $e$ instead. $\mu_0$ is now a measured quantity that still agrees with the old value to ten significant figures, so keep using the round number.

concepts.term: Force Between Two Parallel Currents: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Force Between Two Parallel Currents problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is fields of currents via Biot--Savart and Amp\u00e8re; the working equation is $d\vec B = (\mu_0/4\pi)i\,d\vec L\times\hat{r}/r^2$, $\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec s = \mu_0i_{\text{enc}}$, $B_{\text{sol}} = \mu_0ni$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (tesla) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ (wire at cm, amp) to $1\ \text{T}$ (solenoid); steady currents; Amp\u00e8rian loop needs symmetry.

concepts.term: Force Between Two Parallel Currents: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Force Between Two Parallel Currents lives at $10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ (wire at cm, amp) to $1\ \text{T}$ (solenoid) and the textbook model holds while steady currents; Amp\u00e8rian loop needs symmetry.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Force Between Two Parallel Currents calculation gives seconds when tesla demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ (wire at cm, amp) to $1\ \text{T}$ (solenoid), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Lab cables and the definition of the ampere
examples.problem: Two parallel cable runs, each carrying $i = 10.0$ A in the same direction, sit $d = 5.0$ cm apart. (a) Find the force per meter between them. (b) Verify the defining numbers: the force per meter for two 1 A wires 1.00 m apart.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $F/L = (2\times10^{-7})(100)/0.050 = 4.0\times10^{-4}$ N/m — attractive, because the currents are parallel. A 2.0 m run feels $8.0\times10^{-4}$ N.

steps.label: Definition check
steps.text: With 1 A each and $d = 1.00$ m: $F/L = (2\times10^{-7})(1)(1)/(1.00) = 2.0\times10^{-7}$ N/m — exactly the SI defining value, as it must be.

examples.result: The cables pull together with $4.0\times10^{-4}$ N per meter; at the defining geometry the law returns precisely $2\times10^{-7}$ N/m.

examples.title: Force Between Two Parallel Currents: wire-field check
examples.problem: Find $B = \mu_0I/2\pi r$ at $2.0\ \text{cm}$ from a long wire carrying $15\ \text{A}$.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: $B = 4\pi\times 10^{-7}\times 15/(2\pi\times 0.020)$.

examples.result: $B \approx 1.50\times 10^{-4}\ \text{T}$ circling the wire.

keyTakeaways: $F/L = \mu_0 i_1 i_2/2\pi d$: parallel currents attract, antiparallel currents repel.
The force is just $\vec F = i\vec L\times\vec B$ with the other wire's field doing the pushing.
The SI ampere was defined by this force at 1 m separation, which pinned $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\cdot m/A}$.

quiz.q: Two long wires carry currents in opposite directions. The interaction between them is:
options: Zero, because each wire is electrically neutral
Attractive only if the currents are equal
quiz.explanation: Antiparallel currents repel; the electrical neutrality of the wires is irrelevant to the magnetic force.

quiz.q: Two parallel wires 2.0 cm apart carry 3.0 A each in the same direction. The force per unit length is about:
If one current is doubled and the separation is also doubled, the force per unit length is:
quiz.explanation: The numerator gains a factor of 2 from the current, the denominator a factor of 2 from the distance.

quiz.q: The SI definition of the ampere involves:
options: The number of electrons passing a point per second
The force between two long parallel currents 1 m apart
The charge needed to neutralize one mole of monovalent ions
The field produced at 1 m by a straight wire
quiz.explanation: The classic definition set 1 A so that two such wires 1 m apart pull with $2\times10^{-7}$ N per meter.

intro: Gauss' law converts electric-field symmetry into a one-line answer; Ampère's law does the same for magnetism, replacing a surface integral with a line integral around a closed path. For wires, cylinders, solenoids and toroids it collapses a page of Biot–Savart work into a single equation — and it carries the chapter's deepest message: steady currents are what circulate magnetic field.
objectives: State Ampère's law and assign the sign of the enclosed current with the right-hand rule
Use Amperian loops to find B outside and inside a long current-carrying cylinder
Recognize the symmetries that make Ampère's law a computational tool rather than just a theorem

concepts.statement: **The line integral (circulation) of $\vec B$ around any closed curve equals $\mu_0$ times the net current piercing any surface bounded by the curve:** $$\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec s = \mu_0 i_{enc}.$$ Currents along the right-hand thumb, when the fingers curl along the integration path, count positive.
concepts.detail: The law holds for any steady current distribution (the full Maxwell–Ampère law of Chapter 32 adds a term for changing electric flux). Like Gauss' law it is always true but only instantly useful when symmetry pins $\vec B$ along the path.

concepts.statement: **Choose the loop the symmetry suggests: a concentric circle around a straight wire or cylinder, a rectangle straddling a solenoid, a circle inside a toroid.** On the good loop, $\vec B$ is tangent to the path with constant magnitude, so $\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec s = B(2\pi r)$ and the law reads off $B$ at once.
concepts.detail: Around a long straight wire: $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 i$ gives $B = \mu_0 i/2\pi r$ — the Biot–Savart result without the integration.

concepts.term: Field inside a uniform current distribution
concepts.statement: **If current $i$ is spread uniformly through a cylinder of radius $R$, then inside** $$B = \frac{\mu_0 i}{2\pi R^2}\,r \quad (r \le R),$$ **while outside $B = \mu_0 i/2\pi r$ — as if the whole current ran on the axis.**
concepts.detail: A loop of radius $r$ encloses only the fraction $r^2/R^2$ of the current, so the field grows linearly from zero on the axis to the surface value $\mu_0 i/2\pi R$, then decays as $1/r$ — the magnetic twin of the electric field inside a uniformly charged sphere.

concepts.statement: **Ampère's law constrains only the circulation of $\vec B$ around your loop — a fixed number $\mu_0 i_{enc}$ — regardless of the loop's size.** Enlarge the circle around a wire and $B$ on it drops, but $B(2\pi r)$ stays $\mu_0 i$.
concepts.detail: This is why the law cannot by itself give $B$ for a finite solenoid: no simple closed path there has $\vec B$ constant and tangent everywhere, so the circulation cannot be untangled into one unknown.

concepts.statement: **Solve Ampère's Law problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is fields of currents via Biot--Savart and Amp\u00e8re; the working equation is $d\vec B = (\mu_0/4\pi)i\,d\vec L\times\hat{r}/r^2$, $\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec s = \mu_0i_{\text{enc}}$, $B_{\text{sol}} = \mu_0ni$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (tesla) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ (wire at cm, amp) to $1\ \text{T}$ (solenoid); steady currents; Amp\u00e8rian loop needs symmetry.

examples.title: Field of a bus bar
examples.problem: A cylindrical copper bus bar of radius $R = 2.0$ mm carries a uniformly distributed current of 30 A. Find $B$ at the surface, at $r = R/2$ inside, and at $r = 2R$ outside.

steps.label: Inside at R/2
steps.text: A loop of radius $R/2$ encloses a fraction $(1/2)^2 = 1/4$ of the current and has half the circumference, so $B = (r/R)B_s = 1.5\times10^{-3}$ T — the interior field is linear in $r$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: The inside point at $R/2$ and the outside point at $2R$ give the same field — the profile is a tent peaking exactly at the surface.

examples.result: 3.0 mT at the surface, 1.5 mT at $r = R/2$ inside and at $r = 2R$ outside — linear rise, then $1/r$ decay.

examples.title: Ampère's Law: wire-field check
examples.problem: Find $B = \mu_0I/2\pi r$ at $2.0\ \text{cm}$ from a long wire carrying $20\ \text{A}$.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: $B = 4\pi\times 10^{-7}\times 20/(2\pi\times 0.020)$.

examples.result: $B \approx 2.00\times 10^{-4}\ \text{T}$ circling the wire.

keyTakeaways: $\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec s = \mu_0 i_{enc}$, with the sign fixed by curling the right fingers along the path.
Concentric Amperian circles give the wire field $\mu_0 i/2\pi r$ and the uniform-cylinder interior field $\mu_0 i r/2\pi R^2$ in one step each.
The law always holds but pays off computationally only when symmetry makes $\vec B$ constant and tangent on the loop.

quiz.q: Around a long wire, an Amperian circle is enlarged from $r$ to $2r$. The circulation $\oint \vec B\cdot d\vec s$:
quiz.explanation: The circulation equals $\mu_0 i_{enc}$, and the same current is enclosed — the field on the loop drops as $1/r$ to compensate.

quiz.q: Viewed from above, a circular Amperian path is traversed counterclockwise. A current piercing the loop from below (going away from the viewer) counts as:
options: Positive only if it is the sole current
quiz.explanation: Fingers curled counterclockwise put the right thumb toward the viewer; a current going away from the viewer is antiparallel to it, hence negative.

quiz.q: Inside a uniformly current-carrying cylinder, the field at $r = R/2$ compared to its surface value is:
options: A quarter of the surface value
quiz.explanation: The interior field grows linearly with $r$ because the enclosed current grows as $r^2$ while the path length grows as $r$.

quiz.q: Why does Ampère's law fail to give the field of a short, finite solenoid in one step?
options: A finite solenoid encloses no current
The law is not valid near coils
No simple closed path has B constant and tangent everywhere
Because μ₀ differs inside the winding
quiz.explanation: Without enough symmetry, the circulation cannot be factored into one unknown times a path length.

intro: Stack many current loops into a helix and something wonderful happens inside: every turn pushes the field along the axis, and the exterior fields cancel to nearly zero. The solenoid is the workhorse electromagnet — a uniform field you dial with a current knob. Bend the helix into a ring and the field is trapped entirely in the donut: the toroid, the standard shape when leakage cannot be tolerated.
objectives: Derive $B = \mu_0 n i$ for a long solenoid using a rectangular Amperian loop
Derive $B = \mu_0 iN/2\pi r$ for a toroid and explain why the field vanishes outside the core
Use $n = N/l$ to move between total turns, length, and field strength

concepts.statement: **Inside a long solenoid with $n$ turns per unit length carrying current $i$,** $$B = \mu_0 n i$$ **— uniform across the bore and along the axis, pointing along the right-hand thumb when the fingers curl with the current. Outside, $B \approx 0$ except near the ends.**
concepts.detail: The result is independent of the solenoid's radius: packing more turns per meter compensates exactly for making them smaller. Doubling $n$ and halving $i$ leaves $B$ unchanged.

concepts.statement: **Take a rectangle with one long side of length $l$ inside the bore, parallel to the axis, and the opposite side outside.** The two short sides contribute nothing ($\vec B \perp d\vec s$), the outside side contributes about zero, and the inside side gives $Bl$. The loop is pierced by $nl$ turns, each carrying $i$, so Ampère's law reads $Bl = \mu_0(nl)i$.
concepts.detail: Because the answer does not depend on where inside the bore the long side sits, the interior field is uniform — the argument HRW uses to certify the solenoid as a field-standard device.

concepts.statement: **A toroid with $N$ turns carrying current $i$ has, at radius $r$ within the core,** $$B = \frac{\mu_0 i N}{2\pi r}.$$ **In the central hole and outside the ring, $B = 0$.**
concepts.detail: An Amperian circle inside the core encloses all $N$ turns: $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 N i$. The field is not uniform — it falls as $1/r$ from the inner to the outer edge. Outside the ring, a loop encloses equal numbers of upward and downward piercings (or none at all), so the net enclosed current is zero.

concepts.statement: **The solenoid gives uniformity but leaks field at its ends; the toroid confines the field completely but lets it vary across the core.** A toroid of mean radius $r$ behaves like a solenoid with the same turn density $n = N/2\pi r$ bent into a circle — at the mean radius the two formulas agree exactly.
concepts.detail: Design choice: MRI magnets and lab electromagnets want uniformity (solenoids); transformers and magnetic-core inductors want zero leakage (toroids).

concepts.statement: **Solve Solenoids and Toroids problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is fields of currents via Biot--Savart and Amp\u00e8re; the working equation is $d\vec B = (\mu_0/4\pi)i\,d\vec L\times\hat{r}/r^2$, $\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec s = \mu_0i_{\text{enc}}$, $B_{\text{sol}} = \mu_0ni$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (tesla) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ (wire at cm, amp) to $1\ \text{T}$ (solenoid); steady currents; Amp\u00e8rian loop needs symmetry.

examples.title: Toroid numbers, checked against a solenoid
examples.problem: A toroid has $N = 500$ turns carrying $i = 2.0$ A; its core fills the region from $r = 8.0$ cm to $r = 12.0$ cm. Find $B$ at the mean radius, at the two edges, and compare with the equivalent solenoid.

steps.label: Outer edge
steps.text: At $r = 12.0$ cm: $B = (2\times10^{-7})(1000)/(0.12) = 1.7\times10^{-3}$ T — a drift of about ±25% across the core.

steps.label: Solenoid check
steps.text: Equivalent turn density $n = N/2\pi r = 500/0.628 = 796$ turns/m; $B = \mu_0 n i = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(796)(2.0) = 2.0\times10^{-3}$ T — matching the toroid at its mean radius.

examples.result: 2.0 mT at the mean radius (2.5 mT inner, 1.7 mT outer) — identical to a solenoid of the same turn density bent into a ring.

examples.title: Solenoids and Toroids: wire-field check
examples.problem: Find $B = \mu_0I/2\pi r$ at $2.0\ \text{cm}$ from a long wire carrying $5\ \text{A}$.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: $B = 4\pi\times 10^{-7}\times 5/(2\pi\times 0.020)$.

examples.result: $B \approx 5.00\times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ circling the wire.

keyTakeaways: Long solenoid: $B = \mu_0 n i$ inside, nearly zero outside; direction by the right-hand thumb along the current circulation.
Toroid: $B = \mu_0 iN/2\pi r$ inside the core only; zero in the hole and outside the ring.
The rectangular Amperian loop certifies the solenoid field; the concentric circular loop certifies the toroid field.

quiz.q: A long solenoid has its turns-per-length $n$ doubled while the current $i$ is halved. The interior field is:
quiz.explanation: $B = \mu_0 n i$ depends only on the product $ni$, which is unchanged.

quiz.q: Where is a toroid's magnetic field nonzero?
quiz.explanation: Ampère loops in the hole or outside the ring enclose zero net current.

quiz.q: A toroid has N = 400 turns, i = 1.5 A. Inside the core at r = 0.10 m, B is about:
Across a toroid's core, from the inner edge to the outer edge, the field:
quiz.explanation: The enclosed current is fixed at $Ni$, so $B \propto 1/r$ across the core.

intro: Back away from any current loop — a few radii will do — and its field forgets the shape of the wire and remembers only one vector: the magnetic dipole moment $\mu = NiA$. That single number controls the loop's torque in a field, its energy, and its distant field pattern. It is the bookkeeping unit of everything from compass coils to atomic magnetism.
objectives: Compute the dipole moment $\vec\mu = NiA\,\hat n$ of a coil and orient it with the right-hand rule
Evaluate the on-axis field of a coil, both the exact formula and the far-field dipole form
Connect the loop to the dipole results of Chapter 28: $\vec\tau = \vec\mu\times\vec B$ and $U = -\vec\mu\cdot\vec B$

concepts.term: Magnetic dipole moment of a coil
concepts.statement: **A coil of $N$ turns, area $A$, carrying current $i$, has magnetic dipole moment** $$\mu = N i A,$$ **directed along the unit normal $\hat n$ found by curling the right fingers with the current — the thumb is $\hat n$. SI unit: A·m².**
concepts.detail: Stacking turns multiplies the moment: a 200-turn loop of the same area and current has 200 times the moment of one turn.

concepts.statement: **On the axis of a circular coil of radius $R$, at distance $z$ from the center,** $$B = \frac{\mu_0 N i R^2}{2(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}} \;\xrightarrow{\;z\gg R\;}\; \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\,\frac{\mu}{z^3}.$$ The far-field form is the magnetic dipole field on its axis — the same $1/z^3$ falloff the electric dipole shows, with $\mu = Ni\pi R^2$ playing the role of $qd$.
concepts.detail: At $z = 5R$ the far-field formula overshoots by only about 6%, the size of $(3/2)(R/z)^2$ — the expansion parameter of the dipole approximation.

concepts.statement: **A current loop obeys $\vec\tau = \vec\mu\times\vec B$, has energy $U = -\vec\mu\cdot\vec B$, and radiates the dipole far field — everything an electric dipole does, transposed to magnetism.**
concepts.detail: An orbiting electron is a microscopic current loop with orbital moment $\mu = evr/2$; the Bohr magneton $\mu_B \approx 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{A\cdot m^2}$ sets the scale of atomic magnetism — matter magnetizes by the alignment of these little dipoles.

concepts.term: A Current-Carrying Coil as a Magnetic Dipole: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve A Current-Carrying Coil as a Magnetic Dipole problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is fields of currents via Biot--Savart and Amp\u00e8re; the working equation is $d\vec B = (\mu_0/4\pi)i\,d\vec L\times\hat{r}/r^2$, $\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec s = \mu_0i_{\text{enc}}$, $B_{\text{sol}} = \mu_0ni$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (tesla) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ (wire at cm, amp) to $1\ \text{T}$ (solenoid); steady currents; Amp\u00e8rian loop needs symmetry.

concepts.term: A Current-Carrying Coil as a Magnetic Dipole: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **A Current-Carrying Coil as a Magnetic Dipole lives at $10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ (wire at cm, amp) to $1\ \text{T}$ (solenoid) and the textbook model holds while steady currents; Amp\u00e8rian loop needs symmetry.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a A Current-Carrying Coil as a Magnetic Dipole calculation gives seconds when tesla demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ (wire at cm, amp) to $1\ \text{T}$ (solenoid), recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: A coil as a competitor to Earth's field
examples.problem: A 200-turn coil of radius $R = 2.0$ cm carries $i = 2.0$ A. (a) Find its magnetic dipole moment. (b) Find the on-axis field at $z = 10$ cm, using both the far-field formula and the exact one.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: The far-field value runs 6% high because $z = 5R$ is barely in the asymptotic regime. Either way, the coil rivals Earth's $\sim 5\times10^{-5}$ T field a hand's length from the wire.

examples.result: $\mu = 0.50\ \mathrm{A\cdot m^2}$; $B(10\ \mathrm{cm}) \approx 1.0\times10^{-4}$ T by dipole formula, $9.5\times10^{-5}$ T exactly.

examples.title: A Current-Carrying Coil as a Magnetic Dipole: wire-field check
examples.problem: Find $B = \mu_0I/2\pi r$ at $2.0\ \text{cm}$ from a long wire carrying $10\ \text{A}$.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: $B = 4\pi\times 10^{-7}\times 10/(2\pi\times 0.020)$.

examples.result: $B \approx 1.00\times 10^{-4}\ \text{T}$ circling the wire.

keyTakeaways: $\vec\mu = NiA\,\hat n$ with $\hat n$ set by the right-hand rule; the unit is A·m².
On the axis: exact $\mu_0 NiR^2/2(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}$, far field $\mu_0\mu/2\pi z^3$ — the dipole pattern.
The same $\mu$ governs torque $\mu B\sin\theta$, energy $-\mu B\cos\theta$, and the far field.

quiz.q: A loop lies flat on the page with current circulating clockwise as you view it. Its dipole moment points:
quiz.explanation: Curl the right fingers clockwise and the thumb points into the page.

quiz.q: Keeping area and current fixed, a coil's turns are tripled. Its dipole moment:
quiz.explanation: $\mu = NiA$ is linear in the number of turns.

quiz.q: Moving along a coil's axis from $z$ to $2z$ (both far compared with $R$), the field drops to:
quiz.explanation: The dipole far field falls off as $1/z^3$.

quiz.q: The torque on a magnetic dipole in field $B$ is maximum when the angle between $\vec\mu$ and $\vec B$ is:
quiz.explanation: $\tau = \mu B\sin\theta$ peaks at $\theta = 90°$.

intro: Oersted showed that current makes magnetism; a decade later Faraday ran the logic backward and found that magnetism makes electricity — but only while it changes. The rate at which magnetic flux sweeps through a circuit, not the flux itself, drives an emf. Lenz's minus sign tells the induced current which way to fight, and that fight is energy conservation in disguise.
objectives: Compute magnetic flux $\Phi_B = \int \vec B\cdot d\vec A$ (in webers) through flat surfaces
Apply Faraday's law $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt$ to flux changed by field, area, or orientation
Use Lenz's law to find the direction of the induced current and emf

concepts.statement: **The magnetic flux through a surface is** $$\Phi_B = \int \vec B\cdot d\vec A,$$ **in webers (1 Wb = 1 T·m²).** For a flat area $A$ in a uniform field making angle $\theta$ with the normal, $\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$.
concepts.detail: Flux counts field lines through the surface — nothing more. It can be positive or negative depending on which normal you choose; Faraday's law works with either choice as long as you stay consistent.

concepts.statement: **The emf around a circuit equals minus the rate of change of magnetic flux through it:** $$\mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt},$$ **and for a coil of $N$ turns, $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt$, where $\Phi_B$ is the flux through each turn.**
concepts.detail: Three independent ways to change $\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$: change $B$ (a ramping electromagnet), change $A$ (a loop sliding into or out of a field region), change $\theta$ (a rotating generator). Every power plant uses the third.

concepts.statement: **The induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change in flux that produces it.** Growing flux into the page through a loop drives a counterclockwise current (its own field points out of the page inside the loop); shrinking flux into the page drives a clockwise one.
concepts.detail: The minus sign in Faraday's law is Lenz's law written in algebra. Opposition, not cancellation: the induced field fights the change but never wins completely — a winning loop would violate energy conservation. Note that an emf exists whether or not a circuit is closed; the induced current requires a closed conducting path.

concepts.statement: **A rod of length $L$ sliding at speed $v$, with $v$ perpendicular to $\vec B$ and $L$ perpendicular to both, develops an emf** $$\mathcal{E} = BLv$$ **because it sweeps area at the rate $Lv$.**
concepts.detail: Rail problems close the rod through a resistance; the emf then drives a current $i = BLv/R$ and the field brakes the rod — the full story of section 30-2.

concepts.term: Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Faraday induction with Lenz's sign as energy conservation; the working equation is $\Phi_B = \int\vec B\cdot d\vec A$, $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt$, $U_B = \tfrac12Li^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (webers, volts, henries) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$; the minus sign is energy conservation; $\tau_L = L/R$.

figures.caption: Lenz's law in action. Left: flux into the page grows, so the induced current runs counterclockwise, making its own field out of the page. Right: flux into the page shrinks, so the current runs clockwise, reinforcing it. The galvanometer G registers the direction; in both panels $\mathcal{E} = -d\Phi_B/dt$.

examples.title: Coil in a ramping field
examples.problem: A 50-turn circular coil of area $A = 2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field that points into the page and grows steadily from 0.10 T to 0.60 T in 0.25 s. The coil's resistance is 0.40 Ω. Find the emf and current, and their directions.

steps.label: Rate of change
steps.text: $dB/dt = (0.60 - 0.10)/0.25 = +2.0$ T/s, still into the page.

steps.label: Per-turn emf
steps.text: The flux through each turn changes at $A\,dB/dt = (2.0\times10^{-3})(2.0) = 4.0\times10^{-3}$ Wb/s.

steps.label: Coil emf
steps.text: $|\mathcal{E}| = N\,A\,dB/dt = 50\times 4.0\times10^{-3} = 0.20$ V; then $i = \mathcal{E}/R = 0.20/0.40 = 0.50$ A.

steps.label: Direction
steps.text: Flux into the page is increasing, so by Lenz's law the induced current is counterclockwise — its own field points out of the page inside the coil.

examples.result: 0.20 V and 0.50 A counterclockwise while the field ramps; both drop to zero the instant $dB/dt$ returns to zero.

examples.title: Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law: Faraday numbers
examples.problem: A $300$-turn coil of area $0.010\ \text{m}^2$ sees $B$ rise $0.50\ \text{T}$ in $0.10\ \text{s}$. Find $|\mathcal{E}| = N\,d\Phi_B/dt$.

steps.label: Flux change
steps.text: $\Delta\Phi_B = A\Delta B = 0.010\times 0.50 = 5.0\times 10^{-3}\ \text{Wb}$ per turn.

steps.label: Sign
steps.text: Lenz opposes the rise — the induced $B$ points against the increase.

examples.result: $|\mathcal{E}| \approx 15\ \text{V}$.

keyTakeaways: $\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$ in webers; $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt$ — only the rate matters, never the amount.
Flux can change through $B$, $A$, or $\theta$; a rod sweeping area gives the motional emf $\mathcal{E} = BLv$.
Lenz's law points the induced current against the flux change — nature's built-in opposition, and energy conservation's enforcer.

quiz.q: A stationary circular loop sits in a steady, uniform 0.50 T field perpendicular to its plane. The induced emf is:
options: Equal to the flux through the loop
quiz.explanation: Steady flux means $d\Phi_B/dt = 0$ and therefore $\mathcal{E} = 0$.

quiz.q: The flux through a 10-turn coil changes steadily from 2.0 Wb to 6.0 Wb in 0.10 s. The average induced emf magnitude is:
quiz.explanation: $|\mathcal{E}| = N\,\Delta\Phi/\Delta t = 10\times 4.0/0.10 = 400$ V.

quiz.q: A loop lies in the plane of the page; a field pointing into the page through it is getting weaker. Viewed as drawn, the induced current is:
options: First one way, then the other
quiz.explanation: The induced current must make its own field into the page to oppose the decrease — that requires clockwise circulation.

quiz.q: A 0.25 m rod moves at 4.0 m/s perpendicular to a 0.60 T field. The motional emf between its ends is:

intro: A rod sliding on rails through a magnetic field is the whole story of induction in one picture: flux changes because area changes, current flows, and the field pushes back on the rod. Every joule of work done by whatever keeps the rod moving reappears as heat in the resistance — Lenz's law is energy conservation wearing a minus sign.
objectives: Compute emf, current, and magnetic drag for a rod moving on rails in a uniform field
Do the energy audit: applied mechanical power equals Joule heating
Find the terminal speed under a constant applied force and interpret it as an energy balance

concepts.statement: **A rod of length $L$ sliding at speed $v$ on frictionless rails across a field $\vec B$ (all three mutually perpendicular), with the rails shorted through a resistance $R$:** $$\mathcal{E} = BLv,\qquad i = \frac{BLv}{R},\qquad F = iLB = \frac{B^2L^2v}{R},$$ **the force being a drag that opposes the motion.**
concepts.detail: The drag exists because of Lenz's law: the induced current direction is exactly the one that makes the field push against the rod's motion, never with it.

concepts.statement: **Mechanical power in equals thermal power out: $Fv = i^2R = B^2L^2v^2/R$.** The applied force's work becomes electrical energy carried by the induced current and then heat in the resistance — none lost, none created.
concepts.detail: This is why Lenz's law must hold: if the induced current helped the motion instead of opposing it, the rod would accelerate while generating power — a perpetual-motion machine.

concepts.statement: **Under a constant pulling force $F$, the rod settles at** $$v_t = \frac{FR}{B^2L^2},$$ **where magnetic drag equals the pull. At terminal speed all the input power $Fv_t$ dissipates in $R$.**
concepts.detail: The approach to $v_t$ is exponential, exactly like a falling object reaching terminal velocity under air drag — the equation has the same structure.

concepts.term: Induction and Energy Transfers: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Induction and Energy Transfers problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Faraday induction with Lenz's sign as energy conservation; the working equation is $\Phi_B = \int\vec B\cdot d\vec A$, $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt$, $U_B = \tfrac12Li^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (webers, volts, henries) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$; the minus sign is energy conservation; $\tau_L = L/R$.

concepts.term: Induction and Energy Transfers: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Induction and Energy Transfers lives at $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$ and the textbook model holds while the minus sign is energy conservation; $\tau_L = L/R$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Induction and Energy Transfers calculation gives seconds when webers, volts, henries demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Rail rod driven at constant force — with audit
examples.problem: A rod with $L = 0.20$ m slides on rails through $B = 0.50$ T; the circuit resistance is $R = 0.40$ Ω. A constant force $F = 0.15$ N pulls it. Find the terminal speed, and audit the energy at that speed.

steps.label: Drag check
steps.text: $iLB = (1.5)(0.20)(0.50) = 0.15$ N — exactly the pull, as terminal speed requires.

steps.label: Energy audit
steps.text: Input $Fv_t = (0.15)(6.0) = 0.90$ W; heat $i^2R = (1.5)^2(0.40) = 0.90$ W. The books balance to the watt.

examples.result: The rod tops out at 6.0 m/s, carrying 1.5 A while converting all 0.90 W of pulling power into heat.

examples.title: Induction and Energy Transfers: Faraday numbers
examples.problem: A $400$-turn coil of area $0.010\ \text{m}^2$ sees $B$ rise $0.50\ \text{T}$ in $0.10\ \text{s}$. Find $|\mathcal{E}| = N\,d\Phi_B/dt$.

steps.label: Flux change
steps.text: $\Delta\Phi_B = A\Delta B = 0.010\times 0.50 = 5.0\times 10^{-3}\ \text{Wb}$ per turn.

steps.label: Sign
steps.text: Lenz opposes the rise — the induced $B$ points against the increase.

examples.result: $|\mathcal{E}| \approx 20\ \text{V}$.

keyTakeaways: Moving rod: $\mathcal{E} = BLv$, $i = BLv/R$, drag $F = B^2L^2v/R$ opposing the motion.
Energy conservation reads $Fv = i^2R$; Lenz's law is what guarantees the drag opposes the pull.
Constant force gives terminal speed $v_t = FR/(B^2L^2)$, reached exponentially.

quiz.q: The rod's speed doubles (same field, rod, and rail resistance). The magnetic drag on it:
quiz.explanation: The drag $B^2L^2v/R$ is proportional to the speed.

quiz.q: The rate at which thermal energy appears in the rail resistance equals:
quiz.explanation: Mechanical input converts entirely to heat: $Fv = i^2R$. (The emf is a voltage, not a power.)

quiz.q: Doubling $B$ (at fixed pulling force) changes the terminal speed to:
quiz.explanation: $v_t = FR/(B^2L^2)$ falls as $1/B^2$.

quiz.q: At terminal speed in the worked example, the current was 1.5 A and $R = 0.40$ Ω. The thermal power was:
quiz.explanation: $i^2R = (1.5)^2(0.40) = 0.90$ W — equal to the pulling power $Fv_t$.

intro: Stop thinking of electric fields as the exclusive product of charges. A changing magnetic field creates a curly electric field whose lines close on themselves — no start, no end, no potential to define anywhere. This is Faraday's law restated as a field law, and it is Maxwell's doorway to electromagnetic waves.
objectives: State the field form of Faraday's law, $\oint \vec E\cdot d\vec s = -d\Phi_B/dt$
Find the induced electric field inside and outside a long solenoid with changing current
Explain why the induced field is nonconservative and admits no potential difference

concepts.statement: **A changing magnetic flux through any closed curve drives a circulating electric field along it:** $$\oint \vec E\cdot d\vec s = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}.$$ **For a circular path of radius $r$ concentric with the changing-flux region, $E(2\pi r) = |d\Phi_B/dt|$.**
concepts.detail: The field lines are closed circles around the flux axis — unlike Coulomb fields they never begin or end on charges. A charge transported once around the loop picks up a nonzero emf.

concepts.term: Inside and outside a changing solenoid
concepts.statement: **For a solenoid of radius $R$ with uniform $dB/dt$ inside:** $$E = \frac{r}{2}\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right| \;\; (r \le R), \qquad E = \frac{R^2}{2r}\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right| \;\; (r \ge R).$$ **$E$ rises linearly to the wall, then falls as $1/r$ — it peaks at $r = R$.**
concepts.detail: Inside, the flux through the loop is only $\pi r^2\,dB/dt$ — the changing field within $r$ is all that counts. Outside, the loop catches the entire flux $\pi R^2\,dB/dt$ but spreads it over a longer circumference.

concepts.statement: **Because $\oint \vec E\cdot d\vec s \neq 0$ for induced fields, no potential function exists for them — potential difference is meaningless around a changing flux.**
concepts.detail: Coulomb fields (Chapter 24) are conservative and sourced by charges; induced fields are solenoidal and sourced by changing $\vec B$. In general both coexist: $\vec E_\text{total} = \vec E_\text{Coulomb} + \vec E_\text{induced}$. The induced component is what accelerates electrons in transformers and in the betatron.

concepts.statement: **Solve Induced Electric Fields problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Faraday induction with Lenz's sign as energy conservation; the working equation is $\Phi_B = \int\vec B\cdot d\vec A$, $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt$, $U_B = \tfrac12Li^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (webers, volts, henries) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$; the minus sign is energy conservation; $\tau_L = L/R$.

concepts.term: Induced Electric Fields: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Induced Electric Fields lives at $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$ and the textbook model holds while the minus sign is energy conservation; $\tau_L = L/R$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Induced Electric Fields calculation gives seconds when webers, volts, henries demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: E around a pulsed solenoid
examples.problem: A long solenoid of radius $R = 5.0$ cm carries a current that makes its interior field rise at $dB/dt = +4.0$ T/s into the page. Find the magnitude of the induced electric field at $r = R$, at $r = 2.5$ cm, and at $r = 10$ cm.

steps.label: Direction
steps.text: The flux into the page is increasing, so $\vec E$ circulates counterclockwise — the direction it would drive an opposing current.

examples.result: 0.10 V/m at the wall, 0.050 V/m at $R/2$ inside and at $2R$ outside — the profile is a tent peaking exactly at the solenoid wall.

examples.title: Induced Electric Fields: Faraday numbers
examples.problem: A $200$-turn coil of area $0.010\ \text{m}^2$ sees $B$ rise $0.50\ \text{T}$ in $0.10\ \text{s}$. Find $|\mathcal{E}| = N\,d\Phi_B/dt$.

steps.label: Flux change
steps.text: $\Delta\Phi_B = A\Delta B = 0.010\times 0.50 = 5.0\times 10^{-3}\ \text{Wb}$ per turn.

steps.label: Sign
steps.text: Lenz opposes the rise — the induced $B$ points against the increase.

examples.result: $|\mathcal{E}| \approx 10\ \text{V}$.

keyTakeaways: $\oint \vec E\cdot d\vec s = -d\Phi_B/dt$: changing magnetic flux creates circulating electric field.
Around a solenoid: $E = (r/2)dB/dt$ inside, $E = (R^2/2r)dB/dt$ outside — peak at $r = R$.
The induced field is nonconservative: no potential exists for it, and its lines are closed loops.

quiz.q: For one solenoid with fixed $dB/dt$, the induced $E$ at $r = R/2$ and at $r = 2R$ compare as:
quiz.explanation: Inside: $E = (R/4)dB/dt$; outside: $E = (R^2/4R)dB/dt$ — the same value on both sides of the wall.

quiz.q: If $dB/dt$ inside the solenoid is doubled, the induced $E$ at every point:
quiz.explanation: Both formulas are proportional to $dB/dt$.

quiz.q: A potential function $V$ can be defined for the induced electric field:
options: Always, since E is a field
Never, because the circulation of E is nonzero
quiz.explanation: A potential requires $\oint \vec E\cdot d\vec s = 0$, which the induced field violates.

quiz.q: Around a solenoid with changing current, the induced electric field is largest:
quiz.explanation: Linear growth inside plus $1/r$ decay outside — the peak sits at the wall.

intro: Coil a wire and the magnetic field it produces threads back through its own turns — a device whose flux is proportional to its own current. That proportionality constant is the inductance: pure geometry, measured in henrys, and the electrical inertia of every circuit you will analyze from here on.
objectives: Define inductance $L = N\Phi/i$ and its unit, the henry
Derive $L = \mu_0 n^2 A l$ for a long solenoid and evaluate it for real coils
Treat inductance as a geometric property, independent of the current

concepts.statement: **For a coil (inductor) whose own current $i$ produces flux $\Phi$ through each of its $N$ turns,** $$L = \frac{N\Phi}{i}.$$ **SI unit: the henry, 1 H = 1 Wb/A = 1 T·m²/A.**
concepts.detail: $L$ depends only on the coil's geometry (and any magnetic material inside it), never on the current: doubling $i$ doubles $\Phi$, and the ratio stands still.

concepts.statement: **A long solenoid with $n$ turns per unit length, length $l$, and cross-section area $A$ has** $$L = \mu_0 n^2 A l = \frac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l}.$$
concepts.detail: Derivation: inside, $B = \mu_0 n i$; each turn threads flux $\Phi = BA$; the $N = nl$ turns then give $N\Phi = \mu_0 n^2 A l\,i$. Note the quadratic in $n$: double the turn density and you double both the turns and the flux per turn.

concepts.term: The inductor as a circuit element
concepts.statement: **Circuit symbol: a coil. An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field and, like a capacitor, is defined by a single geometric number — its inductance.**
concepts.detail: Where a capacitor relates charge to voltage ($q = CV$), an inductor relates flux linkage to current ($N\Phi = Li$). The two devices are exact structural twins, which the coming sections exploit over and over.

concepts.statement: **Solve Inductors and Inductance problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Faraday induction with Lenz's sign as energy conservation; the working equation is $\Phi_B = \int\vec B\cdot d\vec A$, $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt$, $U_B = \tfrac12Li^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (webers, volts, henries) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$; the minus sign is energy conservation; $\tau_L = L/R$.

concepts.term: Inductors and Inductance: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Inductors and Inductance lives at $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$ and the textbook model holds while the minus sign is energy conservation; $\tau_L = L/R$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Inductors and Inductance calculation gives seconds when webers, volts, henries demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Inductance of a lab solenoid
examples.problem: A solenoid has 500 turns on a 50 cm length (so $n = 1000$ turns/m) and a cross-section of $A = 4.0\ \mathrm{cm^2}$. Find its inductance, then check it against the flux when $i = 2.0$ A.

steps.label: Field
steps.text: At 2.0 A the interior field is $B = \mu_0 n i = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(10^3)(2.0) = 2.5\times10^{-3}$ T.

steps.label: Consistency
steps.text: $N\Phi = (500)(1.0\times10^{-6}) = 5.0\times10^{-4}$ Wb, and $Li = (2.5\times10^{-4})(2.0) = 5.0\times10^{-4}$ Wb — identical, as the definition requires.

examples.result: The coil is a 0.25 mH inductor; at 2.0 A it links $5.0\times10^{-4}$ Wb of flux.

examples.title: Inductors and Inductance: Faraday numbers
examples.problem: A $300$-turn coil of area $0.010\ \text{m}^2$ sees $B$ rise $0.50\ \text{T}$ in $0.10\ \text{s}$. Find $|\mathcal{E}| = N\,d\Phi_B/dt$.

steps.label: Flux change
steps.text: $\Delta\Phi_B = A\Delta B = 0.010\times 0.50 = 5.0\times 10^{-3}\ \text{Wb}$ per turn.

steps.label: Sign
steps.text: Lenz opposes the rise — the induced $B$ points against the increase.

examples.result: $|\mathcal{E}| \approx 15\ \text{V}$.

keyTakeaways: $L = N\Phi/i$ in henrys; a geometric property of the coil, not of the current.
Long solenoid: $L = \mu_0 n^2 A l$ — quadratic in turns density.
The inductor pairs with the capacitor: flux–current mirrors charge–voltage.

quiz.q: A solenoid's turns-per-length $n$ is doubled (same length and area). Its inductance is:
quiz.explanation: $L = \mu_0 n^2 A l$ is quadratic in $n$.

quiz.q: One henry equals:
quiz.explanation: $L = N\Phi/i$ has units of Wb/A, defined as the henry.

quiz.q: Doubling the current in an inductor:
quiz.explanation: Flux grows proportionally with current; the ratio $N\Phi/i$ is fixed by geometry.

quiz.q: Two otherwise identical solenoids, one twice as long (same $n$). Their inductances compare as:
quiz.explanation: At fixed $n$, $L = \mu_0 n^2 A l$ scales linearly with length.

intro: Flip a switch and a coil fights the change: the growth of its own current changes its own flux, inducing an emf that pushes back. This is why current in an inductor cannot jump — the electrical analogue of mass refusing an instantaneous velocity change.
objectives: State the self-induced emf $\mathcal{E}_L = -L\,di/dt$ and find its direction
Explain why inductor current must be continuous while its voltage can jump
Estimate the emf developed when a current is switched on or interrupted

concepts.statement: **A changing current in an inductor induces in it an emf** $$\mathcal{E}_L = -L\,\frac{di}{dt}$$ **that opposes the change: growing current meets a back-emf; falling current is propped up by a forward emf.**
concepts.detail: This is Faraday's law with $N\Phi = Li$; the minus sign is Lenz's law applied to the coil's own flux. The emf exists even in an isolated superconducting loop — that is how persistent currents survive.

concepts.statement: **Inductance is to current what mass is to velocity: a finite $L$ forbids instantaneous changes of $i$.**
concepts.detail: For steady DC ($di/dt = 0$) the inductor is just a piece of wire; all its drama happens during changes. To change an inductor current at all, a source must supply energy that ends up in the magnetic field (section 30-7).

concepts.statement: **Interrupting an inductor's current quickly makes $|di/dt|$ enormous, and with it the emf $L|di/dt|$.** This is the principle of ignition coils — and the reason relay contacts arc as they open.
concepts.detail: Practical circuits put a freewheeling diode or an RC snubber across inductive loads to give the current a harmless path while it decays.

concepts.statement: **Solve Self-Induction problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Faraday induction with Lenz's sign as energy conservation; the working equation is $\Phi_B = \int\vec B\cdot d\vec A$, $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt$, $U_B = \tfrac12Li^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (webers, volts, henries) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$; the minus sign is energy conservation; $\tau_L = L/R$.

concepts.statement: **Self-Induction lives at $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$ and the textbook model holds while the minus sign is energy conservation; $\tau_L = L/R$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Self-Induction calculation gives seconds when webers, volts, henries demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Back-emf in a relay coil
examples.problem: A relay coil has $L = 20$ mH. Its current rises from 0 to 4.0 A in 2.0 ms when energized. Later, opening the switch interrupts the same current in about 0.10 ms. Find the self-induced emf magnitudes in the two events.

steps.label: Energizing
steps.text: $di/dt = 4.0/0.0020 = 2000$ A/s, so $|\mathcal{E}_L| = (0.020)(2000) = 40$ V — opposing the growth of current.

steps.label: Interpretation

intro: Connect a battery to a resistor and the current jumps to $V/R$. Insert an inductor and the current crawls: it approaches its final value on the timescale $\tau = L/R$, then decays on the same clock when the source is removed. One exponential, two stories — growth and decay.
objectives: Write the RL loop rule and solve it for exponential current growth and decay
Use the time constant $\tau = L/R$ and its 63% and 37% readings
Analyze RL circuits immediately after switching and long after switching

concepts.statement: **Growth (battery $\mathcal{E}$ in series with $R$ and $L$):** $$\mathcal{E} = iR + L\,\frac{di}{dt}.$$ **Decay (source replaced by a plain wire): $L\,di/dt + iR = 0$.**
concepts.detail: The initial slope of the growth curve is $\mathcal{E}/L$ — the inductor starts as a complete bottleneck. Solving the linear equation gives the exponentials of the next concept.

concepts.statement: **Growth:** $i = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$. **Decay:** $i = i_0 e^{-t/\tau}$. **Time constant:** $\tau = L/R$ — at $t = \tau$ the current has climbed to 63% of its final value (or fallen to 37% of its start).**
concepts.detail: At $t = 3\tau$ the current is 95% of the way; by $5\tau$ the circuit is settled for all practical purposes. A bigger $L$ means more sluggishness; a bigger $R$ means less final current but a shorter clock.

concepts.statement: **At the instant of switching, an inductor holds its current — it acts like an open switch if that current was zero. Long after, with $di/dt = 0$, it acts like a plain wire.**
concepts.detail: Continuity of current, not of voltage, is the invariant — this single rule answers most qualitative RL questions instantly.

concepts.statement: **Solve RL Circuits problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is Faraday induction with Lenz's sign as energy conservation; the working equation is $\Phi_B = \int\vec B\cdot d\vec A$, $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt$, $U_B = \tfrac12Li^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (webers, volts, henries) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$; the minus sign is energy conservation; $\tau_L = L/R$.

concepts.statement: **RL Circuits lives at $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$ and the textbook model holds while the minus sign is energy conservation; $\tau_L = L/R$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a RL Circuits calculation gives seconds when webers, volts, henries demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $\Phi_B\sim 10^{-4}$--$10^{-2}\ \text{Wb}$; $L\sim \text{mH}$--$\text{H}$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

intro: Building current in an inductor takes work: the source must push against the back-emf the whole time the current grows. Where does that work go? Into the magnetic field itself. The coil is a storehouse, and $\frac12 Li^2$ is its inventory.
objectives: Derive $U_B = \frac12 Li^2$ from the power balance of an RL circuit
Compute stored energy and the power released during decay
Use the capacitor analogy $\frac12 q^2/C \leftrightarrow \frac12 Li^2$

concepts.statement: **An inductor carrying current $i$ stores** $$U_B = \tfrac12 L i^2.$$
concepts.detail: Derivation: multiplying the RL loop rule by $i$ gives $\mathcal{E}i = i^2R + Li\,di/dt$. The last term is $dU_B/dt$, so $dU_B = Li\,di$, and integrating from 0 to $i$ gives $\frac12 Li^2$. The source heats the resistor and fills the field's store, nothing else.

concepts.statement: **$U_B = \frac12 Li^2$ mirrors the capacitor's $U_E = \frac12 q^2/C$: in both, a state variable squared over a geometric constant, fully recoverable.**
concepts.detail: An ideal LC circuit shuttles the entire inventory back and forth between the two forms (Chapter 31); a discharging RL circuit cashes it out as heat.

concepts.statement: **When the current decays through $R$, $dU_B/dt = -i^2R$: the field's inventory is exactly the heat delivered, $\int i^2R\,dt = \frac12 Li_0^2$.**
concepts.detail: That is why interrupting an inductive current arcs across the gap: the field dumps its stored energy into the first available path, however small.

intro: Divide the solenoid's stored energy by its volume and the coil disappears from the formula: only the field strength survives. Magnetic energy lives in space itself, at a density $B^2/2\mu_0$ — a result true for any field configuration, and half of the energy bookkeeping of electromagnetic waves.
objectives: Derive $u_B = B^2/2\mu_0$ from the solenoid formulas
Evaluate magnetic energy density for laboratory and everyday fields
Combine it with the electric energy density in preparation for electromagnetic waves

concepts.statement: **A magnetic field of magnitude $B$ stores energy at the density** $$u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$$ **per unit volume, in J/m³.**
concepts.detail: Derivation for a solenoid: $U_B = \frac12 Li^2$ with $L = \mu_0 n^2 A l$ and $B = \mu_0 n i$ gives $U_B = (B^2/2\mu_0)(Al)$; divide by the volume $Al$. The result depends only on the local field, so it holds for any $\vec B$, whatever the source — the same logic that freed $u_E = \frac12\varepsilon_0 E^2$ from the parallel-plate capacitor.

concepts.statement: **The energy is stored in space throughout the field region — between transformer cores, around transmission lines, inside an MRI bore — not in the copper wire.**
concepts.detail: Wherever $\vec B$ exists, $u_B$ is banked there; add up $u_B$ over all space and you recover the circuit quantity $\frac12 Li^2$.

concepts.statement: **Total field energy density: $u = \frac12\varepsilon_0 E^2 + B^2/2\mu_0$.** In an electromagnetic wave (Chapter 33) the two terms trade as the wave travels, with $E = cB$ making them equal.
concepts.detail: Magnitudes hint at why technology stores energy magnetically: a 1 T field holds $4\times10^5$ J/m³, while air at its breakdown field (about $3\times10^6$ V/m) supports only about 40 J/m³ of electric energy — a factor of ten thousand.

intro: Bring two coils near each other and a changing current in one induces an emf in the other — no wires, no charges crossing, just field threading turns. The coupling constant between them is the mutual inductance, and its deepest property is a symmetry: M is the same measured either way. Transformers, wireless chargers, and every metal detector live on this number.
objectives: Define mutual inductance via $\mathcal{E}_2 = -M\,di_1/dt$ and compute it for coaxial solenoids
State and use the reciprocity theorem $M_{12} = M_{21}$
Connect coupling to the energy stored in a pair of coupled coils

concepts.statement: **If current $i_1$ in coil 1 produces flux $\Phi_{21}$ through each of the $N_2$ turns of coil 2, then $M = N_2\Phi_{21}/i_1$ and a changing $i_1$ induces** $$\mathcal{E}_2 = -M\,\frac{di_1}{dt}.$$ **Unit: the henry.**
concepts.detail: $M$ depends only on the geometry, separation, and orientation of the pair — never on the currents or their rate of change. It is the two-coil generalization of self-inductance.

concepts.statement: **$M_{12} = M_{21}$: the mutual inductance is identical in both directions.** Drive either coil and measure the emf in the other; you get the same $M$. The proof — from energy conservation — is the masters section below.
concepts.detail: This is not obvious: the flux pattern coil 1 makes in coil 2 looks nothing like the reverse. That one number describes both directions is a deep symmetry of electromagnetism.

concepts.statement: **A coil of $N_2$ turns wrapped tightly around a long inner solenoid ($n_1$ turns per meter, cross-section $A$) has mutual inductance** $$M = \mu_0 n_1 N_2 A.$$
concepts.detail: Only the inner solenoid's field — uniform and contained — contributes; the outer coil's turns catch all of it, each threading $\Phi = \mu_0 n_1 i_1 A$. Ideal nested solenoids are perfectly coupled: $M = \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$.

concepts.statement: **Define $k = M/\sqrt{L_1 L_2}$; then $0 \le k \le 1$, with $k = 1$ only when every field line from one coil links every turn of the other.**
concepts.detail: Iron-core transformers reach $k \approx 0.95$–0.99; well-aligned coaxial coils, $k \approx 0.5$–0.9; distant loose coils, $k \ll 1$. Wireless charging pads and RFID readers live on moderate $k$; leakage flux is what makes real transformers imperfect.

depth.title: Reciprocity: why M₁₂ = M₂₁ — symmetry from energy conservation

blocks.body: Two stationary coils, fixed relative positions. Define $M_{21}$ by $\mathcal{E}_2 = -M_{21}\,di_1/dt$ (drive coil 1, read coil 2) and $M_{12}$ by $\mathcal{E}_1 = -M_{12}\,di_2/dt$ (drive 2, read 1). Nothing in the definitions promises equality — the two flux patterns look completely different from the two ends. Yet experiments always return one number. Energy conservation forces it.

blocks.heading: Neumann reciprocity theorem
blocks.body: For any two stationary filamentary circuits in vacuum (or in any linear magnetic medium), $$M_{12} = M_{21}.$$ The mutual inductance is a property of the pair, not of an order of measurement.

blocks.heading: The two-assembly argument
blocks.body: Bring the system from rest to final currents $(I_1, I_2)$ along two different schedules and demand the same stored energy — legitimate because the magnetic field, and hence the energy, is determined by the final currents alone. **Schedule A:** first raise $i_1: 0 \to I_1$ with coil 2 open. No current flows in coil 2, so only coil 1's source works: $W_1 = \frac12 L_1 I_1^2$. Then raise $i_2: 0 \to I_2$ with coil 1 closed at $I_1$. Coil 2's source supplies $\frac12 L_2 I_2^2$, but coil 1's source must also hold its current against the emf $\mathcal{E}_1 = -M_{12}\,di_2/dt$ induced by the changing $i_2$: the extra power is $-\mathcal{E}_1 I_1 = M_{12} I_1\,di_2/dt$, an extra work $M_{12} I_1 I_2$ over the ramp. Total: $$U_A = \tfrac12 L_1 I_1^2 + \tfrac12 L_2 I_2^2 + M_{12} I_1 I_2.$$ **Schedule B:** raise $i_2$ first, then $i_1$; the same bookkeeping gives $$U_B = \tfrac12 L_1 I_1^2 + \tfrac12 L_2 I_2^2 + M_{21} I_1 I_2.$$ Same final currents, same fields, so $U_A = U_B$; subtracting, $M_{12} = M_{21}$.

blocks.heading: The Neumann formula
blocks.body: Applying Biot–Savart to coil 1 and integrating the resulting flux over coil 2's turns yields the double line integral $$M = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\oint_{1}\oint_{2}\frac{d\vec s_1\cdot d\vec s_2}{|\vec r_1 - \vec r_2|},$$ which is manifestly symmetric under $1 \leftrightarrow 2$ — reciprocity in one line of algebra. For the coaxial solenoid pair of this section only the interior field survives the integral, and either evaluation order returns $M = \mu_0 n_1 N_2 A$.

blocks.heading: How coupled can two coils be?
blocks.body: Writing $k = M/\sqrt{L_1 L_2}$, a Cauchy–Schwarz-type bound on the flux overlap gives $0 \le k \le 1$. Perfect coupling ($k = 1$) requires every field line produced by either coil to link every turn of the other — the ideal-transformer dream; leakage flux is what pushes $k$ below 1 in real devices. Note the corollary: two perfectly coupled ideal coils share one common flux, which is exactly what makes the ideal transformer of Chapter 31 possible.

blocks.heading: Ignition coil
blocks.body: An automotive ignition coil is mutual inductance weaponized: a 12 V battery drives a few hundred primary turns through a switching transistor; interrupting that current (a large $di_1/dt$) induces in the roughly 20,000-turn secondary an emf of 15–30 kV, and the spark plug fires. The turns ratio sets the voltage step-up, while $k \approx 0.95$ sets the efficiency: nearly all of the primary's stored magnetic energy $\frac12 L_1 i_1^2$ reappears across the spark gap. The same physics scaled down runs switch-mode power supplies.

keyTakeaways: $\mathcal{E}_2 = -M\,di_1/dt$ with $M = N_2\Phi_{21}/i_1$ in henrys — geometry only.
$M_{12} = M_{21}$ always; nested ideal solenoids give $M = \mu_0 n_1 N_2 A$ and $k = 1$.
Coupling $k = M/\sqrt{L_1L_2} \le 1$ measures leakage; transformers and wireless chargers are engineered $k$.

quiz.explanation: An iron core funnels nearly all flux through both windings: $k \approx 0.95$–0.99.

intro: Charge a capacitor, connect it to an inductor, and let go: the charge sloshes back and forth at a rate fixed by nothing but $L$ and $C$. The circuit is the electrical twin of a mass on a spring — the same cosine, the same energy trade, and a frequency you dial with components.

Track the exchange between capacitor energy $q^2/2C$ and inductor energy $\frac12 Li^2$

concepts.term: Loop rule to simple harmonic motion
concepts.statement: **Kirchhoff's loop rule around an ideal LC circuit reads** $$L\frac{di}{dt} + \frac{q}{C} = 0,\qquad i = \frac{dq}{dt} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}\,q = 0.$$ **It is the simple-harmonic equation with $\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}$.**
concepts.detail: Signs: as the capacitor discharges, the charge $q$ on the plates decreases while the current grows — $i = dq/dt$ with the sign convention fixed by which plate you label positive. The oscillation frequency $f = \omega/2\pi$ depends on neither the charge nor the current: it is a property of the circuit, like a bell's pitch.

concepts.statement: **With the capacitor fully charged at $t = 0$ (charge $Q$):** $$q = Q\cos\omega t, \qquad i = -\omega Q \sin\omega t.$$ **The current peaks a quarter cycle after the charge, with $I = \omega Q$.**
concepts.detail: The charge is zero exactly when the current is maximum, and vice versa — they trade extremes every quarter period $T/4 = \pi\sqrt{LC}/2$.

concepts.statement: **Capacitor energy $U_E = q^2/2C$ and inductor energy $U_B = \frac12 Li^2$ trade places every quarter cycle while their sum stays exactly** $$U = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = \frac12 LI^2.$$
concepts.detail: Nothing is dissipated: ideal L and C only exchange energy, storing it first as electric field between the plates, then as magnetic field around the coil.

concepts.statement: **$q \leftrightarrow x$, $i \leftrightarrow v$, $1/C \leftrightarrow k$, $L \leftrightarrow m$**: every result of mechanical oscillations translates by direct substitution, including damping once a resistor joins (next section).**
concepts.detail: The analogy explains why heavy coils (large $L$) oscillate slowly and stiff capacitors (small $C$, large $1/C$) oscillate fast — inertia against restoring force.

concepts.statement: **Solve LC Oscillations problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is $LC$/$RLC$ resonance and AC power; the working equation is $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$, $X_L = \omega L$, $X_C = 1/\omega C$, $Z = \sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (ohms, hertz, phase angle) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $f_0\sim \text{kHz}$--$\text{MHz}$ for $\text{mH}$--$\mu\text{F}$; sinusoidal steady state for phasors; peak $I$ at $\omega_d = \omega_0$.
