examples.title: A projector lens
examples.problem: A slide 2.0 cm tall sits 15 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Locate and size the image.

steps.label: Image distance
steps.text: $i = +30$ cm, on the far side — real, because $i > 0$, and light truly passes through it (that is where the screen goes).

steps.label: Magnification
steps.text: $m = -i/p = -30/15 = -2.0$: inverted and doubled.

steps.label: Image height
steps.text: $h’ = mh = (-2.0)(2.0\ \mathrm{cm}) = -4.0$ cm — 4.0 cm tall, upside down on the screen.

examples.result: Real inverted image, 4.0 cm tall, 30 cm beyond the lens — hence the slide must be inserted upside down.

examples.title: Thin Lenses: thin-lens numbers
examples.problem: A converging lens has $f = 10\ \text{cm}$; an object sits at $p = 50\ \text{cm}$. Locate the image via $1/f = 1/p+1/i$.

steps.label: Image
steps.text: $i \approx 12.5\ \text{cm}$ (real, since $i > 0$).

steps.label: Magnification
steps.text: $m = -i/p \approx -0.25$.

examples.result: $i \approx 12.5\ \text{cm}$, $m \approx -0.25$.

keyTakeaways: Thin lenses: $1/p + 1/i = 1/f$ with $m = -i/p$ — converging $f>0$, diverging $f<0$.
Real images form on the far side ($i>0$) and can be caught on a screen; virtual ones share the object’s side.
Lenses in contact add powers: $1/f = 1/f_1 + 1/f_2$ (diopters add).

quiz.q: An object sits at twice the focal length ($p = 2f$) of a converging lens. The image is:
quiz.explanation: Symmetric imaging: $i = 2f$, $m = -1$.

quiz.q: An object is placed inside the focal length of a converging lens. The image is:
quiz.explanation: Like a magnifying glass: $p < f$ gives $i < 0$ and $|m| > 1$.

quiz.q: A diverging lens always forms, for any real object, an image that is:
quiz.explanation: With $f < 0$, $i$ is negative and $|i| < p$ for every $p$: virtual, upright, smaller.

quiz.q: Two thin lenses in contact have $f_1 = 20$ cm and $f_2 = +5.0$ cm (the second converging, the first — check the sign!). Taking both converging, $f_1 = 20$ cm and $f_2 = 5.0$ cm, the combination focal length is:
quiz.explanation: $1/f = 1/20 + 1/5 = 5/20$, so $f = 4.0$ cm: powers add, focal lengths do not.

intro: Instruments are lenses arranged with intent. The eye brings the world onto the retina by accommodation; a simple magnifier lets the eye relax while viewing virtual images up close; the microscope and telescope chain two lenses to stretch angular magnification across nine orders of magnitude in scale — from bacteria to galaxies.
objectives: Model the eye: retina as screen, near point, accommodation, and corrective lenses
Compute simple magnification $m = (25\ \mathrm{cm})/f$ of a magnifier
Compute angular magnifications of compound microscope and refracting telescope

concepts.statement: **A converging lens (cornea plus variable lens) forms a real, inverted image on the retina.** *Accommodation* — tensing the ciliary muscles — shortens the focal length to focus near objects. The *near point* is the closest sharp focus (about 25 cm in a young adult); the *far point* is infinity for a normal eye.

**A diverging lens is prescribed for a myopic (nearsighted) eye whose far point is finite:** the lens images distant objects at the far point. **A converging lens is prescribed for a hyperopic (farsighted) eye whose near point has receded:** it images the near point onto a comfortable closer distance. The power in diopters is just $1/f$.

**A single converging lens used with the image at the viewer’s near point gives** $$M = \frac{25\ \mathrm{cm}}{f}$$ **angular magnification** (25 cm the reference near point). The lens lets the object sit at $f$ or closer while the eye focuses comfortably, enlarging the angle it subtends.

**Objective (short $f_\text{ob}$) makes a real enlarged image of a near object; the eyepiece magnifies that image.** With the tube image at the near point, $$M = -\frac{s}{f_\text{ob}}\cdot\frac{25\ \mathrm{cm}}{f_\text{ey}},$$ with $s \approx$ tube length (17 cm standard) and $P = 25$ cm the near-point distance.

**Objective of long focal length forms a real image of a distant object near its focal plane; the eyepiece magnifies it:** $$M = -\frac{f_\text{ob}}{f_\text{ey}}.$$ The image is inverted, and angular magnification is simply the ratio of focal lengths. Large $f_\text{ob}$ is why observatory refractors were (and are) long tubes.

examples.title: A backyard telescope
examples.problem: A refracting telescope has an objective of focal length 900 mm and an eyepiece of 25 mm. Find its angular magnification, and the magnification of a microscope with $f_\text{ob} = 0.50$ cm, tube distance 17 cm, and $f_\text{ey} = 2.5$ cm.

steps.label: Telescope
steps.text: $M = -f_\text{ob}/f_\text{ey} = -(900\ \mathrm{mm})/(25\ \mathrm{mm}) = -36$.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: The minus sign: the sky appears inverted (astronomers shrug; a correcting prism fixes it for terrestrial use).

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.text: $M = -(34)(10) = -340$: the object appears 340 times larger in angle.

examples.result: Telescope $M = -36$; microscope $M = -340$ — both inverted.

examples.title: Optical Instruments: thin-lens numbers
examples.problem: A converging lens has $f = 10\ \text{cm}$; an object sits at $p = 30\ \text{cm}$. Locate the image via $1/f = 1/p+1/i$.

steps.label: Image
steps.text: $i \approx 15\ \text{cm}$ (real, since $i > 0$).

steps.label: Magnification
steps.text: $m = -i/p \approx -0.5$.

examples.result: $i \approx 15\ \text{cm}$, $m \approx -0.5$.

keyTakeaways: The eye is a variable-f converging system imaging onto the retina; near point ≈ 25 cm, far point ∞ when normal.
Diverging lenses correct myopia, converging lenses correct hyperopia; magnifiers give $M = 25\ \mathrm{cm}/f$.
Microscope: $M = -(s/f_\text{ob})(25\,\mathrm{cm}/f_\text{ey})$; telescope: $M = -f_\text{ob}/f_\text{ey}$ — focal-length ratios do all the work.

quiz.q: The image formed on the retina by a normal eye is:
quiz.explanation: The eye’s lens converges real light through the retina: $m < 0$; the brain re-inverts it.

quiz.q: A farsighted (hyperopic) eye most needs:
quiz.explanation: Hyperopia means the near point is too far out; converging power brings close objects to focus on the retina.

quiz.q: A simple magnifier of focal length 5.0 cm gives (near point 25 cm) an angular magnification of about:
To increase the angular magnification of a refracting telescope, one should:
options: lengthen the objective focal length or shorten the eyepiece focal length
quiz.explanation: $M = -f_\text{ob}/f_\text{ey}$: maximize the ratio. (Tube diameter sets light-gathering, not magnification.)

intro: The formulas of this chapter have been used freely; now they are earned. The three proofs — plane-mirror equality of distances, the spherical-mirror equation, and the single refracting surface — all run on the same engine: ray geometry plus one small-angle approximation. Checking exactly how good that approximation is tells us when spherical optics is trustworthy and when it fails.
objectives: Prove $i = -p$ for a plane mirror from ray geometry
Derive the spherical mirror equation from the geometry of a single reflected ray
Derive $n_1/p + n_2/i = (n_2-n_1)/r$ for a refracting surface, and quantify the small-angle approximation

concepts.statement: **In similar triangles formed by object, image and mirror, the two perpendicular distances are equal.** The right triangles from object tip and image tip to any reflection point share a side along the mirror and equal base angles (law of reflection), so $|i| = p$; the image is behind the mirror ($i < 0$) because the reflected rays diverge as if from there.

**Take a ray from the object tip through the center of curvature C: it reflects back on itself and passes through the image tip.** A second ray to the mirror vertex reflects symmetrically. Comparing triangles and using the exterior-angle relation $\beta = \alpha + \theta$, $\gamma = \alpha + 2\theta$, the small-angle limit yields $1/p + 1/i = 2/r = 1/f$.
concepts.detail: The algebra: eliminating $\theta$ between $\alpha + 2\beta = \gamma + 2\delta$ style angle sums and the arc relation $\tan\alpha \approx \alpha$ etc. gives the result. Its validity is the small-angle assumption — see the third concept.

concepts.statement: **The proofs use $\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta \approx \theta$ (in radians).** The table of errors: $\theta = 10^\circ$: sine 0.02% low, tangent 0.1% low; $\theta = 20^\circ$: 0.01% and 0.2%; $\theta = 30^\circ$: 0.07% and 1.0%; $\theta = 45^\circ$: 0.35% and 5.3%. Rays must stay near the axis — paraxial optics — for the equations to hold.

**When paraxial fails, parallel rays far from the axis reflect inside the focal point.** For a mirror of radius 20 cm, rays at height 1.0 cm cross the axis 9.99 cm from the vertex (deficit 0.01 cm), at 5.0 cm height 9.67 cm, at 8.0 cm height 9.09 cm — a blur, not a point. Parabolic mirrors (and aspheric lenses) fix this exactly, which is why telescopes are parabolas.

**Solve Three Proofs problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is geometric imaging with mirrors and thin lenses; the working equation is $1/f = 1/p+1/i$, $m = -i/p$, $n_1/p+n_2/i = (n_2-n_1)/r$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (centimeters and dimensionless $m$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $f\sim 10\ \text{cm}$ lab lenses; $m\sim -1$ to $+5$; paraxial, thin, small angles; fix one sign convention once.

examples.title: How good is the paraxial approximation?
examples.problem: For a spherical mirror of radius 20 cm ($f = 10$ cm), find where a ray parallel to the axis, hitting at height $h$, crosses the axis after reflection, for $h = 1.0$, 5.0 and 8.0 cm.

steps.label: Ray geometry
steps.text: A parallel ray at height $h$ strikes the mirror where $r^2 = h^2 + s^2$ ($s$ measured along the axis from the center of curvature). The reflected ray crosses the axis at $x = r - r^2/(2s)$ from the vertex.

steps.label: Large h
steps.text: $h = 8.0$ cm: $s = \sqrt{400-64} = 18.33$ cm, $x = 20 - 400/36.67 = 9.09$ cm — nearly a centimeter inside the focal point: spherical aberration in action.

examples.result: Crossing points 9.99, 9.67, 9.09 cm: only near-axis rays honor $f = r/2$.

examples.title: Three Proofs: thin-lens numbers
examples.problem: A converging lens has $f = 10\ \text{cm}$; an object sits at $p = 40\ \text{cm}$. Locate the image via $1/f = 1/p+1/i$.

steps.label: Image
steps.text: $i \approx 13.3\ \text{cm}$ (real, since $i > 0$).

steps.label: Magnification
steps.text: $m = -i/p \approx -0.333$.

examples.result: $i \approx 13.3\ \text{cm}$, $m \approx -0.333$.

keyTakeaways: All three imaging equations follow from ray geometry plus the law of reflection or Snell’s law.
The derivations assume $\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta \approx \theta$ (radians) — excellent below about 10°, poor by 45°.
Off-axis rays miss the focus (spherical aberration); parabolic surfaces fix mirrors exactly.

quiz.q: At $20^\circ$, the small-angle approximation $\tan\theta \approx \theta$ is off by about:
quiz.explanation: $\tan 20^\circ$ is 0.2% below $20^\circ$ in radians; $\sin 20^\circ$ is within 0.01%.

quiz.q: In the mirror-equation derivation, the relation between angles at the mirror is ultimately a statement of:
options: the exterior-angle theorem for triangles plus the law of reflection
quiz.explanation: The angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \theta$ are tied by triangle exterior angles; reflection sets the incidence equal to the reflection angle.

quiz.q: Parallel rays striking a spherical concave mirror far from the axis reflect to points:
quiz.explanation: Spherical aberration: marginal rays cross the axis short of the paraxial focus — a paraboloid is needed for exact focusing.

quiz.q: The plane-mirror proof that $|i| = p$ mostly relies on:
options: similar right triangles and equal reflection angles
quiz.explanation: Two right triangles sharing the mirror-side segment have equal angles, hence equal legs.

intro: What is physics of interference? Rays and shadows were the language of the last chapter, and they hide the most important fact about light: it is a wave. When light passes through narrow openings or across sharp edges it bends and spreads — it diffracts — and when two portions of the same wave overlap they add or cancel to produce patterns of light and dark called interference. This section builds the wave picture the whole chapter runs on: Huygens' principle for propagation, the law of refraction as a wave consequence, what happens to wavelength inside a medium, and the coherence condition that makes interference visible at all.
objectives: State Huygens' principle and use it to derive the law of refraction, $n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$
Compute the speed, wavelength and frequency of light inside a medium of index of refraction $n$
Define coherence and explain why ordinary light sources produce interference only in special arrangements

concepts.statement: **Every point of an advancing wavefront acts as a source of spherical secondary wavelets that spread out at the wave speed; the wavefront a time $t$ later is the envelope — the surface tangent to — all these wavelets.** The construction predicts where the wave goes next, and it works for any wave, water or light.
concepts.detail: Proposed in 1678, it is a geometric recipe rather than a theory: give me a wavefront now and I will draw the wavefront later. It becomes quantitative when each wavelet is drawn with radius $vt$.

concepts.statement: **When a wavefront crosses a boundary between media, the travel times of its two ends fix the bend:** with speeds $v_1 = c/n_1$ and $v_2 = c/n_2$, $$n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2,$$ where $n = c/v$ is the index of refraction.
concepts.detail: Sketch: a plane wavefront of width $w$ meets the surface at angle $\theta_1$. While one end travels a distance $v_1 t$ along the front in medium 1, the other end crosses and travels $v_2 t$ in medium 2; the two right triangles share a hypotenuse, giving $\sin\theta_1/\sin\theta_2 = v_1/v_2 = n_2/n_1$. Dispersion — the slow drift of $n$ with wavelength that prisms exploit — enters simply because $n(\lambda)$ is not constant: each color bends by its own amount.

concepts.statement: **Crossing a boundary cannot change the wave's frequency** — the oscillation handed from medium to medium must stay in step at the interface — so with $v = f\lambda$ in each medium, $$v = \frac{c}{n},\qquad \lambda_n = \frac{\lambda}{n}.$$ The wavelength shrinks in the denser medium; the frequency (and the color you perceive) does not change.
concepts.detail: This $\lambda_n$ is the wavelength that must appear in every film and slit formula when the light travels inside a medium of index $n$.

concepts.statement: **Two waves are coherent if they have the same frequency and a phase difference that stays constant in time.** Only coherent overlapping waves produce a stable interference pattern — fringes that hold still long enough to see.
concepts.detail: Ordinary (thermal) light is emitted in random bursts of about $10^{-8}$ s, so two independent bulbs are coherent only for that flickering instant: their pattern jitters too fast to see. The fix is to derive both interfering waves from the SAME wavefront, as Young did — or to use a laser, whose stimulated emission holds phase over meters.

concepts.statement: **Diffraction — the spreading of a wave around edges and through openings — becomes significant when the opening is comparable in size to the wavelength.** For a window (meters) versus visible light ($\lambda \sim 5\times 10^{-7}$ m), the spreading angle is microscopic and ray optics works; for a 0.1 mm slit it is a few tenths of a degree and the wave cannot be ignored.
concepts.detail: Ray optics is the $\lambda \to 0$ limit of wave optics. This chapter (interference) and the next (diffraction) are the wave-optics chapters; the distinction between them is bookkeeping, not physics.

examples.title: Red light entering water
examples.problem: A laser emits vacuum wavelength $\lambda = 700$ nm. The beam enters water, whose index of refraction is $n = 1.33$. Find the speed, wavelength and frequency of the light in the water.

steps.label: Speed
steps.text: Inside the water the speed is $v = c/n = (2.998\times 10^{8})/1.33 = 2.26\times 10^{8}$ m/s.

steps.label: Wavelength
steps.text: The frequency is fixed at the source, so the wavelength must shrink: $\lambda_n = \lambda/n = (700\ \mathrm{nm})/1.33 = 526$ nm.

steps.label: Frequency
steps.text: In vacuum, $f = c/\lambda = (2.998\times 10^{8})/(700\times 10^{-9}) = 4.28\times 10^{14}$ Hz — unchanged in the water, as the check $v/\lambda_n = (2.26\times 10^{8})/(526\times 10^{-9}) = 4.28\times 10^{14}$ Hz confirms.

steps.label: Period
steps.text: One oscillation takes $T = 1/f = 2.3\times 10^{-15}$ s — a couple of femtoseconds, which is why the wave nature only shows at small scales.

examples.result: In water: $v = 2.26\times 10^{8}$ m/s, $\lambda_n = 526$ nm, $f = 4.28\times 10^{14}$ Hz (unchanged) — the light is still red.

examples.title: Light as a Wave: fringe-spacing check
examples.problem: In Young's setup $\lambda = 550\ \text{nm}$, $d = 0.1\ \text{mm}$, $L = 1.00\ \text{m}$. Find the $m = 1$ fringe position $y = m\lambda L/d$.

steps.label: SI
steps.text: $\lambda = 5.50\times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}$, $d = 0.1\times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}$.

steps.label: Millimeters
steps.text: $y \approx 5.5\ \text{mm}$.

examples.result: $y_1 \approx 5.5\ \text{mm}$ from center.

keyTakeaways: Huygens: a wavefront is the envelope of secondary wavelets of radius $vt$; refraction follows from the changed wave speed, $n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$ with $n = c/v$.
Frequency survives every boundary; speed and wavelength do not: $v = c/n$ and $\lambda_n = \lambda/n$.
Stable interference demands coherent sources — same frequency, fixed phase difference — which is why both slits must be lit by the same incident wave.

quiz.q: Light of vacuum wavelength 600 nm enters glass with index of refraction 1.5. Which quantity stays unchanged?
quiz.explanation: The frequency is fixed by the source; crossing the boundary changes the speed to $c/n$ and the wavelength to $\lambda/n$.

quiz.q: Two light waves can produce a stable interference pattern only if they are coherent, meaning they have:
options: the same frequency and a phase difference that stays constant in time
phases that are both exactly zero
quiz.explanation: Coherence = same frequency + fixed phase difference. Anything else makes the pattern average away.

quiz.q: In Huygens' construction, the wavefront a short time later is:
options: the line through the centers of the wavelets
the envelope — the tangent surface — of the secondary wavelets
any one of the secondary wavelets
the perpendicular bisector of the wavelets
quiz.explanation: Each point emits a wavelet of radius $vt$; the new wavefront is the surface tangent to them all — Huygens' principle.

quiz.q: Wave optics (interference, diffraction) must be used rather than ray optics when:
options: the openings or obstacles are comparable in size to the wavelength
the index of refraction exceeds one
quiz.explanation: Spreading and interference are strongest when the geometry is measured in wavelengths; ray optics is the short-wavelength limit.

intro: In 1801 Thomas Young let sunlight fall on a single pinhole and then on two more pinholes close together, and on a distant screen he saw something Newton's particle picture of light could not explain: alternating bright and dark bands — interference fringes — exactly like overlapping water ripples. Because the two slits are lit by the same wavefront, they act as coherent, in-phase sources, and the waves they send to any point on the screen arrive with a path difference that varies from point to point: bright where the difference is a whole number of wavelengths, dark where it is a half-odd number. This section sets up the geometry and the fringe formulas.
objectives: Describe Young's arrangement and explain why deriving both slits from one wavefront guarantees coherence
Apply the conditions $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ for maxima and $d\sin\theta = (m+\tfrac12)\lambda$ for minima
Compute fringe positions and the fringe spacing $\Delta y = \lambda D/d$ on a screen at distance $D$

concepts.statement: **Monochromatic light first passes a single slit $S$ (the source) and then a double slit $S_1, S_2$ of separation $d$; a viewing screen sits a distance $D$ away, with $D \gg d$.** Both slits sit on the same wavefront, so they are forced into coherence and radiate in phase — the single first slit is what makes the whole experiment work.
concepts.detail: With slits wide compared to $\lambda$ each would diffract too little; with them far apart and independently lit the pattern would jitter away. The geometry — narrow slits, close together, far screen — is the whole trick.

concepts.statement: **Because $D \gg d$, the two rays reaching a point $P$ at angle $\theta$ are effectively parallel, and the lower ray travels farther by** $$\Delta L = d\sin\theta.$$ The construction: drop a perpendicular from one slit onto the other ray; the extra segment between that foot and the second slit is $d\sin\theta$.
concepts.detail: This is the number to watch: everything the two waves do at $P$ — reinforce or cancel — depends only on how many wavelengths fit into $\Delta L$.

concepts.statement: **Constructive interference (bright fringes, maxima):** $$d\sin\theta = m\lambda,\qquad m = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots$$ **Destructive interference (dark fringes, minima):** $$d\sin\theta = (m + \tfrac12)\lambda,\qquad m = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots$$
concepts.detail: $m$ is the order number: the central maximum has $m = 0$ (zero path difference — the waves always arrive in phase there, whatever the wavelength). The first minimum flanking it corresponds to $m = 0$ in the destructive rule, i.e. $d\sin\theta = \lambda/2$.

concepts.statement: **For small angles ($y \ll D$), the $m$-th bright fringe sits at $y_m = m\lambda D/d$, and adjacent bright fringes are separated by** $$\Delta y = \frac{\lambda D}{d},$$ independent of $m$ — evenly spaced teeth.
concepts.detail: Doubling the screen distance doubles the spacing; doubling the slit separation halves it; longer wavelengths spread more than shorter ones. Measuring $\Delta y$, $D$ and $d$ is a classic way to determine $\lambda$ — how Young measured wavelengths a generation before anyone believed the answer.

concepts.statement: **Solve Young's Interference Experiment problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is two-beam interference with coherence; the working equation is $\Delta L = d\sin\theta = m\lambda$, $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\beta/2)$, $2L = m\lambda$ or $(m+\tfrac12)\lambda$ (film), $2d = m\lambda$ (Michelson); every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (meters and nanometers) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $y\sim \text{mm}$ for $\lambda\sim 550\ \text{nm}$, $d\sim 0.1\ \text{mm}$, $L\sim 1\ \text{m}$; coherent, monochromatic source with $L\gg d$; count phase flips on reflection.

figures.caption: Young's double-slit geometry. Monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$ reaches the slits $S_1$ and $S_2$, separated by $d$; the viewing screen is a distance $D$ away (drawing not to scale — in practice $D \gg d$). The two rays to the point $P$ at height $y$ are effectively parallel at angle $\theta$, so the extra distance is the segment $\Delta L = d\sin\theta$, found by the perpendicular construction from $S_1$ onto the lower ray. Here $P$ sits on the $m = 1$ bright fringe, where $d\sin\theta = \lambda$; the curve along the screen sketches the resulting intensity.

examples.title: Fringe spacing and the fifth maximum
examples.problem: Mercury's green line, $\lambda = 546$ nm, illuminates two slits separated by $d = 0.20$ mm, and the screen is $D = 1.30$ m away. Find the fringe spacing and the position of the fifth bright fringe above the center.

steps.label: Fifth fringe
steps.text: $y_5 = 5\Delta y = 5(3.55\ \mathrm{mm}) = 17.7$ mm above the central maximum.

steps.label: Angle check
steps.text: The small-angle assumption holds: $\theta_5 \approx \sin\theta_5 = 5\lambda/d = 5(546\times 10^{-9})/(2.0\times 10^{-4}) = 0.0137$ rad $\approx 0.78^\circ$, so $y = D\tan\theta$ and $D\sin\theta$ agree to four digits.

steps.label: Scale
steps.text: A 3.5 mm spacing over a 1.3 m throw is easily measured with a traveling microscope on the eyepiece — which is exactly how wavelengths were first counted out.

examples.result: Fringes every 3.5 mm; the $m = 5$ maximum sits 17.7 mm from the center line.

examples.title: What changes when the whole apparatus is under water?
examples.problem: The same double-slit setup is submerged in water ($n = 1.33$), with $\lambda = 546$ nm still measured in vacuum. What is the new fringe spacing?

steps.label: Wavelength in water
steps.text: The frequency is fixed, so the wavelength in the water is $\lambda_n = \lambda/n = (546\ \mathrm{nm})/1.33 = 411$ nm.

steps.label: Use the water wavelength
steps.text: The fringe condition counts wavelengths of the light actually in the medium, so $\Delta y = \lambda_n D/d = (411\times 10^{-9})(1.30)/(2.0\times 10^{-4}) = 2.7$ mm.

steps.label: Interpretation
steps.text: Equivalently $\Delta y = \lambda D/(nd)$: immersing the experiment crowds the fringes by the factor $1/n$. Fringe patterns underwater are compressed — a direct measurement of the wavelength in the medium.

examples.result: The spacing shrinks from 3.5 mm to 2.7 mm — the water-shortened wavelength leaves its fingerprint on the pattern.

keyTakeaways: The two rays reaching a distant screen point at angle $\theta$ differ in path by $\Delta L = d\sin\theta$ — bright when this is $m\lambda$, dark when it is $(m+\tfrac12)\lambda$.
Fringe spacing on a far screen: $\Delta y = \lambda D/d$ — proportional to $\lambda$ and $D$, inversely proportional to the slit separation.
The central maximum ($m = 0$) is always bright; measuring $\Delta y$, $d$ and $D$ yields the wavelength.

quiz.q: In a double-slit experiment the slit separation is doubled while $\lambda$ and $D$ stay fixed. The fringe spacing:
quiz.explanation: $\Delta y = \lambda D/d$ is inversely proportional to $d$.

quiz.q: The central maximum ($m = 0$) is always bright, whatever the wavelength, because:
options: both rays travel equal distances and arrive in phase
the center of the screen is closest to both slits
the amplitude doubles exactly at the center
the angle θ is zero so d sin θ = λ
quiz.explanation: At the center the path difference is zero, and the coherent in-phase sources stay in phase there for every wavelength.

quiz.q: The second dark fringe above the central maximum satisfies:
quiz.explanation: Minima occur at $(m+\tfrac12)\lambda$ with $m = 0, 1, \ldots$; the second dark fringe has $m = 1$, giving $3\lambda/2$.

quiz.q: If the screen is moved closer to the slits, the fringes:
options: crowd closer together — the spacing is proportional to D
keep their spacing but grow dimmer
quiz.explanation: $\Delta y = \lambda D/d$ shrinks linearly with the screen distance $D$.

intro: Bright and dark fringes are only half the story: the screen shows a smoothly varying intensity, and its shape — not just the fringe positions — is what a detector actually records. To compute intensity we must add the two electric fields, not the intensities: each wave contributes a sinusoid that we can picture as a rotating phasor, and the intensity is the time average of the squared resultant field. For two slits of equal strength the answer is one cosine-squared: $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$, where $\phi$ is the phase difference the path difference produces. This section builds the phasor tool and the intensity law, and then derives it honestly.
objectives: Represent sinusoidal waves by phasors and add phasors geometrically
Apply $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$ with $\phi = 2\pi d\sin\theta/\lambda$ to find the intensity at any angle
Explain why intensities alone do not add, and predict fringe contrast for unequal slits

concepts.statement: **A phasor is a vector of length equal to a wave's amplitude, rotating counterclockwise at angular frequency $\omega$; its projection on the vertical axis at any instant is the wave's field, $E = E_0\sin(\omega t)$.** Adding waves at a point = placing their phasors tail-to-head and taking the vector sum: the resultant's length is the resultant amplitude, its rotation the common frequency.
concepts.detail: A phase lead $\phi$ is simply the angle between the two phasors. The picture turns the algebra of sinusoids into geometry that can be drawn.

concepts.statement: **A path difference $\Delta L$ corresponds to a phase difference** $$\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\,\Delta L = \frac{2\pi d\sin\theta}{\lambda},$$ because one full wavelength of path is $2\pi$ of phase.
concepts.detail: This is the bridge between the geometry of the last section ($d\sin\theta$) and the intensity of this one ($\phi$). Inside a medium, use the wavelength $\lambda_n$ in the medium.

concepts.statement: **Two coherent waves of equal amplitude give an intensity** $$I = 4I_0\cos^2\!\frac{\phi}{2},$$ where $I_0$ is the intensity either slit alone would produce. Maxima $I = 4I_0$ at $\phi = 2\pi m$; minima $I = 0$ at $\phi = (2m+1)\pi$.
concepts.detail: Not $2I_0$ but $4I_0$ at the peaks, and zero at the troughs: the average over the pattern is $2I_0$, exactly what two independent slits would deliver — interference does not create or destroy light, it redistributes it.

concepts.statement: **For any two overlapping waves, $I = I_1 + I_2 + 2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi$ — the cross term is the whole story of interference.** For incoherent sources $\phi$ wanders randomly, $\langle\cos\phi\rangle = 0$, and the term dies: intensities simply add.
concepts.detail: That is why two flashlights aimed at the same wall give a smoothly doubled brightness and no fringes: their phase difference jitters within nanoseconds, faster than any detector can follow. Coherence is the license to keep the cross term.

concepts.term: Interference and Double-Slit Intensity: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Interference and Double-Slit Intensity problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is two-beam interference with coherence; the working equation is $\Delta L = d\sin\theta = m\lambda$, $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\beta/2)$, $2L = m\lambda$ or $(m+\tfrac12)\lambda$ (film), $2d = m\lambda$ (Michelson); every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (meters and nanometers) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $y\sim \text{mm}$ for $\lambda\sim 550\ \text{nm}$, $d\sim 0.1\ \text{mm}$, $L\sim 1\ \text{m}$; coherent, monochromatic source with $L\gg d$; count phase flips on reflection.

examples.title: Half-maximum intensity: where is it?
examples.problem: For $d = 0.20$ mm, $\lambda = 546$ nm and $D = 1.30$ m, find the intensity at the point on the screen halfway (in position) between the central maximum and the first minimum.

steps.label: Position
steps.text: The first minimum sits at $d\sin\theta = \lambda/2$, i.e. $y = \lambda D/2d = 17.7$ mm; halfway out is $y = \lambda D/4d = 8.9$ mm.

steps.label: Phase there
steps.text: At that point $\Delta L = d\sin\theta = \lambda/4$, so $\phi = 2\pi(\lambda/4)/\lambda = \pi/2$ — a quarter turn between the two phasors.

steps.label: Intensity
steps.text: $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\pi/4) = 4I_0(1/2) = 2I_0$ — exactly half the maximum $4I_0$.

steps.label: Geometry check
steps.text: Two equal phasors $90^\circ$ apart form the sides of a square; their diagonal has length $\sqrt{2}E_0$, and squaring gives $2E_0^2 = 2I_0$ in intensity units — the picture and the formula agree.

examples.result: At 8.9 mm from the center the intensity is $2I_0$ — half the peak — because the cos² profile falls to half exactly one quarter-wavelength of path from a maximum.

examples.title: Interference and Double-Slit Intensity: fringe-spacing check
examples.problem: In Young's setup $\lambda = 550\ \text{nm}$, $d = 0.2\ \text{mm}$, $L = 1.00\ \text{m}$. Find the $m = 1$ fringe position $y = m\lambda L/d$.

steps.label: SI
steps.text: $\lambda = 5.50\times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}$, $d = 0.2\times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}$.

steps.label: Millimeters
steps.text: $y \approx 2.75\ \text{mm}$.

examples.result: $y_1 \approx 2.75\ \text{mm}$ from center.

keyTakeaways: Phase difference from path difference: $\phi = 2\pi\Delta L/\lambda$; then $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$ for two equal coherent slits.
Maxima reach $4I_0$ (amplitudes add before squaring); minima reach zero; the pattern averages $2I_0$.
For incoherent sources the interference term averages away and only $I_1 + I_2$ remains.

quiz.q: At a point where the phase difference between the two waves is $\phi = \pi/2$, the intensity is:
The maxima of the two-slit pattern have intensity $4I_0$ rather than $2I_0$ because:
options: energy is created at the bright fringes
the field amplitudes add before squaring, and $(2E_0)^2$ is four times $E_0^2$
no light at all reaches the dark fringes
each slit’s intensity doubles at a maximum
quiz.explanation: Intensity goes as amplitude squared: two equal amplitudes in phase give double the amplitude and four times the single-slit intensity.

quiz.q: Two phasors of equal length $E_0$ make an angle $\phi = 2\pi/3$ with each other. The amplitude of their sum is:
quiz.explanation: The isosceles phasor triangle has resultant $2E_0\cos(\phi/2) = 2E_0\cos(\pi/3) = E_0$.

quiz.q: Two flashlights aimed at the same wall produce no visible fringes because:
options: their intensities add instead of their fields
the interference term averages to zero when the phase difference wanders randomly — incoherence
their frequencies always differ too much
quiz.explanation: Independent thermal sources hold a fixed phase only for ~$10^{-8}$ s; the cross term $2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi$ averages to zero over any measurement.

depth.title: The double-slit intensity, derived honestly

blocks.heading: Superposition of two coherent waves
blocks.body: At a point $P$ the two slits deliver two sinusoidal fields of the same frequency and — this is the hypothesis that carries everything — a phase difference $\phi$ fixed in time: $E_1 = E_0\sin\omega t$ and $E_2 = E_0\sin(\omega t + \phi)$. Because the wave equation in vacuum-like media is linear, the total field is the algebraic sum of the fields, never the sum of the intensities. Define intensity as proportional to the time average of the field squared; one slit alone then contributes $I_0 = k\langle E_1^2\rangle = \tfrac12 kE_0^2$ for the constant $k$ (in full electromagnetism $k = c\varepsilon_0$). The theorem to prove: the pair delivers $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$. Every hypothesis is visible: equal amplitudes, single frequency, and a phase difference that holds still while we average — coherence, again.

blocks.heading: Adding the sinusoids
blocks.body: Use the sum-to-product identity $\sin A + \sin B = 2\sin\tfrac{A+B}{2}\cos\tfrac{A-B}{2}$ with $A = \omega t + \phi$, $B = \omega t$: $$E = E_1 + E_2 = 2E_0\cos\!\frac{\phi}{2}\;\sin\!\left(\omega t + \frac{\phi}{2}\right).$$ The sum is itself a pure sinusoid — amplitude $2E_0\cos(\phi/2)$, phase $\phi/2$ halfway between its parents. That is the phasor diagram in one line: two arrows of length $E_0$ at angle $\phi$ form an isosceles triangle whose resultant bisects them, with length $2E_0\cos(\phi/2)$. When the phasors oppose ($\phi = \pi$) the triangle closes and the resultant vanishes.

blocks.heading: Averaging to intensity
blocks.body: Square and average over a period of the motion; the identity $\langle\sin^2\rangle = \tfrac12$ kills all time dependence: $$I = k\langle E^2\rangle = k\left(2E_0\cos\frac{\phi}{2}\right)^{\!2}\cdot\frac12 = 4\left(\tfrac12 kE_0^2\right)\cos^2\frac{\phi}{2} = 4I_0\cos^2\frac{\phi}{2}.$$ The endpoints behave: $\phi = 2\pi m$ (path difference $m\lambda$) gives $4I_0$ — four times one slit, not two, because amplitudes add before squaring — and $\phi = (2m+1)\pi$ gives exact darkness. Energy is conserved globally: the $\cos^2$ fringes merely redistribute what two independent slits would spread uniformly at $2I_0$ per point on average.

blocks.heading: Unequal slits and fringe visibility
blocks.body: Drop the equal-amplitude assumption: phasors $E_1$ and $E_2$ still at fixed angle $\phi$. The law of cosines on the phasor triangle gives the resultant amplitude squared directly, $E^2 = E_1^2 + E_2^2 + 2E_1E_2\cos\phi$, and after the same $\tfrac12$ averaging per component: $$I = I_1 + I_2 + 2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\,\cos\phi,$$ the interference term exposed. So $I_{\max} = (\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2})^2$ when the phasors align, $I_{\min} = (\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2})^2$ when they oppose — darkness only for matched beams. The Michelson **visibility** of the fringes, $$V = \frac{I_{\max}-I_{\min}}{I_{\max}+I_{\min}} = \frac{2\sqrt{I_1I_2}}{I_1+I_2},$$ is 1 for equal beams and slides to 0 as one fades: fringe contrast measures beam balance — and, in stellar interferometry, the angular structure of the source itself.

blocks.heading: Numbers: a dim second slit, and fringe widths
blocks.body: Let the second slit pass one quarter the intensity of the first, $I_2 = 0.25I_1$, so $\sqrt{I_1I_2} = 0.5I_1$. Then $I_{\max} = (1+0.5)^2I_1 = 2.25I_1$, $I_{\min} = (1-0.5)^2I_1 = 0.25I_1$ — the dark fringes lift to one-ninth of the bright ones — and $V = 2(0.5)/1.25 = 0.8$. Now return to equal slits with the geometry of this section ($d = 0.20$ mm, $\lambda = 546$ nm, $D = 1.30$ m). Half-maximum intensity demands $\cos^2(\phi/2) = \tfrac12$, i.e. $\phi = \pm\pi/2$: a quarter-wavelength path difference, $y = \pm\lambda D/4d = \pm 8.9$ mm. Each bright fringe is therefore $17.7$ mm wide at half height — exactly half the fringe spacing $\Delta y = \lambda D/d = 35.5$ mm. The cos² profile has equally spaced, equally wide teeth: maxima sit one spacing apart, each half-spacing wide at half height.

blocks.heading: What this derivation did not do
blocks.body: It treated each slit as a point source of uniform strength — no single-slit diffraction envelope. Real slits of finite width $a$ multiply this whole pattern by a broad diffraction factor that dips to zero near $\sin\theta = \lambda/a$, the business of Chapter 36; the $\cos^2$ law is the two-ray interference kernel that survives underneath. It also assumed $\phi$ fixed — over times long compared with the detector's averaging time, and across path differences shorter than the coherence length. Let the source go thermal — phase bursting and re-forming every $10^{-8}$ s — and the cross term averages to zero before any instrument can follow it: the wall glows evenly, and the world mercifully does not look striped.

intro: Shine white light on a soap bubble and colors swim across it; look at a coated camera lens edge-on and a faint purple tint remains. Both are interference from thin films: light reflected from the front and back surfaces of a transparent film recombines, and the film's thickness decides which wavelengths reinforce and which cancel. The new ingredient is a subtle one — a reflection can flip the wave, a phase change of $\pi$ — and it flips only when light bounces off a medium of higher index of refraction. Counting those flips correctly is the entire skill of this section.
objectives: Determine when a reflection flips the wave by half a wavelength (the $\pi$ phase change)
Write the constructive and destructive conditions for a film of thickness $L$ and index $n$ with zero, one or two phase inversions
Apply the results to nonreflecting coatings, soap films and wedge films

concepts.statement: **A wave reflected at the boundary onto a medium of higher index of refraction undergoes a phase change of $\pi$ — equivalent to half a wavelength.** Reflection onto a lower-index medium changes nothing, and the transmitted wave never flips.
concepts.detail: Compare strings: a pulse on a light rope tied to a heavy wall comes back inverted; a pulse meeting a free end reflects upright. Light does the same — the optically 'heavier' (higher-$n$) medium inverts.

concepts.statement: **Near perpendicular incidence the two reflected rays differ by one round trip through the film — a path difference of $2L$ — traveled where the wavelength is $\lambda_n = \lambda/n$.** The total phase difference is $2\pi(2L/\lambda_n)$ plus $\pi$ for each reflection that flipped the wave.
concepts.detail: HRW develops the formulas for near-perpendicular incidence; at oblique incidence the round trip shortens to $2L\cos\theta_2$ measured inside the film, and the same bookkeeping applies.

concepts.statement: **Exactly one flipped reflection (air–film–air, like a soap bubble):** constructive in reflected light when $2L = (m+\tfrac12)\lambda_n$; destructive when $2L = m\lambda_n$. **Zero or two flipped reflections (like a coating on glass, where both reflections hit higher index):** the rules swap — constructive when $2L = m\lambda_n$, destructive when $2L = (m+\tfrac12)\lambda_n$, with $m = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$
concepts.detail: The mnemonic that never fails: count the flips. An odd number of $\pi$ shifts makes half-wavelength thicknesses bright and whole-wavelength thicknesses dark; an even number restores the naive rules. Always reason from the phase sum, never from memorized formulas alone.

concepts.statement: **A film with index between air and lens glass makes BOTH reflections flip, so they cancel when the film is a quarter wavelength thick:** $$L = \frac{\lambda}{4n}.$$ With magnesium fluoride ($n = 1.38$) and $\lambda = 550$ nm, the minimum thickness is about $99.6$ nm — roughly 100 nm, a hundred atoms.
concepts.detail: The cancellation is exact for one wavelength only; across the visible spectrum it is partial, which is why coated lenses reflect a faint purple sheen — red and blue leak back while green dies.

concepts.term: Film colors and the black film
concepts.statement: **In white light each wavelength has its own constructive thickness, so a wedge-shaped film paints bands of color — a contour map of its own thickness.** And a soap film drained to nearly zero thickness looks black: with one $\pi$ shift and no path difference, reflection is destructive for every visible wavelength at once.
concepts.detail: Drain a large soap film and the top turns black just before it bursts: $2L \to 0$ with one flip cancels everything reflected. Newton's rings — the same physics in an air wedge between a lens and a plate — appear as a problem set classic.

examples.title: Designing a nonreflecting coating
examples.problem: A lens of index 1.5 is coated with magnesium fluoride of index $n = 1.38$ to minimize reflection of $\lambda = 550$ nm light (roughly the brightest part of the visual response). Find the minimum coating thickness.

steps.label: Count the flips
steps.text: Air (1.00) → MgF₂ (1.38): reflecting onto higher index — a $\pi$ flip. MgF₂ (1.38) → glass (1.50): again onto higher index — another $\pi$ flip. Two inversions, an even number.

steps.label: Pick the rule
steps.text: With two flips, the reflected rays cancel (destructive in reflection) when $2L = (m+\tfrac12)\lambda_n$. The thinnest choice is $m = 0$: $2L = \lambda_n/2$, i.e. $L = \lambda_n/4$.

steps.label: Wavelength in the film
steps.text: Inside the coating the wavelength is $\lambda_n = \lambda/n = (550\ \mathrm{nm})/1.38 = 399$ nm.

steps.label: Thickness
steps.text: $L = \lambda_n/4 = \lambda/(4n) = 550/(4 \times 1.38) = 99.6$ nm $\approx 100$ nm — about 500 atoms of MgF₂ stacked.

steps.label: Check the other side
steps.text: Light not reflected is transmitted: at this wavelength the coated lens gains transmission — the point of the exercise for camera and binocular objectives with many glass surfaces.

examples.result: A 99.6 nm MgF₂ layer cancels the 550 nm reflection; neighboring wavelengths are only partly canceled, giving the coating its purple tint.

examples.title: Why the soap film glows red (at the right thickness)
examples.problem: A soap-water film ($n = 1.33$) hangs vertically in air. At a spot where the thickness is just right, the reflected white light is strongly red ($\lambda = 600$ nm). Find the thickness, and decide what that thickness does to reflected blue light.

steps.label: Count the flips
steps.text: Air → film: onto higher index — flip. Film → air: onto lower index — no flip. One inversion, odd.

steps.label: Pick the rule
steps.text: One flip: constructive reflection requires $2L = (m+\tfrac12)\lambda_n$. The thinnest strong-red spot is $m = 0$: $2L = \lambda_n/2$, so $L = \lambda/4n$.

steps.label: Same thickness, other colors
steps.text: Destructive reflection at this $L$ needs $2L = m\lambda_n$, so $\lambda = 2Ln = 2(113)(1.33) = 300$ nm — ultraviolet, outside the visible. Within the visible, blue and green are partially suppressed but not extinguished; as gravity drains the film, each thickness sweeps through its own colors until the black of near-zero thickness takes over at the top.

examples.result: A 113 nm film reflects red strongly; the wavelength it would extinguish at that thickness is 300 nm, invisible — so red dominates by default.

keyTakeaways: Reflection onto a higher-index medium flips the wave by $\pi$; onto lower index it does not — count the flips before anything else.
Film conditions use the in-film wavelength $\lambda_n = \lambda/n$ and the round trip $2L$: one flip swaps the constructive and destructive conditions.
A quarter-wave film, $L = \lambda/4n \approx 100$ nm of MgF₂, cancels reflected green light from a lens; a near-zero soap film looks black.

quiz.q: A light wave reflecting from a boundary onto a medium of HIGHER index of refraction undergoes a phase change of:
quiz.explanation: The optically denser medium plays the heavy wall: the reflected wave flips by half a wavelength.

quiz.q: A soap film in air (one phase inversion) shows strong reflection of vacuum wavelength $\lambda$ when its thickness $L$ satisfies, with $m = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$:
quiz.explanation: With one $\pi$ shift, reflection is constructive when the round trip contributes another half wavelength: $2L = (m+\tfrac12)\lambda_n$.

quiz.q: A very thin soap film ($L \approx 0$) viewed in reflected white light looks black because:
options: the film absorbs all colors at that thickness
with one $\pi$ reflection shift and essentially no path difference, reflection is destructive for every wavelength
thin films transmit only ultraviolet light
the front reflection cancels the transmitted light
quiz.explanation: Zero round trip plus one flip: the two reflected rays differ by $\pi$ for all colors at once, so nothing is reflected.

quiz.q: For a nonreflecting MgF₂ coating ($n = 1.38$) on glass, the minimum thickness that cancels 550 nm reflected light is about:
quiz.explanation: Both reflections flip (even count), so cancellation needs $2L = \lambda_n/2$: $L = \lambda/4n = 550/(4\times1.38) \approx 99.6$ nm.

intro: In 1881 Albert Michelson built the most elegant interferometer of them all: a half-silvered mirror, one movable mirror, and two arms. Light is split into two beams that travel out and back along perpendicular paths and are recombined; if the arms differ by half a wavelength the fields cancel, and moving the mirror by that half wavelength sweeps every point of the pattern from bright to dark and back — one fringe. Count fringes while you turn a calibrated screw and you have measured a wavelength in terms of displacement, or a displacement in terms of wavelength: the instrument became the metrologist's ruler, and a century later, the gravitational-wave detector.
objectives: Trace the beams through the beam splitter, compensator plate and two mirrors, and say why the fringes appear
Relate mirror motion to fringe shifts: $\Delta N = 2\Delta d/\lambda$ — one fringe per half wavelength
Describe how interferometry once defined the meter and how LIGO detects gravitational waves

concepts.statement: **Light from a broad source hits a half-silvered glass plate at $45^\circ$ — the beam splitter — which passes half its amplitude to the movable mirror $M_1$ and reflects half to the fixed mirror $M_2$.** The reflected beams return through the splitter and are recombined toward the viewer, where each point of the extended source corresponds to a particular pair of path lengths.
concepts.detail: An identical glass compensator plate sits in one arm so both beams cross the same thickness of glass — without it, the arm through the splitter's backing glass would lag, and white-light fringes (which need every wavelength matched) would be impossible.

concepts.statement: **The two beams recombine with a path difference equal to twice the arm-length difference, $2d$. Moving the mirror by $\Delta d$ changes this by $2\Delta d$, so the pattern shifts by** $$\Delta N = \frac{2\,\Delta d}{\lambda}$$ fringes: every half wavelength of mirror travel sweeps one bright-dark-bright cycle past the crosshairs.
concepts.detail: A tilted, nearly matched mirror pair acts like a thin air wedge (straight fringes); a perfectly matched, perpendicular pair gives concentric rings that collapse or bloom as the mirror moves. Either way, count fringes and you have measured $\lambda$ or $d$ to a fraction of a wavelength.

concepts.statement: **From 1960 to 1983 the meter was defined as exactly 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of the orange radiation of krypton-86** ($\lambda \approx 606$ nm) — a Michelson-type interferometer comparison, pursued by Michelson himself with cadmium light decades earlier.
concepts.detail: The interferometric meter made length metrology a counting experiment, reproducible in any lab; in 1983 the meter was redefined instead by fixing the speed of light, $c = 299{,}792{,}458$ m/s exactly.

concepts.statement: **LIGO's 4 km Michelson arms (with resonant cavities folding the path to over a thousand km) detected in 2015 a gravitational-wave strain of order $10^{-21}$** — a length change of about $10^{-18}$ m, a few thousandths of a proton diameter.
concepts.detail: A passing gravitational wave stretches one arm while squeezing the other; the tiny fringe shift is rescued by laser power, mirror isolation beyond anything in the 1880 design — and by the fact that the Michelson geometry converts length into light intensity, exactly as this section describes.

concepts.statement: **Solve Michelson's Interferometer problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is two-beam interference with coherence; the working equation is $\Delta L = d\sin\theta = m\lambda$, $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\beta/2)$, $2L = m\lambda$ or $(m+\tfrac12)\lambda$ (film), $2d = m\lambda$ (Michelson); every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (meters and nanometers) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $y\sim \text{mm}$ for $\lambda\sim 550\ \text{nm}$, $d\sim 0.1\ \text{mm}$, $L\sim 1\ \text{m}$; coherent, monochromatic source with $L\gg d$; count phase flips on reflection.

examples.title: Measuring a wavelength by counting fringes
examples.problem: A Michelson interferometer is lit by an unknown monochromatic source. The movable mirror is displaced $\Delta d = 0.158$ mm (read off a calibrated micrometer screw), and exactly $N = 500$ fringe shifts are counted at the crosshairs. What is the wavelength?

steps.label: The counting law
steps.text: Each fringe corresponds to a mirror motion of $\lambda/2$: the round-trip path difference must change by a full $\lambda$ to bring the pattern back to the same brightness.

steps.label: Per-fringe motion
steps.text: One fringe per $\Delta d/N = 0.158\ \mathrm{mm}/500 = 316$ nm of mirror travel — so $\lambda/2 = 316$ nm.

steps.label: Sanity check
steps.text: That is essentially the red helium–neon laser line at 632.8 nm — and counting fringes this way is accurate to a small fraction of a fringe, far better than any ruler could hope to be.

examples.result: $\lambda = 632$ nm: half a micron of light measured with a screw, by counting 500 bright-dark cycles.

examples.title: Michelson's Interferometer: fringe-spacing check
examples.problem: In Young's setup $\lambda = 550\ \text{nm}$, $d = 0.15\ \text{mm}$, $L = 1.00\ \text{m}$. Find the $m = 1$ fringe position $y = m\lambda L/d$.

steps.label: Millimeters
steps.text: $y \approx 3.67\ \text{mm}$.

examples.result: $y_1 \approx 3.67\ \text{mm}$ from center.

keyTakeaways: A beam splitter divides amplitude into two arms; recombining them turns any arm-length difference into a fringe pattern.
One fringe per half wavelength of mirror motion: $\Delta N = 2\Delta d/\lambda$ — the basis of precision length measurement and the former definition of the meter.
The same geometry, scaled to 4 km and $10^{-18}$ m sensitivity, is LIGO — interference is still doing the measuring.

quiz.q: In a Michelson interferometer, moving the movable mirror by one full wavelength $\lambda$ shifts the pattern by:
quiz.explanation: Moving the mirror $\lambda$ changes the round-trip difference by $2\lambda$ — two full fringe cycles.

quiz.q: The compensator plate in one arm exists so that:
options: both beams cross the same thickness of glass, keeping the optical paths matched for white light
the mirror can be tilted accurately
the beam splitter does not absorb light
quiz.explanation: One beam would otherwise cross the splitter twice and the other not at all; the compensator equalizes glass paths so all wavelengths stay in step.

quiz.q: A mirror moves 0.100 mm and 400 fringes are counted. The wavelength is:

intro: Light does not simply march past the edge of an opening in straight lines: it spreads, and the spreading is organized into bright and dark bands — a diffraction pattern. A single narrow slit of width $a$ throws onto a distant screen a broad central bright band flanked by far weaker side bands. This section locates those dark fringes exactly, with a one-line condition that ranks among the most useful in optics, and shows why the central band is twice as wide as every other.
objectives: Distinguish Fraunhofer from Fresnel diffraction and explain why a slit of width comparable to the wavelength spreads light
Use $a \sin\theta = m\lambda$ to locate the dark fringes of a single slit
Compute the angular width of the central maximum and its linear width on a distant screen

concepts.statement: **Diffraction is the spreading of a wave into the region of geometrical shadow when it passes an edge or an aperture**, appreciable when the opening is comparable in size to the wavelength $\lambda$. In **Fraunhofer diffraction** the incident and detected waves are effectively plane (screen far away, or a lens used); in **Fresnel diffraction** the wavefront curvature matters.
concepts.detail: This chapter is Fraunhofer throughout: rays from every point of the slit to a given screen point are treated as parallel, which is why a single angle $\theta$ labels the whole pattern.

concepts.statement: **Dark fringes of a single slit lie where the path difference between rays from the slit's two edges is a whole number of wavelengths:** $$a \sin\theta = m\lambda, \qquad m = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$$ When it holds, every wavelet in the top half of the slit has a partner in the bottom half arriving exactly out of phase.
concepts.detail: Note what the formula does not do: it does not locate the maxima. Only the central maximum sits exactly at $\theta = 0$; the side maxima come slightly displaced from the midpoints between minima (next section).

concepts.statement: **The central maximum is twice as wide as any side maximum.** It runs from the $m = 1$ minimum on one side to the $m = 1$ minimum on the other; for small angles its full angular width is $2\lambda/a$ — wider for narrower slits and longer wavelengths.

**Solve Single-Slit Diffraction problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is diffraction limits and grating dispersion; the working equation is $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$, $\theta_R = 1.22\lambda/d$, $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (grating), $2d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (Bragg); every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (radians and lines/mm) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\theta\sim 10^{-3}\ \text{rad}$ for $\lambda/a$; $R = mN\sim 10^4$; Fraunhofer far field; uniform grating spacing.

concepts.statement: **Single-Slit Diffraction lives at $\theta\sim 10^{-3}\ \text{rad}$ for $\lambda/a$; $R = mN\sim 10^4$ and the textbook model holds while Fraunhofer far field; uniform grating spacing.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Single-Slit Diffraction calculation gives seconds when radians and lines/mm demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $\theta\sim 10^{-3}\ \text{rad}$ for $\lambda/a$; $R = mN\sim 10^4$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Width of the central band
examples.problem: Light of wavelength 610 nm falls on a slit of width 0.020 mm. A screen stands 2.0 m away. Where are the first minima, and how wide is the central maximum on the screen?

steps.label: First minimum
steps.text: $\sin\theta_1 = \lambda/a = (610\times10^{-9})/(2.0\times10^{-5}) = 0.0305$, so $\theta_1 = 1.75^\circ$ — small enough that $\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta$ is excellent.

steps.label: Second minimum
steps.text: $\sin\theta_2 = 2\lambda/a = 0.061$, so $\theta_2 = 3.50^\circ$; the first side band spans only $1.75^\circ$, half the central width.

steps.label: On the screen
steps.text: The center-to-minimum distance is $y_1 = D\tan\theta_1 = 2.0 \times 0.0305 = 61$ mm.

steps.label: Full width
steps.text: The central maximum stretches $2y_1 = 12.2$ cm across the screen — some 600 slit widths. Diffraction is not a small correction at this slit size.

examples.result: Minima at $\pm 1.75^\circ$, $\pm 3.50^\circ$, …; the central band is 12.2 cm wide on the 2.0 m screen.

examples.title: Single-Slit Diffraction: single-slit minimum check
examples.problem: A slit of width $a = 0.15\ \text{mm}$ is lit by $550\ \text{nm}$ light. Find the first minimum $a\sin\theta = \lambda$.

steps.label: Small angle
steps.text: $\theta \approx 0.21^\circ$ ($3.67\ \text{mrad}$).

examples.result: $\theta_1 \approx 0.21^\circ$.

keyTakeaways: $a \sin\theta = m\lambda$ locates the minima; only the central maximum lies exactly at $\theta = 0$.
The pattern scales with $\lambda/a$: narrower slit or longer wavelength means wider spread.
The central maximum is twice the angular width of every side maximum and holds nearly all the light.

quiz.q: A single slit of width $a$ is illuminated with wavelength $\lambda$. The first diffraction minimum occurs at angle $\theta$ satisfying:
quiz.explanation: The edge-to-edge path difference is $a\sin\theta$; the slit self-cancels when it equals exactly one wavelength.

quiz.q: The slit width is halved while the wavelength stays fixed. The angular width of the central maximum approximately:
quiz.explanation: Width $\approx 2\lambda/a$ in the small-angle regime, so halving $a$ doubles the spread.

quiz.q: Red light (700 nm) and blue light (450 nm) pass through the same slit. The wider central maximum belongs to:
options: blue, because shorter wavelengths spread more
quiz.explanation: Everything about the angular pattern is a function of the ratio $\lambda/a$; the longer wavelength diffracts more.

intro: Knowing where the dark fringes sit is half a theory; a complete one must say how bright the pattern is at every angle. Divide the slit into many narrow strips, represent each strip's wavelet by a phasor, and watch the phasor chain curl into an arc as the angle grows. The chord of that arc is the resultant amplitude, and one clean limit produces the sinc² law — the workhorse formula of this chapter and of every Fourier analysis to come.
objectives: Build the phasor arc for a single slit and derive $I(\theta) = I_{\max}(\sin\alpha/\alpha)^2$ with $\alpha = (\pi a/\lambda)\sin\theta$
Locate the secondary maxima and state their intensities relative to the central peak
Explain why the central maximum is twice the width of the side maxima

concepts.statement: **Divide the slit into many equal strips and add their wavelets as phasors of equal length, each rotated a fixed step from its neighbor.** At angle $\theta$ the phasors curl into an arc whose full curvature is the edge-to-edge phase difference; defining half of it as $$\alpha = \frac{\pi a}{\lambda}\sin\theta,$$ the resultant amplitude is the chord of an arc of total angle $2\alpha$.

**The single-slit diffraction pattern has intensity** $$I(\theta) = I_{\max}\left(\frac{\sin\alpha}{\alpha}\right)^2, \qquad \alpha = \frac{\pi a}{\lambda}\sin\theta.$$ Zeros at $\alpha = m\pi$ reproduce $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$; at $\theta = 0$ the chord straightens and $\sin\alpha/\alpha \to 1$.
concepts.detail: The arc geometry gives the chord as $2R\sin\alpha$ with arc length $2R\alpha$ — their ratio is exactly $\sin\alpha/\alpha$, so this is the whole derivation.

concepts.statement: **Side maxima occur where the phasor arc wraps one extra half-turn before closing: where $\tan\alpha = \alpha$.** They fall at $\alpha = 1.43\pi, 2.46\pi, 3.47\pi, \ldots$ with intensities only **4.7%, 1.6% and 0.8%** of the central peak — nearly all the diffracted light stays in the central band.
concepts.detail: Note they sit pulled toward the adjacent minimum, not at the midpoints $1.5\pi, 2.5\pi$: the tail of the arc keeps a residue of phase mismatch.

concepts.statement: **Each side maximum spans one unit of $a\sin\theta/\lambda$; the central one spans two.** Successive minima on the same side are separated by $\Delta(a\sin\theta) = \lambda$, while the central band covers from $-\lambda$ to $+\lambda$ — which is also why it collects the lion's share of the energy.

concepts.term: Intensity in Single-Slit Diffraction: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Intensity in Single-Slit Diffraction problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is diffraction limits and grating dispersion; the working equation is $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$, $\theta_R = 1.22\lambda/d$, $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (grating), $2d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (Bragg); every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (radians and lines/mm) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\theta\sim 10^{-3}\ \text{rad}$ for $\lambda/a$; $R = mN\sim 10^4$; Fraunhofer far field; uniform grating spacing.

figures.caption: The single-slit intensity law $I(\theta) = I_{\max}(\sin\alpha/\alpha)^2$ plotted against $a\sin\theta/\lambda$. Dashed verticals mark the minima $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$; the weak secondary maxima, near $\tan\alpha = \alpha$, carry only 4.7%, 1.6% and 0.8% of the central intensity.

examples.title: Half-intensity angle
examples.problem: A slit is 4.0 wavelengths wide ($a = 4.0\lambda$). At what angle does the intensity fall to half its central value?

steps.label: Condition
steps.text: Half the central intensity means $(\sin\alpha/\alpha)^2 = 0.5$, i.e. $\sin\alpha/\alpha = 0.707$.

steps.label: Solve numerically
steps.text: Trial and error gives $\alpha = 1.392$ rad: $\sin 1.392 = 0.9842$ and $0.9842/1.392 = 0.707$ as required.

steps.label: Convert to angle
steps.text: $\sin\theta = (\alpha/\pi)(\lambda/a) = (1.392/\pi)/4.0 = 0.111$, so $\theta = 6.4^\circ$.

steps.label: Perspective
steps.text: The first minimum is at $\sin\theta = \lambda/a = 0.25$ ($\theta = 14.5^\circ$): the peak sags to half height well before the first dark fringe, as the figure shows.

examples.result: $\theta \approx 6.4^\circ$, i.e. $\sin\theta \approx 0.111$ — the sinc² peak is sharply peaked, sagging to half height at about 44% of the way to the first zero.

examples.title: Intensity in Single-Slit Diffraction: single-slit minimum check
examples.problem: A slit of width $a = 0.2\ \text{mm}$ is lit by $550\ \text{nm}$ light. Find the first minimum $a\sin\theta = \lambda$.

steps.label: Small angle
steps.text: $\theta \approx 0.158^\circ$ ($2.75\ \text{mrad}$).

examples.result: $\theta_1 \approx 0.158^\circ$.

keyTakeaways: Phasors of the slit's wavelets form an arc; the chord gives $I = I_{\max}(\sin\alpha/\alpha)^2$ with $\alpha = (\pi a/\lambda)\sin\theta$.
Secondary maxima at $\tan\alpha = \alpha$ carry 4.7%, 1.6%, 0.8% of the peak — the central band dominates.
Minima at $\alpha = m\pi$ are exactly the $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$ condition of the previous section.

quiz.q: In the single-slit intensity formula, the phase variable $\alpha$ equals:
quiz.explanation: $\alpha$ is half the edge-to-edge phase difference across the slit.

quiz.q: The secondary maxima of a single-slit pattern are located at:
options: slightly toward the neighboring minimum from the midpoint, where $\tan\alpha = \alpha$
quiz.explanation: Each side maximum sits just short of the midpoint, where the phasor arc adds one extra half-turn — the condition $\tan\alpha = \alpha$.

quiz.q: Compared with a side maximum, the central maximum is:
quiz.explanation: Minima at $a\sin\theta = \pm\lambda$ bracket the central band: it spans $2\lambda/a$, twice any side band's $\lambda/a$.

intro: Round the aperture and the pattern becomes a bull's-eye: a bright Airy disk ringed with dark circles. Because every real instrument forms images through circular holes — pupils, telescope mirrors, microscope objectives — this is the pattern that sets the ultimate limit on sharpness. Rayleigh's criterion turns it into a single number, and that number governs everything from how far away you can distinguish car headlights to how large astronomers must build their mirrors.
objectives: State the angular radius of the Airy disk, $\sin\theta = 1.22\lambda/d$, for a circular aperture of diameter $d$
Apply Rayleigh's criterion to decide when two point sources are just resolved
Evaluate how aperture size and wavelength limit telescopes, eyes and microscopes

concepts.statement: **A circular aperture of diameter $d$ diffracts plane waves into a central bright disk — the Airy disk — surrounded by dark and bright rings.** The first dark ring lies at $$\sin\theta = 1.22\,\frac{\lambda}{d}.$$ The 1.22 is the first zero of a Bessel function: the price of integrating the sinc² pattern over a disk.
concepts.detail: About 84% of the transmitted light lands inside the first dark ring — the Airy disk is where images actually live.

concepts.statement: **Two point sources are just resolved when the central maximum of one's image falls on the first minimum of the other's** — for a circular aperture, when their angular separation is $$\theta_R = 1.22\,\frac{\lambda}{d}.$$ Smaller $\theta_R$ means finer resolution: enlarge the aperture or shorten the wavelength.

**What limits every optical instrument is the ratio of wavelength to aperture, $\lambda/d$.** The Hubble mirror (2.4 m) gives $\theta_R \approx 2.8\times10^{-7}$ rad at 550 nm — about 0.06 arcsecond; the 10.4 m Gran Telescopio Canarias halves that. Electron microscopes win outright: a 5 pm de Broglie wavelength undercuts visible light by a factor of $10^5$.

**Rayleigh's line is a convention for incoherent sources whose light does not interfere.** Slightly closer sources are still partly distinguishable, and coherent-illumination schemes (and modern computational super-resolution) can beat it — but it remains the honest zeroth-order standard for starlight, and the number printed on telescope spec sheets.

examples.title: Merging headlights
examples.problem: At night, two headlights 1.4 m apart shine toward your dark-adapted pupil of diameter 5.0 mm at wavelength about 550 nm. Beyond what distance do they merge into a single blob?

steps.label: Resolve condition
steps.text: Sources of transverse separation $s$ at range $R$ subtend $\theta = s/R$; resolution requires $s/R \geq \theta_R$.

steps.label: Reality check
steps.text: Glare, aberrations and retinal cell packing usually defeat the eye long before 10 km — this is the physics limit, not the driving test.

examples.result: About 10 km — beyond that, even a perfect eye fuses the two headlights into one.

examples.title: Diffraction by a Circular Aperture: single-slit minimum check
examples.problem: A slit of width $a = 0.1\ \text{mm}$ is lit by $550\ \text{nm}$ light. Find the first minimum $a\sin\theta = \lambda$.

steps.label: Small angle
steps.text: $\theta \approx 0.315^\circ$ ($5.5\ \text{mrad}$).

examples.result: $\theta_1 \approx 0.315^\circ$.

keyTakeaways: A circular aperture diffracts light into an Airy disk whose first dark ring lies at $\sin\theta = 1.22\lambda/d$.
Rayleigh: two sources are just resolved when one's central peak meets the other's first minimum — $\theta_R = 1.22\lambda/d$.
Resolution improves with larger apertures and shorter wavelengths; it depends on $\lambda/d$ and nothing else.

quiz.q: For a circular aperture, the first dark ring of the diffraction pattern lies at:
quiz.explanation: The Bessel-function zero of the circular integral gives 1.22 instead of the single slit's 1.

quiz.q: To resolve a tighter double star, an astronomer should:
options: observe at a longer wavelength for smoother fringes
quiz.explanation: $\theta_R = 1.22\lambda/d$ shrinks with shorter $\lambda$ and larger $d$; altitude helps atmospheric seeing but not diffraction.

quiz.q: The 1.22 in the circular-aperture formula originates in:
options: the two-dimensional diffraction integral over the aperture
an empirical fudge factor for lens flaws
the ratio of circumference to diameter
quiz.explanation: Integrating wavelets over a circular opening produces a Bessel function; its first zero sits at 1.22.

intro: Chapter 35's double slit made fringes of equal brightness — but only because the slits were pretended infinitely narrow. Real slits have width, and each imposes its own single-slit diffraction pattern on the two-slit interference. What lands on the screen is a product: cosine-squared fringes from the pair, riding under the sinc² envelope of each slit — and where the envelope hits zero, whole interference fringes are erased.
objectives: Combine interference and diffraction: $I(\theta) = I_m\cos^2\beta\,(\sin\alpha/\alpha)^2$ with $\beta = \pi d\sin\theta/\lambda$ and $\alpha = \pi a\sin\theta/\lambda$
Predict which interference orders go missing for a given ratio $d/a$
Explain why equal-brightness fringes require very narrow slits

concepts.statement: **Each slit diffracts; the pair interferes.** The screen shows two-slit fringes whose brightness is modulated by the single-slit pattern of each slit: interference supplies the $\cos^2\beta$ factor, diffraction the $(\sin\alpha/\alpha)^2$ envelope — with $d$ the slit separation and $a$ the slit width.

**The double-slit intensity with finite slit widths is** $$I(\theta) = I_m \cos^2\beta\left(\frac{\sin\alpha}{\alpha}\right)^2, \qquad \beta = \frac{\pi d \sin\theta}{\lambda}, \quad \alpha = \frac{\pi a \sin\theta}{\lambda}.$$ Bright fringes still require $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$; envelope zeros still require $a\sin\theta = m'\lambda$.

**When an interference maximum lands exactly on a diffraction minimum, that fringe vanishes — a missing order.** Dividing the two conditions, $m = m'(d/a)$: whenever $d/a$ is an integer $k$, the orders $m = k, 2k, 3k, \ldots$ are missing from the pattern.
concepts.detail: Missing orders are a built-in ruler: counting fringes between the gaps of the central envelope measures $d/a$ directly.

concepts.statement: **As $a \to 0$ the envelope flattens ($\alpha \to 0$ everywhere) and the fringes shine equally** — the idealization Chapter 35 used. Real patterns always betray their envelope: the fringes inside the central band are bright, the next batch dimmer, and so on.

concepts.statement: **Solve Diffraction by a Double Slit problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is diffraction limits and grating dispersion; the working equation is $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$, $\theta_R = 1.22\lambda/d$, $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (grating), $2d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (Bragg); every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (radians and lines/mm) emerges naturally.
