Check the answer against visible $\sim 2\ \text{eV}$ to X-ray $\text{keV}$; $\lambda_c = 2.43\ \text{pm}$; $hf > \Phi$ for emission; uncertainty is statistical over ensembles.

examples.title: Why atoms do not collapse
examples.problem: An electron is confined to an atom-sized region $\Delta x = 0.10$ nm. Estimate the minimum momentum and kinetic energy the confinement forces upon it.

steps.label: Momentum spread
steps.text: $\Delta p \approx \hbar/\Delta x = (1.055\times10^{-34})/(1.0\times10^{-10}) = 1.1\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$.

steps.label: Interpretation
steps.text: Confinement alone forces the electron to carry electron-volts of kinetic energy — the same scale as actual atomic binding energies.

steps.label: The collapse argument
steps.text: Squeeze the electron closer to the nucleus and $\Delta p$ grows as $1/\Delta x$, so $K$ grows as $1/\Delta x^2$ faster than the potential $-e^2/4\pi\epsilon_0 r$ falls: a stable minimum size results — the atom.

examples.result: Δp ≈ 1.1×10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s and K ≈ 3.8 eV: confinement energy sets the atomic scale and forbids collapse.

examples.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle: de Broglie check
examples.problem: An electron is accelerated through $100\ \text{V}$ ($p \approx 5.40\times 10^{-24}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$). Estimate $\lambda = h/p$.

steps.label: Angstroms
steps.text: $\approx 0.123\ \text{nm}$ — atomic scale, hence electron diffraction.

examples.result: $\lambda \approx 0.12\ \text{nm}$.

keyTakeaways: $\Delta x\,\Delta p \geq \hbar$: confinement and momentum sharpness trade off exactly.
Single-slit diffraction of electrons is the principle displayed on a screen.
Uncertainty explains atomic size (confinement energy) and natural linewidths ($\Delta E\Delta t \gtrsim \hbar$).

quiz.q: Narrowing the slit through which electrons pass:
options: increases the spread of their transverse momentum
quiz.explanation: $\Delta p \approx \hbar/\Delta x$: tighter position, wilder momentum.

quiz.q: The uncertainty principle is best described as:
options: a property of waves that matter also obeys
an effect of measurement recoil only
quiz.explanation: Localized wave packets necessarily superpose many wavelengths — Fourier mathematics, not engineering.

quiz.q: An electron is confined to $\Delta x = 1.0$ nm instead of 0.10 nm. The minimum kinetic energy forced by confinement:
quiz.explanation: $K \propto (\Delta p)^2 \propto 1/\Delta x^2$: ten times the width, one-hundredth the energy.

intro: A classical particle with more energy than a gentle upward step in potential energy sails over it every time. A quantum particle does something stranger: even with $E > U_0$ there is a chance it reflects, because its matter wave partially reflects at any abrupt change — exactly as light partly reflects off glass. This section builds the machinery of wave-number matching that tunneling will inherit.
objectives: Analyze a step potential with $E > U_0$: changed wavelength, partial reflection
Compute the reflection and transmission coefficients from wave-number matching
Explain why partial reflection has no classical counterpart for $E > U_0$

concepts.statement: **A step: $U = 0$ for $x < 0$ and $U = U_0 > 0$ for $x \geq 0$.** For $E > U_0$ the classical particle always passes; the quantum wave splits — part transmits with longer wavelength, part reflects.

**Kinetic energy drops from $E$ to $E - U_0$, so the matter wavelength stretches:** $$\lambda_2 = \lambda_1\sqrt{\frac{E}{E-U_0}}.$$ The wave slows in the higher-potential region exactly as light slows in glass — same relation, same cause (speed $v \propto 1/k$ here as $1/n$ there).

**Matching $\psi$ and $d\psi/dx$ at $x = 0$ for incident $e^{ik_1x}$, reflected $r e^{-ik_1x}$ and transmitted $t e^{ik_2x}$ gives** $$R = \left(\frac{k_1-k_2}{k_1+k_2}\right)^2, \qquad T = \frac{4k_1k_2}{(k_1+k_2)^2}, \qquad R + T = 1,$$ with $k = \sqrt{2mK}/\hbar$ in each region.

**Any abrupt change in a wave's medium reflects part of it.** For light, glass; for matter, a sudden jump in potential energy. Smooth the step over many wavelengths and the reflection fades away — abruptness is what scatters.

examples.title: An electron meets a soft barrier edge
examples.problem: An electron with $E = 1.00$ eV meets a step up to $U_0 = 0.75$ eV. Find the reflection and transmission coefficients and the wavelength on each side.

steps.label: Wave-number ratio
steps.text: The transmitted kinetic energy is $E - U_0 = 0.25$ eV, so $k_2/k_1 = \sqrt{0.25/1.00} = 0.50$.

steps.label: Reflection
steps.text: $R = [(1-0.5)/(1+0.5)]^2 = (1/3)^2 = 0.111$ — 11% of the incident electrons bounce back despite having enough energy.

steps.label: Wavelengths
steps.text: $\lambda_1 = 1.226/\sqrt{1.00} = 1.23$ nm and $\lambda_2 = \lambda_1\sqrt{1/0.25} = 2.45$ nm — the wave visibly stretches as it climbs.

examples.result: R = 11%, T = 89%; the wavelength doubles from 1.23 nm to 2.45 nm in crossing.

examples.title: Reflection from a Potential Step: de Broglie check
examples.problem: An electron is accelerated through $100\ \text{V}$ ($p \approx 5.40\times 10^{-24}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$). Estimate $\lambda = h/p$.

steps.label: Angstroms
steps.text: $\approx 0.123\ \text{nm}$ — atomic scale, hence electron diffraction.

examples.result: $\lambda \approx 0.12\ \text{nm}$.

keyTakeaways: At a step with $E > U_0$ the wavelength stretches by $\sqrt{E/(E-U_0)}$ and part of the wave reflects.
Partial reflection at abrupt changes is generic wave physics — classical particles have no such option.

quiz.q: The step-reflection coefficient equals $[(k_1-k_2)/(k_1+k_2)]^2$. If $k_2 = k_1$, it means:
options: there is no step at all (no reflection)
quiz.explanation: Identical wave numbers mean identical regions — nothing to scatter from.

quiz.q: Classically, a particle with $E > U_0$ at a step:
quiz.explanation: Partial reflection is a wave phenomenon with no classical-mechanical counterpart for $E > U_0$.

quiz.q: In the example with $E = 1.00$ eV and $U_0 = 0.75$ eV, the ratio $\lambda_2/\lambda_1$ equals:

intro: Now lower the particle's energy below the barrier: $E < U_0$, so the classically forbidden region. Classical physics is unambiguous — total reflection. Quantum physics is unambiguous too, but different: the wave function does not crash to zero at the barrier edge; it decays exponentially inside and, if the barrier is thin, something survives on the far side. Matter leaks through walls, and this leaking — tunneling — powers nuclear decay, the scanning tunneling microscope, and half of modern electronics.
objectives: Describe the exponential decay of $\psi$ in a classically forbidden region, with $\kappa = \sqrt{2m(U_0-E)}/\hbar$
Apply the tunneling transmission $T \approx e^{-2\kappa L}$ and its sensitivity to barrier width and height
Survey the applications: alpha decay, STM, tunnel diodes

concepts.statement: **Where $E < U(x)$, the Schrödinger equation flips: solutions grow or decay exponentially, $$\psi \propto e^{-\kappa x}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{\sqrt{2m(U_0-E)}}{\hbar}.$$** Only the decaying solution is physical: the probability of finding the particle inside the barrier dies away over a length $1/\kappa$ — small, but not zero.

**For a barrier of height $U_0 > E$ and width $L$, the fraction transmitted is, to high accuracy,** $$T \approx e^{-2\kappa L}, \qquad \kappa = \sqrt{2m(U_0-E)}/\hbar.$$ Double the barrier's width and the exponent doubles — the leak dies exponentially. The full coefficient (see the masters tier) is this exponential times a prefactor of order 1.

**A voltage-biased tip held a fraction of a nanometer from a surface reads the tunneling current $I \propto e^{-2\kappa d}$: a 0.01 nm change in gap $d$ swings the current by about 10%.** Since single atoms are 0.2–0.3 nm tall, the microscope maps them one by one — Binnig and Rohrer's 1981 invention, Nobel 1986.

**Alpha decay is an alpha particle tunneling out of the nucleus** (Gamow, 1928): tiny changes in nuclear barrier energy swing half-lives from microseconds to billions of years. **Tunnel diodes and Josephson junctions** exploit barrier leakage as a circuit element; **proton tunneling** even contributes to DNA mutation. Flash memory writes bits by tunneling electrons through oxide.

figures.caption: Tunneling through a barrier of height $U_0$ and width $L$ for energy $E < U_0$. The wave function oscillates before the barrier, decays exponentially inside as $e^{-\kappa x}$, and emerges with reduced amplitude — a nonzero probability of finding the particle beyond a region classical physics forbids it to enter. $T \approx e^{-2\kappa L}$.

examples.title: Leakage through a thin barrier
examples.problem: An electron with $E = 2.00$ eV faces a barrier of height $U_0 = 5.00$ eV and width $L = 0.70$ nm. Estimate the transmission, and compare with a barrier twice as wide.

steps.label: Transmission
steps.text: $T \approx e^{-12.4} = 4\times10^{-6}$ — one electron in a quarter-million gets through.

steps.label: Doubling the width
steps.text: For $L = 1.40$ nm, $2\kappa L = 24.9$ and $T \approx 1.5\times10^{-11}$: a 26 000-fold collapse from merely doubling $L$.

examples.result: T ≈ 4×10⁻⁶; doubling the width suppresses the leak by four and a half orders of magnitude.

examples.title: Tunneling Through a Potential Barrier: de Broglie check
examples.problem: An electron is accelerated through $100\ \text{V}$ ($p \approx 5.40\times 10^{-24}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$). Estimate $\lambda = h/p$.

steps.text: $\approx 0.123\ \text{nm}$ — atomic scale, hence electron diffraction.

keyTakeaways: In forbidden regions $\psi$ decays as $e^{-\kappa x}$ with $\kappa = \sqrt{2m(U_0-E)}/\hbar$.
$T \approx e^{-2\kappa L}$: transmission is exponentially sensitive to width, height, and particle mass.
Tunneling runs alpha decay, STM imaging, flash memory and Josephson devices.

quiz.q: Inside the barrier ($E < U_0$), the wave function:
quiz.explanation: Only the decaying solution stays normalizable.

quiz.q: Doubling the barrier width (same $U_0 - E$) changes $T$ by:
quiz.explanation: $T \propto e^{-2\kappa L}$: twice the width squares the already tiny factor.

quiz.q: Which change does NOT increase tunneling transmission?
quiz.explanation: Raising $U_0 - E$ raises $\kappa$ and throttles the leak; the other three all help.

quiz.q: The STM achieves atomic resolution chiefly because:
options: the tunneling current varies by ~10% per 0.01 nm of tip–surface gap
the tip is atomically sharp only
quiz.explanation: The exponential $e^{-2\kappa d}$ sensitivity makes the current a ruler for sub-atomic height changes.

depth.title: The transmission coefficient, derived honestly

blocks.heading: Exact transmission for a rectangular barrier
blocks.body: For a particle of energy $E < U_0$ incident on a barrier occupying $0 < x < L$, write $k = \sqrt{2mE}/\hbar$ outside and $\kappa = \sqrt{2m(U_0-E)}/\hbar$ inside. Requiring $\psi$ and $d\psi/dx$ continuous at both edges — four conditions — and eliminating the interior amplitudes gives the exact result $$T = \left[1 + \frac{U_0^2\sinh^2(\kappa L)}{4E(U_0-E)}\right]^{-1}.$$ Because the wave number $k$ is the same on both sides of the barrier, the flux ratio equals the amplitude-squared ratio $|t|^2$. The textbook $e^{-2\kappa L}$ is the opaque-barrier limit of this expression.

blocks.heading: Setting up the four boundary conditions
blocks.body: Take incident amplitude 1: $\psi_I = e^{ikx} + r e^{-ikx}$ for $x<0$; $\psi_{II} = A\cosh(\kappa x) + B\sinh(\kappa x)$ inside (real combination of $e^{\pm\kappa x}$); $\psi_{III} = t\,e^{ikx}$ for $x > L$ — no source on the right, so no incoming wave there. Continuity of $\psi$ and $\psi'$ at $x=0$ and $x=L$ yields four linear equations in $r$, $A$, $B$, $t$. Eliminating $A$ and $B$ (two subtractions) leaves $t$ in terms of hyperbolic functions of $\kappa L$; the algebra is exactly the impedance-matching calculation familiar from transmission lines and coated optics.

blocks.heading: Recovering the exponential law
blocks.body: In the opaque regime $\kappa L \gg 1$, use $\sinh(\kappa L) \approx \tfrac{1}{2}e^{\kappa L}$: $$T \approx \frac{4E(U_0-E)}{U_0^2}\,e^{-2\kappa L} = \frac{16E(U_0-E)}{U_0^2}\cdot\frac{e^{-2\kappa L}}{4}.$$ The prefactor $16E(U_0-E)/U_0^2$ is between 0 and 4 and equals 4 at $E = U_0/2$ — so the honest $T$ can be a small multiple of $e^{-2\kappa L}$, but only in the regime where $e^{-2\kappa L}$ is already minuscule. That is why the exponential alone is an excellent everyday estimate.

blocks.heading: How far off is $e^{-2\kappa L}$?
blocks.body: For the worked numbers above ($E = 2.00$ eV, $U_0 = 5.00$ eV, $L = 0.70$ nm): $\kappa L = 6.21$, so $\sinh(6.21) = 249$ and $\sinh^2 = 6.2\times10^{4}$. Then $$T = \left[1 + \frac{25 \times 6.2\times10^{4}}{4(2)(3)}\right]^{-1} = \frac{1}{6.5\times10^{4}} = 1.5\times10^{-5}.$$ The crude law gave $4\times10^{-6}$; the prefactor $16(2)(3)/25 = 3.8$ explains the difference exactly. For most estimates the exponential alone is fine; for STM calibration the prefactor matters.

blocks.heading: Gamow's alpha-decay theory
blocks.body: An alpha particle rattling inside a nucleus sees a Coulomb barrier of a few tenths of the nuclear radius. Its escape rate is the attempt frequency (about $10^{21}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$) times the transmission through the barrier — obtained by joining exponentials through the sloping Coulomb edge (a WKB integral). The result is the Geiger–Nuttall law: $\log t_{1/2}$ is linear in $1/\sqrt{E}$, spanning half-lives from $10^{-7}$ s (polonium-212) to $10^{17}$ s (uranium-238) — twenty-four orders of magnitude from a few MeV of energy change. Nothing in classical physics can produce such a lever arm; the exponential does.

blocks.heading: Above the barrier, resonances
blocks.body: For $E > U_0$ the same four boundary conditions give $R > 0$ again (above-barrier reflection — the step effect twice), and the transmission oscillates with $L$: full transmission whenever the barrier holds a whole number of half-wavelengths, exactly like a Fabry–Pérot etalon. Quantum-well lasers and resonant tunneling diodes are engineered to sit on these resonances. The tunneling and resonance pictures are the two halves of one scattering theory.

intro: Trap an electron between two impenetrable walls and its matter wave must fit: like a string fixed at both ends, only standing waves survive, and only certain wavelengths — therefore momenta, therefore energies. This is the infinite potential well, the simplest system quantum mechanics solves exactly, and the cleanest place to watch energy quantization emerge from boundary conditions rather than postulates.
objectives: Explain why confinement forces standing-wave matter patterns with discrete wavelengths
Apply $E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2 = n^2E_1$ and compute level spacings
Interpret the nonzero ground-state energy as the uncertainty principle at work

concepts.statement: **An electron trapped between rigid walls at $x = 0$ and $x = L$ (infinite potential outside) has wave functions that vanish at both walls.** The surviving standing de Broglie waves carry $n$ half-wavelengths: $\lambda_n = 2L/n$, so $p_n = nh/2L$.

**The allowed energies of the trapped electron are** $$E_n = \frac{n^2h^2}{8mL^2} = n^2E_1, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$$ with $E_1 = h^2/8mL^2$. Levels climb as $n^2$: the gap from $n$ to $n+1$ grows as $2n+1$.
concepts.detail: Substitute $p = nh/2L$ into $E = p^2/2m$ — the quantization is pure de Broglie plus fitting.

concepts.statement: **The ground state is not zero energy: $E_1 > 0$ always.** Confinement to $\Delta x = L$ forces $\Delta p \geq \hbar/L$, and the accompanying kinetic energy is exactly the uncertainty principle made visible. Nothing trapped can ever be at rest.

**A jump from $n_\text{hi}$ to $n_\text{lo}$ emits a photon of energy** $$hf = E_{n_\text{hi}} - E_{n_\text{lo}} = (n_\text{hi}^2 - n_\text{lo}^2)E_1.$$ The well's spectrum is a fingerprint of its size: smaller traps emit bluer photons.

concepts.term: Energies of a Trapped Electron: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Energies of a Trapped Electron problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is quantized traps with $E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2$ and hydrogen $E_n = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^2$; the working equation is $E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2$, $\psi_n = \sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)$, $E_n = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{eV}$ and nanometers) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $E_1\sim \text{eV}$ for nm wells; $a_0 = 0.529\ \text{\AA}$; infinite-well idealization; $n = 1,2,\dots$ only.

examples.title: An atom-sized trap
examples.problem: An electron is trapped in an infinite well of width $L = 100$ pm (one atomic diameter). Find $E_1$, the photon emitted in the $n = 2 \to 1$ jump, and its wavelength.

steps.label: Wavelength
steps.text: $\lambda = hc/\Delta E = 1240/113 = 11.0$ nm — extreme ultraviolet, ten times bluer than visible light.

steps.label: Scale check
steps.text: Atomic-scale confinement naturally produces electron-volt energies and UV photons — the same arithmetic that runs real atoms.

examples.result: E₁ = 37.7 eV; the 2→1 photon carries 113 eV at λ = 11.0 nm.

examples.title: Energies of a Trapped Electron: well-energy check
examples.problem: An electron is trapped in an infinite well of width $L = 1\ \text{nm}$. Estimate $E_1 = h^2/8mL^2$ in eV.
examples.result: $E_1 \approx 0.376\ \text{eV}$.

keyTakeaways: Fitting $n$ half-wavelengths into width $L$ quantizes momentum and energy: $E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2$.
The ground state energy is never zero — confinement plus the uncertainty principle forbid rest.
Level spacings grow with $n^2$ and shrink as $L^2$ widens: bigger traps, closer levels.

quiz.q: For a particle in an infinite well, doubling $L$ changes the ground energy to:
options: one quarter of its former value

quiz.q: The ratio $E_3/E_1$ for a trapped electron equals:
The ground state energy is nonzero because:
options: confinement forces a momentum spread, hence kinetic energy (the uncertainty principle)
quiz.explanation: Zero momentum spread over the whole box is impossible if the position is confined to it.

intro: The energies are only half the solution of the infinite well; the other half is what the electron is doing inside. The normalized wave functions are standing sine waves, and their squared magnitudes are probability densities: the ground state piles probability in the middle, excited states carve nodes, and expectation values become honest integrals. This is where the Born rule earns its keep as a calculation tool.
objectives: Write and normalize the wave functions $\psi_n = \sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)$
Compute probabilities as areas under $|\psi_n|^2$ for given intervals
Evaluate $\langle x \rangle$ and contrast quantum and classical probability densities

concepts.statement: **The stationary states of the infinite well are** $$\psi_n(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}, \qquad 0 < x < L,$$ zero elsewhere. The prefactor $\sqrt{2/L}$ enforces $\int_0^L |\psi_n|^2 dx = 1$.
concepts.detail: State $n$ has $n - 1$ interior nodes (zeros); the more nodes, the higher the kinetic energy — curvature is kinetic energy in the Schrödinger equation.

concepts.statement: **The probability of finding the electron between $x_a$ and $x_b$ is the area under the density curve:** $$P = \int_{x_a}^{x_b} |\psi_n(x)|^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x}{L} - \frac{1}{2n\pi}\sin\frac{2n\pi x}{L}\right]_{x_a}^{x_b}.$$ Probabilities are areas, never point values: $|\psi|^2$ at a single point contributes nothing.

**The average of repeated position measurements is $\langle x \rangle = \int x|\psi_n|^2 dx$ — which equals $L/2$ for every $n$** by the symmetry of each standing wave about the box's center. A measurement of energy, by contrast, returns exactly $E_n$ every time.

**A classical particle bounces equally everywhere — its density is the flat $1/L$.** The quantum ground state instead peaks at the center and vanishes at the walls; but as $n$ grows the oscillations crowd together and the averaged quantum density flattens toward the classical one — Bohr's correspondence principle in a box.

examples.title: Probability in the left quarter
examples.problem: For the ground state ($n = 1$) of an electron in a well of width $L$, what is the probability of finding it in the left quarter, $0 \leq x \leq L/4$? Compare with $n = 2$.

steps.label: Evaluate for n = 2
steps.text: With $n = 2$ the sine argument is $4\pi x/L$; at $x = L/4$ it is $\pi$, so $P = 1/4 - \sin\pi/(4\pi) = 0.250$.

steps.label: Interpretation
steps.text: The ground state huddles at the center — only 9% in the left quarter — while the first excited state's antinode region makes the first quarter hold exactly its classical share.

examples.result: 9.1% for the ground state; 25.0% for the first excited state.

examples.title: Wave Functions of a Trapped Electron: well-energy check
examples.problem: An electron is trapped in an infinite well of width $L = 1.5\ \text{nm}$. Estimate $E_1 = h^2/8mL^2$ in eV.
examples.result: $E_1 \approx 0.167\ \text{eV}$.

keyTakeaways: $\psi_n = \sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)$; normalization is built into the prefactor.
Probabilities are areas under $|\psi|^2$ — 9.1% for the ground state in the left quarter, 25% for $n = 2$.
$\langle x \rangle = L/2$ for all $n$; high-$n$ densities average to the classical $1/L$.

quiz.q: The wave function $\psi_3$ of an infinite well has how many interior nodes?
quiz.explanation: State $n$ has $n-1$ interior zeros.

quiz.q: The probability of finding the electron exactly at $x = L/2$ (ground state) is:
quiz.explanation: A point has zero width; only areas under $|\psi|^2$ carry probability.

quiz.q: For state $n$, the expectation value $\langle x \rangle$ equals:
quiz.explanation: Each standing wave is symmetric about the box's center.

intro: Real walls are not infinitely high: they are steep hills of finite height $U_0$. Three things change. The electron can no longer count on being trapped — only energies below $U_0$ are bound. The wave functions do not die at the walls — they leak exponentially into them. And every bound level sinks below its infinite-well value, because the leakage effectively widens the box.
objectives: Explain why a finite well binds only a finite number of levels with $E < U_0$
Describe the exponential penetration into the walls and estimate its depth $1/\kappa$
Account for the lowering of bound-state energies relative to the infinite well

concepts.statement: **A finite well: $U = 0$ inside $0 < x < L$ and $U = U_0$ outside.** Bound states have $E < U_0$; any state with $E > U_0$ is unbound (scattering). The number of bound states is finite — roughly the largest $n$ with $n^2E_1^{(\infty)} < U_0$.

**Inside the forbidden walls the wave function decays as $e^{-\kappa x}$ with** $$\kappa = \frac{\sqrt{2m(U_0-E)}}{\hbar},$$ so the probability reaches a characteristic depth $1/\kappa$ beyond the wall. Shallow states (small $U_0 - E$) are the leakiest; deep states barely notice the boundary.

**Because the wave extends past the walls, the effective box is wider than $L$ — and wider boxes mean lower $E_n$.** Every bound level sits below its infinite-well counterpart, with the ground state lowered most in relative terms. Exact values require matching $\psi$ and $\psi'$ numerically (transcendental equations); the trends are rigorous.

concepts.term: An Electron in a Finite Well: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve An Electron in a Finite Well problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is quantized traps with $E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2$ and hydrogen $E_n = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^2$; the working equation is $E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2$, $\psi_n = \sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)$, $E_n = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{eV}$ and nanometers) emerges naturally.

concepts.term: An Electron in a Finite Well: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **An Electron in a Finite Well lives at $E_1\sim \text{eV}$ for nm wells; $a_0 = 0.529\ \text{\AA}$ and the textbook model holds while infinite-well idealization; $n = 1,2,\dots$ only.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a An Electron in a Finite Well calculation gives seconds when $\text{eV}$ and nanometers demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $E_1\sim \text{eV}$ for nm wells; $a_0 = 0.529\ \text{\AA}$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Counting the states of a deep well
examples.problem: An electron occupies a finite well with $L = 100$ pm and $U_0 = 1000$ eV. Using the infinite-well levels as an estimate, how many bound states are there, and how far does the top state penetrate the walls?

steps.label: Infinite-well scale
steps.text: From the previous section, $E_1 = 37.7$ eV for this width, so estimated levels sit at $n^2 \times 37.7$ eV.

steps.label: Bound-state count
steps.text: Require $n^2(37.7) < 1000$: $n < \sqrt{26.5} = 5.2$, so five bound states ($n = 1$ to $5$; $E_5 \approx 943$ eV, just under the rim).

steps.label: Penetration of the top state
steps.text: For $E_5$: $\kappa = \sqrt{2m(U_0-E_5)}/\hbar = \sqrt{2(9.11\times10^{-31})(57)(1.602\times10^{-19})}/(1.055\times10^{-34}) = 3.9\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$, a depth of $1/\kappa = 26$ pm — a quarter of the box width.

steps.label: Contrast
steps.text: The ground state ($U_0 - E \approx 960$ eV) has $1/\kappa \approx 6$ pm: deep states barely leak, shallow ones spill out.

examples.result: Five bound states; the topmost reaches ~26 pm into each wall, the ground state only ~6 pm — and true energies lie slightly below these estimates.

examples.title: An Electron in a Finite Well: well-energy check
examples.problem: An electron is trapped in an infinite well of width $L = 0.5\ \text{nm}$. Estimate $E_1 = h^2/8mL^2$ in eV.
examples.result: $E_1 \approx 1.5\ \text{eV}$.

keyTakeaways: A finite well traps only levels with $E < U_0$ — a finite count, roughly $n^2E_1 < U_0$.
Wave functions leak a depth $1/\kappa = \hbar/\sqrt{2m(U_0-E)}$ into the walls; shallow states leak farthest.
Leakage widens the effective box, lowering every bound energy below the infinite-well value.

quiz.q: Compared with an infinite well of the same width, the finite well's bound energies are:
options: lower, because the wave extends into the walls
quiz.explanation: A longer effective wavelength fits, meaning lower momentum and energy.

quiz.q: The penetration depth $1/\kappa$ into the wall is largest for:
options: the state closest to the rim $U_0$
the state with most interior nodes only
quiz.explanation: $\kappa \propto \sqrt{U_0 - E}$: the smaller the deficit, the deeper the leak.

quiz.q: A finite well has five bound states. A sixth measurement of the energy could yield:
quiz.explanation: Beyond the five bound states, the spectrum is continuous — the electron is free.

intro: Extend the trap to two or three dimensions and the arithmetic multiplies: the wave function factorizes, each dimension carries its own quantum number, and the energies add. New physics appears — distinct states can share one energy, called degeneracy — and so does new technology: quantum dots, tiny boxes whose emitted color is set by their size, are engineered degeneracy-and-confinement playgrounds.
objectives: Write the energies $E = (h^2/8m)(n_x^2/L_x^2 + n_y^2/L_y^2)$ for a rectangular 2D trap
Define degeneracy and count states for square traps from sums of squares
Connect trap size to transition frequencies, as in quantum dots

concepts.statement: **In a rectangular trap the Schrödinger equation separates: $\psi(x, y) = \psi_x(x)\psi_y(y)$, and the energies add.** Each dimension behaves as its own infinite well, labeled by its own quantum number $n_x$, $n_y$ (and $n_z$ in 3D).

**For a rectangular trap of sides $L_x, L_y$:** $$E_{n_x n_y} = \frac{h^2}{8m}\left(\frac{n_x^2}{L_x^2} + \frac{n_y^2}{L_y^2}\right),$$ and for a square ($L_x = L_y = L$) simply $E = (h^2/8mL^2)(n_x^2 + n_y^2)$ — sums of two squares.

**Two different quantum states with the same energy are degenerate.** In a square trap, $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 1)$ share $5(h^2/8mL^2)$ — a two-fold degeneracy from the symmetry of swapping $x$ and $y$. Accidental degeneracies add more: $50 = 1 + 49 = 25 + 25$ gives $(1,7)$, $(7,1)$, $(5,5)$ — three states, one energy.

**A nanometer-scale box for electrons is a quantum dot: its level spacing — hence its absorbed and emitted colors — is tuned by size.** Shrinking the dot from 1 µm to 10 nm raises the fundamental spacing by a factor of $10^4$, from microwaves into the infrared and visible. Semiconductor dots (with effective masses) put this arithmetic to work in lasers, displays and qubits.

examples.title: A menu of levels for a square trap
examples.problem: An electron occupies a square 2D trap with $L = 10$ nm. List the lowest energies in units of $E_0 = h^2/8mL^2$, their quantum numbers, and degeneracies; then find the photon for the $(1,1) \to (2,1)$ transition.

steps.label: Unit of energy
steps.text: From the 1D result scaled to $L = 10$ nm: $E_0 = 37.7\ \mathrm{eV} \times (100\ \mathrm{pm}/10\ \mathrm{nm})^2 = 3.8\times10^{-3}$ eV.

steps.label: Photon
steps.text: $\lambda = hc/\Delta E = 1240/0.0113 = 1.1\times10^{5}$ nm $= 0.11$ mm — far infrared, a microwave-scale transition.

examples.result: 2E₀ (1 state), 5E₀ (2), 8E₀ (1), 10E₀ (2), 13E₀ (2), …; the first excitation emits at λ ≈ 0.11 mm.

examples.title: Two- and Three-Dimensional Electron Traps: well-energy check
examples.problem: An electron is trapped in an infinite well of width $L = 1\ \text{nm}$. Estimate $E_1 = h^2/8mL^2$ in eV.
examples.result: $E_1 \approx 0.376\ \text{eV}$.

keyTakeaways: 2D and 3D traps: energies add one $n^2/L^2$ term per dimension.
Degeneracy: distinct quantum states sharing an energy, beginning with $(1,2)$ ↔ $(2,1)$ in a square trap.
Level spacing scales as $1/L^2$ — the knob that tunes quantum-dot colors.

quiz.q: In a square 2D trap, the states $(1, 3)$ and $(3, 1)$ are:
quiz.explanation: Both carry $n_x^2 + n_y^2 = 10$, and the square's symmetry makes the energies equal.

quiz.q: The ground-state energy of a cubical 3D trap, in units of $E_0 = h^2/8mL^2$, is:
quiz.explanation: Each dimension contributes its own $1^2$: $(1+1+1)E_0 = 3E_0$.

quiz.q: Shrinking a quantum dot from 100 nm to 10 nm multiplies its level spacings by:
quiz.explanation: Spacings go as $1/L^2$: a tenfold shorter side gives a hundredfold boost.

intro: Hydrogen is the only atom nature solves in closed form, and it repays the effort: the Coulomb potential in three dimensions yields the exact energies, the three quantum numbers, and wave functions whose shapes — spheres, dumbbells, cloverleafs — underlie all of chemistry. The levels agree with Bohr's $-13.60$ eV/n², but now they come from the Schrödinger equation, with orbits replaced by probability clouds.
objectives: State the three quantum numbers $n$, $l$, $m_l$ and their allowed values
Use $E_n = -13.60\ \mathrm{eV}/n^2$ to compute transition wavelengths
Describe the ground-state wave function, radial probability, and the Bohr radius

concepts.statement: **Solving the Schrödinger equation for the Coulomb potential labels each state by** $$n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots; \qquad l = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1; \qquad m_l = -l, \ldots, 0, \ldots, +l.$$ The state count for level $n$ (ignoring spin) is $n^2$ — hydrogen's famous degeneracy.

**The bound-state energies are** $$E_n = -\frac{13.60\ \mathrm{eV}}{n^2},$$ with $E = 0$ the ionization threshold. They depend on $n$ alone — the special symmetry of the $1/r$ potential that Bohr guessed and Schrödinger derived.

**The ground state is spherically symmetric, $\psi_{100} \propto e^{-r/a_0}$, with the Bohr radius $a_0 = 52.9$ pm.** The radial probability $P(r) = r^2|R(r)|^2$ peaks exactly at $r = a_0$: the most probable finding-distance reproduces the first Bohr orbit. States with $l > 0$ carry angular shapes (dumbbells for $l = 1$) set by the $Y_l^{m_l}$ angular factors.

**Jumping between levels emits photons $hf = 13.60(1/n_\text{lo}^2 - 1/n_\text{hi}^2)$ eV.** The Lyman series (to $n = 1$) lies ultraviolet, Balmer (to $n = 2$) spans the visible — Hα at 656 nm — and Paschen and beyond fall infrared. Ionizing the ground state takes exactly 13.6 eV.

**Solve The Hydrogen Atom problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is quantized traps with $E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2$ and hydrogen $E_n = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^2$; the working equation is $E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2$, $\psi_n = \sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)$, $E_n = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{eV}$ and nanometers) emerges naturally.

examples.title: The Hα line, exactly
examples.problem: Compute the wavelength of the $n = 3 \to 2$ transition in hydrogen (the red Hα line), and of $n = 2 \to 1$ (Lyman α).

steps.label: Wavelength
steps.text: $\lambda = hc/\Delta E = 1240/1.89 = 656$ nm — the red line that colors hydrogen nebulae.

steps.label: Lyman α
steps.text: $\Delta E = 13.60(1 - 1/4) = 10.2$ eV, so $\lambda = 1240/10.2 = 122$ nm — ultraviolet.

steps.label: Ionization
steps.text: A photon needs $\geq 13.6$ eV ($\lambda \leq 91.2$ nm) to strip the ground-state electron entirely.

examples.result: Hα = 656 nm (red); Lyman α = 122 nm (UV); ionization edge at 91.2 nm.

examples.title: The Hydrogen Atom: well-energy check
examples.problem: An electron is trapped in an infinite well of width $L = 1.5\ \text{nm}$. Estimate $E_1 = h^2/8mL^2$ in eV.
examples.result: $E_1 \approx 0.167\ \text{eV}$.

keyTakeaways: Quantum numbers $n \geq 1$, $l < n$, $|m_l| \leq l$ label the hydrogen states; level $n$ is $n^2$-fold degenerate.
$E_n = -13.60\ \mathrm{eV}/n^2$: the Schrödinger derivation of Bohr's levels.
The ground state $\psi \propto e^{-r/a_0}$ peaks in radial probability at the Bohr radius $a_0 = 52.9$ pm.

quiz.q: For $n = 3$, the allowed values of $l$ are:
quiz.explanation: $l$ runs from 0 up to $n - 1$.

quiz.q: How many hydrogen states share $n = 3$ (ignoring spin)?
The energy needed to ionize hydrogen from its ground state is:
quiz.explanation: Lift the electron from $-13.6$ eV to the $E = 0$ continuum.

intro: Quantum mechanics does not just quantize the magnitude of atomic angular momentum — it quantizes its orientation in space. For a given $l$, the component along any chosen axis takes only $2l + 1$ values, equally spaced: space quantization. Add the electron's intrinsic spin, and atoms acquire the magnetic fingerprints by which spectroscopy, Stern–Gerlach experiments, and the whole periodic table are read.
objectives: Compute orbital angular momentum magnitudes $L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\,\hbar$
Apply space quantization $L_z = m_l\hbar$ and find allowed orientations
Describe electron spin and the Stern–Gerlach evidence

concepts.statement: **An atomic state with orbital quantum number $l$ carries angular momentum of magnitude** $$L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\,\hbar.$$ For $l = 0$ it vanishes exactly — s states orbit nothing, another break with Bohr's imagery of circulating electrons.

**Along any chosen axis (set, say, by a magnetic field) the angular momentum component takes only the values** $$L_z = m_l\hbar, \qquad m_l = -l, \ldots, 0, \ldots, +l$$ — $2l + 1$ orientations and no others. The vector $\vec L$ makes specific angles with the axis, none of which aligns it perfectly: $|m_l|\hbar < \sqrt{l(l+1)}\hbar$ always.

**The electron carries intrinsic angular momentum with spin quantum number $s = 1/2$:** $$S = \sqrt{s(s+1)}\,\hbar = \sqrt{3/2}\,\hbar, \qquad S_z = \pm\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar.$$ Spin is not rotation in space — it is an internal label, the fourth quantum number $m_s$, doubling every state count.

**A beam of silver atoms sent through a nonuniform magnetic field split into two spots — exactly the two $S_z$ values of one unpaired electron.** Space quantization made visible on a plate (1922), before quantum mechanics was even written. Orbital and spin magnetic moments, their coupling, and the addition rules $\vec J = \vec L + \vec S$ generate the fine structure and the multiplet patterns by which atomic spectra are decoded.

concepts.term: Angular Momentum of Atoms: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Angular Momentum of Atoms problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is quantized traps with $E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2$ and hydrogen $E_n = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^2$; the working equation is $E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2$, $\psi_n = \sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)$, $E_n = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{eV}$ and nanometers) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $E_1\sim \text{eV}$ for nm wells; $a_0 = 0.529\ \text{\AA}$; infinite-well idealization; $n = 1,2,\dots$ only.

examples.title: Orientations for $l = 2$
examples.problem: An atomic state has $l = 2$. Find the magnitude of $\vec L$, the possible $L_z$ values, and the smallest allowed angle with the $z$-axis.

steps.label: Magnitude
steps.text: $L = \sqrt{2(3)}\,\hbar = \sqrt{6}\,\hbar = 2.45\hbar$.

steps.label: Components
steps.text: $m_l = -2, -1, 0, +1, +2$: five orientations, $L_z = -2\hbar$ to $+2\hbar$ in steps of $\hbar$.

steps.label: Smallest angle
steps.text: $\cos\theta_\min = L_z/L = 2/\sqrt{6} = 0.816$, so $\theta_\min = 35.3^\circ$.

steps.label: Moral
steps.text: Even the steepest allowed tilt falls short of the axis — $L_z$ can never equal the full magnitude $L$. Angular momentum vectors refuse to line up with any axis.

examples.result: L = 2.45ħ, five $L_z$ values from −2ħ to +2ħ, closest tilt 35.3° from the axis.

examples.title: Angular Momentum of Atoms: well-energy check
examples.problem: An electron is trapped in an infinite well of width $L = 0.5\ \text{nm}$. Estimate $E_1 = h^2/8mL^2$ in eV.
examples.result: $E_1 \approx 1.5\ \text{eV}$.

keyTakeaways: $L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\hbar$ and $L_z = m_l\hbar$ with $2l+1$ allowed orientations — space quantization.
The vector never aligns with the axis: $|m_l|\hbar < \sqrt{l(l+1)}\hbar$ always.
Electron spin ($s = 1/2$, $S_z = \pm\hbar/2$) doubles every state and produced the two-spot Stern–Gerlach pattern.

quiz.q: For $l = 3$, the magnitude of the orbital angular momentum is:
quiz.explanation: $L = \sqrt{3(4)}\,\hbar = \sqrt{12}\,\hbar \approx 3.46\hbar$ — not simply $l\hbar$.

quiz.q: For $l = 1$, the allowed $L_z$ values are:
quiz.explanation: $2l + 1 = 3$ orientations, spaced by $\hbar$.

quiz.q: The Stern–Gerlach experiment split a silver beam into two spots because:
options: the unpaired electron has $s = 1/2$: two $S_z$ orientations
silver atoms are magnetic dipoles of all strengths
the field was nonuniform by accident
quiz.explanation: One unpaired $5s$ electron gives $m_s = \pm 1/2$ — space quantization of spin made visible.

intro: An atom is more than the Bohr hydrogen picture: every electron carries both orbital and spin angular momentum, and each of them drags around a magnetic dipole moment. Because these quantities are quantized, an atom placed in a magnetic field can assume only a discrete menu of orientations. This section assembles the quantum numbers and magnetic moments that the rest of the chapter — Stern–Gerlach, resonance, the periodic table — will use as its vocabulary.
objectives: Compute the magnitude and z component of an electron's orbital and spin angular momentum from the quantum numbers $\ell$, $m_\ell$, $s$ and $m_s$
Relate orbital and spin angular momentum to the corresponding magnetic dipole moments and evaluate the Bohr magneton
Combine orbital and spin contributions into the total angular momentum J of an atom

concepts.statement: A bound electron with orbital quantum number $\ell = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1$ has angular momentum of magnitude $$L = \sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}\,\hbar$$ whose projection on any chosen z axis is restricted to $L_z = m_\ell\hbar$ with $m_\ell = -\ell, \ldots, 0, \ldots, +\ell$ — the vector has length $\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}\,\hbar$ but can never point exactly along z, since $|m_\ell| \le \ell < \sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}$.
concepts.detail: With $\hbar = 1.055\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\cdot s}$, a 2p electron ($\ell = 1$) has $L = \sqrt{2}\,\hbar = 1.49\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\cdot s}$ and allowed projections $L_z = +\hbar, 0, -\hbar$.

concepts.statement: An orbiting electron is a current loop, and its magnetic dipole moment is **antiparallel** to its angular momentum: $$\vec\mu_\mathrm{orb} = -\frac{e}{2m_e}\vec L,\qquad \mu_\mathrm{orb} = \sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}\,\mu_B,$$ where the **Bohr magneton** $\mu_B = eh/4\pi m_e = 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J/T}$ is the natural unit of atomic magnetism.
concepts.detail: Because the electron is negative, the moment points opposite $\vec L$; the ratio $\mu/L$ is called the orbital gyromagnetic ratio and equals $e/2m_e$ to remarkable precision.

concepts.statement: Electrons carry an intrinsic angular momentum with $s = 1/2$: $$S = \sqrt{s(s+1)}\,\hbar = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hbar,\qquad S_z = m_s\hbar = \pm\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar.$$ The spin magnetic moment is twice as effective per unit angular momentum as the orbital one: $\vec\mu_s = -(e/m_e)\vec S$, so $\mu_{s,z} = \mp\mu_B$.
concepts.detail: This factor-of-2 surprise has no classical explanation; it emerges from the Dirac equation of relativistic quantum mechanics and is the reason spin effects dominate the Stern–Gerlach pattern of atoms whose orbital momentum is zero.

concepts.statement: In a real atom the electron's $\vec L$ and $\vec S$ couple into a total $\vec J = \vec L + \vec S$ with $J = \sqrt{j(j+1)}\,\hbar$, where $j = |\ell \pm 1/2|$ for a single electron; only $J$ and one component (say $J_z$) can be sharp at the same time.
concepts.detail: This spin–orbit coupling splits spectral lines into fine-structure doublets — the fingerprint, for example, of the sodium D lines at 589.0 and 589.6 nm.

concepts.statement: **Solve Properties of Atoms problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is atomic angular momentum, X rays and lasers; the working equation is $L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\hbar$, $L_z = m_l\hbar$, $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV$, $\mu_B = 9.27\times 10^{-24}\ \text{J/T}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (tesla and $\text{eV}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\lambda_{\min}\sim 0.01$--$0.1\ \text{nm}$ for $10$--$100\ \text{kV}$; single-electron picture first; Pauli plus Coulomb for many electrons.

examples.title: Magnetic moment of a 2p electron
examples.problem: An electron in a hydrogen atom occupies the 2p state ($n = 2$, $\ell = 1$). Find the magnitude of its orbital angular momentum, its magnetic dipole moment, and the possible values of $L_z$.

steps.label: Setup
steps.text: With $\ell = 1$ the angular momentum magnitude is $L = \sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}\,\hbar = \sqrt{2}\,\hbar$.

steps.label: Numbers
steps.text: $L = 1.414 \times 1.055\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\cdot s} = 1.49\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\cdot s}$.

steps.label: Moment
steps.text: The moment is $\mu_\mathrm{orb} = \sqrt{2}\,\mu_B = 1.414 \times 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J/T}$.

examples.result: $L = 1.49\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\cdot s}$, $\mu_\mathrm{orb} = 1.31\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/T}$, and $L_z \in \{+\hbar, 0, -\hbar\}$.

examples.title: Properties of Atoms: $\lambda_{\min}$ check
examples.problem: An X-ray tube runs at $V = 70\ \text{kV}$. Find $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV = 1240/(V\text{ in volts})\ \text{nm}$.

steps.label: Volts
steps.text: $eV = 70\times 10^3\ \text{eV}$.

examples.result: $\lambda_{\min} \approx 17.7\ \text{pm}$.

keyTakeaways: Orbital angular momentum is quantized in both magnitude ($\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}\hbar$) and projection ($m_\ell\hbar$), with $2\ell+1$ allowed orientations.
Each unit of angular momentum carries a magnetic moment, with the spin gyromagnetic ratio twice the orbital one; the Bohr magneton $\mu_B = 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J/T}$ sets the scale.
Spin is intrinsic and universal: every electron has $s = 1/2$ with only two projections, $\pm\hbar/2$, whatever its orbital state.

quiz.q: For an electron with principal quantum number n = 3, which set of orbital quantum numbers l is allowed?
quiz.explanation: For a given n, l runs from 0 up to n − 1, so n = 3 gives l = 0, 1, 2 (the 3s, 3p, 3d subshells).

quiz.q: How many orientations does the orbital angular momentum vector have for l = 2?
quiz.explanation: $m_\ell$ takes the $2\ell+1 = 5$ values $-2, -1, 0, +1, +2$; the vector can be drawn on five distinct cones about the z axis.

quiz.q: An electron's spin magnetic moment component is related to $S_z$ by $\mu_{s,z} = -(e/m_e)S_z$. Compared with the orbital relation $\mu_\mathrm{orb} = -(e/2m_e)L$, spin magnetism is
options: half as effective per unit angular momentum
quiz.explanation: The spin gyromagnetic ratio $e/m_e$ is exactly twice the orbital ratio $e/2m_e$ — a purely relativistic (Dirac) result with no classical analog.

quiz.q: The Bohr magneton has magnitude
quiz.explanation: $\mu_B = eh/4\pi m_e = 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J/T}$; the first option is the nuclear magneton, smaller by $m_e/m_p \approx 1/1836$.

intro: In 1922 Stern and Gerlach sent a narrow beam of silver atoms through a strongly nonuniform magnetic field and caught them on a glass plate. Classical physics predicts a continuous smear; quantum physics predicts a set of discrete spots. The experiment delivered space quantization to the laboratory — and, because silver atoms have zero orbital angular momentum, the two observed spots revealed the electron's spin.
objectives: Explain why a magnetic dipole feels a net force only in a nonuniform field and compute that force
Trace how the silver-atom ground state reduces the beam to a two-way split governed by spin alone
Interpret the two-spot pattern as direct evidence for space quantization and for $m_s = \pm1/2$

concepts.term: Force on a dipole in a nonuniform field
concepts.statement: In a uniform field a magnetic dipole feels a torque $\vec\tau = \vec\mu \times \vec B$ but no net force. In a field varying along z, the force is $$F_z = -\frac{\partial U}{\partial z} = \mu_z\,\frac{\partial B_z}{\partial z},$$ so atoms with different $\mu_z$ are pushed different amounts — the field acts as a spin sorter.
concepts.detail: A gradient of $10^3\ \mathrm{T/m}$ (about 10 T per mm, achievable between shaped pole pieces) acting on one Bohr magneton gives a force of order $10^{-20}\ \mathrm{N}$ — tiny, but enough over a flight of centimeters to separate the spin populations by millimeters.

concepts.statement: Silver (Z = 47) has the ground-state configuration $[\mathrm{Kr}]\,4d^{10}5s^1$: the 46 inner electrons pair off with zero net angular momentum, so the atom's entire magnetic character comes from the single 5s electron, which has $\ell = 0$ and $s = 1/2$.
concepts.detail: With $L = 0$ the orbital moment vanishes, and only the two spin projections $m_s = \pm1/2$ remain — the beam must split into exactly two parts, not the $2\ell+1 = 1$ of the orbital theory or the continuum of classical physics.

concepts.statement: The Stern–Gerlach result — **two** sharp spots, one deflected toward the strong-field region, one away — is direct experimental proof that the orientation of an atomic magnetic moment is quantized: the projection $\mu_z$ takes only the discrete values $\pm\mu_B$ for silver.
concepts.detail: The 1922 experiment (with the interpretation completed by Uhlenbeck, Goudsmit and others in 1925–26) was the first observation of spin quantization and remains the cleanest demonstration that quantum numbers label real, measurable orientations.

concepts.statement: **Solve The Stern–Gerlach Experiment problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is atomic angular momentum, X rays and lasers; the working equation is $L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\hbar$, $L_z = m_l\hbar$, $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV$, $\mu_B = 9.27\times 10^{-24}\ \text{J/T}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (tesla and $\text{eV}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\lambda_{\min}\sim 0.01$--$0.1\ \text{nm}$ for $10$--$100\ \text{kV}$; single-electron picture first; Pauli plus Coulomb for many electrons.

concepts.term: The Stern–Gerlach Experiment: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **The Stern–Gerlach Experiment lives at $\lambda_{\min}\sim 0.01$--$0.1\ \text{nm}$ for $10$--$100\ \text{kV}$ and the textbook model holds while single-electron picture first; Pauli plus Coulomb for many electrons.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a The Stern–Gerlach Experiment calculation gives seconds when tesla and $\text{eV}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $\lambda_{\min}\sim 0.01$--$0.1\ \text{nm}$ for $10$--$100\ \text{kV}$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

figures.caption: The Stern–Gerlach experiment: silver atoms evaporate from an oven, are collimated into a beam, and pass between asymmetric pole pieces that produce a strong vertical field gradient. A uniform field would merely torque the atoms; the gradient exerts $F_z = \mu_z\,\partial B_z/\partial z$, splitting the beam into two spots on the collector plate — one for each spin projection of the lone 5s electron.

examples.title: Deflection of a silver atom in the magnet
examples.problem: Silver-108 atoms (mass 108 u) travel at 500 m/s through a 3.5 cm magnet with field gradient $\partial B_z/\partial z = 1.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{T/m}$, then fly 0.50 m to the collector. With $\mu_z = \pm\mu_B$, estimate the deflection of one spot.

steps.label: Force
steps.text: $F_z = \mu_B\,(\partial B/\partial z) = (9.27\times10^{-24})(1.0\times10^{3}) = 9.27\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{N}$.

steps.label: Acceleration
steps.text: $m = 108 \times 1.66\times10^{-27} = 1.79\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$, so $a = F/m = 5.18\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

steps.label: Inside the magnet
steps.text: Time in the field: $t_1 = 0.035/500 = 7.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s}$; the atom leaves with $v_z = at_1 = 3.6\ \mathrm{m/s}$, displaced $\tfrac{1}{2}at_1^2 = 0.13\ \mathrm{mm}$.

steps.label: Free flight
steps.text: The remaining 0.50 m takes $t_2 = 1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$, adding $v_z t_2 = 3.6\ \mathrm{mm}$.

examples.result: Each spot sits about 3.7 mm from the axis, so the two spin populations land roughly 7 mm apart — a visible split, matching the millimeter-scale separations Stern and Gerlach photographed.

examples.title: The Stern–Gerlach Experiment: $\lambda_{\min}$ check
examples.problem: An X-ray tube runs at $V = 30\ \text{kV}$. Find $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV = 1240/(V\text{ in volts})\ \text{nm}$.

steps.label: Volts
steps.text: $eV = 30\times 10^3\ \text{eV}$.

examples.result: $\lambda_{\min} \approx 41.3\ \text{pm}$.

keyTakeaways: Only the gradient of $\vec B$ exerts a net force on a dipole: $F_z = \mu_z\,\partial B_z/\partial z$; a uniform field only torques it.
Silver's 46 inner electrons cancel, leaving one 5s electron with $\ell = 0$, $s = 1/2$ — so exactly two spots can appear, and do.
The two-spot pattern is direct evidence for space quantization and for the two spin projections $m_s = \pm1/2$.

quiz.q: A magnetic dipole in a perfectly uniform magnetic field experiences
options: a net force but no torque
a torque but no net force
both a net force and a torque
neither a force nor a torque
quiz.explanation: In a uniform field the two poles feel equal and opposite forces, so only the torque tau = mu × B survives; a net force requires a field gradient.

quiz.q: Silver atoms were chosen for Stern–Gerlach because the ground-state atom has
options: zero orbital angular momentum, so the split comes from the lone 5s electron's spin
quiz.explanation: Ag is [Kr]4d10 5s1: closed inner shells pair to zero, the 5s electron has l = 0, so the only magnetic projection is $\mu_z = \pm\mu_B$ from spin.

quiz.q: If the atoms sent through the Stern–Gerlach magnet had orbital quantum number l = 1 and zero spin, the plate would show
quiz.explanation: The beam splits into $2\ell+1 = 3$ components ($m_\ell = +1, 0, -1$); the historical two-spot count is what betrayed spin 1/2.

quiz.q: In the magnet's field gradient the force on an atom is proportional to
options: the field gradient times the atom's magnetic moment component $\mu_z$
quiz.explanation: $F_z = \mu_z\,\partial B/\partial z$: sorting by $\mu_z$ is exactly why distinct spin projections land at distinct places.

intro: A proton is a spin-1/2 particle with a magnetic moment 660 times smaller than the electron's, so its two orientations in a strong field differ in energy by only a millionth of an electron-volt. Yet radio-frequency photons can flip those spins on resonance, and that flip is the most sensitive signal in medical imaging. Magnetic resonance turns nuclear magnetism into the sharpest diagnostic tool in physics.
objectives: Compute the energy splitting and resonance frequency of proton spins in a magnetic field
Explain the roles of the radio-frequency field, the coil, and spin relaxation in an NMR measurement
Describe how field gradients let magnetic resonance produce spatial images (MRI)

concepts.statement: The proton has spin 1/2 and magnetic moment $\mu_p = 2.79\,\mu_N = 1.41\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{J/T}$, where the nuclear magneton $\mu_N = 5.05\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{J/T}$. In a field $B$ the two orientations differ by $$\Delta E = 2\mu_p B,$$ with the aligned orientation lower in energy.
concepts.detail: At $B = 1.5\ \mathrm{T}$ the splitting is $4.2\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{J}$ — about $2.6\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{eV}$, five orders of magnitude below $k_BT$ at room temperature, so the two populations are nearly equal and only a tiny excess sits aligned.

concepts.statement: Absorption occurs when an applied radio-frequency field supplies photons matched to the splitting: $$hf = \Delta E = 2\mu_p B,\qquad \nu = \frac{2\mu_p B}{h}.$$ Tuning either the frequency or the field and watching the absorption peak is nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR).
concepts.detail: Numerically $\nu = (4.26\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{Hz/T})B$: 42.6 MHz at 1 T, 63.8 MHz at the 1.5 T of a standard MRI magnet.

concepts.statement: A coil driven by an rf generator bathes the sample; when the resonance condition is met, protons absorb energy, flipping from the low orientation to the high one; the same coil (or a second one) then registers the signal as the spins relax back, releasing energy to their surroundings at a tissue-dependent rate.
concepts.detail: The relaxation times — spin–lattice ($T_1$) and spin–spin ($T_2$) — differ between water-rich and fat-rich tissues, which is precisely what MRI images: not proton density alone, but how quickly each voxel forgets the flip.

concepts.term: MRI: gradients make frequency mean position
concepts.statement: Superimposing a controlled linear gradient makes $B$ — and hence the resonance frequency $\nu = 2\mu_p B/h$ — a known function of position, so a Fourier analysis of the received signal assigns every frequency, and therefore every voxel of the patient, its own proton signal.
concepts.detail: By sweeping gradients through all three directions, MRI reconstructs full cross-sectional images without ionizing radiation — one reason it has largely supplanted X-ray tomography for soft tissue.

concepts.statement: **Solve Magnetic Resonance problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is atomic angular momentum, X rays and lasers; the working equation is $L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\hbar$, $L_z = m_l\hbar$, $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV$, $\mu_B = 9.27\times 10^{-24}\ \text{J/T}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (tesla and $\text{eV}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\lambda_{\min}\sim 0.01$--$0.1\ \text{nm}$ for $10$--$100\ \text{kV}$; single-electron picture first; Pauli plus Coulomb for many electrons.

examples.title: Proton resonance in a 1.5 T MRI magnet
examples.problem: Find the photon frequency and energy that flip protons in a 1.5 T field, and compare the population imbalance with $k_BT$ at 300 K.

steps.label: Frequency
steps.text: $\nu = \Delta E/h = 4.23\times10^{-26}/6.626\times10^{-34} = 6.38\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{Hz} = 63.8\ \mathrm{MHz}$ — shortwave radio, not light.

steps.label: Thermal ratio
steps.text: $\Delta E/k_BT = 2.6\times10^{-7}/0.0259 \approx 1.0\times10^{-5}$: out of every million protons only about ten extra are aligned — the tiny surplus MRI must exploit.

examples.result: $\nu = 63.8\ \mathrm{MHz}$ with $2.6\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{eV}$ photons; the aligned excess is only about one part in $10^{5}$, which is why MRI needs strong magnets and clever signal averaging.

examples.title: Magnetic Resonance: $\lambda_{\min}$ check
examples.problem: An X-ray tube runs at $V = 50\ \text{kV}$. Find $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV = 1240/(V\text{ in volts})\ \text{nm}$.

steps.label: Volts
steps.text: $eV = 50\times 10^3\ \text{eV}$.

examples.result: $\lambda_{\min} \approx 24.8\ \text{pm}$.

keyTakeaways: Proton spins in a field B split by $\Delta E = 2\mu_p B$ and resonate at $\nu = 2\mu_p B/h$ — 42.6 MHz per tesla.
The rf photon energy is ~10⁻⁷ eV, far below kT, so the signal rides on a minuscule thermal population imbalance.
Gradient fields turn resonance frequency into a position label, converting NMR into full three-dimensional imaging.

quiz.q: Doubling the magnetic field in a proton NMR experiment does what to the resonance frequency?
quiz.explanation: $\nu = 2\mu_p B/h$ is linear in B; 1.5 T gives 63.8 MHz, so 3.0 T would give 127.6 MHz.

quiz.q: The magnetic moment of the proton is
options: about 660 times smaller than the electron's
equal to the nuclear magneton exactly
larger than the electron's because the proton is heavier
quiz.explanation: $\mu_p = 2.79\,\mu_N$ and $\mu_N/\mu_B = m_e/m_p = 1/1836$, making the proton moment ~660 times weaker than the electron's.

quiz.q: MRI localizes signal in the body primarily by
options: moving the patient through the coil
making the field B position-dependent with gradients, so frequency encodes place
blocking protons outside the plane with lead collimators
quiz.explanation: A linear gradient makes $\nu = 2\mu_p B/h$ vary with position, so the Fourier spectrum of the received signal maps frequency to voxel.

quiz.q: Compared with visible-light photons (~2 eV), the photons that flip proton spins at 1.5 T carry about
quiz.explanation: The flip energy is 2.6×10⁻⁷ eV, about $10^{7}$ times smaller than 2 eV — MRI works with radio waves, not ionizing radiation.

intro: Drop one electron into a one-dimensional trap and it settles into the lowest level. Drop in a second, a third, a thousand, and something new happens: the Pauli exclusion principle forbids crowding, so the electrons stack upward like water filling a jar. The level of the topmost electron — the Fermi energy — will explain everything from the rigidity of metals to the structure of the periodic table.
objectives: State the Pauli exclusion principle and identify the quantum numbers it governs
Fill the levels of an electron trap and locate the Fermi energy of the resulting stack
Extend the one-dimensional filling argument to cubical traps and degenerate levels

concepts.statement: **No two electrons in the same system can occupy the same quantum state.** In a trap each level $n$ (or triple $n_x, n_y, n_z$) already fixes the spatial quantum numbers, so each level holds at most two electrons — one with $m_s = +1/2$, one with $m_s = -1/2$.
concepts.detail: The principle follows from the antisymmetry of the multi-electron wavefunction: swapping two electrons multiplies it by −1, which forces the shared-state amplitude to vanish. It applies to all spin-1/2 particles (fermions), never to photons or helium-4 atoms (bosons).

concepts.statement: For a one-dimensional infinite trap, $E_n = n^2h^2/8mL^2$. With $N$ electrons, fill from the bottom, two per level; for a cubical trap $E = (h^2/8mL^2)(n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2)$ and levels with the same sum, such as $(1,1,2)$, $(1,2,1)$ and $(2,1,1)$, are **degenerate** — three distinct states sharing one energy.
concepts.detail: Degeneracy multiplies capacity: the $(1,1,2)$ family holds six electrons, not two. Counting states, not levels, is the essential bookkeeping of many-electron quantum systems.

concepts.term: Fermi energy of a filled trap
concepts.statement: At $T = 0$ the highest occupied level defines the **Fermi energy** $E_F$: the kinetic energy of the last electron added. For 7 electrons in a 1D trap the first three levels take six electrons and the seventh must sit at $n = 4$, so $E_F = 16E_1$.
concepts.detail: Even at absolute zero the electrons are not at rest — exclusion forces them into a hive of fast motion, the origin of the quantum 'degeneracy pressure' that supports white dwarfs and neutron stars.

concepts.term: Exclusion Principle and Multiple Electrons in a Trap: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Exclusion Principle and Multiple Electrons in a Trap problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is atomic angular momentum, X rays and lasers; the working equation is $L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\hbar$, $L_z = m_l\hbar$, $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV$, $\mu_B = 9.27\times 10^{-24}\ \text{J/T}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (tesla and $\text{eV}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\lambda_{\min}\sim 0.01$--$0.1\ \text{nm}$ for $10$--$100\ \text{kV}$; single-electron picture first; Pauli plus Coulomb for many electrons.

concepts.term: Exclusion Principle and Multiple Electrons in a Trap: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Exclusion Principle and Multiple Electrons in a Trap lives at $\lambda_{\min}\sim 0.01$--$0.1\ \text{nm}$ for $10$--$100\ \text{kV}$ and the textbook model holds while single-electron picture first; Pauli plus Coulomb for many electrons.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Exclusion Principle and Multiple Electrons in a Trap calculation gives seconds when tesla and $\text{eV}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $\lambda_{\min}\sim 0.01$--$0.1\ \text{nm}$ for $10$--$100\ \text{kV}$, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Seven electrons in a one-dimensional trap
examples.problem: An infinite trap has width L = 200 pm. Find $E_1$, then the ground-state configuration, total energy, and Fermi energy of 7 electrons.

steps.label: Filling
steps.text: Two electrons each fill $n = 1, 2, 3$ (six in all); the seventh, excluded from all lower states, occupies $n = 4$.

examples.result: Configuration $(2,2,2,1)$ over levels $n = 1..4$, $E_F = 150\ \mathrm{eV}$, total $E \approx 4.1\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{eV}$ — the trap is a pressure vessel for quantum degeneracy.

examples.title: Exclusion Principle and Multiple Electrons in a Trap: $\lambda_{\min}$ check
examples.problem: An X-ray tube runs at $V = 70\ \text{kV}$. Find $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV = 1240/(V\text{ in volts})\ \text{nm}$.

steps.label: Volts
steps.text: $eV = 70\times 10^3\ \text{eV}$.

examples.result: $\lambda_{\min} \approx 17.7\ \text{pm}$.

keyTakeaways: Exclusion allows two electrons per trap level (one per spin projection); counting states is the key skill.
Degenerate levels in a cubical trap share energy but count separately, multiplying their electron capacity.
The Fermi energy is the energy of the topmost filled level at T = 0 — the signature of a many-fermion system.

quiz.q: The Pauli exclusion principle says that two electrons in the same system cannot share
options: the same set of quantum numbers
the same energy under any circumstance
quiz.explanation: Identical quantum numbers would mean identical quantum states; degenerate states with different quantum numbers may share one energy value.

quiz.q: How many electrons can occupy the n = 2 level of a one-dimensional trap?
quiz.explanation: A 1D level fixes n; the only freedom left is spin, $m_s = \pm1/2$, so two electrons fit.

quiz.q: For 7 electrons in a 1D trap with level energies n²E₁, the Fermi energy is
quiz.explanation: Levels n = 1, 2, 3 hold six electrons; the seventh occupies n = 4, so $E_F = 16E_1$.

quiz.q: The triple (1,1,2) in a cubical trap is part of a set of degenerate states because
options: the sum nx² + ny² + nz² is the same for (1,1,2), (1,2,1) and (2,1,1)
quiz.explanation: Energy depends only on the sum of squared quantum numbers, so any permutation of the same three numbers is degenerate.

intro: A real atom is a three-dimensional trap with a nucleus at its center, and its electrons obey the same stacking rule: two per state, filling in order of energy. Run the stack upward and the architecture of the periodic table appears unbidden — closed shells make noble gases inert, a lone outer electron makes the alkalis reactive, and the transition metals fill an interior d shell while chemistry changes only slowly.
objectives: Write full electron configurations using shell and subshell notation and their capacities
Explain why the 4s subshell fills before 3d and how that shapes the transition metals
Connect the occupancy of the outermost shell to chemical behavior across the table

concepts.statement: States with principal number $n$ form the $K, L, M, \ldots$ shells; each holds subshells $\ell = 0, 1, 2, 3$ ($s, p, d, f$) with capacity $$2(2\ell+1) \quad \text{electrons per subshell,} \qquad 2n^2 \quad \text{per shell.}$$ Thus $K$ holds 2, $L$ holds 8, $M$ holds 18.
concepts.detail: Example — oxygen (Z = 8): $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^4$; the two unpaired 2p electrons with parallel spins are why oxygen is paramagnetic and divalent.

concepts.statement: Electrons fill subshells in order of increasing energy — roughly by increasing $n + \ell$, with lower $n$ winning ties: $1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, \ldots$ The 4s subshell dips **below** 3d because its electrons penetrate the inner shells and feel more of the nuclear charge.
concepts.detail: Consequently potassium (Z = 19) is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,4s^1$, not $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^1$, and the 3d transition series runs from scandium (21) to zinc (30) while the outer 4s electrons do the chemistry.

concepts.statement: A subshell is most stable when full (all states occupied) or half-full with parallel spins (exchange energy); the noble gases have only full subshells, alkalis carry one electron past a closed shell, and halogens lack one electron of closing it — hence their opposite reactivity.
concepts.detail: Hund's rule fills a subshell with parallel spins first: chromium takes $3d^5 4s^1$ and copper $3d^{10}4s^1$ rather than the naive bookkeeping, trading one 4s electron for a half-full or full d subshell.

examples.title: The ground-state configuration of iron
examples.problem: Iron has Z = 26. Write its ground-state electron configuration and identify its valence electrons.

steps.label: Fill in order
steps.text: Order: $1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d$. Fill 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 = 18 electrons through $3p$ (argon core).

steps.label: 4s first
steps.text: The 19th and 20th electrons take $4s^2$; six remain.

steps.label: 3d subshell
steps.text: The last six enter $3d$, giving $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^6\,4s^2$.

steps.label: Count
steps.text: $2+2+6+2+6+6+2 = 26$ ✓; the $3d^6 4s^2$ electrons are the ones that iron lends and shares — the source of its two common oxidation states.

examples.result: Fe: $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^6\,4s^2$ — eight electrons beyond the argon core, six of them in the partially filled 3d subshell.

examples.title: Building the Periodic Table: $\lambda_{\min}$ check
examples.problem: An X-ray tube runs at $V = 30\ \text{kV}$. Find $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV = 1240/(V\text{ in volts})\ \text{nm}$.

steps.label: Volts
steps.text: $eV = 30\times 10^3\ \text{eV}$.

examples.result: $\lambda_{\min} \approx 41.3\ \text{pm}$.

keyTakeaways: Subshell capacities are $2(2\ell+1)$ and shell capacities $2n^2$; configurations are built by filling in order of energy, essentially by increasing $n+\ell$.
4s fills before 3d, which is why period 4 begins with the alkali potassium and why the 3d transition metals have similar outer-shell chemistry.
Chemistry is an outer-shell phenomenon: noble-gas closed shells, alkali singletons and halogen vacancies are direct read-outs of the filling order.

quiz.q: The capacity of an n = 3 shell (M shell) is
Potassium (Z = 19) has its last electron in
quiz.explanation: 4s lies below 3d in energy due to penetration, so K is [Ar]4s1 — placing it under the alkalis in the table.

quiz.q: A nitrogen atom (Z = 7) in its ground state has how many unpaired electrons?
quiz.explanation: N is 1s2 2s2 2p3; Hund's rule gives the three 2p electrons parallel spins, hence three unpaired — the source of its triplet chemistry.

quiz.q: Noble gases are chemically inert because
options: their outermost shells are completely filled
they have no electrons in motion
quiz.explanation: Full subshells leave no low-energy vacancies or loose electrons, so there is little energetic incentive to trade electrons.

intro: Before X rays, the elements were ordered by atomic mass — an ordering with embarrassing exceptions. Moseley's X-ray spectra fixed the ordering for good by tying it to atomic number Z, the count of nuclear protons. The story combines the bremsstrahlung continuum, the sharp characteristic lines of inner-shell vacancies, and a law so clean it assigned Z to every element and predicted the ones still missing.
objectives: Explain the bremsstrahlung continuum and derive its short-wavelength cutoff
Interpret characteristic K lines in terms of electron vacancies and apply Moseley's law
Describe how Moseley re-ordered the periodic table and exposed missing elements

concepts.statement: Electrons accelerated through a potential difference V and slammed into a metal target radiate as they decelerate (braking radiation). The continuum of photon energies cannot exceed the electrons' kinetic energy $eV$, so the spectrum stops at $$\lambda_{\min} = \frac{hc}{eV}.$$ The cutoff is a direct quantum statement: one photon takes all of one electron's energy.
concepts.detail: For V = 35 kV, $\lambda_{\min} = 1240\ \mathrm{eV\cdot nm}/35\,000\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.0354\ \mathrm{nm} = 35.4\ \mathrm{pm}$; the cutoff measures the accelerating voltage from the radiation alone.

concepts.statement: If an incoming electron knocks a K-shell ($n = 1$) electron out of a target atom, an electron from the L shell falls into the vacancy, emitting a $K_\alpha$ photon. Screening by the one remaining K electron makes the effective charge scale as $(Z-1)$, giving Moseley's law: $$\nu_{K\alpha} = (2.48\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{Hz})(Z-1)^2.$$
concepts.detail: The square-root plot of $\nu$ against Z is a straight line to extraordinary accuracy — the first direct measurement of nuclear charge, taken in 1913–14 before the neutron was even suspected.

concepts.statement: Because X-ray frequencies depend on nuclear charge and not on chemistry or mass, Moseley could assign each element an unambiguous integer Z, correct the mass-order anomalies (cobalt must precede nickel, Z = 27 before 28) and show that gaps in the integer sequence corresponded to **undiscovered elements**.
concepts.detail: His table left holes at Z = 43 (technetium), 61 (promethium), 72 (hafnium) and 75 (rhenium); all were later found or purified exactly as predicted. Technetium has no stable isotope at all — the gap was real physics, not missing lab work.
