examples.title: Copper's K-alpha line and an X-ray tube's cutoff
examples.problem: In a 35 kV X-ray tube with a copper target, find the $K_\alpha$ wavelength (Z = 29) and verify it lies beyond the bremsstrahlung cutoff.

steps.label: Cutoff
steps.text: $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV = 1240/35\,000\ \mathrm{eV} = 35.4\ \mathrm{pm}$.

steps.label: Consistency
steps.text: The 154 pm line is well inside the continuum's long-wavelength side and requires the 35 keV electrons to have emptied the K shell (Cu K binding ≈ 9 keV) — both conditions hold.

examples.result: $\lambda_{K\alpha} = 154\ \mathrm{pm}$ — the famous copper line used in crystallography — comfortably beyond the 35.4 pm cutoff set by the tube voltage.

examples.title: X Rays and the Ordering of the Elements: $\lambda_{\min}$ check
examples.problem: An X-ray tube runs at $V = 50\ \text{kV}$. Find $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV = 1240/(V\text{ in volts})\ \text{nm}$.

steps.label: Volts
steps.text: $eV = 50\times 10^3\ \text{eV}$.

examples.result: $\lambda_{\min} \approx 24.8\ \text{pm}$.

keyTakeaways: The bremsstrahlung continuum cuts off at $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV$, a pure quantum effect with no classical counterpart.
Characteristic lines come from inner-shell vacancies; Moseley's $\nu = (2.48\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{Hz})(Z-1)^2$ ties X-ray frequencies to nuclear charge.
Ordering by Z — not by mass — corrected the periodic table's anomalies and predicted elements such as technetium before their discovery.

quiz.q: The minimum wavelength in an X-ray tube's continuum is set by
options: the accelerating voltage, via λmin = hc/eV
the size of the electron beam
quiz.explanation: No photon can carry more energy than eV, so the spectrum stops at $\lambda_\mathrm{min} = hc/eV$ regardless of target.

quiz.q: A K-alpha photon is emitted when
options: an outer electron falls into a K-shell vacancy
quiz.explanation: Removing a K (n = 1) electron leaves a vacancy; an L (n = 2) electron dropping in emits the K-alpha line.

quiz.q: Moseley's law states that the square root of the K-alpha frequency is proportional to
quiz.explanation: Screening by the surviving K electron reduces the effective charge to Z − 1, giving nu proportional to (Z − 1) squared.

quiz.q: Raising the tube voltage V while keeping the same target changes
options: both the cutoff and the K-alpha line
quiz.explanation: The characteristic lines are fixed by the atom's levels; only the bremsstrahlung cutoff (and the intensity) moves with V.

intro: Ordinary light sources emit by spontaneous decay: each atom flashes at random, in a random direction, with a random phase. A laser makes emission obedient — an incoming photon triggers identical photons, in phase, in the same direction — and the result is a beam whose light is as different from a bulb's as a march is from a mob. The trick is a population inversion parked on a metastable state.
objectives: Distinguish spontaneous emission, absorption and stimulated emission, and state the properties of the photons each produces
Explain population inversion and why long-lived metastable states are essential to sustaining it
Trace the pumping cycle of the helium-neon laser and the role of the resonant cavity

concepts.statement: A photon of exactly the transition energy passing an excited atom can trigger the atom's drop to the lower state, emitting a second photon that is a **clone**: same frequency, same phase, same direction, same polarization. Einstein predicted the process in 1917 from thermodynamic bookkeeping — decades before it was observed.
concepts.detail: Where spontaneous emission is isotropic and incoherent, stimulated emission is directional and coherent: each clone can clone again, giving exponential gain along the beam axis.

concepts.statement: Stimulated emission outmuscles absorption only when more atoms populate the upper state than the lower one — a **population inversion**, impossible in thermal equilibrium, since $N_\mathrm{upper}/N_\mathrm{lower} = e^{-\Delta E/k_BT} < 1$ always. Inversions are built on **metastable** states whose forbidden-like transitions make lifetimes long ($\sim 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$ instead of $10^{-8}\ \mathrm{s}$), letting atoms accumulate.
concepts.detail: A pump (electric discharge, flashlamp, another laser, diode current) supplies the energy; the metastable shelf stores it; a three- or four-level ladder keeps the lower laser level nearly empty so the inversion survives.

concepts.statement: In the He-Ne laser a discharge excites helium to a 20.61 eV metastable level; collisions transfer that energy (resonantly, within 0.05 eV) to neon's 20.66 eV metastable level, which sits above a 18.70 eV level. The 20.66 → 18.70 eV cascade radiates **632.8 nm** red light, and mirrors at the tube ends reflect it repeatedly through the gain medium to build the coherent beam.
concepts.detail: One mirror is made ~1–2% transmitting to let the beam escape. The exact output wavelength is selected by the cavity's standing-wave condition and by neon's level structure; other lines (3.39 μm, 1.15 μm) are suppressed by coatings.

concepts.statement: Laser light is close to **monochromatic** (spread by less than one part in 10⁶ with stabilization), **directional** (divergence set by diffraction at the exit aperture) and **coherent** (phases locked across the wavefront and along the beam), which is why it can be focused to a wavelength-scale spot, travel to the Moon and back, and drive interference on human time scales.
concepts.detail: A lightbulb emits photons into $4\pi$ steradians with phase noise; a one-milliwatt laser outperforms it for any task that rewards phase — holography, fiber communication, interferometry, precision cutting.

concepts.statement: **Solve Lasers problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is atomic angular momentum, X rays and lasers; the working equation is $L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\hbar$, $L_z = m_l\hbar$, $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV$, $\mu_B = 9.27\times 10^{-24}\ \text{J/T}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (tesla and $\text{eV}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $\lambda_{\min}\sim 0.01$--$0.1\ \text{nm}$ for $10$--$100\ \text{kV}$; single-electron picture first; Pauli plus Coulomb for many electrons.

examples.title: Photons per second from a 2.5 mW He-Ne beam
examples.problem: A helium-neon laser emits 632.8 nm light at 2.5 mW. Find the photon energy and the rate of photon production.

steps.label: Photon energy
steps.text: $E = hc/\lambda = 1240\ \mathrm{eV\cdot nm}/632.8\ \mathrm{nm} = 1.96\ \mathrm{eV}$.

steps.label: Rate
steps.text: $N/t = P/E = 2.5\times10^{-3}/3.14\times10^{-19} = 8.0\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{photons/s}$.

steps.label: Check the levels
steps.text: The neon cascade 20.66 → 18.70 eV spans 1.96 eV ✓, exactly the 632.8 nm photon.

examples.result: Each photon carries 1.96 eV; the 2.5 mW beam delivers $8.0\times10^{15}$ coherent, in-phase photons every second.

examples.title: Lasers: $\lambda_{\min}$ check
examples.problem: An X-ray tube runs at $V = 70\ \text{kV}$. Find $\lambda_{\min} = hc/eV = 1240/(V\text{ in volts})\ \text{nm}$.

steps.label: Volts
steps.text: $eV = 70\times 10^3\ \text{eV}$.

examples.result: $\lambda_{\min} \approx 17.7\ \text{pm}$.

keyTakeaways: Stimulated emission produces photon clones — same phase, direction, frequency — the seed of all coherent light.
Gain requires a population inversion, which demands pumping and metastable states; thermal equilibrium can never provide it.
In He-Ne, resonant transfer from helium's 20.61 eV metastable to neon's 20.66 eV level drives the 632.8 nm cascade that the cavity amplifies.

quiz.q: The photon emitted by stimulated emission is identical to the triggering photon in
quiz.explanation: The clone is a perfect copy in every wave property — that total identity is what makes laser light coherent.

quiz.q: A population inversion means
options: more atoms in the lower energy state
more atoms in the upper energy state
quiz.explanation: With more atoms up than down, stimulated emission dominates absorption — impossible in thermal equilibrium, so it must be pumped.

quiz.q: Metastable states are crucial in lasers because they
options: have unusually long lifetimes, allowing atoms to accumulate and build an inversion
quiz.explanation: Lifetimes of order 10⁻³ s (versus 10⁻⁸ s for normal states) let the pump stack up atoms and sustain the inversion.

quiz.q: In a He-Ne laser the energy that ultimately becomes 632.8 nm light is delivered to neon atoms by
options: collisions with metastable helium atoms excited by the discharge
quiz.explanation: Helium's 20.61 eV metastable level matches neon's 20.66 eV level almost exactly, so collisional transfer populates the upper laser level.

intro: In 1911 Rutherford's team fired alpha particles at gold foil a few hundred atoms thick and found that about one in eight thousand came straight back. No pudding of positive charge, however dense, could do that. The rebound demanded that all the positive charge of an atom live in a minute, hard core — the nucleus — a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom itself.
objectives: Contrast Thomson's plum-pudding model with Rutherford's nuclear atom and explain what the backscattered alpha particles demanded
Compute the distance of closest approach of an alpha particle to a nucleus and use it to bound the nuclear radius
Summarize the scale hierarchy of nucleus versus atom and its consequences for density

concepts.statement: Alpha particles (charge +2e) scatter off the gold nucleus (charge +79e) through pure Coulomb repulsion; for a head-on approach, conservation of energy converts all initial kinetic energy into electrostatic potential energy at the turning point: $$K = \frac{k(2e)(Ze)}{r_\mathrm{min}}.$$ The observed head-on rebounds — one in about 8000 — match the Coulomb prediction down to distances that set an upper limit on the nuclear radius.
concepts.detail: Because the scattering is Coulombic all the way down to the turning point, deviations from Rutherford's formula at higher alpha energies mark the distance where the alpha actually touches nuclear matter.

concepts.statement: All positive charge and more than 99.9% of the mass of an atom reside in a nucleus of radius about $10^{-14}\ \mathrm{m}$, ten thousand times smaller than the atomic radius $\sim 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$. An atom is mostly empty space: if the nucleus were a marble at midfield, the electrons would be a haze of spectators a kilometer away in every direction.
concepts.detail: Geiger and Marsden counted the angular distribution; Rutherford's 1911 analysis inverted it into a central charge concentrated within a few times $10^{-14}$ m of gold — the birth of nuclear physics.

concepts.statement: Compressing the atom's mass into $10^{-14}\ \mathrm{m}$ gives nuclear densities near $2\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ — a teaspoon would weigh a billion tonnes. Ordinary matter is empty; the mass we feel is a lattice of specks.
concepts.detail: The nucleus achieves this density because the strong force overwhelms Coulomb repulsion at femtometer distances, binding protons and neutrons into a liquid-drop-like ball of essentially constant density (Section 42-8).

concepts.statement: **Solve Discovering the Nucleus problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is nuclear size, binding and the exponential decay law; the working equation is $R = r_0A^{1/3}$, $r_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$, $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (femtometers, becquerels, gray/sieverts) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr; $N\gg 1$ for $e^{-\lambda t}$; $\lambda$ constant in time.

concepts.term: Discovering the Nucleus: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Discovering the Nucleus lives at $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr and the textbook model holds while $N\gg 1$ for $e^{-\lambda t}$; $\lambda$ constant in time.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Discovering the Nucleus calculation gives seconds when femtometers, becquerels, gray/sieverts demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: How close does a 5.0 MeV alpha get to gold?
examples.problem: An alpha particle with kinetic energy 5.0 MeV approaches a gold nucleus (Z = 79) head-on. Find the distance of closest approach and compare it with the gold nuclear radius.

steps.label: Set energies equal
steps.text: At the turning point $K = kq_1q_2/r$: $r_\mathrm{min} = k(2e)(79e)/K$.

steps.label: Handy constant
steps.text: $ke^2 = 1.44\ \mathrm{MeV\cdot fm}$ (with 1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m).

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $r_\mathrm{min} = \dfrac{(2)(79)(1.44\ \mathrm{MeV\cdot fm})}{5.0\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 45.5\ \mathrm{fm} = 4.6\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{m}$.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: The gold radius is $R = 1.2\,A^{1/3}\ \mathrm{fm} = 1.2(197)^{1/3} \approx 7.0\ \mathrm{fm}$ — the alpha turns back six to seven nuclear radii out, so the Coulomb law holds throughout the encounter.

examples.result: $r_\mathrm{min} = 45.5\ \mathrm{fm}$, an upper bound on the nuclear size far above the actual 7 fm radius — exactly the consistency Rutherford needed.

examples.title: Discovering the Nucleus: nuclear-size check
examples.problem: Estimate $R = r_0A^{1/3}$ with $r_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$ for $A = 106$.

steps.label: Radius
steps.text: $R \approx 1.2\times 4.73 = 5.68\ \text{fm}$.

examples.result: $R \approx 5.68\ \text{fm}$.

keyTakeaways: Backscattering of alpha particles requires a small, dense, positively charged core; the plum-pudding model cannot produce it.
The closest approach $r_\mathrm{min} = k(2e)(Ze)/K$ converts alpha energy into a ruler for nuclear size.
The nucleus is ~10⁻¹⁴ m across, 10⁴ times smaller than the atom, with density near 2×10¹⁷ kg/m³.

quiz.q: In Rutherford's experiment, the fraction of alpha particles deflected through large angles was about
quiz.explanation: Only about 1 in 8000 hit nearly head-on; those rebounds were the evidence for a compact nucleus.

quiz.q: The distance of closest approach calculation for an alpha particle and a nucleus assumes
options: all kinetic energy becomes electrostatic potential energy at the turning point
the gold nucleus recoils at light speed
quiz.explanation: At the turning point the radial speed is zero, so $K = k(2e)(Ze)/r_\mathrm{min}$ bounds the interaction as purely Coulombic.

quiz.q: Compared with the atom, the nucleus is roughly
quiz.explanation: 10⁻¹⁴ m versus 10⁻¹⁰ m is a factor of 10⁴ — matter is overwhelmingly empty space.

quiz.q: If the alpha-particle energy is doubled, the distance of closest approach
quiz.explanation: $r_\mathrm{min}$ is inversely proportional to $K$: 10 MeV alphas get within 23 fm of gold.

intro: A nucleus is a bound pack of protons and neutrons, and its single most revealing number is the binding energy per nucleon. The curve of that quantity against mass number — rising steeply, peaking at iron, then sagging slowly — is the energy landscape of all nuclear physics: read it left to right and you have fusion, right to left and you have fission.
objectives: Use the notation Z, N, A and the vocabulary of isotopes and nuclides
Compute nuclear radii and mass densities from the $R = 1.2A^{1/3}\ \mathrm{fm}$ rule
Calculate total and per-nucleon binding energies from atomic masses and read the binding-energy curve to locate where fission and fusion pay off

concepts.statement: A nuclide $^{A}_{Z}X$ has $Z$ protons (defining the element), $N = A - Z$ neutrons, and mass number $A = Z + N$ nucleons. **Isotopes** share Z (¹H, ²H, ³H), **isotones** share N, **isobars** share A. Atomic masses in tables include the electrons, so electron books balance automatically when whole atoms are compared.
concepts.detail: Hydrogen's isotopes earn names — protium, deuterium, tritium — and its two heavy isotopes drive fusion energy: deuterium is forever abundant in seawater, tritium must be bred.

concepts.statement: Charge scattering shows that nuclear volume grows in proportion to A: $$R = r_0 A^{1/3},\qquad r_0 \approx 1.2\ \mathrm{fm}.$$ Constant density follows immediately — nucleons are packed like an incompressible liquid at $\rho \approx 2.3\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, whatever the element.
concepts.detail: From ⁴He to ²³⁸U the radius spans only 1.7 to 7.4 fm; the mass deficit that would otherwise weaken heavy nuclei instead gets packed tight.

concepts.statement: The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of its parts, and the shortfall is the binding energy: $$\Delta E_b = (Z m_H + N m_n - M_X)c^2,$$ with $m_H = 1.007825\ \mathrm{u}$ the hydrogen atom's mass, $m_n = 1.008665\ \mathrm{u}$, and $1\ \mathrm{u}c^2 = 931.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
concepts.detail: Using atomic (not bare-nuclear) masses is legitimate because the Z electrons of the neutral atom appear identically on both sides — a bookkeeping gift that removes the electron mass from every calculation.

concepts.term: The binding energy per nucleon curve
concepts.statement: Dividing $\Delta E_b$ by $A$ and plotting against A: a steep rise through the light nuclides, a broad maximum of **8.79 MeV/nucleon at ⁵⁶Fe**, a near plateau to the middle of the table, and a slow decline to about 7.6 MeV/nucleon at uranium. Energy is released whenever nucleons move **upward** on this curve — light nuclei fusing, heavy nuclei splitting.
concepts.detail: The dip at ⁸Be (7.06 MeV/nucleon) and the double peak at ⁴He (7.07) explain why helium nuclei are the favored ash of both fusion and alpha decay, and the long slow slope beyond iron is why very heavy nuclei are radioactive.

concepts.statement: **Solve Some Nuclear Properties problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is nuclear size, binding and the exponential decay law; the working equation is $R = r_0A^{1/3}$, $r_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$, $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (femtometers, becquerels, gray/sieverts) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr; $N\gg 1$ for $e^{-\lambda t}$; $\lambda$ constant in time.

figures.caption: Binding energy per nucleon versus mass number A. The curve rises steeply to its maximum of 8.79 MeV/nucleon at ⁵⁶Fe, holds nearly flat across the middle of the table, and falls slowly to 7.57 MeV/nucleon at ²³⁸U. Fission gains energy by sliding leftward down the far slope (A ≈ 240 splitting into two fragments near A ≈ 118); fusion climbs the steep left slope by merging light nuclei.

examples.title: Binding energy of the alpha particle
examples.problem: Compute the total binding energy and the binding energy per nucleon of ⁴He, using $m_H = 1.007825\ \mathrm{u}$, $m_n = 1.008665\ \mathrm{u}$, and $M(\mathrm{He}) = 4.002603\ \mathrm{u}$.

steps.label: Mass defect
steps.text: $\Delta m = 4.032980 - 4.002603 = 0.030377\ \mathrm{u}$ — the nucleus weighs less than its parts.

steps.label: Energy
steps.text: $\Delta E_b = (0.030377)(931.5\ \mathrm{MeV}) = 28.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

steps.label: Per nucleon
steps.text: $28.3/4 = 7.07\ \mathrm{MeV/nucleon}$ — remarkably high for so light a nuclide, which is why helium is the standard nuclear ash.

examples.result: $\Delta E_b = 28.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$, or 7.07 MeV per nucleon — a deep early spike on the binding energy curve.

examples.title: Some Nuclear Properties: nuclear-size check
examples.problem: Estimate $R = r_0A^{1/3}$ with $r_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$ for $A = 156$.

steps.label: Radius
steps.text: $R \approx 1.2\times 5.38 = 6.46\ \text{fm}$.

examples.result: $R \approx 6.46\ \text{fm}$.

keyTakeaways: Nuclides are labeled $^{A}ZX$; nuclear volume and mass number go hand in hand through $R = 1.2A^{1/3}$ fm, giving near-constant density.
Binding energy is the mass defect: $\Delta E_b = (Zm_H + Nm_n - M)c^2$ with atomic masses.
The BE-per-nucleon curve peaks at 8.79 MeV at ⁵⁶Fe and falls to ~7.6 MeV at uranium — the two slopes of that peak are where fission and fusion draw their energy.

quiz.q: In the nuclide ¹³¹I (iodine-131), the numbers of protons and neutrons are
quiz.explanation: Iodine has Z = 53, so N = A − Z = 131 − 53 = 78.

quiz.q: The nuclear radius formula $R = 1.2A^{1/3}\ \mathrm{fm}$ implies that nuclear density
options: is approximately the same for all nuclei
quiz.explanation: Volume proportional to A means fixed density, like an incompressible liquid drop of nucleons at ~2.3e17 kg/m³.

quiz.q: The mass of a ⁴He nucleus compared with two protons plus two neutrons is
quiz.explanation: The 0.030377 u defect times c² is the 28.3 MeV binding energy; bound systems always weigh less than their parts.

quiz.q: Why does fission of a uranium nucleus release energy?
options: Uranium nuclei are unstable to the strong force
The fragments have higher binding energy per nucleon than uranium does
The fragments have lower binding energy per nucleon
quiz.explanation: Moving up the BE/A curve (7.57 → about 8.4 MeV/nucleon for the fragments) releases roughly 200 MeV per fission.

intro: Radioactivity was discovered by accident in 1896 and explained only by quantum mechanics: an unstable nucleus is a quantum system that decays at random, with a fixed probability per unit time. From that single assumption flows the exponential decay law, the concept of half-life, and the entire technology of dating, tracers and medical isotopes — the mathematics of this section runs through every one of them.
objectives: Apply the exponential decay law $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and define the decay constant
Relate half-life, mean life and decay constant, and convert fluently among them
Compute activities in becquerels and curies for a given sample

concepts.statement: If each nucleus of a nuclide has a fixed probability $\lambda\,dt$ of decaying in the next $dt$ — independent of its age, its neighbors and its history — then the number of undecayed nuclei falls exponentially: $$N(t) = N_0e^{-\lambda t}.$$ $\lambda$ (the decay constant, in s⁻¹) is the fingerprint of the nuclide.
concepts.detail: Radioactive decay is the archetype of a memoryless process: no amount of waiting makes a remaining nucleus 'due' or 'tired' — every nucleus carries a fresh exponential clock (see the masters tier for the full derivation and its statistics).

concepts.statement: The **half-life** $T_{1/2}$ is the time for half a sample to decay: $$T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \frac{0.693}{\lambda}.$$ The **mean life** $\tau = 1/\lambda$ is the average lifetime of a nucleus; the two differ by the factor ln 2: $T_{1/2} = \tau\ln 2$.
concepts.detail: After $n$ half-lives the population is down by $2^{-n}$: 10% survives at 3.32$T_{1/2}$, 1% at 6.64$T_{1/2}$ — a sample never quite vanishes but effectively fades logarithmically.

concepts.statement: The decay rate, or activity, is $$R = -\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N = R_0e^{-\lambda t},\qquad R_0 = \lambda N_0,$$ measured in becquerels (1 Bq = 1 decay/s) or the older curie ($1\ \mathrm{Ci} = 3.7\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{Bq}$, the activity of one gram of ²²⁶Ra).
concepts.detail: Activity measures decays per second, not energy or danger — a ¹³¹I diagnostic dose and a ²³⁸U pellet can have equal activities and utterly different biological effects (Section 42-7).

concepts.statement: **Solve Radioactive Decay problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is nuclear size, binding and the exponential decay law; the working equation is $R = r_0A^{1/3}$, $r_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$, $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (femtometers, becquerels, gray/sieverts) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr; $N\gg 1$ for $e^{-\lambda t}$; $\lambda$ constant in time.

concepts.statement: **Radioactive Decay lives at $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr and the textbook model holds while $N\gg 1$ for $e^{-\lambda t}$; $\lambda$ constant in time.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Radioactive Decay calculation gives seconds when femtometers, becquerels, gray/sieverts demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Activity of a microgram of iodine-131
examples.problem: Iodine-131 ($T_{1/2} = 8.04$ days) is used in thyroid therapy. Find the decay constant and the initial activity of a 1.0 μg sample.

steps.label: Number of nuclei
steps.text: $N = m/(Am_\mathrm{u}) = 1.0\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{kg}/(131 \times 1.66\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}) = 4.6\times10^{15}$.

steps.label: Perspective
steps.text: That is 4.6 GBq from one microgram — nuclear clocks are ferociously active per unit mass compared with chemical rates.

examples.result: $\lambda = 1.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $R = 4.6\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{Bq}$ (about 0.12 Ci) for 1 μg — the hallmark of a short-lived nuclide.

examples.title: Radioactive Decay: decay-numbers check
examples.problem: Carbon-14 has $T_{1/2} = 5730\ \text{yr}$. Starting from $10^{12}$ nuclei, how many remain after $5730\ \text{yr}$?

steps.label: Remain
steps.text: $N \approx 5.00\times 10^{+11}$ nuclei.

keyTakeaways: Constant decay probability per nucleus gives $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$; the decay constant λ is intrinsic to the nuclide.
$T_{1/2} = \ln2/\lambda$ and $\tau = 1/\lambda$ differ by the factor 0.693.
Activity $R = \lambda N$ follows the same exponential as the population itself and is measured in Bq (or Ci = 3.7×10¹⁰ Bq).

quiz.q: A sample has activity 800 Bq and half-life 10 days. After 30 days its activity is
quiz.explanation: 30 days = 3 half-lives: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 Bq.

quiz.q: The mean life τ of a radioactive nuclide, compared with its half-life, is
quiz.explanation: $T_{1/2} = \tau\ln 2$, so $\tau = T_{1/2}/0.693 \approx 1.44\,T_{1/2}$ — the exponential's long tail raises the average.

quiz.q: Two nuclides have equal numbers of atoms but different decay constants. The one with larger λ has
quiz.explanation: Both $R = \lambda N$ and $1/T_{1/2}$ scale with $\lambda$: fast decayers are hot but brief.

quiz.q: The becquerel is defined as
options: one calorie of absorption per hour
quiz.explanation: 1 Bq = 1 s⁻¹; the curie is 3.7e10 Bq, and the joule-per-kilogram unit is the gray, a dose unit.

depth.title: The decay law, derived and dissected

blocks.heading: The one assumption
blocks.body: Every result of this section flows from a single physical hypothesis: a nucleus of a given nuclide decays with probability $\lambda\,dt$ in the interval $dt$, the same for every nucleus, the same at every moment, unaffected by how long that nucleus has already existed. Quantum mechanically the nucleus sits in a quasi-stationary state whose small coupling to the continuum of final states gives, via Fermi's golden rule, a transition rate $\lambda = \tfrac{2\pi}{\hbar}|\langle f|H'|i\rangle|^2\rho(E_f)$ that is constant because the state is stationary to excellent approximation. Decay has no memory, and no mechanism can 'tickle' a nucleus to make it decay sooner.

blocks.heading: The exponential law
blocks.body: Let $N(t)$ be the number of surviving nuclei. In $dt$ the expected number of decays is $dN = -\lambda N\,dt$ (negative because $N$ falls). Dividing by $N\,dt$ and integrating, $$\int_{N_0}^{N}\frac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\int_0^t dt' \;\Longrightarrow\; \ln\frac{N}{N_0} = -\lambda t \;\Longrightarrow\; N(t) = N_0e^{-\lambda t}.$$ Equivalently the probability that one given nucleus survives to $t$ is $P(t) = e^{-\lambda t}$, and the probability density that it decays at $t$ is the hazard times the survival: $f(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}$.

blocks.heading: Half-life and mean life
blocks.body: Setting $N = N_0/2$ gives $e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} = 1/2$, so $T_{1/2} = \ln2/\lambda$. The mean life comes from averaging $t$ over the decay-time density: $$\tau = \int_0^\infty t\,\lambda e^{-\lambda t}\,dt = \frac{1}{\lambda},$$ where the integral is one integration by parts ($\int te^{-\lambda t}dt = -(t/\lambda + 1/\lambda^2)e^{-\lambda t}$, and both boundary terms vanish). Hence $T_{1/2} = \tau\ln 2$: a half-life is 69% of a mean life, the exponential tail being longer than the median. After one mean life the population is $N_0/e \approx 0.368N_0$.

blocks.heading: Specific activity of a pure nuclide
blocks.body: A sample of pure nuclide $A$ (mass number $A$, atomic mass $\approx A$ u) with mass $m$ carries $N = (m/A)N_A$ nuclei, so its activity is $$R = \lambda N = \frac{m N_A}{A}\,\lambda.$$ Invert it and any measured activity becomes a mass: for ¹³¹I, $\lambda = 9.97\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ gives $R/m = \lambda N_A/A = (9.97\times10^{-7})(6.02\times10^{23})/131 = 4.6\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{Bq/g}$ — one gram of pure iodine-131 is a 4.6-petabecquerel source, and the diagnostic microgram of the worked example is exactly this number scaled down by 10⁶.

blocks.heading: Counting statistics
blocks.body: Whether a given nucleus decays within a window $t$ is a Bernoulli trial with $p = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}$, so $N$ independent nuclei give a binomial distribution with variance $N_0p(1-p)$. For small $p$ (short window or long half-life) the binomial collapses to the Poisson limit in which the number of counts $C$ in time $t$ fluctuates with $\sigma_C = \sqrt{\bar C}$: counting 10,000 decays pins the rate to 1%, while 100 counts leave ±10%. This $1/\sqrt{C}$ law is the price of all nuclear measurement — including the statistical noise visible in every medical scan.

blocks.heading: Why the exponential is unique
blocks.body: The exponential is the only continuous memoryless distribution: if survival to $t_1 + t_2$ equals survival to $t_1$ times survival to $t_2$ from $t_1$ — that is, if age never matters — then $P(t+s) = P(t)P(s)$, whose only continuous solution is $P = e^{-\lambda t}$. This is exactly why nuclei show no wear: the deep quantum state is identical at every instant, so 'aging' has no physical hook to grip. It is also why half-lives spanning 10²⁵ (tellurium-128 to polonium-214) can share one functional form.

blocks.heading: Isotope logistics at the hospital
blocks.body: Technetium-99m, the workhorse of nuclear imaging, has $T_{1/2} = 6.0\ \mathrm{h}$. A hospital that draws 4.0 GBq from its Monday-morning generator and uses nothing until Friday morning, 96 h later, has 16 half-lives of decay: the remaining activity is $4.0\ \mathrm{GBq}/2^{16} = 4.0\ \mathrm{GBq}/65\,536 \approx 61\ \mathrm{kBq}$ — essentially gone, which is why generators are delivered weekly and why short-lived isotopes must be made near where they are used. The same arithmetic, run on ¹⁴C after an organism dies, is the entire logic of Section 42-6.

intro: Alpha decay looks impossible: an alpha particle sits inside the nucleus at an energy far below the Coulomb wall that surrounds it. Classically it can never escape; quantum mechanically it tunnels, and the observed fact that it does — at sharply defined energies and at wildly different rates — is one of the most direct confirmations of barrier penetration.
objectives: Compute the Q value of an alpha decay and explain why Q > 0 is required
Distribute the decay energy between the alpha particle and the recoiling daughter
Explain how tunneling through the Coulomb barrier sets the enormous range of alpha half-lives

concepts.statement: A decay is energetically allowed only if the products are lighter than the parent: $$Q = (M_X - M_Y - M_\alpha)c^2 > 0,$$ computed with atomic masses (the electrons cancel: the parent's $Z$ electrons equal the daughter's $Z-2$ plus the alpha's 2). $Q$ is the total kinetic energy shared by the decay products.
concepts.detail: For ²³⁸U → ²³⁴Th + α, $Q = [238.050788 - 234.043601 - 4.002603]\,\mathrm{u} \times 931.5 = 4.27\ \mathrm{MeV}$ — released as the kinetic energy of the fragments plus a little gamma and internal excitation.

concepts.statement: Momentum conservation with an initially stationary parent fixes the split of kinetic energy: the light alpha takes nearly all of it, $$K_\alpha = Q\,\frac{M_Y}{M_Y + M_\alpha} = Q\,\frac{A-4}{A},$$ with the heavy daughter recoiling backward with $K_Y = Q - K_\alpha$.
concepts.detail: For ²³⁸U: $K_\alpha = 4.27(234/238) = 4.20\ \mathrm{MeV}$, matching the measured alpha line; the thorium daughter carries only 0.07 MeV of recoil.

concepts.statement: The alpha inside the nucleus sits in a potential well whose wall is the Coulomb barrier $U(r) = k(Z_\alpha Z_Y e^2)/r$ — several times taller than $Q$. It escapes only by tunneling, with probability $T \approx e^{-2G}$ governed by the Gamow factor, an integral through the classically forbidden region. Because $T$ is exponentially sensitive to both $Q$ and $Z$, tiny changes in either swing the half-life over dozens of orders of magnitude (the Geiger–Nuttall relation).
concepts.detail: Alpha energies span only 4–9 MeV while half-lives span microseconds to 10¹⁰ years — no classical mechanism can produce that; the exponential of a quantum tunneling probability can, and its observed regularities convinced physicists of barrier penetration by 1928 (Gamow, Gurney, Condon).

concepts.statement: **Solve Alpha Decay problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is nuclear size, binding and the exponential decay law; the working equation is $R = r_0A^{1/3}$, $r_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$, $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (femtometers, becquerels, gray/sieverts) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr; $N\gg 1$ for $e^{-\lambda t}$; $\lambda$ constant in time.

concepts.statement: **Alpha Decay lives at $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr and the textbook model holds while $N\gg 1$ for $e^{-\lambda t}$; $\lambda$ constant in time.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Alpha Decay calculation gives seconds when femtometers, becquerels, gray/sieverts demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Energy and speed of the ²³⁸U alpha
examples.problem: For ²³⁸U → ²³⁴Th + α with Q = 4.27 MeV, find the alpha's kinetic energy and its speed as it emerges.

steps.label: Split
steps.text: $K_\alpha = Q(A-4)/A = 4.27(234/238) = 4.20\ \mathrm{MeV}$; the daughter gets 0.07 MeV.

steps.label: Numbers
steps.text: Numerator $= 1.35\times10^{-12}$; $v = \sqrt{2.03\times10^{14}} = 1.42\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{m/s}$ — about 5% of the speed of light.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Relativistic correction $(v/c)^2/2 \approx 0.1\%$: the nonrelativistic treatment is adequate.

examples.result: $K_\alpha = 4.20\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $v = 1.4\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{m/s}$ — one alpha line per nuclide, the signature of a two-body split.

examples.title: Alpha Decay: nuclear-size check
examples.problem: Estimate $R = r_0A^{1/3}$ with $r_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$ for $A = 256$.

steps.label: Radius
steps.text: $R \approx 1.2\times 6.35 = 7.62\ \text{fm}$.

examples.result: $R \approx 7.62\ \text{fm}$.

keyTakeaways: Alpha decay requires $Q = (M_X - M_Y - M_\alpha)c^2 > 0$, computable entirely from atomic masses.
Momentum conservation hands the alpha nearly all the energy: $K_\alpha = Q(A-4)/A$, giving sharp, discrete alpha lines.
Escape occurs by tunneling through the Coulomb barrier; the exponential sensitivity of the tunneling probability explains the 10¹⁰-year spread of alpha half-lives.

quiz.q: In alpha decay, why may atomic masses be used in computing Q?
options: the electrons are shared equally and simply cancel between the two sides of the balanced equation
the nucleus has no electrons, so none appear
quiz.explanation: The parent's Z electrons reappear as Z − 2 on the daughter plus 2 bound to the alpha: identical electron bookkeeping on both sides.

quiz.q: A heavy parent (A = 240) decays by alpha emission with Q = 6.0 MeV. The alpha's kinetic energy is about
quiz.explanation: $K_\alpha = Q(A-4)/A = 6.0(236/240) = 5.9\ \mathrm{MeV}$ — the light particle takes almost everything.

quiz.q: Alpha half-lives range over enormous values even though alpha energies span only 4–9 MeV because
options: the strong force varies that much
the tunneling probability through the Coulomb barrier is exponential in the energy
quiz.explanation: The Gamow factor is exponentially sensitive to Q and to the daughter charge, magnifying small energy differences into huge lifetime differences.

quiz.q: The ²³⁴Th daughter nucleus recoils with kinetic energy
options: only about 1–2% of Q, by momentum conservation
quiz.explanation: Equal and opposite momenta mean K inversely proportional to mass: the heavy daughter carries only $K_\alpha(m_\alpha/M_\mathrm{daughter}) \approx 1.7\%$ of $Q$.

intro: Beta decay produces not a sharp line but a smear of electron energies — and in 1930 that smear appeared to violate conservation of energy, momentum and angular momentum at once. Pauli's audacious fix was an invisible particle; Fermi built it into a new interaction; the neutrino was caught in 1956 and the weak force became a pillar of the Standard Model.
objectives: Distinguish the three beta modes and write their nuclear equations
Explain how the continuous beta spectrum demands the neutrino
Identify beta decay as the signature of the weak interaction and estimate decay energies

concepts.statement: **Beta-minus:** a neutron converts to a proton, ejecting an electron and an electron antineutrino ($\beta^-$): $n \to p + e^- + \bar\nu_e$. **Beta-plus:** a proton converts to a neutron, ejecting a positron and a neutrino. **Electron capture:** the nucleus swallows an inner orbital electron, $p + e^- \to n + \nu_e$. In each case $A$ is unchanged and $Z$ shifts by one.
concepts.detail: Free protons cannot beta-plus decay (the neutron is heavier); inside a nucleus the binding energies can tilt either way, which is why neutron-rich nuclides beta-minus and proton-rich ones beta-plus or capture.

concepts.term: The continuous spectrum and the neutrino
concepts.statement: In a two-body decay the electron energy would be a single sharp value; instead beta electrons emerge with **all energies from zero up to the endpoint**. Pauli (1930) proposed that a third, undetected particle — the neutrino, neutral and nearly massless — shares the energy at random; Fermi's 1934 theory of the process became the prototype of the weak interaction. Reines and Cowan detected the neutrino directly in 1956.
concepts.detail: Angular momentum also demands it: ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + e⁻ would leave two fermions (integer total spin) violating angular momentum conservation without a third half-integer partner.

concepts.statement: Beta decay changes a quark's flavor (down ↔ up) — a process mediated by the massive $W^\pm$ bosons, whose 80 GeV/c² mass makes the force short-ranged ($\sim10^{-18}\ \mathrm{m}$) and the decays slow: typical beta lifetimes are milliseconds to years, against 10⁻²³ s for strong decays.
concepts.detail: Neutrinos interact so feebly that a light-year of lead would stop only about half of them — which is exactly why the Sun's core is transparent to them and why neutrino astronomy can see the moment of a supernova's collapse.

Check the answer against $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr; $N\gg 1$ for $e^{-\lambda t}$; $\lambda$ constant in time.

examples.title: The tritium endpoint
examples.problem: Tritium beta-decays as ³H → ³He + e⁻ + ν̄ (atomic masses 3.016049 u and 3.016029 u). Find the energy released and the maximum electron energy.

steps.label: Energy
steps.text: $Q = 0.0186\ \mathrm{MeV} = 18.6\ \mathrm{keV}$.

steps.label: Endpoint
steps.text: When the antineutrino takes essentially nothing, the electron gets nearly all of it: $K_\mathrm{max} \approx 18.6\ \mathrm{keV}$ (the heavy ³He takes negligible recoil).

steps.label: Spectrum
steps.text: Most electrons emerge with 5–15 keV; the shape of the tail near 18.6 keV is so clean that the KATRIN experiment uses it to bound the neutrino mass (below ~0.8 eV).

examples.result: $Q = 18.6\ \mathrm{keV}$ sets the tritium endpoint; the continuum of electron energies below it is the neutrino's calling card.

examples.title: Beta Decay: nuclear-size check
examples.problem: Estimate $R = r_0A^{1/3}$ with $r_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$ for $A = 56$.

steps.label: Radius
steps.text: $R \approx 1.2\times 3.83 = 4.59\ \text{fm}$.

examples.result: $R \approx 4.59\ \text{fm}$.

keyTakeaways: Three modes: β⁻ (n → p + e⁻ + ν̄), β⁺ (p → n + e⁺ + ν) and electron capture; A stays fixed while Z shifts by one.
The continuous electron spectrum is explained by three-body kinematics with a third, nearly massless particle — the neutrino.
Beta decay is a weak-interaction flavor change; the heavy W boson makes it slow and short-ranged.

quiz.q: In beta-minus decay the parent nucleus's numbers change as
options: Z decreases by 1, N increases by 1
Z increases by 1, N decreases by 1, A fixed
Z and N both stay the same
quiz.explanation: A neutron becomes a proton: Z up by one, N down by one, mass number unchanged.

quiz.q: The continuous energy spectrum of beta electrons was explained by
options: the neutrino sharing the decay energy as a third particle
quiz.explanation: Pauli's neutrino lets the two light particles split Q randomly, filling every electron energy from zero to the endpoint.

quiz.q: Which conservation law would fail in ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + e⁻ without a neutrino?
quiz.explanation: Two spin-1/2 products cannot combine with the initial integer spin; also energy and momentum conservation appear broken by the missing third body.

quiz.q: Neutrinos interact so weakly with matter that
options: roughly half would pass through a light-year of lead
they cannot be produced in the Sun
quiz.explanation: Their weak-only coupling gives them enormous mean free paths; trillions from the Sun pass through you each second.

intro: Cosmic rays keep the atmosphere stocked with a trace isotope, carbon-14, which living things absorb and maintain at equilibrium with their environment. At death the intake stops and the ¹⁴C clock starts running down at its 5730-year half-life. Measure what is left — by counting decays — and you have a date, one of archaeology's most transformative gifts from physics.
objectives: Explain how cosmic rays sustain atmospheric carbon-14 and how living tissue tracks it
Date a sample from its measured ¹⁴C activity using the decay law
Choose appropriate isotopic clocks for different time scales

concepts.statement: Cosmic-ray neutrons convert atmospheric nitrogen via $^{14}\mathrm{N}(n,p)^{14}\mathrm{C}$; the ¹⁴C oxidizes to CO₂, mixes through the biosphere, and living material holds a steady ratio $^{14}\mathrm{C}/^{12}\mathrm{C} \approx 1.3\times10^{-12}$, decaying and replenished in balance. Death closes the account: the ratio (and hence the activity) then decays with $T_{1/2} = 5730$ y.
concepts.detail: In living carbon this corresponds to about 15 decays per minute per gram; a sample's activity directly measures the surviving fraction.

concepts.statement: With $R_0$ the equilibrium activity of living material and $R$ the measured activity now, $$t = \frac{T_{1/2}}{\ln 2}\,\ln\frac{R_0}{R},$$ the logarithm of the activity ratio run backwards along the exponential.
concepts.detail: The useful range is a few half-lives to about eight (up to ~50,000 years); beyond that the activity sinks below the background and other clocks are needed.

concepts.statement: Longer scales use longer-lived nuclides: potassium–argon ($^{40}\mathrm{K}$, $T_{1/2} = 1.25\times10^{9}$ y) and uranium–lead ($^{238}\mathrm{U}$, $4.47\times10^{9}$ y) date rocks and the Earth itself; the parent-to-daughter **ratio** replaces activity when the daughter accumulates and stays trapped in the mineral.
concepts.detail: Choice of clock is everything: ¹⁴C for a campfire, ²³⁰Th for coral, U–Pb for zircon crystals that closed their chemical systems billions of years ago — each isotope covers the time scale its half-life can resolve.

Check the answer against $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr; $N\gg 1$ for $e^{-\lambda t}$; $\lambda$ constant in time.

examples.title: Dating a bone by carbon-14 activity
examples.problem: A charcoal sample from an archaeological site shows 3.5 ¹⁴C decays per minute per gram of carbon; living carbon gives 15.3. How old is the sample?

steps.label: Numbers
steps.text: $5730/0.693 = 8267$ y per unit logarithm; $t = 8267 \times 1.475 = 1.22\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{y}$.

examples.result: About 12,000 years — the charcoal cooled at the end of the last ice age, deep in the range where ¹⁴C is reliable.

examples.title: Radioactive Dating: decay-numbers check
examples.problem: Carbon-14 has $T_{1/2} = 5730\ \text{yr}$. Starting from $10^{12}$ nuclei, how many remain after $5730\ \text{yr}$?

steps.label: Remain
steps.text: $N \approx 5.00\times 10^{+11}$ nuclei.

keyTakeaways: Cosmic rays maintain atmospheric ¹⁴C; living tissue mirrors the atmospheric ratio, and death freezes the clock.
Age follows from $t = (T_{1/2}/\ln2)\ln(R_0/R)$ — an activity ratio converted to time.
Different isotopes cover different scales: ¹⁴C for millennia, ⁴⁰K and U–Pb for the age of rocks and the Earth.

quiz.q: Carbon-14 is continually produced in the upper atmosphere by
quiz.explanation: The reaction 14N(n,p)14C turns ordinary nitrogen into the clock isotope, which then circulates as CO2.

quiz.q: A sample's 14C activity is one-eighth of the living value. Its age is
quiz.explanation: One-eighth survival = 3 half-lives: t = 3 × 5730 = 17,190 y.

quiz.q: Dating with 14C becomes unreliable beyond roughly 50,000 years mainly because
options: so little 14C remains that its activity falls below background
quiz.explanation: After ~9 half-lives the residual activity is a few decays per hour per gram, swamped by cosmic-ray background and contamination.

quiz.q: For dating a billion-year-old rock, the best choice is
quiz.explanation: Long half-lives (4.5 and 1.25 billion years) match the scale; 14C would have faded to nothing many times over.

intro: The same decays that power reactors and tracer studies also deposit energy in human tissue. Dosimetry measures that deposition — absorbed energy per kilogram — and then weights it by how biologically destructive each radiation type is. Two units, the gray and the sievert, and one table of quality factors, are all the bookkeeping needed to set safety standards.
objectives: Define absorbed dose in grays and rads and compute deposited energies
Apply the RBE weighting to convert absorbed dose to equivalent dose in sieverts
Place typical exposures — background, medical, lethal — on a common scale

concepts.statement: The absorbed dose is energy deposited per unit mass of irradiated material: $$1\ \mathrm{gray\ (Gy)} = 1\ \mathrm{J/kg},\qquad 1\ \mathrm{rad} = 0.01\ \mathrm{Gy}.$$ Absorbed dose is purely physical — it knows nothing of radiation type or biology.
concepts.detail: A whole-body 5.0 Gy of gamma rays deposits 350 J in a 70 kg adult: enough energy to boil a teaspoon of water, yet enough to destroy the bone marrow — dose, not energy, is what matters.

concepts.statement: Radiations differ in biological punch per joule, so dose is weighted by the relative biological effectiveness (RBE, also quality factor): $$\mathrm{equivalent\ dose\ (Sv)} = \mathrm{RBE} \times \mathrm{absorbed\ dose\ (Gy)}.$$ Gamma rays and beta particles have RBE ≈ 1; protons ≈ 2–5; alpha particles internally ≈ 10–20, because their dense ionization trails wreck DNA locally.
concepts.detail: The sievert (and the older rem = 0.01 Sv) is the unit of biological risk; it is the sievert figure, not the gray figure, that radiation-safety limits are written in.

concepts.statement: Natural background delivers about 2–3 mSv per year; a chest X-ray is ~0.1 mSv, a full-body CT scan of order 10 mSv; radiation workers are limited to 20–50 mSv/yr; whole-body equivalent doses of ~4–5 Sv kill about half of those exposed within weeks (the LD50), and brief doses of 10 Sv are invariably fatal.
concepts.detail: Alpha emitters are nearly harmless outside the body (skin stops them) yet vicious when inhaled or ingested — radon gas in basements and plutonium dust in lungs are the classic internal-emitter hazards.
