examples.title: Gamma dose versus internal alpha dose
examples.problem: A 70 kg worker absorbs a uniform whole-body 5.0 Gy of gamma rays (RBE = 1). Separately, a lung tissue sample absorbs 0.10 Gy from inhaled alpha particles (RBE = 20). Compare deposited energies and equivalent doses.

steps.label: Gamma energy
steps.text: $E = (5.0\ \mathrm{J/kg})(70\ \mathrm{kg}) = 350\ \mathrm{J}$ deposited throughout the body.

steps.label: Gamma equivalent
steps.text: $5.0\ \mathrm{Gy} \times 1 = 5.0\ \mathrm{Sv}$ — near the LD50 for whole-body exposure without treatment.

steps.label: Alpha energy
steps.text: For a 0.020 kg lung region absorbing 0.10 Gy: $E = 0.10 \times 0.020 = 2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J}$ — a whisper of energy.

steps.label: Alpha equivalent
steps.text: $0.10\ \mathrm{Gy} \times 20 = 2.0\ \mathrm{Sv}$ to that tissue — comparable damage from 10⁵ times less energy.

examples.result: 350 J of gamma (5.0 Sv whole body) versus 2 mJ of alpha locally (2.0 Sv to the lung): the RBE weighting, not the raw energy, carries the biological story.

examples.title: Measuring Radiation Dosage: nuclear-size check
examples.problem: Estimate $R = r_0A^{1/3}$ with $r_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$ for $A = 156$.

steps.label: Radius
steps.text: $R \approx 1.2\times 5.38 = 6.46\ \text{fm}$.

examples.result: $R \approx 6.46\ \text{fm}$.

keyTakeaways: Absorbed dose: 1 Gy = 1 J/kg (the rad is 0.01 Gy) — a purely physical bookkeeping of deposited energy.
Equivalent dose multiplies by RBE (1 for γ and β, 10–20 for internal alphas) to get sieverts — the unit of biological risk.
Scale for context: ~2–3 mSv/yr background, ~0.1 mSv chest X-ray, ~4–5 Sv LD50 whole body.

quiz.q: An absorbed dose of 2.0 Gy corresponds to deposited energy of
quiz.explanation: The gray is one joule per kilogram of absorbing material; the Sv requires an RBE factor first.

quiz.q: Alpha particles receive a high RBE (10–20) because they
options: deposit dense ionization trails that concentrate damage in cells
quiz.explanation: Short, heavily ionizing tracks mean concentrated, poorly repaired biological damage per joule — the opposite of penetrating gamma rays.

quiz.q: A absorbed dose of 0.05 Gy of beta radiation (RBE = 1) gives an equivalent dose of
quiz.explanation: 0.05 Gy × 1 = 0.05 Sv = 50 mSv — roughly a couple of CT scans' worth of whole-body dose.

quiz.q: Which exposure delivers the larger equivalent dose to tissue?
options: cannot be compared without knowing the half-life
quiz.explanation: 0.1 Gy × 20 = 2.0 Sv beats 1 Gy × 1 = 1.0 Sv — quality factor can outweigh raw dose.

intro: No computer can solve the quantum many-body problem of 238 interacting nucleons exactly, so nuclear physics proceeds by caricature: models that each capture one face of the data. The liquid-drop model treats the nucleus as charged rain and reproduces masses and fission; the shell model, in defiance of that picture, finds evidence for individual nucleons orbiting a central potential — the magic numbers prove both are right about different things.
objectives: State the evidence motivating the collective liquid-drop model and what it explains
Present the magic numbers and the shell-model picture that accounts for them
Explain spin pairing and its consequences for the stability of even-even nuclei

concepts.statement: Because nuclear density is nearly A-independent, Bohr and Wheeler modeled the nucleus as an incompressible, charged droplet: binding energy assembled from a volume term (binding proportional to A), a surface-tension term (underbound surface nucleons, $\propto A^{2/3}$), a Coulomb term (proton repulsion, $\propto Z^2/A^{1/3}$), and a pairing term (Section below). This semi-empirical mass formula predicts binding energies to ~1% and underlies the theory of fission.
concepts.detail: The compound-nucleus picture of reactions — the incident particle is absorbed and its energy shared statistically before re-emission — is the dynamic face of the same collective idea.

concepts.term: Magic numbers and the shell model
concepts.statement: Nuclides with proton or neutron counts equal to **2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, or 126** are anomalously abundant, anomalously tightly bound, and anomalously long-lived; ⁴He (2, 2), ¹⁶O (8, 8), ⁴⁰Ca (20, 20) and ²⁰⁸Pb (82, 126) are 'doubly magic'. The shell model explains them as closed shells of individual nucleons moving in a common potential well with strong spin–orbit coupling — nuclear physics's analogue of noble-gas electron shells.
concepts.detail: Magic-number nuclei also support the idea of an island of stability beyond the known superheavy elements, guiding searches around Z = 114–126, N = 184.

concepts.statement: Nucleons of like type pair their spins to zero, and paired nucleons are extra-bound: **even-even nuclei (even Z, even N) are the most stable and by far the most abundant** — about 160 stable ones. Odd-odd nuclei are so penalized that only four exist in nature in long-lived form (²H, ⁶Li, ¹⁰B, ¹⁴N).
concepts.detail: Between the extremes, odd-A nuclei sit intermediate: one unpaired nucleon supplies the nuclear spin and magnetic moment, which is why only odd-A nuclei show up in NMR and Mössbauer work.

concepts.statement: **Solve Nuclear Models problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is nuclear size, binding and the exponential decay law; the working equation is $R = r_0A^{1/3}$, $r_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$, $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (femtometers, becquerels, gray/sieverts) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr; $N\gg 1$ for $e^{-\lambda t}$; $\lambda$ constant in time.

concepts.statement: **Nuclear Models lives at $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr and the textbook model holds while $N\gg 1$ for $e^{-\lambda t}$; $\lambda$ constant in time.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Nuclear Models calculation gives seconds when femtometers, becquerels, gray/sieverts demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $R\sim \text{fm}$; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2$; $T_{1/2}$ from s to Gyr, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Reading stability from the magic numbers
examples.problem: Using the magic-number lists (2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126), assess ²⁰⁸Pb (Z = 82, N = 126) and ¹³²Sn (Z = 50, N = 82).

steps.label: Lead-208
steps.text: Z = 82 is magic and N = 126 is magic: **doubly magic**, the heaviest known doubly magic nuclide.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.text: ²⁰⁸Pb is stable (the end of the thorium decay chains), extra-tightly bound relative to its neighbors, and spherical with a very low neutron-capture cross section.

steps.label: Tin-132
steps.text: Z = 50 and N = 82 are both magic: doubly magic, though neutron-rich and radioactive — shell closure does not guarantee stability, only extra binding at fixed A.

steps.label: Contrast
steps.text: Its neighbor ¹³³Sn, with one neutron past closure, is markedly less bound per nucleon and decays within days.

examples.result: Both are doubly magic and therefore locally maximally bound; ²⁰⁸Pb is outright stable, ¹³²Sn shows shell closure while still decaying — the magic numbers measure binding structure, not immortality.

examples.title: Nuclear Models: nuclear-size check
examples.problem: Estimate $R = r_0A^{1/3}$ with $r_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$ for $A = 206$.

steps.label: Radius
steps.text: $R \approx 1.2\times 5.91 = 7.09\ \text{fm}$.

examples.result: $R \approx 7.09\ \text{fm}$.

keyTakeaways: The liquid-drop model (volume + surface + Coulomb + pairing terms) reproduces nuclear masses and the energetics of fission.
Magic numbers 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126 mark closed shells of an independent-particle shell model with strong spin–orbit coupling.
Even-even nuclei dominate the stable list because paired like nucleons bind extra-tightly; odd-odd nuclei barely survive.

quiz.q: The liquid-drop model works because
options: nuclear density is nearly independent of A, like an incompressible droplet
quiz.explanation: Volume proportional to A is droplet behavior; surface and Coulomb terms then capture the mass data well.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a magic neutron number?
quiz.explanation: The magic numbers are 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126 — 82 closes a neutron (and proton) shell.

quiz.q: A doubly magic nucleus is one in which
options: both Z and N are magic numbers
A is twice a magic number
it has twice the normal density
quiz.explanation: Closed proton and closed neutron shells together — 4He, 16O, 40Ca, 48Ca, 208Pb — yield exceptional binding and stability.

quiz.q: Stable odd-odd nuclei (odd Z, odd N) are rare because
options: the pairing term leaves two unpaired nucleons, a binding penalty
quiz.explanation: Only 2H, 6Li, 10B and 14N survive the penalty; pairing to zero spin is worth roughly 1-2 MeV of extra binding.

intro: Nudge a uranium-235 nucleus with a slow neutron and it does not merely absorb it — it splits into two medium-mass fragments, a spray of neutrons, and about 200 MeV of energy, three million times the yield per atom of coal burning. Each fission releases the neutrons needed to trigger the next, which is why a lump of fissile material can, if you get the geometry right, power a city.
objectives: Describe the sequence of events in neutron-induced fission of uranium-235
Account for the ~200 MeV energy release from the binding-energy curve and itemize where it goes
Define the multiplication factor and the conditions for subcritical, critical and supercritical chains

concepts.statement: A thermal (slow) neutron absorbed by ²³⁵U forms an excited compound nucleus ²³⁶U* that deforms like a charged liquid drop and splits: $$^{235}\mathrm{U} + n \to {}^{236}\mathrm{U}^* \to X + Y + \bar\nu\,n + \gamma,$$ where $X$ and $Y$ are asymmetric fragments (masses near $A \approx 95$ and $A \approx 140$) and $\bar\nu \approx 2.4$ neutrons are released on average.
concepts.detail: Why slow neutrons? Their de Broglie wavelengths are large, their wavefunctions overlap the nucleus generously, and the fission probability rises steeply as neutron energy falls — which is why reactors go to the trouble of moderating their neutrons.

concepts.statement: Reading the binding energy curve leftward: fragments near $A = 118$ are bound by ~8.4 MeV/nucleon against 7.57 for uranium, so each of the ~235 nucleons gains ~0.85 MeV — about **200 MeV per fission**. Most of it emerges promptly as fragment kinetic energy (~165 MeV); the rest arrives later through beta decays and gamma rays, with ~12 MeV carried off by neutrinos.
concepts.detail: Chemical burning releases a few eV per atom; fission releases ~10⁸ eV per atom. One gram of ²³⁵U (about a paperclip's worth of uranium) delivers $8.2\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$ — several tonnes of TNT.

concepts.statement: Fission neutrons can trigger further fissions; the ratio of new fissions to old ones is the **multiplication factor k**. $k < 1$: subcritical, the chain dies out; $k = 1$: critical, self-sustaining steady power (a reactor's operating point); $k > 1$: supercritical, exponential runaway (a bomb's fuel assembly).
concepts.detail: Control is everything: the fraction of neutrons that leak out, get captured without fission, or are absorbed by poisons determines k, and a reactor is engineered to hover at k = 1 through feedback rather than luck.

concepts.statement: ²³⁵U (0.72% of natural uranium) fissions readily with thermal neutrons; ²³⁸U (99.3%) mostly absorbs fast neutrons without fissioning. But that absorption breeds ²³⁹Pu, which is fissile — the reactor can manufacture its own fuel (Section 43-2).
concepts.detail: The asymmetry of the fragment split is itself physics: symmetric splits would have to pass through more deformed, lower-binding configurations, and the asymmetric channel wins the race to scission.

concepts.statement: **Solve Nuclear Fission problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is fission $Q \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$ and the $p$-$p$ chain $26.7\ \text{MeV}$ per He; the working equation is $Q_{\text{fission}} \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$, $4p\to {}^{4}\!He+2e^++2\nu_e+26.7\ \text{MeV}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{MeV}$ and $\text{MW}\cdot\text{day}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission; $k = 1$ critical; Coulomb barrier needs $10^7\ \text{K}$.

examples.title: One gram of uranium-235 versus coal
examples.problem: Estimate the energy released by complete fission of 1.0 g of ²³⁵U and the mass of coal (30 MJ/kg) delivering the same energy.

steps.label: Count nuclei
steps.text: $N = m/(Am_\mathrm{u}) = 1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}/(235 \times 1.66\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}) = 2.56\times10^{21}$.

steps.label: Coal mass
steps.text: $m_\mathrm{coal} = 8.2\times10^{10}/(3.0\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{J/kg}) = 2.7\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg}$ — about three tonnes.

steps.label: Scale check
steps.text: A 1 GW power plant running a day needs $8.64\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{J}/8.2\times10^{10} \approx 1.05\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ²³⁵U fissioned per day.

examples.result: 1 g of ²³⁵U releases $8.2\times10^{10}$ J, matching ~2.7 tonnes of coal: the factor $3\times10^{6}$ in energy density that defines nuclear fuel.

examples.title: Nuclear Fission: fission-energy check
examples.problem: One mole-equivalent ($10^{24}$ fissions) each releases $200\ \text{MeV}$. How much energy is that?

steps.label: Total
steps.text: $10^{24}\times 3.20\times 10^{-11} = 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$ ($\approx 8.9\ \text{MW}\cdot\text{h}$).

examples.result: $E \approx 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$.

keyTakeaways: Thermal neutrons on ²³⁵U produce asymmetric fragments plus ~2.4 neutrons and ~200 MeV per fission.
The energy gain is the climb up the binding-energy curve from 7.57 to ~8.4 MeV/nucleon, mostly appearing as fragment kinetic energy.
Criticality is the balance of neutron production and loss (k = 1 steady, k > 1 runaway); slow neutrons are the efficient triggers.

quiz.q: The energy released in a single ²³⁵U fission is about
quiz.explanation: About 200 MeV, mostly as kinetic energy of the two fragments, with betas, gammas and neutrinos carrying the remainder.

quiz.q: Thermal (slow) neutrons are preferred for inducing fission in ²³⁵U because
options: their larger de Broglie wavelength gives a much larger fission cross section
quiz.explanation: Slow neutrons overlap the nucleus more effectively; fission probability rises steeply as neutron energy drops, which is why reactors moderate.

quiz.q: A chain reaction with multiplication factor k = 0.9 is
options: subcritical — the chain dies away geometrically
quiz.explanation: Each generation is 90% of the last; the process winds down like compound interest in reverse.

quiz.q: Compared with burning carbon (~5 eV per atom), fission releases roughly
options: a hundred times more energy per atom
quiz.explanation: 200 MeV versus a few eV is a factor of ~4e7 per reaction; per unit fuel mass the ratio is about 3 million.

intro: A nuclear reactor is a kettle with extraordinary bookkeeping: fuel rods supply the fissions, a moderator slows the neutrons so they can find more uranium, control rods swallow whatever excess the reaction offers, and coolant carries away the heat. Around that core lives everything from electricity grids to isotope factories — and the same machine can quietly convert useless uranium-238 into plutonium fuel.
objectives: Identify the essential components of a fission reactor and the function of each
Explain how moderation and delayed neutrons make reactor control possible
Describe breeding: how ²³⁸U captures neutrons to become fissile ²³⁹Pu

concepts.statement: The core contains (1) **fuel** — enriched ²³⁵U (typically 3–4%) in oxide pellets and zirconium-clad rods; (2) a **moderator** — light water, heavy water or graphite — to slow fission neutrons to thermal energies; (3) **control rods** — cadmium or boron, strong neutron absorbers, inserted or withdrawn to trim k; (4) **coolant** carrying the thermal power to turbines; (5) **shielding** against radiation; and (6) emergency systems that flood the core with absorber.
concepts.detail: Heavy water deuterium moderates while absorbing almost nothing, letting natural (unenriched) uranium fuel the CANDU design; light water is cheaper but requires enrichment.

concepts.statement: Neutrons lose energy most efficiently in elastic collisions with nuclei of similar mass, so hydrogen-rich water (or carbon in graphite) tumbles them down to thermal energies in a few dozen collisions. Crucially, about 1% of fission neutrons are **delayed** — emitted by neutron-rich fission fragments seconds after the event — and this small delayed fraction stretches the reactor's time response from milliseconds to seconds, making smooth control physically possible.
concepts.detail: A reactor is engineered so that k exceeds 1 only with the delayed neutrons included; then the power level follows the slow decay of the precursors, and a mechanical control system (and the negative temperature feedback of a well-designed core) can track it.

concepts.statement: Neutrons absorbed in ²³⁸U (rather than in ²³⁵U or the moderator) transmute it: $$^{238}\mathrm{U} \xrightarrow{(n,\gamma)} {}^{239}\mathrm{U} \xrightarrow{\beta^-} {}^{239}\mathrm{Np} \xrightarrow{\beta^-} {}^{239}\mathrm{Pu},$$ and ²³⁹Pu fissions with thermal neutrons just as handily as ²³⁵U. A **breeder reactor** surrounds its core with ²³⁸U (or ²³²Th → ²³³U) and produces more fissile atoms than it burns.
concepts.detail: Since natural uranium is 99.3% ²³⁸U, breeding in principle multiplies the fuel supply by more than a hundred — the resource argument behind fast breeder programs.

concepts.statement: **Solve The Nuclear Reactor problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is fission $Q \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$ and the $p$-$p$ chain $26.7\ \text{MeV}$ per He; the working equation is $Q_{\text{fission}} \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$, $4p\to {}^{4}\!He+2e^++2\nu_e+26.7\ \text{MeV}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{MeV}$ and $\text{MW}\cdot\text{day}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission; $k = 1$ critical; Coulomb barrier needs $10^7\ \text{K}$.

concepts.term: The Nuclear Reactor: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **The Nuclear Reactor lives at $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission and the textbook model holds while $k = 1$ critical; Coulomb barrier needs $10^7\ \text{K}$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a The Nuclear Reactor calculation gives seconds when $\text{MeV}$ and $\text{MW}\cdot\text{day}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Annual fuel budget of a 1 GW thermal reactor
examples.problem: A reactor delivers 1.0 GW of thermal power continuously for a year. How much ²³⁵U must fission, at 200 MeV per fission?

steps.label: Energy per year
steps.text: $E = Pt = (1.0\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{W})(3.15\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}) = 3.15\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{J}$.

steps.label: Fissions
steps.text: Each fission yields $200\ \mathrm{MeV} = 3.2\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$: $N_f = 3.15\times10^{16}/3.2\times10^{-11} = 9.8\times10^{26}$.

steps.label: Mass
steps.text: $m = N_f(235)(1.66\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}) = 3.8\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ²³⁵U fissioned per year.

steps.label: Reality check
steps.text: Real cores load several tonnes, since fuel must be replaced before it fully burns (fission products absorb neutrons) — but the physics bookkeeping stands at about 400 kg per gigawatt-year.

examples.result: About $4\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ²³⁵U fissioned per GW-year — a few hundred kilograms per year, against millions of tonnes of coal for the same energy.

examples.title: The Nuclear Reactor: fission-energy check
examples.problem: One mole-equivalent ($10^{24}$ fissions) each releases $200\ \text{MeV}$. How much energy is that?

steps.label: Total
steps.text: $10^{24}\times 3.20\times 10^{-11} = 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$ ($\approx 8.9\ \text{MW}\cdot\text{h}$).

examples.result: $E \approx 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$.

keyTakeaways: Core components: enriched fuel, moderator (water/graphite/D₂O), cadmium or boron control rods, coolant, shielding.
Delayed neutrons stretch the reactor's response time from milliseconds to seconds — the margin that makes control feasible.
Neutron capture on ²³⁸U breeds ²³⁹Pu through two beta decays; breeder reactors can create more fuel than they consume.

quiz.q: The moderator's job is to
options: slow fast fission neutrons to thermal energies so they fission ²³⁵U efficiently
quiz.explanation: Elastic scattering on light nuclei (H, D, C) tumbles the neutrons down in energy; absorption is the control rods' job.

quiz.q: Delayed neutrons are essential to reactor control because they
options: allow the chain reaction to respond on a seconds timescale rather than milliseconds
quiz.explanation: Emission from beta-decaying fragments seconds later stretches the prompt neutron lifetime into a range mechanical systems can follow.

quiz.q: Control rods are made of cadmium or boron because these
quiz.explanation: Strong absorbers trim the neutron population — pushing k down — and can be inserted to whatever depth the power demands.

quiz.q: In the breeding sequence, ²³⁹U becomes ²³⁹Pu through
quiz.explanation: 238U(n,gamma)239U, then beta-minus to neptunium-239 and beta-minus again to plutonium-239, which is fissile.

intro: In 1972 a French fuel-processing lab noticed that uranium from a mine in Oklo, Gabon, was short of ²³⁵U — as though some of it had already been burned. The only explanation, now universally accepted, is that two billion years ago the ore at Oklo went critical on its own: a natural, water-moderated fission reactor that ran for millennia before anyone existed to observe it.
objectives: Describe the isotopic anomaly that revealed the Oklo natural reactor
Compute the ²³⁵U fraction two billion years ago from the decay law
Explain the groundwater moderation and self-regulation that sustained the reaction

concepts.statement: Uranium from Oklo contained as little as 0.44% ²³⁵U (natural today: 0.72%), and neighboring elements carried the isotopic fingerprints of fission products — for example, neodymium whose isotope ratios match fission yields rather than natural abundances. The inescapable reading: the deposit had hosted sustained fission chains.
concepts.detail: Over a dozen reactor zones have since been mapped at the site; the fission-product isotopes stayed put for two billion years, a natural experiment in radioactive-waste containment that geologists still mine for data.

concepts.statement: ²³⁵U ($T_{1/2} = 7.04\times10^{8}$ y) decays faster than ²³⁸U ($4.47\times10^{9}$ y). Running the exponential decay backward, the ²³⁵U fraction at time $t$ ago is $$f(t) = \frac{f_0e^{+\lambda_{235}t}}{f_0e^{\lambda_{235}t} + (1-f_0)e^{\lambda_{238}t}}$$ — two billion years ago it was about **3.7%**, right in the range of modern enriched reactor fuel.
concepts.detail: At 3.7% enrichment, ordinary water is a sufficient moderator for a critical assembly; at today's 0.72% it is not, which is why the trick cannot repeat in the present epoch.

concepts.statement: Rainwater percolating through the porous ore served as moderator and reflector: more water, better thermalization, more fissions — and the fission heat boiled the water away, throttling the reaction back. This negative feedback cycled the zones between power and shutdown for perhaps 10⁵ years at power levels of order 100 kW thermal.
concepts.detail: The same physics protects modern light-water reactors: a core that heats up loses moderation and shuts itself down — a passive safety feature operating for geological time at Oklo.

concepts.term: A Natural Nuclear Reactor: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve A Natural Nuclear Reactor problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is fission $Q \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$ and the $p$-$p$ chain $26.7\ \text{MeV}$ per He; the working equation is $Q_{\text{fission}} \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$, $4p\to {}^{4}\!He+2e^++2\nu_e+26.7\ \text{MeV}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{MeV}$ and $\text{MW}\cdot\text{day}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission; $k = 1$ critical; Coulomb barrier needs $10^7\ \text{K}$.

concepts.term: A Natural Nuclear Reactor: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **A Natural Nuclear Reactor lives at $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission and the textbook model holds while $k = 1$ critical; Coulomb barrier needs $10^7\ \text{K}$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a A Natural Nuclear Reactor calculation gives seconds when $\text{MeV}$ and $\text{MW}\cdot\text{day}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Uranium-235 abundance two billion years ago
examples.problem: Today ²³⁵U is 0.720% of natural uranium. Using $T_{1/2}(235) = 7.04\times10^{8}$ y and $T_{1/2}(238) = 4.47\times10^{9}$ y, find the ²³⁵U fraction $2.0\times10^{9}$ years ago.

steps.label: Interpretation
steps.text: 3.7% ²³⁵U — enrichment typical of today's commercial reactor fuel, making the ore at Oklo a naturally critical candidate.

examples.result: The ²³⁵U fraction was about **3.7%**, so a water-moderated critical assembly was possible then and is impossible in ore formed today.

examples.title: A Natural Nuclear Reactor: fission-energy check
examples.problem: One mole-equivalent ($10^{24}$ fissions) each releases $200\ \text{MeV}$. How much energy is that?

steps.label: Total
steps.text: $10^{24}\times 3.20\times 10^{-11} = 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$ ($\approx 8.9\ \text{MW}\cdot\text{h}$).

examples.result: $E \approx 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$.

keyTakeaways: Oklo's deficit of ²³⁵U plus fission-product isotope ratios reveal natural reactors that ran ~2×10⁹ years ago.
Differential decay (7.04×10⁸ y versus 4.47×10⁹ y half-lives) put natural uranium at ~3.7% ²³⁵U back then.
Groundwater moderation with boiling feedback self-regulated the zones — the same negative feedback engineered into modern cores.

quiz.q: The first clue pointing to the Oklo natural reactor was
options: uranium ore deficient in ²³⁵U relative to normal natural uranium
quiz.explanation: Some samples held as little as 0.44% 235U versus 0.72% normal — as if part of the fissile inventory had been consumed by fission.

quiz.q: Two billion years ago natural uranium could sustain a chain reaction because
options: the strong force was stronger then
the ²³⁵U fraction (~3.7%) was high enough for water-moderated criticality
there was no water on Earth
quiz.explanation: The shorter half-life of 235U means its relative abundance was far higher in the past, reaching modern-enrichment levels.

quiz.q: At Oklo the reaction was regulated mainly by
options: groundwater boiling away, which removed the moderator
quiz.explanation: Water provided moderation; power output boiled it off; loss of moderation throttled the chain — a natural negative-feedback loop.

quiz.q: The half-lives of ²³⁵U and ²³⁸U are respectively about
quiz.explanation: 235U decays about six times faster; that differential is what enriched ancient ore.

intro: Fusion is the opposite strategy from fission: instead of splitting heavy nuclei down the energy hill, you push light nuclei up the steep left slope of the binding-energy curve. The obstacle is electric — every nucleus repels every other — and the rewards are a hundred times the energy per kilogram of fission, with fuel from seawater and no long-lived ashes. The barrier is beaten by heat and by quantum tunneling: thermonuclear fusion.
objectives: Estimate the Coulomb barrier between light nuclei and compare it with thermal energies
Explain how tunneling and the Maxwell tail make fusion possible at achievable temperatures
Compute the Q value of the deuterium-tritium reaction and compare yields per unit mass with fission

concepts.statement: Two nuclei of charges $Z_1e$ and $Z_2e$, treated as spheres of radius $1.2A^{1/3}$ fm touching, confront a potential hill $$U = \frac{kZ_1Z_2e^2}{r_1 + r_2}.$$ For deuterium on tritium ($R_D + R_T \approx 3.3$ fm) this is about $0.44\ \mathrm{MeV}$; for proton on proton, $0.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$ — yet the gas must be hot enough only that a small fraction of collisions tunnel through.
concepts.detail: At $T = 10^{8}\ \mathrm{K}$, $k_BT$ is only 8.6 keV — fifty times below the D-T barrier. Classically no fusion could occur; the whole subject rests on the Gamow tail of the Maxwell distribution and on barrier penetration.

concepts.statement: A plasma hot and dense enough to fuse must be ionized (no electron shells to cheat the barrier), confined against its own pressure, and kept from its container. The temperature must supply a Maxwell tail of sufficiently energetic ions, and the tunneling probability through the barrier converts the rare fastest collisions into fusion events.
concepts.detail: The reaction rate is the product of two exponentials — a falling Maxwell factor and a rising tunneling factor — whose competition defines the optimal operating temperature for any fuel pair; for D-T that optimum is near $10^{8}\ \mathrm{K}$.

concepts.term: Why D-T is the fuel of first choice
concepts.statement: The reaction $$^{2}\mathrm{H} + {}^{3}\mathrm{H} \to {}^{4}\mathrm{He} + n + 17.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$$ has the largest reactivity at the lowest temperature of any fusion pair: it releases $3.5\ \mathrm{MeV/nucleon}$ — four times fission's yield per nucleon — with deuterium free in the oceans and tritium bred from lithium blankets.
concepts.detail: Deuterium-deuterium fusion (Q ≈ 3–4 MeV per branch) is cleaner and its fuel is inexhaustible, but its cross section peaks at impractibly high temperature — the engineering decision that shaped every controlled-fusion program.

concepts.term: Thermonuclear Fusion: The Basic Process: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Thermonuclear Fusion: The Basic Process problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is fission $Q \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$ and the $p$-$p$ chain $26.7\ \text{MeV}$ per He; the working equation is $Q_{\text{fission}} \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$, $4p\to {}^{4}\!He+2e^++2\nu_e+26.7\ \text{MeV}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{MeV}$ and $\text{MW}\cdot\text{day}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission; $k = 1$ critical; Coulomb barrier needs $10^7\ \text{K}$.

concepts.term: Thermonuclear Fusion: The Basic Process: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Thermonuclear Fusion: The Basic Process lives at $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission and the textbook model holds while $k = 1$ critical; Coulomb barrier needs $10^7\ \text{K}$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Thermonuclear Fusion: The Basic Process calculation gives seconds when $\text{MeV}$ and $\text{MW}\cdot\text{day}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: Barrier and payoff for D-T fusion
examples.problem: Estimate the Coulomb barrier for deuterium-tritium contact, the thermal energy at $10^{8}\ \mathrm{K}$, and the Q value from the masses ($m_D = 2.014102$ u, $m_T = 3.016049$ u, $m_\alpha = 4.002603$ u, $m_n = 1.008665$ u).

steps.label: Height
steps.text: $U = ke^2/r = 1.44\ \mathrm{MeV\cdot fm}/3.24\ \mathrm{fm} = 0.44\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

steps.label: Thermal scale
steps.text: $k_BT = (8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K})(10^{8}\ \mathrm{K}) = 8.6\ \mathrm{keV}$ — 50 times too small classically; tunneling bridges the gap.

examples.result: A 0.44 MeV barrier, 8.6 keV thermal ions, and 17.6 MeV released per reaction — 3.5 MeV per nucleon, four times fission's yield per nucleon.

examples.title: Thermonuclear Fusion: The Basic Process: fission-energy check
examples.problem: One mole-equivalent ($10^{24}$ fissions) each releases $200\ \text{MeV}$. How much energy is that?

steps.label: Total
steps.text: $10^{24}\times 3.20\times 10^{-11} = 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$ ($\approx 8.9\ \text{MW}\cdot\text{h}$).

examples.result: $E \approx 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$.

keyTakeaways: Fusion energy comes from climbing the steep left side of the binding-energy curve, where light nuclei bind progressively tighter.
The Coulomb barrier (~0.4–0.7 MeV at contact) dwarfs thermal energies at 10⁸ K; fusion proceeds through quantum tunneling of the Maxwell-tail ions.
D-T is the easiest pair: Q = 17.6 MeV, 3.5 MeV per nucleon, with deuterium from water and tritium bred from lithium.

quiz.q: The Coulomb barrier between two fusing nuclei is due to
options: electrostatic repulsion of the positive charges
quiz.explanation: Both nuclei are positively charged; only their mutual e²/r repulsion stands between them and the strong force's binding range.

quiz.q: At T = 10⁸ K, $k_BT$ is about 8.6 keV while the D-T Coulomb barrier is ~0.44 MeV. Fusion still occurs because
options: quantum tunneling lets the rare fast Maxwell-tail ions penetrate
the nuclei accelerate in the container
quiz.explanation: Thermonuclear fusion lives on the Gamow tail — the convolution of the Maxwell distribution with the tunneling probability.

quiz.q: The D-T reaction releases 17.6 MeV. Per nucleon involved (5 nucleons), that is
options: 3.5 MeV — about four times fission's yield per nucleon
quiz.explanation: 17.6/5 = 3.5 MeV per nucleon versus ~0.85 MeV/nucleon for fission — the light end of the binding curve is steeper.

quiz.q: A plasma temperature of order 10⁸ K is needed mainly to
options: ionize the fuel and give the Maxwell tail enough fast nuclei
quiz.explanation: Fully ionized fuel with a hot enough energy tail makes the tunneling rate appreciable; nothing material survives contact with the plasma, hence the confinement problem.

intro: The Sun pays for its light the hard way: four protons fuse into one helium nucleus through a chain of reactions so reluctant at its slowest step that each proton waits, on average, billions of years. That bottleneck is why the Sun has burned steadily for 4.6 billion years and will burn for five more — and why the photon warming your face began as gamma rays random-walking out of a 15-million-kelvin core.
objectives: Write the three steps of the proton-proton cycle and its net reaction
Explain why the weak-interaction first step throttles the Sun's burn rate
Compute the Sun's luminosity, mass-conversion rate and hydrogen consumption from the solar constant

concepts.statement: In the Sun's core (T ≈ 1.5×10⁷ K) the dominant chain is $$p + p \to {}^{2}\mathrm{H} + e^+ + \nu,\qquad {}^{2}\mathrm{H} + p \to {}^{3}\mathrm{He} + \gamma,\qquad {}^{3}\mathrm{He} + {}^{3}\mathrm{He} \to {}^{4}\mathrm{He} + 2p.$$ Net: four protons become one ⁴He, two positrons and two neutrinos, releasing **26.7 MeV** (after the positrons annihilate).
concepts.detail: Three of the four protons-to-helium conversions require no weak interaction; it is the first step — turning a proton into a neutron via the weak force — that gates the whole chain.

concepts.term: The bottleneck that stabilizes the Sun
concepts.statement: The first step converts a proton into a neutron and must go through the weak interaction, whose W-boson physics makes it staggeringly rare: a given proton in the solar core waits **of order billions of years** for its fusion. Remove that bottleneck and the Sun would flash like a bomb; with it, the Sun burns at 4×10²⁶ W for ten billion years.
concepts.detail: The cycle also explains the solar neutrino flux: every helium nucleus manufactured deep inside releases exactly two electron neutrinos, giving Earth a continuous 6×10¹⁰ neutrinos per cm² per second beam — the Sun's only unfiltered report from its core.

concepts.term: Energy budget and the CNO alternative
concepts.statement: The Sun's 26.7 MeV per helium nucleus comes out mostly as gamma radiation that scatters (random-walks) outward for ~10⁵ years before reaching the photosphere; about 2% escapes promptly as neutrinos. In stars a few times heavier than the Sun, the carbon-nitrogen-oxygen cycle catalyzes the same net conversion and dominates the luminosity.
concepts.detail: Every step of both cycles climbs the binding-energy curve: ⁴He is bound at 7.07 MeV/nucleon against zero for free protons, and 0.7% of the fused mass converts to energy.

concepts.term: Thermonuclear Fusion in the Sun and Other Stars: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Thermonuclear Fusion in the Sun and Other Stars problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is fission $Q \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$ and the $p$-$p$ chain $26.7\ \text{MeV}$ per He; the working equation is $Q_{\text{fission}} \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$, $4p\to {}^{4}\!He+2e^++2\nu_e+26.7\ \text{MeV}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{MeV}$ and $\text{MW}\cdot\text{day}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission; $k = 1$ critical; Coulomb barrier needs $10^7\ \text{K}$.

concepts.term: Thermonuclear Fusion in the Sun and Other Stars: scales and validity
concepts.statement: **Thermonuclear Fusion in the Sun and Other Stars lives at $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission and the textbook model holds while $k = 1$ critical; Coulomb barrier needs $10^7\ \text{K}$.** Outside that window the formulas above need their next-order corrections, but inside it they predict numbers to the significant figures you carry.
concepts.detail: Use this as a plausibility filter: if a Thermonuclear Fusion in the Sun and Other Stars calculation gives seconds when $\text{MeV}$ and $\text{MW}\cdot\text{day}$ demands meters, or a value orders of magnitude beyond $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission, recheck the setup before trusting the arithmetic.

examples.title: The Sun's fuel bill
examples.problem: The solar constant at Earth is 1.36 kW/m² at a distance of 1.496×10¹¹ m. Find the Sun's luminosity, its rate of mass loss, and its rate of hydrogen consumption.

steps.label: Mass loss
steps.text: $\dot m = L/c^2 = 3.8\times10^{26}/(9.0\times10^{16}) = 4.3\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg/s}$ — four million tonnes of pure energy per second.

steps.label: Protons fused
steps.text: Each helium requires 4 protons and releases 26.7 MeV: $\dot N_{He} = L/(26.7 \times 1.602\times10^{-13}) = 8.9\times10^{37}\ \mathrm{/s}$, so protons fuse at $3.6\times10^{38}\ \mathrm{/s}$.

steps.label: Hydrogen consumed
steps.text: $\dot m_H = (3.6\times10^{38})(1.67\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}) = 6.0\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{kg/s}$ — with 0.7% of it converting to energy, consistent with $\dot m$ above.

examples.result: L = 3.8×10²⁶ W, mass vanishing at 4.3×10⁹ kg/s, hydrogen consumed at 6×10¹¹ kg/s — about 600 million tonnes per second, for billions of years.

examples.title: Thermonuclear Fusion in the Sun and Other Stars: fission-energy check
examples.problem: One mole-equivalent ($10^{24}$ fissions) each releases $200\ \text{MeV}$. How much energy is that?

steps.label: Total
steps.text: $10^{24}\times 3.20\times 10^{-11} = 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$ ($\approx 8.9\ \text{MW}\cdot\text{h}$).

examples.result: $E \approx 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$.

keyTakeaways: The p-p chain nets 4p → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν + 26.7 MeV; the deuterium-forming first step is weak and is the bottleneck.
That billion-year bottleneck is the Sun's stability: weak physics, not fuel supply, sets its lifetime.
L = 3.8×10²⁶ W means 4.3×10⁹ kg/s of mass converted and 6×10¹¹ kg/s of hydrogen fused.

quiz.q: The net result of the proton-proton cycle is
options: 4 protons → 1 alpha particle + 2 positrons + 2 neutrinos + 26.7 MeV
quiz.explanation: Six starting protons appear in the three steps but two come back out: the ledger closes at four in, one helium out, plus positrons and neutrinos.

quiz.q: The slowest step of the p-p cycle is slow because it
options: requires converting a proton into a neutron through the weak interaction
quiz.explanation: p + p → deuterium + positron + neutrino is a weak flavor change; the billions-of-years wait per proton is the Sun's throttle.

quiz.q: In each helium nucleus produced, the fraction of fused mass converted to energy is about
quiz.explanation: 26.7 MeV versus the ~3750 MeV mass of four protons is 0.71% — E = mc² with m a small sliver.

quiz.q: In stars heavier than the Sun, the dominant hydrogen-burning mechanism is
quiz.explanation: The CNO cycle uses carbon as a catalyst for the same net 4p → He conversion and overtakes the p-p chain in hotter cores.

intro: A fusion plasma at 10⁸ K touches nothing and holds nothing: any wall quenches it instantly. Humanity's answer is to fight geometry with physics — magnetic fields weave the charged plasma into doughnut-shaped cages, while laser beams squeeze peppercorn-sized fuel pellets with the intensity of a stellar interior. Both roads must clear the same hurdle: the Lawson criterion, the triple product of density, temperature and confinement time.
objectives: State the Lawson criterion and the parameter regime required for D-T ignition
Explain magnetic confinement in a tokamak, including the roles of toroidal and poloidal fields
Describe inertial confinement and the status of major experiments toward net energy gain

concepts.statement: A burning plasma must confine hot, dense fuel long enough that fusion energy outpaces the energy spent heating it: for D-T at about $2\times10^{8}$ K the requirement is roughly $$n\tau \gtrsim 10^{20}\ \mathrm{s/m^3}$$ — particle density times energy confinement time — with the fuel temperature simultaneously maintained.
concepts.detail: For example, a tokamak plasma at $n = 1\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ (a hundred-thousandth of air density) must hold its heat for about one second; laser fusion instead trades enormous density ($\sim10^{31}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$) for nanosecond confinement.

concepts.statement: Charged particles spiral about magnetic field lines, so a toroidal (doughnut) field can bottle a plasma. Pure toroidal fields drift the particles apart, so a transformer-driven plasma current adds a **poloidal** component — the field lines wind helically around the torus and the plasma stirs itself into stability. Coils, cryogenics and radio-frequency heating complete the machine.
concepts.detail: JET (1997) reached 16 MW of fusion power for 24 MW of heating (gain 0.67) with D-T; ITER, under construction, is designed for Q = 10 — 500 MW out from 50 MW in — the first physics demonstration that a burning plasma can power itself.

concepts.statement: Fire a synchronized fleet of the world's most energetic lasers at a millimeter-scale D-T pellet from all directions: the outer layer ablates, and by rocket-reaction the fuel implodes to stellar densities, fusing before it can fly apart (confinement by inertia alone, ~10⁻¹¹ s). The National Ignition Facility in 2022 achieved the first target gain exceeding unity: 2.05 MJ of laser light in, 3.15 MJ of fusion energy out.
concepts.detail: The NIF result — net gain relative to the laser energy delivered to the target — postdates this textbook's printing and updates it: ignition physics is proven; the wall-plug efficiency of the drivers remains the engineering frontier.

concepts.statement: A power plant needs more than a burning plasma: it must breed its tritium from lithium blankets, extract heat at reactor-grade fluxes, survive neutron bombardment for years, and do it cheaply. These engineering walls, rather than the Lawson criterion, now pace the field — materials that can take the neutron load are the unsolved item on the critical path.
concepts.detail: A 1 GW fusion plant would burn roughly 100 kg of deuterium and a few hundred kilograms of tritium (bred on site) per year — against the 4 million tonnes of coal a coal plant of that size moves annually.

concepts.statement: **Solve Controlled Thermonuclear Fusion problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is fission $Q \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$ and the $p$-$p$ chain $26.7\ \text{MeV}$ per He; the working equation is $Q_{\text{fission}} \approx 200\ \text{MeV}$, $4p\to {}^{4}\!He+2e^++2\nu_e+26.7\ \text{MeV}$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit ($\text{MeV}$ and $\text{MW}\cdot\text{day}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $200\ \text{MeV} \approx 3.2\times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}$ per fission; $k = 1$ critical; Coulomb barrier needs $10^7\ \text{K}$.

examples.title: Energy in one inertial-fusion pellet
examples.problem: A laser-fusion target contains 1.0 mg of D-T fuel (equal numbers of deuterium and tritium atoms). If 30% of it burns, how much energy is released?

steps.label: Reaction pairs
steps.text: Each pair (one D + one T) has mass $5(1.66\times10^{-27}) = 8.3\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$: $N = 1.0\times10^{-6}/8.3\times10^{-27} = 1.2\times10^{20}$ pairs.

steps.label: Energy per pair
steps.text: $17.6\ \mathrm{MeV} = 2.82\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J}$.

steps.label: At 30% burn
steps.text: $E \approx 1.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{J}$ per shot — the energy of about 24 kg of TNT, from a speck of fuel.

examples.result: About $10^{8}$ J per pellet at 30% burn: a power plant would need ~10 shots per second to reach gigawatt scale.

examples.title: Controlled Thermonuclear Fusion: fission-energy check
examples.problem: One mole-equivalent ($10^{24}$ fissions) each releases $200\ \text{MeV}$. How much energy is that?

steps.label: Total
steps.text: $10^{24}\times 3.20\times 10^{-11} = 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$ ($\approx 8.9\ \text{MW}\cdot\text{h}$).

examples.result: $E \approx 3.20\times 10^{+13}\ \text{J}$.

keyTakeaways: Ignition demands the Lawson triple product: $n\tau \gtrsim 10^{20}\ \mathrm{s/m^3}$ at ~2×10⁸ K for D-T.
Tokamaks confine the plasma with helical (toroidal + poloidal) magnetic fields; ITER targets Q = 10.
Inertial confinement compresses pellets to stellar densities for nanoseconds; NIF achieved target gain > 1 in 2022 (2.05 MJ in, 3.15 MJ out).

quiz.q: The Lawson criterion governs which combination of quantities for a fusion plasma?
options: density times confinement time (at adequate temperature)
quiz.explanation: n τ ≥ ~10²⁰ s/m³ for D-T: enough particles, held long enough, hot enough — the triple barrier to ignition.

quiz.q: In a tokamak the poloidal field component exists to
options: counter particle drift so field lines wind helically and confine stably
quiz.explanation: A purely toroidal field lets charges drift to the walls; the induced plasma current's poloidal field twists the lines into stable helices.

quiz.q: Inertial confinement works by
options: holding the plasma in a magnetic bottle for seconds
imploding the fuel so fast it fuses before it can fly apart
using heavy nuclei instead of hydrogen
quiz.explanation: Ablation-driven implosion reaches enormous density; confinement time is the pellet's own disassembly time, ~10⁻¹¹ s.

quiz.q: The 2022 NIF ignition result was significant because
options: fusion energy out (3.15 MJ) exceeded the laser energy delivered to the target (2.05 MJ)
it sustained a plasma for a full day
quiz.explanation: First target gain above unity in the laboratory — proof of ignition physics, though the lasers' wall-plug energy remains far larger.

intro: Faced with hundreds of 'elementary' particles pouring out of accelerators in the 1950s, physicists learned to classify before they could explain. Particles sort by spin, by mass family, by the interactions they feel, and by the conserved charges they carry; antiparticles shadow every one of them. The taxonomy built here is the periodic table of the subnuclear world, and its rows and columns encode the fundamental forces.
objectives: Define antiparticles and describe annihilation and pair production with energy thresholds
Compare the four basic interactions by strength, range and messenger particle
Apply the conservation laws — energy, momentum, angular momentum, charge, baryon and lepton number — to test whether reactions can occur

concepts.statement: Every particle has an **antiparticle** with identical mass and spin but opposite charge (and opposite values of other additive quantum numbers): the positron $e^+$ for the electron, the antiproton for the proton. Particle and antiparticle can annihilate into photons, and a sufficiently energetic photon can create a pair — the threshold being twice the particle mass: $2m_ec^2 = 1.022\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for $e^-e^+$, $2 \times 938.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for $p\bar p$.
concepts.detail: Pair production requires a nearby nucleus to absorb recoil momentum; a lone photon in vacuum cannot conserve both energy and momentum while materializing two particles. Anderson found the positron in cosmic rays in 1932, two years after Dirac's theory demanded it.

concepts.statement: Particle physics recognizes four interactions, each characterized by a messenger: the **strong** (range ~10⁻¹⁵ m, the strongest, binds nuclei), the **electromagnetic** (infinite range, ~10⁻² of the strong, binds atoms), the **weak** (range ~10⁻¹⁸ m, ~10⁻⁵, beta decays and neutrinos) and **gravitation** (infinite range, ~10⁻³⁸ of the strong — irrelevant in particle physics but sovereign over the cosmos).
concepts.detail: A particle participates only in the interactions that couple to its conserved charges: neutrinos feel only the weak force (and gravity), which is why a neutrino can cross light-years of lead; electrons feel electromagnetic and weak but not the strong.

concepts.statement: Any reaction must conserve **energy, momentum, angular momentum, net charge, baryon number and (family-by-family) lepton number**. Interactions differ in what else they conserve: the strong and electromagnetic also conserve strangeness, the weak does not — a hierarchy that predicts which decays are fast (allowed), slow (weak-suppressed) or forbidden outright.
concepts.detail: The proton, being the lightest baryon, cannot decay without violating baryon number conservation — hence its observed lifetime beyond 10³⁴ years, the sharpest constraint on speculative theories.

concepts.term: Fermions and bosons, leptons and hadrons
concepts.statement: Particles of half-integer spin are **fermions** (obeying the exclusion principle); integer-spin particles are **bosons**. By composition: **leptons** (electron, muon, tau and their neutrinos) feel no strong force; **hadrons** feel it and split into **mesons** (quark-antiquark pairs, bosons, e.g. pions) and **baryons** (three quarks, fermions, e.g. protons and neutrons).
concepts.detail: Soaring above both classes sit the **messenger bosons** of Section 44-3 — the photon, the gluons and the W and Z. Very short-lived excited states called resonances live only ~10⁻²³ s, long enough to leave tracks in scattering data but not in detectors.

concepts.term: General Properties of Elementary Particles: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve General Properties of Elementary Particles problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is the Standard Model taxonomy and Hubble expansion; the working equation is $v = Hr$, $H_0 \approx 70\ \text{km/s}\cdot\text{Mpc}$, $E = mc^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (megaparsecs and $\text{GeV}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $H_0^{-1}\sim 14\ \text{Gyr}$; CMB $2.7\ \text{K}$; Standard Model tested to $10^{-12}\ \text{s}$; $v = Hr$ for $z\ll 1$.

examples.title: Pair-production bookkeeping
examples.problem: A 2.00 MeV photon passes a nucleus and converts to an electron-positron pair. How much kinetic energy is shared, and could the same photon instead produce a proton-antiproton pair?

steps.label: Threshold
steps.text: Rest energy needed: $2m_ec^2 = 2(0.511) = 1.022\ \mathrm{MeV}$ (the nucleus absorbs negligible recoil energy).

steps.label: Remainder
steps.text: Kinetic energy for the pair plus recoil: $2.00 - 1.022 = 0.978\ \mathrm{MeV}$, shared between the two particles and (slightly) the nucleus.

steps.label: Proton threshold
steps.text: Producing $p\bar p$ requires $2(938.3) = 1877\ \mathrm{MeV}$ — a gamma ray nearly a thousand times more energetic than this one.

steps.label: Conservation check
steps.text: Charge: photon 0 → e⁻(−1) + e⁺(+1) = 0 ✓; lepton number: 0 → (+1) + (−1) = 0 ✓ — the process is allowed.

examples.result: 0.978 MeV of kinetic energy is released to the pair; a 2 MeV photon is far too feeble to make a proton-antiproton pair.

examples.title: General Properties of Elementary Particles: Hubble check
examples.problem: A galaxy is $100\ \text{Mpc}$ away. With $H_0 \approx 70\ \text{km/s}\cdot\text{Mpc}$, estimate $v = H_0d$.

steps.label: Fraction of $c$
steps.text: $7000/299792 \approx 0.0233c$ — nonrelativistic, so $v = Hd$ holds.

examples.result: $v \approx 7000\ \text{km/s}$.

keyTakeaways: Every particle has an antiparticle; annihilation and pair production respect all conservation laws, with thresholds set by rest masses.
The four interactions rank strong > electromagnetic > weak >> gravity, each with its own range and messenger boson.
Conservation of charge, baryon number and family lepton numbers filters allowed from forbidden reactions — strangeness adds a further test.

quiz.q: The minimum photon energy for electron-positron pair production is
quiz.explanation: Twice the electron rest energy: 2 × 0.511 MeV = 1.022 MeV, supplied near a nucleus for momentum conservation.

quiz.q: Which particle feels ONLY the weak interaction (plus gravity)?
quiz.explanation: Neutrinos carry no electric or color charge — their light-year mean free path in lead is the weakness of the weak interaction made vivid.

quiz.q: Hadrons are the particles that
options: feel the strong force and are made of quarks
quiz.explanation: Hadrons (mesons = quark-antiquark, baryons = three quarks) participate in the strong interaction; leptons do not.

quiz.q: The proton is stable (lifetime > 10³⁴ y) because
options: it is too heavy to decay
it is the lightest baryon, and baryon number conservation forbids any decay channel
no interaction can act on it
quiz.explanation: Decays must go to lighter particles; every lighter final state carries baryon number 0, so a single proton (B = 1) has nowhere to go.

intro: The leptons form a clean set of six, but the hadrons multiplied into a zoo — until strangeness gave the zoo a taxonomy. Assigning quantum numbers to production and decay patterns revealed that hadrons were not elementary at all: their properties pointed inside, to constituents with fractional charge waiting to be named quarks.
objectives: List the six leptons and their neutrinos and apply conservation of the three lepton-family numbers
Distinguish mesons from baryons by quark content and baryon number
Use strangeness conservation to predict which production and decay processes are fast or slow

concepts.statement: The lepton family contains three charged particles — the electron (0.511 MeV/c²), the muon (105.7 MeV/c²) and the tau (1777 MeV/c²) — each paired with its own neutrino. Each family carries a conserved **lepton number** ($L_e$, $L_\mu$, $L_\tau$): particles and neutrinos carry +1, antiparticles and antineutrinos −1.
concepts.detail: Neutrino oscillations (confirmed from atmospheric and solar data — the 2015 Nobel Prize) show neutrinos have tiny, nonzero masses, but below ~1 eV/c²; for all reaction bookkeeping they remain effectively massless.

concepts.statement: Every allowed reaction conserves each family's lepton number separately. Muon decay, $$\mu^- \to e^- + \bar\nu_e + \nu_\mu,$$ checks: $L_\mu$: 1 → 0 + 0 + 1 ✓; $L_e$: 0 → 1 + (−1) + 0 ✓. The observed absence of $\mu^- \to e^- + \gamma$ — the cleanest forbidden decay — is exactly this rule in action.
concepts.detail: Neutrino oscillations do violate individual family numbers in flight (transforming $\nu_e$ into $\nu_\mu$), but total lepton number appears to remain conserved — an open chapter of the field.

concepts.statement: Hadrons split by composition: **mesons** are quark-antiquark pairs ($\pi$, K, ρ, φ…) with baryon number B = 0 and integer spin; **baryons** are three-quark states (p, n, Λ, Σ, Ξ, Ω …) with B = +1 and half-integer spin. Antibaryons ($\bar p$, $\bar \Lambda$…) carry B = −1.
concepts.detail: Baryon number conservation means hadrons can be created and destroyed only in baryon-antibaryon-balanced processes: a proton-proton collision can yield extra pions freely, but extra protons only alongside antiprotons.

concepts.statement: Certain hadrons (the 'strange' ones) are produced copiously in pairs by the strong interaction yet decay only slowly — as if produced easily and destroyed reluctantly. The answer is a new quantum number S, carried by the strange quark ($s$: S = −1; strange antiquarks: S = +1): **strong and electromagnetic interactions conserve S; the weak interaction can change S by 0 or ±1** in a decay.
concepts.detail: The Λ⁰ (uds, S = −1) is born alongside a K (which carries S = +1) in associated production, conserving strangeness; it then decays slowly (weakly) to $p\pi^-$ with ΔS = +1, living 10⁻¹⁰ s instead of the 10⁻²³ s a strong decay would take.

concepts.term: Leptons, Hadrons, and Strangeness: solution protocol
concepts.statement: **Solve Leptons, Hadrons, and Strangeness problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is the Standard Model taxonomy and Hubble expansion; the working equation is $v = Hr$, $H_0 \approx 70\ \text{km/s}\cdot\text{Mpc}$, $E = mc^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (megaparsecs and $\text{GeV}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $H_0^{-1}\sim 14\ \text{Gyr}$; CMB $2.7\ \text{K}$; Standard Model tested to $10^{-12}\ \text{s}$; $v = Hr$ for $z\ll 1$.

examples.title: Strangeness bookkeeping
examples.problem: Test whether these processes are allowed, and if so, at which interaction's speed: (a) $\Lambda^0 \to p + \pi^-$; (b) $\pi^- + p \to K^0 + \Lambda^0$; (c) $\Lambda^0 \to p + \pi^- + \pi^0$ with strong (strangeness-conserving) dynamics.

steps.label: Part (a)
steps.text: Λ⁰(uds) has S = −1; p and π each have S = 0: ΔS = +1. Strangeness is violated, so only the weak interaction can do it — a slow (10⁻¹⁰ s) decay.

steps.label: Part (b)
steps.text: Initial S: π(0) + p(0) = 0. Final: K⁰(d s̄) carries S = +1, Λ⁰ carries S = −1: total 0. S is conserved, so the strong interaction produces this pair copiously — associated production.

steps.label: Part (c)
steps.text: The same ΔS = +1 as (a): no added pion rescues strangeness. This is again a weak process; three-body weak decays are further suppressed by phase space.

steps.label: Also check
steps.text: Charge and baryon number balance in all three (1 → 1 + 0; −1+1 → 0+0; 0 → 1−1+0) ✓ — the strangeness test is what decides the rate.

examples.result: (a) and (c) are allowed but weak-slow; (b) is strong-fast — the very pattern of copious pair production followed by reluctant decay that defined strangeness.

examples.title: Leptons, Hadrons, and Strangeness: Hubble check
examples.problem: A galaxy is $200\ \text{Mpc}$ away. With $H_0 \approx 70\ \text{km/s}\cdot\text{Mpc}$, estimate $v = H_0d$.

steps.label: Fraction of $c$
steps.text: $14000/299792 \approx 0.0467c$ — nonrelativistic, so $v = Hd$ holds.

examples.result: $v \approx 14000\ \text{km/s}$.

keyTakeaways: Six leptons in three families; each family's lepton number is separately conserved in all reactions.
Mesons are quark-antiquark (B = 0); baryons are three-quark states (B = 1) — baryon number conservation forbids proton decay.
Strangeness is conserved by the strong and electromagnetic interactions and changes by ±1 in weak decays, explaining pair production followed by slow individual decay.

quiz.q: The decay μ⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄e + νμ is allowed, while μ⁻ → e⁻ + γ is never seen. The deciding rule is
options: separate conservation of electron and muon lepton numbers
quiz.explanation: The first decay balances $L_e$ and $L_\mu$; the second has $L_\mu$ going from 1 to 0 with no muon-family partner, and $L_e$ from 0 to 1 — doubly forbidden.

quiz.q: A meson is a hadron made of
quiz.explanation: Mesons like the pion and kaon are quark-antiquark pairs with baryon number zero and integer spin.

quiz.q: Strangeness is conserved in
options: strong and electromagnetic interactions but not weak
quiz.explanation: Strange particles are produced in pairs by the strong force (S conserved) but decay individually through the weak force, which may change S by 0 or ±1.

quiz.q: The Λ⁰ (uds, S = −1) decays to p + π⁻ in about 10⁻¹⁰ s rather than 10⁻²³ s because
options: the decay changes strangeness, so it must proceed by the weak interaction
quiz.explanation: Delta S = +1 routes the decay through the weak interaction, slowing it by ~13 orders of magnitude relative to strong timescales.

intro: Every hadron ever measured — hundreds of them — is accounted for by six quarks and their antiquarks, bound by gluons. Three generations, two quarks each, charges +2/3 and −1/3: that is the whole cast of matter, and with the leptons beside them and the four messengers carrying their forces, the Standard Model table is complete down to the last measured particle.
objectives: List the six quarks with their charges, and build hadron charges from quark content
Explain color charge, gluons, confinement and asymptotic freedom
Identify the messenger particles of the four interactions and the place of the Higgs boson in the Standard Model

concepts.statement: Quarks come in six **flavors** in three generations: up $u$ and down $d$ (ordinary matter), strange $s$ and charmed $c$, bottom $b$ and top $t$. Their charges are fractional — $u, c, t$ carry $+\tfrac{2}{3}e$ and $d, s, b$ carry $-\tfrac{1}{3}e$ — and every hadron's charge is just the sum of its constituents: the proton $uud$ has $+\tfrac{2}{3}+\tfrac{2}{3}-\tfrac{1}{3} = +1$; the neutron $udd$ totals 0; $\pi^+ = u\bar d$ carries +1.
concepts.detail: Current masses run from ~2.2 MeV/c² (up) to 173 GeV/c² (top, the heaviest known elementary particle, discovered 1995). Free quarks have never been isolated — quark charges have been confirmed by superconducting-magnetic levitation experiments on oil drops, of all things.

concepts.statement: Quarks carry a strong charge called **color** (three varieties, conventionally red, green, blue) that must combine to white in any observable hadron: three quarks of different colors (baryons) or quark-antiquark color pairs (mesons). The messenger gluons themselves carry color, so the force does not die with distance — pulling quarks apart creates new quark-antiquark pairs instead: **confinement**.
concepts.detail: At short range the opposite happens — **asymptotic freedom**: the color force weakens at high momentum transfer, so deep-scattering experiments see nearly free quarks inside the proton (Gross, Politzer and Wilczek, Nobel 2004).

concepts.statement: Each interaction is carried by its own boson: the **photon** (massless, infinite range) for electromagnetism; **eight gluons** (massless but self-interacting, confined to ~10⁻¹⁵ m) for the strong force; the **W⁺, W⁻ and Z⁰** (massive, 80.4 and 91.2 GeV/c², range ~10⁻¹⁸ m) for the weak force — their mass is what makes the weak force weak. Gravity's hypothetical messenger is the spin-2 **graviton**, not yet observed.
concepts.detail: Messenger particles can be virtual — energy borrowed within the Heisenberg allowance $\Delta E\,\Delta t \sim \hbar$ — which is how forces reach beyond contact and how the weak force's massive messengers enforce its short range.

concepts.statement: Six quarks, six leptons and the messenger bosons (plus the 2012 Higgs boson, 125 GeV/c², whose field gives particles their masses) constitute the **Standard Model** — tested by collider data to extraordinary precision, and silent on gravity, dark matter and neutrino masses. Every prediction of the model that experiments have been able to check has held.
concepts.detail: The Higgs discovery at CERN in 2012 (Nobel 2013) closed the model's open slot; what lies beyond — supersymmetry, string theory, or something unguessed — is the open frontier.

Everything ever observed is built from generation I; generations II and III appear only in high-energy processes and decay back within fractions of a second. Every matter particle also has an antiparticle. Quark masses are 'current' values and are scheme-dependent; neutrino masses are known only to be tiny (below ~1 eV/c²).
