examples.title: Charges from quark content
examples.problem: Predict the charges of (a) the proton, (b) the π⁺ meson, (c) the Ω⁻ baryon, and (d) a hypothetical p p̄ bound state.

steps.label: Pion plus
steps.text: $\pi^+ = u\bar d$: $\tfrac{2}{3}+\tfrac{1}{3} = +1$ ✓ (the anti-down quark, $\bar d$, carries $+\tfrac{1}{3}$).

steps.label: Omega minus
steps.text: $\Omega^- = sss$: three strange quarks at $-\tfrac{1}{3}$ each gives $-1$ — predicted in 1961 by the quark model and found in 1964 with exactly that charge.

steps.label: Protonium
steps.text: $p\bar p$ totals $+1 + (-1) = 0$: an electrically neutral meson-like exotic, which indeed decays promptly into pions.

examples.result: Quark bookkeeping reproduces every hadron charge ever measured — fractional constituents adding to integer (or zero) totals is the model's most austere triumph.

examples.title: Quarks and Messenger Particles: Hubble check
examples.problem: A galaxy is $300\ \text{Mpc}$ away. With $H_0 \approx 70\ \text{km/s}\cdot\text{Mpc}$, estimate $v = H_0d$.

steps.label: Fraction of $c$
steps.text: $21000/299792 \approx 0.07c$ — nonrelativistic, so $v = Hd$ holds.

examples.result: $v \approx 21000\ \text{km/s}$.

keyTakeaways: Six quarks in three generations with charges +2/3 and −1/3; hadron charges (p = uud, n = udd, π⁺ = ud̄) follow by simple addition.
Color charge must combine to white; gluons carry color, giving confinement at long range and asymptotic freedom at short range.
Messengers: photon (EM), eight gluons (strong), W± and Z⁰ (weak, hence its short range); the Higgs (2012) completes the Standard Model, gravity stays outside.

quiz.q: The charge of the up quark is
quiz.explanation: Up-type quarks (u, c, t) carry +2/3 e; down-type (d, s, b) carry −1/3 e — fractional charges never seen in isolation.

quiz.q: Free isolated quarks have never been observed because
options: the color force strengthens with separation, creating new quark-antiquark pairs instead of letting quarks escape
quiz.explanation: Confinement: the gluon's self-interaction keeps the field string taut; pulling hard enough rips new pairs from the vacuum, yielding hadrons only.

quiz.q: The weak interaction is short-ranged (~10⁻¹⁸ m) because
options: its messenger bosons W and Z are massive (~80–91 GeV/c²), so their virtual exchange is limited by the uncertainty principle
quiz.explanation: Range ~ħ/(mc): heavy messengers can be borrowed only briefly, confining the weak force to subnuclear distances.

quiz.q: The Higgs boson, discovered in 2012, is responsible in the Standard Model for
options: giving fundamental particles their masses through coupling to the Higgs field
quiz.explanation: Coupling to the everywhere-present Higgs field is what we call mass; the boson is that field's quantum, found at 125 GeV/c².

intro: Hubble's 1929 discovery that every galaxy recedes from us at a speed proportional to its distance abolished the static universe overnight. Run the expansion backward and you get a hot, dense beginning — a Big Bang — whose afterglow still fills the sky at 2.7 K, whose nuclear furnace set the cosmic hydrogen-helium ratio, and whose present composition is 95% stuff we cannot see: dark matter and dark energy.
objectives: State Hubble's law and use it to convert recession velocities into distances
Summarize the evidence for the Big Bang: redshifts, the cosmic background radiation, and primordial abundances
Describe the roles of dark matter and dark energy in the universe's composition and acceleration

concepts.statement: Galaxies recede with speeds proportional to their distances: $$v = Hr,\qquad H \approx 71\ \mathrm{km/s/Mpc} = 2.3\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.$$ The redshift of spectral lines, $z = \Delta\lambda/\lambda \approx v/c$ for modest speeds, measures $v$; Hubble's law then yields the distance.
concepts.detail: The inverse of H, about $1.4\times10^{10}$ years, sets the age scale of the universe; more refined cosmology (accounting for the change of H with time) gives 13.8 billion years. Expansion has no center: every galaxy sees the same law, like dots on an inflating balloon.

concepts.statement: The universe was once hot, opaque plasma; expansion cooled it until electrons and nuclei combined and light streamed free — and that first light still arrives from all directions, redshifted by a factor ~1100 to a **2.7 K blackbody spectrum** of microwaves. Predicted in 1948, stumbled upon in 1965 (Penzias and Wilson), and mapped to parts-per-million by satellites (COBE, WMAP, Planck), the CMB is the Big Bang's fossil radiation.
concepts.detail: Its tiny temperature ripples are the density seeds of galaxies — the detailed statistics of those fluctuations, fit by cosmological models, is how the universe's inventory is measured.

concepts.statement: In the first few minutes, while the universe was hot and dense enough for nuclear reactions, about a quarter of all mass was fused from hydrogen into helium-4 — the observed ~3:1 hydrogen-to-helium ratio in stars and gas everywhere matches the calculation from first minutes' physics, an independent confirmation of the hot Big Bang.
concepts.detail: The measured abundances of D, ³He and ⁷Li also date the baryon density: ordinary matter amounts to just under 5% of the universe's energy content.

concepts.statement: Galaxies rotate as if held by far more mass than their light shows (Rubin's rotation curves), and gravitational lensing agrees: about **27% of the universe is dark matter**, interacting only gravitationally. And since 1998, observations of distant Type Ia supernovae show the expansion is **accelerating**, driven by **dark energy** — about **68%** of the total budget, whose physical nature is unknown.
concepts.detail: The full ledger: ~5% ordinary matter, ~27% dark matter, ~68% dark energy. The physics that this book has taught — quarks to galaxies — describes the smallest slice of the cosmic pie, and its boundaries are today's frontiers.

concepts.statement: **Solve Cosmology problems by (1) naming the governing principle, (2) writing its equation, (3) substituting numbers with units.** Here the principle is the Standard Model taxonomy and Hubble expansion; the working equation is $v = Hr$, $H_0 \approx 70\ \text{km/s}\cdot\text{Mpc}$, $E = mc^2$; every substitution must carry its units so the final unit (megaparsecs and $\text{GeV}$) emerges naturally.
concepts.detail: HRW 11e tactic: draw the free-body or field sketch first, list knowns with units, solve symbolically and only then substitute numbers. Check the answer against $H_0^{-1}\sim 14\ \text{Gyr}$; CMB $2.7\ \text{K}$; Standard Model tested to $10^{-12}\ \text{s}$; $v = Hr$ for $z\ll 1$.

examples.title: Distance and lookback time from a redshift
examples.problem: A galaxy's hydrogen spectrum shows a redshift z = 0.15 (Δλ/λ = 0.15). Using H = 71 km/s/Mpc, find its recession speed and distance.

steps.label: Speed
steps.text: $v \approx zc = 0.15(3.00\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{km/s}) = 4.5\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{km/s}$ — 15% of light speed.

steps.label: Distance
steps.text: $d = v/H = (4.5\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{km/s})/(71\ \mathrm{km/s/Mpc}) = 6.3\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{Mpc}$.

steps.label: In light-years
steps.text: $1\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 3.26\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{ly}$: $d = 630 \times 3.26\times10^{6} = 2.1\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{ly}$.

steps.label: Lookback
steps.text: Light left the galaxy ~2 billion years ago — well before complex life existed on Earth; telescopes are time machines by necessity.

examples.result: $v = 4.5\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{km/s}$ and $d \approx 630\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 2.1\times10^{9}$ light-years, a two-billion-year lookback.

examples.title: Cosmology: Hubble check
examples.problem: A galaxy is $100\ \text{Mpc}$ away. With $H_0 \approx 70\ \text{km/s}\cdot\text{Mpc}$, estimate $v = H_0d$.

steps.label: Fraction of $c$
steps.text: $7000/299792 \approx 0.0233c$ — nonrelativistic, so $v = Hd$ holds.

examples.result: $v \approx 7000\ \text{km/s}$.

keyTakeaways: Hubble's law v = Hr with H ≈ 71 km/s/Mpc turns measured redshifts into cosmic distances; 1/H ≈ 1.4×10¹⁰ y sets the age scale.
The 2.7 K cosmic microwave background and the universal 3:1 H:He ratio are the hot Big Bang's surviving fingerprints.
The universe is ~5% ordinary matter, ~27% dark matter, ~68% dark energy — and dark energy is accelerating the expansion.

quiz.q: The cosmic microwave background is
options: the redshifted glow of the hot early universe, released when atoms formed
radiation from the Milky Way's center
quiz.explanation: Recombination at ~380,000 years freed the primordial light; cosmic expansion has since stretched it to a 2.7 K microwave blackbody.

quiz.q: The 3:1 hydrogen-to-helium ratio across the universe was produced
options: in stars over billions of years
in the first minutes of the hot Big Bang
quiz.explanation: Primordial nucleosynthesis fused ~25% of the mass into helium-4 before expansion cooled and shut the reactor; stars process only a few percent more.

quiz.q: The main evidence that the universal expansion is accelerating is
options: the dimness of distant Type Ia supernovae, which are farther away than a decelerating universe would place them
quiz.explanation: 1998's supernova surveys found standard candles too faint — too distant — unless the expansion has sped up; the driver is called dark energy.

quiz.q: Dark matter is inferred primarily from
options: gravitational effects such as galactic rotation curves and lensing exceeding what the visible mass allows
quiz.explanation: It neither emits nor absorbs light; its gravity betrays it — Vera Rubin's flat rotation curves are the classic datum.

intro: Physics is the most basic experimental science: it asks how matter, energy, space, and time behave, from quarks to galaxies. Young opens by showing how observation, idealization, and quantitative testing separate physics from pure mathematics and philosophy.
objectives: Describe what physics studies and how experiment tests theory
Distinguish a physical model and idealization from raw observation
Explain why prediction plus measurement is the standard of truth in physics

concepts.statement: Physics studies **matter, energy, and their interactions in space and time**, and every claim must survive confrontation with measurement.
concepts.detail: A theory that predicts $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ lives or dies by dropping objects and timing them, not by elegance alone.

concepts.statement: Modern physics spans **~$10^{-18}\ \mathrm{m}$ (quarks) to ~$10^{26}\ \mathrm{m}$ (observable universe)**, some 44 orders of magnitude.
concepts.detail: Mechanics in Chapters 1–15 lives in the middle scales, but the same laws of motion and energy apply at the extremes with quantum and relativistic corrections.

concepts.statement: An **idealized model** replaces a real system by a simplified version — point mass, massless string, frictionless surface — that keeps the dominant physics.
concepts.detail: A baseball in flight becomes a particle of mass $m$ in uniform gravity; spin and air drag are restored later as corrections.

concepts.statement: Observation suggests a **model**, mathematics develops its **predictions**, and new **measurements** confirm, refine, or falsify it.
concepts.detail: No amount of derivation proves a law; one reproducible disagreement, such as the precession of Mercury before relativity, forces revision.

concepts.statement: Chapters 1–15 are **classical (Newtonian) mechanics plus fluids, waves, and heat**: accurate when speeds satisfy $v \ll c$ and sizes satisfy $L \gg 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}$.
concepts.detail: Young flags from page one where relativity ($v \to c$) and quantum effects (atomic scales) will later take over.

examples.title: Why a model beats a replica
examples.problem: A $0.145\ \mathrm{kg}$ baseball is thrown at $40\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Should air drag be in the first model?

steps.label: Estimate weight
steps.text: Weight is $mg = 0.145 \times 9.8 = 1.42\ \mathrm{N}$.

steps.label: Estimate drag
steps.text: At $40\ \mathrm{m/s}$ drag on a baseball is roughly $1$–$2\ \mathrm{N}$, comparable to weight.

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: For a rough range estimate drop drag first and solve the projectile problem; for a real trajectory restore it as a correction.

examples.result: First model: particle under gravity only. Refined model: add velocity-dependent drag.

examples.title: Prediction versus measurement
examples.problem: A model predicts a fall time of $1.43\ \mathrm{s}$ from $10.0\ \mathrm{m}$. The measured mean is $1.45\ \mathrm{s}$. Is the model wrong?

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: Difference is $0.02\ \mathrm{s}$, about $1.4$%.

steps.label: Ask about uncertainty
steps.text: If the timer resolves $0.01\ \mathrm{s}$ and air drag adds ~$1$%, the gap is expected, not a falsification.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.text: Agreement within estimated uncertainty corroborates the model; a $20$% gap would demand revision.

examples.result: The model stands; uncertainty analysis (Sec 1.5) decides what counts as agreement.

keyTakeaways: Physics is tested by measurement: models predict, experiments decide.
Start with an idealized model that keeps the dominant effect, then refine.
Classical mechanics rules the middle scales; relativity and quanta bound its edges.

quiz.q: Which best describes the role of an idealized model in Young?
options: An exact replica of the real system
A simplified version keeping the dominant physics, refined later
A purely mathematical theorem with no experiment
quiz.explanation: Point masses and frictionless surfaces deliberately omit secondary effects first, then restore them as corrections.

quiz.q: A theory predicting $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ is validated by:
quiz.explanation: Physics is experimental: prediction must survive measurement within uncertainty.

quiz.q: Classical mechanics of Chapters 1–15 is reliable when:
options: Speeds approach $c$ and atoms are involved
Speeds satisfy $v \ll c$ and sizes are far above atomic scales
quiz.explanation: Young states the Newtonian domain explicitly; relativity and quantum mechanics take over outside it.

intro: Young teaches one transferable procedure for every problem in the book: Identify the physics, Set up with diagrams and variables, Execute the mathematics, and Evaluate the answer. This section makes that strategy explicit so later chapters can invoke it by name.
objectives: Apply the Identify–Set up–Execute–Evaluate strategy to any mechanics problem
Translate words into a labeled sketch with knowns, unknowns, and target
Judge an answer by units, magnitude, and limiting cases

concepts.statement: **IDENTIFY:** read the full statement, list knowns and the target, and name the **principle** (for example $\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}$) before touching algebra.
concepts.detail: Ask what is given, what is asked, and which chapter idea governs it; never hunt for an equation that merely contains the right letters.

concepts.term: SET UP with sketch and variables
concepts.statement: **SET UP:** draw the situation, choose **coordinates and symbols** ($x_0$, $v_{0x}$, $t$), and write the governing equations in symbols.
concepts.detail: A labeled axis fixes every sign; subscripts such as $v_{0x}$ distinguish initial $x$-velocity from the unknown $v_x$.

concepts.statement: **EXECUTE:** solve **algebraically for the target symbol**, then substitute numbers with units in one pass.
concepts.detail: Solving $v_x^2 = v_{0x}^2 + 2a_x\Delta x$ for $\Delta x$ before inserting numbers exposes errors and lets units cancel visibly.

concepts.statement: **EVALUATE:** check **units, sign, magnitude, and limits** — does $120\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for a thrown ball make sense?
concepts.detail: Test extremes: setting $\theta = 0$ or $a = 0$ should recover a known simple case; wrong units always mean wrong physics.

concepts.statement: A quick **order-of-magnitude estimate** ($g \approx 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $1\ \mathrm{m/s} \approx 3.6\ \mathrm{km/h}$) catches factor-of-ten slips.
concepts.detail: If the estimate says seconds and the calculation says hours, recheck powers of ten and unit conversions before trusting the algebra.

examples.title: Strategy on a braking car
examples.problem: A car at $20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ brakes with $a_x = -5.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. How far does it travel before stopping?

steps.label: Identify
steps.text: Constant-acceleration kinematics; knowns $v_{0x} = 20\ \mathrm{m/s}$, $v_x = 0$, $a_x = -5.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$; target $\Delta x$.

steps.label: Set up
steps.text: Choose $+x$ forward; use $v_x^2 = v_{0x}^2 + 2a_x\Delta x$.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.text: Units meters, magnitude tens of meters for highway braking — plausible; $a_x \to 0$ correctly gives $\Delta x \to \infty$.

examples.result: $40\ \mathrm{m}$ of stopping distance, verified by units and limits.

examples.title: Catching a unit error
examples.problem: A student reports a sprinter speed as $36\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. What went wrong?

steps.label: Identify
steps.text: Speed must have units of $\mathrm{m/s}$, not $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

steps.label: Set up
steps.text: Likely confused $v$ with $a$, or divided by time twice.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.text: $36\ \mathrm{m/s}$ is $130\ \mathrm{km/h}$ — impossibly fast for a sprinter — so magnitude also fails.

examples.result: Both units and magnitude reject the answer; the EVALUATE step catches it.

keyTakeaways: Name the principle first; never equation-hunt by matching letters.
Draw, choose coordinates, and solve in symbols before substituting numbers.
Every answer must pass units, sign, magnitude, and limiting-case checks.

quiz.q: In Young's strategy, what belongs in SET UP?
options: Plugging numbers into the first equation seen
Sketch, coordinates, symbols, and governing equations in symbols
quiz.explanation: SET UP fixes geometry and signs before any arithmetic; EVALUATE checks limits afterward.

quiz.q: Why solve symbolically before substituting numbers?
options: Algebra first exposes structure and lets units cancel visibly
quiz.explanation: A symbolic target like $\Delta x = -v_{0x}^2/2a_x$ can be checked by units and limits before arithmetic hides errors.

quiz.q: A calculated jet speed of $3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ should be:
options: Rejected on magnitude — jets fly near $250\ \mathrm{m/s}$
quiz.explanation: EVALUATE demands a magnitude sanity check; $3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ is walking pace, not flight.

intro: Mechanics needs only three base quantities — length, mass, and time — and the SI system fixes their units by physical standards. This section defines the meter, kilogram, and second and shows why dimensional consistency is a non-negotiable test of every equation.
objectives: State the SI base units for length, mass, and time
Explain operational standards from artifacts to atomic definitions
Test equations by dimensional consistency

concepts.statement: A **physical quantity** is a number plus a **unit**: $L = 3.00\ \mathrm{m}$ means three times the standard meter.
concepts.detail: Without the unit the number is meaningless; with it, any observer worldwide reproduces the measurement.

concepts.statement: SI mechanics rests on the **meter ($\mathrm{m}$)** for length, **kilogram ($\mathrm{kg}$)** for mass, and **second ($\mathrm{s}$)** for time.
concepts.detail: All other mechanical units derive from these: $1\ \mathrm{N} = 1\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2}$ and $1\ \mathrm{J} = 1\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}$.

concepts.statement: The **second** is $9{,}192{,}631{,}770$ periods of cesium-133 radiation; the **meter** is the distance light travels in $1/299{,}792{,}458\ \mathrm{s}$; the **kilogram** is fixed by the Planck constant.
concepts.detail: Atomic standards replaced bars and cylinders so any equipped lab realizes the same unit without visiting Paris.

concepts.statement: Every term added or equated must carry **identical dimensions**: $[x] = \mathrm{L}$, $[v] = \mathrm{L/T}$, $[a] = \mathrm{L/T^2}$.
concepts.detail: Thus $x = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ passes ($\mathrm{L} = \mathrm{L} + \mathrm{L}$) while $x = vt^2$ fails and is certainly wrong.

concepts.statement: SI **prefixes** scale by tens: $1\ \mathrm{km} = 10^{3}\ \mathrm{m}$, $1\ \mathrm{mm} = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$, $1\ \mathrm{\mu m} = 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$, $1\ \mathrm{nm} = 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}$.
concepts.detail: Young uses centimeters and grams only for conversion practice; dynamics is done in meters, kilograms, and seconds.

examples.title: Checking a kinematics formula
examples.problem: Is $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$ dimensionally consistent?

steps.label: Dimensions of speed squared
steps.text: $[v^2] = (\mathrm{L/T})^2 = \mathrm{L^2/T^2}$; same for $v_0^2$.

steps.label: Dimensions of correction
steps.text: $[a\Delta x] = (\mathrm{L/T^2})(\mathrm{L}) = \mathrm{L^2/T^2}$.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: All three terms are $\mathrm{L^2/T^2}$ — consistent.

examples.result: The equation passes the dimensional test (necessary but not sufficient for correctness).

examples.title: Rejecting a wrong formula
examples.problem: A student proposes $x = v_0 t^2$. Test it.

steps.label: Left side
steps.text: $[x] = \mathrm{L}$.

steps.label: Right side
steps.text: $[v_0 t^2] = (\mathrm{L/T})(\mathrm{T^2}) = \mathrm{L\cdot T}$.

steps.label: Verdict
steps.text: $\mathrm{L} \neq \mathrm{L\cdot T}$ — impossible.

examples.result: Rejected without any numbers; the correct form needs one fewer power of $t$.

keyTakeaways: Mechanics needs only length, mass, time; SI fixes $\mathrm{m}$, $\mathrm{kg}$, $\mathrm{s}$ atomically.
Every number in physics needs its unit to mean anything.
Added or equated terms must share dimensions — a fast, ruthless error filter.

quiz.q: Which triple lists the SI base units for mechanics?
quiz.explanation: Length–mass–time in SI are exactly $\mathrm{m}$, $\mathrm{kg}$, $\mathrm{s}$; newtons and joules are derived.

quiz.q: Why must $x = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ have matching dimensions in each term?
options: Only like dimensions can be added or equated
quiz.explanation: Adding meters to seconds is meaningless; dimensional homogeneity is required of every physical equation.

quiz.q: The modern second is defined by:
quiz.explanation: The second counts $9{,}192{,}631{,}770$ periods of the cesium hyperfine transition — reproducible anywhere.

intro: Unit conversion is algebra, not magic: multiply by one in the form of a conversion factor and let units cancel. This section teaches the chain-link method Young uses on every page, plus density as the first derived quantity.
objectives: Convert reliably between SI, cgs, and British units by chain links
Carry units through every calculation to the final answer
Compute mass and weight from density and volume

concepts.statement: A **conversion factor** such as $\frac{1000\ \mathrm{mm}}{1\ \mathrm{m}}$ equals **$1$**, so multiplying by it changes units, never value.
concepts.detail: Since numerator and denominator name the same length, $2.50\ \mathrm{m} \times (1000\ \mathrm{mm}/1\ \mathrm{m}) = 2500\ \mathrm{mm}$ exactly in value.

concepts.statement: **Chain-link:** string factors so each unwanted unit **cancels diagonally**, leaving only the target unit.
concepts.detail: Hours to seconds: $2.0\ \mathrm{h} \times (60\ \mathrm{min}/1\ \mathrm{h}) \times (60\ \mathrm{s}/1\ \mathrm{min}) = 7200\ \mathrm{s}$.

concepts.statement: Carry **units through every substitution**; the final unit is computed, not guessed.
concepts.detail: In $F = ma = (2.0\ \mathrm{kg})(3.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 6.0\ \mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2} = 6.0\ \mathrm{N}$, the newton emerges from cancellation.

concepts.statement: **Density** is mass per unit volume, $\rho = m/V$, with SI unit $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
concepts.detail: Water at $1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} = 1.00\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$; $1\ \mathrm{g/cm^3} = 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ is the most-used conversion in the chapter.

concepts.statement: **Defined conversions** ($1\ \mathrm{in} = 2.54\ \mathrm{cm}$ exactly) carry **infinite precision**; measured ones inherit uncertainty.
concepts.detail: Use exact factors freely, but a speed limit in $\mathrm{mi/h}$ converted with a measured mile keeps the measurement spread.

examples.title: Sprint speed in SI
examples.problem: A sprinter runs $100\ \mathrm{m}$ in $10.0\ \mathrm{s}$. Express the mean speed in $\mathrm{km/h}$.

steps.label: Chain link
steps.text: $10.0\ \mathrm{m/s} \times (1\ \mathrm{km}/1000\ \mathrm{m}) \times (3600\ \mathrm{s}/1\ \mathrm{h}) = 36.0\ \mathrm{km/h}$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Units collapse to $\mathrm{km/h}$; $36\ \mathrm{km/h}$ matches a $10\ \mathrm{m/s}$ sprint.

examples.result: $10.0\ \mathrm{m/s} = 36.0\ \mathrm{km/h}$.

examples.title: Mass of a gold cube
examples.problem: Gold has $\rho = 19.3\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$. What is the mass of a $2.00\ \mathrm{cm}$ cube?

steps.label: Mass
steps.text: $m = \rho V = 19.3 \times 8.00 = 154.4\ \mathrm{g}$.

steps.label: SI check
steps.text: $154.4\ \mathrm{g} = 0.154\ \mathrm{kg}$; via $19300\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} \times 8.00 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3} = 0.154\ \mathrm{kg}$.

examples.result: About $154\ \mathrm{g}$ ($0.154\ \mathrm{kg}$) — density times volume with units carried.

keyTakeaways: Multiply by one: each conversion factor renames the same quantity.
Cancel units diagonally; the surviving unit is the answer unit.
Density $\rho = m/V$ links mass, volume, and unit systems.

quiz.q: Why is multiplying by $(60\ \mathrm{s}/1\ \mathrm{min})$ legal?
options: Numerator and denominator are the same time, so the factor equals 1
quiz.explanation: A conversion factor renames units without changing value — multiplying by 1 in disguise.

quiz.q: $1\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ equals:
A calculation ending in $\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2}$ has computed:
quiz.explanation: Carrying units through $ma$ produces $\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s^2}$, the definition of the newton.

intro: No measurement is exact: instruments, reading, and the quantity itself all contribute uncertainty. This section separates random from systematic error and teaches the significant-figure rules that keep reported results honest.
objectives: Distinguish random uncertainty from systematic bias
Apply significant-figure rules for products and sums
Round honestly without manufacturing precision

concepts.statement: **Uncertainty** is the doubt about a measurement outcome; **error** in physics usually means this uncertainty, not a mistake.
concepts.detail: A length $25.3 \pm 0.2\ \mathrm{cm}$ asserts the true value very likely lies between $25.1$ and $25.5\ \mathrm{cm}$.

concepts.statement: **Random** uncertainties scatter either way and average down; **systematic** biases push every reading one way and do not average away.
concepts.detail: Parallax misreading is largely random; an unzeroed balance reading $0.5\ \mathrm{g}$ high is systematic and must be corrected.

concepts.statement: **Significant figures** are the digits known reliably plus the first doubtful one; they record precision, not just value.
concepts.detail: $25.3\ \mathrm{cm}$ has three; $0.00450\ \mathrm{m}$ has three (leading zeros never count, trailing zeros after a decimal do).

concepts.statement: For **multiplication and division**, the result carries **as many significant figures as the least precise factor**.
concepts.detail: $3.1416 \times 2.34 = 7.35$ (three figures, set by $2.34$); claiming $7.350$ would invent precision.

concepts.statement: For **addition and subtraction**, the result is cut at the **coarsest decimal place** present in any term.
concepts.detail: $123 + 5.35$ rounds to $128$ at the ones place; $24.68 - 24.61 = 0.07$ keeps only hundredths.

examples.title: Area with honest precision
examples.problem: A plate measures $12.4\ \mathrm{cm}$ by $6.8\ \mathrm{cm}$. Report its area.

steps.label: Multiply
steps.text: $12.4 \times 6.8 = 84.32\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ on the calculator.

steps.label: Apply rule
steps.text: Each factor has three and two figures; the answer keeps two.

examples.result: $84\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ — two significant figures, set by $6.8\ \mathrm{cm}$.

examples.title: Adding lengths
examples.problem: Add $12.5\ \mathrm{m} + 3.42\ \mathrm{m} + 0.238\ \mathrm{m}$.

steps.label: Apply rule
steps.text: Coarsest term $12.5$ stops at tenths.

examples.result: $16.2\ \mathrm{m}$ — tenths place is the last honest digit.

keyTakeaways: Report uncertainty explicitly; error means doubt, not blunder.
Products keep the fewest figures; sums keep the coarsest decimal place.
Never publish precision your inputs do not own.

quiz.q: An unzeroed scale reading $0.5\ \mathrm{g}$ high on every mass is:
quiz.explanation: It shifts all readings one way and survives averaging; only recalibration removes it.

quiz.q: How many significant figures in $0.00450\ \mathrm{m}$?
quiz.explanation: Leading zeros never count; digits run 4, 5, 0 — the trailing zero after the decimal is significant.

quiz.q: $8.2\ \mathrm{m} \times 4.1\ \mathrm{m}$ should be reported as:
quiz.explanation: Two figures in, two figures out: $33.62 \to 34\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

intro: Many exam and real-world questions need only the power of ten, not the exact digit. This section teaches Fermi estimation: replace unknowns by reasonable bounds, compute, and bracket the answer within a factor of a few.
objectives: Construct Fermi estimates from rough but reasoned inputs
Bracket answers between lower and upper bounds
Use powers of ten and unit volumes for counting estimates

concepts.statement: The **order of magnitude** is the power of ten nearest a quantity: $3 \times 10^{5}$ and $8 \times 10^{5}$ are both $\sim 10^{5}$–$10^{6}$.
concepts.detail: Being right within a factor of $3$–$10$ counts as success; the point is scale, not digits.

concepts.statement: **Estimate by bounding:** split the unknown into **countable factors**, guess each within a factor of a few, and **multiply the bounds**.
concepts.detail: Piano tuners in Chicago: population $\times$ households $\times$ pianos per home $\times$ tunings per year $\div$ tunings per tuner — each factor guessed to half an order.

concepts.statement: State **every assumption numerically** so the estimate can be checked and tightened.
concepts.detail: Writing fingernail growth $\sim 1\ \mathrm{mm/month}$ exposes the input to correction; hiding it does not.

concepts.statement: Count large populations by **dividing a total volume by a unit volume**: $N \approx V_{\mathrm{tot}}/V_{\mathrm{one}}$.
concepts.detail: Cells in a body, grains of sand on a beach, and breaths of air in a room all yield to one volume ratio.

concepts.statement: Estimation **cannot replace measurement** where factors cancel or exponents amplify; it gives **scale and sanity checks**.
concepts.detail: A $10$% input error raised to the third power becomes $30$% — fine for orders of magnitude, fatal for precision engineering.

figures.caption: Fermi ladder: $10^{0} \to 10^{3} \to 10^{6} \to 10^{9}$ bracketing an estimate within a factor of ten

examples.title: How many cells in a human?
examples.problem: Estimate the number of cells in a $70\ \mathrm{kg}$ adult.

steps.label: Body volume
steps.text: Density near water: $V \approx 70\ \mathrm{kg}/1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} = 0.07\ \mathrm{m^3}$.

steps.label: Cell volume
steps.text: Typical cell $\sim 10\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ across: $V_{\mathrm{cell}} \sim (10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m})^3 = 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m^3}$.

examples.result: $\sim 10^{13}$–$10^{14}$ cells — correct order; real counts are tens of trillions.

examples.title: Breaths of air in a room
examples.problem: Estimate breaths of air filling a $4 \times 5 \times 3\ \mathrm{m}$ classroom.

steps.label: Room volume
steps.text: $V = 60\ \mathrm{m^3} = 6.0 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{L}$.

steps.label: One breath
steps.text: Tidal volume $\sim 0.5\ \mathrm{L}$.

steps.label: Divide
steps.text: $N \sim 6.0 \times 10^{4}/0.5 = 1.2 \times 10^{5}$ breaths.

examples.result: $\sim 10^{5}$ breaths fill the room.

keyTakeaways: Split unknowns into countable factors and bound each one.
Report orders of magnitude honestly as powers of ten.
Use estimates to check exact calculations, not replace them.

quiz.q: A Fermi estimate is successful when it:
options: Gets the power of ten right within a factor of a few
quiz.explanation: Scale is the product; digits come later from real data.

quiz.q: Best first step for cells in a body?
options: Divide body volume by typical cell volume
quiz.explanation: Unit-volume counting turns an impossible census into one volume ratio.

quiz.q: Why state each assumption numerically?
options: So others can check and tighten each factor
quiz.explanation: Explicit numbers expose weak links; hidden guesses cannot be corrected.

intro: Displacement, velocity, force — none fits in a single number because direction matters. This section introduces vectors geometrically and defines addition and subtraction by the parallelogram and polygon rules that all later dynamics obeys.
objectives: Distinguish vectors from scalars with examples
Add and subtract vectors graphically by tail-to-tip
Interpret the resultant and null vector geometrically

concepts.statement: A **scalar** needs only magnitude ($T = 20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $m = 2\ \mathrm{kg}$); a **vector** needs magnitude **and** direction ($\vec{v}$, $\vec{F}$).
concepts.detail: Speed $10\ \mathrm{m/s}$ is scalar; velocity $10\ \mathrm{m/s}$ due east is a vector — rotating it changes the motion.

concepts.statement: Vectors print as **bold with an arrow** $\vec{A}$; magnitude is $|\vec{A}| = A$, a non-negative scalar.
concepts.detail: In handwriting add the arrow; in print the boldface carries it. $A = 0$ means the null vector, not a missing direction.

concepts.statement: **Place vectors tail to tip; the resultant $\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B}$ runs from the first tail to the last tip.** Order does not matter.
concepts.detail: The parallelogram diagonal and the tip-to-tail polygon give the same $\vec{R}$; Young uses both pictures interchangeably.

concepts.statement: Vector addition is **commutative** $\vec{A}+\vec{B} = \vec{B}+\vec{A}$ and **associative** $(\vec{A}+\vec{B})+\vec{C} = \vec{A}+(\vec{B}+\vec{C})$.
concepts.detail: Any grouping of tail-to-tip chains ends at the same resultant tip — the polygon closes identically.

concepts.statement: **Subtraction** adds the reversed vector: $\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$; $k\vec{A}$ scales length by $|k|$ and flips for $k < 0$.
concepts.detail: $2\vec{A}$ is twice as long in the same direction; $-\vec{A}$ keeps length and reverses direction.

examples.title: Hiking resultant
examples.problem: A hiker walks $3.0\ \mathrm{km}$ east then $4.0\ \mathrm{km}$ north. Find the resultant displacement.

steps.label: Sketch
steps.text: Tail-to-tip right triangle: legs $3.0$ east, $4.0$ north.

steps.label: Direction
steps.text: $\theta = \arctan(4.0/3.0) = 53^{\circ}$ north of east.

examples.result: $5.0\ \mathrm{km}$ at $53^{\circ}$ north of east — the polygon diagonal.

examples.title: Subtracting displacements
examples.problem: Given $\vec{A}$ ($5.0\ \mathrm{m}$ east) and $\vec{B}$ ($3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ east), find $\vec{A} - \vec{B}$.

steps.label: Reverse
steps.text: $-\vec{B}$ points $3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ west.

steps.label: Add
steps.text: Tail-to-tip: $5.0$ east plus $3.0$ west leaves $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ east.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Magnitudes subtract only because directions are antiparallel here; in general use the triangle.

examples.result: $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ east.

keyTakeaways: Vectors carry direction; scalars do not.
Add tail-to-tip; the resultant closes the polygon.
Subtract by adding the reversed vector; scale by stretching or flipping.

quiz.q: Which is a vector?
quiz.explanation: Force needs direction; the other three are fully described by one number plus unit.

quiz.q: Graphically, $\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B}$ is:
options: The arrow from the first tail to the last tip after tail-to-tip placement
quiz.explanation: Tail-to-tip chaining defines addition; the resultant closes the chain.

quiz.q: $\vec{A} - \vec{B}$ equals:
quiz.explanation: Subtraction is addition of the reversed vector — flip $\vec{B}$, then chain.

intro: Graphical addition is intuitive but imprecise. Resolving each vector into perpendicular components turns addition into ordinary arithmetic on numbers — the workhorse method for every equilibrium and projectile problem ahead.
objectives: Resolve a vector into rectangular components from magnitude and angle
Recover magnitude and direction from components
Add vectors analytically via summed components

concepts.statement: The **rectangular components** $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$ are the signed projections of $\vec{A}$ on the axes.
concepts.detail: $\theta$ is measured from $+x$ toward $+y$; components can be negative when the vector points along $-x$ or $-y$.

concepts.statement: Given $(A_x, A_y)$: **$A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$** and **$\tan\theta = A_y/A_x$**, with the quadrant fixed by the signs.
concepts.detail: $A_x < 0$, $A_y > 0$ puts $\vec{A}$ in quadrant II, so $\theta$ lies between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$.

concepts.statement: Add **component by component**: $R_x = A_x + B_x$, $R_y = A_y + B_y$, then $R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}$.
concepts.detail: Two-dimensional geometry collapses to two one-dimensional sums — exact, unlike ruler-and-protractor graphics.

concepts.statement: **Signs carry direction**: $+A_x$ points along $+x$, $-A_x$ along $-x$; swapping $\theta$ by $180^{\circ}$ flips both signs.
concepts.detail: A vector $10\ \mathrm{m}$ at $210^{\circ}$ has $A_x = 10\cos 210^{\circ} = -8.66\ \mathrm{m}$, $A_y = -5.00\ \mathrm{m}$.

concepts.statement: Any perpendicular axes work, but **aligning one axis with the motion or slope** minimizes nonzero components.
concepts.detail: On an incline, $x$ down the plane leaves gravity with two simple projections instead of awkward angles.

examples.title: Components of a pull
examples.problem: A rope pulls with $A = 100\ \mathrm{N}$ at $36.9^{\circ}$ above $+x$. Find $A_x$ and $A_y$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: $\sqrt{80^2 + 60^2} = 100\ \mathrm{N}$ — the 3-4-5 triangle.

examples.result: $A_x = 80.0\ \mathrm{N}$, $A_y = 60.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

examples.title: Adding two forces analytically
examples.problem: $\vec{A} = (80, 60)\ \mathrm{N}$, $\vec{B} = (-20, 30)\ \mathrm{N}$. Find $\vec{R} = \vec{A}+\vec{B}$.

steps.label: Magnitude and angle
steps.text: $R = \sqrt{60^2+90^2} = 108\ \mathrm{N}$; $\theta = \arctan(90/60) = 56.3^{\circ}$ above $+x$.

examples.result: $108\ \mathrm{N}$ at $56.3^{\circ}$ above $+x$.

keyTakeaways: Project with cosine for $x$ and sine for $y$ from $+x$ toward $+y$.
Signs encode quadrant; arctangent alone does not fix direction.
Vector addition is two scalar additions: $R_x$ and $R_y$.

quiz.q: A vector $A = 10\ \mathrm{m}$ at $210^{\circ}$ has components:
quiz.explanation: $\cos 210^{\circ} = -0.866$, $\sin 210^{\circ} = -0.500$ — quadrant III makes both negative.

quiz.q: Given $A_x = -6$, $A_y = 8$, the direction is:
quiz.explanation: $\arctan(8/-6) = -53^{\circ}$, but $(-,+)$ is quadrant II: $180 - 53 = 127^{\circ}$.

quiz.q: To add vectors analytically you:
quiz.explanation: $R_x = A_x+B_x$, $R_y = A_y+B_y$ — geometry becomes arithmetic.

intro: Unit vectors factor direction out of every vector expression. Writing vectors as combinations of the Cartesian triad turns dot and cross products, kinematics, and dynamics into clean component algebra.
objectives: Write vectors in unit-vector form $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{\imath} + A_y\hat{\jmath} + A_z\hat{k}$
Add vectors and scale them in unit-vector notation
Extend components to three dimensions

concepts.statement: **$\hat{\imath}$, $\hat{\jmath}$, $\hat{k}$** are dimensionless vectors of **unit length** along $+x$, $+y$, $+z$.
concepts.detail: $|\hat{\imath}| = |\hat{\jmath}| = |\hat{k}| = 1$ exactly; the hat marks unit magnitude.

concepts.statement: Any vector expands as **$\vec{A} = A_x\hat{\imath} + A_y\hat{\jmath} + A_z\hat{k}$**, with $A = \sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2+A_z^2}$.
concepts.detail: Example: $\vec{A} = 3.0\hat{\imath} - 2.0\hat{\jmath} + 5.0\hat{k}\ \mathrm{m}$ names all three projections at once.

concepts.statement: Add **coefficient by coefficient**: if $\vec{R} = \vec{A}+\vec{B}$ then $R_x = A_x+B_x$, $R_y = A_y+B_y$, $R_z = A_z+B_z$.
concepts.detail: So $(3\hat{\imath}+2\hat{\jmath}) + (-1\hat{\imath}+4\hat{\jmath}) = 2\hat{\imath}+6\hat{\jmath}$.

concepts.term: Unit vector along an arbitrary direction
concepts.statement: The **unit vector along $\vec{A}$** is $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/A$, so $\vec{A} = A\hat{A}$.
concepts.detail: Dividing $(3,4)\ \mathrm{m}$ by $5\ \mathrm{m}$ gives the direction $(0.6\hat{\imath}+0.8\hat{\jmath})$ with no units.

concepts.statement: **$\hat{\imath} \times \hat{\jmath} = \hat{k}$** cyclically: point fingers along $x$, curl toward $y$, thumb gives $z$.
concepts.detail: Young uses right-handed coordinates throughout; a left-handed choice would flip every cross-product sign.

examples.title: Writing a displacement
examples.problem: A displacement has $A_x = -4.0\ \mathrm{m}$, $A_y = 3.0\ \mathrm{m}$, $A_z = 0$. Write it in unit-vector form and find $A$.

steps.label: Expand
steps.text: $\vec{A} = -4.0\hat{\imath} + 3.0\hat{\jmath}\ \mathrm{m}$.

steps.label: Direction unit vector
steps.text: $\hat{A} = (-0.80\hat{\imath} + 0.60\hat{\jmath})$, dimensionless.

examples.result: $\vec{A} = -4.0\hat{\imath}+3.0\hat{\jmath}\ \mathrm{m}$, $A = 5.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

examples.title: Adding in three dimensions
examples.problem: $\vec{A} = 2\hat{\imath}-\hat{\jmath}+3\hat{k}$, $\vec{B} = -\hat{\imath}+4\hat{\jmath}-2\hat{k}$ (meters). Find $\vec{R}$.

steps.label: Assemble
steps.text: $\vec{R} = \hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}+\hat{k}\ \mathrm{m}$, $R = \sqrt{11} = 3.32\ \mathrm{m}$.

examples.result: $\vec{R} = (1,3,1)\ \mathrm{m}$, magnitude $3.32\ \mathrm{m}$.

keyTakeaways: Unit vectors separate magnitude (numbers) from direction (hats).
$\vec{A} = A_x\hat{\imath}+A_y\hat{\jmath}+A_z\hat{k}$ is the standard mechanics shorthand.
Right-handed $\hat{\imath},\hat{\jmath},\hat{k}$ fixes all cross-product signs.

quiz.q: What is $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/A$?
quiz.explanation: Dividing by magnitude strips units and length, leaving pure direction.

quiz.q: $(3\hat{\imath}+2\hat{\jmath}) + (-1\hat{\imath}+4\hat{\jmath})$ equals:
quiz.explanation: Add coefficients: $3-1 = 2$ for $\hat{\imath}$, $2+4 = 6$ for $\hat{\jmath}$.

quiz.q: Right-handed coordinates satisfy:
quiz.explanation: Cyclic right-hand rule: $x$ cross $y$ gives $z$.

intro: Two vectors multiply in two distinct ways: the dot product returns a scalar measuring alignment, and the cross product returns a vector measuring perpendicularity. Both pervade mechanics — work uses the dot, torque and magnetism use the cross.
objectives: Compute dot products geometrically and from components
Compute cross products geometrically and from components
Interpret orthogonality, projection, and area via the two products

concepts.statement: The **dot product** $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\phi$ is a **scalar** measuring parallel alignment ($\phi$ between vectors).
concepts.detail: Parallel vectors give $+AB$; antiparallel give $-AB$; perpendicular give $0$.

concepts.statement: **$\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$**, since $\hat{\imath}\cdot\hat{\imath} = 1$ and mixed hats dot to $0$.
The **scalar projection** of $\vec{A}$ on $\vec{B}$ is $A\cos\phi = (\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B})/B$.
concepts.detail: Work $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s} = Fs\cos\phi$ is exactly this projection times displacement — only the parallel force works.

concepts.statement: The **cross product** $\vec{C} = \vec{A}\times\vec{B}$ has magnitude **$C = AB\sin\phi$** and direction by the **right-hand rule**.
concepts.detail: $\vec{C}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$; $\vec{B}\times\vec{A} = -\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$ (anticommutative).

concepts.statement: **$\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = (A_yB_z-A_zB_y)\hat{\imath} + (A_zB_x-A_xB_z)\hat{\jmath} + (A_xB_y-A_yB_x)\hat{k}$**.
concepts.detail: Cyclic hats: $\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\jmath} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{\jmath}\times\hat{k} = \hat{\imath}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{\imath} = \hat{\jmath}$; self-crosses vanish.

concepts.statement: **$|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|$ is the parallelogram area** spanned by $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$; $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0$ tests **perpendicularity**.
concepts.detail: Torque magnitude $\tau = rF\sin\phi$ and magnetic force $F = qvB\sin\phi$ are cross-product magnitudes in disguise.

figures.caption: Dot uses $\cos\phi$ (parallel part); cross uses $\sin\phi$ (perpendicular part, out of page)

examples.title: Work-style dot product
examples.problem: $\vec{A} = 3\hat{\imath}+4\hat{\jmath}$, $\vec{B} = 2\hat{\imath}-\hat{\jmath}$. Find $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}$ and the angle.
examples.result: Dot $2$; nearly perpendicular ($79.7^{\circ}$).

examples.title: Area-style cross product
examples.problem: $\vec{A} = 4\hat{\imath}$, $\vec{B} = 3\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}$. Find $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$.

steps.label: Formula
steps.text: $C_z = A_xB_y - A_yB_x = 4 \times 3 - 0 = 12$.

steps.label: Vector
steps.text: $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = 12\hat{k}$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: $|C| = AB\sin\phi = 4 \times 4.243 \times \sin 45^{\circ} = 12$ — parallelogram area.

examples.result: $12\hat{k}$ — magnitude $12$, direction $+z$ by the right-hand rule.

keyTakeaways: Dot is a scalar via cosine: $AB\cos\phi = A_xB_x+A_yB_y+A_zB_z$.
Cross is a vector via sine with right-hand direction; order flips sign.
Work projects with the dot; torque and area use the cross.

quiz.q: If $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0$ for nonzero vectors, they are:
quiz.explanation: $AB\cos\phi = 0$ forces $\cos\phi = 0$, i.e. $\phi = 90^{\circ}$.

quiz.q: $\vec{B}\times\vec{A}$ compared with $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$ is:
quiz.explanation: Cross product is anticommutative — swapping fingers reverses the thumb.

quiz.q: $(3\hat{\imath}+0\hat{\jmath}) \cdot (0\hat{\imath}+4\hat{\jmath})$ equals:
quiz.explanation: Perpendicular axes: $(3)(0)+(0)(4) = 0$.

quiz.q: Torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$ is largest when:
quiz.explanation: $|\tau| = rF\sin\phi$ peaks at $\sin\phi = 1$ ($90^{\circ}$).

intro: Atoms bind by sharing, donating, pooling, or faintly attracting electrons: covalent, ionic, metallic, and van der Waals bonds. Potential curves with $eV$-deep minima set bond lengths near angstroms. Bond type predicts conductivity, hardness, and melting at a glance.
objectives: Classify ionic, covalent, metallic, van der Waals bonds
Read bond length and dissociation energy off potential curves
Predict properties from bond type

concepts.statement: **Electron transfer plus Coulomb attraction** (NaCl): large electronegativity gap, conducting melts, brittle crystals.
concepts.detail: Lattice Madelung sums reach $8$ eV per pair.

concepts.statement: **Shared-pair exchange lowering** (H2 $4.5$ eV, diamond): directional, hard, insulating or semiconducting.
concepts.detail: Symmetric spatial states pair with singlet spins by Pauli.

concepts.statement: **Delocalized electron sea over ion cores**: conductive, malleable, lustrous, close-packed.
concepts.detail: Nondirectional pooling allows planes to slide.

concepts.statement: **Induced-dipole $1/r^{6}$ attraction** (Ne, wax): meV depths, soft, low melting.
concepts.detail: Quantum fluctuations correlate dipoles; $r^{-12}$ repulsion balances at contact.

concepts.statement: **Minimum locates $r_{0}$, depth gives $D_{e}$**; curvature gives vibrational $k$ (next section).
concepts.detail: Morse fits interpolate dissociation from spectroscopy.

examples.title: NaCl lattice energy
examples.problem: Estimate NaCl pair Coulomb energy at $r_{0} = 0.281$ nm.

steps.label: Step 2: Lattice
steps.text: Madelung $1.748$ plus repulsion gives $\approx -7.9$ eV per pair in crystal.

steps.label: Step 3: Check
steps.text: Born-Haber $7.6$ eV: Coulomb rules ionic energetics.

examples.result: $-5.1$ eV per pair, $-7.9$ eV in lattice.

examples.title: Bond from curve
examples.problem: Morse minimum $4.5$ eV at $0.074$ nm. Identify bond.

steps.label: Step 1: Depth
steps.text: eV-scale: chemical, not van der Waals meV.

steps.label: Step 2: Length
steps.text: Sub-angstrom: compact H2-like covalent.

steps.label: Step 3: Properties
steps.text: Expect hard gas with $4000+$ K dissociation scale.

examples.result: Covalent H2 bond.

keyTakeaways: Four bonds span eV chemical to meV physical strengths.
Minima give lengths, depths give energies, curvature gives stiffness.
Bond type foretells conductivity and mechanics.

quiz.q: NaCl bonding is chiefly:
quiz.explanation: Full transfer with Coulomb lattice sums.

quiz.q: Deepest typical bond class is:
quiz.explanation: Chemical bonds are eV; physical bonds meV.

quiz.q: Metals conduct because electrons are:
quiz.explanation: Sea electrons accelerate freely under fields.

intro: Molecules rotate in $BJ(J+1)$ ladders and vibrate near $\hbar\omega$, emitting microwave and infrared combs. Line spacings weigh bond lengths to picometers and spring constants to newtons per meter. Selection rules $\Delta J = \pm 1$ shape every branch.
objectives: Write rotational $E_{J} = BJ(J+1)$ with $B = \hbar^{2}/2I$
Extract $r_{0}$ from microwave spacing $2B$
Extract $k$ from vibrational $\hbar\omega$

concepts.statement: **$E_{J} = (\hbar^{2}/2I)J(J+1)$**; absorption lines space **$2B$** ($B$ in energy).
concepts.detail: CO spacing $3.86$ per cm gives $r_{0} = 0.113$ nm.

concepts.statement: **$I = \mu r_{0}^{2} = \hbar^{2}/2B$** inverts spacing to geometry.
concepts.detail: Isotope substitution shifts $\mu$ and confirms assignments.

concepts.statement: **$E_{v} = (v+1/2)\hbar\omega$**, $\omega = \sqrt{k/\mu}$; IR fundamental near $10^{14}$ Hz.
concepts.detail: HCl $2886$ per cm gives $k = 480$ N/m.

concepts.statement: **Rotation $\Delta J = \pm 1$; vibration $\Delta v = \pm 1$ with $\Delta J = \pm 1$** (P/Q/R branches).
concepts.detail: Homopolar H2 lacks dipole rotation lines; Raman fills the gap.

concepts.statement: **$\hbar\omega/2$ shifts reaction barriers**; deuteration slows rates (kinetic isotope effect).
concepts.detail: Heavy bonds sit lower and climb higher.

examples.title: CO bond length
examples.problem: CO microwave spacing $2B = 3.86$ per cm. Find $r_{0}$ ($\mu = 6.86$ u).

steps.label: Step 2: Inertia
steps.text: $I = \hbar^{2}/2B = 1.453 \times 10^{-46}$ kg-m-squared.

examples.title: HCl spring
examples.problem: $\tilde{\nu} = 2886$ per cm for HCl ($\mu = 0.979$ u). Find $k$.

steps.label: Step 1: Omega
steps.text: $\omega = 2\pi c\tilde{\nu} = 5.437 \times 10^{14}$ rad/s.

steps.label: Step 3: Sense
steps.text: Stiff chemical spring, $0.36$ eV steps.

keyTakeaways: Microwave combs space $2B$ and weigh bond lengths.
IR bands step $\hbar\omega$ and weigh bond stiffness.
Selection rules branch every band into P/Q/R.

quiz.q: Rotational absorption lines are spaced by:
quiz.explanation: J to J+1 gaps grow as 2B(J+1); sequence spaces 2B.

quiz.q: Heavier isotope at same bond:
quiz.explanation: Larger I shrinks B = hbar-squared / 2I.

quiz.q: HCl k is about:
quiz.explanation: IR frequency with reduced mass gives chemical stiffness.

intro: Crystals repeat a unit cell on Bravais lattices: cubic families plus hexagonal close packing cover most elements. Coordination, packing fraction, and Miller indices name every plane that diffracts. Defects, vacancies through dislocations, set real strength and color.
objectives: Name SC, BCC, FCC with coordination and packing
Index planes $(hkl)$ and directions $[uvw]$
Classify point, line, and planar defects

concepts.statement: **SC (6, 52 percent), BCC (8, 68 percent), FCC (12, 74 percent)**: coordination plus packing fingerprint each.
concepts.detail: Iron swaps BCC-FCC with temperature; aluminum stays FCC.

concepts.statement: **(hkl) reciprocals of intercepts** name planes; [uvw] name directions; families use braces.
concepts.detail: $(111)$ close-packs FCC; Bragg reads these planes (Chapter 36).

concepts.statement: **FCC/HCP stack $74$ percent dense** (ABC versus AB order); octahedral and tetrahedral holes host alloys.
concepts.detail: Steel carbon sits in iron's holes, hardening it.

concepts.statement: **Vacancies, interstitials, dislocations, grain boundaries** break perfection and set conductivity, strength, color.
concepts.detail: Dislocation glide makes metals ductile; pinning hardens them.

concepts.statement: **Glasses lack long-range order**: sharp Bragg spots blur to halos, bands tail into gaps.
concepts.detail: Same bonds, different organization, different spectra.

examples.title: FCC density of Al
examples.problem: Al FCC $a = 0.405$ nm. Find density.

steps.label: Step 1: Atoms
steps.text: $4$ per cell.

steps.label: Step 3: Density
steps.text: $2698$ kg/m-cubed, matching $2700$ tabulated.

examples.result: $2.70$ g/cm-cubed from lattice alone.

examples.title: Indexing (111)
examples.problem: Plane cuts axes at $(1,1,1)$ cell units. What are indices?

steps.label: Step 2: Meaning
steps.text: Diagonal close-packed plane of the cube.

steps.label: Step 3: Cut at (2,1,inf)
steps.text: Reciprocals $(1/2,1,0) \to (210)$ after clearing.

examples.result: $(111)$ diagonal; scheme generalizes.

keyTakeaways: Bravais plus basis builds every crystal; cubics plus HCP dominate.
Miller $(hkl)$ names Bragg planes.
Defects engineer strength, color, and conduction.

quiz.q: FCC packing fraction is:
quiz.explanation: Close-packed spheres fill about three quarters.

quiz.q: (111) plane intercepts axes at:
quiz.explanation: Equal intercepts invert to equal indices.

quiz.q: Dislocations control:
quiz.explanation: Line-defect motion is macroscopic deformation.

intro: Atomic levels broaden into bands as wells merge: filled valence bands plus empty conduction bands sort every solid. Gap size decides conductor, semiconductor, insulator. Band curvature mints effective masses that drift, absorb, and emit.
objectives: Explain band formation from level splitting with $N$ atoms
Classify solids by gap $E_{g}$ and filling
Define effective mass $m^{\ast}$ from curvature

concepts.statement: **$N$ coupled orbitals split into $N$-state bands**; overlap grows with closeness, splitting with interaction.
concepts.detail: Dimer splits $2$; crystal fans $10^{23}$ into quasi-continua.

concepts.statement: **Overlapping bands conduct; $E_{g} \sim 1$ eV semiconducts; $E_{g} > 3$ eV insulates**; filled bands carry nothing.
concepts.detail: Si $1.12$ eV, GaAs $1.42$ eV, diamond $5.5$ eV, copper overlapped.

concepts.statement: **$m^{\ast} = \hbar^{2}/(d^{2}E/dk^{2})$**: band curvature stands in for inertia, even negative near tops.
concepts.detail: GaAs electrons $0.067m_{e}$ sprint; heavy holes lumber.

concepts.statement: **Missing valence electrons act as positive carriers** with upward-curving energy.
concepts.detail: Current sums electron plus hole drifts; Hall signs reveal both.

concepts.statement: **Direct gaps emit light efficiently** (GaAs LEDs); **indirect need phonons** (Si glows poorly).
concepts.detail: Momentum alignment, not just size, picks optoelectronics.

$m^{\ast}$ and holes rewrite carrier dynamics.

intro: Valence electrons roam as a Fermi gas: $E_{F}$ near $7$ eV, $v_{F}$ near $10^{6}$ m/s, degeneracy pressure holding metals up. Conductivity $\sigma = ne^{2}\tau/m$ prices scattering time $\tau$; heat capacity grows as $T/T_{F}$. Drude plus Fermi explains shine, conduction, and contact potentials.
objectives: State Fermi-Dirac $f(E) = 1/(e^{(E-E_{F})/kT} + 1)$ and $E_{F}$ scale
Derive $\sigma = ne^{2}\tau/m$ qualitatively
Explain work function and contact potential

concepts.statement: **$f(E) = 1/[e^{(E-E_{F})/kT}+1]$**: step at $0$ K smeared over $kT$ at room.
concepts.detail: $T_{F} \sim 80000$ K dwarfs $300$ K: metals stay degenerate.

concepts.statement: **$\sigma = ne^{2}\tau/m$**; resistivity prices collision rate $1/\tau$ from phonons plus impurities.
concepts.detail: Copper $\tau \approx 25$ fs at $300$ K; Matthiessen sums rates.

concepts.statement: **$C_{el} = \gamma T$** with only $T/T_{F}$ electrons active; phonons ($T^{3}$) win except near zero.
concepts.detail: Sommerfeld linear term fingerprints $E_{F}$ density of states.

concepts.statement: **$\phi = E_{vac} - E_{F}$** prices electron escape ($2$-$5$ eV); photoelectric and thermionic currents follow.
concepts.detail: Cesium $2.14$ eV ejects under green; tungsten $4.5$ eV needs heat plus field.

concepts.statement: **Joining metals aligns $E_{F}$**, spilling charge until Volta $\Delta\phi/e$ balances.
concepts.detail: Thermocouples and Schottky barriers are this alignment in action.

examples.title: Copper scattering time
examples.problem: Copper $\sigma = 5.96 \times 10^{7}$ S/m, $n = 8.47 \times 10^{28}$ per m-cubed. Find $\tau$ and mean free path.

steps.label: Step 3: Atoms
steps.text: $\sim 150$ spacings between collisions at room temperature.

examples.problem: What fraction of copper electrons carry heat at $300$ K?

steps.label: Step 2: Meaning
steps.text: Under $1$ percent participate; the Fermi sea is frozen.

steps.label: Step 3: Contrast
steps.text: Classical gas would give $3R/2$ per mole; observed electronic $\sim 1$ percent of that.

examples.result: $0.4$ percent of electrons thermally active.

keyTakeaways: Fermi step at $E_{F}$ (eV scale) governs all metal electrons.
$\sigma = ne^{2}\tau/m$ separates density from scattering.
Work functions and contacts align Fermi seas.

quiz.q: Fermi function at E = $E_{F}$ equals:
quiz.explanation: Exponent zero gives half occupation at any T.

quiz.q: Resistivity rises with T because:
quiz.explanation: Lattice vibration rate grows roughly linearly.

quiz.q: Electronic heat capacity scales as:
quiz.explanation: Only the thermal shell near $E_{F}$ contributes.

intro: A pinch of dopant rewrites conductivity: donors park electrons below the conduction band, acceptors park holes above valence. The law of mass action $np = n_{i}^{2}$ trades electrons against holes. Conductivity $\sigma = e(n\mu_{e} + p\mu_{h})$ spans $10$ orders with doping and temperature.
objectives: Distinguish n-type donors from p-type acceptors with band sketches
Apply $np = n_{i}^{2}$ with $n_{i}$ for Si
Compute $\sigma$ from $n$, $p$, mobilities

concepts.statement: **P in Si donates $45$ meV electrons (n-type); B accepts holes (p-type)**; hydrogenic levels scaled by $\epsilon$, $m^{\ast}$.
concepts.detail: ppm doping beats intrinsic $10^{10}$ per cm-cubed by $10^{6}$.

concepts.statement: **$np = n_{i}^{2}$** in equilibrium; doping raises one carrier and suppresses the other.
concepts.detail: Si $n_{i} = 10^{10}$ per cm-cubed at $300$ K; GaAs $10^{6}$.

concepts.statement: **$\sigma = e(n\mu_{e} + p\mu_{h})$** with mobilities $\mu = e\tau/m^{\ast}$ (Si $1350$/$480$ cm-squared/V-s).
concepts.detail: Resistivity charts span doped-Si $10^{-3}$ to intrinsic $10^{5}$ ohm-cm.

concepts.statement: **Cold freezes dopants out; heat excites across the gap**: extrinsic plateau sits between.
concepts.detail: Devices live on the plateau; sensors exploit the intrinsic rise.

concepts.statement: **Hall sign names the majority carrier**; magnitude weighs $1/ne$.
concepts.detail: Negative Hall: electrons; positive: holes.

$np = n_{i}^{2}$ always; doping trades majority for minority.
Mobility-weighted carriers set $\sigma$ across $10$ orders.

intro: Join p to n and diffusion builds a depletion field that rectifies: forward bias flattens the hill, reverse steepens it. Transistors gate this hill with a third terminal to switch and amplify. Diodes plus transistors are the alphabet of chips.
objectives: Explain built-in $V_{bi}$ and depletion width formation
State diode $I = I_{s}(e^{eV/kT} - 1)$ with forward/reverse behavior
Distinguish BJT current gain from MOSFET gate control

concepts.statement: **$V_{bi} = (kT/e)\ln(N_{a}N_{d}/n_{i}^{2})$** ($\sim 0.7$ V Si): diffusion versus drift balance.
concepts.detail: $N = 10^{16}$ each side gives $0.69$ V.

concepts.statement: **$I = I_{s}(e^{eV/kT}-1)$**: exponential forward, $-I_{s}$ reverse until breakdown.
concepts.detail: $60$ mV per decade at room; $0.7$ V turns Si on.

concepts.statement: **Base current meters collector flow**: $I_{C} = \beta I_{B}$ ($\beta \sim 100$) across a thin base.
concepts.detail: Emitter injects, base steers, collector gathers.

concepts.statement: **Gate voltage inverts a channel** under oxide; drain current follows $V_{GS}$ with (near) zero DC gate current.
concepts.detail: CMOS pairs n- and p-FETs for switch-only dissipation.

concepts.statement: **LEDs forward-inject to emit $hc/E_{g}$; solar cells collect photo-splits** at the same junction reversed.
concepts.detail: Same diode, opposite energy direction.

intro: Cool mercury and resistance vanishes: Cooper pairs condense into one macroscopic wave function with gapped excitations. Meissner expels flux; type-II threads it in quantized vortices to $100+$ T. BCS phonon glue explains low-$T_{c}$; cuprates and hydrides chase room temperature.
objectives: State zero resistance plus Meissner as the two superconducting hallmarks
Distinguish type-I $H_{c}$ from type-II $H_{c1}$, $H_{c2}$
Describe Cooper pairs, gap $2\Delta$, and flux quantization $\Phi_{0}$

concepts.statement: **$\rho = 0$ below $T_{c}$ plus $B = 0$ inside (Meissner)** define superconductivity; perfect conductors lack the second.
concepts.detail: Hg $4.2$ K (1911); NbTi $9.5$ K; YBCO $92$ K; hydrides $250+$ K under pressure.

concepts.statement: **Phonon-mediated $k$-up/$-k$-down pairs** condense with gap **$2\Delta \approx 3.5kT_{c}$** (BCS).
concepts.detail: Gap blocks scattering: no states to scatter into.

concepts.statement: **Type-I expels to $H_{c}$ then quits; type-II admits vortices $H_{c1}$-$H_{c2}$** to $100+$ T.
concepts.detail: MRI NbTi at $5$ T and LHC Nb3Sn at $8$ T are type-II vortex states.

concepts.statement: **$\Phi = n\Phi_{0}$**, $\Phi_{0} = h/2e = 2.07 \times 10^{-15}$ Wb; SQUIDs count single quanta.
concepts.detail: $2e$ charge of pairs halves the flux unit.

concepts.statement: **Cuprates, pnictides, hydrides exceed phonon ceilings** with magnetic or unknown glue; room-$T$ at ambient pressure stays open.
concepts.detail: Mechanism Nobel awaits; applications advance regardless.

steps.text: $2.7$ meV (strong coupling exceeds BCS $3.5$ slightly).

examples.result: $2.2$ meV BCS estimate.

steps.label: Step 3: Pinning
steps.text: Defects pin this lattice to carry loss-free current.

examples.result: $22$ nm vortex lattice.

keyTakeaways: Zero $\rho$ plus Meissner expulsion define the state.
Pairs plus gap explain persistence; vortices extend magnets to $100$ T.
Flux quantizes in $h/2e$ units read by SQUIDs.

quiz.q: Superconductivity requires:
quiz.explanation: Perfect conductors mimic the first, never the second.

quiz.q: Flux quantum is h/2e because carriers are:
quiz.explanation: Pair charge 2e halves the Aharonov-Bohm period.

quiz.q: Type-II magnets reach high field via:
options: Vortex state between Hc1 and Hc2
quiz.explanation: Quantized flux threads without quenching to Hc2.

intro: Technicians meet physics every day in motors, circuits, brakes, and beams, often without naming it. This section makes the case that a working knowledge of a few laws and a disciplined method pays off directly on the job.
objectives: Explain why a technician needs physics even when the job looks purely practical
Identify physics ideas hidden in familiar shop and everyday devices
Describe what studying physics gives you beyond formulas

concepts.term: Physics as the study of matter, motion, and energy
concepts.statement: Physics studies **matter, motion, energy, and their interactions**, expressed as compact laws such as $F = ma$ and $W = Fd$ that predict how things behave.
concepts.detail: Ewen keeps the treatment algebra-based and applied: laws are tools for sizing, measuring, and troubleshooting rather than abstract theory.

concepts.statement: Almost every technical task — wiring a circuit, aligning a belt drive, reading a gauge — **applies a physics law**, whether or not the worker states it.
concepts.detail: The auto mechanic balancing torque against friction, the electrician sizing wire by $P = VI$, and the machinist holding tolerances all use physics quantitatively.

concepts.statement: Physics lets you **predict results before cutting metal**: compute the force, current, or stopping distance first, then verify by measurement.
concepts.detail: That predict-then-verify habit saves material, time, and accidents, and it recurs in every chapter of the book.

concepts.statement: A physical quantity is a **number plus a unit**, such as $12.5\ \mathrm{V}$ or $3.20\ \mathrm{m}$; the number alone means nothing.
concepts.detail: Chapters 1-2 build the unit and substitution habits that make later calculations trustworthy.

concepts.statement: Studying physics builds **quantitative judgment**: estimating orders of magnitude, spotting unreasonable answers, and arguing from data.
concepts.detail: An answer like a $5000\ \mathrm{A}$ lighting circuit or a negative stopping distance should trigger instant suspicion.
