examples.title: Spotting physics in a car stop
examples.problem: A $1200\ \mathrm{kg}$ car slows from $20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to rest. Which physics ideas will Chapters 4-6 use to analyze it?

steps.label: Motion
steps.text: Chapter 4 describes the motion: stopping distance and time follow $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2as$.

steps.label: Force
steps.text: Chapter 5 finds the braking force from $F = ma$ once the acceleration $a$ is known.

steps.label: Energy and momentum
steps.text: Chapter 8 checks the work $W = Fd$ against kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 240{,}000\ \mathrm{J}$, and Chapter 6 frames the impulse $Ft$.

examples.result: One everyday stop uses motion, force, energy, and momentum — the core arc of the course.

examples.title: Number plus unit
examples.problem: A meter reads 12.5. Why is that reading useless until the unit is known?

steps.label: Candidate 1
steps.text: $12.5\ \mathrm{V}$ across a car battery terminal is normal and healthy.

steps.label: Candidate 2
steps.text: $12.5\ \mathrm{A}$ through a lamp cord is a heavy, possibly dangerous load.

steps.label: Rule
steps.text: Same digits, different units, totally different meaning — always record and carry the unit.

examples.result: A measurement is complete only as number times unit.

keyTakeaways: Physics is the working science behind motors, structures, circuits, and machines technicians service.
Its value is prediction: compute first with a law, then verify by measurement.
Every quantity is a number plus a unit, and quantitative judgment starts there.

quiz.q: Why does Ewen argue a technician should study physics?
options: To pass a licensing exam only
Because technical work constantly applies physics laws to real devices
Because shop work never involves measurement
quiz.explanation: The chapter shows motors, brakes, circuits, and structures all run on physics laws the technician must apply.

quiz.q: Which best completes a measurement?
options: A number plus its unit, such as $12.5\ \mathrm{V}$
A unit alone, such as volts
quiz.explanation: A physical quantity is number times unit; either part alone is meaningless.

quiz.q: A car braking analysis will use which chain of ideas?
quiz.explanation: Stopping involves kinematics, $F = ma$, $W = Fd$ versus $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$, and $Ft = \Delta p$.

intro: Modern technology is applied physics made concrete, from the steam engine to the microchip. This section traces that link so the laws ahead feel like the operating principles of the devices around you.
objectives: Relate major technologies to the physics laws behind them
Explain how applied physics turns discovery into devices
Give shop examples of energy conversion governed by physics

concepts.statement: Each technological era rests on physics: **heat engines on thermodynamics, electronics on electromagnetism, computers on quantum solids**.
concepts.detail: Studying the law first makes the device intelligible; studying the device motivates the law.

concepts.statement: Most machines are **energy converters** — chemical to thermal to mechanical to electrical — and every step obeys conservation of energy.
concepts.detail: A power plant, a car engine, and a flashlight battery all illustrate the same bookkeeping: energy in equals energy out plus losses.

concepts.statement: Electric motors, generators, and transformers run on the relation between **current and magnetic field**, quantified later as $F = BIL$ and induced emf.
concepts.detail: The technician who troubleshoots a motor is testing those relations with a meter.

concepts.statement: Vehicles, lifts, and machine tools obey **$F = ma$, $W = Fd$, and $P = W/t$**: force causes acceleration, work moves loads, power sets the rate.
concepts.detail: Horsepower ratings, gear ratios, and brake specifications are these laws in commercial dress.

concepts.statement: This book stresses **applied physics**: use the law to size, predict, and check, leaving deep theoretical derivations to later courses.
concepts.detail: Algebra plus units plus careful measurement carries the whole course.

examples.title: Power plant chain
examples.problem: Trace the energy conversions in a fossil-fuel power plant driving a shop motor.

steps.label: Plant
steps.text: Chemical energy in fuel becomes thermal energy in steam, then mechanical energy in the turbine, then electrical energy in the generator.

steps.label: Shop
steps.text: The motor converts electrical energy back to mechanical energy at the shaft, with heat as loss at each step.

steps.label: Bookkeeping
steps.text: If the generator delivers $500\ \mathrm{kW}$ at $92\%$ efficiency, the shaft input was $500/0.92 \approx 543\ \mathrm{kW}$.

examples.result: Every link is an energy conversion with an efficiency cost — the theme of Chapter 8.

examples.title: Motor current estimate
examples.problem: A $120\ \mathrm{V}$ drill draws $5.0\ \mathrm{A}$. What power does physics predict?

steps.label: Law
steps.text: Electric power is $P = VI$.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: $P = (120\ \mathrm{V})(5.0\ \mathrm{A}) = 600\ \mathrm{W}$.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: About $0.80\ \mathrm{hp}$ input (since $1\ \mathrm{hp} = 746\ \mathrm{W}$) before motor losses.

examples.result: About $600\ \mathrm{W}$ of electrical input — physics predicts the nameplate.

keyTakeaways: Technology advances by applying physics laws to energy conversion and control.
Motors, generators, engines, and lifts each embody mechanics plus electromagnetism.
Applied physics means computing real ratings, currents, and powers with algebra and units.

quiz.q: A car engine plus drivetrain is best described as
options: A chain of energy conversions with losses at each step
quiz.explanation: Chemical to thermal to mechanical with heat and friction losses; conservation always holds.

quiz.q: A $120\ \mathrm{V}$, $5.0\ \mathrm{A}$ drill draws about
quiz.explanation: $P = VI = 120 \times 5.0 = 600\ \mathrm{W}$.

quiz.q: Electric motors and generators both depend on
options: The link between current and magnetic fields
Action at a distance without fields
quiz.explanation: Motor force and generator emf both come from current-field interaction.

intro: Physics does not stand alone: chemistry, biology, and engineering all build on its laws. Seeing those bridges early helps you transfer each formula to allied trades and sciences.
objectives: Describe how physics underlies chemistry, biology, and engineering
Give one cross-field example for each connection
Explain why technicians benefit from seeing those links

concepts.statement: Chemical bonding, gas pressure, and heat of reaction are **electrical forces and energy bookkeeping** at the atomic scale.
concepts.detail: Gas laws ($PV = nRT$), specific heat, and electrochemistry in later chapters are shared physics-chemistry ground.

concepts.statement: Blood pressure, bone levers, optics of the eye, and ultrasound imaging obey **fluid, force, lens, and wave laws**.
concepts.detail: A blood-pressure cuff reads hydrostatic pressure; an X-ray or ultrasound applies wave and photon physics.

concepts.statement: Statics, circuits, heat transfer, and materials selection are **engineering chapters written in physics vocabulary**.
concepts.detail: Beam equilibrium, wire sizing, insulation ratings, and density tables all come from Chapters 1-12 laws.

concepts.statement: Force, energy, power, pressure, and temperature **keep the same units across fields**: $1\ \mathrm{N}$, $1\ \mathrm{J}$, $1\ \mathrm{W}$, $1\ \mathrm{Pa}$, $1\ \mathrm{K}$ mean the same everywhere.
concepts.detail: That shared unit system is what lets a nurse, an electrician, and an engineer trust one another numbers.

concepts.statement: Unit checking, significant digits, and the **predict-compute-verify loop transfer unchanged** to any technical field.
concepts.detail: Learn them once in physics and reuse them in every trade calculation.

examples.title: Three fields, one pressure
examples.problem: Show that tire pressure, blood pressure, and hydraulic pressure are the same quantity.

steps.label: Tires
steps.text: A tire at $220\ \mathrm{kPa}$ pushes outward on every square centimeter with force $F = PA$.

steps.label: Blood
steps.text: $120/80\ \mathrm{mmHg}$ is the same force-per-area idea: $120\ \mathrm{mmHg} \approx 16.0\ \mathrm{kPa}$.

steps.label: Hydraulics
steps.text: A jack lifting with $10\ \mathrm{MPa}$ uses $F = PA$ identically — only the magnitude changes.

examples.result: One definition $P = F/A$, one unit family, three trades.

examples.title: Levers in body and shop
examples.problem: Compare the forearm holding a load with a shop crowbar.

steps.label: Body
steps.text: The biceps pulls a few centimeters from the elbow to support a load $30\ \mathrm{cm}$ out — a third-class lever with $MA < 1$.

steps.label: Shop
steps.text: A crowbar with effort arm $90\ \mathrm{cm}$ and load arm $15\ \mathrm{cm}$ gives $MA = 6$.

steps.label: Common law
steps.text: Both obey moment balance $F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2$ from Chapter 7/10.

examples.result: Anatomy and tools share the same moment law with different trade-offs.

keyTakeaways: Chemistry, life science, and engineering all quantify with physics units and laws.
Pressure, energy, levers, and waves reappear in every technical field.
Mastering units and method once pays off across all of them.

quiz.q: $120\ \mathrm{mmHg}$ blood pressure and $220\ \mathrm{kPa}$ tire pressure share
options: The same quantity $P = F/A$ in convertible units
quiz.explanation: Both are force per area; $1\ \mathrm{mmHg} \approx 133\ \mathrm{Pa}$ converts between them.

quiz.q: The forearm holding a weight and a crowbar both obey
quiz.explanation: Both are levers; equilibrium of moments governs each.

quiz.q: Why do shared SI units matter across fields?
options: They let different trades trust and convert each other numbers
They remove the need for measurement
quiz.explanation: Common units make a joule, pascal, or watt mean the same thing to everyone.

intro: Physics advances by testing theories against measurement and distilling the survivors into laws. This section defines those terms precisely and introduces the step-by-step problem routine used throughout the book.
objectives: Distinguish a theory, a law, and a hypothesis correctly
State how laws are tested and why they remain revisable
Apply the book problem-solving routine to a simple formula

concepts.statement: A **hypothesis** is a testable guess, a **theory** is a well-tested explanatory framework, and a **law** is a concise, repeatedly verified relation such as $F = ma$.
concepts.detail: Laws describe what happens quantitatively; theories explain why within their tested range.

concepts.statement: A law survives only by **agreeing with controlled measurement again and again**, and it stays open to refinement when instruments improve.
concepts.detail: Newton laws rule everyday speeds and sizes; relativity and quantum extend the range without repealing the shop-floor results.

concepts.statement: State the **given data with units, pick the law, solve it symbolically, substitute, and check units and sense** — the five-step habit of Chapters 2-3.
concepts.detail: Writing $v = 20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ rather than bare $20$ catches most errors before they propagate.

concepts.statement: The **units must balance**: both sides of $s = vt$ give meters since $(\mathrm{m/s})(\mathrm{s}) = \mathrm{m}$.
concepts.detail: If they do not, the setup is wrong no matter how careful the arithmetic.

concepts.statement: Every answer needs a **sense check**: sign, size, and unit plausibility against experience before boxing it.
concepts.detail: A car stopping distance of $3\ \mathrm{mm}$ or a negative absolute temperature fails this filter instantly.

figures.caption: The test loop: hypothesis, measurement, law, and the problem routine that applies it
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="The test loop: hypothesis, measurement, law, and the problem routine that applies it" viewBox="0 0 400 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><rect x="20" y="60" width="80" height="50" rx="20"/><rect x="160" y="60" width="80" height="50" rx="4"/><rect x="300" y="60" width="80" height="50" rx="20"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><line x1="100" y1="85" x2="160" y2="85"/><line x1="240" y1="85" x2="300" y2="85"/><path d="M 200 110 L 200 140 L 60 140 L 60 110" fill="none"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="32" y="90">predict</text><text x="172" y="90">measure</text><text x="318" y="90">law?</text><text x="150" y="160">units + sense check</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Using the routine on $s = vt$
examples.problem: A conveyor moves stock at $v = 1.50\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $t = 12.0\ \mathrm{s}$. How far does the stock travel?

steps.label: Given and law
steps.text: $v = 1.50\ \mathrm{m/s}$, $t = 12.0\ \mathrm{s}$; law $s = vt$.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: $s = (1.50\ \mathrm{m/s})(12.0\ \mathrm{s}) = 18.0\ \mathrm{m}$; seconds cancel.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Units give meters as required; $18\ \mathrm{m}$ is a sensible conveyor run.

examples.result: $s = 18.0\ \mathrm{m}$ with units balanced and magnitude reasonable.

examples.title: Catching an error by units
examples.problem: A student writes stopping time $t = v \cdot a$ with $v$ in $\mathrm{m/s}$ and $a$ in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Is it plausible?

steps.label: Check units
steps.text: $(\mathrm{m/s})(\mathrm{m/s^2}) = \mathrm{m^2/s^3}$, not seconds.

steps.label: Repair
steps.text: The correct form $t = v/a$ gives $(\mathrm{m/s})/(\mathrm{m/s^2}) = \mathrm{s}$.

steps.label: Numbers
steps.text: $v = 20\ \mathrm{m/s}$, $a = 5.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ gives $t = 4.0\ \mathrm{s}$, which is sensible.

examples.result: Unit mismatch exposes the error; $t = v/a = 4.0\ \mathrm{s}$ is the correct form.

keyTakeaways: Hypotheses are tested, theories explain, and laws state verified quantitative relations.
Laws hold within tested ranges and are refined, not casually discarded.
Given-units, law, substitution, unit check, sense check solves nearly every problem ahead.

quiz.q: Which ordering is correct?
options: Theory is weaker than a guess
quiz.explanation: Hypotheses are tested into theories; the most compact verified relations are stated as laws.

quiz.q: A student proposes $t = v \cdot a$ for stopping time. The unit check gives
options: $\mathrm{m^2/s^3}$, so the form is wrong; $t = v/a$ is correct
quiz.explanation: Units must balance; only $v/a$ yields seconds.

quiz.q: The final step of every Ewen solution should be
options: Checking units, sign, and order of magnitude
quiz.explanation: A sense check catches sign, size, and unit errors the arithmetic hides.

intro: Every measurement compares an unknown against an agreed standard, and the whole of physics depends on those standards being stable. This section introduces the SI and U.S. customary standards and the base quantities length, mass, and time.
objectives: Name the standard unit for length, mass, and time in SI and U.S. systems
Explain what makes a good physical standard
Convert simple lengths between inches, feet, and meters

concepts.statement: A **standard** is an agreed, reproducible reference — the meter, kilogram, and second in SI — against which all measurements of that kind are compared.
concepts.detail: Modern standards rest on unchanging physics: the meter is defined from the speed of light and the second from atomic transitions.

concepts.statement: SI base units used in this book are the **meter ($\mathrm{m}$) for length, kilogram ($\mathrm{kg}$) for mass, and second ($\mathrm{s}$) for time**, with derived units like the newton built from them.
concepts.detail: SI is decimal throughout, so conversions are powers of ten handled by prefixes.

concepts.statement: Shop work in the U.S. still uses the **inch, foot, yard, mile, pound, and second**, related by $12\ \mathrm{in} = 1\ \mathrm{ft}$ and $5280\ \mathrm{ft} = 1\ \mathrm{mi}$.
concepts.detail: Technicians must convert both ways because drawings, nameplates, and suppliers mix systems.

concepts.statement: Length, mass, and time are **fundamental**; area ($\mathrm{m^2}$), volume ($\mathrm{m^3}$), speed ($\mathrm{m/s}$), and force ($\mathrm{N} = \mathrm{kg \cdot m/s^2}$) are **derived** from them.
concepts.detail: Unit algebra on derived units is the error filter of Chapter 2.

concepts.statement: A good standard is **accessible, invariable, and reproducible** so any equipped lab gets the same value.
concepts.detail: That is why artifact bars gave way to atomic and light-based definitions.

figures.caption: Standards ladder: comparing a shop part against the inch, foot, and meter references
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Standards ladder: comparing a shop part against the inch, foot, and meter references" viewBox="0 0 400 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><line x1="30" y1="120" x2="370" y2="120"/><line x1="30" y1="110" x2="30" y2="120"/><line x1="150" y1="105" x2="150" y2="120"/><line x1="370" y1="110" x2="370" y2="120"/><rect x="60" y="80" width="120" height="30" rx="2"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="30" y="140">0</text><text x="140" y="140">12 in = 1 ft</text><text x="300" y="140">1 m = 39.37 in</text><text x="70" y="100">shop part</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Feet and inches to meters
examples.problem: A shaft is $6\ \mathrm{ft}\ 2\ \mathrm{in}$ long. Express it in meters using $1\ \mathrm{in} = 2.54\ \mathrm{cm}$.

steps.label: Total inches
steps.text: $6 \times 12 + 2 = 74\ \mathrm{in}$.

steps.label: Round
steps.text: Given data to the inch justifies $1.88\ \mathrm{m}$.

examples.result: About $1.88\ \mathrm{m}$ long.

examples.title: Miles to kilometers
examples.problem: A truck route is $85\ \mathrm{mi}$. How many kilometers is that with $1\ \mathrm{mi} = 1.609\ \mathrm{km}$?

steps.label: Set up
steps.text: $85\ \mathrm{mi} \times 1.609\ \mathrm{km/mi}$ so miles cancel.

steps.label: Report
steps.text: About $137\ \mathrm{km}$ at two-significant-digit input.

examples.result: About $137\ \mathrm{km}$.

keyTakeaways: SI measures length, mass, time in meters, kilograms, seconds; U.S. shops add inches, feet, pounds.
Derived units like $\mathrm{N}$ and $\mathrm{m/s}$ are products of base units.
Convert by unity fractions so unwanted units cancel.

quiz.q: The SI base units for length, mass, and time are
quiz.explanation: SI uses $\mathrm{m}$, $\mathrm{kg}$, $\mathrm{s}$; the rest are derived.

quiz.q: $6\ \mathrm{ft}\ 2\ \mathrm{in}$ is about
quiz.explanation: $74\ \mathrm{in} \times 2.54\ \mathrm{cm/in} = 188\ \mathrm{cm}$.

quiz.q: A good measurement standard must be
quiz.explanation: Reproducibility across labs is the whole point of a standard.

intro: The metric system replaces dozens of conversion factors with one idea: prefixes that are powers of ten. Mastering milli, centi, kilo, and mega turns most conversions into decimal-point moves.
objectives: Use the common metric prefixes from milli to mega correctly
Convert within the metric system by powers of ten
Convert between metric and U.S. units for shop quantities

concepts.statement: Prefixes scale the base unit by tens: **milli ($10^{-3}$), centi ($10^{-2}$), kilo ($10^{3}$), mega ($10^{6}$)**, with micro ($10^{-6}$) and nano ($10^{-9}$) for electronics.
concepts.detail: So $1\ \mathrm{km} = 1000\ \mathrm{m}$ and $1\ \mathrm{mm} = 0.001\ \mathrm{m}$ by definition.

concepts.statement: Within SI, **move the decimal point** by the prefix difference: $2.5\ \mathrm{m} = 250\ \mathrm{cm} = 2500\ \mathrm{mm}$.
concepts.detail: Count steps on the prefix ladder rather than memorizing separate factors.

concepts.statement: Key bridges are **$1\ \mathrm{in} = 2.54\ \mathrm{cm}$**, $1\ \mathrm{kg} = 2.205\ \mathrm{lb}$, and $1\ \mathrm{L} = 1.057\ \mathrm{qt}$.
concepts.detail: Ewen tabulates these; memorizing the three above handles most shop problems.

concepts.statement: SI **mass** in kilograms is invariant; **weight** $W = mg$ is a force in newtons that changes with $g$.
concepts.detail: A $10\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass weighs $98.0\ \mathrm{N}$ on earth but far less on the moon.

concepts.statement: Pick the prefix that keeps numbers **between 0.1 and 1000**: $0.0025\ \mathrm{m}$ reads better as $2.5\ \mathrm{mm}$.
concepts.detail: Drawings and meters follow this convention to prevent misread digits.

examples.title: Millimeters to meters on a drawing
examples.problem: A print calls out $850\ \mathrm{mm}$ and $0.045\ \mathrm{Mm}$. Express each in meters.

steps.label: Millimeters
steps.text: $850\ \mathrm{mm} = 850 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 0.850\ \mathrm{m}$.

steps.label: Sense
steps.text: One is a bench dimension, the other a pipeline distance — prefixes keep both readable.

examples.title: Pounds to kilograms
examples.problem: A motor nameplate reads $88\ \mathrm{lb}$. What is its mass in kilograms?

steps.label: Factor
steps.text: $1\ \mathrm{kg} = 2.205\ \mathrm{lb}$, so divide: $88/2.205$.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $88/2.205 \approx 39.9\ \mathrm{kg}$.

steps.label: Weight check
steps.text: $W = mg = 39.9 \times 9.80 \approx 391\ \mathrm{N}$.

examples.result: About $39.9\ \mathrm{kg}$ of mass, weighing $391\ \mathrm{N}$.

keyTakeaways: Metric prefixes are powers of ten; convert by moving the decimal point.
Remember $1\ \mathrm{in} = 2.54\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $1\ \mathrm{kg} = 2.205\ \mathrm{lb}$.
Mass ($\mathrm{kg}$) is invariant; weight ($\mathrm{N}$) depends on $g$.

quiz.q: $2.5\ \mathrm{m}$ equals
quiz.explanation: $1\ \mathrm{m} = 100\ \mathrm{cm}$, so $2.5 \times 100 = 250\ \mathrm{cm}$.

quiz.q: An $88\ \mathrm{lb}$ motor has mass about
quiz.explanation: $88/2.205 \approx 39.9\ \mathrm{kg}$.

quiz.q: Which prefix choice is best for $0.0025\ \mathrm{m}$ on a drawing?
quiz.explanation: $2.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ keeps the number in the readable 0.1-1000 range.

intro: Technicians constantly meet numbers too large or small for plain decimals, from microamperes to megohms. Scientific notation writes every value as a digit factor times a power of ten so arithmetic stays exact and compact.
objectives: Write any number in normalized scientific notation
Multiply, divide, and power numbers in scientific notation
Use the calculator EE key and read its output correctly

concepts.detail: One nonzero digit before the point is the normalization rule examiners check.

concepts.statement: Multiply digit factors and **add exponents**; divide digit factors and **subtract exponents**: $(2.0 \times 10^{5})(3.0 \times 10^{-2}) = 6.0 \times 10^{3}$.
concepts.detail: Renormalize afterward if the digit factor leaves the 1-10 range.

concepts.statement: Raise the digit factor and **multiply the exponent**: $(2.0 \times 10^{3})^2 = 4.0 \times 10^{6}$; for roots divide it.
concepts.detail: Squaring doubles the exponent, which is why areas and $I^2R$ heating jump orders of magnitude.

concepts.statement: The **EE or EXP key** enters powers of ten: $4.72\mathrm{E}{-4}$ means $4.72 \times 10^{-4}$, never $4.72$ times $e$.
concepts.detail: A display of $6.00\mathrm{E}3$ reads $6000$, with the exponent carrying the size.

concepts.statement: To add, first **match exponents**, then add digit factors: $4.0 \times 10^{5} + 3.0 \times 10^{4} = 4.3 \times 10^{5}$.
concepts.detail: Adding raw digit factors at different exponents is the classic notation error.

figures.caption: Powers-of-ten ladder: each step multiplies by 10, digit factor $N$ rides along
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Powers-of-ten ladder: each step multiplies by 10, digit factor N rides along" viewBox="0 0 400 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><line x1="40" y1="75" x2="360" y2="75"/><polygon points="360,75 348,69 348,81" fill="currentColor"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"><line x1="80" y1="65" x2="80" y2="85"/><line x1="160" y1="65" x2="160" y2="85"/><line x1="240" y1="65" x2="240" y2="85"/><line x1="320" y1="65" x2="320" y2="85"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="60" y="60">10⁻³</text><text x="145" y="60">10⁰</text><text x="225" y="60">10³</text><text x="305" y="60">10⁶</text><text x="150" y="110">milli — unit — kilo — mega</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Ohm law with prefixes
examples.problem: Current $I = 4.72 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{A}$ flows through $R = 2.20 \times 10^{3}\ \Omega$. Find $V = IR$.

steps.label: Renormalize
steps.text: $V = 1.0384\ \mathrm{V} \approx 1.04\ \mathrm{V}$.

examples.result: About $1.04\ \mathrm{V}$ across the resistor.

examples.title: Power in a heating element
examples.problem: A $15.0\ \mathrm{A}$ current flows in a $9.60\ \Omega$ element. Compute $P = I^2 R$.

steps.label: Notation
steps.text: $P = 2.16 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{W} = 2.16\ \mathrm{kW}$.

examples.result: $2.16 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{W}$ of heating power.

keyTakeaways: Normalize to one digit before the point: $N \times 10^{n}$, $1 \le N < 10$.
Multiply factors and add exponents; divide factors and subtract.
Match exponents before adding; read EE displays as powers of ten.

quiz.explanation: Multiply $2.0 \times 3.0 = 6.0$ and add $5 + (-2) = 3$.

quiz.q: The normalized form of 0.000472 is
quiz.explanation: One nonzero digit before the point gives $4.72 \times 10^{-4}$.

quiz.q: To add $4.0 \times 10^{5} + 3.0 \times 10^{4}$ you must
options: Convert to a common exponent first

intro: Length is the most-measured quantity in the shop, and its conversions seed every area, volume, and speed calculation later. This section locks in inch-foot-yard-mile and millimeter-centimeter-meter bridges with worked conversions.
objectives: Convert lengths within and between English and metric systems
Select sensible length units for a given job
Solve applied length problems with unit cancellation

concepts.statement: **$12\ \mathrm{in} = 1\ \mathrm{ft}$**, $3\ \mathrm{ft} = 1\ \mathrm{yd}$, $5280\ \mathrm{ft} = 1\ \mathrm{mi}$ — the exact rungs for shop conversion.
concepts.detail: Chain unity fractions so each unwanted unit cancels in turn.

concepts.statement: **$10\ \mathrm{mm} = 1\ \mathrm{cm}$**, $100\ \mathrm{cm} = 1\ \mathrm{m}$, $1000\ \mathrm{m} = 1\ \mathrm{km}$ — decimal steps only.
concepts.detail: A tape reading $2.435\ \mathrm{m}$ is $243.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ or $2435\ \mathrm{mm}$ without any new factor.

concepts.statement: The exact bridge **$1\ \mathrm{in} = 2.54\ \mathrm{cm}$** connects the systems; everything else follows by chaining.
concepts.detail: From it: $1\ \mathrm{m} = 39.37\ \mathrm{in}$ and $1\ \mathrm{mi} = 1.609\ \mathrm{km}$.

concepts.statement: Multiply by **fractions equal to one**, e.g. $\dfrac{2.54\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{in}}$, arranged so unwanted units cancel.
concepts.detail: The surviving unit is the answer unit — a built-in check on the setup.

concepts.statement: A **rule reads to $\pm 0.5\ \mathrm{mm}$**, calipers to $0.02\ \mathrm{mm}$, micrometers to $0.01\ \mathrm{mm}$ — never report more digits than the tool earns.
concepts.detail: Conversion cannot manufacture precision the measurement never had.

examples.title: Blueprint dimension to millimeters
examples.problem: A detail measures $7.25\ \mathrm{in}$ on a scaled print. How wide is it in millimeters?

steps.label: Bridge
steps.text: $7.25\ \mathrm{in} \times 25.4\ \mathrm{mm/in}$.

steps.label: Report
steps.text: Input to three digits gives $184\ \mathrm{mm}$.

examples.result: About $184\ \mathrm{mm}$ wide.

examples.title: Marathon distance check
examples.problem: A race is $26.2\ \mathrm{mi}$. Confirm it is about $42.2\ \mathrm{km}$.

steps.label: Cross-check
steps.text: Via feet: $26.2 \times 5280 = 138{,}336\ \mathrm{ft} = 42{,}169\ \mathrm{m}$.

steps.label: Agree
steps.text: Both routes give $42.2\ \mathrm{km}$ — setup verified.

examples.result: $42.2\ \mathrm{km}$, confirmed two ways.

keyTakeaways: Chain unity fractions; the surviving unit checks your setup.
The $2.54\ \mathrm{cm/in}$ bridge links every length system.
Round converted values to the precision of the original measurement.

quiz.q: $7.25\ \mathrm{in}$ in millimeters is about
Which equals $1\ \mathrm{mi}$?
quiz.explanation: The definition is $5280\ \mathrm{ft} = 1\ \mathrm{mi}$.

quiz.q: A micrometer reading $12.34\ \mathrm{mm}$ converted to meters should be reported as
quiz.explanation: Conversion moves the decimal only; it never adds or drops justified digits.

intro: Area and volume conversions trap students because the linear factor must be squared or cubed. This section derives those factors once and applies them to flooring, tanks, and material estimates.
objectives: Explain why area factors are squared and volume factors cubed
Convert areas and volumes within and across systems
Compute material quantities from area and volume

concepts.statement: If $1\ \mathrm{ft} = 12\ \mathrm{in}$ then **$1\ \mathrm{ft^2} = 144\ \mathrm{in^2}$**; linear factors must be squared for area.
concepts.detail: Likewise $1\ \mathrm{m^2} = 10{,}000\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ since $100^2 = 10{,}000$.

concepts.statement: If $1\ \mathrm{m} = 100\ \mathrm{cm}$ then **$1\ \mathrm{m^3} = 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$**; linear factors must be cubed for volume.
concepts.detail: And $1\ \mathrm{ft^3} = 1728\ \mathrm{in^3}$ from $12^3$.

concepts.statement: **$1\ \mathrm{L} = 1000\ \mathrm{cm^3} = 1.057\ \mathrm{qt}$** connects metric volume to shop liquid measure.
concepts.detail: A gallon is $3.785\ \mathrm{L}$ — the tank-sizing bridge.

concepts.statement: Box $V = lwh$, cylinder **$V = \pi r^2 h$** — the two volume formulas that size nearly every tank and bin.
concepts.detail: Keep radius versus diameter straight: $r = d/2$ before squaring.

concepts.statement: Multiply computed area or volume by a **unit rate** ($\$/\mathrm{ft^2}$, $\$/\mathrm{gal}$) to estimate material cost.
concepts.detail: Waste factors of 5-10 percent are added after the exact geometry.

figures.caption: Why $1\ \mathrm{ft^2} = 144\ \mathrm{in^2}$: a 12-by-12 grid of square inches
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Why 1\ mathrmft^2 = 144\ mathrmin^2: a 12-by-12 grid of square inches" viewBox="0 0 400 170" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><rect x="140" y="15" width="120" height="120"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.7" fill="none"><line x1="170" y1="15" x2="170" y2="135"/><line x1="200" y1="15" x2="200" y2="135"/><line x1="230" y1="15" x2="230" y2="135"/><line x1="140" y1="45" x2="260" y2="45"/><line x1="140" y1="75" x2="260" y2="75"/><line x1="140" y1="105" x2="260" y2="105"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="145" y="152">12 in × 12 in = 144 in² = 1 ft²</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Flooring estimate
examples.problem: A shop floor is $24\ \mathrm{ft}$ by $36\ \mathrm{ft}$. How many square meters of coating are needed?

steps.label: Area
steps.text: $A = 24 \times 36 = 864\ \mathrm{ft^2}$.

steps.label: Convert
steps.text: $1\ \mathrm{ft^2} = 0.092903\ \mathrm{m^2}$, so $864 \times 0.092903 \approx 80.27\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

steps.label: Order
steps.text: Add 5 percent waste: about $84\ \mathrm{m^2}$ to order.

examples.result: About $80.3\ \mathrm{m^2}$ net; order roughly $84\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

examples.title: Cylindrical tank gallons
examples.problem: A cylindrical tank has diameter $1.20\ \mathrm{m}$ and height $2.00\ \mathrm{m}$. What is its capacity in gallons?
examples.result: About $598\ \mathrm{gal}$ capacity.

keyTakeaways: Square the linear factor for area, cube it for volume.
$1\ \mathrm{ft^2} = 144\ \mathrm{in^2}$; $1\ \mathrm{m^3} = 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.
Size boxes with $lwh$ and tanks with $\pi r^2 h$, then convert to sale units.

quiz.q: $1\ \mathrm{ft^2}$ equals
quiz.explanation: Area squares the linear factor: $12^2 = 144$.

quiz.q: A $24 \times 36\ \mathrm{ft}$ floor is about
quiz.explanation: $864 \times 0.092903 \approx 80.3\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

quiz.q: A cylinder of $r = 0.60\ \mathrm{m}$, $h = 2.00\ \mathrm{m}$ holds about
quiz.explanation: $V \approx 2.262\ \mathrm{m^3} = 2262\ \mathrm{L} \approx 598\ \mathrm{gal}$.

intro: Beyond length, the shop measures time, mass, force, pressure, temperature, and angles. This section collects those secondary units and the exact bridges between English and metric forms.
objectives: Convert mass, time, force, and pressure units across systems
Distinguish mass, force, and weight units correctly
Handle temperature and angle units in applied problems

concepts.statement: **$60\ \mathrm{s} = 1\ \mathrm{min}$**, $3600\ \mathrm{s} = 1\ \mathrm{h}$ — the same in both systems, the base of speed and power units.
concepts.detail: Miles per hour to feet per second uses $1\ \mathrm{mi/h} = 1.467\ \mathrm{ft/s}$.

concepts.statement: SI force is the **newton ($1\ \mathrm{N} = 1\ \mathrm{kg \cdot m/s^2}$)**; English force is the **pound ($1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$)**.
concepts.detail: Never state a force in kilograms — kilograms are mass.

concepts.statement: Pressure is force per area: **$1\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \mathrm{N/m^2}$**, with $1\ \mathrm{psi} = 6.895\ \mathrm{kPa}$ and $1\ \mathrm{atm} = 101.3\ \mathrm{kPa}$.
concepts.detail: Gauges in psi convert to SI through kilopascals for $F = PA$ work.

concepts.statement: Intervals convert by factors but readings need offsets: **$T_F = \frac{9}{5}T_C + 32$** and $T_K = T_C + 273.15$.
concepts.detail: A $10\ \mathrm{C^\circ}$ rise is an $18\ \mathrm{F^\circ}$ rise, but $10\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$ is $50\ \mathrm{^{\circ}F}$.

concepts.statement: **$360^{\circ} = 2\pi\ \mathrm{rad}$**, so $1\ \mathrm{rad} \approx 57.3^{\circ}$; rotation chapters use both.
concepts.detail: Revolutions per minute convert via $1\ \mathrm{rev} = 2\pi\ \mathrm{rad}$.

examples.title: Tire pressure to kilopascals
examples.problem: A tire gauge reads $32\ \mathrm{psi}$. Express it in kilopascals.

steps.label: Factor
steps.text: $1\ \mathrm{psi} = 6.895\ \mathrm{kPa}$.

steps.label: Report
steps.text: About $221\ \mathrm{kPa}$ gauge.

examples.result: About $221\ \mathrm{kPa}$.

examples.title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
examples.problem: A curing oven runs at $175\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$. What is that in Fahrenheit?

steps.label: Report
steps.text: About $347\ \mathrm{^{\circ}F}$.

examples.result: $347\ \mathrm{^{\circ}F}$.

keyTakeaways: Forces convert by $1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$; pressures by $1\ \mathrm{psi} = 6.895\ \mathrm{kPa}$.
Temperature readings need the $+32$ offset; intervals do not.
Keep mass ($\mathrm{kg}$) and force ($\mathrm{N}$, $\mathrm{lb}$) units strictly apart.

quiz.q: $32\ \mathrm{psi}$ is about
quiz.explanation: $32 \times 6.895 = 220.6\ \mathrm{kPa}$.

quiz.q: $175\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$ equals
Which unit correctly states a force?
quiz.explanation: Force is $\mathrm{N}$ (SI) or $\mathrm{lb}$ (English); $\mathrm{kg}$ is mass.

intro: No measurement is exact, and honest physics reports only the digits the instrument earns. This section defines significant digits and accuracy, then shows how to round without corrupting results.
objectives: Count significant digits under the standard rules
Distinguish accuracy from instrument resolution
Round converted and computed values correctly

concepts.statement: Significant digits are the **reliably known digits plus one estimated digit**; $12.34\ \mathrm{mm}$ from a caliper carries four.
concepts.detail: Leading zeros never count ($0.00472$ has three); trapped and trailing-with-point zeros do ($40.70$ has four).

concepts.statement: Nonzero digits always count; **zeros between digits count; leading zeros do not; trailing zeros count only with a shown point**.
concepts.detail: So $1005$ has four, $0.0100$ has three, and $500$ is ambiguous without notation.

concepts.statement: **Accuracy** is closeness to the true value, limited by calibration and technique — distinct from how many digits you write.
concepts.detail: An accurate $10.0\ \mathrm{V}$ reading sits near $10.0\ \mathrm{V}$ true; a $10.0000\ \mathrm{V}$ display can still be wrong if uncalibrated.

concepts.statement: Round half up at the cut digit and **round only once, at the end**: $184.15\ \mathrm{mm}$ to three digits is $184\ \mathrm{mm}$.
concepts.detail: Repeated rounding during a chain drifts the answer; carry a guard digit until the end.

concepts.statement: Defined conversions ($12\ \mathrm{in/ft}$) and counted objects have **unlimited digits** and never limit significance.
concepts.detail: Only measured inputs cap the reported digits of a result.

figures.caption: Reading the estimated digit: the pointer falls between marks, so the last digit is judged
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Reading the estimated digit: the pointer falls between marks, so the last digit is judged" viewBox="0 0 400 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><line x1="40" y1="100" x2="360" y2="100"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"><line x1="60" y1="85" x2="60" y2="100"/><line x1="120" y1="85" x2="120" y2="100"/><line x1="180" y1="85" x2="180" y2="100"/><line x1="240" y1="85" x2="240" y2="100"/><line x1="300" y1="85" x2="300" y2="100"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5"><line x1="205" y1="40" x2="205" y2="100"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="55" y="120">10</text><text x="115" y="120">11</text><text x="175" y="120">12</text><text x="235" y="120">13</text><text x="200" y="30">reads 12.4 (4 estimated)</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Counting digits
examples.problem: How many significant digits do $0.00472$, $40.70$, and $1005$ carry?

steps.text: Leading zeros do not count; 4, 7, 2 count: three digits.
Trapped zero plus trailing zero with point count: four digits.
Zeros between nonzeros count: four digits.

examples.result: Three, four, and four significant digits respectively.

examples.title: Rounding a conversion
examples.problem: Convert $7.25\ \mathrm{in}$ ($184.15\ \mathrm{mm}$ raw) to proper digits.

steps.label: Input digits
steps.text: $7.25$ carries three significant digits.

steps.label: Cut
steps.text: Keep three: $184.15 \to 184$ since the next digit 1 rounds down.

steps.label: Report
steps.text: $184\ \mathrm{mm}$ — writing $184.15$ would claim five-digit precision never measured.

examples.result: $184\ \mathrm{mm}$ at honest precision.

keyTakeaways: Count sig digits: nonzeros, trapped zeros, and pointed trailing zeros.
Accuracy is closeness to truth; digits alone do not guarantee it.
Round once at the end; defined factors never limit digits.

quiz.q: How many significant digits does 40.70 carry?
quiz.explanation: 4, 0 (trapped), 7, and the pointed trailing 0 all count.

quiz.q: $184.15\ \mathrm{mm}$ from three-digit input should be reported as
quiz.explanation: Three-digit input justifies three digits: 184.

quiz.q: Accuracy means
quiz.explanation: Accuracy is truth-closeness; resolution is a separate property.

intro: A reading can be repeatable yet wrong: that is the gap between precision and accuracy. This section teaches you to diagnose both from repeated measurements and instrument limits.
objectives: Distinguish precision from accuracy with examples
Estimate precision from repeated readings
State how instrument resolution limits reported digits

concepts.statement: **Precision** is repeatability — the tightness of repeated readings — while accuracy is closeness to the true value.
concepts.detail: Four readings $10.31, 10.33, 10.32, 10.32\ \mathrm{V}$ are precise; whether they are accurate depends on calibration.

concepts.statement: Measurements can be **accurate and precise, precise but biased, accurate-on-average but scattered, or neither** — each pattern points to a different fix.
concepts.detail: Tight-but-off means recalibrate; centered-but-scattered means improve technique or resolution.

concepts.statement: The **spread (max minus min)** of repeats estimates precision: readings spanning $0.05\ \mathrm{mm}$ are precise to about that band.
concepts.detail: Report the mean with uncertainty near half the spread for shop purposes.

concepts.statement: No reading can honestly carry digits **finer than the instrument resolution** — a $1\ \mathrm{mm}$ rule cannot give $0.1\ \mathrm{mm}$ digits.
concepts.detail: The last reported digit is the estimated fraction of the smallest division.

concepts.statement: **Calibration** compares the instrument against a higher standard and corrects systematic bias, restoring accuracy.
concepts.detail: Precision without calibration is precisely wrong — the most expensive kind of error.

examples.title: Diagnosing a caliper set
examples.problem: Four length readings: $25.31, 25.33, 25.32, 25.34\ \mathrm{mm}$. A gauge block says the true length is $25.80\ \mathrm{mm}$. Diagnose.

steps.label: Precision
steps.text: Spread is $0.03\ \mathrm{mm}$ — highly repeatable, precise to about $\pm 0.02\ \mathrm{mm}$.

steps.label: Accuracy
steps.text: Mean $25.325$ versus true $25.80$: bias of about $-0.48\ \mathrm{mm}$ — inaccurate.

steps.label: Fix
steps.text: Precise but biased: recalibrate or apply a $+0.48\ \mathrm{mm}$ correction, not more repeats.

examples.result: Precise but inaccurate — a calibration problem, not a steadiness problem.

examples.title: Resolution honesty
examples.problem: A rule with $1\ \mathrm{mm}$ divisions reads a part near $143\ \mathrm{mm}$. How should it be reported?

steps.label: Estimate
steps.text: Judge tenths of the division: e.g. $143.4\ \mathrm{mm}$ with the 4 estimated.

steps.label: Limit
steps.text: Four digits total is the maximum; $143.42\ \mathrm{mm}$ claims resolution never owned.

steps.label: Report
steps.text: $143.4\ \mathrm{mm}$ with uncertainty about $\pm 0.5\ \mathrm{mm}$.

examples.result: $143.4\ \mathrm{mm}$ is honest; more digits would be fiction.

keyTakeaways: Precision is repeatability; accuracy is truth-closeness; you need both.
Tight-but-off readings need calibration; scattered readings need technique.
Never report digits finer than the instrument resolution earns.

quiz.q: Readings 25.31-25.34 mm against a 25.80 mm true value are
quiz.explanation: Spread $0.03\ \mathrm{mm}$ is tight but the mean sits $0.48\ \mathrm{mm}$ low.

quiz.q: A $1\ \mathrm{mm}$ rule reading should be reported as
quiz.explanation: One estimated digit beyond the division: tenths of a millimeter.

quiz.q: The cure for precise-but-biased readings is
quiz.explanation: Systematic bias is removed by calibration, not by repetition.

intro: Measured data combine through multiplication, division, addition, and powers, and each operation has a digit rule. This section gives those rules and works full technician calculations with honest rounding.
objectives: Apply the product/quotient digit rule correctly
Apply the sum/difference place rule correctly
Complete multi-step shop calculations with end-only rounding

concepts.statement: For $\times$ and $\div$, the result carries **no more significant digits than the weakest input**: $8.45 \times 2.4 = 20$ (two digits).
concepts.detail: Raw $20.28$ must be cut to $20.$ or $2.0 \times 10^{1}$ to show two digits honestly.

concepts.statement: For $+$ and $-$, the result keeps **no place finer than the coarsest input place**: $12.4 + 3.75 = 16.2$ (tenths rule).
concepts.detail: Digits count differently here — decimal place, not digit count, governs.

concepts.statement: Powers and roots **keep the input digit count**: $(2.50)^2 = 6.25$ keeps three digits.
concepts.detail: Squaring does not manufacture certainty; it inherits it.

concepts.statement: Carry **one guard digit through chains** and round only the final answer to its justified digits.
concepts.detail: Early rounding injects up to half a unit of error at every step.

concepts.statement: Every calculation line must **carry and cancel units** alongside digits: $(2.00\ \mathrm{m})(3.0\ \mathrm{m}) = 6.0\ \mathrm{m^2}$.
concepts.detail: Units verify the operation while digits verify the honesty.

figures.caption: Digit rules at a glance: weakest count governs $\times/\div$, coarsest place governs $+/-$
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Digit rules at a glance: weakest count governs times/div, coarsest place governs +/-" viewBox="0 0 400 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><rect x="30" y="30" width="160" height="90" rx="6"/><rect x="210" y="30" width="160" height="90" rx="6"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="12" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="45" y="60">8.45 × 2.4 = 20</text><text x="45" y="85">weakest count wins</text><text x="225" y="60">12.4 + 3.75 = 16.2</text><text x="225" y="85">coarsest place wins</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Plate area with honest digits
examples.problem: A plate measures $8.45\ \mathrm{cm}$ by $2.4\ \mathrm{cm}$. What is its area?

steps.label: Multiply
steps.text: $8.45 \times 2.4 = 20.28\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ raw.

steps.label: Rule
steps.text: Weakest input has two digits ($2.4$), so keep two: $20.\ \mathrm{cm^2}$.

steps.label: Report
steps.text: Write $2.0 \times 10^{1}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ to show two digits unambiguously.

examples.title: Density from three measurements
examples.problem: A block mass $m = 452.0\ \mathrm{g}$ has volume $V = 58.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ from three-digit dimensions. Find density.

steps.label: Rule
steps.text: Three-digit inputs justify three digits: $7.79\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

steps.label: Identify
steps.text: Near iron at $7.87\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ — plausibly steel within error.

examples.result: $7.79\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ — consistent with steel.

keyTakeaways: Multiply/divide: weakest digit count wins; add/subtract: coarsest place wins.
Round once at the end with a guard digit through the chain.
Carry units on every line and let them verify the operation.

quiz.q: $8.45 \times 2.4$ should be reported as
quiz.explanation: Two-digit input caps the product at two digits.

quiz.q: $12.4 + 3.75$ should be reported as
quiz.explanation: Coarsest input place is tenths, so keep tenths.

quiz.q: In a chained calculation you should
options: Carry a guard digit and round only at the end
quiz.explanation: End-only rounding prevents accumulated rounding drift.

intro: Formulas are the working tools of applied physics: each one names a law in symbols. This section teaches you to read those symbols fluently so substitution later is mechanical and safe.
objectives: Read physics symbols as named quantities with units
Rearrange common formulas with basic algebra
Identify which formula fits a stated shop problem

concepts.term: Formula as a law in symbols
concepts.statement: A **formula** states a verified relation compactly, e.g. **$s = vt$** reads distance equals speed times time.
concepts.detail: Every letter stands for a measured quantity with units, never a bare number.

concepts.statement: Standard symbols recur: **$s$ distance, $v$ speed/velocity, $t$ time, $m$ mass, $F$ force, $W$ work, $P$ power** — subscripts like $v_0$ mark initial values.
concepts.detail: Learning this dozen symbols unlocks nearly every formula through Chapter 12.

concepts.statement: Isolate any variable by **undoing operations on both sides**: from $s = vt$ come $v = s/t$ and $t = s/v$.
concepts.detail: Divide both sides by $t$ to free $v$; the units rearrange with the symbols.

concepts.statement: Cover-and-read triangles encode three-variable laws: covering $s$ in $s/vt$ leaves **$v \times t$**, covering $v$ leaves **$s/t$**.
concepts.detail: Triangles speed routine rearrangement but never replace understanding the algebra.

concepts.statement: List **knowns and the wanted unknown**, then pick the law containing exactly those quantities.
concepts.detail: Knowing $F$ and $m$ but wanting $a$ points to $F = ma$ in its $a = F/m$ form.

figures.caption: Cover-and-read triangle for $s = vt$: cover the wanted variable to read its form
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Cover-and-read triangle for s = vt: cover the wanted variable to read its form" viewBox="0 0 400 170" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><line x1="200" y1="25" x2="110" y2="130"/><line x1="200" y1="25" x2="290" y2="130"/><line x1="110" y1="130" x2="290" y2="130"/><line x1="145" y1="85" x2="255" y2="85"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="192" y="65">s</text><text x="150" y="120">v</text><text x="235" y="120">t</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Rearranging $F = ma$
examples.problem: A $1500\ \mathrm{kg}$ car needs acceleration $2.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Which form gives the force, and what is it?

steps.label: Knowns and unknown
steps.text: Known $m$, $a$; want $F$ — the as-written form $F = ma$ already fits.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: $F = (1500\ \mathrm{kg})(2.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 3750\ \mathrm{N}$.

steps.label: Alternate form
steps.text: Had $F$ and $m$ been known, $a = F/m$ would give acceleration.

examples.result: $F = 3750\ \mathrm{N} \approx 3.75\ \mathrm{kN}$ of driving force.

examples.title: Solving power for time
examples.problem: A $750\ \mathrm{W}$ motor does $W = 15{,}000\ \mathrm{J}$ of work. How long does it take, starting from $P = W/t$?

steps.label: Rearrange
steps.text: Multiply by $t$ and divide by $P$: $t = W/P$.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: $t = 15{,}000/750 = 20\ \mathrm{s}$; joules per watt give seconds.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: $750 \times 20 = 15{,}000$ confirms the inversion.

examples.result: $t = 20\ \mathrm{s}$ of running time.

keyTakeaways: Read each symbol as quantity-plus-unit, not a bare letter.
Rearrange with inverse operations on both sides; triangles shortcut routine cases.
Match knowns and unknown to the law containing them.

quiz.q: From $s = vt$, the speed form is
quiz.explanation: Divide both sides by $t$: $v = s/t$ with units $(\mathrm{m})/(\mathrm{s})$.

quiz.q: Known $F$ and $m$, wanting $a$, you use
quiz.explanation: Solving $F = ma$ for $a$ gives $a = F/m$.

quiz.q: A $750\ \mathrm{W}$ motor doing $15{,}000\ \mathrm{J}$ runs for

intro: Substitution is where right setups become right answers — or where dropped units hide errors. This section drills the Ewen habit: replace symbols with data-plus-units, cancel, compute, and round honestly.
objectives: Substitute data with units into any formula
Convert inputs to consistent units before computing
Round the result to justified digits with the correct unit

concepts.statement: Replace each symbol by its **value with units**, e.g. $v = 20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ into $s = vt$, and let the units compute alongside.
concepts.detail: Bare-number substitution forfeits the free error check units provide.

concepts.statement: All inputs must share a **compatible system before substituting**: convert minutes to seconds, kilometers to meters first.
concepts.detail: Mixing $\mathrm{km/h}$ with seconds is the most common substitution failure.

concepts.statement: Cancel units algebraically; the **surviving unit must match the wanted quantity** or the setup is wrong.
concepts.detail: $(\mathrm{m/s})(\mathrm{s}) \to \mathrm{m}$ confirms a distance; anything else rejects it.

concepts.statement: Enter grouped denominators with **parentheses**, keep a guard digit, and re-estimate by mental arithmetic.
concepts.detail: $s = 1/2 \times 9.8 \times 4^2$ needs the square before the halving — order matters.

concepts.statement: Report the computed value **rounded to the weakest input digits with its unit**: $18.0\ \mathrm{m}$, not $18$ or $18.0000$.
concepts.detail: Chapters 1 digit rules apply to every substituted answer.

examples.title: Conveyor distance with minutes
examples.problem: A belt runs at $v = 2.40\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $3.50\ \mathrm{min}$. Find $s = vt$.

steps.label: Unify units
steps.text: $3.50\ \mathrm{min} = 3.50 \times 60 = 210\ \mathrm{s}$.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: $s = (2.40\ \mathrm{m/s})(210\ \mathrm{s}) = 504\ \mathrm{m}$.

steps.label: Round
steps.text: Three-digit input justifies $504\ \mathrm{m}$.

examples.result: The belt advances $504\ \mathrm{m}$.

examples.title: Braking force substitution
examples.problem: A $1200\ \mathrm{kg}$ car decelerates at $6.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the braking force $F = ma$.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: $F = (1200\ \mathrm{kg})(6.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}) = 7200\ \mathrm{N}$.

steps.label: Units
steps.text: $\mathrm{kg \cdot m/s^2} = \mathrm{N}$ confirms a force.

steps.label: Sense
steps.text: $7.20\ \mathrm{kN}$ total, about $1.80\ \mathrm{kN}$ per wheel — plausible.

examples.result: $7.20\ \mathrm{kN}$ of braking force.

keyTakeaways: Convert to consistent units before substituting a single digit.
Substitute value-with-unit and cancel to verify the setup.
Round the final answer to the weakest input digits.

quiz.q: Belt at $2.40\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $3.50\ \mathrm{min}$ advances
quiz.explanation: $3.50\ \mathrm{min} = 210\ \mathrm{s}$; $2.40 \times 210 = 504\ \mathrm{m}$.

quiz.q: First step when inputs mix minutes and seconds is to
options: Convert to one consistent unit system
quiz.explanation: Mixed units guarantee a wrong magnitude unless unified first.

quiz.q: A $1200\ \mathrm{kg}$ car at $6.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ needs braking force

intro: Top technicians solve problems the same way every time, so stress cannot scramble their thinking. This section formalizes the five-step Ewen routine and proves it on motion, force, and power problems.
objectives: Execute the five-step problem-solving routine reliably
Show full written work that earns partial credit
Verify answers by units, sign, and magnitude

concepts.statement: **1. Given/wanted with units. 2. Law. 3. Symbolic solution. 4. Substitution. 5. Unit and sense check** — in that order, every time.
concepts.detail: Skipping straight to numbers is how sign errors and unit mix-ups survive to the answer line.

concepts.statement: Draw a **labeled sketch** and define symbols ($v_0 = 0$, $a = +2.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$) before writing equations.
concepts.detail: The sketch fixes signs and directions that words leave ambiguous.

concepts.statement: Solve the law **in symbols first** ($t = 2s/v$), then substitute once — one arithmetic pass, fewer slips.
concepts.detail: Symbolic form also reveals whether the answer scales sensibly with inputs.

concepts.statement: Make a **rough mental estimate** before computing so the calculator result has something to agree with.
concepts.detail: $1500 \times 2.5$ is about $4000\ \mathrm{N}$; a display of $375$ would then smell wrong.

concepts.statement: Check **units, sign, and order of magnitude**; re-derive by an alternate route when anything feels off.
concepts.detail: A negative time, a force in joules, or a highway speed in $\mathrm{mm/s}$ fails loudly.

examples.title: Full-routine stopping distance
examples.problem: A car at $v_0 = 25.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ brakes at $a = -5.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ to rest. Find stopping distance via $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2as$.

steps.label: Verify
steps.text: Positive, tens of meters at highway speed — estimate $(25^2)/(10) \approx 62$ agrees.

examples.result: Stopping distance $62.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

examples.title: Hoist power check
examples.problem: A hoist lifts $m = 400\ \mathrm{kg}$ by $h = 6.00\ \mathrm{m}$ in $t = 15.0\ \mathrm{s}$. Is a $2.00\ \mathrm{kW}$ motor enough?

steps.label: Work
steps.text: $W = mgh = 400 \times 9.80 \times 6.00 = 23{,}520\ \mathrm{J}$.

steps.label: Power
steps.text: $P = W/t = 23{,}520/15.0 = 1568\ \mathrm{W} \approx 1.57\ \mathrm{kW}$ ideal.

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: $1.57 < 2.00$ with margin for efficiency losses — adequate, pending friction allowance.

examples.result: Ideal $1.57\ \mathrm{kW}$; the $2.00\ \mathrm{kW}$ motor suffices with modest margin.

keyTakeaways: Given, law, symbolic form, substitution, verification — never skip or reorder.
Sketch first to fix signs; estimate to trap calculator slips.
Verify units, sign, and magnitude on every answer.

quiz.q: Stopping from $25.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $5.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ takes about
Why solve symbolically before substituting?
options: One arithmetic pass with visible scaling and fewer slips
It removes the need to check
quiz.explanation: Symbolic form shows structure and needs only one numeric evaluation.

quiz.q: Hoisting $400\ \mathrm{kg}$ by $6.00\ \mathrm{m}$ in $15.0\ \mathrm{s}$ needs ideal power

intro: Some quantities need only a size, but pushes, pulls, and trips need a direction too. This section draws the scalar-vector line and shows the arrow language every later force and motion chapter speaks.
objectives: Distinguish scalar from vector quantities with examples
Represent vectors as scaled arrows with magnitude and direction
Resolve a travel problem into distance versus displacement

concepts.statement: A **scalar** has magnitude only: mass $m = 5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$, temperature $20\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$, time $t = 10\ \mathrm{s}$.
concepts.detail: Scalars combine by ordinary arithmetic regardless of direction.

concepts.statement: A **vector** has magnitude and direction: displacement $30\ \mathrm{km}$ east, force $50\ \mathrm{N}$ at $30^{\circ}$, velocity $v = 20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ north.
concepts.detail: Direction is part of the data — dropping it changes the physics.

concepts.statement: Draw vectors as **arrows with length proportional to magnitude** and orientation showing direction, labeled $\vec{F}$, $\vec{v}$, $\vec{d}$.
concepts.detail: A scale like $1\ \mathrm{cm} = 10\ \mathrm{N}$ turns drawing into measurement.

concepts.statement: **Distance** is path length (scalar); **displacement** is straight-line change of position (vector) with magnitude $\le$ distance.
concepts.detail: Walking $3\ \mathrm{km}$ east then $4\ \mathrm{km}$ north covers $7\ \mathrm{km}$ but displaces only $5\ \mathrm{km}$ northeast-ish.

concepts.statement: **Speed** is the rate (scalar, $50\ \mathrm{km/h}$); **velocity** is rate plus direction ($50\ \mathrm{km/h}$ north).
concepts.detail: Turning at constant speed changes velocity — the seed of Chapter 4 acceleration.

figures.caption: Distance ($7\ \mathrm{km}$ path) versus displacement ($5\ \mathrm{km}$ arrow) for 3 km east plus 4 km north

examples.title: Walker distance versus displacement
examples.problem: A surveyor walks $3.00\ \mathrm{km}$ east, then $4.00\ \mathrm{km}$ north. Find distance walked and displacement magnitude.

steps.label: Distance
steps.text: Scalar sum: $3.00 + 4.00 = 7.00\ \mathrm{km}$ of walking.

steps.label: Displacement
steps.text: Right triangle: $d = \sqrt{3.00^2 + 4.00^2} = \sqrt{25.0} = 5.00\ \mathrm{km}$.

steps.label: Direction note
steps.text: Full displacement is $5.00\ \mathrm{km}$ at $\arctan(4/3) \approx 53.1^{\circ}$ north of east.

examples.result: $7.00\ \mathrm{km}$ walked; $5.00\ \mathrm{km}$ displaced.

examples.title: Force arrow scale
examples.problem: Draw a $50\ \mathrm{N}$ force at $30^{\circ}$ above horizontal with scale $1\ \mathrm{cm} = 10\ \mathrm{N}$.

steps.label: Length
steps.text: $50/10 = 5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ arrow.

steps.label: Direction
steps.text: Protractor $30^{\circ}$ above the $+x$ axis from the tail.

steps.label: Label
steps.text: Mark $\vec{F} = 50\ \mathrm{N}$, $30^{\circ}$ — magnitude and direction both on the drawing.

examples.result: A $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ arrow at $30^{\circ}$ represents the force.

keyTakeaways: Scalars carry size only; vectors carry size plus direction.
Arrows scaled to magnitude make vectors measurable.
Displacement and velocity are vectors; distance and speed are their scalar partners.

quiz.q: Which is a vector?
quiz.explanation: Only the force states magnitude and direction together.

quiz.q: Walking 3 km east then 4 km north gives displacement
quiz.explanation: $\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5\ \mathrm{km}$; 7 km is the distance walked.

quiz.q: Turning a corner at steady speed changes
quiz.explanation: Velocity includes direction, so any turn is a velocity change.

intro: A speedometer number and a velocity arrow are not the same thing, and confusing them wrecks motion analysis. This section fixes average versus instantaneous rates and the sign language of direction.
objectives: Distinguish average from instantaneous speed and velocity
Compute average speed and velocity from distance, displacement, and time
Interpret position-time graphs by slope

concepts.statement: **Average speed** is path length over elapsed time: **$\bar{v} = d/t$** (scalar, e.g. $\mathrm{m/s}$ or $\mathrm{mi/h}$).
concepts.detail: A $240\ \mathrm{km}$ trip in $3.00\ \mathrm{h}$ averages $80.0\ \mathrm{km/h}$ regardless of stops.

concepts.statement: **Average velocity** is displacement over time: **$\bar{\vec{v}} = \Delta\vec{x}/t$** — sign (direction) included.
concepts.detail: A round trip has zero average velocity but nonzero average speed.

concepts.statement: **Instantaneous** speed/velocity is the rate at one instant — what the speedometer shows — found from the **tangent slope** of the position graph.
concepts.detail: Averages cover intervals; the speedometer covers now.

concepts.statement: On an $x$-$t$ graph, **slope is velocity**: steep means fast, flat means stopped, negative slope means returning.
concepts.detail: Curved $x$-$t$ means changing velocity — acceleration, the next section.

concepts.statement: **$1\ \mathrm{m/s} = 3.6\ \mathrm{km/h}$** and $1\ \mathrm{mi/h} = 1.467\ \mathrm{ft/s} = 0.447\ \mathrm{m/s}$ convert rate units.
concepts.detail: $60\ \mathrm{mi/h}$ is $88\ \mathrm{ft/s}$ — the number behind following-distance rules.

figures.caption: Position-time graph: chord slope is average velocity, tangent slope is instantaneous

examples.title: Highway average speed
examples.problem: A truck covers $240\ \mathrm{km}$ in $3.00\ \mathrm{h}$ including a stop. Find average speed, and express it in $\mathrm{m/s}$.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Stops lower the average below the cruising speedometer readings.

examples.result: $80.0\ \mathrm{km/h}$ ($22.2\ \mathrm{m/s}$) average.

examples.title: Round trip velocity
examples.problem: A technician drives $15.0\ \mathrm{km}$ to a site and back in $0.800\ \mathrm{h}$ total. Find average speed and average velocity.

steps.label: Speed
steps.text: Path $30.0\ \mathrm{km}$ over $0.800\ \mathrm{h}$: $37.5\ \mathrm{km/h}$.

steps.label: Velocity
steps.text: Displacement zero (start equals finish): $0\ \mathrm{km/h}$.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.text: Speed accumulates path; velocity only cares endpoints.

examples.result: Average speed $37.5\ \mathrm{km/h}$; average velocity zero.

keyTakeaways: Average speed uses path $d/t$; average velocity uses displacement $\Delta x/t$.
Speedometer and tangent slope give the instantaneous rate.
Convert rates with $1\ \mathrm{m/s} = 3.6\ \mathrm{km/h}$.

quiz.q: $240\ \mathrm{km}$ in $3.00\ \mathrm{h}$ averages
A round trip average velocity is zero because
quiz.explanation: Start equals finish, so $\Delta x = 0$ regardless of path.

quiz.q: On an $x$-$t$ graph the velocity is the
quiz.explanation: Rise (position) over run (time) is velocity at every scale.

intro: Constant acceleration covers vehicles, elevators, and falling bodies with just three equations. This section derives them, applies them to free fall, and works braking and drop problems end to end.
objectives: Apply $v = v_0 + at$, $s = v_0t + \tfrac12at^2$, $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2as$
Solve free-fall problems with $g = 9.80\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$
Choose the equation that skips the unneeded variable

concepts.statement: For constant $a$: **$v = v_0 + at$**, **$s = v_0t + \frac{1}{2}at^2$**, **$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2as$** — each omits one of $s$, $v$, $t$.
concepts.detail: No time wanted? Use the third. No distance wanted? Use the first.

concepts.statement: Neglecting air, falling bodies accelerate at **$g = 9.80\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ downward** ($32.2\ \mathrm{ft/s^2}$), independent of mass.
concepts.detail: Feather-versus-hammer differences are air resistance, not gravity.

concepts.statement: Fix **up positive or down positive once**, then keep $v_0$, $a$, and $s$ signs consistent through all three equations.
concepts.detail: With up positive, free-fall $a = -9.80\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ and dropped $v_0 = 0$.

concepts.statement: Up-and-down flight is **symmetric**: speed at each height matches on rise and fall, and rise time equals fall time to the same level.
concepts.detail: A ball thrown up at $15\ \mathrm{m/s}$ returns at $15\ \mathrm{m/s}$ downward (no air).

concepts.statement: From $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2as$, braking distance grows as **speed squared**: doubling speed quadruples stopping distance.
concepts.detail: That square law is the physics behind speed-limit safety margins.

figures.caption: Free fall strobe: equal-time gaps grow as $1:3:5$, velocity arrows lengthen uniformly
