examples.title: Dropped tool fall time
examples.problem: A wrench drops from a scaffold $45.0\ \mathrm{m}$ up (take down positive, $v_0 = 0$, $a = 9.80\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$). Find fall time and impact speed.

steps.label: Time
steps.text: $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$ gives $t = \sqrt{2s/a} = \sqrt{90.0/9.80} = \sqrt{9.184} \approx 3.03\ \mathrm{s}$.

steps.label: Speed
steps.text: $v = at = 9.80 \times 3.03 \approx 29.7\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

examples.result: Falls $3.03\ \mathrm{s}$, striking at $29.7\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (about $107\ \mathrm{km/h}$).

examples.title: Braking distance at highway speed
examples.problem: A car at $25.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ brakes at $5.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find stopping distance.

steps.label: Pick equation
steps.text: No time wanted: $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2as$ with $v = 0$.

steps.label: Scale note
steps.text: At $50\ \mathrm{m/s}$ this would quadruple to $250\ \mathrm{m}$.

examples.result: Stopping distance $62.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

keyTakeaways: Three equations cover all constant-$a$ motion; pick by the missing variable.
Free fall uses $a = g$ downward for every mass (no air).
Braking distance scales with speed squared.

quiz.q: Drop from $45.0\ \mathrm{m}$: fall time is about
Stopping from $25.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $5.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ needs
Doubling highway speed changes braking distance by
quiz.explanation: $s \propto v_0^2$ from $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2as$.

intro: Throw a ball sideways off a cliff and its horizontal cruise ignores its vertical plunge: the two motions superpose. This section treats projectiles as independent horizontal and vertical constant-acceleration problems.
objectives: Split projectile motion into independent $x$ and $y$ parts
Compute range, height, and flight time for horizontal launches
Describe angled launches and their symmetric trajectories

concepts.statement: Horizontal motion has **$a_x = 0$** (constant $v_x$) while vertical motion has **$a_y = g$ downward** — neither disturbs the other (no air).
concepts.detail: A bullet fired level and a dropped coin hit the ground together from the same height.

concepts.statement: Launched horizontally at $v_x$ from height $h$: **$t = \sqrt{2h/g}$** and **range $R = v_x t$**.
concepts.detail: Time depends only on height; range scales linearly with muzzle speed.

concepts.statement: At launch angle $\theta$: **$v_{0x} = v_0\cos\theta$**, **$v_{0y} = v_0\sin\theta$**; flight time comes from the vertical part, range from $v_{0x} t$.
concepts.detail: Apex occurs where $v_y = 0$; total time is twice the rise time for level landing.

concepts.statement: Constant $v_x$ with uniformly accelerated $y$ traces a **parabola** — symmetric about the apex for level ground.
concepts.detail: Maximum range on level ground occurs at $45^{\circ}$ (no air).

concepts.statement: Real drag **shortens range and breaks symmetry**, especially for light, fast, or spinning projectiles.
concepts.detail: Shop estimates ignore air for dense, slow bodies; ballistics engineers never do.

examples.title: Hose stream range
examples.problem: Water leaves a horizontal nozzle at $v_x = 8.00\ \mathrm{m/s}$ from $h = 1.25\ \mathrm{m}$ above ground. Where does it land?

steps.label: Time
steps.text: $t = \sqrt{2h/g} = \sqrt{2.50/9.80} = \sqrt{0.2551} \approx 0.505\ \mathrm{s}$.

steps.label: Impact speed
steps.text: $v_y = gt = 4.95\ \mathrm{m/s}$; $v = \sqrt{8.00^2 + 4.95^2} \approx 9.41\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

examples.result: Lands $4.04\ \mathrm{m}$ out, striking at $9.41\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

examples.title: Angled ball flight
examples.problem: A ball launches at $v_0 = 20.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$, $\theta = 30^{\circ}$ over level ground. Find flight time and range.

steps.label: Time
steps.text: Rise $t = v_{0y}/g = 1.020\ \mathrm{s}$; total $T = 2.04\ \mathrm{s}$.

steps.label: Range
steps.text: $R = 17.32 \times 2.04 \approx 35.3\ \mathrm{m}$.

examples.result: Airborne $2.04\ \mathrm{s}$; range $35.3\ \mathrm{m}$.

keyTakeaways: Projectiles: uniform $x$, accelerated $y$ — solve each axis separately.
Level horizontal launches obey $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$, $R = v_x t$.
Angled paths are parabolas; $45^{\circ}$ maximizes level range.

quiz.q: Nozzle at $8.00\ \mathrm{m/s}$ from $1.25\ \mathrm{m}$ lands at range
$20.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $30^{\circ}$ over level ground ranges about
Horizontal and vertical projectile motions are
quiz.explanation: $a_x = 0$ while $a_y = g$; neither affects the other.

intro: A force is a push or pull that changes motion, and the first law tells when motion needs no force at all. This section defines force, inertia, and mass, and sets up the free-body habit.
objectives: State Newton first law and define inertia
Relate mass to inertia with examples
Draw a correct free-body diagram for a simple body

concepts.statement: A **force** is a push or pull in a direction, measured in **newtons ($\mathrm{N}$)** or pounds, that tends to accelerate the body it acts on.
concepts.detail: Forces are vectors: $10\ \mathrm{N}$ east and $10\ \mathrm{N}$ west cancel rather than add.

concepts.statement: Without net force, a body **keeps its velocity**: rest stays rest, uniform motion stays uniform — this property is **inertia**.
concepts.detail: Seat-belt injuries and tablecloth tricks are inertia demonstrations, not mysteries.

concepts.statement: **Mass** in kilograms quantifies inertia: harder to accelerate means more mass, independent of location.
concepts.detail: A $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ block resists velocity change twice as strongly as a $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ block anywhere.

concepts.statement: Only the **vector sum (net force)** changes motion; balanced forces leave velocity untouched no matter how large each is.
concepts.detail: A tug-of-war at $500\ \mathrm{N}$ each side produces zero net force and zero acceleration.

concepts.statement: Isolate the body, mark its **center with all external forces as arrows**, and label magnitudes, directions, and axes.
concepts.detail: Internal grips and stresses are omitted — only outside pushes and pulls enter $\sum\vec{F}$.

figures.caption: Free-body diagram: isolated block with weight down, normal up, applied push, and friction back
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Free-body diagram: isolated block with weight down, normal up, applied push, and friction back" viewBox="0 0 400 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><rect x="160" y="80" width="80" height="50"/><line x1="40" y1="130" x2="360" y2="130"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none"><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="200" y2="35"/><line x1="200" y1="130" x2="200" y2="165"/><line x1="240" y1="105" x2="300" y2="105"/><line x1="160" y1="105" x2="110" y2="105"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="206" y="55">N</text><text x="206" y="178">W = mg</text><text x="302" y="110">applied</text><text x="60" y="110">friction</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Belt-ride inertia
examples.problem: A $70.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ passenger rides a bus braking from $12.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Explain the forward lurch with the first law.

steps.label: Before
steps.text: Passenger and bus share $12.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ forward velocity.

steps.label: Braking
steps.text: Brakes exert backward force on the bus, not directly on the passenger.

steps.label: Inertia
steps.text: With no backward force on her yet, she keeps $12.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ — lurching forward relative to the bus until the belt supplies the stopping force.

examples.result: The lurch is continued uniform motion, exactly as the first law predicts.

examples.title: Balanced forces at cruise
examples.problem: A truck cruises at steady $25\ \mathrm{m/s}$ with $3000\ \mathrm{N}$ of driving force. What is the drag force?

steps.label: First law
steps.text: Constant velocity means net force zero.

steps.label: Balance
steps.text: Drag must equal driving force oppositely: $3000\ \mathrm{N}$ backward.

steps.label: Note
steps.text: Large forces act, but their vector sum vanishes.

examples.result: $3000\ \mathrm{N}$ of drag balances the drive.

keyTakeaways: Force is a directed push or pull in newtons; only net force accelerates.
Inertia (mass) keeps velocity without net force — the first law.
Free-body diagrams isolate the body and show every external force.

quiz.q: A truck cruising steadily at $25\ \mathrm{m/s}$ with $3000\ \mathrm{N}$ drive has drag
quiz.explanation: Uniform velocity requires $\sum F = 0$, so drag cancels drive.

quiz.q: The forward lurch under braking is caused by
options: A forward force from the brakes
quiz.explanation: No backward force acts on the passenger until the belt engages.

quiz.q: A free-body diagram shows
options: All external forces on the isolated body
quiz.explanation: External pushes and pulls as arrows on the isolated body.

intro: The second law turns force from a qualitative push into a calculable $F = ma$. This section applies it to vehicles, hoists, and shop loads with strict unit discipline.
objectives: State Newton second law and its unit relation
Compute $F$, $m$, or $a$ from the other two
Solve horizontal dynamics with friction included

concepts.statement: Net force equals mass times acceleration: **$\sum\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$**, so **$1\ \mathrm{N} = 1\ \mathrm{kg \cdot m/s^2}$** by definition.
concepts.detail: Double the net force at fixed mass and acceleration doubles; double the mass and it halves.

concepts.statement: Acceleration points **along the net force**, with magnitude $a = F_{net}/m$ — components obey $\sum F_x = ma_x$ independently.
concepts.detail: Sideways forces never cause forward acceleration.

concepts.statement: Kilograms measure **inertia**; newtons measure **force** — $F = ma$ converts between them but they are never interchangeable.
concepts.detail: A $10\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass needs $98.0\ \mathrm{N}$ to support against gravity, not $10\ \mathrm{N}$.

concepts.statement: Add **signed forces on each axis first**, then apply $a = F_{net}/m$ — never apply $F = ma$ to one force of an opposed pair.
concepts.detail: Thrust minus drag is the accelerating quantity, not thrust alone.

concepts.statement: Gravity exerts **$W = mg$** downward with $g = 9.80\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ — the most common force substituted into $\sum F$.
concepts.detail: A $50.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ crate weighs $490\ \mathrm{N}$ and needs that much upward support to hover.

examples.title: Sports-car driving force
examples.problem: A $1500\ \mathrm{kg}$ car accelerates at $3.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ against $1200\ \mathrm{N}$ of drag. What driving force is needed?

steps.label: Net force
steps.text: $F_{net} = ma = 1500 \times 3.00 = 4500\ \mathrm{N}$ forward.

steps.label: Add drag
steps.text: Drive must supply net plus drag: $4500 + 1200 = 5700\ \mathrm{N}$.

steps.label: Report
steps.text: $5.70\ \mathrm{kN}$ of forward driving force.

examples.result: $5.70\ \mathrm{kN}$ driving force.

examples.title: Forklift load acceleration
examples.problem: A $2000\ \mathrm{kg}$ loaded pallet gets net $800\ \mathrm{N}$ forward. Find $a$ and the speed after $5.00\ \mathrm{s}$ from rest.

steps.label: Sense
steps.text: Slow warehouse pace — consistent with a heavy load and small net force.

examples.result: $0.400\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, reaching $2.00\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

keyTakeaways: $\sum F = ma$ links net force to acceleration with $1\ \mathrm{N} = 1\ \mathrm{kg \cdot m/s^2}$.
Sum signed forces first; thrust alone is not the net force.
Mass is inertia ($\mathrm{kg}$); force is push ($\mathrm{N}$).

quiz.q: $1500\ \mathrm{kg}$ at $3.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ against $1200\ \mathrm{N}$ drag needs drive
quiz.explanation: Net $4500\ \mathrm{N}$ plus $1200\ \mathrm{N}$ drag = $5700\ \mathrm{N}$.

quiz.q: Net $800\ \mathrm{N}$ on $2000\ \mathrm{kg}$ gives acceleration
Acceleration points
quiz.explanation: $\vec{a} = \sum\vec{F}/m$ is parallel to the net force.

intro: Weight is gravity pull on a mass, and it changes with $g$ while mass does not. This section computes weights, compares earth-moon readings, and separates mass, weight, and force units finally.
objectives: Compute weight from mass with $W = mg$
Predict weight changes on the moon and in elevators
Convert weights between newtons and pounds

concepts.statement: **$W = mg$** downward, with $g = 9.80\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ at earth surface — weight is a force in newtons.
concepts.detail: A $70.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ person weighs $686\ \mathrm{N}$ (about $154\ \mathrm{lb}$).

concepts.statement: **Mass never changes with location**; weight scales with local $g$ — moon $g$ is $1.62\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, about one-sixth of earth.
concepts.detail: That $70.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ astronaut still has $70.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ of inertia on the moon but weighs only $113\ \mathrm{N}$.

concepts.statement: **$1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$** converts scale readings; $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of mass weighs $2.205\ \mathrm{lb}$ on earth.
concepts.detail: Scales marked in pounds read force; balances comparing masses read mass.

concepts.statement: In an elevator accelerating upward at $a$, the floor pushes **$N = m(g + a)$** — apparent weight rises; downward $a$ lowers it.
concepts.detail: Free fall ($a = g$ down) gives $N = 0$: true weightlessness feeling with gravity still acting.

concepts.statement: Weight acts at the **center of gravity** of the body — the balance point where the whole $mg$ may be drawn in diagrams.
concepts.detail: Chapter 7 locates that point for beams and composite shapes.

examples.title: Crate weight both ways
examples.problem: A crate has mass $50.0\ \mathrm{kg}$. Find its earth weight in newtons and pounds.

steps.label: Pounds
steps.text: $490/4.448 \approx 110\ \mathrm{lb}$.

steps.label: Moon check
steps.text: On the moon: $50.0 \times 1.62 = 81.0\ \mathrm{N}$ — same mass, one-sixth weight.

examples.result: $490\ \mathrm{N}$ ($110\ \mathrm{lb}$) on earth; $81.0\ \mathrm{N}$ on the moon.

examples.title: Elevator scale reading
examples.problem: A $70.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ person rides an elevator accelerating upward at $2.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. What does the floor scale read?

steps.label: Forces
steps.text: $N - mg = ma$, so $N = m(g + a)$.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: Rest weight $686\ \mathrm{N}$ ($154\ \mathrm{lb}$); now $826\ \mathrm{N}$ ($186\ \mathrm{lb}$) — heavier feeling.

examples.result: Scale reads $826\ \mathrm{N}$ during upward acceleration.

keyTakeaways: $W = mg$ downward; mass is fixed, weight follows local $g$.
$1\ \mathrm{lb} = 4.448\ \mathrm{N}$ bridges scale units.
Accelerating supports change apparent weight via $N = m(g \pm a)$.

quiz.q: A $50.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ crate weighs on earth
On the moon ($g = 1.62$) that crate weighs about
quiz.explanation: $50.0 \times 1.62 = 81.0\ \mathrm{N}$; mass unchanged.

quiz.q: $70\ \mathrm{kg}$ in an elevator accelerating up at $2.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ feels

intro: Real pushes come in opposed pairs — thrust against drag, hoist pull against weight — and only their signed total accelerates. This section practices one-dimensional force totals until the sign habit is automatic.
objectives: Sum collinear forces with correct signs
Solve two-force acceleration problems
Handle vertical hoist and elevator totals

concepts.statement: Pick **one direction positive**, assign signs, then total: **$F_{net} = \sum (\pm F_i)$** before any $F = ma$ step.
concepts.detail: East-positive: $+80\ \mathrm{N}$ thrust with $-30\ \mathrm{N}$ drag gives $+50\ \mathrm{N}$ net.

concepts.statement: Opposed pulls subtract: net equals **larger minus smaller toward the larger side**.
concepts.detail: $400\ \mathrm{N}$ east versus $250\ \mathrm{N}$ west nets $150\ \mathrm{N}$ east.

concepts.statement: Upward-positive hoist problems total as **$F_{net} = T - mg$**, then $a = (T - mg)/m$.
concepts.detail: Tension below weight means downward acceleration, not upward motion necessarily.

concepts.statement: **Zero total means zero acceleration** — constant velocity continues under large but balanced forces.
concepts.detail: Level cruise at any speed is a force balance, not a force absence.

concepts.statement: Convert **all forces to one unit** (all newtons or all pounds) before adding — mixed totals are meaningless.
concepts.detail: $500\ \mathrm{N}$ minus $50\ \mathrm{lb}$ ($222\ \mathrm{N}$) nets $278\ \mathrm{N}$, not $450$ of anything.

examples.title: Tug-of-war acceleration
examples.problem: East team pulls $420\ \mathrm{N}$; west team pulls $380\ \mathrm{N}$ on a $60.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ sled (friction negligible). Find acceleration.

steps.label: Total
steps.text: East positive: $F_{net} = 420 - 380 = +40.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

steps.label: Accelerate
steps.text: $a = 40.0/60.0 \approx 0.667\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ east.

steps.label: Sense
steps.text: Small net of big forces gives gentle acceleration — expected.

examples.result: $0.667\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ toward the east team.

examples.title: Hoist tension check
examples.problem: A $500\ \mathrm{kg}$ load must accelerate upward at $1.50\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. What cable tension is needed?

steps.label: Equation
steps.text: $T - mg = ma$, so $T = m(g + a)$.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: Weight alone is $4900\ \mathrm{N}$; acceleration demands $750\ \mathrm{N}$ more.

examples.result: Tension $5.65\ \mathrm{kN}$.

keyTakeaways: Assign signs first; net force is the signed sum.
Hoist totals read $T - mg = ma$ upward-positive.
Unify force units before totaling.

quiz.q: $420\ \mathrm{N}$ east vs $380\ \mathrm{N}$ west on $60\ \mathrm{kg}$ gives
quiz.explanation: Net $40\ \mathrm{N}$ east; $40/60 = 0.667\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

quiz.q: $500\ \mathrm{kg}$ hoisted upward at $1.50\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ needs tension
Constant velocity under load means the force total is
quiz.explanation: Zero acceleration requires zero net force by $F = ma$.

intro: Forces come in mutual pairs: push on something and it pushes back equally. This section states the third law precisely and uses it to separate action-reaction pairs from balanced forces on one body.
objectives: State Newton third law with the two-body condition
Identify correct action-reaction pairs
Explain propulsion (walking, rockets, propellers) with the third law

concepts.statement: For bodies A and B, **$\vec{F}_{A \mathrm{on} B} = -\vec{F}_{B \mathrm{on} A}$**: equal size, opposite direction, on **different bodies**.
concepts.detail: The book pushes you down exactly as hard as you push it — different bodies, opposite arrows.

concepts.statement: Action-reaction partners **never cancel**: they act on different bodies, so only one enters each free-body diagram.
concepts.detail: Weight (earth on book) pairs with book-on-earth pull — not with the table normal force.

concepts.statement: The table pushing up $N$ on the book pairs with the **book pushing down $N$ on the table** — separate bodies, true pair.
concepts.detail: Book weight and table normal happen to balance numerically at rest but pair elsewhere.

concepts.statement: **Propulsion pushes mass backward to be pushed forward**: feet on ground, propellers on air, rockets on exhaust.
concepts.detail: A $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ exhaust puff thrown back at $200\ \mathrm{m/s}$ carries $1000\ \mathrm{kg \cdot m/s}$ of backward momentum.

concepts.statement: The cart moves because the **horse-ground interaction** (external to horse-plus-cart) has a forward surplus — internal strap forces cancel pairwise.
concepts.detail: Analyze system totals: internal pairs vanish, external remainders accelerate.

examples.title: Book on table pairs
examples.problem: A $2.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ book rests on a table. List the forces on the book and name the pair of each.

steps.label: On the book
steps.text: Weight $19.6\ \mathrm{N}$ down (partner: book pulls earth up $19.6\ \mathrm{N}$); normal $19.6\ \mathrm{N}$ up (partner: book pushes table down $19.6\ \mathrm{N}$).

steps.label: On the book total
steps.text: $19.6 - 19.6 = 0$: at rest as the first law requires.

steps.label: Not a pair
steps.text: Weight and normal act on the same body, so despite balancing they are not third-law partners.

examples.result: Two forces on the book, each paired to a force on another body.

examples.title: Recoil estimate
examples.problem: A $70.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ skater pushes a $30.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ crate, giving it $2.00\ \mathrm{m/s}$. With what speed does she recoil (ice frictionless)?

steps.label: Impulse pair
steps.text: Equal-opposite forces over equal time give equal-opposite momentum changes.

steps.label: Crate momentum
steps.text: $p = 30.0 \times 2.00 = 60.0\ \mathrm{kg \cdot m/s}$ forward.

steps.label: Skater
steps.text: She gains $60.0$ backward: $v = 60.0/70.0 \approx 0.857\ \mathrm{m/s}$ backward.

examples.result: Recoil about $0.857\ \mathrm{m/s}$ opposite the crate.

keyTakeaways: Third-law partners are equal, opposite, and on different bodies.
Same-body balanced forces are equilibrium, not action-reaction.
Propulsion is rearward mass-pushing returned as forward force.

quiz.q: Which is a true third-law pair?
options: Book weight and table normal on the book
Table pushing the book up and the book pushing the table down
Friction and weight on one crate
quiz.explanation: Partners must act on different bodies; only the table-book exchange qualifies.

quiz.q: $70\ \mathrm{kg}$ skater giving $30\ \mathrm{kg}$ crate $2.00\ \mathrm{m/s}$ recoils at
quiz.explanation: $60.0/70.0 = 0.857\ \mathrm{m/s}$ opposite.

quiz.q: A rocket climbs because it
options: Ejects exhaust backward and is pushed forward in return
quiz.explanation: Exhaust-backward pairs with rocket-forward; external force accelerates the system.

intro: Equal-mass collisions in a plane have a beautiful signature: the fragments separate at right angles. This section proves that result from conservation laws and applies component-wise momentum.
objectives: Apply momentum conservation per axis in 2-D
Show equal-mass elastic scattering separates at $90^{\circ}$
Solve a billiard-ball deflection problem

concepts.statement: Momentum conserves **per axis**: $\sum p_x$ before equals $\sum p_x$ after, and likewise $y$ — two independent equations.
concepts.detail: Glancing blows transfer sideways momentum while preserving forward totals.

concepts.statement: An elastic hit of **equal masses with one initially at rest** sends fragments off at **$90^{\circ}$ to each other**.
concepts.detail: Momentum conservation gives $v_0^2 = v_1^2 + v_2^2$ (Pythagoras) while energy gives the same sum — only a right triangle satisfies both.

concepts.statement: Billiard balls approximate the theorem because their **collision is nearly elastic and masses match** — spin and friction cause the small deviations.
concepts.detail: Pool players aim the cue ball deflection using this right-angle expectation.

concepts.statement: For 2-D perfectly inelastic hits, total each axis then recombine: $V_x = (\sum p_x)/M$, $V_y = (\sum p_y)/M$.
concepts.detail: Skid-and-stick car crashes are analyzed exactly this way from skid directions.

concepts.statement: Compare **$\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ totals** before and after to classify the hit as elastic or inelastic.
concepts.detail: Missing energy went to spin, sound, heat, or deformation.

figures.caption: Equal-mass elastic scatter: cue ball and object ball leave at $90^{\circ}$ to each other

examples.title: Billiard scatter check
examples.problem: A $0.170\ \mathrm{kg}$ cue ball at $2.50\ \mathrm{m/s}$ hits an identical ball at rest elastically; the cue ball leaves at $30^{\circ}$ to its path. Find both final speeds via the right-angle rule.

steps.label: Geometry
steps.text: Object ball leaves at $90 - 30 = 60^{\circ}$ on the other side.

steps.label: Solve
steps.text: Right-triangle solution: $v_1 = 2.50\cos 30^{\circ} = 2.165\ \mathrm{m/s}$, $v_2 = 2.50\sin 30^{\circ} = 1.25\ \mathrm{m/s}$; energy $\frac{1}{2}m(2.165^2 + 1.25^2) = \frac{1}{2}m(6.25)$ checks.

examples.result: Cue ball $2.17\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $30^{\circ}$; object ball $1.25\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $60^{\circ}$.

examples.title: Perpendicular momenta sticking
examples.problem: A $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ car east at $10.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ sticks to a $1500\ \mathrm{kg}$ car north at $8.00\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Find the wreck velocity.

steps.label: Components
steps.text: $V_x = 4.00\ \mathrm{m/s}$, $V_y = 4.80\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

steps.label: Recombine
steps.text: $V = \sqrt{16 + 23.04} = 6.25\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $\arctan(4.8/4.0) \approx 50.2^{\circ}$ north of east.

examples.result: $6.25\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $50.2^{\circ}$ north of east.

keyTakeaways: Conserve momentum separately on $x$ and $y$ in plane collisions.
Equal-mass elastic scattering from rest separates at $90^{\circ}$.
Recombine stuck-wreck components with Pythagoras and arctan.

quiz.q: Cue ball $2.50\ \mathrm{m/s}$ deflected $30^{\circ}$ leaves the object ball at speed
quiz.explanation: $v_2 = v_0\sin 30^{\circ} = 1.25\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $60^{\circ}$.

quiz.q: The stuck wreck ($p_x = 10{,}000$, $p_y = 12{,}000$, $M = 2500\ \mathrm{kg}$) moves at
The $90^{\circ}$ rule needs
options: Equal masses, elastic, one initially at rest
quiz.explanation: Both conservation laws coincide into Pythagoras only under those hypotheses.

intro: Real structures carry angled loads that must be split before they can be balanced. This section resolves two-dimensional forces into components and totals them into resultants.
objectives: Resolve angled structural loads into $x$ and $y$ parts
Total concurrent 2-D forces into a resultant
Use the resultant to anticipate the balancing force

concepts.statement: Forces are **concurrent** when their lines of action meet at one point — the single-point tug analyzed by vector sums.
concepts.detail: A ring pulled by three ropes is concurrent; a beam on two supports is not (parallel-force case).

concepts.statement: Replace each angled load by **$F_x = F\cos\theta$**, **$F_y = F\sin\theta$** with correct signs before any balancing.
concepts.detail: A $200\ \mathrm{lb}$ guy wire at $40^{\circ}$ gives $F_x = 153\ \mathrm{lb}$, $F_y = 129\ \mathrm{lb}$.

concepts.statement: **$R_x = \sum F_x$**, **$R_y = \sum F_y$**, $R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}$ — one arrow replacing the set.
concepts.detail: Zero $R$ already means equilibrium; nonzero $R$ names the unbalanced push.

concepts.statement: Chained tip-to-tail, concurrent forces form a **closed polygon if and only if balanced** — the graphical equilibrium test.
concepts.detail: An open gap is the missing equilibrant drawn to scale.

concepts.statement: Keep **one force unit** (all newtons or all pounds) through every resolution and total.
concepts.detail: Mixing $\mathrm{N}$ and $\mathrm{lb}$ inside one sum silently corrupts supports and tensions.

figures.caption: Concurrent ring: three rope pulls resolved on $x$-$y$ axes into $R_x$, $R_y$
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Concurrent ring: three rope pulls resolved on x-y axes into R_x, R_y" viewBox="0 0 400 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"><line x1="200" y1="100" x2="60" y2="100"/><line x1="200" y1="100" x2="340" y2="100"/><line x1="200" y1="100" x2="200" y2="20"/><line x1="200" y1="100" x2="200" y2="170"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none"><line x1="200" y1="100" x2="110" y2="60"/><line x1="200" y1="100" x2="300" y2="70"/><line x1="200" y1="100" x2="200" y2="155"/></g><g fill="currentColor"><circle cx="200" cy="100" r="7"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="90" y="55">rope A</text><text x="302" y="65">rope B</text><text x="208" y="160">load</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Guy-wire components
examples.problem: A guy wire pulls a pole top with $F = 2000\ \mathrm{N}$ at $40^{\circ}$ above horizontal. Find the horizontal and vertical loads on the pole.

steps.label: Meaning
steps.text: The anchor must resist $1532\ \mathrm{N}$ sideways; the pole carries $1286\ \mathrm{N}$ extra compression.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: $\sqrt{1532^2 + 1286^2} \approx 2000\ \mathrm{N}$ — recomposition confirms.

examples.result: $1532\ \mathrm{N}$ horizontal, $1286\ \mathrm{N}$ vertical compression.

examples.title: Two-rope resultant
examples.problem: Ropes pull a ring with $300\ \mathrm{N}$ east and $400\ \mathrm{N}$ at $90^{\circ}$ (north). Find the resultant.

steps.label: Magnitude
steps.text: $R = 500\ \mathrm{N}$ at $\arctan(4/3) = 53.1^{\circ}$ north of east.

steps.label: Balance preview
steps.text: A third rope must supply $500\ \mathrm{N}$ opposite to hold the ring.

examples.result: $500\ \mathrm{N}$ at $53.1^{\circ}$; equilibrant is its opposite.

keyTakeaways: Concurrent forces meet at a point and total by components.
Resolve first with $F\cos\theta$, $F\sin\theta$, then sum axes.
Closed force polygon means balanced; the gap names the missing force.

quiz.q: $2000\ \mathrm{N}$ at $40^{\circ}$ gives horizontal load
$300\ \mathrm{N}$ east plus $400\ \mathrm{N}$ north resultants to
Concurrent means
options: Lines of action meeting at one point
quiz.explanation: One common point of action defines concurrency.

intro: A sign hanging from two cables or a bracket under load stays put only when forces balance on both axes. This section solves concurrent equilibrium with $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$.
objectives: Write equilibrium equations for a concurrent point
Solve symmetric and asymmetric cable tensions
Verify solutions by substitution into both axes

concepts.statement: A concurrent point is in equilibrium **if and only if $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$** — no net push on either axis.
concepts.detail: Two scalar equations solve at most two unknown tensions or angles.

concepts.statement: Cable **tension always pulls away from the point** along the cable — draw every tension arrow outward before resolving.
concepts.detail: Inward arrows reverse signs and wreck both equations.

concepts.statement: Symmetric two-cable hangers share load equally: each carries **$T = W/(2\sin\theta)$** where $\theta$ is the cable angle above horizontal.
concepts.detail: Shallow angles inflate tension: at $10^{\circ}$, each cable carries nearly $2.9W$.

concepts.statement: Solve the **simpler axis first** (often $x$ with one unknown), then carry that value into the other axis.
concepts.detail: Asymmetric hangers need the full pair solved simultaneously.

concepts.statement: The computed balancing force is the **equilibrant $-\vec{R}$**: report magnitude plus the direction it must be applied.
concepts.detail: A strut or cable must physically supply that exact arrow.

examples.title: Symmetric sign hanger
examples.problem: A $200\ \mathrm{N}$ sign hangs from two symmetric cables at $30^{\circ}$ above horizontal. Find each tension.

steps.label: Solve
steps.text: $T = 200\ \mathrm{N}$ per cable.

steps.label: Horizontal check
steps.text: $T\cos 30^{\circ}$ left cancels $T\cos 30^{\circ}$ right — $\sum F_x = 0$ confirmed.

examples.result: $200\ \mathrm{N}$ in each cable — shallow angles cost tension.

examples.title: Bracket with strut
examples.problem: A horizontal cable holds a bracket while a $500\ \mathrm{N}$ load hangs. A strut pushes at $40^{\circ}$ above horizontal into the joint. Find strut force $S$ and cable tension $T$.

steps.label: Vertical
steps.text: $S\sin 40^{\circ} = 500$, so $S = 500/0.6428 \approx 778\ \mathrm{N}$ (compression).

steps.label: Horizontal
steps.text: $T = S\cos 40^{\circ} = 778 \times 0.7660 \approx 596\ \mathrm{N}$.

steps.label: Verify
steps.text: $778\sin 40^{\circ} = 500$ checks; $x$ balanced by the cable.

examples.result: Strut $778\ \mathrm{N}$ compression; cable $596\ \mathrm{N}$ tension.

keyTakeaways: Concurrent equilibrium is two equations: $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$.
Tensions pull outward; symmetric hangers obey $T = W/(2\sin\theta)$.
Shallow suspension angles multiply cable tension steeply.

quiz.q: $200\ \mathrm{N}$ sign on symmetric $30^{\circ}$ cables: each tension is
Strut at $40^{\circ}$ carrying $500\ \mathrm{N}$ vertically needs force
Cable tensions must be drawn
options: Away from the joint along the cable
quiz.explanation: Tension pulls the joint toward the cable anchor — outward from the point.

intro: Pushing a door near its hinges teaches torque intuitively: turning power is force times leverage. This section defines $\tau = Fr$ precisely and works wrench, valve, and door problems.
objectives: Compute torque from force and perpendicular lever arm
Explain the $\sin\theta$ angle dependence
Compare torques in wrench and door examples

concepts.statement: **Torque $\tau = F r_{\perp}$** in $\mathrm{N \cdot m}$ (or $\mathrm{lb \cdot ft}$) measures turning effect about a pivot.
concepts.detail: $50\ \mathrm{N}$ at $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ square-on gives $20.0\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$.

concepts.statement: Only the **perpendicular component** turns: **$\tau = rF\sin\theta$**, where $\theta$ is the angle between the arm and the force.
concepts.detail: Pushing straight into the pivot ($\theta = 0$) turns nothing regardless of force.

concepts.statement: Assign **one sense positive** (often counterclockwise) and keep it through every moment sum.
concepts.detail: Opposite senses subtract — the rotational version of signed force totals.

concepts.statement: Torque is maximized by pushing **perpendicular at the farthest point** — long handle, square angle.
concepts.detail: Angled or choked-up grips waste available force proportionally to $\sin\theta$ and $r$.

concepts.statement: $\mathrm{N \cdot m}$ of torque measures **twist, not energy**: torque times angle (radians) becomes work, but torque alone is not $\mathrm{J}$.
concepts.detail: A tightened-but-unmoving bolt absorbs zero work despite large torque.

figures.caption: Torque geometry: $\tau = rF\sin\theta$ is largest square-on at full handle length
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Torque geometry: tau = rFsintheta is largest square-on at full handle length" viewBox="0 0 400 170" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><circle cx="90" cy="100" r="10"/><line x1="90" y1="100" x2="300" y2="100"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none"><line x1="300" y1="100" x2="300" y2="45"/><line x1="230" y1="100" x2="265" y2="55"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none"><path d="M 120 100 A 30 30 0 0 0 112 85"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="70" y="130">pivot</text><text x="290" y="35">90°: full τ</text><text x="200" y="45">angled: rF sin θ</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Lug-wrench torque
examples.problem: A mechanic pulls $180\ \mathrm{N}$ perpendicular on a $0.450\ \mathrm{m}$ wrench. What torque results, and what force at $0.300\ \mathrm{m}$ matches it?

steps.label: Torque
steps.text: $\tau = 180 \times 0.450 = 81.0\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$.

steps.label: Shorter grip
steps.text: $F = \tau/r = 81.0/0.300 = 270\ \mathrm{N}$ — choking up costs $50\%$ more force.

steps.label: Angle penalty
steps.text: At $60^{\circ}$ the same pull gives $81.0 \times \sin 60^{\circ} \approx 70.1\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$.

examples.result: $81.0\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$; $270\ \mathrm{N}$ needed at $0.300\ \mathrm{m}$.

examples.title: Door push comparison
examples.problem: A $40.0\ \mathrm{N}$ push opens a door $0.800\ \mathrm{m}$ wide. Compare square-on edge push versus $30^{\circ}$ angled push at mid-door ($0.400\ \mathrm{m}$).

steps.label: Best case
steps.text: $\tau = 40.0 \times 0.800 = 32.0\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$.

steps.label: Weak case
steps.text: $\tau = 0.400 \times 40.0 \times \sin 30^{\circ} = 8.00\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$.

steps.label: Ratio
steps.text: One-quarter the turning power — geometry dominates.

examples.result: $32.0$ versus $8.00\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$: push far and square.

keyTakeaways: $\tau = rF\sin\theta$ with $\mathrm{N \cdot m}$ units; perpendicular far pushes win.
Fix a positive rotation sense and sum moments with signs.
Torque is twist, not energy — no motion means no work.

quiz.q: $180\ \mathrm{N}$ on a $0.450\ \mathrm{m}$ wrench square-on gives
quiz.explanation: $180 \times 0.450 = 81.0\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$.

quiz.q: Pushing directly toward the hinge ($\theta = 0$) produces
quiz.explanation: $\sin 0 = 0$: no perpendicular lever arm, no turning.

quiz.q: Matching $81.0\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$ at $0.300\ \mathrm{m}$ needs force

intro: Beams, seesaws, and bridges balance under parallel forces when pushes sum to zero and twists sum to zero. This section solves support reactions with force plus moment equations.
objectives: Write $\sum F = 0$ and $\sum \tau = 0$ for parallel systems
Compute beam support reactions with moments
Choose pivot points that eliminate unknowns

concepts.statement: Parallel systems need **$\sum F = 0$** (no net push) and **$\sum \tau = 0$** about any pivot (no net twist).
concepts.detail: Two equations handle beams with two support reactions.

concepts.statement: Take moments **about one support** so its unknown drops out ($r = 0$), solve for the other, then use $\sum F = 0$ for the first.
concepts.detail: This triangular order avoids simultaneous equations on standard beams.

concepts.statement: Supports share load by **proximity**: a load nearer the left support loads it more, in inverse proportion to the spans.
concepts.detail: Midspan loads split equally; quarter-point loads split 3:1.

concepts.statement: Call **up positive** for forces and pick one moment sense; downward loads and weights enter negative in $\sum F$.
concepts.detail: Consistent signs make the two equations solvable without re-derivation.

concepts.statement: Concentrated loads near midspan produce the **largest moments** and control beam sizing — distribute or support them first.
concepts.detail: Moment grows with span times load, so doubling span quadruples the challenge for uniform load.

figures.caption: Beam on two supports: reactions $R_1$, $R_2$ balance load $W$ via $\sum F = 0$, $\sum\tau = 0$
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Beam on two supports: reactions R_1, R_2 balance load W via sum F = 0, sumtau = 0" viewBox="0 0 400 170" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" fill="none"><line x1="50" y1="80" x2="350" y2="80"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><polygon points="100,110 80,130 120,130"/><polygon points="300,110 280,130 320,130"/><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="100" y2="110"/><line x1="300" y1="80" x2="300" y2="110"/><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="200" y2="40"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="90" y="148">R₁</text><text x="290" y="148">R₂</text><text x="206" y="55">W</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Midspan load reactions
examples.problem: A $6.00\ \mathrm{m}$ beam carries a $3000\ \mathrm{N}$ machine at midspan. Supports at the ends: find $R_1$, $R_2$.

steps.label: Sense
steps.text: Symmetric load splits equally — as expected.

examples.result: $R_1 = R_2 = 1500\ \mathrm{N}$ upward.

examples.title: Offset load reactions
examples.problem: Same $6.00\ \mathrm{m}$ beam; the $3000\ \mathrm{N}$ load sits $1.50\ \mathrm{m}$ from the left support. Find reactions.

steps.label: Rule
steps.text: Near support carries $3\times$ the far one — inverse-span sharing.

keyTakeaways: Parallel equilibrium is $\sum F = 0$ plus $\sum\tau = 0$.
Pivot moments on one support to isolate the other reaction.
Loads split by inverse span proximity.

quiz.q: Midspan $3000\ \mathrm{N}$ on a $6.00\ \mathrm{m}$ beam gives reactions
quiz.explanation: Symmetry splits the load equally.

quiz.q: Load $1.50\ \mathrm{m}$ from the left on a $6.00\ \mathrm{m}$ beam: far (right) reaction is
Taking moments about a support is smart because
options: That reaction moment arm is zero and drops out
quiz.explanation: $r = 0$ kills that unknown moment, isolating the other reaction.

intro: Energy is stored work ready to act — motion holds kinetic, height holds gravitational potential. This section banks both and converts between them quantitatively.
objectives: Compute kinetic energy $\tfrac12mv^2$
Compute gravitational potential $mgh$
Track $KE$-$PE$ exchange in drops and throws

concepts.statement: **Kinetic energy $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$** in joules — motion energy scaling with speed squared.
concepts.detail: A $1200\ \mathrm{kg}$ car at $20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ carries $240{,}000\ \mathrm{J}$; at $40\ \mathrm{m/s}$ it carries $960{,}000$.

concepts.statement: **Potential $PE = mgh$** above a datum — lifted weight banked as joules.
concepts.detail: A $50.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ crate on a $2.00\ \mathrm{m}$ platform holds $980\ \mathrm{J}$.

concepts.statement: Because $KE \propto v^2$, **doubling speed quadruples crash energy** — the quantitative case for speed control.
concepts.detail: Brakes must dissipate four times the heat for twice the speed.

concepts.statement: Only **$PE$ differences matter**: set $h = 0$ anywhere convenient and difference the endpoints.
concepts.detail: Falling $5.00\ \mathrm{m}$ releases $mg(5.00)$ regardless of floor elevation numbers.

concepts.statement: Springs, fuels, batteries, and heat hold **elastic, chemical, electrical, and thermal energy** — same joule, different storage.
concepts.detail: This chapter tracks mechanical accounts; heat losses enter as the missing balance.

examples.title: Car kinetic energy
examples.problem: Find the kinetic energy of a $1500\ \mathrm{kg}$ car at $25.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$, and at $50.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

steps.label: Ratio
steps.text: Four times the energy at twice the speed — square law confirmed numerically.

examples.result: $469\ \mathrm{kJ}$ versus $1.88\ \mathrm{MJ}$.

examples.title: Lifted beam potential
examples.problem: A $800\ \mathrm{kg}$ beam is raised $6.00\ \mathrm{m}$. How much potential is stored?

steps.label: Report
steps.text: About $47.0\ \mathrm{kJ}$ banked.

steps.text: Lowering it can return at most this much (minus friction).

intro: Without friction, mechanical energy only changes form — falling trades height for speed reversibly. This section applies $KE_1 + PE_1 = KE_2 + PE_2$ to drops, coasters, and pendulums.
objectives: State conservation of mechanical energy and its condition
Solve drop and slide speeds with energy balance
Account for friction as energy lost to heat

concepts.statement: With only gravity (and springs) doing work, **$KE_1 + PE_1 = KE_2 + PE_2$** — the total $E = KE + PE$ is constant.
concepts.detail: A $2.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball dropped $5.00\ \mathrm{m}$ trades $98.0\ \mathrm{J}$ of $PE$ for $98.0\ \mathrm{J}$ of $KE$.

concepts.statement: Falling $h$ from rest gives **$v = \sqrt{2gh}$** — mass cancels, height alone sets impact speed.
concepts.detail: From $10.0\ \mathrm{m}$: $v = \sqrt{196} = 14.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for feather and hammer alike (no air).

concepts.statement: With friction, **$E_2 = E_1 - f_k d$**: the missing mechanical energy left as heat.
concepts.detail: A slide ending slower than $\sqrt{2gh}$ predicts names its friction loss in joules.

concepts.statement: A swinging pendulum **trades $PE$ at the top for $KE$ at the bottom** continuously, with total fixed (no air).
concepts.detail: Release height sets bottom speed by $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ regardless of string length.

depth.title: From Newton to Work-Energy: Derivation and Conservative Fields

blocks.heading: Work-energy theorem
blocks.body: For a particle with net force $\vec{F}_{net}$ along path $C$, the work $W_{net} = \int_C \vec{F}_{net}\cdot d\vec{r}$ equals the kinetic change: **$W_{net} = \Delta KE$**. With $\vec{F}_{net} = m\,d\vec{v}/dt$ and $d\vec{r} = \vec{v}\,dt$, the integrand becomes $m\vec{v}\cdot d\vec{v} = d(\frac{1}{2}mv^2)$, and integrating from state 1 to 2 gives $W_{net} = \frac{1}{2}mv_2^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_1^2$ exactly, for any path and any (even non-constant) force.

blocks.heading: Conservative forces and potential
blocks.body: A force is **conservative** when its work between two points is path-independent, equivalently $\oint \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = 0$. Gravity qualifies: $W_{1\to 2} = -mg(h_2 - h_1)$ by direct integration of $-mg\,dy$ regardless of the horizontal route. Defining $PE = mgh$ (up to an additive datum constant) lets that work be written $W_{grav} = -(PE_2 - PE_1)$. Splitting $W_{net} = W_{grav} + W_{other}$ in the theorem gives $\Delta KE = -\Delta PE + W_{other}$, i.e. **$KE_2 + PE_2 = KE_1 + PE_1 + W_{other}$**. Setting $W_{other} = 0$ (no friction, no pushes) yields the conservation law of the section; friction contributes $W_{other} = -f_k d$.

blocks.heading: Why $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ is mass-free
blocks.body: For a free drop, $W_{other} = 0$ and $KE_1 = 0$, so $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh$. Mass divides out before any number is substituted — the cancellation is structural, not coincidental. Numerically, $h = 8.00\ \mathrm{m}$ gives $v = \sqrt{2(9.80)(8.00)} = 12.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for any $m$, and the exchanged energy $mgh$ scales linearly with $m$ ($1.57\ \mathrm{kJ}$ at $20.0\ \mathrm{kg}$). Air drag is nonconservative ($W_{other} < 0$), which is why feathers fall short of this prediction.

blocks.heading: What conservation does not promise
blocks.body: The theorem never claims total energy is mechanical: $W_{other}$ routinely parks energy in heat, sound, and deformation. The first law of thermodynamics extends the ledger so $\Delta KE + \Delta PE + \Delta U_{thermal} + \cdots = W_{in}$, keeping conservation universal while mechanical conservation stays conditional on $W_{other} = 0$. Recognizing which account holds the missing joules is the professional skill behind every efficiency calculation in Chapters 8-10.

intro: Society runs on the same joule whether it comes from coal, river, wind, or sun. This section surveys the sources, compares their densities and trade-offs, and prices a solar contribution.
objectives: List major energy sources with their origins
Compare renewable and nonrenewable trade-offs
Estimate solar and wind contributions quantitatively

concepts.statement: Coal, oil, gas, and uranium are **stock fuels**: concentrated and dispatchable but depletable with waste and emission costs.
concepts.detail: A $1.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ of coal holds roughly $2.4 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{J}$ ($6.7\ \mathrm{kWh}$) of chemical energy.

concepts.statement: Hydro, wind, solar, geothermal, and biomass tap continuing **flows** — inexhaustible but diffuse and variable.
concepts.detail: Peak sun delivers about $1000\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$; a $20\%$-efficient panel yields $200\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$ of it.

concepts.statement: **Watts per square meter** decide land and cost: hydro sites are dense, solar and wind need area, fossil plants need fuel lines.
concepts.detail: A $5.0\ \mathrm{MW}$ solar farm at $200\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$ needs $25{,}000\ \mathrm{m^2}$ of panel.

concepts.statement: Delivered energy is source times **chained efficiencies**: panel $\times$ inverter $\times$ transmission for solar, thermal $\times$ turbine for coal.
concepts.detail: A $35\%$-thermal plant burns $2.86\ \mathrm{J}$ of fuel per joule delivered.

concepts.statement: Variable flows need **storage or backup**: batteries, pumped hydro, or grid exchange shift noon sun to evening load.
concepts.detail: Sizing storage starts from $E = Pt$ for the gap hours — pure Chapter 8 bookkeeping.

steps.label: Value

steps.label: Fuel heat
steps.text: Coal heat needed: $8.64 \times 10^{7}/0.35 \approx 2.47 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{J}$.

examples.result: $24.0\ \mathrm{kWh}$ displacing roughly $10\ \mathrm{kg}$ of coal.

keyTakeaways: Stocks (fossil, nuclear) are dense and dispatchable; flows (sun, wind, water) are clean but variable.
Delivered energy is source times chained efficiencies.

intro: Shafts are rated in rpm, radians, and rim speed — three faces of the same rotation. This section converts among them and relates angular to linear motion at the rim.
objectives: Convert rpm to rad/s and degrees
Compute rim speed from $v = r\omega$
Solve belt-contact speed matching problems

concepts.statement: Rotation is measured in **revolutions, degrees, or radians** with **$1\ \mathrm{rev} = 360^{\circ} = 2\pi\ \mathrm{rad}$**.
concepts.detail: Radians are the working unit because arc length is $s = r\theta$ directly in them.

concepts.statement: **Angular velocity $\omega = \theta/t$** in $\mathrm{rad/s}$; $\mathrm{rpm}$ converts by **$\omega = 2\pi(\mathrm{rpm})/60$**.
concepts.detail: $1750\ \mathrm{rpm} = 183\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ — the standard four-pole motor speed.

concepts.statement: A point at radius $r$ moves at **$v = r\omega$** — outer points fly faster on the same shaft.
concepts.detail: A $0.100\ \mathrm{m}$ wheel at $20.0\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ has rim speed $2.00\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

concepts.statement: **$\alpha = \Delta\omega/t$** in $\mathrm{rad/s^2}$ spins shafts up; constant-$\alpha$ formulas mirror Chapter 4 with $\theta, \omega, \alpha$.
concepts.detail: Reaching $183\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ in $3.00\ \mathrm{s}$ needs $\alpha = 61.0\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}$.

concepts.statement: Rolling or belted surfaces share **equal rim speeds** ($v_1 = v_2$), so $r_1\omega_1 = r_2\omega_2$ — the ratio rule of Sections 9.5-9.7.
concepts.detail: A small driver spins a large pulley slower by the diameter ratio.

intro: Cornering cars, centrifuges, and governors all demand center-seeking force. This section quantifies centripetal $F = mv^2/r$ and sizes curves and spinners safely.
objectives: Compute centripetal force and acceleration
Size safe cornering speeds from $\mu g$
Solve centrifuge and belt-separation problems

concepts.statement: Circular motion at speed $v$, radius $r$ needs center-pointing acceleration **$a_c = v^2/r = r\omega^2$** — direction change, not speedup.
concepts.detail: A car at $20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ on $r = 100\ \mathrm{m}$ pulls $4.00\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ sideways.

concepts.statement: **$F_c = mv^2/r$** must be supplied by grip, tension, or normal force — name the supplier in every problem.
concepts.detail: $1200\ \mathrm{kg}$ in the curve above needs $4800\ \mathrm{N}$ of tire grip.

concepts.statement: The outward fling is **inertia in disguise**, not a new force — free-body diagrams show only the inward supplier.
concepts.detail: Let go of the string and the ball flies tangent, never radially outward.

concepts.statement: Grip caps speed: **$v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu g r}$** from $mv^2/r = \mu mg$ — mass cancels.
concepts.detail: At $\mu = 0.70$, $r = 100\ \mathrm{m}$: $v_{max} = 26.2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ ($94.3\ \mathrm{km/h}$).

concepts.statement: Banked curves tilt the normal inward; strings and walls pull inward — **resolve the supplier radially** to find $F_c$.
concepts.detail: Ideal banking needs no friction at one design speed; grip covers the rest.

steps.text: $4800 < 8232$ — safe with margin; limit speed is $26.2\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

examples.result: Needs $4.80\ \mathrm{kN}$; $8.23\ \mathrm{kN}$ available — safe.

examples.problem: A $0.0100\ \mathrm{kg}$ sample spins at $r = 0.100\ \mathrm{m}$, $\omega = 300\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. Find $F_c$ in newtons and $g$ multiples.

steps.label: Sense
steps.text: Laboratory centrifuges live in the hundreds-to-thousands of $g$ — checked.

keyTakeaways: $a_c = v^2/r$ inward; $F_c = mv^2/r$ must be supplied by a real agent.
There is no outward force on free-body diagrams — only inertia.
Grip-limited speed is $v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu g r}$.

intro: Rotating shafts deliver power as torque times spin rate. This section prices shaft power in watts and horsepower and checks pulley torque against belt tension.
objectives: Compute rotational power with $P = \tau\omega$
Convert shaft power to horsepower
Relate belt tension difference to torque

concepts.statement: **Power $P = \tau\omega$** with $\tau$ in $\mathrm{N \cdot m}$ and $\omega$ in $\mathrm{rad/s}$ gives watts directly.
concepts.detail: $50.0\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$ at $100\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ delivers $5000\ \mathrm{W}$.

concepts.statement: Fixed power trades **torque against speed**: gearing down doubles torque while halving $\omega$.
concepts.detail: That is why low gear climbs hills and high gear cruises.

concepts.statement: Net belt pull $(T_1 - T_2)$ at radius $r$ gives **$\tau = (T_1 - T_2)r$** — slack-side tension subtracts.
concepts.detail: $300\ \mathrm{N}$ tight versus $100\ \mathrm{N}$ slack on $r = 0.150\ \mathrm{m}$ yields $30.0\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$.

concepts.statement: Divide watts by $746$ for **shaft horsepower** — the rating buyers compare.
concepts.detail: $5000\ \mathrm{W}$ is $6.70\ \mathrm{hp}$ at the shaft.

concepts.statement: Motor input exceeds shaft output: **$P_{in} = P_{shaft}/\eta$** with $\eta$ the decimal efficiency.
concepts.detail: A $90\%$-efficient $5.00\ \mathrm{kW}$ shaft needs $5.56\ \mathrm{kW}$ of electricity.

examples.title: Lathe shaft power
examples.problem: A lathe spindle turns at $800\ \mathrm{rpm}$ under $40.0\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$ of cutting torque. Find shaft power.

steps.label: Horsepower
steps.text: $3351/746 \approx 4.49\ \mathrm{hp}$ at the spindle.

examples.result: About $3.35\ \mathrm{kW}$ ($4.49\ \mathrm{hp}$).

examples.title: Belt-drive torque
examples.problem: Belt tensions are $T_1 = 400\ \mathrm{N}$, $T_2 = 150\ \mathrm{N}$ on a $0.200\ \mathrm{m}$ pulley at $30.0\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. Find torque and power.

steps.label: Note
steps.text: Total tension loads bearings; only the difference drives.

examples.result: $50.0\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$; $1.50\ \mathrm{kW}$ transmitted.

keyTakeaways: Shaft power is $P = \tau\omega$ in watts ($/746$ for hp).
Gearing trades torque against speed at fixed power.
Belt torque comes from tension difference times radius.

intro: Belts, chains, and gears all enforce ratio rules between driver and driven. This section derives the inverse speed law and applies it to shop reductions.
objectives: State the inverse speed-diameter rule
Compute driven speeds and directions
Chain two-stage reductions correctly

concepts.statement: No-slip drivers obey **$n_1 d_1 = n_2 d_2$** (speeds $n$, diameters $d$): bigger driven means slower driven.
concepts.detail: A $100\ \mathrm{mm}$ driver at $1750\ \mathrm{rpm}$ spins a $300\ \mathrm{mm}$ pulley at $583\ \mathrm{rpm}$.

concepts.statement: **Open belts keep direction; crossed belts and external gears reverse it** — idlers change direction, not ratio magnitude.
concepts.detail: Meshed external gears always counter-rotate; internal (ring) gears co-rotate.

concepts.statement: Ideal power conservation gives **$\tau_2/\tau_1 = n_1/n_2 = d_2/d_1$** — slow shafts pull harder.
concepts.detail: The $3{:}1$ reduction above triples torque (minus friction).

concepts.statement: Overall ratio is the **product of stage ratios**: $3{:}1$ then $4{:}1$ is $12{:}1$ total.
concepts.detail: Compound drives reach large reductions without absurd single pulleys.

concepts.statement: Real belts **slip 1-3 percent** under load, so driven speed runs slightly below ideal — measure, do not just compute.
concepts.detail: Timing belts and chains eliminate slip where phase matters.

figures.caption: Open-belt drive: $n_1 d_1 = n_2 d_2$, same direction; crossed belt reverses

intro: Gear teeth quantize the ratio rule: tooth counts replace diameters exactly. This section sizes gear trains, distinguishes idlers, and computes train value.
objectives: Compute gear speed ratios from tooth counts
Find train value for multi-pair trains
Predict output direction from mesh count

concepts.statement: Meshed gears obey **$n_1 N_1 = n_2 N_2$** (teeth $N$): the $20$-tooth driver at $900\ \mathrm{rpm}$ spins a $60$-tooth gear at $300\ \mathrm{rpm}$.
concepts.detail: Teeth eliminate slip, so this ratio is exact, not approximate.

concepts.statement: Meshing gears must share **module (tooth size)** and pressure angle — counts set ratio, module sets mesh.
concepts.detail: A $2\ \mathrm{mm}$-module gear cannot mesh a $3\ \mathrm{mm}$-module mate at any count.

concepts.statement: An **idler reverses direction without changing ratio magnitude** — it bridges distance and phase, not value.
concepts.detail: Driver-idler-driven with counts $20$-$30$-$60$ still gives $3{:}1$ overall.

concepts.statement: **Train value $= \prod (N_{driver}/N_{driven})$** per mesh; output speed is input times train value.
**Odd external meshes reverse, even preserve** input direction — count the meshes, not the gears.
concepts.detail: Two external meshes (one idler) preserve direction.

examples.title: Single-pair reduction
examples.problem: A $20$-tooth pinion at $1200\ \mathrm{rpm}$ drives a $75$-tooth gear. Find output speed and torque change.

steps.label: Torque
steps.text: Ideal torque multiplies by $75/20 = 3.75\times$.

steps.label: Direction
steps.text: One external mesh: output counter-rotates.

examples.result: $320\ \mathrm{rpm}$ reversed, $3.75\times$ torque.

examples.title: Two-pair train
examples.problem: Pairs $24/72$ and $18/54$ follow a $900\ \mathrm{rpm}$ input. Find final speed.

steps.label: Direction
steps.text: Two meshes: output matches input direction.

examples.result: $100\ \mathrm{rpm}$ in the input direction.

keyTakeaways: $n_1 N_1 = n_2 N_2$ exactly for meshed gears.
Train value multiplies per-mesh driver/driven ratios.
Idlers bridge and reverse; odd meshes reverse overall.

quiz.q: $20$ teeth at $1200\ \mathrm{rpm}$ driving $75$ teeth gives
quiz.explanation: $1200 \times 20/75 = 320\ \mathrm{rpm}$.

quiz.q: Pairs $24/72$ and $18/54$ on $900\ \mathrm{rpm}$ give
An idler gear primarily
quiz.explanation: Its teeth cancel from the train-value product.

intro: Flat belts connect distant pulleys with quiet, forgiving drives. This section applies the pulley ratio law, computes belt speed and length, and selects open versus crossed layouts.
objectives: Size pulley speeds with $n_1d_1 = n_2d_2$
Compute belt speed from $v = \pi dn$
Estimate belt length for open drives

concepts.statement: Belted pulleys obey **$n_1 d_1 = n_2 d_2$** like gears but with slip — measure critical speeds under load.
concepts.detail: Diameters are pitch diameters where the belt rides, not outside flanges.

concepts.statement: Belt linear speed is **$v = \pi d n$** (consistent units: $d$ in meters, $n$ in rev/s) — one number for the whole loop.
concepts.detail: A $0.150\ \mathrm{m}$ pulley at $20.0\ \mathrm{rev/s}$ runs the belt at $9.42\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

concepts.statement: Open-belt length is approximately **$L \approx 2C + \pi(R + r) + (R - r)^2/C$** for center distance $C$ and radii $R, r$.
concepts.detail: Order the next stock size up and take up slack with adjustment.

concepts.statement: **Crowned pulleys steer belts centerward**; misalignment and overload throw or flip belts regardless of correct ratio.
concepts.detail: Laser alignment and proper tensioning prevent most belt failures.

concepts.statement: Size belts by **power, speed, wrap angle, and service factor** — small pulleys and shock loads demand heavier sections.
concepts.detail: Under-belting slips and burns; over-belting wastes bearings and money.

figures.caption: Belt speed $v = \pi d n$ is uniform around the loop; torque comes from $(T_1 - T_2)r$

examples.problem: A $100\ \mathrm{mm}$ driver at $1750\ \mathrm{rpm}$ runs a $250\ \mathrm{mm}$ fan pulley. Find fan speed and belt speed.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Fan side: $\pi(0.250)(700/60) = 9.16\ \mathrm{m/s}$ — matches.

examples.result: Fan $700\ \mathrm{rpm}$; belt $9.16\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

examples.title: Belt length estimate
examples.problem: Open drive with $R = 0.150\ \mathrm{m}$, $r = 0.060\ \mathrm{m}$, $C = 0.800\ \mathrm{m}$. Estimate $L$.

steps.label: Order
steps.text: Order $2270\ \mathrm{mm}$ stock or next size up with take-up.

examples.result: About $2.27\ \mathrm{m}$ of belt.

keyTakeaways: Pulley speeds obey $n_1d_1 = n_2d_2$ (verify under load for slip).
Belt speed $v = \pi dn$ is loop-uniform.
Estimate open length, order up, tension and align.

Belt speed for $0.100\ \mathrm{m}$ at $29.17\ \mathrm{rev/s}$ is
Crowned pulleys exist to
quiz.explanation: Crowning self-tracks the belt against misalignment.

intro: Every shop machine trades force for distance under one conservation law. This section defines mechanical advantage and efficiency, the two numbers that rate all six simple machines.
objectives: Define ideal and actual mechanical advantage
Compute efficiency from work in and out
Explain why no machine creates energy

concepts.statement: A machine **transfers energy with changed force, distance, or direction** — never creating work, only redirecting it.
concepts.detail: Levers, pulleys, and screws all obey work in equals work out plus losses.

concepts.statement: **Actual $MA = F_{out}/F_{in}$**; **ideal $IMA = d_{in}/d_{out}$** from geometry — friction makes $MA < IMA$ always.
concepts.detail: An $MA = 4$ jack lifts $800\ \mathrm{N}$ with $200\ \mathrm{N}$ of effort.

concepts.statement: **$\eta = W_{out}/W_{in} = MA/IMA$** as a decimal or percent — the fraction of input surviving as useful output.
concepts.detail: $800\ \mathrm{J}$ out of $1000\ \mathrm{J}$ in is $80\%$ efficient.

concepts.statement: **Gaining force costs distance**: $IMA = 4$ means pulling $4\ \mathrm{m}$ of rope per meter lifted — conservation priced per stroke.
concepts.detail: There is no free force; the product $F \times d$ is budgeted.

concepts.statement: Input power must cover **output plus loss rate**: $P_{in} = P_{out}/\eta$ sizes motors driving machines.
concepts.detail: A $1.00\ \mathrm{kW}$ output at $75\%$ needs $1.33\ \mathrm{kW}$ in.

figures.caption: Force-distance trade: small effort over long pull balances large load over short lift
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Force-distance trade: small effort over long pull balances large load over short lift" viewBox="0 0 400 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><line x1="60" y1="60" x2="340" y2="60"/><polygon points="60,60 52,56 52,64" fill="currentColor"/><polygon points="340,60 348,56 348,64" fill="currentColor"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><rect x="300" y="70" width="60" height="40"/><circle cx="100" cy="110" r="12"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="70" y="45">small F, big d</text><text x="280" y="45">big F, small d</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Jack efficiency
examples.problem: A jack lifts $8000\ \mathrm{N}$ by $0.200\ \mathrm{m}$ with $2000\ \mathrm{J}$ of handle work. Find $W_{out}$, $MA$ versus effort $500\ \mathrm{N}$, and efficiency.

steps.label: Efficiency
steps.text: $\eta = 1600/2000 = 0.80 = 80\%$; $400\ \mathrm{J}$ lost to friction.

examples.result: $1.60\ \mathrm{kJ}$ out; $MA = 16$; $80\%$ efficient.

examples.title: Motor sizing through a machine
examples.problem: A hoist must deliver $2.00\ \mathrm{kW}$ of lifting power through gearing at $\eta = 0.75$. What motor input is needed?

steps.label: Horsepower
steps.text: $2667/746 \approx 3.57\ \mathrm{hp}$ — order a $5\ \mathrm{hp}$ frame.

steps.label: Loss
steps.text: $0.667\ \mathrm{kW}$ becomes heat in gears and bearings.

examples.result: About $2.67\ \mathrm{kW}$ input; $5\ \mathrm{hp}$ motor.

keyTakeaways: Machines redirect work; $MA = F_{out}/F_{in}$, $IMA = d_{in}/d_{out}$.
$\eta = W_{out}/W_{in} = MA/IMA$; friction takes the rest.
Force gained is distance paid — always.

quiz.q: $1600\ \mathrm{J}$ out of $2000\ \mathrm{J}$ in is efficiency
$2.00\ \mathrm{kW}$ out at $75\%$ needs input
An $IMA = 4$ machine means
quiz.explanation: Geometry trades distance for force; energy still balances.

intro: The lever is the oldest force amplifier: position the fulcrum and small efforts move great loads. This section classes levers and solves crowbar, plier, and pry problems.
objectives: Classify levers as first, second, or third class
Compute lever MA from arm lengths
Solve torque-balance lever problems

concepts.statement: **First class**: fulcrum between effort and load (crowbar, seesaw). **Second**: load between (wheelbarrow). **Third**: effort between (tweezers, forearm).
concepts.detail: Class sets whether $MA$ exceeds, equals, or trails one.

concepts.statement: Moment balance gives **$IMA = l_{effort}/l_{load}$** and $F_{load} = F_{effort}(l_{effort}/l_{load})$.
concepts.detail: $90\ \mathrm{cm}$ effort versus $15\ \mathrm{cm}$ load gives $IMA = 6$.

concepts.statement: Set **effort moment equals load moment**: $F_e l_e = F_l l_l$ about the fulcrum, with weights of the bar added as needed.
concepts.detail: This is Chapter 7 parallel equilibrium applied to one pivot.

concepts.statement: Third-class levers accept **$MA < 1$ to buy speed and range**: small muscle moves produce large fast hand motions.
concepts.detail: Fishing rods and shovels trade force for tip velocity deliberately.

concepts.statement: The fulcrum carries **effort plus load** (first class, same-side pushes): size pins and pivots for the sum, not just the load.
concepts.detail: $200\ \mathrm{N}$ effort lifting $1200\ \mathrm{N}$ loads the pin with $1400\ \mathrm{N}$.

examples.title: Crowbar nail pull
examples.problem: A crowbar has effort arm $90.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and load arm $15.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. Effort $200\ \mathrm{N}$: what nail force results?

steps.label: Force
steps.text: $F_{nail} = 200 \times 6.00 = 1200\ \mathrm{N}$ (ideal; friction trims it).

steps.label: Pin
steps.text: Fulcrum carries $200 + 1200 = 1400\ \mathrm{N}$.

examples.result: $1.20\ \mathrm{kN}$ on the nail ideally.

examples.title: Wheelbarrow lift
examples.problem: A $400\ \mathrm{N}$ load sits $0.400\ \mathrm{m}$ from the wheel; handles are $1.20\ \mathrm{m}$ out. Find lift force.

steps.label: Feel
steps.text: About $13.6\ \mathrm{kg}$ of lift for a $40.8\ \mathrm{kg}$ load.

examples.result: $133\ \mathrm{N}$ of handle lift.

keyTakeaways: Class by fulcrum-load-effort order; MA is arm ratio.
$F_e l_e = F_l l_l$ solves every lever.
Third class buys speed with $MA < 1$.

quiz.q: Crowbar $90/15\ \mathrm{cm}$ with $200\ \mathrm{N}$ pulls nails with
Wheelbarrow ($400\ \mathrm{N}$ at $0.4\ \mathrm{m}$, handles $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$) needs lift
A fishing rod is third class, meaning it
options: Trades force for tip speed and range
quiz.explanation: Effort between fulcrum and load gives $MA < 1$ with speed gain.

intro: Windlasses, steering wheels, and doorknobs are levers wrapped in a circle. This section rates wheel-and-axle systems by radius ratio and works windlass and screwdriver problems.
objectives: Compute wheel-and-axle MA from radii
Solve windlass lifting problems
Relate handle torque to axle force

concepts.statement: **$IMA = R/r$** (wheel radius over axle radius): the rope winds on the small drum while effort circles the large wheel.
concepts.detail: $R = 30\ \mathrm{cm}$, $r = 5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ gives $IMA = 6$.

concepts.statement: One shaft means **one torque**: $F_{effort}R = F_{load}r$ — solve for any term given three.
concepts.detail: Friction in bearings is the only leakage from this equality.

concepts.statement: Cranks, handwheels, and steering wheels are **wheels with spokes**: crank radius plays $R$ exactly.
concepts.detail: A $40\ \mathrm{cm}$ steering wheel on a $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ pinion gives $IMA = 8$.

concepts.statement: Drum diameter also sets **rope speed and capacity**: small drums lift slowly with thin-rope limits.
concepts.detail: multilayer winding changes effective $r$ — rate the outer layer conservatively.

concepts.statement: Well-greased journal bearings reach **$85$-$95\%$**; dry or loaded bushings fall far below — $MA = \eta \times IMA$.
concepts.detail: Ball bearings on the axle approach the ideal most closely.

examples.title: Windlass well lift
examples.problem: A windlass has crank $R = 0.400\ \mathrm{m}$ and drum $r = 0.0800\ \mathrm{m}$. Effort $120\ \mathrm{N}$: what bucket weight lifts (ideal)?

steps.label: Real
steps.text: At $85\%$ efficiency: $510\ \mathrm{N}$ (about $52\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water plus bucket).

examples.result: $600\ \mathrm{N}$ ideal; $510\ \mathrm{N}$ at $85\%$.

examples.title: Screwdriver torque
examples.problem: A $3.00\ \mathrm{cm}$ handle drives a $0.400\ \mathrm{cm}$ shaft with $25.0\ \mathrm{N}$ of grip force. Find screw torque.

steps.label: Force at rim
steps.text: Torque in: $25.0 \times 0.0300 = 0.750\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$.

steps.label: Ratio view
steps.text: $IMA = 3.00/0.400 = 7.50$ over shaft-surface force.

steps.label: Report
steps.text: $0.750\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$ at the screw — fat handles turn stubborn screws.

examples.result: $0.750\ \mathrm{N \cdot m}$ of screw torque.

keyTakeaways: $IMA = R/r$; torque equality $F_eR = F_lr$ solves windlasses.
Cranks and handwheels are wheels of crank radius.
Real $MA$ is $\eta \times IMA$ after bearing losses.

quiz.q: Crank $0.400\ \mathrm{m}$, drum $0.0800\ \mathrm{m}$, $120\ \mathrm{N}$ lifts ideally
quiz.explanation: $IMA = 5$; $120 \times 5 = 600\ \mathrm{N}$.

quiz.q: Wheel-and-axle torque relation is
quiz.explanation: Shared shaft equalizes torque ideally.
