intro: Pulleys redirect tension and multiply it by rope count. This section counts supporting ropes, separates fixed from movable blocks, and prices real efficiencies.
objectives: Count supporting ropes to find pulley IMA
Solve gun-tackle and luff-tackle tensions
Apply pulley efficiency to predict real effort

concepts.statement: A **fixed pulley changes direction only**: $IMA = 1$, $MA \approx 1$ — convenient, not force-multiplying.
concepts.detail: Flag halyards and hoist redirects are fixed pulleys.

concepts.statement: A **movable pulley doubles force**: $IMA = 2$ because two rope segments share the load.
concepts.detail: $500\ \mathrm{N}$ hangs on two $250\ \mathrm{N}$ segments.

concepts.statement: **$IMA$ equals the number of rope parts supporting the movable block** — count them in the diagram.
concepts.detail: Four supporting parts give $IMA = 4$: pull $4\ \mathrm{m}$ to lift $1\ \mathrm{m}$.

concepts.statement: Ideal effort is **$F = W/n$** for $n$ supporting ropes; real effort is **$F = W/(n\eta)$** with block efficiency.
concepts.detail: A $2000\ \mathrm{N}$ engine on $4$ parts at $80\%$ needs $625\ \mathrm{N}$ of pull.

concepts.statement: Each sheave costs **$3$-$5\%$** in friction: many-part tackles gain force but bleed efficiency per wheel.
concepts.detail: Four-sheave tackles typically land near $75$-$85\%$ overall.

figures.caption: Four-part tackle: $IMA = 4$, effort $F = W/4$ ideally over $4\times$ rope pull
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Four-part tackle: IMA = 4, effort F = W/4 ideally over 4times rope pull" viewBox="0 0 400 170" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><rect x="120" y="20" width="160" height="18" rx="4"/><rect x="150" y="120" width="100" height="18" rx="4"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="none"><line x1="150" y1="38" x2="150" y2="120"/><line x1="190" y1="38" x2="190" y2="120"/><line x1="230" y1="38" x2="230" y2="120"/><line x1="270" y1="38" x2="270" y2="102"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="278" y="115">F</text><text x="160" y="158">W on 4 parts: IMA = 4</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Engine-hoist pull
examples.problem: A $2000\ \mathrm{N}$ engine hangs on a $4$-part tackle at $80\%$ efficiency. What pull is needed, and how much rope for $1.50\ \mathrm{m}$ of lift?

steps.label: Rope
steps.text: Pull $4 \times 1.50 = 6.00\ \mathrm{m}$ of rope.

examples.result: $625\ \mathrm{N}$ pull; $6.00\ \mathrm{m}$ of rope.

examples.title: Movable pulley check
examples.problem: A movable pulley supports $600\ \mathrm{N}$ with $320\ \mathrm{N}$ of effort. Find $MA$ and efficiency.

steps.label: Loss
steps.text: One sheave near $94\%$ — a good ball-bearing block.

keyTakeaways: Fixed pulleys redirect; movable pulleys multiply by rope count.
$IMA$ is supporting-rope count; $F = W/(n\eta)$ really.
Each sheave costs a few percent efficiency.

quiz.q: $2000\ \mathrm{N}$ on 4 parts at $80\%$ needs pull
Lifting $1.50\ \mathrm{m}$ on 4 parts pulls rope
quiz.explanation: Rope distance is $IMA \times$ load distance.

quiz.q: $600\ \mathrm{N}$ on one movable pulley with $320\ \mathrm{N}$ effort is efficiency

intro: Ramps trade a long gentle push for a short brutal lift. This section rates inclined planes by length-over-height and solves skid, dolly, and loading problems with friction noted.
objectives: Compute inclined-plane IMA from $L/h$
Find ideal push force for a given slope
Correct for friction in real pushes

concepts.statement: **$IMA = L/h = 1/\sin\theta$**: a $4.00\ \mathrm{m}$ ramp rising $1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ gives $IMA = 4$.
concepts.detail: Gentler slopes (longer $L$) multiply force more and extend the push proportionally.

concepts.statement: Frictionless push up the slope is **$F = W\sin\theta = W(h/L)$** parallel to the plane.
concepts.detail: $2000\ \mathrm{N}$ up the $4{:}1$ ramp needs $500\ \mathrm{N}$ ideally.

concepts.statement: The plane supports **$N = W\cos\theta$** perpendicular — the base of slope-friction estimates.
concepts.detail: Steeper slopes unload the plane and load the push simultaneously.

concepts.statement: Real pushes add **$f = \mu N = \mu W\cos\theta$** to the ideal: $F_{real} = W\sin\theta + \mu W\cos\theta$.
concepts.detail: Rollers and grease attack the second term directly.

concepts.statement: Two inclines back-to-back make a **wedge** (next section): the same $L/h$ logic splits outward instead of lifting.
concepts.detail: Axes, knives, and doorstops are portable inclines.

examples.title: Loading-ramp push
examples.problem: A $2000\ \mathrm{N}$ crate goes up a $4.00\ \mathrm{m}$ ramp rising $1.00\ \mathrm{m}$. Find ideal push; then with $\mu = 0.20$.
examples.result: $500\ \mathrm{N}$ ideal; $887\ \mathrm{N}$ with friction.

examples.title: Truck-bed ramp choice
examples.problem: A $1.20\ \mathrm{m}$-high bed must keep pushes under $600\ \mathrm{N}$ for a $2400\ \mathrm{N}$ load (ideal). How long a ramp?

steps.label: Reality
steps.text: Friction demands longer or rollers — order $5.5$-$6\ \mathrm{m}$ of ramp.

examples.result: $4.80\ \mathrm{m}$ ideal; longer in practice.

keyTakeaways: $IMA = L/h$; ideal push is $W(h/L)$ along the slope.
Friction adds $\mu W\cos\theta$ to every real push.
Lengthen or roll the load to beat friction.

quiz.q: $2000\ \mathrm{N}$ up a $4\ \mathrm{m}$ ramp rising $1\ \mathrm{m}$ needs ideally
With $\mu = 0.20$ the push above becomes about
The plane supports normal force
quiz.explanation: Perpendicular component of weight.

intro: A screw is an incline wrapped around a cylinder, trading many easy turns for powerful advance. This section derives its large MA and tightens bolts to torque honestly.
objectives: Compute screw IMA from handle radius and pitch
Relate torque to clamping force
Explain self-locking from friction

concepts.statement: One turn advances the pitch $p$ while effort circles $2\pi r$: **$IMA = 2\pi r/p$** — hundreds are routine.
concepts.detail: $r = 0.200\ \mathrm{m}$, $p = 2.00\ \mathrm{mm}$ gives $IMA = 628$.

concepts.statement: Ideal clamp is **$F = F_{effort}(2\pi r/p)$**; real is $\eta \approx 30$-$50\%$ of that after thread friction.
concepts.detail: $50\ \mathrm{N}$ on the $628$-IMA handle ideals $31{,}400\ \mathrm{N}$ of clamp.

concepts.statement: **Pitch** is crest spacing; **lead** is advance per turn ($lead = pitch \times starts$) — multi-start threads advance faster with lower MA.
concepts.detail: Double-start halves the $IMA$ but doubles speed per turn.

concepts.statement: Shallow thread angles let **friction hold the load**: ordinary bolts stay put without back-driving — the flip side of low efficiency.
concepts.detail: Steep ball-screw leads reverse this, back-driving freely and needing brakes.

concepts.statement: Bolt **torque predicts tension only roughly** ($\pm 25\%$) because friction dominates — lubricate consistently and calibrate.
concepts.detail: Critical joints use turn-of-nut or stretch control instead of torque alone.

figures.caption: Screw as wrapped incline: one turn of circumference $2\pi r$ advances pitch $p$
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Screw as wrapped incline: one turn of circumference 2pi r advances pitch p" viewBox="0 0 400 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><polygon points="40,110 360,60 360,90 40,140"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"><line x1="40" y1="110" x2="40" y2="140"/><line x1="360" y1="60" x2="360" y2="90"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="150" y="130">wrapped ramp: rise p per 2πr</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Jack-screw clamp
examples.problem: A press screw has handle $r = 0.250\ \mathrm{m}$, pitch $p = 3.00\ \mathrm{mm}$, effort $60.0\ \mathrm{N}$, efficiency $40\%$. Find clamping force.

steps.label: Real
steps.text: $0.40 \times 31{,}416 = 12{,}566\ \mathrm{N} \approx 12.6\ \mathrm{kN}$.

examples.result: About $12.6\ \mathrm{kN}$ of clamp from a $60\ \mathrm{N}$ hand.

examples.title: Bolt advance count
examples.problem: A $1.50\ \mathrm{mm}$-pitch bolt must advance $18.0\ \mathrm{mm}$. How many turns?

steps.label: Effort distance
steps.text: At $r = 0.150\ \mathrm{m}$ the hand travels $12 \times 2\pi(0.150) = 11.31\ \mathrm{m}$.

steps.label: Trade
steps.text: Eleven meters of easy circling for $18\ \mathrm{mm}$ of crushing advance.

examples.result: $12$ turns; $11.3\ \mathrm{m}$ of hand travel.

keyTakeaways: $IMA = 2\pi r/p$ makes screws the highest-MA simple machine.
Real clamp is $\eta \approx 0.3$-$0.5$ of ideal after thread friction.
Friction self-locks ordinary threads; steep leads need brakes.

quiz.q: Handle $0.250\ \mathrm{m}$, pitch $3.00\ \mathrm{mm}$ gives IMA about
$60\ \mathrm{N}$ on that screw at $40\%$ clamps about
quiz.explanation: $60 \times 524 \times 0.40 = 12.6\ \mathrm{kN}$.

quiz.q: Ordinary bolts stay tight because
options: Thread friction self-locks the shallow helix
quiz.explanation: Low efficiency is the price of holding without back-driving.

intro: Knives, axes, and chisels split by driving a thin incline sideways. This section rates wedges by length-to-thickness and shows why thin, slick wedges split best.
objectives: Compute wedge IMA from length and thickness
Explain splitting-force multiplication
Choose wedge angles for splitting versus holding

concepts.statement: **$IMA = L/t$** (length over max thickness): a $200\ \mathrm{mm}$ wedge $20\ \mathrm{mm}$ thick gives $IMA = 10$.
concepts.detail: Thinner, longer wedges multiply harder and drive deeper per blow.

concepts.statement: Driving force forward becomes **large normal forces sideways** on both faces — the log feels multiples of the maul blow.
concepts.detail: Friction on both faces is the efficiency tax, as with screws.

concepts.statement: Knife and chisel edges are **micro-wedges**: acute angles cut easily but dull fast; obtuse edges endure but push harder.
concepts.detail: Wood-splitting $15^{\circ}$ versus metal-cutting $60^{\circ}$ edges embody the trade.

concepts.statement: Thin slick wedges **split**; thick rough wedges **hold** (doorstops, shims) by friction self-locking.
concepts.detail: Holding wedges reverse the design goal: maximize grip, not advance.

concepts.statement: Mallets deliver **impulse $Ft$** that the wedge converts to splitting work — sharp faces concentrate the stress.
concepts.detail: Stress is force over edge area, so honed edges split at lower blows.

examples.title: Splitting-wedge force
examples.problem: A $250\ \mathrm{mm}$ wedge $25.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ thick is driven with $800\ \mathrm{N}$. Estimate ideal splitting force.

steps.label: Force
steps.text: $F_{split} = 800 \times 10.0 = 8000\ \mathrm{N}$ ideally across the faces.

steps.label: Real
steps.text: At $60\%$ with friction: about $4800\ \mathrm{N}$ still splits green wood.

examples.result: $8.00\ \mathrm{kN}$ ideal; roughly $4.80\ \mathrm{kN}$ real.

examples.title: Doorstop holding
examples.problem: Explain why a rough $10^{\circ}$ rubber doorstop holds but a greased steel one slips.

steps.label: Geometry
steps.text: Both have $IMA = L/t \approx 5.7$ driving in easily.

steps.label: Friction
steps.text: Rubber $\mu \approx 1.0$ self-locks; greased steel $\mu \approx 0.1$ back-drives under the door load.

steps.label: Design
steps.text: Holding wedges maximize $\mu$; splitting wedges minimize it.

examples.result: Friction decides: high-$\mu$ holds, low-$\mu$ slips.

keyTakeaways: Wedge $IMA = L/t$; thin and long splits hardest.
Forward drive becomes multiplied sideways normal force.
Rough wedges hold; slick wedges split.

A doorstop holds best when it is
quiz.explanation: Holding wants friction self-locking, not easy advance.

quiz.explanation: Acute micro-wedges focus force onto tiny area.

intro: Real shop machines chain simple machines: crank to gear to screw to lever. This section multiplies stage advantages into overall MA and traces overall efficiency.
objectives: Multiply stage IMAs into overall IMA
Multiply stage efficiencies into overall efficiency
Analyze a crank-gear-screw press end to end

concepts.statement: **Overall $IMA = \prod IMA_i$** and **overall $MA = \prod MA_i$** — stages multiply, never add.
concepts.detail: Lever $4\times$ times screw $100\times$ gives $400\times$ overall ideally.

concepts.statement: **Overall $\eta = \prod \eta_i$**: $90\%$, $80\%$, $40\%$ stages chain to $28.8\%$ overall.
concepts.detail: The weakest stage dominates — improve it first.

concepts.statement: Size each stage for **compatible force, travel, and speed**: a huge screw MA starved by a tiny crank travel stalls the job.
concepts.detail: Check force, distance, and power continuity at every interface.

concepts.statement: Screw or worm stages can make trains **one-way**: easy forward cranking, locked against back-driving — a safety feature or a nuisance.
concepts.detail: Hoists exploit it; positioning servos must design around it.

concepts.statement: Draw the **power flow with per-stage $IMA$, $MA$, $\eta$** so losses and limits are auditable.
concepts.detail: Nameplate overall ratings must reconcile with the product of stages.

examples.title: Press train overall
examples.problem: A press chains lever $IMA = 5.0$ ($\eta = 0.90$), gears $IMA = 4.0$ ($\eta = 0.85$), screw $IMA = 120$ ($\eta = 0.40$). Find overall $IMA$, $\eta$, and clamp from $80.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

examples.title: Bicycle drive chain
examples.problem: Pedal crank $0.170\ \mathrm{m}$ drives a $44$-tooth ring to a $16$-tooth cog on a $0.340\ \mathrm{m}$ wheel. Find speed versus force trade.

steps.label: Gear
steps.text: Ratio $44/16 = 2.75$: wheel spins $2.75\times$ crank speed.

steps.label: Lever arms
steps.text: Crank $0.170$ versus wheel $0.340$: force at ground is $(0.170/0.340)/2.75 = 0.182\times$ pedal force.

steps.label: Trade
steps.text: Fast gearing: speed multiplied, hill force divided — riders shift to invert it.

examples.result: Ground force $0.182\times$ pedal force at $2.75\times$ cadence rate.

keyTakeaways: Stage IMAs and efficiencies multiply into overall ratings.
Weakest efficiency dominates — fix it first.
Verify force, travel, and power at every interface.

quiz.q: Stages $5 \times 4 \times 120$ give overall IMA
quiz.explanation: $5 \times 4 \times 120 = 2400$.

quiz.q: Stages $90\%$, $85\%$, $40\%$ chain to overall
$80\ \mathrm{N}$ through that press clamps about

intro: Friction is the tax collector on every machine: it trims MA below IMA and turns the difference into heat. This section measures that tax and shows how lubrication and bearings cut it.
objectives: Compute lost work from $IMA$, $MA$ data
Explain friction sources per machine type
Select friction-reduction measures correctly

concepts.statement: **Lost work $= W_{in} - W_{out} = W_{in}(1 - \eta)$** in joules — heat, wear, and noise share it.
concepts.detail: $2000\ \mathrm{J}$ in at $80\%$ loses $400\ \mathrm{J}$ to friction.

concepts.statement: **Sliding friction (threads, wedges, belts) costs far more than rolling friction (bearings, rollers)** — convert slides to rolls where possible.
concepts.detail: Ball screws ($90\%$) crush plain screws ($40\%$) on efficiency for this reason.

concepts.statement: **Boundary, mixed, and full-film lubrication** separate surfaces progressively; correct viscosity and supply sustain the film.
concepts.detail: Dry starts wear most — pre-lube and sealed greasing pay back.

concepts.statement: **Breakaway (static) effort exceeds running effort**: size handles and motors for starting, then cruise efficiently.
concepts.detail: Jacks and winches need their biggest pull on the first stroke.

concepts.statement: **Alignment, tension, and cleanliness restore rated $\eta$**: misaligned belts and gritty threads silently double the friction tax.
concepts.detail: Scheduled inspection is efficiency maintenance, not just reliability.

figures.caption: Efficiency waterfall: input work splits into useful output plus friction heat per stage

examples.title: Tackle heat loss
examples.problem: A tackle takes $W_{in} = 3000\ \mathrm{J}$ to deliver $W_{out} = 2400\ \mathrm{J}$. Find efficiency and heat.

steps.label: Heat
steps.text: $3000 - 2400 = 600\ \mathrm{J}$ warms sheaves and rope.

steps.label: Per lift
steps.text: Ten lifts dump $6000\ \mathrm{J}$ — noticeable warming on small blocks.

examples.result: $80\%$ efficient; $600\ \mathrm{J}$ lost per lift.

examples.title: Screw upgrade payoff
examples.problem: A $10.0\ \mathrm{kN}$ press screw ($IMA = 500$) upgrades from $\eta = 0.35$ to ball-screw $0.90$. Compare handle forces.

steps.label: Payoff
steps.text: Same clamp at $39\%$ of the effort — plus back-drivability to manage.

examples.result: $57.1\ \mathrm{N}$ drops to $22.2\ \mathrm{N}$ of handle effort.

keyTakeaways: Lost work is $W_{in}(1 - \eta)$ — audit it in joules.
Rolling beats sliding; films beat boundary contact.
Size for breakaway; maintain alignment and lubrication.

quiz.q: $3000\ \mathrm{J}$ in, $2400\ \mathrm{J}$ out loses
Upgrading $35\%$ to $90\%$ on $IMA = 500$ changes $10\ \mathrm{kN}$ effort from
The largest friction savings come from
options: Converting slides to rolling with proper lubrication
quiz.explanation: Rolling plus full-film lubrication minimizes the friction coefficient.

intro: Gravity can be mapped as a field: an arrow at every point showing the force a test mass would feel. This section defines $g$ as field strength and traces weight loss with altitude.
objectives: Define gravitational field as force per unit mass
Compute $g$ at altitude with the inverse square
Sketch field lines for earth and two-body regions

concepts.statement: **Field $\vec{g} = \vec{F}/m$** in $\mathrm{N/kg} = \mathrm{m/s^2}$ points toward the source — force per kilogram placed there.
concepts.detail: Earth surface field is $9.80\ \mathrm{N/kg}$ downward everywhere locally.

concepts.statement: Outside a spherical planet, **$g(r) = GM/r^2$** directed centrally — altitude enters through $r = R + h$.
**Lines point inward with density showing strength**: crowded near the surface, sparse far away, ending only on masses.
concepts.detail: Two-body fields show a neutral (zero-force) point between the masses.

concepts.statement: Your **mass feeds the field; the field sets your weight** $W = mg(r)$ — travel changes $g$, never $m$.
concepts.detail: Space-station floating is free fall through a still-strong field, not field absence.

concepts.statement: Multiple masses give **vector sums of fields**: moon plus earth contributions add arrow-to-tail at each point.
concepts.detail: Tides come from the field gradient (difference across earth diameter), not the field itself.

examples.title: $g$ aboard the space station
examples.problem: The station orbits at $h = 400\ \mathrm{km}$ above $R_E = 6380\ \mathrm{km}$. Find $g$ there.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: $89\%$ of surface gravity remains — astronauts float from free fall, not zero-$g$.

examples.result: $g \approx 8.68\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ at station altitude.

examples.title: Earth-moon neutral point
examples.problem: Estimate where earth and moon pulls cancel on the connecting line ($M_E = 81.3\,M_M$, separation $D = 384{,}400\ \mathrm{km}$).

steps.label: Balance
steps.text: $M_E/x^2 = M_M/(D - x)^2$ with $x$ from earth center.

steps.label: Locate
steps.text: $x \approx 346{,}000\ \mathrm{km}$ from earth — about $38{,}400\ \mathrm{km}$ from the moon.

examples.result: Neutral point about nine-tenths of the way to the moon.

keyTakeaways: $g$ is force per unit mass, mapping gravity everywhere.
$g(r) = GM/r^2$ falls slowly — $89\%$ remains at $400\ \mathrm{km}$.
Fields superpose vectorially; gradients drive tides.

quiz.q: $g$ at $400\ \mathrm{km}$ altitude is about
Astronauts float because they are
options: In continuous free fall around earth
quiz.explanation: Strong $g$ still acts; orbit is falling while missing the ground.

quiz.q: The earth-moon neutral point sits
options: About 9/10 of the way to the moon
quiz.explanation: Earth mass dominance pushes cancellation near the moon.

intro: Everything technicians cut, pour, pump, or wire is matter in one of three phases. This section defines matter, mass, and the phase behaviors the next sections detail.
objectives: Define matter, mass, and inertia precisely
Contrast solid, liquid, and gas behavior
Classify phase changes by energy direction

concepts.statement: **Matter** is anything occupying space with mass; **mass** in kilograms measures its inertia and gravitational pull.
concepts.detail: Fields and energy cross space without being matter in this classical sense.

concepts.statement: **Solids hold shape and volume; liquids hold volume but flow; gases fill their container** — molecular freedom increases across the sequence.
concepts.detail: Steel beams, hydraulic oil, and compressed air exemplify the three.

concepts.statement: Bulk behavior comes from **molecular bonding and motion**: bound lattices (solids), sliding neighbors (liquids), free flight (gases).
concepts.detail: Heating feeds molecular motion until bonds yield — melting, then boiling.

concepts.statement: **Melting, freezing, vaporization, condensation, sublimation** trade thermal energy for bonding at fixed temperatures.
concepts.detail: Ice melts at $0\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$ absorbing $334\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}$ without warming.

concepts.statement: Phase decides **containment and hazard**: tanks hold liquids, vessels hold pressure gases, structures rely on solid strength.
concepts.detail: Misjudging phase means burst vessels or collapsed supports.

figures.caption: Three phases: lattice (solid), sliding neighbors (liquid), free flight (gas)

examples.title: Shop phase inventory
examples.problem: Classify: steel beam, hydraulic oil, shop air, welding arc plasma (note), ice coolant.

steps.label: Solids
steps.text: Steel beam and ice hold shape and volume — solids.

steps.label: Fluids
steps.text: Hydraulic oil is liquid (volume fixed, flows); shop air is gas (fills vessels).

steps.label: Beyond
steps.text: The arc is plasma, a fourth high-energy state outside this chapter model.

examples.result: Beam, ice: solid; oil: liquid; air: gas; arc: plasma.

examples.title: Melting energy budget
examples.problem: How much energy melts $5.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ice at $0\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$ ($L_f = 334\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}$)?

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: $Q = mL_f = 5.00 \times 334 = 1670\ \mathrm{kJ}$.

steps.label: Meaning
steps.text: That is $0.464\ \mathrm{kWh}$ of cooling before any warming.

steps.label: Use
steps.text: Ice banks pack this latent capacity into coolers and process loads.

examples.result: $1.67\ \mathrm{MJ}$ absorbed at constant $0\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$.

keyTakeaways: Matter has mass and volume; phases differ in shape freedom.
Molecular bonding versus motion explains solid, liquid, gas.
Phase changes bank or release latent energy at fixed temperature.

quiz.q: Which holds volume but flows?
quiz.explanation: Liquids keep volume while taking the container shape.

quiz.q: Melting $5.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ice absorbs about
Gases differ from liquids by
quiz.explanation: Gas molecules fly free until walls stop them.

intro: Structures stand on solid properties: strength, stiffness, hardness, and ductility. This section defines each and reads material choices off density and strength tables.
objectives: Define stress, strength, elasticity, and hardness
Distinguish ductile from brittle failure
Select materials from property tables

concepts.statement: **Stress $\sigma = F/A$** in $\mathrm{Pa}$ loads material; **strength** is the stress at failure — tension, compression, and shear separately.
concepts.detail: Structural steel yields near $250\ \mathrm{MPa}$ in tension.

concepts.statement: **Elastic** deformation springs back; past the **elastic limit** it stays bent (plastic) and then fractures.
concepts.detail: Springs live elastically; car bodies sacrifice plastically in crashes.

concepts.statement: **Hardness** resists scratching and dents; **ductility** draws into wire without breaking — often traded against each other.
concepts.detail: Quenched steel is hard but brittle; copper is soft but richly ductile.

concepts.statement: **Crystals** (metals, quartz) order atoms in lattices with directional strengths; **amorphous** solids (glass, plastics) freeze disorder.
concepts.detail: Grain and heat treatment tune metal crystals for the job.

concepts.statement: Solids also rate by **conductivity and expansion**: copper wires, aluminum fins, and Invar instruments each exploit one extreme.
concepts.detail: Chapters 14 and 17 quantify those behaviors.

examples.title: Cable stress check
examples.problem: A $5000\ \mathrm{N}$ load hangs on a steel rod of diameter $10.0\ \mathrm{mm}$. Find tensile stress and judge against $250\ \mathrm{MPa}$ yield.

steps.label: Judge
steps.text: $63.7 < 250$ with factor $3.9$ — safe for static load.

examples.result: $63.7\ \mathrm{MPa}$ — safe with margin.

examples.title: Wire ductility choice
examples.problem: Choose between glass rod and copper wire for a bent conductor path.

steps.label: Glass
steps.text: Hard and strong in compression but brittle — bending fractures it.

steps.label: Copper
steps.text: Ductile and conductive — bends without breaking while carrying current.

steps.label: Pick
steps.text: Copper wire; glass only where transparency plus rigidity rule.

examples.result: Copper for bent conductors; property-matched choice.

keyTakeaways: Stress $F/A$ versus directional strengths sizes every part.
Elastic returns; plastic stays; brittle snaps without warning.
Match hardness, ductility, and conductivity to the job.

quiz.q: $5000\ \mathrm{N}$ on $10.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ rod stresses it at about
Past the elastic limit, deformation becomes
quiz.explanation: Yielding leaves permanent set, then fracture.

quiz.q: Bent conductors want
quiz.explanation: Ductility plus conductivity is the copper combination.

intro: Oils, water, and coolants transmit pressure, lubricate, and carry heat because they flow. This section covers viscosity, surface tension, and pressure transmission in liquids.
objectives: Define viscosity and its temperature dependence
Explain surface tension and capillary action
Apply pressure transmission to hydraulic problems

concepts.statement: **Viscosity** is resistance to flow (internal friction): honey high, water low — falling steeply with temperature for oils.
concepts.detail: SAE grades rate that curve so engines start cold yet film hot.

concepts.statement: **Surface tension** skins liquid surfaces (water about $0.073\ \mathrm{N/m}$), beading drops and floating needles.
concepts.detail: Detergents lower it so wash water wets and penetrates.

concepts.statement: **Capillary action** climbs narrow tubes where adhesion beats cohesion — wicks, soils, and solder joints exploit it.
concepts.detail: Finer bores lift higher but carry less volume.

concepts.statement: Confined liquids transmit **pressure undiminished** ($P = F/A$) and add **hydrostatic $\rho g h$** with depth — the hydraulic principle of Chapter 13.
concepts.detail: $1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ of water adds $9.80\ \mathrm{kPa}$.

concepts.statement: Liquids are nearly **incompressible**, so small piston motions pressurize instantly — the hydraulic stiffness advantage over air.
concepts.detail: That stiffness is why jacks lift and brakes bite without sponginess.

examples.title: Hydraulic depth pressure
examples.problem: Find the pressure $2.50\ \mathrm{m}$ deep in oil of density $850\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ (gauge).

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: $P = \rho g h = 850 \times 9.80 \times 2.50$.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $850 \times 24.5 = 20{,}825\ \mathrm{Pa} \approx 20.8\ \mathrm{kPa}$.

steps.label: Sense
steps.text: Less than water ($24.5\ \mathrm{kPa}$) because oil is lighter.

examples.result: About $20.8\ \mathrm{kPa}$ gauge at depth.

examples.title: Oil-grade reasoning
examples.problem: Why does equipment specify $10$W-$30$ multigrade oil?

steps.label: Cold
steps.text: $10$W flows at winter starts, limiting wear when films are thin.

steps.label: Hot
steps.text: $30$ holds viscosity at operating temperature so bearings keep film strength.

steps.label: Viscosity
steps.text: Multigrade chemistry flattens the temperature-viscosity fall.

examples.result: Pumpable cold, protective hot — one oil, both duties.

keyTakeaways: Viscosity resists flow and falls with temperature; grades manage it.
Surface tension and capillarity govern drops, wicks, and solder.
Liquids transmit $P = F/A$ plus $\rho gh$ nearly incompressibly.

quiz.q: Pressure $2.50\ \mathrm{m}$ deep in $850\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ oil is about
Multigrade $10$W-$30$ means
quiz.explanation: Additives flatten the viscosity-temperature curve.

quiz.q: Hydraulics beat pneumatics in stiffness because liquids are
quiz.explanation: Incompressibility transmits motion without spongy delay.

intro: Gases fill, press, and expand with temperature — the behaviors behind tires, tanks, and HVAC. This section previews gas pressure and temperature relations detailed in Chapter 15.
objectives: Explain gas pressure as molecular bombardment
Relate pressure, volume, and temperature qualitatively
Compute gas-mass from density and vessel volume

concepts.statement: **Gas pressure is molecular collisions** with walls — faster or denser molecules hit harder and raise $P$.
concepts.detail: Pumping more molecules into fixed $V$ raises collision rate and pressure together.

concepts.statement: At fixed temperature, **$P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$**: halving volume doubles pressure — squeezing crowds collisions.
concepts.detail: A $10.0\ \mathrm{L}$ tank at $100\ \mathrm{kPa}$ squeezed to $5.00\ \mathrm{L}$ reaches $200\ \mathrm{kPa}$.

concepts.statement: At fixed pressure, **$V/T$ is constant** (kelvin): heating expands gas proportionally.
concepts.detail: Warming $300\ \mathrm{K}$ gas to $450\ \mathrm{K}$ expands it $1.50\times$.

concepts.statement: **$\rho = m/V$** still rules: air near $1.20\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ at standard conditions fills vessels by volume times density.
concepts.detail: A $0.500\ \mathrm{m^3}$ tank holds about $0.600\ \mathrm{kg}$ of air at STP-ish density.

concepts.statement: Gases are **highly compressible** unlike liquids — tanks store large masses by pressure, with temperature swings as the price.
concepts.detail: That is why gas math needs $T$ while hydraulics mostly do not.

examples.title: Tire squeeze check
examples.problem: A $40.0\ \mathrm{L}$ tire cavity at $200\ \mathrm{kPa}$ is compressed (isothermally) to $32.0\ \mathrm{L}$ by loading. Find new pressure.

steps.label: Compute
steps.text: $P_2 = 250\ \mathrm{kPa}$.

steps.label: Note
steps.text: Isothermal ideal; real flexing warms the air and nudges higher.

examples.result: $250\ \mathrm{kPa}$ after compression.

examples.title: Tank air mass
examples.problem: A $0.500\ \mathrm{m^3}$ receiver holds air at density $6.00\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ (pressurized). Find air mass.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: $m = \rho V = 6.00 \times 0.500 = 3.00\ \mathrm{kg}$.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: Five times the $0.600\ \mathrm{kg}$ at ambient density — pressure stores mass.

steps.label: Use
steps.text: Tool runtime follows from this stored mass and flow rate.

examples.result: $3.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ of stored air.

keyTakeaways: Gas pressure is wall bombardment by moving molecules.
$P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$ (Boyle) and $V/T$ fixed (Charles) preview Chapter 15.
Gases store mass by compression; temperature always matters.

quiz.q: $40.0\ \mathrm{L}$ at $200\ \mathrm{kPa}$ squeezed to $32.0\ \mathrm{L}$ (same $T$) reaches
$0.500\ \mathrm{m^3}$ at $6.00\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ holds air mass
quiz.explanation: $m = \rho V = 3.00\ \mathrm{kg}$.

quiz.q: Heating a fixed-pressure gas from $300$ to $450\ \mathrm{K}$
quiz.explanation: $V \propto T$ in kelvin (Charles).

intro: Density is the working property for materials selection: mass packed per volume. This section computes densities, specific gravities, and float-sink verdicts for shop materials.
objectives: Compute density with $\rho = m/V$
Use specific gravity for fast identification
Predict float versus sink in a fluid

concepts.statement: **Density $\rho = m/V$** in $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ (or $\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) packs mass per volume: aluminum $2700$, steel $7860$, water $1000$.
concepts.detail: $1\ \mathrm{g/cm^3} = 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ bridges lab and SI tables.

concepts.statement: **Specific gravity $= \rho/\rho_{water}$** is unit-free: steel $7.86$, aluminum $2.70$, oak $0.70$.
concepts.detail: Below $1.0$ floats in water; above sinks — instant verdicts.

concepts.statement: Weigh the sample, dunk it, and read **displaced volume**: $\rho = m/V_{displaced}$ — Archimedes graduate-cylinder method.
concepts.detail: Irregular castings yield exact volumes no ruler can give.

concepts.statement: **Weight density $= \rho g$** in $\mathrm{N/m^3}$ gives force per volume for load and pressure work.
concepts.detail: Steel weighs $77{,}100\ \mathrm{N/m^3}$ ($7860 \times 9.80$).

concepts.statement: **Low density buys lightness, high density buys compactness**: aircraft aluminum versus flywheel steel versus lead ballast.
concepts.detail: Strength-to-density ratio, not density alone, picks aerospace winners.

figures.caption: Float or sink: body density below fluid floats, above sinks ($\rho$ vs $\rho_{fluid}$)
figures.svg: <svg role="img" aria-label="Float or sink: body density below fluid floats, above sinks (rho vs rho_fluid)" viewBox="0 0 400 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"><line x1="30" y1="70" x2="370" y2="70"/><rect x="30" y="70" width="340" height="60"/></g><g fill="currentColor"><rect x="70" y="45" width="50" height="20" rx="3"/><rect x="250" y="80" width="50" height="20" rx="3"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif"><text x="60" y="130">oak 0.70: floats</text><text x="240" y="130">steel 7.86: sinks</text></g></svg>

examples.title: Block density identification
examples.problem: A block $0.200 \times 0.100 \times 0.0500\ \mathrm{m}$ has mass $2.70\ \mathrm{kg}$. Find density and identify it.

steps.label: Identify
steps.text: Matches aluminum ($2700$); specific gravity $2.70$.

examples.result: $2700\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ — aluminum.

examples.title: Crown-displacement test
examples.problem: A $1.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ part displaces $190\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of water. Find density and float verdict.

steps.label: Density
steps.text: $\rho = 1500\ \mathrm{g}/190\ \mathrm{cm^3} = 7.895\ \mathrm{g/cm^3} = 7895\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$.

steps.label: Identify
steps.text: Near steel $7860$ — plausibly steel within error.

steps.label: Float
steps.text: Specific gravity $7.9 > 1$: sinks in water.

examples.result: $7895\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$; sinks — consistent with steel.

keyTakeaways: $\rho = m/V$; $1\ \mathrm{g/cm^3} = 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
Specific gravity under $1$ floats, over $1$ sinks in water.
Displacement volumetry nails irregular parts.

$1500\ \mathrm{g}$ displacing $190\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ gives density about
Oak ($SG = 0.70$) in water will
quiz.explanation: Below $1.0$ floats with $70\%$ submerged.

intro: The eye is a $2.5$ cm converging system that focuses real inverted images on the retina and lets the brain flip them. Coletta explains accommodation, the near and far points, and the myopia-hyperopia corrections. Every instrument in this chapter mates to this detector.
objectives: Describe cornea-lens-retina imaging with accommodation of eye power
Distinguish myopia from hyperopia and prescribe diverging versus converging lenses
Compute corrective power from $P = 1/f$ in diopters

concepts.statement: Cornea plus lens project a **real inverted** image on the **retina**; ciliary muscles **accommodate** by fattening the lens for near work.
concepts.detail: Most power ($~43$ diopters) comes from the cornea, with the lens adding $15$–$25$ adjustable diopters.

concepts.statement: The **far point** is the farthest sharp distance (infinity when normal) and the **near point** $N$ the closest ($~25$ cm young adult, receding with age).
concepts.detail: Presbyopia stiffens the lens so $N$ drifts past arm's length, requiring readers.

concepts.statement: **Myopia** (nearsight) focuses distant scenes before the retina from excess power or length; **diverging** glasses push the far point back to infinity.
concepts.detail: A $-2.0$ diopter lens ($f = -0.50$ m) corrects a far point stuck at $0.50$ m.

concepts.statement: **Hyperopia** (farsight) focuses behind the retina from weak power or shortness; **converging** lenses add the missing power for near work.
concepts.detail: A $+3.0$ diopter reader supplies what the stiff lens no longer musters.

concepts.statement: Lens power $P = 1/f$ in **diopters** (m$^{-1}$) adds directly: stacked or contact-plus-eye powers sum.
concepts.detail: A $+2.0$ diopter add on a $60$-diopter eye is a $3$ percent boost, enough to pull $N$ back in.

steps.label: Needed image
steps.text: Glasses must put infinity at $d_{i} = -0.80$ m (virtual, same side).

steps.label: Lens
steps.text: A $-1.25$ diopter diverging lens corrects distance vision.

examples.result: $-1.25$ diopters.

examples.title: Reading add
examples.problem: Presbyopia pushes the near point to $1.0$ m. What add images $25$ cm onto $1.0$ m?

steps.label: Object/image
steps.text: $d_{o} = 0.25$ m, $d_{i} = -1.0$ m (virtual near-point image).

examples.result: $+3.0$ diopters.

keyTakeaways: The eye accommodates lens power to hold real images on the retina.
Myopia needs diverging and hyperopia needs converging correction.
Diopter powers $P = 1/f$ add directly.

quiz.q: Myopia is corrected with:
quiz.explanation: Negative power diverges parallel rays as if from the stuck far point.

quiz.q: Accommodation for near vision:
quiz.explanation: Ciliary contraction rounds the lens, shortening $f$ to hold focus.

quiz.explanation: $f = 1/P = 1/2.0 = 0.50$ m converging.

intro: A magnifier lets the eye approach closer than the near point by handing it parallel or easy rays. Coletta derives angular magnification $M = N/f$ for the relaxed eye and $M = 1 + N/f$ with the image at $N$. Short focus means big boost.
objectives: Explain angular size gain versus the naked-eye near point
Apply $M = N/f$ (infinity) and $M = 1 + N/f$ (image at $N$)
Choose focal length for a target magnification

concepts.statement: **Angular magnification** $M = \theta/\theta_{0}$ compares aided angle to the best naked-eye angle $\theta_{0} \approx h/N$ at near point $N = 25$ cm.
concepts.detail: Doubling the angular size doubles retinal image size, the only gain that matters.

concepts.statement: Object at $f$ sends parallel rays (image at infinity) with $M = N/f$.
concepts.detail: A $5.0$ cm lens gives $M = 25/5.0 = 5\times$ with the eye relaxed.

concepts.statement: Pushing the image to $N$ strains accommodation but gains one more: $M = 1 + N/f$.
concepts.detail: The same $5.0$ cm lens reaches $6\times$ with the image at $25$ cm.

concepts.statement: Magnifiers want **short** $f$ and correspondingly strong diopters: $10\times$ needs about $f = 2.5$ cm ($40$ diopters).
concepts.detail: Jeweler's loupes stack short aspheres to hit $20\times$ without crippling aberration.

concepts.statement: Higher $M$ forces the object to $f$, so $20\times$ loupes work millimeters away with tweezers under them.
concepts.detail: Stand magnifiers trade peak $M$ for illuminated working room.

examples.title: Hand lens power
examples.problem: A $4.0$ cm magnifier is used with image at infinity. Find $M$ and required object placement.

steps.label: Placement
steps.text: Object exactly at $f$, $4.0$ cm before the lens.

steps.label: At near point
steps.text: Moving slightly inside raises $M$ to $1 + 6.25 = 7.25\times$.

examples.result: $6.25\times$ relaxed, $7.25\times$ at near point.

examples.title: Design for 10x
examples.problem: What $f$ gives $M = 10\times$ relaxed?

steps.label: Note
steps.text: A thick highly curved lens, as expected for $10\times$.

keyTakeaways: Magnifiers beat the near-point limit by angular gain.
$M = N/f$ relaxed and $1 + N/f$ at near point.
High power demands short focus and close work.

quiz.q: A $10$ cm magnifier relaxed gives $M$ of:
Image-at-near-point versus infinity differs by:
quiz.explanation: $(1 + N/f) - N/f = 1$ exactly.

quiz.q: Raising magnifier power requires:
quiz.explanation: $M = N/f$ grows as $f$ shrinks.

intro: The compound microscope stages two magnifications: an objective makes a big real image and the eyepiece magnifies its angle. Coletta derives $M = -(L/f_{o})(N/f_{e})$ with tube length $L$. Tiny things become visible by multiplication.
objectives: Trace objective real image plus eyepiece angular magnification
Apply $M = -(L/f_{o})(N/f_{e})$ to standard tubes
Explain why illumination and NA matter as much as $M$

concepts.statement: The short-$f$ **objective** images the specimen at lateral $m_{o} = -L/f_{o}$ with tube length $L$ ($~16$ cm).
concepts.detail: A $4.0$ mm objective gives $m_{o} = -160/4.0 = -40\times$ of inverted real size.

concepts.statement: The **eyepiece** works as a magnifier on that real image with $M_{e} = N/f_{e}$.
concepts.detail: A $25$ mm eyepiece contributes $10\times$ of angular gain.

concepts.statement: Overall $M = m_{o}M_{e} = -(L/f_{o})(N/f_{e})$: lateral times angular, negative for inversion.
concepts.detail: $40\times$ objective with $10\times$ eyepiece gives $-400\times$ total.

concepts.statement: **Numerical aperture** $NA = n\sin\alpha$ sets resolution $d \approx 0.61\lambda/NA$, limiting useful $M$ to about $1000\,NA$.
concepts.detail: Oil immersion ($n = 1.5$) lifts $NA$ past $1.3$ and resolves $200$ nm.

concepts.statement: **Empty** magnification beyond $1000\,NA$ enlarges blur without detail: resolution, not $M$, is the microscope's currency.
concepts.detail: A $2000\times$ image from a $0.65$ NA objective shows bigger but not sharper cells.

examples.title: Standard microscope
examples.problem: A microscope has $f_{o} = 8.0$ mm, $f_{e} = 20$ mm, $L = 160$ mm. Find $M$.
examples.result: $-250\times$ inverted.

examples.title: Resolution limit
examples.problem: An $NA = 1.25$ oil objective uses $550$ nm light. Find the smallest resolved spacing.

steps.label: Formula
steps.text: $d = 0.61\lambda/NA$.

steps.label: Meaning
steps.text: Bacteria resolve; viruses need electrons.

examples.result: About $0.27$ micrometers.

keyTakeaways: Objectives magnify laterally and eyepieces angularly in product.
$M = -(L/f_{o})(N/f_{e})$ prices standard tubes.
NA caps useful magnification near $1000\,NA$.

quiz.q: $20\times$ objective with $15\times$ eyepiece gives:
quiz.explanation: Multiply lateral by angular with inversion: $-20 \times 15 = -300\times$.

quiz.q: Oil immersion helps because it:
quiz.explanation: Higher $n$ widens the acceptance cone, shrinking $0.61\lambda/NA$.

quiz.q: Empty magnification means:
quiz.explanation: Past $1000\,NA$ the image grows but diffraction blur grows with it.

intro: Telescopes gather light and stretch angles with long objectives and short eyepieces. Coletta derives $M = -f_{o}/f_{e}$, compares refractors with reflectors, and prices light grasp by aperture area. Astronomy is photon economics.
objectives: Apply telescope $M = -f_{o}/f_{e}$ to refractor combinations
Compare refracting versus reflecting designs and their limits
Explain light-gathering scaling with $D^{2}$

concepts.statement: With objective $f_{o}$ and eyepiece $f_{e}$, $M = -f_{o}/f_{e}$: long focus collects angle, short eyepiece spends it.
concepts.detail: A $900$ mm objective with $15$ mm eyepiece gives $-60\times$.

concepts.statement: **Refractors** use a long converging objective; chromatic aberration and lens sag cap them near $1$ m aperture (Yerkes).
concepts.detail: Different colors focus at different depths because $n$ varies, fringing bright stars.

concepts.statement: **Reflectors** use a concave mirror objective, dodging chromatic error and supporting huge apertures from behind.
concepts.detail: Newtonian, Cassegrain, and Keck segmented designs all fold long $f_{o}$ into compact tubes.

concepts.statement: Brightness scales with area $\pi D^{2}/4$: doubling diameter quadruples photons and reaches $1.5$ magnitudes deeper.
concepts.detail: A $200$ mm scope gathers $100\times$ the pupil's $20$ mm, a $5$-magnitude gain.

concepts.statement: Atmospheric **seeing** ($~1$ arcsec) usually beats diffraction for ground scopes, which is why Hubble and adaptive optics pay off.
concepts.detail: Magnification past the seeing blur only magnifies turbulence.

examples.title: Backyard refractor
examples.problem: A $700$ mm objective with $10$ mm eyepiece observes the Moon. Find $M$ and the Moon's apparent size.

steps.label: Apparent size
steps.text: The $0.5^{\circ}$ Moon spans $70 \times 0.5 = 35^{\circ}$ of apparent angle.

steps.label: Note
steps.text: Eye relief and seeing usually cap useful $M$ near $50\times$ per inch of aperture.

examples.result: $-70\times$.

examples.title: Aperture gain
examples.problem: Compare a $150$ mm scope to the $7.0$ mm dark-adapted pupil.

steps.label: Magnitudes
steps.text: $2.5\log_{10}459 \approx 2.5 \times 2.662 = 6.65$ magnitudes deeper.

steps.label: Meaning
steps.text: Naked-eye $6$th magnitude extends past $12$th.

examples.result: About $460\times$ the light, $6.7$ magnitudes.

keyTakeaways: Telescopes magnify by $-f_{o}/f_{e}$ with long objectives.
Reflectors scale past refractors by avoiding lenses.
Aperture area, not $M$, buys faint objects.

quiz.q: $1000$ mm objective with $25$ mm eyepiece gives:
Doubling telescope diameter at fixed $f$-ratio:
quiz.explanation: Area grows as $D^{2}$.

quiz.q: Large modern research scopes are reflectors because mirrors:
options: Avoid chromatic error and support big sizes
quiz.explanation: Reflection is achromatic and mirrors support from behind, scaling to $10$ m.

intro: No instrument outresolves diffraction: apertures smear points into Airy disks and aberrations warp the rest. Coletta closes with the Rayleigh limit $\theta = 1.22\lambda/D$ and the lens defects opticians fight. Acuity is wave physics plus biology.
objectives: Apply Rayleigh $\theta_{min} = 1.22\lambda/D$ to eyes and instruments
Name spherical, chromatic, and astigmatic aberrations with fixes
Connect retinal sampling to $20/20$ acuity

concepts.statement: Two points resolve when separated by $\theta_{min} = 1.22\lambda/D$: aperture $D$ in wavelengths sets the angle.
concepts.detail: A $3.0$ mm pupil at $550$ nm gives $2.2 \times 10^{-4}$ rad, about one arcminute.

concepts.statement: The **Airy disk** is diffraction's central bright spot ($84$ percent of light) ringed by faint rings, the true image of every point.
concepts.detail: Stars are Airy disks, not points, in every telescope eyepiece.

concepts.statement: **Spherical** surfaces overfocus marginal rays; aspheric figuring or compound correction restores the point.
concepts.detail: Hubble's famous error was spherical aberration fixed by corrective optics.

concepts.statement: **Chromatic** spread focuses blue short of red; achromatic doublets of crown plus flint glass cancel it at two colors.
concepts.detail: Cheap singlets fringe high-contrast edges in blue-yellow.

concepts.statement: $20/20$ vision resolves $1$ arcminute, matching both the pupil's Rayleigh limit and the foveal cone spacing ($~2.5$ micrometers).
concepts.detail: Eye and optics co-evolved to the same limit: bigger pupils would outresolve the cone mosaic.

examples.problem: Find the Rayleigh angle for a $2.5$ mm pupil at $550$ nm and the retinal separation with $f_{eye} = 17$ mm.

steps.text: $s = f\theta = 17 \times 10^{-3} \times 2.68 \times 10^{-4} \approx 4.6 \times 10^{-6}$ m.

steps.text: About $4.6$ micrometers, near foveal cone spacing.

examples.problem: A $130$ mm reflector at $550$ nm: find its diffraction limit in arcseconds.

keyTakeaways: Diffraction caps every aperture at $1.22\lambda/D$.
Spherical and chromatic defects have figured and doublet fixes.
Retinal sampling matches the pupil's optical limit at $20/20$.

quiz.q: Aperture diameter doubles. Diffraction limit:
quiz.explanation: $\theta_{min} \propto 1/D$.

quiz.q: Achromatic doublets fix:
quiz.explanation: Paired glasses cancel focal shift at two wavelengths.

quiz.q: $20/20$ acuity corresponds to about:
quiz.explanation: One arcminute matches pupil diffraction and cone grain together.

intro: The C++ Programming Language is a tour and a reference bound in one volume: 44 chapters arranged in four parts, ordered by increasing abstraction. Stroustrup front-loads three short tours of the language so that you see the whole of C++ before any single feature is studied in depth. This section maps the territory so you can navigate the rest of the book — and this course — deliberately.
objectives: Sketch the four-part structure of the book and the chapters each part contains
Choose the right part of the book for a given programming problem
Explain why the tours (Chapters 2–5) precede the detailed treatments

concepts.statement: **Part I, Introductory material (Chapters 1–5)**, opens with this chapter and continues with three tours of the language plus a tour of utilities and concurrency. **Part II, Basic facilities (Chapters 6–15)**, covers the built-in machinery: types and declarations, pointers, arrays and references, statements, expressions, functions, exception handling, namespaces, and source files and linking. **Part III, Abstraction mechanisms (Chapters 16–29)**, covers classes, construction/copy/move, overloading, derived classes and hierarchies, templates and generic programming, and template metaprogramming. **Part IV, The standard library (Chapters 30–45)**, is the user's view: STL containers, algorithms and iterators, memory and resources, strings, regex, I/O streams, numerics, concurrency, and the C standard library.
concepts.detail: The organizing axis is *level of abstraction*, not history: built-in types first, then user-defined types, then parameterized types, then ready-made library types.

concepts.statement: Chapters 2–5 deliberately present C++ **as it is used by good programmers** — classes, templates, the standard library and concurrency in a few dozen pages each — before any feature gets a full treatment. The rationale: a language cannot be understood as a mere list of features, because its power comes from the combination of features working together.
concepts.detail: You cannot design a class properly without knowing that templates exist, and you cannot appreciate templates without having seen containers. The tours give you the combination first; the later parts supply the detail on demand.

concepts.statement: The book assumes **some programming experience** but *not* prior C. Read Part I linearly as a tutorial; treat Parts II–IV as reference material reached through the table of contents and the index rather than cover to cover.
concepts.detail: Stroustrup's own suggestion for experienced C or Java programmers is to still read the tours first: unlearning habits is harder than learning features, and the tours present the modern style that the detail chapters then justify.

concepts.term: The Structure of This Book: the working contract
concepts.statement: **The Structure of This Book.** Introduction, basic facilities, abstraction mechanisms, the standard library and references. You can claim this section when you can sketch the four-part structure of the book and the chapters each part contains — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 1 (Notes to the Reader); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

concepts.term: The Structure of This Book: deliberate practice
concepts.statement: Work in three passes. First, choose the right part of the book for a given programming problem. Then, explain why the tours (Chapters 2–5) precede the detailed treatments. Finally, test the outcome against the section promise: Four parts ordered by abstraction: introductory tours, basic facilities, abstraction mechanisms, standard library.
concepts.detail: Each pass catches a different class of mistake, and skipping one moves the failure into a larger program where it costs more to diagnose than it would have here.

examples.title: Mapping three questions onto the book
examples.problem: For each of these realistic questions, which chapter(s) answer it, and at what depth?

steps.label: Question 1
steps.text: “I need to sort a vector of structs by a field.” The quick answer is the library tour (4.5, algorithms); the deep answer is Chapter 32 (STL algorithms) with Chapter 33 (iterators) and lambdas from Chapter 11.

steps.label: Question 2
steps.text: “What does the standard actually guarantee about vector growth?” That is Chapter 31 (STL containers) — a Part IV guarantee question; the tours stay silent on purpose.

steps.label: Question 3
steps.text: “How do move semantics really work?” The tour of abstraction (3.3) gives the idea in two pages; Chapter 17 (construction, cleanup, copy and move) gives the mechanism, and Chapter 34 the memory model behind allocation.

steps.label: The pattern
steps.text: Every practical question has a *tour-level* answer you can use today and a *part-level* answer that explains why the quick answer is safe.

examples.result: The book is organized by depth of treatment: tours for use, Parts II–IV for understanding. Read Chapter 1 first, the tours second, then jump.

examples.title: Working through the structure of this book
examples.problem: Introduction, basic facilities, abstraction mechanisms, the standard library and references. Your task: sketch the four-part structure of the book and the chapters each part contains.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: sketch the four-part structure of the book and the chapters each part contains. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Four parts ordered by abstraction: introductory tours, basic facilities, abstraction mechanisms, standard library.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3}; std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — choose the right part of the book for a given programming problem — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: The tours (Chapters 2–5) exist because features only make sense in combination — see the whole before the parts. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Four parts ordered by abstraction: introductory tours, basic facilities, abstraction mechanisms, standard library. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Four parts ordered by abstraction: introductory tours, basic facilities, abstraction mechanisms, standard library.
The tours (Chapters 2–5) exist because features only make sense in combination — see the whole before the parts.
Parts II–IV are reference material: navigate by problem, not by page order.

quiz.q: Which part of the book contains the introductory tours of the language and library?
options: Part II, because tours are basic facilities
quiz.explanation: Part I is the introductory material: Chapter 1 plus the tours of the basics, abstraction, containers and algorithms, and concurrency and utilities.

quiz.q: A reader wants the formal, complete rules for template name binding. Where does that live?
options: Chapter 26 (instantiation) in Part III, the abstraction mechanisms
Part I only — the tours are complete descriptions
Nowhere; templates are specified only by implementations
quiz.explanation: The tours are explicitly incomplete. Templates span Part III (Chapters 23–29); instantiation and name binding is Chapter 26.

quiz.q: Why do the tours precede the detailed chapters?
options: For historical reasons — the tours reproduce the order C++ was standardized in
To keep the page count low by avoiding detail
Because Part II assumes knowledge of the standard library
Because a language cannot be understood as a list of features; its value lies in combinations
quiz.explanation: Stroustrup's stated rationale: features interact, so you need an overview of the whole before any feature's details are meaningful.

quiz.q: Which sequence correctly orders the parts by the abstractions they cover?
options: Standard library → basic facilities → abstraction mechanisms → tours
Abstraction mechanisms → basic facilities → tours → standard library
Tours → basic facilities → abstraction mechanisms → standard library
Basic facilities → tours → standard library → abstraction mechanisms
quiz.explanation: Built-in facilities, then user-defined abstractions, then the ready-made library: the axis is level of abstraction.

intro: C++ was not accreted by accident; it was built against an explicit design brief, and every feature decision in the rest of the book is argued from it. This section states that brief — a systems-programming language supporting multiple paradigms with no room for features that tax code that does not use them — and the two consequences that shape everything else: the zero-overhead principle and the static type system.
objectives: State the design aims of C++ and why no single paradigm is privileged
Apply the zero-overhead principle to judge a proposed feature or design
Explain the role and limits of C compatibility in the design

concepts.statement: **C++ is a general-purpose programming language with a bias toward systems programming that (1) is a better C, (2) supports data abstraction, (3) supports object-oriented programming, and (4) supports generic programming.** It is multi-paradigm by policy: procedures, classes, and templates are all first-class tools, and the design task is to pick the right one for the job, not to force every problem into one idiom.
concepts.detail: This is the canonical formulation Stroustrup gives (echoing The Design and Evolution of C++). “General-purpose with a systems bias” rules out mandatory garbage collection, mandatory run-time checks, and any feature that cannot be implemented efficiently on ordinary hardware.

concepts.statement: **What you don't use, you don't pay for. What you do use, you couldn't hand-code any better.** Abstractions must compile down to code as good as a specialist could write without them: virtual functions cost one indirection *only when you call them virtually*, templates specialize to the exact type used, and unused library features cost nothing at run time.
concepts.detail: The first half is the reason C++ has no universal base class and no mandatory runtime; the second half is the reason `std::sort` beats hand-written loops for inlined element types.

concepts.term: Static type checking as the main safety net
concepts.statement: C++ checks types at **compile time**, and the type system is the primary tool for holding large programs under control: the richer the types you use, the more errors surface as compile-time messages instead of run-time crashes. Type violations are not “undefined unless caught” — the language makes no promise for unchecked memory or type transgressions, so the language's answer is to make the compiler catch what it can before the program runs.
concepts.detail: Small programs can be made to work in almost any language; the hard problem — the one C++ targets — is keeping large programs understandable, and that is where the type system earns its keep.

concepts.term: C compatibility — what it is and is not
concepts.statement: C++ aims for **C compatibility at the source level for the large common subset**, so C libraries and C code can interoperate, but C++ is *not* a superset of C: some C programs are invalid C++, and many accepted-by-both programs mean different things. The book's advice is blunt — from a C background, “leaving C behind” is often the modern C++ move, because many C idioms (arrays, raw pointers, `malloc`, casts, macros) are unsafe micro-optimizations in C++ clothing.
concepts.detail: Together with the library this yields the language-library-system view: an ISO C++ program is written in a language, against a standard library, and atop a compile-link model shared with C. All three layers are part of “knowing C++”.

concepts.term: The Design of C++: the working contract
concepts.statement: **The Design of C++.** Programming styles, type checking, C compatibility and the language-library-system view. You can claim this section when you can state the design aims of C++ and why no single paradigm is privileged — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 1 (Notes to the Reader); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Auditing a design against the zero-overhead principle
examples.problem: Does sorting a `vector<int>` with `std::sort` pay a hidden abstraction tax? Test the claim against the principle's two halves.

steps.label: Step 1: instantiate
steps.text: `std::sort` is a template; used on `vector<int>` it is generated for `int` and `vector<int>::iterator` — the comparisons and the loop overhead can be inlined and optimized for exactly that element type.

steps.label: Step 2: first half
steps.text: Code that never uses `std::sort`, virtual functions, or exceptions at all carries none of their cost — “what you don't use, you don't pay for”.

steps.label: Step 3: second half
steps.text: The generated inner loop is the same compare-and-swap sequence a C programmer would write for an `int` array — “what you do use, you couldn't hand-code any better”.

steps.label: Step 4: contrast
steps.text: A design that boxed each `int` on the heap and called a virtual comparison through a universal base class would violate the principle: every comparison pays an indirection and every element an allocation.

examples.result: The principle is a *test you can apply*: any proposed abstraction must either compile away or provide value visibly greater than its cost.

examples.title: Working through the design of C++
examples.problem: Programming styles, type checking, C compatibility and the language-library-system view. Your task: state the design aims of C++ and why no single paradigm is privileged.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: state the design aims of C++ and why no single paradigm is privileged. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: C++ is general-purpose with a systems bias: better C plus data abstraction, OOP and generic programming — multi-paradigm by design.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3}; std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — apply the zero-overhead principle to judge a proposed feature or design — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Zero-overhead rule: unused features cost nothing; used features cost no more than hand-written code. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: C++ is general-purpose with a systems bias: better C plus data abstraction, OOP and generic programming — multi-paradigm by design. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: C++ is general-purpose with a systems bias: better C plus data abstraction, OOP and generic programming — multi-paradigm by design.
Zero-overhead rule: unused features cost nothing; used features cost no more than hand-written code.
C++ is C-compatible at the interface level, not a superset; many C idioms should be left behind in modern C++.

quiz.q: Which statement is the zero-overhead principle as Stroustrup states it?
options: All abstractions must be paid for by a small constant factor
What you don't use, you don't pay for; what you do use, you couldn't hand-code any better
Run-time checks are worth their cost in all programs
The compiler may insert a garbage collector when heap use is detected
quiz.explanation: Both halves matter: no tax on unused machinery, and no tax on used machinery relative to hand-written specialist code.

quiz.q: Why does C++ reject a mandatory garbage collector as part of the core language?
options: Because it would tax programs that manage resources deterministically — violating the systems-programming bias and zero-overhead rule
Because garbage collection is mathematically unsound
Because collectors cannot be written portably
Because destructors make resource leaks impossible in all cases
quiz.explanation: A mandatory collector is a run-time cost and an unpredictability no real-time or systems program can accept; C++ instead offers deterministic destruction, with optional collectors for those who want them.

quiz.q: “C++ is a better C” is best read as which of the following?
options: C++ accepts every C program unchanged
C++ corrects the C grammar and syntax so old code must be rewritten
C++ programs are always faster than equivalent C programs
C++ improves on C for the areas where C is weak (type safety, abstraction) while remaining close enough for interoperation
quiz.explanation: C++ is not a superset; the aim is compatibility on the common subset so libraries interoperate, while the language pushes toward safer, higher-level styles.

quiz.q: A team argues for treating every entity as an object of a single base class with virtual methods “for uniformity”. Which design rule does this break first?
options: The multi-paradigm rule, because it uses object orientation at all
None — this is exactly how the standard containers are designed
The zero-overhead principle: code that does not need dynamic dispatch would still pay for it
The C compatibility rule, because base classes are not in C
quiz.explanation: A universal base class taxes every use with indirection and uniformity of representation; C++ deliberately has none.

options: `1` in both, because character literals are identical in the two languages
`4` in both, because `int` occupies 4 bytes on every platform
`4` in C and `1` in C++, because C gives character literals type `int` while C++ gives them type `char`
`1` in C and `4` in C++, because C++ widens every literal
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is one token sequence measured by `sizeof` under two language rules. Step 2: The governing rule is the type of a character literal: C assigns it type `int`, while C++ assigns it type `char`, and `sizeof` reports the size of that type. Step 3: Tracing both compilations, the C build measures an `int` and prints `4` on typical platforms, while the C++ build measures a `char` and prints `1`. Step 4: The distractors fail because the literal types genuinely differ, no platform fixes `int` at 4 bytes by standard, and C++ narrows rather than widens here. Step 5: Therefore identical syntax can carry different meanings, which is why C++ is compatible with C on a shared subset rather than being a strict superset.

intro: C++ supports programming at many levels — from raw machine manipulation to type-rich application code — and where you operate is a choice, not a fixed property of the language. This section is Stroustrup's field guide to learning that range: learn by programming, start with the modern style, and retrain your habits deliberately if you come from C or Java.
objectives: Explain why C++ can only be learned by writing programs
List the C habits that modern C++ deliberately leaves behind
Contrast Java programmers' assumptions with C++ value semantics and destruction

concepts.statement: You cannot learn C++ by reading about it: **the only way to learn a programming language is to write programs in it**. Start with the tours, write small complete programs immediately, and use the standard library from the first day so that early programs are useful rather than ceremonial.
concepts.detail: The book is written so this is possible: the tours deliberately use strings, containers and algorithms before defining them, because using the library is how real C++ is learned.

concepts.statement: C++ can express both the **low-level machine view** (pointers, casts, bytes, layout — the C subset's home ground) and the **high-level type-rich view** (user-defined types, containers, algorithms). Both are C++; the design center of the language is the high level, but the low level exists so that abstraction never becomes a wall between you and the machine when you need through it.
concepts.detail: The practical consequence for learning: master the high level first, and reach for the low level deliberately, with a reason, not from habit.

concepts.statement: The C habits to leave behind: fixed-size arrays and pointer arithmetic (use `vector`), `malloc`/`free` (use objects and containers whose lifetimes are managed by constructors/destructors), C-style casts and macros (use templates and `constexpr`), `printf` (use streams), and macro-based constants (use `constexpr`). In C these idioms were tools; in C++ they are the low-level escape hatches that the type system cannot check.
concepts.detail: Stroustrup's warning to C programmers: much of the C you know is a set of unsafe micro-optimizations for 1970s compilers; modern C++ gives the same performance without the unsafety.

concepts.statement: The surprises for Java programmers are structural: C++ has **value semantics** (objects live where you declare them, assignments copy), **deterministic destruction** (destructors run at scope exit — no garbage collector), **no universal root class**, and **`const` as a first-class idea**. Templates do the compile-time work that interfaces and factories do at run time in Java.
concepts.detail: The mental shift: in Java an object is always reached through a reference to heap-allocated memory; in C++ an object *is* its storage, and you choose — stack, member, or free store — per type and per use.

concepts.statement: **Learning C++.** Learning by programming, with suggestions for C++, C and Java programmers. You can claim this section when you can explain why C++ can only be learned by writing programs — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 1 (Notes to the Reader); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Porting a C line counter to C++
examples.problem: Count the lines of an input stream. First the C idiom, then the C++ idiom — compare the failure modes.

steps.label: Step 1: the C version
steps.text: In C: `char line[100]; while (fgets(line, 100, stdin)) ++n;` — a fixed 100-byte buffer, the length limit duplicated as a magic number in two places.

steps.label: Step 2: find the failure
steps.text: A 150-character line is split by `fgets` into two reads, so `n` counts 2 where the text has 1 line. A 99+ character buffer is a silent correctness bug, and any larger reworking risks an overflow.

steps.label: Step 3: the C++ version
steps.text: In C++: `string line; while (getline(cin, line)) ++n;` — `string` owns and grows its own storage, so no size limit exists to get wrong, and `getline` returns the stream, which converts to `bool` exactly when the read fails.

steps.label: Step 4: compare
steps.text: One statement, no buffer, no magic numbers, no overflow class of bugs. This is “leaving C behind”: the C idiom optimized for a 1970s allocator, not for correctness.

examples.result: The port removes an entire bug class (fixed-size buffers) rather than fixing one instance of it — the standard payoff of using the type-rich level.

examples.title: Working through learning C++
examples.problem: Learning by programming, with suggestions for C++, C and Java programmers. Your task: explain why C++ can only be learned by writing programs.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: explain why C++ can only be learned by writing programs. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: C++ is learned by writing programs, and the tours are designed to be programmed along with.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3}; std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — list the C habits that modern C++ deliberately leaves behind — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: From C: replace arrays, `malloc`, casts, macros and `printf` with `vector`, objects, templates, `constexpr` and streams. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: C++ is learned by writing programs, and the tours are designed to be programmed along with. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: C++ is learned by writing programs, and the tours are designed to be programmed along with.
From C: replace arrays, `malloc`, casts, macros and `printf` with `vector`, objects, templates, `constexpr` and streams.
From Java: expect value semantics, deterministic destruction, no root class, and templates doing compile-time genericity.

quiz.q: Which is Stroustrup's position on learning C++?
options: Learn C first, then add classes on top of that base
Write programs from the start, using the standard library early
Read the language definition first; programs come later
Master pointers and memory layout before writing any class
quiz.explanation: The book states that the only way to learn a language is to program in it, and the tours are built so you can use the library from day one.

quiz.q: A C programmer's first instinct is `double buf[256]`. What is the modern C++ replacement in most code?
options: A `vector` or a `string`, which own and grow their storage
A `malloc`'d array, since it can be resized
A raw pointer plus a length variable
A macro that allocates the buffer lazily
quiz.explanation: Fixed-size arrays invite overflow bugs; `vector` and `string` manage size and storage themselves.

quiz.q: Which Java assumption fails immediately in C++?
options: Object assignment copies the object's value — objects are not always heap-allocated references
quiz.explanation: C++ has value semantics: assignment copies, objects live where declared, and only explicitly requested dynamic allocation touches the free store.

quiz.q: Why does C++ have no universal base class like Java's `Object`?
options: Because multiple inheritance already covers that role
It does — `std::object` is the root of the hierarchy
Because it would tax all objects with representation and dispatch they may not need — a zero-overhead violation
Because the standard library forbids it
quiz.explanation: A forced root class means every object carries the root's baggage; C++ keeps built-in types first-class and only pays for polymorphism where it is used.

intro: C++'s design makes sense only against its history: it began in 1979 as “C with Classes”, a Simula-style class mechanism grafted onto C for efficiency, and grew by experiment into an ISO-standard language of two million-plus programmers. This section walks the timeline — Cfront, the 1998 standard with the STL, and the 2011 C++11 revision this fourth edition targets.
objectives: Trace the timeline from C with Classes (1979) to the C++11 standard (2011)
Explain what Simula and C each contributed to the original design
State what C++98 and C++11 each added and why they mattered

concepts.statement: C++ began at Bell Labs in **1979** as a set of extensions to C called **“C with Classes”**, written by Stroustrup for his work on distributed systems. He wanted **Simula's** program organization — classes, inheritance, virtual functions — because it made large programs tractable, but with **C's** efficiency, portability and unfussy deployment, which Simula's run-time systems of the day could not deliver.
concepts.detail: The combination was the design: Simula for structure, C for the machine, and a single-language compile-and-link model so the result could run everywhere C ran.

concepts.statement: The implementation itself was a driving force: a translator (later compiler) named **Cfront**, whose releases paced the language. The name “C++” (Rick Mascitti's suggestion, a play on `++`) dates from 1983; **Cfront 1.0's first commercial release came in 1985**; Release 2.0 (1989) added multiple inheritance; Release 3.0 (1991) added templates and exception handling.
concepts.detail: Each feature was used experimentally for years inside Bell Labs and the user community before standardization — “use it before standardizing it” is the recurring theme of C++'s history.

concepts.statement: **C++98** (ISO/IEC 14882) stabilized thirteen years of industrial practice into a portable standard, and — decisively — **adopted the STL**: the containers, algorithms and iterator framework of Stepanov, Musser and Lee, plus `string`, `complex` and the I/O streams library. The language gained a standard library to match its abstraction mechanisms.
concepts.detail: Standardization converted C++ from a dialect family defined by implementations into a language defined by a document — the difference between “works on my compiler” and “works”.

concepts.statement: After a decade of incremental work, **C++11** nearly doubles the language's effective surface: move semantics and rvalue references, `auto`, range-`for`, uniform `{}` initialization, lambdas, `constexpr`, variadic templates, a defined **memory model with threads, mutexes, atomics and futures**, `unique_ptr`/`shared_ptr`, regular expressions, and `unordered_map`. Stroustrup's summary: it “feels like a new language” while remaining compatible enough to run the world's existing C++ code.
concepts.detail: This fourth edition of the book is a C++11 book: it describes the language as defined by ISO/IEC 14882:2011, with the C++98/03 rules noted only where they differ.

concepts.statement: **History.** The timeline from the early years through the 1998 and 2011 standards. You can claim this section when you can trace the timeline from C with Classes (1979) to the C++11 standard (2011) — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 1 (Notes to the Reader); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.
