examples.title: The temperature program: grow, sort, take the median
examples.problem: Seven temperature readings arrive: 61.5, 63.7, 59.0, 58.1, 57.4, 59.3, 60.9 °C. Run the tour's program — push each into a `vector<double>`, `sort` it, report `temps[temps.size()/2]` — and also compute the mean, checking both by hand.

steps.label: Step 1: fill
steps.text: Seven `push_back` calls grow the vector to `size() == 7`; if capacity ran out along the way, growth relocated the array — the program neither knows nor cares.

steps.label: Step 2: sort
steps.text: `sort(temps.begin(), temps.end())` orders the values ascending: 57.4, 58.1, 59.0, 59.3, 60.9, 61.5, 63.7.

steps.label: Step 3: median, the tour's way
steps.text: `temps[temps.size()/2]` = `temps[3]` = **59.3** — for an odd count 7, index 3 is the exact middle (three below, three above).

steps.label: Step 4: mean as a check
steps.text: Sum: $61.5+63.7+59.0+58.1+57.4+59.3+60.9 = 419.9$; dividing by 7 gives a mean of $59.99$, slightly above the median — the outlier 63.7 pulls the mean up while leaving the middle value alone.

steps.label: Step 5: the even-count caveat
steps.text: With eight readings, `size()/2` is 4 — the fifth of eight, *not* the average of the fourth and fifth; the tour's one-liner is exact only for odd counts, and a correct even-count median needs `(temps[n/2 - 1] + temps[n/2]) / 2`. Knowing when a formula's precondition fails is the point of the check.

examples.result: Median 59.3 °C, mean 59.99 °C: an unknown-length input reduced to order statistics in six lines — vector + sort + index.

examples.title: Working through containers
examples.problem: Vector, map and the container overview. Your task: use `vector`: `push_back`, `[]`, `size()`, and the sort-then-index median pattern.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: use `vector`: `push_back`, `[]`, `size()`, and the sort-then-index median pattern. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `vector` = contiguous free-store array plus three pointers; `push_back` amortized, `[]` unchecked, `at()` checked.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::map<std::string, int> counts; counts[key]++;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain a `vector`'s memory layout and amortized growth — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: `map` is a balanced tree: $O(\log n)$ keyed access and sorted iteration, with `[]` inserting a default value on a miss — `++words[s]` is a word counter. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `vector` = contiguous free-store array plus three pointers; `push_back` amortized, `[]` unchecked, `at()` checked. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `vector` = contiguous free-store array plus three pointers; `push_back` amortized, `[]` unchecked, `at()` checked.
`map` is a balanced tree: $O(\log n)$ keyed access and sorted iteration, with `[]` inserting a default value on a miss — `++words[s]` is a word counter.
Choose by access pattern — `vector` by default; `list` for mid-sequence surgery; `map` or `unordered_map` for keyed access, ordered or not.

quiz.q: In `++words[s];` on a `map<string,int>`, the key `s` was not yet present. What happened?
options: The key was inserted with a random value
The map inserted the pair (`s`, 0), then the increment made it 1
quiz.explanation: `map`'s `[]` default-inserts on a miss — the exact behavior that turns the loop body into a one-statement word counter.

quiz.q: Why does the tour recommend `vector` over `list` by default?
options: Contiguous storage gives cache locality and indexed access; list pays two pointers per element and cannot subscript
Vectors use less memory per element when nearly empty, always
Lists are not part of the standard library
quiz.explanation: Node-based storage scatters elements and forbids subscripting; for the common pattern of append-and-iterate, contiguity wins, and the tour says to switch only for a reason.

quiz.q: What is the complexity of lookup in a `std::map` with n entries?
options: $O(\log n)$ — it is a balanced tree
quiz.explanation: The ordered map is a red-black tree, so search, insert and erase are all logarithmic; the *unordered* map is the hash-based $O(1)$-expected one.

quiz.q: A `push_back` into a full `vector` triggers:
options: Silent loss of the new element
Relocation: allocate a larger array, move the elements across, free the old block — amortized constant time per append
quiz.explanation: Growth is why appending is amortized O(1): occasional linear relocations spread over the many constant-time appends they enable.

quiz.q: A program stores one million records keyed by ID and looks them up constantly, with no need for ordering. Which container choice matches the library guarantees?
options: `std::vector`, because keyed lookup in a vector is logarithmic
`std::list`, because pointer hops are friendly to the cache
`std::map`, because hashing always beats trees for ordered data
`std::unordered_map`, because average lookup is constant time, while `std::map` lookup is logarithmic
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is one million keyed records with lookup-dominated access and no ordering need. Step 2: The governing rules are the container guarantees: `unordered_map` averages constant-time lookup through hashing, `map` offers logarithmic lookup through a balanced tree plus ordering, and sequence containers provide no keyed lookup at all. Step 3: Computing the gap, a tree search needs about twenty comparisons at this size while a hash lookup averages near one probe, so the hashed container removes nearly all per-query work. Step 4: The distractors fail because vectors and lists lack keyed lookup, and the tree pays logarithmic cost precisely to maintain order nobody needs. Step 5: Therefore the hashed container is the matching choice.

intro: Containers hold data; algorithms process it. The tour's central example of the two worlds meeting is the find operation, and the standard library's answer is a separation so clean it looks strange at first: algorithms never ask what container they run on. They take iterators — positions — instead. That one decision is what makes a single sort serve vector, array, list and stream alike.
objectives: Read the half-open iterator range [b:e) and explain what `end()` points to
Use `sort`, `find_if`, `count_if` and `accumulate` with lambdas and function objects
Explain why algorithms-plus-iterators beat member loops and hand-rolled searches

concepts.statement: An **iterator** is a position in a sequence. Every container exposes `begin()` (its first element) and `end()` (the position **one past its last element**), and the standard algorithms operate on the pair `[b:e)` — the **half-open range**: it contains `b` and everything up to but not including `e`. An empty sequence is exactly the pair where `b == e`, which is why every algorithm's loop test is `b != e`. Dereferencing `end()` is not merely wrong — it has no element to be wrong about; it is the *outside* position.
concepts.detail: This convention makes the number of elements in `[b:e)` simply `e − b` for random-access iterators, and lets algorithms describe zero-length inputs without a special case.

concepts.statement: The everyday set from `<algorithm>` and `<numeric>`: `sort(b, e)` orders a range; `stable_sort(b, e)` orders it while preserving the relative order of equal elements; `find(b, e, v)` locates the first element equal to `v`; `find_if(b, e, pred)` locates the first satisfying a predicate; `count_if(b, e, pred)` counts them; `for_each(b, e, f)` applies `f` to each; `accumulate(b, e, init)` (from `<numeric>`) folds the range onto `init` with `+`. A failed `find` returns `e` — “not found” is a position, not a special value.
concepts.detail: `sort` on `n` elements is about $n \log n$ comparisons; `find` is linear and stops early; `accumulate` is the single linear pass that replaces most hand-written sum loops.

concepts.statement: Algorithms take **callable arguments**: a predicate is any object that can be called like a function. A **lambda** writes one inline: `[](const string& a, const string& b) { return a.size() < b.size(); }` — brackets for the capture, then a parameter list, then the body whose value is returned. A **function object** is the class form: `class Less_than { double v; public: Less_than(double vv) : v{vv} { } bool operator()(double x) const { return x < v; } };` — an object carrying state `v` that is called through `operator()`.
concepts.detail: The lambda is not a new kind of entity: it compiles to a function object of exactly this shape, with the capture stored as its members. The tour uses both forms deliberately, one line apart.

concepts.statement: The library's composition rule: a **container** holds a sequence, **algorithms** transform it, and **iterators** are the interface between — so the pieces are independent and recombinable. A hand-written loop names its container and its index arithmetic, and it is wrong once per off-by-one; `find_if(v.begin(), v.end(), pred)` says *what* is wanted and works unchanged on every sequence type, including `istream` and arrays.
concepts.detail: This is the Stepanov STL vision in one sentence: a small set of orthogonal algorithms, uniform over all sequences, is more reuse than any container-specific method list can buy.

concepts.statement: **Algorithms.** Find, sort and the algorithm ideas. You can claim this section when you can read the half-open iterator range [b:e) and explain what `end()` points to — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 4 (A Tour of C++: Containers and Algorithms); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Sort by length, count the long ones
examples.problem: With `vector<string> words = {"the", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumps"};` run: (1) `stable_sort` with the lambda comparing by `size()`; (2) `count_if` counting words longer than 4 characters; (3) `accumulate` summing the lengths.

steps.label: Step 1: lengths
steps.text: The words' lengths are: the=3, quick=5, brown=5, fox=3, jumps=5 — two of length 3 (the, fox in that order) and three of length 5 (quick, brown, jumps in that order).

steps.label: Step 2: stable sort
steps.text: `stable_sort(words.begin(), words.end(), [](const string& a, const string& b) { return a.size() < b.size(); });` orders by length but **preserves the original order among equal lengths**: the → fox → quick → brown → jumps.

steps.label: Step 3: why stable
steps.text: With plain `sort`, the two 3-letter and three 5-letter words could come out in any order — the same length keys give the algorithm no reason to prefer one. `stable_sort`'s guarantee is exactly about this case.

steps.label: Step 4: count
steps.text: `count_if(words.begin(), words.end(), [](const string& s) { return s.size() > 4; });` counts quick, brown and jumps — words strictly longer than 4 characters — giving **3** (the and fox are 3; nothing has length 4).

steps.label: Step 5: accumulate
steps.text: `accumulate(words.begin(), words.end(), 0, [](int s, const string& w) { return s + w.size(); });` folds to $3+5+5+3+5 = 21$ — the total characters, via the four-argument form of the algorithm with a custom fold.

examples.result: Sorted {the, fox, quick, brown, jumps}, count 3, total length 21 — three algorithms, three lambdas, no loop written by hand.

examples.title: Working through algorithms
examples.problem: Find, sort and the algorithm ideas. Your task: read the half-open iterator range [b:e) and explain what `end()` points to.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: read the half-open iterator range [b:e) and explain what `end()` points to. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Algorithms take iterator ranges `[b:e)`; `end()` is one-past-the-last and never dereferenceable; empty is `b == e`.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::map<std::string, int> counts; counts[key]++;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — use `sort`, `find_if`, `count_if` and `accumulate` with lambdas and function objects — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Predicates are callables: lambdas inline, function objects with state; a failed `find`/`find_if` returns `end()`. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Algorithms take iterator ranges `[b:e)`; `end()` is one-past-the-last and never dereferenceable; empty is `b == e`. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Algorithms take iterator ranges `[b:e)`; `end()` is one-past-the-last and never dereferenceable; empty is `b == e`.
Predicates are callables: lambdas inline, function objects with state; a failed `find`/`find_if` returns `end()`.
`sort`/`stable_sort` (order and order-preserving), `find_if`, `count_if`, `accumulate` cover the everyday majority — over any sequence.

quiz.q: For a non-empty container `v`, what does `v.end()` return?
options: An iterator to the position one past the last element — the outside marker that ends the half-open range
quiz.explanation: `[begin(), end())` is half-open: `end()` is not an element at all, which is why `find` can return it to mean “not found”.

quiz.q: After `stable_sort` by `size()` on {"the", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumps"}, what is the second word?
quiz.explanation: Sorted by length: the (3), fox (3), then the three 5-letter words in their original order. Stability kept “fox” after “the” among the equal lengths.

quiz.q: What does `find_if(v.begin(), v.end(), pred)` return when no element satisfies `pred`?
options: The last element, as a fallback
quiz.explanation: “Not found” is a position — the past-the-end iterator — and the caller checks `p != v.end()` to see if anything was found.

quiz.q: The essential difference between `sort` and `stable_sort` is:
options: `stable_sort` preserves the relative order of elements that compare equal; `sort` may reorder them arbitrarily
quiz.explanation: When the comparison key ties (equal lengths, equal dates), stability is the difference between deterministic and arbitrary output order.

intro: The library tour closes with advice that reads as a single strategy: never write below the level the library has already built. Its containers, algorithms and iterators are the product of decades of refinement, and every hand-written loop that replaces a named algorithm is a small bet that you will beat that record — a bet history says you will lose.
objectives: Apply the library-first discipline to containers and algorithms
Justify passing containers by reference and avoiding element copies
Know the complexity contract of the operations you use daily

concepts.statement: The first question on any data-structure or algorithm problem is **“what does the standard library do here?”** — and only a measured shortfall justifies replacing it. The library's components are documented, type-safe, and tuned by implementations competing on their performance; homemade replacements start at zero on all three counts.
concepts.detail: The book's phrasing of the habit: use the library's containers, algorithms and strings in preference to your own — and know them well enough that the question is quick to answer.

concepts.term: Know the costs you are buying
concepts.statement: Using the library is not code-blindness: know each operation's complexity contract — `vector`'s `push_back` amortized constant and its subscript constant; `list`'s insertion constant but its lookup linear; `map`'s operations logarithmic; `unordered_map`'s expected constant — because the container choice *is* the performance decision, made once, at declaration.
concepts.detail: The tour's numbers are worth memorizing: indexing into a `vector` is one pointer computation; reaching the middle of a `list` is half its length in pointer hops.

concepts.term: Algorithms and references over loops and copies
concepts.statement: Write **named algorithms with lambdas** instead of index loops — the name documents intent, and the boundary conditions come with the algorithm. Pass containers **by reference** (by `const&` for reading) so element copies do not silently multiply, and pass large elements the same way — `[](const string& s)` not `[](string s)`.
concepts.detail: The combination of this rule with move semantics is the modern style: `const&` in, move out, algorithms between — the copy count of a well-written function is zero.

concepts.term: Shipping rule for a tour of C++: containers and algorithms
concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Library first: only a measured shortfall justifies hand-rolled containers or searches.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

concepts.term: Review checklist for a tour of C++: containers and algorithms
concepts.statement: Take the objectives as review questions: apply the library-first discipline to containers and algorithms? Then justify passing containers by reference and avoiding element copies? Answer each from the code in front of you, not from memory — the gap between the two answers is the review finding.
concepts.detail: A rule you can derive from the chapter you can also correctly suspend; a rule applied without its reason becomes superstition, so cite the reason in the review note.

examples.title: Replacing a hand-rolled search loop
examples.problem: A code review finds: `int i = 0; while (i < (int)v.size() && v[i] < 10) ++i; if (i < (int)v.size()) use(v[i]); else miss();` — a search for the first element ≥ 10. Rewrite it in the advised style and compare what each version asks the reader to verify.

steps.label: Step 1: audit the loop
steps.text: To trust it you must check four things: the cast, the index bound `i < size()`, the loop condition's predicate direction, and the re-test of the same bound after the loop. Each is a classic off-by-one site, and each must be re-audited at every maintenance touch.

steps.label: Step 2: the rewrite
steps.text: `auto p = find_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [](double x) { return x >= 10; }); if (p != v.end()) use(*p); else miss();` — one statement of intent, one predicate to read.

steps.label: Step 3: what the reader verifies now
steps.text: The predicate (`x >= 10`) and the found-test (`p != v.end()`) — both local, both in the language of the library. Bounds, casts and index arithmetic have ceased to exist.

steps.label: Step 4: generality for free
steps.text: The `find_if` version works unchanged if `v` becomes a `list`, an array, or any sequence exposing iterators — the loop version would need its cast, subscripting and bounds all rewritten.

examples.result: Two conditions to audit instead of four, zero rewrites under container changes — the concrete payoff of algorithms over loops.

examples.title: Reviewing a tour of C++: containers and algorithms code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the library-first discipline to containers and algorithms.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Library first: only a measured shortfall justifies hand-rolled containers or searches.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `std::map<std::string, int> counts; counts[key]++;`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: justify passing containers by reference and avoiding element copies. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Know each operation's complexity contract — the declaration of the container is the performance decision.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Library first: only a measured shortfall justifies hand-rolled containers or searches. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Library first: only a measured shortfall justifies hand-rolled containers or searches.
Know each operation's complexity contract — the declaration of the container is the performance decision.
Prefer named algorithms with lambdas; pass containers by reference and elements by `const&`; count your copies and keep them at zero.

quiz.q: The first response to needing a keyed lookup structure should be:
options: Use `std::map` or `std::unordered_map`, replacing it only if measurement shows a shortfall
Store pairs in a `vector` and linear-search them
Inherit from `std::map` and add the operations you want
Write a hash table tuned to your key type
quiz.explanation: Library-first: the standard associative containers are documented, correct and tuned — a hand-rolled replacement starts far behind and must justify itself.

quiz.q: Why pass containers as `const vector<T>&` rather than by value into a function that only reads them?
options: By value is illegal for containers
Passing by value copies every element on the call; a `const&` binds to the caller's object with no copies
References make the function inline automatically
quiz.explanation: Value semantics means a by-value parameter is a full deep copy — for a million-element vector, an 8 MB copy where a reference would cost a pointer.

quiz.q: Which operation is expected O(1) rather than O(log n) or O(n)?
quiz.explanation: `v[i]` on a vector is a pointer computation — the single address `alloc + i`. Map lookup is logarithmic; the list walk is linear; sort is $n \log n$.

intro: The tour's final stop assembles the modern toolbox: automatic resource management, concurrency, and a shelf of small utilities — pairs, tuples, regular expressions, clocks, and the mathematical library. What unites them is that they are standard: code that used to be hand-rolled or platform-specific is now specified by ISO C++ and behaves identically everywhere. As a tour, this chapter gives each topic just enough depth to be used with confidence; the chapters ahead return to the foundations.
objectives: Define resource and recognize the resource kinds a real program manages
State the single language mechanism C++ uses for every kind of resource
Explain why the standard library — not your own code — is the first candidate for any job

concepts.statement: **A resource is something a program acquires from somewhere and must eventually give back**: memory, file handles, locks, sockets, threads, timers. What makes resources hard is that the number available is finite and the release obligation is easy to forget along the many error paths a program can take.
concepts.detail: Memory is only the most common resource. The chapter's central observation is that every resource — a lock, an open file, an allocation — follows the same acquire/release pattern and therefore deserves one uniform solution.

concepts.statement: **C++ handles every resource the same way: acquire in a constructor, release in a destructor, and let scope determine when the destructor runs.** Because destructors execute on every exit path, the technique scales from a single stack variable to a whole server.
concepts.detail: Other languages bolt special machinery onto the problem — garbage collectors, `finally` blocks, `defer`. C++ builds cleanup into object lifetimes, which the compiler is already tracking for free.

concepts.statement: **Before writing code, look for a standard-library component that already does the job.** Standard components are specified, portable, battle-tested by millions of users, and maintained by the whole community; a hand-rolled replacement starts at zero on all four counts.
concepts.detail: The book's stance is blunt: a reason to avoid the standard library should be articulable, not habitual.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Utilities, resources and concurrency at a glance. You can claim this section when you can define resource and recognize the resource kinds a real program manages — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 5 (A Tour of C++: Concurrency and Utilities); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

concepts.statement: Work in three passes. First, state the single language mechanism C++ uses for every kind of resource. Then, explain why the standard library — not your own code — is the first candidate for any job. Finally, test the outcome against the section promise: A resource is anything acquired that must be released: memory, files, locks, sockets, threads.
concepts.detail: Each pass catches a different class of mistake, and skipping one moves the failure into a larger program where it costs more to diagnose than it would have here.

examples.title: Taking inventory of one function's resources
examples.problem: A web-server request handler must manage: an open socket, three heap buffers, a locked statistics mutex, and a spawned logging thread. How many resources, and what manages them?

steps.label: Step 1: Count
steps.text: Five resources: one file descriptor (the socket), three memory allocations, one lock, one thread.

steps.label: Step 2: Classify the pattern
steps.text: Each is acquired at a point in the code and must be released exactly once — including along early returns and exceptions.

steps.label: Step 3: Match to handles
steps.text: `fstream` or a socket class for the descriptor, `vector` or `unique_ptr` for the buffers, `lock_guard` for the mutex, a joined or detached `thread` object for the thread.

steps.label: Step 4: The payoff
steps.text: Five different resources, one management mechanism — every release is tied to a destructor, not to programmer discipline.

examples.result: Resources come in many kinds; the mechanism that tames them is a single one, which is the subject of the next section.

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: Utilities, resources and concurrency at a glance. Your task: define resource and recognize the resource kinds a real program manages.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define resource and recognize the resource kinds a real program manages. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A resource is anything acquired that must be released: memory, files, locks, sockets, threads.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `auto f = std::async(compute); int r = f.get();` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — state the single language mechanism C++ uses for every kind of resource — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: All resources get the same treatment — constructor acquires, destructor releases, scope sets the lifetime. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A resource is anything acquired that must be released: memory, files, locks, sockets, threads. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A resource is anything acquired that must be released: memory, files, locks, sockets, threads.
All resources get the same treatment — constructor acquires, destructor releases, scope sets the lifetime.
Standard library first: `vector`, `string`, `thread`, `regex` and friends exist so you do not have to write them.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a resource in the chapter's sense?
options: A mutex locked by a thread
quiz.explanation: A `const double` is an automatic object — the compiler manages its storage; nothing was acquired from a finite pool that must be given back. The other three are classic acquire/release obligations.

quiz.q: The single mechanism C++ uses to manage every kind of resource is:
options: Reference counting built into the language
Acquire in a constructor, release in a destructor (RAII)
A garbage collector that runs destructors
quiz.explanation: RAII ties each resource to an object's lifetime; destructors run deterministically at scope exit on every path, including exceptions.

quiz.q: Faced with a new problem, the chapter's first rule is to:
options: write a small class for it
use pointers and manual memory for control
look for a standard-library component that solves it
check what the operating system offers natively
quiz.explanation: The library-first principle: standard components are specified, portable and tested; writing your own needs a stated reason.

intro: Every program manages resources that must be released — and every error path is a chance to forget. This section presents C++'s systematic answer: tie each resource to the lifetime of a handle object. The technique, RAII, together with the two standard smart pointers `unique_ptr` and `shared_ptr` from `<memory>`, turns leaks from coding accidents into design decisions — and the exceptions they cannot prevent.
objectives: State the RAII idiom precisely and explain why destructor-based cleanup is exception-safe
Choose between `unique_ptr` and `shared_ptr` and justify the default
Trace a `shared_ptr` reference count through copies, scope exits and `reset`

concepts.statement: **Acquire the resource in a constructor and release it in the destructor of a handle object.** Because the destructor runs deterministically when the object's scope is left — by fall-through, by `return`, or by a propagating exception — every path from acquisition to release is covered by construction rather than by discipline.
concepts.detail: The standard library is built this way throughout: `vector` frees its elements, `fstream` closes its file, `lock_guard` unlocks its mutex. RAII is not an exotic technique — it is how the library you already use is made safe.

concepts.statement: **A `unique_ptr` owns its object exclusively: there is exactly one owner, the pointer can be moved but never copied, and the object is destroyed when the owner is.** It costs essentially nothing — the generated code matches a raw pointer with the `delete` placed at scope exit.
concepts.detail: `unique_ptr<Record> p {new Record{"Aal"}};` hands ownership to `p`; `return p;` and `f(move(p))` transfer it elsewhere. Passing a `unique_ptr` by value states the ownership transfer in the type itself.

concepts.statement: **A `shared_ptr` shares ownership: the last owner destroyed also destroys the object.** Ownership is tracked by a count in a per-object control block, so `shared_ptr` costs an extra allocation, atomic counter traffic, and — used carelessly — cycles that never release.
concepts.detail: `shared_ptr<Record> p1 {new Record{"Aal"}};` then `auto p2 = p1;` gives two owners, and `p1.use_count()` is now 2. Cycles of `shared_ptr`s are broken with `weak_ptr`, which observes without owning.

concepts.statement: **Default to `unique_ptr`; use `shared_ptr` only when ownership is genuinely shared and lifetimes cannot be ordered.** Most relationships in a program are hierarchical — one owner — and expressing them with `shared_ptr` is both slower and less clear.
concepts.detail: Refactoring a `shared_ptr` down to a `unique_ptr` usually clarifies a design; needing to refactor upward usually means the ownership design was never made explicit.

concepts.statement: **Do not reserve RAII for memory: wrap each resource in a handle type as a matter of course.** The pattern — allocate in the constructor, release in the destructor, deal with copying in the copy operations — is identical for a memory buffer, an open file, a lock, or a socket.
concepts.detail: Outside such handle implementations, pass owners as `unique_ptr`/`shared_ptr` and pass borrows as plain references or non-owning raw pointers.
