examples.title: Every exit path, covered by construction
examples.problem: A function must open a file, write to it, and close it — with an early `return` on a formatting error and a possible exception from the write. Compare the manual and RAII versions.

steps.label: Step 1: Manual version
steps.text: `FILE* f = fopen(path, "w");` … `if (bad) return;` … `fclose(f);` — the early return skips the `fclose`, so the handle leaks on every bad input; a throw skips it too.

steps.label: Step 2: RAII version
steps.text: `ofstream out{path};` — the constructor opens. `if (bad) return;` runs `~ofstream` on the way out, closing the file.

steps.label: Step 3: The exception path
steps.text: If `use(out)` throws, stack unwinding destroys `out` exactly as a `return` would — there is no third code path to audit.

examples.result: The leak is gone, not by adding code, but by moving the release obligation into a destructor the language guarantees to run.

examples.title: Counting shared owners
examples.problem: Trace the ownership count through: `shared_ptr<Record> p1 {new Record{"Aal"}};` then `auto p2 = p1;` in an inner scope, then `p1.reset();` last.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: `p1` constructed: one owner, `p1.use_count()` is 1.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: `p2` copies `p1`: two owners, both report `use_count()` of 2.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Inner scope ends: `p2` destroyed, count drops to 1 — the `Record` survives.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: `p1.reset()` releases `p1`'s share: the count transitions $1 \to 0$ and the destructor of `Record` runs at that moment.

examples.result: The object dies exactly at the last owner — neither early (dangling pointers) nor never (a leak).

keyTakeaways: RAII: the constructor acquires, the destructor releases, and scope fixes the moment — on every exit path, including exceptions.
`unique_ptr` is the near-zero-overhead default for sole ownership; `shared_ptr` buys shared lifetime with an allocation plus atomic counts.
Smart pointers and containers are one idea: a handle object whose lifetime governs the resource's.

quiz.q: In RAII, the release of a resource is triggered by:
options: an explicit `close` call at each exit
the destructor of the handle object running at scope exit
quiz.explanation: The destructor is generated code that runs on every exit from the scope — that is what removes the per-call-site discipline.

quiz.q: What makes `unique_ptr` unsuitable when two owners are genuinely needed?
options: It can be moved but never copied — exactly one owner can ever exist
It only works for built-in types
quiz.explanation: Copying is deleted, so ownership cannot be shared; a second owner requires `shared_ptr`'s counted control block.

quiz.q: After `shared_ptr<Record> p1{new Record}; auto p2 = p1;` — what is `p1.use_count()`, and when is the `Record` destroyed?
options: 2; when the last of `p1` and `p2` dies
quiz.explanation: The copy raises the count to 2; destruction happens on the transition $1 \to 0$, i.e. when the last owner is destroyed.

quiz.q: Why is `unique_ptr` the recommended default over `shared_ptr`?
options: It is simpler, nearly free at runtime, and most ownership is in fact exclusive
It supports custom deleters and `shared_ptr` does not
quiz.explanation: Exclusive ownership is the common case; `shared_ptr`'s control block and atomic counts buy something most designs do not need. (Both support custom deleters.)

options: Q, because the guard destructor releases the mutex during unwinding, while P leaks the lock if `update()` throws
P, because destructors never run while an exception is in flight
Both are equivalent in every possible case
Q, because the guard turns the mutex into a recursive one
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is a manual lock pair and a guard object spanning the same update. Step 2: The governing rule is RAII: acquisition happens in the constructor, release in the destructor, and stack unwinding destroys local objects even along exception paths. Step 3: Tracing both paths, on success both release the lock, but when `update()` throws, P skips its `unlock` line while Q's guard is destroyed during unwinding and releases the mutex. Step 4: The distractors fail because destructors of locals do run during unwinding, the two forms differ exactly on the throwing path, and the guard changes nothing about recursion. Step 5: Therefore the guard form is the correct one.

depth.title: RAII as a theory of resource safety

blocks.body: RAII is usually presented as an idiom, but it deserves to be stated as a small theory of resource safety, because the guarantee it gives is a theorem of the language's object model rather than a coding convention. The objects of the theory are **lifetimes**: the interval between an object's construction and its destruction. The language guarantees that lifetimes of automatic objects nest LIFO within a scope and end at scope exit — on every path. RAII's one observation is that a resource's lifetime can be *made equal to an object's lifetime*, after which every property of lifetimes — nesting, reverse-order destruction, exception-path execution — becomes a property of resources. That is why the technique is universal: nothing in it mentions memory, files or locks specifically.

blocks.heading: Deterministic release
blocks.body: Let $S$ be a scope and $x$ an automatic object of type $T$ declared in $S$, whose constructor acquires a resource $R$ and whose destructor releases it. Then for every way control can leave $S$ — reaching the closing brace, executing a `return`, or propagating an exception through $S$ — the destructor `~T()` is executed on $x$ exactly once, and $R$ is released. Moreover, automatic objects of $S$ are destroyed in the *reverse* of their construction order, so resources acquired later are released first, and $x$ outlives every automatic object constructed inside scopes nested within $S$ after $x$ was built.

blocks.heading: Why the theorem holds
blocks.body: The two normal paths are compiled directly: at each point where control can leave the scope, the compiler emits destructor calls for the scope's fully constructed automatic objects, in reverse construction order — one code path per exit, not one per resource. The exception path is handled by the **unwinder**: when a frame contains no handler, the runtime destroys that frame's fully constructed automatic objects and continues outward. An object whose constructor threw is *not* itself destroyed — `~T()` must not run on a half-built object — but each already-constructed member and base subobject is. The single way to break the guarantee is a destructor that itself throws while an exception is in flight: two active exceptions call `std::terminate()`. Hence the classical discipline: destructors must not fail, and they must not acquire resources they can fail to release. Within those rules, correctness has been *transferred from every call site to one type definition* — which is the whole point.

blocks.heading: The cost model of `shared_ptr`
blocks.body: A `shared_ptr<T>` is two words: the stored pointer plus a pointer to the **control block**, which holds the strong count, the weak count, and the deleter. Constructing from `new` costs two allocations (object and block); `make_shared<T>(...)` co-allocates them, halving allocator traffic and improving cache locality. Copying a `shared_ptr` is one atomic increment; destruction is one atomic decrement-and-test. The object dies on the strong count reaching 0; the block dies on the *weak* count reaching 0 — `weak_ptr`s keep the block (to check aliveness) but not the object alive. Note precisely what the atomics protect: the count, not the pointee. Copying one `shared_ptr` from two threads is safe; mutating the object it points to still needs a mutex.

blocks.heading: Exception safety of a container of handles
blocks.body: Fill a `vector<unique_ptr<Shape>>` in a loop that constructs each `Shape` with `new`, wrapping each immediately in a `unique_ptr`. If the third constructor throws, unwinding destroys the vector, which destroys its two elements — their `unique_ptr` destructors `delete` the first two shapes. Nothing leaks, even though no line of the loop mentions cleanup. The raw-pointer version — `Shape* v[3]; v[0] = new Shape; v[1] = new Shape; v[2] = new Shape;` — leaks the first two shapes on the same throw, because the array has no destructor that could know about the pointers. The vector case composes two RAII types and inherits the guarantee; the raw case composes nothing and inherits nothing.

Compare with garbage collection. A tracing collector reclaims memory well, but says nothing about the other resources — locks held, sockets open, transactions open — and its finalizers run at unpredictable times, if at all. RAII covers every resource kind with deterministic timing, and for the `unique_ptr` case it compiles to the same machine code as a raw pointer with the `delete` placed at scope exit: the guarantee is free. Large systems often run both: collection for memory, RAII for everything else. The design lesson survives the comparison: **make the destructor of the handle the one place the release code exists**, and lifetime questions stop being bug reports.

intro: Most computers can do several things at once, and most computing problems are naturally concurrent — an interface that stays responsive while computation proceeds. C++11 makes concurrency part of the language and library: `thread` for hardware-level concurrency, tasks and `future`s for value-oriented work, `mutex` with `lock_guard` for protecting shared data, and `condition_variable` for waiting. The machinery is not the hard part — the data races that appear when threads share memory are, so they stay front and center.
objectives: Distinguish a task from a thread and say when to prefer each
Define a data race and prevent one with `mutex` plus `lock_guard`
Coordinate producer and consumer with `condition_variable`, and pass results through `future`

concepts.statement: **A `thread` is the mechanism for running a task in the same address space as other tasks.** Construct it from a callable and it starts running immediately; `join()` waits for it to finish; every `thread` must be joined or detached before it is destroyed, or the program terminates.
concepts.detail: `void f() { thread thr{my_task}; thr.join(); }` — the shared address space is both the point (cheap communication) and the hazard (races).

concepts.statement: **A task is an interface to a computation that can run concurrently; `async()` launches a task and returns a `future` — a handle on its result.** `fut.get()` blocks until the value is ready, and an exception thrown inside the task is re-thrown by `get()`. The system decides how many threads to use, so you reason about values, not scheduling.
concepts.detail: Tasks carry both the result and the failure across the concurrency boundary — raw threads do neither without extra plumbing.

concepts.statement: **A data race is two threads accessing the same memory location with at least one write and no synchronization — and it is undefined behavior, not a wrong value.** The fix is mutual exclusion: a `mutex` only one thread can hold, acquired through a `lock_guard` so the critical section releases even on an exception.
concepts.detail: `void increment() { lock_guard<mutex> lck{m}; ++count; }` — the mutex `m` is released at the closing brace, on every path. When in doubt, use a mutex; keep critical sections short.

concepts.statement: **A `condition_variable` lets a thread wait for an event: `wait(lck)` releases the lock and sleeps until another thread calls `notify_one()` or `notify_all()`, then re-acquires the lock.** The standard shape is a queue shared between producers and consumers.
concepts.detail: The consumer loop `unique_lock<mutex> lck{m}; while (queue.empty()) cond.wait(lck); auto msg = queue.front(); queue.pop(); lck.unlock();` — the `while` (not `if`) handles spurious wakeups and races between notification and re-acquisition.

concepts.statement: **Where possible, let concurrent tasks communicate through `future`s and message queues rather than through shared mutable data.** Race-free by construction beats race-free by locking discipline — one less invariant a future maintainer can break.
concepts.detail: This is why `async` plus `future` is the first tool to reach for; raw `thread` plus mutex is the mechanism underneath, kept for when you need the control.

examples.title: Summing a vector with two tasks
examples.problem: Add up `vector<int> v{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8}` using two concurrent tasks and combine their results.

steps.label: Step 1: Split
steps.text: First half `{1,2,3,4}`, second half `{5,6,7,8}` — two ranges over the same storage, no copying.

steps.label: Step 2: Launch
steps.text: `auto f1 = async(accum, &v[0], &v[4], 0);` and `auto f2 = async(accum, &v[4], &v[8], 0);` — each task returns its partial sum through a `future`.

steps.label: Step 4: Combine
steps.text: `return f1.get() + f2.get();` — each `get()` blocks until its task is done, giving $10 + 26 = 36$.

examples.result: 36 — the correct total of 1 through 8, with the partitioning arithmetic checkable by hand: $\frac{8 \times 9}{2} = 36$.

examples.title: A lost-update race, quantified
examples.problem: Two threads each increment a shared `int` counter 500,000 times. What is the final value, with and without synchronization?

steps.label: Step 1: The intended result
steps.text: $2 \times 500{,}000 = 1{,}000{,}000$ — if every increment landed.

steps.label: Step 2: Unprotected
steps.text: `++count` compiles to load, add, store. When both threads interleave loads of the same old value, both write the same new value and an update is lost. Typical observed finals hover near 873,000 — varies run to run, and formally undefined behavior.

steps.label: Step 3: Protected
steps.text: Wrap the increment in `lock_guard<mutex> lck{m}; ++count;` — the loads and stores of any single increment no longer interleave.

steps.label: Step 4: Result
steps.text: Exactly 1,000,000 on every run — correctness restored by exclusion, at the cost of serializing the critical section.

examples.result: 1,000,000 exactly when locked; anything else when raced — including impossible-seeming values, because the race itself is undefined behavior.

keyTakeaways: Threads share an address space; tasks wrap that hazard in value communication — `async` returns a `future` carrying result or exception.
A data race is undefined behavior; the cure is a mutex held via `lock_guard`, never unlocked by hand.
`condition_variable` plus a shared queue is the producer–consumer shape; `wait` releases the lock while sleeping.

quiz.q: A data race is:
options: two threads accessing the same object, at least one writing, with no synchronization — undefined behavior
quiz.explanation: The unsynchronized read/write overlap makes the program's meaning undefined — not merely wrong, but outside the language's guarantees.

quiz.q: When does the `lock_guard` release its mutex?
options: at end of scope — including during exception unwinding
quiz.explanation: The guard is itself an RAII object; its destructor unlocks, so scope exit — normal or exceptional — always releases.

quiz.q: `async(accum, args...)` returns:
options: a new thread handle that must be joined
a `future` whose `get()` yields the result and rethrows any task exception
quiz.explanation: The launch is decoupled from the value: `get()` blocks until the task finishes, delivering either its return value or its exception.

quiz.q: Why does the book prefer tasks to threads?
options: the library chooses the number of threads, and exceptions and results travel through the future — you program with values
quiz.explanation: Tasks express *what* to compute; the system decides *where*. Results and failures flow through one channel instead of ad-hoc shared state.

intro: Between the big containers and the specialized tools sits a shelf of small components the book reaches for constantly: `pair` and `tuple` for heterogeneous bundles, `chrono` for time as a typed quantity, plus function adapters and compile-time type predicates. Individually tiny, together they delete a whole class of bookkeeping code — and of bookkeeping bugs.
objectives: Use `pair` and `tuple` with `get`, `make_pair`/`make_tuple`
Explain a `chrono` duration as a count plus a unit, and time a block with `steady_clock`
Pick the correct clock for measuring intervals versus time-stamping

concepts.statement: **A `pair` holds two values of possibly different types, accessed as `.first` and `.second`.** It is the element type of the associative containers: a `map<K,V>` stores `pair<const K,V>`.
concepts.detail: `make_pair("odd", 1)` builds one without spelling the types; `p.first` is `"odd"`, `p.second` is `1`.

concepts.statement: **A `tuple` is the N-value generalization of `pair`: heterogeneous, its member count and types fixed at compile time, elements reached with `get<i>()`.** The index must be a compile-time constant; `tuple_size` reports the length.
concepts.detail: `auto t = make_tuple("Sue", 25, 63.5);` then `get<0>(t)` is `"Sue"` and `get<1>(t) = 26;` ages her. (Later standards add structured bindings that unpack a tuple into named locals.)

concepts.statement: **A `duration` is a count of ticks together with a compile-time unit; `milliseconds`, `microseconds`, `nanoseconds` are all `duration` specializations.** A `time_point` is a duration measured from a clock's epoch. Unit conversion happens implicitly when exact, and requires `duration_cast` when it could lose information.
concepts.detail: `duration_cast<milliseconds>(t1-t0).count()` reads the integer tick count of an elapsed interval.

concepts.statement: **`steady_clock` never goes backwards — use it for measuring intervals; `system_clock` tracks wall-clock time — use it for time stamps.** Timing with a clock the operating system adjusts mid-measurement produces corrupt intervals.
concepts.detail: The elapsed-time idiom: `auto t0 = steady_clock::now(); do_work(); auto d = steady_clock::now() - t0;` then cast `d` to the unit you want to report.

concepts.statement: **`<type_traits>` supplies compile-time facts about types (`is_integral`, `is_pointer`, `is_class`), and `function`/`bind` adapt callables to a common shape.** These are the small, precisely specified tools that keep generic code from sprouting project-local helpers.
concepts.detail: The section's theme in one line: prefer a tiny standard component with exact semantics to a hand-written one with folklore semantics.

examples.title: Reading and writing a tuple
examples.problem: Given `auto t = make_tuple("Sue", 25, 63.5);`, read each element, change one, and report the length.

steps.label: Step 1: Read
steps.text: `get<0>(t)` is `"Sue"` (a `const char*`-deduced string), `get<1>(t)` is `25`, `get<2>(t)` is `63.5`.

steps.label: Step 2: Write
steps.text: `get<1>(t) = 26;` — `get` returns a reference to the element, so Sue ages.

steps.label: Step 3: Size
steps.text: `tuple_size` reports 3 elements — a compile-time fact, not a stored count.

steps.label: Step 4: Index rule
steps.text: `get<3>(t)` is a compile-time error: index must be constant and in range — mistakes surface before the program runs.

examples.result: A three-element heterogeneous record with compile-time-checked access — no struct declaration, no off-by-one runtime.

examples.title: Timing a loop with `steady_clock`
examples.problem: Measure a 1,000-iteration loop and report the total in microseconds and the per-iteration cost.

steps.label: Step 1: Capture the start
steps.text: `auto t0 = steady_clock::now();` — a `time_point` on the steady clock.

steps.label: Step 2: Run and stop
steps.text: The loop executes; `auto d = steady_clock::now() - t0;` is a `duration` in the clock's native unit.

steps.label: Step 3: Convert
steps.text: `duration_cast<microseconds>(d).count()` returns 412 — a measured total of 412 µs. In nanoseconds that same `d` casts to 412,000.

steps.label: Step 4: Normalize
steps.text: Per iteration: $412\,\mu s / 1000 = 0.412\,\mu s = 412$ ns.

examples.result: Total 412 µs, per-iteration 412 ns — and the arithmetic is forced to be explicit because `chrono` will not silently divide by a count.

keyTakeaways: `pair` and `tuple` bundle heterogeneous values with compile-time indexed access; `make_pair`/`make_tuple` deduce the types.
In `chrono`, time is typed: a duration is a count times a unit, and lossy conversions demand an explicit `duration_cast`.
Measure intervals with `steady_clock`; time-stamp with `system_clock`.

quiz.q: Given `auto t = make_tuple(1, 2.5, "x");`, which expression fails to compile?
quiz.explanation: Tuple indices are compile-time constants in range $0..2$ here; index 3 is out of range and rejected at compile time.

quiz.q: Why is `steady_clock` the right clock for measuring how long something took?
options: it has the highest resolution on every platform
its time points never decrease — operating-system clock adjustments cannot corrupt the interval
it returns a duration rather than a time_point
it counts in nanoseconds by definition
quiz.explanation: Interval measurement needs monotonicity; `system_clock` can jump when the OS resets the time and would corrupt a difference.

quiz.q: `duration_cast<nanoseconds>(milliseconds{5}).count()` is:
quiz.explanation: One millisecond is $10^6$ nanoseconds, so 5 ms is 5,000,000 ns; the conversion is lossless in this direction.

quiz.q: A `map<string,int>` stores its elements as:
quiz.explanation: The key must not be modified through the map, so the stored type pairs a `const` key with the mapped value.

intro: Text is data, and recognizing patterns in text is a recurring job: phone numbers, dates, tags, log lines. The `<regex>` library brings regular expressions into the standard: declare a `regex`, search a `string`, inspect what matched through an `smatch`, rewrite with `regex_replace`. The default grammar is the ECMAScript one, used throughout this section.
objectives: Read and write the core regex notation: classes, quantifiers, groups, alternation
Use `regex_search` with `smatch` to capture submatches
Rewrite text with `regex_replace` and the `$` format markers

concepts.statement: **Character classes (`\d` digit, `\w` word character, `[a-z]` ranges), quantifiers (`*` zero or more, `+` one or more, `?` optional, `{n}` and `{2,4}` counted), grouping `(...)`, and alternation `|`** compose into patterns: `\d{3}-\d{4}` is three digits, a dash, four digits.
concepts.detail: The pattern language is its own small formalism — regex is a notation worth reading fluently, exactly like the math in a physics chapter.

concepts.statement: **`regex_search(s, m, pat)` finds the first substring matching `pat` and fills the `smatch m`: `m[0]` is the whole match, `m[i]` the text of the i-th captured group.** A failed search leaves `m` empty — test the `bool` result before using it.
concepts.detail: Groups are what turn a match into data: wrapping parts of the pattern in `(...)` makes their text addressable as `m[1]`, `m[2]`, ...

concepts.statement: **`regex_replace(s, pat, fmt)` returns a copy of `s` with every match replaced by `fmt`, in which `$&` is the whole match and `$1`, `$2` are the captured groups.** One call performs a global find-and-rewrite.
concepts.detail: Because it rewrites *every* match, the pattern must be anchored carefully — `^` and `\b` (word boundary) are the usual tools.

concepts.statement: **`R"(...)"` is a raw string literal: backslashes are characters, not escapes.** A regex reads as you would write it on paper — `R"(\w{2}\s*=\s*\d+)"` — instead of `"\\w{2}\\s*=\\s*\\d+"`, where every backslash must be escaped for the string before the regex ever sees it.
concepts.detail: In a normal string literal `\d` would be consumed by the compiler as an escape; the raw form passes it through to the regex engine untouched.

concepts.statement: **Regular Expressions.** regex matching in minutes. You can claim this section when you can read and write the core regex notation: classes, quantifiers, groups, alternation — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 5 (A Tour of C++: Concurrency and Utilities); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Extracting a phone number
examples.problem: From `string s = "call 258-3049 today";` extract the phone number and then its two parts, using the pattern `R"(\d{3}-\d{4})"`.

steps.label: Step 1: Search
steps.text: `smatch m; regex pat{R"(\d{3}-\d{4})"}; bool hit = regex_search(s, m, pat);` — `hit` is true; `m[0]` is `"258-3049"`.

steps.label: Step 2: Capture
steps.text: Re-declare `pat2{R"((\d{3})-(\d{4}))"};` — now group 1 grabs the first three digits, group 2 the last four.

steps.label: Step 3: Read the groups
steps.text: `m[1]` is `"258"` and `m[2]` is `"3049"`, while `m[0]` remains the whole `"258-3049"`.

steps.label: Step 4: No match
steps.text: On `"no numbers here"`, `regex_search` returns false and `m` is empty — using `m[0]` without checking would be the bug.

examples.result: Pattern plus two groups: `m[0]` = 258-3049, `m[1]` = 258, `m[2]` = 3049 — the string parsed into data in one search.

examples.title: Reformatting ISO dates
examples.problem: Rewrite every date of the form year-month-day in `"deadline 2025-1-30 firm"` to month/day/year.

steps.label: Step 1: Pattern with groups
steps.text: `regex pat{R"((\d{4})-(\d{1,2})-(\d{1,2}))"};` — year is 4 digits, month and day are 1 or 2.

steps.label: Step 3: Replace
steps.text: `regex_replace(s, pat, "$2/$3/$1")` reorders the groups into month/day/year at every match.

steps.label: Step 4: Result
steps.text: The output string is `"deadline 1/30/2025 firm"` — untouched text passes through, only matches are rewritten.

examples.result: "deadline 1/30/2025 firm" — a global reformat driven entirely by group ordering.

keyTakeaways: `regex` + `regex_search` + `smatch` for finding: `m[0]` is the whole match, `m[i]` the i-th captured group.
`regex_replace` with `$&`, `$1`, `$2` rewrites every match in one pass.
Write patterns as raw strings `R"(...)"` so a backslash in the pattern survives the string literal.

quiz.q: Which string does the pattern `\d{3}-\d{4}` match?
quiz.explanation: Exactly three digits, a dash, exactly four digits — the others have the wrong count on one side or no dash.

quiz.q: After a successful `regex_search` into `smatch m` with pattern `(\d{3})-(\d{4})`, `m[1]` holds:
options: the first captured group — the three digits
quiz.explanation: `m[0]` is the whole match; each parenthesized group contributes `m[1]`, `m[2]`, ... in order of its opening parenthesis.

quiz.q: In a `regex_replace` format string, `$&` denotes:
quiz.explanation: `$&` is the whole matched text; `$1`, `$2`, ... are the groups. That is the full format vocabulary you need for rewrites.

intro: Scientific and engineering code needs more than the arithmetic operators: `<cmath>` supplies the classical functions, `<complex>` makes complex numbers a first-class type, `<random>` separates engines from distributions, `<numeric>` holds the accumulation family, and `<valarray>` offers numeric arrays whose expressions the compiler can optimize. A quick tour of each — plus the precision limits every programmer should be able to quote.
objectives: Use the `<cmath>` function set and distinguish `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `trunc`
Compute with `complex<double>` and with engines-plus-distributions from `<random>`
Quote the precision limits of `float` and `double` from `numeric_limits`

concepts.statement: **The classical mathematical functions — `sqrt`, `pow`, `log`, `exp`, `sin`, `cos`, `abs` — overloaded for `float`, `double` and `long double`, with integral arguments promoted to `double`.** The rounding functions differ in direction: `floor` toward negative infinity, `ceil` toward positive infinity, `trunc` toward zero, `round` to nearest (halves away from zero).
concepts.detail: `floor(-2.5)` is `-3.0` but `trunc(-2.5)` is `-2.0` — the pair that catches the unwary.

concepts.statement: **`complex<double>` supports the full arithmetic with the usual mathematical meaning:** `abs`, `real`, `imag`, `polar`, and complex overloads of `sqrt`, `exp`, `log`. The book's Mandelbrot example is a few lines because the type does the algebra.
concepts.detail: `complex<double> z{3,4};` builds $3+4i$; `abs(z)` is $5$; operators compose exactly as written on paper.

concepts.statement: **An engine produces raw bit sequences; a distribution shapes them into the distribution you asked for.** `default_random_engine re; normal_distribution<double> nd{31.0, 8.0};` — then `nd(re)` yields the next sample from $N(31, 8^2)$.
concepts.detail: `rand()%n` is the anti-pattern: modulo bias plus weak low bits. The engine/distribution split lets you swap either half independently.

concepts.statement: **The accumulation family: `accumulate`, `inner_product`, `partial_sum`, `iota` — generalizations of `+` and `*` over any sequence.** `accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0.0)` sums a `vector<double>`; the *type of the initial value* decides the arithmetic's type.
concepts.detail: Summing a `vector<int>` with initial value `0` overflows as an `int`; with `0.0` it computes in `double` — a one-character fix to a classic bug.

concepts.statement: **`numeric_limits<T>::epsilon()` is the gap between 1.0 and the next representable value: $2^{-23} \approx 1.19\times10^{-7}$ for `float` (24-bit significand, about 6 significant decimal digits) and $2^{-52} \approx 2.22\times10^{-16}$ for `double` (53-bit, about 15).** Every integer up to $2^{53}$ is exact in a `double`; $0.1$ is not.
concepts.detail: Hence `0.1 + 0.2` printing as `0.30000000000000004`: both operands are the nearest representable doubles, and so is their sum.

examples.title: Complex arithmetic, by hand and by machine
examples.problem: Compute the product $(3+4i)(1-2i)$ and the magnitude of $3+4i$ — then write the code.

steps.label: Step 3: Code
steps.text: `complex<double> z{3,4}; complex<double> w{1,-2}; cout << z*w << ' ' << abs(z);`

steps.label: Step 4: Output
steps.text: `(11,-2) 5` — the type prints as an ordered pair and the magnitudes agree with the hand computation.

examples.result: $(11,-2)$ and $5$ — machine and by-hand algebra match exactly.

examples.title: How tall is the histogram peak?
examples.problem: Draw 400 samples from `normal_distribution<double> nd{31.0, 8.0}` into unit-width buckets. Roughly how many land in the bucket containing the mean?

steps.label: Step 1: Density at the mean
steps.text: The normal density peaks at $\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}$ — with $\sigma = 8$: $\frac{1}{8 \times 2.5066} = 0.04987$ per unit.

steps.label: Step 2: Expected count
steps.text: $400 \times 0.04987 \approx 19.9$ — about 20 samples in the central bucket.

steps.label: Step 3: Sanity check
steps.text: Two standard deviations of width ($\sigma/2$ each side) holds about 68% of the mass: $0.68 \times 400 \approx 272$ samples within buckets 23–39.

steps.label: Step 4: Run it
steps.text: `for (int i = 0; i < 400; ++i) { int k = (int)round(nd(re)); if (0 <= k && k < 64) ++h[k]; }` — the observed peak lands near 20.

examples.result: About 20 per bucket at the mean — the arithmetic of the distribution is checkable before the code is run.

keyTakeaways: `<cmath>` and `<complex>` give the classical mathematics with the expected semantics — mind the four rounding directions.
`<random>` is engine times distribution; never `rand()%n`.
`float` carries ~6 significant digits, `double` ~15; integers are exact in a `double` up to $2^{53}$ — but 0.1 is not exact at any size.

quiz.q: `floor(-2.5)` and `trunc(-2.5)` are, respectively:
quiz.explanation: `floor` heads toward negative infinity, `trunc` toward zero — for negatives they differ.

quiz.q: In `normal_distribution<double> nd{31.0, 8.0}; ... nd(re);`, the expression `nd(re)` is:
options: passing the engine to the distribution to obtain the next shaped value
quiz.explanation: The distribution is a functor: give it an engine's raw output and it returns a value with the requested distribution.

quiz.q: `numeric_limits<double>::epsilon()` is approximately:
quiz.explanation: A 53-bit significand makes the gap near 1.0 equal to $2^{-52} \approx 2.22\times10^{-16}$; the float figure is $2^{-23}$.

quiz.q: Why is `rand()%n` discouraged?
options: modulo bias and weak low bits make the distribution wrong
it only works for n below 100
quiz.explanation: The remainder maps unevenly when RAND_MAX+1 is not a multiple of n, and rand's low bits are historically poor — engines plus distributions fix both.

intro: The chapter closes with rules of thumb — the tour distilled into guidance you can apply at code review. Most reduce to a single move: replace hand-rolled resource and concurrency code with the standard machinery the preceding six sections showed. Advice sections read fast precisely because they cost the most when ignored.
objectives: Apply the chapter's advice rules to audit a code fragment
Justify each rule by naming the standard mechanism that replaces the offending code
Recognize situations where the standard tools genuinely do not fit

concepts.statement: **Use standard-library components in preference to your own.** Before writing a string class, a hash table, or a regex matcher, state what the standard one cannot do — the answer is usually nothing.
concepts.detail: This chapter's components — smart pointers, `thread`, `async`, `tuple`, `regex`, `cmath` — exist so that those wheels are never reinvented.

concepts.term: No bare new/delete in application code
concepts.statement: **Keep resource management inside handles: `vector`, `string`, `unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`.** Raw `new` and `delete` scattered through code is where leaks and dangling pointers are born.
concepts.detail: A `new` expression belongs inside the implementation of a handle type; everything above that level passes owners as smart pointers or borrows as references.

concepts.statement: **Prefer tasks — `async` returning a `future` — to threads when you want the result.** Threads are the mechanism; tasks express the computation, with exceptions and return values carried for you.
concepts.detail: Drop to `thread` when you genuinely manage hardware concurrency yourself: long-lived workers, custom scheduling, pinning.

concepts.term: Never throw while holding a lock
concepts.statement: **Code inside a critical section must not let an exception escape.** The `lock_guard` will unlock, but the handler runs while shared data may be in an inconsistent state, and locking discipline leaks into exception handling where nobody planned for it.
concepts.detail: Keep critical sections short and exception-free; compute outside the lock what can be computed outside.

concepts.term: Shipping rule for a tour of C++: concurrency and utilities
concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Default answers: `vector`, `string`, `unique_ptr`, `async`, `regex` — write your own only with a stated reason.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: Auditing a function against the chapter's advice
examples.problem: Review this fragment against the chapter's rules: `int* buf = new int[n]; if (n > 100) return 0; fill(buf, n); thread t{log_stats}; delete[] buf;`

steps.label: Step 1: Leak
steps.text: The early `return` skips `delete[] buf` — violates 'no bare new/delete'. Fix: `vector<int> buf(n);` — release is automatic on every path.

steps.label: Step 2: Thread never joined
steps.text: `t` is destroyed without `join()` or `detach()` — the program terminates. Fix: `t.join()` before return, or express the logging as `async`.

steps.label: Step 3: Hand-rolled fill
steps.text: `fill(buf, n)` reinvents what the library does — fix: the vector initializes, or use `std::fill`/`iota` from `<numeric>`.

steps.label: Step 4: Count
steps.text: Three violations in four lines — each one is a rule from this chapter, and each fix deletes code rather than adding it.

examples.result: The audited version is shorter than the original: `vector<int> buf(n);` plus a joined (or `async`) logging task — every failure mode removed by construction.

examples.title: Reviewing a tour of C++: concurrency and utilities code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the chapter's advice rules to audit a code fragment.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Default answers: `vector`, `string`, `unique_ptr`, `async`, `regex` — write your own only with a stated reason.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `auto f = std::async(compute); int r = f.get();`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: justify each rule by naming the standard mechanism that replaces the offending code. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Bare `new`/`delete` belongs inside handle implementations, never in business code.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Default answers: `vector`, `string`, `unique_ptr`, `async`, `regex` — write your own only with a stated reason. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Default answers: `vector`, `string`, `unique_ptr`, `async`, `regex` — write your own only with a stated reason.
Bare `new`/`delete` belongs inside handle implementations, never in business code.
Concurrency: tasks over threads, short exception-free critical sections, every `thread` joined or detached.

quiz.q: Which fix best applies the chapter's advice to `int* p = new int[n]; ...; delete[] p;` when the function has several early returns?
options: use `vector<int>` (or a smart pointer) so release happens at scope exit
quiz.explanation: The advice is to remove the manual release obligation entirely, not to enumerate every path that needs to remember it.

quiz.q: The advice 'never throw while holding a lock' exists because:
options: exceptions cannot propagate out of threads
a throw can escape a critical section leaving shared data inconsistent, and drags locking into exception handling
locks are destroyed by a throw
quiz.explanation: The guard unlocks — the problem is what the handler then sees and who is prepared for it. Keep critical sections short and non-throwing.

quiz.q: 'Prefer tasks to threads' means:
options: express concurrent work as `async` returning a `future`, unless you need explicit thread control
quiz.explanation: Tasks are the higher-level interface to the same machinery — reach for `thread` when you are managing the concurrency yourself.

intro: C++ is a standardized language: ISO/IEC 14882 defines exactly what a conforming program may rely on, and this book targets the 2011 edition of that document — C++11. Knowing what the standard guarantees, what it leaves to implementations, and what it declares flatly undefined is the difference between portable code and code that merely happens to work on today's compiler. This section reads the fine print.
objectives: Identify the ISO standard document and what it specifies — language and library together
Distinguish implementation-defined, unspecified and undefined behavior
Explain why 'what my compiler does' is not a specification

concepts.statement: **The C++ standard is ISO/IEC 14882; the edition this book implements is C++11 (14882:2011).** It specifies both the language and the standard library in one document — semantics, not implementations: everything observable to a conforming program is fixed, and the rest is deliberately left open.
concepts.detail: A standard is developed through a committee process of proposals and national-body votes, then published by ISO. It is written for compiler writers and expert readers, not as a tutorial.

concepts.statement: **The standard grades every behavior: *implementation-defined* (each implementation must document its choice, e.g. `sizeof(int)`), *unspecified* (no documentation required, e.g. the value of padding bytes), and *undefined* (no guarantees at all, e.g. dereferencing a dangling pointer).** Portable code depends only on the defined core.
concepts.detail: Implementation-defined choices may differ but are at least discoverable; undefined behavior removes the program from the language's protection — the optimizer may do anything.

concepts.statement: **A standard is what makes code portable across compilers, platforms and decades.** Relying on what one implementation happens to do — the size of an `int`, the signedness of a plain `char`, struct padding — is a latent bug for the day the code moves.
concepts.detail: The economic argument: millions of lines of C++ depend on stability, so old guarantees survive even as new standards (C++14, C++17, ...) add facilities.

concepts.statement: **Compilers implement the standard at different rates.** C++98-era implementations are still in the wild, some compilers are mostly C++11, and some lead with experimental facilities. A practical skill is checking which features your toolchain actually provides.
concepts.detail: The book's advice: prefer to write to the standard, and treat features an implementation lacks as a toolchain fact to check, not a reason to write non-standard code.

concepts.term: The ISO C++ Standard: the working contract
concepts.statement: **The ISO C++ Standard.** The standardization process and what it specifies. You can claim this section when you can identify the ISO standard document and what it specifies — language and library together — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 6 (Types and Declarations); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: A portability audit
examples.problem: The line `int base = 100000; int area = base * base;` computes $100{,}000^2$. Is it correct on a typical 32-bit-`int` machine? What does the standard actually guarantee?

steps.label: Step 2: The type's capacity
steps.text: A 32-bit signed `int` tops out at $2^{31} - 1 = 2{,}147{,}483{,}647$ — an order of magnitude too small.

steps.label: Step 3: What the standard says
steps.text: It guarantees only that `int` holds at least 16 bits; on this machine it holds 32 — and $10^{10}$ overflows it. Signed overflow is *undefined behavior*, not a wraparound.

steps.label: Step 4: The fix
steps.text: `long long area = base * 1LL * base;` or `long long area{base} * base;` — 64 bits holds $10^{10}$ trivially (max about $9.2\times10^{18}$).

examples.result: The original is undefined on the very machine it was tested on; the fix depends only on the guaranteed minimum of 64 bits for `long long`.

examples.title: Working through the ISO C++ standard
examples.problem: The standardization process and what it specifies. Your task: identify the ISO standard document and what it specifies — language and library together.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: identify the ISO standard document and what it specifies — language and library together. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: ISO/IEC 14882 defines language and library together; this edition targets C++11.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `constexpr double pi = 3.14159;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — distinguish implementation-defined, unspecified and undefined behavior — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Implementation-defined behavior is documented per implementation; unspecified and undefined behavior are not safety nets. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: ISO/IEC 14882 defines language and library together; this edition targets C++11. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: ISO/IEC 14882 defines language and library together; this edition targets C++11.
Implementation-defined behavior is documented per implementation; unspecified and undefined behavior are not safety nets.
Code that relies on unguaranteed details is a portability bug waiting for the next compiler or platform.

quiz.q: The ISO C++ standard's number, and this book's target edition, are:
quiz.explanation: C++ is standardized as ISO/IEC 14882; the 4th edition of the book is written against the 2011 revision, C++11.

quiz.q: `sizeof(int)` is an example of:
options: implementation-defined behavior — each implementation documents its choice
a value the standard fixes at 4
quiz.explanation: The standard constrains the range (at least 16 bits, and not larger than `long`) but the concrete size is the implementation's documented choice.

quiz.q: A program that depends on how its current compiler pads a struct is relying on:
options: behavior the standard leaves open — a portability risk
quiz.explanation: Padding is left to implementations (and alignment), so the dependence is a latent bug on any machine with different alignment rules.

intro: Every value in a program has a type, and the fundamental types — `bool`, characters, integers, floating point — come with precise guarantees and precise freedom: sizes the standard constrains but does not fix, exact arithmetic on unsigned integers, and approximations in floating point that every engineer must budget for. This section is the field guide: what each type promises, what it costs, and where the traps are.
objectives: State the size guarantees and ordering laws for the fundamental types
Explain unsigned modulo arithmetic and IEEE floating-point precision limits
Distinguish the three character types and choose among them

concepts.statement: **`bool` holds exactly `true` or `false`.** In arithmetic a `bool` promotes to `int` (`true` becomes 1, `false` becomes 0), which is why `count += (x > 0);` tallies the positive entries.
concepts.detail: `sizeof(bool)` is not pinned by the standard — one byte is typical — but its domain is exactly the two truth values.

concepts.statement: **`char`, `signed char` and `unsigned char` are three distinct types; plain `char` is its own type, signed or unsigned by implementation choice.** `sizeof(char)` is 1 by definition — it is the unit of `sizeof` — and a byte is at least 8 bits. For wider text, `char16_t` (UTF-16), `char32_t` (UTF-32) and `wchar_t` hold Unicode characters.
concepts.detail: Treating characters as small integers — as C does — is the source of the signedness surprises; the three-type split exists so plain `char` can stay text.

concepts.term: Integer types and the modulo law
concepts.statement: **Sizes form a non-decreasing chain with each step implementation-dependent:** $1 = \text{sizeof(char)} \le \text{sizeof(short)} \le \text{sizeof(int)} \le \text{sizeof(long)} \le \text{sizeof(long\ long)}$. The minimum guarantees: at least 16 bits for `short` and `int`, 32 for `long`, 64 for `long long`. **Unsigned arithmetic is exact modulo $2^N$; signed overflow is undefined behavior.**
concepts.detail: On a typical 64-bit Linux (LP64): `short` 2, `int` 4, `long` 8, `long long` 8 bytes; on 64-bit Windows, `long` is 4. Use `<cstdint>` names like `int32_t` when a width is a requirement.

concepts.statement: **`float`, `double` and `long double`, with IEEE 754 as the de facto standard: `double` is the default choice, holding integers exactly up to $2^{53}$ and about 15 significant decimal digits; `float` gives about 6.** Numbers like $0.1$ have no exact binary representation at any precision.
concepts.detail: `long double` offers more precision at the cost of memory traffic; prefer `double` until profiling says otherwise.

concepts.statement: **Integer literals can be decimal, hexadecimal (`0x1F`) or octal (leading `0`); suffixes `u`, `l`, `ul` select unsignedness and width; floating literals gain `f` for `float`.** The type of a literal is part of the language, not a property of its digits.
concepts.detail: `0x10` is 16, not a decimal 10 — and `010` is 8, which is why a padded decimal list is a famous bug.

examples.title: Unsigned wraparound, exactly
examples.problem: An 8-bit unsigned counter reads 200. What is 200 + 300 in that type? And 250 + 10?

steps.label: Step 1: The rule
steps.text: Unsigned arithmetic is modulo $2^8 = 256$: the true sum is reduced by multiples of 256 into $[0, 256)$.

steps.label: Step 2: First sum
steps.text: $200 + 300 = 500 = 256 + 244$, so the stored value is 244.

steps.label: Step 3: Second sum
steps.text: $250 + 10 = 260 = 256 + 4$, so the stored value is 4 — not an error, not negative.

steps.label: Step 4: Contrast
steps.text: The same overflow with *signed* 8-bit values would be undefined behavior — the guarantee belongs to the unsigned types only.

examples.result: 244 and 4: unsigned arithmetic is well-defined modular arithmetic, which is why it is the choice for bit-level and range code.

examples.title: The precision ladder, observed
examples.problem: Predict what prints for `0.1f`, and for `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` at `double` precision.

steps.label: Step 1: Why 0.1 is inexact
steps.text: $0.1 = 1/10$ has no finite binary expansion — it is the binary analogue of $1/3$ in decimal.

steps.label: Step 2: Float
steps.text: The nearest `float` to 0.1 is $13421773/2^{24} = 0.100000001490116...$ — printing 0.1f shows the tail of digits.

steps.label: Step 3: Double
steps.text: Each operand rounds to the nearest 53-bit double, so `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004` and the comparison with `0.3` is false.

steps.label: Step 4: The right question
steps.text: Compare with a tolerance: `fabs(a - b) < 1e-12` — or scale to exact integer arithmetic when equality matters.

examples.result: Floating point is a *designed approximation*: exact for integers below $2^{53}$, honest rounding everywhere else, and never silently exact for 0.1.

keyTakeaways: Only the ordering chain and minimum widths are guaranteed; concrete sizes are implementation-defined — use `int32_t`-style names when width matters.
Unsigned arithmetic is exact modulo $2^N$; signed overflow is undefined — never rely on wraparound in signed types.
`double` carries ~15 significant digits and exact integers to $2^{53}$; 0.1 is not exactly representable in binary at any width.

quiz.q: How many distinct types are among `char`, `signed char`, and `unsigned char`?
quiz.explanation: All three exist separately: plain `char` is its own type whose signedness is an implementation choice, distinct from both explicit forms.

quiz.q: In 8-bit unsigned arithmetic, 200 + 300 equals:
quiz.explanation: Modulo $256$: $500 - 256 = 244$. Unsigned overflow is defined as wraparound, not as an error.

quiz.q: The largest integer guaranteed exactly representable in an IEEE 754 `double` is:
quiz.explanation: The 53-bit significand (one implicit bit) keeps every integer up to $2^{53} = 9{,}007{,}199{,}254{,}740{,}992$ exact.

quiz.q: Which relation is guaranteed by the standard?
quiz.explanation: Only the non-decreasing chain is guaranteed; the concrete sizes (4, 8, 2) are all implementation choices on mainstream platforms.

intro: Every name in a program is introduced by a declaration, and the book's first distinction — declaration versus definition — organizes everything from header hygiene to the linker's one-definition rule. The initializer forms carry their own policy: `{}` rejects narrowing conversions that `=` and `()` accept silently. And `auto` lets the compiler deduce the type while guaranteeing initialization, which deletes an entire genre of redundancy and another of bugs.
objectives: Distinguish declaration from definition and apply the one-definition rule
Compare the `=`, `(...)` and `{...}` initializer forms, especially narrowing
Explain what `auto` deduces and why it requires an initializer

concepts.statement: **A declaration introduces a name with a type; a definition additionally provides the entity itself — initialized storage or a body.** `extern int x;` declares; `int x;` defines. Every name must have exactly one definition (the one-definition rule) but may be declared as often as useful.
concepts.detail: This split is why headers contain declarations and exactly one source file contains the definition — the linker matches them.

concepts.statement: **`int a = 7;`, `int a(7);` and `int a{7};` all initialize; only `{}` refuses to narrow.** `double d = 7;` converts silently, but `double d{7};` is fine (widening); `int x = 7.9;` truncates to 7 without complaint, while `int x{7.9};` is a compile-time error.
concepts.detail: Use `{}` as the default for new code: the errors it rejects — lost fractional parts, constants that do not fit — are the ones that cost debugging days.

concepts.statement: **A local variable declared without an initializer holds indeterminate bits — reading it is undefined behavior.** Globals and statics are zero-initialized, which only makes the trap subtler because it disappears in tests that matter less.
concepts.detail: The discipline: never declare a variable before you have a value for it — and initialize at the point of declaration whenever you can.

concepts.statement: **`auto x = expr;` gives `x` the type of `expr`.** It demands an initializer (there is nothing to deduce from otherwise) and guarantees the variable starts with a value. `auto i = 7;` is `int`; `auto d = 7.0;` is `double`; `auto& r = x;` is a reference to `x`'s type.
concepts.detail: In generic code, `auto&&` forwards perfectly; in ordinary code, `auto` removes redundancy like `map<string,int>::iterator it = m.begin();`.

concepts.statement: **`constexpr` marks an entity as usable in constant expressions — values computable by the compiler before the program runs.** A `constexpr int` can serve where a literal is required: an array bound, a template argument, another `constexpr` initializer.
concepts.detail: It is the modern replacement for macros-as-constants: typed, scoped, and evaluated where misuse is a compile error.

examples.title: A narrowing audit
examples.problem: Which of these compile, and which perform silent damage? `int a = 7.9; int b{7.9}; char c = 1000; char d{1000};`

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: `int a = 7.9;` compiles; `a` becomes 7 — the fraction is silently lost.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: `int b{7.9};` is rejected at compile time: `{}` does not narrow a `double` into an `int`.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: `char c = 1000;` compiles on an 8-bit `char` — 1000 does not fit; the stored value is implementation-defined truncation.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: `char d{1000};` is rejected: the constant does not fit the target — again `{}` catches what `=` covers up.

examples.result: Two of the four lines silently corrupt values; `{}` catches both — its entire job is to convert silent loss into compile-time errors.

examples.title: What does `auto` deduce?
examples.problem: Deduce the type and value of `auto a = 7;`, `auto b = 7.0;`, `auto c = 7/2;` and `auto d = 7.0/2;`.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: `auto a = 7;` — the literal 7 is `int`, so `a` is an `int` holding 7.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: `auto b = 7.0;` — the literal is `double`; `b` is a `double`.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: `auto c = 7/2;` — integer division happens *first*: `7/2` is the `int` 3, so `c` is `int` 3, not 3.5.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: `auto d = 7.0/2;` — mixed arithmetic promotes to `double`: `d` is `double` 3.5.

examples.result: `auto` copies the expression's type exactly — including its truncations. The deduction is never the problem; the expression is.

keyTakeaways: A definition is a declaration that provides the entity; the one-definition rule allows many declarations, exactly one definition.
Initialize with `{}` when in doubt: it rejects narrowing that `=` and `()` perform silently.
Reading an uninitialized local is undefined behavior — and `auto` variables are always initialized by construction.

quiz.q: `extern int x;` is:
options: a declaration that is not a definition
quiz.explanation: It announces the name and type but does not set aside storage; some other translation unit must define `x` exactly once.

quiz.q: Which line fails to compile?
quiz.explanation: The braces forbid narrowing from `double` to `int`; the `=` forms convert silently, and widening 7 to `double` is legal in braces.

quiz.q: What is `auto x = 7/2;`?
options: 3 (int) — the integer division happens before deduction
quiz.explanation: `auto` deduces the type of the initialized expression; `7/2` is already the `int` 3, so `x` is an `int`.

quiz.q: Reading the value of an uninitialized local variable is:
quiz.explanation: No value is guaranteed — the standard puts such reads outside the language, and optimizers exploit exactly that.

options: Both are rejected, because fractional literals require `double`
The first compiles holding `7`, while the second is rejected for narrowing
The first is rejected, while the second compiles holding `8`
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is a copy-style initialization and a brace-style initialization from the same fractional literal. Step 2: The governing rule is narrowing control: the `=` form permits narrowing with truncation, while the `{}` form requires a diagnostic when the value cannot be represented exactly. Step 3: Tracing declaration by declaration, `a` initializes through conversion and holds the truncated `7`, while `b` triggers a narrowing diagnostic and the program does not compile. Step 4: The distractors fail because the two forms deliberately differ, fractional literals are valid initializers for `int` under the `=` form, and no rounding to `8` occurs anywhere. Step 5: Therefore braces reject what the equals form silently truncates.

intro: The words object, value, variable and lvalue are the vocabulary of every error message and every design discussion about copying and moving. An object is a piece of memory with a type; a value is what you read from it; an lvalue is an expression that refers to an object that persists, an rvalue one that does not. Get these four words right and half of C++'s reputation for difficulty dissolves.
objectives: Define object, value and variable precisely
Classify expressions as lvalues or rvalues
Explain what `move(x)` changes about an expression's classification

concepts.statement: **An object is a region of memory that holds a value of some type.** Its size, alignment and layout come from the type; its lifetime comes from its storage: automatic (scope), static (program), free store (`new`/`delete`), or temporary (until the end of the full expression).
concepts.detail: Objects are what destructors are called on — the theory of RAII in the previous chapter is exactly a theory of object lifetimes.

concepts.statement: **A value is a set of bits read through a type — the interpretation. A variable is a named object.** The same bits can be values of different types (that is what a union exploits), and a value can exist with no object at all — the literal `42`.
concepts.detail: In the book's phrasing the trio runs: an object is something in memory; a value is the typed content; a variable is a named object.

concepts.statement: **An lvalue refers to an object that persists beyond the expression using it; an rvalue is a value that does not.** Mnemonics from the `=` of assignment: lvalues can appear on the left, rvalues on the right. `*p`, `v[i]`, `s.m` and `++i` are lvalues; `42`, `x+1`, `string("hi")` and `i++` are rvalues.
concepts.detail: The classification decides binding: `T&` accepts lvalues only; `const T&` accepts both; `T&&` accepts rvalues — which is how move semantics finds the temporaries it may harvest.

concepts.statement: **`move(x)` reclassifies the lvalue `x` as an rvalue reference — licensing the receiver to pilfer `x`'s resources.** It moves nothing itself; a move happens only if the receiving constructor or assignment chooses to act on the license. Afterward `x` remains valid but its content is unspecified.
concepts.detail: It is the bridge in the figure below — the controlled way an object's value crosses from the lvalue world into the rvalue world where harvesting is permitted.

concepts.term: Objects and Values: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Objects and Values.** Lvalues, rvalues and lifetimes. You can claim this section when you can define object, value and variable precisely — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 6 (Types and Declarations); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.
