examples.title: Classify eight expressions
examples.problem: With `int x; int* p = &x; vector<int> v(3);` in scope, classify `x`, `x+1`, `*p`, `v[0]`, `42`, `string("hi")`, `++x`, `x++`.

steps.label: Step 1: Names and dereferences
steps.text: `x` names a persistent object — lvalue. `*p` refers to that same object through the pointer — lvalue. `v[0]` names the zeroth element object — lvalue.

steps.label: Step 2: Arithmetic and literals
steps.text: `x+1` computes a temporary value — rvalue. `42` is a literal with no object at all — rvalue. `string("hi")` is a temporary object that dies at the semicolon — rvalue.

steps.label: Step 3: The increments
steps.text: `++x` increments x and yields x itself — lvalue. `x++` yields a *copy* of the old value — rvalue.

steps.label: Step 4: Consequence
steps.text: `int& r1 = x;` and `int& r2 = ++x;` compile; `int& r3 = x+1;` and `int& r4 = x++;` do not — a non-const `T&` cannot bind to an rvalue.

examples.result: Four lvalues (`x`, `*p`, `v[0]`, `++x`) and four rvalues (`x+1`, `42`, `string("hi")`, `x++`) — the binding rules in the figure follow mechanically.

examples.title: Working through objects and values
examples.problem: Lvalues, rvalues and lifetimes. Your task: define object, value and variable precisely.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define object, value and variable precisely. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: An object is a typed region of memory; a value is its typed content; a variable is a named object.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `constexpr double pi = 3.14159;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — classify expressions as lvalues or rvalues — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: lvalues refer to objects that persist (`*p`, `v[i]`, `++i`); rvalues are transient (`42`, `x+1`, `i++`). If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: An object is a typed region of memory; a value is its typed content; a variable is a named object. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: An object is a typed region of memory; a value is its typed content; a variable is a named object.
lvalues refer to objects that persist (`*p`, `v[i]`, `++i`); rvalues are transient (`42`, `x+1`, `i++`).
`move(x)` reclassifies rather than moves — the harvesting happens in the receiver, only if it is written to.

quiz.q: Which of these expressions is an rvalue?
quiz.explanation: `i++` delivers a copy of the old value — a temporary. The other three all refer to objects that persist beyond the expression.

quiz.q: An object is best defined as:
options: a region of memory holding a value of a type
quiz.explanation: Memory plus type — the name is optional (a variable), the value is what is stored, and class instances are just one kind.

quiz.q: `std::move(x)`:
options: reclassifies x as an rvalue reference — the receiver decides whether to move from it
quiz.explanation: It returns an `rvalue` reference to `x`, granting permission; nothing is transferred until a move constructor or assignment acts on it.

quiz.q: Why does `int& r = x+1;` fail to compile?
options: a non-const lvalue reference cannot bind to the temporary result of an expression
quiz.explanation: The sum is an rvalue; binding it to `T&` would let you write through a reference to a dead temporary. `const int&` would accept it and extend its life.

intro: Long type names are a readability tax, and macros are not the answer. C++ offers the alias declaration — `using Pairs = vector<pair<int,int>>;` — which simply names a type without creating a new one, reads left to right, and, unlike the older `typedef`, can be parameterized as a template. Small syntax, big effect on the readability of declarations.
objectives: Write a `using` alias and explain that it introduces a name, not a new type
Decode a complex `typedef` and rewrite it as a `using` alias
Parameterize an alias in a template, and contrast with `#define`

concepts.statement: **`using Pairs = vector<pair<int,int>>;` declares `Pairs` as a synonym for an existing type — no new type is created.** Aliases can be local, appearing in exactly the scope that needs them, and they compose inside other declarations.
concepts.detail: An alias improves clarity exactly when the expanded type is noise: `for (Pairs::iterator p = ps.begin(); ...)` says less than `for (auto p = ps.begin(); ...)` — use aliases for *meaning*, `auto` for *redundancy*.

concepts.statement: **`typedef` is the legacy spelling of the same idea: `typedef vector<pair<int,int>> Pairs;`.** For array, function and pointer-to-function types the declarator syntax reads inside-out, which is why the book prefers the `using` form for anything nontrivial.
concepts.detail: `typedef unsigned long ulong;` is fine either way; the difference bites on complex declarators — see the worked example.

concepts.statement: **A `using` alias can be parameterized: `template<typename T> using Vec = vector<T,My_alloc<T>>;` — a template alias, impossible to express with `typedef`.** Instantiating `Vec<int>` names the whole expanded type.
concepts.detail: This gives libraries a clean way to present customized containers without exposing every default parameter at each use site.

concepts.statement: **A `#define` is preprocessor text substitution: it ignores scope, ignores types, and cannot be scoped to a namespace or a template.** An alias is a language-level name with a type and a scope — everything a textual paste is not.
concepts.detail: The same contrast as `constexpr` versus `#define` constants: the language mechanism participates in checking; the macro does not.

concepts.statement: **Type Aliases.** using declarations and alias templates. You can claim this section when you can write a `using` alias and explain that it introduces a name, not a new type — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 6 (Types and Declarations); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Decoding a classic typedef
examples.problem: What does `typedef void (*Signal_handler)(int);` declare, and what is the `using` spelling?

steps.label: Step 1: Find the name
steps.text: Start at the name being declared: `Signal_handler`.

steps.label: Step 2: Read the declarator
steps.text: `(*Signal_handler)` — it is a pointer; `(int)` at the right — to a function taking an `int`; `void` at the left — returning `void`.

steps.label: Step 3: Assemble
steps.text: `Signal_handler` names the type 'pointer to function taking int, returning void' — the type of a signal callback.

steps.label: Step 4: The alias spelling
steps.text: `using Signal_handler = void(*)(int);` — left side is the new name, right side is the type — no decoding required.

examples.result: The two declarations mean the same thing; the `using` form reads in a straight line, which is why it is the book's preferred syntax.

examples.title: Working through type aliases
examples.problem: using declarations and alias templates. Your task: write a `using` alias and explain that it introduces a name, not a new type.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: write a `using` alias and explain that it introduces a name, not a new type. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `using X = T;` introduces a new name for an existing type — never a distinct type.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `constexpr double pi = 3.14159;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — decode a complex `typedef` and rewrite it as a `using` alias — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Alias templates parameterize the trick, something `typedef` cannot do; both are language-level, unlike `#define`. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `using X = T;` introduces a new name for an existing type — never a distinct type. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `using X = T;` introduces a new name for an existing type — never a distinct type.
Alias templates parameterize the trick, something `typedef` cannot do; both are language-level, unlike `#define`.
Prefer `using` for complex declarators: it reads left to right instead of inside-out.

quiz.q: What does `using Pairs = vector<pair<int,int>>;` introduce?
options: a new type distinct from the vector
another name for an existing type
quiz.explanation: An alias is a synonym: a `Pairs` is a `vector<pair<int,int>>` in every context, including overload resolution.

quiz.q: Which cannot be written with `typedef`?
options: a generic alias taking a template parameter
quiz.explanation: Templates over typedefs are not expressible; `template<typename T> using ...` was added exactly to fill that gap.

quiz.q: Compared with `#define Pairs vector<pair<int,int>>`, the using-alias:
options: respects scope and participates in type checking
quiz.explanation: The macro is blind text replacement; the alias is a scoped, typed name the compiler understands.

intro: The chapter's advice compresses its lessons into reviewable rules: keep types and scopes simple, initialize everything, declare close to use, and let the compiler carry the typing work with `auto` and the `{}` initializer. None of them is decorative — each names a bug class the chapter has just shown how to create.
objectives: Apply the chapter's rules to audit a small code fragment
Explain the uninitialized-variable and integer-division traps in terms of the rules
Choose where `auto` and `{}` improve clarity rather than obscure it

concepts.statement: **Choose the simplest type and the smallest scope that does the job.** A plain `int` loop counter beats a clever template; a local beats a global; a `double` beats a `long double` without a measured reason.
concepts.detail: Complexity in types is paid at every use site — in readability, in error messages, in compile time.

concepts.statement: **Every variable gets an initializer, ideally `{}` at declaration.** Uninitialized reads are undefined behavior, and zero-initialized statics only hide the bug until the variable moves to the stack.
concepts.detail: Corollary: do not declare a variable before you can compute its value — hoisting declarations 'for tidiness' creates the hazard.

concepts.statement: **Declare names in the smallest scope that works, as close to first use as possible.** Locality makes both readers and compilers happier: fewer live variables, shorter proofs of correctness by inspection.
concepts.detail: The same rule scales up: file-scope `static`s and globals are the largest scopes, and the most expensive to reason about.

concepts.statement: **Use `auto` where the type is redundant and `{}` where you want narrowing checked.** The compiler applies both rules perfectly; typing the same thing twice is a chance to disagree with yourself.
concepts.detail: `auto d = 7/2;` still demonstrates the boundary — the compiler deduces faithfully, including the truncation you did not intend.

concepts.term: Shipping rule for types and declarations
concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Smallest scope, simplest type, initializer at declaration — the three habits that prevent most declaration bugs.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: Auditing a fragment
examples.problem: Find the chapter-rule violations in `int total; double avg = n / count; total = total + 1; return avg;`

steps.label: Step 1: Uninitialized read
steps.text: `total` is declared without an initializer and read in `total + 1` — undefined behavior; rule: initialize at declaration.

steps.label: Step 2: Integer division
steps.text: If `n` and `count` are ints, `n / count` truncates *before* the conversion to `double` — `avg` for 7 over 2 becomes 3.0, not 3.5.

steps.label: Step 3: Scope
steps.text: `total` is used only at one point — declaring it there (`int total = 0;` in the smallest scope) removes the read-before-write entirely.

steps.label: Step 4: Fixes
steps.text: `auto avg = double(n) / count;` and `int total = 0;` — two small edits, both moving the work to the compiler or the declaration.

examples.result: The corrected fragment cannot express the original bugs — that is what the advice rules are for.

examples.title: Reviewing types and declarations code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the chapter's rules to audit a small code fragment.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Smallest scope, simplest type, initializer at declaration — the three habits that prevent most declaration bugs.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `constexpr double pi = 3.14159;`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: explain the uninitialized-variable and integer-division traps in terms of the rules. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Reading an uninitialized local is undefined behavior, not zero.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Smallest scope, simplest type, initializer at declaration — the three habits that prevent most declaration bugs. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Smallest scope, simplest type, initializer at declaration — the three habits that prevent most declaration bugs.
Reading an uninitialized local is undefined behavior, not zero.
`auto` removes redundancy and `{}` rejects narrowing; both hand work to the compiler.

quiz.q: The chapter's advice on uninitialized variables is:
options: zero is fine as a default
declare early at the top of the function, initialize later
do not declare a variable until you have a value for it
quiz.explanation: Declaring with the value in hand eliminates the read-before-write window; early declaration exists only to create it.

quiz.q: `double d = 7/2;` gives:
quiz.explanation: Both operands are `int`, so the division truncates to 3, which is then converted to the `double` 3.0 — convert an operand first.

quiz.q: The advice on declarations is to keep them:
options: all at file scope for visibility
in the smallest scope that works, close to first use
in a single block at the top of the function
quiz.explanation: Small scopes shorten the live range of every name, shrinking both the reader's and the compiler's proof burden.

intro: This chapter is the low-level heart of C++: the model of memory as objects at addresses, the pointer as a typed handle to such an address, the array as C's original container, and the reference as the safe re-seating-proof alias. You may write whole programs with `vector` and `string`, but the library itself — and every C interface and ABI you will ever meet — is written in this chapter's vocabulary.
objectives: Describe the pointer model of memory: objects at addresses, pointers as typed handles
State why pointer literacy matters even in code that never declares a pointer
Preview the chapter's three tools: pointers, arrays and references

concepts.statement: **Memory is a sequence of bytes with addresses; every object lives at one, and a pointer `T*` holds the address of an object of type `T`.** A pointer is a machine address given a *type* — the type is what makes `p+1` mean 'the next `T`' rather than 'one byte along'.
concepts.detail: C++ pointers are deliberately close to the hardware — which is exactly why they are the language of interfaces to operating systems, device drivers and C libraries.

concepts.statement: **Containers are implemented with pointers, C interfaces pass arrays as pointers, and library code routinely returns addresses.** You need not write raw pointer loops — you do need to read them, review them, and know which of them are safe.
concepts.detail: The chapter's own examples (a counting loop over a C string, an ownership audit) are the shapes you will encounter in real codebases within your first month.

concepts.statement: **A pointer refers to an object and can be re-seated; an array is a fixed run of objects with no size tag; a reference is an alias that binds once and never changes target.** Choosing among them — and knowing when `vector`, `string` or `span` replaces them all — is the design skill this chapter builds.
concepts.detail: Each tool gets its own section, but the constant theme is *ownership*: who is responsible for the object behind the address.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** The pointer and array model. You can claim this section when you can describe the pointer model of memory: objects at addresses, pointers as typed handles — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 7 (Pointers, Arrays, and References); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

concepts.statement: Work in three passes. First, state why pointer literacy matters even in code that never declares a pointer. Then, preview the chapter's three tools: pointers, arrays and references. Finally, test the outcome against the section promise: A pointer is a typed machine address — the type gives `+1` its meaning and keeps arithmetic honest.
concepts.detail: Each pass catches a different class of mistake, and skipping one moves the failure into a larger program where it costs more to diagnose than it would have here.

examples.title: Where each mechanism appears in the wild
examples.problem: Match pointer, array and reference to their natural occurrences in a real codebase.

steps.label: Step 1: Pointer
steps.text: An optional output parameter — 'compute the value, or return a null pointer on failure' — and a handle returned by a C library such as `fopen`.

steps.label: Step 2: Array
steps.text: A fixed-size table of constants, a buffer arriving from a socket, and every C string — an array of characters terminated by a zero byte.

steps.label: Step 3: Reference
steps.text: An output parameter that always exists (`void bump(int& n)`), and every range-for loop's hidden `auto&` element binding.

examples.result: The three mechanisms are not rivals — each encodes a different promise about identity, size and lifetime, which the rest of the chapter makes precise.

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: The pointer and array model. Your task: describe the pointer model of memory: objects at addresses, pointers as typed handles.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: describe the pointer model of memory: objects at addresses, pointers as typed handles. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A pointer is a typed machine address — the type gives `+1` its meaning and keeps arithmetic honest.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}; int* p = a; int& r = a[0];` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — state why pointer literacy matters even in code that never declares a pointer — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Arrays and pointers are how C interfaces express 'here is a run of objects', so library code uses them constantly. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A pointer is a typed machine address — the type gives `+1` its meaning and keeps arithmetic honest. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A pointer is a typed machine address — the type gives `+1` its meaning and keeps arithmetic honest.
Arrays and pointers are how C interfaces express 'here is a run of objects', so library code uses them constantly.
References are aliases that bind once; they are the high-level face of the same memory model.

quiz.q: A pointer is best described as:
options: a typed handle holding the address of an object
an index into the code segment
quiz.explanation: Address plus type: the address locates the object, the type gives the operations on the pointer their meaning.

quiz.q: Why study pointers if `vector` and `string` exist?
options: containers, ABI boundaries and C libraries exchange raw addresses — you must read that code
the standard library is written without them
quiz.explanation: The containers are *built* from this chapter's machinery, and external interfaces speak it — literacy is not optional.

quiz.q: The three mechanisms of this chapter are:
options: pointers, pointers into arrays, and references
quiz.explanation: Those are the book's own three subsection topics — plus the const and ownership questions that cut across them.

intro: The pointer operations are two unary operators: `&` takes the address of an object, `*` accesses the object a pointer points to. Add the null pointer `nullptr` — the only pointer value that points to no object — and `void*`, the type that holds any object pointer but promises nothing, and you have the complete basic kit. The dangers are equally basic: a null or dangling pointer dereferenced is undefined behavior.
objectives: Use `&` (address-of) and `*` (dereference) correctly
Explain why `nullptr` replaced `0` and `NULL`, and what null checks catch
State what a `void*` can and cannot be used for

concepts.statement: **Unary `&` takes the address of an object; unary `*` dereferences a pointer — accesses the object it points to.** `char c = 'a'; char* p = &c;` makes `p` point at `c`; `*p = 'b';` assigns through `p`, changing `c`.
concepts.detail: Read `char* p` as 'p is a pointer to char' — the declaration mirrors the use: `*p` has type `char`.

concepts.statement: **`nullptr` is the null pointer literal — the value of a pointer that points to no object.** It converts to any pointer type but is not an integer, unlike `0`, and unlike macro `NULL` it cannot collide with an overload taking an `int`.
concepts.detail: Test explicitly: `if (p == nullptr) return;` — and treat the implicit `if (p)` as sugar for exactly that. Dereferencing `nullptr` is undefined behavior.

concepts.statement: **A `void*` holds a pointer to any object type, and in exchange for that generality permits nothing: no dereference, no arithmetic, no type information.** Its legitimate uses are narrow — C library interfaces (`memcpy`, `qsort`) and the lowest level of memory management.
concepts.detail: To use the object you must first cast the `void*` back to a typed pointer — a cast you should be able to justify, because it is where type safety is suspended.

concepts.statement: **`p == q` asks one address question: do these two pointers designate the same object?** Ordering comparisons and subtraction are only meaningful for pointers into the same array — the library's `begin`/`end` machinery relies on exactly that contract.
concepts.detail: Comparing pointers to unrelated objects for order is unspecified; the equality comparison is the only universally safe one.

concepts.statement: **Pointers.** Null, dereferencing and pointer arithmetic. You can claim this section when you can use `&` (address-of) and `*` (dereference) correctly — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 7 (Pointers, Arrays, and References); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: A pointer walk, step by step
examples.problem: `char c = 'a'; char* p = &c; *p = 'b';` — what does each line do to memory?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: `char c = 'a';` places a byte holding 97 (the code for 'a') at some address — say 0x7ffc40.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: `char* p = &c;` stores the value 0x7ffc40 in `p` — a pointer-sized object elsewhere holding c's address.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: `*p = 'b';` writes 98 through the address in `p` — c itself changes; `p` does not move.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: `p = nullptr;` is now legal — `p` points to nothing, and `*p` on the next line would be undefined behavior.

examples.result: After three lines, `c` holds 'b', `p` holds nullptr — the pointer and the object it once addressed are fully decoupled.

examples.title: Working through pointers
examples.problem: Null, dereferencing and pointer arithmetic. Your task: use `&` (address-of) and `*` (dereference) correctly.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: use `&` (address-of) and `*` (dereference) correctly. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `&` yields an address, `*` uses it; the declaration `T* p` mirrors the use `*p`.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}; int* p = a; int& r = a[0];` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain why `nullptr` replaced `0` and `NULL`, and what null checks catch — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: `nullptr` is the null pointer of choice — an explicit test before dereference is the only null check that exists. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `&` yields an address, `*` uses it; the declaration `T* p` mirrors the use `*p`. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `&` yields an address, `*` uses it; the declaration `T* p` mirrors the use `*p`.
`nullptr` is the null pointer of choice — an explicit test before dereference is the only null check that exists.
`void*` erases the type: no dereference, no arithmetic — a C-interface tool, not an application-programming one.

quiz.q: Given `int x = 3; int* p = &x;`, what is `*p`?
quiz.explanation: `p` holds x's address; `*p` follows it and yields the object — the `int` 3.

quiz.q: Why prefer `nullptr` to `0` or `NULL`?
options: 0 is not a valid null pointer value
it has pointer type — no silent integer conversions or overload surprises
quiz.explanation: The literal `0` is an `int` that converts; `nullptr` is a first-class null pointer of its own type, so overloads and templates see it for what it is.

quiz.q: Which operation on a `void*` is legal?
options: passing it to a C library function that takes `void*`
quiz.explanation: Without an element type there is nothing to dereference and no element size to step by — the legal uses are storing and passing it.

options: The behavior is undefined, because the evaluation order is unspecified
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The code given dereferences a pointer with postfix increment and then measures how far the pointer moved. Step 2: The governing rule is precedence: postfix `++` binds tighter than unary `*`, so `*p++` means `*(p++)`, reading through the original pointer and advancing it afterward as one sequenced operation. Step 3: Tracing expression by expression, the stream receives the value `5` through the unmoved pointer, then `p` advances by one element, so the pointer difference is `1`. Step 4: The distractors fail because `6` would need the pointed-to value incremented, `0` would need the pointer frozen, and the single modification is sequenced rather than unsequenced. Step 5: Therefore the program prints `5 1`.

intro: Arrays are the oldest container: a fixed number of elements of one type, laid out contiguously and indexed from zero. Their fatal subtlety is that an array cannot be copied and, when passed to a function, silently becomes a pointer to its first element — the famous decay. Every C string, every buffer, every `main(int argc, char* argv[])` lives inside this rule, and most C/C++ interface bugs trace back to it.
objectives: Declare arrays and index them, with the zero-based convention
Explain array decay and the loss of the element count
Handle C-style strings: the zero terminator and its arithmetic

concepts.statement: **`T a[n]` declares an array of n elements of type T, stored contiguously and indexed `a[0]` through `a[n-1]`.** The size is part of the type and must be a constant expression; the elements are the objects themselves, not pointers to them.
concepts.detail: `char v[6];` reserves six consecutive `char`s; `int a[3] = {1, 2, 3};` initializes them. Out-of-range indexing is undefined behavior — the array carries no bounds of its own.

concepts.statement: **An array of `T` converts to a pointer to its first element: `int arr[10]; int* p = arr;` makes `p` hold `&arr[0]`.** In a parameter list `void f(int arr[])` means `void f(int* arr)` — the brackets are decoration, and the element count is *not* passed.
concepts.detail: This is C compatibility: arrays cannot be passed by value, so the language hands the callee an address instead. The callee must learn the size some other way — a count parameter, a terminator, or `begin`/`end` iterators.

concepts.statement: **A C string is an array of characters terminated by the zero character `\0`.** The literal `"Hello"` is an array of 6 `char`s — five letters plus the terminator — and can be assigned to a `const char*`.
concepts.detail: `strlen("Hello")` is 5 — it counts up to (not including) the terminator, and its cost is O(n) each call, because the length is not stored anywhere.

concepts.statement: **Arrays cannot be copied or assigned with `=`; initialization is the only aggregate operation you get.** Copying is done element-wise in a loop, by `memcpy` — or by using `vector`, which copies itself correctly.
concepts.detail: `auto a2 = a;` does not copy the array — it decays and copies a *pointer*. This single fact is the strongest argument for `std::array` and `vector`.

concepts.statement: **Arrays.** Arrays, strings and the decay problem. You can claim this section when you can declare arrays and index them, with the zero-based convention — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 7 (Pointers, Arrays, and References); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: The sizeof trap
examples.problem: Inside `void f(char arr[])` the code computes `sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0])` to learn the length. With `char buf[] = "Hello";` passed in, what happens?

steps.label: Step 1: At the definition
steps.text: `char buf[] = "Hello";` — `sizeof(buf)` is 6 (five letters plus `\0`), and `strlen(buf)` is 5. Here the idiom would report 6.

steps.label: Step 2: After decay
steps.text: Inside `f`, `arr` is a `char*` — `sizeof(arr)` is the pointer's size, 8 on a 64-bit machine, not 6.

steps.label: Step 3: The broken division
steps.text: `sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0])` computes $8 / 1 = 8$ — the 'length' is a pointer size divided by a char size.

steps.label: Step 4: Why it compiles
steps.text: The types are all consistent — `size_t / size_t` — so nothing warns. The bug is semantic: the array's size never made it into the function.

examples.result: The idiom reports 8 for a 6-byte array: it works only in the scope where the array is complete. The fix is to pass the size, or use `string`/`span`.

examples.title: Working through arrays
examples.problem: Arrays, strings and the decay problem. Your task: declare arrays and index them, with the zero-based convention.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: declare arrays and index them, with the zero-based convention. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Arrays are fixed-size, contiguous and zero-based; the bounds live in the type, not in the object.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}; int* p = a; int& r = a[0];` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain array decay and the loss of the element count — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Decay: `T a[n]` becomes `T*` at every function boundary — the element count must travel separately. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

keyTakeaways: Arrays are fixed-size, contiguous and zero-based; the bounds live in the type, not in the object.
Decay: `T a[n]` becomes `T*` at every function boundary — the element count must travel separately.
C strings end in `\0`: `sizeof("Hello")` is 6 while `strlen("Hello")` is 5.

quiz.q: For `char v[] = "Hello";` — `sizeof(v)` and `strlen(v)` are:
quiz.explanation: The array holds five letters plus the terminator (6 bytes); `strlen` counts characters before the terminator (5).

quiz.q: Inside `void f(char arr[])`, `sizeof(arr)` is:
options: the size of a pointer — the argument decayed
quiz.explanation: The parameter is really a `char*`; the sizeof operator sees the pointer, not the array it came from.

quiz.q: Why do arrays decay when passed to functions?
options: C compatibility: arrays cannot be passed by value, so a pointer to the first element is passed instead
to save memory in the callee
quiz.explanation: The rule is inherited from C — the callee receives an address, and the size information does not come with it.

quiz.q: The root problem with the decayed parameter is:
options: the element count is lost — the callee cannot learn the array's length from it
quiz.explanation: Everything else is recoverable; the missing length is why C interfaces also pass counts (or rely on a terminator).

intro: Pointers come into their own navigating arrays: `p+1` is the next element, `p[i]` is defined as `*(p+i)`, and a pointer may legally be computed to one position past the last element — the exclusive end that the whole standard library's half-open ranges are built on. This section makes pointer arithmetic exact, because exactness here is the difference between a correct loop and undefined behavior.
objectives: Compute pointer arithmetic in elements, and convert to bytes
Explain the one-past-the-end rule and half-open ranges
Read the `count_x` idiom that walks a C string by pointer

concepts.statement: **For `T* p` pointing into an array, `p+n` is the address n *elements* further on — n × `sizeof(T)` bytes.** Subscripting is defined on top of it: `p[i]` means `*(p+i)`, and because arrays decay, `a[i]` for an array is the same `*(a+i)`.
concepts.detail: Only `+`, `-`, and comparisons within the same array are defined — a pointer that leaves the array by more than one-past-the-end, or is dereferenced there, is undefined.

concepts.statement: **Computing the address of the position one past the last element is legal; dereferencing it is not.** `end(v)` is exactly that address, and the convention `for (p = begin(v); p != end(v); ++p)` — a half-open range `[begin, end)` — needs nothing further.
concepts.detail: Why exclusive end: the empty range is `begin == end` (no special case), the length is `end - begin` (one subtraction), and the loop test is `!=` against a computable value.

concepts.statement: **`begin(a)` and `end(a)` return the first element's address and the one-past-the-end address for arrays and containers alike.** They are the bridge that lets the same loop and the same standard algorithms work over both.
concepts.detail: Since `end(a)` is one-past-the-end, it must never be dereferenced — but comparing against it, and subtracting it from `begin(a)`, are exactly what it exists for.

concepts.statement: **Two pointers into the same array subtract to the number of elements between them** (type `ptrdiff_t`), not bytes: with `q = v+4` and `p = v+1`, `q - p` is 3.
concepts.detail: This is the array's length computation — `end(v) - begin(v)` — and the index recovery in searches: `found - v` is the position of `*found`.

concepts.statement: **`while (*p) { if (*p == x) ++count; ++p; }` walks a C string by pointer:** the terminator `\0` is the false value that stops the loop, and `p` advances one character per iteration.
concepts.detail: The null check at the top (`if (p == nullptr) return 0;`) guards the 'points to nothing' case — the same explicit contract every C interface documents.

examples.title: Counting characters by pointer
examples.problem: Trace `count_x("algorithm analysis", 'a')` — the function that walks a C string counting occurrences of a character.

steps.label: Step 1: The string as an array
steps.text: "algorithm analysis" is 18 characters plus the `\0` terminator at index 18 — 19 bytes in all.

steps.label: Step 2: The walk
steps.text: `p` starts at index 0; each iteration compares `*p` with 'a' then `++p` — the loop stops when `*p` is the terminator, whose value 0 is false.

steps.label: Step 3: The hits
steps.text: 'a' occurs at indices 0, 10 and 12 — a-l-g-o-r-i-t-h-m, space, a-n-a-l-y-s-i-s.

steps.label: Step 4: The arithmetic
steps.text: 18 iterations of `++p` (one byte per step for `char`), 3 increments of `count`, 1 final test against the terminator.

examples.result: count_x returns 3 — with every pointer step and every comparison accountably in the trace.

examples.title: Working through pointers into arrays
examples.problem: Navigating arrays with pointers. Your task: compute pointer arithmetic in elements, and convert to bytes.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: compute pointer arithmetic in elements, and convert to bytes. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `p + n` advances n elements (n × `sizeof(T)` bytes); `p[i]` is `*(p+i)` by definition.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}; int* p = a; int& r = a[0];` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain the one-past-the-end rule and half-open ranges — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: One-past-the-end may be computed but never dereferenced; half-open `[begin, end)` ranges are built on it. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `p + n` advances n elements (n × `sizeof(T)` bytes); `p[i]` is `*(p+i)` by definition. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `p + n` advances n elements (n × `sizeof(T)` bytes); `p[i]` is `*(p+i)` by definition.
One-past-the-end may be computed but never dereferenced; half-open `[begin, end)` ranges are built on it.
Pointer subtraction yields an element count — `end(v) - begin(v)` is the length.

quiz.q: With `int* p = v+1` in an int array, `p+2` points to:
quiz.explanation: Addition is in elements: `v+1` advanced one, `+2` two more — `v[3]`, eight bytes on from `v[1]` when ints are 4 bytes.

quiz.q: Which operation is legal (not undefined behavior)?
options: subtracting pointers into two different arrays
ordering two pointers to unrelated objects with `<`
quiz.explanation: The one-past-the-end address exists to be computed and compared; the other three are the classic undefined operations of pointer code.

quiz.q: With `q = v+4` and `p = v+1`, `q - p` is:
quiz.explanation: Subtraction yields the number of elements between the pointers — 3 — independent of `sizeof(T)`.

quiz.q: `p[i]` means:
options: `*(p + i)` — subscripting is defined as pointer arithmetic and a dereference
a copy of the i-th pointer
quiz.explanation: That definition is why subscripts and pointer walks are interchangeable, and why both carry the same out-of-range hazards.

intro: A pointer to a constant promises not to write through the pointer; a constant pointer promises not to change what it points at; a constant pointer to a constant promises both. Const-correctness is a contract system — the declarations document who may modify what — and its reading skill, taught in this section, is decoding the four combinations without hesitation.
objectives: Distinguish `const char*`, `char* const` and `const char* const`
Decode declarations with the read-right-to-left method
Use `const` as an interface contract, not an optimization

concepts.statement: **`const char* p` — p points to a character you promise not to modify through p.** The pointer itself may be re-seated; the pointee may not be written through this name. This is the type of every C string literal.
concepts.detail: `const char* p = "Hello";` compiles; `p[0] = 'h';` does not — the promise is checked by the compiler.

concepts.statement: **`char* const p` — p is a pointer that cannot be re-seated, but the object it addresses may be written through it.** Initialization is the only assignment to p that will ever happen.
concepts.detail: Combine them: `const char* const p` is a fixed pointer to an unmodifiable object — maximal restriction, useful for lookup tables addressed by fixed handles.

concepts.statement: **Decode from the name outward: `const char* const p` reads 'p is a const pointer to a const char'.** Whatever is left of the `*` describes the pointee; whatever is right of it describes the pointer itself.
concepts.detail: The `T const` spelling is equivalent to `const T` — `char const* p` is the same type as `const char* p` — which is why consistency of spelling matters in a codebase.

concepts.statement: **A `const` declaration is an interface promise — 'this code will not modify what this name designates' — that the compiler enforces and every caller can trust.** It also licenses optimization: data known immutable can be shared, cached and folded.
concepts.detail: For compile-time constants use `constexpr`; `const` on a pointer or reference parameter is about the access contract, evaluated at the interface.

concepts.term: Pointers and const: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Pointers and const.** Const-correct pointer types. You can claim this section when you can distinguish `const char*`, `char* const` and `const char* const` — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 7 (Pointers, Arrays, and References); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Classifying four declarations
examples.problem: With `char s[] = "string";` in scope, classify `char* p1 = s;`, `const char* p2 = s;`, `char* const p3 = s;`, `const char* const p4 = s;` — what may change?

steps.label: Step 1: `char* p1`
steps.text: Unrestricted: `p1 = t;` re-seats it, `*p1 = 'c';` writes through it. Both legal, both unchecked.

steps.label: Step 2: `const char* p2`
steps.text: Pointee protected: `p2 = t;` is legal, `*p2 = 'c';` is a compile-time error.

steps.label: Step 3: `char* const p3`
steps.text: Pointer protected: `p3 = t;` is an error, `*p3 = 'c';` is legal — exactly the mirror image of p2.

steps.label: Step 4: `const char* const p4`
steps.text: Both protected: neither assignment compiles; p4 is a fixed window onto an unmodifiable object.

examples.result: Four declarations, two independent restrictions — writing through the pointer and re-seating the pointer — and each declaration is the truth table of those two bits.

Read declarations right to left — everything left of the `*` is about the pointee, everything right is about the pointer.
`const` in a parameter type is a caller-visible contract, checked by the compiler.

quiz.q: `const char* p` means:
options: you cannot write through p to the character, but p can be re-seated
the pointed-to character can never change by any means
quiz.explanation: The restriction is on access through p — other writable paths to the same object may exist; the pointer itself is freely assignable.

quiz.q: Which declaration is a const pointer to a *modifiable* char?
quiz.explanation: The `const` after the `*` binds to the pointer. Note that `char const* p` is just another spelling of the *first* option — pointee protected.

quiz.q: Reading `const char* const p` right to left gives:
options: p is a const pointer to a const char
p is a pointer to a const char that is const
p is const only within its scope
quiz.explanation: Start at the name: p, a const (pointer), to a const (char). Both restrictions are in force.

intro: A raw pointer says where something is — and nothing about whose it is. That silence is the root of leaks, double deletes and dangling pointers: every one of those bugs is an ownership question the type failed to record. This section makes ownership explicit: `unique_ptr` and `shared_ptr` for owning, raw pointers and references only for borrowing, and the dangling-pointer patterns to recognize on sight.
objectives: State the ownership ambiguity of raw pointers and its consequences
Classify pointers as owning or borrowing, and repair each with the right type
Recognize the dangling-pointer bug patterns

concepts.statement: **A raw `T*` records an address but no responsibility: who, if anyone, must delete the object, and when?** The language cannot answer from the type — so in code that relies on convention, the answer lives in comments and folklore, which is to say nowhere.
concepts.detail: The book's framing: when in doubt, make ownership explicit in the type system — an owning smart pointer where there is an owner, a plain non-owning pointer where there is only a view.

concepts.statement: **Express ownership with `unique_ptr` (exactly one owner) or `shared_ptr` (shared, counted ownership); express mere access with a raw pointer or a reference.** The types then answer the delete question mechanically, by destructor.
concepts.detail: The Guideline Support Library adds `owner<T*>` — an annotation marking a raw pointer that does own, for code that cannot yet switch to smart pointers; it documents what the compiler is not yet told.

concepts.statement: **A dangling pointer holds the address of an object that no longer exists.** The classic sources: returning the address of a local, storing a pointer into a container that then reallocates, and deleting an object while aliases to it remain.
concepts.detail: `int* f() { int x = 2; return &x; }` returns the address of a stack slot that dies at the `return` — dereferencing it is undefined behavior, however plausible the value looks.

concepts.statement: **Return by value instead of by pointer; index containers rather than holding element addresses across growth; let `unique_ptr` be the single delete site.** Each fix removes a class of dangles rather than a single instance.
concepts.detail: A `vector` may copy its elements when it grows — addresses into it are loans valid only until the next modifying operation, the lesson behind every iterator-invalidation bug report.

concepts.term: Pointers and Ownership: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Pointers and Ownership.** Who owns what a pointer points to. You can claim this section when you can state the ownership ambiguity of raw pointers and its consequences — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 7 (Pointers, Arrays, and References); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: An ownership audit
examples.problem: Classify every pointer in `Widget* make() { return new Widget; }`, `void use(Widget* w) { render(*w); }`, `int* bad() { int x = 2; return &x; }`, and repair the code.

steps.label: Step 1: make
steps.text: Returns an owner — the caller must delete. Repair: `unique_ptr<Widget> make() { return unique_ptr<Widget>{new Widget}; }` — ownership now travels in the type.

steps.label: Step 2: use
steps.text: Borrows for a call — no delete expected, correct as a raw pointer (or better, a reference, since null is meaningless here).

steps.label: Step 3: bad
steps.text: Returns the address of a dead local — a dangling pointer by construction. Repair: `int bad_fixed() { int x = 2; return x; }` — return the value.

steps.label: Step 4: The audit result
steps.text: One owner expressed, one borrower expressed, one dangle destroyed — three lines, three different ownership facts, each now visible in the signature.

examples.result: The repaired signatures answer the delete question without reading a single function body — which is the entire point of ownership in types.

keyTakeaways: A raw pointer carries an address but no ownership — leaks, double deletes and dangles all stem from that silence.
Own with `unique_ptr`/`shared_ptr`; borrow with raw pointers and references; annotate unconverted owners with `owner<T*>`.
Dangling patterns: address-of-local returned, pointer into a growing container, aliases kept across a delete.

quiz.q: A raw `T*` by itself tells you:
options: nothing about ownership — the central ambiguity of raw pointers
quiz.explanation: Address only. Ownership must come from convention or — better — from the smart-pointer types that encode it.

quiz.q: The bug in `int* f() { int x = 2; return &x; }` is:
options: the returned address outlives the object — x dies at the return
`&x` is a reference, not a pointer
quiz.explanation: The stack slot for x is released at the return; the caller receives a dangling pointer, and using it is undefined behavior.

quiz.q: The book's systematic fix for ownership ambiguity is to:
options: express ownership in types: `unique_ptr`/`shared_ptr` for owners, raw pointers only for borrowing
quiz.explanation: Types are checked; comments are not. The ownership facts move from prose to the signature.

quiz.q: `gsl::owner<T*>` is:
options: a documentation annotation — a raw pointer that owns, for code not yet on smart pointers
quiz.explanation: It marks owning raw pointers so tools (and humans) can see the delete obligation until real smart-pointer types take over.

intro: A reference is another name for an object — `T&` for an lvalue, `T&&` for an rvalue — bound at initialization and never re-seated. References give C++ its natural output parameters and its move machinery in one mechanism: the alias is the object, with no null state, no re-seating, and none of the pointer's syntax tax.
objectives: Define lvalue and rvalue references and their binding rules
Explain why `const T&` binds to temporaries and what that buys
Choose between pointer and reference for parameters, and price the copy

concepts.statement: **`T& r = x;` makes r a second name for x — every use of r is a use of x.** It must be initialized, it can never refer to a different object, and a null reference cannot exist by construction (a dereferenced null pointer is UB *before* it becomes a reference).
concepts.detail: `void increment(int& a) { ++a; }` modifies the caller's object through the alias — the output-parameter idiom, no address-of syntax at the call site.

concepts.statement: **Use a reference when the object always exists and never changes identity; use a pointer when 'no object' or 'another object' are meaningful states.** The re-seating rule is the design hinge: a reference's target is fixed for its life.
concepts.detail: `void f(Record& r)` promises an object; `void g(Record* p)` admits `nullptr` and must be checked. Readers of the first signature start ahead.

concepts.statement: **`const T&` accepts lvalues and rvalues alike, and binds a temporary for the duration of the reference's lifetime.** That is the idiom behind efficient read-only parameters: no copy, no null check, no lifetime hole.
concepts.detail: `const string& s = f();` — the returned temporary lives as long as `s`. The non-const `T&` refuses to bind to an rvalue, which is exactly the error the previous chapter classified.

concepts.statement: **`T&&` binds to rvalues — temporaries whose resources may be harvested instead of copied.** A move constructor takes `T&&`, swaps internals with the expiring source, and leaves it valid but empty; the copy stays untouched.
concepts.detail: `string s2 = move(s1);` — s1 is reclassified as an rvalue, so the move constructor is chosen: its buffer transfers rather than duplicating.

concepts.statement: **`move(x)` does not move — it returns an rvalue reference, a license the receiver may or may not use.** The move itself happens in the chosen constructor or assignment; if no move overload exists, a copy happens and `x` is untouched.
concepts.detail: After a genuine move, the source remains a valid object with unspecified content — destroy it or assign to it, but do not read it.

examples.title: Pricing the pass
examples.problem: A function needs to inspect a `vector<int>` holding 1,000,000 elements. Compare passing by value, by `const&`, and by pointer.

steps.label: Step 1: By value
steps.text: The copy is $10^6$ ints × 4 bytes = 4 MB of allocation and copying — around a millisecond of memory traffic, per call.

steps.label: Step 2: By `const vector<int>&`
steps.text: The reference passes a pointer-sized handle — 8 bytes on a 64-bit machine — no matter the vector's size.

steps.label: Step 3: By pointer
steps.text: The same 8 bytes, plus a null-check obligation and `->` syntax at every use, since 'no vector' is now expressible.

steps.label: Step 4: Decide
steps.text: The function always has a vector to inspect — the reference expresses exactly that, and the 4 MB → 8 B reduction is the design argument, not an optimization footnote.

examples.result: Same observable behavior, a 500,000-fold reduction in bytes copied — and the signature tells the caller which of the three regimes it is entering.

examples.title: Working through references
examples.problem: Lvalue and rvalue references. Your task: define lvalue and rvalue references and their binding rules.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define lvalue and rvalue references and their binding rules. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `T&` is a never-null, never-re-seated alias — the output-parameter type; `const T&` additionally binds temporaries, the read-parameter type.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}; int* p = a; int& r = a[0];` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
