while alternative
steps.text: With `while`, `choice` would have to be primed with a fake non-zero value before the loop so the first test passes — an extra initialization whose only purpose is to satisfy the loop, and a lie about the program state.

steps.label: Cost of misuse
steps.text: Used where the body might legitimately need to run zero times (e.g. empty input), do executes the body once anyway — so the pattern is *first pass guaranteed* or nothing.

examples.result: do-while states the at-least-once contract directly; any while version has to smuggle it in through a primed variable.

keyTakeaways: Match the loop to the shape of the problem: range-for for whole containers, classic for for counted or indexed iteration, while for data-driven top-tested exits, do only when the first pass is guaranteed.
The loop variable of a for-init declaration is scoped to the loop; conditions may also be declarations, keeping tested values out of the surrounding scope.
`break` and `continue` are single-level exits; deep nests need a flag per level, restructuring, or — as a last resort — the goto of 9.6.

quiz.q: To read (without modifying) elements of a large `vector<string> v`, the idiomatic loop head is:
quiz.explanation: `const string&` binds each element without copying it and promises not to modify it — value copies a string per element and a non-const reference needlessly claims write access (and blocks binding temporaries).

quiz.q: A do-statement executes its body:
options: zero or more times, testing the condition first
at least once, because the test comes after the body
quiz.explanation: do-while tests after the body: the first pass always runs even if the condition is false initially — the one property distinguishing it from while.

quiz.q: `continue` inside a `for` loop causes:
options: the next iteration to begin — after running the loop's step expression
the condition to be skipped on the next test
a jump to the enclosing function
quiz.explanation: continue abandons the rest of this pass only; the for's step (e.g. `++i`) still runs before the next condition test — unlike in a while, where continue jumps straight to the test.

quiz.q: Which loop form most directly expresses *keep reading input while it keeps arriving*?
options: a classic for with a counter
quiz.explanation: The exit condition comes from the data, not a counter, and must be tested before the first pass — the while with a stream condition is the textbook idiom.

intro: goto is the assembly-language control flow that survived into C, and C++ keeps it for one reason: some low-level control problems are genuinely clearer with it. The discipline is strict — jump only to a nearby label in the same function, never into a block, and only for the two sanctioned patterns: escaping a deeply nested loop, and jumping backwards to retry an operation.
objectives: State what goto does and the scope rules of labels
Explain the initialization rule that limits where goto may jump
Identify the two disciplined uses and the structured alternatives

concepts.statement: **`goto label;`** transfers control unconditionally to the statement marked **`label:`**. Labels have function scope: a `goto` can only reach a label in the **same function**, forwards or backwards.
concepts.detail: The label syntax is `identifier : statement` — which is exactly why the empty statement earns its keep: before a block's closing brace, a label needs *something* to attach to, and `;` is that something.

concepts.statement: A `goto` may **not jump into a block past the initialization of a variable** — the compiler rejects it, because the variable would come into existence without its initializer having run. Jumping *out* of blocks, freely ending their scopes, is always allowed.
concepts.detail: This is the language defending its own invariant: no object exists whose initialization was bypassed. The same rule protects `switch` jumps — which is why a declaration with an initializer inside a case must be wrapped in its own `{ }` block.

concepts.statement: The sanctioned patterns are narrow: **(1)** a single exit out of a deeply nested loop nest, jumping forward to a label just past the nest; **(2)** a backward jump that *retries* an operation until it succeeds. Anything else — long-distance jumps, jumps between logically unrelated code — is better expressed by restructuring with loops, flags, or functions.
concepts.detail: Note the asymmetry: the sanctioned gotos are local, visible on one screen, and jump to a label that names the intent (`done:`, `retry:`). A goto you have to scroll to understand is already a bug.

concepts.statement: **goto Statements.** goto and its disciplined use. You can claim this section when you can state what goto does and the scope rules of labels — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 9 (Statements); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

concepts.statement: Work in three passes. First, explain the initialization rule that limits where goto may jump. Then, identify the two disciplined uses and the structured alternatives. Finally, test the outcome against the section promise: goto jumps to a label in the same function, forward or backward; labels have function scope only.
concepts.detail: Each pass catches a different class of mistake, and skipping one moves the failure into a larger program where it costs more to diagnose than it would have here.

examples.title: Escaping a nested search
examples.problem: Find the position of `key` in a 2-D array `a[rows][cols]` and stop the moment it is found — with goto and with a flag.

steps.label: With goto
With a flag
The structured winner
steps.text: Wrap the search in a function and `return` the result — the multi-level exit becomes an ordinary return, with no label, no flag and no extra tests: `return make_pair(i, j);` on the spot.

steps.label: Judgment
steps.text: Inside one function, goto is arguably clearest for this shape; once the nest grows or the code is reusable, the function-with-return version wins — which is why advice says *a function is the best structured break*.

examples.result: goto exits the nest in one jump; the flag version is correct but noisier; the extract-a-function version removes the problem the goto was solving.

examples.title: Working through goto statements
examples.problem: goto and its disciplined use. Your task: state what goto does and the scope rules of labels.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: state what goto does and the scope rules of labels. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: goto jumps to a label in the same function, forward or backward; labels have function scope only.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { sum += i; }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain the initialization rule that limits where goto may jump — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: The compiler forbids jumping into a block past an initialization — objects must never exist uninitialized — but jumping out of scopes is unrestricted. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: goto jumps to a label in the same function, forward or backward; labels have function scope only. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: goto jumps to a label in the same function, forward or backward; labels have function scope only.
The compiler forbids jumping into a block past an initialization — objects must never exist uninitialized — but jumping out of scopes is unrestricted.
The two disciplined uses are the forward multi-level loop exit and the backward retry; both keep label and jump within one screen, and both have structured alternatives worth considering first.

quiz.q: Which can a `goto` NOT do?
options: jump out of nested loops to a later label
jump backwards to retry an operation
jump to a label later in the same function
quiz.explanation: Labels have function scope — goto cannot cross function boundaries; that is what function calls and returns are for.

quiz.q: Why does the compiler reject `goto` into a block past `int x = compute();`?
options: goto may only target empty statements
the variable would exist without its initialization having run
quiz.explanation: The initialization rule: control may never bypass an initializer, so that every object in scope has been constructed — the same invariant that protects switch cases.

quiz.q: The chapter's two sanctioned goto patterns are:
options: escaping a nested loop nest, and a backward retry jump
quiz.explanation: Local, intent-named, single-screen jumps for multi-level exit and retry — everything else is better restructured with loops, flags or functions.

intro: Comments and layout are the parts of a program that the compiler throws away and the humans live on. Stroustrup's treatment is short and firm: comments should state intent and rationale, not echo the code; an inaccurate comment is worse than none; and indentation must mirror control structure so that the reader's eye can verify what the compiler enforces invisibly.
objectives: Use the two comment forms and know their limits (no nesting for block comments)
Write comments that state intent, and keep them accurate as code changes
Apply a layout discipline that makes control structure visible

concepts.statement: A `//` comment runs to the end of the line. A `/* ... */` comment may span several lines — but **does not nest**: the first `*/` ends it, so commenting out a block that already contains a block comment breaks.
concepts.detail: To disable code containing `/* */` comments, use `#if 0 ... #endif` (conditional compilation, Chapter 12) rather than wrapping it in another block comment that cannot nest.

concepts.statement: A good comment records what the code **cannot express about itself**: the purpose of a function, class or data structure, the units of a value, the reason an odd-looking expression is correct, and the invariant a loop maintains. `i = i + 1; // add 1 to i` is noise; `// one more failed login: lock the account after 3` is information.
concepts.detail: The test to apply: would a competent reader of C++ who cannot see the surrounding design still misread this code without the comment? If not, delete the comment.

concepts.statement: **A comment that disagrees with the code is worse than no comment**: readers trust prose more than they trust parsing, so a stale comment actively misleads. Whenever code changes, its comments change in the same edit.
concepts.detail: This is the practical reason for commenting *why* rather than *what*: the *what* is duplicated by the code and rots first when the code is tuned; the *why* survives.

concepts.statement: Layout is for humans: indent one level per nested block so the visible structure mirrors the control structure, brace consistently, and let a formatting tool apply the rules mechanically. The compiler ignores every space — the debugger at 3 a.m. does not.
concepts.detail: The classic demonstration is the misleadingly indented dangling-else fragment of 9.4: it compiles, runs, and lies. Consistent layout is the cheapest code review you will ever get.

concepts.term: Comments and Indentation: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Comments and Indentation.** Code that people can read. You can claim this section when you can use the two comment forms and know their limits (no nesting for block comments) — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 9 (Statements); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Rewriting a commented function
examples.problem: This function compiles and works. Improve its comments and layout without touching its behavior.

steps.label: Before
steps.text:
```
// this function takes n and returns the factorial
int f2(int n) {
    int r = 1; // r is the result
    int i; // loop variable
    for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) { // loop from 1 to n
        r = r * i; } // multiply r by i
    return r; } // return r
``` — every comment restates syntax the reader already knows.

steps.label: What the code cannot say
steps.text: The missing information: what *for*? Is overflow a risk? Why multiply and not `std::factorial`-style accumulation? The design intent is absent precisely where the noise is loudest.

steps.label: After
Verification
steps.text: Behavior is identical for every input: the loop `1..n` versus `2..n` both leave `r == n!` because multiplying by 1 is the identity. The overflow bound is real: $12! = 479{,}001{,}600$ fits a 32-bit int, $13! = 6{,}227{,}020{,}800$ does not.

examples.result: Fewer comments, more information: the contract (valid range, overflow bound) and the loop invariant replace six lines of syntax-echo.

examples.title: Working through comments and indentation
examples.problem: Code that people can read. Your task: use the two comment forms and know their limits (no nesting for block comments).

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: use the two comment forms and know their limits (no nesting for block comments). Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `//` runs to end of line; `/* */` spans lines but does not nest — use `#if 0` to disable code containing block comments.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { sum += i; }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — write comments that state intent, and keep them accurate as code changes — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Comment intent, units, invariants and rationale — the things code cannot express; a comment that restates the code is noise that rots into lies. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `//` runs to end of line; `/* */` spans lines but does not nest — use `#if 0` to disable code containing block comments. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `//` runs to end of line; `/* */` spans lines but does not nest — use `#if 0` to disable code containing block comments.
Comment intent, units, invariants and rationale — the things code cannot express; a comment that restates the code is noise that rots into lies.
Indent so the visible structure matches the control structure and let tools enforce it, because layout is the reader's map of the program.

quiz.q: What happens when a `/* ... */` comment contains another `/* ... */` inside it?
options: the compiler reports a nesting error
the inner `/*` is ordinary text; the comment ends at the *first* `*/`
the outer comment extends to the next matching pair
quiz.explanation: Block comments do not nest — the first `*/` closes the comment, so the code after it is live again. This is why #if 0 is the safe way to disable code.

quiz.q: Which comment is the best by the chapter's standard?
options: `// tax is stored in basis points (1/100 of a percent)`
`// this line was changed on Tuesday`
quiz.explanation: It states the units of the data — a fact about the design that the code cannot express and that a reader genuinely needs.

quiz.q: A stale comment that contradicts the current code is:
options: harmless, since the code is what executes
worse than no comment, because readers trust prose and get misled
quiz.explanation: The book's rule: keep comments accurate; a wrong comment actively misleads during maintenance, which is exactly when comments get read.

intro: The chapter closes with its advice list — the distilled rules the preceding sections argued for. They read as common sense only after the arguments: declare late and initialized, match the statement form to the problem's shape, keep selection and loops visible with braces and honest layout, and treat goto as a local, rare, named-intent tool.
objectives: Apply the chapter's rules on declaration placement and initialization
Choose the statement form that makes each control-flow shape most readable
Recognize the discipline that keeps braces, layout and goto honest

concepts.statement: **Don't declare a variable until you have a value to initialize it with** — and then declare it there, in the smallest scope that covers its use. This single habit eliminates uninitialized reads, shrinks the set of live names a reader must track, and lets the optimizer see lifetimes.
concepts.detail: The corollaries: declare loop variables in the for-init, use declarations in conditions when the value is immediately tested, and confine scratch work to explicit blocks.

concepts.term: Match the statement to the shape
concepts.statement: Choose the construct that says *why* you are looping or branching: **range-for** for whole containers, **for** for counted or indexed iteration, **while** for top-tested data-driven exits, **do** only when the first pass is guaranteed, **switch** for selection among enumerated constants, and **if/else** chains otherwise.
concepts.detail: The reader should be able to name the loop's purpose from its head alone — if the head and the purpose disagree, you picked the wrong form.

concepts.statement: Exit loops with their own conditions first; use `break`/`continue` sparingly and locally; keep `goto` for the two sanctioned patterns (nested escape, retry) — never into blocks, never far. When a nest needs a multi-level exit, consider extracting a function so an ordinary `return` does the job.
concepts.detail: The advice is about predictability: every jump statement is a point where the reader loses the thread, so each one must buy its keep.

concepts.statement: Code is read far more often than it is written — by reviewers, debuggers and future you. Braces on all non-trivial branches, indentation that mirrors structure, comments that state intent, and names that carry meaning are all parts of one policy: make the visible program tell the truth about the actual one.
concepts.detail: This is also why the chapter's examples brace even single-statement branches: the cost is two characters now, and the benefit is that no `else` can ever dangle ambiguously.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Declare variables as late as possible and always with an initializer; keep loop counters inside the for-init and tested values inside conditions.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: Auditing a fragment against the advice
examples.problem: List every rule from this chapter that the following fragment violates, and fix it.

steps.label: The fragment
(a) Three top-of-block declarations
steps.text: All three live for the whole function; `i` is only the loop counter and `t` only the count. Advice: declare at first use with initializers — `int t = 0; cin >> t;` and the counter belongs to the for-init.

steps.label: (b) and (c)
steps.text: `max = -1` is a sentinel that breaks if data can hold −1 (a precondition the code cannot check); the counting loop over a whole container is a range-for in disguise: `for (int x : a) if (x > max) max = x;` with `max` initialized to the first element or the type's lowest value.

steps.label: (d) and (e)
steps.text: An unbraced multi-line branch, and a stray `;` after the `if` — the classic empty-statement accident: as written, the `else` pairs with `if (max > 0)` but the semicolon already ended it, making the fragment ill-formed; bracing both branches removes the entire class of error.

examples.result: The repaired version declares three variables at use with initializers, uses a range-for, braces every branch, and deletes the sentinel in favor of an explicit first-element comparison.

examples.title: Reviewing statements code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the chapter's rules on declaration placement and initialization.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Declare variables as late as possible and always with an initializer; keep loop counters inside the for-init and tested values inside conditions.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { sum += i; }`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: choose the statement form that makes each control-flow shape most readable. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Pick the statement whose head states the purpose: range-for for containers, for for counting, while for data-driven exits, do only for guaranteed first pass, switch for enumerated cases.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Declare variables as late as possible and always with an initializer; keep loop counters inside the for-init and tested values inside conditions. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Declare variables as late as possible and always with an initializer; keep loop counters inside the for-init and tested values inside conditions.
Pick the statement whose head states the purpose: range-for for containers, for for counting, while for data-driven exits, do only for guaranteed first pass, switch for enumerated cases.
Brace non-trivial branches, let layout mirror structure, and confine goto to local, intent-named nested-escape and retry jumps — or better, to nothing.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of the chapter's advice?
options: declare a variable when you have a value to initialize it with
prefer range-for when iterating over a whole container
declare all variables at the top of the function for easy lookup
quiz.explanation: The chapter argues the opposite: declarations at the top maximize scope and the uninitialized window — declare at first use, initialized.

quiz.q: For looping over every element of a `map` while modifying each value, the advised form is:
options: a do-while over the map's size
quiz.explanation: Range-for with a non-const reference: the compiler supplies iteration, the reference avoids copying each element, and `auto&` grants the write access the task needs.

quiz.q: The advice on `do` statements is to:
options: prefer them over while because they are faster
use them whenever a loop is needed
avoid them unless the body genuinely must run before the first test
quiz.explanation: A while with its test on top is easier to reason about; do is for the special case where the first pass is required by the problem's shape.

intro: If statements are what a program does, expressions are what it thinks: every value the program computes is computed by an expression. This chapter is organized around three questions — how expressions are built from operators and operands, how the grammar alone decides which operator binds to which operand (precedence), and how the compiler turns mixes of types into one common type (implicit conversions). First the vocabulary: expressions, operands, lvalues, and the crucial difference between grouping and evaluation order.
objectives: Define expression, operator and operand, and classify operators by arity
Distinguish grouping (precedence/associativity) from order of evaluation
Distinguish lvalues from rvalues and say what the distinction is for

concepts.statement: An **expression** is a sequence of operators and operands that specifies a computation. An expression may **produce a value** (`a * b + 1`), **produce side effects** (`++i`), or both (`x = y + 1`). It can also produce nothing useful at all — a stray computation with its result discarded is still an expression.
concepts.detail: In C++ the statement `;` and the expression are separable layers: an expression becomes an expression-statement when terminated by a semicolon (Chapter 9). Everything else in this chapter is about the expression layer itself.

concepts.statement: An **operator** is a token (`+`, `<<`, `[]`, `?:`) that operates on its **operands**. Operators are classified by arity: most are **binary** (`a + b`), a large family is **unary** (`-x`, `*p`, `!ok`), and C++ has exactly one **ternary** operator — the conditional expression `cond ? a : b`. Some symbols do double duty: unary `*` (dereference) is unrelated to binary `*` (multiply).
concepts.detail: Operators are also classified by what they require of their operands and what they yield: arithmetic operators want numbers, `&&`/`||` want conditions and yield `bool`, `<<` shifts bits or writes streams depending on its left operand's type.

concepts.statement: **Precedence and associativity determine grouping only** — which operators bind to which operands. They say nothing about the order in which the subexpressions execute. In `f() + g() * h()` the grouping is `f() + (g() * h())`, but `f` may well run before `g` and `h`. Only `&&`, `||`, `?:` and `,` sequence their parts: `c && f()` guarantees `c` is tested first, and `f()` runs at all only if `c` is true.
concepts.detail: The consequence is a rule of survival: an expression that both reads and writes the same object (`v[i] = i++;`, `f(i, i++)`) relies on unspecified or undefined order and must be split into separate statements.

concepts.statement: An **lvalue** is an expression that refers to an object — a name (`x`), a dereference (`*p`), a subscript (`v[i]`), a string literal — something that (at least in principle) denotes storage. An **rvalue** is a value: `7`, `x + 1`, a function call returning by value. The heritage of the names is *left value* — what can stand on the left of an assignment.
concepts.detail: The distinction drives the language: assignment needs a modifiable lvalue on the left; `&` (address-of) needs an lvalue; and the rvalue/lvalue split is exactly what move semantics (Chapter 11 and 12) exploits to steal from temporaries.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Expressions evaluated. You can claim this section when you can define expression, operator and operand, and classify operators by arity — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 10 (Expressions); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Dissecting one expression
examples.problem: For `x = y + 2 * z`, identify every operator and operand, state the grouping, and point out what precedence does NOT promise.

steps.label: Operators
steps.text: Three binary operators: `=` (assignment), `+` (addition), `*` (multiplication). Operands: `x`, `y`, `2`, `z` are all expressions themselves — a variable name is the simplest expression.

steps.label: Grouping
steps.text: `*` binds tighter than `+`, which binds tighter than `=`, so the parse is `x = (y + (2 * z))` — precedence has already decided this; no parentheses are needed for the compiler to get it right.

steps.label: What precedence does not promise
steps.text: Nothing about when `y` and `z` are read relative to each other. Here both are plain reads so it cannot matter — but if `z` were `f()` and `y` were `g()`, the order of the two calls would be unspecified.

steps.label: Value and effect
steps.text: The expression produces a value — the sum that was assigned — and has a side effect: `x` now holds that value. The statement `x = y + 2 * z;` keeps the effect and discards the value.

examples.result: Grouping `x = (y + (2*z))` is fixed by the grammar; evaluation order of the operand reads is not — harmless here, a bug the moment side effects appear.

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: Expressions evaluated. Your task: define expression, operator and operand, and classify operators by arity.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define expression, operator and operand, and classify operators by arity. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: An expression specifies a computation: it may yield a value, have side effects, or both; operators are unary, binary, or (the conditional) ternary.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int q = x / y; int rem = x % y;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — distinguish grouping (precedence/associativity) from order of evaluation — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Precedence and associativity fix grouping, never evaluation order — only `&&`, `||`, `?:` and `,` sequence their operands. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

keyTakeaways: An expression specifies a computation: it may yield a value, have side effects, or both; operators are unary, binary, or (the conditional) ternary.
Precedence and associativity fix grouping, never evaluation order — only `&&`, `||`, `?:` and `,` sequence their operands.
An lvalue refers to an object; an rvalue is a value — assignment needs a modifiable lvalue on the left, and the distinction is the foundation of move semantics.

quiz.q: In `f() + g() * h()`, what does precedence guarantee?
options: only the grouping `f() + (g() * h())` — nothing about execution order
that the result is an lvalue
quiz.explanation: Precedence and associativity are parsing rules; the compiler may call f, g and h in any order because only the grouping — and not the sequencing — is fixed.

quiz.q: Which of these expressions is an lvalue?
quiz.explanation: `*p` refers to the object p points at — storage you can assign through. A literal, an arithmetic result and a call returning by value are rvalues.

quiz.q: The only ternary operator in C++ is:
quiz.explanation: `cond ? a : b` is the sole operator with three operands — one reason it earns special sequencing rules: exactly one of `a` and `b` is evaluated.

quiz.q: Why is `v[i] = i++;` flagged as a bug?
options: it mixes an lvalue with an rvalue
the order of evaluating `v[i]`'s index and the new `i` is unspecified — which `i` is used is not defined
assignment cannot appear in an expression
quiz.explanation: The write to `i` and the read of `i` for the subscript are unsequenced — grouping cannot help because both uses are of the same object. Split into `++i; v[i] = i;` — or better, one clear statement.

intro: To make expression evaluation concrete, Stroustrup builds a desk calculator: a program that reads arithmetic like `2+3*(4-1)` with variables and computes it. The design lesson is the grammar: precedence and associativity are not a table of arbitrary rules but the visible shape of a little recursive definition — expressions are made of terms, terms of primaries, and the parsing functions mirror the grammar rule by rule. One figure of a parse tree is worth a thousand words about precedence.
objectives: Read the desk calculator grammar and explain why deeper nesting means tighter binding
Trace recursive-descent parsing of an input such as `2+3*4`
Explain the token stream's get/putback lookahead and how the loop in expr() produces left associativity

concepts.statement:
The calculator's grammar, in the book's notation:
```
program:
    end                        // end is end-of-input
expr:
    term
    expr + term                // addition
    expr - term                // subtraction
term:
    prim
    term * prim                // multiplication
    term / prim                // division
prim:
    number                     // floating-point numbers
    name                       // names are looked up
    name = expr                // assignment
    - prim
    ( expr )
```
An expression is a sum of terms; a term is a product of primaries; a primary is a number, a variable, an assignment, a negation, or a parenthesized expression.
concepts.detail: The grammar *is* the precedence table: `*` and `/` sit one level deeper than `+` and `-`, so they bind their operands closer. Parentheses work by making a whole expression a primary — nothing deeper than a primary can be, so parenthesizing is the escape to the top.

concepts.statement: **Recursive descent** gives each grammar rule a function: `expr()` parses an expr by first calling `term()` (which calls `prim()`, which reads a token), then looping while it sees `+` or `-`, folding each new term into the running result. The call tree of the parser mirrors the parse tree of the input.
concepts.detail: The book's loop form handles the left-recursive rule `expr: expr + term` without infinite regress: instead of calling `expr()` on the rest, `expr()` keeps a `left` accumulator and loops — which is also what makes `-` left-associative.

concepts.statement: The parser reads not characters but **tokens** — numbers, names, operators — through a `Token_stream` with `get()` and `putback(t)`. The one-token buffer that `putback` provides is exactly the one-token lookahead the parser needs: `prim()` reads a token to decide what kind of primary it faces, and hands back anything (like a `+`) that belongs to the caller.
concepts.detail: Separating lexing (characters to tokens) from parsing (tokens to structure) is what keeps each function small: `expr()` never sees digits, only whole numbers.

concepts.statement: Because `expr()` folds terms into `left` as it reads left-to-right, `1-2-3` evaluates as `(1-2)-3 = -4` — not `1-(2-3) = 2`. The loop shape of the parser hard-codes left associativity for `-`, `/` and every other non-associative-seeming operator.
concepts.detail: The exception proves the rule: assignment in `prim` (`name = expr`) parses its right side by calling `expr()` recursively, so `x = y = 2` groups `x = (y = 2)` — right-associative, because the recursion is on the right.

concepts.statement: A `name` is looked up in a `map<string,double> table`; `name = expr` evaluates the expression and stores it in the table — which is how the calculator remembers variables across inputs, e.g. `x = 2+3*4` followed later by `x/2 - 1`.
concepts.detail: The assignment rule lives in `prim` because a parenthesized or negated expression may appear on the right — the full expr grammar, recursively.

figures.caption: The parse tree of `2 + 3 * 4` in the desk-calculator grammar. Each nonterminal (expr, term, prim) becomes one function call in the recursive-descent parser. Because the `*` rule lives one level *deeper* in the grammar than `+`, the multiplication `3 * 4` forms a single term that is then added to `2`: value $2 + (3 \times 4) = 14$.

examples.title: Parsing and evaluating 2+3*4
examples.problem: Trace the calculator on the input `2+3*4` — which functions run, in what order, and what value comes back?

steps.label: expr() calls term()
steps.text: `expr()` starts by calling `term()` for its first term. `term()` calls `prim()`, which does `ts.get()` and reads the number token `2`, returning the value $2.0$.

steps.label: term() looks ahead
steps.text: `term()` calls `ts.get()` to see whether a `*` or `/` follows. It sees `+` — not its operator — so it does `putback(+)` and returns $2$.

steps.label: expr() sees the +
steps.text: `expr()` receives `left = 2`, gets the `+`, and calls `term()` again for the right side.

steps.label: The right-hand term
steps.text: The new `term()` calls `prim()` → $3$; then gets `*` — its operator — so it calls `prim()` again → $4$, and folds: $3 \times 4 = 12$. The next token (end) is not `*`, so `term()` returns $12$.

steps.label: expr() finishes
steps.text: `expr()` folds `left = 2 + 12 = 14`, reads the end token, exits its loop, and $14$ is the value of the whole expression.

examples.result: 2+3*4 = 14 — the multiplication happened inside `term()`, before `expr()` ever got to see its operand as a whole: grammar depth *is* precedence.

examples.title: Left associativity: 1-2-3
examples.problem: Why does the calculator (correctly) answer −4 for `1-2-3`, and not 2?

steps.label: First iteration
steps.text: `expr()` gets `left = term() = 1`, reads the first `-`, and immediately calls `term()` for the rest of that operation → $2$, folding `left = 1 - 2 = -1`.

steps.label: Second iteration
steps.text: The loop continues: it reads the second `-`, calls `term()` → $3$, and folds `left = -1 - 3 = -4`.

steps.label: The alternative
steps.text: If the grammar had grouped right — `1-(2-3)` — the answer would be $1-(-1) = 2$. The loop's fold-direction makes subtraction left-associative, matching the C++ rule for `-`.

examples.result: 1-2-3 = (1-2)-3 = -4: the accumulator loop in expr() implements left associativity.

keyTakeaways: The grammar expresses precedence structurally: term (products) nests inside expr (sums), prim inside term — the deeper rule binds its operands tighter.
Recursive descent maps one function per grammar rule; the loop in `expr()` (rather than a recursive call) is what makes `-` and `/` left-associative.
The token stream's `get()`/`putback()` pair gives one token of lookahead, enough for `prim()` to decide what it faces and return what it does not need.

quiz.q: Why does `2+3*4` evaluate to 14 rather than 20 in the calculator?
options: the parser compares operator priorities in a table before parsing
the `*` rule sits deeper in the grammar — the whole `3*4` is parsed as one term before expr() adds
multipation is evaluated by a separate pass
the number 3 is read before the number 2
quiz.explanation: Precedence is grammar shape: term() absorbs 3*4 completely before returning, so expr() adds 2 to 12. Parentheses work by making an expr into a prim — jumping straight to the deepest level.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of `ts.putback(t)`?
options: to record parsed tokens for error reporting
to unread one token so the next `get()` (usually in the caller) returns it again — one token of lookahead
to push results back onto a stack for evaluation
quiz.explanation: When term() reads a `+` that belongs to expr(), it puts it back; expr()'s next get() then sees it. The one-token buffer implements exactly the one-token lookahead the grammar needs.

quiz.q: With the book's grammar, `x = 2` inside the calculator parses its right-hand side by:
options: reading a single number token only
calling expr() recursively, which makes assignment right-associative
looping over numbers and adding them
looking up x in the table first
quiz.explanation: `name = expr` recurses on the full expression grammar, so `x = y = 2` groups as x = (y = 2) — the one right-associative case in the calculator.

quiz.q: In the parse tree of `2+3*4`, the tokens `3` and `4` hang under which nonterminal?
options: expr directly, on both sides of the +
a term that sits as the right operand of the `+`
quiz.explanation: 3*4 is entirely a term: prim(3) and prim(4) under term, term(*) — that subtree is then the right operand of `+` at the top.

intro: The operator summary is the chapter's most consulted page: every operator, its precedence level and its associativity, in one table. Two reading skills unlock it. First, operators in the same box bind equally strongly, and associativity breaks ties. Second — and this is the one everyone gets wrong — the table decides grouping, not order of evaluation, so `f() + g()*h()` still runs f whenever the compiler likes. The tower below is the table drawn to scale: the higher the band, the tighter the grip.
objectives: Read the precedence/associativity table and resolve mixed expressions by hand
Apply associativity to break ties among equally-ranked operators
State precisely what precedence does not determine, and when to parenthesize

concepts.statement: C++ arranges its operators into **precedence levels**; in the table, each box (grouped by horizontal rules) is one level. Operators higher in the table bind their operands more tightly: `a + b * c` parses as `a + (b * c)`, and `*a.b` parses as `*(a.b)` because `.` outranks unary `*`.
concepts.detail: A workable subset, high to low: `::` scope; postfix (`a()`, `a[]`, `.`, `->`, `a++`, `a--`); unary (`++a`, `-a`, `!a`, `~a`, `*a`, `&a`, casts, `sizeof`, `new`, `delete`); `.*` and `->*`; `* / %`; `+ -`; `<< >>`; relational (`< <= > >=`); equality (`== !=`); bitwise `&`, then `^`, then `|`; logical `&&`, then `||`; then the conditional and assignment operators; and finally `,` at the very bottom.

concepts.statement: **Associativity breaks ties** between operators of the same level. Almost all levels associate **left** (`a-b-c` is `(a-b)-c`; `cout << a << b` streams a then b). The right-associative ones are the unary operators, the conditional `?:`, and the assignment family — so `x = y = 0` is `x = (y = 0)`, and `a ? b : c ? d : e` nests on the right.
concepts.detail: The mnemonic: anything that *produces an lvalue-ish result to assign into* associates right; things that *consume values* associate left.

concepts.statement: **The precedence table fixes how expressions parse — nothing else.** In `f() + g() * h()` the grouping is `f() + (g()*h())`, yet the compiler may call `f` first, last, or interleaved. Any code whose answer depends on which subexpression runs first (`v[i] = i++`, `f(i, i++)`) is unspecified or undefined — the table cannot save it.
concepts.detail: The four exceptions — `&&`, `||`, `?:`, `,` — sequence their operands left to right, which is why `p && p->next` is safe when `p` might be null and an `if`-statement cannot be used in an expression.

concepts.statement: Explicit parentheses **override** the table's grouping and, equally important, document intent for readers. Redundant parentheses cost nothing at run time; the book's own examples parenthesize liberally around mixes of `&&`, `||` and comparisons — precisely the levels people misremember.
concepts.detail: The professional rule: memorize the top and bottom of the table (`::`, postfix, unary up high; assignment and `,` at the bottom) and parenthesize everything in between that you have not just verified.

concepts.statement: **Operator Summary.** Precedence, associativity and the full operator table. You can claim this section when you can read the precedence/associativity table and resolve mixed expressions by hand — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 10 (Expressions); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

figures.caption: The operator precedence tower. Each band is one precedence level; higher bands bind tighter, and the arrow beside each band gives its associativity. Note the three-step staircase of the logical/bitwise region — `&` then `^` then `|` below the equality tests, then `&&` then `||` — and the right-associative block of assignment and `?:` near the bottom.
