examples.title: Resolving a precedence chain by hand
examples.problem: With `int i = 4;` evaluate `bool ok = i < 10 && i % 2 == 0;` — group it first, then compute.

steps.label: Group the comparisons
steps.text: Relational (`<`) and equality (`==`) both outrank `&&`, so the parse is `(i < 10) && ((i % 2) == 0)` — and `%` sits above them both, binding `i % 2` first.

steps.label: Right operand
steps.text: `i % 2 == 0` is `(4 % 2) == 0` → `0 == 0` → `true`. Note the classic trap avoided by the table: `==` outranks nothing between it and `&&`, but a programmer who wrote `i % 2 == 0 && ...` without the inner parentheses got them for free.

steps.label: Combine
steps.text: `true && true` → `true`, assigned to `ok`; converting `bool` to `int` later would give $1$.

examples.result: `ok` is true — grouping `(i<10) && ((i%2)==0)` comes straight off the tower without a single parenthesis.

examples.title: Assignment is right-associative
examples.problem: Evaluate `x = y = z = 5;` with all three variables `int`, and explain the grouping.

steps.label: Group
steps.text: Assignment is one precedence level and associates right: the parse is `x = (y = (z = 5))`.

steps.label: Innermost first
steps.text: `z = 5` is an expression whose value is the value assigned, $5$ — so `y = (z = 5)` stores $5$ into `y` and also yields $5$.

steps.label: Outermost
steps.text: `x = ...` stores $5$ into `x`. One semicolon, three assignments, all variables equal $5$.

steps.label: Why it must be right
steps.text: Left grouping `(x = y) = z` would assign to the *result* of `x = y` — for built-ins that result is an rvalue and the code would be ill-formed; right associativity is the only grouping that makes chained assignment legal.

examples.result: x = y = z = 5 → x = (y = (z = 5)); all three end with 5, thanks to assignment's right associativity and its value-producing nature.

keyTakeaways: Operators live in precedence levels — same level means equal strength, and associativity (left for most, right for unary, `?:` and assignment) breaks the tie.
The table determines grouping only; evaluation order of operands is unspecified except for `&&`, `||`, `?:` and `,`.

Parentheses override the table and document intent — redundant grouping costs nothing, while misremembering the bitwise/logical staircase (`&` above `^` above `|`, both above `&&`) silently changes results.

quiz.q: Which groups `a & b == c` the way C++ parses it?
quiz.explanation: Equality (`==`) outranks bitwise `&` in the tower — one of the most misremembered bands, and the reason the book recommends parentheses whenever `&` meets comparisons.

quiz.q: `x = y = z = 5;` sets all three variables because assignment:
options: is an expression yielding the value assigned, and associates right
is a statement that repeats per operand
quiz.explanation: Each `=` yields the assigned value, and the level associates right, so the chain nests x = (y = (z = 5)).

quiz.q: `*p++` — what does the expression do?
options: increments the object p points to, then dereferences
dereferences p, then increments the object
post-increments p, then dereferences the old pointer value
quiz.explanation: Postfix `++` outranks unary `*`, so the grouping is `*(p++)` — the classic idiom for walking an array, and the classic exam trap.

quiz.q: Precedence tells you nothing about:
options: which operand binds to which operator
whether `?:` evaluates its middle or last operand
the grouping of a parenthesized subexpression
quiz.explanation: Which branch of `?:` runs is an *evaluation-order* question (answered: exactly one, chosen by the condition); precedence only says how the text groups.

intro: Some values must be known before the program runs: array sizes, template arguments, case labels, integer template constants. C++11 introduced constexpr to say *this code computes at compile time — check it* rather than hoping a const happens to be initialized by something the compiler can fold. A constexpr function is written like an ordinary function but is guaranteed usable in constant expressions, so the same code serves both worlds — compile-time computation when required, run-time computation otherwise.
objectives: Define constant expression and constexpr, and what constexpr guarantees
Write constexpr functions (single return, literal types, recursion allowed) and use them for array bounds
Distinguish const (do not modify) from constexpr (known at compile time)

concepts.statement: A **constant expression** is an expression that the compiler can evaluate at compile time: literals, `constexpr` variables used in the expression, `constexpr` function calls, and combinations thereof via constexpr operators. It may not contain assignments, increments, or any value that only exists at run time.
concepts.detail: The places that demand constant expressions are exactly the places the compiler must finish a decision before running code: array bounds, case labels, template integer arguments, `static_assert` conditions, and the initializers of other `constexpr` variables.

concepts.statement: A **`constexpr` variable** must be initialized by a constant expression — the compiler enforces it: `constexpr int x = 7 + 3*2;` compiles ( initializer folds to 13), but `constexpr int x = f();` is rejected unless `f` is a `constexpr` function called with constant arguments.
concepts.detail: This is the checking that plain `const` lacks: `const int n = read();` is a perfectly fine read-only variable initialized at run time — legal precisely because `const` promises immutability, not compile-time knowledge.

concepts.statement:
A **`constexpr` function** is one usable in constant expressions: its parameters and return must be of **literal types** (built-ins, pointers, enums, and classes of literal type), and in C++11 its body is effectively a single `return` statement — loops are absent, but **recursion is allowed**:
```
constexpr int fac(int n) { return (n > 1) ? n * fac(n-1) : 1; }
constexpr int f9 = fac(9);          // 362880, computed by the compiler
```
The guarantee is two-way: given constant arguments it must be evaluable at compile time, and no result is cached or magically different at run time.
concepts.detail: The compiler applies the rules where the call needs to be a constant expression; the same `fac` called with a run-time `n` is an ordinary function call executed at run time. (C++14 loosens the single-return rule — loops and locals — but the discipline taught here is the C++11 one the book codifies.)

concepts.statement: A `constexpr` function lives a double life: **at compile time when its value is needed in a constant expression** (an array bound, a case label, another constexpr initializer) and **at run time otherwise**. One definition serves both, with identical semantics — this is what makes constexpr code ordinary code with a guarantee attached, not a separate macro-like language.
concepts.detail: This is the design win over both the pre-C++11 alternatives: the enum hack (no floating point, no arguments) and template metaprogramming (unreadable) — a constexpr factorial reads exactly like a normal one.

concepts.statement: **`constexpr` means *evaluated at compile time*; `const` means *not modified through this name*.** A `constexpr int` is necessarily also `const`; a `const int` need not be constexpr — `const int r = read();` is fine and useless as an array bound, whereas `constexpr int r = fac(4);` is a compile-time 24.
concepts.detail: Rule of thumb from the chapter: use `constexpr` for what should be compile-time (sizes, bounds, mathematical constants), `const` for run-time immutability (parameters, references to data you promise not to change).

examples.title: A compile-time factorial table
examples.problem: Use `fac` to size an array and check the arithmetic by hand.

steps.label: The function
steps.text: `constexpr int fac(int n) { return (n > 1) ? n * fac(n-1) : 1; }` — a single return, recursive, all types literal: legal C++11 constexpr.

steps.label: Array bound
steps.text: `int buf[fac(4)];` — the bound must be a constant expression, so the compiler *must* evaluate `fac(4)` now: $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$ ints, i.e. 96 bytes on a 32-bit-int machine.

steps.label: Check fac(9)
steps.text: The chain: $9 \times 8 = 72$, $72 \times 7 = 504$, $504 \times 6 = 3024$, $3024 \times 5 = 15120$, $15120 \times 4 = 60480$, $60480 \times 3 = 181440$, $181440 \times 2 = 362880$ — so `constexpr int f9 = fac(9);` initializes the constant to $362880$ with zero run-time cost.

steps.label: Run-time use
steps.text: `int n; cin >> n; int r = fac(n);` — the very same function compiles to a plain call; only the *requirement* changed, not the code.

examples.result: fac(4) = 24 sizes the array at compile time; fac(9) = 362880 initializes a constexpr; and fac(n) with run-time n is an ordinary call — one definition, two lives.

examples.title: A physics constant as code
examples.problem: Kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ should be computable both ways. Write it once.

steps.label: The function
steps.text: `constexpr double kinetic(double m, double v) { return 0.5 * m * v * v; }` — literal parameter and return types, single return.

steps.label: Compile-time
steps.text: `constexpr double e = kinetic(2.0, 3.0);` → $0.5 \times 2 \times 9 = 9.0$ folded by the compiler — usable as a template argument or a case value where a `double` is allowed.

steps.label: Run-time
steps.text: `double m = read_mass(); double e2 = kinetic(m, 3.0);` — computed at run time from data that did not exist at compile time, by the same code.

steps.label: What you gained
steps.text: Had `kinetic` been a macro, `kinetic(m+1, 3)` would textually expand to `0.5*m+1*3*3`; as a constexpr function it is typed, scoped, overloadable — and still free when it can be.

examples.result: kinetic(2.0, 3.0) = 9.0 at compile time; the same expression with run-time masses is an ordinary call — type safety in both worlds.

keyTakeaways: A constant expression is one the compiler can evaluate: literals and constexpr things only — it is required for array bounds, case labels and template integer arguments.
A constexpr function is guaranteed usable in constant expressions: literal types in and out, a single return (C++11), recursion allowed; called with run-time arguments it just runs.
constexpr means compile-time evaluation; const means do-not-modify — a const initialized at run time is not a constant expression.

quiz.q: Which initializer makes `constexpr int n = ...;` legal?
quiz.explanation: A constexpr variable's initializer must be a constant expression; calls to constexpr functions with constant arguments qualify, and everything involving run-time data does not.

quiz.q: A `constexpr` function called with arguments only known at run time:
options: compiles and executes as an ordinary function at run time
is evaluated at compile time anyway
quiz.explanation: That is two-phase evaluation: the guarantee applies where a constant expression is *required*; otherwise the same code is a normal run-time call.

quiz.q: The essential difference between `const int r = read();` and `constexpr int r = 42;` is:
options: the first is read-only but initialized at run time; only the second is a compile-time constant
the first cannot be used in expressions
the second may be modified later
quiz.explanation: const promises immutability through the name; constexpr additionally demands and enforces compile-time initialization — which is why only the second can size an array.

quiz.q: In C++11, which is NOT allowed in a constexpr function body?
options: a recursive call to another constexpr function
a local variable modified by a for-loop
quiz.explanation: C++11 constexpr bodies are effectively a single return — loops (and locals they would need) are excluded; C++14 relaxed this, but the book teaches the stricter rule.

intro: C++ inherited from C a machine-near conversion policy: char is just a small int, int and double mix freely, and everything is quietly normalized to a common type before the operator runs. Most of the time this is exactly what you want — 'a'+1 is 98 without ceremony. The chapter's warning is that the same machinery produces three families of silent surprises: promotions that make char arithmetic int arithmetic, usual arithmetic conversions that can turn −1 into the largest unsigned value, and narrowing that throws away high bits and fractions with no diagnostic — unless you initialize with `{}`, which refuses.
objectives: State the integral promotions and what they preserve
Apply the usual arithmetic conversions to predict the common type of a mixed expression
Recognize narrowing and the signed/unsigned trap, and use {} initialization to catch narrowing

concepts.statement: Before an operator runs, operands smaller than `int` are converted to `int` (or `unsigned int` if `int` cannot hold all values, as on 16-bit chars): `char`, `bool`, `short` and their unsigned variants all promote. `'a' + 1` therefore computes in `int`: the character `'a'` has value 97, so the result is $98$ — the character `'b'`.
concepts.detail: Promotions are value-preserving: no information is lost (an `int` holds every `char` value). This is why `sizeof('a' + 1)` is `sizeof(int)`, not 1 — the arithmetic was never done in char.

concepts.statement: When a binary operator gets two different types, both operands are converted to a **common type**: if either is `long double`, both become `long double`; else if either is `double`, both become `double`; else if either is `float`, both become `float`; otherwise both undergo integral promotion and then are widened to the larger (and, if the sizes match and one is unsigned, the unsigned) type. `7/2.0` is `double` division → 3.5; `7/2` is `int` division → 3.
concepts.detail: The result type of the operation is the common type — which is why `double d = 7/2;` stores $3.0$: the division already happened in `int` before any conversion to double, truncating the fraction. Write `7/2.0` or `static_cast<double>(7)/2`.

concepts.statement: A **narrowing conversion** maps a type to one that cannot hold all its values: `double` to `int` (fraction truncated), `long` to `int` (high bits dropped), `int` to `char` (bits beyond 8 dropped). They happen silently in assignments and function calls — `int c = 1000;` then `char ch = c;` leaves `ch` holding $1000 \bmod 256 = 232$ — but `{}`-initialization **rejects** them: `char ch {c};` does not compile.
concepts.detail: The dropped-bits arithmetic: 1000 in binary is 1111101000; keeping the low 8 bits 11101000 gives $128+64+32+8 = 232$. For `double` to `int`, the value is truncated toward zero, never rounded: `int x = 7.9;` is 7.

concepts.statement: When signed meets unsigned of the same size, the **signed operand is converted to unsigned** — so `-1 < 2u` compares $4294967295 < 2$ and is **false**. The same rule ambushes loop bounds: comparing an `int i` against `v.size()` (an unsigned) silently converts `i`; when a container is empty, `v.size() - 1` wraps to the largest value, not −1.
concepts.detail: The defenses from the chapter: avoid mixing signed and unsigned in comparisons; prefer range-for loops (no index at all); and never compute `size() - 1` without checking emptiness first — a back-to-front loop `for (int i = v.size()-1; i >= 0; --i)` needs the emptiness guard *before* the subtraction happens in unsigned arithmetic.

concepts.statement: The `{}` (braced) initialization is the conversion-safe form: it **rejects narrowing** at compile time — `int x {7.9};` and `char c {1000};` are compile errors — which is why the book's advice is to use `{}` for initialization everywhere unless a narrowing is genuinely intended and visible.
concepts.detail: The `=` and `()` forms both narrow silently; `{}` makes the machine check what your eyes might miss. This is the same protection that initializer lists (Chapter 11.3) give to aggregates and containers.

examples.title: Four conversions, four surprises
examples.problem: Predict each value and explain the rule that produced it.

steps.label: Integer division first
steps.text: `double d = 7/2;` → the operands are both `int`, so the division is integer division ($3$), *then* converted: `d` is $3.0$, not 3.5. Fix: `7/2.0` → 3.5.

steps.label: Promotion in action
steps.text: `'a' + 1` → `'a'` promotes to `int` 97, the sum is $98$ — assigning to `char` narrows back to `'b'`. `sizeof('a' + 1) == sizeof(int)` surprises C programmers: in C++ the arithmetic happens in int.

steps.label: Narrowing to char
steps.text: `char c = 1000;` → 1000 does not fit a char's 8 bits; the high bits are dropped: $1000 - 768 = 232$ survives (768 = 3×256). `char c2 {1000};` would refuse to compile — the `{}` form catches it.

steps.label: The unsigned ambush
steps.text: `unsigned u = 2; if (-1 < u)` → `-1` converts to `unsigned int`: all bits set, $4294967295$. The comparison is $4294967295 < 2$ → **false**, against every mathematical intuition.

examples.result: 7/2 → 3 in int then 3.0 as double; 'a'+1 → 98; char(1000) → 232; and −1 < 2u is false: each surprise follows from one rule — normalize to a common type first, silently.

examples.title: The empty-vector off-by-one
examples.problem: Why does `for (int i = 0; i <= v.size() - 1; ++i) cout << v[i];` print nothing for a non-empty `v` but loops ~4 billion times (and crashes) when `v` is empty?

steps.label: The subtraction's type
steps.text: `v.size()` is an unsigned type, so `v.size() - 1` is unsigned arithmetic. For `size() == 3` it is $2$: `i <= 2` works for `i` = 0,1,2 — correct by luck.

steps.label: When size() is 0
steps.text: `0 - 1` in unsigned arithmetic wraps to $2^{32} - 1 = 4294967295$. The condition `i <= 4294967295` holds for essentially every `int i`.

steps.label: What follows
steps.text: The loop reads `v[0]`, `v[1]`, ... of an empty vector — undefined behavior, typically a crash after a few billion nonsense accesses. The bug is invisible on every non-empty test.

steps.label: The repairs
steps.text: Write `i < v.size()` (no subtraction at all), or better the range-for `for (auto& x : v)` — no index, no unsigned, no off-by-one. If a backwards loop is needed, guard emptiness *before* computing `size() - 1`.

examples.result: `size() - 1` on an empty container wraps to 4294967295 — the canonical reason the book says never mix signed and unsigned arithmetic, and never subtract from size() unchecked.

keyTakeaways: Integral promotion converts chars, bools and shorts to int before arithmetic — value-preserving but it changes the type of every small-type expression to int.
The usual arithmetic conversions pick one common type for both operands: any floating type dominates; otherwise the larger, and same-size unsigned wins — so −1 becomes 4294967295 next to a 2u.
Narrowing (double→int, long→int, int→char) is silent with `=` and `()` and a compile error with `{}` — initialize with braces; avoid unsigned in comparisons and never compute size() − 1 unchecked.

quiz.q: `double d = 7/2;` stores:
quiz.explanation: Both operands are int, so integer division gives 3, converted to double afterwards. The common-type rule only widens the operands when one is already floating point.

quiz.q: The value of `'a' + 1` and its type are:
quiz.explanation: 'a' promotes to int 97 and the sum 98 is an int — which happens to be the code of 'b' when narrowed back to char on assignment.

quiz.q: Why is `-1 < 2u` false?
options: the int −1 is converted to unsigned: 4294967295, which is not less than 2
unsigned values are always positive so the comparison is skipped
the comparison is done in floating point
quiz.explanation: The usual arithmetic conversions turn −1 into the largest unsigned int before comparing — the book's canonical example of why signed and unsigned must not mix.

quiz.q: Which initialization refuses to narrow?
quiz.explanation: Braced initialization makes narrowing a compile error; = and () truncate silently (both to 7) and `auto` deduces double — no narrowing at all.

options: `1`, because negative numbers are always smaller
`1`, because the comparison runs in `double` precision
`0`, because `-1` converts to a large unsigned value
The result is unspecified by the standard
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The code given compares a negative `int` against an `unsigned` literal. Step 2: The governing rule is the usual arithmetic conversion: when `int` meets `unsigned int`, the signed operand converts to unsigned, so `-1` becomes the maximum unsigned value. Step 3: Tracing the comparison in the unsigned domain, the converted left side is enormous, which is not less than `1`, so the comparison yields false, printed as `0`. Step 4: The distractors fail because no signed comparison survives the conversion, no floating type participates, and the rule is fully specified rather than open. Step 5: Therefore the program prints `0`.

intro: The chapter's advice on expressions compresses to three habits: parenthesize what you have not verified, keep each expression to one visible side effect, and treat conversions as the boundary where correctness is lost. Every rule here has a bug shown earlier in the chapter behind it — the advice section is just the lesson list.
objectives: Apply the chapter's rules for writing verifiable expressions
Audit code for evaluation-order dependence and signed/unsigned mixing
Choose constexpr and {} initialization as defaults

concepts.statement: **If in doubt, parenthesize.** Redundent grouping is free — the compiler ignores redundant parens, but readers use them as documentation. The levels worth always parenthesizing in source: mixes of bitwise with comparison, mixes of `&&` with `||`, and anything near the assignment block of the tower.
concepts.detail: The inverse also holds: *remove* parentheses you have proven unnecessary during code review, so the remaining ones stay meaningful — a parenthesis that is always there is a parenthesis no one reads.

concepts.statement: Avoid expressions whose value depends on evaluation order: no two writes to the same object in one expression, no read-plus-write (`v[i] = i++`), and never two increments of one variable in an argument list. Split the computation into statements whose order you can see.
concepts.detail: The compiler is free to evaluate subexpressions in any order (10.1), so such code works today and breaks — or silently misbehaves — with the next compiler flag, inlining decision, or platform.

concepts.statement: Conversions are where typed correctness leaks away. Make them visible and intentional: `{}`-initialize so narrowing is rejected, avoid signed/unsigned comparisons (range-for eliminates most indices), and when a conversion is genuinely needed, name it with a cast (Chapter 11.5) rather than letting it happen silently.
concepts.detail: This pairs with 10.4: make what can be compile-time constexpr, so the compiler checks arithmetic it can check and you keep run-time code for the genuinely dynamic parts.

concepts.statement: The advice list's quiet summary: expressions exist to be read. Densely folded one-liners that exploit precedence, conversions and side effects together are a tax on every future reader — including you. A few well-named temporaries beat a heroically unreadable expression, at identical run-time cost.
concepts.detail: The desk calculator is the model: its precedence comes from structure (a grammar of named levels), not from remembering a table — structure that reads is structure that is right.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Parenthesize what you have not verified — grouping you can see is grouping you can audit, and it costs nothing.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: Auditing one dense line
examples.problem: The line `a[i++] = b[j++] + c[k++];` was submitted as a fix. Audit it against the chapter's rules.

steps.label: Side-effect count
steps.text: Three increments in one expression, each a write, none related to the others' values — but all three may interleave in any order with the reads of `i`, `j`, `k`. Here the reads and writes happen to be on different objects, so it is *unspecified* rather than undefined — still unreviewable.

steps.label: What it hides
steps.text: A reader must check three subscript variables and three post-increments to confirm the same element pairing the author intended. There is no comment that could make this cheaper than splitting.

steps.label: The split
Generalize
steps.text: Same audit catches `f(i, i++)` (undefined), `x = x++` (undefined), and `v[i] = ++i;` (unsequenced): any line combining a write with a later read of the same object in the same expression is a bug by construction.

examples.result: One dense line becomes three plain ones with identical behavior on every compiler — and behavior that is now specified, reviewable and testable.

examples.title: Reviewing expressions code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the chapter's rules for writing verifiable expressions.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Parenthesize what you have not verified — grouping you can see is grouping you can audit, and it costs nothing.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `int q = x / y; int rem = x % y;`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: audit code for evaluation-order dependence and signed/unsigned mixing. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Keep to one visible side effect per statement: unsequenced read/write mixes are unspecified or undefined, and they migrate to the worst possible compiler at the worst possible time.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Parenthesize what you have not verified — grouping you can see is grouping you can audit, and it costs nothing. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Parenthesize what you have not verified — grouping you can see is grouping you can audit, and it costs nothing.
Keep to one visible side effect per statement: unsequenced read/write mixes are unspecified or undefined, and they migrate to the worst possible compiler at the worst possible time.
Make conversions deliberate: {} initialization against narrowing, no signed/unsigned comparisons, constexpr where the value should be compile-time.

quiz.q: The chapter's rule on redundant parentheses is:
options: never use them; they slow the compiler down
use them wherever you have not verified the grouping — they are free and document intent
they are only allowed in macros
quiz.explanation: Grouping you can see is grouping you can audit; the cost of redundant parens is zero and the benefit is that readers (including you, later) need not trust memory of the tower.

quiz.q: Which line should definitely be split into statements?
options: `y = f(x, g(x));` where f and g are pure functions
quiz.explanation: It writes i and reads i in the same unsequenced expression — undefined behavior. The others group safely and (in the second) have no side effects at all.

quiz.q: For a loop bound against a container's length, the advice-backed choices are:
options: `i <= v.size() - 1` to include the last element
compare an int against the unsigned size with a cast
`i < v.size()`, or better, a range-for with no index at all
quiz.explanation: Avoid the subtraction (which wraps to 4294967295 when empty) and avoid the signed/unsigned comparison; the range-for removes both hazards structurally.

intro: Chapter 10 catalogued the arithmetic core; this chapter opens with the operators that fit nowhere else: the logical operators with their short-circuit guarantee, the bitwise operators that treat integers as bit patterns, the increment/decrement pair whose prefix and postfix forms differ in what they yield, and the conditional expression — the only ternary operator, and the one way to select a value where a statement cannot go. Each looks trivial; each hides one precise rule worth knowing exactly.
objectives: Distinguish logical from bitwise operators, including their sequencing rules
Predict what prefix and postfix ++/-- yield and when each is appropriate
Use the conditional expression correctly where an if-statement cannot appear

concepts.statement: The logical operators `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not) operate on conditions and yield `bool`. Operands need not be `bool` themselves — each is converted by the *is it nonzero / non-null* rule. Crucially, `&&` and `||` **short-circuit**: the left operand is evaluated first, and the right operand is evaluated only if it can change the outcome.
concepts.detail: Short-circuit is sequencing, not optimization: `p && p->size()` is well-defined for a null `p` precisely because the second operand does not run. `!` is a true operator with no sequencing to do.

concepts.statement: The operators `&` (and), `|` (or), `^` (exclusive or) and `~` (complement) apply the corresponding Boolean function **bit-by-bit** to integer operands — and evaluate both operands with no short-circuit. Shifts `<<` and `>>` move bit patterns: `3 << 2` is $12$ (each shift multiplies by 2), `12 >> 2` is $3$.
concepts.detail: The one-character difference from `&&`/`||` is a classic bug: `1 & 2` is $0$ (bit patterns 01 and 10 share no bits) while `1 && 2` is `true`. In conditions, you almost always want the logical versions; in masks and hardware code, the bitwise ones.

concepts.statement: `++x` **increments x and yields the new value** (an lvalue — the object itself); `x++` increments x but yields a **copy of the old value**. So with `int i = 3;`, `++i` is 4, while `i++` is 3 and leaves `i` at 4 afterwards. The decrement forms are exact mirrors.
concepts.detail: For built-ins the cost is identical; for class types (iterators especially), postfix must construct and return a copy of the old value, so **prefer `++i`** as the idiom unless you specifically need the old value — the postfix `it++` in a `for` loop is a habit, not a requirement.

concepts.statement: **`cond ? e1 : e2`** evaluates `cond`, then exactly one of `e1`, `e2`, and yields it. It is the only ternary operator, and the only way to express selection *inside an expression* — in initializers, arguments, and places a statement cannot go: `int m = a > b ? a : b;`.
concepts.detail: Because the second and third operands are combined into one result, they must have compatible types: `cond ? 1 : 2.0` yields a `double`. And because `?:` is an expression, it nests — but the book's advice stands: if you need more than a pair of simple alternatives, an `if`-statement is clearer.

concepts.statement: Use `&&`/`||` when you mean *condition met* — they yield `bool` and short-circuit. Use `&`/`|`/`^`/`~` when you mean *bit pattern* — they yield the integer type of their operands and always evaluate both sides. A test like `if (a & b)` is legal whenever `a` and `b` are ints, but means *the intersection of their bit patterns is nonzero* — which is a mask test, not the same as `a && b`.
concepts.detail: The exception is deliberate bitflag code, where `(flags & READ_ONLY)` as a condition is idiomatic: the mask intersection *is* the question being asked.

examples.title: A bit-mask round trip
examples.problem: With `unsigned char x = 0xA3;` (binary 10100011), predict the result of: (a) `x & 0xF0`, (b) `x | 0x08`, (c) `x ^ 0xFF`, (d) `x << 1`.

steps.label: Mask off the low nibble
steps.text: `x & 0xF0`: 10100011 AND 11110000 keeps only the four high bits → 10100000 = 0xA0 = 160. The mask selects; the AND keeps the intersection.

steps.label: Set one bit
steps.text: `x | 0x08`: 10100011 OR 00001000 — the 8-bit is already set in 0xA3 (the low nibble is 0011, which includes 8), so the value is unchanged: 0xA3 = 163. OR sets bits; it never clears them.

steps.label: Flip everything
steps.text: `x ^ 0xFF`: XOR with all ones complements every bit → 01011100 = 0x5C = 92. Check: $163 + 92 = 255$ — complementing an 8-bit pattern x gives $255 - x$.

steps.label: Shift left
steps.text: `x << 1`: 10100011 shifted left is 101000110, but an 8-bit `unsigned char` keeps the low 8 bits: 01000110 = 0x46 = 70. Equivalently $(2 \times 163) \bmod 256 = 326 - 256 = 70$ — each left shift doubles, modulo the width.

examples.result: 0xA0, 0xA3, 0x5C, 0x46 — four operators, four different truths about one bit pattern.

examples.title: Prefix vs postfix, one trace
examples.problem: With `int i = 3;` evaluate `a = i++ + ++i;`'s two pieces separately — and then explain why the combined line is banned by the chapter's rules.

steps.label: The postfix piece
steps.text: `j = i++;` → `j` receives the old value 3; afterwards `i` is 4. Postfix yields a copy of the past.

steps.label: The prefix piece
steps.text: `k = ++i;` → `i` becomes 5 first, `k` receives 5. Prefix yields the object's new state.

steps.label: Why the combined line is out
steps.text: `i++ + ++i` writes `i` twice in one expression with no sequencing between the writes — undefined behavior, not just a surprising value. The chapter's rule from 10.6 (one side effect per statement) exists precisely for lines like this.

steps.label: The idiom verdict
steps.text: When the value is discarded — `for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it)` — prefer `++it`: identical cost for ints, cheaper for iterators, and it never makes a reader hunt for an old value that is not used.

examples.result: j = 3, k = 5, and the combined expression is undefined — the pieces are each fine alone; only their unsequenced combination is not.

keyTakeaways: `&&` and `||` yield `bool` and short-circuit their right operands; `&`, `|`, `^`, `~` operate on bit patterns and always evaluate both operands — one character of syntax, completely different semantics.
Prefix `++x` yields the new value (the object itself); postfix `x++` yields a copy of the old value — prefer prefix when the value is unused, especially for iterators.
`?:` is the only ternary operator and the only selection usable inside an expression; it evaluates exactly one branch and both branches must combine to one type.

quiz.q: What is the value of `1 & 2`?
quiz.explanation: Bitwise AND of patterns 01 and 10 has no common bit → 0. The logical `1 && 2` would be true — the one-character difference matters.

quiz.q: Which property do `&&` and `||` have that `&` and `|` lack?
options: they may skip evaluating the right operand
they bind more tightly than comparison
quiz.explanation: Short-circuit evaluation: `p && p->empty()` is safe for a null p because the right operand never runs — that is sequencing, guaranteed by the language.

quiz.q: With `int i = 5;` what does `int j = i++;` leave in `i` and `j`?
quiz.explanation: Postfix increments i to 6 but yields a copy of the old value 5. The prefix `++i` in the same role would have put 6 in both.

quiz.q: The conditional expression `ok ? 1 : 2.0` has result type:
options: `double`, the two branches are combined to a common type
ill-formed — the branches must have identical types
quiz.explanation: The two result operands are converted to a common type (usual arithmetic conversions), just like the operands of a binary operator: int converts to double.

intro: Objects that outlive the function that created them cannot live on the stack; they live on the free store — the memory, managed by `new` and `delete`, whose lifetime you control explicitly. That control is power and it is exactly as dangerous as it is powerful: forget a delete and you leak; delete twice or use after delete and the behavior is undefined. Stroustrup's message is blunt: in application code you should almost never see new/delete — containers and smart pointers manage the store for you, and raw new/delete belongs in the implementation of exactly those low-level components.
objectives: Use new/delete for single objects and new[]/delete[] for arrays, correctly paired
Explain why leaks, dangling pointers and double deletes happen and how RAII containers eliminate them
Describe what happens when allocation fails, and the nothrow alternative

concepts.statement: The **free store** (colloquially, the heap) is the pool of memory from which `new` allocates objects whose lifetime is **not tied to a scope**. A stack variable dies at its closing brace; a free-store object lives from its `new` until its matching `delete` — across function returns, however long you choose.
concepts.detail: That is the entire contract: you, not the scopes of the program, own the object's lifetime. Every rule in this section follows from that one responsibility.

concepts.statement: **`new`** allocates memory *and* constructs an object in it, yielding a pointer: `X* p = new X{args};` allocates one `X` (initializing it with `args`) on the free store. **`delete p`** runs `X`'s destructor and returns the memory. The array forms are `new X[n]` / `delete[] p` — they construct and destroy n elements.
concepts.detail: The pairing rule is absolute: `new` goes with `delete`, `new[]` with `delete[]`. Deleting a `new[]` allocation with plain `delete` (or vice versa) is undefined behavior — the two forms record and expect different bookkeeping for the element count.

concepts.statement: The three classic free-store bugs, all undefined or damaging: a **leak** (allocated, never deleted — the memory is lost until the process ends), a **dangling pointer** (used after `delete`, when the object may already be gone or reused), and a **double delete** (the second `delete` frees memory that may since have been handed to someone else).
concepts.detail: The arithmetic of leaks is unforgiving: a function that allocates `new double[100000]` (800,000 bytes ≈ 0.76 MB) and forgets it leaks 0.76 MB **per call** — 76 GB over 100,000 calls. A desktop app leaking 8 MB per second exhausts 16 GB in under 35 minutes.

concepts.statement: The fix is to give free-store memory an **owner** whose destructor releases it: `vector`, `string` and friends for buffers; **`std::unique_ptr`** for single objects (exactly one owner; the destructor deletes — `unique_ptr<X> p {new X{7}};`, or `make_unique<X>(7)`); **`std::shared_ptr`** when ownership is genuinely shared (a reference count deletes the last copy).
concepts.detail: This is RAII — resource acquisition is initialization — from Chapter 5: the scope owns the handle, the handle owns the resource, and destruction cascades automatically, in the right order, including on exceptions. Application code should read `vector` and `unique_ptr`; the raw `new`/`delete` should hide inside the implementations of such handles.

concepts.statement: When `new` cannot allocate, it throws **`std::bad_alloc`** — by design, because running out of memory is rarely recoverable at the allocation site. The alternative **nothrow `new`** — `new (nothrow) X` — returns `nullptr` instead, for the rare systems code that can meaningfully continue.
concepts.detail: Catching `bad_alloc` everywhere is an anti-pattern: if the machine is out of memory, the handler usually cannot run anyway. Allocate in constructors of owning handles and let the exception propagate — that is the RAII answer.

examples.title: Three ways to own a buffer of doubles
examples.problem: A function needs a million doubles (8 MB with 8-byte doubles) that outlives the call. Show the raw way, the leak it would cause if the early return were taken, and the owning way.

steps.label: Raw new
The leak budget
steps.text: If `something_wrong()` triggers once per second in a long-running server, the process loses 8 MB/s: 480 MB after a minute, every GB in about 2 minutes 8 seconds — the process dies of memory exhaustion without a single wrong answer.

steps.label: Owning it
Single object case
steps.text: For one object: `auto p = make_unique<X>(args);` — the destructor deletes at scope end; ownership can be moved into containers or members, but never copied by accident.

examples.result: The vector/unique_ptr versions are shorter than the raw one, cannot leak on any path, and cost nothing extra at run time — ownership is the design, RAII is the mechanism.

examples.title: Working through free store
examples.problem: new, delete and lifetimes on the heap. Your task: use new/delete for single objects and new[]/delete[] for arrays, correctly paired.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: use new/delete for single objects and new[]/delete[] for arrays, correctly paired. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `new` allocates and constructs, `delete` destructs and frees; arrays need `new[]` matched with `delete[]` — mismatched pairing is undefined behavior.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `auto m = std::min(a, b);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain why leaks, dangling pointers and double deletes happen and how RAII containers eliminate them — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Leaks, dangling pointers and double deletes are the price of manual ownership; each is eliminated by handing the allocation to an owner whose destructor releases it (vector, string, unique_ptr, shared_ptr). If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `new` allocates and constructs, `delete` destructs and frees; arrays need `new[]` matched with `delete[]` — mismatched pairing is undefined behavior. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `new` allocates and constructs, `delete` destructs and frees; arrays need `new[]` matched with `delete[]` — mismatched pairing is undefined behavior.

Leaks, dangling pointers and double deletes are the price of manual ownership; each is eliminated by handing the allocation to an owner whose destructor releases it (vector, string, unique_ptr, shared_ptr).
When allocation fails, `new` throws `std::bad_alloc` (nothrow new returns nullptr); handle exhaustion by owning resources in RAII handles, not by catching everywhere.

quiz.q: Memory allocated with `new X[100]` must be released by:
options: either delete or delete[] — they are synonyms
quiz.explanation: Array and single-object allocations record different bookkeeping; delete[] runs the destructor of every element, plain delete does not — the mismatch is undefined behavior.

quiz.q: What exactly does `X* p = new X{args};` do?
options: allocates raw memory only; construction is a separate call
allocates memory, constructs an X in it with args, and yields a pointer to it
constructs p on the stack and copies it to the heap
returns a reference to the new object
quiz.explanation: new is allocation plus construction as one operation — which is why its inverse, delete, is destruction plus deallocation, and why the pairs must match.

quiz.q: A function that leaks an 8 MB buffer per call and runs once per second will exhaust 16 GB in about:
options: it never will — the OS reclaims leaks
quiz.explanation: 16 GB / (8 MB/s) = 2048 s ≈ 34 minutes. The OS reclaims memory only when the process exits — a leak is lost only for the process's lifetime, which is exactly the problem.

quiz.q: The chapter's advice for managing free-store memory in ordinary application code is:
options: call delete immediately after every use
use containers and smart pointers (vector, string, unique_ptr) so ownership is expressed in types
prefer malloc/free for their clearer semantics
disable exceptions so bad_alloc cannot occur
quiz.explanation: RAII handles: the destructor is the release point, correct on every exit path. Raw new/delete belongs in the implementation of such handles, not in application code.

intro: C++11 made `{}`-lists a universal notation: the same brace syntax initializes variables, arrays, aggregates, containers, function arguments and return values. The mechanism behind the argument and return uses is `std::initializer_list` — a lightweight, immutable view of a temporary array that a function can accept by value. Along with uniformity comes safety: brace initialization rejects narrowing conversions, which is the chapter's main reason for preferring it.
objectives: Use {} lists in initialization, assignment, argument and return positions
Write functions taking std::initializer_list and iterate them
Explain why {} rejects narrowing and how the vector count/element ambiguity is resolved

concepts.statement: A brace-enclosed, comma-separated list of values is usable as an **initializer** (`int a[] {1, 2, 3};`, `vector<int> v {1, 2, 3};`), as a **right-hand side of assignment** (`v = {4, 5};`), as a **function argument** (`f({1, 2});`), and as a **return value** (`return {x, y};` for a pair). One notation, one meaning: *here are the elements*.
concepts.detail: In the range-for, a bare `{}`-list is even a range: `for (int x : {1, 2, 3, 4})` iterates a temporary list — handy in small tests and examples.

concepts.statement: A function accepts a `{}` list by declaring a parameter of type **`std::initializer_list<T>`**. The list object is a lightweight handle — a pair of pointers and a size — to a temporary array of the elements, so passing it **by value is cheap**. Inside, it offers `begin()`/`end()` (so it works with range-for and algorithms) and `size()`; it is read-only: elements cannot be modified through it.
concepts.detail: Example: `double sum(std::initializer_list<double> lst) { double s = 0; for (double x : lst) s += x; return s; }` — then `sum({1, 2, 3, 4})` returns $10$.

concepts.statement: Brace initialization is the **safe** form: it refuses narrowing conversions (10.5). `int x {7.9};` and `int x {some_double};` do not compile, where `int x = 7.9;` silently stores 7. This is the same protection `{}` gives to every initialization position it covers — one more reason to use braces as the default.
concepts.detail: The rule is about *values the compiler can see*: a literal 7.9 or a known double narrows and is rejected; a constant expression the compiler can prove fits (`char c {65};`) is accepted.

concepts.statement: The `{}` list constructor of a container **wins over other constructors** when braces are used — which resolves the famous `vector<int>` pair: `vector<int> v1(3);` is the **count** constructor (three elements, each 0), while `vector<int> v2{3};` is the **list** constructor (one element: 3). Same syntax shape, opposite meanings.
concepts.detail: The moral: with containers, `( )` means *describe the structure* (size, capacity), `{ }` means *here are the elements*. Choosing deliberately between the two pairs of brackets is part of reading modern C++ aloud correctly.

concepts.statement: **Lists.** Initializer lists everywhere. You can claim this section when you can use {} lists in initialization, assignment, argument and return positions — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 11 (Select Operations); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: sum() over an initializer list
examples.problem: Write and trace `sum({1, 2, 3, 4})` and `sum({0.5, 1.5, 2.5})` for the function above.

steps.label: The call
steps.text: `sum({1, 2, 3, 4})` — the braces in the argument position create an `initializer_list<int>`... whose elements then convert to `double` (widening, allowed) because the parameter is `initializer_list<double>`: 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0.

steps.label: The loop
steps.text: The range-for binds `x` to each element in turn: $s = 0 \to 1 \to 3 \to 6 \to 10$. Four passes, `lst.size() == 4` throughout.

steps.label: The floating case
steps.text: `sum({0.5, 1.5, 2.5})` adds $0.5 + 1.5 + 2.5 = 4.5$ — the elements were already `double`, no conversion at all.

steps.label: What is not allowed
steps.text: Assigning through the list: `*(lst.begin()) = 7;` is ill-formed — `initializer_list` is read-only, a view of an immutable temporary, not an out-parameter.

examples.result: sum({1,2,3,4}) = 10; sum({0.5,1.5,2.5}) = 4.5 — argument-position braces work because of initializer_list, and the list itself cannot be written through.

examples.title: vector<int> v(3) versus v{3}
examples.problem: Predict the contents of `vector<int> a(3);` and `vector<int> b{3};` and explain the rule that separates them.

steps.label: Parentheses: the count
steps.text: `vector<int> a(3);` calls the size constructor: 3 elements, each default-initialized to 0 → `{0, 0, 0}`, with `a.size() == 3`.

steps.label: Braces: the elements
steps.text: `vector<int> b{3};` — the `{3}` is an element list, and the list constructor is preferred over every other constructor when braces appear: one element → `{3}`, with `b.size() == 1`.

steps.label: The general rule
steps.text: For a type with an `initializer_list` constructor, `{}`-initialization prefers it. To reach a two-argument structural constructor you must use parentheses: `vector<int> c(3, 7);` is three 7s, while `vector<int> d{3, 7};` is `{3, 7}`.

steps.label: The habit to build
steps.text: Read the two forms aloud as *three empty slots* versus *the single value three* — and in your own code, prefer `{}` whenever you mean elements, since it also refuses narrowing.

examples.result: `a` = {0,0,0}; `b` = {3} — one pair of brackets chooses the count constructor, the other the element list; never write one meaning with the other brackets.

keyTakeaways: A `{}`-list is uniform notation for *the elements*: it initializes arrays and containers, appears as a right-hand side, a function argument and a return value.
Functions accept it as `std::initializer_list<T>` — a cheap by-value view (pointers + size) of a read-only temporary array, iterable with begin()/end().
Brace initialization rejects narrowing, and braces prefer a container's element-list constructor: `vector<int> v(3)` is three zeros, `vector<int> v{3}` is one 3.

quiz.q: A parameter of type `std::initializer_list<double>` is passed by value because:
options: the list is just a lightweight view (a pair of pointers and a size) of the underlying elements
by value copies each element cheaply
the standard forbids references to lists
quiz.explanation: The initializer_list object itself is a tiny handle to a temporary array of the elements; copying the handle is cheap, and the elements themselves are not copied by the pass.

quiz.q: `vector<int> v{3};` produces:
quiz.explanation: Braces select the initializer_list constructor: 3 is the single element. The parentheses form vector<int> v(3) would be three default-initialized elements.

quiz.q: Which initialization compiles?
quiz.explanation: The = form narrows silently (7.9 → 7) — legal but lossy. Every braced version rejects the narrowing it can see: that is precisely why the book prefers braces.

intro: A lambda expression is a function written where you need it — most often as an argument to an algorithm — with the enclosing scope's variables available to its body. Syntactically it is `[capture](parameters) body`; semantically it is the compiler generating a small unnamed function object whose data members are the captures. Get the capture right — what is copied, what is aliased, what happens when the lambda outlives the frame it came from — and lambdas become the cleanest way to hand behavior to code; get it wrong and you have written a time bomb.
objectives: Read and write lambda expressions with value, reference and mixed captures
Explain what a closure is and what mutable changes
Use lambdas as algorithm arguments and recognize capture-lifetime hazards

concepts.statement:
A **lambda expression** has the form **`[capture](parameters) -> return-type { body }`** (the return type is usually deduced). It *is* an expression: it evaluates to an object — a **closure** — that can be called with `(...)` like a function, stored in a variable, or passed as an argument:
```
sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a > b; });   // descending
```
concepts.detail: The book's framing: a lambda is a convenient way of defining a function object at its point of use. Its primary purpose is to specify simple actions to algorithms — the alternative, a named class with an `operator()`, is fifty lines of ceremony for one comparison.

concepts.statement: The **capture list** decides what the body sees of the enclosing scope: `[]` captures nothing; `[=]` captures every used local **by value** (a copy); `[&]` captures every used local **by reference**; `[x, &y]` captures x by value and y by reference; `[&, x]` and `[=, &y]` set the default and list exceptions.
concepts.detail: Capture happens **once, when the lambda expression is evaluated** — it is a snapshot for value captures and a set of aliases for reference captures; later declarations of new locals are not seen by the lambda at all.

concepts.statement: A lambda evaluates to an object of a compiler-generated **unnamed class**: the captures are its data members, and its call operator `operator()(params) const` runs the body. Copying the lambda copies its captured values; calling it runs the body against those members (and whatever reference members alias).
concepts.detail: This is not an implementation trick to know about — it is the *semantics*: the closure is a value, copies are independent, and the constness of `operator()` is what `mutable` removes (see the masters tier below for the full mechanics).

concepts.statement: The call operator of a lambda is `const` by default — the closure may read its value-captured members but not modify them. Adding **`mutable`** after the parameter list removes that constness, so the body may write to its value captures, with the change persisting **between calls of this closure object**.
concepts.detail: `auto next = [n = 0]() mutable { return ++n; };` — each call increments the member: 1, 2, 3, ... Without `mutable` the increment would not compile.

concepts.statement:
The bread-and-butter use is inlining behavior into standard algorithms: a comparator for `sort`, an operation for `for_each`, a predicate for `find_if` or `count_if`:
```
int evens = count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int x) { return x % 2 == 0; });
```
concepts.detail: Since C++14, parameter types may be `auto` (**generic lambdas**): `[](auto a, auto b) { return a < b; }` — the compiler generates a template call operator, one lambda serving many types.

figures.caption: Capture semantics of `[x, &y]`. The closure object holds a **copy** of x (a fresh member, snapshotted when the lambda expression is evaluated) and a **reference** member aliasing the caller's y. Calling `f(10)` runs the body against these members: $3 + 7 + 10 = 20$. Later changes to the outer x do not affect the closure; later changes to y do — and if the enclosing frame dies, the reference dangles.
