steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: C++ has no finally because destructors subsume it: one destructor replaces a release written at every exit path, and it cannot be forgotten. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: RAII ties each resource to an object whose destructor releases it, so every exit — return, break, or a thrown exception — cleans up with zero extra code. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: RAII ties each resource to an object whose destructor releases it, so every exit — return, break, or a thrown exception — cleans up with zero extra code.
C++ has no finally because destructors subsume it: one destructor replaces a release written at every exit path, and it cannot be forgotten.
Constructors report acquisition failures by throwing; destructors must never let an exception escape — a second escaping exception during unwinding calls terminate.

quiz.q: With `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lck(m);` in scope, `process()` throws. What happens to the mutex?
options: The exception machinery leaves it locked; only `catch` can release it
The guard object is destroyed during unwinding, unlocking the mutex
Undefined behavior: locks and exceptions cannot be mixed
quiz.explanation: Unwinding destroys automatic objects — including the guard, whose destructor unlocks. That is the whole point of RAII.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest reason C++ omitted a `finally` construct?
options: It was considered too slow for systems code
Destructors centralize the release once per type, instead of once per exit path, and run on every exit
The keyword was already taken by C
quiz.explanation: A finally clause is cleanup logic duplicated along every exit path; the destructor is written once in the type and dispatched by the scope rules — including the throw path.

quiz.q: An exception escapes a destructor while a first exception is unwinding the stack. What happens?
options: The two exceptions are queued and delivered in order
The first exception is abandoned and the second propagates
The destructor is suspended until the handler runs
quiz.explanation: Two exceptions in flight simultaneously cannot be represented: terminate fires. This is why destructors are implicitly noexcept and must never emit.

quiz.q: In version B of the worked example, a developer adds a fourth early `return`. How many new cleanup lines must they write?
options: Two: an unlock and a close before the return
Zero: the destructors handle every exit path
Four: releases for both resources, plus their exception-path twins
quiz.explanation: A new exit path costs RAII nothing — the return itself triggers the same destructors. That is the structural difference from per-path cleanup.

quiz.q: A function acquires two resources and then throws. Which statement explains why the language needs no `finally` clause?
options: Exceptions are disabled by default, so cleanup code never runs
The `catch` clause in the same function always releases its locals
Resources are reclaimed by the operating system at process exit
Each RAII handle destructor runs during unwinding in reverse order of construction, releasing its resource
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is a function holding two acquired resources when a throw begins unwinding. Step 2: The governing rule is unwinding semantics: fully constructed local objects are destroyed in reverse order of construction while the exception travels outward, and destructors must not themselves throw. Step 3: Tracing the throw, the second handle releases its resource first, then the first handle releases its own, so both acquisitions are undone without any dedicated cleanup clause. Step 4: The distractors fail because exceptions are enabled and active here, no `catch` is needed in the same frame, and process-exit reclamation cannot run timely per-object release. Step 5: Therefore deterministic destruction during unwinding is what replaces a `finally` clause.

intro: A class invariant is what being a valid object means. C++ enforces invariants with one sharp tool: the constructor. If a constructor exits by throwing, the object never existed at all — no destructor runs for it, no caller ever sees a half-made object. This section is about arranging code so that this single mechanism carries the entire weight of error checking.
objectives: Define class invariants and explain why the constructor is the enforcement point
State exactly what runs — and what never runs — when a constructor exits via an exception
Design validation into constructors, and contrast that with the nothrow-construction pattern of resource handles

concepts.statement: An **invariant** is a statement that holds for every object of the class throughout its observable lifetime — the conditions under which the member functions make sense. For a `Date`: year, month and day are in range and the day exists in that month. For a `vector`: the element count never exceeds the allocated capacity.
concepts.detail: The invariant is the class's definition of valid. Every member function may be written *as if* it were true — which is what makes class implementations short and clear instead of defensive.

concepts.statement: **If a constructor exits by an exception, the object never came into existence.** Its own destructor is not run; destructors of its fully constructed members and bases are run; the caller never obtains the object.
concepts.detail: This is the mechanism that enforces invariants: there is no window in which an invalid object exists to be misused. Memory for the object may have been allocated, but if construction fails it is reclaimed — by the operator new machinery and the members' destructors — before anyone can touch it.

concepts.statement: Check everything once, in the constructor; throw on bad input. Thereafter every member function assumes a valid object and states only its own preconditions. Error handling concentrates at the seams where untrusted data enters, instead of being smeared across every operation.
concepts.detail: The dual rule: functions that receive already-validated types (a `Date`, not three ints) need no checking at all. Making invalid values unrepresentable is the cheapest error handling there is.

concepts.statement: Where validation is not the issue, design the invariant so that **construction cannot fail**: `unique_ptr<int> p;` constructs empty (null) — nothing to allocate, nothing to check — and the operations that can fail are separate members (`p.reset(new int[7])` may throw `bad_alloc`).
concepts.detail: The invariant empty-or-owning is achievable with nothing to fail, which is what lets resource handles be used in the exception paths of other code — you can always construct one, unwind always destroys one.

concepts.statement: A violation of an invariant that *should be impossible* — broken by a programming mistake — is a **bug**: `assert` it, or throw a `std::logic_error`. A failure caused by the world — bad input, exhausted memory — is a **runtime error**: throw it and let a caller recover.
concepts.detail: Misclassifying the two poisons the program: throwing for bugs invites handlers that mask them; asserting on user input crashes on data. The standard library splits its exceptions into `logic_error` and `runtime_error` subhierarchies along exactly this line.

examples.title: February 29, checked by a constructor
examples.problem: A `Date(int y, int m, int d)` throws `std::domain_error` unless the day exists in the month. Predict, without running it, what `Date(2024,2,29)`, `Date(1900,2,29)` and `Date(2000,2,29)` do — and what runs if the constructor throws.

steps.label: The leap rule
steps.text: A year is leap iff $y \bmod 4 = 0$ **and** ($y \bmod 100 \neq 0$ **or** $y \bmod 400 = 0$). So the maximum day for February is 28 normally, 29 in a leap year.
$2024 \bmod 4 = 0$ and $2024 \bmod 100 = 24 \neq 0$: leap. Day 29 exists — `Date(2024,2,29)` constructs normally.

$1900 \bmod 4 = 0$ but $1900 \bmod 100 = 0$ and $1900 \bmod 400 = 300 \neq 0$: **not** leap. February has 28 days, so day 29 fails — the constructor throws. This is the classic trap: 1900 is divisible by 4 yet not a leap year.
$2000 \bmod 400 = 0$: leap (the every-400-years exception to the exception). `Date(2000,2,29)` constructs.

steps.label: What a throw runs
steps.text: Suppose `Date` has a `std::string` label member constructed before the validation in the body. On the throw: the member string destructor runs, the operator new storage is reclaimed — but no `Date` destructor runs, because no `Date` ever existed. The caller never sees a half-built object.

examples.result: 2024 and 2000 construct (leap years); 1900 throws — divisible by 100 but not by 400. On any throw: members are destroyed, the object never exists, the caller handles the exception.

examples.title: Working through enforcing invariants
examples.problem: Constructors, exceptions and design. Your task: define class invariants and explain why the constructor is the enforcement point.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define class invariants and explain why the constructor is the enforcement point. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: The invariant is the class definition of valid; the constructor is its enforcement point — a constructor that exits by an exception means the object never existed.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `try { g(); } catch (const std::exception& e) { handle(e); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — state exactly what runs — and what never runs — when a constructor exits via an exception — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: When a constructor throws, destructors of fully constructed members and bases run, but the object itself has no destructor to run, and callers never see it. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: The invariant is the class definition of valid; the constructor is its enforcement point — a constructor that exits by an exception means the object never existed. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: The invariant is the class definition of valid; the constructor is its enforcement point — a constructor that exits by an exception means the object never existed.
When a constructor throws, destructors of fully constructed members and bases run, but the object itself has no destructor to run, and callers never see it.
Validate untrusted data once at the boundary, design resource handles whose construction cannot fail, and distinguish bugs (assert, logic errors) from the world failing (throw, runtime errors).

quiz.q: `Date(1900,2,29)` throws but `Date(2000,2,29)` does not. Why?
options: Both are leap years; the constructor throws for a different reason in 1900
1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400, so it is not a leap year; 2000 is divisible by 400, so it is
Century years never have a February 29 in the Gregorian calendar
quiz.explanation: The leap rule: divisible by 4 AND (not divisible by 100 OR divisible by 400). 1900 fails the second clause; 2000 passes through the mod-400 escape.

quiz.q: A constructor of class X throws after its `std::string` member was fully constructed. What runs?
options: X destructor runs, then the member string destructor
Nothing runs; the memory is simply reclaimed
The member string destructor runs; X never existed, so no X destructor runs
The caller-side handler runs first, then cleanup
quiz.explanation: Fully constructed members and bases are destroyed; the object itself never came into existence, so its destructor is not a thing to run.

quiz.q: Why does `std::unique_ptr<int> p;` (empty construction) never throw?
options: It allocates a null block eagerly
Its invariant — empty or owning — is achievable with nothing to acquire or check
Empty construction throws but is caught by the library
quiz.explanation: The nothrow-construction pattern: the default state costs nothing to establish. Failing operations are separate members (reset, new) that may throw.

quiz.q: A required precondition that a caller violated is best reported as:
options: A runtime_error thrown for the caller to catch and retry
An assert or logic_error — it is a bug, and handlers would only mask it
quiz.explanation: Broken contracts that should be impossible are bugs: assert them in debug, or throw from the logic_error family. Runtime errors are reserved for failures of the world that callers could not have checked.

intro: Now the mechanics: what a throw really does, how handlers are chosen, what the standard exception hierarchy gives you, and what it all costs. The rules are few and exact — exception objects are copies, handlers match first-not-best, rethrow preserves the original, terminate when nobody catches — and each exists to make the safety patterns of the previous sections mechanically sound.
objectives: Apply the matching rules: handler declaration versus exception dynamic type, order of examination, and `catch (...)`
Choose between catching by reference and by value, and use bare `throw;` to rethrow the original exception
Navigate the standard exception hierarchy and state the C++11 cost model for exceptions

concepts.statement: `throw E(args)` constructs (a copy of) the exception object and begins unwinding. A handler `catch (T t)` or `catch (T& t)` matches if the exception's **dynamic** type is `T` or a class derived from `T`. Handlers of one `try` are examined **in order; the first match runs** — not the best match. `catch (...)` matches anything.
concepts.detail: Order the handlers most-derived first: a base-class clause placed earlier silently swallows everything its derived clauses were meant to see.

concepts.statement: Catch as `catch (const std::exception& e)`: the reference binds the actual exception object — no copy, no **slicing** of derived members, and virtual functions like `e.what()` dispatch to the real type. Catching by value copies and slices: the derived part is amputated before the handler sees it.
concepts.detail: Inside a handler, a bare `throw;` rethrows **the original exception object** — preserving its dynamic type — while `throw e;` would copy (and slice, if `e` is caught by value). Use bare `throw;` to pass an exception outward after partial handling.

concepts.statement: All standard exceptions derive from `std::exception`: `logic_error` (`invalid_argument`, `out_of_range`, `length_error`, `domain_error`, `future_error`), `runtime_error` (`range_error`, `overflow_error`, `underflow_error`, `system_error`), and direct children `bad_alloc`, `bad_cast`, `bad_typeid`, `bad_function_call`.
concepts.detail: Derive your own exceptions from `std::exception` (or `std::runtime_error`) so that generic handlers — logging at the top of `main` — can catch, `what()` and rethrow them uniformly.

concepts.statement: The runtime searches outward for a matching handler, popping frames and running their destructors as it goes (**stack unwinding**). If no handler exists, or an exception escapes a `noexcept` function, `std::terminate` is called — for a `noexcept` violation, immediately, without unwinding.
concepts.detail: The search is by *dynamic* type of the exception against the *static* types of handler declarations, scanning scopes and then frames outward — which is why a `try` in a library can recover local failures while letting others pass through untouched.

concepts.statement: On the common implementation (table-driven, "zero-cost" unwinding), a program that throws nothing pays essentially nothing — the cost is moved into static tables consulted only when a throw happens. A `throw` itself costs far more than a `return` (and grows with the number of frames popped), which is irrelevant for rare errors and wrong for hot control flow.
concepts.detail: The design consequence: exceptions are for the exceptional. If a failure is expected on the fast path — a parse loop rejecting most tokens — return codes or expected-style types beat exceptions; `noexcept` additionally lets the compiler drop unwind bookkeeping around calls it knows cannot fail.

examples.title: First match, not best match
examples.problem: `v.at(7)` on a size-5 `vector` throws `std::out_of_range`. For each handler list, say which clause runs: (A) `catch (std::out_of_range&)` then `catch (std::logic_error&)`; (B) `catch (std::logic_error&)` then `catch (std::out_of_range&)`; (C) `catch (std::exception&)` only; (D) `catch (std::range_error&)` only.

steps.label: The type chain
steps.text: `std::out_of_range` derives from `std::logic_error`, which derives from `std::exception`. `std::range_error` derives from `std::runtime_error` — a *sibling* branch: it does not match at all.

steps.label: List A
steps.text: The first clause matches the dynamic type exactly: the `out_of_range` handler runs. The `logic_error` clause never gets consulted — correct style, most-derived first.

steps.label: List B
steps.text: The first clause matches too (a base-class reference binds the derived object): the `logic_error` handler runs, **even though a more specific clause sits right below it**. Compiles fine, silently wrong intent — the classic ordering bug.

steps.label: List C
steps.text: The single base clause matches and runs. One coarse handler is fine when all it does is log `e.what()` and rethrow with `throw;` — the rethrow still carries the original `out_of_range` object.

steps.label: List D
steps.text: No clause matches — `range_error` is on the runtime_error branch. The exception propagates out of the `try` entirely, unwinding further frames until another handler or `std::terminate`.

examples.result: A: out_of_range clause. B: logic_error clause — first match wins, order is semantics. C: exception clause. D: nothing matches, the exception escapes the try block.

examples.title: Working through throwing and catching exceptions
examples.problem: The mechanics and the cost model. Your task: apply the matching rules: handler declaration versus exception dynamic type, order of examination, and `catch (...)`.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: apply the matching rules: handler declaration versus exception dynamic type, order of examination, and `catch (...)`. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Handlers match by the exception dynamic type against declaration types, are examined in order, and the FIRST match runs — put derived-class handlers before base-class ones.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `try { g(); } catch (const std::exception& e) { handle(e); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — choose between catching by reference and by value, and use bare `throw;` to rethrow the original exception — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Catch by const reference to avoid copying and slicing; rethrow the original with a bare throw; derive your own exception types from std::exception. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Handlers match by the exception dynamic type against declaration types, are examined in order, and the FIRST match runs — put derived-class handlers before base-class ones. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Handlers match by the exception dynamic type against declaration types, are examined in order, and the FIRST match runs — put derived-class handlers before base-class ones.
Catch by const reference to avoid copying and slicing; rethrow the original with a bare throw; derive your own exception types from std::exception.
The zero-cost model makes non-throwing code free; a throw is far costlier than a return and grows with frames popped — exceptions are for the exceptional, not for control flow.

quiz.q: Handlers `catch (std::logic_error&)` then `catch (std::out_of_range&)`; an `out_of_range` is thrown. Which runs?
options: `out_of_range` — the most specific match is preferred
`logic_error` — handlers are examined in order and the first match runs
Ambiguous: the compiler rejects the pair
quiz.explanation: Matching is first-match-wins, not best-match: the base-class clause matches the derived exception and runs; the specific clause below is dead code. Order handlers most-derived first.

quiz.q: `catch (std::exception e)` catches an `out_of_range` by value. What is lost?
options: The exception can no longer be rethrown
The derived part is sliced off: e is a plain exception, and any copied state of out_of_range is gone
quiz.explanation: By-value catching copies into the static type of the declaration, amputating the derived portion. Catch by const reference — `catch (const std::exception& e)` — instead.

quiz.q: Inside a handler, what does a bare `throw;` do?
options: Rethrows the original exception object, preserving its dynamic type
Throws a copy of the caught object, sliced to the declared type
Clears the exception and returns normally
quiz.explanation: Bare throw re-activates the exception currently being handled — the original object, original type. throw e; by contrast copies (and slices, if caught by value).

quiz.q: Under the table-driven (zero-cost) implementation model:
options: Every function call pays a small tax to support potential throws
Both normal and exceptional paths cost the same
Code that never throws pays essentially nothing; the cost lives in static tables consulted only when a throw actually happens
Throws are as cheap as returns by mandate of the standard
quiz.explanation: The zero-cost model moves unwinding information out of the hot path entirely; a throw is expensive relative to a return, which is fine for rare errors and wrong for control flow.

intro: Now the chapter cashes in its philosophy: a small `vector`, built the way the standard one is, whose every operation states and keeps a guarantee. Two ideas do the work — `vector_base`, a resource handle for raw memory, and `reserve`, which moves-if-safe and copies otherwise so that `push_back` keeps the strong guarantee even while elements are in transit.
objectives: Explain the vector_base split and how its destructor makes buffer management exception-safe
Trace reserve and push_back step by step, identifying the commit point and the fallback to copying
Compute the amortized cost of growth and distinguish checked from unchecked access

concepts.statement: `vector_base` is the raw-memory layer: an allocator plus three pointers — `elem` (start of elements), `space` (one past the last constructed element), `last` (end of storage) — with a destructor that unconditionally destroys elements and deallocates. size is `space - elem`; capacity is `last - elem`.
concepts.detail: Separating it from `vector` gives the buffer a handle whose destructor frees it *even while an exception is in flight* — RAII applied to raw memory. The invariant `elem <= space <= last` is what every operation must preserve.

concepts.statement: Growth is: allocate a new `vector_base` with capacity `max(2*capacity, needed)`; **move** the elements into it if their move is `noexcept`, **copy** otherwise; swap the three pointers; let the old base's destructor clean up the old buffer.
concepts.detail: The two-phase structure — build the new arrangement aside, then swap — is the strong guarantee made executable. If anything throws before the swap, the vector still points at its untouched old buffer.

concepts.statement: After ensuring space, `push_back` constructs the new element at `space`, then increments `space`. The commit is a single construction: if it throws, the size is unchanged — the vector gained nothing and lost nothing.
concepts.detail: Every step before the construction (reallocation, transfer) is already exception-safe; the construction itself is the last, only, and atomic visible effect.

concepts.statement: `at(i)` validates `0 <= i < size()` and throws `std::out_of_range`; `operator[](i)` is unchecked — the caller has already validated, so no test runs (at most a debug-build `assert`).
concepts.detail: Offering both is the design: pay for the check exactly on the paths where the index is untrusted. The out-of-range call to `operator[]` is a precondition violation — a bug, not an error to handle.

concepts.statement: Implement `a = b` as: make a temp copy of `b`'s elements, `swap` it into `a`, let the temp destroy the old state. Self-assignment is safe for free, and any throw happens while `a` is still intact — the strong guarantee without a special case.
concepts.detail: This copy-and-swap shape reuses the machinery of `reserve`: it is the same theorem (build aside, commit by swap) applied to assignment instead of growth.

examples.title: The arithmetic of doubling
examples.problem: An empty `vector` (capacity 0) receives 1000 `push_back`s. The growth policy doubles capacity, first allocation is 1, and each reallocation moves (nothrow move) exactly the current size. How many allocations occur, how many element moves in total, and what is the amortized move count per push?

steps.label: When reallocation happens
steps.text: A push that finds size == capacity triggers reserve. With doubling: pushes 1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, 65, 129, 257, 513 — the capacities before them are 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512.

steps.label: Count allocations
steps.text: Eleven pushes trigger reserve: 11 allocations, taking capacity 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024. The 1000th push never reallocates again — capacity 1024 suffices.

steps.label: Count moves
steps.text: Each reallocation moves the current size: $0+1+2+4+8+\cdots+512 = 2^{10} - 1 = 1023$ element moves in total.

steps.label: Amortize
steps.text: $1023/1000 \approx 1.02$ moves per push. In general, for $n$ pushes the total is below $2n$ (the worst case is just past a doubling: $n = 2^k + 1$ gives $2^{k+1} - 1 < 2n$) — each element is moved at most about once per *doubling of the whole vector*, which is the sense in which growth is free.

steps.label: The slack
steps.text: The price is memory: final capacity 1024 for 1000 elements — 24 spare slots, under 2.4% overhead, and the next 24 pushes cost no allocation at all.

examples.result: 1000 pushes: 11 allocations, 1023 element moves, amortized about 1.02 moves per push — bounded by 2n in general, with 2.4% capacity slack at the end.

examples.title: Working through a vector implementation
examples.problem: An industrial-strength vector with exceptions. Your task: explain the vector_base split and how its destructor makes buffer management exception-safe.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: explain the vector_base split and how its destructor makes buffer management exception-safe. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: vector_base owns the raw buffer, so its destructor frees memory even when an exception is mid-flight — RAII under the vector itself.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `try { g(); } catch (const std::exception& e) { handle(e); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — trace reserve and push_back step by step, identifying the commit point and the fallback to copying — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: reserve builds the new arrangement aside, moves if noexcept and copies otherwise, then commits with a nothrow pointer swap: push_back inherits the strong guarantee. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: vector_base owns the raw buffer, so its destructor frees memory even when an exception is mid-flight — RAII under the vector itself. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: vector_base owns the raw buffer, so its destructor frees memory even when an exception is mid-flight — RAII under the vector itself.
reserve builds the new arrangement aside, moves if noexcept and copies otherwise, then commits with a nothrow pointer swap: push_back inherits the strong guarantee.
Doubling growth makes 1000 pushes cost 1023 element moves (under 2n always); at() validates and throws out_of_range while operator[] trusts the caller.

quiz.q: An empty `vector` with pure doubling receives 1000 `push_back`s (first allocation capacity 1). How many element moves total?
options: It depends on the heap state
quiz.explanation: Moves happen at each reallocation, moving the current size: 1+2+4+...+512 = 2^10 - 1 = 1023. The bound is under 2n for any n.

quiz.q: Why keep the buffer in a separate `vector_base` class rather than directly in `vector`?
options: To reduce the size of the vector object by one pointer
Because its destructor frees the buffer even while an exception is unwinding — raw memory gets a RAII handle of its own
To allow vector to inherit from the allocator
Because templates cannot contain raw pointers
quiz.explanation: During reserve, a vector_base holds the new (or old) buffer; if anything throws, its destructor still destroys elements and deallocates — the exception-safety of the whole design rests on it.

quiz.q: During `reserve(8)` on a capacity-4 vector with nothrow-move elements, who frees the OLD buffer?
options: The caller, via an explicit delete
A temporary vector_base whose destructor runs as it goes out of scope — after the swap made it owner of the old buffer
quiz.explanation: The swap passes old-buffer ownership to the local base; its destructor (running normally or during unwinding) destroys the old elements and deallocates.

quiz.q: Which statement about `at()` versus `operator[]` is the design intent?
options: at() is always preferred because safety is free
operator[] throws std::out_of_range only in debug builds
at() validates and throws out_of_range for untrusted indices; operator[] is unchecked because the caller has already validated — the out-of-range call is a precondition violation, a bug
Both are checked; at() is simply faster
quiz.explanation: TC++PL provides both on purpose: pay the validation cost exactly where indices are untrusted; treat an out-of-range operator[] as a bug (assert), not an error to recover from.

intro: The chapter's rules of thumb compress its philosophy into checkable habits. Three of them carry most of the weight: design error handling as part of the interface from the start; throw to report an unmet promise and catch only what you can handle; and prefer RAII to any amount of manual cleanup.
objectives: Recite the chapter's core advice on when to throw, when to assert, and when to use ordinary control flow
Explain why error handling must be designed in from the start rather than retrofitted
Audit a small design against the advice list and justify each verdict

concepts.statement: **Error handling is part of the interface, so it must be designed when the interface is designed** — which guarantee each operation offers is as contractual as its postconditions. Retrofitting guarantees into working code is a redesign, not a patch.
concepts.detail: The practical form: for each operation, write down which of basic/strong/nothrow it offers and why callers need that. The audit takes minutes on a whiteboard and months to reverse.

concepts.term: Throw to report, catch to recover
concepts.statement: **Throw an exception to indicate you cannot perform an assigned task; catch an exception only if you can handle it.** Do not use `throw` for ordinary control flow — it is far costlier than a `return` and it scatters the logic; do not write catch-alls that swallow errors and continue as if nothing happened.
concepts.detail: The corollary: exceptions are for the exceptional. A parser rejecting most tokens on its fast path wants a return code or an expected-style type, not a throw per failure.

concepts.statement: **Never write cleanup that a resource handle could own.** Every acquire/release pair — memory, locks, files, sockets, transactions — belongs in a class whose destructor releases it, so every exit path, including throws, is correct by construction.
concepts.detail: The advice closes the loop with the rest of the chapter: exceptions make code with RAII *more* robust than code without them, because the destructor path is the one path that cannot be forgotten.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Design error handling with the interface: which guarantee each operation offers is a contract, and retrofitting is redesign.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

concepts.statement: Take the objectives as review questions: recite the chapter’s core advice on when to throw, when to assert, and when to use ordinary control flow? Then explain why error handling must be designed in from the start rather than retrofitted? Answer each from the code in front of you, not from memory — the gap between the two answers is the review finding.
concepts.detail: A rule you can derive from the chapter you can also correctly suspend; a rule applied without its reason becomes superstition, so cite the reason in the review note.

examples.title: Auditing a design against the advice
examples.problem: A colleague's `read_config(path)` returns an error code, locks a mutex manually, and `delete`s a `new char[4096]` buffer on each of its three exits. Audit it with the chapter's checklist and prescribe the rewrite.

steps.label: Resource audit
steps.text: Two acquire/release pairs managed by hand (mutex, buffer) across 3 exit paths = 6 cleanup sites, and one wrong `delete` (missing `[]`) besides. Verdict: wrap both — `std::lock_guard`, `std::unique_ptr<char[]>` — per the RAII law.

steps.label: Failure classification
steps.text: Config files are missing or malformed in the field — a runtime error the caller may recover from (default config, user prompt). Verdict: throw `std::runtime_error` with context, not an error code callers will ignore.

steps.label: Guarantee choice
steps.text: Callers hold partially-built state across this call. Verdict: offer the strong guarantee — build the parse in a temporary and commit by move, the copy-and-commit shape of 13.2/13.6.

steps.label: Frequency check
steps.text: Read once at startup: cost of a throw is irrelevant. (Had this been per-frame hot code, the verdict on error codes would flip.)

steps.label: Who recovers
steps.text: The GUI wants to prompt; the service wants to log and die. Both catch `std::runtime_error` where context exists — impossible with an ignored return code.

examples.result: Rewrite: lock_guard + unique_ptr (0 cleanup sites), throw runtime_error on malformed input, temp-then-commit for the strong guarantee — each verdict is a direct application of the checklist.

examples.title: Reviewing exception handling code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: recite the chapter’s core advice on when to throw, when to assert, and when to use ordinary control flow.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Design error handling with the interface: which guarantee each operation offers is a contract, and retrofitting is redesign.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `try { g(); } catch (const std::exception& e) { handle(e); }`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: explain why error handling must be designed in from the start rather than retrofitted. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Throw to report an unmet promise, catch only what you can handle, and keep throws off hot paths where failures are expected.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Design error handling with the interface: which guarantee each operation offers is a contract, and retrofitting is redesign. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Design error handling with the interface: which guarantee each operation offers is a contract, and retrofitting is redesign.
Throw to report an unmet promise, catch only what you can handle, and keep throws off hot paths where failures are expected.
Any acquire/release pair belongs in a resource handle — exceptions then strengthen code, because destructor cleanup is the one path that cannot be forgotten.

quiz.q: Which practice does the chapter explicitly reject?
options: Catching only exception types you can actually handle
Using `throw` for the ordinary flow of a loop that frequently takes that branch
Documenting which guarantee each operation offers
quiz.explanation: Exceptions are for the exceptional: a frequently-taken branch thrown as control flow pays the unwinding cost on the hot path and obscures the logic. Use ordinary returns there.

quiz.q: Why is retrofitting error handling into a finished design costly?
options: It cannot be done without changing the ABI
Guarantees shape interfaces — which operations can throw, what state callers may rely on — so adding them later forces redesign of every caller that guessed otherwise
The compiler caches old exception specifications
It is not costly; this is a style preference
quiz.explanation: The guarantees are interface contracts, not implementation details. Callers written against unspecified behavior have already guessed; changing the guess breaks them.

quiz.q: The single most load-bearing habit from the chapter is:
options: Catching every exception as early as possible
Wrapping every acquire/release pair in a resource handle so cleanup runs on every exit path
Avoiding exceptions in favor of error codes
quiz.explanation: RAII makes every exit path — return, break, throw — correct by construction. Everything else in the chapter is policy; this one is the mechanism.

intro: Real programs are not written; they are composed — from libraries written by people who never met, at different times, with no shared naming authority. The central problem of scale is making that composition possible: how do names chosen by strangers coexist in one program? This chapter's answer is the namespace, and the section before the mechanism itself is about why the older answers failed.
objectives: State the composition problem: separately developed libraries must interoperate without a global naming authority
Evaluate the pre-namespace solutions — prefixes, macros, long names — and say why each fails
Distinguish what a module must provide (a coherent interface plus hidden implementation) from what a file or a class provides

concepts.statement: Software is built by composing independently developed parts, and **no global authority coordinates their names**. Two libraries will both define `Node`, `list`, `print` — not through carelessness, but because each is a natural name within its own context. A module mechanism must let names coexist without requiring the authors to have known about each other.
concepts.detail: The deeper requirement behind the naming one: a library must also keep its implementation details out of the way — what a user of the library cannot name, the user cannot break or depend on.

concepts.statement: A module is a coherent set of services presented through an **interface** (the declarations users need) and implemented by an **implementation** (the definitions users should never see). What users see is exactly what the module author intends them to see — and nothing more.
concepts.detail: In C++ the class already does this at the type level (member names are scoped by the class; `private` keeps implementation out). The namespace extends the same idea to any set of names: functions, types, constants, templates — the module is a design unit, not a file.

concepts.statement: The C tradition attacked clashes with **prefixes** (`pthread_`, `str`-functions), the preprocessor with **macros** (`#define`), and convention with **long unique names**. Prefixes are verbose, unenforced and cannot group a family of overloads; macros are untyped, unscoped text substitution that silently rewrites unrelated code; long names punish every reader for a collision that may never happen.
concepts.detail: What none of them offer: a scope that can be opened and closed by the compiler, searched selectively, extended later, and composed with overloading. That shopping list becomes the namespace specification.

concepts.statement: Whatever the design documents say, the *enforceable* interface of a module in C++ is what its declarations make visible: the names, their types, and their access — classes control access to members; namespaces control which names are visible from where.
concepts.detail: Chapter 15 adds the physical layer: the header is the interface *as seen by the compiler*, and separate compilation is what lets the interface be shared while implementations stay private.

concepts.statement: **Composition Problems.** Why modules and names must be managed. You can claim this section when you can state the composition problem: separately developed libraries must interoperate without a global naming authority — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 14 (Namespaces); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: The two-Node project
examples.problem: A build combines a text library (`text.h`: `class Node`, `class Link`, `void print(std::ostream&, const Node&)`) and a graph library (`graph.h`: `struct Node`, `struct Link`, `void draw(const Node&)`). One new translation unit includes both headers. Predict every compile error and price the two candidate fixes.

steps.label: Diagnose
steps.text: Two definitions of `Node` and two of `Link` appear at the same (global) scope: **2 redefinition errors**. The functions do not clash at all — `print` and `draw` are different names, and two functions of the same name would merely form an overload set (they take different parameter types).

steps.label: Fix A — rename
steps.text: Make the text library use `TextNode`. Say `Node` appears at 60 sites inside the library: 60 edits, every one breaking third-party clients that compiled against the old names — the collision is exported to everyone downstream.

steps.label: Fix B — namespaces
steps.text: Wrap each header once: `namespace Text { /* as before */ }` and `namespace Graph { /* as before */ }`: **2 lines per header**, zero internal edits. Users write `Text::Node` or `Graph::Node`, or bring one name in with a using-declaration at a use site.

steps.label: Price it
steps.text: Rename: about 120 use-site edits across both libraries (60 + 60) plus all client code, and binary compatibility is gone. Namespaces: 4 lines changed, and code that does not mention the colliding name is untouched.

examples.result: Namespaces remove both collisions with 4 changed lines and zero client edits; renaming touches roughly 120 sites and breaks every existing user of both libraries.

examples.title: Working through composition problems
examples.problem: Why modules and names must be managed. Your task: state the composition problem: separately developed libraries must interoperate without a global naming authority.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: state the composition problem: separately developed libraries must interoperate without a global naming authority. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Composition is the norm: independently written libraries must coexist with no global naming authority, so the module mechanism must make name coexistence automatic.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `namespace Lib { int version(); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — evaluate the pre-namespace solutions — prefixes, macros, long names — and say why each fails — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Prefixes, macros and long names are workarounds that are verbose, untyped or unenforced — none gives a compiler-managed scope that also groups overloads. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Composition is the norm: independently written libraries must coexist with no global naming authority, so the module mechanism must make name coexistence automatic. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Composition is the norm: independently written libraries must coexist with no global naming authority, so the module mechanism must make name coexistence automatic.
Prefixes, macros and long names are workarounds that are verbose, untyped or unenforced — none gives a compiler-managed scope that also groups overloads.
A module is an interface plus a hidden implementation; in C++ the class provides it for types and the namespace for any set of names.

quiz.q: A translation unit includes both `text.h` and `graph.h`, each defining `class Node` at global scope. What happens?
options: The linker merges the two Node classes
The second definition silently shadows the first
A redefinition error at compile time
Undefined behavior; it compiles and misbehaves
quiz.explanation: Two definitions of the same name at one scope are a compile-time redefinition error — the collision is at least loud, which is the problem the section wants solved rather than merely reported.

quiz.q: Why is `#define MAX_COUNT 100` a poor substitute for namespace discipline?
options: It is untyped, unscoped text substitution: it rewrites any later occurrence of those letters, including in unrelated code and strings
The preprocessor runs after the compiler
quiz.explanation: A macro has no scope, no type and no respect for context — it renames everything, everywhere, before the compiler ever parses the result.

quiz.q: The two libraries also define `print(std::ostream&, const TextNode&)` and `print(std::ostream&, const GraphNode&)`. Once the parameter types differ, these functions:
options: Clash: the same name can only be defined once
Form an overload set — which is precisely the composition behavior wanted, and namespaces keep it under control
Are resolved by the linker at random
quiz.explanation: Same name, different parameter types: an overload set. The composition problem is about uncontrolled collisions, and overloading is the controlled, compiler-checked version of name sharing.

intro: A namespace is a named scope: a way to group declarations so they do not pollute the global namespace, while remaining reachable by qualification, by explicit import of one name, or implicitly through the types of the arguments you call with. The rules here — qualification, using-declarations, using-directives and argument-dependent lookup — are the daily grammar of every large C++ codebase.
objectives: Define namespaces, their openness across files, and qualified access with the scope resolution operator
Distinguish using-declarations from using-directives, and place each where it is safe (never a directive in a header)
Explain argument-dependent lookup and why generic code and operators depend on it

concepts.statement: `namespace Chrono { /* declarations */ }` places every declaration inside a new named scope. Members are named by **qualification**: `Chrono::Date`. A namespace is **open**: it may be reopened and extended in the same or other files, even other translation units — standard headers are all members of `std` this way.
concepts.detail: Nesting is ordinary scoping: `Lib::V2::f` reads outside-in. The global scope is spelled with a leading `::` (`::x` is the global `x`, whatever local `x` shadows).

concepts.statement: A **using-declaration** imports one name: `using std::string;` makes `string` mean `std::string` in this scope. A **using-directive** opens the whole namespace: `using namespace std;` makes every name of `std` reachable from this scope. Declarations are safe almost anywhere; directives belong in implementation files — **never in headers**, where they would apply to every includer and could change the meaning of later code.
concepts.detail: Both are transition tools: the goal is code that qualifies (`std::sort`) or imports selectively (`using std::swap;` before a `swap(x, y)` call), so that a reader can see which names come from where.

concepts.statement: When calling `f(x)` where `x`'s type is a member of namespace `N`, the lookup set for `f` **includes `N`** — the namespace of an argument contributes candidates. This is why `cout << d` finds `Chrono`'s `operator<<` with no qualification and no using-declaration at all.
concepts.detail: ADL is the glue between namespaces and overloading: operators (which cannot be qualified in call syntax) and customization points like `swap` rely on it entirely. It is also why your operators belong in the same namespace as their class — that is where ADL will look for them.

concepts.statement: An **unnamed namespace** `namespace { /* ... */ }` has internal linkage: its members are invisible outside this translation unit — the modern replacement for file-`static`. A **namespace alias** `namespace Cur = Lib::V2;` binds a short name to a long or versioned one, at one place.
concepts.detail: Aliases are the standard versioning mechanism: flip one alias and every `Cur::`-qualified call site follows; see 14.4.

concepts.statement: Using-declarations for the same function name from different namespaces **merge into one overload set** (if their signatures differ). A using-directive does the same, but ambiguities — including those created later by library growth — are detected only at the call site.
concepts.detail: This is composition at the function level: `A::f(int)` and `B::f(double)` can coexist as candidates, with the usual overload resolution picking per call — the worked example runs the numbers.

examples.title: Three calls, one merged overload set
examples.problem: Given `namespace A { int f(int); }` and `namespace B { double f(double); }`, plus `using A::f; using B::f;` in one function: which function runs for `f(1)`, `f(2.5)` and `f('a')`?

steps.label: The set
steps.text: The two using-declarations merge `A::f(int)` and `B::f(double)` into a single overload set of two candidates, visible as plain `f` in this scope.

steps.label: f(1)
steps.text: Candidates: `A::f(int)` needs an exact match; `B::f(double)` needs int-to-double conversion. Exact match wins: **A::f(int)**.

steps.label: f(2.5)
steps.text: Symmetric: `B::f(double)` is exact, `A::f(int)` would need double-to-int conversion. **B::f(double)** runs.

steps.label: f('a')
steps.text: Neither is exact: `char` to `int` is an **integral promotion**; `char` to `double` is a **floating-integral conversion**. Promotions rank better than conversions: **A::f(int)** runs — the same rule that keeps `'a' + 1` integer arithmetic.

steps.label: Why no ambiguity
steps.text: Ambiguity would require two equally-good candidates, e.g. two exact matches or two same-rank conversions. With one int and one double overload, every arithmetic argument resolves — 0 ambiguous calls in 3.

examples.result: A::f(int); B::f(double); A::f(int) — the merged overload set resolves all three calls by the standard ranking: exact, then promotion, then conversion.

examples.title: Working through namespaces
examples.problem: Namespace definition and use. Your task: define namespaces, their openness across files, and qualified access with the scope resolution operator.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define namespaces, their openness across files, and qualified access with the scope resolution operator. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A namespace is an open named scope: reopened across files and translation units, its members reached by qualification or selective using-declarations.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `namespace Lib { int version(); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — distinguish using-declarations from using-directives, and place each where it is safe (never a directive in a header) — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Import one name with a using-declaration where it aids readability; keep using-directives to implementation files and out of headers entirely. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A namespace is an open named scope: reopened across files and translation units, its members reached by qualification or selective using-declarations. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A namespace is an open named scope: reopened across files and translation units, its members reached by qualification or selective using-declarations.
Import one name with a using-declaration where it aids readability; keep using-directives to implementation files and out of headers entirely.
ADL searches the namespaces of a call's argument types — which is how operators and swap are found without qualification, and why they live beside their class.

quiz.q: Why is `using namespace std;` at global scope in a header forbidden by the house rules?
options: It slows down compilation of every includer by orders of magnitude
It injects all of std into the global namespace of every translation unit that includes it — directly or transitively — creating ambiguity and changing the meaning of later code
It makes every std function inline
quiz.explanation: A using-directive in a header applies to every includer, who never chose it. New std names would then shadow or collide with local names — the exact composition failure namespaces were invented to fix.

quiz.q: In the worked example, `f('a')` resolved to `A::f(int)` rather than `B::f(double)`. Why?
options: Declarations earlier in the set win
int parameters are always preferred over double
The char-to-int integral promotion outranks the char-to-double conversion in overload resolution
It is ambiguous and the call is ill-formed
quiz.explanation: Neither candidate is exact, so resolution falls to ranking: promotions (char to int) beat conversions (char to double) — the same ladder every other overload resolution uses.

quiz.q: How does `cout << d` for a `Chrono::Date d` find the right `operator<<` without any qualification or using-declaration?
options: Operators are always found in the global namespace
Every operator is a member of std
Argument-dependent lookup adds the namespaces of the arguments — std for cout, Chrono for d — to the candidate set
The compiler guesses from the file name
quiz.explanation: ADL: each argument contributes its namespace to the search, where the member operator<< of std and the free Chrono::operator<< are both found as candidates.

quiz.q: Which statement about namespace openness is correct?
options: A namespace may be opened only once per file
A namespace may be reopened across files and translation units; the definitions accumulate into one namespace
Reopening a namespace in a second translation unit is an ODR violation
Once closed, a namespace is sealed
quiz.explanation: Every standard header reopens std. The namespace is a logical scope, not a file-boundary artifact — which is what lets a library distribute its interface across many headers.

intro: Namespaces are the mechanism; modularization is the discipline. The design question is where to draw module boundaries, what to expose at each boundary, and how to keep interfaces small enough to change. The rules are few — minimize, do not expose implementation, keep interfaces strongly typed and stable — and every one of them is about who is allowed to depend on what.
objectives: Design module boundaries: a module expresses a coherent concept, not a file or a single class
Apply interface minimization and justify it in terms of what clients may come to depend on
Keep implementation details out of interfaces and interfaces stable across implementation change

concepts.term: A module is a design unit
concepts.statement: A module is a set of declarations representing **one coherent concept** — not a file, not a class, not a layer cake. The Chrono module is "calendar time"; its interface is `Date`, its ordering, its arithmetic and its I/O — no more.
concepts.detail: The test of coherence: can you describe the module in one sentence a user of the whole system understands? If the description is a list, the module is a grab bag and should be split.

concepts.statement: **Expose only what users need — the smallest set of names that does the job.** Every name in the interface is a promise: it must keep working, forever, because someone will call it. Names you never exposed you can still change freely.
concepts.detail: The asymmetry is the economics: adding a name to an interface later is cheap; removing one is a breaking change for every client. When in doubt, leave it out — an interface is easier to grow than to shrink.

concepts.statement: **What users cannot see, they cannot depend on.** Helper functions, tables and algorithms belong in an implementation namespace (or an unnamed namespace in the .cpp file), not beside the interface; exposing them couples every client to a detail you intended to replace.
concepts.detail: The physical leak is the subtler one: private members and private helper types still appear in the class definition and pull their headers into every client — the include-graph cost that chapter 15 attacks with firewalls.

concepts.statement: **Let types do the checking.** A function taking `const Date&` rejects nonsense at compile time that three `int` parameters would defer to runtime validation — the invariant machinery of chapter 13 starts with an interface that makes invalid values unrepresentable.
concepts.detail: Ties back to error handling: if the type system filters the impossible, the exceptions that remain to throw are the genuinely exceptional.

concepts.statement: The interface should change far more slowly than the implementation. Organize so the changes you expect — algorithms, representation, performance work — touch only implementation namespaces, and the interface names survive untouched.
concepts.detail: This is why versioning (14.4) and interface minimization interact: a smaller surface is a smaller thing to keep stable, and a stable surface is the module's contract with the future.

examples.title: Shrinking a draft interface
examples.problem: A draft Chrono interface exposes 15 names: `Date`, `year`, `month`, `day`, `operator==`, `operator<`, `operator<<`, `to_string`, `from_string`, plus helpers `is_leap`, `month_length`, `day_of_week`, `normalize`, `epoch_days`, `validate`. Audit the list: which names belong in the public interface?

steps.label: What users need
steps.text: Construct and inspect dates (`Date`, `year`, `month`, `day`), order and compare (`operator==`, `operator<`), print and parse (`operator<<`, `to_string`, `from_string`): 9 names carry the whole service.

steps.label: What is implementation
steps.text: `is_leap`, `month_length`, `normalize`, `epoch_days`, `validate` are machinery: a user who calls `is_leap` directly has coupled to the Gregorian representation — exactly the detail the module exists to hide (proleptic calendars, day-count conventions and all).

steps.label: The judgement call
steps.text: `day_of_week` is genuinely useful — but it is derived data, and it is the kind of name that grows relatives (`iso_week_day`, `weekday_name`). Verdict: keep it out until a user needs it; adding later is compatible, removing is not.

steps.label: Move, do not delete
steps.text: The 6 helpers go to `namespace Chrono::impl` (or an unnamed namespace in the .cpp). They remain available to the module itself — and invisible to clients, who cannot form dependencies they cannot name.

steps.label: Count the saving
steps.text: 15 exposed names shrink to 9 — a 40% reduction in the surface that must stay stable, bought with one namespace relocation and zero loss of service.

examples.result: Keep 9 names; retire 6 into an implementation namespace. Every retired name is a design decision that stays reversible.

examples.title: Working through modularization and interfaces
examples.problem: Designing module boundaries. Your task: design module boundaries: a module expresses a coherent concept, not a file or a single class.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: design module boundaries: a module expresses a coherent concept, not a file or a single class. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A module is a coherent concept expressed as a small interface; it is not a file or a class — files are the physical concern of chapter 15.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `namespace Lib { int version(); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — apply interface minimization and justify it in terms of what clients may come to depend on — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Minimize: every interface name is a promise to keep it working; adding later is cheap, removing breaks clients — so leave out what is merely useful. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A module is a coherent concept expressed as a small interface; it is not a file or a class — files are the physical concern of chapter 15. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A module is a coherent concept expressed as a small interface; it is not a file or a class — files are the physical concern of chapter 15.
Minimize: every interface name is a promise to keep it working; adding later is cheap, removing breaks clients — so leave out what is merely useful.
Implementation helpers belong in implementation namespaces where clients cannot name them; strongly typed parameters let the compiler reject what runtime validation would otherwise throw.

quiz.q: Which names belong in a module interface?
options: All public, private and helper names, for documentation value
Only the names users need to get the module's service done — the smallest such set
Only class names; functions never belong in an interface
Whatever is easiest to implement first
quiz.explanation: Minimization is the economics of promises: each exposed name must work forever, so the interface is the minimum that delivers the service — nothing more.

quiz.q: A colleague argues `is_leap` should stay in the public interface because users keep asking for it. The chapter's strongest counter is:
options: It is too slow to be public
Exposing it couples users to the calendar representation the module exists to hide; a user who cannot name it cannot depend on it
Leap years will be abolished eventually
Only operators can be interface members
quiz.explanation: Every name in the interface is a commitment. is_leap is representation machinery — a user who calls it has bypassed the abstraction boundary the module was drawn to enforce.

quiz.q: Why does an interface change more slowly than an implementation?
options: Interface files are larger and compile slower
Because clients depend on interface names and must not break, while implementation namespaces can change invisibly
It does not; both change together
quiz.explanation: The interface is the contract; the implementation is a detail behind it. That asymmetry is the whole point of drawing the boundary.

intro: Composition at scale is the payoff chapter: libraries in their own namespaces, glued together with qualification at boundaries, pass-through re-exports, versioned sub-namespaces, and ADL doing the operator wiring. The techniques here are how million-line systems absorb a new library version without touching a thousand files.
objectives: Compose libraries by qualifying at boundaries and importing selectively inside function scopes
Use pass-through using-declarations to build facades, and namespace aliases to version and migrate
Explain how ADL plus overloading provides the wiring for composed generic code (swap, operators)

concepts.statement: Compose libraries by keeping names in their namespaces and **qualifying where they meet** — `Chrono::Date d;` in application code — with using-declarations (`using Graph::Node;`) admitted inside a function that uses the name heavily. The book's own style: fully qualified in interfaces, local imports inside implementation functions.
concepts.detail: The rule keeps provenance readable: a reader of a 50-line function can see, per name, which library it came from — something a file-wide using-directive destroys.

concepts.statement: A namespace can re-export names it does not define: `namespace App { using Chrono::Date; using Text::Token; }` builds a **facade** — clients of App see one coherent interface assembled from several libraries, without knowing (or compiling against) the partition.
concepts.detail: Pass-through is how mature platforms hide internal structure: the facade is the published interface; the sub-libraries behind it can be repartitioned without touching clients.

concepts.statement: Publish versions as sibling namespaces — `namespace Lib { namespace V2 { /* ... */ } }` — and bind the choice in **one alias**: `namespace Current = Lib::V2;`. Clients that qualify with `Current::` migrate to the new version when the one alias line changes; clients that pinned `Lib::V1` are untouched.
concepts.detail: The arithmetic is the argument: one edit versus one edit per call site (the worked example counts 200). Real libraries additionally use `inline namespace` to keep old spellings working during a transition.

concepts.statement: Generic code composes because of ADL: `swap(x, y)` finds the user overload in x's namespace without any declaration at the call site; operators are found the same way. Customization points live *with their types*, and libraries interoperate without common headers.
concepts.detail: This is the quiet miracle of the standard library: `std::sort` can call *your* swap for your type because the lookup reaches into your namespace through the arguments — no registration, no inheritance.

concepts.statement: Move old global-namespace code into namespaces gradually: wrap new development in its namespace, keep a header of using-declarations that re-exports the old global names, and remove aliases as callers are updated. The build never breaks mid-migration.
concepts.detail: The same one-alias-at-a-time discipline as versioning: each step compiles and tests, and the global namespace drains slowly instead of exploding.

examples.title: Migrating 200 call sites with one alias
examples.problem: A library publishes `Lib::V2::f` with a changed (source-compatible) implementation; 200 call sites currently use `Lib::V1::f` through an alias `namespace Current = Lib::V1;`. Compare the migration cost of the alias mechanism against direct qualification, then trace how `cout << d` finds a Date's operator without any of it.

steps.label: Direct migration
steps.text: If each call site spelled `Lib::V1::f` literally, the move to V2 is 200 textual edits, each a chance to typo a version prefix — plus review of all 200 diffs.

steps.label: Alias migration
steps.text: All 200 sites spell `Current::f`. The migration is **1 line** — `namespace Current = Lib::V2;` — followed by a rebuild and the V2 test suite. A site needing V1 semantics pins `Lib::V1` explicitly and is unaffected.

steps.label: The arithmetic
steps.text: 1 edit + rebuild versus 200 edits + review: the alias mechanism converts an O(call sites) migration into an O(1) one — the reason versioning belongs in the design, not the release checklist.

steps.label: ADL on the side
steps.text: Meanwhile `cout << d` (a `Lib::V2::Date`) resolves with zero qualification: ordinary lookup finds no candidate at the call site; ADL adds `std` (for `cout`) and `Lib::V2` (for `d`); `Lib::V2::operator<<` is found there and selected.

steps.label: Why this scales
steps.text: The version switch is centralized (one alias), while the operator wiring is decentralized (ADL finds it wherever the type lives). Composition needs both properties at once.

examples.result: One alias line migrates 200 call sites (versus 200 edits), and ADL finds the V2 operator<< with no using-declarations anywhere — versioning centralized, lookups local.

examples.title: Working through composition using namespaces
examples.problem: Namespaces at scale. Your task: compose libraries by qualifying at boundaries and importing selectively inside function scopes.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: compose libraries by qualifying at boundaries and importing selectively inside function scopes. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Compose by qualifying at boundaries and importing selectively within function scopes, so every name’s provenance stays readable.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `namespace Lib { int version(); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — use pass-through using-declarations to build facades, and namespace aliases to version and migrate — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Pass-through using-declarations build facades over several libraries; versioned sub-namespaces plus a single alias turn per-call-site migrations into one-line switches. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Compose by qualifying at boundaries and importing selectively within function scopes, so every name’s provenance stays readable. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Compose by qualifying at boundaries and importing selectively within function scopes, so every name's provenance stays readable.
Pass-through using-declarations build facades over several libraries; versioned sub-namespaces plus a single alias turn per-call-site migrations into one-line switches.
ADL makes libraries interoperate without common headers: swap and operators are found through their argument types, wherever those types live.

quiz.q: A library ships `Lib::V2` while 200 sites call `Current::f`, where `Current` is an alias for `Lib::V1`. To migrate all sites to V2:
options: Edit all 200 call sites to spell `Lib::V2::f`
Change the one alias definition to `namespace Current = Lib::V2;` and rebuild
Recompile the library with a special flag
quiz.explanation: The alias is the single point of version binding: one line flips all 200 sites. Directly-qualified sites — those that pinned V1 on purpose — are untouched.

quiz.q: What does `namespace App { using Chrono::Date; }` accomplish?
options: It moves Date out of Chrono, deprecating the old name
It makes App::Date a pass-through name for Chrono::Date — a facade that re-exports without defining
It copies the Date class into App
It makes Date private to App
quiz.explanation: A using-declaration re-exports: App::Date is the same entity as Chrono::Date. Facades assemble one published interface from several libraries behind it.

quiz.q: Why does `std::sort` find a user-defined `swap` for a user type `W` in namespace `Wlib`?
options: All swaps are members of std
The user must open namespace std and add the overload
ADL: the call `swap(x, y)` with a `Wlib::W` argument adds Wlib to the lookup set, where the user swap is found
sort calls it through a virtual function
quiz.explanation: Customization points work through the argument types: the namespace of W contributes candidates, so libraries interoperate with no registration and no common header.

intro: The chapter's advice compresses the mechanism into habits: name namespaces for what they provide, keep using-directives out of interfaces, and use namespaces to express structure rather than to save typing. Every rule has the same target — readable composition.
objectives: Recite the house rules on namespace naming, placement of using-directives and depth of nesting
Explain the connection between namespace structure and physical module structure
Spot the standard namespace-misuse smells in a code review

concepts.statement: **A namespace name should say what it provides** — `Chrono`, `Geometry`, `Net` — not who wrote it, where it sits in a directory tree, or the project codename. The name is the one-sentence description of the module from 14.3, compressed to a word.
concepts.detail: The test of coherence from 14.3 applies verbatim: if you cannot name the namespace in one plain word or two, the module is probably a grab bag that wants splitting.

concepts.statement: **Never place a using-directive in a header or any other interface.** It applies to every includer, who never chose it, and any later library growth can turn it into ambiguity far from the cause. Using-declarations of individual names are the interface-safe import.
concepts.detail: In an implementation file, a using-directive is a defensible local convenience — the damage is then confined to a scope the author owns and reads.

concepts.statement: **Use namespaces to express design structure** — libraries, versions, implementation detail — not to shorten names or to group whatever files happen to sit together. Deep nesting is a smell: more than two or three levels usually means physical layout leaking into logical design.
concepts.detail: The mirror-image rule also holds: do not put everything in the global namespace to save the two characters of qualification — composition, not brevity, is what the mechanism buys.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Name namespaces for the service they provide — Chrono, Geometry, Net — because the namespace name is the module description compressed to a word.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

concepts.statement: Take the objectives as review questions: recite the house rules on namespace naming, placement of using-directives and depth of nesting? Then explain the connection between namespace structure and physical module structure? Answer each from the code in front of you, not from memory — the gap between the two answers is the review finding.
concepts.detail: A rule you can derive from the chapter you can also correctly suspend; a rule applied without its reason becomes superstition, so cite the reason in the review note.

examples.title: A code review in three smells
examples.problem: Review this header: it opens with `using namespace std;` and `using namespace Chrono;` at global scope, declares `namespace proj_utils { /* 40 unrelated helpers */ }`, and defines `namespace A { namespace B { namespace C { void f(); } } }`. Identify the violations and prescribe fixes.

steps.label: Smell 1 — directives in an interface
steps.text: Two using-directives at global scope in a header: every includer inherits all of std and Chrono, and any future name in either can collide with the includer's own names. Fix: delete both; qualify in the declarations (`std::string`, `Chrono::Date`) or import single names with using-declarations *inside* the functions that need them.

steps.label: Smell 2 — the grab bag
steps.text: `proj_utils` holds 40 unrelated helpers: a name that describes neither service nor concept — the one-sentence test fails immediately. Fix: split along the concept boundaries (parsing, io, math), each in its own namespace with a speakable name.

steps.label: Smell 3 — nesting as directory tree
steps.text: A::B::C almost always mirrors a folder structure that the build system, not the design, created. Three levels of qualification for one function is directory leakage. Fix: flatten to one meaningful namespace, or make the outer levels version facades per 14.4 — never a mirror of the file tree.

steps.label: Count the fallout
steps.text: Three violations, three fixes — and every fix is local: delete-and-qualify, split, flatten. No client code changes beyond qualification, which is the sign the structure was decorative rather than load-bearing.

examples.result: Directives removed (qualify instead), the grab bag split into concept namespaces, the directory mirror flattened: three smells, three local fixes, zero client breakage beyond requalification.

examples.title: Reviewing namespaces code
