examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: recite the house rules on namespace naming, placement of using-directives and depth of nesting.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Name namespaces for the service they provide — Chrono, Geometry, Net — because the namespace name is the module description compressed to a word.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `namespace Lib { int version(); }`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: explain the connection between namespace structure and physical module structure. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Never put a using-directive in a header; import single names with using-declarations, and keep directives to implementation files if at all.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Name namespaces for the service they provide — Chrono, Geometry, Net — because the namespace name is the module description compressed to a word. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Name namespaces for the service they provide — Chrono, Geometry, Net — because the namespace name is the module description compressed to a word.
Never put a using-directive in a header; import single names with using-declarations, and keep directives to implementation files if at all.
Namespaces express design structure (libraries, versions, implementation detail); deep nesting and grab-bag namespaces are physical layout leaking into logic.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest reason `using namespace std;` must not appear in a header?
options: It silently applies to every current and future includer, who never chose it — future std growth can break their code at a distance
It prevents include guards from working
quiz.explanation: The directive's scope is whoever includes the header: an open-ended commitment on behalf of strangers, plus a time bomb — every new std name becomes a potential ambiguity far from the cause.

quiz.q: A namespace named `team_foundation_common_utils` holding 80 helpers violates:
options: The one-concept rule: the name describes neither a service nor a concept, so the namespace is a grab bag that should be split
quiz.explanation: The namespace name is the module description in one word. A name that lists neither service nor concept — just provenance — announces a module boundary drawn by convenience, not design.

quiz.q: Acceptable use of a using-directive is:
options: At global scope in a widely-included header
Inside a namespace published as a library interface
Inside an implementation .cpp file or a single function scope the author owns, where the blast radius is bounded
quiz.explanation: Confine the blast radius: within a translation unit (or better, a function), the author both chose the import and reads all the code it can affect.

intro: A C++ program is not what the compiler sees — the compiler sees one translation unit at a time and has no idea your other files exist. The program is assembled later, by the linker, out of object files. Understanding that split — and the header/source convention that makes declarations identical across translation units — is what separates compiling programs from building them.
objectives: Define translation unit and explain what the compiler does and does not see
Explain #include as textual splicing and the declaration/definition distinction that makes it work
Read and predict linker errors: undefined reference and multiple definition

concepts.statement: After preprocessing (all `#include` directives spliced in, macros expanded), **one source file is one translation unit (TU)** — the complete unit the compiler translates into an object file. The compiler never sees two TUs at once; "the program" is a linker-time concept.
concepts.detail: This is the root fact of physical design: every rule about headers, declarations and linkage exists to let independently compiled fragments agree with each other without ever being seen together.

concepts.statement: `#include "stack.h"` **splices the header's text into the translation unit** before compilation. The compiler does not know files, projects or headers — it simply parses the resulting stream. Headers exist so that the same declarations reach every TU **identically, by construction**.
concepts.detail: The convention follows: declarations the world needs go in a `.h`; definitions stay in a `.cpp`. The language does not enforce the split — nothing stops you defining functions in a header except the linker, soon.

concepts.statement: A **declaration** introduces a name and its type (`void push(int);`); a **definition** additionally provides the body or storage (`void push(int) { /* ... */ }`). The One-Definition Rule: every entity may be defined **at most once per program**; it may be declared many times, and every declaration must agree.
concepts.detail: Class definitions, inline functions and templates are the exceptions — each TU that uses them needs a (token-identical) definition, which is exactly why they live in headers.

concepts.statement: The linker merges object files and libraries, resolving each cross-TU reference: every **undefined reference** must be matched by exactly one definition among the objects and libraries, and each **strong definition** must occur only once. Failures are reported at link time — undefined reference (no definition found) or multiple definition (two found).
concepts.detail: Note the timing: these are not compile errors. The compiler checked each TU in isolation; only the linker holds the whole symbol table and can see the mismatch.

concepts.statement: Separate compilation buys: **incremental rebuilds** (change one `.cpp`, recompile one TU, relink), **interface enforcement** (the header is the published contract), and **binary distribution** (ship object files and headers, keep the source).
concepts.detail: The price is bookkeeping: the include graph (15.3) decides what must be rebuilt, and the linkage rules (15.2) decide what may be shared. The chapter's remaining sections are those two bills, paid in order.

Only the linker ever sees the whole program.

examples.title: The price of touching a header
examples.problem: A project has 20 translation units, each taking 2 s to compile, plus a 1 s link. Compare the full rebuild time after (a) a change to one `.cpp` file only, and (b) a change to a header included by all 20. Explain the difference.

steps.label: Change a .cpp
steps.text: Only its TU is stale: 1 compile (2 s) + link (1 s) = **3 s**. The other 19 object files are reused as-is — that is what separate compilation buys.

steps.label: Change a header
steps.text: The header text is spliced into all 20 TUs, so all 20 are stale: 20 compiles ($20 \times 2$ s) + link = **41 s**.

steps.label: Why the asymmetry
steps.text: A TU depends on everything textually spliced into it, and transitively on everything those headers include. Editing a definition inside `stack.cpp` changes no spliced text elsewhere; editing `stack.h` changes the text of every includer — and the compiler cannot know the edit was harmless.

steps.label: The design consequence
steps.text: This is why 15.3 obsesses over shrinking include graphs: a header reached by all TUs multiplies every edit into a project-wide rebuild, and a header reached by none multiplies nothing.

examples.result: Source-file change: 3 s. Header change: 41 s — nearly 14 times more — because the header is textually present in all 20 translation units.

examples.title: Working through separate compilation
examples.problem: Translation units and linkage. Your task: define translation unit and explain what the compiler does and does not see.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define translation unit and explain what the compiler does and does not see. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: One .cpp plus its spliced headers is one translation unit; the compiler translates TUs in isolation, and the program exists only at link time.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int main(int argc, char* argv[]) { return 0; }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain #include as textual splicing and the declaration/definition distinction that makes it work — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Declarations are shared via headers (textual splicing); definitions are unique per program — at most one, with class/inline/template definitions replicated identically where needed. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: One .cpp plus its spliced headers is one translation unit; the compiler translates TUs in isolation, and the program exists only at link time. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: One .cpp plus its spliced headers is one translation unit; the compiler translates TUs in isolation, and the program exists only at link time.
Declarations are shared via headers (textual splicing); definitions are unique per program — at most one, with class/inline/template definitions replicated identically where needed.
Cross-TU mismatches are linker errors, not compiler errors: undefined reference (no definition found), multiple definition (two found).

quiz.q: What exactly does the compiler see when you compile `user.cpp`?
options: All files of the project, plus the project manifest
One translation unit: user.cpp after preprocessing, with every #include spliced in textually
The .cpp files only; headers are read by the linker
quiz.explanation: The preprocessor pastes the headers into the source; the compiler parses that one stream. It has no notion of your other files — that is the entire point of separate compilation.

quiz.q: The build fails with: undefined reference to `push(int)`. What is the cause?
options: A syntax error in the header declaring push
Some translation unit called push, but no object file or library supplied to the linker contains its definition
push was declared twice in the same header
push was declared static in the wrong file
quiz.explanation: The compiler was satisfied by the declaration (that is all it needs to generate the call); the linker, holding all symbol tables, found no definition among the supplied objects and libraries.

quiz.q: A project rebuild is triggered by editing a single header included by every translation unit. Why must every object file be rebuilt?
options: The header's mtime invalidates all files by convention
The header's text is spliced into every TU, so every TU's input changed — the compiler cannot assume the edit was semantically harmless
Headers are recompiled themselves into a shared cache
The linker cannot mix object files of different ages
quiz.explanation: Compilation is a pure function of the TU text. Change the text anywhere and the TU must be retranslated — correctness cannot be assumed from intent.

quiz.q: Which statement about the One-Definition Rule is correct?
options: Every name may be defined once per translation unit
Every entity may be defined at most once per program; declarations may repeat, but class and inline definitions may replicate token-identically across TUs
Definitions may appear only in headers
The ODR is enforced by a linker warning only
quiz.explanation: One definition per program is the rule; the class/inline/template exception allows the identical definition in each TU that needs it — which is precisely why they live in headers.

intro: Linkage is the rulebook for names crossing translation-unit boundaries — or being forbidden from crossing. External linkage lets a definition in one TU serve a reference in another; internal linkage keeps a name private to its TU; and the initialization order of the globals that linkage shares is the classic C++ trap this section teaches you to sidestep.
objectives: Classify names as having external or internal linkage, and choose the right one deliberately
Explain inline as an ODR escape hatch — a definition allowed to replicate across TUs — not merely an optimization hint
Diagnose the initialization-order problem for nonlocal variables and fix it with function-local statics

concepts.statement: A name with **external linkage** can be used from translation units other than the one that defines it: ordinary functions and mutable namespace-scope variables. The definition lives in one TU; declarations in the header let others reference it, and the linker unites them.
concepts.detail: This is the default for functions and variables at namespace scope — the "shared" setting, and the reason a missing `static` can accidentally export an internal helper into the program's symbol space.

concepts.statement: A name with **internal linkage** is local to its translation unit: entities in an **unnamed namespace**, namespace-scope names declared `static`, and namespace-scope `const`/`constexpr` variables (internal by default). Two TUs may define same-named internals independently — they are different objects.
concepts.detail: That last clause is why `constexpr int size = 10;` can live safely in a header: each TU gets its own copy, which is exactly what a constant wants.

concepts.statement: **`inline` means: this definition may appear identically in multiple translation units.** The linker merges them; only the rule that all definitions must be token-identical (and mean the same) keeps it sound. Inlining as an optimization is the compiler's business — `inline` is the ODR permission slip that makes header-defined functions legal.
concepts.detail: C++17 added `inline` variables for the same purpose; before that, class `static constexpr` members were the loophole. Every header-resident function or template relies on this rule.

concepts.statement: Within a translation unit, namespace-scope objects are initialized **in order of definition**. Across translation units, the order is **unspecified**. So a global constructed in TU-a that reads a global defined in TU-b has a 50/50 chance of reading an uninitialized object.
concepts.detail: The fix is construct-on-first-use: wrap the global in a function returning a reference to a **function-local static** — initialized the first time control passes through it (and thread-safe since C++11), so the order problem disappears for every caller.

concepts.statement: `extern "C" { /* ... */ }` declares its contents to have **C language linkage**: names are unmangled (or C-mangled), so C and C++ code can interoperate. A C-linkage function cannot be overloaded — the C world has one symbol per name.
concepts.detail: Headers meant for both languages gate the block: `#ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { #endif` ... so C compilers skip what only C++ needs.

examples.title: The initialization-order fiasco, defused
examples.problem: TU-a defines `Registry reg("main");` whose constructor reads settings from TU-b's global `Config cfg;`. What can go wrong, and what one-line shape fixes it for every number of translation units?

steps.label: The dependency
steps.text: reg's constructor reads cfg. Within TU-b, cfg is initialized in definition order; within TU-a, reg too. **Across** the two TUs, no order is specified.

steps.label: The failure
steps.text: If the linker/run order initializes reg before cfg — 1 of the 2 possible orders — the constructor reads an object whose constructor has not run: undefined behavior, typically garbage settings or a crash that appears only on some builds.

steps.label: The fix
steps.text: Replace the global in TU-b with `const Config& cfg() { static Config c; return c; }`. The function-local static initializes the first time control passes through it — after TU-a's reg, before TU-a's reg, it does not matter which.

steps.label: Why it is safe
steps.text: Initialization order becomes *demand-driven*: whoever reaches cfg() first constructs it, on that thread, exactly once (C++11 guarantees thread-safety here). With N dependent TUs there are N! possible orders, and every one of them is now correct.

steps.label: The costs
steps.text: One guard check per access (a load-and-branch, branch-predicted to nothing after the first call) and the loss of "plain global" syntax: `cfg().setting` instead of `cfg.setting` — the standard trade in code that must not depend on link order.

examples.result: Before: 2 orders, 1 broken. After: every order works — demand-driven initialization scales to any number of TUs.

examples.title: Working through linkage
examples.problem: Internal, external and no linkage. Your task: classify names as having external or internal linkage, and choose the right one deliberately.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: classify names as having external or internal linkage, and choose the right one deliberately. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: External linkage shares a name across TUs (one definition, many references); internal linkage — unnamed namespaces, static, const/constexpr at namespace scope — keeps it TU-private.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int main(int argc, char* argv[]) { return 0; }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain inline as an ODR escape hatch — a definition allowed to replicate across TUs — not merely an optimization hint — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: inline is an ODR permission slip: the definition may replicate token-identically across TUs; that legality is what makes header-defined functions and templates possible. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: External linkage shares a name across TUs (one definition, many references); internal linkage — unnamed namespaces, static, const/constexpr at namespace scope — keeps it TU-private. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: External linkage shares a name across TUs (one definition, many references); internal linkage — unnamed namespaces, static, const/constexpr at namespace scope — keeps it TU-private.
inline is an ODR permission slip: the definition may replicate token-identically across TUs; that legality is what makes header-defined functions and templates possible.
Cross-TU initialization order is unspecified: wrap globals in functions returning function-local statics, and the order problem vanishes for every caller.

quiz.q: Two translation units each define `static int count = 0;` at namespace scope. What exists in the program?
options: One shared count; the linker merges them
Two independent objects — internal linkage keeps each name private to its TU
quiz.explanation: `static` at namespace scope (or an unnamed namespace) gives internal linkage: the same spelling in two TUs denotes two different objects. That is the privacy the mechanism is for.

quiz.q: What does `inline` primarily promise about a function definition?
options: The compiler will expand calls inline
The definition may appear in multiple TUs, and the linker will merge them, provided the definitions are token-identical
The function cannot be called through a pointer
quiz.explanation: inline is the ODR escape hatch that legalizes header-resident definitions. Speed is a compiler decision orthogonal to the keyword.

quiz.q: A global object's constructor in TU-a reads a namespace-scope variable defined in TU-b. What does the standard guarantee about the order?
options: Variables initialize in alphabetical order of file name
TU-a's objects always initialize first, since it appears first on the link line
Nothing — the cross-TU order is unspecified; the read may happen before TU-b's variable is constructed
The linker delays all constructors until main begins
quiz.explanation: Only within a single TU is order defined (definition order). Across TUs it is unspecified — which is why the construct-on-first-use idiom exists.

quiz.q: `const Config& cfg() { static Config c; return c; }` defuses that problem because:
options: Function-local statics are initialized on first pass through the declaration, so every caller — whatever the TU order — constructs it on first use
Static locals are initialized at load time before main
The compiler hoists the static to a global
quiz.explanation: Demand-driven initialization: order of use now determines order of construction, and C++11 makes it thread-safe. The unspecified link order becomes irrelevant.

intro: Headers are where the chapter's rules become house discipline: what may live in a header, how guards make repeated inclusion harmless, and why the include graph — not the code — decides your build times. A header is a promise to every includer; these rules are how you keep the promise cheap.
objectives: Classify what belongs in a header (declarations, types, inline/constexpr, templates) and what must never be there
Explain include guards, self-containment, and the include-what-you-use rule
Read an include graph, cut edges with forward declarations, and reason about rebuild cascades

concepts.statement: A header holds the interface: named namespaces, type definitions, function and variable **declarations**, `inline` and `constexpr` function definitions, templates, and constants users need. It must **not** contain: definitions of ordinary functions or variables, `using`-directives at global scope, or macros beyond unavoidable necessity.
concepts.detail: The test is the ODR: whatever the header holds gets spliced into every includer, so anything that would be multiply-defined if repeated must stay out — unless its form (inline, class definition, template) explicitly permits replication.

concepts.statement: Wrap every header: `#ifndef STACK_H / #define STACK_H / /* ... */ / #endif`. The second and later inclusions of `stack.h` in one TU become no-ops, so **diamond-shaped include graphs are harmless** — the second textual copy of a class definition would otherwise be a redefinition error.
concepts.detail: `#pragma once` is the widespread shortcut for the same purpose; the guard macro's name should encode the file's identity, since guards collide by macro name.

concepts.statement: **A header must compile alone** — the test is a TU containing nothing but its include. Symmetrically, every file should **directly include what it uses**, never relying on names that arrive transitively through someone else's header.
concepts.detail: The two rules kill the two classic shocks: "this header errors unless you include string first" and "my build broke because a third-party header stopped pulling in vector for me."

concepts.statement: The `#include` relation between files is a directed **acyclic** graph: an included file cannot transitively include its includer. Every edge in a header drags the entire subgraph into **every includer, transitively** — the graph, not the code, determines what a header change rebuilds.
concepts.detail: The firewall technique: when a header needs a type only as a pointer or reference, replace its `#include` with a **forward declaration** (`struct Node;`) — the edge disappears, and the whole subgraph behind it stays out of downstream builds.

concepts.statement: A `using namespace std;` in a header is injected into the global namespace of **every translation unit that includes it directly or transitively** — hundreds of names, every one a future ambiguity. It is the single most forbidden line a header can contain.
concepts.detail: The chapter's phrasing of the general rule: what a header holds is interface, and a directive changes the meaning of the includer's own code — something an interface must never do.

figures.caption: Figure 15.2 — An include graph. Solid edges are #include (a textual splice, so the whole subgraph travels along); the dashed edge is one a forward declaration cuts — stack.h needs Node only as a pointer, so `struct Node;` suffices and node.h stays out of every downstream build. examples.title: Diamonds, guards, and saved lines
examples.problem: `geometry.h` is 80 lines and defines `class Point`. Ten translation units include `stack.h`, and `stack.h` includes `geometry.h` (it mentions `Point` only as `Point*`); `main.cpp` includes both `stack.h` and `util.h`, and `util.h` also includes `geometry.h`. Predict the failure without guards, and the splice savings after replacing `stack.h`'s include with a forward declaration.

steps.label: The diamond
steps.text: From `main.cpp`, two paths reach `geometry.h`: via `stack.h` and via `util.h`. With no guard, the TU receives **two textual copies** of `class Point` — the second is a redefinition error.

steps.label: Guards on
steps.text: `#ifndef GEOM_H` makes the second splice a no-op: 2 paths, **1 copy**, the diamond compiles. This is the entire reason guards are not optional.

steps.label: Count the splices
steps.text: Before the cut: 10 TUs receive `geometry.h` via `stack.h` (plus `main.cpp` via `util.h`): roughly $10 \times 80 + 80 = 880$ spliced lines across the build.

steps.label: Cut the edge
steps.text: `stack.h` mentions `Point` only as `Point*` — a pointer to an incompletely-known type is fine. Replace its `#include "geometry.h"` line with `struct Point;`: the 10 `stack.h`-includers stop pulling `geometry.h` entirely.

steps.label: Count again
steps.text: After the cut only the 2 TUs that use `Point` by value (via `util.h`) still include it: $2 \times 80 = 160$ spliced lines. The edit saves about 720 spliced lines per build — and every future change to `geometry.h` now rebuilds 2 TUs instead of 11.

examples.result: Guards turn 2 copies into 1 (no redefinition error); the forward declaration cuts the spliced text from about 880 to 160 lines and shrinks the rebuild set for geometry.h from 11 TUs to 2.

examples.title: Working through using header files
examples.problem: What belongs in a header. Your task: classify what belongs in a header (declarations, types, inline/constexpr, templates) and what must never be there.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: classify what belongs in a header (declarations, types, inline/constexpr, templates) and what must never be there. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Headers hold interfaces: declarations, types, inline/constexpr definitions and templates — never ordinary definitions or using-directives.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int main(int argc, char* argv[]) { return 0; }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain include guards, self-containment, and the include-what-you-use rule — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Include guards make repeated splicing a no-op, so diamonds are legal; self-containment (a header compiles alone) and include-what-you-use make builds robust. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Headers hold interfaces: declarations, types, inline/constexpr definitions and templates — never ordinary definitions or using-directives. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Headers hold interfaces: declarations, types, inline/constexpr definitions and templates — never ordinary definitions or using-directives.
Include guards make repeated splicing a no-op, so diamonds are legal; self-containment (a header compiles alone) and include-what-you-use make builds robust.
The include graph decides rebuild cost: forward declarations cut edges, and an edge cut anywhere removes a whole subgraph from every downstream build.

quiz.q: Without include guards, `main.cpp` reaches `geometry.h` by two include paths. What happens?
options: The linker merges the two copies of class Point
The preprocessor skips the second copy automatically
The TU contains two definitions of class Point: a redefinition error
The build succeeds with two distinct Point types
quiz.explanation: Each #include splices text again; the second definition of Point at the same scope is a compile-time redefinition error — exactly what #ifndef guards exist to prevent.

quiz.q: When may a header replace `#include "node.h"` with a forward declaration `struct Node;`?
options: Never: complete types are always required
When the header mentions Node only through pointers or references — incomplete types suffice there
Only if node.h is in the standard library
quiz.explanation: Pointers and references to incomplete types are legal, so the edge — and the whole subgraph behind it — can be cut from every downstream build. By-value use, member access or sizeof requires the complete type.

quiz.q: A header compiles only when the includer includes `string` before it. Which rule did its author break?
options: Self-containment: a header must compile alone — everything it needs must be in its own include list
The include-what-you-use rule for the includer only
quiz.explanation: The self-containment test — a TU whose only line is including the header — is the house standard. A header that only compiles after preparatory includes exports fragility to every user.

quiz.q: Which line must never appear in a header?
quiz.explanation: A using-directive in a header is injected into the global namespace of every includer — including transitively — changing the meaning of code the author has never seen.

intro: The program is the outermost shell: how a run starts (nonlocal objects before main), what arguments and environment arrive through main, and how termination returns control to the operating system. Small rules, but they answer the questions every systems programmer eventually hits at 2 a.m. — what ran before main, and what exactly does exit() clean up?
objectives: Use `int main(int argc, char* argv[])` correctly: the argv layout, the exit status contract, and option parsing
Describe program startup and termination: nonlocal initialization before main, and the different cleanup of return-from-main, exit() and abort()
Interoperate with C and other languages through language linkage

concepts.statement: `int main()` or `int main(int argc, char* argv[])` is the program's entry point. `argv[0]` is the program name (or an empty string), `argv[1]` through `argv[argc-1]` are the arguments, and `argv[argc]` is guaranteed to be a null pointer. The returned `int` is the **exit status** the OS receives: `0` (or `EXIT_SUCCESS`) means success, a nonzero value (e.g. `EXIT_FAILURE`) means failure.
concepts.detail: A program that never returns from main returns 0 implicitly. Scripts, make and CI read this status — a tool that succeeds but forgets to return 0 breaks every pipeline above it.

concepts.statement: Walk `argv` in a loop from index 1; options conventionally start with `-` and are read with a `switch` on the option character; operands are everything else. Report malformed input early, print usage, and return a nonzero status.
concepts.detail: The book's compiler example is exactly this shape: a `for` over `argv`, a `switch` on `*arg` with cases per option, error messages that name the offending argument.

concepts.statement: **Before `main`:** namespace-scope objects are constructed (in definition order per TU, cross-TU order unspecified — 15.2). **Return from `main`:** main's locals are destroyed, then static objects' destructors run, and the return value becomes the exit status. **`exit(n)` from anywhere:** static destructors run, but locals of intervening frames do **not** — the stack is not unwound. **`abort()`:** no cleanup at all.
concepts.detail: The exit()-vs-return distinction matters in library code: a function that ends the program by `exit` skips destructors of the objects it and its callers hold — a resource leak at shutdown that never shows up in tests that return normally.

concepts.statement: Each process also inherits an **environment**: a map of strings (`getenv`, `putenv` in `<cstdlib>`) set by the parent, visible to every child — out-of-band configuration that arrives alongside `argv`.
concepts.detail: Because it is inherited, the environment is how a parent process configures a whole tree of children without threading a flag through every command line — and why a stale `PATH` or `LC_ALL` produces behavior no source file explains.

concepts.term: Linking with C and other languages
concepts.statement: Wrap foreign declarations in `extern "C" { }` — C language linkage, no name mangling — so C object files link with C++ ones. Headers shipped to both languages gate the block with `#ifdef __cplusplus` so C compilers skip what is only for C++.
concepts.detail: This is the bridge to the ecosystem: OS APIs, database drivers and math libraries are C at the ABI level, and `extern "C"` is the toll gate.

examples.title: Walking the command line
examples.problem: A tool is invoked as `./sum -v 10 20 30` and elsewhere as `./sum` and `./sum 5`. For each invocation, give argc, the parse the loop performs, the output, and the exit status the shell sees.

steps.label: Invocation 1
steps.text: `argc = 5`: argv[0] is `./sum`, argv[1] is `-v`, argv[2..4] are `10`, `20`, `30`. The loop: i=1 sees a leading `-` — the `v` sets verbose; i=2..4 see no dash — accumulate 10+20+30. Output (verbose): `total: 60`. Status: `EXIT_SUCCESS`, i.e. 0.`

steps.label: Invocation 2
steps.text: `argc = 1`: the loop body never runs, total stays 0. A tool that got no operands should say so — print usage to stderr and return `EXIT_FAILURE` (1), rather than silently succeed with 0.

steps.label: Invocation 3
steps.text: `argc = 2`: one operand, no options: total = 5; no output unless verbose. Status 0. Note argv[argc] is the guaranteed null terminator — the loop can also stop on `argv[i] == nullptr` instead of comparing to argc.

steps.label: The status contract
steps.text: The shell combines statuses: `./sum -v 10 20 30 && next-step` runs next-step because 0 means success. One broken return value — success but returning 1, or failure but returning 0 — breaks every such pipeline.

examples.result: argc=5: verbose, total 60, status 0. argc=2: total 5, status 0. argc=1: usage message, status 1 — the exit status is part of the interface, same as the output.

examples.title: Working through programs
examples.problem: From source files to programs. Your task: use `int main(int argc, char* argv[])` correctly: the argv layout, the exit status contract, and option parsing.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: use `int main(int argc, char* argv[])` correctly: the argv layout, the exit status contract, and option parsing. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: argv[0] is the program name, argv[1..argc-1] the arguments, argv[argc] a null pointer; the int returned from main is the exit status the OS receives (0 = success).

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int main(int argc, char* argv[]) { return 0; }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — describe program startup and termination: nonlocal initialization before main, and the different cleanup of return-from-main, exit() and abort() — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Before main, nonlocal objects construct (per-TU order, cross-TU unspecified); return from main destroys locals and statics, exit() skips the stack, abort() cleans up nothing. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: argv[0] is the program name, argv[1..argc-1] the arguments, argv[argc] a null pointer; the int returned from main is the exit status the OS receives (0 = success). Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: argv[0] is the program name, argv[1..argc-1] the arguments, argv[argc] a null pointer; the int returned from main is the exit status the OS receives (0 = success).
Before main, nonlocal objects construct (per-TU order, cross-TU unspecified); return from main destroys locals and statics, exit() skips the stack, abort() cleans up nothing.
extern "C" gives declarations C linkage so C object files interoperate; the environment (getenv/putenv) is inherited, out-of-band configuration.

quiz.q: For `./sum -v 10 20 30`, what is `argc` and `argv[1]`?
quiz.explanation: argc counts the program name: 5 total. argv[0] is the name, so argv[1] is the first real argument, the option -v; the numbers sit at argv[2..4].

quiz.q: What is the crucial difference between returning from main and calling `exit(0)` from deep in the call stack?
options: return destroys main's locals and the static objects; exit() runs static destructors but does NOT unwind the stack — locals of intervening frames are never destroyed
exit() is faster because it skips all destructors including static ones
quiz.explanation: exit terminates without unwinding: statics are destroyed in reverse construction order, but automatic objects in the abandoned frames are skipped — a leak at shutdown invisible to tests that return normally.

quiz.q: A C library ships `frobnicate.h`. For C++ clients, its declarations must be wrapped in:
options: `extern "C" { }` — C language linkage, so names are unmangled and match the C object files
quiz.explanation: C++ mangles names to encode types for overloading; extern "C" turns that off so the C++ reference resolves to the C symbol.

intro: The chapter's closing advice turns the machinery into habits: match files to modules, keep headers self-contained, distrust nonlocal variables, and treat the exit status as part of your program's interface. Each rule buys a specific, predictable failure mode you stop having.
objectives: Apply the header/source discipline: interface in the header, implementation in the source, one module per boundary
Justify the distrust of nonlocal variables and the construct-on-first-use alternative
Audit a small header against the chapter's checklist and fix every violation

concepts.statement: **The physical decomposition (files) should mirror the logical one (modules from chapter 14)**: a module's published declarations in one header, its definitions in a matching source, implementation helpers in an unnamed namespace. When files and modules drift apart, neither is findable.
concepts.detail: The corollary of minimality: one module, one header — a header is a unit of inclusion and therefore of rebuild; merging modules into one header couples their users' build times for no design reason.

concepts.statement: **Guard every header; make it self-contained; include what you use; put nothing in it that a definition rule forbids.** The audit is mechanical — a TU containing only `#include "your.h"` must compile — and it should run in CI before every merge.
concepts.detail: The inverse discipline is just as mechanical: a `.cpp` includes its own header first, proving self-containment at every compile, then what else it uses.

concepts.statement: **Avoid dependencies among nonlocal variables** — cross-TU initialization order is unspecified (15.2). Where a global is genuinely needed, wrap it as a function-local static behind an accessor, and pay the one-branch guard without complaint.
concepts.detail: The advice pairs with chapter 13: nonlocal state is also what makes exception-safety and thread-safety hard. Every global removed is a proof obligation deleted.

concepts.term: Shipping rule for source files and programs
concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Files should mirror modules: interface declarations in one guarded, self-contained header; definitions in the matching source; helpers in unnamed namespaces.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

concepts.term: Review checklist for source files and programs
concepts.statement: Take the objectives as review questions: apply the header/source discipline: interface in the header, implementation in the source, one module per boundary? Then justify the distrust of nonlocal variables and the construct-on-first-use alternative? Answer each from the code in front of you, not from memory — the gap between the two answers is the review finding.
concepts.detail: A rule you can derive from the chapter you can also correctly suspend; a rule applied without its reason becomes superstition, so cite the reason in the review note.

examples.title: Auditing one bad header
examples.problem: Review this `config.h`: it lacks guards, defines `int default_port = 8080;` and `bool parse(const char* s) { /* 30 lines */ }` at namespace scope, opens with `using namespace std;`, and needs `std::string` but includes nothing. Find every violation and fix them.

steps.label: Violation 1 — no guard
steps.text: Any TU reaching config.h twice (a diamond) gets a redefinition of `parse`. Fix: `#ifndef CONFIG_H / #define CONFIG_H / ... / #endif` — three lines, total immunity.

steps.label: Violation 2 — definitions
steps.text: `default_port` and `parse` are defined in a header: every includer gets a copy, and the linker reports multiple definition. Fix: declare in the header (`extern int default_port;`, `bool parse(const char* s);`), define in `config.cpp` — or make them `inline`/`constexpr` if the header really is their home.

steps.label: Violation 3 — the directive
steps.text: `using namespace std;` in a header injects all of std into every includer's global namespace — the forbidden line of 15.3. Fix: delete it; qualify `std::string` where used.

steps.label: Violation 4 — not self-contained
steps.text: The header uses `std::string` but relies on someone else having included `<string>` first. Fix: `#include <string>` at the top; the proof is a TU compiling with only `#include "config.h"`.

steps.label: Tally
steps.text: Four violations, four fixes, all local to the header plus one new `.cpp`. The interesting part: without fixing them, every symptom appears somewhere else — in includers' builds and at link time, never in the header's own authoring TU.

examples.result: Guard added; the two definitions moved (or marked inline); the directive deleted; <string> included. The header is now self-contained and safe to include from anywhere, in any order, twice.

examples.title: Reviewing source files and programs code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the header/source discipline: interface in the header, implementation in the source, one module per boundary.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Files should mirror modules: interface declarations in one guarded, self-contained header; definitions in the matching source; helpers in unnamed namespaces.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `int main(int argc, char* argv[]) { return 0; }`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: justify the distrust of nonlocal variables and the construct-on-first-use alternative. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: A TU that includes only your header must compile — self-containment and include-what-you-use are CI-checkable, not stylistic.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Files should mirror modules: interface declarations in one guarded, self-contained header; definitions in the matching source; helpers in unnamed namespaces. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Files should mirror modules: interface declarations in one guarded, self-contained header; definitions in the matching source; helpers in unnamed namespaces.
A TU that includes only your header must compile — self-containment and include-what-you-use are CI-checkable, not stylistic.
Avoid dependencies among nonlocal variables (cross-TU order is unspecified); wrap needed globals in function-local statics behind accessors.

quiz.q: A header defines `int count = 0;` at namespace scope and is included by two translation units. What does the build produce?
options: Two distinct counts, which is usually the intended design
A multiple-definition error from the linker
A warning at compile time, then one shared variable
quiz.explanation: Each TU gets its own definition with external linkage; when the linker tries to fold the two objects together, the duplicate strong symbol is an error. Declare (extern) in the header, define in one .cpp.

quiz.q: Why is a namespace-scope variable in a header an initialization-order hazard even after fixing the linkage problem?
options: It is not: fixing linkage fixes everything
Cross-TU initialization order is unspecified, so any global in another TU that reads it during construction may see it uninitialized
Headers are read before source files by the build system
Global variables are initialized after main begins
quiz.explanation: Two rules bite separately: linkage (how many objects exist) and initialization order (when they construct). The second is unspecified across TUs — hence the construct-on-first-use idiom.

quiz.q: The cheapest CI-checkable proof of header self-containment is:
options: Code review by the module owner
A translation unit whose only line is #including the header, compiled on every build
quiz.explanation: If a TU containing nothing but the include compiles, the header brings everything it needs — the definition of self-containment, executed as a test rather than asserted in review.

intro: The class is C++'s fundamental tool for building new types, and this chapter is where the machinery starts. A class ties a representation — the data members holding an object's state — to the operations that may touch that state, and hands the result to users as one named concept. Everything later in the book depends on the vocabulary fixed here: members, access control, invariants, and the contrast between concrete classes and the abstract, hierarchy-based ones of chapters 20 and 21.
objectives: Define a class as a user-defined type and list what a class definition contains
Separate a class' interface from its implementation and explain why users depend only on the interface
State the invariant idea and distinguish concrete classes from abstract classes

concepts.statement: A **class is a user-defined type**: a named bundle of a *representation* (data members holding state) plus *operations* (member functions) defining how that state may be read and changed. The class definition is a blueprint — each object gets its own copy of the data members, while the member function code is stored once.
concepts.detail: Built-in types are given by the language; classes are how programmers add types with equal citizenship. A well-designed `Date` or `complex` is meant to be as easy to use as an `int`.

concepts.statement: The **interface** of a class is what users see — the declaration of its public operations. The **implementation** is everything else: the private data members and the bodies of the member functions. Access control (`public` / `private`) lets the compiler enforce the split.
concepts.detail: Users of `Date` need only the interface: how to construct one, read the month, ask for the next day. Switching the implementation to days-since-epoch instead of `y`/`m`/`d` changes none of their code — that separation is the reason for the wall.

concepts.statement: A **concrete class**'s representation is part of its definition, so its objects can live on the stack, copy and move cheaply, and be used without pointers or virtual functions — `complex`, `vector` and `Date` are examples. An **abstract class** hides its representation behind an interface, typically reached through a pointer.
concepts.detail: The distinction is one of design style, not a language rule — both are classes. This chapter is about concrete classes; abstract types and hierarchies come in chapters 20 and 21.

concepts.statement: An **invariant** of a class is a statement about an object's state that holds from the end of construction to the start of destruction — in particular whenever a member function is not executing. The constructor's job is to establish it; every member function must preserve it.
concepts.detail: For `Date`, the invariant is that `y`, `m`, `d` form a valid calendar date (no Feb 30, no month 13). Once established, no public operation may leave the object violating it — that is what separates a class from a bare struct of data.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** What classes are for. You can claim this section when you can define a class as a user-defined type and list what a class definition contains — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 16 (Classes); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: One definition, three roles
examples.problem: Annotate a small `Date` class: which parts are interface, which are implementation, and what invariant does it promise?

steps.label: The definition
steps.text: `class Date { public: Date(int yy, Month mm, int dd); int day() const; void add_day(int n); private: int y; Month m; int d; };` — everything from `public:` up to `private:` is the interface; the rest is representation.

steps.label: Interface
steps.text: Constructing a `Date`, reading `day()`, asking for `add_day(n)` — these operations are all users may depend on.

steps.label: Implementation
steps.text: The three data members and the body of `add_day` are implementation details; user code cannot even name `d.m`.

steps.label: Invariant
steps.text: `(y, m, d)` is a valid date — checked by the constructor, maintained by `add_day`, so no caller ever meets a Feb 30.

examples.result: Interface for users, implementation for the maintainer, invariant as the contract between them — the whole class idea in one definition.

examples.problem: What classes are for. Your task: define a class as a user-defined type and list what a class definition contains.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define a class as a user-defined type and list what a class definition contains. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A class ties a representation to the operations allowed on it; each object holds its own state, the code is shared.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `class Date { public: Date(int d); private: int day; };` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — separate a class' interface from its implementation and explain why users depend only on the interface — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Users program against the public interface only — the private implementation can change without breaking them. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A class ties a representation to the operations allowed on it; each object holds its own state, the code is shared. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A class ties a representation to the operations allowed on it; each object holds its own state, the code is shared.
Users program against the public interface only — the private implementation can change without breaking them.
An invariant is established once by the constructor and preserved by every member function; it is what separates a class from a struct of public data.

quiz.q: A class invariant is a rule that…
options: holds only while the constructor is running
is true of an object's state between member function calls, established by the constructor
is checked automatically by the compiler at every assignment
applies only to classes with virtual functions
quiz.explanation: The constructor establishes it and every member must leave it true. The compiler does not understand invariants — checking them is the class author's job.

quiz.q: Which is a property of a concrete class in Stroustrup's sense?
options: Its representation is part of its definition and its objects are usable directly, like built-in types
It must be accessed through a pointer to an implementation
It must have a virtual destructor
quiz.explanation: `complex`, `vector` and `Date` are concrete: cheap on the stack, no indirection, no virtuals required. Pointer-mediated use is the abstract-class style.

quiz.q: Code that uses class `Date` depends on:
options: the order of the data members
the implementation of each member function
quiz.explanation: That is the interface/implementation split: private members and function bodies may change freely as long as the interface stays stable.

quiz.q: Changing the private part of a well-designed class…
options: requires rewriting user code that never mentions it
silently changes the meaning of user code
is impossible once the class is used elsewhere
does not require changes to code that uses only the public interface
quiz.explanation: Users cannot name private members, so they cannot depend on them — recompilation may be needed, but their code does not change.

intro: Class basics are the mechanics. A class contains members of several kinds, access specifiers carve it into public interface and private representation, and `const` member functions promise read-only access. The section closes with the deliberate escape hatches — `mutable` for caches and `friend` for close collaborators — plus the `this` pointer that quietly threads through every call.
objectives: Read and write a class definition using members, access specifiers and nested types
Write `const` member functions and explain what they promise — and when `mutable` relaxes it
Use the `this` pointer and `friend` declarations deliberately rather than accidentally

concepts.statement: A class can contain **data members** (the state), **member functions** (the operations) and **nested types** such as an `enum` used by the interface — collectively, the *members*. Each object gets its own copy of the data members; member functions are stored once and told which object via `this`.
concepts.detail: Stroustrup's `Date` nests `enum class Month { jan = 1, feb /* … */, dec };` inside the class. Users write `Date::Month::mar`, which keeps month names out of the global namespace and makes a month a distinct type, not an `int`.

concepts.statement: **`public:`** members form the interface — usable by everyone. **`private:`** members form the representation — usable only by the class' own members and friends. **`protected:`** is `private` plus derived classes (meaningful only with inheritance, chapter 20). The only difference between `class` and `struct` is the default: `class` defaults to private, `struct` to public.
concepts.detail: Access control is per class, not per object: one `Date`'s member functions may read another `Date`'s private members. The wall separates users from implementers, not objects from each other.

concepts.statement: A member function declared with a trailing `const` — `int day() const { return d; }` — promises not to modify the object's observable state. Only `const` member functions may be called on a `const` object; a class whose operations are all non-const cannot be used through `const` at all.
concepts.detail: The promise is enforced mechanically: inside a `const` member function `this` is a `const Date*`, so writing to members is a compile-time error. `const` is part of the function's type — a `const` and a non-`const` version can overload (the standard `operator[]` pair).

concepts.statement: A member declared **`mutable`** may be modified inside a `const` member function. Use it only for state invisible to the logical state of the object — caches, memoization, statistics — never for anything the invariant speaks about.
concepts.detail: Example: `Date::string_rep()` that formats lazily may keep `mutable bool cache_valid; mutable string cache;` — the date never logically changes, so the function is `const`, yet the cache is filled on first call.

concepts.statement: Every non-static member function receives an implicit parameter **`this`** — a pointer to the object it was invoked on — so `d.add_day(1)` means `Date::add_day(&d, 1)` inside. A **`friend`** declaration grants a named function or class access to the private representation; friendship is given by the class, never taken.
concepts.detail: Typical uses: symmetric binary operators (chapter 18) and two classes that are genuinely one design. A friend that is not part of the class' logical interface is a design smell — the wall now has a door in it.
