examples.title: The same buffer, two ways
examples.problem: A `Buffer` owns `char* p; int n;`. Write it under the rule of five, then rewrite it under the rule of zero using `std::vector<char>`, and compare what the compiler writes for each.

steps.label: Step 1: rule of five
steps.text: `explicit Buffer(int n) : p{new char[n]}, n{n} { } ~Buffer() { delete[] p; }` plus a correct copy constructor, copy assignment, `noexcept` move constructor and `noexcept` move assignment — roughly 15 careful lines, each one a chance to leak, double-delete or forget `noexcept`.

steps.label: Step 2: rule of zero
steps.text: `class Buffer2 { std::vector<char> buf; public: explicit Buffer2(int n) : buf(n) { } };` — zero special members declared.

steps.label: Step 3: what the compiler writes for Buffer2
steps.text: Generated copy = memberwise through `vector`'s copy (allocate + n byte copies); generated move = `vector`'s `noexcept` pointer hand-off; generated destructor frees; generated assignments likewise — all correct, all already tested library code.

steps.label: Step 4: count and compare
steps.text: For a 4096-byte buffer the runtime costs are identical: copy = one 4 KiB allocation + 4 KiB of copying; move = a few machine words. The difference is 15 lines of your code vs 1 — and the zero version cannot get the details wrong.

examples.result: Rule of zero by default; rule of five only when a bare resource or a subtle invariant forces your hand — and then all five, deliberately, with `=default` where the generated one was right anyway.

examples.title: Working through generating default operations
examples.problem: The rules of zero and the big five. Your task: list the six generated operations and their generated meanings.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: list the six generated operations and their generated meanings. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Six operations, generated with memberwise semantics (copy, move) and reverse-order destruction — correct by construction for composed classes.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `Widget w; Widget v = std::move(w);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — apply the suppression and deletion rules to any class declaration — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Taking over one changes the rules for the rest: moves vanish behind a destructor or copy declaration; declaring a move deletes the copies. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Six operations, generated with memberwise semantics (copy, move) and reverse-order destruction — correct by construction for composed classes. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Six operations, generated with memberwise semantics (copy, move) and reverse-order destruction — correct by construction for composed classes.
Taking over one changes the rules for the rest: moves vanish behind a destructor or copy declaration; declaring a move deletes the copies.
Rule of zero: compose from resource-owning members and declare nothing; rule of five: once you declare any one, define or `=default`/`=delete` all of them.

quiz.q: You declare `~Buffer()` and nothing else. Which best describes the compiler's response?
options: copy operations are still generated (deprecated), but the move operations are NOT — your `Buffer` now copies where it could have moved
all five other operations are still generated as before
moves are deleted: using one is a compile error
quiz.explanation: A destructor signals resource management, so generated moves are suppressed for safety — and the class silently degrades to copy behavior, the classic performance trap.

quiz.q: The rule of zero works because the generated operations…
options: apply only to classes with no data members
delegate to the members' own operations, which already get copy, move and destruction right
quiz.explanation: Memberwise semantics mean a class composed of `string`/`vector`/`unique_ptr` members inherits their correctness — nothing for you to write.

quiz.q: A copy constructor declared `=delete` means that…
options: the class cannot be constructed at all
the compiler writes a slower copy instead
any use of the copy constructor is a compile-time error — as with `unique_ptr`
copies are allowed only for temporaries
quiz.explanation: Deleted functions stay in overload resolution and fail loudly when chosen — the mechanism that makes move-only types safe.

quiz.q: The generated destructor destroys members…
options: in reverse declaration order, after the destructor body
in the order of the member initializer lists across the class
in alphabetical order of member names
quiz.explanation: Mirror-image of construction: body first (members still alive), then members last-declared-first.

depth.title: The generated-default-operations rules, exactly

blocks.body: Before C++11 there were four implicitly generated operations — default constructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, destructor — and one rule: generation unless you declared your own. Move semantics forced the committee to interlock *six* operations without breaking the billions of lines of C++98 already deployed. The result is a compromise, and every clause of it is a decision you can reconstruct: make the dangerous combination a hard error, keep the historically common one compiling, and let the rest follow from memberwise semantics. Knowing *why* each rule reads as it does is what separates memorizing the table from being able to derive it.

blocks.heading: Generation and suppression
blocks.body: Let `X` be a class. **(a) Default constructor**: implicitly declared iff `X` has no user-declared constructor of any kind. **(b) Copy constructor**: declared unless `X` has a user-declared copy constructor, move constructor or move assignment; it is *defined as deleted* if `X` has a user-declared move operation; its generation is *deprecated* (but still happens) if `X` has a user-declared copy assignment or destructor. **(c) Copy assignment**: symmetric — declared unless user-declared copy assignment, move constructor or move assignment exists; deleted given a user-declared move operation; deprecated given a user-declared copy constructor or destructor. **(d) Move constructor and move assignment**: declared only if `X` has no user-declared copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment *or* destructor. **(e) Destructor**: declared unless user-declared. Independently of all the above, any generated operation that would be ill-formed for a member — e.g. copy assignment when a member is a reference or `const` — is *deleted*. Deprecation is not suppression: the deprecated functions still exist and work.

blocks.heading: Why the rules are asymmetric on purpose
blocks.body: **Declaring any constructor removes the default constructor** because you have taken over initialization policy: what would 'construct from nothing' even mean for `Vector(int)`? A guess. **Declaring a move operation deletes the copies** because a hand-written move only exists when the class manages resources non-trivially — and there, a memberwise copy of a raw handle would give two owners and a double delete. The committee chose a *compile-time error* over a silent, expensive, occasionally fatal copy. **Declaring a destructor or copy operation merely suppresses moves** (falling back to copies) for exactly the opposite reason: C++98 code with destructors was everywhere, and had moves been deleted, no recompilation campaign would have survived. So the asymmetry maps onto risk: hard error where the bug is likely (user move + generated copy), quiet fallback where history demanded it (user destructor + no moves). Note the one surprise in row 5 of the table: a user destructor does *not* remove the generated default constructor — a destructor is not a constructor.

blocks.heading: The performance cliff, quantified
blocks.body: Take a `Buffer` with 4 KiB payloads and one hand-written destructor — moves silently suppressed. Grow a `std::vector<Buffer>` to $n = 1{,}000{,}000$ elements by `push_back`: geometric doubling performs about $2n = 2{,}000{,}000$ element transfers in total. With working moves, each transfer is the object's few machine words (say 24 bytes): about $2 \times 10^6 \times 24\ \text{B} \approx 48$ MB of traffic. With moves suppressed, each transfer deep-copies: $2 \times 10^6 \times 4096\ \text{B} \approx 8.2$ GB of `memcpy`, plus about two million extra heap allocations and frees. One added destructor line — invisible in review — costs roughly a 170-fold traffic increase and a much larger wall-clock factor from allocation. The fix is mechanical: `Buffer(Buffer&&) noexcept = default; Buffer& operator=(Buffer&&) noexcept = default;` (or just follow the rule of zero), and the numbers collapse back to 48 MB.

blocks.heading: Composing the rules: how zero-rule classes get away with it
blocks.body: The rules *compose through members*, which is the whole reason the rule of zero works. `unique_ptr` deletes its copy and declares its move, so a class holding one gets its copy operations deleted automatically and its move operations generated (memberwise move through a movable member is well-formed). A class holding a `std::mutex` — neither copyable nor movable — becomes immovable itself; a `lock_guard` member quietly propagates 'no copy, no move'. The same propagation deletes a generated copy assignment for any class with a reference or `const` member, because such a member cannot be assigned. When you audit a class, read its members first: the special members it will receive are exactly what its members are willing to provide.

The deprecation marks are the standard's way of saying 'this compiles, but it should not have to.' Core Guidelines rule C.21 turns the table into policy: *if you define or `=delete` any default operation, define or `=delete` all five* — `=default` counts as defining. And notice what no declaration can take from you: the destructor is generated even in the last row of the table, because every object must be destructible no matter what else was suppressed or deleted.

intro: The chapter's distilled guidance: let the compiler write the special members (rule of zero), take over all five when you must, make moves `noexcept`, prefer `{}` initialization, and keep destructors exception-free. The list is short because the rules underneath are mechanical — once you know them.
objectives: Decide, for a given class, whether to write zero or five special members
Apply the initialization and `noexcept` advice to new code
Recognize destructor-related traps before they ship

concepts.statement: Design classes so that no special member is needed: resource-owning members (`string`, `vector`, `unique_ptr`, file handles) carry the weight. Reach for the rule of five only when a bare resource or a subtle invariant leaves no alternative.
concepts.detail: The strongest form of the advice: a class with no bare resources reads like a class of values, and value semantics are the easiest to reason about and test.

concepts.statement: If you declare any of destructor, copy or move operations, define or `=delete` all five. The suppression rules of 17.6 otherwise rewrite your class' behavior behind your back — typically, your destructor just cost you your moves.
concepts.detail: A declaration you added 'for logging' is still a declaration: state your intent for the whole set, even if four of the five are `=default`.

concepts.statement: Mark move constructors and move assignments **`noexcept`** — containers pay you back with real moves during growth. Initialize with **`{}`**: narrowing errors and vexing parses become compile-time errors instead of runtime surprises.
concepts.detail: Together the two habits remove the two classic silent-degradation modes: copy-instead-of-move, and 'it compiled with `=` but meant something else'.

concepts.statement: Never throw from a destructor; never call one by name (`delete` and scope exit do it); and ensure every resource a constructor acquires has exactly one release path — the constructor/destructor pair is the unit of resource management.
concepts.detail: A destructor that logs, flushes or unlocks should absorb failures itself; one that throws during unwinding kills the process (17.2).

concepts.term: Shipping rule for construction, cleanup, copy, and move
concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Default to the rule of zero: compose from resource-owning members and declare no special members; take over all five only when forced.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: Auditing `File_handle`
examples.problem: Review `class File_handle { FILE* f; public: File_handle(const char* n) : f{std::fopen(n, "r")} { if (!f) throw std::runtime_error{"open failed"}; } ~File_handle() { std::fclose(f); } };` against the advice list.

steps.label: Step 1: the acquisition pair ✓
steps.text: The constructor acquires and *fails loudly* — the invariant 'f points to an open file' holds or the object never exists. The destructor releases on every exit path. Core RAII done.

steps.label: Step 2: the missing five ✗
steps.text: Copying would `fclose` the same `FILE*` twice. The class declares a destructor, so its moves are suppressed too — by 17.6 it silently degrades to (broken) copying.

steps.label: Step 3: the fix
steps.text: Declare the whole set: copies `=delete`; moves defined (transfer `f`, null the source) and `noexcept` — or better, store a `std::ifstream` and declare nothing at all (rule of zero).

steps.label: Step 4: the payoff
steps.text: Users write `File_handle h{"data.txt"};` and cannot leak, double-close, or forget to check — the class carries the discipline they would otherwise have to remember.

examples.result: Four audit questions — paired? all five? moves `noexcept`? destructor quiet? — are the chapter's advice in checklist form.

examples.title: Reviewing construction, cleanup, copy, and move code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: decide, for a given class, whether to write zero or five special members.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Default to the rule of zero: compose from resource-owning members and declare no special members; take over all five only when forced.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `Widget w; Widget v = std::move(w);`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: apply the initialization and `noexcept` advice to new code. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Any special-member declaration triggers the 17.6 rules — state your intent for the whole set, and make moves `noexcept` so containers actually move.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Default to the rule of zero: compose from resource-owning members and declare no special members; take over all five only when forced. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Default to the rule of zero: compose from resource-owning members and declare no special members; take over all five only when forced.
Any special-member declaration triggers the 17.6 rules — state your intent for the whole set, and make moves `noexcept` so containers actually move.
Destructors never throw, are never called by name, and pair one-to-one with constructor acquisitions; `{}` initialization keeps the build-time surprises coming (the good kind).

quiz.q: The best first response for a class whose members already manage their own resources is:
options: declare none of them — the rule of zero
write all six special members by hand for clarity
derive it from a base class with virtual functions
quiz.explanation: Generated operations delegate to the members; composed of well-behaved members, the class needs nothing written.

quiz.q: Which operation should essentially never be invoked by name in normal code?
quiz.explanation: Scope exit, `delete` and unwinding invoke destructors; naming one is for placement-`new` specialists only.

quiz.q: Move operations should be marked `noexcept` because:
options: it documents the contract only; behavior is unchanged
containers grow with moves only when the move cannot throw — otherwise they copy for exception safety
the compiler deletes moves that can throw
quiz.explanation: A throwing move mid-reallocation would lose data; a copy leaves the source intact. No `noexcept` label, no moves — just silent copies.

intro: Overloading is one name with several meanings, selected by the types of the arguments — never by the return. It exists so that a concept can keep its natural notation across types: `+` adds `int`s, `double`s and `complex`es alike, and library types can meet user expectations without new syntax. All of the machinery runs at compile time, which is why overloading costs nothing at run time and forgives nothing at compile time.
objectives: Define overloading and the role argument types play in selecting among same-named functions
Rank the conversion categories used to choose a best match
State what overload resolution cannot do — overloading on return type, run-time selection

concepts.statement: **Overloading** lets several functions share a name with different parameter lists; the compiler selects among them by the argument types at each call site. When several functions or operators share a name, the choice among them — *overload resolution* — happens entirely at compile time.
concepts.detail: Two overloads that differ only in return type are an error: the return type is not part of the selection, so the compiler could never choose between them.

concepts.statement: The point is uniformity of notation for uniform meaning: users write `z1 + z2` for complex addition rather than `add(z1, z2)`, and `cout << x` rather than a family of `print_int`, `print_double`, … functions. The name carries the concept; the argument types pick the implementation.
concepts.detail: This is why overloading matters most for operator overloading (18.2–18.3) and for generic programming, where one template name must mean the same thing across many types.

concepts.statement: (1) **Name lookup** collects the candidate set from the visible scopes. (2) The **viable** candidates are those with the right number of parameters and arguments convertible to the parameter types. (3) The **best match** wins: a candidate that is better than every other in at least one argument and at least as good in all of them. If two candidates each win one argument, the call is *ambiguous* — a compile-time error.
concepts.detail: Member functions, non-members and (for operators) the built-in meanings all compete in the same pool — which is where chapter 18's subtlest examples come from.

concepts.statement: For ranking a single argument: **exact match** beats **integral or floating promotion** (`char` to `int`, `float` to `double`), which beats a **standard conversion** (`char` to `double`, `int` to `double`), which beats a **user-defined conversion** — at most one — which beats matching an ellipsis `...`.
concepts.detail: Exact match includes only trivial adjustments (array-to-pointer, qualification). Promotion beats conversion is the fact that decides most textbook resolution puzzles.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Operators as a design tool. You can claim this section when you can define overloading and the role argument types play in selecting among same-named functions — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 18 (Overloading); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Resolve four calls by hand
examples.problem: Given only `void f(int);` and `void f(double);` in scope, determine which function is chosen — or ambiguity — for `f(5)`, `f('a')`, `f(3.0f)` and `f(true)`.

steps.label: Step 1: f(5)
steps.text: Exact match for `f(int)` — no conversion anywhere, decision made.

steps.label: Step 2: f('a')
steps.text: No `f(char)`; `char` to `int` is an *integral promotion*, while `char` to `double` is a *standard conversion*. Promotion outranks conversion → `f(int)` (with argument value 97).

steps.label: Step 3: f(3.0f)
steps.text: No `f(float)`; `float` to `double` is the *floating-point promotion*, `float` to `int` a standard conversion. Promotion wins → `f(double)`.

steps.label: Step 4: f(true)
steps.text: `bool` to `int` is an integral promotion → `f(int)` receives 1; `f(double)` would need a standard conversion and loses.

examples.result: `f(int)`, `f(int)`, `f(double)`, `f(int)` — promotion beat conversion every time the two overloads offered the choice.

examples.problem: Operators as a design tool. Your task: define overloading and the role argument types play in selecting among same-named functions.

keyTakeaways: One name, several parameter lists: the argument types select the overload, at compile time; return type never participates.
Resolution: lookup builds the candidates, viability filters by arity and convertibility, best match wins or the call is ambiguous.
Per-argument ranking: exact > promotion > standard conversion > user-defined conversion (one) > ellipsis.

quiz.q: Two functions with the same name and identical parameter lists but different return types:
options: are a compile-time error — return type is not part of overload selection
select the overload by the context of the return value
quiz.explanation: Callers do not always use the return, so it cannot drive selection; the two declarations simply clash.

quiz.q: For `f('a')` with overloads `f(int)` and `f(double)` only, which is called?
options: `f(int)` — `char` to `int` is a promotion and outranks the conversion to `double`
quiz.explanation: Integral promotion (char to int) beats the standard conversion char to double — the classic ranking fact.

quiz.q: Overload resolution happens:
options: at run time, using the dynamic types of the arguments
at compile time, using the static types of the arguments
quiz.explanation: It is pure compile-time machinery — zero run-time cost, and run-time polymorphism is an entirely different mechanism (virtual functions, chapter 20).

quiz.q: A call is reported *ambiguous* when:
options: no candidate has the right number of parameters
two viable candidates each convert an argument better than the other, so neither is best
an argument is a class type
a candidate is declared in a namespace
quiz.explanation: Best match must dominate in one argument and tie or win in all others; mutual domination means no winner — the compiler refuses to guess.

options: `f(int)`, because `char` to `int` is a promotion while `char` to `double` is a conversion, and promotions rank higher
`f(double)`, because floating types always outrank integer types
The call is ambiguous, because both candidates need one conversion
Neither is viable: character arguments require an exact match
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is a call with a `char` argument against `int` and `double` overloads. Step 2: The governing rule is overload ranking: exact match beats promotion, and promotion beats general conversion. Step 3: Tracing the candidates, `char` to `int` is an integral promotion while `char` to `double` is a floating conversion, so the promotion path wins and `f(int)` is selected. Step 4: The distractors fail because no type family outranks another wholesale, the two sequences differ in rank so no ambiguity arises, and conversions make both candidates viable. Step 5: Therefore the integer overload is selected.

intro: An operator function is just a function with a strange name — `operator+`, `operator[]`, `operator()` — that the compiler calls when it sees the corresponding operator applied to operands of your types. The rules are strict where they must be: you cannot invent operators, and precedence, associativity and arity are fixed. The reward: types like `complex` and the containers that read like the built-ins.
objectives: Declare operator functions for binary, unary, subscript and call operators
Apply the member-versus-nonmember rules, including the four member-only operators
Distinguish prefix from postfix `++`/`--` and explain the return-value difference

concepts.statement: For every operator `@`, a function named **`operator@`** can be declared — as a member (`a.operator@(b)`) or a non-member (`operator@(a, b)`), and both forms compete in overload resolution. Only *existing* operators can be overloaded: there is no `operator**` for exponentiation.
concepts.detail: Precedence, associativity and the number of operands are those of the built-in operator — overloading adds meanings, never syntax. `operator+` for two `complex` values still binds exactly as tightly as `a + b` always did.

concepts.statement: **`=` (assignment), `[]` (subscript), `()` (call) and `->` (dereference) must be member functions** — their left operand must be the object itself, with identity. Everything else is free: symmetric binary operators (`==`, `+`, `*`) are best as non-members, so both operands take conversions with equal rights.
concepts.detail: Conversion operators (18.4) are members by the same logic. The `->` operator is the odd one out: it may return a pointer or another class with its own `operator->`, so smart pointers chain.

concepts.statement: `::` (scope), `.` and `.*` (member access), `?:` (conditional), `sizeof`, `alignof`, `typeid`, `noexcept` and the cast operators (`static_cast` and friends) **cannot be overloaded** — their meaning is wired into the type system itself.
concepts.detail: The committee kept these fixed because their operands are type names or because their behavior could not be meaningfully replaced (what would an overloaded `?:` even select between?).

concepts.statement: Prefix is **`T& operator++()`** — increments the object and returns it by reference. Postfix is **`T operator++(int)`**: the dummy `int` parameter exists purely to distinguish the two forms; the function saves the old value, increments, and returns the *old* value by value.
concepts.detail: So `++c` means 'increment, use the new value' (a reference, no copy), while `c++` means 'use the old value (a copy), increment' — the built-in semantics exactly, and the reason `++c` is the preferred spelling in loops.

concepts.statement: `operator[]` gives a container class built-in feel for element access — the checked version throws `std::out_of_range` rather than reading arbitrary memory. `operator()` takes any number of arguments and turns objects into *function objects*, the foundation of the standard algorithms' flexibility.
concepts.detail: A `const` and a non-`const` subscript pair (chapter 16's const-overloading) gives read access on `const` objects and write access on mutable ones — the standard container idiom.

figures.caption: Figure — Overload resolution for `a @ b`: candidate operator functions (member and non-member forms, plus the built-in meanings) are gathered by lookup, filtered for viability, and ranked per argument — exact, promotion, standard, user-defined conversion (at most one), ellipsis — with a unique best match required or the call is rejected as ambiguous.

examples.title: Prefix, postfix and checked subscript, traced
examples.problem: For `struct Counter { int n = 0; Counter& operator++() { ++n; return *this; } Counter operator++(int) { Counter old = *this; ++n; return old; } };` trace `Counter c; int a = c++; int b = ++c;` — then show the checked subscript idiom.

steps.label: Step 1: int a = c++; (n starts at 0)
steps.text: Postfix runs: `old` snapshots `{n: 0}`, `n` becomes 1, and the snapshot is returned → `a == 0`, `c.n == 1`.

steps.label: Step 2: int b = ++c;
steps.text: Prefix runs: `n` becomes 2 and `*this` is returned (no copy) → `b == 2`, `c.n == 2`. Note the types: prefix returns a reference, postfix returns a value — one copy per postfix use.

steps.label: Step 3: checked subscript
steps.text: `double& Vector::operator[](int i) { if (i < 0 || size() <= i) throw std::out_of_range{"Vector::operator[]"}; return elem[i]; }` — `v[v.size()]` throws instead of reading the next object in memory.

steps.label: Step 4: the const companion
steps.text: Adding `double operator[](int i) const` gives read access on `const Vector`s — read-only subscript on read-only objects, the container idiom.

examples.result: `a == 0, b == 2`, and out-of-range access is a catchable exception, not undefined behavior.

keyTakeaways: Operator functions are named `operator@`; only existing operators, with their built-in precedence, associativity and arity — `=`, `[]`, `()` and `->` must be members.
`::`, `.`, `.*`, `?:`, `sizeof`, `alignof`, `typeid`, `noexcept` and the casts cannot be overloaded at all.
Prefix `++` returns the updated object by reference; postfix `++(int)` returns the old value by value; checked `operator[]` trades a branch for the elimination of undefined behavior.

quiz.q: Which operator must be defined as a member function?
quiz.explanation: `=`, `[]`, `()` and `->` require the left operand to be the object; the others — including `==` and `<<` — work better as non-members anyway.

quiz.q: Which of these cannot be overloaded?
quiz.explanation: The conditional operator's meaning depends on evaluating exactly one branch — the type system keeps it for itself, along with `::`, `.`, `sizeof` and friends.

quiz.q: The declaration `Counter operator++(int)` defines:
options: the prefix increment, returning a reference
the postfix increment — the `int` is a dummy parameter, and the old value is returned by value
an increment that takes a count
quiz.explanation: The parameter exists only to give postfix a different signature from `T& operator++()`. It is never used, and is conventionally left unnamed.

quiz.q: Overloading `operator+` for `complex` operands changes the precedence of `+` in `a + b * c`:
options: not at all — precedence and associativity are fixed by the language
only if the operator is a non-member
quiz.explanation: Overloading adds meanings for user-defined operands; the grammar of expressions is untouchable.

intro: The chapter's showcase puts the machinery to work: a `complex<T>` supporting `+`, `*`, `+=`, mixed arithmetic with scalars, and output — reading exactly like the built-in numeric types. Two decisions carry the design: compound assignment (`+=`, `*=`) as the primitive member, and free `+`/`*` built on top of it, with by-value parameters so conversions reach both operands equally.
objectives: Read the `complex` class: representation, constructor and accessors
Explain why `operator+=` is a member while `operator+` is not
Do complex arithmetic by hand — the numbers the operators encode

concepts.statement: `template<class T> class complex { T re, im; public: complex(const T& r = {}, const T& i = {}) : re{r}, im{i} { } /* … */ T real() const { return re; } T imag() const { return im; } };` — two data members, one constructor with default arguments (so `complex{1,2}`, `complex{1}` and `complex{}` all construct), const accessors. A concrete class in chapter 16's sense: no virtuals, cheap to copy.
concepts.detail: The representation is deliberately exposed *through accessors only* — users cannot put the two doubles into an invalid state, and the class stays small enough to copy like an `int`.

concepts.statement: `complex& operator+=(complex a) { re += a.re; im += a.im; return *this; }` — a member, modifying `*this`, returning `*this` by reference (mirroring the built-in `+=`). Then `operator+` is written *from* it: `complex operator+(complex a, complex b) { return a += b; }` — non-member, by value, so conversions apply to both operands with equal rights.
concepts.detail: This layering is the chapter's central design lesson: define the essential operation that needs privileged access (`+=` reads `re`, `im`), then express the rest in terms of it. `a += b` inside `operator+` is legal because `a` is a local by-value copy nobody else needs.

concepts.statement: `z + 2.0` and `2.0 + z` both work: the `double` converts to `complex<double>` via the converting constructor, and *one* `operator+` serves both orders. The templated converting constructor `template<class X> complex(const complex<X>&)` brings `complex<float>` into `complex<double>` the same way.
concepts.detail: This is exactly why `operator+` must not be a member: a member `+` would only convert its right operand, and `2.0 + z` would fail while `z + 2.0` worked — an asymmetry users would hate.

concepts.statement: For $z = a + bi$: the **modulus** is $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ and the **argument** is $\arg z = \operatorname{atan2}(b, a)$. Neither needs member status — helpers reading `real()` and `imag()` suffice, keeping the class minimal.
concepts.detail: The rule the operators encode: $(a+bi)(c+di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i$ — one temporary for the new real part avoids re-reading `re` after overwriting it.

concepts.statement: `operator+` returns a `complex` by value — two doubles, trivially moved (chapter 17). The by-value parameters are equally deliberate: each is a fresh copy the function may consume (`a += b` mutates the copy), so no self-aliasing cases exist and the code stays branch-free.
concepts.detail: Return-by-value + move semantics means users write `z3 = z1 * z2;` with no hidden allocation at all — the whole expression is a few floating operations.

examples.title: Hand-computing what the operators do
examples.problem: Evaluate `complex<double> z1{3, 4}; complex<double> z2{1, -2}; complex<double> z3 = z1 * z2;` and `complex<double> z4 = z1 + 2;` by hand, and compute `|z1|` and `arg z1`.

steps.label: Step 1: the multiply formula
steps.text: $(a+bi)(c+di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i$ with $a=3, b=4, c=1, d=-2$.

steps.label: Step 3: imaginary part
steps.text: $ad + bc = 3 \cdot (-2) + 4 \cdot 1 = -6 + 4 = -2$. So `z3 == complex{11.0, -2.0}` — and the member `operator*=` computes exactly these, keeping `re` in a temporary until both parts are done.

steps.label: Step 4: the mixed add
steps.text: `z1 + 2` — the literal converts to `complex<double>{2, 0}`, then `operator+` adds: real $3 + 2 = 5$, imaginary $4 + 0 = 4$ → `{5, 4}`.

steps.label: Step 5: modulus and argument
steps.text: $|z_1| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ — the 3-4-5 triangle; $\arg z_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(4, 3) \approx 0.9273$ radians (about 53.13 degrees).

examples.result: `z3 = {11, -2}`, `z4 = {5, 4}`, `|z1| = 5`, `arg z1 ≈ 53.13°` — thin operators over school algebra, with types that carry the rules.

examples.title: Working through a complex number type
examples.problem: Classic operator overloading in action. Your task: read the `complex` class: representation, constructor and accessors.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: read the `complex` class: representation, constructor and accessors. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `complex` is two doubles plus accessors: a concrete type whose constructor's default arguments make `complex{1,2}`, `complex{1}` and `complex{}` all work.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `Complex operator+(Complex a, Complex b) { return a += b; }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain why `operator+=` is a member while `operator+` is not — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: `+=` and `*=` are members returning `*this`; `+` and `*` are non-members built on them with by-value parameters, so `2.0 + z` works exactly like `z + 2.0`. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `complex` is two doubles plus accessors: a concrete type whose constructor's default arguments make `complex{1,2}`, `complex{1}` and `complex{}` all work. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `complex` is two doubles plus accessors: a concrete type whose constructor's default arguments make `complex{1,2}`, `complex{1}` and `complex{}` all work.
`+=` and `*=` are members returning `*this`; `+` and `*` are non-members built on them with by-value parameters, so `2.0 + z` works exactly like `z + 2.0`.
The operators encode $(a+bi)(c+di) = (ac-bd) + (ad+bc)i$ — verify by hand: $(3+4i)(1-2i) = 11-2i$.

quiz.q: The product $(2+i)(3-i)$ equals:
quiz.explanation: Real: $2\cdot3 - 1\cdot(-1) = 7$; imaginary: $2\cdot(-1) + 1\cdot3 = 1$ — the same two expressions the member `operator*=` computes.

quiz.q: Why is `operator+` for `complex` a non-member taking its parameters by value?
options: so conversions apply to *both* operands equally — `2.0 + z` works exactly like `z + 2.0`
because a member cannot return a value
quiz.explanation: A member `+` would convert only the right operand, breaking symmetry; by-value copies are also free to be consumed by the `+=` inside.

quiz.q: `complex<double>& operator+=(complex a)` returns:
options: a reference to the right-hand operand
a reference to `*this`, mirroring the built-in `+=` so it can chain
a copy of the old value
quiz.explanation: Assignment-flavored operators return the (updated) left operand by reference — the built-in pattern, and what makes `z1 += z2 += z3` meaningful.

quiz.q: The expression `z1 + 2` compiles and gives `{5, 4}` because:
options: the literal `2` converts to `complex<double>{2, 0}` via the converting constructor, then the single `operator+` applies
`2` is stored as the imaginary part
quiz.explanation: One converting constructor plus one operator serves all mixed arithmetic — no explosion of overloads, and both orders symmetric.

intro: Constructors convert *into* your type; conversion operators convert *out* of it. Both can fire implicitly, and having both directions at once makes ordinary expressions ambiguous — the chapter's cautionary tale. `explicit` is the brake: it keeps a constructor from converting implicitly, or a conversion operator from firing anywhere a boolean is not obviously wanted.
objectives: Define conversions both into and out of a class type
Use `explicit` to prevent implicit conversions — including the `explicit operator bool` idiom
Diagnose the classic two-way conversion ambiguity

concepts.statement: A constructor taking one effective argument — `complex(double)` — defines an implicit conversion **from** its argument type **into** the class: wherever a `complex` is expected, a plain `double` silently becomes one. This is precisely how `z + 2` works.
concepts.detail: The conversion is the *whole point* for math-like types, and a hazard for container-like ones — which is why the chapter pairs this idea with `explicit`.

concepts.statement: A member function of the form **`operator T() const`** converts the object **to** `T`. `operator double()` on a `complex` would let it flow into arithmetic as its real part — convenient, and treacherous: it silently discards the imaginary part.
concepts.detail: Conversion operators are necessarily member functions (18.2's identity requirement, again). For output-style conversion, a named function like `real()` is safer than an operator that fires without being called.

concepts.statement: **`explicit complex(double)`** stops the implicit conversion path: `complex z = 3;` no longer compiles, while `complex z{3};` still does. **`explicit operator bool()`** (C++11) is the idiomatic middle ground — the conversion fires in condition contexts like `if (p)` but not in accidents like `int n = p;`.
concepts.detail: Rule of thumb: make single-argument constructors `explicit` unless implicit conversion is genuinely part of the class' value semantics (as with `complex`).

concepts.statement: An implicit conversion sequence applies **at most one user-defined conversion** — a constructor or a conversion operator — possibly surrounded by standard conversions on either side. `A → B → C` through two class conversions is never done silently; the programmer must name one of the steps.
concepts.detail: This keeps meaning under control: with two implicit user conversions chained, almost any expression could mean almost anything, and every overload set would explode.

concepts.statement: With **both** `complex(double)` and `operator double()` in place, `z + 2.0` has two equally good readings: `operator+(complex, complex)` after converting the literal, or `operator+(double, double)` after converting `z`. Each candidate is exact in one argument and user-converted in the other — neither is better, so the call is **ambiguous**: a compile-time error.
concepts.detail: The cure is one-directional conversion: delete `operator double()` and expose the value as a named function (`z.real()`), or make the constructor `explicit`. Libraries that keep both directions are unusable in arithmetic — a design lesson, not just a language quirk.

examples.title: The ambiguous addition
examples.problem: Given `class complex { public: complex(double r = 0, double i = 0); operator double() const; /* … */ };` and `complex z1{1, 2};`, what happens for `complex z2 = z1 + 2.0;` — and what if both operands are complex?

steps.label: Step 1: the candidates
steps.text: For `z1 + 2.0`, resolution gathers the user `operator+(complex, complex)` and the built-in `operator+(double, double)` — both are viable.

steps.label: Step 2: reading A (complex + complex)
steps.text: `z1` matches exactly; the literal `2.0` needs one user-defined conversion — the constructor `complex(double)`.

steps.label: Step 3: reading B (double + double)
steps.text: `2.0` matches exactly; `z1` needs one user-defined conversion — `operator double()` (silently dropping the imaginary part 2).

steps.label: Step 4: the tie
steps.text: Each candidate is better in one argument and worse in the other: neither is the best match → the call is **ambiguous**, a compile-time error. (For `z1 + z3` there is no tie: `operator+(complex, complex)` is exact in *both* arguments and wins outright.)

steps.label: Step 5: the fix
steps.text: Remove `operator double()` and offer `z1.real()` instead — one direction of implicit conversion, no ambiguity, no silent loss of the imaginary part.

examples.result: Two viable readings, one dead program — implicit conversion must be one-directional, or the arithmetic you meant to enable becomes unexpressible.

examples.title: Working through type conversion
examples.problem: Conversions to and from your types. Your task: define conversions both into and out of a class type.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define conversions both into and out of a class type. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A single-argument constructor converts into the class; `operator T() const` converts out; at most one user-defined conversion fires in any implicit sequence.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `Complex operator+(Complex a, Complex b) { return a += b; }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — use `explicit` to prevent implicit conversions — including the `explicit operator bool` idiom — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: `explicit` disables implicit use of a constructor or conversion operator — `explicit operator bool()` keeps `if (p)` while forbidding `int n = p;`. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A single-argument constructor converts into the class; `operator T() const` converts out; at most one user-defined conversion fires in any implicit sequence. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A single-argument constructor converts into the class; `operator T() const` converts out; at most one user-defined conversion fires in any implicit sequence.
`explicit` disables implicit use of a constructor or conversion operator — `explicit operator bool()` keeps `if (p)` while forbidding `int n = p;`.
Conversion in both directions at once makes expressions like `z + 2.0` ambiguous — the compiler refuses, and it is right to.

quiz.q: With both `complex(double)` and `operator double()` declared, the expression `z + 2.0` is:
options: resolved to `operator+(complex, complex)` — the exact match on the left wins
resolved to `operator+(double, double)` — the exact match on the right wins
ambiguous: each candidate wins one argument, so neither is best — compile-time error
evaluated left to right, first conversion first
quiz.explanation: Best match must dominate: here each reading converts exactly one argument via a user-defined conversion, so the comparison ties and the compiler rejects the call.

quiz.q: An `explicit operator bool()` on a stream allows:
quiz.explanation: Explicit conversion operators fire only where a boolean is clearly required (conditions, `!`, `&&`, `||`) — the accidental conversions are compiled away.

quiz.q: How many user-defined conversions may one implicit conversion sequence apply?
quiz.explanation: Standard conversions may bracket it, but only one constructor or conversion operator fires implicitly — the rule that keeps overload sets sane.

quiz.q: A constructor `Vector(int)` without `explicit`:
options: implicitly converts `int` to `Vector` — so `Vector v = 7;` compiles
quiz.explanation: That is the definition of a converting constructor; when it is not part of the design, `explicit` turns the surprise into a compile error.

quiz.q: A class `Score` provides both a non-explicit constructor `Score(int)` and a conversion operator `operator int()`. What follows for code that mixes `Score` values with integers?
options: The constructor path always wins every overload contest
The conversion operator path always wins every overload contest
Calls may turn ambiguous or surprising as two user-defined conversion sequences compete, so one direction should be marked explicit
Every use of `+` with a `Score` is ill-formed
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is a type convertible implicitly in both directions with plain integers. Step 2: The governing rule is conversion budgeting: overload resolution admits at most one user-defined conversion per sequence, and when inward and outward paths both qualify, competing sequences can tie or pick surprising winners. Step 3: Tracing a mixed expression, the compiler may convert the integer into a `Score` or the `Score` into an integer with neither sequence outranking the other, producing ambiguity or silent behavior shifts. Step 4: The distractors fail because neither direction dominates by rule, and many expressions remain well-formed while meaning something unintended. Step 5: Therefore one direction should be explicit unless both implicit paths are genuinely wanted.

intro: The advice column condenses the chapter: operators earn their keep only by keeping their promises. Use the conventional meanings, mirror the built-ins' behavior (return types, self-modification, evaluation), keep symmetric operators non-member, and treat implicit conversions as the loaded convenience they are.
objectives: Apply the conventional-meaning rule when designing operators
Match built-in semantics for return types and mutation
Decide member versus non-member and implicit versus explicit by principle

concepts.statement: If you overload `+`, it should add. `==` should be an equivalence relation; `<` a strict weak ordering; `*` multiplication. Surprising meanings — `*` as 'repeat the string' — defeat the purpose of notation, because readers *assume* the conventional meaning, and code that looks right while being wrong is worse than code that looks wrong.
concepts.detail: When the operation you want has no conventional operator, use a named member function: honest syntax beats clever syntax.

concepts.statement: `+=` modifies its left operand and returns `*this` by reference; `+` computes a new value without modifying either operand; postfix `++` yields the old value by value; assignment forms chain (`a = b = c`). Deviations compile and confuse — including you, a month later.
concepts.detail: Also mirror *evaluation* behavior: do not overload `&&`, `||` or `,` at all, because their built-in short-circuit and sequencing guarantees cannot survive becoming function calls — both operands would evaluate, in unspecified order.

concepts.statement: The built-in `&&` and `||` evaluate their second operand only when needed; the comma operator sequences. An overloaded version is a plain function call: *both* operands are evaluated and the guarantee is gone. The semantics silently change — a real bug factory, not a style issue.
concepts.detail: This is the one operator-design rule with no exceptions in practice: no library in the standard does it, and neither should you.

concepts.statement: Make `==`, `+`, `*` non-members so conversions apply equally to both operands — `2 + z` as legal as `z + 2`. And define implicit conversions only where the value semantics are genuine (`double` to `complex`); when in doubt, `explicit` — a conversion that surprises is worse than a named function call.
concepts.detail: The two rules are one rule: conversion-rich types need non-member symmetric operators, and conversion-poor types need neither.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Operators must keep their conventional meanings — `+` adds, `==` is an equivalence, `<` orders — or the notation actively misleads.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: Design review: three operators for String
examples.problem: A proposal adds `String operator*(const String& s, int n)` (repeat n times), `int operator<(const String& a, const String& b)` (compare lengths) and `String& operator+(String a, const String& b)` (return the first operand). Which survive review?

steps.label: Step 1: operator* for repeat
steps.text: No multiplication is happening; readers will expect numeric meaning — reject as an operator and provide a named member `s.repeat(n)` instead.

steps.label: Step 2: operator< returning int on lengths
steps.text: `<` must return `bool` and be an ordering consistent with `==` on content; a length comparison surprises every reader and quietly breaks sorted containers that expect lexicographic order. Reject: return `bool`, compare contents.

steps.label: Step 3: operator+ returning a reference to a by-value parameter
steps.text: The parameter dies at return — a dangling reference, undefined behavior. And `+` must produce a *new* value (modifying the left operand is `+=`'s job). Reject: `String operator+(const String&, const String&)` by value.

steps.label: Step 4: the survivors
steps.text: A by-value, non-member `operator+`; a `bool`-returning lexicographic `operator<`; a named `repeat(n)` — every operator keeps the promise its syntax makes.

examples.result: All three rejected designs compiled; none kept the conventional promise — that is the review criterion.

examples.title: Reviewing overloading code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the conventional-meaning rule when designing operators.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Operators must keep their conventional meanings — `+` adds, `==` is an equivalence, `<` orders — or the notation actively misleads.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `Complex operator+(Complex a, Complex b) { return a += b; }`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: match built-in semantics for return types and mutation. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Mirror built-in behavior: `+=` mutates and returns `*this`, `+` returns a fresh value, postfix yields the old value; never overload `&&`, `||` or `,`.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Operators must keep their conventional meanings — `+` adds, `==` is an equivalence, `<` orders — or the notation actively misleads. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Operators must keep their conventional meanings — `+` adds, `==` is an equivalence, `<` orders — or the notation actively misleads.
Mirror built-in behavior: `+=` mutates and returns `*this`, `+` returns a fresh value, postfix yields the old value; never overload `&&`, `||` or `,`.
Symmetric binary operators belong outside the class so conversions reach both operands; make conversions `explicit` unless value semantics are genuine.

quiz.q: Why does the advice forbid overloading `&&`?
options: it cannot be a member function
the overloaded version evaluates both operands — the built-in short-circuit guarantee is lost
quiz.explanation: An operator function is just a call: arguments are evaluated before it runs, so `p && p->safe()` would dereference a null pointer the built-in would never touch.

quiz.q: For a class with a converting constructor, `==` should be a non-member because:
options: conversions then apply to both operands equally — `2 == z` works like `z == 2`
quiz.explanation: A member `==` converts only the right operand, producing asymmetric surprise — the same reasoning as `+` on `complex`.

quiz.q: An `operator==` for a type should:
options: return the number of equal members
be an equivalence relation — reflexive, symmetric, transitive — and consistent with `!=`
quiz.explanation: Users and the standard algorithms both *assume* equivalence semantics; anything else corrupts every abstraction built above the type.

intro: Operator overloading lets a user-defined type meet the built-in types on their own grammar: `m[i]`, `p->m`, `++it` read naturally only if the class supplies the operators behind them. This chapter gathers the operators that need special care — subscripting, dereferencing, increment and decrement, the call operator — and then assembles all of them in one place: a small but complete `String` class, together with the friend mechanism that grants carefully chosen nonmembers access to the representation.
objectives: State which operators cannot be overloaded at all and which must be non-static member functions
Apply the chapter's design rule: a user-defined operator should mirror the semantics of the built-in type
Set up the String case study by listing what a resource-owning class must define to behave like a built-in type

concepts.statement: **Precedence, grouping and arity are fixed for every type.** However `operator+` is defined for a Matrix, `a*b+c` still groups as `(a*b)+c`, a unary `+` still takes exactly one operand, and the programmer may not invent new operator tokens — the set of operators is closed.
concepts.detail: The only freedom left is what an operator does with its operands, which is why the chapter insists that meaning be chosen well.

concepts.statement: `operator=` (assignment), `operator[]` (subscripting), `operator()` (function call), `operator->` (dereferencing) and conversion operators must be non-static member functions of the class of their first operand. All other operators may be defined as nonmember functions.
concepts.detail: Members get the right operands by construction: `a[i]` invokes a member of `a`, and the updating operators (`=`, `+=`, `++`) mutate their left operand.

concepts.term: As close to a built-in as possible
concepts.statement: The goal for these operators is a user-defined type that behaves **as close to a built-in type as its semantics allow and as users expect**: a `String` should support subscripting, concatenation and comparison the way the library `string` does, so a user needs to know only what the operators mean for the type — never how they are spelled.
concepts.detail: The flip side is the chapter's discipline: an operator whose meaning users cannot guess from the notation is a design bug, however clever the implementation.

concepts.statement: The operators `::` (scope resolution), `.` (member selection), `.*` (member selection through pointer-to-member) and `?:` (conditional expression) cannot be overloaded — nor can `sizeof`, `typeid` or the named casts.
concepts.detail: They are protected because language machinery depends on them: `.` and `::` govern name lookup itself, and `?:` carries sequencing guarantees an overload could not honor.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Special operators. You can claim this section when you can state which operators cannot be overloaded at all and which must be non-static member functions — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 19 (Special Operators); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Why symmetric binary operators are nonmembers
examples.problem: A complex type can be constructed from an int. Show why `operator+` for complex must be a free function if both `z+2` and `2+z` are to work.

steps.label: Member version
steps.text: As a member `complex complex::operator+(const complex&)`, the expression `z+2` compiles: the right operand converts to complex by the constructor. But `2+z` fails — the left operand 2 is an int, and member operators are looked up only in the left operand's class; the implicit conversion is never applied to a left operand.

steps.label: Nonmember version
steps.text: With `complex operator+(const complex& a, const complex& b)` both operands are on equal footing: in `2+z` the int converts to complex(2) first, then the operator runs. Both orders compile and both mean exact complex addition.

steps.label: General rule
steps.text: Symmetric binary operators (arithmetic, equality, streaming) become nonmembers so that either operand can convert; mutating and asymmetric ones (`+=`, `=`, `[]`, `->`) stay members.

examples.result: `z+2` and `2+z` both work and both call the same function — exactly the built-in behavior the chapter asks you to preserve.

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: Special operators. Your task: state which operators cannot be overloaded at all and which must be non-static member functions.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: state which operators cannot be overloaded at all and which must be non-static member functions. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Overloading changes what an operator computes, never its precedence, grouping or operand count

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `Widget* p = new Widget; delete p;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — apply the chapter's design rule: a user-defined operator should mirror the semantics of the built-in type — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: `=`, `[]`, `()` and `->` must be non-static member functions; symmetric binary operators are best as free functions If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Overloading changes what an operator computes, never its precedence, grouping or operand count Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Overloading changes what an operator computes, never its precedence, grouping or operand count
`=`, `[]`, `()` and `->` must be non-static member functions; symmetric binary operators are best as free functions
The design goal is a class that behaves predictably like a built-in type — an operator whose meaning must be explained should not exist

quiz.q: You overload `operator+` for a Matrix class. Which of these can you not change?
options: The algorithm that computes the sum
Whether + is a member or a free function
quiz.explanation: Precedence and grouping belong to the grammar of expressions, not to the meaning of an operator; the implementation, the operand types and member-ness are all in the programmer's hands.

quiz.q: Which operator must be defined as a non-static member function?
quiz.explanation: Subscripting, assignment, function call and dereferencing with `->` are reserved to member functions; the others may be nonmembers.

quiz.q: Which of these operators can never be overloaded?
quiz.explanation: Member selection through a pointer to member, like `.` and `::`, is not overloadable — unlike `->`, which smart pointers define routinely.

quiz.q: According to the chapter's rule, `operator+` for a Money class should
options: subtract, to keep Money cheap to implement
add, mirroring what + means for built-in types
be defined only if Money also overloads *
quiz.explanation: Operators should be defined only when their meaning is obvious — and the obvious meaning is the built-in one. Anything else defeats the purpose of the notation.

intro: Subscripting, dereferencing and increment each carry a contract inherited from the built-in types, and each has a canonical implementation shape. The book's examples make the shapes concrete: an `Assoc` class whose `operator[]` returns a reference so that `++price[buf]` updates the table, smart pointers whose `operator->` is applied recursively until it reaches a real pointer, and prefix/postfix `++` distinguished by a dummy int parameter.
objectives: Implement operator[] that supports both reading and writing, as the book's Assoc does
Implement the dereference pair operator* / operator-> for smart-pointer and iterator classes
Distinguish prefix from postfix operator++ and explain why &&, || and the comma operator must not be overloaded

concepts.statement: `operator[]` must be a member and, for containers, returns a **reference to the element**: the book's `double& Assoc::operator[](const string&)` walks a vector of `(name, value)` pairs and, for a missing key, appends a `Pair{s,0}` and returns a reference to the new element — so `++price[buf]` both creates and counts.
concepts.detail: Returning the value instead of a reference would make `++price[buf]` increment a temporary and silently leave the table unchanged.

concepts.statement: `operator->` must be a member; the expression `p->m` is interpreted as `(p.operator->())->m`, and the compiler applies `operator->` **recursively** until the result is an ordinary pointer, on which the built-in member access finally runs. Smart pointers pair it with `operator*`: `*p` yields the object, `p->m` reaches its members.
concepts.detail: That recursion is what lets chains such as `p->next->val` work when every link is a smart pointer.

concepts.statement: Prefix `operator++()` updates the object and returns a reference to the updated object. Postfix `operator++(int)` takes a **dummy int**, saves the old value, updates, and returns the saved copy by value. The int argument is never used — it exists only to give the two forms distinct signatures.
concepts.detail: The contract: `p++` and `++p` leave the object in the same state and differ only in the value they deliver — increment operators must increment, just as + must add.

concepts.statement: `operator[]` accepts at most one operand, so a multi-dimensional Matrix uses the **call operator**: `m(i, j)` selects row i, column j. The same `operator()` is what turns ordinary objects into function objects.
concepts.detail: Alternatively `m[i]` can return a proxy row object with its own `operator[]` — at the cost of an extra class.

concepts.statement: The built-in `&&` and `||` evaluate the left operand first and skip the right when the result is settled; the built-in comma operator guarantees left-to-right sequencing. A user-defined version loses all three: both operands are always evaluated, in unspecified order.
concepts.detail: The book's verdict is blunt: do not overload `&&`, `||` or the comma operator — the notation lies about what it does.

examples.title: Word frequencies with Assoc
examples.problem: Count the occurrences of each word in the input `the cat sat on the mat the end` using the book's associative-array class, `class Assoc { struct Pair { string name; double val; }; vector<Pair> vec; public: double& operator[](const string&); };`

steps.label: Step 1: The lookup
steps.text: `operator[]` scans vec for the name; on a hit it returns a reference to that Pair's val, on a miss it appends `Pair{s,0}` and returns a reference to the new element's val — the value 0 is the default the caller then updates.

steps.label: Step 2: The driver
steps.text: `while (cin >> buf) ++price[buf];` — eight words are read; the first `the` is not found, a Pair with val 0 is appended, and the ++ makes it 1.

steps.label: Step 3: The tally
steps.text: Distinct names after the run: the, cat, sat, on, mat, end — six entries. Counts: the appears 3 times; each of the other five appears once. Check: 3 + 5 = 8 words read.

steps.label: Step 4: The cost
steps.text: Each lookup is a linear scan of vec: the run does $\Theta(n)$ work per word for n distinct names. The standard-library `map` keeps the same interface with $O(\log n)$ lookups — the book's point is that the operator makes both feel identical to use.

examples.result: Six pairs stored; `the` maps to 3, every other name to 1; the sum of all values equals the word count, 8. `operator[]` returning `double&` is what makes the one-line driver work.

examples.title: Reading *it++ — prefix and postfix traced
examples.problem: An iterator over `int a[] = {10, 20, 30};` provides prefix and postfix `operator++`. Trace `auto v = *it++;` followed by `++*it;` and `++it;`.

steps.label: Step 1: Postfix binds tighter
steps.text: `*it++` parses as `*(it++)`. Postfix `it++` saves the old iterator, advances it to a[1], and returns the saved copy by value — the dereference reads the OLD position: v == 10.

steps.label: Step 2: Prefix on the element
steps.text: `++*it` parses as `++(*it)`: it now points at a[1] (20), so the element itself is incremented — a[1] becomes 21.

steps.label: Step 3: Prefix on the iterator
steps.text: `++it` advances to a[2] and returns a reference to the iterator itself (no copy is made); a subsequent `*it` reads 30.

examples.result: v == 10; the array now reads {10, 21, 30} and the iterator sits on a[2]. Postfix returns the old value by value; prefix returns `*this` by reference — that is the entire difference between the two forms.

keyTakeaways: An `operator[]` that must support writing returns a reference to the stored element, never a copy
`p->m` means `(p.operator->())->m`, applied recursively until an ordinary pointer appears
Prefix ++ returns the updated object by reference; postfix ++ takes a dummy int and returns the old value by value; `&&`, `||` and comma must not be overloaded at all

quiz.q: `double& operator[](const string& s)` is called with a word not yet in the table. What does `++price[buf]` do?
options: It throws, because the key does not exist
A new Pair {s, 0} is appended and the ++ makes its val 1
The vector is cleared and the word becomes the only entry
quiz.explanation: The miss branch appends a zero-valued pair and returns a reference to it; the ++ then operates on that reference, so the count becomes 1 — exactly how the word-frequency driver works.

quiz.q: `p` is an object of a smart-pointer class whose `operator->` returns a raw `T*`. What does `p->draw()` mean?
quiz.explanation: The overload of -> yields a pointer (or another class object); the compiler keeps applying operator-> until it reaches an ordinary pointer, then uses built-in member access.

quiz.q: How does the compiler distinguish a postfix `operator++` declaration from a prefix one?
options: By the return type: postfix returns by value
Postfix takes a dummy int parameter that is never used
Postfix must be a nonmember function
Postfix is declared with two pluses: `operator++++`
quiz.explanation: The int argument exists purely to give the two forms different signatures; inside, postfix saves the old value, updates, and returns the saved copy.

quiz.q: Why does the book forbid overloading `&&`, `||` and the comma operator?
options: They must be members, and members cannot be binary
User versions lose short-circuit evaluation and the guaranteed sequencing of built-in use
They are reserved for operands of type bool only
The standard library already overloads them
quiz.explanation: The built-in operators evaluate the left operand first and may skip the right; an overload becomes a normal function call — both operands evaluated, in unspecified order — so the notation promises what the code does not deliver.

options: Both `p` and `q` hold the advanced iterator
`p` holds the original position while `q` holds the advanced one, and postfix typically costs an extra copy
`p` holds the advanced position while `q` holds the original
Both expressions are undefined when applied to iterators
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is one postfix and one prefix increment on the same iterator sequence. Step 2: The governing rules are the canonical signatures: prefix returns the advanced iterator by reference, while postfix returns the original value by value, which forces a spare copy. Step 3: Tracing statement by statement, `p` snapshots the starting position as `it` advances once, then `++it` advances again with `q` observing the twice-advanced position. Step 4: The distractors fail because the two forms deliberately return different positions, and both are well-defined operations on iterators. Step 5: Therefore postfix preserves the old position at a copying cost while prefix yields the new one.

intro: Everything the chapter has taught comes together in a small class that behaves the way a string should. The book's `String` is a deliberately simplified `std::string`: two data members — a pointer and a size — one invariant, all five special member functions, subscripting, concatenation and stream output. Each member is a few lines; together they are a complete review of what a class that owns memory must do, and a checklist for the rule of five.
objectives: State and use the String invariant: ptr points to an array of sz+1 characters whose last is the terminator
Write all five special member functions for a pointer-owning class (the rule of five)
Build free operator+ on top of member operator+=, and contrast checked access with unchecked subscripting

concepts.statement: **If `ptr` is not nullptr, it points to an array of `sz+1` characters and `ptr[sz] == 0`.** An empty String has `sz == 0` and `ptr == nullptr`. Every member preserves the invariant — and the trailing terminator is what makes `c_str()` and stream output trivial.
concepts.detail: The data members are `char* ptr; int sz;` — 16 bytes on a typical 64-bit ABI (8 for the pointer, 4 for the size, 4 of padding).

concepts.statement: A class that owns a resource must define, or deliberately delete, **destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor and move assignment**. The compiler's defaults would copy the pointer member by member — two Strings would then own one array and both destructors would `delete[]` it.
concepts.detail: The book's version of the rule: if a class has a pointer member, it usually needs these five operations — or it should hold a `string`/`vector` instead and need none of them.

concepts.statement: The move constructor copies `ptr` and `sz` into the new object, then zeroes the source (`a.ptr = nullptr; a.sz = 0;`) — $O(1)$, no allocation, and the source is left in a state safe to destroy and to assign to. The copy constructor instead allocates a fresh array and `memcpy`s all `sz+1` bytes — $O(sz)$.
concepts.detail: Moves are what let a function return a String by value without copying the characters: the return value is constructed by stealing.

concepts.statement: `char& operator[](int n)` is unchecked — C++ does not range-check built-in arrays either, and the book keeps the same zero-cost rule for String. The checked alternative, `at(n)`, throws `out_of_range` for a bad index; the standard `string` offers exactly this pair.
concepts.detail: The C++ philosophy in one contrast: the safe version exists, but you say so — you don't pay for the check unless you ask for it.

concepts.statement: The member `String& operator+=(const String&)` does the growing in place — new array, copy, append, delete old. The free function `String operator+(const String& a, const String& b)` then has a two-line body: copy `a`, `+=` `b`, return — and the copy out is a move, not another allocation.
concepts.detail: The member mutates; the nonmember makes a fresh object. That division of labor keeps every concatenation expression working with a single grown buffer.
