examples.title: Four constructions, counted
examples.problem: Trace every heap allocation in `String s{“Stroustrup”}; String t{s}; String u{std::move(s)}; String w = t + "!";`

steps.label: Step 1: From a C string
steps.text: `strlen` finds 10 characters, so `new char[11]` and `memcpy` of 11 bytes — ten letters plus the terminator — give s its invariant.

steps.label: Step 2: Copy
steps.text: `String t{s}` allocates its own 11 bytes and copies them: two independent objects, two arrays — destroying either one leaves the other intact.

steps.label: Step 3: Move
steps.text: `String u{std::move(s)}` allocates nothing: it copies the pointer and size (12 bytes on the stack) and sets `s.ptr = nullptr`, `s.sz = 0`. The source is safe to destroy and safe to assign to; it just has no characters.

steps.label: Step 4: Concatenation
steps.text: `t + "!"` first materializes the right operand as a 2-byte array, then operator+ copies t (11 bytes), and `+=` grows it to `new char[12]`, copying 10 letters, then writes '!' and the terminator: "Stroustrup!" with sz == 11.

examples.result: Exactly four allocations, totaling 11 + 11 + 2 + 12 = 36 bytes, and four `delete[]` calls at scope exit — one per array, no leaks and no double deletes.

examples.title: Why copy assignment allocates before it deletes
examples.problem: The naive assignment body `delete[] ptr; ptr = new char[a.sz+1]; memcpy(...)` has two failure modes. Repair it.

steps.label: Failure 1: self-assignment
steps.text: `s = s` runs `delete[] ptr` first, then memcpy reads from the freed array — undefined behavior caused by the object's own valid expression.

steps.label: Failure 2: exception safety
steps.text: If `new char[a.sz+1]` throws after the delete, s is left with a dangling ptr and the invariant is destroyed with no way to repair it.

steps.label: The fix
steps.text: Check, then allocate-and-copy before releasing: `if (this != &a) { char* p = new char[a.sz+1]; memcpy(p, a.ptr, a.sz+1); delete[] ptr; ptr = p; sz = a.sz; }` — on any throw, s is untouched; on success, every intermediate state is a valid String.

examples.result: The order check, allocate, copy, delete, rewire leaves the object never-half-assigned — the same discipline the standard-library strings implement.

keyTakeaways: The invariant `ptr[sz] == 0` (with an 11th byte) is what every String member buys and maintains
A pointer member drags in the rule of five: destructor, copy and move constructors, copy and move assignment — all five appear in this one class
`+=` is the member that grows; the free `+` copies its left operand, appends, and returns by value — which is then moved

quiz.q: For a String with sz == 10, what does the invariant say about `ptr[10]`?
options: It holds the terminating 0 — the array was allocated with 11 cells
It holds a pointer to the next String
quiz.explanation: The constructor allocates `sz+1` characters and copies the terminator, so `ptr[sz] == 0` always holds for a non-empty String — c_str() and operator<< depend on it.

quiz.q: `String u{std::move(s)}` just completed. What is true of s?
options: s is unusable until reassigned and must not be destroyed
s.ptr == nullptr and s.sz == 0 — safe to destroy, safe to assign to
s is a copy of u sharing its array
quiz.explanation: The move constructor steals the representation and zeroes the source, leaving the moved-from object in a valid empty state.

quiz.q: Why is `operator+` for String a free function while `operator+=` is a member?
options: So + can be built as a copy-and-append, while += mutates its left operand *this
Because + must be a friend of std::string
quiz.explanation: `+=` updates the object it is applied to — a member's job; `+` produces a fresh value from operands on equal footing, which is the nonmember pattern for symmetric operators.

quiz.q: The compiler-generated copy constructor for String would
options: refuse to compile, forcing you to write one
copy ptr member by member — two Strings owning one array, and a double delete at scope exit
quiz.explanation: Copying a raw pointer copies the address, not the array: both objects' destructors would `delete[]` the same memory — exactly why the rule of five exists.

intro: Encapsulation is not a sealed vault: a class can name trusted collaborators. A friend declaration grants a specific function — or every member of a specific class — access to private members, and only the granting class can issue the invitation. Friends are how `operator<<` reaches String's `ptr` and `sz`, and how a Matrix-times-Vector product can touch two representations while belonging to neither class.
objectives: Declare friend functions and friend classes, and explain what friendship does and does not grant
Implement operator<< for String as a friend
State the three negative properties of friendship — not transitive, not inherited, not reciprocal

concepts.statement: A declaration inside the class body — `friend ostream& operator<<(ostream&, const String&);` — makes that specific nonmember function a **friend**: it may use the class's private members. A friend is not a member: there is no `this`, and the granting does not make the friend visible to users of the class — it must be declared like any other function.
concepts.detail: A friend declaration may itself be a definition, but such inline definitions are found only through argument-dependent lookup.

concepts.term: Why the stream operators are friends
concepts.statement: `operator<<` cannot be a member of String — its left operand is an `ostream`, not a String — yet it needs the representation to stream the characters. Nonmember with representation access is precisely the friend case: it loops `s.ptr[0] .. s.ptr[s.sz-1]` and writes them.
concepts.detail: Returning `ostream&` is what lets output chain: `cout << s << "!";` applies the operator left to right.

concepts.term: A friend of two classes: Matrix times Vector
concepts.statement: Consider `Vector operator*(const Matrix&, const Vector&)`. The product belongs to neither class, but it must index both representations — so the book declares it a friend **in both classes** and defines it once. This is the canonical cure for 'which class should own this operator?'
concepts.detail: The alternative — making it a member of one — misleads readers about symmetry and usually forces accessors that weaken the representation's privacy anyway.

concepts.statement: **Friendship is neither transitive, nor inherited, nor reciprocal.** The friend of my class is not thereby the friend of my friends; a friend of a base is not a friend of a derived class; and my being your friend does not make you mine. A class can also be a friend (`friend class Matrix;`) and a member of another class can be named individually.
concepts.detail: Because the grant is explicit, local and revocable only by editing the granting class, friendship is a precision tool — not a hole punched in encapsulation at random.

concepts.statement: **Friends.** Friends and their disciplined use. You can claim this section when you can declare friend functions and friend classes, and explain what friendship does and does not grant — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 19 (Special Operators); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Matrix times Vector, verified
examples.problem: With `operator*` declared a friend of both Matrix and Vector, compute M times v for v = (1, 2, 3, 4) and rows of M = (1,2,3,4), (2,3,4,5), (3,4,5,6), (4,5,6,7).

steps.label: Step 1: The code shape
steps.text: `class Matrix; class Vector { double v[4]; friend Vector operator*(const Matrix&, const Vector&); }; class Matrix { double v[4][4]; friend Vector operator*(const Matrix&, const Vector&); };` — one function, declared twice as a friend, defined once.

steps.label: Step 4: Row 3
steps.text: (4,5,6,7)·v = 4 + 10 + 18 + 28 = 60 — sixteen multiply-adds in total, four per component.

examples.result: M times v = (30, 40, 50, 60). The function touched `m.v[i][j]` and `x.v[j]` — private in two classes — without either class owning it or exposing an accessor.

examples.title: operator<< as a friend of String
examples.problem: Write and trace the output operator for the String class of 19.3.

steps.label: Step 1: The declaration
steps.text: Inside class String: `friend ostream& operator<<(ostream& os, const String& s);` — the only place the invitation can be issued.

steps.label: Step 2: The definition
steps.text: `ostream& operator<<(ostream& os, const String& s) { for (int i = 0; i != s.sz; ++i) os << s.ptr[i]; return os; }` — exactly sz characters are written.

steps.label: Step 3: The trace
steps.text: For the String of 19.3, ten characters S, t, r, o, u, s, t, r, u, p stream out — the loop stops before ptr[10], so no terminator is printed; returning os lets the next << continue the line.

examples.result: Printing works without a c_str() call and without any public accessor for ptr — a nonmember that needed the representation and got it by name, not by breaking the class open.

keyTakeaways: A friend declaration grants representation access to a named function or class — it grants neither membership nor visibility to users
Symmetric operators that need the representation of two classes (Matrix times Vector) are friends of both and members of neither
Friendship is not transitive, not inherited and not reciprocal — the grant is explicit, local and one-directional

quiz.q: Which statement about friendship is FALSE?
options: It must be declared by the class that grants it
A friend of a base class is automatically a friend of its derived classes
It is not transitive: your friend's friend is not your friend
It is not reciprocal: friending someone does not make them friend you back
quiz.explanation: Friendship is never inherited — a friend of a base has no special access to a derived class. The other three are the defining properties of the mechanism.

quiz.q: Why must `operator<<` for String be a nonmember?
options: Because its left operand is an ostream, not a String
Because ostream is a final class
quiz.explanation: A member operator's left operand is always an object of its own class; the stream must come first in the expression, so the operator lives outside String and is declared a friend to reach ptr and sz.

quiz.q: `friend class Matrix;` appears inside class Vector. This means
options: Vector is a friend of Matrix
Every member function of Matrix may access Vector's private members
Matrix and Vector share a vtable
quiz.explanation: The declaration grants the whole class Matrix the access rights of a friend of Vector — one-directional: Vector gets nothing in Matrix.

quiz.q: The Matrix-times-Vector `operator*` is declared a friend of both classes because
options: friend functions run faster than members
it needs the representations of both classes and belongs to neither
operators must be friends when they return a class type
Matrix and Vector cannot have public members
quiz.explanation: Membership would misrepresent the operator's symmetry — the product is no more a Matrix operation than a Vector operation — while accessors would widen the representation's exposure instead of narrowing it to one named function.

intro: The chapter closes with Stroustrup's rules of thumb, and they are short because they are meant to be applied: define operators only where the meaning is obvious; keep that meaning close to the built-in one; supply operators in families; never overload the three whose built-in behavior you cannot reproduce; and treat a pointer member as an alarm bell that rings for the rule of five.
objectives: Apply the conventional-meaning test before adding any operator to a class
Supply operators in families so users can reason by analogy (== with !=, the full ordering with <)
Run the rule-of-five audit on any class with a pointer member

concepts.statement: **Define an operator only if its meaning is obvious and natural.** `+` adds, `==` compares, `[]` subscripts — anything a reader must stop and look up is a misuse of the notation, and ordinary named functions would serve better.
concepts.detail: The chapter pairs this with the mirror rule: keep the semantics close to what the built-in operator does, including convention (subscripting starts at 0).

concepts.statement: A class with `==` should also provide `!=`; a class with `<` should provide the full ordering (`>`, `<=`, `>=`); a class with `+` should provide `+=`. Users reason by analogy, and a half-finished family breaks the analogy — often where the compiler cannot catch it.
concepts.detail: Define the family members in terms of each other (`!=` as the negation of `==`) so the meanings cannot drift apart.

concepts.statement: **Never overload `&&`, `||` or the comma operator.** Their built-in meanings — short-circuit evaluation and guaranteed sequencing — cannot be reproduced by a function call, and code that looks like it short-circuits but does not is a trap for every reader.
concepts.detail: This rule, like the fixed precedence, protects the reader of an expression first and the writer second.

concepts.term: A pointer member rings the alarm
concepts.statement: If a class has a pointer member, it probably needs the destructor, the copy and move constructors, and the copy and move assignments — or a comment explaining why not. The better cure is often to hold a `string`, `vector` or smart pointer instead and need none of the five.
concepts.detail: The String class is the worked proof: five hand-written members, each of which a `std::string` member variable would have made unnecessary.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Define an operator only when its meaning is obvious, and keep that meaning close to the built-in one** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: Auditing a broken handle class
examples.problem: Find every defect in `class Bad { char* p; public: Bad(const char* s) : p{new char[strlen(s)+1]} { strcpy(p, s); } ~Bad() { delete[] p; } };`

steps.label: Step 1: Count the resources
steps.text: Each constructor allocates exactly one array; the destructor frees one. Balanced so far — the class is one correct operation away from disaster.

steps.label: Step 2: Copy construction
steps.text: `Bad b2{b1};` uses the compiler-generated copy constructor, which copies p bitwise: b1.p == b2.p. At scope exit both destructors `delete[]` the same array — a double delete, undefined behavior.

steps.label: Step 3: Copy assignment
steps.text: `b2 = b3;` copies the pointer over b2's, so b2's original array is never freed (a leak) and b2, b3 now share one array (a future double delete). One operation, two defects.

steps.label: Step 4: The repair
steps.text: Either write all five special members, exactly as String does — or delete them, or replace `p` with a `std::string` member and let the compiler's generated members be correct for free.

examples.result: One missing set of five members produced a leak and a double delete on three lines of ordinary use; the audit trail is exactly the rule-of-five checklist.

examples.title: Reviewing special operators code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the conventional-meaning test before adding any operator to a class.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Define an operator only when its meaning is obvious, and keep that meaning close to the built-in one

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `Widget* p = new Widget; delete p;`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: supply operators in families so users can reason by analogy (== with !=, the full ordering with <). Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Deliver operators in families: == with !=, the orderings with <, + with +=, defined in terms of each other

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Define an operator only when its meaning is obvious, and keep that meaning close to the built-in one Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Define an operator only when its meaning is obvious, and keep that meaning close to the built-in one
Deliver operators in families: == with !=, the orderings with <, + with +=, defined in terms of each other
Never overload &&, || or comma; and treat a pointer member as the trigger for the rule of five — or for a redesign around string, vector or a smart pointer

quiz.q: A class X provides `operator==` but not `operator!=`. Following the chapter's advice, you should
options: leave it — users can write !(a == b)
also provide !=, so the family is complete and analogous to the built-ins
make != a friend of the class
quiz.explanation: Operators come in families; users reason by analogy with built-in types. The one-line member `!=` (the negation of ==) completes the contract the notation promised.

quiz.q: Which of these must never be overloaded?
quiz.explanation: An overloaded && cannot reproduce short-circuit evaluation — both operands get evaluated in unspecified order — so the notation lies. `[]`, `->` and `()` are the chapter's everyday tools.

quiz.q: A class's only data member is `char* p`. The book's first question about that class is
options: why is p not a std::string — or where are the five special member functions?
why does the class have no friends?
quiz.explanation: A pointer member is the rule-of-five trigger: either the class wraps a resource and needs destructor, copies and moves, or it should hold a string/vector/unique_ptr and need none of them.

intro: Inheritance came to C++ from Simula together with the class concept itself: objects of different kinds respond to the same request, and the code making the request never names the kinds. A derived class adds members to those of its base — `class Circle : public Shape` says a Circle is a kind of Shape, usable wherever a Shape is expected. This chapter builds the machinery: virtual functions and override control, the type-field technique they replace, abstract classes, the three levels of base access, and pointers to members.
objectives: Read a derived-class declaration and say exactly what a derived object contains and converts to
Distinguish interface inheritance (substitutability) from implementation reuse
Connect the chapter's pieces: virtual functions, abstract classes, access control, pointers to members

concepts.statement: `class D : public B { ... };` declares D **derived from** base B. A D object contains a B subobject plus D's new members; unhidden B members are used directly in D. The key conversions are free: a `D*` converts to a `B*` and a `D&` to a `B&`, which is what lets Shape code drive Circle objects.
concepts.detail: A class may have several direct bases (chapter 21) and may itself be derived from; the result is a directed acyclic graph, not a tree.

concepts.statement: Stroustrup took the class/derived-class mechanism from **Simula**, the simulation language whose worldview is exactly the hierarchy worldview: a program is a set of objects of many kinds, and variation between kinds is expressed by derivation plus overriding rather than by case analysis.
concepts.detail: The Manager-and-Employee shape of the idea: a Manager is an Employee (name, department, hire date) plus a group and a level — same type of thing, more facilities.

concepts.statement: Two distinct goods: **interface inheritance** — code written against B keeps working for every present and future D, unmodified and un-recompiled; and **implementation reuse** — D's members use B's members instead of restating them. The first is the deep one: the substitutability that lets libraries ship hierarchies that user code extends.
concepts.detail: Confusing the two is the classic misuse: inheriting to grab a base's functions, without any is-a relationship, couples the classes for no behavioral gain.

concepts.statement: Public inheritance means **is-a**: every D must be usable wherever a B is expected, through B's interface, without surprises. Circle is-a Shape; a Car has-an Engine (member); a Stack may be implemented-in-terms-of a list (containment or private derivation) — but a Stack is-not-a list.
concepts.detail: The square-and-rectangle trap is the standard counterexample: a Square with set_edge is not substitutable for a Rectangle with independent set_width and set_height, whatever the geometry suggests.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Inheritance from Simula. You can claim this section when you can read a derived-class declaration and say exactly what a derived object contains and converts to — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 20 (Derived Classes); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Classifying six type relationships
examples.problem: Decide for each pair: public inheritance, plain membership (composition), or neither — (1) Circle/Shape, (2) Car/Engine, (3) Manager/Employee, (4) Stack/list, (5) Square/Rectangle with independent edge setters, (6) Flight/Airplane.

steps.label: Steps 1 and 3: is-a
steps.text: A Circle is a Shape and a Manager is an Employee — every operation of the base applies meaningfully to the derived, so both get public inheritance and the substitution it licenses.

steps.label: Steps 2 and 6: has-a
steps.text: A Car has an Engine; a Flight (probably) has an Airplane — whole and part, not kind and kind. A private member is the right tool; inheriting would let an engine stand in for the car.

steps.label: Step 4: implemented-in-terms-of
steps.text: A Stack can be built on a list, but a Stack is not a list (no indexing, no middle insertion exposed) — containment, or at most private derivation, keeps the reuse without asserting substitutability.

steps.label: Step 5: the trap
steps.text: Square inherits Rectangle only if the rectangle interface (independent width and height) is honestly honored by a square. With set_width and set_height, it is not — the pair fails is-a and should not share a public hierarchy.

examples.result: Two is-a pairs (public inheritance), two has-a pairs (members), one implemented-in-terms-of (containment or private inheritance), one trap — the classification is the whole design skill in miniature.

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: Inheritance from Simula. Your task: read a derived-class declaration and say exactly what a derived object contains and converts to.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: read a derived-class declaration and say exactly what a derived object contains and converts to. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A derived class contains a base subobject and converts implicitly to base pointers and references — that conversion is where polymorphism enters

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `struct Shape { virtual void draw() const = 0; virtual ~Shape() = default; };` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — distinguish interface inheritance (substitutability) from implementation reuse — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Inheritance and virtual functions arrived from Simula; their job is expressing variation between kinds without case analysis If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A derived class contains a base subobject and converts implicitly to base pointers and references — that conversion is where polymorphism enters Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A derived class contains a base subobject and converts implicitly to base pointers and references — that conversion is where polymorphism enters
Inheritance and virtual functions arrived from Simula; their job is expressing variation between kinds without case analysis
Public inheritance asserts is-a; has-a and implemented-in-terms-of are membership relationships, not inheritance

quiz.q: After `class Circle : public Shape { ... };`, which statement is TRUE?
options: A Circle object contains a Shape subobject and a `Circle*` converts to a `Shape*`
Shape's constructors are inherited by Circle
Circle can no longer define data members
quiz.explanation: Derivation adds to: the derived object embeds the base, and the derived-to-base pointer conversion is implicit — the conversion that lets Shape code operate on a Circle.

quiz.q: Which language contributed the class-derivation mechanism that C++ inherited?
quiz.explanation: Classes, derivation and virtual functions came from Simula, the simulation language; C++ kept the mechanism and re-grounded it in static typing and zero-overhead use.

quiz.q: The is-a test for public inheritance demands that
options: the derived class share all of the base's data members
every derived object be usable wherever a base is expected, through the base's interface, without surprises
the two classes have the same name for their constructors
quiz.explanation: Substitutability is the contract: if any use through the base's interface would surprise, the relationship is has-a or implemented-in-terms-of instead — the Square/Rectangle trap being the canonical failure.

intro: A derived class declares what it adds and, function by function, what it redefines. `virtual` marks a base member for run-time selection; `override` asks the compiler to prove that a redefinition really overrides; `final` stops the chain deliberately. Construction runs base-first and destruction runs it base-last, and copy and move have their own rules that trip the unwary — most famously slicing.
objectives: Declare a derived class overriding virtuals with override, and predict which function a call through a base pointer selects
Trace construction and destruction order through a hierarchy, including virtual calls made from constructors
Explain the exact signature rules for overriding and what final forbids

concepts.statement: `class Circle : public Shape { public: void draw() const override; void rotate(int) override {} private: Point x; int r; };` — Circle is derived from Shape, adds data members x and r, and overrides the virtuals draw and rotate. Unhidden Shape members are used as if they were Circle's own.
concepts.detail: The book's flavor: `Circle(Point p, int rr) : x{p}, r{rr} {}` — the base has no data to initialize here, so only members appear in the initializer list.

concepts.statement: A member function declared `virtual` in a base can be **overridden** in a derived class, and when called through a base pointer or reference it is the override belonging to the object's dynamic type that runs — chosen at run time, from the object, not from the static type of the pointer.
concepts.detail: The design decision C++ makes: the base-class author decides which operations are customizable; a derived redefinition of a non-virtual merely hides and never reaches callers through the base.

concepts.statement: `override` after a declarator makes the compiler verify a matching base virtual — same name, same parameter list, same const-ness, and a return type that is identical or covariant. `final` forbids further overriding of that virtual (or, on a class, any derivation from it). Both are C++11 additions that turn silent mistakes into compile errors.
concepts.detail: The classic catch: `void rotate(double)` does not override `virtual void rotate(int)` — it hides it, and calls through the base silently run the base version. One word, `override`, makes that a compile-time error.

concepts.statement: A derived object is built **bottom-up**: the base subobject first (its members, then its constructor body), then the derived class's members, then the derived constructor body. Destruction runs exactly in reverse. Inside a base constructor or destructor, virtual calls resolve at that level — the derived part does not exist yet or no longer does.
concepts.detail: This is why a base can be abstract yet still have a constructor: it runs as part of every derived construction, even though no standalone base object can be created.

concepts.statement: Copying a derived object into a base variable copies **only the base subobject** — the Circle-ness is sliced off. Assignment is no rescue: copy assignment is never virtual and cannot change an object's dynamic type. That is why hierarchies are used through pointers and references, never by value.
concepts.detail: `void f(Shape s);` called with a Circle is either a compile error (Shape abstract) or, for a concrete base, a silent slice — both are design smells; the correct parameter is `const Shape&`.

examples.title: Rotating a square, and not rotating a circle
examples.problem: A Square stores its corner points; rotation by angle $\theta$ maps $(x, y)$ to $(x\cos\theta - y\sin\theta,\ x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta)$. Rotate the corner (3, 4) by 90 degrees, then rotate a Circle by the same 90 degrees through a `Shape*`.

steps.label: Step 1: Substitute
steps.text: With $\theta = 90°$, $\cos\theta = 0$ and $\sin\theta = 1$, so the map collapses to $(x, y) \mapsto (-y, x)$ — quarter turn counterclockwise.

steps.label: Step 2: Rotate the corner
steps.text: (3, 4) maps to (−4, 3). The distance from the origin is preserved: $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5 = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + 3^2}$ — the square stays a square.

steps.label: Step 3: Dispatch through the base
steps.text: `Shape* p = &sq; p->rotate(90);` runs Square's override and moves the points. `p = &c; p->rotate(90);` runs Circle's override — the empty no-op `{}` — because a circle is invariant under rotation.

steps.label: Step 4: One call site, two behaviors
steps.text: The two calls have identical machine code at the call site; the difference lives in the objects, which is the entire point of virtual functions.

examples.result: The square's corner (3, 4) moves to (−4, 3) while the circle does nothing — same expression, `p->rotate(90)`, dispatched from each object's own class.

examples.title: The birth and death of a Circle
examples.problem: Trace the constructor and destructor calls for `Circle c{Point{1,2}, 5};` in a hierarchy where Shape has a constructor body and Circle initializes x and r.

steps.label: Construction, bottom-up
steps.text: Shape's base subobject is built first — its members (here only the vptr machinery) and then Shape's constructor body. Only then: Circle's members in declaration order (x from Point{1,2}, then r from 5), and finally Circle's constructor body.

steps.label: Destruction, top-down
steps.text: At scope exit the order is exactly reversed: ~Circle body, then members (r, x), then ~Shape — the base is destroyed last.

steps.label: The virtual-call caveat
steps.text: If Shape's constructor calls `this->draw()`, the call resolves to Shape's draw — Circle's part does not exist yet. The same happens in ~Shape, for the mirror reason. Overridable behavior is simply not available during base construction and destruction.

examples.result: Base, members, body on the way in; body, members, base on the way out — and no virtual dispatch past the level currently being constructed or destroyed.

keyTakeaways: A virtual call through a base pointer selects the override from the object's dynamic type — the decision is made at run time, from the object
`override` turns the accidental-hide bug into a compile error; `final` deliberately stops overriding or derivation
Build bottom-up, destroy top-down; inside base constructors and destructors, virtual calls stay at the base level; and copying a derived object into a base slices it

quiz.q: `class D : public B` declares `void f(double)` intending to override B's `virtual void f(int)`. What happens?
options: It overrides f for double arguments only
It hides — it is not an override, so calls through a B pointer still run B::f(int); with `override` it would not compile
The two functions overload each other within B
quiz.explanation: The parameter lists differ, so no override exists: D's function merely hides B's by name, and a call through the base uses the base version — the silent bug that `override` exists to catch.

quiz.q: During destruction of a Circle, when does the `~Shape` body run relative to ~Circle's body?
options: After it — derived bodies first, base last
quiz.explanation: Destruction is the exact reverse of construction: the derived destructor body runs while the object is still whole, then its members, then the base's destructor.

quiz.q: Shape's constructor calls `this->draw()` while a Circle is being constructed. Which draw runs?
options: Circle::draw — the object is already a Circle
Shape::draw — during base construction, virtual dispatch resolves at the base level
The call is a compile error
quiz.explanation: The derived part does not exist yet, so dispatch cannot reach it; the call resolves as if the object were exactly the class under construction. The same holds in destructors.

quiz.q: `void f(Shape s);` is called with a Circle and Shape is a concrete base class. What happens?
options: The Circle is passed by reference
The argument is sliced: only Shape's subobject is copied into s
A Circle is constructed inside f
quiz.explanation: Pass by value copies the base subobject only — the derived members are sliced away. (Had Shape been abstract, the compiler would have refused the parameter outright.) Either way, the fix is `const Shape&`.

Step 1: The code given calls one virtual and one non-virtual member through a base pointer to a derived object. Step 2: The governing rules are the two dispatches: virtual calls resolve on the dynamic type through the table, while non-virtual calls resolve on the static type at compile time. Step 3: Tracing call by call, `p->who()` dispatches to `Child::who` printing `C`, and `p->id()` binds to `Base::id` printing `b`, for a total of `Cb`. Step 4: The distractors fail because the virtual call ignores the static type, the hiding non-virtual never overrides, and each call follows its own dispatch rule. Step 5: Therefore the program prints `Cb`.

depth.title: Virtual functions and the object layout they imply

blocks.body: Separate the two types every polymorphic pointer has. The **static type** of `p` in `Shape* p` is Shape — it is fixed by the declaration and known to the compiler. The **dynamic type** of `*p` is the type of the object actually created, known only where `new` ran. Virtual dispatch is the rule that certain calls consult the second, not the first. The deep problem is that C++ compiles translation units separately and has no global program database: when it compiles `p->draw()`, it cannot enumerate every class that will ever derive from Shape, so it cannot bind the call to a single address. The standard implementation solves this by moving the missing information **into the object itself** — every polymorphic object carries a pointer to its class's dispatch data.

blocks.heading: The final-overrider rule
blocks.body: Let B declare f virtual, and let p have static type `B*` pointing to an object whose dynamic type is D. Then the call `p->f(args)` invokes the **final overrider** of `B::f` in D: the override closest to D on the derivation path from D up to B. If no class on that path (starting at D) overrides f, the final overrider is `B::f` itself. Two consequences follow immediately: virtual-ness is transitive, since an override is implicitly virtual whether or not it repeats the keyword — so overriding propagates through intermediate classes; and the rule is per-object, so two Shape pointers in the same expression can dispatch two different functions from identical call sites.

blocks.heading: From the rule to two instructions
blocks.body: Dispatch by dynamic type needs a per-class table of function addresses and a per-object link to that table. Hence the **vtable object model**: for each polymorphic class, the compiler lays out one static table — one slot per virtual function, conventionally in declaration order; for each object, a hidden **vptr**, conventionally at offset zero, pointing at its class's table. (Real ABIs such as the Itanium ABI put an offset-to-top and a `type_info` pointer just before slot 0 — the RTTI hook used later.) The call `p->draw()` then compiles to roughly: `mov rax, [rdi]` — load the vptr from the object; then `call [rax]` — index slot 0 and jump through it. The exact slot numbering is an implementation detail, but the shape is universal: **two dependent loads and one indirect call**. This is also why an override must match the base signature exactly: a function that merely hides (a differently-typed parameter, a missing const) never occupies the slot — the table still holds the base's address, and the call silently runs the wrong code.

blocks.heading: A Circle, byte by byte
blocks.body: With `Point` = two ints, a typical 64-bit layout is: Shape = one vptr, `sizeof(Shape) == 8`. Circle = vptr at bytes [0,8), the Point x at [8,16), `int r` at [16,20), padding to [20,24) — `sizeof(Circle) == 24`. Circle's vtable has three slots in declaration order: slot 0 `Circle::draw`, slot 1 `Circle::rotate` (the empty no-op body), slot 2 `Shape::~Shape`. Square's table has the same shape — `Square::draw`, `Square::rotate`, `Shape::~Shape` — the destructor entry shared because neither class declares its own. Now the costs become concrete: `p->draw()` with p pointing at a Square is a load, an indexed load, an indirect jump to Square::draw. And slicing has a byte count: `Shape s = c;` copies 8 of 24 bytes — everything the base knows about. `*sp = c;` through a `Shape&` calls Shape's assignment (never virtual) and assigns only the base subobject: assignment can never change an object's dynamic type, which is why the language does not even try to let it.

blocks.heading: Destructors and RTTI live in the same table
blocks.body: Deleting through a base pointer must run the derived destructor — that is a virtual call too, which is why a class meant as a polymorphic base needs a `virtual` destructor (the ABIs actually store two destructor entries: the complete-object and the deleting destructor, so that `delete p` frees the right amount). The `type_info` pointer hanging off the vtable is the second product of the same machinery: `typeid` and `dynamic_cast` read it — which is exactly why only polymorphic types (types with a vptr) can be dynamically cast down a hierarchy. Dispatch and RTTI are two uses of one table.

blocks.heading: The price list
blocks.body: Per class: one vtable plus `type_info` in static storage — off the hot path. Per object: one vptr, 8 bytes on a 64-bit ABI — a Shape grows from 0 bytes of overhead to 8 the moment it gains its first virtual function. Per call: two dependent loads plus an indirect branch, and the optimizer cannot inline through the indirect target — for trivial bodies the lost inlining, not the branch, dominates. Hardware cooperates well: the loads hit L1 and branch predictors learn monomorphic call sites. And the zero-overhead principle survives intact — a class with no virtual functions stores no vptr and runs no table lookups; you pay only for the polymorphism you actually use.

intro: The point of a hierarchy is that one piece of code can drive many types: `rotate_all` walks a vector of Shape pointers and every object rotates itself the right way. Stroustrup compares this with the older technique — a type field plus a switch statement in every operation — and the comparison is the chapter's best design lesson. The section ends where the mechanism begins: the vtable, which is the switch the compiler writes for you.
objectives: Write polymorphic algorithms such as draw_all and rotate_all over vectors of base pointers
Contrast the type-field-and-switch design with virtual dispatch, listing exactly what must change when a new type joins each design
Explain the vtable implementation of virtual dispatch well enough to reason about its cost

concepts.statement: Code that works on a hierarchy stores (smart) base pointers and never names the concrete types: `void rotate_all(vector<Shape*>& vs, int d) { for (auto* p : vs) p->rotate(d); }`. The function was written, compiled and debugged before Pentagon existed — and needs no edit, no recompile, no source access when Pentagon arrives.
concepts.detail: Modern style prefers `vector<unique_ptr<Shape>>` so ownership and polymorphism come together; the dispatch argument is identical.

concepts.statement: The pre-inheritance design: every object carries a discriminant — `enum Kind { circle, triangle, square };` with a `kind()` accessor — and every operation is a function containing a **switch over the field**: one branch per kind, maintained by hand in every operation that cares.
concepts.detail: The field must be kept consistent with the data layout, every switch must list every kind, and no compiler checks that an operation's switch was updated when a kind was added.

concepts.statement: A virtual function is **a switch statement the compiler writes, indexes and keeps consistent for you** — the object itself selects its case. Adding a type-field kind means editing every switch in every operation; adding a derived class means writing one new class, and the existing operations keep working unmodified.
concepts.detail: The book's deeper point: data and the functions maintaining it should live together. In the switch design the knowledge of circle-ness is smeared across every operation; in the hierarchy it is in Circle.

concepts.statement: Each polymorphic class gets one static **vtable** — an array of the addresses of its virtual functions' final overriders — and each object starts with a **vptr** to its class's table. A virtual call loads the vptr, indexes the declared slot, and jumps: $O(1)$ time, a couple of instructions, but an indirect jump the optimizer cannot inline through.
concepts.detail: The vtable is why virtual dispatch is cheap and uniform: the alternative — searching a class DAG at each call — is what dynamic languages pay for late binding, and C++ precomputes it into a flat table per class.

concepts.statement: **Class Hierarchies.** Type fields versus virtual functions. You can claim this section when you can write polymorphic algorithms such as draw_all and rotate_all over vectors of base pointers — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 20 (Derived Classes); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Adding Pentagon: switch design versus hierarchy design
examples.problem: A drawing program has four shape operations (draw, rotate, move, center) and three shapes. Compare the cost of adding Pentagon under the type-field design and under the class-hierarchy design.

steps.label: Type-field design
steps.text: Four operation functions each contain a switch over `kind()` with three cases. Adding Pentagon means adding an enum value and editing four switches — four separate source edits, and the compiler cannot flag an operation you forgot to update: a missed case just falls through with the default behavior.

steps.label: Hierarchy design
steps.text: One new class with four overrides. Nothing existing changes — `rotate_all` and its siblings were compiled long ago and drive Pentagon unmodified the first time it appears in a container.

steps.label: The compiler as checklist
steps.text: If the interface is abstract (20.4) and you forget one of the four overrides, Pentagon stays abstract and `new Pentagon{...}` fails to compile — the miss is loud, not silent.

steps.label: The count
steps.text: Type-field: 4 edits, 0 compile-time checks. Hierarchy: 1 new type, 4 compiler-enforced overrides.

examples.result: The hierarchy turns 'did every operation learn about the new kind?' from a code-review question into a type question — which is why the book calls a virtual function a switch the compiler writes and checks for you.

examples.title: Working through class hierarchies
examples.problem: Type fields versus virtual functions. Your task: write polymorphic algorithms such as draw_all and rotate_all over vectors of base pointers.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: write polymorphic algorithms such as draw_all and rotate_all over vectors of base pointers. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Polymorphic algorithms store base pointers and never name concrete types — they work unchanged for types written later

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `struct Shape { virtual void draw() const = 0; virtual ~Shape() = default; };` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — contrast the type-field-and-switch design with virtual dispatch, listing exactly what must change when a new type joins each design — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: The type-field design scatters knowledge of each kind across every switch and has no compiler check for forgotten cases If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Polymorphic algorithms store base pointers and never name concrete types — they work unchanged for types written later Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Polymorphic algorithms store base pointers and never name concrete types — they work unchanged for types written later
The type-field design scatters knowledge of each kind across every switch and has no compiler check for forgotten cases
Virtual dispatch is one vtable index — a couple of instructions, $O(1)$, not inlinable — and the switch-equivalent is maintained by the compiler, not by you

quiz.q: `rotate_all` was compiled long ago. A Pentagon class is added today. What makes `p->rotate(d)` rotate the pentagon correctly inside that old code?
options: The linker patches rotate_all with the new class list
Each Pentagon object carries a vptr selecting Pentagon's vtable entry for rotate
rotate_all is recompiled as a template
The compiler resolves rotate at link time from the static type
quiz.explanation: The dispatch data lives in the object: the vptr points at Pentagon's vtable, whose rotate slot holds Pentagon's override. The call site is unchanged and needs no knowledge of the new class.

quiz.q: In the type-field design, adding a new kind to a program with k operations each containing a switch over the kind requires
options: up to k edits — one case per switch, with no compiler check that any of them was made
no edits: the switches grow automatically
rewriting every operation as a template
quiz.explanation: Every switch that should know about the new kind must be edited by hand; a missed case compiles and silently does the wrong default thing.

quiz.q: The machine-level cost of one virtual call, relative to a direct call, is essentially
options: a search of the class graph at run time
two dependent loads and an indirect jump, with inlining through the call no longer possible
a system call into the loader
proportional to the number of derived classes
quiz.explanation: The vtable is flat: load vptr, index the slot, jump. The constant-time lookup is the design win; losing inline expansion is the real cost for trivial bodies.

quiz.q: Which change lets a new shape join a program WITHOUT touching the code of `rotate_all`?
options: Adding a new value to the type-field enum
Deriving a new class from Shape and overriding its virtuals
quiz.explanation: The hierarchy is open for extension: a new derived class plugs into existing base-pointer code through its own vtable. The enum route edits every switch; removing virtual disables dispatch entirely.

intro: Make every Shape operation pure virtual and Shape becomes what the book calls an abstract class: a common interface with no objects of its own. Abstract classes are how C++ states 'these are the operations every shape must provide'; the derived classes provide the implementations, and users hold pointers and references to the interface only. It is the hinge between this chapter's machinery and chapter 21's design questions.
objectives: Declare pure virtual functions and explain exactly what = 0 makes illegal
Use an abstract class as an interface: instantiate only its concrete derived classes
Distinguish degrees of abstractness, from a pure interface to a partially implemented base

concepts.statement: A virtual function with the declarator suffix `= 0` — `virtual void draw() const = 0;` — is a **pure virtual**: it must be overridden (transitively) before any object of the class can be created. A pure virtual may even be given a definition, callable only with explicit qualification — rare, occasionally useful for shared default behavior.
concepts.detail: The `= 0` is read 'is implemented elsewhere': the base states the contract, some derived class supplies the body.

concepts.statement: A class with one or more pure virtual functions is **abstract**: no objects of it can be created. Pointers and references to it are fine and are the whole point — `vector<Shape*>` and parameters of type `Shape&` are how users touch the hierarchy. Its constructor still runs in every derived construction, and its destructor should be virtual like any polymorphic base's.
concepts.detail: The classic interface: `class Shape { public: virtual Point center() const = 0; virtual void move(Point to) = 0; virtual void draw() const = 0; virtual void rotate(int angle) = 0; virtual ~Shape() {} };`

concepts.statement: Abstractness is a dial, not a switch. At one end sits the **pure interface**: no data, every operation pure — Shape here. At the other, a base with data and default implementations plus a few pure virtuals — the derived classes inherit the common parts and finish the contract. What you choose fixes who may rely on what.
concepts.detail: The pure interface keeps implementations fully interchangeable; a stateful base shares code but couples every derived class to the shared representation.

concepts.statement: Users program against the abstract class; implementers derive from it. A new implementation (a Triangle, a new window system's slider) does not disturb a single line of user code — this is the 'program to the interface' discipline the next chapter turns into design method.
concepts.detail: The compiler enforces the contract at both ends: an implementation missing a pure override is itself abstract and cannot be instantiated.

concepts.statement: **Abstract Classes.** Pure virtual functions and interfaces. You can claim this section when you can declare pure virtual functions and explain exactly what = 0 makes illegal — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 20 (Derived Classes); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: A mixed collection, computed through the interface
examples.problem: Extend the Shape interface with `virtual double area() const = 0;`, then total the areas of `Circle(Point{0,0}, 2)` and `Square(Point{1,1}, 3)` held through Shape pointers.

steps.label: Step 1: The interface grows by one line
steps.text: Adding the pure virtual instantly makes Circle and Square abstract again — every concrete derived class now fails to compile where it is constructed until it overrides area. The compiler is the migration checklist.

steps.label: Step 2: The overrides
steps.text: Circle: `double area() const override { return 3.14159 * r * r; }` — for r = 2, that is $4\pi \approx 12.57$. Square: `double area() const override { return double(edge) * edge; }` — for edge = 3, that is 9.

steps.label: Step 3: The user code
steps.text: `double total = 0; for (auto* p : shapes) total += p->area();` — no name Circle or Square appears anywhere in the loop, and the values dispatched are $12.5664$ and $9$.

steps.label: Step 4: The total
steps.text: $12.5664 + 9 = 21.5664 \approx 21.57$ — and a Pentagon dropped into the container tomorrow joins the sum without any edit to the loop.

examples.result: About 21.57 square units, computed by one loop over base pointers; the interface owns the arithmetic's existence, the objects own its value.

Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `= 0` makes a virtual pure: it must be overridden before an object can be created, and the class owning it is abstract

steps.label: Step 3: vary

keyTakeaways: `= 0` makes a virtual pure: it must be overridden before an object can be created, and the class owning it is abstract
Abstract classes are instantiated never and referenced everywhere — they are the interface users code against
Adding a pure virtual makes every existing concrete derived class fail to compile until it complies — extension with the compiler as the checklist

quiz.q: Given `class Shape { public: virtual void draw() const = 0; };`, which declaration is an error?
quiz.explanation: An abstract class has no objects — only pointers and references to it. Defining a Shape by value is a compile-time error listing the pure virtuals; all three indirect uses are exactly the intended ones.

quiz.q: A pure virtual function may be given a function body. That body is callable
options: through a base pointer, like any override
only with explicit qualification, as in Derived::base-style calls
quiz.explanation: A definition for a pure virtual is legal and occasionally useful for shared default code, but the function is still pure: ordinary dispatch never selects it — it must be reached by naming it explicitly.

quiz.q: Circle overrides 3 of Shape's 4 pure virtuals and defines no other virtuals. Then
options: Circle is concrete; the fourth operation uses Shape's
Circle is itself abstract — objects cannot be created until the missing override exists
the missing function becomes a type field
the program links but crashes on the first call
quiz.explanation: A class is abstract if it inherits any un-overridden pure virtual. The failure is at compile time, at the point someone tries to create a Circle — loud, local and fixable.

quiz.q: The chapter calls an abstract class 'a class with no objects but' — complete the point:
options: plenty of pointers and references: it is the interface through which users see every implementation
quiz.explanation: The absence of objects is precisely what makes it a pure contract: every access goes through a base pointer or reference, so implementations remain interchangeable behind it.

intro: Inheritance comes with its own access control, and it answers one question: who may use the base's members through the derived class? Public derivation keeps is-a intact; protected and private derivation make the base an implementation detail. Inside the classes, `protected` opens a channel to derived classes that ordinary users never get — powerful, and in Stroustrup's judgment usually a design error when applied to data. The `using`-declaration rounds out the toolbox: un-hiding base members, inheriting constructors, adjusting access.
objectives: Predict the legality of member access from inside a derived class, from outside, and through each derivation level
Choose between public, protected and private derivation for a given relationship
Use using-declarations: to un-hide base overloads, to inherit constructors, and to widen access deliberately

concepts.statement: `class D : public B` — is-a preserved: B's public members are public in D and a `D*` converts to `B*` everywhere. `class D : protected B` — public and protected members of B become protected in D. `class D : private B` (the default for `class`) — they become private: the base is an implementation detail and the conversion is hidden from users. `struct` derivation defaults to public.
concepts.detail: By far the most common is public — and it is the only one that expresses substitution; the other two are implementation inheritance.

concepts.statement: A `protected` member of B is accessible to B's own member functions and to the member functions (and friends) of classes derived from B — but not to ordinary users. Stroustrup's verdict on **protected data**: usually a design error, because every derived class is then coupled to the representation; prefer protected member functions and private data.
concepts.detail: Protected data trades the encapsulation you already had for a convenience the interface could have provided safely.

concepts.statement: Access control limits **permission, not visibility**. Name lookup finds private members all the same — they participate in overload resolution and can create ambiguities — but using them outside their permitted context is an error. You cannot hide a member by access alone.
concepts.detail: The C++ model: if a name can be seen, the compiler reasons about it; whether it may be used is a separate, checkable question.

concepts.statement: A declaration of `f` in D hides **all** base members named f — `void f(double)` in D hides even `B::f(int)`; overloading does not cross scopes. A `using B::f;` declaration in D brings the whole base family back into scope alongside D's own, so overload resolution sees both.
concepts.detail: The same syntax in D's public section — under private inheritance — deliberately re-exposes chosen base members to users.

concepts.statement: Constructors are never inherited automatically, but a derived class can adopt them: `class D : public B { public: using B::B; };` gives D a constructor for each B constructor, each initializing the B subobject then D's members. The destructor and the copy/move operations are never adopted this way — D always gets its own.
concepts.detail: It is the tool for 'D is B plus data members with their own initializers', removing a page of forwarding one-liners.

examples.title: The access audit, counted
examples.problem: Audit every access in `class B { public: void pub(); protected: void prot(); private: void priv(); };` `class D : public B { void use(); };` — from inside `D::use()` and from user code holding a D.

steps.label: Inside D::use()
steps.text: `pub()` legal (public in B, inherited public); `prot()` legal (protected extends to derived classes); `priv()` illegal — private means B's own members and friends only. Two of three.

steps.label: Outside, through a D object
steps.text: `d.pub()` legal; `d.prot()` illegal (protected is invisible to users); `d.priv()` illegal. One of three.

steps.label: Switch to private derivation
steps.text: Now `class Secret : private B {}`: inside Secret::use() all three calls are legal — access within the class ignores derivation level — but outside, `s.pub()` fails and, crucially, `B* b = &s;` fails too: the is-a conversion is not exported.

steps.label: Selective re-exposure
steps.text: Adding `public: using B::pub;` inside Secret makes `s.pub()` legal again while everything else stays sealed — access as a dial, not a wall.

examples.result: Six audited uses, three legal under public derivation; private derivation seals users out entirely until a using-declaration opens exactly the members you choose.

examples.problem: public, protected, private and using declarations. Your task: predict the legality of member access from inside a derived class, from outside, and through each derivation level.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: predict the legality of member access from inside a derived class, from outside, and through each derivation level. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Public derivation preserves is-a; protected and private derivation keep the base as an implementation detail and hide the conversion

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `struct Shape { virtual void draw() const = 0; virtual ~Shape() = default; };` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — choose between public, protected and private derivation for a given relationship — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Protected members reach derived classes but not users — and protected data is usually a design error; prefer protected functions If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

keyTakeaways: Public derivation preserves is-a; protected and private derivation keep the base as an implementation detail and hide the conversion
Protected members reach derived classes but not users — and protected data is usually a design error; prefer protected functions
`using B::f` un-hides a hidden overload family, `using B::B` inherits constructors, and a public using-declaration can re-expose members under private inheritance

quiz.q: `class D : private B { ... };` — which is TRUE outside D's member functions?
options: D is substitutable for B: any D converts to B freely
A D* does not convert to B* implicitly — the base is an implementation detail
B's protected members become public in D
D cannot have any public members of its own
quiz.explanation: Private derivation turns the base into an implementation detail: users neither see B's members nor get the derived-to-base conversion — D is-implemented-in-terms-of B, not is-a B.

quiz.q: A protected member of B is accessible
options: only to B's own members and friends
to B's members, friends, and the members of classes derived from B — but not to ordinary users
quiz.explanation: Protected is the family channel: derived classes get it, the outside world does not — which is why it suits member functions and, in Stroustrup's judgment, suits data badly.

quiz.q: `class D : public B` declares `void f(double)`; B has `void f(int)`. A user calls `d.f(3)`. What runs?
options: B::f(int) — the base version is preferred
D::f(double) — D's declaration hides the base family, so 3 converts to double
The call is ambiguous and rejected
Nothing: hiding makes the call ill-formed
quiz.explanation: A name declared in D hides all base members of that name — overloading does not cross scopes — so the int argument converts and D::f(double) runs. `using B::f;` would restore both.

quiz.q: `using B::B;` in a public section of D causes
options: D to inherit B's constructors — one D constructor per B constructor
B's assignment operators to be inherited
quiz.explanation: Constructors can be adopted by using-declaration only; destructors and the copy/move operations are never inherited — D always has its own.

intro: Sometimes the thing to parameterize over is not a value but a member: run this member function on that object; read that data member. C++ splits the problem in two — `&X::a` is a pointer to the member a of any X, and the member is reached through an object with `.*` or `->*`. A pointer-to-member is an offset-like creature belonging to no particular object, which is exactly why ordinary pointers cannot do the job.
objectives: Declare and use pointers to data members and to member functions
Explain why .* and ->* exist: members need a this, which the object supplies at use time
Build a table of member-function pointers and call through it, with virtual dispatch intact

concepts.statement: `int X::* p = &X::a;` declares p a **pointer to an int member of X**. It names which member, not where: applied to an object x with `x.*p` — or to a `X*` px with `px->*p` — it designates that object's a. The value stored is offset-like, so the same p serves every X.
concepts.detail: Read `int X::*` right to left: pointer to member of X with type int — an ordinary `int*` would claim to point at an int that exists somewhere on its own.

concepts.statement: `void (X::*pf)(int) = &X::f;` — pf names X's member function f. It is invoked bound to an object: `(x.*pf)(3)` or `(px->*pf)(3)`. **The parentheses are mandatory**: `.*` binds more loosely than the function call, so `x.*pf(3)` would try to call pf and apply .* to the result.
concepts.detail: No object, no call — the member function needs a this, and the object at use time provides it.

concepts.term: Why an ordinary function pointer will not do
concepts.statement: A member function is not a standalone function: it runs on an object and reads its `this`. A bare address of 'the code' is not enough — for virtual members the code depends on the object's class, and for any member the object must be named. The pointer-to-member plus the object at use time supplies both halves.
concepts.detail: It is the same split virtual dispatch makes implicitly; `.*` and `->*` make it explicit, chosen by the programmer at run time.

concepts.statement: The classic use: a menu or protocol table mapping names or events to members. With `using Pstd_mem = void (Std_interface::*)();` one writes `vector<Pstd_mem> ops = { &Std_interface::start, &Std_interface::suspend, &Std_interface::shutdown };` and runs `(p->*op)()` for every op on every object p — calling through a pointer-to-member of a **virtual** member still dispatches on the object's dynamic type.
concepts.detail: It is dispatch-table code you write yourself — the honest alternative when the table's rows must be chosen at run time rather than by class.

concepts.term: Pointers to Members: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Pointers to Members.** Pointers to function and data members. You can claim this section when you can declare and use pointers to data members and to member functions — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 20 (Derived Classes); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: One selector, two objects, nine dispatched calls
examples.problem: Given `struct X { int a{7}; int b{9}; void f(); };`, exercise pointers to members on two objects, then run a three-by-three member-function table.

steps.label: Data members
steps.text: `int X::* pi = &X::a; X x; X* p = &x;` — `x.*pi` is 7 and `p->*pi` is 7 (same member, two syntaxes). After `pi = &X::b;`, `x.*pi` is 9: the selector changed, the object did not.

steps.label: A second object
steps.text: Declare `X y` with a == 5: `y.*pi` is 5 — the same pi applied to a different object yields that object's member. This is the offset nature of the value.

steps.label: The function-member table
steps.text: For three users (objects of a class with virtuals start, suspend, shutdown) and the three-entry `ops` table, `for (auto* p : users) for (auto op : ops) (p->*op)();` makes 3 times 3 = 9 dispatched calls — one loop body, no switch.

steps.label: Virtual members still dispatch
steps.text: If a user's dynamic type overrides suspend, the `(p->*op)()` call runs the override: binding through a pointer-to-member preserves virtual dispatch on the object.

examples.result: 7, 7, 9, 5 from the data-member runs and 9 dispatches from the table — members selected at run time and applied to objects that supply the this.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain why .* and ->* exist: members need a this, which the object supplies at use time — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.
