keyTakeaways: `int X::*` and `void (X::*)(int)` name members, not addresses; the object at use time supplies them via `.*` and `->*`
`(x.*pf)(3)` needs its parentheses — `.*` binds more loosely than the function call
Member-function tables drive menus and protocols without switches, and calls through them remain virtual

quiz.q: Why must `(x.*pf)(3)` be parenthesized?
options: `.*` is not a legal operator otherwise
Because .* binds more loosely than the function call, `x.*pf(3)` would call pf first and misparse
Because pf is a member of x
Because pointers to members cannot take arguments
quiz.explanation: Without the parentheses the call binds to pf alone — which is not a callable — so the language requires the explicit grouping of bind-then-call.

quiz.q: `int X::* pi = &X::a;` — what does pi hold?
options: The address of the a member of some specific object
An offset-like selector naming which member of any X, applied with .* or ->*
A pointer to a function returning int
quiz.explanation: A pointer to member belongs to the class, not to an object: it records which member, and yields a particular object's instance of it only once bound with .* or ->*.

quiz.q: Calling a virtual member function through a pointer-to-member — `(p->*pf)()` — does what?
options: Fails to compile for virtual functions
Still dispatches virtually, on the dynamic type of *p
Calls the base class version always
quiz.explanation: The pointer-to-member selects the member; the call through it is an ordinary member invocation on the object — so the object's vtable still decides which override runs.

intro: The chapter's advice compresses its lessons into rules aimed at the two things that go wrong in practice: an override that isn't (silent base-call bugs that `override` was invented to catch) and inheritance used for convenience rather than substitutability. Run the audit — virtual destructor, override everywhere, no type fields — and most hierarchies stay out of trouble.
objectives: Apply the hierarchy audit: virtual destructor, override on every override, no type fields
Explain why virtual calls from constructors and destructors are a trap
Choose among public/protected/private inheritance and plain composition using the is-a test

concepts.term: Virtual functions instead of type fields
concepts.statement: Where a class's behavior varies by kind, use virtual functions — not a type field with switches in every operation. The compiler maintains the dispatch; new kinds join without touching old operations; forgetting an override of a pure virtual is a compile error, not a silent default.
concepts.detail: Keep the type-field technique for genuinely closed sets where every operation is written in one place anyway.

concepts.statement: Express the contract of a hierarchy as an abstract class with pure virtuals, and program against it — users see the interface, implementations derive from it. Keep the interface minimal and complete: users should never need to downcast to get their job done.
concepts.detail: An interface users must downcast around is under-designed; an interface with knobs for one implementation is over-designed (the fat-interface smell of chapter 21).

concepts.term: A polymorphic base needs a virtual destructor
concepts.statement: If a class is meant to be derived from and used through base pointers, give it a `virtual` destructor — otherwise `delete p` through the base pointer is undefined behavior and typically skips the derived destructor, leaking whatever it would have freed.
concepts.detail: It is the one member whose virtual-ness the base author must remember even when the base owns no data — `virtual ~Shape() {}` appears in every example for exactly this reason.

concepts.term: No virtual calls from constructors and destructors
concepts.statement: During base construction and destruction the object is exactly the class being built or torn down — virtual calls resolve at that level, surprising readers who expected derived behavior. Factor such calls into ordinary functions the derived class can call after construction instead.
concepts.detail: Two companion rules: mark every override with `override` so the compiler checks it, and remember `final` when overriding must stop.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Give every polymorphic base a virtual destructor — deleting through it is otherwise undefined** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: The audit finds three bugs
examples.problem: A hierarchy ships with (1) Shape lacking a virtual destructor while users do `Shape* p = new Circle{...}; delete p;`, (2) Circle's `void rotate(double)` where Shape declares `virtual void rotate(int)`, and (3) a leftover `kind()` field with a switch from a port of the old design. Audit all three.

steps.label: Bug 1: the wrong delete
steps.text: Without a virtual destructor, `delete p` is undefined behavior — in practice ~Circle does not run, so anything Circle's destructor would release leaks. Fix: `virtual ~Shape() {}` in the base — one line, checked forever after.

steps.label: Bug 2: the hidden override
steps.text: `void rotate(double)` does not match `virtual void rotate(int)`: it hides, not overrides, and `p->rotate(90)` silently runs Shape's version — the object rotates wrong or not at all. Adding `override` makes the compiler reject the mismatch today rather than the debugger find it next month.

steps.label: Bug 3: the fossil switch
steps.text: The `kind()` accessor and the switch inside `Shape::print` are now shadow behavior parallel to the virtuals — two sources of truth that will disagree when a new shape arrives. Replace: a `virtual void print() const` overridden per class, delete the field.

examples.result: Three one-line classes of fix — a virtual destructor, an override specifier, a virtual replacing a switch — and the hierarchy's remaining failure modes are design questions, not latent bugs.

examples.title: Reviewing derived classes code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the hierarchy audit: virtual destructor, override on every override, no type fields.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Give every polymorphic base a virtual destructor — deleting through it is otherwise undefined

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `struct Shape { virtual void draw() const = 0; virtual ~Shape() = default; };`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: explain why virtual calls from constructors and destructors are a trap. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Write `override` on every override and expect no virtual calls to reach derived behavior during construction or destruction

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Give every polymorphic base a virtual destructor — deleting through it is otherwise undefined Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Give every polymorphic base a virtual destructor — deleting through it is otherwise undefined
Write `override` on every override and expect no virtual calls to reach derived behavior during construction or destruction
Replace type fields and switches with virtuals; program users against the abstract interface and keep it minimal

quiz.q: Shape has NO virtual destructor. A user executes `Shape* p = new Circle{...}; delete p;`. Per the book's advice this is
options: fine — the compiler calls both destructors
undefined behavior: make ~Shape virtual so the delete dispatches to ~Circle
a memory leak only, otherwise fine
illegal C++ — the new expression would not compile
quiz.explanation: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer whose destructor is not virtual is undefined behavior — the fix is the rule: a base used polymorphically gets `virtual ~Shape() {}`.

quiz.q: Calling a virtual function from a base-class constructor dispatches to
options: the base class's version — the derived part does not exist yet
a pure virtual call and crashes
the function in the translation unit that linked first
quiz.explanation: During base construction the object's dynamic type is the base; overrides are unavailable — which is why the advice is to keep virtual calls out of constructors and destructors entirely.

quiz.q: Which is the chapter's recommended default for expressing 'these operations vary by kind'?
options: A kind enum plus a switch in each operation
Virtual functions and an abstract base interface
Pointers to members as the dispatch table
quiz.explanation: Virtuals are the compiler-maintained switch: new kinds need no edits to old operations and forgotten overrides are compile errors, not silent defaults.

intro: Chapter 20 built derivation one base at a time; real systems grow a whole graph of classes, and the graph itself is a design artifact. Stroustrup opens this chapter with the two questions that organize it: what should classes share — a common interface — and how should they share it — implementation by inheritance or by membership. The answers produce the interface/implementation split of §21.2, and then, when one class must honor two contracts at once, multiple inheritance, with the stream family as the working example.
objectives: Say what a class hierarchy is for: a common interface plus shared implementation across a set of related classes
Distinguish interface inheritance (substitutability) from implementation inheritance (reuse of data and code) as the two reasons to derive
Recognize when a set of variants is open — hierarchy territory — and when it is closed and better served without derivation

concepts.statement: A **class hierarchy** is a set of classes ordered by derivation, together with the design decisions that graph encodes: which operations are common to all of them (the **interface**) and which data and function bodies are shared along the edges (the **implementation**). With more than one base allowed, the shape is a **directed acyclic graph — a lattice** — not a tree: a class can be reached along several paths, which is exactly what §21.3 is about.
concepts.detail: Users touch the hierarchy through its root interface — `Shape*`, `istream&` — while each node below supplies its own representation. The graph, not any single class, is the unit of design.

concepts.statement: Every inheritance edge exists for one or both of two goods. **Interface inheritance**: code written against the base keeps working, unmodified and un-recompiled, for every class derived from it — substitutability. **Implementation inheritance**: the derived class reuses the base's data and function bodies instead of restating them. The design discipline of this chapter is asking, for each edge, which of the two you want — because the answer dictates whether the derivation should be public, private, or a member instead.
concepts.detail: Chapter 20 introduced the pair in passing; here it becomes the organizing principle of the whole design.

concepts.statement: The `Shape` family from the tour and chapter 20 settled the interface question: users hold `Shape*` and call `draw()`, `center()`, `move()`, `rotate()`, and each kind of shape overrides them. What is *not* settled is where the **representation** lives — which node owns the center point, the radius, the vertex list — and how much of it can be shared between classes rather than restated per class.
concepts.detail: That question is the chapter's engine: answering it splits one classical tree into an interface hierarchy plus implementation hierarchies, and ends in multiple inheritance when a class must draw on two of them at once.

concepts.statement: A hierarchy earns its keep only when the set of variants is **open**: new classes (a `Pentagon`, next year's `Audio_shape`) must join without editing or recompiling the code that uses the base interface. When the set of alternatives is **closed and known** — fixed by the problem, a handful at most — a tagged union, a `switch`, or a single class with a representation pointer is simpler and faster than derivation.
concepts.detail: The chapter's discussion of alternatives makes the same point from the other end: inheritance is one tool for expressing variation, not the only one.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Using hierarchies well. You can claim this section when you can say what a class hierarchy is for: a common interface plus shared implementation across a set of related classes — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 21 (Class Hierarchies); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: From design brief to base class
examples.problem: Version 1 of a drawing tool must support circles, polygons and text; shapes are drawn to a screen or a printer; and customers will add shape kinds the authors cannot foresee. Decide the root class.

steps.label: Step 1: Start from the uses, not the nouns
steps.text: List the loops user code writes over a heterogeneous collection: render (`draw`), reposition (`move`), query (`center`), transform (`rotate`). Four operations, one per loop body — these are the interface candidates.

steps.label: Step 2: Which can the base implement?
steps.text: None: each depends on the representation a derived class chooses. So all four become pure virtual, plus the virtual destructor every polymorphic base needs — four pure virtuals and an empty virtual destructor, zero bodies, zero data.

steps.label: Step 3: What may the base store?
steps.text: Nothing. A `Point center` member would tax an image-backed shape that keeps no center; representation belongs in the derived classes, one per kind, chosen freely.

steps.label: Step 4: Open or closed?
steps.text: Customer extension makes the set of shapes open — they derive from the published interface and user code never notices. The medium is not a kind of shape at all: it varies per operation, so it travels as a parameter of `draw`, not as classes in the hierarchy.

examples.result: A data-free abstract root — four pure virtual declarations, a virtual destructor, and nothing else — with media handled as arguments. The interface is exactly the uses, no more.

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: Using hierarchies well. Your task: say what a class hierarchy is for: a common interface plus shared implementation across a set of related classes.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: say what a class hierarchy is for: a common interface plus shared implementation across a set of related classes. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A class hierarchy is a DAG whose nodes share a root interface and, along its edges, implementation — the graph, not any class, is the design unit

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `struct Circle : Shape { void draw() const override; };` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — distinguish interface inheritance (substitutability) from implementation inheritance (reuse of data and code) as the two reasons to derive — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Every derivation edge should declare its purpose: interface inheritance for substitutability, implementation inheritance for reuse If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A class hierarchy is a DAG whose nodes share a root interface and, along its edges, implementation — the graph, not any class, is the design unit Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A class hierarchy is a DAG whose nodes share a root interface and, along its edges, implementation — the graph, not any class, is the design unit
Every derivation edge should declare its purpose: interface inheritance for substitutability, implementation inheritance for reuse
Derivation pays when the variant set is open; closed sets of alternatives are better expressed without it

quiz.q: With multiple inheritance allowed, the shape of a class hierarchy is best described as:
options: A tree — each class has exactly one direct base
A directed acyclic graph — a class can be reached along several paths
A linear list of classes ordered by object size
An unordered set with no structure
quiz.explanation: Several direct bases make the derivation relation a DAG (Stroustrup calls it a lattice); the same class can be reached through different paths, which is what produces the duplication problems of §21.3.

quiz.q: A class derives from another mainly to reuse its protected data and helper functions, with no substitutability intended. Which relationship is being expressed?
quiz.explanation: Reuse of state and code is implementation inheritance; substitutability through the public interface is the other, different good. The distinction decides whether the derivation is public at all.

quiz.q: A parser's token set is fixed at six kinds by the language grammar and can never grow. The chapter's guidance suggests:
options: A deep hierarchy with one class per token kind
Deriving all six tokens from a Token base so users can extend them later
Making Token a virtual base of all six kinds
A closed representation such as a tagged union or a switch, not derivation
quiz.explanation: Hierarchies earn their keep on open variant sets. A set fixed by the grammar is closed — a tagged union and switch (or a single class) is simpler and has no virtual-call overhead.

intro: Chapter 20 told you what derivation *is*; this section is about what each edge is *for*. Stroustrup's central move is to separate **interface inheritance** — public derivation from an abstract base that owns a contract — from **implementation inheritance** — deriving to reuse state and code, properly done through a private or protected base or, better, a member. The section builds the Shape example into that split, states when composition beats inheritance, and shows why the deep taxonomic 'classical' hierarchies of the 1980s aged badly: one tree can encode only one classification criterion.
objectives: Separate interface inheritance from implementation inheritance and map each to public versus private/protected derivation or membership
Apply the composition-first rule and name the three powers that justify private inheritance over a member
Diagnose classical-taxonomy failure: the Square/Rectangle trap and the class-count arithmetic of independent criteria

concepts.statement: **Interface inheritance** is public derivation from a class used as a pure contract: the base is (typically) abstract, carries its operations as pure virtuals plus a virtual destructor, and holds **no data**. The public edge asserts substitutability — every derived object is usable wherever a base is expected — and users of the hierarchy hold base pointers and references *only*.
concepts.detail: The Shape interface of chapter 20 is the template: `virtual Point center() const = 0; virtual void move(Point to) = 0; virtual void draw() const = 0; virtual void rotate(int) = 0;` and a virtual destructor. Every operation user code needs uniformly, and nothing else.

concepts.statement: **Implementation inheritance** is derivation in order to reuse the base's data and function bodies. It should be kept out of the public interface: `class Circle : public Shape, protected Point` would take the interface from Shape publicly and reuse `Point`'s storage and move machinery as an implementation detail. Stroustrup's warning: the implementation hierarchy is plumbing — a reader of the public interface should not have to know it exists.
concepts.detail: The alternatives the chapter weighs for a circle's center: a `Point` member (plain composition, default choice), a protected/private `Point` base (derivation as reuse), or — rejected — putting the `Point` in `Shape` itself, which taxes every present and future shape with state it may not need.

concepts.statement: The default way to use a class's services is **membership**: represent commonality with plain classes and compose them. Reach for private inheritance only when a member cannot do the job — when the derived class must **override a virtual function** of the implementation, must reach the implementation's **protected members**, or must exploit the **empty-base optimization**. The relationships decide: is-a → public derivation; has-a → member; implemented-in-terms-of → member, or private inheritance; uses-a → a function argument, no inheritance at all.
concepts.detail: Membership also wins the housekeeping: it can be hidden behind a pointer (a compilation firewall), can appear multiple times, and never advertises the arrangement in the base list of a public interface.

concepts.statement: A **classical hierarchy** organizes classes by taxonomy: `Shape → Polygon → Rectangle → Square`, `Shape → Ellipse → Circle`. It couples interface and implementation in one tree and hard-codes a single classification criterion — so independent criteria multiply leaf classes as a *product*, and substitutability traps (Square inheriting `Rectangle`'s independent `set_width`/`set_height`) hide inside the geometry. Stroustrup's redesign: shallow public interface hierarchies for the uses, implementation detail in members or private bases.
concepts.detail: The test is behavioral, not taxonomic: if code holding `Rectangle*` can call `set_width(3)` and leave the height untouched, a Square is not a Rectangle whatever Euclid says.

concepts.term: Design of Class Hierarchies: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Design of Class Hierarchies.** Interfaces, implementation inheritance and composition. You can claim this section when you can separate interface inheritance from implementation inheritance and map each to public versus private/protected derivation or membership — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 21 (Class Hierarchies); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Two independent criteria: the class-count arithmetic
examples.problem: A graphics tool has 3 kinds of geometry (circle, polygon, text) and 3 output media (screen window, PostScript file, printer), varying independently. Compare the classical single-inheritance design with an interface/implementation split — today, and after additions of each kind.

steps.label: Step 1: Classical
steps.text: A class occupies one node of the tree, and each edge encodes one criterion, so a leaf must fix BOTH: leaves are the product $3 \times 3 = 9$ — Circle-on-screen, Circle-on-printer, …, Text-on-printer — each carrying geometry code *and* medium code.

steps.label: Step 2: Split
steps.text: Keep two hierarchies: a public interface side with the 3 geometric kinds implementing `Shape`, and an implementation side with 3 media classes. A shape is drawn by delegating to its medium, or by deriving from one class of each side: $3 + 3 = 6$ classes.

steps.label: Step 3: Add a fourth medium
steps.text: Classical grows by one leaf per kind: $9 \to 12$. The split grows by one class: $6 \to 7$. Add a fourth kind next quarter: classical $12 \to 16$, split $7 \to 8$.

steps.label: Step 4: Add a whole third criterion
steps.text: Suppose interactivity becomes a criterion with 2 values (interactive vs. static). Classical leaves multiply to $4 \times 4 \times 2 = 32$; the split needs $4 + 4 + 2 = 10$ classes. Product growth versus sum growth.

examples.result: 9 versus 6 today, 16 versus 8 after one addition of each: single-inheritance trees encode one criterion per edge, so independent criteria multiply leaves; separate hierarchies keep them additive.

examples.title: Working through design of class hierarchies
examples.problem: Interfaces, implementation inheritance and composition. Your task: separate interface inheritance from implementation inheritance and map each to public versus private/protected derivation or membership.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: separate interface inheritance from implementation inheritance and map each to public versus private/protected derivation or membership. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Keep the public base a pure interface — pure virtuals plus a virtual destructor, no data; representation belongs to implementations

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `struct Circle : Shape { void draw() const override; };` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — apply the composition-first rule and name the three powers that justify private inheritance over a member — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Default to members; private inheritance is the reserved tool for overriding the implementation's virtuals, protected access, and the empty-base optimization If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Keep the public base a pure interface — pure virtuals plus a virtual destructor, no data; representation belongs to implementations Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Keep the public base a pure interface — pure virtuals plus a virtual destructor, no data; representation belongs to implementations
Default to members; private inheritance is the reserved tool for overriding the implementation's virtuals, protected access, and the empty-base optimization
A classical taxonomy hard-codes one criterion: with $k$ independent criteria, single inheritance needs the product of the counts where split hierarchies need the sum

quiz.q: A team debates how a Stack should reuse a list's machinery. Which consideration would justify `class Stack : private list` rather than a `list` member?
options: They want the list's operations visible in Stack's public interface
Stack must override a virtual function of the list implementation, use its protected members, or exploit the empty-base optimization
They want two independent lists inside one Stack
They want Stack objects to convert implicitly to list
quiz.explanation: Those three powers — overriding, protected access, EBO — are the only ones a member cannot supply. Visibility of base operations and implicit conversion are what public derivation would give, which is exactly what is not wanted here.

quiz.q: Why does `class Square : public Rectangle` fail the chapter's test when Rectangle offers independent `set_width` and `set_height`?
options: Because squares have no width or height
Because Rectangle lacks a virtual destructor
Because a square cannot store its edge length
Because code holding `Rectangle*` could set the width without the height — the square invariant breaks, so the derived class no longer honors the base contract
quiz.explanation: Public inheritance asserts substitutability. A setter that leaves the object an inconsistent square contradicts Rectangle's contract through the base interface — a design failure the signature check cannot catch.

quiz.q: A system has 4 geometric kinds and 5 output media, two independent criteria. The interface/implementation split needs how many classes where the classical design needs $4 \times 5 = 20$?
quiz.explanation: Split hierarchies are additive: $4 + 5 = 9$ classes, against the 20 leaves of the product — the chapter's arithmetic for why one tree per criterion, not one tree for everything.

quiz.q: Which base is closest to the chapter's ideal interface root?
options: class Shape { public: virtual void draw() const = 0; virtual ~Shape() {} protected: Point c; };
class Shape { public: virtual void draw() const { /* blank screen */ } };
class Shape { public: virtual void draw() const = 0; virtual void move(Point to) = 0; virtual ~Shape() {} };
class Shape { public: void draw() const; };
quiz.explanation: Pure virtuals plus a virtual destructor and no data: option A taxes every derived class with a center it may not need, B silently supplies a wrong default body, and D is not even polymorphic.

depth.title: A taxonomy of derivation: interface, implementation, and the space between

blocks.body: Every derivation edge answers two independent questions: **what crosses the edge** — operations only, or operations plus state — and **who is allowed to see the edge** — public, protected, or private. Crossing the two dimensions yields the taxonomy this chapter argues from. (1) The **pure interface**: a public base that is nothing but pure virtuals and a virtual destructor. (2) The **abstract base with defaults**: public, essentially stateless, some operations implemented for the derived classes to inherit. (3) The **concrete public base**: public with state — the classical style, sound only while every derived class can honor the base's invariants. (4) The **implementation base**: private or protected derivation, state and code reused but invisible to users of the derived class. (5) The **member**: composition, no inheritance at all. (6) **Friendship** — not derivation, but the strongest grant of representation access. Design, in this chapter, is choosing cells deliberately rather than drifting into them.

blocks.heading: Soundness of a public derivation (the substitutability condition)
blocks.body: Let $B$ be a class whose public interface carries, for each operation $f$, a documented contract $S(f)$: preconditions, postconditions, and the invariants $f$ may rely on. The public derivation `class D : public B` is **sound** if and only if (i) every operation of $B$'s interface, invoked through a `B*` or `B&` denoting a `D` object, terminates with an outcome consistent with $S(f)$ — refinement is allowed, contradiction is not — and (ii) every invariant $B$'s own operations rely on holds for each `D` object before and after every call. The compiler verifies none of this: the override check of chapter 20 tests signature compatibility, which is necessary but not sufficient — `Square::set_width` satisfies the signature and demolishes the contract. Substitutability is a design review, not a compile step.

blocks.heading: Why classical hierarchies multiply classes
blocks.body: Let a family of concepts be described by $k$ independent criteria, the $i$-th taking $n_i$ values. Single inheritance places each class at one node of a tree, so each edge can encode exactly one criterion and every leaf must fix all of them: the leaves are the Cartesian product $\prod_{i=1}^{k} n_i$. With $k = 2$ and $n_1 = n_2 = 3$: $3 \times 3 = 9$ classes. Grant each criterion its own edge — multiple inheritance, or composition — and the count becomes $\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i$: here $3 + 3 = 6$. Add a third criterion with $n_3 = 2$ and the product jumps to $3 \times 3 \times 2 = 18$ while the sum is $3 + 3 + 2 = 8$: multiplicative versus additive growth. This arithmetic is the engine behind the advice to organize interfaces by *use*: a use-driven interface tends to be a one-criterion tree, which is exactly what a tree encodes well.

blocks.heading: Circle's center: member, private base, or data in the root
blocks.body: Take `struct Point { int x, y; };` — 8 bytes on a typical 64-bit machine. (a) **Member**: `class Circle : public Shape { Point c; int r; /* … */ };` — the center is private representation, and `move` is written once: `void move(Point to) { c = to; }`. (b) **Private base**: `class Circle : public Shape, private Point { int r; /* … */ };` — the layout is identical (the `Point` subobject occupies the same 8 bytes), but `x` and `y` now sit in Circle's scope and Point's `move` serves every class built this way; the cost is that the base list advertises the arrangement. (c) **Data in the root** `Shape` — rejected: every shape, image-backed ones included, pays the 8 bytes and owns the invariant. The empty case sharpens the choice: for `struct Empty {};`, `class A { int id; Empty e; };` occupies $4 + 1$ bytes padded to **8**, while `class B : Empty { int id; };` occupies **4** — the empty-base optimization is the one layout fact that can force private inheritance over membership.

Membership wins the default case, so why does the language keep private derivation at all? Three powers a member cannot give: the derived class may **override the base's virtual functions** (a member is called, never overridden); it may **use the base's protected members**; and it may **vanish** through the empty-base optimization. Against them stand the costs: appearing in the base list couples the classes visibly, and readers are surprised by derivation used for reuse. The advice section's ordering is explicit — represent commonality as a plain class first; reach for private inheritance only when one of the three powers is actually needed. The same discussion carries the older warning: **protected data** is a design smell, because it shares raw representation with every present and future derived class; protected *functions* — services offered to implementers — are the defensible use.

blocks.heading: The two-hierarchy architecture, and the single-class alternative
blocks.body: The chapter's designs converge on one architecture: a small **public interface hierarchy** (abstract roots like `Shape` or `basic_istream`) through which users program, and one or more **implementation hierarchies** — representation families, `Point`-style helpers, buffers — that the public classes own privately, as bases or members. The standard library's stream family is the worked instance: users see `basic_iostream`'s interface; the `basic_ios` state and the `streambuf` doing the actual I/O are shared machinery behind it (§21.3). The chapter also names the alternative: collapse the public hierarchy to **a single class holding a pointer to its representation** — the envelope/letter or pimpl shape. You gain value semantics and a compilation firewall; you pay one indirection per operation, and the set of representations must be closed behind that one class's constructors. Choose the split hierarchies when the variant set must stay open; choose the single class when stability and value semantics dominate.

intro: Most classes need only one base — but some concepts are genuinely two things at once: a bidirectional stream is an input stream *and* an output stream, and a shape that persists itself is a shape that also knows a file. Multiple inheritance gives a class several direct bases, and with it two problems the single-inheritance world never sees: names found through two bases (ambiguity) and the same base reached along two paths (duplication). The stream family — `istream`, `ostream`, `iostream`, sharing `basic_ios` — is the canonical solution: virtual bases, resolved.
objectives: Declare classes with several direct bases and predict their subobjects, conversions and construction order
Resolve cross-base name ambiguities with qualification and using-declarations, and state exactly when a clash becomes an error
Explain the iostream diamond and the role of virtual bases: one shared subobject, constructed by the most-derived class

concepts.statement: A class may have several direct bases: `class D : public A, public B { };` — the list gives each base its own access specifier (private by default for a `class`). A `D` object contains **both base subobjects**; a `D*` converts implicitly to an `A*` and to a `B*` — the two results need not even compare equal as addresses, since each points at its own subobject at its own offset. The uses: combining **interfaces**, combining an **interface with an implementation**, and — rarely and carefully — combining two implementations.
concepts.detail: Construction runs in the order the bases are declared (destruction in reverse); members and the constructor body follow, exactly as in the single-base case of chapter 20.

concepts.statement: If two bases offer the same member name, a use of that name through the derived object is **ambiguous** — an error at the point of use, and only there: `c.f()` with both `A::f` and `B::f` in scope is rejected. The fixes: qualify explicitly — `c.A::f()` or `c.B::f()` — or bring one candidate in with a using-declaration (`using A::f;`) in the derived class. The same rule governs conversions: with a base reached twice (non-virtually) through two paths, even converting `D*` to `B*` is ambiguous. If the two paths reach the *same* subobject — the virtual-base case below — the lookup finds one member and there is no ambiguity.
concepts.detail: Note the ordering the language rules impose: ambiguity is diagnosed before access control, so hiding one candidate behind `private` does not rescue the other. A clash that is never used is not an error.

concepts.statement: The classic worked example is the iostream family. `basic_istream` supplies the input area (`operator>>`, `get`, `read`), `basic_ostream` the output area (`operator<<`, `put`, `write`), and a stream that both reads and writes — `basic_iostream` — derives from **both**: `class basic_iostream : public basic_istream, public basic_ostream { /* … */ };`. But both parents also keep stream state (the good/fail/eof bits, the attached buffer), and that state must be **one thing**, or end-of-file observed by a read would be invisible to the next write through the same object. Hence the diamond: both `basic_istream` and `basic_ostream` declare `basic_ios` a **virtual base**, and `basic_iostream` contains exactly one `basic_ios` subobject.
concepts.detail: The file streams extend the pattern: `basic_ifstream : basic_istream`, `basic_ofstream : basic_ostream`, `basic_fstream : basic_iostream` — each still sharing the single state its iostream side owes to the virtual base.

concepts.statement: `class D : public virtual B { };` makes B a **virtual base**: however many inheritance paths reach B, the final object contains **exactly one** B subobject, shared by all of them. Two rules follow. Construction: the **most-derived class** constructs the virtual base, before all non-virtual bases; the initializers for B written in intermediate classes are ignored when those classes are not most-derived — which is why virtual bases are best given default constructors, with the most-derived class initializing explicitly when it needs more. Layout: the shared subobject is placed once (typically at the end of the most-derived object), so its offset varies with the complete type — reaching it through a base-class pointer loads the virtual-base offset from the vtable. That indirection is the cost of sharing.
concepts.detail: Without `virtual`, the diamond is duplicated state and ambiguous conversions; with it, one state and one construction — bought with layout indirection and construction discipline. The standard pays that price in every stream object rather than let one stream disagree with itself.

concepts.statement: **Multiple Inheritance.** Multiple base classes and their conflicts. You can claim this section when you can declare classes with several direct bases and predict their subobjects, conversions and construction order — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 21 (Class Hierarchies); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Auditing the diamond: layout arithmetic, state by state
examples.problem: Model the streams: `struct IOS { int state; };`, plus `Istream` (a virtual `get`, an `int cnt`) and `Ostream` (a virtual `put`, an `int cnt`), each deriving `public virtual IOS`, and `Iostream : public Istream, public Ostream`. On a typical 64-bit implementation — vptr $8$ bytes, int $4$, alignment $8$, a virtual base laid out at the end of the most-derived object (the GCC/Clang Itanium model) — compute both designs.

steps.label: Step 1: The non-virtual design
steps.text: `Istream_nv : public IOS` is vptr $8$ + state $4$ + cnt $4$ = $16$ bytes, its state at offset $8$. `Iostream_nv` places the `Istream_nv` subobject at offset $0$ and the `Ostream_nv` subobject at offset $16$: $16 + 16 = 32$ bytes holding **two** state words, at offsets $8$ and $24$.

steps.label: Step 2: Why two words is a defect
steps.text: A read that hits end-of-file sets eofbit in the istream-side word; the next write consults the ostream-side word and believes the stream is still good — the object disagrees with itself. Even `if (io)` becomes ambiguous, because two base subobjects offer the conversion.

steps.label: Step 3: The virtual design, one class
steps.text: `Istream_v : public virtual IOS` is vptr $8$ + cnt $4$ + state $4$ = $16$ — the shared base is placed last, at offset $12$. Same size as the non-virtual single class.

steps.label: Step 4: The virtual diamond
steps.text: In `Iostream_v`, the Istream part (vptr at $0$, cnt at $8$) is followed by the Ostream part at offset $16$ (vptr at $16$, cnt at $24$), and the **single shared** state word lands at offset $28$: $12 + 4 + 12 + 4 = 32$ bytes, one state subobject.

steps.label: Step 5: The bill
steps.text: The size is the same $32$ — padding absorbed the bookkeeping, because the vtable carries the virtual-base offset rather than a dedicated pointer field. The price is paid elsewhere: reaching the state through an `Istream*` now means loading that offset from the vtable at run time, and the most-derived `Iostream_v` alone constructs `IOS`.

examples.result: Two designs, both 32 bytes: the non-virtual diamond carries two divergent states at offsets $8$ and $24$; the virtual diamond carries one shared state at offset $28$. Correctness, not size, decides — and the sharing costs one indirection.

examples.title: Working through multiple inheritance
examples.problem: Multiple base classes and their conflicts. Your task: declare classes with several direct bases and predict their subobjects, conversions and construction order.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: declare classes with several direct bases and predict their subobjects, conversions and construction order. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `class D : public A, public B` gives D two base subobjects and both pointer conversions — the hierarchy becomes a true DAG

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `struct Circle : Shape { void draw() const override; };` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — resolve cross-base name ambiguities with qualification and using-declarations, and state exactly when a clash becomes an error — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Name clashes across bases are ambiguities at the point of use: qualify (`x.A::f()`) or resolve with a using-declaration; a clash never used is not an error If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `class D : public A, public B` gives D two base subobjects and both pointer conversions — the hierarchy becomes a true DAG Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `class D : public A, public B` gives D two base subobjects and both pointer conversions — the hierarchy becomes a true DAG
Name clashes across bases are ambiguities at the point of use: qualify (`x.A::f()`) or resolve with a using-declaration; a clash never used is not an error
A virtual base is one shared subobject constructed by the most-derived class — the standard's `basic_ios` keeps an iostream's state single

quiz.q: In the standard, why is `basic_ios` declared a virtual base of `basic_istream` and `basic_ostream`?
options: To make stream objects smaller than single inheritance could
So that `basic_iostream` — deriving from both — contains exactly one stream-state subobject: end-of-file seen by a read is seen by the next write through the same object
To let streams be copied cheaply
Because virtual functions require virtual bases
quiz.explanation: Without the virtual base, the diamond would hold two copies of the state and the read side would disagree with the write side. Virtual inheritance is what keeps the state single — size is not the issue.

quiz.q: `class BB : public A, public B {}` where both A and B declare `int f();`. Then `BB b; b.f();` is:
options: a compile-time error: ambiguous — qualify as `b.A::f()`, or introduce a using-declaration choosing one candidate
fine — `A::f` is called because A is listed first
a run-time choice made through the vtable
quiz.explanation: Lookup finds two different members in two base subobjects, so the use is ambiguous at compile time. Declaration order and derivations rescue nothing; qualification or a using-declaration does.

quiz.q: In `class D : public B1, public B2`, where both B1 and B2 virtually derive from V, who initializes V when a D is created?
options: B1 — the first base in declaration order initializes V
V is constructed twice, once along each path
The most-derived class D initializes V; the initializers for V written in B1 and B2 are ignored
No class initializes V — virtual bases self-construct
quiz.explanation: Virtual bases are constructed by the most-derived class, before the non-virtual bases. That is why virtual bases should have default constructors, and why intermediate classes' V-initializers only apply when they themselves are most-derived.

quiz.q: Under the section's layout model (vptr $8$, int $4$, alignment $8$), how many state subobjects does the NON-virtual diamond `Iostream_nv : Istream_nv, Ostream_nv` contain, and where?
options: Two — one per base subobject, at offsets $8$ and $24$
quiz.explanation: Each base subobject embeds its own copy: the Istream part's state at offset $8$, the Ostream part's at $24$ — duplication that virtual inheritance exists to remove, leaving the single shared word at offset $28$.

intro: The chapter closes, like every chapter in TC++PL, with a set of rules. They compress the design method: find the commonality and express it as a minimal abstract interface; keep implementation out of the public graph; prefer composition; reserve multiple inheritance for combining interfaces, and virtual bases for genuinely shared state. This section states the rules and — more useful — shows how to run them as an audit over a flawed hierarchy.
objectives: Apply the design order: interface first, minimal, abstract and data-free
Choose correctly among public inheritance, membership, private inheritance and plain function arguments using the relationship rules
Deploy multiple inheritance and virtual bases within the chapter's limits: interfaces combine freely; shared state needs virtual bases

concepts.statement: Start from the **uses**: enumerate the operations user code needs through the base, make exactly those the abstract interface — pure virtuals plus a virtual destructor — and stop. Every extra operation is a permanent tax on every present and future implementer, and every data member in the root forces a representation choice on classes that never asked for it. An interface is a contract drafted on behalf of classes you will never see: minimal beats convenient.
concepts.detail: The companion test is extension: write a use, then design the next derived class against the interface as a trial. If it forces edits to user code, the interface is wrong.

concepts.statement: **is-a** → public inheritance. **has-a** → a member. **uses-a** → a function argument — no inheritance at all. **implemented-in-terms-of** → a member, or private inheritance when the three special powers are needed: overriding the implementation's virtuals, its protected members, or the empty-base optimization. The default is membership; derivation is a decision, not a reflex.
concepts.detail: These four relationships, applied edge by edge over the class graph, are the whole of hierarchy design in one line — the rest of the advice is commentary.

concepts.statement: Multiple inheritance is sound and idiomatic for **combining interfaces** (`basic_iostream`) and for combining an interface with a private implementation; it turns hazardous when two bases both contribute **state**, because the derived object now owns two half-implementations that must be kept consistent. Virtual bases are the tool of last resort: use them when the shared state is genuinely one thing — a stream's flags — never as a preventive habit.
concepts.detail: A virtual base costs every use an indirection and moves construction to the most-derived class; reach for it when the duplication is a correctness problem, not a style problem.

concepts.statement: A hierarchy is designed for the classes that are **not in it yet**. The audit questions: can a new derived class be added without touching user code or sibling classes? Does every operation of the base still make sense for it? Does it need to override, or would a member have expressed the relationship better? A design that only fits the classes you have today is a taxonomy, not an interface.
concepts.detail: This is the operational form of the substitutability condition: each prospective derived class is a test case for the public contract.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Design the interface first, from the uses: minimal, abstract, data-free — each operation is a permanent commitment** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: A four-defect hierarchy audit
examples.problem: Find and fix the design defects in this sketch for a shape editor: `class Shape { public: virtual void draw() const { /* blank screen */ } protected: Point c; int col; }; class Rectangle : public Shape { public: void set_width(int); void set_height(int); }; class Square : public Rectangle {}; class File_shape : public Shape, public File { public: void draw() const; };` — where `File` is a class offering `read`, `write` and `sync`.

steps.label: Defect 1: state in the root
steps.text: `c` and `col` make Shape an implementation, not an interface: every shape pays the layout and the invariant — including image-backed shapes with no center. Fix: pure virtuals and a virtual destructor only; representation moves into the classes that have it.

steps.label: Defect 2: a default draw body
steps.text: A blank-screen default silently does the wrong thing for any new shape that forgets to override. Make `draw` pure: the compiler becomes the migration checklist instead of the bug report.

steps.label: Defect 3: Square from Rectangle
steps.text: Independent `set_width` and `set_height` through a `Rectangle*` can break the square invariant — the substitutability condition fails. Fix: do not derive; both classes can implement the Shape interface directly, or share a private polygon implementation base.

steps.label: Defect 4: File as a public base
steps.text: A `File_shape` is not a File: the public edge lets user code upcast to `File*` and call `read`/`write`/`sync` on a shape. It is implemented-in-terms-of a file — fix: make `File` a member (or at most a private base).

examples.result: The repaired design: a data-free pure interface at the root, Square decoupled from Rectangle, and File demoted from the public graph to an implementation detail — four applications of the relationship rules, four classes that no longer lie.

examples.title: Reviewing class hierarchies code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the design order: interface first, minimal, abstract and data-free.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Design the interface first, from the uses: minimal, abstract, data-free — each operation is a permanent commitment

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `struct Circle : Shape { void draw() const override; };`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: choose correctly among public inheritance, membership, private inheritance and plain function arguments using the relationship rules. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: is-a → public derivation; has-a → member; uses-a → argument; implemented-in-terms-of → member, or private inheritance for its three special powers

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Design the interface first, from the uses: minimal, abstract, data-free — each operation is a permanent commitment Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Design the interface first, from the uses: minimal, abstract, data-free — each operation is a permanent commitment
is-a → public derivation; has-a → member; uses-a → argument; implemented-in-terms-of → member, or private inheritance for its three special powers
Combine interfaces with multiple inheritance; reserve virtual bases for genuinely shared state — and judge every hierarchy by the derived classes not yet written

quiz.q: Per the chapter's advice, the first move when designing a new hierarchy is to:
options: Decide the data members of the root class
Design the interface from the uses — the operations user code needs through the base — before any representation
Pick the deepest taxonomy that fits the domain concepts
Make every class derive from a common Object root
quiz.explanation: Interfaces are drafted from uses; representation follows. Starting from data or taxonomy produces exactly the classical-hierarchy failure mode the chapter dismantles.

quiz.q: Which relationship justifies public inheritance?
options: is-a — substitutability through the base interface
quiz.explanation: Public derivation asserts substitutability. The other three relationships call for a member, a function argument, or at most a private base — never a public edge.

quiz.q: Which statement matches the chapter's advice on multiple inheritance and virtual bases?
options: Combine interfaces freely with public bases; combine implementation state from two bases only with care — and use a virtual base when the state must genuinely be shared
Avoid multiple inheritance in all forms; single inheritance plus composition always suffices
Make every base virtual as a matter of hygiene
Prefer repeated non-virtual bases so each subobject keeps its own copy of the state
quiz.explanation: The streams show the pattern: interfaces combine cleanly, duplicated state breaks invariants, and the virtual base is the surgical fix for shared state — not a default. Blanket rules in either direction contradict the chapter.

intro: A `Shape*` can point to any shape the program will ever define — that is the whole point of the interface — but it also means the compiler has deliberately forgotten which one. Run-time type information (RTTI) is the machinery for getting that knowledge back at run time: `dynamic_cast` to ask whether an object really is of some class, and `typeid` to ask exactly what its type is. Stroustrup introduces RTTI as a fallback: virtual functions should always be the first tool, and this chapter is about the situations where they are not enough.
objectives: Explain why an upcast to a base-class interface discards static type information, and why virtual functions alone cannot recover it
Name the two RTTI mechanisms — `dynamic_cast` for navigation and `typeid` for identification — and the distinct questions each answers
Recognize the classic motivating problems, such as object I/O, where the exact type of an object must be recovered at run time

concepts.statement: RTTI is information about the **run-time type of an object** that a program can inspect after the object has been handed over through a base-class interface. C++ exposes two mechanisms: `dynamic_cast` for checked navigation of a class hierarchy (§22.2) and `typeid` for exact-type queries (§22.5).
concepts.detail: The information is attached to polymorphic objects — implementations store it beside the virtual function table — which is why RTTI works only where virtual functions do: a class with no virtual functions has no run-time type record to consult.

concepts.statement: Upcasting — using a `Circle` where a `Shape` is expected — is the act that makes object-oriented programming work, and it is also the act that **discards the static type** of the object. A virtual call recovers *behavior* for the questions the interface designer anticipated, but it can never answer questions like "which exact class is this?" or "does this object also belong to that other class?"
concepts.detail: The canonical example is object I/O: an object is written to a stream as a sequence of bytes, and the program that reads it back sees only bytes plus a base-class pointer — the exact type must be recovered before the data can be interpreted. Equality comparison across a heterogeneous hierarchy raises the same problem.

concepts.statement: `dynamic_cast` answers "**is this object of class T, or of a class derived from T?**" and delivers a usable `T*` (or `T&`) when the answer is yes. `typeid` answers "**what is the exact type of this object?**" and delivers a `const type_info&` naming that one class.
concepts.detail: The distinction matters: a `Smiley` derived from `Circle` passes `dynamic_cast<Circle*>` but fails `typeid(*p) == typeid(Circle)`. Use `dynamic_cast` when you intend to *use* the object as a `T`; reach for `typeid` only when the exact type itself is the information you need.

concepts.term: RTTI as a fallback, not a feature
concepts.statement: The question "which kind of object is this?" is usually better answered by **redesigning the interface** — adding a virtual function, or reorganizing which class owns which responsibility. RTTI exists for the cases where you cannot change the classes: other people’s libraries, interfaces fixed by the system, and persistent data laid down long ago.
concepts.detail: This is why the chapter is short and the advice section stern: most designs that lean heavily on RTTI are using it to patch a missing virtual function, and the patches rot as the hierarchy grows.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** RTTI at a glance. You can claim this section when you can explain why an upcast to a base-class interface discards static type information, and why virtual functions alone cannot recover it — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 22 (Run-Time Type Information); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Where the type disappears
examples.problem: Trace a `Circle` object through a base-class interface and identify exactly what information survives and what is lost.

steps.label: Construct
steps.text: `Circle c;` — the static type of `c` is `Circle`; every member of `Circle` is directly accessible.

steps.label: Upcast
steps.text: `Shape& r = c;` — a legal, implicit upcast. The static type of `r` is now `Shape&`; everything only `Circle` declares is invisible through `r`.

steps.label: Virtual call
steps.text: `r.draw()` compiles and runs `Circle::draw` — dynamic dispatch recovers the *behavior*, because `draw()` is one of the questions `Shape` was designed to answer.

steps.label: Unanticipated question
steps.text: If `Shape` has no `radius()`, then `r.radius()` does not compile — the interface simply does not carry that knowledge, even though the object has a radius.

steps.label: Object I/O
steps.text: Write `r` to a file and read it back as a `Shape*`: the stream contains bits only. Nothing virtual can be called before the exact type is known — the type itself must be reconstructed first.

examples.result: Virtual dispatch answers the questions the interface designer anticipated; RTTI exists for the questions nobody anticipated — starting with "what type is this object, so that I may even call one of its functions?"

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: RTTI at a glance. Your task: explain why an upcast to a base-class interface discards static type information, and why virtual functions alone cannot recover it.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: explain why an upcast to a base-class interface discards static type information, and why virtual functions alone cannot recover it. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: An upcast deliberately discards the static type of an object; virtual functions recover anticipated behavior, not arbitrary type knowledge

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `if (auto p = dynamic_cast<Derived*>(base)) { p->extra(); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — name the two RTTI mechanisms — `dynamic_cast` for navigation and `typeid` for identification — and the distinct questions each answers — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: `dynamic_cast` asks about membership in a class family; `typeid` asks for exact identity — choose the weaker question that suffices If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: An upcast deliberately discards the static type of an object; virtual functions recover anticipated behavior, not arbitrary type knowledge Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: An upcast deliberately discards the static type of an object; virtual functions recover anticipated behavior, not arbitrary type knowledge
`dynamic_cast` asks about membership in a class family; `typeid` asks for exact identity — choose the weaker question that suffices
RTTI is available only for polymorphic types, because the run-time type record lives beside the virtual function table

quiz.q: Which single act discards the static type of a derived object in C++?
options: Upcasting it through a base-class interface
Calling a pure virtual function on it
quiz.explanation: Assigning or binding a derived object to a base-class pointer or reference is precisely the conversion that forgets the derived type — by design, since that is what lets one interface serve every derived class.

quiz.q: Which RTTI facility answers "is this object a T or something derived from T"?
quiz.explanation: `dynamic_cast<T*>(p)` performs exactly this checked membership test at run time, returning a valid `T*` on success and `nullptr` on failure.

quiz.q: The chapter’s canonical motivating problem for recovering exact types at run time is
options: Object I/O: reconstructing objects of unknown exact type from a stream
quiz.explanation: A reader that receives raw bytes plus a base-class pointer must first learn the exact type before it can meaningfully call any virtual function on the reconstructed object.

quiz.q: Why is RTTI restricted to polymorphic types?
options: Because the run-time type information is stored beside the virtual function table
Because only virtual classes have addresses
Because the standard library forbids it otherwise
Because non-virtual classes cannot be derived from
quiz.explanation: The run-time type record is tied to the vtable; a class with no virtual functions has no vtable, so there is nowhere for the compiler to hang the type information that `dynamic_cast` and `typeid` consult.

intro: Class hierarchy navigation is the primary legitimate use of RTTI: given a base-class pointer, recover a pointer to a more specific part of the hierarchy, safely. `dynamic_cast` is a *conditional* conversion — it consults the object’s own type record, succeeds only when the object really is of the target class, and reports failure in a way the program can branch on. The section also fixes the vocabulary: upcasts, downcasts, and the cross-casts that only `dynamic_cast` can perform.
objectives: Use `dynamic_cast<T*>` to test and convert a base-class pointer, employing the declaration-in-condition idiom
State what `dynamic_cast` does on failure for pointers (`nullptr`) and references (`std::bad_cast`), and why the two differ
Distinguish upcasts, downcasts and cross-casts, and explain why only `dynamic_cast` can perform a checked cross-cast

concepts.statement: `dynamic_cast<T*>(p)` examines the object that `p` points to at run time; if that object is a `T` or a class derived from `T`, the result is a valid `T*`; otherwise the result is **`nullptr`**. The recommended idiom puts the cast in the condition so the pointer’s scope matches its guarantee: `if (Circle* pc = dynamic_cast<Circle*>(ps)) { /* pc is valid */ }`.
concepts.detail: If `p` is itself `nullptr`, the result is a null `T*`. A `dynamic_cast` that merely converts to an accessible base (an upcast) needs no run-time check at all and always succeeds.

concepts.statement: For references, `dynamic_cast<T&>(r)` succeeds under the same condition and otherwise **throws `std::bad_cast`** — because a reference cannot be null, there is no failure value to return, so failure must be an exception.
concepts.detail: Use the pointer form when failure is an expected branch of the logic, and the reference form when failure means a broken program invariant and an exception (with its stack unwinding) is the honest response.

concepts.statement: `static_cast<Circle*>(ps)` converts the pointer **without any run-time check**: it simply trusts you, at zero cost. If `ps` actually pointed to a `Square`, every subsequent member access through the result is undefined behavior — a lying pointer that compiles cleanly.
concepts.detail: The trade is explicit: `dynamic_cast` pays a run-time lookup against the object’s type record for a guarantee; `static_cast` pays nothing and guarantees nothing. In template and low-level code `static_cast` has honest uses, but as a hierarchy tool it is a trap.

concepts.statement: Given `class MI : public Left, public Right`, converting a `Left*` that points to an `MI` object into a `Right*` is a **cross-cast**. Whether it can succeed, and by what address adjustment, depends on the actual object’s layout — known only at run time — so this is a job for `dynamic_cast` alone.
concepts.detail: `static_cast` cannot even express it (the types are siblings, not related up or down), and `reinterpret_cast` would produce a wrong address by simply re-labeling the pointer. `dynamic_cast<Right*>(pl)` succeeds exactly when the pointed-to object really does contain a `Right` part, and returns the adjusted address of that subobject.

concepts.statement: `dynamic_cast<void*>(p)` yields a pointer to the **most derived object** of whatever `*p` is — usable as an identity key, since two such casts on the same object always yield the same address. All checked forms require the source type to be polymorphic (at least one virtual function).
concepts.detail: This "which complete object am I a part of?" query is the machinery that makes interfaces, garbage collectors and persistence systems possible; it cannot be faked with a plain cast because multiple inheritance makes the most-derived address a run-time fact.

figures.caption: Class hierarchy navigation with `dynamic_cast`. Left: in a single hierarchy an upcast is implicit and always safe, a downcast is the checked conditional conversion (`nullptr` for pointers, `std::bad_cast` for references), and types in unrelated branches cannot be cast to one another at all. Right: with multiple inheritance, converting a `Left*` into a `Right*` — a cross-cast — depends on the actual object’s layout, so only `dynamic_cast` can perform it.

examples.title: Six casts on one Smiley
examples.problem: Given the hierarchy `Shape` ← { `Circle` ← `Smiley`, `Square` } and the declaration `Shape* ps = new Smiley;`, predict the outcome of each cast.

steps.label: Upcast
steps.text: `dynamic_cast<Shape*>(ps)` — non-null without any run-time check: every `Smiley` is a `Shape`, and casting to an accessible base always succeeds.

steps.label: Downcast to a true base
steps.text: `dynamic_cast<Circle*>(ps)` — non-null: a `Smiley` IS-A `Circle`, so the returned pointer addresses the `Circle` subobject of the most derived object.

steps.label: Downcast to the wrong branch
steps.text: `dynamic_cast<Square*>(ps)` — `nullptr`: a `Smiley` has no `Square` part. The null test is the branch: `if (Square* q = dynamic_cast<Square*>(ps))` protects every use of `q`.

steps.label: Identity
steps.text: `dynamic_cast<void*>(ps)` — the address of the complete `Smiley` object. Any other `dynamic_cast<void*>` applied to any pointer into the same object yields this same address.

steps.label: Reference form
steps.text: `dynamic_cast<Square&>(*ps)` — throws `std::bad_cast`: there is no null reference to return, so failure must throw.

steps.label: The trap
steps.text: `static_cast<Square*>(ps)` — compiles, "succeeds", and lies: the pointer was never checked, and the first `Square` member access through it is undefined behavior.

examples.result: Two forms of failure (`nullptr`, `std::bad_cast`), one identity query (`void*`), one guaranteed success, and one silent trap — the complete decision table for one line of hierarchy.

examples.title: Working through class hierarchy navigation
examples.problem: dynamic_cast and safe downcasts. Your task: use `dynamic_cast<T*>` to test and convert a base-class pointer, employing the declaration-in-condition idiom.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: use `dynamic_cast<T*>` to test and convert a base-class pointer, employing the declaration-in-condition idiom. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `dynamic_cast<T*>(p)` is a conditional conversion: valid `T*` if the object is a `T`, `nullptr` otherwise; the reference form throws `std::bad_cast` instead

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `if (auto p = dynamic_cast<Derived*>(base)) { p->extra(); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — state what `dynamic_cast` does on failure for pointers (`nullptr`) and references (`std::bad_cast`), and why the two differ — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: The declaration-in-condition idiom ties the pointer’s scope to the validity of its guarantee If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

keyTakeaways: `dynamic_cast<T*>(p)` is a conditional conversion: valid `T*` if the object is a `T`, `nullptr` otherwise; the reference form throws `std::bad_cast` instead
The declaration-in-condition idiom ties the pointer’s scope to the validity of its guarantee
Cross-casts between sibling bases of a multiply-derived object depend on run-time layout — only `dynamic_cast` performs them, and `static_cast` cannot even express them

quiz.q: `Shape* ps` points to a `Square`. What does `dynamic_cast<Circle*>(ps)` do?
quiz.explanation: For pointer targets, failure is a null pointer so that the caller can branch on it; the object is in the wrong branch of the hierarchy, so the checked conversion reports "no".

quiz.q: Why does the reference form `dynamic_cast<T&>(r)` throw rather than return something on failure?
options: References are slower to convert than pointers
The compiler cannot inspect a referenced object
There is no null reference, so failure has no representable return value
Throwing keeps the exception table warm
quiz.explanation: A reference cannot be null, so the "failed conversion" outcome must be delivered some other way — `std::bad_cast` is that signal.

quiz.q: You hold a `Left* pl` that points to an object actually derived from both `Left` and `Right`. Which conversion to `Right*` is guaranteed correct?
quiz.explanation: The cross-cast needs the address of the `Right` subobject inside the actual object — a layout fact known only at run time, which is exactly what `dynamic_cast` consults.

quiz.q: The idiom `if (Tool* t = dynamic_cast<Tool*>(p)) { /* use t */ }` is preferred mainly because
options: the pointer’s scope exactly matches the region where it is guaranteed valid
it is faster than storing the result separately
it works for non-polymorphic classes too
quiz.explanation: The variable declared in the condition is in scope only inside the dependent statement — precisely where the cast is known to have succeeded; there is no way to use it before checking.

intro: A virtual function call selects the code to run from the dynamic type of exactly one object. But many interesting operations — intersecting two shapes, evaluating an expression node, comparing two objects — depend on the dynamic types of *two* operands. The chapter presents two answers: hand-built double dispatch, and the Visitor pattern, which achieves the same effect with one virtual call plus ordinary overload resolution and no RTTI at all.
objectives: Explain why a single virtual call cannot select an operation from the dynamic types of two objects
Implement double dispatch: a virtual call on the first operand followed by a call on the second with `*this` statically typed
Structure the Visitor pattern — `accept(Visitor&)` plus `visit` overloads — and trace both dispatches step by step

concepts.statement: A virtual call performs **single dispatch**: the function is chosen from one object’s dynamic type. An operation over two polymorphic objects — `intersect(circle, square)`, or evaluating one node against another — needs a choice from the *pair* of dynamic types, and the language has no direct syntax for that.
concepts.detail: The brute-force fix is a `dynamic_cast` chain over the second operand inside each virtual override: for $n$ and $m$ classes that is up to $n \times m$ type tests, each a possible run-time cost and a place to forget a case. Double dispatch and visitors remove the type tests entirely.

concepts.statement: Dispatch twice: the first virtual call `a.op(b)` discovers `a`’s type; inside that override, call `b.op2(*this)` — and now `*this` is **statically typed as the concrete class**, so the second virtual call dispatches on `b` while the first choice is already fixed.
concepts.detail: The catch is coupling: every class must know the interface of every other class it can interact with, so the "member" version of double dispatch scales badly when new classes keep arriving. That is what the visitor decouples.

concepts.statement: Each element class defines `virtual void accept(Visitor& v) { v.visit(*this); }`; a `Visitor` declares one `visit` overload per element type. Inside `Num::accept`, `*this` has type `Num&`, so the compiler picks `visit(Num&)` — **the second dispatch is done by ordinary overload resolution**, using the type information the first (virtual) dispatch established.
concepts.detail: The pattern is double dispatch without RTTI: no `dynamic_cast`, no `typeid`, no type tags — just virtual functions plus overloading, both of which the compiler already implements perfectly.

concepts.statement: The visitor machinery carries the type information in the **static type of `*this`**: by the time `v.visit(*this)` is compiled, the element class is known, so the pair (element, operation) is pinned by two ordinary language mechanisms — a virtual call and an overload resolution.
concepts.detail: This is the general lesson of the section: type-driven selection is cheapest when it is pushed into the type system itself; run-time type interrogation is what you fall back on when the structure cannot be arranged to carry the types.

concepts.statement: With a visitor, **adding a new operation** means writing one new `Visitor` class — nothing existing changes. **Adding a new element class** means adding a `visit` overload to the `Visitor` interface and editing every existing visitor to implement it.
concepts.detail: Compare plain virtual functions, where the trade is reversed: new types are free, new operations touch every class. Choose the pattern by which axis changes more often — that decision, not the mechanics, is the design content of the pattern.

figures.caption: The Visitor pattern as double dispatch. The call `e.accept(ev)` (step 1) is a virtual call, so it runs on the concrete element — `Num`, `Times` or `Plus`. Inside `accept`, the static type of `*this` *is* that concrete class, so `v.visit(*this)` (step 2) is resolved by ordinary overload resolution, pinning the (element, operation) pair without any run-time type query. Finally `visit` itself is virtual (step 3), so the concrete visitor — here an `Evaluator` — executes.
