examples.title: Evaluating 3 + 4 × 5 with a visitor
examples.problem: An expression tree `Plus(Num(3), Times(Num(4), Num(5)))` must be evaluated by a visitor `Evaluator`. Trace every dispatch and verify the arithmetic.

steps.label: The call
steps.text: `Evaluator ev; double r = root.accept2(ev);` — the root is held as `Expr*`, its dynamic type is `Plus`.

steps.label: First dispatch
steps.text: `root.accept(ev)` is virtual, so `Plus::accept` runs — the element half of the pair is now known.

steps.label: Second dispatch
steps.text: `Plus::accept` executes `v.visit(*this)` where `*this` is a `Plus&`; overload resolution — at compile time — selects `Evaluator::visit(Plus&)`. No type was queried at run time.

steps.label: Recurse
steps.text: `visit(Plus&)` visits both children; the right child is a `Times`, so the same two-step dance lands in `Evaluator::visit(Times&)`.

steps.label: Leaves and arithmetic
steps.text: `visit(Num&)` yields `4` and `5`, so `Times` computes $4 \times 5 = 20$; `Plus` computes $3 + 20 = 23$.

examples.result: The visitor evaluates the tree to 23 using two virtual dispatches plus compile-time overloading — zero `dynamic_cast`, zero `typeid`, and the (element, operation) pair fixed twice without a single run-time type test.

examples.title: Working through double dispatch and visitors
examples.problem: The visitor pattern with double dispatch. Your task: explain why a single virtual call cannot select an operation from the dynamic types of two objects.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: explain why a single virtual call cannot select an operation from the dynamic types of two objects. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Single virtual dispatch chooses from one object’s dynamic type; binary operations need the pair, which is the double-dispatch problem

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `if (auto p = dynamic_cast<Derived*>(base)) { p->extra(); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — implement double dispatch: a virtual call on the first operand followed by a call on the second with `*this` statically typed — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: In `accept(Visitor& v) { v.visit(*this); }` the static type of `*this` is the concrete element class, so the second dispatch is plain overload resolution If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Single virtual dispatch chooses from one object’s dynamic type; binary operations need the pair, which is the double-dispatch problem Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Single virtual dispatch chooses from one object’s dynamic type; binary operations need the pair, which is the double-dispatch problem
In `accept(Visitor& v) { v.visit(*this); }` the static type of `*this` is the concrete element class, so the second dispatch is plain overload resolution
Visitors reverse the extensibility axis: new operations are one new class; new element types require editing every visitor

quiz.q: A virtual function call selects the code to run using
options: the static types of all arguments
the dynamic type of exactly one object
the return type of the function
the most-derived class of every object in scope
quiz.explanation: The virtual mechanism consults the vtable of the object on which the call is made — one object, one dynamic type. That limitation is exactly why double dispatch needs a second mechanism.

quiz.q: Inside `Num::accept(Visitor& v) { v.visit(*this); }`, which overload of `visit` is selected?
options: `visit(Num&)`, chosen at compile time by overload resolution
Whichever overload was called most recently
quiz.explanation: The static type of `*this` inside `Num::accept` is `Num&` — the compiler therefore resolves the call to `visit(Num&)` while compiling `Num::accept`, before the program ever runs.

quiz.q: Which change forces you to edit existing Visitor implementations?
options: Adding a new concrete visitor class
Adding a new element class to the hierarchy
quiz.explanation: A new element class needs a new `visit` overload in the Visitor interface, and every visitor must implement it; a new operation is just a new visitor class that leaves existing code untouched.

quiz.q: What performs the *second* dispatch in the Visitor pattern?
options: Ordinary overload resolution on the statically-typed `*this`
A second virtual table lookup keyed by the visitor
quiz.explanation: By the time `v.visit(*this)` is compiled, `*this` has the concrete element’s type, so the compiler’s normal overload resolution picks the pair — no run-time type information is consulted.

intro: What happens if a constructor calls one of its own virtual functions? The answer is a rule every C++ programmer must own: during construction and destruction, an object behaves as if it were of the class currently being constructed — virtual calls, `dynamic_cast` and `typeid` inside a constructor of `B` see a `B`, never the derived override. The rule looks like a defect until you see what it prevents: calling code that touches members that do not exist yet.
objectives: State the rule: during construction and destruction an object behaves as if it were of the class currently being constructed
Explain the mechanism — vtable-pointer installation order — and the safety rationale that motivates it
Choose the standard workarounds: passing information to the base constructor, or post-construction initialization

concepts.statement: During the construction of an object of class `X`, the object **behaves as if it were exactly an `X`**: a virtual function called from `X`’s constructor (or destructor) is resolved to `X`’s version, never to an override in a class derived from `X`. Destruction follows the same rule in reverse order.
concepts.detail: The rule covers all the RTTI machinery: `typeid(*this)` inside `B::B()` is `typeid(B)`, and a `dynamic_cast` inside the constructor sees a `B` as well. The "object" is being built bottom-up through the hierarchy, and each level sees only itself.

concepts.statement: Each constructor installs the vtable pointer for its own class before running its body, and the derived class’s members are **not initialized until the base constructor has finished**. Calling the derived override would execute code that reads members whose initializers have not run yet — so the language simply does not do it.
concepts.detail: The sequence for `D d;` is: `B`’s vptr → `B`’s member initializers → `B`’s constructor body → `D`’s vptr → `D`’s member initializers → `D`’s constructor body. Destruction unwinds this exactly in reverse, so a virtual call from `B`’s destructor also gets `B`’s version.

concepts.term: Pass information up, do not ask down
concepts.statement: The fix when a base needs data that a derived override would have computed: **give the base constructor the information as arguments**. Constructors should take what they need rather than call a virtual function on a half-built object to ask for it.
concepts.detail: The chapter’s recurring example is a shape whose constructor wants to establish its center: pass the center (or the arguments to compute it) to the base constructor explicitly. The interface documents the dependency, and the object never runs code that outruns its own construction.

concepts.statement: When a genuinely virtual initialization is unavoidable, **construct minimally, then initialize**: create the object, then call an (often virtual) `init()` on the fully constructed object. The pattern is common in frameworks that must create objects before configuring them.
concepts.detail: Its cost is that an object exists in a not-yet-usable state — every member function must cope with that window. Use it when constructor arguments cannot express the setup; otherwise prefer the one-phase, argument-passing style.

concepts.term: Construction and Destruction: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Construction and Destruction.** Virtual functions in constructors. You can claim this section when you can state the rule: during construction and destruction an object behaves as if it were of the class currently being constructed — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 22 (Run-Time Type Information); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: What does this program print?
examples.problem: Predict the output of a base constructor that calls a virtual function which the derived class overrides, and explain why the answer is the safe one.

steps.label: The code
steps.text: `struct B { B(); virtual void trace(); }; struct D : B { D() : member{7} { } void trace() override; int member; };` with `B::B() { trace(); }` and `D d;` in `main`.

steps.label: Construction order
steps.text: Storage is obtained; `B::B()` runs first. At this moment the vptr points at `B`’s table, and `D::member` is uninitialized memory.

steps.label: The call
steps.text: Inside `B::B()`, the object is a `B`: `trace()` resolves to `B::trace`, so the program prints what `B::trace` prints — not `D::trace`.

steps.label: The counterfactual
steps.text: Had `D::trace` been called, it would have read `member` before `member{7}` ran — garbage. The rule exists precisely to make that impossible.

steps.label: After construction
steps.text: Later, `d.trace()` dispatches normally and prints the derived message with `member = 7`; only *during* `B::B()` is the override invisible.

examples.result: The base constructor’s virtual call prints the base version. The override exists but does not participate until the derived constructor has run — the same reason `typeid(*this)` inside `B::B()` is `typeid(B)`.

examples.title: Working through construction and destruction
examples.problem: Virtual functions in constructors. Your task: state the rule: during construction and destruction an object behaves as if it were of the class currently being constructed.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: state the rule: during construction and destruction an object behaves as if it were of the class currently being constructed. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: During a constructor or destructor, an object behaves as if it were of the class currently being constructed — virtuals, `typeid` and `dynamic_cast` all see that class

steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `if (auto p = dynamic_cast<Derived*>(base)) { p->extra(); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain the mechanism — vtable-pointer installation order — and the safety rationale that motivates it — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: The rule prevents derived code from touching members that have not been initialized yet If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

keyTakeaways: During a constructor or destructor, an object behaves as if it were of the class currently being constructed — virtuals, `typeid` and `dynamic_cast` all see that class
The rule prevents derived code from touching members that have not been initialized yet
The cure for a base that needs data is constructor arguments, or failing that, post-construction (two-phase) initialization

quiz.q: Inside `B::B()` a call to a virtual function `f()` that `D` overrides resolves to
quiz.explanation: The vptr installed at this moment is `B`’s, and the object genuinely is a `B`-under-construction: the call lands in `B::f`, which is exactly what keeps derived members from being read before their initialization.

quiz.q: The main reason the rule exists is that
options: virtual calls are too slow in constructors
derived class members are not initialized while the base constructor runs
the vtable has not been allocated yet at all
constructors cannot be member functions of the same class
quiz.explanation: A derived override would be entitled to use derived members; those members do not yet hold their values until the derived constructor’s initializers run — so the language forbids the situation rather than the crash.

quiz.q: A base constructor needs a value that depends on the derived class. The chapter’s preferred fix is to
options: call a pure virtual function and implement it in the derived class
pass the needed information as arguments to the base constructor
quiz.explanation: Taking the data as constructor arguments states the dependency in the interface and never runs code that outruns the state of construction.

quiz.q: What does `typeid(*this)` report inside `D`’s destructor body (with base `B`)?
options: `typeid(B)`, because destruction has reached the base
`typeid(D)`, because the object was born a `D`
quiz.explanation: During `D`’s own destructor body the object is still (as far as the machinery is concerned) a `D`; it becomes a `B` only when `B`’s destructor begins. The type slides down the hierarchy as destruction proceeds — construction slides up through it.

intro: Where `dynamic_cast` asks a question about family membership, `typeid` asks for the name of the thing itself: `typeid(x)` produces a `const type_info&` describing the type of `x` — the dynamic type when `x` is a polymorphic lvalue, the static type otherwise. The section covers what `type_info` offers, how `std::type_index` turns it into a container key, and the traps that catch almost everyone once.
objectives: Use `typeid` on expressions and types, and predict when it reports the dynamic rather than the static type
Read a `type_info`: `name()`, `==`, `before()`, `hash_code()`, and use `std::type_index` as a container key
Avoid the classic `typeid` traps: applying it to the pointer instead of the object, and dereferencing a null pointer

concepts.statement: `typeid(e)` yields a reference to a `const std::type_info` describing the type of `e`. If `e` is a **polymorphic lvalue** — a reference to an object of a class with virtual functions — the description is the object’s **dynamic type**; for every other operand, including all non-polymorphic expressions and all types used directly, it is the **static type**.
concepts.detail: The operand is not evaluated unless it is a polymorphic glvalue, so `typeid(f())` with a non-polymorphic return type never calls `f` — a useful and occasionally surprising rule.

concepts.statement: The handle `typeid` returns: `name()` gives an **implementation-defined string** (often mangled), `==` and `!=` test exact type identity, `before()` provides an ordering for sorting, and `hash_code()` supports unordered containers. A `type_info` cannot be copied — hold it by reference or through `std::type_index`.
concepts.detail: Two `type_info`s compare equal exactly when they describe the same type — `operator==` is the identity test to use in code. Never compare `name()` strings across implementations: the spelling is not portable.

concepts.statement: `std::type_index` (header `<type_index>`) wraps a `type_info&` with `operator<` and a hash specialization, turning types into **keys for maps and unordered maps**: `std::map<std::type_index, std::string> registry;` then `registry[typeid(*p)]` looks up data by the object’s dynamic type.
concepts.detail: This is the standard pattern for per-type tables: name-to-factory registries, per-type debug counters, and the type tags that object I/O systems write into their streams.

concepts.statement: Three mistakes account for nearly all `typeid` bugs: applying it to the **pointer** instead of the object (`typeid(p)` describes `Shape*`, not the shape); **dereferencing null** (`typeid(*p)` with `p == nullptr` throws `std::bad_typeid`); and forgetting that `typeid` is **exact** — a derived object does not equal its base, where `dynamic_cast` would succeed.
concepts.detail: The exactness trap interacts badly with type switches: replacing virtual dispatch with `typeid` comparisons silently drops every class derived from the one you tested for — the subject of the next section.

concepts.statement: **Type Identification.** typeid and type_info. You can claim this section when you can use `typeid` on expressions and types, and predict when it reports the dynamic rather than the static type — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 22 (Run-Time Type Information); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: A typeid trace on one Smiley
examples.problem: Given `Shape* ps = new Smiley;` (with `Smiley : public Circle`), evaluate six `typeid` expressions and one `dynamic_cast`.

steps.label: The pointer
steps.text: `typeid(ps)` — describes the pointer itself: `Shape*`. No dereference, no dynamic lookup; the static type of the expression is all `typeid` sees.

steps.label: The object
steps.text: `typeid(*ps)` — `ps` is dereferenced and the object is polymorphic, so the dynamic type is reported: `Smiley`.

steps.label: Identity checks
steps.text: `typeid(ps) == typeid(Shape*)` is true; `typeid(*ps) == typeid(Smiley)` is true.

steps.label: The exactness trap
steps.text: `typeid(*ps) == typeid(Circle)` is **false** — a `Smiley` is derived from `Circle`, but not equal to it. Yet `dynamic_cast<Circle*>(ps)` succeeds: membership and identity are different questions.

steps.label: A registry
steps.text: With `std::map<std::type_index, std::string> names;` initialized for each concrete shape, `names[typeid(*ps)]` retrieves the entry stored under the `Smiley` key — the per-type-table pattern.

examples.result: Three true facts, one false-by-design comparison, and one keyed lookup: `typeid` answers identity, `dynamic_cast` answers substitutability, and the Smiley row shows both in action.

quiz.q: `Shape* ps` points to a `Smiley` (derived from `Circle`). What is the value of `typeid(*ps) == typeid(Circle)`?
options: True, because Smiley is a Circle
False — the dynamic type is Smiley, and typeid is exact
quiz.explanation: `typeid` tests exact identity, not substitutability: the dynamic type is `Smiley`, which is not the same type as `Circle` — even though `dynamic_cast<Circle*>(ps)` would succeed.

quiz.q: Which expression yields a `const type_info&` describing the object a polymorphic pointer `p` targets?
quiz.explanation: Dereferencing produces a polymorphic lvalue, which is the one case where `typeid` consults the run-time type of the object rather than the static type of the expression.

quiz.q: Why does the standard library provide `std::type_index`?
options: To provide ordering and hashing so types can be map keys
quiz.explanation: `type_info` itself has no `operator<` and cannot be stored by value; `type_index` wraps a reference to it with the ordering and hash that `std::map` and `std::unordered_map` require.

quiz.q: `Shape* p = nullptr;` — what does `typeid(*p)` do?
quiz.explanation: For a polymorphic operand the implementation must consult the object; there is none, so the operation throws `std::bad_typeid` rather than fabricating a type.

intro: RTTI is occasionally essential and often misused, and this section is Stroustrup’s audit of which is which. The legitimate uses share one signature: an object arrives through an interface that could not possibly have anticipated what you need to do with it. The classic misuse is subtler than it looks — replacing a virtual function with a chain of exact-type tests — and it fails not stylistically but structurally, the moment someone derives a new class.
objectives: Recognize the legitimate uses of RTTI: object I/O, interfaces you cannot change, and operations their designers never anticipated
Diagnose the classic misuse — type switches replacing virtual functions — and prove exactly how it breaks
Use the interface-retrieval idiom with `dynamic_cast` when the base interface cannot be extended

concepts.statement: RTTI earns its keep when the type information was **genuinely lost by an interface that could not be extended**: object I/O and persistence (reconstructing the exact type from a stream), libraries whose classes you cannot modify, and operations on objects that the interface designer never anticipated.
concepts.detail: The common thread: you hold a base-class reference and need knowledge the interface does not carry — and you cannot add a virtual function to fix that. If you can change the classes, you should.

concepts.term: The classic misuse: the type switch
concepts.statement: Replacing a virtual function with exact-type tests — `if (typeid(*p) == typeid(Circle)) draw_circle(p); else if (typeid(*p) == typeid(Square)) ...` — duplicates the class hierarchy in code: every operation must enumerate every class, and every new class must edit every operation.
concepts.detail: The fatal flaw is structural, not cosmetic: `typeid` is exact, so a class derived from `Circle` matches neither branch and silently falls through, while the virtual function it replaced would have dispatched correctly. The switch also loses to the vtable on every axis — type safety, extensibility, and speed.

concepts.statement: When you cannot modify a hierarchy but need a service its base does not offer, query the object for the interfaces it supports: `if (Interactive* i = dynamic_cast<Interactive*>(p)) i.handle_event(e);` — a loop of `dynamic_cast` tests, each one retrieving a capability the object may or may not have.
concepts.detail: This is the pattern behind component systems and interfaces like query-interface: the base stays minimal, and capabilities are discovered by checked conversion. It is legitimate precisely when the set of capabilities is open-ended and the classes are not yours to change.

concepts.statement: Before writing any `dynamic_cast`, ask: (1) **Do I need an operation or a type?** An operation belongs in a virtual function. (2) **Do I need the exact type or membership in a family?** Membership is `dynamic_cast`; only true identity needs `typeid`. (3) **Could the designer have anticipated this need?** If yes — and if you own the classes — extend the interface instead.
concepts.detail: Only when all three answers come back "no reasonable alternative" is the RTTI use clean. A design where most type queries survive those questions is doing interface retrieval by necessity, not by habit.

concepts.term: Uses and Misuses of RTTI: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Uses and Misuses of RTTI.** When dynamic_cast is a design smell. You can claim this section when you can recognize the legitimate uses of RTTI: object I/O, interfaces you cannot change, and operations their designers never anticipated — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 22 (Run-Time Type Information); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Why the type switch breaks, with arithmetic
examples.problem: A `draw(Shape*)` implemented as a `typeid` chain must handle a hierarchy of shapes including `Circle` and a new `Smiley : public Circle`. Count the edits and find the silent failure.

steps.label: The switch
steps.text: `if (typeid(*p) == typeid(Circle)) draw_circle(p); else if (typeid(*p) == typeid(Square)) draw_square(p); else throw std::runtime_error("bad shape");`

steps.label: Feed it a Smiley
steps.text: A `Smiley` IS-A `Circle` for substitution, but `typeid(*p) == typeid(Circle)` is false — the comparison is exact. And it is not a `Square` either.

steps.label: The failure
steps.text: The chain falls through to the final `else` and throws at run time — or, in the version without the else, draws nothing at all. No compiler diagnostic mentions it.

steps.label: Count the edits
steps.text: With $n = 20$ shape classes and $m = 15$ operations, the switch style costs on the order of $n \times m = 300$ branch bodies to review; the virtual-function style costs $n + m = 35$ functions, each written once, in one place.

steps.label: The virtual version
steps.text: `p.draw()` — a `Smiley` inherits or overrides `draw` and renders correctly with zero edits to existing code; adding a shape touches nothing downstream.

examples.result: The type switch is not merely inelegant — it is incorrect the day the hierarchy grows, and the failure is silent. That, not style, is why it heads the misuse list.

examples.title: Working through uses and misuses of RTTI
examples.problem: When dynamic_cast is a design smell. Your task: recognize the legitimate uses of RTTI: object I/O, interfaces you cannot change, and operations their designers never anticipated.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: recognize the legitimate uses of RTTI: object I/O, interfaces you cannot change, and operations their designers never anticipated. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Legitimate RTTI shares one signature: the type was lost through an interface that could not be extended — object I/O, foreign libraries, unanticipated operations

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `if (auto p = dynamic_cast<Derived*>(base)) { p->extra(); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — diagnose the classic misuse — type switches replacing virtual functions — and prove exactly how it breaks — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Type switches duplicate the hierarchy in code and break silently on derived classes, because `typeid` is exact If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Legitimate RTTI shares one signature: the type was lost through an interface that could not be extended — object I/O, foreign libraries, unanticipated operations Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Legitimate RTTI shares one signature: the type was lost through an interface that could not be extended — object I/O, foreign libraries, unanticipated operations
Type switches duplicate the hierarchy in code and break silently on derived classes, because `typeid` is exact
Interface retrieval — a loop of `dynamic_cast` capability probes — is the honest pattern when the classes are not yours to change

quiz.q: A new class `Smiley : public Circle` arrives. Which existing test still recognizes a Smiley object pointed to by `Shape* p`?
quiz.explanation: `dynamic_cast` asks about family membership and succeeds for derived classes; `typeid` demands exact identity and fails for `Smiley` — which is precisely how the type switch rots.

quiz.q: When is the interface-retrieval idiom (a loop of `dynamic_cast` probes) justified?
options: Whenever it saves writing a virtual function
When you cannot modify the base classes but need capabilities they do not expose
When the hierarchy has exactly two levels
quiz.explanation: The pattern exists for hierarchies you do not own: the base interface stays minimal, and callers discover capabilities by checked conversion. If you own the classes, adding the virtual function is the better design.

quiz.q: The root problem with replacing virtual dispatch by a `typeid` chain is that
options: `typeid` is slower than a virtual call
it duplicates the hierarchy in code and silently mishandles newly derived classes
quiz.explanation: Every operation must enumerate every class — the hierarchy is maintained twice — and because comparisons are exact, a newly derived class falls through the tests with no diagnostic.

intro: The chapter closes with its rules of thumb. They compress the whole argument: virtual functions first, the weakest RTTI question that answers the need, no virtual calls from constructors expecting derived behavior, and type queries isolated in a few well-documented places where their cost and fragility are visible.
objectives: Apply the chapter’s rules of thumb to choose among virtual functions, `dynamic_cast` and `typeid`
Justify each rule by the concrete failure mode it prevents
Recognize the restricted niche where RTTI is the correct engineering choice

concepts.statement: When the same action applies to every object of a class, **use a virtual function** — dynamic dispatch is type-safe, extensible to derived classes, and as fast as the mechanism allows. Reach for RTTI only when the type itself, not a behavior, is what you need.
concepts.detail: The rule follows from the misuse analysis: a type query hard-codes the set of classes, while a virtual function lets the set grow. Design effort spent moving work from type tests into the interface is repaid every time the hierarchy changes.

concepts.statement: When you must ask a type question, ask the **weaker** one: `dynamic_cast` asks membership in a family and keeps working for derived classes; `typeid` demands exact identity and breaks the moment someone derives.
concepts.detail: Escalate to `typeid` only for genuine identity questions — registries keyed by exact type, debugging output, and the type tags of object I/O — where "derived from" would be the wrong answer.

concepts.term: Never call a virtual from a constructor expecting the derived version
concepts.statement: During construction and destruction the object is of the class currently being built or destroyed — a virtual call from a constructor gets the local version, not the override. Pass needed information as constructor arguments instead.
concepts.detail: This rule closes the one gap that looks like RTTI but is really construction order: even `typeid` and `dynamic_cast` inside a constructor see the class under construction.

concepts.statement: Confine type queries to **a few well-documented functions** — the object I/O layer, the interface-retrieval helpers — so the rest of the system stays ignorant of type questions and their fragility.
concepts.detail: A design with `dynamic_cast` scattered through its logic is a design where every new class must be checked against every cast site; isolation makes that cost visible and local, and keeps the type switches honest by putting them where they belong.

concepts.term: Shipping rule for run-time type information
concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Virtual functions first; RTTI only when the type itself — not a behavior — is the information needed** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: A design review in three questions
examples.problem: An editor over the shape hierarchy has three new requirements. Apply the diagnosis questions to pick the right mechanism for each.

steps.label: Requirement A
steps.text: "Draw every shape": an operation, uniform across classes we own — question 1 says virtual function. `draw()` already exists; nothing to add.

steps.label: Requirement B
steps.text: "Select only the circles for the circle-tool": a capability probe over a hierarchy we own but a service `Shape` should not carry — `dynamic_cast<Circle*>(p)` in the selection filter, and derived circle-like classes still qualify.

steps.label: Requirement C
steps.text: "Log the exact class name of each shape as it is destroyed": true identity for debugging — `typeid(*p)` fed to a `std::map<std::type_index, int>` counter in the destructor of the logging wrapper.

steps.label: The audit
steps.text: No `typeid` switches dispatching behavior; the one `dynamic_cast` lives in a single filter function; the `type_index` table is part of the logging subsystem and documented as such.

examples.result: Three requirements, three different mechanisms, chosen by the questions — operation versus type, family versus identity, anticipated versus not.

examples.title: Reviewing run-time type information code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the chapter’s rules of thumb to choose among virtual functions, `dynamic_cast` and `typeid`.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Virtual functions first; RTTI only when the type itself — not a behavior — is the information needed

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `if (auto p = dynamic_cast<Derived*>(base)) { p->extra(); }`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: justify each rule by the concrete failure mode it prevents. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Ask the weaker question: `dynamic_cast` for family membership, `typeid` only for exact identity

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Virtual functions first; RTTI only when the type itself — not a behavior — is the information needed Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Virtual functions first; RTTI only when the type itself — not a behavior — is the information needed
Ask the weaker question: `dynamic_cast` for family membership, `typeid` only for exact identity
Isolate type queries in a few documented functions, and never expect derived behavior from virtuals in constructors

quiz.q: A new operation must apply uniformly to every shape in a library you own. The first choice is
quiz.explanation: An operation over classes you control belongs in the interface: virtual dispatch stays correct as classes are added and derived, which no type test achieves.

quiz.q: A filter must pick out every Circle, including classes derived from Circle. The best tool is
options: a C-style cast followed by a check
quiz.explanation: Membership in a family is exactly the `dynamic_cast` question; the exact-type comparison would silently drop derived classes.

quiz.q: Which rule protects you from the constructor trap of §22.4?
options: Pass needed information as constructor arguments instead of calling virtuals
quiz.explanation: The object during base construction is the base class; any derived-dependent service is unavailable — so supply the data through the constructor interface, or initialize after construction.

intro: Templates are C++’s mechanism for parameterized types and functions: a class or a function that takes types and constant values as parameters. From a template plus a set of arguments, the compiler generates — instantiates — a specific class or function, fully type-checked at the moment of generation. This one idea powers the containers, iterators and algorithms of the standard library, and it is the foundation on which generic programming (chapter 24) is built.
objectives: Define template, template argument, instantiation and specialization, and their relationships
List the kinds of template parameters — types, non-type constants, and templates — and what may serve as an argument
Explain the zero-run-time-overhead claim, and the compile-time and code-size price it is paid with

concepts.statement: A template is a class or function **parameterized by a set of types and/or integers**. From the template and a set of template arguments, the compiler generates a class or function — an instantiation. The generic definition is written once and serves every argument set.
concepts.detail: Templates are the compile-time twin of the function call: a call passes run-time values to one body; an instantiation passes compile-time types and constants to one definition. Everything a template computes, it computes while the program compiles.

concepts.statement: A parameter can be a **type** (`template<typename T>`), a **constant value** of integral, pointer or reference type (`template<int N>`, `template<typename T, T* root>`), or a **template itself**. Arguments must be known at compile time: types, `constexpr` values, and addresses.
concepts.detail: A value argument lets the type carry a size or policy — `std::array<int, 3>` — while keeping everything checkable and inlinable. Template template arguments, and the variadic forms of chapter 25, extend the same idea.

concepts.statement: A template plus a set of arguments names a **specialization**: `std::vector<int>`. Two specializations with different arguments are **distinct, unrelated types** — there are no conversions between `vector<int>` and `vector<double>` — and each gets its own code, generated on demand for the members actually used.
concepts.detail: This is the central accounting fact of templates: nothing exists until it is instantiated, and then it exists exactly and type-correctly for that argument set. The compiler does not generate "generic object code"; it generates specific, optimized code per specialization.

concepts.term: Zero overhead — and where the cost lands
concepts.statement: Everything the template mechanism does happens at compile time, so the generated code is **as fast as hand-written code for that type** — abstraction without run-time loss. The price is paid at build time: template definitions must be visible wherever they are used (§23.7), each specialization adds code, and instantiation-heavy code can dominate compile times.
concepts.detail: Code bloat — many specializations of near-identical code — is the classic risk; disciplined use of the standard library and explicit instantiation (§23.7) keeps it in check. The trade is the deliberate opposite of run-time polymorphism: pay at compile time, run for free.

concepts.statement: A preprocessor macro is textual substitution with no scope, no types and no overloading. A template is a **checked, scoped, overloadable language construct**: each instantiation passes name lookup, type checking and optimization on the substituted code.
concepts.detail: That is why `std::max`, `std::swap` and the containers could be built as templates: the mechanism preserves everything the type system knows, where a macro would discard it.

figures.caption: Template instantiation as code generation. The template is written once; each set of template arguments, together with the template, is compiled into a distinct specialization. `vector<int>` and `vector<string>` are separate, fully type-checked types with their own generated member code — and members that are never used are not generated at all.

examples.title: One template, three instantiations, one error
examples.problem: Given a function template `sum` over a `std::vector`, count the specializations the compiler generates and predict where the error appears.

steps.label: The template
steps.text: `template<typename T> T sum(const std::vector<T>& v) { T s {}; for (const T& x : v) s += x; return s; }`

steps.label: Call 1
steps.text: `sum(std::vector<int>{1,2,3})` instantiates `sum<int>` and computes $1+2+3 = 6$.

steps.label: Call 2
steps.text: `sum(std::vector<double>{1.5, 2.5})` instantiates a *different* function, `sum<double>`, and computes $1.5+2.5 = 4.0$.

steps.label: Call 3
steps.text: `sum(std::vector<std::string>{"a","b"})` instantiates `sum<std::string>`; the same `+=` line is now string concatenation: `"a" + "b"` gives `"ab"`.

steps.label: The error
steps.text: Add `struct Empty {};` and call `sum(std::vector<Empty>{})`: the body requires `Empty += Empty`, which does not exist. The error is reported **at the instantiation** — the point of use — not at the template definition (§23.3).

examples.result: Three working specializations from one definition, each its own type-checked function — and a fourth use that fails precisely where the argument meets the body.

examples.title: Working through introduction and overview
examples.problem: Templates at a glance. Your task: define template, template argument, instantiation and specialization, and their relationships.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define template, template argument, instantiation and specialization, and their relationships. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A template plus a set of arguments names a specialization; different arguments give distinct, unrelated types

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<typename T> T larger(T a, T b) { return (a < b) ? b : a; }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — list the kinds of template parameters — types, non-type constants, and templates — and what may serve as an argument — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Template parameters are types, compile-time constants, or templates — never run-time values If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A template plus a set of arguments names a specialization; different arguments give distinct, unrelated types Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A template plus a set of arguments names a specialization; different arguments give distinct, unrelated types
Template parameters are types, compile-time constants, or templates — never run-time values
Instantiation is a compile-time, code-generating, type-checking step: abstraction with zero run-time overhead, paid for in build time

quiz.q: What does the compiler produce from a template together with a set of arguments?
options: A run-time object of the template class
An instantiation: a specific class or function for exactly those arguments
quiz.explanation: Instantiation generates real, specific code — the template is a compile-time factory of classes and functions, not a run-time construct.

quiz.q: Which statement about `std::vector<int>` and `std::vector<std::string>` is correct?
options: They are the same type with different contents
They are distinct, unrelated types, each with its own generated members
One converts implicitly to the other
quiz.explanation: Each template plus arguments names a separate specialization: no conversions exist between them, and their members and code are generated independently.

quiz.q: Which of these can NOT be a template argument?
options: A value read from input at run time
quiz.explanation: Arguments must be known at compile time — types, constant expressions, addresses. Run-time values are parameters of function calls, never of templates.

quiz.q: The "zero-overhead" claim for templates means
options: the generated code is as efficient as hand-written code for the same type
the compiler never generates duplicate code
quiz.explanation: All the work — substitution, checking, specialization — happens at compile time, so at run time the instantiated code matches what a programmer would have written by hand for that type; the costs are compile time and code size, not execution speed.

intro: The chapter’s worked example is a `String` parameterized over its character type: `template<typename C> class String`. One template then serves `char`, `wchar_t`, and user-defined character types such as a Japanese character class — with the same operations, the same short-string optimization, and checked element-wise conversions between different character types. The example shows what "written once, used for many types" really costs: the template body becomes a list of requirements on `C`.
objectives: Read the `String<C>` template definition and extract the implicit requirements it places on `C`
Explain how member-template constructors convert between `String` specializations, element by element
Describe how user-defined character types plug in through overloaded helper functions

concepts.term: The design: String of any character type
concepts.statement: `template<typename C> class String` holds a sequence of `C`. The design carries over from the `String` of chapter 19 — counted representation, and a **short-string optimization** with `short_max = 15`, so strings of up to 15 characters live inside the object with no free-store allocation — with only the element type turned into a parameter.
concepts.detail: The point of the example: nothing about a string’s logic depends on characters being 8-bit. Storage, copying, comparison, concatenation and searching all work for any element type that supports a handful of operations.

concepts.statement: The template body **is** the requirements list. Reading `String<C>` top to bottom, `C` needs: default construction, copy construction, assignment, destruction (for storage); `==` and `<` (for `find`, sorting, comparisons); output streaming (for printing); and convertibility to other character types where the converting constructors are used.
concepts.detail: This is the key skill the chapter teaches before concepts arrive formally (§24.3): to read a template as a contract, asking at every operation "which type must support this, and what must it mean?"

concepts.statement: A constructor can itself be a template: `template<typename C2> String(const String<C2>&);` converts a string of one character type into a string of another, **element by element**. Because it is a template, one definition handles every pair of character types — there is no combinatorial list of `String<char>`-from-`String<wchar_t>`, `String<char>`-from-`String<Kana_char>`, … constructors.
concepts.detail: In the book’s design the element conversion is *checked at run time* by a small helper: if some element of the source cannot be represented in the target character type, the conversion throws `std::bad_cast`. Conversions between arbitrary types, unlike built-in narrowing, cannot all be validated at compile time.

concepts.statement: Operations the standard library only provides for `char` are supplied as **overloads**: the library’s `strlen` works for C strings, and a user defining `Kana_char` adds `int strlen(const Kana_char*);` plus the operators on `Kana_char` — after which `String<Kana_char>` works unchanged.
concepts.detail: This is dependency injection at the type level: the template never names a specific helper, it uses the operations, and overload resolution finds the right one per character type. (In practice one also writes a `size()` member and iterates, avoiding C-style helpers entirely.)

concepts.term: A Simple String Template: the working contract
concepts.statement: **A Simple String Template.** A first class template. You can claim this section when you can read the `String<C>` template definition and extract the implicit requirements it places on `C` — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 23 (Templates); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: A string of anything
examples.problem: Construct and convert `String` specializations for several character types, tracking sizes, allocations and failure points.

steps.label: Short string
steps.text: `String<char> s1("chair");` — length 5, and $5 \le 15 = $ `short_max`, so the characters live in the object’s internal array: no allocation happens.

steps.label: Long string
steps.text: A 40-character string exceeds `short_max`, so the representation allocates on the free store — the same policy as chapter 19, now for any `C`.

steps.label: Convert
steps.text: `String<wchar_t> s2(s1);` selects the member-template constructor: each `char` element is converted to `wchar_t`; the length is still 5.

steps.label: User characters
steps.text: `String<Kana_char> ks("...");` uses the user’s `strlen(const Kana_char*)` overload to measure the length — in characters, not bytes — before copying elements.

steps.label: Failure
steps.text: Converting a `String<wchar_t>` containing a character with no representation in `Kana_char` runs the checked element conversion and throws `std::bad_cast` mid-copy.

examples.result: One class template serves every alphabet; conversions between alphabets are element-wise, generated once for every pair, and fail loudly rather than silently producing garbage.

options: So a single definition converts from every other `String` specialization, rather than one constructor per pair

A specialization of the whole `String` class

quiz.q: With `short_max = 15`, constructing `String<char> s("chair")` (5 characters)

quiz.explanation: Length 5 does not exceed the short-string threshold, so the internal array is used — the short-string optimization inherited from chapter 19’s design, now generalized to any `C`.

intro: When is a template checked? Twice. At the point of definition the compiler checks everything it can — syntax, scoping, and every name that does not depend on a template parameter. Everything that does depend on one is checked at the point of instantiation, after the arguments are known. The consequence shapes the whole subject: a template error is never purely in the template, nor purely in the argument — it is in the combination.
objectives: Describe the two times a template is checked: at definition and at instantiation
Classify which errors are caught at each point, with examples
Explain why a template error implicates the template definition and its argument together, and how that shapes error messages and design

concepts.statement: A template is checked **once at its definition** — syntax, scoping, and all expressions that do not depend on a template parameter — and **again at each instantiation**, where dependent expressions are checked after the arguments have been substituted.
concepts.detail: A template that is never used is still checked once: misspell a non-dependent name and the definition fails to compile even with no instantiations anywhere in the program.

concepts.statement: At the definition the compiler verifies everything independent of the parameters: matching braces and semicolons, that non-dependent names like `std::vector` exist and are used correctly, that calls with fully known arguments type-check, and that the return statements are consistent **for the forms that can be judged without knowing `T`**.
concepts.detail: This is deliberately conservative: only what is provably wrong for every possible `T` can be rejected here. `s += x;` with `T s` and `T x` might be fine for every useful `T` — the compiler cannot know yet.

concepts.statement: An expression that depends on `T` is only checkable when `T` is known. The resulting failure — "no `operator+` for `X`" — belongs to **the combination of the template and its argument**: `sum<std::vector<int>>` is fine and `sum<std::vector<Empty>>` is an error, and neither the template nor `Empty` is wrong on its own.
concepts.detail: This is why template error messages arrive as long instantiation backtraces: the compiler reports the point of use, walks back through the instantiations that led there, and shows the substituted code that failed. Reading them is a learned skill; writing templates that produce short errors is a design skill (§24.4).

concepts.statement: Late checking can be tamed three ways: **minimize requirements** so fewer arguments can fail (chapter 24’s lifting); **state requirements early** — `static_assert` predicates at the top of the template fire at the interface with a message naming the missing requirement; and **keep instantiation points close to the cause** so the backtrace is short.
concepts.detail: The chapter’s strategy in one sentence: what cannot be checked at definition time should at least be checked at the front door, before the body is instantiated and the diagnosis becomes an archaeology dig.

concepts.statement: **Type Checking.** Templates and type errors at instantiation. You can claim this section when you can describe the two times a template is checked: at definition and at instantiation — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 23 (Templates); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: One template, two successes, one failure
examples.problem: Predict exactly when the compiler accepts or rejects each use of `template<typename T> T twice(T x) { return x + x; }`.

steps.label: Definition
steps.text: The body `return x + x;` is well-formed C++ *syntax*, and nothing in it can be rejected at definition time — `T` might support `+`.

steps.label: Use 1
steps.text: `twice(21)` — `T = int`, and `21 + 21 = 42` compiles and runs.

steps.label: Use 2
steps.text: `twice(2.5)` — `T = double`, `2.5 + 2.5 = 5.0`; a distinct specialization, checked independently.

steps.label: Use 3
steps.text: `twice(std::string("ab"))` — `T = std::string`, and `+` is concatenation: `"ab" + "ab"` = `"abab"`.

steps.label: Use 4
steps.text: `struct X {}; twice(X{});` — no `operator+(X, X)` exists, so this use fails **at its own instantiation point**, citing the substituted expression `x + x`.

examples.result: The template is innocent, `X` is innocent, and the pair is guilty: two-phase checking means the error can only be found where they meet.

A template error is in the combination of template and argument — neither alone is wrong
Tame late checking by minimizing requirements and stating them early with `static_assert` at the interface

quiz.q: The expression `s += x;` (with `T s`, `T x`) inside a template is checked
options: when the template is instantiated, with `T` known
never — dependent expressions are not checked
quiz.explanation: Whether `+=` exists between two `T` objects is unknowable until `T` is; the check happens at the instantiation, on the substituted code.

quiz.q: Which error IS caught at template-definition time?
options: A misspelled non-dependent name such as `std::vectorr`
Calling a member that only some `T` have
quiz.explanation: Non-dependent names are looked up and checked where the template is defined — a typo like `std::vectorr` fails even if the template is never used.

quiz.q: The compile error "no operator+ for X" from a template means
options: the template definition is ill-formed and must be rewritten
the argument type `X` is ill-formed and must be fixed
the combination of this template and this argument is invalid — the requirements and the type do not meet
quiz.explanation: Two-phase checking pins the failure to the meeting point: the same template works for other types, and the same type works with other templates; together they lack one operation.

quiz.q: The most effective way to surface template requirement failures early is
options: comment the requirements carefully and hope
put `static_assert` predicate checks at the top of the template so failures report at the interface
instantiate every template with every known type
quiz.explanation: A `static_assert` naming the missing requirement fires at the point of use, before the body is instantiated — converting an archaeology dig into a one-line diagnosis (the technique §24.4 develops fully).

intro: A class template is a family of classes, and each member of the family lives once per specialization. This section covers the mechanics of defining those members: the out-of-class syntax that names the specialization, the member type aliases that make generic code possible, static members that are per-specialization by construction, and member templates — members that are themselves parameterized, which is how conversions between specializations are written.
objectives: Define members of a class template inside and outside the class body, using the correct syntax
Use member type aliases and static members, and state precisely what "per specialization" means
Write member templates for conversions between specializations, and explain the role of friends

concepts.statement: A member defined outside its class template must name the specialization: `template<typename T> void vector<T>::push_back(const T& x) { /* ... */ }` — the `vector<T>::` prefix is what the definition belongs to, and `T` is in scope throughout. Members defined inside the class are implicitly inline and, the book’s style notes, read better.
concepts.detail: The definition itself is a template: it is not code yet, only a recipe from which the compiler emits one `push_back` per `vector<T>` actually used.

concepts.statement: The conventional names — `using value_type = T;`, `using iterator = ...;` — let generic code say `typename C::value_type` and work for **every** container. This traits convention is the foundation of the standard library’s uniformity.
concepts.detail: The `typename` is required in dependent contexts (`typename C::value_type`) because before `C` is known the compiler cannot know that `value_type` names a type. §23.6 shows how an alias template hides this housekeeping.

concepts.statement: Each specialization of a class template gets its **own** static members: `vector<int>::count` and `vector<string>::count` are different objects, defined out-of-line as `template<typename T> int vector<T>::count = 0;` and initialized once per specialization used.
concepts.detail: This is the type-level analogue of per-class statics: the family has one shared member per member of the family — and it composes with the instantiation-on-demand rule (an unused specialization’s static is never emitted).

concepts.statement: A member can itself be a template: the conversion constructor `template<typename C2> String(const String<C2>&);` of §23.2 is exactly this, and assignment can follow the same pattern. A **friend** declaration grants a nonmember access while staying outside the class — useful for operators like `operator==` that compare specializations.
concepts.detail: Friends may be templates or name particular specializations; they provide access, not membership. The combination "member template for conversions, friend operators for comparisons" is the standard shape for family-wise value types like `String`.

concepts.term: Class Template Members: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Class Template Members.** Members of class templates. You can claim this section when you can define members of a class template inside and outside the class body, using the correct syntax — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 23 (Templates); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Counting with per-specialization statics
examples.problem: A `Tracer<T>` counts its live objects with a static member. Predict the three counter readings.

steps.label: The definition
steps.text: `template<typename T> struct Tracer { static int live; Tracer() { ++live; } ~Tracer() { --live; } };` and out-of-line: `template<typename T> int Tracer<T>::live = 0;`

steps.label: Instantiate
steps.text: `Tracer<int> a, b;` — both share `Tracer<int>::live`, which goes $0 \to 1 \to 2$. There is exactly one such object in the program.

steps.label: A second family member
steps.text: `Tracer<double> c;` — a *different* static, `Tracer<double>::live`, goes $0 \to 1$; the `int` counter is untouched.

steps.label: Scope end
steps.text: When `b` is destroyed, `Tracer<int>::live` falls to 1; destroying `c` returns `Tracer<double>::live` to 0. Each specialization keeps its own books.

examples.result: Readings: `Tracer<int>::live` is 2 then 1; `Tracer<double>::live` is 1 then 0 — one static per specialization, each initialized once, each emitted only if used.

quiz.q: The prefix `vector<T>::` in `template<typename T> void vector<T>::push_back(const T& x) { }` exists to
options: name the specialization whose member is being defined
quiz.explanation: A class template is a family; an out-of-line member definition must say which family member it belongs to, and `vector<T>::` does exactly that, with `T` still a template parameter.

quiz.q: How many objects is `vector<int>::size_count` (a static member) compared with `vector<double>::size_count`?
options: The same one object, shared by all specializations
Two distinct objects — one per specialization used
One per instance of the class
None — statics are not allowed in templates
quiz.explanation: Static members belong to a class, and `vector<int>` and `vector<double>` are different classes of the family: each specialization gets its own static, emitted only if that specialization is used.

quiz.q: Why do containers conventionally define `using value_type = T;`?
options: It is required by the compiler
So generic code can say `typename C::value_type` uniformly, for every container
It replaces the need for constructors
quiz.explanation: The alias gives a single name to "the element type" across the whole zoo of containers — the naming convention that one generic algorithm can rely on for all of them.

quiz.q: A constructor declared `template<typename C2> String(const String<C2>&);` inside `String<C>` is
options: a member template: one constructor definition covering conversion from every other specialization
a partial specialization of the class
quiz.explanation: Members of a class template may be templates themselves; this one is instantiated per source character type, which is how one definition serves every conversion pair.

intro: Function templates are the most-used template form, because their arguments are deduced from the call: you write `max(1, 2)`, not `max<int>(1, 2)`. This section covers the deduction rules — and their sharp edges: deduction is conservative, uses no user-defined conversions, and fails loudly when two arguments disagree about `T`. It closes with the accumulator-parameter idiom that reappears throughout the standard library.
objectives: Write function templates and read the deduction of `T` from the function arguments
Predict ambiguity errors such as `max(1, 2.5)` and repair them with explicit qualification or casts
Use an accumulator parameter — as in `sum(first, last, val)` — to decouple element type from arithmetic type

concepts.statement: A function parameterized over types and values, called like an ordinary function: `template<typename T> const T& max(const T& a, const T& b) { return a < b ? b : a; }` — `max(2, 3)` deduces `T = int` and instantiates the function for it.
concepts.detail: Function templates interact with ordinary overloading as one overload set: a plain function that matches exactly beats a template needing deductions, which is a common way to specialize a hot case.

concepts.statement: Each template parameter used in the parameter list is deduced from the corresponding argument, and only **exact-ish matches** participate: array-to-pointer decay and top-level `const` adjustments, but **no user-defined conversions and no arithmetic promotions applied to `T`**. Independent deductions of the same parameter must agree.
concepts.detail: The conservatism is deliberate: silent `int`→`double`→`T`-style surprises would make generic code unpredictable. Where mixing is wanted, the caller states the intent — with an explicit template argument, a cast, or a second parameter.

concepts.statement: `max(1, 2.5)` **does not compile**: the first argument deduces `T = int`, the second `T = double`, and the two deductions conflict. The fixes are explicit — `max<double>(1, 2.5)` (both converted to `double`, result `2.5`) — or giving the template two parameters, or overloading for the mixed case.
concepts.detail: The error message typically shows both candidates for `T`, which is the deduction machinery being transparent rather than broken. It is a feature wearing an error’s clothes.

concepts.statement: Template arguments may be supplied explicitly, left to right: `sum<double>(b, e, 0)` fixes `T = double` (or the first parameter) and lets the rest be deduced. Use it when a parameter appears **only in the return type**, or when deduction would pick a type you do not want.
concepts.detail: Because arguments bind left to right, put the parameters you intend to specify explicitly first in the template’s parameter list — an interface-design rule the standard library follows (e.g. `std::accumulate` lets the accumulator type be chosen by its third argument instead).

concepts.statement: In `template<typename Iter, typename Val> Val sum(Iter first, Iter last, Val s)`, the initial value’s type **chooses the arithmetic**: pass `0` and the sum is `int`; pass `0.0` and every addition happens in `double`, avoiding overflow and absorbing fractions. The value is passed in, not default-constructed — so `Val` needs only `+=`, not a default constructor.
concepts.detail: This is the shape of `std::accumulate` and of most numeric generic algorithms: the accumulator is part of the *interface*, which keeps the requirements on the element type minimal (it need only convert to `Val` and add into it).

examples.title: Deducing, conflicting, and choosing the accumulator
examples.problem: For `std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}` and the `sum` template above, evaluate four calls.

steps.label: Call 1
steps.text: `sum(v.begin(), v.end(), 0)` — `Iter` is `std::vector<int>::iterator`, `Val` is `int`; the running value goes $0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15$ — the call returns the `int` 15.

steps.label: Call 2
steps.text: `sum(v.begin(), v.end(), 0.0)` — only `Val` changes: the additions run in `double`: $0.0, 1.0, 3.0, 6.0, 10.0, 15.0$ — returns `15.0`. For a hundred-million-element `int` vector this is the difference between silent overflow and a correct total.

steps.label: Call 3
steps.text: `sum(v.begin() + 1, v.end(), 0.0)` — iterator arithmetic selects a subrange: elements $2, 3, 4, 5$ sum to $14.0$. The same template, a different pair of iterators.

steps.label: The failure
steps.text: `max(1, 2.5)` on its own does not compile — conflicting deductions for `T`. `max<double>(1, 2.5)` converts the first argument and returns `2.5`.

examples.result: 15 (`int`), 15.0 (`double`), 14.0 (subrange) — one template, three behaviors chosen entirely by the arguments — and one deliberate error repaired by one explicit template argument.
