quiz.q: What does `max(1, 2.5)` do, given `template<typename T> const T& max(const T&, const T&);`?
options: Fails to compile — deductions for `T` conflict
Returns 2.5 after converting both to double automatically
quiz.explanation: Deduction applies no arithmetic conversions: the first argument forces `T = int`, the second `T = double`, and the conflict is an error. State your intent with `max<double>(1, 2.5)`.

quiz.q: For `sum(v.begin(), v.end(), 0.0)` over a `std::vector<int>`, what is `Val`?
options: `double`, from the third argument — which also sets the arithmetic of every addition
`void`, since it is inferred from context
quiz.explanation: The accumulator parameter is deduced only from the initial value: `0.0` makes `Val = double`, so the whole computation runs in `double` regardless of the elements’ type.

quiz.q: Why is the starting value passed in as an argument rather than created inside as `T s = T();`?
options: It is faster to pass an int
Passing it lets the caller choose the accumulator type and keeps the requirements on `Val` minimal — no default constructor needed
quiz.explanation: The argument chooses `Val` explicitly (0 vs 0.0 vs an empty string) and the template then needs only `+=` on `Val` — a smaller requirement set, the theme of the next chapter.

quiz.q: Which conversions may be applied while deducing a template parameter `T` from a function argument?
options: Only decay (array/function to pointer) and top-level `const` adjustments
quiz.explanation: Deduction is deliberately exact: beyond decay and `const` trimming, no conversions are applied, so every deduction is unambiguous — and conflicts surface as errors at the call site.

options: `x` is the `int` `2`, because the second argument truncates
`x` is the `double` `2.5`, because the first argument promotes
The call fails: deduction finds conflicting types for `T`, and no conversion applies during deduction
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The code given passes an `int` and a `double` to a single-parameter template. Step 2: The governing rule is deduction exactness: each argument must match the parameter to deduce the same `T`, and ordinary conversions are not consulted while deducing. Step 3: Tracing the deduction, the first argument proposes `T = int` while the second proposes `T = double`, the proposals conflict, and the call is rejected rather than coerced. Step 4: The distractors fail because no truncation or promotion happens during deduction, and the compiler never silently prefers one proposal. Step 5: Therefore the call fails until written with an explicit argument such as `bigger<double>(1, 2.5)`.

intro: C++11 finally gave templates a parameterized synonym: the alias template, written with `using`. A template alias introduces no new type — it is pure naming, so `Vec<int>` and `std::vector<int>` are the same type everywhere — but it removes the boilerplate of long dependent names and lets part of a template’s argument list be fixed while the rest stays variable.
objectives: Write alias templates with `using`, and contrast them with `typedef`, which cannot be parameterized
Explain alias-as-pure-synonym: no new type, no new members, no specialization of an alias
Apply aliases to shorten dependent names such as `typename String<C>::iterator`

concepts.statement: `template<typename T> using Vector = std::vector<T, My_alloc<T>>;` declares a synonym parameterized by `T`: `Vector<int>` is exactly `std::vector<int, My_alloc<int>>`. This is the mechanism the language lacked when `typedef` could not be templated.
concepts.detail: The `using` spelling is the modern form for plain synonyms too — `using iterator = typename C::iterator;` reads left-to-right and works in templates where decades of `typedef` syntax did not compose.

concepts.statement: An alias introduces **no type**: `Vector<int>` *is* `std::vector<int, My_alloc<int>>` — interchangeable in declarations, overload sets and template arguments; there are no conversions because there is no second type; and an alias **cannot be specialized** (one specializes what the alias names, not the alias).
concepts.detail: The contrast to keep straight: a wrapper class `template<typename T> struct Box { std::vector<T> v; };` *is* a new type needing member access and conversions; an alias is only a shorter spelling of an existing one.

concepts.statement: `template<typename C> using String_iterator = typename String<C>::iterator;` packages the `typename` and the qualification into one name — users write `String_iterator<char> p;` and never see the plumbing that says `String<C>::iterator` is a type dependent on `C`.
concepts.detail: This is the most common industrial use: alias templates clean up the `typename X<T>::abc` spatter that generic code otherwise accumulates, and they document intent ("this is the iterator of a `String`") better than the raw form.

concepts.statement: An alias can fix some arguments and leave the rest as parameters: `template<typename T> using String_map = std::map<std::basic_string<T>, std::vector<T>>;` — one name for "maps from strings of some character type to vectors of it," reusable wherever that shape recurs.
concepts.detail: Combined with defaulted template arguments, this covers most uses of the "policy-laden" long names — `std::map<K, V, C, A>` with defaults — without any macro trickery.

concepts.statement: **Template Aliases.** Alias templates. You can claim this section when you can write alias templates with `using`, and contrast them with `typedef`, which cannot be parameterized — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 23 (Templates); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: An alias renames; a wrapper creates
examples.problem: Show that a template alias produces the *same* type where a wrapper class produces a *different* one, and use the alias to simplify a dependent name.

steps.label: The alias
steps.text: `template<typename T> using Vec = std::vector<T>;` — then `Vec<int> v{1, 2, 3};` declares a plain `std::vector<int>`.

steps.label: Same type
steps.text: A function `void take(std::vector<int>&);` accepts `v` directly, and `std::vector<int>* q = &v;` compiles with no cast: there is nothing to convert.

steps.label: The wrapper
steps.text: `template<typename T> struct Wrap { std::vector<T> v; };` — `Wrap<int> w;` does *not* convert: `take(w)` fails to compile, and only `take(w.v)` works, because `Wrap<int>` is a genuinely new type.

steps.label: Dependent name
steps.text: `template<typename C> using Str_it = typename String<C>::iterator;` — `Str_it<char> p = s.begin();` works, with the `typename` machinery hidden inside the alias.

examples.result: Aliases rename existing types (no casts, no conversions, no specialization); wrappers manufacture new ones (members, casts, conversions). Choose renaming when the goal is only readability.

examples.title: Working through template aliases
examples.problem: Alias templates. Your task: write alias templates with `using`, and contrast them with `typedef`, which cannot be parameterized.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: write alias templates with `using`, and contrast them with `typedef`, which cannot be parameterized. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `template<typename T> using X = ...;` declares a parameterized synonym — the templated `typedef` the language lacked

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<typename T> T larger(T a, T b) { return (a < b) ? b : a; }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain alias-as-pure-synonym: no new type, no new members, no specialization of an alias — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: An alias is pure naming: same type, no new members, no specialization of the alias itself If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `template<typename T> using X = ...;` declares a parameterized synonym — the templated `typedef` the language lacked Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `template<typename T> using X = ...;` declares a parameterized synonym — the templated `typedef` the language lacked
An alias is pure naming: same type, no new members, no specialization of the alias itself
The workhorse use is shortening dependent names such as `typename String<C>::iterator`

quiz.q: After `template<typename T> using Vec = std::vector<T>;`, the types `Vec<int>` and `std::vector<int>` are
options: different types with an implicit conversion
the same type — the alias is pure naming
quiz.explanation: A template alias introduces no type at all; `Vec<int>` is simply another spelling of `std::vector<int>`, interchangeable in every context.

quiz.q: Which can NOT be done with a template alias?
options: Fix some template arguments while leaving others open
Add member functions to the named template
Hide the `typename` in a dependent name
quiz.explanation: An alias has no type of its own — it cannot add members, change behavior, or be specialized; everything it names behaves exactly as before.

quiz.q: In `template<typename C> using String_iterator = typename String<C>::iterator;`, why is the word `typename` required?
options: It names the template parameter’s keyword, like `class`
Because `String<C>::iterator` is a dependent name: before `C` is known, the compiler cannot know it names a type
Because aliases must end in a type
quiz.explanation: Dependent names are ambiguous until instantiated — `iterator` could be a static member — so the compiler requires `typename` to be told this one is a type; the alias then hides that detail from users.

intro: Where do template definitions live? The compiler can only instantiate what it can see, so the general rule is blunt: template definitions go in header files. The exceptions are the explicit instantiation mechanisms — a definition that generates the specialization once, in exactly one translation unit, and the `extern template` declaration that promises it exists and suppresses local generation everywhere else. Together they are the knobs for template compile time and code size.
objectives: Explain why template definitions must be visible at the point of instantiation — the inclusion model
Use explicit instantiation definitions and `extern template` declarations to control code generation
Organize a real project’s template code: headers for the generic, one translation unit for the hot specializations

concepts.statement: To instantiate a template, the compiler must see its **full definition** — unlike a normal function, which compiles from a declaration and links later. So template definitions belong in headers, included wherever the template is used, unless explicit instantiation makes the body visible indirectly.
concepts.detail: This is why the standard library is almost entirely headers, and why the book’s rule is stated so flatly: put template definitions in a header unless you have a specific, measured reason to do otherwise.

concepts.statement: Generating `sum<std::vector<int>::iterator, double>` is **code generation with the arguments substituted**, not an ordinary call: the compiler needs the body in the very translation unit that triggers the instantiation. A declaration alone says the template exists; it cannot produce the specialization.
concepts.detail: A declaration does suffice when the specialization is explicitly instantiated somewhere else — which is exactly the contract the next two mechanisms make explicit.

concepts.statement: The pair of forms: `template class String<char>;` is an **explicit instantiation definition** — generate the specialization here, in this translation unit, once; and `extern template class String<char>;` is an **explicit instantiation declaration** — the specialization is generated elsewhere, so do not generate it here.
concepts.detail: The same two forms exist for function templates (`template void f<int>(int);` and `extern template void f<int>(int);`). The definition must appear in exactly one translation unit; declaring `extern` in the header and defining in one `.cpp` is the standard arrangement.

concepts.statement: Without `extern template`, every translation unit that uses a specialization emits the members it uses, and the linker folds the duplicates (vague linkage). With it, the same members are emitted **once**: N translation units using `String<char>` go from emitting up to $N \times M$ candidate bodies (M = members used) to emitting them exactly M times.
concepts.detail: The compile-time win is the usual motivation — skipped code generation and smaller object files for the hot specializations — at the cost of one extra file to maintain and the risk of forgetting the single definition. Apply it to the few specializations that dominate build times, not to every instantiation.

concepts.term: Source Code Organization: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Source Code Organization.** Where templates live and how they compile. You can claim this section when you can explain why template definitions must be visible at the point of instantiation — the inclusion model — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 23 (Templates); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Taming fifty translation units
examples.problem: A `String<char>` template with 8 used member functions is included in 50 `.cpp` files. Count the candidate function bodies before and after explicit instantiation.

steps.label: Baseline
steps.text: Definitions are in the header; implicit instantiation in each translation unit emits the members it uses — up to $50 \times 8 = 400$ candidate bodies for the linker to fold into 8.

steps.label: The arrangement
steps.text: Put `extern template class String<char>;` in the header, next to the template; put `template class String<char>;` in one dedicated `string_inst.cpp`.

steps.label: After
steps.text: Each of the 50 translation units sees the declaration, skips code generation for `String<char>`, and the 8 bodies are emitted once, in `string_inst.cpp`: the candidate count falls from 400 to 8.

steps.label: The caveats
steps.text: All 50 still parse the template header — templates are visible wherever used — so this trims *generation*, not parsing; and the explicit definition must exist exactly once, or the linker (best case) objects.

examples.result: 400 candidate bodies become 8, object files shrink, and links speed up — the standard treatment for the few instantiations that measurably dominate a build.

keyTakeaways: Template definitions live in headers: the compiler must see the body in the translation unit that triggers instantiation
`template class String<char>;` generates the specialization once; `extern template class String<char>;` suppresses local generation elsewhere
The win is skipped code generation (up to an N-fold reduction in candidate bodies) and smaller objects — parsing still happens everywhere

quiz.q: Why must a template definition be visible (typically: in a header) at the point of use?
options: The linker requires all code in headers
The compiler must substitute the arguments into the full body to generate the specialization there
Templates are macros and must be expanded first
quiz.explanation: Instantiation is code generation: producing `sum<int*>` needs the body in that translation unit, which is why template code is organized around inclusion rather than declaration-plus-link.

quiz.q: What does `extern template class String<char>;` do?
options: Promises the specialization is generated in another translation unit and suppresses local generation
quiz.explanation: It is the explicit instantiation *declaration*: every translation unit that sees it skips generating `String<char>`’s members, relying on the one translation unit containing the explicit definition.

quiz.q: Where must the matching `template class String<char>;` (the explicit instantiation definition) appear?
options: In every translation unit that uses it
In the header, before the `extern` declaration
quiz.explanation: The definition generates the specialization; duplicating it in several translation units violates the one-definition rule for that specialization, so it lives in a single designated file.

quiz.q: With explicit instantiation in place, what cost do all translation units still pay?
options: Parsing the template definitions in the header
A run-time indirection on every call
quiz.explanation: `extern template` removes code *generation*, not code *visibility*: each translation unit still parses the template definitions it includes.

intro: The chapter’s rules of thumb compress its two arguments: templates earn their complexity only by raising the level of abstraction, and requirements should be designed — stated, minimized, checked — even when the language (as of C++11) could not state them for you. The advice also tells you when not to write a template at all.
objectives: Apply the design rules: abstraction level, minimal and stated requirements, standard components first
Organize template source code so instantiation is visible and build costs are controlled
Recognize when a template is the wrong tool for a need

concepts.term: Use templates to raise the level of abstraction
concepts.statement: A template should express **the same design for many types** — one generic `String` instead of six per-alphabet classes, one `sum` instead of one loop per container. If only one or two concrete types will ever be used, a plain class or function is simpler and should win.
concepts.detail: The standard library sets the bar: a handful of templates serving thousands of types. That is the shape of a template that has earned its keep; a template used once is indirection with no return.

concepts.statement: Even without language support, write templates against **minimal, precisely stated requirements**, and check them at the interface (`static_assert`, §24.4; real `requires` clauses in C++20). The requirements are the design; the syntax is bookkeeping.
concepts.detail: This discipline is what makes the difference between a template that fails with a one-line error at the call site and one that fails forty frames deep in its own guts.

concepts.statement: Template definitions live in headers (§23.7); for the specializations that dominate build time, add `extern template` and one explicit instantiation; and prefer fewer, well-chosen template parameters. **Measure** compile time before and after — the costs are real but localized.
concepts.detail: The complementary habit is to keep templates small and composable: several small templates instantiate and inline better than one monster template carrying every policy.

concepts.statement: Before writing a container, string, algorithm or utility template, check whether the standard library already has it — its components are lifted, tuned and constrained by the best concept engineering available. Write your own templates only at a genuine abstraction frontier.
concepts.detail: The advice is not deference but economics: the standard templates have been compiled, profiled and debugged on more code than any one project will ever see; a replacement must beat that on its merits.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Templates exist to raise the level of abstraction — one design serving many types; one-or-two types is not a template problem** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: A four-question review of a home-made Stack
examples.problem: A team proposes `template<typename T> struct Stack` with a linked-list representation, used with three element types across 12 translation units. Review it with the chapter’s rules.

steps.label: Abstraction
steps.text: Used with 3 types and likely more — the generic form is justified; the rules would have said "just write a class" only for a single hard-coded element type.

steps.label: Requirements
steps.text: What does `Stack<T>` need of `T`? Copy construction and destruction — no `==`, no default construction, no ordering. Stating that keeps it usable for types that cannot be default-constructed.

steps.label: Standard first
steps.text: `std::stack<T>` on `std::deque<T>` already provides the abstraction, tested and tuned — the home-made version must win on something measurable to be worth its maintenance.

steps.label: Organization
steps.text: Definition in `Stack.h`; since `Stack<int>` dominates build time in 12 files, add `extern template class Stack<int>;` in the header and one explicit instantiation in `Stack.cpp` — candidate bodies drop from $12 \times M$ to $M$.

examples.result: Either adopt `std::stack`, or keep the custom template with its requirements stated, its definition in a header, and its hot instantiation declared `extern` — each rule pulling its own weight.

examples.title: Reviewing templates code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the design rules: abstraction level, minimal and stated requirements, standard components first.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Templates exist to raise the level of abstraction — one design serving many types; one-or-two types is not a template problem

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `template<typename T> T larger(T a, T b) { return (a < b) ? b : a; }`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: organize template source code so instantiation is visible and build costs are controlled. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: State and check minimal requirements at the interface, even without language support for concepts

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Templates exist to raise the level of abstraction — one design serving many types; one-or-two types is not a template problem Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Templates exist to raise the level of abstraction — one design serving many types; one-or-two types is not a template problem
State and check minimal requirements at the interface, even without language support for concepts
Definitions in headers, `extern template` for the hot specializations, and the standard library checked first

quiz.q: The strongest signal that you should NOT write a class template is
quiz.explanation: A template with exactly one realistic argument type is unearned generality: write the concrete class, and template it only when a second real type arrives.

quiz.q: By default, where do template definitions belong?
options: In headers, included wherever the template is instantiated
quiz.explanation: The compiler needs the full body at the point of instantiation — the inclusion model; explicit instantiation is the targeted exception, not the default.

quiz.q: Before writing your own generic container, the chapter’s advice says to
options: inherit from the closest standard container
check the standard library first — its components are already lifted, tuned and constrained
template it on the allocator only
write it as a macro instead
quiz.explanation: The standard templates are the survivors of decades of instantiation, profiling and concept engineering; a replacement must beat them on measured merits.

intro: The standard library's power — one `sort` for every container, one `accumulate` for every sequence — did not come from clever code. It came from a discipline called **generic programming**: lifting concrete algorithms so they work for any type that satisfies precisely stated requirements, with no loss of run-time efficiency. This chapter names that discipline and splits it into its two halves — the lifting of algorithms (24.2) and the formulation of concepts (24.3–24.4).
objectives: Define generic programming as the book uses the term and distinguish it from ordinary code reuse
Explain the zero-overhead demand that generic abstractions must satisfy
Describe how the STL decoupled algorithms from containers through the sequence abstraction

concepts.statement: **Generic programming is the design of algorithms and data structures so that they work for a family of types** — those meeting the requirements the algorithm states — rather than for one concrete type. It has two inseparable activities: *lifting* concrete algorithms into generic ones, and formulating the discovered requirements precisely as **concepts**.
concepts.detail: The generality is bought entirely at compile time: the template machinery, not run-time polymorphism, delivers it.

concepts.statement: The generic version must be **as fast as the concrete version written for the specific type** — what you do not use, you do not pay for; what you do use, you could not hand-write better. Instantiation plus inlining must collapse the abstraction so that the generated code matches handwritten code.
concepts.detail: This is why the STL uses templates and compile-time dispatch rather than virtual functions: a virtual call per element would tax every loop.

concepts.statement: Stepanov's observation behind the STL: algorithms and containers can be **decoupled by a small set of concepts** — iterators presenting sequences — so that one `sort`, one `find`, one `accumulate` serves `vector`, `list`, raw arrays, and streams alike.
concepts.detail: The chapter studies how such generality is actually found, using the humble summation function as the running specimen.

concepts.statement: The working method of generic programming: **(a)** start from a concrete, correct algorithm; **(b)** lift it by removing accidental dependencies one at a time; **(c)** record each removal as a named requirement — a concept. Sections 24.2 and 24.3 perform (b) and (c) on the same example.
concepts.detail: The order matters: requirements discovered by lifting are real; requirements invented in the abstract usually are not.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** What generic programming is. You can claim this section when you can define generic programming as the book uses the term and distinguish it from ordinary code reuse — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 24 (Generic Programming); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: The 3×3 explosion a template family prevents
examples.problem: A program needs `sum`, `find`, and `count` over three storage shapes: `vector<int>`, `double[1000]`, and a linked list of readings. Compare writing these concretely against writing them generically.

steps.label: Concrete accounting
steps.text: Three algorithms times three data shapes is $3 \times 3 = 9$ handwritten functions; at about 6 lines each that is roughly 54 lines of near-duplicate code, each line a chance to differ.

steps.label: Generic accounting
steps.text: Three algorithms written once as templates (`accumulate`, `find`, `count`, about 10 lines each); the compiler instantiates exactly the 9 specializations the program uses, on demand.

steps.label: Maintenance
steps.text: A bug found in a concrete `find` must be fixed in 3 places and re-tested 3 times; a bug in the generic `find` is fixed once, in the single definition every instantiation shares.

steps.label: Performance check
steps.text: Instantiating the generic `accumulate` for `double[1000]` produces the same loop a handwritten double sum would — the abstraction exists only at compile time, satisfying the zero-overhead demand.

examples.result: Nine functions become three, fixed once and instantiated freely — the two economic arguments (code volume, maintenance) plus the performance guarantee are the case for generic programming.

quiz.q: What best characterizes generic programming as this chapter defines it?
options: Writing macros that work for many types
Code reuse through inheritance from a common base class
Lifting algorithms to work for any type meeting precisely stated requirements, at zero run-time cost
quiz.explanation: Generality is achieved by lifting plus precisely stated requirements (concepts), and the abstraction must cost nothing at run time — the zero-overhead demand.

quiz.q: The chapter insists a lifted algorithm instantiated for `int` should be:
options: as fast as a handwritten int-specific version — abstraction at zero overhead
about twice as slow, the price of generality
faster, because templates get optimized more aggressively
unpredictable — performance is not a concern here
quiz.explanation: Instantiation plus inlining must collapse the abstraction; if the generic code ran slower, the abstraction would be the wrong one.

quiz.q: What lets one `sort` serve `vector<int>`, `deque<double>`, and raw arrays alike?
options: The iterator/sequence abstraction: every container and array can be presented as a `[b:e)` range
quiz.explanation: The STL decoupling: algorithms are written against sequences of positions, not against container types — the small set of iterator concepts does the unifying.

intro: Generic algorithms are not written in a flash of abstraction — they are **lifted**, one deliberate step at a time, from concrete code that is already understood. This section performs the canonical lift, the book's running example: a function that sums the elements of a `vector<int>`, generalized step by step until it *is* the standard library's `std::accumulate`. Watch what each step removes — and what each removal exposes as a requirement.
objectives: Perform the four lifts that turn a concrete sum into the generic `accumulate`
State the requirements each lift discovers on the iterator and the accumulator
Explain the half-open `[b:e)` sequence notation and why the initial value determines the accumulator type

concepts.statement: **Lifting** is removing the *accidental* properties of a concrete algorithm — the type of its elements, the way it traverses data, what it accumulates with, the operation it applies — while keeping its essential computation. Each removal is safe only when the removed capability is replaced by a requirement on a parameter.
concepts.detail: Lifting is how requirements are discovered rather than guessed: the set of expressions that survive is exactly the algorithm's requirement set.

concepts.statement: A sequence is passed as a pair of positions with `e` **one past the last element**; the empty sequence is `b == e`, and `e` itself is never dereferenced. No size member and no container type are needed.
concepts.detail: Half-open ranges make sub-ranges free (`v.begin()+1, v.end()`), terminate loops by inequality alone, and extend naturally to stream iterators that have no "last element" to name in advance.

concepts.statement: What an algorithm needs is exactly **the set of expressions that survive lifting**: `first != last`, `*first`, `++first` on the traversal position, and `val + *first` on the accumulator. A concept is these expressions plus their intended meaning.
concepts.detail: This is why concept names read like expression summaries: `Equality_comparable` means "has `==` with sensible semantics".

concepts.statement: When the combining **operation itself becomes a parameter**, `accumulate(b, e, init, op)` — the four-argument form of `std::accumulate` — the sum becomes a general *fold*: the same code computes products, maxima, and concatenations. The initial value's type **is** the accumulator type: `accumulate(b, e, 0L)` sums into `long`, escaping `char`/`short` overflow.
concepts.detail: Choosing `init = 0` sums; choosing `init = 1` with `a*b` multiplies — the initial value is part of the algorithm's contract, not a detail.

concepts.term: Algorithms and Lifting: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Algorithms and Lifting.** From concrete to generic algorithms. You can claim this section when you can perform the four lifts that turn a concrete sum into the generic `accumulate` — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 24 (Generic Programming); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

figures.caption: The lifting staircase of §24.2: from `int sum(const vector<int>&)` to `accumulate(b, e, init, op)`. Each lift deletes one accident — the element type, the container, the operation itself — and each deletion leaves a requirement behind: `T + T` and `0 → T` on the element type, `++`/`*`/`!=` on the iterator, `op(val, *b)` for the fold. Four small lifts turn five concrete lines into the standard library's `std::accumulate`.

examples.title: Lifting sum all the way to accumulate
examples.problem: Start from a concrete summation and lift it four times, naming the requirement each lift exposes; then run the result on verifiable data.

steps.label: Level 0 — concrete
steps.text: `int sum(const vector<int>& v) { int s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < (int)v.size(); ++i) s += v[i]; return s; }` — three accidents: the element type is `int`, the traversal is `vector` indexing, and the accumulator is `int`.

steps.label: Lift 1 — the element type
steps.text: `template<class T> T sum(const vector<T>& v)` with the same loop: now `T s = 0` and `s += v[i]` expose a requirement — `T` supports `+` and initialization from 0. But `vector<short>` still overflows: the accumulator remains welded to the element type.

steps.label: Lift 2 — the traversal
steps.text: Replace indexing with positions: `for (auto p = v.begin(); p != v.end(); ++p) s += *p;` — the traversal requirements become visible as expressions: `!=`, unary `*`, and `++` on the position.

steps.label: Lift 3 — the container
steps.text: `template<class Iter, class T> T sum(Iter first, Iter last, T s) { while (first != last) { s = s + *first; ++first; } return s; }` — the vector is gone: any `[b:e)` range works, and the accumulator type `T` is now chosen by the caller. Renamed, this is `std::accumulate`.

steps.label: Lift 4 — the operation
steps.text: Pass the combining operation as a parameter: `s = op(s, *first)`. Sum becomes the general fold — products, maxima, concatenations — the four-argument `std::accumulate(b, e, init, op)`.

steps.label: Runs
steps.text: Over `{1,2,3,4,5}` with init 0: 15. Over `{1, ..., 100}` with init 0: 5050 (Gauss: $100 \times 101 / 2$). Over the chars `'a'`…`'e'` (ASCII 97–101) with an `int` init of 0: 495 — the accumulator outgrows the element type. Over `{2,3,4,5,6}` with init 1 and `a*b`: 720; with init 0 the result is 0 — the initial value is part of the contract.

examples.result: Four lifts turn five concrete lines into the general fold. The requirements discovered — `!=`, `*`, `++` on the iterator; `+` (then `op`) on the accumulator — are exactly the raw material of the concepts in the next section.

examples.title: Working through algorithms and lifting
examples.problem: From concrete to generic algorithms. Your task: perform the four lifts that turn a concrete sum into the generic `accumulate`.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: perform the four lifts that turn a concrete sum into the generic `accumulate`. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Lifting removes accidents (element type, container, traversal, operation); each removal leaves a named requirement behind.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<typename In> int total(In first, In last);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — state the requirements each lift discovers on the iterator and the accumulator — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: The half-open `[b:e)` range is the canonical sequence interface: empty means `b == e`, `e` is never dereferenced, sub-ranges are free. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Lifting removes accidents (element type, container, traversal, operation); each removal leaves a named requirement behind. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Lifting removes accidents (element type, container, traversal, operation); each removal leaves a named requirement behind.
The half-open `[b:e)` range is the canonical sequence interface: empty means `b == e`, `e` is never dereferenced, sub-ranges are free.
Requirements are the surviving expressions (`!=`, `*`, `++`, `+`); with `op` as a parameter, sum generalizes to the fold `std::accumulate`, and `init`'s type chooses the accumulator.

quiz.q: Why is `T s = 0;` in the templated sum a discovered dependency?
options: It is not — 0 works for every type
It forces T to be a floating-point type
It requires convertibility from 0 and keeps the accumulator tied to the element type — summing shorts into a short overflows
quiz.explanation: Initialization from 0 is an unstated requirement on `T`, and the accumulator inherits the element type until the caller is allowed to choose it — the overflow trap motivates the next lift.

quiz.q: In `[b:e)` notation, the empty sequence is expressed as:
quiz.explanation: Half-open means `e` is one past the last element, so an empty sequence has the two positions equal — no sentinel value or size member needed.

quiz.q: Which expression in the lifted `accumulate` is the source of the requirement on the accumulator type `Val`?
quiz.explanation: The accumulator requirement comes from combining: `val + *first` must be well-formed and assignable back to `Val` — the iterator requirements come from the other three expressions.

quiz.q: `accumulate(p, p+5, 1, [](int a, int b){ return a*b; })` over the array `{2,3,4,5,6}` returns:
quiz.explanation: The fold multiplies: $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 \cdot 6 = 720$. With the natural-for-sum init 0 the answer would be 0 — the initial value must match the operation.

intro: Lifting only half works if the requirements it discovers stay implicit in the code. A **concept** names them: a compile-time predicate on template arguments that says precisely which expressions must compile and what may be assumed about them. Concepts, with their companion **axioms**, are the vocabulary in which generic algorithms are specified, checked, selected among, and — most of all — understood.
objectives: Define a concept and read the ideal concept-annotated template notation
Distinguish checkable requirements from axioms, and Semiregular from Regular
Explain multi-argument (relational) concepts such as `Equality_comparable<T, U>`

concepts.statement: A **concept** is a named set of requirements on one or more template arguments: which expressions must be valid (the syntactic requirements) and what may be assumed about their behavior (the semantic requirements). A concept is a predicate — a type either satisfies it or does not — evaluated at compile time. The ideal notation makes it part of the template head:
concepts.detail: `template<Sequence S, Number N> N sum(S s, N n);` reads 'sum takes a sequence and a number'; a `requires Arithmetic<Value_type<S>, N>()` clause can refine the relation between them. Concepts buy better error messages, concept-based overloading, and honest documentation of what an algorithm needs.

concepts.statement: An **axiom** is a semantic requirement stated as an assumed property rather than a checked expression: for `Arithmetic`, $a + b = b + a$; for copy, that a copy equals the original and does not alias it. The compiler generally **cannot** check axioms; they document meaning, guide optimization, and can be exercised by testing.
concepts.detail: Requirements say "this must compile"; axioms say "and here is what you may rely on". Generic code that exploits only axioms, never accidents, stays correct for every satisfying type.

concepts.statement: **Regular** is the book's fundamental concept: a type that *behaves like an `int`* — default constructible, copy and move constructible and assignable, swappable, and equality-comparable. **Semiregular** is Regular without `==`. Nearly every algorithm at least copies its arguments, so Semiregular is the floor of value semantics.
concepts.detail: The iterator and arithmetic concepts all presuppose value behavior; thinking of objects as values (rather than as handles to shared state) is what makes generic code composable.

concepts.statement: Concepts may relate **several** types: `Equality_comparable<T, U>` requires `t == u` and `u == t` to make sense; `Arithmetic<T, U>` requires `t + u`, `t * u` and friends with a sensible result; `Common<T, U>` names a type both convert to (how `string` and `char*` are compared).
concepts.detail: Almost every interesting generic operation relates two types — the sequence's element type and the accumulator, the compared pair — so two-type concepts are the norm, not the exception.

concepts.statement: **Concepts.** The requirements vocabulary. You can claim this section when you can define a concept and read the ideal concept-annotated template notation — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 24 (Generic Programming); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Auditing candidate types against sum's requirements
examples.problem: The lifted `accumulate` requires of its iterator: `p != q`, `*p`, `++p` (an input iterator); and of its accumulator `Val`: `val + *p` assignable back to `Val`. Which candidates can call it?

steps.label: `int*` over an array
steps.text: `!=`, `*`, `++` all hold; `0 + *p` is fine. Works — and `accumulate(a, a+4, 0L)` widens the accumulator to `long`, the caller choosing the arithmetic.

steps.label: `list<double>::iterator`
steps.text: Node-hopping traversal supports exactly `!=`, `*`, `++`. Works — the whole point of the iterator abstraction discovered by lifting.

steps.label: A stream iterator over `int`
steps.text: Single-pass positions over input support the three operations; reading `5 10 15 20` yields $5+10+15+20 = 50$. Works — `[b:e)` needs no last element in memory.

steps.label: `back_insert_iterator<vector<int>>`
steps.text: Fails: it is write-only. `*p = x` compiles, but `val + *p` must *read* through the iterator, and there is no readable element. Requirements have direction and meaning, not just shape.

steps.label: `std::ostream` used as the iterator
steps.text: Fails outright: no `*p`, no `++p`, no `p != q`. This is the failure the next section catches with a *named* requirement instead of a cascade of errors.

examples.result: Three passes show the breadth one lifted algorithm gains; two failures show that a concept is a predicate with direction and semantics — write-only traversal and no traversal are both genuine "does not satisfy".

examples.title: Working through concepts
examples.problem: The requirements vocabulary. Your task: define a concept and read the ideal concept-annotated template notation.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define a concept and read the ideal concept-annotated template notation. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A concept is a compile-time predicate naming syntactic and semantic requirements; the ideal notation puts it in the template head (`template<Sequence S, Number N>`).

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<typename In> int total(In first, In last);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — distinguish checkable requirements from axioms, and Semiregular from Regular — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Axioms state semantics the compiler cannot check ($a + b = b + a$); they document meaning, license optimization, and are testable. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A concept is a compile-time predicate naming syntactic and semantic requirements; the ideal notation puts it in the template head (`template<Sequence S, Number N>`). Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A concept is a compile-time predicate naming syntactic and semantic requirements; the ideal notation puts it in the template head (`template<Sequence S, Number N>`).
Axioms state semantics the compiler cannot check ($a + b = b + a$); they document meaning, license optimization, and are testable.
Regular ("behaves like an int") is the baseline; relational concepts like `Equality_comparable<T, U>` and `Common<T, U>` capture cross-type operations.

quiz.q: Which of these is an axiom rather than a compiler-checkable requirement?
options: `p != q` must be valid for iterators
$a + b = b + a$ for the Arithmetic concept
quiz.explanation: The commutativity of `+` is a semantic assumption — no compiler checks it — while the others are expression-level requirements that either compile or do not.

quiz.q: A Regular type is one that:
options: behaves like an int: default constructible, copyable, assignable, and comparable with `==`
cannot be used as a template argument
quiz.explanation: Regular is the value-semantics baseline — everything an `int` can do; Semiregular is the same minus equality.

quiz.q: Why do concepts such as `Equality_comparable<T, U>` take two type parameters?
options: To express operations across two types, such as comparing a `string` with a C-style string
To double the cost of checking
quiz.explanation: Relational concepts capture whether cross-type expressions make sense — exactly the element-type/accumulator relation in `sum`.

quiz.q: In the ideal notation `template<Sequence S, Number N> N sum(S s, N n);` the names `Sequence` and `Number` are:
options: class names to be derived from
concepts: compile-time predicates constraining the template arguments
quiz.explanation: They stand in for requirement sets — the notation the book wants, and the one later standardized (in C++20) as template constraints.

quiz.q: A generic algorithm is lifted from a concrete version, and its hidden requirements are named in one place so misuse is diagnosed at the call. What is that named set of requirements?
options: An allocator, because every generic algorithm allocates
A concept: a compile-time predicate on template arguments stating the required operations and associated types
A virtual base class, because generics need runtime dispatch
A macro, because requirements cannot be named in the language
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is a lifted algorithm whose assumptions about its types were discovered step by step. Step 2: The governing rule is the concept: a named compile-time predicate over template arguments that states required operations, associated types, and semantics, checked where the template is used. Step 3: Applying it, a call with an unsuitable type fails early at the requirement boundary with a readable diagnostic instead of deep inside the template body. Step 4: The distractors fail because allocation is orthogonal to requirements, runtime bases would erase the compile-time genericity, and the mechanism is a language facility rather than text substitution. Step 5: Therefore the named requirements are a concept.

intro: C++11 shipped without language support for concepts, so the book shows how to get most of the value with pure library machinery: concepts as `constexpr` predicates, expression tests that ask "does this compile?", `static_assert` for *checking*, and `enable_if` for *selection*. This section is the bridge between the ideal notation of 24.3 and the code that compiles — and it is where concept-based overloading becomes possible (and painful).
objectives: Build a concept as a `constexpr bool` predicate from traits and expression tests
Contrast `static_assert` checking (diagnosis) with `enable_if`/`Requires` selection (overload removal)
Trace how two `advance` overloads are chosen by concept, and why the weaker guard needs a hand-written complement

concepts.statement: In C++11 a concept is emulated by a `constexpr` function returning `bool`, composed from smaller predicates: `Regular<T>()` is `Semiregular<T>() && Equality_comparable<T>()`, and `Semiregular` is assembled from `is_copy_constructible`-style type traits.
concepts.detail: The predicates compose with `&&` and `!` exactly as concepts do in the ideal notation; what is lost is not expressiveness but the compiler's automatic *use* of the structure.

concepts.statement: To ask whether an expression compiles, provide **two overloads of a probe**: one viable only if the expression is well-formed (selected by `decltype` on the expression), and a catch-all returning a `substitution_failure` marker. Substitution failure is not an error (SFINAE), so "does not compile" becomes "returns `false`":
concepts.detail: `Has_plus<int>()` is `true`; for a `Date` with no `operator+`, `Has_plus<Date>()` is `false` — a question answered at compile time, never a hard error by itself.

concepts.statement: Assert the predicate inside the template: `static_assert(Input_iterator<Iter>(), "sum(): Iter must be an input iterator");`. The error surfaces **at instantiation, naming the requirement**, instead of as a cascade inside the loop body.
concepts.detail: This is diagnosis only: the check fires after the template has already been selected — it cannot redirect the call to another implementation.

concepts.statement: Put the predicate in the *signature*, via the alias `template<bool B, typename T = void> using Requires = std::enable_if<B,T>;` — when the concept fails, `Requires<C>()` is an ill-formed return type and **substitution failure removes the whole function from the overload set**.
concepts.detail: Selection, not diagnosis: this is what makes concept-based overloading possible — and what forces the hand-negated guards examined below.

concepts.term: Making Concepts Concrete: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Making Concepts Concrete.** Emulating concepts in C++11. You can claim this section when you can build a concept as a `constexpr bool` predicate from traits and expression tests — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 24 (Generic Programming); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

figures.caption: A concept gate on instantiation. The compiler evaluates the concept predicates — `Input_iterator<Iter>() && Number<Val>()` — at compile time. Types that pass (raw pointers, container iterators, stream iterators) get a real instantiation; a type that fails (`std::ostream` used as an iterator) trips the `static_assert` inside the body, which names the requirement rather than burying the error in the loop. The same predicate placed in the signature via `Requires`/`enable_if` makes the overload vanish instead — selection rather than diagnosis.
