examples.title: Two advances, chosen by concept
examples.problem: `advance(p, n)` should use `p += n` for random-access iterators and `n` increments otherwise. Select between them in C++11 with `Requires` guards, and trace both calls — plus the failure mode the design must avoid.

steps.label: The overloads
steps.text: `template<class I> Requires<Random_access_iterator<I>()> advance(I& p, int n) { p += n; }` and `template<class I> Requires<Input_iterator<I>() && !Random_access_iterator<I>()> advance(I& p, int n) { while (n--) ++p; }`

steps.label: `list<string>::iterator` by 5
steps.text: The concept predicate `Random_access_iterator` is `false` for it, so the first overload's return type is ill-formed and SFINAE removes it. The second guard evaluates `true && !false` — viable. Result: 5 increments, 5 iterator operations.

steps.label: `vector<int>::iterator` (or `double*`) by 5
steps.text: Random-access holds, so the first overload is viable; the second guard is `true && !true` — `false` — and that overload is removed. Result: a single `p += 5`, one iterator operation.

steps.label: The failure you must design away
steps.text: Drop the `!Random_access_iterator<I>()` complement and the second guard is `true` for a `vector` iterator too: two viable overloads with identical parameter lists, no concept-based tie-breaker in C++11 — the call is **ambiguous**, a compile-time error.

examples.result: Concept selection picks the algorithm, not just the answer: 5 operations versus 1. The complement guard is the C++11 programmer's responsibility — the price of emulating what the language did not yet order automatically.

examples.title: Working through making concepts concrete
examples.problem: Emulating concepts in C++11. Your task: build a concept as a `constexpr bool` predicate from traits and expression tests.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: build a concept as a `constexpr bool` predicate from traits and expression tests. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: C++11 emulates concepts with `constexpr bool` predicates assembled from traits and SFINAE expression tests (`Has_plus`).

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<typename In> int total(In first, In last);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — contrast `static_assert` checking (diagnosis) with `enable_if`/`Requires` selection (overload removal) — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: `static_assert` checks — it diagnoses at instantiation; `enable_if`/`Requires` selects — it removes the overload. Two different jobs. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: C++11 emulates concepts with `constexpr bool` predicates assembled from traits and SFINAE expression tests (`Has_plus`). Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: C++11 emulates concepts with `constexpr bool` predicates assembled from traits and SFINAE expression tests (`Has_plus`).
`static_assert` checks — it diagnoses at instantiation; `enable_if`/`Requires` selects — it removes the overload. Two different jobs.
Overloads distinguished only by concept guards need hand-complemented conditions (`&& !Random_access_iterator<I>()`) because C++11 has no constraint ordering.

quiz.q: `static_assert`-based concept checking differs from `enable_if` because `static_assert`:
options: removes the function from the overload set
reports a clear error at instantiation but leaves the overload set unchanged
checks the requirements at run time
can only be used inside class templates
quiz.explanation: It is diagnosis after selection: the template has already been chosen when the assertion fires — it cannot send the call elsewhere.

quiz.q: Why does the weaker `advance` overload in C++11 need `Requires<Input_iterator<I>() && !Random_access_iterator<I>>` rather than just `Requires<Input_iterator<I>>`?
options: C++11 has no automatic constraint ordering: for a random-access iterator both overloads would be viable with identical parameter lists, and the call would be ambiguous
Because random-access iterators fail the `Input_iterator` predicate
To make the template compile faster
quiz.explanation: With both guards true for a random-access iterator, ordinary overload resolution finds no tie-breaker between constraints — the complement makes the guards complementary over the whole domain.

quiz.q: For a type `X` with no `operator+`, the predicate `Has_plus<X>()` returns `false` because:
options: the program is ill-formed and compilation stops
an exception is thrown at run time
the expression probe's substitution fails, so by SFINAE only the catch-all overload survives — returning the failure marker
quiz.explanation: The probe has two overloads: one selected by `decltype` when `x + y` compiles, and a catch-all returning the `substitution_failure` type; failure of substitution is not an error, so the question has an answer.

quiz.q: Given `template<bool B, typename T = void> using Requires = std::enable_if<B,T>;`, the declaration `Requires<Arithmetic<T>()> double algo(T);` is:
options: a function template enabled only for class types
a function template whose return type exists only when the concept holds — otherwise the overload is removed from consideration
quiz.explanation: When the predicate is false, substituting into `enable_if` fails, the declaration is ill-formed, and SFINAE drops it from the candidate set — selection by concept.

depth.title: Concept-based overloading resolution

blocks.body: The problem `enable_if` solves is deeper than error messages. With unconstrained templates, *every* signature matches every call, so when two generic implementations of the same operation exist, overload resolution has only conversion ranking to separate them — and among exact matches that ranking is degenerate. The result is the classic "ambiguous call" for anything but a strictly better conversion. Concepts restore a meaningful partial order on templates: implementations become candidates only for the argument types that satisfy their requirements, and a *more constrained* implementation can be preferred over a less constrained one. The C++11 emulation achieves the first half (candidacy) through SFINAE and misses the second half (preference), which is exactly where its pain lives.

blocks.heading: Constrained overload selection (C++11 emulation)
blocks.body: Let $f_1$ and $f_2$ be function templates with identical parameter lists, distinguished only by their constraint guards $C_1$ and $C_2$ — boolean expressions over concept predicates placed in the return type via `Requires`. For a call with deduced argument type $A$: **(1) Removal.** During template argument deduction each guard is evaluated; if it yields `false`, the substitution of the deduced arguments into the signature fails, and by the SFINAE rule $f_i$ is silently removed from the candidate set. **(2) No ordering.** If both guards hold, both candidates are exact matches on identical parameter lists and ordinary overload resolution finds **no tie-breaker between constraints**: the call is ambiguous unless the guards were constructed to be *complementary* over the intended domain ($C_1(A) \Rightarrow \lnot C_2(A)$ for all $A$). **(3) C++20 subsumption (for contrast).** If $C_1 \Rightarrow C_2$ holds as a syntactic implication over atomic predicates and conjunctions, and $C_2 \Rightarrow C_1$ does not, then $f_1$ is *more constrained* and is preferred — the tie-breaker the emulation cannot provide.

blocks.heading: The iterator lattice and the advance guards
blocks.body: Define the lattice $\mathrm{Input} \subset \mathrm{Forward} \subset \mathrm{Bidirectional} \subset \mathrm{RandomAccess}$, each level adding requirements: Forward adds multi-pass copyability, Bidirectional adds `--p`, RandomAccess adds `p + n`, `p += n`, `p[n]`, and `p < q`. Consequently $\mathrm{RandomAccess}(I) \Rightarrow \mathrm{Input}(I)$ — the lattice is a chain of implications. The `advance` family must place its fast implementation on the top of the lattice and its fallback below: the fast guard is the atomic predicate $R = \mathrm{RandomAccess}(I)$, and the fallback guard must be $\mathrm{Input}(I) \land \lnot R$. Complementarity now follows structurally: for every $I$, exactly one of $R$, $\mathrm{Input}(I) \land \lnot R$ holds, so exactly one candidate survives — selection is total. Had the fallback been guarded by $\mathrm{Input}(I)$ alone, then for a random-access $I$ both $R$ and $\mathrm{Input}(I)$ would hold, both candidates would be exact matches, and by part (2) of the theorem the call would be ambiguous.

blocks.heading: Tracing three calls, with costs
blocks.body: Take `advance(p, 1000)`. **`p` a `list<int>::iterator`:** $R$ is false — the fast overload is removed; the fallback guard is true, so 1000 increments execute: 1000 iterator operations, $O(n)$. **`p` a `double*`:** $R$ is true — the fast overload is viable; the fallback guard is $\mathrm{Input} \land \lnot R = \mathrm{true} \land \mathrm{false}$, so it is removed; one `+=` executes: 1 operation, $O(1)$. **The design error:** if the `!R` complement is forgotten, the `double*` call sees two viable candidates; the compiler reports ambiguity at the *call site*, a thousand miles from either definition. The concept selection is not cosmetic — it chooses between algorithms whose complexities differ by a factor of $n$.

The emulation's fragility has a precise technical name: C++11 partial ordering of function templates compares *parameter types*, and two overloads whose parameters are identical differ only in an invented return type — `enable_if<A>` versus `enable_if<B>` are unrelated types to partial ordering, whatever $A$ and $B$ mean. Worse, two *logically* equivalent guards written differently — `Input_iterator<I>() && Bidirectional_iterator<I>()` versus `Bidirectional_iterator<I>()` — are not recognized as related at all, so an accidental overlap between guards silently becomes ambiguity for some argument types. The concept is also written twice: once in the guard, once (as a `static_assert` or comment) in the body, and the two copies can drift. C++20 subsumption repairs all three defects at once by reading the boolean structure of `requires`-clauses instead of comparing types.

blocks.heading: Rules for surviving the C++11 emulation
blocks.body: **(1)** Order every overload family most-constrained first, and make each weaker guard the explicit complement of everything above it ($\ldots \land \lnot R$). **(2)** Name each concept once as a `constexpr` predicate and reuse that name verbatim — never retype the underlying expression, or two spellings of one concept will fail to match. **(3)** Use `static_assert` when diagnosis is the whole job (no alternative implementation exists); use `Requires` only when selection among overloads is intended. **(4)** Record the axioms as comments beside the predicates: the compiler cannot check $a + b = b + a$, but the next maintainer must know it is assumed. These habits are exactly what the language later automated — which is the strongest evidence they were the right habits.

intro: The chapter closes with Stroustrup's rules of thumb for genericity. Their common thread: **genericity is earned** — by lifting in small steps from code that works, by stating requirements minimally and completely, by testing with types that have nothing beyond what the concept requires, and by writing down the semantics the type system cannot express.
objectives: Apply the lift-don't-rewrite method to a concrete algorithm
Explain concept minimality and completeness, and how minimal types expose hidden requirements
Recognize over-requiring idioms such as ordered iteration where inequality suffices

concepts.statement: Begin with a concrete, correct algorithm; generalize by **removing one accident at a time**, re-checking after each lift. A leap straight to "fully general" code usually smuggles in unmet assumptions from the original — the four small lifts of 24.2 are the model.
concepts.detail: Each lift must leave a nameable requirement behind; if you cannot name what you now need, you have not finished the lift.

concepts.statement: A concept should name **exactly** what the algorithm uses: if you can drop a requirement and the algorithm still compiles and works, it was not a requirement; if the algorithm uses an operation the concept does not mention, the concept is incomplete and the documentation lies.
concepts.detail: Minimal concepts maximize the set of usable types — the entire economic point of genericity.

concepts.statement: Verify generic code against types that satisfy the concept **and nothing more** — a hand-rolled iterator, not `vector`'s full-featured one. Hidden dependencies surface as errors on the minimal type instead of as silent limits on your users.
concepts.detail: `list` iterators are the standard probe: they famously lack `<`, so any accidental ordering requirement is caught immediately.

concepts.statement: Write the axioms next to the predicates — the compiler cannot check $a + b = b + a$, but the reader, the tester, and (in a concepts-aware compiler) the optimizer all rely on them. Code that documents its assumptions is the deliverable of generic programming.
concepts.detail: In C++11 the axiom lives in a comment beside the `constexpr` predicate; the design intent survives unchanged into language-supported concepts.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Lift in small steps from concrete, correct code; every lift must leave its requirement explicit and named.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: A requirements audit of find
examples.problem: Audit this almost-generic algorithm against the concept rules: which requirement is accidental, and what does removing it cost?

steps.label: The suspect
steps.text: `template<class Iter, class T> Iter find(Iter first, Iter last, const T& val) { while (first < last && *first != val) ++first; return first; }` — plausible, and subtly wrong.

steps.label: Probe with a minimal type
steps.text: Test with `list<int>` iterators — types that satisfy input iteration and nothing more. It fails: `list<int>::iterator` has no `<`. The accidental requirement is exposed exactly where the advice predicted.

steps.label: Diagnose
steps.text: Termination never needed *ordering* of positions — only *inequality*. The `<` was a habit carried over from index-based loops, over-requiring an ordered (random-access-style) position and excluding lists, streams, and any node-based traversal.

steps.label: Fix and verify
steps.text: Change to `while (first != last && *first != val) ++first;`. Searching `{27, 51, 34, 96}` for 34: three termination checks (`!=`), two value comparisons, two increments — returns the position of 34 (index 2); the requirement drops from "ordered iterator" to plain input iterator.

examples.result: One operator swapped, one requirement deleted, a whole family of sequences admitted. That trade — an audit finding an unneeded capability and replacing it with a stated, weaker one — is the daily work of generic programming.

examples.title: Reviewing generic programming code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the lift-don’t-rewrite method to a concrete algorithm.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Lift in small steps from concrete, correct code; every lift must leave its requirement explicit and named.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `template<typename In> int total(In first, In last);`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: explain concept minimality and completeness, and how minimal types expose hidden requirements. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Keep concepts minimal (drop what is not needed) and complete (name everything used), and test with minimal types — `list` iterators expose accidental ordering.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Lift in small steps from concrete, correct code; every lift must leave its requirement explicit and named. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Lift in small steps from concrete, correct code; every lift must leave its requirement explicit and named.
Keep concepts minimal (drop what is not needed) and complete (name everything used), and test with minimal types — `list` iterators expose accidental ordering.
Record axioms beside the predicates; and remember the fold's contract: `init = 0` sums, `init = 1` multiplies.

quiz.q: A `find` written with `first < last` instead of `first != last`:
options: over-requires ordered iterators — it rejects list iterators, although termination needs only inequality
is more efficient for all containers
is required by the standard library interface
has no effect on which sequences can use it
quiz.explanation: The ordering of positions was never needed for the algorithm's meaning — `!=` needs only an input iterator, `<` demands random-access-style positions.

quiz.q: Why test generic code with types that satisfy the concept and nothing more?
options: Because minimal types optimize better at run time
To catch hidden requirements the concept does not document — the real dependency leaks out as an error on the minimal type
Because the standard library requires it
quiz.explanation: Full-featured types silently satisfy requirements you never declared; only a minimal type makes an undocumented dependency visible.

quiz.q: A requirement that you can drop while the algorithm still compiles and works:
options: was not a requirement — concepts should be minimal, naming only what is needed
should always be converted into an axiom
quiz.explanation: Minimality: every requirement you can delete widens the family of usable types at no cost — keep exactly what the algorithm uses.

intro: A template supplies one general implementation for every argument set — the **primary template**. But the best implementation for all types is often not the best implementation for a specific type: comparing two C-style strings should compare characters, not addresses, and a `vector<bool>` wants bits, not one byte per element. **Specialization** lets the compiler substitute a better definition for chosen template arguments while the user-visible interface stays exactly the same.
objectives: Explain what a specialization overrides and why the primary template alone is not always enough
Identify full and partial specializations and state the priority order among them
Say which template kinds support partial specialization and which must be handled differently

concepts.statement: The template as originally defined — `template<class T> class Vector { /* ... */ };` — is the **primary**: the definition used for every argument combination not claimed by a specialization. It is deliberately the most general and most conservative implementation.
concepts.detail: Everything the template family offers must be expressible through the primary's interface, because that is the interface users write against.

concepts.statement: A **specialization** is an alternative definition of a template for a specific set of template argument values, written with an empty `template<>` list (a full specialization) or a reduced parameter list (a partial specialization). The compiler — not the programmer at the call site — selects it by matching the template arguments.
concepts.detail: Selection is entirely compile-time: a specialization costs nothing at run time and changes nothing about how users invoke the template.

concepts.statement: The two honest motives are a **better implementation** — bit-packing for `vector<bool>`, `strcmp` for `const char*`, a more efficient algorithm for a type that supports it — and **genuinely different semantics** that the general implementation would silently get wrong (comparing pointers when the user means strings).
concepts.detail: A third, technical motive appears in template metaprogramming: a full specialization is the standard way to write the terminating case of a recursive template.

concepts.statement: **Specialization does for templates what virtual overriding does for hierarchies — but selected by type at compile time.** The caller writes the same `less(a, b)` call and gets the implementation the compiler deems best for the actual argument types, with no indirection and no run-time decision.
concepts.detail: The price is symmetric too: like a derived class overriding a base, a specialization is extra code that must stay semantically consistent with what it replaces.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Specialization at a glance. You can claim this section when you can explain what a specialization overrides and why the primary template alone is not always enough — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 25 (Specialization); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: The pointer-comparison trap
examples.problem: The primary `template<class T> bool less(const T& a, const T& b) { return a < b; }` is instantiated for `T = const char*`. The literals "apple" and "zebra" happen to be stored at addresses 0x7ffd0004 and 0x7ffd0000. What does `less("apple", "zebra")` return?

steps.label: Primary at work
steps.text: With `T = const char*`, the primary compares the two pointer values with `<` — it computes `0x7ffd0004 < 0x7ffd0000`.

steps.label: Pointer arithmetic
steps.text: That comparison is `false`: the address holding "apple" is 4 bytes *higher* than the one holding "zebra".

steps.label: The intended meaning
steps.text: Alphabetically "apple" < "zebra"; `strcmp("apple", "zebra")` is negative, so the answer a string-comparing `less` must give is `true`.

steps.label: The fix
steps.text: A full specialization — `template<> bool less<const char*>(const char* a, const char* b) { return strcmp(a, b) < 0; }` — reclaims the intended semantics with zero changes at call sites.

examples.result: The primary silently compares addresses; a specialization restores the meaning users assume — same call, different (correct) implementation, chosen at compile time.

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: Specialization at a glance. Your task: explain what a specialization overrides and why the primary template alone is not always enough.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: explain what a specialization overrides and why the primary template alone is not always enough. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A template is a family of definitions: the primary covers the general case, specializations override chosen argument sets with the same interface.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<typename T> struct Traits; template<> struct Traits<char>;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — identify full and partial specializations and state the priority order among them — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Specialize for better algorithms or representations — or to correct semantics the primary would silently get wrong, as with `less<const char*>`. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A template is a family of definitions: the primary covers the general case, specializations override chosen argument sets with the same interface. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A template is a family of definitions: the primary covers the general case, specializations override chosen argument sets with the same interface.
Specialize for better algorithms or representations — or to correct semantics the primary would silently get wrong, as with `less<const char*>`.
Selection among the primary and its specializations happens entirely at compile time, from the template arguments alone.

quiz.q: The primary `less` above is used with `T = const char*`. What does the call actually compare?
options: The characters of the two strings, lexicographically
The addresses where the two string literals are stored
The lengths of the two strings
Nothing — the call fails to compile
quiz.explanation: `const char*` is a pointer, so the primary's `a < b` compares the two addresses — which says nothing about the strings they point to.

quiz.q: A specialization differs from a run-time override mainly because it:
options: is selected by the dynamic type of an object at run time
is selected by matching template arguments at compile time and keeps the primary's interface
may change the number of function parameters
removes the primary template from the program
quiz.explanation: Selection is pattern matching on the template arguments during compilation; the user-visible interface is unchanged.

quiz.q: In template metaprogramming, a full specialization is typically used to:
options: provide the terminating case of a recursive template
convert value parameters to type parameters
quiz.explanation: Recursion over template arguments stops when a full specialization matches — the metaprogramming analog of a base case.

quiz.q: Which is a legitimate motive for specializing, as opposed to just using the primary?
options: The argument type admits a better representation or algorithm, or needs different semantics
Specializations are required for every template to compile
It lets users pick implementations at run time
quiz.explanation: Specialization exists for better algorithms and representations, and for argument sets whose intended semantics differ — never for run-time choice.

intro: Before you can specialize anything you must know exactly what a template can be parameterized by. C++ offers three kinds of template parameters — types, values, and templates — and three ways to supply arguments: writing them explicitly, relying on defaults, and (for function templates) letting the compiler deduce them from the call. This vocabulary governs everything else in the chapter.
objectives: Classify the three kinds of template parameters and list the legal value-parameter types
Apply the rules for default template arguments across declarations
Explain how function template arguments are deduced and when they must be written explicitly

concepts.statement: A template parameter list can hold three kinds of parameters: **type parameters** (`template<class T>`, equivalently `template<typename T>`), **value parameters** (`template<int N>`, also pointers, references, and `std::nullptr_t`), and **template parameters** (`template<template<class> class C>`), and a single template may mix all three.
concepts.detail: Type parameters consume argument types; value parameters consume compile-time constants; template parameters consume class templates.

concepts.statement: **A value argument must be a constant expression**: `Buffer<char, 512>` works, `Buffer<char, n>` with a run-time `n` is an error, and `Buffer<char, 512*2>` works because `1024` is still a constant expression. Legal value parameter types: integral and enumeration types, pointers to objects and functions, lvalue references, member pointers, and `std::nullptr_t`.
concepts.detail: Floating-point and class-type value parameters are not allowed in this edition of the language (C++20 later relaxed both). Address arguments must have external linkage.

concepts.statement: **Defaults** are written with `=`: `template<class T = int, int N = 128> class Buffer { /* ... */ };` makes `Buffer<>` mean `Buffer<int, 128>`. A default may refer to preceding parameters; a given parameter may be given a default only once, and defaults can be added in a later redeclaration of the same template.
concepts.detail: Specializations do not get their own defaults — the defaults of a specialization are those of the primary template.

concepts.statement: A **template template parameter** is a parameter that is itself a class template: `template<class T, template<class> class C> class X { C<T> c; };`. In this edition the argument must match the pattern exactly, so `std::vector` — really `template<class T, class A = allocator<T>> class vector` — does not match `template<class> class C`; you must write the pattern with its defaulted parameter included (C++17 later relaxed the matching rule).
concepts.detail: Template template parameters let the *structure* of a container, not just its element type, be an argument.

concepts.statement: **Function template arguments are deduced from the call**: `min(2, 3)` deduces `T = int` and instantiates `min<int>`; `min(2.7, 3.1)` deduces `T = double`. When deduction is impossible — `min(2, 3.5)` deduces `T = int` from one argument and `T = double` from the other — write the argument explicitly: `min<double>(2, 3.5)`.
concepts.detail: Deduction applies only to function templates in this edition; class template arguments must be named or defaulted (C++17 later added class template argument deduction).

examples.title: Sizing a ring buffer with a value parameter
examples.problem: Given `template<class T, int N> struct Ring { T buf[N]; int count = 0; };`, compute `sizeof(Ring<char, 512>)` and `sizeof(Ring<double, 100>)`, and decide the legality of `Ring<char, 2*512>` and of `Ring<char, n>` where `n` is an `int` read at run time.

steps.label: Ring<char, 512>
steps.text: 512 chars = $512 \times 1 = 512$ bytes, plus the 4-byte `int` member, gives 516; alignment is 4, so `sizeof` is exactly 516 bytes.

steps.label: Ring<double, 100>
steps.text: $100 \times 8 = 800$ bytes plus 4 = 804; alignment 8 rounds up to 808 bytes.

steps.label: Ring<char, 2*512>
steps.text: `2*512` evaluates to the constant 1024 — still a constant expression, so this is legal and identical in type to `Ring<char, 1024>`.

steps.label: Ring<char, n>
steps.text: A value read at run time is not a constant expression — ill-formed, rejected before any code is generated.

examples.result: Value parameters push array sizes into the type: `sizeof` is exact arithmetic (516 and 808 here), and any run-time quantity is refused at the door.

examples.title: Working through template parameters and arguments
examples.problem: Type, value and template parameters. Your task: classify the three kinds of template parameters and list the legal value-parameter types.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: classify the three kinds of template parameters and list the legal value-parameter types. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Three parameter kinds: types, values (constant expressions only), and templates.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<typename T> struct Traits; template<> struct Traits<char>;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — apply the rules for default template arguments across declarations — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Defaults may refer to earlier parameters, may be added in later declarations, and belong to the primary — specializations inherit them. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

keyTakeaways: Three parameter kinds: types, values (constant expressions only), and templates.
Defaults may refer to earlier parameters, may be added in later declarations, and belong to the primary — specializations inherit them.
Function template arguments deduce from the call; when deduction conflicts, qualify explicitly (`min<double>(2, 3.5)`).

quiz.q: Which of these cannot be a value template parameter in this edition of the language?
quiz.explanation: Floating-point (and class-type) value parameters were not allowed until C++20; integral types, pointers, and references were always legal.

quiz.q: Given `template<class T = int, int N = 128> class Buffer;`, the name `Buffer<>` means:
options: an incomplete type until arguments are given
quiz.explanation: Empty angle brackets trigger the defaults: `T = int` and `N = 128`.

quiz.q: Why does `template<class T, template<class> class C> class X` reject `std::vector` as the second argument?
options: `std::vector` has a second (allocator) parameter, and this edition requires the parameter lists to match exactly
template template arguments must be passed as values
class templates cannot nest inside other templates
quiz.explanation: C++11 matching is exact: `vector`'s extra defaulted `allocator<T>` parameter defeats the one-parameter pattern; the pattern must spell the defaulted parameter out.

quiz.q: A single-parameter `min` template is called as `min(2, 3.5)`. What happens?
options: `T` is deduced as `double` for both arguments
the `int` is converted to `double` before deduction
deduction fails — one argument wants `T = int`, the other `T = double`
the call is resolved to the primary at run time
quiz.explanation: Deduction performs no implicit conversion between argument types; each argument must deduce the same `T`. The fix is `min<double>(2, 3.5)`.

intro: A template definition is really a *set* of alternative definitions: the primary, plus any specializations you declare. Given a use like `Vector<Shape*>`, the compiler runs a deterministic selection procedure over that set — exact full match first, then partial patterns, most specialized wins, ties are errors. This section makes the procedure precise and shows the classic trick of implementing one specialization on top of another.
objectives: Write full and partial specializations with correct syntax
Apply the most-specialized-wins selection rule, including the ambiguity error
Explain how a partial specialization can be implemented over a full one, and why specializations must be declared before use

concepts.statement: **Full specialization** pins every template argument. The empty `template<>` announces that no parameter remains free: `template<> class Vector<void*> { /* ... */ };` for a class, or `template<> bool less<const char*>(const char* a, const char* b) { return strcmp(a, b) < 0; }` for a function.
concepts.detail: A full specialization is an ordinary class or function that happens to carry the template's name and interface.

concepts.statement: **Partial specialization** fixes some arguments and leaves others as a pattern: `template<class T> class Vector<T*> { /* ... */ };` handles every `Vector<X*>` while leaving `Vector<int>` to the primary. **Only class templates (and class members) can be partially specialized — function templates cannot**; overload functions instead.
concepts.detail: The pattern is matched structurally against the argument list; a partial specialization with no free parameters is ill-formed (that would be a full specialization).

concepts.statement: Among the primary and all specializations whose patterns match a given set of arguments, the compiler selects **the most specialized**: a full specialization beats any partial, a more specific partial beats a less specific one. If two partial specializations match and neither is more specialized than the other, the use is an **ambiguity error** at compile time.
concepts.detail: This mirrors overload resolution's partial ordering — the compiler never guesses between two incomparable matches.

concepts.statement: The classic space-saver: implement the partial specialization of `Vector<T*>` on top of the full specialization `Vector<void*>` — `template<class T> class Vector<T*> : private Vector<void*> { /* cast at the interface */ };`. All the storage-and-growth machinery is compiled once, in `Vector<void*>`; each `Vector<X*>` adds only a thin, type-safe wrapper.
concepts.detail: Without this trick, `Vector<Shape*>`, `Vector<int*>`, and every other pointer instantiation would each grow their own copy of the machinery.

concepts.statement: A specialization must be declared **before the first use that would trigger an implicit instantiation** of that specialization, in every translation unit. Use the primary in one file and the specialization in another and the program violates the one-definition rule in a way no diagnostic is required to catch.
concepts.detail: Practical consequence: put specializations in the same header as the primary template they specialize.

figures.caption: Selecting an implementation for `Vector<Shape*>`: no full specialization matches, the partial `Vector<T*>` does (with `T = Shape*`), so it wins over the primary. A full specialization would have beaten it; two equally good partials would be an ambiguity error. The partial is itself implemented over the full specialization `Vector<void*>`, so all pointer element types share one storage implementation.

examples.title: Routing four instantiations through a specialization set
examples.problem: A program provides the primary `Vector<T>`, the partial specialization `Vector<T*>` (privately built over a full specialization `Vector<void*>`), and that full specialization `Vector<void*>`. Which definition serves `Vector<void*>`, `Vector<Shape*>`, `Vector<int>`, and `Vector<char>`?

steps.label: Vector<void*>
steps.text: The argument list matches the full specialization exactly — the full is used (it outranks the partial `T*` pattern, which would also match).

steps.label: Vector<Shape*>
steps.text: No full specialization matches (`Vector<void*>` matches only itself); the partial `Vector<T*>` matches with `T = Shape` — the partial is used, and its storage lives in the shared `Vector<void*>` base.

steps.label: Vector<int>
steps.text: No full matches; the partial pattern requires a pointer as the element type and `int` is not one — the primary template is used.

steps.label: Vector<char>
steps.text: Same reasoning as `int`: no match but the primary.

examples.result: Four uses, one interface, three distinct implementations chosen by pattern matching — and every pointer element type shares a single storage implementation.

examples.title: Working through specialization
examples.problem: Specializing for better code. Your task: write full and partial specializations with correct syntax.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: write full and partial specializations with correct syntax. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Full specialization pins all arguments (`template<>`); partial specialization fixes a pattern (`Vector<T*>`); the most specialized match wins and ties are errors.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<typename T> struct Traits; template<> struct Traits<char>;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — apply the most-specialized-wins selection rule, including the ambiguity error — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Class templates may be partially specialized; function templates may not — use overloading to reach the same effect for functions. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Full specialization pins all arguments (`template<>`); partial specialization fixes a pattern (`Vector<T*>`); the most specialized match wins and ties are errors. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Full specialization pins all arguments (`template<>`); partial specialization fixes a pattern (`Vector<T*>`); the most specialized match wins and ties are errors.
Class templates may be partially specialized; function templates may not — use overloading to reach the same effect for functions.
A specialization must be declared before any use that would instantiate it, in every translation unit — otherwise an undetectable one-definition violation.

quiz.q: `template<class T> class Vector<T*> { /* ... */ };` is best described as:
quiz.explanation: One argument of the pattern is fixed structurally (pointer-ness) while `T` remains free — the definition of a partial specialization.

quiz.q: With the primary `Vector<T>`, the partial `Vector<T*>`, and the full `Vector<void*>` in scope, which definition serves `Vector<Shape*>`?
options: None — the use is an ambiguity error
quiz.explanation: No full specialization matches `Vector<Shape*>`; the partial pattern matches with `T = Shape`, and a matching partial outranks the primary.

quiz.q: Why is the partial specialization `Vector<T*>` implemented over the full specialization `Vector<void*>`?
options: So that all pointer element types share one storage implementation instead of growing one each
Because partial specializations cannot have their own members
quiz.explanation: The heavy machinery is compiled once inside `Vector<void*>`; every `Vector<X*>` adds only a thin type-safe interface on top.

quiz.q: Two partial specializations both match a use, and neither is more specialized than the other. The result is:
options: The compiler picks the one declared first
The compiler picks the one with fewer parameters
The primary template is silently used
quiz.explanation: The selection rule only ranks comparable specializations; an unrankable tie is diagnosed as an error rather than guessed.

intro: Specialization is a sharp tool. Every specialization is extra code that must be written, tested, and kept semantically synchronized with the primary as it evolves. The professional defaults are: let the general implementation carry the load, specialize only when measurement or meaning demands it — and then make the specialization a drop-in replacement.
objectives: Decide when specialization is and is not warranted
Apply the drop-in contract to any specialization you write
Choose correctly among overloading, specializing, and the standard-library exception

concepts.term: Specialize only for a proven reason
concepts.statement: **The default answer is the primary.** Every specialization is code you write, test, document, and keep synchronized with the primary as it evolves. Specialize when measurement shows a win, or when the semantics of an argument type genuinely differ from what the primary assumes.
concepts.detail: A misplaced specialization also removes the general implementation from consideration for exactly those types that would have been fine with it.

concepts.statement: **A specialization must satisfy the primary's documented semantics** — same operations, same meanings, comparable complexity: `less<const char*>` still means "less", `swap` still exchanges values. Anything else turns a type-correct program into a wrong one.
concepts.detail: Treat the primary's specification as a contract every specialization signs, exactly as a derived class honors its base class's contract.

concepts.statement: For **function** templates, prefer overloading: overload resolution's partial ordering handles "more specialized" robustly, and explicit function specializations do not even participate in overload resolution. For **class** templates, specialization is the only mechanism. One sanctioned exception: you may not add new templates to namespace `std`, but you *may* specialize `std` templates for your own types.
concepts.detail: `std::hash`, `std::less` and friends are the designed customization points of the standard library.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Default to the primary; specialize when measurement or a genuine semantic difference demands it.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

concepts.statement: Take the objectives as review questions: decide when specialization is and is not warranted? Then apply the drop-in contract to any specialization you write? Answer each from the code in front of you, not from memory — the gap between the two answers is the review finding.
concepts.detail: A rule you can derive from the chapter you can also correctly suspend; a rule applied without its reason becomes superstition, so cite the reason in the review note.

examples.title: Specializing std::hash — the sanctioned exception
examples.problem: You want to store `Vertex` objects in a `std::unordered_set<Vertex>`. `std::hash` has no definition for user types. What is the legal way to teach the library about `Vertex`?

steps.label: What is wanted
steps.text: `unordered_set<Vertex>` needs two things from the type: a hash function object and `operator==` for equality.

steps.label: What is forbidden
steps.text: Adding new templates or overloads to namespace `std` is reserved for the library itself — user code may not do it.

steps.label: What is allowed
steps.text: Specializing a `std` template *for a user-defined type* is explicitly permitted: open `std` and write `template<> struct hash<Vertex> { std::size_t operator()(const Vertex& v) const { return v.h; } };`.

steps.label: The rest
steps.text: `operator==` is not a `std` template — it goes next to `Vertex`, in your own namespace, where the library finds it.

examples.result: Specialization is the *only* way to customize a closed namespace like `std` — the one place where "prefer overloading" must yield.

examples.title: Reviewing specialization code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: decide when specialization is and is not warranted.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Default to the primary; specialize when measurement or a genuine semantic difference demands it.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `template<typename T> struct Traits; template<> struct Traits<char>;`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: apply the drop-in contract to any specialization you write. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: A specialization is a drop-in: same operations, same meanings, comparable cost — the primary’s contract holds.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Default to the primary; specialize when measurement or a genuine semantic difference demands it. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Default to the primary; specialize when measurement or a genuine semantic difference demands it.
A specialization is a drop-in: same operations, same meanings, comparable cost — the primary's contract holds.
Prefer overloading for function templates; reserve specialization of `std` templates for user-defined types — the sanctioned exception.

quiz.q: You need a better `swap` for your own type in your own namespace. What is the right tool?
options: A `swap` function in the same namespace as your type
A new overload added to namespace `std`
Deriving your type from a swappable base
quiz.explanation: Generic code that needs the customization looks it up next to the type; adding to `std` is forbidden, and specializing `std::swap` defeats the lookup idiom that generic code uses.

quiz.q: The drop-in contract says a specialization must:
options: preserve the primary's documented semantics and interface
delegate every operation back to the primary
quiz.explanation: Same operations, same meanings, comparable complexity — otherwise type-correct programs silently misbehave.

quiz.q: Why keep specializations rare even when they are correct?
options: Each is separate code to maintain and keep synchronized with the evolving primary
quiz.explanation: Maintenance cost is linear in the number of specializations, and a stale one violates the drop-in contract silently.

intro: A template is not code — it is a recipe the compiler turns into code, and that act is **instantiation**. Two questions dominate this chapter: *when* the compiler generates a definition (and how you can control it with explicit instantiation), and *what names inside the template mean* — because a template is defined once, used far away, yet must not mean something different at every use. The answers are what let templates scale from one student file to millions of lines.
objectives: Define instantiation and distinguish the class-template and function-template cases
Explain on-demand, partial instantiation and what it implies for error checking
Frame the two governing questions: when code is generated and what names mean

concepts.statement: **Instantiation is generating a definition from a template plus a set of template arguments**: calling `sort(v)` on a `vector<int>` causes the compiler to stamp out `sort` specialized to those iterator types; naming `Vector<int>` where a complete type is needed stamps out the class. The program's code comes from the compiler applying recipes, not from the source text alone.
concepts.detail: Both class templates and function templates are instantiated — but only the parts actually used.

concepts.statement: **A template is instantiated only when used, and only the parts used.** A `Vector<T>` whose `sort()` member requires `<` on its element type compiles fine for a type without `<`, as long as nobody calls `sort()` on that instantiation. This is what makes generic libraries usable with types their authors never anticipated.
concepts.detail: Corollary: an error inside an unused member function is never diagnosed — templates are checked only along the paths actually taken.

concepts.statement: **When** — which contexts trigger instantiation, at which point of the program the generated definition logically lives (the point of instantiation), and how to force or suppress generation explicitly. **What names mean** — the binding rules that decide, for every name in a template, which declaration it names. Both have precise answers; they are the rest of the chapter.
concepts.detail: Both questions exist because a template's definition and its uses live in different scopes, files, and often different projects.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Instantiation at a glance. You can claim this section when you can define instantiation and distinguish the class-template and function-template cases — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 26 (Instantiation); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

concepts.statement: Work in three passes. First, explain on-demand, partial instantiation and what it implies for error checking. Then, frame the two governing questions: when code is generated and what names mean. Finally, test the outcome against the section promise: A template is a recipe; the compiler writes the code when a specialization is actually needed.
concepts.detail: Each pass catches a different class of mistake, and skipping one moves the failure into a larger program where it costs more to diagnose than it would have here.

examples.title: Counting the bodies the compiler writes
examples.problem: One translation unit contains the calls `max(1, 2)`, `max(2.7, 3.1)`, `max('a', 'b')` and, later, `max(1, 2)` again. It also creates a `list<int>` object, calls `push_back` on it twice, and never calls `list<int>::sort`. How many template bodies does the compiler generate?

steps.label: The max calls
steps.text: Three distinct argument sets — {int, int}, {double, double}, {char, char} — so three instantiations; the repeated `max(1, 2)` reuses the already-generated `max<int>`.

steps.label: The class
steps.text: Creating the `list<int>` object requires a complete type, so the class is instantiated — but only the members actually called get function bodies.

steps.label: push_back
steps.text: Called twice, but both calls name the same specialization `list<int>::push_back` — one body.

steps.label: sort
steps.text: Never called, never instantiated: even if its body would fail to compile for `int`, no diagnostic is owed.

examples.result: Four function bodies (three `max` + one `push_back`) plus one class layout — instantiation is per *use*, never per template.

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: Instantiation at a glance. Your task: define instantiation and distinguish the class-template and function-template cases.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: define instantiation and distinguish the class-template and function-template cases. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A template is a recipe; the compiler writes the code when a specialization is actually needed.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `extern template class std::vector<int>;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain on-demand, partial instantiation and what it implies for error checking — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Instantiation is on demand and partial: only used members come into existence. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A template is a recipe; the compiler writes the code when a specialization is actually needed. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A template is a recipe; the compiler writes the code when a specialization is actually needed.
Instantiation is on demand and partial: only used members come into existence.
Two rules govern quality: when definitions are generated, and which declaration each name inside the template binds to.

quiz.q: Which statement about a template is accurate?
options: It is compiled into ordinary code once and shared by all argument sets
It is a recipe from which the compiler generates code for specific argument sets when needed
It is interpreted at run time
It is expanded textually at each use like a macro
quiz.explanation: No code for `max<int>` exists until an instantiation of it is required — and the compiler, not the preprocessor, does the work.

quiz.q: `list<My_type>` has a member `sort()` that requires `>` on the element type, but no one ever calls it. The program:
options: fails to compile for any `My_type` without `>`
compiles only if `My_type` derives from a sortable base
quiz.explanation: On-demand instantiation touches only used members; the unused `sort()` never comes into existence for that type.

quiz.q: A translation unit contains `max(1, 2)` and, one hundred lines later, `max(1, 2)` again. The compiler generates:
options: one body, reused by the second call
one body per call site after inlining
no body — calls are expanded inline by the preprocessor
quiz.explanation: Both calls name the same specialization `max<int>`; the second finds the first instantiation already in place.

intro: The language is exact about when a template must be instantiated: a class template where a context requires a **complete type**, a function template when it is **called** (or its address taken). It is equally exact about *where* the generated definition logically lives — the **point of instantiation** — and it hands you two manual controls: explicit instantiation, and the `extern template` declaration that suppresses implicit instantiation in all but one translation unit.
objectives: List the contexts that trigger implicit instantiation of class and function templates
State the point-of-instantiation rules for classes and functions
Control code generation with explicit instantiation and `extern template`

concepts.statement: **A class template is instantiated where a complete type is required**: defining an object, `new`, `sizeof`, member access. A mere `Vector<int>* p;` or an `extern Vector<int> v;` mentions the name without needing the layout — no instantiation. A function template is instantiated when it is **called** or when its address is taken.
concepts.detail: This is why you can pass around pointers and references to not-yet-instantiated templates freely.

concepts.statement: The **POI** is the place in the source where the generated definition logically lives. For a class template used in a namespace-scope declaration, immediately **before** that declaration; for a function template called there, at the **end of the translation unit** — which is why a function template may be defined *below* its caller in the same file. Instantiations may use templates that get their own POIs in turn, and every POI for the same specialization must produce an equivalent definition.
concepts.detail: POIs are the mechanism behind "declare above, define below" for function templates — and behind the rule that a class template must be complete above its use.

concepts.statement: `template class Vector<int>;` in a translation unit generates `Vector<int>` and its members **there and now**; `template bool less<int>(int, int);` does the same for a function. Use it to place a single instantiation in a dedicated source file instead of letting every user generate their own.
concepts.detail: Explicit instantiation of a class also instantiates its member functions and static members (member templates wait until used).

concepts.statement: `extern template class Vector<int>;` — an explicit instantiation **declaration**: a promise that the definition is generated in some other translation unit, so implicit instantiation is suppressed here. Put it in the header, pair it with one explicit instantiation in one `.cpp`, and heavyweight template code is compiled once instead of in every user file.
concepts.detail: A C++11 addition; the standard library uses it for its own heavyweight instantiations such as `basic_string<char>`.

concepts.statement: Templates are checked at two levels: at the **definition**, syntax and every non-dependent name are checked — enough to catch typos early; at each **instantiation**, dependent names are checked against the actual arguments. An error deep in a member function is diagnosed only if some instantiation actually needs that member.
concepts.detail: This explains the otherwise-mysterious placement of template diagnostics — sometimes far from the line that triggered them.

examples.title: One instantiation, many translation units
examples.problem: `Vector<int>` is used in 10 translation units, and its heavy member `sort_all()` is called in 3 of them. Describe what the compiler and linker do, with and without explicit control.

steps.label: Without control
steps.text: Each of the 3 translation units implicitly instantiates `sort_all<int>` at its own point of instantiation — three generations of identical code. The linker (comdat merging) keeps exactly one body in the program.

steps.label: Header change
steps.text: The header gains `extern template class Vector<int>;` — implicit instantiation of `Vector<int>` and its members is now suppressed in every file that includes it.

steps.label: One dedicated file
steps.text: A single Vector.cpp says `template class Vector<int>;` — one generation, one body, one place to set a breakpoint.

steps.label: Net effect
steps.text: Compile-time work drops from 3 generations to 1; the program binary is unchanged, because the linker already merged the duplicates.

examples.result: The explicit-instantiation-declaration pattern is a build-time and code-discipline tool, not a size tool — you save redundant generation, not bytes.

examples.title: Working through template instantiation
examples.problem: How compilers generate code. Your task: list the contexts that trigger implicit instantiation of class and function templates.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: list the contexts that trigger implicit instantiation of class and function templates. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Classes instantiate where a complete type is required; functions when called or addressed — never for a mere pointer or extern declaration.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `extern template class std::vector<int>;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — state the point-of-instantiation rules for classes and functions — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: POI: immediately before the namespace-scope use for a class; end of the translation unit for a called function template. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Classes instantiate where a complete type is required; functions when called or addressed — never for a mere pointer or extern declaration. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Classes instantiate where a complete type is required; functions when called or addressed — never for a mere pointer or extern declaration.
POI: immediately before the namespace-scope use for a class; end of the translation unit for a called function template.
`template class Vector<int>;` forces generation; `extern template class Vector<int>;` promises it lives elsewhere — one generation instead of many.

quiz.q: What does `Vector<int>* p = nullptr;` alone cause?
options: Full instantiation of `Vector<int>` and its members
Instantiation of only the declaration-related members
Nothing — a pointer does not require the complete type
quiz.explanation: Naming a pointer to an instantiation needs no object layout, so the compiler is not required to instantiate the class there.

quiz.q: As this chapter models it, the point of instantiation of a function template called in a translation unit is:
options: immediately after the enclosing declaration, or the end of the translation unit
in the header where the template was declared
quiz.explanation: The end-of-TU rule is what lets a function template be defined below its caller in the same file; class templates, by contrast, instantiate before their use.

quiz.q: A header contains `extern template class Vector<int>;` and exactly one .cpp contains `template class Vector<int>;`. Ten other translation units use `Vector<int>`. How many times is the heavy member code generated?
options: One — in the dedicated .cpp; the others reuse it
Zero — the linker generates it on demand
quiz.explanation: The instantiation declaration suppresses implicit generation in the users; the single explicit instantiation in the dedicated file is the one generation.

quiz.q: `Vector<T>` contains a member `draw_3d()` with a syntax error, but no instantiation ever uses it. The error:
options: is reported when the template is defined
is reported only in debug builds
quiz.explanation: Weak checking: unused members are never instantiated, so their bodies are never fully checked.

intro: The hard question: a template is defined once but used with types defined elsewhere, by code written elsewhere, in files that may not exist when the template is written — so which declaration does each name in the template body refer to? The answer composes from exactly **four contexts** and deliberately excludes the place where the template happens to be *used*: templates are not macros. The masters tier below formalizes the two-phase lookup and ADL machinery that makes this work.
objectives: Classify names in a template as dependent or non-dependent and state when each binds
List the four contexts template names can come from — and the excluded fifth
Use `typename`, `.template`, and `this->` to make dependent names resolvable

concepts.statement: A name is **dependent** if its meaning could change with a template parameter — `T::value_type`, `f(t)` with `T t`, `obj.m` where `obj` has a type that depends on a parameter. Everything else is **non-dependent**. Dependent names are resolved at instantiation; non-dependent names are bound **at the definition** and never re-bound.
concepts.detail: The classification is made once, at the definition, and it decides everything that follows.

concepts.statement: A name in a template can come from: **(1)** the template's own declarations — parameters, members, locals; **(2)** the scope of the template **definition** — enclosing namespaces and globals, where non-dependent names bind; **(3)** the **dependent base classes** — members of `B<T>`, reachable only via `this->` or qualification; **(4)** the **declaration contexts of the template arguments** — the namespaces of the argument types, reached for dependent calls by **ADL** (argument-dependent lookup). The point of use is not on the list.
concepts.detail: Deliberate design: a template's meaning is fixed by its definition plus its arguments — so it means the same thing in every translation unit that uses it.

concepts.term: Non-dependent names bind at the definition
concepts.statement: **A non-dependent name binds to the declarations visible where the template is defined — permanently.** A global `g()` visible at the template's definition is what `g()` means inside it, in every instantiation, no matter what other `g` exists at any call site. This is exactly what distinguishes templates from macros: no capture by the point of use.
concepts.detail: If you need a template to use something declared later, declare it before the template — or make it reachable through the arguments.

concepts.statement: The compiler cannot know whether the dependent qualified name `T::iterator` names a type or a static member until instantiation — so **you must say**: `typename T::iterator it;` declares a variable. Likewise `obj.template f<int>()` tells the parser that the dependent `f` is a template, so the `<` starts an argument list rather than a comparison.
concepts.detail: A dependent name is assumed to name a value unless it is qualified by `typename` (for types) or `template` (for member templates).

concepts.statement: Unqualified lookup **does not search a base class that depends on a template parameter** — at definition time that base could be specialized to anything. In `template<class T> struct Derived : Base<T> { void g() { draw(); } };` the call to `draw()` fails — write `this->draw();` (or `Base<T>::draw();`, or a `using Base<T>::draw;`) to make the name dependent and resolve it at instantiation against the actual base.
concepts.detail: The `this->` form preserves virtual dispatch; the qualified `Base<T>::draw()` form disables it — choose deliberately.

figures.caption: The four binding contexts for a name used inside a template: the template's own declarations, the definition scope (non-dependent names — phase 1), the dependent bases (reached through `this->`), and the argument declarations (reached by ADL — phase 2). The point of use — where a template happens to be called — is never consulted: that is what makes a template mean the same thing everywhere.
