examples.title: Tracing operator<< through the two phases
examples.problem: Namespace `Geo` declares `class Coord` and `std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream&, const Coord&)`. Separately, someone writes `template<class T> void dump(const T& t) { std::cout << t; }`. A user calls `dump(c)` for a `Geo::Coord`. Why does the call compile, although `operator<<` for `Coord` is visible neither inside `dump` nor in namespace `std`?

steps.label: Phase 1 — at dump's definition
steps.text: `std::cout` is non-dependent: it binds to the `std::ostream` object declared in `<iostream>`. But `std::cout << t` has a dependent argument `t`, so the operator name is **not** bound yet — the call is postponed.

steps.label: Phase 2 — at the instantiation
steps.text: With `T = Geo::Coord`, the candidate set is ordinary lookup at the definition context (no `std` operator accepts a `Coord`) together with ADL over the arguments' associated entities.

steps.label: ADL computes the associates
steps.text: The left argument `std::ostream` associates namespace `std`; the right argument `const Geo::Coord&` associates namespace `Geo` — the innermost enclosing namespace of the class.

steps.label: Resolution
steps.text: `Geo::operator<<(std::ostream&, const Coord&)` is the unique candidate, and the call binds to it.

examples.result: The template author never mentioned `Geo`; the author of `Coord` never mentioned the template; the call resolves anyway — that is the ADL contract.

examples.title: Working through name binding
examples.problem: Where names come from in templates. Your task: classify names in a template as dependent or non-dependent and state when each binds.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: classify names in a template as dependent or non-dependent and state when each binds. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Non-dependent names bind at the definition and never change; dependent names resolve at each instantiation.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `extern template class std::vector<int>;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — list the four contexts template names can come from — and the excluded fifth — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: The four contexts: the template itself, the definition scope, dependent bases (via `this->`), and the arguments’ namespaces (via ADL) — never the point of use. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Non-dependent names bind at the definition and never change; dependent names resolve at each instantiation. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Non-dependent names bind at the definition and never change; dependent names resolve at each instantiation.
The four contexts: the template itself, the definition scope, dependent bases (via `this->`), and the arguments' namespaces (via ADL) — never the point of use.
`typename`, `.template`, and `this->` exist because the compiler cannot classify dependent names until instantiation — you must annotate them.

quiz.q: A template is defined with a global `void g()` visible at its definition. A user's translation unit declares its own `void g(int)` and then instantiates the template, whose body calls `g()`. Which `g` is called?
options: The user's `g(int)`, because it is closer to the use
The global `g()` visible at the definition
quiz.explanation: The name is non-dependent, so it was bound at the definition, permanently — the point of use cannot rebind it.

quiz.q: Inside a template, `T::iterator` must be named as a type in a declaration. The correct spelling is:
quiz.explanation: Until instantiation the compiler cannot know that the dependent qualified name names a type; `typename` says so.

quiz.q: In `template<class T> struct D : B<T> { void g() { draw(); } };` the call to `draw()` fails to compile. Why?
options: Unqualified lookup never searches a base that depends on a template parameter
quiz.explanation: At definition time the dependent base is an unknown specialization, so unqualified lookup skips it — write `this->draw();` to resolve at instantiation.

quiz.q: ADL finds `Geo::operator<<(std::ostream&, const Coord&)` because:
options: the operator is declared in the same namespace as `Coord`, an argument of the dependent call
the template definition includes a Geo header
the linker searches all translation units
quiz.explanation: For a dependent call, the associated namespaces of the argument types are searched — `Coord`'s namespace is `Geo`, where the operator lives.

depth.title: Two-phase lookup and argument-dependent lookup, formally

blocks.body: The designer's problem: a template must be checked as strictly as ordinary code, yet work with types its author never saw — and mean the same thing in every translation unit that uses it. Two-phase lookup is the resolution. Every name in a template is classified at the definition as **dependent** (its meaning could vary with a template parameter) or **non-dependent**. Non-dependent names get one meaning, fixed forever at the definition. Dependent names get a meaning *composed* at each instantiation from exactly two ingredients: the definition context and the declaration contexts of the arguments. The point of use is excluded by construction — precisely the property macros lack, and the reason a template can be maintained independently of its users.

blocks.heading: The two-phase lookup theorem
blocks.body: Let $N$ be a name used in a template $F$ with parameters $T_1, \dots, T_n$. **Phase 1, at the definition of $F$:** $F$ is checked for syntactic well-formedness; every name is classified as dependent or non-dependent; every non-dependent name is looked up against the declarations visible at the definition and **bound permanently**. **Phase 2, at each instantiation `F<A1, ..., An>`:** each dependent name is resolved anew — a qualified name `Q::m` is looked up in the scope that the (now concrete) `Q` denotes, and an unqualified function name in a dependent call is looked up by the ordinary lookup rules *restricted to the definition context*, together with **argument-dependent lookup** over the associated namespaces and classes of the argument types. A non-dependent call uses only phase 1's binding. No lookup consults the lexical context of the use, the point of instantiation, or anything else.

blocks.heading: Why the point of use is powerless
blocks.body: Declare `int a = 0;` at namespace scope, then `template<class T> void bump() { ++a; }`, then user code that declares its own `double a = 3.14;` before calling `bump<int>()`. The `a` inside `bump` was bound at the definition — to the global `int` — and phase 2 cannot rebind it, because `a` is not dependent. The user's `a` is never a candidate. Contrast a macro: `#define BUMP() (++a)` expands where it is used and captures whatever `a` is in scope there. This exclusion is the entire difference in maintainability between templates and preprocessor tricks — and the reason the standard forbids a template's meaning to depend on where it is instantiated. To influence a template, you must be in its definition's scope or be one of its arguments; there is no third door.

blocks.heading: Computing the associated entities
blocks.body: For a call $f(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ whose name is unqualified, ADL computes, for each argument's type $X_i$, its **associated entities**: a **class type** contributes itself (friends and nested members matter) plus its innermost enclosing namespace, plus, recursively, the associated entities of every base class; a **class template specialization** contributes the entities of the template's own declaration plus those of each template argument; an **enumeration** contributes its enclosing class (if a member) or its innermost enclosing namespace; **pointers and arrays** contribute their pointee's or element's entities, and a **function type** the union over its parameters and return type. The candidate set for the call is the union of ordinary lookup (for dependent calls, restricted to the definition context) and every function found in those entities. Worked: for `Geo::Coord` the associated set is exactly {Geo}; for `std::vector<Geo::Coord>` it is {std, Geo} — so a call `f(v)` on such a vector searches *both* namespaces even though the caller never named either.

blocks.heading: The swap two-step — the idiom ADL forces
blocks.body: Suppose `Big_matrix` holds $10{,}000$ doubles — $80{,}000$ bytes — behind two members and is copy-only. The generic `std::swap` performs three copies: $3 \times 80{,}000 = 240{,}000$ bytes of traffic. Its author writes `swap(Big_matrix&, Big_matrix&)` next to the class, exchanging the two 16-byte handles: about 48 bytes moved. Now compare spellings inside a generic algorithm. `std::swap(a, b)` is a *qualified* call: resolved entirely within `std`, no ADL — the compiler silently picks the $240{,}000$-byte version. `using std::swap; swap(a, b);` puts the generic into the definition context, and the unqualified call lets ADL contribute the author's version, which overload resolution prefers — a 5,000-fold reduction in bytes moved, from one spelling change. Every customization point in the standard library must be invoked this way.

ADL fires only for unqualified function *calls*. An algorithm that takes a function object — `for_each(b, e, my_fun)` — invokes `my_fun(*p)` as an object's call operator: no namespace search, no surprises, typically inlinable. This is one reason the standard library passes function objects by value and why generic code prefers them to function pointers. A bare overloaded function *name*, by contrast, denotes an entire overload set that template argument deduction cannot narrow — pass it with an explicit type or wrap it in a lambda.

blocks.heading: Designing for the model
blocks.body: Three habits make two-phase lookup work for you rather than against you. **(1) Keep a type and its operations in one namespace** — ADL binds them into any template that receives the type; this is how `operator<<`, `swap`, and `begin`/`end` are found. **(2) Expose customization points the way `std` does**: call unqualified, after a `using`-declaration of your general fallback, so the caller's better match wins by ADL. **(3) When a template must use an operation the argument type may not have, take the operation as an explicit parameter** (a policy object or a function argument) rather than hunting for it — explicit beats implicit, and the failure becomes a clear "no such parameter" instead of a lookup mystery. The C++20 ranges library formalized (2) as customization point objects; the underlying lookup semantics are unchanged.

intro: The binding rules reward a small, explicit vocabulary of habits: minimize what a template needs, make the remaining needs findable, and follow the customization-point idiom when you write generic code yourself. Diagnosing failures gets easy once you ask which phase the error came from.
objectives: Apply the minimum-dependency rule when designing templates
Use the customization-point idiom in your own generic code
Diagnose the two classic binding failures by the phase they occur in

concepts.statement: **The fewer names a template uses, the more types it works with** — and the fewer name-binding surprises it can have. Declare everything the template needs *before* the definition, or make it reachable through the arguments. Every name is a type requirement in disguise.
concepts.detail: This is the same discipline that makes algorithms in the standard library work with minimal iterator requirements.

concepts.statement: **If a template needs an operation on its argument type, put that operation where ADL will find it: in the same namespace as the type.** Do not rely on a global function that happens to be visible in your header — that works today and breaks when the header is included from somewhere else.
concepts.detail: Co-locating a type with its operations is not style; it is what makes the phase-2 lookup succeed for every user.

concepts.statement: In generic code, invoke customizable operations as `using std::swap; swap(a, b);` — the `using` supplies the general fallback into the definition context, and the unqualified call lets ADL find a better match from the argument's namespace. A qualified `std::swap(a, b)` disables this and silently picks the generic.
concepts.detail: Whatever your library's equivalent of `swap` is, the same two-line shape applies.

concepts.statement: **A template error at definition time is a non-dependent problem** — a misspelled or undeclared name, a missing header. **An error at instantiation time involves a dependent name** — the argument type is missing something: a missing `typename`, a missing `this->`, a missing operation.
concepts.detail: Read the error's location first, the message second; the phase tells you which half of the model to suspect.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Minimize the names a template uses — each one is a type requirement in disguise.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: Diagnosing the dependent-base failure
examples.problem: `template<class T> struct Base { void draw() const; };` and `template<class T> struct Derived : Base<T> { void report() { draw(); } };` fail to compile with "draw was not declared in this scope". Why, and what are the fixes?

steps.label: Why it fails
steps.text: At `Derived`'s definition, unqualified lookup for `draw` searches `Derived` and the enclosing scopes — but not `Base<T>`, because a base that depends on a template parameter could be specialized to anything, so the compiler refuses to guess.

steps.label: Fix 1 — this->
steps.text: `this->draw();` makes the name dependent: it is resolved at instantiation, against the actual `Base<T>` — and it preserves virtual dispatch if `draw` is virtual.

steps.label: Fix 2 — qualification
steps.text: `Base<T>::draw();` also works, but suppresses virtual dispatch — it always calls the base's version.

steps.label: Fix 3 — using-declaration
steps.text: `using Base<T>::draw;` inside `Derived` brings the name into scope once, keeping later unqualified calls clean.

examples.result: Prefer `this->` for member lookup in template hierarchies: it fixes the lookup and keeps the run-time behavior you expect.

examples.title: Reviewing instantiation code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the minimum-dependency rule when designing templates.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Minimize the names a template uses — each one is a type requirement in disguise.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `extern template class std::vector<int>;`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: use the customization-point idiom in your own generic code. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Customization points are invoked `using std::swap; swap(a, b);` — never `std::swap(a, b)`.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Minimize the names a template uses — each one is a type requirement in disguise. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Minimize the names a template uses — each one is a type requirement in disguise.
Customization points are invoked `using std::swap; swap(a, b);` — never `std::swap(a, b)`.
Definition-time errors mean non-dependent problems; instantiation-time errors mean a dependent name is missing something.

quiz.q: Your generic algorithm needs a swappable type. The correct spelling inside the algorithm is:
quiz.explanation: The `using` puts the general fallback into the definition context; the unqualified call lets ADL find a user version specialized for the argument type. A qualified call would disable ADL.

quiz.q: A name in a template that does not mention any parameter is looked up:
options: at each instantiation, in the caller's scope
at the definition, against the declarations visible there
quiz.explanation: Non-dependent names bind at the definition, permanently — this is what makes templates independent of their points of use.

quiz.q: Calling `Base<T>::draw()` instead of `this->draw()` inside a derived template is risky because:
options: it suppresses virtual dispatch, always calling the base version
it binds at the point of use
quiz.explanation: Qualification names the base's implementation directly — if `draw` is virtual and overridden, the override is bypassed.

intro: C++ gives you two grand mechanisms for making one piece of code serve many needs: **parameterization** — templates, resolved at compile time — and **derivation** — class hierarchies with virtual functions, resolved at run time. They are not rivals but a pair of axes: real designs place the interface in a hierarchy, the implementation in templates, and sometimes use a template parameter *as a base class*. This chapter is about choosing and combining them deliberately.
objectives: Position templates and class hierarchies as the two variation mechanisms of C++
State the cost axis of each mechanism
Name the three combination patterns this chapter develops

concepts.statement: **Parameterization varies behavior at compile time**: all types and values are known during compilation, every call can be statically checked and inlined, and no per-object overhead exists. The cost is paid in code — each argument set can produce a distinct body.
concepts.detail: This is the mechanism of the standard library's containers and algorithms.

concepts.statement: **Derivation varies behavior at run time**: one interface, many implementations, selected by an object's dynamic type through a vtable. The cost is an indirection per call and a vptr per object; the gain is mixing types not known until execution — and substitutability without recompiling call sites.
concepts.detail: This is the mechanism of the classic object-oriented interface hierarchies.

concepts.statement: The chapter's repertoire: **hierarchies whose members are templates** (a template derived from a template or from an instantiation), **templates whose parameters are base classes** (mixins), and the everyday blend — **generic containers of pointers to base classes** (`vector<unique_ptr<Shape>>`).
concepts.detail: Most real systems use all three simultaneously; the skill is knowing which mechanism owns which decision.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Parameterization and hierarchy together. You can claim this section when you can position templates and class hierarchies as the two variation mechanisms of C++ — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 27 (Templates and Hierarchies); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

concepts.statement: Work in three passes. First, state the cost axis of each mechanism. Then, name the three combination patterns this chapter develops. Finally, test the outcome against the section promise: Parameterization varies behavior at compile time; derivation with virtual functions varies it at run time.
concepts.detail: Each pass catches a different class of mistake, and skipping one moves the failure into a larger program where it costs more to diagnose than it would have here.

examples.title: Drawing shapes both ways
examples.problem: A graphics program must draw collections of shapes. Compare the run-time design (`vector<Shape*>` with a virtual `draw()`) against the compile-time design (a template `draw_all` over containers of concrete shapes), for two concrete types `Circle` and `Square`.

steps.label: Run-time path
steps.text: `vector<Shape*> v; for (Shape* p : v) p->draw();` — exactly one loop body is compiled; every call is an indirection through the vtable; the vector can mix circles, squares, and types added later.

steps.label: Compile-time path
steps.text: `draw_all(circles)` and `draw_all(squares)` over a `vector<Circle>` and a `vector<Square>` — two instantiations of `draw_all`, one per element type; every call is direct and inlinable.

steps.label: Accounting
steps.text: Run-time: 1 body + 1 vtable per shape class + 8-byte vptr per object. Compile-time: 2 bodies, 0 bytes per object, no vtables.

steps.label: The real question
steps.text: Are the types of the elements known when the loop is compiled? If the user picks shapes with a mouse at run time, only the virtual design can answer.

examples.result: Same algorithm shape, different economics — the chapter teaches you to pick the mechanism consciously, not by habit.

keyTakeaways: Parameterization varies behavior at compile time; derivation with virtual functions varies it at run time.
The mechanisms compose in both directions: templates over hierarchies, and template parameters as base classes.
The everyday blend is a container template holding pointers to a base class — generic outside, polymorphic inside.

quiz.q: Which mechanism selects among implementations at run time?
quiz.explanation: Only the dynamic dispatch of virtual functions can choose an implementation after the program has started; the other three are compile-time.

quiz.q: A `vector<Shape*>` filled with `Circle`s and `Square`s, drawn through a virtual `draw()`, exercises:
options: both — a template for the container, virtual functions for the elements
quiz.explanation: The container is a class template instantiation; the element behavior is chosen by dynamic type — the standard combination.

quiz.q: A generic algorithm instantiated over N distinct element types produces:
options: one body shared by all N types
one body per call site, always
quiz.explanation: Each distinct set of template arguments can yield a distinct instantiation — the code-growth side of the compile-time mechanism.

intro: The decision rule is refreshingly mechanical. If the exact type is known at compile time, prefer templates: static checking, direct inlinable calls, no per-object cost. If the type is known only at run time — the user picks shapes with a mouse — you need virtual functions: one body, dispatch through a vptr, heterogeneous collections. And one combination is so standard it is the default shape of C++ code: a container template holding pointers to a base class.
objectives: Apply the criterion: templates when the type is known at compile time, virtual functions when it is not
Quantify the costs: per-type bodies and no per-object overhead, versus one body with a vptr and an indirection
Combine the mechanisms: generic containers of base-class pointers

concepts.statement: **When the types are not known until run time, use virtual functions; when they are known at compile time, use templates.** Templates give better type checking and better run-time performance; hierarchies give run-time flexibility and code growth that is independent of the number of types.
concepts.detail: Almost every detailed rule in this chapter is a corollary of this one question: *when is the actual type known?*

concepts.statement: Each distinct set of template arguments can produce a distinct body: an algorithm instantiated over $N$ element types yields up to $N$ code paths (code bloat when unmanaged). In exchange, every call is direct — typically inlined — and objects carry no vptr.
concepts.detail: The standard countermeasure is centralized explicit instantiation (Chapter 26), not abandonment of templates.

concepts.statement: One body per operation and one vtable per class; every object carries a **vptr — 8 bytes on a 64-bit implementation** — and every call is one indirection. The number of derived classes can grow without touching the call sites: run-time substitutability templates cannot offer.
concepts.detail: The vtable itself is tiny by comparison: $k$ virtual functions cost $k$ pointers of static data per class.

concepts.statement: `Circle*` converts to `Shape*`, but **`vector<Circle>` is not a `vector<Shape>`** and does not convert to one: a template demands exact argument types. The standard combination is therefore a container of (smart) pointers to the base: `vector<unique_ptr<Shape>>` — generic container, polymorphic elements.
concepts.detail: The reason is structural: `vector<Shape>` would have to accept elements of size `sizeof(Shape)`, which `Circle` might exceed.

concepts.statement: Use **hierarchies for interfaces** — what varies at run time, must stay binary-stable, or must mix in one container. Use **templates for implementations** — algorithms, containers, policies. The standard library is exactly this shape: iterator interfaces consumed by template algorithms.
concepts.detail: A graphics editor should mirror it: a `Shape` hierarchy for the interface, template algorithms over containers of shapes.

figures.caption: The mechanism matrix. Templates choose implementations at compile time and pay per-type code; virtual functions choose at run time and pay a vptr plus an indirection per object. A template cannot select its own argument at run time — that cell falls back to the hierarchy. CRTP uses a base-class template parameter to obtain static dispatch inside a hierarchy-shaped design.

examples.title: A million points: vptr arithmetic
examples.problem: Compare `struct P { double x, y; };` with `struct VP { virtual void draw() const; double x, y; };` for 1,000,000 objects: memory footprint and the cost of drawing each one.

steps.label: P
steps.text: Two doubles: $2 \times 8 = 16$ bytes per object; a million objects occupy $16{,}000{,}000$ bytes.

steps.label: VP
steps.text: The vptr adds 8 bytes and alignment stays at 8: $8 + 16 = 24$ bytes per object; a million occupy $24{,}000{,}000$ bytes.

steps.label: Difference
steps.text: $8{,}000{,}000$ bytes — 50% more memory, spent entirely on the vptr that enables run-time dispatch.

steps.label: Calls
steps.text: A template `draw(p)` resolves to a direct, inlinable call; `p->draw()` on `VP` loads the vptr, loads the vtable slot, and jumps indirectly.

examples.result: When the type is known at compile time, the template path saves the vptr and the indirection; when it is not, the 8 bytes and the indirection are the price of run-time choice.

examples.title: Working through parameterization and hierarchy
examples.problem: Choosing templates or virtual functions. Your task: apply the criterion: templates when the type is known at compile time, virtual functions when it is not.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: apply the criterion: templates when the type is known at compile time, virtual functions when it is not. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Templates: compile-time choice, better checking, inlinable calls; code grows with the number of argument sets.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<typename Base> struct Logged : Base { };` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — quantify the costs: per-type bodies and no per-object overhead, versus one body with a vptr and an indirection — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Virtual functions: run-time choice, one body per operation, an 8-byte vptr and one indirection per object on 64-bit implementations. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Templates: compile-time choice, better checking, inlinable calls; code grows with the number of argument sets. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Templates: compile-time choice, better checking, inlinable calls; code grows with the number of argument sets.
Virtual functions: run-time choice, one body per operation, an 8-byte vptr and one indirection per object on 64-bit implementations.
`vector<Circle>` is not a `vector<Shape>` — combine via `vector<unique_ptr<Shape>>`: template container, hierarchical elements.

quiz.q: A paint program lets the user select shapes with the mouse at run time and draw them. Which mechanism must the drawing loop use?
options: A template instantiated per shape type
A virtual function call through a base pointer
quiz.explanation: The concrete type is not known until run time — precisely the case virtual dispatch exists for; a template cannot select its argument then.

quiz.q: Why is passing a `vector<Circle>` to a function expecting `vector<Shape>&` an error?
options: Templates require exact argument types — there is no container covariance
Vectors cannot be passed by reference
quiz.explanation: Template arguments do not convert along inheritance paths; the standard workaround is a container of pointers to the base.

quiz.q: On a 64-bit implementation, the per-object price of virtual dispatch is:
options: a vptr of 8 bytes plus an indirection per call
quiz.explanation: Each object carries one vptr (8 bytes); the vtable itself is static data shared by all objects of the class.

quiz.q: Which is a cost that grows with the number of *element types*, rather than with the number of classes?
quiz.explanation: Each distinct set of template arguments can yield a distinct body — instantiation count grows with argument sets, not with the class hierarchy.

intro: Hierarchies can be built out of templates in three classic shapes: derive an ordinary class from a specific instantiation (`class D : public B<int>`), derive a template from a template (`D2<T>` from `B<T>`), and derive from a base supplied as a **template parameter** — which turns the base class itself into a policy knob. Virtual functions work inside class templates, with one notable prohibition.
objectives: Write the three derivation forms: from an instantiation, template from template, and from a base parameter
State what virtual-function support is and is not allowed inside class templates
Use a parameterized base class as a compile-time implementation policy

concepts.statement: `class D1 : public B<int> { /* ... */ };` — once instantiated, `B<int>` is an ordinary class, so this is plain derivation: `D1` sees `B<int>`'s public interface, and a `D1*` converts to `B<int>*`.
concepts.detail: Use it to hang a domain-specific class on a general library component without re-parameterizing.

concepts.statement: `template<class T> class D2 : public B<T> { /* ... */ };` — the same argument flows to the base: `D2<int>` derives from `B<int>`, `D2<double>` from `B<double>`. Each instantiation is an independent class with an independent base; they share source, not type.
concepts.detail: This is how class templates extend other class templates without fixing their element type.

concepts.term: The base as a policy parameter
concepts.statement: `template<class T, class Base = std::vector<T>> class Stack : private Base { /* push, pop via the base */ };` — implementation by derivation: swap `vector`, `deque`, or a fixed-size buffer by naming it, with the public interface untouched. The base is part of the type, chosen at compile time and checked where used.
concepts.detail: Derivation used this way is parameterization in disguise — hence the chapter title.

concepts.statement: **Allowed**: a class template may have virtual functions; each instantiation is a distinct class with its own vtable. **Forbidden**: a *member function template* cannot be virtual — the compiler would need a vtable entry for every instantiation of it that could ever exist, which is unknowable.
concepts.detail: Virtual functions and templates compose; virtual function templates do not.

concepts.statement: Inside such hierarchies, conversion follows the instantiated classes: `D2<int>*` converts to `B<int>*`, but nothing relates `D2<int>` to `B<double>` or to `D2<double>` — template arguments do not convert along the way (the same rule that keeps `vector<Circle>` from being a `vector<Shape>`).
concepts.detail: When you need mixed collections, you need a non-template base class — or pointers to one.

examples.title: One stack, three containers — policy arithmetic
examples.problem: Given `template<class T, class Base = std::vector<T>> class Stack : private Base { public: void push(const T& x) { Base::push_back(x); } /* ... */ };`, compare `Stack<int>`, `Stack<int, std::deque<int>>`, and `Stack<int, Fixed<int, 64>>` where `Fixed` is `template<class T, int N> struct Fixed { T buf[N]; int n = 0; };`.

steps.label: Default policy
steps.text: `Stack<int>` with the default base `std::vector<int>`: `sizeof` = 24 bytes on a 64-bit implementation (three machine words) — the empty derived class adds nothing on top of its base.

steps.label: Deque policy
steps.text: `Stack<int, std::deque<int>>`: typically 80 bytes — same public interface, same four operations, different internal structure.

steps.label: Fixed policy
steps.text: `Fixed<int, 64>` holds $64 \times 4 + 4 = 260$ bytes; `Stack<int, Fixed<int, 64>>` is those 260 bytes — a stack whose capacity is now a compile-time fact.

steps.label: What is absent
steps.text: No virtual functions anywhere: `push` calls the base directly — an inlinable call with no vptr in any object.

examples.result: One interface over interchangeable implementations chosen at compile time — derivation used as parameterization.

examples.title: Working through hierarchies of class templates
examples.problem: Template base classes and derived classes. Your task: write the three derivation forms: from an instantiation, template from template, and from a base parameter.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: write the three derivation forms: from an instantiation, template from template, and from a base parameter. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `B<int>` is an ordinary class once instantiated — derive from it directly; `D2<T>` from `B<T>` pairs each derived instantiation with the matching base.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<typename Base> struct Logged : Base { };` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — state what virtual-function support is and is not allowed inside class templates — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Virtual functions live happily in class templates — but a member function template can never be virtual. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `B<int>` is an ordinary class once instantiated — derive from it directly; `D2<T>` from `B<T>` pairs each derived instantiation with the matching base. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `B<int>` is an ordinary class once instantiated — derive from it directly; `D2<T>` from `B<T>` pairs each derived instantiation with the matching base.
Virtual functions live happily in class templates — but a member function template can never be virtual.
Deriving from a template parameter makes the base itself a policy: one `Stack` over `vector`, `deque`, or a fixed buffer.

quiz.q: Given `template<class T> class D2 : public B<T> { /* ... */ };`, the class `D2<double>` derives from:
quiz.explanation: The same argument flows to the base: `D2<double>` is an ordinary class derived from the instantiation `B<double>`.

quiz.q: Which construct is ill-formed inside a class template?
quiz.explanation: A member function template cannot be virtual: the compiler would need a vtable slot for every instantiation of it that could ever appear.

quiz.q: The `Stack` example changes its storage from `vector` to `deque` by:
options: redeclaring the class at run time
quiz.explanation: The base is a template parameter — the policy is part of the type, selected where the type is named.

quiz.q: In the same setup, which conversion is valid?
quiz.explanation: Conversion follows the instantiated classes: `D2<int>` derives from `B<int>`, and template arguments never convert along the way.

intro: The final step in combining the two mechanisms: derive a class from **its own template arguments** — each argument supplies a feature layer, a *mixin*. With variadic templates the core class can take any number of layers; the empty ones cost nothing thanks to the empty-base optimization; and every distinct combination of layers is a distinct, statically-checked type.
objectives: Write a mixin-composed class whose bases are its template parameters
Predict object layouts using the empty-base optimization
Contrast mixin composition with run-time, interface-based composition

concepts.statement: A **mixin** is a small class contributing one feature — data plus the operations on it — composed by deriving a core class from it: `template<class... Bases> class Point : public Bases... { double x, y; /* ... */ };`. `Point<Label, Color>` is a point carrying a label and a color, with every layer's operations available on the whole object.
concepts.detail: The mixin supplies the feature; the core supplies the identity; the composition is the type.

concepts.statement: `class Point : public Bases...` expands the parameter pack into the base-clause list. Bases initialize left-to-right in the order written, with the core members constructed after them; destruction reverses the order. The same base appearing twice in the list is an error — and can be detected by a compile-time check over the pack.
concepts.detail: Ordering matters for layout: `Point<Label, Color>` and `Point<Color, Label>` are different types with different layouts.

concepts.statement: **A base class with no data occupies no storage in its derived class** (implementations apply this universally). `Point<Plain>` — with `struct Plain { };` — is exactly as large as `Point<>`: 16 bytes for the two doubles. This is what makes behavior-only mixins free.
concepts.detail: `std::vector<int>` stays 24 bytes while carrying an allocator for the same reason: the (empty) allocator is a base.

concepts.statement: Each distinct list of bases is a **distinct type**: features are baked in at compile time, every call is direct, and nothing can be added or removed at run time. You trade run-time flexibility for zero dispatch cost and full static checking.
concepts.detail: This is the §27.2 criterion applied at feature granularity rather than element-type granularity.

concepts.statement: The run-time alternative — an interface hierarchy with a virtual function per feature — costs a vptr per object plus an indirection per feature call, but allows any object to mix features at run time. Mixins cost compilation and fix the feature set at compile time.
concepts.detail: Choose by the same question as always: is the feature set known at compile time?

examples.title: The bytes behind Point<Label, Color>
examples.problem: Given `struct Plain { };`, `struct Color { int r, g, b; };`, `struct Label { std::string s; };` (32 bytes on a typical 64-bit implementation), and `template<class... Bases> class Point : public Bases... { double x, y; };`, compute the size of `Point<>`, `Point<Plain>`, `Point<Color>`, and `Point<Label, Color>`.

steps.label: Point<>
steps.text: The two doubles alone: $2 \times 8 = 16$ bytes.

steps.label: Point<Plain>
steps.text: The empty base occupies 0 bytes (empty-base optimization): still 16 bytes — composing a behavior-only mixin changed nothing.

steps.label: Point<Color>
steps.text: The base subobject is 12 bytes; the members need 8-byte alignment, so they land at offset 16 and the total is $16 + 16 = 32$ bytes.

steps.label: Point<Label, Color>
steps.text: Label occupies 32 bytes, Color the next 12 — bases end at offset 44; members align to offset 48, so the total is $48 + 16 = 64$ bytes.

examples.result: Mixins add exactly the data they carry — 16 → 16 → 32 → 64 — and empty ones are free; a comparable interface-based design would add a vptr to every point.

examples.problem: Mixin-style composition. Your task: write a mixin-composed class whose bases are its template parameters.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Empty bases cost nothing (EBO): `Point<Plain>` = `Point<>` = 16 bytes; `std::vector<int>` stays 24 bytes while carrying an allocator. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `template<class... Bases> class Point : public Bases...` composes features at compile time; each list of bases is a distinct type. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `template<class... Bases> class Point : public Bases...` composes features at compile time; each list of bases is a distinct type.
Empty bases cost nothing (EBO): `Point<Plain>` = `Point<>` = 16 bytes; `std::vector<int>` stays 24 bytes while carrying an allocator.
Mixins trade run-time flexibility for zero dispatch cost and full static checking — the §27.2 criterion at feature granularity.

quiz.q: With `class Point { double x, y; };` as the core and `struct Plain { };`, what is `sizeof(Point<Plain>)`?
options: 24 bytes — the base costs a vptr
16 bytes — the empty base costs nothing
Undefined — empty bases are not allowed
quiz.explanation: The empty-base optimization lets an empty base occupy zero storage, so the size equals the core: 2 doubles = 16 bytes.

quiz.q: What happens with `Point<Label, Label>` (the same mixin twice)?
options: The two Labels share their storage
The program is ill-formed — a class cannot be a direct base twice
It works, but the layout is unspecified
quiz.explanation: Specifying the same class as a direct base more than once is an error — one reason to check the pack for duplicates.

quiz.q: When are a mixin's features attached to the object?
options: At run time, when the feature is first used
At compile time — the list of bases is part of the type
quiz.explanation: Mixin composition is a compile-time act: every distinct combination of layers is a distinct class.

quiz.q: `std::vector<int>` remains 24 bytes on a 64-bit implementation despite carrying an allocator because:
options: the allocator is stored in a global table
the allocator is an empty base and the empty-base optimization applies
allocators are not stored at all
vectors store pointers to their allocators
quiz.explanation: The (empty) allocator is a base class of the vector's internal representation; EBO makes it occupy no storage.

intro: A short discipline for using both mechanisms well: match the mechanism to when the type is known, compose interfaces by hierarchy and implementations by template, and watch instantiation growth. When in doubt, the criterion of 27.2 decides — and the numbers confirm it.
objectives: Decide between templates and hierarchies using the type-availability criterion
Apply the division of labor: interfaces by hierarchy, implementations by template
Recognize and control instantiation growth

concepts.term: Match the mechanism to the question
concepts.statement: **Ask first: is the actual type known at compile time?** If yes — templates (static checking, inlining, no vptr). If no — virtual functions (the only mechanism that can choose then). Everything else in the chapter is a corollary of this one question.
concepts.detail: Performance arguments matter, but they follow the criterion; they do not replace it.

concepts.term: Interfaces by hierarchy, implementations by template
concepts.statement: Put the run-time interface — what varies dynamically and must stay stable — into a base class with virtual functions. Put the algorithms and data structures over that interface into templates (`vector<unique_ptr<Shape>>` plus template algorithms). Parameterize policies by base classes when you need compile-time interchange.
concepts.detail: The standard library's own shape: stable iterator interfaces, generic template algorithms.

concepts.statement: Each type combination can generate a distinct body: $N$ element types through a heavy template can mean $N$ heavy bodies. Centralize instantiations with explicit instantiation (Chapter 26) and measure before templating what a virtual call was handling fine.
concepts.detail: Code bloat is real but manageable; unmeasured fear of it is just as damaging as ignoring it.

concepts.term: Shipping rule for templates and hierarchies
concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Ask first: is the actual type known at compile time? Everything else follows.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

concepts.term: Review checklist for templates and hierarchies
concepts.statement: Take the objectives as review questions: decide between templates and hierarchies using the type-availability criterion? Then apply the division of labor: interfaces by hierarchy, implementations by template? Answer each from the code in front of you, not from memory — the gap between the two answers is the review finding.
concepts.detail: A rule you can derive from the chapter you can also correctly suspend; a rule applied without its reason becomes superstition, so cite the reason in the review note.

examples.title: Auditing a design choice
examples.problem: A CAD application redraws about 40,000 shapes of 6 concrete types every frame; the shapes live together in a heterogeneous collection selected by the user. A reviewer proposes replacing the `Shape` hierarchy with a template `draw(const T&)` per concrete type. Evaluate.

steps.label: The criterion
steps.text: The element types are known only at run time — they arrive in a mixed collection chosen by the user — so a per-type template *cannot* be selected at the draw loop. The hierarchy is the right mechanism.

steps.label: What the template version would cost
steps.text: Six separate containers or a `variant` switch, six call sites, more code for identical behavior — and still a run-time dispatch somewhere to find the right one.

steps.label: What the hierarchy costs
steps.text: vptrs: $40{,}000 \times 8 = 320{,}000$ bytes ≈ 0.32 MB; vtables: 6 classes with a handful of virtuals each — a few hundred bytes of static data; one indirect call per draw, negligible next to rasterization.

steps.label: Where templates belong here
steps.text: The math kernel, the container policies, the algorithms over containers of concrete types known at compile time — everywhere the criterion says yes.

examples.result: Keep the hierarchy for drawing; spend templates where the types are compile-time knowledge — the criterion decides, the arithmetic confirms.

examples.title: Reviewing templates and hierarchies code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: decide between templates and hierarchies using the type-availability criterion.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Ask first: is the actual type known at compile time? Everything else follows.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `template<typename Base> struct Logged : Base { };`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: apply the division of labor: interfaces by hierarchy, implementations by template. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Interfaces by hierarchy, implementations by templates; policies by parameterized bases.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Ask first: is the actual type known at compile time? Everything else follows. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Ask first: is the actual type known at compile time? Everything else follows.
Interfaces by hierarchy, implementations by templates; policies by parameterized bases.
Instantiation growth is real: $N$ types through a heavy template can mean $N$ bodies — centralize with explicit instantiation and measure.

quiz.q: The fastest reliable way to decide between a template and a virtual function for an operation is to ask:
options: which one is shorter to write
whether the actual type is known at compile time
whether the class has a destructor
which one the standard library uses more
quiz.explanation: Compile-time knowledge selects the template path (checking, inlining, no vptr); run-time knowledge forces virtual dispatch.

quiz.q: The "standard combination" for storing user-selected polymorphic objects is:
options: a template array of concrete objects
a container template over pointers to a base class
a base class containing a template array
a union of all concrete types
quiz.explanation: `vector<unique_ptr<Shape>>`: the container is generic, the elements are polymorphic — each mechanism doing what it is best at.

quiz.q: A heavy template instantiated for $N$ element types across many translation units risks:
options: $N$ bodies of code bloat unless centralized with explicit instantiation
no risk — the linker deduplicates everything
quiz.explanation: Each argument set can generate its own body; `extern template` declarations and one explicit instantiation keep it to one.

intro: Metaprogramming is programming whose subject is the program itself: code that computes new types, compile-time constants, or decisions about which definitions exist, all before the program ever runs. C++ does this with the template system — a language of types and constant expressions running inside the compiler — plus constexpr, which lets ordinary functions execute at compile time. Done well, it moves work and errors from run time to compile time: a units system that rejects meters-plus-seconds, a tuple whose element types are computed, a standard library that adapts itself to its element types. Done badly, it produces incomprehensible error messages and hour-long builds. This chapter is about doing it well.
objectives: Explain what can be computed at compile time: values, types, and which definitions exist
Recognize metaprogramming already at work in the standard library: `tuple`, `array`, type traits, container internals
Weigh the benefits — type safety, performance, expressiveness — against compile-time cost and opaque error messages

concepts.statement: **Metaprogramming is computation about programs.** A C++ metaprogram computes types, values and code selections during compilation; its results are ordinary declarations and constants in the final program. Templates (types and non-type arguments, specialization) and constant expressions (`constexpr`) are the machinery.
concepts.detail: The two halves: computing values — where a `constexpr` function reads like normal code — and computing types or selecting declarations, where templates are unavoidable. Stroustrup's aim for the chapter is techniques that raise the level of abstraction without losing type safety or performance.

concepts.statement: **A metaprogram can produce (1) a value, (2) a type, or (3) a choice among declarations.** Values come from `constexpr` functions and template constants; types come from type functions (templates with nested `::type`); declaration selection comes from overload resolution steered by `enable_if` and friends.
concepts.detail: The whole chapter is an elaboration of these three: sections 28.2–28.3 build the value and type machinery, 28.4 selects declarations, 28.5–28.6 assemble heterogeneous lists of arbitrary length, and 28.7 puts it all to work catching physical unit errors.

concepts.statement: **Template instantiation with recursion and specialization can compute anything an ordinary program can — with compile time and compiler memory as the only budget.** Compilers therefore cap instantiation depth (commonly around 1024 levels) as a safety valve.
concepts.detail: Turing-completeness is a fact, not a license: the chapter's recurring discipline is to use the simplest mechanism that computes what you need, because compile time is real time and deep template machinery taxes every rebuild of every user.

concepts.statement: **You metaprogram every day without writing templates:** `std::tuple` is a compile-time heterogeneous list; `std::array` takes its size as a template argument; `std::common_type` computes arithmetic result types; every container's internal machinery (allocator handling, iterator traits, `enable_if`-based constraints) is metaprogramming working for you.
concepts.detail: The chapter rebuilds small versions of exactly these artifacts — a tuple, units, conditional definitions — to show that the machinery inside the standard library is learnable, not magic.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Computation at compile time. You can claim this section when you can explain what can be computed at compile time: values, types, and which definitions exist — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 28 (Metaprogramming); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: A first metaprogram: compile-time factorial
examples.problem: Compute 10! during compilation, and make any wrong constant refuse to compile.

steps.label: The constexpr function
steps.text: `constexpr int fac(int n) { return n > 1 ? n * fac(n - 1) : 1; }` — called with constant arguments, the compiler evaluates the recursion right there; when called with run-time arguments, the same code runs at run time. One definition, two lives.

steps.label: Use it in a constant expression
steps.text: `static_assert(fac(10) == 3628800);` — the compiler performs the whole recursion while instantiating nothing and emitting no code. A wrong value is a compile-time error, not a failed test.

steps.label: Know the limits
steps.text: The machine arithmetic, not the technique, is the limit: `fac(12) == 479001600` is the largest that fits a 32-bit `int` (2,147,483,647); `fac(13)` would need 6,227,020,800 and overflows.

steps.label: Why not a template?
steps.text: A `Factorial<N>` template computes the same number (section 28.3) but only for constant N and at the cost of N instantiations — the `constexpr` function is the chapter's preferred tool for pure value computation.

examples.result: fac(10) = 3,628,800, computed entirely by the compiler; the `static_assert` documents the value and enforces it forever.

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: Computation at compile time. Your task: explain what can be computed at compile time: values, types, and which definitions exist.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: explain what can be computed at compile time: values, types, and which definitions exist. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Metaprogramming computes values, types and declaration choices at compile time via templates and `constexpr`.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<bool B, typename T, typename F> struct Pick;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — recognize metaprogramming already at work in the standard library: `tuple`, `array`, type traits, container internals — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: The payoff: errors like adding meters to seconds become compile-time errors, and work moves from run time to build time. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Metaprogramming computes values, types and declaration choices at compile time via templates and `constexpr`. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Metaprogramming computes values, types and declaration choices at compile time via templates and `constexpr`.
The payoff: errors like adding meters to seconds become compile-time errors, and work moves from run time to build time.
The costs are real: compile time, template-depth limits, and famously impenetrable error messages — prefer the simplest mechanism that works.

quiz.q: Metaprogramming in C++ computes, at compile time:
options: types, values, and which declarations exist
quiz.explanation: The three results of template metaprogramming: a value, a type, or a selection among declarations.

quiz.q: Which is a genuine benefit of metaprogramming argued in this chapter?
options: It removes the need for templates
Dimension errors like adding meters to seconds are rejected before the program runs
quiz.explanation: Compile-time checking of program invariants — units being the flagship example of section 28.7 — is the benefit worth paying for.

quiz.q: The statement `static_assert(fac(10) == 3628800);` demonstrates that:
options: fac runs in a separate thread
the compiler evaluated the call before the program exists
the value is checked at run time
quiz.explanation: A static_assert requires a constant expression: the compiler must have computed fac(10) already, and a wrong value would break the build.

intro: An ordinary function takes values and returns values. A type function takes types — and possibly values — and returns types or values computed from them. They are the vocabulary of metaprogramming: given an iterator, what is the type it points to? Given two numeric types, what should their arithmetic use? C++ expresses type functions as class templates with nested names, made palatable by alias templates; the standard library ships a whole library of them in `<type_traits>` and `iterator_traits`. This section builds a few by hand to see the machinery, then points at the standard ones.
objectives: Define type functions as templates with nested `::type` or `::value` members, and call them through alias templates
Implement type functions with template specialization, for example removing references
Use the standard type functions from `<type_traits>` and `iterator_traits`

concepts.statement: **A type function maps types (and values) to types or values, computed at compile time by a template.** The canonical shapes: a class template with a nested `type` (a 'metafunction returning a type') or a nested `value` ('returning a value').
concepts.detail: You have used one since day one: `iterator_traits<Iter>::value_type` maps any iterator to its element type. Type functions are how generic code asks questions about its arguments that cannot be asked any other way.
`Remove_ref<int&>::type` matches the `T&` case with `T = int`, so it is `int`. This is exactly how the standard `std::remove_reference` (and much of `<type_traits>`) is built.

concepts.term: Alias templates make type functions usable
concepts.statement:
**An alias template hides the `typename ... ::type` noise:**
```
template<typename T>
using Remove_ref_t = typename Remove_ref<T>::type;
```
Now `Remove_ref_t<int&>` is a plain type name users can write without remembering the `typename`.
concepts.detail: The standard library adopted this convention in C++14 — `std::remove_reference_t`, `std::enable_if_t` — precisely because it makes type functions read like functions. This is one of the few metaprogramming habits with no downside.

concepts.statement: **A type predicate is a type function returning a truth value.** Class form: a nested `value` of type `std::integral_constant<bool,b>` (e.g. `std::is_integral<T>::value`); function form: `template<typename A, typename B> constexpr bool Same() { return std::is_same<A,B>::value; }`.
concepts.detail: The function form reads better in conditions — `if (Same<T,int>())` — and Stroustrup prefers it in presentation code; the class form is what composes with other templates and what `<type_traits>` ships.

concepts.statement: **Reach for `<type_traits>` before writing your own:** `remove_reference`, `decay`, `conditional<B,A,F>`, `common_type`, `enable_if` — plus `iterator_traits` for iterators, a specialization-backed facade that works for class iterators and raw pointers alike.
concepts.detail: `std::conditional<std::is_signed<T>::value, long, unsigned>::type` picks a type; `std::common_type<int,double>::type` is `double`. Hand-rolled versions exist in this chapter to teach the mechanism, not to replace the library.

examples.title: A type function in use: sum any iterator's elements
examples.problem: Write one `sum(first, last)` that returns a variable of the iterator's element type — working for arrays, `vector`, `list` — and check it on real data.

steps.label: Go through a type function
steps.text: `template<typename Iter> using Value_type = typename std::iterator_traits<Iter>::value_type;` — an alias template naming the element type of any iterator.

steps.label: Use it like any type
steps.text: `template<typename Iter> Value_type<Iter> sum(Iter first, Iter last) { Value_type<Iter> s{}; while (first != last) s += *first++; return s; }`

steps.label: Instantiate with a pointer
steps.text: `int a[] {1,2,3,4}; auto s = sum(a, a+4);` — here `Iter` is `int*`, which has no members, so `Iter::value_type` would not compile. But `iterator_traits<int*>` is a specialization that yields `int`, so `s` starts at 0 and the answer is 10.

steps.label: Instantiate with a class iterator
steps.text: The same function called with `std::vector<double>` iterators returns a `double` summing the elements — no overloads, no run-time type machinery, one template.

examples.result: A single generic `sum`: the accumulator's type is computed by a type function, transparently for pointers and class iterators alike.

examples.title: Working through type functions
examples.problem: Computing on types. Your task: define type functions as templates with nested `::type` or `::value` members, and call them through alias templates.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — implement type functions with template specialization, for example removing references — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: The computation is specialization: primary template as default, partial specializations as pattern-matched cases. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

keyTakeaways: Type functions are templates with nested `::type` (types) or `::value` (values); alias templates (`using X_t = ...`) are their user-friendly spelling.
The computation is specialization: primary template as default, partial specializations as pattern-matched cases.
The standard library ships the common cases in `<type_traits>` and `iterator_traits` — use them before rolling your own.

quiz.q: `std::iterator_traits<int*>::value_type` is:
quiz.explanation: A specialization of the trait for raw pointers yields the pointed-to type, which is exactly why generic algorithms work on arrays.

quiz.q: With `template<typename T> using R = typename Remove_ref<T>::type;` (the two-specialization version), what does `R<int&>` name?
quiz.explanation: The `T&` partial specialization matches with `T = int`, and its `type` is the bare `int`.

quiz.q: Which specialization matches `Remove_ref<int&&>`?
quiz.explanation: The rvalue-reference pattern is the most specialized match for an rvalue reference type.

quiz.q: By the standard library convention, a type predicate exposes its result as:
options: a nested `::value` usable in constant expressions (derived from `std::integral_constant`)
quiz.explanation: `std::is_integral<T>::value` and friends are `integral_constant`s that work in template arguments, static_asserts and other constant expressions.

intro: A metaprogram needs selection and repetition just like any program, but the machine it runs on is the compiler: selection is specialization matching, and iteration is recursion that terminates at a specialization. Modern C++ softens this — constexpr functions give ordinary `if` and loops for value computation, and `if constexpr` selects at compile time inside normal-looking code. The chapter's discipline throughout is economy: use the simplest mechanism that computes what you need, and stop.
objectives: Select between types with specializations, `std::conditional`, and `if constexpr`
Drive compile-time recursion to a base-case specialization, and say what stops it
Choose the simplest mechanism: constexpr functions for values, templates only when types are involved

concepts.detail: `Select<(sizeof(T) > 4), T, long>::type` grows the arithmetic type when `T` is small: a decision made during compilation with zero run-time trace. `if constexpr` is the modern, readable spelling for code selection; the class template remains the tool when a TYPE is the result.

concepts.statement:
**A template refers to itself with a smaller argument; a specialization halts the chain**
```
template<unsigned long N>
struct Factorial { static constexpr unsigned long value = N * Factorial<N-1>::value; };
template<>
struct Factorial<0> { static constexpr unsigned long value = 1; };
```
concepts.detail: Instantiating `Factorial<5>` forces `Factorial<4>`, which forces `Factorial<3>`... down to the base case `Factorial<0>`; then the values fold back up. The recursion happens in the compiler's instantiation machinery — the program contains only the final constants.

concepts.statement: **Every level of template recursion is a class the compiler must instantiate, check and (usually) emit metadata for.** Compilers cap instantiation depth — commonly around 1024 — and deep chains inflate compile times and memory even when legal.
concepts.detail: A compile-time loop over a million values belongs in a `constexpr` function (a loop, not a recursion); template recursion is for when the loop's counter must steer TYPES. The chapter treats compile-time cost as a design constraint, not an afterthought.

concepts.statement: **Stroustrup's rule of thumb: compute values with constexpr functions; use template metaprogramming when — and only when — the result must be a type or must select a declaration.**
concepts.detail: A factorial as a constexpr function is shorter, reads like code, and reuses the same code at run time for a dynamic `n`. The template version exists to be composed with other templates — that is its only excuse.

concepts.statement: **Control Structures.** Compile-time selection and recursion. You can claim this section when you can select between types with specializations, `std::conditional`, and `if constexpr` — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 28 (Metaprogramming); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Unroll the metaprogram: Factorial<5>
examples.problem: List the instantiations the compiler performs for `Factorial<5>::value`, and the values computed.

steps.label: Force the chain
steps.text: `Factorial<5>::value` writes `5 * Factorial<4>::value`; to know that, the compiler must instantiate `Factorial<4>`, which needs `Factorial<3>`, then `Factorial<2>`, then `Factorial<1>`, then `Factorial<0>`.

steps.label: The base case stops it
steps.text: `Factorial<0>` is a full specialization; its `value` is the literal 1, so instantiation ends there: five recursive classes plus one base class.

steps.label: Fold back up
steps.text: Working back outward: `Factorial<1>::value` = 1·1 = 1; `Factorial<2>` = 2·1 = 2; `Factorial<3>` = 3·2 = 6; `Factorial<4>` = 4·6 = 24; `Factorial<5>` = 5·24 = 120.

steps.label: Verify at zero cost
steps.text: `static_assert(Factorial<5>::value == 120);` — and the emitted program contains the single constant 120, no classes, no calls.

examples.result: `Factorial<5>::value == 120`: five recursive instantiations, one base case, one constant in the binary.

examples.title: Working through control structures
examples.problem: Compile-time selection and recursion. Your task: select between types with specializations, `std::conditional`, and `if constexpr`.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: select between types with specializations, `std::conditional`, and `if constexpr`. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Selection at compile time: specializations for types, `std::conditional`, or `if constexpr` for code.

steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `template<bool B, typename T, typename F> struct Pick;` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — drive compile-time recursion to a base-case specialization, and say what stops it — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify

keyTakeaways: Selection at compile time: specializations for types, `std::conditional`, or `if constexpr` for code.
Repetition at compile time is recursion that must terminate at a base-case specialization — and every level costs the compiler.
Reach for constexpr functions when a value is wanted; templates only when types or declaration choices are the result.

quiz.q: What terminates compile-time recursion in a template like `Factorial<N>`?
options: a full specialization supplying the base case
quiz.explanation: A full (or partial) specialization that does not refer to itself is the stop condition; depth limits only catch the failure to provide one.

quiz.q: `std::conditional<false, int, double>::type` is:
quiz.explanation: Conditional picks the third argument when the condition is false — here `double`.

quiz.q: You need a compile-time VALUE (not a type) from simple recursive arithmetic. The chapter's advice is to first reach for:
quiz.explanation: Values are what constexpr functions are for; the template version only pays when types or declaration selection are involved.

quiz.q: Instantiating `Factorial<1000>` with only `Factorial<0>` as a base case will most likely:
options: hit the compiler's template instantiation depth limit (or consume enormous compile time)
be fine — a thousand small classes is nothing
quiz.explanation: 999 levels of instantiation is at or beyond most compilers' default depth caps, and is slow even when allowed.

options: `double`, because both branches are instantiated into the result
`int`, because the boolean selects the first branch at compile time
The alias is ill-formed: types cannot be computed
`bool`, because the condition value leaks into the result
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is a type alias computed from a boolean and two candidate types. Step 2: The governing rule is compiler-time selection: `conditional<B, T, F>::type` names `T` when `B` is true and `F` otherwise, with no runtime branch involved. Step 3: Tracing the computation, the condition is `true`, so the nested `type` names `int`, and `T` becomes a plain alias for `int`. Step 4: The distractors fail because selection discards the unused branch from the result, type computation is the entire subject of metaprogramming, and the boolean never becomes part of the named type. Step 5: Therefore `T` is `int`.

intro: Sometimes the right move is not choosing between two definitions but having a definition exist only when a condition holds — switching a declaration on or off. That is conditional definition, and enable_if is its tool: a type function whose member `type` exists only when its predicate is true, so a template written in terms of it silently vanishes from the overload set when the predicate fails. Before C++20 concepts this was the standard library's universal constraining mechanism, and it still explains how constrained interfaces work under the hood.
objectives: Implement `enable_if` from two template declarations and explain why the missing member disqualifies the overload
Constrain function templates with `Enable_if` in the return type
Relate `enable_if` to SFINAE and to the C++20 `requires` clause that supersedes it

concepts.statement: **A declaration that exists only if a compile-time predicate is satisfied.** The mechanism: `enable_if<B, T>` has a member `type` if and only if `B` is true — when `B` is false there simply is no such member, and any use of it is an error.
concepts.detail: Used bare, that error stops the compilation. Used inside a template signature, the error happens during overload-resolution substitution — which, by the SFINAE rule, removes the candidate instead of failing the build.

concepts.statement:
**Two declarations are the whole trick**
```
template<bool B, typename T = void>
struct enable_if {};                    // no ::type when B is false

template<typename T>
struct enable_if<true, T> { using type = T; };
```
The primary template defines nothing; the specialization for `true` defines the member.
concepts.detail: The standard library also provides the palatable alias `std::enable_if_t<B,T>`, and the chapter defines its own: `template<bool B, typename T = void> using Enable_if = typename enable_if<B,T>::type;` — used below exactly as the book uses it.

concepts.statement: **Substitution Failure Is Not An Error:** during overload resolution, if substituting the deduced arguments into a candidate's SIGNATURE fails, that candidate is quietly removed from consideration. The program is ill-formed only if no candidate survives.
concepts.detail: This C++ rule from the earliest standards is what `enable_if` rides on: the failure must occur in the immediate context of the substitution (a missing member like `enable_if<false>::type`), not in the function body — body errors remain ordinary errors.

concepts.statement:
**Use `Enable_if` as the return type to give each overload a condition**
```
template<typename T>
constexpr Enable_if<std::is_signed<T>::value, T>
abs(T x) { return x < 0 ? -x : x; }

template<typename T>
constexpr Enable_if<std::is_unsigned<T>::value, T>
abs(T x) { return x; }
```
concepts.detail: For any `T`, at most one of these declarations exists — no ambiguity is possible, and code like `abs(p)` for a pointer `p` is rejected instead of silently doing something strange. An `Enable_if` can also ride in an extra defaulted template parameter when the return type is unavailable (constructors, conversions).

concepts.statement: **C++20 concepts and `requires` clauses say the same thing readably:** `template<typename T> requires std::is_signed_v<T> T abs(T x);` — and the standard library has switched its constraints machinery accordingly.
concepts.detail: Knowing `enable_if` still matters: it is what runs under `std::enable_if`-based libraries you will read for a decade, and it explains precisely why a template 'does not exist' for certain arguments.

examples.title: Selecting abs at compile time
examples.problem: With only the signed and unsigned `Enable_if` overloads above, trace the calls `abs(-7)`, `abs(7u)` and `abs(3.5)`.

steps.label: abs(-7)
steps.text: `T = int`; `std::is_signed<int>::value` is true, so the first overload exists and computes `-(-7) = 7`. For the second overload the substitution fails — `enable_if<false>` has no `::type` — and SFINAE drops it silently.

steps.label: abs(7u)
steps.text: `T = unsigned`; the roles swap: the unsigned overload exists and returns 7u unchanged (an unsigned value is never negative), and the signed one vanishes.

steps.label: abs(3.5)
steps.text: `T = double` — `is_signed<double>` is false (it is a floating type, not a signed integer) and `is_unsigned<double>` is false as well. BOTH overloads disappear, and the call is ill-formed: a clear error at the call site, before any code runs.

steps.label: Extending the set
steps.text: Adding `template<typename T> constexpr Enable_if<std::is_floating_point<T>::value, T> abs(T x) { return x < 0 ? -x : x; }` completes the family — conditional definitions compose side by side.

examples.result: Each call finds exactly one abs; a type nobody thought of fails compilation with 'no matching function' rather than computing nonsense at run time.

SFINAE — substitution failure in the immediate context of a candidate signature drops the candidate — is the rule that makes conditional definition work.
C++20 `requires` clauses express the same constraints readably; `Enable_if` remains the machinery to understand.

quiz.q: `enable_if<false, T>` is a class with:
options: no member `type` — so using it in a template signature is a substitution failure
quiz.explanation: The primary template is empty; only the `true` specialization defines `type`. Absence of the member is the entire mechanism.

quiz.q: SFINAE means that during overload resolution:
options: a substitution failure in a candidate's signature quietly drops that candidate from the overload set
the first overload declared always wins
quiz.explanation: Failure in the immediate context of substitution removes only that candidate; a hard error occurs just if no candidate survives.
