intro: A tuple is the canonical metaprogram: a heterogeneous list whose length and element types are known only at compile time, so only the template system can build it. The design insight is to treat the tuple as a recursive data structure — head plus tail — exactly like a Lisp list, with each tail stored as a base-class subobject. One declaration and one specialization give storage, construction and copying for lists of any length; access functions then peel heads off by recursion. std::tuple is this idea at industrial strength.
objectives: Define a tuple as a recursive head-and-tail template terminated by an empty base case
Explain why storing the tail as a base-class subobject gives correct layout and what the empty-base optimization buys
Access element N by recursive descent through the base classes

concepts.statement: **A tuple is an ordered heterogeneous sequence whose length is part of its type:** `Tuple<int,double,char>` — three elements, no more, no less. Variadic template parameters make the length a template argument list.
concepts.detail: Where a `vector` is a run-time list of one type, a tuple is a compile-time list of many types: it can never grow, and every element's type and location are known to the compiler while building the program.

`Tuple<int,double,char>` is a head `int` attached to `Tuple<double,char>`, which is a head `double` attached to `Tuple<char>`, which is a head `char` attached to the empty `Tuple<>`. Construction peels the head off the argument list and forwards the rest down the same chain.

concepts.statement: **The tail IS a base-class subobject of the tuple — the class hierarchy and the list structure are the same object.** Each element lives in its own class, and the empty-base optimization makes empty tails free: `Tuple<char>` can be exactly one byte, because `Tuple<>` adds nothing.
concepts.detail: This is the same economy `std::tuple` exploits: stateless element types (empty comparators, empty allocators) occupy no storage when they sit in base subobjects.

`Get<1>::get(t)` casts to the base (dropping one head), then `Get<0>` peels the next one. Every offset is a compile-time constant, so the recursion unrolls to plain member access on a known subobject.

concepts.statement: **`std::make_tuple(1, 2.5, 'x')` builds one; `std::get<1>(t)` reads element 1; `std::get<double>(t)` reads by type; C++17 structured bindings `auto [i, d, c] = t;` destructure it.** The standard version adds perfect forwarding, swap, comparison, `std::tie` — but the storage and access ideas are exactly the ones above.
concepts.detail: Stroustrup's point in building a small tuple first: what looks like magic in the library is two templates and one specialization. The library's work is polish, not different machinery.

figures.caption: The recursive layout of `Tuple<int, double, char>`. examples.title: Build and probe a three-element tuple
examples.problem: Construct `Tuple<int,double,char> t{1, 2.5, 'x'};` and describe its storage, then retrieve each element.

steps.label: Construction cascades
steps.text: The constructor takes `(1, 2.5, 'x')`, stores `head = 1` (an `int`), and forwards `(2.5, 'x')` to the base `Tuple<double,char>`; that one stores `2.5` and forwards `('x')`; `Tuple<char>` stores `x` and forwards `()` to the empty `Tuple<>` — the chain ends.

steps.label: Layout
steps.text: Three subobjects stack up: a `Tuple<>` (empty — the empty-base optimization charges nothing for it) inside `Tuple<char>` inside `Tuple<double,char>` inside `Tuple<int,double,char>`. The class hierarchy and the list are literally the same shape.

steps.label: Access
steps.text: `Get<0>::get(t)` peels the outer head: 1, an `int`. `Get<1>::get(t)` casts down to the `Tuple<double,char>` subobject and peels: 2.5, a `double`. `Get<2>::get(t)` descends twice and peels: `x`, a `char`.

steps.label: Out-of-range is a type error
steps.text: `Get<3>::get(t)` tries to descend past `Tuple<>`, which matches no `Tuple<T,Rest...>` pattern — there is no such subobject, and the program does not compile. The length encoded in the type is enforced by the type system, not by a run-time size check.

examples.result: t holds exactly 1, 2.5 and 'x' in three stacked subobjects; every access compiles to member selection at a compile-time-known offset.

keyTakeaways: A tuple is a compile-time list: head member plus tail base class, terminated by the empty `Tuple<>` specialization.
Inheritance doubles as storage — the tail is a subobject, and the empty-base optimization makes empty tails free.
Element access is a recursive descent through base classes; out-of-range access fails to compile.

quiz.q: `Tuple<int,double,char>` inherits directly from:
quiz.explanation: The tail — everything after the head — is the direct base class: here `Tuple<double,char>`.

quiz.q: The recursion of the tuple design ends at:
quiz.explanation: `Tuple<>` stores nothing and derives from nothing: it is the base case that stops both construction and access.

quiz.q: `Get<1>::get(t)` on `Tuple<int,double,char> t{1,2.5,'x'}` returns:
quiz.explanation: One cast down to the base drops the int head; `Get<0>` then peels the double.

quiz.q: Thanks to the empty-base optimization, `sizeof(Tuple<char>)` can be as small as:
options: sizeof(char) — the empty `Tuple<>` base adds nothing
quiz.explanation: An empty base subobject need not occupy storage, so the whole stack collapses to the single char.

intro: A function that must take any number of arguments of any types needs a mechanism beyond fixed parameter lists: the variadic template, whose ellipsis declares a parameter pack that absorbs zero or more arguments. Packs are expanded by an ellipsis after a pattern — the heart of the feature — and because a pack has no first element, you process it by recursion, peeling one argument at a time. Together with perfect forwarding, variadic templates are how `emplace`, `make_shared`, `make_tuple` and `thread` take arbitrary argument lists without losing type information on the way in.
objectives: Declare, pass and expand parameter packs with the ellipsis
Process packs head-first with recursion plus an empty overload, and size them with `sizeof...`
Forward packs intact with `std::forward<Args>(args)...`, and simplify accumulation with C++17 fold expressions

concepts.statement: **`template<typename T, typename... Tail> void f(T head, Tail... tail)` declares a pack; the pattern followed by `...` expands it.** In `f(tail...)` the pattern is `tail` — it becomes the comma-separated list of the remaining arguments.
concepts.detail: Expansion works on any pattern containing the pack: `g(h(args)...)` applies h to each argument and passes the results; `std::forward<Args>(args)...` forwards each argument with its own type. The ellipsis is not a loop — it is a pattern rewrite the compiler performs textually, keeping every type.

concepts.statement:
**A pack has no first element, so peel: process the head, recurse on the tail, and let an empty overload close the chain**
```
template<typename T, typename... Tail>
void f(T head, Tail... tail)
{
    g(head);         // do something to the head
    f(tail...);      // pass the rest on
}

void f() { }         // the empty pack: nothing to do
```
concepts.detail: Every nonempty call peels exactly one argument and recurses with a pack one shorter; the zero-argument overload ends the descent. This idiom — the book's canonical variadic pattern — is also exactly how the tuple constructor of the previous section consumes its arguments.

This is the pattern inside `std::make_shared`, `std::make_tuple` and `std::thread`: constructor arguments travel from the caller to a far-away construction site with zero copies and zero information loss.

concepts.statement: **`sizeof...(args)` is the number of elements in the pack — a compile-time constant. And C++17 fold expressions collapse the whole recursion into one expression:** `(v + ... + 0)` sums, `(f(args), ...)` calls `f` on each argument.
concepts.detail: TC++PL 4e predates folds (C++17); its C++11 answer to 'do this to every argument' is the peeling recursion above. Both live side by side in modern code — folds for accumulation, peeling when each step needs its own function body.

concepts.statement: **Variadic Templates.** Packs and folds. You can claim this section when you can declare, pass and expand parameter packs with the ellipsis — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 28 (Metaprogramming); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: sum() by fold and by recursion
examples.problem: Compute `sum(1, 2, 3, 4)` with a fold expression and with the peeling recursion, and check it at compile time.

steps.label: The fold
steps.text: `template<typename... T> constexpr int sum(T... v) { return (v + ... + 0); }` — for arguments 1, 2, 3, 4 this expands right-associated: `1 + (2 + (3 + (4 + 0))) = 10`. The trailing `0` makes the empty call legal: `sum()` is 0.

steps.label: The recursion
steps.text: Peeling form: the first call processes head 1 and recurses with (2,3,4); that call processes 2 and recurses with (3,4); then 3 and (4); then 4 and (); the empty overload ends the chain — four heads, one terminator.

steps.label: Compile-time check
steps.text: `constexpr int s = sum(1, 2, 3, 4); static_assert(s == 10);` — the fold is one constant expression; the recursion unrolls to four nested calls, all gone by the time the program runs.

steps.label: Counting
steps.text: `sizeof...(v)` is 4 here, and after one peel it is 3 — usable anywhere a constant expression is, including `Enable_if` predicates and `static_assert` messages.

examples.result: Both designs yield 10; the fold writes it as one expression, the recursion as one function per argument plus an empty case.

quiz.q: Inside `template<typename T, typename... Tail> void f(T head, Tail... tail)`, the call `f(tail...)` passes:
quiz.explanation: The ellipsis expands the pattern `tail` into the comma-separated list of the arguments not yet consumed.

quiz.q: After the first call of the peeling recursion with five arguments, `sizeof...(tail)` is:
quiz.explanation: One head was peeled; four arguments remain in the pack, and `sizeof...` reports it at compile time.

quiz.q: The fold expression `(v + ... + 0)` for v = 1, 2, 3, 4 evaluates as:
quiz.explanation: A binary right fold associates to the right around the init value 0 — which is also what makes sum() well-formed.

quiz.q: `std::forward<Args>(args)...` expands to:
options: one call forwarding the whole pack as a single argument
a run-time loop over the arguments

quiz.explanation: The pattern is `std::forward<Args>(args)` — repeated once per pack element with the matching type.

intro: The chapter's showpiece is a small library where the type system does physics: quantities carry their dimensions as template parameters, so a program that adds meters to seconds — or passes seconds to a function expecting meters — is rejected at compile time. The exponents of meters, kilograms and seconds become three int template parameters; multiplication and division add and subtract them; addition demands exact equality. The real-world justification is famous and expensive: in 1999 NASA lost the $125M Mars Climate Orbiter because one team's code produced pound-force seconds where another expected newton-seconds.
objectives: Model dimensions as integer template parameters on `Unit`, and wrap magnitudes in `Quantity`
Define `+` and `*` whose signatures themselves enforce dimensional analysis
Appreciate both the power and the admitted limits of the book's toy units system

concepts.detail: `Quantity<Unit<1,0,0>>` is a length; `Quantity<Unit<0,0,1>>` a time; `Quantity<Unit<1,0,-1>>` a velocity, meters per second — seconds to the power −1. The dimension of every value is written in its type, where the compiler can check it.
`2.0s + 2.0m` is not a wrong answer; it is no function to call. The mismatch between `Unit<0,0,1>` and `Unit<1,0,0>` cannot even be expressed as an instantiation of this template.

m/s × s is m: `Unit<1,0,-1>` times `Unit<0,0,1>` instantiates `Unit<1+0, 0+0, -1+1> = Unit<1,0,0>`. The dimensional algebra runs entirely in the template argument lists — pure compile-time integer arithmetic, for free.

concepts.statement:
**Quantities multiply and add correctly while the program is still being compiled**
```
constexpr Quantity<Unit<0,0,1>>  t{2.0};    // 2 s
constexpr Quantity<Unit<1,0,-1>> v{2.0};   // 2 m/s
constexpr auto d = v * t;                  // a length: 4 m
static_assert(d.v == 4.0);

d + v;    // error: Unit<1,0,0> vs Unit<1,0,-1> — no operator+
```
concepts.detail: Everything here — the multiplication, the unit arithmetic, the comparison — is a constant expression. The compiler has just checked a physics equation before emitting a single instruction.

concepts.statement: **Stroustrup is explicit that this is a demonstration, not an industrial units library.** It has no scaled or prefixed units (m vs km vs inch all collapse to 'length'), no angle or currency dimensions, no dimension names in error messages, no I/O beyond raw doubles.
concepts.detail: A production system represents dimension sets as compile-time lists and scale factors as `std::ratio`s. The chapter's point stands regardless: the techniques of 28.2–28.6 are enough to make dimensional errors uncompilable — the rest is engineering.

examples.title: distance = velocity × time, checked by the compiler
examples.problem: With the library above, evaluate `v * t` for v = 3 m/s and t = 2 s; then explain why adding a time to the result cannot compile.

steps.label: Types in play
steps.text: v is `Quantity<Unit<1,0,-1>>` (m/s) and t is `Quantity<Unit<0,0,1>>` (s) — their dimensions live in their types.

steps.label: The product instantiates
steps.text: `operator*` is instantiated with M1=1, K1=0, S1=−1, M2=0, K2=0, S2=1. The result type is `Unit<1+0, 0+0, −1+1>` — that is, `Unit<1,0,0>`: meters.

steps.label: Value
steps.text: 3.0 × 2.0 = 6.0, so d is 6 m; because everything is `constexpr`, the whole computation can happen during compilation, and `static_assert(d.v == 6.0)` proves it.

steps.label: A units bug, made uncompilable
steps.text: `d + t;` would need an `operator+` with `Unit<1,0,0>` equal to `Unit<0,0,1>` in both arguments — no such instantiation exists, so the compiler rejects the line at the call site. The pound-force-second/newton-second class of error (the Mars Climate Orbiter loss) becomes a red squiggle before the program exists.

examples.result: d = 6 m with all dimensional algebra done in template arguments; mixing units does not type-check at all.

Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Dimensions as template parameters: `Unit<M,K,S>` and `Quantity<U>` put units in the type system where the compiler polices them.

keyTakeaways: Dimensions as template parameters: `Unit<M,K,S>` and `Quantity<U>` put units in the type system where the compiler polices them.
`operator+` exists only between identical units; `operator*` adds exponents — the signatures enforce dimensional analysis.
The book admits the system is a demonstration — no prefixes, no scaled units — but dimensional errors become compile-time errors, which is the whole idea.

quiz.q: `Quantity<Unit<1,0,-1>>` represents:
quiz.explanation: Meters to the first power and seconds to the −1: meters per second.

quiz.q: The type of `v * t`, with v of `Unit<1,0,-1>` and t of `Unit<0,0,1>`, is:
quiz.explanation: Multiplication adds exponents: seconds cancel (−1+1 = 0), leaving pure meters.

quiz.q: The expression `2.0s + 2.0m` fails because:
options: no `operator+` instantiation exists for two different Unit types
the units library forbids SI base units in sums
quiz.explanation: The signature demands the same `Unit<M,K,S>` on both arguments; two different units leave no candidate function.

quiz.q: Which limitation does the book itself acknowledge for this units system?
options: It does not handle scaled or prefixed units such as km vs m
It only works at run time
It requires operator overloading that C++14 removed
quiz.explanation: No prefixes, no scale factors, no derived-name sugar — a demonstration of techniques, not an industrial library.

intro: The chapter closes with Stroustrup's own advice, and its flavor is restraint: metaprogramming is a means to correctness and expressiveness, not an end in itself. The rules compress the chapter's hard-won habits — check them before writing your next template, and especially before writing someone else's next template for them.
objectives: Adopt rules that keep metaprogramming worth its costs
Recognize when plain constexpr functions or library traits suffice
Use `static_assert` and unit-style typing to catch errors before run time

concepts.term: Let the compiler find the errors
concepts.statement: **Prefer code that fails to compile over code that fails at run time.** Anything expressible as a type rule — dimensional analysis, extent compatibility, iterator requirements — is checked free of charge on every build.
concepts.detail: The units example is the pattern: encoding the invariant in types turned a class of run-time mistakes into "no matching function." What can be a type, should be a type.

concepts.statement: **Compute values with constexpr functions; use templates when — and only when — the result must be a type or must select a declaration.**
concepts.detail: A `constexpr` factorial reads like code, reuses at run time, and costs one function; a template factorial costs N instantiations and only works for constants. The same test applies to every 'should this be a template?' decision.

concepts.statement: **Reach for `<type_traits>`, `iterator_traits`, `conditional`, `common_type` and friends before writing your own**, and `Enable_if` (today: `requires`) for conditional definition.
concepts.detail: The library versions are tested, documented and understood by readers; a hand-rolled `Remove_ref` in application code is a smell unless the standard one is somehow lacking.

concepts.statement: **Hide metaprogramming behind narrow, conventional interfaces.** Users of your tuple write `get<1>(t)`, never `Get<1>::get(t)`; the machinery stays an implementation detail. Excessive template trickery is a design smell, and deep instantiation chains are a build-time tax on everyone downstream.
concepts.detail: Aim `static_assert`s with readable messages at the entry of a deep metaprogram, so misuse fails with one clear line instead of a screen of template gibberish.

concepts.statement: **`static_assert` plus `constexpr` objects give a zero-run-time test suite for metaprograms:** `static_assert(fac(10) == 3628800)` documents the expected value and enforces it on every compile.
concepts.detail: Compile-time assertions cannot be skipped, flake, or run out of order — they run before the program exists. They are also documentation that cannot go stale.

examples.title: The advice applied: a units-checked kinematics function
examples.problem: Write $d = vt + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ so that it cannot be called with mismatched units, and evaluate it for v = 3 m/s, a = 2 m/s², t = 2 s.

steps.label: Types first
steps.text: v is `Quantity<Unit<1,0,-1>>`, a is `Quantity<Unit<1,0,-2>>`, t is `Quantity<Unit<0,0,1>>`; and t*t is `Unit<0,0,2>` — square seconds come out of the same multiplication machinery.

steps.label: The expression
steps.text: `auto d = v*t + Quantity<Unit<0,0,0>>{0.5} * a * t * t;` — the half is dimensionless (`Unit<0,0,0>`), products add exponents left to right, and the final `+` demands both sides be `Unit<1,0,0>`: meters. They are, or it does not compile.

steps.label: Numbers
steps.text: vt = 3 × 2 = 6 m; a t² = 2 × 4 = 8; half of that is 4 m; total d = 6 + 4 = 10 m — with every intermediate unit checked by the compiler as the expression instantiates.

steps.label: What misuse looks like
steps.text: Passing a time where a velocity is expected does not produce a wrong answer silently — it produces 'no operator+' or 'could not deduce' at the call site. The 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter class of bug is now a compile error.

examples.result: d = 10 m, dimensionally guaranteed: the signature of each operator is a proof that the units line up.

examples.title: Reviewing metaprogramming code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: adopt rules that keep metaprogramming worth its costs.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Encode invariants in types so the compiler enforces them — the units example is the model.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `template<bool B, typename T, typename F> struct Pick;`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: recognize when plain constexpr functions or library traits suffice. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: constexpr functions for values, library traits before hand-rolled ones, templates only when types or declaration selection demand them.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Encode invariants in types so the compiler enforces them — the units example is the model. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Encode invariants in types so the compiler enforces them — the units example is the model.
constexpr functions for values, library traits before hand-rolled ones, templates only when types or declaration selection demand them.
Hide the machinery behind clean interfaces, and use `static_assert` as a free, incorruptible test suite.

quiz.q: To compute a compile-time value, the chapter's advice says to first try:
quiz.explanation: constexpr functions read like code, cost one function instead of N instantiations, and reuse at run time.

quiz.q: The advice section treats excessive template trickery as:
options: fine because the compiler optimizes it away
a design smell — interfaces should not leak implementation techniques
quiz.explanation: Clever machinery behind clean interfaces is engineering; clever machinery leaking into user code is a smell that taxes every reader and rebuild.

quiz.q: In a metaprogram, `static_assert` acts as:
options: a compile-time test that documents and checks expected results
a substitute for testing I/O code
quiz.explanation: It runs before the program exists, cannot be skipped, and doubles as documentation that cannot go stale.

intro: Chapter 29 applies everything the book has built — templates, operator overloading, initializer lists, move semantics, the metaprogramming of Chapter 28 — to one serious, real-world design: a numerical matrix library. Not because the world needs another matrix library, but because a matrix forces the questions every library designer faces: what should the user be able to write (mathematical notation), what must the implementation deliver (contiguous storage, zero-copy views, near-optimal loops), and where do those demands fight? The result, Matrix<T,N>, is the book's capstone design study.
objectives: State the design goals for Matrix<T,N>: N dimensions at compile time, element types as parameters, several subscript styles, useful arithmetic
Recognize the tension between mathematical elegance and implementation efficiency that the chapter navigates
Read the sample usage that the rest of the chapter implements

concepts.statement: **A template for N-dimensional numerical matrices:** `Matrix<double,2>` is a 2-D matrix (rows and columns), `Matrix<double,1>` behaves like a `vector` with matrix-style operations, and `Matrix<char,3>` is a 3-D block of chars. The element type and the number of dimensions are compile-time template parameters; the EXTENTS (3 rows, 4 columns) are chosen at run time, at construction.
concepts.detail: That split is the central design decision: dimension count affects the type system machinery (variadic subscripting, slice dimensionality), while extents are just data — an array of sizes carried in each object.

concepts.statement: **The chapter sets out five aims:** (1) N-dimensional matrices with N a template parameter; (2) element types as template parameters; (3) conventional subscripting — elements, rows, columns, slices — without copying; (4) useful matrix arithmetic (`+`, `-`, scalar `*`, matrix product, `apply`); (5) near-optimal performance for a simple, readable design.
concepts.detail: Explicitly not goals: a complete linear-algebra system (no eigenvalues, no factorizations), sparse-matrix support, or parallelism. The chapter wants the design and implementation techniques, kept honest and complete enough to actually use.

concepts.statement:
**The target usage reads like the math**
```
Matrix<double,2> A = {  {2, 1, -1},  {-3, -1, 2},  {-2, 1, 2}  };
Matrix<double,1> b = { 8, -11, -3 };
Matrix<double,1> x = solve(A, b);        // 29.5's Gaussian elimination

A(1,2) = 7;                             // element access
Matrix<double,1> r = A[1];              // a row, viewed not copied
```
concepts.detail: Everything in this tour — the initializer lists, the element indexing, the row view, the solver — is built from the techniques of the preceding chapters. The rest of the chapter makes it real, one layer at a time.

concepts.statement: **A matrix is the classic vehicle for C++ design questions:** where to draw the interface/implementation line (operators in front, descriptors underneath), how to alias safely (views borrow, owners copy), when checked access is worth it, and how to make a template general without making it slow.
concepts.detail: Stroustrup's framing: by the end you have seen how a professional-grade library component is shaped — and you have written most of one yourself.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** A matrix as a real design. You can claim this section when you can state the design goals for Matrix<T,N>: N dimensions at compile time, element types as parameters, several subscript styles, useful arithmetic — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 29 (A Matrix Design); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: The one-minute tour
examples.problem: Given `Matrix<double,2> m = { {1,2,3}, {4,5,6}, {7,8,9} };`, read an element, a row and a slice, and scale the matrix.

steps.label: Element
steps.text: `m(1,2)` is 8: row index 1, column index 2, zero-based — the middle row {4,5,6} contributes its third entry.

steps.label: Row
steps.text: `m[1]` is a view of the whole middle row {4,5,6} — a `Matrix_ref<double,1>` borrowing m's storage, not a copy of it.

steps.label: Scale
steps.text: `m2 = 3*m;` produces a new 3×3 matrix with every element tripled: {3,6,9},{12,15,18},{21,24,27}; extents are checked and match (3 and 3).

steps.label: The promise
steps.text: Nothing here allocates per element access, and nothing copies except the operations that visibly make new matrices. The rest of the chapter earns those two sentences.

examples.result: Elements, rows, scaling — the whole interface surface in four lines, on one 3×3 test matrix.

Design aims: N-D generality, several subscript styles without copying, useful arithmetic, near-optimal performance — but deliberately not a full linear-algebra system.
The chapter doubles as a course in library design: interface/implementation separation, views vs. owners, checked vs. unchecked access.

quiz.q: In `Matrix<T,N>`, which is fixed at compile time?
options: the extents (number of rows and columns)
the number of dimensions N and the element type T
quiz.explanation: Extents are run-time data carried by each object; N and T are template parameters and therefore part of the type.

quiz.q: `Matrix<double,1>` is best described as:
options: a 1-D matrix behaving much like a vector
a matrix forced to have one row
an error — N must be at least 2
quiz.explanation: 1-D matrices support the same subscripting/view/arithmetic machinery and serve as the vector type of 29.5.

quiz.q: Which is NOT among the chapter's stated design goals for Matrix?
options: a complete industrial linear-algebra package (eigenvalues, sparse, parallel)
near-optimal performance for a simple design
quiz.explanation: The chapter explicitly disclaims completeness: no factorizations, no sparse or parallel support — techniques over features.

intro: The heart of the design is the subscripting interface: users must reach individual elements, grab whole rows and columns, carve sub-matrices with slices, and construct from nested initializer lists — all without copying data. This section fixes that interface and the small set of supporting types that make it uniform: Matrix_ref for borrowed views, slice descriptors for rectangular regions, and the degenerate Matrix<double,0> that is its own element.
objectives: Use the three access styles: elements `m(i,j)`, rows/columns via `m[i]` and named views, and slice-based sub-matrices
Explain why `operator()` takes all indices at once while `operator[]` yields a lower-dimensional view
Construct matrices from extents and from nested initializer lists, with ragged lists rejected

concepts.statement: **A Matrix owns its elements and carries a descriptor of their arrangement.** Constructed from extents — `Matrix<double,2> m(3,4)` makes 3 rows × 4 columns — or from nested initializer lists: `Matrix<double,2> m = { {1,2,3}, {4,5,6} };`.
concepts.detail: The members are a `Matrix_slice<N>` (start, extents, strides — see 29.4) and a handle to the elements, default-initialized to zero for arithmetic types. Copy is deep; move is a constant-time steal of the handle.

concepts.statement: **`m(i,j)` returns a reference to the element at row i, column j — all indices at once, variadic:** `T& operator()(Args... dims)` computes the offset through the descriptor and indexes the elements. `Matrix<T,0>` is the degenerate case: a 0-dimensional matrix IS its element, and its `operator()` takes zero indices.
concepts.detail: Why `()` rather than `[]` for elements: `operator[]` takes ONE argument, so `m[i][j]` would need an intermediate proxy for every access — and that proxy reads wrongly for N ≠ 2. A single call with all indices needs no proxy and adapts naturally to any dimension count; subscripts can be checked (in debug builds) before touching memory.

concepts.statement: **`m[i]` views the i-th row — a `Matrix_ref<T,N-1>` that borrows storage; named views do the rest:** a column of a 2-D matrix, and slice-based sub-matrices: a `slice(i,n)` names the n elements starting at index i along one dimension, so `m(slice(1,2), slice(1,2))` carves the 2×2 block of rows 1–2 and columns 1–2 — still an alias, never a copy.
concepts.detail: Every one of these returns a `Matrix_ref` (a descriptor plus a raw pointer — 29.4); writing through a view writes the matrix. Slices were chosen over iterators for sub-matrix selection because they describe a rectangular region of ANY dimension with the same three numbers: start, extent, stride.

concepts.statement: **A `Matrix_ref<T,N>` is (almost) a Matrix that does not own its elements:** same descriptor machinery, same subscript styles, but a borrowed pointer instead of owned storage — the same relationship that `string_view` and `span` bear to their owners.
concepts.detail: Views are how the library does 'look at part of the data' cheaply and safely: the price is that the user must keep the owner alive, exactly as with any borrowed-range type.

concepts.statement: **Nested brace lists construct matrices with the shape checked:** the `Matrix_initializer<T,N>` machinery unwinds the nesting recursively, requires the structure to be perfectly rectangular, and derives the extents — `{ {1,2,3}, {4,5,6} }` yields a 2×3. A ragged list like `{ {1,2}, {3} }` throws rather than guessing.
concepts.detail: This is Chapter 28 metaprogramming at work: the initializer's type encodes the nesting depth, and a small trait (`Matrix_init<T,N>`) recognizes `initializer_list` chains of exactly the right depth for N dimensions.

examples.title: Access patterns on a 3×3
examples.problem: For `Matrix<double,2> m = { {1,2,3}, {4,5,6}, {7,8,9} };` read elements, a row and a slice, and confirm the extents.

steps.label: Elements
steps.text: `m(0,0)` is 1, `m(1,2)` is 8, `m(2,2)` is 9 — indices are (row, column), zero-based.

steps.label: Row view
steps.text: `m[1]` aliases the middle row {4,5,6}: it is a `Matrix_ref`, so `m[1](0) = 40;` also changes `m(1,0)` — one storage, two ways in.

steps.label: Slice
steps.text: `m(slice(1,2), slice(1,2))` carves rows 1–2 and columns 1–2: the 2×2 block { {5,6}, {8,9} } — still aliased, still no copy.

steps.label: Extents
steps.text: `m.extent(0)` is 3 (rows) and `m.extent(1)` is 3 (columns); the elements live contiguously as 9 doubles, and every view above is descriptor arithmetic on them.

examples.result: One object, three views into it — elements, rows and slice blocks all alias the same contiguous storage.

quiz.explanation: Row 1 is {4,5,6}; column 2 of that row is 8. Indices are zero-based (row, column).

quiz.q: The interface uses `operator()` rather than `operator[]` for elements because:
options: a single call takes all N indices at once, avoiding chained proxies that only fit 2-D
quiz.explanation: `operator[]` takes one argument; N-dimensional access through it would need proxy objects — one variadic `()` call handles any N.

quiz.q: Along one dimension, `slice(1,2)` selects:
options: rows 1 through 2 of the other dimension
quiz.explanation: A slice is (start, extent): here indices 1 and 2 — two entries beginning at 1.

quiz.q: A `Matrix_ref` differs from a `Matrix` because it:
options: owns a copy of the elements
aliases (borrows) the elements through a slice descriptor, adding no ownership
quiz.explanation: Views borrow: same subscript machinery, but the storage belongs to someone else — like `span` over a `vector`.

intro: With subscripting in place, arithmetic is where the design pays for itself: `+` and `-` are element-wise with extents checked, scalar multiplication scales every element, `apply` runs any function over the whole matrix, and the matrix product multiplies 2-D matrices with the classical triple loop. The chapter is equally clear about what it does not do — no expression templates to fuse operations, no general N-dimensional tensor contraction — keeping every line readable and every allocation visible.
objectives: Use element-wise `+`, `-`, compound assignment, scalar `*`, and `apply`
Compute matrix products with the extents check that guards them
Say what the design deliberately omits — expression templates, general tensor products — and why

concepts.statement: **`a + b` and `a - b` produce a new matrix with the same extents**, each element the sum or difference of the corresponding pair; `a += b` and friends assign in place. Both operands' extents must match exactly — enforced by an `assert` at run time, because extents are run-time data.
concepts.detail: The natural spelling is a loop over `m.begin()..m.end()` or nested index loops; either way the whole implementation of `operator+` is a few lines, thanks to the uniform access machinery of 29.2.

concepts.statement: **`m * 2.0` scales every element; `m.apply(f)` calls `f` on each element in place; `apply(m, f)` returns the transformed copy.** The scalar version is itself `apply` in disguise, `m.apply([](double& x){ x *= 2.0; })`.
concepts.detail: Because `apply` takes any callable, one line buys you absolute values, rounding, clamping — the standard unary functions of `<cmath>` applied across a matrix. Element access stays behind the descriptor, so the loops need no special cases for rows or views.

Loop order matters for speed: with row-major storage, making `j` (the b-column index) the inner stride-touching loop keeps both `b(k,j)` and `res(i,j)` walking contiguous memory — the i-k-j ordering shown is the cache-friendly one. The chapter keeps the loops plain and near-optimal rather than clever and opaque.

concepts.statement: **No expression templates:** `C = A*B + D` computes and allocates the product `A*B` first, then adds `D`. **No general N-D product:** multiplication is defined for 2-D matrices only — an N-dimensional tensor contraction machinery would dwarf everything else in the chapter.
concepts.detail: The omissions are the design's honesty: fusing loops buys constant factors at the cost of a second, invisible language; real heavy numerics belongs to a BLAS-backed library. The chapter's target is near-optimal WHILE readable.

concepts.term: Matrix Arithmetic Operations: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Matrix Arithmetic Operations.** Slices, views and arithmetic. You can claim this section when you can use element-wise `+`, `-`, compound assignment, scalar `*`, and `apply` — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 29 (A Matrix Design); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: A 2×3 times 3×2 product, by hand and by code
examples.problem: With `A = { {1,2,3}, {4,5,6} }` and `B = { {7,8}, {9,10}, {11,12} }`, compute `A*B` element by element, and count the arithmetic.

steps.label: Shape
steps.text: `A` is 2×3, `B` is 3×2 — the inner extents chain (3 = 3), so the result is 2×2.

steps.label: Cost
steps.text: Each of the 4 result entries is an inner product of length 3: 3 multiplies + 3 adds = 6 flops, so $2\times m\times n\times p = 2\times 2\times 3\times 2 = 24$ flops in all — for large shapes the $\Theta(n^3)$ cubic growth is the reason the loop order (and real BLAS libraries) matter.

examples.result: `A*B` is { {58, 64}, {139, 154} } — every entry verifiable by hand, 24 flops total.

examples.title: Working through matrix arithmetic operations
examples.problem: Slices, views and arithmetic. Your task: use element-wise `+`, `-`, compound assignment, scalar `*`, and `apply`.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: use element-wise `+`, `-`, compound assignment, scalar `*`, and `apply`. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `+`, `-`, `+=` are element-wise with matching extents asserted at run time; `*` by a scalar scales; `apply(f)` maps any function over the elements.

steps.label: Step 2: build

intro: Now the lid comes off. Every Matrix<T,N> is two things: a handle to its elements plus a Matrix_slice<N> — the small descriptor that maps N subscripts to an offset. Computing that offset is the entire implementation: a row-major 2-D matrix stores rows end to end, so a 3×4 matrix has strides {4,1} and element (i,j) sits at offset 4i+j. Every access style of 29.2 — elements, rows, slices, Matrix_refs — reduces to arithmetic on descriptors.
objectives: Define `Matrix_slice<N>` and its three members: start, extents, strides
Compute element offsets for row-major matrices, including strided column walks
Explain `Matrix<T,0>`, `Matrix_ref` and the `begin()`/`end()` iterator pair

concepts.detail: A `Matrix` owns elements and a slice; a `Matrix_ref` holds a slice and someone else's pointer. Two objects share ALL the subscript machinery precisely because both are a slice plus a way to reach elements.

concepts.statement:
**Element (i₁, …, i_N) lives at flat offset**
$$\text{loc} = \text{start} + i_1 \cdot \text{strides}[0] + \cdots + i_N \cdot \text{strides}[N{-}1]$$
**— one multiply-add per dimension, no searches, no branches.** The default layout is row-major (C-style): the last dimension has unit stride, and each stride going up is the product of the extents below it.
concepts.detail: For a 3×4 matrix: strides = {4,1}, so m(2,1) is at 2·4 + 1·1 = 9. A row view is a slice with stride 1 and extent 4; a COLUMN view is stride 4, extent 3 — the descriptor language covers both without special cases.

concepts.statement: **A zero-dimensional matrix is just its element.** The specialization stores a single `T`; subscripting with zero indices returns it. That one class is what lets generic code recurse cleanly: each row of an N-D matrix is (N−1)-D, down to 0-D.
concepts.detail: Degenerate cases that work are the measure of a general design — `Matrix<double,0>` is why `m[i]` of a 1-D matrix can yield the element itself rather than a view, and why the initializer-list machinery can bottom out.

concepts.statement: **`m[i]` is a `Matrix_ref<T,N-1>` whose slice is the i-th slab of `m`'s slice; a slice expression rewrites extents and strides in O(1).** No element is touched to build a view — carving a sub-matrix costs three numbers per dimension.
concepts.detail: This is the implementation of 29.2's promise that views never copy: `m(slice(1,2), slice(1,2))` adjusts start by 1·strides[0] + 1·strides[1], sets extents to {2,2} and inherits the strides — arithmetic, not data movement.

concepts.statement: **`begin()` and `end()` iterate over all elements in storage (row-major) order** — which makes `range-for` and the standard algorithms work on matrices — while subscript access through `()` can be checked or bare depending on build.
concepts.detail: The chapter keeps checks cheap: indices are validated against extents where debugging needs it, and move semantics make returning matrices from functions free — a moved Matrix is a slice-and-pointer steal, O(1) whatever the element count.

examples.title: Offsets in a 3×4
examples.problem: For `Matrix<double,2> m(3,4);` in the default row-major layout, locate `m(2,1)`, `m(1,3)`, and the elements of column 2.

steps.label: Descriptor
steps.text: start = 0, extents = {3,4}, strides = {4,1}: the last dimension is unit stride, and each row is 4 elements.

steps.label: m(2,1)
steps.text: offset = 2·4 + 1·1 = 9 — the tenth double of the flat array. In general $(i,j)$ sits at $4i + j$.

steps.label: m(1,3)
steps.text: offset = 1·4 + 3·1 = 7. Cross-check: row 1 owns offsets 4–7, and column 3 is its last entry — 7. ✓

steps.label: Column 2
steps.text: The entries `m(0,2)`, `m(1,2)`, `m(2,2)` live at offsets 2, 6, 10: same column index, rows four apart — a stride-4 walk through the flat array. That is exactly the descriptor a column view carries: start = 2, extents = {3}, strides = {4}.

examples.result: Every access is offset arithmetic: (i,j) → 4i+j for the whole 3×4 matrix; columns cost nothing extra because they are just a different stride.

quiz.explanation: offset = 2·strides[0] + 3·strides[1] = 2·4 + 3·1 = 11.

quiz.explanation: The element sequence is the flat storage order — which is what makes range-for and standard algorithms work directly.

intro: The payoff of the whole design is numerical: solving Ax = b by Gaussian elimination. The idea is two centuries old — eliminate below the diagonal by subtracting scaled rows, then back-substitute — but doing it in floating point adds one crucial refinement: partial pivoting, always dividing by the largest available pivot, obtained by swapping rows. The chapter uses its own Matrix type to write both the naive and the pivotal solver, and closes with the numerical programmer's catechism: never trust an untested floating-point algorithm.
objectives: Carry out forward elimination and back-substitution on a small system, by hand
Explain partial pivoting and why the naive solver fails or loses accuracy
Test numerical code the way the chapter does: generate the answer first, then recover it

concepts.detail: The matrices are passed BY VALUE on purpose: elimination destroys its operands, so each solver works on its own copies and returns the solution — the caller's data is untouched.

concepts.statement: **For each column k = 0 … n−2, subtract a multiple of row k from every row below it, choosing the multiple to zero out column k:** row_i ← row_i − (a(i,k)/a(k,k))·row_k, applied to the augmented row including b. After n−1 columns the matrix is upper triangular.
concepts.detail: Each elimination step is a whole-row operation — exactly what Matrix rows-as-views make natural: `m(i,k)` indexing and row subtraction are descriptor arithmetic over contiguous storage, with no copies of the matrix.

concepts.statement: **Before eliminating with column k, find the row p ≥ k with the largest |a(p,k)| and swap rows p and k (b entries included), then eliminate using that pivot.** The naive version divides by a(k,k) whatever its size: a zero pivot crashes the algorithm, and a tiny one amplifies rounding error catastrophically.
concepts.detail: The swaps cost only comparisons and element moves, and they rescue essentially all practical systems — the chapter's `pivotal_elimination` differs from `classical_gaussian_elimination` by exactly this inner search-and-swap.

concepts.statement:
**Read the unknowns off the triangular system bottom-up:**
$$x_{n-1} = \frac{b_{n-1}}{a(n{-}1,\,n{-}1)}, \qquad x_i = \frac{b_i - \sum_{j>i} a(i,j)\,x_j}{a(i,i)}$$
— each step needs only the row already reduced and the unknowns already found.
concepts.detail: The inner sum is an inner product of row i's upper part with the partially built x — a one-line loop over `Matrix` elements, again contiguous in storage.

concepts.statement: **The chapter's discipline: pick the answer x first, compute b = A·x with the matrix product of 29.3, solve, and compare** — including deliberately nasty (tiny-pivot, ill-conditioned) systems that expose the difference between the classical and pivotal solvers.
concepts.detail: A solve that compiles tells you nothing: the same lines run accurately with pivoting and fail without it. Numerical correctness is an empirical property, tested — never assumed — and singular systems should be detected and reported (the chapter throws on a zero pivot) rather than allowed to return garbage.

examples.title: A 3×3 solved with partial pivoting
examples.problem: Solve $$2x + y - z = 8, \qquad -3x - y + 2z = -11, \qquad -2x + y + 2z = -3$$ by pivotal Gaussian elimination.

steps.label: Pivot on column 0
steps.text: Available magnitudes: |2|, |−3|, |−2| — the largest is −3 in row 1, so swap rows 0 and 1: (−3, −1, 2 | −11) becomes the pivot row.

steps.label: Pivot on column 1
steps.text: Candidates |1/3| and |5/3|: swap rows 1 and 2 so the pivot is 5/3. Eliminate: row 2 ← row 2 − (1/5)·row 1: (0, 0, 1/5 | −1/5).

steps.label: Back-substitute
steps.text: From the last row: (1/5)z = −1/5, so z = −1. Then (5/3)y + (2/3)(−1) = 13/3 gives (5/3)y = 5, so y = 3. Finally −3x − 3 + 2(−1) = −11 gives −3x = −6, so x = 2.

examples.result: x = 2, y = 3, z = −1 — every step is a row operation the Matrix library performs on views, and every equation verifies.

quiz.q: Partial pivoting exists to:
options: reduce the operation count below cubic
avoid zero or near-zero pivots that crash the algorithm or amplify rounding error
quiz.explanation: Dividing by the largest available pivot keeps multipliers ≤ 1 in size and keeps elimination numerically honest.

quiz.q: After forward elimination, the coefficient matrix has become:
quiz.explanation: All entries below the diagonal have been zeroed; the unknowns can then be read from the bottom up.

quiz.q: With `Vector = Matrix<double,1>` and the solvers of this section, the call `pivotal_elimination(A, b)`:

refuses non-square A at compile time

intro: The standard library is what turns C++ from a powerful language into a productive one: ready-made, efficient answers to the problems virtually every program faces — storage, traversal, sorting, I/O, time, text, concurrency. This chapter is the map of that territory before the book descends into each region in detail.
objectives: List the major parts of the standard library and say what each contributes
Explain how the design ideals — generality, uniformity, economy — shape the library's interfaces
Classify a given programming task into the library component that serves it

concepts.statement: The library spans a dozen domains: **run-time language support** (dynamic memory, RTTI), **the C standard library** with minor modifications, **strings and I/O**, a **framework of containers, iterators and algorithms** (the STL), **numerical computation** (`complex`, `valarray`, random numbers), **regular expression matching**, **concurrency** (`thread`, `mutex`, `future`), plus general **utilities** (time, function objects) and **locale** support.
concepts.detail: The book's own tour spends a chapter on each part; the point of the summary is to know what exists before designing anything yourself.

concepts.statement: The **Standard Template Library** — the framework of generic **containers, iterators and algorithms** designed by Alexander Stepanov and colleagues, later adopted as the centerpiece of the ISO C++ library: roughly a dozen containers, some sixty algorithms, glued together by five iterator categories.
concepts.detail: The STL's defining move is the separation: algorithms never know which container they serve, only the iterator category — one `sort` works for every container that can be randomly accessed.

concepts.statement: Library facilities aim to be **general** (usable for any element type meeting minimal requirements), **uniform** (predictable naming and conventions across all components) and **economical** (zero-overhead: you do not pay for what you do not use).
concepts.detail: Stroustrup's practical corollary: the standard components are typically more efficient, more correct and better tested than what you can write yourself in the time you have.

concepts.statement: Features migrate between language and library as experience accumulates: what many users need and can be supplied without special syntax becomes a library component; what the compiler must understand stays in the language. The boundary is a design decision, not an accident.
concepts.detail: Examples: `string` is library, not language; `initializer_list` needed language support but is library machinery; `thread` arrived only when hardware made concurrency mainstream.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** What the library provides and why. You can claim this section when you can list the major parts of the standard library and say what each contributes — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 30 (Standard Library Summary); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Matching tasks to library components
examples.problem: A program must (1) keep a million (name, phone) records searchable by name, (2) produce a report sorted by phone, (3) parse dates like “Mar 30, 2026” from user input, (4) time a slow function, and (5) run the parsing on a worker thread. Which library parts do you reach for?

steps.label: Step 1: Lookup structure
steps.text: An `unordered_map<string, Phone>` gives expected $O(1)$ lookup by name; a `map` would instead give $O(\log n)$ lookup plus alphabetical iteration.

steps.label: Step 2: Sorted report
steps.text: Copy the records into a `vector<pair<Phone, Name>>` and `sort` with a comparator on the phone field — $O(n \log n)$.

steps.label: Step 3: Dates
steps.text: `<regex>` — build a `regex`, apply `regex_match` to each line, and read the captures.

steps.label: Step 4: Timing
steps.text: `<chrono>` — take `steady_clock::now()` before and after, subtract, and print the `duration`.

steps.label: Step 5: Concurrency
steps.text: `<thread>` — run the parse in a `thread` and `join` it, guarding shared results with a `mutex` from `<mutex>`.

examples.result: Every subtask lands on an existing, tuned component — the mark of knowing the library is that nothing here is designed from scratch.

quiz.q: Which part of the library is the framework of containers, iterators and algorithms?
quiz.explanation: The Standard Template Library — Stepanov's framework — is one part of the larger standard library; the others are separate parts.

quiz.q: A library design that must work for any element type meeting minimal requirements is called:
quiz.explanation: Generality is the ideal of serving any suitable type; uniformity is consistent conventions; economy is the zero-overhead principle.

quiz.q: Which component answers “time a slow function”?
quiz.explanation: `steady_clock` is the monotonic clock intended for interval measurement; `system_clock` can jump and is for wall-clock time.

quiz.q: In this chapter's view, replacing a library component with a hand-written one is usually:
options: more code, more bugs, rarely faster
quiz.explanation: The library's templates are tuned, inlinable and battle-tested; hand-rolled versions lose on all three counts.

intro: Every standard-library facility is reached through a header. This section fixes the naming rules, the namespace rules, and the subtle difference between the `<c...>` and `<...h>` spellings of the C library — the details that decide whether `std::sqrt` or bare `sqrt` compiles.
objectives: Use the header-naming conventions and locate each facility in the right header
Distinguish `<cmath>`-style from `<math.h>`-style headers and their namespace effects
Avoid the classic header pitfalls: missing includes and polluting `using` directives

concepts.statement: Standard headers carry **no file extension**: `#include <vector>`, `#include <string>`, `#include <algorithm>`. Every name they declare lives in **namespace `std`** (except `std` itself and the C macros, which have no namespace).
concepts.detail: The headers are not file names in any guaranteed sense — they are names the preprocessor resolves as the implementation sees fit.

concepts.statement: Each C standard-library header `xxx.h` reappears as `<cxxx>`: `<cmath>`, `<cstdlib>`, `<cstring>`, … **The `<math.h>` spelling puts its names in the global namespace and possibly in `std`; the `<cmath>` spelling puts them in `std` and possibly in the global namespace.**
concepts.detail: The two spellings are therefore not symmetric — and portable C++ code says `std::sqrt`, which works under either, rather than relying on which direction the leakage goes.

concepts.statement: A working mental map: containers have headers named after them (`<vector>`, `<list>`, `<map>`, `<unordered_map>`, …); the algorithms live in `<algorithm>` (numeric ones in `<numeric>`); iterators and their adaptors in `<iterator>`; function objects and adaptors in `<functional>`; `size_t`, `ptrdiff_t`, `nullptr_t` in `<cstddef>`.
concepts.detail: When a name fails to compile, the missing header is the first suspect — the compiler's “not declared” is usually “not included”.

concepts.statement: Never put a using-directive (`using namespace std;`) in a header or before an `#include`: it reopens the namespace for **every** includer, silently inviting ambiguities and name capture.
concepts.detail: Inside a function or a source file the directive is a style choice; at global scope in a header it is a defect.

concepts.statement: **Headers.** How the library is included. You can claim this section when you can use the header-naming conventions and locate each facility in the right header — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 30 (Standard Library Summary); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Diagnosing three compile-time failures
examples.problem: A small program (a) calls `std::find(v.begin(), v.end(), 7)` and fails to compile; (b) calls `sqrt(2.0)` having included `<cmath>` and fails; (c) includes `<string.h>` and calls `std::strlen` — should that work?

steps.label: Case a
steps.text: `find` is declared in `<algorithm>`, not alongside the container — add `#include <algorithm>`. The rule “algorithms live in `<algorithm>`” is absolute.

steps.label: Case b
steps.text: `<cmath>` guarantees the name in `std`; the unqualified `sqrt` is only available under the `.h` spelling or by the (unspecified) leakage — write `std::sqrt(2.0)`.

steps.label: Case c
steps.text: `<string.h>` is the C header: it puts `strlen` in the global namespace and only *possibly* in `std`, so `std::strlen` is not portable — use `<cstring>` with `std::`, or plain `strlen`.

steps.label: Moral
steps.text: All three failures are header or namespace mismatches, not logic errors: the compiler is enforcing the library's naming discipline.

examples.result: One include and two spellings fixed the whole program — the fix was knowing the rules, not debugging.

examples.problem: How the library is included. Your task: use the header-naming conventions and locate each facility in the right header.

steps.label: Step 2: build

keyTakeaways: Standard headers have no extension and declare their names in namespace `std`.
`<math.h>` pollutes the global namespace (and possibly `std`); `<cmath>` declares in `std` (and possibly the global one) — prefer `<c...>` plus qualified names.
Algorithms are in `<algorithm>`/`<numeric>`, never in the container headers; never place `using namespace std;` in a header.

quiz.q: Which header declares `std::find`?
quiz.explanation: All the non-numeric algorithms, `find` included, live in `<algorithm>`; containers only supply the iterators you pass to them.

quiz.q: `<math.h>` versus `<cmath>`:
options: `<math.h>` puts names in the global namespace and possibly in `std`; `<cmath>` puts them in `std` and possibly in the global one
the two are identical in every respect
quiz.explanation: This is the chapter's exact statement — the leakage is only guaranteed in one direction for each spelling.

quiz.q: `using namespace std;` at global scope in a header is:
options: a pollution hazard for every includer — avoid it
quiz.explanation: The directive reopens `std` in every translation unit that includes the header, capturing names unpredictably.

quiz.q: For `std::strlen`, the portable include is:
quiz.explanation: `<cstring>` guarantees the names in `std`; `<string.h>` guarantees them only in the global namespace.

intro: Before the library can offer containers and algorithms it must underpin the language itself: the types the core mentions by name (`size_t`, `nullptr_t`), the numeric limits of the machine, allocation failure and initializer lists. These facilities are the bedrock the rest of the library stands on.
objectives: Name the headers that provide core-language support and say what each contributes
Use `numeric_limits` to query type properties instead of hard-coding platform constants
Avoid the unsigned-arithmetic traps that `size_t` and `ptrdiff_t` set

concepts.statement: **`<cstddef>`** (`size_t`, `ptrdiff_t`, `nullptr_t`), **`<limits>`** (`numeric_limits`), **`<new>`** (`bad_alloc`, `set_new_handler`), **`<typeinfo>`** (`type_info`, `bad_cast`, `bad_typeid`), **`<exception>`** (`exception`, `terminate`), **`<initializer_list>`**, plus the C inheritance `<cstdarg>`, `<csetjmp>`, `<csignal>`, `<cstdlib>`, `<ctime>`.
concepts.detail: These are not “utilities you may use” — they are the declarations the language semantics refer to.

concepts.statement: `std::size_t` is the **unsigned** type returned by `sizeof` and by every container's `size()`; `std::ptrdiff_t` is the **signed** type of pointer subtraction. A container of $n$ elements has valid subscripts $0 \ldots n-1$.
concepts.detail: The classic trap: `v.size() - 1` on an *empty* container computes $0 - 1$ in unsigned arithmetic — a huge number near $2^{32}$ or $2^{64}$, never $-1$.

concepts.statement: A template exposing each built-in type's properties: `numeric_limits<int>::max()` and `::min()`, `::digits10`, `::is_signed`; for floating types also `::epsilon()` and `::has_infinity()`. It replaces the C macros (`INT_MAX`, `DBL_MAX`) with one uniform, overloadable interface.
concepts.detail: For `double`, `digits10` is 15 — about fifteen significant decimal digits round-trip exactly — and `epsilon()` is $2^{-52} \approx 2.22\times10^{-16}$, the spacing of `double`s near 1.

concepts.statement: The type behind the brace syntax `vector<int> v {1, 2, 3}`: a lightweight view of an array of `const T` that the compiler constructs automatically when a function takes an `initializer_list<T>` parameter.
concepts.detail: It is how variadic-looking brace lists reach constructors and `min({a, b, c})`-style overloads without templates.

concepts.statement: **Language Support.** Support for language features and limits. You can claim this section when you can name the headers that provide core-language support and say what each contributes — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 30 (Standard Library Summary); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Limits in action: the overflow-safe midpoint
examples.problem: A binary search over `int` data must compute the midpoint of `lo = 1500000000` and `hi = 2000000000`. Show why `(lo + hi) / 2` is wrong, and fix it.

steps.label: The overflow
steps.text: $lo + hi = 3.5\times10^{9} > 2\,147\,483\,647$: signed overflow — **undefined behavior**, typically a wrapped negative midpoint.

steps.label: The floating cousin
steps.text: For `double`, remember `digits10 == 15` significant digits and `epsilon()` $\approx 2.22\times10^{-16}$ before trusting an `==` on computed reals.

examples.result: Midpoint 1,750,000,000 computed without overflow — the general lesson: query `numeric_limits` instead of assuming a 32-bit two's-complement world.

examples.problem: Support for language features and limits. Your task: name the headers that provide core-language support and say what each contributes.

steps.label: Step 1: restate

Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `<cstddef>`, `<limits>`, `<new>`, `<typeinfo>` and `<exception>` declare the types the core language itself depends on.

steps.label: Step 2: build

keyTakeaways: `<cstddef>`, `<limits>`, `<new>`, `<typeinfo>` and `<exception>` declare the types the core language itself depends on.
`size_t` is unsigned: `v.size() - 1` wraps on an empty container instead of becoming $-1$.
`numeric_limits<T>` is the portable source of every platform constant — max, min, digits10, epsilon.

quiz.q: `numeric_limits<int>::max()` for the usual 32-bit two's-complement `int` equals:
quiz.explanation: One less than $2^{31}$: the sign bit halves the positive range — the fact that makes `(lo + hi)` overflow.

quiz.q: For an empty `vector` v, the expression `v.size() - 1` yields:
options: a huge unsigned value near $2^{32}$ or $2^{64}$
quiz.explanation: `size()` is unsigned; $0 - 1$ wraps modulo $2^{32}$ or $2^{64}$ — defined behavior, disastrous value.

quiz.q: `set_new_handler`, which lets you intercept out-of-memory, is declared in:
quiz.explanation: `<new>` declares `bad_alloc` and `set_new_handler`; `<exception>` holds the base class and `terminate`.

quiz.q: The braced list in `vector<int> v {1, 2, 3}` has type:
quiz.explanation: The compiler builds an `initializer_list<int>` over a temporary array of `const int` and hands it to the constructor.

intro: The standard library reports errors by exceptions, but it is deliberately stingy: most operations communicate through return values or preconditions, and exceptions are reserved for what return values cannot express. This section maps exactly what the library throws, when, and what it never throws.
objectives: Draw the standard exception hierarchy and place `out_of_range`, `length_error` and `bad_alloc` correctly
Predict which library operations throw and which leave errors unchecked
State the basic, strong and no-throw exception-safety guarantees

concepts.statement: All standard exceptions derive from `std::exception`. **`logic_error`** covers errors a caller could in principle detect before running — `invalid_argument`, `length_error`, `out_of_range`, `domain_error`; **`runtime_error`** covers errors detectable only at run time — `range_error`, `overflow_error`, `underflow_error`. Beside them sit `bad_alloc` (`<new>`) and `bad_cast`/`bad_typeid` (`<typeinfo>`).
concepts.detail: A too-large request (say, a `reserve` beyond policy) reports `length_error`; an out-of-range index on a *checked* access reports `out_of_range`.

concepts.statement: Very little, by design: `vector::at`, `map::at` and `bitset`'s checked conversions throw `out_of_range`; `new` throws `bad_alloc`; `dynamic_cast` of references throws `bad_cast`; a `bitset::to_ulong` too large to fit throws `overflow_error`. Everything else — in particular `v[i]` — **checks nothing**.
concepts.detail: Rationale: the library cannot know whether a caller has already validated the index; unchecked access keeps the zero-overhead principle intact.

concepts.statement: A library operation offers the **basic guarantee** (on failure, invariants hold, no leaks, the object is in some valid state), the **strong guarantee** (failure leaves the object exactly as before — `push_back` when a copy throws mid-reallocation), or the **no-throw guarantee** (`swap`, `pop_back`, destructors — never let these throw).
concepts.detail: Code written to the strong guarantee can retry; code written to the basic guarantee must be able to continue with a valid-but-changed object.

concepts.term: Unchecked by default, checked by request
concepts.statement: The library's error-handling philosophy splits access in two: the fast, unchecked path (`[ ]`, iterators) assumes the caller has established validity; the checked path (`at()`) pays a comparison and a branch to convert a logic error into a catchable exception.
concepts.detail: An uncaught exception terminates the program via `terminate`; that is the intended fate of a violated precondition that nobody handled.

concepts.statement: **Error Handling.** Exceptions from the library's point of view. You can claim this section when you can draw the standard exception hierarchy and place `out_of_range`, `length_error` and `bad_alloc` correctly — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.

examples.title: at() versus [ ]
examples.problem: For `vector<int> v {0, 10, 20, 30, 40}`, contrast `v[5] = 1;` with `v.at(5) = 1;` — and with `v[4]` / `v.at(4)`.

steps.label: Valid index
steps.text: `v[4]` and `v.at(4)` both yield `40` — fast path and checked path agree when the index is legal.

steps.label: Subscript out of range
steps.text: `v[5]` writes past the end: **undefined behavior** — heap corruption, a crash, or nothing at all; no exception is thrown.

steps.label: Checked access
steps.text: `v.at(5)` throws `std::out_of_range` (a `logic_error`), so `catch (std::out_of_range&)` — or `catch (std::exception&)` — handles it; `e.what()` returns an implementation-defined message.

steps.label: Choosing
steps.text: Use `[ ]` where the index is already known valid (a loop bounded by `v.size()`); use `at()` where the index arrives from outside the program's control.

examples.result: One index error, two contracts: undefined behavior on the fast path, a precise exception on the checked path — pick per call site, not by habit.

Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `out_of_range` and `length_error` are `logic_error`s; `overflow_error` and `underflow_error` are `runtime_error`s; `bad_alloc` sits on its own branch.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `double m = std::numeric_limits<double>::max();` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: The library throws only from checked operations (`at`, `new`, `dynamic_cast`); `v[i]` is unchecked by design. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

keyTakeaways: `out_of_range` and `length_error` are `logic_error`s; `overflow_error` and `underflow_error` are `runtime_error`s; `bad_alloc` sits on its own branch.
The library throws only from checked operations (`at`, `new`, `dynamic_cast`); `v[i]` is unchecked by design.
Know which guarantee an operation gives — basic, strong or no-throw — before writing recovery code.

quiz.q: `v.at(99)` on a five-element `vector` throws:
quiz.explanation: `at` is the checked access: it throws `out_of_range`, a subclass of `logic_error`.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a `logic_error` subclass?
quiz.explanation: `overflow_error` belongs to the `runtime_error` branch — a numeric condition only detectable at run time.

quiz.q: “Failure leaves the object exactly as it was before the operation” is the:
quiz.explanation: The strong guarantee permits retry; the basic guarantee only promises a valid state, and the no-throw guarantee promises no failure at all.

quiz.q: `v[7]` on a five-element `vector`:
quiz.explanation: Unchecked subscripting is the zero-overhead path; only `at` validates.

intro: The chapter closes with Stroustrup's rules of thumb, which compress the library into a decision procedure: what to reach for first, what to distrust, and what never to write by hand. They are short because the earlier sections earned them.
objectives: Apply the “know the library first” discipline to new programming tasks
Justify preferring standard components over hand-rolled ones with cost and correctness arguments
Recognize when library advice overrides performance intuition

concepts.term: Know the library before you write
concepts.statement: **Do not re-invent the wheel: before writing a container, algorithm or utility, check the library** — it is probably there, already tested and tuned. Reading the library's table of contents is part of design.
concepts.detail: The corollary cuts the other way: do not turn to non-standard or hand-built code until the standard has demonstrably failed you.

concepts.statement: Hand-written code is not automatically faster: the library's templates are specialized by iterator category and inlined by the compiler, so a library `sort` routinely beats hand-written quicksort and a `vector` beats hand-managed arrays in real programs.
concepts.detail: Measure before believing — but start from the library side, where the surprises are usually pleasant.

concepts.statement: Every standard algorithm and container operation carries a documented complexity — $O(n)$ for `find`, $O(n \log n)$ for `sort`, $O(\log n)$ for a `map` lookup. Treat these as binding contracts you may reason with, not folklore.
concepts.detail: This is what makes “the library is fast enough” a design argument rather than a hope.

concepts.term: Shipping rule for standard library summary
concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Check the library before writing any container, algorithm or utility yourself.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

concepts.term: Review checklist for standard library summary
concepts.statement: Take the objectives as review questions: apply the “know the library first” discipline to new programming tasks? Then justify preferring standard components over hand-rolled ones with cost and correctness arguments? Answer each from the code in front of you, not from memory — the gap between the two answers is the review finding.
concepts.detail: A rule you can derive from the chapter you can also correctly suspend; a rule applied without its reason becomes superstition, so cite the reason in the review note.

examples.title: The cost of not using the library
examples.problem: A team hand-writes a bubble sort for 10,000 records while a colleague uses `std::sort`. Compare the comparison counts.

steps.label: Bubble sort
steps.text: average/worst case $\frac{n(n-1)}{2} = \frac{10^4(10^4-1)}{2} \approx 5\times10^7$ comparisons.

steps.label: std::sort
steps.text: worst case $O(n \log n)$: about $10^4 \times \log_2(10^4) \approx 10^4 \times 13.3 \approx 1.3\times10^5$ comparisons.

steps.label: Ratio
steps.text: $5\times10^7 / 1.3\times10^5 \approx 370$ — three orders of magnitude, before counting the bugs a hand-rolled sort accumulates.

steps.label: Beyond speed
steps.text: The library version also accepts any element type with a strict weak ordering, and is exercised daily by millions of programs.

examples.result: ≈370× fewer comparisons — the advice “prefer the standard library” is quantitative, not aesthetic.

examples.title: Reviewing standard library summary code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the “know the library first” discipline to new programming tasks.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Check the library before writing any container, algorithm or utility yourself.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `double m = std::numeric_limits<double>::max();`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: justify preferring standard components over hand-rolled ones with cost and correctness arguments. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Trust the documented complexity guarantees — they are contracts you can reason with.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Check the library before writing any container, algorithm or utility yourself. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Check the library before writing any container, algorithm or utility yourself.
Trust the documented complexity guarantees — they are contracts you can reason with.
Hand-written code is rarely faster and never better tested than the standard equivalent.

quiz.q: For n = 10,000, `std::sort` makes about how many comparisons?
quiz.explanation: $n \log_2 n \approx 10^4 \times 13.3 \approx 1.3\times10^5$ — versus $5\times10^7$ for bubble sort.

quiz.q: Your first move when a program needs a hash table is:
options: avoid the question with parallel arrays
quiz.explanation: The library already supplies the tuned, tested hash table; hand-rolling is the last resort, not the first.

quiz.q: A standard algorithm's documented complexity is:
quiz.explanation: The complexity is part of the standard's contract — you may rely on it in design.

intro: A container is an object that holds other objects, manages their storage and lifetime, and offers access through a uniform interface. This chapter tours the standard containers — the part of the library programmers touch most — and builds the vocabulary for choosing among them.
objectives: Define what counts as a standard container and what the container interface promises
Explain the STL's three-part separation of containers, iterators and algorithms
Reason about element ownership: copying, moving and destroying containers

concepts.statement: A container **owns its elements**: it constructs them (by copy or move) as they are inserted and destroys them as they are erased or as the container itself is destroyed. All elements share one type; a container is characterized by how it stores elements and which operations it offers for accessing them.
concepts.detail: Because containers hold values, element types should behave as values too — follow the rule of five, or better, the rule of zero.

concepts.statement: Stepanov's design: **containers hold data, algorithms process sequences, iterators connect the two.** An algorithm never sees a container — only a pair of iterators — so one `sort` serves every container that can supply random-access iterators.
concepts.detail: This is why the container and algorithm chapters can be read independently: their contract is entirely expressed in iterator categories.

concepts.statement: To live in a container an element type must be copy- or move-constructible; keys of ordered associative containers must support `<` (a strict weak ordering); keys of unordered containers need a hash function and `==`.
concepts.detail: A type with a copy constructor that throws can still be stored — but see the exception-safety consequences in chapter 30.

concepts.statement: The containers fall into three structural families — **sequence** (order is where you insert), **ordered associative** (order is key order, a balanced tree), **unordered associative** (no order, hash buckets) — plus three **adaptors** that restrict an ordinary container to a specialized interface.
concepts.detail: Choosing a container is choosing a data structure, and the choice is dominated by one question: which operations must be fast?

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Containers at a glance. You can claim this section when you can define what counts as a standard container and what the container interface promises — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 31 (STL Containers); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Word count in one screen
examples.problem: Read whitespace-separated words and print each word with its count, alphabetically. How much data-structure machinery does the container carry for you?

steps.label: Step 1: Choose
steps.text: Key → value with alphabetical iteration ⇒ `map<string, int>`.

steps.label: Step 2: Fill
steps.text: `for (string w; cin >> w;) ++m[w];` — `m[w]` returns the count, inserting 0 the first time a word is seen.

steps.label: Step 3: Report
steps.text: `for (auto& p : m) cout << p.first << ' ' << p.second;` — iteration follows key order because the tree is sorted.

steps.label: Step 4: Why it works
steps.text: Insertion is $O(\log n)$: $n = 100{,}000$ words cost about $100\,000 \times 17 \approx 1.7\times10^6$ key comparisons in total.

examples.result: A dozen lines replace a hand-managed sorted array plus resize and rebalance code — the container does the data-structure engineering.
