keyTakeaways: A container owns its elements: copies in, destruction out; elements must be copy or move constructible.
Containers, iterators and algorithms are strangers to one another by design — iterators are the only contract.
Three families — sequence, ordered associative, unordered associative — plus three adaptors cover the whole vocabulary.

quiz.q: What does it mean that a container “owns” its elements?
options: it may store references to stack objects
it constructs them on insert and destroys them on erase or destruction
elements are shared with the container's owner
elements are always heap-allocated outside the container
quiz.explanation: Ownership is lifetime control: erasing an element destroys it; destroying the container destroys everything left in it.

quiz.q: In the STL design, algorithms access container contents:
options: through iterator pairs naming a half-open sequence
quiz.explanation: The iterator pair is the entire contract — the algorithm knows nothing about the container.

quiz.q: A word counter that must print alphabetically needs a:
options: `unordered_map` — order is irrelevant to the task
`map<string, int>` — sorted iteration is the product
quiz.explanation: Ordered iteration is `map`'s defining feature; the hash table would print in bucket order.

intro: The eleven standard containers fall into three structural families plus three adaptors. Choosing among them is choosing a data structure — and the choice is dominated by one question: which operations must be fast? The taxonomy below is the map; the complexity numbers are the terrain.
objectives: Classify the standard containers into sequence, ordered associative and unordered associative families
Match each family's internal structure to its complexity guarantees
Choose between `map`, `unordered_map` and sorted `vector` from measured complexity, not habit

concepts.statement: **`vector`, `array`, `deque`, `list`, `forward_list`** — element order is the order you choose by where you insert. `vector`/`array` store elements contiguously ($O(1)$ subscripting); `deque` supports $O(1)$ push/pop at **both** ends; `list`/`forward_list` are linked (insert/erase anywhere in $O(1)$ given a position, but no subscripting).
concepts.detail: `array` is the fixed-size, non-allocating `vector`; `forward_list` is the minimal singly-linked list, kept deliberately free of even a `size()` operation.

concepts.statement: **`map`, `multimap`, `set`, `multiset`** — ordered by key using `<` (or a user comparator), implemented as balanced binary trees in every major implementation: find, insert and erase in $O(\log n)$, iteration in key order. `map` stores (key, value) pairs; `set` stores keys alone; the `multi` variants allow duplicate keys.
concepts.detail: Worst case is the point: $O(\log n)$ is guaranteed — no adversarial input, no hash-flood behavior.

concepts.statement: **`unordered_map`, `unordered_multimap`, `unordered_set`, `unordered_multiset`** — hash tables: expected $O(1)$ find/insert/erase, worst case $O(n)$; iteration order is unspecified and can change when a rehash occurs. Keys need a hash and `==` rather than `<`.
concepts.detail: Implementation as buckets is exposed: `bucket_count()`, `load_factor() = size()/bucket_count()`, and rehashing when the load exceeds `max_load_factor()`.

concepts.statement: Default to `map` unless you have a measured reason: it needs only `<`, iterates in order, and has a firm worst case. Use `unordered_map` for pure lookup performance on simple, well-hashed keys — remembering that hashing a long `string` costs a scan of the whole string, so the speedup shrinks as keys grow.
concepts.detail: The book's rule of thumb is exactly this asymmetry: `unordered_map` wins averages, `map` wins predictability and order.

concepts.statement: Containers hold **copies** (or moves): insert an object and the container stores its own element — later mutation of the original does not touch the stored one. There is no common `Object` base class; containers are not part of a class hierarchy at all.
concepts.detail: To share, store pointers — `vector<Shape*>` — or better, smart pointers: `vector<unique_ptr<Shape>>`.

examples.title: The cost of 100,000 lookups
examples.problem: From a dictionary of $n = 100{,}000$ entries, perform 100,000 random lookups by key. Compare `map`, `unordered_map` and an unsorted `vector` of pairs.

steps.label: map
steps.text: Each lookup is $O(\log_2 n)$: $\log_2 10^5 \approx 17$ key comparisons, so about $1.7\times10^6$ comparisons total — guaranteed, adversarial input or not.

steps.label: unordered_map
steps.text: Expected 1–2 bucket probes per lookup: roughly $2\times10^5$ hash evaluations plus probes — the fastest average.

steps.label: Unsorted vector
steps.text: A linear scan pays $n/2 = 5\times10^4$ comparisons on average per lookup: $5\times10^9$ total — four orders of magnitude worse than the tree.

steps.label: Sorted vector
steps.text: Binary search would pay the same 17 comparisons per lookup as `map` — but inserting a new word then costs $O(n)$ element moves.

examples.result: map ≈ $1.7\times10^6$, unordered_map ≈ $2\times10^5$, unsorted vector ≈ $5\times10^9$ operations: the data-structure choice is worth four orders of magnitude.

examples.title: Working through container overview
examples.problem: Sequence, associative and unordered containers. Your task: classify the standard containers into sequence, ordered associative and unordered associative families.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: classify the standard containers into sequence, ordered associative and unordered associative families. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Sequence containers order by insertion position; ordered associatives by key; unordered associatives by nothing at all.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::vector<int> v; v.reserve(64); v.push_back(1);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — match each family's internal structure to its complexity guarantees — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Ordered containers guarantee $O(\log n)$; unordered containers average $O(1)$ but degrade to $O(n)$. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Sequence containers order by insertion position; ordered associatives by key; unordered associatives by nothing at all. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Sequence containers order by insertion position; ordered associatives by key; unordered associatives by nothing at all.
Ordered containers guarantee $O(\log n)$; unordered containers average $O(1)$ but degrade to $O(n)$.
Default to `map` over `unordered_map` unless measurement says otherwise — order and predictability are features.

quiz.q: Which container gives $O(1)$ average lookup by key with no ordering guarantee?
quiz.explanation: The hash table averages constant time; iteration order is unspecified and changes on rehash.

quiz.q: In the chapter's taxonomy, `deque` is a:
quiz.explanation: `deque` inserts at the ends by position — a sequence container with $O(1)$ push/pop at both ends.

quiz.q: Keys in an ordered associative container compare with:
options: `<` — a strict weak ordering, by default
quiz.explanation: `<` (with a strict weak ordering) is the ordered family's requirement; hashing belongs to the unordered family.

quiz.q: `unordered_map` iteration order is:
options: unspecified — and a rehash can change it
quiz.explanation: Bucket order is an implementation detail; rehashing rearranges it, which is why the standard leaves it unspecified.

quiz.q: Lookups by key dominate, order does not matter, and the table holds 200,000 entries. Which choice matches the container guarantees?
options: `std::unordered_map`, with average constant-time lookup and no ordering
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is a large keyed table with lookup-dominated access and no ordering requirement. Step 2: The governing rules are the structural guarantees: hash tables average constant-time lookup without order, balanced trees give logarithmic lookup with order, and sequence containers offer no keyed lookup. Step 3: Applying the numbers, hashing averages near one probe per query while the tree needs about eighteen comparisons, so the hashed container removes nearly all per-query work. Step 4: The distractors fail because trees never reach constant time, and neither sequence container hashes by key. Step 5: Therefore the unordered container is the matching choice.

intro: All containers share a common interface — constructors, assignment, swap, size queries, iterators and comparison — plus family-specific operations. Knowing what is common lets you write code that works across containers; knowing where members beat generic algorithms keeps it fast.
objectives: List the operations common to every standard container
Explain why member operations such as `map::find` outperform their generic counterparts
Distinguish the insert, emplace and push families and their copy-versus-in-place semantics

concepts.statement: Every container offers: default, element-count, iterator-range and initializer-list constructors; copy and move assignment; `swap`; `==`/`!=` and `<`/`<=`/`>`/`>=` (lexicographic elementwise comparison); `size()`, `empty()`; `begin()`/`end()`; and `max_size()` — the sole exception being `forward_list`, which omits `size()` to stay minimal.
concepts.detail: Comparison is lexicographic: the first differing pair of elements decides; a shorter prefix makes the shorter container smaller.

concepts.statement: A member knows the container's internal structure: `map::find` descends the tree in $O(\log n)$, while `std::find` on the same `map` walks the sequence in $O(n)$. **If a container offers an operation as a member, prefer the member.**
concepts.detail: The same logic ranks `list::sort` above `std::sort` for lists — the generic sort cannot even run there (it needs random access).

concepts.statement: `insert` copies or moves an existing object into the container; `emplace`/`emplace_back` **construct the element in place** from the argument list — no temporary is created. `push`/`pop` are the adaptor names for insert/erase at the restricted end.
concepts.detail: `emplace_back(args...)` is exactly “construct a `T` from `args` directly at the end of the buffer” — for expensive-to-move element types this is a real win.

concepts.statement: Every container's iteration is the half-open sequence $[b, e)$: `e` designates one-past-the-last element; an empty container has `begin() == end()`; and loops test `p != e` — never `p < e`, which is meaningless for node iterators.
concepts.detail: The convention is inherited from C pointer arithmetic and is what lets empty sequences need no special cases.

concepts.statement: **Operations Overview.** The common container interface. You can claim this section when you can list the operations common to every standard container — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 31 (STL Containers); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Member find versus generic find on a million-entry map
examples.problem: A `map<int, string>` holds $10^6$ entries. Compare `m.find(k)` with `std::find(m.begin(), m.end(), pair)` for locating one entry.

steps.label: Member
steps.text: `m.find(k)` descends the tree: $\log_2 10^6 \approx 20$ comparisons; returns an iterator in $O(\log n)$.

steps.label: Generic
steps.text: `std::find` sees only a bidirectional sequence of pairs: it walks left to right, so about $n/2 = 5\times10^5$ pair comparisons on average.

steps.label: Why
steps.text: The generic algorithm cannot know it is walking a tree — iterators expose the sequence, not the structure. Even `std::lower_bound` on a `map` pays $O(n)$ iterator movement for its $O(\log n)$ comparisons.

steps.label: Contrast
steps.text: For a **sorted `vector<int>`** of $10^6$ elements, `std::lower_bound` does 20 comparisons and 20 pointer jumps — the generic algorithm matches the member because here the structure *is* a sequence.

examples.result: 20 versus 500,000 comparisons — same container, same key: the member exploits the tree; the generic code cannot.

keyTakeaways: Constructors, assignment, `swap`, size queries, lexicographic comparisons and `begin`/`end` are the universal container interface.
Member operations exploit internal structure (`map::find`, `list::sort`); generic algorithms see only a sequence — prefer the member when it exists.
`emplace` constructs in place; `insert` and `push` copy or move an existing object.

quiz.q: Which operation is NOT provided for `forward_list`?
quiz.explanation: `forward_list` omits `size()` deliberately — keeping track of the count would cost time and space a C-style singly linked list never pays.

quiz.q: Why prefer `map::find` over `std::find` on a `map`?
options: the generic one requires sorted input
no reason — they are the same
the member descends the tree — $O(\log n)$ versus the generic $O(n)$ walk
quiz.explanation: The member knows the structure; the generic algorithm is structure-blind and must traverse.

quiz.q: `emplace_back(args...)` differs from `push_back(x)` by:
options: constructing the element in place from the arguments — no temporary
quiz.explanation: Emplacement forwards the arguments to the element constructor at the final location; the push version first materializes the object.

quiz.q: Container comparison `v1 < v2` is defined:
quiz.explanation: Elementwise lexicographic order — the same rule `strcmp` and dictionary ordering follow.

intro: This is the field guide: the individual containers, their internal layouts, and the guarantees each makes. `vector` dominates practice; the others exist for the jobs its contiguity cannot do. Along the way we meet the rule that silently breaks real programs: what container mutation does to outstanding iterators and pointers.
objectives: Explain `vector`'s growth strategy and its amortized $O(1)$ `push_back`
State what `list`, `map`, `set` and the unordered containers trade away to gain their special guarantees
Apply the iterator-invalidation rules that follow from each container's memory layout

concepts.statement: Elements in **contiguous** memory: subscripting is a pointer computation, $O(1)$; insert/erase at the end is $O(1)$ amortized (and $O(n)$ anywhere else, by shifting). When full, a `push_back` allocates a larger buffer (growth factor typically 2 or 1.5), moves every element, and frees the old buffer — `reserve(n)` preempts the whole dance. `array<T, N>` is the fixed-size version: no allocation, no growth, ever.
concepts.detail: Contiguity is why `vector` is the default: cache locality and pointer arithmetic in one property.

concepts.statement: Doubly/singly linked nodes: insert/erase **anywhere** in $O(1)$ given a position; iterators and references stay valid while other elements are inserted or erased; no subscripting; `forward_list` lacks even `size()` to stay as cheap as a hand-written C list. `splice` stitches whole lists together in $O(1)$.
concepts.detail: The price is memory per element (two pointers for `list`) and poor locality — a `list` trades the cache for pointer stability.

concepts.statement: A balanced tree of (key, value) pairs: find/insert/erase in $O(\log n)$, iteration in key order, `equal_range` for a `multimap`'s duplicate keys. The subscript `m[k]` **inserts** a default value when `k` is absent — the classic trap when you only meant to look.
concepts.detail: Read-only lookup uses `find` or `at` (the latter throws `out_of_range`); subscript is a mutating operation.

concepts.statement: The tree stores keys alone: a sorted collection — unique in `set`, possibly repeated in `multiset` — with $O(\log n)$ membership tests and `lower_bound`/`upper_bound` range queries on the sorted order.
concepts.detail: A `set` of 1,000 elements answers “is x present” in at most 10 comparisons; an unordered set does it in about 1 hash probe.

concepts.statement: Hash tables: $`bucket_count()` buckets, `load_factor() = size()/bucket_count()`, and automatic **rehash** when the load exceeds `max_load_factor()` (default 1.0). A rehash invalidates every **iterator** but no **pointer or reference** — nodes are relinked, not moved. Average $O(1)$; worst $O(n)$ under pathological hashing.
concepts.detail: You can `reserve(n)` (which sets the bucket count) to pre-empt rehashing, just as with `vector` memory.

Growing 1, 2, 4, …, $2^k$ costs $2^k - 1$ moves, about one move per element: the amortized $O(1)$ guarantee.

examples.title: The arithmetic of doubling
examples.problem: Push $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$ elements one at a time into an empty `vector<int>`. Count total element moves (a) with default doubling growth, (b) with `reserve(1048576)` first.

steps.label: Growth law
steps.text: Buffer sizes run 1, 2, 4, …, $2^{20}$; moving from $2^k$ to $2^{k+1}$ costs $2^k$ element moves.

steps.label: Total
steps.text: $1 + 2 + 4 + \dots + 2^{19} = 2^{20} - 1 = 1\,048\,575$ moves over the whole process.

steps.label: Per element
steps.text: $\frac{2^{20}-1}{2^{20}} < 1$ move per `push_back` — exactly the meaning of **amortized $O(1)$**.

steps.label: Memory churn
steps.text: For 4-byte ints the final buffer is 4 MiB, and all transient buffers together allocated another ~4 MiB before being freed.

steps.label: With reserve
steps.text: `v.reserve(1048576)` up front: zero moves, one allocation — amortization becomes zero-cost.

examples.result: 1,048,575 moves versus 0 — `reserve` converts amortized cost into no cost whenever the final size is known.

depth.title: Container guarantees: the iterator and reference invalidation rules

blocks.body: Every container operation carries a second, less visible contract: which of the three kinds of handles into its elements — **iterators**, **pointers** and **references** — still designate a live element afterwards. The C++ standard states this exactly, per container and per operation; anything else is undefined behavior. Because generic code composes operations across call boundaries, these rules are what make multi-step container programs *programs* rather than accidents: the STL's flexibility is usable only because invalidation is specified, not incidental.

blocks.heading: The invalidation rules (C++11)
blocks.body: **`vector`/`array`**: an insertion forces reallocation exactly when it would exceed `capacity()`; reallocation invalidates **every** iterator, pointer and reference. Without reallocation, insertion invalidates all handles **at or after** the insertion point (those before survive). Erasure invalidates everything at or after the erase point. **`deque`**: insertion at either end invalidates all iterators but **no references**; insertion or erasure in the middle invalidates everything; erasure at an end invalidates only the erased elements. **`list`, `forward_list`, `map`, `set`, `multimap`, `multiset`**: insertion invalidates **nothing**; erasure invalidates only the erased element. **`unordered_map`, `unordered_set`, …**: insertion invalidates iterators **iff** it triggers a rehash — references and pointers survive, because nodes are relinked, not moved; erasure invalidates only the erased. **`swap`** (all containers): invalidates nothing — but every handle now designates elements of the *other* container.

blocks.heading: Why the rules follow from memory layout
blocks.body: Each rule is a lemma about storage. (1) **Contiguity**: a `vector`'s elements live in one buffer; reallocation moves the buffer itself, so every address into it dangles — no handle survives. Insertion without reallocation shifts the tail one slot: a shifted element is *moved into* a new position, so old references point at the vacated slot, while handles to elements before the point are untouched. (2) **Nodes**: `list`, `forward_list`, `map` and `set` allocate each element in its own node; insertion links new nodes and never disturbs old ones — no handle can break, and only erasure frees a node. (3) **Segmentation and buckets**: a `deque` iterator caches the segment map, which an end-push may reallocate — iterators break, while the segments (and the references into them) stay. An unordered container's iterator remembers its bucket: a rehash rebuilds the bucket table, so all iterators break, while each element node keeps its address — which is precisely why references survive a rehash but iterators do not. The table is not to be memorized; it is the memory layouts stated as promises.

blocks.heading: One push too far
blocks.body: Take `vector<int> v; v.reserve(8);` and push until `size() == 8`. Save `int* p = &v[3];` and `auto it = v.begin();`. Now `v.push_back(x);` forces reallocation (say, to capacity 16): eight element moves — and both `p` and `it` now point into the freed buffer. Reading `*p` is a heap-use-after-free that AddressSanitizer flags instantly and an unsanitized build may silently accept. Had `capacity()` been 16 beforehand, both handles would still be valid: the rule is **capacity-conditional, not operation-conditional** — which is why `reserve` is a correctness tool, not merely an optimization.

blocks.heading: Idioms the rules buy
blocks.body: Three corollaries run through real code. (1) The **erase-loop**: `for (auto it = c.begin(); it != c.end(); ) if (pred(*it)) it = c.erase(it); else ++it;` — `erase` returns the successor because the old successor was invalidated; `it++` after `erase` is undefined for a `vector`. (2) **Stable-address selection**: keep pointers into elements across later insertions only in node containers (`list`, `set`, `map`) — or in a `vector` you have pre-`reserve`d, or in an `unordered_map`, whose references survive even a rehash. (3) **Shrinking**: the swap idiom `vector<int>(v).swap(v)` leaves `v` with capacity equal to size, releasing the spare memory a history of growth left behind.

Note what *invalidated* means: not a stale but readable value — **undefined behavior**, with no defined way even to compare or copy the dead iterator. The invalidation rules are the library's memory-safety envelope: they circumscribe which compositions of operations constitute a program. Sanitizers (ASan, UBSan) and debug-mode standard libraries exist precisely because compilers cannot diagnose these violations statically — the guarantees are real, but only the disciplined get them.

keyTakeaways: `vector`: contiguous, $O(1)$ amortized end-insertion, $O(n)$ mid-insertion; reallocation invalidates everything.
`list` buys iterator stability and $O(1)$ splice at the price of locality; `map`/`set` buy order at $O(\log n)$; unordered containers buy speed at the price of order.
Invalidation follows layout: contiguous buffers break on reallocation, nodes never break on insertion, buckets break iterators but not references.

quiz.q: `vector::push_back` when `size() < capacity()`:
options: invalidates no iterators — no reallocation happens
quiz.explanation: With headroom, `push_back` writes into existing storage: no reallocation, nothing invalidated.

quiz.q: Which operation leaves ALL iterators valid?
quiz.explanation: Node containers invalidate nothing on insertion; the other three each invalidate (at least some) iterators.

quiz.q: `m[k]` on a `map` when `k` is absent:
options: is a pure lookup — no insertion
inserts a default value and returns a reference to it
quiz.explanation: The subscript inserts `Value{}` first; `at` is the throwing lookup, `find` the non-throwing one.

quiz.q: The default `max_load_factor` of an unordered container is:
quiz.explanation: Load factor = size / bucket_count; at the default threshold 1.0, growth triggers a rehash — invalidating iterators but not references.

intro: `stack`, `queue` and `priority_queue` are not containers but **container adaptors**: deliberately restricted interfaces over an ordinary container. They exist to make dangerous flexibility impossible — you cannot accidentally scan a stack, and the compiler enforces that.
objectives: Explain what an adaptor is and which underlying containers each one accepts
Use `priority_queue`'s heap interface and reason about its $O(\log n)$ costs
Recognize the interface restrictions as design, not omission

concepts.statement: `stack<T, C>`, `queue<T, C>` and `priority_queue<T, C>` wrap any container `C` meeting their needs and expose only the restricted operations — `push`, `pop`, and the peek — with **no iteration at all**. Defaults: `deque<T>` for `stack` and `queue`, `vector<T>` for `priority_queue`.
concepts.detail: The restrictions are contractual: a type that cannot be misused needs no comments defending it.

concepts.statement: **`stack`**: LIFO — `top()`, `push()`, `pop()`, all $O(1)$; works over `vector`, `list` or `deque`. **`queue`**: FIFO — `front()`/`back()`, `push` at the back, `pop` from the front, $O(1)$; it needs `push_front`, so **`vector` cannot underlie it** — a compile-time requirement failure, not a runtime one.
concepts.detail: Like `pop_back`, these `pop`s return `void`: returning the popped element would cost an extra copy and leave you holding a moved-from object on exception paths.

concepts.statement: A **max-heap** by default: `top()` is the largest element in $O(1)$; `push` and `pop` are $O(\log n)$ sift-up/sift-down. A comparator flips the order — `priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>` makes a min-heap. No iteration, no `find` — deliberately.
concepts.detail: The same machinery is exposed for raw arrays in `<algorithm>` as `make_heap`, `push_heap`, `pop_heap`.

concepts.statement: A binary heap is an array in which element $i$'s children sit at $2i+1$ and $2i+2$: no pointers, perfect cache behavior, one `swap` chain per update. That is why `priority_queue` defaults to `vector` — the adaptor's cost model *is* the array's.
concepts.detail: Priority scheduling, Dijkstra's algorithm and event queues are all “extract-the-best repeatedly,” which is exactly a heap's shape.

concepts.statement: **Container Adaptors.** stack, queue and priority_queue. You can claim this section when you can explain what an adaptor is and which underlying containers each one accepts — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 31 (STL Containers); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Tracing a priority queue
examples.problem: Insert 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6 into `priority_queue<int>`; show the heap array after each push, then the pop order.

steps.label: push 3, 1
steps.text: `[3]`, then `[3, 1]` — 1 does not exceed its parent 3, no swap.

steps.label: push 1
steps.text: `[4, 1, 3, 1]` — new 1 sits below parent 1, no swap.

steps.label: push 5
steps.text: Sifts past 1, then past 4: `[5, 4, 3, 1, 1]`.

steps.label: Cost
steps.text: The i-th push does at most $\lfloor \log_2 i \rfloor$ swaps; the bound sums to $0+1+1+2+2+2+2+3 = 13$ — this sequence used 7.

steps.label: Drain
steps.text: Pops emit 9, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 1 — descending order, each pop one sift-down.

examples.result: `top()` is 9; the eight pushes cost 7 swaps (bound 13); draining yields the elements in descending order.

keyTakeaways: Adaptors wrap a container and cut its interface down to a discipline: LIFO, FIFO, or extract-the-best.
`queue` needs `push_front`, so `vector` cannot underlie it; `priority_queue` defaults to `vector` because a heap is an array.
`priority_queue`: `top` $O(1)$, `push`/`pop` $O(\log n)$ — and no iteration by design.

quiz.q: The default underlying container for `stack` is:
quiz.explanation: Both `stack` and `queue` default to `deque`; `priority_queue` defaults to `vector`.

quiz.q: `vector` cannot underlie a `queue` because it lacks:
quiz.explanation: A queue pops from the front; `vector` has no `push_front`, so the requirement fails at compile time.

quiz.q: `priority_queue::pop()` costs:
quiz.explanation: Removing the root moves the last element to the top and sifts it down a path of length at most $\log_2 n$.

quiz.q: In the 0-based array form of a binary heap, the children of index $i$ are at:
quiz.explanation: 0-based indexing puts the children of $i$ at $2i+1$ and $2i+2$; the parent of $i$ is $(i-1)/2$.

intro: The container chapter's rules of thumb compress a hundred pages of trade-offs into a handful of defaults you can apply without re-deriving the analysis each time. They are the difference between choosing a container and merely using the one you know.
objectives: Adopt the defaults — `vector` first, member operations over generic ones
Justify container choices with named complexity and invalidation guarantees
Apply sizing discipline (`reserve`) and know when adaptors document design

concepts.statement: **Use a `vector` unless you have a reason not to**: it is compact, cache-friendly, has the best-tested code paths and subscripting. Every other container is an answer to a specific need — splicing, stable iterators, ordered iteration, hash lookup — and should be chosen by naming that need.
concepts.detail: The corollary: if you cannot name why a container beats `vector` for your workload, you have not chosen yet.

concepts.term: Know the guarantees you rely on
concepts.statement: Every container choice should be one sentence long and contain its complexity and invalidation behavior: “`list`, because I hold iterators across erasure”; “`unordered_map`, because lookup dominates and the keys hash well.”
concepts.detail: The standard publishes both tables — relying on them is not optional knowledge but the whole basis of the choice.

concepts.statement: Call `reserve(n)` when the final element count is known: it converts doubling-scaled reallocation churn into a single allocation — and, per the invalidation rules, keeps existing iterators and pointers valid.
concepts.detail: The same advice applies to `unordered_map::reserve`, which sets the bucket count and pre-empts a rehash.

concepts.statement: Adaptors exist because restricting an interface makes errors impossible: prefer a `stack` over a `vector` you promise (only in a comment) to use LIFO-only. The type system enforces what comments merely request.
concepts.detail: The same philosophy reappears throughout the library: `string_view` ranges, `const` iterators, `unique_ptr`'s move-only handle.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Default to `vector`; name the reason for anything else.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

examples.title: Picking containers for five jobs
examples.problem: Match each job to a container with a one-sentence justification: (1) undo history, (2) a unique word index printed alphabetically, (3) a cache keyed by URL, (4) a print spooler, (5) a scheduler that always runs the highest-priority waiting task.

steps.label: Step 1: Undo history
steps.text: `stack<Action>` — strict LIFO, and the restricted interface documents the design.

steps.label: Step 2: Word index
steps.text: `set<string>` (or `map<string, int>` with counts) — sorted iteration is the product, $O(\log n)$ per insertion.

steps.label: Step 3: URL cache
steps.text: `unordered_map<URL, Record>` — point lookups dominate; iteration order is irrelevant.

steps.label: Step 4: Print spooler
steps.text: `queue<Job>` — FIFO fairness, $O(1)$ at both ends.

steps.label: Step 5: Scheduler
steps.text: `priority_queue<Task>` — extract-the-best each step ($O(\log n)$); with `greater<Priority>` if the smaller value wins.

examples.result: Five data-structure decisions, each one sentence with its complexity named — that is what the advice buys.

examples.title: Reviewing STL containers code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: adopt the defaults — `vector` first, member operations over generic ones.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Default to `vector`; name the reason for anything else.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `std::vector<int> v; v.reserve(64); v.push_back(1);`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: justify container choices with named complexity and invalidation guarantees. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: State every choice with its complexity and invalidation guarantee in the same breath.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Default to `vector`; name the reason for anything else. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Default to `vector`; name the reason for anything else.
State every choice with its complexity and invalidation guarantee in the same breath.
`reserve` when the size is known; prefer adaptors when the discipline they enforce is the design.

quiz.q: The default container when in doubt is:
quiz.explanation: Compact, contiguous, cache-friendly and best tested — everything else needs a stated reason.

quiz.q: You hold iterators to elements while other elements are erased elsewhere in the same sequence. Choose:
quiz.explanation: Node containers invalidate only the erased element's handles; a `vector` erase invalidates everything at and after the point.

quiz.q: `reserve(1000)` before 1000 `push_back`s eliminates:
options: all element moves and the reallocation
quiz.explanation: One allocation up front: zero moves — and iterators taken after the reserve stay valid throughout.

intro: The standard algorithms are the payoff of the STL's separation: some sixty generic functions that traverse, transform, search and sort any sequence an iterator pair can name. This chapter is the field guide to them — what exists, what it costs, and what it demands of your data.
objectives: Describe what the standard algorithms offer and where they are declared
Explain the sequence-based (iterator-pair) interface and why it beats container-based design
Read an algorithm's complexity guarantee as part of its contract

concepts.statement: Generic functions, mostly in `<algorithm>` (the numeric ones in `<numeric>`), operating on **sequences**: searching (`find`), counting, reordering (`sort`, `reverse`, `rotate`), mutating (`copy`, `transform`, `replace`, `remove`), set operations on sorted ranges, extrema (`min_element`, `minmax_element`) and numeric folds (`accumulate`, `inner_product`).
concepts.detail: Each is a template over iterator types — one definition, instantiable for every sequence that meets its requirements.

concepts.statement: An algorithm's input is a **sequence** $[b, e)$ — a pair of iterators — never a container object. The same `sort` therefore serves a `vector`, a built-in array, a `string`'s characters or a stream buffer: nothing about the container is known or needed.
concepts.detail: This is the STL's central economy: N containers × M algorithms become N + M implementations instead of N × M.

concepts.term: The cost is part of the contract
concepts.statement: Every algorithm carries a standard-mandated complexity: `find` is $O(n)$, `sort` is $O(n \log n)$, `binary_search` is $O(\log n)$ on sorted input, `merge` is $O(n+m)$. Choosing an algorithm is choosing a cost model you may rely on.
concepts.detail: The standard counts in the currency of the iterator's category — comparisons, assignments and iterator steps.

concepts.statement: Algorithms demand the **weakest iterator category** they can get away with: `find` needs only input iterators, `reverse` bidirectional, `sort` random access. The weaker the demand, the more containers — and streams — an algorithm serves.
concepts.detail: A `list` cannot be `std::sort`ed (its iterators are bidirectional); it gets a member `sort` instead, which exploits the links.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** The algorithms at a glance. You can claim this section when you can describe what the standard algorithms offer and where they are declared — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 32 (STL Algorithms); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: One sort, three data sources
examples.problem: Sort the same five values whether they live in a built-in array, a `vector`, or the characters of a `string`. Show the identical shape of the three calls.

steps.label: Built-in array
steps.text: `double a[5] {30.0, 10.0, 20.0, 50.0, 40.0}; sort(a, a + 5);` — pointers are iterators, so the raw array is a first-class sequence.

steps.label: vector
steps.text: `sort(v.begin(), v.end());` — same algorithm, iterator type now a class.

steps.label: string
steps.text: `sort(s.begin(), s.end());` on "cabde" yields "abcde" — characters are elements like any other.

steps.label: Why one definition serves all
steps.text: Each call instantiates the template for a different iterator type: three specializations, zero runtime dispatch, no virtual functions.

examples.result: Three iterator types, one algorithm — the entire STL in miniature.

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: The algorithms at a glance. Your task: describe what the standard algorithms offer and where they are declared.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: describe what the standard algorithms offer and where they are declared. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Algorithms take iterator pairs naming half-open sequences — never containers.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()); auto it = std::find(v.begin(), v.end(), k);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain the sequence-based (iterator-pair) interface and why it beats container-based design — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Every algorithm's complexity is a standard-mandated promise, not folklore. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Algorithms take iterator pairs naming half-open sequences — never containers. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Algorithms take iterator pairs naming half-open sequences — never containers.
Every algorithm's complexity is a standard-mandated promise, not folklore.
Each algorithm demands the weakest iterator category it can — that is why one definition serves arrays, containers and streams alike.

quiz.q: The first two arguments to a standard algorithm are usually:
options: iterator pairs naming a half-open sequence
quiz.explanation: The sequence $[b, e)$ is the universal interface; containers are merely one way to produce it.

quiz.q: `std::sort` requires which iterator category?
quiz.explanation: Jumping to pivot positions needs $p + n$ arithmetic — random access only.

quiz.q: The numeric folds like `accumulate` are declared in:
quiz.explanation: `<numeric>` holds `accumulate`, `inner_product`, `partial_sum` and `iota`.

quiz.q: An algorithm is written to demand the weakest category it can because:
options: it serves every sequence with those operations — generality
quiz.explanation: Weaker requirements enlarge the set of sequence types the algorithm accepts — the STL's core economy.

intro: Beneath the sixty names lies one design: inputs are sequences, outputs are sequences, behavior is customized by function arguments, and every operation carries a mandated complexity. This section reads that design as a set of rules you can apply to any algorithm you meet.
objectives: Read an algorithm signature: input sequence(s), function arguments, output iterator, return value
Predict output-space requirements and know when insert iterators supply them
Use the complexity table to choose among algorithms with identical results

concepts.statement: Almost every algorithm is `alg(first, last, [first2, last2,] [value or predicate,] [out])`: the sequence arguments come first, the customization — values, predicates, comparators — after, and writing algorithms return the one-past-the-end iterator of what they produced.
concepts.detail: Read new signatures in that order and nothing in `<algorithm>` will surprise you.

concepts.statement: Algorithms accept **predicates** (`bool`-returning callables) and operations as arguments: `find_if(b, e, pred)`, `count_if`, `sort(b, e, cmp)`. Callables are passed **by value** — make them cheap to copy and free of side effects that depend on call order.
concepts.detail: The callable may be a function pointer, a function object or a lambda — chapter 33 covers the machinery.

concepts.term: Output space is the caller's duty
concepts.statement: `copy`, `transform` and friends write through an **output iterator** and never grow anything: the destination must have room for $n$ elements — or be an insert iterator that supplies its own storage. Writing past the room is undefined behavior, not a checked error.
concepts.detail: This is the design consequence of sequence-based interfaces: the algorithm cannot see the container, so it cannot resize it.

concepts.statement: Mandated costs you can rely on: linear scans $O(n)$; `sort` $O(n \log n)$; `nth_element` $O(n)$ on average; `merge` $O(n+m)$; the binary-search family $O(\log n)$ on sorted input; `minmax_element` at most $\frac{3n}{2} - 2$ comparisons.
concepts.detail: The cheat-sheet figure below is the exam version of the standard's tables — every row is a promise.

concepts.statement: The same name adapts to what the iterator can do: `distance(p, q)` is one subtraction for a `vector` iterator but a counted walk for a `list` iterator; `advance(p, n)` likewise. The category tag selects the implementation at **compile time** — no virtual dispatch.
concepts.detail: This is how one generic name provides the cheap algorithm where possible without penalizing the rest.

examples.title: Auditing a complexity claim
examples.problem: Verify by counting: (a) worst-case `find` on $n = 1000$; (b) `std::sort`'s comparator calls on $n = 1000$; (c) a hand-written bubble sort on the same data.

steps.label: find
steps.text: The value is absent ⇒ exactly $n = 1000$ element comparisons (plus 1001 iterator comparisons for the loop).

steps.label: sort
steps.text: A counting comparator reports about $n \log_2 n \approx 1000 \times 9.97 \approx 9966$ comparisons — introsort keeps its $O(n \log n)$ worst case.

steps.label: bubble
steps.text: Reversed input costs $\frac{n(n-1)}{2} = 499{,}500$ comparisons — 50× `sort`'s count.

steps.label: Read the table
steps.text: The cheat-sheet figures are what the standard owes you: measured counts may land anywhere at or below the bound, never above it in complexity class.

examples.result: 1,000 vs ≈9,966 vs 499,500 comparisons — the complexity table, verified in integers.

examples.title: Working through algorithms
examples.problem: The algorithms and their design. Your task: read an algorithm signature: input sequence(s), function arguments, output iterator, return value.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: read an algorithm signature: input sequence(s), function arguments, output iterator, return value. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Signatures read: sequence(s) first, customization next, output iterator last; writing algorithms return the new end.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()); auto it = std::find(v.begin(), v.end(), k);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — predict output-space requirements and know when insert iterators supply them — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: The caller guarantees output space — or passes an insert iterator. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

keyTakeaways: Signatures read: sequence(s) first, customization next, output iterator last; writing algorithms return the new end.
The caller guarantees output space — or passes an insert iterator.
Complexity is mandated per algorithm: the table is a contract, verified by counting.

quiz.q: `copy(b, e, out)` with `out` a plain iterator into an **empty** `vector`:
options: is undefined: the destination must already have room for $n$ elements
quiz.explanation: Sequence-based algorithms cannot resize anything they cannot see; room is the caller's promise.

quiz.q: Predicates are passed to algorithms:
quiz.explanation: By value — hence the rule to keep them small, pure and cheap to copy.

quiz.q: `distance(p, q)` on `list<int>` iterators costs:
quiz.explanation: Bidirectional iterators support no subtraction, so the distance is measured by incrementing.

intro: The read-only algorithms ask questions of a sequence without changing it: does it contain a value, how many pass a test, where is the first match, are two sequences equal. They are the safest tools in the library — and the ones you will call most.
objectives: Select among the find, count and `all_of`-family for the question being asked
Trace the short-circuit behavior of the question-asking algorithms
Use `for_each`'s returned function object to carry state out of a traversal

concepts.statement: `find(b, e, v)` — the first element `==` to v; `find_if(b, e, pred)`; `find_if_not`. All return **`e` when nothing matches** — so always test the result against `e` before dereferencing. Linear $O(n)$, short-circuiting at the first hit.
concepts.detail: The pattern `auto p = find(v.begin(), v.end(), x); if (p != v.end()) ...` is the library's “is it there, and where” in one call.

concepts.statement: `count(b, e, v)` returns the number of elements `==` to v; `count_if(b, e, pred)` counts predicate hits. A full $O(n)$ pass with no early exit — counting cannot stop early.
concepts.detail: Both return a difference-type integer, so counting an empty range yields 0, never an error.

concepts.statement: C++11 whole-sequence predicates: `all_of(b, e, p)` is true iff p holds for **every** element, `any_of` iff for at least one, `none_of` iff for none. Each scans left to right and **stops at the first element that decides the answer**.
concepts.detail: `all_of` halts on the first false; `any_of` on the first true — the same short-circuit as `&&` and `||`, lifted to sequences.

concepts.statement: Applies its function to each element and **returns the function** — so a stateful functor's accumulated data comes back in the return value. It is the generic traversal when no more specific algorithm states your intent.
concepts.detail: Returning the (possibly mutated) functor is what makes `for_each` a poor man's `accumulate` with arbitrary state.

concepts.statement: `equal(b1, e1, b2)` — element-by-element `==`, with the second range's sufficiency the caller's promise; `mismatch` returns the **first differing pair** as a pair of iterators; `search(b, e, b2, e2)` finds the first occurrence of the second sequence **as a contiguous subsequence** of the first.
concepts.detail: These are the comparison queries: whole-sequence equality, first difference, and subsequence location.

examples.title: Asking six questions of one vector
examples.problem: For `vector<int> v {3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6}` (whose elements sum to 31): count the evens, find the first value above 5, test “all odd”, test “any at least 8”, and total the elements with a stateful functor.

steps.label: count_if
steps.text: Even predicate `x % 2 == 0` matches 4, 2 and 6 ⇒ **3** — a full 8-element scan.

steps.label: find_if
steps.text: First value > 5: 3, 1, 4, 1, 5 all fail, then **9 at index 5** — six predicate calls, short circuit.

steps.label: all_of odd
steps.text: 3 ✓, 1 ✓, 4 ✗ ⇒ **false after 3 calls** — the first counterexample ends the scan.

steps.label: any_of ≥ 8
steps.text: 3, 1, 4, 1, 5 fail, then 9 ✓ ⇒ **true after 6 calls**.

steps.label: for_each sum
steps.text: A functor `Sum{0}` accumulates $3+1+4+1+5+9+2+6 = 31$ and is handed back as `for_each`'s return value.

examples.result: 3 evens; first >5 is `v[5] == 9`; all-odd false; any ≥ 8 true; sum 31 — every query answered with its exact cost.

examples.title: Working through nonmodifying sequence algorithms
examples.problem: find, count, all_of and friends. Your task: select among the find, count and `all_of`-family for the question being asked.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: select among the find, count and `all_of`-family for the question being asked. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `find`-family results must be tested against `end()` before use; they stop at the first hit.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()); auto it = std::find(v.begin(), v.end(), k);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — trace the short-circuit behavior of the question-asking algorithms — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: `all_of`/`any_of`/`none_of` short-circuit exactly as `&&`/`||` do. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `find`-family results must be tested against `end()` before use; they stop at the first hit. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `find`-family results must be tested against `end()` before use; they stop at the first hit.
`all_of`/`any_of`/`none_of` short-circuit exactly as `&&`/`||` do.
`for_each` returns its function object — the standard way to carry state out of a traversal.

quiz.q: If `find(b, e, v)` finds nothing it returns:
options: `e`, the end iterator — always test against it
quiz.explanation: The end iterator is the universal “not found”; dereferencing it is undefined behavior.

quiz.q: `all_of(b, e, p)` stops scanning when it:
options: meets the first element where p is false
quiz.explanation: One false element decides the conjunction — short-circuit, exactly like `&&`.

quiz.q: You recover a stateful functor's accumulated data after `for_each` by:
quiz.explanation: `for_each` returns the function it applied, mutations and all.

quiz.q: `equal(b1, e1, b2)` assumes:
options: the second range is at least as long as the first — an unchecked promise
quiz.explanation: Only the first range has an end; the caller guarantees the second can keep up.

options: `0`, because `find` throws when the value is missing
`1`, because a miss returns the end iterator
`9`, because `find` returns the sought value itself
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The code given searches a three-element vector for an absent value and compares the result with the end iterator. Step 2: The governing rule is the search contract: read-only searches return an iterator to the first match, or the past-the-end iterator when nothing matches, and callers must test before dereferencing. Step 3: Tracing the scan, positions holding `1`, `2`, and `3` all mismatch `9`, so the returned iterator equals `v.end()`, the comparison yields true, and the stream prints `1`. Step 4: The distractors fail because the algorithm reports misses by value rather than by throwing, the returned iterator is valid, and the sought value is never materialized. Step 5: Therefore the program prints `1`.

intro: Modifying algorithms write into output sequences: copying with a transformation, replacing, reordering, removing. Their most famous subtlety is that removing never shrinks anything — the erase–remove idiom exists because of it, and because algorithms cannot see the container they are cleaning.
objectives: Use copy/transform/replace/fill/generate with correct output space
Explain why `remove` and `unique` return an iterator instead of shrinking the container
Apply the erase–remove idiom and the reverse/rotate/shuffle reorderings

concepts.statement: `copy(b, e, out)` copies elements unchanged (the overloaded `copy_if` filters by a predicate); `transform(b, e, out, f)` applies a unary operation (or a binary one over two input ranges) while copying. All are $O(n)$ and return the new end of the output.
concepts.detail: `copy` is the workhorse of the iterator adaptors: with a `back_inserter` it becomes “append everything”.

concepts.statement: `remove(b, e, v)` **cannot shrink the container** — it holds only iterators, not the container object. It moves the kept elements forward and returns the new logical end; elements beyond are unspecified leftovers. Shrink explicitly: `c.erase(remove(c.begin(), c.end(), v), c.end())` — the **erase–remove idiom**. `unique` follows the same rule for adjacent duplicates.
concepts.detail: The rule is the price of sequence-based design: no container in sight, no `size()` to change.

concepts.statement: `replace(b, e, old, new)` (and `replace_if`) overwrite matching elements in place; `fill(b, e, v)` assigns v to every element; `generate(b, e, g)` assigns `g()`'s successive results. All $O(n)$, all in place — no output iterator needed.
concepts.detail: They write only into elements that already exist, so no capacity question ever arises.

concepts.statement: `reverse(b, e)` flips in place ($\frac{n}{2}$ swaps, bidirectional iterators); `rotate(b, m, e)` makes `m` the new first element — a circular shift and the heart of insertion sort's inner loop; `shuffle(b, e, engine)` produces a uniformly random permutation from a random-number engine (its deprecated ancestor `random_shuffle` is gone).
concepts.detail: `rotate`'s return value — the new position of the old first element — makes cycles composable.

concepts.statement: `move(b, e, out)` moves elements out through an output iterator: the source remains valid but its element values are unspecified. This is the C++11 underpinning of transferring a buffer's contents without copies.
concepts.detail: Combined with move iterators (ch33), whole containers can be relocated at the cost of pointer fix-ups rather than deep copies.

examples.title: Erase–remove, element by element
examples.problem: From `vector<int> v {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}`, remove all odd values via `remove_if` and then `erase`. Trace the buffer.

steps.label: Call
steps.text: `auto it = remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int x) { return x % 2; });`

steps.label: The pass
steps.text: Read 1 (odd, skip); keep 2 → write at index 0; skip 3; keep 4 → index 1; skip 5; keep 6 → index 2.

steps.label: Logical view
steps.text: `v == {2, 4, 6, ?, ?, ?}` with `it` pointing at index 3 — the tail still holds leftover values, and they are **unspecified**: never relied on.

steps.label: Erase
steps.text: `v.erase(it, v.end());` ⇒ `v == {2, 4, 6}`, `size() == 3`, capacity unchanged (still 6).

steps.label: Cost
steps.text: $n$ reads and at most $n$ writes — here exactly 3 keep-writes, one linear pass.

examples.result: v = {2, 4, 6} with size 3 and capacity 6: the algorithm moved the frontier, the erase reclaimed the size.

examples.title: Working through modifying sequence algorithms
examples.problem: transform, copy, remove and shuffle. Your task: use copy/transform/replace/fill/generate with correct output space.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: use copy/transform/replace/fill/generate with correct output space. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `remove`/`unique` return the new logical end — the container's `erase` must finish the job.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()); auto it = std::find(v.begin(), v.end(), k);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary

keyTakeaways: `remove`/`unique` return the new logical end — the container's `erase` must finish the job.
`transform` applies an operation while copying; `replace`/`fill`/`generate` overwrite in place.
`rotate` is the circular shift; `shuffle` is the uniform random permutation; `move` relocates without copies.

quiz.q: After `remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 0)` on `v = {0, 1, 0, 2}` (size 4), `v.size()` is:
quiz.explanation: Remove never changes the container — only the logical frontier moves; the erase finishes the job.

quiz.q: The complete idiom is:
quiz.explanation: Algorithm moves the frontier; the member reclaims the tail — together, one idiom.

quiz.q: `unique` removes:
options: all duplicates, anywhere in the sequence
nothing — it is a pure query
quiz.explanation: One pass can only compare neighbors — sort first if you want all duplicates removed.

quiz.q: `transform(b, e, out, f)` differs from `copy` by:
options: applying f to each element as it is written
quiz.explanation: Same traversal, same output rules — one function application per element along the way.

intro: Sorting converts lookup cost into comparison cost once, and buys every later question at logarithmic price. This section covers the sort family, the binary-search family that demands sorted input, and merge with the set operations that compose sorted sequences.
objectives: Choose among sort, stable_sort, partial_sort and nth_element by what you actually need
Apply lower_bound/upper_bound/equal_range and state their requirements
Merge sorted sequences and compute set operations with the right preconditions

concepts.statement: `sort(b, e)` orders the sequence with `<` (or a comparator) in $O(n \log n)$; it is **not stable** — equivalent elements may swap places. `stable_sort` preserves the relative order of equivalent elements, at $O(n \log n)$ comparisons with $O(n)$ extra memory (degrading to $O(n \log^2 n)$ if the allocator refuses).
concepts.detail: Implementation-wise, `sort` is introsort — quicksort that falls back to heapsort when recursion goes too deep — hence the $O(n \log n)$ **worst case**.

concepts.statement: `partial_sort(b, mid, e)` sorts only the first `mid − b` elements — the smallest ones, in order — in about $O(n \log m)$. `nth_element(b, n, e)` puts the element that belongs at position n there, with everything before ≤ it and after ≥ it, in $O(n)$ on average: quickselect, the top-k workhorse.
concepts.detail: Need the 10 smallest in order? `partial_sort`. Need the median or a split point? `nth_element` — no full sort required.

concepts.statement: On a **sorted** sequence: `lower_bound(b, e, v)` — the first element **≥** v; `upper_bound` — the first **>** v; `equal_range` — both as a pair; `binary_search` — a mere bool. $O(\log n)$ comparisons on random-access iterators (halving steps degrade on weaker categories — see ch33).
concepts.detail: `equal_range`'s `[lower, upper)` pair is the idiom for “all elements equal to v”: its length is the multiplicity.

concepts.statement: `merge(b1, e1, b2, e2, out)` weaves two sorted runs into one sorted output in $O(n+m)$; `inplace_merge` does it inside one sequence. `includes`, `set_union`, `set_intersection`, `set_difference` and `set_symmetric_difference` compute set algebra on **sorted** inputs, all in $O(n+m)$.
concepts.detail: Sorted order is what makes set algebra linear: two cursors advance monotonically, each element examined once.

concepts.statement: `partition(b, e, p)` splits in place — true-elements first, false-elements after — in $O(n)$: the engine of quicksort. `is_partitioned` tests, and `partition_point` finds the boundary of an already-partitioned range in $O(\log n)$: binary search over a predicate.
concepts.detail: `stable_partition` keeps the relative order within each half, at the cost of extra memory.
