options: the first capture of each match
the pieces *between* matches — the splitting idiom
quiz.explanation: −1 selects the complement of the pattern: the text the separators did not touch.

quiz.q: Incrementing an `sregex_iterator` performs:
options: a fresh `regex_match` on the whole input
a `regex_search` starting where the previous match ended
a copy of the previous match
a jump to the input's end
quiz.explanation: That is exactly the progression that makes matches non-overlapping and the loop exhaustive.

quiz.q: The lifetime rule for the iterators is:
options: they own a copy of the pattern
the `regex` object must outlive them — they store a pointer to it
they must be destroyed before the input
quiz.explanation: Declare the regex before the loop; a temporary pattern is the classic dangling-pointer crash.

intro: Everything character-specific in the regex engine is delegated to a traits class: classification, case folding, digit values, collation. `regex_traits<char>` implements the pattern language over the standard locale, and the same engine serves wide and custom character types through different traits. You will rarely write one — but this section is why you could.
objectives: Say what the traits parameter of `basic_regex` supplies
Explain how `icase` matching works through `translate_nocase`
Recognize the one sanctioned way to bend character classes to an unusual alphabet

concepts.statement: `basic_regex<C, Tr>` separates the *pattern language* from the *character set* it runs on: everything that touches actual characters — classification (`[[:alpha:]]`, `\w`), case folding, digit values, collation — is delegated to the traits class `Tr`. `regex_traits<char>` and `regex_traits<wchar_t>` are the provided specializations; both implement the language over `std::ctype` of the imbued locale, which is why the same `regex` machinery serves `regex`, `wregex` and beyond.
concepts.detail: Traits are the 'policy' of the regex world: the engine's state machine, backtracking and capture logic are policy-free.

concepts.statement: The catalogue: a `char_class_type` (a bitmask of character classes); `lookup_classname` (name → mask) and `isctype` (character against mask) — the pair behind every named class; `translate` and `translate_nocase` (single-character equivalences used for matching — where `icase` folds); `value(c, base)` (the numeric value of a digit character, used by escapes and counted repetitions); `transform`/`transform_primary` (sort-key equivalents of strings, needed for locale-correct ranges like `[a-z]`); `imbue`/`getloc` for locale handling.
concepts.detail: The engine calls these; it never inspects characters directly. That is the entire seam along which behavior is customized.

concepts.statement: Because the policy is external, the *same engine* serves `char`, `wchar_t` and custom character types, and locale behavior is not frozen into the machine. A custom traits class is the sanctioned way to bend the alphabet: treat `'_'` as a word character in `\w`, add folded pairs to case-insensitive matching, or adapt the classes to a non-ASCII set. You pay for the flexibility once, when writing the traits; every pattern after that inherits it.
concepts.detail: The book's own example instantiates the regex machinery over different character types — the engine never notices.

concepts.statement: **regex_traits.** Customizing regex. You can claim this section when you can say what the traits parameter of `basic_regex` supplies — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 37 (Regular Expressions); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

concepts.statement: Work in three passes. First, explain how `icase` matching works through `translate_nocase`. Then, recognize the one sanctioned way to bend character classes to an unusual alphabet. Finally, test the outcome against the section promise: `basic_regex<C, Tr>` delegates every character-level decision to traits; the engine is policy-free.
concepts.detail: Each pass catches a different class of mistake, and skipping one moves the failure into a larger program where it costs more to diagnose than it would have here.

examples.title: Case folding through traits
examples.problem: How does matching built with `regex::icase` compare 'Q' with 'q' — and why is that a traits concern rather than an engine concern?

steps.label: The mechanism
steps.text: With `icase`, the engine compares `translate_nocase(a) == translate_nocase(b)` instead of `a == b` — each character is folded once, and the folds are compared.

steps.label: The default fold
steps.text: For `regex_traits<char>` over the classic locale, `translate_nocase` is essentially `tolower` on both bytes: 'Q' (0x51) and 'q' (0x71) both fold to 0x71 — equal.

steps.label: The engine never learned what a letter is
steps.text: Swap in a traits class that folds differently — more pairs, different pairs — and the same engine folds differently, because the comparison goes through the policy, not through the machine.

steps.label: Classes too
steps.text: Character *classes* are equally external: `\w` is an `isctype(c, mask)` call, which is why a custom traits can widen or narrow what counts as a word character.

examples.result: Matching is equality; *which things are equal* is policy — and policy lives in traits.

examples.title: Working through regex_traits
examples.problem: Customizing regex. Your task: say what the traits parameter of `basic_regex` supplies.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: say what the traits parameter of `basic_regex` supplies. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: `basic_regex<C, Tr>` delegates every character-level decision to traits; the engine is policy-free.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::regex pat(word); bool hit = std::regex_search(line, pat);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain how `icase` matching works through `translate_nocase` — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: `lookup_classname`/`isctype` implement named classes; `translate_nocase` implements `icase`; `value` and `transform` cover digits and collation. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: `basic_regex<C, Tr>` delegates every character-level decision to traits; the engine is policy-free. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: `basic_regex<C, Tr>` delegates every character-level decision to traits; the engine is policy-free.
`lookup_classname`/`isctype` implement named classes; `translate_nocase` implements `icase`; `value` and `transform` cover digits and collation.
Custom traits are the sanctioned way to adapt the alphabet — the same engine then serves the custom character type.

quiz.q: The second template parameter of `basic_regex` supplies:
options: the character-level policy: classification, folding, digit values, collation
quiz.explanation: Everything touching actual characters is delegated; the engine itself is generic.

quiz.q: `lookup_classname` and `isctype` together implement:
options: named character classes such as the alpha class
quiz.explanation: One maps a class name to a bitmask, the other tests a character against that mask.

quiz.q: With `regex::icase`, two characters match when:
quiz.explanation: Folding through the traits function is the whole of case-insensitive matching.

intro: The chapter's advice is about where regexes pay and where they betray: build them once and write them as raw strings; pick match, search or replace by intent; and know that regular languages cannot carry nested structure — tokens yes, grammar no.
objectives: Apply the construction discipline: raw strings, built once, outside loops
Choose the right function family for validation, extraction and transformation
Recognize the structural limit of regular languages

concepts.statement: Construct the `regex` outside loops — compilation is the expensive part, matching is cheap. And write patterns as raw string literals: `R"(\d{5})"` rather than `"\\d{5}"`, so the pattern on the page is the pattern the machine compiles. Every doubled backslash is one more chance for a maintainer to halve or double it wrongly.
concepts.detail: A pattern hidden inside a loop is a silent tax of parse-and-build on every iteration — often the difference between milliseconds and seconds.

concepts.statement: Validate with `regex_match`; extract with `regex_search` or the iterators; transform with `regex_replace` — whose format splices do most rewriting jobs without post-processing. For plain splitting, the token iterator with −1 beats manual `find` loops. Reach for non-greedy quantifiers when structure demands them — the §37.1 `<a><b>` case is the canonical example.
concepts.detail: Most regex bugs are intent bugs: the wrong verb for the job, not a wrong pattern inside the right verb.

concepts.statement: Regular expressions match *regular* languages — flat patterns, no nesting. HTML with balanced tags, arithmetic with nested parentheses, C++ itself: not regular, and forcing them into a regex produces monsters that half-work. Use regex for tokens and shapes; use (recursive) grammars and real parsers for structure. And in hot paths, measure: the convenience has a price, and `optimize` plus hoisting is how you pay less of it.
concepts.detail: The book's own regular-expression chapters are followed by parsing chapters — the boundary between them is exactly this rule.

concepts.statement: Before code that uses this chapter is done, check it against the summary: **Compile once, outside loops; write patterns as raw strings so backslashes survive untouched.** A second reader should be able to point at each clause of that sentence in the code.
concepts.detail: Advice sections collect the rules whose violation caused real bugs; each rule here is the cheapest known way to avoid its bug class.

concepts.statement: Take the objectives as review questions: apply the construction discipline: raw strings, built once, outside loops? Then choose the right function family for validation, extraction and transformation? Answer each from the code in front of you, not from memory — the gap between the two answers is the review finding.
concepts.detail: A rule you can derive from the chapter you can also correctly suspend; a rule applied without its reason becomes superstition, so cite the reason in the review note.

examples.title: The pattern, made readable
examples.problem: A date pattern was written as `regex pat {"\\d{2}/\\d{2}/\\d{4}"};` — correct, but every edit risks a backslash error. Restate it by the chapter's rules.

steps.label: What the escapes cost
steps.text: Each `\\` in the literal is one real backslash reaching the engine — correct, but the reader must un-double in their head on every line, and a maintainer who 'fixes' one to a single backslash silently changes `\d` (digit class) into `d` (the letter).

steps.label: The raw form
steps.text: `regex pat {R"(\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{4})"};` — character for character what the engine compiles: digit-digit, slash, digit-digit, slash, digit-digit-digit-digit. Page and pattern can no longer disagree.

steps.label: The placement
steps.text: And the `regex` lives at namespace or function-static scope — outside any loop that uses it — so it compiles once per run, not once per call.

examples.result: Same machine, one readable form, zero construction in loops — the advice in two moves.

examples.title: Reviewing regular expressions code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the construction discipline: raw strings, built once, outside loops.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Compile once, outside loops; write patterns as raw strings so backslashes survive untouched.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `std::regex pat(word); bool hit = std::regex_search(line, pat);`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: choose the right function family for validation, extraction and transformation. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Match to validate, search to extract, replace to transform; token iterator with −1 to split.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Compile once, outside loops; write patterns as raw strings so backslashes survive untouched. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Compile once, outside loops; write patterns as raw strings so backslashes survive untouched.
Match to validate, search to extract, replace to transform; token iterator with −1 to split.
Regular languages have no nesting — tokens and shapes for regex, structure for grammars.

quiz.q: The chapter's advice about `regex` construction is:
options: hoist construction out of loops — compilation is the expensive part
always pass the pattern string directly to the match functions
quiz.explanation: The regex object is a compiled machine; rebuilding it per iteration re-pays the build cost every time.

quiz.q: A pattern that must match arbitrarily nested parentheses is:
options: not expressible as a regular expression — use a grammar/parser
quiz.explanation: Nesting is exactly the structure regular languages lack; backreferences add nothing structural.

quiz.q: Raw string literals are preferred for patterns because:
options: the pattern appears exactly as written — no escape doubling
quiz.explanation: What you read is what the machine gets — the whole point of a pattern's notation.

intro: The iostream library is C++'s framework for moving characters between a program and the outside world — terminals, files, strings, sockets — with formatting and error handling built in. Its central idea is the stream: a uniform abstraction that hides the differences between devices, so the same `<<` and `>>` code works everywhere. Stroustrup's design goals were type safety, extensibility to user-defined types, and efficiency good enough for real systems. This chapter follows the library from the top of its class hierarchy down to the character buffers that touch the operating system.
objectives: Describe the stream abstraction and the split between formatting (stream classes) and transport (buffers)
Explain why iostream I/O is type-safe where C stdio is not
Name the four standard streams and their intended uses

concepts.statement: **A stream is a source or sink of characters.** Input streams produce characters (from a keyboard, a file, a string); output streams consume them; the iostream library gives every stream the same interface regardless of what is behind it.
concepts.detail: The key separation of concerns: the *stream classes* (`istream`, `ostream`, ...) format and convert values, while a *stream buffer* (§38.6) performs the actual character transport to and from the device.

concepts.statement: The operators `<<` (output) and `>>` (input) are **overloaded on the type of their right-hand operand, so the conversion to characters is chosen at compile time**. A classic `printf` mismatch such as passing a `char*` to `%d` compiles and corrupts memory; `cout << name` where no matching operator exists is a compile-time error.
concepts.detail: Every operation knows the type it is dealing with. There is no run-time format string to drift out of sync with the argument list — the class of bugs that has haunted C programs since the 1970s is structurally impossible.

concepts.statement: **Users define `<<` and `>>` for their own types** — a `Date`, a `complex<double>`, a `Point` — and those operators immediately work with every kind of stream: files, strings, the console. That uniformity is what makes the hierarchy of §38.2 valuable.
concepts.detail: The library ships with the built-in types handled; everything else is ordinary overloading, with no library changes required.

concepts.statement: **`cin`** — standard input (from `stdin`); **`cout`** — standard output (to `stdout`); **`cerr`** — standard error, **unbuffered**, for immediate error messages; **`clog`** — standard logging, buffered. Wide-character variants `wcin`, `wcout`, `wcerr` complete the set.
concepts.detail: Unbuffered means every character written to `cerr` is handed to the operating system immediately — exactly what you want when the next event might be a crash.

concepts.statement: **Introduction.** Streams at a glance. You can claim this section when you can describe the stream abstraction and the split between formatting (stream classes) and transport (buffers) — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 38 (I/O Streams); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: printf vs. cout — the type-safety argument
examples.problem: A program must print a person's name (a string) and age (an int). Show how the C and C++ mechanisms differ when the programmer swaps the arguments by mistake.

steps.label: Step 1: The C attempt
steps.text: `printf("%s %d\n", age, name);` — the arguments are swapped: `age` is printed as a string (undefined behavior — typically garbage or a crash) and the compiler cannot warn reliably, because `printf` takes `...` and checks nothing.

steps.label: Step 2: Why the compiler is silent
steps.text: Variadic C functions receive no type information at all; the conversion performed is dictated entirely by the format string at run time.

steps.label: Step 3: The C++ equivalent
steps.text: `std::cout << age << ' ' << name << "\n";` — overload resolution picks `operator<<(int)` and the string overload at compile time. Had `name` lacked a matching operator, the program would simply not compile.

examples.result: The iostream design moves the run-time format/argument agreement problem into the type system: what used to be a crash becomes a compile-time error.

examples.title: Working through introduction
examples.problem: Streams at a glance. Your task: describe the stream abstraction and the split between formatting (stream classes) and transport (buffers).

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: describe the stream abstraction and the split between formatting (stream classes) and transport (buffers). Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: A stream is a uniform character source/sink; stream classes format, stream buffers transport.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `if (std::cin >> x) { use(x); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain why iostream I/O is type-safe where C stdio is not — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: `<<` and `>>` are ordinary overloaded operators — type safety and extensibility fall out of the type system. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: A stream is a uniform character source/sink; stream classes format, stream buffers transport. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: A stream is a uniform character source/sink; stream classes format, stream buffers transport.
`<<` and `>>` are ordinary overloaded operators — type safety and extensibility fall out of the type system.
Use `cerr` (unbuffered) for urgent diagnostics, `clog` for logging, `cout` for normal output.

quiz.q: Which statement best captures the division of labor in the iostream library?
options: The stream classes format and convert values; stream buffers handle character transport to devices
The stream buffers format values; the stream classes talk to the operating system
`cin` handles all input and `cout` handles all output
The `<<` operator formats and the `>>` operator transports
quiz.explanation: Formatting and conversion live in the stream class hierarchy; `basic_streambuf` and its derived classes move characters to and from devices (§38.6).

quiz.q: Why is `cout << p` for a user type `p` guaranteed to be type-checked?
options: The library scans the value for format specifiers
The compiler resolves a specific overload of `operator<<` for the type of `p`
`p` is always converted to a string first
quiz.explanation: Type safety comes from ordinary overload resolution at compile time — no operator found means a compile error, not a run-time crash.

quiz.q: You need an error message to reach the screen immediately, before a likely crash. Which stream and why?
options: `cerr`, because it is unbuffered — characters are handed to the OS immediately
`cout`, because it is the default destination
`cin`, because errors are read, not written
quiz.explanation: `cerr` is unbuffered by design; buffered output can still be sitting in a buffer when the process dies.

intro: The iostream framework is a small class hierarchy — small enough to memorize. At the top sits `ios_base`, which holds everything that is independent of the character type: stream state, formatting flags, and the locale. Below it, templated on the character type, `basic_ios` adds the link to a stream buffer, and the input/output/file/string classes hang off that. Knowing the shape of this hierarchy tells you what you can safely pass to a function that logs.
objectives: Draw the iostream class hierarchy from `ios_base` down to the file and string streams
Say what each level contributes: state, buffer link, input, output
Use the typedefs (`istream`, `ofstream`, ...) and explain the diamond under `basic_iostream`

concepts.statement: **`ios_base`** holds the stream *state* (`goodbit`, `failbit`, `eofbit`, `badbit`), the *formatting information* (base, precision, width, flag set) and the *locale*. Because none of that depends on the character type, it is a plain class, not a template.
concepts.detail: `flags()`, `precision()` and `width()` all live here — the formatting state that §38.4 manipulates.

concepts.statement: **`basic_ios`** adds everything that needs to know the character type: the managed pointer to a **`basic_streambuf`** (`rdbuf()`), the fill character, `tie()`, and `narrow`/`widen`. It is here that `imbue()` installs a new locale (§39.2).
concepts.detail: A stream object is a formatting front end; the buffer it points to does the real transport — one object, two cooperating classes.

concepts.statement: **`basic_istream<charT, traits>`** provides formatted input (`>>`, `get()`, `getline()`, `read()`, `ignore()`, `peek()`); **`basic_ostream`** provides output (`<<`, `put()`, `write()`); **`basic_iostream`** multiply inherits both, giving a stream that reads and writes the same character source (a file opened for I/O, a string).
concepts.detail: Multiple inheritance is used because an iostream *is-a* read stream and *is-a* write stream — a classic diamond with the shared `basic_ios` base above.

concepts.statement: **`basic_ifstream`/`basic_ofstream`/`basic_fstream`** derive from the corresponding stream classes, add `open()`/close management, and own a **`basic_filebuf`**; **`basic_istringstream`/`basic_ostringstream`/`basic_stringstream`** do the same for an in-memory **`basic_stringbuf`**, plus `str()` access to the string.
concepts.detail: These are the classes you instantiate: they bundle a stream and its buffer so construction opens the source and destruction closes it (RAII, as in Chapter 5).

concepts.statement: `istream` = `basic_istream<char, char_traits<char>>`, `ostream` = `basic_ostream<char, ...>`; prefix `w` for `wchar_t`: `wistream`, `wofstream`, `wstringstream`, ... The naming runs through the buffers too: `streambuf` = `basic_streambuf<char, ...>`.
concepts.detail: Almost all code mentions only the `char` typedefs; the template machinery exists so wide characters and custom traits work with zero library redesign.

figures.caption: The iostream class hierarchy. Template parameters (`charT`, `traits`) are elided after the first level; every class exists for `char` (typedefs `istream`, `ostream`, ...) and `wchar_t` (`wistream`, ...). The dashed link is the `rdbuf()` pointer by which `basic_ios` delegates transport to a `basic_streambuf` (§38.6).

examples.title: One logging function, three destinations
examples.problem: Write a single function that appends a message to any output destination — console, file, or an in-memory string — and use all three.

steps.label: Step 1: The function
steps.text: `void log_event(std::ostream& os, const std::string& msg) { os << msg << "\n"; }` — it accepts a reference to the base `ostream`, so any derived stream can be passed (polymorphism).

steps.label: Step 2: Console
steps.text: `log_event(std::cout, "session start");` — the formatted characters go to the terminal.

steps.label: Step 3: File
steps.text: `std::ofstream log{"run.log", std::ios::app}; log_event(log, "session start");` — the same call appends to the file; destruction of `log` closes it.

steps.label: Step 4: String
steps.text: `std::ostringstream buf; log_event(buf, "session start"); std::string line = buf.str();` — the characters are captured in `line` for later use.

examples.result: Because `ofstream` and `ostringstream` are both kinds of `ostream`, one function covers all three sinks — the whole point of the hierarchy.

quiz.explanation: State and formatting are character-type independent, so they live in the non-template root `ios_base`; the typed layer starts at `basic_ios`.

quiz.q: What does `basic_ios` add over `ios_base`?
options: The managed link to a `basic_streambuf`, plus `tie()`, `fill()` and the character-typed state
The locale and the formatting flags
quiz.explanation: `basic_ios` is where the character type enters — including the `rdbuf()` pointer that carries out the actual transport.

quiz.q: `std::ifstream` is derived from ...
quiz.explanation: The file stream classes derive from the corresponding basic stream classes and add an owned file buffer plus `open()` management.

quiz.q: `std::stringstream` exists so that ...
options: strings can be written to files
a stream that reads and writes can operate on an in-memory `std::string`
quiz.explanation: A `stringstream` is a `basic_iostream` over a `basic_stringbuf`: you get full stream I/O over a string in memory.

intro: Streams report trouble in their state, not by throwing. Every stream carries four state bits that record what went wrong, and every operation checks them before doing anything — a failed stream stays failed until you clear it. This design makes the canonical read loop `while (is >> x)` both idiomatic and safe, and it explains why forgetting to test the result of an input is the classic I/O bug.
objectives: Read and set the four stream state bits and know what each means
Explain the idiom `if (cin >> x)` and the failure behavior of formatted input
Enable and use stream exceptions, and recover a failed stream with `clear()` plus `ignore()`

concepts.statement: Each stream carries a state composed of four bits: **`goodbit`** (zero — no error), **`eofbit`** (end of input reached), **`failbit`** (an operation failed: the characters did not form a valid value for the target type), **`badbit`** (a corrupted stream or buffer — a serious error). Queries: `good()`, `eof()`, `fail()`, `bad()`, `rdstate()`.
concepts.detail: `fail()` is true whenever `failbit` *or* `badbit` is set — failure subsumes badness, so testing `!fail()` is the general 'is the stream usable' check.

concepts.term: How state gets set — and stays
concepts.statement: **A failed operation leaves the stream in a failed state, and subsequent operations on a failed stream do nothing.** A formatted extraction that cannot parse the characters sets `failbit` (and since C++11 writes 0 to the arithmetic target — never rely on that); reaching the end of input during a read sets `eofbit`; only `clear()` restores operation.
concepts.detail: The fail-sticky design is deliberate: a stream in a bad state would otherwise produce cascading garbage; silence is safer.

concepts.statement: Since C++11 streams provide **`explicit operator bool`** — `if (cin >> x)` works because `>>` returns the stream by reference, and the stream converts to `bool` as `!fail()`. Chained extractions `cin >> a >> b` stop at the first failure for the same reason.
concepts.detail: The `explicit` qualifier rules out accident-prone implicit conversions; before C++11 the same effect was achieved with the 'safe bool' idiom.

concepts.statement: By default streams never throw. **`is.exceptions(mask)`** arms a state mask: when a subsequent operation sets a bit in the mask, an **`ios_base::failure`** (derived from `std::system_error` since C++11) is thrown. `exceptions()` with no argument reads the current mask; a `clear()` that lands in the mask throws too.
concepts.detail: A common policy: keep `failbit`/`eofbit` as ordinary control flow and throw only on `badbit` — parsing attempts to recover, but a broken stream surfaces loudly.

concepts.statement: **Error Handling.** Stream state and exceptions. You can claim this section when you can read and set the four stream state bits and know what each means — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 38 (I/O Streams); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Reading integers with failure and recovery
examples.problem: Input is the string `"10 20 30 forty 40"` (delivered by an `istringstream`). Sum every integer, surviving the word in the middle.

steps.label: Step 1: First pass
steps.text: `for (int x; is >> x;) sum += x;` — extracts 10, 20 and 30; the next extraction of an `int` sees the letter `f`, sets `failbit`, and stops. `sum` is 60.

steps.label: Step 2: Diagnose
steps.text: `is.fail()` is true but `is.eof()` is false — a parse failure, not end of input, so recovery is reasonable.

steps.label: Step 3: Recover
steps.text: `is.clear();` resets the state; `is.ignore(std::numeric_limits<std::streamsize>::max(), ' ');` discards characters up to and including the next space, removing `forty`.

steps.label: Step 4: Resume
steps.text: A second identical loop extracts 40 and then ends cleanly at end-of-input. Final `sum` = 60 + 40 = **100**.

examples.result: Robust input = test after every read, then clear-and-skip past the offending characters. Without `clear()` the stream would have stayed silent forever.

quiz.q: In `while (cin >> x)`, what exactly terminates the loop?
options: `fail()` becomes true — failure or end of input stops the extraction, and the conversion to `bool` yields false
quiz.explanation: The contextually converted `operator bool` tests `!fail()`; both a parse failure and hitting end-of-input set `failbit` (often together with `eofbit`).

quiz.q: An `int` extraction meets the characters `"t4"`. What is the state after?
options: `failbit` set; the characters remain unread, pending `clear()` and `ignore()`
Nothing is wrong — the extraction reads 4
quiz.explanation: No digit could be converted, so the extraction fails immediately; the input characters stay in the stream for a later skip.

quiz.q: You want a genuinely broken (bad) stream to throw `ios_base::failure`, while parsing failures remain flag-based. What do you set?
quiz.explanation: The `exceptions` mask selects which state bits throw; arming only `badbit` leaves parsing failures as ordinary flags.

quiz.q: After a failed extraction, which sequence can make the stream usable again?
options: Just `ignore()` — skipping input resets the state
`clear()` to reset the state, then `ignore()` to remove the offending characters
Close and reopen the stream — there is no other way
quiz.explanation: `clear()` resets the bits; `ignore()` then removes the bad characters that caused the failure — either alone is not enough.

intro: I/O operations split into formatted (converting values to and from character sequences) and unformatted (moving raw characters). Formatting is governed by a small amount of per-stream state — base, precision, width, fill and a flag set — usually touched through manipulators such as `std::hex` and `std::setprecision`. Files add the last piece: opening with modes, and letting the stream's destructor close.
objectives: Choose between formatted (`<<`, `>>`) and unformatted (`get`, `write`, `read`, `getline`) operations
Predict output from the formatting state: base, precision, width, fill, and the manipulators that set them
Open files with the right mode flags and know why `app` differs from `ate`

concepts.statement: `operator<<` converts values to character sequences under the current format state; `operator>>` parses characters into typed values, skipping leading whitespace by default (`skipws`). Unformatted operations — `put(c)`, `write(p, n)` on output; `get()`, `getline()`, `read()`, `ignore()`, `peek()`, `unget()` on input — move characters with no conversion; `gcount()` reports how many characters the last unformatted input took.
concepts.detail: The free function `getline(is, s)` reads a line into a `std::string` and discards the newline — the everyday tool for line-oriented input.

concepts.statement: Three flag groups — **basefield** (`dec`/`hex`/`oct`), **floatfield** (`fixed`/`scientific`/`defaultfloat`), **adjustfield** (`left`/`right`/`internal`) — plus **precision** (how many digits to show), the **width** of the next field, and the **fill** character. Everything persists except width: **`width` is reset to 0 after every output operation** and must be re-set (`setw`) for each field.
concepts.detail: That asymmetry is the number-one formatting gotcha: base, precision and fill are sticky; width is not.

concepts.statement: Manipulators are the ergonomic interface to that state: `std::hex`, `std::fixed`, `std::setprecision(9)`, `std::setw(12)`, `std::setfill('*')`, `std::boolalpha`, `std::showbase` (print `0x` for hex), `std::uppercase`, `std::left`. **`std::endl` inserts a newline *and flushes*; a plain `"\n"` does not** — prefer it when you do not need the flush.
concepts.detail: `std::ws` skips whitespace on input; `ends` writes a terminating zero into char arrays (a `string`-era relic).

concepts.statement: `ifstream`, `ofstream` and `fstream` wrap a `basic_filebuf` with `open()` and `close()`; construction opens, destruction closes, `is_open()` tests. Modes combine: **`in`**, **`out`**, **`trunc`** (discard existing content), **`ate`** (seek to end after opening), **`app`** (append: *every* write goes to the end), **`binary`** (no end-of-line translation).
concepts.detail: `app` vs `ate`: `ate` positions once after opening (you may then seek back), while `app` forces each write to the current end regardless of any seeks.

concepts.statement: **I/O Operations.** Formatting, manipulators and files. You can claim this section when you can choose between formatted (`<<`, `>>`) and unformatted (`get`, `write`, `read`, `getline`) operations — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 38 (I/O Streams); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Formatting one number six ways
examples.problem: The double `1234.5678` and the int `255` must appear in a report: with the default format, with 9 significant digits, fixed with 2 decimals, scientific, right-aligned in a field of width 12, and hex with the base shown. Predict each output.

steps.label: Step 1: Default
steps.text: `std::cout << 1234.5678;` — the default precision is 6 significant digits: prints `1234.57`.

steps.label: Step 2: More digits
steps.text: `std::cout << std::setprecision(9) << 1234.5678;` → `1234.5678` — the value needs only 8 significant digits, so 9 restore it exactly.

steps.label: Step 3: Fixed
steps.text: `std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << 1234.5678;` → `1234.57` — precision now counts digits *after* the decimal point.

steps.label: Step 4: Scientific
steps.text: `std::cout << std::scientific << std::setprecision(6) << 1234.5678;` → `1.234568e+03` — six digits after the point, exponent form.

steps.label: Step 5: A field
steps.text: `std::cout << std::defaultfloat << std::setprecision(9) << std::setw(12) << 1234.5678;` → three spaces then `1234.5678` — 9 characters in a field of 12, right-aligned by default. The next output would no longer be padded: width was consumed.

steps.label: Step 6: Hex
steps.text: `std::cout << std::hex << std::showbase << 255;` → `0xff` — the base shows, digits are lowercase (add `std::uppercase` for `0XFF`).

examples.result: Formatting state is sticky (base, precision, fill) — except width, which must be set per field. Every output above is exactly what the state dictates.

options: The field width — it is reset to 0 after each output operation
quiz.explanation: `setw` applies to the next output only; base, precision and fill persist until changed.

intro: Stream iterators make an input stream look like a sequence and an output stream look like an algorithm's destination — the bridge between the iostream framework and the STL. With `istream_iterator<int>` the standard algorithms (`copy`, `accumulate`, `sort`) can consume console or file input directly, and `ostream_iterator<int>` lets them produce output. The buffer-level `istreambuf_iterator` family does the same job with no formatted-input layer at all.
objectives: Construct and use `istream_iterator<T>` and `ostream_iterator<T>` with algorithms
Explain when an input iterator becomes the end-of-stream sentinel
Contrast `istreambuf_iterator` with the formatted iterator — and copy a file with either

concepts.statement: An input iterator constructed from a stream: `std::istream_iterator<int> in{cin};`. **Constructing it triggers the first `>>` read**, each `++` reads the next value, and dereferencing (`*in`) returns the value read. A value-initialized `istream_iterator<T>{}` is the **end-of-stream sentinel** — and any iterator whose extraction has failed compares equal to it.
concepts.detail: So the classic range is `copy(istream_iterator<int>{is}, {}, back_inserter(v));` — the second `{}` reads as 'until extraction fails'.

concepts.statement: An output iterator that writes values with `<<`; a second constructor argument becomes the separator written after each value: `ostream_iterator<int> out{cout, "\n"};` produces one number per line.
concepts.detail: It lets `copy(v.begin(), v.end(), ostream_iterator<int>{cout, " "})` print a container — no hand-written loop, no off-by-one.

concepts.statement: The pair (stream iterator, end sentinel) is an STL range, so **any algorithm that accepts input iterators works on I/O**: `accumulate` to total a file of numbers, `find` to search a log, `sort` once the values are collected into a container first.
concepts.detail: The pattern is always the same: read lazily until an extraction fails, at which point the iterator silently becomes the sentinel and the algorithm stops.

concepts.statement: **`istreambuf_iterator<char>`** and **`ostreambuf_iterator<char>`** iterate the stream's *buffer* — no whitespace skipping, no parsing, no formatting: exactly the characters in the file. `copy(istreambuf_iterator<char>{is}, {}, ostreambuf_iterator<char>{os});` copies a file character-for-character.
concepts.detail: With `istream_iterator<char>` you would need `is >> noskipws` to approximate that — and still pay the formatted-input layer for every character.

concepts.statement: **Stream Iterators.** istream_iterator and ostream_iterator. You can claim this section when you can construct and use `istream_iterator<T>` and `ostream_iterator<T>` with algorithms — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 38 (I/O Streams); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

examples.title: Totalling a file of numbers with algorithms only
examples.problem: The file `nums.txt` contains one line: `2 3 5 7 11`. Read it into a vector, sum it with `accumulate`, and write it back one number per line — no explicit loops.

steps.label: Step 1: Read
steps.text: `std::ifstream is{"nums.txt"}; std::vector<int> v; std::copy(std::istream_iterator<int>{is}, {}, std::back_inserter(v));` — five extractions succeed; the sixth hits end-of-input, fails, and the iterator equals the sentinel, ending the copy. `v` = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11}.

steps.label: Step 2: Sum
steps.text: `int total = std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0);` — 2 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 11 = **28**.

steps.label: Step 3: Write
steps.text: `std::copy(v.begin(), v.end(), std::ostream_iterator<int>{std::cout, "\n"});` — prints 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, each followed by a newline.

examples.result: Three statements, no loops: the stream iterators turned a file into a range and a range into output.

intro: Below the formatting layer sits `basic_streambuf`: the abstract class that actually moves characters, usually in blocks, between memory and a device. The design is two little memory windows — a get area you read from and a put area you write to — plus virtual functions (`underflow`, `overflow`, `sync`) that derived buffers (`filebuf`, `stringbuf`, your own device buffers) override to talk to real devices. Understanding the pointer protocol explains both the speed of buffered I/O and how to build new devices.
objectives: Explain the split: stream classes format, `basic_streambuf` transports
Name the get-area and put-area pointers and the events that trigger `underflow()` and `overflow()`
Use `rdbuf()` for whole-buffer operations and justify why it is the fast way to copy

concepts.statement: **`basic_streambuf<charT, traits>`** is the abstract device interface: the stream classes never touch a device — they ask their buffer (`rdbuf()`) for characters. The standard provides `basic_filebuf` (files) and `basic_stringbuf` (strings); user-defined buffers implement anything from terminals to network sockets.
concepts.detail: This is §38.1's separation made concrete: formatting policy in one class family, transport mechanism in another — either can vary independently.

concepts.statement: Output characters accumulate in an array delimited by three pointers: **`pbase`** (start), **`pptr`** (next free position), **`epptr`** (end). `sputc` writes at `pptr` and advances it; when `pptr` reaches `epptr` the buffer calls the virtual **`overflow()`**, which in `basic_filebuf` writes the whole area out with one large operation and makes room again.
concepts.detail: `xsputn` moves whole blocks in one call — the bulk path used by `write()` and by `os << is.rdbuf()`.

concepts.statement: Input is served from an array delimited by **`eback`** (start), **`gptr`** (current position), **`egptr`** (end). Reads advance `gptr`; when it reaches `egptr`, the virtual **`underflow()`** is invoked to refill the area from the device — a `basic_filebuf` fills it with one big read. `sungetc`/`sputbackc` step `gptr` back for ungetting.
concepts.detail: `in_avail()` reports how many characters are buffered without touching the device; `uflow()` is underflow plus advance.

concepts.statement: **`overflow()` and `underflow()` return `traits::eof()` to report trouble** — end of input is a normal outcome signalled by failing to refill, not by throwing. `sync()` flushes the put area to the device (what `endl`, `flush` and destruction ultimately call); `xsgetn`/`xsputn` are the bulk character moves.
concepts.detail: Consequence: end-of-input is discovered lazily, one read too late — hence the eofbit-after-failure pattern of §38.3.

concepts.statement: `is.rdbuf()` yields the buffer pointer, and **`os << is.rdbuf()` copies all remaining characters through the bulk path** — no per-character formatting layer, typically the fastest way to copy a stream. If zero characters are copied, the insertion sets `failbit` on `os`.
concepts.detail: The buffer stays owned by its stream: `rdbuf()` is for using, not for deleting — `basic_streambuf` has a protected destructor, like the locale facet of §39.3.

figures.caption: Stream buffer architecture. The stream object formats values and hands characters to its `rdbuf`. Output fills the put area (`pbase`..`epptr`); when it is full, `overflow()` writes the block to the device. Input drains the get area (`eback`..`egptr`); when it is exhausted, `underflow()` reads a new block. Buffering converts many small character operations into a few large device transfers.

examples.title: Two ways to copy a file — and why one wins
examples.problem: A large text file must be copied with iostreams. Compare the naive character loop against the single-statement buffer copy.

steps.label: Step 1: Naive
steps.text: `char c; while (is.get(c)) os.put(c);` — every character travels through the formatted layer: `get` checks state and calls the buffer (possibly a virtual `underflow`), `put` calls `sputc` (possibly a virtual `overflow`). Millions of tiny operations.

steps.label: Step 2: Buffer copy
steps.text: `os << is.rdbuf();` — the filebuf hands whole blocks (typically thousands of characters) from its get area to the device, in essentially `memmove` plus a few system calls.

steps.label: Step 3: Why
steps.text: The per-character state checks and virtual calls are amortized over a block instead of being paid once per byte — the same reason C's `stdio` beats raw `read()` per byte.

steps.label: Step 4: A peek inside
steps.text: On an `istringstream` holding `"42x"`: `is >> n` reads 42 and stops at `x`; `is.peek()` returns `x` without moving `gptr`; `is.get()` consumes it and `gcount()` reports 1 — the pointer protocol of the figure, visible from the stream interface.

examples.result: Same output bytes; the buffer copy is commonly several times faster. Stroustrup's rule: formatted I/O for values, raw buffers for bulk.

examples.title: Working through buffering
examples.problem: Stream buffers under the hood. Your task: explain the split: stream classes format, `basic_streambuf` transports.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: explain the split: stream classes format, `basic_streambuf` transports. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Streams format; stream buffers transport — devices appear only below `basic_streambuf`.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `if (std::cin >> x) { use(x); }` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — name the get-area and put-area pointers and the events that trigger `underflow()` and `overflow()` — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Put area: `pbase`/`pptr`/`epptr` with `overflow()`; get area: `eback`/`gptr`/`egptr` with `underflow()`; `sync()` flushes. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Streams format; stream buffers transport — devices appear only below `basic_streambuf`. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Streams format; stream buffers transport — devices appear only below `basic_streambuf`.
Put area: `pbase`/`pptr`/`epptr` with `overflow()`; get area: `eback`/`gptr`/`egptr` with `underflow()`; `sync()` flushes.
Bulk operations (`xsputn`, `os << is.rdbuf()`) win because block moves amortize the per-character overhead.

quiz.q: What happens when `pptr` reaches `epptr` during an output operation?
options: `overflow()` is called to flush and rearrange the put area
The buffer doubles its size automatically
quiz.explanation: A full put area triggers the virtual `overflow()`, which in a `filebuf` writes the block out and makes room.

quiz.q: Which call refills the get area when `gptr` has reached `egptr`?
quiz.explanation: `underflow()` is the virtual that fetches the next block from the device; `setg()` is what it uses internally to publish the new pointers.

quiz.q: Why is `os << is.rdbuf()` the fast way to copy a file?
options: It uses a larger disk cache
It moves whole blocks through the buffer, skipping the per-character formatting layer
quiz.explanation: The insertion of a `streambuf*` uses the bulk path (`xsputn`), so block moves replace millions of single-character operations.

quiz.q: How does a streambuf report failure or end-of-input from `underflow()`?
quiz.explanation: The protocol is a return value, not an exception: end of input is a normal outcome signalled by failing to refill.

intro: A handful of rules prevent most real-world I/O bugs: define operators for your own types, test the stream after every input, send diagnostics where they survive failures, and prefer the safe idioms — string streams over `sprintf`, `'\n'` over `endl`, `rdbuf()` for bulk copies. This closing section collects the chapter's practice into a checklist you can apply to any I/O code.
objectives: Apply the chapter's rules for user-defined types and error reporting
Choose `"\n"` vs `endl`, string streams vs `sprintf`, formatted vs unformatted I/O
Write the canonical robust read loop with testing, clearing and recovery

concepts.statement: **Define `operator<<` and `operator>>` for each user-defined type you want to print or read.** This is the extension point the whole design exists for — one pair of functions, and the type works with every stream in the library.
concepts.detail: Keep the operators minimal: stream the parts in a natural order and leave layout decisions to the caller's manipulators.

concepts.statement: **After `is >> x`, verify `is` before using `x`.** The `while (is >> x)` form makes the check the loop condition. Using a value after a failed extraction is the classic I/O bug: garbage or zeros propagate silently.
concepts.detail: Check even for values you 'know' are there — file formats drift, users edit files, disks truncate.

concepts.term: Format as needed, not as a habit
concepts.statement: **Prefer `'\n'` to `endl`** — `endl` flushes on every line, a pure performance loss on large outputs. When you must change format state in a function, **restore it** before returning: global format changes leak across call boundaries.
concepts.detail: Flush when you need the data visible — before a long computation, before reading a prompt response, on the error path — not by reflex.

concepts.statement: **Error messages go to `cerr`** — unbuffered, so nothing is lost if the process dies, and separate from `stdout` so piped program data is not polluted.
concepts.detail: C libraries that print errors to `stdout` corrupt piped output; the stream design gives you the two channels for free.

concepts.statement: **To build a string, format into an `ostringstream`** (`buf << "(" << x << ", " << y << ")"`, then `s = buf.str()`), never into a fixed `char` buffer with `sprintf` — the latter is a buffer overflow waiting to happen. To parse a string, read it back through an `istringstream`.
concepts.detail: The same goes for values going into GUIs, databases and logs: format in memory, hand over a `std::string`.

examples.title: The robust reader, assembled
examples.problem: Read whitespace-separated integers from a stream until exhaustion, summing the good ones and tolerating (while reporting) bad tokens — the full §38.3 recovery pattern.

steps.label: Step 1: Loop
steps.text: `for (int x; is >> x;) sum += x;` — consumes every well-formed integer.

steps.label: Step 2: On failure
steps.text: If `is.eof()`, the input is done — a clean end. Otherwise a bad token is next: `is.clear();` then `is.ignore(std::numeric_limits<std::streamsize>::max(), ' ');` skips past it.

steps.label: Step 3: Repeat until exhausted
steps.text: Wrap steps 1–2 in `while (is)` — the outer loop ends only on a clean end-of-input.

steps.label: Step 4: Trace
steps.text: Input `"10 20 30 forty 40"` → 10+20+30, fail at `forty`, recover, read 40 → sum **100**, one bad token reported.

examples.result: A reader that cannot be derailed by malformed input — the pattern to reuse for any structured format.

examples.title: Reviewing I/O streams code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the chapter's rules for user-defined types and error reporting.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Define `<<`/`>>` for your types; test the stream after every extraction.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `if (std::cin >> x) { use(x); }`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: choose `'\n'` vs `endl`, string streams vs `sprintf`, formatted vs unformatted I/O. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: `'\n'` unless you need the flush; `cerr` for diagnostics; string streams, never `sprintf`.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Define `<<`/`>>` for your types; test the stream after every extraction. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Define `<<`/`>>` for your types; test the stream after every extraction.
`'\n'` unless you need the flush; `cerr` for diagnostics; string streams, never `sprintf`.
Recoverable input: fail → `clear()` → `ignore()` past the bad token → resume.

quiz.q: You output a large table and performance matters. `endl` or `'\n'` between rows — and why?
options: `'\n'` — `endl` also flushes the buffer on every row, which costs system calls for no benefit
quiz.explanation: `endl` = newline + flush; in a big loop the flushes dominate. Flush deliberately, not by habit.

quiz.q: Why write diagnostics to `cerr` rather than `cout`?
options: It is unbuffered (survives crashes) and keeps error text out of the program's data stream on `stdout`
`cerr` is buffered, so it is faster
`cout` cannot be written to during errors
quiz.explanation: Two channels: `stdout` for program output (pipeable), `cerr` for immediate diagnostics.

quiz.q: A colleague suggests `sprintf` into `char buf[32]`. The iostream answer is:
options: Format into an `ostringstream` and take `str()` — no fixed size, no overflow
Write to `cout` and read it back
quiz.explanation: In-memory formatting grows with the data; a fixed buffer is an overflow bug with a delay fuse.

intro: A program that works in Copenhagen must also work in Cairo and Chicago: the same double 1234.56 must print as 1,234.56 or as 1.234,56, names must sort by the local alphabet, and dates, currency and even the question of which characters count as letters all vary. Stroustrup's solution is to treat cultural conventions as data rather than logic: each convention is encapsulated in a facet, facets are collected into a locale, and I/O streams are parameterized by the locale they are imbued with. This section frames the problem; the rest of the chapter builds the machinery.
objectives: Explain why culture-dependent behavior must be isolated from program logic
List the kinds of cultural difference a program can meet
Describe the locale/facet division of the standard library

concepts.statement: **Keep the program logic culture-independent and confine the culture-dependent behavior to the I/O layer.** The core computes with abstract values — the double 1234.56, a timestamp, an amount in cents — while conventions such as decimal points, digit grouping, date layout and currency symbols belong to the input/output code, where the locale machinery can reach them.
concepts.detail: Cultural conventions are *data*, not logic: each is a facet, facets are collected in a locale, and a stream's formatting is driven by the locale it is imbued with.

concepts.statement: The differences a program meets: **character classification** (is a character a letter — depends on the alphabet), **numeric punctuation** (decimal point `.` or `,`, thousands separators, digit grouping), **date and time layout** (`Dec 25, 2015` vs `25/12/2015` vs ISO `2015-12-25`), **currency** (symbol, placement, sign conventions), **collation** (the ordering used to sort names) and **messages** (translated user-visible strings).
concepts.detail: The book's striking example is Danish: `aa` is alphabetized as the letter they write after `z`, so Aarhus sorts *after* Zurich in a Danish phone book.

concepts.statement: A **locale** is an object representing a set of cultural conventions; it is implemented as a container of **facets**, each holding one aspect of that culture (number punctuation, character classification, collation, …). The standard library supplies a set of standard facets, a programmer can add new ones, and I/O streams are imbued with locales so that `<<` and `>>` format according to the imbued conventions.
concepts.detail: The default is the classic locale, named `"C"` after the C language's home conventions: period decimal point, no digit grouping, byte-order sorting.

concepts.term: Handling Cultural Differences: the working contract
concepts.statement: **Handling Cultural Differences.** Why locales exist. You can claim this section when you can explain why culture-dependent behavior must be isolated from program logic — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 39 (Locales); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

concepts.statement: Work in three passes. First, list the kinds of cultural difference a program can meet. Then, describe the locale/facet division of the standard library. Finally, test the outcome against the section promise: Culture-dependent behavior belongs in the I/O layer; the core computes with invariant values.
concepts.detail: Each pass catches a different class of mistake, and skipping one moves the failure into a larger program where it costs more to diagnose than it would have here.

examples.title: Sorting a Danish phone book
examples.problem: Order the two names "Aarhus" and "Zurich" first under the classic C locale, then under a Danish locale. What differs?

steps.label: Step 1: classic locale
steps.text: Collation is byte order: the first bytes decide, `A` (65) < `Z` (90), so "Aarhus" sorts before "Zurich".

steps.label: Step 2: Danish locale
steps.text: In Danish the digraph "aa" is collated as the letter that follows `z` — the city's name is read as "Århus" — so "Zurich" now sorts before "Aarhus".

steps.label: Step 3: What changed
steps.text: The strings are untouched; only the collation rule was swapped, by taking the `collate` facet from a different locale. The sort algorithm itself is identical.

examples.result: Same two names, opposite orders: the strings are the data, the ordering rule is a facet (the exact locale name — e.g. `da_DK.UTF-8` — is implementation-defined).

examples.title: Working through handling cultural differences
examples.problem: Why locales exist. Your task: explain why culture-dependent behavior must be isolated from program logic.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: explain why culture-dependent behavior must be isolated from program logic. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Culture-dependent behavior belongs in the I/O layer; the core computes with invariant values.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `std::locale loc(tag); std::cout.imbue(loc);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — list the kinds of cultural difference a program can meet — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Conventions differ in classification, numeric punctuation, dates, currency, collation and messages. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Culture-dependent behavior belongs in the I/O layer; the core computes with invariant values. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Culture-dependent behavior belongs in the I/O layer; the core computes with invariant values.
Conventions differ in classification, numeric punctuation, dates, currency, collation and messages.
A locale collects facets; each facet owns one cultural aspect; streams consult the imbued locale.

quiz.q: In the classic C locale "Aarhus" sorts before "Zurich" (65 < 90). In a Danish locale the order reverses because:
options: In Danish, "aa" is collated as the letter following "z", so "Aarhus" is read last
Danish compares UTF-16 code units rather than bytes
The C locale compares string lengths first
quiz.explanation: Danish treats the digraph "aa" as the letter written after "z" — a collation fact, invisible to byte-order comparison.

quiz.q: Which property of a program should be *invariant* across cultures?
options: The numeric value parsed into a double
quiz.explanation: The whole design keeps the computed value culture-independent; only its textual presentation varies, driven by facets.

quiz.q: The mechanism C++ uses to carry a set of cultural conventions is:
options: a set of preprocessor macros per target market
a per-country set of compiled string tables
quiz.explanation: A locale is a container of facets; streams are imbued with locales to control formatting and parsing.

intro: Class locale is the hub of the model — and it is deliberately tiny: a copyable handle to a set of facets, nothing more. All the cultural knowledge lives in the facets; the locale selects, owns and shares them. This section covers the object model: cheap copying, immutability, names and equality, the classic and global locales, and how a stream gets its locale.
objectives: Use named, classic, global and environment locales, and know which names are portable
State the immutability and equality rules of class locale
Tie a stream to a locale with `imbue()` and read it back with `getloc()`

concepts.statement: A **locale** is a small object acting as a handle to a set of facets; **copying a locale is cheap** (the facets are shared and reference-counted), so locales are passed by value. All cultural information lives in the facets — the locale itself only selects and owns them. `loc.name()` returns the locale's name, or `"*"` if the locale was constructed rather than named.
concepts.detail: This is why `imbue()` takes a locale by value and `getloc()` returns one by value: nobody worries about ownership.

concepts.statement: **A locale is immutable.** You never modify a locale; you construct new ones from existing ones — installing a facet, combining locales, or taking a category from another locale. Two locales `a` and `b` compare equal iff one is a copy of the other, or both have names and the names are equal; a constructed (unnamed) locale is equal only to its own copies.
concepts.detail: Immutability is what makes sharing safe: a stream, your code and a facet table can all hold the same locale, and nobody can change it under anyone else's feet.

concepts.term: The classic, global and environment locales
concepts.statement: `locale::classic()` returns the locale named **"C"** — the neutral default: `.` decimal point, no grouping, byte-order collation. `locale("")` constructs the **user's preferred locale** from the environment. `locale::global(loc)` installs `loc` as the **global locale** (the default for newly created streams), returns the previous global, and — if `loc` has a name — also sets the C library's locale. Existing streams such as `cin` and `cout` are *not* affected by a global change.
concepts.detail: A stream carries its own locale: set it with `imbue(loc)` and read it with `getloc()` — every subsequent operation uses it.

concepts.statement: **Class locale.** The locale object model. You can claim this section when you can use named, classic, global and environment locales, and know which names are portable — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.
concepts.detail: This section belongs to Chapter 39 (Locales); later sections in the chapter use it without restating it, so the contract compounds.

concepts.statement: Work in three passes. First, state the immutability and equality rules of class locale. Then, tie a stream to a locale with `imbue()` and read it back with `getloc()`. Finally, test the outcome against the section promise: A locale is a cheap, immutable handle to a shared set of facets; construct new ones, never modify.
concepts.detail: Each pass catches a different class of mistake, and skipping one moves the failure into a larger program where it costs more to diagnose than it would have here.

examples.title: Three prints of one number
examples.problem: Print `double x = 1234567.89;` with `cout << x` under the default locale, an `en_US.UTF-8` locale, and a `de_DE.UTF-8` locale. What appears on screen?

steps.label: Step 1: default
steps.text: A fresh `cout` is imbued with the classic locale: no grouping, `.` decimal point — output `1234567.89`.

steps.label: Step 2: US
steps.text: `cout.imbue(locale("en_US.UTF-8"));` — `numpunct` supplies thousands separator `,` and grouping `'\003'` (groups of three): `1,234,567.89`.

steps.label: Step 3: German
steps.text: `cout.imbue(locale("de_DE.UTF-8"));` — decimal point `,`, separator `.`: `1.234.567,89`.

steps.label: Step 4: What stayed fixed
steps.text: `x` is the same double throughout; only the punctuation changed. (Names beyond `"C"` and `""` are implementation-defined; these are the conventional POSIX spellings.)

examples.result: One value, three renderings: `1234567.89`, `1,234,567.89`, `1.234.567,89` — the choice is a facet's, not the algorithm's.

quiz.q: `locale("")` constructs:
options: a locale with no facets at all
the user's preferred locale, taken from the environment
quiz.explanation: The empty string asks the implementation for the environment's preferred locale — the standard's only other guaranteed name besides "C".

quiz.q: Right after `locale::global(locale("de_DE.UTF-8"));` executes, `cout << 1234567.89` prints:
options: `1.234.567,89` — cout follows the new global locale
`1234567.89` — existing streams keep their own imbued locale
an implementation-defined string, since the call was illegal
quiz.explanation: The global locale is the default for *newly created* streams; cin, cout and friends keep the locale they were imbued with.

quiz.q: Two locales `a` and `b` compare equal (`a == b`) iff:
options: they hold facet objects at the same addresses
every facet in `a` has a counterpart in `b` with identical behavior
equality is left implementation-defined for unnamed locales
one is a copy of the other, or both have names and the names are equal
quiz.explanation: Copies are always equal; otherwise two *named* locales are equal exactly when their names match. A constructed (unnamed) locale equals only its own copies.

intro: Facets are where the locale model earns its keep as an extension mechanism. A facet encapsulates one cultural aspect behind a family of virtual functions; the standard defines about a dozen families, and you can add your own by deriving from an existing one. The key questions are how a locale finds a facet (by id), how you install yours (with `new`, into a constructed locale), and how locales are combined.
objectives: Explain what a facet is and how `use_facet`/`has_facet` find it by id
Add a user-defined facet by deriving from a standard facet
Compose locales with the facet constructor, `combine()` and categories

concepts.statement: A **facet** encapsulates one cultural aspect. Every facet derives from `locale::facet`, and each facet family carries a static member `id` of type `locale::id` identifying it inside a locale. `use_facet<F>(loc)` looks the facet up by `F::id` and returns a `const F&`; `has_facet<F>(loc)` tests presence without throwing — `use_facet` throws `bad_cast` when the family is absent.
concepts.detail: The reference is const because a locale's meaning is fixed at construction: facets are never modified in place.

concepts.statement: The set of facets in a locale is **open-ended**: derive your own facet (from an existing facet family, or from `locale::facet` with an `id` member) and install it — `locale loc(l, new My_facet);` constructs an unnamed copy of `l` with your facet in place of the family it implements. No standard class is edited; the locale model extends itself.
concepts.detail: The virtual functions with the `do_` prefix are the customization points: a facet derived from `numpunct<char>` overrides `do_decimal_point()`, `do_thousands_sep()`, `do_grouping()`, and the public non-virtuals forward to them.

concepts.statement: `locale(l, new F)` — a copy of `l` with `F` replacing `l`'s facet of that family. `loc.combine<F>(other)` — a copy of `loc` with the `F` facet taken from `other`. `locale(l1, l2, cat)` — a copy of `l1` with all facets of category `cat` (e.g. `locale::numeric`, `locale::time`) taken from `l2`.
concepts.detail: A typical composition: an otherwise-English locale with German number formatting — `locale(loc_en, loc_de, locale::numeric)`.

concepts.statement: **Class facet.** Facets as extension points. You can claim this section when you can explain what a facet is and how `use_facet`/`has_facet` find it by id — and can say what would go wrong if you could not.

Finally, test the outcome against the section promise: `use_facet<F>(loc)` is a lookup by `F::id`; `has_facet` tests, `use_facet` throws `bad_cast` when absent.
concepts.detail: Each pass catches a different class of mistake, and skipping one moves the failure into a larger program where it costs more to diagnose than it would have here.

examples.title: A user-defined number format
examples.problem: Print numbers with a blank as thousands separator — `12345678.9` as `12 345 678.9` — without touching the decimal point or any other convention.

steps.label: Step 1: Derive
steps.text: `class My_punct : public numpunct<char> { public: explicit My_punct(size_t r = 0) : numpunct<char>(r) {} protected: char do_thousands_sep() const override { return ' '; } string do_grouping() const override { return "\003"; } };` — only the separator and grouping are overridden; `do_decimal_point()` keeps the classic `.`.

steps.label: Step 2: Install
steps.text: `cout.imbue(locale(cout.getloc(), new My_punct));` — the locale constructor takes ownership of the new facet and builds a copy of cout's locale with it under the key `numpunct<char>::id`.

steps.label: Step 3: Use
steps.text: Every later `cout << x` goes through `num_put`, which consults the stream's `numpunct`: separator `' '`, grouping `'\003'` (groups of three).

steps.label: Step 4: Verify
steps.text: 8 integer digits group as 12 | 345 | 678 with the blank, and the fraction keeps the classic point: `12 345 678.9`.

examples.result: `cout << 12345678.9` prints `12 345 678.9` — three lines of code, no standard class modified, and the stream's locale did the rest.
