examples.title: Three rewrites, measured
examples.problem: Take three C++98 idioms, rewrite each in C++11, and count what disappears.

steps.label: Rewrite 1: Iteration
steps.text: C++98: `for (std::map<std::string,int>::iterator p = m.begin(); p != m.end(); ++p) use(p->first, p->second);` — a 35-character type name spelled at the loop head. C++11: `for (auto& e : m) use(e.first, e.second);` — three lines become one and the type name vanishes.

steps.label: Rewrite 2: The algorithm argument
steps.text: C++98 sorts by a named functor: a struct with an `operator()`, defined away from the call, then passed by name — six lines and a page-flip. C++11: `sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const string& a, const string& b) { return a.size() < b.size(); });` — the ordering lives at the call site and inlines.

steps.label: Rewrite 3: Returning a big object
steps.text: Returning a `vector<string>` of 1,000 strings of 100 characters: a C++98 copy duplicates every buffer — 1,000 allocations and roughly 101,000 bytes moved, about 0.1 ms. The C++11 move hands over three pointers per string instead — a few hundred nanoseconds, about four orders of magnitude less work, with the same source code (`return v;`) thanks to overload resolution on rvalue-ness.

examples.result: One iterator spelling, one functor, and one deep copy gone — each rewrite deletes exactly the kind of code reviewers have to squint at, which is the pattern of the whole C++11 delta.

examples.title: Working through C++11 extensions
examples.problem: What C++11 added over C++98. Your task: explain what move semantics and rvalue references change about returning and growing objects.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: explain what move semantics and rvalue references change about returning and growing objects. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: Move semantics (rvalue references) makes returning and growing objects cheap — the enabler of C++11's value-style APIs.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int legacy(int n);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — list the major language and library families added in C++11 and their purpose — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Lambdas, auto, decltype, and range-for delete the boilerplate and the giant type spellings of C++98. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: Move semantics (rvalue references) makes returning and growing objects cheap — the enabler of C++11's value-style APIs. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: Move semantics (rvalue references) makes returning and growing objects cheap — the enabler of C++11's value-style APIs.
Lambdas, auto, decltype, and range-for delete the boilerplate and the giant type spellings of C++98.
The memory model plus atomics and threads is the foundational addition; uniform initialization and variadic templates round out the language core.

quiz.q: What single C++11 addition made a portable thread library possible at all?
options: The memory model — the formal definition of what one thread is guaranteed to see when another writes.
quiz.explanation: Without a memory model, compilers are free to reorder and cache memory operations; atomics and mutexes have semantics only because C++11 first defined the model they sit on (chapter 41).

quiz.q: What do rvalue references (`T&&`) enable?
options: Move semantics — taking resources from expiring objects instead of deep-copying them.
Aliasing the same object under two names.
quiz.explanation: An rvalue reference binds to objects whose value need not be preserved, so the move constructor may steal its guts — a vector move is three pointer assignments.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a C++11 feature?
quiz.explanation: Concepts were the headline feature of C++20; C++11 shipped without them and used tag dispatch and SFINAE instead.

quiz.q: What does `enum class` mainly buy over a plain enum?
options: Scoped enumerator names and no implicit conversion to int — no silent surprises.
quiz.explanation: A scoped enum's enumerators do not leak into the enclosing scope, and values do not silently convert to integers — closing two classic bug families at once.

intro: The C and C++ committees parted company in 1989 and have met separately ever since; the languages overlap heavily but neither contains the other. The differences are not accidents — almost every one exists to make C++'s type discipline possible — and each is a porting bug waiting for the unwary. This section is the checklist.
objectives: Predict which valid C programs a C++ compiler will reject, and why the rejection is deliberate
Explain the type-system differences: void* conversions, character literal types, string literal constness
Use extern "C" and the common subset to build headers and libraries that serve both languages

concepts.statement: Every incompatibility in this section is deliberate: C++ trades C's silent permissiveness for compile-time error detection — implicit `void*` conversions, unconverted character literals, unchecked empty parameter lists. The price is that some correct C programs need small, mechanical edits to become C++.
concepts.detail: TC++PL's stance: the differences are 'minor' in count but not in kind — each removes a silent assumption a C compiler makes on the programmer's behalf.

concepts.statement: In C, `malloc`'s `void*` result converts implicitly to any object pointer; C++ requires a cast. In C a character literal has type `int`, so `sizeof('a')` is `sizeof(int)` (typically 4); in C++ it is `char` — `sizeof('a') == 1`. A C string literal is `char[N]`; a C++ literal is `const char[N]`, and binding it to `char*` is at best deprecated. File-scope `const` has external linkage in C, internal in C++.
concepts.detail: The `const` linkage rule means a `const int x;` at file scope needs an initializer in C++ but is a common tentative declaration pattern in C.

concepts.statement: C++ reserves about 80 identifiers C uses freely (`class`, `new`, `delete`, `template`, `this`, `namespace`, ...). C keeps a separate **tag namespace** (`struct S` and an ordinary identifier `S` can coexist); in C++ the tag *is* an ordinary type name. Empty parentheses `f()` mean 'unspecified arguments' in C but 'no arguments' in C++ — C must write `f(void)`. Tentative definitions (`int x; int x;`) are legal C and a redefinition error in C++. `goto` may not jump over an initialization in C++.
concepts.detail: The K&R one-argument-defines-at-a-time style also shows the difference: old-style C definitions without prototypes are rejected by C++ outright.

concepts.term: Features C has and C++ lacks
concepts.statement: Variable-length arrays (`int a[n]` with run-time n), the `restrict` qualifier, C99 designated initializers (`{ .x = 1 }` — C++20 adopts a restricted form), compound literals, `_Generic` type dispatch, and flexible array members. C++ answers each differently: `vector`, implementation extensions, member initializers, and overloading.
concepts.detail: These are the reason 'compile it as C++' fails on modern C codebases: C99-era code assumes features the C++ committee consciously declined to import (until C++20 partially relented on designated initializers).

concepts.statement: `extern "C" { ... }` gives declarations **C linkage**: the function keeps its unmangled C symbol, so C code, C compilers, and dlsym-style lookups can all find it. Headers shared between the languages wrap their declarations in `#ifdef __cplusplus` guards; overloading and classes cannot cross the boundary, but pointers to plain data and to functions pass freely.
concepts.detail: A C function can never be overloaded if it is to keep C linkage; and the objects crossing the boundary should be of layout-compatible types — PODs or standard-layout structs.

examples.title: One line, two languages
examples.problem: This line is legal C and rejected by every C++ compiler. Diagnose it, fix it both ways, and note the two hidden numbers a shared codebase must know.

steps.label: Step 1: The line
steps.text: `int* p = malloc(10 * sizeof(int));` — in C, `malloc` returns `void*` and the assignment converts it implicitly; in C++ that conversion is ill-formed, and the compiler stops right there.

steps.label: Step 2: Two fixes
steps.text: The portable form adds the cast — `int* p = (int*)malloc(10 * sizeof(int));` — legal in both languages. The C++-native form is `int* p = new int[10];` (or better, `vector<int> v(10);`), which also constructs and deallocates correctly.

steps.label: Step 3: The hidden numbers
steps.text: Write `printf("%zu", sizeof('a'));` through both compilers: C prints `4` (a character literal has type int), C++ prints `1` (type char). Same source, different language, different answer — the classic shared-codebase interview question.

steps.label: Step 4: The linking half
steps.text: A function `double rate(int);` compiled by a C++ compiler gets a mangled name encoding its parameter types; C code linking against it finds no symbol. Wrapping the declaration in `extern "C"` suppresses the mangling so both sides agree on the one name — the same mechanism a shared header automates with `#ifdef __cplusplus`.

examples.result: Diagnosis (implicit void* conversion), two fixes (cast for common-subset code, new for C++-only), one measurable divergence (sizeof of a character literal), and the linkage rule that makes the last mile work.

examples.title: Working through C/C++ compatibility
examples.problem: Real differences between the languages. Your task: predict which valid C programs a C++ compiler will reject, and why the rejection is deliberate.

steps.label: Step 1: restate
steps.text: Restate the goal in the section’s terms: predict which valid C programs a C++ compiler will reject, and why the rejection is deliberate. Write down the guarantee you will rely on — for this chapter it is: C++ deliberately rejects some valid C: implicit void* conversions, tentative definitions, VLAs, restrict, and unconverted character literals.

steps.label: Step 2: build
steps.text: Build the smallest program that exercises it. Start from this skeleton and adapt it: `int legacy(int n);` Compile it before adding anything else, so later errors are attributable to later changes.

steps.label: Step 3: vary
steps.text: Change one thing at a time — explain the type-system differences: void* conversions, character literal types, string literal constness — and recompile after each change, so each diagnostic maps to exactly one decision.

steps.label: Step 4: verify
steps.text: Check the result against the takeaway: Same source, different meaning: sizeof('a') is 4 in C and 1 in C++; file-scope const has different linkage; () means different things. If the program satisfies it with no extra machinery, stop — extra machinery would tax code that does not need it.

examples.result: The section’s lesson survives contact with the compiler: C++ deliberately rejects some valid C: implicit void* conversions, tentative definitions, VLAs, restrict, and unconverted character literals. Small, compiled, varied, checked — that is the whole method.

keyTakeaways: C++ deliberately rejects some valid C: implicit void* conversions, tentative definitions, VLAs, restrict, and unconverted character literals.
Same source, different meaning: sizeof('a') is 4 in C and 1 in C++; file-scope const has different linkage; () means different things.
extern "C" plus the common subset is the standard interop kit: one unmangled symbol per function, layout-compatible types across the boundary.

quiz.q: What happens to `int* p = malloc(10 * sizeof(int));` in each language?
options: Legal C, rejected by C++ — a void* does not implicitly convert to int*.
quiz.explanation: C permits the implicit conversion from void*; C++ requires an explicit cast (or new) — a deliberate removal of an unsound silent conversion.

quiz.q: What does `sizeof('a')` yield in C and in C++?
options: C: typically 4 (a character literal has type int); C++: 1 (type char).
quiz.explanation: C inherits its promotion rules from pre-ANSI practice; C++ made the literal a char so overloading on character type works — same syntax, different types.

quiz.q: Which feature exists in C but not in (pre-C++20) C++?
options: Variable-length arrays (and restrict, and C99 designated initializers).
quiz.explanation: The C committee added VLAs, restrict, and designated initializers in C99; C++ consciously declined, offering vector and (later) a restricted initializer form instead.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of `extern "C"`?
options: It makes the function inline across translation units.
It renames the function to a C++-style mangled symbol.
It marks the function as deprecated for C callers.
It gives the function C linkage — an unmangled symbol that C code can link to.
quiz.explanation: Name mangling encodes parameter types; extern "C" suspends it so the symbol the C++ compiler emits is the one the C compiler expects — the hinge of every mixed codebase.

intro: The chapter closes with advice that is really a migration strategy: keep C code compiling as C++ from day one, keep the boundary between the languages narrow and explicit, and never write in the C subset what the language you are using exists to improve. Each rule converts a compatibility trap into a deliberate, visible decision.
objectives: Apply the compile-early, compile-often strategy for C code in a C++ project
Structure a dual-language header with include guards and extern "C" correctly
Explain why programming in the C subset of C++ is a false economy

concepts.statement: Get C code compiling under a C++ compiler early, and keep it compiling in both languages — the compiler then flags every silent difference (implicit conversions, missing prototypes, tentative definitions) as it appears, instead of letting it become an archaeology dig years later.
concepts.detail: The inverse rule is just as important: do not 'fix' the warnings by casting them into silence — fix the code, or the compatibility check stops checking anything.

concepts.statement: Isolate the C interface behind a thin façade of RAII types: a `File` class owning `FILE*`, a `std::string` boundary converting with `.c_str()`, a `vector` behind the pointer-and-count API. The C lives in one directory; the rest of the program stays C++.
concepts.detail: The façade is also the natural place for the error checks the C API omits — turning return codes into exceptions exactly once, at the boundary.

concepts.term: Program in C++, not the C subset
concepts.statement: You can write C with a C++ compiler, and sometimes you must — but resource handles, `string`, `vector`, and exceptions exist precisely so you do not have to. A project that forbids its own facilities re-imports every bug class the C++ library was designed to remove.
concepts.detail: TC++PL's formulation is about intent: the C subset is for interoperating with C, not a dialect to write new systems in.

concepts.statement: Maintain the checklist: implicit `void*` casts, `sizeof('a')`, string literal constness, reserved keywords, tag namespaces, tentative definitions, `goto` over initialization, VLAs and `restrict`. When a dual-language header misbehaves, it is almost always one of these — and a wrong guess hides it further.
concepts.detail: The shared-subset dialect is learnable in an afternoon; what it costs is remembering that two compilers read the same line differently, and knowing which line.

concepts.statement: The standard does not guarantee that code compiled by different compilers — or even different versions of one compiler — links. The safe common denominator across vendors is the C ABI: `extern "C"` functions plus standard-layout data across the boundary, with anything richer created through a factory function.
concepts.detail: This is why plugin systems and OS interfaces are C APIs even when their implementations are C++ — the C ABI is the one interface every toolchain agrees on.

examples.title: One header, two languages
examples.problem: Write a geometry header that compiles as C under a C compiler and as C++ under a C++ compiler, exporting one function to both.

steps.label: Step 1: The skeleton
steps.text: `#ifndef GEOM_H / #define GEOM_H / #ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { #endif ... #ifdef __cplusplus } #endif / #endif` — the include guard is identical in both languages; `__cplusplus` is defined only by C++ compilers.

steps.label: Step 2: The declarations
steps.text: Inside the guarded region, plain common-subset declarations only: `typedef struct { double r; } Circle; double area(const Circle* c);` — pointers to layout-compatible data and functions with C linkage cross the boundary; references, classes, and overloads cannot.

steps.label: Step 3: What each compiler sees
steps.text: The C compiler sees two plain declarations. The C++ compiler additionally wraps them in `extern "C"`, so the definition — even if compiled as C++ — receives an unmangled symbol with C calling convention, and a C-built library links against it without knowing C++ exists.

steps.label: Step 4: The C++ side's freedom
steps.text: The implementation file compiles as C++ and may use `vector`, templates, and exceptions internally — the boundary constrains only the declared interface, which is exactly why it stays maintainable.

examples.result: One file, two compilers, one ABI: the pattern underlying every C library that ships a C++ binding, and the standard layout of system headers on every platform.

examples.title: Reviewing compatibility code
examples.problem: You are reviewing a colleague’s change that uses this chapter’s facilities. Your task: apply the compile-early, compile-often strategy for C code in a C++ project.

steps.label: Step 1: inventory
steps.text: List every use of this chapter’s facilities in the change. For each, write the rule it must satisfy — starting with: Keep C code compiling as C++ from the start — the compiler becomes a continuous compatibility checker.

steps.label: Step 2: probe
steps.text: Probe the riskiest use with a minimal program built on `int legacy(int n);`. If the probe surprises you, the rule behind it is load-bearing.

steps.label: Step 3: question
steps.text: Ask the chapter’s questions of the code: structure a dual-language header with include guards and extern 'C' correctly. Record where the code answers and where it stays silent.

steps.label: Step 4: rule
steps.text: Turn each silence into a review note that cites the reason, not just the rule: Contain the C interface behind RAII wrappers and one narrow boundary; use extern 'C' and the common subset in shared headers.

examples.result: The review ends with findings tied to reasons: Keep C code compiling as C++ from the start — the compiler becomes a continuous compatibility checker. Advice applied with its reasons is engineering; without them it is taste.

keyTakeaways: Keep C code compiling as C++ from the start — the compiler becomes a continuous compatibility checker.
Contain the C interface behind RAII wrappers and one narrow boundary; use extern "C" and the common subset in shared headers.
Write new code in full C++: the C subset re-imports the bug classes the library exists to remove.

quiz.q: What is the first move when a C++ project needs to absorb a C library?
options: Rewrite it from scratch in a modern language.
Get it to compile as C++ early and keep it compiling in both — the compiler then surfaces every silent difference.
Compile it as C forever and link with extern "C" only at the end.
Convert all its functions to classes before reading them.
quiz.explanation: Early dual compilation turns compatibility from a one-time porting project into a standing invariant the compiler enforces for free.

quiz.q: In a header shared by C and C++ code, what is the role of `#ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" {`?
options: To include the declarations twice for safety.
To disable the include guard for C.
So the same header compiles as C, while a C++ compiler additionally sees the declarations wrapped in C linkage — one symbol, callable from both.
quiz.explanation: The macro `__cplusplus` is defined only by C++ compilers; the guard lets one source of truth serve both languages with the right linkage on each side.

quiz.q: What is the book's stance on writing new code in the C subset of C++?
options: It is the recommended style for systems work.
It compiles, but you re-import C's bug classes — use `string`, `vector`, RAII, and exceptions where you can.
It is required for portability to embedded targets.
It always produces smaller and faster code.
quiz.explanation: The C subset exists for interop, not as a dialect for new systems; every facility it declines to use is a bug class it volunteers to keep.

intro: Every page you open is the result of cooperation between clients and servers across the internet, mediated by names, addresses, and a transfer protocol. This section traces that journey from the physical internet to DNS resolution, HTTP message exchange, and the anatomy of a URL. Master these ideas and the rest of web development has a place to stand.
objectives: Distinguish clients from servers and explain what the internet provides beneath the web
Trace DNS resolution from a hostname to an IP address through resolvers and records
Describe the parts of an HTTP request and response including methods and status codes
Dissect a URL into scheme, host, port, path, query, and fragment

concepts.statement: The **internet** is a global network of networks that routes packets between machines using the `IP` protocol, while the **web** is an application that runs on top of it using `HTTP`. A **client** such as a browser initiates requests, and a **server** listens for those requests and returns responses. The same machine can play both roles at different times, but the request always flows from client to server.
concepts.detail: Packets travel through routers and ISPs independently and are reassembled at the destination, which is why the web survives individual link failures.

concepts.statement: The **Domain Name System** translates human hostnames like `example.com` into numeric `IP addresses` that routers understand. Your browser asks a **recursive resolver**, which walks from **root** to **TLD** to **authoritative** nameservers, following `A` and `AAAA` records to the answer. Successful answers are **cached** at each level with a `TTL` so repeat visits skip the full walk.
concepts.detail: DNS caching is why a first visit can feel slower than later ones, and why DNS changes can take time to propagate worldwide.

concepts.statement: Every web exchange is a **request** carrying a `method`, a `path`, `headers`, and an optional `body`, answered by a **response** carrying a `status code`, `headers`, and a `body`. Common methods include `GET` for retrieval, `POST` for creation, and `PUT`, `PATCH`, and `DELETE` for updates and removal. Status codes are grouped by class, with `2xx` for success, `3xx` for redirection, `4xx` for client errors, and `5xx` for server errors.
concepts.detail: HTTP itself is stateless, so features like logins are layered on with cookies, tokens, and sessions that the client resends on every request.

concepts.statement: Plain `HTTP` sends headers and bodies readable by anyone on the path, so the modern web uses **HTTPS**, which wraps HTTP inside a `TLS` encrypted tunnel. During the **TLS handshake** the server proves its identity with a **certificate**, the two sides agree on keys, and everything after is **confidential and tamper-evident**. Browsers warn against plain HTTP sites because logins and cookies sent over them can be intercepted directly.
concepts.detail: Certificates are issued by trusted certificate authorities and are validated against the hostname, which is why a name mismatch triggers a full-page warning.

concepts.statement: A **URL** names one resource with the shape `scheme://host:port/path?query#fragment`, for example `https://example.com:443/docs/search?q=dns#results`. The `scheme` selects the protocol, the `host` names the server, and the optional `port` selects the service on that host. The `path` locates the resource, the `query` carries `key=value` parameters, and the `fragment` scrolls to a section without ever being sent to the server.
concepts.detail: Query strings are visible in history and logs, so secrets belong in headers or bodies rather than in the URL.

examples.title: Trace a first visit to a site
examples.problem: Follow what happens when you type https://example.com/articles into a fresh browser and press Enter.

steps.label: Step 1: Resolve the name
steps.text: The browser asks its configured resolver for `example.com`. The resolver walks root to TLD to authoritative servers, receives an `A` record with the server IP, and caches it under its `TTL`.

steps.label: Step 2: Open a secure channel
steps.text:
```bash
# conceptually, the browser now does:
# 1. TCP connect to the IP on port 443
# 2. TLS handshake, verify certificate for example.com
# 3. Send the HTTP request inside the encrypted tunnel
```
Port `443` is the default for HTTPS, so no port appears in the typed URL, and the certificate check ties the encryption to the hostname.

steps.label: Step 3: Request and response
steps.text:
```html
<!-- the request line and headers the browser sends --> <!-- GET /articles HTTP/1.1 --> <!-- Host: example.com --> <!-- the server answers: HTTP/1.1 200 OK + HTML body -->
```
The server returns `200 OK` with an HTML body, and the browser renders it while fetching subresources referenced by the markup.

examples.result: One typed address triggers DNS resolution, a TCP plus TLS connection, one HTTP exchange, and then a cascade of follow-up requests driven by the returned HTML.

examples.title: Dissect a URL with query and fragment
examples.problem: Break https://shop.example.com:443/search?q=keyboard&sort=price#top into its six parts and state what each part does.

steps.label: Step 1: Scheme, host, and port
steps.text: `https` selects encrypted HTTP, `shop.example.com` is the DNS hostname, and `443` is the explicit default HTTPS port. Removing the default port would leave the meaning unchanged.

steps.label: Step 2: Path and query
steps.text: `/search` routes to the search handler on the server, while `q=keyboard&sort=price` passes two parameters the handler reads. The server may return different HTML or JSON for different query values.

steps.label: Step 3: Fragment
steps.text:
```html
<!-- the browser never sends #top to the server -->
<section id="top">Deals of the day</section>
```
After the response arrives, the browser scrolls to the element with `id="top"` locally, with no second request.

examples.result: Scheme, host, and port locate the service, path and query select and parameterize the resource, and the fragment is purely a client-side scroll target.

keyTakeaways: The internet moves packets by IP address while the web exchanges resources by HTTP between clients and servers.
DNS resolves hostnames through root, TLD, and authoritative servers, with TTL-based caching at every level.
HTTP pairs a method plus path plus headers with a status code plus headers plus body on every exchange.
HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS so identities are verified and traffic is confidential and tamper-evident.
URLs split into scheme, host, port, path, query, and fragment, and only the fragment stays entirely client-side.

quiz.q: Which order does a recursive DNS resolver follow to resolve a new hostname?
quiz.explanation: The resolver walks down the hierarchy from root to TLD to the authoritative server for the domain, caching the answer for repeat visits.

quiz.q: A server returns status 404. What does that mean?
options: Client error: the requested resource was not found
quiz.explanation: Codes in the 4xx range report client-side errors, and 404 specifically means the path did not match any known resource.

quiz.q: Which part of a URL is never sent to the server?
quiz.explanation: The fragment is resolved locally by the browser to scroll to an element id, so it never appears in the HTTP request.

quiz.q: Why does HTTPS protect a login form while plain HTTP does not?
options: HTTPS compresses the password so it cannot be read
HTTPS wraps the exchange in a TLS tunnel with a verified certificate so traffic is encrypted
HTTPS stores passwords on the server instead of the client
HTTPS blocks all third-party scripts automatically
quiz.explanation: TLS negotiates encryption after verifying the server certificate, making headers and bodies confidential and tamper-evident in transit.

quiz.q: A site first visit takes noticeably longer to start than repeat visits, and after the team moves to new hosting addresses some users keep reaching the old server for a while. Which mechanism explains both observations?
options: TCP slow start delaying every single connection
DNS answers cached at resolvers for their TTL: the first lookup walks the hierarchy while repeats reuse the stored record, and stale copies persist until the TTL lapses
Browsers re-download the page markup only on the first paint
TLS certificates expiring between one visit and the next
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is a slow first resolution, fast repeats, and lingering old addresses after a hosting move. Step 2: The governing rule is resolver behavior: a recursive resolver walks from root to TLD to authoritative servers for A and AAAA records, then caches the answer at each level for its TTL. Step 3: Tracing the three cases, the first visit pays the full walk, repeats reuse the cached record, and the address change stays invisible to holders of unexpired copies until their TTL lapses. Step 4: The distractors fail because transport startup affects every connection equally, markup fetching is unrelated to name resolution, and certificate lifetimes operate on a different timescale. Step 5: Therefore TTL-bounded DNS caching explains both the speedup and the slow migration.

intro: A browser is an operating system for web pages: it fetches resources, parses HTML and CSS, runs JavaScript, and paints pixels many times per second. Understanding the critical rendering path explains why some pages feel instant and others stutter. Browser DevTools then let you watch every step and fix what is slow or broken.
objectives: List the stages of the critical rendering path from navigation to paint
Explain how the DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, and paint relate
Use the Elements, Console, and Network panels of DevTools for inspection
Diagnose a slow or broken page by reading status codes, timing, and console errors

concepts.statement: Loading a page follows a **pipeline**: navigation and DNS plus TLS, then fetching `HTML`, then parsing it into the `DOM` while fetching `CSS` into the `CSSOM`. The browser combines both trees into the **render tree**, runs **layout** to compute geometry, then **paints** pixels and **composites** layers. JavaScript can pause parsing or invalidate layout, which is why script placement and size dominate load performance.
concepts.detail: Anything that delays the first three stages delays everything after, so fast HTML delivery and small stylesheets matter most.

concepts.term: DOM, CSSOM, and the render tree
concepts.statement: The **DOM** is the parsed tree of `HTML elements`, the **CSSOM** is the parsed map of `style rules`, and the **render tree** contains only the boxes that will actually display. Nodes with `display: none` enter the DOM but are excluded from the render tree, while `visibility: hidden` nodes stay in the tree but paint nothing. DevTools shows the live DOM, which scripts may have already changed from the original source.
concepts.detail: View Source shows the bytes from the server while the Elements panel shows the live tree after parsing and scripting.

concepts.statement: In the **layout** step the browser computes the `width`, `height`, and position of every render-tree box from CSS. In the **paint** step it fills in `color`, `borders`, `shadows`, and text, and in the **composite** step it draws cached `layers` in order. Animating `transform` and `opacity` is cheap because it reuses painted layers, while animating `width` or `top` forces fresh layout and paint.
concepts.detail: Jank usually means scripts or styles keep invalidating layout instead of staying on compositor-friendly properties.

concepts.statement: Browser **DevTools** expose the pipeline: the `Elements` panel inspects and edits live HTML and CSS, the `Console` runs `JavaScript` and surfaces errors, and the `Network` panel lists every request with its `status`, `size`, and `timing`. The `Performance` and `Lighthouse` tabs record frames and score loading health. Learning these four panels covers the large majority of daily debugging.
concepts.detail: Edits made in the Elements panel apply instantly but vanish on reload, which makes them ideal for experiments before touching source files.

concepts.statement: A plain `<script>` tag **blocks parsing** until it downloads and executes, while `async` lets parsing continue and runs the script when ready, and `defer` waits until parsing finishes in order. Stylesheets block rendering until loaded because the browser refuses to paint without the `CSSOM`. Placing scripts at the end of `body` or marking them `defer` keeps first paint early without losing functionality.
concepts.detail: Render-blocking chains are the most common cause of blank-screen delays on otherwise simple pages.

examples.title: Read a Network waterfall
examples.problem: A page loads slowly. Use the Network panel to decide whether HTML, CSS, or a script is the bottleneck.

steps.label: Step 1: Open and reload
steps.text: Open DevTools with `F12` or `Cmd+Option+I`, select the `Network` panel, enable `Disable cache`, and reload. Each row is one request with status, size, and a timing bar.

steps.label: Step 2: Read the waterfall
steps.text: A long dark bar before the first byte means slow `TTFB` on the server or network, while a long light bar means a large download. A script row that starts early but ends late is blocking everything below it.

steps.label: Step 3: Act on the evidence
steps.text:
```html
<!-- before: blocks parsing until analytics.js arrives -->
<script src="analytics.js"></script>
<!-- after: parsing continues, script runs when ready -->
<script src="analytics.js" defer></script>
```
Adding `defer` or moving the tag lets the render tree build earlier while preserving execution order.

examples.result: The waterfall turns a vague slow feeling into a named culprit and a one-line fix that can be verified by reloading and comparing timings.

examples.title: Fix a broken style with the Elements panel
examples.problem: A button should be blue but renders gray. Find the losing rule without guessing.

steps.label: Step 1: Inspect the node
steps.text: Right-click the button and choose Inspect to jump to it in the `Elements` panel. The `Styles` pane lists every matching rule with losing declarations struck through.

steps.label: Step 2: Toggle and edit live
steps.text: Uncheck candidate declarations and edit values inline until the button turns blue. The page updates instantly because you are editing the live `CSSOM`.

steps.label: Step 3: Check the Console

examples.result: Inspection replaces guesswork: the struck-through rules show exactly which selector lost, and the live edit becomes the patch.

keyTakeaways: Navigation, HTML parsing, CSSOM building, render tree, layout, paint, and composite form the rendering pipeline.
The DOM holds all parsed nodes while the render tree holds only boxes that will display.
Animating transform and opacity stays on the compositor while width and position force costly relayout.
DevTools Elements, Console, Network, and Performance panels expose each pipeline stage.
Plain scripts block parsing while async and defer keep first paint early.

quiz.q: Which sequence correctly orders the rendering stages?
options: DOM and CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, composite
quiz.explanation: Parsing produces the DOM and CSSOM, which combine into the render tree, and only then do layout, paint, and composite compute and draw pixels.

quiz.q: An element has display: none. Where does it appear?
options: In the DOM and the render tree
In the DOM but not the render tree
quiz.explanation: The node still parses into the DOM but generates no box, so the render tree excludes it entirely.

quiz.q: Why is animating width slower than animating transform?
options: Width cannot be animated at all
Width changes force layout and paint while transform reuses composited layers
quiz.explanation: Geometry changes invalidate layout for surrounding boxes, while transform and opacity only move already-painted layers.

quiz.q: What does adding defer to a classic script tag do?
options: It prevents the script from running
It downloads in parallel and executes after HTML parsing in order
It inlines the script into the HTML
It moves execution to a web worker
quiz.explanation: Deferred scripts never block parsing and still execute in document order once the DOM is complete.

intro: Professional web work rests on three tools: a code editor for writing, a terminal for running, and a package manager for reusing the work of others. This section sets up VS Code, teaches the handful of shell commands behind every tutorial, and explains how Node, npm, and package.json fit together. The goal is a project folder you can run, install into, and script.
objectives: Configure VS Code with extensions, settings, and formatting for web files
Navigate, create, and manage files from the terminal with core shell commands
Explain the roles of Node, npm, npx, and package.json in a web project
Add, run, and script dependencies in a fresh project folder

concepts.term: VS Code as a web bench
concepts.statement: Visual Studio Code is a **file-first editor**: it opens a `folder`, previews a `live server`, and extends through **extensions** for languages, linting, and formatting. The **command palette** under `Ctrl+Shift+P` runs every command by name, and `settings.json` pins choices like `tab size` and `format on save`. A shared extension list keeps a team editing identically.
concepts.detail: Format-on-save with a single formatter ends most style debates before they start.

concepts.statement: The **terminal** runs text commands against the file system, with the **shell** interpreting each line and the **working directory** deciding what relative paths mean. Core verbs include `pwd` to show where you are, `ls` to list, `cd` to move, `mkdir` and `touch` to create, and `rm` and `mv` to remove and rename. Flags like `ls -la` modify behavior, and the `up arrow` plus `Tab` recall and complete earlier commands.
concepts.detail: Every deploy, build, and git command in later chapters is just these same shell mechanics aimed at a new program.

concepts.statement: Node.js is a **JavaScript runtime** outside the browser built on the `V8` engine, and **npm** is its **package registry plus installer**. Running `npm install <pkg>` records the dependency in `package.json` and downloads it into `node_modules`, while `npx <pkg>` executes a package binary without a global install. Version numbers follow **semver** like `1.4.2`, where each position signals breaking, feature, or fix changes.
concepts.detail: Prefer npx for one-off tools and local installs for project tools so every machine builds with the same versions.

concepts.statement: The `package.json` file is the **manifest** of a project: its `name`, `version`, `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, and `scripts` table. A script like `"dev": "vite --port 3000"` turns `npm run dev` into a memorable alias for a long command. The `package-lock.json` file then **pins exact versions** so installs reproduce byte for byte on other machines.
concepts.detail: Commit the manifest and the lockfile but never hand-edit the lockfile or commit node_modules.

concepts.statement: A minimal project pairs an `index.html` entry page with `styles.css` and `app.js` assets plus `package.json` for tooling. A `.gitignore` file excludes generated output like `node_modules` and `dist` from version control. The `README.md` documents how to `install`, `run`, and `build`, so a stranger can start the project with three commands.
concepts.detail: Small, conventional layouts scale because every tool in the ecosystem already expects these filenames.

examples.title: Start a project from zero
examples.problem: Create a folder, turn it into an npm project, and serve a page with a dev script.

steps.label: Step 1: Scaffold the files
steps.text:
```bash
mkdir hello-web && cd hello-web
npm init -y
touch index.html styles.css app.js
ls -la
```
`npm init -y` writes a default `package.json`, and `ls -la` confirms the new files including hidden ones.

steps.label: Step 2: Add a script
steps.text: Add a `scripts` entry that serves the folder, then run it with `npm run dev`. The script is now the documented way to start the project on any machine.

steps.label: Step 3: Verify in the browser
steps.text: Open the served address, confirm the page loads, and inspect it with DevTools. The loop of edit, save, and reload is now in place.

examples.result: A reproducible project exists: anyone cloning it runs install plus the dev script and sees the same page.

examples.title: Install and use a library
examples.problem: Add a date library to the project and use it from a page script without a global install.

steps.label: Step 1: Install the package
steps.text:
```bash
npm install date-fns
npm list date-fns
```
The dependency lands in `dependencies` and the exact tree is pinned in `package-lock.json`.

steps.label: Step 2: Run a one-off tool
steps.text:
```bash
npx prettier --write .
```
`npx` fetches and runs the formatter without polluting the global environment, formatting every web file in place.

steps.label: Step 3: Import from app.js

examples.result: The library is a recorded, pinned, local dependency rather than a mystery global, so builds stay repeatable.

keyTakeaways: VS Code plus the command palette, extensions, and format-on-save form a consistent web bench.
A few shell verbs plus flags, history, and completion cover most daily terminal work.
Node runs JavaScript outside the browser while npm installs and npx executes packages.
package.json declares metadata, dependencies, and scripts while the lockfile pins exact versions.
Conventional files plus a README let any newcomer install, run, and build the project.

quiz.q: What is the difference between npm and npx?
options: npm edits images while npx edits video
npm installs packages into a project while npx executes package binaries without a global install
quiz.explanation: Install with npm so the dependency is recorded, and execute one-off or local binaries with npx to avoid global installs.

quiz.q: Which files should be committed to version control?
quiz.explanation: The manifest and lockfile reproduce the exact tree, while generated folders and outputs are rebuilt and stay ignored.

quiz.q: What does npm run dev do?
options: It always starts a production server
It runs the dev entry from the scripts table of package.json
quiz.explanation: Scripts map short names to full commands, so dev can mean a Vite server in one project and something else in another.

quiz.q: Which terminal command shows the current working directory?
quiz.explanation: pwd prints the working directory that relative paths resolve against, while ls lists and cd changes it.

intro: Git records the history of your files so experiments are cheap and mistakes are reversible, while GitHub hosts that history for collaboration. This section builds the mental model of repositories, commits, and branches, then walks the GitHub Flow teams use daily. You will finish able to branch, commit, push, and open a pull request with confidence.
objectives: Explain repositories, working trees, staging, commits, and remotes
Create branches, switch between them, and merge work back to main
Push, pull, and clone to synchronize local and GitHub repositories
Open and review a pull request following the GitHub Flow

concepts.statement: A **repository** is a folder plus a `.git` database that records every **commit**, where each commit is a **snapshot** with a message, an author, and a parent pointer. The **working tree** holds your editable files, the **staging area** holds the exact set bound for the next snapshot, and `HEAD` names the currently checked-out commit. History is therefore a linked chain you can inspect, rewind, and share.
concepts.detail: Because commits store snapshots rather than diffs, checking out any point in history restores the complete tree instantly.

concepts.statement: A **branch** is a movable pointer to one commit, so creating a branch with `git branch` or `git switch -c` costs almost nothing. Commits advance only the current branch, and `git merge` joins two lines of history by creating a **merge commit** or fast-forwarding the pointer. **Merge conflicts** mark overlapping edits with `<<<<<<<` fences for a human to resolve and commit.
concepts.detail: Short-lived feature branches keep main releasable because half-finished work never lands there directly.

concepts.statement: A **remote** like `origin` is a named URL for a hosted copy, and `git clone` copies a whole repository including history from that URL. `git push` publishes local commits upward, while `git pull` fetches remote commits and merges them into the current branch. The `main` branch on GitHub is the shared source of truth that every teammate synchronizes against.
concepts.detail: Push and pull are explicit so developers review what leaves and enters their machine instead of syncing silently.

concepts.statement: The **GitHub Flow** is a five-step loop: **branch** from `main`, **commit** small steps, **push** the branch, open a **pull request**, then **merge** after review and checks. A **pull request** is a proposal page showing `diffs`, `checks`, and `comments` where teammates request changes. Merging deletes the topic branch and advances `main` by exactly the reviewed commits.
concepts.detail: Small pull requests with green checks merge quickly, while giant ones stall because no reviewer can hold the whole diff in mind.

concepts.statement: A good commit is **atomic** with an **imperative message** like `Add hero image`, so `git log` reads as instructions already carried out. The `.gitignore` file keeps generated paths such as `node_modules` and `.env` out of history before they ever get staged. Secrets committed by accident must be **rotated**, not just deleted, because history preserves every version forever.
concepts.detail: Atomic commits make reverts safe: one revert undoes one idea instead of tangling several features together.

examples.title: Ship a feature with GitHub Flow
examples.problem: Add a footer to the site on a branch and land it through a reviewed pull request.

steps.label: Step 1: Branch and commit
steps.text:
```bash
git switch -c add-footer
git add index.html
git commit -m "Add site footer"
git log --oneline -3
```
The branch pointer carries the new snapshot while `main` stays untouched and releasable.

steps.label: Step 2: Push and open the request
steps.text: Push with `git push -u origin add-footer` and open a pull request against `main`. The diff, checks, and description give reviewers everything in one page.

steps.label: Step 3: Merge and clean up
steps.text: After approval, merge the request on GitHub, then run `git switch main` and `git pull` locally. Deleting the topic branch leaves history with one clean merge.

examples.result: The footer reaches main only as a reviewed, tested, atomic unit, and the branch that carried it disappears.

examples.title: Resolve a merge conflict
examples.problem: Main and your branch both edited the same line of the page title. Merge without losing either change.

steps.label: Step 1: Attempt the merge
steps.text: Run `git merge main` on your branch and read the conflict notice naming the file. Git pauses the merge instead of guessing which edit should win.

steps.label: Step 2: Edit the fences
steps.text:
```html

StudyVerse

``` Open the file, choose or combine the wording, and remove every fence marker so the markup parses again.

steps.label: Step 3: Finish the merge
steps.text: Stage with `git add` and commit to complete the merge, then verify with `git log --oneline --graph -5`. The graph now shows the join explicitly.

examples.result: The conflict becomes a deliberate human decision recorded as a merge commit rather than a silent overwrite.

keyTakeaways: Repositories store snapshots as commits chained through parents with HEAD marking checkout.
Branches are cheap pointers and merges join lines of history with explicit merge commits.
Clone, push, and pull move history between local machines and the origin remote.
GitHub Flow ships every change as a reviewed pull request merged into main.
Atomic messages plus gitignore keep history readable and free of generated files and secrets.

quiz.q: What does the staging area do?
options: It holds the exact set of changes bound for the next commit
quiz.explanation: Staging lets a commit contain precisely the reviewed files rather than everything touched in the working tree.

quiz.q: A merge reports a conflict. What should you do?
options: Delete the repository and clone again
Open the marked files, choose the correct content, remove fences, stage, and commit
Ignore the fences and commit anyway
quiz.explanation: Conflicts pause the merge so a human can reconcile overlapping edits and record the decision as the merge commit.

quiz.q: Which sequence matches the GitHub Flow?
options: Branch, commit, push, pull request, merge after review
Commit directly to main and skip review
quiz.explanation: Work happens on a topic branch that is pushed and proposed as a pull request before reviewed code reaches main.

quiz.q: A secret was committed by accident. What is the correct response?
options: Delete the line in a new commit and move on
Rotate the secret and purge it from history because old commits still contain it
Add the secret to gitignore only
quiz.explanation: History preserves every version, so the exposed value must be revoked even after the file is cleaned.

intro: Some pages are fixed files while others are assembled per visitor, and knowing which you need decides your hosting and tooling. This section contrasts frontend and backend roles with static and dynamic rendering, surveys hosting options, and ends with your first deploy. You will publish a static page and learn how to update it safely.
objectives: Contrast frontend and backend responsibilities in a web application
Compare static files, server rendering, and client rendering with tradeoffs
Choose a host for a static site and explain domains, DNS, and TLS setup
Deploy a static page and publish an update through a repeatable flow

concepts.statement: The **frontend** is the code that runs in the browser — `HTML`, `CSS`, and `JavaScript` — and owns layout, interaction, and presentation. The **backend** is code that runs on servers, owning `databases`, `authentication`, and business rules behind an `API`. The two meet over HTTP, with the frontend requesting data and the backend answering with guarded, validated results.
concepts.detail: Keeping secrets and validation on the backend matters because every byte sent to the browser can be read and replayed.

concepts.statement: A **static site** is a set of **prebuilt files** served exactly as stored, with no per-request computation. Because responses are identical for everyone, they cache on **CDNs** at the edge and load quickly under traffic spikes. Blogs, docs, and portfolios stay static until a page genuinely needs per-user or per-request data.
concepts.detail: Static does not mean motionless: shipped JavaScript can still fetch data and animate after the fixed files arrive.

concepts.statement: **Server-side rendering** builds `HTML` per request on the server, so first paint arrives with content but every visit costs compute. **Client-side rendering** ships a small shell plus `JavaScript` that fetches data and builds the DOM in the browser, which delays first content but scales serving to static edges. Many frameworks **hybridize**, prerendering shared pages statically while server rendering only personalized routes.
concepts.detail: Choose per route rather than per project: marketing pages prerender well while dashboards favor client fetching behind a login.

concepts.statement: Static hosts like `GitHub Pages`, `Netlify`, and `Vercel` serve a folder globally and attach free `TLS certificates` automatically. Pointing a custom domain means adding a `DNS record` such as a `CNAME` or `A` record from your registrar to the host. **Propagation** plus certificate issuance can take minutes to hours, after which both the bare and `www` names should redirect to one canonical HTTPS URL.
concepts.detail: One canonical domain with forced HTTPS avoids duplicate-content and mixed-content faults from the start.

concepts.term: Deploy pipeline for a static page
concepts.statement: A repeatable deploy is **commit**, **push**, and **publish**: push `main` and let the host **build** and invalidate its `cache` automatically. Preview deploys give every pull request its own `URL` for review before merging to production. Rolling back is checking out or reverting to the last good commit and pushing again, which restores the previous files exactly.
concepts.detail: If a deploy is not reproducible from a clean clone plus install plus build, it is a ritual rather than a pipeline.

examples.title: Decide static versus dynamic
examples.problem: Two projects arrive: a conference site and a team task board. Choose the rendering approach for each.

steps.label: Step 1: List data needs
steps.text: The conference site shows the same schedule to everyone, while the board shows per-user tasks behind a login. Shared content favors prebuilt `HTML`, and per-user content needs an `API` plus identity.

steps.label: Step 2: Choose per route
steps.text: Ship the conference site as a **static** build on a CDN for speed and cheap scale. Build the board with **client rendering** against an authenticated API, prerendering only the public marketing route.

steps.label: Step 3: Note the escape hatch
steps.text:
```html
<!-- static shell that hydrates with live data -->
<main id="app">Loading schedule…</main>
<script src="app.js" defer></script>
```
Even the static choice keeps a `script` slot so later dynamic widgets can mount without replatforming.

examples.result: Same toolbox, different split: static where content is shared and dynamic where data is personal.

examples.title: Deploy a first page
examples.problem: Publish a local index.html to a public HTTPS URL and then ship an update.

steps.label: Step 1: Prepare the folder
steps.text: Confirm `index.html` loads locally with no absolute file paths and that only source files are present. A clean folder prevents broken asset links after upload.

steps.label: Step 2: Publish
steps.text:
```bash
 git init
 git add index.html styles.css app.js
 git commit -m "Launch first static page"
 git push -u origin main
```
Pushing `main` triggers the host build, which publishes the folder to a public address and provisions its certificate.

steps.label: Step 3: Update safely
steps.text: Edit locally, verify in the browser, commit, and push again, then check the live URL and roll back with a revert if anything looks wrong. Every release is now one reviewed push.

examples.result: The page is live on HTTPS with a repeatable update path: edit, commit, push, and verify.

keyTakeaways: Frontend owns presentation in the browser while backend owns data, identity, and rules on servers.
Static files cache at the edge and scale cheaply because every visitor gets identical bytes.
Server rendering paints content early at compute cost while client rendering fetches and builds late.
Custom domains need a DNS record plus automatic TLS with one canonical HTTPS redirect.
Repeatable deploys are commit plus push plus automatic build, with previews and reverts built in.

quiz.q: When is a static site the best choice?
options: Content identical for every visitor such as docs or event pages
Apps needing per-request database writes on every view
quiz.explanation: Identical bytes for everyone cache perfectly on CDNs, which is exactly the static strength.

quiz.q: What distinguishes server-side rendering from client-side rendering?
options: SSR builds HTML per request on the server while CSR builds the DOM in the browser from fetched data
They are two names for the same technique
quiz.explanation: The split is where HTML is assembled: on the server before delivery versus in the browser after fetching.

quiz.q: What does pointing a custom domain at a static host require?
options: A DNS record toward the host plus TLS issuance with one canonical HTTPS URL
quiz.explanation: DNS routes the name to the host, which then provisions and renews the certificate for that name.

quiz.q: How should a broken static deploy be rolled back?
options: Edit files directly on the CDN
Revert to the last good commit and push so the host rebuilds that snapshot
Wait for caches to expire randomly
quiz.explanation: Because deploys track git, restoring the previous snapshot and pushing republishes the known-good files.

intro: HTML is a language of elements built from tags, attributes, and text, parsed into a document with strict rules about nesting and structure. This section covers syntax, the doctype, and the split between head metadata and body content. Get this skeleton right and every later chapter has a valid page to style and script.
objectives: Write well-formed elements with correct tag, attribute, and nesting syntax
Explain the purpose of the doctype and the lang attribute on html
Separate head metadata from body content and place each tag correctly
Add charset, viewport, title, and description meta tags to a document

concepts.statement:
An **element** is a unit of meaning built from a **start tag**, content, and an **end tag**, such as `

hello

`, with **attributes** carrying extra data as `name="value"` pairs inside the start tag. **Void elements** like `` and `
` have no end tag because they cannot contain content. Whitespace between attributes is required, and attribute values should always be **quoted** so special characters parse predictably.
concepts.detail: Tags describe structure while attributes configure it, which is why the same img tag shows different pictures through different src values.

concepts.statement: The `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration is a **history-triggered switch** that tells the browser to parse the page in **standards mode** with modern layout rules. It is not an element, carries no attributes, and must be the **first line** of the document. Omitting it drops the browser into **quirks mode**, where old box-model bugs return and CSS behaves inconsistently.
concepts.detail: One line at the top prevents an entire family of cross-browser layout mysteries.

concepts.statement: Every page wraps content in `<html lang="en">`, which holds exactly one `<head>` for **metadata** and one `<body>` for **visible content**. The `lang` attribute names the page language for **screen readers** and search engines. Scripts, styles, and metadata belong in the head or at the end of the body, but never as loose text directly inside `html`.
concepts.detail: Assistive technology announces the language and switches pronunciation from this single attribute.

concepts.statement: Three head tags shape every render: `<meta charset="utf-8">` selects the **character encoding**, `<meta name="viewport">` sets the **mobile layout width**, and `<title>` names the **tab and bookmark**. Declaring `charset` first avoids mojibake, and the viewport tag with `width=device-width` stops phones from shrinking desktop layouts. The head also hosts linked `stylesheets` and `scripts` plus social preview tags.
concepts.detail: Pages missing the viewport tag look tiny on phones because the browser assumes a desktop-width canvas.

concepts.statement:
Elements must **nest strictly**: inner elements close before outer ones, so `text` is valid while overlapping tags are not. Block containers like `
` and `

` may hold inline content like `` and ``, but **paragraphs cannot contain** block children such as headings or divs. When markup overlaps, the **parser repairs** it by closing and reopening elements, which moves nodes somewhere surprising.
concepts.detail: Validation catches nesting faults early because the repaired DOM rarely matches the intended outline.

examples.title: Build a minimal valid document
examples.problem: Write the smallest HTML5 page that passes validation and renders predictably on phones.

steps.label: Step 1: Doctype and language
steps.text:
```html Hello page

Hello, web.

``` The doctype triggers standards mode, `lang` names the language, and `charset` comes before any content bytes.

steps.label: Step 2: Check head versus body
steps.text: Metadata such as `title` and `meta` sits in the head, while the visible `p` sits in the body. Nothing visible leaks into the head and no metadata litters the body.

steps.label: Step 3: Validate
steps.text: Paste the file into the Nu Html Checker and fix any reported nesting or missing-tag errors. A green validation pass means the parser needs no repairs.

examples.result: A compact skeleton now guarantees standards mode, correct encoding, mobile sizing, and a named tab.

examples.title: Repair an overlapping-nesting bug
examples.problem: A paragraph was written to hold a div, and the layout breaks. Diagnose and fix it.

steps.label: Step 1: Spot the violation
steps.text:
```html

Intro text

Note

``` The `p` element accepts only phrasing content, so a `div` child violates the content model.

steps.label: Step 2: Predict the repair
steps.text: The parser closes the paragraph before the div and drops the stray closing tag, producing siblings instead of a parent and child. Styles targeting `p div` therefore never match.

steps.label: Step 3: Rewrite validly
steps.text:
```html

Intro text

Note
``` Siblings inside a `section` preserve the visual order with a DOM that matches the stylesheet.

examples.result: Replacing illegal nesting with explicit siblings aligns the DOM, the styles, and the author intent.

keyTakeaways: Elements combine tags, quoted attributes, and content, with void elements taking no end tag.
The doctype must lead the file to keep browsers in standards mode.
html wraps one head for metadata and one body for visible content with a lang attribute.
Charset, viewport, and title tags control encoding, mobile layout, and tab naming.
Strict nesting matters because the parser silently repairs overlapping or illegal children.

quiz.q: What does <!DOCTYPE html> do?
options: It switches the browser into standards mode for modern parsing and layout
quiz.explanation: The doctype is a historical switch: present means standards mode, absent means quirks mode with legacy bugs.

quiz.q: Where do <title> and <meta charset> belong?
quiz.explanation: Head holds metadata about the document while body holds visible content, so title and charset live in the head.

quiz.q:
Why is

Text

Note

invalid?
options: Paragraphs cannot contain block-level children like div
quiz.explanation: The p content model allows only phrasing content, so the parser closes the paragraph early and repairs the tree.

quiz.q: Why quote all attribute values?
options: Quoted values parse predictably when they contain spaces or special characters
Unquoted values are a security feature
Quotes are required only in CSS
quiz.explanation: Quotes delimit exactly where a value ends, preventing spaces and symbols from splitting it into new tokens.

intro: Most pages are headings, paragraphs, lists, and links arranged in a meaningful order. This section teaches the text elements that carry document meaning and the link patterns that connect pages. Done well, the markup reads like an outline even with styles disabled.
objectives: Apply the heading hierarchy from h1 to h6 without skipping levels
Mark paragraphs, emphasis, code, and quotations with inline semantics
Choose between ordered, unordered, and description lists for grouped content
Write links with correct href values, targets, and accessible names

concepts.statement: Headings from `<h1>` to `<h6>` form the **document outline**, with exactly one `h1` naming the page and deeper levels **nesting in order** without skips. Screen readers and search engines navigate by this outline, treating headings as a table of contents. Using headings for **sizing rather than structure** destroys that map, since visual size belongs to `CSS`.
concepts.detail: Skipping from h1 to h4 confuses assistive tech because the missing levels imply sections that do not exist.

concepts.statement:
The `

` element wraps a **block of prose**, while inline elements mark meaning inside it: `` for **strong importance**, `` for **stress emphasis**, and `` for **code mentions**. Quotations use `

` for **block quotes** with a `cite` source and `` for **inline quotes**. Line breaks with `
` are for verse and addresses only, never for paragraph spacing.
concepts.detail: Strong and em convey meaning to assistive tech, unlike bold and italic styling which only change appearance.

concepts.statement: Lists group related items where each `<li>` is one member: `<ul>` marks an **unordered** set, `<ol>` marks an **ordered** sequence with `start` and `type` controls, and `<dl>` pairs **terms** in `<dt>` with **definitions** in `<dd>`. Navigation menus, breadcrumbs, and steps are all lists because their items belong together. Nesting a full `ul` or `ol` inside a parent `li` builds sub-steps correctly.
concepts.detail: Announcing list counts helps screen reader users, which stray divs pretending to be lists never provide.

concepts.statement: The `<a>` element turns its content into a **hyperlink** whose `href` names the destination: absolute `https://` URLs for other sites, **root-relative** `/docs` paths for same-site pages, and `#id` **fragments** for in-page jumps. The `target="_blank"` value opens a new tab and should pair with `rel="noopener"` for **process isolation**. **Descriptive link text** like `Read the install guide` replaces bare `click here` so the purpose survives out of context.
concepts.detail: Fragment links need a matching id on the destination element, otherwise the jump silently lands at the top.

concepts.statement: Small elements prevent big misunderstandings: `<time datetime="2026-05-01">` gives machines a **parseable date**, `<abbr title="...">` expands an **abbreviation**, and `<mark>` highlights a **relevant passage**. Escaping with `<`, `>`, and `&` shows literal **angle brackets** instead of starting new tags. These details make prose robust for search, translation, and assistive tools.
concepts.detail: Human-readable dates vary by locale, so the datetime attribute carries the canonical value for sorting and calendars.

examples.title: Outline an article correctly
examples.problem: Structure a recipe page with a title, two sections, steps, and an ingredient list.

steps.label: Step 1: Headings in order
steps.text:
```html

Lemon Cake

Ingredients

Method

Step details

``` One `h1` names the page, `h2` sections divide it, and `h3` subdivides without skipping from `h1` to `h3`.

steps.label: Step 2: Lists for groups
steps.text: Ingredients become a `ul` of `li` items while method steps become an `ol`, so numbering and bullets carry meaning rather than decoration.

steps.label: Step 3: Inline meaning
steps.text: Mark the oven setting with `<strong>` for importance and the pan size with `<code>` so both survive as semantics, not just styling.

examples.result: The page outline reads as title, two sections, and a subsection even in a screen reader rotor or text-only view.

examples.title: Write links that survive anywhere
examples.problem: Add external, internal, and in-page links to a docs page with safe behavior.

steps.label: Step 1: Three href shapes
steps.text: ```html MDN reference Install guide Jump to troubleshooting ``` Absolute, root-relative, and fragment destinations each match their use: off-site, same-site, and same-page.

steps.label: Step 2: Safe new tabs
steps.text: External links that need a new tab add `target="_blank"` with `rel="noopener"` so the opened page cannot reach back into the opener.

steps.label: Step 3: Name the purpose
steps.text: Link text describes the destination instead of the mechanics, so a list of links read aloud still makes sense.

examples.result: Every link resolves correctly, opens safely, and announces a purpose that needs no surrounding context.

keyTakeaways: One h1 plus ordered h2 through h6 headings form the navigable document outline.
Paragraphs hold prose while strong, em, code, blockquote, and q mark inline meaning.
Unordered, ordered, and description lists group items that belong together.
Hrefs use absolute, root-relative, or fragment forms with descriptive link text.
Target blank links need rel noopener, and dates and abbreviations need machine-readable attributes.

quiz.q: Which heading pattern is correct?
options: One h1, then h2 sections, then h3 subsections in order
Multiple h1 elements per section for sizing
quiz.explanation: Headings nest in order without skips so assistive tech and search can reconstruct the document outline.

quiz.q:
When should
be used?
options: For line breaks inside verse or addresses where the break is content
quiz.explanation: Breaks encode meaningful line endings, while paragraph and section spacing belongs to CSS margins.

quiz.q: What is wrong with click here?
options: The text describes mechanics instead of the destination and fails out of context
quiz.explanation: Link text should name the destination so it stays useful in link lists and screen reader rotors.

quiz.q: Which list fits a glossary of terms and definitions?
quiz.explanation: Description lists pair each term in dt with its definition in dd, which is exactly the glossary shape.

intro: Images carry product photos, diagrams, and delight, but each one costs bytes and layout stability. This section teaches img essentials, meaningful alt text, figure captions, and the responsive picture system. You will serve sharp images on every screen without shipping desktop weight to phones.
objectives: Write img elements with src, alt, width, and height for stable layout
Compose alt text that replaces the image purpose for non-sighted users
Use figure and figcaption to bind images to their captions
Serve responsive images with srcset, sizes, picture, and modern formats

concepts.statement: The `` element embeds a raster image through its **`src`** address, and it is a **void element** with no end tag. Including **`width` and `height`** attributes reserves the aspect box before bytes arrive, preventing **cumulative layout shift** as images load. The `loading="lazy"` attribute defers **below-the-fold** images until scroll approaches, while `decoding="async"` keeps decoding off the main thread.
concepts.detail: Reserving the box is a performance fix: content stops jumping once image dimensions are known upfront.

concepts.statement: The **`alt`** attribute replaces the image when it cannot be seen, so it should state the **purpose**, not the pixels. Informative images get concise functional text like `alt="Golden lemon cake on a plate"`, while **decorative** images take an empty `alt=""` so assistive tech skips them. Complex charts need a short alt plus a nearby **text equivalent** such as a table or described summary.
concepts.detail: Good alt completes the sentence formed by surrounding content, while redundant phrases like image of waste the listener time.

concepts.statement: The `<figure>` element groups an **image with its caption**, and `<figcaption>` holds the **visible explanation** of that image. Captions can credit sources, explain trends, or link to data, keeping the association explicit for browsers and assistive tech. A figure may hold multiple images plus one caption when they form a single **illustrated unit**.
concepts.detail: Caption text is visible to everyone while alt stays invisible, so they complement rather than duplicate each other.

concepts.statement: The **`srcset`** attribute lists **candidate files** with `w` width descriptors, and **`sizes`** tells the browser how wide the image will render at each viewport. The browser then picks the **smallest sufficient file** given viewport width and `device pixel ratio`, saving mobile data without blurring desktop screens. A plain `src` remains as the **fallback** for older parsers.
concepts.detail: Width descriptors plus sizes beat pixel-density descriptors for fluid layouts because they account for rendered CSS width.

concepts.statement: The `` element wraps multiple `` options plus a fallback ``, switching by **`media` queries** or **`type`** format support. Serving **`AVIF`** first, then **`WebP`**, then `JPEG` or `PNG` gives each browser the **smallest format** it understands. **Art direction** uses media sources to crop differently on narrow screens, while format switching keeps the same crop in lighter bytes.
concepts.detail: Modern formats can halve file size at equal quality, which directly improves loading scores on image-heavy pages.

examples.title: Make an image stable and accessible
examples.problem: Add a hero photo of a cake so layout never jumps and screen readers get its purpose.

steps.label: Step 1: Size the box
steps.text: ```html ``` Explicit `width` and `height` reserve a box with the right aspect ratio, and `figcaption` carries the visible story.

steps.label: Step 2: Write purpose alt
steps.text: The alt names the dish and setting rather than listing pixels or repeating the caption. A decorative divider elsewhere on the page would instead use `alt=""`.

steps.label: Step 3: Choose loading
steps.text: Hero images stay `eager` because they fill the first viewport, while gallery images below switch to `loading="lazy"`.

examples.result: The photo appears without shifting text, announces its purpose aloud, and shows a caption to sighted readers.

examples.title: Serve responsive formats
examples.problem: Ship one sharp image to phones, tablets, and desktops without wasting bytes.
