keyTakeaways: Background layers stack top-first with size, position, and fallback colors.
Gradients are image values that paint stripes and scrims without files.
Borders take layout space while outlines draw focus rings without reflow.
Layered soft shadows create depth that stays cheap when static.
Styles, Computed, and box overlays pinpoint missed versus losing rules.

quiz.q: In background-image with two layers, which paints on top?
quiz.explanation: Layers stack with the first listed uppermost, ending in the background color at the bottom.

quiz.q: Why use outline rather than border for focus rings?
options: Outlines draw outside the border without shifting layout
quiz.explanation: Focus indication should never reflow neighbors, which outside-the-box outlines guarantee.

quiz.q: A rule is missing entirely from the Styles pane. What does that mean?
options: Its selector never matched the inspected element
It is always a browser bug
quiz.explanation: Only matching rules appear, with losers struck through, so absence proves non-matching.

quiz.q: How do you draw a crisp stripe with a gradient?
options: Give adjacent stops the same position for a hard edge
quiz.explanation: Coincident stop positions stop blending and switch color instantly at that line.

intro: Typography is the voice of a page: before a visitor reads a single word, the choice of typeface, size, weight and spacing tells them whether the site is playful or serious, cheap or premium. This section builds the full font and text toolkit — families and fallbacks, fluid sizes, weights, line and letter spacing, alignment, decoration and the readability rules that keep long passages comfortable.
objectives: Compose font-family stacks with generic fallbacks and system stacks
Size type with rem units, fluid clamp() scales and a clear hierarchy
Control weight, line-height and letter-spacing for legible text
Align, decorate and transform text without harming readability

concepts.statement: The **font-family** property takes an ordered list of typefaces, ending in a **generic family** such as `serif`, `sans-serif` or `monospace`, so the browser walks the list until it finds an installed face. A classic stack like `Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif` prefers Georgia, falls back to Times New Roman, and guarantees a serif rendering even on bare systems. Quote multi-word names such as `"Segoe UI"` and always keep the generic keyword last, because a stack with no generic can end in an unpredictable default.
concepts.detail: System stacks like `system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif` skip downloads entirely by using the operating system’s own interface face, which is fast and feels native on every device.

concepts.term: Sizing type with rem and fluid clamp()
concepts.statement: The **root-relative `rem`** unit sizes text against the `html` font size, so `1rem` equals the root size and `1.25rem` scales with a single user or author change to that root. Body copy around `1rem` with headings stepped up a modular scale keeps hierarchy consistent, while **fluid type** with `clamp()` such as `font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.2rem + 2vw, 2.75rem)` lets a heading grow with the viewport between sane minimum and maximum bounds. Prefer `rem` over `px` for text so browser font-size preferences and zoom keep working.
concepts.detail: Set `html { font-size: 100%; }` to respect the user default, then build every text size in `rem` or `clamp()` expressions so one root change rescales the whole page proportionally.

concepts.term: Weight, style and the variable range
concepts.statement: The **font-weight** property selects the thickness of glyphs, either with keywords `normal` and `bold` or with the numeric scale `100` through `900` where `400` is regular and `700` is bold. Numeric weights only render when the loaded face actually ships them, otherwise the browser synthesizes or rounds to the nearest available cut, which is why a `font-weight: 600` headline can look identical to `700` with a two-weight web font. The companion **font-style** property toggles `italic` and `oblique`, and variable fonts expose the whole weight continuum through one file instead of discrete cuts.
concepts.detail: Load only the weights you use and match every `font-weight` you declare to a shipped cut, because each extra cut is render-blocking download weight for zero visual gain.

concepts.statement: The **line-height** property sets the leading between baselines, and a unitless value such as `line-height: 1.5` is the professional default because it scales with the element’s own font size and inherits as a pure ratio. Body copy reads best between `1.4` and `1.7`, headings can tighten toward `1.1`, and **letter-spacing** with small `em` values such as `letter-spacing: 0.02em` opens up caps or small text while negative values draw display type together. Use `em` for spacing so the tracking stays proportional when the font size changes, and reach for `word-spacing` or `text-wrap: balance` for headline polish.
concepts.detail: Unitless `line-height` inherits as a multiplier while `em` or percentage values inherit as a computed length, so a unitless ratio is almost always the safer, more predictable choice.

concepts.statement: The **text-align** property positions lines within their block with `left`, `right`, `center` and `justify`, while **text-decoration** underlines, overlines or strikes text and **text-transform** recases it to `uppercase` or `capitalize` without touching the source. Long-form readability then depends on **measure and contrast**: lines of roughly forty five to seventy five characters, left-aligned body copy, generous line height, and color pairs that pass WCAG contrast keep readers comfortable. Centered paragraphs and justified narrow columns look decorative but tire the eye, so reserve centering for headings and short hero lines.
concepts.detail: Constrain article bodies with `max-width: 65ch` and `line-height: 1.6` to land measure and leading in the comfortable zone on every screen with two declarations.

keyTakeaways: End every font-family stack with a generic family so text always has a designed fallback.
Size body copy in rem and headings in clamp() so user preferences and viewports both work.
Declare only font weights you actually load, and prefer unitless line-height ratios.
Track small caps and labels with em letter-spacing; keep body copy left-aligned.
Cap article measure near 65ch with generous leading for comfortable long-form reading.

quiz.q: Why must a font-family stack end with a generic family like sans-serif?
options: The CSS parser rejects stacks without one
It guarantees a designed category fallback when no named face is installed
It loads a web font automatically
quiz.explanation: The browser walks the list in order; the generic keyword ensures the last resort is a serif, sans-serif or monospace face rather than an unpredictable browser default.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of clamp(1.75rem, 1.2rem + 2vw, 2.75rem) over a fixed rem size for a heading?
options: It scales fluidly with the viewport while enforcing a minimum and maximum
It changes the typeface at breakpoints
It fixes cumulative layout shift by itself
quiz.explanation: The middle preferred value grows with viewport width while the first and last arguments clamp the result, giving fluid scaling between legible bounds.

quiz.q: Why is unitless line-height: 1.5 preferred over line-height: 1.5em for body text?
options: It renders larger in all browsers
It inherits as a pure ratio that rescales with each element’s font size
quiz.explanation: Unitless values inherit as multipliers, so children with different font sizes keep proportional leading; em values inherit as a fixed computed length that can crowd larger child text.

quiz.q: Which combination best supports long-form readability?
options: Justified narrow columns with tight leading
Centered paragraphs at full viewport width
Left-aligned copy, measure near 65ch, line-height around 1.6, strong contrast
Uppercase body copy with negative letter-spacing
quiz.explanation: Left alignment gives a steady reading edge, the ch-capped measure keeps lines in the comfort range, generous leading separates lines, and contrast keeps glyphs legible.

intro: Lists and links are the working furniture of the web: navigation menus, article bullets, breadcrumbs and calls to action are all lists of links wearing different outfits. This section covers list markers and counters, the link-state order that keeps interactive feedback predictable, modern underline control, and the navigation patterns that turn a plain unordered list into a robust menu.
objectives: Style list markers, positions and custom counters with ::marker
Apply the LVHA link-state order for predictable feedback
Control underlines with offset, thickness and skip behavior
Build accessible horizontal navigation from a plain list

concepts.statement: The **list-style-type** property chooses the marker glyph — `disc`, `circle`, `square`, decimal `1`, `lower-roman`, `upper-alpha` and friends — while **list-style-position** decides whether the marker hangs `outside` the content box or sits `inside` it. The `outside` default keeps multi-line items aligned on a straight text edge with markers in the margin, whereas `inside` pulls markers into the flow so wrapped lines start beneath the bullet. The **list-style** shorthand bundles type, position and an optional `list-style-image` in one declaration.
concepts.detail: Reset default indentation deliberately with `margin: 0; padding-left: 1.5rem;` so custom markers align identically across browsers instead of inheriting each engine’s own list chrome.

concepts.statement: The **::marker** pseudo-element styles the bullet or number itself — `color`, `font-size` and `content` — without touching the item text, so `li::marker { color: #6366f1; font-weight: 700; }` recolors every bullet in one rule. For bespoke numbering, **CSS counters** with `counter-reset`, `counter-increment` and `content: counter(step)` in `::before` build chapter numbers, step badges or nested outlines that native `ol` types cannot express. Counters live on any element and nest with `counters(step, ".")` for dotted section numbers.
concepts.detail: Prefer `::marker` for simple recoloring since it keeps native list semantics and alignment, and reach for counters only when the design needs text, shapes or numbering the marker cannot draw.

concepts.statement: Links carry four classic states — **`:link`**, **`:visited`**, **`:hover`** and **`:active`** — and they must be written in that **LVHA order** so each later rule can override the earlier ones at equal specificity. The mnemonic **LoVe HAte** encodes the sequence: unvisited, visited, hover, active, with `:focus` typically grouped alongside hover for keyboard parity. Disordering them lets `:link` override `:hover`, which silently kills hover feedback and is one of the oldest CSS gotchas on record.
concepts.detail: Modern practice adds `:focus-visible` to the hover group so mouse users see no ring while keyboard users keep a strong indicator, satisfying both aesthetics and accessibility.

concepts.statement: The **text-decoration** family gives fine control: `text-decoration-line`, `text-decoration-color`, `text-decoration-style` with `wavy` or `dotted`, plus **text-decoration-thickness** and **text-underline-offset** for weight and clearance. A rule like `text-underline-offset: 4px` lifts the stroke off descenders for legibility, and `text-decoration-skip-ink: auto` lets the line gap around glyphs. These beat the old `border-bottom` underline hack because they wrap across line breaks and follow text direction automatically.
concepts.detail: Animate `text-decoration-color` or background-size underlines rather than thickness for hover effects, since color and background transitions stay on the cheap compositing path.

concepts.statement: Professional navigation starts as a semantic **unordered list of anchors** inside a `nav` landmark, then CSS removes bullets, lays items out with **flexbox**, and styles the **current page** with `aria-current="page"` rather than a presentational class. Spacing comes from `gap`, padding on the anchors enlarges the tap target to at least forty four pixels, and `:hover`, `:focus-visible` and the current-page style give three distinguishable states. This structure degrades to a clean vertical list with no CSS and announces itself correctly to screen readers.
concepts.detail: Mark the active link with `aria-current="page"` so assistive technology announces it, then hook the visual treatment to the selector `[aria-current="page"]` to keep state and style in one source of truth.

keyTakeaways: Use ::marker for simple bullet styling and CSS counters for bespoke numbering.
Write link states in LVHA order — :link, :visited, :hover, :active — or hover feedback breaks.
Control underlines with thickness, offset and skip-ink instead of border hacks.
Build navigation as a ul of anchors in a nav landmark with aria-current on the active link.
Pair :hover with :focus-visible so mouse and keyboard users each get correct feedback.

quiz.q: What breaks if you write a:hover before a:link and a:visited at equal specificity?
options: The :link and :visited rules override :hover, killing hover feedback
quiz.explanation: Equal-specificity rules resolve by source order, so LVHA puts hover after link and visited precisely so hover wins while pointing.

quiz.q: Which approach recolors every bullet without disturbing item alignment?
quiz.explanation: The ::marker pseudo-element targets the marker glyph alone, leaving item text color and the hanging outside alignment untouched.

quiz.q: Why prefer text-underline-offset over a border-bottom underline?
options: Text decorations wrap across line breaks and follow text direction automatically
quiz.explanation: Decoration underlines are part of text layout so they fragment across wrapped lines and rtl text correctly, while a bottom border is a single box edge.

quiz.q: How should the current page be marked in a list-based nav?
options: With a bold class and nothing else
With aria-current="page" on the anchor, styled via an attribute selector
By removing the anchor and using plain text
With a title attribute on the nav
quiz.explanation: The aria-current attribute announces the active page to screen readers, and hooking styles to the same attribute keeps the announced and visual states synchronized.

intro: Custom properties — the feature universally called CSS variables — turn scattered magic values into a named design-token system that cascades, inherits and can be rewritten at runtime. This section covers declaring tokens, how scoping and the cascade shape them, fallback values that keep components resilient, theme switching with dark mode, and live updates from JavaScript.
objectives: Declare --tokens on :root and consume them with var()
Predict variable values through scoping, inheritance and cascade
Write fallbacks including nested var() chains for resilient components
Switch themes with data attributes and update tokens from JavaScript

concepts.statement: A **custom property** is any property whose name begins with a double dash, such as `--brand: #4f46e5;`, and it is consumed with the **`var()`** function as in `color: var(--brand)`. Tokens are conventionally declared on **`:root`** so every element inherits them, with names grouped by role — `--color-brand`, `--space-md`, `--radius-lg` — forming a design-token dictionary. Unlike preprocessor variables, custom properties are live cascade participants that DevTools can inspect and override per element.
concepts.detail: Name tokens by purpose rather than value, so `--color-danger` survives a rebrand while `--red` becomes a lie the moment the palette changes.

concepts.statement: Custom properties **inherit** like ordinary properties and obey the **cascade**, so a `--brand` set on `:root` flows everywhere until a nearer rule overrides it for its subtree. Redefining the token inside `.card { --brand: #0ea5e9; }` recolors only that card and its descendants, which makes scoped theming a one-line override instead of a selector rewrite. Specificity, order and origin resolve competing definitions exactly as they do for `color` or `margin`, because variables are properties first and values second.
concepts.detail: Scope overrides to the smallest subtree that needs them so a component theme never leaks sideways into unrelated siblings.

concepts.statement: The **fallback** second argument of `var()` supplies a safety net: `color: var(--brand, #4f46e5)` renders the hex value whenever `--brand` is undefined or invalid. Fallbacks **nest**, so `color: var(--button-bg, var(--brand, #4f46e5))` walks a preference chain from component token to global brand to hard default. This pattern lets shared components ship working defaults while pages opt into narrower tokens only where they define them.
concepts.detail: Treat every consumed token in a reusable component as optional-with-fallback so the component renders sensibly even in pages that define none of its variables.

concepts.term: Theming with data attributes and media queries
concepts.statement: Theme switching means **redefining the same tokens** under a different selector, typically `[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: #0f172a; --ink: #e2e8f0; }` toggled by one attribute on `html`, with components referencing only the tokens. The **`prefers-color-scheme`** media query seeds the initial theme from the operating system, while the explicit attribute lets the user override it and persist the choice. Because only token definitions change, every component repaints consistently with no per-component dark rules.
concepts.detail: Combine both signals by defaulting the attribute from the media query in a tiny startup script, then honoring stored user choice over the system preference thereafter.

concepts.statement: JavaScript reads and writes tokens through **`setProperty`** and **`getComputedStyle`**, as in `root.style.setProperty("--brand", "#7c3aed")`, which repaints every consumer instantly without touching individual elements. This powers live theme pickers, density toggles and animation parameters driven by scroll or pointer position. The complementary **`@property`** rule registers a token with a syntax, initial value and inheritance flag, unlocking type-checked transitions and animations of variables that plain unregistered tokens cannot interpolate.
concepts.detail: Set tokens on the narrowest ancestor that needs the change and prefer `@property` registration when animating a variable, since registered types interpolate smoothly instead of flipping discretely.

examples.title: Drive tokens live from JavaScript
examples.problem: Add a settings panel where a color input recolors the brand everywhere and a density toggle compacts spacing — with choices persisted across visits.

steps.label: Step 1: Markup with controls
steps.text:
```html
<label>Brand <input type="color" id="brandPicker" value="#4f46e5"></label>
<button id="themeToggle">Toggle dark mode</button>
```
Two controls cover the requirements: a native color input for the brand and a button flipping the theme attribute.

steps.label: Step 2: Update tokens and persist
Step 3: Seed from the operating system

examples.result: Brand and theme become runtime state: instant repaints from token writes, OS-aware defaults, and user choices that survive reloads.

keyTakeaways: Declare --tokens on :root and consume them with var() for a single source of truth.
Variables inherit and cascade, so scoped redefinitions theme subtrees with one rule.
Give components nested var() fallbacks so they render without every token defined.
Theme by redefining tokens under [data-theme] seeded from prefers-color-scheme.
Update tokens from JS with setProperty and register animatable tokens with @property.

quiz.q: What does color: var(--brand, #4f46e5) do when --brand is undefined?
options: The declaration is dropped as invalid
It inherits --brand from the parent anyway
quiz.explanation: The second var() argument is a fallback used whenever the named custom property is missing or invalid at the point of use.

quiz.q: Why does redefining --brand inside .card recolor only that card?
options: Custom properties are scoped to the stylesheet that defines them
They inherit and cascade, so the nearer definition wins for that subtree
The card creates a new stacking context
quiz.explanation: Variables are ordinary cascading properties: the .card definition overrides :root for descendants of the card while the rest of the page keeps the root value.

quiz.q: What is the cleanest dark-mode architecture with custom properties?
options: Duplicate every component rule inside a dark media query
Redefine the same tokens under [data-theme="dark"] so all consumers repaint
Swap stylesheets with JavaScript per component
quiz.explanation: Since components reference tokens rather than literal colors, redefining the token set once repaints everything consistently with no per-component dark rules.

quiz.q: What does root.style.setProperty("--brand", value) accomplish?
options: It edits the CSS file on disk
It updates the live token so every var(--brand) consumer repaints instantly
It only affects the next created element
It registers the property for animation
quiz.explanation: Inline custom property values on the root cascade to all inheriting consumers, so one write repaints the whole design; registration for animation is the separate @property job.

quiz.q: A theme system defines `:root { --brand: teal; }` while a dark panel overrides `--brand: amber` on its own class. A button inside the panel uses `color: var(--brand, teal);`. Which color shows, and what is the fallback for?
options: Teal: the `:root` value always wins everywhere
Teal: the declared fallback overrides the cascade
Amber: the closer custom-property value wins through the cascade, and the fallback applies only when `--brand` is undefined
Nothing renders: variables cannot change per subtree
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is a global token, a subtree override, and a use site with a fallback. Step 2: The governing rules are that custom properties cascade and inherit like ordinary properties so the closest definition wins, and that the `var()` fallback applies only when the variable is undefined or guaranteed-invalid. Step 3: Tracing the button, `--brand` resolves through the panel override to amber since that definition is nearer than `:root`, the fallback is ignored because the variable is defined, and the text renders amber. Step 4: The distractors fail because `:root` loses to nearer definitions, fallbacks never override live values, and per-subtree tokens are the entire point of the feature. Step 5: Therefore the panel override wins and the fallback stays dormant.

intro: System fonts are instant but generic; web fonts give a site its typographic identity at the cost of downloads that can block rendering and shift layout. This section makes web fonts production-safe: declaring faces with @font-face, choosing display strategies, preloading critical cuts, adopting variable fonts, and neutralizing the layout shift that font swaps cause.
objectives: Declare web fonts with @font-face, src formats and descriptors
Choose font-display strategies for the right blocking tradeoff
Preload critical cuts and connect early to font origins
Contain layout shift with fallbacks, metrics overrides and variable fonts

concepts.statement: The **`@font-face`** rule registers a family name with one or more **`src`** files plus descriptors — **`font-weight`**, **`font-style`**, **`font-stretch`** and **`unicode-range`** — that tell the browser exactly which characters and cuts each file covers. A modern declaration lists **`woff2`** first with a `format("woff2")` hint and keeps older formats only where legacy support demands them. Splitting by weight and by `unicode-range` subsets lets pages download just the Latin cut they need instead of the entire world’s glyphs.
concepts.detail: Serve fonts from your own origin when possible so caching, subsetting and cache lifetimes stay under your control rather than a third party’s.

concepts.statement: The **`font-display`** descriptor controls the render-blocking tradeoff during download: **`swap`** paints fallback text immediately then swaps when the face arrives, **`fallback`** allows only a brief swap window, and **`optional`** uses the web font solely when already cached. Body copy almost always wants **`swap`** so content is never invisible, while decorative display faces can accept `fallback` or `optional` to avoid a jarring late swap. The dreaded invisible-text flash comes from the default blocking behavior that `swap` explicitly disables.
concepts.detail: Pair `swap` with a well-matched fallback stack so the interim render already resembles the final design and the swap feels like a refinement rather than a jump.

concepts.statement: The **`preload`** resource hint with `as="font"`, `type="font/woff2"` and `crossorigin` tells the browser to fetch the critical roman cut before CSS parsing discovers it, shaving a full round trip off first paint. A companion **`preconnect`** to the font origin warms up DNS, TLS and congestion state so the fetch starts without handshake delay. Preload at most one or two cuts — the above-the-fold roman and perhaps its bold — because every preloaded file competes with hero images and scripts for early bandwidth.
concepts.detail: Always include the `crossorigin` attribute on font preloads since fonts fetch anonymously by default, and a mismatched CORS mode double-downloads the file.

concepts.statement: A **variable font** packs an entire design space — weight, width, slant, optical size — into one file addressed by axes such as **`wght`** and **`wdth`**, requested with `font-weight: 100 900` ranges in `@font-face` and tuned per element or animated smoothly. One variable file replaces a dozen static cuts, collapsing both transfer size and request count while enabling fluid weight animation impossible with discrete files. Fine control comes from **`font-variation-settings`**, though standard properties like `font-weight` should carry everyday styling so the cascade keeps working.
concepts.detail: Prefer the standard `font-weight` and `font-stretch` properties over raw `font-variation-settings` for ordinary styling, reserving the low-level setting for axes with no CSS property mapping.

concepts.statement: Swapping faces shifts layout whenever the fallback and web font disagree on **metrics**, so production setups harmonize them with **`size-adjust`**, **`ascent-override`** and **`descent-override`** in a fallback `@font-face` that reshapes the system face to the web font’s box. Google Fonts’ `display=swap` URLs plus a metric-matched fallback stack keep **Cumulative Layout Shift** near zero even on slow connections. Always declare explicit `width` and `height` or aspect boxes around font-dependent hero areas so the swap refines glyphs without moving surrounding content.
concepts.detail: Generate the override percentages from the two faces’ published metrics and verify with Lighthouse CLS audits on throttled connections, since eyeballing on fast office wifi hides the shift real users feel.

examples.title: Ship Inter with swap and a metric-matched fallback
examples.problem: A marketing page wants the Inter typeface for headings and body with no invisible text, fast first paint, and negligible layout shift on swap.

Step 2: Preload the critical cut
steps.text:
```html
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.example.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" as="font" type="font/woff2" href="/fonts/inter-latin-400.woff2" crossorigin>
```
Preconnect warms the origin and preload fetches the roman cut early, since body copy renders before any bold headline matters.

steps.label: Step 3: Metric-matched fallback stack

examples.result: Text paints immediately in a metrically compatible fallback, Inter swaps in with near-zero shift, and only two subset files ever download.

examples.title: Adopt one variable font for the whole scale
examples.problem: A dashboard ships six static weights of a grotesque face; replace them with a single variable file that still styles through normal font-weight declarations.

Step 2: Style with standard properties

examples.result: Six downloads collapse to one, arbitrary grades become available, and weight itself turns into an animatable design dimension.

keyTakeaways: Declare faces with @font-face, woff2 first, split by weight and unicode-range.
Use font-display: swap for body copy so text never sits invisible.
Preload only the critical roman cut with crossorigin, plus preconnect.
Prefer one variable font over many static cuts for size and fluid grades.
Neutralize swap shift with metric-matched fallbacks using size-adjust and overrides.

quiz.q: What does font-display: swap guarantee during font download?
options: The browser waits for the font before painting any text
Fallback text paints immediately and swaps when the face arrives
The font downloads with highest network priority
quiz.explanation: Swap sets a zero block period: text renders in the fallback face at once, then upgrades to the web font on arrival instead of hiding.

quiz.q: Why must font preload links carry the crossorigin attribute?
options: Fonts fetch with anonymous CORS mode, and a mismatch double-downloads the file
It restricts the font to one page
quiz.explanation: Font fetches use CORS anonymous mode; a preload without matching crossorigin creates a separate cache entry and the file downloads twice.

quiz.q: What is the main delivery advantage of a variable font?
options: One file covers continuous weight and width ranges, replacing many static cuts
quiz.explanation: Axes like wght address the whole design space from one resource, collapsing request count and bytes while enabling intermediate grades.

quiz.q: How do size-adjust and ascent-override reduce layout shift?
options: They delay the swap until idle time
They reshape the fallback face’s metrics to match the web font so lines keep their boxes
They subset the font to fewer glyphs
quiz.explanation: Harmonizing the fallback box with the web font’s metrics means the swap changes glyph shapes without reflowing line breaks or container heights.

intro: Form controls are the least cooperative citizens of CSS: inputs, selects, checkboxes and buttons arrive with heavy native chrome, ignore inherited fonts, and vary by operating system. This section tames them — forcing font inheritance, designing visible focus rings, styling placeholders, and building buttons and inputs that look identical in every modern browser.
objectives: Force font, color and sizing inheritance into native controls
Design :focus-visible rings that survive brand styling
Style placeholders, labels and validation states accessibly
Normalize buttons, inputs and selects to one visual language

concepts.statement: Form elements do **not** inherit typography by default: `button`, `input`, `select` and `textarea` render in the operating system’s widget font unless told otherwise. The one-line reset `font: inherit` — or the trio `font-family: inherit; font-size: 100%; line-height: inherit` — forces controls to adopt the page’s type, and `color: inherit` extends the treatment to text color. Skipping this step leaves mismatched micro-type where every label says the brand face but every field speaks the OS default.
concepts.detail: Apply the inheritance reset globally to all four control families at the top of the stylesheet so no dynamically injected field ever escapes it.

concepts.statement: The **`:focus-visible`** pseudo-class shows a focus indicator exactly when keyboard or assistive-technology users need one, staying hidden for mouse clicks that already carry positional context. A robust ring pairs **`outline`** with **`outline-offset`**, as in `outline: 3px solid #4f46e5; outline-offset: 2px`, so the indicator clears the element edge at any contrast ratio. Never remove outlines without supplying an equivalent, because `outline: none` with no replacement strands keyboard users with zero orientation.
concepts.detail: Test every ring by tabbing through the form with the mouse untouched, and verify the ring survives Windows High Contrast and forced-colors modes.

concepts.statement: The **`::placeholder`** pseudo-element styles hint text inside empty fields — `color`, `opacity` and `font-size` — but placeholders must never replace **labels**, since hint text vanishes on input and many browsers render it at low contrast. Every control needs a real **`label`** element bound by `for` and `id`, with placeholders reserved for short format examples like a date pattern. Keep placeholder contrast above the faint browser default and disable the temptation to stuff instructions solely into disappearing text.
concepts.detail: Pair each placeholder example with a persistent label and, where format matters, an `aria-describedby` hint so screen readers announce the requirement without depending on vanishing text.

concepts.statement: Consistent controls start by neutralizing native chrome with **`appearance: none`** where appropriate, then rebuilding with explicit `padding`, `border`, `border-radius`, `background` and a shared height scale. Unifying `border-width`, focus, hover, disabled and invalid states across `input`, `select`, `textarea` and `button` produces one visual language instead of four OS dialects. The **`accent-color`** property then tints checkboxes, radios, ranges and progress bars to the brand with a single declaration, sparing custom-drawn replacements for most designs.
concepts.detail: Define one control height scale and one border treatment as tokens, then compose every control from them so sizing and state feedback stay synchronized.

concepts.term: Validation states that help, not punish
concepts.statement: Helpful validation styles **`:invalid`** and **`:valid`** only after interaction — combining them with `:user-invalid` or a `.touched` class — so pristine fields are not painted red on page load. Pair the border treatment with an **inline message** element referenced by `aria-describedby`, using `aria-invalid="true"` for programmatic state, because color alone excludes color-blind users. Success styling should whisper while error styling speaks clearly, with icons plus text rather than hue as the carrier of meaning.
concepts.detail: Delay error visuals until blur or submit so users are guided rather than scolded, and always announce errors in text that persists beside the field.

keyTakeaways: Apply font: inherit to buttons, inputs, selects and textareas or type will mismatch.
Show strong :focus-visible rings with outline plus offset; never remove outlines bare.
Use real labels for every control; keep placeholders as short format examples.
Normalize controls with shared padding, borders and accent-color for one language.

quiz.q: Why do form controls need an explicit font: inherit rule?
options: They cannot display web fonts otherwise
They default to the OS widget font instead of inheriting page typography
Inheritance is disabled in forms by the HTML parser
quiz.explanation: Buttons, inputs, selects and textareas start in the operating system widget face, so only an explicit inheritance rule brings them into the page type system.

quiz.q: What is the key advantage of :focus-visible over :focus for rings?
options: It shows the indicator for keyboard users while staying quiet for mouse clicks
quiz.explanation: The :focus-visible heuristic matches focus that needs a visible indicator — typically keyboard and assistive-tech interaction — avoiding redundant rings on mouse clicks.

quiz.q: What is wrong with using a placeholder as the only label?
options: Hint text disappears on input and often fails contrast, leaving the field unlabeled
quiz.explanation: Vanishing hint text plus low-contrast defaults strand both memory and screen-reader users; a persistent label element is the accessible name.

quiz.q: How should :invalid styling avoid punishing users on page load?
options: Style :invalid only after interaction via :user-invalid or a touched class
quiz.explanation: Gating error paint behind interaction keeps pristine fields neutral, so red appears as guidance after real input rather than a scolding on arrival.

intro: Every CSS layout scheme is an answer to one question: where does this box go when nobody tells it otherwise. This section starts from normal flow and the display types that shape it, detours through floats and their modern replacements, then masters the five positioning schemes — the toolkit behind dropdowns, modals, sticky headers and every overlay on the web.
objectives: Describe normal flow and choose block, inline and inline-block display
Contain floats with clear and modern flow-root clearing
Position elements with relative, absolute, fixed and sticky schemes
Manage overlap with containing blocks, z-index and stacking contexts

concepts.statement: In **normal flow**, block boxes stack vertically and fill their container width while **inline** boxes run with the text line, wrapping where it wraps. The **`display`** property moves elements between these worlds: `block` for sections and paragraphs, `inline` for runs within lines, and **`inline-block`** for boxes that size like blocks yet sit in the line, such as buttons or badges. Modern layouts layer flex and grid on top of flow rather than replacing it, so paragraphs, headings and form stacks still rely on these defaults.
concepts.detail: Reach for `inline-block` when an element needs width, height and vertical padding but must stay in the text line, like a pill badge inside a sentence.

concepts.statement: The **`float`** property pulls an element to the `left` or `right`, letting following text wrap around it — the original mechanism behind magazine-style image wraps and the earliest column grids. Floated elements leave normal flow, so containers collapse around them unless **cleared** with `clear: both` or contained with the modern **`display: flow-root`**, which establishes a fresh block formatting context. The classic **clearfix** hack with a clearing `::after` pseudo-element solved the same collapse before `flow-root` made one declaration sufficient.
concepts.detail: Reserve floats for text wrap and legacy maintenance today, since flexbox and grid build columns with alignment, ordering and equal heights that floats never offered.

concepts.statement: Setting **`position: relative`** offsets a box from its flow position with `top`, `right`, `bottom` and `left` while preserving its original footprint in the layout. The companion **`position: absolute`** removes the box from flow entirely and anchors it to its nearest **positioned ancestor** — the closest parent with any non-static position — which is why patterns pair `position: relative` on the card with `absolute` on its badge. Without a positioned ancestor, absolute offsets resolve against the initial containing block, effectively the viewport-sized page area.
concepts.detail: Give the intended anchor `position: relative` with no offsets to create a positioning context that moves nothing yet contains every absolute child.

concepts.statement: **Fixed** positioning anchors an element to the **viewport**, so headers, chat buttons and modal backdrops stay put while the page scrolls beneath them. **Sticky** positioning is the hybrid: `position: sticky` with a `top` threshold behaves like relative until the scroll position reaches the offset, then sticks like fixed within its parent’s bounds and releases at the parent edge. Sticky table headers and section navs use this clamping naturally, but any ancestor with `overflow: hidden` or a transform clips the stick range and silently disables the effect.
concepts.detail: Pair sticky elements with a `top` value plus a background and `z-index` so content sliding underneath never shows through or overlaps the stuck bar.

concepts.term: Containing blocks, z-index and stacking contexts
concepts.statement: An absolutely positioned box resolves its offsets against its **containing block**, and the **`z-index`** property orders overlapping positioned boxes along the depth axis, with larger values painting above smaller ones. Crucially, several properties — `opacity` below one, `transform`, `filter`, `isolation: isolate` — spawn new **stacking contexts** that trap descendants’ `z-index` values inside, so a huge `z-index` inside one context can never escape above a sibling context. The fix is structural: order the contexts themselves and keep modal layers as high-level siblings rather than nesting them inside transformed cards.
concepts.detail: When a `z-index` value seems ignored, inspect ancestors for stacking-context creators first, since the trap almost always sits one level above the element being raised.

keyTakeaways: Normal flow stacks blocks and runs inlines; display moves boxes between behaviors.
Contain floats with display: flow-root and prefer flex or grid for columns.
Anchor absolute children by giving the intended parent position: relative.
Use sticky for in-flow clamping and fixed for viewport-pinned chrome.
Order stacking contexts, not just z-index values, when overlap misbehaves.

quiz.q: What does display: flow-root do for a container with floated children?
options: It removes the floats from the page
It creates a block formatting context that contains the floats so the parent wraps them
It converts floats to flex items
quiz.explanation: The new formatting context forces the container to account for floated descendants, curing the classic collapsed-parent without clearfix markup.

quiz.q: An absolutely positioned badge lands relative to the page instead of its card. What is missing?
options: The badge needs a higher z-index
The card needs a non-static position such as relative to become the containing block
quiz.explanation: Absolute offsets resolve against the nearest positioned ancestor, so the card must establish that context with relative or another non-static scheme.

quiz.q: When does position: sticky actually stick?
options: After its scroll position reaches the declared offset, until its parent edge releases it
Only with a z-index above one hundred
quiz.explanation: Sticky behaves as relative until the threshold offset meets the scroll position, then clamps like fixed within the parent bounds.

quiz.q: A child with z-index 9999 still paints below a sibling card. What is the likely cause?
options: z-index values above one thousand are invalid
An ancestor created a stacking context that traps the child below the sibling context
z-index only works on flex items
quiz.explanation: Properties like opacity, transform and filter spawn contexts that confine descendants, so ordering must be fixed at the context level.

intro: Flexbox is the one-dimensional layout engine: a row or a column of items that distribute space, align and wrap with a handful of declarations. This section covers the container-versus-item split, the main and cross axes that explain every alignment property, wrapping, the flex sizing shorthand, and the ordering and gap patterns behind navbars, card rows and centered heroes.
objectives: Distinguish flex container properties from flex item properties
Explain main-axis versus cross-axis alignment choices
Size items with flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis and the shorthand
Build navbars, centered heroes and wrapping card rows

concepts.term: Flex containers and the two axes
concepts.statement: Declaring **`display: flex`** turns an element into a **flex container** whose children become **flex items** laid along the **main axis** with the **cross axis** perpendicular to it. The **`flex-direction`** property aims the main axis — `row`, `row-reverse`, `column` or `column-reverse` — which simultaneously decides the cross direction, so every alignment choice flows from this one setting. Row layouts align horizontally first and vertically second, while column layouts invert that priority entirely.
concepts.detail: Sketch the two axes before writing alignment code, since naming the main direction first makes every subsequent property choice obvious.

concepts.statement: The **`flex-wrap`** property decides whether items squeeze onto one line with `nowrap` or spill onto multiple lines with `wrap` and `wrap-reverse`, and the **`flex-flow`** shorthand bundles direction plus wrap as in `flex-flow: row wrap`. Wrapping converts a flex row into a responsive grid-like band that needs no media queries, with each line then aligned independently. Combined with flexible bases, wrap gives card rows that collapse gracefully from four columns to one.
concepts.detail: Default to `flex-flow: row wrap` for card collections so overflow becomes a new aligned row instead of a clipped or squished line.

concepts.statement: **`justify-content`** distributes space along the **main axis** with `flex-start`, `center`, `flex-end`, `space-between`, `space-around` and `space-evenly`, while **`align-items`** positions items along the **cross axis** with `stretch`, `center`, `flex-start` and `baseline`. The companion **`align-content`** only matters across multiple wrapped lines, spacing the rows themselves. Centering both axes — `justify-content: center; align-items: center` — is the canonical flexbox centering recipe for heroes and empty states.
concepts.detail: Remember the axis mapping, not the physical direction: justify always works the main axis, so in a column layout it centers vertically.

concepts.term: Growing, shrinking and the flex shorthand
concepts.statement: Three properties size each item: **`flex-grow`** claims shares of free space, **`flex-shrink`** surrenders shares when space runs short, and **`flex-basis`** sets the starting size before distribution. The **`flex`** shorthand bundles them — `flex: 1` means grow fully from a zero base, `flex: 0 0 12rem` fixes an item at twelve rems, and `flex: auto` grows from content size. Misunderstood shrink is the classic overflow culprit: long unbreakable content with `flex-shrink: 0` forces its siblings off the line.
concepts.detail: Allow text items to shrink and add `min-width: 0` so long words and nested elements can actually compress instead of bursting the row.

concepts.statement: The **`order`** property reorders items visually without touching source order, **`align-self`** overrides cross-axis alignment per item, and **`gap`** injects uniform gutters that margins never managed cleanly. Together they express the standard patterns: space-between navbars, vertically centered media objects, and equal-height cards with bottom-pinned actions via `margin-top: auto`. Keep `order` cosmetic only, because screen readers and tab order still follow the source sequence.
concepts.detail: Use `gap` for all inter-item spacing and reserve margins for alignment tricks like auto margins that push one item to the far edge.

Use flex-flow: row wrap plus flexible bases for self-responsive rows.
Pin card footers with margin-top: auto inside column-direction cards.

quiz.q: In a column-direction flex container, what does justify-content: center do?
options: Centers items vertically along the column main axis
Stretches items to fill the container
quiz.explanation: Flex direction aims the main axis, so in column mode justify-content distributes vertical space while align-items handles the horizontal cross axis.

quiz.q: What does flex: 1 1 16rem declare?
options: Fixed sixteen-rem width with no flexibility
Grow and shrink shares of one from a sixteen-rem starting basis
Order sixteen with one line of wrap
quiz.explanation: The three values are grow, shrink and basis: the item starts at sixteen rems, claims free space and surrenders space equally with siblings.

quiz.q: How do you pin a button to the bottom of variable-height flex cards?
options: Make each card a column flex container and give the button margin-top: auto
Add align-content: flex-end to the grid
quiz.explanation: Auto margins absorb free space in the flex direction, so an auto top margin inside a column card shoves the action to the base.

quiz.q: Why should order be used only for cosmetic reordering?
options: Screen readers and keyboard tab order still follow source order
quiz.explanation: Order changes paint position alone, so visual order that contradicts source order confuses assistive technology and keyboard users.

quiz.q: A dialog must center horizontally and vertically inside its row-direction overlay, and one child should absorb leftover horizontal space. Which declaration set does it?
options: `display: flex; flex-direction: column; justify-content: center;` on the overlay
`display: flex; align-items: stretch;` on the child alone
`display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;` on the overlay plus `flex: 1;` on the growing child
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The data given is a row-direction flex container needing two-axis centering plus one expanding child. Step 2: The governing rules are axis mapping in row mode, `justify-content` placing along the horizontal main axis and `align-items` along the vertical cross axis, with `flex: 1` letting a child absorb free main-axis space. Step 3: Applying the set, the overlay centers the dialog on both axes while the flagged child grows to consume leftover width without disturbing the centering of the rest. Step 4: The distractors fail because a column switch redefines the axes, stretch alone centers nothing, and no `float: center` value exists. Step 5: Therefore the two-axis centering plus growth set is the correct one.

intro: Where flexbox lays out in one dimension, grid commands two: rows and columns together, with explicit placement, named areas and overlapping layers. This section builds the full grid model — tracks, lines and areas, explicit versus implicit grids, placement and spanning, and the judgment call of when grid rather than flexbox is the right instrument.
objectives: Define tracks with fr, repeat and minmax for fluid two-dimensional layouts
Place items with lines, spans and named grid areas
Control implicit rows and dense auto-placement for dynamic content
Choose grid versus flexbox for any layout task

concepts.term: Tracks, fr units and repeat with minmax
concepts.statement: A grid **track** is one row or column defined in **`grid-template-columns`** and **`grid-template-rows`**, and the **`fr`** unit apportions leftover space as fractions after fixed tracks are satisfied. The **`repeat()`** function stamps recurring patterns such as `repeat(12, 1fr)`, while **`minmax()`** bounds each track between a floor and ceiling like `minmax(12rem, 1fr)`. Together, `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(14rem, 1fr))` yields a self-responsive card grid that needs no media queries at all.
concepts.detail: Size flexible tracks with `fr` and guard content tracks with `minmax()` so long words narrow the track to a floor instead of bursting the grid.

concepts.statement: **Grid lines** are the numbered boundaries between tracks, and items attach to them with **`grid-column`** and **`grid-row`** using start and end lines or the **`span`** keyword. A declaration like `grid-column: 1 / span 8` starts at line one and covers eight tracks, while `grid-column: 1 / -1` stretches full-bleed from first to last line. Explicit placement overrides automatic flow exactly where the design needs a hero to span or a sidebar to dock.
concepts.detail: Prefer `span` for component widths and negative `-1` for full-bleed bands so layouts survive column-count changes without renumbering.

concepts.statement: The **`grid-template-areas`** property draws the layout as ASCII art — `"header header" "sidebar main" "footer footer"` — and items dock into it with **`grid-area`** names, making page skeletons readable at a glance. Retargeting the same names inside a media query rearranges the whole page by rewriting the drawing rather than touching item rules. Areas also document intent: a glance at the template reveals the design in a way line numbers never do.
concepts.detail: Keep area names semantic like main and sidebar so the template reads as the page outline and restacks by editing strings alone.

concepts.term: Explicit versus implicit grids and auto flow
concepts.statement: The **explicit grid** is what templates declare; any items beyond it spawn the **implicit grid**, whose track sizes come from **`grid-auto-rows`**, **`grid-auto-columns`** and **`grid-auto-flow`**. Setting `grid-auto-rows: minmax(8rem, auto)` keeps dynamically added cards uniform, while `grid-auto-flow: dense` backfills holes left by spanning items at the cost of visual-versus-source order gaps. Understanding this split explains why extra items sometimes size unexpectedly — they live in implicit territory.
concepts.detail: Always declare `grid-auto-rows` on dynamic grids so user-added or CMS-fed items inherit designed sizing instead of content-height accidents.

concepts.statement: The decision rule is dimensional: **grid** aligns content along **two axes at once** — page skeletons, card matrices, overlapping hero layers declared with `grid-template-columns` — while **flexbox** distributes along **one axis** — navbars, button rows, centered stacks. Grid controls the container’s columns and rows from the parent; flexbox lets items negotiate space along a line. Real pages compose both: grid frames the regions, flexbox arranges the furniture inside each region.
concepts.detail: When items must line up in both directions at once, choose grid; when they flow in one direction with wrapping, choose flexbox.

Place with lines and span; stretch full-bleed with 1 / -1.

Choose grid for two-axis alignment, flexbox for one-axis flow.

quiz.q: What does repeat(auto-fill, minmax(14rem, 1fr)) accomplish?
options: As many fourteen-rem-minimum columns as fit, sharing leftover space equally
Fourteen rows of one fraction each
quiz.explanation: Auto-fill stamps columns until the container fills, minmax floors each at fourteen rems, and fr stretches survivors across remaining space.

quiz.q: How does grid-column: 1 / -1 behave?
options: It spans from the first line to the last, going full-bleed across columns
It moves the item to row minus one
quiz.explanation: Negative line indexes count back from the explicit grid end, so -1 always means the final boundary regardless of column count.

quiz.q: Why restack layouts by rewriting grid-template-areas in a media query?
options: Item rules stay untouched since docking is by name, so the whole page rearranges by editing the drawing
quiz.explanation: Because items attach via grid-area names, redefining the area strings alone repositions everything without per-item overrides.

quiz.q: When is grid the right choice over flexbox?
options: For a single row of buttons
When items must align along rows and columns simultaneously
For vertical centering of one element
quiz.explanation: Two-axis alignment — shared columns plus shared rows, overlap, spanning — is grid territory; one-directional distribution belongs to flexbox.

quiz.q: A layout needs a header spanning two columns with a sidebar and content row below it. Which grid code expresses that?
options: Three nested flex rows with fixed pixel widths
`grid-template-areas: 'head head' 'side main';` with each child assigned its area, so the header spans both tracks
`grid-template-columns: 1fr;` with all children stacked in one track
Absolute positioning with hard-coded offsets for every box

Step 2: The governing rules are named areas: each quoted string is a row, each name is a cell, repeating a name spans tracks, and children claim cells through their assigned area. Step 3: Tracing the declaration, `head head` stretches the header across both columns while `side main` splits the row below, and each child lands by name without any line arithmetic. Step 4: The distractors fail because fixed pixels cannot share leftover space, a single track cannot express two columns, and absolute offsets break flow and responsiveness. Step 5: Therefore the named-areas declaration with a repeated header name is the correct expression.

intro: Responsive design is the discipline of one codebase serving every screen, from a watch-wide viewport to an ultrawide monitor. This section builds the mobile-first workflow: fluid foundations that need no queries, min-width breakpoints that enhance upward, container queries that let components respond to their own box, and responsive images that serve the right pixels to each device.
objectives: Build fluid foundations with percentages, max-width and clamp()
Write mobile-first media queries with min-width breakpoints
Scope responsive behavior with container queries
Serve right-sized images with srcset, sizes and picture

concepts.statement: The cheapest responsiveness needs no queries at all: **percentages** and **`max-width`** let content fill small screens and stop sprawling on large ones, while **`clamp()`** interpolates type and spacing fluidly between bounds. A container with `width: min(100%, 70rem)` plus grid or flex children that wrap covers most layouts before any breakpoint fires. Breakpoints should resolve genuine design stress, not substitute for a fluid base that never needed them.
concepts.detail: Exhaust fluid tools — flexible grids, wrapping, clamp and max-width caps — before adding the first media query, and many pages will need only a handful.

concepts.statement: In the **mobile-first** workflow, base styles target the smallest screen and **`min-width`** queries layer enhancements upward, as in `@media (min-width: 48rem)` unlocking two columns only where they fit. This keeps phones on the leanest CSS, guarantees content works without any query matching, and makes each breakpoint purely additive. Choosing breakpoints from **content stress** — where the design actually breaks — beats memorizing device widths that obsolesce every hardware cycle.
concepts.detail: Add a breakpoint exactly where the layout strains, name it by intent in a comment, and let device diversity fall wherever the content dictates.

concepts.statement: Classic **breakpoints** restack grids, reveal sidebars and scale type at widths like forty and sixty four rems, but modern queries also test **features** such as `orientation`, `prefers-color-scheme` and `prefers-reduced-motion`. The **range syntax** `@media (width >= 48rem)` reads as plain comparison and composes cleanly with `and` for bounded ranges. Feature queries adapt to user preference and device capability rather than raw size, which is the deeper half of responsiveness.
concepts.detail: Combine width ranges with preference features so layouts adapt to both the viewport and the human holding it.

concepts.statement: **Container queries** with `@container` let a component respond to its **own box** instead of the viewport, so the same card renders compact in a sidebar and expansive in main content from identical markup. Declaring `container-type: inline-size` on the wrapper establishes the query context, and `@container (min-width: 24rem)` restyles internals when that box — not the window — crosses the threshold. This finally decouples reusable components from page position, the limitation viewport queries could never escape.
concepts.detail: Establish containment on the component wrapper and write container rules for internal arrangement, keeping viewport queries for page-level skeleton changes.

concepts.term: Responsive images with srcset and picture
concepts.statement: The **`srcset`** attribute offers the browser multiple resolutions or widths of one image while **`sizes`** declares the rendered slot width, letting the engine pick the cheapest sufficient file for the viewport and pixel density. The **`picture`** element goes further, swapping art direction — a cropped portrait on phones versus a panorama on desktop — plus next-generation formats with built-in fallback sources. Without these, phones download desktop-sized hero images, the single largest mobile performance tax on image-heavy pages.
concepts.detail: Describe every content image with width-based srcset plus sizes, and reserve picture for art-direction swaps or format upgrades with built-in fallbacks.

keyTakeaways: Build fluid with percentages, max-width caps and clamp() before any query.
Write mobile-first CSS enhanced upward with min-width breakpoints at content stress.
Use range syntax and feature queries for preferences as well as widths.
Give reusable components container queries so slots, not viewports, drive them.
Describe images with srcset plus sizes and art-direct with picture.

quiz.q: What is the core mobile-first rule?
options: Write desktop styles first, then undo them for phones
Base styles target small screens; min-width queries add enhancements upward
Hide content on phones with display: none
quiz.explanation: Small-screen-first bases guarantee working content with no query matched, and min-width layers keep every breakpoint purely additive.

quiz.q: What problem do container queries solve that viewport queries cannot?
options: They let a component adapt to its own box so identical markup behaves correctly in different slots
quiz.explanation: Viewport queries see only the window, so a sidebar card and a main-column card look identical to them; container queries respond to each wrapper box.

quiz.q: What do srcset and sizes together let the browser do?
options: Pick the cheapest sufficient file for the rendered slot, viewport and density
quiz.explanation: Width descriptors enumerate candidates while sizes declares the slot, so the engine computes and fetches the optimal resource.

quiz.q: When should the picture element be used instead of a plain img with srcset?
options: When art direction differs per viewport, such as a portrait crop versus a panorama
quiz.explanation: Picture swaps whole sources by media condition, enabling different compositions per breakpoint rather than different resolutions of one composition.

intro: Layout ends where geometry begins: measuring boxes, understanding the viewport they live in, and choreographing scroll. This section covers the viewport meta tag and modern viewport units, coordinate systems with getBoundingClientRect, sticky and smooth scrolling, overflow patterns including scroll snap, and scroll-driven reveals with IntersectionObserver.
objectives: Configure the viewport meta tag and choose modern viewport units
Measure elements with getBoundingClientRect across coordinate systems
Build sticky, smooth and snap scrolling experiences
Reveal content on scroll with IntersectionObserver

concepts.statement: The **viewport meta tag** `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` tells mobile browsers to size the layout viewport to the device width instead of shrinking a desktop page into a zoomed-out miniature. CSS then sizes against it with **viewport units**: classic **`vw`** and **`vh`** plus the 2026-stable small, large and **dynamic** variants — **`svh`**, **`lvh`** and **`dvh`** — where `100dvh` tracks the visible height as mobile chrome shows and hides. Full-height heroes built on `100vh` strand content behind browser bars; `100dvh` follows the visible area instead.
concepts.detail: Ship the meta tag on every page and default full-height sections to `min-height: 100dvh` so mobile browser chrome never covers content.

concepts.statement: The **`getBoundingClientRect()`** method returns an element’s box as viewport-relative `top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left`, `width` and `height`, remeasured live on every call. These **client coordinates** differ from **page coordinates**, which add scroll offset, and from **`offsetTop`** chains that measure against positioned ancestors. Scroll math therefore pairs the rect with **`window.scrollY`** — as in `rect.top + window.scrollY` for document position — choosing the system that matches whether the goal is viewport visibility or document location.
concepts.detail: Call getBoundingClientRect at the moment of need inside scroll or click handlers, since cached rects go stale the instant anything scrolls or resizes.

concepts.term: Sticky, smooth scrolling and scroll margin
concepts.statement: **Sticky** section navs clamp within their parents while **`scroll-behavior: smooth`** animates anchor jumps instead of teleporting, and **`scroll-margin-top`** offsets landing positions so fixed headers never cover the target heading. Together they produce documentation-style navigation: clicking a table-of-contents link glides to the section with breathing room below the bar. Honor **`prefers-reduced-motion`** by disabling smooth scrolling for users who request minimal movement.
concepts.detail: Give every anchor target a `scroll-margin-top` matching the fixed header height plus a cushion so jumps land readable on the first try.

concepts.statement: The **`overflow`** property decides how boxes handle excess content — `visible`, `hidden`, `scroll`, `auto` and the per-axis `overflow-x` and `overflow-y` splits — with `auto` showing scrollbars only when needed. **Scroll snap** with **`scroll-snap-type`** on the scroller plus **`scroll-snap-align`** on children magnetizes carousels and full-screen decks to clean stopping points. Horizontal snap carousels with `scroll-snap-type: x mandatory` deliver app-like paging with zero JavaScript.
concepts.detail: Prefer `overflow: auto` over `scroll` so scrollbars appear only when content actually overflows, avoiding permanently disabled chrome.

concepts.statement: The **`IntersectionObserver`** API fires callbacks when elements cross viewport thresholds, enabling scroll reveals, lazy image swaps and infinite lists without scroll-event math on the main thread. Observing sections with a modest threshold and unobserving after the first reveal runs entrance animations exactly once at minimal cost. Unlike scroll listeners that compute geometry every frame, the observer lets the browser batch visibility work off the critical path.
concepts.detail: Unobserve each target after its reveal and choose thresholds near one quarter visible so animations trigger while content is still entering.

The meta tag establishes the mobile layout viewport while sticky keeps the index clamped beside the scrolling article.

Measure with getBoundingClientRect and convert with scroll offsets deliberately.
Combine sticky, smooth scroll and scroll-margin for polished anchor navigation.
Use overflow: auto plus scroll snap for native-feeling carousels.

quiz.q: Why does a mobile page render as a shrunken desktop miniature?
options: The viewport meta tag is missing, so the layout viewport stays at desktop width
quiz.explanation: Without width=device-width the mobile browser lays out near desktop width and scales down; the meta tag aligns the layout viewport to the device.

quiz.q: What coordinates does getBoundingClientRect() return?
options: Viewport-relative client coordinates remeasured on each call
Offsets against the nearest positioned ancestor
quiz.explanation: The rect describes the box against the current viewport, so adding window.scrollY converts to document position and cached values stale on scroll.

quiz.q: Why pair scroll-behavior: smooth with scroll-margin-top on targets?
options: The margin offsets landings so fixed headers do not cover the jumped-to heading
Smooth scrolling requires margins by spec
quiz.explanation: Smooth animates the journey while scroll-margin reserves space at the destination, clearing sticky or fixed chrome above the target.

quiz.q: What is the main performance advantage of IntersectionObserver over scroll listeners?
options: The browser batches visibility checks off the critical path instead of running geometry math per scroll event
quiz.explanation: Observers delegate intersection computation to the browser runtime, avoiding per-frame rect math and layout thrash in main-thread handlers.

intro: Transitions are the smallest unit of interface motion: a property glides from one value to another when state changes, making hovers, focus and toggles feel physical instead of abrupt. This section covers the transition properties, which properties animate cheaply on the compositor, easing and delay craft, trigger patterns from classes to hover, and the accessibility duty to respect reduced motion.
objectives: Write transition shorthand with property, duration, easing and delay
Choose cheap transform and opacity animations over layout properties
Shape feel with timing functions from ease to cubic-bezier and steps
Gate motion behind prefers-reduced-motion for accessible interfaces

concepts.statement: A transition needs four ingredients: **`transition-property`** naming what animates, **`transition-duration`** timing the glide, **`transition-timing-function`** shaping its acceleration, and **`transition-delay`** postponing the start. The **`transition`** shorthand bundles them as in `transition: background-color 200ms ease, transform 200ms ease`, with comma-separated entries animating independent properties on different curves. Declaring the transition on the base state — not the hover rule — ensures the glide runs in both directions, out and back.
concepts.detail: List each animated property explicitly rather than using `all`, so later style additions never accidentally inherit animation they were never designed for.

concepts.statement: **`transform`** and **`opacity`** animate **cheaply** because the compositor can interpolate them on the GPU without reflowing layout or repainting pixels. Animating **layout properties** such as `width`, `height`, `margin` or `top` is **expensive**: every frame recalculates geometry for the element and potentially its whole subtree, dropping frames on modest devices. The professional habit is reframing effects compositely — slide with `translate` instead of `left`, fade with `opacity` instead of `display`, grow with `scale` instead of `width`.
concepts.detail: When an effect seems to demand a layout property, look for the composite equivalent first, since sixty-frame motion lives or dies on this substitution.

concepts.statement: The **timing function** sculpts velocity across the duration: **`ease`** starts fast and lands softly, **`ease-out`** decelerates into rest, **`ease-in`** accelerates away, and **`linear`** holds constant speed. Custom **`cubic-bezier()`** curves draw bespoke acceleration for brand-feel motion, while **`steps()`** jumps discretely for sprite flips and typewriter ticks. Short UI feedback lives near two hundred milliseconds with `ease-out` landings; entrances may run slightly longer, exits slightly shorter, matching physical expectation.
concepts.detail: Reserve `ease-in` for exits that accelerate away and `ease-out` for entrances that settle, since motion that lands softly reads as deliberate rather than mechanical.

concepts.term: Triggers: hover, focus, classes and interruption
concepts.statement: Transitions fire whenever a transitioned property’s value **changes**, however the change arrives: **`:hover`** and **`:focus-visible`** for pointer and keyboard feedback, **class toggles** from JavaScript for menus and dialogs, or **attribute flips** like `aria-expanded` for disclosed panels. Because the transition lives on the base rule, **interrupting** mid-glide — hovering off halfway — smoothly reverses from the current value instead of snapping. Toggling one class that restyles many properties choreographs whole-panel motion from a single state bit.
concepts.detail: Drive multi-property choreography from one class or attribute so state stays singular while presentation animates across every affected property.

concepts.statement: The **`prefers-reduced-motion`** media query signals users who need minimal animation, and honoring it is an accessibility **requirement**, not decoration: `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` should collapse durations, disable glides, or snap to end states. Vestibular-sensitive users experience parallax and large-area motion as nausea or disorientation, so essential state changes must remain legible with motion removed. Design every transition as an enhancement layered over an instant change that already communicates fully.
concepts.detail: Wrap all non-essential transitions in a reduced-motion guard that forces near-zero durations, keeping meaning carried by state rather than movement.

Animate transform and opacity; reframe layout effects compositely.

quiz.q: Why must the transition declaration live on the base rule rather than :hover?
options: The base placement animates both the forward and reverse changes
quiz.explanation: Transitions run when a listed property changes value; on the base rule the property is transitioned in both directions, while hover-only placement animates just the entry.

quiz.q: Why is animating width considered expensive while animating transform is cheap?
options: Layout properties force geometry recalculation each frame, while transform and opacity interpolate on the compositor
quiz.explanation: Compositor-handled properties avoid reflow and repaint, sustaining sixty frames where per-frame layout work drops them.

quiz.q: What does transition: background-color 200ms ease, transform 200ms ease-out express?
options: Two properties animating on independent curves over the same duration
A two-second delay before anything animates
A keyframe animation, not a transition
quiz.explanation: Comma-separated entries give each property its own duration and timing function, decoupling color crossfade from motion feel.

quiz.q: What must happen inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)?
options: Animations should run longer for clarity
Non-essential motion collapses to none or near-zero while state stays legible
quiz.explanation: Sensitive users need state communicated without vestibular-triggering movement, so motion becomes an enhancement over an already-clear instant change.

intro: Transforms reshape elements without disturbing layout: moving, scaling, rotating and skewing boxes in two and three dimensions while siblings hold their ground. This section covers the transform functions, the origin they pivot around, true 3D with perspective, GPU compositing and will-change discipline, and the order sensitivity that makes combined transforms predictable.
objectives: Apply translate, scale, rotate and skew for layout-free movement
Aim effects with transform-origin for pivots and zooms
Build 3D scenes with perspective, rotate axes and preserve-3d
Manage compositing cost with will-change discipline

concepts.statement: The **`transform`** property applies geometric functions that move pixels without reflowing layout: **`translate()`** slides, **`scale()`** grows or mirrors, **`rotate()`** spins around the origin, and **`skew()`** slants axes for oblique effects. A rule like `transform: translateY(-4px) scale(1.02)` lifts and enlarges a card while siblings never shift, because transforms paint after layout completes. Individual properties **`translate`**, **`rotate`** and **`scale`** now offer the same effects as independent cascade-friendly declarations.
concepts.detail: Prefer the individual translate, rotate and scale properties when transitions must animate one axis without disturbing the others’ values.

concepts.statement: The **`transform-origin`** property sets the pivot around which scaling and rotation happen, defaulting to the element center at `50% 50%`. Zooming toward a corner wants `transform-origin: top left`, clock hands pivot at `bottom center`, and door-swing panels rotate around `left center`. Because percentages resolve against the element’s own box, origins track responsive sizing automatically where fixed offsets would drift.
concepts.detail: Set the origin explicitly on every rotation and scale that pivots anywhere but center, since the default silently misplaces edge-anchored effects.

concepts.statement: Three-dimensional transforms add depth axes: **`rotateX()`** and **`rotateY()`** tip planes backward and sideways, **`translateZ()`** pushes toward the viewer, and **`perspective()`** or the `perspective` property supplies the vanishing-point distance that makes depth visible. The **`transform-style: preserve-3d`** declaration keeps children in a shared 3D space so card faces can sit back to back, while **`backface-visibility: hidden`** hides the mirrored reverse of flipped faces. Without perspective, 3D rotations flatten into what looks like ordinary 2D skew.
concepts.detail: Apply perspective on the scene parent and preserve-3d on the flipping element, keeping depth context and flipped faces in their correct layers.

concepts.statement: Transformed elements earn their own **compositor layers** promoted to the **GPU**, which is why transform animation sustains sixty frames while layout animation stutters. The **`will-change`** property hints upcoming animation as in `will-change: transform`, letting the browser promote early — but each layer costs memory, so blanket `will-change` on dozens of elements exhausts mobile GPUs. The discipline is narrow and temporary: hint the animating few, then remove the hint when motion ends.
concepts.detail: Add will-change just before animation starts via a class or script, and clear it on transition end so layers collapse back and memory is released.

concepts.statement: Transform functions compose **right to left** as nested coordinate systems, so `transform: translateX(2rem) rotate(45deg)` slides then spins the moved frame, while `rotate(45deg) translateX(2rem)` spins first and slides along the rotated axis — visibly different destinations. Reading the list as successive frames around the element explains every surprise: each function redefines the axes its successors inherit. Fixed orders per component plus comments naming the intent keep combined transforms maintainable.
concepts.detail: Freeze one canonical order per component — typically translate, then rotate, then scale — and reorder only deliberately with a comment explaining the new frame sequence.
