examples.title: Maximum-likelihood coin bias from ten tosses
examples.problem: Seven heads appear in ten tosses. Estimate the head probability by maximum likelihood and by moments.

steps.label: Step 1: Likelihood shape
steps.text: The likelihood `$L(p) = p^{7}(1-p)^{3}$` times `$\binom{10}{7}$` peaks where log-likelihood derivative `$7 \div p - 3 \div (1-p)$` vanishes. Solving gives `$\hat{p} = 7 \div 10 = 0.7$`, the observed proportion.

steps.label: Step 2: Moments agree here
steps.text: Bernoulli mean is `$p$` itself, so matching `$\bar{X} = 0.7$` reproduces `$\hat{p} = 0.7$`. Agreement is typical for single-parameter location problems, not a general rule.

steps.label: Step 3: Report with honesty
steps.text: The point estimate `$0.7$` carries standard error `$\sqrt{0.21 \div 10} \approx 0.145$`, so the interval view of the next section matters more than the lonely number.

examples.result: Both methods give `$\hat{p} = 0.7$` with standard error about `$0.145$`.

examples.title: Score an estimator by bias and MSE
examples.problem: An estimator of `$\theta = 10$` has expected value `$10.5$` and variance `$0.25$`. Compute its bias and MSE, confirmed by script.

steps.label: Step 1: Bias
steps.text: Bias is `$10.5 - 10 = 0.5$`, a systematic overshoot of half a unit. Sign matters for correction even though MSE squares it away.

steps.label: Step 2: MSE in code
steps.text:
```python
bias, var = 0.5, 0.25
mse = var + bias ** 2
print(bias, mse)  # 0.5 0.5
```
The script prints `0.5 0.5`: MSE `$0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5$`, split evenly between wiggle and miss.

steps.label: Step 3: Compare fairly
steps.text: A competing unbiased estimator with variance `$0.6$` loses despite zero bias, since `$0.6 > 0.5$`. MSE is the single scoreboard behind such choices.

examples.result: Bias `$0.5$` with MSE `$0.5$`, beating any unbiased estimator of variance above `$0.5$`.

keyTakeaways: Random samples are i.i.d. draws while statistics are data functions estimating population parameters.
MSE equals variance plus squared bias, the single scoreboard ranking competing estimators.
The `$n - 1$` divisor makes `$S^{2}$` unbiased for `$\sigma^{2}$`, paying one degree of freedom.
Maximum likelihood maximizes `$L(\theta)$` while moments match averages, agreeing on `$\hat{p} = x \div n$`.

quiz.q: Which quantity is a statistic rather than a parameter?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Parameters describe the unseen population. Step 2: Statistics compute from the seen sample. Step 3: Only the sample mean uses observed data. Step 4: The rest are fixed unknowns to estimate.

quiz.q: An estimator has bias `$0.2$` and variance `$0.21$`. What is its MSE?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Square the bias: 0.2 squared gives 0.04. Step 2: Add the variance 0.21. Step 3: The total is 0.25. Step 4: Variance alone would underreport by the squared bias.

quiz.q: Why does `$S^{2}$` divide by `$n - 1$` instead of `$n$`?
options: To offset centering by the sample mean and stay unbiased
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Deviations center on estimated x-bar, not true mu. Step 2: That centering shrinks the raw scatter systematically. Step 3: Dividing by n minus 1 inflates exactly enough. Step 4: The result targets sigma squared on average.

quiz.q: Twelve successes in `$20$` Bernoulli trials give which MLE of `$p$`?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The Bernoulli MLE is the sample proportion. Step 2: Divide 12 by 20. Step 3: The quotient is 0.6. Step 4: Moments match the same value here.

intro: Point estimates gain meaning only with stated uncertainty, which confidence intervals supply as ranges with calibrated coverage. Normal theory with known spread uses z-values while estimated spread switches to t-values, and proportions get their own standard-error form. This section constructs all three interval types, interprets coverage honestly, and shows what narrows or widens the band.
objectives: Build z-intervals for means with known spread and read their margins
Switch to t-intervals when spread is estimated and state the degrees of freedom
Form proportion intervals and explain width drivers and coverage meaning

concepts.statement: A **95 percent confidence interval** is a random range covering the fixed parameter in about 95 of 100 repetitions, centering at the estimate plus or minus a `cover` margin. Coverage describes the procedure across repeats, never the probability that one computed interval caught its target. Wider confidence demands wider intervals, the price list read directly off the critical values.
concepts.detail: Ninety-five percent coverage with 99 percent confidence needs the larger `$2.576$` multiplier, visibly widening every band.

concepts.term: z-interval for the mean with known spread
concepts.statement: With known `$\sigma$`, the interval **`$\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma \div \sqrt{n}$`** centers at the sample mean with standard-error-scaled `zint` margin. The `$95$` percent multiplier `$z = 1.96$` is the working constant of applied statistics. Quadrupling `$n$` halves the width, the square-root return on sampling effort.
concepts.detail: Mean `$50$` with `$\sigma = 10$` and `$n = 100$` gives `$50 \pm 1.96$`, the canonical chalkboard interval.

concepts.statement: Replacing `$\sigma$` by `$s$` swaps `$z$` for **`$t_{n-1}$`** with `$n - 1$` degrees of freedom, widening bands to pay for the extra estimation in the `tint` adjustment. Heavy uncertainty at tiny `$n$` inflates `$t$` far above `$1.96$`, while large samples merge `$t$` back into `$z$`. Normal or near-normal data justify the swap; heavy skew calls for larger samples first.
concepts.detail: With `$n = 5$`, the 95 percent `$t$` value `$2.776$` exceeds `$z$` by over forty percent, the small-sample penalty made visible.

concepts.statement: Proportions use **`$\hat{p} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p}) \div n}$`**, with the estimated spread inside the `pint` margin. Validity needs enough successes and failures, classically at least five of each, so the normal approximation holds. Near-zero or near-one proportions switch to exact or Wilson intervals rather than forcing the symmetric form.
concepts.detail: Polling `$400$` voters at `$\hat{p} = 0.6$` gives margin about `$0.048$`, the familiar plus-or-minus five points of headline polls.

concepts.statement: **Width shrinks** with larger `$n$` and smaller confidence, and grows with spread and confidence level in the `width` trade table. Overlapping intervals do not settle significance by themselves, and a narrow interval around a biased estimate misleads with confidence. Design effort therefore targets the dominant width driver: usually sample size, sometimes measurement noise.
concepts.detail: To halve a poll margin at fixed confidence requires four times the respondents, the quadratic cost of precision.

examples.title: z-interval for a production mean
examples.problem: A sample of `$n = 100$` has `$\bar{x} = 50$` with known `$\sigma = 10$`. Build the 95 percent interval.

steps.label: Step 1: Standard error
steps.text: Divide spread by root size: `$10 \div \sqrt{100} = 1$`. Each observation contributes, but the root law compresses their joint power.

steps.label: Step 2: Margin and band
steps.text: Multiply by `$1.96$` for margin `$1.96$`, giving `$(48.04, 51.96)$`. The interval spans roughly four units around the estimate.

steps.label: Step 3: Honest interpretation
steps.text: The procedure covers the true mean in 95 of 100 repeats; this particular band either does or does not. Width halves only at `$n = 400$`, pricing precision explicitly.

examples.result: 95 percent interval `$(48.04, 51.96)$` around `$\bar{x} = 50$`.

examples.title: Poll margin for a proportion
examples.problem: Of `$n = 400$` voters, `$240$` favor a proposal. Build the 95 percent interval for the true share with a script.

steps.label: Step 1: Sample share
steps.text: The estimate is `$\hat{p} = 240 \div 400 = 0.6$`. Successes and failures both exceed five comfortably, licensing the normal form.

steps.label: Step 2: Margin in code
steps.text:
```python
import math
p, n = 0.6, 400
se = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
margin = 1.96 * se
print(round(se, 4), round(margin, 4))  # 0.0245 0.048
```
The script prints `0.0245 0.048`: standard error `$0.0245$` with margin `$0.048$`, giving `$(0.552, 0.648)$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Read the headline
steps.text: Sixty percent plus or minus about five points keeps the entire band above half, so majority support is established at this confidence. Halving the margin would need sixteen hundred respondents.

examples.result: 95 percent interval `$(0.552, 0.648)$` with margin about `$0.048$`.

keyTakeaways: Intervals center at the estimate plus or minus margin, with coverage describing repeat behavior.
Known-spread means use `$\bar{x} \pm z\sigma \div \sqrt{n}$` with `$1.96$` at 95 percent.
Estimated spread switches to `$t_{n-1}$`, wider at small `$n$` and merging into `$z$` when large.
Proportion margins scale with `$\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p}) \div n}$`, and quadrupling `$n$` halves width.

quiz.q: A 95 percent z-interval with `$n = 100$` is `$4$` wide. About how wide at `$n = 400$` with the same `$\sigma$`?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Width scales with 1 over root n. Step 2: Quadrupling n halves the root factor. Step 3: Half of 4 is 2. Step 4: Doubling n instead would give about 2.83.

quiz.q: Why is a 95 percent t-interval with `$n = 6$` wider than the z-interval from the same data?
options: t tables are misprinted for small n
Degrees of freedom remove all variance
Estimating spread adds uncertainty priced by heavier t tails
quiz.explanation: Step 1: z-intervals assume sigma known exactly. Step 2: t-intervals estimate sigma by s from 6 points. Step 3: That extra estimation widens bands via t at 5 degrees. Step 4: As n grows t sinks back onto z.

quiz.q: What does 95 percent coverage mean for one computed interval `$(3.1, 4.2)$`?
options: The procedure catches mu in 95 of 100 repeats
Ninety-five percent of data fall inside
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Mu is fixed, the interval was random before sampling. Step 2: Coverage describes the method across repeats. Step 3: About 95 of 100 such bands cover mu. Step 4: This band either covers or misses; no probability remains.

quiz.q: A proportion interval needs validity. Which check applies before using the normal form?
options: The sample must exceed the population
At least five successes and five failures
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Normal approximation needs enough of both outcomes. Step 2: The classic floor is five successes and five failures. Step 3: Near-boundary shares need exact methods instead. Step 4: Sample never exceeds its population.

intro: Hypothesis tests convert data into decisions with controlled error rates, extending interval logic to accept-or-reject verdicts. The null hypothesis faces the data through a test statistic, p-values measure surprise, and named sampling distributions supply the reference scales. This section builds z and t tests for means, chi-square goodness of fit, F comparisons of spread, and the error taxonomy behind them all.
objectives: State null and alternative hypotheses with rejection regions and p-values
Run z and t tests for means and interpret Type I and Type II errors
Apply chi-square goodness of fit and F variance-ratio tests correctly

concepts.statement: The **null** `$H_{0}$` states the default under challenge while the **alternative** `$H_{1}$` states the change to detect, and a **test statistic** compresses data into one number compared against its `h0` null distribution. Rejection regions hold the most surprising values at total probability `$\alpha$`, the significance level. Two-sided regions split `$\alpha$` across both tails for change in either direction.
concepts.detail: Testing `$\mu = 100$` against `$\mu \ne 100$` rejects for large `$|z|$`, while `$\mu > 100$` rejects only for large positive `$z$`.

concepts.term: p-values with Type I and II errors
concepts.statement: The **p-value** is the null probability of data at least as extreme as observed, rejecting `$H_{0}$` when it falls below `$\alpha$` in the `pval` decision rule. **Type I error** falsely rejects truth at rate `$\alpha$` while **Type II error** misses real effects at rate `$\beta$`, with **power** `$1 - \beta$` as the detection chance. Bigger samples and bigger effects both raise power at fixed `$\alpha$`, the design levers of every experiment.
concepts.detail: A p-value of `$0.03$` rejects at `$\alpha = 0.05$` but not at `$\alpha = 0.01$`, showing significance is always relative to the chosen level.

concepts.term: z and t tests for means
concepts.statement: **z-tests** standardize with known `$\sigma$` while **t-tests** studentize with estimated `$s$` and `$n - 1$` degrees of freedom in the `ttest` pair. One-sample tests face a benchmark, two-sample tests compare groups, and paired tests difference matched units before testing once. Assumptions run from normality for tiny samples down to large-sample robustness, checked by plots before verdicts.
concepts.detail: A two-sample statistic near `$2.1$` with large `$n$` clears the `$1.96$` bar, declaring the group gap significant at five percent.

concepts.statement: **Goodness of fit** sums **`$\sum (O - E)^{2} \div E$`** over categories, referring the total to `$\chi^{2}$` with `$k - 1 - m$` degrees of freedom for `$k$` cells and `$m$` estimated parameters in the `chi2` recipe. Large totals signal observed counts straying beyond sampling wobble from the claimed model. Each expected count should reach at least five, merging sparse cells before testing.
concepts.detail: Counts `$(30, 50, 20)$` against `$(25, 50, 25)$` give `$\chi^{2} = 2$` on `$2$` degrees, far below the `$5.99$` bar.

concepts.term: F ratio for spreads with nonparametric backup
concepts.statement: The **F statistic** `$F = s_{1}^{2} \div s_{2}^{2}$` compares two variances against `$F$` tables indexed by both degrees of freedom in the `ftest` check. Normality matters more here than for means, so skewed data reroute to robust Levene-style or rank procedures. When distributions resist all parametric shapes, **nonparametric** sign and rank tests decide by orderings rather than values.
concepts.detail: An `$F$` near one supports equal spread while values far above one indict the numerator group as more variable.

figures.caption: Two-sided $z$-test at $\alpha = 0.05$: rejection past $\pm 1.96$ shades both tails while the observed $z = 1.5$ lands inside, so $H_{0}$ stands.

examples.title: z-test of a shifted production mean

steps.label: Step 1: Standardize
steps.text: The standard error is `$10 \div 5 = 2$`, so `$z = (103 - 100) \div 2 = 1.5$`. The sample sits one and a half errors above the benchmark.

steps.label: Step 2: Compare with critical values
steps.text: Two-sided five percent testing rejects past `$\pm 1.96$`, and `$1.5$` falls inside. The p-value `$2(1 - \Phi(1.5)) \approx 0.1336$` exceeds `$0.05$`, confirming the verdict numerically.

steps.label: Step 3: Phrase the conclusion
steps.text: Evidence is insufficient to reject `$H_{0}$` at five percent; the mean may still exceed `$100$`, but these data do not establish it. A larger sample could shrink the error enough to flip the call.

examples.result: `$z = 1.5$` with p-value about `$0.1336$`: keep `$H_{0}$` at `$\alpha = 0.05$`.

examples.title: Chi-square test of a claimed split
examples.problem: Counts `$(30, 50, 20)$` face the claimed split `$(25, 50, 25)$`. Test fit at `$\alpha = 0.05$` with a script.

steps.label: Step 1: Chi-square total
steps.text: Cell contributions are `$(30-25)^{2} \div 25 = 1$`, `$0$`, and `$(20-25)^{2} \div 25 = 1$`, totaling `$\chi^{2} = 2$`. All expected counts clear five, so the reference distribution applies.

steps.label: Step 2: Degrees and bar in code
steps.text:
```python
obs = [30, 50, 20]
exp = [25, 50, 25]
chi2 = sum((o - e) ** 2 / e for o, e in zip(obs, exp))
print(chi2)  # 2.0 against 5.99 on df = 2
```
The script prints `2.0` against the five percent bar `$5.99$` on `$3 - 1 = 2$` degrees.

steps.label: Step 3: Verdict
steps.text: Since `$2 < 5.99$`, the data fit the claimed split adequately at five percent. Rejection would need far larger cell surprises.

examples.result: `$\chi^{2} = 2$` on `$2$` degrees below `$5.99$`: the split stands.

keyTakeaways: Tests pit `$H_{0}$` against `$H_{1}$` through statistics with `$\alpha$`-sized rejection regions.
p-values reject below `$\alpha$`, while Type I errors run at `$\alpha$` and power at `$1 - \beta$`.
Means use z with known spread and t with estimated spread across one, two and paired designs.
Fit sums `$(O-E)^{2} \div E$` against chi-square while spreads compare through `$F = s_{1}^{2} \div s_{2}^{2}$`.

quiz.q: A test returns p-value `$0.02$` at `$\alpha = 0.05$`. What is the decision?
options: Reject `$H_{0}$` since p is below alpha
The test is invalid without the raw data
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Compare p 0.02 against alpha 0.05. Step 2: Smaller p means more surprising under H0. Step 3: Below alpha triggers rejection. Step 4: Rejection flags evidence, not proof of H1.

quiz.q: Which error is controlled directly at the significance level `$\alpha$`?
options: Type I error of false rejection
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Alpha sizes the rejection region under H0. Step 2: Landing there when H0 holds is false rejection. Step 3: That mistake is Type I by definition. Step 4: Beta instead needs power analysis with an effect size.

quiz.q: Goodness of fit on `$4$` categories with no estimated parameters uses how many degrees of freedom?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Start from cell count 4. Step 2: Subtract 1 for the total constraint. Step 3: Subtract 0 estimated parameters. Step 4: The reference is chi-square on 3 degrees.

quiz.q: Two sample variances `$s_{1}^{2} = 12$` and `$s_{2}^{2} = 3$` give which F statistic for testing equal spread?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Form the ratio of sample variances. Step 2: Divide 12 by 3 to get 4. Step 3: Large F values indict unequal spread. Step 4: Tables with both degrees of freedom judge significance.

depth.title: Neyman-Pearson and duality of tests and intervals

blocks.body: For simple $H_{0}: \theta = \theta_{0}$ versus $H_{1}: \theta = \theta_{1}$ the **Neyman Pearson** lemma states that the most powerful size $\alpha$ test rejects for large likelihood ratio $\Lambda = L(\theta_{1})/L(\theta_{0}) > k$, with randomized boundary when needed. Under monotone likelihood ratio the one sided test $T > c$ is uniformly most powerful by Karlin Rubin. Duality inverts tests to sets: $C(x) = \\{\theta_{0} : x \text{ accepts } H_{0}\\}$ is a $1-\alpha$ confidence set, and every confidence procedure inverts to a family of tests. Power $1-\beta$ and size $\alpha$ trade through sample size $n$.

Let $\phi^{\ast} = 1_{\\{\Lambda > k\\}}$ with $E_{0}[\phi^{\ast}] = \alpha$ and let $\phi$ be any competing size $\alpha$ test. Then $(\phi^{\ast} - \phi)(\Lambda - k) \geq 0$ pointwise, since $\phi^{\ast} = 1$ exactly where $\Lambda > k$. Integrating against $L_{0}$ gives $\int (\phi^{\ast} - \phi)(L_{1} - k L_{0}) \geq 0$, so $E_{1}[\phi^{\ast}] - E_{1}[\phi] \geq k(\alpha - \alpha) = 0$. Hence $\phi^{\ast}$ maximizes power. The threshold $k$ is the Lagrange multiplier for the size constraint, and sufficiency lets $\Lambda$ depend only on sufficient statistics by factorization.

Inversion builds intervals: accept $|\bar{X} - \mu_{0}| \leq z_{1-\alpha/2} \sigma/\sqrt{n}$ for each $\mu_{0}$ and collect survivors to get $\bar{X} \pm z_{1-\alpha/2} \sigma/\sqrt{n}$. Reported $p = \inf \\{\alpha : \text{reject at } \alpha\\}$ is the smallest size allowing rejection. Power analysis sizes $n$ from $(\sigma(z_{1-\alpha} + z_{1-\beta})/\delta)^{2}$ for shift $\delta$. Multiplicity breaks naive $p$ values: Bonferroni divides $\alpha$ by the number of tests while Benjamini Hochberg controls false discovery rate, the modern response to replication and $p$ hacking concerns.

intro: Regression fits lines through scattered data by least squares, turning cloud trends into slopes, intercepts and predictions. The normal equations deliver closed-form coefficients while correlation scores the linear strength. This section derives the least-squares line, reads residuals for model health, and warns prediction beyond the data range.
objectives: Fit least-squares lines from summary sums with slope and intercept formulas
Compute correlation and interpret its strength without causal overreach
Check residuals for curvature and respect prediction boundaries

concepts.statement: Least squares chooses intercept `$a$` and slope `$b$` minimizing **`$\mathrm{SSE} = \sum (y_{i} - a - bx_{i})^{2}$`**, the total squared vertical miss in the `sse` objective. Squaring penalizes large misses hardest and keeps the mathematics differentiable everywhere. Vertical misses assume `$x$` is fixed and `$y$` carries the noise, the regression direction that matters for prediction.
concepts.detail: Minimizing absolute misses instead would give robust median-style fits at the price of harder computation.

concepts.term: Normal equations with slope and intercept
concepts.statement: Zeroing both partial derivatives gives slope **`$b = S_{xy} \div S_{xx}$`** and intercept **`$a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$`**, where `$S_{xx}$` and `$S_{xy}$` sum squared and cross deviations in the `slope` solution. The fitted line always passes through `$(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$`, the balance point of the cloud. One pass over the data accumulating five sums then closes the whole fit.

**Correlation** **`$r = S_{xy} \div \sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}$`** standardizes the slope into `$[-1, 1]$`, with `$r^{2}$` reporting the response variance fraction explained in the `corr` gauge. Steep slopes on tight clouds score near `$\pm 1$` while shapeless clouds score near zero regardless of scale. Significance testing divides `$r$` by its standard error, since `$0.8$` on six points proves less than on six hundred.
concepts.detail: The four-point example scores `$r = 0.8$`, with `$64$` percent of variation explained linearly.

concepts.statement: **Residuals** `$e_{i} = y_{i} - \hat{y}_{i}$` should scatter randomly about zero, and any curve or fan in their plot indicts the straight-line model through the `resid` lens. Curved bands call for transformations or polynomials while widening fans call for weighted fits. Numerical summaries never substitute for this one picture, which exposes structure that `$r$` alone hides.
concepts.detail: A U-shaped residual band around a fitted line advertises a missing quadratic term louder than any statistic.

concepts.statement: **Extrapolation** beyond observed `$x$` gambles that the line continues where no data checks it, while interpolation inside the range inherits the fit guarantees in the `extrap` boundary. Far-out predictions compound slope uncertainty with model-form risk, the two multipliers of embarrassment. Honest reporting pairs each forecast with its interval, widening with distance from `$\bar{x}$`.
concepts.detail: Predicting at `$x = 5$` from data ending at `$4$` is mild, but projecting to `$x = 50$` invites structural breaks.

figures.caption: Least-squares line $\hat{y} = 1.5 + 0.8x$ through four points with $r = 0.8$: vertical residual ticks show the squared misses that SSE totals.

derivations.title: Least-Squares Normal Equations for a Line
derivations.statement: Derivation of $b = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}$ and $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$ by minimising $\mathrm{SSE} = \sum_{i}(y_{i} - a - bx_{i})^{2}$
prerequisites: Squared-error objective $\mathrm{SSE}(a,b)$ in slope $b$ and intercept $a$
Stationary point of a convex quadratic is its global minimiser
Sample means $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ with centred sums $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$

steps.label: Step 1: Write the squared-error objective
steps.explanation: Measure fit by total squared vertical miss, which penalises large deviations hardest while staying differentiable everywhere. This choice works because squaring makes the objective a convex paraboloid in $a$ and $b$ with a single bowl bottom. Vertical misses encode the modelling assumption that $x$ is fixed and $y$ carries noise.

steps.label: Step 2: Zero the intercept partial derivative
steps.explanation: Differentiate termwise in $a$, bringing down a factor of $-2$ times each residual. Setting this to zero works because at the bowl bottom every directional slope must vanish. Dividing by $-2n$ gives $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$, so the line passes through the cloud centre.

steps.label: Step 3: Zero the slope partial derivative
steps.explanation: Differentiate termwise in $b$, where the chain rule leaves an extra $x_{i}$ factor on each term. This second stationarity condition works because the minimum must be flat in the $b$ direction as well. Together the two zero-derivative equations form the $2 \times 2$ normal system for $a$ and $b$.

steps.label: Step 4: Solve the normal system for slope and intercept
steps.explanation: Substitute $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$ into the slope equation and collect $b$ terms, which centres the data and decouples the unknowns. This elimination works because centred cross sums $S_{xy}$ and $S_{xx}$ absorb all mean-level shifts. Positivity of $S_{xx}$ for nonconstant $x$ guarantees a unique minimiser rather than a ridge.

derivations.result: The minimisers are $b = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}$ and $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$, meaning the best line passes through the mean point with slope equal to the ratio of cross to horizontal spread.

examples.title: Least-squares line through four points
examples.problem: Fit `$\hat{y} = a + bx$` to `$(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 4)$` by least squares.

steps.label: Step 2: Slope and intercept
steps.text: Slope `$b = 4 \div 5 = 0.8$` with intercept `$a = 3.5 - 0.8 \times 2.5 = 1.5$`, so `$\hat{y} = 1.5 + 0.8x$`. The line passes through `$(2.5, 3.5)$` as theory demands.

steps.label: Step 3: Residual glance
steps.text: Fitted values `$2.3, 3.1, 3.9, 4.7$` leave residuals `$-0.3, -0.1, 1.1, -0.7$` summing to zero. No curve pattern appears across four points, so the line stands.

examples.result: Fitted line `$\hat{y} = 1.5 + 0.8x$` with zero-sum residuals.

examples.title: Correlation, explained variance and a forecast
examples.problem: For the same four points compute `$r$`, the explained fraction, and forecast at `$x = 5$` with a script.

steps.label: Step 1: Spread of y
steps.text: Squared deviations of `$y$` give `$S_{yy} = 2.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 + 0.25 = 5$`. Both clouds spread equally here, simplifying the ratio.

steps.label: Step 2: Correlation in code
steps.text:
```python
sxx, syy, sxy = 5.0, 5.0, 4.0
r = sxy / (sxx * syy) ** 0.5
print(round(r, 4), round(r ** 2, 4))  # 0.8 0.64
```
The script prints `0.8 0.64`: correlation `$0.8$` with `$64$` percent of variance explained linearly.

steps.label: Step 3: Forecast with caution
steps.text: At `$x = 5$` the line gives `$1.5 + 4 = 5.5$`, just past the data edge at `$4$`. Mild extrapolation is defensible; distant projection would need model evidence beyond four points.

examples.result: Correlation `$0.8$`, explained fraction `$0.64$`, forecast `$5.5$` at `$x = 5$`.

keyTakeaways: Least squares minimizes `$\sum (y_{i} - a - bx_{i})^{2}$`, fixing `$x$` and charging vertical misses.
Slope `$b = S_{xy} \div S_{xx}$` with `$a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$` puts the line through the cloud center.
Correlation `$r$` in `$[-1, 1]$` scores linear strength with `$r^{2}$` explained.
Residual plots expose curvature while extrapolation beyond data gambles on untested structure.

quiz.q: Summary sums give `$S_{xx} = 10$` and `$S_{xy} = 30$` with `$\bar{x} = 2$`, `$\bar{y} = 9$`. What is the least-squares line?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Slope is 30 divided by 10, giving 3. Step 2: Intercept is 9 minus 3 times 2, giving 3. Step 3: The line is 3 plus 3x. Step 4: It passes through (2, 9) as required.

quiz.q: A fit reports `$r = -0.9$`. What does it mean?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Magnitude 0.9 sits near the 1 endpoint. Step 2: That signals a tight linear cloud. Step 3: The minus sign makes it decreasing. Step 4: Causation stays unproven regardless of strength.

quiz.q: Residuals against `$x$` form a clear U shape. What is indicated?
options: A missing quadratic curve in the model
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Good fits leave structureless residual scatter. Step 2: A U shape is systematic structure. Step 3: Curvature points at a quadratic term. Step 4: Adding x squared should straighten the plot.

quiz.q: Data span `$x$` from `$10$` to `$20$`. Which forecast is safest?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Inside-range prediction is interpolation. Step 2: x equal to 15 sits centrally in the data. Step 3: Far points extrapolate untested structure. Step 4: Hence 15 inherits fit guarantees the others lack.

intro: Axler begins with coordinates before abstraction, so this section follows the same road from the concrete lists of $\mathbb{F}^{n}$ to the abstract axioms of a vector space. Complex numbers enter first because the deepest theorems need scalars in which every polynomial splits, and the single rule $i^{2} = -1$ rebuilds all of complex arithmetic. The vector space axioms then distil the familiar rules of coordinate arithmetic into a short list of requirements shared by arrows, functions and polynomials alike.
objectives: Compute with complex numbers from `$i^{2} = -1$` and add and scale lists in `$\mathbb{F}^{n}$` coordinate by coordinate
State the vector space axioms and test a proposed addition and scalar multiplication against them
Prove the elementary consequences `$0v = 0$`, `$a0 = 0$` and `$(-1)v = -v$` from the distributive law

concepts.statement: A **complex number** is `$a + bi$` with `$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$`, and every product is rebuilt from the single rule `$i^{2} = -1$` together with the usual arithmetic laws, which is why Axler tells the reader never to memorize the product formula. The `complexpair` view keeps real and imaginary parts separate, while `$\overline{a + bi} = a - bi$` and `$|a + bi|^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$` record conjugation and size. Because `$\mathbb{R}$` sits inside `$\mathbb{C}$` as `$a + 0i$`, real arithmetic is just the special case that never leaves the real axis.
concepts.detail: Axler 1.1 motivates `$i$` as a square root of `$-1$` obeying ordinary rules, then verifies `$i^{2} = -1$` from the product definition rather than assuming it.

concepts.statement: A **list** of length `$n$` is an ordered `$n$`-tuple `$(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n})$`, and `$\mathbb{F}^{n}$` is the set of all such lists with entries in `$\mathbb{F}$`, where `$\mathbb{F}$` means `$\mathbb{R}$` or `$\mathbb{C}$`. Addition and scalar multiplication act **coordinate by coordinate** through the `coordwise` rule `$\lambda(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}) = (\lambda x_{1}, \ldots, \lambda x_{n})$`. Coordinatewise multiplication of two lists is deliberately excluded, because experience shows it leads nowhere, while scalar multiplication carries the whole subject.
concepts.detail: Axler 1A builds `$\mathbb{F}^{n}$` first so that every later axiom looks like a familiar coordinate fact written abstractly.

concepts.statement: A **vector space** is a set `$V$` with an addition and a scalar multiplication obeying commutativity, associativity, an additive identity `$0$`, additive inverses, a multiplicative identity `$1$`, and the distributive and compatibility laws, all collected in the `vspace` axioms of Axler 1B. The two distributive laws are the only bridge between addition and scaling, so every proof joining the two operations must cross them. Arrows in the plane, lists in `$\mathbb{F}^{n}$`, functions and polynomials all satisfy the same list, which is exactly why one theory covers them all.
concepts.detail: Addition takes two vectors to a vector while scalar multiplication takes a scalar and a vector to a vector, and confusing the two roles is the most common beginner slip.

concepts.term: Unique zero, unique inverses and the three small laws
concepts.statement: Every vector space has a **unique additive identity** and every vector a **unique additive inverse**, proved in Axler 1.26 and 1.27 by the two-identity squeeze `$0^{\prime} = 0^{\prime} + 0 = 0$`. From distributivity alone follow `$0v = 0$`, `$a0 = 0$` and `$(-1)v = -v$`, the `zerolaws` numbered 1.30 through 1.32. All three proofs run the same trick of expanding `$0$` as `$0 + 0$` and cancelling, so learning one proof teaches all three.
concepts.detail: In `$0v = 0$` the left zero is the scalar `$0 \in \mathbb{F}$` while the right zero is the vector `$0 \in V$`, a distinction Axler flags explicitly.

concepts.term: Scalars are numbers, vectors are not
concepts.statement: In Axler’s setup `$\mathbb{F}$` always means the scalars `$\mathbb{R}$` or `$\mathbb{C}$`, while elements of `$V$` are **vectors** even when they look like functions or polynomials, and the `scalarvec` discipline never multiplies two vectors together. The **dot product** of Chapter 6 will multiply two vectors to get a scalar, but that is a later structure rather than part of the axioms. Keeping the two sorts straight makes every subspace test and every linearity check mechanical.
concepts.detail: When `$\mathbb{F}^{n}$` is later called an inner product space, Axler assumes the Euclidean product unless told otherwise, as fixed in 6.4.

examples.title: Multiply complex numbers the Axler way
examples.problem: Evaluate `$(2 + 3i)(4 + 5i)$` from the single rule `$i^{2} = -1$` together with the distributive and commutative laws, as in Axler 1.2, and confirm the real and imaginary parts with a short script.

steps.label: Step 1: Distribute over the sum
steps.text: Treat `$3i$` as `$3$` times `$i$` and expand: `$(2 + 3i)(4 + 5i) = 2(4 + 5i) + 3i(4 + 5i) = 8 + 10i + 12i + 15i^{2}$`. No memorized product formula is used, only distributivity and commutativity.

steps.label: Step 2: Collapse the square and check by script
steps.text:
```python
a, b = 2, 3
c, d = 4, 5
real = a*c - b*d
imag = a*d + b*c
print(real, imag)  # -7 22
```
Since `$i^{2} = -1$`, the term `$15i^{2}$` becomes `$-15$`, and the script confirms the real part `$-7$` and the imaginary part `$22$` from the coordinate formulas.

steps.label: Step 3: Read off the answer
steps.text: Collecting terms gives `$(2 + 3i)(4 + 5i) = -7 + 22i$`. Setting `$a = c = 0$` with `$b = d = 1$` in the same computation yields `$i^{2} = -1$`, closing the loop Axler describes.

examples.result: The product equals `$-7 + 22i$`, derived from `$i^{2} = -1$` with no memorized formula.

examples.title: Prove that zero times any vector is zero
examples.problem: Starting only from the vector space axioms, prove `$0v = 0$` for every `$v \in V$` (Axler 1.30), saying each time which zero is meant.

steps.label: Step 1: Expand the scalar zero
steps.text: Write the scalar `$0$` as `$0 + 0$` and use distributivity: `$0v = (0 + 0)v = 0v + 0v$`. This step is the only place the axioms enter, since distributivity is the sole bridge between addition and scaling.

steps.label: Step 2: Cancel from both sides
steps.text: Add the additive inverse of `$0v$` to both sides to get `$0 = 0v$` by associativity and the inverse law. The `$0$` on the left of `$0v$` is the scalar zero, while the final `$0$` is the zero vector.

steps.label: Step 3: Note the reusable pattern
steps.text: The same expand-and-cancel trick proves `$a0 = 0$` by expanding the vector `$0 = 0 + 0$`, and proves `$(-1)v = -v$` by checking that `$v + (-1)v = 0$`. One trick therefore covers Axler 1.30 through 1.32.

examples.result: `$0v = 0$` for every `$v \in V$`, with the scalar zero on the left and the vector zero on the right.

keyTakeaways: Complex arithmetic needs only `$i^{2} = -1$` plus ordinary laws, and `$\mathbb{R}$` sits inside `$\mathbb{C}$` as `$a + 0i$`.
`$\mathbb{F}^{n}$` adds and scales coordinate by coordinate, while products of two lists are deliberately excluded.
The axioms bridge addition and scaling only through distributivity, so every mixed proof must use it.
Unique zero, unique inverses, `$0v = 0$`, `$a0 = 0$` and `$(-1)v = -v$` all follow from expand-and-cancel.

quiz.q: Using only `$i^{2} = -1$`, what is `$(2 + 3i)(4 + 5i)$`?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Distribute to get `$8 + 10i + 12i + 15i^{2}$`. Step 2: Replace `$i^{2}$` by `$-1$` to turn `$15i^{2}$` into `$-15$`. Step 3: Combine `$8 - 15 = -7$` with `$10i + 12i = 22i$`. Step 4: The remaining options forget the sign flip, drop the cross terms, or add coordinates instead of multiplying.

quiz.q: In Axler’s notation, what does `$\mathbb{F}$` stand for?
options: Either `$\mathbb{R}$` or `$\mathbb{C}$`, fixed for the whole discussion
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Recall Axler works over real and complex scalars side by side. Step 2: The symbol `$\mathbb{F}$` abbreviates whichever of the two is in force. Step 3: It never means vectors, integers, or finite fields in this book. Step 4: Hence the discussion fixes `$\mathbb{F}$` as `$\mathbb{R}$` or `$\mathbb{C}$`.

quiz.q: For `$v$` in a vector space, `$0v$` equals which vector?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Expand the scalar as `$0 = 0 + 0$`. Step 2: Distribute to get `$0v = 0v + 0v$`. Step 3: Cancel `$0v$` from both sides to leave `$0 = 0v$`. Step 4: The surviving zero is the vector zero, not `$v$` or `$-v$`.

quiz.q: Why does Axler refuse to multiply two lists of `$\mathbb{F}^{n}$` coordinate by coordinate?
options: It makes scalar multiplication impossible to define
It forces every vector space to be infinite-dimensional
Experience shows that definition is not useful for the subject
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Nothing in the axioms forbids inventing a list product. Step 2: Axler reports that experience shows the definition leads nowhere. Step 3: Scalar multiplication, not list multiplication, drives the theory. Step 4: So the book defines only the useful operation.

intro: A subspace is a subset that is a vector space in its own right, inheriting addition and scaling from the parent space. The whole axiom list collapses to three quick checks, namely that the subset holds the zero vector and stays closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Sums of subspaces then replace unions, because the union of two subspaces is almost never a subspace while their sum is the smallest subspace containing both.
objectives: Apply the three-condition subspace test to subsets of `$\mathbb{F}^{n}$` and to function spaces
Decide shifted-hyperplane questions of the form `$x_{1} + 2x_{2} + 3x_{3} = b$` by the value of `$b$`
Compute sums of subspaces and explain why unions usually fail while sums always work

concepts.statement: A subset `$U$` of `$V$` is a **subspace** if it is itself a vector space with the same additive identity, addition and scalar multiplication as `$V$`, which is Axler’s `sub` definition 1.33. The empty set is never a subspace, since a vector space must contain at least an additive identity. The smallest subspace of `$V$` is `$\{0\}$` and the largest is `$V$` itself.
concepts.detail: Some authors say linear subspace for the same notion, and Axler notes the two terms mean exactly the same thing.

concepts.statement: A subset `$U$` of `$V$` is a subspace if and only if it passes the **three conditions** `$0 \in U$`, sums stay inside so `$u, w \in U$` implies `$u + w \in U$`, and `$au \in U$` for all `$a \in \mathbb{F}$` and `$u \in U$`, the `subtest` numbered 1.34. The zero condition may be traded for nonemptiness, because scaling any member by `$0$` manufactures `$0$`. Associativity, commutativity and distributivity need no checking since they are inherited from `$V$`.
concepts.detail: The proof uses 1.32 to get inverses as `$(-1)u$`, so every member of `$U$` has its additive inverse inside `$U$`.

concepts.statement: The set `$\{(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}) \in \mathbb{F}^{4} : x_{3} = 5x_{4} + b\}$` is a subspace if and only if `$b = 0$`, which is Axler’s `shiftb` example 1.35 with the same verdict for `$x_{1} + 2x_{2} + 3x_{3} = b$` and `$f^{\prime}(2) = b$`. A nonzero shift pushes `$0$` outside the set and breaks both closure laws at once. **Homogeneous** conditions pass the test while shifted ones fail it, and spotting the shift is the fastest point on the page.
concepts.detail: Continuous functions on `$[0, 1]$`, differentiable functions on `$\mathbb{R}$`, and null sequences in `$\mathbb{C}^{\infty}$` pass for the same reason: limits, sums and scalings preserve the defining property.

concepts.statement: The **sum** `$V_{1} + \cdots + V_{m}$` is the set of all `$v_{1} + \cdots + v_{m}$` with `$v_{k} \in V_{k}$`, the `subsum` definition 1.36. It is the **smallest subspace** containing every summand: each `$V_{k}$` sits inside it by padding with zeros, and any subspace holding all summands must hold all their finite sums, which is 1.40. Sums are the vector-space analogue of unions of sets, because the smallest subspace containing given subspaces is their sum.
concepts.detail: In Axler 1.37 the `$x$`-axis plus the `$y$`-axis of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$` sums to the `$xy$`-plane `$\{(x, y, 0)\}$`.

concepts.statement: The **union** of two subspaces is rarely a subspace, since the sum of a vector from each side usually escapes both, which is why Axler works with sums rather than unions. The subspaces of `$\mathbb{R}^{2}$` are exactly `$\{0\}$`, the lines through the origin, and `$\mathbb{R}^{2}$`, with the analogous list of points, lines and planes through the origin in `$\mathbb{R}^{3}$`. The `lineorigin` slogan is that through-the-origin is the whole test in low dimensions.
concepts.detail: Proving those low-dimensional lists are complete needs the independence tools of the next chapter, so Axler postpones the hard direction.

figures.caption: A line through `$0$` passes the subspace test because sums and scalar multiples stay on it, while a shifted line fails at once since `$0$` is missing from the set.

examples.title: The hyperplane test: subspace only when b is zero
examples.problem: For `$b \in \mathbb{F}$`, decide for which `$b$` the set `$U_{b} = \{(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}) \in \mathbb{F}^{3} : x_{1} + 2x_{2} + 3x_{3} = b\}$` is a subspace of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`.

steps.label: Step 1: Test the zero vector
steps.text: The zero vector `$(0, 0, 0)$` satisfies the condition only when `$b = 0$`, since `$0 + 2(0) + 3(0) = 0$`. Any nonzero `$b$` already fails the first of the three conditions, so `$U_{b}$` can be a subspace only for `$b = 0$`.

steps.label: Step 2: Verify closure when b is zero, with a numeric check
steps.text:
```python
u = (1, -2, 1)
v = (0, 1, 3)
def lhs(w):
    return w[0] + 2*w[1] + 3*w[2]
w = tuple(2*x + 3*y for x, y in zip(u, v))
print(lhs(u), lhs(v), lhs(w))  # 0 0 0
```
Both `$u$` and `$v$` satisfy `$x_{1} + 2x_{2} + 3x_{3} = 0$`, and the script confirms their combination `$2u + 3v$` does too. In symbols, adding two solutions adds the left sides `$0 + 0 = 0$`, and scaling multiplies `$0$` by `$a$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Conclude with the slogan
steps.text: Homogeneous linear conditions pass the test while shifted ones fail it, so `$U_{b}$` is a subspace if and only if `$b = 0$`. The same argument settles Axler’s `$x_{3} = 5x_{4} + b$` and `$f^{\prime}(2) = b$` families.

examples.result: `$U_{b}$` is a subspace of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$` exactly when `$b = 0$`.

examples.title: Add the x-axis and the y-axis in `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`
examples.problem: Let `$U = \{(x, 0, 0) : x \in \mathbb{F}\}$` and `$W = \{(0, y, 0) : y \in \mathbb{F}\}$` in `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`. Describe `$U + W$` by proving both inclusions, as in Axler 1.37.

steps.label: Step 1: Guess the plane
steps.text: Adding `$(x, 0, 0)$` to `$(0, y, 0)$` gives `$(x, y, 0)$`, so every sum lands in the `$xy$`-plane `$P = \{(x, y, 0)\}$`. Hence `$U + W \subseteq P$`.

steps.label: Step 2: Split an arbitrary point of the plane
steps.text: Conversely, `$(x, y, 0) = (x, 0, 0) + (0, y, 0)$` writes each point of `$P$` as a member of `$U$` plus a member of `$W$`. Hence `$P \subseteq U + W$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Appeal to the smallest-subspace fact
steps.text: Both inclusions give `$U + W = P$`, and 1.40 guarantees the sum is a subspace without further checks. The third coordinate stays `$0$` because neither summand can produce one.

examples.result: `$U + W = \{(x, y, 0) : x, y \in \mathbb{F}\}$`, the coordinate plane of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`.

keyTakeaways: A subset is a subspace exactly when it holds `$0$` and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
Shifted conditions such as `$x_{1} + 2x_{2} + 3x_{3} = b$` give subspaces only for `$b = 0$`.
`$V_{1} + \cdots + V_{m}$` is the smallest subspace containing every summand.
Unions of subspaces are rarely subspaces, so the theory adds subspaces instead of uniting them.

quiz.q: Which triple is Axler’s subspace test?
options: Contains `$0$`, closed under addition, closed under scalar multiplication
Closed under products, quotients, and powers
Spans the space and is linearly independent
quiz.explanation: Step 1: A subspace must be a vector space with the inherited operations. Step 2: The inherited laws make associativity and distributivity automatic. Step 3: Only the identity and the two closure properties need checking. Step 4: Products, finiteness and spanning are irrelevant to the test.

quiz.q: The set `$\{(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}) : x_{1} + 2x_{2} + 3x_{3} = 4\}$` is a subspace of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$` for which reason?
options: It is, because the condition is linear
It is, because it contains infinitely many vectors
It is, because sums of solutions stay solutions
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Test `$0$` first: `$0 + 2(0) + 3(0) = 0 \ne 4$`. Step 2: The missing zero already disqualifies the set. Step 3: Adding two solutions would give `$4 + 4 = 8$`, breaking closure too. Step 4: Only the homogeneous version with `$0$` on the right is a subspace.

quiz.q: What is the union of the two coordinate axes in `$\mathbb{R}^{2}$`?
options: Not a subspace, since `$(1, 0) + (0, 1)$` escapes both axes
A subspace, because each axis is a subspace
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Each axis alone passes the subspace test. Step 2: Form `$(1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1)$` from one member of each. Step 3: The sum lies on neither axis, so closure fails. Step 4: Hence unions need not be subspaces even when both parts are.

quiz.q: The sum `$U + W$` of two subspaces is which subspace?
options: The largest subspace contained in both `$U$` and `$W$`
The union `$U \cup W$` with extra points filled in
The smallest subspace containing both `$U$` and `$W$`
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Padding with zeros shows `$U$` and `$W$` sit inside `$U + W$`. Step 2: Any subspace holding both must hold all their finite sums. Step 3: So every competing subspace contains `$U + W$`. Step 4: That double inclusion is exactly the smallest-containing claim of 1.40.

intro: A direct sum is a sum with unique decomposition, so each vector splits into summands in exactly one way. For two subspaces the test is beautifully simple, since the sum is direct exactly when the intersection holds only the zero vector. With three or more summands pairwise trivial intersections are not enough, and only the zero-decomposition test decides.
objectives: State the unique-decomposition definition of a direct sum and use the `$\oplus$` notation correctly
Apply the two-subspace intersection test `$U \cap W = \{0\}$` in both directions
Use the zero-only test for three or more summands and reproduce the standard nonexample

concepts.statement: The sum `$V_{1} + \cdots + V_{m}$` is a **direct sum**, written `$V_{1} \oplus \cdots \oplus V_{m}$`, when every element has exactly one representation `$v_{1} + \cdots + v_{m}$` with `$v_{k} \in V_{k}$`, which is the `dsum` definition 1.41. The circled plus serves as a certificate that uniqueness has been checked. Direct sums are the vector analogue of disjoint unions, with the zero vector shared by all parts instead of disjointness.
concepts.detail: Uniqueness for every vector is a strong demand, which is why the next two tests reduce it to checks on `$0$` alone.

concepts.term: Zero-only condition for a direct sum
concepts.statement: A sum is **direct** if and only if the only way to write `$0$` as `$v_{1} + \cdots + v_{m}$` is the trivial one with every `$v_{k} = 0$`, the `zerotest` numbered 1.45. Subtracting two rival decompositions of one vector produces a zero-decomposition, so triviality for `$0$` forces uniqueness everywhere. Checking one vector instead of all of them is the whole point of the result.
concepts.detail: The proof subtracts `$v = v_{1} + \cdots + v_{m} = u_{1} + \cdots + u_{m}$` to get `$0 = (v_{1} - u_{1}) + \cdots + (v_{m} - u_{m})$` and concludes term by term.

concepts.statement: For two subspaces the sum `$U + W$` is a **direct sum** if and only if `$U \cap W = \{0\}$`, the `twotest` numbered 1.46. Forward, a shared nonzero `$v$` gives the rival zero-writing `$0 = v + (-v)$`; backward, `$0 = u + w$` forces `$u = -w$` into the intersection and hence to `$0$`. No simpler test exists, and it is the workhorse of every dimension-addition argument.
concepts.detail: Axler stresses the analogy: disjointness of sets becomes trivial intersection, because two subspaces can never be disjoint as both hold `$0$`.

concepts.term: Pairwise trivial meets are not enough
concepts.statement: With three or more summands it is **not enough** that each pair meets trivially, as Axler’s `pairwarn` nonexample 1.44 shows with `$V_{1}$` the `$xy$`-plane, `$V_{2}$` the `$z$`-axis and `$V_{3}$` the diagonal `$\{(0, y, y)\}$`. All three pairwise intersections equal `$\{0\}$`, yet `$0 = (0, 1, 0) + (0, 0, 1) + (0, -1, -1)$` is a second zero-writing alongside all zeros. The moral is to test the full sum against 1.45 rather than testing pairs.
concepts.detail: The three subspaces still sum to all of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`, since `$(x, y, z) = (x, y, 0) + (0, 0, z) + (0, 0, 0)$`, so spanning does not imply directness.

concepts.term: Model direct sums: planes, lines and axes
concepts.statement: The **models** to memorize are `$\mathbb{F}^{3} = U \oplus W$` with `$U = \{(x, y, 0)\}$` and `$W = \{(0, 0, z)\}$` from 1.42, and `$\mathbb{F}^{n} = V_{1} \oplus \cdots \oplus V_{n}$` with `$V_{k}$` nonzero only in slot `$k$` from 1.43, the `axesum` pair. Each coordinate lands in exactly one summand, which makes both the spanning and the uniqueness visible at a glance. Every abstract direct sum behaves like these coordinate models after a choice of bases.
concepts.detail: Verifying 1.42 means splitting `$(x, y, z) = (x, y, 0) + (0, 0, z)$` and noting only `$0$` lies in both parts.

examples.title: Split every vector of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$` along a plane and a line
examples.problem: With `$U = \{(x, y, 0)\}$` and `$W = \{(0, 0, z)\}$` in `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`, prove `$\mathbb{F}^{3} = U \oplus W$` (Axler 1.42) and test the splitting on `$(4, 5, 6)$`.

steps.label: Step 1: Split an arbitrary vector
steps.text: Write `$(x, y, z) = (x, y, 0) + (0, 0, z)$`, with the first piece in `$U$` and the second in `$W$`. Hence every vector of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$` is a sum, so `$\mathbb{F}^{3} = U + W$`.

steps.label: Step 2: Check the intersection and confirm by script
steps.text:
```python
v = (4, 5, 6)
u = (v[0], v[1], 0)
w = (0, 0, v[2])
print(u, w)  # (4, 5, 0) (0, 0, 6)
print(u[0]+w[0], u[1]+w[1], u[2]+w[2])  # 4 5 6
```
A vector in both `$U$` and `$W$` has the form `$(0, 0, 0)$` only, so `$U \cap W = \{0\}$`, and the script rebuilds `$(4, 5, 6)$` from its two pieces.

steps.label: Step 3: Conclude directness
steps.text: By 1.46 the trivial intersection makes the sum direct, so `$\mathbb{F}^{3} = U \oplus W$`. The decomposition above is therefore the only one possible.

examples.result: `$\mathbb{F}^{3} = U \oplus W$`, with `$(4, 5, 6) = (4, 5, 0) + (0, 0, 6)$` as the unique splitting.

examples.title: Three subspaces that sum to `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$` but not directly
examples.problem: With `$V_{1} = \{(x, y, 0)\}$`, `$V_{2} = \{(0, 0, z)\}$` and `$V_{3} = \{(0, y, y)\}$` in `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`, show the sum is all of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$` yet not a direct sum (Axler 1.44).

steps.label: Step 2: Exhibit two zero-writings
steps.text: The zero vector splits trivially as `$(0, 0, 0) + (0, 0, 0) + (0, 0, 0)$`, but also as `$(0, 1, 0) + (0, 0, 1) + (0, -1, -1)$`, and each piece lies in the matching subspace. Two writs of `$0$` violate 1.45.

steps.label: Step 3: Draw the lesson
steps.text: All three pairwise intersections are `$\{0\}$`, yet the triple sum is not direct. Pairwise tests never suffice beyond two summands.

examples.result: The sum is `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$` but not `$V_{1} \oplus V_{2} \oplus V_{3}$`, since `$0$` decomposes in two ways.

keyTakeaways: A sum is direct exactly when every vector, equivalently `$0$` alone, decomposes in only one way.
`$U + W$` is direct if and only if `$U \cap W = \{0\}$`.
Pairwise trivial intersections do not make a triple sum direct, as Axler 1.44 shows.
Coordinate planes, lines and axes are the models every direct sum imitates.

quiz.q: What does `$V_{1} \oplus \cdots \oplus V_{m}$` assert beyond `$V_{1} + \cdots + V_{m}$`?
options: The summands are pairwise disjoint as sets
Each element has exactly one representation `$v_{1} + \cdots + v_{m}$`
Each summand equals the whole space
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The plain sum only promises existence of a decomposition. Step 2: The circled plus adds uniqueness for every vector. Step 3: Disjointness is impossible since all parts share `$0$`. Step 4: So the extra content is exactly the one-way splitting.

quiz.q: For subspaces `$U$` and `$W$`, `$U + W$` is a direct sum exactly when which condition holds?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: This is the two-subspace test of 1.46. Step 2: A shared nonzero `$v$` builds the rival writing `$0 = v + (-v)$`. Step 3: Conversely `$0 = u + w$` pushes `$u$` into the intersection. Step 4: Trivial intersection is therefore equivalent to directness.

quiz.q: In Axler 1.44, why is `$V_{1} + V_{2} + V_{3}$` not a direct sum of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`?
options: The three subspaces fail to span `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`
One of the three is not a subspace
The pairwise intersections are all nonzero
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Spanning holds, so existence is not the issue. Step 2: Each piece of the displayed sum lies in its matching subspace. Step 3: Together with all zeros this gives two writings of `$0$`. Step 4: By 1.45 the sum is not direct despite trivial pairwise meets.

quiz.q: Axler writes `$\mathbb{F}^{n} = V_{1} \oplus \cdots \oplus V_{n}$` with `$V_{k}$` nonzero only in slot `$k$`. What makes this a direct sum?
options: Each coordinate belongs to exactly one summand, fixing the splitting
The union of the `$V_{k}$` already equals `$\mathbb{F}^{n}$`
Summation order can be rearranged freely
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Slot `$k$` of a vector can only come from `$V_{k}$`. Step 2: That pins every summand of every decomposition. Step 3: Spanning is clear since coordinates assemble the vector. Step 4: Pinned pieces plus spanning give the unique splitting.

intro: Functions and polynomials are vectors too, with addition and scaling performed pointwise and coefficient by coefficient. Classical calculus facts such as the continuity of sums become subspace statements, and a degree cap turns polynomials into finite-dimensional spaces. The section closes with a first glimpse of quotients, where a whole subspace is collapsed to a single zero.
objectives: Verify function subspaces such as continuous, differentiable and vanishing-at-a-point families
Work inside `$\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})$` and `$\mathcal{P}_{m}(\mathbb{F})$` using degree arithmetic
Describe cosets `$v + U$` and preview the quotient collapse of `$U$` to zero

concepts.statement: For a set `$S$`, the **function space** `$\mathbb{F}^{S}$` holds all functions `$S \to \mathbb{F}$`, added and scaled **pointwise** by `$(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$` and `$(af)(x) = a f(x)$`, the `funcspace` convention of Axler 1B. Pointwise rules inherit every vector axiom from `$\mathbb{F}$` at each input separately. A function is therefore an `$S$`-tuple with possibly infinitely many coordinates.
concepts.detail: Axler writes `$\mathbb{R}^{[0, 1]}$` for real functions on the unit interval and `$\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}}$` for all real functions of a real variable.

concepts.statement: A **polynomial** with coefficients in `$\mathbb{F}$` is a function `$p(z) = a_{0} + a_{1}z + \cdots + a_{m}z^{m}$`, its **degree** is the top index with `$a_{m} \ne 0$`, and `$\mathcal{P}_{m}(\mathbb{F})$` keeps degrees at most `$m$`, the `polydeg` trio of Axler 2.10 through 2.12. Sums and scalings never raise the degree, so each `$\mathcal{P}_{m}(\mathbb{F})$` is a subspace while the exact-degree set is not. The full `$\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})$` is infinite-dimensional, the first example at 2.14.
concepts.detail: The zero polynomial gets degree `$-\infty$` by convention so that degree arithmetic never breaks on it.

concepts.statement: **Continuous** real functions on `$[0, 1]$` form a subspace of `$\mathbb{R}^{[0, 1]}$`, differentiable functions on `$\mathbb{R}$` form a subspace of `$\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}}$`, and `$\{f : f^{\prime}(2) = b\}$` is a subspace only for `$b = 0$`, the `calcsub` list of Axler 1.35. Each claim reuses one calculus linearity fact: sums of continuous functions are continuous and derivatives scale by constants. Analysis supplies the closure proofs while algebra supplies the frame.
concepts.detail: Verifying the differentiable case uses that `$(cf)^{\prime} = c f^{\prime}$` for constants `$c$`, exactly the scaling law in disguise.

concepts.statement: The set of complex **null sequences**, those with limit `$0$`, is a subspace of `$\mathbb{C}^{\infty}$`, the `nullseq` example 1.35. Limits add and scale, so the defining property survives both operations. Sequence spaces are the natural habitat of shift operators, which return as invertibility counterexamples in Chapter 19.
concepts.detail: Convergence to `$0$` is a homogeneous condition, so the shifted family with limit `$b \ne 0$` fails exactly like every shifted hyperplane.

concepts.statement: The **coset** `$v + U = \{v + u : u \in U\}$` translates a subspace, and the **quotient** identifies each coset with one point, collapsing all of `$U$` to a single zero, the `coset` preview of Chapter 19. Two vectors share a coset exactly when their difference lies in `$U$`. Dimension drops by `$\dim U$`, so quotients count what remains after ignoring `$U$`.
concepts.detail: Modulo the `$z$`-axis, the vectors `$(1, 2, 3)$` and `$(1, 2, 7)$` name the same coset since their difference `$(0, 0, -4)$` lies in the axis.

figures.caption: Two real functions `$f$` and `$g$` with their pointwise sum `$f + g$`: addition in `$\mathbb{R}^{[0, 1]}$` happens one input at a time, exactly like adding coordinates.

examples.title: Functions vanishing at zero form a subspace
examples.problem: Prove `$U = \{f \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}} : f(0) = 0\}$` is a subspace of `$\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}}$` by checking the three conditions directly.

steps.label: Step 1: Check the zero function
steps.text: The zero function `$z(x) = 0$` satisfies `$z(0) = 0$`, so `$z \in U$` and `$U$` is nonempty with its identity present. The homogeneous value `$0$` on the right is doing all the work.

steps.label: Step 2: Close under addition and scaling, with a numeric check
Step 3: Conclude
steps.text: All three conditions hold with the inherited operations, so `$U$` is a subspace. Replacing `$0$` by any nonzero value would break the argument at once.

examples.result: `$U$` is a subspace of `$\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}}$`, since vanishing at `$0$` is a homogeneous linear condition.

examples.title: Degree caps are subspaces, exact degrees are not
examples.problem: Show `$\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$` is a subspace of `$\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$`, but the set `$E$` of polynomials of degree exactly `$2$` is not.

steps.label: Step 1: Verify the cap
steps.text: Adding two polynomials of degree at most `$2$` cannot create `$x^{3}$` terms, and scaling never raises degree. The zero polynomial qualifies, so `$\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$` passes all three checks.

steps.label: Step 2: Break the exact-degree set twice
steps.text: The zero polynomial has no degree `$2$`, so `$0 \notin E$`. Worse, `$x^{2} + x$` and `$-x^{2} + 1$` both lie in `$E$` while their sum `$x + 1$` drops to degree `$1$`, breaking closure under addition.

steps.label: Step 3: Name the pattern
steps.text: At-most conditions are homogeneous and survive, while exact-equality conditions shatter under addition. Degree caps behave like the `$b = 0$` hyperplanes of the previous section.

examples.result: `$\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$` is a subspace; the exact-degree set `$E$` fails the zero test and the sum test.

keyTakeaways: Function spaces add and scale pointwise, making each input behave like one coordinate.
Degree caps `$\mathcal{P}_{m}(\mathbb{F})$` are subspaces while exact-degree sets are not.
Continuity, differentiability and null limits are homogeneous, hence subspace-forming, conditions.
Cosets `$v + U$` preview quotients, where `$U$` collapses to zero and dimension drops.

quiz.q: What are the operations on the function space `$\mathbb{R}^{[0, 1]}$`?
options: Pointwise addition and pointwise scalar multiplication
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Axler defines `$(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$` for every input `$x$`. Step 2: Scaling is likewise `$(af)(x) = a f(x)$` at each point. Step 3: Composition and convolution are different operations with different theories. Step 4: So the vector structure is purely pointwise.

quiz.q: Which polynomial set is a subspace of `$\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$`?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The cap keeps degrees at most `$2$` under sums and scalings. Step 2: Exact degree `$2$` loses `$0$` and breaks under `$x^{2} + (-x^{2}) = 0$`. Step 3: Fixed leading coefficients break under addition of two such polynomials. Step 4: The value condition at `$0$` is a nonzero shift, failing the zero test.

quiz.q: Why do continuous functions on `$[0, 1]$` form a subspace of `$\mathbb{R}^{[0, 1]}$`?
options: Every continuous function is a polynomial
Continuity is preserved under sums and scalar multiples
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Sums of continuous functions are continuous by basic analysis. Step 2: Scalar multiples preserve continuity the same way. Step 3: The zero function is continuous, completing the three checks. Step 4: Finiteness of the interval and differentiability play no role.

quiz.q: Two vectors share the coset `$v + U$` exactly when which relation holds?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Write the cosets as `$v + U$` and `$w + U$`. Step 2: Equality means `$w = v + u$` for some `$u \in U$`. Step 3: Rearranging gives `$w - v = u \in U$`. Step 4: So coset membership tests differences, not sums.

intro: The span of a list is the set of all its linear combinations, the smallest subspace containing the list. A list is independent when only the trivial combination gives zero, and the Linear Dependence Lemma pinpoints the first vector that leans on its predecessors. The workhorse inequality then says an independent list can never outgrow a spanning list.
objectives: Form spans of lists and test whether a target vector lies in a given span
Apply the Linear Dependence Lemma to locate the first redundant vector of a list
Use the length inequality to bound independent lists by spanning lists

concepts.statement: A **linear combination** of `$v_{1}, \ldots, v_{m}$` is any `$a_{1}v_{1} + \cdots + a_{m}v_{m}$` with scalars `$a_{k} \in \mathbb{F}$`, and the **span** is the set of all of them, the `lincomb` pair of Axler 2A. The span of the empty list is `$\{0\}$` by convention, since no combination can produce anything else. Spans are tailor-made subspaces: every span is a subspace, and it is the smallest one holding the list.
concepts.detail: To test membership, write the target as a combination with unknown scalars and solve; inconsistency means the target lies outside the span.

concepts.term: Span is the smallest containing subspace
concepts.statement: The **span** of a list is the smallest subspace containing every vector of the list, so any subspace holding the list must swallow all their combinations too. A list **spans** `$V$` when its span equals `$V$`, which says every vector of `$V$` is reachable as some combination. The `spanmin` slogan is that spanning means reachable and minimality means nothing smaller suffices.
concepts.detail: The standard basis spans `$\mathbb{F}^{n}$` because `$(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}) = x_{1}e_{1} + \cdots + x_{n}e_{n}$` reaches every list.

concepts.statement: A list `$v_{1}, \ldots, v_{m}$` is **linearly independent** when the only scalars with `$a_{1}v_{1} + \cdots + a_{m}v_{m} = 0$` are `$a_{1} = \cdots = a_{m} = 0$`, the `indep` definition 2.15. A list is **linearly dependent** when it is not independent, which is 2.17. Independence says no vector is wasted; dependence says at least one vector leans on the others.
concepts.detail: Any list containing `$0$` is dependent, and any list with a repeated vector is dependent, since `$1v + (-1)v = 0$` is then nontrivial.

concepts.statement: If `$v_{1}, \ldots, v_{m}$` is dependent, then some `$v_{j}$` lies in the span of the earlier vectors `$v_{1}, \ldots, v_{j-1}$`, and deleting that `$v_{j}$` leaves the span unchanged, the `deplemma` numbered 2.19 with its span-preserving sequel 2.20. The proof takes a shortest nontrivial relation and solves for its last nonzero coefficient. Choosing the **smallest** such `$j$` makes the earlier vectors independent, which is exactly how redundancy gets isolated.
concepts.detail: Axler 2.21 runs this on four vectors of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`, finding the first one that leans on its predecessors.

concepts.term: Independent lists never outgrow spanning lists
concepts.statement: In a finite-dimensional space the length of every independent list is **at most** the length of every spanning list, the `lenineq` numbered 2.22. Hence no list longer than three is independent in `$\mathbb{R}^{3}$` and no list shorter than four spans `$\mathbb{R}^{4}$`, the 2.23 and 2.24 corollaries. The proof repeatedly swaps spanning vectors for independent ones via the lemma, and the swap must terminate because the spanning list is finite.
concepts.detail: This single inequality forces all bases to share one length, which is how dimension becomes well defined in the next section.

figures.caption: The span of `$v_{1}$` and `$v_{2}$` is the full plane they grid, while `$v_{3} = v_{1} + v_{2}$` leans on them and adds nothing new to the span.

examples.title: A dependent triple in `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`, exposed
examples.problem: Show `$(2, 3, 1)$`, `$(1, -1, 2)$`, `$(7, 3, 8)$` is linearly dependent in `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$` by finding an explicit relation (Axler 2.18), and confirm it by script.

steps.label: Step 1: Propose unknown scalars
steps.text: Seek `$a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}$`, not all zero, with `$a_{1}(2, 3, 1) + a_{2}(1, -1, 2) + a_{3}(7, 3, 8) = (0, 0, 0)$`. Three vectors in `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$` need not be dependent, so the relation must be earned, not assumed.

steps.label: Step 2: Verify the relation by script
steps.text:
```python
a1, a2, a3 = 2, 3, -1
v1 = (2, 3, 1)
v2 = (1, -1, 2)
v3 = (7, 3, 8)
combo = tuple(a1*x + a2*y + a3*z for x, y, z in zip(v1, v2, v3))
print(combo)  # (0, 0, 0)
```
The coefficients `$2, 3, -1$` combine the three vectors to `$0$` coordinate by coordinate, and the script checks all three slots at once.

steps.label: Step 3: Read the lemma’s conclusion
steps.text: Since `$2(2, 3, 1) + 3(1, -1, 2) - (7, 3, 8) = 0$`, the third vector equals `$2v_{1} + 3v_{2}$` and lies in the span of its predecessors. Deleting it keeps the span by 2.20.

examples.result: The triple is dependent with relation `$2v_{1} + 3v_{2} - v_{3} = 0$`, so `$v_{3}$` is redundant.

examples.title: Find the first redundant vector in `$\mathbb{F}^{2}$`
examples.problem: In `$\mathbb{F}^{2}$`, consider `$(1, 0)$`, `$(0, 1)$`, `$(1, 1)$`. Use the length inequality to predict dependence, then locate the smallest leaning index.

steps.label: Step 1: Invoke the length bound
steps.text: The list `$(1, 0)$`, `$(0, 1)$` already spans `$\mathbb{F}^{2}$` with length two, so by 2.22 no list of length three is independent. Dependence is guaranteed before any arithmetic.

steps.label: Step 2: Test each prefix
steps.text: The first vector alone is independent, and the pair `$(1, 0)$`, `$(0, 1)$` is independent since `$a(1, 0) + b(0, 1) = (a, b) = 0$` forces `$a = b = 0$`. The third vector is the first candidate for leaning.

steps.label: Step 3: Write the dependency
steps.text: Indeed `$(1, 1) = (1, 0) + (0, 1)$`, so `$j = 3$` is the smallest leaning index and deleting `$(1, 1)$` preserves the span. The lemma’s smallest-`$j$` clause is sharp here.

examples.result: The list is dependent with smallest leaning index `$j = 3$`, since `$(1, 1)$` is the sum of its predecessors.

keyTakeaways: The span is the set of all linear combinations and the smallest subspace holding the list.
Independence means only the trivial combination gives `$0$`; any `$0$` or repeat forces dependence.
The Dependence Lemma puts a redundant vector in the span of its predecessors without shrinking the span.
Independent lists are bounded by spanning lists, so `$\mathbb{R}^{3}$` holds no independent four-list.

quiz.q: Which vector lies in the span of `$(1, 0)$` and `$(0, 1)$` in `$\mathbb{F}^{2}$`?
options: No vector with both coordinates nonzero
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The span holds all `$a(1, 0) + b(0, 1) = (a, b)$`. Step 2: Every pair `$(a, b)$` arises this way, so the span is all of `$\mathbb{F}^{2}$`. Step 3: In particular `$(3, -4) = 3(1, 0) - 4(0, 1)$`. Step 4: The remaining options confuse span with the bare list.

quiz.q: A list `$v_{1}, \ldots, v_{m}$` is linearly independent when which statement holds?
options: The list spans the whole space
The list contains the zero vector
quiz.explanation: Step 1: This is the definition 2.15 verbatim. Step 2: A nontrivial killing relation is dependence, not independence. Step 3: Spanning is a separate property about reachability. Step 4: Containing `$0$` forces dependence, the opposite claim.

quiz.q: The Dependence Lemma says a dependent list has which feature?
options: Some `$v_{j}$` lies in the span of `$v_{1}, \ldots, v_{j-1}$`
It must contain exactly one redundant vector
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Take a shortest nontrivial relation killing the list. Step 2: Its last nonzero coefficient lets you solve for that vector. Step 3: All other vectors in the relation precede it. Step 4: Deleting it keeps the span, confirming genuine redundancy.

quiz.q: Why is no list of length four independent in `$\mathbb{R}^{3}$`?
options: The standard basis has length three and spans, so 2.22 caps independence at three
Independence is undefined beyond length three
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The standard triple spans `$\mathbb{R}^{3}$` with length three. Step 2: The length inequality 2.22 bounds every independent list by every spanning list. Step 3: Hence independent lists have length at most three. Step 4: This is Axler’s example 2.23 exactly.

intro: A basis is an independent spanning list, the minimal skeleton that coordinatizes the whole space. Every spanning list trims down to a basis and every independent list extends to one, so bases are never in short supply. The miracle is that all bases share one length, and that invariant length is the dimension.
objectives: Test bases with the unique-representation criterion and write coordinates in a basis
Trim spanning lists to bases and extend independent lists to bases
Compute dimensions of `$\mathbb{F}^{n}$`, `$\mathcal{P}_{m}(\mathbb{F})$` and `$\{0\}$`, and split spaces as `$V = U \oplus W$`

concepts.statement: A **basis** of `$V$` is a list that is linearly independent and spans `$V$`, the `basis` definition 2.26. The **standard basis** `$e_{1}, \ldots, e_{n}$` of `$\mathbb{F}^{n}$` has `$1$` in slot `$k$` and `$0$` elsewhere, as in 2.27. Bases are the coordinate systems of linear algebra: fix one and every vector becomes a unique coefficient list.
concepts.detail: The lists `$1, z, \ldots, z^{m}$` form a basis of `$\mathcal{P}_{m}(\mathbb{F})$`, and `$1, z, z^{2}, \ldots$` is not a basis of `$\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{F})$` in the finite-list sense without care.

concepts.statement: A list is a basis if and only if every `$v \in V$` has **exactly one** representation `$v = a_{1}v_{1} + \cdots + a_{n}v_{n}$`, the `basiscrit` numbered 2.28. Spanning gives existence while independence gives uniqueness, so the criterion fuses the two defining properties. Coordinates are well defined precisely because of this result.
concepts.detail: Two rival writings would subtract to a nontrivial relation killing the list, contradicting independence.

concepts.term: Trimming to a basis and extending to one
concepts.statement: Every **spanning list trims** to a basis by deleting leaning vectors one at a time, which is 2.30, and every **independent list extends** to a basis by adjoining spanning vectors that keep independence, which is 2.32. Hence every finite-dimensional space **has** a basis, which is 2.31. The `trimtext` pair means bases can be built from above or from below.
concepts.detail: Axler 2.32 extends `$(2, 3, 4)$`, `$(9, 6, 8)$` with `$(0, 1, 0)$` to a basis of `$\mathbb{F}^{3}$`, a model extension to imitate.

concepts.statement: The **dimension** `$\dim V$` is the length of any basis, well defined because 2C proves all bases share one length, the `dimdef` invariant. Consequently `$\dim \mathbb{F}^{n} = n$`, `$\dim \mathcal{P}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) = m + 1$` and `$\dim \{0\} = 0$`. Dimension turns structural questions into integer comparisons, which is the engine of every rank argument later.
concepts.detail: The empty list is a basis of `$\{0\}$`, which is why the zero space has dimension zero rather than one.

concepts.statement: Every subspace of a finite-dimensional space is **finite-dimensional**, with dimension at most the parent’s, which is 2.25. Moreover each subspace `$U$` pairs with some `$W$` so that `$V = U \oplus W$`, the `subdim` complement 2.33 built by extending a basis of `$U$`. Dimension therefore adds across complements: `$\dim V = \dim U + \dim W$`.
concepts.detail: The complement is not unique: a line in the plane pairs with any other line through the origin except itself.
