examples.title: Build a room chat round trip
examples.problem: A study room needs instant messages both ways with join, broadcast, and clean leave handling.

steps.label: Step 1: Connect and join
Step 2: Receive and send
Step 3: Leave cleanly
steps.text: Call close with a normal code on view teardown and remove the socket from the room map server side. Freed slots keep presence accurate.

examples.result: Members see each post near instantly with correct presence and no leaked waits.

examples.title: Fan out game moves fairly
examples.problem: A quiz game must broadcast each move to all players without polling delays or duplicate delivery.

steps.label: Step 1: Publish one frame
steps.text:
```bash
# server fans one publish to room members
# room-7 members: 24 sockets share one move frame
```
One publish fans out to the whole room in one server action.

steps.label: Step 2: Order with sequence
steps.text: Stamp each move with a room sequence so late joiners sort correctly. Clients ignore replays below their high water mark.

steps.label: Step 3: Guard overload
steps.text: Throttle move rate per socket and queue per reader to bound memory. Loud clients cannot stall the room.

examples.result: All players share one ordered move stream with bounded server cost.

keyTakeaways: An Upgrade handshake promotes HTTP into a persistent frame pipe.
Either side may send frames at any time with low overhead.
Browser sockets need open guarded sends and explicit closes.
Servers add rooms, broadcast, history, and backpressure for real rooms.

quiz.q: What does the WebSocket handshake accomplish?
options: It upgrades a plain HTTP connection into a persistent bidirectional pipe
quiz.explanation: Step 1: It starts as HTTP. Step 2: Upgrade asks to switch. Step 3: Acceptance promotes the wire. Step 4: Frames then flow freely.

quiz.q: When may each side send a frame?
options: At any time after open without reasking
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The pipe stays open. Step 2: No ask precedes each write. Step 3: Both directions interleave. Step 4: Hence real time conversation works.

quiz.q: Why guard browser sends on open state?
options: Early sends before open would be lost, so queue until ready
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Construction is async. Step 2: Open fires when ready. Step 3: Prior writes have no pipe. Step 4: Queueing preserves first messages.

quiz.q: A chat needs rooms, presence, and history across drops. What must the server add beyond raw pipes?
options: Room maps plus broadcast plus backlog replay with identity resume
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Pipes alone lack groups. Step 2: Room maps track members. Step 3: Broadcast fans publishes. Step 4: Backlog plus identity heal drops.

intro: Polling, streams, and sockets all work, but they cost very different amounts at scale. This section selects by direction, latency budget, audience size, and operational appetite. You will defend the cheapest sufficient choice and know exactly what would force an upgrade.
objectives: Compare polling, streams, and sockets by direction and latency
Size audience and frequency costs before committing to pipes
State upgrade triggers that move a feed up the ladder

concepts.statement: Choose by **direction** first using `one way` versus two way need. Read only news fits streams while conversational rooms need `sockets`, and rare reads fit plain ticks. Direction eliminates two of three options before any tuning.
concepts.detail: Ask whether clients publish through the same channel since yes forces sockets immediately.

concepts.statement: A **latency** budget names the oldest acceptable `news` in seconds. Minute tolerance admits polling, second tolerance favors streams, and sub second interaction demands `sockets`. Budgets turn taste debates into measurable thresholds.
concepts.detail: Write the budget as a number in the ticket and test worst case lag against it under load.

concepts.statement: Multiply **audience** by update `frequency` to size hits, streams, or frame rate. Polling cost scales with ticks times viewers while broadcast streams share one write across many readers. Math reveals when cheap per unit choices become expensive in aggregate.
concepts.detail: Estimate peak viewers times peak rate and compare polling hits against one broadcast fan out.

concepts.statement: Each rung adds **operations** burden from plain `HTTP` to held streams to stateful socket fleets. Polling needs only endpoints, streams need held connections, and sockets need rooms plus sticky routing plus `scale` out. Appetite for on call complexity should match product need.
concepts.detail: Start on the lowest rung that meets direction plus latency and climb only on measured pain.

concepts.statement: Protocol **push** for assets differs from `live` data pushes for app state. Early HTTP versions could push files the browser would soon ask for, which helped page speed but never delivered app events. Do not confuse asset push with streams or `sockets` for live features.
concepts.detail: Treat asset push as page optimization history and choose streams or sockets for live app data.

examples.title: Keep a dashboard on ticks
examples.problem: A fleet dashboard with hundreds of viewers tolerates thirty second data and must minimize operations.

steps.label: Step 1: Check direction and budget
Step 2: Size the tick
steps.text: Four hundred viewers times two asks per minute is eight hundred hits per minute of cheap cached reads. No held connections or room state is needed.

steps.label: Step 3: Record the trigger
steps.text: Note that sub five second alerts or tenfold audience growth would force a move to streams. Until then ticks stay cheapest.

examples.result: Ticks meet the contract with trivial operations and a written upgrade trigger.

examples.title: Move a live scoreboard to streams
examples.problem: A scoreboard with thousands of readers needs second level goals but no fan posting.

steps.label: Step 1: Rule out sockets
steps.text:
```bash
# direction: server to screen only
# budget: about one second
# audience: thousands of readers
```
One way plus second budget plus large audience favors broadcast streams.

steps.label: Step 2: Broadcast once
steps.text: One server write fans to thousands of open streams instead of thousands of ticks hammering the endpoint. Frequency spikes cost one frame, not a storm.

steps.label: Step 3: Keep sockets in reserve
steps.text: Chat beside the scores would still need sockets, but scores alone do not pay that tax. Split features by direction rather than bundling.

examples.result: Streams deliver second level scores to crowds with one broadcast per event.

keyTakeaways: Direction decides first: read only to streams or ticks, converse to sockets.
Latency budgets of minutes, seconds, or instant map to ticks, streams, or sockets.
Audience times frequency math exposes when cheap units turn costly.
Asset push history must not be confused with live app data channels.

quiz.q: Which need forces sockets over streams?
options: Clients must publish through the same live channel
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Streams flow one way. Step 2: Publishing needs the reverse path. Step 3: Sockets provide both ways. Step 4: Therefore converse features force sockets.

quiz.q: A feed tolerates minute old data for a small team. What fits?
options: Simple interval polling on cached reads
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Budget is loose. Step 2: Audience is small. Step 3: Ticks meet both cheaply. Step 4: Heavier pipes add needless ops.

quiz.q: Why multiply audience by frequency?
options: To size aggregate load and compare ticks versus one broadcast
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Unit cost misleads. Step 2: Aggregate reveals storms. Step 3: Broadcast shares writes. Step 4: Math picks the cheaper shape.

quiz.q: What is the disciplined upgrade rule?
options: Start on the cheapest rung meeting direction plus latency, climb only on measured pain with a recorded trigger
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Name direction plus budget. Step 2: Pick cheapest fit. Step 3: Record what breaks it. Step 4: Climb only when measures trip the trigger.

intro: Clients and servers trade contact lists, orders, and settings as text long before they render a pixel. This section compares delimited, markup, and object notations for structure, size, and parsing. You will choose the leanest safe encoding and validate it against a schema.
objectives: Contrast flat delimited rows with nested markup and object trees
Parse safely with DOM versus streaming versus native object tools
Validate payloads against schemas before trusting their shape

concepts.statement: Comma separated **values** encode rows with line breaks and `comma` split columns. An optional first row names fields for human clarity. The shape suits simple tables but collapses on nested or optional structure.
concepts.detail: Use CSV for flat exports with stable columns and quote fields that contain separators or line breaks.

concepts.statement: The **markup** language wraps data in `elements` plus attributes you define yourself. One `root` holds nested children such as grouped address parts, which flat rows cannot express. Namespaces plus schemas plus validators make cross service contracts explicit.
concepts.detail: Define element vocabularies per domain and validate inbound documents before mapping them to app objects.

concepts.statement: A **DOM** parser builds a `tree` for random access at memory cost, while a streaming parser fires `events` while walking once. Trees suit small to medium documents with cross references, while event walks suit huge feeds that never fit comfortably in memory. Libraries exist per language so hand parsing is rarely needed.
concepts.detail: Choose tree parsing for small config style files and event parsing for large feeds processed in order.

concepts.statement: Object **notation** uses braces plus quoted `keys` plus colon values with arrays for lists. Strings plus numbers plus booleans plus nested objects cover most web payloads without open and close tag weight. Native `parse` plus direct embedding make browser handling almost free.
concepts.detail: Prefer JSON for browser APIs and config where human readability plus tiny size plus native parsing all matter.

concepts.statement: A **schema** states required `properties` plus types plus nesting rules for a family of documents. Validators reject malformed payloads at the boundary before faulty data poisons logic. Both markup and object worlds offer schema dialects with the same gatekeeping role.
concepts.detail: Check every inbound payload against its schema in tests and at runtime boundaries, failing closed on mismatch.

examples.title: Trade contacts as flat rows
examples.problem: A newsletter tool needs a tiny export of names plus phones plus mails with no nesting.

steps.text:
```csv
firstname,lastname,phone,email
John,Doe,01234567,john@example.com
Paula,Doe,01234567,paula@example.com
```
Line breaks split records while commas split fields with an optional header row.

steps.label: Step 2: Read with a library
steps.text: Split lines then fields with a tested CSV reader that honors quotes and escapes. Hand splitting breaks on quoted commas.

steps.label: Step 3: Know the ceiling
steps.text: Adding grouped addresses or optional nested parts forces a move to markup or object trees. Flat rows cannot grow nesting without hacks.

examples.result: Flat contact exports stay tiny and readable until nesting requirements force a richer shape.

examples.title: Exchange nested contacts safely
examples.problem: A service must send grouped address parts with typed numbers and validate shape before processing.

steps.label: Step 1: Encode as objects
Step 2: Validate the shape
steps.text: Check required keys plus value types against a shared schema before mapping to domain objects. Reject mismatches closed with a clear error.

steps.label: Step 3: Choose markup when needed
steps.text:
```html
<!-- markup alternative with custom elements -->
<!-- contacts root, contact child, address group -->
```
Markup suits extensible cross service vocabularies with namespaces and mixed content.

examples.result: Nested contacts travel leanly as objects with schema gates, with markup reserved for extensible contracts.

keyTakeaways: CSV suits flat stable tables while nesting needs markup or object trees.
Trees give random access at memory cost while event walks stream huge files.
JSON pairs lean syntax with native browser parsing for web APIs.
Schemas plus validators reject malformed payloads at the boundary.

quiz.q: When does CSV suffice?
options: Deeply nested documents with optional groups
Flat tables with stable columns and no nesting
quiz.explanation: Step 1: CSV has rows plus separators only. Step 2: It lacks nesting. Step 3: Stable flat tables fit that shape. Step 4: Richer needs force other formats.

quiz.q: What distinguishes tree parsing from event parsing?
options: Tree builds a full model for random access while events walk once with low memory
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Trees hold the whole model. Step 2: That enables jumps but costs memory. Step 3: Events fire while walking. Step 4: Walks suit huge ordered feeds.

quiz.q: Why does JSON dominate browser APIs?
options: Lean braces plus native parse plus direct embedding keep it small and easy
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Syntax is compact. Step 2: No closing tags bloat size. Step 3: Browsers parse natively. Step 4: Together they lower cost and code.

quiz.q: A payload gains grouped optional address parts. What is the principled move?
options: Cram nesting into flat rows with hacks
Move to a nested tree shape with a schema and validate at the boundary
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Flat rows cannot express groups. Step 2: Trees model nesting naturally. Step 3: Schemas state the contract. Step 4: Validators enforce it before logic runs.

intro: Photos, logos, animations, and diagrams each punish the wrong encoding with bloat or blur. This section tours photographic, graphic, animated, vector, and modern unified formats. You will match color depth, transparency, animation, and scaling needs to the right container.
objectives: Separate photographic lossy needs from graphic lossless needs
Compare palette limits, transparency, and animation support
Explain vector scaling and modern unified compression

concepts.statement: The **photo** format compresses continuous tone images with `lossy` tuned quality. Millions of colors survive while file size falls as quality drops, which suits camera shots with gradients. Sharp text plus flat logos blur and band under the same treatment.
concepts.detail: Export photos at the lowest quality that still looks clean at display size and keep a lossless master.

concepts.statement: The **palette** format caps images at `256` colors for crisp flat areas. Small logos plus icons compress well while photos posterize, and frame sequences enable simple `animation`. Basic transparency is binary rather than smooth.
concepts.detail: Reserve this format for tiny flat animations and move rich motion to video or modern containers.

concepts.statement: Portable **graphics** span palette plus true color plus `alpha` depths. Eight bit mode mirrors palette economy for flat art while twenty four bit mode covers photos without loss. An extra channel adds smooth `transparency` levels for overlays and soft edges.
concepts.detail: Use palette mode for flat UI art and true color plus alpha for graphics needing smooth see through.

concepts.statement: Scalable **vectors** describe lines plus curves plus shapes in `XML` text rather than pixels. Any size renders crisply since math redraws the shapes, and style plus `animation` integrate with page code. Logos plus icons plus diagrams thrive as resolution free assets.
concepts.detail: Draw logos and icons as vectors and style them with page styles for theme aware crisp rendering.

concepts.statement: The modern **unified** format offers `lossless` plus lossy modes near a third smaller than older twins. One container covers photos plus graphics plus `transparency` plus animation, which simplifies pipelines. Fallbacks plus support checks still matter for older viewers.
concepts.detail: Serve the modern container first with classic fallbacks and verify support data before relying on it alone.

Step 3: Animate cheaply

keyTakeaways: Continuous tone photos favor tuned lossy compression over lossless weight.
Flat art favors palette or lossless modes with smooth alpha when needed.

quiz.q: Why do photos favor JPG style lossy compression?
options: Photos contain smooth gradients where tuned loss saves bytes invisibly
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Photos hold continuous tone. Step 2: Human eyes forgive tuned loss there. Step 3: Size falls sharply. Step 4: Hence lossy fits photos.

quiz.q: What caps the classic palette animation format?
options: About two hundred fifty six colors with binary transparency
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Palette means indexed color. Step 2: Eight bits allow limited entries. Step 3: Transparency is coarse. Step 4: Photos and soft edges suffer.

quiz.q: What makes vectors resolution free?
options: They store shape math that redraws at any size
quiz.explanation: Step 1: No pixel grid is stored. Step 2: Lines plus curves define art. Step 3: Renderers rasterize per size. Step 4: Edges stay crisp at all scales.

quiz.q: A logo must stay crisp from favicon to billboard with theme tints. What fits best?
options: A single low quality photo export
A palette bitmap with binary transparency
A vector asset styled by page code
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Need spans huge scale range. Step 2: Bitmaps pixelate when enlarged. Step 3: Vectors redraw per size. Step 4: Page styling adds theme tints freely.

intro: Knowing formats is half the job, and choosing between them under size, quality, and support pressure is the other half. This section turns the comparison matrix into decision rules for photos, graphics, transparency, and motion. You will serve responsive images with modern first sources and reliable fallbacks.
objectives: Apply the compression, color, transparency, and animation matrix
Serve responsive sizes with modern first sources and fallbacks
Weigh tooling and support data when adopting new containers

concepts.statement: The **matrix** rows map each format to `compression` plus color depth plus `transparency` plus animation plus scaling. Lossy rows trade quality for bytes while lossless rows preserve edges exactly. Reading across one need at a time yields a shortlist in seconds.
concepts.detail: Filter first by must have features like smooth alpha or motion, then by size among survivors.

concepts.statement: The **quality** dial trades visible fidelity for `bytes` along a curve unique per image. Photo exports fall fast with little visual cost before cliffs appear, while flat art cliffs arrive immediately. Testing at display size finds the knee where savings stop being free.
concepts.detail: Export three quality steps and pick the lowest that still looks clean at real display size.

concepts.statement: Responsive **images** pair `srcset` plus sizes so browsers pick sufficient `pixels` for the slot. Small screens download small files while dense screens get extra density without waste. Art direction variants crop differently per breakpoint when layout demands it.
concepts.detail: Generate two to three widths per image and let the browser match slot plus density automatically.

concepts.statement: A **picture** wrapper lists modern `source` entries before a classic `img` fallback. Capable browsers take the smaller unified file while others ignore unknown types and render the fallback. Support tables plus real device tests gate full reliance on new containers.
concepts.detail: List modern sources first with correct type attributes and always keep a classic fallback image.

concepts.statement: Editors from **Affinity** to free `GIMP` tune exports while vector tools shape logos. Tiny icons may inline as Base sixty four `data` URIs to save requests, which trades cacheability for fewer round trips. Support references confirm which browsers accept each container before launch.
concepts.detail: Inline only sub kilobyte icons as data URIs and keep larger art as cacheable files with far future headers.

keyTakeaways: Filter by must have alpha, motion, and scaling before comparing bytes.
Dial quality at display size to find the knee where savings stop being free.
Responsive widths plus modern first sources cut payloads across devices.
Inline only tiny icons while keeping larger art cacheable with fallbacks.

quiz.q: What is the correct first filter when choosing a format?
options: Must have features like smooth alpha, motion, or scaling
quiz.explanation: Step 1: List hard needs. Step 2: Drop rows lacking them. Step 3: Compare size among survivors. Step 4: Support checks finalize the pick.

quiz.q: How do responsive width sets save bytes?
options: They force desktop files on phones
They let browsers fetch sufficient pixels for slot plus density
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Slots differ by screen. Step 2: Sets offer widths. Step 3: Browsers match need. Step 4: Small screens skip large files.

quiz.q: Why keep a classic fallback beside modern sources?
options: Older viewers ignore unknown types and need a renderable image
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Support varies. Step 2: Unknown types are skipped. Step 3: The fallback renders. Step 4: Coverage stays universal.

quiz.q: A diagram needs crisp edges plus transparency plus huge scale range. What wins?
options: True color plus alpha bitmap only
Vector art with fallback bitmap for ancient viewers
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Scaling demands vectors. Step 2: Edges need lossless shapes. Step 3: Styling handles tints. Step 4: Fallback covers ancient viewers.

intro: Moving pictures and sound turn pages into players with their own controls and tracks. This section wires native video and audio elements with multi source fallbacks and accessible captions. You will configure playback attributes and drive custom controls through a tiny media interface.
objectives: Embed video and audio with native players and fallback sources
Configure autoplay, controls, loop, mute, poster, and preload wisely
Add caption tracks and script custom controls accessibly

concepts.statement: The **video** element renders a built in `player` with timeline plus volume plus fullscreen. A `src` file suffices when one container covers the audience, while nested `source` children offer alternates per browser. Fallback text inside covers viewers without media support.
concepts.detail: Start with one widely supported container and add alternates only for measured gaps in the audience.

concepts.statement: A **container** holds timed media while the `codec` compresses the pictures and sound inside. File extensions name containers while type attributes name the `MIME` contract the browser checks. Matching both avoids downloads that can never play.
concepts.detail: Declare correct MIME types on sources and servers so browsers skip unplayable options without fetching.

concepts.statement: Boolean **attributes** tune `autoplay` plus controls plus loop plus `muted` plus preload plus poster. Controls expose usable chrome,muted plus autoplay satisfy motion policies, and `poster` plus preload shape first paint and data cost. Defaults should respect data, motion, and sound etiquette.
concepts.detail: Avoid autoplay with sound and preload only what the view likely plays to respect data plans.

concepts.statement: The **audio** element mirrors video with a compact `player` for sound only. Multiple `source` children with MIME types cover format splits while controls expose play plus seek plus volume. Scripting uses the same play plus `pause` verbs as video.
concepts.detail: Treat audio configuration like video minus dimensions, with identical fallback and scripting patterns.

concepts.statement: Text **tracks** add captions plus `chapters` for access and navigation. The media interface exposes `play` plus pause plus seek plus volume for custom chrome wired to buttons. Custom controls must stay keyboard reachable with visible focus and labels.
concepts.detail: Ship captions for speech content and mirror every custom button to the underlying media verb with labels.

examples.problem: A course video must play across browsers with captions and a poster before start.

steps.text: ```html ``` The browser picks the first playable MIME while poster paints early.

steps.label: Step 2: Add the caption track

Controls on plus sound restraint plus poster shape usable first paint.
Containers hold media while codecs compress, and types must match both.
Caption tracks plus labeled scripted controls keep media accessible.

quiz.q: How does the browser choose among multiple sources?
options: It downloads all files at once
It picks the first playable MIME type and skips the rest
It picks the largest file always
It asks the user to choose a codec
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Sources list options in order. Step 2: Types declare playability. Step 3: The browser tests each. Step 4: First playable wins.

quiz.q: Why pair autoplay with muted when autoplay is truly needed?
options: Policies allow silent motion while blocking unexpected sound
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Sound on load harms users. Step 2: Browsers gate it. Step 3: Silent motion passes. Step 4: Users then opt into sound.

quiz.q: What do caption tracks add?
options: Accessible speech plus cues plus navigation aid
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Speech needs text form. Step 2: Tracks carry it. Step 3: Viewers read or search it. Step 4: Access plus comprehension rise.

quiz.q: A custom video skin must match native access. What is required?
options: Divs with no labels are enough
Real labeled buttons with focus calling play plus pause plus volume verbs
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Custom chrome replaces native. Step 2: Verbs stay the same. Step 3: Buttons plus labels expose them. Step 4: Focus plus state keep parity.

intro: Every web app splits work between what you see and what persists, but the lines can be drawn in many places. This section layers presentation, logic, persistence, and data so each owns one job. You will place classic server rendering and modern client rendering on the same layered map.
objectives: Name the four classic layers and their single responsibilities
Contrast two tier client server with multi tier decompositions
Place classic versus modern rendering on the layered map

concepts.statement: A **layered** design stacks `presentation` plus logic plus persistence plus data with downward calls only. Presentation owns look plus input, logic owns calculations plus rules, persistence owns database access, and data owns `storage`. Each layer hides its internals behind a narrow contract.
concepts.detail: Enforce downward calls and mock lower layers to test upper layers in isolation.

concepts.statement: The **two tier** core splits `client` frontend from central `server` backend over a network protocol. Clients ask, servers process with files or databases, and answers return to the asker. Either side may itself be layered further without breaking the contract.
concepts.detail: Keep the protocol boundary explicit so web, mobile, and script clients can share one server.

concepts.statement: Multi **tier** growth subdivides client plus `server` into finer physical or logical units. Classic apps split the server into presentation plus business plus persistence plus data, while modern apps move much presentation to the `client`. More tiers add clarity at the cost of more hops.
concepts.detail: Add tiers only when a layer strains ownership and measure hop latency after each split.

concepts.statement: Classic **rendering** builds HTML on the `server` with templates while modern rendering builds it in the `browser` from data. The book shows presentation sliding clientward as single page apps mature, with JSON or markup crossing the wire accordingly. Architecture diagrams must state where HTML birth happens.
concepts.detail: Label who builds HTML in every diagram since caching, SEO, and interactivity all hinge on that choice.

concepts.statement: A **peer** design gives every `node` equal client plus server duties with direct links. No central server exists, which contrasts sharply with the central `server` of client server designs. Web apps rarely choose this shape but should recognize it when integrating decentralized pieces.
concepts.detail: Reserve peer shapes for decentralized sync and keep request response discipline for classic web features.

examples.title: Layer a contacts app
examples.problem: A contacts app mixes SQL inside button handlers and must gain testable boundaries.

steps.label: Step 1: Assign the four jobs
Step 2: Enforce direction
steps.text: Presentation calls logic, logic calls persistence, and persistence touches data. No layer reaches upward for shortcuts.

steps.label: Step 3: Test by layer
steps.text: Mock the store to test validation and mock the table to test the store. Failures point at one layer instead of the whole app.

examples.result: Button code renders and delegates while rules and storage evolve independently with passing tests.

examples.title: Place rendering for a marketing site
examples.problem: A marketing site debates server templates versus a client app and needs the tradeoff stated plainly.

steps.label: Step 1: Map classic flow
steps.text:
```bash
browser asks -> server templates HTML -> browser paints
# best for content heavy, SEO sensitive pages
```
HTML birth on the server favors first paint and indexing.

steps.label: Step 2: Map modern flow
steps.text:
```bash
browser app asks -> server sends JSON -> app builds HTML
# best for interactive dashboards after login
```
HTML birth in the browser favors rich interaction after data arrives.

steps.label: Step 3: Choose per surface

keyTakeaways: Four layers separate interface, rules, access, and storage with downward calls.
Two tier client server centers on a protocol boundary sharable by many clients.
Multi tier growth clarifies ownership at the price of extra hops.
Diagrams must state where HTML is born to reason about cache and SEO.

quiz.q: What does the persistence layer own?
options: Database access behind a narrow contract
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Layers split jobs. Step 2: Presentation owns UI. Step 3: Logic owns rules. Step 4: Persistence abstracts database access.

quiz.q: What defines the two tier core?
options: Client frontend plus central server backend over a protocol
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Two parts exist. Step 2: Client asks. Step 3: Server processes and answers. Step 4: Protocol joins them.

quiz.q: How do classic and modern rendering differ?
options: Classic builds HTML on the server, modern builds it in the browser from data
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Both use layers. Step 2: Classic templates on server. Step 3: Modern apps render client side. Step 4: Wire carries pages versus data accordingly.

quiz.q: SQL lives inside click handlers. What is the layered fix?
options: Move rules to logic and access to persistence with downward calls
Merge all layers into one file
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Handlers own UI only. Step 2: Rules belong to logic. Step 3: Access belongs to persistence. Step 4: Downward calls restore testability.

intro: Small teams love one deployable while large products strain against it. This section travels from modular monoliths through service layers to microservices, reusable components, microfrontends, and message brokers. You will match team size, scale needs, and frontend reuse to the right distributed shape.
objectives: Contrast monolith simplicity with distributed scale and cost
Separate service, microservice, component, and microfrontend ideas
Choose messaging via broker versus direct calls deliberately

concepts.statement: A **monolith** ships one `deployable` unit with layered code inside. One build plus one environment keeps early delivery fast, while growth risks tangled dependencies and single stack lock in. Modularity inside delays the pain without adding network cost.
concepts.detail: Keep internal module boundaries strict and deploy as one unit until scale or team size forces a split.

concepts.statement: A **service** layer carves reusable `services` behind a `gateway` with a broker for chatter. Teams own services independently and scale hot ones separately, while the gateway routes and the broker decouples. Network plus versioning plus observability become the new price.
concepts.detail: Introduce services per bounded capability with versioned contracts and gateway routing from day one.

concepts.statement: Micro **services** push smallness plus independent `data` ownership to the limit for extreme scale. Each unit scales out with load balancing and deploys alone, which suits streaming scale products. Dozens of units demand serious platform maturity most small apps lack.
concepts.detail: Adopt micro units only when independent scaling plus team autonomy outweigh the heavy platform cost.

concepts.statement: Reusable **components** share UI widgets across apps while `microfrontends` split the interface by feature with backend mates. Component reuse via web components or frameworks cuts duplication, while feature slices enable independent `frontend` deploys. One reuses pieces, the other reuses delivery independence.
concepts.detail: Share widgets as components first and split delivery by feature only when teams collide on release trains.

concepts.statement: A **broker** routes `messages` centrally to cut direct dependencies while point to point calls couple callers to callees. Brokers ease extension with new consumers at the cost of infra plus latency, while direct calls stay simple but tangle as channels multiply. Service designs favor brokers while tiny systems favor directness.
concepts.detail: Count channels before choosing since broker overhead pays off only as direct links multiply.

examples.problem: A five person team ships a shop and fears premature service sprawl will stall features.

steps.label: Step 1: Modularize inside
Step 2: Ship one unit
steps.text: One build plus one deploy keeps environments and rollbacks trivial. Observability stays single pane while velocity stays high.

steps.label: Step 3: Name the split trigger
steps.text: Record that sustained team collision or hot catalog scaling forces extraction. Until measures trip, the monolith remains the honest choice.

examples.result: Features ship fast with clear internals and a written trigger for future extraction.

examples.title: Split checkout for scale
examples.problem: Checkout saturates a shop monolith on sale days while catalog idles, and teams block each other.

steps.label: Step 1: Carve the capability
steps.text:
```bash
# gateway routes /checkout to checkout service
# checkout owns its data plus queue
```
Gateway plus owned data let checkout scale and deploy alone.

steps.label: Step 2: Decouple with messages

Services trade network and platform cost for independent scale and ownership.
Components reuse widgets while microfrontends reuse independent delivery.
Brokers cut direct dependencies at infrastructure cost worth paying as channels grow.

quiz.q: What is the main early advantage of a monolith?
options: Single build plus single environment with minimal deploy cost
quiz.explanation: Step 1: One unit ships. Step 2: One env configures. Step 3: Deploys stay trivial. Step 4: Speed dominates early.

quiz.q: What new costs arrive with services?
options: Network hops plus versioning plus observability across units
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Calls cross networks. Step 2: Contracts version. Step 3: Failures need tracing. Step 4: Platform maturity becomes mandatory.

quiz.q: How do microfrontends differ from shared components?
options: Components share widgets while slices split interface by feature for independent delivery
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Components are pieces. Step 2: Slices are delivery units. Step 3: Pieces cut duplication. Step 4: Slices cut release coupling.

quiz.q: A tiny team with modest traffic asks for dozens of microservices. What is the principled answer?
options: Stay modular monolithic until team or scale measures force extraction
Delete all tests to fund services
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Count teams and load. Step 2: Weigh platform cost. Step 3: Modularity gives clarity cheaply. Step 4: Split only on tripped triggers.

intro: Views must show data without gluing themselves to storage details. This section separates model, view, and their mediators across three classic patterns. You will trace user input through controller, presenter, and view model shapes and pick the decoupling your framework expects.
objectives: Separate model state from view presentation in all three patterns
Trace input flow through controller, presenter, and view model
Map classic server versus modern client placements correctly

concepts.statement: The **model** holds data plus rules while the `view` renders state plus captures input. All three patterns keep this split so one model can feed many presentations. Testing and redesign both improve once storage stops dictating pixels.
concepts.detail: Model pure data plus rules with no widget imports so views can be swapped without touching state.

concepts.statement: A **controller** coordinates via routing plus `validation` plus model updates plus view selection. Users touch the view, the controller checks input, mutates the model, and picks the next `template`. Views may still observe models directly in this looser coupling.
concepts.detail: Route to one controller per action and keep view picking plus validation inside it, not in templates.

concepts.statement: A **presenter** enforces full separation where `view` never touches `model`. All talk flows through the presenter, which also pushes model changes back to the display. The extra rigor eases isolated testing at the cost of more mediator code.
concepts.detail: Hide the model behind presenter methods and assert view behavior through presenter doubles in tests.

concepts.statement: A **view model** exposes bindable `fields` mirroring editable widgets with two way `binding`. Typing in a box updates the field while code changes to the field repaint the box automatically. One binding declaration replaces manual sync code both ways.
concepts.detail: Bind each editable widget once and keep formatting plus validation in the view model, not in handlers.

concepts.statement: Classic **placement** hosts the trio on the `server` with routing plus template engines answering requests. Modern **placement** moves the trio into the `browser` as apps fetch data and patch the document interface. The pattern travels while the network boundary shifts.
concepts.detail: State where the trio lives in each feature since data fetching plus rendering strategies follow that home.

examples.title: Route a classic form submission
examples.problem: A contact form posts to the server and must validate, store, and render the next page cleanly.

steps.label: Step 1: Route to control
Step 2: Validate and update
steps.text: The controller rejects bad input with the form view plus errors and persists good input to the model. Views never write storage directly.

steps.label: Step 3: Render via template
steps.text: A template engine merges view markup with model data into HTML for the response. The client paints the answered page.

examples.result: Form flow stays ordered with validation plus storage plus rendering each in its home.

examples.title: Bind an editor without sync spaghetti
examples.problem: A profile editor copies field values back and forth manually and drifts out of sync.

steps.label: Step 1: Expose bindable fields
Step 2: Type both ways
steps.text: User edits update fields while code updates repaint widgets automatically. No handler copies values either direction.

steps.label: Step 3: Validate centrally
steps.text: Rules live on the view model so both typed and programmatic changes face identical checks. The view stays thin and honest.

examples.result: Editor state stays single sourced with sync declared once instead of copied everywhere.

keyTakeaways: Models own data plus rules while views own pixels plus input in all variants.
Controllers route and validate with looser view to model links.
Presenters isolate strictly with all traffic through the mediator.
View models replace manual sync with declared two way bindings.

quiz.q: What does the model own across all three patterns?
options: Data plus business rules independent of presentation
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Split is the goal. Step 2: State plus rules group together. Step 3: Pixels stay in views. Step 4: Hence models stay UI free.

quiz.q: How does a presenter differ from a classic controller?
options: It forbids direct view to model contact and pushes changes itself
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Controllers allow some direct links. Step 2: Presenters close them. Step 3: All talk crosses the mediator. Step 4: Tests isolate more cleanly.

quiz.q: What does two way binding buy an editor?
options: Automatic sync both ways from one declaration
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Widgets mirror fields. Step 2: Typing updates fields. Step 3: Field writes repaint widgets. Step 4: One binding replaces sync code.

quiz.q: A team needs maximal view isolation for testing. Which mediator fits?
options: Presenter with all view model traffic through it
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Goal is isolation. Step 2: Controllers allow some links. Step 3: Presenters forbid direct contact. Step 4: Therefore presenters maximize test seams.

intro: Good architectures are written down before they are debated. This section records decisions with context, options, consequences, and reversibility so future teams understand the why. You will write short decision records with fitness checks that warn when assumptions rot.
objectives: Write concise records with context, options, and consequences
Judge reversibility to size process versus speed correctly
Define fitness checks that signal when to revisit a choice

concepts.statement: A **record** captures title plus `context` plus options plus decision plus `consequences` in one page. Context states forces, options weigh at least two roads, and consequences own the tradeoffs. Future readers learn why without excavating chat history.
concepts.detail: Keep each record to one page with dated status so the log stays readable as it grows.

concepts.statement: Strong **options** compare at least `two` roads on cost plus latency plus `complexity`. Naming the road not taken preserves honesty about what was sacrificed. Reviewers trust choices whose downsides are stated plainly.
concepts.detail: Score each option on the same three axes so comparisons stay fair across records.

concepts.statement: Reversible **choices** deserve lightweight `notes` while one way doors deserve prototypes plus reviews. A library swap reverses in an afternoon while a data split does not. Sizing process to reversibility keeps speed where safe and rigor where stuck.
concepts.detail: Label each decision reversible or one way and match ceremony to that label explicitly.

concepts.statement: A **fitness** check watches a `metric` that guards the decision over time. Latency budgets plus error rates plus deploy pain signal when assumptions rot. Tripped checks reopen the record instead of letting drift harden into folklore.
concepts.detail: Attach one numeric guard per record with owner plus review date for automatic revisit.

concepts.statement: A **living** log stays beside `code` with numbered entries plus superseded links. New records link prior ones they refine or reverse, which turns history into a chain rather than a pile. Teams onboard by reading the log instead of interrogating elders.
concepts.detail: Number records sequentially and link supersedes relations so the chain tells the story.

examples.title: Record staying monolithic
examples.problem: A team must defend one deployable today while keeping the door open for services later.

steps.label: Step 1: Frame context and options
steps.text:
```bash
# context: five devs, modest traffic, sale spikes
# options: modular monolith vs checkout service now
```
Forces plus roads make the debate concrete.

steps.label: Step 2: Decide with consequences
steps.text: Pick modular monolith for speed while owning coupling risk plus extraction cost later. Name checkout scale as the known limit.

steps.label: Step 3: Guard the bet
steps.text: Set fitness guards on deploy lead time plus checkout latency plus team collision count. Trips reopen the record toward extraction.

examples.result: The log defends today with honesty and triggers tomorrow without drama.

examples.title: Revisit on tripped guard
examples.problem: Checkout latency trips its guard during a sale and the old record must guide action, not blame.

steps.label: Step 1: Read the chain
Step 2: Propose the reversal
steps.text: Draft extraction of checkout with gateway plus owned data plus broker events. Cite the tripped metric as the reason, not urgency.

steps.label: Step 3: Supersede cleanly
steps.text: Mark the old record superseded with a forward link and date the new guard review. History stays a chain of reasons.

examples.result: The team extracts with context intact and a fresh guard watching the new shape.

keyTakeaways: One page records hold context, options, decision, and consequences.
Stated tradeoffs plus the road not taken build reviewer trust.
Reversibility sizes ceremony from light notes to full reviews.
Numeric fitness guards reopen records before drift hardens.

quiz.q: What belongs in a decision record?
options: Context plus options plus decision plus consequences with status
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Future teams need why. Step 2: Context states forces. Step 3: Options show roads. Step 4: Consequences own tradeoffs.

quiz.q: How should reversibility shape process?
options: Light notes for reversible, rigorous review for one way doors
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Reversals differ in cost. Step 2: Cheap reversals need speed. Step 3: Costly ones need rigor. Step 4: Match ceremony to label.

quiz.q: What is a fitness check?
options: A metric guard that reopens the record when assumptions rot
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Decisions age. Step 2: Metrics watch them. Step 3: Trips signal rot. Step 4: Records reopen on signal.

quiz.q: Why link superseded records instead of deleting them?
options: To keep history as a chain that teaches why roads changed
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Deletion erases why. Step 2: Links preserve chain. Step 3: Newcomers read evolution. Step 4: Trust grows with honest history.

intro: Phones run code from stores, browsers, and hybrids that blur the line. This section compares native, web, and hybrid routes by capability, reach, cost, and distribution. You will recommend the cheapest route that still reaches required hardware and store presence.
objectives: Contrast native, web, and hybrid builds by skill, cost, and reuse
Weigh hardware access plus performance against reach and maintenance
Choose distribution via store versus URL for the product need

concepts.statement: A **native** app compiles per operating system with `Kotlin` or Swift plus platform kits. Full hardware access plus top `performance` come at the price of separate codebases plus specialized skills. Stores distribute installs with platform trust.
concepts.detail: Choose native when max fidelity plus hardware depth outweigh duplicate builds and hiring cost.

concepts.statement: A **web** app ships HTML plus CSS plus `JS` from a `URL` rendered in mobile browsers. One codebase plus instant updates trade against limited `hardware` reach plus browser chrome instead of install feel. Standards expand access yearly but trail native depth.
concepts.detail: Choose web for broad reach plus instant deploys when hardware needs stay within browser APIs.

concepts.statement: A **hybrid** app wraps web code in a native `shell` with a `view` rendering engine. Web skills ship installable apps with partial hardware bridges, landing between native and web on both power and cost. Lowest common denominator APIs may leave platform gems untapped.
concepts.detail: Choose hybrid to reuse web skills for store presence while auditing which hardware gaps truly matter.

concepts.statement: Every route trades **capability** against `reach` against cost with no free corner. Native maximizes capability at duplicate cost, web maximizes reach at capability cost, and hybrid balances with `medium` totals. Naming the binding constraint picks the corner honestly.
concepts.detail: Write the binding constraint first since it eliminates two routes before feature debate starts.

concepts.statement: Store **distribution** offers discovery plus trust plus `install` presence with review gates. URL **distribution** offers instant link sharing plus zero review with `update` speed. Product need for presence versus speed decides the channel before code does.
concepts.detail: Require store presence for trust sensitive installs and URL speed for content plus campaign reach.

examples.title: Pick for a camera heavy workout app
examples.problem: An app needs continuous sensor plus camera plus offline sets with store trust for payments.

steps.label: Step 1: Name the constraint
steps.text:
```bash
need: sensors + camera + offline + store trust
binding: hardware depth + presence
```
Depth plus trust eliminate pure URL delivery.

steps.label: Step 2: Price the routes
steps.text: Native meets every hardware need at duplicate build cost while hybrid covers most at medium cost. Web trails on background capture and feel.

steps.label: Step 3: Recommend with reason
steps.text: Recommend native, or hybrid only if the hardware audit proves bridges suffice. Record the audit so scope growth triggers revisit.

examples.result: Hardware depth plus store trust justify native cost with a documented hybrid fallback test.

examples.title: Pick for a content campaign site
examples.problem: A campaign needs link sharing to millions with daily content tweaks and no hardware beyond location.

steps.label: Step 1: Name the constraint
Step 2: Check capability
steps.text: Browser location APIs cover the need while central deploys update all viewers at once. No store review blocks the launch.

steps.label: Step 3: Recommend with reason
steps.text: Recommend mobile web with responsive polish and shareable URLs. Skip store cost until install presence becomes a requirement.

examples.result: One web codebase reaches millions instantly with updates that land centrally.

keyTakeaways: Native buys depth and speed at duplicate builds and specialist cost.
Web buys one codebase and instant updates at limited hardware depth.
Hybrid reuses web skills for installs at middle power and cost.
Binding constraints on hardware, presence, and speed pick the route.

quiz.q: When does native justify its cost?
options: When hardware depth plus top performance plus store trust are binding
When updates must bypass review daily
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Native costs duplicate builds. Step 2: It returns depth plus speed. Step 3: Trust comes via stores. Step 4: Binding needs must warrant that price.

quiz.q: What is the core web advantage?
options: One codebase with instant central updates across platforms
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Code lives centrally. Step 2: One version runs widely. Step 3: Edits land at once. Step 4: Reach plus speed dominate.

quiz.q: What limits hybrid builds?
options: Generic bridges may miss platform specific depths
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Hybrids bridge APIs. Step 2: Bridges target common ground. Step 3: Gems stay native only. Step 4: Audits must confirm coverage.

quiz.q: A team needs store presence plus web skills but modest hardware. What fits?
options: Hybrid shell with web content and bridged hardware
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Presence demands install. Step 2: Skills are web only. Step 3: Hardware is modest. Step 4: Hybrid matches all three.

intro: One codebase must look intentional from small phones to wide monitors. This section sets the viewport, queries capabilities with media rules, and reshapes grid layouts by breakpoint. You will build mobile first so growth adds rather than amputates.
objectives: Set the viewport so mobile browsers size pages correctly
Write media queries with features and breakpoints for real devices
Reshape flexible grids mobile first across screen bands

concepts.statement: The **viewport** tag tells mobile browsers the layout `width` plus initial `scale` to use. Without it phones shrink desktop layouts into thumbnails, while with it the page fills device width at readable scale. Every responsive page starts with this one line.
concepts.detail: Set width to device width with an initial scale of one and verify no sideways scroll on small phones.

concepts.statement: A **media** rule wraps `CSS` that applies only when its query matches. Classic types split `screen` from print, while modern queries test width plus orientation plus resolution. Matched rules cascade normally with the rest of the sheet.
concepts.detail: Isolate print tweaks from screen tweaks so paper output never inherits phone layout hacks.

concepts.statement: Media **features** like `min-width` plus max width gate rules by capability. **Breakpoints** mark widths where layout must morph, often near common device bands. Content should pick breaks where it strains, not where devices happen to sit.
concepts.detail: Add a break where lines grow unreadable or cards crush, then name it by content reason.

concepts.statement: Flexible **grids** with fractional `tracks` plus wrapping reflow across bands. Named `areas` let header plus main plus sidebar restack by simply rewriting the template per query. One markup order serves all sizes while CSS reorders visually.
concepts.detail: Define areas once then rewrite templates per band so markup stays stable while layout morphs.

concepts.statement: Mobile **first** ships the narrow `layout` as default then enhances upward with min width layers. Desktop first does the reverse and often amputates under pressure, while mobile first adds delight as space allows. Constraints first yield focus that survives expansion.
concepts.detail: Write base styles for narrow screens and add min width layers for larger bands only.

examples.title: Fix a shrunken phone page
examples.problem: A page looks like a tiny desktop thumbnail on phones with unreadable text and sideways scroll.

steps.label: Step 1: Declare the viewport
steps.text:
```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```
Device width plus unit scale let the layout fill phones correctly.

steps.label: Step 2: Stack the base
steps.text: Lay header plus main plus sidebar plus footer in one column as the default narrow style. No query is needed for the base.

steps.label: Step 3: Verify by resizing
steps.text: Open on a phone profile and confirm readable text with no sideways scroll. Only then add wider bands.

examples.result: Phones gain a readable stacked page instead of a shrunken thumbnail.

examples.title: Grow a grid across bands
examples.problem: A stacked phone layout must become two columns on tablets and three on desktops without markup forks.

steps.label: Step 1: Name the areas
Step 2: Add the bands
Step 3: Keep content led
steps.text: Adjust break values where cards strain rather than copying device specs blindly. Content comfort outranks device fashion.

examples.result: One markup morphs from stack to columns exactly where content needs room.

keyTakeaways: Viewport declaration makes mobile sizing intentional instead of shrunken.
Media rules gate styles by type and capability with normal cascade.
Breaks belong where content strains, named by reason rather than device.
Mobile first base plus min width layers grow layouts without forks.

quiz.q: What breaks without a viewport tag on phones?
options: Pages shrink to desktop thumbnails instead of filling width
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Phones default wide. Step 2: Layout scales down. Step 3: Text turns tiny. Step 4: The tag fixes width plus scale.

quiz.q: What do min-width queries express?
options: Enhancements that apply at and above a width band
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Feature tests width. Step 2: Min means at least. Step 3: Rules add upward. Step 4: Base stays mobile.

quiz.q: Why prefer content led breakpoints?
options: Layouts morph where strain appears rather than at arbitrary device pixels
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Content varies. Step 2: Strain points differ. Step 3: Device lists age fast. Step 4: Comfort led breaks endure.

quiz.q: A layout crushes cards at mid widths. What is the disciplined fix?
options: Add a min-width band that reflows the grid where strain shows
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Strain marks the break. Step 2: Keep markup stable. Step 3: Rewrite template per band. Step 4: Test live across sizes.

intro: Web skills can ship truly native feeling apps without learning platform languages. This section explains the learn once bridge that maps shared logic onto native widgets. You will read the entry file, respect the no HTML rule, and style with native friendly sheets.
objectives: Explain shared logic plus native widget mapping clearly
Read the entry file with view, text, and style sheet roles
Respect platform differences while reusing web thinking

concepts.statement: Learn **once** reuse means shared `JS` logic plus idioms drive both major platforms. One mental model for state plus layout transfers while the toolchain renders truly native `widgets`. Teams ship twice the reach without twice the languages.
concepts.detail: Invest in shared state plus navigation design since those transfer most cleanly across platforms.

concepts.statement: A **bridge** maps shared declarations onto native `View` plus text plus image controls. Pixels are drawn by the platform, not by a browser engine, which preserves feel plus accessibility. The same declaration yields platform true controls per side.
concepts.detail: Prefer provided widgets over custom drawing so feel plus accessibility stay platform true.

concepts.statement: The **entry** file exports an `App` function returning element trees. `View` boxes contain, `Text` shows strings, and a style `Sheet` holds layout rules. Changing copy hot reloads the running device view for instant feedback.
concepts.detail: Keep the entry small with screen components separate so hot reload stays instant as the app grows.

concepts.statement: Platform builds accept no raw **HTML** elements since output is native `code`, not pages. Familiar tag names do not exist here even though JSX `mixing` looks similar. Styling names echo web CSS while running through native layout.
concepts.detail: Translate div thinking into View plus Text plus image widgets and verify on both platforms early.

concepts.statement: Assisted **tooling** scaffolds projects plus serves `previews` to devices and emulators. Templates plus scripts hide native build pain while preserving eject paths to full control. Beginners validate ideas on hardware before owning native toolchains.
concepts.detail: Start assisted for speed and eject only when native modules or build control demand it.

examples.title: Read the hello world entry
examples.problem: A newcomer opens the generated entry and must map each import to its UI job.

steps.label: Step 1: Map the imports
Step 2: Read the tree
steps.text: View centers children while Text shows the greeting and StatusBar tunes the top bar. The App function returns this tree for the runtime to mount.

steps.label: Step 3: Edit and watch

intro: Ideas become apps when they run on hardware and pass store gates. This section initializes projects, previews on emulators and devices, and builds release bundles. You will run the script set confidently and package for publishing without mystery.
objectives: Initialize projects and read the generated file map
Preview on emulators, browsers, and hardware efficiently
Build release bundles and approach store publishing cleanly

concepts.statement: Project **init** scaffolds config plus `assets` plus entry plus package manifests. Assets hold media, entry boots the tree, and manifests pin `dependencies` plus scripts. Reading the map first prevents edits in generated corners.
concepts.detail: Inspect entry plus manifest plus config before adding screens so generated wiring stays intact.

concepts.statement: Npm **scripts** alias `start` plus platform previews plus eject. Start serves the tool UI, platform flags open matching `emulators`, and web preview runs in a browser tab. One vocabulary drives every preview surface.
concepts.detail: Learn start plus platform flags first since they cover daily preview loops end to end.

concepts.statement: An **emulator** mimics a device on the `workstation` for fast layout checks. Real `hardware` reveals touch plus sensors plus performance truth that emulation approximates. Use emulators for speed and hardware for sign off.
concepts.detail: Pass layout on emulators then confirm gestures plus load on real devices before release.

concepts.statement: Release **builds** bundle JS plus assets into signed `packages` per store. Versioned manifests plus icons plus splash plus permissions feed the packager, which outputs installable artifacts. Separate debug and release configs to avoid leaking dev settings.
concepts.detail: Bump versions per release and audit permissions plus secrets before packaging for stores.

concepts.statement: Store **publishing** adds review plus listings plus `rollout` control beyond the binary. Screenshots plus descriptions plus categories face human gates, while staged rollouts limit blast radius. Web previews never face this gate, which explains timeline gaps.
concepts.detail: Prepare listings plus test accounts early since review queues dwarf build times.

intro: Style sheets sprawl until variables and nesting restore order. This section compiles preprocessor sources into plain style sheets with watch driven feedback. You will centralize tokens, nest with discipline, and split code into partials with source maps for debugging.
objectives: Compile sources to style sheets with watch and directory builds
Centralize design tokens in variables with clean references
Nest selectors plus split partials without over specificity

concepts.statement: A **preprocessor** translates enriched `source` into plain `CSS` during builds, not at runtime. Linked pages consume only the generated sheet while sources stay as authorship truth. Watch mode recompiles on save for instant feedback.
concepts.detail: Compile named sources to named outputs and keep generated files out of hand edits.

concepts.statement: A **variable** names one `value` once for reuse across many declarations. Fonts plus brand colors live centrally so a rebrand edits one line instead of dozens. Typed values cover numbers plus strings plus colors plus lists plus `maps`.
concepts.detail: Tokenize repeated values early and reference variables instead of pasting literals.

concepts.statement: Rule **nesting** derives child `selectors` from parent context automatically. Lists plus items plus nested items read as their DOM shape without retyping long chains. Depth beyond two or three levels breeds over specific `selectors` that resist override.
concepts.detail: Nest to mirror structure but flatten when depth exceeds three levels or reuse suffers.

concepts.statement: Small **partials** split tokens plus base plus components into focused `files` joined by modern `use` imports. Each file owns one concern while the entry composes the sheet in order. Namespaced imports prevent global collisions as the system grows.
concepts.detail: Split by concern with an entry that imports in dependency order and namespaces shared tokens.

concepts.statement: Compiler **maps** link generated `CSS` lines back to source lines for DevTools. Newer brace `syntax` suits CSS authors while older indented syntax suits minimalists, with identical power. Editor highlighting plus linked sources make debugging feel source native.
concepts.detail: Ship maps in development and click through to source lines when inspecting applied rules.

intro: Static tokens only start the story, and logic finishes it. This section branches themes, loops repetitive grids and icons, and computes with built in plus custom functions. You will generate families of rules from data instead of hand writing each cousin.
objectives: Branch themes with conditional compilation for light and dark modes
Generate families with each, counted, and conditional loops
Compute with module functions plus custom reusable functions

concepts.statement: A **branch** compiles one `block` or another by boolean test. A theme flag selects light tokens or dark tokens so one source ships either skin. Only the taken branch reaches the generated `sheet`, which keeps output lean.
concepts.detail: Gate theme skins plus feature variants on flags so dead alternatives never bloat the sheet.

concepts.statement: An **each** loop walks a `list` binding each value in turn. Icon names generate matching classes plus image paths without copy paste. Interpolation injects the current value into `selectors` plus URLs cleanly.
concepts.detail: Collect variant names in one list and generate their rules with a single each block.

concepts.statement: Counted **loops** repeat by index with `to` excluding the end and `through` including it. Conditional `while` loops repeat until a test fails for data driven widths. Choosing the right bound avoids off by one families.
concepts.detail: Prefer counted loops for grids and while loops for growing scales with explicit termination.

concepts.statement: Namespaced **modules** group color plus string plus `math` plus list plus map helpers. Imports like color plus math load only needed powers, and calls like mix plus max compute values at `compile` time. Modern code favors modules over legacy globals.
concepts.detail: Import the narrow module needed per file and call helpers for computed values, not hand math.

concepts.statement: A **custom** function names reusable `calc` with params plus return for domain math. A sum helper totals dynamic lengths while nested lists feed batch generation. Debug prints trace values during `compile` without touching output.
concepts.detail: Extract repeated calculations into named functions with clear params and return the computed value.

intro: Reuse separates tidy systems from pasted ones. This section contrasts inheritance that merges selectors with mixins that inject declarations, plus operators that compute fluid grids. You will bottle media query management and button variants into callable abstractions.
objectives: Contrast extend merging with mixin injection for reuse
Compute fluid layouts with operators and calc correctly
Abstract media handling and variants into callable patterns

concepts.statement: Inheritance via **extend** merges selectors into one shared `rule` for common declarations. Base button plus special plus submit variants group their shared core while keeping deltas separate. Merged output stays compact when variants truly share `semantics`.
concepts.detail: Extend only for genuinely shared semantics since unrelated grouping harms readability.

concepts.statement: A **mixin** injects its `declarations` into each including rule via `include`. Error plus warning boxes duplicate the marker core with distinct backgrounds, which favors flexibility over selector `merging`. Params plus defaults later turn mixins into configurable factories.
concepts.detail: Prefer mixins for skinnable patterns where each use may diverge with params.

concepts.statement: Math **operators** compute widths plus gutters from `variables` at compile time. Division needs function safe `calc` handling while multiply plus add size fluid columns from base widths. Computed numbers land as finished values in output `CSS`.
concepts.detail: Compute grid math from base widths and verify finished values in output before shipping.

concepts.statement: A media **manager** mixin centralizes `breakpoints` behind named calls. Components include tablet or desktop wrappers instead of pasting raw queries, which keeps bands consistent. One map owns widths while many callers reuse `names`.
concepts.detail: Bottle each band once behind a named mixin and call it everywhere instead of pasting queries.

concepts.statement: Choose **merging** for identical `cores` and injection for diverging `skins`. Extend compacts truly shared meaning while mixins duplicate safely for parameterized variety. Misapplied merging couples strangers while misapplied injection bloats twins.
concepts.detail: Ask whether variants share meaning or merely look alike before picking the reuse tool.

Step 2: Extend the core

intro: Small demos forgive mess that large teams cannot. This section scales Sass with layered architecture, build integration, and a clear path to modern CSS. You will organize seven folders with intent, automate reloads, and migrate variables without breaking themes.
objectives: Organize large systems with layered folders and strict imports
Integrate builds with directory watch plus live reload helpers
Migrate thoughtfully to modern CSS while keeping Sass strengths

concepts.statement: A **seven** folder layout splits abstracts plus base plus `components` plus layout plus pages plus themes plus vendors. Tokens plus mixins live in abstracts while real rules live outward in order. The entry imports layers so `cascade` stays predictable at scale.
concepts.detail: Adopt the full split once partial counts pass a dozen and enforce import order in review.

concepts.statement: Directory **watch** compiles whole `source` trees to output trees on save. Live reload helpers refresh browsers on sheet change, which closes the edit see loop. Together they turn large systems into small feedback `loops`.
concepts.detail: Watch source to output directories and pair with reload tooling for instant visual feedback.

concepts.statement: Classic **rivals** share variables plus nesting plus `mixins` with taste level differences. Sass leads on modules plus community depth, while leaner dialects suit existing pipelines. Concepts transfer, so teams should honor incumbent `choices` over relitigation.
concepts.detail: Learn concepts deeply and respect incumbent picks since migration cost dwarfs syntax taste.

concepts.statement: Native **custom** properties now offer runtime `theming` plus cascade plus JS updates. Compile time tokens still win for math plus branching plus dead code removal, while runtime props win for live theme `switches`. Hybrids keep build power with runtime flexibility.
concepts.detail: Keep computed design math in Sass while exposing live theme knobs as custom properties.

concepts.statement: Large **systems** rot through deep nesting plus merged strangers plus `global` leaks. Lint depth plus forbid unrelated extension plus namespace shared `tokens` to keep growth linear. Reviews guard the entry order like API surface.
concepts.detail: Lint nesting depth plus import order and reject global leaks that couple distant features.

intro: Matrices store linear information in rectangular arrays, and almost every later topic in this volume leans on fluent matrix algebra. This section fixes the vocabulary of special matrix types and the rules for addition, multiplication, transpose and trace. The non-commutativity of multiplication and the shape-compatibility check cause more slips than any other pair of facts in the chapter.
objectives: Classify symmetric, skew-symmetric, orthogonal, idempotent, triangular and diagonal matrices from defining identities
Multiply conformable matrices and explain why order matters with a concrete counterexample
Apply transpose, trace and identity rules to simplify matrix expressions

concepts.statement: A square matrix is **symmetric** when it equals its own transpose, `$A^T = A$`, so entry `$a_{ij}$` mirrors `$a_{ji}$` for every pair, while it is **skew-symmetric** when `$A^T = -A$`, which forces every diagonal entry to vanish since `$a_{ii} = -a_{ii}$`. The `transpose` operation reflects across the main diagonal, and every square matrix splits uniquely into a symmetric plus a skew-symmetric part via `$A = \frac{1}{2}(A + A^T) + \frac{1}{2}(A - A^T)$`. Any sum of the form `$B + B^T$` is symmetric and any difference `$B - B^T$` is skew-symmetric, a construction used constantly in later proofs.
concepts.detail: Diagonal entries of a skew-symmetric matrix are always zero, and `$A^T$` applied twice returns `$A$`, so symmetry can be tested in one glance at off-diagonal pairs.

concepts.statement: An **orthogonal** matrix has orthonormal columns, equivalently `$Q^T Q = I$` so that `$Q^T = Q^{-1}$` and length is preserved under `$x \mapsto Qx$`, while an **idempotent** matrix obeys `$A^2 = A$` and an **involutory** matrix obeys `$A^2 = I$`. The `diag` family contains diagonal matrices with nonzero entries allowed only on the main diagonal, upper-triangular matrices with zeros below it, and lower-triangular matrices with zeros above it. Identity `$I$`, zero `$O$`, and scalar matrices `$cI$` sit at the intersection of these families and act as the neutral elements of multiplication and addition.
concepts.detail: Products of upper-triangular matrices stay upper-triangular with multiplied diagonal entries, so triangular determinants and eigenvalues are read directly off the diagonal.

concepts.term: Multiplication needs conformable shapes and does not commute
concepts.statement: The product `$AB$` exists only when the column count of `$A$` equals the row count of `$B$`, and the **order matters**: in general `$AB \ne BA$`, and one side may exist while the other does not. The `matmul` entry rule is `$c_{ij} = \sum_{k} a_{ik} b_{kj}$`, a dot product of row `$i$` of `$A$` with column `$j$` of `$B$`. Scalar multiplication `$cA$` scales every entry and does commute with everything, which is why scalars can be pulled through products but matrices cannot be reordered.
concepts.detail: Before multiplying, write the shapes as `$(m \times n)(n \times p) = m \times p$`; a mismatch of inner dimensions means the product is undefined, not zero.

concepts.statement: Reversal governs products: **transpose reverses order** via `$(AB)^T = B^T A^T$` and, when inverses exist, `$(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}$`, while sums stay in order with `$(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T$`. The **trace** sums diagonal entries as `$\mathrm{tr}(A) = \sum_{i} a_{ii}$` and obeys the cyclic rule `$\mathrm{tr}(AB) = \mathrm{tr}(BA)$` even though `$AB \ne BA$`. The `trace` is linear with `$\mathrm{tr}(A + B) = \mathrm{tr}(A) + \mathrm{tr}(B)$` and `$\mathrm{tr}(cA) = c\,\mathrm{tr}(A)$`, facts used to compute eigenvalue sums without solving any polynomial.
concepts.detail: Cyclicity extends to three factors as `$\mathrm{tr}(ABC) = \mathrm{tr}(CAB)$`, but arbitrary permutations are not permitted, only cyclic rotations.

concepts.statement: Experts read the **shapes first and the entries second**: the shape line `$(m \times n)$` decides existence, output size, and which identities even type-check, while entry arithmetic comes only after. The `identity` `$I_n$` must carry the correct size for each product, since `$AI_m = A$` requires `$m$` to match the column count of `$A$`. Most algebra slips are shape slips, such as adding matrices of different sizes or writing `$A^2$` for a non-square `$A$`.
concepts.detail: Powers `$A^k$`, polynomials `$p(A)$`, and exponentials `$e^A$` are defined only for square matrices, because only squares stay conformable under self-multiplication.

examples.title: Multiply two small matrices and expose non-commutativity
examples.problem: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Compute `$AB$` and `$BA$`, and confirm they differ.

steps.label: Step 1: Check shapes
steps.text:
```text
A is 2x2, B is 2x2 -> both products AB and BA exist, each 2x2
c(ij) = row i of A dot column j of B
```
Both matrices are square of the same size, so shape permits multiplication in either order, and the outputs are both `$2 \times 2$`.

steps.label: Step 2: Compute AB entry by entry
steps.text: Row one of `$A$` dotted with columns of `$B$` gives `$c_{11} = 1 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 1 = 2$`, `$c_{12} = 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 1 = 3$`; row two gives `$c_{21} = 0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 = 1$` and `$c_{22} = 0 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1 = 1$`. Hence $$AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ using the `matmul` row-dot-column rule.

steps.label: Step 3: Compute BA and compare
steps.text: Reversing the order gives `$d_{11} = 0 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 0 = 0$`, `$d_{12} = 0 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 1 = 1$`, `$d_{21} = 1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 0 = 1$`, `$d_{22} = 1 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 1 = 3$`, so $$BA = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \ne AB$$ The two products share the trace `$3$` but differ in every off-diagonal story, a clean witness that order matters.

examples.result: $$AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ while $$BA = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ so multiplication does not commute.

examples.title: Test symmetry, orthogonality and trace in one pass
examples.problem: For $$M = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ decide whether `$M$` is symmetric or skew-symmetric, test orthogonality via `$M^T M$`, and compute `$\mathrm{tr}(M)$` and `$\mathrm{tr}(M^T M)$`.

steps.label: Step 1: Transpose test
steps.text:
```text
M^T = [0 1; -1 0] = -M  -> skew-symmetric
Diagonal of M is (0, 0) as required
Symmetric test M^T = M fails
```
Since `$M^T = -M$`, the matrix is **skew-symmetric** and not symmetric, with the mandatory zero diagonal `$0, 0`.

steps.label: Step 2: Orthogonality check
steps.text: Form `$M^T M = (-M)(M) = -M^2$`; direct multiplication gives `$M^2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$`, so `$M^T M = I_2$`. The `orthogonal` identity holds, meaning columns are orthonormal and `$M^T = M^{-1}$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Traces
steps.text: The trace `$\mathrm{tr}(M) = 0 + 0 = 0$` as every skew-symmetric trace must vanish, while `$\mathrm{tr}(M^T M) = \mathrm{tr}(I_2) = 2$` counts the squared column lengths. The two traces together confirm skew-symmetry plus orthogonality in numbers.

examples.result: `$M$` is skew-symmetric and orthogonal with `$\mathrm{tr}(M) = 0$` and `$M^T M = I_2$`.

keyTakeaways: Symmetric means `$A^T = A$` and skew-symmetric means `$A^T = -A$` with zero diagonal; every square splits into one of each.
Orthogonal means `$Q^T Q = I$`, idempotent means `$A^2 = A$`, triangular means zeros on one side of the diagonal.
Products need matching inner dimensions and do not commute: `$AB \ne BA$` in general.
Reversal rules `$(AB)^T = B^T A^T$` and cyclic trace `$\mathrm{tr}(AB) = \mathrm{tr}(BA)$` organize all simplification.

quiz.q: If `$A$` is any square matrix, which claim about `$B = A + A^T$` and `$C = A - A^T$` is correct?
quiz.explanation: First transpose each combination using linearity of transpose. Next `$B^T = A^T + A = B$` shows symmetry while `$C^T = A^T - A = -C$` shows skew-symmetry. Finally the diagonal of `$C$` must vanish, confirming the classification.

quiz.q: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ Which statement about `$AB$` versus `$BA$` holds?
options: Both exist and both equal the zero matrix
quiz.explanation: First note both factors are `$2 \times 2$` so both orders are conformable. Next compute `$AB$` whose second column picks out column structure of `$A$` scaled by `$B$`. Then compute `$BA$` which instead combines rows of `$A$`. Finally compare entries: the two results differ, so order matters.
