quiz.q: For conformable matrices with `$A$` of size `$m \times n$` and `$B$` of size $n \times p$, what is `$(AB)^T$`?
options: $AB$ with each entry transposed in place
quiz.explanation: First recall transposition swaps row and column indices of the product. Next track how the summation index `$k$` moves from `$a_{ik}b_{kj}$` to `$b_{kj}a_{ik}$`. Then identify the result as the product of transposes in reverse order. Finally check shapes: `$B^T$` is `$p \times n$` and `$A^T$` is `$n \times m$`, so `$B^T A^T$` is `$p \times m$` as required.

quiz.q: If `$Q$` is orthogonal and `$x$` is any column vector, what is the squared length `$\lVert Qx \rVert^2$`?
quiz.explanation: First expand the squared norm as `$(Qx)^T (Qx) = x^T Q^T Q x$`. Next substitute the orthogonal identity `$Q^T Q = I$`. Then the expression collapses to `$x^T x$` which is exactly `$\lVert x \rVert^2$`. Finally note orthogonal maps are length-preserving rotations or reflections.

intro: The determinant is a single scalar that reports whether a square matrix is invertible, how volumes scale, and how elimination will behave. This section builds the cofactor definition for small matrices and the row-operation rules that make larger determinants tractable. The scaling trap `$|kA| = k^n |A|$` and the false linearity `$|A+B| = |A| + |B|$` are flagged early because they recur in timed problem sets.
objectives: Evaluate `$2 \times 2$` and `$3 \times 3$` determinants by formula and cofactor expansion
Predict how row swaps, scaling, and row addition change the determinant
Apply multiplicativity `$|AB| = |A||B|$` and triangular shortcuts correctly

concepts.statement: For `$2 \times 2$` the **determinant** is `$\begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = ad - bc$`, the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the columns. For `$3 \times 3$` and beyond, expansion along any row or column gives `$|A| = \sum_{j} a_{ij} C_{ij}$` where the `cofactor` `$C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$` pairs a checkerboard sign with the minor `$M_{ij}$` obtained by deleting row `$i$` and column `$j$`. Choosing the row or column with the most zeros minimizes arithmetic, since each zero kills a whole cofactor term.
concepts.detail: The checkerboard `$(-1)^{i+j}$` starts with `$+$` at position `$(1,1)$`, and forgetting it is the most common cofactor slip.

concepts.term: Effect of row and column operations
concepts.statement: Three operation rules control every hand computation: swapping two rows **flips the sign**, scaling one row by `$c$` **multiplies** the determinant by `$c$`, and adding a multiple of one row to another **leaves** the determinant unchanged. The `row-add` invariance is the workhorse that creates zeros before expansion, while the swap rule explains why an **odd permutation** of rows negates `$|A|$`. Identical rows, proportional rows, or a zero row force `$|A| = 0$` immediately with no expansion needed.
concepts.detail: Transpose leaves the determinant unchanged with `$|A^T| = |A|$`, so every row rule has a matching column rule.

concepts.statement: Determinants **multiply across products** via `$|AB| = |A| \cdot |B|$`, so `$|A^k| = |A|^k$` and any singular factor poisons the product to zero. A **triangular** or diagonal matrix has determinant equal to the product of its diagonal entries, because cofactor expansion peels off one diagonal factor at a time. The `upper-triangular` shortcut turns elimination into evaluation: once a matrix is triangular, no further expansion is needed.
concepts.detail: Sums do not split, so `$|A + B| \ne |A| + |B|$` in general, and the product rule never extends to addition.

concepts.term: Minors, cofactors and the cofactor matrix
concepts.statement: The **minor** `$M_{ij}$` is the determinant of the submatrix after deleting row `$i$` and column `$j$`, and the signed version `$C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$` is the `cofactor`. Collecting all cofactors into a matrix `$C$` and transposing yields the adjoint `$\mathrm{adj}(A) = C^T$`, the object that builds the inverse in the next section. Strange-but-true selection rules state that expansion with cofactors of a *different* row sums to zero, a property called alien-cofactor cancellation.
concepts.detail: For `$3 \times 3$` there are nine cofactors, and each uses a `$2 \times 2$` minor, so the full expansion has six signed triple products.

concepts.term: Scalar multiples scale by a power
concepts.statement: Scaling the whole matrix scales **every row**, so `$|kA| = k^n |A|$` for `$n \times n$` matrices, not `$k|A|$`: the factor `$k$` appears once per row. The `determinant` is linear in each single row separately (multilinear), which is exactly why one-row scaling gives one factor of `$k$` while whole-matrix scaling gives `$n$` of them. Confusing `$|kA|$` with `$k|A|$` undercounts by `$k^{n-1}$`, a costly slip on matrices of size three and above.
concepts.detail: Consequences include `$|-A| = (-1)^n |A|$`, so odd-sized matrices flip sign under global negation while even-sized ones do not.

examples.title: Evaluate a 3x3 determinant with a zero-creating step
examples.problem: Compute $$|A| = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}$$ by first simplifying, then expanding along the best line.

steps.label: Step 1: Choose the method
steps.text:
```text
Best line: row 1 has a zero already (entry a(13) = 0)
Plan: expand along row 1 directly, two live cofactors
Signs on row 1: + - +
```
Row one already contains a zero, so expansion costs only two `$2 \times 2$` minors instead of three.

steps.label: Step 2: Write the two cofactors
steps.text: Expansion gives `$|A| = 2 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} - 1 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{vmatrix} + 0$`. The `cofactor` signs `$+$`, `$-$` come from `$(-1)^{1+j}$`, and the zero term drops out entirely.

steps.label: Step 3: Finish the arithmetic
steps.text: The minors evaluate to `$4 - 1 = 3$` and `$2 - 0 = 2$`, so `$|A| = 2 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot 2 = 4$`. A nonzero value reports an invertible matrix with volume scale `$4$`.

examples.result: The determinant equals `$4$`, so `$A$` is invertible.

examples.title: Use row operations to triangularize before evaluating
examples.problem: Compute $$|B| = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 5 & 7 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$$ by creating zeros with row addition, tracking the determinant at each move.

steps.label: Step 1: Clear below the pivot
steps.text:
```text
R2 <- R2 - 2*R1   (det unchanged)
R3 <- R3 - R1     (det unchanged)
New matrix: [1 2 3; 0 1 1; 0 -1 -2]
```
Both moves are `row-add` operations, so the `determinant` is unchanged and no sign or scale correction is owed.

steps.label: Step 2: Clear once more
steps.text: Add row two to row three via `$R_3 \gets R_3 + R_2$`, again determinant-preserving, reaching $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$$ The matrix is now **upper-triangular**, so the determinant is the diagonal product.

steps.label: Step 3: Read the diagonal
steps.text: Diagonal entries `$1, 1, -1$` multiply to `$-1$`, hence `$|B| = -1$`. No swaps or scalings occurred, so no sign flip or factor contaminates the reading.

examples.result: After determinant-preserving row additions, `$|B| = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot (-1) = -1$`.

keyTakeaways: Expand along the row or column with the most zeros using `$|A| = \sum_j a_{ij} C_{ij}$` with `$C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$`.
Swap flips sign, single-row scaling scales once, and row addition preserves `$|A|$`; duplicate or proportional rows give zero.
Products multiply as `$|AB| = |A||B|$` and triangular determinants are diagonal products.
Whole-matrix scaling obeys `$|kA| = k^n |A|$`, and `$|A+B|$` never splits into `$|A| + |B|$`.

quiz.q: What is $$\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}~?$$
quiz.explanation: First expand along row one, which already holds a zero. Next evaluate the two live minors `$3$` and `$2$`. Then combine as `$2 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot 2 = 4$`. Finally note the nonzero value signals invertibility.

quiz.q: Matrix `$A$` is `$3 \times 3$` with `$|A| = 2$`. What is `$|3A|$`?
quiz.explanation: First recall whole-matrix scaling hits every one of the `$n = 3$` rows. Next apply `$|kA| = k^n |A|$` with `$k = 3$`. Then compute `$3^3 \cdot 2 = 27 \cdot 2$`. Finally arrive at $54$, not `$6$`.

quiz.q: Starting from `$A$`, matrix `$B$` is formed by swapping rows one and two, then adding twice row one to row three. If `$|A| = 5$`, what is `$|B|$`?
quiz.explanation: First the swap multiplies the determinant by `$-1$`, taking `$5$` to `$-5$`. Next the row-addition move `$R_3 \gets R_3 + 2R_1$` leaves the determinant unchanged. Then no scaling occurred, so no further factor applies. Finally `$|B| = -5$`.

quiz.q: If `$A$` and `$B$` are `$n \times n$` with `$|A| = 0$`, what is `$|AB|$`?
quiz.explanation: First invoke multiplicativity `$|AB| = |A| \cdot |B|$`. Next substitute `$|A| = 0$`. Then the product is `$0 \cdot |B| = 0$` regardless of `$B$`. Finally conclude a singular factor always poisons the product.

intro: Inverses undo matrix multiplication, adjoints build them from cofactors, and rank measures how much independent information a matrix carries. This section unites the adjoint-inverse formula with the two practical rank computations: minors and echelon form. Rank then becomes the single number that predicts consistency, invertibility, and solution dimension in the next section.
objectives: Compute inverses via `$A^{-1} = \mathrm{adj}(A)/|A|$` and detect singular matrices
Find rank by largest nonzero minor and by row-echelon pivot count
State invertibility equivalences linking determinant, rank, rows and columns

concepts.statement: For square `$A$` with `$|A| \ne 0$`, the **inverse** is `$A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|} \mathrm{adj}(A)$` where the `adjoint` is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. Each entry of the inverse therefore divides a signed minor by the determinant, which is why a zero determinant makes inversion impossible. The formula also gives `$A \cdot \mathrm{adj}(A) = |A| I$`, valid even for singular matrices.
concepts.detail: For `$2 \times 2$` this collapses to swapping diagonal entries, negating off-diagonals, and dividing by `$ad - bc$`.

concepts.statement: A square matrix is **singular** when `$|A| = 0$`, admitting no inverse, and **invertible** (nonsingular) when `$|A| \ne 0$`. The `inverse` when it exists is unique and obeys `$(A^{-1})^{-1} = A$` plus `$(A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T$`. Invertibility is equivalent to full rank, independent columns, independent rows, and a trivial null space containing only the zero vector.
concepts.detail: Numerically, a tiny but nonzero determinant still inverts in theory yet amplifies rounding error, a conditioning warning beyond the binary singular label.

concepts.statement: The **rank** `$\rho(A)$` is the size `$r$` of the largest square submatrix with nonzero determinant, so rank is found by testing minors from large to small. A `minor` of size `$r+1$` vanishing everywhere while some `$r$`-minor survives certifies rank `$r$`. Rank zero occurs only for the zero matrix, and rank never exceeds either dimension of the matrix.
concepts.detail: For a `$3 \times 4$` matrix, test the four `$3 \times 3$` minors first: any nonzero one proves full row rank `$3$` at once.

concepts.statement: Row operations preserve rank, so reduction to **row-echelon form** reveals rank as the count of nonzero rows, equivalently the count of `pivot` positions. The `echelon` staircase has each leading entry to the right of the one above, and zero rows sink to the bottom. This method scales to large matrices where minor-hunting would need combinatorially many determinants.
concepts.detail: Column operations also preserve rank, so mixed reduction is permitted when only the rank number, not the solution set, is wanted.

concepts.statement: Rank obeys the **ceiling** `$\rho(A) \le \min(m, n)$` for `$m \times n$` matrices, with equality called **full rank**. The `rank` of a product obeys `$\rho(AB) \le \min(\rho(A), \rho(B))$`, so multiplication never creates independence. A tall matrix can have full column rank while a wide matrix can have full row rank, but only square full-rank matrices earn inverses.
concepts.detail: Rank one matrices factor as `$uv^T$`, an outer product whose columns are all multiples of `$u$` and whose rows are all multiples of `$v^T$`.

examples.title: Invert a 2x2 matrix and verify the product
examples.problem: Find the inverse of $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$$ and verify `$AA^{-1} = I$`.

steps.label: Step 1: Determinant first
steps.text:
```text
|A| = 4*6 - 7*2 = 24 - 14 = 10 (nonzero -> invertible)
2x2 shortcut: swap diagonal, negate off-diagonal, divide by |A|
```
The nonzero value `$10$` licenses inversion, and its size will divide every entry of the `inverse`.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply the shortcut
steps.text: Swap `$4$` and `$6$`, negate `$7$` and `$2$`, then divide by `$10$` to get $$A^{-1} = \frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix} 6 & -7 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 & -0.7 \\ -0.2 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix}$$ This is the `$2 \times 2$` face of `$A^{-1} = \mathrm{adj}(A)/|A|$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Verify
steps.text: Multiply `$AA^{-1}$`: top-left `$4(0.6) + 7(-0.2) = 2.4 - 1.4 = 1$`, top-right `$4(-0.7) + 7(0.4) = -2.8 + 2.8 = 0$`, and similarly the second row gives `$0$` and `$1$`. The product is $I_2$, confirming the inverse.

examples.result: $$A^{-1} = \frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix} 6 & -7 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$$ with `$|A| = 10$`.

examples.title: Find rank by echelon form
examples.problem: Determine `$\rho(A)$` for $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ using elimination.

steps.label: Step 1: Eliminate
steps.text:
```text
R2 <- R2 - 2*R1  ->  [0 0 0]
R3 <- R3 - R1    ->  [0 -2 0]
Swap R2 and R3 to restore staircase
```
Row two is a multiple of row one, so it collapses to zeros and contributes no `pivot`.

steps.label: Step 2: Read the staircase
steps.text: After the swap the echelon form is $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ with pivots in columns one and two. The `echelon` nonzero-row count is `$2$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Cross-check by minors
steps.text: All `$3 \times 3$` determinants vanish since `$|A| = 0$` by proportional rows, but the minor deleting row two and column three gives `$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -2 \ne 0$`. Largest surviving minor has size $2$, confirming `$\rho(A) = 2$`.

examples.result: Rank `$\rho(A) = 2$` with one dependency from the doubled row.

keyTakeaways: Invert by `$A^{-1} = \mathrm{adj}(A)/|A|$` when `$|A| \ne 0$`; zero determinant means singular with no inverse.
Rank is the largest surviving minor size, equal to the echelon pivot count.
Invertible is equivalent to full rank, nonzero determinant, and independent rows and columns.
Rank obeys `$\rho(AB) \le \min(\rho(A), \rho(B))$` and `$\rho(A) \le \min(m,n)$`.

quiz.q: If $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$$ what is `$A^{-1}$`?
options: Does not exist since `$A$` is singular
quiz.explanation: First compute `$|A| = 24 - 14 = 10 \ne 0$` so the inverse exists. Next swap diagonal entries and negate off-diagonals to form the adjoint. Then divide every entry by `$10$`. Finally the first option matches while the divisor `$38$` has no basis.

quiz.q: A `$4 \times 5$` matrix has every `$3 \times 3$` minor equal to zero but some `$2 \times 2$` minor nonzero. What is its rank?
quiz.explanation: First recall rank is the largest surviving minor size. Next all size-three minors vanish, so rank is below `$3$`. Then a surviving size-two minor proves rank is at least `$2$`. Finally rank equals `$2$` exactly.

quiz.q: Which condition is equivalent to `$A$` (square) being invertible?
options: Some row is a linear combination of the others
The adjoint `$\mathrm{adj}(A)$` is the zero matrix
quiz.explanation: First eliminate singularity: `$|A| = 0$` is the opposite of invertibility. Next dependent rows force zero determinant, also opposite. Then full rank `$\rho(A) = n$` matches nonzero determinant and independent rows. Finally a zero adjoint occurs only for rank below $n - 1$, never for invertible matrices.

quiz.q: If `$A$` is `$3 \times 3$` with `$|A| = 4$`, what is `$|A^{-1}|$`?
quiz.explanation: First use `$AA^{-1} = I$` with determinants on both sides. Next `$|A| \cdot |A^{-1}| = |I| = 1$`. Then substitute `$|A| = 4$` to get `$4 \cdot |A^{-1}| = 1$`. Finally `$|A^{-1}| = \frac{1}{4}$`.

intro: Linear systems ask which vectors `$x$` satisfy `$Ax = b$`, and the answer depends on a race between the coefficient rank and the augmented rank. This section states the consistency conditions, contrasts homogeneous with non-homogeneous systems, and compares Cramer rule against elimination. Counting solutions without fully solving is the headline skill.
objectives: Apply the consistency conditions to predict zero, one, or infinitely many solutions
Solve small systems by Cramer rule and by Gaussian elimination
Distinguish homogeneous trivial-only from nontrivial cases via rank

concepts.statement: Let `$\rho(A)$` be the coefficient rank and `$\rho([A \mid b])$` the **augmented** rank. The system is **consistent** exactly when the ranks agree, and then the solution is unique if `$\rho(A) = n$` (unknowns count) or infinite with `$n - \rho(A)$` free variables if `$\rho(A) < n$`. The `augmented` matrix appends `$b$` as an extra column, and disagreement `$\rho([A \mid b]) = \rho(A) + 1$` means `$b$` points outside the column space.
concepts.detail: Counting solutions needs only the two ranks and `$n$`: no full solve is required to answer zero, one, or infinite.

concepts.term: Homogeneous systems and the trivial solution
concepts.statement: The **homogeneous** system `$Ax = 0$` is always consistent because `$x = 0$` (the trivial solution) works, with the only question being uniqueness. It admits **nontrivial** solutions exactly when `$\rho(A) < n$`, equivalently `$|A| = 0$` for square systems. The `nullspace` of `$A$` is the full solution set, a subspace of dimension `$n - \rho(A)$`.
concepts.detail: More unknowns than equations (`$n > m$`) forces nontrivial solutions, since rank cannot exceed `$m$`.

concepts.statement: For a square system with `$|A| \ne 0$`, **Cramer rule** gives each unknown as a ratio `$x_i = |A_i| / |A|$` where `$A_i$` replaces column `$i$` of `$A$` by `$b$`. The `determinant` in the denominator is shared across all unknowns, so one `$|A|$` plus `$n$` modified determinants solve the whole system. The rule collapses when `$|A| = 0$`, and it costs `$n+1$` determinants, making it a theory tool rather than a large-system algorithm.
concepts.detail: Cramer rule proves uniqueness cleanly but elimination wins on arithmetic for size four and above.

concepts.term: Gaussian elimination to echelon and back substitution
concepts.statement: Forward elimination applies `row-add`, swap, and scale moves to reach an **upper-triangular** (echelon) form, tracking that swaps flip determinant signs while row-adds preserve solution sets. **Back substitution** then solves from the last equation upward, dividing by each `pivot` in turn. A zero pivot with nonzero right-hand side exposes inconsistency, while a full zero row exposes a free variable.
concepts.detail: Gauss-Jordan continues to reduced echelon with ones on pivots, reading the solution without a separate backward pass.

concepts.statement: Each missing pivot creates one **free variable** that can be chosen arbitrarily, with the remaining basic variables expressed in terms of it. The `parametric` solution `$x = x_p + t_1 v_1 + \cdots$` separates one particular solution from the homogeneous directions. Rank deficiency `$n - \rho(A)$` therefore counts the degrees of freedom, not just the vague label infinite.
concepts.detail: A unique solution has zero free variables, and an inconsistent system has none either, since inconsistency means no solution at all.

derivations.title: Cramer Rule for Two Equations in Two Unknowns
derivations.statement: Derivation of $x = \frac{\Delta_{x}}{\Delta}$ and $y = \frac{\Delta_{y}}{\Delta}$ for $ax + by = e$ and $cx + dy = f$ with $\Delta = ad - bc \ne 0$
prerequisites: Determinant of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $\Delta = ad - bc$
Elimination moves preserve the solution set of $Ax = b$
Unique solution exists exactly when $\Delta \ne 0$

steps.label: Step 1: Eliminate $y$ to isolate $x$
steps.explanation: Multiply the first equation by $d$ and the second by $b$, then subtract, so the $y$ terms cancel exactly because both become $bdy$. This works because equal quantities subtracted from equal quantities keep equality, leaving a single equation in $x$ with coefficient $ad - bc$. The combination is chosen precisely to force the $y$ coefficient to zero.

steps.label: Step 2: Eliminate $x$ to isolate $y$
steps.explanation: Multiply the first equation by $c$ and the second by $a$, then subtract, so the $x$ terms cancel exactly because both become $acx$. This mirrors the previous step with the roles exchanged, which is legitimate for the same equality-preserving reason. The surviving $y$ coefficient is again $ad - bc$ up to sign, giving $\Delta_{y}$ on the right.

steps.label: Step 3: Divide by the nonzero determinant
steps.explanation: Because $\Delta \ne 0$ is assumed, division by $\Delta$ is valid and yields a single candidate pair. This step works since a nonzero scalar multiple can be cancelled from both sides of an equation without changing its truth. If $\Delta$ were zero this division would be impossible, which is why the hypothesis is essential.

steps.label: Step 4: Read numerators as replaced-column determinants
steps.formula: $$\Delta_{x} = \begin{vmatrix} e & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix}, \quad \Delta_{y} = \begin{vmatrix} a & e \\ c & f \end{vmatrix}$$
steps.explanation: Expanding each $2 \times 2$ determinant reproduces $ed - bf$ and $af - ce$ respectively, so the elimination numerators are exactly the determinants of matrices with one column replaced by constants on the right side. This identification works because the determinant formula is defined by the same cross products that elimination produced. Hence each unknown is a ratio of two determinants.

derivations.result: For $\Delta \ne 0$, $x = \frac{\Delta_{x}}{\Delta}$ and $y = \frac{\Delta_{y}}{\Delta}$, meaning each unknown is the determinant with its column replaced by constants divided by the shared coefficient determinant.

examples.title: Solve a 2x2 system by Cramer rule
examples.problem: Solve $$\begin{aligned} 2x + y &= 5 \\ x + 3y &= 5 \end{aligned}$$ using determinant ratios.

steps.label: Step 1: Determinant of A
steps.text:
```text
A = [2 1; 1 3], b = [5; 5]
|A| = 2*3 - 1*1 = 5 (nonzero -> unique solution)
A_x replaces col 1 by b; A_y replaces col 2 by b
```
The shared denominator `$|A| = 5$` is nonzero, so **Cramer rule** applies and exactly one solution exists.

steps.label: Step 2: Modified determinants
steps.text: Form `$|A_x| = \begin{vmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 5 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 15 - 5 = 10$` and `$|A_y| = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 5 \end{vmatrix} = 10 - 5 = 5$`. Each `determinant` replaces one column of `$A$` by `$b$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Divide
steps.text: Ratios give `$x = 10/5 = 2$` written properly as `$x = \frac{10}{5} = 2$` and `$y = \frac{5}{5} = 1$`. Substitution checks: `$4 + 1 = 5$` and `$2 + 3 = 5$`.

examples.result: The unique solution is `$x = 2$`, `$y = 1$`.

examples.title: Detect inconsistency from the augmented rank
examples.problem: Determine the solution count for $$\begin{aligned} x + y + z &= 1 \\ 2x + 2y + 2z &= 4 \\ x - y + z &= 0 \end{aligned}$$ without finding any solution.

steps.label: Step 1: Build the augmented matrix
steps.text:
```text
[A|b] = [1 1 1 | 1; 2 2 2 | 4; 1 -1 1 | 0]
Suspect: row 2 is twice row 1 on the left only
```
The left block of row two doubles row one, but `$4 \ne 2 \cdot 1$` on the right, the classic parallel-plane signal.

steps.label: Step 2: Eliminate
steps.text: Subtract `$2R_1$` from `$R_2$` to get `$[0 \; 0 \; 0 \mid 2]$`, the row `$0 = 2$` which is impossible. Coefficient rank stays `$2$` from rows one and three, but the `augmented` rank rises to `$3$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Conclude
steps.text: Since `$\rho(A) = 2 \ne 3 = \rho([A \mid b])$`, the consistency condition fails and the system has **no solution**. Geometrically two of the planes are parallel and distinct.

examples.result: Ranks disagree (`$2$` versus `$3$`), so the system is inconsistent with zero solutions.

keyTakeaways: Consistent exactly when `$\rho(A) = \rho([A \mid b])$`; unique if rank equals $n$, otherwise `$n - \rho(A)$` free variables.
Homogeneous `$Ax = 0$` always admits `$x = 0$`, plus nontrivial solutions exactly when rank drops below `$n$.
Cramer rule `$x_i = |A_i|/|A|$` needs `$|A| \ne 0$` and costs `$n+1$` determinants.
Zero pivot rows read as `$0 = c$` (inconsistent) or `$0 = 0$` (free variable).

quiz.q: For `$Ax = b$` with `$A$` of size $3 \times 3$, suppose `$\rho(A) = 2$` and `$\rho([A \mid b]) = 3$`. How many solutions?
quiz.explanation: First compare the two ranks: `$2 \ne 3$` so consistency fails. Next recall agreement is necessary and sufficient for any solution. Then mismatch means `$b$` lies outside the column space. Finally the count is zero solutions.

quiz.q: The homogeneous system with $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ has how many solutions?
quiz.explanation: First rows one and two are proportional, so `$|A| = 0$`. Next rank is `$2$` since rows one and three are independent. Then `$n - \rho = 3 - 2 = 1$` free variable remains. Finally homogeneous systems are always consistent, so solutions form a line through the origin.

quiz.q: By Cramer rule, the solution of $$\begin{aligned} 2x + y &= 5 \\ x + 3y &= 5 \end{aligned}$$ is:
quiz.explanation: First compute `$|A| = 6 - 1 = 5$`. Next `$|A_x| = 15 - 5 = 10$` giving `$x = \frac{10}{5} = 2$`. Then `$|A_y| = 10 - 5 = 5$` giving `$y = \frac{5}{5} = 1$`. Finally verify `$2 + 3 = 5$` in the second equation.

quiz.q: A system of `$2$` equations in `$4$` unknowns has `$\rho(A) = \rho([A \mid b]) = 2$`. The solution set is:
quiz.explanation: First ranks agree so the system is consistent. Next free variables count `$n - \rho = 4 - 2 = 2$`. Then two independent homogeneous directions span the solution offset. Finally the general solution is a `$2$-dimensional flat, a plane through a particular point.

depth.title: Fredholm alternative and the four subspaces

blocks.body: The **Fredholm alternative** decides solvability of $Ax = b$ without solving. Let $A$ be $m \times n$ with rank $r$. Then $Ax = b$ is solvable exactly when $y^{T} b = 0$ for every $y$ with $A^{T} y = 0$, equivalently $\mathrm{rank}(A) = \mathrm{rank}([A \, b])$. Moreover $\mathrm{rank}(A) + \dim \ker(A) = n$ and $\mathrm{rank}(A) + \dim \ker(A^{T}) = m$, so the four subspaces have dimensions $r$, $n - r$, $r$ and $m - r$. The condition $y^{T} b = 0$ says $b$ has no component in the left nullspace.

Necessity is one line: if $Ax = b$ and $A^{T} y = 0$ then $y^{T} b = y^{T} A x = (A^{T} y)^{T} x = 0$. Sufficiency follows from orthogonal complements. The row space equals $(\ker A)^{\perp}$ and the column space equals $(\ker A^{T})^{\perp}$ under the standard dot product, with inclusion upgraded to equality by the dimension count $\dim \mathrm{range}(A) = r = m - \dim \ker(A^{T})$. Hence any $b$ orthogonal to $\ker(A^{T})$ lies in the range. The augmented rank test is this geometry in computational form.

When the test fails, the **normal equations** $A^{T} A \hat{x} = A^{T} b$ still give the least squares projection, and the Moore Penrose pseudoinverse selects the minimum norm minimizer via the singular value decomposition $A = U \Sigma V^{T}$. Finite dimensions make the range closed, so the alternative is sharp. In infinite dimensions it breaks: compact operators can have nonclosed range, and the index $\dim \ker - \dim \mathrm{coker}$ becomes Fredholm theory, the gateway to integral equations $u - \lambda K u = f$ and the Riesz Schauder theorems.

intro: Eigenvalues expose the directions along which a matrix acts by pure scaling, reducing complicated transformations to stretches and flips. This section builds the characteristic equation, eigenspaces, and the trace-determinant shortcuts that read eigenvalues without full expansion. Symmetric and triangular matrices receive special treatment because their spectra are visible almost immediately.
objectives: Form `$|A - \lambda I| = 0$` and solve for eigenvalues, then find eigenvectors
Apply trace-equals-sum and determinant-equals-product checks to spectra
State the symmetric and triangular eigenvalue shortcuts and their eigenvector consequences

concepts.statement: A scalar `$\lambda$` is an **eigenvalue** with nonzero vector `$v$` when `$Av = \lambda v$`, equivalently when `$A - \lambda I$` is singular so that `$|A - \lambda I| = 0$`. The `characteristic` polynomial `$p(\lambda) = |A - \lambda I|$` has degree `$n$` for `$n \times n$` matrices, and its roots counted with multiplicity are the full spectrum. Each eigenvalue is found first, and only then are eigenvectors solved from `$(A - \lambda I)v = 0$`.
concepts.detail: The zero vector never counts as an eigenvector, though `$\lambda = 0$` is a legitimate eigenvalue exactly when `$A$` is singular.

concepts.statement: For fixed `$\lambda$`, the solution set of `$(A - \lambda I)v = 0$` plus the zero vector forms the **eigenspace** `$E_\lambda$`, a subspace whose dimension is the geometric multiplicity. The `eigenspace` is the null space of $A - \lambda I$, so its dimension equals `$n - \rho(A - \lambda I)$`. Eigenvectors from distinct eigenvalues are always linearly independent, which is why enough distinct eigenvalues guarantee diagonalizability later.
concepts.detail: Geometric multiplicity never exceeds algebraic multiplicity, and a strict shortfall marks a defective eigenvalue.

concepts.term: Trace is the sum and determinant is the product
concepts.statement: The **spectral checks** state `$\mathrm{tr}(A) = \lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n$` and `$|A| = \lambda_1 \cdots \lambda_n$` with multiplicities included. The `trace` identity follows from matching the `$\lambda^{n-1}$` coefficient of the characteristic polynomial, and the product identity follows by setting `$\lambda = 0$`. Any claimed spectrum that fails either check is wrong before further work begins.
concepts.detail: A zero eigenvalue forces $|A| = 0$, and a negative determinant for odd `$n$` forces an odd count of negative real eigenvalues.

concepts.statement: A **triangular** or diagonal matrix wears its eigenvalues on the diagonal, since `$|A - \lambda I|$` stays triangular with diagonal entries `$a_{ii} - \lambda$`. The `diagonal` case decouples completely: `$e_1, \dots, e_n$` are eigenvectors with eigenvalues `$a_{11}, \dots, a_{nn}$`. Repeated diagonal entries still diagonalize here, unlike general matrices where repetition may defect.
concepts.detail: Reading eigenvalues off a triangular diagonal is instant, but eigenvectors still require solving each singular system.

concepts.term: Real symmetric spectra are fully real
concepts.statement: A real **symmetric** matrix has all eigenvalues real, and eigenvectors from distinct eigenvalues emerge automatically orthogonal. The `symmetric` guarantee removes complex arithmetic from the spectrum entirely, a sharp contrast with general real matrices whose complex eigenvalues arrive in conjugate pairs. Orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices in the next section rests entirely on this reality plus orthogonality.
concepts.detail: Skew-symmetric real matrices mirror this with purely imaginary eigenvalues, and orthogonal matrices confine theirs to the unit circle `$|\lambda| = 1$`.

examples.title: Compute the full spectrum of a 2x2 matrix
examples.problem: Find all eigenvalues and one eigenvector each for $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

steps.label: Step 1: Characteristic polynomial
steps.text:
```text
A - λI = [4-λ 1; 2 3-λ]
|A - λI| = (4-λ)(3-λ) - 2 = λ^2 - 7λ + 10
Roots: λ = 5 and λ = 2
```
The quadratic `$\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = 0$` factors as `$(\lambda - 5)(\lambda - 2)$`, giving the **eigenvalues** `$5$` and `$2$`.

steps.label: Step 2: Eigenvector for λ = 5
steps.text: Solve `$(A - 5I)v = 0$`, i.e. `$-x + y = 0$` with `$2x - 2y = 0$` redundant, so `$y = x$`. Choosing `$x = 1$` yields `$v_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$`, and `$Av_1 = 5v_1$` checks out.

steps.label: Step 3: Eigenvector for λ = 2 and checks
steps.text: Solve `$(A - 2I)v = 0$`, i.e. `$2x + y = 0$`, giving `$v_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$`. Spectral checks pass: sum `$5 + 2 = 7 = \mathrm{tr}(A)$` and product `$10 = |A|$`.

examples.result: Eigenvalues `$5$` and `$2$` with eigenvectors `$[1, 1]^T$` and `$[1, -2]^T$` up to scaling.

examples.title: Read a triangular spectrum and test independence
examples.problem: For $$T = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$$ list eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicities and decide whether three independent eigenvectors exist.

steps.label: Step 1: Read the diagonal
steps.text:
```text
T is upper-triangular -> eigenvalues are diagonal entries
λ = 2 (twice), λ = 7 (once)
Trace check: 2 + 2 + 7 = 11 = tr(T)
```
The **triangular** shortcut gives the spectrum with no polynomial work, and the `trace` sum `$11$` confirms the listing.

steps.label: Step 2: Eigenspace for λ = 7
steps.text: Solving `$(T - 7I)v = 0$` gives full rank `$2$` in the coefficient part, leaving a one-dimensional space spanned by a vector with nonzero third component. Geometric multiplicity is `$1$`, matching algebraic `$1$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Eigenspace for λ = 2
steps.text: Here `$T - 2I$` has only one independent row beyond zeros in a way that leaves rank `$2$`, so nullity is `$3 - 2 = 1$` against algebraic `$2$`. The shortfall means only two independent eigenvectors exist in total, so `$T$` is defective.

examples.result: Spectrum `$2, 2, 7$` but only two independent eigenvectors: defective, not diagonalizable.

keyTakeaways: Solve `$|A - \lambda I| = 0$` for eigenvalues, then `$(A - \lambda I)v = 0$` for eigenvectors; zero vector never qualifies.
Verify every spectrum with `$\sum \lambda_i = \mathrm{tr}(A)$` and `$\prod \lambda_i = |A|$`.
Triangular spectra sit on the diagonal; symmetric spectra are real with orthogonal eigenspaces.
Geometric multiplicity `$\le$` algebraic multiplicity; a shortfall means defective.

quiz.q: The eigenvalues of $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ are:
quiz.explanation: First form `$|A - \lambda I| = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10$`. Next factor as `$(\lambda - 5)(\lambda - 2)$`. Then roots are `$5$` and `$2$`. Finally the trace check `$7$` and determinant check `$10$` both pass.

quiz.q: A `$3 \times 3$` matrix has trace `$6$` and eigenvalues `$1$` and `$2$` plus one unknown. The unknown eigenvalue is:
quiz.explanation: First apply `$\mathrm{tr}(A) = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3$`. Next substitute `$6 = 1 + 2 + \lambda_3$`. Then solve `$\lambda_3 = 3$`. Finally note no determinant data was needed.

quiz.q: Eigenvalues of every upper-triangular matrix are:
options: Always all equal to the trace
quiz.explanation: First `$A - \lambda I$` stays upper-triangular with diagonal `$a_{ii} - \lambda$`. Next its determinant is the product `$\prod (a_{ii} - \lambda)$`. Then zeros occur exactly at `$\lambda = a_{ii}$`. Finally multiplicities follow diagonal repetition.

quiz.q: If `$Av = \lambda v$` with `$v \ne 0$` and `$k$` is a positive integer, what is `$A^k v$`?
quiz.explanation: First apply `$A$` once to get `$\lambda v$`. Next each further application pulls out one more factor `$\lambda$`. Then after `$k$` rounds the accumulated scalar is `$\lambda^k$`. Finally the direction `$v$` is unchanged.

depth.title: Characteristic polynomials over general fields

blocks.body: Scalars $\lambda$ with $A v = \lambda v$ for nonzero $v$ are exactly the roots of $p_{A}(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$. If $p_{A}(\lambda) = \prod_{j} (\lambda_{j} - \lambda)^{a_{j}}$ over an algebraic closure, then $\mathrm{tr}(A) = \sum_{j} a_{j} \lambda_{j}$ and $\det(A) = \prod_{j} \lambda_{j}^{a_{j}}$. For each eigenvalue the **geometric multiplicity** $g_{j} = \dim \ker(A - \lambda_{j} I)$ satisfies $1 \leq g_{j} \leq a_{j}$, where $a_{j}$ is the algebraic multiplicity. Triangular matrices display the spectrum on the diagonal, and diagonalizable matrices attain $g_{j} = a_{j}$ for all $j$.

Over $\mathbb{C}$ every $A$ is unitarily triangularizable as $A = Q T Q^{\ast}$ with $T$ upper triangular, by induction on invariant subspaces. Then $\det(A - \lambda I) = \prod_{k} (t_{kk} - \lambda)$, so eigenvalues are diagonal entries counted with multiplicity. The trace and determinant formulas follow from the constant and leading coefficients of $p_{A}$. The inequality $g_{j} \leq a_{j}$ holds because $g_{j}$ independent eigenvectors extend to a basis in which $A - \lambda_{j} I$ has a zero block of size $g_{j}$, forcing $(\lambda_{j} - \lambda)^{g_{j}}$ to divide $p_{A}(\lambda)$.

blocks.heading: A shear with one eigenline but a double root
blocks.body: The shear $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ has $p_{A}(\lambda) = (2 - \lambda)^{2}$, so $\lambda = 2$ has algebraic multiplicity $2$. Solving $(A - 2I)v = 0$ gives $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} v = 0$, hence $v$ is a multiple of $(1, 0)^{T}$ and $g = 1 < 2 = a$. No two independent eigenvectors exist, so $A$ cannot diagonalize. This gap $g < a$ is the precise obstruction: diagonalizability is the statement that the gaps close for every eigenvalue, equivalently that the minimal polynomial splits with distinct linear factors.

intro: Cayley-Hamilton lets a matrix satisfy its own characteristic equation, turning high powers and inverses into low-degree polynomial arithmetic. Diagonalization goes further by changing basis until the matrix becomes diagonal. This section pairs the power-reduction tool with the exact diagonalizability test and the special symmetric guarantee.
objectives: State Cayley-Hamilton and use it to reduce `$A^3$` and above to lower-degree expressions
Test diagonalizability via independent eigenvector count and minimal polynomial splitting
Diagonalize `$2 \times 2$` matrices explicitly as `$A = PDP^{-1}$`

concepts.statement: Every square matrix **satisfies its own characteristic equation**: if `$p(\lambda) = |A - \lambda I|$`, then `$p(A) = O$` upon replacing `$\lambda$` by `$A$` and constants by scalar matrices. The `characteristic` polynomial of degree `$n$` thus yields a relation expressing `$A^n$` through `$I, A, \dots, A^{n-1}$`. All higher powers reduce recursively, so no power ever escapes the span of the first `$n$` powers.
concepts.detail: For `$2 \times 2$` with `$p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - t\lambda + d$`, the relation is `$A^2 = tA - dI$` with trace `$t$` and determinant `$d$`.

concepts.term: Inverse and powers from the characteristic relation
concepts.statement: When `$|A| \ne 0$`, the constant term of `$p(A) = O$` is nonzero and can be rearranged to isolate `$I$`, giving `$A^{-1}$` as an explicit polynomial in `$A$` with no elimination. The `inverse` of a `$2 \times 2$` follows in one line, and repeated reduction computes `$A^3, A^4, e^A$` truncated series terms purely by substitution. Singular matrices still satisfy `$p(A) = O$` but yield no inverse, since the constant term vanishes.
concepts.detail: This polynomial route shines for small matrices and theory questions, while elimination wins for large numerical inverses.

concepts.statement: A matrix `$A$` is **diagonalizable** exactly when it owns `$n$` linearly independent eigenvectors, equivalently when `$A = PDP^{-1}$` with `$D$` diagonal and `$P$` holding the eigenvectors as columns. The `diagonal` entries of `$D$` are the eigenvalues matched to their columns of $P$, and powers collapse to `$A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$`. Distinct eigenvalues always suffice but are not necessary, since repeated eigenvalues may still supply full eigenspaces.
concepts.detail: Defective matrices fail the count and admit only Jordan form, never a pure diagonal `$D$`.

concepts.statement: Matrices related by `$B = P^{-1}AP$` are called **similar** and share eigenvalues, trace, determinant, rank, and characteristic polynomial. The `similar` transform is a change of basis, so it preserves the underlying linear map while changing its coordinate description. Diagonalization is the quest for the most similar-to-diagonal representative of the map.
concepts.detail: Eigenvectors transform as $w = P^{-1}v$, so similar matrices have matched, not identical, eigenvectors.

concepts.statement: Every real symmetric matrix is **orthogonally diagonalizable**: there exists orthogonal `$Q$` with `$A = QDQ^T$` and real diagonal `$D$`. The `orthogonal` diagonalizer has orthonormal eigenvector columns, so inversion is free via `$Q^{-1} = Q^T$`. This spectral decomposition underlies quadratic forms, principal axes, and covariance analysis.
concepts.detail: Repeated eigenvalues cause no defect here, because symmetric eigenspaces always achieve full dimension.

examples.title: Reduce A cubed with Cayley-Hamilton
examples.problem: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ Use Cayley-Hamilton to express `$A^3$` through `$I$` and `$A$`, then evaluate.

steps.label: Step 1: Characteristic polynomial
steps.text:
```text
Triangular -> eigenvalues 1 and 3
p(λ) = (λ-1)(λ-3) = λ^2 - 4λ + 3
Cayley-Hamilton: A^2 - 4A + 3I = O
```
The **characteristic** relation gives `$A^2 = 4A - 3I$`, the reduction rule for all higher powers.

steps.label: Step 2: Multiply up once
steps.text: Multiply by `$A$` to get `$A^3 = 4A^2 - 3A$`, then substitute `$A^2$` again: `$A^3 = 4(4A - 3I) - 3A = 13A - 12I$`. The `polynomial` reduction keeps degree below two at every stage.

steps.label: Step 3: Evaluate
steps.text: Insert `$A$` and `$I$` to get $$A^3 = 13\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - 12\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 26 \\ 0 & 27 \end{bmatrix}$$ Diagonal entries `$1^3$` and `$3^3$` confirm the triangular power rule.

examples.result: `$A^3 = 13A - 12I$`, numerically `$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 26 \\ 0 & 27 \end{bmatrix}$`.

examples.title: Diagonalize a 2x2 matrix as PDP inverse
examples.problem: Diagonalize $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ from the previous section as `$A = PDP^{-1}$` and write `$A^2$` via `$D$`.

steps.label: Step 1: Assemble P and D
steps.text:
```text
Eigenvalues: 5 and 2
v1 = [1; 1] for λ=5, v2 = [1; -2] for λ=2
P = [v1 v2], D = diag(5, 2)
```
Columns of `$P$` are eigenvectors in the order matching the `diagonal` of `$D$`, and `$|P| = -3 \ne 0$` confirms independence.

steps.label: Step 2: Invert P
steps.text: Using the `$2 \times 2$` shortcut, $$P^{-1} = \frac{1}{-3}\begin{bmatrix} -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2/3 & 1/3 \\ 1/3 & -1/3 \end{bmatrix}$$ written with fractions `$\frac{2}{3}$`, `$\frac{1}{3}$`, `$-\frac{1}{3}$` in KaTeX. Then `$A = PDP^{-1}$` holds by construction.

steps.label: Step 3: Square via D
steps.text: Powers hit only `$D$`: `$A^2 = PD^2P^{-1}$` with `$D^2 = \mathrm{diag}(25, 4)$`. One short multiplication recovers `$A^2$` without squaring `$A$` directly.

examples.result: With `$P = [v_1 \; v_2]$` and `$D = \mathrm{diag}(5,2)$`, `$A = PDP^{-1}$` and `$A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$`.

keyTakeaways: Cayley-Hamilton `$p(A) = O$` reduces every `$A^n$` to degree below `$n$`, and yields `$A^{-1}$` as a polynomial when `$|A| \ne 0$`.
Diagonalizable exactly with `$n$` independent eigenvectors; then `$A = PDP^{-1}$` and `$A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$`.
Similarity preserves eigenvalues, trace, determinant, rank and characteristic polynomial.
Real symmetric matrices always admit `$A = QDQ^T$` with orthogonal `$Q$` and real `$D$`.

quiz.q: Matrix `$A$` has characteristic `$p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3$`. Which matrix identity holds?
options: No relation: the theorem applies only to symmetric matrices
quiz.explanation: First state Cayley-Hamilton: `$p(A) = O$`. Next substitute `$A$` for `$\lambda$` and `$3I$` for `$3$`. Then `$A^2 - 4A + 3I = O$` follows directly. Finally the theorem needs no symmetry hypothesis.

quiz.q: If `$A = PDP^{-1}$` with `$D = \mathrm{diag}(2, -1)$`, what is `$A^3$`?
quiz.explanation: First expand `$A^3 = PDP^{-1}PDP^{-1}PDP^{-1}$`. Next adjacent `$P^{-1}P$` pairs cancel to `$I$`. Then only `$PD^3P^{-1}$` survives. Finally cube the diagonal: `$2^3 = 8$` and `$(-1)^3 = -1$`.

quiz.q: A `$3 \times 3$` matrix has eigenvalue `$2$` of algebraic multiplicity `$3$` but eigenspace dimension `$1$`. It is:
quiz.explanation: First count independent eigenvectors: only `$1$` from the short eigenspace. Next diagonalizability needs `$3$` independent eigenvectors. Then algebraic `$3$` versus geometric `$1$` marks defect. Finally no change of basis can repair the missing directions.

quiz.q: Which property is preserved under similarity `$B = P^{-1}AP$`?
quiz.explanation: First similarity is a basis change of the same linear map. Next eigenvalues solve `$|A - \lambda I| = 0$` which is invariant. Then trace and determinant follow as spectral sums and products. Finally entries and eigenvector coordinates do change with basis.

depth.title: Cayley-Hamilton beyond hand computation

blocks.body: Every square $A$ annihilates its own characteristic polynomial: if $p_{A}(s) = \det(sI - A) = s^{n} + c_{n-1} s^{n-1} + \cdots + c_{0}$ then $p_{A}(A) = A^{n} + c_{n-1} A^{n-1} + \cdots + c_{0} I = 0$. Consequently the **minimal polynomial** $m_{A}$, the monic polynomial of least degree with $m_{A}(A) = 0$, divides $p_{A}$ and shares exactly the same irreducible factors. Powers $A^{k}$ for $k \geq n$ and, when $A$ is invertible, $A^{-1} = -c_{0}^{-1}(A^{n-1} + \cdots + c_{1} I)$ reduce to degree below $n$.

One clean proof uses density: diagonalizable matrices are dense over $\mathbb{C}$, since a matrix with $n$ distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable and arbitrarily small perturbations separate repeated eigenvalues. The identity $p_{X}(X) = 0$ is obvious on diagonalizable $X = S D S^{-1}$ because it holds on each eigenvalue, and both sides depend continuously on the entries of $X$. Hence the identity persists on the closure, all matrices. The classical adjugate proof writes $(sI - A) \, \mathrm{adj}(sI - A) = p_{A}(s) I$ as a polynomial identity in $s$ and equates operator coefficients.

The theorem turns high powers into Krylov arithmetic: $e^{A}$, resolvents $(sI - A)^{-1}$ and recurrences $x_{k+1} = A x_{k}$ all collapse to polynomials of degree below $n$. Numerically the Faddeeva LeVerrier recursion extracts the coefficients $c_{k}$ alongside the adjugate, while control theory uses $p_{A}(A) = 0$ to prove that the controllability matrix $[B \, A B \, \cdots \, A^{n-1} B]$ already spans every reachable direction. The rational canonical form refines the picture: invariant factors interpolate between $m_{A}$ and $p_{A}$.

intro: Vector spaces abstract the familiar rules of arrows and function spaces into span, independence, basis and dimension. Rank-nullity then ties the shape of a matrix to the dimensions of its row space and null space. This section supplies the geometry behind elimination: pivots count basis vectors, free variables count null directions.
objectives: Test sets for span, independence, subspace closure and basis status
Compute dimension and coordinates relative to a basis
Apply rank-nullity `$\mathrm{rank} + \mathrm{nullity} = n$` to solution geometry

concepts.statement: The **span** of vectors is the set of all their linear combinations `$c_1 v_1 + \cdots + c_k v_k$`, and a **subspace** is a subset closed under addition and scalar multiplication containing the zero vector. The `span` of any set is automatically the smallest subspace holding it. Lines and planes through the origin qualify, while translated lines missing the origin do not.
concepts.detail: Column space and null space are the two subspaces attached to every matrix, living in `$\mathbb{R}^m$` and `$\mathbb{R}^n$` respectively.

concepts.statement: Vectors are **independent** when `$c_1 v_1 + \cdots + c_k v_k = 0$` forces every `$c_i = 0$`, and **dependent** when some nontrivial relation exists. The `independent` test runs elimination on the matrix with these vectors as columns: full column rank means independent. Any set containing the zero vector or a repeated vector is dependent at once.
concepts.detail: In $\mathbb{R}^n$, any `$n+1$` vectors are automatically dependent, since rank cannot exceed `$n$`.

concepts.statement: A **basis** is an independent spanning set, so every vector has unique coordinates `$x = c_1 b_1 + \cdots + c_n b_n$` relative to it. The `basis` size is fixed for a space and called its **dimension**, with `$\dim(\mathbb{R}^n) = n$`. The standard basis `$e_1, \dots, e_n$` gives raw components, while eigenbases and orthogonal bases simplify maps and projections.
concepts.detail: To extend an independent set to a basis, adjoin vectors outside the current span one at a time until spanning holds.

concepts.statement: For `$m \times n$` matrix $A$, **rank plus nullity equals `$n$`**: `$\rho(A) + \dim(\ker A) = n$`, where nullity counts free variables. The `nullity` measures the solution space of $Ax = 0$, so each pivot removes one null direction. Full column rank `$\rho = n$` forces nullity zero and a trivial-only homogeneous solution.
concepts.detail: Row rank equals column rank, so the same `$\rho$` serves both the row space in `$\mathbb{R}^n$` and the column space in `$\mathbb{R}^m$`.

concepts.term: Coordinates depend on the basis, geometry does not
concepts.statement: The same vector carries **different coordinate tuples** under different bases, related by an invertible change-of-basis matrix `$[x]_C = P^{-1}[x]_B$`. The `coordinates` are labels while span, independence and dimension are intrinsic geometry. Confusing a coordinate tuple with the vector itself is why basis-change slips occur.
concepts.detail: Choosing an eigenbasis diagonalizes the coordinate map, turning iteration `$x_{k+1} = Ax_k$` into independent scalar recurrences.

examples.title: Test independence and build a basis
examples.problem: In $\mathbb{R}^3$, test `$v_1 = (1,0,0)$`, `$v_2 = (1,1,0)$`, `$v_3 = (1,1,1)$` for independence, and express `$x = (2,3,4)$` in this basis.

steps.label: Step 1: Elimination test
steps.text:
```text
Columns matrix: [1 1 1; 0 1 1; 0 0 1]
Already upper-triangular, pivots in all 3 columns
Determinant = 1 (nonzero) -> independent
```
Three pivots in three columns certify **independence**, and since three independent vectors in `$\mathbb{R}^3$` must span, they form a `basis`.

steps.label: Step 2: Solve for coordinates
steps.text: Write `$c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2 + c_3 v_3 = x$`: bottom row gives `$c_3 = 4$`, middle gives `$c_2 + c_3 = 3$` so `$c_2 = -1$`, top gives `$c_1 + c_2 + c_3 = 2$` so `$c_1 = -1$`. Back substitution up the triangular system yields coordinates `$(-1, -1, 4)$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Verify
steps.text: Recombine `$-v_1 - v_2 + 4v_3 = (-1-1+4, -1+4, 4) = (2, 3, 4)$`. Uniqueness of basis coordinates guarantees no second triple works.

examples.result: Independent, hence a basis, with `$[x]_B = (-1, -1, 4)$`.

examples.title: Apply rank-nullity to a solution space
examples.problem: Matrix `$A$` is `$4 \times 5$` with `$\rho(A) = 3$`. Find the nullity and describe `$Ax = 0$` geometrically.

steps.label: Step 1: Rank-nullity
steps.text:
```text
n = 5 columns, rank = 3
nullity = n - rank = 5 - 3 = 2
Free variables: 2; pivots: 3
```
The formula `$\rho + \mathrm{nullity} = n$` converts one rank number into the full solution dimension.

steps.label: Step 2: Geometry
steps.text: Two free variables span a **two-dimensional** subspace (a plane through the origin) in `$\mathbb{R}^5$`. Every solution is `$x = s u_1 + t u_2$` with basis null vectors `$u_1, u_2$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Consistency remark
steps.text: The column space has dimension `$3$` inside $\mathbb{R}^4$, so non-homogeneous `$Ax = b$` is solvable only for `$b$` in that `$3$-dimensional subspace. Rank counts solvability directions while `nullity` counts solution freedom.

examples.result: Nullity `$2$`: solutions form a plane `$x = su_1 + tu_2$` in `$\mathbb{R}^5$`.

keyTakeaways: Span is all linear combinations; subspaces must contain zero and close under both operations.
Independence means only the trivial relation; `$n+1$` vectors in `$\mathbb{R}^n$` always depend.
Basis gives unique coordinates; size equals dimension.
Rank-nullity `$\rho + \mathrm{nullity} = n$` splits unknowns into pivot versus free counts.

quiz.q: Which triple forms a basis of `$\mathbb{R}^3$`?
quiz.explanation: First the triple with zero third components spans only a plane, so it fails spanning. Next any set holding the zero vector is dependent at once. Then the proportional pair is dependent. Finally the triangular triple has determinant `$1$`, hence independent and spanning.

quiz.q: For a `$5 \times 7$` matrix of rank $4$, the nullity (dimension of `$Ax = 0$) is:
quiz.explanation: First identify `$n = 7$` columns. Next apply `$\rho + \mathrm{nullity} = n$`. Then `$4 + \mathrm{nullity} = 7$`. Finally nullity equals `$3$`, meaning three free variables.

quiz.q: Vectors `$v_1, v_2, v_3$` in `$\mathbb{R}^3$` are dependent. Which must hold?
options: One of them is a linear combination of the others
quiz.explanation: First write the nontrivial relation `$c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + c_3v_3 = 0$`. Next some `$c_i \ne 0$` divides through. Then that vector is expressed via the rest. Finally spanning and rank claims need not hold for dependent sets.

quiz.q: The null space `$\ker(A)$` is best described as:
options: All `$b$` for which `$Ax = b$` is solvable
The set of pivot columns of $A$
quiz.explanation: First the defining equation is `$Ax = 0$`. Next closure under addition and scaling follows from linearity. Then zero belongs and the set is a subspace of `$\mathbb{R}^n$`. Finally it collapses to zero only at full column rank.

intro: LU decomposition splits `$A$` into a unit-lower times an upper factor so that each right-hand side costs only two triangular solves. Doolittle fixes unit diagonal on `$L$` while Crout puts it on $U$, and partial pivoting extends the idea to every invertible matrix. This section derives the factor patterns and the forward-back substitution routine.
objectives: Factor small matrices in Doolittle `$A = LU$` form by multiplier inspection
Solve `$Ax = b$` through `$Ly = b$` then `$Ux = y$` without inverting
State when `$LU$` exists directly and when row swaps `$PA = LU$` are needed

concepts.statement: The **Doolittle** factorization writes `$A = LU$` with `$L$` unit-lower-triangular (ones on the diagonal) and `$U$` upper-triangular. The `multiplier` `$l_{ij}$` below the diagonal records the elimination factor used to clear column `$j$` from row $i$, while `$U$` is the resulting echelon form. For `$2 \times 2$` with $a_{11} \ne 0$, the factors are immediate: `$l_{21} = a_{21}/a_{11}$` written as `$l_{21} = \frac{a_{21}}{a_{11}}$`, `$u_{11} = a_{11}$`, `$u_{12} = a_{12}$`, `$u_{22} = a_{22} - l_{21}u_{12}$`.
concepts.detail: The decomposition is unique when it exists, because the unit diagonal on `$L$` removes the scaling ambiguity between factors.

concepts.statement: The **Crout** form instead puts ones on `$U$` and lets `$L$` carry the diagonal, while **Cholesky** handles symmetric positive-definite `$A$` as `$A = GG^T$` with lower-triangular `$G$`. The `Crout` choice suits certain derivations, and `Cholesky` halves storage and work for covariance-type matrices. All three share the same elimination multipliers, differing only in where diagonal scaling is parked.
concepts.detail: Cholesky needs positive pivots throughout; a non-positive pivot aborts the factorization and reports indefiniteness.

concepts.statement: Once $A = LU$, solving `$Ax = b$` splits into **forward** `$Ly = b$` solved top-down via `$y_i = b_i - \sum_{j < i} l_{ij} y_j$`, then **back** `$Ux = y$` solved bottom-up. The `forward` pass costs about `$\frac{n^2}{2}$` operations and the back pass the same, far below a fresh elimination per right-hand side. Repeated `$b$` vectors reuse one factorization, which is the economic point of the method.
concepts.detail: Unit diagonal on `$L$` means no division in the forward pass, only multiply-subtract steps.

concepts.statement: Direct `$LU$` without swaps exists exactly when all **leading principal minors** are nonzero, so every elimination pivot is available in order. With **partial pivoting** every invertible matrix factors as `$PA = LU$` where `$P$` records row swaps. The `pivot` strategy swaps the largest-magnitude candidate into place, guaranteeing stability and existence together.
concepts.detail: A zero leading minor forces at least one swap, but `$PA = LU$` still succeeds as long as `$A$` is invertible.

concepts.term: One factorization serves many right-hand sides
concepts.statement: Factorization dominates cost at about **two-thirds `$n^3$`** operations, while each triangular solve costs only order `$n^2$`. The `reuse` principle therefore favors `$LU$` whenever several `$b$` vectors share one $A$, such as time stepping or load cases. Computing `$A^{-1}$` explicitly is wasteful by comparison, costing several solves plus denser storage.
concepts.detail: Determinant follows free from `$U$`: `$|A| = \pm \prod u_{ii}$` with the sign from the recorded swaps.

examples.title: Doolittle factorization of a 3x3 matrix
examples.problem: Factor $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 3 \\ 8 & 7 & 9 \end{bmatrix}$$ as `$A = LU$` in Doolittle form.

steps.label: Step 1: First column multipliers
steps.text:
```text
Pivot u11 = 2
l21 = 4 over 2 = 2,  l31 = 8 over 2 = 4
Clear column 1 (U rows update, L records multipliers)
```
Pivots must be nonzero; `$u_{11} = 2$` qualifies, giving integer `multiplier` values `$2$` and `$4$`.

steps.label: Step 2: Schur update and second pivot
steps.text: Subtracting yields working rows `$[0, 1, 1]$` and `$[0, 3, 5]$` in `$U$`, so the next pivot is `$u_{22} = 1$` with `$l_{32} = \frac{3}{1} = 3$`. Elimination records `$3$` in `$L$` and clears to `$[0, 0, 2]$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Assemble
steps.text: Collecting gives $$L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \qquad U = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ and `$LU$` multiplies back to `$A$, verified entry by entry.

examples.result: Doolittle factors as above with `$|A| = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 = 4$`.

examples.title: Solve a system with two triangular passes
examples.problem: Using the factors above, solve `$Ax = b$` for `$b = (2, 7, 23)^T$` written `$b = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 7 \\ 23 \end{bmatrix}$`.

steps.label: Step 1: Forward Ly = b
steps.text:
```text
L unit lower -> no divisions
y1 = 2
y2 = 7 - 2*y1 = 3
y3 = 23 - 4*y1 - 3*y2 = 6
```
Top-down `forward` substitution peels off one multiplier row at a time, producing `$y = (2, 3, 6)^T$`.

steps.label: Step 2: Back Ux = y
steps.text: Bottom-up from `$2x_3 = 6$` gives `$x_3 = 3$`, then `$x_2 + x_3 = 3$` gives `$x_2 = 0$`, then `$2x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 2$` gives `$x_1 = -\frac{1}{2}$`. Each step divides by the diagonal `pivot` of `$U$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Check
steps.text: Insert into `$A$` with `$x_1 = -\frac{1}{2}$`, `$x_2 = 0$`, `$x_3 = 3$`: row one gives $-1 + 0 + 3 = 2$, row two gives $-2 + 0 + 9 = 7$, row three gives $-4 + 0 + 27 = 23$. All three equations check, confirming `$x = (-\frac{1}{2}, 0, 3)^T$`.

examples.result: Forward then back substitution yields `$y = (2,3,6)^T$` and the triangular path to `$x$`.

keyTakeaways: Doolittle `$A = LU$` stores multipliers in unit `$L$` and the echelon in `$U$`; `$l_{ij} = a_{ij}^{(j)}/u_{jj}$`.
Solve via `$Ly = b$` top-down then `$Ux = y$` bottom-up; each pass costs about `$n^2/2$`.
Direct `$LU$` needs nonzero leading principal minors; otherwise factor `$PA = LU$` with swaps.
One factorization serves all right-hand sides; determinant is `$\pm \prod u_{ii}$`.

quiz.q: Doolittle factors of $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ are:
quiz.explanation: First pivot `$u_{11} = 2$` is nonzero. Next multiplier `$l_{21} = \frac{4}{2} = 2$`. Then `$u_{22} = 3 - 2 \cdot 1 = 1$`. Finally only the second option multiplies back to `$A$`.

quiz.q: After factoring $A = LU$, solving for a new `$b$` requires:
quiz.explanation: First the factors already encode elimination. Next `$Ly = b$` runs top-down in order `$n^2$`. Then `$Ux = y$` runs bottom-up. Finally no refactorization is needed for any new right-hand side.

quiz.q: Direct `$LU$` without row swaps is guaranteed iff:
options: All leading principal minors are nonzero
quiz.explanation: First each elimination pivot equals a ratio of successive leading minors. Next a zero minor forces a zero pivot in order. Then swaps become unavoidable. Finally nonzero minors at every stage are exactly the condition.

quiz.q: If `$PA = LU$` with one row swap and `$U$` diagonal `$(2, 3, 5)$`, then `$|A|$` equals:
quiz.explanation: First `$|P| = -1$` for a single swap. Next `$|L| = 1$` since `$L$` is unit triangular. Then `$|U| = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 = 30$`. Finally `$|A| = -|U| = -30$` via `$|P||A| = |L||U|$`.

intro: First-order equations relate a function to its first derivative, and the separable and homogeneous classes solve by direct integration after the right rearrangement. This section builds the separation move, the `$y = vx$` substitution for homogeneous forms, and the handling of initial data and lost constant solutions. Recognizing these two forms on sight is the fastest skill in the differential-equations toolkit.
objectives: Solve separable equations by `$\int \frac{dy}{g(y)} = \int f(x)\,dx$` including initial-value problems
Detect homogeneous `$F(y/x)$` forms and apply `$y = vx$` to separate them
Recover constant solutions lost during division and validate answers by substitution

concepts.statement: An equation is **separable** when it factors as `$\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x)g(y)$`, so dividing by `$g(y)$` and integrating gives `$\int \frac{dy}{g(y)} = \int f(x)\,dx + C$`. The `separable` move treats `$\frac{dy}{dx}$` as a ratio of differentials, collects `$y$` terms left and `$x$` terms right, then integrates each side independently. Absolute values from `$\int \frac{dy}{y} = \ln|y|$` merge into the constant `$C$` or a positive factor `$C_1 = e^C$`.
concepts.detail: Always record zeros of `$g(y)$` first: each root `$y = c$` with `$g(c) = 0$` is a constant solution that division by `$g(y)$` would erase.

concepts.statement: An equation is **homogeneous** of degree zero when the right side depends only on the ratio `$v = \frac{y}{x}$`, i.e. `$\frac{dy}{dx} = F\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)$`, equivalently when `$M$` and `$N$` in `$M\,dx + N\,dy = 0$` are homogeneous of the same degree. The `homogeneous` test rescales: `$M(tx, ty) = t^n M(x, y)$` and `$N(tx, ty) = t^n N(x, y)$` with a shared `$n$`. Sums like `$x^2 + xy + y^2$` pass with `$n = 2$`, while `$x^2 + y$` mixes degrees and fails.
concepts.detail: Every term must carry the same total power of `$x$` and `$y$`; constants and mixed-degree sums break homogeneity.

concepts.statement: Setting `$y = vx$` with `$\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}$` converts every homogeneous equation into the **separable** form `$x\frac{dv}{dx} = F(v) - v$`. The `substitution` trades the ratio structure for a product structure, and separation `$\int \frac{dv}{F(v) - v} = \int \frac{dx}{x}$` finishes the work. Back-substitution `$v = \frac{y}{x}$` restores the answer to `$x$` and `$y$`.
concepts.detail: The companion `$x = uy$` suits equations cleaner in `$\frac{dx}{dy}$`, chosen whenever `$N$` is simpler than `$M$`.

concepts.statement: The **general solution** carries one arbitrary constant `$C$` for a first-order equation, a **particular solution** fixes `$C$` from initial data `$y(x_0) = y_0$`, and a **singular solution** meets the equation but lies outside the general family. The `particular` value follows from substituting `$x_0, y_0$` into the general form and solving for `$C$`. Singular cases typically arise as envelopes or as the divided-out zeros `$g(c) = 0$` from separation.
concepts.detail: Existence and uniqueness hold near `$x_0$` when `$f$` and `$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$` are continuous there, so a crossing of two solutions signals a continuity failure.

concepts.statement: Every division by a **variable expression** risks deleting solutions, so the audit habit is: list zeros first, divide second, reattach lost constants third. The `audit` also covers logarithms, which demand positive arguments handled by `$|y|$` or piecewise signs. A final substitution check of the answer into the original equation catches sign and constant slips in one pass.
concepts.detail: Writing `$\ln|y| = x + C$` as `$y = \pm e^C e^x$` and folding `$\pm e^C$` into a nonzero `$C_1$` keeps the family complete including sign flips.

examples.title: Separable equation with initial data
examples.problem: Solve `$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2x}{y}$` with `$y(0) = 3$`.

steps.label: Step 1: Audit and separate
steps.text:
```text
No zeros of g(y) = 1/y at finite y; y = 0 excluded from domain
Multiply: y dy = 2x dx
Integrate: y^2 over 2 = x^2 + C
```
No constant solution is lost since `$\frac{1}{y}$` vanishes nowhere, and the `separable` split `$y\,dy = 2x\,dx$` is valid for `$y \ne 0$`.

steps.label: Step 2: General solution
steps.text: Integration gives `$\frac{y^2}{2} = x^2 + C$`, or `$y^2 = 2x^2 + C_1$` with `$C_1 = 2C$`. Taking roots yields `$y = \pm\sqrt{2x^2 + C_1}$`, two branches of one family.

steps.label: Step 3: Particular branch
steps.text: Data `$y(0) = 3 > 0$` selects the positive branch with `$9 = C_1$`, so `$y = \sqrt{2x^2 + 9}$`. Differentiation confirms `$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2x}{\sqrt{2x^2+9}} = \frac{2x}{y}$`.

examples.result: General `$y^2 = 2x^2 + C_1$`; particular `$y = \sqrt{2x^2 + 9}$`.

examples.title: Homogeneous equation via y = vx
examples.problem: Solve `$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^2 + y^2}{xy}$` for `$x > 0$`.

steps.label: Step 1: Confirm homogeneity
steps.text:
```text
Numerator x^2 + y^2 has degree 2; denominator xy has degree 2
Right side = x/y + y/x = 1/v + v with v = y/x
Homogeneous degree zero confirmed
```
Both numerator and denominator are degree $2$, so the ratio depends only on `$v = \frac{y}{x}$`.

steps.label: Step 2: Substitute and separate
steps.text: With `$y = vx$`, `$v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1}{v} + v$`, so `$x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1}{v}$`. The `substitution` cancels `$v$` on both sides, leaving `$v\,dv = \frac{dx}{x}$`, which integrates to `$\frac{v^2}{2} = \ln x + C$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Return to x and y
steps.text: Back-substitution gives `$\frac{y^2}{2x^2} = \ln x + C$`, or `$y^2 = 2x^2(\ln x + C)$`. The candidate `$y = 0$` meets the original equation only at isolated points, so no global constant solution was lost.

keyTakeaways: Separate as `$\int dy/g(y) = \int f(x)\,dx$`, but list zeros of `$g$` before dividing.
Homogeneous means `$dy/dx = F(y/x)$`; `$y = vx$` gives `$x\,dv/dx = F(v) - v$`.
Initial data selects branch and constant; verify by substituting back.
Continuity of `$f$` and `$\partial f/\partial y$` governs uniqueness near `$x_0$`.

quiz.q: The general solution of `$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2x}{y}$` is:
options: $\ln y = x^2 + C$ only, with no other branch
quiz.explanation: First separate as `$y\,dy = 2x\,dx$` for `$y \ne 0$`. Next integrate to `$\frac{y^2}{2} = x^2 + C$`. Then clear denominators to `$y^2 = 2x^2 + C_1$`. Finally absorb `$2$` into the constant, matching the first option.

quiz.q: Which equation is homogeneous of degree zero?
quiz.explanation: First test each right side under scaling `$(x, y) \to (tx, ty)$`. Next only the second is unchanged since numerator and denominator are both degree `$2$`. Then the others mix degrees or carry constants. Finally write it as `$\frac{1}{v} + v$` with `$v = \frac{y}{x}$`.

quiz.q: Under $y = vx$, the equation `$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x} + \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2$` becomes:
quiz.explanation: First substitute `$\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}$` and `$\frac{y}{x} = v$`. Next the equation reads `$v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = v + v^2$`. Then cancel `$v$` from both sides. Finally $x\frac{dv}{dx} = v^2$, separable in `$v$` and `$x$`.

quiz.q: Solving `$\frac{dy}{dx} = y^2$` by separation, which constant solution must be reattached alongside the general family?
quiz.explanation: First note `$g(y) = y^2$` has zero `$y = 0$`. Next division by `$y^2$` assumes `$y \ne 0$`. Then `$y = 0$` meets `$\frac{dy}{dx} = y^2$` since both sides vanish. Finally the general `$y = \frac{-1}{x + C}$` never takes the value zero, so it must be listed separately.

intro: Linear first-order equations add a `$y$` term to the derivative, and the integrating factor collapses the left side into a single product derivative. Bernoulli equations look nonlinear but linearize under `$z = y^{1-n}$`. This section turns both classes into routine quadrature with careful attention to the standard form and the `$n = 0, 1$` edge cases.
objectives: Rewrite equations in standard form `$\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$` and compute `$\mu = e^{\int P\,dx}$`
Solve linear equations completely via `$\frac{d}{dx}(\mu y) = \mu Q$` plus initial data
Reduce Bernoulli equations with `$z = y^{1-n}$` and handle `$n = 0, 1$` directly

concepts.statement: A first-order equation is **linear** when it fits `$\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$` with `$y$` and `$\frac{dy}{dx}$` to the first power and no products `$y\frac{dy}{dx}$`. The `standard` form demands coefficient `$1$` on `$\frac{dy}{dx}$`, so dividing by the leading coefficient is step zero. Terms like `$y^2$`, `$\sin y$`, or `$y\frac{dy}{dx}$` immediately disqualify linearity.
concepts.detail: Bernoulli equations `$\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)y^n$` are the near-linear neighbors, linear exactly when `$n = 0$` or `$n = 1$`.

concepts.statement: Multiplying by `$\mu(x) = e^{\int P(x)\,dx}$` turns the left side into an exact derivative: `$\frac{d}{dx}(\mu y) = \mu Q$`. The **integrating factor** is never unique, since any nonzero constant multiple works, and the simplest choice drops the constant of integration inside the exponent. The `integrating` identity follows from `$\frac{d}{dx}(\mu y) = \mu\frac{dy}{dx} + y\frac{d\mu}{dx}$` with `$\frac{d\mu}{dx} = \mu P$` by construction.
concepts.detail: For constant $P(x) = a$, the factor is `$e^{ax}$`, and for `$P(x) = \frac{k}{x}$` it is `$x^k$`, two instances worth memorizing.

concepts.statement: The pipeline is: divide into **standard form**, compute `$\mu$`, multiply through, collapse to `$\frac{d}{dx}(\mu y) = \mu Q$`, and integrate `$y = \frac{1}{\mu}\left(\int \mu Q\,dx + C\right)$`. The `pipeline` fails loudly if `$P$` or `$Q$` blow up at the initial point, signaling a restricted interval of validity. Initial data `$y(x_0) = y_0$` applied after integration selects the single curve through that point.
concepts.detail: Definite integration from `$x_0$` to `$x$` bakes the initial value in directly and avoids a separate constant-solving round.

concepts.statement: For `$\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)y^n$` with $n \ne 0, 1$, dividing by `$y^n$` and setting `$z = y^{1-n}$` yields a **linear** equation `$\frac{dz}{dx} + (1-n)P(x)z = (1-n)Q(x)$`. The `Bernoulli` substitution differentiates as `$\frac{dz}{dx} = (1-n)y^{-n}\frac{dy}{dx}$`, which is exactly the combination produced by division. Constant solutions `$y = 0$` (for `$n > 0$) may be lost in division and need reattachment.
concepts.detail: The values `$n = 0$` and `$n = 1$` need no substitution: they are already linear and separable-linear respectively.

concepts.statement: The solution is valid on intervals where `$P$` and `$Q$` stay **continuous**, with division points and zeros of `$\mu$` excluded. The `domain` containing `$x_0$` and bounded by the nearest discontinuity is the guaranteed interval from the existence theorem. Extending formulas across a singular point without fresh constants manufactures false global solutions.
concepts.detail: Factors like `$x^k$` from `$P = \frac{k}{x}$` split the line into `$x > 0$` and $x < 0$, each carrying its own constant.

derivations.title: Integrating-Factor Solution of Linear First-Order Equations
derivations.statement: Derivation of $y = \frac{1}{\mu}\left(\int \mu Q \, dx + C\right)$ with $\mu = e^{\int P \, dx}$ for $\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$
prerequisites: Product rule $\frac{d}{dx}(\mu y) = \mu \frac{dy}{dx} + y \frac{d\mu}{dx}$
Exponential derivative $\frac{d}{dx}e^{A(x)} = A^{\prime}(x)e^{A(x)}$
Standard linear form $\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$

steps.label: Step 1: Demand a product derivative
steps.explanation: Seek a positive multiplier $\mu$ such that $\mu P$ equals $\frac{d\mu}{dx}$, because then the left side matches the product-rule expansion of $\frac{d}{dx}(\mu y)$. This requirement works since it is a separable equation for $\mu$ whose solution is the exponential of the integral of $P$. Any nonzero constant multiple would also work, so the simplest choice drops the constant.

steps.label: Step 2: Multiply and collapse the left side
steps.explanation: Multiplying the standard form by $\mu$ gives $\mu \frac{dy}{dx} + \mu P y = \mu Q$. The left side is exactly $\frac{d}{dx}(\mu y)$ by the product rule plus the defining property of $\mu$ from the previous step. This collapse works because $\mu$ was engineered to supply the missing $y \frac{d\mu}{dx}$ piece.

steps.label: Step 3: Integrate the collapsed equation
steps.explanation: Integrate both sides with respect to $x$, which inverts the outer derivative on the left by the fundamental theorem of calculus. This works because $\mu Q$ is assumed continuous on the interval of interest, so its antiderivative exists. The constant $C$ records the one degree of freedom of a first-order equation.

steps.label: Step 4: Divide by the nonzero factor
steps.explanation: Since $\mu$ is an exponential it never vanishes, so division by $\mu$ is safe on the whole interval. This final division works because it isolates $y$ while preserving equality, converting quadrature into an explicit solution. The formula separates the forced response from the homogeneous term $\frac{C}{\mu}$.

derivations.result: With $\mu = e^{\int P \, dx}$, $y = \frac{1}{\mu}\left(\int \mu Q \, dx + C\right)$, meaning the linear equation reduces to one quadrature after the product-derivative collapse.

examples.title: Linear equation with polynomial factor
examples.problem: Solve `$\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{2}{x}y = x^2$` for `$x > 0$`.

steps.label: Step 1: Read P and build mu
steps.text:
```text
Standard form already (coeff 1 on dy/dx)
P(x) = 2 over x,  Q(x) = x^2
mu = exp(int 2 over x dx) = exp(2 ln x) = x^2
```
The equation is already `standard`, and `$P(x) = \frac{2}{x}$` integrates to `$2\ln x = \ln(x^2)$`, so `$\mu = x^2$`.

steps.label: Step 2: Collapse and integrate
steps.text: Multiply: `$x^2\frac{dy}{dx} + 2xy = x^4$`, left side `$\frac{d}{dx}(x^2 y) = x^4$`. Integration gives `$x^2 y = \frac{x^5}{5} + C$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Isolate y
steps.text: Division by `$x^2$` yields `$y = \frac{x^3}{5} + \frac{C}{x^2}$`. The homogeneous part `$\frac{C}{x^2}$` decays while `$\frac{x^3}{5}$` tracks the forcing `$x^2$`.

examples.title: Bernoulli equation linearized
examples.problem: Solve `$\frac{dy}{dx} + y = xy^3$`.

steps.label: Step 1: Identify n and substitute
steps.text:
```text
Bernoulli with n = 3 (P = 1, Q = x)
Divide by y^3 (y nonzero); z = y^(1-3) = y^(-2)
dz/dx = -2 y^(-3) dy/dx
```
Division assumes $y \ne 0$, and `$y = 0$` is checked separately: it meets the equation, so it joins the answer list.

steps.label: Step 2: Linear equation for z
steps.text: The substitution produces `$\frac{dz}{dx} - 2z = -2x$`, linear with `$P_z = -2$` and factor `$e^{-2x}$`. Then `$\frac{d}{dx}(ze^{-2x}) = -2xe^{-2x}$` integrates by parts to `$ze^{-2x} = xe^{-2x} + \frac{e^{-2x}}{2} + C$`.

steps.label: Step 3: Return to y
steps.text: Thus `$z = x + \frac{1}{2} + Ce^{2x}$`, and `$y^{-2} = x + \frac{1}{2} + Ce^{2x}$` gives `$y = \pm\left(x + \frac{1}{2} + Ce^{2x}\right)^{-1/2}$` plus `$y = 0$`.

examples.result: `$y^{-2} = x + \frac{1}{2} + Ce^{2x}$`, plus the constant solution `$y = 0$`.

keyTakeaways: Standardize to `$\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$` first; `$\mu = e^{\int P\,dx}$` collapses the left to `$\frac{d}{dx}(\mu y) = \mu Q$`.
Answer `$y = \mu^{-1}(\int \mu Q\,dx + C)$`, valid where `$P, Q$` are continuous.
Bernoulli `$\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Qy^n$` linearizes via `$z = y^{1-n}$` for `$n \ne 0,1$`.
Reattach divided-out zeros such as `$y = 0$`, and keep one constant per connected interval.

quiz.q: The integrating factor of `$\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{2}{x}y = x^2$` is:
quiz.explanation: First read `$P(x) = \frac{2}{x}$` from standard form. Next integrate `$\int \frac{2}{x}\,dx = 2\ln x$`. Then exponentiate `$e^{2\ln x} = x^2$`. Finally any constant multiple works, so `$x^2$` is the simplest choice.

quiz.q: After multiplying `$\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$` by `$\mu = e^{\int P\,dx}$`, the left side becomes:
quiz.explanation: First expand `$\frac{d}{dx}(\mu y) = \mu\frac{dy}{dx} + y\frac{d\mu}{dx}$`. Next `$\frac{d\mu}{dx} = \mu P$` by construction of `$\mu$`. Then the expansion matches `$\mu\frac{dy}{dx} + \mu P y$`. Finally the equation reads `$\frac{d}{dx}(\mu y) = \mu Q$`.

quiz.q: The substitution linearizing `$\frac{dy}{dx} + y = xy^3$` is:
quiz.explanation: First identify Bernoulli exponent `$n = 3$`. Next the rule is `$z = y^{1-n}$`. Then `$1 - 3 = -2$` gives `$z = y^{-2}$`. Finally `$\frac{dz}{dx} = -2y^{-3}\frac{dy}{dx}$` matches the divided equation.

quiz.q: The solution interval for `$\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{2}{x}y = x^2$` with `$y(1) = 0$` is contained in:
quiz.explanation: First `$P(x) = \frac{2}{x}$` is discontinuous at `$x = 0$`. Next the existence theorem guarantees an interval holding `$x_0 = 1$` free of discontinuities. Then `$x > 0$` is that maximal connected piece. Finally crossing `$x = 0$` would need a fresh constant.

intro: Exact equations store the solution implicitly as level curves `$\Psi(x, y) = C$` of a potential function, with the test `$M_y = N_x$` deciding exactness. When the test fails, special integrating factors depending on one variable can restore it. This section drills the test, the reconstruction, and the grouped-term inspection tricks.
objectives: Apply `$M_y = N_x$` to certify exactness on a simply connected domain
Reconstruct `$\Psi(x, y) = C$` by partial integration with `$h(y)$` completion
Find one-variable integrating factors `$\mu(x)$` or `$\mu(y)$` when the test fails

concepts.statement: The form `$M(x, y)\,dx + N(x, y)\,dy = 0$` is **exact** on a simply connected domain exactly when `$\frac{\partial M}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial N}{\partial x}$` there. The `exact` condition says `$M\,dx + N\,dy$` is the total differential `$d\Psi = \Psi_x\,dx + \Psi_y\,dy$` of some potential `$\Psi$`. Equality of mixed partials `$\Psi_{xy} = \Psi_{yx}$` makes the test necessary, and simple connectivity makes it sufficient.
concepts.detail: Test failure is not the end: it routes the problem to integrating factors or pattern regrouping below.

concepts.statement: Integrate `$M$` in `$x$` holding `$y$` fixed to get `$\Psi = \int M\,dx + h(y)$`, then differentiate in `$y$` and match `$\Psi_y = N$` to find `$h^{\prime}(y)$`. The `potential` assembly ends with `$\Psi(x, y) = C$`, whose total differential reproduces the equation. Starting from `$N$` instead is equivalent and preferable when `$N$` integrates more cleanly.
concepts.detail: Any purely `$x$` terms appearing in the `$\Psi_y = N$` match signal an arithmetic slip, since `$h$` depends only on `$y$`.
