examples.problem: A first-order reaction is 40% complete in 50 minutes. Find the rate constant and the time for 90% completion.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: 40% complete means 60% remains: $\frac{[A]_t}{[A]_0} = 0.6$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Half-life: $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{0.0102} \approx 68$ min.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: 90% completion: $t = \frac{2.303}{0.0102}\log\frac{1}{0.1} = \frac{2.303 \times 1}{0.0102} \approx 226$ min — about 3.3 half-lives, as expected.

examples.result: $k \approx 0.0102$ min$^{-1}$, $t_{1/2} \approx 68$ min, 90% completion $\approx 226$ min.

examples.title: Rate from stoichiometry
examples.problem: For $2\text{N}_2\text{O}_5 \to 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$, the rate of NO$_2$ formation is 0.0072 mol L$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$. Find the rates of N$_2$O$_5$ consumption and O$_2$ formation.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Write the unique rate $r$: $-\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]}{dt} = \frac{1}{4}\frac{d[\text{NO}_2]}{dt} = \frac{d[\text{O}_2]}{dt}$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: N$_2$O$_5$ consumption: $\frac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]}{dt} = -2r = -0.0036$ mol L$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$ — rate of disappearance 0.0036.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: O$_2$ formation equals $r$ directly (coefficient 1): 0.0018 mol L$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$.

examples.result: N$_2$O$_5$ disappears at 0.0036, O$_2$ forms at 0.0018 mol L$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$.

keyTakeaways: Rate $= -\frac{1}{\nu}\frac{d[\text{reactant}]}{dt}$: stoichiometric coefficients normalise all species to one rate.
Rate law exponents come from experiment; order need not match coefficients.
First order: $t_{1/2} = 0.693/k$ independent of concentration; zero order: linear decay, $t_{1/2} \propto [A]_0$.
Temperature feeds the Boltzmann tail; catalysts lower $E_a$ without touching equilibrium.

quiz.q: For a first-order reaction, the half-life is 20 min. The time for 75% completion is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: 75% completion leaves 25% = one quarter. Step 2: One quarter is two halvings: $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}$. Step 3: Two half-lives $= 2 \times 20 = 40$ min. Step 4: Constant half-life makes first-order bookkeeping purely multiplicative.

quiz.q: The units of the rate constant of a zero-order reaction are
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Zero-order rate: $r = k$. Step 2: Rate units are mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$. Step 3: So $k$ inherits exactly those units. Step 4: s$^{-1}$ belongs to first order; L mol$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ to second.

quiz.q: Increasing temperature increases reaction rate mainly because
options: the fraction of molecules with energy above $E_a$ increases
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Activation energy is a property of the reaction route, not the temperature. Step 2: The Boltzmann distribution’s high-energy tail grows rapidly with $T$. Step 3: More collisions then clear the unchanged barrier. Step 4: Order and units are structural, not thermal, properties.

quiz.q: A catalyst accelerates a reaction by
options: shifting the equilibrium to the right
quiz.explanation: Step 1: A catalyst is unmoved matter — it cannot add heat. Step 2: It offers an alternative mechanism with a smaller $E_a$. Step 3: Concentrations are untouched, and equilibrium position is unchanged. Step 4: Forward and reverse rates rise equally — equilibrium arrives sooner, not further right.

prerequisites: Electronic configuration and quantum numbers (Unit 2)
Nuclear charge and shielding (Slater intuition helps but not required)
intro: The periodic table is not a list — it is a map of electron configuration. When Moseley ordered elements by atomic number instead of mass, the anomalies vanished and the modern law emerged: properties are a **periodic function of atomic number**. The s, p, d and f blocks are simply where the differentiating electron lands, and from that single fact flow the trends — radius, ionisation energy, electronegativity — that engineering assessment tests every single year.
objectives: State the modern periodic law and describe the present form of the table (periods, groups, blocks)
Identify the s, p, d and f blocks from electronic configuration and predict period and group
Explain why hydrogen and helium are placement puzzles and where they sit
Predict element type (representative, transition, inner-transition, noble gas) from position

concepts.statement: The physical and chemical properties of elements are a **periodic function of their atomic number** — the count of protons, which fixes electron count and hence configuration.
concepts.detail: Mendeleev ordered by atomic mass, leaving anomalies (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I) and gaps he bravely predicted (eka-silicon = Ge). Moseley’s X-ray work showed atomic number is the true ordering principle; the anomalies dissolved. Periodicity arises because shells fill in repeating patterns — the outermost configuration repeats every 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 electrons.

concepts.statement: Seven periods (1–7) and 18 groups (1–18, IUPAC); groups 1–2 + He make the s block, 3–12 the d block, 13–18 the p block, and the lanthanide/actinide rows the f block.
concepts.detail: Period number = highest principal quantum number being filled. First period (2 elements), second and third (8), fourth and fifth (18 — d block begins), sixth and seventh (32 — f block). Group 18 closes every period with a noble gas. The long form’s 18-column shape IS the filling order written sideways.

concepts.statement: The block is decided by where the differentiating (last) electron enters: s block $ns^{1-2}$, p block $ns^2np^{1-6}$, d block $(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{1-2}$, f block $(n-2)f^{1-14}$.
concepts.detail: Worked pattern: $Z = 26$ (Fe) $= [\text{Ar}]3d^64s^2$ — differentiating electron in 3d, so d block, period 4, group 8. For d block, group $= (\text{d electrons}) + (\text{s electrons})$ when that total is 3–12. Exceptions Cr ($3d^54s^1$) and Cu ($3d^{10}4s^1$) still land correctly in groups 6 and 11.

concepts.statement: Hydrogen sits in group 1 though it belongs to no natural family — it can lose one electron (like alkalis), gain one (like halogens), or share; helium’s $1s^2$ places it in the s block but its closed shell earns it a group-18 seat.
concepts.detail: Hydrogen’s ambiguity: placed above Li by electron count, above F by one-electron-short-of-duet, sometimes floated alone. He is the only s-block noble gas. Lanthanides and actinides are pulled out to avoid an unbearable 32-column table — an aesthetic choice, not a chemical one.

concepts.statement: Across a period, nuclear charge grows with the same shell — radius falls, ionisation energy and electronegativity rise; down a group, new shells dominate — radius rises, ionisation energy falls.
concepts.detail: Every trend question reduces to a tug-of-war between nuclear charge (pulls electrons in) and shielding (pushes them out). Small anomalies (IE of O < N from paired-electron repulsion in O’s 2p$^4$) are the classic engineering assessment twist — half-filled shells have extra stability.

examples.title: Locating an element from Z
examples.problem: An element has $Z = 35$. Find its electronic configuration, block, period and group, and predict its family behaviour.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Differentiating electron lands in 4p: p block, period 4 (highest $n = 4$).

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Group = 12 (filled s + d up to Zn) + 5 p electrons $=$ 17.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Group 17 halogen ($p^5$, one short of octet): bromine — a volatile red liquid, strong oxidiser, forms Br$^-$ readily.

examples.result: Bromine: $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^24p^5$, p block, period 4, group 17.

examples.title: Anomaly reasoning: first IE of N vs O
examples.problem: The first ionisation enthalpy of nitrogen is higher than that of oxygen despite oxygen’s greater nuclear charge. Explain.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Configurations: N is $2p^3$ (half-filled, one electron per orbital), O is $2p^4$ (one pair + two singles).

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Half-filled subshells exchange-stabilise and spread electron repulsion minimally.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: In oxygen, removing one 2p electron un-pairs the doublet — the paired-electron repulsion makes that electron easier to strip.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Net: $\text{IE}_1(\text{N}) > \text{IE}_1(\text{O})$ — the classic exception sitting between the general rise across period 2.

examples.result: Half-filled stability of N and pair-repulsion in O invert the expected order.

keyTakeaways: Modern law: properties repeat periodically with atomic number (electron configuration), not mass.
Block = where the differentiating electron enters; period = highest $n$; group follows the filling arithmetic.
Period 4/5 have 18 elements, 6/7 have 32; f block lives in the detached lanthanide/actinide rows.
Trends are a nuclear-charge vs shielding tug-of-war, with half-filled-shell anomalies as the assessment twist.

quiz.q: The element with configuration $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^24p^3$ belongs to
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The differentiating electron enters 4p — p block. Step 2: Period 4 (highest $n = 4$). Step 3: Group $= 10 (3d) + 2 (4s) + 3 (4p) = 15$. Step 4: The element is As (arsenic), a group-15 pnictogen.

quiz.q: Mendeleev’s periodic table improved on earlier attempts mainly by
options: leaving gaps for undiscovered elements and predicting their properties
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Atomic number came later (Moseley). Step 2: Electron configuration came later still (Bohr). Step 3: Mendeleev’s genius was obeying periodicity even when mass order argued — and leaving gaps (eka-boron, eka-aluminium, eka-silicon) later filled perfectly. Step 4: The f-block separation is a modern long-form refinement.

quiz.q: The number of elements in the fourth period is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Period 4 fills 4s, 3d, 4p. Step 2: That is $2 + 10 + 6 = 18$ orbitals’ worth of electrons. Step 3: Eighteen elements, K through Kr. Step 4: 8 belongs to periods 2 and 3; 32 to periods 6 and 7.

quiz.q: Helium is placed in group 18 because
options: it is an s-block element by configuration
its duplet is a closed, chemically inert shell like other noble gases
quiz.explanation: Step 1: By configuration He is $1s^2$ — technically s block. Step 2: But its filled shell makes it monatomic and inert, the defining noble-gas character. Step 3: Chemical behaviour outweighs the mechanical filling label. Step 4: He is the only s-block resident of group 18 — the table’s acknowledged exception.

prerequisites: Hybridisation and VSEPR shapes (Unit 3 bonding)
Basics of nomenclature from school chemistry
intro: Carbon is tetravalent and small — the two facts that build a chemistry of millions of compounds. Its four bonds point tetrahedrally ($sp^3$), trigonal-planarly ($sp^2$) or linearly ($sp$), giving organic molecules their three-dimensional personalities. organising this zoo are **functional groups** (the reactive sites) and **homologous series** (families differing by CH$_2$), the two classification tools every engineering assessment organic question silently assumes.
objectives: Explain tetravalency and the geometry of $sp^3$, $sp^2$ and $sp$ carbon centres
Classify organic compounds by functional group, including halo, oxygen, nitrogen and sulfur families
Use homologous series to generate formulas and predict gradations in properties
Distinguish saturated versus unsaturated, aliphatic versus aromatic, and ring versus chain skeletons

concepts.statement: Carbon forms **four covalent bonds** by promoting a 2s electron to 2p; the resulting orbitals hybridise to $sp^3$ (109.5° tetrahedral), $sp^2$ (120° trigonal) or $sp$ (180° linear).
concepts.detail: $sp^3$: methane, diamond’s network. $sp^2$: ethene’s planar double bond, graphite’s sheets, benzene’s ring. $sp$: ethyne’s linear triple bond. Bond strength and shortness rise $sp^3 < sp^2 < sp$, and acidity of attached C–H follows the same order (more s character holds electrons closer) — the isomer-counting and acidity questions both hang off this geometry ladder.

concepts.statement: A **functional group** is the atom or substructure that dictates a molecule’s characteristic reactions: halo ($-$X), alcohol ($-$OH), ether ($-$O$-$), aldehyde ($-$CHO), ketone ($-$CO$-$), carboxylic acid ($-$COOH), ester ($-$COOR$-$), amine ($-$NH$_2$), nitrile ($-$CN), nitro ($-$NO$_2$), thiol ($-$SH), sulfonic acid ($-$SO$_3$H).
concepts.detail: Functional group = reactivity + suffix in nomenclature. The same carbon skeleton wearing different groups behaves like different people in different jobs. Recognising the group is step zero of every engineering assessment organic problem — name it, and half the reaction map is already written.

concepts.statement: A **homologous series** is a family of compounds with the same functional group, successive members differing by $-$CH$_2\ -$; general formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$ (alkanes), $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}$ (alkenes/cycloalkanes), $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n-2}$ (alkynes), $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}\text{O}$ (alcohols/ethers) and so on.
concepts.detail: Members show gradual property trends (boiling point climbs ~20–30 K per CH$_2$ as dispersion grows) and identical chemistry. Any two adjacent members differ in molar mass by exactly 14 u — the fingerprint for "which pair is homologous?" questions.

concepts.statement: By structure: **chain** (acyclic) versus **ring** (cyclic); **saturated** (single bonds only) versus **unsaturated** (C=C, C≡C); **aliphatic** versus **aromatic** (cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, Hückel $4n+2$ π electrons).
concepts.detail: Aromaticity checklist on benzene: ring ✓, planar ✓, cyclic conjugation ✓, 6 π electrons $= 4(1)+2$ ✓ — aromatic and exceptionally stable. Cyclooctatetraene (8 π, non-planar) and cyclobutadiene (4 π, antiaromatic) fail. Heterocycles (pyridine, furan) can also qualify — oxygen’s lone pair in furan counts toward the six.

concepts.statement: Names encode structure: root (meth-, eth-, prop- for carbons) + saturation infix (-an-, -en-, -yn-) + suffix for the senior functional group ($-$ol, $-$al, $-$one, $-$oic acid) + prefixes for substituents and juniors groups (bromo-, nitro-, hydroxy-).
concepts.detail: Order of seniority (memorise): carboxylic acid > ester > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine. The senior group takes the suffix and the lowest locant; everything else prefixes alphabetically. Isomer counting (structural: chain, position, functional, tautomer; stereo: geometric, optical) rides on this scaffolding and is a permanent engineering assessment fixture.

examples.title: Identifying a homologous pair
examples.problem: Which pairs are homologous: (a) CH$_3$OH and C$_2$H$_5$OH, (b) C$_2$H$_4$ and C$_3$H$_6$, (c) CH$_3$CHO and CH$_3$COCH$_3$, (d) C$_2$H$_6$ and C$_3$H$_8$?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Homology = same functional group + mass difference exactly 14 u ($-$CH$_2\ -$).

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: (a) Two alcohols, 32 vs 46 u: differ by CH$_2$ — homologous. (b) Two alkenes, 28 vs 42: homologous. (d) Two alkanes, 30 vs 44: homologous.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (c) Ethanal (aldehyde, 44 u) versus propanone (ketone, 58 u): mass differs by 14 but the functional groups differ — a functional-isomer trap, NOT homologous.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Verdict: (a), (b) and (d) are homologous pairs; (c) is the classic impostor.

examples.result: Homologous: (a), (b), (d). Pair (c) mixes an aldehyde with a ketone.

examples.title: Writing the general formula member
examples.problem: Write the molecular formula of the fifth member of the alkyne family and name it.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Alkynes: $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n-2}$, with $n = 2$ the first member (ethyne — $n = 1$ would leave 0 H).

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Fifth member: $n = 6$, so $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{2(6)-2} = \text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Straight-chain name: hex-1-yne (older: 1-hexyne).

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Check: two fewer H than hexene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$) — one triple bond’s worth — exactly as the general formula promises.

examples.result: Fifth alkyne: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}$, hex-1-yne.

keyTakeaways: Tetravalent carbon hybridises $sp^3/sp^2/sp$ → tetrahedral/planar/linear geometries.
Functional groups define family, suffix and reactivity — identify them first in every problem.
Homologues: same group, $+$CH$_2$, $+$14 u, gradual property trends.
Aromatic = cyclic + planar + conjugated + $4n+2$ π electrons; benzene is the 6-π prototype.

quiz.q: The shape of the carbon skeleton in ethene is governed by
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Ethene, C$_2$H$_4$, has one C=C per carbon. Step 2: Three $sp^2$ orbitals form the σ framework (two C–H + one C–C) in a plane at 120°. Step 3: The unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways for the π bond, locking planarity. Step 4: $sp^3$ belongs to methane’s tetrahedron; $sp$ to ethyne’s line.

quiz.q: Which pair represents functional isomers?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Functional isomers share the same molecular formula but carry different functional groups. Step 2: Propanal (CH$_3$CH$_2$CHO, aldehyde) and propanone (CH$_3$COCH$_3$, ketone) are both C$_3$H$_6$O. Step 3: Propan-1-ol/propan-2-ol are positional isomers (same group, different spot); butane/2-methylpropane are chain isomers. Step 4: Ethanol and methanol differ by CH$_2$ — homologues, not isomers.

quiz.q: The general formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\text{O}_2$ fits
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Two oxygens suggest $-$COOH or $-$COOR$-$. Step 2: Acetic acid CH$_3$COOH: C$_2$H$_4$O$_2$ — $n = 2$ gives H$_4$. Step 3: Methyl formate HCOOCH$_3$ is also C$_2$H$_4$O$_2$ — the ester twin. Step 4: Alcohols/ethers are C$_n$H$_{2n+2}$O; aldehydes/ketones C$_n$H$_{2n}$O.

quiz.q: A compound is cyclic, planar, fully conjugated and has 10 π electrons. It is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Hückel rule: aromatic requires $4n + 2$ π electrons. Step 2: $10 = 4(2) + 2$ — the magic number for $n = 2$. Step 3: Ring, planarity and conjugation are already satisfied. Step 4: Naphthalene (10 π) is aromatic; 4 or 8 π in a planar ring would be anti-aromatic instead.

prerequisites: Functional-group classification (Unit 14 section 1)
Basic nomenclature: alkane/alkene/alkyne roots and suffixes
intro: Hydrocarbons — just carbon and hydrogen — are organic chemistry’s trunk from which all families branch. Alkanes are the saturated backbone, lazy and substitution-only; alkenes and alkynes carry π-bond reactivity that makes them addition magnets; arenes add the aromatic stability wildcard. Mastering their **IUPAC names, isomer counts and preparation routes** is the entry ticket to every engineering assessment organic question.
objectives: Classify hydrocarbons (alkane, alkene, alkyne, arene; saturated vs unsaturated) and name them by IUPAC rules
Count structural isomers of small alkanes and draw geometric (cis/trans, E/Z) isomers of alkenes
Describe laboratory preparations: alkane (decarboxylation, hydrogenation), alkene (dehydration, dehydrohalogenation), alkyne (dehydrohalogenation of dihalides)
Summarise the characteristic reaction classes: free-radical substitution, electrophilic addition, Markovnikov and anti-Markovnikov routes

concepts.statement: **Alkanes** $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$ (saturated, single bonds); **alkenes** $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}$ (one C=C); **alkynes** $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n-2}$ (one C≡C); **arenes** contain a benzene ring.
concepts.detail: Degree of unsaturation (DoU) from a formula: $\text{DoU} = \frac{2C + 2 - H}{2}$ (ignore O; add H for halogens; subtract H for N). C$_4$H$_6$: DoU 2 — one triple or two doubles or a double + a ring. DoU is the fastest formula-to-structure probe in the assessment arsenal.

concepts.statement: Find the longest chain carrying the senior feature → number from the end giving lowest locants (multiple bond wins ties) → name substituents alphabetically: 4-methylhex-2-ene, not 3-methylhex-4-ene.
concepts.detail: The double/triple bond position must ALWAYS be stated for enes and ynes. Lower-sum rule operates on the set of locants (2,3,5 beats 2,4,5), compared lexicographically, not by sum alone in modern IUPAC — but lowest-set-in-order keeps assessment answers consistent.

concepts.statement: Chain isomers (butane vs 2-methylpropane), position isomers (but-1-ene vs but-2-ene), and for alkenes **geometric isomerism** when each C of the double bond carries two different groups: cis/trans or E/Z by CIP priority.
concepts.detail: Isomer counts to memorise: C$_4$H$_{10}$ → 2, C$_5$H$_{12}$ → 3, C$_6$H$_{14}$ → 5, C$_7$H$_{16}$ → 9. But-2-ene’s cis/trans pair is the smallest geometric pair; but-1-ene cannot show it (one carbon has two H). Restricted rotation of the π bond is the physical cause — breaking it costs ~260 kJ/mol.

concepts.statement: Alkanes: decarboxylation ($\text{RCOONa} + \text{NaOH} \xrightarrow{\text{soda lime}} \text{RH}$), hydrogenation of unsaturates, Wurtz coupling ($2\text{RX} + 2\text{Na} \to \text{R\!-\!R}$). Alkenes: acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols and dehydrohalogenation of haloalkanes (Saytzeff — most substituted alkene wins). Alkynes: double dehydrohalogenation of vicinal/geminal dihalides with strong base.
concepts.detail: Kolbe electrolysis gives alkanes from carboxylates; Lindlar’s poisoned catalyst or Na/NH$_3$ tames the alkyne hydrogenation to cis or trans alkenes respectively. Preparation questions love conditions: concentrated H$_2$SO$_4$ at 443 K dehydrates ethanol; alcoholic KOH eliminates while aqueous KOH substitutes — one word decides the product.

concepts.statement: Alkanes undergo **free-radical substitution** (halogenation, $h\nu$); alkenes/alkynes undergo **electrophilic addition** (HX, X$_2$, H$_2$O with Markovnikov orientation; HBr + peroxide gives anti-Markovnikov); benzene undergoes **electrophilic substitution** (nitration, sulfonation, halogenation, Friedel–Crafts).
concepts.detail: Markovnikov: H adds to the hydrogen-richer carbon, carbocation stability dictating (3° > 2° > 1°). Peroxide effect (Kharasch) reverses HBr only — not HCl or HI. The stability order and its rearrangements power elimination-versus-addition predictions throughout the assessment.

examples.title: Naming by the rules
examples.problem: Provide the IUPAC name of CH$_3$CH(CH$_3$)CH=CHCH$_3$.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Longest chain containing C=C has five carbons: pent-ene base.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Number from the right end (closest to the double bond): bond at C2; methyl then lands at C4.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Name: 4-methylpent-2-ene. Numbering the other way would give pent-3-ene — forbidden (lowest double-bond locant dominates).

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Stereochemistry check: the C2=C3 carbons each carry H plus carbon groups, so (E)-/(Z)-4-methylpent-2-ene are both possible.

examples.result: 4-methylpent-2-ene (with E/Z stereoisomers possible).

examples.title: Dehydrohalogenation product
examples.problem: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is heated with alcoholic KOH. Predict the major product and the rule used.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Alcoholic KOH → elimination (dehydrohalogenation), not substitution.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: β-hydrogens exist on two carbons: removal from the ethyl side or from either of two methyl groups.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Saytzeff: the more substituted alkene dominates — removing the ethyl-side H gives 2-methylbut-2-ene (trisubstituted), while methyl-side removal gives 2-methylbut-1-ene (disubstituted).

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Major: 2-methylbut-2-ene; the mechanism is E2, anti-periplanar H and Br.

examples.result: Major product 2-methylbut-2-ene by Saytzeff’s rule.

keyTakeaways: Formulas: alkane C$_n$H$_{2n+2}$, alkene C$_n$H$_{2n}$, alkyne C$_n$H$_{2n-2}$; DoU = (2C+2−H)/2.
IUPAC: longest senior chain, lowest locants, double bond beats substituents in ties.
Geometric isomerism needs two different groups on EACH doubly bonded carbon.
Alcoholic KOH eliminates (Saytzeff), aqueous KOH substitutes — conditions decide the family.

quiz.q: The IUPAC name of $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}=$CH$_2$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Five-carbon chain containing the double bond: pent-ene. Step 2: Number from the CH$_2$ end so the bond gets locant 1. Step 3: The branch (CH$_3$)$_2$CH puts a methyl at C4: 4-methylpent-1-ene. Step 4: Numbering from the other end would give the double bond locant 4 — never acceptable when 1 is possible.

quiz.q: Which alkene shows geometrical isomerism?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Geometric isomerism requires each double-bond carbon to carry two DIFFERENT groups. Step 2: Propene: one carbon has H,H — fails. Step 3: But-1-ene: terminal carbon has H,H — fails; 2-methylpropene: one carbon has CH$_3$,CH$_3$ — fails. Step 4: But-2-ene: each carbon holds H and CH$_3$ — the classic cis/trans pair.

quiz.q: Ethanol heated with concentrated H$_2$SO$_4$ at 443 K gives
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Concentrated H$_2$SO$_4$ at high temperature dehydrates alcohols. Step 2: Ethanol loses H and OH from adjacent carbons as water. Step 3: The π bond forms: ethene. Step 4: At the LOWER temperature of 413 K the same reagent gives diethyl ether — temperature is the switch.

quiz.q: HBr added to propene in the presence of peroxides gives mainly
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Peroxides switch the mechanism to free-radical addition (Kharasch effect). Step 2: Br· adds first, placing the radical on the more substituted carbon. Step 3: H then attaches there overall — Br ends up on the terminal carbon: 1-bromopropane. Step 4: The peroxide effect works for HBr only, never HCl or HI.

prerequisites: Mole concept and stoichiometry (Unit 1)
Mass, volume and density arithmetic
intro: Every quantitative statement about a solution — a titration result, a Raoult’s-law plot, a colligative-property sum — opens with a concentration term. engineering assessment asks 25 chemistry questions for 100 marks with +4 for a correct answer and −1 for a wrong one, and a good share of them are one-step concentration numericals lifted almost line-by-line from NCERT. That is exactly why chemistry is the fastest-scoring subject on the paper: the formulas are short and the arithmetic honest. This lesson drills the four NCERT terms — molarity, molality, mole fraction and the percentage/`ppm` family — and the density bridge that converts any one of them into another.
objectives: Define molarity, molality, mole fraction and the mass/volume percentage terms and compute each from raw data
Interconvert molarity, molality and mole fraction using the solution’s density
Decide which concentration terms survive a temperature change and justify the choice
Solve dilution and mixing problems with $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$

concepts.statement: A **solution** is a homogeneous mixture whose **solute** (lesser component) is dispersed at the molecular level in the **solvent** (greater component); each concentration term is a different bookkeeping choice — per volume of solution (`molarity`), per mass of solvent (`molality`), per moles of all species (`mole fraction`) or per mass/volume of solution (percentages).
concepts.detail: No single term suits every experiment. Volumetric glassware makes molarity the lab workhorse, but volume drifts with temperature, so the physical chemistry ahead (Raoult’s law, colligative properties in the later sections of this unit) demands molality and mole fraction, which are immune to heating. Spotting which term a question silently assumes is half the mark.

concepts.statement: **Molarity** $M$ is moles of solute per litre of solution: $M = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution}}(\text{L})}$, units mol L$^{-1}$; dilution obeys $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$.
concepts.detail: Dilution problems assume only solvent is added, so moles of solute are untouched while volume grows. For mixing two solutions of the same solute, total moles over total volume gives the final molarity. Watch the unit: 250 mL must become 0.25 L before dividing — the commonest silly slip on the assessment.

concepts.statement: **Molality** $m$ is moles of solute per kilogram of **solvent** (not solution!): $m = \frac{n_{\text{solute}} \times 1000}{w_{\text{solvent}}(\text{g})}$, units mol kg$^{-1}$.
concepts.detail: Mass neither expands nor contracts, so molality is temperature-independent — the assertion–reason staple of this unit. The solvent-only denominator is the trap: 1 mol of solute in 1 kg of solvent is exactly 1 molal, but that same solution poured into a 1 L flask is not 1 molar.

concepts.statement: **Mole fraction** $x_A = \frac{n_A}{n_A + n_B}$ is dimensionless with $x_A + x_B = 1$; **mass %** $= \frac{w_{\text{solute}}}{w_{\text{solution}}} \times 100$; **volume %** $= \frac{V_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution}}} \times 100$; trace levels use ppm $= \frac{w_{\text{solute}}}{w_{\text{solution}}} \times 10^{6}$.
concepts.detail: Mole fraction and mass % ignore temperature; volume % does not, because liquid volumes are not strictly additive on mixing (ethanol + water contracts). `ppm` is the water-quality unit — hardness ions, fluoride and dissolved pollutants live there.

concepts.statement: Density links mass and volume: $d = \frac{\text{mass of solution}}{\text{volume of solution}}$ in g mL$^{-1}$. On a 1 L basis, $m = \frac{1000\ M}{1000\ d - M M_1}$ and $M = \frac{10 \times (\%\ w/w) \times d}{M_1}$, where $M_1$ is the molar mass of the solute.
concepts.detail: The 1-litre basis makes every conversion mechanical: mass of solution $= 1000d$ g, mass of solute $= M \times M_1$ g, so mass of **solvent** $= (1000d - MM_1)$ g. Divide moles by solvent mass in kg for molality, or convert solvent mass to moles for the mole fraction. Reverse the flow to climb from molality back to molarity.

examples.title: Dilution bookkeeping
examples.problem: 4.0 g of NaOH ($M = 40$ g/mol) is dissolved and made up to 250 mL. Find the molarity, and the molarity after 500 mL of water is added.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Moles of NaOH: $n = \frac{4.0}{40} = 0.10$ mol.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Dilution: $M_2 = \frac{M_1V_1}{V_2} = \frac{0.40 \times 250}{750} = 0.133$ M — the final volume is $250 + 500 = 750$ mL.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Check the invariant: moles $= 0.133 \times 0.75 = 0.10$ mol — unchanged, exactly as dilution demands.

examples.result: 0.40 M initially; 0.133 M after adding 500 mL of water.

examples.title: Molarity to molality via density
examples.problem: A 2.0 M NaOH solution has density 1.10 g/mL. Calculate its molality and the mole fraction of NaOH. ($M_{\text{NaOH}} = 40$, $M_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = 18$ g/mol)

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
1 L of solution:  mass = 1000 x 1.10 = 1100 g
NaOH in it:        2.0 mol x 40 = 80 g
water (solvent):   1100 - 80 = 1020 g = 1.02 kg
```

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Note the direction: molality ($1.96 < 2.0$) fell below molarity because part of the solution’s mass is solute, shrinking the solvent base.

examples.result: $m = 1.96$ mol kg$^{-1}$; $x_{\text{NaOH}} \approx 0.034$.

examples.title: From mass percent to molarity
examples.problem: A commercial reagent is 10% glucose by mass with density 1.04 g/mL ($M_{\text{glucose}} = 180$ g/mol). Find its molarity.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Take 100 g of solution: 10 g glucose $= \frac{10}{180} = 0.0556$ mol.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Volume of that solution: $\frac{100}{1.04} = 96.2$ mL $= 0.0962$ L.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Shortcut cross-check: $M = \frac{10 \times (\%\ w/w) \times d}{M_1} = \frac{10 \times 10 \times 1.04}{180} = 0.578$ M ✓ — identical, as it must be.

examples.result: The 10% (w/w) glucose solution is about 0.58 M.

keyTakeaways: Molarity = mol per litre of solution (temperature-dependent); molality = mol per kg of solvent (temperature-independent).
Mole fractions are dimensionless, temperature-proof and sum to 1 for a binary solution.
Density bridge on a 1 L basis: solvent mass $= 1000d - MM_1$ g — the key to every interconversion.
Dilution never changes moles of solute: $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$.
ppm scales trace concentrations: $\frac{w_{\text{solute}}}{w_{\text{solution}}} \times 10^{6}$.

quiz.q: Which concentration term changes when a solution is heated from 25 °C to 35 °C?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Heating expands the solution’s volume. Step 2: Molarity divides moles by litres of solution, so it falls as volume grows. Step 3: Molality divides by solvent mass, mole fraction by moles, mass % by mass — none involve volume. Step 4: Only molarity among these is temperature-dependent.

quiz.q: Water must be added to 250 mL of 2.0 M NaOH to make it 0.50 M. The volume of water to be added is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Moles of NaOH stay fixed at $2.0 \times 0.250 = 0.5$ mol. Step 2: Final volume for 0.50 M: $V_2 = \frac{0.5}{0.5} = 1.0$ L. Step 3: Water added $= 1000 - 250 = 750$ mL. Step 4: 1000 mL is the final volume, not the added water — the classic mix-up.

quiz.q: The mole fraction of glucose in a solution of 18 g glucose ($M = 180$) in 178.2 g water ($M = 18$) is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: $n_{\text{glucose}} = \frac{18}{180} = 0.1$ mol. Step 2: $n_{\text{water}} = \frac{178.2}{18} = 9.9$ mol. Step 3: $x = \frac{0.1}{0.1 + 9.9} = \frac{0.1}{10} = 0.01$. Step 4: 0.1 would forget to include the solute moles in the denominator’s total.

quiz.q: A 10% (w/w) aqueous NaCl solution contains
options: 10 g NaCl in 100 g of water
10 g NaCl in 100 g of solution
10 g NaCl in 100 mL of solution
10 mL NaCl in 100 mL of solution
quiz.explanation: Step 1: w/w means mass of solute divided by mass of the whole solution. Step 2: 10% w/w = 10 g NaCl per 100 g of solution, which contains 90 g of water. Step 3: If it were 10 g per 100 g of water, the solution would mass 110 g and the percentage would fall to about 9.1%. Step 4: The solvent is 90 g, not 100 g — the persistent misconception.

prerequisites: Electronic configuration and subshell filling (Unit 2)
The modern periodic table’s blocks (Unit 9 section 1)
intro: Six groups, 38 elements, one governing configuration: the **p block** is where the periodic table’s chemistry turns vivid — acids and bases, oxidants and reductants, inert gases and reactive metals all live here. Since the 2024 syllabus rationalisation the testing agency trimmed the group-wise descriptive detail, so the modern engineering assessment paper (25 chemistry questions, 100 marks, +4 for a hit, −1 for a miss) tests the **grammar** of the block — configurations, family names, oxidation states — through short NCERT-line questions. Chemistry stays the fastest-scoring subject of the paper when this grammar is automatic. This section fixes the $ns^2np^{1–6}$ skeleton and the family map it generates, leaving the detailed trends to the next two sections.
objectives: Write the general p-block configuration $ns^2np^{1–6}$ and deduce block, group, period and valence electrons of any element from its $Z$
Name the six families from group 13 to 18 with their valence-electron counts
Predict the common oxidation states of each family, including the group − 2 companion state
Introduce the inert pair effect as the reason heavier p-block elements prefer lower oxidation states

concepts.statement: The **p-block elements** have their differentiating (last) electron entering a p orbital; they occupy **groups 13–18**, where the p subshell fills from $np^1$ to $np^6$, giving the general outer configuration $ns^2np^{1–6}$.
concepts.detail: A p subshell holds six electrons, so filling it spawns six columns of the table. Helium sits in group 18 by its inert behaviour but its $1s^2$ configuration is pure s block — the acknowledged misfit the assessment likes to probe. The lightest true p-block element is boron, because period 2 is the first that owns a 2p subshell.

concepts.statement: Families to own: **13** boron family (3 valence electrons), **14** carbon family (4), **15** pnictogens (5), **16** chalcogens (6), **17** halogens (7), **18** noble gases (8) — for the p block, valence electrons = group number − 10.
concepts.detail: Group arithmetic: group = 10 + (s electrons) + (p electrons). For $Z = 33$: $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^24p^3$ gives $10 + 2 + 3 = 15$ — arsenic, a metalloid of the pnictogens. The metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) straddle the staircase inside the block: metals dominate the bottom-left, non-metals the top-right.

concepts.statement: The highest positive state equals the **number of valence electrons**; each family also shows a state two lower (group − 2) where the $ns^2$ pair stays unused: $+3/+1$ (13), $+4/+2$ (14), $+5/+3$ (15), $+6/+4/+2$ (16), $+7/+5/+3/+1$ (17), $0$ (18).
concepts.detail: Fluorine breaks the ladder — only −1, never positive, because nothing is more electronegative. Oxygen sticks mainly to −2. The heavier noble gases do form compounds (Xe reaches $+2$, $+4$, $+6$ and $+8$ as in XeF$_2$ and XeO$_3$), so "inert gas" is a dated label. Negative states appear only on the right side’s non-metals (N$^{3–}$, O$^{2–}$, F$–$).

concepts.statement: Down each group the **$ns^2$ pair participates less and less** in bonding, so the lower oxidation state wins for the heavyweights: Tl$^+$ over Tl$^{3+}$, Pb$^{2+}$ over Pb$^{4+}$, Bi$^{3+}$ over Bi$^{5+}$.
concepts.detail: Cause: poor shielding by the intervening filled $d$ and $f$ subshells raises the effective nuclear pull on the outer $s$ pair, binding it tighter. Within group 13, aluminium is dominantly +3 while thallium is dominantly +1 — the assessment’s favourite one-line illustration. The full map of how these states shift across periods and down groups belongs to section 10.2.

concepts.statement: A 20-second loop for any p-block $Z$: configuration → differentiating electron in p → **block** → highest $n$ = **period** → group = 10 + s + p electrons → family, valence count and common states.
concepts.detail: Drill example $Z = 52$: $[\text{Kr}]4d^{10}5s^25p^4$ → p block, period 5, group 16, six valence electrons, states −2, +4, +6 — tellurium. Automating this loop converts at least one guaranteed configuration question into a free mark every year.

examples.title: Locating an element from Z
examples.problem: An element has $Z = 52$. Write its electronic configuration and deduce its block, period, group, family and common oxidation states.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: The differentiating electron lands in 5p: p block, and the highest principal quantum number $n = 5$ fixes period 5.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Group $= 10 + 2 (5s) + 4 (5p) = 16$ — the chalcogen family with six valence electrons.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: States: −2 (gaining a full octet), +4 and +6 (sharing all or four valence electrons) — the element is tellurium, a metalloid used in alloys and semiconductors.

examples.result: Tellurium: $[\text{Kr}]4d^{10}5s^25p^4$, p block, period 5, group 16 (chalcogen), states −2, +4, +6.

examples.title: Inert pair in action: the missing PbI$_4$
examples.problem: PbCl$_4$ can be prepared, but PbI$_4$ does not exist. Explain using oxidation states and the inert pair effect.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Lead: $[\text{Xe}]4f^{14}5d^{10}6s^26p^2$ — the $+4$ state must deploy the reluctant $6s^2$ pair, so Pb(IV) is a strong oxidant.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: I$–$ is a strong reductant; it hands electrons back to Pb(IV), reducing it to the inert-pair-stable Pb$^{2+}$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Any Pb(IV)–iodide bond self-destructs: $\text{Pb}^{4+} + 2\text{I}^- \to \text{Pb}^{2+} + \text{I}_2$ — so PbI$_4$ collapses to PbI$_2$ plus iodine.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: With the less reducing Cl$–$, PbCl$_4$ survives (though it is still unstable and decomposes on warming) — the reductant strength of the halide anion decides.

examples.result: PbI$_4$ cannot exist: the inert-pair-stabilised Pb$^{2+}$ plus oxidising iodide to I$_2$ is the preferred outcome.

keyTakeaways: p block = groups 13–18, outer configuration $ns^2np^{1–6}$; valence electrons = group − 10.
Group = 10 + s + p electrons; period = highest $n$; helium is the s-block resident of group 18.
Highest oxidation state = valence electron count; the group − 2 state rides on the inert pair effect.
Heavier elements prefer lower states: Tl$^+$, Pb$^{2+}$, Bi$^{3+}$ beat Tl$^{3+}$, Pb$^{4+}$, Bi$^{5+}$ in stability.

quiz.q: The general outer electronic configuration of group 15 elements is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Group 15 = 10 + 2 + p electrons, so p electrons = 3. Step 2: The configuration is $ns^2np^3$ — five valence electrons. Step 3: $ns^2np^1$ is group 13, $ns^2np^5$ is group 17, $ns^2np^4$ is group 16. Step 4: N, P, As, Sb, Bi are the pnictogens with this signature.

quiz.q: The element with $Z = 33$ belongs to
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Fill: $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^24p^3$ (18 + 10 + 2 + 3 = 33). Step 2: Differentiating electron in 4p → p block, and $n = 4$ gives period 4. Step 3: Group $= 10 + 2 + 3 = 15$. Step 4: The element is arsenic — a group-15, period-4 metalloid; period 3 would end its p subshell at $Z = 18$.

quiz.q: The most common oxidation state of lead in its stable compounds is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Lead is group 14: $6s^26p^2$, so +4 uses all four valence electrons. Step 2: The inert pair effect binds the $6s^2$ pair tightly down the group. Step 3: Pb$^{2+}$ (pair unused) is therefore the stable state; Pb(IV) compounds are oxidising and easily reduced. Step 4: +6 is impossible for group 14; 0 is the free element, not a compound state.

quiz.q: Which element placed in group 18 is NOT a p-block element by electronic configuration?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Group 18 is otherwise the p$^6$ terminus of each period. Step 2: Ne, Ar and Kr are indeed $ns^2np^6$. Step 3: Helium is $1s^2$ — only two electrons in an s subshell, no p electrons at all. Step 4: He sits in group 18 purely for its closed-shell inertness; by configuration it belongs to the s block.

prerequisites: Electronic configuration of atoms (Unit 2)
Position of the d block in the periodic table (Unit 9)
intro: The **d block** occupies the periodic table’s waist and behaves like a bridge — hence "transition": its properties grade smoothly between the fiercely electropositive s-block metals and the p-block’s mixed personalities. One structural fact — a partially filled d subshell — detonates into eight characteristic fingerprints, from the colours of gemstones to the magnets in headphones. engineering assessment’s 25-question, 100-mark chemistry paper (+4 per correct, −1 per wrong) reliably parks a question on configurations or the Zn/Cd/Hg exclusion, drawn straight from NCERT lines — quick marks that keep chemistry the fastest-scoring subject of the three.
objectives: Define transition elements through the partially filled d subshell in the atom or its common ions
Write configurations of the 3d series and rationalise the chromium and copper exceptions
Argue why Zn, Cd and Hg are d-block elements but not transition elements
Connect the eight characteristic properties to their d-electron origin and describe typical occurrences

concepts.statement: A **transition element** possesses a partially filled d subshell in the elemental atom **or** in at least one common oxidation state: the 3d series Sc–Zn, 4d Y–Cd, 5d La, Hf–Hg (and the incomplete 6d row Ac, Rf–Cn).
concepts.detail: All transition elements are d-block elements, but the converse fails: **Zn, Cd, Hg** carry $d^{10}$ in both the atom and their common +2 ion — nowhere is a d subshell partially filled — so NCERT excludes them from strict transition status. Their tell-tale signs: colourless ions, diamagnetism and a single fixed oxidation state.

concepts.statement: General configuration $(n-1)d^{1–10}ns^{1–2}$; the two 3d celebrities are **Cr** $= [\text{Ar}]3d^54s^1$ and **Cu** $= [\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^1$.
concepts.detail: Why the exceptions: exactly half-filled or fully filled d subshells gain exchange-energy stability and symmetric charge distribution that beats the naive aufbau fill. The 4d and 5d rows show many more anomalies (Nb $4d^45s^1$, Pd $4d^{10}5s^0$, Pt $5d^96s^1$) because those subshells are closer in energy. On ionisation, **4s electrons leave first**: Fe$^{2+}$ is $3d^6$, never $3d^44s^2$.

concepts.statement: The d block sits **between** the s and p blocks, and its chemistry transits between them: s-block-like metallic reactivity softening toward p-block covalency, with the d electrons supplying the gradient.
concepts.detail: Expect intermediate behaviour in practice — moderately reactive metals, several oxidation steps, a strong appetite for complex formation. The literal filling order also transitions: ns fills before (n−1)d, which fills before np — the d subshell is the interlude between the two ends of the period.

concepts.statement: Most d-block metals occur in the combined state as oxides, sulfides, carbonates and silicates: hematite $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$, pyrolusite $\text{MnO}_2$, rutile for Ti, chalcopyrite $\text{CuFeS}_2$, sphalerite $\text{ZnS}$; only gold, platinum and some silver/copper occur native.
concepts.detail: The consequence is metallurgical: extraction of this block is reduction-dominated — sulfide ores are roasted to oxides first, then reduced with carbon or aluminium (thermite), and the most reactive members need electrolysis. Occurrence explains why the industry around this block centres on furnaces rather than evaporation ponds.

concepts.statement: Partially filled d orbitals deliver: **variable oxidation states** (Mn spans +2 to +7), **coloured ions** (d–d transitions, Cu$^{2+}$ blue), **paramagnetism** with $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM for $n$ unpaired electrons, **catalysis** (Fe–Haber, $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$–contact, Ni–hydrogenation), **complex formation**, **interstitial compounds**, **alloys** and **high melting points** — Zn, Cd, Hg being the low-melting exceptions.
concepts.detail: Each property maps to d structure: unpaired electrons feed magnetism and metallic-bond strength; vacant d orbitals plus high charge density invite lone-pair donation (complexes, catalytic surfaces); tiny atoms (H, C, N) slip into lattice voids giving hard, non-stoichiometric interstitial compounds; similar radii let atoms swap lattice sites, hence alloys. Warning: the purple of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is a charge-transfer colour, NOT d–d — the standard trap.

examples.title: Configuration, ion and magnetism of iron
examples.problem: Write the configurations of Fe ($Z = 26$) and Fe$^{2+}$, count the unpaired electrons, and compute the magnetic moment.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
Fe   : [Ar] 3d6 4s2
Fe2+ : [Ar] 3d6      (4s electrons leave first)
unpaired d electrons = 4
```

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Fe$^{2+}$: $3d^6$ — Hund’s rule places five singly first, the sixth pairs up, leaving 4 unpaired electrons.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Magnetic moment: $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.9$ BM.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Fe$^{3+}$ would be $3d^5$ — all five unpaired — giving $\mu = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.9$ BM; the moment is a direct d-electron census.

examples.result: Fe: $[\text{Ar}]3d^64s^2$; Fe$^{2+}$: $[\text{Ar}]3d^6$ with 4 unpaired electrons, $\mu \approx 4.9$ BM.

examples.title: The Zn exclusion argument
examples.problem: Zinc is a d-block element yet is not counted among transition elements, and Zn$^{2+}$ salts are white. Explain.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Zn ($Z = 30$): $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^2$ — the d subshell is completely filled in the atom.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: The only common ion, Zn$^{2+}$, is $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}$ — still fully filled: no partially filled d subshell anywhere.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: By the strict definition Zn fails the test; the same argument excludes Cd ($4d^{10}$) and Hg ($5d^{10}$).

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: With no partially filled d, no d–d transition is possible — Zn$^{2+}$ compounds are colourless (white salts) and diamagnetic, and zinc shows only the +2 state.

examples.result: Zn is d-block by position but not transition by definition; its filled $d^{10}$ shells cost it colour, magnetism and variable valence.

keyTakeaways: Transition = partially filled d in the atom or a common ion; Zn, Cd, Hg are the excluded d$^{10}$ trio.
General configuration $(n-1)d^{1–10}ns^{1–2}$; Cr and Cu break it for half/fully filled stability; 4s ionises before 3d.
The eight fingerprints (states, colour, magnetism, catalysis, complexes, interstitials, alloys, high mp) all trace to d electrons.
Magnetic census: $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM — count unpaired d electrons first.
Most d-block metals occur as oxides/sulfides; extraction is reduction chemistry.

quiz.q: The ground-state electronic configuration of chromium ($Z = 24$) is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Naive aufbau gives $3d^44s^2$ — option one, the trap. Step 2: A half-filled $3d^5$ maximises exchange energy and symmetry. Step 3: One 4s electron is promoted: $[\text{Ar}]3d^54s^1$ — six singly occupied orbitals. Step 4: $3d^64s^2$ is iron’s configuration (26 electrons), not chromium’s 24.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a d-block element but NOT a transition element?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Check the d subshell of the atom and its common ions. Step 2: Fe, Cu and Ni all have partially filled d subshells in some common state (Cu$^{2+}$ is $3d^9$). Step 3: Zn is $3d^{10}$ as atom and Zn$^{2+}$ is $3d^{10}$ — never partially filled. Step 4: Zinc keeps its d-block seat by position but loses transition status by the strict definition.

quiz.q: The number of unpaired electrons in Fe$^{2+}$ ($3d^6$) is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Six d electrons enter five d orbitals by Hund’s rule. Step 2: Five orbitals each take one electron first. Step 3: The sixth must pair, leaving 4 unpaired spins. Step 4: 5 belongs to Fe$^{3+}$ ($3d^5$, all unpaired); 6 would need six orbitals, which d does not have.

quiz.q: Transition metals and their compounds serve as catalysts mainly because they
options: are always in the gaseous phase
have vacant d orbitals and variable oxidation states that adsorb and activate reactants
quiz.explanation: Step 1: A catalyst must bind reactants and offer an easier route. Step 2: Vacant d orbitals accept lone pairs, adsorbing molecules on the metal surface. Step 3: Variable oxidation states shuttle electrons without net consumption (Fe in Haber, $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ in contact process, Ni in hydrogenation). Step 4: Filled d subshells (Zn, Cd, Hg) make poor catalysts — and low melting points have nothing to do with catalysis.

prerequisites: Oxidation-number bookkeeping (Unit 7)
Lewis acids and bases, lone pairs (Unit 3)
intro: By 1890 chemists could write formulas like CoCl$_3$·6NH$_3$ but not explain them — why did only some of the chloride precipitate with silver nitrate? **Alfred Werner** answered with two kinds of valence, one ionisable and one directional, and single-handedly founded coordination chemistry (the first Nobel Prize in inorganic chemistry, 1913). His vocabulary — ligand, coordination number, denticity, chelation — is the working language of this unit and of the bioinorganic chemistry engineering assessment adores. Across the paper’s 25 chemistry questions (100 marks, +4/−1), a definitional or counting question from this vocabulary appears nearly every year as a direct NCERT-line read — cheap marks that keep chemistry the fastest-scoring subject.
objectives: State Werner’s postulates of primary (ionisable, oxidation-state) and secondary (non-ionisable, directional) valence
Dissect any complex into central metal ion, ligands, coordination sphere, counter ions and coordination number
Compute the metal’s oxidation number from charge bookkeeping of the coordination sphere
Classify ligands by denticity, recognise ambidentate cases and explain why chelation stabilises complexes

concepts.statement: Metals show **two kinds of valence**: the **primary valence** equals the oxidation state, is ionisable and is satisfied by negative ions; the **secondary valence** equals the coordination number (CN), is non-ionisable, is satisfied by ligands and is **directional** — it fixes the geometry (CN 6 → octahedral, CN 4 → tetrahedral or square planar).
concepts.detail: The silver-nitrate evidence: CoCl$_3$·6NH$_3$ releases 3 mol AgCl per mol (so [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]Cl$_3$), CoCl$_3$·5NH$_3$ releases 2 ([Co(NH$_3$)$_5$Cl]Cl$_2$) and CoCl$_3$·4NH$_3$ only 1 ([Co(NH$_3$)$_4$Cl$_2$]Cl). Only ions outside the coordination sphere precipitate — the counting experiment that made the theory unanswerable.

concepts.statement: In $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$: square brackets mark the **coordination sphere** (non-ionisable); Co is the **central metal ion**; NH$_3$ and the inner Cl$–$ are **ligands**; the two outer Cl$–$ are **counter ions**; the CN is 6 and the complex ion carries +1.
concepts.detail: The number of ions a formula releases in solution equals counter ions plus one (the complex ion itself) — three for this salt, measurable by conductivity or colligative methods. Everything inside the brackets survives in water as a unit; everything outside dissociates like any ordinary salt.

concepts.statement: A **ligand** is a Lewis base donating a lone pair to the metal (a Lewis acid); **denticity** counts the donor atoms it uses: monodentate (H$_2$O, NH$_3$, Cl$–$, CO), bidentate (ethylenediamine `en`, oxalate ox$^{2–}$), polydentate (EDTA$^{4–}$ is hexadentate: 2 N + 4 O).
concepts.detail: Denticity counts donor atoms, not the total atoms of the ligand — that is why $[\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3–}$ has CN 6, not 3. Chosen ligands must carry the lone pair at the right spacing: `en` (ethane-1,2-diamine) donates through both nitrogen atoms, wrapping five-membered rings around the metal.

concepts.statement: An **ambidentate** ligand owns two different donor atoms but binds through only one at a time: CN$–$ through C (cyano) or N (isocyano), NO$_2^-$ through N (nitro –NO$_2$) or O (nitrito –ONO).
concepts.detail: Binding through the alternative atom generates linkage isomerism — pairs like $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{NO}_2]^{2+}$ (yellow, nitro) and $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{ONO}]^{2+}$ (red, nitrito). The isomerism itself is treated in section 12.2; here the assessment only wants the donor-atom discrimination.

concepts.statement: When a polydentate ligand grips the **same metal through two or more donor atoms**, it forms rings called a **chelate** — and chelates are markedly more stable than the equivalent collection of monodentate ligands.
concepts.detail: Thermodynamics favours ring closure largely through entropy: one EDTA molecule replacing six water molecules raises the particle count. $[\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3–}$ locks three five-membered rings around iron; EDTA therapy exploits the same claw (Greek chēlē) to pull toxic lead out of blood. This is why titrations and biological metal sites overwhelmingly use chelating ligands.

concepts.statement: A **double salt** (Mohr’s salt $\text{FeSO}_4·(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4·6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, potash alum) dissociates completely in water and shows all tests of its constituent ions; a **complex** ($\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$) retains the complex ion intact — no free Fe$^{2+}$ or CN$–$ tests.
concepts.detail: The distinction is behavioural, not structural: both crystallise as single phases. Add Fe$^{3+}$ to each solution — Mohr’s salt answers with the deep thiocyanate red of free Fe$^{3+}$; ferrocyanide gives Prussian blue only through the intact $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4–}$ unit. "Does the identity survive in water?" is the assessment’s one-line discriminator.

examples.title: Dissecting [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$Cl]Cl$_2$
examples.problem: For $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$, identify the coordination sphere, ligands, counter ions, coordination number, the oxidation state of cobalt, and the number of ions furnished in solution.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
[ Co (NH3)5 Cl ] Cl2
  |    |     |    \__ 2 counter Cl- (ionisable)
  |    |     \__ 1 coordinated Cl- (non-ionisable)
  |    \__ 5 ammine ligands (denticity 1 each)
  \__ central ion, coordination number 6
```

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Ligands: five neutral NH$_3$ plus one coordinated Cl$–$; CN = 5 + 1 = 6 (an octahedral complex).

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Oxidation state: $x + 5(0) + (-1) = +2$ for the complex ion, so $x = +3$ — Co(III).

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: In water: 1 complex ion + 2 chloride ions = 3 ions per formula unit — matching Werner’s 2 mol AgCl per mol of this, his CoCl$_3$·5NH$_3$.

examples.result: Co(III), CN 6, [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$Cl]$^{2+}$ + 2 Cl$–$: three ions in solution, two of them ionisable chlorides.

examples.title: Counting the ionisable chlorides
examples.problem: 0.1 mol each of CoCl$_3$·6NH$_3$, CoCl$_3$·5NH$_3$ and CoCl$_3$·4NH$_3$ is separately treated with excess AgNO$_3$. Predict the AgCl formed and write the modern formulas.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Only chlorides outside the coordination sphere precipitate — count the ions Werner could not.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: CoCl$_3$·6NH$_3$ = $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]\text{Cl}_3$: 3 free Cl$–$ → 0.3 mol AgCl.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: CoCl$_3$·5NH$_3$ = $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$: 2 free Cl$–$ → 0.2 mol AgCl; CoCl$_3$·4NH$_3$ = $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]\text{Cl}$: 1 → 0.1 mol AgCl.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: The one chloride "missing" at each step simply moved inside the sphere — every NH$_3$ that drops out is replaced by an inner chloride, keeping Co(III) and CN 6 constant.

examples.result: 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1 mol AgCl respectively — the precipitation series that proved the coordination sphere.

keyTakeaways: Primary valence = oxidation state (ionisable); secondary valence = coordination number (directional, non-ionisable).
Only ions outside the brackets precipitate with AgNO$_3$ — Werner’s counting argument.
Denticity counts donor atoms: en and ox$^{2–}$ are bidentate, EDTA$^{4–}$ hexadentate; CN = ligands × denticity.
Oxidation state from charge bookkeeping: $x + \sum(\text{ligand charges}) = \text{sphere charge}$.
Double salts lose their identity in water; complex ions survive it; chelate rings buy entropy-driven stability.

quiz.q: In Werner’s theory, the secondary valence of a metal ion corresponds to its
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Werner split valence into two kinds. Step 2: Primary valence = oxidation state, satisfied by ionisable anions. Step 3: Secondary valence = coordination number, satisfied by ligands and directional (fixes geometry). Step 4: Counter ions and unpaired electrons play no part in his classification.

quiz.q: 0.1 mol of CoCl$_3$·5NH$_3$, i.e. $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$, is treated with excess AgNO$_3$. The amount of AgCl formed is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: AgCl precipitates only from ionisable chlorides. Step 2: The two Cl$–$ outside the brackets are ionisable; the one inside is coordinated. Step 3: 0.1 mol of salt gives 2 × 0.1 = 0.2 mol AgCl. Step 4: 0.3 mol belongs to $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]\text{Cl}_3$, one chloride further out.

quiz.q: The coordination number of Fe in $[\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3–}$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Identify the ligand: oxalate, C$_2$O$_4^{2–}$. Step 2: Each oxalate binds through two oxygen donor atoms — bidentate. Step 3: CN = 3 ligands × 2 donor atoms = 6 (octahedral, three chelate rings). Step 4: Answering 3 counts ligands, not donor atoms — the classic denticity trap.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an ambidentate ligand?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Ambidentate means two different possible donor atoms, one used at a time. Step 2: NO$_2^-$ can bind through N (nitro, –NO$_2$) or O (nitrito, –ONO). Step 3: `en` and EDTA$^{4–}$ are chelating polydentate ligands that always use all their donor atoms; H$_2$O is monodentate. Step 4: NO$_2^-$ binding either way generates linkage isomers.

prerequisites: Boiling point, vapour pressure and states of matter (school physics/chemistry)
Intermolecular forces and solubility basics (Unit 5 helps)
intro: Organic reactions are messy by nature — they stop short, run sideways and leave by-products, so the product must be **purified** before it can be melted, weighed or characterised. Every technique in this section is one physical property exploited: solubility, volatility, sublimability or adsorption. engineering assessment’s practical-leaning questions — within the paper’s 25 chemistry questions worth 100 marks at +4/−1 — usually ask which technique suits which mixture, a direct NCERT-line read that makes this some of the cheapest marks on the paper. Chemistry stays the fastest-scoring subject when you can name the right apparatus in ten seconds.
objectives: Select a purification technique by matching the exploitable physical-property difference of a mixture
Describe crystallization, sublimation and simple, fractional, steam and reduced-pressure distillation with one application each
Explain differential extraction and why several small extractions beat a single large one
State the principle of chromatography and contrast adsorption with partition chromatography

concepts.term: Purification is a decision, not a recipe
concepts.statement: Choose the technique from the **property gap**: solubility difference → crystallization; boiling-point difference → distillation; sublimability → sublimation; distribution between immiscible solvents → differential extraction; differential adsorption/partition → chromatography — thermal sensitivity then modifies the choice.
concepts.detail: The assessment almost never says "crystallize this"; it describes a mixture and expects the property gap to trigger the method. Boiling points within a few kelvin demand a fractionating column; a compound that decomposes before boiling forces reduced pressure; a compound immiscible with but volatile in steam invites steam distillation.

concepts.statement: **Crystallization** exploits a solubility gap: dissolve the impure solid hot to saturation, cool slowly, and pure crystals grow while the (minor) impurity stays dissolved in the mother liquor.
concepts.detail: A good solvent dissolves the compound well when hot and poorly when cold, does not react with it, and keeps the impurity soluble even cold. The trick is that the impurity is present in small quantity, so it never reaches saturation — the whole method rests on concentration, not just solubility. Decolourising with animal charcoal before filtration handles coloured impurities.

concepts.statement: **Sublimation** passes a solid straight to vapour on heating and redeposits it as crystals on a cold surface; it separates sublimable camphor, naphthalene, benzoic acid, anthracene or iodine from non-sublimable residue.
concepts.detail: These solids have appreciable vapour pressure below their melting points, so heating drives the solid ⇌ vapour equilibrium fully to vapour; the cold finger (inverted funnel with wet filter paper) recrystallises it. A camphor–common salt mixture is the standard lab demo — salt stays behind in the dish.

concepts.statement: **Simple distillation** for a large boiling-point gap (chloroform 334 K vs aniline 457 K); **fractional distillation** for close-boiling liquids via the repeated condensation cycles of a fractionating column (acetone 329 K vs methanol 338 K); **distillation under reduced pressure** for liquids that decompose below their b.p. (glycerol); **steam distillation** for steam-volatile compounds immiscible with water (aniline–water, o-nitrophenol).
concepts.detail: Steam distillation works because an immiscible mixture boils when the **sum** of the vapour pressures hits 1 atm — so the organic distils well below its normal boiling point, protected from decomposition. Fractionating columns multiply the simple-distillation cycle; each theoretical plate is one vaporisation–condensation round that enriches the vapour in the more volatile component.

concepts.statement: **Differential extraction** moves a solute between immiscible solvents in a separating funnel: the distribution coefficient $K = \frac{C_{\text{organic}}}{C_{\text{water}}}$ decides how much transfers per shake, and the organic layer is dried over anhydrous $\text{CaCl}_2$ or $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$ after separation.
concepts.detail: The counter-intuitive arithmetic: extracting with two half-portions of ether leaves less solute behind than one full portion of the same total volume, because each extraction multiplies the remaining fraction by $\frac{V_{\text{water}}}{V_{\text{water}} + K V_{\text{org}}}$. "Many small shakes beat one big soak" is the lab and assessment rule.

concepts.statement: **Chromatography** separates by differential migration over a stationary phase under a mobile phase: **adsorption chromatography** (column and TLC on silica gel or alumina) and **partition chromatography** (paper, where water held on the paper is the stationary phase); on a plate, $R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}$.
concepts.detail: TLC reads a reaction at a glance — spots located under UV or in an iodine chamber; a strongly adsorbed compound crawls (low $R_f$), a weakly adsorbed one runs with the front (high $R_f$). Column chromatography scales the same principle to grams, as in separating plant pigments. Adsorption is a surface competition; partition is a solubility equilibrium between two liquids — know which mechanism your question assumes.

examples.title: Choosing the technique
examples.problem: Suggest the purification method for: (a) camphor contaminated with common salt, (b) chloroform mixed with aniline, (c) acetone mixed with methanol, (d) aniline from an aniline–water mixture.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
(a) camphor + NaCl   -> sublimability gap  -> sublimation
(b) CHCl3 + aniline   -> b.p. gap 334/457 K -> simple distillation
(c) acetone/methanol  -> b.p. gap 329/338 K -> fractional distillation
(d) aniline + water   -> immiscible + steam-volatile -> steam distillation
```

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: (a) Camphor sublimes on gentle heating and re-forms on the cold funnel; non-volatile NaCl stays in the dish.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (b) The 123 K boiling-point gap lets chloroform distil off cleanly, leaving aniline behind; (c) the 9 K gap is too small for one plate, so the fractionating column supplies many.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: (d) Aniline boils at 457 K but co-distils with steam below 373 K because the vapour pressures add — no decomposition, no high heat.

examples.result: (a) sublimation, (b) simple distillation, (c) fractional distillation, (d) steam distillation.

examples.title: Reading a TLC plate
examples.problem: On a silica TLC run, the solvent front travelled 7.2 cm; spot A moved 2.9 cm and spot B moved 5.0 cm. Find both $R_f$ values and say which compound is adsorbed more strongly.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: $R_f = \frac{\text{spot distance}}{\text{front distance}}$ — always a number between 0 and 1.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: A spends more time stuck on the polar silica, so it travels less — A is the more strongly adsorbed compound.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Under identical conditions $R_f$ is a reproducible identity tag for the compound — the basis of purity checks on reaction mixtures.

examples.result: $R_f(A) = 0.40$, $R_f(B) = 0.69$; A is adsorbed more strongly on silica.

examples.title: Extraction arithmetic: two small beats one big
examples.problem: 2.0 g of a solute is dissolved in 100 mL water. Its distribution coefficient between ether and water is $K = 4$. Compare one extraction with 100 mL ether against two extractions with 50 mL each.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Fraction left in water per extraction $= \frac{V_w}{V_w + K V_{\text{ether}}}$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: One 100 mL extraction: $\frac{100}{100 + 4 \times 100} = \frac{1}{5}$, so $2.0 \times \frac{1}{5} = 0.40$ g stays behind — 1.60 g recovered.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Each 50 mL extraction: $\frac{100}{100 + 4 \times 50} = \frac{1}{3}$, so after two, $2.0 \times (\frac{1}{3})^2 = 0.22$ g stays behind — 1.78 g recovered.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Same 100 mL of ether, 0.18 g more solute recovered — the multiplicative logic that makes "many small extractions" the standing lab instruction.

examples.result: One 100 mL extraction leaves 0.40 g; two 50 mL extractions leave 0.22 g — two small extractions win.

keyTakeaways: Match the property gap to the method: solubility → crystallization, b.p. → distillation, sublimability → sublimation, distribution → extraction, adsorption → chromatography.
Close boiling points need a fractionating column; thermal fragility needs reduced pressure; steam volatility + immiscibility need steam.
Steam distillation boils when $p_{\text{organic}} + p_{\text{water}} = 1$ atm — always below 373 K.
$R_f = \frac{\text{distance by spot}}{\text{distance by front}}$; strong adsorption ⇒ low $R_f$.
Extraction: several small portions beat one large portion at equal total solvent.

quiz.q: Aniline is separated from an aniline–water mixture by
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Aniline and water are immiscible. Step 2: Aniline is steam-volatile, and the pair boils when the vapour pressures add to 1 atm. Step 3: The mixture distils below 373 K, far under aniline’s 457 K boiling point. Step 4: Simple/fractional distillation would heat aniline to 457 K — unnecessary and risky.

quiz.q: Acetone (b.p. 329 K) and methanol (b.p. 338 K) are best separated by
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The boiling points differ by only 9 K. Step 2: One vaporisation–condensation cycle cannot enrich the vapour enough. Step 3: A fractionating column provides many cycles (theoretical plates), stepwise enriching the more volatile acetone. Step 4: Steam distillation needs immiscibility with water; crystallization applies to solids.

quiz.q: A liquid that decomposes below its normal boiling point is best purified by
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Lowering the external pressure lowers the boiling point. Step 2: The liquid then boils at a temperature below its decomposition point. Step 3: Glycerol, which decomposes on strong heating, is the textbook case. Step 4: Steam distillation needs steam volatility plus immiscibility; sublimation applies to solids.

quiz.q: In a TLC run the solvent front travels 6.0 cm and a spot travels 3.6 cm. The $R_f$ value is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: $R_f = \frac{\text{distance by spot}}{\text{distance by front}}$. Step 2: $\frac{3.6}{6.0} = 0.6$. Step 3: 1.67 inverts the ratio — $R_f$ can never exceed 1. Step 4: 0.36 would use the front distance as numerator.

prerequisites: Functional groups and IUPAC nomenclature (Unit 14)
Markovnikov addition to alkenes (Unit 15)
intro: Swap an –OH for a halogen and carbon becomes a leaving-group artist: **haloalkanes and haloarenes** are the pivot of synthetic organic chemistry. The C–X bond’s measurable personality — length, enthalpy, dipole moment — predicts everything downstream, and engineering assessment interrogates exactly those orders. Among the paper’s 25 chemistry questions (100 marks, +4/−1), halogen-compound items are usually NCERT-line fact checks — reagent choice, bond orders, preparation routes — which is why this unit rewards revision more than genius and keeps chemistry the fastest-scoring subject of the three.
objectives: Classify halogen compounds as haloalkanes or haloarenes, and by carbon class (1°, 2°, 3°) and position (vinylic, allylic, benzylic)
Write the general preparation routes: from alcohols (HX, PX$_3$/PX$_5$, SOCl$_2$), from hydrocarbons (halogenation, HX addition) and by halogen exchange (Finkelstein, Swarts)
Explain the bond-length, bond-enthalpy and dipole-moment trends of the C–X bond and the reactivity order R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F
Contrast the C–X bond of haloarenes with that of haloalkanes using resonance and hybridisation

concepts.statement: **Haloalkanes** carry X on an $sp^3$ carbon (alkyl, allylic, benzylic); **haloarenes** carry X directly on an aromatic $sp^2$ carbon; both classify further by halogen count and by the substitution class (1°, 2°, 3°) of the carbon bearing X.
concepts.detail: Position matters as much as family: CH$_2$=CH–Cl (vinylic) and C$_6$H$_5$–Cl (aryl) resist substitution, while allylic (CH$_2$=CH–CH$_2$Cl) and benzylic (C$_6$H$_5$CH$_2$Cl) halides react briskly — resonance-stabilised intermediates. Physical sheet: boiling points climb R–F < R–Cl < R–Br < R–I with van der Waals bulk, branching lowers them, haloalkanes shun water (no H-bonding) but love organic solvents; CH$_2$Cl$_2$, CHCl$_3$ and CCl$_4$ are all denser than water.

concepts.statement: Alcohol → halide via $\text{R–OH} + \text{HX} \to \text{R–X} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ (reactivity HI > HBr > HCl; HCl needs anhydrous ZnCl$_2$), or via phosphorus halides $3\text{R–OH} + \text{PX}_3 \to 3\text{R–X} + \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3$, or via $\text{R–OH} + \text{SOCl}_2 \to \text{R–Cl} + \text{SO}_2 + \text{HCl}$.
concepts.detail: SOCl$_2$ (thionyl chloride) is the connoisseur’s choice: both by-products are **gases** that bubble out, leaving the alkyl chloride pure — no aqueous workup, no side products. For iodides, red phosphorus with I$_2$ generates PI$_3$ in situ. The Lucas reagent (conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl$_2$) doubles as the 1°/2°/3° diagnostic from Unit 17.

concepts.statement: Alkanes + X$_2$ under $h\nu$ give **free-radical substitution** (industrial but unselective); alkenes + HX give Markovnikov **addition** (propene → 2-bromopropane; peroxides flip HBr to anti-Markovnikov); X$_2$ addition gives vicinal dihalides; haloarenes come from benzene + X$_2$/FeX$_3$ or from diazonium salts via Sandmeyer (Cu$_2$X$_2$/HX) or KI.
concepts.detail: Radical halogenation of alkanes is a synthetic mess — every H is a target, so mixtures dominate unless the molecule has one kind of hydrogen (methane → chloromethane for the chemical industry). The diazonium route is the clean laboratory path to haloarenes, and it is the only easy way to fluoroarenes (Balz–Schiemann-style replacements) — detail reserved for Unit 18’s diazonium section.

concepts.statement: **Finkelstein**: R–Cl/R–Br + NaI in dry acetone → R–I (NaCl/NaBr precipitate drives it, Le Chatelier); **Swarts**: R–X + AgF (or Hg$_2$F$_2$, CoF$_2$) heated → R–F.
concepts.detail: Direct fluorination of hydrocarbons is violent and unselective, so fluoroalkanes are made by swapping the halogen instead — the Swarts route to the freon family. Finkelstein’s precipitation trick only works in dry acetone, where NaI dissolves but NaCl/NaBr do not — a solvent-detail the assessment checks.

concepts.statement: Bond enthalpy falls C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I (452 > 351 > 293 > 215 kJ/mol) while length grows (139 < 177 < 193 < 214 pm), so **reactivity rises** R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F; yet dipole moments of the methyl halides order $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl} > \text{CH}_3\text{F} > \text{CH}_3\text{Br} > \text{CH}_3\text{I}$.
concepts.detail: The dipole paradox: C–F is the most polar bond, but its short bond length shrinks the charge separation — dipole moment is charge × distance, so the longer C–Cl wins. Learn both orders separately: bond enthalpy governs substitution reactivity, dipole moment governs polarity questions. Both are favourite engineering assessment ordering questions.

concepts.statement: In haloarenes, the halogen lone pair delocalises into the ring: the C–X bond gains **partial double-bond character** — shorter (169 pm vs 177 pm in chloroethane), stronger, less polar — so haloarenes resist nucleophilic substitution spectacularly.
concepts.detail: Two reinforcing reasons: resonance ties the carbon to the halogen, and the $sp^2$ carbon is more electronegative than $sp^3$, pulling bond electrons toward itself and dulling the carbon’s positive charge. Chlorobenzene laughs at NaOH at room temperature and only reacts under brutal conditions (623 K, ~300 atm) — the punchline of many engineering assessment assertion–reason items.

examples.title: Reagent selection for clean conversions
examples.problem: Choose reagents for the cleanest conversion of: (a) propan-1-ol → 1-chloropropane, (b) 2-methylpropan-2-ol → 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, (c) ethanol → iodoethane.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
(a) CH3CH2CH2OH + SOCl2  -> CH3CH2CH2Cl + SO2 + HCl (both gases!)
(b) (CH3)3COH + conc. HCl / anhyd. ZnCl2  -> (CH3)3CCl  (instant, 3°)
(c) C2H5OH + red P + I2  -> C2H5I (PI3 generated in situ)
```

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: (a) SOCl$_2$ wins because SO$_2$ and HCl escape as gases, handing over the pure chloride; PCl$_5$ also works but leaves POCl$_3$ to wash out.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (b) The 3° carbocation forms instantly, so plain conc. HCl with ZnCl$_2$ (Lucas conditions) converts it at once — no stronger reagent needed.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: (c) HI alone overalkylates; red P + I$_2$ meter the iodide delivery as PI$_3$, the standard clean route to iodoalkanes.

examples.result: (a) SOCl$_2$, (b) conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl$_2$, (c) red phosphorus + I$_2$.

examples.title: The dipole-moment paradox
examples.problem: The C–F bond is more polar than C–Cl, yet CH$_3$Cl (1.86 D) has a slightly larger dipole moment than CH$_3$F (1.85 D). Explain, and give the full order for methyl halides.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Dipole moment is a product: $\mu = q \times d$ — charge separation times bond length.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: C–F is short (139 pm): high polarity multiplied by a tiny distance gives a slightly smaller $\mu$ than C–Cl’s 177 pm distance.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Down the group the charge keeps falling while length grows; the length effect caps out, so the net order is $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl} > \text{CH}_3\text{F} > \text{CH}_3\text{Br} > \text{CH}_3\text{I}$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Moral: bond polarity and molecular dipole moment are different quantities — the assessment’s favourite bait conflates them.

examples.result: Order: CH$_3$Cl (1.86) > CH$_3$F (1.85) > CH$_3$Br (1.83) > CH$_3$I (1.64 D) — charge × distance wins.

examples.title: Why chlorobenzene resists substitution
examples.problem: Chloroethane reacts with aqueous NaOH readily at reflux, but chlorobenzene does not react even on prolonged boiling. Explain using resonance and hybridisation.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: In chlorobenzene the chlorine lone pair delocalises into the ring: contributing structures put a C=Cl double bond on the C–Cl linkage.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: The bond shortens (169 pm vs 177 pm in chloroethane) and strengthens — cleaving it costs much more energy.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: The $sp^2$ carbon is also more electronegative, so the carbon’s positive charge (the nucleophile’s target) is muted.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Net: chlorobenzene needs 623 K and ~300 atm of NaOH to react at all, while chloroethane — a long, weak, polar $sp^3$ C–Cl bond — substitutes easily.

examples.result: Resonance-driven partial double-bond character plus $sp^2$ carbon make aryl C–Cl short, strong and nearly apolar — substitution stalls.

keyTakeaways: Haloalkanes = X on $sp^3$ carbon; haloarenes = X on aryl $sp^2$ carbon — the hybridisation decides reactivity.
Best lab routes: SOCl$_2$ for R–Cl (gaseous by-products), red P + X$_2$ for R–I, Finkelstein (NaI/acetone) and Swarts (AgF) for exchange.
Reactivity order R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F follows falling bond enthalpy, not dipole moment.
Dipole moments: $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl} > \text{CH}_3\text{F} > \text{CH}_3\text{Br} > \text{CH}_3\text{I}$ — charge × distance.
Aryl C–X: resonance gives partial double-bond character (169 pm) — chlorobenzene needs 623 K/300 atm to substitute.

quiz.q: The order of reactivity of haloalkanes toward nucleophilic substitution is
