Iron is won by CO in stacked stages ($\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 \to \text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4 \to \text{FeO} \to \text{Fe}$) with limestone fluxing silica; copper refines itself ($2\text{Cu}_2\text{O} + \text{Cu}_2\text{S} \to 6\text{Cu} + \text{SO}_2$).
Al$_2$O$_3$ out-sits carbon on the Ellingham chart at all practical temperatures, so aluminium comes from fused-salt electrolysis — quantified by Faraday's law with a sacrificial carbon anode.

quiz.q: Aluminium oxide cannot be reduced by carbon in a blast furnace because
options: the $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ Ellingham line lies below the C/CO lines at all attainable temperatures
aluminium is volatile and escapes the furnace
the reaction is too exothermic to control
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Carbon reduction is thermodynamically allowed only above the temperature where the C$\to$CO line dips beneath the metal-oxide line. Step 2: The $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ line lies so low that no attainable furnace temperature makes $\Delta G^\circ(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{C})$ negative. Step 3: Hence aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of alumina in molten cryolite instead. Step 4: Alumina's very high melting point (2072 $^\circ$C), not volatility, is what cryolite circumvents.

quiz.q: In the bessemerisation reaction $2\text{Cu}_2\text{O} + \text{Cu}_2\text{S} \to 6\text{Cu} + \text{SO}_2$, the reducing agent is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: A reducing agent is itself oxidised. Step 2: In $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$, sulphur sits at $-2$; in the product $\text{SO}_2$ it is $+4$ — sulphur is oxidised, so $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$ donates electrons. Step 3: Copper in $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ falls from $+1$ to $0$, accepting those electrons. Step 4: This internal redox is why the process is called *self*-reduction: the ore's own sulphide refines its own oxide, and the reaction is exothermic enough to sustain the converter temperature.

quiz.q: On an Ellingham diagram, the lines for $2\text{Zn} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{ZnO}$ and similar metal oxidations slope upward because
options: $\Delta S^\circ < 0$: gaseous oxygen is consumed, lowering the entropy
$\Delta G^\circ$ must always increase with temperature
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The slope of a $\Delta G^\circ$-vs-$T$ line is $-\Delta S^\circ$. Step 2: Metal oxidation consumes 1 mol of $\text{O}_2$(g) and produces only condensed phases, so $\Delta S^\circ$ is distinctly negative. Step 3: Slope $= -\Delta S^\circ > 0$: the line climbs, meaning the oxide becomes *less* stable as temperature rises — which is exactly what makes high-temperature reduction possible. Step 4: The sign of $\Delta H^\circ$ sets the intercept, not the slope.

quiz.q: In the thermite reaction $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{Al} \to \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{Cr}$, aluminium works as reductant because
options: the $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ formation line lies below the $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$ line, making the overall $\Delta G^\circ$ negative
the reaction is slow and therefore favourable
chromium is more electropositive than aluminium
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Reverse one oxidation and add the other: $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3 \to 2\text{Cr}$ (up its own line) plus $2\text{Al} \to \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ (down aluminium's line). Step 2: The net $\Delta G^\circ$ is the vertical gap between the two Ellingham lines, $\Delta G^\circ(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3) - \Delta G^\circ(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3)$. Step 3: Since aluminium's line lies far lower, the difference is positive and the net $\Delta G^\circ$ is negative — thermodynamically spontaneous and highly exothermic. Step 4: In fact aluminium is among the most electropositive (reactive) metals, which is precisely *why* it sits below chromium on the chart; the last option states the opposite.

prerequisites: Solubility product and the common-ion effect (chem-a6-s4)
Acid–base equilibria, pH and buffers (chem-a6-s5)
Redox basics and precipitation reactions from the mole-concept chapter (chem-a1)
intro: Qualitative inorganic analysis is the advanced engineering assessment syllabus's laboratory course on paper: eleven cations are separated into five groups by nothing deeper than solubility products and the common-ion effect, yet the scheme rewards exactly the multi-step deductive reasoning the assessment prizes. Every group reagent is an equilibrium argument in disguise — acidic $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ suppresses sulphide ion so completely that only ultra-insoluble sulphides fall, while ammonium chloride holds hydroxide down so magnesium stays in solution. Master the logic, not the list, and any flowchart question becomes an exercise.
objectives: Reproduce the five-group scheme: group reagent, member cations, precipitate formulae and colours

Explain each separation quantitatively with $K_{sp}$ and the common-ion effect — why acidic $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ catches only Group II and why $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ must precede $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$
Deduce the cations present in a mixture from a described sequence of observations, and name the confirmatory tests for Fe$^{3+}$, Cu$^{2+}$, Zn$^{2+}$, Ba$^{2+}$, Ca$^{2+}$
Apply Group I separations: PbCl$_2$ in hot water, AgCl in ammonia, and the interplay with Group II lead

concepts.statement: Cations are precipitated in sequence: **Group I** with dilute HCl (AgCl white, $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ white, PbCl$_2$ white); **Group II** with $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ in dilute HCl (CuS black, HgS black, PbS black, $\text{Bi}_2\text{S}_3$ brown, CdS yellow); **Group III** with $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ in presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ ($\text{Fe(OH)}_3$ reddish brown, $\text{Cr(OH)}_3$ green, $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ white gelatinous); **Group IV** with $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ in ammoniacal medium (ZnS dirty white, MnS buff); **Group V** with $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$ in $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}/\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ (BaCO$_3$, CaCO$_3$ white), with Mg$^{2+}$ remaining in solution.
concepts.detail: The order is a solubility ladder, not an arbitrary convention: each reagent is chosen to catch the *most* insoluble remaining members while leaving the rest dissolved. Because PbCl$_2$ is moderately soluble (about 1 g per 100 mL cold water), lead leaks past Group I into Group II as PbS — the standard "split personality" the assessors love. At every stage, precipitate (carries the group) and filtrate (carries everything else) must both be tracked; flowchart questions test exactly this double bookkeeping.

concepts.term: Why acidic H₂S precipitates only Group II
concepts.statement: $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ is a weak diprotic acid: $[\text{S}^{2-}] = \frac{K_{a1}K_{a2}[\text{H}_2\text{S}]}{[\text{H}^+]^2}$. In 0.3 M HCl the common ion $\text{H}^+$ crushes $[\text{S}^{2-}]$ to about $10^{-22}$ M — low enough that only sulphides with $K_{sp} \lesssim 10^{-30}$ (CuS, HgS, PbS, $\text{Bi}_2\text{S}_3$, CdS) can exceed their solubility products; ZnS and MnS ($K_{sp} \sim 10^{-22}$) stay dissolved. In ammoniacal medium $[\text{S}^{2-}]$ rebounds by over $10^{10}$-fold and Group IV falls.
concepts.detail: This is the common-ion effect doing real analytical work: the *same reagent* (hydrogen sulphide) is made selective simply by fixing the pH. Quantitatively, precipitation begins when the ionic product $[M^{2+}][\text{S}^{2-}]$ exceeds $K_{sp}$ — with $[\text{S}^{2-}] \approx 10^{-22}$ M a cation needs $K_{sp}$ below roughly $10^{-24}$ (at millimolar $M^{2+}$) to precipitate at all, and the residual $[\text{S}^{2-}]$ also sets how *completely* it precipitates. Assertion–reason items probe both directions: "H$_2$S precipitates CuS but not ZnS in acid because CuS is more soluble" — false as stated; it is *less* soluble, and that is why it falls.

concepts.statement: Before adding $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ for Group III, $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ is added: the common ion $\text{NH}_4^+$ suppresses the dissociation of the weak base, holding $[\text{OH}^-]$ low enough that only the very insoluble hydroxides of Fe$^{3+}$, Al$^{3+}$ and Cr$^{3+}$ precipitate, while Mg(OH)$_2$ (relatively soluble) stays in solution for Group V.
concepts.detail: Without $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$, concentrated ammonia would dump enough hydroxide to precipitate $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ (and even traces of Mn/Zn hydroxides), wrecking the group separations that follow. The amphoteric pair is then split inside Group III: $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ and $\text{Cr(OH)}_3$ dissolve in excess NaOH (as $[\text{Al(OH)}_4]^-$ and $[\text{Cr(OH)}_4]^-$) while $\text{Fe(OH)}_3$ does not — the first diagnostic fork in the group. Chromyl-chloride and Prussian-blue tests then pin the individual members.

concepts.statement: The Group I chlorides separate cleanly: **PbCl$_2$ dissolves in hot water** (retreating on cooling as needles) and so leaves AgCl and $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ behind; **AgCl dissolves in $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$** as $[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$ and re-precipitates on acidification with HNO$_3$; **$\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ turns black with ammonia** (disproportionation to Hg and $\text{HgNH}_2\text{Cl}$).
concepts.detail: Hot water exploits PbCl$_2$'s steeply temperature-dependent solubility; the ammonia test exploits complex formation ($K_f \approx 10^{7}$ for the diamminesilver ion) versus mercury(I)'s disproportionation $\text{Hg}_2^{2+} \to \text{Hg}^{2+} + \text{Hg}$. Lead that reaches Group II is caught as black PbS and confirmed as yellow PbCrO$_4$ (soluble in NaOH, unlike BaCrO$_4$). The assessment pattern: a described colour change with one reagent, then ask which cation — so the *differential* behaviour, not the precipitate colours alone, is the memory target.

concepts.statement: Fe$^{3+}$ + $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$ $\to$ deep-blue **Prussian blue** $\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3$; Cu$^{2+}$ + $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$ $\to$ chocolate-brown $\text{Cu}_2[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$; Ba$^{2+}$ + $\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$ $\to$ yellow $\text{BaCrO}_4$ (insoluble in acetic acid); Ca$^{2+}$ + ammonium oxalate $\to$ white $\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$; Zn$^{2+}$ + potassium ferrocyanide $\to$ white/bluish ppt soluble in NaOH; Mg$^{2+}$ + $\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4/\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ $\to$ white crystalline $\text{Mg(NH}_4)\text{PO}_4$; flame tests: Ca brick-red, Ba apple-green.
concepts.detail: Each confirmatory test is itself a small equilibrium or redox story: Prussian blue is a mixed-valence iron(II/III) hexacyanometallate; the chromate test for barium works in dilute acetic acid because $\text{BaCrO}_4$ is far less soluble than $\text{CaCrO}_4$; the calcium oxalate test fails for barium only after barium has been removed — sequence matters. Mn$^{2+}$ is confirmed by oxidation to purple permanganate with $\text{PbO}_2$/conc. HNO$_3$ or sodium bismuthate. Remember the colours as *pairs* (reagent $\to$ colour) — the assessment almost always describes the observation and asks for the inference.

examples.title: Reading a flowchart: two cations from six observations
examples.problem: A mixture of two salts in water gives the following results: (i) no precipitate with dilute HCl; (ii) no precipitate when $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ is passed in acidic medium; (iii) a gelatinous reddish-brown precipitate with $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{NH}_4\text{OH}$, insoluble in excess NaOH; (iv) after removing that precipitate, no precipitate with $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ in ammoniacal medium; (v) a white precipitate with $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$ in presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}/\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$, which dissolves in acetic acid and gives no precipitate with $\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$ but a white precipitate with ammonium oxalate; (vi) the flame test is brick-red. Identify the cations and suggest a confirmatory test for each.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Observations (i) and (ii) rule out Group I (no Ag$^+$/Hg$_2^{2+}$/Pb$^{2+}$) and Group II (no Cu$^{2+}$/Hg$^{2+}$/Bi$^{3+}$/Cd$^{2+}$) — the acidic medium would have caught their sulphides.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Observation (iii) is textbook Group III: gelatinous reddish-brown $\text{Fe(OH)}_3$ with $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}/\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$. The colour already excludes white $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ and green $\text{Cr(OH)}_3$, and insolubility in excess NaOH excludes the amphoteric pair — Al$^{3+}$ and Cr$^{3+}$ hydroxides would have dissolved as $[\text{Al(OH)}_4]^-$/$[\text{Cr(OH)}_4]^-$. So Fe$^{3+}$ is present.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Observation (iv) clears Group IV: no Zn$^{2+}$, Mn$^{2+}$ (no dirty-white ZnS or buff MnS in the alkaline sulphide medium).

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Observation (v) is Group V: a white carbonate among Ba$^{2+}$/Ca$^{2+}$. Dissolution in acetic acid readies the solution for the pair of differential tests — no yellow $\text{BaCrO}_4$ with $\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$ excludes barium; the white oxalate ppt identifies Ca$^{2+}$, and the brick-red flame (vi) seals it.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Confirmatory tests: Fe$^{3+}$ with $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$ gives Prussian blue, $\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3$; Ca$^{2+}$ is already confirmed by ammonium oxalate ($\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$) plus the flame. Conclusion: the mixture contains Fe$^{3+}$ and Ca$^{2+}$ (for instance $\text{FeCl}_3$ and $\text{CaCl}_2$).

examples.result: The cations are Fe$^{3+}$ (Group III, reddish-brown gelatinous hydroxide) and Ca$^{2+}$ (Group V, oxalate + brick-red flame); no Group I, II or IV cations are present.

examples.title: The Ksp arithmetic behind the Group II / Group IV split
examples.problem: Saturated $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ provides $[\text{S}^{2-}] \approx 10^{-22}$ M in 0.3 M HCl, but about $10^{-6}$ M in ammoniacal solution. Given $K_{sp}(\text{CuS}) \approx 10^{-35}$ and $K_{sp}(\text{ZnS}) \approx 10^{-22}$, show that Cu$^{2+}$ (taken as 0.01 M) precipitates in acid while Zn$^{2+}$ (0.01 M) does not, and that Zn$^{2+}$ precipitates completely in the ammoniacal medium.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Precipitation condition: ionic product $[M^{2+}][\text{S}^{2-}] > K_{sp}$. In acid, with $[\text{S}^{2-}] = 10^{-22}$ M, the IP for a 0.01 M cation is $10^{-2} \times 10^{-22} = 10^{-24}$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Copper in acid: $10^{-24} \gg 10^{-35}$, so CuS precipitates massively. The residual copper left dissolved is $[\text{Cu}^{2+}] = \frac{K_{sp}}{[\text{S}^{2-}]} = \frac{10^{-35}}{10^{-22}} = 10^{-13}$ M — quantitative separation.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Zinc in acid: the threshold concentration is $[\text{Zn}^{2+}]_{min} = \frac{10^{-22}}{10^{-22}} = 1$ M, far above the 0.01 M on offer; equivalently $\text{IP} = 10^{-24} < K_{sp} = 10^{-22}$. No ZnS forms — Group IV stays dissolved with the filtrate.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Zinc in ammoniacal medium: $[\text{S}^{2-}] = 10^{-6}$ M, so the IP becomes $10^{-2} \times 10^{-6} = 10^{-8} \gg 10^{-22}$ — precipitation is violent, and the residual zinc is $\frac{10^{-22}}{10^{-6}} = 10^{-16}$ M: essentially complete.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: The pH lever moved $[\text{S}^{2-}]$ by sixteen orders of magnitude ($10^{-22} \to 10^{-6}$), swinging zinc from "cannot precipitate" to "cannot stay dissolved" — the entire group scheme in one equilibrium. This is why the acid strength before passing $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ must be controlled: too much acid and even CdS leaks; too little and ZnS crashes early.

examples.result: In acid: CuS precipitates (residual $[\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 10^{-13}$ M) while ZnS cannot ($[\text{Zn}^{2+}]$ would need to exceed 1 M); in ammonia: ZnS precipitates completely (residual $10^{-16}$ M).

keyTakeaways: The five groups are a $K_{sp}$ ladder: chlorides $\to$ acid-insoluble sulphides $\to$ hydroxides $\to$ alkaline sulphides $\to$ carbonates, each reagent catching only what cannot stay dissolved.
The same $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ is selective purely by pH: $[\text{S}^{2-}] \sim 10^{-22}$ M in 0.3 M acid (Group II only) versus $\sim 10^{-6}$ M in ammonia (Group IV) — a $10^{16}$-fold swing.
$\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ before $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is a buffer instruction: it suppresses $[\text{OH}^-]$ so Mg$^{2+}$ survives to Group V while Fe$^{3+}$/Al$^{3+}$/Cr$^{3+}$ hydroxides fall.

Differential behaviour, not colour alone, identifies cations: PbCl$_2$ hot-water solubility, AgCl in ammonia, $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ blackening, Prussian blue for Fe$^{3+}$, chromate-vs-oxalate for Ba$^{2+}$/Ca$^{2+}$.

quiz.q: A solution gives no precipitate with dilute HCl. Which cation can nevertheless still be present?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Dilute HCl is the Group I reagent — it precipitates AgCl, $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ and PbCl$_2$. Step 2: No precipitate therefore excludes all Group I cations. Step 3: $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is a Group II cation, caught only later by $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ in acidic medium (black CuS), so it sails through the HCl step. Step 4: Note the converse trap: Pb$^{2+}$ *usually* precipitates in Group I but partially leaks into Group II because PbCl$_2$ is noticeably soluble in cold water.

quiz.q: A white precipitate obtained with dilute HCl dissolves completely in hot water and reappears as needle-shaped crystals on cooling. The cation is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Only Group I members give precipitates with dilute HCl, so the cation is among Pb$^{2+}$, Ag$^+$, $\text{Hg}_2^{2+}$. Step 2: PbCl$_2$ solubility rises steeply with temperature (~0.7 g/100 mL cold to ~3.3 g/100 mL hot), so it dissolves in hot water and recrystallises as needles on cooling. Step 3: AgCl and $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ are insoluble in hot water; their differential reagent is ammonia (AgCl dissolves, $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ blackens). Step 4: Ba$^{2+}$ never precipitates with HCl at all — its group reagent is ammonium carbonate.

quiz.q: Ammonium chloride is added *before* ammonium hydroxide while testing for Group III cations because
options: the common ion $\text{NH}_4^+$ keeps $[\text{OH}^-]$ low, so Mg(OH)$_2$ does not precipitate along with the Group III hydroxides
it complexes Fe$^{3+}$ and prevents its precipitation
quiz.explanation: Step 1: $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is a weak base; its dissociation is suppressed by the common ion $\text{NH}_4^+$ from the strong-ish electrolyte $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$. Step 2: The resulting $[\text{OH}^-]$ is low — a buffered, mildly basic medium. Step 3: Only hydroxides with very small $K_{sp}$ (Fe$^{3+}$, Al$^{3+}$, Cr$^{3+}$) exceed their solubility products; $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, relatively soluble, waits in solution for its own Group V test. Step 4: Far from preventing precipitation, the buffer *ensures selective* precipitation — and it has no redox role.

quiz.q: A reddish-brown precipitate from Group III gives a deep-blue colouration with potassium ferrocyanide. The cation confirmed is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The reddish-brown gelatinous Group III precipitate is $\text{Fe(OH)}_3$, already pointing to Fe$^{3+}$. Step 2: With $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$, Fe$^{3+}$ forms Prussian blue, $\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3$, an intense deep-blue mixed-valence precipitate. Step 3: Fe$^{2+}$ gives a white ferrocyanide that *turns* blue on standing/oxidation, while its classical deep-blue test uses ferricyanide (Turnbull's blue); Cu$^{2+}$ gives a chocolate-brown ferrocyanide. Step 4: The colour of the hydroxide plus the blue ferrocyanide test jointly pin ferric iron.

prerequisites: Structure of benzene and the mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution (chem-a18-s1)
Resonance and electronic effects (+M, −M, +I, −I) from organic basics (chem-a16)
Acid strength and the stabilisation of charged intermediates by delocalisation
intro: Put one substituent on a benzene ring and it dictates the fate of the next: where the incoming electrophile lands and how fast it arrives. Electron-donating groups such as $-\text{OH}$ and $-\text{NH}_2$ flood the ring with electron density — ortho/para attack, faster reaction — while electron-withdrawing groups like $-\text{NO}_2$ starve it and redirect attack to the meta position. advanced engineering assessment tests the concept three ways at once: predicting products, ranking rates, and — hardest of all — planning multi-step syntheses where the *order* of substitution is the whole answer.
objectives: Classify substituents as activating/ortho–para, deactivating/meta, or the halogen special case (deactivating yet ortho–para)
Predict the major product (and significant minor products) of electrophilic substitution on monosubstituted benzenes, including steric bias toward para
Rank reactivity toward a fixed electrophile (e.g. nitration) across substituted rings and match conditions to activation level
Design two-step syntheses on benzene where the target isomer is reachable only by choosing the correct order of substituent installation

concepts.statement: Groups that donate electron density by resonance ($-\text{OH}$, $-\text{NH}_2$, $-\text{OR}$, $-\text{NHR}$, $-\text{NR}_2$) or hyperconjugation/induction ($-\text{R}$ alkyl, $-\text{aryl}$) are **activating ortho/para directors**: they accelerate electrophilic substitution and steer the new group to the 2- and 4-positions.
concepts.detail: The reason lives in the arenium ($\sigma$) complex: for ortho or para attack, one resonance form places the positive charge on the carbon bearing the substituent, where the donor's lone pair can stabilise it by delocalisation ($+M$). Meta attack never generates that stabilised form. Strength ladder for nitration ease: $-\text{NH}_2 > -\text{OH} > -\text{OR} > $ alkyl $> $ H. Practical fingerprint: phenol and aniline nitrate with *dilute* $\text{HNO}_3$ at room temperature (aniline's $-\text{NH}_2$ must be protected as the acetanilide in practice, or the oxidising acid wrecks it).

concepts.statement: Groups that withdraw electron density by resonance ($-\text{NO}_2$, $-\text{CN}$, $-\text{CHO}$, $-\text{COR}$, $-\text{COOH}$, $-\text{COOR}$, $-\text{CONH}_2$) or strongly by induction ($-\text{NR}_3^+$, $-\text{CCl}_3$) are **deactivating meta directors**: substitution slows and the new group enters the 3-position.
concepts.detail: For ortho/para attack on such a ring, a resonance form of the arenium ion places the cation *adjacent* to the electron sink — a violently destabilised structure; meta attack avoids that resonance form entirely, so meta is the least-bad option, not an actively good one. Hence meta products always need harsher conditions (nitrobenzene requires conc. $\text{HNO}_3$/conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ near 370–380 K, versus ~330 K for benzene), and second nitrations of deactivated rings are slow. Ranking deactivation for nitration: $-\text{NO}_2 > -\text{CHO} \approx -\text{COR} > -\text{COOH} > $ halogens.

concepts.statement: Halogens are the **only deactivating ortho/para directors**: their strong $-I$ effect drains electron density overall (slower reaction than benzene), yet their lone pairs still delocalise into the ring ($+M$) and specifically stabilise the ortho/para $\sigma$-complexes.
concepts.detail: Chlorobenzene nitrates about 30 times slower than benzene yet gives a mixture of 4-chloronitrobenzene (major) and 2-chloronitrobenzene — never the meta product in significant amount. The apparent contradiction dissolves once "rate" (governed by net electron density, dominated by $-I$) is separated from "orientation" (governed by which $\sigma$-complex is best stabilised, where $+M$ wins). This single concept generates a steady supply of assertion–reason questions, so be ready to defend both halves independently.

concepts.statement: On a disubstituted benzene, **the strongest activator controls the orientation**; if two groups direct to the same position it is favoured, if they conflict the activating group wins; and positions between two meta-related substituents (crowded) are strongly disfavoured sterically. Bulky substituents or electrophiles bias toward para over ortho.
concepts.detail: For example, in $p$-nitrotoluene further substitution is steered by $-\text{CH}_3$ (the activator) to positions 2 and 6 (ortho to methyl, meta to nitro — the directors *agree*), whereas in $m$-dinitrobenzene the only sites both groups will tolerate are 2/4/6... in practice a third nitration is extremely hard. Steric rule of thumb: electrophiles the size of $\text{SO}_3$ (sulphonation) or $text{-tert-butyl}$ (FC with isobutylene) show heavy para preference. Also recall that sulphonation is *reversible*, so $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$ occasionally serves as a temporary blocking group to force para selectivity — a favourite Advanced synthesis trick.

concepts.statement: Because the first substituent installed directs the second, **the target isomer fixes the sequence**: to place two groups meta, install the meta-directing relationship by putting the *director-last* logic in reverse — introduce the group that becomes the meta director first (or create it by transformation, e.g. oxidising $-\text{CH}_3$ to $-\text{COOH}$). To place them ortho/para, install the o/p director first.
concepts.detail: Worked logic: (a) $p$-bromonitrobenzene requires bromination *then* nitration (Br directs nitro para); nitration *then* bromination would give the meta isomer. (b) $m$-nitrobenzoic acid requires benzoic acid *before* nitration — reached from toluene by oxidation, since $-\text{COOH}$ is a meta director; nitrating toluene first and then oxidising instead yields the para isomer. Remember the constraints: Friedel–Crafts reactions fail on strongly deactivated rings (nitrobenzene, benzoic acid) and on rings bearing $-\text{NH}_2$ (Lewis-acid complexation) — a wrong route can be impossible, not just clumsy.

examples.title: Three nitrations, three verdicts
examples.problem: Predict the product(s) and comment on conditions for the nitration of (a) phenol, (b) nitrobenzene, (c) toluene.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: (a) Phenol: $-\text{OH}$ is the strongest simple activating o/p director — its lone pair delocalises into the ring, stabilising the arenium ion at ortho/para. With *dilute* $\text{HNO}_3$ at room temperature phenol gives a mixture of o-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol (separable by steam distillation: the ortho isomer is steam-volatile thanks to intramolecular H-bonding, the para isomer is not).

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: With concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ phenol over-nitrates to 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid) — the ring is so activated that all three activated positions (2, 4, 6 — every position ortho or para to $\text{OH}$) are exhausted. Mild conditions are not a stylistic choice; they are the only way to stop at mononitration.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (b) Nitrobenzene: $-\text{NO}_2$ is a powerful deactivating meta director; for ortho/para attack the $\sigma$-complex would place positive charge adjacent to the positively-polarised nitro nitrogen — intolerable. Meta attack avoids that structure, so with conc. $\text{HNO}_3$/conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and heat ($\sim$ 370 K) the product is $m$-dinitrobenzene, in low yield and slowly.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: (c) Toluene: $-\text{CH}_3$ activates by hyperconjugation and directs o/p; nitration at ordinary temperature gives a mixture of o-nitrotoluene and p-nitrotoluene (para usually the larger fraction because the methyl group crowds the ortho positions) with negligible meta.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Rate comparison for the same electrophile: phenol $\gg$ toluene $>$ benzene $>$ nitrobenzene — matched exactly by the conditions each needs (dilute/room-temperature for the first, heated fuming acids for the last). Orientation and activation are two readings of the same $\sigma$-complex energetics.

examples.result: (a) o- + p-nitrophenol with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$; picric acid with excess; (b) $m$-dinitrobenzene under forcing conditions; (c) o- + p-nitrotoluene, para major.

examples.title: Two isomers, one starting material: order of operations
examples.problem: Starting from benzene, devise syntheses of (i) $m$-nitrobenzoic acid and (ii) $p$-nitrobenzoic acid, and explain why the orders cannot be swapped.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: (i) Meta target $\Rightarrow$ nitration must occur on a ring already bearing the meta director. Route: benzene $\xrightarrow{\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}/\text{AlCl}_3}$ toluene $\xrightarrow{\text{hot KMnO}_4}$ benzoic acid $\xrightarrow{\text{conc. HNO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4}$ $m$-nitrobenzoic acid. The $-\text{COOH}$ group (formed by oxidising methyl) withdraws by $-M$ and directs the nitro to position 3.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: (ii) Para target $\Rightarrow$ nitration must occur while the ring still carries the o/p director. Route: benzene $\to$ toluene (FC alkylation) $\xrightarrow{\text{HNO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4}$ mixture of o- and p-nitrotoluene (isolate the para isomer) $\xrightarrow{\text{hot KMnO}_4}$ $p$-nitrobenzoic acid — the oxidation is untouched by the nitro group and converts the director after it has done its job.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Why (i) cannot run as nitrate-then-oxidise: nitrating toluene first gives o/p isomers (the $-\text{CH}_3$ director), and oxidising those delivers the *para* (or ortho) nitro acid — the wrong isomer for target (i). The meta relationship can only be created by nitrating last.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Why the "obvious" alternative — nitrate benzene first, then attach the carbon chain — fails twice over: nitrobenzene is too deactivated for Friedel–Crafts alkylation (the arenium ion cannot form on a ring carrying $-\text{NO}_2$), and benzoic-acid derivatives also poison the $\text{AlCl}_3$ catalyst.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: General principle extracted: the isomer you want *is* a sequencing instruction. Transforming a group in place ($-\text{CH}_3 \to -\text{COOH}$) flips it from o/p director to meta director — a "director switch" that unlocks isomers otherwise unreachable in two steps.

examples.result: (i) FC methylation $\to$ oxidation $\to$ nitration gives the meta isomer; (ii) FC methylation $\to$ nitration (para) $\to$ oxidation gives the para isomer; the orders are not interchangeable.

keyTakeaways: Donors ($-\text{OH}$, $-\text{NH}_2$, $-\text{OR}$, alkyl) activate and direct o/p; withdrawers ($-\text{NO}_2$, carbonyls, $-\text{CN}$, $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$) deactivate and direct meta — both follow from which $\sigma$-complex resonance forms are stabilised or wrecked.
Halogens are the exception that proves the rule: net deactivating ($-I$) yet o/p-directing ($+M$) — keep rate and orientation arguments separate.
The strongest activator rules disubstituted rings, and sterics push bulky electrophiles/para sites; positions between two substituents are disfavoured.
Synthesis is sequencing: create the directing relationship first (or switch a group in place, like $-\text{CH}_3 \to -\text{COOH}$), and remember FC fails on deactivated rings.

quiz.q: Which of the following substituents is deactivating yet directs incoming electrophiles to the ortho and para positions?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Separate the two properties: net rate effect (activation) and orientation. Step 2: $-\text{Cl}$ has a strong $-I$ (deactivates: chlorobenzene nitrates ~30 times slower than benzene) but its lone pairs delocalise into the ring ($+M$), stabilising exactly the ortho/para $\sigma$-complexes. Step 3: $-\text{NO}_2$ deactivates and directs meta; $-\text{OH}$ and $-\text{CH}_3$ activate and direct o/p. Step 4: Thus $-\text{Cl}$ (and F, Br, I) are the unique deactivating-o/p class.

quiz.q: The major product of mononitration of anisole (methoxybenzene) is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: $-\text{OCH}_3$ is a strong $+M$ donor and therefore an activating o/p director. Step 2: The electrophile therefore lands at positions 2 and 4; the para site wins statistically and sterically (the methoxy group crowds both ortho positions), so $p$-nitroanisole dominates with some $o$-nitroanisole. Step 3: Meta product is not formed in significant amount because meta attack forfeits the resonance stabilisation the methoxy lone pair offers the o/p $\sigma$-complex. Step 4: Trinitration needs excess nitrating agent and far harsher treatment; demethylation is not part of aromatic nitration.

quiz.q: Which group directs electrophilic substitution to the meta position?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Meta directors are resonance or strong inductive withdrawers — carbonyl-attached groups top the list. Step 2: $-\text{COCH}_3$ withdraws by $-M$ (the carbonyl oxygen pulls electron density through the C=O), so ortho/para $\sigma$-complexes place positive charge beside the electron sink and meta attack is favoured. Step 3: $-\text{CH}_3$ (hyperconjugation), $-\text{OH}$ and $-\text{NHCOCH}_3$ (lone-pair donors) are all o/p directors — acetamido is merely a *weaker* activator than $-\text{NH}_2$ because the nitrogen lone pair is shared with its own carbonyl. Step 4: Acetanilide nitration consequently gives $p$-nitroacetanilide, not the meta product.

quiz.q: Benzoic acid is nitrated with conc. $\text{HNO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. The major product is
options: benzoic acid does not undergo nitration
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The $-\text{COOH}$ group withdraws electron density by $-M$ (and $-I$), deactivating the ring and directing meta. Step 2: For ortho/para attack, a resonance form of the $\sigma$-complex puts the cation on the carbon adjacent to the carboxyl — strongly destabilised; meta attack never generates that form. Step 3: The electrophile therefore enters position 3, giving $m$-nitrobenzoic acid as the dominant product, though slowly and with heating. Step 4: "No reaction" is wrong — deactivated rings still substitute under forcing conditions; only Friedel–Crafts reactions are effectively forbidden on them.

prerequisites: Derivatives of standard functions and the chain rule (math-a12-s1, math-a12-s2)
Continuity on closed intervals (math-a11-s2)
Monotonicity from the sign of the first derivative (math-a12-s5)
intro: Differentiation answers local questions; the mean value theorems convert it into global statements about a whole interval. Rolle's theorem promises a flat tangent somewhere between two equal heights, Lagrange's mean value theorem (LMVT) promises a tangent parallel to the end-point chord, and both — though pure existence results — become sharp tools: they count roots, prove inequalities like $\frac{x}{1+x} < \ln(1+x) < x$, and police the extrema of functions whose derivative vanishes for reasons you must interrogate. advanced engineering assessment rarely asks "state the theorem"; it asks you to *use* it three steps into a problem.
objectives: State Rolle's theorem and LMVT precisely, check their hypotheses on a given function, and find the guaranteed point(s) $c$ explicitly
Use Rolle's theorem to bound the number of real roots of an equation via roots of the derivative
Convert LMVT into inequalities by bounding $f'$ on an interval, and apply it to $\ln$, $e^x$, trigonometric and power functions
Audit functions for global extrema: critical points, endpoints and points of non-differentiability, with the second-derivative test as a fallible shortcut

concepts.statement: If $f$ is **continuous on $[a, b]$**, **differentiable on $(a, b)$**, and $f(a) = f(b)$, then there exists at least one $c \in (a, b)$ with $$f'(c) = 0.$$ Geometrically: between two equal heights the graph has a horizontal tangent.
concepts.detail: The hypotheses are *sufficient*, not necessary — $f(x) = x^3$ on $[-1, 1]$ has $f(-1) \ne f(1)$ yet still a flat tangent at 0. The assessment standard is the converse probe: on $f(x) = |x|$ over $[-1, 1]$, continuity and equal endpoint values hold, but differentiability fails at 0 — and indeed no horizontal tangent exists, so each hypothesis earns its place. Typical task: verify all three conditions, then solve $f'(x) = 0$ and confirm the roots land inside the *open* interval.

concepts.statement: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, there exists $c \in (a, b)$ such that $$f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}.$$ Equivalently $f(b) = f(a) + (b-a)f'(c)$: somewhere the tangent is parallel to the chord joining the endpoints.
concepts.detail: Rolle is the special case $f(a) = f(b)$ (chord slope zero). LMVT is the tool for *estimates*: if $m \le f'(x) \le M$ throughout $(a, b)$, then $m(b-a) \le f(b) - f(a) \le M(b-a)$. It also grounds monotonicity: $f' > 0$ on an interval makes every chord slope positive, so $f$ is strictly increasing. advanced engineering assessment numericals hide $c$ inside nastier algebra (roots like $c = \sqrt{ab}$ from applying LMVT to $\ln x$ or $\sqrt{x}$), so practise the pattern $f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ solved for $c$.

concepts.statement: Between any two distinct real roots of a differentiable function lies a root of its derivative. Consequently, if $f'$ has **no** real root in an interval, $f$ has **at most one** root there; if $f'$ has at most $k$ roots, $f$ has at most $k + 1$ roots.
concepts.detail: Contrapositive thinking: to show an equation has at most one solution, exhibit a derivative that never vanishes (monotone function). To show it has *at least* one, use the intermediate value property of continuous functions on a sign change — the two arguments together pin the count exactly. Classic instance: $e^x = x + 1$ — since $f'(x) = e^x - 1$ vanishes only at $x = 0$ and $f(0) = 0$ is already the global minimum (as $f$ decreases then increases), the root is unique.

concepts.statement: Apply LMVT to a well-chosen $f$ on $[a, b]$ and squeeze the unknown $c$: for $x > 0$, $$\frac{x}{1+x} < \ln(1+x) < x,$$ from LMVT on $f(t) = \ln(1+t)$ over $[0, x]$, where $\ln(1+x) = \frac{x}{1+c}$ with $0 < c < x$.
concepts.detail: Because $\frac{1}{1+x} < \frac{1}{1+c} < 1$ for $0 < c < x$, the single LMVT identity spawns both bounds. The same template on $f(t) = \sqrt{t}$ over $[x, x+1]$ gives $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+1}} < \sqrt{x+1} - \sqrt{x} < \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$, and on $f(t) = \sin t$ it gives $|\sin a - \sin b| \le |a - b|$. Recognise the signature: any inequality comparing a function increment with a product of an interval length and a derivative bound is an LMVT production.

concepts.statement: A continuous function on a closed interval attains its global max and min, and they occur only at (i) interior points with $f' = 0$, (ii) interior points where $f'$ fails to exist, or (iii) the endpoints. The **second-derivative test** ($f'' > 0$: local min, $f'' < 0$: local max) is a shortcut that fails when $f'' = 0$.
concepts.detail: Three landmines: $f'(c) = 0$ does not imply an extremum ($x^3$ at 0); extrema can sit at non-differentiable points ($|x|$ at 0); and $f''(c) = 0$ is inconclusive ($x^4$ has a minimum at 0, $-x^4$ a maximum, $x^3$ neither) — fall back on the sign change of $f'$. For closed-interval problems, *always* tabulate endpoint values alongside critical values; advanced engineering assessment's "greatest value of $f(x) = x^3 - 12x + 5$ on $[0, 3]$" style questions are decided by the endpoints more often than students expect.

examples.title: Verifying Rolle's theorem and catching both points
examples.problem: Verify the hypotheses of Rolle's theorem for $f(x) = x^3 - 4x$ on $[-2, 2]$, find every $c$ whose existence it guarantees, and interpret the answer on the graph.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Hypotheses: $f$ is a polynomial, so it is continuous on $[-2, 2]$ and differentiable on $(-2, 2)$; and $f(-2) = -8 + 8 = 0 = f(2) = 8 - 8$. All three conditions hold, so at least one $c$ exists.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Solve $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \approx \pm 1.155$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Both candidates lie strictly inside $(-2, 2)$, so Rolle's theorem actually delivers *two* points: $c = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $c = +\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ — the theorem guarantees "at least one", and here the count is two.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Graph reading: the curve runs from $(-2, 0)$ up to a local max at $(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, f(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}))$, down through the origin to a local min at $(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, f(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}))$, and back up to $(2, 0)$ — the chord from $(-2,0)$ to $(2,0)$ is horizontal, and both horizontal tangents are parallel to it.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Root-count cross-check: $f$ has roots $-2, 0, 2$ — three roots — and indeed $f'$ has (at least) $3 - 1 = 2$ roots, exactly the pair we found. Rolle's root-counting corollary is the same statement read backwards.

examples.result: Rolle applies (polynomial continuity/differentiability, $f(-2) = f(2) = 0$); $c = \pm\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$, the two local-extremum points where the tangent is horizontal.

examples.title: Proving $\frac{x}{1+x} < \ln(1+x) < x$ with LMVT
examples.problem: Using Lagrange's mean value theorem, prove that for every $x > 0$, $$\frac{x}{1+x} < \ln(1+x) < x,$$ and deduce the behaviour of $\ln(1+x)$ relative to $x$ as $x \to 0^+$.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Choose $f(t) = \ln(1+t)$ on $[0, x]$ with $x > 0$: it is continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on the open one, with $f'(t) = \frac{1}{1+t}$ — LMVT applies.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: LMVT gives some $c \in (0, x)$ with $\frac{f(x) - f(0)}{x - 0} = f'(c)$, i.e. $\ln(1+x) = \frac{x}{1+c}$, since $f(0) = \ln 1 = 0$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Squeeze the hidden $c$: from $0 < c < x$ we get $1 < 1 + c < 1 + x$, hence $\frac{1}{1+x} < \frac{1}{1+c} < 1$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Multiply through by $x > 0$: $\frac{x}{1+x} < \frac{x}{1+c} < x$, and the middle term *is* $\ln(1+x)$ — the inequality is proved. (For $-1 < x < 0$ the same run with reversed signs yields the same displayed inequality.)

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Deduction: as $x \to 0^+$ both bounds $\to 0$, so $\ln(1+x) \to 0$ and $\ln(1+x) \sim x$ — the first-order approximation that also explains $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\ln(1+x)}{x} = 1$ without l'Hôpital. The identical template on $\tan^{-1}t$ gives $\frac{x}{1+x^2} < \tan^{-1}x < x$ for $x > 0$.

examples.result: LMVT on $[0, x]$ converts $\ln(1+x)$ into $\frac{x}{1+c}$ with $0 < c < x$; squeezing $c$ yields $\frac{x}{1+x} < \ln(1+x) < x$ for all $x > 0$.

keyTakeaways: Rolle needs all three hypotheses — continuity on $[a,b]$, differentiability on $(a,b)$, $f(a) = f(b)$; LMVT drops only the last.
Both are existence results, but solving $f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ pins $c$ down explicitly — always check it lies in the open interval.
Root counting: roots of $f'$ interleave roots of $f$; a derivative with no roots means at most one root, and IVP + sign change supplies existence.
LMVT on $\ln(1+t)$, $\sqrt{t}$, $\sin t$, $\tan^{-1}t$ manufactures the standard inequalities — recognise "increment vs derivative $\times$ interval" as its signature.

quiz.q: Rolle's theorem is *not* applicable to $f(x) = |x|$ on $[-1, 1]$ because
options: $f$ is not differentiable at $x = 0$, an interior point
the function has no zero in $(-1, 1)$
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Check the hypotheses in order: $|x|$ is continuous everywhere, so continuity holds. Step 2: $f(-1) = 1 = f(1)$, so the equal-endpoints condition also holds. Step 3: But $\frac{|x| - 0}{x}$ has left limit $-1$ and right limit $+1$ at $x = 0$: $f$ is not differentiable at the interior point 0 — the failing hypothesis. Step 4: Consistently, no horizontal tangent exists on $(-1,1)$, showing the hypothesis cannot be dropped. (The "no zero" option misreads Rolle — it requires equal endpoint values, not zeros.)

quiz.q: The number of values of $c \in (0, 2)$ guaranteed... : for $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2x$ on $[0, 2]$, Rolle's theorem delivers how many points $c$ with $f'(c) = 0$?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: $f$ is a polynomial and $f(0) = 0$, $f(2) = 8 - 12 + 4 = 0$: Rolle applies. Step 2: $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x + 2 = 0$ gives $x = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 24}}{6} = 1 \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$. Step 3: Numerically $x \approx 0.42$ and $x \approx 1.58$, and both lie in $(0, 2)$. Step 4: So the theorem's "at least one" is realised as exactly two points — matching the root count $f(x) = x(x-1)(x-2)$ with three roots guaranteeing at least two critical points.

quiz.q: For $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ on $[1, 4]$, the value of $c$ satisfying LMVT is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: $\sqrt{x}$ is continuous on $[1,4]$ and differentiable on $(1,4)$, so LMVT applies. Step 2: Chord slope: $\frac{f(4) - f(1)}{4 - 1} = \frac{2 - 1}{3} = \frac{1}{3}$. Step 3: $f'(c) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{c}} = \frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow \sqrt{c} = \frac{3}{2} \Rightarrow c = \frac{9}{4}$. Step 4: Check $1 < \frac{9}{4} < 4$ $\checkmark$ — the point where the tangent slope equals the chord slope sits at $x = 2.25$, not at the midpoint, because $\sqrt{x}$ flattens as $x$ grows.

quiz.q: The number of real roots of the equation $e^x = x + 1$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Define $f(x) = e^x - x - 1$; we need its zeros. Step 2: Existence: $f(0) = 1 - 0 - 1 = 0$, so $x = 0$ is a root. Step 3: Uniqueness via monotonicity: $f'(x) = e^x - 1$, which is negative for $x < 0$, zero at $x = 0$ and positive for $x > 0$ — so $f$ strictly decreases up to $x = 0$ and strictly increases after it. Step 4: Hence $f(0) = 0$ is the global minimum and the graph touches the axis exactly once: one real root. Alternatively, by Rolle: two roots would force a root of $f'$ strictly between them; $f'$ vanishes only at 0, where $f = 0$ — so a second root is impossible.

prerequisites: Indefinite integration by substitution, partial fractions and by parts (math-a13-s2, math-a13-s3)
Definite integrals as limits of Riemann sums (math-a13-s4)
Even, odd and periodic functions (math-a1-s5) and the limit $\lim_{x\to0^+} x\ln x$
intro: The fundamental theorem turns integration from an infinite summation into antiderivative bookkeeping — but the properties of the *definite* integral are where advanced engineering assessment actually lives. The king property $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(a+b-x)\,dx$ alone cracks integrals that no antiderivative table touches; even–odd and periodic symmetries turn $[-a, a]$ and $[0, nT]$ into half- or $n$-fold copies; and the Leibniz rule differentiates integrals whose limits are functions. Add the limit-of-sums reading and the same theory evaluates things like $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n!}{n^n}\right)^{1/n}$ in four lines.
objectives: Apply the king property and its add-both trick to evaluate symmetric integrals such as $\int_0^\pi \frac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx$
Exploit even/odd symmetry and periodicity to shrink integration domains before computing anything
Differentiate integrals with variable (or functional) limits via the Leibniz rule $\frac{d}{dx}\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}f(t)\,dt = f(v)v' - f(u)u'$
Recognise Riemann sums — especially $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}f\left(\frac{r}{n}\right) \to \int_0^1f(x)\,dx$ — and use them to evaluate sequence limits

concepts.statement: By definition $\int_a^b f = -\int_b^a f$, and integration is additive over adjacent intervals: $\int_a^b f + \int_b^c f = \int_a^c f$. Combined with linearity, $\int_a^b(\alpha f + \beta g) = \alpha\int_a^bf + \beta\int_a^bg$.
concepts.detail: These bookkeeping rules look trivial but power the "split at the awkward point" strategy: integrate $|x|$ or $\{x\}$ (fractional part) by splitting where the formula changes, and handle piecewise-defined integrands interval by interval. A signed area below the axis counts negative — so $\int_0^{2\pi}\sin x\,dx = 0$ even though the "area" is 4; only $\int|f|$ gives unsigned area. Most Advanced "find the area" traps are really sign-discipline traps.

concepts.statement: For any integrable $f$ on $[a, b]$, $$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(a + b - x)\,dx.$$ Adding the two forms gives the working tool: $$2I = \int_a^b\left[f(x) + f(a+b-x)\right]dx,$$ which is decisive whenever the sum simplifies.
concepts.detail: The substitution $x \mapsto a + b - x$ reverses the direction of travel, leaving the integral's value untouched. On $[0, \pi]$ it converts $\sin x \to \sin x$, $\cos x \to -\cos x$, $\tan x \to -\tan x$; on $[0, \pi/2]$ the partner $\frac{\pi}{2} - x$ swaps $\sin \leftrightarrow \cos$. The classic strikes when the integrand pairs an $x$ (odd under the swap) with a symmetric factor: $\int_0^\pi x f(\sin x)\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2}\int_0^\pi f(\sin x)\,dx$. Also the fraction trick: $\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\sqrt{\tan x}+\sqrt{\cot x}}dx$ pairs with its mirror to sum to 1, forcing $I = \pi/4$ without any antidifferentiation.

concepts.statement: For even $f$: $\int_{-a}^{a}f = 2\int_0^{a}f$; for odd $f$: $\int_{-a}^{a}f = 0$. For $f$ with period $T$: $\int_0^{nT}f = n\int_0^{T}f$ for any positive integer $n$, and more generally $\int_a^{a+T}f = \int_0^{T}f$ for *any* $a$.
concepts.detail: Odd cancellation is the fastest zero in the business — spot it before integrating anything on a symmetric interval: $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}x^3\cos^2x\,dx = 0$ on sight. The period rule explains why $\int_0^{4\pi}|\sin x|\,dx = 4\int_0^{\pi}|\sin x|\,dx$ — wait, $|\sin x|$ has period $\pi$, so it equals $4 \times 2 = 8$. Note $\sin x$ itself has period $2\pi$ but $|\sin x|$ only $\pi$: always integrate the *smallest* period before multiplying. Mixed integrands should be decomposed into symmetric parts first, since $f(x) = \frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2} + \frac{f(x)-f(-x)}{2}$ splits any function into even + odd.

concepts.statement: Fundamental theorem: if $f$ is continuous and $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt$, then $F'(x) = f(x)$. Leibniz extension: for differentiable limits, $$\frac{d}{dx}\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}f(t)\,dt = f(v(x))\,v'(x) - f(u(x))\,u'(x).$$
concepts.detail: Read it as "top limit contributes plus, bottom limit contributes minus". When the dummy variable itself depends on $x$ (e.g. $\int_0^{x^2}\cos(t^2)\,dt$ — no, that one is fine; but $\int_0^{x}\frac{f(t)}{...}$... in general $\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}g(x, t)\,dt$), first substitute to freeze the inner $x$, or split $\int_0^{x^2} = \int_0^{\text{const}} + \int_{\text{const}}^{x^2}$. The theorem's existential power: $F(x) = \int_0^x\frac{\sin t}{t}dt$ *is* a perfectly good function even though no elementary antiderivative exists — questions exploit exactly this by asking about $F'$ or $F''$ instead of $F$.

concepts.term: Definite integrals as limits of sums
concepts.statement: The defining limit survives as a computational tool: $$\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}f\!\left(\frac{r}{n}\right), \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{b-a}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}f\!\left(a + \frac{r(b-a)}{n}\right).$$
concepts.detail: Recognition drill: any limit of the form $\lim\sum \frac{1}{n}f(\frac{r}{n})$ with the number of terms growing like $n$ is a disguised $\int_0^1$. The flagship example takes logarithms first — $\left(\frac{n!}{n^n}\right)^{1/n}$ becomes $\exp\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum\ln\frac{r}{n}\right] \to \exp\int_0^1\ln x\,dx = e^{-1}$ — turning an intractable product into an improper integral evaluated by a one-limiter integration by parts. Similarly $\lim\frac{1^p + 2^p + \cdots + n^p}{n^{p+1}} = \int_0^1x^p\,dx = \frac{1}{p+1}$.

examples.title: The king property on $\int_0^\pi \frac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx$
examples.problem: Evaluate $$I = \int_0^{\pi}\frac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx.$$

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Apply the king substitution $x \to \pi - x$: $\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$ and $\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x$, so $$I = \int_0^{\pi}\frac{(\pi - x)\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx.$$

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Add the two expressions for $I$: $$2I = \int_0^{\pi}\frac{x\sin x + (\pi - x)\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx = \pi\int_0^{\pi}\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx.$$ The lone $x$ has cancelled — the entire point of the manoeuvre.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Substitute $t = \cos x$, $dt = -\sin x\,dx$: as $x$ runs $0 \to \pi$, $t$ runs $1 \to -1$, so $$\int_0^{\pi}\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx = \int_{1}^{-1}\frac{-dt}{1+t^2} = \int_{-1}^{1}\frac{dt}{1+t^2}.$$

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: The integrand $\frac{1}{1+t^2}$ is even, so the integral is $2\int_0^1\frac{dt}{1+t^2} = 2[\tan^{-1}t]_0^1 = 2\cdot\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2}$.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Therefore $2I = \pi\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi^2}{2}$, giving $I = \frac{\pi^2}{4} \approx 2.47$. Sanity check: the integrand is positive on $(0, \pi)$ (both $x$ and $\sin x$ are), and a value between $0$ and $\pi \times \frac{\pi}{4} \approx 2.47$-ish bounds is plausible.

examples.title: A sequence limit as a Riemann sum: $\left(\frac{n!}{n^n}\right)^{1/n}$
examples.problem: Evaluate $$L = \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n!}{n^n}\right)^{1/n}.$$

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Take logarithms to convert the product into a sum: write $A_n = \left(\frac{n!}{n^n}\right)^{1/n} = \left(\frac{1}{n}\cdot\frac{2}{n}\cdots\frac{n}{n}\right)^{1/n}$, so $$\ln A_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\ln\frac{r}{n}.$$

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Recognise the Riemann signature: $\frac{1}{n}$ times a sum of $f\left(\frac{r}{n}\right)$ with $n$ terms, where $f(x) = \ln x$ on $(0, 1]$. Hence $\lim\ln A_n = \int_0^1\ln x\,dx$ — an improper integral, since $\ln x \to -\infty$ at 0.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Evaluate: $\int_0^1\ln x\,dx = \lim_{a\to0^+}\left[x\ln x - x\right]_a^1 = (0 - 1) - \lim_{a\to0^+}(a\ln a - a) = -1 - 0 = -1$, using $\lim_{a\to0^+}a\ln a = 0$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Exponentiate: $L = e^{\lim\ln A_n} = e^{-1} = \frac{1}{e} \approx 0.368$.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Plausibility: $\frac{n!}{n^n}$ is the probability that a random function from an $n$-set to itself is a permutation... more simply, $\left(\frac{n!}{n^n}\right)^{1/n}$ is the geometric mean of $\frac{1}{n}, \frac{2}{n}, \ldots, \frac{n}{n}$, which should sit well below the arithmetic mean $\frac{n+1}{2n} \to \frac{1}{2}$ — and $0.368 < 0.5$ as expected (AM–GM in the limit).

keyTakeaways: King property $\int_a^bf(x)dx = \int_a^bf(a+b-x)dx$; add both copies to kill odd factors like a lone $x$ — it evaluates integrals no antiderivative can.

Odd on symmetric interval $\Rightarrow$ 0 immediately; even $\Rightarrow$ double the half; periodic $f$ with period $T$: $\int_0^{nT}f = n\int_0^{T}f$ (use the smallest period — $|\sin x|$ has period $\pi$).
Leibniz rule: derivative of $\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}f$ is $f(v)v' - f(u)u'$ — upper limit in, lower limit out, minus sign attached.
$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}f(\frac{r}{n}) \to \int_0^1f$: after taking logs, products like $(n!/n^n)^{1/n}$ collapse to $e^{\int_0^1\ln x\,dx} = 1/e$.

quiz.q: The value of $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\left(x^3 + x\cos x + \sin^4x\right)dx$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Split by symmetry: $x^3$ is odd and $x\cos x$ is (odd)$\times$(even) = odd, so both integrate to 0 over the symmetric interval. Step 2: $\sin^4x$ is even, so the integral equals $2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^4x\,dx$. Step 3: Wallis formula: $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^4x\,dx = \frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{3\pi}{16}$. Step 4: Doubling gives $\frac{3\pi}{8}$. Choosing 0 forgets that only the *odd* parts cancel — the even term survives.

quiz.q: The value of $\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\sqrt{\tan x}+\sqrt{\cot x}}\,dx$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: King substitution $x \to \frac{\pi}{2} - x$ swaps $\tan x \leftrightarrow \cot x$, so the mirror integrand is $\frac{\sqrt{\cot x}}{\sqrt{\tan x}+\sqrt{\cot x}}$. Step 2: Call the original $I$; the substitution proves $I$ also equals the mirror integral, and adding them: $2I = \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sqrt{\tan x}+\sqrt{\cot x}}{\sqrt{\tan x}+\sqrt{\cot x}}dx = \int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Step 3: Hence $I = \frac{\pi}{4}$ — no antiderivative was ever needed. Step 4: This "fraction pairs to 1" pattern works for any $\frac{g(x)}{g(x)+g(a+b-x)}$ over $[a, b]$.

quiz.q: If $F(x) = \int_0^{x^2}\frac{dt}{1+t^3}$, then $F'(1) =$
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The upper limit is a function of $x$, so apply the Leibniz rule: $F'(x) = f(v(x))\cdot v'(x) - f(0)\cdot 0$ with $f(t) = \frac{1}{1+t^3}$ and $v(x) = x^2$. Step 2: $F'(x) = \frac{1}{1+(x^2)^3}\cdot 2x = \frac{2x}{1+x^6}$. Step 3: At $x = 1$: $F'(1) = \frac{2}{1+1} = 1$. Step 4: The common error $\frac{1}{2}$ comes from evaluating $f(1) = \frac{1}{2}$ and forgetting the factor $v'(1) = 2$ from the chain rule on the limit.

quiz.q: The value of $\int_0^{4\pi}|\sin x|\,dx$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: $|\sin x|$ is periodic with period $\pi$ (not $2\pi$ — the absolute value folds the negative lobes up). Step 2: The interval $[0, 4\pi]$ contains exactly 4 periods... $\frac{4\pi}{\pi} = 4$ periods, so the integral is $4\int_0^{\pi}|\sin x|\,dx$. Step 3: On $[0, \pi]$, $\sin x \ge 0$, so $|\sin x| = \sin x$ and the integral is $[-\cos x]_0^{\pi} = 2$. Step 4: Total $= 4 \times 2 = 8$. Choosing 0 treats the *unsigned* integrand like $\sin x$ itself, whose signed integral over full periods vanishes.

prerequisites: Vector and Cartesian equations of straight lines in space (math-a10-s2)
Dot and cross products of vectors (math-a15-s2)
Scalar triple product and coplanarity (math-a15-s3)
intro: Two lines in a plane either meet or run parallel; in space they can do neither — they can be **skew**, passing each other on non-intersecting, non-parallel tracks like two flight paths at different altitudes. For skew lines the natural question is "how close do they get?", and the answer is beautiful: the shortest segment is perpendicular to both lines, its direction is the cross product of the two direction vectors, and its length comes from one scalar triple product. advanced engineering assessment wraps this in three-step problems — test coplanarity, compute the distance, and (hardest) find the line of shortest distance itself.
objectives: Classify a pair of lines in space as intersecting, parallel, coincident or skew, using $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2$ and the scalar triple product

Compute the shortest distance between skew lines, $d = \frac{|(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2)|}{|\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2)|}$, and between parallel lines, $d = \frac{|(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\times\vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}$
Find the point of intersection of two coplanar non-parallel lines by solving parametric equations and *verifying* the third coordinate
Construct the equation of the line of shortest distance between two skew lines using the cross-product direction

concepts.statement: Two lines in space are **skew** if they are neither parallel nor intersecting — equivalently, no single plane contains both. Direction vectors of skew lines are not parallel ($\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 \ne \vec{0}$), yet the lines never meet.
concepts.detail: The definitive test is two-stage: first, if $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \vec{0}$ the lines are parallel (distinct or coincident — decide by checking a point of one against the other); second, for non-parallel lines compute the scalar triple product $(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2)$: zero means coplanar, and coplanar non-parallel lines must intersect; nonzero means skew. Train lines on opposite sides of a river and adjacent edges of a tetrahedron (e.g. $AB$ and $CD$) are the canonical physical pictures of skew.

concepts.statement: For skew lines $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2$, the shortest distance is $$d = \frac{\left|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2)\right|}{\left|\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2\right|}.$$ The minimising segment is perpendicular to both lines and points along $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2$.
concepts.detail: Why it works: the joining vector $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1$ can be resolved along the common normal $\hat{n} = \frac{\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2}{|\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2|}$ and perpendicular to it; the components perpendicular to $\hat{n}$ can be absorbed by sliding along the two lines (changing $\lambda, \mu$), so the *unremovable* separation is exactly the projection $(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot\hat{n}$ — the formula. The numerator is the volume of the parallelepiped on the three vectors; the denominator is the area of its base; the quotient is its height, which is precisely the gap between the two "floor planes" containing the lines.

concepts.statement: For parallel lines with common direction $\vec{b}$, the shortest distance is $$d = \frac{\left|(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\times\vec{b}\right|}{\left|\vec{b}\right|},$$ the height of the parallelogram built on the joining vector and the direction.
concepts.detail: This is *not* the skew formula degenerated — the skew formula dies here because $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2 = \vec{0}$ zeroes the denominator. Instead project: the distance is the component of $\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1$ perpendicular to $\vec{b}$, which the cross product extracts after dividing by $|\vec{b}|$. Advanced papers deliberately mix a parallel pair among skew pairs; applying the triple-product formula to the parallel pair is a guaranteed zero. (Coincident lines: the same formula yields $d = 0$ automatically.)

concepts.statement: Two lines are coplanar **iff** $$(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2) = 0,$$ i.e. the determinant $$\begin{vmatrix} x_2-x_1 & y_2-y_1 & z_2-z_1 \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2\end{vmatrix} = 0$$ vanishes. Coplanar + non-parallel $\Rightarrow$ intersecting; coplanar + parallel $\Rightarrow$ parallel or coincident.
concepts.detail: The practical recipe for the intersection point: parametrise both lines, equate the $x$ and $y$ coordinates, solve for the two parameters, then *verify the $z$ coordinate* — consistency means intersection; contradiction means the lines are skew despite the first two equations having a "solution". This verification step is where most marks are lost, because equating two coordinates always produces parameter values; only the third decides whether the points coincide. The Cartesian determinant is the same triple product in components — pick whichever form the data makes cheaper.

concepts.statement: Between two skew lines there is a **unique common perpendicular**; it meets each line at one foot, has direction $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2$, and its length is the shortest distance. Its equation can be built as the line through one foot with direction $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2$.
concepts.detail: To find the feet: let them be $\vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2$ and impose perpendicularity to both directions: $(\vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2 - \vec{a}_1 - \lambda\vec{b}_1)\cdot\vec{b}_1 = 0$ and $(\cdot)\cdot\vec{b}_2 = 0$ — two linear equations in $\lambda, \mu$. A slicker route passes through the plane family: the SD line is the intersection of plane $\Pi_1$ (containing line 1, parallel to $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2$) with plane $\Pi_2$ (containing line 2, parallel to $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2$), each built from a scalar triple product condition. This "common perpendicular as line of intersection of two planes" is the version advanced engineering assessment asks when it wants more than a distance.

examples.title: Shortest distance between two skew lines
examples.problem: Find the shortest distance between the lines $$L_1:\ \vec{r} = (\hat{i} + \hat{j}) + \lambda(2\hat{j} + \hat{k}), \qquad L_2:\ \vec{r} = (2\hat{j} - \hat{k}) + \mu(\hat{i} + \hat{k}).$$

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Extract the data: $\vec{a}_1 = (1, 1, 0)$, $\vec{b}_1 = (0, 2, 1)$; $\vec{a}_2 = (0, 2, -1)$, $\vec{b}_2 = (1, 0, 1)$. First, $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2 = (2\cdot1 - 1\cdot0,\ 1\cdot1 - 0\cdot1,\ 0\cdot0 - 2\cdot1) = (2, 1, -2) \ne \vec{0}$, so the lines are not parallel.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Scalar triple product: $(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2) = (-1)(2) + (1)(1) + (-1)(-2) = -2 + 1 + 2 = 1 \ne 0$ — the lines are skew (non-coplanar), so the distance formula applies.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Magnitude of the cross product: $|\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$. Hence $$d = \frac{|1|}{3} = \frac{1}{3}.$$

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Interpretation: the common perpendicular has direction ratios $(2, 1, -2)$ and length $\frac{1}{3}$; had the triple product come out 0, the lines would have been coplanar (intersecting, since not parallel) and the "shortest distance" would simply be 0.

examples.result: The lines are skew with shortest distance $d = \frac{1}{3}$ unit, along direction $(2, 1, -2)$.

examples.title: Coplanarity test and the intersection point — the third-coordinate check
examples.problem: Show that the lines $L_1:\ \frac{x}{1} = \frac{y}{1} = \frac{z}{1}$ and $L_2:\ \frac{x-1}{1} = \frac{y-2}{2} = \frac{z-3}{3}$ are coplanar, and find their point of intersection.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Data: $\vec{a}_1 = (0,0,0)$, $\vec{b}_1 = (1,1,1)$; $\vec{a}_2 = (1,2,3)$, $\vec{b}_2 = (1,2,3)$. Cross product: $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2 = (1\cdot3 - 1\cdot2,\ 1\cdot1 - 1\cdot3,\ 1\cdot2 - 1\cdot1) = (1, -2, 1) \ne \vec{0}$: not parallel.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Coplanarity: $(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2) = (1,2,3)\cdot(1,-2,1) = 1 - 4 + 3 = 0$. The lines are coplanar, and being non-parallel they intersect.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Parametrise: $L_1$: $(x,y,z) = (\lambda,\lambda,\lambda)$; $L_2$: $(x,y,z) = (1+\mu,\ 2+2\mu,\ 3+3\mu)$. Equate the first two coordinates: $\lambda = 1 + \mu$ and $\lambda = 2 + 2\mu$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Solve: subtracting gives $0 = 1 + \mu$, so $\mu = -1$ and then $\lambda = 0$. Both parameters found — now the mandatory check on the third coordinate: $\lambda = 3 + 3\mu = 3 - 3 = 0$ $\checkmark$ — consistent, so the lines genuinely meet.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Intersection point: with $\lambda = 0$, $L_1$ gives $(x, y, z) = (0, 0, 0)$; on $L_2$, $\mu = -1$ gives $(1-1, 2-2, 3-3) = (0,0,0)$ $\checkmark$. The two "solutions" agree — the lines pass through the origin. If step 4 had failed, the parameters from the first two coordinates would have been a mirage and the lines skew.

examples.result: The lines are coplanar (triple product $1 - 4 + 3 = 0$) and intersect at the origin $(0, 0, 0)$.

keyTakeaways: Two-stage classification: $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2 = \vec{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ parallel; otherwise the triple product $(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2)$ decides — zero: coplanar (hence intersecting); nonzero: skew.

Skew distance: $d = \frac{|(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2)|}{|\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2|}$ — numerator = parallelepiped volume, denominator = base area, quotient = height between the lines.
Parallel lines need the *other* formula $d = \frac{|(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\times\vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}$ — the skew formula divides by zero there.
When hunting an intersection, equate two coordinates, solve, then verify the third: agreement $\Rightarrow$ intersection point; disagreement $\Rightarrow$ skew (the classic trap).

quiz.q: The direction ratios of the line of shortest distance between two lines with direction vectors $\vec{b}_1 = (1, 0, -1)$ and $\vec{b}_2 = (0, 1, -1)$ are
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The common perpendicular is directed along $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2$. Step 2: Compute $(1,0,-1)\times(0,1,-1) = (0\cdot(-1) - (-1)\cdot1,\ (-1)\cdot0 - 1\cdot(-1),\ 1\cdot1 - 0\cdot0) = (1, 1, 1)$. Step 3: Hence the shortest-distance segment has direction ratios $(1, 1, 1)$ — equivalently direction cosines $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1,1,1)$. Step 4: The other options are sign flips of the same vector — but as *ratios* only exact proportionality counts, and $(1,-1,1)$ is not proportional to $(1,1,1)$.

quiz.q: The shortest distance between the line through $(0,0,0)$ with direction $(1,2,2)$ and the line through $(1,2,3)$ with direction $(2,4,4)$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The directions are proportional ($(2,4,4) = 2(1,2,2)$), so the lines are parallel — the skew formula is unusable and the cross-product-with-single-direction formula applies. Step 2: Joining vector $\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1 = (1,2,3)$. Step 3: $(1,2,3)\times(1,2,2) = (2\cdot2 - 3\cdot2,\ 3\cdot1 - 1\cdot2,\ 1\cdot2 - 2\cdot1) = (-2, 1, 0)$, with magnitude $\sqrt{4+1} = \sqrt5$. Step 4: Distance $= \frac{\sqrt5}{|(1,2,2)|} = \frac{\sqrt5}{3}$.

quiz.q: The lines $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2$ (with $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2 \ne \vec{0}$) are coplanar if and only if
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Coplanar means the joining vector lies in the plane spanned by the two directions — i.e. the three vectors $\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1, \vec{b}_1, \vec{b}_2$ are linearly dependent. Step 2: Linear dependence of three vectors is exactly the vanishing of their scalar triple product. Step 3: Hence the condition $(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2) = 0$; a nonzero value measures (up to the base area) the perpendicular gap between the two lines — i.e. skewness. Step 4: $\vec{b}_1\cdot\vec{b}_2 = 0$ merely says the lines are perpendicular in direction, which is compatible with being skew.

quiz.q: If $(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2) = 0$ and $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2 \ne \vec{0}$, then the two lines
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Vanishing triple product means the joining vector and both directions are coplanar — the two lines lie in one plane. Step 2: The added condition $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2 \ne \vec{0}$ means the directions are not parallel. Step 3: Two non-parallel coplanar lines must cross exactly once: unique intersection point. Step 4: Parallel lines would need $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2 = \vec{0}$ (excluded), skew lines would need a nonzero triple product (excluded), and coincidence is a special case of parallelism.

prerequisites: Combining like terms and the distributive property
Order of operations with integers and fractions
intro: Algebra is the biggest slice of the Math assessment — about 35% of all 44 questions — and one-variable linear equations are where it starts. Every item here rewards fluency: solve fast, solve accurately, and know instantly when an equation has no solution or infinitely many. The built-in Desmos calculator can do much of the arithmetic, but reading equation structure is what the test is really buying.
objectives: Solve multistep linear equations fluently, including ones with parentheses, fractions, and variables on both sides
Create a linear equation from a word context and interpret its solution in that context
Recognize when a linear equation has no solution or infinitely many solutions by comparing structure
Choose strategically among algebra, Desmos graphing, and plugging in answer choices

concepts.statement: A **solution** of an equation is a value of the variable that makes the statement true: substituting $x = 3$ into $2x + 1 = 7$ gives $7 = 7$.
concepts.detail: the assessment items test the definition itself: "If $x = 4$ is a solution of $3x + k = 14$, what is $k$?" — substitute and solve ($k = 2$). Substitution is also the fastest error check on student-produced response items, where no answer choices exist to lean on.

concepts.statement: Move in this order: **distribute, collect like terms, isolate the variable** with inverse operations, keeping both sides balanced — $2(x - 3) + 4 = 10$ becomes $2x - 6 + 4 = 10$, then $2x = 12$, then $x = 6$.
concepts.detail: Fractions clear instantly when you multiply every term by the common denominator: $\frac{x}{3} + \frac{x}{4} = 7$ becomes $4x + 3x = 84$ after multiplying by $12$, so $x = 12$. In Desmos you can instead graph $y = \frac{x}{3} + \frac{x}{4}$ with $y = 7$ and read the intersection.

concepts.statement: If the variable terms cancel and leave a **false number statement**, the equation has **no solution**: $3(x + 2) = 3x + 5$ reduces to $6 = 5$.
concepts.detail: Distribute first to see it: $3x + 6 = 3x + 5$ gives $6 = 5$, never true. For "which equation has no solution" stems, compare the $x$-coefficients — equal coefficients with unequal constants means no solution. Graphing both sides in Desmos shows two parallel lines that never meet.

concepts.statement: If everything cancels to a **true statement** such as $4 = 4$, every value of $x$ works: the equation is an **identity**, like $2(x + 3) = 2x + 6$.
concepts.detail: The parameter version is a the assessment staple: "For what value of $k$ does $kx + 12 = 3x + 2k + 6$ have infinitely many solutions?" Match the $x$-coefficients ($k = 3$) and the constants ($12 = 2k + 6$, so $k = 3$); the two conditions agree, so $k = 3$.

concepts.statement: Before grinding algebra, scan the format: **graph both sides in Desmos** for a solve-item, or **plug the answer choices** back in — test whether a candidate $x = 4$ balances $3x + 2 = 14$ before doing any algebra.
concepts.detail: Student-produced response ("grid-in") items leave you no choices, so algebra or Desmos must finish them. Practicing all three routes — algebra, graphing, back-solving — across separate sessions is deliberate distributed practice: it keeps each method fast instead of over-fitting to one.

examples.title: A tank fills (student-produced response style)
examples.problem: A storage tank already contains 200 gallons of water. Water is pumped in at a constant rate of 15 gallons per minute. How many minutes does it take for the tank to hold 725 gallons?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
m = minutes ; amount = 200 + 15m ; set equal to 725
```
Let $m$ be minutes pumped. The tank holds the initial amount plus rate times time: $200 + 15m = 725$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Subtract 200 from both sides to isolate the variable term: $15m = 525$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Check in context: $200 + 15(35) = 200 + 525 = 725$ gallons. The answer $35$ is a clean grid-in value.

examples.result: $m = 35$ minutes.

examples.title: Designing an identity
examples.problem: For what value of $k$ does the equation $kx + 12 = 3x + 2k + 6$ have infinitely many solutions?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
collect: (k - 3)x = 2k - 6 ; identity => both sides zero
```
Gather $x$-terms on the left and constants on the right: $kx - 3x = 2k + 6 - 12$, that is $(k - 3)x = 2k - 6$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: For every $x$ to satisfy the equation, the $x$-coefficient must be zero: $k - 3 = 0$, so $k = 3$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: The constant side must then also vanish: $2k - 6 = 0$ gives $k = 3$ — consistent, not conflicting.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: With $k = 3$ the equation reads $3x + 12 = 3x + 12$, true for every real $x$.

keyTakeaways: A solution makes the equation true — substitution is the universal check and often the fastest route on parameter items.
Clear fractions by multiplying through by the common denominator, distribute carefully, and keep both sides balanced.
Cancel and compare structure: false number statement means no solution; true number statement means infinitely many.
Rotate methods — algebra, Desmos graphing, back-solving — in distributed practice so each stays sharp for the format the item demands.

quiz.q: Which of the following equations has no solution?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Expand each left side. Step 2: Choice A gives $2x + 10 = 2x + 10$ — an identity with infinitely many solutions. Step 3: Choice B gives $2x + 10 = 2x + 5$, which reduces to $10 = 5$, a false statement, so no value of $x$ works. Step 4: Choices C and D each reduce to $x = 0$, a single solution.

quiz.q: A phone plan costs $\$35$ per month plus $\$0.10$ per minute of talk time. One month's bill is $\$52.50$. How many minutes were used?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Model the bill: $35 + 0.10m = 52.50$. Step 2: Subtract the fixed fee: $0.10m = 17.50$. Step 3: Divide by $0.10$: $m = 175$. Step 4: Check: $35 + 17.50 = 52.50$. The trap $525$ comes from dividing the whole bill by $0.10$ and forgetting the fee.

quiz.q: How many solutions does $3(x - 4) + 2x = 5x - 12$ have?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Distribute: $3x - 12 + 2x = 5x - 12$. Step 2: Combine like terms: $5x - 12 = 5x - 12$. Step 3: The two sides are identical, so every $x$ satisfies the equation. Step 4: That is the signature of infinitely many solutions.

quiz.q: If $7 - 2(x + 1) = 4x + 9$, what is the value of $x$?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Distribute the negative carefully: $7 - 2x - 2 = 4x + 9$. Step 2: Simplify the left side: $5 - 2x = 4x + 9$. Step 3: Collect: $-4 = 6x$, so $x = -\frac{2}{3}$. Step 4: The answer $\frac{2}{3}$ is the sign slip from dropping the negative when dividing.

prerequisites: Solving one-variable linear equations (Section 1.1)
Plotting ordered pairs in the $xy$-plane
intro: Two-variable linear equations are the assessment's bridge between algebra and graphs. You will compute slope, read intercepts, spot parallel and perpendicular pairs, and translate a real relationship — cost, distance, temperature — into $Ax + By = C$ or $y = mx + b$. Desmos makes every one of these visual, and the fastest test-takers graph first and compute second.
objectives: Switch between standard form $Ax + By = C$ and slope-intercept form $y = mx + b$
Compute and interpret slope and $x$- and $y$-intercepts from two points, a table, or a graph
Use slopes to identify parallel and perpendicular lines
Model a linear relationship in context and evaluate it

concepts.statement: **Standard form** is $Ax + By = C$; solving for $y$ exposes the slope-intercept view with slope $-\frac{A}{B}$ and $y$-intercept $\frac{C}{B}$.
concepts.detail: A favorite the assessment stem hands you $6x + 3y = 12$ and asks for the slope — rearrange to $y = -2x + 4$ instead of misreading the coefficients. Questions like "what is $y$ when $x = 2$?" need no rearranging at all: substitute directly into the standard form.

concepts.statement: The **slope** between points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ is $m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ — change in output over change in input.
concepts.detail: Consistency is everything: subtract in the same order top and bottom. The classic slope trap flips one order, turning the true $m = \frac{7 - 3}{2 - 9} = -\frac{4}{7}$ into the false $+\frac{4}{7}$. In context, slope is a rate with units — dollars per hour, miles per gallon — and the assessment answer choices include the inverted unit rate as bait.

concepts.statement: The **$y$-intercept** is where $x = 0$ — the starting amount in context; the **$x$-intercept** is where $y = 0$ — when the quantity reaches zero.
concepts.detail: Compute the $x$-intercept of $y = \frac{3}{4}x - 9$ by solving $0 = \frac{3}{4}x - 9$, which gives $x = 12$. Graph-style stories hide these: "at what time did the tank empty?" is an $x$-intercept question wearing a narrative.

concepts.statement: **Parallel** lines share slope: $m_1 = m_2$. **Perpendicular** lines have slopes multiplying to $-1$: $m_1 m_2 = -1$, so flip the fraction and change the sign.
concepts.detail: Perpendicular to $y = \frac{2}{3}x + 5$ needs slope $-\frac{3}{2}$, not $-\frac{2}{3}$. Horizontal lines ($m = 0$) and vertical lines ($x = a$, undefined slope) are perpendicular to each other — an the assessment favorite in disguise.

concepts.statement: Translate stories directly into $y = mx + b$: **$m$ is the per-unit rate, $b$ is the fixed starting value** — then evaluate or extrapolate with the model.
concepts.detail: Two data points determine a linear model. In Desmos, enter the points in a table and type $y_1 \sim m x_1 + b$ to fit the line instantly — a smart on-screen check of paper-and-pencil work.

examples.title: Pricing a print job
examples.problem: A copy shop charges a one-time setup fee plus a per-page rate. An order of 30 pages costs $\$9.50$, and an order of 70 pages costs $\$17.50$. What is the total cost of a 120-page order?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
points (30, 9.50) and (70, 17.50) ; slope = per-page rate
```
Treat the orders as points on a line with $x$ = pages and $y$ = dollars: $(30, 9.50)$ and $(70, 17.50)$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Slope is the per-page rate: $m = \frac{17.50 - 9.50}{70 - 30} = \frac{8}{40} = 0.20$ dollars per page.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Use one point to find the setup fee: $9.50 = 0.20(30) + b$, so $b = 3.50$. The model is $y = 0.20x + 3.50$.
