Summaries must be accurate, complete, proportional.
If a choice needs an unstated assumption, eliminate it.

quiz.q: A main-idea choice that covers only the first paragraph is wrong because it is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The main idea must govern the WHOLE text. Step 2: First-paragraph-only choices are the too-narrow flank. Step 3: Grammar and register are not at issue here. Step 4: Scope is the criterion being tested.

quiz.q: A detail choice that states something true in reality but never mentioned in the passage must be
options: kept if it matches the topic
quiz.explanation: Step 1: the assessment reading is a closed-book, closed-universe exercise. Step 2: The passage is the only admissible evidence. Step 3: Real-world truth without textual support fails the "according to the text" standard. Step 4: Eliminate without regret.

quiz.q: The fastest reliable way to find a passage’s central idea is usually to
options: weigh the first and last sentences plus repeated concepts
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Authors open with the thesis or close with the takeaway. Step 2: Repeated concepts mark sustained emphasis. Step 3: Paragraph count and sentence length are structural noise. Step 4: First + last + repetition triangulates the spine efficiently.

quiz.q: In summary items, giving a minor example the prominence of the thesis makes an answer wrong by failing
quiz.explanation: Step 1: A summary must mirror the passage’s weight distribution. Step 2: Inflating an aside distorts the text’s shape even if every word is accurate. Step 3: That is a proportion failure, distinct from factual inaccuracy. Step 4: Correct summaries respect the author’s emphasis ratios.

prerequisites: Central-idea reading (section 2.1)
Basic chart, table and line-graph literacy
intro: The digital the assessment quietly handed R&W students a lab instrument: informational graphics. **Command of Evidence** comes in two flavours — textual (which quotation or finding best supports a conclusion?) and quantitative (which table cell, bar or trend supports the claim — or completes the table consistently?). Both are about the marriage of claims and their proof.
objectives: Test each answer choice as a mini-premise for the stated conclusion
Read tables and bar graphs for exact values, trends and comparisons
Distinguish results that support a claim from results merely consistent with it
Complete tables so every row follows the stated rule

concepts.statement: For "which finding, if true, would best support the conclusion" items, place each choice as a premise before the conclusion and ask: does the conclusion now FOLLOW more forcefully? Only one choice adds genuine support; the others are unrelated or weakly consistent.
concepts.detail: Support is directional: the finding must make the conclusion MORE LIKELY, not merely coexist with it. Strong support closes an alternative explanation or quantifies the claimed pattern. Distractors typically support a DIFFERENT conclusion the passage also mentions — the borrowed-evidence trap.

concepts.statement: Read the graphic’s title, axes and units FIRST; then answer exactly what the stem asks — a value, a comparison, a trend direction, or a difference — citing specific cells or bars.
concepts.detail: Most quantitative errors are question-misreads: the stem asks for the LARGEST INCREASE and the student picks the LARGEST VALUE. Underline the comparison words in the stem. For line graphs, trend = direction over the labelled interval; for bar charts, watch legend order before declaring "taller means more of what".

concepts.statement: Table-completion items give a rule (each row’s quantities follow a stated relationship) and a partially filled table; the correct completion preserves the rule across every row, not just the visible ones.
concepts.detail: Strategy: express the rule as an arithmetic sentence (e.g., total = restored + lost), compute the missing quantity from any complete row to calibrate, then test each choice against the incomplete row. The wrong choices satisfy the table’s surface pattern while breaking the stated rule — or vice versa.

concepts.statement: A claim is supported only by data that would be DIFFERENT if the claim were false — data that discriminates between the claim and its rivals; data consistent with every rival explanation is not evidence.
concepts.detail: This is the deep logic the assessment tests: a study finding "bees visited both flower types" does not support "bees prefer red flowers" — the finding fits preference for blue too. Look for the asymmetry: the right answer should be surprising under the negation of the claim.

examples.title: Textual evidence selection
examples.problem: Claim to support: "The restoration programme has been effective." Which finding, if true, would most directly support the claim? (A) The river’s history of pollution is long documented (B) Native fish abundance in restored stretches rose 40% while unmanaged stretches stayed flat (C) Volunteers enjoyed participating (D) Restoration programmes are popular worldwide

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Identify the claim’s key term: "effective" — effective at WHAT? Restoration implies ecological recovery.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: The discriminating evidence must show recovery AND attribute it to the programme — a comparison group does exactly that: restored vs unmanaged stretches.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (B) provides a 40% rise with a control comparison; the flat control rules out "the river recovered anyway".

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: (A) is background, (C) testimonial, (D) general praise — all consistent with failure. Answer: (B).

examples.result: (B) — differential recovery with a control directly supports effectiveness.

examples.title: Quantitative support from a graph
examples.problem: A line graph shows Arctic sea-ice extent (million km²) for 1980–2020, declining from ~7.5 to ~4.5 with year-to-year wiggles. Claim: "Sea-ice extent has steadily declined since 1980." Which statement about the graph best supports the claim? (A) The 2012 point is the lowest shown (B) The overall trend slopes downward across the four decades despite annual fluctuations (C) The y-axis begins at zero (D) Sea ice reflects sunlight

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: The claim has two parts: downward direction + persistence ("steadily... since 1980").

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Support must address the TREND across the full interval, absorbing the fluctuations.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (B) states exactly that; (A) is a single-year fact that fits a noisy plateau too; (C) is graph hygiene; (D) is outside science.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Answer: (B) — trend with fluctuation acknowledged.

examples.result: (B) the downward four-decade trend, fluctuations included.

keyTakeaways: Support = makes the conclusion follow; consistency alone is not evidence.
Read title, axes, units first; underline the stem’s comparison words.
Table completions must satisfy the stated rule for every row.
The best evidence discriminates the claim from its rivals (control groups, trends).

quiz.q: A finding that is consistent with a claim whether the claim is true OR false is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Evidence must be asymmetric — expected if the claim holds, surprising if it fails. Step 2: A finding compatible with both outcomes discriminates nothing. Step 3: That is precisely weak/no support. Step 4: Counterexamples point the OTHER way, against the claim.

quiz.q: The stem asks which city had the largest INCREASE in ridership. You should look for
options: the difference between the two years for each city
the city with the largest population
quiz.explanation: Step 1: "Increase" is a change quantity, not a level. Step 2: Compute year-2 minus year-1 per city. Step 3: The tallest bar may belong to a city that was already high and flat. Step 4: Question-word discipline prevents the classic value/change swap.

quiz.q: In a textual-evidence item, a quotation that supports a DIFFERENT claim made in the passage is
options: irrelevant to the task and automatically ungrammatical
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The stem names one specific conclusion. Step 2: Evidence for another conclusion, however accurately quoted, misses the target. Step 3: This is the borrowed-evidence trap, the most popular wrong-answer design in this skill. Step 4: Accuracy of quotation is necessary, never sufficient.

quiz.q: For a table-completion item, the safest procedure is to
options: express the stated rule arithmetically and test each choice against it
pick the row with the fewest blanks
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The item defines a rule binding the columns. Step 2: Translate it into an equation (e.g., total = a + b). Step 3: Only the choice satisfying the equation for the incomplete row (and consistent with complete rows) survives. Step 4: Esthetics like round numbers are noise.

prerequisites: Central-idea and evidence skills (2.1, 2.2)
Conditional logic: if A then B, contrapositive reasoning
intro: "Which choice most logically completes the text?" — the **Inferences** stem. You are handed an argument with the last step missing and must supply the ONLY conclusion the evidence licenses. Not the most interesting conclusion, not the one you believe: the one that must follow if the passage is true.
objectives: Treat the passage as a set of premises; derive what must follow
Keep inference scope inside the passage’s qualifiers ("most", "in this region")
Eliminate choices that add new information or overgeneralise
Apply contrapositive logic to conditional statements

concepts.statement: An inference is correct when it MUST be true given the passage — the strongest statement supported without adding any assumption; the assessment rewards logical necessity, not creativity.
concepts.detail: Think of each passage as two or three premises with a slot after them. The correct answer is the least controversial sentence that could occupy the slot. If you can say "well, not necessarily" about a choice, it is out — that phrase is your elimination trigger.

concepts.statement: Words like "most", "typically", "in this sample", "between 1850 and 1870" shrink claims; a correct inference respects every qualifier, while an overgeneralising choice quietly drops them.
concepts.detail: "Most respondents preferred tea" licenses "more than half of respondents preferred tea" — nothing about the population, nothing about coffee haters. Watch for choices that upgrade "most" to "all", stretch "this sample" to "the species", or extend a time window. The expansion may be millimetres — but millimetres decide answers.

concepts.statement: From "if P then Q" you may validly infer "if not-Q then not-P"; you may NOT infer "if Q then P" (converse) or "if not-P then not-Q" (inverse) — the assessment builds distractors from exactly these two fallacies.
concepts.detail: Passage: "If a manuscript used the iron-gall ink, it predates 1600." Correct inference: a manuscript dated 1700 did not use iron-gall ink. Wrong: a pre-1600 manuscript used iron-gall (converse — other inks existed); wrong: post-1600 manuscripts never used iron gall elsewhere (inverse + scope stretch).

concepts.statement: When premises carry numbers, correct inferences respect interval logic: "more than 30" excludes exactly 30; "at least half" includes exactly half; combined premises bound, never pinpoint, unless arithmetic forces it.
concepts.detail: Classic the assessment pattern: "The archive holds 2,400 letters; more than half were catalogued before 1990; exactly 1,100 are from artists." From these: at least 1,201 catalogued early, so at most 1,199 late; letters from non-artists = 1,300 exactly. Choices offering "exactly 1,250 early" or "most letters are from artists" fail the arithmetic. Translate statements into inequalities on scratch paper.

examples.title: Completing a research argument
examples.problem: Passage: "A theatre troupe’s 1597 ledger lists payments for costumes, scenery and a 'pyrotechnist’ — yet the play performed that season is a quiet domestic comedy. Archivists therefore concluded that the troupe's records include expenditures for a SECOND production whose text is now lost. Therefore, ___" Which completion is best supported? (A) all Elizabethan theatres staged lost plays (B) the troupe staged at least one additional play that season beyond the comedy (C) pyrotechnics were common in domestic comedies (D) the ledger is unreliable

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Premises: fireworks-related staff + scenery costs exist; the known play needs neither; archivists posit a lost second production.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: The licensed conclusion keeps the troupe’s scope and the "at least one" quantity: another production happened.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (A) inflates one troupe to all theatres; (C) contradicts the "quiet comedy" framing; (D) attacks the evidence the argument uses.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Answer: (B) — the minimal necessary conclusion.

examples.result: (B) the troupe mounted at least one more production that season.

examples.title: Numerical inference
examples.problem: Passage: "Of the 400 survey respondents, at least 70% commute by bike at least once a week, and exactly 150 respondents commute ONLY by bike." Which statement must be true? (A) Exactly 280 respondents bike weekly (B) At most 250 respondents sometimes use another mode (C) 150 respondents never bike (D) A majority commute only by bike

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Bike-weekly $\geq 280$ (not exactly — "at least"). Only-bike = 150 exactly.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Sometimes-other = weekly-bikers minus only-bikers $\geq 280 - 150 = 130$; non-weekly-bikers $\leq 120$. Careful: "at most 250 sometimes use another mode" — the 400 total includes non-bikers who use other modes: non-weekly $\leq 120$ plus sometimes-other $\geq 130$ gives other-mode users between 130 and 250. At most 250 is forced by 400 − 150 only-bikers.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (A) upgrades "at least" to "exactly"; (C) non-bikers $\leq 120$, not 150; (D) 150 < half of 400 — a minority, so false.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Answer: (B) — since 150 ride only by bike, at most 250 can involve another mode.

examples.result: (B) at most 250 respondents use any other mode.

keyTakeaways: Correct = must be true, no added assumptions; "not necessarily" eliminates.
Qualifiers carry the answer — never let choices drop or upgrade them.
Contrapositive valid; converse and inverse are the assessment bait.
Translate numeric premises into inequalities before comparing choices.

quiz.q: "If the comet is visible tonight, the sky is clear." Which inference is valid?
options: The sky is clear, so the comet is visible
The sky is not clear, so the comet is not visible tonight
The comet is not visible, so the sky is not clear
The sky is clear, so it will rain
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The premise is "visible → clear". Step 2: Its contrapositive is "not clear → not visible" — valid. Step 3: Choice (A) is the converse fallacy; choice (C) is the inverse fallacy. Step 4: Only the contrapositive preserves truth.

quiz.q: A passage states "most of the gallery’s paintings are landscapes." A choice reading "all of the gallery’s paintings are landscapes" should be
options: chosen if the gallery is small
kept if no other choice fits
quiz.explanation: Step 1: "Most" means more than half, possibly not all. Step 2: "All" claims universality the passage never grants. Step 3: That upgrade is the standard overgeneralisation trap. Step 4: Eliminate — strength beyond the evidence is a fault, not a virtue.

quiz.q: The best mental test for an inference choice is
options: "Must this be true if the passage is true?"
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Inference = logical necessity from premises. Step 2: The necessity test catches every over-reach. Step 3: Interest and popularity are rhetorical, not logical criteria. Step 4: Length correlates with distractor design, not truth.

quiz.q: "Fewer than 12 volunteers attended each session." Which must be true?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: "Fewer than 12 per session" bounds every session below 12. Step 2: So no session reached 12 — the direct restatement. Step 3: Exactly 11 is possible but not forced; decline is a trend claim the data does not make; total volunteers is unconstrained. Step 4: Restatements of bounds are the safest licensed inferences.

prerequisites: Recognising independent versus dependent clauses
The comma, semicolon and period as boundary tools
intro: Sentence boundaries are the traffic rules of Standard English. **Boundaries** items hand you a text with a blank at a clause junction and four options that splice the same clauses together with different punctuation and conjunctions. Your job: identify whether each side is a full sentence, then choose the legal join — and only one is legal.
objectives: Test any clause for independence: subject + finite verb + complete thought
Join independent clauses correctly: comma + FANBOYS, semicolon, or period
Punctuate supplements — nonessential phrases, appositives, interrupters — with comma pairs or dashes
Spot and fix fragments, run-ons, comma splices, and unwanted boundary punctuation

concepts.statement: Cover one side of the junction and read the other alone: if it could stand as a sentence (subject + conjugated verb + complete thought), it is an **independent clause**; if it leans ("because...", "which...", "walking to school"), it is a fragment on its own.
concepts.detail: Everything in Boundaries flows from this test. IC + IC requires a real join (,FANBOYS / ; / .). IC + fragment tolerates no boundary punctuation between them. Run-ons and comma splices are simply the two illegal ways of refusing this rule — the two most tested errors on the assessment.

concepts.statement: Two independent clauses may be joined by a **comma followed by a coordinating conjunction** (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) or by a **semicolon alone**; a comma alone is a splice, nothing is a run-on.
concepts.detail: The semicolon implies close logical connection — a fine stylistic choice the assessment tests directly. Colons may also join ICs when the second explains the first, but only after a complete sentence. Watch for the "comma + conjunctive adverb" trap: "however, therefore, moreover" are NOT FANBOYS — they need a semicolon before them ("...; however, ...").

concepts.statement: Nonessential material — appositives ("my mentor, Dr. Chen,"), participial phrases, and interrupters — must be **bracketed symmetrically**: comma-comma, dash-dash, or parentheses; a single comma of a pair is an error.
concepts.detail: Test essential vs nonessential by deletion: if the sentence survives without the material, cut it out mentally and check the remaining punctuation — pairs must close. Names after proper nouns, "such as" examples, and "which" clauses are usually nonessential; "that" clauses usually essential (no commas).

concepts.statement: A correct boundary answer sometimes adds NOTHING: subject-verb-object needs no comma between subject and verb, no comma before a direct object, and no punctuation splitting verb from its required complement.
concepts.detail: The assessment loves a comma between a long subject and its verb ("The biologist who spent decades in Antarctica, discovered...") — always wrong. Equally beloved: a comma cordoning off a necessary "that" clause. When in doubt, read the sentence aloud: breath needs are not punctuation rules, but friction usually marks a boundary error.

examples.title: Choosing the legal join
examples.problem: Text: "The lighthouse was automated in 1987 ___ the last keeper retired to the village below." Choices: (A) 1987, the (B) 1987; the (C) 1987 the (D) 1987, therefore the

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Test both sides: "The lighthouse was automated in 1987" — independent. "The last keeper retired to the village below" — independent.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: IC + IC demands a real join. (A) comma alone = splice. (C) nothing = run-on. (D) comma + "therefore" = still a splice (however/therefore need a semicolon).

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (B) semicolon: a legal, stylistically apt join for two closely related statements.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Answer: (B).

examples.result: (B) "1987; the" — semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.

examples.title: Appositive punctuation
examples.problem: Text: "The festival honours Ada Lovelace ___ the first programmer ___ whose analytical engine notes anticipated modern computing." Choices for blank 1: (A) Lovelace, the ... (B) Lovelace the ... For blank 2: (C) programmer, whose (D) programmer whose

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: "the first programmer" renames Ada Lovelace — a nonessential appositive needing paired punctuation.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Blank 1 must open the comma: (A). Then "whose..." continues the supplement; the pair must close after "programmer": choose (C) with the closing comma.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Deletion test: "The festival honours Ada Lovelace whose... computing" still works — the supplement is truly nonessential, commas legal.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Combined answer: (A) + (C): "Ada Lovelace, the first programmer, whose..."

examples.result: Paired commas around the appositive: "Ada Lovelace, the first programmer, whose..."

keyTakeaways: Run the independence test on each side of every boundary blank.
IC + IC: comma+FANBOYS, semicolon, or period — never a bare comma or nothing.
Nonessential material gets symmetrical bracketing; one open comma without its partner is an error.
Sometimes the right answer adds no punctuation at all — never punctuate subject-verb or verb-object.

quiz.q: Which is a comma splice?
options: The rain stopped, and we left
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Both clauses are independent. Step 2: A comma alone between ICs is a splice — choice (C). Step 3: (A) has comma + FANBOYS "and" — legal. (B) semicolon — legal. (D) period — legal. Step 4: Spotting the missing conjunction is the whole game.

quiz.q: "However", "therefore" and "moreover" join two independent clauses only when preceded by
quiz.explanation: Step 1: These are conjunctive adverbs, not conjunctions. Step 2: They cannot legally follow a bare comma between ICs. Step 3: The rule: "...; however, ..." or "... . Therefore, ...". Step 4: A comma before "however" mid-splice is the assessment’s most-planted trap.

quiz.q: A long subject must never be separated from its verb by
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Subject and verb form one grammatical unit. Step 2: Length tempts writers to breathe with a comma — Standard English forbids it. Step 3: Semicolons and dashes equally cannot intrude there. Step 4: The correct boundary answer often simply omits punctuation.

quiz.q: Nonessential phrases should be set off with
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Supplements are grammatically removable islands. Step 2: Islands need matching shores: open and close with the same mark. Step 3: A lone comma leaves the sentence structurally open. Step 4: Deletion test first, then check BOTH brackets.

prerequisites: Subject–verb identification under intervening phrases
Pronoun basics: antecedent, case, agreement
intro: The second Conventions skill polishes the inside of sentences: **Form, Structure, and Sense**. The assessment plants agreement, tense, pronoun and modifier traps inside otherwise fluent prose, then asks which choice makes the text conform. Because the errors hide between the subject you see and the verb you reach, the discipline is structural: find the true grammatical core before judging any form.
objectives: Match verbs to true subjects across intervening phrases and indefinite pronouns
Keep tense, mood and voice consistent with the passage’s temporal frame
Resolve pronoun–antecedent agreement and case (I/me, who/whom) errors
Place modifiers beside what they modify and fix possessive/plural/contraction confusions

concepts.statement: To find the true subject, mentally delete every phrase between subject and verb: "The collection of rare stamps (was/were) sold" — cross out "of rare stamps" — the subject is "collection", singular: **was**.
concepts.detail: Intervening plural nouns are the assessment’s favourite camouflage. Also immune to camouflage: indefinite pronouns — each, every, either, neither, anyone, everyone, somebody, nobody — are ALWAYS singular; "none" and "some" match their noun of reference. "Either of the routes is passable." Memorise the singular list cold.

concepts.statement: Verb tense must fit the passage’s time frame and stay consistent unless a genuine time shift occurs; historical commentary uses present tense ("the author argues"), while narrated events follow their own sequence (past perfect for the earlier of two past events).
concepts.detail: The digital the assessment tests tense mainly through consistency and logic: a paragraph in past tense suddenly offering "will" needs cause. Watch perfect forms: "had painted" only when another past event follows as a reference point. Conditional pairs: "If the funding were approved, the dig would proceed" — hypothetical = were + would.

concepts.statement: A pronoun agrees with its antecedent in number (the committee ... it, NOT they) and person; case follows function — subjects take I/we/who, objects take me/us/whom; possessives (its, their) never carry apostrophes.
concepts.detail: Ambiguity is also tested: a pronoun with two possible antecedents is wrong even when agreeable. Case shortcut for compound objects: strip the other person — "gave tickets to (Asha and) me" survives; "to I" collapses. Who/whom: he-answer → who, him-answer → whom ("Who called? He did." / "Whom did you call? ... him.").

concepts.statement: A modifier sits next to what it describes — a dangling or misplaced modifier describes the wrong noun; and the assessment’s lexical traps: its/it’s, their/there/they’re, your/you’re, whose/who’s, fewer (countable) vs less (uncountable), comparative vs superlative.
concepts.detail: Dangling test: the noun after the opening participle must be its doer — "Walking through the museum, the paintings amazed her" fails (paintings don’t walk). Comparative vs superlative: two items → -er/more; three or more → -est/most. "Between the two routes, the shorter one..." — never "shortest" of two. Countability: fewer delays, less traffic.

examples.title: Intervening phrase trap
examples.problem: Text: "The array of sensors ___ the bridge’s vibration in real time." Choices: (A) monitors (B) monitor (C) have monitored (D) are monitoring

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Find the core: "The array ___ the vibration." Cross out "of sensors".

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Subject = "array" (singular), despite the plural noun beside it.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Present-tense context ("in real time") wants (A) monitors; (B) and (D) agree with "sensors" — the camouflage; (C) adds a perfect form nothing in the passage licenses.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Answer: (A) monitors.

examples.result: (A) "The array of sensors monitors..."

examples.title: Pronoun case in a compound
examples.problem: Text: "The director awarded the fellowship to Priya and ___." Choices: (A) I (B) me (C) myself (D) mine

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: The pronoun is the object of "awarded to" — an object slot.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Strip trick: "awarded the fellowship to me" — correct; "to I" collapses.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: "Myself" is reflexive — legal only when subject and object are the same person; "mine" is possessive.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Answer: (B) me.

examples.result: (B) "to Priya and me" — object case throughout.

keyTakeaways: Delete intervening phrases to expose the true subject; each/every/neither/everyone are singular.
Tense must be consistent and logically sequenced; hypotheticals use were + would.
Pronouns: agree with the antecedent, take the right case, and refer unambiguously.
Modifiers hug their nouns; know the confusion pairs and countability rules.

quiz.q: "Neither of the essays ___ the required sources." The correct verb is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: "Neither" is an indefinite pronoun — always singular. Step 2: Cross out "of the essays": the subject is "neither". Step 3: Singular subject needs "cites". Step 4: The plural noun in the phrase is pure camouflage.

quiz.q: Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?
options: Rushing to finish, Maya left her notes on the tram
Rushing to finish, the notes were left on the tram
Maya, rushing to finish, left her notes on the tram
Left on the tram, the notes were reprinted
quiz.explanation: Step 1: An opening participle must describe the subject that follows. Step 2: In (B), the subject is "the notes" — notes cannot rush. Step 3: (A) and (C) put the rusher (Maya) as subject; (D) reassigns logically (notes were left). Step 4: (B) dangles.

quiz.q: Correct: "The data show that the eruption was ___ of the two events."
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Two events are compared. Step 2: Two-item comparisons take the comparative: "the more violent". Step 3: Superlative "most" needs three or more. Step 4: "Violenter" is not a word — data never licenced it.

quiz.q: In "its/it’s careful design", the correct choice for the possessive sense is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Possessive "its" is one of the pronoun family (his, hers, its) that never takes an apostrophe. Step 2: "It’s" is exclusively the contraction of "it is/it has". Step 3: "Its’" does not exist in Standard English. Step 4: Substitution test — "it is careful design" fails, so possessive "its" stands.

prerequisites: Clause relationships: addition, contrast, cause–effect (Boundaries helps here)
Transition vocabulary bank
intro: Transitions are logical hinges: one blank, and the whole sentence must swing the right way. **Transitions** items give two statements and four candidate connectors — "however", "therefore", "in other words", "for example" — and exactly one matches the TRUE relationship between the statements. The discipline: name the relationship before shopping for the word.
objectives: Classify the statement pair’s logical relationship before reading choices
Master the assessment’s transition families: addition, contrast, cause–effect, exemplification, emphasis, sequence, restatement
Detect scope mismatches: contrast words before agreeing statements, additions between opposites
Distinguish near-synonymous transitions by their exact logical contracts

concepts.statement: Cover the choices, read statement 1, read statement 2, and say the relationship aloud in plain words ("same idea continued", "opposite", "consequence", "example of") — only then uncover and match.
concepts.detail: This reverses the fatal habit of plugging choices in one by one and nodding at whatever sounds smooth. Every wrong transition sounds smooth read aloud; only the pre-named relationship discriminates. Two minutes of relationship taxonomy saves the whole item family.

concepts.statement: **Addition** (moreover, furthermore, in addition, also); **contrast** (however, nevertheless, on the contrary, in contrast, still); **cause–effect** (therefore, thus, consequently, as a result, hence); **exemplification** (for example, for instance, specifically); **restatement** (in other words, that is, namely); **sequence** (first, then, finally, subsequently); **emphasis** (indeed, in fact).
concepts.detail: The assessment’s favourite confusions sit INSIDE families: "on the contrary" contradicts a negative statement and substitutes the truth — stronger than "however"’s mere contrast; "for instance" introduces an example while "namely" introduces a specification of something already named. Learn the contracts, not just the vibes.

concepts.statement: "However" signals that statement 2 pushes back on statement 1; "admittedly"/"granted" signal that statement 2 CONCEDES before an implied rebuttal — the assessment tests this directionality by placing the pivot word mid-argument.
concepts.detail: Read the pair with the pivot blanked: "The evidence is voluminous. ___ , it is circumstantial." The second statement LIMITS the first — that is concession-contrast: "However"/"Nevertheless"/"Granted" all fit; "Moreover" (addition) and "Therefore" (consequence) break the logic. Direction is decided by which statement is the point and which is the pressure.

concepts.statement: If statement 2 could begin "for instance" — it instantiates statement 1 (exemplification); if it could begin "as a result" — it follows from statement 1 (cause–effect); mixing these two families is the most common two-way elimination on the test.
concepts.detail: Test by reordering: an example can be swapped for a different instance without breaking the logic; a consequence cannot be swapped at will because it is CAUSED. "The storm damaged the pier. ___ , the ferry route closed." — the closure results from the damage: therefore/consequently. "The museum bans flash. ___ , guards patrol the galleries" — patrol illustrates enforcement: for example.

examples.title: Naming before matching
examples.problem: Text: "The startup’s app reached a million downloads in its first year. ___ , the company struggled to convert users into paying subscribers." Choices: (A) Moreover (B) However (C) For instance (D) In other words

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Name the relationship: downloads boomed — but revenue lagged. Statement 2 pressures statement 1: contrast.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Match: (A) moreover = addition (logic runs same way — no); (C) for instance = example (no instance follows); (D) in other words = restatement (different claim, not a paraphrase).

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (B) however = contrast — the only word honouring the push-back.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Answer: (B) However.

examples.result: (B) "However" — popularity versus monetisation is a contrast.

examples.title: Inside-family discrimination
examples.problem: Text: "Cephalopods edit their own RNA. ___ , an octopus can retune its neurons to temperature changes within hours." Choices: (A) Therefore (B) For example (C) On the contrary (D) Meanwhile

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Relationship: the octopus sentence INSTANTIATES the general claim — exemplification.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Screen: (A) therefore = consequence — the octopus is not caused by the general fact; (C) on the contrary = contradiction — the example agrees; (D) meanwhile = simultaneous contrast — no time conflict exists.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (B) for example: one species illustrating the class claim.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Swap test: a squid example would work equally well — confirming exemplification over consequence. Answer: (B).

examples.result: (B) "For example" — species-level instance of the class claim.

keyTakeaways: Name the relationship BEFORE reading any choice — plug-in-and-nod is the trap.
Know all seven families and their exact contracts.
Contrast pushes back; concession yields before rebutting — direction matters.
Swap test distinguishes example (swappable) from consequence (caused).

quiz.q: Statement 2 restates statement 1 in simpler words. The blank needs
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Restatement is its own family. Step 2: "In other words" (or "that is", "namely") signals a paraphrase. Step 3: However contrasts; for instance exemplifies; consequently concludes. Step 4: Same proposition, new phrasing — restatement only.

quiz.q: "The bridge was reinforced in 2018. ___ , inspectors still flagged corrosion in 2023." The best transition is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Repair happened — yet problems persisted: contrast with concession flavour. Step 2: "Nevertheless" honours the push against expectation. Step 3: "Therefore" makes corrosion a result of reinforcement — absurd; "moreover" runs the same direction; "namely" specifies a name. Step 4: Answer: nevertheless.

quiz.q: A transition choice that is grammatically smooth but reverses the logical direction should be
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Transition items test logic, not music. Step 2: Smoothness is universal among distractors. Step 3: Only the pre-named relationship discriminates. Step 4: Logic-first, always.

quiz.q: Which pair belongs to the SAME logical family?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Families: contrast (however, in contrast), cause–effect (therefore, consequently), exemplification (for example, specifically), addition/sequence (moreover, first). Step 2: (B) pairs two exemplifiers. Step 3: Every other option crosses family lines. Step 4: Answer: for example / specifically.

prerequisites: Sentence-combining practice from Boundaries (3.1)
Concision instinct: spotting redundancy
intro: The final R&W skill is the most practical: you receive a student’s bullet-point notes and a rhetorical goal — "emphasise the contrast", "present the finding and its limitation", "introduce the artist with her signature technique" — and must craft the ONE sentence that uses the right notes, in the right order, with no fluff. It is writing under orders, the assessment’s miniature editorship.
objectives: Parse the rhetorical goal before reading the notes or choices
Select only the note content the goal requires — no more, no less
Order information to serve the goal (emphasis first, context first, or contrast-second)
Cut redundancy and wordiness; prefer the shortest choice that fully achieves the goal

concepts.statement: Read the goal sentence twice ("Which choice most effectively accomplishes the goal of ___?"), underline its requirement verbs, and only then skim the notes — the goal is the rubric against which every choice is graded.
concepts.detail: The goal names the deliverable: to compare, to introduce, to emphasise a contrast, to state a cause. Choices fail by missing the target relationship, including irrelevant notes, or burying the required emphasis. Underlining goal verbs turns a fuzzy writing task into a checklist.

concepts.statement: Every bullet is optional inventory: correct answers deploy exactly the notes the goal needs; distractors smuggle in irrelevant detail or drop a load-bearing fact.
concepts.detail: If the goal is "explain why the dig was delayed", the notes about the site’s discovery year are cargo — attractive, tested, wrong. Conversely, a delay goal answered without the flood note fails completeness. For each choice, audit: which notes does it use? Which does the goal demand? Set equality or elimination.

concepts.statement: English grants end-position and main-clause status the greatest emphasis; goals like "highlight the surprise" are met by putting the surprising content in the main clause (or at the end), not in a subordinate "although..." pocket.
concepts.detail: Compare: "Although the manuscript was unsigned, scholars attribute it to the monastery’s best scribe" (emphasis on attribution) versus "Although scholars attribute it to the monastery’s best scribe, the manuscript is unsigned" (emphasis on anonymity). Same facts, opposite spotlights — the assessment grades the spotlight, not the facts.

concepts.statement: Among choices that achieve the goal, the shortest complete one wins; redundancy patterns include doubled synonyms ("end result", "plan ahead for the future"), restated ideas, and empty openers ("It is a fact that...").
concepts.detail: Concision is not brevity at all costs — a choice that is shorter but drops a goal-required note loses to a longer complete one. The rule: shortest among ADEQUATE options. Common the assessment redundancies: "annual per-year", "past history", "combine together", "basic fundamentals". Also eliminate meta-language ("this essay will discuss...") in favour of direct statement.

examples.title: Synthesis with a contrast goal
examples.problem: Notes: • Rani manufacturers’ guild funded the 1521 bridge • bridge rebuilt in stone in 1589 • wooden original survived only 30 years. Goal: "emphasise how briefly the original bridge served." (A) The Rani manufacturers’ guild funded the bridge, which was rebuilt in stone in 1589. (B) Though the stone bridge dates to 1589, the wooden original served for just three decades. (C) Bridges in the region were often wooden before 1600. (D) The guild funded the 1521 bridge, and builders used wood.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Goal keywords: "briefly", "original". Required notes: wooden original’s short life; stone rebuild as the contrast frame.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: (A) mentions the rebuild but never the brevity — goal miss. (C) is off-notes generalisation. (D) has no dates, no duration, no contrast.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (B) frames stone as the concession and the wooden lifespan as the main point — emphasis exactly where the goal demands.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Concision audit: (B) is also the tightest. Answer: (B).

examples.result: (B) "Though the stone bridge dates to 1589, the wooden original served for just three decades."

examples.title: Redundancy elimination
examples.problem: Goal: "state the finding concisely." Notes: • study observed bees for two summers • bees visited blue flowers 60% more often than red. (A) Over the course of two consecutive summer seasons, researchers observed and witnessed bees visiting blue flowers 60% more often. (B) Bees visited blue flowers 60% more often than red. (C) Blue flowers were visited more often, 60% more, by bees, in the study. (D) The two-summer study found that bees visited blue flowers 60% more often than red flowers.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Goal needs: the finding (60% preference) — the study duration is optional context, not emphasised.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: (A) doubles verbs ("observed and witnessed") and inflates duration — redundant. (C) is tangled and splits the statistic awkwardly. (B) is shortest but drops the red-flower comparison target and any study framing — arguably adequate, but (D) keeps the comparative basis AND stays clean.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Between (B) and (D): "60% more often" needs a "than" — (B) supplies it, but (D) does too, plus attribution. The goal "state the finding" is fully met by (D) with minimal extra weight; (B)’s missing comparison object makes it less precise.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Answer: (D) — complete, attributed, concise.

examples.result: (D) "The two-summer study found that bees visited blue flowers 60% more often than red flowers."

keyTakeaways: Read the goal first; its verbs are the grading rubric.
Audit which notes each choice uses — relevance beats completeness of inventory.
Emphasis lives in main clauses and end position; match it to the goal.
Shortest ADEQUATE choice wins; redundancy patterns are drilled answers.

quiz.q: The first thing to read in a Rhetorical Synthesis item is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The goal defines success for the sentence. Step 2: Reading choices first invites being charmed by fluent but off-target options. Step 3: Notes are inventory; the goal is the order form. Step 4: Goal-first, always.

quiz.q: A choice that uses an irrelevant note from the list should be
options: kept if it is the longest
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Synthesis grades relevance to the goal. Step 2: Every note is optional inventory, not a checklist. Step 3: Irrelevant detail dilutes the requested emphasis. Step 4: Grammar cannot redeem off-goal content.

quiz.q: "The end result was a final completion of the finished project" fails mainly by
quiz.explanation: Step 1: "End result", "final completion", "finished project" each double their noun. Step 2: The sentence says "result" three times. Step 3: That layered restatement is textbook redundancy. Step 4: No boundary or agreement error exists — it is wordiness, not grammar.

quiz.q: To emphasise a surprising fact, place it
options: in a subordinate clause starting with "although"
in the main clause, ideally at the end
at the start of a "because" clause
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Main clauses carry the assertion; end position carries the punch. Step 2: "Although" pockets content as concession — de-emphasis. Step 3: Parentheses signal afterthought. Step 4: "Because" clauses give reasons, not spotlight. Answer: main clause, end position.

prerequisites: Sets and set operations (languages are sets of strings)
Directed graphs (states and transitions form one)
intro: Theory of Computation contributes about 6–8 marks, and the paper reliably opens with finite automata — designing or minimizing a DFA, converting an NFA by subset construction, or reading the language of a regular expression. The items are MCQ/MSQ on language membership and equivalence, and NAT on state counts. This section covers the machine definitions, the constructions, and the closure facts needed to reason about all of them.
objectives: Define DFAs and NFAs formally and trace the acceptance of specific strings
Convert NFAs (with ε-moves) to equivalent DFAs by subset construction, computing ε-closures
Move between regular expressions and automata and read off the language of an expression
Apply closure properties of regular languages and minimize DFAs by merging indistinguishable states

concepts.statement: A **DFA** is $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ with a *total* transition function $\delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q$; $M$ accepts $w$ iff the extended transition $\delta^*(q_0, w) \in F$, and $L(M)$ is the set of accepted strings.
concepts.detail: Totality is part of the definition — a design with missing transitions is an NFA, so incomplete DFAs are completed with a trap (dead) state that loops on everything and is non-accepting. The minimal DFA of a regular language is unique up to state renaming, which is why "how many states must a DFA for L have" has a single right answer.

concepts.statement: An **NFA** maps each (state, symbol) to a *set* of states and accepts $w$ if **some** path on $w$ from $q_0$ ends in $F$; an ε-NFA additionally may follow ε-edges, formalised by the ε-closure.
concepts.detail: NFAs are easier to design but no more powerful: the subset construction converts any NFA to a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states, with up to $2^n$ states — and this blow-up is unavoidable in the worst case. For an ε-NFA, close every subset under ε before and after reading each symbol; when the initial subset is $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(\{q_0\})$, accepting DFA states are those subsets intersecting F.

concepts.statement: **Kleene's theorem**: a language is regular iff some finite automaton accepts it iff some regular expression denotes it; RE → ε-NFA via Thompson gadgets, DFA → RE via state elimination.
concepts.detail: Working identities: $\emptyset + R = R$, $\varepsilon R = R$, $R^* = \varepsilon + RR^*$, and $(a+b)^* = (a^*b^*)^*$. To read a dense expression like $(0+1)^*1(0+1)$, parse the mandatory core: some 1 with exactly one symbol after it — strings whose second symbol from the right is 1.

concepts.statement: Regular languages are closed under **union, concatenation, star, complement, intersection, difference, reversal and homomorphism** — the whole regular-expression/automaton toolbox.
concepts.detail: Complement: flip accepting and non-accepting states of a *complete* DFA — doing this on an NFA is wrong because acceptance there is existential. Intersection: product construction on DFAs, never syntactic intersection of expressions. Not closed under: infinite (countable) unions, subsets, and languages like $\{a^{2^n}\}$ or "strings of prime length" — the standard non-regular exhibits for the pumping lemma in a later section.

concepts.statement: **Delete unreachable states, then merge states no distinguishing string separates**: $p \equiv q$ iff for every $w$, exactly one of $\delta^*(p, w), \delta^*(q, w)$ is in $F$; the resulting minimal DFA is unique (Myhill–Nerode).
concepts.detail: Table-filling algorithm: first mark all (accepting, non-accepting) pairs; repeatedly mark a pair whose successors on some symbol are already marked. A state count worth memorising: the minimal DFA for "binary strings ending with w" has exactly $|w| + 1$ states — 3 for ending in 01, 4 for ending in 011.

concepts.statement: **Count what the machine must remember**: a suffix window of length $k$ forces about $2^k$ states, and "the k-th symbol from the end is 1" needs $2^k$ DFA states though it has an NFA with only $k + 1$ states.
concepts.detail: That $2^k$ versus $k+1$ gap is the canonical proof that subset construction is tight — the graduate assessment asks exactly this. Before drawing, decide the memory contents (e.g., "the parity of 1s seen" = 2 states; "the last two symbols" = 4 states plus a start), then check reachability; unreachable memory states never appear in the minimal machine.

examples.title: Design and prove minimal: strings containing 01
examples.problem: Design a DFA for $L = \{w \in \{0,1\}^* : 01 \text{ is a substring of } w\}$, prove it minimal, and describe its complement language.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
A: no progress yet (start)
B: a 0 was just seen (waiting for 1)
C: 01 has been seen (accepting sink)
```
The machine must remember its progress towards the pattern: A (nothing useful seen), B (last symbol was 0, pattern may complete on a 1), C (pattern seen — accept forever).

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Transitions: $A: 0 \to B, 1 \to A$; $B: 0 \to B, 1 \to C$; $C: 0 \to C, 1 \to C$. The function is total, so this is a genuine DFA.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Minimality by distinguishing strings: ε versus 0 — appending 1 gives "1" (rejected) versus "01" (accepted); 0 versus 01 — appending ε leaves 0 rejected and 01 accepted. So A, B, C are pairwise distinguishable and no 2-state DFA suffices.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Complement: swap accepting and non-accepting states of this complete DFA — the result accepts strings with **no** 01 substring, which is exactly the language $0^*1^*$ (all 0s must precede all 1s).

examples.result: A 3-state DFA (states A, B, C as above, only C accepting) recognises L; it is minimal, and the complement of L is $0^*1^*$.

examples.title: Subset construction: NFA for strings ending in "ab"
examples.problem: An NFA over $\{a, b\}$ has states $q_0$ (start), $q_1$, $q_2$ (sole accepting state) and transitions: on $a$: $q_0 \to \{q_0, q_1\}$; on $b$: $q_0 \to \{q_0\}$ and $q_1 \to \{q_2\}$; $q_2$ has no outgoing transitions. Convert it to an equivalent DFA.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Start state of the DFA is the singleton set $\{q_0\}$ (there are no ε-moves; otherwise we would take $\varepsilon$-closure of $\{q_0\}$). Call it A.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text:
```text
A = {q0}:  a -> {q0,q1} = B     b -> {q0} = A
B = {q0,q1}: a -> {q0,q1} = B   b -> {q0} U {q2} = C
C = {q0,q2}: a -> {q0,q1} = B   b -> {q0} = A
```
Compute transitions subset by subset: from B on b, $q_0$ returns to $\{q_0\}$ while $q_1$ moves to $\{q_2\}$, and the union is $\{q_0, q_2\} = C$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Accepting DFA states are the subsets containing the NFA accepting state $q_2$: only C. All three subsets A, B, C are reachable (A start, B via a, C via ab), so the DFA has exactly 3 states.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: The result is already minimal — the language is "ends with ab", whose minimal DFA needs $|w| + 1 = 3$ states; subset construction happened to produce it directly here (in the worst case it can produce $2^n$ states).

examples.result: DFA: states $A = \{q_0\}$, $B = \{q_0, q_1\}$, $C = \{q_0, q_2\}$; transitions A—a→B, A—b→A, B—a→B, B—b→C, C—a→B, C—b→A; only **C accepts**.

keyTakeaways: A DFA needs a total transition function — complete partial designs with a trap state before claiming DFA-hood.
Subset construction: DFA states are sets of NFA states; worst case $2^n$ states, and this bound is tight.
Complement only by flipping a complete DFA; intersection via the product construction.
Minimal DFA for "ends with w" has $|w| + 1$ states; "k-th symbol from the end is 1" needs $2^k$ states versus $k + 1$ for an NFA.

quiz.q: The minimum number of states in a DFA accepting all binary strings that **end with 011** is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The machine must track its progress through the suffix 011. Step 2: The progress states are: nothing matched, matched 0, matched 01, matched 011 — four states. Step 3: The minimal DFA for "ends with w" has exactly $|w| + 1$ states, and $|011| + 1 = 4$. Step 4: Three states would only track a 2-symbol suffix.

quiz.q: In the worst case, converting an n-state NFA to an equivalent DFA by subset construction can produce
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Each DFA state is a subset of the n NFA states. Step 2: There are at most $2^n$ subsets, and all can be reachable. Step 3: The "k-th symbol from the end is 1" family shows the bound is tight. Step 4: Hence $2^n$ is the correct worst case.

quiz.q: Which statement about regular languages is FALSE?
options: The union of two regular languages is regular
The complement of a regular language is regular
The intersection of two regular languages is regular
Every countable union of regular languages is regular
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Union is closed by the NFA construction or by the + operator on expressions. Step 2: Complement is closed via the complete-DFA state flip. Step 3: Intersection follows from De Morgan on union and complement, or the product construction. Step 4: Countable unions can escape regularity: $\{a\} \cup \{a^2\} \cup \{a^3\} \cup \cdots$ unions up to $a^*$, but e.g. singletons $\{a^{2^n}\}$ union to a non-regular language — closure fails.

quiz.q: The regular expression $(0 + 1)^*1(0 + 1)$ over the alphabet $\{0,1\}$ denotes exactly the set of strings
options: whose second symbol from the right is 1
whose second symbol from the left is 1
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Parse the expression: any prefix, then a mandatory 1, then exactly one more symbol. Step 2: So every accepted string has length ≥ 2 and its second-to-last symbol is forced to be 1. Step 3: The last symbol is free — strings may end in 0, ruling out "end with 1". Step 4: The first symbols are unconstrained by $(0+1)^*$, so nothing is forced at the left.

prerequisites: Fractions, decimals and place value
Prime factorisation of integers
intro: the defence research establishment’s Stage-I screening test packs roughly 20 quantitative-aptitude questions into a 100-mark paper with 0.25 negative marking per slip, so speed on number systems is survival. HCF, LCM, surds and indices look elementary but hide most of the time traps in Section A. This section drills the shortcuts that turn two-minute calculations into twenty-second ones.
objectives: Apply divisibility and remainder rules to shortcut Stage-I computation
Compute HCF and LCM from prime factorisations and decode which one a word problem wants
Simplify, rationalise and compare surds without decimal approximation
Resolve indices quickly, including unit-digit problems via digit cyclicity

concepts.statement: A number $n$ is divisible by 3 or 9 when its **digit sum** is; by 4 or 8 when its last two or three digits are; and by 11 when the alternating digit sum is. Under a fixed modulus, remainders add and multiply: $(a + b) \bmod n$ and $(a \cdot b) \bmod n$ can be computed from $a \bmod n$ and $b \bmod n$ alone.
concepts.detail: This residue arithmetic is the engine behind "find the remainder of $17^{200}$ divided by 9" questions — reduce the base first ($17 \equiv 8 \equiv -1$), then the power. Trap: the rule for 11 needs the alternating sum of digits, not the plain digit sum.

concepts.term: HCF and LCM as prime powers
concepts.statement: The **HCF** takes the lowest power of each common prime; the **LCM** takes the highest power of every prime present. For two numbers $a$ and $b$: $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = a \times b$.
concepts.detail: For fractions: HCF $= \frac{\text{HCF of numerators}}{\text{LCM of denominators}}$ and LCM $= \frac{\text{LCM of numerators}}{\text{HCF of denominators}}$. The product identity holds only for two numbers — with three numbers it fails, which is exactly where the assessment sets its trap.

concepts.term: Decoding HCF and LCM word problems
concepts.statement: "**Greatest number** that divides $a$ and $b$ leaving remainder $r$" is HCF$(a - r,\ b - r)$; "**smallest number** divisible by …" or "ring/beep together again" is the LCM.
concepts.detail: Variant: "greatest number dividing $a$ and $b$ leaving the same remainder" — the answer is HCF$(b - a)$ constrained below $r$ when remainders $r_1 \ne r_2$ but their difference is constant, use HCF$(a - r_1,\ b - r_2)$. When remainders differ, never subtract a fixed number from both without checking the difference logic.

concepts.statement: A **surd** is an irrational root such as $\sqrt{2}$. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate to rationalise: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}} = \frac{\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b}}{a - b}$.
concepts.detail: To compare surd options, raise both sides to a common power (square for square roots, cube for cube roots) instead of estimating decimals. Trap: $\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} \ne \sqrt{a + b}$ and $\sqrt{a}\sqrt{b} = \sqrt{ab}$ is valid only for non-negative reals.

concepts.statement: Index laws give $a^m a^n = a^{m+n}$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ and $a^0 = 1$. Unit digits **cycle**: 2, 3, 7 and 8 repeat every 4 powers; 4 and 9 every 2; 0, 1, 5 and 6 never change.
concepts.detail: For "unit digit of $7^{95}$", reduce the exponent modulo the period: $95 \bmod 4 = 3$, third member of the cycle $7, 9, 3, 1$ gives 3. Shortcut when the exponent is a multiple of the period: use the last member of the cycle, not the first.

examples.title: Greatest number leaving a fixed remainder
examples.problem: Find the greatest number that divides 245 and 1029 leaving remainder 5 in each case.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: A divisor that leaves remainder 5 must divide the differences exactly: $245 - 5 = 240$ and $1029 - 5 = 1024$. So the answer is the **HCF of 240 and 1024**.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Factorise: $240 = 2^4 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ and $1024 = 2^{10}$. The HCF keeps the lowest power of each common prime: $2^4$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: HCF $= 16$. Verify both divisions: $245 = 16 \times 15 + 5$ and $1029 = 16 \times 64 + 5$ — both leave exactly 5, confirming the answer in under thirty seconds.

examples.result: Greatest such number is 16.

examples.title: Bells that ring together (LCM signature)
examples.problem: Telemetry beacons on a defence-research test range beep every 6, 8, 10 and 12 minutes. They beep together at 07:00 hours. When do they next beep together?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: "Together again" is the signature of an **LCM** problem — the common cycle of the four periods.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Factorise: $6 = 2 \cdot 3$, $8 = 2^3$, $10 = 2 \cdot 5$, $12 = 2^2 \cdot 3$. The LCM takes the highest powers: $2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 = 120$ minutes.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: They coincide every 120 minutes $= 2$ hours, so from 07:00 the next joint beep falls at 09:00 hours.

examples.result: 09:00 hours — after LCM = 120 minutes.

keyTakeaways: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers; HCF takes the lowest prime powers, LCM the highest.
"Greatest number that divides … leaving remainder r" is HCF(a − r, b − r); "smallest number divisible by …" is the LCM.
Unit digits cycle: 2, 3, 7, 8 repeat every 4 powers; 4 and 9 every 2; 0, 1, 5, 6 are constant — reduce the exponent modulo the period.
Rationalise surds with the conjugate and compare irrational options by squaring rather than decimal guessing.

quiz.q: The unit digit of $3^{47}$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The cycle of 3 is $3, 9, 7, 1$ with period 4. Step 2: Reduce the exponent: $47 = 4 \times 11 + 3$, so take the 3rd member. Step 3: The unit digit is 7. Step 4: Choosing 9 forgets to discard the completed cycles; choosing 1 uses the 4th member.

quiz.q: The HCF of two numbers is 11 and their LCM is 7700. If one number is 275, the other is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Use the product identity HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers. Step 2: Product $= 11 \times 7700 = 84700$. Step 3: Other number $= 84700 \div 275 = 308$. Step 4: Check: $275 = 25 \times 11$ and $308 = 28 \times 11$, so the HCF is indeed 11.

quiz.q: The smallest number which when divided by 12, 16 and 18 leaves remainder 5 in each case is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Such a number is 5 more than a common multiple of 12, 16, 18, so first find the LCM. Step 2: $12 = 2^2 \cdot 3$, $16 = 2^4$, $18 = 2 \cdot 3^2$, giving LCM $= 2^4 \cdot 3^2 = 144$. Step 3: Answer $= 144 + 5 = 149$. Step 4: The other options are not 5 above any common multiple — 149 alone satisfies all three divisions.

quiz.q: The value of $\frac{\sqrt{5} + \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{5} - \sqrt{3}}$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $\sqrt{5} + \sqrt{3}$. Step 2: The denominator becomes $5 - 3 = 2$. Step 3: The numerator becomes $(\sqrt{5} + \sqrt{3})^2 = 8 + 2\sqrt{15}$, so the value is $\frac{8 + 2\sqrt{15}}{2} = 4 + \sqrt{15}$. Step 4: Picking $4 - \sqrt{15}$ means you squared a difference instead of a sum.

prerequisites: Basic arithmetic operations
English alphabet positions (A = 1 … Z = 26)
intro: Reasoning supplies the second block of about 20 questions in the defence research establishment’s 100-mark Stage-I screening, where a wrong answer costs 0.25 marks and a slow one costs the paper. Analogies, classification and series reward pattern vocabulary more than raw calculation. Scientists at defence-research laboratories read signatures — of signals, materials and code — and this section trains exactly that muscle.
objectives: Name the relation in an A : B :: C : D analogy before scanning options
Isolate the single discriminating attribute in odd-one-out classification
Crack number and letter series with difference, ratio and positional engines
Decide quickly when a guess is worth the 0.25-mark penalty

concepts.statement: An **analogy** A : B :: C : ? is solved by naming the relation between A and B in one phrase — function (knife : cut), degree (warm : hot), part–whole (chapter : book), worker–tool (surgeon : scalpel) — then applying the same phrase to C.
concepts.detail: Trap: options often fit a second-best relation. If A : B is "country : capital", reject options pairing a country with its currency. Order matters too: feather : bird (part : whole) is not bird : feather.

concepts.statement: In **odd-one-out** problems, three options share one structural attribute — divisibility, being a perfect square, taxonomic family — and exactly one breaks it. Find the shared attribute first, not the odd option.
concepts.detail: Test each option against candidate attributes in turn (all prime? all cubes? all vehicles with wheels?). Trap: superficial similarity — four words may all be metals while three are ferrous; the discriminator is chemistry, not metalness.

concepts.statement: Work the ladder: first **differences**, then second differences, then ratio between consecutive terms, then alternating rules, then $n^2 \pm k$ or $n^3 \pm k$ patterns.
concepts.detail: If terms roughly double, jump straight to the multiplicative engine ($a_{n+1} = 2a_n \pm k$). Mixed engines are common: $\times 3, \div 2$ alternating. Always verify the discovered rule on every given term — the last term you check is the one the assessor bent.

concepts.statement: Write letters as positions A = 1 to Z = 26. The anchor word **EJOTY** fixes E = 5, J = 10, O = 15, T = 20, Y = 25; a letter’s mirror position is $27 - n$.
concepts.detail: For skip patterns, convert the letters to positions and inspect the gaps — A, C, F, J, O has gaps 2, 3, 4, 5. Trap: alphabetical direction can reverse mid-series; recompute from positions rather than reciting the alphabet.

concepts.statement: With +1 per correct answer and −0.25 per error, a **blind guess** on 4 options has expectation $\tfrac{1}{4}(1) + \tfrac{3}{4}(-0.25) = +0.0625$ — barely positive — while **eliminating two options** lifts it to $+0.375$.
concepts.detail: So elimination, not bravado, is the strategy: spend the first pass only on questions where one option dies instantly, and bank the remaining time for the series you can actually crack.

examples.title: Series with a doubling-difference engine
examples.problem: Find the next term: 5, 11, 23, 47, 95, ?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
5, 11, 23, 47, 95, ?
diffs:  6, 12, 24, 48
```
First differences are $6, 12, 24, 48$ — doubling each time, so the next difference is $96$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Next term $= 95 + 96 = 191$. Cross-check with the multiplicative reading: each term is twice the previous plus one, and $2 \times 95 + 1 = 191$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Two independent engines agreeing certifies the pattern — do this check before committing when 0.25 negative marking is live.

examples.result: 191 (differences double; equivalently each term = 2 × previous + 1).

examples.title: Classification with a defence flavour
examples.problem: Find the odd one out: Mirage 2000, Sukhoi Su-30MKI, Tejas, BrahMos.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Name the majority class: Mirage 2000, Su-30MKI and Tejas are all **fighter aircraft** flown by the Indian Air Force.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Test BrahMos against that attribute: it is a supersonic cruise missile built by the India–Russia joint venture, not an aircraft.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: The discriminating attribute is airframe versus missile; everything else (defence platform, the defence research establishment association) is shared and therefore useless as a discriminator.

examples.result: BrahMos — a cruise missile among fighter aircraft.

keyTakeaways: Name the analogy relation in one phrase before looking at the options; reject options that fit a different relation.
Odd-one-out turns on a single structural attribute shared by three options — find the attribute, not the stranger.
Series ladder: differences → second differences → ratios → alternating and power patterns; verify on every term.
EJOTY and mirror positions (27 − n) make letter series arithmetic instead of recitation.

quiz.q: Complete the series: 8, 24, 12, 36, 18, ?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The jump 8 → 24 is ×3 and 24 → 12 is ÷2. Step 2: The alternating rule is ×3, ÷2, ×3, ÷2. Step 3: Apply ×3 to 18 to get 54. Step 4: Choosing 27 applies ÷2 instead — the wrong half of the cycle.

quiz.q: Find the odd one out: 27, 64, 125, 218
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Test the perfect-power attribute. Step 2: $27 = 3^3$, $64 = 4^3$, $125 = 5^3$. Step 3: $218 \ne 6^3 = 216$ — it misses the cube by 2, a deliberate near-miss trap. Step 4: Hence 218 is the odd one.

quiz.q: Thermometer : Temperature :: Barometer : ?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Name the relation: instrument : quantity it measures. Step 2: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure. Step 3: Humidity is measured by a hygrometer and wind by an anemometer. Step 4: Rainfall correlates with pressure but is not what the instrument reads.

quiz.q: Complete the letter series: A, C, F, J, O, ?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Convert to positions: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. Step 2: Gaps are 2, 3, 4, 5 — increasing by one each step. Step 3: Next gap is 6, giving position 21. Step 4: Position 21 is U (T = 20, U = 21).

prerequisites: Indian polity and geography basics
Defence organisation overview (the defence research establishment, armed forces, HAL, BARC)
intro: About a fifth of the defence research establishment’s Stage-I screening marks sit in General Awareness — roughly 20 questions scored at +1 with 0.25 negative marking and a strong defence-and-S&T tilt. Current affairs decay faster than any other section, so method matters more than memory dumps. This section shows what to track, for how long before the assessment, and how to answer with elimination when the fact escapes you.
objectives: Scope preparation to the rolling twelve-month window the paper actually samples
Classify every question into one of five event families and recall its fixed question signature
Track defence and space developments (the defence research establishment tests, inductions, exercises, space-agency missions) at assessment depth
Anchor current facts to static GK so each new fact stabilises an old one

concepts.statement: Cover current affairs from **January of the year before the assessment** to the assessment month — roughly a rolling twelve-month band — using one monthly compilation plus a one-page revision sheet per month.
concepts.detail: Older events resurface only when they set a "first" (first indigenous carrier, first National Space Day) or an anniversary. Trap: coaching compilations front-load trivia; the assessment samples names, dates, venues and firsts, not commentary.

concepts.statement: Nearly every current-affairs question belongs to one of **five families** — summits and conferences, appointments, schemes and policies, agreements and MoUs, reports and indices — and each family asks a fixed signature: host venue, officeholder, parent ministry, signatories, or issuer and India’s rank.
concepts.detail: Build a five-column tracker and file one line per event. When a question appears, identify the family first — it tells you which attribute is being asked before you read the options.

concepts.statement: the defence research establishment papers weight **defence and space developments** heavily: missile and system flight-tests, inductions into service, joint exercises and space-agency missions. Record system, agency, date/window and the first-of-its-kind tag.
concepts.detail: Typical items: Agni-Prime and BrahMos extensions flight-tested from the Odisha coast, INS Vikrant commissioned as the first indigenously built aircraft carrier, Tejas Mk1A orders, Malabar with all four Quad navies, Chandrayaan-3’s south-pole landing. Trap: confuse the developer (the defence research establishment versus HAL versus private DPSU) and the question flips.

concepts.statement: Hook every current fact to a **static fact**: summit city → state and river, scheme → ministry and launch year, satellite → orbit type and launch centre.
concepts.detail: One current line then answers two papers’ worth of questions — the current one and a static one. Example: Chandrayaan-3 anchors 23 August, the lunar south pole, Shiv Shakti Point, LVM3 launcher and Sriharikota in a single row of notes.

concepts.statement: Dates and pairings often **self-eliminate** through chronology — a summit host cannot repeat in consecutive years, a scheme’s ministry rarely changes, and option pairs that swap two entities kill each other.
concepts.detail: With +1 / −0.25 marking, eliminating two options makes guessing strongly profitable (+0.375 expectation); eliminating none leaves it marginal. Spend eight seconds on elimination before either guessing or skipping.

examples.title: Summit question via the presidency cycle
examples.problem: The 18th G20 Leaders’ Summit adopting the New Delhi Declaration was hosted in which city, and when?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Classify the family: international summit → recall the presidency cycle. India held the G20 presidency from December 2022 to November 2023, so the leaders’ summit fell in that window.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: The 18th Leaders’ Summit was hosted on 9–10 September 2023 at **Bharat Mandapam**, Pragati Maidan, New Delhi.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Anchor the extras while you are there: the theme was "Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — One Earth, One Family, One Future" and the African Union was admitted as a permanent G20 member at this summit — both reusable facts.

examples.result: New Delhi — 9–10 September 2023, at Bharat Mandapam.

examples.title: Defence item via tag elimination
examples.problem: Which of the following correctly describes Agni-Prime? (A) a submarine-launched cruise missile (B) a canisterised surface-to-surface ballistic missile (C) an anti-tank guided missile (D) an air-to-air missile.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Tag the family: the Agni series are strategic **surface-to-surface ballistic missiles** developed by the defence research establishment — half the options die on family name alone.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Eliminate (A): submarine-launched systems belong to the K-family; eliminate (D): Astra is the defence research establishment’s air-to-air missile; eliminate (C): Nag is the anti-tank guided missile.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Option (B) survives and carries the distinguishing detail: Agni-Prime is canisterised, two-stage and solid-propellant, first flight-tested from the Odisha coast in June 2021.

examples.result: Option (B) — a canisterised surface-to-surface ballistic missile.

keyTakeaways: Prepare a rolling twelve-month window ending at the assessment month; older items matter only as firsts and anniversaries.
Five event families — summits, appointments, schemes, agreements, reports/indices — each with a fixed question signature (venue, person, ministry, signatories, issuer/rank).
Defence and space items carry outsized weight: record system, agency, date and the first-of-its-kind tag.
Anchor current facts to static GK so one row of notes answers both current and static questions.

quiz.q: The 28th UN Climate Change Conference (COP28, 2023) was hosted by
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Family: summit → attribute: host country. Step 2: COP28 ran from 30 November to 13 December 2023 at Expo City, Dubai, UAE. Step 3: Egypt hosted COP27 (2022, Sharm El-Sheikh) and Azerbaijan hosted COP29 (2024, Baku) — classic adjacent-year distractors. Step 4: Hence the UAE is correct.

quiz.q: Chandrayaan-3’s Vikram lander achieved India’s first lunar soft landing on
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Separate launch from landing — 14 July 2023 is the LVM3 launch from Sriharikota. Step 2: Vikram soft-landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023. Step 3: 2 September 2023 is INS Vikrant’s commissioning date, a planted cross-domain trap. Step 4: The date is now commemorated as National Space Day.

quiz.q: INS Vikrant, commissioned in September 2022, is significant because it is
options: India’s first aircraft carrier, acquired from the United Kingdom in 1961
India’s first indigenously designed and built aircraft carrier
a nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine built at Visakhapatnam
a defence-research-built stealth frigate for coastal defence
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Read the qualifier "commissioned in September 2022" — that is the Cochin Shipyard-built carrier. Step 2: Designed by the Navy’s Directorate of Naval Design, it is the first indigenously designed and built Indian aircraft carrier (about 45,000 tonnes). Step 3: The 1961 INS Vikrant of the same name was acquired from the UK — option A confuses the two ships. Step 4: Submarines (Arihant class) and frigates are different programmes entirely.

quiz.q: Exercise Malabar, in its current format, is a naval exercise involving
options: India, the USA, Japan and Australia
India, France, the UAE and the USA
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Malabar began in 1992 as an India–US bilateral exercise. Step 2: Japan became a permanent participant in 2015 and Australia rejoined in 2020. Step 3: It now regularly sails all four Quad navies. Step 4: Options with Russia, Singapore or France mix in exercises those navies actually run with India elsewhere.

prerequisites: Parts of speech
Simple sentence structure (subject, verb, object)
intro: The English section of the defence research establishment’s Stage-I screening carries about 20 of the 100 marks, and grammar questions are its fastest-scoring subset under the 0.25 negative-marking regime. Articles, tenses and agreement are also the foundation for the descriptive Stage-II discipline papers, where marks are lost to imprecise prose. Master the rules here and error-spotting becomes a checklist rather than a gamble.
objectives: Choose a/an/the by the initial sound of the following word
Select tenses from time markers such as since, for, by the time and next week
Make verbs agree with the grammatical head of the subject, ignoring intervening phrases
Apply the proximity rule and collective-noun judgement in error-spotting items

concepts.statement: Use **an** before a vowel sound and **a** before a consonant sound: an hour (silent h), a university (/yu/), an M.Tech (/em/), a one-rupee coin (/wʌn/). Use **the** for second mention, unique objects, superlatives, rivers, mountain ranges, holy books and organisations.
concepts.detail: Trap: spell the word, pay with marks — "an MLA", "a European", "an SOS" all follow the ear. Also compare: "the fewer the mistakes" type fixed phrases keep the in parallel slots.

concepts.statement: **Since** + point of time and **for** + duration demand perfect tenses; a past clause after "by the time" forces past perfect in the main clause; scheduled events take the simple present or "will".
concepts.detail: Never use a future form after when, before, after, as soon as in a time clause: "she will call when she lands", not "when she will land". Trap: "since 2018" pairs with present perfect (continuous), never simple past.

concepts.statement: The verb agrees with the **head** of the subject phrase, not the nearest noun: "the list of items is", "each of the scientists has", "one of the missiles is".
concepts.detail: Each, every, either, neither and many a are singular even when followed by plural nouns. "A number of + plural" takes plural, but "the number of + plural" stays singular — a favourite paired option.

concepts.statement: With **either … or / neither … nor**, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: "neither the soldiers nor their commander was aware". Collectives (team, committee) stay singular when acting as one unit and turn plural only when members act separately.
concepts.detail: Test: "the committee has issued its report" (unit) versus "the committee were divided among themselves" (members). Trap: distance between subject and verb — the assessor inserts long phrases precisely to hide the head.

concepts.statement: A **four-sweep protocol**: (1) underline the subject–verb pair of each clause, (2) check tense consistency against the time markers, (3) check articles and prepositions, (4) prefer the smallest correction among options.
concepts.detail: In part-labelled questions, mentally delete prepositional phrases between subject and verb before judging. Most tested errors are agreement (C position), tense (B/C position) or article (A position) — sweep in that order.

examples.title: Spotting the intervening-phrase trap
examples.problem: Spot the error: "Each of the scientists (A) working on the seeker module (B) have submitted (C) their test reports (D)."

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Strike out the intervening phrase "of the scientists working on the seeker module" — the subject is **Each**, which is always singular.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: The plural noun "scientists" sits inside a prepositional phrase and cannot govern the verb; its only job is to lure the ear.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Correct part (C): "have" becomes "has". The later "their" reflects modern singular usage and is not the tested error.

examples.result: Error in part C — "have" must become "has".

examples.title: Articles and tense in one sentence
examples.problem: Fill in the blanks: "The scientist is ___ M.Tech from a leading engineering institute and ___ (work) at the Bengaluru laboratory since 2018; next week she ___ (present) her findings to the review board."

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Article by sound: "M.Tech" is read /em tech/, beginning with a vowel sound — "**an** M.Tech", exactly like "an hour" and opposite to "a university" (/yu/).

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: "Since 2018" plus a continuing action demands the present perfect continuous: "**has been working**" (simple "has worked" is also accepted).

steps.label: Step 3
