steps.text: "Next week" points to scheduled future — "will present" is the standard key, with the simple present acceptable for timetabled events.

examples.result: an M.Tech; has been working; will present.

keyTakeaways: a/an follows the initial sound: an hour, a university, an M.Tech, a one-rupee coin.
The verb agrees with the grammatical head, not the nearest noun: "the list of items is", "each of the scientists has".
since + point and for + duration demand perfect tenses; "by the time" + past event forces past perfect.
With either … or / neither … nor the nearer subject rules; collectives stay singular unless members act separately.

quiz.q: "One of my friends ___ going to the test range tomorrow."
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The head of the subject is "one", singular. Step 2: "of my friends" is a prepositional phrase and cannot control the verb. Step 3: Hence "is going". Step 4: "are" and "were" fall for the nearest-noun trap.

quiz.q: "Neither the soldiers nor their commander ___ aware of the ambush."
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Apply the proximity rule for neither … nor. Step 2: The nearer subject is "commander", singular. Step 3: The tense is past, so the answer is "was". Step 4: "were" agrees with the distant plural instead of the near singular.

quiz.q: "He is ___ honest officer who holds ___ M.Tech degree." Choose the pair of articles.
quiz.explanation: Step 1: "honest" begins with a silent h — the sound is vowel-initial, so "an honest". Step 2: "M.Tech" is read /em tech/, again vowel-initial, so "an M.Tech". Step 3: Both slots take "an". Step 4: Any "a" choice spells the word instead of listening to it.

quiz.q: "By the time the flight trial ended, the defence research establishment team ___ the telemetry anomaly."
quiz.explanation: Step 1: "By the time + past event" triggers the past perfect in the main clause. Step 2: The isolation preceded the trial’s end. Step 3: Hence "had isolated". Step 4: "has isolated" clashes with the past anchor, and plain "isolated" loses the sequence the sentence is signalling.

prerequisites: Decibel and link-budget arithmetic
Antenna gain basics (ece-d7-s5)
intro: The defence research establishment Stage-II Electronics & Communication paper devotes 60 descriptive marks to the discipline (plus 15 for research aptitude in the legacy pattern), and microwave line-of-sight systems are its most defence-flavoured topic — every radar and telemetry link is an LOS design problem. Doppler shifts, path loss and Fresnel clearance are the working equations of the defence research establishment radar and communication laboratories. This section builds the link-budget and Doppler toolkit the paper tests.
objectives: Compute radio-horizon distances and size tower heights for LOS hops
Apply the Friis equation and the dB free-space path-loss formula to close a link budget
Compute radar Doppler shifts for approaching and receding targets
Apply the 60% first-Fresnel-zone clearance rule during path profiling

concepts.term: Radio horizon of an LOS link
concepts.statement: With standard atmospheric refraction (effective earth radius $4/3$ times the true radius), the **radio-horizon** distance is $d(\text{km}) \approx 3.57\,(\sqrt{h_t} + \sqrt{h_r})$ with antenna heights in metres.
concepts.detail: Doubling a tower height does not double its horizon — the square root sees to that. Trap: adding the two horizon distances (not the heights) gives the maximum hop length; questions love swapping the two operations.

concepts.term: Free-space path loss and the Friis equation
concepts.statement: **FSPL** in decibels: $\text{FSPL} = 92.45 + 20\log_{10} f_{(\text{GHz})} + 20\log_{10} d_{(\text{km})}$, and the Friis balance reads $P_r = P_t + G_t + G_r - \text{FSPL}$ (all dB/dBm/dBi).
concepts.detail: Each doubling of distance or frequency adds 6 dB of loss. Trap: the constant 92.45 belongs to the GHz–km combination; mixing units with the 32.45 (MHz–km) version is a standard planted error.

concepts.term: Doppler shift in radar and links
concepts.statement: A target with radial velocity $v$ produces a **Doppler shift** $f_d = \frac{2v}{\lambda}$ — the factor 2 from the two-way monostatic path. Approaching targets raise the received frequency; receding targets lower it.
concepts.detail: One-way communication links shift by only $\frac{v}{\lambda}$. Trap: use the radial (line-of-sight) velocity component, never the ground speed, unless the geometry is head-on; tangential motion produces no Doppler.

concepts.statement: The first Fresnel-zone radius at a point along the path is $F_1 = 17.3 \sqrt{\dfrac{d_1 d_2}{f D}}$ metres ($d_1, d_2, D$ in km, $f$ in GHz); keep at least **60% of $F_1$** obstacle-free to avoid diffraction loss.
concepts.detail: The 60% rule keeps added loss below roughly 6 dB in typical geometry. Trap: the worst obstruction point is mid-path where $F_1$ is largest — profile the whole path, not just the endpoints.

concepts.statement: Design order: fix hop length from tower heights (radio horizon) → compute FSPL → close the budget for $P_r$ → subtract receiver threshold to obtain **fade margin** → check availability targets and diversity needs.
concepts.detail: Descriptive marks live in the ordering and the units. Defence practice: telemetry hops between range stations budget generous fade margins because monsoon multipath and k-factor fades strike precisely during trials.

examples.title: Doppler shift of a closing target
examples.problem: A 10 GHz tracking radar locks a target closing head-on at 300 m/s. Find the Doppler shift and the received echo frequency. What changes if the target recedes at the same speed?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{f} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{10^{10}} = 0.03$ m.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Monostatic radar sees the two-way effect: $f_d = \dfrac{2v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2 \times 300}{0.03} = 20$ kHz.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: A closing target raises the frequency: the echo returns at $10\,\text{GHz} + 20\,\text{kHz} = 10.00002$ GHz. A receding target flips the sign — the echo would come back at $10\,\text{GHz} - 20\,\text{kHz}$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Note the factor-of-two: a one-way communication link at the same closing speed would shift by only $v/\lambda = 10$ kHz — the radar’s round trip doubles the Doppler.

examples.result: Doppler shift $= +20$ kHz (closing); echo at 10.00002 GHz. Receding flips the sign to −20 kHz.

examples.title: Closing a 6 GHz microwave link budget
examples.problem: A 6 GHz LOS microwave hop of 50 km uses a 1 W transmitter (30 dBm) and 20 dBi dishes at both ends. Compute the free-space path loss and received power, and judge the margin against a −90 dBm receiver threshold.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Write the loss formula with the GHz–km constant: $\text{FSPL} = 92.45 + 20\log_{10} 6 + 20\log_{10} 50$ dB.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Evaluate the logs: $20\log_{10} 6 \approx 15.56$ dB and $20\log_{10} 50 \approx 33.98$ dB, so FSPL $\approx 92.45 + 15.56 + 33.98 \approx 142$ dB.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Close the Friis budget: $P_r = 30 + 20 + 20 - 142 = -72$ dBm.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Fade margin $= -72 - (-90) = 18$ dB — comfortable in clear air, and exactly the reservoir a heavy monsoon fade will consume.

examples.result: FSPL ≈ 142 dB; received power −72 dBm; fade margin 18 dB.

keyTakeaways: Radio horizon: $d(\text{km}) \approx 3.57(\sqrt{h_t} + \sqrt{h_r})$ for heights in metres — add horizon distances, not heights.
FSPL(dB) $= 92.45 + 20\log f_{(\text{GHz})} + 20\log d_{(\text{km})}$; each doubling of distance or frequency adds 6 dB.
Monostatic radar Doppler $f_d = 2v/\lambda$: approaching raises, receding lowers the carrier; one-way links shift by $v/\lambda$ only.
Keep at least 60% of the first Fresnel zone clear — mid-path, where $F_1$ peaks, is the critical profile point.

quiz.q: A 10 GHz radar tracks a target receding at 150 m/s. The Doppler shift is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Wavelength $\lambda = 0.03$ m at 10 GHz. Step 2: Two-way shift magnitude $f_d = 2 \times 150 / 0.03 = 10$ kHz. Step 3: Receding motion lowers the received frequency, so the shift is −10 kHz. Step 4: The +20 kHz option doubles the speed as well as the sign.

quiz.q: The radio horizon of a 64 m tower (standard refraction) is about
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Apply $d = 3.57\sqrt{h}$ km. Step 2: $\sqrt{64} = 8$. Step 3: $d = 3.57 \times 8 = 28.56$ km. Step 4: The 35.7 km option squares to 100 m — a planted height swap.

quiz.q: Doubling the distance of a free-space link changes the path loss by
quiz.explanation: Step 1: FSPL contains the term $20\log_{10} d$. Step 2: Doubling $d$ adds $20\log_{10} 2 \approx 6$ dB. Step 3: The same 6 dB applies per doubling of frequency. Step 4: +12 dB would be a quadrupling of distance.

quiz.q: To avoid diffraction loss on a microwave path, at least this fraction of the first Fresnel zone should be kept clear:
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The first Fresnel zone is the ellipsoid of half-wavelength path excess around the ray. Step 2: Practical planning keeps 0.6 $F_1$ clear of obstacles. Step 3: That limits the additional diffraction loss to a few dB. Step 4: Demanding full clearance over-engineers towers at real cost.

prerequisites: Three-phase phasor basics (ee-d2-s2)
Faraday's law and magnetic circuits (ee-d10-s2)
intro: Synchronous machines anchor the electrical-machines area of the defence research establishment Stage-II Electrical paper — 60 descriptive discipline marks plus the 15-mark research-aptitude component in the legacy recruitment pattern. Every the defence research establishment runs alternators in its DG sets and test bays, so EMF equations and regulation calculations carry direct laboratory relevance. Expect numerical questions built on $N_s = 120f/P$ and $E = 4.44\, k_w f \Phi T$.
objectives: Compute synchronous speed and machine frequency from pole count and rpm
Apply the alternator EMF equation to rated-voltage calculations
Predict voltage regulation from the synchronous-impedance phasor diagram at lagging and leading loads
State the four synchronisation conditions and the role of the synchronous condenser

concepts.statement: A synchronous machine locks to the supply frequency at the **synchronous speed** $N_s = \dfrac{120f}{P}$ rpm, and conversely a driven alternator generates $f = \dfrac{PN_s}{120}$ Hz.
concepts.detail: A 50 Hz, 4-pole machine must run at 1500 rpm; a 12-pole machine at 500 rpm. Trap: more poles means slower speed — options pairing high pole counts with high speeds invert the relation.

concepts.statement: The RMS phase EMF is $E = 4.44\, k_w f \Phi T$ volts, where $\Phi$ is flux per pole, $T$ the series turns per phase and $k_w = k_d k_p$ the **winding factor** pricing distribution and chording.
concepts.detail: The 4.44 is $\sqrt{2}\pi/2$ in disguise — the same constant as the transformer EMF equation, because both sweep sinusoidal flux past a winding. Trap: $T$ counts series turns per phase, not conductors; using conductors $Z$ requires $E = 2.22\, k_w f \Phi Z$.

concepts.statement: Armature current produces an MMF that distorts the main field: **lagging** power-factor loads demagnetise (reduce the resultant flux), **leading** loads magnetise (strengthen it), and unity-power-factor loads act mainly cross-magnetising.
concepts.detail: This is why regulation is positive at lagging PF and can go negative at leading PF. Trap: reactive current along the quadrature axis is what modifies flux — pure active current mostly twists it.

concepts.statement: **Regulation** $= \dfrac{E_0 - V}{V} \times 100\%$. Predicted from the synchronous impedance $Z_s = R_a + jX_s$: $E_0 = \sqrt{(V\cos\phi + I R_a)^2 + (V\sin\phi \pm I X_s)^2}$ with $+$ for lagging, $-$ for leading loads.
concepts.detail: The EMF (synchronous-impedance) method overestimates regulation (pessimistic); the MMF and ASA methods lean optimistic; the ZPF (Potier) triangle method is the accurate one — a favourite ordering question.

concepts.statement: Before closing the breaker, match the incoming alternator to the bus on four counts: **voltage magnitude, frequency, phase sequence and phase angle** — checked with a synchroscope (or dark-lamp method).
concepts.detail: Closing out of synchronism produces damaging torques and stator currents. Related assessment gem: an overexcited synchronous motor running unloaded draws leading current and behaves as a **synchronous condenser** — a rotating VAR source for power-factor correction.

examples.title: Speed and EMF of a 12-pole alternator
examples.problem: A 3-phase, 50 Hz, 12-pole alternator has 200 series turns per phase, a winding factor of 0.96 and 40 mWb of flux per pole. Find the synchronous speed, the phase EMF and the line EMF for a star connection.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Synchronous speed $N_s = \dfrac{120f}{P} = \dfrac{120 \times 50}{12} = 500$ rpm — the prime mover must hold exactly this speed to stay on frequency.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Phase EMF: $E_{ph} = 4.44\, k_w f \Phi T = 4.44 \times 0.96 \times 50 \times 0.04 \times 200$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: $E_{ph} = 1704.96 \approx 1705$ V; the star connection scales line voltage by $\sqrt{3}$: $E_L \approx 2951$ V $\approx 2.95$ kV.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Sensitivity check: EMF is linear in each of $\Phi$, $f$ and $T$ — doubling the flux alone doubles the EMF, a favourite one-mark extension.

examples.result: $N_s = 500$ rpm, $E_{ph} \approx 1705$ V, $E_L \approx 2.95$ kV (star).

examples.title: Regulation at 0.8 lagging power factor
examples.problem: A 3-phase star-connected alternator delivers 100 A at 6.6 kV line voltage and 0.8 power factor lagging. With synchronous reactance 5 Ω per phase and negligible armature resistance, estimate the no-load EMF and the voltage regulation.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Phase voltage $V = \dfrac{6600}{\sqrt{3}} = 3810.5$ V; with $\cos\phi = 0.8$, $\sin\phi = 0.6$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: With $R_a = 0$, the synchronous-impedance phasor gives $E_0 = \sqrt{(V\cos\phi)^2 + (V\sin\phi + I X_s)^2} = \sqrt{3048.4^2 + (2286.3 + 500)^2}$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Regulation $= \dfrac{4130 - 3810.5}{3810.5} \times 100 \approx 8.4\%$ — positive, exactly as lagging armature reaction demagnetising predicts.

examples.result: $E_0 \approx 4130$ V per phase; regulation $\approx 8.4\%$ (positive at lagging PF).

keyTakeaways: $N_s = 120f/P$ rpm and $f = PN_s/120$ — a 12-pole 50 Hz alternator must spin at 500 rpm.
Phase EMF $E = 4.44\, k_w f \Phi T$ with $k_w = k_d k_p$; the constant is the transformer’s, the winding factor is the addition.
Lagging loads demagnetise (positive regulation); leading loads magnetise (regulation can go negative); unity loads act cross-magnetising.
Synchronise on voltage, frequency, phase sequence and phase angle; an overexcited idling synchronous motor is a synchronous condenser supplying VARs.

quiz.q: A 50 Hz, 4-pole synchronous machine runs at
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Apply $N_s = 120f/P$. Step 2: $N_s = 120 \times 50 / 4 = 1500$ rpm. Step 3: 3000 rpm belongs to a 2-pole machine at 50 Hz. Step 4: More poles — slower synchronous speed.

quiz.q: Armature reaction in an alternator is magnetising when the load power factor is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Reactive armature current along the quadrature axis modifies the main flux. Step 2: Leading current produces MMF that aids the field — magnetising. Step 3: Lagging current opposes it — demagnetising. Step 4: Unity-PF load mainly distorts the field (cross-magnetising).

quiz.q: A 6-pole alternator driven at 1000 rpm generates a frequency of
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Invert the speed relation: $f = PN/120$. Step 2: $f = 6 \times 1000 / 120 = 50$ Hz. Step 3: 60 Hz would need 1200 rpm at 6 poles. Step 4: The $120$ in the formula converts pairs of poles per revolution into per-minute cycles.

quiz.q: An overexcited synchronous motor running on no load, drawing leading current, is called a
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Overexcitation makes the synchronous machine supply reactive power even without mechanical load. Step 2: Idling, it draws a leading (capacitive) current. Step 3: Used this way it is a synchronous condenser — a rotating VAR source for power-factor correction. Step 4: A static VAR compensator does similar duty with thyristor-switched reactors and capacitors, no rotating machine.

prerequisites: Pure-substance properties and phase change (me-d3-s1)
Basic integral calculus for computing work
intro: Thermodynamics opens the propulsion-and-energy stream of the defence research establishment Stage-II Mechanical paper — 60 descriptive discipline marks alongside the 15-mark research-aptitude section in the legacy recruitment pattern. Missile propulsion, wind-tunnel drives and test-rig power all trace back to the three laws. The assessor’s favourite is the Carnot bound: the fastest route to full marks, and the easiest to fumble with a Celsius slip.
objectives: Apply the first law $Q - W = \Delta U$ to closed systems and cycles with a consistent sign convention
State and interconvert the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius forms of the second law
Compute Carnot efficiency and refrigerator/heat-pump COPs in absolute temperature
Use the entropy inequality to classify processes as reversible, irreversible or impossible

concepts.statement: If bodies A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with body C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other — the **transitivity** that makes temperature a measurable property and thermometry possible.
concepts.detail: Assessment use: justify why a thermometer reading is meaningful at all. Trap: the zeroth law defines equality of temperature, not its direction of flow — that is the second law’s business.

concepts.term: First law for a closed system
concepts.statement: The **first law** balances energy with heat positive into the system and work positive out of it: $Q - W = \Delta U$. Over a cycle $\oint dU = 0$, hence $\oint \delta Q = \oint \delta W$ — net heat equals net work.
concepts.detail: The law is a bookkeeping identity, not a direction: it cannot forbid the impossible engine. Traps: boundary work is $W = \int p\,dV$ only for quasi-equilibrium processes; in a free expansion into vacuum $W = 0$ though volume changes.

concepts.statement: **Kelvin-Planck**: no cyclic device converts heat from a single reservoir entirely into work. **Clausius**: heat does not flow unaided from a colder to a hotter body. The two statements are logically equivalent; both forbid a perpetual-motion machine of the second kind (PMM-2).
concepts.detail: A heat engine must therefore reject heat — the condenser in a power plant and the exhaust of a missile engine are thermodynamic necessities, not design flaws. Trap: PMM-1 violates the first law; PMM-2 violates the second — options swap them.

concepts.statement: No engine between reservoirs at $T_H$ and $T_L$ beats $\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \dfrac{T_L}{T_H}$, independent of the working substance — temperatures in **kelvin**. Companion coefficients: $\text{COP}_R = \dfrac{T_L}{T_H - T_L}$ and $\text{COP}_{HP} = \dfrac{T_H}{T_H - T_L} = \text{COP}_R + 1$.
concepts.detail: The killer trap: using °C. Between 227°C and 27°C the true bound is $1 - 300/500 = 40\%$, while the Celsius computation suggests about 88%. Also: raising $T_H$ or lowering $T_L$ both help, but lowering the sink is usually the harder engineering problem.

concepts.statement: The **Clausius inequality** $dS \ge \dfrac{\delta Q}{T}$ holds with equality only for reversible heat transfer; consequently $\Delta S_{\text{universe}} > 0$ for every real (irreversible) process and a reversible adiabatic process is isentropic ($\Delta S = 0$).
concepts.detail: Entropy of a system may fall — a refrigerator cools its contents — but only by exporting more entropy elsewhere. Trap: "adiabatic" alone does not mean isentropic; friction makes real adiabatic processes entropy-generating.

examples.title: Carnot engine between 600 K and 300 K
examples.problem: A Carnot engine absorbs 2 kJ of heat per cycle from a 600 K reservoir and rejects to a 300 K sink. Find the efficiency, the work output and the heat rejected. What efficiency would a 250 K sink allow?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Efficiency $\eta = 1 - \dfrac{T_L}{T_H} = 1 - \dfrac{300}{600} = 0.5$ — with temperatures already absolute.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Work $W = \eta Q_H = 0.5 \times 2 = 1$ kJ; rejected heat $Q_L = Q_H - W = 1$ kJ.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Lowering the sink to 250 K gives $\eta = 1 - \dfrac{250}{600} = 0.583$ — 58.3%, showing why rejection temperature is a prime design lever in propulsion and electronics cooling.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Interpretation: no real engine between the same reservoirs, however finely built, can exceed these numbers — Carnot is a bound, not a tuning target.

examples.result: $\eta = 50\%$, $W = 1$ kJ, $Q_L = 1$ kJ; a 250 K sink lifts the bound to 58.3%.

examples.title: First law for a process and a cycle
examples.problem: A sealed actuator cylinder on a missile test rig receives 800 J of heat while its gas expands doing 300 J of work. Separately, the rig’s working fluid completes a cycle with heat interactions of +60 kJ and −30 kJ. Find $\Delta U$ for the expansion and the net work over the cycle.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: First law (heat-in positive, work-by positive): $\Delta U = Q - W = 800 - 300 = 500$ J for the expansion.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: The gas stores 500 J more internal energy — observable as a temperature rise at fixed composition.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Over a complete cycle the fluid returns to its initial state, so $\oint dU = 0$ and $W_{\text{net}} = Q_{\text{net}} = 60 - 30 = 30$ kJ.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Cross-read: the cycle converts 30 of the 60 kJ absorbed into work — a 50% conversion, permissible only because heat is rejected to a colder sink, as the second law demands.

examples.result: $\Delta U = +500$ J for the expansion; cyclic net work $= 30$ kJ.

keyTakeaways: First law (closed system): $Q - W = \Delta U$; over a cycle $\Delta U = 0$, so net heat equals net work.
Kelvin-Planck and Clausius are equivalent faces of the second law; together they outlaw PMM-2 while the first law outlaws PMM-1.
$\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - T_L/T_H$ in kelvin — the °C slip turns 40% into 88% and full marks into zero.
$\text{COP}_R = T_L/(T_H - T_L)$ and $\text{COP}_{HP} = \text{COP}_R + 1$; both degrade as the temperature gap widens.

quiz.q: A Carnot engine works between 227°C and 27°C. Its efficiency is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Convert to absolute temperature: $T_H = 500$ K, $T_L = 300$ K. Step 2: $\eta = 1 - 300/500 = 0.4$. Step 3: The 88% option is the Celsius trap $1 - 27/227$. Step 4: 60% and 20% fail even the Kelvin arithmetic.

quiz.q: The COP of a Carnot refrigerator operating between 300 K and 250 K is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Refrigerator COP removes heat from the cold reservoir: $\text{COP}_R = T_L/(T_H - T_L)$. Step 2: $\text{COP}_R = 250/50 = 5$. Step 3: The value 6 is the heat-pump COP $T_H/(T_H - T_L) = 300/50$. Step 4: COPs exceed 1 legitimately — they move heat, they do not create it.

quiz.q: A perpetual-motion machine of the second kind (PMM-2) violates
options: both the first and second laws
quiz.explanation: Step 1: PMM-2 extracts work cyclically from a single reservoir, conserving energy in the process. Step 2: Energy bookkeeping is intact, so the first law is satisfied. Step 3: It contradicts the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law. Step 4: PMM-1, which creates energy from nothing, is the one violating the first law.

quiz.q: In a reversible adiabatic (isentropic) process, the entropy change of the system is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Adiabatic means $\delta Q = 0$, so the Clausius inequality gives $dS \ge 0$. Step 2: Reversibility forces the equality $dS = \delta Q / T = 0$. Step 3: Hence $\Delta S = 0$ — the process is isentropic. Step 4: The $c_p \ln(T_2/T_1)$ form is only one piece of the ideal-gas entropy change, which the pressure term cancels exactly along $pv^\gamma = \text{const}$.

prerequisites: Modular arithmetic and gcd
Binary and hexadecimal number bases
intro: Cybersecurity is Area 6 of Paper 2 in the defence research establishment Stage-II CSE assessment — 60 descriptive discipline marks plus the 15-mark research-aptitude component in the legacy recruitment pattern — and it is the most the defence research establishment-native topic on the syllabus. Secure tactical datalinks, classified networks and cryptographic key management are daily business in defence laboratories. This section covers the principles, the mathematics of RSA and hashes, and the PKI that binds it together.
objectives: Classify attacks against the CIA triad together with authentication and non-repudiation
Work RSA end-to-end on small numbers: key generation, encryption, decryption and the factoring basis
Distinguish hashes, MACs and digital signatures, and verify signatures with public keys
Explain certificates, CA chains and why TLS combines asymmetric key exchange with AES session traffic

concepts.term: The CIA triad and its extensions
concepts.statement: Security goals are classed as **confidentiality** (only authorised parties read the data), **integrity** (no undetected tampering) and **availability** (the service works when needed); defence practice adds **authentication** (who) and **non-repudiation** (cannot deny sending).
concepts.detail: Map every attack to a violated property: eavesdropping → confidentiality, log tampering → integrity, DDoS → availability. Trap: encrypting a message guarantees none of the others — an attacker can still delete or replay ciphertext.

concepts.statement: **Symmetric** ciphers use one shared key for both directions; AES operates on 128-bit blocks with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys and is orders of magnitude faster than public-key cryptography. The hard problem is distributing the key securely.
concepts.detail: Kerckhoffs’s principle governs design: the system’s security must survive the algorithm being public — secrecy lives only in the key. Trap: key size alone does not make security; a misused 256-bit AES mode (e.g. ECB on structured data) leaks patterns.

concepts.statement: **RSA** publishes $n = pq$ and $e$, keeps $d$ with $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\phi(n)}$; encryption is $c = m^e \bmod n$ and decryption $m = c^d \bmod n$. Its security rests on the difficulty of factoring the modulus $n$.
concepts.detail: ECC delivers comparable security with far smaller keys (roughly 256-bit ECC ≈ 3072-bit RSA), which matters for constrained battlefield radios. Trap: RSA encrypts a bounded block — bulk data always goes symmetric.

concepts.statement: A cryptographic **hash** such as SHA-256 is one-way and collision-resistant: any input maps to a fixed 256-bit digest from which nothing is recovered. A **digital signature** applies the signer’s private key to the hash; anyone verifies it with the public key.
concepts.detail: Signing the hash (not the whole message) is what makes signatures fast. Verification proves integrity, origin and non-repudiation. Trap: a MAC uses a shared secret — it authenticates but cannot prove origin to a third party.

concepts.statement: A **certificate** (X.509) binds an identity to a public key under a certification authority’s signature; trust chains from a root CA through intermediates to the end entity. TLS uses this to agree an AES session key via asymmetric (or ECDHE) exchange, then encrypts bulk traffic symmetrically.
concepts.detail: The hybrid pattern answers the assessment’s recurring "why both?" — asymmetric solves key distribution, symmetric supplies the speed. Defence networks layer this with segmentation, HSM-held keys and certificate pinning.

examples.title: RSA on assessment-sized numbers
examples.problem: Bob publishes the public key $(n = 33, e = 7)$. Alice sends the message $m = 5$. Verify that the private key is $d = 3$, encrypt $m$, and confirm decryption recovers 5.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: With $p = 3$, $q = 11$: $\phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1) = 20$. Check $ed = 7 \times 3 = 21 \equiv 1 \pmod{20}$ — so $d = 3$ is the matching private exponent.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Encrypt: $c = m^e \bmod n = 5^7 \bmod 33$. Repeated squaring: $5^2 = 25$, $5^4 = 625 \equiv 31$, so $5^7 = 5^4 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 5 \equiv 31 \times 25 \times 5 \equiv 14$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Decrypt: $m = c^d \bmod n = 14^3 \bmod 33 = 2744 \bmod 33 = 5$ — the plaintext returns intact.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Scale check: real systems use 2048–3072-bit moduli; breaking $n = 33$ needs only a glance at its factors — the mathematics is identical, the factoring is not.

examples.result: Ciphertext $c = 14$ travels; decryption with $d = 3$ restores $m = 5$.

examples.title: Why brute force is the wrong attack on AES-128
examples.problem: Estimate the time to brute-force a 128-bit AES key at $10^{12}$ keys per second, and state what this implies about how adversaries actually attack the defence research establishment-grade systems.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Key space $= 2^{128} \approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}$ keys.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: At $10^{12}$ keys/s: $t = \dfrac{3.4 \times 10^{38}}{10^{12}} = 3.4 \times 10^{26}$ s, and with $3.15 \times 10^7$ s per year, $t \approx 1.1 \times 10^{19}$ years.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: The universe is about $1.4 \times 10^{10}$ years old — exhaustive search is out of reach by roughly nine orders of magnitude even at planetary hardware scale.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Conclusion for the answer: real attacks target implementations — side channels, weak randomness, key management and people — so security engineering concentrates there rather than on longer keys.

examples.result: ≈ $10^{19}$ years at $10^{12}$ keys/s; key search is infeasible, so attacks target implementation and key management.

keyTakeaways: CIA triad — confidentiality, integrity, availability — plus authentication and non-repudiation; map every attack to the property it violates.
RSA: publish $n = pq$ and $e$, keep $d$ with $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\phi(n)}$; security rests on factoring hardness.
Sign with the private key, verify with the public key; hashing the message first makes signatures fast and tamper-evident.
Kerckhoffs’s principle: secrecy lives only in keys; TLS is hybrid — asymmetric setup, AES for bulk traffic.

quiz.q: The security of RSA rests primarily on
options: the difficulty of factoring large semiprime integers
the difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem
quiz.explanation: Step 1: RSA publishes $n = pq$; recovering $d$ requires $\phi(n)$, which requires factoring $n$. Step 2: Discrete logarithms underpin Diffie-Hellman, DSA and ECC instead. Step 3: Lattices power newer post-quantum schemes. Step 4: Hash collisions break signatures’ collision resistance, a different property.

quiz.q: A digital signature is created with the
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Signing must be possible only by the signer — so it uses the key only the signer holds. Step 2: Anyone can verify with the matching public key. Step 3: That asymmetry is what delivers non-repudiation. Step 4: The CA’s key signs certificates, which bind identities to public keys.

quiz.q: An attacker silently alters a transmitted mission log. Which property is primarily violated?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The log was readable throughout, so confidentiality held. Step 2: The service stayed up, so availability held. Step 3: The data’s trustworthiness — integrity — is what tampering breaks. Step 4: Non-repudiation concerns denial of authorship, not alteration in transit.

quiz.q: Kerckhoffs’s principle states that
options: security must depend only on the secrecy of the key, never of the algorithm
algorithms must remain classified to stay secure
longer keys always guarantee secure systems
encryption and hashing are interchangeable operations
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Assume the adversary knows the full design — only the key stays secret. Step 2: Published algorithms survive open attack, which is how AES earned trust. Step 3: Key length helps but cannot rescue a broken construction or a leaked key. Step 4: Hashing is one-way and keyless — never a substitute for encryption.

prerequisites: Sets, relations and functions (Discrete Structures)
Proof by induction and contradiction basics
intro: Theory of Automata is the Semester 4 abstract core, and its Unit 1 is the highest-scoring unit of the subject: construct a DFA for a language, convert an NFA to a DFA by subset construction, then minimise — these three tasks recur in five straight years of the state technical universities papers, usually 10–14 marks combined. The section treats finite automata as the mathematics of finite memory.
objectives: Write a DFA as the five-tuple $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ and read the extended transition function
Construct DFAs for arithmetic and pattern languages such as binary multiples of 3 or strings ending in 01
Convert any NFA to an equivalent DFA via subset construction with the $2^n$ bound
Minimise a DFA by removing unreachable states and refining equivalence partitions; state the role of Kleene’s theorem and the pumping lemma

concepts.statement: A **deterministic finite automaton** is $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ — a finite state set, input alphabet, transition function $\delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q$, start state and accepting set $F$; the language accepted is $L(M) = \{w : \hat{\delta}(q_0, w) \in F\}$.
concepts.detail: Assessments demand the formal tuple before the diagram. A common error is an incomplete transition table — in a DFA every (state, symbol) pair must have exactly one target; if your table has holes you have really designed an NFA.

concepts.statement: A **nondeterministic FA** allows $\delta : Q \times \Sigma \to 2^Q$ (a set of targets, possibly empty) plus **ε-transitions** that fire without consuming input; the NFA accepts when **any** run of choices reaches a final state.
concepts.detail: NFAs are easier to design but no more powerful — by Kleene’s theorem DFAs, NFAs and regular expressions all define exactly the regular languages. Students lose marks claiming NFAs recognise more; they only express the same class more concisely.

concepts.statement: **Subset construction** converts an NFA over states $Q$ into a DFA whose states are subsets of $Q$: start from the ε-closure of $\{q_0\}$ and set $\delta'(S, a) = \epsilon\text{-closure}\left(\bigcup_{q \in S} \delta(q, a)\right)$; a DFA state is accepting when it contains an NFA final state.
concepts.detail: Only reachable subsets are ever built, so practical blow-up is small even though the worst case is $2^n$. Forgetting the ε-closure when starting or moving is the most common conversion error; the deterministic version of this assessment task usually has no ε-moves at all.

concepts.statement: To **minimise a DFA**: (1) drop unreachable states; (2) partition states into final versus non-final; (3) repeatedly split any class whose states send some symbol into different classes; the fixed point is the unique minimal DFA (up to isomorphism) whose states are the Myhill–Nerode equivalence classes.
concepts.detail: Papers hand you a 5–6 state DFA to minimise. Work a table of successive partitions and cite minimality and uniqueness for full marks; merging two states that some string distinguishes is the fatal error.

concepts.statement: **Kleene’s theorem**: a language is regular iff some finite automaton accepts it iff some regular expression denotes it. The **pumping lemma** — for regular $L$ there is a length $p$ such that $w = xyz$ with $|xy| \le p$, $|y| \ge 1$ and $xy^iz \in L$ for every $i$ — proves languages like $\{0^n1^n\}$ **not** regular.
concepts.detail: The pumping lemma is a necessary condition for regularity, never a sufficient one; using it to prove a language regular earns zero. Assessments want the contrapositive argument: if for every valid decomposition some $i$ pumps the word out of the language, the language cannot be regular.

examples.title: DFA for binary strings divisible by 3
examples.problem: Construct a DFA over $\{0, 1\}$ accepting exactly the binary representations of numbers divisible by 3 (including 0), and check it on $1001$ and $101$.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Model the memory: the only fact a finite automaton can track about the number read so far is its remainder $r \in \{0, 1, 2\}$. Take states $q_0, q_1, q_2$ for the three remainders, start $q_0$, accepting set $\{q_0\}$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Appending a digit $d$ maps the value $N$ to $2N + d$, so the remainder updates as $r \mapsto (2r + d) \bmod 3$. This gives the table: $q_0$: $0 \to q_0$, $1 \to q_1$; $q_1$: $0 \to q_2$, $1 \to q_0$; $q_2$: $0 \to q_1$, $1 \to q_2$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text:
```text
1001 (= 9):  q0 -1-> q1 -0-> q2 -0-> q1 -1-> q0   accept
```
Trace $1001_2 = 9$: it ends in $q_0$, and indeed $9 = 3 \times 3$ is divisible by 3.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text:
```text
101 (= 5):   q0 -1-> q1 -0-> q2 -1-> q2           reject
```
Trace $101_2 = 5$: it ends in $q_2$, rejected since $5 \bmod 3 = 2$. The automaton is already minimal — the three remainders are pairwise distinguishable (the suffix 0 leads $q_0$ to acceptance but $q_1$ to rejection).

examples.result: A three-state DFA with transition $r' = (2r + d) \bmod 3$ and single accepting state $q_0$; accepts 1001 (9), rejects 101 (5).

examples.title: NFA to DFA by subset construction
examples.problem: Convert the NFA $N$ for strings over $\{0, 1\}$ ending in $01$ — states $\{A, B, C\}$, start $A$, final $\{C\}$, with $\delta(A,0) = \{A, B\}$, $\delta(A,1) = \{A\}$ and $\delta(B,1) = \{C\}$ — into an equivalent DFA.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: The DFA start state is the singleton $\{A\}$. On 0 it reaches $\{A\} \cup \{B\} = \{A, B\}$; on 1 it stays at $\{A\}$. Name the new subset $S_1 = \{A, B\}$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: From $S_1$: on 0, $\delta(A,0) \cup \delta(B,0) = \{A, B\} = S_1$; on 1, $\{A\} \cup \{C\} = \{A, C\}$ — name it $S_2$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: From $S_2$: on 0 back to $S_1$; on 1 back to $\{A\}$. No new subsets appear, so the DFA has the three states $\{A\}, \{A,B\}, \{A,C\}$, with $S_2$ accepting because it contains the NFA final state $C$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text:
```text
0101:  {A} -0-> {A,B} -1-> {A,C} -0-> {A,B} -1-> {A,C}   accept
```
Check $w = 0101$: it ends in the accepting subset, and 0101 indeed ends in 01. The resulting DFA is minimal at three states.

examples.result: DFA states $\{A\}, \{A,B\}, \{A,C\}$ with accepting state $\{A,C\}$ — three states, no subset blow-up.

keyTakeaways: A DFA is the tuple $(Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ with a total, single-valued $\delta$; the NFA relaxes both to sets and ε-moves.
Design trick: states equal the finite memory of the problem — the remainder mod 3, or the last symbols seen.
Subset construction builds DFA states as subsets of NFA states; worst case $2^n$, accepting means containing an NFA final state.
Minimisation = drop unreachable states then refine partitions; the minimal DFA is unique, and the pumping lemma proves non-regularity — never regularity.

quiz.q: The minimum number of states in a DFA accepting binary strings whose value is divisible by 3 is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: A DFA has finite memory, so it can only track the current remainder. Step 2: Divisibility by 3 needs three distinguishable remainders 0, 1 and 2. Step 3: The states for remainders 0 and 1 are distinguished by the suffix 0 — from remainder 0 it keeps you accepting, from remainder 1 it moves you to 2, rejecting. Step 4: Fewer than three states would merge two remainders and misclassify some multiple.

quiz.q: During subset construction, an NFA with $n$ states can require up to how many DFA states?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Each DFA state is a subset of the NFA state set. Step 2: An $n$-state NFA has $2^n$ subsets. Step 3: Adversarial NFAs make every subset reachable, achieving the bound. Step 4: In practice only reachable subsets are constructed, so most conversions stay small.

quiz.q: Which of these languages is regular?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Test for finite memory — can a fixed number of states capture what must be remembered? Step 2: Substring detection needs only "have I seen 01 yet", so a three-state DFA accepts it. Step 3: Balanced counting ($0^n1^n$), string copying ($ww$) and quadratic lengths all need unbounded memory and fall to pumping-lemma proofs. Step 4: Hence only the substring language is regular.

quiz.q: When minimising a DFA, the initial partition places which states together?
options: states whose labels share a letter
all accepting states together and all non-accepting states together
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Two states are equivalent if no suffix distinguishes them. Step 2: The empty string already distinguishes accepting from non-accepting states. Step 3: So refinement starts from finals versus non-finals and splits classes whose members behave differently on some symbol. Step 4: The process stops when no class splits, leaving the Myhill–Nerode classes.

prerequisites: What constitutes software: programs, data and documentation
Experience of any team project whose requirements changed midway
intro: Software Engineering and Project Management opens with the surest 10 marks in the paper: compare SDLC models and select one for a given scenario — the question the state technical universities have reused, with fresh scenarios, across the last five years. Unit 1 also carries the agile short notes (Scrum events, XP practices) that appear as 3–5 mark sub-questions.
objectives: Name the SDLC phases common to every model and the work products of each
Compare waterfall, incremental/iterative, RAD, spiral and agile on requirements volatility, risk and delivery speed
Justify model selection for scenario questions using explicit criteria
Describe Scrum roles, artifacts and timeboxed events, plus the core XP practices

concepts.statement: Every SDLC model organises **requirements analysis → design → implementation → testing → deployment → maintenance**, with software understood as programs **plus documentation and procedures**; the models differ only in how they order, repeat or overlap these phases.
concepts.detail: Assessments ask which phase an activity belongs to (SRS = requirements; unit, integration, system and acceptance testing = testing) and the maintenance types — corrective, adaptive, perfective and preventive — as a short note. Maintenance consuming the majority of lifetime cost is a favourite one-liner.

concepts.statement: The **waterfall** flows one direction through frozen, sign-off stages — requirements → design → code → test → maintain; it suits stable, well-understood and safety-critical work, but change after sign-off is expensive because repair cost grows steeply downstream.
concepts.detail: Its V-model variant pairs each development phase with a test level (requirements with acceptance, design with integration, code with unit) — worth one diagram line. The standard criticism: working software appears only at the end, so late requirement errors are catastrophic.

concepts.statement: **Incremental** delivery builds the system as usable slices — core first, feature increments after; **iterative** refinement reworks the same product through cycles; **RAD** (James Martin) compresses delivery into 60–90-day cycles using heavy user involvement (JAD workshops), reusable components and 4GL/CASE tools.
concepts.detail: Contrast with waterfall: early working software and easier feedback, but good architects are needed to slice increments cleanly. RAD fails when performance or scalability is critical or users cannot be collocated — that trade-off sentence is exactly what earns marks.

concepts.statement: Boehm’s **spiral** loops through four quadrants — (1) determine objectives and constraints, (2) evaluate alternatives, **identify and resolve risks**, (3) develop and verify, typically via a prototype, and (4) plan the next loop — making it a **risk-driven** meta-model whose radius reflects cumulative cost.
concepts.detail: The keyword is risk: every assessment answer must show the risk quadrant doing prototyping or simulation before major commitment. It suits large, novel, first-of-a-kind systems; critics note it is costly and demands risk-assessment expertise.

concepts.term: The agile family: XP and Scrum
concepts.statement: **Agile** values individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration and responding to change (the Manifesto); **XP** practices include pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, small releases and on-site customer; **Scrum** fixes roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers), artifacts (product backlog, sprint backlog, increment) and timeboxed events — sprints of at most one month, sprint planning, the 15-minute daily scrum, sprint review and retrospective.
concepts.detail: Know the timeboxes (daily scrum 15 minutes; planning, review and retrospective scale with sprint length — 8, 4 and 3 hours for a one-month sprint) and one-line purposes. Confusing the Product Owner (decides what to build) with the Scrum Master (guards the process) is the classic MCQ trap.

examples.title: Selecting the model for four projects
examples.problem: Recommend an SDLC model with a one-line justification for: (i) control software for a nuclear reactor, (ii) a startup’s e-commerce app whose requirements change weekly, (iii) the company’s first AI-based imaging product on unproven technology, (iv) an in-house payroll system similar to one the vendor has built thrice before.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Fix the criteria: requirement volatility, project risk, need for documentation or certification, user availability and schedule pressure.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: (i) Stable, precisely specified, safety-critical → **waterfall/V-model**: complete documentation and verification before deployment outweigh flexibility. (ii) Volatile requirements and fast market feedback → **agile (Scrum)**: sprints absorb weekly change and ship working increments.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (iii) Novel technology with huge technical risk → **spiral**: each loop prototypes and retires the biggest risk before major investment is committed.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: (iv) Known problem, reusable components, tight schedule → **RAD**: reuse plus JAD workshops deliver a working system in a short cycle. Write each answer as model plus criterion — assessors award the marks for the justification, not the label alone.

examples.result: (i) waterfall/V-model, (ii) agile-Scrum, (iii) spiral, (iv) RAD — each keyed to its dominant selection criterion.

examples.title: One Scrum sprint, end to end
examples.problem: A seven-member team works in two-week sprints. Walk through every Scrum event of one sprint, giving its timebox and its output.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: **Sprint planning** (at most 4 h for a two-week sprint): the team selects high-priority items from the product backlog into the sprint backlog and commits to a sprint goal.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Throughout the sprint, the **daily scrum** (15 minutes, same time every day): each developer answers what I did, what I will do and what blocks me — a synchronisation among developers, not a status report to managers.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: At sprint end, the **sprint review** (at most 2 h) demonstrates the potentially shippable **increment** to stakeholders and collects feedback that re-orders the product backlog.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: The **sprint retrospective** (at most 1.5 h) inspects the process itself — what worked, what to improve — closing the loop before the next planning event; timeboxes scale down from the one-month reference.

examples.result: Planning (≤ 4 h) → daily scrums (15 min each) → review (≤ 2 h, increment demonstrated) → retrospective (≤ 1.5 h, process improvements).

keyTakeaways: All models share requirements → design → code → test → deploy → maintain; they differ in ordering and repetition.
Waterfall for stable, documented, safety-critical work; incremental and RAD for fast, reuse-heavy delivery.
The spiral is risk-driven: objectives → risk resolution → development → planning, loop after loop.
Scrum = roles (PO, SM, developers) + artifacts (backlogs, increment) + timeboxed events (15-minute daily scrum, sprint of at most one month).

quiz.q: The SDLC model organised explicitly around risk analysis is the
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Recall each model’s organising principle — sequence, reuse speed, verification, risk. Step 2: The spiral’s second quadrant explicitly identifies and resolves risks through prototyping on every loop. Step 3: Waterfall and the V-model handle stable requirements while RAD compresses the schedule. Step 4: Hence the spiral is called risk-driven.

quiz.q: Waterfall is most appropriate when
options: requirements are expected to change monthly
the technology is unproven and risky
requirements are well understood and stable
users are unavailable but markets shift weekly
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Waterfall freezes each stage behind a sign-off. Step 2: That is safe only when requirements are clear and unlikely to change. Step 3: Evolving needs would force costly re-entry into finished stages. Step 4: Risky technology suggests the spiral; shifting markets suggest agile.

quiz.q: The daily scrum timebox is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The daily scrum is a short synchronisation for the developers. Step 2: The Scrum Guide fixes it at 15 minutes, held daily at the same time and place. Step 3: Other events scale with sprint length — planning up to 8 hours for a one-month sprint. Step 4: Treating it as a lengthy status meeting for managers is the anti-pattern.

quiz.q: Which pair lists XP practices?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: XP is an agile method built on engineering practices. Step 2: Pair programming and test-driven development (write the failing test first) are signature XP practices, along with continuous integration and small releases. Step 3: The first option lists Scrum events and the third lists Scrum artifacts. Step 4: JAD workshops and 4GL tools belong to RAD.

prerequisites: Straight-line equations and partial derivatives (Engineering Mathematics I)
Basic probability and expected value
intro: Machine Learning enters the B.Tech CSE scheme in Semester 6, and its Unit 1 is the dependable scorer: classify the learning paradigm of a scenario, then derive or numerically fit a least-squares line and run gradient-descent steps — the repeated the state technical universities pattern over the last five years. The unit also introduces logistic regression as the bridge to classification.
objectives: Classify tasks as supervised (regression or classification), unsupervised or reinforcement learning with justified labels
Fit $y = a + bx$ by least squares using the normal equations and predict at a new point
Run and analyse gradient-descent updates, including learning-rate failure modes
Explain logistic regression: sigmoid hypothesis, decision boundary and cross-entropy loss

concepts.statement: **Supervised learning** trains on labelled pairs $(x, y)$ — **regression** for continuous targets, **classification** for discrete labels; **unsupervised learning** finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering, dimensionality reduction, association rules); **reinforcement learning** learns a **policy** from delayed **rewards** through interaction with an environment.
concepts.detail: The scenario question — spam filtering, customer segmentation, game playing — is worth 2 marks every session; label by the signal present: labels → supervised, none → unsupervised, rewards → reinforcement.

concepts.term: Linear regression and the normal equations
concepts.statement: With hypothesis $h_\theta(x) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x$ and cost $J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}(h_\theta(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)})^2$, the minimiser satisfies the **normal equations**: $b = \frac{m\sum xy - \sum x \sum y}{m\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2}$ and $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$ (vector form $\theta = (X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty$).
concepts.detail: Numericals supply 3–4 points and ask for the line and one prediction — tabulate $\sum x$, $\sum y$, $\sum xy$ and $\sum x^2$ first. Swapping the numerator pair or dropping $m$ are the classic slips; note that $a = \bar y - b\bar x$ means the fitted line always passes through the centroid.

concepts.statement: **Batch gradient descent** iterates $\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_j}$ — for MSE this is $\theta_1 := \theta_1 - \frac{\alpha}{m}\sum (h_\theta(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)})\,x^{(i)}$ — with the learning rate $\alpha$ controlling stability; all parameters update **simultaneously**.
concepts.detail: Assessments ask for 2–3 iterations on a toy cost function. Diagnosis rules: too small $\alpha$ = slow crawl, too large $\alpha$ = oscillation or divergence. Gradient descent also scales to large feature counts where the normal-equation matrix inverse at $O(n^3)$ does not.

concepts.statement: For binary labels, **logistic regression** squashes a linear score through the sigmoid $g(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \in (0, 1)$, modelling $P(y = 1 \mid x) = g(\theta^T x)$ with **decision boundary** $\theta^T x = 0$ and cost $J = -\frac{1}{m}\sum [y \log h + (1 - y)\log(1 - h)]$ — **cross-entropy, not MSE**.
concepts.detail: Know $g(0) = 0.5$, $g(2) \approx 0.88$ and $g(-z) = 1 - g(z)$. Why not MSE: the squared error on a sigmoid is non-convex with vanishing gradients, while cross-entropy is convex for this model. Despite the name it is a classifier, not a regressor.

concepts.statement: **Underfitting (high bias)** = too simple a hypothesis; **overfitting (high variance)** = fitting noise, shown by a widening train-versus-test gap; defences are more features (fixes bias), more data or regularisation $J + \lambda\sum \theta_j^2$ (fixes variance), judged always on a held-out **test split** never used for training.
concepts.detail: Short-note questions want the overfitting sketch, the two curves and one remedy each. Reporting training accuracy as performance is the flagged error — the test set must stay untouched until final evaluation.

examples.title: Least-squares line and prediction
examples.problem: Fit a straight line $y = a + bx$ by least squares to the data (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5) and predict $y$ at $x = 4$.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Tabulate the sums: $m = 3$, $\sum x = 6$, $\sum y = 10$, $\sum xy = 2 + 6 + 15 = 23$ and $\sum x^2 = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Slope: $b = \frac{m\sum xy - \sum x \sum y}{m\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2} = \frac{69 - 60}{42 - 36} = \frac{9}{6} = 1.5$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Intercept: $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} = \frac{10}{3} - 1.5 \times \frac{6}{3} = 0.333$, so the fitted line is $\hat{y} = 0.33 + 1.5x$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Prediction at $x = 4$: $\hat{y} = 0.333 + 6 = 6.33$. The residuals at the data points are $+0.17$, $-0.33$ and $+0.17$, and the line passes through the centroid $(2, 10/3)$ as the normal equations guarantee.

examples.result: $\hat{y} = 0.33 + 1.5x$; the predicted value at $x = 4$ is about $6.33$.

examples.title: Gradient descent iterations
examples.problem: Run three iterations of gradient descent on $J(w) = (w - 3)^2$ starting from $w_0 = 0$ with $\alpha = 0.1$, and explain what happens if $\alpha = 1$.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: The update rule is $w := w - \alpha \cdot 2(w - 3)$. First step: $w_1 = 0 - 0.1 \times 2(0 - 3) = 0.6$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Each step multiplies the gap to the optimum by $(1 - 2\alpha) = 0.8$, so $w_k = 3 - 3(0.8)^k \to 3$ — steady geometric convergence.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: With $\alpha = 1$ the update becomes $w := 6 - w$: the iterates oscillate $0, 6, 0, 6, \ldots$ forever — the too-large learning-rate failure mode that assessments want named.

examples.result: $w_1 = 0.6$, $w_2 = 1.08$, $w_3 = 1.464$, converging to 3 geometrically; $\alpha = 1$ oscillates without ever converging.

keyTakeaways: Labels → supervised (regression or classification); no labels → unsupervised; rewards → reinforcement.
Least-squares line: $b = \frac{m\sum xy - \sum x\sum y}{m\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2}$ with $a = \bar y - b\bar x$, always through the centroid.
Gradient descent $\theta := \theta - \alpha\nabla J$: small $\alpha$ crawls, large $\alpha$ oscillates or diverges; updates are simultaneous.
Logistic regression outputs $g(\theta^Tx) \in (0, 1)$ probabilities with boundary $\theta^Tx = 0$ and the convex cross-entropy loss.

quiz.q: Grouping a shop’s customers into segments without any labelled categories is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Look for the training signal — labels or rewards. Step 2: Neither is provided, only customer feature vectors. Step 3: Discovering groups in unlabelled data is clustering, an unsupervised task. Step 4: Supervised learning would need segments already labelled by someone.

quiz.q: For the least-squares fit on the data (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), the slope $b$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Tabulate $\sum x = 6$, $\sum y = 10$, $\sum xy = 23$, $\sum x^2 = 14$, $m = 3$. Step 2: Numerator $= 3(23) - 6(10) = 9$. Step 3: Denominator $= 3(14) - 36 = 6$, so $b = 1.5$. Step 4: The value $0.33$ is the intercept $a$ — the classic mix-up.

quiz.q: The sigmoid $g(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$ satisfies
quiz.explanation: Step 1: At $z = 0$ we have $e^{0} = 1$, so $g(0) = 1/2$. Step 2: As $z \to \infty$, $e^{-z} \to 0$ and $g \to 1$. Step 3: As $z \to -\infty$, $g \to 0$ while staying positive. Step 4: Hence the output is a probability in the open interval $(0, 1)$ — never negative and never equal to 1.

quiz.q: Training accuracy 99% but test accuracy 62% indicates
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Compare train and test performance — the large gap is the signature. Step 2: The model memorised the training data including its noise. Step 3: That is overfitting, i.e. high variance; remedies are more data, regularisation or a simpler model. Step 4: Underfitting would show poor scores on both sets.

prerequisites: KCL and KVL for simple resistive circuits
Matrix multiplication and transpose
Two-terminal elements: resistors and ideal sources as branches
intro: Every Network Analysis paper (the state technical university KEC303 / the state technical university Semester 3) begins with the graph: strip the elements away and keep only the connection pattern. Topology decides how many independent KCL and KVL equations you must write before any numbers appear. Mastering tree, incidence, tie-set and cut-set matrices turns messy mesh and nodal analysis into a mechanical procedure worth easy marks.
objectives: Draw the graph of a network and count tree branches, links and independent loops for any connected graph
Write the reduced incidence matrix $A$ and use the formulations $A i_b = 0$ (KCL) and $v_b = A^T v_n$ (KVL)
Construct fundamental tie-set and cut-set matrices from a chosen tree and state their sizes
Solve the nodal equations of a resistive network straight from the incidence formulation

concepts.statement: A **directed graph** replaces every two-terminal element by a **branch** joining two **nodes**; a **tree** is any connected subgraph containing all $n$ nodes but no closed path, and it always has **$n - 1$ twigs** with the remaining **$b - n + 1$ links** forming the co-tree.
concepts.detail: Every link added to the tree closes exactly one loop, so a connected graph has exactly $b - n + 1$ independent loops and $n - 1$ independent node equations. Assessments love the counting question "how many links / twigs / loops" — draw the graph, never guess from the circuit diagram. Sources stay in as branches here; killing sources is the Thevenin exercise of Section 10.2, a completely different operation.

concepts.statement: The **reduced incidence matrix** $A$ is $(n-1) \times b$ with $a_{kj} = +1$ if branch $j$ leaves node $k$, $-1$ if it enters and $0$ otherwise; KCL becomes $A i_b = 0$ and branch voltages follow node voltages as $v_b = A^T v_n$.
concepts.detail: The rank of $A$ is $n - 1$ for a connected graph because the reference-node row is dropped. Sign conventions must stay consistent — one flipped arrow and the matrix system turns singular. Choosing the reference at the node with the most branches shortens the algebra, a trick worth marks in long problems.

concepts.statement: Each **link** of the co-tree closes exactly one **fundamental loop** through the tree; collecting orientations row-wise gives the $(b-n+1) \times b$ **tie-set matrix** $B$, and KVL reads $B v_b = 0$ with loop currents entering as $i_b = B^T i_L$.
concepts.detail: The f-loop direction is fixed by its own link. Substituting Ohm law and $i_b = B^T i_L$ produces the familiar mesh-resistance equations — mesh analysis is just tie-set analysis on the natural tree of a planar graph. The orthogonality $B A^T = 0$ is a favourite two-mark proof.

concepts.statement: A **cut-set** is a minimal set of branches whose removal splits the graph into two parts; each **twig** defines one fundamental cut-set, giving the $(n-1) \times b$ **cut-set matrix** $Q$ with KCL as $Q i_b = 0$ and $v_b = Q^T v_t$.
concepts.detail: The f-cut-set direction is set by its twig, and $Q$ is the machine form of "total current leaving a supernode is zero". Numericals ask sizes: $Q$ is $(n-1) \times b$ and $B$ is $(b-n+1) \times b$, with $Q B^T = 0$ linking them. Twig voltages as variables generalise node analysis.

concepts.statement: The number of possible trees of a **complete graph** on $n$ nodes is $n^{n-2}$ (Cayley), e.g. $4^2 = 16$ trees for four nodes; when voltage sources or floating elements break the pure admittance pattern, nodal analysis upgrades to **modified nodal analysis (MNA)**.
concepts.detail: MNA appends extra rows for the branch currents that cannot be eliminated (voltage-source currents), keeping the incidence-based structure intact — SPICE works this way. The counting question "trees of a complete graph with 4 nodes" (answer 16) appears verbatim in the state technical university papers; remember each such tree has $n - 1 = 3$ twigs.

examples.title: Topology bookkeeping of a five-node graph
examples.problem: A connected network graph has $n = 5$ nodes and $b = 8$ branches. Find the number of twigs, links, independent loops, the rank of the incidence matrix, and the sizes of the fundamental tie-set and cut-set matrices.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
twigs = n - 1 = 4 ; links = b - n + 1 = 8 - 5 + 1 = 4
```
A tree on 5 nodes always uses $n - 1 = 4$ twigs; the remaining $8 - 4 = 4$ branches are the links of the co-tree.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Each link closes exactly one independent loop, so the graph has $b - n + 1 = 4$ fundamental loops — exactly the number of independent KVL equations mesh analysis will need.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: KCL supplies $n - 1 = 4$ independent node equations, and the reduced incidence matrix $A$ is $(n-1) \times b = 4 \times 8$ with rank $4$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Hence $B$ is $4 \times 8$ (one row per link) and $Q$ is $4 \times 8$ (one row per twig); the check $BA^T = 0$ must hold identically, a 30-second self-verification in the assessment.

examples.result: 4 twigs, 4 links, 4 independent loops, rank $A = 4$; $B$ is $4\times8$ and $Q$ is $4\times8$.

examples.title: Nodal analysis from the incidence formulation
examples.problem: A 5 A current source feeds node 1 of a network whose conductances are $G_{10} = 1\ \text{S}$ (node 1 to ground), $G_{12} = 2\ \text{S}$ (between nodes 1 and 2) and $G_{20} = 2\ \text{S}$ (node 2 to ground). Find both node voltages.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
node 1: (1+2)V1 - 2V2 = 5 ; node 2: -2V1 + (2+2)V2 = 0
```
Pick node 0 as reference. The node-admittance form $A Y_b A^T v_n = i_s$ gives $3V_1 - 2V_2 = 5$ and $-2V_1 + 4V_2 = 0$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: The second equation gives $V_1 = 2V_2$; substitute into the first: $3(2V_2) - 2V_2 = 4V_2 = 5$.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Hence $V_2 = 1.25$ V and $V_1 = 2.5$ V.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: KCL check at node 1: current down $G_{10}$ is $2.5 \times 1 = 2.5$ A and current towards node 2 is $2(2.5 - 1.25) = 2.5$ A — exactly the injected 5 A.

examples.result: $V_1 = 2.5$ V and $V_2 = 1.25$ V, with the source current fully accounted for by KCL.

keyTakeaways: A tree on $n$ nodes has $n-1$ twigs; the co-tree holds the $b-n+1$ links, and each link defines one independent loop.
The incidence matrix encodes both laws: $Ai_b = 0$ for KCL and $v_b = A^Tv_n$ for KVL, with rank $n-1$.
Tie-set matrix $B$ ($(b-n+1)\times b$) carries KVL $Bv_b = 0$; cut-set matrix $Q$ ($(n-1)\times b$) carries KCL $Qi_b = 0$; always $BA^T = 0$.
A complete graph $K_n$ has $n^{n-2}$ spanning trees — 16 for four nodes, 125 for five.

quiz.q: A connected graph has 15 branches and 9 nodes. The number of links is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Links are the co-tree branches, $b - n + 1$. Step 2: Substitute: $15 - 9 + 1 = 7$. Step 3: The twigs number $n - 1 = 8$, which is the planted distractor. Step 4: Links plus twigs must total 15 branches, confirming $7 + 8 = 15$.

quiz.q: The rank of the reduced incidence matrix of a connected graph with 6 nodes is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Dropping the reference node leaves $n - 1$ independent rows. Step 2: Those rows are independent KCL equations at the remaining nodes. Step 3: Hence rank $= 6 - 1 = 5$. Step 4: Rank 6 is impossible because all six node rows sum to zero.

quiz.q: The number of possible trees of a complete graph with four nodes is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Cayley formula: spanning trees of $K_n$ equal $n^{n-2}$. Step 2: With $n = 4$: $4^2 = 16$. Step 3: Each tree has 3 twigs, so twig-counting alone undercounts. Step 4: 64 is the $4^3$ exponent trap.

quiz.q: Which matrix equation is the node form of Kirchhoff current law?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: KCL is a statement about currents meeting at nodes. Step 2: Each row of the incidence matrix sums branch currents at one node, giving $Ai_b = 0$. Step 3: $Bv_b = 0$ is KVL and $v_b = A^Tv_n$ maps node voltages to branch voltages. Step 4: $Q i_b = 0$ is the cut-set version of KCL, but the canonical node form is $Ai_b = 0$.

prerequisites: Elementary calculus: integrating decaying exponentials
Complex exponentials $e^{j\omega t}$ and the Euler formula
Unit step $u(t)$ and unit impulse basics
intro: Signals & Systems (KEC403 / the state technical university Semester 4) opens by sorting every signal into classes: continuous or discrete, periodic or not, energy or power. University papers test exactly these classification drills — periodicity of a sum, energy of a decaying exponential, stability of a system — because a wrong class means every later formula (Fourier, Laplace, z) is misapplied. This section builds the sorting machinery the whole semester reuses.
objectives: Classify signals as continuous/discrete, periodic/aperiodic, energy/power and deterministic/random
Compute signal energy $E = \int |x(t)|^2 dt$ and test periodicity for both CT sums and discrete sinusoids
Test systems for linearity, time-invariance, causality and BIBO stability
Explain why $e^{j2n}$ is not periodic although $e^{j2t}$ is — the classic assessment trap

concepts.statement: A **continuous-time signal** $x(t)$ is defined for every $t$; a **discrete-time signal** $x[n]$ exists only at integer indices $n$, and when amplitudes are also quantised the signal is fully **digital**.
concepts.detail: Deterministic signals are given by formula; random signals (noise) only by statistics. Sampling turns CT into DT while quantisation discretises amplitude — two different operations that students constantly swap in viva questions. Chapters 14.4 and 16 chain them: sample first, quantise second.

concepts.statement: $x(t)$ is **periodic** if $x(t + T) = x(t)$ for some $T > 0$; a sum of sinusoids is periodic iff the ratio of any two periods is **rational**, with $T_0$ the LCM. For $x[n] = \cos(\Omega_0 n)$ periodicity needs $\frac{\Omega_0}{2\pi} = \frac{p}{q}$ rational, giving $N = q$ samples.
concepts.detail: The killer trap: $e^{j2t}$ is periodic with $T = \pi$, but $e^{j2n}$ is NOT periodic because $\frac{2}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{\pi}$ is irrational — no integer N reproduces the sample sequence. Assessment favourite: $\cos(0.3\pi n)$ has $\frac{0.3\pi}{2\pi} = \frac{3}{20}$, so $N = 20$.

concepts.statement: **Energy** $E = \lim_{T \to \infty} \int_{-T/2}^{T/2} |x(t)|^2 dt$ and **power** $P = \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T} \int_{-T/2}^{T/2} |x(t)|^2 dt$; an energy signal has finite $E$ (then $P = 0$), while a periodic signal has finite $P$ with $E \to \infty$.
concepts.detail: $tu(t)$ is neither — its energy and power both blow up. For $x(t) = Ae^{-at}u(t)$ with $a > 0$: $E = \frac{A^2}{2a}$; for $A\cos\omega_0 t$: $P = \frac{A^2}{2}$. Papers ask "classify the signal" — compute $E$ first, then $P$, and quote both numbers.

concepts.statement: A system is **linear** iff homogeneity and additivity both hold; it is **time-invariant** iff $x(t) \to y(t)$ implies $x(t - t_0) \to y(t - t_0)$ for every shift $t_0$.
concepts.detail: $y(t) = x(2t)$ is linear but time-varying (a shift before compression becomes a doubled shift after it). The amplitude modulator $y(t) = x(t)\cos\omega_c t$ is also linear but time-VARYING: the carrier samples a different value at the shifted instant. The integrator $y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} x(\tau) d\tau$ is linear, time-invariant and causal — the standard all-true example.

concepts.statement: A system is **causal** when the output never anticipates the input ($h(t) = 0$ for $t < 0$ for LTI systems) and **BIBO stable** iff $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |h(\tau)| d\tau < \infty$ (CT) or $\sum_k |h[k]| < \infty$ (DT).
concepts.detail: $h(t) = e^{-2t}u(t)$ is stable since $\int_0^{\infty} e^{-2t} dt = \frac{1}{2}$; $u(t)$ is NOT BIBO stable even though a step input gives a bounded-looking output — the definition demands a bounded output for EVERY bounded input, and any bounded non-decaying input accumulates without limit. Test the impulse response, never one lucky input.

examples.title: Energy of a one-sided exponential
examples.problem: Classify $x(t) = 3e^{-2t}u(t)$ as an energy or power signal and compute its energy.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
E = integral of 9 e^{-4t} dt from 0 to infinity = 9/4
```
Square the signal: $|x(t)|^2 = 9e^{-4t}$ for $t \ge 0$ and zero elsewhere, so $E = \int_0^{\infty} 9e^{-4t} dt$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Evaluate: $E = 9 \left[ \frac{e^{-4t}}{-4} \right]_0^{\infty} = 9 \times \frac{1}{4} = 2.25$ J (normalised to 1 $\Omega$).

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Because $E$ is finite, $P = 0$ and $x(t)$ is an energy signal; in general $Ae^{-at}u(t)$ stores $E = \frac{A^2}{2a}$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Scaling check: amplitude 1 would give $E = \frac{1}{4}$, and tripling amplitude multiplies energy by 9 — the square law assessors exploit to build distractors.

examples.result: $E = 2.25$ J and $P = 0$: an energy signal.

examples.title: Periodicity of CT sums and DT sinusoids
examples.problem: Find the fundamental period of $x(t) = 2\cos(\frac{\pi t}{4}) + 3\sin(\frac{\pi t}{8})$ and of $x[n] = \cos(0.3\pi n)$; is $e^{j2n}$ periodic?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Continuous-time terms: $T_1 = \frac{2\pi}{\pi/4} = 8$ s and $T_2 = \frac{2\pi}{\pi/8} = 16$ s.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: The ratio $\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{1}{2}$ is rational, so the sum is periodic with $T_0 = \mathrm{lcm}(8, 16) = 16$ s.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Discrete case: $\frac{\Omega_0}{2\pi} = \frac{0.3\pi}{2\pi} = \frac{3}{20}$ is rational, so $x[n]$ is periodic with $N = 20$ samples — the digital frequency must be a rational multiple of $2\pi$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: For $e^{j2n}$: $\frac{2}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{\pi}$ is irrational, so no integer $N$ satisfies $e^{j2(n+N)} = e^{j2n}$; it is aperiodic even though its continuous twin $e^{j2t}$ has period $\pi$.

examples.result: $T_0 = 16$ s; $N = 20$ samples; $e^{j2n}$ is not periodic.

keyTakeaways: A CT sum is periodic only for rational period ratios, with $T_0$ the LCM; a DT sinusoid is periodic only when $\frac{\Omega_0}{2\pi}$ is rational.
Energy signals have finite $E$ and zero $P$; periodic signals are power signals with infinite energy.
$y(t) = x(2t)$ and $y(t) = x(t)\cos\omega_c t$ are linear but time-varying — the two most-tested time-invariance failures.
BIBO stability means $\int |h| < \infty$ (or $\sum |h[k]| < \infty$), verified on the impulse response itself.

quiz.q: The energy of $x(t) = e^{-3t}u(t)$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Square first: $|x(t)|^2 = e^{-6t}$. Step 2: Integrate: $E = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-6t} dt = \frac{1}{6}$. Step 3: The shortcut $E = \frac{1}{2a}$ with $a = 3$ gives the same $\frac{1}{6}$. Step 4: $\frac{1}{3}$ is the trap of integrating $e^{-3t}$ before squaring.

quiz.q: The fundamental period of $x[n] = \cos(0.25\pi n)$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: For DT sinusoids compute $\frac{\Omega_0}{2\pi}$. Step 2: $\frac{0.25\pi}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{8}$ is rational with denominator 8. Step 3: Hence $N = 8$ samples. Step 4: Had the ratio been irrational, "not periodic" would be the answer — as with $e^{j2n}$.

quiz.q: Which of these discrete-time signals is NOT periodic?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Periodicity needs $\frac{\Omega_0}{2\pi}$ rational. Step 2: $\frac{\pi/3}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{6}$ gives $N = 6$; $\frac{0.2\pi}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{10}$ gives $N = 10$; $\frac{0.5\pi}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{4}$ gives $N = 4$. Step 3: $\frac{2}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{\pi}$ is irrational, so $e^{j2n}$ never repeats. Step 4: A constant phase offset never affects periodicity.

quiz.q: The system $y(t) = x(t)\cos(\omega_0 t)$ is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Scaling and additivity pass, so the system is linear. Step 2: A shifted input gives $x(t-\tau)\cos\omega_0 t$. Step 3: The shifted output is $x(t-\tau)\cos\omega_0(t-\tau)$, which differs because the carrier samples a different value. Step 4: This is the AM modulator — linear but time-varying.

prerequisites: Fourier series of periodic signals (preview of ECE Section 14.3)
Trigonometric integrals and the Parseval idea
Logarithm and decibel arithmetic
intro: Analog Communication (KEC401 / the state technical university Semester 4) starts where signals end: every message must be measured in watts and spectra before any modulation is designed. Papers open with a Fourier-series numerical — harmonic amplitudes of a square wave — then a power or noise computation in dB and dBm. These marks come quickly once the three tools (series, Parseval and $N = kTB$) are automatic.
objectives: Expand a periodic waveform into trigonometric or exponential Fourier series and sketch its line spectrum
Apply the Parseval power theorem to split total power among harmonics
Convert powers between watts, dB and dBm without sign or factor errors
Compute thermal noise $N = kTB$ and signal-to-noise ratio in dB

concepts.term: Fourier series and the line spectrum
concepts.statement: A periodic $x(t)$ of period $T$ expands as $x(t) = a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (a_n \cos n\omega_0 t + b_n \sin n\omega_0 t)$ with $\omega_0 = \frac{2\pi}{T}$; the **line spectrum** plots harmonic amplitude against $n f_0$, lines spaced $\frac{1}{T}$ apart.
concepts.detail: Symmetry halves the work: even $x$ keeps only $a_n$, odd $x$ only $b_n$, and half-wave symmetry kills the even harmonics. The bipolar square wave of levels $\pm A$ carries harmonics $\frac{4A}{n\pi}$ on odd $n$ only — the $\frac{4}{\pi}$ factor and odd-only pattern are the most quoted results in communication assessments.

concepts.statement: The compact form $x(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n e^{jn\omega_0 t}$ with $c_n = \frac{1}{T} \int_T x(t) e^{-jn\omega_0 t} dt$ gives **two-sided spectra**, $c_{-n} = c_n^{*}$ for real signals and $|c_n| = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{a_n^2 + b_n^2}$.
concepts.detail: Each trigonometric harmonic splits into $\pm n f_0$ lines of half amplitude. The standing trap: quoting $a_n$ where $|c_n|$ was asked (or vice versa) loses a factor of two — check whether the question says one-sided or two-sided spectrum before writing numbers.

concepts.statement: Total normalised power $P = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} |c_n|^2 = a_0^2 + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (a_n^2 + b_n^2)$ — **power splits additively over harmonics**.
concepts.detail: For the $\pm A$ square wave, $P = A^2$ with about 81% in the fundamental and 90% once the third harmonic is added — the Parseval answer to "what fraction of power survives a band-limiting filter". Channel truncation causes distortion exactly computable this way.

concepts.statement: Power ratios use $\text{dB} = 10 \log_{10} \frac{P_2}{P_1}$ and absolute power uses **dBm**, $\text{dBm} = 10\log_{10} \frac{P}{1\ \text{mW}}$; halving power is $-3$ dB and a decade is 10 dB.
concepts.detail: Voltage ratios across equal impedances use $20\log$. Traps that cost marks: adding dB means multiplying powers; dBm + dB stays dBm; doubling voltage is $+6$ dB. Anchor values to memorise: 1 mW is 0 dBm, 1 W is $+30$ dBm and 1 $\mu$W is $-30$ dBm.

concepts.term: Thermal noise, SNR and noise figure
concepts.statement: Available **thermal noise** power is $N = kTB$ with $k = 1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K, giving the anchor $-174$ dBm/Hz at $T_0 = 290$ K; the **noise figure** $F = \frac{SNR_{in}}{SNR_{out}} \ge 1$ means, in dB, $SNR_{out} = SNR_{in} - NF$.
concepts.detail: Every doubling of bandwidth adds 3 dB of noise — the shortcut $-174 + 10\log B$ is expected in assessments. The Friis cascade $F = F_1 + \frac{F_2 - 1}{G_1} + \cdots$ shows stage one dominating, which is why the low-noise amplifier sits first in every receiver chain.

examples.title: Harmonics and power of a square wave
examples.problem: A square wave switching between $\pm 5$ V has a period of 1 ms. Compute the amplitudes of the first three odd harmonics, the total normalised power, and the percentage of power carried by the fundamental.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text:
```text
odd harmonics only : a_n = 4A / (n pi) , A = 5 V
```
Half-wave symmetry keeps only odd harmonics with $a_n = \frac{4A}{n\pi}$: $a_1 = \frac{20}{\pi} = 6.37$ V, $a_3 = \frac{20}{3\pi} = 2.12$ V and $a_5 = \frac{20}{5\pi} = 1.27$ V.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Normalised power of the wave itself: mean-square of $\pm 5$ V is $P = A^2 = 25$ W.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Fundamental power by Parseval: $P_1 = \frac{a_1^2}{2} = \frac{(6.37)^2}{2} = 20.3$ W, i.e. $\frac{20.3}{25} \approx 81\%$ of the total.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Adding the third harmonic: $P_{1+3} = \frac{8A^2}{\pi^2}(1 + \frac{1}{9}) = 22.5$ W, so 90% of the power sits below $3f_0 = 3$ kHz — the Parseval justification for band-limiting channels.

examples.result: $a_1 = 6.37$ V, $a_3 = 2.12$ V, $a_5 = 1.27$ V; total power 25 W with about 81% in the fundamental.

examples.title: Thermal noise floor and SNR
examples.problem: A receiver of 200 kHz bandwidth operates at 290 K. If the delivered signal power is $-91$ dBm, find the thermal noise power in dBm and the SNR.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: In watts: $N = kTB = 1.38\times10^{-23} \times 290 \times 2\times10^5 = 8.0\times10^{-16}$ W.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Shortcut check: $-174 + 10\log_{10}(2\times10^5) = -174 + 53 = -121$ dBm — identical.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Hence $SNR = S - N = -91 - (-121) = 30$ dB, a 1000:1 power ratio; any front-end noise figure subtracts directly from this figure.

examples.result: $N \approx -121$ dBm and $SNR = 30$ dB.

keyTakeaways: A $\pm A$ square wave carries odd harmonics $\frac{4A}{n\pi}$ with total power $A^2$ and roughly 81% in the fundamental.
