Step 3: Any skew then momentarily synthesizes a code near full scale or zero, far from both endpoints of a nominally 1-LSB step, so the output spikes before settling. Step 4: The other options toggle only one or two switches, so no large intermediate excursion is possible; the major carry remains the classic worst case.

prerequisites: Sampling and quantization fundamentals (Section 1)
DAC output mapping (Section 2)
Comparator operation and priority encoding
intro: Given a code, how fast can you produce it? The flash converter answers "immediately" by brute force — a bank of comparators sniffing every decision level at once — while the successive-approximation converter answers "in N steps" by running a binary search with a DAC and a single comparator in a feedback loop. Between them they define the speed-resolution frontier of analog-to-digital conversion, and assessments favor this section because the numbers are crisp: $2^N - 1$ comparators, one clock cycle, N clock cycles, throughput $f_{clk}/N$. The quiet hero is the sample-and-hold, without which the SAR search corrupts its own earlier decisions. This section sizes the flash hardware, traces the SAR register bit by bit, compares conversion times numerically, and states the track-and-hold requirements that any serious design must write down.
objectives: Size the comparator bank, resistor string and encoder of an N-bit flash converter
Trace a complete successive-approximation search cycle by cycle
Compute conversion times and maximum throughputs for flash and SAR converters
Specify acquisition, aperture and droop requirements of the track-and-hold front end

concepts.statement: A flash ADC compares the input against **all $2^N - 1$ decision levels simultaneously**: a resistor string of $2^N$ equal resistors between the reference rails feeds $2^N - 1$ latched comparators, and a priority encoder collapses their thermometer code into an N-bit result — one clock cycle per conversion.
concepts.detail: Every comparator whose threshold lies below $V_{in}$ fires, so the comparator outputs form a thermometer — a row of 1s above a row of 0s — and the encoder need only find the boundary. Real parts add bubble logic because a metastable comparator can fire out of sequence near the transition. The price of parallelism is input capacitance: $2^N - 1$ comparator input pairs load the source directly, which is why flash inputs are usually buffered.

concepts.statement: Each extra bit **doubles the comparator count** — 63 at 6 bits, 255 at 8 bits, 1,023 at 10 bits — along with input capacitance and static power, which is why practical flash converters stop near 8 bits.
concepts.detail: Two more bits quadruple the bank, the reference-string loading and the die area, while each comparator still burns bias current whether it toggles or not — flash power is roughly static, not conversion-rate-dependent. The family survives where nothing else is fast enough: oscilloscope front ends, optical receivers and direct RF sampling at hundreds of megasamples to gigasamples per second, at 4–8 bits of resolution.

concepts.statement: The successive-approximation register runs a **binary search on the code**: set the MSB, let the internal DAC present $2^{N-1}$ to one comparator, keep the bit if the DAC level is below the held input, clear it otherwise, then descend bit by bit — N trials yield the N-bit code.
concepts.detail: Register, internal DAC and one comparator form a feedback loop that is exactly the bisection method in hardware: each trial halves the remaining voltage uncertainty, so after N trials the residual is below one LSB. The elegance is the scaling — doubling resolution adds one clock cycle and one DAC bit, not another few hundred comparators — which is why SAR dominates the 8-to-18-bit, kilo-to-megasample middle ground of data acquisition.

concepts.statement: Flash converts in **one clock cycle**; SAR converts in **N clock cycles** (plus optional acquisition and status cycles), so a SAR’s maximum sampling rate is about $$f_{sample} \le \frac{f_{clk}}{N}, \qquad T_{conv} = \frac{N}{f_{clk}}.$$
concepts.detail: Reference numbers worth memorizing: a 10-bit SAR at 2 MHz takes 5 µs per conversion (200 ksamples/s); a 12-bit SAR at 1 MHz takes 12 µs (about 83 ksamples/s); an 8-bit flash at 20 MHz takes 50 ns (20 Msamples/s). Assessment problems routinely pair these with a channel budget — when one ADC is multiplexed across M channels, divide the throughput by M before answering.

concepts.statement: The track-and-hold (sample-and-hold) acquires the input to the required accuracy, then **freezes it for the whole conversion**; its acquisition time, aperture delay, aperture jitter and droop set the front-end limits of the ADC.
concepts.detail: Acquisition to N bits needs about $0.7N$ RC time constants of settling — 8.3 τ for 12 bits — before the hold command. Aperture jitter converts to a hard SNR ceiling (the formula arrives in Section 5), and droop — the decay of the held voltage through leakage on the hold capacitor — must stay under ½ LSB for the conversion duration, which sizes the capacitor against leakage current. SAR cannot function without the frozen sample, because every bit decision must be judged against the same value; flash needs no dedicated hold at low resolution since its comparators do the sampling, though a track-and-hold still sharpens the effective sampling instant.

concepts.statement: Flash owns the **few-bit, gigasample corner**; SAR owns the **8–18-bit, kilo-to-megasample middle ground** where energy per conversion matters — a straight resolution-speed-power trade.
concepts.detail: A SAR’s cost grows gently: one more bit adds a clock cycle and a DAC element, and its power scales with conversion rate, so idling is cheap. A flash bank pays statically in comparators, reference string and clock distribution no matter how slowly it samples. In selection questions, the standard answers line up: multiplexed industrial sensing and general data acquisition point to SAR; instantaneous waveform capture at low resolution points to flash; the two families bracket the pipeline and sigma-delta options of the next section.

examples.title: Sizing a flash converter
examples.problem: Specify the comparator bank and resistor string for a 6-bit flash ADC, and determine the hardware growth if two more bits are needed.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Decision levels: a 6-bit converter has $2^6 = 64$ codes, hence $2^6 - 1 = 63$ transitions to detect → 63 comparators.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Reference divider: a string of $2^6 = 64$ equal resistors between the reference rails provides the 63 taps (each tap one comparator threshold).

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: For 8 bits: $2^8 - 1 = 255$ comparators and $2^8 = 256$ string resistors, with the encoder widening from 63-line thermometer logic to 255-line.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Growth: $\frac{255}{63} \approx 4$ — two added bits quadruple the bank, the input capacitance and the static power, which is why flash rarely passes 8 bits.

examples.result: 6-bit: 63 comparators + 64 resistors; 8-bit: 255 + 256 — a ×4 hardware increase for just two bits.

examples.title: Conversion-time comparison
examples.problem: Compare the conversion time and maximum throughput of (a) a 10-bit SAR clocked at 2 MHz with one bit decision per cycle, and (b) an 8-bit flash clocked at 20 MHz with one cycle per conversion. What would the SAR achieve at 20 MHz?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: SAR: $T_{conv} = N/f_{clk} = \frac{10}{2\ \text{MHz}} = 5\ \mu\text{s}$, so the maximum throughput is $\frac{1}{5\ \mu\text{s}} = 200$ ksamples/s.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Flash: $T_{conv} = \frac{1}{20\ \text{MHz}} = 50$ ns, so 20 Msamples/s.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Ratio: the flash is 100× faster in throughput, despite its lower resolution.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Same clock: the SAR at 20 MHz would take $\frac{10}{20\ \text{MHz}} = 0.5\ \mu\text{s}$ → 2 Msamples/s — still 10× behind the flash, because SAR pays N cycles per sample while flash pays one.

examples.result: SAR 5 µs / 200 ksamples/s; flash 50 ns / 20 Msamples/s; even at 20 MHz the SAR reaches only 2 Msamples/s.

examples.title: Cycle-by-cycle SAR trace
examples.problem: A 3-bit SAR ADC with a 0–5 V range digitizes a steady 3.3 V input. Trace the register, the internal DAC and the comparator through every cycle.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Cycle 1 — set MSB: DAC presents 100 → $1 \times \frac{5}{2} = 2.500$ V. Comparator: input 3.3 V > 2.5 V → keep the bit.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Cycle 2 — try the next bit: DAC presents 110 → 3.750 V. Now 3.3 V < 3.75 V → clear the bit back to 0.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Cycle 3 — last bit: DAC presents 101 → 3.125 V. Since 3.3 V > 3.125 V → keep the bit.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Final code 101, DAC level 3.125 V. The residual error is $3.3 - 3.125 = 0.175$ V = 0.28 LSB, and measured from the code centre (3.4375 V) only 0.22 LSB — comfortably inside the ±½ LSB quantization band.

examples.result: Final code 101 (3.125 V DAC level); the 0.175 V residual is 0.28 LSB, within one LSB of the true input and 0.22 LSB from the code centre.

keyTakeaways: Flash = $2^N - 1$ comparators + $2^N$ resistor string + priority encoder, one clock cycle per conversion — fastest family, but area, capacitance and power double with every bit, capping it near 8 bits.
SAR = one comparator + internal DAC + successive-approximation register performing a binary search: N clock cycles, $T_{conv} = N/f_{clk}$, throughput ≈ $f_{clk}/N$.
The track-and-hold is mandatory for SAR: acquisition must settle (~0.7N time constants) before the search, and droop must stay under ½ LSB for its duration.
Numbers to carry: 8-bit flash → 255 comparators; 12-bit SAR at 1 MHz → 12 µs (≈83 ksamples/s); 10-bit SAR at 2 MHz → 5 µs (200 ksamples/s); multiplexing divides throughput by the channel count.

quiz.q: An 8-bit flash ADC requires how many comparators?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: A flash converter needs one comparator per decision level. Step 2: The number of transitions between $2^8 = 256$ codes is $2^8 - 1 = 255$. Step 3: 256 is the resistor count (or the code count) — the classic distractor. Step 4: So the design uses 255 comparators, 256 string resistors and one priority encoder.

quiz.q: A 12-bit SAR ADC uses a 1 MHz clock and settles one bit per clock cycle. Its conversion time is about
quiz.explanation: Step 1: A SAR needs one clock cycle per bit decision. Step 2: $T_{conv} = N/f_{clk} = \frac{12}{1\ \text{MHz}} = 12\ \mu\text{s}$. Step 3: The matching throughput is $\frac{1}{12\ \mu\text{s}} \approx 83$ ksamples/s. Step 4: 12 ms would mean a millisecond per bit — a units slip; and even at the same clock a flash part would finish in a single 1 µs cycle.

quiz.q: A SAR ADC can complete its binary search correctly only if
options: the reference voltage is larger than the input
the input is held constant during the N decision cycles (track-and-hold)
the comparator is clocked N times faster than the internal DAC
the input changes by exactly one LSB per cycle
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Each bit decision compares the input against an internal DAC level. Step 2: If the input moves mid-search, a bit kept or cleared against an earlier level no longer describes the final value — earlier decisions corrupt the code. Step 3: The track-and-hold freezes one sample for the whole search so all N comparisons are consistent. Step 4: Reference sizing and comparator speed affect accuracy and maximum clock rate, not the logical validity of the search.

quiz.q: A 6-bit flash converter and a 16-bit SAR converter both run from a 10 MHz clock (flash: one cycle per conversion; SAR: one bit per cycle). Their approximate conversion times are
quiz.explanation: Step 1: One clock period at 10 MHz is 100 ns. Step 2: The flash converts in a single cycle: 100 ns. Step 3: The 16-bit SAR needs 16 cycles: $16 \times 100\ \text{ns} = 1.6\ \mu\text{s}$. Step 4: 16 µs would correspond to a 1 MHz clock — the common slip of mixing up clock rates between the two parts.

prerequisites: Op-amp integrator circuits
Flash and SAR conversion times (Section 3)
Sampling theorem and oversampling (Section 1)
intro: When the signal is a slow, noisy, near-DC sensor voltage and the requirement is digits of accuracy rather than speed, two architectures take over. The dual-slope integrating converter — the heart of every bench digital multimeter — wins precision not from exotic components but from a cancellation: the same clock counts the run-up and the run-down, so R, C and most offsets drop out of the result, and integrating over whole mains periods nulls 50/60 Hz pickup exactly. The sigma-delta converter attacks from the opposite direction, trading speed for resolution by massively oversampling a deliberately coarse (often 1-bit) quantizer, shaping its noise out of band, and digitally decimating — the route to 16–24 bits in audio and instrumentation. The pipeline family fills the high-speed middle ground between these and the flash/SAR pair of Section 3. Assessment questions here revolve around run-down counts, oversampling-ratio arithmetic, the dB-per-octave rules of noise shaping, and latency-versus-throughput reasoning.
objectives: Explain the run-up/run-down charge balance of the dual-slope converter and compute its counts
Choose integration times that null 50 Hz and 60 Hz interference
Compute oversampling ratio and the ENOB gains of noise shaping
Contrast dual-slope, sigma-delta and pipeline converters on speed, resolution and latency

concepts.statement: The integrator first ramps on the input for a fixed count $N_1$ (run-up), then ramps back on a reference of opposite polarity while a counter measures $N_2$ (run-down); charge balance gives $$\frac{V_{in}}{V_{ref}} = \frac{N_2}{N_1}.$$
concepts.detail: Run-up integrates $-V_{in}/RC$ for $T_1 = N_1 T_{clk}$; run-down integrates $+V_{ref}/RC$ until the integrator crosses zero, taking $T_2 = N_2 T_{clk}$. Equal and opposite integrals force $V_{in}T_1 = V_{ref}T_2$, and because both times are counted with the same clock, the reading depends only on the count ratio and $V_{ref}$ — R, C and long-term clock accuracy cancel, and a zero-input cycle auto-zeros offsets. That cancellation is the precision trick: multimeter-grade digits from modest parts, at a few readings per second.

concepts.statement: Choosing the run-up time equal to the mains period — **20 ms for 50 Hz, 16.7 ms for 60 Hz, 100 ms to null both** — makes the integral of the periodic interference exactly zero, because whole cycles cancel.
concepts.detail: A sinusoid (or any periodic waveform with zero mean) integrates to zero over an integer number of periods, so mains pickup contributes no net charge to the run-up. The rejection is a notch at the line frequency and its harmonics, degrading gracefully if the line drifts from nominal. The cost is speed: a 100 ms run-up means at most a few readings per second even before run-down — ideal for a voltmeter, hopeless for audio, and one more reminder that precision-DC and bandwidth are different products.

concepts.statement: Sampling at $\text{OSR} = \frac{f_s}{2f_B}$ times the Nyquist rate spreads the fixed quantization-noise power across a wider band, so the in-band share falls: **+3 dB (½ bit) per doubling of OSR**; a decimation filter then removes the out-of-band noise and returns the rate to $2f_B$.
concepts.detail: The total quantization-noise power (set by the LSB) does not change; oversampling merely spreads it over $f_s/2$ instead of $f_B$, so the fraction landing in-band scales as $1/\text{OSR}$. The digital decimation filter — typically a sinc/CIC structure — averages the stream and resamples it down. The honest limitation: ½ bit per octave means +2 bits costs a 16× rate increase, which is why plain oversampling stops being practical quickly and noise shaping takes over.

concepts.statement: A sigma-delta ADC wraps an integrator (loop filter) around a coarse — often **1-bit** — quantizer whose output drives a 1-bit feedback DAC; the loop pushes quantization noise toward $f_s/2$ (noise shaping, first-order NTF $(1 - z^{-1})$), buying about **+9 dB (1.5 bits) per octave of OSR**, or +15 dB (2.5 bits) for a second-order loop.
concepts.detail: The 1-bit output stream is a pulse-density copy of the input; digital decimation turns OSR stream bits into each output word. Two properties carry the family: the 1-bit feedback DAC has only two levels, so it is inherently linear and the converter is inherently monotonic; and the noise-shaping slope is set by loop order, so resolution scales with sample rate rather than with component matching. In round figures, a first-order 1-bit modulator at OSR = 64 delivers roughly 8–9 effective bits, and every doubling of the rate adds 1.5 more — the arithmetic assessment items probe (worked example 2).

concepts.statement: A pipeline ADC chains low-resolution stages, each resolving a few bits, subtracting them with an internal DAC and **amplifying the residue** for the next stage; samples flow stagewise, so throughput is one result per clock **after an N-stage latency**.
concepts.detail: Digital redundancy lets each stage’s comparators be sloppy — the next stage absorbs the error — which is what makes 12–16 bits at tens to hundreds of Msamples/s affordable. Latency is the fine print: the first result emerges only after every stage has handled its first sample, so in a streaming acquisition the delay is invisible, but inside a fast digital control loop N clocks of delay erode phase margin. The pipeline thus fills the gap between SAR (to ~10 Msamples/s) and flash (few bits, gsamples/s), at power that scales with both stages and rate.

concepts.statement: The families partition the design space: **dual-slope** (slow, line-rejecting, 4½–8 digits), **sigma-delta** (16–24 bits, Hz-to-kHz bandwidth), **SAR** (8–18 bits, kS to ~10 MS/s), **pipeline** (10–16 bits, 10s–100s MS/s), **flash** (≤ 8 bits, gsamples/s).
concepts.detail: Given a bandwidth, a resolution and a power budget, the architecture choice is almost automatic — and "name the architecture" is a standard selection-assessment and interview pattern. Sensors and DC metrology point to dual-slope or sigma-delta; multiplexed industrial acquisition points to SAR; communications and imaging front ends point to pipeline; the few-bit, lowest-latency corner belongs to flash. Power tracks the map too: SAR energy scales with conversions, flash burns statically, sigma-delta trades clock rate for bits at microwatt levels.

examples.title: Dual-slope numerics and mains rejection
examples.problem: A dual-slope ADC counts at 100 kHz with a fixed run-up of $N_1 = 2{,}000$ counts against $V_{ref} = 2.000$ V. (a) Find the run-down count for $V_{in} = 1.500$ V. (b) Why does this run-up reject 50 Hz pickup?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Clock period $T_{clk} = 10\ \mu\text{s}$, so the run-up lasts $T_1 = 2000 \times 10\ \mu\text{s} = 20$ ms — exactly one 50 Hz period.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Charge balance: $N_2 = N_1 \cdot \frac{V_{in}}{V_{ref}} = 2000 \times \frac{1.5}{2.0} = 1500$ counts.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Run-down duration $T_2 = 1500 \times 10\ \mu\text{s} = 15$ ms; the full conversion takes at most $20 + 15 = 35$ ms, allowing at least ~28 readings per second.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Rejection: any 50 Hz pickup integrates to zero over whole periods, so it adds no net charge during run-up — the reading is immune to the mains.

examples.result: $N_2 = 1{,}500$ counts; the 20 ms run-up places an exact null at 50 Hz (use 100 ms to null 50 and 60 Hz together).

examples.title: Oversampling arithmetic
examples.problem: A 20 kHz audio band is sampled at 2.56 MHz by a sigma-delta modulator. (a) What is the OSR? (b) How many effective bits does first-order noise shaping add over the coarse quantizer, and how many more with second order? (c) What sample rate would buy 3 additional first-order bits?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Oversampling ratio: $\text{OSR} = \frac{f_s}{2f_B} = \frac{2.56\ \text{MHz}}{2 \times 20\ \text{kHz}} = \frac{2.56\ \text{M}}{40\ \text{k}} = 64$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Octaves available: $\log_2 64 = 6$ doublings of the rate.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: First order gains 1.5 bits per octave: $6 \times 1.5 = +9$ effective bits; second order gains 2.5 per octave: $6 \times 2.5 = +15$ bits.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Three more bits at 1.5 bits/octave require $\frac{3}{1.5} = 2$ octaves → a ×4 rate: $4 \times 2.56\ \text{MHz} = 10.24\ \text{MHz}$.

examples.result: OSR = 64 (six octaves): +9 effective bits first order, +15 second order; quadrupling the rate to 10.24 MHz buys three more first-order bits.

examples.title: Pipeline latency versus throughput
examples.problem: A 10-stage pipeline ADC runs at 125 MHz. What are its throughput and conversion latency, and how do they compare with a 10-bit SAR clocked at 1 MHz?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Throughput: one sample enters and one result leaves per clock, so 125 Msamples/s.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Latency: the first result must traverse all 10 stages, $10 \times 8\ \text{ns} = 80$ ns after that sample entered.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: The SAR comparison: 10 bits at 1 MHz cost 10 µs per conversion → 100 ksamples/s, so the pipeline delivers 1,250× the sample rate at the same resolution.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Interpretation: in streaming acquisition the 80 ns latency is invisible, but in a fast digital control loop it delays the loop by 10 clock cycles — a real stability consideration that throughput numbers hide.

examples.result: 125 Msamples/s throughput with 80 ns (10-stage) latency; the SAR delivers 100 ksamples/s — the pipeline trades latency for over three orders of magnitude in throughput.

keyTakeaways: Dual-slope: $N_2 = N_1 V_{in}/V_{ref}$ — the reading is a ratio of counts, immune to R, C and clock-rate errors, with offsets removed by auto-zero; slow (tens of ms) but multimeter-precise.
Make run-up 20 ms (50 Hz), 16.7 ms (60 Hz) or 100 ms (both) and periodic interference integrates to exactly zero — the line-rejection notch every voltmeter uses.

Sigma-delta: OSR = $f_s/2f_B$; plain oversampling gains 3 dB/octave, first-order shaping 9 dB (1.5 bits), second order 15 dB (2.5 bits) — and the 1-bit feedback DAC makes the converter inherently monotonic.
Pipeline: throughput one result per clock, latency N stages — streaming-friendly but control-loop-hostile; it occupies the 10–16 bit, 10s–100s Msamples/s gap between SAR and flash.

quiz.q: A dual-slope ADC runs up for a fixed 2,000 counts with $V_{ref} = 4.0$ V. For $V_{in} = 1.0$ V the run-down count is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Charge balance gives $V_{in}T_1 = V_{ref}T_2$, hence $N_2 = N_1\frac{V_{in}}{V_{ref}}$. Step 2: $N_2 = 2000 \times \frac{1.0}{4.0} = 500$ counts. Step 3: The run-down is shorter than the run-up because the input is smaller than the reference — the slopes ratio directly. Step 4: 8,000 inverts the ratio, which would require $V_{in}$ four times the reference.

quiz.q: A dual-slope ADC best rejects 50 Hz mains pickup when the run-up time is
options: exactly 20 ms or an integer multiple of it
as short as possible, so interference cannot accumulate
randomized from one conversion to the next
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The integrator output depends on the time-average of the input over the run-up. Step 2: Any zero-mean periodic waveform averages to zero over whole numbers of periods. Step 3: 20 ms is exactly one 50 Hz period (16.7 ms is one 60 Hz period; 100 ms covers both). Step 4: 50 ms spans 2.5 periods, so a residual half-period of interference survives — only integer multiples null.

quiz.q: Doubling the oversampling ratio of a first-order sigma-delta modulator improves its in-band SQNR by about
quiz.explanation: Step 1: First-order noise shaping yields about 1.5 bits of resolution per octave of OSR. Step 2: Converting to decibels, $1.5 \times 6.02 \approx 9$ dB. Step 3: 3 dB is the gain of plain oversampling without shaping, and 15 dB belongs to a second-order loop. Step 4: So every doubling of the sample rate buys 9 dB — 1.5 bits — of in-band resolution.

quiz.q: A 10-stage pipeline ADC clocked at 125 MHz produces
options: one result every 10 clock cycles, and never more often
one result every clock cycle once the pipe is full, after about 10 cycles of latency
one result every 80 ns with zero startup latency
quiz.explanation: Step 1: In a pipeline, every stage works on a different sample during the same clock period. Step 2: Once all stages hold samples, one finished result emerges per clock — 125 Msamples/s. Step 3: But the first result appears only after the first sample traverses all 10 stages: $10 \times 8$ ns = 80 ns of latency. Step 4: The last option names the right number but wrongly claims zero latency — throughput and latency are different properties, and pipeline latency is exactly N stages.

prerequisites: Quantization and LSB arithmetic (Section 1)
Converter architectures of Sections 3 and 4
Decibels and rms noise basics
intro: A converter that meets its resolution on paper can still be wrong by several LSBs in the field: the transfer curve shifts, its slope drifts, steps go missing, and the sampling instant wobbles. The error vocabulary — offset, gain, INL, DNL, missing codes, monotonicity — is the language of every converter datasheet and of essentially every data-converter question in selection assessments, because it separates resolution (how many codes exist) from accuracy (how close each code is to the truth). This section defines each error with the transfer-graph picture that makes it intuitive, then quantifies the dynamic limits — aperture jitter’s SNR ceiling and sample-and-hold droop. It closes by assembling the full data-acquisition chain from sensor to digital word, and with the selection reasoning — resolution versus speed versus power — that decides which architecture a system actually gets.
objectives: Define, measure and convert offset and gain errors into LSB units
Read DNL and INL from a transfer characteristic and detect missing codes and non-monotonicity
Budget aperture jitter and sample-and-hold droop against a target SNR
Assemble a sensor-to-digital data-acquisition chain and select a converter from resolution-speed-power trade-offs

concepts.statement: **Offset error** is the parallel shift of the whole transfer curve from the ideal: the measured output when the code should produce exactly zero (or, for an ADC, the shift of every transition threshold), expressed in LSBs.
concepts.detail: On the transfer graph, the ideal staircase passes through the origin and the actual staircase is displaced vertically by the same amount at every code — same step heights, wrong address. Sources include op-amp and comparator input offsets and switch leakage. Offset is fully calibratable: measure the zero-scale point and subtract. A converter can have flawless step uniformity yet sit 5 LSBs off — resolution and accuracy are independent specifications, and conflating them is the classic assessment trap.

concepts.statement: **Gain error** is the deviation of the transfer-curve slope from ideal after offset is removed: the difference between the measured and ideal full-scale span, in LSBs or percent.
concepts.detail: Graphically, the staircase rotates about the (offset-corrected) zero point — the top codes land progressively too high or too low. Sources are reference tolerance, feedback-resistor mismatch and current-source scaling. Gain error is the second of the two calibratable errors: a two-point endpoint calibration removes offset first, then scales the span. What calibration cannot remove is curvature — the bow of the staircase that remains is the integral nonlinearity below.

concepts.statement: **Differential nonlinearity** measures each code step against the ideal 1 LSB: $\text{DNL}(k) = \frac{W_k}{\text{LSB}} - 1$; a code with $\text{DNL} \le -1$ LSB has zero (or negative) width and is a **missing code**.
concepts.detail: On the transfer graph the ideal staircase has equal treads of exactly 1 LSB; DNL is the tread-width error, code by code — for an ADC, the width between adjacent transition thresholds, for a DAC, the output step between adjacent codes. A width of 0.5 LSB is DNL = −0.5; a width of zero means the transition jumps straight past the code, which never appears in the output stream. The "no missing codes" guarantee requires DNL > −1 LSB everywhere, and weighted-resistor DACs with a mismatched MSB are the textbook way to violate it.

concepts.statement: **Integral nonlinearity** is the deviation of the code centres from the ideal straight line (endpoints or best-fit), in LSBs — the running accumulation of DNL — and **INL within ±½ LSB guarantees monotonicity**.
concepts.detail: Draw the straight line through the calibrated endpoints; INL is the bow of the staircase away from that line, and because each code’s position error is the sum of all preceding step errors, worst-case |INL| is the quoted number. Monotonicity — the output never reverses direction as the code increases — requires every step to be non-negative, i.e. DNL ≥ −1 LSB everywhere. It is not a cosmetic spec: a non-monotonic feedback DAC inside a control loop or an ADC’s internal loop creates spurious zero crossings and can force oscillation or hysteresis, so guaranteed-monotonic architectures (R-2R with matched units, segmented current steering) earn their premium.

concepts.statement: Timing uncertainty $t_j$ at the sampling instant limits SNR to $$\text{SNR}_{jitter} = -20\log_{10}\!\left(2\pi f_{in} t_j\right)\ \text{dB},$$ while the held value may droop by at most ½ LSB over the conversion: $\text{droop} < \frac{\text{LSB}/2}{T_{conv}}$.
concepts.detail: Intuition: sampling a sine of slope $2\pi f_{in}V$ with a timing error $t_j$ produces a voltage error near the slope times the jitter; taking rms values yields the formula. Landmark numbers: a 1 MHz input sampled with 1 ns rms jitter caps SNR at 44 dB — barely 7 bits, whatever the datasheet says; holding 12 bits (74 dB) at 2 MHz demands about 16 ps. Droop is the hold-side twin: leakage current discharging the hold capacitor must stay under ½ LSB for the conversion duration, which sizes the capacitor, while a larger capacitor slows acquisition — the compromise every sample-and-hold designer negotiates (worked example 3).

concepts.statement: A canonical DAQ chain runs **sensor → signal conditioning (amplify, filter, isolate) → multiplexer → sample-and-hold → ADC → digital processing**, and the converter is chosen from a resolution-speed-power-cost table, with multiplexing sharing one ADC across channels at the price of per-channel rate.
concepts.detail: Conditioning scales the sensor span onto the converter range and hosts the anti-alias pole(s); the economics of one MUX + one S/H + one ADC give per-channel rate = total throughput ÷ channels (8 channels on a 100-ksample/s converter → 12.5 ksamples/s each). When inter-channel phase matters — power quality, vibration analysis — per-channel sample-and-holds capture all channels simultaneously and pay for the extra capacitors. Selection reasoning: DC precision with line rejection → dual-slope; audio and precision sensors → sigma-delta; general multiplexed acquisition → SAR; high-speed streaming → pipeline; lowest latency at few bits → flash. Power then breaks ties: SAR scales with conversion count, flash burns statically, sigma-delta trades clock rate for bits.

examples.title: Offset and gain from a two-point measurement
examples.problem: An 8-bit 0–5 V DAC (LSB = 19.53 mV) measures +25 mV at code 0 and 5.015 V at code 255. Find the offset error and the gain error in LSBs.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Offset: the code-0 output should be 0 V, so the offset is $+25$ mV $= \frac{25}{19.53} = +1.28$ LSB.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Actual span between the endpoints: $5.015 - 0.025 = 4.990$ V; ideal span for the same codes: $255 \times 19.53\ \text{mV} = 4.980$ V.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Gain error = (actual span − ideal span) in LSBs: $\frac{4.990 - 4.980}{0.01953} = \frac{9.5\ \text{mV}}{19.53\ \text{mV}} = +0.49$ LSB.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Calibration order: subtract the 25 mV offset first, then rescale by $\frac{4.980}{4.990} = 0.9980$ to correct gain; whatever error remains is pure curvature — the INL, which no two-point calibration can touch.

examples.result: Offset = +1.28 LSB and gain error = +0.49 LSB; two-point calibration removes both, leaving only the INL bow.

examples.title: DNL and INL from a transition table
examples.problem: A 3-bit 0–4 V ADC (LSB = 0.5 V) has measured transition thresholds at 0.55, 0.95, 1.45, 1.70, 2.20, 2.95 and 3.55 V (ideal: 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5 V). Compute the code widths, worst DNL, worst INL, and state whether any code is missing.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Code widths between adjacent transitions: code 001: $0.95 - 0.55 = 0.40$ V; 010: 0.50 V; 011: 0.25 V; 100: 0.50 V; 101: 0.75 V; 110: 0.60 V.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: DNL = width/LSB − 1: $-0.2, 0, -0.5, 0, +0.5, +0.2$ LSB; worst magnitude 0.5 LSB (code 011).

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: INL at each transition = (measured − ideal)/LSB: $+0.1, -0.1, -0.1, -0.6, -0.6, -0.1, +0.1$ LSB; worst magnitude 0.6 LSB.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Consistency check — INL is the running sum of DNL: at the fourth transition, $+0.1 + (-0.2 + 0 - 0.5) = -0.6$ LSB, matching the direct deviation.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Verdict: every width is positive, so no code is missing and the staircase never reverses (monotonic); but the −0.6 LSB bow would fail a ±½ LSB INL specification.

examples.result: Worst DNL = −0.5 LSB (code 011), worst INL = −0.6 LSB (transitions 4–5); no missing codes, monotonic — yet outside a ±½ LSB INL spec.

examples.title: Aperture-jitter and droop budget for 12 bits at 2 MHz
examples.problem: A 12-bit system samples a 2 MHz signal (74 dB SQNR target) with a 12 µs SAR conversion and a 5 V range. Find (a) the maximum rms aperture jitter and (b) the minimum hold capacitance if total leakage is 1 nA.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Jitter bound: $t_j = \frac{10^{-\text{SNR}/20}}{2\pi f_{in}} = \frac{10^{-74/20}}{2\pi \times 2 \times 10^6}$.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Evaluate: $10^{-3.7} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}$ and $2\pi \times 2\times 10^6 = 1.257 \times 10^7$, so $t_j = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-4}}{1.257 \times 10^7} = 15.9$ ps rms.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Droop budget: $\text{LSB} = \frac{5}{4096} = 1.22$ mV, so ½ LSB = 0.61 mV over 12 µs → droop $< \frac{0.61\ \text{mV}}{12\ \mu\text{s}} \approx 51$ V/s.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Hold capacitor: $C = \frac{I}{dV/dt} = \frac{1\ \text{nA}}{51\ \text{V/s}} \approx 20$ pF — and acquisition through, say, 1 kΩ must still settle 8.3 τ ($\approx 0.18\ \mu\text{s}$ for 22 pF), comfortably inside the 12 µs window.

examples.result: (a) $t_j \le 16$ ps rms; (b) $C_{hold} \ge 20$ pF (choose 22 pF with margin), trading droop against acquisition settling.

keyTakeaways: Offset = parallel shift of the transfer curve (read at zero scale); gain = slope error of the span after offset removal — both calibratable in software, and both distinct from resolution.
DNL is the per-code step error ($W_k/\text{LSB} - 1$): DNL ≤ −1 LSB means a missing code; INL is the accumulated bow of the curve, and ±½ LSB INL guarantees monotonicity.
Aperture jitter caps SNR at $-20\log_{10}(2\pi f_{in} t_j)$ — 1 MHz with 1 ns jitter is only 44 dB — while droop must stay under ½ LSB per conversion, sizing the hold capacitor against leakage.

The DAQ chain is sensor → conditioning → (MUX → S/H →) ADC → digital; multiplexing divides throughput by the channel count, and architecture follows the resolution-speed-power map: dual-slope, sigma-delta, SAR, pipeline, flash.

quiz.q: A converter’s datasheet lists DNL = −1.5 LSB at code 176. This means
options: code 176 never appears at the output — it is missing
the converter runs 1.5 times too slowly at that code
quiz.explanation: Step 1: $\text{DNL}(k) = W_k/\text{LSB} - 1$ measures the width of code k. Step 2: DNL of −1 LSB already means zero width — the code is skipped entirely. Step 3: −1.5 LSB is beyond that: the transition overshoots and code 176 never appears in the output stream. Step 4: Offset is a whole-curve shift, not a per-code width error — a different specification altogether.

quiz.q: A 1 MHz sinusoid is sampled with 1 ns rms aperture jitter. The jitter-limited SNR is about
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The jitter ceiling is $\text{SNR} = -20\log_{10}(2\pi f_{in} t_j)$. Step 2: $2\pi \times 10^6 \times 10^{-9} = 6.28 \times 10^{-3}$. Step 3: $-20\log_{10}(6.28 \times 10^{-3}) \approx 44$ dB. Step 4: That is barely 7 effective bits — at high input frequencies the clock jitter, not the resolution, sets the ceiling.

quiz.q: An 8-channel data-acquisition system multiplexes one 100 kSPS ADC across all channels. The per-channel sampling rate is
quiz.explanation: Step 1: One converter serves 8 channels in round-robin fashion. Step 2: The total throughput of 100 kSPS is shared equally, giving $\frac{100}{8} = 12.5$ kSPS per channel. Step 3: 800 kSPS is the impossible direction — multiplexing divides the per-channel rate, never multiplies it. Step 4: The hidden divide-by-channel-count is the standard trap in DAQ numericals; check for it before answering.

quiz.q: A DAC whose output never decreases as the input code increases is called
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Monotonicity is the property that every code increment produces a non-negative output step. Step 2: It requires DNL ≥ −1 LSB at every code, since a negative step would reverse the output direction. Step 3: INL within ±½ LSB is a sufficient condition, because it bounds how far the curve can bow. Step 4: It matters practically because a non-monotonic DAC in a feedback or control loop creates spurious zero crossings and can force oscillation.

prerequisites: Percentages, ratio–proportion and averages (Sections 2 and 3)
Fraction–decimal–percent conversion fluency
intro: Data interpretation is the highest-yield block of any engineering selection assessment’s quantitative section: a single table or chart anchors three to five questions, so two minutes spent understanding the data once is repaid across every mark that follows. The formats are predictable — tables, multi-bar and stacked-bar charts, pie charts, line graphs and caselets — and so are the question verbs: share, growth, ratio, average, difference. Nearly every computation is percentage-basing of one kind or another, which means the real skill is identifying the correct base before touching the numbers. Screening papers add one more layer: the numbers are chosen to reward approximation, so a candidate who rounds 4,980 to 5,000 and 19.8% to 20% finishes three sets in the time a precise calculator finishes one. This lesson works through one full table set, one pie chart and one line-chart set in exactly that spirit.
objectives: Base every percentage on the correct total — row, column or grand total — before computing
Read multi-bar and stacked-bar charts, and convert pie sectors between degrees, fractions and percents
Extract average annual growth and ratio-of-slopes comparisons from line charts, separating percentage change from absolute change
Convert caselet narratives into self-built tables, and judge when to approximate or skip a set entirely

concepts.statement: Every table question is a fraction in disguise — decide the **base** first: a cell against its row total, a cell against its column total, or a cell against the grand total. “Hardware’s share in 2024” is $\frac{\text{Hardware in 2024}}{\text{Total in 2024}}$ — never the 2021 total, never the four-year company-wide total.
concepts.detail: Write the fraction in words before substituting numbers: most distractors are manufactured by using a nearby but wrong base (a different year’s total, or the row total instead of the column total). Quick self-checks: the shares of one column must add to 100%, and shares of the same row across years can move even when the raw value rises — a falling share with rising revenue is the classic “both true” reading. When two fractions share the same base, compare them by numerators alone; when bases differ, cross-multiply rather than divide: comparing $\frac{200}{600}$ with $\frac{230}{750}$ is settled by $200 \times 750 = 150{,}000$ versus $230 \times 600 = 138{,}000$ — no division anywhere.

concepts.statement: In a **grouped (multi-bar)** chart, bars stand side by side within each category, so the eye compares across groups; in a **stacked** bar, segments pile on top of one another, so a category’s value is the *height of its upper boundary*, and the segment’s size is the **difference of consecutive boundaries**.
concepts.detail: The stacked-bar trap: the visually largest top segment is not necessarily the largest category, because segments start at different heights — read boundary differences, not segment prominence. Always check three things before computing: the axis units (crore versus lakh is a factor of 100), any axis break (a bar that looks twice as tall may be far more than twice as large), and whether the bars show absolute values or percentages (a 100%-stacked chart has equal total heights by construction). In grouped charts, draw the comparison the question asks — pairing bars within a group — rather than comparing bar heights across distant groups.

concepts.statement: A pie chart maps the whole to the full circle: $360^{\circ} = 100\%$, so $1\% = 3.6^{\circ}$ and a sector of angle $\theta$ is the fraction $\frac{\theta}{360^{\circ}}$ of the total: $$\text{amount} = \text{total} \times \frac{\theta}{360^{\circ}}, \qquad \theta = \frac{\text{part}}{\text{total}} \times 360^{\circ}.$$
concepts.detail: Memorise the fraction shortcuts and the degree equivalents together: 45° = 12.5% = 1/8, 60° = 16⅔% = 1/6, 90° = 25% = 1/4, 120° = 33⅓% = 1/3, 135° = 37.5% = 3/8, 180° = 50% = 1/2. Converting through fractions (not decimals) keeps the arithmetic mental: a 72° sector of ₹45,000 is $\frac{72}{360} = \frac{1}{5}$ of the total, instantly ₹9,000. The manufactured error is treating the angle as a percentage — 72° is 20% of the circle, not 72% — and forgetting that “per cent distribution” charts still need the caption’s grand total to convert shares into amounts.

concepts.term: Line charts: growth, slopes and averages
concepts.statement: Average annual **absolute** growth $= \frac{\text{last} - \text{first}}{\text{number of intervals}}$; **percentage** growth always divides by the value at the start of the interval. With equal time spacing, the **ratio of slopes equals the ratio of growth rates** — a line twice as steep grows twice as fast in absolute terms.
concepts.detail: Count intervals, not plotted points: five annual points span four years of growth, and dividing by five understates the rate by exactly that factor. The largest absolute rise is rarely the largest percentage rise, because big bases dilute rates — screening sets deliberately place the two answers side by side to catch the confusion. When a paper asks for the average annual *growth rate* over a period, the compound form $\left(\frac{\text{final}}{\text{initial}}\right)^{1/n} - 1$ is meant only when stated; otherwise compute the arithmetic average of the year-on-year percentages. On stacked line charts (two series on one axes), compare slopes segment by segment before comparing heights.

concepts.statement: A **caselet** is a data set told in prose. Convert it immediately into a small table or a set of relations: assign one variable per unknown, translate each sentence into exactly one equation, and only then attempt the questions.
concepts.detail: When the narrative gives only percentages and ratios (no absolute total), assume a convenient base of 100 units — the unknown total cancels out of every share, ratio and percentage question. Example: “a plant makes only items A and B; A is 40% of output; defect rates are 2% on A and 5% on B” becomes a two-row table over 100 units (A = 40, B = 60) giving defects $0.8 + 3.0 = 3.8$, so 3.8% of all units are defective. The classic caselet trap is hidden double-counting — “20% of the women and 30% of the men” needs the men:women split before any blending, which is exactly the weighted-average work of Section 3.

concepts.statement: Round to factor-friendly numbers **before** multiplying — 19.8% of 25,300 is close enough to $0.20 \times 25{,}000 = 5{,}000$ when the answer options are spaced 10% apart. When options differ by only 1–2%, the set demands exact work; when they differ by 10% or more, approximation is the intended method.
concepts.detail: Timed-paper triage rules: skip a set when (i) it needs long chained exact computations with tightly clustered options, (ii) the caselet carries more than three interdependent unknowns, or (iii) you have already spent its time budget (roughly one and a half to two minutes per question). Mark it and return on the second pass — DI answers rarely depend on earlier skipped work, so the cost of deferring is near zero. When rounding, control the error direction: rounding one quantity up and the other down is safe when you only need to *eliminate* options; if you must land *between* two options, round both in the same direction and correct at the end.

examples.title: A full set on a company revenue table
examples.problem:
A company’s revenue (₹ lakh) by product line over four years:

```text
Product line   2021   2022   2023   2024
Hardware        240    300    360    450
Software        160    220    310    420
Services        200    230    270    330
Total           600    750    940   1200
```

(i) What was Hardware’s share of total revenue in 2024? (ii) By what percent did Software revenue grow from 2021 to 2024? (iii) In which year was Services’ share of total revenue the lowest?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Read the structure first: rows are product lines, columns are years, and the Total row is the base for every share question — shares are computed **within one column**, against that year’s total.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: (i) Hardware share in 2024 $= \frac{450}{1200} = \frac{3}{8} = 37.5\%$. Simplify before dividing: $450 : 1200 = 3 : 8$, and $\frac{3}{8} = 0.375$ is a known conversion.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (ii) Software growth $= \frac{420 - 160}{160} \times 100 = \frac{260}{160} \times 100 = 162.5\%$ — the base is the 2021 value, the starting point of the interval, not the average and not the ending value.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: (iii) Services’ share by year: $\frac{200}{600} = 33.3\%$, $\frac{230}{750} = 30.7\%$, $\frac{270}{940} = 28.7\%$, $\frac{330}{1200} = 27.5\%$ — strictly falling, so the lowest share falls in **2024** even though the raw revenue rose every single year.

examples.result: (i) 37.5%; (ii) 162.5%; (iii) 2024 — Services’ share falls every year while its revenue rises.

examples.title: A pie-chart household budget
examples.problem: A household’s monthly budget of ₹72,000 is shown as a pie chart with sector angles: Housing 120°, Food 90°, Transport 60°, Savings 45°, Others 45°. (i) How much goes to Housing? (ii) What percent of the budget is Savings? (iii) What is the ratio of Housing to Food expenditure?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Check the chart closes: $120 + 90 + 60 + 45 + 45 = 360^{\circ}$, so no hidden “miscellaneous” remainder is folded into the sectors.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: (i) Housing fraction $= \frac{120}{360} = \frac{1}{3}$, so Housing $= 72{,}000 \times \frac{1}{3} = ₹24{,}000$. The shortcut list does it instantly: 90° is a quarter, so 120° is a third.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (ii) Savings: $\frac{45}{360} = \frac{1}{8} = 12.5\%$ — 45° is half of 90°, and half of a quarter is one eighth.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: (iii) Housing : Food $= \frac{120}{360} : \frac{90}{360} = 120 : 90 = 4 : 3$ — the common denominator 360 cancels, so ratios of sectors equal ratios of angles.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Verify with money: ₹24,000 : ₹18,000 = 4 : 3, and the five amounts $24{,}000 + 18{,}000 + 12{,}000 + 9{,}000 + 9{,}000$ re-add to ₹72,000 — the cheapest possible error check on any pie set.

examples.title: Line chart: same percentage, different absolute
examples.problem: Sales of two product models (₹ crore): Model A rose from 40 to 52 to 64 to 76 across 2020–2023; Model B rose from 20 to 26 to 32 to 38 in the same years. (i) What is Model A’s average annual (absolute) growth? (ii) Compare the percentage growth of the two models over the period. (iii) What happens to the absolute gap between them?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: (i) Average annual growth of A $= \frac{76 - 40}{3} = \frac{36}{3} = ₹12$ crore per year — four plotted points span three intervals, the classic off-by-one trap.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: (ii) Model A: $\frac{76 - 40}{40} = \frac{36}{40} = 90\%$. Model B: $\frac{38 - 20}{20} = \frac{18}{20} = 90\%$. Identical percentage growth — the two lines keep the same relative shape.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Slope check: A gains 12 per year, B gains 6 per year, so the slope ratio is $2 : 1$ — A grows twice as fast in absolute terms, exactly as the widening gap between the lines shows.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: (iii) The gap grows from $40 - 20 = ₹20$ crore to $76 - 38 = ₹38$ crore: equal percentage growth on unequal bases widens the absolute difference, which is why “percentage change” and “absolute change” questions sit side by side in the same set.

examples.result: (i) ₹12 crore per year; (ii) both grew 90% — equal; (iii) the gap widens from ₹20 crore to ₹38 crore.

keyTakeaways: Fix the base before computing — cell ÷ its column total for shares, start-of-interval value for growth; every distractor comes from a wrong base.
Pie charts: 360° = 100%, so 1% = 3.6°; know 45° = 12.5%, 60° = 16⅔%, 90° = 25%, 120° = 33⅓%, and convert through fractions, not decimals.
Line charts: count intervals not points, compare growth by ratio of slopes, and never confuse the largest absolute rise with the largest percentage rise.
Turn caselets into tables over a convenient 100-unit base, round before multiplying when options are 10% apart, and skip exact-demanding sets until the second pass.

quiz.q: A company’s 2023 revenue was ₹940 lakh in total, of which Software contributed ₹310 lakh, Hardware ₹360 lakh and Services the rest. Software’s share of the year’s revenue, to the nearest whole percent, is:
quiz.explanation: Step 1: The base is the 2023 column total, ₹940 lakh. Step 2: Share $= \frac{310}{940} \approx 0.330$. Step 3: To the nearest whole percent that is 33%. Step 4: 38% is Hardware’s share ($\frac{360}{940}$) and 29% is Services’ ($\frac{270}{940}$) — reading the wrong row or wrong base supplies the distractors.

quiz.q: In a pie chart of a ₹45,000 monthly expense budget, the education sector subtends 72°. The amount spent on education is:
quiz.explanation: Step 1: 360° represents the whole ₹45,000, so 1° is worth $\frac{45{,}000}{360} = ₹125$. Step 2: Education $= 72^{\circ} \times 125 = ₹9{,}000$. Step 3: Fraction route: $\frac{72}{360} = \frac{1}{5}$, and $\frac{45{,}000}{5} = 9{,}000$. Step 4: ₹7,200 is the trap of treating 72° as 16% instead of converting properly ($1\% = 3.6^{\circ}$, so 72° is 20%); ₹10,000 would be an 80° sector.

quiz.q: Over three years, product P’s sales rose from ₹40 crore to ₹76 crore while product Q’s rose from ₹20 crore to ₹38 crore. Which statement is correct?
options: P grew by a larger percentage than Q
Q grew by a larger percentage than P
Both grew by the same percentage, but the absolute gap widened
Both grew by the same percentage, and the absolute gap stayed the same
quiz.explanation: Step 1: P’s percentage growth $= \frac{76 - 40}{40} = \frac{36}{40} = 90\%$. Step 2: Q’s $= \frac{38 - 20}{20} = \frac{18}{20} = 90\%$ — equal. Step 3: The absolute gap moves from $40 - 20 = 20$ crore to $76 - 38 = 38$ crore, so it widens. Step 4: Equal relative growth on unequal bases always widens the absolute gap — the steeper-looking line is steeper only in absolute terms.

quiz.q: Using sensible rounding, the best estimate of 19.8% of 25,300 is:
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Round both numbers toward easy factors: 19.8% ≈ 20% and 25,300 ≈ 25,000. Step 2: Compute $0.20 \times 25{,}000 = 5{,}000$. Step 3: Check the error: the exact value is $0.198 \times 25{,}300 = 5{,}009$ — within 0.2% of the estimate. Step 4: 5,500 and 6,000 overshoot by 10–20%, far outside the rounding error; when options are spaced that widely, approximation is the intended method.

prerequisites: Linear and quadratic equations, including two-variable systems
Number properties: signs, parity, powers and fractions
intro: Data sufficiency turns testing inside out: instead of asking for a value, it asks whether the value could be found. Two numbered statements accompany every question, and your job is to decide which statement — or which combination — pins the answer down. Aptitude screening papers favour the format because it punishes auto-pilot solving: the strongest candidates stop computing the moment sufficiency is settled, saving half the time the question appears to demand. The same philosophy powers quantity comparison — Column A versus Column B — where the fourth choice, “cannot be determined”, is correct exactly when the relationship changes across the values the variables are allowed to take. Both formats live or die on traps: negatives, zero, fractions between 0 and 1, and even powers that hide signs.
objectives: Apply the standard sufficiency answer pattern, mapping the five classic options onto the four choices used here
Run the decision tree in order — statement 1 alone, statement 2 alone, both together — without ever solving more than sufficiency requires
Answer quantity comparisons by probing boundary values: negative, zero, fraction, one and a large number
Recognise the four classic traps: negative values, zero, fractions that flip inequalities, and even powers that hide signs

concepts.statement: A data-sufficiency item supplies a question and two numbered statements, and asks which statements determine the answer. The classic five-option pattern — statement 1 alone; statement 2 alone; both together; each alone; neither — is compressed in this course to four choices: **(A)** statement 1 alone is sufficient, **(B)** statement 2 alone is sufficient, **(C) both together are needed**, **(D) each alone is sufficient**.
concepts.detail: “Sufficient” means the statements force exactly one answer to the question asked — a unique number for a value question, or a definite YES (or a definite NO) for a yes/no question; a definite negative answer settles a question just as firmly as a positive one. In the full five-option format a fifth choice, “neither even together”, exists; the four-choice adaptation used here simply guarantees the combined statements always settle the question, so read the printed mapping before starting. Two failure modes to avoid: answering the underlying question instead of the sufficiency question, and forgetting that the statements are to be taken as true — you judge whether they *determine* the answer, not whether they are plausible.

concepts.statement: Work in fixed order: **test statement 1 alone** (physically cover statement 2), then **test statement 2 alone**, then combine. If both work alone the answer is (D); if exactly one works alone it is (A) or (B); if neither works alone, combine before answering (C).
concepts.detail: Covering the unused statement with a finger is not a gimmick — statements leak, and half of all errors come from letting statement 2 colour the judgement of statement 1. Keep the survivors: if statement 1 alone narrows x to two candidates, that narrowing is gold when you later combine — you only test the survivors, not all values. The logical obligation behind (C) is strict: you may answer (C) only after showing that *each* statement alone fails; a single missed case that one statement handles alone converts a correct (C) into a trap. Symmetrically, answering (A) or (B) requires the statement to work for every allowed case, not just the first one you tried.

concepts.statement: The question is “could you find it?”, not “what is it?” — once a statement forces a unique answer, stop; the numerical value is irrelevant. Two independent linear equations in two unknowns are sufficient without solving them, and a quadratic with a nonzero discriminant is **not** sufficient unless a statement selects between its two roots.
concepts.detail: The timing dividend is real: in the pen-and-notebook example below, subtracting the two statements settles the pen price without ever computing the notebook price — a sufficiency judgement made in one line. “Insufficient”, likewise, is best proven by counterexample: to show a statement fails, exhibit one allowed case giving YES and another giving NO. Counterexamples, not algebra, are the fast exit. One boundary case deserves respect: a statement that is true for *every* possible case (like “2n is even” for integer n) separates nothing and is therefore never sufficient, no matter how true it sounds.

concepts.statement: A quantity-comparison item gives **Column A** and **Column B** with shared constraints, and four fixed choices: Column A is greater; Column B is greater; the two are equal; **the relationship cannot be determined** from the information given. The fourth choice is correct precisely when the allowed values produce more than one of the first three outcomes.
concepts.detail: The solving routine: plug one friendly value and note the winner, then hunt for a value that flips or ties the result. If two probes give different winners, the answer is “cannot be determined” and you are finished — a third probe is wasted time. Only when every allowed value gives the same verdict (or all tie) may you choose one of the first three. The most common error is over-claiming: after testing 2 and 3 (both making Column A win), candidates declare Column A greater — but the constraint “x is a real number” also admits −1, 0 and ½, where the verdict may flip. Read the constraint as the exact set of values you are allowed to probe.

concepts.statement: **Negatives**: $-3 > -5$ and squaring is not order-preserving across signs; **zero**: equal to itself, annihilates products, collapses exponents ($x^0 = 1$); **fractions between 0 and 1**: squaring shrinks them, so $x^2 < x$ — the inequality verdict flips; **even powers**: $x^2 = 25$ admits $x = \pm 5$, so even powers, absolute values and even roots all hide signs.
concepts.detail: Each trap lives at a specific boundary, which is why the probe list below is short and fixed. Reciprocals add one more flip: for positives, $0 < a < b$ implies $\frac{1}{a} > \frac{1}{b}$. Inequalities reverse when multiplied or divided by a negative number: $-2x < 6$ becomes $x > -3$. And respect the root convention: $\sqrt{25}$ denotes the principal root 5, never −5, while the *equation* $x^2 = 25$ keeps both roots — statements quoting a square root are silently handing you sign information that statements quoting a square are not.

concepts.statement: For any comparison over loosely constrained variables, probe in this order: a **positive integer** (usually 2), a **fraction** (½), **zero**, a **negative** (−1 or −2), and a **large number** (10 or 100). The first probe that flips the outcome settles “cannot be determined”; if all agree, look for an algebraic confirmation before committing.
concepts.detail: Why this set: zero kills products and exponents, fractions reverse squaring, negatives reverse powers and inequalities, and large numbers expose asymptotic behaviour — between them they cover all four traps. Probes must respect the constraints: given $0 < x < 1$, zero and negatives are forbidden and the probe set shrinks to ½, 0.9 and 0.99; given “x is a nonzero integer”, ½ drops out. When the quantity involves two variables, vary them independently (x = 2, y = 3 then x = 3, y = 2) — symmetric-looking quantities are exactly where order flips hide.

examples.title: Pens and notebooks — both together, and nothing more
examples.problem:
A shop sells only pens and notebooks, each at a fixed whole-rupee price. What is the price of one pen?

(1) 3 pens and 2 notebooks together cost ₹79.
(2) 5 pens and 2 notebooks together cost ₹117.

Choose: (A) statement 1 alone; (B) statement 2 alone; (C) both together needed; (D) each alone sufficient.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Cover statement 2. Statement 1 is one equation, $3p + 2n = 79$, in two unknowns: $(p, n) = (21, 8)$ satisfies it ($63 + 16 = 79$), and so does $(19, 11)$ ($57 + 22 = 79$). Two different pen prices — not sufficient.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Cover statement 1. Statement 2 alone has the same defect: $5p + 2n = 117$ is satisfied by $(21, 6)$ ($105 + 12 = 117$) and by $(23, 1)$ ($115 + 2 = 117$). Two pen prices again — not sufficient.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Combine: subtract statement 1 from statement 2, $(5p + 2n) - (3p + 2n) = 117 - 79$, so $2p = 38$ and $p = ₹19$ — a unique pen price, so together the statements are sufficient.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Note what was never computed: the notebook price (₹11) is irrelevant to the question asked, and stopping at sufficiency — the answer is (C) — skipped the second half of the solve entirely.

examples.result: (C) — both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone.

examples.title: Even powers hide the sign
examples.problem:
What is the value of the real number $x$?

(1) $x^2 = 49$.
(2) $x > 0$.

Choose: (A) statement 1 alone; (B) statement 2 alone; (C) both together needed; (D) each alone sufficient.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Statement 1 alone: $x^2 = 49$ has **two** real roots, $x = 7$ and $x = -7$. Squaring destroyed the sign, so the value is not unique — not sufficient. The reflex “x = 7” is precisely the trap being tested.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Statement 2 alone: $x > 0$ leaves infinitely many candidates — not sufficient.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Together: statement 2 selects the positive root, $x = 7$, uniquely — sufficient, so the answer is (C).

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Generalise: pair $x^2 = 49$ with *any* sign information — $x < 0$, $x > 5$, $x + y > 0$ with $y$ known — and the combination becomes sufficient. “Even power plus one sign fact” is the standard (C) pattern; “even power alone” is the standard trap.

examples.result: (C) — together they force $x = 7$; neither statement alone.

examples.title: Quantity comparison: $x^3$ versus $x$
examples.problem: $x$ is a real number. **Column A:** $x^3$. **Column B:** $x$. Which is greater?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Probe a positive integer: $x = 2$ gives $8 > 2$ — Column A wins this round.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Probe a fraction: $x = \frac{1}{2}$ gives $\frac{1}{8} < \frac{1}{2}$ — Column B wins. The outcome has flipped, so no single verdict can survive.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Map the rest quickly: $x = -2$ gives $-8 < -2$ (Column B); $x = -\frac{1}{2}$ gives $-\frac{1}{8} > -\frac{1}{2}$ (Column A); and $x \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ ties the columns. Every one of the four outcomes occurs.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Since more than one outcome occurs across allowed values, the answer is the fourth choice — the relationship **cannot be determined**. Had the constraint been $x > 1$, Column A would win everywhere; had it been $0 < x < 1$, Column B would — the unconstrained version is the trap, and the boundary probes are the defence.

examples.result: Cannot be determined — all four relationships occur for different real $x$.

keyTakeaways: Sufficiency means the statements force exactly one answer — a definite YES or NO qualifies for yes/no questions; stop computing the moment uniqueness is assured.
Run the decision tree with the unused statement physically covered; never answer (C) until each statement alone has failed, and never (A)/(B) on a single favourable case.
In quantity comparison, two probes with different winners settle “cannot be determined” instantly — probe 2, ½, 0, −1 and 10 in that order, respecting the constraints.
The four traps live at the boundaries: negatives, zero, fractions between 0 and 1, and even powers — test each before declaring a winner.

quiz.q:
What is the value of $x$?

(1) $5x - 12 = 3x + 4$.
(2) $x^2 = 100$ and $x < 0$.

Options: (A) statement 1 alone is sufficient; (B) statement 2 alone is sufficient; (C) both together are needed; (D) each alone is sufficient.
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Statement 1 alone: $5x - 3x = 4 + 12$, so $2x = 16$ and $x = 8$ — a unique value, sufficient. Step 2: Statement 2 alone: $x^2 = 100$ gives $x = \pm 10$, and $x < 0$ selects $x = -10$ uniquely — sufficient. Step 3: Each statement independently determines $x$, so the answer is (D). Step 4: The trap is stopping at statement 1’s simplicity and never testing statement 2 — the sign condition there is doing real work.

quiz.q:
Is the integer $n$ even?

(1) $n^2$ is even.
(2) $2n$ is even.

Options: (A) statement 1 alone is sufficient; (B) statement 2 alone is sufficient; (C) both together are needed; (D) each alone is sufficient.
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Statement 1 alone: parity is preserved under multiplication — an odd $n$ would give odd $n^2$ — so $n^2$ even forces $n$ even. A definite YES: sufficient. Step 2: Statement 2 alone: $2n$ is even for **every** integer $n$, so the statement separates nothing — not sufficient. Step 3: Only statement 1 decides, so the answer is (A). Step 4: The trap is reading “2n is even” as evidence about $n$ — statements true for all cases carry zero information.

quiz.q: If $0 < a < 1$, which is greater: **Column A:** $a^2$ or **Column B:** $a$?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: A number strictly between 0 and 1 shrinks when squared: $0.5^2 = 0.25 < 0.5$. Step 2: Algebraically, $a - a^2 = a(1 - a)$, and both factors are positive when $0 < a < 1$, so $a > a^2$ always. Step 3: Column B is greater for every allowed value — no probe can flip it, so “cannot be determined” is wrong here. Step 4: Without the constraint, $x = 2$ would flip the verdict — the fraction condition is exactly what pins the answer down.

quiz.q: Which is greater: **Column A:** 45% of 80, or **Column B:** 80% of 45?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: Column A: $0.45 \times 80 = 36$. Step 2: Column B: $0.80 \times 45 = 36$. Step 3: The columns are equal — multiplication is commutative, so $x\%$ of $y$ always equals $y\%$ of $x$. Step 4: The intuition “a bigger percentage of a bigger number must be bigger” misleads here: the percentage and the base swap exactly, and the products tie.

prerequisites: Photon energy $E = h\nu$ and energy-level diagrams from atomic physics
Wave optics: interference and standing waves
intro: A laser is not a source of energy but a reorganiser of it: atoms that would otherwise glow at random are persuaded to emit in step, and the resulting beam is coherent, monochromatic, directional and intense enough to cut steel. The physics rests on three light–matter interactions — absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission — whose equilibrium balance Einstein analysed in 1917, decades before anyone built a device. Two engineering ingredients turn the physics into light: population inversion, achieved by pumping atoms into a metastable state, and an optical resonator that feeds photons back through the inverted medium until gain beats loss. This section builds the full chain — stimulated emission, inversion, resonator, threshold — and closes with the property set that makes lasers useful, plus a first look at how a glass fibre traps light by total internal reflection. The two sections that follow work through real laser systems and the complete fibre-communication design.
objectives: Distinguish absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission, and state how the Einstein A and B coefficients balance them at equilibrium
Explain population inversion, the role of metastable states, and why at least three energy levels are needed for pumping
Compare three-level and four-level pumping schemes and derive the round-trip threshold condition of an optical resonator
State the four hallmark properties of laser light and describe, qualitatively, how a fibre guides light by total internal reflection

concepts.statement: For two atomic levels $E_1 < E_2$ separated by $\Delta E = h\nu$: **absorption** lifts an atom from 1 to 2 by destroying a photon; **spontaneous emission** drops $2 \to 1$ creating a photon at a random time, in a random direction and phase; **stimulated emission** drops $2 \to 1$ when triggered by a passing photon of frequency $\nu$, producing a **second photon identical in frequency, phase, direction and polarisation** — the trigger emerges with a clone.
concepts.detail: Spontaneous emission is the ordinary glow of a lamp: incoherent, emitted in all directions, from excited states that live only about $10^{-8}$ s. Stimulated emission is the multiplier of optics — one photon in, two indistinguishable photons out — and repeated passes through an inverted medium give $2 \to 4 \to 8 \cdots$, exponential amplification. It is this photon “family”, cloned from a common ancestor and therefore sharing one phase front, that makes laser light coherent: the beam is not merely bright, it is organised.

concepts.statement:
With $N_1, N_2$ atoms in the two levels and radiation energy density $ho(
u)$ at the transition frequency, the rates are: absorption $= B_{12} N_1 ho(
u)$, stimulated emission $= B_{21} N_2 ho(
u)$, spontaneous emission $= A_{21} N_2$. Thermal equilibrium (absorption balancing both emission channels) forces $B_{12} = B_{21}$ and $ rac{A_{21}}{B_{21}} \propto 
u^3$ — spontaneous emission dominates ever more strongly as frequency rises.
concepts.detail: Two consequences drive all laser design. First, because $B_{12} = B_{21}$, a photon meeting an excited atom is exactly as likely to trigger emission as a photon meeting a ground-state atom is to be absorbed — which process wins is decided purely by which population is larger, nothing else. Second, the $\nu^3$ law says that at optical frequencies equilibrium is overwhelmingly spontaneous; making stimulated emission win requires raising the photon density $\rho(\nu)$ inside the cavity enormously above its thermal value, which is precisely what the resonator mirrors are for.

concepts.statement: A **population inversion** exists when $N_2 > N_1$ for the lasing pair — more atoms in the upper level than the lower — so that stimulated emission out-runs absorption and the medium amplifies light at $\nu = \Delta E/h$. Achieving it requires the upper level to be **metastable**: an excited state with an unusually long lifetime, about $10^{-3}$ s, some $10^{5}$ times longer than an ordinary excited state, in which atoms can accumulate.
concepts.detail: Metastability comes from selection rules: transitions to lower states are quantum-mechanically forbidden or weak, so the state decays slowly and behaves as a storage shelf for excitation. Inversion is impossible to sustain in a strict two-level system pumped at the transition frequency: as $N_2$ approaches $N_1$, absorption and stimulated emission rates become equal and net gain vanishes — at best you equalise the populations. Three or more levels break the deadlock by pumping atoms up through one pair of levels and letting them lase down a different pair, with the metastable shelf as the middle stop.

concepts.statement: **Three-level scheme:** pump atoms from the ground level into a broad absorption band; they drop rapidly and radiationlessly to a metastable level, and lase from there back to the ground level — inversion requires **more than half** of all atoms to sit in the metastable level. **Four-level scheme:** pump to a band, decay to the metastable upper level, lase down to a *lower level that sits above the ground state* and empties to the ground within nanoseconds — so almost every pumped atom contributes to inversion.
concepts.detail: The arithmetic explains the design split. In a three-level laser the lower lasing level is the ground state, which is always crowded, so the pump must excite over 50% of all atoms — demanding intense flashlamp pumping and yielding pulsed operation. In a four-level laser the lower lasing level is nearly empty by construction, so a modest continuous pump holds inversion; that is why four-level systems (helium–neon, Nd:YAG) run continuously on milliwatts to watts where ruby needs kilowatt flashes. The pump source can be light (flashlamp or another laser), an electrical discharge, or, for diode lasers, injected current.

concepts.statement: Two facing mirrors — one fully reflecting ($R_1$), one partially transmitting ($R_2$) — turn the inverted medium into an oscillator: photons traverse repeatedly, and each round trip multiplies the intensity by $R_1 R_2 e^{2gL}$ for medium gain coefficient $g$ and cavity length $L$. **Lasing threshold** is the condition that this factor equal 1: $$g_{\text{th}} = \frac{1}{2L}\ln\frac{1}{R_1 R_2}.$$ Above threshold, stimulated emission grows until it depletes the inversion, and the partial mirror leaks the output beam.
concepts.detail: The resonator also defines the light it amplifies: the cavity length must hold an integer number of half-wavelengths, $L = q\lambda/2$, selecting narrow longitudinal modes and narrowing the spectrum; transverse modes shape the beam profile. Feedback raises the photon density — the $\rho(\nu)$ of the Einstein balance — by orders of magnitude over a single pass, letting stimulated emission overwhelm spontaneous emission along the axis. The few spontaneously emitted photons that happen to run exactly along the axis are the seeds that get amplified into the beam; the resonator is what makes a weak random event into the dominant output.

concepts.term: The four laser properties and the fibre bridge
concepts.statement: **Coherence** — the photons share one phase front, so interference survives metres of path difference; **directionality** — divergence is diffraction-limited, $\theta \sim \frac{\lambda}{D}$ for aperture $D$, typically milliradians; **monochromaticity** — spectral width $\Delta\lambda$ is a fraction of a nanometre, set by the transition plus cavity modes; **intensity** — power packed into the narrowest angular and spectral slice light can occupy. A glass fibre with core index $n_1$ inside cladding of index $n_2 < n_1$ guides light by **total internal reflection**: rays reaching the core–cladding wall beyond the critical angle $\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$ reflect without loss and are channelled for kilometres (Section 3 does the full design).
concepts.detail: Each property is exploited downstream: coherence enables holography (Section 2), directionality and intensity enable cutting and LIDAR, monochromaticity limits pulse spreading in fibres, and diode lasers matched to the fibre windows enable communication links. Contrast a filament lamp: hundreds of nanometres wide, all directions, random phase, brightness limited by the source temperature. The laser wins not by making more energy but by concentrating its power into the narrowest possible region of the space of light — direction, frequency and phase all at once.

examples.title: Why pumping is unavoidable: the thermal fraction
examples.problem: For the red 632.8 nm transition of a neon-based gas laser, estimate the fraction of atoms occupying the upper level in thermal equilibrium at 300 K. ($h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}$ m/s, $k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K.)

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Photon energy: $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.0 \times 10^{8})}{632.8 \times 10^{-9}} = \frac{1.99 \times 10^{-25}}{6.33 \times 10^{-7}} \approx 3.14 \times 10^{-19}$ J $\approx 1.96$ eV.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Thermal energy scale: $kT = (1.38 \times 10^{-23})(300) \approx 4.14 \times 10^{-21}$ J $\approx 0.026$ eV — the level gap is about 76 times larger.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Boltzmann ratio: $\frac{N_2}{N_1} = e^{-\Delta E/kT} = e^{-75.9}$. Converting with $e^{-x} = 10^{-x/2.303}$: $\frac{75.9}{2.303} \approx 33$, so $\frac{N_2}{N_1} \approx 10^{-33}$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Interpretation: about one atom in $10^{33}$ occupies the upper level — thermal agitation at room temperature cannot populate a visible transition at all. Every laser must therefore pump atoms upward by design; inversion is an engineered state, never a natural one.

examples.result: $N_2/N_1 \approx e^{-76} \approx 10^{-33}$ — effectively zero; pumping is indispensable.

examples.title: The 50% barrier in a three-level laser
examples.problem: A three-level laser contains $N = 10^{20}$ active atoms, all initially in the ground state, and the lower lasing level **is** the ground state. (i) What minimum number of atoms must occupy the metastable level before any net amplification occurs? (ii) If the pump drives the metastable population to 75% of N, what is the inversion ratio $N_2/N_1$?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Net gain requires the stimulated rate to exceed the absorption rate: $B_{21}N_2 > B_{12}N_1$, and with $B_{12} = B_{21}$ this reduces to $N_2 > N_1$ — a purely population condition.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: (i) The pumped band empties immediately into the metastable level, so $N_1 + N_2 = N$. Then $N_2 > N_1$ means $N_2 > \frac{N}{2}$: at least $5 \times 10^{19}$ atoms must be lifted — the 50% barrier that makes three-level lasers power-hungry.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: (ii) At $N_2 = 0.75N$: $N_1 = 0.25N$, so $\frac{N_2}{N_1} = \frac{0.75}{0.25} = 3$, and the inversion density is $N_2 - N_1 = 0.5N = 5 \times 10^{19}$ atoms contributing to gain.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Contrast the four-level case: with the lower lasing level empty ($N_1 \approx 0$), even $10^{-4}$ of the atoms in the metastable level would give an enormous ratio $N_2/N_1$ — the essential economy of four-level design.

examples.result: (i) More than half — $5 \times 10^{19}$ of the $10^{20}$ atoms; (ii) $N_2/N_1 = 3$, inversion density $0.5N$.

examples.title: Round-trip threshold gain
examples.problem: A laser cavity of length $L = 50$ cm has a total reflector ($R_1 = 1.00$) and an output mirror with $R_2 = 0.95$. Ignoring all other losses, find the threshold gain coefficient $g_{\text{th}}$ of the medium.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: One round trip (length $2L = 1.0$ m) multiplies the intensity by the two mirror reflections and the medium gain: factor $= R_1 R_2\,e^{2gL} = 0.95\,e^{g}$, since $2gL = 1.0 \times g$ here.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Threshold is the condition that the round trip neither grows nor decays — the factor equals 1: $R_1R_2\,e^{2gL} = 1$.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Reading: the medium must supply about 5% intensity gain per metre just to balance the 5% leak through the output mirror. Real cavities add absorption and scattering losses, raising the requirement; and since $g_{\text{th}} \propto \frac{1}{L}$, a longer cavity spreads the fixed mirror loss over more gain length and demands less gain per metre.

examples.result: $g_{\text{th}} \approx 0.051$ m$^{-1}$ — about 5% net gain per metre.

keyTakeaways: Stimulated emission clones the trigger photon in frequency, phase, direction and polarisation — one photon in, two indistinguishable photons out — while spontaneous emission is random in all four.
