quiz.explanation: Products of linear maps are linear: W10 · … · W1 is one effective matrix. Outputs still exist and gradients do not vanish identically — the model simply loses all the power depth was supposed to add.

quiz.q: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight by...
options: Finite differences, perturbing one weight at a time
Applying the chain rule backward from the loss, reusing each layer's error signal
Solving the normal equations for the network
quiz.explanation: Backprop is the chain rule arranged so shared sub-expressions (the deltas) are computed once per layer. Finite differences would need one forward pass per weight — exactly the cost backpropagation exists to avoid.

quiz.q: A neuron has weights (0.5, -0.5), bias 0, and a sigmoid activation. What is its output for input (2, 2)?
quiz.explanation: z = 0.5·2 + (−0.5)·2 + 0 = 0, and σ(0) = 0.5. Symmetric weights on a symmetric input cancel; the other values would require a nonzero pre-activation.

quiz.q: Deep networks largely replaced sigmoid hidden units with ReLU because...
options: ReLU outputs are always between 0 and 1
ReLU's gradient is a nonzero constant for positive inputs, so it does not saturate
ReLU removes the need for biases
quiz.explanation: Sigmoid derivatives peak at 0.25 and vanish in the tails, so stacked layers multiply vanishing factors. ReLU passes gradient 1 for z > 0, which combats vanishing gradients; the loss stays nonconvex and biases remain useful.

intro: Unsupervised learning has no labels to lean on, so evaluation shifts to internal geometry and careful downstream metrics. K-means partitions by distance, PCA compresses by variance, and precision, recall, and F1 quantify classifier quality from raw counts. This section ties the threads together with numbers you can check by hand.
objectives: Run k-means by hand through its assignment and update steps
Compute silhouette, precision, recall, and F1 from raw counts
Explain why PCA's principal directions are eigenvectors of the covariance matrix

concepts.statement: Minimizes within-cluster scatter $J = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{x \in C_i} \lVert x - \mu_i \rVert^2$ by alternating between assigning points to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids as cluster means.
concepts.detail: Each half-step strictly decreases $J$, so the loop converges — but only to a local optimum that depends on initialization, hence restarts or k-means++. The user must choose $k$ (elbow or silhouette), and Euclidean clusters come out convex, so rings and moons defeat it.

concepts.statement: For point $i$: $s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max(a(i), b(i))}$, where $a(i)$ is the mean distance to its own cluster and $b(i)$ the mean distance to the nearest other cluster.
concepts.detail: Values lie in $[-1, 1]$: near +1 means the point sits snug inside its cluster, near 0 means it is on a boundary, and negative means it is probably assigned to the wrong cluster. The average silhouette across points is a standard internal criterion for choosing $k$.

concepts.statement: Projects data onto the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix with the largest eigenvalues; the first principal component is the direction of maximum variance.
concepts.detail: Centering the data first is essential. Eigenvalue $\lambda_j$ equals the variance captured along eigenvector $v_j$, so keeping the top $m$ eigenvectors is the best rank-$m$ linear compression in squared-error terms. PCA is unsupervised — high-variance directions need not be class-discriminative.

concepts.statement: TP = true positives, FP = negatives predicted positive, FN = positives predicted negative, TN = true negatives — the four outcomes of binary classification.
concepts.detail: Every standard metric is a ratio of these counts, which is why you should always read them off the matrix. The positive class is whatever you declare it to be (spam, disease, defect), and swapping classes trades the roles of precision and recall.

concepts.statement: Precision $= TP / (TP + FP)$ — of the flagged, how many were right. Recall $= TP / (TP + FN)$ — of the real cases, how many were found. $F1 = 2PR / (P + R)$.
concepts.detail: F1 is the harmonic mean, dominated by the smaller of the two, so you cannot buy a high F1 with one strong component. Raising the decision threshold trades recall for precision; the F-beta family lets you weight one side heavier.

concepts.statement: The covariance matrix is symmetric positive semi-definite, so its eigenvectors are orthogonal and its eigenvalues are non-negative variances along those axes.
concepts.detail: Orthogonality is what makes principal components uncorrelated — projecting onto them decorrelates the data. The trace of the covariance equals total variance equals the sum of eigenvalues, which is exactly how explained-variance ratios are computed.

examples.title: Precision, Recall, and F1 from a Confusion Matrix
examples.problem: A spam classifier evaluated on 100 emails produces TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 30. Compute precision, recall, F1, and accuracy.

steps.label: Precision
steps.text: $P = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 50 = 0.80$ — of the flagged emails, 80% truly were spam.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: $R = TP / (TP + FN) = 40 / 60 \approx 0.667$ — two-thirds of the real spam was caught.

steps.label: F1
steps.text: $F_1 = 2PR / (P + R) = 2(0.80)(0.667) / 1.467 \approx 0.727$ — pulled toward the weaker side.

steps.label: Accuracy
steps.text: $(TP + TN) / 100 = 70 / 100 = 0.70$, which hides the 20 missed spams that F1 exposes.

examples.title: Finding the First Principal Component
examples.problem: A centered 2D dataset has a covariance matrix with 2 on the diagonal and 1 off the diagonal. Find the first principal component and the variance it explains.

steps.label: Set up the eigenproblem
steps.text: Solve $\det(C - \lambda I) = (2 - \lambda)^2 - 1 = 0$ for the covariance matrix $C$.

steps.label: Solve for eigenvalues
steps.text: $(2 - \lambda)^2 = 1$ gives $\lambda = 3$ or $\lambda = 1$; total variance $= 3 + 1 = 4$.

steps.label: First eigenvector
steps.text: For $\lambda = 3$: $(C - 3I)v = 0$ gives $-v_1 + v_2 = 0$, so $v \propto (1, 1)$, normalized to $(1, 1) / \sqrt{2}$.

steps.label: Explained variance
steps.text: The first component carries $3 / (3 + 1) = 75\%$ of the variance; projecting onto $(1,1)/\sqrt{2}$ compresses the data with least squared loss.

examples.result: PC1 = (1, 1)/√2 with eigenvalue 3 — 75% variance explained

keyTakeaways: K-means alternates nearest-centroid assignment with mean recomputation and converges only to a local optimum; choose k with the silhouette or elbow.
Precision answers 'of the flagged, how many were right'; recall answers 'of the real cases, how many were found'; F1 is their harmonic mean.
PCA keeps the top-eigenvalue eigenvectors of the centered covariance matrix — an orthogonal basis ordered by explained variance.

quiz.q: You run k-means 10 times on the same data and get noticeably different clusterings. The most likely explanation is that...
options: k-means has a bug unless results are identical
The algorithm converged to different local optima from different initializations
Euclidean distance is undefined for this data
The value of k was too small
quiz.explanation: k-means only guarantees convergence to a local minimum of J, and which one depends on the starting centroids — which is exactly why restarts or k-means++ initialization are standard practice.

quiz.q: A point has silhouette s = −0.4. What does that mean?
options: It is deep inside its own cluster
It is on average closer to a neighboring cluster than to its own — likely misassigned
It is exactly on a cluster boundary
quiz.explanation: A negative silhouette means b(i) < a(i): the point's average distance to its own cluster exceeds the distance to the nearest other cluster. s = 0 is the boundary case and +1 is snug; values must lie in [−1, 1].

quiz.q: PCA is applied to centered data with covariance eigenvalues 5, 3, and 0.2. Keeping the first two components explains what fraction of the variance?
quiz.explanation: Total variance = 5 + 3 + 0.2 = 8.2, so the first two components give 8 / 8.2 ≈ 97.6%. The 61% figure is what keeping only the first component would give; the others match no partial sum.

quiz.q: A classifier produces TP = 30, FP = 20, FN = 10. What are precision and F1?
quiz.explanation: Precision = 30/50 = 0.60; recall = 30/40 = 0.75; F1 = 2(0.60)(0.75)/1.35 = 0.9/1.35 ≈ 0.67. The 0.75 figure is recall, not precision, and F1 is dragged toward the weaker side.

quiz.q: A dataset has 99% negatives. A trivial classifier that always predicts negative scores 99% accuracy. Which measurement exposes its uselessness?
options: Training loss on the majority class
Recall on the positive class, which is 0
quiz.explanation: The all-negative rule never flags a positive: TP = 0, so recall = 0 and precision is zero or undefined — F1 collapses. Accuracy hides this under class imbalance, which is exactly why precision and recall reporting matters.

intro: Ensembles win by combining many weak, diverse learners: bagging averages variance away, while boosting reweights training toward the hard cases. Bayesian learning supplies the probability machinery underneath, from naive Bayes to posterior updating. Both come with crisp formulas you can evaluate by hand.
objectives: Explain why bagging reduces variance while boosting reduces bias
Carry out one full round of AdaBoost weight updates numerically
Apply Bayes rule to turn a prior and a likelihood into a posterior

concepts.statement: Train the same learner on $B$ bootstrap resamples of the data and average (or majority-vote) the predictions: $\hat{f}(x) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_b \hat{f}^{(b)}(x)$.
concepts.detail: Bootstrap sampling decorrelates the base models by feeding each a different perturbed dataset. Averaging $B$ roughly independent, equally noisy models shrinks prediction variance by about a factor of $B$ while leaving bias unchanged — which is why high-variance, low-bias learners like deep trees are the classic base model.

concepts.statement: Bagged decision trees plus random feature subsets: at each split, only a random sample of features (classically about $\sqrt{d}$) may be considered.
concepts.detail: The extra randomness attacks the one failure mode bagging cannot fix — correlated trees making the same mistakes. Out-of-bag samples give a free validation estimate, and per-split feature sampling keeps individual trees weak enough to disagree usefully.

concepts.statement: Builds an additive model $F_T(x) = \sum_t \alpha_t h_t(x)$ sequentially: each new weak learner focuses on the examples the current ensemble gets wrong.
concepts.detail: Each round reweights the training set, fits a weak learner (often a depth-1 stump), and adds it with weight proportional to its accuracy. Because later learners chase errors, boosting drives bias down; but it eagerly fits hard examples, so label noise can drag it into overfitting.

concepts.statement: With weighted round error $\epsilon_t$, the learner weight is $\alpha_t = \frac{1}{2} \ln \frac{1 - \epsilon_t}{\epsilon_t}$ and example weights update as $w_i \leftarrow w_i \, e^{-\alpha_t y_i h_t(x_i)}$, then renormalize.
concepts.detail: Misclassified points ($y_i h_t(x_i) = -1$) are multiplied by $e^{+\alpha_t} > 1$ and grow; correct points shrink by $e^{-\alpha_t}$. A learner with $\epsilon_t = 0.5$ is coin-flip useless and gets $\alpha_t = 0$; the classic algorithm stops or reweights when error reaches 0.5.

concepts.statement: $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A) P(A)}{P(B)}$ — the posterior is the likelihood times the prior, divided by the evidence.
concepts.detail: It is the bookkeeping identity for flipping conditional probabilities. With rare events, a highly accurate test can still yield a small posterior: the false-positive population of the healthy majority can outweigh the true positives of the rare condition.

concepts.statement: Averaging independent models cancels uncorrelated errors (variance falls); sequentially correcting errors removes systematic mistakes (bias falls).
concepts.detail: Bagging is the variance weapon — combine strong, unstable learners. Boosting is the bias weapon — combine weak, stable learners in an adaptive order. This is also why bagging parallelizes trivially while boosting is inherently sequential.

examples.title: One Round of AdaBoost Weight Updating
examples.problem: Round 1 of boosting runs on 10 samples with uniform weights 0.1 each. The weak learner misclassifies 2 samples. Update the weights for round 2.

steps.label: Round error
steps.text: 2 of 10 equally weighted samples are wrong: $\epsilon_1 = 2 \times 0.1 = 0.2$.

steps.label: Up-weight the wrong
steps.text: Misclassified weights multiply by $e^{\alpha_1} = e^{0.5 \ln 4} = \sqrt{4} = 2$: each goes $0.1 \to 0.2$.

steps.label: Down-weight the right
steps.text: Correctly classified weights multiply by $e^{-\alpha_1} = 0.5$: each goes $0.1 \to 0.05$.

steps.label: Normalize
steps.text: Sum $= 2(0.2) + 8(0.05) = 0.8$; divide through: misclassified $\to 0.25$ each, correct $\to 0.0625$ each.

examples.result: Misclassified weights end at 0.25 vs 0.0625 — a 4:1 focus ratio for round 2

examples.title: Bayes Rule with a Rare Disease
examples.problem: A disease has 1% prevalence. A test has 99% sensitivity (P(positive | disease) = 0.99) and a 5% false-positive rate. If a random person tests positive, what is the probability they have the disease?

steps.label: Posterior
steps.text: $P(D \mid +) = 0.0099 / 0.0594 = 1/6 \approx 0.167$ — the 99% sensitivity is outweighed by the 99% healthy population.

examples.result: P(disease | positive) ≈ 0.167 (about 17%)

keyTakeaways: Bagging leaves bias alone but cuts variance roughly like 1/B for decorrelated models; random forests force that decorrelation with random feature subsets.
In AdaBoost, misclassified weights grow by a factor of e^{alpha_t} each round, and alpha_t = 0.5·ln((1−e)/e) weights the learner in the final vote.
Bayes rule turns priors and likelihoods into posteriors — with rare conditions, even highly accurate tests yield surprisingly low posteriors.

quiz.q: Which ensemble construction most directly reduces the variance of the final predictor?
options: Bagging with bootstrap resamples and averaged predictions
Increasing the learning rate of a single network
quiz.explanation: Averaging over bootstrap samples cancels uncorrelated errors, shrinking variance while bias is untouched. Boosting targets bias; the other two are single-model tweaks with no averaging effect.

quiz.q: Random forests improve on plain bagged trees primarily by...
options: Restricting each split to a random feature subset, which decorrelates the trees
Using a validation set to pick the best single tree
Weighting trees by their training accuracy
quiz.explanation: Bagged trees stay correlated because dominant features get chosen everywhere; random feature subsets force different trees to explore different structure, which is what makes the average effective.

quiz.q: In an AdaBoost round the weighted error is e = 0.3. What is the learner weight alpha?
quiz.explanation: α = ½ ln(0.7/0.3) = ½ ln(2.33) ≈ 0.42. The 0.85 distractor forgets the ½ factor, and 0.30 just echoes the error.

quiz.q: A spam filter: P(spam) = 0.4, P(word | spam) = 0.9, P(word | not spam) = 0.1. Given the word appears, what is P(spam | word)?
quiz.explanation: Numerator 0.9 × 0.4 = 0.36; evidence 0.36 + 0.1 × 0.6 = 0.42; posterior = 0.36/0.42 ≈ 0.86. The 0.90 option ignores the prior and the false-positive mass; 0.50 would require equal priors and symmetric likelihoods.

quiz.q: Label noise flips a few training labels. Which ensemble is more likely to overfit those mislabeled points, and why?
options: Bagging, because bootstrap samples concentrate on them
Boosting, because it exponentially reweights hard (including mislabeled) examples each round
Both equally, since they are both ensembles
quiz.explanation: AdaBoost treats persistently misclassified points as the most important ones and keeps inflating their weights — genuine noise gets chased forever. Bagging's resampling dilutes noise instead of focusing it.

intro: Choosing a model is itself a skill: you need a trustworthy estimate of future performance before the future arrives. This section covers the telltale signs of overfitting, the mechanics of k-fold cross-validation, and how to run a disciplined model-selection experiment. The worked example selects a kNN hyperparameter from CV scores.
objectives: Diagnose overfitting and underfitting from train and validation curves
Explain how k-fold cross-validation spends data efficiently and where it can mislead
Select a model and hyperparameters using validation evidence rather than training accuracy

concepts.statement: Choosing among algorithms and hyperparameters using held-out or cross-validated performance, never the training metric alone.
concepts.detail: The core discipline: any score used to make a choice has been optimized against and is therefore optimistic; a final untouched test set (or nested cross-validation) is needed for an honest estimate. Selection compares candidate configurations; assessment reports the chosen one's expected error.

concepts.statement: The model captures noise and idiosyncrasies of the training set: training error keeps falling while validation error rises, opening a generalization gap.
concepts.detail: Classic signs: a large train-validation gap, wild coefficients or boundaries, and performance that degrades as capacity grows past a point. Cures include more data, regularization, lower capacity, early stopping, and ensembling. The opposite failure, underfitting, shows both errors high and close together.

concepts.statement: Split the data into $k$ folds; train on $k-1$ folds and validate on the held-out fold, rotating so every example is validated exactly once, then average the $k$ scores.
concepts.detail: Each model trains on about $(k-1)/k$ of the data, so folds are reused and scores share training data — the estimate has lower bias than a single split but the fold scores are not independent. Leave-one-out (k = n) maximizes training data per fold but is expensive and returns highly correlated fold scores.

concepts.statement: With squared loss, expected test error decomposes into bias² + variance + irreducible noise; capacity buys bias reduction at the price of variance.
concepts.detail: Underfitting means high bias and low variance; overfitting means low bias and high variance. Regularization moves you along this frontier rather than escaping it — the art is stopping at the validation minimum, not the training minimum.

concepts.statement: Stratified folds preserve class proportions in every train and validation split; all preprocessing must be fit inside each fold to avoid leakage.
concepts.detail: With a 5% positive class, plain random folds can leave a validation fold nearly empty of positives. Leakage — fitting scalers, imputers, or feature selection on the full dataset before splitting — quietly inflates CV scores because validation information seeps into training.

examples.title: Selecting k in kNN with 5-Fold Cross-Validation
examples.problem: 5-fold CV accuracies for kNN on the same data: k = 1 gives [0.70, 0.72, 0.68, 0.71, 0.69]; k = 5 gives [0.78, 0.80, 0.76, 0.79, 0.77]; k = 20 gives [0.75, 0.74, 0.76, 0.75, 0.75]. Training accuracy for k = 1 is 1.00. Which k should be selected?

steps.label: Flag the overfit candidate
steps.text: k = 1 hits 1.00 on training data but 0.70 in CV — a 0.30 gap, the classic variance signature of memorization.

steps.label: Flag the over-smoothed candidate
steps.text: k = 20 drops to 0.75: the neighborhood is now so large it blends classes together, so bias is creeping up.

steps.label: Select
steps.text: k = 5 maximizes CV accuracy; report it as the choice and reserve a final untouched test set for the honest number.

examples.result: Choose k = 5 (mean CV accuracy 0.78)

keyTakeaways: A big train-validation gap flags overfitting; both errors high and close together flags underfitting.
K-fold CV reuses data across folds — great for selection, but fold scores are correlated and the winner's CV score is optimistic.
Hyperparameters are chosen on validation or CV evidence; the test set is spent exactly once, at the end.

quiz.q: Training accuracy is 0.99 and validation accuracy is 0.71, and the gap grows with more training. Diagnosis?
options: Underfitting — the model is too simple
Overfitting — the model memorizes the training data including its noise
The validation set is too large
This is healthy behavior for a good model
quiz.explanation: Near-perfect training performance with mediocre validation performance is the signature of memorization. Underfitting would show both accuracies low and close; the fix here is regularization or more data, not more capacity.

quiz.q: In 5-fold cross-validation with 500 examples, how many examples are in each validation fold, and how often is each example used for validation?
quiz.explanation: 500/5 = 100 held out per round; the rotation guarantees each example lands in the validation fold exactly once across the five rounds.

quiz.q: Compared with 10-fold CV, leave-one-out CV typically has...
options: Lower bias but higher variance and much higher cost
Lower variance because it uses more folds
quiz.explanation: LOOCV trains on nearly all the data, so its estimate is less pessimistic (lower bias), but each fold's model is nearly identical, making fold scores highly correlated (higher variance), and it needs n full trainings.

quiz.q: A dataset has 3% positives. Which cross-validation setup is most appropriate for a classifier?
options: Plain 10-fold CV — randomness will handle it
Stratified k-fold so every fold keeps about 3% positives
LOOCV, because rare classes need maximum training data
quiz.explanation: Stratification guarantees each validation fold carries the class mix; unstratified folds can randomly contain almost no positives, making fold scores meaningless. A single split wastes data and is noisier still.

intro: Regression fits real-valued outputs by minimizing squared error, and its geometry — projections, norms, eigenvectors — is the same geometry behind dimensionality reduction. This section derives the least-squares solution, works it on three data points, and connects ridge, lasso, and SVD to PCA. The through-line: penalize complexity to buy generalization.
objectives: Derive and compute the ordinary least-squares solution on real numbers
Contrast ridge (L2) and lasso (L1) penalties and their effects on coefficients
Explain how the SVD of centered data recovers PCA's directions and variances

concepts.statement: Minimizes $\lVert y - Xw \rVert^2$ over weights $w$; the normal equations $X^T X w = X^T y$ give the closed form $\hat{w} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y$ when $X^T X$ is invertible.
concepts.detail: Geometrically, $X \hat{w}$ is the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto the column space of $X$. The solution is unique exactly when the features are linearly independent; collinear features make $X^T X$ singular, and the minimal-norm solution is selected via the pseudo-inverse.

concepts.statement: Minimizes $\lVert y - Xw \rVert^2 + \lambda \lVert w \rVert_2^2$, shrinking the OLS solution to $\hat{w} = (X^T X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^T y$.
concepts.detail: The penalty makes the system invertible even under collinearity and pulls coefficients toward zero without ever setting them exactly to zero. Cross-validation picks $\lambda$; as it approaches 0 ridge returns OLS, and as it grows the estimate approaches zero — a continuous bias-for-variance trade.

concepts.statement: Minimizes $\lVert y - Xw \rVert^2 + \lambda \lVert w \rVert_1$, which drives some coefficients exactly to zero, performing feature selection.
concepts.detail: The L1 ball has corners on the axes, so the constrained least-squares solution often lands exactly on a sparse point — unlike the round L2 ball, which only grazes smoothly. Prefer lasso when few features are believed to matter; ridge usually wins for dense weak signals and prediction stability.

concepts.statement: $X = U \Sigma V^T$ factors any matrix into orthonormal $U$, a diagonal $\Sigma$ of singular values, and orthonormal $V^T$.
concepts.detail: For centered data, the right singular vectors (columns of $V$) are the principal directions, and the singular values satisfy $\sigma_j^2 = (n-1) \lambda_j$ with covariance eigenvalues $\lambda_j$. Truncating to the top $m$ singular values gives the best rank-$m$ approximation of $X$ — PCA and low-rank modeling are the same computation.

concepts.statement: For a square matrix $A$, $Av = \lambda v$ means the direction $v$ is only scaled, never rotated, by $A$; $\lambda$ is the eigenvalue.
concepts.detail: Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors — the covariance matrix is symmetric, which is why principal directions form an orthonormal basis. The spectral theorem behind this is the reason PCA decorrelates features.

concepts.statement: Penalties shrink the effective capacity of a model: they restrict $w$ to a ball around the origin, deliberately trading bias for variance.
concepts.detail: The same idea appears as weight decay in neural networks, shrinkage priors in Bayesian regression, and cost-complexity pruning in trees. What changes is the geometry — L2 balls, L1 diamonds, tree penalties — and therefore what kind of simplicity you get.

examples.title: Least Squares on Three Points
examples.problem: Fit the line y = a + bx by ordinary least squares to the points (0, 1), (1, 3), and (2, 3).

steps.label: Intercept
steps.text: $a = (\sum y - b \sum x) / n = (7 - 3) / 3 \approx 1.333$.

examples.title: Ridge Shrinks the OLS Estimate
examples.problem: A single data point (x, y) = (1, 3) means OLS would fit w = 3. Ridge minimizes J(w) = (3 − w)² + 2w². What is the ridge estimate, and what happens as the penalty changes?

steps.label: Objective
steps.text: $J(w) = (3 - w)^2 + 2w^2$ — squared error plus the $\lambda = 2$ penalty.

steps.label: Solve
steps.text: $w = 1$; OLS alone gives $w = 3$, so the penalty shrank the estimate by two-thirds.

steps.label: Limits
steps.text: As $\lambda \to 0$, $w \to 3$ (OLS); as $\lambda \to \infty$, $w \to 0$ — ridge interpolates between fit and simplicity.

examples.result: w = 1.0 — the L2 penalty shrinks the OLS estimate from 3 toward 0

keyTakeaways: OLS solves the normal equations and is unique only when features are linearly independent; ridge's λI repairs exactly that failure.
L1 corners make lasso sparse (feature selection); L2 smoothness keeps ridge dense but stabilizes collinear data.
The SVD of centered data is PCA in disguise: V holds the directions, the squared singular values scale the variances, and truncation is the compression.

quiz.q: You need a linear model that automatically discards irrelevant features by zeroing their coefficients. Which penalty do you choose?
options: No penalty — OLS already zeroes irrelevant features
quiz.explanation: The L1 diamond's corners sit on the axes, so solutions frequently have exact zeros. Ridge shrinks everything smoothly but keeps all features, and plain OLS gives small nonzero coefficients to irrelevant features.

quiz.q: The matrix X^T X is nearly singular because two features are almost collinear. What does ridge regression do about it?
options: Adds λI, conditioning the system and shrinking coefficients
Drops one of the collinear features automatically
Sets both coefficients to exactly zero
quiz.explanation: X^T X + λI has eigenvalues bounded below by λ, so the inverse exists and the coefficients stabilize. Dropping features is lasso-like behavior under special conditions; exact zeroing is not an L2 property.

quiz.q: For centered data X = U Σ V^T, the principal component directions are...
quiz.explanation: V's columns are the right singular vectors, identical to the covariance eigenvectors. U's columns span the row space of the scores, and singular values are scalars, not directions.

quiz.q: One data point (x, y) = (1, 3). OLS would fit w = 3. Ridge minimizes (3 − w)² + 2w². What is the ridge estimate?
quiz.explanation: dJ/dw = −2(3 − w) + 4w = 6w − 6 = 0 gives w = 1: the penalty pulls the fit toward zero. The 1.5 option is what λ = 1 would give, and 3.0 ignores the penalty entirely.

quiz.q: Why does truncating the SVD to the largest m singular values give the same result as PCA with m components?
options: Both algorithms are randomized with the same seed
SVD also centers the data automatically
They only coincide when m equals the number of features
PCA's eigenproblem on X^T X is solved exactly by V and the squared singular values, so both optimize the same rank-m projection
quiz.explanation: X^T X = V Σ² V^T, so the right singular vectors are the eigenvectors and the squared singular values are the eigenvalues — the two procedures compute the identical subspace. Centering must be done before either method, and the equivalence holds for any m.

intro: Requirements engineering turns vague stakeholder wishes into precise, testable statements of what the system must do and how well it must do it. Its disciplines — elicitation, specification of functional and non-functional needs, and traceability — are where project failures are quietly born or prevented. The craft is making every requirement verifiable and every decision traceable.
objectives: Distinguish functional from non-functional requirements and write both verifiably
Choose elicitation techniques for different stakeholder and uncertainty situations
Use a traceability matrix to detect orphan requirements and untested behavior

concepts.statement: A statement of what the system shall do — a service, input, output, or behavior — typically written as 'The system shall X'.
concepts.detail: Examples: 'The system shall export a report as PDF' or 'The system shall reject passwords shorter than 12 characters'. Functional requirements define the problem's verbs; each should be atomic, unambiguous, and independently testable.

concepts.statement: A constraint on how well the system performs its functions: performance, security, usability, reliability, scalability, maintainability, portability.
concepts.detail: The fatal mistake is writing NFRs as adjectives — 'fast', 'secure', 'user-friendly' — which can neither pass nor fail a test. A good NFR binds a metric, a threshold, and a condition, such as 95% of search requests completing within 300 ms under 500 concurrent users. NFRs often conflict (security vs usability) and need explicit prioritization.

concepts.statement: Structured ways to surface requirements: interviews, workshops, observation, document analysis, prototyping, and surveys.
concepts.detail: Stakeholders describe what they think they do; observation captures what they actually do — the gap is where hidden requirements live. Prototypes and storyboards are the cheapest way to resolve ambiguity early because they force concrete reactions instead of abstract opinions. Quality attributes need targeted questioning, since nobody volunteers that the system must stay maintainable.

concepts.statement: Recorded links from each requirement forward to design elements, code, and tests (forward traceability) and backward to their stakeholder origin (backward traceability).
concepts.detail: The traceability matrix makes three audits mechanical: does every requirement have a design and a test; does every test trace to a requirement (no gold-plating); does every implemented feature trace to a requirement (no scope creep). When a requirement changes, the matrix lists exactly which artifacts to revisit — that is impact analysis.

concepts.statement: Validation asks 'are we building the right system' (does it meet stakeholder intent); verification asks 'are we building the system right' (does it match the specification).
concepts.detail: A perfectly implemented spec that solves the wrong problem verifies green and validates red. Reviews, prototypes, and acceptance-criteria walkthroughs validate; formal checks and test tracing verify. Ambiguity — such as 'up to 50 users' — is the enemy of both.

concepts.statement: Agile requirement units of the form 'As a role, I want a capability, so that I get a benefit', made testable by given/when/then acceptance criteria.
concepts.detail: Stories deliberately defer detail to conversation — the card is a promise to talk, not a contract. Acceptance criteria turn the story into pass/fail checks the product owner agrees to; a story without them is not ready for implementation.

examples.title: Turning Vague Requirements into Verifiable Ones
examples.problem: A stakeholder submits three requirements: 'The system shall respond quickly to searches', 'Passwords must be secure', and 'Users shall reset a forgotten password via email'. Rewrite them so each can pass or fail a test.

steps.label: Classify each statement
steps.text: Password reset is a behavior — functional. Response speed and password security are quality constraints — non-functional.

steps.label: Make latency measurable
steps.text: '95% of search requests complete within 300 ms, measured at 500 concurrent users on production-equivalent hardware.'

steps.label: Make security operational
steps.text: 'Passwords are at least 12 characters, screened against a known-breach list, and stored as salted memory-hard hashes; accounts lock after 5 failed attempts in 15 minutes.'

steps.label: Make the functional one atomic
steps.text: 'The system shall email a single-use reset link that expires after 15 minutes; a used or expired link is rejected.'

examples.result: One atomic functional requirement plus two measurable NFRs, each with a pass/fail threshold

examples.title: Spotting an Orphan Test with a Traceability Matrix
examples.problem: A traceability matrix links requirements to modules and tests: R1 (login) maps to M1 (auth service) and tests T1, T2. R2 (password reset) maps to M2 (email service) and test T3. Test T4 exercises email retry after timeout but traces to no requirement. What should the team do?

steps.label: Audit the requirement rows
steps.text: Every requirement has a module and at least one test — no orphan requirements on that axis.

steps.label: Audit the test columns
steps.text: T4 traces to nothing: it is an orphan test, and M2's failure-handling behavior exists only as test code.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: Either a real requirement is missing (notifications must be reliable) or the team is gold-plating beyond agreed scope.

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: If retries matter, add R3 'The system shall retry failed notification emails up to 3 times' and link T4 to it; otherwise delete T4.

examples.result: T4 is an orphan test — add requirement R3 or drop the test

keyTakeaways: Functional means what the system does; non-functional means how well — and only measurable NFRs can be tested.
Observation and prototyping surface the requirements stakeholders cannot articulate in interviews.
A traceability matrix turns coverage, scope-creep, and change-impact questions into table lookups.

quiz.q: 'The system shall complete a funds transfer within 2 seconds at the 99th percentile.' This is best classified as...
quiz.explanation: It constrains how well a transfer performs, not what a transfer is — the behavior (transfer funds) stays functional. It is testable precisely because metric, threshold, and percentile are pinned.

quiz.q: Why must 'The system shall be easy to use' be rewritten before it can serve as a requirement?
options: It is not measurable, so no test can pass or fail it
Usability is a design decision, not a requirement
Only functional requirements belong in specifications
quiz.explanation: Requirements need acceptance criteria, and 'easy' has no threshold. Rewrite with a metric, for example 90% of new users completing checkout in under 3 minutes without assistance. Usability can absolutely be a requirement — just a quantified one.

quiz.q: During elicitation, users describe a tidy daily process, but watching them work reveals a spreadsheet full of workarounds. What does this gap signal?
options: The users are unreliable and should be excluded
Hidden requirements the stated process omits — capture and prioritize them
quiz.explanation: Divergence between stated and observed practice is the classic marker of tacit requirements; observation exists to find exactly this. The workarounds encode real constraints the new system must handle or replace.

quiz.q: In a traceability matrix, a test case exists that links to no requirement. What does this indicate?
options: Gold-plating — work not requested by any stakeholder requirement
The matrix was filled out incorrectly
quiz.explanation: Tests without requirement parents mean someone built behavior nobody asked for — scope creep or gold-plating. The fix is to either justify it with a (possibly missing) requirement or remove the behavior.

quiz.q: A team builds exactly to specification, passes every specified test, and the customer still rejects the result. Which requirements-engineering failure is this?
options: Verification without validation — the spec was implemented right but was the wrong spec
quiz.explanation: Building the system right (verification) succeeded while building the right system (validation) failed — elicitation missed the true stakeholder needs. This is why prototypes and early customer walkthroughs are part of requirements validation.

intro: Design turns requirements into structure, and UML gives that structure a shared visual language: class diagrams for static relationships, sequence diagrams for message flow over time, and state diagrams for event-driven behavior. Underneath the notation sit two criteria that decide whether a design survives change: cohesion high, coupling low. This section reads the diagrams and applies the criteria.
objectives: Read and construct class, sequence, and state machine diagrams for a small system
Judge a design using cohesion and coupling criteria
Refactor a low-cohesion, high-coupling module into focused services

concepts.statement: Static structure: boxes with name, attribute, and operation compartments, connected by associations carrying multiplicities (1, 0..1, 1..*, *), plus generalization arrows for is-a and diamonds for whole-part relationships.
concepts.detail: Composition (filled diamond) binds the part's lifetime to the whole — delete the order and its line items die; aggregation (hollow diamond) is a looser whole-part link. Multiplicity at an association end counts how many objects at that end relate to one object at the other: an Order has 1..* OrderLines, each Line referring to exactly 1 Product.

concepts.statement: Time-ordered interactions: vertical lifelines for objects, horizontal messages drawn left to right in chronological order, with activations and dashed returns.
concepts.detail: It answers 'who talks to whom, in what order' for one scenario — ideal for verifying a use case's flow or an API contract. Solid arrows with filled heads are synchronous calls, open heads are asynchronous messages, and alt/opt/loop frames encode conditionals and repetition.

concepts.statement: Event-driven behavior of one object: states as rounded boxes, transitions labeled event [guard] / action, with an initial pseudostate and a final state.
concepts.detail: Use it when an object's response depends on its history — an Order that ignores 'ship' while pending but accepts it while paid. Guards such as [stock > 0] gate transitions, and actions run on transitions or on state entry and exit. Missing and unreachable states are this diagram's classic defects.

concepts.statement: The degree to which a module's elements serve a single purpose; high cohesion means one module, one mind-sized responsibility.
concepts.detail: A class that validates, charges, emails, and updates inventory has low cohesion — its name cannot say what it does. High cohesion concentrates change: a change to notification logic touches only the notifier. Functional cohesion, where elements cooperate toward one function, is the strongest kind.

concepts.statement: The degree of interdependence between modules; low coupling means a module can be understood and changed without touching its neighbors.
concepts.detail: Coupling spreads through concrete types, global state, and wide interfaces; it is reduced by narrow interfaces, dependency injection, and depending on abstractions. Low coupling does not mean no communication — it means few, explicit, contract-based touchpoints.

concepts.statement: Each module should hide a design decision behind a stable interface, exposing what clients need and nothing more.
concepts.detail: This is the mechanism behind low coupling: if a database choice or algorithm is invisible behind an interface, swapping it is a local change. Design-to-interface plus dependency injection operationalizes it — callers name the abstraction, and wiring supplies the implementation.

examples.title: Refactoring a God Class for Cohesion and Coupling
examples.problem: An OrderManager class validates orders, charges credit cards, sends confirmation emails, and updates inventory. It directly instantiates PaymentGateway, SmtpClient, and InventoryDatabase; six other modules call OrderManager for all four jobs. Diagnose the design flaws and restructure.

steps.label: Diagnose cohesion
steps.text: Four unrelated responsibilities in one class — low cohesion; its name cannot describe its purpose.

steps.label: Diagnose coupling
steps.text: Concrete dependencies created inside the class plus six modules routed through one god object — high, hidden coupling.

steps.label: Split by responsibility
steps.text: Create OrderValidator, PaymentService, NotificationService, and InventoryService — one purpose each (high cohesion).

steps.label: Invert the dependencies
steps.text: Each service exposes a narrow interface and receives its collaborators from outside; callers depend on the abstractions.

steps.label: Verify the fix
steps.text: A change to email formatting now touches NotificationService alone, and swapping payment providers touches one wiring point.

examples.result: Four single-purpose services behind narrow interfaces — change becomes local

keyTakeaways: Class diagrams capture static structure, sequence diagrams capture time-ordered message flow, and state machines capture event-driven lifecycles.
High cohesion concentrates responsibility; low coupling isolates change — together they make modification local instead of viral.
Depend on narrow abstractions and inject implementations; that is how information hiding is engineered in practice.

quiz.q: You need to model how a browser, web server, and payment gateway exchange messages during checkout, in chronological order. Which diagram fits best?
quiz.explanation: Sequence diagrams show lifelines and time-ordered messages between objects — exactly an interaction protocol. Class diagrams are static, and state machines model one object's internal lifecycle.

quiz.q: An Order object accepts a 'ship' event only when it is in the 'paid' state and ignores it in 'pending'. Which model captures this most directly?
options: A class diagram with a ship() operation
A sequence diagram with an alt fragment
A state machine diagram with states and guarded event transitions
quiz.explanation: History-dependent responses to events are the definition of stateful behavior — states plus event and guard transitions. An alt fragment could show one scenario's branching, but not the object's full lifecycle.

quiz.q: In a class diagram, an association from Order to OrderLine reads: 1 Order relates to 1..* OrderLines; each OrderLine belongs to exactly 1 Order. What does the 1..* end express?
options: An Order may exist with no lines
OrderLine is a subclass of Order
Every Order has at least one and possibly many OrderLines
quiz.explanation: Multiplicity at the OrderLine end counts lines per Order: one-or-more. Zero-or-many (*) would allow empty orders, and subclassing is a generalization arrow, not an association end.

quiz.q: A module named ReportManager generates reports, emails them, archives PDFs, and logs audit events. What design smell is loudest?
options: High coupling to the email server
Low cohesion — four unrelated responsibilities in one module
quiz.explanation: One name cannot cover four purposes: that is low cohesion by definition. Coupling may also be poor, but the module's own mixed responsibility is the primary smell — split by responsibility first, then fix dependencies.

quiz.q: Why is low coupling valued so highly in design?
options: It reduces the number of features the product needs
It eliminates the need for testing
It makes changes local: few, explicit interfaces mean modifications do not cascade through the system
quiz.explanation: Low coupling bounds the blast radius of a change and lets modules evolve independently behind stable contracts. It says nothing about feature count, testing, or raw speed — those are separate concerns.

intro: Testing is structured sampling of behavior: levels place tests at unit, integration, system, and acceptance scope, while black-box and white-box techniques decide which cases to generate from specifications or code. Coverage metrics turn 'did we test enough' into counting. The subtle part — worked below — is that covering every statement can still leave branches and paths unexercised.
objectives: Place tests correctly across unit, integration, system, and acceptance levels
Design black-box and white-box test cases from specifications and code
Distinguish statement, branch, and path coverage on a concrete function

concepts.statement: Unit tests exercise one module in isolation; integration tests verify interfaces between modules; system tests check the assembled product against requirements; acceptance tests confirm stakeholder readiness.
concepts.detail: Each level catches what the others cannot: units catch logic errors cheaply, integration catches contract mismatches like wrong formats or orderings, system catches emergent and non-functional failures, and acceptance catches a built-right-but-wrong product. Fix cost rises steeply with level — hence the push to find defects low.

concepts.statement: Test cases derive from the specification, not the code: inputs and expected outputs are chosen with no knowledge of internal structure.
concepts.detail: Core techniques are equivalence partitioning — one representative per class of inputs that should behave alike — and boundary value analysis, testing the edges (0, max, min, off-by-one) because that is where bugs cluster. Black-box can find missing behavior: the code cannot be tested for what it never implemented.

concepts.statement: Test cases derive from the code's structure — control flow, conditions, data flow — aiming to exercise branches, paths, and definition-use chains.
concepts.detail: Its strength is proving the existing logic is executed; its blind spot is omission, since it cannot detect behavior the code never had. Typical criteria are statement, branch, condition, and path coverage, with tooling that instruments code to measure what the suite actually reached.

concepts.statement: The fraction of executable statements executed by the test suite; 100% means every statement ran at least once.
concepts.detail: It is the weakest structural criterion: a statement can run under conditions that never test its alternatives, and unexercised else-branches stay dark. Satisfying it is a floor, not a goal — it subsumes nothing but itself.

concepts.statement: The fraction of decision outcomes exercised: each if, while, or case must be evaluated both true and false at least once.
concepts.detail: Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage — taking both edges of every decision forces every statement to run. It still misses condition interactions: a decision like (a && b) can show both outcomes while a is always false, masking bugs in how b is used; condition and modified-condition criteria target that gap.

concepts.statement: Re-running existing tests after changes to confirm that unchanged behavior stays unchanged.
concepts.detail: Every fix risks breaking a neighbor, and the regression suite is the safety net that makes refactoring and continuous integration possible. Selection is the practical problem: run everything (safe, slow) or prioritize by code proximity and failure history (fast, riskier).

examples.title: Statement Coverage Is Not Branch Coverage
examples.problem: A method computes a label from two independent checks: it sets sign = 'neg' when a < 0 (otherwise 'nonneg'), then sets grade = 'pass' when score >= 60 (otherwise 'fail'). Test T1 runs the method with a = -5 and score = 70. What does T1 cover, and what is still missing?

steps.label: Trace T1
steps.text: Both conditions are true; every statement — both default assignments, both conditions, both then-arms — executes: 6 of 6 statements = 100% statement coverage.

steps.label: Count branch outcomes
steps.text: Only the true edges run; the two false edges never do: 2 of 4 outcomes = 50% branch coverage.

steps.label: Add T2
steps.text: Running with a = 3 and score = 50 takes both false edges, lifting branch coverage to 100%.

steps.label: What remains dark
steps.text: The mixed paths (true/false and false/true) never execute — path coverage is still 50%, so any interaction between the two checks goes untested.

examples.result: T1 alone: 100% statement, 50% branch; T1 + T2: 100% branch, 50% path

keyTakeaways: Unit, integration, system, and acceptance levels target defects at successively larger scope; finding them low is cheapest.
Black-box designs cases from the spec (equivalence classes, boundaries); white-box designs them from the code's structure.
Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage; 100% statement coverage can coexist with 50% branch coverage.

quiz.q: Defects like 'module A sends XML but module B expects JSON' are targeted by which test level?
quiz.explanation: Interface-contract mismatches appear only when modules meet — that is integration testing's specific quarry. Unit tests mock the neighbor, and acceptance tests check stakeholder value, not inter-module formats.

quiz.q: A suite achieves 100% statement coverage on a module. Which claim follows?
options: Every statement executed at least once, but some branch outcomes may be untested
All paths through the module were executed
quiz.explanation: Statement coverage only promises execution: one test can run every statement without ever taking an else edge. Branch coverage is strictly stronger, and path coverage stronger still — and none of them prove correctness.

quiz.q: A specification says the system accepts quantities 1 to 100. Which black-box test set is most appropriate?
quiz.explanation: Equivalence classes are invalid (< 1), valid (1 to 100), and invalid (> 100); boundaries are where off-by-one bugs live: 0, 1, 100, 101 (2 and 99 add inner checks). Testing all 100 values wastes the effort that partitioning saves.

quiz.q: White-box testing alone cannot find which class of defect?
options: A loop that iterates one time too few
A feature the specification demands but the code never implemented
A condition that inverts a flag
quiz.explanation: White-box measures the code that exists; missing functionality leaves no structure to cover — only specification-derived (black-box) cases can expose absence. The other three are all visible in control flow.

quiz.q: A method contains two independent if-statements, each with two outcomes. What is the minimum number of test cases for full branch coverage?
quiz.explanation: One test making both conditions true takes both then-edges; a second making both false takes both else-edges — 4 branch outcomes in 2 tests. Full path coverage, however, needs all four combinations (TT, TF, FT, FF), that is, 4 tests.

intro: Project management chooses a lifecycle to fit requirements volatility, estimates effort with models like COCOMO, and manages risk as a scored, prioritized list. Quality attributes — reliability, maintainability, security, performance — are the product-side NFRs made operational. This section works a COCOMO estimate and a risk ranking on real numbers.
objectives: Choose between plan-driven and agile lifecycles from requirement stability and context
Compute effort, schedule, and staffing with basic COCOMO
Rank risks by probability-times-impact exposure and name quality attributes precisely

concepts.statement: Sequential phases — requirements, design, implementation, verification, maintenance — each completing before the next begins, with documents as phase gates.
concepts.detail: It works when requirements are stable and well understood, the domain is safety- or contract-critical, and rework is expensive relative to upfront analysis. Its weakness is late feedback: the customer sees working software only at the end, so a wrong early decision surfaces at maximum cost.

concepts.statement: Iterative, incremental delivery in short timeboxes: each iteration produces a potentially shippable increment, and feedback reprioritizes the backlog.
concepts.detail: Agile trades predictability of plan for adaptability to learning; it shines when requirements evolve or the product is novel. The cost is discipline: without continuous integration, testing, and an empowered product owner, technical debt accumulates silently and velocity decays.

concepts.statement: Basic organic mode: $E = 2.4 \, (KLOC)^{1.05}$ person-months and schedule $T = 2.5 \, E^{0.38}$ months; average staff is $E / T$.
concepts.detail: KLOC is estimated size in thousands of delivered source lines, and the exponent above 1 says effort grows superlinearly with size because of communication overhead. Intermediate and detailed modes multiply by cost drivers — product complexity, personnel capability, tool support. The outputs are calibration, not prophecy: re-estimate as size knowledge improves.

concepts.statement: Identify risks, assess each as exposure = probability × impact, prioritize by exposure, plan mitigations with triggers, and monitor.
concepts.detail: A risk matrix plots probability against impact, and the top-right corner demands active mitigation (reduce probability), contingency (reduce impact), or both. Risks are future-tense and uncertain — the payment API may ship late — unlike issues, which have already happened. Untreated top risks silently become the schedule's hidden buffer.

concepts.statement: Measurable properties of the running system and its codebase: performance, reliability, availability, security, usability, maintainability, portability.
concepts.detail: External attributes (performance, usability) are visible to users at runtime; internal attributes (maintainability, testability, modularity) show up as the cost of change. They conflict — caching versus freshness, security versus usability — so architectures must trade them explicitly, using tactics like redundancy for reliability or authentication layers for security.

concepts.statement: The accumulated future cost of shortcuts taken under schedule pressure: ship the quick fix now, pay interest as slower change later.
concepts.detail: Debt can be strategic — a deliberate prototype loan to learn fast — or reckless, like shipping with no tests into a tangled module. The interest is real: every change to a debt-laden area costs more, and velocity decays until the principal is repaid by refactoring. That is why refactoring time must be budgeted, not begged for.

examples.title: A Basic COCOMO Estimate
examples.problem: A basic COCOMO organic-mode project is estimated at 10 KLOC. Estimate effort, schedule, and average team size using E = 2.4 × (KLOC)^1.05 person-months and T = 2.5 × E^0.38 months.

steps.label: Effort
steps.text: $E = 2.4 \times 10^{1.05} \approx 2.4 \times 11.22 \approx 26.9$ person-months.

steps.label: Schedule
steps.text: $T = 2.5 \times 26.9^{0.38} \approx 2.5 \times 3.49 \approx 8.7$ months.

steps.label: Average staff
steps.text: $E / T \approx 26.9 / 8.7 \approx 3.1$ people.

steps.label: Sanity-check
steps.text: Re-estimate when the size estimate firms up: if scope creeps to 20 KLOC, effort roughly doubles to about 56 person-months.

examples.result: ≈ 27 person-months, ≈ 8.7 months of schedule, ≈ 3 people average

examples.title: Ranking Risks by Exposure
examples.problem: Three identified risks: R1 'a key developer leaves' (probability 0.3, impact 4 on a 1–5 scale), R2 'the third-party payment API ships late' (probability 0.5, impact 4), R3 'the UI framework deprecates a widget we use' (probability 0.6, impact 1). Rank them and propose responses.

steps.label: Score each risk
steps.text: Exposure = probability × impact: R1 = 0.3 × 4 = 1.2; R2 = 0.5 × 4 = 2.0; R3 = 0.6 × 1 = 0.6.

steps.label: Rank
steps.text: R2 (2.0) > R1 (1.2) > R3 (0.6) — R2 sits top-right in the risk matrix even though R3 is the most likely.

steps.label: Mitigate R2
steps.text: Reduce probability and impact: early integration spike, a sandboxed mock, contract tests, and a fallback provider behind an interface.

steps.label: Mitigate R1, accept R3
steps.text: R1: cross-training, pairing rotation, documented handover. R3: cheap to monitor — wrap the widget and accept the residual risk.

examples.result: Priority R2 (2.0) > R1 (1.2) > R3 (0.6): mitigate the top two, accept-and-monitor R3

keyTakeaways: Waterfall fits stable, contract-driven scope; agile fits evolving scope — both demand disciplined engineering either way.
Basic COCOMO organic mode: E = 2.4·(KLOC)^1.05 person-months, T = 2.5·E^0.38 months, staff = E/T; treat the outputs as calibrated ranges.
Risk exposure = probability × impact drives priority, and quality attributes conflict, so they must be traded deliberately.

quiz.q: Using basic COCOMO in organic mode, the effort for a 20 KLOC project is closest to...
quiz.explanation: E = 2.4 × 20^1.05 ≈ 2.4 × 23.2 ≈ 56 person-months. The 48 figure forgets the superlinear exponent (2.4 × 20 = 48), and 24 roughly halves the correct value.

quiz.q: A regulated medical device with fixed, documented requirements and formal certification. Which lifecycle is the better default?
options: Plan-driven (waterfall-style) with document gates and formal reviews
Any lifecycle, since the choice does not affect certification
quiz.explanation: Stable requirements plus certification evidence argue for plan-driven: traceable documents and staged verification map directly to regulatory review. Agile is possible with heavy tailoring, but plan-driven is the natural default here.

quiz.q: Risk R has probability 0.5 and impact 4 on a 1–5 scale; risk S has probability 0.1 and impact 5. Which has higher exposure and should be mitigated first?
options: S, because its impact is maximal
They are equal since both involve a 5
Cannot be compared — probability and impact are incommensurable
quiz.explanation: Exposure multiplies: R = 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 versus S = 0.1 × 5 = 0.5, so R dominates despite S's worse worst case. Prioritizing by worst-case impact alone chases rare catastrophes while likely ones bleed the project.

quiz.q: Maintainability is classified as which kind of quality attribute?
options: External, visible to end users at runtime
Internal, affecting the cost of change rather than runtime behavior
quiz.explanation: Maintainability is internal: users never see it directly, but developers pay it on every change. Performance and usability are external and visible; functionality is what the system does, not how changeable it is.

quiz.q: A team skips writing tests to hit a deadline. In quality-management terms, what have they created?
options: Technical debt — a shortcut whose interest is slower future change
quiz.explanation: Deliberate shortcuts that borrow from the future are technical debt, and the interest arrives as regressions and slower feature work. Repayment is refactoring plus test backfill, best done in budgeted slices.

prerequisites: What a requirement is (a statement of what the system must do or a property it must have)
intro: Every failed project post-mortem eventually stumbles onto the same root cause: nobody asked the right people the right questions. Elicitation is the disciplined art of extracting what stakeholders actually need — which is rarely what they first say. This section covers the core technique toolbox and the stakeholder analysis that decides where to aim it.
objectives: Identify the full stakeholder set of a system — including indirect stakeholders like maintainers and regulators, not just end users
Classify stakeholders on a power/interest grid and choose an engagement strategy for each class
Select and sequence elicitation techniques (interviews, workshops, observation, document analysis) to fit each stakeholder group
Explain why observation and ethnography catch tacit knowledge that interviews systematically miss
Probe past stated solutions to uncover underlying needs

concepts.statement: A **stakeholder** is anyone who affects the success of the system, or whom the system's operation affects. Beyond obvious users this includes customers (who pay), operators, maintainers, testers, regulators, auditors, and adjacent system owners whose data or workflows you will touch.
concepts.detail: The classic elicitation failure is sampling only direct users. A medication-tracking system that forgets the night-shift nurses who do the actual barcode scanning, or the pharmacy technician who reconciles discrepancies, will be resented by exactly the people whose compliance it needs.

concepts.statement: Map each stakeholder by **power** (ability to influence the outcome) against **interest** (degree of involvement in day-to-day concerns). High power + high interest → **manage closely**; high power + low interest → **keep satisfied**; low power + high interest → **keep informed**; low power + low interest → **monitor**.
concepts.detail: The grid drives engagement budget. A regulator has enormous power but little interest in your internals: send compliance summaries, do not drag them into weekly workshops. A nurse has high interest and modest power: involve deeply, because their goodwill determines adoption.

concepts.statement: **Closed questions** (How many orders per day? Which report do you run first?) fix vocabulary and quantify, but bias the answer by pre-selecting the option space. **Open questions** (Walk me through what happens when a shipment is late.) let stakeholders reveal what you did not think to ask about. Skilled elicitors open with open questions and close with closed ones to quantify what the open ones surfaced.
concepts.detail: Interviews remain the workhorse technique: cheap, one-to-one, safe for politically sensitive admissions a stakeholder would never make in a group. Their weakness is the same one-to-one isolation — contradictions between stakeholders surface only after you compare notes.

concepts.statement: A **facilitated workshop** brings stakeholders — ideally from conflicting functions — into one room with a neutral facilitator, a timed agenda, and a scribe, to elicit, negotiate, and agree requirements at speed. Its great advantage is that contradictions surface immediately, in the room, instead of in month four.
concepts.detail: Discipline keeps it honest: park off-agenda items in a visible parking lot, enforce round-robin turns so quiet experts speak, and record decisions with explicit owner and date. Without a neutral facilitator, workshops degenerate into dominance by whoever has the loudest voice or the best title.

concepts.statement: **Observation** embeds the analyst in the workplace to watch real work as it happens; **ethnography** is its long-form version, studying the culture and informal practices of a work community. Both attack the same gap: the difference between **work-as-documented and work-as-done**.
concepts.detail: People cannot articulate tacit knowledge — the post-it note on the monitor, the informal phone call that resolves a shipment problem, the workaround done in a spreadsheet because the official tool is unusable. Asking about it returns the official story; watching it reveals the truth. The cost is high analyst time, so observe a representative sample, not everyone.

concepts.statement: Before meeting anyone, mine what exists: forms, spreadsheets, procedure manuals, incident reports, tickets, and the data schemas of systems you will integrate with. Documents show the **as-is vocabulary** and volumes, and often contain the exceptions list that nobody remembers in interviews.
concepts.detail: Treat documents as evidence of the past, not requirements for the future. A form that must be filled in triplicate because a 1990s carbon-copy process demanded it is a candidate for elimination, not automation.

concepts.statement: Stakeholders describe their problems as **solutions**: 'we need a bigger screen for the schedule' is really 'we cannot see tomorrow's schedule from across the room'. Elicitation that records demanded features verbatim ships a solution to a misdiagnosed problem. The analyst's job is to ask **why** until the underlying need — the goal the solution serves — is exposed.
concepts.detail: The folk version is the customer who asks for a faster horse when the need is faster transportation. A useful probe: 'If this feature worked perfectly tomorrow, what would you be able to do that you cannot do today?'

examples.title: Choosing an elicitation mix for a hospital medication-tracking app
examples.problem: You are eliciting requirements for a tablet app that tracks medication administration at a 400-bed hospital. Stakeholders so far mentioned by the sponsor: doctors and the IT director. Devise a stakeholder analysis and a technique plan.

steps.label: Step 1: Enumerate the stakeholder chain
steps.text: Walk the medication from prescription to patient: **doctors** (prescribe), **pharmacists** (verify, dispense), **day and night shift nurses** (administer and scan), **pharmacy technicians** (reconcile stock), **patients** (receive), plus **maintenance/IT** (device fleet), the **regulator** (controlled-substance reporting), and **billing**. Eight groups, not two.

steps.label: Step 2: Place them on the power/interest grid
steps.text: Nurses: high interest, low power → keep informed and involve deeply. Regulator: high power, low interest → keep satisfied via compliance summaries. IT director and head pharmacist: high power, high interest → manage closely, sit on the steering group. Patients: low/medium on both → monitor via representative feedback.

steps.label: Step 3: Assign techniques by group
steps.text: Nurses get **observation** across both shifts — tacit workarounds live there, and night shift is documented nowhere. Doctors and pharmacists get **workshops** together, because their requirements (override rules, verification windows) conflict and must be negotiated face to face. The regulator gets targeted **interviews** plus **document analysis** of the existing controlled-substance report format.

steps.label: Step 4: Cross-validate
steps.text: Compare findings across techniques: the observation notes say nurses photograph the screen at shift change — an undocumented handover need that no interview mentioned. Feed it back into the workshop as a new requirement candidate.

examples.result: A single technique cannot cover an eight-group stakeholder landscape. Observation captures tacit practice, workshops force conflicting parties to converge, interviews handle the powerful-but-detached, and document analysis anchors volumes and vocabulary. The mix — and the cross-checks between them — is the method.

keyTakeaways: Stakeholders extend far beyond end users: operators, maintainers, regulators, and adjacent system owners can each veto success.
The power/interest grid converts a stakeholder list into an engagement budget: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor.
Open questions discover; closed questions quantify — sequence open-first, closed-last inside each interview.
Observation and ethnography exist because work-as-documented and work-as-done differ, and the gap is where the real requirements hide.
Stakeholders speak in solutions; the analyst keeps asking why until the underlying need is exposed.

quiz.q: Interviews with hospital pharmacists all describe the drug-reconciliation process one way, but when an analyst spends a shift on the ward, the actual process includes an informal phone call to the dispensary that nobody mentioned. Which elicitation gap does this illustrate?
options: Interviews are too expensive for requirements work
Work-as-documented differs from work-as-done, and tacit practice is invisible to interviews but visible to observation
The pharmacists were deliberately hiding information from the analyst
Document analysis would have revealed the phone call in the procedure manual
quiz.explanation: Tacit, informal work is exactly what observation and ethnography were invented to catch — people cannot articulate what they do on autopilot, and the official procedure manual would omit it by definition. Option (d) is backwards: the manual documents the official story. The problem was never cost or dishonesty, so (a) and (c) misdiagnose.

quiz.q: A national drug-safety regulator has enormous influence over whether your medication app can ship, but no interest in its user interface or feature set. On the power/interest grid, what is the right engagement strategy?
options: Manage closely — invite them to every weekly design workshop
Monitor — ignore them until the product is finished
Keep satisfied — send compliance summaries and targeted updates, but do not consume their patience with UI debates
Keep informed — add them to the monthly internal newsletter
quiz.explanation: High power + low interest → keep satisfied: give them what they need to say yes, without burning their limited attention on details they do not care about. Dragging them into workshops (a) wastes the scarcest resource you have with them; ignoring them (b) risks a late, total veto; a passive newsletter (d) is the treatment for low-power, high-interest stakeholders.

quiz.q: During requirements interviews, an analyst asks: 'How many medication administrations does a typical nurse handle per shift, and what fraction are urgent?' What kind of question is this, and what is its main risk?
options: Open question — risk of overwhelming the interviewee
Closed question — risk of biasing the answer by pre-selecting the option space
Hypothetical question — risk of introducing requirements the stakeholders never wanted
Leading question — risk that the nurse refuses to answer
quiz.explanation: It fixes the vocabulary and demands a number: closed. Closed questions quantify beautifully but can only collect answers within the frame the analyst already imagined — if the real problem is shift handover rather than urgency rates, this question never surfaces it. That is why interviews should open with open questions and close with closed ones.

quiz.q: In a facilitated workshop about override rules, the senior consultant talks over the junior pharmacist every time she starts to disagree, and the group converges on the consultant's position. What is the correct facilitation response?
options: Accept the consensus — seniority usually implies better knowledge of edge cases
End the workshop and switch to one-on-one interviews permanently
Use round-robin turn-taking and direct questions so quieter experts speak, and record the pharmacist's concern as an open issue with an owner
Escalate to the sponsor to have the consultant removed from the project
quiz.explanation: Dominance and groupthink are known workshop failure modes with known fixes: enforced turn-taking, direct questions by name, and a visible parking lot that keeps disagreements alive instead of drowning them. The pharmacist's dissent is data — junior staff often own the exception cases. Abandoning workshops (b) throws away their cross-stakeholder convergence benefit; both (a) and (d) treat symptoms by destroying information.

quiz.q: A warehouse manager tells you: 'We need a bigger monitor at the packing station.' Which response best practices need-driven elicitation?
options: Record the requirement: the system shall support a bigger monitor at packing stations
Ask whether a curved or flat monitor would be preferred, to make the requirement testable
Ask what the manager would be able to do with the bigger monitor that cannot be done today, to expose the underlying need
Reject the request because solution proposals do not belong in a requirements document
quiz.explanation: Stakeholders speak in solutions; the analyst's probe is why — what goal would the bigger screen serve? The real need might be reading the pick list from a distance, solvable by font size, projection, or reorderable layouts. Recording the solution verbatim (a) ships a misdiagnosis; refining the solution (b) polishes the wrong requirement; and a flat rejection (d) loses the signal instead of translating it.

prerequisites: Basic idea of a requirement as a testable statement
The difference between a wish and a verifiable statement
intro: 'The system shall be fast and user-friendly' is not a requirement — it is a horoscope. The single most valuable skill in requirements writing is separating what the system does (functional) from how well it must do it (non-functional), and then making the how-well measurable enough to fail a test. This section builds that skill.
objectives: Distinguish functional requirements from non-functional requirements and classify borderline cases correctly
Map non-functional requirements onto a quality-attribute taxonomy covering performance, availability, security, usability and maintainability
Rewrite vague quality statements as measurable requirements using the stimulus–environment–response pattern
Explain why non-functional requirements, more than functional ones, drive architectural decisions

concepts.statement: A **functional requirement** (FR) states what the system shall do: a mapping from inputs and preconditions to outputs and postconditions. 'The system shall generate a monthly sales report grouped by region' is functional — you can verify it by performing the action and inspecting the output.
concepts.detail: FRs define behavior. They are usually verifiable by direct observation: do the thing, check the result. If a statement cannot be verified by any conceivable observation of system behavior, it is not a functional requirement — it is either a non-functional property or a wish.

concepts.statement: A **non-functional requirement** (NFR) constrains *how well* the system must perform its functions, or constrains its development and operation: response time, throughput, availability, security, usability, maintainability, portability. The engineering term for the measurable subset of these is **quality attribute**.
concepts.detail: NFRs are often global — they apply to every feature at once — which is why they are easy to state and easy to forget. A checkout button that works and a checkout button that responds in 200 ms under Black-Friday load are two different engineering problems with one functional requirement between them.

concepts.statement: A working taxonomy of product quality attributes: **performance** (latency, throughput, capacity), **availability** (uptime, recovery time), **security** (authentication, authorization, confidentiality, auditability), **usability** (learnability, error rate, task completion), **reliability** (fault tolerance, failure rate), **maintainability** (modifiability, testability), and **portability** (installability, adaptability). International software-quality standards (the ISO 25010 family) formalize this ladder.
concepts.detail: The taxonomy's job is completeness pressure: walking each attribute against each feature asks 'what is the latency requirement for this? the failure mode? the audit trail?' — surfacing NFRs nobody volunteered.

concepts.statement: Make an NFR measurable by specifying three things: the **stimulus** (the operation or event), the **environment** (the conditions under load, at peak, degraded), and the **response with a measure** (a numeric threshold and how it is measured). Template: 'When [stimulus] under [environment], the system shall [response] within [measured threshold].'
concepts.detail: Example rewrite: 'The system shall be fast' becomes 'When a customer submits the payment form (stimulus) while the site is serving 5,000 concurrent sessions (environment), the confirmation page shall render in at most 2 seconds at the 95th percentile, measured at the browser (response + measure).' Now it can fail a load test — which is the whole point.

concepts.statement: **A requirement that cannot be verified by some defined procedure is not a requirement — it is a wish.** Every requirement must carry, explicitly or by obvious construction, a verification method: inspection, demonstration, test, or analysis. An NFR without a number and a measurement context cannot be tested, so it cannot be violated, so it silently controls nothing.
concepts.detail: Wishes are not harmless. They create the illusion of agreement — marketing, engineering and the customer each privately define 'user-friendly' differently, and the disagreement detonates at acceptance time, the most expensive possible moment.

concepts.statement: Functional requirements shape *what modules exist*; non-functional requirements shape *how they are structured and connected*. Two systems with identical features — one targeting 99.99% availability, one running on a single office server — deserve radically different architectures. When the NFRs arrive late, the architecture built for the FRs must be torn apart to absorb them.
concepts.detail: This is why eliciting performance, availability and security targets *early* is cheap insurance: adding redundancy to a design is a drawing change; adding it to shipped code is an excavation. The costliest requirements to discover late are almost always non-functional ones.

examples.title: Turning horoscopes into requirements
examples.problem: A draft specification for an online pharmacy contains these three statements: (a) 'The system shall be user-friendly.' (b) 'The system shall respond quickly to searches.' (c) 'The system shall be secure.' Rewrite each as a measurable, testable requirement.

steps.label: (a) Usability — define the user and the task
steps.text: User-friendliness must become an observable human outcome: 'A customer who has never used the site before, given only the packaging of a common medication, shall locate and add the correct 10-tablet pack to the cart within 90 seconds in moderated usability testing, with an error rate under 10% across 20 representative participants.' The stimulus is the task, the environment is a first-time user, the response measure is time plus error rate.

steps.label: (b) Performance — add load and a percentile
steps.text: 'Quickly' becomes: 'When a customer submits a search query while 2,000 concurrent users are active, the results page shall display the top 10 matching products within 1.5 seconds at the 95th percentile, measured server-side.' The percentile matters: an *average* of 1.5 s lets 1 user in 10 wait 10 seconds while the average still passes.

steps.label: (c) Security — decompose into concrete controls
steps.text: 'Secure' is a family, not a property.
