Decompose: 'All traffic shall be encrypted in transit (TLS 1.3 or later)'; 'Passwords shall be stored using a salted adaptive hash (bcrypt, cost factor 12 or higher)'; 'Every access to a prescription record shall be authenticated and written to an append-only audit log with user, timestamp and record id'; 'Sessions shall expire after 30 minutes of inactivity.' Each is verifiable by inspection or test.

steps.label: Attach verification methods
steps.text: (a) → demonstration/usability test. (b) → load test in a staging environment at specified concurrency. (c) → configuration inspection plus penetration test plus audit-log review. Now each statement can *fail*, which is what makes it a requirement rather than decoration.

examples.result: The rewrites share one skeleton: stimulus (who does what) + environment (under which load/conditions) + response (observable outcome with a number and a measurement point). Any NFR that cannot be coaxed into this skeleton needs another round of elicitation, not a place in the specification.

keyTakeaways: Functional requirements define what the system does; non-functional requirements constrain how well, and they are usually global across all features.
Walk a quality-attribute taxonomy (performance, availability, security, usability, maintainability, portability) against every feature to surface NFRs nobody volunteered.
The measurable form of an NFR is stimulus + environment + response with a numeric threshold, measurement point and percentile.
If no defined procedure can verify a statement, it is a wish, not a requirement — and wishes detonate at acceptance time.
NFRs drive architecture far more than functional requirements do; discovering them late is the most expensive kind of discovery.

quiz.q: Classify this statement for a train-ticketing site: 'When the daily-sales report is requested between 06:00 and 09:00, the system shall generate it from the overnight warehouse within 60 seconds at the 95th percentile.'
options: Functional — it describes generating a report
Both — the report generation is functional, the 60-second bound is a non-functional constraint on that function
Neither — percentiles make it a statistical estimate, not a requirement
quiz.explanation: The sentence bundles both: the *existence* of report generation is functional; the *time bound under stated conditions* is a performance (non-functional) constraint. This bundling is normal in practice — good specifications just keep the two kinds separately taggable so coverage and testing can be tracked per kind. (b) misses the functional half; (d) is wrong because a percentile is precisely what makes the bound measurable.

quiz.q: Which rewrite of 'The system shall be easy to maintain' is the best measurable requirement?
options: The system shall be designed with clean, well-commented code that any developer can understand
The system shall use industry-standard frameworks so maintenance is straightforward
A developer familiar with the codebase shall be able to add support for a new payment provider by changing at most 3 modules, with no change outside the payment subsystem, within 5 working days
The system shall pass a code review by the architecture board before each release
quiz.explanation: Maintainability becomes measurable when expressed as a *change scenario with a bounded blast radius and effort*: stimulus (new payment provider), environment (a developer who knows the system), response (≤3 modules, none outside the payment subsystem, ≤5 days). Options (a) and (b) restate the wish with new adjectives — still nothing a test can fail; (d) measures process compliance, not maintainability of the product.

quiz.q: A team's load test shows their search averages 800 ms while serving 1,000 concurrent users, and the requirement reads: 'Search shall respond within 1.5 seconds on average under normal load.' A stakeholder complains that users are frequently waiting 6 seconds. Which requirement-writing flaw does this expose?
options: The threshold is too loose and should have been 500 ms
An average without a percentile hides the tail: 1-in-20 users can wait far longer while the average still passes
The load level of 1,000 users was unrealistically low
The requirement should have specified the server hardware
quiz.explanation: Averages are a property of the *distribution*, and user pain lives in the *tail*. With heavy skew — a few multi-second outliers — the mean stays comfortable while real users suffer. The fix is a high percentile (p95 or p99) with the load and measurement point stated. (a), (c) and (d) may all be true-ish, but none addresses the actual flaw: the statistic chosen cannot see the pain the requirement exists to bound.

quiz.q: Marketing demands 'the system must be secure' and refuses to elaborate. Engineering proceeds, ships, and six months later a breach forces an emergency redesign of session handling and logging. Which lesson is the primary takeaway?
options: Security cannot be specified in requirements and must be handled reactively
Marketing should not talk to engineers about quality goals

A monolithic NFR like 'secure' hides a family of concrete, testable requirements (encryption, authentication, audit, session management) that must be elicited and specified early — precisely because they shape architecture
The breach proves the developers were not skilled enough to implement security correctly
quiz.explanation: 'Secure' decomposes into verifiable controls: encryption in transit and at rest, authentication and authorization rules, audit logging, session expiry, input validation. Each is testable, and each constrains architecture — retrofitting them into shipped code is an excavation, exactly what happened. The failure was in elicitation and specification, not in the concept of security requirements (a) or anyone's competence (d).

quiz.q: Two candidate systems have identical feature lists. System A targets 99.99% monthly availability; System B targets office-hours availability on a single server. What correctly describes their requirements sets?
options: Their functional requirements differ, so their features cannot really be identical
Their non-functional requirements differ so strongly that their appropriate architectures will likely differ — redundant deployment, failover and replication for A versus a single-node design for B
Availability targets affect operations only, not architecture or design
System B's requirements are incomplete because every system must target 99.99%
quiz.explanation: Identical FRs plus radically different NFRs should produce different architectures: 99.99% availability is about 4.4 minutes of downtime per month and practically demands redundancy, health checking, failover and replicated state. The NFR is the architectural driver. (c) inverts the truth; (d) confuses a business decision with a universal law; (a) contradicts the premise.

prerequisites: Functional vs non-functional requirements
The idea of a stakeholder or user role
intro: A requirements specification is a communication device before it is a contract: it must let a stakeholder confirm you understood, and let a developer build without guessing. Use cases and user stories are the two dominant modeling forms, and they are complementary rather than competing — one captures interaction detail, the other drives iteration planning. This section covers both, plus the document conventions that hold them together.
objectives: Write a well-formed use case with actor, preconditions, a numbered main success scenario and extension branches
Write user stories in role–capability–benefit form and evaluate them with the INVEST criteria
Attach concrete acceptance criteria in Given–When–Then form
Choose between use cases and user stories based on audience and purpose
Describe the standard structure of a software requirements specification document

concepts.statement: A **use case** is a named interaction between an **actor** (a role external to the system) and the system itself, pursuing a goal. It consists of a **precondition** (state that must already hold), a numbered **main success scenario** (the happy path, actor step, system step, alternating), and **extensions** (numbered branches handling everything that can go wrong at each step), ending in a **postcondition**.
concepts.detail: The discipline of extensions is where use cases earn their keep. 'Withdraw cash' with no extension for insufficient funds, wrong PIN, or a card reported stolen is a demo script, not a specification. Rule of thumb: for every step, ask what could fail here — every answer is an extension with its own outcome.

concepts.statement: Canonical field set: **Name** (verb phrase, e.g. 'Withdraw cash'), **Primary actor** (role, not job title), **Precondition**, **Main success scenario** (numbered 1..n, alternating actor/system), **Extensions** (referenced by step number: '3a. PIN incorrect: system displays error, allows 2 retries, then retains card'), **Postcondition**, optional **Trigger** and **Frequency**.
concepts.detail: Numbered steps make extensions attachable — '2a' unambiguously means 'the failure of step 2'. Use one sentence per step in actor-verifies-system rhythm, and keep the main scenario at 3–10 steps; if it grows past that, you are writing several use cases.

concepts.statement: A **user story** is a short placeholder for a conversation, written: **As a** ⟨role⟩, **I want** ⟨capability⟩ **so that** ⟨benefit⟩. The story is not the requirement — the requirement is the story plus the conversation it provokes plus the acceptance criteria that result.
concepts.detail: Stories deliberately omit interaction detail so they can be written fast, prioritized by business value, and fitted into a fixed iteration. That omission is a feature at planning time and a bug at build time — which acceptance criteria exist to repair.

concepts.statement: A healthy story is **I**ndependent (orderable without deadlock), **N**egotiable (states a need, not a bundled solution design), **V**aluable (delivers benefit a stakeholder cares about), **E**stimable (understood enough to size), **S**mall (completable within one iteration), **T**estable (has a clear pass/fail). Violations are diagnostic: too big → split; solution-baked → renegotiate; untestable → elicit acceptance criteria first.
concepts.detail: Most INVEST failures trace to two habits: stories that are really tasks ('build the database table' — valuable to no user) and stories that are really epics ('manage inventory' — not small). Both are fixable by returning to the role-capability-benefit sentence.

concepts.statement: Each story carries concrete pass/fail conditions, typically phrased **Given** ⟨initial context⟩, **When** ⟨action/event occurs⟩, **Then** ⟨observable outcome⟩. Example: 'Given my cart holds 3 items and I am logged out, When I proceed to checkout, Then I am asked to log in and, on success, my cart is preserved.'
concepts.detail: Given–When–Then maps directly onto automated tests — which is the point: a story whose acceptance criteria cannot be written in this form is usually not yet understood, and discovering that before coding is the cheapest possible moment.

concepts.statement: A conventional **software requirements specification (SRS)** organizes: (1) introduction — purpose, scope, definitions; (2) overall description — product perspective, user classes, operating and constraint environment; (3) external interface requirements — UI, hardware, software, communication; (4) functional requirements, numbered for traceability (e.g. REQ-104); (5) non-functional requirements by quality attribute; (6) constraints and rationale. Standards lineage runs through IEEE 830 and its successors.
concepts.detail: The numbering is not bureaucracy — REQ-104 is what a traceability matrix, a change request and a test case will all cite. Numbers turn prose into referencable engineering objects.

concepts.statement: Use cases capture **interaction structure** for stakeholders who must validate the flow; stories capture **planning units** for teams who deliver in iterations; acceptance criteria capture **verification** for testers. Mature teams keep all three: a story for the iteration board, the use case as its backing detail, and Given–When–Then clauses lifted from the use-case extensions as its tests.
concepts.detail: Choosing one form religiously costs you its complement's strengths. Use-case extensions are literally a pre-written list of negative test cases; stories shorn of that backing are where forgotten edge cases go to live.

examples.title: One need, two forms: ATM cash withdrawal
examples.problem: Model the ATM cash-withdrawal capability twice: as a use case for the bank's operations team to validate, and as a user story with acceptance criteria for an iteration board.

steps.label: Use case, header
steps.text: **Name:** Withdraw cash. **Primary actor:** Cardholder. **Precondition:** Card is valid and account is accessible. **Trigger:** Cardholder inserts card and requests withdrawal.

steps.label: Use case, main success scenario
steps.text: 1. Cardholder inserts card. 2. System prompts for PIN. 3. Cardholder enters PIN. 4. System validates PIN and prompts for amount. 5. Cardholder enters amount. 6. System checks balance, debits account, instructs dispenser, and prints receipt. 7. Cardholder takes card and cash. **Postcondition:** Account debited, dispenser log written, card returned.

steps.label: Use case, extensions
steps.text: 3a. PIN incorrect: system shows error and reprompts; after 3 consecutive failures system retains card and ends session. 5a. Amount not a permitted denomination multiple: system explains valid amounts and reprompts. 6a. Insufficient balance: system shows available balance, offers a lower amount or cancel. 6b. Dispenser jam: system rolls back the debit, logs the fault, and tells the cardholder to contact the bank. 0a. Card reported stolen (checked at step 2): system retains card immediately and notifies the fraud service.

steps.label: The same need as a story
steps.text: As a cardholder, I want to withdraw cash from my account at an ATM so that I can pay at cash-only places without visiting a branch. Note what the story deliberately does not contain: no flows, no extensions — those live in the use case.

steps.label: Acceptance criteria, lifted from extensions
steps.text: Given three consecutive wrong PINs, When the third wrong PIN is entered, Then the card is retained and the fraud service is notified. Given a balance of 40 and a request of 100, When the request is submitted, Then the system shows the available balance and offers to withdraw 40 or cancel. Given a dispenser jam after debit, When the fault is detected, Then the debit is rolled back and the cardholder sees a contact-the-bank message. Each Given–When–Then is an extension from step 3, turned into a test.

examples.result: The use case gives operations something to validate in full, including every failure branch; the story gives the board something to size and prioritize; the acceptance criteria — harvested straight from use-case extensions — give the testers their cases. Same requirement, three coordinated views.

keyTakeaways: A use case is actor + goal + numbered main success scenario + extensions for every failure, framed by pre- and postconditions.
Extensions are the specification's real content — and, rewritten as Given–When–Then clauses, they become the test list for free.
A user story is a placeholder for a conversation: role, capability, benefit — negotiable by design, never a disguised task or design.
INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) is a diagnostic checklist; each violation names its own fix.
Numbered requirements in a structured SRS (interfaces, FRs, NFRs by attribute, constraints) make change control and traceability possible.

quiz.q: Review this story: 'As a user, I want the system to use a Redis cache with a 60-second TTL on the product catalogue so that pages load faster.' What is the primary INVEST violation?
options: Not Small — implementing a cache cannot fit in one iteration
Not Negotiable — the story bakes a specific technical solution into what should be a negotiable statement of need
Not Valuable — page load speed does not matter to users
Not Estimable — the team cannot possibly size caching work
quiz.explanation: The story dictates the solution (Redis, 60-second TTL) instead of the need (fast catalogue pages). That removes the team's ability to negotiate *how*, and couples the product backlog to an implementation detail that may change. The need form: 'As a shopper, I want product pages to load within 1.5 seconds so that I can browse quickly' — the cache becomes one possible design discussed at build time. The other three criteria are plausibly satisfiable here.

quiz.q: In the 'Withdraw cash' use case, where should 'PIN entered incorrectly' be recorded?
options: In the main success scenario, as a step the actor may perform
As an extension branch labeled 3a, referenced to the main-scenario step it disrupts
In the precondition, which should read 'the PIN is correct'
In a separate use case called 'Enter wrong PIN'
quiz.explanation: Extensions attach to numbered main-scenario steps — 3a means 'step 3 failed in this specific way' — carrying their own handling and outcome. Putting failure paths in the main scenario (a) destroys the happy-path readability; moving them into preconditions (c) hides them from validation; and separate use cases (d) shatter one coherent interaction into fragments nobody can review as a whole.

quiz.q: Your backlog contains the story: 'As a warehouse manager, I want to manage inventory.' The team cannot estimate it and it has sat unchanged for three sprints. What is the correct next action?
options: Force an estimate by making the team play planning poker until they converge
Mark the story as blocked on the product owner and leave it in the backlog

Recognize it violates Small (and likely Estimable), and split it along real user goals — e.g. receive stock, adjust counts after a cycle count, view low-stock alerts — each with its own acceptance criteria
Rewrite it as a technical task so the developers can size it
quiz.explanation: This is an epic wearing a story costume: 'manage inventory' is a whole capability area. The INVEST failure is Small (with Estimable as its symptom), and the cure is splitting along user goals, each slice independently valuable and testable. Forcing estimates (a) measures the symptom; (b) parks it without a fix; (d) converts it into a non-user-valuable task, which trades one violation for another.

quiz.q: Which acceptance criterion is written well enough to automate as a test?
options: The search feature should be helpful and return relevant products
Given the catalogue contains products A, B and C with prices 10, 20 and 30, When the user searches for a price range of 15–25, Then exactly product B is listed and A and C are not
The search shall be tested by the QA team before each release
Search results must load quickly even when many people use the site
quiz.explanation: Only the Given–When–Then form is mechanically checkable: fixed initial state (products A, B, C with stated prices), a precise triggering action (search for range 15–25), and an exact expected outcome (B listed, A and C not) that a test can assert. The others fail as automation inputs — 'relevant' and 'helpful' (a) name qualities with no oracle, 'tested by QA' (c) describes process rather than pass/fail, and 'quickly' (d) has no number to assert against.

quiz.q: A telecom client must formally sign off detailed interaction behavior for a billing dispute flow, including every error branch; a startup is planning the same kind of feature in two-week iterations. Which modeling choice fits each?
options: Both should use user stories only — detailed models are waste
Both should write full use cases — stories are too informal to build from
The telecom client needs use cases (validation-grade interaction detail with extensions); the startup fits user stories with acceptance criteria (planning-grade placeholders for conversation)
Neither needs written requirements; prototypes replace both
quiz.explanation: The choice is governed by purpose and audience: contractual validation with non-developer stakeholders demands the stepwise, extension-complete form of use cases; iteration planning inside a responsive team needs lightweight, negotiable placeholders with Given–When–Then backing. Both extremes — stories-only (a) and cases-everywhere (b) — pay one audience's cost at the other's expense, and (d) discards specification entirely.

prerequisites: Requirements specification basics (use cases, stories, acceptance criteria)
intro: A specification can be beautifully written and still be wrong — validation is how you find that out while it is still cheap to fix. Reviews put human eyes and checklists on the document; prototypes put a tangible almost-product in front of stakeholders and let their reactions do the talking. Both attack the same enemy: the gap between what was written and what was meant.
objectives: Distinguish validation (building the right product) from verification (building the product right)
Run a requirements review or walkthrough with roles, checklists and ambiguity-detection techniques
Choose between throwaway and evolutionary prototyping based on what the prototype must answer
Anticipate the characteristic failure modes of prototypes: misplaced stakeholder confidence and missing non-functional coverage

concepts.statement: **Validation** asks *are we building the right product?* — does this specification capture the stakeholders' real needs? **Verification** asks *are we building the product right?* — does the artifact conform to its specification? Requirements work lives almost entirely in validation; testing of code against requirements is verification.
concepts.detail: The distinction matters because the two fail differently. A perfectly implemented feature that nobody needed passes verification and fails validation — and validation failures discovered at delivery are the most expensive defects in software, because everything built on top of the wrong requirement is also wrong.

concepts.statement: A **review** (or its lighter cousin, the **walkthrough**) gathers reviewers to examine the specification against explicit checklists: Is every requirement testable? Unambiguous? Consistent with the others? Traceable to a stakeholder or goal? Complete for the stated scope? A **walkthrough** is author-led and informal; an **inspection** is moderator-led, role-assigned and defect-logging, with metrics.
concepts.detail: Effectiveness comes from roles and preparation: assign one reviewer to hunt ambiguity, one to hunt conflicts with other documents, one to read as a tester asking 'how would I verify this?'. Reviewers who read in advance and come with written findings beat a room improvising around a projector, every time.

concepts.statement: Have several reviewers read each critical requirement **independently** and write down what they believe it mandates, *before* any group discussion. Then compare the written interpretations: any divergence between competent readers is an ambiguity in the requirement — not a comprehension failure in the reviewer.
concepts.detail: Group discussion synchronizes interpretation too early: the first person to voice a reading anchors everyone, and the ambiguity hides successfully. Writing first, comparing second, converts ambiguity from an argument into a detected defect. For grammar-level suspects, parse the sentence and check each plausible attachment of modifiers and conjunctions.

concepts.statement: A **prototype** is a partial representation of the system, built to answer specific open questions about requirements — not to ship. It ranges from paper sketches and clickable mockups to running code with fake data. Its value is that stakeholders react to something concrete far more honestly than they speculate about the abstract.
concepts.detail: The prototype is an elicitation and validation instrument: its design should start from a list of questions it must answer (Is this checkout flow understandable? Do nurses trust this scan confirmation screen?) — a prototype without questions is a demo, and demos validate nothing.

concepts.statement: **Throwaway** (rapid) prototypes are built to answer questions and then discarded — the answers inform the real specification and implementation. **Evolutionary** prototypes are built to production quality from the start and grow into the delivered system, requirement by requirement. Choose throwaway when the open questions are about *what* is needed; choose evolutionary only when the requirements are stable enough that *growing* code is not a trap.
concepts.detail: Throwaway earns its discipline: because it will be discarded, it can fake everything — hard-coded results, no error handling, no performance — so it answers questions in days. Evolutionary demands real engineering up front; if you pretend a throwaway-quality build is evolutionary, you have invented the classic trap: shipping the prototype.

concepts.statement: Two systematic risks: (1) **misplaced confidence** — stakeholders see a polished mockup with three happy-path screens and read it as '90% done', or developers become emotionally unable to discard a throwaway build; (2) **surface bias** — prototypes naturally exercise look-and-feel and interaction, while performance, security, recovery and data-volume questions stay invisible, because none of them can be seen on a screen.
concepts.detail: Counter-measures: label prototype fidelity explicitly (paper mockup ≠ working software), schedule the discard date for throwaway builds, and pair every prototype cycle with an explicit checklist of the non-functional questions the prototype deliberately does *not* answer. A prototype that raises false confidence is worse than no prototype.

examples.title: Validating a checkout redesign: review plus throwaway prototype
examples.problem: An online grocer's specification for a redesigned checkout is drafted. Analytics suggest customers abandon at the delivery-slot step, but nobody can explain why. Devise a validation plan.

steps.label: Step 1: Review before building anything
steps.text: Run a moderator-led review of the draft specification. One reviewer reads as a tester ('how would I verify each requirement?'), one hunts cross-document conflicts, three perform independent written readings of the critical requirements and compare interpretations. The comparison surfaces that 'the system shall offer the customer a delivery slot' has two live readings — one slot preselected vs. a choice of slots — a defect found in an afternoon rather than in production.

steps.label: Step 2: Define the prototype's question list
steps.text: The open questions are about *what* customers need at the slot step — comprehension of the slot grid? trust that the slot is held? price transparency? These are what/UX questions, not stability questions, so a **throwaway** prototype is the right instrument.

steps.label: Step 3: Build low-fidelity, cheaply
steps.text: A clickable mockup with hard-coded slots — three variants of the slot-selection screen. Nothing is real: no persistence, no payment, deliberately fake data. Total build: days. Explicitly label every screen 'mockup — not working software'.

steps.label: Step 4: Put it in front of real customers
steps.text: Moderated sessions with 8–10 customers who abandoned real carts. Watch them attempt to pick a slot; the reactions are the data. Variant B (price shown per slot up front) is understood instantly; variant A produces frowns and re-reading — a strong signal that slot-price surprise was the abandonment driver.

steps.label: Step 5: Discard, and write what was learned into the specification
steps.text: The mockup is deleted on its scheduled date. The specification gains a measurable requirement: 'When a delivery slot carries a premium, the price delta shall be displayed beside the slot before selection' — plus acceptance criteria lifted from the observed confusions. The prototype's product was never the code; it was that sentence.

examples.result: Review caught an ambiguity in hours; the throwaway prototype converted an unexplained analytics mystery into a specific, testable requirement in days. Neither instrument shipped, and that was the plan: validation exists to change the specification while it is still cheap to change.

keyTakeaways: Validation asks if you are building the right product; verification asks if you are building the product right — requirements defects are validation failures and cost the most when found late.
Effective reviews assign roles and preparation; walkthroughs are informal, inspections are measured.
Independent written readings before discussion turn ambiguity into a detectable defect instead of a silent disagreement.
Choose throwaway prototyping for what-questions (needs, UX comprehension) and reserve evolutionary prototyping for stable, well-understood requirements.
Prototypes systematically hide non-functional issues and breed misplaced confidence — label fidelity, schedule the discard, and state explicitly what the prototype cannot answer.

quiz.q: A team delivers a feature that matches its specification exactly, is bug-free, and passes every acceptance test — yet customers ignore it because the underlying workflow need was misjudged. What failed, and where should it have been caught?
options: Verification failed; unit tests should have been stricter
Validation failed; requirements validation (reviews, prototypes with real stakeholders) should have caught the misjudged need before implementation
Both failed equally; the fault is shared between testers and developers
Nothing failed — the process worked and the market simply changed
quiz.explanation: Perfect conformance to a wrong specification is a validation failure by definition: the product was built right but is not the right product. The instruments for catching it — stakeholder reviews, prototypes in front of real users — exist precisely at the requirements stage. Stricter testing (a) polishes conformance to the same wrong target.

quiz.q: During a specification review, five engineers read the requirement 'The system shall notify the manager and auditor of failed transactions above 500' and write down what it mandates. Three interpretations emerge: both people notified about the same events; the manager for failures above 500 and the auditor for all failures; notifications of transactions above 500 that failed, but read as failures of transactions whose *total* exceeds 500. What has the review demonstrated, and what is the fix?
options: The engineers need better training in reading specifications
The requirement is ambiguous; rewrite it to disambiguate attachment and scope — and record the divergence as a review defect
The requirement is fine; the majority interpretation (2 of 3) should be adopted and the outlier reviewers overruled
The specification should drop the notification requirement entirely
quiz.explanation: Diverging interpretations by competent readers *is* the definition of ambiguity, and the independent-writings-then-compare technique exists to expose exactly this. The fix is a rewrite that pins down who is notified, of what, under which threshold semantics. Majority vote (c) institutionalizes one guess; blaming readers (a) and deleting the feature (d) both discard the signal the review worked to produce.

quiz.q: A startup's product requirements are genuinely unstable — the team is still discovering what customers want in a social scheduling tool. Which prototyping strategy fits, and why?
options: Evolutionary: build production-quality code and grow it as understanding improves
Throwaway: build cheap fakes to answer each round of what-questions, discard, and write the answers into the specification
None: unstable requirements mean prototyping is impossible until the market research finishes
Evolutionary, but with the prototype built in a cheaper programming language to save money
quiz.explanation: Instability is the textbook trigger for throwaway: each discovery cycle needs fast, fake answers, not production-quality structure that will be wrong in three weeks and is psychologically hard to delete. Evolutionary prototyping (a, d) invests engineering rigor into requirements that have not stabilized yet — you end up either shipping debris or paying to rebuild. (c) inverts the logic: instability is exactly when prototyping earns its keep.

quiz.q: After a sleek clickable prototype demo, the sponsor says: 'This looks nearly finished — we can launch next month, right?' The prototype is a three-screen happy-path mockup with hard-coded data. What is the best response?
options: Agree to the timeline, since the screens are indeed finished

Explain that the mockup answers look-and-feel questions only, walk through what is deliberately fake (data, error paths, payment, performance, security), and re-anchor scope with a fidelity statement and a non-functional question list
Refuse to demo prototypes to sponsors in the future
Immediately start hardening the prototype's code so it can actually ship
quiz.explanation: Misplaced confidence is a known prototype failure mode with a known counter: explicit fidelity labeling plus a stated list of what the prototype does not answer — the entire non-functional space (performance, security, recovery, data volume) is invisible on screens. Option (d) is the classic trap of shipping the throwaway; (c) throws away the demo's real value; (a) converts an illusion into a project commitment.

quiz.q: Which review technique most directly increases the chance of catching an ambiguous requirement, as opposed to merely confirming the specification is tidy?
options: Checking that every requirement has a unique identifier and correct formatting
Confirming the document follows the standard template section order
Multiple reviewers writing independent interpretations of each critical requirement and comparing them before any discussion
Verifying that all reviewers attended the meeting and signed the attendance sheet
quiz.explanation: Ambiguity is invisible to formatting and process checks (a, b, d) — a perfectly formatted sentence can still mandate two behaviors. Only divergence between independent readers exposes it: if two competent readers write two different interpretations, the requirement itself is defective. That is why interpretations are written *before* discussion, so anchoring cannot synchronize them into false agreement.

prerequisites: Requirements specification and numbered requirement identifiers
intro: Requirements do not end when the document is approved — they live for years, absorbing change requests while design, code and tests pile up around them. Requirements management is the machinery that keeps that from becoming chaos: baselines that define what 'approved' means, change control that gates every mutation, and traceability that lets you answer the two questions that matter — did we build everything we promised, and if this changes, what else breaks?
objectives: Explain what a requirements baseline is and why changes to it need formal control
Walk a change request through impact analysis using traceability links
Build and read a requirements traceability matrix, using it to find orphans, gaps and affected tests
Choose requirement attributes (rationale, source, priority, verification method, status) that make management possible

concepts.statement: A **baseline** is a formally reviewed and agreed version of the requirements set, frozen as the reference point for further work. Once baselined, requirements change only through **change control** — never by silent editing. Baselines give the project a stable definition of 'what we are currently building' and a measurement point for scope growth.
concepts.detail: Baselining too early is as harmful as too late: freeze a half-baked set and every clarification must ride the change-control machinery, breeding either bureaucracy or (worse) the quiet uncontrolled edits the process was meant to prevent. Baseline when the set is validated and stable enough to plan against.

concepts.statement: Every proposed change to a baselined requirement enters a defined loop: **submit** (problem, proposed change, urgency) → **impact analysis** (which design elements, code modules, tests, documents and schedule are affected, at what cost) → **decision** (approve, reject, or defer) by a change control board or the empowered owner → **implement and update** (requirement, affected artifacts, traceability links) → **notify** affected parties.
concepts.detail: Impact analysis is the intellectual core of the loop and is only as good as your traceability — without links, 'what breaks if we change this?' is answered by memory and optimism. The board itself can be one product owner on a small project; what is non-negotiable is that the questions (impact, cost, alternatives) get asked before the answer.

concepts.statement: **Requirements traceability** is the ability to follow the life of a requirement, in both directions. **Forward traceability** runs from requirements to design, code and tests (was every requirement allocated and verified?). **Backward traceability** runs from artifacts back to requirements (why does this test exist? which requirement mandated this module? — exposing gold-plating).
concepts.detail: Pre-traceability extends the chain further back: every requirement should link to its source — the stakeholder, goal or regulation that justifies it. A requirement with no origin story is un-defendable during prioritization: when the cut line comes, nobody knows what dying stakeholder need would die with it.

concepts.statement: A **traceability matrix** is a table: rows are requirements (by id), columns are the artifacts they should connect to — design elements, code modules, test cases (and optionally source stakeholder and rationale). A filled cell asserts 'this artifact exists because of this requirement'; an empty cell in a required column is a defect: a **missing allocation** (row with no design/test) or an **orphan artifact** (test with no requirement).
concepts.detail: In practice the matrix lives as links in a requirements management tool or fields in issue trackers rather than a literal spreadsheet, but the reasoning is identical: the matrix is a coverage computation over the relationship graph, and every hole is either a gap (unbuilt promise) or gold-plating (unpromised build).

concepts.statement: Manage requirements by attaching structured metadata to each: unique **id**, **source** (stakeholder or regulation), **rationale** (why it exists), **priority** (e.g. MoSCoW: Must/Should/Could/Won't), **verification method** (test, inspection, demonstration, analysis), **status** (proposed, approved, implemented, verified, dropped), and **version/change history**. The id makes it referencable; the attributes make it discussable.
concepts.detail: Rationale is the highest-value, most-skipped attribute: it is the only one that lets a future maintainer distinguish 'this is load-bearing' from 'this was somebody's guess in 2022'. Writing one sentence of why, at the moment of capture, costs nothing then and prevents tragic deletions later.

concepts.statement: Traceability is bought with maintenance effort: every link is a thing to update when either end changes, so link at the **coarsest granularity that still answers your management questions** — typically requirement to design element to test suite, not requirement to individual line of code. Fine-grained link farms are accurate for one sprint and dead weight forever after.
concepts.detail: Decide what questions you must answer (audit coverage? impact of change X? regulatory evidence?) and trace exactly enough to answer them. An unused traceability graph is not free insurance; it is a slow-motion tax on every future edit.

examples.title: A traceability matrix, worked: finding the orphan and surviving the change
examples.problem: A food-delivery app has four baselined requirements: R1 (place an order), R2 (track courier on a map), R3 (rate a delivery), R4 (all payment attempts shall be logged for audit). Current artifacts: design elements D1 (ordering service), D2 (tracking service), D3 (notification service), plus tests T1, T2, T3, T5. Build the matrix, audit it, then run the change request: 'Track courier location only to the neighborhood level for privacy.'

steps.label: Step 1: Lay out the matrix
steps.text: Rows R1–R4; columns Design and Tests. R1 → D1, T1. R2 → D2, T2. R3 → D3, T3. R4 → (design?) T5. Each cell is an assertion that the artifact exists because of the requirement.

steps.label: Step 2: Audit the rows (forward coverage)
steps.text: R4 has test T5 but **no design element** — the audit log has no owning component; it is being implemented, apparently, as scattered print statements. That is a missing allocation: the row caught it. Also compare with the pre-traceability view: R4's source is the payment regulation; note it in the Source column.

steps.label: Step 3: Audit the columns (backward coverage)
steps.text: Every design element maps to some requirement (D1←R1, D2←R2, D3←R3). Tests: T1←R1, T2←R2, T3←R3, T5←R4 — but **T4 maps to nothing**. T4 is an orphan test: it clicks the courier's exact coordinates on the map. Either a requirement was forgotten (R2 says 'track' — maybe precision belongs there) or T4 tests gold-plating nobody asked for. Flag it for the change board.

steps.label: Step 4: Run the change request through impact analysis
steps.text: Change CR-9 (neighborhood-level tracking) touches R2. Follow the matrix: R2 → D2 (tracking service: new privacy-preserving location blur at the edge) → T2 (assertions on exact coordinates must be rewritten for neighborhood polygons) → T4 (the orphan — now definitively dies, it tested the exact behavior being removed). Also scan for conflicts: R4 is unaffected; a new NFR candidate is born — 'courier identity shall not be derivable from blurred coordinates' — submitted as R5 via the same change process.

steps.label: Step 5: Update and re-baseline
steps.text: The board approves CR-9 with R5 attached. Update R2's text and version, add row R5 with source CR-9, link it to a new test T6, mark T4 retired-with-rationale. The matrix stays square: every row filled, every column justified.

examples.result: The matrix found one missing design allocation (R4), one orphan test (T4), and then converted a privacy change request into a bounded, evidence-based impact list — D2, T2, T4 — plus a new requirement the change itself exposed. That is requirements management doing its job: change with accounted consequences, never silent edits.

keyTakeaways: A baseline is the agreed, frozen reference version of the requirements; after it exists, changes ride the change-control loop, never silent edits.
Impact analysis — the heart of change control — is only as strong as the traceability links it traverses.
Forward traceability proves every requirement was allocated and verified; backward traceability exposes orphans and gold-plating.
Empty cells in a traceability matrix are defects: a row without tests is an unverified promise, a test without a requirement is an orphan.
Capture rationale and source per requirement; link at the coarsest granularity that answers your actual management questions.

quiz.q: In a traceability audit of a scheduling system, test T-17 exercises the drag-and-drop calendar editor, but no requirement in the baseline mentions drag-and-drop. What has the audit found, and what are the possible truths behind it?
options: A missing allocation — a requirement exists but was never designed
An orphan test — either a requirement was never written for a genuinely wanted behavior, or the feature is gold-plating built beyond the agreed scope
A forward-traceability failure — the requirement cannot be traced to its stakeholder source
Proof that the test suite is complete, since extra tests cannot hurt
quiz.explanation: A test with no justifying requirement is an orphan: either the team built and tested a real need without ever writing it down (a specification gap — the requirement should be added via change control) or they built unrequested scope (gold-plating). (a) describes the opposite hole — requirement present, design absent. And extra tests are not free or harmless: they must be maintained, and they silently encode requirements nobody agreed to.

quiz.q: Mid-project, a stakeholder asks a developer to 'just tweak' the export report to include margins per region, and the developer quietly does it. Which two mechanisms existed precisely to prevent this, and what specifically went wrong?
options: Baselining and change control; the change bypassed impact analysis and approval, so affected design, tests, schedule and other stakeholders were never assessed
Prototyping and validation; the change was implemented without a throwaway prototype first
Elicitation and workshops; the need should have been discovered in the original interviews
Traceability matrices and test coverage; the change broke the matrix's row-column symmetry
quiz.explanation: Post-baseline, every change goes through submit → impact analysis → decision → implement → notify. The quiet tweak skipped all of it: no cost estimate, no check of which tests assert the old format, no decision by the empowered owner, no notification of downstream consumers. The deeper costs are process corrosion — once quiet edits are tolerated, the baseline stops meaning anything. The other options misidentify the violated mechanisms.

quiz.q: A safety-critical medical device must demonstrate to auditors that every requirement was implemented and verified, and trace every design element back to a requirement that justifies it. Which traceability directions does this demand?
options: Forward only — requirements to tests is sufficient for auditors
Backward only — tests to requirements is sufficient for auditors
Both forward (every requirement allocated to design and verified by tests) and backward (every design element and test justified by a requirement) — full bidirectional coverage
Neither — auditors only review the final test report
quiz.explanation: The two demands are different queries over the same graph: 'everything promised was built and verified' is forward traceability; 'everything built exists because of a promise' is backward traceability, and it is what exposes gold-plating and unjustified features in regulated settings. Either direction alone answers only half the audit.

quiz.q: During deprioritization of requirements for a release cut, the team cannot explain why requirement R-31 ('orders shall be repriceable before dispatch') exists or whom it serves. Which missing requirement attribute is responsible, and what should it have contained?
options: The verification method — how R-31 would be tested
The priority — whether R-31 was a Must or a Could
The source and rationale — which stakeholder or goal motivated R-31 and why, without which no defensible keep-or-cut decision is possible
The version number — which edit created R-31
quiz.explanation: Source and rationale are exactly the attributes that make prioritization defensible: with them, cutting R-31 becomes 'we are choosing to disappoint the warehouse manager's reconciliation goal, knowingly'; without them it is a coin flip that may delete a load-bearing need. Verification method, priority and version all matter for other decisions — but none explains *why R-31 exists at all*.

quiz.q: A team maintains requirement-to-line-of-code traceability links — 40,000 of them — and spends days after each refactor repairing the graph, which nobody queries at that granularity. What is the correct adjustment?
options: Automate the link repair and keep all 40,000 links, since more traceability is always safer
Drop traceability entirely; it has proven too expensive for the team
Re-granularize to the coarsest level that answers the team's actual questions — typically requirement to design component to test suite — and delete the line-level links
Freeze the codebase so refactors stop breaking the links
quiz.explanation: Traceability should exist to answer named management questions (impact of change, coverage for audits, orphan detection) at the least granularity that suffices. Line-level links that nobody queries are pure carrying cost — they buy no additional answer over component-level links. (a) automates waste; (b) over-corrects, discarding the questions' answers along with the excess; (d) inverts the relationship: the process serves the product, not the reverse.

prerequisites: Requirements specification basics
The idea of requirement verification (test, inspection, demonstration, analysis)
intro: The three silent killers of specifications are ambiguity (two readers, two systems), inconsistency (two requirements, no possible system) and incompleteness (nobody asked what happens when the disk fills). None of them shows up in a spelling check, and all of them surface as production defects months later. This section is the diagnostic toolkit: taxonomies of ambiguity, systematic conflict detection, and completeness heuristics that find the requirements you never wrote.
objectives: Classify ambiguity into lexical, syntactic, semantic and pragmatic layers, with a test for each
Detect weak words and replace them with measurable statements
Find direct and indirect conflicts between requirements — including NFR-against-FR conflicts
Apply completeness heuristics (boundary analysis, error enumeration, input/output/state checks) to expose missing requirements
Repair an ambiguous requirement by enumerating readings and choosing one deliberately

concepts.statement: A requirement is **ambiguous** when two competent readers can derive different systems from it. Ambiguity is reader-relative: the author always knows what they meant, which is precisely why authors are the worst ambiguity detectors — independent readers with written interpretations are the instrument that works.
concepts.detail: The economic damage of ambiguity is deferred disagreement: the analyst, the developer and the tester each resolve it silently and differently, and the divergence is discovered at integration or acceptance — the three most expensive places in the project to have a conversation that should have cost one email in week two.

concepts.statement: Four layers: **lexical** — a word with multiple dictionary senses ('file' the document vs. file the tool; 'period' the interval vs. the punctuation); **syntactic** — the grammar allows multiple attachments ('The system shall record the transaction and notify the manager and the auditor' — who exactly is notified of what?); **semantic** — inherently vague quantifiers and adjectives ('several', 'appropriate', 'efficient', 'user-friendly'); **pragmatic** — meaning depends on unstated context ('The report shall be generated daily' — which timezone's day? sent or merely created?).
concepts.detail: The layers have different fixes: lexical and syntactic yield to rewriting and glossaries; semantic vagueness yields only to measurable thresholds; pragmatic gaps yield to context specification — timezone, environment, actor identity. Diagnosing the layer tells you which fix to reach for.

concepts.statement: Scan the specification for a standing list of vagueness markers and treat each hit as a defect to repair: *adequate, appropriate, efficient, sufficient, user-friendly, easy, fast, robust, flexible, minimal, maximal, several, some, few, generally, typically, if needed, as required, support (unquantified), enable (unquantified)*, and the notorious *etc.* Each is a placeholder for a number, a list, or a decision that someone still owes the document.
concepts.detail: The scan is cheap enough to run as a checklist item in every review, and it finds a striking fraction of semantic ambiguity in minutes. Every hit gets one of two treatments: replace with a measurable bound, or add a decision task — 'who must decide what several means, by when?'

concepts.statement: Two requirements are **inconsistent** when no system can satisfy both. **Direct conflicts** contradict on the same subject (R1: sessions expire after 5 minutes; R2: sessions last 8 hours). **Indirect conflicts** contradict only through an unstated assumption or a shared resource (an FR demanding all errors displayed in real time, plus an NFR that the UI thread never blocks — satisfiable together only with engineering effort nobody budgeted). **Temporal conflicts** hold at different times (a migration requirement that both preserves all history and deletes personal data after 30 days).
concepts.detail: Conflicts cluster where documents never meet: NFRs written by one group contradicting FRs written by another; global constraints ('all logs shall be human-readable') colliding with local needs ('logs shall be encrypted at rest'); regulatory requirements colliding across jurisdictions. Cross-document reviews exist because conflicts do not live inside single paragraphs.

concepts.statement: Detect by construction: maintain a **shared glossary** (kills lexical drift), cross-check every global NFR against every FR it constrains, and tabulate requirements that mention the same entity or resource. Resolve by making the trade-off explicit and routing it to the empowered owner: **prioritize** (one wins, with rationale recorded), **scope-condition** (each holds under different conditions — 5-minute expiry for admin consoles, 8 hours for warehouse terminals), or **negotiate a third requirement** that satisfies both interests.
concepts.detail: The cardinal rule: never resolve a conflict by silent averaging or by letting the developer pick at build time. The resolution is a decision with a rationale, recorded as such — future maintainers will otherwise re-litigate it, wrongly.

concepts.statement: You cannot prove completeness, but you can attack it from fixed directions. Per requirement: **boundary analysis** — what happens at, just inside, just outside every limit (order of 0 items? of 10,000?); **error enumeration** — for every step and every external dependency, ask what happens when it fails (payment gateway down, network lost mid-transaction, disk full). Per system: every input is used, every output is produced, every state is reachable and exitable, every user class has its requirements, every entity has create/read/update/delete/archive behavior. Per domain: legal, regulatory and environmental constraints enumerated, not assumed.
concepts.detail: The single most productive question in the toolkit is the failure question: 'what should the system do when X fails?' applied to every step, every call, every human actor. Happy paths write themselves; the missing requirements hide almost exclusively in the unhappy ones.

concepts.statement: No specification is provably complete — completeness can only be asserted *relative to a stated frame*: scope statement, list of user classes, list of external interfaces, failure-question checklist. The professional move is to make the frame explicit ('this specification covers the four named user classes and the eleven external interfaces; everything else is out of scope') so that gaps are detectable as violations of the frame rather than invisible omissions.
concepts.detail: This reframes reviews: instead of the unanswerable 'is it complete?', ask 'against this frame — these user classes, these interfaces, these failure questions — is anything missing?'. The question becomes answerable, and the answer becomes actionable.

examples.title: Repairing an ambiguous requirement
examples.problem: A ticketing specification contains: 'The system shall allow a customer to save an order and retrieve it later.' Production incidents show three teams built three behaviors from this one sentence. Diagnose and repair it.

steps.label: Step 1: Enumerate the readings
steps.text: Independent readings diverge: (i) *save* = persist for the current browser session only, (ii) *save* = persist to the customer's account for 30 days, (iii) *save* = persist indefinitely until deleted; and for *retrieve*: (a) only the saving customer may retrieve, (b) any agent on the account may retrieve; and *order*: complete orders only, or in-progress carts too. Crossed out, that is 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 defensible systems from one sentence.

steps.label: Step 2: Classify the ambiguities
steps.text: Lexical/pragmatic: 'save' has an unstated duration and location (account vs. session) — a context gap. Semantic: 'later' is unbounded — a weak word. Pragmatic: 'customer' — which role, exactly, when accounts have multiple agents?

steps.label: Step 3: Choose deliberately, with the stakeholder
steps.text: The business decision: orders persist to the customer's account for 30 days, then auto-archive; any agent listed on the account may retrieve them; both completed orders and in-progress carts are saveable. These are product decisions, not analyst guesses — route each to the empowered owner.

steps.label: Step 4: Rewrite measurably
steps.text: 'REQ-207: A customer shall be able to save an in-progress cart or a completed order to their account. Saved items shall persist for 30 calendar days from last modification, computed in the account's registered timezone, then be archived and recoverable only by support request. Any agent named on the account may list and retrieve saved orders; retrieval shall restore item, quantity and pricing as of retrieval time.' Every reading that caused an incident is now pinned.

steps.label: Step 5: Add the guardrails
steps.text: Push the fixed vocabulary into the shared glossary (save = persist-to-account-30-days), and add acceptance criteria at the boundary: day 29, day 30, day 31 post-modification — the three tests that fail if anyone quietly re-ambiguates the rule.

examples.result: Twelve systems hidden in one sentence, collapsed to one by enumerating readings, classifying each ambiguity layer, deciding deliberately, and rewriting with numbers, timezone and role identity. Plus boundary tests at the freshly quantified edges — because every new number creates a new edge that deserves a test.

examples.title: Catching an indirect conflict before it ships
examples.problem: A ride-sharing app's specification includes: R1 (FR): 'Every fare adjustment shall be displayed to the passenger within 1 second of the driver submitting it.' R2 (NFR): 'The passenger app shall consume at most 2% battery per hour of idle waiting.' No single sentence contradicts another. Is the set consistent?

steps.label: Step 1: Cross-check every global NFR against every FR
steps.text: R1 demands a push channel that can wake the app within a second, at any time. R2 demands the idle app do almost nothing. Both are satisfiable — but only via specific mechanisms (persistent socket vs. periodic polling), and polling at a 1-second cadence blows the battery budget by an order of magnitude.

steps.label: Step 2: Expose the hidden assumption
steps.text: The conflict is indirect: it lives in the *mechanism space*, not the sentences. Whoever wrote R2 assumed a low-frequency sync design; whoever wrote R1 assumed an always-on channel. The requirements do not conflict — the implied designs do, for naive implementations.

steps.label: Step 3: Resolve by scoped conditions
steps.text: Resolution: R1 holds while the app is in the foreground or a ride is active (when the push channel is open anyway); during idle waiting, adjustments sync on app-open with a visible freshness indicator. Record the decision and rationale; the trade-off (immediacy vs. battery) is now a documented product choice instead of a build-time coin flip.

examples.result: Indirect conflicts are invisible to sentence-by-sentence review — only the systematic NFR×FR cross-check, plus surfacing the mechanism each requirement silently assumes, finds them. The output is not a winner but a scoped resolution with rationale: the only form of conflict resolution that survives the next maintainer.

keyTakeaways: Ambiguity means two competent readers derive different systems; authors cannot detect it in their own text — independent written readings can.
Diagnose the ambiguity layer — lexical, syntactic, semantic, pragmatic — because each layer has a different fix (glossary, rewrite, measurable threshold, context specification).
Weak words (adequate, efficient, user-friendly, several, etc.) are standing defect markers; each is an unpaid decision, a missing number or an unfinished list.
Conflicts can be indirect — NFR against FR through a shared mechanism or resource — so cross-check every global constraint against every affected behavior, not just sentence against sentence.

Completeness is only ever checklist-relative: boundary values, failure of every step and dependency, input/output/state coverage, user classes, interfaces — make the frame explicit and audit against it.

quiz.q: A specification states: 'The system shall record the transaction and notify the manager and the auditor.' One developer notifies both parties about every transaction; another notifies the manager about every transaction and the auditor only about failed ones. Which ambiguity layer is this, and what is the fix?
options: Lexical ambiguity — replace the word 'transaction' with a glossary term

Syntactic ambiguity — the conjunction chain allows multiple attachments; rewrite with explicit per-recipient scope ('notify the manager of every recorded transaction; notify the auditor of every failed transaction')
Semantic ambiguity — 'notify' is a vague verb needing a measurable threshold
Pragmatic ambiguity — the timezone of 'record' is unspecified
quiz.explanation: The sentence's grammar does not pin what each 'and' conjoins — whether the auditor joins the notify list or the failure condition — so two parses survive. The fix is a rewrite that names each recipient and their triggering condition explicitly. Lexical fixes (a) address word senses, semantic fixes (c) address unquantified vagueness, and (d) addresses context gaps — none of which is the defect here.

quiz.q: Which of these specification fragments should a weak-word scan flag first?
options: The system shall reject login attempts after 5 consecutive failures within 10 minutes
The report shall be generated daily at 02:00 server time and emailed to the operations list
The system shall provide adequate performance under typical load conditions
Every order shall carry a UTC timestamp with millisecond precision
quiz.explanation: 'Adequate' and 'typical' are weak words — two unquantified decisions masquerading as a requirement: no number for latency or throughput, no definition of the load environment, hence no possible test. The other three fragments are what repaired requirements look like: bounded counts, named schedules, explicit timezone and precision.

quiz.q: Two requirements from different teams: R1 — 'All stored logs shall be encrypted at rest.' R2 — 'The audit log shall be directly human-readable by compliance staff without decryption tooling.' What is the status of this pair, and what is the appropriate resolution path?
options: Consistent — encryption and readability can trivially coexist

A direct conflict: as written, no log can be both encrypted at rest and directly human-readable without decryption; route to the empowered owners to prioritize, scope-condition, or negotiate a third design (e.g. encrypted at rest with a compliance viewing console that decrypts on authorized access)
An indirect conflict through an unstated performance assumption
Not a requirements issue — developers will figure it out during implementation
quiz.explanation: As stated the pair is unsatisfiable — the classic NFR-vs-NFR/FR direct conflict that appears when security and compliance requirements are written by separate groups. Resolution must be an explicit, recorded decision: one requirement wins, conditions split the cases, or a third design satisfies both interests. Deferring to implementation (d) delegates a security-and-compliance product decision to whoever writes the code that week.

quiz.q: A specification says: 'When the payment gateway is unreachable, the system shall handle it appropriately.' Which completeness heuristic, applied here, generates the real requirement the sentence is hiding?
options: Boundary analysis — test the statement at gateway timeouts of exactly 30 seconds

The failure-question heuristic: for every external dependency, specify detect, degrade, retry, and recover — e.g. within how long unavailability is detected, how many retries at what spacing, what the customer sees (queue vs. reject vs. retry-later), how orders persist meanwhile, and how the queue drains on recovery
Input/output coverage — verify every payment input field is used somewhere
User-class coverage — confirm both guests and registered customers can pay
quiz.explanation: 'Handle it appropriately' is an unpaid decision about failure behavior, and the failure-question heuristic — detect, degrade, retry, recover, for every dependency — is exactly the checklist that forces those decisions into explicit requirements. Boundary analysis (a) polishes numbers once they exist; (c) and (d) are other valuable heuristics that do not touch this gap.

quiz.q: A reviewer claims a specification is complete. What is the strongest professionally defensible response?
options: Agree — if every requirement in it is testable and none are ambiguous, the document is complete
Ask complete relative to what frame: which user classes, external interfaces, failure questions and boundary cases were enumerated — then audit the document against that explicit checklist
Disagree on principle — no specification is ever complete, so the claim is always false
Run a spell-check and grammar pass; completeness follows from correct prose
quiz.explanation: Completeness is checklist-relative: it can only be assessed against an explicit frame — enumerated user classes, interfaces, failure questions, boundary values. With the frame stated, gaps become detectable violations; without it, 'complete' is an unfalsifiable feeling. (a) conflates testability and unambiguity (internal qualities) with completeness (a relational one); (c) is technically true but useless — it abandons the audit instead of framing it; (d) polishes prose, not coverage.

quiz.q: During review, three independent readers interpret 'The system shall support image uploads' as: (1) any image format the browser can produce, (2) JPEG and PNG only, (3) images up to any size. What is the correct next action?
options: Take a vote among the readers and adopt the majority interpretation as the requirement
Ask the original author what they meant and consider the ambiguity resolved

Record a defect, classify the ambiguity (semantic — 'support' and implicit limits are unquantified), and drive a decision: which formats, what maximum size, at what resolution, verified how — then rewrite with the numbers
Leave it as is — at implementation time the developers will choose the most reasonable interpretation
quiz.explanation: Three competent readers, three systems: that is a detected ambiguity defect, and the professional response is repair, not arbitration. 'Support' is the canonical unquantified weak word — the rewrite must name formats, size bounds and failure behavior, each a stakeholder decision. Voting (a) institutionalizes a guess; the author's intent (b) does not bind the stakeholders who will use the system; and (d) delegates the product decision to build time, which is how the incident reports get written.

prerequisites: Basic familiarity with components, modules and deployment
intro: A pile of diagrams is not architecture documentation — a set of views, each answering a specific stakeholder question, is. The classic 4+1 view model and the modern C4 model both rest on the same insight: no single picture can serve a database administrator, an ops engineer and a product lead at once. And underneath the pictures sits the artifact that keeps architecture honest over time: the humble decision record.
objectives: Define software architecture as structures of elements, relations and properties — the set of decisions that are hard to change later
Describe the 4+1 view model (logical, process, development, physical, plus scenarios) and map stakeholder questions to views
Navigate a system with the C4 model's zoom levels: context, containers, components, code
Write an architecture decision record capturing context, decision, consequences and status
Explain why rationale is the most valuable — and most perishable — part of architectural documentation

concepts.statement: **Software architecture** is the set of structures of a system: its **elements** (modules, components, connectors, data), the **relations** among them, and the **properties** they must maintain — together with the principal design decisions that produce them. Operationally: architecture is the collection of decisions that are expensive to change after code exists (process boundaries, data ownership, trust zones, technology choices).
concepts.detail: The decisions framing is the useful one day-to-day. Choosing a message broker or drawing a service boundary is architecture; choosing a loop structure is not — not because one is more technical, but because one costs a quarter to reverse and the other costs an afternoon. Architecture is where the expensive-to-change decisions live.

concepts.statement: Kruchten's model documents a system through four coordinated views plus scenarios binding them: the **logical view** (end-user functionality; domain decomposition for engineers who own features), the **process view** (runtime: concurrent processes, their interactions, synchronization, failure behavior — for integrators and performance engineers), the **development view** (module organization, layers, build and ownership — for the programmers), and the **physical view** (deployment: processes mapped to processors, network links — for ops). The **+1 scenarios** walk through each view to verify they are consistent with real usage.
concepts.detail: The model's power is stakeholder routing: the DBA's questions live in logical-plus-data views, the SRE's in the physical view, the feature team's in development and logical. A review that cannot say which view a diagram belongs to will have the wrong audience arguing about the wrong picture.

concepts.statement: C4 documents a system as four zoom levels, each a box-and-line diagram at fixed vocabulary: **Context** — the system as one box among its users and external systems; **Container** — the separately runnable things inside it (web app, API, single-page app, database, message queue); **Component** — the major building blocks inside one container; **Code** — the classes inside one component, usually left to IDEs and UML where useful at all.
concepts.detail: The levels kill the two chronic documentation failures: diagrams that mix runtime boxes with build-time boxes, and diagrams with no stated zoom. Rule: every box in a given C4 diagram is the same *kind* of thing, every line means the same *kind* of interaction, and every diagram is titled with its level. Most teams need context and container diagrams maintained religiously, components for hot areas only, and code almost never.

concepts.statement: An **ADR** is a short, immutable document capturing one decision: **Title** and date, **Status** (proposed, accepted, superseded by ADR-14...), **Context** — the forces in play: constraints, requirements, options considered, **Decision** — what was chosen and concretely what will be done, **Consequences** — what becomes easier, what becomes harder, what we now must live with. Superseded ADRs are never deleted; they are marked, leaving the decision's full history legible.
concepts.detail: The context section is the payload: six months later, nobody remembers why Kafka was rejected — only that 'we do not use Kafka'. ADRs convert that tribal rule back into a re-evaluable decision with its original forces attached. Keep them short (a page), numbered, and stored beside the code so they survive reorganizations.

concepts.term: Views are stakeholder routing, not redundancy
concepts.statement: Multiple views are not repeated documentation — they are **different answers to different questions asked by different people**. The question determines the view: 'Which servers talk to the payment zone?' → physical. 'What happens at runtime when the cart service times out?' → process. 'Who owns this module and what can it depend on?' → development. 'What does the customer see as features?' → logical.
concepts.detail: Practical corollary: documentation effort should follow stakeholder questions, not completeness ideals. An internal tool with one team and one server needs context and container diagrams; a regulated multi-region platform needs all four views plus ADRs for every zone boundary. Write for the questions that will actually be asked.

concepts.statement: Structural diagrams rot because structure changes with every sprint; **rationale rots invisibly** because nobody edits it — it just becomes false as its context changes. The defense is pairing: keep current-structure views cheap and regenerable (close to code, ideally derived from it), and keep decisions in immutable ADRs whose supersession chain is itself the history of the architecture.
concepts.detail: A wrong diagram is detectable by comparing it to reality; a wrong-but-unrecorded rationale is undetectable until someone builds on a constraint that no longer holds — which is how the next team 'fixes' a design decision that was protecting them from an outage mode nobody remembers.

examples.title: Documenting a food-delivery platform: two C4 levels and one ADR
examples.problem: You inherit a food-delivery platform with no architecture documentation. Teams keep breaking each other by changing shared contracts, and new engineers take weeks to understand what talks to what. Produce the minimum documentation set that fixes both problems.

steps.label: Level 1: Context diagram
steps.text: One box: FoodDelivery Platform. Around it: Customer app (person), Courier app (person), Restaurant portal (person), Payment gateway (external system), Maps API (external system), SMS provider (external system). Every line is labeled with what crosses it: 'order requests', 'payment authorizations', 'location queries', 'dispatch texts'. This single diagram answers the new-engineer questions: what is this system, who uses it, what does it depend on.

steps.label: Level 2: Container diagram
steps.text: Inside the platform box: Web SPA, Order API, Dispatch service, Courier location service, Notifications service, PostgreSQL (orders), Redis (live location), Message queue. Lines show real interactions: Order API → queue → Dispatch service; Courier location service → Redis; Dispatch → Notifications → SMS provider. This is the diagram that stops contract-breaking changes: the queue's message schema is visibly a shared contract between three containers.

steps.label: Skip what you do not need yet
steps.text: Component-level diagrams for the Order API only — it is the hotspot everyone touches. Code-level diagrams: none; the IDE does that job. Two-and-a-half diagrams, maintained, beat twenty that are all stale.

steps.label: The ADR for the decision the diagram cannot show
steps.text: **ADR-07 — Async dispatch via message queue.** Status: Accepted. Context: dispatch was initially synchronous in the Order API; a dispatch outage took down order placement entirely; peak-hour latency doubled under load; the team considered synchronous retries and a queue. Decision: dispatch becomes asynchronous — Order API publishes an OrderPlaced event to the queue and returns; Dispatch service consumes at its own pace; message schema is a versioned contract. Consequences: order placement survives dispatch outages (+); eventual consistency — couriers see orders seconds later (+/−); the message schema is now a coupling point needing versioning discipline (−); dead-letter handling and monitoring are now mandatory (−).

steps.label: Wire the documentation into the workflow
steps.text: Container diagram lives in the repo beside the code, updated in the same PR that changes a container boundary. ADRs are numbered files; the schema-change checklist includes 'update ADR-07's contract version'. Staleness is combated by proximity, not by policy memos.

examples.result: Two C4 levels answer the structural questions new engineers and change-reviewers actually ask; one ADR preserves the reason the queue exists — the outage-driven context that nobody will remember in a year. The set is small enough to maintain, which is the only documentation set that survives.

keyTakeaways: Architecture = elements, relations, properties, and the expensive-to-change decisions that fix them; the decision framing tells you what is architectural and what is not.
4+1 routes stakeholder questions to views: logical (functionality), process (runtime), development (modules), physical (deployment), with scenarios checking cross-view consistency.
C4 gives four zoom levels — context, container, component, code — with fixed vocabulary per level; most systems need the first two maintained religiously.
An ADR captures context, decision and consequences for exactly one choice; superseded records are marked, never deleted — the supersession chain is the architecture's memory.
Diagrams rot visibly, rationale rots invisibly: keep structure views near the code and cheap to regenerate, and keep the why in immutable ADRs.

quiz.q: The operations lead asks: 'Which physical machines can initiate connections into the payment-processing network zone?' Which architectural view answers this question directly?
options: The logical view — it shows user-facing functionality
The process view — it shows concurrent processes and their synchronization
The physical view — it maps runtime processes onto processors and network links, which is exactly where zone boundaries and connection directions live
The development view — it shows module organization and build dependencies
quiz.explanation: Deployment topology — which node talks to which node, across which network — is the physical view's exclusive subject. The logical view answers feature questions, the process view answers runtime-concurrency questions, and the development view answers code-organization questions. Routing the question to the right view is half of what view models teach.

quiz.q: In a C4 container diagram of a streaming platform, which set of boxes is correct at that zoom level?
options: User, Session, PlaybackController, PlaylistRepository — the classes of the domain model
React SPA, Edge API, Transcoder service, Kafka, PostgreSQL — the separately runnable processes and data stores that together form the system
The streaming platform (one box), viewers (one box), ad exchange (one box), CDN (one box) — the system and its external actors
PaymentGateway, InvoiceGenerator, TaxCalculator — one container's internal building blocks
quiz.explanation: A container diagram's boxes are things you can separately run and deploy: SPAs, APIs, services, databases, queues — option (b) exactly. Option (a) is code-level, (c) is the context level (system + externals as single boxes), and (d) is component level inside one container. Mixing zoom levels in one diagram is the documentation sin C4 exists to prevent.
