quiz.q: Eighteen months after a platform was built, a new engineer proposes replacing its message queue with direct synchronous calls, believing the queue is pointless complexity. Which documentation artifact would most directly prevent this mistake, and how?
options: An up-to-date container diagram, showing the queue exists between the order and dispatch services

An ADR recording the context — the outage that motivated the queue, the alternatives considered, and the consequences accepted — so the proposal is evaluated against the original forces rather than in ignorance of them
A logical view showing the end-user functionality the queue supports
A sprint-by-sprint changelog of every modification to the messaging code
quiz.explanation: The diagram shows *that* the queue exists — the ADR shows *why*, including the outage and the trade-offs consciously accepted (eventual consistency, schema versioning). The engineer's proposal may still be right if the original forces have changed — but only an ADR makes that a reasoned re-decision instead of an unwitting regression. Structure documents what; rationale documents why-for.

quiz.q: In the 4+1 view model, what role do the '+1' scenarios play with respect to the other four views?
options: They replace the need for any runtime documentation, since scenarios are executable
They serve as integration checks — walking a concrete end-to-end usage through logical, process, development and physical views exposes inconsistencies between them
They are user manuals for the testers and play no architectural role
They document only the non-functional requirements, which the four views ignore
quiz.explanation: A single scenario — say, 'customer places an order during a payment-gateway outage' — must be traceable through all four views: the functionality (logical), the concurrent processes and failure handling (process), the modules implementing it (development), and the machines it runs on (physical). If the walk breaks — the process view has a retry the logical view never mentions — an inconsistency between views is exposed. That cross-view glue is the '+1's entire job.

quiz.q: A team's wiki has 30 detailed architecture diagrams, but every one is at least six months stale and engineers distrust them. What is the soundest corrective strategy?
options: Mandate that architects review all 30 diagrams monthly for accuracy
Delete architecture documentation entirely and rely on verbal knowledge transfer

Shrink to the few diagrams that answer real recurring stakeholder questions (typically C4 context + container), store them beside the code so structure changes update them in the same PR, and capture the why in ADRs
Regenerate all 30 diagrams automatically from the codebase every night
quiz.explanation: Documentation that is not trusted is worse than none, and 30 diagrams cannot be kept honest by review meetings. The durable fix is fewer diagrams chosen by stakeholder question, versioned with the code so they change when the code changes, plus ADRs for rationale (which diagrams never carry). (b) discards the genuine value; (a) is a maintenance treadmill that has already failed; (d) can derive structure but never rationale, and regenerates noise nobody asked about.

prerequisites: Non-functional requirements as architectural drivers
Components and connectors at runtime
intro: An architectural style is a packaged set of structural decisions with a known quality profile — pick pipes-and-filters and you have bought incremental throughput at the price of interactivity; pick microservices and you have bought independent deployment at the price of a distributed system. This section tours the load-bearing styles and, more importantly, the trade-off discipline for choosing among them.
objectives: Define an architectural style as a vocabulary of components and connectors plus constraints, with a characteristic quality profile
Explain layered, pipes-and-filters and event-driven styles: their strengths, and their specific failure modes
Analyze the monolith vs microservices decision as a trade-off among deployment independence, data consistency and operational complexity
Diagnose the distributed-monolith anti-pattern from its symptoms
Select a style (or hybrid) by scoring candidates against the 2–3 dominant quality-attribute drivers

concepts.statement: An **architectural style** is a family of structures defined by a **vocabulary** of component and connector types (filter, pipe, layer, publisher, subscriber), **constraints** on how they may be combined (no layer skipping, filters do not share state), and a resulting **quality profile** — a predictable bundle of qualities the style delivers well and delivers badly.
concepts.detail: Styles are pre-made decision bundles. That is their value and their danger: value, because a style imports decades of accumulated wisdom about its sweet spots; danger, because it imports the failure modes too, and teams that adopt a style for its brochure qualities meet its fine print in production.

concepts.statement: The system is organized into an ordered stack of **layers**, each providing services to the layer above and consuming services only from the layer below — presentation, application logic, domain logic, persistence being the canonical four. Strengths: **separation of concerns**, swappable implementations behind layer interfaces, teams organized by layer. Costs: performance overhead from pass-through calls, and the chronic failure mode of **layer leakage** — bypassing the stack for convenience until every layer knows about everything.
concepts.detail: Two laws of layers worth memorizing: strict layering (call only the layer immediately below) maximizes substitutability; relaxed layering (call any lower layer) trades it for fewer pass-through hops. Choose per layer boundary, explicitly — and enforce with lint rules and architecture tests, because layers decay silently one shortcut at a time.

concepts.statement: Computation is a pipeline of independent **filters**, each reading a stream from its input **pipe**, transforming it, and writing to its output pipe — with no shared state between filters. Strengths: **incremental, streaming throughput** (filters run concurrently as data flows), composability of transformations, easy parallelization. Costs: no natural interactivity (a data-flow model, not a request model), error handling across the chain is awkward, and filters are coupled by the data format flowing in the pipes.
concepts.detail: The style dominates data processing — compilers (lexing → parsing → optimization → code generation), ETL, media transcoding, log analysis — and is wrong for interactive interfaces, where the user is not a stream. Its signature weakness is format coupling: changing the pipe schema touches every filter downstream, so schema versioning is the pipe-line's central discipline.

concepts.statement: Components communicate indirectly: **publishers** emit named events without knowing who (if anyone) consumes them; a broker delivers events to **subscribers** that registered interest. Strengths: extreme **decoupling of senders from receivers**, easy extensibility (add a subscriber, touch no publisher), resilience of producers to consumer slowness or failure. Costs: **debugging is genuinely harder** — no call stack follows an event across a broker; ordering and delivery semantics (at-least-once, exactly-once) become explicit engineering obligations; consumers must be idempotent under redelivery; and **eventual consistency** replaces immediate feedback.
concepts.detail: The observability tax is the price most teams under-estimate: correlation ids that propagate through every event, dead-letter queues with real runbooks, and dashboards that can answer 'did event X get processed, and if not, why'. Without that instrumentation, an event-driven system is a distributed system with the lights off.

concepts.statement: A **monolith** packages all functionality into one deployable unit: in-process calls, one transaction boundary, one release train — simplest to develop, debug and transactionally protect, but every change redeploys everything and scaling is all-or-nothing. **Microservices** decompose by business capability into independently deployable services with private data: independent scaling, releases and technology per service — purchased with network failure modes, distributed transactions and sagas, eventual consistency, and a heavy operations platform (containers, service discovery, tracing, orchestrated deploys).
concepts.detail: The honest decision rule: microservices buy **organizational scaling** (many teams shipping independently without queuing on one another) more than they buy technical elegance. A team of eight running twelve services is paying distributed-system tax without the organizational dividend. Conway's law cuts both directions: your architecture will grow to look like your communication structure, so choose the structure you can staff.

concepts.statement: The worst of both worlds arrives when services are split physically but not logically: synchronous call chains where every request fans through five services (all the latency and failure coupling of distribution, none of the independent deployability), shared databases reached around the service boundary, and releases that must still be coordinated across teams. Symptoms: deploys require a synchronized rollout of multiple services; one service's outage cascades through the chain; 'temporary' shared tables age into permanence.
concepts.detail: The cure is boundary hygiene: services own their data exclusively (no cross-service table reads), synchronous chains are collapsed or replaced with events where eventual consistency is tolerable, and each service is independently deployable *in practice* — verified by actually deploying them independently, not by asserting it in a diagram.

concepts.statement: Choose styles by enumeration and scoring, not by fashion: (1) identify the 2–3 **dominant quality-attribute drivers** from the requirements (throughput? modifiability of processing stages? independent team deployment? 99.99% availability?); (2) list candidate styles and hybrids; (3) score each candidate against each driver, noting sensitivities — where the style fights the requirement; (4) verify the fine print — the failure modes the style imports are acceptable. The style that wins on the drivers must also survive its own cost column.
concepts.detail: Real systems are almost always hybrids: a pipes-and-filters core for the data path, an event bus for integration, a modular monolith for the transactional core that does not need distribution. Purity is not a quality attribute; the drivers are the drivers.

examples.title: Choosing a style for an IoT telemetry platform
examples.problem: Design the architecture for a platform ingesting telemetry from 50,000 factory sensors. Requirements: (1) ingest at 200,000 events/second; (2) new analytic jobs (rolling averages, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance) added every few weeks without touching running code; (3) raw data replayable into new analytics; (4) a configuration dashboard for engineers — interactive, low volume. Drivers and style choices?

steps.label: Step 1: Identify the dominant drivers
steps.text: Driver one: **throughput at scale** (200k events/s). Driver two: **modifiability of the processing stages** — new analytics without redeploying the pipeline. Driver three: **replayability** — raw events retained and re-processable. The dashboard is real but minor: interactive, low volume, boring.

steps.label: Step 2: Map drivers to styles
steps.text: Throughput + stage modifiability + replay is the exact quality profile of **pipes-and-filters**: ingest → decode → validate → route → per-analytic fan-out, each filter independently replaceable, run concurrently as streams. Replay is satisfied by one crucial pipe choice: an **append-only durable log** (Kafka-style) as the spine — raw events are retained, and every new analytic is a new consumer group that replays history from the beginning.

steps.label: Step 3: Add event-driven where decoupling pays
steps.text: New analytics added weekly, without touching producers: consumers **subscribe** to the log's topics — publishers (the ingest filters) neither know nor care how many analytics subscribe. That is publish–subscribe semantics, and it is exactly why requirement (2) is satisfied by construction rather than by discipline.

steps.label: Step 4: Keep the boring parts boring
steps.text: The configuration dashboard: an interactive request/response application. Give it a small **layered** service (presentation → application → data) with its own database, reading config changes the pipeline picks up via a control topic. No distribution where none is needed — the dashboard has no throughput driver and joins no event flow.

steps.label: Step 5: Audit the fine print
steps.text: The style's costs, accepted deliberately: schema evolution on the log is a contract — every event format is versioned, old consumers tolerate new fields; ordering is per-partition, documented per analytic; dead-letter topics with runbooks for poison events; end-to-end tracing via correlation ids, because no stack trace will ever cross the broker.

examples.result: A hybrid, chosen driver by driver: pipes-and-filters on a durable log spine for throughput, replay and stage modifiability; pub-sub semantics for zero-touch extensibility; a small layered service for the interactive dashboard. Every acceptance carries its fine print — versioned schemas, per-partition ordering, dead-letter runbooks — acknowledged up front rather than discovered in an incident.

keyTakeaways: A style is a vocabulary + constraints + a predictable quality profile: it imports decades of wisdom and its specific failure modes together.
Layers buy separation and substitutability at the cost of pass-through overhead and silent layer leakage; enforce layering with tooling, not hope.
Pipes-and-filters owns streaming throughput, composability and replay (especially over a durable log); it is wrong for interactivity and pays format coupling in the pipes.
Event-driven buys decoupling and extensibility at the price of observability, delivery semantics, idempotent consumers and eventual consistency.
Microservices primarily buy organizational scaling; a distributed monolith — synchronous chains, shared data, coordinated releases — pays the tax without the dividend.
Select styles by scoring candidates against the 2–3 dominant quality drivers, then verify the imported failure modes are acceptable; real systems are deliberate hybrids.

quiz.q: A team must process nightly clickstream dumps: read compressed logs, parse, clean, join with a product catalogue, aggregate, and emit reports. The stages change monthly as analysts experiment. Which style fits best, and why?
options: Layered — the cleaning, joining and aggregating map naturally to presentation, logic and persistence layers
Pipes-and-filters — independent stream transformations, composable and individually replaceable as analytics evolve, running concurrently for throughput
Event-driven pub-sub — publishers of click events decouple from subscriber analytics
Microservices — each transformation becomes an independently deployable service with its own database
quiz.explanation: This is the pipes-and-filters sweet spot verbatim: a data-flow computation through replaceable transformations — the compiler/ETL shape. Layers (a) model request/response separation of concerns, not stream composition; pub-sub (c) is about runtime decoupling of unknown consumers, while here the chain is a known, ordered pipeline; (d) pays distributed-system tax (network serialization of entire streams, cross-service joins) for a deployment independence the monthly-change requirement never asked for.

quiz.q: A retailer's system: the web checkout synchronously calls the inventory service, which synchronously calls the pricing service, which synchronously calls the promotion service — all in the request path; all four must be deployed in a coordinated weekly release; the promotion database is read directly by the inventory service 'temporarily'. What is the diagnosis?
options: A well-formed microservices architecture — synchronous calls between services are standard practice
A distributed monolith: physical distribution without logical independence — cascading latency and failure, coordinated releases, and boundary-violating shared data
An event-driven architecture missing a message broker
A layered architecture with too many layers
quiz.explanation: Every symptom is the distributed-monolith signature: a synchronous chain couples availability and latency of four services; the coordinated weekly release proves there is no independent deployability; direct database access around the service boundary destroys data ownership. The system pays full distributed-systems tax for none of the benefit. (a) mistakes the symptom for the design; (c) and (d) name different styles entirely.

quiz.q: Why is debugging characteristically harder in an event-driven architecture than in a layered monolith?
options: Because events are always slower than function calls

Because no call stack spans the broker: control flow is scattered across asynchronous consumers, delivery may be delayed or reduplicated, and reconstructing what happened requires correlation ids and event logs rather than a debugger
Because event-driven systems cannot have automated tests
Because brokers do not support encryption of message payloads
quiz.explanation: The monolith's stack trace is a complete causal narrative; the broker severs it — publishers cannot know consumers, delivery is asynchronous and possibly at-least-once, so causality must be reconstructed from instrumentation: correlation ids propagated in every event, consumed-offset tracking, dead-letter inspection. The difficulty is an architectural property, not a tooling gap (a) or a testing impossibility (c).

quiz.q: A five-person startup is building its first product — a booking platform expected to reach a few thousand users in year one. The tech lead proposes twelve microservices 'to be ready to scale'. What is the soundest architectural counsel?
options: Agree — rewriting a monolith into microservices later is prohibitively expensive

Propose a well-modularized monolith with clean internal boundaries: at this scale the dominant risks are product-market discovery and speed of iteration, and microservices' distributed-system and operational tax buys nothing the team can use — while disciplined module boundaries preserve the later extraction option
Compromise on six microservices, splitting the difference
Adopt microservices but outsource operations to a cloud provider, eliminating the tax
quiz.explanation: Microservices buy independent deployment and team scaling — dividends that require multiple teams to pay off, which five people cannot be. At this stage the monolith's in-process simplicity maximizes iteration speed, and the real hedge for the future is internal modularity: clean seams are what make later extraction mechanical. (a) overstates rewrite cost relative to daily tax paid; (c) splits a bad decision, not the difference; (d) outsources infrastructure, not the failure-mode, consistency and design burden.

quiz.q: In a layered system, the UI layer directly queries the persistence layer 'just for this one report', skipping the application and domain layers. Over two years this happens eleven more times. What has been lost, and what is the practical defense?
options: Nothing important — relaxed layering is a documented variant with no costs

Substitutability and separation of concerns erode: the UI now knows the database schema, so schema changes and logic changes ripple into screens; the defense is automated enforcement — architecture tests and lint rules that fail the build on layer violations
Only performance has suffered; adding caching will restore the architecture
The system has become a pipes-and-filters architecture, which must be documented as such
quiz.explanation: Each shortcut is locally rational and globally corrosive: layer leakage couples the top of the stack to the bottom, destroying the ability to change either independently — the exact benefit layers exist to provide. Because leakage is silent and incremental, the only effective defense is automated boundary enforcement in CI: a rule that turns 'just this once' into a build failure. Reviewer vigilance alone reliably loses this war of attrition.

quiz.q: A team choosing an architectural style scores four candidates against their drivers: throughput (weight: high), modifiability of processing stages (weight: high), interactive responsiveness (weight: medium). Pipes-and-filters wins on the first two but scores badly on interactivity. What is the correct interpretation and action?
options: Reject pipes-and-filters — a style must win on every quality attribute
Accept pipes-and-filters — winning the two dominant drivers is what matters, and a good score on a medium-weight attribute is optional

Accept pipes-and-filters for the data path, and satisfy interactive responsiveness with a separate layered service — a deliberate hybrid that scores well on all three, acknowledging the style's known weakness rather than ignoring it
Average the three scores and pick the style with the highest mean
quiz.explanation: The scenario is a hybrid signature: the dominant drivers belong to the streaming data path, the medium driver belongs to a different subsystem with different needs. Splitting the architecture lets each part use the style whose profile fits it — the standard real-world outcome. (a) demands a style that does not exist; (b) ignores a real requirement; (d) lets a medium-weight driver dilute the dominant ones arithmetically — drivers are not fungible.

prerequisites: Interfaces and polymorphism
Coupling and cohesion basics
intro: Design patterns are named, packaged micro-architectures: each one is a context-problem-solution triple with documented consequences. Their real power is as much vocabulary as mechanism — 'wrap it in an adapter' compresses a design conversation into three words. This section covers the essential catalog entries, their consequences you will actually feel, and — just as important — the discipline of not using them.
objectives: Define a design pattern as a named context-problem-solution triple with consequences, and explain why the vocabulary matters
Apply Strategy, Observer, Factory Method and Adapter to the problems they are shaped for, and state each one's costs
Diagnose the Singleton's failure modes: hidden global state, testability, and concurrent initialization
Distinguish Adapter from Facade by intent (converting an interface vs. simplifying one)
Recognize pattern over-application and apply the restraint tests before paying a pattern's complexity cost

concepts.statement: A **design pattern** is a named, reusable solution template for a recurring design problem, specified as: **context** (the situation), **problem** (the forces in tension), **solution** (the structure of classes/objects and their collaboration), and — decisively — **consequences** (what the pattern costs and what it trades away). The classic Gang-of-Four catalog organizes them as **creational** (object creation: Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Singleton, Prototype), **structural** (composition: Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Composite, Proxy), and **behavioral** (interaction: Strategy, Observer, Command, Template Method, State, Iterator).
concepts.detail: The name is half the value: a shared vocabulary turns a paragraph of explanation into a phrase ('make ShippingCost a Strategy'), makes reviews faster, and encodes the solution's consequences as tribal knowledge attached to the name. A team without the vocabulary rediscovers the patterns anonymously — and inherits their costs without their names.

concepts.statement: **Context:** a class needs one of several interchangeable algorithms or policies, selected at runtime. **Problem:** hard-coding the variants as conditionals (`if region == 'EU' ... else if region == 'US' ...`) scatters the algorithm families across every caller and makes adding a variant a shotgun-edit. **Solution:** define a `Strategy` interface with one method; implement one class per variant; the client holds a Strategy reference and delegates. **Consequences:** adding a variant becomes one new class, zero caller edits (+); callers must know which strategies exist to choose one (−); more classes to navigate (−); overkill when the policy is genuinely stable and singular (−).
concepts.detail: The tell-tale smell is a `switch` on a type code that appears in multiple methods of the same class — the same discriminator branching again and again. Each branch cluster is a Strategy (or a State, if the branches represent object lifecycle rather than a selectable policy) waiting to be extracted.

concepts.statement: **Context:** one object's state change must notify an open-ended set of dependent objects. **Problem:** the subject should not know every dependent's concrete class — that couples publisher to all subscribers and hard-codes the extension set. **Solution:** the subject holds a list of `Observer` interfaces and calls `notify()` on each; observers register and deregister themselves. **Consequences:** adding a subscriber touches no publisher code (+); publishers and subscribers stay loosely coupled (+); notification ordering is typically unspecified — order-dependent observers harbor latent bugs (−); un-registered observers leak (the **lapsed listener** problem) (−); cascading updates can ripple through observer graphs unpredictably (−).
concepts.detail: Observer is the pattern behind every event system, pub-sub API and reactive framework — but in its raw form it is also a memory-leak and race-condition generator. Modern practice delegates its mechanics to framework event buses or reactive streams that handle registration lifecycle and threading, keeping the decoupling and outsourcing the sharp edges.

concepts.statement: **Context:** a framework or client code must create objects, but the concrete type should be decided by a subclass or configuration. **Problem:** instantiating `new ConcreteProduct()` binds the client to a concrete class, defeating abstraction. **Solution:** define a creator with a factory method returning the `Product` interface; subclasses override the method to return their concrete product; client code stays written against the abstraction. **Consequences:** clients are insulated from concrete types and construction complexity (+); families of related products plug in cleanly (+); you grow parallel class hierarchies — each product extension needs a matching creator (−); for one or two stable types it is ceremony (−).
concepts.detail: The modern classics shorthand: a constructor returning an interface, a registry keyed by type, or a dependency-injection container all deliver the same essential service — 'decide the concrete type somewhere other than the use site'. When a language has first-class functions, a factory is often just a function that returns the right implementation.

concepts.statement: **Context:** you must use an existing component, but its interface is not the one your code expects — a third-party library, a legacy module, an external service. **Problem:** rewriting either side couples you to code you do not own or cannot safely change. **Solution:** an **Adapter** class implements the interface the client expects and internally translates each call to the legacy interface (and each result back). **Consequences:** systems with incompatible interfaces interoperate without source changes (+); the mapping is localized and testable (+); every new operation needs adapter plumbing (−); a leaky adaptation exposes the adaptee's model anyway (−).
concepts.detail: Distinguish from **Facade** by intent: an Adapter *converts* one interface into another, preserving operation-for-operation semantics; a Facade *simplifies* a complex subsystem behind a new, smaller interface. Adapter is a translator between equals; Facade is a front door over a maze. Same structural shape — object wrapping another — entirely different reasons.

concepts.statement: **Context:** exactly one instance of a class must exist, globally accessible (a config store, a connection pool). **Solution:** a private constructor, a static instance, and a global access point. **Consequences, honestly:** the instance is **global mutable state** — hidden dependencies that bypass constructor signatures; **unit tests cannot isolate themselves** — one test's mutations bleed into the next, and there is no clean way to inject a fake; **initialization order and thread safety** become load-bearing concerns (lazy vs. eager init, double-checked locking subtleties); and it ** Singleton-ifies scalability away** — the single instance becomes an assumption woven through every caller.
concepts.detail: The standard modern replacements: dependency injection with a single configured instance (same effect, explicit dependency), or a module-level immutable value in languages with real modules. Then 'singleton' becomes a lifecycle decision made at the composition root, testable by swapping what is composed — rather than a hard-coded property of the class reachable from anywhere.

concepts.statement: A pattern is complexity purchased for flexibility — so run the restraint tests before buying: (1) **The variability test**: is there a *second* concrete variant, or a scheduled one? Patterns solve variation; one implementation with an interface is speculative generality. (2) **The change-frequency test**: will the varying dimension actually change, or is it stable in this domain? (3) **The cost-of-change test**: if a future change would be a mechanical 20-minute edit without the pattern, the pattern's premium is not justified. Rule of thumb: **write the simple thing; extract the pattern when the second variant actually arrives** — refactoring tools make that extraction cheap precisely so you can defer it.
concepts.detail: Pattern over-application ('patternitis') is the failure mode of teams who learned patterns as a syllabus rather than as responses to forces: everything becomes an Abstract Factory; simple data flow vanes behind five layers of Strategy. The mature question is never 'which pattern fits here?' but '**does this problem have the forces this pattern answers?**' — and usually the honest answer is no.

examples.title: Killing a switch statement with Strategy, and integrating a legacy tax engine with an Adapter
examples.problem: An e-commerce checkout contains: (a) a `calculateShipping(order)` method with a growing `switch` over regions — EU, US, APAC — each branch with its own formula, duplicated in `estimateDeliveryDate` with the same switch; (b) a mandatory legacy tax engine with a hostile interface (`computeTax(amountCents, regionCode, dateInt)`) the team must keep calling. Region count is about to grow from 3 to 7. Apply patterns where they pay.

steps.label: Step 1: Verify the forces warrant Strategy
steps.text: Variability test: 7 concrete variants, real and scheduled — passes. Change-frequency test: regions change every quarter — passes. The same region discriminator branching in multiple methods is the classic smell: each branch is a policy that wants to be an object.

steps.label: Step 2: Extract the Strategy
steps.text: Define `interface ShippingStrategy { calculateShipping(o: Order): Money; estimateDeliveryDate(o: Order): DateRange; }` — note both methods move behind the interface, because they vary along the same axis. Implement `EuShipping`, `UsShipping`, `ApacShipping`. The checkout class holds a `ShippingStrategy` resolved from region by a factory/registry lookup. The two switch statements collapse to one strategy resolution point.

steps.label: Step 3: Reap and pay the consequences
steps.text: Reap: adding region 4 through 7 is now four new classes with zero edits to checkout code; each region's rules are unit-tested in isolation; the two-method duplication is structurally impossible. Pay: five files where there was one; a reader must now know the Strategy vocabulary; strategy selection is a new place to be wrong (a mis-registered strategy silently no-ops).

steps.label: Step 4: Wrap the tax engine in an Adapter
steps.text: The domain wants `TaxResult calculate(TaxOrder): TaxOrder` in domain terms; the legacy wants `computeTax(amountCents, regionCode, dateInt)` in its terms. `LegacyTaxEngineAdapter implements TaxCalculator`: it translates domain objects to the legacy's integers and codes, calls the engine, and converts the raw return into a `TaxResult`. All units, codes and date-format conversions live in exactly one tested place.

steps.label: Step 5: Test at the seam
steps.text: The adapter is the seam: unit tests verify the translation (e.g. 19.99 → 1999 cents, round-trip, timezone of dateInt); the domain tests use a fake `TaxCalculator` and never touch the legacy engine. When the engine is eventually replaced, the adapter is deleted and its successor written against the same `TaxCalculator` interface — checkout code does not notice.

examples.result: Strategy paid for itself because the variability was real (7 variants, quarterly change) — the two switch statements collapsed into pluggable policies. The Adapter quarantined the hostile legacy interface behind a domain-shaped one, making the eventual replacement a one-file change. Both decisions passed the restraint tests before the complexity was purchased — which is the entire discipline.

keyTakeaways: A pattern is a named context-problem-solution triple with consequences; the shared vocabulary is as valuable as the structure, and the consequences are the fine print.
Strategy replaces repeated switching over a discriminator with interchangeable policy objects — worth it only when the variants are real and changing.

Observer decouples publishers from an open subscriber set, at the price of ordering ambiguity, lapsed-listener leaks and cascading updates; modern event frameworks are Observer with the sharp edges managed.
Factory Method (and its functional/DI descendants) moves the choice of concrete type away from the use site; Adapter converts interfaces you do not own — Facade simplifies ones you do.
Singletons trade testability and explicit dependencies for convenience; dependency injection of a single configured instance achieves the goal without the global state.
Before applying any pattern, run the restraint tests — variability, change frequency, cost of deferred extraction — and prefer extracting the pattern when the second variant actually arrives.

quiz.q: A pricing module selects discount rules at runtime among five interchangeable algorithms chosen by customer tier, and marketing adds a new tier roughly monthly. Which pattern fits, and what is its most relevant consequence here?
options: Singleton — guarantees one pricing engine exists

Strategy — interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, so the monthly tier is one new class with no edits to the pricing module; consequence: client code must still resolve which strategy applies per tier
Observer — the pricing engine should publish discount events to subscribers
Adapter — the discount algorithms have incompatible interfaces needing translation
quiz.explanation: Interchangeable runtime-selected algorithms is Strategy verbatim, and the monthly addition lands in the pattern's sweet spot: new class, zero caller edits. The consequence named in the option is real and relevant — selection logic still lives somewhere. Observer (c) addresses notification, not selection; Adapter (d) addresses incompatible existing interfaces, not pluggable variants; Singleton (a) is unrelated to the problem.

quiz.q: A GUI framework keeps a global `ApplicationConfig` Singleton. Tests that change config values in one test bleed into later tests, and a parallel-test runner produces order-dependent failures. What is the root cause and the sound fix?
options: The tests are badly written; each test should save and restore the Singleton's fields manually

Root cause: Singleton is global mutable state — hidden dependencies and shared lifetime that defeat test isolation; fix: inject configuration through constructors/context, with a single configured instance created at the composition root so tests construct their own
Make the Singleton thread-safe with double-checked locking
Run tests strictly sequentially and alphabetically, removing the order dependence
quiz.explanation: The test bleed is the Singleton's documented consequence surfacing: state with global lifetime cannot be isolated per test, because nothing owns its creation. Dependency injection restores ownership — each test builds (or fakes) its own config, and the single instance becomes a runtime decision at the composition root. (a) treats symptoms in every test forever; (c) addresses races, not isolation; (d) institutionalizes the fragility.

quiz.q: Your payment subsystem expects a `PaymentGateway` interface, but must now use a third-party SDK whose interface is entirely different (different method names, amounts in pence rather than decimal currency, asynchronous callbacks rather than returns). Which pattern, and what exactly does it NOT do for you?
options: Facade — it will simplify the SDK behind a friendlier interface

Adapter — a class implementing `PaymentGateway` that translates calls, units and callback style; it does NOT redesign the SDK or absorb semantic mismatches (declined vs. errored, idempotency rules) — those differences must be mapped explicitly and tested
Observer — subscribe to the SDK's callbacks and republish them
Strategy — select between gateways at runtime
quiz.explanation: Interface conversion between a required port and a foreign API is Adapter's exact purpose — signature, units, and synchronous-to-callback bridging all live in one tested class. But adapters translate interfaces, not semantics: whether the SDK's 'declined' maps to your 'rejected' or 'error', and how idempotency keys behave, are business mappings the pattern cannot infer. Facade (a) is the wrong intent — simplification, not conversion; (c) and (d) address different problems.

quiz.q: In an event-driven UI, a `ChartPanel` subscribes to a `StockTicker` but is never unsubscribed when the panel closes; heap profiling shows thousands of retained dead panels. What is this failure and the standard cure?
options: The lapsed-listener problem — a consequence of Observer: the subject retains references to observers that forgot to deregister; cure: unsubscribe on disposal (dispose/unmount hooks), or use weak references / a framework event bus that manages registration lifecycle
Observer ordering — assign priorities to observers
A Strategy leak — the wrong charting strategy was selected
quiz.explanation: The subject's subscriber list is a strong reference: an observer that never deregisters is kept alive — and keeps receiving events — indefinitely. This is the Observer pattern's classic memory leak, and the cures are structural: deterministic unsubscribe in disposal paths, or delegating registration lifecycle to infrastructure that does it for you. Throttling (a) changes frequency, not retention; ordering (c) is a different Observer consequence.

quiz.q: A developer proposes: 'Let us wrap our single, stable CSV exporter in a Strategy interface with an Abstract Factory for creating exporters, so we can add PDF and XLSX later.' What is the disciplined response?
options: Approve — anticipating future formats is exactly what patterns are for

Challenge with the restraint tests: there is currently one variant and no scheduled second; the cost of *deferring* is one mechanical extraction when PDF actually arrives (cheap with refactoring tools) — so write the simple exporter, and extract the pattern when the second variant is real
Approve, but only the Strategy interface — drop the Abstract Factory
Reject permanently — CSV export will never need variants
quiz.explanation: This is speculative generality: paying a pattern's complexity premium for flexibility with no confirmed demand. The restraint tests expose it — variability test fails (one variant), cost-of-change test fails (extraction later is mechanical and cheap). Note the response is defer, not never (d): when the second exporter arrives, the extraction is precisely the moment the pattern's cost starts buying something. And (c) keeps half the speculative machinery for the same failed justification.

quiz.q: Which distinguishing question best separates Adapter from Facade when you are wrapping an existing subsystem?
options: Is the wrapper a class or a set of functions?
Is the wrapper stateless or stateful?
What is the intent: converting an existing interface to one the client already expects (Adapter), versus designing a new, simpler front-door interface over a complex subsystem (Facade)?
Does the wrapped subsystem use third-party code or our own code?
quiz.explanation: Structurally the two patterns are near-identical — an object delegating to wrapped collaborators — so intent is the only reliable discriminator, and GoF organize them by intent for exactly this reason. Adapter: the client's expected interface already exists and the wrapper conforms to it, operation-for-operation. Facade: the client-facing interface is newly designed to be smaller and simpler than the subsystem's real surface. Ownership (d) and shape questions (a, b) do not separate them.

prerequisites: Interfaces and polymorphism
Basic idea of runtime components vs. build-time modules
intro: Ask an architect 'is this design good?' and the honest answer is always a question: 'good at what?' The most useful at-what is the cost of change — and coupling and cohesion are the two dials that determine it. This section makes those dials precise, then adds the principle that operationalizes them: depend on abstractions you own, and let details plug into them.
objectives: Distinguish component-and-connector thinking (runtime) from module thinking (build time), and identify connectors in a design
Define coupling precisely, rank its forms by damage, and recognize each in code scenarios
Define cohesion, rank its forms, and diagnose low-cohesion modules
State and apply the dependency inversion principle, including who should own the abstraction's interface
Reason about change impact — ripple size — as the practical measure of a design's quality

concepts.statement: In component-and-connector (runtime) thinking, a **component** is a principal unit of runtime computation or state (a service, a process, a database, an in-process object with responsibilities), and a **connector** is the interaction mechanism between components: a synchronous call, an HTTP request, a message on a queue, a database connection, a shared file. Connectors are architecture — choosing 'call' versus 'queue' changes latency, failure and concurrency semantics more than most code changes.
concepts.detail: The module view (build time: which source units exist and may depend on which) and the C&C view (runtime: what talks to what, how) are different graphs that must stay consistent — every runtime interaction implies a build-time dependency somewhere, but the maps are not the same, and designs fail when one is changed without the other.

concepts.statement: **Coupling** is the degree of interdependence between two modules: how much must be known, and must change, on one side when the other changes. Ranked from most to least damaging: **content coupling** (one module reaches into another's internals — modifying another's data or jumping into its middle); **common coupling** (modules share global data — any reader breaks when the shared meaning shifts); **control coupling** (one module passes a flag that decides the other's control flow — the caller must understand the callee's decision tree); **stamp coupling** (passing a whole data structure when only part is used — reader and writer now share the structure's evolution); **data coupling** (passing exactly the data needed — the healthy baseline).
concepts.detail: The ranking is a triage guide: content and common coupling are architecture-threatening; control and stamp coupling are friction worth removing opportunistically; data coupling is the target state, not a pathology. Zero coupling is neither possible nor the goal — the goal is that dependencies are narrow, explicit and point at stable things.

concepts.statement: **Cohesion** is how strongly the elements of one module belong together — the degree to which its responsibilities form a single, nameable purpose. Ranked from weakest to strongest: **coincidental** (a 'utils' bag — parts related by nothing but the file they landed in), **logical** (one interface, unrelated implementations chosen by flag), **temporal** (grouped only by when they run — init/shutdown), **procedural** (a sequence of steps, in one module only because they follow each other), **communicational** (operations over the same data — find-by-id and update-by-id), **sequential** (each part's output feeds the next's input), **functional** (all elements contribute to one single, statable function — the target).
concepts.detail: The practical cohesion test: can you complete the sentence 'the responsibility of this module is to ___' with one verb phrase that names no 'and'? A module whose purpose statement needs 'and' (and also '...') is a module with more than one reason to change — and more than one reason to be touched by more than one team.

concepts.statement: An **interface** is the surface a component exposes; a **contract** is the full obligation set behind it: **syntactic** (signatures and types), **semantic** (preconditions, postconditions, invariants — what the operation *means*), **quality-of-service** (latency bounds, availability, freshness guarantees) and **error behavior** (which failures are signaled how, and what state the component is left in). Two components whose connectors agree syntactically but disagree semantically compile happily and fail at 3 a.m.
concepts.detail: Contract maturity is a design deliverable: undocumented contracts get re-invented by every consumer, slightly differently. Writing down even informally — 'returns within 50 ms p99; blocks never; on timeout, exactly-once side effects are NOT guaranteed' — is the difference between an interface and an accident report form.

concepts.statement: High-level policy modules should not depend on low-level detail modules; **both should depend on abstractions** — and the abstraction should be shaped by the high-level module's needs, i.e. **the interface belongs to the consumer's domain, not the provider's**. 'Inversion' names the reversal of the source-code arrow: instead of Policy → details, you have Policy → interface ← details (the details depend on the interface, implementing it).
concepts.detail: The ownership clause is what makes the principle bite. A `PaymentService` should define the narrow `PaymentGateway` interface *it* needs (`charge(order, amount)`), and the Stripe adapter, the PayPal adapter and the test fake implement *that* — not the reverse, where the service imports the gateway vendor's sprawling SDK interface and inherits its churn. When the abstraction serves the policy, swapping or faking the detail is mechanical; when it serves the vendor, the vendor's next release is your refactor.

concepts.term: Change impact as the master metric
concepts.statement: Coupling and cohesion are not virtues in themselves — they are the levers behind the measurable question that matters: **when a likely change arrives, how many modules must be touched, and how far does the ripple travel?** A design is good to the extent that expected changes stay local: one high-cohesion module edited, its stable interface intact, its dependents untouched. Track 'files touched per feature' and 'blast radius of the last ten changes' and you have an empirical architecture health metric, not an aesthetic.
concepts.detail: This reframes the two dials: low coupling keeps strangers out of your change; high cohesion keeps the change inside one neighborhood. When a one-requirement change routinely edits seven modules (the 'shotgun surgery' smell), that is the system reporting, through its diff statistics, exactly where the architecture has failed.

examples.title: Inverting a payment dependency — and measuring the win in blast radius
examples.problem: An order service directly constructs and calls a concrete `StripeGateway` class from the vendor SDK: it imports the SDK's types, converts Money to the vendor's unit (integer pence) inline, and parses vendor error codes in six places. Tests run against Stripe's sandbox (slow, flaky, occasionally billed). A second gateway must be added next quarter. Diagnose and repair.

steps.label: Step 1: Diagnose the coupling
steps.text: The order service is **content-coupled to vendor semantics**: it knows pence, vendor error enums, and the SDK's type vocabulary. The dependency arrow is Policy → VendorDetail, exactly what dependency inversion exists to reverse. Cohesion is also leaking — currency conversion and error translation are payment-domain concerns living inside order-placement code.

steps.label: Step 2: Design the abstraction in the consumer's language
steps.text: The order service defines what it needs — `interface PaymentGateway { charge(payment: PaymentRequest): PaymentResult; refund(paymentId: PaymentId): RefundResult; }` — with `PaymentRequest` in domain types (Money, not pence; domain reason codes, not vendor enums). Note the ownership: this interface lives in the order domain's module, and says nothing about Stripe.

steps.label: Step 3: Push details behind an adapter
steps.text: `StripeGatewayAdapter implements PaymentGateway`: pence conversion, SDK invocation, error-code mapping — all of it in one file, unit-tested exhaustively (19.99 → 1999; vendor 'card_declined' → domain `PaymentRejected`). A `PayPalGatewayAdapter` next quarter is a parallel file. The order service never imports either vendor again.

steps.label: Step 4: Reap the testability dividend
steps.text: A `FakeGateway` implements the interface in twenty lines: programmable results, recorded calls, no network. Order-service tests become fast and deterministic — 'when payment is rejected, the order transitions to OnHold and the customer sees the saved cart' is now a millisecond unit test, not a sandbox integration roulette.

steps.label: Step 5: Measure the blast radius, before and after
steps.text: Before: swap-vendor change = edits throughout the order service (six error-parsing sites, conversions, imports). After: swap-vendor = compose a different adapter at the composition root; order service diff: zero files. Adding the fake for tests: zero production files. The likely changes — new gateway, new test scenario — now land in one module each. That diff statistic *is* the proof the design works.

examples.result: The inversion moved vendor knowledge from six scattered sites into one adapter behind a consumer-owned interface. Coupling dropped from content-level to data-level (a narrow, domain-typed call), the order service regained cohesion (it now contains only order logic), and both expected future changes — new gateway, new tests — became single-file edits. Blast radius is the scoreboard.

keyTakeaways: Runtime architecture is components (computation and state) joined by connectors (call, request, message, shared store) — connector choice is a design decision of the first rank.
Coupling forms, most-to-least damaging: content, common, control, stamp, data — triage the first two architecturally, polish the rest opportunistically.
Cohesion is whether a module has one nameable purpose; a purpose statement requiring 'and' predicts multiple reasons to change.
Contracts go beyond syntax: semantics, quality-of-service and error behavior are what connectors actually agree on.
Dependency inversion: both policy and detail depend on an abstraction shaped by — and owned by — the policy side; adapters then make details swappable and fakeable.
The master metric is change impact: good designs keep expected changes local, measurable as files-touched and ripple-extent per real change.

quiz.q: Module A passes its entire 40-field `CustomerRecord` to Module B, which uses only 3 fields (email, tier, region). Later, a new field `consentFlags` is added to the record, and Module B must be recompiled and re-reviewed even though it never reads the new field. What coupling form is this, and what is the minimal fix?
options: Content coupling — Module B should reach into the record through accessors
Stamp coupling — pass only the 3 needed values (or a small parameter object), so B depends on exactly what it uses and nothing else
Data coupling — this is already the healthy baseline; no action needed
Common coupling — move the record to a global store
quiz.explanation: Passing a whole structure while using a fragment is stamp coupling: B's world grows whenever the record grows, coupling it to the evolution of 37 fields it does not care about. The fix is narrowing the interface to the needed data — which reduces it to data coupling. (a) misdiagnoses (no internals are being violated), (c) mislabels the problem as health, and (d) would make things dramatically worse.

quiz.q: A module named `Utils` contains: date formatting, a CSV parser, retry-with-backoff logic, and a helper that resizes images. Which cohesion level is this, and what is the practical consequence?
options: Functional cohesion — everything is a utility function
Sequential cohesion — output of the parser feeds the formatter

Coincidental cohesion — the parts are related by nothing but the file they share; consequence: every team with any need touches this one module, it accretes dependencies on everything, and any change risks breaking unrelated callers
Communicational cohesion — all functions communicate through parameters
quiz.explanation: A grab-bag module has no organizing principle: its elements are together coincidentally. The consequence is structural: Utils depends on (and is depended on by) nearly everyone, becomes a merge-conflict magnet, and its blast radius makes refactoring terrifying — which is why utils modules only ever grow. The cure is distributing each part to a module defined by its real purpose (parsing, retry policy, formatting).

quiz.q: Applying the dependency inversion principle to a report generator that currently imports a specific PDF vendor SDK: which arrangement is the correct inversion, and why does interface ownership matter?
options: Keep importing the SDK but wrap every call in a try-catch — errors no longer propagate, so the dependency is managed
Create a `PdfExporter` interface in the vendor's package and have the report generator depend on it, since the vendor knows PDF best

Define the exporter interface in the report generator's own module — shaped around what reporting needs (render(document) → bytes) — and implement it with a vendor adapter that plugs in; the interface serves the policy, so the vendor's SDK churn stops touching report code
Invert the call direction: have the vendor SDK call the report generator
quiz.explanation: DIP is the arrow reversal Policy→Detail becoming Policy→Abstraction←Detail, and the ownership clause is decisive: an abstraction owned by the consumer contains only what the consumer needs and is stable when the vendor churns. Option (b) fails exactly there — a vendor-owned interface drags vendor vocabulary into policy code regardless of wrapping. (a) confuses error handling with decoupling; (d) misreads inversion as call-direction.

quiz.q: In a runtime component-and-connector description of a web system, which of these is a *connector* rather than a component?
options: The PostgreSQL database holding user profiles
The message queue carrying order events from the storefront to the fulfillment service
quiz.explanation: Connectors are the interaction mechanisms — the queue, the HTTP call, the JDBC session — while components are the principals doing computation and holding state: services, databases, engines. Classifying the queue as a connector is what makes its architectural weight visible: swapping it, or its delivery semantics, changes interaction properties across the system rather than any one component's internals.

quiz.q: Over ten features, a team's diffs show that adding any new product feature edits seven modules: catalog, pricing, cart, checkout, notification, reporting, and an integration layer. Which smell is this, and what does it indicate about the architecture?
options: Shotgun surgery — low cohesion along feature lines: the modules are organized around technical layers rather than feature responsibilities, so every change ripples across all of them; high coupling measured empirically
The God class anti-pattern — one module must be doing everything
Healthy layering — features are supposed to touch every layer
Data coupling — parameters are being passed too narrowly
quiz.explanation: One conceptual change, seven scattered edits is shotgun surgery — the empirical signature that the module boundaries do not align with change axes. The diffs are the evidence that coupling is high and cohesion is misaligned, regardless of what the architecture diagram claims. (b) would show the opposite pattern: one file growing enormous. (c) confuses touching layers with touching every module in every layer.

quiz.q: Two components agree perfectly at the type level: the caller sends `getUser(id: UserId): UserProfile`. Yet in production the caller treats an absent user as a returned null, while the callee signals absence by throwing a typed exception. Which contract layer failed, and what is the lesson?
options: Syntactic — the signatures should have used a different language

Semantic and error-behavior — the interface matched but the meaning of 'user not found' was never agreed; type agreement is the weakest layer of a contract, and semantic mismatches compile cleanly and fail at runtime
Quality-of-service — latency must have differed between the components
No failure — exceptions and null checks are interchangeable
quiz.explanation: The contract's semantic and error-behavior clauses — what absence *means* and how it is *signaled* — were never specified, and the type system had nothing to say about them. This is the canonical demonstration that syntax is the floor of a contract, not its substance: two components can agree on types while agreeing on nothing else that matters at 3 a.m.

prerequisites: Quality attributes and measurable non-functional requirements
Architectural views: components and connectors
intro: You cannot weigh an architecture on a scale — but you can interrogate it with scenarios, and that interrogation has a disciplined form. Scenario-based evaluation converts abstract qualities ('scalable', 'secure') into concrete stimulus–environment–response triples, then walks the architecture through them, exposing the points where one quality is bought with another's coin. The method's real output is not a score; it is the list of risks and trade-off points you would otherwise meet for the first time in production.
objectives: Express quality attributes as scenarios in stimulus–environment–response form, with a measurable response measure
Build a utility tree that organizes and prioritizes scenarios by (importance, difficulty)
Walk through the steps of an architecture trade-off analysis method (ATAM-style evaluation)
Identify sensitivity points and trade-off points in an architecture under scenario analysis
Classify findings as risks or non-risks and explain why the documented rationale is the primary deliverable

concepts.statement: A quality attribute becomes evaluable when written as a **scenario** with six parts: **source** (who/what initiates), **stimulus** (the event arriving), **artifact** (which part of the system is stimulated), **environment** (the conditions: normal, peak, degraded), **response** (what the system does), and **response measure** (the number that makes pass/fail decidable). Example: 'During the peak season sale (environment), a surge of 50,000 concurrent checkouts (stimulus, source: customers) hits the order service (artifact); the service shall shed non-critical load and complete 99% of checkouts within 3 seconds (response, measure).'
concepts.detail: The response measure is what separates an evaluation scenario from a wish. 'Handles load gracefully' cannot be walked through an architecture; '99% within 3 seconds while degrading recommendations first' can — the design either has a load-shedding policy and a degradation hierarchy, or it does not.

concepts.statement: A **utility tree** organizes and prioritizes scenarios before analysis: root = overall utility; second level = quality attributes (performance, availability, security, modifiability, usability); third level = attribute refinements (latency vs. throughput; integrity vs. confidentiality); leaves = concrete scenarios, each labeled **(importance, difficulty)** — typically H/M/L on both. Scenarios with high importance and high difficulty form the **focus set** the evaluation actually analyzes; the tree is pruned, or the evaluation drowns.
concepts.detail: The tree is the political heart of the exercise: stakeholders argue about importance *before* architecture is on the table, so the prioritization reflects business value rather than the presenter's agenda. It also bounds scope honestly — the final report must state which scenarios were analyzed and which were deferred, making the evaluation's coverage explicit rather than implied.

concepts.statement: The architecture trade-off analysis method, in its essential sequence: (1) **present the method** — process, roles, outputs; (2) **present business drivers** — goals, constraints, dominant qualities; (3) **present the architecture** — views, components, connectors, decisions; (4) **elaborate and prioritize scenarios** — typically by building the utility tree; (5) **analyze the architecture** against the focus scenarios — identify architectural decisions, classify each as a **sensitivity point**, **trade-off point**, **risk**, or **non-risk**; (6) **brainstorm additional scenarios** to stress the design from angles the tree missed; (7) **present the results** — risks, non-risks, sensitivity and trade-off points, and the themes that connect them.
concepts.detail: Step 5 is the engine, and it is a group reasoning exercise, not a formula: for each focus scenario, walk the architecture — which component receives the stimulus, what connectors carry it, what decisions govern the response — and record every place where a decision significantly helps or hurts the measured response. The artifacts that matter are the decision list and its classification, because those are what the method's outputs (risks, trade-offs) are made of.

concepts.statement: A **sensitivity point** is a property of the architecture to which a quality-attribute response is significantly sensitive: a decision such that changing it moves the measured response materially (database connection-pool size materially moves peak throughput; the synchronous fraud check in the checkout path materially moves p99 latency). A **trade-off point** is a sensitivity point for *multiple attributes in opposite directions*: the decision helps one quality and hurts another (caching authorization decisions helps latency, hurts security freshness; synchronous validation helps integrity, hurts availability).
concepts.detail: Trade-off points are the crown jewels of an evaluation: they are the exact coordinates where the architecture spends one stakeholder's quality to buy another's, and they mark the decisions that management — not architects alone — should ratify, because they are business decisions wearing technical clothing.

concepts.statement: A **risk** is an architectural decision that threatens a quality objective under some scenario ('the single shared database is a risk to the availability scenario requiring checkout to survive analytics failures'). A **non-risk** is a decision that, after analysis, is explicitly deemed safe — recorded with its reasoning and the assumptions it rests on ('the read-only catalogue replica suffices for the browsing-load scenario, *assuming* replica lag stays under 30 seconds'). Non-risks matter because their assumptions, written down, can later be checked — and silently rotted assumptions are how yesterday's safe decisions become tomorrow's outages.
concepts.detail: Both are logged as one-line numbered findings during analysis, with the scenario and decision referenced. The numbered log is the evaluation's ledger: every claim the evaluation makes traces to a decision-scenario pair, which is what distinguishes evaluation from opinion.

concepts.statement: The ATAM's most durable output is not the risk list — it is the **conversation**: stakeholders forced to articulate what they value, architects forced to articulate why the design is what it is, both groups discovering mismatches while the design is still a set of drawings. Teams that emerge from an evaluation knowing their own trade-off points make better decisions daily thereafter; the report is the residue, the shared model is the product.
concepts.detail: This explains the method's heavyweight-versus-lightweight spectrum: a full multi-day ATAM with many stakeholders suits systems whose failure is catastrophic; a half-day scenario walkthrough by four people captures much of the value for a mid-size service. The scenarios-and-walkthrough core scales down gracefully — the parts you must never drop are measurable scenarios and decision-classified findings.

examples.title: A mini-evaluation of an e-commerce checkout
examples.problem: Evaluate a checkout architecture: a web SPA → a monolithic Order service (containing cart, pricing, and payment orchestration) → a PostgreSQL database, plus a synchronous third-party fraud-scoring API called in the payment path, and an in-memory session cache for authorization data. Focus scenarios from the utility tree: P1 (H, H) 'peak sale: 20,000 concurrent checkouts, 99% complete within 3 s p99'; A1 (H, H) 'fraud API outage: checkout remains available in degraded mode'; S1 (H, M) 'permission change takes effect for a user within 60 s'; M1 (M, H) 'add a new payment provider without touching cart or pricing code'. Walk the analysis.

steps.label: Step 1: Walk P1 (peak-load latency)
steps.text: Trace the stimulus through the architecture: SPA → Order service → synchronous fraud API → database. Findings: the **synchronous fraud call in the request path** is a sensitivity point for P1 — p99 checkout latency is capped by the fraud API's p99 (you have coupled your latency to a network you do not control). The **single PostgreSQL instance** is a sensitivity point for P1 and A1: every scenario's throughput ceiling is its connection pool and write capacity. Classify: both logged as risks — R-1 (fraud-call latency coupling) and R-2 (single-database contention under peak).

steps.label: Step 2: Walk A1 (fraud-API outage)
steps.text: Question: what happens today when the fraud API is down? Answer in the design: the call fails, the exception propagates, checkout fails. R-1 doubles: the coupling is an availability risk too — a third party's outage is our outage. The walk also surfaces the missing decision: no degraded mode exists (no policy like 'queue orders under 200 for manual review'). Logged as R-3: no load-shedding/degradation hierarchy exists for third-party failure.

steps.label: Step 3: Walk S1 (permission freshness)
steps.text: Authorization data lives in an **in-memory cache**. Trace: admin changes a role → database updated → caches still stale until expiry. Finding: the **cache TTL** is a sensitivity point for S1 — freshness improves as TTL shrinks; but the same TTL is a sensitivity point for P1 in the *opposite* direction (shorter TTL → more database reads → worse peak latency). This is a textbook **trade-off point**: T-1, cache TTL trades security freshness against performance. Trade-off points are management decisions: which stakeholder wins, and by how much, gets ratified, not assumed.

steps.label: Step 4: Walk M1 (add payment provider)
steps.text: The monolith contains cart, pricing, and payment orchestration in one deployable. Adding a provider is a code change inside the same unit — no independent deployment concern at this scale (non-risk), but the analysis asks: does payment code share tables with cart code? The architect confirms a clean module boundary with a `PaymentGateway` seam. Logged as **NR-1 (non-risk)** with its assumption stated: 'modifiability of payment is safe *assuming* the module boundary rule survives future hires — enforce with an architecture test.' The assumption is now checkable.

steps.label: Step 5: Report themes
steps.text: Themes connect the findings: (1) *third-party coupling* — R-1, R-3: one architectural cause (synchronous unmanaged dependency), two scenarios hurt; candidate mitigations: timeout + circuit breaker + degraded-mode policy. (2) *The shared database* — R-2: candidate mitigations: read/write split, analytics offload. (3) *The TTL trade-off* — T-1: needs a product decision (proposed: 60 s TTL matches S1 exactly; measure the P1 cost in load test). The evaluation ends with a prioritized, evidence-linked agenda — and four people now share one model of why this system is shaped as it is.

examples.result: One half-day walkthrough produced three risks, one trade-off point and one assumption-bearing non-risk — each traceable to a decision-scenario pair. The trade-off point (cache TTL) was escalated to its rightful owners as a business decision; the theme analysis collapsed five findings into three architectural causes. No score was assigned, and none was needed: the agenda is the deliverable.

keyTakeaways: Quality attributes become evaluable only as scenarios: source, stimulus, artifact, environment, response, response measure — the measure makes pass/fail decidable.
The utility tree prioritizes scenarios by (importance, difficulty) before architecture enters the room; the high-high pairs form the focus set.
ATAM-style analysis walks each focus scenario through the architecture, classifying every significant decision as sensitivity point, trade-off point, risk, or non-risk.
Sensitivity points move one quality materially; trade-off points move two in opposite directions — those are business decisions in technical clothing, and belong to management.
Record non-risks with their assumptions so they can be checked later; rotted assumptions are how safe decisions become outages.

The evaluation's durable product is the shared understanding — stakeholders who know their system's trade-off points — and the method scales down gracefully to a half-day walkthrough with four people.

quiz.q: Which of these is a properly formed quality-attribute scenario suitable for architecture evaluation?
options: The system should be highly scalable to support future growth
Security must be a first-class concern in the design

During the annual sale (environment), 30,000 concurrent users submit orders (stimulus) against the order service (artifact); it shall accept and confirm 99.5% of them within 2 seconds at p99 (response with measure), by degrading recommendation lookups first
The architecture will use microservices because they scale well
quiz.explanation: Only option (c) contains the six load-bearing parts, including the decisive ones: the environment (annual sale), the numeric response measure (99.5% within 2 s at p99), and a degradation policy that can be traced through the design. (a) and (b) are aspirations — nothing in the architecture can be walked against them; (d) is a solution assertion, which scenarios exist precisely to avoid.

quiz.q: In an evaluation, the team discovers that decreasing the session-cache TTL improves security freshness but increases database load and worsens peak latency. How should this finding be classified and handled?
options: A risk — the cache should simply be removed
A non-risk — caches always involve this tension, so nothing need be recorded

A trade-off point — one architectural decision (the TTL) is a sensitivity point for two qualities in opposite directions; it should be escalated for a deliberate, documented business decision, not left as an implementation detail
A sensitivity point for security only; the latency effect is a separate, unrelated finding
quiz.explanation: One decision, two qualities, opposite directions: that is the definition of a trade-off point — and the reason it belongs to management rather than to whichever developer configures the cache. Escalation means the choice is made consciously with both stakeholders present and recorded with rationale. (a) prescribes a fix before the trade-off is even decided; (b) discards the finding and its checkable assumptions; (d) artificially splits one decision into two findings, hiding the trade it embodies.

quiz.q: In an ATAM-style evaluation, immediately after the architecture is presented and the utility tree built and prioritized, what is the next step?
options: Assign the architecture a final quality score

Analyze the architecture against the high-priority focus scenarios — walking each scenario through components and connectors, and classifying the significant decisions as sensitivity points, trade-off points, risks and non-risks
Rewrite the architecture to fix the risks found so far
Brainstorm an entirely new set of stakeholders to redo the prioritization
quiz.explanation: The method's engine follows prioritization: scenario-by-scenario analysis that produces classified findings. (a) is the classic category error the method exists to prevent — architectures are not scored, they are interrogated; (c) confuses evaluation with redesign (mitigation happens after, informed by the findings); (d) re-litigates the input to avoid the analysis. Scenario brainstorming does appear in the method — but as a later step that *stresses* the design from angles the tree missed, not as a redo.

quiz.q: During analysis, the team records: 'NR-4: the read-only catalogue replica is sufficient for browsing-load scenarios, assuming replica lag remains under 5 seconds.' Why record a non-risk at all, and why phrase the assumption explicitly?
options: Non-risks pad the report so the findings list looks balanced

Because a non-risk documents that a decision was analyzed and deemed safe *under stated assumptions* — making the assumptions explicit converts them into checkable claims; when traffic grows and lag creeps to 40 seconds, the evaluation record shows exactly which assumption rotted and what to revisit
Because auditors require an equal number of risks and non-risks
To protect the architect from blame if the decision later fails
quiz.explanation: A non-risk is a claim with a shelf life: safe *now*, under conditions *x*. Recording the conditions makes the rot detectable — monitoring can watch replica lag against the stated 5-second bound, and when the assumption fails, the response is targeted rather than forensic. Without the record, the failure arrives as a mystery; with it, as a known broken contract. The other options describe bureaucracy or blame management, which the method does not trade in.

quiz.q: A five-person team is deciding whether to run a full multi-day ATAM with 20 stakeholders on their new internal reporting tool. What is the soundest counsel?
options: Yes — every architecture deserves full-method evaluation regardless of context
No — evaluation should only happen after the system has run in production for six months

Scale the method to the stakes: a half-day scenario walkthrough (utility tree with a handful of scenarios, walk the focus set, log risks/trade-offs/non-risks) by the team plus one outside voice captures most of the value; reserve the full multi-stakeholder ATAM for systems whose failure is costly enough to justify it
Skip evaluation entirely — small teams know their architecture and informal knowledge suffices
quiz.explanation: The method's core — measurable scenarios, a walked architecture, classified findings — scales down gracefully and is where nearly all the value lives; the heavyweight ceremony (many stakeholders, multiple days, dedicated facilitation) is justified by consequence-of-failure, not by principle. (a) applies a one-size process; (b) inverts the timing — the whole point is evaluating while change is cheap; (d) abandons the cheap insurance a walkthrough provides.

quiz.q: An evaluation of an order system finds: R-1 'the synchronous inventory call in the payment path is a risk to the checkout-availability scenario'; R-2 'the same synchronous call is a risk to peak-latency'; R-5 'no circuit breaker exists on the inventory dependency'. What analytic move does the findings-to-themes step perform on these?
options: It averages the risk severities into a single score for the synchronous call
It deletes R-5 as a duplicate of R-1

It recognizes a common architectural cause — an unmanaged synchronous third-party dependency — so one mitigation (timeout + circuit breaker + degraded mode) addresses multiple findings, converting a scattered list into a prioritized agenda
It reassigns each risk to the team that wrote the relevant code
quiz.explanation: Theme analysis is the synthesis step: findings that share an architectural cause are grouped, revealing that several scenario failures trace to one decision — which makes mitigation leveraged rather than piecemeal. That is how a half-day evaluation produces an agenda of three causes instead of a backlog of fifteen symptoms. (a) manufactures a false precision the method rejects; (b) discards a distinct, decision-level finding; (d) converts analysis into blame routing.

prerequisites: Coupling, cohesion and change impact
The idea of automated regression tests as a safety net
intro: Technical debt is the most useful metaphor in software engineering and the most misused: it explains why the quick-and-dirty path costs more later, but only if you remember that interest accrues only where change passes through. This section makes the metaphor precise, catalogs the refactorings that pay debt down, and works through the strangler-fig strategy — the pattern for replacing legacy systems without betting the company on a rewrite.
objectives: Define technical debt precisely, with principal (rework cost) and interest (recurring drag) separated
Classify debt with the quadrant: deliberate vs inadvertent, prudent vs reckless — and respond differently to each class
Prioritize debt paydown by interest rate (change hotspots), not by size or aesthetics
Execute named refactorings from the catalog (extract method, move method, replace conditional with polymorphism) under test protection
Plan a strangler-fig migration: seams, routing, incremental cutover, parallel run, retirement

concepts.statement: **Technical debt** is the implied future cost of choosing a quicker solution now instead of a better one that would take longer. Its **principal** is the cost of the eventual rework — rewriting the hack into the clean design. Its **interest** is the recurring drag: every change that passes through the messy area costs extra time, extra bugs, extra fear. The metaphor's discipline: debt is not 'bad code' — it is *borrowed speed that accrues cost only where future change flows through the borrowed region*.
