Abbe: error = offset × tan(tilt). Micrometers comply; calipers do not — hence their accuracy gap.
A 30 mm offset with 0.1° of tilt already produces 52 µm of error — geometry beats graduation as the accuracy limiter.

quiz.q: A measuring instrument holds its scale 25 mm to the side of the displacement axis. If the guidance tilts by 0.2° during measurement, the resulting Abbe error is about:
quiz.explanation: $e = 25 \times \tan 0.2° = 25 \times 0.00349 = 0.0873$ mm ≈ 87 µm. Missing the mm-to-µm conversion by a factor of ten gives the 8.7 µm distractor.

quiz.q: Which of these instruments best satisfies the Abbe principle?
quiz.explanation: In a micrometer the dimension, the spindle axis and the thimble scale are all collinear — Abbe's requirement. Calipers, rules and offset-scribe height gauges all measure displaced from their scale axis.

quiz.q: A gauge block is classified as which type of standard?
quiz.explanation: Its defining quantity is the distance between the two end faces — the archetypal end standard, wringable and accurate to a tenth of a micron. Line standards live between engraved graduations.

quiz.q: The metre is currently defined as:
options: the length of a platinum-iridium bar in Sevres
the distance light travels in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second
one ten-millionth of the distance from pole to equator
quiz.explanation: Since 1983 the metre is fixed by defining the speed of light. The krypton definition ruled 1960-1983; the artefact bar and the Earth-quadrant definition are the older, less reproducible ancestors.

quiz.q: The essential function of a comparator is to:
options: measure absolute lengths from a built-in scale
compare a dimension against a reference standard with high amplification
quiz.explanation: Comparators have no absolute scale of their own — they are difference amplifiers zeroed on a reference (typically slip gauges), which is exactly why their accuracy can exceed their size and cost.

intro: The vernier caliper and the micrometer are the workhorses of dimensional measurement — and their least counts are pure arithmetic, not marketing. Add the sine bar for angles (it is just trigonometry with roller centres), the autocollimator for straightness over metres, and angle gauges that build to seconds of arc, and linear-and-angular measurement is fully equipped.
objectives: Derive and compute least counts of vernier calipers and micrometers from their scale construction
Read a full vernier or micrometer measurement including zero error
Set up and compute sine-bar angles from slip-gauge stacks, and know its accuracy envelope
Explain the autocollimator principle and its role in straightness, flatness and small-angle measurement

concepts.statement: **LC = 1 main-scale division − 1 vernier-scale division.** The classic metric caliper: 50 vernier divisions span 49 main divisions → 1 VSD = 0.98 MSD → **LC = 0.02 mm** (with 1 mm MSDs). Reading = main-scale reading to the left of the vernier zero + (coinciding vernier division) × LC.
concepts.detail: A vernier works because graduations drift out of step: at the k-th vernier line the cumulative mismatch is k × LC, and the coincidence of lines marks exactly k × LC beyond the last main graduation. Zero error (vernier zero right/left of main zero) must be added or subtracted algebraically.

concepts.statement: **LC = pitch ÷ number of thimble divisions.** Standard metric: pitch 0.5 mm, 50 divisions on the thimble → **LC = 0.01 mm**. Reading = sleeve (whole + half mm, the half-mm line appears below the datum) + thimble × 0.01. Faster screw pitch (2 mm, 100 divisions) keeps the same 0.01; digital micrometers resolve 0.001 mm.
concepts.detail: Fringes of technique that actually matter: use the ratchet/friction stop (standard measuring force ~5-10 N), check zero with the anvils closed, wipe faces. The 0.5 mm pitch two-start? — no, one start; the sleeve simply carries two datum rows, one for whole and one for half millimetres.

concepts.statement: Two equal rollers, centre distance L (100 or 200 mm standard), one propped on a slip-gauge stack: $\sin\theta = h/L$. Example: L = 100 mm, stack 50 mm → $\theta = 30°$. Best below **45°** — since $dh = L\cos\theta\,d\theta$, near 90° a tiny height error explodes into a large angle error.
concepts.detail: The sine bar measures an angle against a length standard — that is its beauty and its limitation. For steep angles, complement it (measure 90° − θ) or use an angle gauge/autocollimator stack instead.

concepts.statement: A collimated light beam reflects off a flat mirror mounted on the object; a tilt $\theta$ of the mirror deflects the reflected beam by **2θ**, displacing the image on a graduated eyepiece/photodetector. Sensitivities reach a **tenth of an arc-second**, and the instrument reads tilt, which is why sweeping a mirror along a straightedge or surface plate yields **straightness and flatness profiles** (integrating tilt into height).
concepts.detail: Straightedge calibration: step the mirror/pedestal along by equal spans, record tilt each step, integrate differences to height deviations; close the loop or least-squares the line. The same instrument with a polygon mirror calibrates rotary tables and dividing heads to arc-second level.

concepts.statement: Angle-gauge blocks (degrees, minutes, seconds series) stack **additively or subtractively** — a 13-piece set can build any angle in steps of 3 seconds of arc. The **clinometer** (spirit level on a rotatable vernier circle) reads inclination of surfaces directly to a minute or so; **spirit levels** resolve ~10 arc-seconds per division for machine setting.
concepts.detail: Angle gauges carry a wedge symbol showing direction; stacking with alternating directions subtracts — e.g., 30° + 1° laid against 3° builds 28°, and seconds blocks trim the remainder. They are to angles what slip gauges are to lengths.

examples.title: A full vernier reading
examples.problem: On a metric vernier caliper (LC = 0.02 mm), the main scale reads 37 mm to the left of the vernier zero, and the 18th vernier division coincides. With jaws closed, the vernier zero sits 0.04 mm (two divisions) to the right of the main zero. What is the true dimension?

steps.label: Zero error
steps.text: Vernier zero right of main zero with closed jaws = **positive zero error** of +0.04 mm.

steps.label: Correction
steps.text: True = raw − zero error = 37.36 − 0.04 = 37.32 mm.

steps.label: Watch the sign convention
steps.text: Right-of-zero with closed jaws means the instrument over-reads, hence subtract; if the vernier zero had sat left, the error would be negative and the correction additive.

examples.result: 37.32 mm — the zero check is the 10-second habit that separates a measurement from a guess.

examples.title: Setting 30 degrees on a sine bar
examples.problem: A 100 mm sine bar must be set to 30°. Compute the stack, build it, and assess the angle sensitivity to a ±1 µm stack error.

steps.label: Trigonometry
steps.text: $h = L\sin\theta = 100\sin 30° = 50.000$ mm.

steps.label: Stack
steps.text: From a standard set: 40 + 9.5 + 0.5 = 50.000 mm (three blocks), wrung and placed under the far roller.

steps.label: Sensitivity
steps.text: $dh = L\cos\theta\,d\theta$: at 30°, 1 µm of height error gives $d\theta = 0.001/(100 \times 0.866) = 1.15 \times 10^{-5}$ rad ≈ **2.4 arc-seconds**.

steps.label: Envelope
steps.text: Sub-arc-second accuracy is therefore possible at modest angles with calibrated blocks — and increasingly expensive as θ → 90° (cos θ → 0 inflates everything).

examples.result: Stack 50.000 mm exactly; ±1 µm on the stack costs about ±2.4 arc-seconds at 30°.

keyTakeaways: LC(vernier) = 1 MSD − 1 VSD (49:50 construction → 0.02 mm); LC(micrometer) = pitch/thimble divisions (0.5/50 → 0.01 mm).
Read = main + coincidence × LC, then algebraically correct the zero error measured with closed anvils/jaws.
Sine bar: $\sin\theta = h/L$ — a length-based angle standard, accurate below 45° and exponentially sensitive beyond.
Autocollimator: mirror tilt θ deflects the beam 2θ; integrating equal-step tilts yields straightness/flatness to sub-arc-second.
Angle gauges stack additively and subtractively to 3-second resolution — slip gauges for angles.

quiz.q: A vernier caliper has 1 mm main-scale divisions, and 50 vernier divisions coincide with 49 main-scale divisions. Its least count is:
quiz.explanation: 1 VSD = 49/50 = 0.98 mm, so LC = 1 − 0.98 = 0.02 mm. The 0.01 mm answer belongs to the micrometer, and 0.05 to the older 20-division vernier construction.

quiz.q: A micrometer screw has a pitch of 0.5 mm and its thimble carries 50 divisions. Its least count is:
quiz.explanation: One thimble division advances the spindle 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm. Digital versions with an extra decade give 0.001 mm, but the classical mechanical instrument stops at 0.01.

quiz.q: A 100 mm sine bar uses a slip-gauge stack of exactly 50 mm under one roller. The angle set is:
quiz.explanation: $\sin\theta = h/L = 50/100 = 0.5 \Rightarrow \theta = 30°$. A stack of 70.7 mm would give 45° — the other memorable pair.

quiz.q: In the worked vernier example, the raw reading was 37.36 mm and the closed-jaw zero error was +0.04 mm. The corrected dimension is:
quiz.explanation: A positive zero error means the caliper over-reads, so subtract: 37.36 − 0.04 = 37.32 mm. Adding instead (37.40) is the classic sign flip.

quiz.q: An autocollimator is best described as an instrument that:
options: collimates light to measure long distances directly
measures small angular tilts of a mirror via the 2θ deflection of a reflected beam
compares angles against a sine bar
quiz.explanation: Its bread and butter is tiny angles: a mirror tilt of θ swings the returned beam by 2θ, which the graduated reticle or detector converts to arc-seconds — and stepping that mirror along a bed integrates tilts into a straightness profile.

intro: Interchangeable manufacture relies on holding every mating feature inside a stated tolerance zone and verifying that zone economically on the shop floor. This section connects the limit-and-fit system to the gauges that police it, the surface-texture parameters that describe finish, and the way tolerances stack through an assembly.
objectives: Explain hole-basis and shaft-basis fit systems and select a fit for a given function
Compute extreme clearances and worst-case tolerance stacks for multi-part assemblies
Apply Taylor's principle when specifying GO and NO-GO gauge forms
Compute Ra and Rz from measured profile data and choose the parameter that matches the surface function

concepts.statement: **Hole-basis**: the hole tolerance zone sits at basic size with fundamental deviation H (lower limit on basic size), and the shaft zone is varied to obtain the fit.
concepts.detail: It is the default because holes are produced with fixed-size tooling - drills, reamers and punches - while shafts can be turned or ground to any zone. One H7 hole can be paired with shaft deviations a, g, k, n or p to give clearance, transition or interference fits from the same tooling.

concepts.statement: **Shaft-basis**: the shaft zone stays at basic size (fundamental deviation h, upper limit on basic size) and the hole zone is varied to select the fit.
concepts.detail: Choose it when one finished shaft - ground bar stock or a spindle - carries several components needing different fits, since re-machining the common shaft for each fit is impractical while boring each hole to its own zone is routine.

concepts.statement: For nominal sizes up to 500 mm the tolerance unit is $i = 0.45·D^(1/3) + 0.001·D$ µm (D in mm), and each IT grade is a fixed multiple of i: IT5 = 7i, IT6 = 10i, IT7 = 16i, IT8 = 25i.
concepts.detail: Each step up the IT scale widens the zone by about 60%, so IT7 is roughly 1.6 times IT6. Mating features are usually toleranced in the IT5 to IT11 band; IT12 and coarser are left to non-critical features and raw material.

concepts.statement: A **GO** gauge must check every dimension and feature of the workpiece simultaneously and in full form, while a **NO-GO** gauge must check only one dimension or feature at a time.
concepts.detail: The GO gauge is a replica of the mating part: a full-length plug detects taper and ovality that point contacts would miss. A full-form NO-GO plug could be blocked by the small axis of an oval hole and never reveal that its other axis is beyond the minimum-metal limit, so NO-GO elements are shortened or segmented to touch one surface at a time.

concepts.statement: $R_a$ is the arithmetic mean of the absolute profile deviations from the mean line over a sampling length; $R_z$ is the largest peak-to-valley height within the evaluation length.
concepts.detail: Ra averages and is therefore stable between instruments, which is why it dominates drawings; Rz responds to deep scratches and isolated peaks that govern fatigue and sealing. Typical bands: turning 0.8-6.3 µm Ra, grinding 0.1-0.8 µm Ra, lapping and polishing below 0.1 µm Ra.

concepts.statement: A new GO gauge is made slightly beyond the maximum-material limit with a wear allowance of about 5-10% of the work tolerance, and it is retired once wear carries it back past that limit.
concepts.detail: A GO plug for a hole is made marginally larger than the hole minimum; rubbing wear steadily reduces its size toward and then past the limit, at which point it would begin to accept undersized holes and must be withdrawn.

examples.title: Fit analysis - 25 mm H7/g6 running fit
examples.problem: A 25 mm journal runs in a bushed housing bored to 25H7 (+0.021/0 mm) with the journal ground to 25g6 (-0.007/-0.020 mm). Determine the minimum and maximum clearance and classify the fit.

steps.label: Hole limits
steps.text: 25.000 to 25.021 mm - the H deviation pins the lower limit to basic size, the signature of the hole-basis system.

steps.label: Shaft limits
steps.text: 24.980 to 24.993 mm, from the -0.020 lower and -0.007 upper deviations.

steps.label: Maximum clearance
steps.text: Largest hole minus smallest shaft: 25.021 - 24.980 = 0.041 mm.

steps.label: Minimum clearance
steps.text: Smallest hole minus largest shaft: 25.000 - 24.993 = 0.007 mm.

examples.result: Clearance always lies between 0.007 mm and 0.041 mm - a close-running clearance fit on the hole basis.

examples.title: Worst-case and statistical tolerance stack
examples.problem: A housing recess is 60.20 ±0.05 mm deep and receives three blocks of 20.00 ±0.02, 15.00 ±0.03 and 25.00 ±0.04 mm. Find the guaranteed gap by worst-case stacking and the statistical estimate if the four tolerances are independent.

steps.label: Worst-case spread
steps.text: ±(0.05 + 0.02 + 0.03 + 0.04) = ±0.14 mm if every part sits at a limit simultaneously.

steps.label: Worst-case gap
steps.text: 0.20 ± 0.14 mm, so the gap lies between 0.06 mm and 0.34 mm and never closes.

steps.label: Statistical spread
steps.text: Root-sum-square of independent tolerances: √(0.05² + 0.02² + 0.03² + 0.04²) = √0.0054 ≈ ±0.073 mm, giving 0.13 to 0.27 mm at high confidence.

examples.result: Guaranteed gap 0.06 to 0.34 mm by worst case; statistical estimate 0.13 to 0.27 mm.

keyTakeaways: Use the hole-basis system unless one shaft must carry parts with different fits - then hold the shaft at h and vary the holes.
Taylor's principle: GO gauges are full-form and simultaneous; NO-GO gauges touch one feature at a time.
Worst-case stacking guarantees assembly but tightens every part; RSS stacking relaxes tolerances at the cost of a small statistical risk.
Ra averages the profile and is the default drawing parameter; Rz exposes the peaks and valleys that govern fatigue and sealing.

quiz.q: A 40H7 hole (+0.025/0 mm) is mated with a 40g6 shaft (-0.009/-0.025 mm). What is the maximum clearance?
quiz.explanation: Maximum clearance = upper hole limit - lower shaft limit = 0.025 - (-0.025) = 0.050 mm; the minimum clearance is 0 - (-0.009) = 0.009 mm.

quiz.q: According to Taylor's principle, how must a NO-GO gauge be designed?
options: As a full-form replica of the mating part, like the GO gauge
So that it contacts only one dimension or feature of the work at a time
Longer than the GO gauge so it can detect taper
With looser tolerances than the GO gauge since it rejects fewer parts
quiz.explanation: A full-form NO-GO plug could be blocked by the small axis of an oval hole and never reveal that the other axis exceeds the limit; contacting one surface at a time prevents such missed rejections.

quiz.q: Profile deviations from the mean line at five sampled points are +1.4, -1.6, +2.4, -2.6 and +0.4 µm. What are Ra and Rz for this sampling length?
options: Ra = 0 µm because the deviations average out, and Rz = 2.4 µm
quiz.explanation: Ra uses absolute values: (1.4 + 1.6 + 2.4 + 2.6 + 0.4)/5 = 1.68 µm. Rz is the peak-to-valley height: 2.4 - (-2.6) = 5.0 µm.

quiz.q: Blocks of 30 ±0.03, 20 ±0.02 and 10 ±0.05 mm stack in a recess 60.20 ±0.06 mm deep. What is the minimum gap by worst-case analysis?
quiz.explanation: Nominal gap = 60.20 - 60.00 = 0.20 mm; worst-case deviation = ±(0.06 + 0.03 + 0.02 + 0.05) = ±0.16 mm, so the minimum gap = 0.20 - 0.16 = 0.04 mm.

quiz.q: One ground shaft made from drawn bar stock carries two bushes requiring different fit classes. Which fit system applies, and why?
options: Hole-basis, since drills and reamers come in fixed sizes
Shaft-basis, since the common shaft is kept at basic size and each hole takes its own zone
Either system, because the fit class does not depend on the system
Neither, since bushings are always selectively assembled
quiz.explanation: With several fits on one shaft it is cheaper to hold the shaft at basic size (deviation h) and bore each bushing to its own fundamental deviation - the shaft-basis system.

intro: Threads, gears and machine tools carry functional surfaces that no plain micrometer can read directly. This section works the wire methods that convert a thread's effective diameter into a single over-wires reading, the gear measurements that isolate tooth thickness and runout, and the laser interferometer that maps machine tool geometry to sub-micrometre accuracy.
objectives: Determine thread effective diameter from best-wire measurements and judge the result against nominal
Select between chordal-thickness, span and composite checks for gear teeth
Explain laser interferometric calibration of linear, angular and straightness errors of machine tools

concepts.statement: For a symmetric thread of pitch P and half-flank angle α, the best wire touches both flanks exactly on the pitch line when $w = P/(2·cos α)$ - 0.5774P for a 60° metric thread.
concepts.detail: At best-wire contact the over-wires reading is insensitive to small flank-angle errors, because the shift of the contact points compensates geometrically. Oversize or undersize wires sit off the pitch line and require correction terms in the evaluation.

concepts.statement: For a 60° thread the micrometer reading over three wires is $M = E + 3w - 0.866P$, so the effective diameter is $E = M - 3w + 0.866P$.
concepts.detail: Two wires rest in the lower grooves and one in the upper groove, held by a wire holder; the constant 0.866 arises from (P/2)·cot 30°. The two-wire variant places wires in opposed grooves on a floating-carriage machine, which cancels measurement-pressure effects and reaches the highest accuracy for master gauges.

concepts.statement: The gear tooth vernier measures tooth thickness along the pitch-circle chord; for a standard gear the nominal thickness is $t = π·m/2$.
concepts.detail: The vertical slide is set to the chordal addendum so the jaws straddle one tooth exactly at the pitch circle. Because the setting references the tooth tip, tip wear or profile error corrupts the reading, which limits the accuracy of the method.

concepts.statement: A span micrometer (flange micrometer) across k teeth reads $W_k = m·cos α·[(k - 0.5)·π + z·inv α]$, a length fixed by the base circle.
concepts.detail: For z = 20, m = 2 and α = 20° with k = 3: W = 1.8794 × (2.5π + 20 × 0.0149) ≈ 15.321 mm. A deviation ΔW corresponds to a tooth-thickness change ΔW/cos α, and since the anvils bear on the involute flanks the tooth tip never enters the datum.

concepts.statement: A ball seated in successive tooth spaces against a fixed stop measures radial runout, while rolling the gear against a master gear records the total composite error in one trace.
concepts.detail: The double-flank rolling test sums eccentricity, pitch and profile errors into a single radial-displacement record - ideal for production screening. Span or individual-pitch measurements are then applied to diagnose which element actually failed.

concepts.statement: A frequency-stabilised He-Ne laser (λ ≈ 632.8 nm) counts interference fringes - one per λ/2 of travel - to measure axis displacement with uncertainty near 0.1 ppm.
concepts.detail: Linear optics calibrate positioning accuracy and repeatability; angular optics read pitch and yaw; straightness optics map guideway deviation; squareness follows from two straightness runs at right angles. Air temperature, pressure and humidity enter through the refractive-index correction, and all results are referred to 20 °C.

concepts.statement: Running circular interpolation with a telescoping ballbar between spindle and table records radial deviation, exposing backlash, squareness and servo mismatch in one polar plot.
concepts.detail: Steps at the quadrant reversals indicate lost motion; an egg-shaped plot elongated along a diagonal indicates squareness error; ellipticity along the machine axes points at scale mismatch; lobing near 45° points at servo gain mismatch between axes.

examples.title: Effective diameter of an M10 × 1.5 thread by best wires
examples.problem: An external M10 × 1.5 thread is measured over three best-size wires with a thread micrometer reading M = 10.290 mm. Find the best wire size and the effective diameter, and compare it with the nominal d2 = 9.026 mm.

steps.label: Comparison
steps.text: The thread is 9.026 - 8.991 = 0.035 mm, or 35 µm, below nominal pitch diameter.

examples.result: E ≈ 8.991 mm - about 35 µm under nominal.

examples.title: Fringe counting on a 300 mm axis
examples.problem: A laser interferometer with λ = 632.8 nm checks a 300 mm traverse. How many fringes pass the detector, and what length does one fringe represent?

steps.label: Fringe value
steps.text: The optical path changes by twice the table motion, so one fringe = λ/2 = 316.4 nm = 0.3164 µm.

steps.label: Scale context
steps.text: If the wavelength compensation holds to 1 ppm, the accumulated scale uncertainty over 300 mm is only 0.3 µm.

examples.result: About 948 167 fringes, each worth 0.3164 µm of travel.

keyTakeaways: Best-size wires (0.5774P on 60° threads) seat on the pitch line, making the over-wires result immune to small flank-angle errors.
E = M - 3w + 0.866P converts any three-wire reading of a metric thread into effective diameter.
Span measurement beats the tooth vernier whenever the tooth tip cannot be trusted, because its datum is the base circle.
Laser interferometry delivers sub-micrometre machine-tool calibration only when air-index and thermal corrections are applied.

quiz.q: An M8 × 1.25 thread is checked with best-size wires (w = 0.7217 mm) and the micrometer reads M = 8.271 mm. What is the effective diameter?
quiz.explanation: E = M - 3w + 0.866P = 8.271 - 2.165 + 1.083 = 7.188 mm, which equals the nominal pitch diameter d2 = 8 - 0.6495 × 1.25 ≈ 7.188 mm, so the thread is on nominal size.

quiz.q: Why are best-size wires specified for thread measurement?
options: They maximise the micrometer reading for sensitivity
They contact the flanks exactly on the pitch line so flank angle errors do not affect the result
They are the largest wires that fit inside the thread groove
They cancel out pitch errors of the thread
quiz.explanation: At w = P/(2·cos α) each wire touches both flanks at the pitch-line crossing, so small deviations of flank angle shift the contact points in a way that cancels out of the effective-diameter evaluation.

quiz.q: Which gear measurement is referenced to the base circle and therefore insensitive to errors of the tooth tip?
options: Chordal thickness with a gear tooth vernier
Base tangent (span) measurement across k teeth
Optical projection of the whole tooth profile
quiz.explanation: The span micrometer contacts the involute flanks, and Wk is measured between parallel tangent planes related to the base circle, so the tooth tip never serves as a datum.

quiz.q: A laser interferometer (λ = 632.8 nm) counts 3161 fringes during an axis move. Approximately how far did the table travel?
quiz.explanation: L = N·λ/2 = 3161 × 0.3164 µm ≈ 1000 µm = 1.000 mm, since each fringe corresponds to half a wavelength of travel.

quiz.q: A ballbar test shows sharp steps in the polar plot exactly at the axis reversal points. What does this indicate?
quiz.explanation: Offsets where motion reverses direction are the signature of lost motion (backlash); squareness shows as an egg-shaped plot and servo mismatch as lobing near 45°.

intro: Statistical quality control replaces exhaustive checking with decision rules built on data: control charts separate common-cause noise from assignable causes, acceptance sampling quantifies the risk attached to every lot decision, and capability indices say whether the process can hold the tolerance at all. This section computes each of these from realistic numbers.
objectives: Construct and interpret p-chart control limits from pooled inspection data
Read an OC curve and quantify producer's and consumer's risks for a sampling plan
Compute Cp and Cpk from process data and choose between re-centring and variation reduction

concepts.statement: Control charts place 3-sigma limits about a centre line computed from the process itself; a stable process plots inside them 99.73% of the time, so a point outside flags an assignable cause.
concepts.detail: For variables, the X-bar and R chart pair tracks mean and spread together. Supplementary run rules - nine points on one side of the centre line, or two of three beyond 2 sigma - catch sustained shifts that single-point limits miss.

concepts.statement: For subgroup size n and pooled fraction defective p, $UCL = p + 3√(p(1-p)/n)$ and $LCL = p - 3√(p(1-p)/n)$; a negative LCL is set to zero.
concepts.detail: The fraction p must be the long-run pooled estimate over all subgroups, never a single day's value. When subgroup sizes differ, limits are computed per subgroup and the chart takes a stair-stepped form; when n is constant and defectives are counted directly, the np chart is simpler.

concepts.statement: The operating characteristic curve of a sampling plan (n, c) plots the acceptance probability $P_a$ against the incoming fraction defective p.
concepts.detail: The producer's risk α is the chance of rejecting a lot at the AQL; the consumer's risk β is the chance of accepting a lot at the LTPD. Increasing n at fixed c steepens the curve between those points, while increasing c shifts the whole curve toward more acceptance.

concepts.statement: $C_p = (USL - LSL)/(6σ)$ measures spread alone, while $C_{pk} = min(USL - μ, μ - LSL)/(3σ)$ penalises an off-centre mean.
concepts.detail: A Cp of 1.33 is the usual minimum for a capable process. A wide gap between the two indices is a centring problem, so re-target the mean before attacking variation. Estimate σ from within-subgroup statistics such as R-bar/d2 so that between-subgroup drift is not folded into capability.

concepts.statement: Six-sigma performance allows a 1.5σ long-term mean shift, which caps the defect rate near 3.4 per million opportunities.
concepts.detail: With no shift at all, a 6σ spread against the tolerance corresponds to about two defects per billion; the 1.5σ allowance is an empirical provision for drift that accumulates between control actions.

concepts.statement: A double sampling plan decides on a smaller first sample and draws a second sample only when the first falls in an indecisive band, cutting average sample size for the same OC protection.
concepts.detail: Good lots usually clear on the first sample, so inspection effort concentrates on lots of doubtful quality. The price is administrative complexity and a plan that is harder to explain and administer on the floor.

examples.title: p-chart limits from 25 days of data
examples.problem: Twenty-five daily samples of n = 200 switches yield 500 defectives in total. Build the fraction-defective chart and judge a day that reports 38 defectives.

steps.label: The suspect day
steps.text: 38/200 = 0.19 exceeds UCL = 0.164, so that day is out of control and needs an assignable-cause investigation.

examples.result: Centre line p = 0.10, UCL = 0.164, LCL = 0.036; a day at 19% defective is out of control.

examples.title: Capability of a grinding operation
examples.problem: Ground pins average μ = 10.020 mm with within-subgroup σ = 0.010 mm against a specification of 10.000 ± 0.050 mm. Compute Cp and Cpk and prescribe the fix.

steps.label: Centring check
steps.text: USL - μ = 0.030 mm while μ - LSL = 0.070 mm, so the mean leans toward the upper limit.

steps.label: Action
steps.text: Re-centre to 10.000 mm; with the same spread both indices become 1.67 and no reduction of σ is required.

examples.result: Cp = 1.67, Cpk = 1.00 - the process is off-centre, not too variable.

keyTakeaways: Chart limits come from pooled process data, never from the specification; only capability uses the tolerance.
Set a negative p-chart LCL to zero, and recompute limits for each subgroup when n varies.
The OC curve is the complete signature of a sampling plan; larger n at the same c lowers the consumer's risk.
Cp versus Cpk separates the two remedies of quality work: reduce variation versus re-centre the mean.

quiz.q: Forty samples of n = 100 parts contain 160 defectives in total. What are the 3-sigma p-chart limits?
options: UCL = 0.099 and LCL = 0, since the computed LCL is negative
UCL = 0.099 and LCL = -0.019, plotted directly on the chart

quiz.q: A process reports Cp = 1.8 and Cpk = 0.9. What is the correct diagnosis and remedy?
options: Variation is excessive; invest in variation reduction
Spread is adequate but the mean is off-centre; re-centre the process
Both spread and centring are unacceptable
Impossible, since Cpk cannot be smaller than Cp
quiz.explanation: Cp proves the 6σ spread fits the tolerance with room to spare; the gap to Cpk is pure displacement of the mean, so re-centring is the cheap and correct fix.

quiz.q: For the single sampling plan n = 50, c = 1, the probability of zero defectives at p = 0.05 is 0.077 and of exactly one defective is 0.202. What is the lot acceptance probability?
quiz.explanation: Pa = P(0) + P(1) = 0.077 + 0.202 = 0.279; the plan accepts only about 28% of lots that run 5% defective.

quiz.q: Holding the acceptance number c fixed while increasing the sample size n does what to the OC curve?
options: Flattens it and raises the consumer's risk
Steepens it near the indifference point and lowers β at the LTPD
Shifts the whole curve to the right toward more acceptance
quiz.explanation: More samples at the same c make acceptance fall off faster as quality worsens: the curve steepens, the consumer's risk at the LTPD drops, and inspection cost rises.

quiz.q: Which σ should be used when computing capability indices for a process run with X-bar and R charts?
options: The overall standard deviation of all parts ever measured
The within-subgroup estimate, such as R-bar divided by d2
The standard deviation of the subgroup means
quiz.explanation: Capability is a potential measure: σ from within-subgroup variation (R-bar/d2 or s-bar/c4) excludes assignable between-subgroup drift, which belongs to control rather than inherent capability.

intro: A measurement is a decision, and every decision carries uncertainty. This section matches instruments to tolerance grades, assembles an error budget from its components, and follows the calibration chain that connects a shop-floor micrometer to the definition of the metre.
objectives: Select measuring instruments for a tolerance grade using the rule of ten and the Abbe principle
Combine uncertainty components into a budget and evaluate a test uncertainty ratio
Describe the traceability chain from working gauges to national standards

concepts.statement: The measuring process should be at least ten times - and never less than four times - more precise than the tolerance it is asked to verify.
concepts.detail: A ±0.05 mm free tolerance suits a caliper (±0.02 mm); a ±0.02 mm fit tolerance calls for a micrometer (±0.004 mm); ±0.005 mm demands a bench comparator with gauge blocks; below that, interferometry or a length measuring machine takes over. The 4:1 floor is usually written as a minimum test uncertainty ratio.

concepts.statement: Maximum length-measuring accuracy requires the scale axis to be collinear with the measured dimension; an offset l and a tilt θ create a first-order sine error $l·sin θ$.
concepts.detail: The micrometer satisfies Abbe because spindle, anvil and work share one line; the vernier caliper violates it because its slide sits offset from the jaw faces, so guidance errors amplify with beam length. Comparators restore Abbe by nulling the part against a collinear gauge-block stack.

concepts.statement: Independent uncertainty components combine by root-sum-square, $u_c = √(u_1² + u_2² + ...)$, and the expanded uncertainty reported at roughly 95% confidence is $U = 2·u_c$.
concepts.detail: Typical entries: the calibration certificate of the instrument (Type B), repeatability from repeated readings (Type A), resolution or quantisation half-width, thermal effects, and probing-force variation. Improving the largest term moves the whole budget; improving a small one changes nothing.

concepts.statement: A length responds to temperature as $ΔL = L·α·ΔT$; with steel at α ≈ 11.5 ppm/K, a 100 mm gauge warmed by 6 K grows 6.9 µm.
concepts.detail: Dimensional results are referred to 20 °C, so either measure at that temperature or correct both part and gauge. Differential expansion - part, gauge and scale at different temperatures or with different α - is what actually corrupts a comparison; hand heat, lamps and warm spindles are the usual culprits.

concepts.statement: Traceability is an unbroken, documented chain of calibrations, each with stated uncertainty, linking a workshop measurement to the SI unit through national metrology institutes.
concepts.detail: A micrometer is calibrated against working gauge blocks; those are calibrated against reference blocks by an accredited laboratory; the reference blocks are interferometrically compared at the national institute; and the metre itself is realised from an iodine-stabilised laser. Uncertainty accumulates at every transfer, which is why reference-grade blocks carry smaller uncertainties than shop blocks.

concepts.statement: Reference standards are reserved for calibrating other standards, while working standards are used day-to-day on the shop floor and are checked against the references at fixed intervals.
concepts.detail: The interval is chosen so that expected wear or drift between calibrations stays comfortably inside the stated uncertainty of the working standard. Gauge blocks embody the split: grades K and 0 serve as references, while grades 1 and 2 serve as working standards.

examples.title: Error budget and TUR for a ±6 µm tolerance
examples.problem: A 25-50 mm micrometer checks a feature toleranced ±6 µm (span 12 µm). The budget lists calibration 1.0 µm, thermal 0.8 µm, repeatability 0.6 µm and resolution 0.5 µm. Compute the combined and expanded uncertainties and the test uncertainty ratio.

steps.label: Expand
steps.text: U = 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 µm at approximately 95% confidence.

steps.label: TUR
steps.text: TUR = tolerance span/U = 12/3.0 = 4:1 - the customary minimum.

steps.label: Verdict
steps.text: The 4:1 ratio passes minimum practice but misses the rule of ten; a bench comparator with grade 0 blocks would shrink the dominant calibration term.

examples.result: u_c = 1.5 µm, U = 3.0 µm (k = 2), TUR = 4:1 - acceptable at the floor.

examples.title: Thermal correction to 20 °C
examples.problem: A 100 mm steel gauge block is compared on a bench at 26 °C, with gauge and part both at α = 11.5 ppm/K. What correction refers the result to 20 °C?

steps.label: Expansion
steps.text: ΔL = L·α·ΔT = 100 mm × 11.5 ppm/K × 6 K = 6.9 µm (1.15 µm per kelvin).

steps.label: Sign
steps.text: The block is longer than its 20 °C length, so subtract 6.9 µm from the comparison result.

steps.label: Differential note
steps.text: Had gauge and part shared the same α and the same temperature, the growth would cancel in the comparison; the residual error is the differential expansion, zero only when both match.

examples.result: Subtract 6.9 µm: a 100.0069 mm reading at 26 °C is 100.0000 mm at 20 °C.

keyTakeaways: Pick the instrument by tolerance: the rule of ten is the target and a 4:1 test uncertainty ratio is the floor.
Abbe alignment separates instruments that can verify tight tolerances from those that only indicate size.
Error budgets combine by root-sum-square and are quoted expanded with k = 2; attack the largest component first.
A result is traceable only through an unbroken, documented calibration chain to the SI, with uncertainty growing at each transfer.

quiz.q: A feature is toleranced ±0.02 mm. Under the rule of ten, what instrument precision is the target and what is the practical choice?
quiz.explanation: One tenth of the tolerance is ±0.002 mm; a micrometer with 0.001 mm resolution and a few µm of uncertainty meets it, while a caliper with ±0.02 mm of uncertainty barely matches the tolerance itself.

quiz.q: An error budget lists independent components of 1.0, 0.8 and 0.6 µm. What is the combined standard uncertainty?
quiz.explanation: u_c = √(1.0² + 0.8² + 0.6²) = √2.00 = 1.41 µm; budgets add in quadrature, so the result is smaller than the arithmetic sum of 2.4 µm.

quiz.q: A 100 mm steel part with α = 11.5 ppm/K is measured at 25 °C. What is its thermal error relative to the 20 °C reference?
quiz.explanation: ΔL = L·α·ΔT = 100 mm × 11.5 ppm/K × 5 K = 5.75 µm - larger than many of the tolerances it might be checked against.

quiz.q: Which statement defines a traceable measurement?
options: It was checked against any gauge available in the shop
It is linked to the SI unit by an unbroken chain of calibrations, each with stated uncertainty
It was taken by a qualified inspector using a labelled instrument
It matches the nominal dimension on the drawing
quiz.explanation: Traceability demands documented comparisons through working and reference standards up to the national institute, with each transfer carrying its own uncertainty.

quiz.q: Why does a vernier caliper violate the Abbe principle while an outside micrometer does not?
options: Its scale is shorter than the jaw span
Its measuring jaws are offset from the scale axis, so jaw tilt produces a sine error
It reads with a vernier rather than a digital scale
Its jaws are hardened less than micrometer anvils
quiz.explanation: The micrometer measures along the spindle axis, collinear with the work; the caliper jaw faces sit at an offset l from the beam, so a tilt θ adds l·sinθ to every reading.

intro:
A science experiment is an argument arranged as apparatus. The question becomes a hypothesis — a specific, testable prediction — and the apparatus is designed so that the world itself can say no: one factor is varied, everything else is held fixed or distributed evenly, and a comparison group absorbs every influence except the one under test. This lesson builds that argument from its vocabulary out: the three kinds of variable, the control group and the placebo it receives, the blinding that keeps expectation out of the data, and the statistical backbone — randomisation, replication and blocking — that lets a difference in means count as evidence rather than luck. It closes with the ladder every result climbs: hypothesis, theory, law, and the falsifiability that makes the whole structure scientific.

**Why this matters.** Science sections test design literacy more than content: given an experiment, identify the variable that was manipulated, the group that was cheated of treatment, the flaw that lets a confounder in. The vocabulary is small, the questions are predictable, and the same words — control, blind, replicate — carry through biology, chemistry, physics and statistics alike.
objectives: Explain hypothesis: testable prediction from a question
Explain hypothesis versus theory versus law
Explain independent, dependent and controlled variables
Explain control groups and the placebo effect
Explain blinding: single, double and why it matters
Explain randomisation, replication and blocking
Explain reliability, validity and sources of error
Explain falsifiability as the line around science

concepts.statement: A specific, testable prediction stating an expected relationship between variables — "plants receiving fertiliser X grow taller in four weeks than unfertilised plants." Testable means an observation could in principle prove it wrong; "plants grow best" is too vague to fail, which is exactly its defect.

A hypothesis is a single testable prediction. A theory is a broad explanatory framework supported by many independent lines of evidence — it explains why patterns occur. A law describes a pattern, usually mathematically, without explaining its mechanism. Theories do not "graduate" into laws; they do different jobs. Everyday "just a theory" inverts the scientific usage.

The factor the experimenter deliberately varies — the dose, the temperature, the light level. Plotted on the horizontal axis. An experiment with two independently varied factors is factorial; most introductory questions keep one.

The measured outcome expected to respond to the independent variable — height, reaction time, yield. Everything that could affect it but is not being studied must be controlled or randomised, or it becomes a confounder.

The comparison group that receives no active treatment — or an inert placebo where expectation itself could act. It anchors the counterfactual: without it, improvement cannot be attributed to the treatment, because untreated groups improve too, sometimes dramatically (regression to the mean).

Single-blind: participants do not know their assignment, killing expectation effects. Double-blind: the experimenters interacting with participants do not know either, killing measurement and treatment bias. The placebo effect is genuine physiology — expectation changes outcomes — which is why the inert comparison is not cruelty but calibration.

Random assignment distributes every known and unknown nuisance factor evenly between groups. Replication — enough experimental units — lets chance differences average out and gives errors a measurable size. Blocking groups similar units (same soil plot, same litter) so comparisons happen within blocks, removing a known nuisance factor from the noise. A matched-pairs design blocks by pairing each subject with itself: before-and-after, or two treatments in random order.

concepts.term: Hypothesis: testable prediction from a question
concepts.statement: Reliability and validity name the two ways a measurement can disappoint. Reliability is repeatability: the same procedure on the same subject gives the same reading — unreliability shows up as scatter and is fought with replication and better instruments. Validity is truthfulness: the measurement measures the concept it claims to — a questionnaire on "screen time" that forgets phones under-measures, and a study whose only subjects are volunteers of one age has narrow external validity, whatever its internal logic. A result can be perfectly reliable and invalid — a precise reading of the wrong thing — which is why exam questions asking "what is the flaw here?" are usually pointing at a validity hole, not noise.

The theory ladder deserves its honest restatement, because it is the most misused vocabulary in science. Hypotheses are tested; a hypothesis that survives many independent, risky tests becomes part of a theory — an integrated explanation with scope far beyond any single experiment, like germ theory or evolution. Laws summarise what happens under stated conditions — ideal gas behaviour at low pressure — without supplying mechanism. A theory explaining why gas laws hold (molecular motion) is not on a path to become a law; explanation and description are different products. And the boundary of the whole enterprise is falsifiability: a claim arranged so no observation could refute it has left the territory where experiments can adjudicate.

The exam staples: confusing the independent variable (varied) with the dependent one (measured); calling any second group a "control" when it also differs in conditions — the control must differ ONLY in the treatment; reading "failed to reject" as "proved the hypothesis"; and treating correlation between two measured variables as an experiment at all — with no assignment and no manipulation, design vocabulary does not apply. And never say a theory is "just" a hypothesis: the ladder misreading is itself a tested item.

examples.title: Auditing a plant-growth experiment
examples.problem: Experimental Design: Hypotheses, Controls and the Theory Ladder — worked through step by step

steps.label: Claim
steps.text: fertiliser X increases tomato yield. Design so far: 20 plants in a sunny window get X; 20 plants in a dim corridor get nothing; all watered daily.

steps.label: Independent variable
steps.text: fertiliser X. Dependent variable: yield. Confounder spotted immediately: light differs between groups — the design cannot attribute any difference to X.

steps.label: Repair 1 — control group
steps.text: 20 plants in the SAME sunny window, no fertiliser. Now the comparison isolates X.

steps.label: Repair 2 — randomisation
steps.text: assign the 40 window positions to treated/untreated plants by coin flip, so position-in-window, pot history and plant vigour distribute evenly.

steps.label: Repair 3 — replication and blocking
steps.text: several trays (blocks) each containing treated and untreated plants, so a tray-level quirk (draft, heater) becomes a between-block difference, not a treatment effect. More plants per group narrows the error bars.

steps.label: Repair 4 — blinding where possible
steps.text: whoever measures height records readings for pots labelled only with codes. Measurement stays blind even though gardeners know the assignment.

steps.label: Falsifiability check
steps.text: the hypothesis names a direction and a timeframe — if treated plants show no excess yield after four weeks, it is disconfirmed. A hypothesis that accommodates any result was never scientific.

keyTakeaways: Next: the social-sciences evidence lesson — how causal inference works when experiments are impossible.
Then: Nonverbal Reasoning — the same controlled-comparison instinct applied to figures.
Reference reading: OpenStax Introductory Statistics, Ch. 1 (Sampling and Data — experimental design and ethics).
A hypothesis is specific and falsifiable; theories explain, laws describe.
One independent variable, one measured outcome, everything else controlled or randomised.
The control group anchors the counterfactual; placebos calibrate expectation.
Blinding removes bias; randomisation, replication and blocking remove noise and known nuisances.
Reliable is not valid: precise measurement of the wrong thing is the classic flaw.

quiz.q: In a drug trial, Group A receives the drug, Group B an identical-looking tablet with no drug. Group B is:
quiz.explanation: The inert tablet makes B the placebo control — the anchor for what would happen without treatment, including expectation effects. The dependent variable is the measured outcome, not a group.

quiz.q: A study finds students given a new app score higher — but the app group knew they were receiving the "innovation". The missing safeguard is:
quiz.explanation: Knowledge of assignment is an expectation effect; blinding participants — or giving the comparison group a plausible inert alternative — is the designed remedy. More subjects do not remove expectation bias.

quiz.q: Which statement about theories and laws is correct?
options: A theory becomes a law once enough evidence accumulates
A law explains mechanisms; a theory merely describes
A theory is a broad explanation; a law describes a pattern without explaining it
Laws are hypotheses that survived testing
quiz.explanation: The two do different jobs and do not convert into each other. Option 3 is the inverted, incorrect folk version; the rest swap the definitions.

quiz.q: Field plots differ in soil quality across a slope. The design that removes this nuisance factor is:
options: block by soil zone — compare treatments only within each zone
quiz.explanation: Blocking groups similar units so treatment comparisons occur within a soil zone; the zone effect cancels. Replication alone leaves the confounder in place, and blinding addresses bias, not field heterogeneity.

intro:
Situational judgement tests put you inside a workplace dilemma — a colleague cutting a corner, a distressed client, a task outside your competence — and score the quality of your response. The scenarios change per profession; the tested structure does not. Three values recur: integrity (honesty and probity even when silence is easier), perspective taking (reading the stakes of every party, especially the most vulnerable), and teamwork (clear communication inside the role hierarchy). Across every marking scheme, one pattern sorts good answers from brilliant ones: do what you can at your own level, then escalate through the proper channel — and never let a patient, client or public interest be quietly sacrificed to colleague comfort or your own convenience.

**Why this matters.** These items are scored against consensus judgements of experienced professionals, which makes them learnable: the professional consensus follows visible principles, not hidden taste. The same principles govern real workplaces — whether to report a mistake, how to correct a senior colleague, when to say no — so the practice transfers to reference requests, interviews and the first year of any job.
objectives: Explain integrity and probity: honesty under pressure
Explain escalation: when and to whom to raise concerns
Explain perspective taking: stakes for each party
Explain patient-centred and client-centred reasoning
Explain teamwork: roles, handover, communication
Explain confidentiality and disclosure boundaries
Explain rating scales: appropriateness versus effectiveness
Explain the accountability-first framework

concepts.statement: Truthfulness as a default: record events accurately, admit your own errors promptly, never falsify or sign for what you did not verify, and refuse instructions to mislead — even small ones, even from seniors. The marker’s intuition: a small dishonesty tolerated is a large one rehearsed.

The canonical best response to a problem beyond your authority: address what is safe at your level, then raise it with the appropriate senior or responsible body, and follow through. Skipping levels, going straight to anonymous public complaint while private channels remain, or doing nothing are all marked down — the ladder has a middle and the middle is where the best answers live.

Before rating any action, inventory the stakeholders and their stakes: the person affected, their family, colleagues, the institution, the public. The best responses protect the most vulnerable stake first; the worst dismiss someone’s distress as overreaction or trade a client’s interest for team harmony.

In care-flavoured scenarios, the service user’s welfare and autonomy outrank staff convenience. Explain rather than do unto, check understanding, respect refusals from a competent adult, and never let embarrassment or busyness decide what the person is told.

Good answers communicate early, through the right channel, in the right tone: ask before assuming, delegate to competence rather than convenience, hand over fully (what, status, next step), and correct colleagues privately where possible — publicly only when the risk is immediate.

Information gained in a professional role is not gossip. Share it within the team on a need-to-know basis, with consent where possible, and break it only for defined reasons — imminent serious harm, legal duty, or safety of others — and then through the proper channel, not the group chat.

Many schemes rate actions on two axes: appropriateness (is it the right thing — ethics, policy) and effectiveness (does it achieve the aim). Asking a distracted senior for an urgent decision may be effective but inappropriate; documenting a concern and waiting may be appropriate but ineffective at that moment. Top-rated actions usually pair both: act at your level AND escalate, honestly AND kindly.

concepts.term: Integrity and probity: honesty under pressure
concepts.statement: The fastest marking heuristic, confirmed across schemes: look for the option that combines honesty with action. Doing nothing, "staying out of it", and handling it alone beyond your competence are near-universal bottom ratings. Confrontation without proportion, and whistleblowing that skips every internal channel, are near-universal partial marks. Full marks typically belong to responses that protect the affected person now, record the facts accurately, and route the problem to the person whose job it is — in that order.

concepts.term: Escalation: when and to whom to raise concerns
concepts.statement: Perspective-taking items reward the same inventory stated as a habit. Before judging any action in a scenario, name the parties and the stakes: the user or client (safety, dignity, information), you (competence, honesty, workload), colleagues (fairness, morale), institution (rules, reputation, risk). Watch for the built-in asymmetry markers: scenarios are written so the cheapest convenient option is usually the one that sacrifices the least powerful party — the tired colleague’s shortcut lands on the patient; the skipped explanation lands on the family. When an option’s cost is borne by someone absent from the conversation, treat that as a flag, and let the response that informs and involves them rise.

Five reliable traps: choosing loyalty to colleagues over the affected person — consensus always ranks the vulnerable party first; confusing "not my job" with professional boundaries (boundaries say whom to route to, not whether to care); skipping the private-first conversation; treating confidentiality as absolute when defined safety exceptions exist — and its mirror, breaking it casually; and answering as yourself under exam-day anxiety rather than as the trained professional the scheme assumes. When torn between two options, the one that both protects the person AND keeps an accurate record is nearly always the better rating.

examples.title: One scenario, four responses, four ratings
examples.problem: Situational Judgement: Integrity, Perspective Taking and Teamwork — worked through step by step

steps.label: Scenario
steps.text: during a busy shift you notice a senior colleague documenting a safety check that you did not see performed. Nothing has gone wrong yet.

steps.label: Response A
steps.text: say nothing — the colleague is senior and nothing bad happened. Bottom rating: integrity failure; an unrecorded check is a live risk, and silence leaves no accurate record.

steps.label: Response B
steps.text: publicly accuse the colleague of falsifying records in front of the team. Partial: the concern is right, the channel is wrong — disproportionate, damages team function, no accurate account gathered first.

steps.label: Response C
steps.text: check the facts (was the check perhaps done before you arrived?), then speak to the colleague privately: "I could not see the check logged as done — can we make sure it is completed and recorded?" If it is resolved and recorded, no further step may be needed. Top rating: honest, proportionate, direct, preserves the team.

steps.label: Response D
steps.text: the colleague dismisses the question and the record remains uncompleted. Now escalate to the shift lead, stating facts only. Also top rating — C was correct at its level, and this is correct at the next level: the ladder continues.

steps.label: The pattern
steps.text: A fails on integrity, B fails on proportion and channel, C and D pair honesty with the right channel at the right level — the consensus-rated best actions.

keyTakeaways: Before: Applying Principles — the same rule-to-case logic in normative form.
Next: the stress and coping lesson — managing your own state is part of professional judgement.
Reference reading: the official situational-judgement test framework and good-medical-practice style guidance published by admissions and regulator bodies.
Integrity first: honest records, prompt disclosure, no small falsities.
Escalate through the ladder: act at your level, then route upward with facts.
Inventory stakeholders; protect the most vulnerable stake first.
Communicate early, privately where possible, completely when handing over.
Pair appropriateness with effectiveness — the top rating does both.

quiz.q: You realise you made a small error in a submitted report. Nobody has noticed. The best-rated action is:
options: wait — if no one notices, no harm done
correct it quietly in the next revision without mention
report the error promptly, state its impact, and propose the correction
mention it casually weeks later in conversation
quiz.explanation: Integrity plus action: prompt, honest disclosure with an impact statement and a fix. Silent correction (B) hides a process failure; waiting (A) leaves stakeholders acting on wrong information.

quiz.q: A distressed client asks a question you cannot answer and you are mid-shift alone at the desk. The most appropriate FIRST action:
options: guess an answer to be helpful
acknowledge the question, say you will find out, and contact the responsible colleague or source
tell them no one can help today
research it yourself after your shift
quiz.explanation: Honesty about limits plus immediate routing through the proper channel. Guessing violates integrity; deferral without acknowledgment abandons the client.

quiz.q: A colleague consistently misses handover information. Your team’s work is slipping. Best-rated sequence:
options: raise it privately with the colleague, agree a fix, and if it continues, involve the supervisor
report them to the supervisor immediately
compensate silently by doing their part yourself
mention it in the group chat so everyone knows
quiz.explanation: The ladder in order: lowest appropriate level first, proportionate and private; escalation only if the problem persists. Immediate reporting is disproportionate; silent compensation conceals a team risk; public shaming damages the team.

quiz.q: An action is rated "appropriate but ineffective" most likely because it:
options: is honest but does not actually resolve or route the problem
breaks a rule to solve the problem
protects the client at staff expense
quiz.explanation: Appropriateness tracks ethics and policy; effectiveness tracks outcome. Documenting-and-waiting is the classic honest-but-inert option — the fix is pairing it with action at your level or the next one.

intro:
Nonverbal reasoning strips language out of logic and leaves pure pattern: a row of figures obeying a hidden rule, one figure breaking it, or a matrix whose missing cell the rule determines. The method that beats these items is not an eye for patterns but a checklist: inventory the attributes each figure can vary — shape family, element count, rotation, shading, size, position — then track which attribute changes and how between consecutive frames. Every rule a test uses is some combination of those six attributes changing, staying, or trading off, so a systematic scan finds in seconds what intuition finds by luck. This lesson builds the inventory, the three item formats, and the two-feature tracking habit that separates fast solvers from flatterers.

**Why this matters.** Figural items are the purest measure of controlled comparison on any reasoning paper: no vocabulary, no prior knowledge, just rule-finding under time. The inventory method also generalises — it is the same disciplined attribute-scanning that powers debugging, diagram reading and data checking in every technical job.
objectives: Explain the attribute inventory: shape, count, rotation, shading, size, position
Explain series: what changes, what stays
Explain analogies: A is to B as C is to —
Explain odd-one-out and rule detection
Explain figure formation and decomposition
Explain tracking two features at once
Explain systematic elimination over intuition

concepts.statement: The six axes every figure can vary along: shape family (which forms appear), count (how many of each), rotation (orientation and its step), shading (filled, empty, hatched, colour), size (large, small, growing), position (arrangement, overlap, distance). Scan in this fixed order every time — a fixed order beats a smart glance because it cannot be skipped by panic.

Four or five frames evolve; find the next. The rule is a per-attribute schedule: count increases by one, rotation advances 45 degrees clockwise, shading alternates. Read each attribute across the row separately — series rules are almost always one or two attributes changing while the rest stay fixed.

A is to B as C is to —: the first pair demonstrates the transformation; apply the SAME transformation to C. The discipline is naming the transformation explicitly ("rotate 90 degrees, add a dot") before looking at options; options are built to contain each single-step half of the transformation, so partial matches abound.

One frame violates the rule the others share. Find the rule first from the majority — what four frames hold constant — then test the fifth against it. Scanning for the constant is faster than scanning for the difference: violations hide, constants advertise.

Which combination of pieces assembles into the target shape — mentally decompose the target (a notch here, a diagonal there) and match parts, watching for mirrored pieces that look right but fit wrong. Dissect the target’s outline first; the outline’s corners tell you which candidate edges must meet.

Most medium and hard items vary two attributes at once, often in opposite directions (count rises while size falls). Holding two schedules in mind is the trained skill: name both aloud ("plus one arrow, minus one square"), and check the answer satisfies BOTH, because every option satisfies one.

concepts.term: The attribute inventory: shape, count, rotation, shading, size, position
concepts.statement: Time discipline is part of the method. First pass on any item: one full inventory scan, then commit to the best-supported rule; if no rule emerges within the scan, eliminate options that fail the strongest single attribute (count is usually decisive) and choose among survivors. Marking a hard item and moving on is correct strategy — figural sets are dense and evenly weighted, so three easy items beat one stubborn matrix. The trained habit is trusting the inventory over the impression: an option that "looks right" but violates one named attribute is wrong, and an option that looks odd but satisfies every schedule is right.

Odd-one-out items reward the same inventory run against the majority. Four frames share a rule — interior cross present, rotation multiples of 60 degrees, two elements — and the fifth breaks exactly one attribute. Find the constant set first, and prefer the simplest rule that fits all four: with count, rotation and shading all available, the common rule is usually one attribute, and the violation is one attribute. When two frames both look odd, widen the rule: a rule covering four frames that brands two as violators is mis-stated — recheck rotation steps and cumulative counts before trusting either candidate.

The classic losses: fixing on the first attribute that changes and ignoring the second schedule — the standard hard-item trap; treating rotation as linear past a completed cycle; reading mirrored pieces as fitting in formation items; and impression-based elimination, where an option "looks right" while violating one named attribute. Against all of these the defence is the same: name the schedules out loud, check the answer against BOTH, and never let appearance overrule an attribute you have explicitly tracked.

examples.title: A two-feature series, decoded
examples.problem: Nonverbal Reasoning: Shape Attributes, Series and Rule Detection — worked through step by step

steps.label: Frames
steps.text: (1) one large filled triangle pointing up; (2) two medium filled triangles, the leading one pointing up; (3) three small filled triangles, the leading one pointing up; (4) four small empty triangles, leading one pointing up.

steps.label: Inventory scan — count
steps.text: 1, 2, 3, 4 → next has five. Size: large, medium, small, small → suspects: size stopped mattering; not the rule. Shading: filled, filled, filled, empty → suspect a switch at the end.

steps.label: Re-scan shading against count
steps.text: the number of EMPTY triangles is 0, 0, 1, 2 → next has three empty (and two filled, since five total). The size anomaly was a distractor; the real second feature is cumulative emptying.

steps.label: Rotation
steps.text: leading triangle points up in every frame → constant, ignore.

steps.label: Answer requirement
steps.text: five small triangles, three empty and two filled, leading triangle up. Options that show five filled triangles fail the empty-count schedule; options with four fail the count schedule.

steps.label: The habit generalises
steps.text: when one schedule seems to break, re-scan the odd attribute as a CUMULATIVE quantity rather than a per-frame state — that single reinterpretation unlocks most "impossible" series.

keyTakeaways: Before: Experimental Design — the same controlled-comparison instinct in scientific form.
Next: mathematics sequences and series — the numeric twin of figural series.
Revision cue: invent a five-frame series varying two attributes, then solve it a day later from cold.
Inventory six attributes in a fixed order: shape, count, rotation, shading, size, position.
Series rules are per-attribute schedules; re-scan breaking attributes as cumulative counts.
Analogies require naming the full transformation and applying every component.
Odd-one-out: find the majority rule first, then the single violating attribute.
Hard items hide in the second feature — track two schedules and check both.

quiz.q: A series shows a square rotating 90 degrees clockwise each frame. The fifth frame’s orientation is:
options: same as the first — the cycle resets after four
rotated 450 degrees — continue past the cycle
quiz.explanation: Rotation is modular: 90-degree steps over four frames return to the start, so frame five matches frame one. Options built on linear rotation past 360 ignore the cycle.

quiz.q: In an analogy item, A to B adds one circle and doubles the shading stripes. C has two circles. The correct D must:
options: have three circles AND doubled stripes
match whichever option looks most like B
quiz.explanation: The transformation has two components; the analogy applies BOTH to C: two circles become three, and the stripe count doubles. Options honouring one component are the standard distractors.

quiz.q: Five frames share: even element count, top-right rotation, no shading. A candidate odd-one-out differs in shading but fits count and rotation. You should:
options: confirm it as the odd one — any single violation suffices
recheck: a rule violation must also be consistent with the others being regular
reject it — shading is not in the inventory
quiz.explanation: Odd-one-out needs exactly one attribute violating the majority rule; the shading frame fits every other attribute, so it is the violator. Option 2’s worry applies when TWO frames look odd.

quiz.q: The core reason for scanning attributes in a fixed order is:
options: fixed order is faster for easy items only
it prevents attribute-blindness under time pressure — every axis gets checked
it avoids the need to track two features
quiz.explanation: Panic narrows attention to one salient attribute; a fixed scan guarantees the second feature is seen — and hard items hide in exactly that second feature.

intro:
Coded inequality questions hide a tiny logic engine inside a substitution puzzle: symbols such as @, #, % or & stand in for “greater than”, “less than”, “equal to” and their compound forms, and the task is to decide which conclusions about the underlying order must follow. Nothing in the topic needs speed-reading tricks or lucky guesses — it is the mathematics of order relations dressed in costume. Decode the symbols, lay the statements into a single chain, and test each conclusion against what the chain guarantees. Done in that order, the questions are among the fastest, most reliable marks in any reasoning section; done out of order — reading coded conclusions against coded statements — they become guesswork.

**Why this matters.** The entire method reduces to one geometric picture: a number line with the elements placed left-to-right, and arrows that must all point the same way for information to travel. Transitivity — if A > B and B > C then A > C — is the property that lets a chain carry a conclusion from end to end; the direction-reversal rule (A > B but C < B) is the property that stops it. Every classification of a conclusion — definitely true, definitely false, cannot say, either-or — falls out of whether the chain connects the two elements with an unbroken same-direction path and whether the connectors are strict (>, <) or generous (≥, ≤). Master the picture once and every question, coded or plain, becomes the same three-step routine.
objectives: Explain decoding a symbol-to-meaning map first
Explain order relations: transitivity and direction
Explain combining statements into one chain
Explain the direction-reversal breaking point
Explain how ≥ and ≤ change what is definite
Explain either-or conclusions and complementary pairs
Explain conclusion validation against the chain

concepts.statement: The legend converting each code symbol to its real meaning (for example @ → >, # → <, $ → =, % → ≥, & → ≤). Always rewrite the statements in standard symbols before thinking; never reason on the codes.

A comparison relation between elements. The chains used here are transitive — A > B and B > C force A > C — which is the property that makes chains informative. In formal terms the relations studied are (partial or total) orderings: reflexive or irreflexive variants aside, antisymmetry and transitivity are what give an order its shape.

The combined picture after decoding: statements joined through shared elements, written as one line such as A > B ≥ C = D < E. A conclusion between two elements is legitimate exactly when a same-direction path joins them.

A position where the direction reverses, as in A > B < C. Information cannot cross it: nothing definite follows between A and C — each of A > C, A < C and A = C remains possible, so any definite claim is wrong.
Strict connectors (>, <) pin an order; generous ones (≥, ≤) leave a choice. Chaining through ≥ yields a definite ≥ and nothing sharper: A ≥ B ≥ C guarantees A ≥ C but neither A > C nor A = C alone.

Two conclusions that are individually unprovable but jointly exhaustive — for example “A > B” and “A = B” when the chain guarantees only A ≥ B. Exactly one of them must hold, so the answer is “either I or II follows”. They require the same two elements, and neither may be provable alone.

Decode before you think — the rule has no exceptions. Read the legend once and write the meaning of every symbol in the margin; then rewrite all statements in standard notation, checking the direction of each as you go, because coded legends deliberately reverse intuitions (“@ means greater than” on one paper may mean less than on the next). A code for “not equal to” deserves special respect: ≠ gives no direction at all, so a statement P ≠ Q contributes order nothing — it may decorate a conclusion’s options but can never help build a chain. After decoding, the conclusions must be decoded too: a conclusion written in codes is read against the chain only after conversion to standard symbols. Every one of the classic errors — “treating ≥ as >”, “assuming transitivity across disconnected statements”, “reading coded conclusions directly” — is at bottom a decode-order error.

Build the chain next. List the statements, find the shared elements and splice them into one line — P > Q, Q = R, R > S becomes P > Q = R > S. Two kinds of combination are safe. Same-direction transitivity: every strict step compounds, so P > Q > R gives P > R, and any run of ≥ steps gives a definite ≥ across the run. Equality substitution: an = merges its two elements into interchangeable labels, so P > Q = R is exactly P > R with a spare name. One combination is never safe: opposite-facing connectors around a shared element — P > Q alongside R < Q, or P ≥ Q alongside Q < R — leave the outer pair unordered, because concrete numbers make all three outcomes possible (take P = 10, R = 5; P = 5, R = 10; P = R = 7 with suitable Q). The chain line makes the breaking point visible; trust it over any feeling.

Generous connectors demand accounting. Read A ≥ B as a fork: either A > B or A = B, with neither branch guaranteed. Chaining through a fork can only promise the fork’s own generosity: A ≥ B ≥ C guarantees A ≥ C, but the sharper claims A > C and A = C are each merely possible — a case exists for both. A strict step anywhere in the run sharpens everything after it: A > B ≥ C forces A > C (the strictness propagates forward), and A ≥ B > C does too. So the one-line rule: a run of connectors is as strong as its weakest strict member — if any link in the run from X to Y is strict, the conclusion is strict; if all are generous, the conclusion is generous; if a link is equality, elements merge. This single sentence resolves every “definitely” question about ≥ chains without a table.

Conclusions then classify into four verdicts. Definitely true: the chain carries an unbroken same-direction path with the right strength (P > R from P > Q = R > S; P ≥ R from P ≥ Q ≥ R). Definitely false: the chain carries the opposite path — “P < R” is false when P > R is guaranteed. Cannot say: no path joins the pair, or every path crosses a breaking point (P > Q, Q < R leaves P–R open). Either-or: the pair of conclusions uses the same two elements, neither is individually definite, and together they exhaust the guaranteed relation — the canonical case is “P > R” and “P = R” when the chain proves only P ≥ R; the mirror case is “P ≤ R” with “P = R” when only P ≤ R is proved. Mark either-or only when both conditions hold; a conclusion that is outright false cannot join the pair.

Reading coded conclusions against coded statements — decode everything first, including the conclusions. Crossing a breaking point: A > B < C licenses nothing about A and C, however tempting. Promoting ≥ to >: a generous chain proves only a generous conclusion, and the sharper claim is always a coin-flip case. Reversing a decoded symbol — A > B is B < A, not B > A. Assuming transitivity across statements that share no element, or across a “not equal” code, which carries no direction at all. And awarding either-or when one conclusion is outright false or the two conclusions mention different element pairs — complementarity needs same elements, individual unprovability and joint exhaustiveness, all three.

examples.title: Worked Example — One Full Coded Question, Start to Finish
examples.problem: Coded Inequalities: Decoding Order Statements into Valid Conclusions — worked through step by step

steps.label: Legend
steps.text: @ → >, % → ≥, $ → =, # → <. Statements: A % B, B @ C, C $ D, D # E. Conclusions: I. A @ D; II. A @ E; III. C % E.

steps.label: Decode statements
steps.text: A ≥ B, B > C, C = D, D < E. Rewrite the chain: A ≥ B > C = D < E.

steps.label: Mark the breaking point
steps.text: between D and E the direction flips (< after the descending run) — no definite statement can cross it.

steps.label: Test I (A > D)
steps.text: path A ≥ B > C = D carries one strict link (B > C), so strictness propagates: A > D. TRUE.

steps.label: Test II (A > E)
steps.text: every A–E path crosses the D–E breaking point. CANNOT SAY.

steps.label: Test III (C ≥ E)
steps.text: the only path is C = D < E, which actually proves C < E — the opposite. FALSE. Verdict: only I follows.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: none — the order-relations core is built from scratch here. Follow with the critical-reasoning lesson for conclusion-testing habits in verbal arguments, and the order-and-ranking style puzzles that extend chains with positions. Primary reading: SATHEE, IIT Kanpur (Ministry of Education initiative), “Inequality (Coded Inequalities) — Theory & Concepts”, sathee.iitk.ac.in — the decode-then-chain method, combination rules and either-or conditions; H. Kwong, A Spiral Workbook for Discrete Mathematics, section 7.4 “Partial and Total Ordering”, math.libretexts.org (CC BY-NC-SA) — the reflexive/antisymmetric/transitive properties behind order relations.
Decode first: rewrite statements and conclusions in standard symbols; a “not equal” code contributes no direction.
Splice statements into one chain; the chain is the single source of truth for every verdict.
Same-direction runs compound by transitivity; opposite-facing connectors create a breaking point that nothing definite crosses.
Strictness propagates: one strict link sharpens the whole run; a run of ≥ proves only ≥.
Four verdicts: definitely true, definitely false, cannot say, either-or (complementary pairs on the same two elements).
The routine — decode, chain, test, classify — turns the whole topic into repeatable 60-second questions.

quiz.q: Statements: M > N, N > O. Conclusions: I. M > O; II. O < M. Which follows?
quiz.explanation: The chain M > N > O proves M > O; conclusion II restates the same fact in reverse wording (O < M ≡ M > O). Both follow.

quiz.q: Statements: P ≥ Q, Q = R. Which single conclusion is definitely true?
quiz.explanation: A ≥ run through an equality keeps only the generous strength: P ≥ R holds in both branches (P > R or P = R), but neither sharper claim is guaranteed.

quiz.q: Statements: X > Y, Z < Y. What can be concluded about X and Z?
quiz.explanation: Both statements face Y from opposite directions — a breaking point at Y. X > Z, X < Z and X = Z are all consistent with the data, so nothing definite follows.

quiz.q: Statements: A > B ≥ C. Conclusion: A > C. This conclusion is…
options: true, because one strict link sharpens the run
quiz.explanation: A > B is strict and the strictness propagates through the generous B ≥ C, so A > C is definite. Had both links been ≥, only A ≥ C would follow.

quiz.q: A chain guarantees exactly A ≥ B. Conclusions: I. A > B; II. A = B. The correct verdict is…
quiz.explanation: Neither branch of the fork is provable alone, but one must hold — same two elements, jointly exhaustive. That is the complementary-pair (either-or) case.

intro:
Every memory starts fading the moment you stop using it.
