Baroreceptors in the neck sense beat-to-beat drift and retune heart rate and vessel width within seconds, while kidneys and hormones adjust the set point over days. Readings that stay above 130/80 quietly damage vessels, heart, brain, and kidneys.

The textbook shortcut "arteries carry oxygen-rich blood" fails twice on the right side: the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein returns oxygen-rich blood — circuit names describe direction from the heart, not oxygen content. A second mix-up is reading blood pressure backwards: the upper number is the systolic surge, the lower one the diastolic resting pressure.
One full heartbeat — ventricular contraction (systole) followed by relaxation and refilling (diastole).
An upper chamber that receives blood returning to the heart.
A lower pumping chamber; the left ventricle has the thickest wall.
Blood ejected by one ventricular contraction, about 70 milliliters at rest.
Stroke volume times heart rate — total blood flow delivered per minute.
Microscopic vessel with one-cell-thick walls where gases and nutrients are exchanged.
Peak arterial pressure during ventricular contraction, the upper blood-pressure number.

examples.title: Worked example — The Heart and Circulation: One Pump, Two Circuits
examples.problem: How much blood the heart delivers per minute at rest.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: each contraction ejects about 70 milliliters and a resting heart beats roughly 72 times per minute, so 70 × 72 ≈ 5,040 milliliters per minute.

examples.result: about five liters per minute — the whole blood volume — while hard exercise can push stroke volume and rate to deliver over 20 liters to working muscles.

keyTakeaways: A stethoscope reading of valve sounds flags narrowing or leaks long before symptoms appear.
Treating high blood pressure — lifestyle first, then drugs — sharply cuts stroke and heart-failure risk.
Stents and bypass grafts reopen blocked coronary arteries during heart attacks.
Endurance training lowers resting heart rate toward 40-50 beats per minute with a larger stroke volume.
Pacemakers and replacement valves mechanically substitute for failing parts of the pump.

quiz.q: Which chamber pumps oxygen-rich blood to the entire body?
quiz.explanation: The left ventricle drives the systemic circuit; its extra-thick wall exists for exactly that job.

quiz.q: The heart's valves are essential because they:
options: secrete hormones that raise blood pressure
keep blood flowing one way so it cannot reverse
quiz.explanation: One-way valves convert rhythmic squeezing into directed flow — without them the pump merely sloshes blood.

quiz.q: A stroke volume of 70 milliliters and a heart rate of 72 give a cardiac output of about:
quiz.explanation: 70 × 72 ≈ 5,040 milliliters — roughly the entire blood volume moved each minute.

quiz.q: Capillary walls are one cell thick mainly to:
options: minimize the diffusion distance for gases and nutrients
quiz.explanation: Exchange happens fastest across the thinnest barrier — withstanding pressure is the arteries' job.

intro:
You can hold your breath for a minute, but the body will not allow two: every cell runs on oxygen delivered moment to moment. Breathing works by pressure differences, exchange happens across a barrier thinner than tissue paper, and delivery rides on a molecule built to grab oxygen in the lungs and release it in hungry tissue. This topic follows one oxygen molecule from open air to a mitochondrion — and the carbon dioxide making the return trip.

**Why this matters.** The gas-exchange surface folded into your chest totals about 70 square meters — a sheet that would floor a good-sized apartment — and the heart sends the entire blood volume past it every minute. Asthma, emphysema, pneumonia, and altitude sickness are each a failure at a different stage of the journey traced here.
objectives: Explain breathing driven by pressure differences
Explain alveoli: where air meets blood
Explain hemoglobin: the oxygen courier
Explain carbon dioxide, bicarbonate, and pH
Explain automatic control from the brainstem

concepts.statement: Air moves because the chest makes room for it. When the diaphragm dome flattens and the ribs lift, chest volume grows, the pressure inside drops below atmospheric, and air flows in; when the muscles relax, the lungs' own elastic recoil squeezes the air back out. Quiet exhalation is passive — recoil does the work — while deep breathing recruits rib muscles to drive air out as well as in.

The airways branch some twenty-three generations before ending in about 480 million alveoli: thin-walled sacs wrapped so tightly in capillaries that blood practically touches air. The barrier between them is under a micrometer thick, so oxygen diffuses down its partial-pressure gradient into blood while carbon dioxide diffuses out — each exchange completed in a fraction of a second. A soapy coating called surfactant keeps the wet sacs from collapsing shut.

Oxygen dissolves poorly in water, so plasma alone would carry almost nothing. Red cells are instead packed with hemoglobin, and each molecule carries four iron-bearing heme groups able to bind four oxygen molecules. Fully loaded blood holds about 200 milliliters of oxygen per liter — roughly fifty times what plasma dissolves — and unloads it fastest exactly where tissue is warm, acidic, and metabolically busy.

Carbon dioxide rides home mostly as bicarbonate. An enzyme inside red cells, carbonic anhydrase, converts it to carbonic acid, which splits into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions that hemoglobin mops up. This chemistry ties breathing directly to blood pH: breathing faster blows the gas off and raises pH, breathing too slowly lets pH fall — the reason hyperventilation makes fingertips tingle.

The system runs on autopilot from the brainstem. Rhythm generators in the medulla set the basic pace, while chemoreceptors — central ones bathing in brain fluid, others in the major arteries — monitor carbon dioxide, the true controlled variable, with oxygen as a backup alarm. That is why the agony of a held breath is driven by rising carbon dioxide long before oxygen actually runs low.

Two ideas mislead beginners. First, air is not sucked in by the lungs — the chest expands, pressure falls, and the atmosphere pushes air in; the lungs simply follow the chest wall. Second, the urge to breathe comes mainly from rising carbon dioxide, not falling oxygen — which is why hyperventilating before an underwater swim is dangerous: it delays the warning signal while oxygen stores keep falling.
The dome of muscle whose flattening enlarges the chest and draws air in.
A thin-walled air sac, one of about 480 million, where gas exchange with capillaries occurs.
A phospholipid coating that lowers surface tension so alveoli do not collapse.
The four-part oxygen carrier that fills red blood cells.
The share of total gas pressure contributed by one gas, which sets diffusion direction.
The dissolved form in which most carbon dioxide travels in plasma.
A sensor of blood or brain-fluid chemistry that feeds back on breathing rate.

examples.title: Worked example — Breathing and Gas Exchange: From Air to Cell
examples.problem: How much oxygen the bloodstream delivers each minute at rest.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: arterial blood carries about 200 milliliters of oxygen per liter bound to hemoglobin, and the heart circulates about 5 liters per minute.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: 200 milliliters per liter times 5 liters per minute equals 1,000 milliliters of oxygen in transit, of which resting tissues consume roughly 250 milliliters.

examples.result: about one liter per minute delivered with a fourfold reserve — the margin hard exercise draws on when cardiac output and extraction must rise to meet a demand near 4 liters.

keyTakeaways: Ventilators take over the pressure cycle when the diaphragm or its brainstem control fails.
Pulse oximeters estimate hemoglobin saturation through the skin in seconds.
Asthma inhalers open constricted airways; emphysema destroys alveolar walls and shrinks the exchange surface.
Carbon monoxide kills by occupying hemoglobin's oxygen seats — treated with pure oxygen.
Weeks at altitude raise red-cell counts to compensate for thin air.

quiz.q: Inhalation happens because:
options: the lungs actively suck air inward
chest expansion drops internal pressure below atmospheric, pushing air in
oxygen diffuses into the chest cavity
the diaphragm squeezes air up from the stomach
quiz.explanation: Muscles enlarge the chest; the pressure drop lets the atmosphere push air in — the lungs ride along.

quiz.q: Most oxygen in blood travels:
options: bound to hemoglobin inside red cells
quiz.explanation: Hemoglobin's four heme groups carry the load — about fifty times what plasma alone could dissolve.

quiz.q: The strongest everyday drive to breathe comes from:
options: rising carbon dioxide and falling pH
quiz.explanation: Carbon dioxide is the tightly controlled variable; oxygen only becomes a major drive when quite low.

quiz.q: Most carbon dioxide returns to the lungs as:
quiz.explanation: Roughly 70 percent rides as bicarbonate, formed by carbonic anhydrase inside red cells.

intro:
A sandwich is worthless to your cells until it has been dismantled. The digestive system is a nine-meter disassembly line that grinds food, douses it in acid, and attacks it with a suite of specialist enzymes, until nothing remains but molecules small enough to cross the intestinal wall. This topic walks the tract from mouth to large intestine, names the enzymes and their targets, and shows why the liver gets first claim on every absorbed nutrient.

**Why this matters.** Coeliac disease, ulcers, lactose intolerance, and reflux are all failures at specific stations of the line — and each is managed by understanding which step misfires. Medicine's most common gut prescriptions, from antacids to enzyme replacements, are direct applications of this anatomy.
objectives: Explain a nine-meter disassembly line
Explain mechanical and chemical digestion
Explain enzymes: each a specialist
Explain absorption in the small intestine
Explain the liver as processing hub

concepts.statement: The tract runs from mouth through esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine — about nine meters coiled into the abdomen — with salivary glands, pancreas, and gallbladder emptying in through side ducts. Its wall carries the enteric nervous system, a local mesh of some 500 million neurons that coordinates the peristaltic waves and mixing contractions pushing contents along, largely without consulting the brain.

Teeth shear and grind, the stomach churns, and segmentation contractions mix — but all of that is only preparation. Chemical digestion is hydrolysis: enzymes add water across bonds to split starches into sugars, proteins into amino acids, and fats into fatty acids. The tract's true product is not the mush passing through but the molecules small enough to be absorbed from it.

Each enzyme has a target and a workplace. Salivary amylase starts on starch in the mouth; pepsin attacks proteins in stomach acid near pH 2, strong enough to kill most swallowed microbes; pancreatic amylase, proteases like trypsin, and lipase finish the job in the small intestine, arriving with sodium bicarbonate to neutralize the acid. Bile salts from the liver emulsify fat into droplets small enough for lipase to attack.

Nearly all uptake happens in the small intestine, whose lining is pleated into villi and microvilli — the brush border — multiplying the absorptive surface many times over. Sugars and amino acids cross on specific transporters into capillaries; digested fats reassemble into droplets that enter lymph vessels. The large intestine then reclaims water and salts, and its bacterial flora ferments whatever remains.

Absorbed nutrients travel the portal vein straight to the liver, which gets first claim: it stores glucose as glycogen, packages and ships fats, builds plasma proteins, and detoxifies alcohol, drugs, and ammonia. Between meals it drips glycogen back out as glucose, holding blood sugar steady — the body's metabolic customs house.

Digestion and absorption are different jobs in different places: the stomach digests protein but absorbs almost nothing — alcohol being a notable exception — while nearly all uptake is small-intestine work. And the gallbladder only stores bile; the liver makes it. Removing a gallbladder rarely stops digestion, it just makes an especially fatty meal harder to process.
Wave-like muscle contractions that propel contents along the tract.
Splitting a molecule by adding water across the bond — how food polymers are broken down.
The stomach's protein-digesting enzyme, active only in strong acid.
Liver-made salts that emulsify fat into droplets exposed to lipase.
A finger-like fold of the small-intestine lining, itself covered in microvilli.
The microvilli layer carrying the final digestive enzymes and transporters.
The vessel carrying nutrient-rich blood from the intestine to the liver first.

examples.title: Worked example — The Digestive System: From Meal to Molecule
examples.problem: The fate of the starch in a slice of bread.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: starch is a chain of glucose units, split by amylases and finished by brush-border enzymes.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: salivary amylase begins in the mouth; stomach acid pauses it; pancreatic amylase resumes in the duodenum, yielding the two-sugar maltose; brush-border maltase then releases free glucose, which transporters carry into villus cells and on into the portal vein.

examples.result: within about two hours a plant polymer has become glucose in the blood — stored as liver glycogen or shipped out as fuel.

keyTakeaways: Lactase enzyme tablets replace what lactose-intolerant guts no longer make.
Ulcer therapy pairs acid-suppressing drugs with antibiotics against Helicobacter pylori.
In coeliac disease, gluten flattens the villi and absorption collapses until gluten is removed.
Bariatric surgery reshapes the tract to limit intake and absorption for severe obesity.
Dietary fiber feeds the colonic bacteria that finish digestion in the large intestine.

quiz.q: Most nutrient absorption occurs in the:
quiz.explanation: Villi and the brush border give the small intestine its enormous uptake surface.

quiz.q: Pepsin works best:
quiz.explanation: Pepsin is adapted to stomach acid near pH 2; pancreatic enzymes instead need the alkaline duodenum.

quiz.q: Bile's role in fat digestion is to:
options: chemically split fats into fatty acids
emulsify fat into droplets that lipase can attack
quiz.explanation: Bile salts break fat into tiny droplets — multiplying surface area — while lipase does the actual splitting.

quiz.q: Blood leaving the intestine travels first to the:
quiz.explanation: The portal vein gives the liver first access to absorbed nutrients before anything reaches the general circulation.

intro:
Two fist-sized kidneys filter roughly 180 liters of fluid from your blood each day — the entire plasma volume dozens of times over — deciding ion by ion what to keep and what to discard. Around them, the endocrine system broadcasts slower chemical instructions through the bloodstream. Together they hold the body's internal sea of water, salts, sugar, and calcium within the narrow ranges chemistry demands. This topic covers the nephron's filter-and-reclaim engineering, water balance by hormone, and the feedback loops that run the show.

**Why this matters.** Chronic kidney disease and diabetes are among the world's fastest-growing chronic conditions, and both are failures of balance — one of filtration, one of hormonal feedback. Dialysis, sodium labels, thyroid tests, and glucose meters are all applications of the machinery described here.
objectives: Explain the nephron: filter and tubule
Explain filtration, reabsorption, secretion
Explain osmoregulation by ADH
Explain hormones as chemical messengers
Explain negative feedback: the master pattern
Explain the kidneys as endocrine organs

concepts.statement: Each kidney packs about a million nephrons, its functional units. Blood enters the glomerulus, a knot of capillaries under pressure, and fluid is forced across a filter into a capsule, then flows along a tubule whose successive sections decide — through transporters and channels — what returns to the blood and what drains on toward the bladder as urine.

About 180 liters of fluid filter through each day, yet only a liter or two leaves as urine: more than 99 percent is reabsorbed. Glucose is normally recovered completely, salts are tuned to the body's needs, and wastes like urea are left behind or actively secreted into the tubule. Urine is the fine-tuned residue of the filtrate, not the filtrate itself.

Sweat through an afternoon or skip water and the blood concentrates; osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus fire within minutes, triggering thirst and the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the posterior pituitary. ADH inserts water channels into the kidney's collecting ducts, letting water be retracted from the forming urine — which is why dehydration shrinks urine volume and darkens its color.

Endocrine glands release hormones into the bloodstream, where they reach every cell but act only on cells carrying the matching receptor. Insulin commands glucose uptake in muscle and fat while the brain runs on other rules; adrenaline acts in seconds, thyroid hormone over days. Where nerves send addressed electrical signals, hormones are chemical broadcasts steering metabolism, growth, reproduction, and mood.

The master pattern is negative feedback: a hormone's effects feed back to shut off its own release. The pancreas senses glucose, secretes insulin, glucose falls, and insulin secretion stops — a loop holding blood sugar near 5 millimoles per liter. The pituitary reads thyroid hormone levels and dials its own TSH up or down to hold metabolic rate on target. Positive feedback exists too, but mainly for events that must run to completion, like childbirth's oxytocin spiral.

The kidneys are endocrine organs in their own right. Falling oxygen delivery prompts them to release erythropoietin, the hormone ordering the marrow to make more red blood cells; low blood flow prompts renin, launching a cascade that raises blood pressure and salt retention. And the adrenal glands sit perched on top of the kidneys, managing sodium via aldosterone — a constant conversation between filter and gland.

The kidney filters, but the tubule decides: raw filtration alone would waste 180 liters a day and dump glucose, so the real work is selective reabsorption. A second misconception is that hormones act everywhere they reach — only cells with the right receptor respond, which is why one hormone can have opposite effects in different organs. And the pituitary is a manager, not a boss: it answers to the hypothalamus above it and to feedback from the glands below.
The kidney's functional unit — a glomerulus filter plus a tubule that reclaims what the body keeps.
The high-pressure capillary knot where filtration begins.
Reclaiming filtered water and solutes from the tubule back into blood.
Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) — inserts water channels to concentrate urine.
A loop in which a hormone's own effect turns its release back down.
The kidney hormone that orders marrow to build red blood cells.
The pancreatic hormone driving glucose uptake, held steady by negative feedback.

examples.title: Worked example — Kidneys, Hormones and the Body's Balance
examples.problem: How the body defends its water balance through a hot afternoon with nothing to drink.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: osmoreceptors plus ADH conserve water by concentrating urine.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: sweating raises the solute concentration of blood; hypothalamic osmoreceptors fire, ADH rises from the posterior pituitary, water channels open in the collecting ducts, and more water is reabsorbed before urine leaves — while the same signal drives you to find a drink.

examples.result: urine output falls toward half a liter a day and darkens, thirst sharpens, and plasma concentration stays near normal until water arrives.

keyTakeaways: Dialysis artificially filters wastes when nephrons fail, typically three sessions a week.
Insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitors engineer the feedback loop that diabetes breaks.
Thyroid check-ups start with TSH — reading the pituitary feedback loop to locate the fault.
Erythropoietin treats the anemia of kidney failure — and is banned as a blood-doping drug.
Dehydration darkens urine; ADH-suppressing alcohol explains the morning-after thirst.

quiz.q: Roughly how much fluid do the two kidneys filter per day?
quiz.explanation: The full plasma volume filters dozens of times a day — 180 liters — of which over 99 percent is reabsorbed.

quiz.q: ADH conserves water mainly by:
options: inserting water channels in the kidney's collecting ducts
quiz.explanation: ADH opens water channels so the collecting duct reabsorbs more water, concentrating the urine.

quiz.q: Insulin secretion switches off when:
options: blood glucose falls back toward normal
quiz.explanation: Negative feedback: the hormone's own effect — falling glucose — is the off switch at the pancreas.

quiz.q: Which hormone do the kidneys release when oxygen delivery runs low?
options: Erythropoietin, ordering more red blood cells
quiz.explanation: Erythropoietin from the kidneys stimulates the marrow — the basis of both anemia therapy and blood doping.

intro:
Take one step and a committee of 206 bones, a hundred movable joints, and more than 600 skeletal muscles fires in sequence — a machine that also happens to be alive, self-repairing, and rebuilt while you sleep. This topic covers that machinery at organ scale: the skeleton as frame and mineral bank, joints as bearings, muscles as engines that can only pull, and the cellular crew that remodels the whole apparatus decade after decade.

**Why this matters.** Osteoporosis, back injury, arthritis, and most sports damage are failures of this machinery's design limits — levers loaded wrong, bearings worn out, remodeling tipped the wrong way. Physiotherapy, joint replacement, and safe-lifting rules are applied biomechanics.
objectives: Explain the skeleton: 206 bones, two divisions
Explain joints: the body's bearings
Explain bones and muscles as levers
Explain muscles pull; pairs oppose
Explain motor units grade the force
Explain living bone, constantly remodeled

concepts.statement: The 206 bones divide into an axial skeleton — skull, spine, and rib cage shielding brain and organs — and an appendicular skeleton of limbs and their girdles. Bone is not inert framing: it stores about 99 percent of the body's calcium, and the marrow inside it manufactures every red blood cell and many immune cells you own.

Bones meet at joints ranging from the fused, immovable sutures of the skull to the freely moving synovial joints of shoulder, hip, knee, and fingers. In a synovial joint, glass-smooth cartilage coats the mating surfaces, a capsule of slippery fluid keeps friction near zero, and ligaments — tough collagen straps — hold the bones aligned while allowing the joint's designed motion.

Muscle-bone systems are levers: the bone is a rigid bar, the joint a fulcrum, the muscle's pull an effort, and the load a resistance. Most human joints, like the elbow, work as third-class levers — the biceps attaches only a few centimeters past the joint while the hand carries its load ten times farther out. The design trades raw force for speed and range of motion.

A muscle can only shorten and pull, never push, so movement needs opposing teams: the biceps bends the elbow while the triceps straightens it, and balance between such pairs is what physiotherapy restores. Collagen cables called tendons clamp muscle to bone; the Achilles tendon stretches under load and snaps back, recycling energy with every running stride like a spring.

A whole muscle is thousands of fibers, each wired to one motor neuron — together a motor unit. The nervous system grades force two ways: firing the units it has recruited more rapidly, and recruiting additional units, smallest first, as demand climbs. In a maximal lift every available unit is active; a faint tremor is recruitment flickering on and off at the edge of that command.

Bone is constantly rebuilt: osteoblasts deposit new tissue where mechanical load is high, osteoclasts dissolve it where it is not, and the entire skeleton turns over roughly every ten years. Loading drives the building — which is why bone fades during bed rest. When resorption outruns deposition for years, as after menopause, the result is osteoporosis: bones with normal chemistry but thinning architecture.

Muscles pull and never push — every "pushing" motion you make is another muscle pulling from the other side. Tendons and ligaments are not interchangeable: tendon joins muscle to bone, ligament joins bone to bone. And lifting a heavy box with a bent spine turns the back into the worst lever in the body, which is the entire logic of lifting with the knees and a straight back.
The skull, spine, and rib cage — the central protective frame.
A freely movable joint with cartilage surfaces, a lubricating capsule, and ligaments.
Tough collagen strap binding bone to bone across a joint.
Collagen cable transmitting muscle pull to bone.
One motor neuron and the set of muscle fibers it commands.
Effort between fulcrum and load — fast, wide movement at the cost of force.
Bone thinning from years of resorption outpacing deposition.

examples.title: Worked example — Muscles, Bones and the Machinery of Movement
examples.problem: How hard the biceps must pull to hold a 10-kilogram dumbbell in the hand.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: in a third-class lever, effort close to the fulcrum is multiplied across the longer load distance.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: the biceps inserts about 5 centimeters from the elbow while the load sits about 35 centimeters out at the hand, so the muscle must supply 35/5 = 7 times the load's force — 10 kg × 9.8 N/kg × 7 ≈ 690 newtons.

examples.result: holding a modest weight costs the muscle roughly seventy kilograms-force — the price your arm pays for fast, far-reaching movement instead of brute strength.

keyTakeaways: DXA scans measure bone density as the standard screen for osteoporosis.
Joint replacement swaps worn cartilage surfaces for metal and plastic bearings.
ACL reconstruction rebuilds the knee's stabilizing ligament from a tendon graft.
Loading bones through resistance exercise keeps remodeling tilted toward deposition across life.
Ergonomics redesigns tools and lifts so joints work mid-range, where levers are safest.

quiz.q: Bones are tied to other bones by:
quiz.explanation: Ligament is bone-to-bone; tendon is muscle-to-bone — a distinction with surgical consequences.

quiz.q: Holding a dumbbell, the biceps must pull with far more force than the load itself because:
options: the bone absorbs most of the force
it attaches close to the elbow fulcrum, a third-class lever
gravity is stronger at the hand
quiz.explanation: The short effort arm and long load arm multiply the required muscle force — the trade for speed and reach.

quiz.q: The nervous system raises whole-muscle force mainly by:
options: making each fiber contract beyond its maximum
recruiting more motor units and firing them faster
quiz.explanation: Force grading is recruitment and firing rate — individual fibers are all-or-none.

quiz.q: Osteoporosis develops when:
options: resorption by osteoclasts outruns deposition for years
quiz.explanation: The remodeling balance tips toward dissolution, leaving bones light and brittle though chemically normal.

intro:
Your body carries more microbial cells than it has human ones, and the world beyond carries more still. The three great kinds of microbe — bacteria, viruses, and fungi — differ from one another more deeply than you differ from a mushroom, and those differences decide everything about the diseases they cause and the drugs that fight them. This field guide covers what each is made of, how each multiplies, and how each makes you sick.

**Why this matters.** Which kind of microbe is causing an illness decides nearly everything about treatment: antibiotics touch only bacteria, antivirals only viruses, antifungals only fungi. Most "stomach flu" is viral — demanding antibiotics for it buys side effects and resistance while touching nothing responsible.
objectives: Explain bacteria: independent single cells
Explain viruses: hijackers in a coat
Explain fungi: recyclers with chitin walls
Explain a size ladder for the invisible
Explain three ways to cause disease

concepts.statement: A bacterium is a complete, self-sufficient cell a few micrometers long: DNA floating free in the cytoplasm, ribosomes building protein, and a tough wall of peptidoglycan holding shape. Most divide by binary fission — copy the DNA, split in two — and some manage a division every 20 minutes, letting a single cell found a colony of millions before nightfall. Thousands of species inhabit your body; only a handful are pathogens.

A virus is not a cell at all: a stretch of DNA or RNA folded into a protein coat, sometimes wrapped in a stolen membrane, a few dozen nanometers across. It has no metabolism and cannot reproduce alone. Instead it injects its genome into a living cell and reprograms the host's ribosomes into building virus parts, which assemble and burst out — usually killing the cell. Influenza, measles, and SARS-CoV-2 all run this racket.

Fungi are eukaryotes with chitin-reinforced walls — closer kin to you than to any bacterium. They grow as budding yeasts or as thread-like hyphae that push through soil or skin, digest food outside their bodies, and spread by hardy spores. Many are indispensable — bread, beer, and penicillin — while a few cause trouble: Candida yeasts flare when immunity dips, and dermatophytes cause the itchy ringworms of skin and nail.

concepts.term: A size ladder for the invisible
concepts.statement: Scale keeps the field guide organized. Viruses are far smaller than bacteria — a tenth to a twentieth across, and thousands of times lighter — so a single bacterial cell can host an entire viral factory; bacteria are about a tenth the size of your cells; yeasts approach your own cells in size. That is why a surgical mask blocks virus-laden droplets, but only the immune system clears viruses already inside cells.

Each kind sickens in its own way. Bacteria release toxins — cholera's flood of diarrhea, tetanus's rigid spasms — or inflame tissue directly; viruses kill cells and provoke immune responses whose side effects feel like the illness itself; fungi colonize surface tissue and provoke irritation. The mechanism predicts the cure: antibacterials sabotage bacterial-only machinery, antivirals block stages of the viral life cycle, and antifungals attack fungal targets like the chitin wall.

Antibiotics do nothing to viruses and never have — a virus has no wall, no bacterial ribosome, nothing for the drug to grip. Nor are microbes villains by default: the overwhelming majority are harmless or essential, and most infections are decided as much by the host's immune response as by the microbe. Finally, viruses sit outside biology's formal definition of life — not quite object, not quite organism.
Bacterial reproduction — DNA copied, cell split in two.
The cross-linked sugar-protein mesh of bacterial walls, penicillin's target.
The protein coat enclosing a viral genome.
An agent that can reproduce only inside a host cell — every virus, by definition.
A fungal filament; masses of them form a mycelium.
A dormant, near-indestructible bacterial survival capsule.
A bacterial poison that does damage apart from the organism itself.

examples.title: Worked example — Bacteria, Viruses, Fungi: A Field Guide to the Microbial World
examples.problem: How fast a food-contaminating bacterium can multiply from a few cells.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: binary fission doubles the population every generation time.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: Salmonella dividing every 30 minutes gains ten doublings in five hours — 10 cells become about 10,000 — and twenty doublings by ten hours carry the colony past ten million.

examples.result: exponential growth turns a contaminated crumb into an infectious dose overnight — the arithmetic behind every refrigeration rule ever written.

keyTakeaways: The Gram stain, unchanged since 1884, still sorts bacteria into wall types that predict antibiotic response.
Antivirals against HIV and influenza target viral enzymes that human cells lack.
Yogurt, bread, beer, cheese, and penicillin are all microbial biotechnology.
Culture plates and PCR assays name the microbe and reveal which drugs it fears.
Hospital sterilization targets endospores that survive boiling and shrug off disinfectants.

quiz.q: Which microbe cannot reproduce outside a living host cell?
quiz.explanation: A virus is an obligate intracellular parasite — no metabolism, no reproduction without hijacking a cell.

quiz.q: Bacterial cell walls are built mainly of:
quiz.explanation: Peptidoglycan is unique to bacteria — which is exactly what penicillin attacks.

quiz.q: A bacterium dividing every 20 minutes grows from one cell to over a thousand in about:
quiz.explanation: Ten doublings take 200 minutes — just over three hours — and two to the tenth is 1,024.

quiz.q: Ringworm, despite the name, is caused by:
quiz.explanation: Dermatophyte fungi — the misnomer stuck centuries before anyone could see the cause.

intro:
In 1943 a rose thorn could kill; by 1960 penicillin had made such deaths a rarity. That shield is leaking. Bacteria resistant to our best drugs now collect in hospitals, farms, and waterways, and every careless prescription runs an evolutionary experiment with the stakes counted in lives. This topic covers how antibiotics work, how resistance evolves and spreads, and what stewardship — in clinics, on farms, and at the pharmacy counter — actually requires.

**Why this matters.** The World Health Organization ranks antimicrobial resistance among the top ten threats to global health, with projections near ten million extra deaths a year by mid-century if trends hold. It is the clearest example of evolution happening on a human timescale — with human fingerprints all over the selection pressure.
objectives: Explain what antibiotics actually attack
Explain selection in fast-forward
Explain the resistance toolbox
Explain genes that travel: plasmids
Explain stewardship: keeping the drugs working

concepts.statement: Antibiotics work by attacking machinery that bacteria have and you do not. Penicillins and their relatives block the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so walls burst as the cell grows; tetracyclines jam the bacterial ribosome; fluoroquinolones corrupt bacterial DNA enzymes. Human cells share none of these targets — which is why the drugs can cure without killing you, and why they have nothing at all to grip on a virus.

Every large bacterial population already contains mutants — one in a million, one in a hundred million — that shrug off a given drug by sheer luck of mutation. The antibiotic kills their rivals, and the survivors inherit the infection: natural selection, the principle from the evolution lesson, compressed into days inside a single patient. An under-dosed or abandoned course gives the hardy minority extra rounds to multiply.

Resistance has a toolbox. Enzymes like beta-lactamase chemically shred penicillin's ring; efflux pumps expel drugs before they act; target molecules mutate shape so the drug no longer fits; biofilms shelter whole communities behind slime. Some mechanisms cost the bacterium little to carry, so they persist even after the drug disappears — resistance, once selected, does not conveniently evaporate.

The alarming part is horizontal gene transfer: bacteria pass DNA around, even across species. A resistance gene riding a plasmid — a small ring of DNA — can move from harmless gut flora into a pathogen in a single conjugation event. Genes travel, not just lineages: that is how resistance born in farm animals surfaces in hospital superbugs, and why one hospital's problem becomes every hospital's problem.

Stewardship means keeping the drugs working: prescribe only for bacterial infections, narrow the drug once the laboratory names the culprit, complete the prescribed course, and never demand antibiotics for colds or flu. The One Health frame adds the farm — roughly two-thirds of the world's antibiotic tonnage feeds animals, a vast selection tank with pipes running straight into human medicine.

Resistance develops in bacteria, not in patients: "I've become resistant to amoxicillin" confuses the target of selection. Stopping a course early usually selects the hardiest minority — the opposite of the folk advice that finishing breeds immunity in you. And resistance rarely reverses on its own: remove the drug and the genes often persist at low cost, waiting for the next round.
A drug that kills or slows bacteria by targeting machinery human cells lack.
A bacterial enzyme that destroys penicillin-family drugs.
A molecular bouncer ejecting drugs from the bacterial cell.
A transferable DNA ring that can carry resistance between bacteria.
Movement of genes between organisms, not just down lineages.
Coordinated practice — right drug, right dose, right duration — to preserve antibiotic effectiveness.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, the emblematic resistant pathogen.

examples.title: Worked example — Antibiotics and the Rise of Resistance
examples.problem: Why a standard amoxicillin course can end in a resistant rebound infection.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: antibiotics impose selection — susceptible cells die, and pre-existing resistant variants inherit the field.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: in a bacterial population of a billion cells, resistance already present at one in a million means about a thousand resistant cells stand ready; the drug clears the rest, and doubling every half hour, the survivors rebuild a billion within roughly ten hours.

examples.result: the rebound infection is fully resistant — selected, not created, by the drug — and every cell inheriting the plasmid carries the same shield into the next patient.

keyTakeaways: MRSA — methicillin-resistant Staph aureus — remains the classic hospital superbug, fought with hygiene plus last-line drugs.
Rapid diagnostics name the pathogen in hours, letting doctors narrow broad-spectrum therapy early.
New beta-lactamase inhibitors are paired with old penicillins to outflank the shredding enzymes.
EU rules now ban routine antibiotic growth promotion in livestock to shrink the selection tank.
Drug development incentives — push funding and pull prizes — aim to refill a thinning pipeline.

quiz.q: Penicillin kills bacteria by:
options: preventing peptidoglycan cell-wall cross-linking so cells burst
quiz.explanation: Weakened walls rupture as the bacterium grows — a target human cells simply do not have.

quiz.q: Resistance can leap between bacterial species mainly because:
options: bacteria inherit it only from parents
resistance genes on plasmids move horizontally between species
quiz.explanation: Plasmid transfer moves genes across species boundaries — even between harmless and pathogenic bacteria.

quiz.q: Antibiotics fail against colds because:
options: cold viruses mutate too fast for any drug
viruses have none of the bacterial machinery the drugs attack
quiz.explanation: No wall, no bacterial ribosome — nothing for the drug to grip. The mismatch is structural, not dose-related.

quiz.q: A course stopped too early tends to:
options: select for the hardiest resistant minority
quiz.explanation: The most susceptible cells die first; stopping then leaves the toughest ones alive to repopulate.

intro:
You are outnumbered in your own body. Roughly 38 trillion bacterial cells ride along — about as many as your own cells — with the overwhelming majority packed into the colon. Far from passive passengers, they digest food you cannot, manufacture vitamins, train your immune system, and defend their territory against invaders. This topic tours the microbiome: who lives where, what they do for you, what reshuffles the community, and what medicine is learning to do about it.

**Why this matters.** A disturbed community — dysbiosis — now links to conditions from recurrent C. difficile colitis to allergies, inflammatory bowel disease, and obesity. Fecal transplants cure repeat C. difficile at rates no single antibiotic matches, which is why clinicians have begun treating the microbiome as an organ in its own right.
objectives: Explain who lives where: the census
Explain services rendered: fiber, vitamins, defense
Explain how the tenancy is set
Explain dysbiosis: when balance breaks
Explain fecal transplants and engineering the flora

concepts.statement: The residents are mostly bacteria — dominated by the phyla Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes — plus archaea, fungi, and viruses. Each body site keeps its own climate: oily skin, an acidic stomach home to a mere handful of hardy species, and the oxygen-poor colon, the metropolis. Your genome is fixed; the microbiome shifts measurably with every change of diet — a garden replanted by each meal.

The rent is paid in chemistry. Gut bacteria ferment fiber your enzymes cannot touch into short-chain fatty acids — especially butyrate, the preferred fuel of colon cells and a calming signal to the immune system. They synthesize vitamin K and several B vitamins, and by filling every niche they crowd out arriving pathogens. Breast milk even carries specialized sugars the baby cannot digest: food shipped for the tenants.

The founding community arrives at birth — vaginal microbes for most babies, skin microbes by cesarean — and antibiotics, diet, and environment reshuffle it for life. High-fiber diets feed the fermenters; processed, low-fiber diets starve them. Each antibiotic course is clear-cut logging in a rainforest that may not fully regrow: repeated courses can thin the community's diversity, in some cases permanently.

When diversity collapses, trouble follows. The clearest case: antibiotics wipe out the fiber-fermenters, and toxin-producing Clostridioides difficile explodes into life-threatening colitis. Weaker but replicated links extend to inflammatory bowel disease, allergies, obesity, and mood, where the gut-brain axis runs chemical traffic in both directions — serotonin's building blocks among the freight.

concepts.term: Fecal transplants and engineering the flora
concepts.statement: The bluntest therapeutic tool is the fecal microbiota transplant: filtered stool from a screened donor, delivered by capsule or colonoscope, restoring an entire working ecosystem in a single dose. It cures roughly 85-90 percent of recurrent C. difficile — far beyond any single drug. Next in the pipeline: rationally defined microbe cocktails and engineered strains that dispense drugs or consume toxins.

The word "probiotic" on a label promises little: most commercial strains are transient visitors that rarely colonize, and the right strain for one condition is wrong for another. Correlation is not causation — many microbiome-disease links remain associations still under investigation. And a healthy microbiome means diverse and stable, not merely numerous: quality of the community, not headcount, is what counts.
The full community of microbes inhabiting a body site, plus their genes.
An organism living on or in a host without harming it.
Fatty acids like butyrate made by bacterial fermentation of fiber.
A fiber or compound that feeds existing beneficial microbes.
Live microorganisms consumed with intent to improve the community.
A harmful imbalance or diversity loss in the microbiome.
Transfer of a donor's stool community to restore a patient's flora.

examples.title: Worked example — The Microbiome: Your Trillion Tenants
examples.problem: What actually happens to the fiber in a bowl of beans.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: gut bacteria ferment fiber that human enzymes cannot break.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: species like Bifidobacterium split the complex carbohydrates into short-chain fatty acids; butyrate is burned on the spot by colon cells, while acetate and propionate enter the circulation and influence liver metabolism and appetite signaling.

examples.result: an "indigestible" carbohydrate becomes fuel, colon-cell nourishment, and metabolic signaling — fiber is nutrition for two organisms at once, you and your tenants.

keyTakeaways: Fecal microbiota transplantation is approved therapy for recurrent C. difficile infection.
Probiotic yogurts deliver live cultures; prebiotic fibers feed the ones already there.
Newborn vitamin K shots bridge the gap until the colon flora establishes itself.
Germ-free mice and gut-on-chip models let researchers test microbes one species at a time.
Personalized nutrition projects predict glucose responses from an individual's microbiome.

quiz.q: Most of the body's microbial residents live in the:
quiz.explanation: The oxygen-poor colon is the metropolis — dark, fibrous, and densely populated.

quiz.q: Butyrate is produced when gut bacteria:
quiz.explanation: Fermentation of dietary fiber yields short-chain fatty acids — the colon cells' main fuel.

quiz.q: Fecal microbiota transplantation is most clearly curative for:
quiz.explanation: Restoring the whole ecosystem beats the pathogen in a way single drugs cannot — an approved therapy for repeat cases.

quiz.q: A prebiotic differs from a probiotic in that it is:
options: fiber that feeds the microbes already present
quiz.explanation: Prebiotics are the food; probiotics are the organisms — the meal versus the guests.

intro:
Gregor Mendel counted his way to the laws of inheritance: some 28,000 pea plants over eight years in a monastery garden, tracking seed shape, flower color, and stem length across generations. From the ratios alone he deduced that traits are carried by paired factors that separate cleanly into eggs and pollen and recombine at random. Published in 1866 and ignored for 34 years, Mendel's laws still anchor genetics — this topic covers the two laws, the square that applies them, and the family trees that extend them.

**Why this matters.** Genetic counseling for cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell trait, and Huntington's disease is applied Mendelism: the same ratios that fell out of monastery peas tell an expecting couple their odds. Punnett-square arithmetic is the working toolkit of clinics, breeding programs, and identity labs alike.
objectives: Explain genes come in pairs, one per parent
Explain the law of segregation
Explain the law of independent assortment
Explain punnett squares and probability
Explain dominance and its variants
Explain reading family pedigrees

concepts.term: Genes come in pairs, one per parent
concepts.statement: Every gene comes in two copies — alleles — one on each member of a chromosome pair, one inherited from each parent. Mendel saw the logic without ever seeing a chromosome: crossing pure tall with pure short peas gave all tall offspring, yet the short factor had not vanished, for it resurfaced in the grandchildren. The lesson: an organism's appearance (phenotype) and its genetic makeup (genotype) are different things.

The law of segregation: during the formation of eggs and sperm, the two alleles of each gene separate, and each gamete receives exactly one. A plant carrying one tall and one short allele makes equal numbers of each type of gamete — the fairness of a coin flip — and at fertilization, chance reassembles the pair.

The law of independent assortment: pairs of alleles for different genes are handed out independently, so the allele a seed gets for height says nothing about its allele for seed color. The independence holds only for genes on different chromosomes, or far apart on the same one — a boundary Mendel could not have known he was brushing against. Where it holds, trait ratios multiply like probabilities.

The Punnett square turns the laws into arithmetic. Cross two heterozygotes (Tt × Tt): the grid yields one TT, two Tt, and one tt — a 3:1 ratio of phenotypes when one allele dominates, and a 1:2:1 ratio of genotypes. Stack two traits and the ratios multiply into the classic 9:3:3:1 dihybrid pattern Mendel tabulated. Probability, not blending, is the grammar of inheritance.

Dominance is a biochemical outcome, not a tug of war. In incomplete dominance, one red and one white allele yield pink flowers; in codominance, both appear separately, as the A and B antigens on AB blood; and a recessive disease allele usually means one working copy is enough for health. Humans carry some 20,000 genes — a slot, in each of them, where alleles can differ.

Pedigrees hang the laws on family trees. Autosomal recessive traits like cystic fibrosis skip generations and can strike two entirely healthy carriers; dominant traits like Huntington's disease appear in every generation, each child of an affected parent at 50 percent risk. Squares for males, circles for females, shading for the affected — and behind every pedigree, Mendel's ratios at work.

Dominant does not mean common — Huntington's is dominant and rare, while type O blood is recessive and everywhere. Recessive does not mean weak: it means the trait shows only in the absence of a working allele. And independent assortment fails for linked genes — neighbors on the same chromosome travel together, the very exception that first let geneticists map genes onto chromosomes.
One of the alternative forms a gene can take in a population.
The actual pair of alleles an organism carries.
The observable trait, which may mask one of the alleles present.
Carrying two different alleles of a gene.
The two alleles of a gene separate into separate gametes, one each.
Allele pairs for different genes are inherited independently — when not linked.
A grid computing the genotypes and ratios expected from a cross.

examples.title: Worked example — Mendel's Laws: How Traits Travel Between Generations
examples.problem: The risk that two unaffected carriers of cystic fibrosis have an affected child.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive — only the double-recessive genotype is affected.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: both carrier parents are Cc. The Cc × Cc Punnett square gives CC, Cc, Cc, and cc — one cc combination in four.

examples.result: a 25 percent chance of an affected child per pregnancy, a 50 percent chance of a carrier like the parents, and 25 percent of a non-carrier — Mendel's 3:1 arithmetic running in a modern clinic.

keyTakeaways: Carrier screening for recessive diseases counsels couples with Mendelian odds before pregnancy.
Plant and animal breeding still runs on segregation ratios and selection indices.
DNA paternity and forensic tests track alleles as Mendelian markers across generations.
Classroom corn ears showing 9:3:3:1 kernel ratios demonstrate assortment on a single cob.
The royal hemophilia pedigree traced a recessive X-linked allele across Victorian Europe.

quiz.q: Two heterozygous parents (Tt × Tt) are crossed. What fraction of offspring shows the recessive phenotype?
quiz.explanation: One tt combination in four — the signature 3:1 phenotypic ratio.

quiz.q: Independent assortment fails when two genes:
options: sit close together on the same chromosome
quiz.explanation: Linked genes travel together through meiosis — recombination only occasionally breaks the pair.

quiz.q: In codominance, a heterozygote:
options: expresses both alleles distinctly, as in AB blood
quiz.explanation: Both products are made side by side — A and B antigens together, not a blend of them.

quiz.q: A pedigree showing healthy parents with affected siblings, skipping generations, suggests:
quiz.explanation: Unaffected carriers producing affected children is the classic recessive signature.

intro:
Life on Earth is not a smear of intermediates but a world of discrete kinds — and the discreteness is the work of speciation, the process by which one lineage splits into two that can no longer exchange genes. It is evolution's grand product, the process that turned one ancestral population into an estimated eight million kinds. This topic covers how biologists delimit species, the barriers that keep lineages apart, the geographic and genetic routes by which splits happen, and the trees that display the results.

**Why this matters.** Speciation is where evolutionary theory meets the courtroom and the farm: species concepts decide which populations get endangered-species protection, and whether wolves and dogs are one species or two. Crop wild relatives are separated from crops by exactly the barriers described here — and sometimes not.
objectives: Explain what a species is — and when it blurs
Explain prezygotic barriers: stopping the meeting
Explain postzygotic barriers: stopping the heirs
Explain allopatric: divided by geography
Explain sympatric: divided without moving
Explain phylogenetic trees: reading the branches

concepts.term: What a species is — and when it blurs
concepts.statement: The biological species concept defines a species as a population whose members breed with each other but not — in nature — with outsiders, its boundary maintained by the absence of gene flow. It works cleanly for animals but blurs elsewhere: bacteria trade genes without mating, fossils cannot be test-bred, and ring species interbreed neighbor-to-neighbor while the two ends refuse each other. Biologists carry several concepts because nature refuses to carry only one.

Barriers acting before fertilization are the cheapest. Populations may never meet — separate ponds, separate host plants — or may breed in different seasons or hours, court with songs or scents the other population does not recognize, or fail at mating mechanically. Each barrier is a lane closure; stacked together, they end traffic between two gene pools before any egg is wasted.

When mating still happens, barriers act after it. Hybrid embryos may die early; hybrids may be viable but sterile, like the mule; or the second generation may collapse, failing to survive or reproduce. Each wasted mating is an evolutionary dead end, and selection then favors sharper prezygotic barriers — one reason sibling species often differ most in their mating signals.

The classic route is geographic: a river changes course, an island breaks away, a glacier splits a grassland in two. The separated halves evolve independently — by drift and by selection on their own conditions — until reunion no longer produces working hybrids. The two squirrel species facing each other across the Grand Canyon split exactly this way, a textbook case of allopatry.

Splitting without a map change is rarer but real. In plants, a chromosome-doubling error creates a polyploid that cannot mate successfully with its parent species — instantly, in one generation, a new species. In animals, sympatric splits usually ride on ecological specialization: hawthorn flies that colonized apple orchards now breed on a different fruit at a different time, drifting apart while living side by side.

The result of all this splitting is a phylogeny — a tree whose branch points are speciation events and whose leaves are living species. Shared derived traits diagnose real branches, and branch lengths can measure time. Modern trees are computed from DNA sequences, and reading one is reading a family album: every fork in the canopy is a population that once split, most often never to rejoin.

Speciation is not an individual transforming — no animal hatches as a new species; it is a population-level change in who breeds with whom. The boundary is often a long gray zone of partial interbreeding, so "two species or one" can be genuinely unanswerable. And barriers evolve as by-products of divergence: evolution does not aim to make species — species fall out as consequences.
A species defined by interbreeding within, and reproductive isolation from, other groups.
Movement of alleles between populations through interbreeding — the glue of a species.
A barrier acting before fertilization — timing, behavior, anatomy, or habitat.
A barrier acting after fertilization — hybrid inviability or sterility.
Splitting promoted by geographic separation of populations.
Extra chromosome sets, instantly creating reproductive barriers in plants.
A branching diagram of lineages whose forks are speciation events.

examples.title: Worked example — How New Species Are Born
examples.problem: How bread wheat became a species unable to breed with its own ancestors.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: sympatric speciation by polyploidy — chromosome doubling breaks mating compatibility in a single step.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: about 10,000 years ago, hybridization between two wild grasses gave a sterile plant; chromosome doubling restored pairing at 28 chromosomes (emmer wheat); a later second hybridization and another doubling produced bread wheat at 42.

examples.result: bread wheat cannot exchange genes with any of its three parent species — a new species born of a counting error, now sown across more of the planet than any wild grass.

keyTakeaways: Polyploid crops — wheat, cotton, strawberry — are human-adopted species born from chromosome doubling.
Lake Victoria cichlids diversified into hundreds of species within a single lake basin.
Hawthorn flies colonizing apple orchards record a sympatric split now in progress.
Endangered-species law turns on species delimitation — the red wolf's legal status is a species-concept case.
DNA-based phylogenies settled that the hippopotamus is the whale's closest living relative.

quiz.q: The biological species concept rests on:
options: potential to interbreed, with no gene flow outward
quiz.explanation: Who breeds with whom — not looks — draws the boundary, wherever the test can be applied at all.

quiz.q: A mule, healthy but sterile, exemplifies:
quiz.explanation: The horse-donkey mating succeeds; the barrier strikes the hybrid itself — sterility after fertilization.

quiz.q: Allopatric speciation begins with:
quiz.explanation: Physical separation halts gene flow; divergence then accumulates independently on each side.

quiz.q: Polyploid speciation is most frequent in:
quiz.explanation: Plants tolerate chromosome doubling — and can self-fertilize or double again to escape sterility.

intro:
Somewhere between six and seven million years ago, an African ape population split in two: one branch leads to today's chimpanzees and bonobos, the other to every human being who has ever lived. The story of that second branch is written in fragmentary skeletons, chipped stones, and — only since 2010 — in DNA recovered from the bones themselves. This topic traces the main chapters, from Lucy's small-brained bipedality to the global species reading this sentence.

**Why this matters.** Human evolution was never a ladder. For most of the last three million years, several hominin species shared the planet at once; Homo sapiens is the last branch standing, not the summit of a staircase. Every new fossil nudges the details without shaking the outline — and ancient DNA now settles disputes fossils never could.
objectives: Explain hominins: the walk comes first
Explain lucy and the australopithecines
Explain the Homo lineage: brain meets tools
Explain sapiens, Neanderthals, and interbreeding
Explain out of Africa
Explain reading the evidence: fossils, stone, DNA

concepts.statement: The first defining trait was underfoot. Bipedalism — habitual walking on two legs — predates big brains, tools, and language by millions of years, visible in four-million-year-old Ardipithecus bones and in the Laetoli footprints, an upright pair's trail preserved in volcanic ash some 3.6 million years ago. Freed hands, energy-cheap walking, and a view over the grass came before everything else.

The most famous fossil, Lucy — an Australopithecus afarensis from Ethiopia, 3.2 million years old — stood barely a meter tall with a brain near 400 cubic centimeters: a chimpanzee-sized brain riding on a human-style pelvis, spine, and knees. Australopithecines kept long arms suited to climbing, ate everything from fruit to tubers, and their kind persisted across Africa for well over a million years.

concepts.term: The Homo lineage: brain meets tools
concepts.statement: By 2.4 million years ago, larger brains and the first sharp stone tools mark Homo habilis. Homo erectus, appearing near 1.9 million years ago, had a tall striding body, a brain approaching 1,000 cubic centimeters, and the range to walk out of Africa into Asia — the first globetrotter. Through the ice ages, brain volume climbed toward the modern average of about 1,350 cubic centimeters as toolkits diversified, fire spread, and hunting grew serious.

Homo sapiens enters the African fossil record near 300,000 years ago at Jebel Irhoud, Morocco. Meanwhile, Europe and Asia belonged to the Neanderthals — heavy-browed, cold-adapted hunters — and to the Denisovans, known almost entirely from DNA. The groups met: most people with non-African ancestry carry 1-4 percent Neanderthal DNA, and a Denisovan version of the altitude gene EPAS1 helps Tibetans live above 4,000 meters.

Genetics, fossils, and archaeology agree on the outline: a main dispersal out of Africa around 60,000-70,000 years ago reached Australia by about 50,000 years ago and the Americas by around 15,000. Earlier excursions left fossils and stone tools but no descendants in today's gene pool. Every living population descends from African ancestors — legible in the diversity of African genomes, deeper than anywhere else on Earth.

concepts.term: Reading the evidence: fossils, stone, DNA
concepts.statement: The evidence stacks in independent layers. Fossils give anatomy and radiometric dates; tools, hearths, and art give behavior; ancient DNA, first recovered from Neanderthal bones in 2010, gives migrations and interbreeding directly. When a discovery moves a date or adds a branch, the genetic clock and the stones move with it — the sign of a story that keeps checking out.

The march-of-progress cartoon is wrong twice over: evolution has no direction or goal, and humans did not descend from any living ape — chimpanzees are cousins, not ancestors, both lines having evolved since the split. "Missing link" is a relic phrase; the bush is richly populated. And human genetic variation does not sort into deep continental lineages: most of humanity's diversity lies within Africa, and the rest of the world carries only a subset of it.
Any species on the human side of the split from the chimpanzee lineage.
Habitual upright walking on two legs — the earliest hominin signature.
The genus of Lucy: small-brained, upright-walking African hominins.
The tall, wide-ranging hominin of the last two million years.
The cold-adapted Eurasian hominin that interbred with sapiens.
Dating divergence by counting neutral mutations that accumulate at steady rates.
Genetic material recovered from fossils, readable at scale since 2010.

examples.title: Worked example — From Lucy to Us: The Story of Human Evolution
examples.problem: How DNA itself dates the split between the human and chimpanzee lineages.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: the molecular clock — neutral mutations accumulate at a roughly steady rate per lineage.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: the two genomes differ at about 1.2 percent of DNA positions; at roughly 0.1 percent per million years per lineage, the two lines together close that gap in about six million years.

examples.result: a split near six million years ago, matching the oldest putative hominin fossils — independent clocks vouching for one another.

keyTakeaways: Ancient DNA extracted from bones now tests migration and interbreeding claims directly.
Rift Valley fieldwork keeps adding branches — Homo naledi was announced only in 2015.
EPAS1, an inherited Denisovan gene, helps Tibetans thrive at extreme altitude.
Neanderthal-derived immune and skin genes still influence disease risk and drug response.
Argon and uranium dating anchor each fossil's age within a few percent.

quiz.q: The earliest defining trait of the hominin lineage was:
quiz.explanation: Upright walking shows up millions of years before brains expanded — the feet came first.

quiz.q: Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) is famous for showing:
options: a chimp-sized brain on a bipedal body
quiz.explanation: About 400 cubic centimeters of brain on a human-style pelvis and knees — walking long before thinking much.

quiz.q: Most people with non-African ancestry carry:
quiz.explanation: Interbreeding with Neanderthals left a measurable signature in non-African genomes.

quiz.q: The main Homo sapiens dispersal from Africa occurred roughly:
quiz.explanation: Earlier humans left Africa too, but the dominant ancestry of living non-Africans traces to that late dispersal.

intro:
Animals are multicellular consumers — they eat other organisms, lack the rigid walls and chloroplasts of plants, and bind their cells together with the protein collagen. From that single shared decision, evolution has assembled over thirty phyla: sponges that pump, jellyfish that sting, worms that burrow, squid that solve problems, and everything with a backbone. This tour walks the major body plans — symmetry, layers, cavities — and the phyla built from them.

**Why this matters.** Arthropods alone — insects, spiders, crustaceans — account for more than 80 percent of all described animal species. Chordates, the phylum containing every fish, bird, and mammal, are a rounding error by headcount. Familiarity is not importance, and reading the tree corrects the eye.
objectives: Explain what makes an animal an animal
Explain symmetry and the rise of a head end
Explain germ layers and body cavities
Explain the phylum tour: sponges to chordates
Explain protostomes, deuterostomes, and your kin

concepts.term: What makes an animal an animal
concepts.statement: Animals are heterotrophs: they obtain energy and carbon by eating, not by photosynthesis. Their cells lack walls, letting them squeeze, change shape, and form muscles and nerves; collagen glues the tissues together. Almost all animals develop from a blastula embryo and move under their own power at some stage of life — the sponges, permanently anchored, mark the base of the tree.

concepts.term: Symmetry and the rise of a head end
concepts.statement: Sponges are asymmetrical. Cnidarians — jellyfish, anemones, corals — are radial, built like wheels with many identical spokes and no front or back. The decisive invention is bilateral symmetry: a head-to-tail axis with mirrored sides, which pairs muscles for directed crawling and concentrates sense organs at the front that travels first — cephalization. From flatworms to falcons, that is the layout.

Embryos build from germ layers. Cnidarians are diploblastic — two tissue layers; all bilaterians are triploblastic, adding a middle mesoderm that becomes muscle, bone, heart, and kidney. Many also excavate a coelom, a fluid-filled cavity between gut and body wall that cushions organs and gives muscles a hydrostatic scaffold to push against — the trick behind an earthworm's crawl.

concepts.term: The phylum tour: sponges to chordates
concepts.statement: The tour, briefly. Sponges (Porifera) filter-feed without nerves or muscles; cnidarians sting with explosive harpoon cells; flatworms (Platyhelminthes) are thin enough to need no cavity; roundworms (Nematoda) molt and occur in staggering numbers; mollusks (Mollusca) run from snails to octopuses, the most intelligent invertebrates; annelids (Annelida) add segmented bodies; arthropods dominate on jointed legs and chitin armor; echinoderms like starfish run on hydraulic water-vascular systems; and chordates get a notochord, a hollow dorsal nerve cord, and a post-anal tail at some stage.

Bilaterians split deep by one embryological detail: which opening of the early gut becomes the mouth. In protostomes — arthropods, mollusks, annelids — the first opening becomes the mouth. In deuterostomes — echinoderms and chordates — it becomes the anus, and the mouth opens second. The startling consequence: by development, you are more closely related to a starfish than to a lobster, resemblance notwithstanding.

Evolution is not a ladder from sponge to human: phyla are separate, contemporaneous strategies, and the sponge lineage is as "evolved" as you are — just aimed elsewhere. "Worm" describes a shape, not a lineage: flatworms, roundworms, and annelids are about as distantly related as three animals can be while still being worms. And vertebrates are a subphylum of chordates — a branch of a branch, not a peer of the phyla.
A major branch of the animal family tree, ranked below kingdom.
A body organized around an axis with many identical parts, as in jellyfish.
A head-to-tail axis with mirrored sides, enabling directed movement.
The concentration of sense organs and neurons at the leading end.
A fluid-filled body cavity cushioning organs and enabling hydrostatic movement.
A bilaterian whose embryonic first gut opening becomes the mouth.
The stiffening rod along the back of chordates, ancestral to the spine.

examples.title: Worked example — The Animal Kingdom: A Tour of Body Plans and Phyla
examples.problem: How animal species are distributed across phyla.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: diversity is wildly uneven across body plans.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: of roughly 1.5 million described animal species, arthropods account for over a million; mollusks about 85,000; chordates about 70,000 — and mammals, for all their prominence, only some 6,500.

examples.result: a randomly chosen animal is almost certainly an arthropod, most likely an insect — the familiar vertebrate cast is a statistical fringe.

keyTakeaways: Coral reefs — cnidarian skeletons — shelter perhaps a quarter of marine species on under one percent of the ocean floor.
Soil-transmitted worm infections affect well over a billion people, driving tropical-medicine programs.
Octopus cognition research has rewritten ideas about invertebrate intelligence — and cephalopod welfare rules.
Tunicate and lancelet genomes illuminate how the vertebrate body was assembled.
Insect monitoring programs track ecosystem health, since arthropods respond fastest to change.

quiz.q: Animals differ from plants and fungi fundamentally in that they:
options: eat other organisms and lack cell walls
quiz.explanation: Heterotrophy plus wall-less, collagen-bound cells — the traits behind muscles and nerves.

quiz.q: Cephalization is:
options: the concentration of sense organs at a head end
the formation of a body cavity
quiz.explanation: Bilateral bodies travel head-first, so sensors and neurons gather at the front.

quiz.q: In deuterostomes, the embryo's first opening becomes:
options: the anus, with the mouth forming second
quiz.explanation: Mouth-second development groups echinoderms with chordates — starfish are your kin, lobsters are not.

quiz.q: Insects, spiders, and crabs belong to the phylum:
quiz.explanation: Jointed appendages plus a chitin exoskeleton define Arthropoda, the most speciose phylum.

intro:
Every living cell runs on one accounting trick: capture energy from food, bank it briefly as ATP, spend it instantly on work. Biochemistry, the branch that studies the molecules running inside organisms, traces that currency through its whole economy — how glucose is dismantled step by step, where the electron transport chain fits, why the true yield is about 30-32 ATP per glucose rather than the 36 older textbooks quote, and how enzymes make all of it fast enough to matter. This is the respiration half of the energy story; photosynthesis, the other half, lives in Botany.

**Why this matters.** Metabolic logic explains why you cannot sprint for a mile, why cyanide kills in minutes, and why statins lower cholesterol: nearly every drug target in the body is an enzyme sitting on one of these pathways.
objectives: Explain aTP: the spent-and-recycled currency
Explain glycolysis, Krebs cycle, electron transport
Explain chemiosmosis: gradients before ATP
Explain real accounting: 30-32 ATP per glucose
Explain enzymes and activation energy
Explain michaelis-Menten kinetics
Explain catabolism and anabolism integrated

concepts.statement: ATP is a nucleotide carrying two extra phosphates, and snapping off the last one releases about 30.5 kilojoules per mole. Cells couple that hydrolysis to reactions that would otherwise not run — contracting a muscle, pumping calcium. The pool holds seconds of supply, so a resting adult recycles roughly her own body weight of ATP daily.

Glycolysis is the oldest and most conservative module: ten enzyme steps in the cytosol split one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvates, yielding a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH. It needs no oxygen, which is why it predates the atmosphere's oxygen and why your muscles can still work in short anaerobic bursts — with pyruvate diverted to lactate to regenerate NAD+.

Aerobic cells hand pyruvate to the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix. After pyruvate dehydrogenase trims pyruvate to an acetyl group, each two-carbon acetyl joins oxaloacetate and the cycle turns twice per glucose, producing per turn 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 ATP-equivalent, with carbon leaving as CO2. The cycle doubles as a parts depot, its intermediates siphoned off to build amino acids and heme.

The payoff comes at the inner membrane. NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the transport chain's complexes, which pump protons outward and leave oxygen as the final electron acceptor, producing water. The stored gradient then drives protons back through ATP synthase — chemiosmosis, Peter Mitchell's radical idea before it won the 1978 Nobel Prize. Measured ratios give about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2, which enters later in the chain and pumps less.

None of it runs at useful speed without enzymes. An enzyme lowers the activation energy of a reaction by stabilizing its transition state; it never changes the reaction's equilibrium or makes an unfavorable one spontaneous. Because each enzyme molecule works on one substrate at a time, reaction rate climbs with substrate concentration and then saturates — the shape Michaelis and Menten captured in 1913, where Km is the substrate concentration at half-maximal velocity.

Finally, the modules are wired together. Catabolism — breaking molecules down — feeds anabolism, building them up, through shared intermediates: citrate from the Krebs cycle becomes the carbon source for fatty-acid synthesis, and glycolysis runs backward as gluconeogenesis when blood sugar dips. Insulin and glucagon flip the switches, and the AMP-activated kinase acts as the low-fuel alarm that idles expensive synthesis when ATP runs short.
$$C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6\,O_2 \rightarrow 6\,CO_2 + 6\,H_2O \quad (\Delta G \approx -2870\ \text{kJ/mol})$$
concepts.detail: Complete oxidation of one glucose releases about 2,870 kilojoules; the cell banks roughly a third of it as ATP and lets the rest go as heat.

concepts.statement: $$4\,\text{ATP}_{\text{direct}} + 10\,\text{NADH}\times 2.5 + 2\,\text{FADH}_2\times 1.5 = 30{-}32\,\text{ATP}$$
concepts.detail: Four substrate-level ATP plus oxidative phosphorylation at the measured ratios — 32 with the efficient malate-aspartate shuttle, 30 with the cheaper glycerol-3-phosphate one.
Reaction velocity rises with substrate concentration and saturates at Vmax; Km is the substrate level that gives half of Vmax, a proxy for binding tightness.

concepts.statement: The classic error is quoting 36-38 ATP: modern measurements of the ATP synthase and proton-pumping stoichiometry give about 30-32. ATP is also not stored fuel like fat — it is a recycled middleman holding seconds of supply. Enzymes are catalysts, not magicians: they change speeds, never whether a reaction is favorable. And oxygen does not get glued onto carbon to make ATP — it only accepts spent electrons at the end of the chain.
Adenosine triphosphate — the phosphorylated nucleotide whose hydrolysis powers cellular work.
The ten-step cytosolic split of glucose to two pyruvates; net 2 ATP and 2 NADH, no oxygen required.
The mitochondrial cycle oxidizing acetyl groups to CO2 while loading electrons onto NADH and FADH2.
Using a proton gradient across a membrane to drive ATP synthase.
The inner-membrane complexes that pass electrons to oxygen and pump protons.
In Michaelis-Menten kinetics, the substrate concentration at half-maximal velocity.
The energy hill between reactants and transition state, lowered by enzymes.

examples.title: Worked example — Biochemistry: The Cell's Energy Economy
examples.problem: The total ATP a cell extracts from one glucose molecule, using the efficient shuttle.

steps.label: Recall the tallies
steps.text: glycolysis nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH; pyruvate dehydrogenase makes 2 NADH; two turns of the Krebs cycle make 2 ATP, 6 NADH, and 2 FADH2 — 10 NADH and 2 FADH2 in all reach the chain.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: direct ATP is 2 + 2 = 4; oxidation gives 10 NADH at 2.5 each = 25, and 2 FADH2 at 1.5 each = 3.

examples.result: 4 + 25 + 3 = 32 ATP per glucose — or 30 if the cytosolic NADH enter via the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle, which is why the honest figure is a range of 30-32.

keyTakeaways: Cyanide and carbon monoxide poison the chain's oxygen-facing complex, halting ATP production within minutes; antidotes out-compete the poison.
Brown fat uncouples the gradient on purpose, leaking protons to make heat instead of ATP; it keeps infants and hibernating mammals warm.
Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, lowering blood cholesterol for millions of patients.
Tumors absorb glucose and ferment it even with oxygen present — the Warburg effect — which is exactly what a PET scan visualizes.
Brewing and bioethanol depend on yeast running glycolysis to ethanol when oxygen is withheld.

quiz.q: Glycolysis of one glucose molecule directly nets:
quiz.explanation: It costs 2 ATP to prime the sugar and earns 4 back, for a net of 2 ATP plus 2 NADH.

quiz.q: What does oxygen actually do in aerobic respiration?
options: It binds glucose to start glycolysis
It accepts electrons at the end of the transport chain, forming water
It carries protons across the inner membrane
quiz.explanation: Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor; without it the chain backs up and ATP synthesis stops.

quiz.q: In the Michaelis-Menten equation, Km equals:
options: the substrate concentration giving half of Vmax
the activation energy of the reaction
quiz.explanation: Km is read off the curve as the substrate level at which velocity reaches half its saturating value.

quiz.q: Why do current textbooks quote 30-32 ATP per glucose rather than 36-38?
options: because glycolysis makes less ATP than believed
because P/O ratios are about 2.5 per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2, with shuttle costs subtracted
because oxygen is scarce in cells
because the Krebs cycle skips two turns
quiz.explanation: Measured stoichiometries and the cost of importing cytosolic NADH lower the older, rounder numbers.

intro:
