Follow immediately with the quadratics lesson — this lesson’s factorising is that lesson’s first solving method — and then with simultaneous equations and graph-sketching topics. Primary reading: OpenStax, Intermediate Algebra 2e, ch.1 “The Language of Algebra” for the vocabulary and ch.9’s factoring review for the patterns (openstax.org, CC BY-NC-SA).
Anatomy: terms, coefficients (sign included), degrees (highest wins).
Collect like terms — identical letter parts only, signs carried.
Expand with the distributive law; double brackets give four products.
Factorise in order: common factor, named patterns, factor pair of c summing to b.
Rearrange: reverse order, symmetric operations, factor the target out when it repeats.
Equations are solved; identities (≡) are shown — different commands entirely.

quiz.q: In the expression 5x³ − 2x + 8, what is the coefficient of x and the degree of the expression?
quiz.explanation: The x-term is −2x, so its coefficient is −2 (sign included); the highest term degree is 3, which is the expression’s degree.

quiz.q: Expand and simplify (x − 3)(x + 5).
quiz.explanation: Four products: x² + 5x − 3x − 15 = x² + 2x − 15. Middle coefficient = 5 + (−3) = 2; constant = 5 × (−3) = −15.

quiz.q: Factorise 4x² − 25.
quiz.explanation: Difference of squares: 4x² = (2x)² and 25 = 5², so a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) with a = 2x, b = 5.

quiz.q: Rearrange p = 2(a + b) to make b the subject.
quiz.explanation: Divide both sides by 2 first (a + b = p/2), then subtract a: b = p/2 − a, which equals (p − 2a)/2. Reverse order, symmetric operations.

quiz.q: Which statement is an identity rather than an equation?
quiz.explanation: It holds for every x — an expansion pattern stated as a fact, marked with ≡. The others hold only for specific values and are solved.

intro: Quadratic equations are the boundary between school arithmetic and real algebra: the first equation type whose solutions are not obvious, and the template for every higher-degree technique that follows. Projectile heights, areas, revenue curves — when one quantity is the square of another plus a linear term, a quadratic models it. The examinable skill set is compact and fixed: put the equation in standard form, choose among four solving methods, read the discriminant to know how many solutions exist, and switch to vertex form when the question asks for a maximum or minimum. This lesson covers all four moves and the decision rule between them.
objectives: Explain standard form ax² + bx + c = 0
Explain solving by factorising
Explain the square-root property
Explain completing the square: the recipe and why it works
Explain the quadratic formula and its four-step use
Explain the discriminant and the number of solutions
Explain choosing the fastest method
Explain vertex form and applications

concepts.statement: Standard form is ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0 — everything moved to one side, zero on the other. Every method begins here, and most lost marks on quadratics are lost before any solving: a sign dropped while moving terms poisons everything downstream. Rearrange first, identify a, b and c, then solve.

Method one, factorising, uses the algebra lesson’s machinery: x² − x − 12 = 0 factorises to (x − 4)(x + 3) = 0, and a product is zero only when a factor is zero — so x = 4 or x = −3. Fast and clean when the factor pair is friendly. Method two, the square-root property, handles the missing-middle-term shape: x² = k gives x = ±√k (both roots!), and a(x − h)² = k gives x = h ± √(k/a). The habit to keep: a square root always carries a plus-or-minus — forgetting the negative root is the single most common answer-killing slip on this method.

Completing the square rewrites any quadratic so the x appears exactly once, squared: x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² + (c − b²/4). The recipe, when the leading coefficient is 1: take half of b, square it, add and subtract that square, then regroup. For x² + 6x + 2 = 0: half of 6 is 3, squared is 9, so x² + 6x + 2 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 2 = (x + 3)² − 7; setting this to zero gives (x + 3)² = 7 and x = −3 ± √7. When the leading coefficient is not 1, divide the whole equation by a first — OpenStax’s Intermediate Algebra makes the same point: completing the square requires a = 1, so make it so.

concepts.term: Completing the square: the recipe and why it works
concepts.statement: Why the maneuver works: (x + b/2)² expands to x² + bx + b²/4 — the square of half of b is exactly the constant that completes x² + bx into a perfect square. Adding and subtracting b²/4 changes nothing while creating that square. Beyond solving, the form pays twice: (x − h)² + k is the vertex form of the parabola, handing over the turning point (h, k) directly, and it is the launchpad from which the quadratic formula is derived.

concepts.term: The quadratic formula and its four-step use
concepts.statement: Method four works on every quadratic: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a). OpenStax drills a four-step procedure: write the equation in standard form and identify a, b, c; write the formula; substitute; simplify — and then CHECK the solutions by substitution. Worked example from the same text: 2x² + 9x − 5 = 0 has a = 2, b = 9, c = −5, giving x = (−9 ± √(81 + 40))/4 = (−9 ± 11)/4, so x = 1/2 or x = −5. The formula is an equation — start every line with x =, and keep the whole numerator over the whole denominator.

concepts.term: The discriminant and the number of solutions
concepts.statement: The discriminant b² − 4ac counts the solutions before any arithmetic: positive — two distinct real roots; zero — exactly one (a repeated root; the parabola touches the axis); negative — no real roots (two complex ones). So b² − 4ac = 9 − 4(1)(−4) style questions are answered by inspection after computing one number. The method-choice strategy rounds out the toolkit, in OpenStax’s order: try factorising first if the factors are easy; use the square-root property if the shape fits; otherwise the quadratic formula — and completing the square is the method you fall back on when you must SHOW the vertex or the derivation. Applications tie it together: projectile height h = −16t² + v₀t questions ask “when is h = 0?” (solve) or “what is the maximum height?” (vertex form, or −b/2a for the time).

Solving before reaching standard form — always gather to ax² + bx + c = 0 first. Dropping the ± on square roots, in the square-root property and the formula alike. Halving b twice or forgetting to divide by a before completing the square when a ≠ 1. Writing the formula with only part of the numerator over 2a — the whole of −b ± √(b² − 4ac) sits over 2a. Announcing one solution when the discriminant is negative and “no real solutions” was meant — complex roots still exist. Answering maximum-height questions with roots instead of the vertex. And skipping the check — substitution catches sign slips the algebra hid.

examples.title: Worked Example — One equation, method decision live
examples.problem: Quadratics: Four Ways to Solve, One Formula to Rule Them — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Solve 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0. Standard form already; a = 2, b = −4, c = −3.

steps.label: Method check
steps.text: factorising — factors of 2 × (−3) summing to −4? −6 and 2 give −4, but 2x² + 2x − 6x − 3 resists clean grouping (2x(x+1) − 3(2x+1)) — not friendly. Square-root property: no isolated square. So: quadratic formula.

steps.label: Discriminant read
steps.text: b² − 4ac = 16 + 24 = 40 > 0 — two distinct real roots, as found. (If it had been 0, the equation would collapse to one root; negative, none.)

steps.label: Vertex bonus
steps.text: x = −b/2a = 4/4 = 1; f(1) = 2 − 4 − 3 = −5. Vertex (1, −5) — the minimum, since a > 0. The same numbers, read two ways.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: the algebraic-notation-and-manipulation lesson — factorising and rearranging are this lesson’s first and third methods. Follow with function-graphing topics (the parabola as a function’s picture) and, later, the derivative lesson, whose critical points generalize the vertex. Primary reading: OpenStax, Intermediate Algebra 2e §9.2 “Solve Quadratic Equations by Completing the Square” and §9.3 “Solve Quadratic Equations Using the Quadratic Formula”, with §9.5’s projectile applications (openstax.org, CC BY-NC-SA).
Standard form first: ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0; identify a, b, c.
Factorise when friendly; square-root property when a square stands alone — both roots.
Complete the square: half of b, squared, added and subtracted; divide by a first if needed.
Formula: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a — four steps, then check.
Discriminant trichotomy: positive two, zero one, negative none.
Vertex from −b/2a: maxima and minima live there, not at the roots.

quiz.q: Solve x² = 49.
quiz.explanation: Square-root property: x = ±√49 = ±7. Every square root in solving carries both signs — the negative root is the classic dropped solution.

quiz.q: What number completes the square for x² + 10x + 3?
quiz.explanation: Half of b = 5; squared = 25. x² + 10x + 25 = (x + 5)², so the expression becomes (x + 5)² − 22.

quiz.q: For 3x² + 2x + 5 = 0, the discriminant is
quiz.explanation: b² − 4ac = 2² − 4(3)(5) = 4 − 60 = −56. Negative discriminant means the parabola never meets the x-axis — no real roots.

quiz.q: According to the standard method-choice strategy, which equation is best solved by the square-root property?
quiz.explanation: The shape (x − h)² = k is the square-root property’s home turf: x − 3 = ±√12 directly. The others suit factorising or the formula.

quiz.q: A ball’s height is h = −16t² + 40t. What is its maximum height?
quiz.explanation: Maxima need the vertex, not the roots: t = −b/2a = 1.25 s, h(1.25) = −16(1.5625) + 50 = 25. Solving h = 0 finds landing time, not peak.

intro: Sets are the containers of mathematics and logic is its grammar; both supply the precise vocabulary every later subject borrows — functions map between sets, probability measures them, proofs argue in logical forms. Yet the vocabulary itself is often assumed rather than taught, which is why phrases like “if and only if” or “at least one” trip otherwise strong students. This lesson fixes the vocabulary in place: what a set is and how to draw one, what the five connectives mean, how conditionals split into converse, inverse and contrapositive, and how the two languages — sets and statements — mirror each other through De Morgan’s laws.
objectives: Explain roster and set-builder forms
Explain membership, subsets and set equality
Explain venn diagrams and two-set regions
Explain union, intersection and complement
Explain counting with the inclusion-exclusion formula
Explain statements, negation and quantifiers
Explain and, or, not: compound statements
Explain conditionals: converse, inverse, contrapositive
Explain necessary and sufficient conditions
Explain de Morgan's laws in logic and in sets

concepts.statement: The treatment follows the open textbook Contemporary Mathematics (OpenStax), whose first two chapters give exactly this ground floor: Chapter 1 runs from basic set concepts through subsets and Venn diagrams to set operations with two and three sets; Chapter 2 runs from statements and quantifiers through compound statements and truth tables to equivalent statements, De Morgan’s laws and logical arguments. Everything below is that material in exam-ready form, with the notation compressed to what assessments actually use.

A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects — well-defined meaning membership is decidable: either 3 belongs to the set of odd numbers or it does not, with no arguing. Two notations define sets. Roster form lists elements between braces: A = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Set-builder form states the membership condition: A = {x | x is a natural number less than 5}. Membership uses ∈ (3 ∈ A) and non-membership ∉ (7 ∉ A). The empty set ∅ has no elements; the cardinality n(A) counts them, so n(A) = 4 and n(∅) = 0. One caution the assessments love: order and repetition do not matter in roster form — {1, 2, 2, 3} is just {1, 2, 3} — and the empty set is not the same as the set containing zero.

A is a subset of B, written A ⊆ B, when every element of A is also an element of B; it is a proper subset, A ⊂ B, when B additionally has elements A lacks. Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set — two conventions worth memorizing because true/false questions target them directly. Equality of sets is mutual containment: A = B exactly when A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A. Fixing a universal set U — the universe of discourse for the problem, say all students in a school — lets you define the complement A′: everything in U outside A. n(A′) = n(U) − n(A), the single most-used counting fact in this topic.

The union A ∪ B is everything in A or B (or both); the intersection A ∩ B is everything in both; two sets are disjoint when A ∩ B = ∅. Venn diagrams turn these definitions into pictures: two overlapping circles inside the universal-set rectangle carve the plane into four regions — A only, B only, both, neither — and every counting problem is a matter of filling those regions from the inside out: intersection first, then the “only” regions by subtraction. The inclusion-exclusion formula compresses the picture: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B); the subtraction corrects the double-count of the overlap. With three sets the diagram has eight regions and the principle is unchanged — fill the innermost overlap first — though the full formula adds and subtracts three more terms.

The set operations mirror the logical connectives, which is no accident: “in A ∪ B” means “in A or in B”, and “in A ∩ B” means “in A and in B”. Keep that dictionary in your pocket — every logic law below has a set twin, and exam questions exploit the translation in both directions, most often through the complement laws (A ∪ A′ = U, A ∩ A′ = ∅) and through De Morgan’s set form.

A logical statement is a declarative sentence that is definitively true or false — questions (“is it raining?”), commands (“close the door”) and opinions without a truth condition do not qualify. Negation flips the truth value: the negation of “the door is open” is “the door is not open”, and negation of a negation restores the original. Quantified statements bring generality: “all A are B”, “no A are B”, “some A are B” (where “some” means at least one). Their negations are the exam’s favourite trap, so memorize the pair: the negation of “all are” is “some are not” — NOT “none are”; the negation of “some are” is “none are”; the negation of “no A are B” is “some A are B”. One bird that is not a raven kills “all birds are ravens”, but does not touch “no birds are ravens” — it proves that one false.

Compound statements join simpler ones with “and” (∧, the conjunction — true only when both parts are true), “or” (∨, the disjunction — true when at least one part is true, the inclusive reading that formal logic always takes), and “not” (¬). Truth tables list every case, and their four-line tables for two statements are the ground truth from which every equivalence below is verified. The conditional “if p then q” (p → q) gets its own table: it is false only when p is true and q is false — the one case where the promise was broken. When the hypothesis is false the conditional is vacuously true, a convention that feels strange and is tested constantly.

From a conditional p → q, three variants are formed by juggling p and q with negation: the converse q → p (conditions swapped), the inverse ¬p → ¬q (both negated), and the contrapositive ¬q → ¬p (swapped and negated). Exactly one variant is logically equivalent to the original: the contrapositive. “If it is a swan then it is a bird” is the same claim as “If it is not a bird then it is not a swan” — but NOT the same as “If it is a bird then it is a swan” (the converse), the single most common logic error in student writing and in option lists. To disprove a conditional, exhibit a case with p true and q false; to prove it, assume p and derive q — the contrapositive route counts as a proof because of the equivalence.

The same conditional carries the language of conditions: p is a sufficient condition for q when p → q (p alone guarantees q), and q is a necessary condition for p under the same arrow (q must hold for p to have any chance). So “being in A ∩ B is sufficient for being in A”, while “being in A is necessary for being in A ∩ B”. The biconditional p ↔ q — “p if and only if q” — holds when both arrows hold, making each condition both necessary and sufficient; set-wise it is equality, A = B.

concepts.term: De Morgan's laws in logic and in sets
concepts.statement: De Morgan’s laws close the mirror between the two languages: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q — negation flips and with ors and ors with ands. The set twins: (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′ and (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′. Finally, an argument is a chain of conditionals, and validity means the conclusion follows from the premises by form alone. The two workhorse forms: modus ponens (p → q, p, therefore q) and modus tollens (p → q, ¬q, therefore ¬p — contrapositive reasoning in action). The classic invalid look-alike, affirming the consequent (p → q, q, therefore p) is just the converse error wearing a suit.

Forgetting the subtraction in inclusion-exclusion — the overlap gets counted twice. Reading “some” as “not all” in formal logic; it means at least one, possibly all. Swapping in the converse when the contrapositive is called for. Misnegating quantified statements: “not all” is “some are not”, never “none are”. Treating a false-hypothesis conditional as false — it is vacuously true, the only false row being p true with q false. Filling Venn diagrams from the outside in, which garbles the “only” regions; always start from the innermost overlap.

examples.title: Worked Example — A survey counted by regions, a claim tested by contrapositive
examples.problem: Sets and Logical Terms: The Grammar of Precise Mathematics — worked through step by step

steps.label: Survey
steps.text: in a class of 40, n(Maths) = 22, n(Physics) = 18, and 8 students take both. How many take neither?

steps.label: Fill the Venn regions from the inside
steps.text: both = 8; Maths only = 22 − 8 = 14; Physics only = 18 − 8 = 10.

steps.label: Union
steps.text: n(Maths ∪ Physics) = 14 + 8 + 10 = 32 — check against the formula: 22 + 18 − 8 = 32.

steps.label: Neither = complement of the union
steps.text: 40 − 32 = 8 students. Every survey question is this recipe with different costumes.

steps.label: Logic check
steps.text: the claim “if a student takes Maths then she takes Physics” is false — the 14 Maths-only students are counterexamples. Its contrapositive “if she does not take Physics then she does not take Maths” is equally false; its converse is a different (also false) claim. Same diagram, two languages.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is a foundations lesson. Follow with the probability topics (events are sets, and “or”/“and” become union/intersection with rules attached) and the critical-reasoning lesson for arguments in natural language. Primary reading: OpenStax, Contemporary Mathematics, ch.1 “Sets” and ch.2 “Logic” (openstax.org, CC BY-NC-SA) — sections 1.1-1.5 and 2.1-2.7 cover everything here with fuller truth tables.
Sets: roster or set-builder; ∈ membership; n(A) counts; ∅ is a subset of everything.
Venn regions fill from the overlap out; n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
“And” is true only jointly; “or” is inclusive; → fails only when p true, q false.
Negate “all are” as “some are not”; negate “some are” as “none are”.
Only the contrapositive is equivalent; the converse is the classic decoy.
Sufficient writes p → q; necessary is q under the same arrow; both = biconditional.

quiz.q: Which statement about subsets is true by convention?
options: the empty set is a subset of no set
every set is a proper subset of itself
the empty set is a subset of every set
quiz.explanation: Vacuously, ∅ has no element outside any set, so ∅ ⊆ B for every B. Repetition never increases cardinality: {1, 2, 2, 3} = {1, 2, 3}, n = 3.

quiz.q: In a group, n(A) = 15, n(B) = 12 and n(A ∩ B) = 5. How many are in at least one of A, B?
quiz.explanation: Inclusion-exclusion: n(A ∪ B) = 15 + 12 − 5 = 22. Forgetting the subtraction — answer 27 — double-counts the five in both.

quiz.q: What is the negation of “all smartphone cameras have wide lenses”?
options: no smartphone cameras have wide lenses
all smartphone cameras lack wide lenses
some smartphone cameras do not have wide lenses
some smartphone cameras have wide lenses
quiz.explanation: “All are” dies on a single counterexample, so its negation is “some are not”. Answer 3 states something the original already implies — the classic decoy.

quiz.q: The statement “if a number is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by 3” is true. Which variant is guaranteed true as well?
options: if divisible by 3, then divisible by 6 (converse)
if not divisible by 6, then not divisible by 3 (inverse)
if not divisible by 3, then not divisible by 6 (contrapositive)
quiz.explanation: Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original. The converse is false (6 does not divide 3), and the inverse is its equivalent — equally false here.

quiz.q: In the sentence “passing the practical exam is necessary for certification”, which logical form is stated?
quiz.explanation: “q is necessary for p” writes as p → q — no certificate can exist unless the practical is passed. “Passing implies certification” would additionally make it sufficient — that stronger reading is the biconditional error.

intro: Limits tell you where a function is heading; continuity asks whether it actually arrives. The syllabus treats this as a diagnostic skill: given a function, locate every point of discontinuity, classify each one, and — where the discontinuity is removable — repair the function by redefining a single value. That final step, redefining the function to fill a hole, is the distinctive move of this topic. It converts an abstract limit computation into a concrete construction: you write down a slightly enlarged function that agrees with the original everywhere except one point, and at that one point takes the value the limit demands.
objectives: Explain three conditions for continuity at a point
Explain removable versus non-removable discontinuities
Explain redefining a function to fill a hole
Explain cancelling common factors to expose the limit
Explain confirming continuity after the repair
Explain jump and infinite discontinuities cannot be patched

concepts.term: Three conditions for continuity at a point
concepts.statement: The classification matters because it tells you which repairs are possible. A removable discontinuity is a hole the graph could have: the function approaches a single finite limit from both sides, but the value at the point is missing or wrong. Patch it and the function becomes continuous there. A jump discontinuity — the left and right limits both exist but disagree — is a tear, not a hole; no single value at the point can match both sides at once. An infinite discontinuity, where the function blows up, is beyond patching entirely. So the first job is always the same: compute the one-sided behaviour and decide which of the three worlds you are in.

OpenStax’s Calculus Volume 1 (§2.4) states that f is continuous at a point a exactly when three conditions hold together: f(a) is defined; the limit of f(x) as x approaches a exists; and that limit equals f(a). Every discontinuity is the failure of at least one condition, and the type of failure names the type of discontinuity. If f(a) is undefined or disagrees with a limit that does exist, the discontinuity is removable. If the two one-sided limits exist but differ — as with the piecewise function −x² + 4 for x ≤ 3 and 4x − 8 for x > 3 at the seam x = 3, where the left limit is −5 and the right limit is 4 — the discontinuity is a jump. If a one-sided limit is infinite — as with (x + 2)/(x + 1) at x = −1, where the denominator dies — the discontinuity is infinite.

concepts.term: Redefining a function to fill a hole
concepts.statement: One subtlety the classification hides: a function can fail continuity at a point even when nothing dramatic happens nearby. The function f(x) = sin(x)/x has limit 1 as x approaches 0, and OpenStax’s Example 2.28 shows that the enlarged function with f(0) = 1 is perfectly continuous at 0 — the original was merely missing its value. By contrast, a rational function like (x − 1)/(x² + 2x) is continuous on its whole domain (−∞, −2) ∪ (−2, 0) ∪ (0, ∞); the excluded points are where continuity fails. Polynomials, by the way, never fail: a polynomial is continuous everywhere, which is why holes in rational functions always trace back to a cancelled or zeroed denominator, never to the polynomial numerator alone.

concepts.term: Cancelling common factors to expose the limit
concepts.statement: To remove a removable discontinuity at x = a, compute the limit L of f as x approaches a, then declare a new function that equals f everywhere except at a, and takes the value L at a. The classic worked case from OpenStax Example 2.26: f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2). Both numerator and denominator vanish at x = 2, so f(2) is undefined — condition 1 fails. Factor the numerator: (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2). For every x ≠ 2 the factors cancel, leaving x + 2, whose limit as x approaches 2 is 4. The limit exists; only the value is missing. Define f(2) = 4 and the enlarged function is continuous at 2. The hole has been filled with the one point the formula was hiding.

Piecewise definitions ask the same question in reverse. Suppose a syllabus-style function is given as (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3 with some value c assigned at x = 3, and you must find the c that makes the whole thing continuous. Cancel to x + 3, take the limit, and the answer is c = 6. The general recipe is mechanical: compute the limit the pieces approach, then set the odd piece’s value to match. Always finish by confirming continuity after the repair — re-run the three conditions on the enlarged function. The limit must exist (it did by construction), the value must equal it (you set it), and the point must belong to the domain (you just defined it). Three ticks, and the repair is certified.

Cancelling a factor and forgetting that the cancellation is illegal at the zero itself — the simplified formula x + 2 is only equal to the original for x ≠ 2, which is exactly why the original needed a repair. Calling every hole "removable" without checking that the two-sided limit exists: if the one-sided limits disagree (jump) or diverge (infinite), no value helps. Confusing "f is undefined at a" with "the limit does not exist at a" — Example 2.26 has the former but not the latter. Also beware the opposite slip on piecewise seams: a function can be defined at the seam (condition 1 passes) yet still be discontinuous because the pieces fail to meet (condition 2 fails). Finally, do not claim continuity of a repaired function beyond the point you repaired — confirm the rest of the domain separately.

examples.title: Worked Example — Classify, then repair, then confirm
examples.problem: Removing Discontinuities: Finding and Filling the Holes — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2). Evaluate at the suspect point: f(2) is undefined, so continuity fails at x = 2 regardless of anything else.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: compute the limit. Factor and cancel for x ≠ 2: f(x) = x + 2, so the limit as x → 2 is 4. A finite two-sided limit exists — the discontinuity is removable, not jump, not infinite.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: repair. Define the enlarged function g with g(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2 and g(2) = 4.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: confirm. g(2) = 4 is defined; the limit is 4; the limit equals the value. All three conditions hold, so g is continuous at 2 — and everywhere else, since away from 2 it is a polynomial (x + 2).

steps.label: Contrast
steps.text: h(x) = (x + 2)/(x + 1) at x = −1. The denominator vanishes with no cancelling factor in the numerator, and the one-sided limits run to ±∞. No value assigned at −1 can fix an infinite limit — the discontinuity is infinite and non-removable.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: the derivative-as-a-limit lesson for limit mechanics and the algebra of factoring. Follow with the linearization lesson to see what continuity guarantees near a repaired point, and the concavity lesson for how the second derivative reads a graph’s shape. Primary reading: OpenStax, Calculus Volume 1, §2.4 "Continuity" (openstax.org, CC BY-NC-SA) — Examples 2.26 through 2.34 are the canonical drill set, and the Composite Function Theorem there explains why limits pass through continuous wrappers like cos.
Continuity at a: f(a) defined, limit exists, limit = f(a) — all three or it fails.
Failure modes: value missing or wrong → removable; one-sided limits differ → jump; a one-sided limit unbounded → infinite.
Repair recipe: factor, cancel, take the limit L, set f(a) = L, then re-confirm all three conditions.
Rational holes come from cancelled denominators; polynomials are always continuous on ℝ.
sin(x)/x with f(0) = 1 is the model repair: the formula was one point short of continuous.
Jumps and infinite breaks are non-removable — no single value can satisfy both sides or an unbounded limit.

quiz.q: What makes a discontinuity at x = a removable rather than jump or infinite?
options: f(a) is the largest value nearby
the two-sided limit exists and is finite, but f(a) is missing or wrong
the left and right limits are both infinite
quiz.explanation: Removable means the limit exists and is finite but the point’s value is absent or mismatched — a fillable hole. Jump means the one-sided limits exist but differ; infinite means a one-sided limit is unbounded. Neither of those can be fixed by setting one value.

quiz.q: For f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2), which redefinition makes the function continuous at x = 2?
quiz.explanation: Cancel the common factor: for x ≠ 2 the function equals x + 2, whose limit at 2 is 4. Setting f(2) = 4 makes the value meet the limit — the repair OpenStax demonstrates in Example 2.26.

quiz.q: A piecewise function gives −x² + 4 for x ≤ 3 and 4x − 8 for x > 3. What kind of discontinuity sits at the seam x = 3?
options: jump — the one-sided limits (−5 and 4) disagree
none — the function is continuous there
quiz.explanation: The left limit is −(3)² + 4 = −5 and the right limit is 4(3) − 8 = 4. Both are finite but unequal, so no single value at x = 3 can match both sides: a jump discontinuity, which no redefinition can remove.

quiz.q: After repairing a removable discontinuity by setting g(a) = L, what is the correct final step?
options: re-check all three continuity conditions for g at a
take the derivative of g at a
confirm the limit is the largest value of g nearby
state that confirmation is unnecessary once a value is assigned
quiz.explanation: The syllabus explicitly includes "confirming continuity after removal": verify g(a) is defined, the limit exists, and they are equal. Assignment without confirmation risks matching the limit with the wrong value or leaving the point outside the domain.

quiz.q: Why can no redefinition repair the infinite discontinuity of (x + 2)/(x + 1) at x = −1?
options: because the one-sided limits are unbounded, so no finite value can equal the limit
because the numerator also vanishes there
because rational functions are never continuous
quiz.explanation: Repair requires the limit to exist and be finite. Near x = −1 the denominator tends to 0 while the numerator tends to 1, so the function diverges to ±∞ from the two sides — there is no limit to assign.

intro: Every smooth curve, viewed through a microscope, looks like its tangent line. Linearization turns that observation into a computational tool: if you know a function’s value and derivative at one convenient point a, you can approximate its values at all nearby points using nothing more than a straight line — no calculator required. The syllabus pairs this with differentials, the same idea written in the language of small changes: estimate how much the output moves when the input wobbles by a little dx. Together these form the standard unit on approximating values with tangent lines and linearization at a point, and they power the applied question every exam loves: if a measurement is off by this much, how far off is the computed answer?
objectives: Explain linearization L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a)
Explain tangent-line approximation of nearby values
Explain differentials dy = f′(x) dx
Explain relative and percentage error estimation
Explain accuracy decays with distance from the anchor
Explain the (1 + x)^n ≈ 1 + nx micro-approximation

concepts.statement: The formula is short enough to memorise and worth understanding rather than memorising. The tangent line to f at x = a passes through the point (a, f(a)) with slope f′(a). Its point-slope equation is y = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a). OpenStax’s Calculus Volume 1 (§4.2) names the right-hand side the linearization of f at a, written L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a), and states the approximation as f(x) ≈ L(x) for x near a. Why it works: near a, the tangent hugs the curve — both share the same value at a and the same slope there, so their gap is genuinely second-order small, shrinking much faster than the distance from a. Why it eventually fails: as x travels away from a, the curve bends while the line does not, and the gap widens. Approximation quality is always a story about distance from the anchor point.

The drill has four moves. Choose an anchor a where f is easy to evaluate exactly and a’s neighbour x is genuinely close. Compute f(a) and f′(a). Assemble L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a). Evaluate L at the awkward input. OpenStax’s flagship example: approximate √9.1. Take f(x) = √x with anchor a = 9, where f(9) = 3 and f′(x) = 1/(2√x) so f′(9) = 1/6. Then L(x) = 3 + (x − 9)/6, and √9.1 ≈ 3 + 0.1/6 ≈ 3.0167. The true value is 3.01662… — five digits of accuracy from one derivative. The same template with f(x) = sin x anchored at π/3 (where sin(π/3) = √3/2 and cos(π/3) = 1/2) gives sin 62° ≈ 0.88348, and the anchor a = 0 on f(x) = (1 + x)^n collapses to the famous micro-approximation (1 + x)^n ≈ 1 + nx, which prices (1.01)³ ≈ 1.03 instantly.

Differentials re-phrase the same line in increment language. For y = f(x), define dx as an independent small change in the input and dy = f′(x) dx as the resulting change predicted along the tangent. The ratio dy/dx recovers the derivative — the notation is doing double duty — but the productive reading is predictive: dy is what the output change would be if the graph were its tangent. OpenStax works y = x² + 2x at x = 3 with dx = 0.1: dy = (2x + 2)dx = 8 × 0.1 = 0.8, while the true change Δy = f(3.1) − f(3) = 0.81. The tangent’s prediction misses by 0.01, the size of the ignored curvature — small precisely because dx is small.

Where the syllabus docks real weight is measurement error. If a quantity a is measured with a small error dx, the computed f(a) carries error approximately Δy ≈ dy = f′(a) dx — the derivative is a sensitivity coefficient converting input error into output error. Divide by the size of the output to get the relative error |dy/y|, and multiply by 100 for the percentage error. The logic explains everyday surprises: measuring a radius slightly wrong poisons a sphere’s volume three times as strongly in relative terms, because V = (4/3)πr³ differentiates to dV = 4πr² dr, so dV/V = 3 dr/r. A half-percent radius error is a one-and-a-half-percent volume error — the exponent is the error multiplier, a shortcut worth internalising for any power-law quantity.

Anchoring at a point that is easy but distant — the tangent at a = 1 says √9.1 ≈ 5.05, and the method’s accuracy guarantee never applied at that distance. Mixing up dy and Δy: dy is the tangent’s prediction (0.8 in OpenStax’s y = x² + 2x example), Δy is the true change (0.81); exams ask for both, distinguished. Forgetting to square the error multiplier for power laws — area carries twice the input’s relative error, volume three times. Reporting percentage error as a decimal (0.015 instead of 1.5%). And differentiating with respect to the wrong variable in applied word problems: identify which measured quantity carries the dx before computing anything.

examples.title: Worked Example — Anchor choice and error propagation
examples.problem: Linearization and Differentials: The Tangent as a Calculator — worked through step by step

steps.label: Part A
steps.text: estimate √9.1. Anchor a = 9 (perfect square, adjacent to 9.1). f′(x) = 1/(2√x), so f′(9) = 1/6.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Assemble L(x) = 3 + (1/6)(x − 9). Evaluate at x = 9.1: L = 3 + 0.1/6 ≈ 3.0167 — matching OpenStax’s value, and within 0.0001 of the true √9.1.

steps.label: Part B
steps.text: y = x² + 2x measured at x = 3 with dx = 0.1. dy = (2x + 2)dx = 8(0.1) = 0.8; the actual Δy = 0.81. Report dy as the estimate and note the 0.01 curvature shortfall.

steps.label: Part C
steps.text: a rod’s length is measured as 10 cm with possible error 0.05 cm; its area scales as L². Relative error in area ≈ 2 × (0.05/10) = 1%, by the power-law rule dA/A = 2 dL/L.

steps.label: Sanity check
steps.text: in each case the anchor was easy to evaluate exactly and the probe point was close. Had we anchored √x at 1 to approximate √9.1, the line 1 + (x − 1)/2 predicts 5.05 — a disaster, because 9.1 is nowhere near the anchor.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: the derivative-as-a-limit lesson for f′ fluency. Follow with the concavity-and-second-derivative lesson to quantify exactly when the tangent overshoots (concave down) or undershoots (concave up), and the removing-discontinuities lesson for the continuity backdrop that makes local approximation legitimate. Primary reading: OpenStax, Calculus Volume 1, §4.2 "Linear Approximations and Differentials" (openstax.org, CC BY-NC-SA) — the √9.1, sin 62° and (1.01)³ examples are the canonical drill set.
L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a): value at the anchor, slope at the anchor, straight line beyond.
Four-move drill: easy anchor, f(a) and f′(a), assemble L, evaluate at the awkward point.
Differentials: dy = f′(x) dx predicts output change; Δy is the truth dy approximates.
Error relay: input error dx becomes output error f′(a) dx; relative error |dy/y|; power-law exponents multiply it.
Accuracy is local — near a it is excellent, and it decays as the curve bends away from the line.

quiz.q: What is the linearization L(x) of f at x = a?
quiz.explanation: It is the tangent line at a in point-slope form: value f(a) at the anchor plus slope f′(a) times the horizontal offset. Options B and C drop the value or the slope; option D is circular.

quiz.q: Using the tangent at a = 9, what is the estimate of √9.1?
quiz.explanation: L(x) = 3 + (x − 9)/6 gives 3 + 0.1/6 ≈ 3.0167 — OpenStax’s worked value, accurate to about four decimal places.

quiz.q: For y = (1 + x)³, the linearization at a = 0 gives which approximation?
quiz.explanation: The general rule (1 + x)^n ≈ 1 + nx comes from f(0) = 1 and f′(0) = n; for n = 3 this prices (1.01)³ ≈ 1.03, matching OpenStax’s example.

quiz.q: A measurement error dx in the input produces what estimated error in f(a)?
options: no error can be estimated without the second derivative
quiz.explanation: The differential dy = f′(a) dx is the tangent’s prediction of the output change; the second derivative governs how wrong that prediction is, not the first-order estimate itself.

quiz.q: The radius of a sphere is measured with 0.5% relative error. Roughly what relative error does the volume inherit?
quiz.explanation: V = (4/3)πr³ is a power law with exponent 3, so dV/V = 3 dr/r — the relative error triples to about 1.5%. Exponents are error multipliers.

quiz.q: When does a linearization start giving poor estimates?
options: when x moves far from the anchor a, so curvature accumulates
quiz.explanation: The tangent matches the curve in value and slope only at a; away from a the graph bends and the line does not, so the gap grows. A large slope merely stretches the line — the failure is about distance and curvature.

intro: The first derivative tells you which way a graph climbs; the second derivative tells you how the climbing itself changes — whether the curve is bending upward like a cup or downward like a dome. That bending is concavity, and it answers questions the first derivative cannot: is this slowing growth still growth, is this minimum really the bottom of a valley, where does a trend genuinely change character? The syllabus packages three skills under this heading — determining concavity, locating points of inflection, and using the Second Derivative Test to classify extrema — and all three run off one instrument: the sign of f″, the derivative of the derivative.
objectives: Explain concave up means f′ increasing; concave down means f′ decreasing
Explain test for Concavity via the sign of f″
Explain points of inflection where concavity flips
Explain second Derivative Test for local extrema
Explain the inconclusive f″(c) = 0 case
Explain critical points versus inflection candidates

concepts.term: Concave up means f′ increasing; concave down means f′ decreasing
concepts.statement: OpenStax’s Calculus Volume 1 (§4.5) builds the definition from the first derivative rather than from pictures: f is concave up over an interval where f′ is increasing, and concave down where f′ is decreasing. That framing is worth savouring, because it converts concavity into a problem you already know how to solve — checking whether a function (here f′) is increasing — which is what the Test for Concavity (Theorem 4.10) formalises: if f″(x) > 0 on an interval, f is concave up there; if f″(x) < 0, concave down. Geometrically, concave-up curves sit above their tangent lines (slopes steepening), concave-down curves sit below them (slopes flattening). A parabola y = x² is concave up everywhere because f″ = 2 never changes sign; y = x³ switches from concave down to concave up at the origin, because f″ = 6x flips sign there.

concepts.term: Test for Concavity via the sign of f″
concepts.statement: A point (a, f(a)) is a point of inflection when f changes concavity at a and f is continuous at a. Two consequences follow immediately. First, candidates for inflection live only where f″(x) = 0 or f″ is undefined — a continuous function cannot switch from f″ > 0 to f″ < 0 without passing through zero (or breaking), by the same reasoning that pins critical points. Second, and more treacherous: f″(a) = 0 is necessary, not sufficient. The function must actually change concavity at a. For y = x⁴, f″ = 12x² is zero at 0 but never negative — the curve is concave up on both sides of 0, so the origin is not an inflection point, just a flat moment in a cup. Always test the sign of f″ on each side before declaring a flip.

concepts.term: Points of inflection where concavity flips
concepts.statement: The same sign-chart discipline that classifies critical points classifies inflection candidates. OpenStax’s Example 4.17 runs it on f(x) = x³ − 3x² − 9x − 1: f′(x) = 3x² − 6x − 9 = 3(x − 3)(x + 1), so the critical points are x = −1 and x = 3; f is increasing on (−∞, −1), decreasing on (−1, 3), increasing on (3, ∞) — a local maximum at x = −1 and a local minimum at x = 3. Now the second derivative f″(x) = 6x − 6 vanishes at x = 1, is negative to its left and positive to its right, so (1, f(1)) is the inflection point where the dome gives way to the cup — and note it sits neatly between the max and the min, as it must for a cubic.

concepts.term: Second Derivative Test for local extrema
concepts.statement: The test converts concavity at a critical point into a classification. Suppose f′(c) = 0. If f″(c) > 0, the curve is concave up at c, so c is a local minimum — the curve bends up away from the point. If f″(c) < 0, the curve is concave down at c, so c is a local maximum. In Example 4.17: f″(−1) = −12 < 0 confirms the local max at x = −1, and f″(3) = 12 > 0 confirms the local min at x = 3 — no sign chart needed once the second derivative is evaluated. The test’s fine print is the case f″(c) = 0 (or undefined): the test is inconclusive, and you fall back to the first-derivative sign chart. The two standard counters show why: for y = x⁴, f″(0) = 0 yet 0 is a minimum; for y = x³, f″(0) = 0 and 0 is neither max nor min. Identical second-derivative readings, different verdicts — the test genuinely cannot see the difference.

OpenStax’s Example 4.18 shows the machinery surviving rough terrain: f(x) = 5x^(1/3) − x^(5/3) has f′(x) = 5(1 − x^(4/3))/(3x^(2/3)), with critical points at x = −1, x = 0 and x = 1 — including a point where f′ is undefined because of the cube-root denominator. The sign analysis gives a local minimum at x = −1, a local maximum at x = 1, and no extremum at x = 0 despite f′(0) being undefined, because f′ does not change sign there. The lesson generalises: critical points (f′ zero or undefined) are candidates, sign behaviour is the judge, and the second derivative is a fast judge when it is available and nonzero.

Treating f″ = 0 as an inflection guarantee — x⁴ at the origin is the standing counterexample; a sign change in f″ is the requirement. Running the Second Derivative Test at a point where f′ ≠ 0 — the test only speaks at critical points. Applying it where f″(c) = 0 and "guessing minimum because cup-shaped nearby" — the inconclusive case demands the first-derivative chart. Confusing critical points (f′ = 0 or undefined) with inflection candidates (f″ = 0 or undefined) — they are different suspect lists from different derivatives. And forgetting continuity in the inflection definition: a concavity flip across a break in the graph is not an inflection point.

examples.title: Worked Example — Full classification of a cubic
examples.problem: Concavity and the Second Derivative Test — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: f(x) = x³ − 3x² − 9x − 1. First derivative: f′(x) = 3x² − 6x − 9 = 3(x − 3)(x + 1). Critical points: x = −1, x = 3.

steps.label: Concavity
steps.text: f″(x) = 6x − 6, zero at x = 1, negative on (−∞, 1), positive on (1, ∞). So f is concave down then concave up, and (1, f(1)) is the inflection point.

steps.label: Second Derivative Test
steps.text: f″(−1) = −12 < 0 → concave down at the critical point → local maximum at x = −1.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: f″(3) = 12 > 0 → concave up at the critical point → local minimum at x = 3. (Values: f(−1) = 6, f(3) = −26.)

steps.label: Counter-check for the inconclusive case
steps.text: g(x) = x⁴ has g′(0) = 0, g″(0) = 0 — test silent. First-derivative chart shows g′ negative left and positive right of 0: minimum after all. h(x) = x³ shows h′ positive on both sides: no extremum.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: the derivative-as-a-limit lesson and comfort with sign charts. Follow with the linearization lesson — concavity tells you whether a tangent approximation over- or under-shoots — and, for the fuller curve-sketching picture, pair with your algebra volume’s polynomial-analysis sections. Primary reading: OpenStax, Calculus Volume 1, §4.5 "Derivatives and the Shape of a Graph" (openstax.org, CC BY-NC-SA) — Theorem 4.10 and Examples 4.17–4.18 are the canonical drills.
Concave up = f′ increasing; concave down = f′ decreasing.
Test for Concavity: f″ > 0 → up, f″ < 0 → down (Theorem 4.10).
Inflection = concavity flip with continuity; candidates at f″ = 0 or undefined, confirmed by sign change.
Second Derivative Test: at f′(c) = 0, f″(c) > 0 → min, f″(c) < 0 → max, f″(c) = 0 → inconclusive (fall back to f′ signs).
x⁴ and x³ at 0 are the standing counters to "f″ = 0 decides".
Critical points and inflection candidates are different suspect lists — one from f′, one from f″.

quiz.q: By definition, f is concave up on an interval exactly when…
options: f′ is increasing on the interval
the graph lies above the x-axis
quiz.explanation: OpenStax defines concavity through the slope’s behaviour: concave up means f′ increasing (slopes steepening), which the Test for Concavity then detects via f″ > 0. Positivity of f itself is irrelevant — a cup can live below the axis.

quiz.q: If f″(c) > 0 and f′(c) = 0, the Second Derivative Test classifies c as…
quiz.explanation: f″(c) > 0 means concave up at c — the curve bends upward from a stationary point, the picture of a valley bottom. Hence local minimum.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x³ − 3x² − 9x − 1, where does the inflection point sit?
quiz.explanation: f″(x) = 6x − 6 changes sign at x = 1, so concavity flips there — between the local max at −1 and the local min at 3.

quiz.q: f″(a) = 0. Which conclusion is valid?
options: nothing yet — f″ = 0 is only a candidate; a sign change in f″ across a is required for inflection, and the extremum question needs other tools
quiz.explanation: x⁴ (minimum at 0) and x³ (no extremum at 0) both have zero second derivative there: f″(a) = 0 alone decides nothing. Inflection needs an actual concavity change; extrema need the First-Derivative Test when the second is silent.

quiz.q: A function’s critical point has f′ undefined but f defined. What is the right workflow?
options: discard the point — the test needs f′ = 0
sign-chart f′ around the point; if f′ changes sign, classify by direction (and only then consider f″ if it exists)
declare it an inflection point automatically
declare it a local maximum automatically
quiz.explanation: Example 4.18’s x = 0 is exactly this case: f′ undefined, no extremum, because f′ keeps its sign. Candidates come from f′ zero or undefined; verdicts come from sign behaviour.

quiz.q: Which pair correctly matches curve behaviour with tangent-line position?
options: concave up: graph above its tangents; concave down: graph below
concave up: graph below its tangents; concave down: graph above
both concavities: graph crosses its tangents
tangent position is unrelated to concavity
quiz.explanation: Steepening slopes (f″ > 0) pull the curve above each tangent; flattening slopes (f″ < 0) drop it below. This picture is also why linearization errors have a sign: the concavity lesson feeds directly into the tangent-approximation lesson.

intro:
Mensuration is the arithmetic of measuring the world: how much fence a field needs (perimeter), how much seed (area), how much water a tank holds (volume), how much paint its walls take (surface area). Exam questions test three skills at once: choosing the right formula for the shape, combining formulas for compound figures, and keeping units honest through the calculation. This lesson builds all three on the same principle — every formula is a picture you can re-derive — and works through the shapes that dominate question banks: rectilinear figures, circles with their arcs and sectors, and the standard solids from prisms to spheres. The masters volumes own the axioms of geometry; here the subject is measurement arithmetic done fast and done right.

**Why this matters.** Mensuration marks are lost in three predictable ways, and each is fixable with a habit rather than more memory. First, wrong formula for the shape — usually cone versus pyramid, or slant height versus height. Second, compound-shape panic — cured by the add-and-subtract strategy, where every composite figure is simple shapes joined or with holes punched in. Third, unit slips — converting centimetres to metres by dividing by 100 even when the quantity is an area or a volume, where the conversion is 10,000 or 1,000,000. The unit of the answer (cm, cm², cm³) tells you which quantity you are computing; examiners deliberately plant the trap, and the habit of checking units against the question turns the trap into a free mark.
objectives: Explain perimeter and area of rectilinear figures
Explain circles: circumference, area, arcs and sectors
Explain prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres
Explain surface area versus volume: units give the game away
Explain compound shapes: the add-and-subtract strategy
Explain unit conversion: one square metre is 10,000 square centimetres

concepts.statement: Perimeter is the walk around the boundary; area is the coverage. Rectangle: P = 2(l + w), A = lw. Triangle: A = ½ × base × height (any side as base, height perpendicular to it); Heron's formula A = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)) with s the semi-perimeter, when only the three sides are known. Parallelogram A = bh; trapezium A = ½(a + b)h with a and b the parallel sides.

Circumference C = 2πr, area A = πr². An arc is a fraction of the circumference and a sector a fraction of the area, both proportional to the central angle θ: arc = (θ/360) × 2πr, sector area = (θ/360) × πr². The chord's perpendicular bisector passes through the centre — the fact behind most "find the radius from a chord" questions.

A prism has the same cross-section all the way through: volume V = (area of cross-section) × length; surface area = 2 × (cross-section area) + (perimeter of cross-section) × length. A cylinder is the circular prism: V = πr²h, total surface area = 2πr² + 2πrh (two discs plus the rolled rectangle).

Pyramid: V = ⅓ × (base area) × height. Cone: V = ⅓πr²h, curved surface = πrl where l is the slant height with l² = r² + h², total surface = πrl + πr². Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³, surface area = 4πr². Hemisphere: half of each, plus a disc πr² if closed.

Break composites into named shapes and add; for shapes with holes or cut-outs, subtract. For composite solids (a cylinder topped by a hemisphere), volume adds, but surface area needs care — the surfaces where solids join disappear from the outside.

Lengths scale by 100 per metre-to-centimetre step, areas by 100² = 10,000, volumes by 100³ = 1,000,000. One cubic metre is 1,000 litres; one litre is 1,000 cm³. The final unit declared in the question — cm² versus cm³ — tells you whether you owe an area or a volume.

concepts.term: Perimeter and area of rectilinear figures
concepts.statement: Rectilinear figures reward one idea above all: the perpendicular height. A triangle's area is half the base times the height — not "a side times a side" — and the height is the perpendicular drop onto that base, outside the triangle for obtuse shapes just as legally as inside. Heron's formula handles the case with three sides given: compute the semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c)/2 and take the square root of s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c) — clunky but bulletproof, and worth checking against the ½ × base × height answer when both are available. Parallelograms shear rectangles (base times perpendicular height), and trapezia average the parallel sides before multiplying by the height: ½(a + b)h. A useful sanity reflex on any area answer: rough the figure against a grid of its own side lengths, and reject answers that could not hold, say, four copies of an obvious inscribed rectangle.

concepts.term: Circles: circumference, area, arcs and sectors
concepts.statement: Circles introduce proportionality to the toolkit. Circumference and area both scale with the radius — linearly for circumference, quadratically for area, which is why doubling the radius quadruples the area (a favourite ratio question: two circles with radii in ratio 2:3 have areas in ratio 4:9). Arcs and sectors are proportional slices of the circle, cut by the central angle: a 60-degree arc is one-sixth of the circumference, and its sector is one-sixth of the area — the same fraction, because the fraction depends only on the angle. Reverse questions are equally common: given an arc length and radius, recover the angle by dividing; given a sector's area, walk back to the angle. Chord problems lean on one fact: the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it, which converts "find the radius" into a right-triangle exercise — half the chord and the perpendicular distance are two legs, the radius the hypotenuse.

concepts.term: Prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres
concepts.statement: Solids are the prism idea plus exceptions. The prism formula — volume is cross-section area times length — explains cylinders (circular cross-section: πr²h) and every extruded shape; its surface area is the two end faces plus the "label" around the middle (perimeter of the cross-section times the length: for the cylinder, the rolled rectangle 2πrh). Pyramids and cones carry the one-third: each is exactly a third of the prism or cylinder standing on the same base with the same height — a fact you can verify by pouring sand, and a formula you should never confuse with the prism's. The cone's curved surface unrolls into a sector of radius equal to the slant height l, giving πrl; keep l and h strictly separate (l² = r² + h²), because question banks bait the swap. The sphere closes the set with the only formulas worth a dedicated slot: V = (4/3)πr³ and S = 4πr² — surface area exactly four great circles, a fact that doubles as a check. For composites, add volumes freely, but subtract the hidden faces from surface area: a hemisphere sitting on a cylinder hides both the cylinder's top disc and the hemisphere's flat one.

concepts.term: Surface area versus volume: units give the game away
concepts.statement: Units are the last mile, and they are where careful students still slip. Conversion factors chain by the power of the quantity: 1 metre = 100 centimetres, so 1 m² = 10⁴ cm² and 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³ — a square metre is not a hundred square centimetres, and a tank "2 m by 1 m by 50 cm" must be converted to common units before multiplying. Capacity rides on volume: 1 m³ = 1,000 litres and 1 litre = 1,000 cm³, so a 20 cm cube holds 8,000 cm³ = 8 litres. Rates link the systems: mass = volume × density (a water tank's weight from its litre count), cost = area × rate per square metre (painting, tiling, turfing), and flow = volume ÷ time (filling a pool). The professional habit is dimensional bookkeeping — write the unit beside every factor as you substitute, cancel what cancels, and let the surviving unit tell you whether the question is answered or a conversion is still owed.

Using the vertical height where the slant height is owed — the cone's curved surface needs l with l² = r² + h², never h. Halving the wrong quantity in a trapezium — ½(a + b)h averages the parallel sides, it does not halve the height. Treating 1 m² as 100 cm² — the conversion squares: 10,000; and 1 m³ is 1,000,000 cm³. Doubling a radius and expecting the area to double — areas scale with r². Adding surface areas across a joint without subtracting the hidden faces. Dropping the one-third from pyramids and cones, the most mechanical formula loss in the topic. And answering in the unit the question never asked for — a capacity answer in cubic metres, a paint answer in square centimetres; declare the unit, convert deliberately, then box.

examples.title: Worked Example — A Composite Water Tank, From Volume to Paint
examples.problem: Mensuration and Calculation: Perimeter, Area, Surface Area and Volume — worked through step by step

steps.label: Shape
steps.text: a closed cylindrical tank of radius 1 m and height 2 m, topped by a hemispherical lid of the same radius. Question: capacity in litres, and metal area for a one-coat paint estimate.

steps.label: Volume
steps.text: cylinder πr²h = π × 1² × 2 = 2π ≈ 6.283 m³; hemisphere (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)π ≈ 2.094 m³; total ≈ 8.377 m³.

steps.label: Convert to capacity
steps.text: 8.377 m³ × 1,000 = 8,377 litres — the litres conversion is part of the answer, not decoration.

steps.label: Surface area (outside only)
steps.text: cylinder's curved wall 2πrh = 4π; hemisphere's curve 2πr² = 2π; the base disc πr² = π. The cylinder's top disc and the hemisphere's flat face are hidden — subtracted by construction.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Total surface ≈ 4π + 2π + π = 7π ≈ 21.99 m²; paint for one coat at 10 m² per litre ≈ 2.2 litres.

steps.label: Unit audit
steps.text: volume answer in m³ → litres (×1,000); area answer in m² (no conversion owed); both declared before boxing — the habit that survives examiner traps.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: confident arithmetic with squares and roots. Follow with the percentage-ratio mental-math lesson for the rate questions (cost per m², fill rates) and the data-chart reading lesson for measurement questions wearing table clothes. Primary reading: OpenStax, Contemporary Mathematics and Prealgebra 2e geometry and measurement chapters (openstax.org, CC BY — perimeter, area, surface area, volume and unit-conversion sections); the masters volume's combined "Algebra, Geometry, Mensuration & Trigonometry Basics" section for the underlying axioms this lesson applies.
Rectilinear: rectangle 2(l+w)/lw; triangle ½bh or Heron; trapezium ½(a+b)h — perpendicular height everywhere.
Circle: C = 2πr, A = πr²; arc and sector are angle-fractions (θ/360) of each; the perpendicular from centre to chord bisects it.
Prism/cylinder: V = cross-section × length; SA = 2 ends + perimeter × length (cylinder: 2πr² + 2πrh).
Pyramid/cone: one-third of the matching prism/cylinder (cone V = ⅓πr²h, curved SA = πrl, l² = r² + h²). Sphere: (4/3)πr³ and 4πr².
Composites: volumes add; surface areas add minus hidden faces.
Units: ×100 per length step, ×10⁴ per area step, ×10⁶ per volume step; 1 m³ = 1,000 litres = 10⁶ cm³; declare the unit before boxing.

quiz.q: Two circles have radii in the ratio 2 : 3. The ratio of their areas is…
quiz.explanation: Area scales with the square of the radius, so the ratio 2 : 3 squares to 4 : 9 — the classic proportional-slice question.

quiz.q: A sector of a circle of radius 6 cm has central angle 60°. Its area is…
quiz.explanation: The sector is 60/360 = one-sixth of the circle; full area is π × 6² = 36π, so the sector is 6π cm².

quiz.q: A cone has radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. Its slant height is…
quiz.explanation: l² = r² + h² = 9 + 16 = 25, so l = 5 cm — the 3-4-5 right triangle hiding inside every such cone question.

quiz.q: A 20 cm cube holds how much water?
quiz.explanation: Volume 20³ = 8,000 cm³; one litre is 1,000 cm³, so the cube holds 8 litres — capacity conversion as a named step.

quiz.q: A hemisphere sits exactly on a cylinder's top. The composite's surface area excludes…
options: the cylinder's top disc and the hemisphere's flat face
quiz.explanation: Joined surfaces disappear from the outside: the two circular faces in contact are hidden, while the curved wall, base and dome all remain.

intro:
A single average hides most of what a data set can tell you. The tools of this lesson — quartiles, the cumulative frequency curve, the five-number summary and the box plot — exist to expose the rest: how the data spread, where the middle half sits, how the two halves skew, and which points deserve suspicion. They are also the standard bridge between raw numbers and honest claims: before any inference is drawn, an examiner wants evidence that you can describe a distribution graphically and numerically, and that you know the difference between a value in the 90th percentile and a score of 90 percent. This lesson builds that toolkit exactly once, from ordering the data to fencing off outliers.

**Why this matters.** Everything here follows one move: put the data in order. Quartiles, percentiles, the ogive and the box plot are all different views of the same ordered list, so the skills stack instead of multiplying. Learn the median-of-halves rule for quartiles, learn to read three positions off an ogive, learn the five values that draw a box — and you can answer construction questions, interpretation questions and comparison questions with the same three facts.
objectives: Explain ordering data and the percentile index formula
Explain quartiles from the lower and upper halves
Explain cumulative frequency tables and the ogive
Explain the five-number summary
Explain box plot anatomy and the interquartile range
Explain the 1.5 × IQR outlier fences
Explain reading skewness from a box plot
Explain comparing two distributions

concepts.statement: The value below which a given percentage of the ordered data falls. The 90th percentile means 90 percent of scores are at or below yours — it is a position, not a mark. Universities use percentiles to compare applicants; the 75th-percentile SAT cut-off translates into a specific score only through the score distribution.

One of the three values Q1, Q2, Q3 that cut ordered data into four equal parts; Q2 is the median. About one quarter of the data falls at or below Q1, one half at or below Q2, three quarters at or below Q3.
The spread of the middle 50 percent of the data: IQR = Q3 − Q1. Because it ignores the tails, it is a resistant measure of spread — unaffected by extreme values — and the base unit for outlier tests.

Minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum: the five ordered values from which a box plot is constructed. Two distributions with equal means can still differ hugely in their five-number summaries — which is the point of computing one.

The graph of running totals: cumulative frequency plotted against the upper boundary of each class. Reading across at n/4, n/2 and 3n/4 and then down gives Q1, the median and Q3 — the curve is a quartile-reading machine.
A value more than 1.5 × IQR below Q1 or above Q3. It requires further investigation — it may be an error, an abnormality, or the most interesting data point in the set.

concepts.term: Ordering data and the percentile index formula
concepts.statement: Quartiles by the median-of-halves rule. Order the data; find the median. For a data set of 14 observations, the median is the mean of the 7th and 8th values. Then split: Q1 is the middle value of the lower half (the first 7 values), Q3 the middle of the upper half (the last 7). The OpenStax worked set — 1; 1; 2; 2; 4; 6; 6.8; 7.2; 8; 8.3; 9; 10; 10; 11.5 — gives median 7, Q1 = 2, Q3 = 9, so the middle half of the data lies between 2 and 9. For percentiles beyond the quartiles, use the index formula: compute i = (k/100)(n + 1) for the kth percentile of n values; if i is an integer, the percentile is the ith ordered value, and if not, average the values at the two nearest positions. For 29 ages, the 70th percentile is the 21st value (i = 0.70 × 30 = 21), while the 83rd sits between the 24th and 25th, averaging 71 and 72 to give 71.5.
$$IQR = Q_3 - Q_1,\qquad \text{lower fence} = Q_1 - 1.5\times IQR,\qquad \text{upper fence} = Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR$$
concepts.detail: The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle 50 percent of ordered data. Values beyond the two fences are flagged as potential outliers — the rule box plots use to draw whiskers to the last non-flagged value and plot dots beyond.

concepts.term: Quartiles from the lower and upper halves
concepts.statement: Cumulative frequency and the ogive. Build a table whose final column adds the class frequencies as you go: each row’s cumulative value answers “how many observations are at most this class boundary?”. Plot those running totals against the upper class boundaries and join with a smooth curve — the ogive. Three horizontal reads then return the summary values: across from n/2, down to the x-axis for the median; across from n/4 and 3n/4 for Q1 and Q3. The same table also answers direct questions — how many scored below 60, what proportion cleared 80 — which is why cumulative frequency is the practical form of the percentile idea for grouped data. With unequal class widths, plot against boundaries (not midpoints) and keep the running total honest; the curve, not the table’s raw frequencies, is what you read.

concepts.term: Cumulative frequency tables and the ogive
concepts.statement: The box plot draws the five-number summary. A box spans Q1 to Q3 — the middle 50 percent of the data — with a line at the median; whiskers run from the box ends to the smallest and largest values (or to the last values inside the outlier fences, with dots marking flagged extremes). What the picture encodes is concentration and skew: a median line off-centre inside the box signals skew, whisker lengths expose tail heaviness, and the box’s height is the IQR made visible. Two box plots on a common scale make comparison immediate: the OpenStax day-class and night-class test scores share similar medians (74.5 versus 81) but wildly different boxes (IQR 26.5 versus 11) — the day class varies far more, whatever its average.

Reading a percentile as a mark: the 90th percentile is a position in the ordered data, not 90 percent correct. Ignoring convention clashes: calculators, software and exam boards use slightly different quartile rules — the median-of-halves method is the taught standard, so know which one your syllabus examines and stay consistent. Flagging every extreme dot as an error: the 1.5 × IQR rule marks values for investigation, not deletion — the most interesting datum is often the outlier. Believing the whiskers hold “the other half” of the data: the box already holds the middle half; whiskers reach to extremes, tails included. And building the ogive from midpoints or raw frequencies instead of upper boundaries and running totals — the curve then answers questions it was never drawn to answer.

examples.title: Worked Example — Five Numbers, Two Fences, One Verdict
examples.problem: Quartiles, Cumulative Frequency and Box Plots — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Day class scores (ordered, 20 values) give five-number summary: min 32, Q1 56, median 74.5, Q3 82.5, max 99. Night class: min 25.5, Q1 78, median 81, Q3 89, max 98.

steps.label: IQRs
steps.text: day = 82.5 − 56 = 26.5; night = 89 − 78 = 11. The day class’s middle half is more than twice as wide.

steps.label: Day fences
steps.text: 56 − 1.5 × 26.5 = 16.25 and 82.5 + 1.5 × 26.5 = 122.25. No score lies outside, so no outliers.

steps.label: Night fences
steps.text: 78 − 1.5 × 11 = 61.5 and 89 + 1.5 × 11 = 105.5. The scores 45 and 25.5 fall below 61.5 — two potential outliers to investigate.

steps.label: Verdict
steps.text: similar centres, very different spreads; the night class is tightly packed with two low stragglers, the day class broadly spread. That is a complete comparison in five numbers and two fences.

steps.label: Step 6
steps.text: The same test on 13 house prices (median 488,800; Q1 308,750; Q3 649,000; IQR 340,250; upper fence 1,159,375) flags the 5,500,000 listing as a potential outlier — real-estate data’s classic long right tail.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: measures of centre and spread (mean, median, range, standard deviation) from the descriptive-statistics chapters of the master statistics volume. Follow with the normal distribution, where percentiles reappear as z-scores, and the charts-reading lesson for the graphical side of data handling. Primary reading: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e, sections 2.3 “Measures of the Location of the Data” and 2.4 “Box Plots” (openstax.org, CC BY-NC-SA) — the source of both worked data sets used here.
Order the data once: quartiles, percentiles, the ogive and the box plot are four views of the same ordered list.
Median-of-halves gives Q1 and Q3; the index formula i = (k/100)(n + 1) locates any percentile, averaging adjacent values when i is not an integer.
IQR = Q3 − Q1 measures the middle 50 percent and is resistant to extremes.
Ogive: cumulative frequency against upper class boundaries; read n/4, n/2, 3n/4 across and down for Q1, median, Q3.
Box plot = five-number summary: box spans Q1–Q3, line at median, whiskers to extremes (or fence-adjacent values, dots beyond).
Outlier fences: Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR — flag, investigate, never auto-delete.

quiz.q: For the 14-observation set 1; 1; 2; 2; 4; 6; 6.8; 7.2; 8; 8.3; 9; 10; 10; 11.5, the first quartile is…
quiz.explanation: The median is 7 (mean of the 7th and 8th values); the lower half is 1; 1; 2; 2; 4; 6; 6.8, whose middle value is 2. So Q1 = 2.

quiz.q: Scoring in the 90th percentile on an exam means…
options: you answered 90 percent of questions correctly
90 percent of scores are at or below yours
you scored 90 more than the mean
your score is 90 percent of the maximum
quiz.explanation: Percentiles are positions in the ordered distribution, not percentages of correct answers — a weak exam with low scores could still put a modest mark in the 90th percentile.

quiz.q: A value is flagged as a potential outlier when it lies…
options: outside the box of a box plot
beyond Q3 + 1.5 × IQR or below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR
more than 2 standard deviations from the mean
outside the whiskers of any chart
quiz.explanation: The 1.5 × IQR fences define potential outliers; whiskers extend only to the last values inside the fences, with dots beyond — the standard box-plot convention.

quiz.q: To read the median and quartiles from an ogive, you…
options: read vertically at n/2, n/4 and 3n/4 cumulative frequency
read the upper class boundaries directly
quiz.explanation: The ogive plots cumulative totals, so horizontal lines at n/4, n/2 and 3n/4 intersect the curve at x-values equal to Q1, the median and Q3.

intro:
Most numerical claims now arrive as pictures: a bar chart in a report, a line graph of prices, a pie chart of budget shares, a dashboard joining three tables and two trends. Data interpretation is the skill of getting the numbers back out of the picture correctly — reading what is plotted, against what scale, in what units — and then computing exactly what was asked, which is often not the number on the page but a change, a share, a ratio or a comparison derived from several sources at once. This lesson covers the standard chart families and the arithmetic each invites, then the discipline of reading multiple sources together, and finally the visual tricks that make honest data lie.

**Why this matters.** Interpretation questions rarely test calculation difficulty; they test precision of reading. The marks are lost in the first ten seconds — reading the wrong axis, missing that one table is in thousands and the other in millions, comparing a percentage to a percentage point, or treating a pie share of one year as a share of another year’s larger total. Build a fixed reading ritual — title, units, axes, legend, source, note — and the arithmetic that follows is the easy part.
objectives: Explain bar charts: comparison across categories
Explain line graphs: trend, slope and rate of change
Explain pie charts: shares, sector angles and totals
Explain histograms versus bar charts
Explain frequency polygons and time series
Explain percentage change and share arithmetic
Explain reading several sources together
Explain misleading axes and scales

concepts.statement: How often a category or class occurs, and that count as a fraction of the total. Bar charts display either; the relative form lets two data sets of different sizes be compared on one axis.

The angle a pie slice occupies: share × 360°. A quarter is 90°, an eighth is 45° — computing the angle is the fastest way to check whether a drawn pie is even drawn honestly, and exam questions ask for angles as often as for percentages.

Data recorded in time order and best shown as a line graph: the horizontal axis is time, and the slope between two points is the rate of change — steeper means faster, downward means decline, flat means stable.

Grouped bars put two or more series side by side within each category for direct comparison; stacked bars place them on top of one another to show composition of a total. Reading a stacked chart for a middle segment means subtracting — the segment’s height, not its top edge, is its value.

(new − old) ÷ old × 100. It is signed and always taken on the old value. A rise from 50 to 75 is a 50 percent increase; a fall from 75 back to 50 is a 33.3 percent decrease — the asymmetry that exam questions exploit.

A line graph joining the midpoints of histogram bars — the same distribution drawn for comparison of several data sets on one set of axes, and the form OpenStax uses to bridge histograms and line graphs.

Bar charts compare categories. The vertical axis carries the counts (with units!), the horizontal the categories, and the bars’ heights — read against gridlines, not eyeballed — are the data. Two reading habits pay for themselves: first, check whether the categories are ordered by value or by something else (alphabetical, chronological); a chart may be sorted to make a point, and the tallest bar is not always adjacent to the second-tallest. Second, for grouped bars, fix which colour or shade is which series before reading any number; for stacked bars, remember the middle segments must be recovered by subtraction — the top of a segment is cumulative, the segment is a difference. Horizontal bar charts do the same job with long category labels; nothing about the arithmetic changes.

concepts.term: Line graphs: trend, slope and rate of change
concepts.statement: Line graphs show change. With time on the horizontal axis, the graph’s slope between two points is the rate of change between them, so questions about “when did it grow fastest” are slope questions — steepest segment, not largest value. Extrapolation beyond the plotted range is assumption, not reading; interpolation between points is legitimate only as far as the sampling justifies. When two lines share an axis, check the units and the baseline before comparing slopes — a truncated axis (starting at 90 rather than 0) exaggerates slopes and is the most common honest-looking distortion in published charts. Frequency polygons and time-series graphs are line graphs too, with the same slope discipline; the only new idea is that the polygon’s vertices are class midpoints.

concepts.term: Pie charts: shares, sector angles and totals
concepts.statement: Pie charts show shares of one total. Every slice is a fraction of the whole, so a pie without a stated total is half-invisible: 25 percent of what? The arithmetic the chart invites is angle-and-share conversion — a sector of 54° is 54/360 = 15 percent; a share of 18 percent of 2,400 units is 432 units — and comparison caution: slices from two different pies (different years, different totals) cannot be compared by angle alone, because the underlying totals moved. Pie charts hide small differences and degrade past five or six categories, which is why they attract both exam questions and criticism; when precise comparison among many categories is the point, a bar chart is the honest tool.

Histograms are not bar charts. A histogram groups a continuous variable into class intervals and the bars touch, because the scale is numeric and continuous — whereas bar-chart categories are discrete and separated. With unequal class widths, honest reading requires frequency density (frequency ÷ class width): the area of each bar, not its height, carries the count, and a naive height read on a stretched final bin is the classic error. The rest of the toolkit is the multi-source discipline: real questions join a table to a chart to a paragraph, often in different units. Convert everything to one unit first (thousands to millions; percentages to fractions), locate the raw numbers each source supplies, and compute only the derived quantity asked — a growth rate from two rows of a table, a share from one chart applied to a total from another, a difference between two slices across years.

Reading the wrong axis in two-axis charts — always match a series to its labelled scale before quoting any number. Assuming categories are sorted by value; many charts sort alphabetically or chronologically, so rank by reading, not by position. Adding percentages that belong to different totals — 30 percent of 2024’s sales and 25 percent of 2025’s do not sum to anything meaningful.
