steps.text: If the central government must set a new national standard for a hazardous substance, the umbrella Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 supplies the power.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: If the factory emits greenhouse gases, no domestic cap applies directly — the relevant frame is India’s NDC under the Paris Agreement and NAPCC missions.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.text: match medium → statute → adjudicator; treaty items quote goals and dates, not factory scenarios.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: none. The unit feeds the Comprehension passages (environmental prose is a favourite) and any Geography/Sociology course on development. Primary reading: United Nations SDG pages (sdgs.un.org — goal list, targets, 2030 Agenda); OpenStax Biology 2e ch.47 "Conservation Biology and Biodiversity" (openstax.org, CC BY) for the biodiversity and pollution framing; India’s Environment (Protection) Act 1986 text (indiacode.nic.in) and the UNFCCC Paris Agreement page for the treaty mechanics.
Interaction: renewable vs non-renewable resources; carrying capacity is environmental, footprint is demand; IPAT = Population × Affluence × Technology.
Sustainable development (Brundtland 1987): present needs without compromising future generations.
Air pollutants: PM2.5 (cardio-respiratory), SO₂/NOₓ (acid rain, smog), CO (haemoglobin), O₃ (irritant), lead (neurotoxin); WHO ≈ 7 million premature deaths a year from air pollution.
Water: pathogens, arsenic/fluoride, eutrophication; soil: pesticides, heavy metals, e-waste; noise ≥ 80-85 dB harms hearing.
MDGs 8 (2000-2015) → SDGs 17 goals, 169 targets (2016-2030), universal, 5 Ps.
Disasters: hazard + vulnerability = disaster; NDMA (2005) apex in India; Sendai 2015-2030 for prevention.
Law and treaties: Water 1974, Air 1981, EPA 1986 (Bhopal), NGT 2010; Stockholm 1972, Montreal 1987, Rio 1992, Kyoto 1997, Paris 2015.

quiz.q: The Sustainable Development Goals consist of:
quiz.explanation: SDGs: 17 goals and 169 targets under the 2030 Agenda, universal across countries; the 8-goal set was the MDGs (2000-2015).

quiz.q: Which pollutant-health pairing is correct?
options: CO — binds haemoglobin reducing oxygen delivery
PM2.5 — mainly a skin disease agent
Ozone — central-nervous-system toxin from leaded petrol
quiz.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin; PM2.5 penetrates lungs and blood (cardio-respiratory disease); ground-level ozone is a respiratory irritant; hearing damage is noise’s effect; lead is the neurotoxin.

quiz.q: The treaty that phases out ozone-depleting substances and is universally ratified is:
quiz.explanation: Montreal phased out CFCs and is the first universally ratified treaty in UN history; Kyoto targets greenhouse gases, Paris sets NDCs, Stockholm was the declaration that started the process.

quiz.q: India's Environment (Protection) Act was enacted in 1986 largely in response to:
quiz.explanation: The 1984 Bhopal gas leak exposed gaps in hazardous-substance regulation; the 1986 umbrella Act filled them. Stockholm (1972) inspired the earlier Water/Air Acts’ era.

quiz.q: Under the Paris Agreement, each country’s pledged contribution is called a:
quiz.explanation: Paris runs on nationally determined contributions (NDCs) — voluntary pledges reviewed collectively; Annex I targets and CDM belong to Kyoto’s architecture.

intro:
The global carbon budget is the balance sheet of the carbon cycle: human emissions from fossil fuels and land-use change, minus what ocean and land sinks reabsorb, leaves the rest to pile up in the atmosphere. Carbon flows between reservoirs — air, ocean, soils, vegetation, rocks — through fluxes that dwarf human emissions yet stayed balanced for millennia. Today roughly 45 percent of each year's emissions stay airborne, and tracking the rest is a core task of climate science.

**Why this matters.** Every net-zero pledge and offset scheme is an attempt to balance this budget, which for a given warming limit shrinks each year emissions continue.
objectives: Explain reservoirs and fluxes
Explain the airborne fraction
Explain ocean solubility and biological pumps
Explain terrestrial biosphere uptake
Explain residence time of a CO2 pulse
Explain budget imbalance

concepts.statement: A reservoir is a carbon store; a flux is the transfer rate between stores. The ocean holds about 38,000 gigatonnes of carbon, and soils plus vegetation over twice the atmosphere's 880 — but only fluxes crossing into and out of the air change the greenhouse effect.

The airborne fraction is the share of each year's human emissions that stays in the atmosphere after sinks take their cut. Averaged since 1959 it sits near 45 percent, wobbling upward in hot, dry El Nino years; a persistent rise would signal saturating sinks.

The ocean absorbs CO2 two ways. The solubility pump dissolves gas into cold water and overturning circulation carries it to the deep; the biological pump has plankton fix carbon into sinking organic matter.

Land ecosystems absorb another 30 percent, mostly where photosynthesis exceeds respiration in regrowing forests. Because the service depends on water, nutrients and biomass, droughts, fires and deforestation can flip regions from sink to source within a season.

concepts.term: Residence time of a CO2 pulse
concepts.statement: An individual molecule spends only a few years airborne, but the excess from a pulse lingers far longer: re-equilibrating with the deep ocean takes centuries to millennia. That is why CO2 cuts pay off slowly while methane cuts act within decades.

Adding emissions and subtracting the best sink estimates should reproduce measured growth, and it never does exactly. The small leftover is the budget imbalance — a diagnosis of uncertainty that pushes better sensors, flux towers and carbon-observing satellites.
$$\Delta C_{\text{atm}} = E_{\text{ff}} + E_{\text{luc}} - S_{\text{ocean}} - S_{\text{land}}$$
concepts.detail: Atmospheric growth equals fossil plus land-use emissions minus ocean and land uptake; the mismatch with measured growth is the imbalance.

concepts.statement: $$AF = \frac{\Delta C_{\text{atm}}}{E_{\text{ff}} + E_{\text{luc}}}$$
concepts.detail: The share of each year's human emissions that remains airborne — near 45 percent since 1959.

concepts.statement: Sinks delay warming rather than cancel it — much of the absorbed carbon re-equilibrates with the air over centuries. The airborne fraction is a diagnostic, not a constant, and it moves with climate variability. And confusing gigatonnes of carbon with CO2 rescales every figure by 3.67.
A reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases over a stated period.
The percentage of annual human emissions remaining in the atmosphere.
Dissolution of CO2 into cold seawater and its transport to depth.
Plankton fixing carbon that sinks to the deep ocean.
How long a molecule, or a pulse’s excess, persists in a reservoir.
One billion tonnes of carbon; multiply by 3.67 to express it as CO2.

examples.title: Worked example — Carbon Sinks and the Global Carbon Budget
examples.problem: Carbon Sinks and the Global Carbon Budget — worked through step by step

steps.label: Identify
steps.text: atmospheric growth for a year with fossil emissions 10.0 GtC, land-use 1.1, ocean sink 2.7 and land sink 3.3 GtC.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: the budget equation, atmospheric growth = total emissions − total sink uptake.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: emissions total 11.1 GtC, sinks remove 6.0 GtC, so predicted growth is 5.1 GtC; measurements show 5.0 GtC.

examples.result: the airborne fraction is 5.0/11.1 ≈ 45 percent, and the 0.1 GtC gap is the budget imbalance.

keyTakeaways: Remaining-budget estimates that anchor net-zero deadlines in climate policy
Carbon markets, where verification of real sink uptake decides whether a credit is genuine
Ocean acidification forecasts, since absorbed CO2 shifts seawater chemistry
Peatland and coastal 'blue carbon' restoration strengthening the land sink

Where next — Tackle this once the greenhouse effect and basic chemistry feel solid. Natural follow-ons are ocean acidification, climate feedbacks and the mitigation pathways that spend the remaining budget.
Growth in the air = fossil + land-use emissions − ocean sink − land sink.
About 45 percent stays airborne; the ocean takes a quarter, land roughly 30 percent.
Cold waters and plankton exports make the ocean a vast but slow sink.
Molecules cycle in years, but a pulse persists for centuries to millennia.
The budget imbalance audits how well we know the sinks.

quiz.q: Emissions total 11 GtC and the sinks absorb 6 GtC. Atmospheric growth is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Growth is emissions minus uptake: 11 − 6 = 5 GtC.

quiz.q: An emission pulse warms for centuries though each molecule leaves the air within years because:
options: molecules are constantly re-emitted to replace the ones removed
removing molecules is fast, but rebalancing the excess with the deep ocean is slow
CO2 is permanently trapped in the stratosphere
sinks absorb only methane, never CO2
quiz.explanation: The molecule exchanges quickly, but the added inventory re-equilibrates with the deep ocean over centuries.

quiz.q: The budget imbalance is best described as:
options: the mismatch between predicted and measured atmospheric growth after sink estimates
emissions from unreported fossil-fuel use only
the forest share of total uptake
quiz.explanation: It is the residual when emissions minus estimated sinks fails to match the observed increase — a measure of uncertainty.

intro:
Planetary boundaries define a 'safe operating space' for humanity: nine Earth-system processes — climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows, ocean acidification, atmospheric aerosol loading, stratospheric ozone and novel entities — each with a quantified level judged unsafe to cross. Proposed by Johan Rockstrom and colleagues in 2009 and updated since, the framework treats the stable Holocene as the only envelope our civilisations know. The 2023 assessment judged six of the nine boundaries already transgressed.

**Why this matters.** The framework converts scattered scientific warnings into one comparable dashboard that governments, companies and cities use to steer environmental targets — the biophysical backbone of science-based targets and doughnut economics.
objectives: Explain nine boundary processes
Explain boundary versus threshold
Explain tipping elements and hysteresis
Explain zone of increasing risk
Explain novel entities
Explain safe and just boundaries

concepts.statement: Each process is tracked by a control variable: atmospheric CO2 concentration for climate, phosphorus flow to the sea for biogeochemical flows, aragonite saturation for ocean acidification. A measurable control variable turns an abstract warning into a monitorable number for the whole process.

The true tipping threshold is usually unknown, so boundaries are deliberately set below the best estimate as a buffer — precaution in numerical form. Society stays inside a zone science can still vouch for, paying a modest premium against cascading change.

Systems such as the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, the Amazon rainforest and the Atlantic overturning circulation can flip into self-reinforcing alternative states. Hysteresis means returning the driver below the threshold does not guarantee the system returns.

Between the boundary and the true threshold lies the zone of increasing risk, where damage grows but collapse is not expected. Climate occupied that zone for decades; honestly framing that uncertainty is a feature of the framework, not a flaw.

Novel entities — plastics, pesticides, PFAS, engineered organisms — are released faster than science can test their effects. The control variable is assessment capacity, so zero untested release is the only provably safe value.

The 2023 'safe and just' analysis added distribution: significant harm to people appears near 1 °C of warming, well below the biophysical limits. The boundaries become a scoreboard of who bears the damage, not only of Earth's state.
$$T = \frac{X_{\text{current}}}{X_{\text{boundary}}}$$
concepts.detail: A control variable divided by its boundary value; above 1 means the process is outside the safe space. In 2023, nitrogen fixation (about 150 Tg per year against a 62 Tg boundary) scored about 2.4.

concepts.statement: Boundaries are guard-rails, not cliff edges — crossing one does not mean instant collapse, and staying inside guarantees nothing. The nine processes interact, so land change pushes climate and freshwater together. The numbers are expert judgements with real uncertainty, which is exactly why the buffers exist.
A suggested safe limit for an Earth-system process, set below the expected threshold.
The measurable quantity chosen to track a boundary process.
A subsystem that can shift into a self-reinforcing alternative state.
A system's failure to retrace its original path when a driver is reversed.
The span between boundary and threshold where the uncertainty of harm grows.
Synthetic chemicals and organisms released faster than they can be tested for harm.

examples.title: Worked example — Planetary Boundaries and Safe Operating Space
examples.problem: Whether industrial nitrogen fixation, about 150 Tg per year, sits inside its boundary of 62 Tg per year.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: the transgression ratio divides the current control variable by its boundary value, with 1 marking the safe edge.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: T = 150/62 ≈ 2.4 — well past 1 and deep in the red zone of the boundary diagram.

examples.result: nitrogen is among the most transgressed boundaries, flagging eutrophication risk and arguing for cuts in fertiliser and combustion nitrogen losses.

keyTakeaways: Corporate science-based target setting for water, land and biodiversity footprints
Doughnut economics dashboards pairing planetary limits with social foundations for cities
National and international environmental assessments framing policy against biophysical limits
Teaching and communication tools that make Earth-system limits visible at a glance

Where next — Come here with solid grounding in climate science and ecology — the carbon budget topic pairs naturally. Next steps are earth-system modelling, resilience theory, and the governance instruments that might keep humanity inside the safe space.
Nine processes, each with a measurable control variable, define the safe operating space.
Boundaries sit below uncertain thresholds on purpose — precaution as a buffer.
Tipping elements plus hysteresis make some transgressions effectively irreversible.
The 2023 assessment found six of nine boundaries transgressed, with nitrogen deepest in the red.
'Safe and just' adds distribution: harm to people starts well before biophysical collapse.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the nine planetary boundary processes?
quiz.explanation: Volcanoes are natural drivers outside the framework; boundaries track human-stressed processes.

quiz.q: A boundary is deliberately set below the best estimate of the actual threshold to:
options: make the boundary diagram look symmetric
provide a safety margin for scientific uncertainty
quiz.explanation: The gap is a precautionary buffer, since thresholds are uncertain and some changes are effectively irreversible.

quiz.q: Hysteresis matters for boundary policy because:
options: systems return instantly once a driver is reversed
a system that has tipped may stay tipped even if the driver is reduced
it makes measurements cheaper to collect
quiz.explanation: Self-reinforcing alternative states make prevention far cheaper than reversal.

intro:
A healthy soil is not dirt but a living ecosystem — minerals, organic matter, roots, fungi, bacteria and animals — that cycles nutrients, stores water and resists erosion. Soil health names that capacity; regenerative agriculture is the toolkit that rebuilds it after decades of organic-matter mining: cover crops, minimal tillage, diverse rotations, compost and managed grazing. Since roughly 95 percent of food calories trace back to soil, the subject underpins sustainable food systems, and its central currency is soil organic matter.

**Why this matters.** Degraded soils erode faster than they form, threatening yields within a generation, while regenerating them improves drought tolerance and water quality. Practices that build soil carbon also pull CO2 out of the atmosphere.
objectives: Explain soil organic matter
Explain aggregate structure and tilth
Explain the soil food web
Explain cover cropping
Explain minimal tillage
Explain carbon sequestration and its limits

concepts.statement: Organic matter — living roots and microbes, dead residues, humus — is only 2 to 5 percent of soil by weight yet drives most function: holding water, feeding microbes and releasing nutrients slowly.

Mineral particles cling into crumbs around roots and fungal threads, creating pores that admit air and water. Good tilth lets roots push easily and rain soak in; compaction from heavy machinery collapses the network and starves it of oxygen.

Bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes and earthworms form a food web that mineralises nutrients from organic matter. Mycorrhizal fungi trade phosphorus and water to plant roots for sugars — a partnership some crops cannot grow well without.

Keeping living roots in the ground year-round protects aggregates from rain impact, captures leftover nitrogen and pumps fresh carbon underground. The cover crop is terminated before the cash crop, returning biomass as mulch and food for the web.

Ploughing flushes oxygen into the profile, letting microbes burn stored carbon while the mixing destroys fungal networks and aggregates. No-till drills seed through residue instead, trading immediate weed control for long-term structure.

Building soil carbon is slow — tenths of a tonne per hectare per year — and each soil has a saturation ceiling set by texture and climate. Gains reverse when practices stop, so permanence matters as much as totals.
$$\text{SOM} \approx 1.72 \times \text{SOC}$$
concepts.detail: The Van Bemmelen factor: organic matter is roughly 58 percent carbon, so multiply carbon by 1.72.

concepts.statement: $$C_{\text{stock}} = \rho_b \cdot d \cdot f_{OC}$$
concepts.detail: Carbon per square metre: bulk density times sampling depth times the organic-carbon fraction; multiply by 10,000 for tonnes per hectare.

concepts.statement: No practice regenerates every soil: no-till in cold, wet clay can depress yields, and cover crops need water that drylands cannot always spare. Soil carbon saturates and reverses, so permanence beats headline rates. And 'regenerative' is not a certification — without measurement it slides into marketing.
The living, dead and decayed biological fraction of soil; roughly 58 percent carbon.
The physical condition of soil as roots experience it: structure, porosity, workability.
The soil’s ability to hold and trade positively charged nutrients on clay and organic surfaces.
A fungal symbiosis on plant roots that trades phosphorus and water for sugars.
A non-cash crop grown to protect and feed the soil between main crops.
Dry soil mass per unit volume; high values mean compaction.

examples.title: Worked example — Soil Health and Regenerative Agriculture
examples.problem: Soil Health and Regenerative Agriculture — worked through step by step

steps.label: Identify
steps.text: the organic matter and carbon stock of a 30 cm soil with bulk density 1.3 t/m3 and 1.6 percent organic carbon.

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: SOM ≈ 1.72 × SOC, and stock = bulk density × depth × carbon fraction.

steps.label: Apply them
steps.text: SOM ≈ 1.72 × 1.6 ≈ 2.75 percent; stock = 1.3 × 0.3 × 0.016 = 0.00624 t C per m2, or 62.4 tonnes per hectare.

examples.result: raising carbon by 0.5 percentage points would store about 19.5 tonnes per hectare — a decade-scale project, not a season of work.

keyTakeaways: Carbon-farming programmes that pay for verified soil carbon gains
Drought planning, since each extra point of organic matter lifts water holding
Nutrient-pollution control, as cover crops capture leftover fertiliser before it leaches
Erosion control on slopes, where structure and surface cover keep soil in place

Where next — Start here with basic biology and chemistry — photosynthesis and nutrient cycles are the only prerequisites. Next: composting systems, integrated nutrient management, water in soils, then agroecology at landscape scale.
Organic matter is the currency: 2–5 percent of weight drives water, nutrients and biology.
Aggregates built by roots and fungi create the pores that roots and rain depend on.
Cover crops keep the food web fed year-round; tillage burns its capital.
SOM ≈ 1.72 × SOC; carbon stock = bulk density × depth × carbon fraction.
Sequestration is slow, saturating and reversible — permanence defines its value.

quiz.q: A lab reports 2 percent soil organic carbon. Total organic matter is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Multiply carbon by the Van Bemmelen factor: 2 × 1.72 ≈ 3.4 percent organic matter.

quiz.q: Ploughing depletes soil organic matter mainly because:
options: it removes nutrients directly from the field
the flush of oxygen lets microbes rapidly oxidise stored carbon
it raises bulk density above 2 t/m3
it kills earthworms and nothing else
quiz.explanation: Tillage aerates the profile, and the microbial bloom burns stored carbon while breaking aggregates.

quiz.q: Mycorrhizal fungi help crops mainly by:
options: trading phosphorus and water to roots for sugars
quiz.explanation: The fungus extends the root’s reach for immobile phosphorus in exchange for plant carbon.

intro:
The water cycle is Earth's endlessly repeating distillery: the sun evaporates about 500,000 cubic kilometres of water each year, mostly from the oceans, and rain and snow return nearly all of it. Of the planet's water, 97 percent is salty; of the fresh remainder, two-thirds is locked in ice and nearly all the rest is groundwater. Rivers, lakes and soil moisture — the pools civilisation actually drinks from — hold a sliver of one percent.

**Why this matters.** More than two billion people face high water stress for part of every year, and agriculture claims roughly 70 percent of all withdrawals. Every drought response, irrigation plan and river treaty is applied hydrology.
objectives: Explain reservoirs and residence times
Explain evaporation, condensation and precipitation
Explain runoff and infiltration
Explain groundwater and aquifers
Explain watersheds and the water balance
Explain physical and economic water scarcity

concepts.statement: Every pool of water, from the ocean to a leaf, is a reservoir linked to the others by fluxes of evaporation, rain, rivers and groundwater. Residence time — how long a molecule stays put — is stock divided by throughflow: about 3,000 years in the deep ocean, centuries to millennia in aquifers, but only nine days in the atmosphere, which holds barely a week and a half of the world's rain.

Solar energy drives the engine. Evaporation from the oceans supplies about 86 percent of the total, and the vapour releases its latent heat when it condenses into clouds — a planetary heat pump moving energy toward the poles. Globally, precipitation balances evaporation almost exactly, but the two are offset in space and time: the sea loses more than it gains, and the land runs a surplus that rivers carry back.

Where rain strikes the ground it either infiltrates into soil or runs off across the surface, and that split decides everything downstream. Infiltration depends on texture, plant cover and how wet the profile already is; intense rain on baked or paved ground becomes overland flow that carves gullies and floods rivers. Hydrologists call soil moisture and the water plants transpire green water, and the rivers, lakes and aquifers feeding taps blue water.

Below the water table every crack and pore is saturated, and geology organises this hidden ocean into aquifers — unconfined ones recharged quickly from above, confined ones sealed between impermeable layers. Half the world's drinking water comes from underground. Some, such as the Ogallala beneath the American Great Plains, hold fossil water recharged thousands of years ago; pumping them is mining, because what is withdrawn will not return on any human timescale.

A watershed is the entire land area draining to one outlet, and the natural accounting unit for water: for any catchment, precipitation equals evapotranspiration plus streamflow plus the change in storage. The equation looks trivial, but each term is hard to measure — evapotranspiration cannot be observed directly over large areas, and storage shifts silently underground. Closing the balance is the everyday craft of hydrology.

Scarcity comes in two kinds. Physical scarcity means a basin's renewable water is already over-allocated — the Colorado, the Indus and the rivers feeding the Aral Sea no longer arrive in most years. Economic scarcity means water exists but money, infrastructure or institutions cannot deliver it, the situation across much of sub-Saharan Africa. The Falkenmark index flags stress below 1,700 cubic metres per person per year, absolute scarcity below 500.
$$P = ET + Q + \Delta S$$
concepts.detail: Precipitation equals evapotranspiration plus runoff plus storage change; averaged over years, the storage term shrinks toward zero.

concepts.statement: $$T_r = \frac{S}{\bar{Q}}$$
concepts.detail: Time a molecule spends in a reservoir: stock divided by mean throughflow — days in the atmosphere, millennia in the deep ocean.

concepts.statement: $$F = \frac{R}{N}$$
concepts.detail: Renewable water per person per year; below 1,700 cubic metres signals stress, below 500 absolute scarcity.

concepts.statement: Water withdrawn is not water consumed — most irrigation and cooling water returns to the cycle, warmer or saltier but not gone. Averages mislead: a basin can be wet on paper yet run short every summer, because timing and storage decide scarcity. And groundwater depletion stays invisible until wells fail.
The return of water to the atmosphere by evaporation and transpiration through plants.
Passage of water from the surface into the soil; its rate sets the runoff-infiltration split.
A water-bearing layer of rock or sediment; fossil aquifers are not recharged on human timescales.
The depth below which soil and rock pores are saturated.
Blue water flows in rivers, lakes and aquifers; green water sits in soil and passes through plants.
Renewable water per person per year; 1,700 cubic metres marks stress, 500 scarcity.

examples.title: Worked example — The Water Cycle and Freshwater Scarcity
examples.problem: The annual runoff of a 2,000 square-kilometre catchment with 1,100 mm of rain, 600 mm of evapotranspiration and negligible storage change, plus per-capita supply for its 3 million residents.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: the water balance Q = P − ET, and the Falkenmark index, renewable supply divided by population.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: Q = 1,100 − 600 = 500 mm of runoff, or 0.5 m over 2.0 billion square metres, giving 1.0 billion cubic metres a year; shared among 3 million people that is about 333 cubic metres each.

examples.result: the basin yields about one cubic kilometre of blue water a year, and at 333 cubic metres per person it sits deep in absolute scarcity, below the 500 line.

keyTakeaways: Reservoir and hydropower scheduling that turns snowpack forecasts into release plans
Irrigation design and crop choice in basins where every cubic metre is allocated
City water-supply planning blending rivers, groundwater and desalination
Transboundary treaties, from the Nile to the Mekong, dividing shared river flows

Where next — Within this domain, follow with soil health — organic matter is the catchment's hidden sponge — and planetary boundaries, which counts freshwater among the transgressed limits. Climate modelling explains why a warmer atmosphere intensifies floods and droughts.

quiz.q: The atmosphere holds about 13,000 cubic kilometres of water and precipitation removes 505,000 each year. Average residence time is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Stock over throughflow: 13,000 ÷ 505,000 of a year is about nine days.

quiz.q: A catchment receives 900 mm of rain and loses 650 mm to evapotranspiration. Annual streamflow is about:
quiz.explanation: With storage steady, Q = P − ET = 900 − 650 = 250 mm.

quiz.q: Economic water scarcity describes a situation where:
options: rivers have run completely dry across the region
groundwater is being pumped faster than rain recharges it
water is present but money, infrastructure or institutions fail to deliver it
per-capita supply exceeds 1,700 cubic metres per year
quiz.explanation: Physical scarcity is over-allocation of supply; economic scarcity is a delivery failure.

quiz.q: Pumping the Ogallala aquifer faster than it recharges is best described as:
options: raising the water table by reducing pressure
a closed loop returning every pumped litre
water mining of fossil groundwater that cannot return on human timescales
quiz.explanation: Fossil aquifers recharge over millennia; overdraft is mining, like extracting ore.

intro:
The renewable energy transition is the attempt to move the world's energy system — still more than 80 percent fossil-fuelled — onto sunlight, wind, water, biomass and the Earth's internal heat. Solar and wind are now the cheapest new electricity in most of the world, so the hard questions have moved to grids, storage, heavy industry and sheer speed: electricity is only about one-fifth of final energy, and the rest — steel, cement, shipping, heating, flying — must be electrified or reinvented.

**Why this matters.** Three-quarters of greenhouse-gas emissions come from energy. How fast coal retires, how fast heat pumps and electric vehicles scale, and how well grids absorb variable wind and sun largely decide how much the planet warms.
objectives: Explain primary energy, final energy and electricity
Explain variable generation from sun and wind
Explain capacity factor
Explain storage, grids and flexibility
Explain learning curves and cost declines
Explain system integration and stranded assets

concepts.term: Primary energy, final energy and electricity
concepts.statement: Energy statistics separate primary energy — the raw fuel pulled from nature — from final energy delivered to consumers. A coal plant converts about 38 percent of its fuel into power and discards the rest as waste heat, while a solar array delivers its output directly. That asymmetry makes 'renewable share of electricity' and 'renewable share of energy' very different numbers, and mixing them up exaggerates progress.

concepts.term: Variable generation from sun and wind
concepts.statement: Solar and wind are called variable because weather, not demand, sets their output. Their fuel is free, so every kilowatt-hour they generate displaces the most expensive fossil plant running — solar now routinely pushes midday wholesale prices toward zero, the 'duck curve' etched into California's grid. But the energy arrives on nature's schedule, and a calm, overcast winter week is the stress test a power system must survive.

A plant's capacity factor is its average output divided by its nameplate rating. Utility solar runs 15-25 percent, onshore wind 25-45 percent, offshore wind 50 percent or more, while nuclear sustains about 90 and gas near 50. Capacity factor is not efficiency — it records how often and how hard a plant runs. Comparing megawatts without capacity factors is the fastest way to misjudge an energy plan.

Matching variable supply to demand takes flexibility. Lithium-ion batteries smooth hours-long swings, yet pumped hydro still stores most of the world's grid electricity. Long-distance transmission lets windy plains serve distant cities, demand response shifts consumption into sunny hours, and surplus output can be curtailed — deliberately spilled. The unsolved frontier is seasons: banking summer's solar for a windless week in February, likely through hydrogen.

Each doubling of cumulative solar-panel production has cut module cost by roughly 20 percent — Wright's law, now repeating in wind turbines, batteries and electrolyisers. Module prices fell from over 100 dollars per watt in the mid-1970s to well under 30 cents today, which is why deployment, not invention, became the main lever: every gigawatt built makes the next one cheaper.

The last quarter of a decarbonised grid is far harder than the first half. Firm low-carbon sources — nuclear, hydro, geothermal — plus long-duration storage must cover extended lulls, and grids must supply the inertia that spinning turbines once provided free. Meanwhile utilities and oil regions face stranded assets: infrastructure worth billions that climate policy may render unprofitable before the end of its paying life.
$$CF = \frac{E_{\text{actual}}}{P_{\text{rated}} \times 8760}$$
concepts.detail: Actual annual energy divided by what the nameplate rating would produce running flat-out all 8,760 hours of a year.

concepts.statement: $$C_n = C_0 \left( \frac{n}{n_0} \right)^{-b}$$
concepts.detail: Cost falls by a constant fraction per doubling of cumulative production n; a 20 percent learning rate means b ≈ 0.32.

concepts.statement: $$LCOE = \frac{\sum_{t=0}^{T} \frac{I_t + M_t}{(1+r)^t}}{\sum_{t=0}^{T} \frac{E_t}{(1+r)^t}}$$
concepts.detail: Discounted lifetime costs divided by discounted lifetime generation — the price per megawatt-hour a plant must earn to break even.

concepts.statement: Nameplate capacity is not energy: a gigawatt of solar is roughly a quarter-gigawatt of average power. LCOE hides the integration costs — storage, transmission, curtailment — that climb with renewable share. And clean electricity is only the beginning: steel, cement, aviation and shipping will not decarbonise by plugging into a socket.
Energy in raw fuels before conversion; fossil plants waste most of it as heat.
Average output divided by nameplate capacity; how hard a plant runs.
The weather-driven variability of solar and wind output, unrelated to demand.
Discounted lifetime cost over lifetime generation; the break-even price per megawatt-hour.
The fall in unit cost as cumulative production doubles; about 20 percent per doubling for solar.
Deliberately spilling available renewable output the grid cannot absorb.
Fossil infrastructure whose value collapses before the end of its life.

examples.title: Worked example — The Renewable Energy Transition
examples.problem: The solar capacity, running at a 20 percent capacity factor, that delivers the annual energy of a 1,000 MW nuclear plant at 90 percent.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: annual energy equals nameplate capacity times capacity factor times 8,760 hours.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: the reactor generates 1,000 × 0.90 × 8,760 ≈ 7,880 GWh a year; matching that with solar requires 7,880 ÷ (8,760 × 0.20) = 4,500 MW of panels.

examples.result: about 4.5 GW of solar matches 1 GW of nuclear in yearly energy — but it arrives only in daylight, so firm capacity, storage or overbuild must cover the nights.

keyTakeaways: National decarbonisation pathways that phase out coal while keeping the lights on
Corporate power-purchase agreements funding new wind and solar farms at fixed prices
Grid-operator planning for resource adequacy, storage tenders and transmission
Off-grid solar-and-battery systems delivering first-time electricity to remote villages

Where next — Within this domain, pair with carbon sinks and the global carbon budget to see how fast the transition must run, and with nuclear fission technology for firm low-carbon power. Learning-curve economics links onward to manufacturing and industrial policy.

quiz.q: A 300 MW wind farm runs at a 35 percent capacity factor. Its annual generation is closest to:
Under a 20 percent learning rate, each doubling of cumulative production makes the cost:
options: fall to 80 percent of its previous level
fall to 20 percent of its previous level
quiz.explanation: The learning rate is the cost drop per doubling: 20 percent cheaper, leaving 80 percent.

quiz.q: The central challenge solar and wind pose to grid operators is that:
options: their fuel is expensive and volatile in price
they cannot be connected to transmission networks
their output follows weather rather than demand
quiz.explanation: Variability, not cost: supply and demand must balance every second.

quiz.q: Renewables supply 30 percent of a country's electricity, itself about 20 percent of final energy. The renewable share of total energy is roughly:
quiz.explanation: 0.30 × 0.20 = 0.06, about six percent — electrifying heat and transport matters as much as cleaning the grid.

intro:
Life on Earth has endured five mass extinctions — the worst, at the end of the Permian 252 million years ago, erased roughly 90 percent of marine species. Many biologists warn a sixth is under way, this one caused by a single species. Measured extinction rates run tens to hundreds of times the natural background, and monitored wild vertebrate populations have fallen by more than two-thirds since 1970. Biodiversity is not scenery: it is the machinery of pollination, soil formation, water purification and every food web.

**Why this matters.** About 75 percent of leading food crops depend partly on animal pollinators, and the services ecosystems provide each year have been valued above global GDP. Extinction is also the one environmental loss that is permanent — nothing regrows a vanished species.
objectives: Explain biodiversity from genes to ecosystems
Explain background versus mass extinction
Explain the HIPPO drivers
Explain ecosystem services and functioning
Explain extinction debt and trophic cascades
Explain protected areas and rewilding

concepts.statement: Biodiversity is the variety of life at every scale: genetic diversity within species that lets populations adapt, the richness and evenness of species themselves, and the variety of ecosystems — coral reefs, wetlands, old-growth forest. About two million species are formally described and several million more await description, mostly insects and microbes. Most species vanish before we ever knew they existed.

Extinction is natural: the fossil record suggests a background rate near 0.1 to 2 extinctions per million species-years. Mass extinctions are the exceptions — sudden events that swept away more than 75 percent of species, each followed by millions of years of recovery. Amphibians and other assessed groups are now disappearing tens to hundreds of times faster, which is why researchers speak of a sixth extinction in progress.

Conservationists rank the causes with the acronym HIPPO: Habitat destruction, Invasive species, Pollution, human Population growth and Overharvesting — with climate change layered on as an accelerant. Habitat loss leads everywhere, from cleared tropical forest to drained wetlands. Invasive rats, fungi and water hyacinth devastate islands and freshwaters; pollution runs from plastics to nitrogen; and overharvesting empties the ocean of large predators.

Species are working parts, not ornaments. Insects pollinate three-quarters of leading food crops; forests, wetlands and soils filter water and store carbon; predators hold pests and disease in check. Grassland experiments show the pattern: more diverse plots are more productive, more stable under drought and recover faster. Ecosystems tolerate some loss — the 'rivet popper' imagines an aircraft shedding rivets — but nobody knows which removal releases the wing.

Damage arrives with delay. When habitat shrinks to fragments, populations persist for decades below viable size — the extinction debt committed by past land clearing. Remove a keystone species and the effects cascade: hunting sea otters unleashed urchins that mowed down Pacific kelp forests, and without wolves, elk stripped Yellowstone's riverbanks until reintroduction let willows return. Ecosystems are webs, and cutting one strand deforms the whole.

The standard response is protection. About 17 percent of land and 8 percent of ocean lie in protected areas, and the Kunming-Montreal framework pushes toward 30 percent of each by 2030. Protection works only with enforcement and connectivity — 'paper parks' guard lines on maps, and isolated reserves slowly lose species they cannot replenish. Rewilding goes further, reinstating missing species and processes: beavers engineering wetlands, wolves shaping herds.

concepts.detail: Species count grows with area raised to an exponent z, typically 0.15-0.35; doubling habitat adds species, never doubles them.

concepts.statement: $$\frac{\Delta S}{S_0} = 1 - \left( \frac{A}{A_0} \right)^{z}$$
concepts.detail: Fraction of species ultimately lost when habitat shrinks from A0 to A, by the power law.

concepts.statement: $$E_{\text{MSY}} = \frac{N_{\text{ext}}}{S \cdot T} \times 10^{6}$$
concepts.detail: Extinctions per million species-years, the currency for comparing today with the fossil record.

concepts.statement: Charismatic megafauna absorb most conservation money while insects and plants — the actual workhorses — decline unnoticed. Species counts say nothing about abundance: populations can collapse while the species technically survives. Protected areas without rangers are paper parks, and planting trees is not restoring an ecosystem. Above all, there is no undoing extinction.
The variety of life at genetic, species and ecosystem levels.
The natural pace of extinction, roughly 0.1-2 per million species-years.
Habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, population, overharvesting — the main extinction drivers.
Future losses already committed by past habitat destruction.
A species whose influence on its ecosystem is vastly disproportionate to its abundance.
The power law linking species count to area.
Restoring ecosystems by reinstating missing species and natural processes.

examples.title: Worked example — Biodiversity and the Sixth Extinction
examples.problem: The fraction of species ultimately lost when 90 percent of a region's habitat is cleared, with z = 0.25.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: by the species-area relationship, surviving species scale as the remaining habitat fraction raised to z.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: survivors ÷ original = (0.10)^0.25 ≈ 0.56, so about 56 percent of species persist and 100 − 56 = 44 percent are committed to extinction.

examples.result: clearing 90 percent of habitat dooms not 90 but roughly 44 percent of species — a debt paid out as the last fragmented populations fade.

keyTakeaways: Reserve and corridor design that applies island biogeography to park networks
Red List assessments steering scarce conservation funding toward the most threatened species
Farm pollinator programmes — hedgerows, cover crops, fewer pesticides — protecting yields
Rewilding projects rebuilding food webs, from wolves in Yellowstone to beavers in Europe

Where next — Within this domain, planetary boundaries treats biosphere integrity as a core transgressed limit and soil health explores the biodiversity beneath our feet. The species-area logic leads into island biogeography and reserve design.

quiz.q: Doubling the area of a habitat with species-area exponent z = 0.25 raises its species count by about:
quiz.explanation: The multiplier is 2^0.25 ≈ 1.19 — a 19 percent increase.

quiz.q: The leading driver of species loss worldwide today is:
quiz.explanation: Habitat loss tops the HIPPO ranking; the others are secondary on average.

quiz.q: A keystone species is one that:
options: has the largest population in the ecosystem
appeared earliest in the fossil record
can thrive in any habitat it is moved to
disproportionately shapes the ecosystem relative to its abundance
quiz.explanation: Sea otters and wolves are classic examples: removing them reorganises entire food webs.

quiz.q: Extinction debt refers to:
options: the cost of running protected areas
species already doomed by past habitat loss although still extant today
the loss of genetic diversity within a single crop
quiz.explanation: Fragmented populations linger for decades, so past destruction keeps claiming species.

intro:
The ocean is one connected body of water covering 71 percent of the planet and holding 97 percent of its water — and it is never still. Winds drag its surface into great circular gyres, while differences in temperature and salinity drive a slow overturning that carries water on thousand-year journeys from the North Atlantic to the Pacific. The same water quietly absorbs roughly a quarter of each year's carbon emissions, changing its own chemistry as it does. This intermediate Earth Systems lesson covers the currents, the chemistry and the life they support — and why what happens in the ocean never stays in the ocean.

**Why this matters.** The ocean sets Earth's climate thermostat, feeds over three billion people who rely on seafood for a major protein source, and is acidifying as it absorbs our CO2. Fisheries, storms and coastlines all answer to how the water moves.
objectives: Explain one ocean, wind-driven gyres
Explain thermohaline circulation: the conveyor
Explain upwelling: the ocean fertilizer pumps
Explain salinity and the carbonate buffer
Explain acidification under way
Explain vertical zones of life

concepts.statement: Surface currents are the wind's work. Persistent trade winds and westerlies drag water into five great subtropical gyres — clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, counterclockwise in the south. Their western edges run fast, narrow and deep: the Gulf Stream off Florida moves some 30 million cubic meters of water per second, over a hundred Amazon rivers, carrying tropical heat that keeps Western Europe milder than its latitude suggests.

The deep circulation is driven by density. In the Greenland and Labrador seas, cold water chilled and salted by winter ice formation sinks and creeps south along the ocean floor; the loop resurfaces in the Pacific and Indian oceans centuries later. This thermohaline conveyor redistributes heat planet-wide, and its Atlantic arm — the AMOC — is watched closely because meltwater freshening the North Atlantic could weaken it.

Where wind blows surface water away, cold, nutrient-rich water rises to replace it: upwelling. The coasts off Peru, California and Namibia are upwelling engines — nitrate and phosphate from the deep fertilize plankton blooms that feed the world's richest fisheries, including the Peruvian anchoveta. A few percent of ocean area supplies roughly a fifth of the marine fish catch. When trade winds slacken in an El Nino, the pump stalls and the anchoveta fishery collapses.

Seawater is a broth of dissolved ions averaging 35 grams of salt per kilogram — mostly sodium and chloride — wrapped in a self-regulating buffer. Added CO2 reacts with water and carbonate to form bicarbonate, which is why the ocean can absorb about a quarter of human emissions. The buffer is not free: the reaction consumes the carbonate ions that shelled life needs.

Since pre-industrial times the surface ocean's pH has slipped from about 8.2 to 8.1 — a 0.1-unit drop meaning roughly 30 percent more hydrogen ions. Oyster hatcheries on the U.S. West Coast have already lost broods to corrosive upwelled water, and corals build more slowly as carbonate declines. High-emission projections reach 0.3 units by 2100, a near-doubling of acidity.

Life sorts by depth. Phytoplankton, the base of nearly every marine food web, live in the sunlit top 100 to 200 meters; below, the twilight zone runs on the rain of debris from above — the biological pump detailed in our carbon-budget lesson. Even the sunless floor surprises: hydrothermal vents discovered in 1977 host tube worms and shrimp farmed by chemosynthesis, no sunlight required.

The ocean absorbing CO2 is not a harmless free service — the buffering that protects pH consumes carbonate. Surface gyres (wind-driven, fast) and the thermohaline conveyor (density-driven, millennium-slow) are different machines. And the pH change from 8.2 to 8.1 looks tiny because the scale is logarithmic — each 0.1 is about a 30 percent jump in acidity.
A large wind-driven circular surface current around an ocean basin.
The global overturning driven by density — sinking cold, salty water and slow deep return flows.
The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation — the conveyor's Atlantic arm, a key climate knob.
Wind-driven rise of cold, nutrient-rich water that fertilizes surface life.
The pH decline caused by absorbed CO2 reacting to form carbonic acid and bicarbonate.
The sunlit upper 100-200 meters where photosynthesis powers marine food webs.
Building biomass from chemical energy, as at hydrothermal vents, with no sunlight.

examples.title: Worked example — The Global Ocean: Currents, Chemistry and Life
examples.problem: What a further 0.3-unit drop in ocean pH by 2100 would mean for acidity.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: pH is logarithmic — a shift of n units multiplies the hydrogen-ion concentration by 10 to the power n.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: 10^0.3 ≈ 2.0, so the hydrogen-ion concentration very nearly doubles.

examples.result: a "mere" 0.3-unit fall is a near-doubling of acidity — which is why shell-building organisms track CO2 emission scenarios so closely.

keyTakeaways: Fisheries agencies watch El Nino and upwelling indices to set anchoveta and sardine quotas
Oyster and clam hatcheries on the Pacific coast now monitor pH and carbonate daily
Climate scientists track AMOC indicators because a weaker conveyor would reshape European weather
Coral-reef managers pair local pollution control with global CO2 projections for reef survival
Shippers and sailors still ride the Gulf Stream and Agulhas currents to save fuel and days

quiz.q: Western Europe is milder than its latitude suggests largely because:
options: It is closer to the equator
The Gulf Stream carries tropical heat northward
Its winds blow only from the south
quiz.explanation: The Gulf Stream and its extension release enormous amounts of tropical heat to the North Atlantic atmosphere.

quiz.q: Upwelling zones support huge fisheries because rising water brings:
quiz.explanation: Deep water is cold but nutrient-rich; fertilized phytoplankton feed everything above them.

quiz.q: The pH drop from 8.2 to 8.1 means the ocean is now about:
quiz.explanation: The scale is logarithmic: 0.1 units is roughly a 30 percent increase in hydrogen-ion concentration.

quiz.q: Hydrothermal-vent communities are powered by:
quiz.explanation: Bacteria oxidize hydrogen sulfide from the vents, feeding ecosystems that never see the Sun.

intro:
Every crop you have ever eaten is a human invention. Wheat, rice, maize and potatoes all descend from wild plants remade by ten thousand years of selection by farmers who mostly had no idea what genes were. Modern crop science does the same job with far more precision: crossing, selecting, and since the 1990s directly adding or editing DNA. This core lesson traces the arc from domestication through Mendelian breeding, hybrid seed and the Green Revolution to today's GM debate — and shows how agronomists measure whether any of it is working, in tonnes per hectare.

**Why this matters.** Agriculture must roughly double food production by 2050 on little extra land, under shifting climates and evolving pests. Which breeding tools we use — and who controls seed — shapes food prices, farm livelihoods and wild-land conversion.
objectives: Explain domestication: the first genetic engineering
Explain breeding by selection
Explain hybrid vigor and yearly seed buying
Explain the Green Revolution
Explain gM crops: what they are, what is debated
Explain yield gaps and closing them

concepts.statement: Domestication began independently in a dozen-odd centers, from the Fertile Crescent's wheat and barley to Mexico's maize — a scrawny wild grass called teosinte transformed into full ears of corn. The domestication syndrome repeated everywhere: seeds stopped shattering from the stalk, dormancy and bitterness fell away, and harvestable parts swelled. A few regulatory gene changes did much of the work.

Selection is breeding's engine. Early farmers simply kept seed from the best plants; modern breeders do it deliberately — cross two parents, then walk the fields choosing offspring generation after generation, guided now by DNA markers linked to disease resistance or drought tolerance rather than by eye alone. Local landraces, shaped by centuries of farmer selection, remain a reservoir of adaptive genes.

concepts.term: Hybrid vigor and yearly seed buying
concepts.statement: Cross two genetically different inbred lines and the first generation can outgrow both parents — heterosis, or hybrid vigor, typically worth 10 to 30 percent in maize. The boost does not persist: the second generation reshuffles genes and yields crash, which is why farmers replant fresh F1 seed each season. The biology created the seed industry's business model.

The Green Revolution bundled genetics with agronomy. Norman Borlaug's semi-dwarf, rust-resistant wheats, bred at CIMMYT in Mexico, went to India and Pakistan in the mid-1960s and — with fertilizer and irrigation — turned looming famines into grain surpluses; Borlaug won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize. IR8, the 1966 "miracle rice," did the same across Asia.

concepts.term: GM crops: what they are, what is debated
concepts.statement: GM crops add genes rather than selecting existing ones. Bt corn and cotton carry a bacterial protein toxic to specific insects, cutting insecticide spraying; herbicide-tolerant varieties simplified weed control. The debate is real on both sides: pests have evolved Bt resistance where refuge plantings were skipped, weeds have followed glyphosate into resistance, and seed ownership concentrates in a few companies — while decades of evidence show no special danger from the technique itself. Newer gene-edited crops, built with the CRISPR tools explained in our genetics lesson, mostly tweak a plant's own genes and face lighter regulation.

Progress is measured in yield: tonnes per hectare. U.S. maize averages about 11 t/ha with contest plots above 16, while Sub-Saharan African maize averages under 2. The yield gap — actual minus attainable yield — closes as much through agronomy, seed access and soil care as through new genetics.

Hybrid is not GMO: hybrid vigor comes from crossing inbred lines, a technique organic farmers happily use, while GM inserts or edits specific genes. Yield growth also stalled in several regions after the Green Revolution — genetics alone cannot outrun degraded soils and hotter summers. And a record yield in a contest plot says nothing about what average farmers can afford.
The recurring changes — no shattering, less bitterness, bigger seeds — that mark a domesticated plant.
A locally adapted crop population improved by generations of farmer selection.
Hybrid vigor — the F1 outperforming both inbred parents.
First-generation cross of two inbred lines; uniform and vigorous, but its seed cannot be saved profitably.
The 1960s-70s yield leap from semi-dwarf varieties plus fertilizer and irrigation.
A plant engineered to produce a bacterial protein toxic to specific insect pests.
The difference between actual farm yield and the attainable yield with best local practice.

examples.title: Worked example — Crop Science: From Domestication to Disease Resistance
examples.problem: The yield gap for a region whose farmers average 3.0 tonnes of maize per hectare where attainable yield with best local practice is 6.5.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: yield gap = attainable − actual; farmers' realized share = actual / attainable.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: gap = 6.5 − 3.0 = 3.5 t/ha; realized share = 3.0 / 6.5 ≈ 0.46, so about 46 percent of attainable yield is captured.

examples.result: over half the potential is unrealized — usually a seed, water, pest or soil-fertility problem to diagnose field by field before any new variety is even discussed.

keyTakeaways: Seed companies run hundreds of trial plots a year to pick next season's hybrids
Gene banks such as CIMMYT's wheat collection preserve wild relatives for future breeding
Plant pathologists race new stem rust strains like Ug99, breeding resistance before it spreads
Seed certification laws guarantee that the hybrid in the bag matches its label
Extension services demo trial yields to close local yield gaps farmer by farmer

quiz.q: Farmers buy new hybrid seed every year because:
options: The F2 generation loses vigor as genes reshuffle
quiz.explanation: Segregation in the second generation breaks up the combination that made the F1 outperform — yields crash.

quiz.q: The Green Revolution depended primarily on:
options: Semi-dwarf disease-resistant varieties plus fertilizer and irrigation
quiz.explanation: Borlaug's wheats and IR8 rice only paid off as a package with nutrients and controlled water.

quiz.q: Bt corn reduces insecticide spraying because:
options: It produces a bacterial protein toxic to its target pests
quiz.explanation: The engineered Cry protein kills chewing caterpillars like corn borers — the plant is its own pesticide.

quiz.q: A region yields 3.0 t/ha against an attainable 6.5. The yield gap and realized share are:
quiz.explanation: Gap = 6.5 − 3.0 = 3.5 t/ha; realized share = 3.0/6.5 ≈ 46 percent.

intro:
Conservation has two jobs: protect what remains, and put back what was lost. The second job — restoration — has grown from hobby to global industry: the United Nations declared 2021-2030 the Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, and the Bonn Challenge aims to bring 350 million hectares under restoration. The science begins with a simple observation: damaged land does not stay damaged. It recovers along a predictable relay called succession, and restoration is the art of steering it. This core lesson covers that sequence, the choice between letting nature heal itself and helping actively, and the rewilding experiments — from Yellowstone wolves to English beavers — that test how much of an ecosystem you actually need.

**Why this matters.** Restoration is now central to climate policy (nature-based carbon), water security and the 30x30 global target of protecting 30 percent of land and ocean by 2030. Done well it multiplies biodiversity; done badly it is expensive green paint.
objectives: Explain succession: nature recovery sequence
Explain setting restoration targets
Explain passive restoration: removing the stressor
Explain active restoration and reintroduction
Explain trophic rewilding: Yellowstone and beavers
Explain measuring recovery, not just acres

concepts.statement: After a disturbance, life returns in an orderly relay. Bare lava or glacier scrape starts from scratch — primary succession, lichens first and soil building over centuries. A logged forest or abandoned farm keeps its soil, so secondary succession runs faster: weeds and grasses in year one, shrubs by five, pioneer trees by twenty, and in the eastern United States a mature hardwood forest after a century or two.

Good restoration needs a target: a reference ecosystem — often a nearby intact site or historical records — and goals stated as structure (which species, how many layers), function (nutrient cycling, water storage) and resilience. "Make it green" is not a target; a monoculture of one fast-growing exotic tree is green and still an ecological desert.

The cheapest restoration is often to stop the harm and wait: fence livestock off the stream, end logging, remove drainage. Studies comparing methods repeatedly find passive recovery can match active planting at a fraction of the cost — but only where the stressor is truly gone and seeds can still reach the site. On land cleared for decades, waiting is not enough.

Active restoration adds what nature cannot deliver fast: seeding and planting natives, rebuilding hydrology, reintroducing species. Costa Rica did it at national scale — forest cover fell to about 21 percent by 1987, then rebounded past half the country through protection and assisted regrowth, reversing one of the world's fastest deforestation curves.

Trophic rewilding restores the animals that shape ecosystems from the top. In 1995, 41 gray wolves were released in Yellowstone; elk stopped loitering in open river valleys, willows and aspen regrew, beavers recolonized, and their ponds drew birds and fish — a trophic cascade still studied and debated. In Europe, beavers are reintroduced as ecosystem engineers whose dams slow floods, recharge groundwater and build wetlands free of charge; England's Devon trial measured real flood-peak reduction downstream.

Restoration is measured, not announced: species richness against the reference, indicator species returning, functions like decomposition and stream shade, plus survival of what was planted. The flagship caution is "plant a tree" arithmetic — single-species plantations can tick an acreage box (and a carbon credit) while supporting less biodiversity than the degraded land they replaced. The 30x30 target will be judged on function, not geometry.

Planting is not restoring: rows of one exotic species store carbon yet starve wildlife. Restoring while the original stressor — overgrazing, drainage, pollution — still operates wastes money, which is why passive "stressor removal first" is the field's golden rule. And expecting a pristine past ignores that climate has moved the goalposts; many projects now aim for novel but functional ecosystems.
Recovery on ground that kept its soil, from weeds to mature forest over decades to centuries.
The intact site or historical record a restoration project measures itself against.
Removing the stressor — fencing, stopping logging — and letting succession do the work.
Planting, seeding, earthworks and species reintroductions where nature cannot recover alone.
Indirect effects rippling from a predator's return, as wolves changed elk behavior and then rivers' vegetation.
A species, like the beaver, that physically rebuilds habitat for many others.
A functioning new assemblage with no historical analogue, often the realistic target under climate change.

examples.title: Worked example — Restoration and Rewilding: Putting Ecosystems Back Together
examples.problem: What an abandoned cornfield in the eastern U.S. will look like at 2, 15 and 60 years, and how a restorationist would steer it.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: secondary succession runs annual weeds → perennial herbs and shrubs → pioneer trees → mature hardwoods, because soil and a nearby seed source remain.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: year 2 brings ragweed and crabgrass; year 15, broomsedge, shrubs and first pines; year 60, a young hardwood stand with oaks establishing beneath. Steering: knock back invasives early, plant native hardwoods to skip decades, leave snags and logs for habitat.

examples.result: natural recovery delivers a young forest by mid-century; targeted planting reaches the reference community decades sooner at modest cost.

keyTakeaways: Mine-reclamation law obliges companies to rebuild soils and native vegetation after closure
Dam removal — over 2,000 U.S. dams since 2012 — lets rivers and salmon runs re-connect
Cities convert vacant lots to native meadows with passive restoration and seed mixes
Peatland rewetting in Europe and Southeast Asia cuts both biodiversity loss and fire risk
Carbon-market standards increasingly demand native diversity, not just planted stems, before paying out

quiz.q: Passive restoration is most likely to succeed when:
options: The original stressor is removed and a seed source remains nearby
The land has been cleared for a century
All native species are locally extinct
quiz.explanation: Nature's relay is fast when soil and seeds survive — stop the harm and succession does the labor for free.

quiz.q: The Yellowstone wolf return is celebrated mainly as:
options: A trophic cascade that reshaped vegetation and rivers
quiz.explanation: Wolf-avoidance behavior changed elk browsing, letting willows and aspen recover and beavers return — effects still debated in detail.

quiz.q: Beavers are called ecosystem engineers because:
options: Their dams physically create wetlands used by many species
quiz.explanation: One animal's construction reworks hydrology — ponds, flood storage and habitat that would cost millions to build.

quiz.q: The core criticism of single-species tree plantations counted as "restoration" is:
options: They meet acreage targets while restoring little biodiversity or function
quiz.explanation: Monocultures can earn carbon credits yet support less life than the degraded land they replaced — the trap 30x30 must avoid.

intro:
You put the bin out at night and it vanishes by morning — and for most people the story of waste ends there. Behind that vanishing act sits one of civilization's largest logistics operations: collection trucks, transfer stations, sorting facilities, engineered landfills and incinerators, all sized to the flow of material a city discards every day. This core lesson follows your rubbish from kerb to final destination, and asks the question modern waste management obsesses over: how much of that material can be kept in use instead of buried?

**Why this matters.** Waste is a design failure made visible. Every tonne of rubbish is raw material, energy and embodied labor discarded — and the systems that collect, sort and process it decide whether those values are recovered or lost for centuries.
objectives: Explain collection economics dominate the system
Explain engineered landfills: liners, leachate, gas
Explain waste-to-energy trade-offs
Explain recycling as a commodity business
Explain contamination and National Sword
Explain organics diversion and composting
Explain circular economy and producer responsibility

concepts.statement: The first and most expensive step is getting waste from millions of doors to anywhere at all. Collection — trucks, crews, routes — typically consumes half of a municipal waste budget, which is why cities obsess over route density and bin design. Once collected, waste is compacted and hauled to transfer stations, loaded onto larger vehicles, and moved in bulk to the distant facilities that handle it: landfill, incinerator or recycling plant. Geography matters; transport costs shape every design decision downstream.

The modern sanitary landfill is nothing like the town dump of memory. Its base is sealed with compacted clay plus a plastic geomembrane, layered like a bathtub; a network of pipes collects leachate, the contaminated liquid percolating through the waste, and treats it as wastewater. Decomposing organic matter generates landfill gas — roughly half methane — which capture wells either flare or burn for energy. Monitoring wells surround the site for decades after closure, because a landfill is not finished when full: it is a slow bioreactor and a long-term liability.

Burning waste shrinks it to about a tenth of its volume and can recover energy — waste-to-energy plants supply district heating in Copenhagen and electricity elsewhere. The controversies are real: combustion flue gases need scrubbers, fabric filters and activated carbon to control acid gases, particulates and dioxins, and the fly ash left over requires secure disposal. Whether incineration counts as recovery or disposal — and whether it quietly undermines recycling by demanding fuel — remains a live policy fight.

Recycling is a commodity business wearing an environmental halo. In single-stream systems everything recyclable goes in one bin; at the materials recovery facility, conveyors, screens, magnets, optical sorters and people separate paper, card, plastics, glass and metals into bales sold to processors. Everything hinges on contamination: one greasy pizza box can downgrade a batch of cardboard, and wishcycling — tossing questionable items in hopefully — does real damage. In 2018 China's National Sword policy slashed the contamination it would accept in imported bales, crashing commodity prices and forcing Western nations to build domestic capacity and confront how little plastic marked recyclable actually is.

Organics — food scraps and yard waste — form the largest single slice of municipal waste and the most damaging in landfill, where they decompose into methane. Composting returns them to soil as humus; anaerobic digestion captures the methane as biogas for energy first. Source-separated organics collections are the quiet workhorses of high-diversion cities like San Francisco and Milan, because no sorting technology can scrub mixed food waste out of plastic film.

The endgame is upstream design. The waste hierarchy ranks options from best to worst — reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose — and every step up the list beats the one below it. Circular-economy thinking pushes producers to take responsibility for products at end of life, a principle already law for packaging across much of Europe, and to design for disassembly and for materials that survive recycling loops rather than degrade through them.
$$\text{MRR} = \frac{m_{\text{recovered}}}{m_{\text{collected}}} \times 100\%$$
concepts.detail: The share of collected material actually processed back into products, rather than landfilled or burned.

concepts.statement: $$D = \frac{m_{\text{recycled}} + m_{\text{composted}}}{m_{\text{generated}}} \times 100\%$$
concepts.detail: Total diversion from disposal: recycling plus organics recovery, over everything generated.

concepts.statement: The label recyclable describes a possibility, not a promise — whether something is actually recycled depends on your local facility and the market for the bale. Wishcycling contaminates loads and raises costs. Diversion statistics can be gamed by counting incineration as recovery. And exporting waste to poorer countries long propped up Western recycling rates — an exit the world is closing.
Liquid that has percolated through waste; collected by landfill pipes and treated.
The plastic liner sealing a modern landfill base above compacted clay.
Materials recovery facility — the sorting plant turning mixed recyclables into saleable bales.
Wrong or dirty material in a recycling stream, degrading or destroying batch value.
China's 2018 import crackdown that collapsed markets for contaminated recyclables.
Microbial breakdown of organics in sealed tanks, yielding biogas.
Rules making producers fund or manage end-of-life handling of their products.

examples.title: Worked example — Waste: Where It Goes After the Bin
examples.problem: Recycling and diversion rates for a city generating 100,000 tonnes of municipal waste a year — 30,000 t set out as recyclables, of which the sorting facility sells 24,000 t of clean material, plus 20,000 t of organics composted.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: recycling rate = material actually recycled over total generated; diversion adds composting on top.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: recycling = 24,000/100,000 = 24 percent. Diversion = (24,000 + 20,000)/100,000 = 44 percent. The facility's process yield is 24,000/30,000 = 80 percent — 6,000 t were too contaminated to sell.

examples.result: 44 percent diverted, 56 percent still needing landfill or incineration — and improving that means attacking both the 6,000 t of contamination and the 50,000 t never separated at all.

keyTakeaways: Landfill gas capture systems powering generators or feeding pipelines
Waste-to-energy plants providing district heating for whole districts
Deposit-return schemes achieving above 90 percent container return in Germany and Scandinavia
Extended producer responsibility laws financing packaging recycling from producer fees
City organics programs — San Francisco and Milan collect food waste separately from nearly every household

quiz.q: Leachate is:
options: contaminated liquid that has percolated through the landfill
quiz.explanation: Rain and moisture moving through waste pick up pollutants; liners and collection pipes keep it out of groundwater.

quiz.q: China's National Sword mattered because it:
options: sharply restricted contaminated recyclable imports, crashing Western recycling markets
quiz.explanation: For decades the West's recycling depended on Chinese buyers; the 2018 contamination limits ended that and forced domestic capacity.

quiz.q: A city generates 100,000 t of waste; 24,000 t are sold as clean recyclables and 20,000 t composted. Its diversion rate is:
quiz.explanation: (24,000 + 20,000)/100,000 = 44 percent — the 80 percent figure is the sorting facility's process yield, not the city's rate.

quiz.q: The waste hierarchy ranks options, from best to worst, as:
quiz.explanation: Not producing waste beats reusing it, which beats recycling it — energy recovery and disposal are the last resorts.

intro:
Air pollution is the world's largest environmental health risk — linked by the World Health Organization to roughly seven million early deaths a year, more than traffic accidents and malaria combined. Yet unlike climate change, its damage is local, fast and reversible: shut the sources off and the air clears within days. This lesson is about health-relevant pollution, not carbon — the particles and gases that attack lungs and hearts, the weather that traps them, and the engineering that scrubs them out of exhausts and smokestacks.

**Why this matters.** Every major city's air today is the product of a century of pollution-control engineering. London's lethal fogs, Los Angeles's brown haze and the removal of lead from gasoline were all solved, or measurably improved, once the chemistry was understood. The history proves the tools work.
objectives: Explain criteria pollutants: PM2.5, NOx, SO2, O3, CO
Explain london coal smog versus photochemical smog
Explain temperature inversions as lids
Explain health evidence down to no safe threshold
Explain scrubbers, precipitators, catalytic converters
Explain air Quality Index and indoor air

concepts.term: criteria pollutants: PM2.5, NOx, SO2, O3, CO
concepts.statement: Regulators track a handful of criteria pollutants. Fine particles, PM2.5, are smaller than 2.5 micrometres — thirty side by side span a hair's width — and slip past the body's defenses into deep lungs and blood. Nitrogen oxides come from any high-temperature combustion; sulfur dioxide from burning sulfur-bearing coal and oil; carbon monoxide from incomplete burning. Ozone is different: a secondary pollutant emitted by no chimney at all, cooked in sunlight from NOx and volatile organic compounds — which is why it peaks on hot afternoons downwind of cities.

concepts.term: London coal smog versus photochemical smog
concepts.statement: The two great smog disasters teach two chemistries. London, December 1952: coal smoke plus fog plus a stagnant anticyclone, sulfur dioxide dissolving into droplets, a week of lethal air and on the order of 12,000 excess deaths — the disaster that produced clean-air legislation. Los Angeles from the 1940s: a different beast, photochemical smog with no smokestacks, traced by chemist Arie Haagen-Smit to sunlight reacting with car exhaust to make ozone and the brown haze of nitrogen dioxide. One chemistry needed cleaner fuel; the other needed catalytic converters.

Geography and weather decide who suffers. Normally air cools with altitude; a temperature inversion puts warm air atop cold, sealing the cold layer like a lid. The Los Angeles basin traps marine air behind mountains; Delhi and Beijing suffer winter inversions that stack a city's emissions into a shallow layer; the 1952 London fog sat under one for days. The same emissions under a brisk wind are a non-event — which is why air quality is as much meteorology as chemistry.

concepts.term: health evidence down to no safe threshold
concepts.statement: The evidence that particles kill is among the strongest in environmental epidemiology. The Harvard Six Cities study followed over 8,000 people for more than a decade and found death rates rising steadily with fine-particle exposure, with cardiovascular disease — heart attacks and strokes — dominating, not just lung trouble: PM2.5 inflames arteries and stresses the heart. Crucially, harm is found down to the lowest measurable levels. There is no established safe threshold, only steeper and flatter risks.

The engineering toolbox is mature. Electrostatic precipitators charge particles and collect them on plates, removing over 99 percent of fly ash from power-station flue gas; fabric baghouses filter like giant vacuum bags. Flue-gas desulfurization — scrubbing — sprays limestone slurry to pull sulfur dioxide out as gypsum. The three-way catalytic converter, mandatory on gasoline cars since the 1980s, oxidizes carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons while reducing NOx, cutting each by more than 90 percent. And removing lead from gasoline — finished worldwide only in 2021 — stands as the all-time win: a neurotoxin simply eliminated.

concepts.term: Air Quality Index and indoor air
concepts.statement: Public information runs on the Air Quality Index, which converts measured concentrations into a 0-500 scale with color categories, computed pollutant by pollutant and reported as the worst of them. Indoor air matters more than most people think: across much of the world the worst exposure is cooking smoke inside homes, while in wealthy countries the main indoor threats are radon seeping from soil, cooking particles and volatile organics from products. You spend most of your life indoors; outdoor monitoring networks see none of it.
$$I = \frac{I_{hi} - I_{lo}}{C_{hi} - C_{lo}}\,(C - C_{lo}) + I_{lo}$$
concepts.detail: A pollutant concentration C is mapped linearly onto the index scale within its breakpoint band.

concepts.statement: Ground-level ozone has nothing to do with the ozone layer — one is a harmful pollutant, the other a protective shield. Masks marketed for pollution vary wildly; only well-fitted respirators filter fine particles. A clean week proves nothing about a city's average. And indoor air, invisible to monitoring networks, is where much of the exposure actually happens.
Particles under 2.5 micrometres, penetrating deep into lungs and entering the bloodstream.
A pollutant formed in the air by reactions — like ozone — rather than emitted directly.
Warm air atop cold, sealing a city's emissions under a lid.
Sunlight-driven chemistry of NOx and volatile organics producing ozone and haze.
Device charging particles so they collect on oppositely charged plates.
Exhaust device oxidizing CO and hydrocarbons while reducing NOx.
Index mapping pollutant concentrations to a 0-500 health-advice scale.

examples.title: Worked example — Air Pollution: Sources, Smog and Solutions
examples.problem: The AQI for a PM2.5 reading of 55 micrograms per cubic metre, using U.S. breakpoints in which the band 35.5-55.4 maps to index values 101-150, unhealthy for sensitive groups.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: interpolate linearly across the band — index rises from 101 to 150 as concentration rises from 35.5 to 55.4.

examples.result: AQI 149 — the very top of the unhealthy-for-sensitive-groups band, one unit below the level where everyone, not just sensitive groups, is advised to reduce outdoor exertion.

keyTakeaways: Three-way catalytic converters on every gasoline vehicle sold since the 1980s and 90s
Scrubbers and precipitators fitted to coal-fired power stations
Low-emission zones and London's Ultra Low Emission Zone charging
Air-quality alerts modifying school sports and outdoor work on bad days
