HEPA filtration and public clean-air rooms during wildfire smoke episodes

quiz.q: PM2.5 is especially dangerous because the particles:
options: are small enough to reach deep lungs and the bloodstream
quiz.explanation: At 2.5 micrometres they bypass the airways' filters, inflaming lung tissue and entering blood — hence cardiovascular effects.

quiz.q: Ground-level ozone is called a secondary pollutant because:
options: it comes only from power plants
it forms in sunlight from NOx and volatile organics rather than being emitted directly
it is less harmful than other pollutants
quiz.explanation: No chimney emits ozone; sunshine cooks it from precursor gases, so it peaks on hot afternoons downwind of traffic.

quiz.q: The 1952 London smog and Los Angeles photochemical smog differed mainly in that:
options: London was coal smoke and sulfur in fog; LA was sunlight chemistry acting on vehicle exhaust
London was ozone while LA was smoke
LA's haze came from sulfur dioxide industry
quiz.explanation: Two different chemistries, two different cures: cleaner fuel for one, catalytic converters and vapor controls for the other.

quiz.q: A temperature inversion worsens pollution by:
options: placing warm air above cold and trapping pollutants in a shallow layer
quiz.explanation: The warm lid stops the vertical mixing that would normally dilute emissions — geography and weather decide who suffers.

intro:
Cities mostly feel like they happened by accident, yet almost every street you walk was shaped by deliberate decisions — a zoning map, a road width, a parking rule, a transit line someone fought over in a council chamber. Urban planning is the design practice behind those choices: the discipline that decides where homes, shops and factories may go, how people move among them, and what the public realm between buildings feels like. Why cities exist at all — the economics of agglomeration — belongs to urban sociology; this lesson is about the designer's toolkit.

**Why this matters.** Planning's core insight is that land use and transport form one feedback loop. Build a highway and development spreads to fill it; add a metro line and density crowds around the stations. Cities do not stay put when you plan them — they respond.
objectives: Explain zoning and its critique
Explain land use-transport feedback loop
Explain induced demand
Explain 15-minute city and complete streets
Explain parking minimums and their cost
Explain nIMBY, YIMBY and participation

concepts.statement: Zoning — dividing a city into districts by permitted use — is planning's sharpest instrument and its most criticized. American zoning traces to Euclid v. Ambler (1926), where the Supreme Court upheld separating uses; the aftermath was decades of single-use districts, apartment bans and minimum lot sizes that priced out all but detached houses. The critique is now mainstream: single-use zoning produces car-dependent sprawl, strips street life and functions as exclusion by other means. Reform responds by legalizing mixed use and the 'missing middle' of small apartment buildings.

The loop runs both ways. New roads briefly relieve congestion — then cheaper car travel invites longer trips, further-out development and abandoned alternatives until congestion returns: induced demand, the finding that traffic grows to fill the capacity built for it. The same logic reversed explains transit-oriented development: put rail stations where you want density, and the density arrives. Planning is less about predicting this loop than about deciding which future you want it to produce.

Contemporary urbanism has a direction: proximity. The 15-minute city, championed by Carlos Moreno and applied across Paris, aims for daily needs — home, work, school, food, care — within a short walk or cycle. Complete-street design gives every mode a safe place, replacing the car-only section with sidewalks, protected bike lanes and crossings. Barcelona's superblocks push the same logic: through traffic is routed around clusters of blocks whose interior streets become plazas and play space.

The humblest lever may be parking. Cities across North America long required each building to provide set amounts of off-street parking; the cost — tens of thousands of dollars per structured space — was quietly bundled into rents, subsidizing driving and hollowing out walkable form. Cities from Buffalo to Minneapolis have abolished their minimums outright, discovering that when parking is no longer forced, less of it is built and land goes to homes instead. Prices, it turns out, work better than mandates.

Plans collide with politics. Public hearings let those who dislike change — often existing homeowners — block it, the dynamic behind NIMBY obstruction of new housing; the YIMBY counter-movement argues abundance is the cure. Done well, participation is not a veto but co-design: charrettes where residents shape projects early, and participatory budgeting where neighborhoods spend real money. The planner's craft is telling the difference between hearing everyone and being captured by the loudest.

The everyday toolkit is quieter than the debates. Comprehensive plans set long-term direction; codes translate it into rules — use-based Euclidean codes versus form-based codes that regulate building shape, frontage and street relationship instead of activity. Floor-area limits, setbacks, height districts and design guidelines together decide, long before an architect appears, whether a street becomes a wall of garage doors or a line of shopfronts.
$$\text{FAR} = \frac{A_{\text{floors}}}{A_{\text{lot}}}$$
concepts.detail: Total buildable floor area as a multiple of the lot area — the single number that most determines urban density.

concepts.statement: Treat no plan as neutral: a technical-sounding rule — setback, parking count, height cap — encodes a choice about who can live there. Do not copy solutions across cultures; what works in Copenhagen may fail in Karachi. Beware participation that hears only the loudest, and master plans that assume the city will not respond to what is built. Planning errors are durable — a road width outlives the meeting that chose it by a century.
Legal division of land into districts with permitted uses and development rules.
New road capacity generating new traffic until congestion returns.
Proximity planning: daily needs reachable within a short walk or cycle of home.
Streets designed for safe use by pedestrians, cyclists and transit, not just cars.
Mandated quantity of off-street parking per building type — now being abolished in many cities.
Floor area permitted as a multiple of lot area.
Regulation by building form and street relationship rather than land use.

examples.title: Worked example — Urban Planning: Designing Cities That Work
examples.problem: What a 2,000 square-metre lot can hold under FAR 3.0, and how much land a common parking requirement of one space per 100 square metres of floor area would consume.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: allowed floor area = FAR x lot area; spaces required = floor area / 100; each space with aisles occupies about 30 square metres.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: floor area = 3.0 x 2,000 = 6,000 m², requiring 60 spaces = 1,800 m² of parking — nearly the whole site.

examples.result: the parking requirement effectively consumes the lot, forcing an underground level or structured podium costing far more than the land — the arithmetic behind parking reform.

keyTakeaways: Paris rolling out 15-minute-city service geography school by school
Barcelona superblocks reclaiming interior streets as public space
Minneapolis and Buffalo eliminating parking minimums citywide
Transit-oriented development crowding density around new metro stations
Road diets converting four-lane arterials into safer three-lane complete streets

quiz.q: Induced demand means that:
options: added road capacity tends to fill with new traffic
quiz.explanation: Cheaper travel invites longer trips and further-out development, so congestion returns — capacity is not a cure.

quiz.q: The 15-minute city aims to:
options: cap city speed limits at 15 km/h
place daily needs within a short walk or cycle of home
limit commutes to 15 minutes by car
quiz.explanation: Proximity is the goal — bringing services and work to neighborhoods rather than moving people across the city.

quiz.q: A 2,000 m² lot under FAR 3.0 may contain at most:
quiz.explanation: FAR multiplies lot area by the ratio: 3.0 x 2,000 = 6,000 m² across all floors.

quiz.q: Critics argue single-use zoning mainly produces:
options: car-dependent sprawl and exclusionary low density
too many shopfronts on residential streets
quiz.explanation: Separating homes from everything else forces driving for every errand and bans affordable building types — sprawl by design.

intro:
Every hour, more energy from sunlight reaches Earth than humanity uses in a year. Photovoltaics harvest that bounty: slabs of purified silicon that turn photons directly into electricity with no moving parts, no combustion and no fuel. A solar farm is silent, modular and nearly free to run; the engineering lives in converting sunlight efficiently and handling the fact that the sun sets. This lesson covers the silicon cell's physics, the efficiency ceiling no single-junction panel escapes, competing panel technologies, solar-thermal plants, and the capacity-factor realities of where solar fits.

**Why this matters.** Photovoltaic modules are now the cheapest electricity in most of the world. Understanding why they work — and what physics limits them — separates genuine constraints from solvable ones, and explains why a laboratory curiosity of 1954 now dominates new power-plant construction.
objectives: Explain the photovoltaic effect at a p-n junction
Explain band gap losses and the Shockley-Queisser ceiling
Explain crystalline silicon, thin film and perovskite tandems
Explain inverters, tracking and temperature derating
Explain concentrated solar-thermal with molten-salt storage
Explain capacity factor and intermittency realities

concepts.term: the photovoltaic effect at a p-n junction
concepts.statement: The photovoltaic effect is a junction phenomenon. Silicon is doped with two impurities: phosphorus atoms donate spare electrons to one layer, making it n-type, while boron atoms leave electron vacancies — holes — in the other, making it p-type. At the junction, electrons diffuse across until an internal field builds up. A photon with enough energy knocks an electron loose, and that field sweeps the electron one way and the hole the other before they recombine. Collect the separated charges and you have current — a battery driven by light.

concepts.term: band gap losses and the Shockley-Queisser ceiling
concepts.statement: Not every photon is that useful. Silicon's band gap — the minimum energy to free an electron — is about 1.1 electron-volts. Infrared photons carry less and pass straight through; ultraviolet photons carry far more, but the excess is shed as heat within picoseconds, a loss called thermalization. The Shockley-Queisser analysis of 1961 tallied these losses and found a hard ceiling near 32 percent at silicon's band gap. Lab cells nudge 27 percent and commercial modules run 20 to 23 — close to a limit set by quantum mechanics.

concepts.term: crystalline silicon, thin film and perovskite tandems
concepts.statement: Panel technology has consolidated around crystalline silicon. Monocrystalline modules are sliced from single-crystal ingots drawn from molten silicon — the efficiency leaders at 21 to 23 percent; polycrystalline modules, cast from cheaper blocks, trail slightly. The alternative is thin film: micrometre layers of cadmium telluride or CIGS chemicals on glass, using a hundredth of the semiconductor. The frontier is the tandem: a perovskite layer stacked on silicon, each harvesting a different slice of the spectrum, already past 33 percent in the lab.

A module is only the start of a system. Cells are wired into strings feeding inverters that convert direct current to grid-ready alternating current at the maximum-power point. Single-axis trackers that follow the sun east to west lift yield 15 to 25 percent on utility farms. Heat is the quiet enemy: crystalline output falls about 0.35 percent per degree of cell temperature, so panels on a hot roof underperform the nameplate rating, stamped at a cool 25 degrees under a standard 1,000 watts per square metre.

Photovoltaics is not the only way to harvest the sun. Concentrated solar-thermal plants aim thousands of mirrors at a receiver, heating a fluid to hundreds of degrees and driving a steam turbine — curved troughs or heliostat fields. The trump card is cheap heat storage: Spain's Gemasolar tower kept generating after dark by banking energy in molten salt at 565 degrees, and modern plants ship six to fifteen hours of storage — dispatchable solar, something a bare panel cannot do. The catch is cost: photovoltaics plus batteries usually undercuts it.

One number captures solar's system reality: the capacity factor, actual annual output over round-the-clock output at full rating — 15 to 25 percent for utility farms. The fuel is free but arrives on nature's schedule: nothing at night, less each winter at high latitudes, and midday surges that bend California's demand curve into the shape of a duck. Modules, meanwhile, ride a learning curve — each doubling of cumulative production has cut cost roughly 20 percent, a story the renewable-transition lesson follows; it is enough that modules fell from over one hundred dollars per watt in the 1970s to under thirty cents.
$$\eta = \frac{P_{\text{mp}}}{G \times A}$$
concepts.detail: Maximum-power output divided by the irradiance G falling on the module's area A — the fraction of sunlight converted to electricity.

concepts.statement: $$P = P_{\text{STC}}\left[1 + \gamma\,(T_{\text{cell}} - 25)\right]$$
concepts.detail: Real output at cell temperature, with the silicon temperature coefficient gamma near minus 0.35 percent per degree.

concepts.statement: Higher efficiency does not mean better economics: a cheap 21-percent module beats an exotic 30-percent one on cost per kilowatt-hour. Nameplate ratings assume cool test conditions a rooftop rarely provides. A solar farm delivers energy, not availability — divide claims of capacity by roughly five. And dirty panels bleed money: desert dust can shave output by double digits.
Boundary between differently doped layers whose built-in field separates photo-generated charges.
Minimum photon energy that frees an electron; silicon's is about 1.1 electron-volts.
The roughly one-third efficiency ceiling on any ideal single-junction cell.
Loss, as heat, of photon energy beyond the band gap.
Device converting module DC to grid AC at the maximum-power point.
Panel harvesting light on both faces.
Tanks of hot nitrate salt banking solar heat for after sunset.

examples.title: Worked example — Solar Energy: How Photovoltaics and Solar Thermal Actually Work
examples.problem: A 400-watt module's efficiency (area 1.9 square metres), its output with cells at 60 degrees, and its annual yield at five peak-sun-hours per day.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: efficiency is rating over irradiance times area; hot output applies the derating with gamma = -0.0035; yield = rating x peak-sun-hours x 365 x 0.85 for system losses.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: efficiency = 400/(1,000 x 1.9) = 21 percent. At 60 degrees: 400 x (1 - 0.0035 x 35) = 351 watts. Yield = 400 x 5 x 365 x 0.85 = 620 kWh per year.

examples.result: the panel loses 12 percent of its rating to heat at peak summer sun and delivers about 620 kilowatt-hours a year — a capacity factor near 18 percent.

keyTakeaways: Rooftop arrays offsetting household consumption under net metering
Utility-scale farms of hundreds of megawatts
Floating solar on reservoirs — cooler panels, less evaporation
Solar water heaters on tens of millions of roofs
Molten-salt tower plants delivering solar electricity after sunset

Where next — Pair with the wind-energy lesson — the other pillar of variable renewables — and the renewable-transition lesson for how grids absorb them. The dams lesson in Engineering covers hydropower, the dispatchable renewable.

quiz.q: In a photovoltaic cell, the p-n junction's job is to:
options: heat the silicon so electrons flow faster
separate light-generated electrons and holes before they recombine
reflect unused photons back into the cell
convert direct current into alternating current
quiz.explanation: Photon absorption frees electron-hole pairs; the junction's field sweeps them apart before they recombine.

quiz.q: The Shockley-Queisser limit caps single-junction silicon cells near one-third efficiency mainly because:
options: silicon is too rare to purify further
sub-bandgap photons pass through and above-bandgap energy is lost as heat
wires and contacts consume the remainder
sunlight is too weak at Earth's surface
quiz.explanation: A fifth of sunlight arrives below silicon's band gap and much of the rest arrives with excess energy that thermalizes — only the matched slice converts well.

quiz.q: A 400 W module with a -0.35 percent per degree coefficient runs at a cell temperature of 45 degrees. Its output is about:
quiz.explanation: P = 400 x (1 - 0.0035 x 20) = 372 W — heat subtracts from the nameplate.

quiz.q: Concentrated solar-thermal plants compete with photovoltaics mainly by offering:
options: cheap heat storage that generates after sunset
quiz.explanation: Molten-salt storage makes their electricity dispatchable — though photovoltaics plus batteries usually wins on cost.

intro:
Wind is second-hand sunlight: the sun heats land and sea unevenly, pressure differences try to even things out, and air rushes from one place to another. One to two percent of the solar energy reaching Earth becomes wind's kinetic energy, and modern turbines skim it back out of the sky — a single offshore unit now spans 230 metres of rotor and rates 15 megawatts. This lesson covers lift and the Betz ceiling, turbine anatomy, farm siting and wakes, and offshore versus onshore.

**Why this matters.** Together with solar, wind is decarbonizing electricity faster than any other technology. Its engineering story — cube laws, height and rotor scale — explains why turbines grew twenty-fold in thirty years, and why a farm is a puzzle of spacing, wakes and weather.
objectives: Explain wind power scales with the cube of speed
Explain lift-driven blades on tall towers
Explain the Betz limit on rotor efficiency
Explain turbine anatomy: pitch, gearbox, yaw
Explain wake losses and farm siting
Explain offshore foundations and floating platforms

concepts.term: wind power scales with the cube of speed
concepts.statement: The power available in wind scales with the cube of its speed: double the wind and eight times the power flows through the same disc of air. It also scales with air density and with swept area, which is why rotors grow — doubling diameter quadruples the catch. Height matters nearly as much: surface friction slows the air, so wind speed rises roughly ten percent for each doubling of height over open terrain. The cube law turns that modest gain into a third more power — the arithmetic behind ever-taller towers.

A turbine blade is a rotating wing. Rather than being pushed like a paddle, the blade is an airfoil that deflects the flow, creating lift roughly perpendicular to the oncoming air — the wing physics the aerodynamics lesson in Engineering develops in full. The geometry is surprising: tips travel at six to ten times wind speed, so each section meets air dominated by the blade's own motion — hence the twist that keeps every station at its best angle. Three blades have become standard — enough solidity to catch the energy without excess material or noise.

concepts.term: the Betz limit on rotor efficiency
concepts.statement: No rotor can harvest all the wind's energy, and the reason is elegant: air that surrendered all its kinetic energy would stop dead and pile up behind the machine. In 1919 Albert Betz treated the rotor as a permeable disk and found extraction is maximized when air leaves at one third of its arrival speed — at most 16/27, or 59.3 percent, can ever be captured. Modern rotors reach power coefficients of 0.45 to 0.50, about three quarters of that ceiling; the rest is lost to the air's own rotation and blade-tip vortices.

Inside the nacelle is a small power station. Pitch motors rotate each blade about its long axis — feathering them in storms, fine-tuning angles around the operating point. Most designs use a gearbox stepping the rotor's 10 to 15 revolutions per minute up to generator speed, though direct-drive machines couple a huge slow magnet generator straight to the hub. Yaw motors swing the nacelle to face the wind, and the controller starts production near 3 metres per second, reaches full rating around 12, and shuts down near 25.

A wind farm is a study in interference. Every turbine extracts energy and leaves behind a slower, turbulent wake, so a machine downwind of a badly spaced neighbour loses 10 to 20 percent of its output — hence rows spaced five to ten rotor diameters apart, staggered across the prevailing wind. Siting begins with the resource: masts or lidar measure a site for a year or more, because a ten percent error in average wind speed becomes a thirty percent error in energy.

Offshore is wind's frontier. Sea wind is stronger and steadier — capacity factors of 45 to 55 percent against 25 to 40 onshore — and there are no neighbours to object. The price is paid underwater: monopiles for shallow sites, steel jackets for deeper water, floating platforms tethered beyond about 60 metres. Integration remains the challenge: output follows weather, not demand, so operators lean on forecasting, curtailment and storage — the renewable-transition lesson's system-level story.

concepts.detail: Kinetic power flowing through a rotor disc of area A; air density rho matters, but the cubed wind speed v dominates.
The maximum fraction of wind power any rotor can extract, reached when the flow slows to one third of its arrival speed.

concepts.statement: The cube law punishes sloppy comparison: a site averaging 6 rather than 7 metres per second loses a quarter of its energy. Turbines do kill birds and bats — far fewer than cats or buildings — but siting on migration corridors and bat activity needs real care. The claim that turbines never repay their embodied energy is a myth; payback takes six to twelve months. And never judge a fleet by one calm day — the grid sees thousands of machines averaged over a continent.
Fraction of available wind power a rotor captures; modern machines reach 0.45 to 0.50.
Blade-tip speed divided by wind speed; efficient rotors run six to ten.
Energy-depleted, turbulent zone downwind of a turbine.
Giant steel tube hammered into the seabed as a shallow-water foundation.
Step-up transmission converting slow rotor turns to generator speed.
Rotating blades about their long axis to trim power or shed storms.
Actual annual output over nameplate potential — offshore 45 to 55 percent.

examples.title: Worked example — Wind Energy: Turbines, Farms and the Physics of Harvesting Wind
examples.problem: The power a 236-metre-rotor turbine delivers in an 11-metre-per-second wind at power coefficient 0.42, plus its annual energy at 50 percent capacity factor.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: available power = 0.5 x rho x A x v-cubed, with A = pi x D-squared / 4; delivered = Cp x available.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: A = pi x 118 x 118 = 43,700 square metres. Available power = 0.5 x 1.225 x 43,700 x 1,331 = 35.7 MW. Delivered = 0.42 x 35.7 = 15 MW.

examples.result: the rating is the physics — 42 percent of a 36-megawatt wind, 71 percent of the Betz ceiling — and annual yield is 15 x 8,760 x 0.5 = 66 GWh.

keyTakeaways: North Sea offshore farms powering coastal Europe
Onshore wind belts of the American Great Plains and Inner Mongolia
Repowering 1990s farms with fewer, taller, more productive turbines
Wind-plus-storage hybrids bidding firmer power into markets
Farmland lease income — crops growing beneath 150-metre rotors

Where next — Pair with the solar lesson and the renewable-transition lesson for storage and grids. The aerodynamics lesson in Engineering develops the wing physics; the dams lesson covers hydropower, the firm counterpart.

quiz.q: Doubling wind speed, all else fixed, changes the available power by a factor of:
quiz.explanation: Speed enters the power expression cubed — the most consequential fact in wind engineering.

quiz.q: The Betz limit exists because:
options: air that lost all its energy could not flow away to make room for more
the tower blocks part of the wind
quiz.explanation: Air must keep moving to carry energy through; slowing it to a third of arrival speed is the optimum.

quiz.q: Turbine blades are twisted and tapered mainly so that:
options: they look elegant from the ground
each section meets the air at its best angle despite different speeds
quiz.explanation: Tips travel several times faster than roots; the twist keeps every station's angle of attack in the productive range.

quiz.q: Offshore farms achieve higher capacity factors than onshore mainly because:
options: sea winds are stronger and steadier over the low-friction surface
quiz.explanation: Smooth open water means faster, less turbulent wind at hub height.

intro:
Plastics are the defining material of the last century: light, durable, cheap, moldable into any shape — and stubbornly permanent in the wrong places. Humanity has produced over nine billion tonnes of the stuff since 1950, and nearly all of it still exists somewhere, because the same carbon chains that make plastics useful make them nearly immune to the microbes that recycle everything else. This lesson treats plastics as materials: what they are, the families behind the resin codes, why they persist, what microplastics and additives are doing, and why recycling them has proved so hard.

**Why this matters.** Almost every product you touched today contains plastic, and almost none of it was recycled. Understanding the material — not just the guilt — is the precondition for judging bans, bioplastics and circular-economy promises honestly.
objectives: Explain polymers: chains of monomers
Explain thermoplastics versus thermosets
Explain the resin-code families
Explain persistence as chemistry, not conspiracy
Explain microplastics and nurdles
Explain additive migration
Explain the recycling-reality problem

concepts.statement: A plastic is a polymer: long molecules built by chaining thousands of small units, monomers, into strands that entangle like cooked spaghetti. Chemistry controls the chain: polyethylene is just ethylene gas linked into chains of different lengths — short and branched for flexible films, long and straight for stiff jugs. Thermoplastics can be melted and reshaped repeatedly; thermosets — Bakelite, epoxies, polyurethanes — are cross-linked into one giant molecule and never truly melt again; elastomers stretch and snap back. High strength-to-weight, chemical inertness and barrier properties all fall out of this architecture.

The chasing-arrows numbers mark six workhorse families plus a catch-all. PET, code 1, is bottles and polyester fibre. HDPE, 2, is the stiff, forgiving stuff of milk jugs and pipes. PVC, 3, is window frames, cable insulation and flooring — cheap and tough, and the plastic environmental regulators like least, both for its chlorine chemistry and its reliance on additives. LDPE, 4, is films and bags. PP, 5, survives boiling water: food tubs, caps, syringes. PS, 6, is foam and cutlery. Code 7 means everything else — polycarbonate, nylon, ABS — and to a sorter, effectively nothing.

Persistence is chemistry, not conspiracy. Synthetic polymers are new on evolutionary timescales, and no microbe has evolved the enzymes needed to chew carbon backbones it never met. Sunlight does attack the chains — ultraviolet photodegradation — but the result is not disappearance: plastic fragments into ever-smaller pieces. A bottle estimated to last centuries does not vanish; it shatters into sand-sized grains. Rivers then deliver the debris: an estimated eight to twelve million tonnes of plastic reach the ocean each year, most of it from land.

Below five millimetres, debris counts as microplastic. Some starts small — nurdles, the pre-production pellets shipped around the world by the billion, and the synthetic fibres a single wash sheds from a fleece. The rest is weathered fragments. Microplastics have been found from the Mariana Trench to Arctic ice to human blood; lab animals exposed to them show inflammation, but the honest reading of human-health evidence is that it is still developing. The ecological record is starker, and in the North Pacific garbage patch nearly half the mass is discarded fishing gear, not consumer waste.

Pure polymer rarely ships alone. Plasticizers make PVC flexible, flame retardants meet fire codes, stabilizers block sunlight, pigments colour everything — and because additives are blended in rather than chemically bonded, they migrate out. Phthalates and bisphenol A, common in vinyls and historic can linings, are endocrine disruptors at very low doses, which is why regulators have chased them for decades. Additives also poison recycling: a 'plastic' bottle may carry a dozen trace chemicals that survive every remelt, complicating any return to food contact.

The material explains the recycling letdown. Of all plastic ever made, about nine percent has been recycled, twelve percent incinerated, and the rest landfilled or loose in the environment. Mechanical recycling remelts, but every heat cycle shortens the chains, so bottles become fibre, fibre becomes carpet, carpet becomes landfill — a cascade, not a circle. Multilayer films and mixed resins defeat sorting outright. Bio-based PLA composts only in industrial digesters; drop it in the sea and it lasts like any other plastic. The fix being pursued is design: mono-material packaging that can loop cleanly.
$$\Delta M = P - R - I$$
concepts.detail: Annual growth of the plastic stock equals production P minus genuine recycling R and incineration I; degradation is effectively zero on human timescales.

concepts.statement: 'Biodegradable' without a standard means little: PLA breaks down in an industrial composter, not in the ocean or a garden. Oxo-degradable bags just fragment faster into microplastic. Compostable and recyclable are different streams — a PLA cup contaminates a PET bale. And obsessing over straws while ignoring fishing gear and tyre wear misses where much of the mass actually comes from.
Small building-block molecule; polymers are chains of thousands of them.
Cross-linked polymer — epoxy, Bakelite — that chars rather than remelts.
The number 1-7 stamped on plastic goods; names the family, never promises recyclability.
UV-driven chain breaking that embrittles and fragments plastic rather than dissolving it.
Plastic pieces under five millimetres — weathered debris or intentionally shed material.
Pre-production pellet shipped in bulk; a major spill category worldwide.
Plasticizer, pigment or stabilizer blended into polymer — and free to migrate out.

examples.title: Worked example — Plastics: The Polymer Century
examples.problem: How fast the world's plastic stock grows at today's rates — production 400 million tonnes a year, 9 percent recycled, 12 percent incinerated — and what share of all-time plastic still sits in landfills or nature.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: only recycled and burned material leaves the stock; everything else accumulates, because degradation is negligible.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: recycled = 0.09 x 400 = 36 Mt; incinerated = 0.12 x 400 = 48 Mt; accumulation = 400 - 36 - 48 = 316 Mt per year.

examples.result: the stock grows by 316 million tonnes annually — roughly a tonne for every 25 people on Earth, each year — and about 79 percent of all plastic ever made remains landfilled or loose in the environment.

keyTakeaways: Deposit-sourced PET bottles looping back into food-grade bottles in Norway and Germany
Minimum-recycled-content laws creating demand for recovered material
Single-use-plastic bans on bags, straws and cutlery across dozens of countries
Fishing-gear recovery schemes targeting the largest ocean-plastic source
Mono-material redesign of flexible packaging for recyclability

Where next — The companion lessons finish the story: recycling systems covers the sorting machinery and the markets, and the waste lesson follows the streams themselves. Materials science in Engineering explains how chain structure governs strength.

quiz.q: Thermosets such as epoxy differ from thermoplastics because they:
options: are cross-linked into one network and never truly remelt
quiz.explanation: Cross-links weld the chains together; heat chars the network instead of letting it flow.

quiz.q: Plastics persist in the environment mainly because:
options: microbes never evolved enzymes to break down these synthetic carbon backbones
quiz.explanation: These molecules are evolutionarily new; sunlight only fragments them into smaller pieces.

quiz.q: With 400 Mt produced, 9 percent recycled and 12 percent incinerated, annual accumulation is about:
quiz.explanation: 400 minus 36 recycled minus 48 burned leaves 316 Mt joining the standing stock every year.

quiz.q: By mass, the North Pacific garbage patch is dominated by:
quiz.explanation: Nets, ropes and other gear are nearly half the patch's mass — consumer single-use items are the visible minority.

intro:
A recycling symbol on a package is not a promise — it is a hypothesis. The claim becomes true only if a sorting facility can separate the material, a buyer will pay for the bale, and a processor can turn it into something someone wants. This lesson is about the machinery and the markets in that middle stretch: how materials-recovery facilities actually sort, why some streams loop while others stall, what contamination does to economics, the difference between closed loops and downcycling, and the deposit and producer-responsibility systems built to keep material clean.

**Why this matters.** China's 2018 import crackdown forced wealthy countries to discover how fragile their recycling chains were. The difference between a recycling rate and a recycling reality is made — or lost — on the sorting floor and at the bale scale.
objectives: Explain the MRF as an un-mixing factory
Explain eddy currents, magnets and trommels
Explain near-infrared optical sorting
Explain bale purity and contamination economics
Explain closed loops versus downcycling cascades
Explain deposit-return and eco-modulated fees

concepts.term: the MRF as an un-mixing factory
concepts.statement: A single-stream materials recovery facility is a factory for un-mixing. Mixed recyclables ride conveyors into rotating trommel drums, where small objects — shards, caps, food scraps — fall through the holes while cardboard rides over the top. Disc screens flick paper up and let containers drop through. Overhead magnets lift steel cans off the belt. Nonferrous metals then meet the eddy-current separator: a spinning magnet array induces electric currents in aluminium, and those currents generate an opposing magnetic field that physically flings cans off the belt into a chute — electromagnetism doing the sorting. Whatever survives meets the optical sorters.

Near-infrared optical sorters are the modern heart of the line. A sensor sweeps the belt with infrared light, and each polymer family reflects a characteristic fingerprint back — PET reads differently from HDPE, which reads differently from polypropylene. The instant a target is identified, a bank of high-speed air jets blasts it off the belt mid-flight, hundreds of picks per minute. The blind spot is colour: carbon-black plastic absorbs the infrared and reads as nothing at all. Density finishes the job in float-sink tanks, where polyethylene and polypropylene float while PET, PVC and glass sink to their own streams.

Material physics decides what can loop. Metals loop forever: remelting aluminium takes about 95 percent less energy than smelting ore, which makes the can the crown jewel — it can return to the shelf as a new can in about six weeks. Glass recycles endlessly but is heavy, so transport often eats the value, though cullet does lower melting temperatures in the furnace. Paper survives only four to six loops before its fibres shorten into sludge. PET and HDPE recycle well when clean; flexible film wraps the machinery into shutdown, and multilayer laminates — the chip packet, several plastics fused into one — are effectively beyond sorting.

Everything trades on bale purity. Buyers pay by grade — the percentage of target material — and reject anything below specification, so one greasy or mixed load can downgrade a whole bay. The mixing arithmetic is brutal, and tanglers do the rest: hoses, cords and film wrap around screens and shafts, stopping the line for hours while workers cut them free. Wishcycling — the hopeful toss of unrecyclables into the bin — converts directly into that downtime. The lesson every facility learns is that quality is made at the source, not recovered at the end of the belt.

Two fates await sorted material. Closed loops return like for like — bottle to bottle, can to can — but food-grade recycled PET demands super-clean processes or source material clean enough to start with. Downcycling cascades instead: bottle to fibre, fibre to carpet, carpet to landfill within two or three turns. Deposit-return schemes attack the problem at the source: a 10-to-25-cent refund pushes container return above 90 percent in Norway and Germany, and the reverse-vending stream is so clean it can feed food-grade loops directly. Extended producer responsibility goes further still, charging producers fees modulated by how recyclable their packaging is — money that finances the whole collection system.
$$p_{\text{mix}} = \frac{\sum_i m_i\,p_i}{\sum_i m_i}$$
concepts.detail: The purity of a blended bale is the mass-weighted average of its streams — clean material diluted by dirty loses grade for everyone.

concepts.statement: Collected is not recycled: tonnages counted at the kerb overstate what actually sells. Single-stream convenience buys participation at the price of contamination. Chemical recycling — dissolving or pyrolyzing plastics back toward feedstock — may yet rescue mixed streams, but its energy bills and yields remain unproven at scale. And no sorting technology, however clever, can fix a package designed to be unsortable.
The plant where mixed recyclables are separated, graded and baled for sale.
Device inducing currents in nonferrous metals so their opposing fields fling them off the belt.
Sensor reading infrared fingerprints of polymers, with air jets ejecting the targets.
Density separation in which plastics divide by whether they float.
The purity percentage of a sorted bale — the number buyers pay on.
Film, cords or hoses that wrap sorting machinery into downtime.
Refund scheme keeping beverage containers separate and clean enough for food-grade loops.

examples.title: Worked example — Recycling Systems: How Materials Actually Loop Back
examples.problem: Whether a facility should blend 1,200 kilograms of PET baled at 97 percent purity with 800 kilograms from a contaminated route at 62 percent, against a buyer's 90-percent specification.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: blended purity is the mass-weighted average of the streams mixed.

examples.result: the blend misses the 90-percent spec. Kept separate, the 97-percent bale sells at grade while the dirty stream is downgraded alone; mixing would have destroyed fourteen points of the clean material's value.

keyTakeaways: Reverse vending machines at Norwegian and German supermarkets returning over 90 percent of containers
Optical-sorter retrofits lifting facility purity after the 2018 import crackdown
Eco-modulated producer fees rewarding mono-material packaging design
Aluminium closed loops remelting cans back into cans within weeks
Food-grade rPET plants supplying bottle-to-bottle brands

Where next — This is the middle lesson of three: the plastics lesson explains the materials themselves and the waste lesson follows the streams. For the same sorting logic at industrial scale, see separation processes in Chemical Engineering.

quiz.q: An eddy-current separator captures aluminium by:
options: inducing currents whose opposing magnetic field flings it off the belt
suction cups on a robotic arm
quiz.explanation: Spinning magnets induce eddy currents in the metal; the currents' own fields repel and eject the pieces — electromagnetism as a sorter.

quiz.q: Carbon-black plastic defeats optical sorters because it:
options: is too heavy for the belt
absorbs the near-infrared light the sensor reads
quiz.explanation: No reflection, no fingerprint — the sorter sees nothing where the black tray passes, which is why designers are moving away from carbon black.

quiz.q: Mixing 1,200 kg of 97-percent-pure PET with 800 kg at 62 percent produces a bale of about:
quiz.explanation: (1,164 + 496)/2,000 = 83 percent — below spec, which is exactly why streams are kept apart.

quiz.q: Deposit-return schemes lift recycling quality mainly because:
options: they fine people for buying drinks
returned containers arrive pre-sorted and clean, feeding closed loops
quiz.explanation: A small refund separates beverage containers from the general stream at the source — the cleanliness that food-grade reuse requires.

intro:
A river can swallow a certain load of waste and heal itself; push past that load and the very process of decay turns lethal. Water pollution is mostly an overdose problem: nutrients that overfeed, toxins that accumulate, and pathogens riding along. This lesson follows the chemistry and ecology of polluted natural waters — how nutrients strangle lakes and coastal seas into dead zones, where the toxins come from and why they climb food chains, and why groundwater contamination stays hidden for decades. The engineering fix — treatment plants — has its own lesson.

**Why this matters.** Nutrient pollution is among the most widespread water-quality failures on Earth, and dead zones now number in the hundreds. Understanding the mechanism explains why the cure is upstream agriculture and sewage management, not anything you can do in the ocean itself.
objectives: Explain eutrophication: blooms then oxygen collapse
Explain dead zones and seasonal stratification
Explain point versus nonpoint sources
Explain methylmercury and biomagnification
Explain pFAS and the parts-per-trillion era
Explain slow-motion groundwater plumes

concepts.statement: The choking sequence starts with fertilizer. Nitrogen and phosphorus are the limiting nutrients of aquatic life, so when runoff and sewage effluent rich in both reach a lake or bay, algae bloom in huge proportions. The bloom itself is not the kill: when it dies, bacteria decompose the mats and consume dissolved oxygen, dropping the water below the two milligrams per litre that fish require — hypoxia. Summer stratification seals the trap, because warm surface water floats on the cold depths until autumn mixing, so deep water stays suffocated for months. Lake Erie collapsed this way in the 1970s and recovered only after nutrient limits were imposed.

Where a big river drains farm country, the damage reaches the sea. The Mississippi collects runoff from 41 percent of the continental United States and delivers it to the Gulf of Mexico, where each summer a hypoxic zone of 10,000 to 20,000 square kilometres forms. The Baltic suffers the largest human-caused zone, and more than 400 such sites have been reported worldwide, roughly doubling each decade since the 1960s. The remedy is unglamorous: load budgets that cut the nitrogen and phosphorus entering at the source.

Regulation divides sources, and the division matters. Point sources — pipes, outfalls, factory discharges — are visible, permittable, and were largely tamed by the U.S. Clean Water Act after rivers famously caught fire. Nonpoint sources — fertilizer washing off fields, manure from feedlots, urban stormwater — have no pipe to permit. Only about half the nitrogen farmers apply is ever taken up by the crop; the rest runs off or leaches downward. That is why four decades of water law cleaned the pipes while the Gulf dead zone persisted, and why modern remedies target cover crops, buffer strips and precision application.

Metals poison differently: in tiny doses, invisibly, by accumulating. Mercury from coal combustion settles into water, and bacteria in oxygen-poor sediment convert it to methylmercury, a form living tissue absorbs but cannot readily shed. Each step up the food chain concentrates it roughly tenfold, so long chains multiply water concentrations a hundred-thousand-fold — tuna and swordfish carry mercury advisories while the seawater around them meets standards. Minamata, Japan, proved the endpoint in the 1950s: industrial mercury in seafood poisoned thousands. Abandoned mines add an acidic legacy: pyrite exposed to air and water generates sulfuric acid and orange iron precipitate that sterilizes streams.

The newest concern is a family of forever chemicals. PFAS build water- and grease-repellent products — firefighting foam, nonstick coatings, weatherproof fabric — and the carbon-fluorine bonds that make them useful make them nearly indestructible, so they now appear in the blood of people and wildlife worldwide, with drinking-water limits set in parts per trillion. Groundwater is pollution in slow motion: hidden, moving metres per year, contaminated for decades before anyone samples it. Fuel from leaking tanks, solvents and septic nitrate form plumes that cleanups chase for generations; Bangladesh's naturally arsenic-bearing tube wells remain the starkest case, exposing tens of millions.

Lead pipes add a municipal chapter. When Flint, Michigan switched water sources in 2014 without corrosion control, river water stripped the protective scale inside old pipes and carried lead into taps — a treatment-chemistry failure, not a source failure. The broader arc is encouraging where enforced: rivers that once burned now hold fish, because point sources were forced to clean up. The stubborn remainder — nutrients, plastics, forever chemicals — is woven into agriculture and consumer products, which is why water pollution has migrated from a pipe problem to a land-use problem.
$$\text{BMF} = \frac{C_{\text{predator}}}{C_{\text{prey}}}$$
concepts.detail: Concentration ratio across one trophic step; a chain of tenfold steps multiplies to enormous enrichment in top predators.

concepts.statement: Dilution is not the solution for anything that bioaccumulates — the ocean dilutes mercury while food chains re-concentrate it. Clear water is not clean water: a dead zone's water can be glass-clear, because nothing lives to cloud it. Treated sewage is not nutrient-free sewage; conventional treatment handles organics, not the nitrogen and phosphorus that feed blooms. And groundwater contamination is invisible until wells reveal it, decades late.
Over-enrichment of water by nutrients, triggering blooms and oxygen depletion.
Dissolved oxygen below 2 milligrams per litre — too little for most aquatic life.
The scarcest essential nutrient, usually nitrogen or phosphorus, whose arrival triggers growth.
Diffuse pollution from fields and streets, with no single pipe to permit.
Microbially converted mercury that bioaccumulates up food chains.
Persistent fluorinated chemicals repelling water and grease; regulated in parts per trillion.
Contaminated groundwater body migrating slowly from its source.

examples.title: Worked example — Water Pollution: Nutrients, Toxins and Dead Zones
examples.problem: The methylmercury concentration in a top predator, given seawater at 1 part per trillion and a five-step food chain concentrating tenfold at each step.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: each trophic transfer multiplies concentration by the biomagnification factor, here ten.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: 1 ppt x 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 = 100,000 ppt = 100 parts per billion = 0.1 parts per million in predator tissue.

examples.result: 0.1 ppm is a third of the way to the 0.3 ppm fish advisory — the arithmetic behind tuna limits for pregnant women, from water that itself passes standards.

keyTakeaways: Total-maximum-daily-load budgets driving Chesapeake Bay and Gulf cleanup plans
Tertiary sewage treatment stripping nitrogen and phosphorus before discharge
Cover crops and riparian buffer strips cutting farm runoff at the source
Fish-consumption advisories for mercury in long-lived predators
Drinking-water limits for PFAS set in parts per trillion

Where next — Two lessons bracket this one: air pollution for the atmospheric side of environmental health, and water treatment for the engineering that turns tainted sources into safe taps. The water cycle lesson covers the flows beneath it all.

quiz.q: The order of events in eutrophication is:
options: nutrients arrive, algae bloom, blooms die, decomposition strips the oxygen
oxygen falls first, then the algae bloom
algae bloom, nutrients arrive, fish leave
quiz.explanation: The bloom is the symptom; the kill comes when bacteria decompose it and consume the dissolved oxygen.

quiz.q: Dead zones are worst in summer because:
options: fish eat more in warm water
warm surface water stratifies, sealing the depths from re-aeration
quiz.explanation: The warm lid blocks mixing with oxygen-rich surface water until autumn turnover — months of suffocation below.

quiz.q: With water at 1 ppt and five tenfold trophic steps, top-predator tissue reaches about:
quiz.explanation: Ten to the fifth gives 100,000 ppt = 0.1 ppm — a third of the consumption advisory from water that passes standards.

quiz.q: Groundwater contamination is hard to manage mainly because:
options: it flows rapidly to the sea
plumes move metres per year and go undetected for decades
quiz.explanation: Out of sight and slow, a plume is usually discovered long after the spill — and cleanup spans generations.

intro:
After every flood, heatwave and wildfire comes the same question: was this climate change? For most of the twentieth century science could only shrug — no single event, the honest answer went, could be attributed. Since the early 2000s that has changed: a new discipline now answers with numbers, publishing peer-reviewed estimates of how much human influence altered the odds of a specific disaster, sometimes within weeks of it happening. This advanced lesson covers how probabilistic event attribution works, which hazards attribute confidently and which resist, the distinction between detection and attribution, and how the IPCC phrases what it knows.

**Why this matters.** Attribution numbers now shape lawsuits, insurance pricing and international loss-and-damage talks — money and justice turn on the answer. Reading a headline like 'made 150 times more likely' requires knowing where the number comes from and what it does and does not claim.
objectives: Explain probabilistic event attribution
Explain risk ratio and attributable fraction
Explain confidence by hazard class
Explain detection versus attribution
Explain clausius-Clapeyron water-vapour scaling
Explain calibrated IPCC uncertainty language

concepts.statement: The core trick is comparing two worlds. Using large ensembles of climate-model simulations — many alternate histories of the same planet — researchers compute how often an event of at least the observed severity occurs in the world as it is, with human emissions, versus a counterfactual world without them. The comparison is anchored to observations, with models validated for the region and season in question. The result is a risk ratio: if a heatwave that was once a one-in-a-thousand-year event now comes every fifty years, human influence has made it twenty times more likely. The method was first applied to the 2003 European heatwave, found to have been at least doubled in likelihood by our emissions.

The complementary statistic is the fraction of attributable risk. If the pre-industrial probability is P0 and today's is P1, the risk ratio is P1/P0, and FAR is one minus P0/P1 — the share of today's risk that traces to human influence. A 150-fold increase in likelihood yields a FAR of 99.3 percent. Everything depends on defining the event: duration, spatial footprint and the variable chosen all change the answer, which is why careful studies test several definitions and report the spread rather than one number chosen for drama.

Confidence tracks the physics. Heatwaves attribute best: large, slow-moving, and thermodynamically pushed — the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome was found virtually impossible without human influence. Heavy rainfall follows close behind, because warmer air holds about seven percent more water vapour per degree of warming, so record downpours attribute robustly unless circulation shifts fight the signal. Droughts are mixed, depending on region and on whether rainfall or soil moisture is meant. Tropical cyclones are harder — rare, small next to a model grid, dominated by internal variability — so intensification and heavier rain attribute with confidence, but not every storm's existence. Tornadoes and severe convective storms remain beyond reliable attribution.

The discipline rests on an older distinction. Detection is the observation that something has changed beyond the range of natural variability — a trend in the data. Attribution is the explanation, done by fingerprinting: simulations driven by natural factors alone cannot reproduce observed warming, while simulations that add human forcings can. Event attribution extends the logic from averages to extremes, asking the same question of one storm's odds rather than a century's trend. Weather forecasting predicts what happens next; attribution asks what we made more likely — and the machinery of both has its own lesson.

Findings arrive calibrated. The IPCC's vocabulary maps fixed probability bands onto words — virtually certain, very likely, likely, medium confidence. Its sixth assessment found human influence has made heat extremes more frequent and intense virtually certainly, heavy precipitation more likely than not over most land, and intense tropical cyclones more likely, while severe-convective-storm trends earned only low confidence. The final discipline is separating hazard from harm: attribution quantifies the change in weather, not in damage. More people and property in floodplains inflate losses with no climate change at all, so honest studies attribute the hazard and leave exposure to the accountants.
$$\text{RR} = \frac{P_1}{P_0}$$
concepts.detail: How many times more likely an event of given severity is in today's climate than in the counterfactual without human emissions.

concepts.statement: $$\text{FAR} = 1 - \frac{P_0}{P_1}$$
concepts.detail: The share of current event risk owed to human influence; 0.95 means nineteen twentieths of it.

concepts.statement: Attribution is probabilistic, never a simple 'caused by' — the honest phrasing is 'made X times more likely.' Do not attribute the damage bill: exposure and vulnerability move it as much as weather does. Beware single-model numbers and cherry-picked event definitions; robust studies use ensembles and test their definitions. And do not expect skill where physics offers little signal — a single tornado will never attribute the way a heatwave does.
Comparing model worlds with and without human emissions to quantify an event's changed odds.
Probability of the event today over its probability in the counterfactual climate.
Fraction of attributable risk — the share of current probability owed to human influence.
Observing a change beyond natural variability, before any cause is assigned.
Matching observed change patterns to simulations with and without each forcing.
Many simulations of the same climate, providing the statistics of rare events.
Air's water-holding capacity rising about 7 percent per degree of warming.

examples.title: Worked example — Extreme Weather in a Warming World: The Science of Attribution
examples.problem: The risk ratio and attributable fraction for a heatwave that model ensembles say occurs once per 20 years today but was once per 1,000 years in the pre-industrial climate.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: RR = P1/P0 and FAR = 1 - P0/P1, with probabilities the reciprocals of return periods.

examples.result: the event is 50 times more likely because of human influence, and 98 percent of its present-day risk is attributable — numbers a court or an adaptation planner could act on.

keyTakeaways: World Weather Attribution rapid studies published within weeks of disasters
Attribution evidence entering climate lawsuits against fossil-fuel producers
Return-period recalibration of drainage and dam design standards
Insurers repricing hazard distributions that no longer hold still
Loss-and-damage finance debates grounded in quantified responsibility

Where next — This lesson sits between two others: the storm-and-forecast lessons for the meteorology of the events themselves, and the climate-models lesson for the simulation machinery. The carbon-budget lesson covers the emissions driving it all.

quiz.q: Event attribution quantifies human influence by comparing:
options: simulations of the world as it is with a counterfactual lacking human emissions
this year with the year before
quiz.explanation: Two model worlds — fact and counterfactual — supply the two probabilities whose ratio measures our influence.

quiz.q: An event once per 1,000 years now occurs once per 20. The fraction of attributable risk is:
quiz.explanation: RR = 50, so FAR = 1 - 1/50 = 0.98 — ninety-eight percent of the risk is human-made.

quiz.q: Heatwaves attribute more confidently than tropical cyclones because they are:
options: large-scale and thermodynamically driven, so models resolve them well
quiz.explanation: A broad, slow shift in the temperature distribution is exactly what warming physics predicts and grids can capture.

quiz.q: Record downpours intensify in a warming world mainly because warmer air:
options: holds about 7 percent more water vapour per degree
quiz.explanation: Clausius-Clapeyron scaling is thermodynamics, not modelling — the most trustworthy line in the field.

intro:
A bare-rock Earth reflecting 30 percent of sunlight would sit at about 255 kelvin, or minus 18 degrees Celsius — a frozen planet. The real Earth averages 15 degrees, and the difference between those two numbers is written by the atmosphere. But how much does the planet warm when we add carbon dioxide? Not by a fixed recipe: the initial nudge of extra greenhouse gas triggers feedback processes inside the climate system that amplify or dampen the response. This intermediate lesson defines radiative forcing, tours the major feedbacks, and explains where the famous sensitivity numbers come from.

**Why this matters.** Every carbon budget, every projection and every policy target translates through climate sensitivity. If feedbacks sum near zero, doubled CO2 warms the planet modestly; because they sum strongly positive, the globe is heading for roughly three degrees of warming per doubling — the single most consequential number in climate policy.
objectives: Explain radiative forcing defined at the top of the atmosphere
Explain cO2 forcing grows as the logarithm of concentration
Explain positive and negative feedback processes
Explain water vapor, ice–albedo and lapse-rate feedbacks
Explain cloud feedback as the leading uncertainty
Explain equilibrium climate sensitivity for doubled CO2
Explain tipping points when feedbacks take over

concepts.term: Radiative forcing defined at the top of the atmosphere
concepts.statement: Radiative forcing is the initial response of radiative fluxes at the top of the atmosphere: the change in the radiative balance for a specific process — greenhouse gases, aerosols, solar output — with everything else held constant. Positive forcing warms, negative cools. For carbon dioxide the forcing grows with the logarithm of concentration, ΔF = 5.35 × ln(C/C0) watts per square meter, where C0 is a reference level. The log arises because the strongest absorption bands saturate first: each extra part per million matters less than the last. Doubling from the pre-industrial 280 ppm to 560 ppm gives ΔF = 5.35 × ln(2) ≈ 3.7 W/m² — the benchmark forcing of climate science.

concepts.term: CO2 forcing grows as the logarithm of concentration
concepts.statement: A climate feedback is a process that amplifies (positive) or dampens (negative) the initial temperature response to a forcing. The strongest damper is built into physics itself: a warmer planet radiates as the fourth power of temperature (Stefan–Boltzmann), so it sheds heat faster the hotter it gets. Holding everything else fixed, the 3.7 W/m² of doubled CO2 would settle at about 1.2 degrees of warming — the no-feedback sensitivity. Everything interesting in climate prediction is the sum of what happens next.

The biggest amplifier is water vapor. Warmer air evaporates more water from the oceans, and because water vapor is itself a powerful greenhouse gas — the atmosphere’s most important infrared absorber alongside CO2 — the extra vapor traps more heat and warms the surface further. Water vapor cannot act as a forcing on human timescales: its lifetime is days, and its concentration is set by temperature. It is the feedback that roughly doubles whatever the CO2 push started, which is why the EPA calls it the most important positive feedback.

concepts.term: Water vapor, ice–albedo and lapse-rate feedbacks
concepts.statement: Ice and snow add a second amplifier, the ice–albedo feedback. Earth reflects about 30 percent of sunlight (albedo ≈ 0.3); melt bright surfaces and the planet darkens, absorbs more solar radiation, and melts more ice — a loop that runs in reverse to amplify cooling into ice ages. Partly offsetting it, the lapse-rate feedback is negative: as the surface warms, the vertical temperature profile adjusts so that more radiation escapes to space from the warm lower atmosphere, damping the response. Clouds remain the wild card — they both reflect sunlight (cooling) and trap infrared (warming), and their net feedback sign varies by type and altitude, which is why cloud feedback dominates the spread in model projections.

concepts.term: Cloud feedback as the leading uncertainty
concepts.statement: Climate sensitivity is the total warming or cooling from one forcing after all feedbacks act. The bookkeeping is compact: if f is the net feedback factor, the equilibrium warming is ΔT = ΔT0/(1 − f), where ΔT0 is the no-feedback response. With ΔT0 ≈ 1.2 °C for doubled CO2 and f near 0.6–0.7, the result lands near 3 °C — the equilibrium climate sensitivity that assessment reports place in a likely range of about 2.5 to 4 °C. Net feedbacks being significantly positive is what turns a 3.7 W/m² nudge into a three-degree world; and where feedbacks cross into self-drive — permafrost carbon, ice-sheet collapse, circulation changes — scientists speak of tipping points, thresholds beyond which change continues without further forcing.

concepts.detail: Forcing from a CO2 concentration C relative to reference C0; doubling gives 3.7 W/m².

concepts.statement: $$\Delta T_{eq} = \frac{\Delta T_0}{1 - f}$$
concepts.detail: Equilibrium temperature response ΔT0 (≈1.2 °C for doubled CO2, no feedbacks) amplified by the net feedback factor f; f → 1 means runaway.

concepts.statement: Forcing and feedback are roles, not substances: CO2 injected deep in geological time or by humans acts as forcing, while water vapor acts as feedback because temperature controls its amount. A positive feedback does not mean instant runaway — runaway requires the feedback factor to approach one, far from today’s 0.6–0.7. And equilibrium sensitivity is not the warming you see this decade: transient response lags because oceans absorb heat for centuries.
The change in top-of-the-atmosphere radiative balance caused by one driver, with the rest of the system held fixed.
A process that amplifies (positive) or dampens (negative) the temperature response to a forcing.
Warming → more evaporation → more atmospheric water vapor → more greenhouse trapping; the largest positive feedback.
Melting ice lowers reflectivity, increasing absorbed sunlight and further melting; amplified in both warming and cooling directions.
Negative feedback from changes in the atmospheric vertical temperature profile as the surface warms.
The global warming eventually reached per doubling of CO2, feedbacks included — likely near 3 °C.
A threshold beyond which a feedback-dominated part of the system keeps changing without further forcing.

examples.title: Worked example — Climate Feedbacks and Sensitivity: Why Warming Amplifies
examples.problem: The forcing and equilibrium warming when CO2 rises from 280 to 420 ppm (today’s level).

steps.label: Apply the forcing formula
steps.text: ΔF = 5.35 × 0.405 ≈ 2.2 W/m² — about 60 percent of the doubling benchmark, a direct consequence of the logarithm.

steps.label: Fold in feedbacks
steps.text: with the no-feedback response of about 1.2 °C per 3.7 W/m², this forcing alone gives ≈ 0.7 °C; with the observed net feedback factor f ≈ 0.65, ΔT = 0.7/(1 − 0.65) ≈ 2 °C.

examples.result: today’s concentration already commits the system to roughly two degrees of eventual equilibrium warming — the gap between committed and realized warming is the ocean’s thermal inertia, not an absence of feedbacks.

keyTakeaways: Remaining carbon budgets are computed by dividing allowable warming by sensitivity — a better-constrained ECS means a sharper emissions deadline
Ice-age paleoclimate serves as a natural experiment: glacial–interglacial cycles record the feedback sum (CO2, ice sheets, dust) at planetary scale
Solar geoengineering proposals are judged against feedback logic — masking forcing while leaving feedbacks intact still leaves the system sensitive
Weather-forecast ensembles and climate models perturb feedback parameters to span the plausible sensitivity range
Arctic monitoring tracks the ice–albedo loop in real time as sea-ice minimum records fall decade after decade

quiz.q: Why does CO2 radiative forcing grow only logarithmically with concentration?
options: Because the strongest absorption bands saturate first, so extra gas matters progressively less
Because the oceans absorb the difference
Because sunlight weakens as CO2 rises
quiz.explanation: Central absorption wavelengths fill in first; additional CO2 acts mostly on the band edges, giving the ln(C/C0) dependence.

quiz.q: Water vapor is classified as a feedback rather than a forcing because:
options: It is not a greenhouse gas
Its concentration is controlled by temperature, with a lifetime of days
quiz.explanation: Humans do not directly load the atmosphere with water vapor on climate timescales; temperature sets its abundance, so it amplifies the initial push.

quiz.q: With no feedbacks at all, doubled CO2 would warm Earth by about:
quiz.explanation: The bare Stefan–Boltzmann response to 3.7 W/m² is roughly 1.2 °C; feedbacks lift the equilibrium value to near 3 °C.

quiz.q: Which feedback is currently the largest source of uncertainty in climate sensitivity?
quiz.explanation: Clouds both cool (reflect sunlight) and warm (trap infrared); their net response to warming varies by type and altitude and dominates the spread among models.

intro: The ICT unit tests operational literacy: the abbreviations a teacher meets daily, the difference between an intranet and the internet, the etiquette of e-mail and conferencing, and — India-specific — the alphabet soup of national digital-education platforms. Five or so questions per paper, most of them one-mark classification items. The risk is over-familiarity: candidates mix up SWAYAM (courses) with SWAYAM PRABHA (TV channels) or DIKSHA (school teachers) with the National Digital Library (all readers). This lesson separates the platforms, then wires the underlying computing vocabulary.
objectives: Explain iCT versus information technology
Explain hardware, software and storage basics
Explain common abbreviations and terminology
Explain internet versus intranet
Explain e-mail mechanics and etiquette
Explain audio- and video-conferencing
Explain sWAYAM and the four-quadrant model
Explain sWAYAM PRABHA, NPTEL, DIKSHA, NDL, e-PG Pathshala, NAD
Explain e-governance models
Explain iCT in research workflow

concepts.statement: Definition first. Information and communication technology (ICT) is the extension of information technology (IT) that stresses unified communications and the convergence of telephony, broadcast media, audio-visual systems and computer networks — IT handles information (compute and store), ICT adds the communication layer that moves it. For a teacher or researcher the practical scope is: devices and their parts, networks and protocols, the services that ride them (web, mail, conferencing, cloud), and the institutional platforms that deliver education and governance.

Hardware basics the unit assumes: the CPU (central processing unit — the arithmetic and control core, with ALU and control unit inside), memory in two roles — RAM (random access memory, volatile working memory) and ROM (read-only memory, non-volatile firmware) — plus input/output devices and external storage. Storage runs HDD (magnetic) → SSD (flash) → optical and USB media; capacity units climb bit → byte (8 bits) → KB → MB → GB → TB. Software splits into system software (operating systems — Windows, Linux, Android; drivers, utilities) and application software (browsers, office suites, LMS); open-source licences make software free to use, modify and redistribute, proprietary licences do not.

The recurring abbreviation set: HTTP/HTTPS (web transfer protocols — the S is TLS-encrypted), FTP (file transfer), TCP/IP (the internet’s core transport/internetworking protocols), URL (uniform resource locator — the web address), WWW (the hypertext service on the internet), DNS (the domain-name system translating names to IP addresses), ISP (internet service provider), LAN/WAN/MAN (local, wide, metropolitan area networks), Wi-Fi (wireless LAN standard family), Bluetooth (short-range pairing), VPN (virtual private network), HTML (page markup), PDF (portable document format), OTP (one-time password), ICT’s own institutional acronyms (below). File-size and speed arithmetic — a 2 GB file over a 10 Mbps link — occasionally appears as an aptitude item.

The internet is the global public network of networks speaking TCP/IP; the intranet is an organisation’s private version of the same technology, firewalled for members only, often carrying the institution’s portals, policies and internal applications. (An extranet extends an intranet selectively to partners.) The web is not the internet — it is one service (hypertext over HTTP) among many (e-mail, DNS, file transfer). Browsers render pages; search engines index them (search tips: exact phrases in quotes, site: filters, evaluating sources — authority, currency, provenance — which doubles as the research unit’s skill). Cloud computing delivers storage and computation over the network (SaaS/PaaS/IaaS in ascending flexibility); the practical teaching examples are Google Drive-type storage, shared documents and hosted LMS platforms.

E-mail runs client-to-server-to-server via SMTP (sending) and IMAP or POP3 (retrieval). Mechanics worth marks: To (primary recipients), Cc (carbon copy — visible), Bcc (blind copy — hidden from other recipients), subject discipline, attachments (size limits, compression), and the reply/reply-all decision. Etiquette is examinable: concise subject lines, plain professional tone, no shouting in capitals, minimal reply-all, attachment named properly, and privacy — never expose others’ addresses by mass-Cc. Audio- and video-conferencing are synchronous many-point communication over the network: the underlying standards (Voice over IP; H.323/SIP historically), the platform features (screen share, breakout rooms, recording, chat, mute control), and their classroom role — flipped and blended learning, remote lectures, virtual labs and viva. Asynchronous alternatives (recorded lectures, forums) trade immediacy for access across time zones and bandwidths.

The national platforms the unit names, separated by function. SWAYAM (Study Webs of Active Learning for Young Aspiring Minds, launched 2017) is the national MOOC platform delivering free courses from Class 9 to post-graduation in four quadrants — video lectures, reading material, self-assessment tests, discussion forum — with certification through proctored exams and credit transfer permitted up to 40 per cent of a programme per UGC (Credit Framework for Online Learning Courses) rules. SWAYAM PRABHA is the companion group of DTH television channels (the 34-channel network under the PM eVIDYA umbrella of one-class-one-channel) for learners without bandwidth. NPTEL (National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning, from 2003, IITs + IISc) is the engineering-and-science content engine whose courses feed SWAYAM. DIKSHA (Digital Infrastructure for Knowledge Sharing, 2017) is the school-teacher-and-student platform of the school-education ministry — QR-coded "energised textbooks" and teacher training. e-PG Pathshala hosts postgraduate e-texts and e-content across subjects; the National Digital Library of India (NDLI, IIT Kharagpur) aggregates e-books and resources across all levels; the National Academic Depository (NAD) stores digital academic awards (degrees, marksheets); Shodhganga is the ETD repository for Indian PhD theses, Shodhgangotri for research proposals; Virtual Labs run remote experiments; e-Yantra supports embedded-systems education; and the Academic Bank of Credits (ABC) under NEP 2020 stores credit records for transfer. Memory hook: SWAYAM teaches, PRABHA broadcasts, NPTEL engineers, DIKSHA schools, e-PG postgraduates, NDLI libraries, NAD deposits, Shodhganga archives theses.

ICT and governance (e-governance) closes the unit. The service models are G2C (government to citizen — certificates, tax filing), G2B (business — licensing, tenders), G2G (inter-agency), G2E (employee); the delivery pillars are the Digital India programme (2015), Aadhaar-based authentication, UPI payments, and portal one-stop shops (National Scholarship Portal, e-Pathshala, SWAYAM’s own exam registration). Benefits the exam lists: transparency, reduced discretion and queueing, audit trails, inclusion through vernacular interfaces; risks: the digital divide (access, bandwidth, literacy, gender gap), data privacy, and cybersecurity hygiene — strong passwords, two-factor authentication, phishing awareness — which also belongs to every teacher’s professional responsibility.

Treating the web and the internet as synonyms — the web is one service on the internet. Swapping SWAYAM (online courses) and SWAYAM PRABHA (TV channels). Putting DIKSHA (school education) where SWAYAM (higher education) belongs. Saying intranet when an organisation-wide public-facing portal is meant, or VPN when only a firewall-protected internal network is described. Mixing RAM (volatile) and ROM (permanent). And forgetting the 40 per cent credit-transfer cap for SWAYAM courses — the number shows up in statement-style items.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: none — foundations level. This lesson pairs with res-research-methodology-hypothesis-sampling (the ICT-in-research workflow) and edu-higher-education-system-india (NEP 2020’s ABC and digital architecture). Primary reading: Wikipedia, "Information and communication technology" (definition and convergence framing); SWAYAM official pages (swayam.gov.in — the four quadrants and credit framework); Ministry of Education digital-initiative pages (education.gov.in) for SWAYAM PRABHA, DIKSHA, NDLI, NAD and e-PG Pathshala descriptions.
ICT = IT plus the communication layer; convergence of computing, telecom and broadcast.
RAM is volatile working memory; ROM permanent; storage climbs KB → MB → GB → TB.
Internet is the global TCP/IP network; intranet is private; the web is HTTP hypertext, one service among many.
Mail: SMTP sends, IMAP/POP3 retrieve; Bcc hides recipients; etiquette is professional brevity.
Conferencing is synchronous (VoIP, screen-share, breakout rooms); recorded media serve asynchronous learning.
Platforms: SWAYAM (MOOCs, four quadrants, 40 per cent credit cap), PRABHA (TV), NPTEL (IIT content), DIKSHA (schools), NDLI (library), e-PG Pathshala (PG texts), NAD (awards), Shodhganga (theses).
E-governance: G2C/G2B/G2G/G2E; benefits transparency and access; risks the digital divide and privacy.

quiz.q: A university’s internal portal, reachable only on campus credentials, running web technology behind a firewall, is best described as:
quiz.explanation: Private web technology restricted to an organisation’s members is an intranet; an extranet would extend selected access to outside partners.

quiz.q: Which platform is the national MOOC system whose courses follow the four-quadrant model?
quiz.explanation: SWAYAM delivers courses in four quadrants (video, reading, self-assessment, discussion); SWAYAM PRABHA is its DTH television counterpart, DIKSHA serves school education, e-PG Pathshala hosts PG e-content.

quiz.q: In an e-mail, the field that hides recipients from one another is:
quiz.explanation: Bcc (blind carbon copy) conceals the list; Cc recipients are visible to all.

quiz.q: The protocols for sending and retrieving e-mail are, respectively:
quiz.explanation: SMTP moves mail out; IMAP/POP3 retrieve it. HTTP/HTML belong to the web, FTP to file transfer.

quiz.q: Shodhganga is the national repository for:
options: Indian PhD theses (electronic theses and dissertations)
quiz.explanation: Shodhganga (INFLIBNET) archives Indian doctoral theses; Shodhgangotri holds research proposals; credits live in the ABC; channels are SWAYAM PRABHA.

intro:
Two questions face every computer-science student and every phone owner, and this lesson takes both. The first is how to think like a computer scientist — the discipline called computational thinking: turning a messy problem into a form a machine can execute, through decomposition, pattern recognition and abstraction, expressed finally as an algorithm you can write as pseudocode or draw as a flowchart. The second is what life online does to you and to society — the digital footprint you leave, the attackers who phish for it, and the impacts (digital divide, e-waste, new law) that computing has stamped on the world. The two halves share a premise: computing is now a civic competence, not a vocational one, and the exam syllabus (CUET, CBSE Computer Science and Informatics Practices) treats it that way. The programming that builds on the first half continues elsewhere in this domain; this lesson is the foundation and the conscience.

**Why this matters.** The algorithm half trains the reasoning every paper tests — tracing loops, spotting off-by-one errors, judging efficiency — without which programming is guesswork. The digital-citizen half is now examined in its own right and matters more with each passing year: the footprint you are building right now is permanent, the attacks are engineered, and the law (IT Act, DPDP) assigns real penalties to both attackers and careless data-handlers.
objectives: Explain computational thinking: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction
