This pairing, stable and inefficient at once, is the theoretical scandal of the game. It kills the comforting assumption that whatever rational actors converge on must somehow be for the best.

concepts.term: Iteration and the shadow of the future
concepts.statement: Repeat the game indefinitely and the calculus changes, because today’s defection now has a price tomorrow. Robert Axelrod’s computer tournaments around 1980 showed that in such settings nice strategies — those that never defect first — systematically outperformed aggressive ones. The shadow of the future is what makes cooperation rational; when the relationship has no tomorrow, the one-shot logic returns.

The tournament winner, submitted by psychologist Anatol Rapoport, was tit-for-tat: cooperate first, then copy whatever the partner did last round. Axelrod distilled its success into four properties — nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear. It never exploits anyone, never lets exploitation pass unanswered, returns to cooperation after a single punishment, and is easy for any strategy to model and to trust.

Beyond iteration, cooperation escapes through reputation systems, binding contracts with external enforcement, small-group monitoring, and communication that converts the game into a coordination problem. Institutional design — trade courts, verification regimes, environmental treaties with monitoring — is largely the craft of taking prisoner’s-dilemma payoffs and re-engineering them into games where cooperation is safe.

concepts.detail: A dilemma exists when the temptation payoff T (defecting against a cooperator) beats the mutual reward R, which beats mutual punishment P, with the sucker’s payoff S last; if 2R > T + S, mutual cooperation also beats taking turns exploiting each other.

concepts.statement: $$w \geq \frac{T - R}{T - P}$$
concepts.detail: With strategies that punish defection, cooperation can be sustained when the weight w of future interaction is at least this ratio: the short-term gain from exploiting, T − R, must be outweighed by the discounted long-run cost of landing in punishment, T − P. Make the future matter enough, and cooperation is self-interest.

concepts.statement: The commonest confusion is reading the dilemma as a claim that humans are selfish; it is a claim about payoff structure, not psychology, and real people often cooperate even where theory predicts defection. The second is mixing one-shot and repeated play: almost everything interesting — reputation, retaliation, forgiveness — exists only when the game has a future. Third, not every conflict is a dilemma: chicken and the stag hunt have different orderings and different cures.
A move that is best regardless of what the other player chooses.
A pair of strategies from which neither player gains by switching alone.
An outcome that leaves everyone at least as badly off as some alternative.
The table listing every player’s payoff for every combination of moves.
The weight of future rounds in current decisions; what repetition adds to a game.
Open with cooperation, then mirror the partner’s previous move.
Any setting where individually rational choices aggregate into a worse collective result.

examples.title: Worked example — Game Theory of Cooperation: The Prisoner’s Dilemma
examples.problem: Two rival drink shops each choose Advertise or Stay quiet; advertising costs money but steals customers, so each earns more by advertising whatever the other does — a disguised prisoner’s dilemma.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: with defection (here, Advertise) dominant for both players, the unique Nash equilibrium is mutual defection, even though both shops earn more when both stay quiet.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: each shop compares payoffs pair by pair — if the rival advertises, advertising limits the damage; if it stays quiet, advertising grabs the market — so both advertise.

examples.result: the shops settle into a low-profit advertising war, the commercial twin of mutual defection; regulation or a self-enforcing agreement is needed to reach the quiet equilibrium both secretly prefer.

keyTakeaways: Climate policy: emission pledges are dilemma-shaped, which is why treaties add measurement, reporting and verification to lengthen the shadow of the future.
Trade: tariff spirals and their institutional cures, from dispute-settlement panels to bound commitments.
Arms control: verification regimes exist precisely to make the cooperative outcome observable and the temptation payoff risky.
Antitrust economics: cartel members face a standing temptation to shave prices, so collusion requires monitoring and punishment strategies.
Biology: reciprocal altruism in grooming primates and vampire-bat blood sharing as naturally selected tit-for-tat.

Where next — No prerequisites beyond comfort with a two-by-two table — this is core-tier rational choice theory. Follow with Nash equilibrium in general, then the stag hunt and chicken for contrasting structures, then collective action theory. Axelrod’s The Evolution of Cooperation is the classic bridge to biology and political science.
Payoffs ordered T > R > P > S make unilateral defection tempting and mutual punishment stable.
The one-shot equilibrium is mutual defection: individually rational, collectively poor.
Repetition casts a shadow of the future that can make cooperation self-enforcing.
Tit-for-tat: be nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear.
Institutions — reputation, contracts, verification — are payoff engineering.

quiz.q: In a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma, what is the unique Nash equilibrium?
quiz.explanation: Defection dominates for both players, so mutual defection is the only stable outcome — even though both would prefer cooperation.

quiz.q: Tit-for-tat won Axelrod’s tournaments largely because it…
options: never defected first, retaliated once, then forgave
quiz.explanation: Its four properties — nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear — let it harvest cooperation from cooperators without being exploitable.

quiz.q: Cooperation becomes sustainable in the repeated dilemma mainly when…
options: the future matters enough relative to immediate gains
quiz.explanation: A sufficient weight on future interaction makes the long-run cost of punished defection exceed the short-run temptation gain.

intro:
The human mind is a marvel that errs in patterns. In the early 1970s Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky began studying how people judge probabilities, and found not random mistakes but systematic ones — predictable errors they traced to mental shortcuts called heuristics. Judgments were made as if by rough rules of thumb: start from a number and adjust, recall whatever comes easily, judge by resemblance. Their research programme, later the foundation of behavioural economics, reframed rationality itself as a scarce resource the mind budgets carefully.

**Why this matters.** Biases are not curiosities; they move markets, medicine and negotiation. Doctors over-reading screening tests, investors holding losers too lovingly, negotiators anchored by the first offer — all are documented, priced and sometimes exploited. Because the errors are systematic, they can be anticipated, measured and designed around, which makes the study of bias one of the few directly profitable branches of psychology.
objectives: Explain heuristics and two systems of thinking
Explain anchoring and insufficient adjustment
Explain availability and vividness
Explain representativeness and base-rate neglect
Explain framing effects and loss aversion
Explain confirmation bias and motivated reasoning
Explain debiasing and decision hygiene

concepts.term: Heuristics and two systems of thinking
concepts.statement: Kahneman later popularised a two-system picture of the mind: System 1 fires instantly, effortlessly and intuitively, while System 2 is slow, deliberate and lazy. Heuristics are System 1’s tools — brilliant frugality when stakes are small and worlds are familiar, misleading when a problem demands arithmetic. The crucial claim is that biases are byproducts of otherwise adaptive machinery: a shortcut honed for foraging and social life meets casino odds or Bayesian inference and stumbles in characteristic ways.

In the 1974 wheel-of-fortune experiment, a rigged spin left participants staring at the number ten or sixty-five before they estimated the percentage of African nations in the United Nations. The high-anchor group guessed around forty-five; the low-anchor group around twenty-five — dragged toward a number both knew was random. Anchoring survives money, expertise and explicit warnings: even a fabricated list price changes what later offers feel reasonable, because adjustment away from the anchor is habitually too small.

Frequency is judged by ease of recall, and ease is not neutral. Plane crashes are filmable; asthma deaths are not, and studies of perceived lethality find tornadoes rated deadlier than asthma while strokes are wildly underrated. News coverage acts as a distortion field: after heavy reporting of a rare event, probability estimates climb regardless of the true base rate. Vividness, recency and emotion — not frequency — decide what springs to mind, and what springs to mind decides what seems likely.

Asked whether a quiet, poetry-loving woman is a librarian or a nurse, most people answer by resemblance — how librarian-like she is — and ignore how many more nurses exist. In Kahneman and Tversky’s engineer-and-lawyer study, personality sketches moved predictions even when participants were told the person came from a group that was ninety per cent engineers. Judged by fit rather than by prior odds, resemblance functions as an automatic substitute for Bayes’ rule, and the bigger picture — the base rate — quietly drops out.

Tversky and Kahneman’s Asian disease problem offered identical outcomes in two costumes: a plan that “saves 200 of 600 lives” versus one under which “400 will die”. Majorities chose the certain saving in the gain frame but gambled in the loss frame. Prospect theory formalised the asymmetry: losses hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains please, so the description of a choice — not merely its content — steers the decision. Framing is why ninety-per-cent-lean meat outsells ten-per-cent-fat.

In Wason’s 2-4-6 task, people given a hidden rule to discover usually proposed number triples that confirmed their first guess and almost never tested cases that could refute it. Confirmation bias is the search for support rather than diagnosis, and motivated reasoning sharpens it when identity is at stake — the smarter you are, the better you argue for your own side. This is why partisan debates rarely converge: both camps are running confirmation searches on opposite evidence pools.

Awareness alone is weak medicine — the bias blind spot means people spot biases in others more readily than in themselves. What works is procedure: premortems that legitimise doubt before decisions lock, checklists, outside views that replace gut forecasts with reference-class base rates, and choice architecture that sets helpful defaults. Kahneman called this decision hygiene — you cannot disinfect intuition, but you can build institutions that quarantine its most predictable failures.
$$P(H \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}$$
concepts.detail: The probability of a hypothesis after seeing evidence equals the prior, P(H), times how expected the evidence is if the hypothesis holds, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

concepts.statement: The commonest error is treating every heuristic as a defect: in many real environments fast-and-frugal rules match or beat complex models, a point Gerd Gigerenzer presses against the biases school. A second is overconfidence in the catalogue itself — several famous effects, from ego depletion to some priming results, have failed replication, so check before you cite. Third, knowing the names confers no immunity: the bias blind spot persists in experts, and debiasing works through procedures, not lectures.
A fast, effort-saving rule of thumb that substitutes an easy question for a hard one.
Estimates dragged toward an initial value, even when that value is known to be arbitrary.
Judging frequency or probability by how easily instances come to mind.
Ignoring prior probabilities when judging how well evidence fits a category.
A reversal of preference produced by describing the same outcomes as gains or as losses.
The asymmetry by which losses loom roughly twice as large as equivalent gains.
Readily detecting biases in others while remaining blind to the same biases in oneself.

examples.title: Worked example — Cognitive Biases: The Bugs in Human Judgment
examples.problem: A condition affects 1 woman in 1,000; a screening test detects every true case but falsely flags 5% of healthy women. Given a positive result, how likely is the condition?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: Bayes’ theorem — the answer depends on the prior (1 in 1,000) as much as on the test; a positive result is evidence, not a verdict.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: in 1,000 women, about 1 true case tests positive, while 5% of the 999 healthy women — roughly 50 — also test positive. So 51 positives arrive, only 1 of them real.

examples.result: the probability is about 1 in 51, just under 2% — yet most laypeople and many clinicians guess near 95%, the signature error of base-rate neglect.

keyTakeaways: Medicine: natural-frequency formats for screening results, decision aids and second opinions counter base-rate neglect and availability-driven overdiagnosis.
Finance: the disposition effect — selling winners too early and losers too late — traced to loss aversion, and tamed by disciplined rebalancing rules.
Negotiation and pricing: first offers work as anchors, so list prices, pre-sale discounts and “regular prices” are engineered artefacts rather than facts.
Policy design: defaults in pension enrolment and organ-donation registries exploit inertia benevolently — choice architecture that outperforms persuasion.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is the core-tier entry to judgment under uncertainty. Pair it with cognitive dissonance in this subject to see motivated reasoning from the inside, then read Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow at a chapter a sitting. Follow with prospect theory’s formal curves, Gigerenzer’s ecological rationality as the loyal opposition, and the nudge literature for institutional design.

quiz.q: In the wheel-of-fortune experiment, participants who saw the spin land on 65 rather than 10 subsequently…
options: estimated higher numbers of African nations in the UN
adjusted fully away from the random number
guessed identically to a no-spin control group
quiz.explanation: Even a visibly random anchor pulls estimates toward itself, because adjustment away from the anchor is systematically insufficient.

quiz.q: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people; a test with no missed cases and a 5% false-positive rate comes back positive. The best estimate of the disease probability is…
quiz.explanation: Of roughly 51 positive results per 1,000 people, only 1 is a true case — about 1 in 51, just under 2%.

quiz.q: The Asian disease problem shows that preference reversals occur when…
options: identical outcomes are described as gains versus losses
quiz.explanation: People become risk-averse for gains and risk-seeking for losses, so equivalent framings of the same outcome produce opposite choices.

quiz.q: Which practice is the clearest example of debiasing through procedure rather than awareness?
options: Reading a list of named biases before a meeting
Running a premortem that asks the team to write why the plan failed
Repeating the decision until it feels right
quiz.explanation: Premortems institutionalise the search for disconfirming evidence — a structural counter to confirmation bias — whereas mere awareness does not immunise.

intro:
One person’s recycling does not cool the planet, and one herder’s restraint does not save the pasture. Groups face problems whose solution benefits everyone but whose cost falls on whoever moves first — a structure that makes inaction individually rational even when it dooms the group. Mancur Olson and Garrett Hardin turned this ancient dilemma into modern social science, and Elinor Ostrom, by studying the communities that beat it, rewrote the ending.

**Why this matters.** Climate change, overfished oceans, groundwater depletion, congested roads and antibiotic resistance are all commons problems wearing different clothes. The vocabulary of collective action tells you why voluntary appeals underperform, when prices and quotas work, and why some communities govern shared resources without either — the difference between a policy fight and a solved problem.
objectives: Explain public goods and the free-rider problem
Explain olson’s logic of collective action
Explain hardin’s tragedy of the commons
Explain common-pool resources and subtractability
Explain ostrom’s design principles
Explain the spectrum of governance solutions

concepts.term: Public goods and the free-rider problem
concepts.statement: A public good is defined by two traits: non-excludability — you cannot keep anyone from benefiting once it exists — and non-rivalry — one person’s use does not diminish another’s. National defence, clean air and lighthouses are the classics. The combination is toxic for supply: each person enjoys the good whether or not they paid, so rational individuals withhold contributions and wait for others. The free-rider problem is why public radio stations beg and armies are funded by taxes.

In The Logic of Collective Action (1965), Olson argued that large groups cannot achieve their common interests by voluntary action alone: the larger the group, the smaller each member’s stake in the outcome and the easier it is to ride free. Organisation survives on selective incentives — union insurance, professional credentials, member discounts — private rewards bundled with the public good. His sharpest theorem, the exploitation of the great by the small, notes that big players carry alliances while small ones quietly underpay.

Hardin’s 1968 essay told of a pasture open to all. Each herder gains the full benefit of one more animal, while the cost of overgrazing is divided among every herder, so each rationally adds animals “in a society that believes in the freedom of the commons.” The pasture dies not from villainy but from impeccable individual arithmetic. Hardin’s prescription — “mutual coercion mutually agreed upon” — made the essay one of the most cited, and most contested, in twentieth-century social science.

A common-pool resource is rival but hard to exclude people from — the diagonal opposite of a public good. Groundwater, fisheries, forests and the atmosphere are subtractable: what one user takes, the others cannot. That single distinction organises all of resource policy. Public goods such as weather forecasts need subsidy; private goods need only markets; common-pool resources need institutions, because open access plus subtraction equals the tragedy.

Elinor Ostrom’s Governing the Commons (1990) examined Swiss alpine pastures, Spanish irrigation communities, Japanese mountain forests and coastal fisheries that had thrived for centuries under rules the users themselves made. Her design principles — clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, participation in rule-making, monitoring by accountable users, graduated sanctions, cheap conflict resolution and rights to organise recognised from above — predict success closely: miss several, and the commons tends to fail. The 2009 Nobel Prize crowned the finding: self-governance is a genuine third way.

Between market and state lies a menu. Privatisation gives each user a stake — dividing rangeland into fenced plots, or issuing individual transferable quotas in fisheries. Regulation caps use directly — seasons, licences, emissions standards. Prices work where meters exist — road charges, carbon taxes. And communal governance succeeds where boundaries are visible and users depend on the resource long-term. The craft is matching the instrument to the good’s biology and the group’s capacity; every option fails somewhere.

concepts.term: Private versus social payoff of one more animal
concepts.statement: $$u = B - \frac{C}{n} \;(\text{herder}), \qquad U = B - C \;(\text{society})$$
concepts.detail: Adding one animal returns its full benefit B to a single herder while the overgrazing cost C is spread across all n users, so each individual adds animals well past the social optimum.

concepts.statement: $$\delta \geq \frac{T - R}{T - P}$$
concepts.detail: When users meet repeatedly, restraint is self-enforcing if the discount factor δ — how much tomorrow matters — exceeds the ratio of the temptation to defect to the total loss from mutual defection.

concepts.statement: First error: reading Hardin as the last word. He himself refined the essay into “the tragedy of the unmanaged commons”, and Ostrom documented hundreds of durable exceptions. Second, confusing public goods with commons — rivalry is the difference, and it changes the remedy. Third, romanticising self-governance: communal regimes fail too, usually where boundaries blur or monitoring lapses. And the tragedy is not a population parable — it is about incentives, not headcount.
A good that is non-excludable and non-rival, and therefore chronically undersupplied by voluntary payment.
Someone who benefits from a collective effort while avoiding its costs.
A private reward or penalty tied to participation that makes contributing individually rational.
A rival good from which exclusion is costly, such as a fishery or aquifer.
The property that each unit taken by one user is unavailable to the others.
Ostrom’s empirical regularities in the rules of long-enduring commons institutions.
The weight a decision-maker places on future payoffs relative to present ones.

examples.title: Worked example — Collective Action and the Tragedy of the Commons
examples.problem: In a fishery of 20 identical boats, an extra day of fishing earns a skipper €3,000 but depletes the stock at a future cost of €4,000 to the fleet. Will an individually rational skipper fish the extra day?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: the private cost of the extra day is the social cost divided by the number of users, C/n, while the gain lands undivided on one boat.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: the skipper’s cost is €4,000 ÷ 20 = €200 against a €3,000 gain — a private net of +€2,800. Society’s ledger reads €3,000 − €4,000 = −€1,000 per extra day.

examples.result: every skipper adds the day, and the fishery slides toward collapse; only boundaries, quotas or fleet-level governance reattach the full €4,000 to the decision.

keyTakeaways: Climate policy: carbon pricing and cap-and-trade convert the atmosphere’s invisible cost into a private one, while treaties grapple with free riding among nations.
Fisheries management: individual transferable quotas, as in New Zealand and Iceland, have turned collapse-prone fleets into rights-holding stewards.
Antibiotic stewardship: resistance is a pooled resource spent with every prescription — hence hospital guidelines and limits on agricultural use.
Groundwater and irrigation: from Spanish huertas to Californian adjudications, courts and user associations write the rules that pumps cannot.

Where next — This topic builds on the prisoner’s dilemma in this subject — read that first if you have not. Then follow with Elinor Ostrom’s Governing the Commons, the single most rewarding book on the theme, and Hardin’s 1968 essay as a brisk counterpoint. Mechanism design and public-choice theory are the natural next tiers for the mathematically inclined.

quiz.q: According to Olson, large groups most reliably achieve collective goals when they…
options: offer selective incentives that make membership privately worthwhile
quiz.explanation: In large groups each member’s contribution is negligible and invisible, so organisation needs private-side rewards such as insurance or credentials.

quiz.q: Why does each herder keep adding animals to the open pasture?
options: The full benefit of an extra animal is private while its grazing cost is shared by all
Herd sizes are fixed by tradition
Animals multiply faster than pastures can recover
quiz.explanation: The asymmetry between private benefit and socialised cost makes overgrazing individually rational — the tragedy’s engine.

quiz.q: Which of Ostrom’s design principles most directly targets free riding?
options: Clear boundaries defining who may use the resource
Monitoring and graduated sanctions enforced by accountable users
quiz.explanation: Monitoring and graduated sanctions make violations detected and punished at proportionate cost — the institutional antidote to free riding.

quiz.q: A common-pool resource differs from a public good because it is…
options: rival in consumption though often hard to exclude from
quiz.explanation: Subtractability — what one user takes, the others lose — is the defining difference, and the reason commons need institutions.

intro:
In 2008, humanity crossed a quiet threshold: for the first time, more than half of us lived in cities. The pull is ancient and economic at once. Cities are expensive, crowded and loud, yet they concentrate the two things nothing else produces on the same scale — opportunity and other people. Understanding why cities exist means understanding agglomeration: the strange, robust fact that clustering people and firms in one place multiplies what they can do.

**Why this matters.** Housing crises, transit investments, regional decline and the geography of innovation are all agglomeration problems in disguise. If density itself generates productivity, zoning that forbids it destroys wealth invisibly; if cities scale superlinearly, the century of urbanization ahead will be faster, richer and more eventful than countryside arithmetic suggests.
objectives: Explain agglomeration economies: sharing, matching, learning
Explain increasing returns and the urban trade-off
Explain the bid-rent gradient
Explain zipf’s law and the urban hierarchy
Explain superlinear scaling of city life
Explain urbanism as a way of life

concepts.statement: Alfred Marshall, writing in 1890, heard “the mysteries of the trade” hanging “in the air” of industrial districts. Modern economics decomposes his insight into three mechanisms. Sharing: firms pool specialised suppliers, infrastructure and a deep labour market. Matching: workers and jobs, founders and funders find each other faster where candidates are dense. Learning: ideas leak, imitate and recombine across corridors and cafés. Duranton and Puga’s formulation — sharing, matching, learning — remains the cleanest summary of why co-location pays.

concepts.term: Increasing returns and the urban trade-off
concepts.statement: Agglomeration exhibits increasing returns: doubling a cluster more than doubles certain benefits, which is why economic geography is lumpy rather than smooth. Against this stands the price of proximity — rent, congestion, crime, disease. Cities sit where the two curves balance, which explains both skylines and sprawl: Manhattan stacks floors because land at the centre is worth stacking on, while cheap land at the edge pulls development outward. A city’s shape is the visible residue of this tug-of-war.

The Alonso–Muth–Mills model formalises the gradient: land value falls predictably with distance from the centre, because each extra metre of travel costs more while each saved metre is worth more to whoever values centrality most. Retailers outbid residents for the core; manufacturers, needing space, take the ring beyond; agriculture holds the margin where land is cheapest. Concentric rings of land use — however disguised by history and geography — are the model’s fingerprint.

concepts.term: Zipf’s law and the urban hierarchy
concepts.statement: Line up a country’s cities by population and a startling regularity appears: the second city is about half the first, the tenth about a tenth. Zipf’s law, the rank-size rule, holds roughly for many countries and centuries, and its explanation is still debated. The leading candidate, Gibrat’s law — cities grow in proportion to their size, so random shocks compound — generates Zipf distributions naturally. The deviations are informative too: a nation whose second city is far smaller than the rule predicts usually has a primate capital.

A team led by Luís Bettencourt and Geoffrey West found that urban quantities scale as power laws of population: socioeconomic outputs — wages, patents, GDP — scale with an exponent near 1.15, so a city twice the size delivers roughly ten to fifteen per cent more per resident, while infrastructure scales sublinearly, needing less road and wire per head. The same exponent, though, amplifies crime and disease. Cities are social reactors: bigger runs hotter, in output and in trouble alike.

concepts.term: Urbanism as a way of life
concepts.statement: Louis Wirth’s 1938 essay “Urbanism as a Way of Life” listed the sociological ingredients: size, density, heterogeneity. Georg Simmel had already described the psychic result in 1903 — the metropolis hammers the nerves until the dweller adopts a blasé attitude, a protective flatness toward strangers, exchanged for unprecedented freedom from village scrutiny. Urban ties become segmental and role-based; the neighbour is a stranger and the stranger a potential ally. Wirth’s determinism has been qualified — urban villages persist — but the tension he named is real.
$$\text{rank} \times \text{population} \approx \text{constant}$$
concepts.detail: The tenth-largest city is roughly one-tenth the size of the largest; the product of rank and size is stable across many countries and eras.

concepts.statement: $$Y = Y_0 N^{\beta}, \qquad \beta \approx 1.15$$
concepts.detail: Socioeconomic outputs Y grow faster than population N; each doubling of city size raises per-capita output by roughly ten to fifteen per cent, with crime and disease scaling similarly.

concepts.statement: Correlation is not causation: cities may select ambitious people rather than transform them, and wage premiums partly reflect sorting. Zipf’s law is an approximation, sensitive to how city boundaries are drawn, and primate-city deviations are common in politically centralised nations. Superlinear scaling is contested in its details and is an average across thousands of cities, not a law any one city obeys. And Wirth’s picture of urban alienation has aged: Herbert Gans’s urban villages showed strong local ties thriving inside the metropolis.
Productivity gains that arise when firms and people locate near one another.
The informal spread of ideas and know-how across firms and workers in a cluster.
The decline in land value with distance from a central point of access.
Zipf’s observation that a city’s population is inversely proportional to its rank.
The tendency of urban outputs to grow faster than population, with exponent above one.
A country’s dominant city, far larger than the rank-size rule predicts.
In Wirth’s sense, the distinctive way of life produced by size, density and heterogeneity.

examples.title: Worked example — Why Cities Exist: Agglomeration and Urban Life
examples.problem: The largest city of a country holds 8 million people; its fourth-largest holds 1.1 million. Is the urban hierarchy close to Zipf’s prediction?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: the rank-size rule predicts a city’s population as the largest city’s population divided by its rank.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: with the top city at 8 million, the expected size of the fourth city is 8,000,000 ÷ 4 = 2 million; the observed 1.1 million is barely half that.

examples.result: the hierarchy is steeper than Zipf predicts — a signature of primate-city dominance, where the capital monopolises political and economic functions and secondary cities are undersized.

keyTakeaways: Housing and zoning policy: if density creates agglomeration value, height limits and minimum lot sizes tax productivity as surely as they preserve character.
Regional development: subsidies that scatter firms across a province fight the clustering economics; cluster-based policy works with the gradient, not against it.
Transport investment: agglomeration benefits accrue to accessibility, which is why transit lines between co-located firms and workers can outperform their ridership models.
Public health planning: density amplifies both innovation and epidemic spread — from nineteenth-century cholera maps to modern outbreak modelling.

Where next — Prerequisites: comfort with graphs and percentages. Pair with the collective action topic in this subject — congestion and NIMBY disputes are commons problems — and with Durkheim, whose division of labour explains why city dwellers need strangers. Then read Jane Jacobs’s The Death and Life of Great American Cities and Edward Glaeser’s Triumph of the City; Krugman’s new economic geography is the mathematical frontier.

quiz.q: Marshall’s remark that “the mysteries of the trade” are “in the air” refers to which agglomeration mechanism?
options: Improved matching in thick labour markets
Cheaper land at the urban core
quiz.explanation: Ideas drifting between nearby firms and workers — the learning mechanism — is what Marshall’s phrase captured.

quiz.q: According to the bid-rent model, land use arranges itself so that…
options: the activities valuing accessibility most occupy the central land they outbid others for
land values are uniform within a city
quiz.explanation: Land goes to the highest bidder, and whoever gains most from centrality — typically commerce — pays most at the core.

quiz.q: The largest city of a country has 8 million residents. Zipf’s rule predicts the fifth-largest city is about…
quiz.explanation: 8,000,000 ÷ 5 = 1.6 million — the rank-size rule divides the top city’s population by its rank.

quiz.q: Superlinear scaling means that when a city doubles in population, per-capita outputs such as patents and wages…
options: fall by about fifteen per cent
rise by roughly ten to fifteen per cent
quiz.explanation: With an exponent near 1.15, doubling population multiplies per-capita output by 2 raised to the power 0.15 — an increase of roughly ten to fifteen per cent.

intro:
Developmental psychology asks how a squalling newborn becomes a banker, a baker and eventually a grandmother — and what changes, holds steady and trades places along the way. The field once stopped at childhood; today it spans the whole lifespan, tracking infancy's leaps, adolescence's identity work, midlife's reorganizations and old age's quiet negotiations. Its findings are remarkably practical: they tell teachers what a six-year-old can grasp, tell parents what a clinging toddler is actually doing, and tell societies when an aging worker is best retrained rather than replaced. Six frameworks organize the journey.

**Why this matters.** Development is not a script that unfolds; it is an interaction between a growing brain and the people, places and expectations around it. That is why the same toddler turns out differently in different households, and why investments in children, schools and elder care repay themselves in ways economics is only beginning to price.
objectives: Explain piaget's four stages of cognitive growth
Explain vygotsky: the zone of proximal development
Explain attachment and the secure base
Explain erikson's psychosocial crises
Explain fluid and crystallized intelligence
Explain aging: plasticity, reserve, compensation

concepts.term: Piaget's four stages of cognitive growth
concepts.statement: Jean Piaget watched his own children and concluded that thinking grows in four leaps. Sensorimotor infants (zero to two) learn through action and grasp object permanence — hidden things persist. Preoperational children (two to seven) command symbols and language yet fail conservation: juice poured into a taller glass seems "more". Concrete operational children (seven to eleven) master conservation and logic on real objects; formal operational adolescents reason about abstractions. Replication has softened the boundaries — infants show surprise at impossible events earlier than Piaget credited — but the sequence survives.

concepts.term: Vygotsky: the zone of proximal development
concepts.statement: Lev Vygotsky, who died at thirty-seven in 1934, saw development as social before it is individual. His zone of proximal development is the gap between what a child can do alone and what she can do with help; growth happens inside that zone, not beyond it. Teachers therefore scaffold — the term is Jerome Bruner's — withdrawing support as competence rises. Children's private speech, once dismissed as egocentric chatter, works as self-coaching that goes silent and inward.

John Bowlby, drawing on Konrad Lorenz's imprinting goslings, argued that infants are biologically primed to bond with a caregiver who is reliably available. Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation staged separations and reunions and found patterns: secure infants (about six in ten) explore, using the caregiver as a secure base, and settle on reunion; avoidant infants feign indifference; resistant infants cling and fight. A disorganized pattern was added later. Styles echo into adult romance — as tendencies, never as destinies.

Erik Erikson stretched the map across the whole life: eight psychosocial stages, each a crisis between a strength and its failure — trust against mistrust in infancy, identity against role confusion in adolescence, intimacy against isolation in young adulthood, generativity against stagnation in midlife, integrity against despair at the end. Adolescence got the deepest reworking: James Marcia showed identity arrives in statuses — achieved, in moratorium, foreclosed or diffused — rather than in one leap.

Adulthood brought a surprise: intelligence splits in two. Fluid intelligence — novel problem solving, processing speed — peaks in the twenties and slides slowly afterward. Crystallized intelligence — vocabulary, factual knowledge, professional judgment — keeps rising into the sixties. K. Warner Schaie's Seattle Longitudinal Study followed thousands of adults for decades and found declines begin later than cross-sectional snapshots claim, because each cohort is better educated than the last.

An aging brain is not simply a smaller one. Denise Park's scaffolding theory of aging describes compensation: as some regions slow, others are recruited to share the load, and performance holds until reserve runs short. Reserve is trainable — education, complex work and exercise delay dementia symptoms by years. Structural plasticity persists too: London taxi drivers who learned "the Knowledge" grew larger posterior hippocampi, sculpted by unaided navigation.

Three habits distort the picture. Stage ages are averages, not deadlines — the underlying change is continuous. Cross-sectional age comparisons exaggerate decline by mixing generations of different schooling. And attachment categories are risk indicators, not personality types: temperament, later relationships and culture all bend the path. Above all, "critical period" rarely means "only window" — most capacities keep a sensitive, not sealed, period.
Knowing that objects continue to exist when out of sight; the sensorimotor milestone.
Understanding that quantity survives changes of shape or container; achieved in the concrete operational stage.
The band between what a learner can do alone and with guidance; where teaching works.
Ainsworth's image of the attachment figure as a safe platform from which to explore.
Erikson's eight age-graded crises between a strength and its failure.
Speed and flexibility on novel problems; peaks in early adulthood.
Accumulated knowledge and skill; grows into late life.

examples.title: Worked example — How Minds Grow: Developmental Psychology Across the Lifespan
examples.problem: A five-year-old watches juice poured from a short wide glass into a tall thin one and insists the tall glass now holds "more" — what is going on, and what should a teacher expect?

steps.label: Recall the framework
steps.text: Piaget's preoperational stage (two to seven) is marked by centration — locking onto one dimension, here height — and by failure of conservation.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: she centers on the visible change (the water line rose) and cannot yet mentally reverse the pouring or compensate across height and width, so her claim follows from how her cognition works, not from stubbornness.

examples.result: normal preoperational thinking. Expect conservation near the concrete operational stage around seven, and teach measurement through pouring and counting, not lectures.

keyTakeaways: Curriculum design: concrete materials before abstraction in early grades, following Piagetian sequencing.
Pediatrics and parenting programs: milestone checklists and attachment-based interventions in early-childhood clinics.
Teacher training: scaffolding inside the zone of proximal development as the operating logic of tutoring.
Elder care: lifelong learning and exercise programs built on cognitive-reserve research that delays dementia symptoms.
Policy: the case for early-childhood investment rests on how heavily development front-loads its sensitive periods.

quiz.q: Object permanence — knowing a hidden toy still exists — emerges in which Piagetian stage?
quiz.explanation: Grasping that unseen things persist is the crowning achievement of the sensorimotor period, before symbolic thought begins.

quiz.q: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, a securely attached infant…
options: cries without pause and cannot explore
explores using the caregiver as a secure base and settles on reunion
clings and resists comfort at reunion
quiz.explanation: Security shows in the balance: exploration away from the caregiver plus comfort-seeking back — the secure base at work.

quiz.q: A sixty-two-year-old finds crossword vocabulary still growing while novel puzzle speed dips. This pattern is…
options: fluid falling while crystallized holds or rises
quiz.explanation: The classic adult dissociation: processing speed declines while knowledge-based intelligence keeps accruing.

quiz.q: Erikson's crisis of adolescence is…
quiz.explanation: Adolescence is Erikson's identity workshop; intimacy follows only once identity is somewhat settled.

intro:
In 1956 psychology changed its subject: from rats and levers to people and information. George Miller measured the mind's holding capacity at seven items, plus or minus two; Allen Newell and Herbert Simon programmed a computer to prove logic theorems; Noam Chomsky's review of B. F. Skinner dismantled behaviorism's account of language. The cognitive revolution that followed studies the mind as a system that attends, stores, retrieves and thinks, testing each piece with reaction times, errors and recall. This lesson tours that architecture: the small workbench of working memory, the vast warehouse beneath it, and the narrow door between them.

**Why this matters.** Every interface, syllabus, checklist and courtroom procedure implicitly prices the mind's limits. Designers who respect a four-chunk workbench and a single-channel attention system build things people can actually use; those who do not build expensive mistakes and confident eyewitnesses who are wrong.
objectives: Explain working memory: the mind's small workbench
Explain long-term memory: episodic, semantic, procedural
Explain depth of processing at encoding
Explain attention as a bottleneck
Explain inattentional and change blindness
Explain schemas: memory with priors

concepts.term: Working memory: the mind's small workbench
concepts.statement: Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed in 1974 that short-term memory is not a shelf but a workbench. Working memory couples a silent supervisor — the central executive — with subordinate stores: the phonological loop rehearses speech (why long words are harder to keep) and the visuospatial sketchpad holds images; an episodic buffer was added in 2000 to bind content into episodes. Capacity is a handful of chunks — Nelson Cowan estimates four — and chunking stretches it: chess masters recall real positions brilliantly and random ones poorly.

Endel Tulving divided long-term memory into episodic (dated, autobiographical events) and semantic (facts stripped of occasion), alongside procedural memory for skills. The split is written into Henry Molaison's tragedy: surgery in 1953 removed his hippocampi to stop seizures and erased his ability to form new episodic memories — yet he slowly learned mirror-drawing, improving day after day while insisting he had never seen the task. Memory is several systems, and they fail separately.

Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart showed in 1972 that memory is fixed at encoding by depth, not repetition alone. Judging whether a word is printed in capitals barely leaves a trace; judging whether "chicken" fits "the cook served the ___" produces far better recall. Meaning is the glue. How to convert this into study schedules is the business of the Study Skills lessons on spaced repetition and retrieval practice; here the finding stands on its own.

Colin Cherry demonstrated the cocktail-party problem in 1953 with dichotic listening: repeat one ear's speech aloud and the other ear's content vanishes, though your own name may break through. Donald Broadbent modeled a filter admitting one channel; Anne Treisman softened it into attenuation; late-selection theorists moved the filter past meaning. Nilli Lavie's load theory reconciled the camps: perception runs wide and automatic until capacity fills, then narrows to one stream.

Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked viewers to count basketball passes in a 1999 video; roughly half never saw a person in a gorilla suit stroll through the scene. Inattentional blindness is not laziness — attention is a budget, and unattended stimuli do not reach awareness. Its cousin, change blindness, left people failing to notice a swapped conversation partner in a doorway experiment. The felt richness of vision is a confidence trick memory plays.

Frederic Bartlett had shown the way in 1932: British students retold a Native American tale, "The War of the Ghosts", and each retelling rationalized the strange parts toward the storyteller's own schemas — organized packages of expectation. Perception and memory are inference from priors: fast and efficient, and systematically bent toward the familiar. A predicting brain is a slightly distorting one.

Working memory span is not intelligence — it predicts, but loosely. "Seven plus or minus two" described 1950s digit recall, not everything; the modern chunk estimate is nearer four. Attention is not one spotlight: practiced skills run with little budget at all. And memory is not a recording — it is rebuilt on retrieval, which is why confident recollections can be wrong in detail while feeling perfect.
The limited workbench that holds and manipulates information in the moment.
The speech-and-sound store of working memory, kept alive by inner rehearsal.
Baddeley's later addition that binds working-memory content into integrated episodes.
Tulving's system for dated, personally experienced events.
Memory for skills; survives hippocampal damage that erases episodes.
Craik and Lockhart's finding that deeper, meaning-based encoding yields stronger memory.
Failure to perceive a visible, unexpected stimulus while attention is engaged elsewhere.

examples.title: Worked example — Memory, Attention and Thinking: Cognitive Psychology
examples.problem: Why can a receptionist reliably take a seven-digit phone number but not a sixteen-digit tracking code, and what should she do about the code?

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: working memory holds about four chunks in the phonological loop, maintained by rehearsal; longer strings overflow within seconds.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: split the code into meaningful groups — dates, repeated pairs, triplets like area codes — rehearse each group aloud, and write it down immediately to offload storage.

examples.result: chunking plus immediate offloading turns an impossible string into a manageable one; without them, overflow is guaranteed no matter how hard she concentrates.

keyTakeaways: Interface design: menus, forms and dashboards chunked to respect a four-chunk limit before anything else.
Eyewitness practice: interviews built around reconstructive memory — open questions first, no leading details.
Aviation and medicine: checklists and alarms engineered around attention's single-channel limits.
Education: cognitive-load theory sequences worked examples before problem solving for novices.
Clinical assessment: working-memory tests help distinguish attention disorders from motivation problems.

quiz.q: Molaison (H.M.) improved at mirror-drawing across days while denying any memory of practicing. Which system kept working?
quiz.explanation: Skill learning rides on procedural memory and survived his hippocampal loss, while episodic memory of the practice sessions did not.

quiz.q: People remember fewer long words than short words. This word-length effect implicates…
quiz.explanation: Rehearsal takes time: longer words take longer to say, so fewer fit within the loop's fading window.

quiz.q: Half of viewers miss a gorilla suit while counting basketball passes. This is…
quiz.explanation: Attention was budgeted to the counting task; the unexpected visitor never reached awareness — perception requires attention, not just eyes.

quiz.q: Bartlett's "War of the Ghosts" retellings demonstrated that…
quiz.explanation: Each retelling rationalized the unfamiliar toward the teller's expectations — memory as reconstruction, not playback.

intro:
Every known society ranks its members — by wealth, honor, birth or clout — and every such ranking outlives the individuals inside it. Social stratification is the name for this structured inequality: not the fact that people differ, but that their differences are patterned, passed on and defended. Sociologists ask three questions of any hierarchy. What is being ranked? How open is movement between ranks? And what stories make the ranking feel legitimate? The answers separate caste from class, estate from market, and all three from the gentler fictions of merit.

**Why this matters.** Where you sit in a stratification system predicts your health, schooling, lifespan and even your stress hormones more reliably than your personal choices do. That is why inequality statistics are fought over like territory: they measure who gets what, and the maps rarely flatter the stories societies tell about themselves.
objectives: Explain structured inequality and its alleged functions
Explain weber: class, status, party
Explain caste, estate and class systems
Explain mobility regimes and their mechanics
Explain status attainment: how advantage travels
Explain gini-style measurement of inequality

concepts.term: Structured inequality and its alleged functions
concepts.statement: Kingsley Davis and Wilbert Moore argued in 1945 that inequality is functional: important, demanding positions must pay more to attract the talented into them. Melvin Tumin's 1953 rejoinder cut deep — rewards track power more than importance (compare nurses to celebrities), and inequality itself wastes talent by denying the poor the training their ability deserves. The exchange, still unfinished, frames every debate about executive pay.

Max Weber distinguished three dimensions of ranking that need not coincide. Class is market position — income, skills, property — shaping one's life chances. Status is honor: the prestige of a surname, a profession, a way of life. Party is organized power, the capacity to act in concert. A lottery winner buys class overnight but not status; an indebted aristocrat holds status without class; a party functionary wields power while lacking both.

Systems differ in how ranks are assigned. In caste systems position is ascribed at birth and sealed by endogamy — India's jati order, formally outlawed by the 1950 Constitution yet resilient, and apartheid South Africa are the canonical cases. Estate orders, like feudal Europe's clergy, nobility and commons, made rank legal. Class systems rank by market position, in principle open to achievement; slavery stands as the extreme closed system. In practice pure types blur: every class system leaks ascription through the back door.

Pitirim Sorokin founded mobility studies in 1927 with distinctions still in use: vertical against horizontal movement, and intergenerational (child versus parents) against intragenerational (within one career). Structural mobility moves whole strata — industrialization lifted millions into white-collar work with no individual virtue required — while exchange mobility shuffles individuals within a fixed structure. "Rags to riches" tales describe exchange mobility, which in most countries is rarer than the tales imply.

Peter Blau and Otis Dudley Duncan's 1967 study of American occupations traced how advantage travels: father's education and occupation shape the child's schooling, and schooling shapes the child's occupation far more than origins directly do. Education is the hinge of transmission — which is why school funding and admissions are fought like class battles. Later work added sticky floors, glass ceilings and Raj Chetty's census-scale maps of mobility by neighborhood.

Inequality is measured, not just felt. The Lorenz curve plots cumulative income against cumulative population; the Gini coefficient summarizes it, running from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (a single holder of everything). Advanced economies range from roughly 0.25 to 0.4; South Africa exceeds 0.6. Income and wealth Ginis differ sharply — wealth concentrates harder — and any single number hides the distribution's shape.

Income is not wealth — a salary and a portfolio rank differently, and wealth concentrates harder. The Gini compresses a distribution into one number: two societies with identical Ginis can be shaped utterly differently. Occupational classes are not lived classes, and self-identified class mixes identity with position. And "meritocracy", coined by Michael Young in 1958 as satire, names a legitimating story as much as a mechanism.
Structured, enduring inequality in rewards and life chances across a society.
Weber's term for the probabilities of obtaining goods and opportunities given one's market position.
A collectivity ranked by honor and shared style of life, independent of money.
Position assigned at birth or by force of law rather than achieved.
Movement between strata, vertical or horizontal, within or across generations.
Stratum shifts caused by changes in the economy rather than individual effort.
Inequality measure from 0 (equal) to 1 (one holder of all income).

examples.title: Worked example — Class, Status and Power: Social Stratification
examples.problem: Compare two ten-household villages — in A, nine families earn 10 units and one earns 90; in B, all ten earn 19 — using a Kuznets-style ratio of the top tenth's income share to the bottom four-tenths' share.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: shares are incomes over totals; the ratio expresses how many times the top slice out-earns the bottom slice.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: in A, total income is 180: the top tenth holds 90/180 = 50 per cent, the bottom four-tenths hold 40/180 = about 22 per cent, a ratio of 2.25. In B every share equals its population share, so the ratio is 10/40 = 0.25.

examples.result: village A's top tenth out-earns its bottom four-tenths nine times over, versus an even 0.25 in B — one household produced steep, measurable inequality.

keyTakeaways: Tax and transfer design: Gini and top-share statistics anchor redistribution debates and progressivity schedules.
Education policy: the mobility hinge — early-childhood access and school funding fight transmission.
Corporate governance: pay-ratio disclosure ties CEO compensation to the median worker's.
Development monitoring: the World Bank and OECD track Ginis to compare societies and eras.
Public health: the Whitehall studies found civil-service grade predicted mortality — status gradients get under the skin.

quiz.q: A lottery winner gains money overnight but no old-school prestige. Weber would say class changed while…
quiz.explanation: Class is market position and moves with money; status is honor and must be granted, not bought — the two dimensions come apart.

quiz.q: The defining feature of a caste system is…
quiz.explanation: Caste assigns position at birth and closes exits, above all through rules about who may marry whom.

quiz.q: A Gini coefficient of 0 means…
quiz.explanation: Zero Gini means every unit of population holds the same share of income — the Lorenz curve sits on the diagonal.

quiz.q: Blau and Duncan found the strongest link between a father's occupation and his son's ran through…
quiz.explanation: Origins shape schooling, and schooling largely carries the effect onward — the transmission hinge.

intro:
Society holds together less by force than by routines nobody remembers inventing. Institutions are those routines grown durable: families that raise the young, religions that sanctify shared life, laws, schools and markets that let strangers cooperate. Douglass North called them the rules of the game — humanly devised constraints that structure interaction. Peter Berger and Thomas Luckmann described how habitual actions harden into roles and get legitimated by stories until they feel natural. This lesson reads that skeleton through its two oldest members — family and religion — then asks what happens when it shifts or snaps.

**Why this matters.** Institutional analysis explains why imported laws fail abroad, why some villages manage commons and others cannot, and why "just change the policy" so often disappoints. Rules on paper are the visible tenth of an institution; the norms and enforcement beneath decide what the rules mean.
objectives: Explain institutions as rules of the game
Explain family forms and functions
Explain religion: glue, gearbox and typology
Explain the secularization debate
Explain path dependence and institutional change
Explain anomie: when institutions fail

concepts.term: Institutions as rules of the game
concepts.statement: North's rules come in three layers: formal rules (statutes, constitutions), informal norms (customs, shame) and enforcement (courts, neighbors). Their function is to reduce uncertainty so that strangers can plan — you marry, save and specialize because rules make others predictable. And the court is not the institution: an organization is a player; the institution is the rules it plays under.

Family systems vary along dimensions anthropologists mapped long ago: residence (patrilocal, matrilocal, neolocal), descent (most societies patrilineal; the Khasi of Meghalaya reckon through mothers) and composition, from extended households to nuclear ones. William Goode argued that industrialization pushes the conjugal, nuclear family forward because mobility needs portability. Whatever the form, the functions persist — socializing children, pooling income, organizing care — so "the decline of the family" usually describes rearrangement, not exit.

Religion, as Durkheim saw, works by dividing the sacred from the profane and regenerating belonging in ritual (the Durkheim lesson in this subject treats his collective conscience). As an organization it takes shapes Ernst Troeltsch and Max Weber sorted into a typology: the church, accommodated to society at large; the sect, a voluntary breakaway demanding commitment; denominations between those poles; new religious movements at the edge. Robert Bellah added civil religion — the quasi-sacred rites, texts and martyrs nations cultivate around themselves.

Peter Berger predicted in 1967 that modernity would dissolve the sacred canopy; by 1999 he was editing a book on the desecularization of the world. Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart reconciled the facts with their existential security thesis: where life feels secure, religiosity thins; where it stays precarious, it does not — secular Europe beside a devout Global South. Grace Davie's "believing without belonging" caught the European pattern: faith persists while church attendance drains away.

Institutions change slowly and unevenly because each carries its history. Path dependence locks early choices in — welfare states built on Bismarck's payroll contributions still behave differently from those built on general revenue. Family life shows punctuated change instead: the second demographic transition brought delayed marriage, cohabitation and low fertility to country after country, without any decree ordering it.

When institutions lose legitimacy, Durkheim's anomie follows — norms blur and expectations fail. Distrust taxes every transaction; corruption fills the enforcement gaps where courts cannot reach. Development agencies learned this the hard way: importing formal rules into institutional voids produces paperwork without prediction, because the informal layer and the enforcement were never built.

Do not confuse organizations with institutions, or intended functions with actual ones — Robert Merton insisted on latent functions and dysfunctions. "The family is collapsing" conflates change with breakdown: forms churn while functions persist. Secularization is a pattern with mapped exceptions, not a universal law. And institutions are not automatically benign: segregation and caste are institutions too, durable for exactly the reasons that make law durable.
Enduring rules, norms and roles that structure social interaction.
The process by which habitual practice hardens into taken-for-granted rules.
A household of kin across generations, as against the conjugal or nuclear unit.
Troeltsch and Weber's sorting of religious bodies by their accommodation to society.
Bellah's term for the quasi-sacred rituals and symbols a nation wraps around itself.
The long-run weakening of religion's authority over society and belief.
The constraint of present choices by the accumulated weight of past ones.

examples.title: Worked example — Family, Religion and Institutions: The Skeleton of Society
examples.problem: Will a city's new participatory-budgeting assembly become a real institution or remain a one-off event?

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: institutions are durable rules plus norms, roles and enforcement that reduce uncertainty by making behavior predictable.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: check the layers — formal rules (who proposes, who votes, spending thresholds), norms (public justification, no backroom deals), roles (district delegates, secretariat) and enforcement (published, auditable records).

examples.result: if the cycle repeats and sanctions bite, it institutionalizes; if winners defect or records stay closed, it remains an event — an organization without an institution behind it.

keyTakeaways: Constitutional design: founders write the rules of the game knowing they will not always be the players.
Welfare policy: pension and childcare design reshapes family forms, often faster than culture does.
Development practice: programs now budget for institution-building, not just equipment and training.
Organizational management: onboarding, rituals and role clarity are institutionalization in miniature.
Family law: custody, adoption and inheritance rules track — and sometimes lead — changing family forms.

quiz.q: Douglass North's "rules of the game" refers to…
options: the organizations that staff a society
humanly devised constraints that structure interaction
quiz.explanation: Institutions — formal rules, informal norms and their enforcement — constrain interaction; organizations are the players, not the game.

quiz.q: Troeltsch and Weber's church-sect typology distinguishes…
options: an accommodated religious body from a voluntary breakaway
quiz.explanation: The church is embedded in and accommodated to society; the sect is a smaller, voluntary, higher-commitment withdrawal from it.

quiz.q: Norris and Inglehart's existential security thesis predicts religiosity declines where…
quiz.explanation: Where survival is effectively guaranteed, the demand for religious reassurance thins; precarious lives keep it high.

quiz.q: "Believing without belonging" (Davie) describes…
options: European faith persisting while church attendance drains
quiz.explanation: Davie's phrase caught the European mismatch between private belief and institutional participation.

intro:
In 1974 a Lisbon coup began what Samuel Huntington called democracy's third wave; within two decades electoral democracy reached Latin America, Eastern Europe, the Philippines, South Africa and beyond, and some declared history's ideological contests over. Since the mid-2000s the tide has run the other way. The lesson of both eras is the same: regime type is a spectrum, not a wall between full democracies and naked dictatorships. Classifying regimes — by their rules, their elections and their power — is comparative politics' foundational skill, and this lesson builds it.

**Why this matters.** Most of the world's people live between the poles. Whether aid flows, sanctions bite or treaties get honored depends heavily on how a regime is classified — and the newest form of breakdown arrives not in tanks but in amendments, appointments and licensing decisions that each look lawful alone.
objectives: Explain dahl's polyarchy: contestation and participation
Explain electoral systems and their consequences
Explain hybrid regimes and competitive authoritarianism
Explain waves of democratization
Explain backsliding by legal means
Explain measuring regimes

concepts.statement: Robert Dahl's 1971 study of polyarchy cut regimes along two axes: public contestation — can opposition organize, speak and win? — and inclusive participation — who may vote? Cross them and the spectrum fills: closed hegemonies (neither), competitive oligarchies (contestation without inclusion), inclusive hegemonies (voting without choice) and polyarchy (both). Joseph Schumpeter supplied the minimalist floor: democracy as the competitive struggle for the people's vote.

Electoral rules shape party systems. Maurice Duverger's law holds that single-member, winner-take-all districts push toward two parties, while proportional representation lets many survive. Consequences ripple outward: proportional systems elect more women and mirror vote shares but build coalition cabinets; majoritarian systems manufacture clear winners at the price of disproportionality and wasted votes. Arend Lijphart sorted the whole toolbox into majoritarian and consensus democracies; mixed systems like Germany's bolt the two together.

Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way named the gray zone competitive authoritarianism: real elections occur, but incumbents tilt the field with state media, captured courts, selective regulation and blurred state-party lines. It differs from full autocracy, because contestation survives, and from democracy, because the tilt is decisive. The toolkit is legalistic — laws amended, agencies staffed, referees replaced — which is why observers watching for coups often miss the change.

Huntington counted three long waves of democratization — the 1820s, 1945 and 1974 — each followed by a reverse wave. Seymour Martin Lipset's modernization finding, that wealth and democracy travel together, was sharpened by Adam Przeworski's team: above a certain income, no democracy in their dataset had yet fallen. Growth is no guarantee and poverty a heavy tax; the correlation is probabilistic, and oil-funded states are the standing exception.

Nancy Bermeo catalogued the new coups: executive aggrandizement — sitting leaders legally weakening checks, term by term — has displaced old-style tanks and stolen election nights. Courts are packed, term limits stretched, media bought, NGOs regulated. Polarization feeds the process, because supporters accept damage to institutions when the alternative feels worse. Erosion is gradual enough that each step alone looks defensible.

A measuring industry tracks it all. Freedom House scores political rights and civil liberties into Free, Partly Free and Not Free; the V-Dem project codes hundreds of indicators per country from expert judgments; Polity anchored a longer series from minus ten to plus ten. The indices disagree at the edges — and the disagreements are themselves data about what "democracy" is being defined to mean.

Beware the binary: most countries live between the poles, and hybrid regimes can hold for decades in either direction. Indices measure different things — an electoral democracy can score well on voting and poorly on rights — so read the components, not the headline. Modernization is correlation, not clockwork: growth neither guarantees democracy nor excuses its absence.
Dahl's term for a regime with high public contestation and broad inclusive participation.
The extent to which opposition can organize and realistically win power.
Single-member districts favor two-party systems; proportional rules favor many parties.
Regimes with real but tilted elections, per Levitsky and Way.
Bermeo's term for legal, incremental weakening of checks by sitting incumbents.
Huntington's name for the democratization surge that began in 1974.
The Varieties of Democracy project, coding hundreds of indicators per country per year.

examples.title: Worked example — Democracies, Autocracies and Everything in Between
examples.problem: A country holds regular elections in which an opposition wins a third of the legislature, yet state media give the incumbent near-total coverage, the election commission is staffed by loyalists and the constitutional court was expanded to outvote its critics — what is it?

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: Dahl's two dimensions, and Levitsky and Way's competitive authoritarianism — contestation exists but the playing field tilts.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: contestation is present (the opposition wins seats) and participation is broad, so it is not a closed hegemony; but media, referees and courts tilt the field decisively, so it is not a polyarchy.

examples.result: a hybrid — competitive authoritarian — regime: formal democracy's machinery, minus the level ground that makes the machinery mean anything.

keyTakeaways: Election observation: checklists now audit the playing field before polling day, not just the count on it.
Constitutional drafting: designers engineer term limits and appointment rules with backsliding in mind.
Democracy assistance: budget lines for independent media, parties and audit institutions, not just elections.
Investment risk: regime-type indices feed sovereign ratings and political-risk premiums.
News literacy: asking "which dimension is being degraded this month?" turns vague alarm into analysis.

quiz.q: Dahl's two dimensions of polyarchy are…
quiz.explanation: Who may take part, and whether the contest is real — crossing the two generates the whole spectrum of regimes.

quiz.q: Duverger's law links single-member districts to…
quiz.explanation: Winner-take-all districts punish third parties whose votes are wasted, squeezing the system toward two contenders.

quiz.q: Competitive authoritarianism, per Levitsky and Way, is defined by…
options: elections held on a tilted playing field
quiz.explanation: Contestation survives in form while state resources, media and referees are bent toward the incumbent.

quiz.q: Bermeo found today's most common form of democratic breakdown is…
quiz.explanation: Incumbents now erode checks through legal, incremental steps rather than seizing power in one stroke.

intro:
Why did a world war begin in 1914 over a Sarajevo assassination, and why did a colder, deadlier rivalry never fire its weapons? Why do nations that could fight instead trade? International Relations theory offers competing lenses rather than one answer. All share a premise: the international system has no referee — no world government stands above states to enforce rules or rescue the weak. From that single fact, three great traditions derive very different worlds. The legal machinery of treaties is covered in the International Law lessons; this one is about the explanations beneath them.

**Why this matters.** Sanctions, alliances, trade wars and arms races are all run by people using some theory of why states act. Knowing the three lenses lets you read a strategy document, an op-ed or a defense budget and identify which assumptions are doing the work — and what the author is not watching.
objectives: Explain anarchy and the security dilemma
Explain realism: power and balance
Explain liberalism: trade, institutions, democratic peace
Explain constructivism: ideas all the way down
Explain polarity and systemic stability
Explain theory as a lens, not a verdict

concepts.statement: Anarchy means the absence of hierarchy, not the presence of chaos. With no enforcer, states rely on self-help — their own capabilities — and worry about relative gains even in cooperation. John Herz and Robert Jervis formalized the security dilemma: measures one state takes to feel safer (a missile shield, a border garrison) read as menace to its neighbors, who respond in kind, and the spiral feeds itself. The prisoner's dilemma lesson in this subject models the trap precisely.

Realism descends from Thucydides through Hans Morgenthau, whose 1948 Politics Among Nations defined politics as interest defined as power. Kenneth Waltz's 1979 structural turn located causes in the system itself: states balance against power, and the number of great powers matters — bipolarity, he argued, is stabler than multipolarity, with fewer great-power pairs to misread. Offensive realists like John Mearsheimer expect states to maximize power, not merely match it; power-transition theorists locate war risk in the moment a challenger nears parity.

Liberalism finds cooperation rational even under anarchy. Immanuel Kant's 1795 sketch of perpetual peace paired republics, commerce and international law; Michael Doyle's democratic peace finding — established democracies almost never fight one another — remains the field's closest thing to an empirical law. Robert Keohane showed in After Hegemony that institutions endure because they lower transaction costs and stretch the shadow of the future: repeated games reward keeping promises. Interdependence, in Keohane and Joseph Nye's phrase, makes war expensive without making it impossible.

concepts.term: Constructivism: ideas all the way down
concepts.statement: Constructivism, carried into the mainstream by Alexander Wendt's 1992 article, starts from a slogan: "Anarchy is what states make of it." Threat is not fixed by structure but produced by identity — the United Kingdom's warheads alarm Washington less than North Korea's, as Wendt put it. Norms travel: Martha Finnemore and Kathryn Sikkink traced how ideas cascade from entrepreneurs to tipping points, delegitimizing the slave trade and stigmatizing chemical weapons long before enforcement caught up.

Polarity names the distribution of power. A unipolar moment followed the Cold War, as Charles Krauthammer called it; hegemonic stability theory held that a single leader underwrites open trade — Charles Kindleberger blamed the Great Depression partly on Britain's exit and America's hesitation. Multipolarity returns when challengers rise, and with it the classic question: do many poles dampen war through flexibility, or feed it through miscalculation?

concepts.term: Theory as a lens, not a verdict
concepts.statement: Theory earns its keep as a disciplined lens. One event, three readings: a rising power builds a blue-water navy. Realists see a power transition and hedge; liberals see interdependence raising the price of any adventure and negotiate; constructivists ask whether the rising state identifies as defender or reviser of the order before calling the ships a threat. Parsimony is bought with accuracy, so analysts triangulate.

Theories are lenses, not laws — none predicted 1989 cleanly, as Stephen Walt conceded. Do not read anarchy as lawlessness: norms and treaties order much of daily international life. The democratic peace has surviving disputes over cause, and young democracies are not covered by the finding. And paradigm loyalty ages badly — most working analysts mix lenses, then argue about the mixture.
The absence of a common superior above states; the system's ordering principle.
Defensive measures that threaten others and provoke countermeasures, spiraling without ill intent.
The realist expectation that states counter concentrations of power.
The finding that established democracies rarely fight one another.
Keohane and Nye's world of multiple channels and mutual sensitivities among states.
The view that identities and norms, not just material power, shape state behavior.
The number of great powers: unipolar, bipolar or multipolar.

examples.title: Worked example — Why Nations Fight and Trade: International Relations Theory
examples.problem: Two states impose tariffs on each other's semiconductors — what does each lens predict and recommend?

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: realism weighs relative gains and security spillovers; liberalism weighs joint losses and institutional remedies; constructivism weighs identity and domestic narratives about the other.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: the realist expects escalation where chip capacity feeds military power and advises hedging; the liberal expects both sides to lose and recommends negotiated, rules-anchored settlement that lengthens the shadow of the future; the constructivist asks who each public believes the other to be before predicting.

examples.result: the lenses identify different causal motors, so they monitor different indicators — capability shifts, trade shares and national narratives respectively.

keyTakeaways: Grand strategy: any defense white paper's assumptions reveal one of the three lenses at work.
Risk analysis for multinationals: sanctions, chokepoints and polarity scenarios priced into supply chains.
Institutional design: treaty bodies and dispute systems built to lengthen shadows of the future.
Foreign-policy journalism: diagnosing which lens an op-ed uses is half its critique.
Forecasting practice: structured lenses beat intuition about escalation and restraint.

quiz.q: In IR theory, anarchy means…
options: no authority above states to enforce rules
quiz.explanation: Anarchy names the structure — no referee — not a prediction of chaos; order can exist without a world government.

quiz.q: Wendt's "anarchy is what states make of it" means…
options: anarchy can be abolished by treaty
identities and ideas shape whether anarchy becomes threat
quiz.explanation: The same distribution of power reads as danger or friendship depending on the identities states hold — enemies are made, not found.

quiz.q: The democratic peace finding holds that…
options: established democracies rarely fight each other
quiz.explanation: Democracies fight non-democracies readily enough; the near-absence is in wars between pairs of established democracies.

quiz.q: Waltz argued bipolarity is stabler than multipolarity because…
options: there are fewer great-power pairs to misread
quiz.explanation: Two blocs make deterrence calculations clearer; many powers multiply the possible confrontations and the chances of miscalculation.

intro:
Cities concentrate people and then sort them. The sorting happens one lease, one loan and one moving truck at a time.
