quiz.explanation: Wineburg's finding: fact-checkers judge credibility by consulting the wider web first, not by studying the page itself.

intro:
Strikes, sit-ins, mass marches, hashtag storms: social movements are organized challenges mounted by people outside regular institutions, and they are how most large social change has actually arrived — suffrage, labor protections, civil rights, environmental law. Sociology's question is why scattered grievances so rarely become movements, and what machinery turns them into sustained campaigns that rewrite law and custom. (The free-rider logic of group action is its own lesson; this one is about organizations, not dilemmas.)

**Why this matters.** Grievance is everywhere; movements are rare. Understanding the machinery — resources, opportunities, frames and repertoires — separates hero narratives from actual causation, and tells you which of today's campaigns have the parts that historically produced change.
objectives: Explain resource mobilization
Explain political opportunity structure
Explain diagnostic, prognostic, motivational framing
Explain repertoires of contention
Explain cycles of protest
Explain movements in the social media era

concepts.statement: The modern field begins with a reversal. Classical theory assumed grievances and then collective anger; John McCarthy and Mayer Zald's 1977 resource mobilization argument noted that grievances are a constant, so they cannot explain anything: what varies is organization — money, staff, offices, mailing lists, professional cadres, and the social infrastructure from which supporters can actually be mobilized. Aldon Morris's study of the civil rights movement made the point concrete: Black churches supplied the movement's communication network, meeting places, funds and leadership, which is why Montgomery happened where it did.

Structure supplies the timing. Political opportunity structure — developed by Sidney Tarrow and Doug McAdam — holds that movements surge when the environment opens: divided elites, new allies, shifting electoral coalitions, relaxed repression. McAdam's Political Process and the Development of Black Insurgency (1982) traced the sit-in wave of 1960 to the New Deal's expansion of Black political leverage, the migration that concentrated voters in northern cities, and Brown v. Board's signal that the courts might move. The same grievance under a closed structure produces quiescence.

Movements also do interpretive work. Robert Benford and David Snow's framing analysis splits it into tasks: diagnostic framing names the problem and assigns blame; prognostic framing proposes the remedy; motivational framing supplies the reason to act now despite risk. The 1960s civil rights frame — full citizenship, dignity, American values honored at last — became a master frame that later movements recycled for women's rights, disability rights and indigenous claims. A movement without a coherent frame is a crowd with grievances.

What movements actually do is drawn from a repertoire of contention — Charles Tilly's term for the historically specific toolkit of learned performances: the charivari and grain seizure of old Europe, the strike, the public meeting, the demonstration, the petition of the national era. Repertoires change slowly and are inherited more than invented; people protest the way their grandparents did, until a period of innovation — the sit-in, the freedom ride — adds tools that spread rapidly. Today's toolkit adds the boycott, the occupation and the hashtag campaign.

Movements arrive in waves. Tarrow's protest cycles describe the pattern: early victories recruit moderates and bystanders, radicalization follows as demands escalate, countermobilization organizes against, and the cycle closes in exhaustion, repression or institutionalization — movement organizations becoming lobbying groups, with Frances Piven and Richard Cloward's warning that organization domesticates disruption just as disruption without organization cannot sustain gains. Outcomes are slow: movement-shaped policy usually lands a decade or more after the streets empty.

concepts.term: Movements in the social media era
concepts.statement: The social media era lowered coordination costs and changed the mix. Tahrir Square, #MeToo and Black Lives Matter mobilized at speeds the older machinery could not match; Zeynep Tufekci's Twitter and Tear Gas (2017) supplies the caveat — digital tools let movements scale before building durable organization, so they are easier to start and harder to finish, and the same cheap tools serve surveillance and countermovements equally well. Slacktivism is the wrong lesson; capacity-without-organization is the right one.

Grievance does not equal movement — most grievances never mobilize. Do not romanticize either disruption or organization: each fails differently, per Piven and Cloward. Social media cut costs for all sides, including movements you may oppose. The machinery is morally neutral — nativist and supremacist campaigns have used it as effectively as civil rights. And attribution is genuinely hard: outcomes take decades, many actors share credit, and counterfactual histories cannot be run.
McCarthy and Zald's thesis that organization and resources, not grievances, decide movement success.
The openings — divided elites, new allies, relaxed repression — that permit movements to surge.
A dominant interpretive template, like the civil rights frame, later adapted by other movements.
Tilly's inherited toolkit of protest performances available in a given era.
The wave pattern of rising mobilization, radicalization, countermobilization and closure.
Movement organizations converting into interest groups that lobby rather than disrupt.
Campaigning built on platform coordination, with Tufekci's scale-without-organization caveat.

examples.title: Worked example — Social Movements: How Change Happens
examples.problem: Read the Montgomery bus boycott (1955-56) through the four-part framework rather than the hero narrative.

steps.label: Resources
steps.text: the Women's Political Council had mimeographed leaflets ready within hours; churches, car pools and northern fundraising supplied the infrastructure McCarthy and Zald would later theorize.

steps.label: Political opportunity
steps.text: Brown v. Board (1954) had signaled judicial openness; rising Black electoral weight in northern cities gave national politicians a reason to care.

steps.label: Framing
steps.text: riders were cast as dignified citizens claiming constitutional rights, not lawbreakers — diagnostic, prognostic and motivational work fused in King's sermons.

steps.label: Repertoire
steps.text: the boycott, an old labor weapon, adapted to city buses; disciplined nonviolence turned provocation into sympathetic coverage.

steps.label: Outcome and beyond
steps.text: Browder v. Gayle (1956) ended bus segregation, and the boycott's infrastructure — organizations, trained cadres, networks — seeded the campaigns of the next decade.

keyTakeaways: Advocacy and NGO strategy, where resource mobilization is the business model.
Labor organizing, from recognition strikes to gig-economy campaigns.
Movement-countermovement dynamics in abortion and gun politics — same mechanics, opposite aims.
Digital campaign design that builds organization, not just audience.
Historical analysis of policy change, from suffrage to environmental regulation.

quiz.q: McCarthy and Zald's core claim is that…
options: grievances cause movements when strong enough
grievances are constant; resources and organization decide mobilization
quiz.explanation: Since grievance is everywhere, the variable that explains movements is the organization that can act on it.

quiz.q: A political opportunity structure opens when, for example…
options: elites split and new allies become available
quiz.explanation: Openings like divided elites or shifting coalitions lower the cost of mobilizing — McAdam's preconditions for 1960.

quiz.q: Benford and Snow's framing tasks are…
quiz.explanation: Name the problem and blame, propose the remedy, and supply the reason to act now.

quiz.q: Tufekci's warning about digital movements is that they…
options: scale fast without building durable organization
quiz.explanation: Cheap tools compress mobilization without the organizational construction slow movements once required — easier to start, harder to finish.

intro:
People differ, and they differ consistently: the friend who was organized at twelve is organized at fifty. Personality psychology is the study of these stable patterns — how to describe them, measure them, and know what they do. After a century of competing systems, the field converged on a finding so replicated it now anchors the discipline: five broad dimensions capture most of the stable variation in human personality. (Trait psychology is a different program from judgment biases and attitude change — this is who people are, not how they err.)

**Why this matters.** The Big Five predicts outcomes at a distance no rival framework approaches: longevity, divorce, job performance, mental-health risk — modestly but relentlessly, across decades and cultures. It is also the yardstick that exposes popular typologies: when a test disagrees with itself across five weeks, it is not measuring a trait.
objectives: Explain the lexical hypothesis and the dictionary sweep
Explain oCEAN: five dimensions, not types
Explain conscientiousness and openness as outcome predictors
Explain rank-order stability rises with age
Explain the maturity principle
Explain traits predict modestly but consistently
Explain dimensional scores versus typologies

concepts.term: The lexical hypothesis and the dictionary sweep
concepts.statement: The route ran through the dictionary. The lexical hypothesis holds that anything important about human difference gets named, so in 1936 Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert swept English dictionaries for trait terms and emerged with about 4,500. Raymond Cattell factor-analyzed the list toward sixteen dimensions; later replications — Fiske, Tupes and Christal, Warren Norman — kept collapsing toward five. Paul Costa and Robert McCrae's 1985 NEO-PI-R gave the five names, items and a research industry. Factor analysis of different languages and samples kept landing on the same five: a convergence rare in psychology.

Two dimensions carry much of the predictive load. Conscientiousness — orderliness, self-discipline, dutifulness, deliberation — is the strongest non-cognitive predictor of school grades, job performance in most occupations, and even longevity: high scorers live years longer, partly through healthier behavior. Openness to experience — curiosity about ideas and art, appetite for novelty — predicts training success and creative achievement. The two sit loosely at odds in populations: fast-and-loose versus checked-and-thorough, each suited to different environments.

concepts.term: Conscientiousness and openness as outcome predictors
concepts.statement: Extraversion is reward sensitivity: sociability, assertiveness, positive emotion — the dopamine-flavored dimension. Agreeableness is cooperation style: trust, compassion, modesty — low scorers compete, high scorers harmonize, and both strategies have niches. Neuroticism is threat sensitivity: the tendency toward anxiety, irritability and self-consciousness under stress, the personality variable closest to the anxiety-and-depression lesson's vulnerability factor. High neuroticism roughly doubles the risk of common mental disorders; it is the trait clinicians meet first.

Measurement is deliberately dull: many statements, rating scales, aggregation. Single items are noisy; thirty cancel the noise. The validity evidence is unusually rich — self-reports agree with friends' and spouses' ratings at correlations near .5, and spouse ratings predict some outcomes better than self-reports do. The structure replicates in dozens of languages, though in small-scale subsistence societies the factors fray, a live debate about how universal the five are versus products of literate, complex societies.

Traits are both stable and on the move. Rank-order stability — does your position among your peers hold? — rises from correlations around .3 in childhood to above .7 by the fifties. Mean levels drift systematically: on average people gain conscientiousness and agreeableness and shed neuroticism from adolescence through middle age, the maturity principle. Personality is not fixed at thirty, but it becomes increasingly set — and the competing claims that it is destiny fail in both directions.

What traits predict, they predict modestly: correlations of .1 to .3 with most outcomes, small per decision but compounding over hundreds of them. The person-situation debate — Walter Mischel's 1968 complaint that behavior correlates with traits at barely .30 — dissolved through aggregation and through if-then signatures: people are consistently shy with strangers and bold with friends. Beyond the five, the HEXACO model adds honesty-humility, and the dark triad — narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy — maps onto low agreeableness with attitude. What the Big Five does not do is explain the traits: description is not cause.

The standard errors: treating typologies as science (the Myers-Briggs sorts continuous dimensions into either-or boxes, and half of retest-takers flip at least one letter within weeks); reading traits as destiny (they are base rates); using personality as an excuse (low conscientiousness describes a problem, it does not license it); judging someone's traits from their worst visible day (states masquerade as traits); and assuming one true self hides under the data. Traits describe the center of a distribution that variance still lives in.
The premise that important human differences get encoded in language — hence the dictionary sweep.
The replicated five-dimension structure of stable personality variation.
How well your position among peers holds over time; it rises with age.
The average drift toward more conscientiousness and agreeableness, less neuroticism, across adulthood.
Mischel's .30 ceiling for trait-behavior correlations, later dissolved by aggregation.
The six-factor alternative adding honesty-humility to the standard five.
Narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy — low-agreeableness variants with attitude.

examples.title: Worked example — The Big Five: A Field Guide to Human Personality
examples.problem: Two job candidates bring identical skills, one high in conscientiousness with moderate extraversion, the other low C and high E — what does the model actually forecast?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: conscientiousness is the strongest trait predictor of long-horizon performance; extraversion predicts interview warmth more than output reliability.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: expect steadier delivery and fewer missed deadlines from the high-C candidate — a correlation of roughly .2 to .3 with performance, modest but real — while the high-E candidate interviews warmer and may shine where sociability is the job itself.

examples.result: use traits as base rates, not verdicts — the model narrows the prior, and the probation period collects the evidence a questionnaire never will.

keyTakeaways: Personnel selection pairs conscientiousness and integrity testing with structured interviews — measurement over gut feel.
Clinical practice uses the five-factor model to describe personality problems dimensionally, replacing checklists with extremity.
Couple research finds neuroticism the strongest divorce predictor — and assortative mating on the traits everywhere.
Self-development works by situation selection: choosing environments that fit traits beats remolding the traits.
Longitudinal research adjusts for personality when estimating what programs and treatments actually change.

Where next — Pairs with the cognitive-biases and dissonance lessons — judgment and attitude change, the field's other programs. Follow with the intelligence lesson for cognitive individual differences, and the research-methods toolkit for reliability and validity. Next: personality disorders, HEXACO, and behavioral genetics.

quiz.q: The lexical hypothesis motivated which research move?
quiz.explanation: If important differences get named, the trait vocabulary is sitting in the dictionary — Allport and Odbert went and collected it.

quiz.q: Which trait is the strongest personality predictor of longevity and job performance?
quiz.explanation: Discipline and dutifulness compound: healthier behavior, fewer missed deadlines, years of life.

quiz.q: The maturity principle describes how people, on average,
options: gain conscientiousness and agreeableness through adulthood
revert to adolescent traits in old age
quiz.explanation: Mean levels drift — calmer, more dependable, more caring — even while rank order stays put.

quiz.q: The core measurement flaw in type-based tests like the MBTI is:
quiz.explanation: Cutting a continuous distribution at the midpoint makes near-half of people flip types on retake — the signal is in the score, not the box.

intro:
An IQ score is the most reliable and best-validated number psychology has ever produced — and the most misused. It began as a schoolteacher's tool for finding children who needed help, became a legal instrument of exclusion, and settled into its modern role: a strong but partial statistical predictor of school and work outcomes. Understanding what the tests measure, and what they cannot, is prerequisite to using them or defending against their use.

**Why this matters.** Scores predict academic achievement at correlations near .5 — better than any other single psychological measure — and general mental ability is among the best single predictors of training success. The same numbers justified sterilization laws. An instrument this powerful and this compromised must be understood, not waved away.
objectives: Explain g and the positive manifold
Explain deviation IQ: scores as positions, not quantities
Explain reliability before validity
Explain the Flynn effect
Explain heritability is not immutability
Explain predictive bias versus score gaps
Explain fluid and crystallized abilities

concepts.statement: In 1904 Charles Spearman noticed that children's grades in dissimilar subjects all correlated positively — the positive manifold. Every cognitive test since shows it: people who do well at vocabulary tend, on average, to do well at matrices and memory span. Spearman attributed the shared variance to g, general intelligence, and tests differ mostly in how heavily they load on it — abstract reasoning most, rote memory least. Modern models split g into fluid ability, for novel problems, and crystallized, for accumulated knowledge, then fan into a dozen broad abilities.

concepts.term: Deviation IQ: scores as positions, not quantities
concepts.statement: A score is manufactured precision. Test makers norm items on representative thousands, so a raw score becomes a percentile against a population. And since the original mental-age arithmetic broke in adulthood, the Wechsler scales fixed deviation IQ: mean 100, standard deviation 15 — 68 percent of people between 85 and 115. Reliability runs above .9 (retake and expect your score within a few points) and validity against later achievement nears .5 — psychometric gold by any measurement standard, which is why armies, schools and clinics still buy it.

In the 1980s James Flynn found that raw scores had risen roughly three points per decade across the twentieth century in every country with records — the Flynn effect, large enough that tests must be renormed to keep the mean at 100. Explanations still compete: nutrition, schooling, increasingly cognitively demanding environments, test familiarity. Norway's conscript data sharpened the puzzle — brothers raised together show the same generational gains as unrelated men, pointing to environment rather than changing gene pools. In several Nordic countries the rise has now quietly reversed.

Within affluent populations, IQ differences run perhaps 50 percent heritable in childhood, rising toward 70 percent by adulthood — the counterintuitive Wilson effect, as people increasingly select environments that fit their inclinations. Two cautions govern everything. Heritability describes a population's variance, not an individual's fate. And heritable does not mean immutable: height is 90 percent heritable and still rose with nutrition. The Scarr-Rowe hypothesis adds that heritability shrinks under deprivation — poverty suppresses expression — so the same fraction means different things in different societies.

The history is the dark half. Alfred Binet built the first test explicitly to identify schoolchildren needing support, and warned against fixed readings of it. Henry Goddard's Ellis Island classifications mislabeled immigrants by language and culture; Lewis Terman's genetic confidence and the 1917 Army tests fed the eugenics movement, sterilization statutes and the 1924 immigration quotas. The technical question — do the tests underpredict minority performance? — has a mostly reassuring answer: predictive bias by group is small in modern instruments. Score gaps between groups are real, have narrowed, and their causes remain contested terrain.

Alternative structures sell better than they test. Howard Gardner's multiple intelligences are influential in education but weakly supported psychometrically — the abilities correlate, which is the very phenomenon g names. Sternberg's triarchic theory fares little better formally; emotional intelligence shows some incremental validity in its ability-based form. The honest summary: beyond g, specific aptitudes add real predictive value for specific outcomes — spatial ability for engineering, for instance — but no rival framework has displaced the general factor in a century of trying.
$$\mathrm{IQ} = 100 + 15z, \qquad z = \frac{\mathrm{raw} - \mu_{\mathrm{peers}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{peers}}}$$
concepts.detail: Your score is your raw performance expressed in standard deviations from the peer mean, rescaled so 100 is average and 15 is one step.

concepts.statement: The standing confusions: IQ as a substance you have an amount of (it is a relative position, and the Flynn effect proves positions move); heritability as immutability (see: height); the single score as complete description (narrow abilities matter for narrow outcomes); colloquial bias conflated with the technical test of underprediction; and ranking groups as if scores settled causes. The ratio-IQ hangover — an adult with the mind of a twelve-year-old — is a category error, not a measurement.
The shared variance behind the positive correlations among all cognitive tests.
The finding that all mental tests correlate — the phenomenon g explains.
Score as standard deviations from the age-peer mean: mean 100, standard deviation 15.
The roughly three-point-per-decade rise in raw scores across the twentieth century.
The fraction of population variance attributable to genetic difference — not individual fate.
The heritability of IQ rising from childhood into adulthood.
The technical question of whether tests underpredict outcomes for a group.

examples.title: Worked example — Intelligence and IQ: What the Tests Actually Measure
examples.problem: A man scores 130 on a Wechsler test — what is that, concretely, and what is it not?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: deviation IQ rescales standard deviations — 130 is exactly z = +2.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: the normal distribution puts z = +2 at about the 98th percentile — roughly one in fifty of his age peers scores higher. The old mental-age reading, a mind like a nineteen-year-old's, is meaningless because raw ability stops tracking age after the teens — which is precisely why the ratio formula was abandoned.

examples.result: 130 is a well-measured position in a distribution, predictive of training success — not a quantity of brain, a fixed ceiling, or a verdict on worth.

keyTakeaways: Psychoeducational assessment uses cognitive batteries to diagnose learning disabilities and design support.
Military placement runs on the ASVAB — the direct descendant of the 1917 Army tests.
Serial cognitive testing tracks dementia, where the change matters more than the level.
Personnel meta-analyses rank general mental ability among the best single predictors of training performance.
Forensic cases still turn on IQ thresholds, execution eligibility included — numerology with stakes.

Where next — Pairs with the research-methods toolkit — correlation, reliability, validity, norms — and the education lesson for what schools do with scores. The Big Five lesson covers the non-cognitive side of individual differences. Next: behavioral genetics, expertise and deliberate practice, and the history of eugenics.

quiz.q: The positive manifold refers to:
quiz.explanation: Vocabulary, matrices, memory span — everything correlates. g is the name for the shared variance.

quiz.q: A deviation IQ of 115 means:
options: one standard deviation above the age mean
quiz.explanation: The Wechsler rescaling makes 15 points one standard deviation — 115 is the 84th percentile.

quiz.q: The Flynn effect is:
options: raw score gains of about three points per decade
quiz.explanation: Every country with records gained points across the twentieth century — the moving target tests must renorm against.

quiz.q: Heritability is not immutability is best illustrated by:
options: height: 90 percent heritable, yet it rose with nutrition
the reversal of the Flynn effect
quiz.explanation: A trait can be highly heritable in a population and still shift when the environment shifts — the two facts coexist.

intro:
Ask a room of sociologists who you know, and you have asked a serious question. Social life has a shape — not just the people, but the pattern of ties between them — and that pattern quietly decides what information reaches you, what norms hold you, and what opportunities you ever hear about. Network analysis shifted sociology from attributes, like your class and your attitude, to structure, like your position — and the results have been among the field's most portable findings. (The business lesson on network effects explains markets tipping to winner-take-all — a different phenomenon entirely.)

**Why this matters.** Granovetter's weak-tie finding — that acquaintances, not close friends, carry most job leads — has been confirmed across decades and countries. Position in a network predicts outcomes individual traits cannot: the same person, differently connected, meets a different life.
objectives: Explain strong ties, weak ties and redundancy
Explain the small-world property
Explain bonding versus bridging social capital
Explain homophily: selection versus influence
Explain diffusion thresholds and S-curves
Explain complex contagion
Explain network poverty

concepts.term: Strong ties, weak ties and redundancy
concepts.statement: Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper began with job-changers in Newton, Massachusetts. The counterintuitive result: of those who found work through contacts, the majority heard it from people they saw rarely — weak ties. The logic is structural. Close friends know each other's worlds; their information is redundant. An acquaintance bridges to a different cluster and returns novel news. Strong ties give you devotion; weak ties give you reach — and the strategic resource is the bridge, not the bond.

Stanley Milgram's 1967 chain-letter experiment asked Nebraskans to route a letter to a Boston stockbroker through acquaintances; completed chains averaged about six hands (though fewer than a quarter completed — a caveat often lost in the retelling). Duncan Watts and Steven Strogatz later showed why: a few long-range shortcuts stitched into clustered networks collapse the world's distances. Facebook's planetary graph now measures average separation at about 3.5 steps. The mathematics of graphs belongs to the math library; sociology's version asks what actually flows across those steps.

Robert Putnam's Bowling Alone (2000) popularized social capital — the value embedded in relationships — and the crucial split. Bonding capital ties similar people tightly: ethnic associations, churches, old friends — solidarity, favors, getting by. Bridging capital spans difference: civic leagues, professional ties — information, opportunity, getting ahead. Communities rich in one can starve in the other, and the poor are disproportionately network-poor, isolated in clusters that connect to little — a structural amplifier of inequality the stratification lesson knows well.

Similarity clusters people — birds of a feather — a tendency Paul Lazarsfeld and Robert Merton named homophily. It has two faces that are brutally hard to separate: do your friends shape you, or did you choose them? Health behaviors appear to spread through networks — Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler reported obesity and happiness cascades — but later methodological work showed that unmeasured similarity can mimic contagion. Network methods find real effects; smoking-cessation interventions through networks can work. They also demand humility about the selection-influence problem.

Everett Rogers' Diffusion of Innovations charted how new things move through a population — innovators, early adopters, majority, laggards — along an S-curve, slow while a behavior looks strange and fast once it looks normal. Granovetter's threshold models explain the shape: each person adopts when enough contacts already have. And Damon Centola's experiments found a twist — simple information spreads best through long, thin networks, but behaviors that need reinforcement, like a new diet or a norm, spread best through clustered ones: complex contagion. Matching the network to the thing spreading is public health's daily bread.

The mistakes: networking as schmoozing (weak ties need maintenance, not charisma — the value is the bridge itself); assuming contacts are wealth (a phone full of numbers is not a network of edges); treating six degrees as a promise (paths exist; using them is costly and often inappropriate); blaming the internet alone for echo chambers (homophily predates modems by millennia); and over-reading contagion studies whose methods cannot separate influence from similarity.
An infrequent, low-intimacy relationship valued for the novel information it bridges.
High local clustering combined with short global paths, via a few shortcuts.
Dense ties within a group — solidarity and support, getting by.
Ties across groups — novelty and opportunity, getting ahead.
The clustering of similar people — the confounder of network influence.
Behaviors needing multiple reinforcing contacts, spreading through clustered ties.
Isolation in clusters with few outward bridges — the structural face of disadvantage.

examples.title: Worked example — Social Networks: The Hidden Structure of Social Life
examples.problem: Two unemployed accountants hunt for work — one asks five close friends, the other activates twenty acquaintances. What does network theory predict?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: close friends cluster together and share information; acquaintances bridge clusters, and bridges are where novel leads live.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: the five friends mostly work in the same firms and hear the same postings; the twenty weak ties span perhaps a dozen organizations and industries. Granovetter's result forecasts most interviews arriving through the fringe of the second network — including contacts the accountant barely remembers.

examples.result: job search is network design before it is resume polish — and the time to build weak ties is long before the layoff notice.

keyTakeaways: Employee-referral programs are Granovetter institutionalized — referred candidates are cheaper to source and stay longer.
Network-based health interventions in Honduran villages spread adoption faster by seeding well-connected community members.
Microfinance groups — Grameen's circles — use existing ties as social collateral for loans.
Libraries, parks and other social infrastructure deliberately manufacture bridging ties across class lines.
Platform feeds are homophily engines with dials — a design choice with civic consequences.

Where next — Pairs with the collective-action lesson — threshold logic is their shared engine — and the stratification lesson for how network poverty reproduces advantage. The business lesson's network effects explain markets, not people. Next: social media network analysis, organizational networks, and Klinenberg's social infrastructure.

quiz.q: Granovetter's job-finders mostly heard about their jobs from:
quiz.explanation: Close contacts share one's information pool; the acquaintance's bridge to another cluster is what carries news.

quiz.q: Bridging social capital differs from bonding because bridging ties:
options: connect across groups and deliver novel information
quiz.explanation: Bonding gets you by; bridging gets you ahead — the external edge is the information edge.

quiz.q: The Christakis-Fowler contagion findings are best read today as:
options: settled proof that networks cause obesity
methodologically contested — homophily can mimic contagion
proof that networks do not matter
quiz.explanation: Similar friends growing similar without influence produces the same signature — identification remains the field's open problem.

quiz.q: Complex contagion means a behavior spreads best when:
options: multiple contacts reinforce it, favoring clustered networks
quiz.explanation: Reinforced behaviors need social proof from several directions — Centola's clustered networks beat thin ones.

intro:
What counts as a crime is a social decision: alcohol was a felony during Prohibition, and much of what your grandparents' society punished is legal now. Deviance — rule-breaking against a group's norms — is not a fixed category of acts but a moving boundary, and sociology's founding insight was to study the boundary, the rule-makers and the reactions rather than only the rule-breakers. (How courts process cases is the law library's territory; this is the social machinery around them.)

**Why this matters.** The United States ran history's largest incarceration experiment: the imprisonment rate roughly quintupled after 1970, making it the world's leading jailer — while about two-thirds of released prisoners are rearrested within three years. Whether punishment reduces crime, and what does instead, is a trillion-dollar question with actual evidence, some of it surprising.
objectives: Explain durkheim: deviance is normal and functional
Explain merton's strain and five adaptations
Explain labeling and secondary deviance
Explain social disorganization and collective efficacy
Explain certainty beats severity
Explain the mass incarceration experiment
Explain desistance and what reduces reoffending

concepts.term: Durkheim: deviance is normal and functional
concepts.statement: Émile Durkheim argued the scandalous: crime is normal — every known society has it, and a sudden disappearance would signal something broken, not perfected. It is even functional: punishing it performs the norms publicly, a community rallied around a verdict is watching its rules draw themselves, and yesterday's deviance is often tomorrow's law — labor organizing, civil disobedience. The Durkheim lesson owns the theory of social facts; the point here is its application, that moral outrage around crime is itself a social fact with consequences.

Robert Merton's 1938 strain theory located crime in a mismatch: the culture commands success goals for everyone, while the structure blocks legitimate means for some. He catalogued five adaptations — conformity; innovation, accepting goals while rejecting means, the thief; ritualism, abandoning goals while keeping means; retreatism, rejecting both; rebellion, replacing both. Crime concentrates where the goal is loudest and the ladder is shortest — a structural reading that still organizes what is known about neighborhoods and opportunity.

Howard Becker's Outsiders (1963) moved deviance from the act to the audience: nothing is inherently deviant until someone with the power to define says so — moral entrepreneurs like temperance crusaders manufacture rules. Labeling does real work after the fact. The kid processed through juvenile court now carries a record, a stigma and a changed self-concept, sliding from primary deviance, the act, into secondary deviance, the career. The policy implication — that formal processing can make young offenders worse, and diversion can beat court — has support in randomized evaluations.

The Chicago School mapped delinquency by neighborhood and found rates stayed high in the same districts across generations of entirely different residents. Shaw and McKay's explanation was social disorganization: poverty, turnover and heterogeneity weaken the informal social control — eyes on the street, neighbors who intervene — that keeps order without police. Robert Sampson's modern update, collective efficacy, explains why some poor neighborhoods are safe and some comfortable ones are not: shared trust plus willingness to intervene for the common good. The broken-windows era translated this into order-maintenance policing, with mixed evidence and real costs.

Deterrence's own evidence is awkward for the tough-on-crime instinct. Certainty of punishment deters; severity barely does — after Cesare Beccaria's eighteenth-century hunch was finally tested, long sentences proved weak brakes while the probability of being caught moves behavior. Clearance rates tell the story: with roughly one in eight burglaries solved, decade-long sentences are discounted to near-irrelevance. What reduces recidivism looks boring — cognitive-behavioral programs with 20-odd percent reductions, prison education, employment bridges, and age itself: most offenders simply desist by their forties.

The American experiment: imprisonment rose roughly fivefold from the early 1970s to the 2000s — two million people — driven by the drug war, mandatory minimums and parole restriction, with Black Americans imprisoned at roughly five times the white rate. It bought some crime reduction in the 1990s, though how much is contested — the decline had many claimants, lead exposure among them — and the marginal returns turned negative as more low-risk offenders were cycled through. Since 2009 the rate has fallen by roughly a quarter, and the reform debate — sentencing changes, collateral consequences, focused deterrence — is now mainstream rather than fringe.

The recurring errors: reasoning from rare, horrifying cases to policy (moral panic's signature); equating severity with deterrence (certainty does the work); explaining crime entirely by individual character while neighborhoods keep their rates across generations of residents; crediting any single policy with the 1990s crime drop (its causes are contested and plural); and the symmetrical fatalisms — that nothing works, and that prisons are hotels. Both survive contact with the evidence badly.
Behavior that violates a group's norms — a property of the boundary, not the act.
Merton's mismatch between culturally commanded goals and structurally available means.
Becker's insight that audiences with power define deviance — and definitions shape careers.
Rule-breaking organized around a stigmatized identity, downstream of the label.
Sampson's trust plus willingness to intervene — the variable that orders neighborhoods.
Discouragement by threat; effectiveness runs through certainty far more than severity.
The ordinary aging-out of crime that most offenders eventually do.

examples.title: Worked example — Deviance and Crime: The Sociology of Rule-Breaking
examples.problem: A burglar in a neighborhood with a 12 percent clearance rate faces five-year mandatory sentences — will severity deter him, and what would?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: expected punishment is probability times severity, and evidence says certainty carries the deterrent weight.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: five years discounted by 0.12 is about seven months of expected time — and burglars, like everyone, respond to the odds, not the abstract maximum. Doubling clearance toward 25 percent doubles expected punishment without touching the statute book; collective efficacy and hot-spots patrols are how that happens without a police state.

examples.result: the deterrent lever is investigation and visibility — and the neighborhood with shared trust is the one where a burglar is seen at all.

keyTakeaways: Hot-spots policing concentrates patrol where a small fraction of addresses produces most calls.
Focused-deterrence programs, like Boston's Operation Ceasefire, pair offers of help with credible group-level sanctions.
Restorative-justice conferences modestly cut reoffending and raise victim satisfaction.
Risk-need-responsivity rules match supervision intensity and programming to assessed risk.
Ban-the-box and record-sealing laws attack the collateral consequences that block desistance.

Where next — Pairs with the Durkheim lesson for the underlying theory and the law-and-governance library for courts and evidence rules. Follow the collective-action lesson for threshold logic in riots and protest waves. Next: procedural justice and legitimacy, drug policy history, and comparative penology — Norway's rehabilitative model.

quiz.q: Merton's 'innovation' adaptation means:
options: accepting success goals while using illegitimate means
going through the motions without believing
quiz.explanation: The innovator wants the culturally mandated success and, blocked from legitimate means, takes the shortcut.

quiz.q: Labeling theory's core claim is that deviance lies in:
options: the reaction of audiences with power to define
quiz.explanation: Becker: nothing is deviant until rule-makers with the power to define treat it so — and the label then reshapes the person.

quiz.q: The best-supported deterrent variable is:
quiz.explanation: Beccaria's hunch, confirmed: the odds of being caught move behavior; the length of the sentence barely does.

quiz.q: Collective efficacy predicts neighborhood safety because it captures:
options: informal social control — trust plus willingness to intervene
quiz.explanation: It is the modern refinement of Shaw and McKay: some poor districts are safe because neighbors act, and some rich ones are not.

intro:
Two numbers — the births and the deaths per thousand people — quietly explain most of modern population history. Every nation that industrializes has passed, or is passing, through the same sequence: high and balanced, death falling, birth following, and a new equilibrium that is no longer growing. The demographic transition is demography's central regularity, and the arithmetic behind it — rates, structures, momentum — is what pension systems, school planners and climate models run on. (Where people live and why is the companion geography lesson's subject; this one is the rates.)

**Why this matters.** The world is mid-transition: population growth peaked at about 2.1 percent per year in 1968 and has slowed to under 1 percent, while two-thirds of humanity now lives in countries below replacement fertility. The twenty-first century's population story is aging and shrinking, not explosion — and almost every institution is unprepared.
objectives: Explain crude rates and natural increase
Explain four stages of transition
Explain replacement fertility (2.1)
Explain age pyramids as autobiographies
Explain dependency ratio and the dividend
Explain population momentum
Explain shrinking societies

concepts.statement: The vital arithmetic: the crude birth rate and crude death rate are annual births and deaths per thousand population, and their difference is the rate of natural increase — 30 per thousand equals 3 percent growth, a doubling time of roughly 23 years by the 70-over-growth rule. Migration adds or subtracts on top; its push-and-pull mechanics are the migration lesson's. Fertility is counted per woman as the total fertility rate, with 2.1 as replacement — the extra tenth covers those who die before reproducing.

The model's stages read like compressed history. Stage one — both rates high and roughly equal — was all of humanity until about 1750, growth near zero. Stage two: death falls first, through sanitation, food security and vaccination, while births stay high — populations explode, as Europe did in the nineteenth century and much of sub-Saharan Africa late in the twentieth. Stage three: births follow downward as children survive, cities grow, women educate and contraception spreads. Stage four: both low, growth near zero — most industrial countries today. A disputed fifth stage has fertility sinking below replacement into decline; the sequence is descriptive, its timing has varied enormously, and no country reversed it by decree.

An age pyramid — males one side, females the other, by five-year cohorts — is a population's autobiography. A wide base means high fertility and built-in growth; a bulge records a baby boom, or its echo; a notch records famine, war or policy. Japan's near-rectangle, top-heavy and narrowing, is stage five in silhouette. Median age summarizes the shape: Niger about sixteen, Japan near fifty — the same planet.

The dependency ratio counts the young and old per hundred working-age adults, tracking the transition like a needle. Stage-two societies carry crushing child dependency; as fertility falls, the bulge reaches working age while child numbers shrink — the demographic dividend, a generation-long window when dependents are few and workers abundant. East Asia's miracle was partly this arithmetic — analysts credit a third or so of its growth to the dividend — but only where jobs, schooling and savings absorbed the bulge. Latin America fumbled part of its window: a dividend is a chance, not a guarantee.

The strangest trap: populations with young age structures keep growing for decades after fertility hits replacement, because the pyramid's base is so wide that even replacement-level mothers outnumber their own mothers. Momentum carried the world from six billion in 1999 toward eight in 2022 even as global fertility fell near 2.3. UN projections now put the peak near 10.3 billion in the 2080s — the momentum spending itself out.

The far side is here first in East Asia and Europe. Fertility below 2.1 means every generation smaller than its parent — South Korea's 0.7 roughly halves each one — and pay-as-you-go pensions, built on growing cohorts, meet the mathematics: Japan's workers per pensioner fell from ten in the 1950s toward two. Responses exist, all hard: later retirement, immigration (contested everywhere), and pro-natal spending, which nudges fertility by hundredths, not halves. Population decline is not collapse — but fast aging strains every institution built for young populations, and speed matters more than direction.

concepts.detail: Dependents per hundred working-age adults — child and old-age pressure in one number.

concepts.statement: $$t_2 \approx \frac{70}{r\,\%}$$
concepts.detail: At r percent annual growth, the population doubles in about 70-over-r years — 3 percent growth doubles in 23.

concepts.statement: The recurring mistakes: Malthusian determinism (fertility fell fastest exactly where famine was forecast — the model describes, it does not doom); treating the stages as prophecy (timings have varied fivefold; Africa is not one demographic story); reading overpopulation as today's crisis when two-thirds of humanity already sits below replacement; blaming or crediting single policies for fertility (China's birth rate kept falling after the one-child policy ended); and assuming decline buys sustainability — aging societies still consume, with fewer workers to build the transition.
Annual live births per thousand population.
Birth rate minus death rate — the growth migration does not touch.
Average children per woman across a lifetime; 2.1 is replacement.
The generation-long window of low dependency when the bulge works.
Growth baked into young age structures even at replacement fertility.
Young plus elderly per hundred working-age adults.
Males and females by age cohort — a population's autobiography in one chart.

examples.title: Worked example — The Demographic Transition: The Arithmetic of Populations
examples.problem: A stage-two country posts CBR 45, CDR 15, with 44 percent of its population under fifteen and 3 percent over sixty-four — growth rate, doubling time and dependency burden?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: natural increase is the rate difference divided by ten; the dependency ratio is dependents per hundred of working age.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: (45 − 15)/10 = 3 percent growth, doubling in 70/3 ≈ 23 years. The working-age share is 53 percent, so DR = (44 + 3)/53 ≈ 89 — nearly one dependent per worker, overwhelmingly children.

examples.result: schools are the crisis and the investment. Forty years later, stage three-four with CBR 18, CDR 8 and the bulge working, the ratio falls toward 50 — the dividend window, open or squandered.

keyTakeaways: School systems plan classroom cohorts a decade out from today's birth counts — Kenya builds while Japan closes.
Pension reform indexes retirement ages to life expectancy to steady the worker-pensioner ratio.
Labor and immigration policy is quietly becoming demography policy, like it or not.
Health systems shift capacity from obstetrics to chronic and geriatric care along the transition.
Climate and resource models run on population paths — the UN's projections feed IPCC scenarios.

Where next — Pairs with the population-geography lesson — where people live — and the stratification lesson for who ages poor. The reproductive-health lesson covers the contraception that carried stage three. Next: the epidemiologic transition, pension economics, and China's demographic reversal.

quiz.q: Stage two of the transition is defined by:
options: death rates falling while births stay high
quiz.explanation: Sanitation and vaccination cut mortality first; the birth rate lags for a generation — that lag is the explosion.

quiz.q: Replacement fertility is about:
quiz.explanation: Two to replace the parents, plus a tenth for mortality before reproductive age.

quiz.q: The demographic dividend opens when:
options: the baby-bulge reaches working age while child dependency falls
quiz.explanation: Few dependents, many workers — for one generation. East Asia caught the window; Latin America partly missed it.

quiz.q: Population momentum means growth continues after fertility hits replacement because:
options: young age structures keep births numerous for decades
quiz.explanation: The wide base supplies abundant future parents — even replacement behavior grows a young population.

intro:
In 1951 an experiment asked people to judge which line matched a sample — a task a child gets right alone — and a third of the answers bent toward a unanimous group. The classic social-influence studies, from Asch through Milgram to the bystander experiments, are pop culture's favorite horror stories, and they are genuinely important once their real finding is extracted: situations have reliable power over behavior, more than the people inside them predict. This lesson is that extraction — the sibling of the dissonance lesson's attitude-change program, and its frequent partner.

**Why this matters.** From boardrooms to emergencies, the situational lens is applied psychology's best tool: if behavior follows the shape of the room, redesign the room. The one-ally and speak-last procedures that tame conformity are cheap, tested, and almost never used.
objectives: Explain informational versus normative influence
Explain asch: unanimity and the power of one ally
Explain milgram's variations: what actually moves obedience
Explain groupthink: symptoms and antidotes
Explain crowds as shared identity, not lost selves
Explain diffusion of responsibility and the bystander effect
Explain situations can be designed

concepts.statement: Solomon Asch's line judgments: facing a unanimous majority giving an obviously wrong answer, about 75 percent of participants conformed at least once, and roughly a third of all critical trials bent. The decomposition is the point — informational influence, taking others as evidence when unsure, versus normative influence, the cost of standing out even when sure. And the finding's best half: one dissenting ally, even a stranger giving a different wrong answer, collapses conformity to near five percent. Unanimity, not group size, was doing almost all the work.

concepts.term: Asch: unanimity and the power of one ally
concepts.statement: Stanley Milgram's obedience studies asked teachers to deliver shocks for wrong answers: 65 percent went to the maximum 450 volts. The variations matter more than the headline — obedience fell to 30 percent when the teacher had to force the learner's hand, and to under 10 percent with two peers who refused first, shifting as well with proximity and setting. Interpretation has evolved from blind obedience to engaged followership: most participants were distressed, and most complied while trying to do the job well. The critiques — demand characteristics, sampling, and the ethics debates that followed — reshaped research ethics itself.

concepts.term: Milgram's variations: what actually moves obedience
concepts.statement: The Stanford Prison Experiment ended after six days when guards turned cruel, and it became the textbooks' exhibit on the power of roles. It has since aged badly as evidence: archival work shows guards were coached toward toughness, and volunteers for a prison study scored higher on aggression than average. A 2006 BBC partial replication inverted it — the guards failed to identify with their role and the prisoners won. The durable lesson inverted with it: roles shape behavior when people identify with the role, which makes identity, not loss of self, the mechanism.

Irving Janis extracted groupthink from the Bay of Pigs fiasco: cohesive groups seeking unanimity suppress dissent and outperform nothing. The symptoms — illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship, mindguards shielding the leader from bad news, illusion of unanimity — map onto Asch's mechanism, and the antidotes are procedural because the cause is structural: the leader states preferences last, a devil's advocate is assigned and rotated, outside review is mandatory. Same fix as the one ally.

concepts.term: Crowds as shared identity, not lost selves
concepts.statement: Gustave Le Bon's 1895 mob — humans losing themselves in crowds — dominated a century, but the evidence refined it. Anonymous Halloween trick-or-treaters took more candy when alone, yet Stephen Reicher's crowd work shows crowds enforcing their own shared norms: sports crowds police themselves when treated as communities, and confrontational policing manufactures the disorder it fears. The bystander story parallels: after the Kitty Genovese murder — whose famous thirty-eight-witnesses account was substantially wrong — Darley and Latané showed helping collapses as perceived bystanders multiply, with 75 percent of people alone reporting smoke within two minutes against 10 percent who believed four others were present. Responsibility diffuses; naming a helper undoes it.

concepts.term: Diffusion of responsibility and the bystander effect
concepts.statement: The synthesis is neither cynicism nor exoneration. Situations do have main effects — but the effects respond to design: unanimity broken, responsibility assigned, leaders speaking last, norms made visible. The errors live at the extremes — people are sheep (a single ally flattened Asch's effect) and I would never, the fundamental attribution error the biases lesson owns, applied to yourself first. The studies' replication record is honestly mixed; the situational principle it supports has survived every test.

The standard misuses: quoting headline numbers as constants (Milgram's variations ran from 10 to 65 percent; the Genovese account was wrong; Zimbardo's guards were coached); concluding people are sheep (one ally flattens conformity — the sheep finding is about unanimity); skipping the ethics lesson these studies forced into existence; and deploying the cynicism version — everyone conforms — as an excuse for rooms where nobody was ever asked. The deepest misuse is reading these as verdicts on humanity rather than instructions for design.
Conforming to be liked and accepted, even against one's own perception.
Taking others' behavior as evidence about reality.
Janis's mode of cohesive decision-making that suppresses dissent for unanimity.
Each bystander's felt obligation shrinking with their number.
The modern reading of Milgram: complying while trying to serve a legitimate-seeming goal.
The crowd's organizing principle in Reicher's account — behavior follows the group one identifies with.
Society's overreaction to a deviance episode — Durkheim's boundary ritual at full volume.

examples.title: Worked example — Conformity, Obedience and the Power of the Situation
examples.problem: A leadership team keeps approving flawed launches — meetings where everyone senses trouble and nobody says it. Apply the conformity toolkit concretely.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: normative influence and groupthink suppress dissent under unanimity; procedures, not courage campaigns, break it.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: the CEO now speaks last on any proposal; a rotating devil's advocate must argue the strongest case against; anonymous pre-reads collect objections before the room converges; and one member is named the obligated dissenter per decision — Asch's ally, institutionalized.

examples.result: dissent stops being a character trait of the brave and becomes a role in the process — the finding of 1951, deployed as calendar policy.

keyTakeaways: Intelligence agencies institutionalized red teams and devil's advocates after analytic failures.
Bystander-training programs teach designation — you, in the red jacket, call for help — to defeat diffusion.
Dialogue-based crowd policing at football matches measurably reduced disorder in European field trials.
Jury research finds a single dissenting juror transforms deliberation from verdict-confirmation to evidence-testing.
Whistleblower channels and speak-up training are groupthink insurance with compliance teeth.

Where next — Pairs with the cognitive-dissonance lesson — attitude change is its sibling program — and the biases lesson for the fundamental attribution error. The research-methods toolkit covers the ethics regime these studies created. Next: persuasion science, leadership psychology, and the crowd-safety engineering of mass events.

quiz.q: In Asch's studies, the single most powerful reducer of conformity was:
quiz.explanation: Conformity collapsed from about a third of trials to near five percent — the room only had to stop being unanimous.

quiz.q: Milgram's variations showed obedience fell most when:
options: the learner sat in another room
peers refused first and the teacher had to force the learner's hand
quiz.explanation: Peer disobedience plus physical proximity pushed full obedience under 10 percent — the situation, not the person's character, carried the result.

quiz.q: The bystander effect is primarily an effect of:
quiz.explanation: Darley and Latané: each additional perceived bystander shrinks any one person's felt obligation to act.

quiz.q: Reicher's crowd findings suggest that crowds:
options: act on shared identity and enforce group norms
quiz.explanation: Crowds are not melted individuals; they are groups with identities — which is why respectful policing produces peaceful ones.

intro:
A bank enrolled over a million customers in insurance they never asked for and opened accounts in their names without consent — crimes by any statute — yet no executive served a day in jail. Meanwhile a teenager caught with a pocketful of a cheap drug could lose a decade. Deviance, crime and punishment look like a moral ledger written in stone; sociology reads them as a social document, edited constantly by whoever holds the pen. This lesson covers the machinery: how societies define rule-breaking, how formal and informal control enforce the rules, what the major theories say about why people break them, and how the criminal justice system — police, courts, corrections — processes what society hands it.

**Why this matters.** What a society criminalizes, and how hard it punishes, distributes freedom and suffering at trillion-dollar scale: the United States holds the world's largest prison population — roughly 2.3 million people behind bars, with another four million on probation or parole — while corporate wrongdoing of far greater dollar value routinely ends in fines. Understanding deviance and social control is understanding who writes the rules, who gets caught by them, and why the same act can be a felony, a faux pas or a civil right depending on the decade.
objectives: Explain deviance as relative norm violation
Explain formal and informal social control
Explain sanctions: positive, negative, formal, informal
Explain conflict theory: crime and unequal power
Explain neutralization, association and social bonds
Explain crime typologies: street, corporate, victimless
Explain reading crime statistics honestly
Explain police, courts and corrections

concepts.statement: Deviance is a violation of established contextual, cultural or social norms — the folkways of everyday etiquette, the mores a community treats as moral necessities, or codified law itself — a formulation owed to William Graham Sumner in 1906. The category is famously relative. Listening to music on the way to class is normal; during the lecture it is rude; on the witness stand it is contempt of court. Whether an act counts as deviant depends on the setting, the audience and the actor, and the boundary moves over time — cannabis traveled from folk remedy to "Marijuana Menace" to legal recreational purchase within a century. Deviance is not automatically negative, either: Rosa Parks committing the "crime" of keeping her seat is now taught to schoolchildren as civic virtue.

When norms are violated, societies respond with social control — the regulation and enforcement of norms — in pursuit of social order, the predictable backdrop on which daily life depends. The instruments are sanctions, and they come in two crossed varieties. Informal sanctions emerge in face-to-face interaction: a smile for the stranger who helps carry groceries, a cold stare for the loud talker in a quiet car. Formal sanctions are official and organizational: a commendation for a soldier, expulsion for a student who breaks a conduct code, a parking fine, a prison sentence. The two-by-two matters because most everyday conformity is enforced not by police and courts but by the cheap, constant machinery of approval and disapproval — which is why dissolving community ties tends to precede rising crime.

Three paradigms explain why deviance happens. Functionalists treat it as, improbably, useful: Durkheim argued that punishing deviance publicly reaffirms the violated norms — "a crime is a crime because we condemn it" — and the Durkheim lesson in this subject develops that theory. Merton's strain theory located deviance in the gap between culturally commanded goals, such as financial success, and legitimately available means; the companion deviance lesson works through his five adaptations and the Chicago School's social disorganization account of crime concentrating where poverty and turnover have dissolved informal control. The functionalist question is always: what does the rule, or its breaking, do for the system?

concepts.term: Conflict theory: crime and unequal power
concepts.statement: Conflict theorists flip the question: who writes the rules, and who benefits? Marx's shadow hangs over the approach — the wealthy, who control production, also shape government, law and enforcement to protect their position. C. Wright Mills named the result the power elite: a small circle of executives, politicians and commanders whose interests are baked into what counts as criminal in the first place. The evidence is not subtle. The FBI counted about 15 billion dollars lost to burglary, larceny and vehicle theft in 2009; Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme alone destroyed on the order of 50 billion — yet street crime is what fills the prisons. The crack-versus-powder disparity is the classic exhibit: federal law made 50 grams of crack carry the same ten-year mandatory sentence as 500 grams of cocaine powder, a 100-to-1 ratio tracking the class of each drug's users, softened to 18-to-1 only in 2010. The 1994 crime bill — mandatory minimums, three-strikes laws, prison funding — then produced the mass incarceration of Black and Hispanic Americans that sociologists study as a policy outcome rather than a crime statistic.

Symbolic interactionism moves deviance from the act to the audience. Labeling theory — Becker's statement, Lemert's primary-versus-secondary deviance and master status — is developed in the companion lesson; two extensions matter here. Sykes and Matza's techniques of neutralization catalog how rule-breakers deflect labels: denial of responsibility, denial of injury, denial of the victim, condemnation of the condemners, and appeal to higher loyalties — the vocabulary of "I was owed it" heard wherever rule-breaking is rationalized. Sutherland's differential association theory holds that deviance is learned from close others who model it and supply opportunities, which is why a parent's conviction predicts a child's criminality decades later. Hirschi's control theory inverts the question entirely: deviance is what happens when the bonds of attachment, commitment, involvement and belief snap.

Crime is the subset of deviance that violates official law and is punishable through formal sanctions, and sociology sorts it several ways. Violent crimes use force or its threat — murder, rape, armed robbery; nonviolent property crimes — larceny, car theft, vandalism — do not. Street crime, the visible kind committed in public space, dominates the news; corporate crime — embezzlement, insider trading, identity theft — does quieter damage on a grander scale. Victimless crimes, like underage drinking or sex work, have no complaining victim beyond the participant, though the label is contested: defenders of such laws argue society itself is harmed. Hate crimes add a distinct element — target selection by race, religion, gender identity or similar — and are badly undercounted: victimization surveys find roughly 205,000 episodes a year where police records show fewer than 9,000 incidents.

All crime statistics are constructions with known blind spots. The FBI's Uniform Crime Reports aggregate police data from about 17,000 agencies — comprehensive on what reaches the police, silent on what victims never report; its successor system, NIBRS, captures richer detail per incident. The Bureau of Justice Statistics' National Crime Victimization Survey asks around 160,000 people directly and accordingly finds more crime than the UCR; neither captures everything, and the unmeasured remainder is the dark figure. The perception data are the kicker: violent crime in the United States has mostly declined since its early-1990s peak, yet majorities tell pollsters it is rising — an error researchers trace to crime-saturated news and police dramas, and a standing lesson that fear of crime is a social fact in its own right.

The criminal justice system — the organization that exists to enforce a legal code — has three branches. Police enforce laws across fragmented jurisdictions: federal agencies such as the FBI and ATF work narrow mandates, state police patrol highways, local departments handle the daily volume; there is no single national force. Courts decide guilt and set penalties — trial courts with judge and jury, appellate review for the losing side, state supreme courts at the top. Corrections supervises both the convicted and the accused awaiting trial: at the end of 2018 about 2.3 million Americans were incarcerated and 6.4 million — one adult in forty — were under some form of correctional supervision. The vocabulary matters: jails confine locally and pre-trial, prisons hold sentences longer than a year, probation is supervised time instead of prison, and parole is supervised release after serving part of a sentence.

First, deviance and crime are overlapping circles, not synonyms — most deviance is legal and plenty of law-breaking is normalized. Second, do not equate legality with morality: the civil-rights era's illegal sit-ins are the canonical case. Third, severity of punishment is not deterrence — evidence prices certainty of being caught, not sentence length (the companion lesson has the research). Fourth, resist media-driven perception: American crime rates fell for decades while fear did not. And "victimless" is a claim, not a fact — every category in the typology is contested terrain, which is exactly why the sociology of the boundary exists.
Violation of contextual, cultural or social norms — folkways, mores or codified law.
The regulation and enforcement of norms, formal and informal, in pursuit of social order.
A reward or punishment for conforming to or violating norms; formal or informal.
Mills's term for the small circle of wealthy and influential who shape what counts as criminal.
Sutherland's theory that deviance is learned from close others who model and enable it.
Hirschi's account of deviance as the snapping of bonds — attachment, commitment, involvement, belief.
Illegal act whose only apparent victim is the participant; the label itself is contested.
The police, courts and corrections apparatus that enforces a society's legal code.

examples.title: Worked Example — Reading a Sentencing Disparity
examples.problem: Under the 1986 federal law, possession of 50 grams of crack cocaine carried a ten-year mandatory minimum, while the same sentence for powder cocaine required 500 grams. What does the arithmetic reveal, and how would each paradigm read it?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: conflict theory treats law as shaped by the groups empowered to write it; the ratio between penalties for pharmacologically near-identical drugs measures whose conduct is being discounted.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: 500 ÷ 50 = 100 — a hundred-fold disparity at a moment when crack was concentrated in poor Black urban neighborhoods and powder cocaine among wealthier white users. The Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 cut the ratio to 18-to-1.

examples.result: a functionalist calls the law boundary-maintenance; a conflict theorist calls it class legislation with a racial signature — the 100-to-1 figure is now a standard exhibit in both literatures.

keyTakeaways: Sentencing reform: mandatory-minimum rollbacks and retroactive crack-sentencing fixes are direct applications of conflict analysis.
Corporate accountability: deferred-prosecution deals and individual-liability debates track the street-versus-suite enforcement gap.
Decriminalization: cannabis, gambling and sports betting show the deviance boundary moving in real time — and who profits from the move.
Statistical literacy: comparing UCR, NIBRS and NCVS findings before believing a crime-wave headline.
Reentry policy: record-sealing and rights restoration attack the labels that outlive sentences.

quiz.q: Music on the bus is fine, in a lecture it is rude, at the witness stand it is contempt. This illustrates that deviance is…
options: relative to context, audience and actor
quiz.explanation: The same act changes meaning with setting and audience — deviance is a social judgment, not a property of acts.

quiz.q: A parking fine is best classified as a…
quiz.explanation: Formal sanctions are official and organizational; a fine is a punishment, so it is negative and formal.

quiz.q: Conflict theorists read the 100-to-1 crack-versus-powder sentencing ratio mainly as…
options: law shaped by the interests of the powerful who write it
quiz.explanation: Mills and Marx both point the same way: rule-makers write rules that protect rule-makers, and the penalty gap tracked the class of each drug's users.

quiz.q: Sutherland's differential association predicts crime can run in families because…
options: deviance is learned from close others who model it and open opportunities
quiz.explanation: Deviance is a socialization product — longitudinal work found parental conviction the strongest childhood predictor of adult offending.

quiz.q: The key distinction between jail and prison is…
options: jails hold local, short-term and pre-trial detainees; prisons hold sentences over a year
quiz.explanation: Jails are small and local, run by counties; prisons are state or federal facilities for longer sentences.

quiz.q: The National Crime Victimization Survey reports more crime than the Uniform Crime Reports because it…
options: captures crimes victims never reported to police
quiz.explanation: Self-report surveys surface the unreported share of crime — part of the dark figure the police data cannot see.

intro:
Ask any classroom to divide itself by race and everyone moves with quiet confidence — the categories feel as real as the floor. Ask geneticists to mark those boundaries in the genome and the project dissolves: human variation is gradual, overlapping and mostly shared across groups. Race is real the way money and borders are real — because societies act as if it were, and those actions build neighborhoods, schools, prisons and bank accounts around it. Sociology's task is to hold both truths at once: race is not biology, and race is absolutely a social fact with measurable, durable consequences for health, wealth, safety and belonging.

**Why this matters.** Nearly every contested policy question — immigration, policing, school assignment, voting rights, census design — turns on racial and ethnic categories and what a society does with them. You cannot follow the argument, on any side, without knowing what the categories are, where they came from, and how sociologists trace their effects. This lesson deliberately treats the racial and ethnic dimensions; the stratification lesson covers the class axis they intersect with.
objectives: Explain race as social construction
Explain ethnicity and pan-ethnic identities
Explain minority groups: power, not numbers
Explain stereotypes, prejudice, discrimination
Explain individual versus institutional racism
Explain intersection theory
Explain models of intergroup relations
Explain from assimilation to genocide

concepts.statement: Sociologists define race as a grouping of humankind based on shared physical or social qualities that a particular society considers significant — emphasis on the society. The historical categories were literal pseudoscience: Johann Friedrich Blumenbach sorted human skulls into five color-coded races in the eighteenth century, a taxonomy whose vocabulary lingered for two hundred years. The major professional associations — in anthropology, sociology and psychology alike — have since formally rejected biological race concepts, and the claims stacked on them have not survived evidence: measured Black-White IQ gaps shrink sharply as educational access equalizes, which points to nurture, not nature. None of this makes race unreal in daily life. It makes it a social construction — produced, maintained and occasionally revised by institutions from the census to the courthouse.

Ethnicity is shared culture: practices, norms, values and beliefs, often carried by a common language, religion or set of traditions. It is not race — Irish, Italian, Jewish and Serbian Americans can all sit inside the "White" box while keeping distinct ethnicities — and it is not national origin: Vietnam alone recognizes 54 ethnic groups. Identities also scale up: associated groups sometimes form pan-ethnic identities such as "Asian American" or "Latino", labels embraced by some members, rejected by others, and deployed differently in Houston than in the family home abroad. The growing number of people checking multiple race boxes on the census, and Tiger Woods's self-coined "Cablinasian", are reminders that identity is plural, situational and increasingly self-authored.

A minority group, in Louis Wirth's 1945 definition, is any group singled out from the rest of society for differential and unequal treatment — a definition about power, not arithmetic. Under apartheid, Black South Africans were an overwhelming numerical majority governed by a White population that was about 11 percent of the country. Wagley and Harris supplied the classic five markers: unequal treatment and reduced power over one's life, distinguishing physical or cultural traits, involuntary membership, awareness of subordination, and high rates of in-group marriage. Scapegoat theory, descending from Dollard's frustration-aggression work, explains one recurring use of the category: dominant groups displace unfocused frustration onto whoever is handy — Jewish Germans under Hitler, immigrants in hard economic times — and law has often ratified the targeting.

The everyday machinery runs stereotype → prejudice → discrimination. Stereotypes are oversimplified generalizations about groups; they are rarely invented fresh, being recycled from last century's targets onto this century's immigrants. Prejudice is the belief layer — prejudgments held without grounding experience, self-sealed by confirmation bias, in which every confirming anecdote counts and every disconfirming statistic does not. Discrimination is the action layer: redlining, biased hiring, the historical "No Irish Need Apply" sign. The layers can come apart — the unprejudiced discriminator who unthinkingly follows a biased system, the prejudiced nondiscriminator who holds beliefs but serves anyone — and they can stack into racism: beliefs plus practices plus institutional power arranged so one racial category is systematically advantaged. Sociologists split that further into individual and systemic racism, racial profiling, colorism within groups, and the color-blind racism that declares the problem solved by refusing to name it. Peggy McIntosh's image of privilege as an "invisible weightless knapsack" of unasked-for provisions captures why dominant groups so often fail to notice the arrangement.

Each paradigm takes a cut. Functionalism asks what racism does: Rose answered that its dysfunctions are wasted talent and the steep cost of maintaining artificial boundaries — think of running duplicate, unequal school systems — while Nash noted it is functional for the dominant group, morally licensing inequality as slaveholders once did. Symbolic interactionism studies the manufacture of belief: Blumer argued prejudice forms in interactions among the dominant, who assemble an abstract picture of the subordinate from media and hearsay — the culture of prejudice everyone is marinated in. Conflict theory traces outcomes to power: Jim Crow, disenfranchisement and wage ceilings; the surgical technician Vivien Thomas, classified and paid as a janitor for years while he helped develop a technique that saved "blue babies". Intersection theory, articulated by Crenshaw and developed by Collins, insists the layers cannot be studied one at a time: the prejudice aimed at a White woman and at an Asian woman in poverty are different objects.
