examples.title: Worked example — Greece and Rome: The Classical Inheritance
examples.problem: Why do political theorists call sortition, rather than elections, the most democratic device the Athenians used?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: elections select the distinguished and well-funded; the lot gives every eligible citizen an equal chance — which is what demokratia, people-power, names.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: Athens filled its Council of 500 and its large juries by lot and paid for service so the poor could attend; generals and treasurers, needing skill, were elected — the modern dilemma reversed.

examples.result: modern systems elect nearly everything, Athens lotted nearly everything; "democracy" has named different machines in different centuries, and the choice is live again in citizens' assemblies.

keyTakeaways: Constitutional design: separation of powers, vetoes and term limits descend from Roman fear of concentrated office.
Citizens' assemblies: Ireland, France and others now use randomly selected panels — sortition revived — for contested questions such as abortion and climate policy.
Legal systems: civil codes from France to Latin America descend from Justinian's sixth-century compilation of Roman law.
Vocabulary: senate, republic, politics, tyrant and democracy itself are Greek and Latin loans still structuring political speech.
Heritage disputes: the Parthenon marbles controversy turns on what modern states owe the classical heritage they hold.

quiz.q: In the Athenian view, elections were…
options: aristocratic, favouring the notable and well-funded
quiz.explanation: Sortition was the democratic device; elections were seen as selecting the distinguished few.

quiz.q: The Roman Republic gave way to empire chiefly because…
options: commanders gained armies more loyal to themselves than to the state
quiz.explanation: Career generals with private loyalty from their troops — Caesar above all — outmatched republican institutions.

quiz.q: The year 476 CE conventionally marks…
options: the deposition of the last western Roman emperor
the founding of the Byzantine empire
quiz.explanation: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus; the eastern empire continued until 1453.

quiz.q: Justinian's codification of Roman law matters today because…
options: it is the ancestor of most continental European legal systems
it was the first written law anywhere
quiz.explanation: The Corpus Juris Civilis (529-534 CE) was received by medieval and modern Europe as the model of a civil code.

intro:
Between 1914 and 1945, two global wars killed between 80 and 100 million people, ended five empires, industrialised genocide and closed with the first and only use of nuclear weapons in war. The two conflicts are properly one story: the peace that ended the first poisoned the ground under the second. This lesson traces the cascade from a double assassination in Sarajevo to the United Nations order — the system that, for all its failures, has kept great-power war at bay since 1945.

**Why this matters.** The world you live in was built from the rubble: the UN Charter, human rights law, the war-crimes court in The Hague, the nuclear standoff, the welfare state and the end of empires all date from these decades. Every current debate about alliance commitments, deterrence, appeasement or intervention is argued with examples drawn from 1914, 1938 or 1945.
objectives: Explain the July crisis: alliance cascade in 1914
Explain industrial war and the mobilised home front
Explain versailles: a peace that failed
Explain from appeasement to 1939
Explain the deadliest war in history
Explain 1945 and the new order

concepts.term: The July crisis: alliance cascade in 1914
concepts.statement: On 28 June 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, in Sarajevo. What followed was machinery, not accident: Austria's ultimatum to Serbia, mobilisation timetables that turned diplomacy into countdown, and alliance commitments — Germany backing Austria, Russia backing Serbia, France backing Russia — that turned a Balkan quarrel into general war within five weeks. Germany's Schlieffen Plan, attacking France through Belgium, brought Britain in on 4 August.

concepts.term: Industrial war and the mobilised home front
concepts.statement: The result was war at factory scale. Machine guns, quick-firing artillery and barbed wire made defence decisive: at Verdun and on the Somme in 1916, attackers advanced a few kilometres at the cost of hundreds of thousands of lives — the British Army lost 57,470 men on the Somme's first day alone. Behind the lines, whole societies were mobilised: women in the shell factories, rationing, propaganda, and by 1918 an influenza pandemic that killed more people than the war itself.

The Treaty of Versailles (1919) ended the war by blaming it: Article 231 assigned Germany sole responsibility, and reparations were set at 132 billion gold marks. Germany lost territory, colonies and its fleet; the German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and Russian empires were gone. The League of Nations, the peace's great hope, never included the United States and could not stop Japan in Manchuria (1931) or Italy in Ethiopia (1935). Keynes, resigning from the British delegation, predicted the consequences in print.

The Depression after 1929 shattered faith in liberal democracy; in Germany it handed power to Hitler in 1933. Britain and France, haunted by the trenches, chose appeasement — the Rhineland, then Austria, then the Sudetenland at Munich in 1938. When Hitler broke Munich and seized the rest of Czechoslovakia, the strategy died. The Nazi-Soviet pact of 23 August 1939 removed Germany's two-front fear; on 1 September German armies crossed into Poland, and two days later Britain and France declared war.

The second war outdid the first in every dimension: perhaps 60 to 70 million dead, half of them civilians. Its defining crime was the Holocaust — the industrialised murder of six million Jews and millions of Roma, disabled people, Slavs, political prisoners and others — uncovered as Allied armies advanced. Momentum swung at Stalingrad (1942-43) and Midway (1942); D-Day opened the western front in June 1944; and in August 1945 atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, ending the war and opening the nuclear age.

The victors built deliberately: the United Nations (charter 1945), the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), the Nuremberg trials that named crimes against humanity, and the Bretton Woods economic institutions. Europe's empires began dissolving at once, and the anti-Hitler alliance split into the Cold War — yet the core achievement held. No war between great powers has recurred since 1945; historians still argue whether the cause is institutions, nuclear terror or luck.

Avoid single-cause explanations: the thesis blaming Germany alone, and the mirror claim that everyone stumbled in blindly, both flatten the evidence. Do not read 1914 as inevitable — the same alliance system had survived earlier crises. "Appeasement is always wrong" is an overlearned lesson; Munich also bought Britain a year of rearmament. And keep the Holocaust at the centre of 1939-45, not as a footnote to a military story: the genocide was a war aim, not a by-product.
Germany's pre-war strategy: knock out France quickly via Belgium, then turn east — invasion on a timetable.
Warfare mobilising entire societies — economies, labour, food, propaganda — erasing the soldier-civilian line.
The Versailles "war guilt" clause assigning Germany responsibility for the war and grounding reparations.
British and French policy of concession to Hitler, 1936-38, discredited at and after Munich.
The Nazi genocide: six million Jews and millions of others murdered in factories of death.
The 1945-46 prosecutions of Nazi leaders, establishing individual liability for crimes against humanity.

examples.title: Worked example — The World Wars: Causes, Courses and Consequences
examples.problem: Explain how a five-week crisis in July 1914 became a world war rather than a third Balkan war.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: the mechanisms were rigid alliance commitments and mobilisation timetables that ran faster than diplomacy could.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: Austria's ultimatum drew Russian mobilisation in defence of Serbia; German war plans required attacking France before Russia was ready, and the route through Belgium activated a British guarantee; each government's locally rational steps composed an unstoppable sequence.

examples.result: the war was not "caused" by any single decision but by an architecture — the lesson institutional designers have drawn ever since, from the UN Charter to crisis hotlines.

keyTakeaways: International law: Nuremberg's precedent underwrites the International Criminal Court's jurisdiction over war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Security design: NATO and the UN Security Council are institutional answers to the alliance-cascade problem of 1914.
Nuclear policy: the entire doctrine of deterrence descends directly from Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
Memory politics: disputes over monuments, museums and curricula for both wars still shape national identity across Europe and Asia.
Economic statecraft: sanctions and reparations debates still cite the Versailles cautionary tale about punitive peace terms.

quiz.q: The immediate trigger of World War I was…
options: the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo
quiz.explanation: The Sarajevo assassination of 28 June 1914 set the alliance and mobilisation machinery in motion.

quiz.q: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles…
options: assigned Germany sole war guilt, grounding reparations
banned German rearmament in the air
quiz.explanation: The "war guilt" clause justified the 132-billion-mark reparations bill and German resentment alike.

quiz.q: Munich (1938) is remembered today chiefly for…
options: the failed British-French concession of the Sudetenland to Hitler
quiz.explanation: The surrender of the Sudetenland, aimed at "peace for our time", became the standing indictment of appeasement.

quiz.q: A central institutional innovation of the post-1945 order was…
options: the abolition of empires by treaty
the Nuremberg precedent of individual liability for crimes against humanity
quiz.explanation: For the first time, state office offered no immunity from prosecution for genocide and aggression.

intro:
In 1914 a handful of European empires governed most of Africa and much of Asia. By 1975 the map had been remade: more than a hundred new states, most born between India's midnight of 15 August 1947 and Portugal's African collapse in 1974-75. Decolonization was the largest transfer of political power in history, achieved by negotiation, mass movement and war alike — and it created the geopolitical category we now call the Global South. This lesson follows the endings, the new states' first decades, and the arguments about what colonialism left behind.

**Why this matters.** Two-thirds of the world's states and most of its population live in countries whose borders, languages and institutions were shaped by empire and independence struggles. Migration corridors, debt debates, resource conflicts, the politics of the United Nations and the vocabulary of postcolonial criticism are unintelligible without this history — which is to say, the news is unintelligible without it.
objectives: Explain empire weakened from within
Explain india 1947: freedom and partition
Explain ghana to 1960: Africa's wave
Explain bandung and non-alignment
Explain hard births: borders, coups and proxy wars
Explain legacies and the Global South

concepts.statement: The world wars broke the empires' aura of permanence. Indian, Senegalese and Algerian troops fought for France and Britain in both wars; the Atlantic Charter of 1941 proclaimed self-determination, awkwardly for colonial powers; and by 1945 Britain was effectively bankrupt, while Japan's early victories had shattered the myth of European invincibility from Manila to Jakarta. Anti-colonial leaders — Gandhi, Nehru, Nkrumah, Ho Chi Minh — were seasoned organisers with global platforms.

Britain's largest possession left first and most traumatically. Mass campaigns — the Salt March of 1930, Quit India in 1942 — had made the Raj ungovernable at acceptable cost, and a war-drained Britain negotiated. The price was partition: on 15 August 1947 India and Pakistan were born, and the division of Punjab and Bengal uprooted twelve to fifteen million people amid killing that took hundreds of thousands to a million lives. The new states stayed in the Commonwealth; the wound has never closed.

Ghana's independence in March 1957 — Kwame Nkrumah declaring it meaningless unless linked to the liberation of all Africa — lit the fuse. Seventeen African states followed in 1960 alone, France's territories mostly by negotiated transfer and Britain's by hurry; Algeria was the exception, winning independence in 1962 after an eight-year war whose torture and counterinsurgency scandalised France itself. By the mid-1970s the European empires were finished.

In April 1955, twenty-nine Asian and African nations met at Bandung, Indonesia — Nehru, Nasser, Sukarno and Zhou Enlai in the same hall — to stake out a third way between the American and Soviet blocs; the Non-Aligned Movement formalised at Belgrade in 1961. Its members were anything but uniform, but the bloc gave the "Third World" (a coinage from 1952) voting power in a United Nations growing from 51 members in 1945 toward today's 193 — where Resolution 1514 (1960) declared colonialism a violation of human rights.

concepts.term: Hard births: borders, coups and proxy wars
concepts.statement: The new states inherited borders drawn in Berlin (1884-85) with no reference to the people inside them, plus economies built to export raw materials. The first decades were brutal: Congo's prime minister Patrice Lumumba was murdered in 1961 with foreign complicity; coups multiplied as armies became the one functioning institution; Biafra's attempted secession starved (1967-70); and Cold War patrons armed proxy wars from Angola to Vietnam. Decolonization did not end intervention — it changed its form.

Yet the balance is not only tragedy. Literacy and life expectancy across the Global South rose faster after 1950 than in any previous half-century; India held together as a democracy; and the postcolonial critique — from Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth (1961) to Said's Orientalism (1978) — rebuilt how the world understands power and culture. Debates over debt, extraction and museum collections are the empire's afterlife, conducted in the vocabulary decolonization created.

Do not tidy the story into Europeans granting freedom to grateful subjects: independence was taken — by strikes, boycotts, wars and votes — at real cost. Avoid romanticising either side: some liberation movements became one-party states, and some new rulers turned on their own. "Third World" began as a geopolitical label, not a poverty ranking. And remember the timeline's range: the main wave ran 1947 to 1975, but Hong Kong waited until 1997 — the chapter is not closed.
The 1947 division of British India into India and Pakistan, displacing twelve to fifteen million people amid mass violence.
Leader of Ghana's independence (1957) and advocate of pan-African liberation; later coined "neocolonialism".
The 1955 meeting of twenty-nine Asian and African states that founded the non-aligned third way.
The bloc formalised at Belgrade in 1961 by states formally outside both Cold War alliances.
The 1960 UN declaration that colonialism violates human rights and must end unconditionally.
The postcolonial world's collective name, emphasising shared structural position more than geography.

examples.title: Worked example — Decolonization and the Making of the Global South
examples.problem: Why did British decolonization in Ghana (1957) take a decade of negotiation while French decolonization in Algeria (1962) took eight years of war?

steps.label: Recall the governing variable
steps.text: legal status and the settler question — Algeria was legally part of France with a million European settlers; the Gold Coast was a colony with no settler class blocking majority rule.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: Ghana's movement could win elections and inherit a functioning administration under Nkrumah; in Algeria, settler interests and French national identity made compromise nearly impossible, and the FLN fought until Paris conceded.

examples.result: decolonization's course was set less by imperial ideology than by each territory's status and settler presence — the same logic explains why Kenya and Zimbabwe came late and violently.

keyTakeaways: United Nations politics: the General Assembly's transformation from 51 to 193 members is mostly the decolonization story, and its voting blocs descend from Bandung.
Development economics: aid, debt relief and commodity-dependence debates all begin from colonial economic structures.
Migration policy: postcolonial ties shape today's migration corridors from South Asia, Africa and the Caribbean to Europe.
Museum restitution: returns of Benin bronzes and other artefacts turn on colonial-era acquisition records.
Language and education: the continuing role of English, French and Portuguese in law, universities and publishing is a measurable imperial legacy.

quiz.q: The largest single-year wave of African independence came in…
quiz.explanation: Seventeen African states, mostly French and British colonies, became independent in 1960.

quiz.q: Partition in 1947 refers to…
options: the split of British India into India and Pakistan
quiz.explanation: The division of Punjab and Bengal displaced twelve to fifteen million people amid mass killing.

quiz.q: The Bandung Conference (1955) is remembered for…
options: uniting Asian and African states around non-alignment
quiz.explanation: Twenty-nine states met to chart a course independent of both Cold War blocs, seeding the Non-Aligned Movement.

quiz.q: Algeria's independence (1962) was won by war rather than negotiation chiefly because…
options: it was legally part of France with a large settler population
France had no interest in Algeria
quiz.explanation: Algeria's constitutional status and its million European settlers made negotiated majority rule nearly impossible.

intro:
Philosophy's second-oldest question, after what there is, is how we know it. Epistemology — from episteme, knowledge — asks what knowledge is, where it comes from and how much of it we can have. For two millennia the standard answer was tidy: knowledge is justified true belief. Then in 1963 a three-page paper demolished the tidy answer, and the discipline has been rebuilding ever since. This lesson runs the main line from Plato's definition through the rationalist-empiricist wars to Kant's synthesis and today's debates about reliability, testimony and doubt.

**Why this matters.** Every practice that claims to produce knowledge — science, courts, journalism, medicine, machine learning — runs on an implicit epistemology: rules for what counts as evidence, how much justification is enough and who is entitled to testify. When those rules fail, the failure is epistemological: the cold-case conviction built on a lab's false positive, the study that replicated on nobody. Studying the theory makes the practice visible.
objectives: Explain knowledge as justified true belief
Explain gettier's counterexamples
Explain rationalism: reason as the source
Explain empiricism: experience as the source
Explain kant's two-source synthesis
Explain justification after Gettier

concepts.statement: Plato's dialogues entertain and reject several definitions of knowledge, but the analysis that stuck is the triad: to know that p, you must believe p, p must be true, and you must be justified in believing it. A lucky guess hits truth without knowledge; a well-evidenced falsehood is belief without truth; a prejudice is belief without justification. Each condition excludes something, and for twenty centuries the trio looked jointly sufficient.

In 1963 Edmund Gettier published, in the journal Analysis, two terse counterexamples. In the classic case, Smith has strong evidence that Jones owns a Ford and will get the job; he infers "the man who will get the job owns a Ford". Jones does not get the job — Smith does — and Smith, by coincidence, happens to own a Ford. The belief is true and justified, yet the justification is disconnected from what makes it true. Nobody wants to call it knowledge; the literature has been proposing fourth conditions ever since.

The rationalists — Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz — held that the mind's own resources supply substantive knowledge. Descartes' Meditations (1641) doubted everything doubtable until it hit bedrock: cogito, ergo sum, the one belief that cannot be false while believed. From such certainties, plus proofs of a non-deceiving God, rationalism hoped to derive the world's basic structure — extension, motion, mathematics — a priori, before and independent of experience.

The empiricists answered that nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses. Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690) modelled the mind as white paper written on by experience; Hume, sharpest of the three, pushed empiricism to its crisis: observation gives us habits, not necessities, so even causation and induction — the machinery of science — lack rational foundation. His Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748) is still the sceptic's manual.

Kant reported that Hume woke him from "dogmatic slumber". The Critique of Pure Reason (1781) split the difference: experience supplies the matter of knowledge, but the mind supplies the form — space, time and causality are the a priori frame through which any experience must arrive. Synthetic a priori truths, like mathematics, hold necessarily of experience without deriving from it. The rebuild preserved science while denying that reason can know things as they are in themselves.

Twentieth-century epistemology multiplied strategies. Reliabilism (Alvin Goldman) counts a belief as knowledge when produced by a reliable process, whatever the believer can inspect; internalists insist justification must be accessible from inside. The regress argument — what justifies the justifiers? — bottoms out in Agrippa's trilemma: infinite regress, circle, or foundations. Testimony, once an embarrassment, is now central: most of what anyone knows — history, geography, physics — is taken on other people's word, structured by trust.

Do not confuse knowledge with certainty — the first is a status requiring truth, the second a feeling. Gettier cases refute the three-condition analysis, not the concept of knowledge. Keep rationalism and empiricism as ideal types: Kant, Hume and Descartes each cross the lines. And resist treating scepticism as an enemy to be beaten: brains in vats and dreaming arguments are diagnostic tools, stress-testing what any theory of knowledge must assume.
The classical analysis: knowledge requires belief, truth and adequate justification.
Cases where a belief is justified and true yet not knowledge, because justification is unconnected to the truth-maker.
Knowledge independent of experience, versus knowledge derived from it.
Locke's "white paper" model of the mind before experience writes on it.
Kant's category: necessary truths that extend knowledge, such as mathematics and the framework of experience.
The view that a belief counts as knowledge when formed by a reliable process, whether or not the believer can cite it.
Justification chains must end in dogmatic foundations, circularity or infinite regress.

examples.title: Worked example — Epistemology: What Can We Know?
examples.problem: Test a belief against the justified-true-belief analysis, then show why Gettier breaks it.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Recall the three conditions — belief, truth, justification — and Gettier's addition: the justification must be appropriately connected to the truth.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: a farmer reads a reliable almanac forecasting early rain, believes it, and the rain does come early — because of a stalled storm system the almanac knew nothing about. Justified, believed, true; but the forecast's method is not why it rained.

examples.result: by the classical criteria the farmer "knows"; by any post-Gettier standard he does not — exactly the kind of case the missing fourth condition is meant to exclude.

keyTakeaways: Machine learning: classifiers are judged by reliability, applying reliabilist thinking to artificial knowers.
Law: standards of proof, from "beyond reasonable doubt" to "preponderance of evidence", are institutional thresholds of justification.
Journalism: source verification and correction policies are applied epistemology under deadline.
Science: peer review and replication exist because testimony must be structured before it can carry knowledge.
Medicine: evidence hierarchies, from expert opinion to randomised trials, are a working theory of justification.

quiz.q: The classical analysis defines knowledge as…
quiz.explanation: Belief, truth and justification — each excluding guesses, falsehoods and mere conviction.

quiz.q: Gettier cases show that…
options: justified true belief is not sufficient for knowledge
quiz.explanation: A belief can be justified and true by luck, the justification unconnected to what makes it true — so a fourth condition is needed.

quiz.q: Kant's answer to Hume holds that…
options: the mind supplies the a priori forms through which experience arrives
reason alone knows things in themselves
quiz.explanation: Space, time and causality are the mind's contribution — which is why science is possible and metaphysics is fenced in.

quiz.q: Agrippa's trilemma says chains of justification must end in…
options: self-evident foundations, circularity or infinite regress
quiz.explanation: Every attempt to justify the justifiers runs into one of the three dead ends — hence competing theories of where to stop.

intro:
Nothing is closer to you than your own experience — the taste of coffee, the ache of a tooth, the felt redness of red — and nothing is harder to explain. The philosophy of mind asks how mental life fits into the physical world: whether the mind is a substance, a program, a brain process or something else entirely. This advanced lesson runs the main theories — dualism, behaviourism, identity theory, functionalism — and then the problem that has dominated the field since the 1990s: why all this processing should feel like anything at all.

**Why this matters.** The questions are no longer seminar games. Whether an artificial system could suffer, what makes a patient in a coma a person, whether octopuses deserve welfare protection, and whether free will survives neuroscience are all philosophy-of-mind questions with law, medicine and engineering budgets attached. The vocabulary you need to argue about them — dualism, functionalism, qualia — is exactly what this lesson supplies.
objectives: Explain the mind-body problem and Cartesian dualism
Explain ryle's ghost and the identity theory
Explain functionalism: mind as what the mind does
Explain the hard problem and qualia
Explain intentionality and the Chinese Room
Explain consciousness theories today

concepts.term: The mind-body problem and Cartesian dualism
concepts.statement: Descartes divided reality into thinking substance and extended substance, and immediately met the objection Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed on him in 1643: how can an unextended mind move an extended body? Causal interaction across categories is mysterious, and dualism's mechanism never recovered. Yet the intuition driving it — that experience is not obviously a physical thing — survives every attempt at burial.

concepts.term: Ryle's ghost and the identity theory
concepts.statement: Gilbert Ryle's The Concept of Mind (1949) mocked dualism as "the ghost in the machine", a category mistake: the mind is not a second thing inside the body but a pattern in what people do. Behaviourism ruled psychology for a generation; then U. T. Place and J. J. C. Smart proposed the identity theory: mental states just are brain states, as water is H2O. The analogy held until multiple realizability raised its head.

concepts.term: Functionalism: mind as what the mind does
concepts.statement: Hilary Putnam's move was to define mental states by role rather than material: pain is whatever state is typically caused by tissue damage and causes avoidance, distress and belief — an organisational job description. Minds are multiply realizable, so a functional duplicate should have the same mental life whatever it is made of, neuron or silicon. Functionalism became cognitive science's philosophical backbone, and the default answer to "what is a mind?"

In 1995 David Chalmers named the residue every functional account leaves: the hard problem of consciousness. Explaining discrimination, report and integration — the "easy" problems, hard but tractable — still does not explain why there is something it is like to undergo them. The redness of red — qualia — seems left over however complete the mechanistic story. Chalmers' thought experiment of a zombie twin, molecule-for-molecule identical yet dark inside, argues that consciousness does not logically follow from the physical facts.

John Searle's Chinese Room (1980) targeted functionalism's favourite case: a man in a room follows rules for manipulating Chinese symbols and passes for a fluent correspondent, yet understands nothing. Syntax, however elaborate, is not semantics — the mind's aboutness, its intentionality, is not symbol-shuffling. The argument is contested at every joint, but it fixed the burden of proof: show me where the understanding would be.

The present field is a bazaar. Global workspace theory (Baars, Dehaene) treats consciousness as information broadcast across the brain; integrated information theory (Tononi) assigns it a mathematical quantity, phi; Crick and Koch hunted its neural correlates; panpsychism, respectable again, treats experience as fundamental to matter, while illusionists reply that consciousness as classically conceived is the brain's user-illusion. No result is settled, and every camp claims the evidence.

Do not confuse the easy problems (functions, reports, access) with the hard problem — solving all the easy ones would not obviously touch the hard one. "Conceivable" does not straightforwardly mean "possible"; the zombie argument leans hard on that bridge. Functionalism explains cognition, not yet phenomenology — treat claims otherwise with suspicion. And beware false certainty in both directions: neither "science has explained consciousness" nor "it never can" is a report from the frontier.
Descartes' thesis that mind and body are distinct substances; strained by the interaction problem.
The view that mental states are identical to brain states, as water is identical to H2O.
The thesis that the same mental state can be realised in very different physical substrates.
The view that mental states are defined by causal role — what they do — not by their composition.
Chalmers' name for explaining why physical processing is accompanied by subjective experience at all.
The felt qualities of experience — what red looks like, what pain feels like.
Searle's 1980 argument that symbol manipulation alone is not understanding.

examples.title: Worked example — The Philosophy of Mind: Consciousness and Its Puzzles
examples.problem: Evaluate multiple realizability as an objection to identity theory.

steps.label: Recall the claim
steps.text: mental states are identical to brain states as water is identical to H2O — and identities hold necessarily, in every possible case.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: if an octopus, a hypothetical silicon system and a human can all realise pain while differing grossly in physical make-up, pain cannot be identical to any one physical state type; the identity would have to be claimed per species or per instance.

examples.result: type identity fails as a general theory, and functionalism inherits the field by defining mental states by role — though whether roles capture experience is precisely the hard problem.

keyTakeaways: AI ethics: whether machine systems could deserve moral consideration turns on functionalism versus the hard problem.
Medicine: theories of consciousness inform diagnostic standards for coma, vegetative and minimally conscious states.
Animal welfare: the 2012 Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness drew on this literature to extend moral concern across species.
Neurolaw: assessments of responsibility and conscious intent increasingly cite findings about will and awareness.
Meditation research: first-person reports are being formalised as data, reviving introspection under experimental discipline.

quiz.q: Elisabeth of Bohemia's objection to Descartes concerned…
options: how an immaterial mind could causally move a body
quiz.explanation: The interaction problem: causal commerce between unextended and extended substances is inexplicable.

quiz.q: Multiple realizability embarrasses identity theory because…
options: the same mental state seems realisable in very different physical systems
quiz.explanation: If octopus, silicon and human pains share nothing physical, pain cannot be identical to one physical state type.

quiz.q: The "hard problem" of consciousness is…
options: explaining why processing is accompanied by subjective experience at all
quiz.explanation: Chalmers' distinction: functions are hard but tractable; the existence of experience is the residue.

quiz.q: Searle's Chinese Room concludes that…
options: running the right program is not sufficient for understanding
quiz.explanation: Syntax is not semantics: symbol manipulation, however fluent, lacks the aboutness of genuine understanding.

intro:
For most of our species' time on Earth, art has been made — ochre, charcoal, carved bone — but only in the last five thousand years has anyone written about it, so the first thirty millennia must be read from the objects alone. This lesson traces the long arc from torch-lit caves to the Gothic cathedrals of the twelfth century, treating art history as the study of how images, buildings and objects carried meaning: for worship, for power, for the dead. Each era's way of seeing was also a way of thinking, and the objects are the evidence.

**Why this matters.** Walk through any museum and you are walking this arc in reverse: the same conventions — profile heads, ideal bodies, saints in glass — are still doing work in logos, film and games. Art history trains the skill of asking what an image was for, in whose interest it was made and what it assumed; no other discipline teaches you to interrogate the visible so systematically.
objectives: Explain the cave painters and their purposes
Explain egypt: art that worked forever
Explain greece: the measured ideal
Explain rome: engineering as expression
Explain the icon and the theology of light
Explain gothic: building as theology

concepts.term: The cave painters and their purposes
concepts.statement: Chauvet (found 1994, painted around 36,000 years ago) and Lascaux (found 1940, around 17,000) hold horses, lions and aurochs drawn with a fluency that destroyed the old idea of clumsy beginnings. The painters worked deep inside torch-lit chambers, grinding ochre and charcoal and sometimes exploiting the rock's own relief — which rules out mere decoration. Explanations compete: hunting magic, shamanic vision (David Lewis-Williams' theory), a mythic teaching space. The honest verdict: the purpose is lost; the skill is not.

Egyptian art ran on rules fixed early and kept for three thousand years: heads in profile, shoulders frontal, the body drawn to a canon of proportions from a fixed grid so it would read perfectly for eternity. Scale signalled rank — on the Narmer palette (c. 3100 BCE) the king is largest, the servants smallest. Art was equipment for the afterlife first and an aesthetic object barely: tomb paintings, shabti figures and the Book of the Dead were machines for continuing to live.

Greek artists pursued the ideal body with something close to mathematics. The kouros statues evolve within a century from a stiff Egyptian stance to the weight-shifted balance of contrapposto; Polykleitos' Doryphoros (c. 440 BCE) embodied his written Canon, a system of harmonious proportion. Above them rose the Parthenon (447-432 BCE), its columns subtly curved and inclined to correct the eye's own distortions — idealism, but idealism engineered.

Rome's genius was to treat engineering as art. The Pantheon (completed c. 126 CE) spans a 43.3-metre dome in unreinforced concrete — still the world's largest — with its oculus spinning sunlight around the interior; the Colosseum (80 CE) stacked the Greek orders as ornament on a concrete entertainment machine. Roman portraiture went the other way entirely: veristic busts, wrinkles and warts, the individual set against the Greek ideal.

concepts.term: The icon and the theology of light
concepts.statement: Constantine's empire moved its capital east and its art inward. Hagia Sophia (537 CE) replaced mass with light — a dome, contemporaries said, suspended from heaven by a golden chain — and gold mosaic without weight or shadow. Icons, panel paintings of Christ, the Theotokos and the saints, functioned as windows onto their prototypes; that is precisely why the iconoclast controversies (726-843) fought over whether veneration passed through the image into idolatry.

Around 1144, Abbot Suger rebuilt the abbey church of Saint-Denis outside Paris with pointed arches, ribbed vaults and walls dissolved into stained glass: lux nova, new light — his theology of divine radiance made structural. Chartres (rebuilt 1194-1220) and its successors used flying buttresses to peel the roof's thrust away from the walls, filling them instead with blue-and-red stories of salvation. The Gothic cathedral was architecture as argument: light is divine, and the building is a machine for concentrating it.

Do not read "primitive" as "beginner" — Chauvet's lions are as observant as any academy drawing. Egyptian conventions were choices, not inability: ask what the convention was for. "Gothic" began as a Renaissance insult for a style with its own rigorous logic. And keep function in view: a cathedral, an icon and a cave painting were made to work — worship, protection, memory — not to hang in museums; judging them by museum values is anachronism.
Iron-rich earth pigment, ground and heated by cave painters for a range of reds and yellows.
A fixed system of ideal bodily measure — the Egyptian grid, Polykleitos' ratios.
The weight-shifted pose that released Greek statues from frontal stiffness.
Hyper-individualised Roman portraiture, wrinkles and all, against Greek idealisation.
A panel image of holy figures, venerated as a window onto its prototype.
Suger's "new light": divine radiance entering worshipers through stained glass.
The external arch carrying a Gothic roof's thrust, freeing the wall to become glass.

examples.title: Worked example — From Caves to Cathedrals: The First Thirty Thousand Years of Art
examples.problem: Explain how the Gothic cathedral's structural innovations and its theology reinforce one another.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Recall the innovations — pointed arch, ribbed vault, flying buttress — and the theology of God-as-light, from pseudo-Dionysius through Suger.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: the pointed arch directs weight more steeply downward than the semicircular Roman arch; ribs concentrate loads onto piers; buttresses externalise the thrust, so the wall stops carrying the roof and can become glass.

examples.result: structure liberates glass, glass delivers coloured light, and Suger's inscription at Saint-Denis says it outright — the material raises the mind to truth.

keyTakeaways: Conservation science: cave-climate control at Lascaux (closed to visitors since 1963) and laser cleaning of Chartres are materials-science problems.
Archaeology: Chauvet's radiocarbon and uranium-thorium dating recalibrated the whole timeline of image-making.
Architecture education: the pointed arch and buttress logic taught in every structures course descend from Suger's masons.
Heritage disputes: the Parthenon marbles question is art history's most public ethics case.
Digital heritage: photogrammetry now records at-risk monuments, from Palmyra to Notre-Dame after the 2019 fire.

quiz.q: The paintings at Chauvet date to roughly…
quiz.explanation: Chauvet is about twice as old as Lascaux, making fluent image-making far older than was once believed.

quiz.q: Egyptian figures show the head in profile and shoulders frontal because…
options: each body part appears in its most recognisable view, serving the image's function
quiz.explanation: The canon displayed each part most legibly — clarity for eternity outranked a single moment of seeing.

quiz.q: The Pantheon's dome is remarkable because it…
options: is the tallest structure on Earth
remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever built
quiz.explanation: Forty-three metres of unreinforced Roman concrete, uncopied for nearly two millennia.

quiz.q: Abbot Suger's "lux nova" refers to…
options: the theology of divine light expressed through stained glass
quiz.explanation: At Saint-Denis, structure was theology: walls become glass so that divine light could flood the worshiper.

intro:
In the 1420s an architect demonstrated a trick for showing depth on a flat panel; within a generation painters could construct a convincing window onto three-dimensional space, and European seeing changed. This lesson follows the five-century run from Brunelleschi's perspective through the High Renaissance, the Baroque, the Impressionists' fragmentation of that window and the modernists' decision to break it — ending with abstraction and the question of what art even is. The thread is not styles succeeding styles but one long renegotiation of what a picture owes to the world.

**Why this matters.** The camera in your phone is a Renaissance instrument: its lens implements the single-point perspective that Alberti described in 1435, and every 3D game engine solves the same projection. Modern advertising, cinema and museums are equally downstream of this story. Knowing how the window was built — and then deliberately broken — is visual literacy for a culture that now spends hours a day inside engineered images.
objectives: Explain the perspective revolution
Explain high Renaissance confidence
Explain baroque theatre
Explain realism to impressionism
Explain cezanne to abstraction
Explain the question "what is art?"

concepts.statement: Filippo Brunelleschi's lost demonstration panels (c. 1420s) showed Florence's baptistery in mathematically exact recession; Leon Battista Alberti codified the method in Della pittura (1435): a single vanishing point, the picture as a window. Masaccio's Trinity fresco (c. 1427) applied it with startling illusion. Perspective was more than technique — it made the viewer's eye the measure of the world, a humanism you could draw with a ruler.

In the two decades around 1500, Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael turned technique into statement. Leonardo's Last Supper (1495-98) fixes its vanishing point in Christ's head, choreographing psychology through geometry; Michelangelo's David (1504) scales the classical ideal to civic monument; Raphael's School of Athens (1511) stages antiquity's thinkers in a perspective architecture painted for the pope who was rebuilding Rome itself.

The Counter-Reformation wanted drama, and Caravaggio supplied it: tenebrism — zones of paint-lit darkness — turning the Calling of Saint Matthew (1600) into theatre, saints in contemporary dress and dirty feet. Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa (1652) makes marble billow and swoon; Artemisia Gentileschi's Judith Slaying Holofernes lends the old subject a physical conviction no male rival matched. The Baroque is art as event, aimed at the body rather than the diagram.

The nineteenth century stripped the varnish. Courbet painted stone-breakers and rural funerals, refusing gods and goddesses; Manet's Olympia (1865) replaced the goddess with a modern Parisian and a stare. In April 1874 the painters the Salon had rejected exhibited independently, and the critic Louis Leroy mocked Monet's Impression, Sunrise (1872) — accidentally naming the movement. They painted outdoors, in broken colour, chasing light itself; the camera, freed from copying duties, had quietly changed the job description.

Paul Cezanne — "treat nature by the cylinder, the sphere, the cone" — rebuilt painting as construction, and Picasso and Braque radicalised the approach into Cubism: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) shatters the picture window into several viewpoints at once. Kandinsky exhibited largely abstract works by 1911; Malevich's Black Square (1915) and Mondrian's grids pressed further. The subject of painting was becoming painting itself — its planes, its colour, its edges.

In 1917 Marcel Duchamp submitted a urinal signed "R. Mutt" to an exhibition; Fountain asked whether art is a matter of making or of choosing and naming. The question governed the century that followed — Dada's anti-art, Warhol's Brillo boxes, conceptual works where the idea outranks the object — and defines the contemporary pluralism where a performance, an algorithm-trained image and a cave-descended painting share one conversation. The Renaissance opened a window; modern art asked who is looking, and why.

Avoid the progress myth: art history is not a race toward photographic accuracy — the Egyptians were not failing at perspective, they were succeeding at something else. "Renaissance" and "Baroque" are later labels covering mixed, overlapping practices. Impressionism was not sloppiness — broken colour was precise optics under study. And abstraction was not the death of skill: look at the drawings underneath before believing the anecdote.
The single point where parallel receding lines converge in one-point perspective.
Caravaggio's extreme chiaroscuro: small zones of light in engulfing darkness.
The official French exhibition whose rejections produced the Impressionist show of 1874.
Painting outdoors, directly before the motif — the Impressionist practice.
Unmixed strokes placed side by side so the viewer's eye blends them at distance.
Picasso and Braque's fracture of the single viewpoint into simultaneous planes.
Duchamp's category: an ordinary object chosen, signed and displaced into art.

examples.title: Worked example — Renaissance to Modernism: How Seeing Changed
examples.problem: Contrast the role of the viewer in Albertian perspective and in Cubism.

steps.label: Recall the two schemes
steps.text: perspective constructs a single fixed eye-point before a window; Cubism superimposes multiple viewpoints simultaneously.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: in Masaccio's Trinity the spectator stands where the vanishing point dictates, seeing the scene from exactly one place; in Picasso's Demoiselles, no single standpoint can account for the fractured faces — the painting shows what several positions know at once.

examples.result: the Renaissance viewer is a stable measuring eye; the modern viewer is a moving, assembling intelligence — a philosophical shift carried entirely by geometry.

keyTakeaways: Computer graphics: real-time rendering engines implement the projective geometry Alberti described; the camera lens is perspective made hardware.
Museums and the market: blockbusters and immersive digital exhibitions monetise different halves of this same tradition.
Authentication law: attribution disputes over works from Caravaggio to Warhol turn on the connoisseurship this history trains.
Photography and film: lens-based media inherited, and then escaped, the single-point perspective painting devised.
Design education: foundation courses still teach perspective, colour and composition as the grammar this tradition wrote.

quiz.q: Alberti codified single-point perspective in…
quiz.explanation: His treatise defined the picture as a window with a single vanishing point — the method Brunelleschi had demonstrated.

quiz.q: The name "Impressionism" originated as…
options: a critic's mocking review of Monet's Impression, Sunrise
quiz.explanation: Louis Leroy's 1874 sneer at "Impressionism" was adopted by the painters it mocked.

quiz.q: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) is significant as…
options: the first nude in Western art
the break toward Cubism and the shattering of single-point perspective
quiz.explanation: Picasso's brothel scene fractured space and the tradition simultaneously — the point of no return for modern art.

quiz.q: Duchamp's Fountain (1917) primarily challenged…
options: the assumption that art must be made rather than chosen and named
quiz.explanation: The ready-made relocated art from craft to selection and context — the question contemporary art still argues.

intro:
The traditions now called Hindu, Buddhist, Confucian and Daoist emerged between roughly 1500 and 400 BCE from the Ganges to the Yellow River, and today they shape the daily life of most of Asia: temple festivals, village shrines, civil-exam ethics and family ritual. Studying them descriptively — what practitioners believe, do and dispute — requires unlearning the assumption that a religion needs a single founder, creed or god. This lesson surveys the major Eastern traditions, as a scholar rather than a partisan.

**Why this matters.** A billion and a half people live inside these traditions, and their concepts now circulate globally — karma in casual English, mindfulness in clinics, yin-yang in logos. Knowing what the terms actually mean, and where the traditions disagree, is basic cultural literacy for medicine, business, diplomacy and reading the news. It is also the corrective for a century of Western caricature: "Eastern spirituality" as one bland, ancient wisdom.
objectives: Explain a shared vocabulary: dharma, karma, samsara
Explain hinduism: many paths, one aim
Explain the Buddha's diagnosis of suffering
Explain buddhism's spread and its vehicles
Explain confucius: the ethics of relationship
Explain the Dao and the art of unforced action

concepts.term: A shared vocabulary: dharma, karma, samsara
concepts.statement: Several Indian traditions share a grammar. Samsara: the cycle of birth, death and rebirth in which all sentient beings are caught. Karma: not fate but a causal principle — intentional actions, including mental ones, have consequences that shape future lives. Dharma: the order or duty that varies by tradition, and in Hindu usage by caste and stage of life. And moksha, liberation: ending the cycle altogether. Whether any self persists through the cycle is where the traditions split.

"Hinduism" is a Persian-derived umbrella (from Sindhu, the Indus) for practices consolidated over three and a half millennia: the Vedic hymns (composed c. 1500-500 BCE), the philosophical Upanishads, the epics Ramayana and Mahabharata with its Bhagavad Gita, and centuries of temple worship and devotional (bhakti) practice directed to Vishnu, Shiva and the Goddess. There is no single founder, creed or church: orthopraxy outranks orthodoxy, and schools disagree — Advaita Vedanta holds the self and ultimate reality one, dualists dissent.

The historical Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama, taught in the Ganges basin around the fifth century BCE. His Four Noble Truths form a diagnosis: life is pervaded by dukkha, suffering; it has a cause, craving; the cause can cease; and the Eightfold Path — right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration — is the way. The goal, nirvana, "blows out" the fires of greed, hatred and delusion and ends rebirth. The Buddha set aside metaphysical puzzles, comparing them to a man shot with an arrow demanding the archer's identity before accepting treatment.

After Ashoka's patronage in the third century BCE, Buddhism spread along the trade corridors described in this section's Silk Road lesson: south as Theravada into Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia; east as Mahayana, with its bodhisattvas who postpone nirvana to save others, into China, Korea and Japan; and as Vajrayana into Tibet. It receded in India by 1200 CE, absorbed by the tradition it had left; its global spread since is the newest chapter.

Kong Fuzi — Confucius, 551-479 BCE — taught amid warring states; the Analects, his remembered sayings, made social order the central task: the cultivation of ren, humaneness, through li, ritual propriety, beginning in the five relationships of ruler-subject, father-son, husband-wife, elder-younger and friend-friend. The junzi, exemplary person, is made by study and practice, not born. For two millennia Confucian learning anchored East Asian education, exams and family ethics.

concepts.term: The Dao and the art of unforced action
concepts.statement: The Daodejing, a terse classic attributed to Laozi, and the playful Zhuangzi teach the Dao — the way things move, beyond naming — and wu wei, unforced action: water yields yet carves canyons. Where Confucianism perfects the social grid, the Daoist classics distrust it, urging natural spontaneity instead. In practice the two have coexisted for two millennia: the same scholar could pass state examinations on Confucius and retire to paint mountains as a Daoist.

Do not file these as "Eastern thought", one single thing: a Theravada monk, a Shaiva priest and a Confucian scholar agree on almost nothing, including whether gods exist. Karma is not fate, and rebirth is not the transmigration of a fixed soul — Buddhism denies exactly that self. "Hinduism" as one label is barely two centuries old for three and a half millennia of practice. And keep the stance descriptive: this lesson reports what traditions claim, which is scholarly method, not endorsement or attack.
The cycle of birth, death and rebirth binding all sentient beings.
The causal principle that intentional actions condition future experience and rebirth.
Liberation from samsara — the final aim of most Indian traditions.
The Buddha's diagnosis: suffering, its cause in craving, its cessation, and the path.
The "blowing out" of greed, hatred and delusion that ends rebirth.
Confucian humaneness or co-humanity, cultivated through relationship and ritual.
Daoist unforced action, aligned with the way things naturally move.

examples.title: Worked example — Hinduism, Buddhism and the Eastern Traditions
examples.problem: Explain the difference karma makes to Buddhist ethics compared with a rule-based scheme.

steps.label: Recall the principle
steps.text: karma is a causal law, not a judge — intentional actions condition future experience, and the Eightfold Path trains intention itself.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: where a commandment tradition asks "is this act permitted?", the Buddhist question is "what mental state is this act training?" — generosity practised from compassion strengthens dispositions that ripen in this and future lives.

examples.result: Buddhist ethics is a habituation ethics of agents-in-progress across many lives — closer in spirit to Aristotle's training of character (see the virtue ethics lesson) than to a law code.

keyTakeaways: Clinical psychology: mindfulness-based stress reduction and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy are secularised Buddhist practices now in trials.
Global wellness: yoga as taught worldwide is largely posture-work extracted from a Hindu ascetic framework — a live case study in tradition change.
Education policy: mindfulness programmes in schools raise ongoing debates about extraction, context and consent.
Diplomacy and business: East Asian negotiation cultures are shaped by Confucian relational ethics and Daoist indirection.
Bioethics: Buddhist and Confucian frameworks inform organ-donation and end-of-life debates in Japan, Taiwan and Thailand.

quiz.q: In the Buddhist analysis, the cause of suffering is…
options: the caste one is born into
quiz.explanation: The second Noble Truth locates dukkha's origin in thirst or craving, which the path extinguishes.

quiz.q: Karma refers to…
options: the causal consequences of intentional actions
quiz.explanation: It is a law of moral causation — deeds, including mental acts, condition future experience.

quiz.q: Theravada and Mahayana differ chiefly on…
options: the ideal — the arhat's liberation versus the bodhisattva who delays nirvana to save others
quiz.explanation: Mahayana made the compassionate bodhisattva the model; Theravada kept the arhat's individual liberation.

quiz.q: The Confucian five relationships define…
options: a mystical union with the Dao
the social bonds through which humaneness is cultivated
quiz.explanation: Ethics begins in the family and office: ren grows through ritualised, reciprocal relationships.

intro:
Judaism, Christianity and Islam trace their family line to one figure: Abraham, the patriarch who — so Genesis and the Quran both recount — answered a call to leave his homeland for a land promised by one God. Together they count roughly four billion adherents and centuries of coexistence and crusade, studied here descriptively: texts, practices, institutions and splits. That history is inseparable from world history — law, calendars, art, war and the vocabulary of the modern West.

**Why this matters.** From weekend rhythms to courtroom oaths, from the Israel-Palestine conflict to bioethics committees, the Abrahamic framework structures much of public life on every continent. Understanding what each tradition actually claims — and where the claims interlock — is prerequisite knowledge for journalism, diplomacy, law and simply reading the news without the distortions of caricature.
objectives: Explain abraham and the covenant idea
Explain judaism: Torah, exile and rabbinic renewal
Explain christianity: from movement to creed
Explain the church divides: 1054 and 1517
Explain islam: the five pillars and the Quran
Explain shared lineage, entangled history

concepts.statement: The covenant — a binding agreement between God and a people — organises all three. In the Hebrew Bible, God promises Abraham descendants and land, seals a covenant with Israel at Sinai, its sign circumcision. Christianity reads itself as the covenant renewed through Christ; Islam presents Muhammad as restoring Abraham's pure monotheism; the Quran calls Abraham a muslim, one who submits. One ancestor, three claims to the promise.

concepts.term: Judaism: Torah, exile and rabbinic renewal
concepts.statement: Judaism's arc runs from temple to book. The Temple in Jerusalem — destroyed by Babylon in 586 BCE, rebuilt, destroyed again by Rome in 70 CE — had been the sacrificial centre; after the catastrophe, rabbinic Judaism rebuilt life around Torah study, synagogue prayer and halakha, producing the Mishnah (c. 200 CE) and the vast Talmuds. Shabbat, the weekly rest built into creation, and the festival cycle structure the year; diaspora communities carried the tradition worldwide.

Jesus of Nazareth (c. 4 BCE to c. 30 CE) preached in Galilee and Judea; after his crucifixion his followers proclaimed him risen, and Paul's missions carried the movement to Gentiles. By 313 the Edict of Milan ended Roman persecution; in 325 the Council of Nicaea fixed the creed — the Son "of one substance" with the Father — settling and creating doctrine at once. The bishop of Rome became the pope; in three centuries Christianity had travelled from sect to empire.

The church's unity was always contested. In 1054 Rome and Constantinople excommunicated each other — the Great Schism between Catholicism and Orthodoxy, driven by papal authority, language and the filioque clause added to the creed. In 1517 Martin Luther's ninety-five theses against indulgences ignited the Reformation: scripture alone, faith alone — and the printing press made it unstoppable. Protestantism fragmented further — Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Anabaptist — and the map of Europe was redrawn in blood and confession.

concepts.term: Islam: the five pillars and the Quran
concepts.statement: Islam begins with Muhammad (c. 570-632 CE), whose recitations, standardised as the Quran within decades of his death, are held to be God's speech. The hijra, his migration from Mecca to Medina in 622, opens the Islamic calendar. The five pillars structure practice: shahada (the testimony), salat (five daily prayers), zakat (alms), sawm (the Ramadan fast) and hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca). After Muhammad's death, the succession split the community — Sunnis following consensus, Shi'a following Ali's line, a division deepened most painfully at Karbala in 680.

The three faiths borrowed, fought and lived together. Islamic philosophy carried Aristotle into the Latin universities; Jewish communities flourished and suffered under both Christian and Muslim rule; medieval Spain's convivencia, destroyed in 1492, remains the standing case study. Christians and Jews are "People of the Book" (ahl al-kitab) in Islamic law. The shared scriptural core makes the resemblance genuine even where politics turned murderous: these are arguments inside one grammar — which is why they can be so intense.

Do not rank the traditions by age or truth — the scholarly stance is descriptive, and each community's self-understanding is data. "Judeo-Christian" erases Islam from a family it belongs to; "Abrahamic" can over-flatten real differences. Islam did not borrow wholesale from Judaism any more than Christianity did — each claims continuity and correction. And avoid treating the splits of 1054, 1517 and the Sunni-Shi'a divide as sudden schisms: each was centuries in the making.
A binding agreement between God and a people — the organising idea of all three faiths.
The five books of Moses, the first and most authoritative section of the Tanakh.
The rabbinic commentary tradition (Mishnah plus Gemara) governing Jewish life after the Temple's fall.
The council that fixed the creed defining the Son as "of one substance" with the Father.
The Islamic practices: testimony, prayer, alms, fasting and pilgrimage.
Muhammad's 622 CE migration from Mecca to Medina, year one of the Islamic calendar.
The Islamic succession divide: community consensus versus the line of Ali.

examples.title: Worked example — Judaism, Christianity and Islam: The Abrahamic Faiths
examples.problem: What makes the Abrahamic religions a family, despite their doctrinal disagreements?

steps.label: Recall the shared elements
steps.text: one God, a covenant structure, a prophetic line that includes Abraham and Moses, scripture, and linear sacred history.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: all three claim to continue or restore the covenant of Abraham; all read history as moving toward divine purpose rather than cycling; and each canonises the earlier tradition's figures — Moses in all three, Jesus as prophet in Islam, the Hebrew Bible as Christianity's Old Testament.

examples.result: "family" names common descent and mutual reference, not agreement — which is precisely why their disputes take the intense form they do: arguments inside one shared grammar.

keyTakeaways: Interfaith work: hospitals, militaries and prisons train Jewish, Christian and Muslim clergy for shared chaplaincy.
Law: Sabbath observance, halakha and sharia inform accommodation cases from diet to dress in secular courts.
Calendars: the common era, the Islamic hijri calendar and the Jewish lunar calendar still schedule global life and markets.
Diplomacy: Jerusalem's politics cannot be read without the shared geography of the holy that all three claim.
Art history: Islamic aniconism versus Christian icon traditions shape what each civilisation's museums hold.

quiz.q: The covenant with Abraham matters to all three faiths because…
options: each tradition claims to continue or restore it
quiz.explanation: Judaism lives the covenant of Sinai; Christianity reads it renewed in Christ; Islam restores Abraham's pure monotheism.

quiz.q: Rabbinic Judaism emerged after…
options: the Roman destruction of the Temple in 70 CE
quiz.explanation: With the sacrificial centre gone, the rabbis rebuilt Judaism around Torah, synagogue and law — the Mishnah and Talmud.

quiz.q: The Great Schism of 1054 divided…
quiz.explanation: Rome and Constantinople excommunicated each other over papal authority, language and the filioque clause.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five pillars of Islam?
quiz.explanation: The pillars are testimony, prayer, alms, fasting and pilgrimage — circumcision is customary, not one of the pillars.

intro:
Suppose you promise to visit a friend in hospital and a better invitation arrives: are you free to break the promise because the alternative evening is more pleasant, or does the promise bind you regardless of outcomes? Normative ethics asks what makes actions right and wrong, and modern debates revolve around three families: consequentialism, which judges acts by their outcomes; deontology, which judges them by duties, rights and the character of the act itself; and virtue ethics, which asks what a person of good character would do. This lesson covers the first two families and two further challengers — virtue ethics has its own lesson on Aristotle's eudaimonia.

**Why this matters.** Every serious moral dispute in public life — vaccine mandates, autonomous vehicles, whistleblowing, taxation — is implicitly a fight between these frameworks. Naming the theory behind an intuition shows exactly where you and your opponent disagree: usually over what kind of fact counts as morally relevant, not over the facts themselves.
objectives: Explain consequentialism: rightness by outcomes
Explain bentham's hedonic calculus, Mill's higher pleasures
Explain kant's categorical imperative
Explain the Euthyphro dilemma for divine command
Explain care ethics and the partiality challenge
Explain trolley cases as theory probes

concepts.statement: Consequentialism holds that the rightness of an act depends solely on the goodness of its outcomes. Its most influential form is utilitarianism, launched by Jeremy Bentham in An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789): pain and pleasure are our sovereign masters, and the right act is the one that maximizes aggregate happiness. Bentham even proposed a hedonic calculus, scoring pleasures by intensity, duration, certainty and extent. John Stuart Mill's Utilitarianism (1861) refined the doctrine, insisting that pleasures differ in quality as well as quantity — better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.

concepts.term: Bentham's hedonic calculus, Mill's higher pleasures
concepts.statement: Deontology, from the Greek deon, duty, locates rightness in the act itself. Immanuel Kant's Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785) begins from the good will, the only thing good without qualification, and expresses moral law as categorical imperatives — commands that hold unconditionally, unlike hypothetical imperatives tied to what you want. Two formulations anchor the system: act only on maxims you could will as universal laws (a lying promise fails, since universalized promising would destroy the institution), and treat persons always as ends in themselves, never merely as means.

The oldest rival framework grounds morality in the will of God: an act is right because God commands it. Plato staged its central problem in the Euthyphro (c. 399 BCE): is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because they love it? If the first, morality stands independent of divine will; if the second, it risks arbitrariness — could cruelty become right by decree? Leibniz pressed the arbitrariness worry; modern defenders such as Robert Merrihew Adams answer that God's commands track a necessarily loving nature.

concepts.term: The Euthyphro dilemma for divine command
concepts.statement: In the 1980s a third challenge arrived from psychology. Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice (1982) argued that Lawrence Kohlberg's stage theory of moral development, built on justice and abstract principle, measured one voice — the one his studies coded as male — while girls tended to reason through relationships, responsibility and context. Nel Noddings and others developed this into care ethics: morality grows out of caring relationships and responsiveness to particular others, not out of impartial formulae, a direct challenge to both systems' prized impersonality.

concepts.term: Care ethics and the partiality challenge
concepts.statement: The families divide on a clean line. Consequentialism is agent-neutral: everyone's welfare counts equally and my own projects get no special weight. Deontology is typically agent-relative: my duties and my integrity can forbid what would maximize value — Bernard Williams pressed this with his integrity objection and his case of Jim and the Indians. Trolley problems, introduced by Philippa Foot in 1967 and extended by Judith Jarvis Thomson, became the standard probe for where intuitions switch from counting lives to respecting constraints.

Utilitarianism is not egoism — the calculus counts everyone's pleasure, never just the agent's. Deontology is not legalism: duties can conflict, and Kantians debate which wins. The categorical imperative is not the golden rule — it tests universalizability, not your preferences. And the theories are lenses, not tribes: most working ethicists are pluralists who concede each framework captures something real. Treating a rival theory as monstrous is usually the first symptom of not understanding it.
The view that the rightness of an act depends solely on the value of its outcomes.
Bentham and Mill's consequentialism: the right act maximizes overall happiness or welfare.
Bentham's procedure for scoring pleasures by intensity, duration, certainty and extent.
Kant's unconditional command: act only on universalizable maxims and treat persons as ends.
Plato's question whether the good is good independently of God's commanding it.
Gilligan and Noddings' relational ethics of responsiveness, context and particular others.
Whether morality weighs everyone's interests equally or lets duties attach specially to the agent.

examples.title: Worked example — Ethics: Consequentialism, Deontology and Beyond
examples.problem: Run one case through two frameworks and see precisely where they diverge.

steps.label: The case
steps.text: a runaway trolley will kill five track workers; you can pull a lever diverting it onto a side track, where it will kill one worker — Foot's original 1967 setup.

steps.label: The utilitarian calculation
steps.text: five deaths are worse than one; with no morally relevant difference between the workers, pulling the lever maximizes expected welfare and is obligatory.

steps.label: The Kantian constraint
steps.text: the humanity formulation forbids using the one worker merely as a means to save the five, and the duty not to kill the innocent does not yield to arithmetic — so the lever stays untouched.

steps.label: Read the result
steps.text: the theories disagree not about the facts but about what kind of fact matters, outcomes versus constraints. A rule utilitarian may reply that a rule permitting such diversions still maximizes welfare, showing the debate is live inside consequentialism too.

keyTakeaways: Public policy: cost-benefit analysis, including the value of a statistical life used in transport and environmental regulation, is institutionalized utilitarianism.
Technology ethics: autonomous vehicles encode trade-offs between passengers and pedestrians — trolley problems shipped in software.
Medicine: pandemic triage protocols allocate scarce ventilators by expected benefit, then hedge with deontological safeguards against discrimination.
Business: stakeholder theory borrows Kantian language of dignity; critics reply that a firm that never weighed consequences would not survive a quarter.
Animal welfare: Peter Singer's Animal Liberation (1975) revived Bentham's question — not can they reason, but can they suffer?

quiz.q: Bentham's utilitarian standard judges actions by…
options: their tendency to maximize pleasure and minimize pain
the virtue of the agent's character
quiz.explanation: The greatest happiness principle scores acts by their contribution to aggregate pleasure — for Bentham, a matter of arithmetic.

quiz.q: Kant's humanity formulation requires that we…
options: treat persons always as ends in themselves, never merely as means
follow the rule a virtuous person would follow
obey the commands of a loving God
quiz.explanation: Persons have a dignity beyond price; using one merely as an instrument is for Kant the paradigm moral error.

quiz.q: The Euthyphro dilemma challenges divine command theory by asking…
options: whether the good is good independently of God's commanding it
quiz.explanation: Either morality pre-exists the command, or it becomes arbitrary — both horns trouble a simple command theory.

quiz.q: Gilligan's In a Different Voice (1982) argued that Kohlberg's stages…
options: privileged justice reasoning and missed a voice of care and relationship
quiz.explanation: Gilligan found that reasoning through relationships and responsibility was being scored as less developed rather than differently developed.

intro:
Western philosophy is not the only tradition to have argued systematically about reality, self and knowledge. Between roughly 800 BCE and 500 CE, India and China produced systems of extraordinary rigor — debates over whether the self exists, what language can capture, and how to live, conducted through arguments rather than revelation. This lesson treats them as philosophy: claims defended with reasons. It focuses on metaphysics and argument; the practices and social history of the same traditions are covered in the lesson on Eastern religions.

**Why this matters.** These systems are not museum pieces. Advaita's analysis of consciousness, Madhyamaka arguments against essences and Confucian role ethics are active participants in contemporary philosophy of mind, ethics and cognitive science — and they reopen questions you thought were settled, such as whether there is a self to be found at all.
objectives: Explain brahman and atman in the Upanishads
Explain shankara's Advaita non-dualism
Explain the Buddha's argument against a self
Explain nagarjuna and emptiness
Explain confucian role ethics and rectified names
Explain daoist wu wei and perspectivism

concepts.term: Brahman and atman in the Upanishads
concepts.statement: The Upanishads (c. 800-200 BCE), dialogues appended to the Vedic ritual texts, ask what underlies world and self. Their central claim: Brahman, ultimate reality, is identical with atman, the innermost self — the formula tat tvam asi, you are that, spoken by the sage Uddalaka to his son Svetaketu in the Chandogya Upanishad. Yajnavalkya in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad locates the self in consciousness itself, present through waking, dream and deep sleep, and teaches by subtraction: neti, neti — not this, not this.

Shankara (eighth century CE) systematized this inheritance into Advaita Vedanta: reality is non-dual, and the appearance of many things is the work of ignorance, avidya. His argument is one of adequacy: a changing world can be experienced only against an unchanging witness of awareness, and that witness cannot itself become an object. Rivals inside Vedanta dissented — Ramanuja's eleventh-century Vishishtadvaita held that selves and world are real, though inseparable from God: a structured unity, not a featureless one.

concepts.term: The Buddha's argument against a self
concepts.statement: The Buddha (fifth century BCE) turned the analysis against the self. In the anatta doctrine a person is only five aggregates — body, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness — and none is a permanent owner. The argument runs from control and impermanence: anything genuinely self would be stable and obedient, and nothing observed is. The Milindapanha adds the chariot: no single part is the chariot, nor the parts apart from their arrangement — a person is a name for a process, not a substance hidden inside it. Nagarjuna (c. 150 CE) radicalized this into emptiness, sunyata: in the Mulamadhyamakakarika he argues that whatever arises dependently lacks intrinsic essence — emptiness means absence of independent existence, not a void.

Confucian philosophy, from the Analects (fifth century BCE), is an ethics without a metaphysical self: what you are is constituted by your roles and relations. Its doctrine of the rectification of names, zhengming, is a logic of social reality — government fails when a father does not act as a father, a ruler as a ruler. Two heirs split on human nature: Mencius (372-289 BCE) argued we have inborn sprouts of compassion that ritual cultivation grows into virtue; Xunzi (c. 310-235 BCE) countered that nature is unruly and ritual is deliberate artifice — the debate that organized Chinese ethics for two millennia.

concepts.term: Confucian role ethics and rectified names
concepts.statement: The Daoist classics argue in the opposite direction. The Daodejing opens by surrendering language: a Dao that can be spoken is not the constant Dao, since naming carves what is intrinsically whole. Zhuangzi (fourth century BCE) dramatizes perspectivism — the butterfly dream asks what grounds your certainty of being a man who dreamed he was a butterfly rather than the reverse — and the butcher Cook Ding embodies wu wei: skill so aligned with the grain of things that effort disappears, a proto-analysis of expert coping.

Do not file these as timeless wisdom rather than arguments — Shankara and Nagarjuna are as analytically demanding as any scholastic. Emptiness is not nothingness: denying essences is not denying tables. Advaita is one school of Vedanta, not Hindu philosophy as a whole, which also contains fierce dualists and theists. And Eastern philosophy is a surveyor's convenience — the Kyoto school in Japan and Islamic falsafa lie east of these systems and belong to none of them. Keep this lesson's arguments and the religions lesson's practices in view together: two lenses, not rivals.
Ultimate reality in the Upanishads — the one existence and consciousness underlying plurality.
The innermost self; Upanishadic non-dualism identifies it with Brahman (tat tvam asi).
The Buddha's no-self doctrine: persons are processes of five aggregates, not owners of a soul.
Nagarjuna's emptiness — absence of intrinsic, independent existence; things arise dependently.
Confucian rectification of names: social order requires that names and conduct match.
Daoist unforced action: effective doing aligned with how things naturally move.
Mencius's innate tendencies — compassion, shame, deference, discernment — that cultivation grows into virtue.

examples.title: Worked example — Eastern Philosophy: The Great Systems
examples.problem: Does the person have a soul — a permanent, independent self?

steps.label: Recall the framework
steps.text: the Buddhist analysis of the five aggregates and the Milindapanha's chariot argument.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: search each aggregate in turn — body, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. None is permanent, none fully controllable, none findable apart from the process; the self cannot be located as a part, and apart from the parts there is no person left over, just as no chariot exists over and above its wheels and axle.
