Explain memos, circulars and notices
Explain email etiquette for institutional contexts
Explain the précis: one-third rule, own words, title

concepts.statement: Sender's address, date, receiver's name/address, subject line, salutation, body, complimentary close, signature block. The body runs purpose → particulars → action requested: what you want, the facts that justify it, and exactly what the reader should do, with dates and account or reference numbers concrete.

Address the reader by name ("Dear Ms Rao") and close "Yours sincerely"; address the office ("Dear Sir or Madam") and close "Yours faithfully". The close mirrors the salutation — the single most-tested convention in letter formats.

The formality level of vocabulary and grammar. Formal register: no contractions, no slang or idioms, no emotive language, measured modals ("I would be grateful if you could…"), complete sentences, concrete nouns. Courtesy is strategic: firmness about the remedy, politeness about the person.

Internal one-page instruments. A memo has a header block — To, From, Date, Subject — no salutation, one topic, and an explicit action line with a deadline. A circular broadcasts one announcement to many readers; a notice posts an event with time, place and authority. All three prize brevity and scannability.

A subject line that names the topic, a greeting and sign-off even in short notes, one topic per email, paragraphs that survive a two-second skim, attachments named and mentioned in the text, cc reserved for people who need to know, reply-all restraint, and no typing in capitals — the written equivalent of shouting.

A faithful condensation of a passage to roughly one-third of its length, in the précis-writer's own words, keeping the argument and dropping examples, repetition and digression, written in the third person, with a title. The test is whether a reader of the précis alone would leave with the passage's claims and none of its padding.

concepts.term: Formal letter anatomy: block layout, salutation, close
concepts.statement: The formal letter is the genre's backbone, and its layout is a convention you simply own. Top left: the sender's address (no name above your own address in the block style), then the date; below, the receiver's name, designation and address; then a subject line that names the business in a phrase — "Request for stop-payment on cheque no. 441207" — because the subject line is how the letter gets routed and retrieved. The salutation mirrors your knowledge of the reader: "Dear Sir or Madam" when unknown (closing "Yours faithfully"), "Dear Ms Rao" when named (closing "Yours sincerely"). The first paragraph states the purpose in one sentence; the middle paragraphs carry the particulars — dates, amounts, reference numbers, what happened, what you have already tried; the final paragraph states the action sought and a courteous deadline. Sign, then print your name below. Every part exists because someone downstream files, routes or acts on it.

Three letter types cover most exam and desk situations. The enquiry letter asks: it frames the question precisely, states what you already know, and closes with the specific information requested and the response channel. The complaint letter escalates politely: facts first (date, time, place, transaction reference), then the problem's effect, then the remedy sought — refund, correction, replacement — then a deadline and the escalation path if it passes ("I shall refer the matter to the Banking Ombudsman under the RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme if unresolved within thirty days"). Never insult; the reader is rarely the person who caused the problem. The application letter sells: the position and its source in the first line, the fit in the second paragraph (two or three proof-points drawn from the advertisement's own language), availability, and a request for interview. All three share the register rules: formal, concrete, courteous — and all three end with an unmistakable ask.

Internal instruments trade ceremony for speed. The memo strips to a header — To, From, Date, Subject — and a body that does one job: announce, explain, request. Its discipline is the one-topic rule and the action line ("Please send the Q2 figures to me by Thursday, 5 p.m."); anything that needs discussion is a meeting, not a memo. Circulars broadcast one announcement to many — an office holiday, a policy change — written once for simultaneous reading, with dates and authority named. Notices post events for a public board: heading, date, body with the five Ws, signature of the authority. Email then carries all of it at internet speed, which is precisely why its conventions matter more, not less: the subject line is the envelope, the greeting and sign-off are the clothes, the two-second-skim paragraph structure is the body language, and reply-all restraint is the office citizenship test. An email that says what its attachment is, asks exactly one question, and names its deadline replaces three phone calls.

The précis is the odd instrument of the family — an act of reading as much as writing — and it has its own discipline. Read the passage thrice: once for sense, once to mark the argument's skeleton (thesis, moves, conclusion), once to choose your own words. Compress to about one-third — the ratio is tested — by deleting examples, illustrations, repetition, rhetorical questions and digressions, and by folding lists into categories. Keep the third person and your own words: lifted phrases read as failure to understand. Preserve proportion (the passage spends most words on its main claim; so should you) and add a title — a phrase that names the argument. The mark scheme in banking and administrative papers scores content (all main points, nothing invented), organisation (logical, linked), language (accurate, own words) and the one-third discipline; a précis that is merely a copy with words crossed out scores none of them.

Pairing "Dear Sir or Madam" with "Yours sincerely" — the close mirrors the salutation, and this is the most-tested convention on the paper. Writing complaints in anger: emotive language converts a fixable error into a defensive reader; facts, references and a deadline do the work. Letting memos grow salutations and second topics — the header replaces the salutation and the one-topic rule is the point. Treating email as casual by default — institutional email keeps greeting, sign-off, subject discipline and reply-all restraint. Breaking the précis ratio (a "summary" of 250 words from 300), lifting the original's phrases, inventing claims the passage never made, or forgetting the title — each is a named mark-scheme deduction. And burying the ask: every letter, memo and email must end with an unmistakable action for a named reader by a stated time.

examples.title: Worked Example — A Complaint Letter That Gets a Refund
examples.problem: Business Correspondence: Formal Letters, Memos, Email and the Précis — worked through step by step

steps.label: Collect the facts before writing
steps.text: ATM ID, branch, date and time (14 October 2026, 11:42 a.m.), amount debited (2,000) without cash dispensed, transaction reference number from the slip or alert, account number.

steps.label: Lay out the letter
steps.text: sender address, date, the Branch Manager's designation and branch address, subject line "Complaint regarding ATM debit without cash dispensation — A/c no. 0123…".

steps.label: Open with purpose
steps.text: "I wish to report a failed ATM transaction in which my account was debited but no cash was dispensed."

steps.label: Paragraph of particulars
steps.text: the machine, the time, the amount, the reference number, the fact that the card was returned and no alert credit followed — the evidence trail.

steps.label: State the remedy and the clock
steps.text: "I request reversal of the erroneous debit within the prescribed timeline; failing which I shall escalate to the Banking Ombudsman under the Reserve Bank's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021." Close "Yours faithfully" — the salutation was "Dear Sir or Madam".

steps.label: Précis check on any draft
steps.text: facts kept, adjectives deleted, third person if summarising the episode for a file, title "Failed ATM Transaction and Refund Request" — one-third length.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: none — though the punctuation-mechanics lesson polishes the surface of everything written here. Follow with the argument-essay lesson for the long-form descriptive paper and the cohesion lesson for paragraph-level flow. Primary reading: Business Communication for Success (Open Textbook Library / LibreTexts — the communication process, channel choice, and professional letter/memo conventions read directly); RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021 complaint-route pages (cms.rbi.org.in) for the banking escalation path used in the worked example; NCERT/CBSE functional-writing conventions for the block-layout letter and précis mark schemes used in Indian descriptive papers.
Letter anatomy: sender address, date, receiver, subject line (routes the letter), salutation, purpose → particulars → action, close, signature.
Close mirrors salutation: named reader → "Yours sincerely"; office → "Yours faithfully".
Register: no contractions, no slang, no emotives; concrete nouns and reference numbers; firm on remedy, courteous on people.
Three letters: enquiry (asks precisely), complaint (facts → effect → remedy → deadline → escalation), application (position-source → fit → availability).
Internal instruments: memo (To/From/Date/Subject, one topic, action line), circular (one announcement to many), notice (five Ws, authority).
Email: subject names the topic, greeting/sign-off always, one question, attachment named, reply-all restraint. Précis: one-third, own words, third person, titled, proportion kept.

quiz.q: Your letter begins "Dear Sir or Madam". The correct complimentary close is…
quiz.explanation: Unnamed recipient ("Dear Sir or Madam") pairs with "Yours faithfully"; a named recipient ("Dear Ms Rao") pairs with "Yours sincerely".

quiz.q: What does the subject line of a business letter most directly enable?
options: routing and retrieval of the letter
quiz.explanation: The subject line names the business in a phrase so that the letter can be routed to the right desk and retrieved later — which is why it should carry reference numbers.

quiz.q: The correct one-topic discipline for a memo requires all of the following EXCEPT…
options: an explicit action line with a deadline
quiz.explanation: Memos drop the salutation — the header block replaces it; they keep one topic and end in a clear action line.

quiz.q: A précis of a 300-word passage should be roughly…
options: 100 words, in the writer's own words, with a title
75 words, in the original's best phrases
the full argument re-copied with examples removed
quiz.explanation: The tested ratio is one-third — 100 words for 300 — in the writer's own words and in the third person, with a title, keeping claims and dropping examples and digressions.

quiz.q: In a complaint letter about a failed ATM transaction, the escalation line citing the RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme serves to…
options: state the consequence of missing the remedy deadline
quiz.explanation: Escalation is stated as a consequence — polite, factual, dated — not as a threat; the evidence trail (reference numbers, dates) still does the real work.

intro:
Punctuation is not decoration; it is the traffic system of a sentence. Every mark either separates things that must not blur together — items in a list, clauses with different jobs — or signals the relationship between them: cause, aside, possession, omission. Standardised English tests treat the marks as a closed set of rules with predictable distractors, which makes mechanics one of the highest-yield skills on the paper: a handful of distinctions, tested over and over, with no ambiguity once the underlying grammar is visible. This lesson builds that grammar-first view: find the clause boundary or the possessor first, then choose the mark.

**Why this matters.** Mechanics questions are the most mechanical points on an English or writing section — literally. The tested rules are finite, the wrong options recur (the comma splice, the possessive its, the colon after an incomplete clause), and every rule here transfers to every essay you will ever write. There is no other topic with this ratio of learnable rules to marks available.
objectives: Explain commas: lists, clauses, appositives
Explain comma splices and how to fix them
Explain semicolons join independent clauses
Explain colons announce what follows
Explain apostrophes: possession versus contraction
Explain its versus it’s, whose versus who’s
Explain dashes for interruption, parentheses for aside
Explain unnecessary punctuation as an error class

concepts.statement: A group of words with a subject and a verb that can stand alone as a sentence. Every comma and semicolon rule is stated against this unit: what separates two of them, what cannot, and what a comma is allowed to do inside one.

Two independent clauses joined by only a comma — "The results were clear, the study ended early." Fix by period, semicolon, or a coordinating conjunction after the comma. Tests present this constantly, dressed as style; it is a grammar error with three legal repairs.

Joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction, or separates complex list items that already contain commas. Neither side may be a fragment: if what follows the semicolon cannot stand alone, the mark is wrong.

Announces: a list, an explanation, a quotation — but only after a complete independent clause. "The trial had one flaw: no control group." Compare the wrong "The flaw was: no control group", where the clause before the colon is incomplete.

Marks possession (the study’s findings) or omission in a contraction (doesn’t). Never marks a simple plural. Pronouns have their own possessive forms without apostrophes — its, whose, their — so "the team lost it’s lead" doubles an error: wrong word and wrong logic.

Parentheses tuck away an aside the sentence survives without; dashes punch it into view and can also set off an abrupt turn. On tests the choice between dash pair and parenthesis pair usually turns on emphasis, but both marks must come in pairs when both sides are removable.

A tested error class of its own: a comma between subject and verb, between verb and object, or after a coordinating conjunction joining clauses. The mark is wrong because no grammatical boundary exists at that point — no rule licenses inserting one.

The comma rules compress into four questions. Is it a list? Use commas between items, and note that a comma before the final and is the serial comma — a house-style choice, not a tested error either way, unless the list items themselves would blur. Is it two independent clauses? Then a comma alone is illegal; it needs a conjunction or must yield to a semicolon. Does the clause open the sentence? An introductory phrase or subordinate clause takes a comma before the main clause begins. Is it extra information? An appositive or non-essential modifier takes a comma pair — and the pair is the test: if the sentence loses nothing when the between-commas material is lifted out, the commas belong there; if lifting it breaks the meaning, the clause is essential and takes no commas.

concepts.term: Comma splices and how to fix them
concepts.statement: Test strategy leans on one habit: locate the grammatical joints before reading the options. Find the subjects and verbs; mark the clause boundaries; decide whether a modifier is essential. With the joints mapped, most mechanics questions collapse — three of four options violate a rule you can name, and the correct answer follows from the boundary, not from ear. Read-aloud checks catch rhythm but not rules: tests deliberately include options that sound smooth and violate a boundary, and options that sound stiff and are correct.

The recurring traps: trusting rhythm over clause structure — splice-heavy prose sounds natural in speech; apostrophising every plural ending in s; using a colon after an incomplete clause; and deleting only one dash or parenthesis of a pair, leaving an unbalanced aside. Also beware the "correct but unnecessary" distractor: a mark can be wrong not because it breaks a rule but because no boundary exists for it to mark.

examples.title: Four sentences, four decisions
examples.problem: Punctuation Mechanics: Commas, Semicolons, Apostrophes and Dashes — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: "The experiment failed the sample was contaminated." Two independent clauses, no mark: a fused sentence. Legal repairs — semicolon ("failed; the sample"), comma plus conjunction ("failed, because the sample..." making the second part subordinate), or a period. A bare comma remains illegal.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: "The study which took three years was published." The modifier is non-essential — the study is identified without it — so it needs a comma pair: "The study, which took three years, was published." No commas would only be right if the clause were essential: "Any study which takes three years deserves funding."

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: "The lab published its findings; it’s clear the samples were its’." First its: correct possessive pronoun. Second it’s: contraction of it is, correct in place. Third: wrong — possessive pronouns never take apostrophes.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: "The report had one recommendation: retrain every analyst." Colon legal — a complete clause precedes it. Compare "The recommendation was: retrain..." — the preceding verb phrase is not an independent clause, so the colon fails.

keyTakeaways: Before: any reading-strategy lesson — mechanics questions reward the same slow, structural reading.
Next: Paired Passages and Authorial Choices — the reading half of the same sections.
Revision cue: take any paragraph and name the job of every mark; the ones you cannot justify are your gap list.
Find the clause boundaries first; the marks follow from the grammar.
Comma splices are illegal — repair with semicolon, conjunction or period.
Colons need a complete clause before them; semicolons need one on each side.
Apostrophes mark possession or omission, never plain plurals; its and whose are already possessive.
Unnecessary punctuation is an error class: no boundary, no mark.

quiz.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The trial ended early, the data was inconclusive.
The trial ended early; the data was inconclusive.
The trial ended early; and the data was inconclusive.
The trial, ended early; the data was inconclusive.
quiz.explanation: Two independent clauses: the semicolon joins them legally. Option 1 is a comma splice; option 3 puts a conjunction after a semicolon with no second list item to justify it; option 4 splits a subject from its verb.

quiz.q: Where does a colon belong: "The design had one weakness ( ) no control group."?
options: nowhere — this sentence cannot take a colon
quiz.explanation: The clause "The design had one weakness" is complete, so a colon can announce the appositive explanation. No other position follows a complete clause.

quiz.q: Which pair uses apostrophes correctly?
options: The committee published it's report; who's responsible is unclear.
The committee published its report; who's responsible is unclear.
The committee published its' report; whose responsible is unclear.
The committee published it's report; whose responsible is unclear.
quiz.explanation: Its is the possessive pronoun; who’s is the contraction of who is. The possessive forms its and whose never take apostrophes.

quiz.q: "My supervisor who studied in Nairobi reviewed the draft." The error is:
options: a missing pair of commas, if the clause is non-essential
no error — the sentence is correct as written
quiz.explanation: If the writer has only one supervisor, the clause is extra information and needs a comma pair. With several supervisors, the clause identifies which one and takes no commas — the essential/non-essential test decides.

intro:
Paired-passage sets hand you two texts on the same question and then ask about each of them — and, more treacherously, about their relationship. The skill is bookkeeping under time pressure: for each passage separately, hold the author’s view, the evidence offered, and the tone; only then model the relationship — do they agree, disagree, address different questions, or one qualify the other? Reading tests also probe the craft beneath the content: why this structural choice, why that word, what is the author doing by opening with an anecdote. Those authorial-choice questions reward the same habit from the other direction: treating every textual feature as a decision with a purpose.

**Why this matters.** Paired sets carry double the questions of a single passage, and the cross-passage items are where reading sections are designed to separate scores: the wrong answers are built from true statements about the wrong text. The authorial-choice items, meanwhile, reward a reusable lens — every paragraph you read anywhere can be asked what it is doing, not just what it says.
objectives: Explain per-passage reading: view, evidence, purpose
Explain relationship classes: agree, qualify, oppose, extend
Explain point-of-view attribution in paired texts
Explain authorial choices: structure, diction, tone
Explain purpose questions and the evidence behind them
Explain cross-passage traps: similarity is not agreement
Explain annotating for the questions, not the content

concepts.statement: After reading Passage 1, one sentence in your own words: "P1: author believes X, because Y, tone Z." Do the same for Passage 2 before touching the cross-passage questions. Every relationship item is answered from these two lines, not by rereading both texts in a panic.

The standard taxonomy of paired texts: agreement (same conclusion), opposition (direct conflict), qualification (P2 accepts P1 in part, limits it in part), extension (P2 develops P1’s point further), independence (different questions, no real contact). Most wrong options mislabel the class — an extension misread as disagreement, a qualification misread as full agreement.

In paired sets, knowing WHO holds a view is half the marks. Both authors quote experts and cite critics; an option that credits P2’s author with P1’s cited scientist’s claim is a classic trap. Anchor every claim to its holder: the author, the author’s source, or the author’s opponents.

A deliberate craft decision: opening with a scene, repeating a phrase, choosing "claimed" over "showed", structuring as problem-then-response. The testable claim is function — what the choice does to the reader’s understanding or attitude — never just a description of the feature itself.

Tone answers must be provable from word choice: "measured" because the author hedges with might and some, "admiring" because the adjectives are uniformly positive. If you cannot point to two or three words that create the tone, the answer is an inference too far.

Two passages can share facts, cite the same study, even share values, and still disagree about the conclusion those facts support. The relationship question is about claims, not topics: agreement requires the same bottom line, not the same subject matter.

The workflow that survives time pressure is strict passage-first ordering. Read Passage 1 and its own questions before starting Passage 2 — most formats allow this and it halves the working-memory load. When the cross-passage questions arrive, answer them from the two summary lines: the relationship class first, then verify with one line-location per passage. For authorial-choice items, translate the question into function language before looking at options — "why does the author list three failed attempts?" becomes "what does the list establish?" — and then reject any option that merely restates content ("to describe three attempts") rather than naming the function ("to show the problem resisted easy solutions, setting up the breakthrough").

concepts.term: Relationship classes: agree, qualify, oppose, extend
concepts.statement: The same machinery powers per-passage analysis in argument-heavy sets. "Analyzing each passage in the pair" items ask what each text is doing at a given point — conceding, pivoting, dismissing a rival reading — and reward labelling paragraphs by function as you read: background, evidence, counterargument, rebuttal. A pair read this way yields the relationship for free: two texts whose final paragraphs are rebuttal-shaped are usually in opposition; one that ends by granting the other’s strongest point before narrowing its claim is a qualification. Structure is the fastest honest signal of relationship, faster than hunting for vocabulary of agreement and disagreement.

Three recurring losses: reading both passages together from the start and blending the views into one hybrid author; answering cross-passage items from memory instead of the summary lines, which is exactly how true-statements-about-the-wrong-text get chosen; and answering choice questions with content restatement — "the author mentions X" is never the function of mentioning X. A fourth, quieter one: treating a shared topic as shared ground.

examples.title: Mapping a disagreement set
examples.problem: Paired Passages and Authorial Choices: Reading Two Texts at Once — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Passage 1 argues rewilding projects succeed when they restore a single keystone species; evidence: two reserves where reintroduced predators rebalanced ecosystems. Tone: confident, promotional.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Passage 2 argues the same projects fail when exported carelessly; evidence: one reserve where a reintroduced predator devastated naive prey. Tone: cautious, corrective.

steps.label: Summary lines
steps.text: P1 keystone restoration works; P2 keystone restoration is fragile and context-bound. Both accept keystone importance — the disagreement is about generalising.

steps.label: Relationship class
steps.text: qualification, not opposition. P2 does not claim keystone restoration is wrong; it limits the scope of P1’s success claim.

steps.label: Trap option
steps.text: "P2 rejects the scientific basis of P1" — no: P2 cites the same mechanism. Another: "Both agree rewilding is always beneficial" — no: P2’s existence is a caveat.

steps.label: Step 6
steps.text: Authorial-choice item on P2’s single-example structure: the function is to undercut generalisation — one vivid failure counts as evidence about the danger of exporting results, which is exactly the passage’s thesis.

keyTakeaways: Before: Skimming and Scanning for Timed Reading — the locating skills this lesson builds on.
Next: Applying Principles — the reasoning half of the same verbal sections.
Revision cue: take any two editorials on one question and write the two summary lines plus the relationship class.
Summarise each passage separately before modelling any relationship.
Relationship classes: agree, oppose, qualify, extend, independent.
Anchor every claim to its holder — author, source or opponent.
Authorial-choice answers name functions, not content.
Structure, especially the endings, is the fastest relationship signal.

quiz.q: Passage 1: social media harms teen attention. Passage 2: the evidence is weaker than claimed, but heavy use correlates with worse sleep. What is the relationship?
options: full agreement — both criticise social media
qualification — P2 partly accepts, partly limits P1’s claim
independence — the passages address different topics
quiz.explanation: P2 accepts that some harm exists (sleep pathway) but rejects the strength of the general claim — the signature of qualification. Shared topic is not agreement; scepticism is not defence.

quiz.q: An authorial-choice question asks why the author opens Passage 1 with a farmer’s anecdote. The best answer will:
options: describe what happens in the anecdote
name the function: grounding an abstract claim in a concrete stakeholder
state whether the anecdote is literally true
quiz.explanation: Choice questions test function. Content restatement is the built-in distractor; truth-value is irrelevant; the conclusion is a different question.

quiz.q: In a paired set, an option says "P2’s author would agree that reserve reintroductions are risk-free." The summary lines say P2: reintroductions are fragile. The option is:
options: correct — P2 discusses risks so it must accept the opposite
correct — both passages cite the same scientists
wrong — it contradicts P2’s stated position
undeterminable — the passages never mention risk
quiz.explanation: The summary line settles it: fragility is the opposite of risk-free. Shared citations do not transfer agreement, and the passages plainly do discuss risk.

quiz.q: The fastest honest signal for a relationship question under time pressure is:
options: the structural shape of each text’s ending — rebuttal, concession, extension
how many sources each author cites
quiz.explanation: Endings carry the claim: a rebuttal ending signals opposition, a conceding-then-narrowing ending signals qualification. Shared vocabulary is topical, not logical.

intro:
Some reasoning questions hand you a rule instead of a fact-pattern to evaluate: a principle — "public resources should go where they do the most good" — and a set of cases, asking which case the principle justifies, or which principle best explains a decision already made. The skill is neither arithmetic nor reading comprehension but structured matching: extract exactly what the principle requires, permits and excludes, then test each case against that scope. It is the everyday grammar of policy, law and professional ethics — the same operation, at tiny scale, that courts and regulators perform when they fit a rule to a situation.

**Why this matters.** Principle questions are where strong readers still lose marks, because the wrong options are attractive sentences — humane, sensible, plausible — that simply fall outside the principle’s scope. Learning to test scope mechanically converts a vibes exercise into a checklist, and the same checklist is the core of professional judgement in every field that runs on written rules.
objectives: Explain principles: general norms stated in words
Explain matching scope: what the principle covers
Explain justify-the-action and conform-to questions
Explain the most-principled-action standard
Explain underlying-principle extraction
Explain scope traps: too broad, too narrow, wrong domain
Explain counterexample testing

concepts.statement: A general normative statement — what ought to be done, valued or prioritised — not a fact. "Libraries should be free at the point of use" prescribes; "libraries cost cities money" describes. Principle questions test movement between the general norm and particular cases.

The principle is given; the task is to find the case it genuinely supports. The winning option must be covered by the principle’s terms — the right actor, the right kind of resource, the right kind of benefit — not merely made more attractive by it.

The case is given; the task is to name the principle that best explains it. The correct principle must fit the decision’s actual hinge, not a peripheral feature: if the decision turned on avoiding harm, a principle about efficiency is wrong even if efficiency was present.

The range of cases a principle covers, fixed by its words. "Children should be vaccinated" covers children, not adults; "public libraries should be free" covers public libraries, not museums. Most wrong options fail here — either stretching the scope (too broad) or shrinking it by importing conditions the principle never stated (too narrow).

When several options are defensible, the question is comparative: which action is most justified by the principle’s terms. A tie means you have misread scope — usually one option fits a further element of the principle the others ignore.

The quickest scope check: try to construct a case inside the option’s wording that the principle would not cover, or a case the principle clearly covers that the option excludes. If the option survives both directions, it matches.

concepts.term: Principles: general norms stated in words
concepts.statement: The mechanical procedure has four steps. One: restate the principle as actor + action + beneficiary + condition, marking every qualifier — only, always, public, direct. Two: do the same for each candidate case. Three: align element by element; a mismatch on any marked qualifier disqualifies. Four: when two options survive, prefer the one that accounts for more of the principle’s content — the residual difference is usually the test-maker’s intended discriminator. Throughout, resist importing your own principles: the question is what THIS principle commits you to, and the answer may be a policy you personally dislike.

concepts.term: Matching scope: what the principle covers
concepts.statement: Reverse-direction questions — extracting the principle a decision rests on — reward the same ledger read backwards. Ask: what general rule, if accepted, would make THIS choice the right one and neighbouring choices wrong? A hospital that triages by survivability rather than by queue position acts on the principle that scarce treatment should maximise lives saved — not on principles about seniority, payment or compassion that might also be present in the scene. The distractors in these items are principles that are true, even admirable, but orthogonal to the decision’s hinge; the counterexample test exposes them, because you can vary the orthogonal factor and watch the decision stay fixed.

The big four: importing your own values and answering what should be rather than what this principle licenses; ignoring single-word qualifiers like only and always that carry the entire scope; letting the actor slide — a principle about what governments should do says nothing about private firms; and mistaking a true-but-irrelevant principle for the underlying one in reverse-direction items. Name the failed element in every rejection and the method stays honest.

examples.title: Scope alignment on a funding principle
examples.problem: Applying Principles: From Rule to Case — worked through step by step

steps.label: Principle
steps.text: "A city should fund preventive health programmes only when they reach populations that lack alternatives." Marked elements: city (actor); fund preventive health (action); only (exclusive condition); lack alternatives (condition on recipients).

steps.label: Case A
steps.text: funding a rural mobile clinic serving villages with no pharmacy. Actor: city — assume a city-run programme counts. Recipients lack alternatives. Covered.

steps.label: Case B
steps.text: funding a downtown gym subsidy for office workers with three nearby gyms. Action fits (preventive health) but "lack alternatives" fails. Not covered.

steps.label: Case C
steps.text: a private charity funding night clinics. The action and condition fit, but the actor is not the city — the principle says nothing about what charities should do. Not covered.

steps.label: Case D
steps.text: funding an ambulance service — emergency care, not prevention. Wrong action class. Not covered.

steps.label: Answer
steps.text: A alone. Note how each rejection names one failed element — that named-element habit is what makes the method fast under exam conditions.

keyTakeaways: Before: the critical-reasoning lesson — argument anatomy is the substrate principles live in.
Next: Paired Passages and Authorial Choices — the same sections’ reading half.
Then: Situational Judgement — principle application applied to professional dilemmas.
Revision cue: take one household rule and map its scope: actor, action, conditions, boundaries.
Restate principles as actor + action + beneficiary + conditions.
Mark qualifiers — only, always, public — they are the scope.
Justify questions: the case must be covered, not flattered.
Underlying-principle questions: match the decision’s hinge.
Counterexample tests at both boundaries expose wrong options fast.

quiz.q: Principle: "Schools should teach coding only with tools students can use at home." Which action does it justify?
options: A school teaching coding with licensed classroom-only software
A school teaching coding with free browser-based tools
A library running evening coding classes for adults
quiz.explanation: The browser tools are usable at home — the only condition is satisfied, and the actor and action fit. Classroom-only software violates the condition; the library changes the actor; the ban acts on nothing the principle permits.

quiz.q: A council reroutes buses to serve a new hospital despite longer average commutes. The underlying principle is best captured as:
options: public transport should minimise total travel time
transport should prioritise access to essential services
buses should follow the shortest physical routes
hospitals should be built near city centres
quiz.explanation: The decision accepts longer commutes to reach an essential service — the hinge is access priority, not efficiency (A and B’s rival), route mechanics or planning advice.

quiz.q: The fastest test for whether an option is covered by a principle is:
options: whether you can build a counterexample at either boundary of its wording
whether the option restates the principle verbatim
quiz.explanation: Boundary counterexamples expose scope mismatches — a case the option covers but the principle excludes, or vice versa. Attractiveness and popularity are precisely what distractors trade on.

quiz.q: Two options both fit the principle. The tie-breaking habit is:
options: pick the one that satisfies more of the principle’s stated elements
pick the first one you read
pick the one with more conditions added
quiz.explanation: When a true tie seems to occur, one option usually honours an extra marked element (only, direct, public) that the other ignores — the intended discriminator.

intro:
Forty minutes, at least 250 words, and a question designed so that no answer is ever simply right: that is IELTS Writing Task 2, and it is the purest form of a family of exam tasks that also includes the TOEFL Academic Discussion post (about ten minutes and one hundred words, answering a professor's question while reacting to classmates) and the GRE's thirty-minute Analyze an Issue essay — the task ETS kept when it retired "Analyze an Argument" in September 2023. Every variant rewards the same underlying competence: take a position, defend it with organized evidence, acknowledge the strongest objection, and land the reader somewhere deliberate. This lesson builds that competence as a repeatable procedure — how to convert a prompt into a thesis in ninety seconds, how to architect the essay before writing it, how paragraphs carry arguments, and how to self-score against the official rubrics the examiners use.

**Why this matters.** The argument essay is the highest-leverage single task on these exams: one IELTS Task 2 essay is worth twice the marks of Task 1, the TOEFL discussion post is a fifth of the entire writing score, and the GRE essay is a standalone section reported to admissions committees. Beyond exams, the same move set — claim, support, concede, rebut — is what law-school memos, funding applications and engineering design justifications are made of. Writing under a clock merely removes the illusion that thinking and drafting can be separated.
objectives: Explain thesis: the one-sentence claim everything serves
Explain essay architecture: stance, roadmap, body, verdict
Explain evidence: examples, data and reasoning from first principles
Explain counterargument and rebuttal: the strongest-opposition move
Explain paragraph roles and the point-proof-comment cycle
Explain rubric self-scoring: task response and development
Explain timed drafting: the plan-first protocol
Explain short-form argument: the discussion-post answer

concepts.statement: One sentence stating your actual position on the prompt — specific enough that a reasonable person could disagree with it. "Education is important" is not a thesis; "Free university tuition helps the economy overall, but only when places are limited by merit rather than wealth" is.
An explicit admission that the opposing side has a real point. Conceding a minor point costs nothing and buys credibility for the rebuttal that follows.
The move that explains why your position survives the concession — usually by weighing: the opposing point is real but smaller, rarer, or addressable.
A sentence or clause signalling the essay's plan — "I will argue X for two reasons, before addressing the strongest objection" — which examiners reward under Coherence and Cohesion.

concepts.term: Thesis: the one-sentence claim everything serves
concepts.statement: Everything begins with the ninety-second prompt conversion. Exam prompts almost always contain two or three contestable terms — "free", "merit", "helps" — and a question type that tells you the shape of the answer. "To what extent do you agree" wants a calibrated stance, not a yes/no. "Discuss both views and give your own opinion" is legally obliged by its own wording to cover both sides before stating yours. The professional habit is to underline the two or three load-bearing words, decide your position on them, and write the thesis as a single sentence that answers the exact question asked. Writers who skip this step commonly produce essays that are fluent and off-prompt — the fastest route to a Task Response penalty in the IELTS band descriptors, which explicitly reward "addresses all parts of the task" and penalize positions that drift from the question.

concepts.term: Essay architecture: stance, roadmap, body, verdict
concepts.statement: Architecture comes next, and the counterintuitive rule is that the thinking happens before the prose. A four-paragraph default handles nearly every prompt: an introduction that rephrases the question and lands the thesis; body paragraph one carrying your strongest reason with its evidence; body paragraph two carrying either the second reason or the counterargument-plus-rebuttal, depending on which the prompt demands; and a conclusion that restates the position in fresh words and states what follows from it. For "discuss both views" prompts the middle expands to two paragraphs — one per view — before the verdict paragraph gives your own opinion. Planning time is not lost time: five minutes spent listing the thesis, the two body-paragraph topics and one concrete example each routinely saves ten minutes of mid-essay stalling, because the writer never has to decide what comes next while simultaneously managing grammar.

concepts.term: Evidence: examples, data and reasoning from first principles
concepts.statement: Within each body paragraph, the point-proof-comment cycle does the carrying. The point is the paragraph's topic sentence — a claim, in your words. The proof is the evidence: a concrete example, a statistic you actually remember, or reasoning from a principle the reader already accepts. The comment is the sentence that explains how the proof supports the point — the step examiners call "development" and novice writers skip, assuming the example speaks for itself. It never does. "For instance, students in Germany pay almost no tuition" is not an argument; "For instance, students in Germany pay almost no tuition, yet German universities maintain international rankings — evidence that removing fees does not by itself degrade quality" is. The comment sentence is where the writer's thinking becomes visible, and it is the single most reliable marker distinguishing band-7-plus IELTS essays from band-6 work.

concepts.term: Counterargument and rebuttal: the strongest-opposition move
concepts.statement: Evidence under exam conditions deserves honest treatment: you will not remember true statistics, and examiners do not fact-check specifics — but invented precision reads as fragile. The robust forms are generic-but-real examples ("public universities in several European countries", "studies of childhood vaccination programmes"), reasoning from shared principles (incentives, fairness, long-term versus short-term effects), and hypotheticals clearly flagged as such ("consider a student from a low-income district..."). What weakens an essay is stacking three thin examples instead of developing one, or citing numbers so specific they invite skepticism. One example explored to its consequences beats three listed and abandoned — depth is what the "extended and supported" language of the band descriptors is scoring.

concepts.term: Paragraph roles and the point-proof-comment cycle
concepts.statement: The counterargument move deserves its own rehearsal because it separates confident writers from defensive ones. The pattern is four beats: name the objection fairly ("Critics argue that free tuition mainly benefits the middle class, who would attend university anyway"); concede its truth ("This is partly fair — subsidy does flow to families who could pay"); rebut by weighing ("but the alternative — means-tested fees — creates its own disincentives and administrative cost, and the fair-access gains outweigh the leak"); and tie back to the thesis. Note what the pattern avoids: straw-manning the opposition, conceding everything, or "rebutting" by merely repeating your earlier paragraph. Rebuttals weigh, they do not shout. Practised once per practice essay, the move becomes available automatically in the exam hall — and it directly feeds the GRE issue rubric, whose top scores go to essays that "address possible objections" as a matter of course.

concepts.term: Rubric self-scoring: task response and development
concepts.statement: Timing and self-scoring close the loop. A workable clock for IELTS Task 2 is five minutes planning, thirty drafting, five editing — with the editing pass spent on thesis visibility, paragraph openings and verb-tense slips rather than rewording half the essay. For the TOEFL discussion post the whole cycle compresses to ten minutes: ninety seconds reading the professor's prompt and one classmate's post, a minute deciding a position that adds something new rather than echoing the thread, and the rest drafting roughly a hundred words that state a stance, give one reason with brief support, and respond explicitly to the classmate you quoted. Self-scoring then uses the real criteria: IELTS publishes its four band descriptors (Task Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy — the middle two get their own lessons in this field), the GRE issue rubric rewards quality of reasoning over position taken, and the TOEFL writing rubric scores relevant content and elaboration. Grading your own practice essays against the published descriptors, brutally, is the fastest known way to move a band.

Writing before planning, which guarantees mid-essay stalling and structural drift. Answering the question you wish had been asked instead of the one printed. Listing three thin examples instead of developing one. Straw-manning the opposing view — examiners read fairness as maturity. Saving the opinion for the conclusion in a prompt that demands it throughout ("give your own opinion" means the essay is yours from the first paragraph). And treating the word count as a floor to pad to rather than a scope to fill with developed ideas — padding shows.

examples.title: Worked Example — Prompt to Outline in Five Minutes
examples.problem: The Argument Essay: Thesis, Evidence and Counterargument — worked through step by step

steps.label: Prompt
steps.text: "Some people believe university education should be free for everyone. Others think students should pay, because personal benefit justifies personal cost. Discuss both views and give your own opinion."

steps.label: Contestable terms underlined
steps.text: "free", "everyone", "personal benefit". Question type: discuss-both-views, so both sides must get a full paragraph before my verdict.

steps.label: Thesis drafted
steps.text: "Universities should be publicly funded at the point of use, because the benefits spill well beyond the individual graduate — but means-tested contribution after graduation is a defensible compromise."

steps.label: Outline
steps.text: intro with thesis; body 1 — the free case (access, graduate-tax effect, comparisons with public schooling); body 2 — the paying case (personal return, capacity funding); body 3 — rebuttal weighing both (graduate-contribution schemes as synthesis); conclusion restating the calibrated position.

steps.label: Clock
steps.text: 5 minutes planning produced all five paragraph topics and one example each (German tuition, UK loan system, graduate taxes) — drafting now has no decisions left to make.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: the Library's critical-reasoning lesson — analysing arguments is the mirror image of writing them, and its premise-conclusion anatomy makes your own essays sturdier. Follow-ons: the cohesion-and-lexical-resource lesson for the sentence-level craft this lesson assumes, the skimming-and-scanning lesson for the reading half of these exams, and the long-turn speaking lesson for the same argument skills performed aloud.
Convert the prompt in ninety seconds: underline contestable terms, match the question type, draft a one-sentence thesis that answers exactly what is asked.
Plan five minutes before drafting: thesis, body-paragraph topics, one concrete example per paragraph — no decisions left for mid-essay.
Default architecture: introduction with thesis, two or three body paragraphs, conclusion in fresh words; "discuss both views" adds a paragraph per view.
Run the point-proof-comment cycle in every body paragraph; the comment sentence is scored development.
Prefer one developed example to three abandoned ones; keep evidence generic-but-real and flag hypotheticals.
Rehearse the four-beat counterargument: name fairly, concede partly, rebut by weighing, tie back to thesis.
Use a fixed clock (5-30-5 for IELTS Task 2; roughly 1.5-8-0.5 for the TOEFL post) and self-score against the published band descriptors.

quiz.q: The fastest route to a low Task Response score is an essay that is…
options: fluent and well-written but not answering the question asked
quiz.explanation: The band descriptors reward essays that address all parts of the task; drifting from the prompt fails it regardless of prose quality.

quiz.q: The "comment" in the point-proof-comment cycle exists to…
options: show how the evidence supports the claim — the development examiners score
quiz.explanation: Evidence never speaks for itself; the explaining sentence is where development becomes visible.

quiz.q: A strong rebuttal characteristically…
options: denies the objection has any merit
concedes the point fully and moves on
weighs the objection against your case and shows it is smaller, rarer or addressable
quiz.explanation: Rebuttals weigh rather than deny — fair concession plus proportion is what earns top reasoning marks.

quiz.q: For the TOEFL Academic Discussion post, the highest-value opening move is…
options: summarizing the professor's lecture at length
taking a clear position that adds something new to the thread, then supporting it
agreeing with the most detailed classmate
quiz.explanation: The rubric rewards relevant, elaborated contribution to the discussion — echo posts score lower than additive ones.

intro:
Two of the four IELTS Writing band descriptors are named Coherence and Cohesion and Lexical Resource and Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and the same qualities hide inside every other essay or discussion-post rubric under plainer names — organization, word choice, sentence control. They are also the three qualities most candidates believe they cannot improve in the final weeks, because they feel like talent. They are not: each decomposes into a small set of learnable devices. Coherence is whether the reader can reconstruct your logic; cohesion is the mechanical stitching — pronouns, connectors, repeated key nouns — that lets them; lexical resource is the range and precision of vocabulary; grammatical range and accuracy is the spread of sentence shapes executed without slips. This lesson takes the four apart and rebuilds them as concrete moves with a three-minute editing pass at the end.

**Why this matters.** These descriptors together are worth half of the IELTS writing band and roughly half of the TOEFL discussion-post rubric — but their reach is far wider. Every email that gets answered, every report that gets acted on and every essay that earns its marks runs on the same machinery: a reader who never has to ask "what is this paragraph about?" or "what does this sentence connect back to?". The devices here are small, free and transferable to every language you write in.
objectives: Explain coherence: the logic a reader can follow
Explain cohesion: the words that stitch sentences together
Explain topic sentences and the given-new contract
Explain reference chains, substitution and ellipsis
Explain conjunctions that signal the logical move
Explain lexical resource: range, collocation and paraphrase
Explain grammatical range and accuracy: variety under control
Explain the three-minute editing pass

concepts.statement: The invisible quality: information arranged so the reader always knows what is being discussed and why. Coherence is achieved by paragraph planning and logical order, and cohesion merely makes it visible on the surface.

Any word or pattern that ties one sentence to the next: reference pronouns (this, these, such), substitution (one, do so), ellipsis (deliberate omission), conjunctions (however, therefore) and lexical chains (repeating or varying key nouns).

The sentence-level rhythm of fluent prose: begin with information the reader already holds (the "given"), end with the new point. New information then becomes the given of the next sentence — prose that obeys this flows without effort.

Words that native usage pairs: "heavy rain" not "strong rain", "reach a decision" not "arrive a decision". Lexical resource scores reward collocations precisely because they are the fingerprint of real exposure to a language.

concepts.term: Coherence: the logic a reader can follow
concepts.statement: Start with the unit that carries both descriptors at once: the paragraph. A competent exam paragraph opens with a topic sentence that announces the paragraph's claim in plain words, develops it through two to four sentences of support, and closes either by drawing the implication or handing to the next topic. The topic sentence is not decoration — it is the reader's handle on everything beneath it. Underneath, the given-new contract governs sentence order: "Vocational training has one decisive advantage. That advantage is speed: a plumbing certificate takes two years, a physics degree six." The second sentence opens with "that advantage" — the given — and spends the rest of the sentence delivering the new point. Compare the disorienting alternative: "Speed is one decisive advantage of vocational training, since a plumbing certificate takes two years and a physics degree six." Same words, wrong order; the reader must jump backward to find what "speed" is doing. Essay writers who obey given-new get coherence credited without ever using a fancy connector.

concepts.term: Cohesion: the words that stitch sentences together
concepts.statement: Cohesion then supplies the visible thread, and its devices sort into a short taxonomy worth memorizing. Reference: pronouns and demonstratives point back — "these costs", "such a policy", "this" standing for a whole preceding sentence. Substitution and ellipsis: "more people cycle than do so" and "some cities invest; others do not" — the omitted verb is still heard. Conjunctions: the logical-signalling layer, best learned as a signal-to-meaning table — "however, nevertheless, on the other hand" announce contrast; "therefore, consequently, as a result" announce consequence; "for instance, specifically" announce support; "admittedly, granted" announce concession; "moreover, in addition" announce accumulation. The scorer is watching whether the connector matches the actual logical move: a "furthermore" pasted onto a contrast reads as a mechanical chain, which is exactly what the band descriptors mean by cohesion that is "used mechanically". The final device, lexical chaining, is the most underestimated: key nouns return in varied dress — "tuition fees ... the policy ... free education" — keeping the topic visible without robotic repetition.

concepts.term: Topic sentences and the given-new contract
concepts.statement: Lexical resource is scored on three axes: range (enough different words to avoid strain), precision (the right word, including collocations) and paraphrase (restating prompt language in your own words). The paraphrase axis matters most immediately, because the first sentence of any exam essay must rephrase the question — copying it verbatim is penalized as memorized language. Practical technique: build three-word variation ladders for the prompt's key nouns before drafting ("students ... learners ... graduates"; "free tuition ... publicly funded places ... removing fees"). Precision grows from collocation study, not from exotic vocabulary: examiners consistently reward accurate ordinary words ("implement a policy", "pose a risk") over misused impressive ones ("utilize" bolted onto every sentence is a known band-6 signature). A useful discipline is the one-per-paragraph rule: allow yourself exactly one ambitious word choice per paragraph, check it, and keep the rest clean — ambitious vocabulary that misfires costs more than plain vocabulary that never slips.

Grammatical range and accuracy is the most misunderstood descriptor because candidates read "range" as "long sentences". What the descriptors actually reward is a spread of sentence types — simple, compound, complex, and the inverted or participle-opened sentence used sparingly — each executed accurately. One controlled complex sentence per paragraph ("Because graduates earn more over a lifetime, the public investment repays itself") does more for the score than a three-line sentence with a broken clause. Accuracy, meanwhile, is dominated by a short list of high-frequency errors: subject-verb agreement after long subjects, article choice, tense consistency in the past, and comma splices. The professional response is not to write less but to keep an error inventory — the same three or four mistakes in every essay you write — and aim the final editing pass straight at them.

concepts.term: Conjunctions that signal the logical move
concepts.statement: That editing pass is the lesson's payoff move, and it fits in three minutes. Minute one: read only the first sentence of every paragraph — do they announce the argument? Is the thesis still visible? Minute two: scan for your personal error inventory (agreement, articles, tense) and comma splices. Minute three: check connectors — no two paragraphs should open with the same linker, and every "however" should genuinely mark a contrast. Deliberately not rewording: wholesale rephrasing in the last minutes manufactures fresh errors faster than it fixes old ones. The pass is targeted, short and unglamorous, and it routinely moves essays half a band because the descriptors for cohesion and accuracy are precisely what it touches.

Connector stuffing — a "furthermore" before every sentence scores as mechanical cohesion. Pronouns with no clear ancestor ("this causes problems" — what does "this" stand for?). One idea per paragraph abandoned after a single sentence, starving development. Memorized introduction templates copied onto prompts they do not fit. Treating "range" as licence for multi-clause monsters, which multiply agreement errors. And skipping the error inventory: almost every writer repeats the same three mistakes, and not knowing yours makes the editing pass blind.

examples.title: Worked Example — Rewriting a Choppy Paragraph
examples.problem: Coherence, Cohesion and Lexical Resource: Writing That Reads Smoothly — worked through step by step

steps.label: Before
steps.text: "Free tuition is good. Students do not have debt. Students study harder. Government spends money. Government has less money for hospitals." Five sentences, zero connections — the reader assembles the logic alone.

steps.label: Step 1 — order by logic
steps.text: benefit to students first, cost to the state second. Step 2 — stitch: reference pronouns, one contrast connector, one consequence connector.

steps.label: After
steps.text: "Free tuition removes the debt that shapes graduates' early careers, and for that reason alone students can choose fields for interest rather than salary. Many also study more effectively without paid work competing for their hours. The state, however, pays directly: every subsidized place is money unavailable for hospitals or schools. The question, therefore, is not whether the cost exists but whether the benefits outrun it."

steps.label: Tally
steps.text: reference ("that", "for that reason"), contrast ("however"), consequence ("therefore"), lexical chain ("free tuition ... subsidized place ... the cost"), given-new flow sentence to sentence — every descriptor touched in four sentences.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: the argument-essay lesson in this field, which produces the drafts this lesson polishes. Follow-ons: the skimming-and-scanning lesson for the reading side of timed exams, and the critical-reasoning lesson — its paragraph-level anatomy of claims is what your topic sentences are modelling from the writing side.
Every paragraph: plain topic sentence, two to four support sentences, closing implication or handover.
Obey given-new: open with what the reader holds, end with the new point.
Cohesive toolkit: reference, substitution, ellipsis, matching conjunctions, lexical chains.
Learn conjunctions as a signal-to-meaning table and let each one mark a real logical move.
Lexical resource = range, collocation, paraphrase; build variation ladders for prompt nouns; one ambitious word per paragraph.
Grammar range = a spread of sentence types executed cleanly; keep a personal error inventory.
Edit three minutes: paragraph openings, then error inventory, then connectors — never wholesale rewording.

quiz.q: Coherence and cohesion are related but distinct because…
options: cohesion is the visible stitching, coherence the underlying logical order
they are two names for vocabulary range
quiz.explanation: Plan the logic (coherence), then make it visible with reference, conjunctions and lexical chains (cohesion).

quiz.q: The given-new contract says sentences flow best when they…
options: always begin with the newest idea
open with known information and end with the new point
quiz.explanation: Ending on the new point lets it become the given of the next sentence — the engine of fluent prose.

quiz.q: In lexical resource, examiners consistently reward…
options: accurate ordinary collocations and clean paraphrase over misused "impressive" words
quiz.explanation: Precision and collocation carry the score; misfired ambitious words are the classic band-6 signature.

quiz.q: The three-minute editing pass deliberately does NOT…
options: verify connectors match the logical move
quiz.explanation: Wholesale rewording manufactures fresh errors; the pass is targeted at structure, known errors and linkers.

intro:
IELTS Academic Reading gives you three long passages, forty questions and sixty minutes — no time to read every word twice, and no marks for elegant comprehension. TOEFL reading items similarly test whether you can locate stated facts fast, spot the negative-factual question ("All of the following are true EXCEPT..."), and compress a passage into a summary or table. The ACT Reading section runs forty questions in thirty-five minutes across four passages, and its main-idea questions reward the same first-minute survey. The exam boards themselves prescribe the technique in their official materials: skimming for gist and scanning for detail, two different eye-movements doing two different jobs. This lesson trains both as deliberate procedures — when to survey, when to hunt, how questions disguise the words you scanned for, and how to spend the error budget a timed section really is.

**Why this matters.** On every one of these exams, timing — not difficulty — is the reported cause of lost marks: candidates who comprehend perfectly run out of clock because they read everything at the same speed. Reading at adjustable speed is also the everyday skill: a researcher triaging thirty papers, a lawyer finding the clause that matters, a doctor scanning a chart all run the same two gears. The exam just makes the cost of staying in first gear visible.
objectives: Explain skim: building a thirty-second map of a passage
Explain main idea: titles, bookends and repetition
Explain scan: anchoring on names, numbers and keywords
Explain question-first or passage-first: matching strategy to task
Explain paraphrase radar: questions rarely reuse the text's words
Explain negative-factual items: EXCEPT and NOT questions
Explain summary and table completion: facts into frames
Explain pacing protocol and the error budget

concepts.statement: Reading for structure and gist at high speed — title, first sentences of paragraphs, the final paragraph — producing a mental map: what the passage is about, its stance, and where each part sits. Used once, before questions.
Reading for location, not meaning: eyes sweep for specific anchors — names, dates, numbers, capitalized terms — and stop only when the anchor appears. Used per question.
The concrete token a question hands you to search with. Proper nouns, numbers and technical terms are ideal anchors because the passage cannot paraphrase them away; abstract phrases are poor ones.

A question asking which option is NOT stated or is EXCEPT-ed. All three true options are in the passage — the exam is testing whether you can verify each option against the text instead of pattern-matching the first plausible one.

concepts.term: Skim: building a thirty-second map of a passage
concepts.statement: Skimming has a definite anatomy, and practising it as anatomy is what makes it fast. First the title and any subheading — they set the topic frame. Then the opening paragraph, read at near-full speed: writers state their subject and intent there. Then the first sentence of every body paragraph, where academic and journalistic English puts its topic sentence; the rest of each paragraph is skipped entirely on the first pass. Then the closing paragraph, where the conclusion or implication lives. Done in under a minute for a typical exam passage, this produces a skeleton — topic, stance, the three or four supporting movements — that you spend the rest of the section hanging details onto. Two habits spoil it: sliding into full reading ("just this one paragraph..."), which destroys the time advantage, and skipping the survey entirely to go question-first on a hard passage, which forces re-reading later. Main-idea questions, the staple of the ACT and TOEFL, are answered almost directly by the survey: the main idea lives in the title, the bookends and the repeated concern of the topic sentences — never in one dramatic sentence buried mid-passage.

concepts.term: Main idea: titles, bookends and repetition
concepts.statement: Scanning is the other gear, and it works only when you let the question do the aiming. Each question supplies anchors; the procedure is to fix them in mind — especially numbers, names and capitalized or technical terms, which the passage usually prints identically — and sweep the relevant paragraph region until they light up. Then, and only then, do you switch to normal reading for the two or three lines around the hit, because the answer almost always sits in the sentence containing the anchor or the one after it. Where scanning goes wrong is in the gap between the question's words and the passage's words: exam boards deliberately paraphrase. The question says "the introduction of the policy"; the passage said "when the scheme came into force". Only the anchor survives paraphrase — "policy" became "scheme", but a date or a name cannot be swapped. This is why anchor-first works and keyword-literalism fails, and it is the single most trainable micro-skill in timed reading: expecting the paraphrase instead of being defeated by it.

concepts.term: Scan: anchoring on names, numbers and keywords
concepts.statement: Question-first or passage-first is the strategy fork, and the right branch depends on the item type. Fact-location items (TOEFL factual information, IELTS matching information) are question-first: the question hands you the anchor, so survey briefly, then hunt. Summary-completion and fill-in-a-table items are passage-structure tasks: they compress the whole passage or one section into gaps, so build the skim map first, then scan per gap — the table's own headings and row labels are additional anchors that tell you where each fact must have come from. Global items (main idea, author's purpose, best title) come last and cost almost nothing: the survey already answered them. Leaving global questions for the end also exploits a property of these sections — by the time you have located ten facts, the passage's shape is twice as clear as it was after the first skim.

concepts.term: Question-first or passage-first: matching strategy to task
concepts.statement: The negative-factual item deserves special drill because it inverts reflexes. "The author mentions the 1994 survey for all of the following reasons EXCEPT" — now every option must be verified against the passage, and three verifications are as much work as one. The efficient protocol: scan to the anchor region, then check options one at a time against that region only; the three supported ones cluster near the anchor, and the intruder is the option whose content you cannot find anywhere near it. The classic trap is the option that is true in real life or true elsewhere in the passage but not connected to the asked-about anchor — the exam is testing whether "true" and "mentioned for this reason" are different claims. Marking the three confirmed options as you verify them turns a chaotic memory task into a checklist.

concepts.term: Paraphrase radar: questions rarely reuse the text's words
concepts.statement: Pacing closes the system. IELTS's official advice is roughly twenty minutes per passage-set; a workable error budget is to refuse any single question more than ninety seconds — at the limit, mark, guess and move, because one stubborn question can cost two answerable ones later. Answer sheets and transfer time, where they exist, are part of the budget, not an afterthought. And the section-level habit that separates consistent scorers from streaky ones: never leave blanks (these exams do not subtract for wrong answers on reading), because a scanned guess at an anchored question is right far more often than chance. Practise the whole loop under the clock from the first week — untimed skimming practice builds the wrong reflexes — and keep an error log distinguishing "did not know the word" from "never found the line": the second category is what this lesson eliminates, and it is usually the larger one.

Reading everything at one speed — the defining timing failure. Keyword-literalism: scanning for the question's exact words when the passage reworded them. Going question-first on hard passages without any survey, then re-reading three times. Missing the paraphrase and concluding the information is not there. In EXCEPT items, choosing an option that is true-but-irrelevant to the anchor. Ignoring the clock until minute fifteen. And practising untimed: the skills are speed skills and only transfer under the clock.

examples.title: Worked Example — One Passage-Set Under the Clock
examples.problem: Skimming and Scanning: Reading Strategy for Timed Exams — worked through step by step

steps.label: Passage
steps.text: "The revived tradition of street-food night markets in Taiwanese cities" — 850 words, 13 questions, 20 minutes.

steps.label: Minute 0-1 — skim
steps.text: title sets topic; opening paragraph says the markets revived after 2000s municipal promotion; topic sentences track economy, tourism policy, and a debate about authenticity; final paragraph predicts consolidation.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Q1-6 fact-location, question-first: "In which year did Kaohsiung open its first regulated night market?" — anchors "Kaohsiung", "regulated"; scan hits line 22; read two lines; answer found in 35 seconds.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Q7-9 summary completion: the frame's own row labels ("economic role", "government policy") route the scans; paraphrase radar required — passage said "municipal subsidies", gap asked about "official financial support".

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Q10-12 negative-factual: anchor "tourism campaign" region; verify options a-b-d confirmed in two sentences, option c found nowhere nearby — marked NOT-mentioned after a checklist sweep.

steps.label: Step 6
steps.text: Q13 main idea, zero new reading: the survey already answered it — municipal revival policy reshaped an inherited tradition. Total: 17 minutes, 2 minutes review, no blanks.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is an entry-level strategy lesson, though comfortable grammar speed helps. Follow-ons: the true-false-can't-tell lesson in this field for the judgement layer on top of located facts, the long-turn speaking lesson for the listening-and-speaking half of the same exams, and the argument-essay lesson for the writing half.
Skim once per passage: title, opening, first sentences, closing — a skeleton under a minute.
Main-idea questions are answered by the survey: title, bookends, repeated concern of topic sentences.
Scan per question with concrete anchors — names, dates, numbers survive paraphrase; abstract phrases do not.
Expect the paraphrase: the answer sits where the anchor is, in reworded language.
Fact-location items are question-first; summary and table items are structure-first.
EXCEPT/NOT items: verify each option against the anchor region as a checklist.
Cap any question near ninety seconds; never leave blanks; practise only under the clock.

quiz.q: Skimming a passage for structure means reading…
options: title, opening paragraph, first sentences of body paragraphs, and the closing paragraph
quiz.explanation: The skeleton lives in the bookends and topic sentences; mid-paragraph detail is skipped on the first pass.

quiz.q: Proper nouns, dates and numbers are the best scanning anchors because…
options: the passage rarely paraphrases them, while abstract phrases get reworded
they are always in the final paragraph
quiz.explanation: Questions paraphrase concepts but cannot swap a name or a date — anchors survive the paraphrase.

quiz.q: In a negative-factual (EXCEPT) item, the efficient protocol is to…
options: pick the option that sounds least likely
verify each option against the anchor region, confirming the three supported ones
quiz.explanation: Three options are stated and one is not; a checklist sweep near the anchor exposes the intruder.

quiz.q: The recommended error budget in a timed reading section says…
options: spend unlimited time on hard questions to be sure
cap any single question near ninety seconds, then mark, guess and move
answer only questions you are certain about
quiz.explanation: One stubborn question can cost two answerable ones; there is no penalty for wrong answers on these reading sections, so never leave blanks.

intro:
UCAT Verbal Reasoning compresses a hard discipline into a brutal format: a passage of a few hundred words, four statements, and three possible verdicts on each — True, False, or Can't Tell — at roughly two minutes for the set. CLAT's English section asks the same skill in gentler dress (what is the author's tone, which conclusion is best supported), and LSAT Reading Comprehension's author-attitude questions are the same judgement at leisure. The discipline itself is textual epistemology: separate what the passage says from what is plausible, and decide verdicts on textual evidence alone. This lesson builds the three-verdict logic from the ground up, then adds the judgement layer that rides on it — fact versus opinion, tone and attitude markers, and how far a conclusion can run before it overreaches the page.

**Why this matters.** These judgements are the daily work of any profession that consumes documents: the clinician reading a trial report, the lawyer reading a witness statement, the analyst reading a claim in a filing, the citizen reading a claim on social media. UCAT tests it because medicine drowns in literature where "the study did not say that" is a patient-safety skill. The exam's three-verdict format is just the cleanest training rig ever built for asking one question: how do you know?
objectives: Explain the three-verdict rule: the text is the only witness
Explain true: explicitly supported, not merely plausible
Explain false: explicitly contradicted by the text
Explain can’t tell: neither — and outside knowledge is the trap
Explain fact, opinion and inference on the page
Explain tone and attitude markers: the author between the lines
Explain drawing conclusions without overreaching
Explain scope qualifiers: all, some, only, tend to

concepts.statement: The passage explicitly supports the statement — its information is stated or follows by a small, safe step from what is stated. Plausibility alone never earns a True.
The passage explicitly contradicts the statement — some textual detail runs directly against it. A statement that merely cannot be confirmed is NOT False; see Can’t tell.

The passage neither states nor contradicts the claim. The information gap, not your ignorance, is the verdict — the passage itself does not settle it. Bringing in outside knowledge to break the tie is the format's signature error.

Words that set claim size: all, some, most, only, always, tends to, may. Verdicts hinge on them — a passage supporting "some cities" does not support "most cities", and "only" is almost always a trap.

concepts.term: The three-verdict rule: the text is the only witness
concepts.statement: The three-verdict rule begins with a boundary decision that feels alien to well-read candidates: the passage is the only witness. Everything you know from elsewhere — the real-world fact, the textbook answer, the sensible prior — is inadmissible. UCAT's own materials are explicit that the passages are self-contained, and several of its published trap statements are true-in-reality but unmentioned-in-text, engineered precisely to catch candidates answering from memory instead of from the page. The practical procedure for every statement is therefore fixed: locate the relevant text region (the skimming-and-scanning lesson's anchoring does this job), read it properly, and only then compare statement against text. Never read the statement first and then go looking for confirmation — that is how outside knowledge sneaks in, dressed as recognition.

concepts.term: True: explicitly supported, not merely plausible
concepts.statement: True is a higher bar than it looks. The statement is True when the passage explicitly says it, or when it follows from the text by a step so small the passage clearly owns it — converting "sales doubled between 2010 and 2012" into "sales were higher in 2012 than in 2010" is safe.
