Both are the system admitting its own difficulty and engineering a fix — use them shamelessly.

concepts.term: A learning order that actually works
concepts.statement: The order that works: hiragana first, two weeks of grid, handwriting and reading until recall is automatic, because everything else is written over it. Katakana second — same sounds, new shapes — consolidated by decoding loanword menus. Kanji third and indefinitely: learn characters as assemblies of components, pair each with vocabulary words rather than abstract readings, and let spaced repetition schedule the reviews. Read real text early; furigana exists precisely so beginners can.

The classic mistake is attacking all three scripts at once and stalling in month one — sequence them: kana, then kanji. The second is romaji dependence: staying in transcription delays the ear and the eye from doing real work. Third, memorising kanji stroke by stroke as pictures instead of assemblies of components — the difference between two thousand passwords and a few hundred parts. And beware one-to-one thinking: kanji are not words; 食堂 is one word built from two characters.
A writing system whose characters each encode one syllable-type beat, like hiragana and katakana.
The timing unit of Japanese; each kana represents one mora, the basic beat of the language.
Characters borrowed from Chinese that carry meaning and both Sino-Japanese and native readings.
The imported Chinese reading of a kanji and the native Japanese reading matched to it.
Hiragana following a kanji to express inflection, as the べます of 食べます.
Small kana printed beside a kanji to indicate its reading.
The 2,136 characters designated for everyday literacy in Japan.

examples.title: Worked example — Hiragana, Katakana and Kanji: How Japanese Writing Works
examples.problem: Label every character of 私はコーヒーを飲みます by script and state what each one is doing.

steps.label: Recall the division of labour
steps.text: kanji for content stems, hiragana for grammatical glue, katakana for loanwords.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: 私 watashi, “I”, is kanji; は wa is a hiragana particle marking the topic; コーヒー kōhī, “coffee”, is katakana because the word is a Dutch loan; を o is a hiragana particle marking the object; 飲 is the kanji stem of “drink”; みます -mimasu is hiragana carrying tense and politeness.

examples.result: three scripts, six jobs, no redundancy — one sentence is a wiring diagram of what each script is for.

keyTakeaways: Manga and anime: many series print furigana over nearly every kanji, making them free graded readers for learners.
Menus and signage: katakana loanwords let a traveller read コーヒー, ビール and エレベーター on sight once the script is known.
Names: given names in kanji carry meanings parents chose, and official forms include a space for how each is read.
Typing: a Japanese IME converts typed romaji through kana to kanji, so writing is choosing candidates, not drawing strokes.
Certification: the JLPT language exams and the Kanji Kentei both grade reading levels by which characters a text uses.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — start here for Japanese. Follow with the particles lesson, which turns these characters into sentences, then verb conjugation and politeness registers. Drill apps make the first fortnight of kana a game; after that, furigana-graded readers keep the kanji campaign fed.

quiz.q: The job of hiragana in a Japanese sentence is…
options: carrying grammar: particles, inflections and native words
quiz.explanation: Kanji carry content stems, katakana the foreign, and hiragana the grammatical glue between them.

quiz.q: コーヒー is written in katakana because…
options: it is a foreign loanword, from Dutch koffie
it is a native Japanese word
quiz.explanation: Katakana is the script for loanwords, foreign names, onomatopoeia and emphasis.

quiz.q: The small kana printed beside a difficult kanji to show its pronunciation are called…
quiz.explanation: Furigana give the reading of a character in context — the built-in support system of learner texts.

quiz.q: The recommended learning order for the writing system is…
options: kanji first, because it is hardest
quiz.explanation: Hiragana underlies every textbook and pronunciation guide; katakana reuses its sounds; kanji is the long campaign fed by real reading.

intro:
Words look atomic but are assembled. Cats contains two pieces — cat, a meaning, and -s, “more than one”. Unbelievable contains three: un- “not”, believe and -able “capable of being”. Morphology is the study of this hidden assembly line: the units languages build words from and the rules that order them. Etymology, elsewhere in this section, traces where words came from over the centuries; morphology studies the machinery that is still running today — and every fluent speaker already owns one.

**Why this matters.** Every plural noun, tensed verb and derived adjective you have ever produced was computed by these rules, not stored one by one — which is why you can make sense of words you have never met, like unfriendable or decaffeinate. Morphology also explains why a single Turkish word can translate an English phrase. For learners it is the difference between memorising a thousand forms and learning a stem plus a system.
objectives: Explain the morpheme: the smallest unit of meaning
Explain free and bound morphemes
Explain inflection: grammar without new words
Explain derivation: building new words
Explain compounding and word structure
Explain language types: isolating to fusional

concepts.term: The morpheme: the smallest unit of meaning
concepts.statement: The morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning or grammatical function — smallest, because cat cannot be cut further without leaving sounds that mean nothing, and a unit, because cat and -s each contribute. The counting test is not syllables: crocodile is three syllables but one morpheme, while cats is one syllable but two morphemes. Silent and unstressed material misleads English eyes; the structural cut, not the sound, is what counts.

Free morphemes stand alone as words: book, run, green. Bound morphemes must attach: plural -s, past -ed, -ness, re-, un-. Some bound items are roots that never surface independently — Latin -ceive in receive and perceive has no life of its own in English. Speakers feel the difference instantly, and morphology names it: green is a word; the -en of greenen is not, and cannot be. Function words like the and of are free but grammatical — same toolkit, different shelf.

Inflection adjusts a word's grammar without changing what it is: cat and cats, walk and walked, she and her. Number, case, tense, aspect and person — the bookkeeping categories — arrive as inflections, and each language has only a small, closed set of them. Inflected forms share one dictionary entry: walks is still walk. English is inflection-poor; Spanish verb tables and Turkish case endings run the same machinery at far higher volume.

Derivation builds different words, often changing word class: happy the adjective becomes happiness the noun; modern becomes modernise; read becomes readable; agree becomes disagree. Derivational affixes form an open, productive set — -gate caught on after Watergate — and they stack in a fixed order: un-believ-ab-ly works, belie-un-ably does not. Where inflection changes grammar, derivation changes identity, and the derived word earns its own dictionary entry.

Compounding welds free morphemes into single words: blackboard, laptop, smartphone. English marks the seam with stress — a BLACKbird is a species, a black BIRD is any dark bird — and compounds drift toward meanings no sum of parts predicts. German industrialises the process, Mandarin builds nearly its whole vocabulary this way, and blending, clipping and back-formation add further word-formation routes whose histories the etymology lesson covers.

Languages distribute the work differently. Isolating Mandarin runs close to one morpheme per word and leans on compounding. Agglutinative Turkish, Finnish and Swahili chain long strings of clearly separated affixes: ev-ler-im-de means “in my houses” — four morphemes, each visible. Fusional Latin, Russian and Spanish compress several meanings into single endings — Latin -rum marks feminine, plural and genitive at once. English sits mid-spectrum: nearly isolating in inflection, exuberant in derivation and compounding.

Three confusions cause most errors. Morpheme is not syllable: chased is one syllable, two morphemes; crocodile the reverse. Inflection is not derivation: a new dictionary entry means derivation; the same word in a different grammatical setting means inflection. And English is not the norm: it is unusually morpheme-light, so learners of Spanish, Finnish or Turkish must deliberately rebuild the habit of hearing endings as meaningful.
The smallest unit of language carrying meaning or grammatical function.
A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, like book or green.
A morpheme that must attach to another, like plural -s or negative un-.
Variation of a word's form for grammar — number, tense, case — without creating a new word.
Word-building with affixes that changes meaning or class, producing a new dictionary entry.
A word formed by joining two free morphemes, as blackboard joins black and board.
Chaining clearly separable affixes, one meaning each, as Turkish ev-ler-im-de, “in my houses”.

examples.title: Worked example — Morphology: How Languages Build Words
examples.problem: Parse the English word unbelievably and the Turkish word evlerimde completely — every morpheme, its type and its contribution.

steps.label: Recall the toolkit
steps.text: free versus bound; inflection versus derivation; in agglutination, one affix does exactly one job.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: un- (bound, derivational, negation) + believe (free root) + -able (bound, derivational, verb to adjective) + -ly (bound, derivational, adjective to adverb). Turkish: ev “house” + -ler plural + -im “my” + -de “in” — three bound suffixes in a row, each with one job.

examples.result: four morphemes in each word, but the English ones layer into class-shifting derivation while the Turkish ones snap together like bricks — derivation versus agglutination in a single comparison.

keyTakeaways: Language teaching: the tense endings and plural markers drilled first in every course are morphology, organised into a syllabus.
Search and machine translation: lemmatisation reduces walked and walking to walk so that queries and documents match.
Lexicography: one dictionary entry per word forces editors to rule on inflection versus derivation case by case.
Translation practice: a single Turkish or Inuktitut word often equals an English phrase, and morpheme counts drive the work.
Word games: Scrabble legality, crosswords and spelling bees all turn on which derived forms count as real words.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is core-tier linguistics and pairs directly with the etymology lesson, which covers word origins and word-formation history. Follow with the phonology of whichever language you are learning, and with typology across language families. The habit to build: meet a long word, cut it into morphemes before reaching for the dictionary.

quiz.q: How many morphemes are in unbelievably?
quiz.explanation: un- + believe + -able + -ly: negation, root, “capable of being”, and the adverbial ending.

quiz.q: Which of these is inflection rather than derivation?
quiz.explanation: Walked is the same verb marked for tense; the others are new words with their own dictionary entries.

quiz.q: A language that chains long strings of clearly separated affixes, one meaning each, is…
quiz.explanation: Agglutination: Turkish ev-ler-im-de assembles “in my houses” like bricks, every seam visible.

quiz.q: Cats versus crocodile shows that…
options: morphemes can outnumber syllables and vice versa
quiz.explanation: Cats is one syllable but two morphemes; crocodile is three syllables but one morpheme.

intro:
Say “REcord”, then “reCORD” — same segments, different word, and the difference is pure melody. Prosody is the layer of speech that operates above vowels and consonants: pitch, loudness, length and rhythm, stretched across syllables and phrases. It is why you can hear a question without catching its words, why sarcasm survives when the joke does not, and why a foreign accent sounds foreign even when every individual sound is correct. The segments carry the dictionary; prosody carries everything else.

**Why this matters.** Prosody is the most audible and least taught layer of language. A learner with perfect vowels but wrong stress still sounds — and sometimes means — wrong, because listeners gauge questions, irony and emphasis almost entirely from the tune. It is also where meaning lives without words: caregivers understand infants, and friends understand a flat “fine.”, from melody alone. If you have ever misread the tone of a text message, you know exactly how much rides on this layer.
objectives: Explain prosody: the music above the segments
Explain word stress and contrastive pairs
Explain stress-timed versus syllable-timed rhythm
Explain intonation: tunes that carry meaning
Explain focus: highlighting the new information
Explain tone and pitch accent across languages

concepts.term: Prosody: the music above the segments
concepts.statement: Prosodic properties are suprasegmental: they belong to stretches larger than a single sound. A syllable can be high or low, long or short, heavy or light, and these settings pattern over whole words and phrases. Phoneticians bundle them as stress (prominence), rhythm (timing) and intonation (the tune of the phrase). The layers are separable in the laboratory and in performance: hum a sentence's melody while discarding its consonants and vowels, and listeners can still recognise the phrase's shape.

In English, word stress is contrastive: REcord is a noun, reCORD a verb; PERmit is a document, perMIT is to allow. Stress arrives as a bundle — higher pitch, greater length and a full vowel — while unstressed vowels reduce toward the schwa of “about”. Some languages fix stress on a predictable syllable, Czech on the first, Polish on the next-to-last; English and Russian place it unpredictably, which is why learners must memorise the stress of every new word along with its spelling.

Languages also divide time differently. In stress-timed English, German or Russian, stressed syllables recur at roughly even intervals and unstressed syllables compress between them — English speakers swallow syllables wholesale, which is why “I wanna go” is natural speech. In syllable-timed Spanish, Italian or French, syllables take roughly equal time — the machine-gun impression English ears report. Japanese runs on morae, equal beats smaller than syllables. The categories are tendencies, not laws, but they explain most of what “sounding fluent” means.

Intonation assigns tunes to phrases, and tunes carry speech-act meaning. English yes-no questions typically end rising (“You're coming?”); statements fall; lists rise on every item except the last, which falls to close. A statement delivered with a final rise sounds uncertain or asks for confirmation — uptalk. And sarcasm is intonation's proof of power: “Well, that went GREAT”, flat, low and stretched, means precisely its opposite. No word changed; the tune flipped the sentence.

Nuclear stress marks the new information. “MARY baked the cake” answers who; “Mary baked the CAKE” answers what. Given, old information is deaccented — the melody drops it — because the listener already holds it. Misplaced stress confuses: stressing “baked” implies someone doubts the baking happened. Languages differ in machinery — some mark focus with particles or word order — but every language must tell the listener where the news is, and English does it with the tune.

concepts.term: Tone and pitch accent across languages
concepts.statement: Where prosody and phonology fully merge, pitch becomes part of the word. In tone languages — the subject of the Tonal Languages lesson in this section — every syllable carries a stored pitch pattern. Pitch-accent languages are the middle case: Japanese allows roughly one accent per word, a pitch drop separating háshi “chopsticks” from hashí “bridge”. English stress is a feeble cousin built mostly of loudness and vowel quality. The continuum runs from melody decorating words to melody being the words.

The first error is equating stress with loudness — it is a bundle of pitch, length and vowel quality, so shouting an unstressed syllable fixes nothing. Second, treating intonation as pure emotion: tunes carry grammar — questionhood, closure, focus — not just feeling. Third, over-generalising English: wh-questions in English fall rather than rise, and many languages mark questions with particles instead of tunes. Finally, refusing the schwa — unreduced unstressed vowels are the most durable accent habit English learners fossilise.
The melodic layer of speech — pitch, length, loudness and rhythm — operating above segments.
A property belonging to stretches larger than one sound, such as stress or intonation.
The relative prominence of one syllable, marked by pitch, length and full vowel quality.
The reduced neutral vowel of unstressed syllables, the first sound of “about”.
A timing pattern in which stressed syllables recur at roughly equal intervals.
The most prominent stress in a phrase, placed on the new information.
A system in which one accentual pitch drop per word distinguishes meanings, as in Japanese.

examples.title: Worked example — Prosody: The Melody of Speech
examples.problem: The sentence “She said she'd call” — what changes as stress moves through it, and what does the tune add?

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: nuclear stress selects the new information; intonation supplies stance — sarcasm uses flat, stretched, low contours.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: “SHE said...” contradicts doubts about who; “she SAID...” implies she only said it; “she said she'd CALL” marks calling, not texting, as the issue. Delivered as “Well, she CALLed...” with lengthened fall-rise pitch, the speaker implies the call somehow fell short.

examples.result: one string of words, at least four messages — stress selects the news, the tune supplies the attitude. Those are the two jobs prosody performs in every sentence you speak.

keyTakeaways: Language teaching: stress-placement and compression drills fix the “perfect vowels, foreign accent” plateau faster than more segment work.
Speech technology: synthetic voices sound natural or robotic almost entirely on prosody — tune, timing and pauses, not segments.
Texting and email: stripped of melody, writing borrows punctuation, emoji and a flat “fine.” to reconstruct the tune readers cannot hear.
Public speaking: deliberate pitch variation and pausing are what keep monotone delivery from losing an audience.
Accent coaching: “sounds foreign” judgments are usually prosodic — wrong stress and rhythm with flawless consonants still reads as accent.

Where next — Prerequisites: basic phonetics — vowels, consonants and the notion of a minimal pair. Pair this with the Tonal Languages lesson, which treats pitch inside words in depth; this topic covers the melody above them. Follow with the phonology of whichever language you are learning, and train your ear by humming sentences before repeating their segments.

quiz.q: REcord versus reCORD demonstrates that English word stress is…
quiz.explanation: The noun and verb differ only in stress placement — a minimal pair in the prosodic dimension.

quiz.q: In “Mary baked the CAKE”, the capitals mark…
options: the nuclear stress on the new information
quiz.explanation: Nuclear stress lands on the news of the sentence; old information is deaccented because the listener already has it.

quiz.q: Sarcasm — “Well, that went GREAT” — is evidence that…
options: intonation can reverse meaning on its own
quiz.explanation: The words stay identical; a flat, stretched, low contour flips the sentence to its opposite.

quiz.q: Japanese háshi versus hashí illustrates…
options: pitch accent — one pitch drop distinguishing words
quiz.explanation: A single accentual pitch drop, moving between syllables, separates “chopsticks” from “bridge”.

intro:
French looks intimidating on the page and is mostly rules in disguise. Final consonants usually fall silent — petit sounds like “puh-tee” — and three vowels travel through the nose: the endings of bon, vin and un are pure nasal sounds with no n pronounced at all. Add one gender system, two verbs, and a politeness register, and the first week of French is genuinely survivable. Bonus for anyone who has wrestled Spanish: where Spanish splits “to be” into ser and estar, French collapsed the pair into a single verb — the hardest choice in Romance grammar simply does not exist.

**Why this matters.** French is spoken natively on five continents, works as an official language of the UN, the EU and the African Union, and supplied roughly a third of English vocabulary. That last fact makes it the highest-yield second language for English speakers: gouvernement, bibliothèque and animal are already in your head, waiting only for pronunciation rules to unlock them. Learn the sound system once and thousands of words arrive free.
objectives: Explain the sound world: pure vowels and nasals
Explain silent finals, liaison and elision
Explain gender and the article system
Explain être and avoir: the first two verbs
Explain tu, vous and the bonjour ritual
Explain survival phrases for the first week

concepts.term: The sound world: pure vowels and nasals
concepts.statement: Keep French vowels pure and tense: never let café glide into “kay-ay”. The nasal vowels have no English equivalent — an (as in the first syllable of “an encore” minus the n), on (rounded, like “song” without the ng), in/un (fronted and tight) — made by sending the vowel through the nose while the tongue stays in vowel position. The French r is a soft gargle at the back of the mouth. And u differs from ou by lip-shape alone: say “ee” with lips rounded as for “oo” — that is tu; tout is plain “too”.

Final consonants are usually silent, with a short list of usually-pronounced exceptions — c, r, f, l, memorised as CaReFuL. Liaison revives a silent consonant before a vowel: les amis runs together as “lay-zah-mee”, vous avez as “voo-zah-vay”. Elision shrinks je and la before vowels — j'aime, l'ami — and the h of l'hôtel is silent, which is why it elides. Adopt these two habits and spoken French stops sounding like one long unbreakable word.

Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and the article is its handle: le livre, la table, les livres, with the plural -s heard only through liaison. Gender is not reliably predictable from meaning — la moustache is a feminine moustache, le problème a masculine problem — so learn each noun with its article, never bare, and the problem dissolves. Some pairs genuinely contrast: un tour is a stroll, une tour a tower; un mode is a mode, une mode a fashion.

concepts.term: être and avoir: the first two verbs
concepts.statement: Two verbs do most of the load-bearing. être, to be: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. avoir, to have: j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont. Both are irregular — learn them as chants, not tables. The pronoun set is je, tu, il, elle, on (the everyday “we”), nous, vous, ils, elles; identity runs through c'est — “c'est Marie” — and possession through de: le livre de Marie. With these two verbs you can already say who you are, what you have and how you feel.

concepts.term: tu, vous and the bonjour ritual
concepts.statement: Politeness runs on one choice and one ritual. Vous is the formal and plural “you”; tu is intimate. Default to vous with strangers, shopkeepers and elders, and accept the invitation “on peut se tutoyer” when it comes. The ritual is bonjour: entering a shop or arriving at a counter without it reads as genuinely rude in France, while with it, almost anything is forgivable. Bonsoir replaces it in the evening; merci, s'il vous plaît and excusez-moi oil every exchange.

concepts.term: Survival phrases for the first week
concepts.statement: The survival kit: bonjour, merci, s'il vous plaît, au revoir. Je m'appelle... introduces you, with enchanté as the reply. Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît orders; l'addition, s'il vous plaît closes the meal. Où est la gare? asks the way; combien ça coûte? asks the price. Je ne parle pas français — parlez-vous anglais? buys honesty and help, and je ne comprends pas, répétez s'il vous plaît repairs the line when it breaks.

The classic English accent keeps three habits: letting vowels glide (a pure “eh” in café, never “ay-ee”), pronouncing final consonants (petit ends in “tee”), and skipping the nasals by saying a real n (bon is one nasalised sound, not “bon-n”). Grammar-wise, the durable error is learning nouns bare and guessing gender later — always memorise le or la with the word. And mind the registers: tutoyer a stranger or a functionary reads as presumptuous; vous is never wrong.
A vowel produced with airflow through the nose, as in bon, vin and un — no n consonant is pronounced.
Sounding a normally silent final consonant before a following vowel, as in les amis.
Dropping a final vowel before another vowel, marked by an apostrophe: je + aime → j'aime.
The classification of every French noun as masculine or feminine, signalled by its article.
The little word that carries gender and number: le, la, les, un, une, des.
The tu versus vous choice that indexes social distance and formality.
A word shared between languages by descent or borrowing, like government and gouvernement.

examples.title: Worked example — French Foundations: Pronunciation, Articles and First Phrases
examples.problem: Order breakfast politely in a Paris café, entirely in French, and understand what comes back.

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: bonjour opens; je voudrais + article + noun orders; un and une must match gender; s'il vous plaît closes the request; tunes rise on questions.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: enter with “Bonjour!”; order “Je voudrais un café au lait et un croissant, s'il vous plaît” — checking that un, not une, agrees with masculine croissant; the server's rising-tune “Autre chose ?” is audible as a question before the words are parsed; close with “Non, merci — l'addition, s'il vous plaît”.

examples.result: the whole exchange ran on greeting, voudrais, article agreement and please/thank-you — the four moves of first-week French, with liaison in s'il and silent finals in croissant doing their quiet work.

keyTakeaways: Travel: greetings, ordering and asking prices cover cafés, stations and hotels in every French-speaking country.
Menus: quiche, croissant, café au lait, hors d'oeuvre — English borrowed the vocabulary already; pronunciation is the only new skill.
Etiquette: bonjour on entry and merci on exit is the French social contract; visitors who keep it are forgiven nearly everything else.
Cognate harvest: government, restaurant, important, animal — a third of English vocabulary turns out to be French with an accent.
Media: films, chansons and slow-news broadcasts (RFI, for example) turn passive vocabulary into listening comprehension within weeks.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is the first French lesson. Follow with present-tense conjugation (-er verbs run on one template), then adjective agreement. The ser versus estar lesson in this section explains what French collapsed; ten minutes of daily slow-French listening tunes the nasals faster than any table can.

quiz.q: The nasal vowel at the end of bon is produced by…
options: pronouncing a clear n after the vowel
sending the vowel through the nose with no n consonant
raising the tongue to the palate
quiz.explanation: The vowel itself is nasalised; the letter n signals the nasal quality and is never released as a consonant.

quiz.q: Les amis is pronounced with a z sound because of…
options: liaison — the silent s sounds before a vowel
quiz.explanation: Liaison revives the silent final consonant when the next word begins with a vowel.

quiz.q: The correct way to order one croissant is…
quiz.explanation: Croissant is masculine, and the article must agree — the reason nouns are always learned with their articles.

quiz.q: Spanish has ser and estar; French…
options: uses être for both — one verb covers essence and state
splits them into être and avoir
quiz.explanation: French collapsed the Latin pair into a single être, removing the choice that defines early Spanish.

intro:
Mandarin looks uncrackable from outside — an alphabet-free wall of squares — but it opens with three keys. First, tones: every syllable carries one of four pitch shapes, and the shape is part of the word. Second, characters: they are not pictures but assemblies, built from a few hundred recurring parts, most hinting at meaning or sound. Third, pinyin: the romanisation on every sign, keyboard and textbook — read by rules, never by English instincts. One lesson cannot teach Mandarin, but it can teach you how the system is put together, which changes everything about learning it.

**Why this matters.** Mandarin has more native speakers than any other language, and its difficulty is front-loaded: the first month is steeper than Spanish's and the fifth year flatter. Knowing the architecture — tones as part of words, characters as component assemblies, pinyin as a tool rather than a spelling — replaces intimidation with a map. Learners who drill tone pairs aloud from day one and learn characters through components consistently outpace those who memorise strokes and hope.
objectives: Explain four tones and a neutral one
Explain pinyin: read the rules, not the letters
Explain radicals: the meaning inside characters
Explain phonetic components: sound hints in the square
Explain simplified versus traditional scripts
Explain compounding and the first phrases

concepts.term: Four tones and a neutral one
concepts.statement: Every full Mandarin syllable carries a tone: mā, high and level; má, rising; mǎ, dipping; mà, falling — mother, hemp, horse, scold. Unstressed syllables take a light neutral tone, as in the second half of xièxie, thanks. Tones are not emotion and not optional: to a native listener, mà is as distant from mā as “bat” is from “pat”. The Tonal Languages lesson in this section treats the phonology in depth; for foundations, the work is minimal pairs spoken aloud — má against mǎ — until the pitch shapes attach themselves to words.

concepts.term: Pinyin: read the rules, not the letters
concepts.statement: Pinyin looks like English and is not. Its letters obey Mandarin rules: q is a soft “ch” (qī, seven), x a whispery “sh” (xǐ, wash), c is “ts” (cài, vegetable), zh a richer “j”. The vowel of shi, si and ci is a buzzed retroflex nothing like the i of “see”. Aspiration is flipped: p, t and k are puffy with breath, while b, d and g are plain. The diacritics carry the tones — mā má mǎ mà — so a syllable's melody is written into its spelling. Master these rules once, or every word you read aloud will be wrong in a predictable way.

Characters assemble from components, and the most meaningful one is called the radical. 氵 marks water: hǎi 海, sea; xǐ 洗, wash; lèi 泪, tears. 木 is wood and trees; 口 is mouth — eat, drink, call; 心 is heart — feeling, memory, thinking. Roughly two hundred radicals organise the dictionary and chunk the 3,000-plus characters of genuine literacy into families. Nobody memorises three thousand arbitrary symbols; learners read wholes the way you read “unbelievably” — as assembled parts.

concepts.term: Phonetic components: sound hints in the square
concepts.statement: Most characters — perhaps four in five — are phono-semantic compounds: one component hints at meaning, another at sound. 妈 mā, mother, is 女, woman (meaning), plus 马 mǎ, horse (sound). 青 qīng helps spell 清 qīng, clear water, 请 qǐng, request, and 情 qíng, feeling. The hints are weather forecasts, not guarantees — sounds drifted across centuries and dialects — but they cut the memorisation load enormously. Character logic is exactly this: meaning part plus sound part, guessed before confirmed.

One language, two scripts. The simplified characters used in mainland China and Singapore were standardised in the 1950s and 60s to speed literacy: 爱 drops strokes from 愛, 门 from 門. Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau and many overseas communities keep traditional forms. Readers of one recognise much of the other; writers must commit to a target. Choose by where you will use the language, and check which script a textbook, app or dictionary uses before buying it.

Mandarin builds words by compounding, transparently: 电 diàn, electricity, plus 脑 nǎo, brain, gives 电脑, computer; 电话 is “electric speech”, a telephone; 火车 is “fire vehicle”, a train. Each morpheme keeps its meaning across words, so vocabulary compounds — learn fifty characters and hundreds of words unlock. First phrases run on the same logic: nǐ hǎo 你好, “you good”, hello; xièxie 谢谢, thanks; duìbuqǐ 对不起, sorry; wǒ jiào... 我叫, “I am called”; duōshao qián? 多少钱, how much; wǒ bù míngbái 我不明白, I do not understand.

Reading pinyin as English is the first and worst error — “xiè” is not “zee” and “qī” is not “key”. The second is treating tones as decoration to add later: fossilised toneless Mandarin is the hardest accent to repair. Third, memorising characters stroke by stroke instead of as component assemblies — the difference between three thousand passwords and two hundred puzzle pieces. Fourth, buying materials in the wrong script for your target region. And remember that pinyin is a learning and typing tool, not the language: fluency lives in characters and ears.
A pitch pattern stored as part of a word's identity; Mandarin has four tones plus a neutral one.
The standard romanisation of Mandarin — rule-governed, but never to be read with English letter values.
The meaning-bearing component of a character, used to organise dictionaries: 氵 water, 口 mouth.
A character combining a meaning component with a sound-hinting component, like 妈 mā, mother.
The stroke-reduced standard script of mainland China and Singapore, introduced from the 1950s.
The older full-stroke script retained in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau and many diaspora communities.
Word-formation by joining morphemes — Mandarin's main strategy, as in 电 + 话, “electric speech”.

examples.title: Worked example — Mandarin Foundations: Tones, Characters and First Phrases
examples.problem: Given 电 diàn, “electricity”, the radical 火, “fire”, and 话 huà, “speech”, infer the meanings of 电话, 火车 and 电灯.

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: characters compound meaning with meaning, and most real words are two-character compounds of stable morphemes.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: 电话 = diàn + huà = “electric speech” → telephone. 火车 = huǒ + chē = “fire vehicle” → train, named for steam. 灯 dēng pairs the fire radical with a sound component and means lamp, so 电灯 is an electric lamp — and 电脑, “electric brain”, confirms the pattern.

examples.result: five characters and one radical produced five real words — the arithmetic that makes Mandarin vocabulary accelerate instead of accumulate.

keyTakeaways: Travel: signage, station names and menus are bilingual with pinyin, so reading rules plus survival phrases carry a trip.
Typing: every phone keyboard converts typed pinyin into characters, so writing Mandarin is choosing among candidates, not drawing strokes.
Study paths: the HSK proficiency exams sequence characters and vocabulary by level, and graded readers pace the climb to real texts.
Business: name cards, script choice and simplified-versus-traditional materials are regional decisions with real stakes.
Heritage learning: background speakers often read well but type better — pinyin fluency is their bridge back into the characters.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is the first Mandarin lesson. Follow with the Tonal Languages lesson for the phonology of tone, then character study proper: the two to three thousand characters of real literacy, learned through components and spaced repetition. Drill tone pairs aloud from the first day; the ear will not learn what the mouth never attempts.

quiz.q: In pinyin, the letter q represents a sound closest to…
quiz.explanation: qī, “seven”, begins like “chee”; pinyin letters follow Mandarin rules, not English values.

quiz.q: The 氵 component in 海 (sea) and 洗 (wash) is a…
options: phonetic hint for the sound hǎi
quiz.explanation: Radicals carry the meaning family — water in this case — and organise dictionaries around it.

quiz.q: Mandarin builds most of its vocabulary by…
options: compounding morphemes, as in 电 + 话, telephone
quiz.explanation: Stable morphemes compound into transparent words: electricity plus speech gives telephone.

quiz.q: The four tones of Mandarin are best described as…
options: four pitch patterns stored as part of each word
quiz.explanation: Tone is lexical, not expressive: mā, má, mǎ and mà are four different words to a native ear.

intro:
The oldest story we have is about a king who could not accept death. Gilgamesh, carved on clay tablets in Mesopotamia four thousand years ago, already contains friendship, hubris, flood and grief; the Iliad and the Odyssey, sung in Greek around the eighth century BCE, still define what a hero is. Epic is where literature begins — and it did not begin as writing at all, but as performance, rhythm and trained memory. Understanding how these poems were made is understanding what a book was before books.

**Why this matters.** Epic is the root system of nearly everything you have read or watched: the hero's arc that Hollywood engineers, the invocation that opens Paradise Lost, the in medias res cold open of every prestige drama. It is also the first evidence of how humans stored culture before hard drives — in formula, metre and memory. To read Gilgamesh and Homer knowing how they were built is to watch humanity invent literature in real time.
objectives: Explain literature before writing: the oral poet
Explain gilgamesh: the first recorded epic
Explain the Homeric question and the formula
Explain epic conventions: invocation, in medias res, epithet
Explain the hero: kleos, nostos and mortality
Explain what writing changed

concepts.term: Literature before writing: the oral poet
concepts.statement: Before writing, the poet was the storage medium. Epics lived in performance: a singer with an instrument, a toolkit of ready-made phrases, and an audience with expectations. Rhythm and repetition were engineering, not ornament — metrical patterns made thousands of lines memorable. Composition happened in delivery: the singer re-created the story each time from structural bones and stock phrases, never reproducing the same text twice, because there was no text. Literature begins inside this performance tradition, not outside it.

The Epic of Gilgamesh reached its standard Babylonian version around 1200 BCE, from Sumerian poems up to a millennium older. Gilgamesh, king of Uruk — two-thirds god, one-third man — is tamed by the wild man Enkidu; together they slay the guardian of the Cedar Forest; the gods answer with Enkidu's death; and Gilgamesh, terrified, crosses the waters of death to ask the flood-survivor Utnapishtim how to escape dying. The answer is that he cannot. It is literature's first great meditation on mortality — and its flood story predates Noah's by centuries.

concepts.term: The Homeric question and the formula
concepts.statement: Who was Homer, and how were the Iliad and Odyssey made? Milman Parry's 1930s fieldwork on South Slavic oral singers supplied the answer. The signature Homeric devices — “swift-footed Achilles”, “rosy-fingered Dawn” — are metrical spare parts, each shaped to fit a given slot in the dactylic hexameter line. The oral-formulaic theory, completed by Albert Lord's The Singer of Tales, showed the poems could be composed in performance without writing. The monumental versions we read were probably dictated in the new Greek alphabet: performance caught and frozen at a moment of transition.

concepts.term: Epic conventions: invocation, in medias res, epithet
concepts.statement: The genre announces itself with a fixed toolkit. The invocation — “Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles” — calls a Muse and states the theme. In medias res: the Iliad opens in the war's tenth year; the Odyssey begins with its hero trapped on Calypso's island while his son searches for him. The fixed epithet, the catalog of massed ships, the extended epic simile, the visible gods who intervene — all were listeners' signposts and the singer's scaffolding, and literary epics from Virgil to Milton adopted them as homage.

concepts.term: The hero: kleos, nostos and mortality
concepts.statement: Two Greek words name the epics' engines. Kleos, glory won in song, is what Achilles buys with a short life — the Iliad's tragic bargain. Nostos, homecoming, is the Odyssey's drive: ten years of wandering, a wife holding off suitors, a kingdom to reclaim. Both poems run mortality as the unstated price — the gods are immortal and bored; humans matter because they die. This journey pattern — departure, trial, return — is the raw material that Campbell's monomyth later systematised; the comparative mythology lesson in Humanities takes that story forward.

Writing did not kill the epics; it canonised them. A dictated text could outlive its dialect, its singer, its occasion — rhapsodes now performed a fixed Homer, and Alexandrian librarians edited him into the versions we inherit. Virgil, composing the Aeneid in writing two decades before the Common Era, deliberately wrote himself into the lineage; Beowulf, Dante and Milton follow. Literature became a portable, quotable object — the prerequisite for criticism, canon and school. The epic tradition is the record of that shift: performance becoming text, text becoming heritage.

Do not read epics as novels: they are amplified performance texts, and their repetition, catalogs and formulae are features of oral engineering, not padding. Do not insist on a single historical Homer — the formulaic make-up of the poems is precisely what complicates that picture. Do not call Gilgamesh “the first book”: older Sumerian poems fed it, and the standard version was compiled over centuries. And do not skip the invocation and catalogs to get to the story — in epic, the frame is part of the story.
Building verse in performance from metrical formulas and story-patterns, without a fixed text.
A long narrative poem of heroic action, performed or written, centring figures of communal importance.
A fixed, formulaic phrase — “swift-footed Achilles” — shaped to fit the metre.
Opening in the middle of the action, at a late point in the story's chronology.
The opening appeal to a Muse to authorise and enable the telling.
Glory won in song — the imperishable fame that repays a mortal hero's death.
Homecoming, the Odyssey's driving pattern and the root of “nostalgia”.

examples.title: Worked example — From Gilgamesh to the Odyssey: The Birth of Literature
examples.problem: Read the opening of the Odyssey as an engineering document — which conventions are deployed, and to what effect?

steps.label: Recall the toolkit
steps.text: invocation, statement of theme, in medias res, fixed epithet, the Muse as authority.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: “Tell me, O Muse, of the man of many turns...” — the invocation outsources authority to the goddess; the theme arrives at once: the man, his wanderings, his crew; “many turns” is a fixed epithet doing double work, characterising both Odysseus' mind and travels; the poem then jumps in medias res — year ten, everyone else home, the hero trapped — creating the gap the whole poem exists to close.

examples.result: in about twenty lines the performance contract is signed — who speaks, what the story is, where we are in it, and what the hero is like. Oral technology working at full pressure.

keyTakeaways: Reading the epics today: Emily Wilson's 2017 Odyssey — the first English translation by a woman — and modern Gilgamesh editions make four-thousand-year-old poems newly readable.
Screenwriting: the cold open, the flashback structure and the journey plot are epic conventions still earning money in every multiplex.
Ancient history: epics are evidence — for Bronze Age warfare, ships, palaces and values — read critically alongside archaeology.
Comparative literature: Gilgamesh, Homer, the Mahabharata and Beowulf together frame the question of what makes a story epic.
Creative writing: studying formula and variation teaches the deepest lesson the epics hold — constraints generate fluency.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — start world literature here. Follow with the comparative mythology lesson in Humanities, which follows the hero's journey from these epics to Campbell and Hollywood, and the literary devices lesson in this section for the close-reading toolkit. Wilson's Odyssey and a good Gilgamesh translation are the two first books to actually read.

quiz.q: The oral-formulaic theory of Parry and Lord explains Homeric epithets as…
options: metrical spare parts for composing verse in performance
proof of a single written draft
quiz.explanation: Each formula fits a metrical slot, letting the singer compose fluently without a fixed text.

quiz.q: Opening a poem in medias res means beginning…
options: with an invocation of the Muse
in the middle of the action
quiz.explanation: The Iliad starts in the war's tenth year; the Odyssey with its hero already years into his return.

quiz.q: Achilles' choice between a long life and kleos dramatises…
options: the tension between mortality and imperishable fame
the wrath of the gods against Troy
quiz.explanation: Kleos is glory in song — the only immortality a mortal can buy, and the Iliad prices it in years.

quiz.q: The standard Babylonian Gilgamesh is remarkable for containing…
options: a flood narrative centuries older than Noah's
a signed contract with the singer
quiz.explanation: Utnapishtim's flood predates the Genesis account by centuries — one of literature's earliest echoes across cultures.

intro:
Open a German newspaper and meet the family: Haus, Wasser, Mutter, Buch, trinken — English and German descend from the same Germanic ancestor, so hundreds of words sit side by side wearing slightly different clothes. The grammar that frightens beginners is largely English grammar before it wore smooth: Old English carried cases too, and German still wears them openly. Learn the four cases, the verb-second rule and a page of pronunciation laws, and German stops being a wall of capitalised Nouns and becomes the most approachable major language an English speaker can study.

**Why this matters.** German has the most native speakers in the European Union and remains a working language of science, engineering and philosophy. For English speakers it offers the biggest cognate harvest of any major language, while its cases and word order teach — better than any textbook — how inflection can carry the meaning that English assigns to position.
objectives: Explain pronunciation you can trust
Explain gender: der, die, das
Explain four cases on the articles
Explain verb-second word order
Explain verb-final subordinate clauses
Explain cognates and false friends

concepts.statement: German spelling keeps its promises. The famous clusters have fixed values: ei sounds like the “i” of “ice” (nein, mein); ie like “ee” (vier, Bier); eu and äu like “oy” (heute, Häuser). Of the consonants, w is English v (Wasser), v is f (Vater), z is “ts” (Zeit), sch is “sh”, j is English y (ja), and ß is simply a sharp double s (Straße). The umlauts pull vowels forward: ü is “ee” said with lips rounded for “oo” — the same trick as the French u — while ö rounds an “eh”. The ch after a, o and u is a throaty rasp (Buch); after i and e, a hiss (ich).

Every noun is der (masculine), die (feminine) or das (neuter), and the article is the handle you actually use — so learn nouns with their article from the first day, never bare. Gender is grammatical, not natural: das Mädchen, “the girl”, is neuter, because the suffix -chen makes any noun neuter. The suffixes are your friends: -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft and -tion are reliably feminine (die Zeitung, die Freiheit); -chen and -lein are neuter. Plurals are less tidy than in Spanish or Italian — umlauts, -e, -er, -en or -s, chosen noun by noun — but the plural article is always die.

Four cases mark who does what to whom, and they ride on the articles: nominative for subjects, accusative for direct objects, dative for indirect objects, genitive for possession. In Der Mann gibt dem Kind das Buch — “the man gives the child the book” — dem marks the recipient and das the thing given; because endings carry the roles, the phrases can be shuffled for emphasis and the sentence survives. Only the masculine article changes between nominative and accusative (der → den); dative and genitive demand memorisation, and dative plurals add an -n (mit den Kindern).

German main clauses are verb-second. The finite verb claims the second slot no matter what opens the sentence: Heute regnet es, “today it rains”; Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin, “tomorrow travel I to Berlin”. Time phrases, places and even objects can be fronted for emphasis — but whichever element leads, the verb stays second and the subject slides to third. English speakers must practise this actively, because their instinct puts the subject first; behind the verb, the middlefield follows tendencies like time before manner before place.

Subordinators — weil (because), dass (that), wenn (if, when) — change the grammar: the finite verb drops to the very end. Ich weiß, dass er morgen kommt is literally “I know that he tomorrow comes”. Infinitives and past participles also collect at the end (Ich möchte ein Buch kaufen, “I want to buy a book”), so a German sentence often delays its resolution like a suspense novel. Fluent German is largely the management of these two orders: verb-second in main clauses, verb-final in subordinate ones.

The cognate harvest is enormous: Hand, Land, Wasser, Apfel, Vater, Haus, trinken, schlafen. But harvest carefully — the false friends bite. Also means “so, thus”, not “also”; bekommen means “get, receive” (Ich bekomme ein Geschenk, “I receive a present”); Gift means poison; brav means well-behaved; Chef means boss. Germans capitalise every noun, which at least makes the traps easy to spot.

The first trap is treating German as English with capital nouns: the word order is engineered, and ignoring verb-second marks a speaker instantly. The second is guessing gender from meaning — das Mädchen breaks the rule that seems obvious. Third, forgetting the dative plural -n (mit den Kindern, not mit die Kinder). Fourth, trusting false friends — ordering confidently with bekommen and praising the Gift. And keep the vowels honest: ei is not “ee”, however tired you are.
The der/die/das classification of every German noun, signalled by its article.
An ending-set marking a noun phrase’s role — nominative, accusative, dative or genitive.
The main-clause rule that the finite verb occupies the second position, whatever leads.
A clause introduced by weil, dass, wenn and their kin, where the verb falls to the end.
The fronted, rounded vowels ä, ö and ü, and the diacritic that writes them.
A look-alike word with a different meaning, like bekommen, “receive”.
A word shared by descent, like Haus and house.

examples.title: Worked example — German Foundations: Cases, Word Order and Cognates
examples.problem: Assemble — in correct German order — “Tomorrow my sister gives her friend a watch”, then embed the same statement under dass.

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: verb-second in the main clause; dative for the recipient (ihrem Freund), accusative for the thing given (eine Uhr); a time phrase may lead.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: front the time phrase — Morgen; the verb takes slot two — schenkt; subject third — meine Schwester; then dative before accusative — ihrem Freund eine Uhr.

examples.result: “Morgen schenkt meine Schwester ihrem Freund eine Uhr.” Embedded: “Ich freue mich, dass meine Schwester ihrem Freund morgen eine Uhr schenkt” — the verb now falls to the very end.

keyTakeaways: Nominative: der Mann, die Frau, das Kind — subjects.
Accusative: den Mann, die Frau, das Kind — direct objects.
Dative: dem Mann, der Frau, dem Kind — recipients; den Kindern in the plural.
Genitive: des Mannes, der Frau, des Kindes — possession, “of the man”.
Business and science in the EU’s largest economy: German is the most widely spoken native language of Europe.
The academic tradition: psychology, physics and philosophy were written in German for two centuries.
Cognate-powered vocabulary growth: thousands of transparent relatives bring reading speed early.
Music and literature: lieder, Goethe, Kafka and Mann in the original.
Grammar transfer: German cases train the reflexes that Russian, Latin and Greek will later demand.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is the first German lesson. Follow with present-tense conjugation and adjective endings, which extend the case system you just met. The Spanish and French foundations lessons sit beside this one; for a second case-marking language, continue to the Russian foundations lesson in this section.

quiz.q: In “Heute gehe ich ins Kino”, why does ich come after gehe?
options: The verb-second rule puts the finite verb in slot two, pushing the subject to third
quiz.explanation: Whatever opens the clause — here heute — the finite verb claims the second position and the subject follows.

quiz.q: In “Der Mann gibt dem Kind das Buch”, dem Kind is…
options: the dative recipient of the book
quiz.explanation: Dem marks dative — the child receives; das Buch is the accusative thing given.

quiz.q: “Ich bekomme ein Geschenk” means…
quiz.explanation: Bekommen is the classic false friend: it means get or receive, not become.

quiz.q: Das Mädchen, “the girl”, is grammatically…
quiz.explanation: Suffix beats meaning: -chen and -lein are always neuter — gender is grammatical, not natural.

intro:
Hindi is one of the world’s largest languages by total speakers, and its script looks like temple ornament until you learn its logic — at which point Devanagari behaves like a machine for reading. The grammar rewires two habits: the verb goes last, the opposite of English, and verbs and adjectives carry the gender of their subjects. Nothing in it is harder than what you once did with English before the age of six; it is only arranged differently.

**Why this matters.** Hindi shares its spoken core with Urdu, so learning one opens the other; Bollywood dialogue, India’s officialdom and a vast diaspora all run on it. And the script’s fit between letter and sound is close to perfect: once the letters are yours, you can pronounce any written word — including ones you have never met — on sight.
objectives: Explain devanagari: the abugida principle
Explain the inherent vowel and its matras
Explain retroflex and aspirated consonants
Explain sOV order and postpositions
Explain gender agreement in verbs and adjectives
Explain hindi and Urdu: one speech, two scripts

concepts.statement: Devanagari is an abugida: each consonant letter comes with a built-in short “a”. क is ka, not k — that is the inherent vowel. To change it, attach a matra, a vowel sign clipped around the letter: कि is ki, कू is kū, के is ke. To kill the vowel entirely, add the virama (्) below the letter: क् is plain k. A horizontal headline called the shirorekha runs along the top of every word, linking its letters into one visual unit — the clothesline the letters hang from.

concepts.term: The inherent vowel and its matras
concepts.statement: Decode the greeting: नमस्ते namaste. Letter by letter: न na, then म ma, then स् — sa with its vowel killed by the virama — and finally ते, ta with the e-matra. Na-mas-te, “I bow to you”, the universal hello. Independent vowel letters open words where no consonant precedes them: आप āp, the formal “you”. Read चाय chāy, tea, and कॉफ़ kophī, coffee — the extra dots (nukta) mark sounds borrowed from Persian and English, like f and z.

Two consonant families do work English never asks of consonants. Retroflex consonants — ट ठ ड ढ, transliterated ṭ and ḍ — curl the tongue tip back to the roof of the mouth, contrasting with the soft dentals त थ द ध, tongue against the teeth. And aspiration, a burst of breath after the consonant, separates words: पल pal is “moment”, फल phal is “fruit”. English speakers produce both kinds of sound but never use the difference to tell words apart; in Hindi the difference is load-bearing, exactly as the tonal contrasts of Mandarin are.

Word order is subject–object–verb: मैं सेब खाता हूँ (maiṃ seb khātā hūñ) — “I apple eat”, with the verb closing the sentence, always. Role-words follow the noun instead of preceding it: Hindi has postpositions where English has prepositions — में “in”, पर “on”, के साथ “with” — so मेरे घर में (mere ghar meṃ) is “in my house”, literally “my house in”. Japanese, in the particles lesson of this section, runs precisely the same geometry with different machinery.

concepts.term: Gender agreement in verbs and adjectives
concepts.statement: Verbs and adjectives agree with the gender of their subject. A man says मैं चाय पीता हूँ (maiṃ chāy pītā hūñ), a woman says मैं चाय पीती हूँ (pītī hūñ) — both mean “I drink tea”; only the verb ending moves. Adjectives shift the same way: अच्छा लड़का (achhā laḍkā), “good boy”, becomes अच्छी लड़की (achhī laḍkī), “good girl”. Learn every noun with its gender, exactly as the French and German lessons of this section demand with theirs.

concepts.term: Hindi and Urdu: one speech, two scripts
concepts.statement: Politeness is graded. Three “you”s calibrate distance: आप āp for respect and strangers, तुम tum for friends, तू tū for intimacy. Stock phrases: नमस्ते namaste, hello and goodbye; आप कैसे हैं? (āp kaise haiṃ), “how are you?”; धन्यवाद dhanyavād, thank you; कृपया kṛpayā, please; माफ़ कीजिए māf kījiye, excuse me; कितना है? (kitnā hai?), how much is it?; मुझे नहीं पता (mujhe nahīṃ patā), I don’t know. Default upward to आप — the etiquette of Spanish usted, with one more step.
concepts.detail: Hindi and Urdu are one spoken language — Hindustani — in two official dresses. Hindi draws its learned vocabulary from Sanskrit and writes Devanagari; Urdu draws from Persian and Arabic and writes the flowing Nastaliq script. India and Pakistan maintain the two registers as separate official standards; Bollywood dialogue lives happily between them. The writing-systems lesson in this section returns to this pair as its most consequential example: a language is not its script.

concepts.statement: The first and worst error is reading क as “k” — every consonant carries its “a” until a virama or matra says otherwise. The second is confusing कि and की: the first is “that”, a conjunction; the second is “of”, a possessive — different words entirely. Third, imposing English order: the verb belongs at the end. Fourth, treating gender agreement as decoration — dropping it is as audible as dropping the -s of Spanish verbs. Last, flattening retroflex and aspirated consonants into English ones quietly turns each word into another word.
A script whose consonant letters carry an inherent vowel, modified by diacritics.
The default short “a” built into every Devanagari consonant.
A vowel sign attached to a consonant letter to replace its inherent vowel.
The diacritic that kills a consonant’s inherent vowel, as in स्.
Subject–object–verb word order — the verb closes the sentence.
A role word that follows its noun — Hindi’s mirror of English prepositions.
Verbs and adjectives taking endings that match the gender of what they describe.

examples.title: Worked example — Hindi Foundations: Devanagari, Word Order and Agreement
examples.problem: Read the word नमस्ते aloud from its letters, then build “I drink tea” for a male and a female speaker.

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: every consonant carries an inherent “a” unless a matra or the virama changes it; the verb goes last; the verb agrees with the speaker’s gender.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: नमस्ते = न na + म ma + स् (virama-killed sa) + ते (ta with e-matra) → namaste. The sentence: मैं (I) + चाय (tea) + पीता हूँ (drink-masculine + am) → मैं चाय पीता हूँ; the feminine speaker swaps पीता for पीती.

examples.result: you decoded an unfamiliar word letter by letter and built one grammatical sentence twice — the two skills Devanagari and agreement demand from the first day.

keyTakeaways: Travel in India: greetings, prices and directions run on the phrases above plus numbers.
Bollywood and music: songs arrive subtitled in Devanagari and romanisation alike — reading opens the lyrics.
Heritage learning: the script reconnects diaspora speakers to print, signage and ceremony.
The Urdu bridge: shared grammar and speech make the second register cheap once the first exists.
Yoga and mantra traditions: their pronunciation rests on exactly the retroflex and aspirated contrasts taught here.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — start here for Hindi. Follow with verb conjugation across tenses and the oblique case that postpositions trigger. The Japanese particles lesson teaches the same verb-final geometry with a different mechanism, and the writing-systems lesson places Devanagari among the scripts of the world.

quiz.q: The letter क, standing alone, is read…
quiz.explanation: The inherent short “a” rides along until a matra or the virama changes it.

quiz.q: मैं सेब खाता हूँ (maiṃ seb khātā hūñ) displays which word order?
quiz.explanation: Subject, object, verb — the mirror image of English, and the norm for the language family.

quiz.q: पल (pal, “moment”) and फल (phal, “fruit”) differ in…
options: aspiration — the breath burst after the consonant
quiz.explanation: The added puff of air is the entire difference — aspiration is contrastive in Hindi.

quiz.q: Hindi and Urdu…
options: share a spoken core but differ in script and vocabulary sources
quiz.explanation: One speech, two dresses: Devanagari with Sanskrit learning versus Nastaliq with Perso-Arabic learning.

intro:
Arabic builds its vocabulary on an idea most languages never use: the root. Three consonants carry a core meaning, and patterns — fixed moulds of vowels and affixes — sculpt them into words. Kitāb, maktab, maktaba and kātib are all one root, K-T-B, “writing”, in four different jobs. Add a script that runs right to left and mostly writes consonants, plus a formal standard living beside a family of spoken dialects, and you have the three ideas that organise everything else about the language.

**Why this matters.** Arabic gives roughly four hundred million people their first language across more than twenty countries, is one of the UN’s six official languages, and is the liturgical language of the Quran’s nearly two billion Muslims. And its root system is the most elegant word-engine among major languages: learn one root honestly, and a dozen words arrive pre-assembled.
objectives: Explain the triliteral root system
Explain patterns: reusable word moulds
Explain the script: right to left, connected
Explain short vowels left unwritten
Explain sun and moon letters
Explain diglossia: the standard and the dialects

concepts.statement: Take the triliteral root K-T-B, whose meaning core is writing. Kataba means “he wrote” — the bare past verb. Kitāb is “book”, the result of writing. Maktab is “office, desk” — literally the place where writing happens. Maktaba is “library, bookshop”, the place with a lot of it. Kātib is “writer, clerk”, the person who does it, and maktūb, “written”, also means “letter” and by extension “fate”. The root itself never appears alone — only slotted into patterns, which is why Arabic dictionaries are organised by root: you look up maktaba under K-T-B.
$$\text{K-T-B} \;\text{+}\; \text{maCCaC} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{maktab}$$
concepts.detail: A triliteral root slots into a pattern: the root supplies the meaning core (“write”), the pattern supplies the category and shape (maCCaC, a noun of place), and the composite is a word — maktab, “place of writing”. Swap the root, keep the mould: D-R-S gives madrasa, “school”.

concepts.statement: The script runs right to left, in a cursive that joins letters inside words — each letter has up to four shapes depending on position, but they are variations on one skeleton, learned once. There are 28 letters, no capitals, and three long vowels that are written (ā, ū, ī) — but the three short vowels, a, i and u, are normally left off the page entirely. The skeleton كتب might read kataba, “he wrote”, or kutiba, “it was written”. Diacritics called harakāt supply the vowels where they matter most — the Quran, children’s books, learner texts — but ordinary print expects the reader to fill them in from grammar and context, exactly as English readers choose the pronunciation of “read”.

concepts.term: The script: right to left, connected
concepts.statement: The definite article is al-, welded onto its word. Before the “sun” letters — t, n, r, s, sh, z and their kin — the l assimilates to the following sound: الشمس ash-shams, “the sun”, is pronounced with sh-sh, no l at all. “Moon” letters keep it: القمر al-qamar, “the moon”. The rule is automatic once the ear knows it, and it explains why transliterations swing between al-, as-, ar- and ash-.

Charles Ferguson named diglossia in 1959, and Arabic was his exhibit A: a formal standard — Modern Standard Arabic, descended from Classical Arabic — coexists with a family of natively spoken vernaculars. The standard rules news, literature, formal speech and the Quran; Egyptian Arabic (Cairo’s film industry made it the most widely understood), Levantine, Gulf and Maghrebi rule the street and the kitchen. Children grow up speaking a dialect and meet the standard at school as a written register. The practical strategy: Modern Standard Arabic for reading and news, one dialect — usually Egyptian or Levantine — for speaking, and no illusions that one “Arabic” covers both.

Grammar opens gently: there is no present-tense “to be” — البيت كبير (al-bayt kabīr), “the house big”, means “the house is big” — and possession is a chain, the iḍāfa: بيت الرجل (bayt al-rajul), “house of-the-man”, is “the man’s house”. The sounds include a family English lacks: خ kh as in Bach, a breathy ḥ, the pharyngeal ع ʿayn — a voiced squeeze deep in the throat — غ gh like a French r, a deep ق q, and the “emphatic” ṭ, ṣ and ḍ that darken neighbouring vowels. First phrases: السلام عليكم (as-salāmu ʿalaykum), “peace be upon you”, answered وعليكم السلام (wa ʿalaykumu s-salām); شكرا (shukran), thanks; من فضلك (min faḍlik), please; كم؟ (kam?), how much?; لا أفهم (lā afham), I don’t understand.

Do not expect the short vowels on the page — supplying them is the reader’s job. Do not read left to right; the habit is deeper than you think. Do not assume one Arabic: the standard-only learner is silent in a Cairo café, and the dialect-only learner cannot read a newspaper. Do not treat the root as a word — it never stands alone. And do not pronounce the article of ash-shams as “al-shams” — the assimilation is not optional.
A usually three-consonant skeleton carrying a meaning core, like K-T-B, “write”.
A fixed mould of vowels and affixes that turns a root into a word of a given category.
The coexistence of a formal standard and native vernaculars with distinct social jobs.
A script writing consonants, with vowels mostly left to the reader.
Optional diacritics marking short vowels, used in the Quran and learner texts.
Letter classes deciding whether the article al- assimilates (ash-shams) or stays (al-qamar).
The possessive chain “X of Y”, as in bayt al-rajul, “the man’s house”.

examples.title: Worked example — Arabic Foundations: Roots, Script and Diglossia
examples.problem: Given the root D-R-S, “study”, predict the words for lesson, school and teacher — then check the logic against the K-T-B family.

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: roots never surface alone; patterns are reusable moulds; maCCaC names the place of the action.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: dars, “lesson”, from the simple noun pattern; madrasa, “school”, from the place pattern — where studying happens; mudarris, “teacher”, from the pattern naming the one who makes the action happen.

examples.result: all three are filed under D-R-S in the dictionary, and madrasa sits in the same mould as maktaba — the pattern transferred, the root supplied new meaning. One root learned, a classroom of words received.

keyTakeaways: Travel across twenty-plus countries: greetings and numbers in the standard plus one dialect carry the day.
Media: newspapers and satellite news run on Modern Standard Arabic — the written register is uniform from Rabat to Muscat.
Quranic study: the classical register, fully vowel-marked, is the tradition’s core discipline.
Vocabulary arithmetic: every new word reinforces the dozens of relatives sharing its root.
Cross-linguistic credit: Arabic loanwords — algebra, algorithm, alcohol — are already in your English.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — start here for Arabic. Follow with the letter forms in their four positions, then verb patterns in past and present. The writing-systems lesson classifies Arabic’s script among the world’s systems, and the Hindi lesson shows a script built on the opposite principle.

quiz.q: Maktab and maktaba are both filed in the dictionary under…
quiz.explanation: Root, not first letter: Arabic dictionaries are organised by consonant skeleton.

quiz.q: In ordinary printed Arabic, the short vowels are…
options: normally unwritten, supplied by the reader
quiz.explanation: Harakāt appear in the Quran and learner texts; ordinary print leaves the vowels to grammar and context.

quiz.q: الشمس (ash-shams, “the sun”) shows that…
options: the article’s l assimilates before sun letters
quiz.explanation: Sun letters assimilate the l of al-; moon letters like q leave it standing.

quiz.q: Diglossia in Arabic means…
options: a formal standard for written life alongside natively spoken dialects
quiz.explanation: Ferguson’s term: Modern Standard Arabic and the vernaculars divide the labour of daily life.

intro:
Korean hands you the friendliest writing system on Earth. Hangul, promulgated in 1446, was designed rather than evolved: its letters encode the shapes of the mouth making the sounds, and they pack into tidy syllable blocks learnable in a weekend. The grammar, meanwhile, is verb-final with particles marking roles — the same geometry as Japanese — and its signature system is politeness: every sentence announces the social relationship between speaker and listener.

**Why this matters.** Korean is the language of a leading global economy and of film, drama and music exported worldwide, and its layered politeness means register grammar is not decoration but the spine of the language. Best of all, the script barrier that slows learners of Japanese and Mandarin simply does not exist here: Hangul was engineered to be learnable, and it keeps that promise.
objectives: Explain hangul: a featural alphabet
Explain syllable blocks, not letter rows
Explain three-way consonant contrast
Explain speech levels and honorifics
Explain sOV order with particles
Explain the verb-ending engine

concepts.statement: Before 1446 Koreans wrote in Classical Chinese; King Sejong’s committee published Hangul — first called Hunminjeongeum, “the correct sounds for the instruction of the people” — and literacy became a matter of days rather than years. The letters are featural: their shapes draw the speech organs. ㅁ m pictures two lips; ㅅ s the teeth; ㄴ n the tongue tip at the ridge; ㅇ ng an open throat; ㄱ g the tongue root closing on the back of the mouth. Add a stroke and the sound gains a puff of breath (ㄱ g → ㅋ k); double the letter and it tightens (ㄱ → ㄲ kk).

Letters — jamo — do not stand in a row; they pack into square blocks, one per syllable: 한 han assembles ㅎ h + ㅏ a + ㄴ n, and 글 geul assembles ㄱ g + ㅡ eu + ㄹ l. The script’s own name, 한글 hangeul, is therefore two blocks. Reading runs left to right, top to bottom within each block. Twenty-four basic jamo cover the whole language, and automatic reading arrives within a month of honest practice — the promise of the design, kept.

Korean consonants come in plain, aspirated and tense triplets — ㄷ d, ㅌ t, ㄸ tt — where English keeps only the first two, and only half the time. The tense series squeezes the throat; the aspirated series adds a burst of breath; the distinctions separate words, so they are not accent polish. The vowels include ㅓ eo and ㅡ eu, unrounded sounds with no English equivalents, and there is no f or v — which is how “fighting!” becomes 파이팅 (paiting).

Every Korean sentence chooses a speech level. The workhorse is the polite 해요체, ending verbs in -아/어요: 안녕하세요 annyeonghaseyo, hello. Formal settings — news, presentations — use 하십시오체 with -ㅂ니다: 감사합니다 gamsahamnida, thank you. Close friends and younger family get banmal, the plain register: 고마워 gomawo, thanks; using it uninvited is the fastest way to sound rude in the language. Honorifics reach deeper than endings: the infix -시- and the suffix -님 elevate the person being spoken about. Default politely upward and wait to be invited down — the etiquette of Spanish usted, systematised.

Word order is subject–object–verb, with particles marking roles: 저는 김치를 먹어요 (jeoneun kimchireul meogeoyo) — “I-topic kimchi-object eat-polite”. 는/은 marks the topic, 를/을 the object, 이/가 the subject, 에 and 에서 places and times. The verb closes the sentence without exception, and whatever context supplies gets dropped: 밥 먹었어? — “rice ate?” — is a complete, standard greeting. The Japanese particles lesson in this section teaches the identical geometry; the machinery differs in detail.

The verb is the sentence. Endings stack on a stem: polite -아/어요, past -았/었어요, future -(으)ㄹ 거예요; questions rise in intonation without changing a word. “To be” is 이에요/예요; “to have” does not exist — you say the thing exists: 시간 있어요? (sigan isseoyo?), “time exists?”, means “do you have time?”. Korean grammar is one stem and a wardrobe of endings, which makes the first hundred hours systematic and the second hundred expressive.

The first mistake is treating Hangul like kanji — it is an alphabet in blocks, learnable in a weekend, not a decade. The second is skipping the register decision: banmal picked up from dramas and aimed at a stranger lands as rudeness. The third is dropping particles early because the sentence survives — it survives because natives know what was meant; you will not. Fourth, trusting romanisation: eo and eu are not exotic spellings of o and u but different vowels. And ㄹ is one letter flapping between l and r — neither, and both.
The Korean script, designed in the 1440s, whose letters encode the shapes of the speech organs.
The individual letters of Hangul, packed into syllable blocks.
A script whose letter shapes depict how the sounds are articulated.
A register of verb endings keyed to formality — polite, formal, plain (banmal).
Grammar, like the -시- infix, that elevates the person being spoken about.
A short word after a noun marking its role — topic, subject, object.
Subject–object–verb order; the verb closes every Korean sentence.

examples.title: Worked example — Korean Foundations: Hangul, Politeness and Verb-Last Order
examples.problem: Build “I study Korean tomorrow” in the polite register, then shift it to formal and to banmal, and honorify a professor doing the studying.

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: subject plus topic particle; object plus object particle; verb last with its register ending; -시- elevates a respected subject.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: 저는 (I-topic) + 내일 (tomorrow) + 한국어를 (Korean-object) + 공부해요 (study-polite). Formal: 공부합니다. Banmal: 공부해. The professor: 교수님은 한국어를 공부하세요.

examples.result: one stem, 공부하-, four sentences, four social relationships — the register system in miniature, built by endings alone.

keyTakeaways: K-dramas and K-pop: subtitles fade once blocks read at speed and register differences become audible.
Travel and business in Korea: the politeness choice is the first impression a visitor makes.
TOPIK, the proficiency exam, sequences exactly these registers and particles.
Heritage learning: reconnection often starts with the weekend Hangul takes to reacquire.
Typing: a Korean keyboard is a jamo grid, and blocks assemble as you type.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — start here for Korean. Follow with verb conjugation across tenses and the honorific vocabulary that pairs with -시-. The Japanese lessons in this section cover the same verb-final grammar in another language; the writing-systems lesson places Hangul in the world typology as the one featural script.

quiz.q: Hangul letter shapes were designed to depict…
options: the speech organs making the sound
quiz.explanation: Lips, teeth, tongue and throat are drawn in the letters — a featural script.

quiz.q: One block, like 한 han, encodes…
quiz.explanation: Jamo assemble into one square per syllable; words are strings of blocks.

quiz.q: Using banmal with a stranger is…
options: rude — the plain register belongs to intimates
quiz.explanation: Banmal presumes closeness; uninvited, it oversteps — default politely upward instead.

quiz.q: In 저는 김치를 먹어요 (jeoneun kimchireul meogeoyo), the particle 를 marks…
quiz.explanation: 를/을 marks the direct object; 는 marks the topic; the politeness lives in the verb ending.

intro:
Russian is a language of disguised familiarity. The alphabet looks alien until you notice that a third of its letters are Greek in disguise and another third are straight allies — А, К, М, О, Т. Underneath sit two systems English shed centuries ago: six cases marking who does what to whom, and verbal aspect dividing every action into process and completion. Cyrillic yields in a week; the cases and the aspect pair become the long, rewarding campaign.

**Why this matters.** Russian is the most spoken Slavic language and the gate to a literary canon — Pushkin, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky — examined in the World Literature lessons of this section. Its case system trains the reflexes Latin once taught, and its aspect system will change how you think about time in every language you know afterwards.
objectives: Explain cyrillic: letters that lie
Explain vowel reduction and the soft sign
Explain six cases, one noun
Explain word order freed by case
Explain aspect: imperfective versus perfective
Explain no articles, no present “to be”

concepts.statement: Thirty-three letters, most with one sound each. The allies behave: А a, К k, М m, О o, Т t. The deceivers look Latin but sound Russian: В is v (so РОССИЯ reads “Rossiya”), Н is n, Р is r, С is s, У is u, Х is kh. Read КАФЕ — kafe — and МЕТРО — metro — and you have used the system already. Two signs make no sound of their own: the soft sign Ь palatalises, softens, the consonant before it (мать, mat’, “mother”), and the rare hard sign Ъ separates a prefix from its root.

concepts.term: Vowel reduction and the soft sign
concepts.statement: Two laws govern fluent speech. Unstressed о drifts toward “a”: молоко, “milk”, sounds like “malako” — do not trust the spelling.
