And voiced consonants devoice at word end: город, “city”, ends like “gorat”. The vowels я, е, ё, ю, и palatalise the consonant before them or open with a y-glide at a word’s start (я = ya). Russian stress is mobile and unpredictable — mark it when you learn each word, the same discipline English imposes on learners.

Six cases mark roles, so endings — not positions — carry the grammar. Nominative names the subject and greets you in dictionaries. Accusative takes the direct object. Genitive means “of”, and swallows the object of negation: нет времени (nyet vremeni), “no time”. Dative marks the recipient. Instrumental says “by means of”: писать ручкой (pisat’ ruchkoy), “to write with a pen”. Prepositional lives after в, на, о — in, on, about. Adjectives, pronouns and nouns decline together, a three-layer agreement sandwich the German lesson builds in miniature.

Watch one noun travel. Книга, “book”: Это книга (Eto kniga), “this is a book” — nominative. Я читаю книгу (Ya chitayu knigu), “I am reading the book” — accusative. У меня нет книги (U menya net knigi), “I have no book” — genitive under negation. Книга на столе (Kniga na stole), “the book is on the table” — prepositional. Because the endings do the work, word order floats free for emphasis — the syntax lesson in this section explains exactly why.

Russian verbs come in aspect pairs: читать/прочитать (chitat’/prochitat’), read; писать/написать (pisat’/napisat’), write; делать/сделать (delat’/sdelat’), do. The imperfective is the verb of process and habit: я читал книгу (ya chital knigu), “I was reading the book”. The perfective is the verb of the completed whole: я прочитал книгу (ya prochital knigu), “I read the book — finished, cover to cover”. The perfective has no present tense, because completion cannot be happening right now. Choosing aspect is the daily decision of Russian speech — the local equivalent of Spanish ser versus estar, examined in this section’s Spanish lessons.

There is no “a” or “the”: Это книга means “this is a book” or “the book” — context decides. The present tense of “to be” simply vanishes: Он врач (On vrach), “he is a doctor”; Москва — столица (Moskva — stolitsa), “Moscow is the capital”. Past and future reappear (был, budet). The cognates flow — кофе coffee, чай tea, метро metro, банк bank, музей museum, университет university — with one warning label: магазин (magazin) is a shop, not a magazine.

Reading Cyrillic with Latin values is the first trap — РСТ is “RST”, not “pct”; В is v, always. The second is trusting spelling over reduction: unstressed о is “a” everywhere but slow, careful speech. Third, ignoring aspect: English has one past where Russian insists on two, and using the perfective for habits is an error no listener misses. Fourth, dragging English word order around when the endings let you rearrange. Fifth, skipping soft signs — мать and its hard-sign cousin are different words entirely.
The alphabet of Russian and other Slavic languages, derived from Greek in the ninth century.
An ending-set marking a noun phrase’s role; Russian has six.
The grammar of completed versus ongoing action; Russian verbs come in pairs.
The aspect of completed wholes; it has no present tense by definition.
The aspect of processes and habits, with all three tenses.
Softening a consonant with a y-glide, written with the soft sign or iotated vowels.
Unstressed о drifting toward “a”, as in молоко, “malako”.

examples.title: Worked example — Russian Foundations: Cyrillic, Cases and Aspect
examples.problem: Follow the word “book” through a short story that exercises four cases and both aspects.

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: nominative names, accusative takes, genitive is demanded by negation, prepositional sits after “on”; imperfective is process, perfective is completion.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: declare it — Это книга, nominative. Read it — Я читаю книгу, accusative. Lose it — У меня нет книги, genitive. Then set it in past time two ways: Я читал книгу весь вечер, “I was reading the book all evening” (imperfective), against Вчера я прочитал книгу, “yesterday I finished the book” (perfective).

examples.result: one noun, four shapes, and two pasts where English keeps one — the case and aspect systems doing exactly the jobs endings exist for.

keyTakeaways: Reading the canon: Pushkin, Tolstoy and Chekhov in the original — the World Literature lessons show what waits.
Science and space: a large research literature still lives in Russian.
Travel across Eurasia: Russian serves as a lingua franca across the post-Soviet space.
Grammar training: the case system builds reflexes that transfer to Latin, German and Greek.
Cognate harvest with care: magazine versus магазин is the warning label on the free words.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — take Cyrillic first, then the present tense. Follow with the past tense, where aspect first bites, and pair this lesson with the German foundations lesson for a lighter case system. The Russian Novel lesson in World Literature is the payoff shelf.

quiz.q: The Cyrillic letter Н sounds like…
quiz.explanation: The Latin look-alikes deceive: Н is n, Р is r, В is v, С is s.

quiz.q: Я читал книгу versus Я прочитал книгу: the second sentence…
options: reports the reading as completed, cover to cover
quiz.explanation: Прочитать is perfective — the whole, finished action; читал leaves it in process.

quiz.q: “У меня нет времени” (U menya net vremeni) uses the genitive because…
quiz.explanation: Нет plus genitive is the negation formula — “there is no time”.

quiz.q: “Он врач” (On vrach) translates as…
quiz.explanation: The present-tense copula is simply omitted — literally “he doctor”.

intro:
Every human language is built from the same raw material: air from the lungs, shaped by a tube of muscle and cartilage. Phonetics is the anatomy of that shaping — the study of how speech sounds are made, travel and land. Its twin, phonology, asks how languages organise sounds into contrasts; the tonal-languages and prosody lessons in this section live on that side of the border. This lesson is the foundation both of them assume: the sounds themselves.

**Why this matters.** Your accent in any new language is decided here, and so is your ability to hear one. The International Phonetic Alphabet — one symbol per sound for every language on Earth — turns pronunciation from guesswork into data: dictionaries, textbooks and wiktionaries all speak it. And the vocal tract you own is the same instrument every speaker owns; the “impossible” sounds of other languages are mostly unmapped, not unavailable.
objectives: Explain the vocal tract as instrument
Explain consonants: voicing, place, manner
Explain vowels: height, backness, rounding
Explain the International Phonetic Alphabet
Explain minimal pairs and contrast
Explain sounds English does not own

concepts.statement: Trace the airflow. The lungs push; the larynx holds the vocal folds, which can buzz — voicing — or rest. Feel it: put a fingertip to your throat and alternate ssss and zzzz. Same mouth, same breath; only the buzz differs. Above the larynx the tube bends through the pharynx into the mouth, roofed by the hard and soft palate — the velum, which opens the nose for m, n and ng or seals it for everything else. The tongue is the main mover, with tip, blade, body and root; the lips and teeth finish the toolkit.

A consonant is a cell in a three-way grid: voicing, place, manner. Place is where the narrowing happens — bilabial (p, b, m), labiodental (f, v), dental and interdental (the th of think), alveolar (t, d, s, n, l), postalveolar (sh), palatal (y), velar (k, g) and glottal (h). Manner is how narrow — stops (p, t, k) close the airway completely; fricatives (s, f, th) leave a turbulent gap; affricates (ch) do stop-then-fricative; nasals lower the velum; liquids (l, r) and glides (w, y) barely narrow at all. Name any consonant in three words: ʃ, the sh of ship, is a voiceless postalveolar fricative; ŋ, the ng of sing, is a velar nasal — which English allows only at the end of syllables.

Vowels narrow nothing; the tongue body sculpts the resonating tube instead, along three axes. Height: close vowels like i and u lift the tongue; open a drops it. Backness: i and e sit front; u and o back. Rounding: u rounds the lips; i does not. The IPA vowel chart is this space drawn as a trapezium. Languages sample it differently — Spanish and Japanese run on five vowels, a e i o u; English stocks a dozen-plus, including the schwa ə of “about”, its most common vowel of all, and gliding diphthongs like the “ai” of “price”.

The International Phonetic Association published its alphabet in 1888 on one principle: one symbol, one sound, cross-linguistically, forever. Transcription sits in slashes: “sin” is /sɪn/, “sing” /sɪŋ/. The symbols are not English letters in costume — ʃ, θ, ɣ and ʁ are citizens of their own — and ː marks length while ˈ marks stress. The payoff: with the chart and this lesson’s grid, you can pronounce a word of any language from its dictionary entry on sight, including languages you have never heard spoken. English “colonel” and “kernel” meet as /ˈkɜːrnəl/; the spelling was never the sound.

What makes two sounds different in a language? The minimal pair: two words differing in exactly one sound — pin versus bin, ship versus sip, bat versus bet. Pairs prove the contrast is real; everything else is physics without meaning. The p of English “pin” carries a puff of air that the p of “spin” lacks; English treats them as one phoneme, and speakers barely hear the difference. In Hindi, Thai, Korean and Mandarin, that puff separates words — the Hindi and Korean lessons of this section trade on exactly this line. And beyond any one inventory: clicks in Xhosa and Zulu, ejectives in Georgian and Quechua, the pharyngeal ʿayn of Arabic — all producible, with practice, by the standard-issue vocal tract.

The first error is believing your language’s inventory is the universal one — it is a dialect of the mouth, not its constitution. The second is trusting spelling: English orthography records the sound of Chaucer’s England, which is why “ghoti” can be argued to spell “fish”. The third is confusing phonetics with phonology — physical description versus a language’s contrast system; aspiration is phonetics in English, phonology in Hindi. And the vowel chart is a map, not a menu: cardinal vowels are reference points, not a claim that your accent sits exactly on them.
The study of how speech sounds are produced by the vocal tract.
Vocal-fold buzzing — the s–z difference felt at the throat.
Where the airflow is narrowed — bilabial, alveolar, velar, glottal.
How the airflow is narrowed — stop, fricative, nasal, liquid, glide.
Two words differing in exactly one sound, proving the contrast is meaningful.
The one-symbol-one-sound notation for every language’s sounds, born 1888.
The neutral reduced vowel ə, the most common vowel in English.

examples.title: Worked example — The Sounds of Speech: Phonetics and the IPA
examples.problem: Name three sounds precisely by their coordinates, and transcribe one English word fully.

steps.label: Recall the toolkit
steps.text: for a consonant, voicing, place, manner; for a vowel, height, backness, rounding; for a word, symbol by symbol.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: ð — the th of “this” — is a voiced dental fricative; x — the ch of German Bach — a voiceless velar fricative; ʁ, the French r, a voiced uvular fricative. And “phonetics” comes out /fəˈnɛtɪks/: f, schwa, stressed ɛ, t, ɪ, k, s.

examples.result: three coordinates plus a chart named any sound asked of you — the working method of every phonetician and every good pronunciation dictionary.

keyTakeaways: Language learning: minimal-pair listening drills build the categories an accent actually depends on.
Pronunciation dictionaries and wiktionaries: IPA entries for any word in any language, free to read.
Speech-language pathology: assessment and therapy run on articulatory description.
Accent coaching and dialect description: actors and linguists map accents with the same grid.
Speech technology and fieldwork: recognisers, synthesizers and the documentation of endangered languages all begin with transcription.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is the entry point of the Phonetics & Phonology subject. Follow with the prosody lesson, the melody above these segments, and the tonal-languages lesson, pitch inside words — both assume exactly this toolkit. For any language you study next, find its vowel chart and consonant grid first.

quiz.q: The difference between ssss and zzzz is…
quiz.explanation: The mouth shape is identical; the vocal folds buzz for z and rest for s.

quiz.q: ŋ, the final sound of “sing”, is a…
quiz.explanation: Tongue back against the soft palate, velum lowered — and never syllable-initial in English.

quiz.q: A minimal pair, like ship and sip, demonstrates…
options: that the two sounds contrast meanings in that language
quiz.explanation: One sound of difference, one word of difference: the cleanest proof of contrast.

quiz.q: The most common vowel in English speech is…
quiz.explanation: Unstressed syllables reduce to ə — the first vowel of “about” and the last of “sofa”.

intro:
Consider two strings of words. “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” means nothing at all, yet every English speaker recognises it as a flawless sentence. Rearrange the same words — “Ideas sleep colorless green furiously” — and the sentence vanishes while the words survive. The difference is syntax: the rule system that builds sentences out of words, running independently of whether the result makes sense. Every fluent speaker executes it thousands of times a day without stating a rule.

**Why this matters.** Syntax is what lets a finite brain produce sentences it has never heard: there is no longest sentence, and no dictionary of sentences is needed. It is also where languages differ most visibly — German parks the verb second, Japanese saves it for last, Russian lets endings free the order. Learn constituents, trees and movement once, and every language’s grammar becomes describable.
objectives: Explain constituency: words that travel together
Explain tree diagrams and structural ambiguity
Explain recursion: sentences without a ceiling
Explain agreement and government
Explain movement: questions and passives
Explain word-order typology
Explain case and particles versus position

concepts.statement: Sentences are not strings but hierarchies. [The little dog] [buried [a bone] [in the garden]] groups words into constituents — phrases behaving as single units — and three tests prove the grouping. Substitution: a pronoun replaces a whole phrase and nothing else — “it” stands in for “a bone”, never for “buried a”. Movement: constituents travel as blocks — “A bone, the little dog buried in the garden”. Standalone answer: asked what the dog buried, a speaker answers “A bone”. Words that move, shrink and answer together belong together.

The hierarchy is drawn as a tree: the sentence splits into a noun phrase and a verb phrase, each splits again, and the words hang as leaves. Trees explain what word order cannot: structural ambiguity. “Old men and women” has two trees — old [men and women], only the men are old, against [old men] and [women], where the women need not be. “I saw the man with the telescope” toggles between seeing through the telescope and seeing a man who carries one — only the brackets decide.

The engine of the system is recursion: rules whose output can contain their own input. A noun phrase may hold a prepositional phrase, and a prepositional phrase must hold a noun phrase — so the loop can run forever: “the dog [in the yard [behind the house [at the end of the lane]]]”. A finite rule set therefore generates sentences of unbounded length; every speaker can parse “This is the dog that worried the cat that killed the rat that ate the malt” on first hearing. But centre-embed the same recursion — “The rat the cat the dog chased killed ate the malt” — and grammar stays legal while working memory collapses: grammaticality and parsability are different things.
$$NP \rightarrow Det\;N\;(PP), \qquad PP \rightarrow P\;NP$$
concepts.detail: A noun phrase may contain a prepositional phrase, which must contain a noun phrase — the loop makes the system unbounded: finite rules, infinitely many sentences.

concepts.statement: Words inside a sentence must coordinate. Agreement copies features between connected words: English verbs agree with their subjects — “she walks” versus “they walk” — while German determiners and adjectives agree with their nouns in gender, case and number, as the German lesson tracks in full. Government runs the other way: a verb or preposition demands a case form from its dependents, as Russian verbs rule their objects. Together they are the wiring that holds distant parts of a tree together.

Constituents also move. English questions are statements with one phrase promoted to the front and a gap left behind: “What did the dog bury __?” moves the object from its slot. The passive runs the machinery in the other direction: “A bone was buried __ by the dog” promotes the object to subject and demotes the agent to a by-phrase. Movement explains why question order and statement order feel like one grammar — and supplies a long-distance constituency test: what moves as a block is a constituent.

Languages divide the labour between order and marking. English encodes who does what to whom almost entirely by position — swap “dog” and “man” and the bite reverses. Verb-final Japanese marks roles with particles, and case-rich Russian lets the endings carry them — exactly why the Russian lesson’s книга can wander the sentence while the meaning stands still: when endings do the work, order is freed for emphasis. Verb-final is the most common order worldwide, with verb-second German and free-order Latin filling out the typology. Syntax is universal; its strategies are not.

The first error is equating syntax with word order: order is the surface; the hierarchy is the grammar. The second is treating tree diagrams as reality — they are models, useful and revisable, not photographs of the brain. Third, assuming every language owns English’s categories: many manage without articles. Fourth, confusing grammaticality with sense — “colorless green ideas” is the standing reminder that the two are independent. And length is not complexity: right-branching sentences grow easily, but centre-embed three clauses and native speakers stall.
A word or group of words functioning as a single unit.
A diagram of a sentence’s hierarchy, from sentence to word.
A rule whose output can contain its own input.
One string, two trees, two meanings — as in “old men and women”.
The copying of features like number or gender between words.
Relocating a constituent, as in questions and passives.
How languages encode grammatical roles: position, particles or case.

examples.title: Worked example — Syntax: How Sentences Are Built
examples.problem: Give “The dog buried a bone in the garden” its hierarchical structure, then interrogate and passivise it.

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: find the verb; group its arguments; test the groups; then move the object.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: the verb buried splits the sentence into subject [the dog] and verb phrase [buried a bone in the garden]; “a bone” substitutes with it and fronts alone, so it is a constituent; “in the garden” fronts too and attaches inside the verb phrase.

examples.result: S → [NP the dog] [VP buried [NP a bone] [PP in [NP the garden]]]. Question: “What did the dog bury in the garden?” Passive: “A bone was buried in the garden by the dog.” One tree, three sentences.

keyTakeaways: Language learning: transfer errors — verb-second ignored, verb-final anticipated — are syntax errors, and typology predicts them.
Translation: interpreters re-bracket and re-order, because trees, not strings, correspond.
Computing: compiler parse trees descend from this tradition — the Theory of Computation lessons formalise it.
Clinical linguistics: agrammatic aphasia prunes the tree, sparing words while wrecking structure.
Editing: rhythm, subordination and clarity are tree management under another name.

Where next — Prerequisites: the morphology lesson — syntax assembles what morphology manufactures. Follow with the semantics and pragmatics lesson, and read the German, Japanese and Russian foundations lessons to watch verb-second, particle-marking and case-freed order in daily use.

quiz.q: “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” demonstrates that…
options: syntax is independent of meaning — well-formed nonsense
quiz.explanation: Every rule of English syntax is satisfied while sense is entirely absent.

quiz.q: “A bone, the dog buried in the garden” shows that “a bone” is…
options: a constituent — it moves as one block
quiz.explanation: Movement is a constituency test: only constituents front as units.

quiz.q: “I saw the man with the telescope” is ambiguous because…
options: the prepositional phrase can attach to the verb phrase or the noun phrase
quiz.explanation: Two trees, one string: the telescope belongs to the seeing or to the man.

quiz.q: Russian word order floats free largely because…
options: case endings, not positions, mark who does what to whom
quiz.explanation: When endings carry the roles, order is released for emphasis.

intro:
“Can you pass the salt?” is, literally, a question about the capabilities of your arm. Nobody answers “Yes” and continues eating — everyone passes the salt. Human utterances carry two layers at once: semantics, the meaning encoded in words and sentences, and pragmatics, the meaning a speaker produces with those words in a context. The first is a property of the language; the second is an act of communication. Drawing the border between them is one of linguistics’ liveliest enterprises.

**Why this matters.** Every conversation runs two computations simultaneously: what the sentence means, and what the speaker means by uttering it here and now. The machinery is invisible until it misfires — in cross-cultural encounters, in text messages sent without a tune (the prosody lesson’s complaint), and above all in translation, where semantics usually survives crossing but pragmatics must be rebuilt by hand.
objectives: Explain reference versus sense
Explain lexical relations: antonymy, hyponymy
Explain compositionality
Explain grice’s maxims and implicature
Explain speech acts and felicity conditions
Explain deixis and presupposition
Explain politeness and indirectness

concepts.statement: Frege’s founding distinction: an expression’s reference is what it points at; its sense is the way it presents that thing. “The morning star” and “the evening star” both refer to Venus, but by different routes — and the Babylonian astronomers who discovered that the two names share one planet made an astronomical discovery, not a linguistic one. Sense is why two expressions can denote one thing yet differ in what they reveal — and why learning a language means learning senses, not just references.

Word meanings live in webs. Perfect synonyms barely exist: big and large overlap until you meet a large number and a big brother. Antonyms come in two kinds — gradable pairs like hot and cold, which permit lukewarm and let “not hot” fall short of cold, and complementary pairs like dead and alive, which allow no middle. Hyponymy is containment: tulip and rose are hyponyms of flower. Meronymy is part-hood: wheel is a meronym of car. These relations power thesauruses and the vocabulary webs good learners build.

The meaning of a whole is computed from the meanings of its parts plus the syntax that assembles them — Frege’s principle of compositionality, and the reason productivity works. “The dog bit the man” and “The man bit the dog” draw on identical vocabulary; only the structure differs, and so does the news. You have never heard “The ostrich apologised to the dentist”, yet you understand it instantly. Idioms are the famous leaks — “kick the bucket” is stored whole, not computed.
$$\mathrm{meaning}(S) = f\big(\mathrm{meaning}(w_1), \ldots, \mathrm{meaning}(w_n),\ \mathrm{structure}(S)\big)$$
concepts.detail: A sentence’s meaning is a function of its words’ meanings plus the structure that assembles them — why “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” differ in news from the same vocabulary.

concepts.statement: Grice noticed that conversation runs on cooperation: speakers try to be informative (Quantity), truthful (Quality), relevant (Relation) and clear (Manner). Because hearers assume the maxims hold, flouting them generates meaning beyond the words — implicature. “Some students passed” implicates that not all did: a cooperative speaker with better news would have given it. The laboratory test is cancellation: “Some students passed — in fact, all of them” remains coherent, so “not all” was implicature, not entailment; an entailment cannot be cancelled at all. Implicature is where understatement, sarcasm and tact live.

Austin observed that utterances do things. “I promise”, “I apologise”, “I now pronounce you married” do not describe — they perform. A speech act has three faces: the locution (the words uttered), the illocutionary force (what is done in saying them — a request, a warning) and the perlocutionary effect (what the saying achieves — frightening, persuading). Performatives can misfire when felicity conditions fail: only the right person with the right authority can launch a ship by name, which is why strangers cannot marry you.

Context is not scenery; it is wiring. Deictics — I, you, here, now, tomorrow, come — anchor their meaning to the speaker, place and moment of utterance: a note reading “Meet me here tomorrow” is nearly uninterpretable when found later. Presupposition smuggles assumptions aboard: “Have you stopped drinking coffee?” takes for granted that you drank it, which is why cross-examining lawyers love the question. Indirectness scales with imposition — “Would you mind possibly…?” — and cultures divide the labour differently: the Korean and Hindi lessons show politeness grammaticised as speech levels and graded “you”s.

Literalism is the standing trap: answering “Can you…?” about ability instead of acting, or sending “fine.” without a tune. Second, the dictionary fallacy: definitions approximate a word’s use; sense lives in contexts and collocations. Third, exporting the maxims wholesale — cultures weigh informativeness, directness and politeness differently, and German directness is efficiency, not insult. Fourth, confusing entailment with implicature: only implicatures cancel. And resist over-reading: sometimes “it’s cold” is a weather report, and cold is just cold.
What an expression denotes — the thing it points at.
The way an expression presents its reference; morning star and evening star differ here.
The principle that the meaning of the whole is computed from parts plus structure.
What a sentence guarantees to be true if it is; uncancellable.
Meaning generated beyond the words by flouting a maxim; cancellable under test.
An utterance viewed as an action — promising, requesting, warning.
Meaning anchored to speaker, place and time, as in here, now, tomorrow.

examples.title: Worked example — Meaning: Semantics and Pragmatics
examples.problem: Analyse “It’s cold in here”, said to a roommate sitting beside an open window, on both layers.

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: semantics fixes the literal, truth-evaluable content; pragmatics asks what the speaker is doing, via the maxims and speech-act force.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: literally, the sentence reports the room’s temperature — true or false as it stands. But relevance rules out a weather bulletin: the roommate controls the window, so the utterance flouts Relation and implicates a request — close the window.

examples.result: cancel it — “It’s cold in here, but don’t shut the window; I want the air” — and the request evaporates while the temperature report stands. Two layers, computed in order and separable on demand.

keyTakeaways: Translation: the words cross easily; the politeness, indirectness and deixis must be rebuilt for the target culture.
Language teaching: textbook “How are you?” is a greeting, not a question — learners need pragmatics, not just grammar.
Computing: the NLP lessons cover machine meaning for words; computing implicature is the frontier.
Law: contracts are speech acts — offer, acceptance, warranty — whose felicity conditions courts police.
Daily diplomacy: requests, refusals and sarcasm repair are pragmatics under pressure.

Where next — Prerequisites: the syntax lesson, whose structures feed the compositional machine. Follow with the sociolinguistics lesson — meaning in society — and reread the Spanish ser versus estar lesson to watch predication semantics doing daily work. Grice’s “Logic and Conversation” is among the field’s most readable papers.

quiz.q: “The morning star” and “the evening star” have…
options: the same reference but different senses
quiz.explanation: Both denote Venus; the routes differ — Frege’s founding case.

quiz.q: “Some students passed — in fact, all of them” is coherent, which shows “not all” was…
options: an implicature — cancellable, hence not literal
quiz.explanation: Cancellation is the laboratory: what cancels cleanly was never entailed.

quiz.q: “I now pronounce you husband and wife” fails when said by a stranger because…
options: felicity conditions — authority and circumstances — are unmet
quiz.explanation: Performatives succeed only under the right conditions; the wrong speaker misfires.

quiz.q: A note reading “Meet me here tomorrow” frustrates a later finder because of…
options: deixis — anchors to an unknown speaker, place and day
quiz.explanation: Deictics point from a moment of utterance that has gone missing.

intro:
You do not speak one way. The voice you use with your grandmother is not the voice of a job interview or a group chat, and you police them without ever being taught the rules. Sociolinguistics studies language as a social instrument: who says what to whom, and what the saying says about the sayer. Its founding joke is also its thesis — “a language is a dialect with an army and a navy”, attributed to Max Weinreich — because the line between dialect and language is drawn by power, not by grammar.

**Why this matters.** Accent and dialect are the most openly policed social differences left in polite society: rated in interviews, weighed in courtrooms, corrected in classrooms. Linguistically, every variety — every one — is a complete, rule-governed system. Sociolinguistics supplies the evidence for that claim and the tools for seeing how speech stratifies by class, situation and allegiance.
objectives: Explain language versus dialect: the army-and-navy line
Explain registers and style-shifting
Explain overt and covert prestige
Explain labov’s department stores
Explain code-switching as competence
Explain standardisation: how a dialect becomes the rule
Explain lingua francas and endangerment

concepts.term: Language versus dialect: the army-and-navy line
concepts.statement: The textbook test for language versus dialect is mutual intelligibility: one language if speakers understand each other, two if not. Reality argues back. Danes, Norwegians and Swedes largely understand one another yet speak three languages; Mandarin and Cantonese share almost nothing when spoken yet count as dialects of Chinese inside one state. Hindi and Urdu — the Hindi lesson of this section — are one spoken core with two standards and two scripts, and Serbian, Croatian and Bosnian repeat the lesson. Intelligibility measures speech; language boundaries are drawn by armies, academies and printers.

Every speaker also commands registers — situation-bound varieties running from news-anchor formality to kitchen ease, from legalese to the telegraphic grammar of texting. Shifting between them is universal, fast and mostly unconscious; speakers caught mid-shift repair within a syllable. Some languages grammaticise the ladder entirely: the Korean lesson’s speech levels and the Hindi lesson’s three “you”s are registers built into the verb system itself.

Varieties carry social exchange rates. Overt prestige belongs to the standard — school, media, interviews — while covert prestige belongs to local loyalty: the hometown accent that proves you kept faith. William Labov made the measurement famous in 1966, walking three New York department stores and asking where to find something on the “fourth floor”. The pronunciation of r rose with the store’s prestige tier, and rose again when shoppers repeated the phrase carefully — class and style visible in a single consonant, and, Labov argued, change entering the language from below.

Multilinguals routinely mix languages, and the mixing is skilled, not confused. Tag-switching drops in a phrase; intersentential switching alternates sentences; intrasentential switching — “Estoy tired” — builds one sentence from two grammars, with the matrix language supplying the frame. Speakers switch by situation and by effect: quoting, joking, signalling expertise or intimacy. Spanglish and Hinglish — Bollywood’s home register — are not broken languages but creative, rule-governed repertoires; describing them as failure measures the listener, not the speaker.

How does a dialect become the standard? Selection — the court’s or the capital’s variety is chosen, never by ballot. Codification — grammars, dictionaries and academies fix it; the Real Academia Española has been at the work since 1713. Elaboration — it is equipped for science, law and government. Acceptance — schools and media install it as the nation’s voice. Standard English is London’s dialect as fixed by early printers — a choice with power, not a grammar with truth. “Ain’t” was once as respectable as “isn’t”.

concepts.term: Standardisation: how a dialect becomes the rule
concepts.statement: Most of humanity is multilingual, and languages meet constantly. Lingua francas — English today; Latin, Sanskrit and Swahili in their days — serve as bridges between them. Contact also threatens: of roughly seven thousand living languages, perhaps forty per cent are endangered, kept going by dwindling generations of speakers. Revival is possible but rare — Hebrew is the spectacular full recovery, while Welsh and Māori language-nest schools show partial successes. Language policy — official status, schooling, media slots — is where linguistics becomes law.

The first error is the correctness fallacy: the standard is one dialect with institutional backing, not the grammar the universe issued. The second is hearing error where there is system — African American English marks habitual aspect with be (“she be working” means she works regularly), a rule many school grammars lack. Third, calling code-switching failure: it requires two grammars, not zero. Fourth, assuming monolingualism is normal — it is a quirk of large, powerful states. And covert prestige is real: mocking the standard proves its critics have somewhere else to belong.
A variety of a language marked by region or social group, in accent, grammar and words.
A variety chosen by situation rather than community — the interview voice, the group-chat voice.
The standard’s institutional value versus the local variety’s value as a loyalty signal.
A speaker’s movement between varieties as attention and audience change.
Skilled alternation between languages within a conversation or a sentence.
Selection, codification, elaboration and acceptance — the making of a standard language.
A bridge language used between speakers of different mother tongues.

examples.title: Worked example — Language in Society: Dialects, Prestige and Code-Switching
examples.problem: How do you demonstrate that a single sound carries social meaning — cheaply and fast?

steps.label: Recall the design
steps.text: pick a variable that varies in the community, post-vocalic r in a largely r-less city; pick institutions that sort by class; elicit the word naturally, then elicit it again carefully.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: Labov asked floor locations in Saks (upper), Macy’s (middle) and S. Klein (working-class), pretending to mishear so shoppers repeated “fourth floor” — then scored each r.

examples.result: r-fulness climbed with store tier and with attention to speech — class and style surfacing in one consonant, the founding demonstration that social structure lives inside the sound system and is measurable in an afternoon.

keyTakeaways: Education: teaching the standard while respecting the vernacular — bidialectalism — beats shaming learners for the variety they own.
Hiring and services: accent ratings seep into interviews, rentals and sentencing; knowing the mechanism is the defence.
Speech technology: systems trained on standard varieties fail the speakers who need them most — fairness is a sociolinguistic problem.
Localisation: translating registers — the marketing voice, the legal voice — matters as much as translating words.
Policy and revival: official status, schooling and media slots decide which of the seven thousand survive.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is the entry point of the Sociolinguistics subject. The Korean and Hindi lessons show politeness grammaticised; the Arabic lesson’s diglossia is standard-versus-vernacular in its purest form. Follow with the historical-linguistics lesson: change from below is where society and history meet inside sound.

quiz.q: The army-and-navy quip means that the boundary between language and dialect is drawn by…
options: social and political power rather than grammar
quiz.explanation: Mandarin and Cantonese are “dialects”; Danish and Swedish are languages — the difference is states, not speech.

quiz.q: In Labov’s department-store study, the pronunciation of r…
options: rose with the store’s class tier and again with careful repetition
quiz.explanation: Class and style both surfaced in one consonant — prestige measurable in an afternoon.

quiz.q: Intrasentential code-switching, as in “Estoy tired”, is…
options: rule-governed bilingual composition of one sentence
quiz.explanation: It demands both grammars at once, with the matrix language supplying the frame — competence, not confusion.

quiz.q: A register differs from a dialect because it is…
options: chosen by situation, within a single speaker’s repertoire
quiz.explanation: Dialects belong to communities; registers are switches inside one speaker, flipped by setting.

intro:
An English speaker of the year 1000 is unintelligible today; Chaucer, six centuries back, needs footnotes; Beowulf, ten, is a foreign language. Yet a Spanish, an Italian and a Portuguese speaker at one table can half-follow each other’s sentences. Languages change constantly — in sound, grammar and vocabulary — and the changes are regular enough that the unwritten past can be reconstructed from living speech. The etymology lesson followed single words; this one follows whole systems — and the method that builds family trees.

**Why this matters.** Language change is not decay — every generation’s speech is a complete system — and its regularity is the closest thing historical linguistics has to laws of motion. From regular correspondences, linguists have reconstructed languages no one ever wrote down, predicted sounds later dug out of clay tablets, and mapped the migrations behind half of humanity’s languages.
objectives: Explain sound change and the Great Vowel Shift
Explain analogy: taming the irregular
Explain grammaticalization: words into endings
Explain the comparative method, step by step
Explain the world’s language families
Explain tree versus wave: inheritance and diffusion
Explain pidgins and creoles

concepts.term: Sound change and the Great Vowel Shift
concepts.statement: Sound change is regular: it sweeps the vocabulary, consulting no word’s meaning or dignity. The clearest demonstration is the Great Vowel Shift, roughly 1400 to 1700, when English long vowels rotated like queue-jumpers, each dragging the next: Middle English “meece” [meːs] became mice and “hoos” [hoːs] became house. Spelling had been fixed by the new printing presses while the rotation was still under way — which is why English letters still point at vowel positions their sounds abandoned centuries ago. Grimm’s law — Latin pater matching English father — is the same lawfulness across branches; the etymology lesson shows it at work.

Sound change is blind and regular; speakers are pattern-hungry, and analogy tames the wreckage. Old English had hundreds of strong verbs building their pasts by vowel change; the bulk were levelled to -ed — holp became helped, kine became cows — while the seventy-odd survivors live on by sheer frequency. Children saying “goed” are not erring; they are running the analogical engine that has always pruned the language. The same force drags opaque words toward transparent shapes, re-cutting “a napron” into “an apron”.

Grammar itself is congealed vocabulary. Words worn down in frequency and force become function words, then affixes, then vanish into endings. English “going to”, a verb of motion, is now the future marker gonna. The French future je chanterai fuses an infinitive with Latin habere, “to have” — literally “sing-have”. French negation pas began as the noun “step”, in “he doesn’t walk a step”, and has shouldered ne aside entirely. English -ly descends from a word meaning “body, form”. The cycle — content word, function word, affix — runs in every language.

concepts.term: The comparative method, step by step
concepts.statement: The discipline’s engine is a procedure. First, assemble candidate cognates across related languages from stable vocabulary — kinship, numbers, body parts. Second, align correspondences sound by sound: what matters is not resemblance but systematic matching, the etymology lesson’s much/mucho trap. Third, reconstruct the ancestral sound for each correspondence set, judging direction by where the innovations cluster. Fourth, demand regularity: the reconstruction must hold across the whole lexicon or be abandoned. The trophy: Saussure, young in the 1870s, deduced that Proto-Indo-European needed consonants no one had seen — and when Hittite was deciphered decades later, there they were.

Run the method worldwide and the seven thousand living languages sort into families. Indo-European — some 450 languages and nearly half of humanity — spans Germanic, Romance, Slavic, Indo-Iranian, Celtic, Hellenic, Baltic, Armenian and Albanian, plus the extinct Anatolian and Tocharian branches. Sino-Tibetan, Afro-Asiatic (Arabic, Hebrew, Hausa, Amharic), Niger-Congo — some fifteen hundred mostly tonal languages spread by the Bantu expansions — and Austronesian, from Taiwan to Madagascar to Easter Island, the widest pre-modern spread on Earth, are the other giants. Turkic, Dravidian, Japonic and Koreanic follow; Basque stands alone, an isolate older than the Indo-European arrival in Europe.

concepts.term: Tree versus wave: inheritance and diffusion
concepts.statement: The family tree models inheritance — a parent language splitting into daughters. The wave model models diffusion: features spreading neighbour to neighbour across family lines, as in the Balkans, where Greek, Albanian, Bulgarian and Romanian share postposed articles despite belonging to different branches. Both are true; neither suffices alone. Contact can even ignite new languages: a pidgin born of trade is spare by design, but children raised on one grammaticise it into a creole — Haitian Creole and Tok Pisin are full languages with French and English parents respectively.

Resemblance is still not kinship — across seven thousand languages, chance lookalikes are guaranteed (the etymology lesson’s much/mucho rule stands). Do not read decay into change: every stage of every language was complete. Do not trust the tree alone — English is Germanic by inheritance yet half Romance by borrowing. Do not accept shortcut comparisons: lumping languages by surface similarity, without regular correspondences, built castles that fell on inspection. And date proto-languages with humility — the honest error bars span millennia.
A reconstructed ancestor, marked with an asterisk because it is inferred, never attested.
Languages shown by regular correspondences to descend from one proto-language.
The rotation of English long vowels, roughly 1400–1700, fossilised in spelling.
Remodelling irregular forms on productive patterns, as holp gave way to helped.
The drift by which content words become function words and affixes.
Change spreading area by area across family lines, as in the Balkans.
A full language nativised from a pidgin by a generation of children.

examples.title: Worked example — How Languages Change: Sound, Grammar and Family Trees
examples.problem: Run the comparative method on words that survive in one modern family, and let it recover their common source.

steps.label: Assemble the set — “horse”
steps.text: Spanish caballo, Portuguese cavalo, Italian cavallo, French cheval, Romanian cal.

steps.label: Align and check the correspondences
steps.text: Latin ca- repeatedly pairs with French cha- (campus → champ, cantare → chanter, castellum → château) while Spanish keeps ca-; Latin -ll- yields Italian -ll-, Spanish -ll-, French and Romanian -l. Each branch owns its own sound law.

steps.label: Reconstruct and verify
steps.text: the correspondences converge on *caballu — and Latin, attested in texts, confirms it: caballus, the everyday “horse” that shouldered classical equus aside. One ancestor, five branch-specific laws; run on dead ends with no texts, the same procedure reconstructs Proto-Indo-European.

keyTakeaways: Reading the past: the distance from Beowulf to Chaucer to Shakespeare is measured in these changes.
Learning arithmetic: know one Romance or Germanic language and the next arrives pre-discounted — cognates follow sound laws.
Heritage: the family tree tells you which branch your home language sits on, and who its cousins are.
Prehistory: Proto-Indo-European words for wheels and wool date the family after those inventions.
Classification: surveys and translation pipelines begin from the family tree.

Where next — Prerequisites: the etymology lesson, which follows words; this lesson follows systems. Follow with sociolinguistics — change from below is where the laboratory meets the street — and the writing-systems lesson for what carries the families on the page. The foundations lessons for German, Russian, Hindi and Arabic put cognates and family membership in your mouth.

quiz.q: English spelling and pronunciation disagree largely because…
options: the Great Vowel Shift rotated the long vowels after spelling standardised
quiz.explanation: The presses froze the letters while the vowels moved.

quiz.q: French je chanterai (“I will sing”) preserves a fossil of…
quiz.explanation: The future ending grew from “sing-have”: grammaticalization in an ending.

quiz.q: Saussure’s reconstructed consonants for Proto-Indo-European were vindicated when…
options: Hittite was deciphered and showed them
quiz.explanation: The laryngeals he inferred from vowels alone turned up in Hittite clay.

quiz.q: The Balkan sharing of postposed articles illustrates…
options: the wave model — diffusion across family lines
quiz.explanation: Greek, Albanian, Bulgarian and Romanian are not one family, yet share the feature.

intro:
Speech is ancient; writing is an invention so difficult that humans managed it independently only a handful of times — Mesopotamia by about 3200 BCE, Egypt, China, Mesoamerica. Nearly every script in use descends from those few sparks (the Humanities lessons trace cuneiform’s birth in the account office). What differs dramatically is what a single character encodes: a morpheme, a syllable, or one lone sound. That choice — the typology — turns every unfamiliar script from a wall of decoration into a finite, learnable system.

**Why this matters.** Know the typology and you can budget: an alphabet yields in days, a syllabary in weeks, a logographic system in years. It also settles the deepest confusion — a script is not a language. Hindi and Urdu are one speech written two ways; Latin serves hundreds of tongues from Vietnamese to Finnish. Script is the clothing; language is the body.
objectives: Explain the typology: what a character encodes
Explain logographic systems: morphemes on the page
Explain syllabaries: one character, one syllable
Explain alphabets: the Greek vowel invention
Explain abjads and abugidas
Explain hangul: the one featural script
Explain a language is not its script

concepts.term: The typology: what a character encodes
concepts.statement: Classify by the unit. Logographic systems write morphemes: Chinese characters (hanzi) each carry a morpheme of sound-plus-meaning — 日 rì, sun; 木 mù, tree; 林 lín, two trees, forest; 明 míng, sun beside moon, bright. Japanese borrowed them as kanji — the Japanese writing lesson covers the aftermath. But characters are not pictures of ideas: the great majority are phono-semantic compounds pairing a meaning component with a sound component — 妈 mā, mother, is woman plus horse, the horse contributing only its pronunciation ma. Morphemic writing suits Mandarin, whose one-syllable morphemes by the thousand would drown an alphabet in homographs.

concepts.term: Logographic systems: morphemes on the page
concepts.statement: A syllabary writes whole syllables, one character each. Japanese kana — forty-six base signs — is the textbook case, matched to a language of simple beats. Sequoyah, a Cherokee monolingual who saw alphabetic writing’s power without being able to read it, invented a Cherokee syllabary in 1821; literacy in the nation leapt within years. Linear B wrote Greek in syllables three thousand years before anyone could read them again. Syllabaries fit languages with a few hundred syllable types; English, with clusters like strengths, would need a warehouse of signs.

Alphabets segment the syllable and award consonants and vowels separate letters. The step happened essentially once: around the eighth century BCE, Greeks took the Phoenician abjad and repurposed letters for vowels — alpha and beta are aleph, “ox”, and beth, “house”, fossils of older pictographs. Latin descends through Etruscan; Cyrillic was built from Greek for the Slavs, and the Russian lesson unwraps it. The ideal is a few dozen letters mapping transparently to sound; reality runs from shallow Spanish and Finnish to deep English and French — the phonetics lesson explains why spelling became a museum.

An abjad writes the consonant skeleton and leaves vowels to the reader: Arabic كتب may read kataba, “he wrote”, or kutiba, “it was written” — the Arabic lesson shows the harakāt diacritics that supply vowels where they matter, and why the system suits a language whose word families live in consonant roots like K-T-B. Hebrew belongs here too, and so did Phoenician, the ancestor of the whole Western tradition. Abjads look under-specified to alphabet readers and run beautifully once grammar fills the gaps.

An abugida writes consonants with a built-in vowel and modifies it with diacritics. Devanagari, the Hindi lesson’s subject, is the model: क is ka by default, a matra makes कि ki, and the virama kills the vowel to क् k. Thai, Burmese, Khmer and Tibetan descend from ancient Brahmi on this plan; Ethiopic runs on the same principle independently.

One script encodes more than sound identity: Hangul’s letters draw the speech organs themselves — the Korean lesson presents the world’s one featural script, whose jamo pack into square blocks, 한 han. Systems also mix: a Japanese sentence runs kanji for stems, hiragana for grammar, katakana for the foreign — three scripts, six jobs. English, an alphabet, still keeps logograms in service: 2, 8, &, %, read as words. Direction is convention — left to right for most, right to left for Arabic and Hebrew, vertical columns for traditional Chinese and Japanese, and early Greek boustrophedon, turning like an ox ploughing.

concepts.term: A language is not its script
concepts.statement: The principle that organises it all: a script is a technology, not the language itself. One language may wear many scripts — Hindi–Urdu is the consequential case, one spoken core dressed in Devanagari and Nastaliq; Serbo-Croatian wrote itself Latin and Cyrillic; Turkey switched scripts by a single 1928 law. One script may dress many languages — Latin carries Vietnamese, an Austroasiatic language, and Finnish, a Uralic one; Arabic dresses Persian and Urdu with extra letters for sounds it lacks. Decipherment proves the point from the far side: Ventris showed Linear B was Greek; Knorozov cracked the Maya mix of word-signs and syllables; the Humanities lessons carry the Rosetta Stone story.

Stop calling characters pictures: most are phonetic compounds, and 妈 contains a horse for its sound alone. Retire the ladder myth — no script is more “advanced”; each suits its language’s structure, and Mandarin’s homophones make characters earn their keep. Do not read family trees off scripts: Vietnamese writes Latin but speaks Austroasiatic. Do not assume your reading direction is natural. And no alphabet maps sound perfectly — English orthography is an archive, read for fossils in the phonetics lesson.
A written sign carrying a morpheme — sound and meaning together.
A script with one character per syllable, like Japanese kana or Cherokee.
A script granting consonants and vowels separate letters — the Greek innovation.
A consonantal script whose vowels are mostly left to the reader.
A script whose consonants carry an inherent vowel altered by diacritics.
A script whose letter shapes depict articulation — Hangul, uniquely.
Recovering the language and system of an unread script, as Ventris did for Linear B.

examples.title: Worked example — Writing Systems of the World: Alphabets, Abjads and Beyond
examples.problem: Classify five scripts on sight — Arabic كتب, Devanagari नमस्ते, Korean 한글, Japanese 食べます, Chinese 森林 — with the diagnostic for each.

steps.label: Recall the diagnostic ladder
steps.text: what does the smallest character encode — morpheme, syllable, or single sound? If sound: are vowels full letters, absent, or inherent but modifiable?

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: كتب writes consonants with vowels unwritten — an abjad. नमस्ते shows consonant letters fused with vowel signs — an abugida. 한글 decomposes into featural jamo packed per syllable. 食べます mixes a meaning-character with syllabic kana. 森林 packs one morpheme per character.

examples.result: five systems, five answers to one question — how much language does a character carry? None of the five tells you what family its users speak.

keyTakeaways: Study budgeting: alphabet weekend, kana fortnight, characters years — the typology sets the calendar.
Typing: Korean jamo keyboards, Chinese pinyin input and Japanese IME conversion all solve typology problems.
Romanisation: pinyin versus Wade-Giles gave the world Beijing and Peking for one city.
Literacy policy: Turkey’s 1928 switch and Japan’s jōyō list show states steering scripts.
Archaeology: decipherment — Linear B, Maya — turns writing back into history.

Where next — Prerequisites: none. The Japanese writing, Hindi, Arabic, Korean and Russian lessons each open one system in depth; this lesson is the map that files them. Follow with the historical-linguistics lesson to see how scripts ride — and sometimes outlive — the families that carry them.

quiz.q: Arabic, which writes كتب with the vowels unwritten, is…
quiz.explanation: The consonant skeleton carries the root; grammar and context supply the vowels.

quiz.q: Devanagari क versus कि shows…
options: an abugida: an inherent vowel replaced by diacritics
quiz.explanation: Each consonant owns a default “a” until a matra swaps it or a virama kills it.

quiz.q: The horse in 妈 mā, “mother”, is there…
options: to supply the sound ma — most characters are phono-semantic compounds
quiz.explanation: The woman carries meaning; the horse carries pronunciation.

quiz.q: Hindi and Urdu demonstrate that…
options: a language is not its script — one speech, two scripts
quiz.explanation: One spoken core dresses in Devanagari and Nastaliq: clothing, not body.

intro:
Two readers close the same novel. One calls it a romance about a plain governess who marries well; the other calls it a record of empire whose happy ending is funded by colonial money — and both are reading Jane Eyre. The literary-devices lesson handed you the microscope: metaphor, irony, imagery, named and evidenced. This lesson supplies the slides. Critical schools are lenses — standing questions you can put to any text — and criticism is the discipline of arguing from evidence toward meaning, not the art of issuing star ratings.

**Why this matters.** A lens is a thesis machine: ask a text the feminist question or the postcolonial question and the essay writes its own outline. Lenses explain why intelligent readers disagree so productively, why canons get rebuilt every generation, and why film essays and book commentary run on fifty-year-old theory whether they name it or not.
objectives: Explain criticism versus reviewing
Explain formalism and the intentional fallacy
Explain psychoanalytic readings
Explain marxist criticism and ideology
Explain feminist criticism and the male gaze
Explain postcolonial criticism and writing back
Explain reader-response and interpretive communities

concepts.statement: Reviewing is a consumer report: is this worth your evening? Criticism is an argument: what is this text doing, how, and what does it mean? The discipline requires three moves in lockstep — a claim, quoted evidence, and reasoning that connects them; close reading, trained by the devices lesson, supplies the middle move. A verdict without evidence is taste; evidence without an argument is a quiz.

Russian Formalism and its Anglo-American heir, the New Criticism, made the text sovereign: meaning lives in the words on the page, not in the author’s biography or the reader’s tears. Wimsatt and Beardsley named two bans: the intentional fallacy (a stated purpose cannot settle interpretation) and the affective fallacy (a reader’s response cannot either). The formalist reads for tension, irony, paradox and pattern; Shklovsky’s defamiliarization — art’s job is to make the stone stony again — explains why literature slows what habit automatises.

Freud read dreams as texts and texts as dreams: condensation, displacement, symbols returning the repressed. Psychoanalytic criticism treats characters as systems of desire and defence, and, more subtly, reads the text’s own unconscious — its gaps, repetitions and obsessions, the things it cannot say and therefore keeps saying. Lacan sharpened the tool: the unconscious is structured like a language, and desire works by metaphor and metonymy. Hamlet’s delay, Poe’s entombments — the method surfaces what the plot buries.

Marxist criticism asks what the text does with class and labour: who works, who owns, whose interests are served, and what is made to look natural that is actually historical. Literature belongs to the superstructure — produced by economic relations and producing ideology in return; Gramsci’s hegemony names the soft rule by which culture wins consent. The method reads Dickens’s workhouses, the marriage market’s economics, and the quiet idealisation of inherited money.

concepts.term: Feminist criticism and the male gaze
concepts.statement: Feminist criticism asks who speaks, acts and desires — and who merely inspires. Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own imagined Shakespeare’s equally gifted sister dead in obscurity for want of money and a door that locked; Beauvoir answered that one is not born, but becomes, a woman. The tradition grew three organs: recovering the writers the canon misplaced (Showalter’s gynocriticism), theorising women’s writing (Cixous), and analysing representation — where Mulvey’s male gaze put cinema’s camera in male desire, and Butler’s gender-as-performance opened into queer theory.

Said’s Orientalism (1978) argued that “the East” is a Western construction that then helped govern real Easterners — the Humanities empire lessons tell the history; the method reads it inside texts. Spivak asked whether the subaltern can speak at all within imperial discourse; Bhabha described mimicry and hybridity, the colonised subject who becomes almost the same and thereby menacing. And the literature writes back: Achebe prosecuted Conrad’s Heart of Darkness as an offensive and deplorable book for Africa and Africans, and Rhys handed the silenced Creole wife of Jane Eyre her own novel.

Reader-response criticism relocates meaning from page to event: texts are completed by readers, and readers are trained by institutions. Iser mapped the gaps every reader must fill; Jauss set texts against the horizon of expectations their first readers brought; Fish’s interpretive communities explain why the same poem reads differently in a church and a seminar. The school’s danger — anything means anything — is checked by its own insight: communities, not individuals, set what counts as evidence.

The straitjacket: a lens that finds capitalism in every text and contradiction in none is not reading, it is reciting. Evidence-free theory-speak is the second failure — quotation still outranks vocabulary. Presentism is the third: historicise before you judge, or you will merely congratulate yourself across a century. Lenses are tools, not teams: formalism has no political agenda, and Marxism no monopoly on truth. And the death of the author licenses new readings, not the abandonment of evidence.
Argument from quoted evidence — the shared core of every school.
Wimsatt and Beardsley’s ban on settling meaning by authorial intention.
Shklovsky’s term for art’s slowing of what habit automatises.
The picture of the social world a culture presents as natural.
Mulvey’s term for visual narrative structured around male desire.
Said’s name for the Western construction of “the East” that helped govern it.
Fish’s term for the institution that trains readers in what counts as evidence.

examples.title: Worked example — Literary Criticism: Lenses and Schools
examples.problem: Read the proposal scene of Jane Eyre through three lenses without letting any swallow the others.

steps.label: Formalist pass
steps.text: the proposal happens under a chestnut tree that lightning splits that same night — the symbol system commenting on the marriage before the reader can; the fire imagery around Rochester concentrates here and is answered by ice the morning after.

steps.label: Feminist pass
steps.text: Jane insists on speaking as an equal — “equal — as we are!” — but her equality is pending an inheritance the plot must supply; the marriage is legally a transfer of property, and the chapter knows it.

steps.label: Postcolonial pass
steps.text: the obstacle is already in the attic — Bertha Mason, the Creole wife whose Jamaican fortune made Rochester rich, silenced and confined. Rhys’s Wide Sargasso Sea is this reading novelised.

examples.result: three lenses, three proposals — and the scene grows larger with each. The critic’s job is calibrated attention, not a verdict.

keyTakeaways: Essay writing: a lens converts a topic into a question, and a question into a thesis.
Rereading: old favourites under new lenses repay the time — the book you loved at sixteen is not the book at forty.
Media literacy: the gaze, the ideology and the franchise are the same concepts at cinema scale.
Canon debates: what gets taught, translated and anthologised is argued in these terms.
Adaptation: every film version of a classic is a critical reading made visible.

Where next — Prerequisites: the literary-devices lesson for the evidence toolkit and the epic-tradition lesson for the texts being argued over. Pair with the Humanities lessons on mythology and decolonisation, where Campbell and Said wait in their home territory. The exercise that pays: take one novel you know cold and interrogate it with three lenses.

quiz.q: The intentional fallacy holds that…
options: a stated intention cannot settle what a text means — the words are the evidence
quiz.explanation: The New Critics banned appeals to authorial purpose.

quiz.q: Rhys’s Wide Sargasso Sea is “writing back” because it…
options: answers Jane Eyre by giving Bertha Mason — the silenced Creole wife — her own story
is a sequel to Jane Eyre
quiz.explanation: The postcolonial revision hands the marginalised figure narration and a history of her own.

quiz.q: Mulvey’s male gaze describes…
options: visual narrative structured around the male viewer’s desire
quiz.explanation: Camera, framing and story position the look as male.

quiz.q: Fish’s interpretive communities explain disagreements as…
options: trained by institutions — communities read by different rules
quiz.explanation: Readers arrive trained; the community certifies a reading.

intro:
A short paragraph, five options, ninety seconds: that is the critical reasoning question, and it decides large slices of the LSAT (logical reasoning is half the scored test since Logic Games were dropped in August 2024), CLAT's Logical Reasoning section, GMAT verbal and CAT's VARC paper. The skill is constant across all of them: read a compact argument, find its load-bearing parts, and judge what would make it stronger, weaker or untenable. This lesson builds that skill as a system — argument anatomy first, then the assumption test that powers it, then each question family with its own method — following the question-type taxonomy of LSAC and GMAC official prep materials. It is a different discipline from reading comprehension, which the Library's reading lessons cover on long passages, and from formal symbolic logic, which belongs to the aptitude reasoning chapters.

**Why this matters.** Critical reasoning is the most trainable section on any aptitude test — scores move tens of percentiles with method, not genius — and the same anatomy (claim, support, unstated bridge) is the backbone of legal reasoning, editorial reading and business cases. CLAT passages, LSAT prompts and GMAT arguments are built from the same dozen patterns; learn the patterns and the questions become recognisable rather than mysterious.
objectives: Explain premise-conclusion-assumption anatomy
Explain indicator words and argument mapping
Explain the negation test for assumptions
Explain strengthen and weaken: the evidence gap
Explain inference: must be true
Explain flaws and the classic fallacies
Explain paradox and resolution
Explain method and role-of-statement questions

concepts.statement: Every argument has three parts. The conclusion is the claim being pushed — the point the arguer wants you to accept. The premises are the stated reasons offered for it. The assumptions are the unstated links: statements that must be true for the premises to actually support the conclusion. Train yourself to find the conclusion first, using indicator words: therefore, thus, so, consequently, it follows that, clearly, the answer is. Premise indicators: because, since, given that, as shown by, after all, for. Assumptions never appear in the text — that is what makes them the exam's favourite target, because an argument can look airtight and still stand on a hidden plank that one new fact can kick away.

The single most powerful technique in the section is the negation test for assumptions. Take a candidate assumption, negate it, and ask whether the argument still stands. If the negation destroys the conclusion, the candidate is a genuine assumption — a necessary condition. If the argument survives the negation, the candidate was merely a nice-to-have, and it is the wrong answer. Example: "The new expressway must be causing the town's traffic surge — average journey times through town rose 12 per cent in the year since the expressway opened, and expressway users are exempt from the town's congestion charge." Candidate: "The expressway did not merely replace a faster route that closed the same year." Negate it — suppose the old ring road did close the same year — and the whole inference collapses: that is the assumption. Candidate: "The congestion charge is unpopular." Negate it: the argument does not care. One negation kills, the other does not — the test tells you which is load-bearing, and answer options for assumption questions are designed so that two or three survive everything except the negation test.

Strengthen and weaken questions run on the evidence gap: the space between what the premises establish and what the conclusion needs. The method is to state the gap as a question — "the argument assumes WHAT about the link between the data and the claim?" — and then find the option that closes (strengthen) or widens (weaken) that exact gap. Two disciplines matter. Attack the reasoning, not the topic: an option that merely expresses dislike of the conclusion, or adds an unrelated fact, is out of scope. And direction matters: a weaken answer supplies new information that makes the conclusion less likely — typically an alternative explanation, a sampling flaw, or a reversal of the causal arrow. The six classic weaken moves: alternative cause (something else did it), reverse causation (the effect produces the supposed cause), sampling bias (the data come from an unrepresentative slice), confounder (a third factor drives both), timing (the correlation predates nothing useful), and threshold (the change is too small to matter). Every correct weaken answer on these tests is one of those six wearing a story.

concepts.term: Strengthen and weaken: the evidence gap
concepts.statement: Inference questions invert the relationship: instead of a conclusion to attack, you get premises and must find what must be true — the answer is the one statement that cannot be false if the passage is true. The discipline is closure: no outside knowledge, no probability talk, nothing about the future beyond what the text guarantees. Wrong answers are usually could-be-true statements — plausible, consistent with the passage, but not forced by it — or exaggerations that upgrade "some" to "most". If the passage says "every participant who improved had slept more than seven hours", it does not follow that sleep caused improvement (that would be a causal trap), nor that most participants improved (scope creep), only that no improver slept seven hours or fewer. Method-of-argument and role-of-statement questions ask you to describe the structure instead of evaluating it — "the argument proceeds by" or the boldfaced-statement format of the GMAT, where you classify each highlighted sentence as premise, conclusion, counterpoint, evidence against a rival view, or concession before attack. For those, the map you drew while finding the conclusion is already the answer key.

Flaw questions name the gap, and the same fallacies recur so often they should be recognised on sight. Ad hominem: attacking the person (a scientist funded by industry, so wrong — perhaps suspect, not thereby wrong). Straw man: restating an opponent's claim in a weaker form and demolishing that. False dilemma: presenting two options as exhaustive when others exist. Post hoc ergo propter hoc: after it, therefore because of it — the rooster crows before dawn. Correlation-as-causation, the parent fallacy of the last two, with its third-variable and reverse-causal children. Hasty generalisation: three data points to a universal claim. Slippery slope: one modest step presented as inevitably ending in catastrophe. Circular reasoning: the conclusion smuggled in as a premise. Equivocation: a key word shifting meaning mid-argument. Appeals to authority, popularity and tradition fill out the list. LSAT answer choices rarely name them; they say "takes for granted that..." (an assumption) or "fails to consider that..." (an overlooked possibility) — you still need the pattern to spot which one.

Paradox and resolution questions present two facts that seem not to fit together — "the pharmacy's generic sales rose after a price rise, though generics are supposed to be price-sensitive" — and ask for the fact that reconciles both. The answer must make both statements true, not explain one away; typically it introduces a changed constraint (a branded rival rose faster, the price rise funded wider availability). Timing strategy is the last pillar: budget roughly ninety seconds to two minutes per question, read the question stem before the stimulus so you know the task, predict an answer before reading options, and treat elimination as the method — four wrong answers, each wrong for a nameable reason (out of scope, wrong direction, too strong, wrong comparison), leave one standing. When a question passes your budget, flag it and move; the section rewards the disciplined more than the heroic, and flagged questions answered in the last minutes are answered with fresh eyes.

Reading the stimulus before the stem wastes your first pass — always know the task first. Choosing an answer because it is true of the world rather than true of the argument: outside knowledge is out of scope even when correct in reality. Confusing weaken with refute: the right answer makes the conclusion less likely, not impossible. Falling for causal language in inference questions — correlation in the premises never licenses causation in the answer. Missing direction reversals ("most" versus "some", "could" versus "must") planted in the options. And spending four minutes on one heroic question: the section is a points-per-minute game, and the flag-and-return discipline is worth more marks than any single battle.
The claim an argument exists to establish — find it first, using therefore, thus, so, clearly.
An unstated statement that must be true for the premises to support the conclusion; the exam's favourite target.
Negate a candidate assumption; if the argument collapses, it is the assumption. The section's sharpest tool.
The space between what premises show and what the conclusion needs; strengthen closes it, weaken widens it.
Inference standard: the only answer that cannot be false if the passage is true — no probability, no outside knowledge.
The classic weaken move: a second explanation for the same correlation.
Assuming that because B followed A, A caused B — after it, therefore because of it.
Refuting a weakened restatement of an opponent's position instead of the position itself.
The most common wrong-answer crime: true or plausible material that the argument never depends on.

Critical reasoning reduces to four moves, drilled until they are reflexes: find the conclusion, expose the assumption, measure the gap, eliminate by name. Everything else — the fallacy labels, the question families, the timing discipline — is scaffolding around those moves. Ten questions a day with full written elimination reasons, for two weeks, is the standard preparation arc; the students who write why each wrong option is wrong are the ones who stop falling for the same trap twice.

examples.title: Worked Example — Weaken with Full Elimination
examples.problem: Critical Reasoning: Breaking Down Arguments for Exams — worked through step by step

steps.label: Read the stem first — it says weaken. Stimulus
steps.text: "The city's new bike-share scheme must be reducing traffic congestion. Since the scheme launched in April, average commute times have fallen 9 per cent, and bike-share trips now exceed 20,000 a day. The council should therefore double the fleet to cut congestion further."

steps.label: Map the argument
steps.text: conclusion — the scheme is reducing congestion (and should be doubled). Premises — commute times fell since April; ridership is 20,000 trips a day. The gap — did the scheme cause the fall, and would more bikes mean less congestion? Note the argument rides entirely on a post hoc correlation.

steps.label: Predict before looking
steps.text: a weaken answer shows something else caused the fall, or shows the correlation does not mean what it claims. Keep that prediction in mind as the standard.

steps.label: Eliminate by name
steps.text: (A) commute times also fell 8 per cent in comparable cities with no bike-share — supplies an alternative cause; keep, it hits the exact gap. (B) most riders previously walked or took the bus, not cars — attacks the mechanism, tempting; hold. (C) the scheme costs the council 40 lakh a year — irrelevant to causation; eliminate, out of scope. (D) bike-share membership grew every month — strengthens; wrong direction; eliminate. (E) the city also resynchronised its traffic signals in May — another alternative cause; hold.

steps.label: Choose between survivors by directness
steps.text: (B) says riders were not drivers, so substitution is limited — but 20,000 trips could still include enough car-switchers, and the conclusion could survive with reduced effect. (E) is an alternative cause but only one corridor's worth. (A) is the strongest: a matched comparison group showing the same fall without any scheme makes the causal claim close to unsupportable. Answer (A) — and note that if the question had said strengthen, the answer would have been a fact making (A)-style explanations impossible, such as times holding steady in cities without schemes while the city's fell 9 per cent.

keyTakeaways: Exam practice: do official LSAT and GMAT questions untimed first to install the method, then timed sets of ten to install the pace.
Legal reasoning: CLAT's rule-application passages are assumptions and strengthen questions wearing robes — identify the rule, the fact gap and the inference.
Editorial literacy: the fallacy list turns op-ed pages and cable news into drills — find the conclusion, find the gap, name the move.
Business writing: the strengthen test is a pre-mortem for your own proposals — attack your argument the way a weaken question would.
Interviews and case studies: "what would change your mind?" is the negation test in conversational form.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is core-tier reasoning. Pair it with the reading-and-literacy lessons for comprehension of long passages (the other half of CLAT and CAT verbal) and the aptitude reasoning chapters for formal logic, syllogisms and coding patterns. Official LSAC and GMAC prep materials are the source of the most exam-faithful practice questions; editorial pages are the best free gymnasium.

quiz.q: "Sales rose every quarter since the new logo launched, so the logo drove the growth." The argument assumes…
options: nothing else changed that could plausibly drive sales over the same period
quiz.explanation: Negate it — suppose a tariff cut or a rival's exit happened the same quarter — and the inference collapses. That is the assumption by the negation test.

quiz.q: Which fact most weakens: "Our town's recycling rate doubled after the awareness drive, so the drive worked"?
options: neighbouring towns without any drive saw recycling rates double the same year
the town has a young population
recycling is good for the environment
quiz.explanation: A matched comparison group with the same change and no treatment is the strongest possible alternative-cause evidence.

quiz.q: "Every student who scored above 90 attended all the revision sessions." It must follow that…
options: some who attended all sessions scored above 90
no student who scored above 90 missed a revision session
