quiz.explanation: Only the restatement is forced. The causal reading (sessions raise scores) and the scope exaggerations (that any attendee scored above 90, or that most did) go beyond what "every high scorer attended" guarantees.

quiz.q: Restating an opponent's position in a deliberately weaker form and attacking that is called…
quiz.explanation: The straw man refutes something nobody claimed; ad hominem attacks the person, false dilemma forces two options, post hoc confuses sequence with cause.

intro:
The foundations lesson gave French its sound and its first phrases; this lesson hands over the engine — the verb system. French endings carry person and number, the ending classes follow three infinitive patterns, a handful of irregular verbs do a disproportionate share of the work, and the main past tense is built by stacking two verbs together. None of it is arbitrary: each pattern recurs across hundreds of verbs, so four or five shapes cover most of everyday speech.

**Why this matters.** Verb endings are where French learners either converge or stall: they decide whether you are understood as saying “I speak”, “you spoke” or “we will speak” — three different conversations. They are also the backbone of proficiency-exam grammar sections worldwide, from school papers to the CEFR-based tests that gate study and work visas.
objectives: Explain three conjugation classes: -er, -ir, -re
Explain the silent-ending pattern of French speech
Explain four essential irregulars: être, avoir, aller, faire
Explain negation as a sandwich: ne … pas
Explain near future: aller + infinitive
Explain passé composé: auxiliary + past participle
Explain the être-verbs of motion and reflexives

concepts.statement: Regular verbs split into three classes by infinitive ending. The -er class — parler, manger, donner — is the giant, covering the large majority of French verbs, and it conjugates with one stem and six endings: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. Notice that four of the six are silent in speech: je parle, tu parles, il parle and ils parlent all sound identical — context and pronouns carry the grammar. The -ir class — finir, choisir, grandir — inserts -iss- in the plural: finis, finis, finit, finissons, finissez, finissent. The -re class — attendre, vendre, répondre — drops the ending entirely in the singular: attends, attend, attend (tu/il forms identical, no -s in the il form), then -ons, -ez, -ent return in the plural.

concepts.term: The silent-ending pattern of French speech
concepts.statement: Four irregulars are worth memorising cold because they double as auxiliary and scaffolding verbs. être (to be): suis, es, est, sommes, êtes, sont. avoir (to have): ai, as, a, avons, avez, ont. aller (to go): vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont — note the singular forms swap in a v-. faire (to do/make): fais, fais, fait, faisons, faites, font. With these four plus the -er pattern you can already narrate most of a day: je suis fatigué, j’ai un train, je vais au marché, je fais la cuisine.

concepts.term: Four essential irregulars: être, avoir, aller, faire
concepts.statement: Negation wraps the verb like a sandwich: ne before the conjugated verb, pas after — je ne parle pas, il n’a pas (the ne drops to n’ before a vowel). In compound tenses the sandwich closes around the auxiliary, not the participle: je n’ai pas parlé. Learners who speak the words but forget the wrapper still communicate; those who master it early avoid relearning later. Related daily grammar: questions by intonation (tu parles ?) or est-ce que, and the near future formed with aller plus an infinitive — je vais parler, “I am going to speak” — which is often the first tense learners actually use, precisely because it needs no new endings.

concepts.term: Negation as a sandwich: ne … pas
concepts.statement: The default past is the passé composé: a conjugated auxiliary (avoir, occasionally être) plus a past participle. Participles mostly form on the infinitive stem: -er gives -é (parlé), -ir gives -i (fini), and -re gives -u (attendu), with famous short forms — faire → fait, prendre → pris, mettre → mis, dire → dit. With avoir, the participle never agrees with the subject. With être, the participle agrees: elle est allée, ils sont allés. The être auxiliary serves a closed club — movement and change-of-state verbs (aller, venir, partir, arriver, entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, naître, mourir, rester, tomber, devenir, and their kin) — plus all reflexive verbs (elle s’est levée). Choosing the wrong auxiliary is the classic learner error, but the club’s membership rule — motion or change of state — makes it predictable.

One more habit breaks English speakers in: French has no present progressive. “I am speaking” is je parle, full stop — the Wikibooks grammar puts it bluntly: the present indicative does the job, and constructions translating “am -ing” word-for-word are wrong. Beyond the two tenses here, the ladder continues: imparfait for habitual or ongoing past description (parlais), futur simple for formal prediction (parlerai), and the subjunctive after expressions of necessity and emotion (il faut que je parle). Each rung reuses the same stem logic, so the -er/-ir/-re patterns learned now keep paying out.
$$\text{passé composé} = \underbrace{\text{avoir (default)} \;|\; \text{être (motion/reflexive)}}_{\text{conjugated, carries negation}} + \text{participe passé}$$
concepts.detail: The auxiliary is conjugated for person and tense and hosts the ne…pas sandwich; the participle follows — agreeing with the subject only when the auxiliary is être.

concepts.statement: Sounding out every ending — most singular -er endings are silent, and pronouns carry the distinctions. Using avoir with the motion club (j’ai allé is wrong; je suis allé). Making the avoir-participle agree (elle a fini, never finie for the subject). Translating the English progressive literally. And forgetting that ne…pas wraps the conjugated verb — in compound tenses, that is the auxiliary, not the participle.
The infinitive-ending family (-er, -ir, -re) that determines a regular verb’s endings.
The helper verb (avoir or être) conjugated to build the compound past.
The verb form (-é, -i, -u families plus irregulars) combined with the auxiliary.
The closed set of motion/change-of-state verbs that take être and agree in the compound past.
The two-part negation wrapping the conjugated verb (or auxiliary).
aller + infinitive; the everyday way to express upcoming intentions.
The imperfect past, used for habitual, ongoing or descriptive past actions.

examples.title: Worked example — French Verbs: Three Endings, Four Rebels and the Compound Past
examples.problem: Build the French for “she did not finish her homework yesterday”, using finir.

steps.label: Recall the machinery
steps.text: finir is -ir class; the compound past needs an auxiliary; finir takes avoir; negation wraps the auxiliary.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: participle fini; auxiliary a (elle a); sandwich: n’a … pas; assemble: elle n’a pas fini ses devoirs hier.

examples.result: no participle agreement with avoir, the ne…pas hugs the auxiliary, and the time word sits at the end — every rule in one sentence, and the shape transfers to hundreds of -ir verbs.

keyTakeaways: Everyday narration: emails, postcards and voicemails lean on present, near future and passé composé alone.
Proficiency-exam grammar sections test exactly these patterns: ending choice, auxiliary choice, agreement.
Reading comprehension: recognising participles (fini, pris, fait) unlocks most narrative prose.
Travel logistics: je vais partir, nous sommes arrivés — transport announcements speak in compound pasts.
Recipe and instruction language, where the vous imperative of -er verbs (ajoutez) is a regular-verb ending in disguise.

Where next — Prerequisites: the French foundations lesson for sound rules and articles. Follow with the Spanish and German verb lessons to see how sibling Romance and Germanic systems solve the same problems, and the morphology lesson for the general theory of endings. Grounding texts: Wikibooks’ French grammar (verbs chapters) and any standard beginner French course grammar.
Three classes — -er (dominant), -ir (-iss- in plural), -re (bare singular) — six endings each.
Singular -er endings are silent; pronouns do the disambiguating.
être, avoir, aller, faire are the four irregulars that build everything else.
ne … pas sandwiches the conjugated verb; the near future is aller + infinitive.
Passé composé = avoir (default) or être (motion/reflexive) + participle; only être triggers agreement.

quiz.q: Which verb is conjugated: vous ______ au cinéma (aller)?
quiz.explanation: Aller’s plural forms are allons, allez, vont; vous takes allez.

quiz.q: The past of “they (masculine) went out” is…
quiz.explanation: Sortir belongs to the être club: auxiliary sont, participle sortis agreeing in gender and number.

quiz.q: In elle n’a pas parlé, the ne…pas wraps…
options: nothing — it splits around both verbs
quiz.explanation: Negation attaches to the conjugated element, which in compound tenses is the auxiliary.

intro:
The foundations lesson covered German’s cases and cognates; this lesson takes the verb machinery, which is where German earns its reputation. The system is strict — one stem, six endings, a bracketed sentence — but it is also deeply regular: learn the pattern for one verb and you own thousands. The exceptions concentrate in a small set of high-frequency verbs that repay memorising many times over.

**Why this matters.** German packs meaning into prefixes — aufstehen, verstehen, bekommen are three different verbs wearing the same stem — so prefix behaviour is the key to vocabulary growth. And the perfect-tense word order (auxiliary second, participle last) is the single most recognisable signature of German syntax.
objectives: Explain regular endings on one stem: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en
Explain stem-vowel changes: du gibst, du fährst
Explain separable prefixes and the sentence bracket
Explain inseparable prefixes and the no-ge- participle
Explain modal verbs with a bare infinitive at the end
Explain perfect tense: haben/sein + Partizip II
Explain präteritum for the small verbs

concepts.statement: Regular verbs conjugate by adding six endings to the stem (infinitive minus -en): ich lerne, du lernst, er lernt, wir lernen, ihr lernt, sie lernen. Only the du and er/sie/es forms differ from the stem-plus-ending ideal — where the stem ends in -t or -d or a consonant cluster, an extra -e- slides in to keep it pronounceable: du arbeitest, er arbeitet. A small set of strong verbs changes the stem vowel in the du and er forms: geben → du gibst, er gibt; fahren → du fährst, er fährt; nehmen → du nimmst, er nimmt; lesen → du liest, er liest. English keeps a fossil of this in sing/sang/sung — German just kept the living system.

concepts.term: Stem-vowel changes: du gibst, du fährst
concepts.statement: The sentence bracket is German’s signature move. In a main clause the conjugated verb claims second position (V2), and any unhooks a separable prefix, which flies to the sentence’s end: aufstehen → Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf, “I get up at six” — the bracket closes with auf. The same bracket holds infinitives (Ich kann heute nicht kommen) and participles. Subordinate clauses pull the whole verb to the end: …, weil ich früh aufstehe. Separable prefixes are a common, stressed set — ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, mit-, vor-, zu-, zurück- — and each re-verbs the stem: anrufen (call), einkaufen (shop), mitnehmen (bring along).

concepts.term: Separable prefixes and the sentence bracket
concepts.statement: Inseparable prefixes behave in mirror image: be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp-, miss- stay welded to the verb, carry no stress, and — crucially — forbid the ge- of the participle: verstehen → verstanden, besuchen → besucht, bekommen → bekommen. Spotting the prefix class therefore tells you the participle shape before you have conjugated anything. A third group, verbs ending in -ieren (studieren, telefonieren), also drops the ge-: studiert. This is the short list of German morphology that rewards fifteen minutes of memorising with lifetime returns.

concepts.term: Inseparable prefixes and the no-ge- participle
concepts.statement: Modal verbs — können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen(möchten) — conjugate irregularly in the singular (ich kann, du kannst, er kann with no ending on er) and, when they govern another verb, push that bare infinitive to the bracket’s end: Ich muss heute arbeiten, “I must work today”. They are also the exception to spoken-German perfect habits: the modals, haben, sein and es gibt prefer the simple Präteritum even in speech — ich konnte, ich hatte, ich war — because their perfect forms would need a double infinitive (ich habe kommen müssen), which exists but is heavy. So: small verbs take the old simple past; everything else takes the perfect.

concepts.term: Modal verbs with a bare infinitive at the end
concepts.statement: The everyday past is the Perfekt: haben or sein plus the Partizip II in final position. Weak verbs build ge- + stem + -t (lernen → gelernt); strong verbs build ge- + (possibly changed) stem + -en (sprechen → gesprochen); verbs with an inseparable prefix or -ieren drop the ge- as above. Auxiliary choice follows meaning: haben for transitive and most verbs; sein for movement from A to B and change of state — gehen, fahren, fliegen, aufstehen, werden, bleiben, sein itself. Ich habe gegessen, but ich bin gegangen. The participle agrees with nothing, which is a small mercy; the auxiliary does all the agreeing, and the perfect covers most conversational past-tense needs.
$$\text{weak: } ge + \text{stem} + t \quad | \quad \text{strong: } ge + \text{stem}^{\pm\text{vowel}} + en \quad | \quad \text{be-/ver-/er-/ent-/…-verbs and -ieren: no } ge-$$
concepts.detail: Three participle shapes cover the lexicon; the prefix class of the verb decides whether the ge- appears at all.

concepts.statement: Sending the separable prefix into the bracket and then forgetting to close it. Adding ge- to inseparable verbs — it is verstanden, never geverstanden. Using haben where movement demands sein. Putting the bare infinitive after a modal anywhere but the bracket’s end. And using the Perfekt for haben/sein/modals in speech — ich war, ich hatte, ich konnte are what Germans actually say.
Strong-verb vowel shift in the du/er forms (geben → du gibst, fahren → du fährst).
A stressed prefix (auf-, ein-, mit-, …) that detaches and closes the sentence bracket.
An unstressed prefix (be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp-, miss-) welded to the verb; no ge- in the participle.
The frame formed by the conjugated verb in second position and its dependent (prefix, infinitive, participle) at the end.
können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen — conjugated irregularly, governing a bare infinitive at the end.
The perfect-tense participle: ge-…-t (weak), ge-…-en (strong), no ge- with inseparable prefixes and -ieren.
The simple past, reserved in speech for haben, sein and the modals.

examples.title: Worked example — German Verbs: Stem Changes, Separable Prefixes and the Perfect
examples.problem: Say “Yesterday I went shopping (and bought bread)” using einkaufen and kaufen.

steps.label: Recall the machinery
steps.text: einkaufen is separable → bracket; kaufen is weak → Partizip II gekauft; movement/shopping takes sein in the perfect by convention with einkaufen.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: Ich bin gestern eingekauft (prefix at the end closes the bracket); for the bread with haben: Ich habe Brot gekauft.

examples.result: two past clauses, one bracket, one ge- participle suppressed where the prefix forbids it — in one sentence pair, the whole verb system in miniature.

keyTakeaways: Everyday conversation, where the perfect + modal + bracket structure is the default grammar of speech.
Proficiency-exam writing sections, which score exactly these: ending accuracy, prefix behaviour, participle formation.
Vocabulary tripling: one stem plus ten prefixes is eleven verbs — ver-, be-, ent- families grow fast.
Reading signs and announcements: geschlossen, verboten, abgefahren — participles are public furniture.
Workplace German: meeting verbs (besprechen, vorbereiten, einladen) are inseparable/separable showcases.

Where next — Prerequisites: the German foundations lesson for cases and the V2 rule it introduces. Follow with the French verb lesson for a sibling system that solves the past with two auxiliaries too, and the morphology lesson for the theory behind stems and affixes. Grounding texts: Wikibooks’ German grammar (verbs chapters) and the verb pages of any standard beginner German course.
One stem, six endings; only du/er forms deviate, and strong verbs shift the vowel there.
Separable prefixes fly to the sentence end and close the bracket; inseparables stay welded.
Partizip II: ge-…-t (weak), ge-…-en (strong), no ge- with be-/ver-/er-/ent- and -ieren.
Modals take bare infinitives at the end; in speech they, haben and sein prefer the Präteritum.
Everyday past = haben (default) or sein (movement/state change) + participle in final position.

quiz.q: The correct participle of verstehen is…
quiz.explanation: Inseparable prefixes forbid the ge-; the strong participle is verstanden.

quiz.q: Ich ______ morgen nach Berlin (fahren, perfect tense)…
quiz.explanation: Fahren expresses movement, so the perfect auxiliary is sein: ich bin gefahren.

quiz.q: In “Ich muss heute früh aufstehen”, the bracket closes with…
quiz.explanation: The modal holds position two; the governed bare infinitive (here with its separable prefix intact) sits at the end.

intro:
The writing-system lesson covered scripts; the particles lesson covered how Japanese marks roles; this lesson covers the verbs themselves — and they are friendlier than the writing suggests. A Japanese verb never changes for person or number: 飲む (nomu, drink) means I, you, we or they drink; the sentence ends in the verb; and every form is built by regular inflection for tense, polarity and politeness. Master three groups and a handful of sound rules, and you can conjugate nearly the whole language.

**Why this matters.** Japanese politeness is built into the verb, not added around it: choosing ます-form versus plain form is a social act performed dozens of times per minute. The te-form, meanwhile, is the hinge of half the language’s most useful patterns — requests, progressives, permission — which is why textbooks race learners toward it.
objectives: Explain verbs inflect for tense and politeness, never for person
Explain group 1 (u-verbs) vs Group 2 (ru-verbs) vs the two irregulars
Explain the ます polite system and its negative/past
Explain plain forms and the dictionary form
Explain te-form: the connective of Japanese
Explain sound changes: く→いて, む/ぶ/ぬ→んで, る/つ/う→って
Explain politeness levels from casual to keigo

concepts.term: Verbs inflect for tense and politeness, never for person
concepts.statement: Verbs divide into three groups. Group 2 — the ru-verbs — end in the vowel row る and conjugate by simply dropping it: 食べる → 食べます (eat → polite eat), 食べない (negative), 食べた (past). Group 1 — the u-verbs — end in a consonant plus a u-vowel (買う, 書く, 飲む, 話す) and conjugate by shifting that final syllable to its i-row twin before ます: 買う → 買います (kau → kaimasu), 書く → 書きます (kaku → kakimasu), 飲む → 飲みます (nomu → nomimasu), 話す → 話します (hanasu → hanashimasu — note す becomes し, shi). Group 3 is two verbs, irregular and indispensable: する (suru, do → します shimasu) and 来る (kuru, come → 来ます kimasu). A verb ending in る is usually a ru-verb, but a set of u-verbs wears る too (帰る kaeru → 帰ります kaerimasu) — the dictionary mark and practice settle them.

concepts.term: Group 1 (u-verbs) vs Group 2 (ru-verbs) vs the two irregulars
concepts.statement: The ます system gives four core forms with total regularity: present affirmative ます, present negative ません, past affirmative ました, past negative ませんでした. 行きます (go), 行きません (do not go), 行きました (went), 行きませんでした (did not go). The plain forms — dictionary form, -nai negative, -ta past — carry the same tense information without the politeness marker, and they are the forms dictionaries list and casual conversation lives in: 行く, 行かない, 行った. Learners who meet textbooks first speak ます-form everywhere; learners who meet anime first speak plain everywhere — Japanese fluency needs both registers and the judgment to switch.

concepts.term: The ます polite system and its negative/past
concepts.statement: The te-form is the connective tissue. For ru-verbs, it is the ます-stem plus て: 食べて, 見て. For u-verbs, four sound-change families: final く→いて and ぐ→いで (書く→書いて, 泳ぐ→泳いで); す→して (話す→話して); む/ぶ/ぬ→んで (飲む→飲んで, 遊ぶ→遊んで, 死ぬ→死んで); る/つ/う→って (食べる is Group 2, but 乗る→乗って, 待つ→待って, 買う→買って). The te-form alone does little, but compounds: お願い pattern 〜てください (please do), progressive 〜ている (doing / in a state — 知っている, to know, literally “has been knowing”), permission 〜てもいい, linking clauses “and then” (朝起きて、顔を洗って、出かけた). One form, five high-frequency grammars.

concepts.term: Plain forms and the dictionary form
concepts.statement: Politeness is a layered architecture. The plain and ます contrast is the first layer (teineigo, polite speech); Japanese adds honorific keigo — sonkeigo to elevate the listener’s actions (召し上がる for eat), kenjougo to humble your own (いただく, 参る). Everyday learners need awareness, not mastery: use ます-form with strangers, teachers, shops; plain form with family, close friends, and inside casual writing; and remember that politeness attaches to WHO the action benefits, not just to formality. Verb-final word order plus the politeness engine gives Japanese its famous rhythm: topic, roles, then the verb — ending in ます or its plain twin — that tells you when the sentence was over.

Two habits seal the system. First, particles and verbs share the load: は/が/を mark who does and what receives (the particles lesson), and the verb closes the frame — 私はコーヒーを飲みます — so no ending change for person ever arrives. Second, the past tense splits between ました (polite) and -た (plain) without any of the agreement anxiety of European languages: no gender, no number, no auxiliary stacking for the everyday past. Japanese verbs are the rare grammar that is easier than its script — and the script is learnable too, which is the encouragement the writing lesson ends on.
$$\text{u-verb: } \text{final う-row syllable} \to \text{i-row twin} + ます \quad (\text{ru-verb: drop る} + ます)$$
concepts.detail: Group 1 verbs shift the final syllable to its i-row (く→き, む→み, す→し) before ます; Group 2 verbs just drop る. Every other form builds on these stems.

concepts.statement: Classifying every る-verb as Group 2 — 帰る, 走る, 要る are u-verbs (帰ります, not 帰ます). Applying the te-form sound change to ru-verbs, which simply take て. Using 〜ている wherever English uses “is -ing” — Japanese often prefers the plain result state (知っている for “I know”). Mixing plain and ます forms mid-conversation with the same person without signalling a register change. And expecting person endings — they never come; the particles carry the roles.
Verb whose final syllable is a consonant + u-vowel; conjugates by shifting to the i-row before ます.
Verb ending in the る vowel row; conjugates by dropping る.
The connective form powering requests, progressives, permission and clause linking.
The polite verb system: ます / ません / ました / ませんでした.
Dictionary, -nai and -ta forms; casual register and dictionary listing.
The te-form + いる progressive/state pattern, covering both “is doing” and “is in a state”.
The honorific layer (sonkeigo, kenjougo) that elevates and humbles actions beyond the ます level.

examples.title: Worked example — Japanese Verbs: Three Groups, the te-Form and the Politeness Engine
examples.problem: Conjugate 飲む (drink) through polite negative, polite past, and te-form, then say “I am drinking coffee now”.

steps.label: Recall the machinery
steps.text: 飲む is a Group 1 u-verb ending む; the む family maps to んで in the te-form and み in the ます-stem.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: polite 飲みます; negative 飲みません; past 飲みました; te-form 飲んで; progressive uses ている → 今、コーヒーを飲んでいます.

examples.result: one stem (のみ-) generated three polite forms, and the te-form opened the progressive — four grammars from one sound rule, with zero person endings anywhere.

keyTakeaways: Daily conversation: ます-form with strangers and shops; plain form among friends — the register switch is constant.
Proficiency-test grammar sections, which drill group identification, te-form sound changes and ている states.
Asking and responding: 〜てください requests and 〜てもいい permission run daily logistics.
Describing states: 結婚している (is married), 行っている (has gone) — the progressive that doubles as resultative.
Workplace survival: understanding keigo even while speaking plain-polite, and spotting the humble いたします.

Where next — Prerequisites: the particles lesson for は/が/を and the writing lesson to read the examples. Follow with the French and German verb lessons for contrastive views of how languages encode person, and the prosody lesson for pitch accent. Grounding texts: the verb chapters of standard beginner Japanese courses (the Genki tradition) and Wikibooks’ Japanese grammar.
Three groups: ru-verbs drop る; u-verbs shift the last syllable to the i-row; する and 来る are irregular.
ます system: ます / ません / ました / ませんでした — four forms, total regularity.
Plain forms (dictionary, -nai, -ta) are the casual register and the base for te-form.
te-form sound changes: く→いて, ぐ→いで, す→して, む/ぶ/ぬ→んで, る/つ/う→って.
Politeness is lexical and layered — ます first, keigo later; verbs never mark person.

quiz.q: The polite present of 書く (write) is…
quiz.explanation: く shifts to its i-row き before ます: 書きます. (書いています would be the progressive te-form.)

quiz.q: The te-form of 飲む is…
quiz.explanation: The む/ぶ/ぬ family maps to んで: 飲んで. (飲んでいる is the progressive built on it.)

quiz.q: How many person endings does a Japanese verb have?
options: zero — verbs never agree with the subject
quiz.explanation: Tense, polarity and politeness inflect; person and number never do — particles mark the roles.

intro:
The ser/estar lesson handled the two ways to be; this lesson handles everything else — the full Spanish verb engine. Spanish endings do the work pronouns would otherwise do, three infinitive classes organise the system, a beautiful irregularity (the stem-changing “boot verbs”) adds texture, and the language keeps two different past tenses because Spanish grammar insists completed events and ongoing background deserve separate grammar. It is the most regular of the major Romance engines, and its patterns transfer straight to French and Italian later.

**Why this matters.** Spanish is the second-most-spoken native language on earth, and its verb endings are the difference between hablo (I speak), habló (he/she spoke) and hablaré (I will speak) — three tenses, one letter. Proficiency tests, school curricula and workplace Spanish all drill exactly this machinery.
objectives: Explain three infinitive classes: -ar, -er, -ir
Explain endings that carry person and number
Explain stem-changing boot verbs: e→ie, o→ue, e→i
Explain irregular first-person forms: -go, -zco
Explain preterite versus imperfect aspect
Explain only -ir verbs stem-change in the preterite
Explain agreement lives on nouns and adjectives, not verbs

concepts.statement: Regular verbs conjugate by stripping the infinitive ending (-ar, -er, -ir) and adding the person endings. The -ar template (hablar): -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. The -er template (comer): -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en. The -ir template (vivir): same as -er except nosotros/vosotros take -imos/-ís. Because every ending encodes person and number, subject pronouns are optional and usually dropped — como already means “I eat”, and adding yo is for emphasis or contrast, not clarity. This is the load-bearing difference from English: the ending IS the subject.

concepts.term: Endings that carry person and number
concepts.statement: Boot verbs are the signature irregularity: in certain verbs the stem vowel shifts in all forms except nosotros and vosotros. Plot the changed and unchanged forms on a conjugation table and the changes form a boot shape. Three families: e→ie (pensar → pienso, piensas, piensa, pensamos, pensáis, piensan), o→ue (poder → puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden), and e→i (pedir → pido, pides, pide, pedimos, pedís, piden), plus the lone u→ue (jugar → juego). The logic: the stress-bearing vowel mutates, and only the weak nosotros/vosotros forms escape. Dozens of high-frequency verbs live here — querer, cerrar, entender, dormir, volver, contar — so the boot is not decoration; it is daily speech.

concepts.term: Stem-changing boot verbs: e→ie, o→ue, e→i
concepts.statement: A second irregularity concentrates in the first person singular: many verbs are regular everywhere except the yo form. The -go family: tener → tengo, hacer → hago (with the silent-h spelling change), salir → salgo, poner → pongo, decir → digo. The -zco family (verbs whose infinitive ends in a vowel + -cer/-cir): conocer → conozco, conducir → conduzco. Learners who memorise the yo-forms separately — tengo, hago, conozco — neutralise most of Spanish’s apparent irregularity in one sitting, because the other five forms stay regular.

Spanish keeps two past tenses, and the choice is aspectual, not temporal. The preterite (hablé, comí, vivió) frames events as completed: bounded, counted, done — fue ayer, “it happened yesterday”. The imperfect (hablaba, comía, vivía) paints background: ongoing, habitual, unbounded — comía todos los días, “I used to eat every day”. The contrast shines in combination: leía cuando sonó el teléfono — “I was reading (background, imperfect) when the phone rang (event, preterite)”. Classic minimal pairs encode worldview: supe (I found out) versus sabía (I knew), pude (I managed to) versus podía (I was able to). Tests drill this relentlessly because no English tense pair maps onto it.

One wrinkle completes the picture: in the preterite, only -ir verbs stem-change, and only in the third-person forms — pedir → pidió, pidieron; dormir → durmió, durmieron — while -ar and -er verbs never do. The system’s regularity is remarkable otherwise: the future and conditional attach whole endings to the entire infinitive (hablaré, comería), and compound habits like ir + a + infinitive (voy a comer) offer the near future with zero new endings. Agreement, meanwhile, stays where the Romance languages put it: gender and number live on nouns and adjectives — the ser/estar lesson’s territory — never on the verb.
$$\text{stem change in: } \{yo,\ t\acute{u},\ \acute{e}l,\ ellos\} \qquad \text{unchanged in: } \{nosotros,\ vosotros\}$$
concepts.detail: The stressed stem vowels mutate (e→ie, o→ue, e→i, u→ue) wherever stress falls on the stem; the weak nosotros/vosotros endings pull stress onto the ending, so the stem survives there intact.

concepts.statement: Pronouncing or writing every pronoun — the endings already say yo, tú, nosotros. Stem-changing in the nosotros/vosotros forms — the boot leaves them alone. Stem-changing an -ar or -er verb in the preterite — only -ir verbs do, and only in él/ellos forms. Treating the two pasts as interchangeable tenses rather than aspects — comí (I ate it) and comía (I used to eat) are different claims about reality. And forgetting the yo-form irregulars (tengo, hago, conozco), which are Spanish’s most common single-letter surprises.
The -ar, -er or -ir infinitive ending that sets a verb’s person endings.
A stem-changing verb whose mutation covers all forms except nosotros/vosotros, tracing a boot on the table.
e→ie, o→ue, e→i (and u→ue for jugar) under stress in the present tense.
A first-person-only surprise: -go (tengo, hago) or -zco (conozco) families.
The completed-event past: bounded, counted, done.
The background past: ongoing, habitual, unbounded.
The shape an action is given — bounded vs ongoing — as distinct from when it happened.

examples.title: Worked example — Spanish Verbs: Endings, Boot Verbs and Two Pasts
examples.problem: Say “I was reading when the phone rang”, choosing between the two past tenses for each verb.

steps.label: Recall the aspect rule
steps.text: background, ongoing scene → imperfect; completed, punctual event → preterite.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: leer (ongoing background) → leía; sonar (single completed event) → sonó — and sonar is a boot verb in the present, but -ar verbs never stem-change in the preterite, so it is simply sonó.

examples.result: Leía cuando sonó el teléfono — the sentence’s shape is itself the lesson: imperfect paints, preterite acts.

keyTakeaways: Everyday conversation across twenty-plus countries — the endings do the subject’s job, fast speech drops the pronouns.
Proficiency-test grammar sections: ending tables, boot verbs, and preterite-versus-imperfect narratives are the core drills.
Travel Spanish: past-tense storytelling (what happened, what you needed) runs on the preterite/imperfect pair.
Song lyrics and telenovelas, where aspect shifts (sabía → supe) carry emotional turns.
Learning French or Italian afterward — the -ar/-er/-ir logic maps onto their conjugation classes almost one-to-one.

Where next — Prerequisites: the ser/estar lesson for the two “to be”s and the survival-Spanish lesson for context. Follow with the French verb lesson — sibling Romance logic — and the morphology lesson for the general theory of endings. Grounding texts: Wikibooks’ Spanish grammar (verb chapters) and the stem-changing/past-tense pages of any standard Spanish course.
Three classes — -ar, -er, -ir — with endings that carry person and number, so pronouns are optional.
Boot verbs shift e→ie, o→ue, e→i under stress; nosotros/vosotros escape.
Irregular yo-forms (-go, -zco) are memorisable in one sitting and cover most of the irregularity.
Two pasts by aspect: preterite completes, imperfect paints — leía cuando sonó el teléfono.
Only -ir verbs stem-change in the preterite, and only in él/ellos forms.

quiz.q: The correct nosotros form of poder is…
quiz.explanation: The o→ue boot skips nosotros — stress falls on the ending -emos, so the stem survives: podemos.

quiz.q: “He found out yesterday” (saber, completed event) is…
quiz.explanation: Completed discovery takes the preterite third person: supo. Sabía would mean he already knew (background).

quiz.q: Which verb stem-changes in the preterite third person?
quiz.explanation: Only -ir verbs stem-change in the preterite: pedir → pidió. The others stay regular.

intro:
A literary passage is a different machine from the news article or the argument excerpt. It does not advance a claim you can underline; it builds an experience — a stretch of invented time peopled by characters whose motives you must read between the lines. The questions that follow such passages therefore probe different skills: not "what is the main argument" but "what does the narrator reveal despite himself", "why does the author place the revelation here", "what does the image of the locked door mean". This lesson covers the moving parts of fiction and the reading habits that answer those questions reliably.

**Why this matters.** Reading-comprehension sections increasingly draw on literary and narrative extracts, and readers trained only on expository text misread them predictably — hunting for a thesis that is not there. The devices behind the prose have their own lesson; this one is about the reading: tracking who tells the story, what changes, and what the text implies without saying.
objectives: Explain what literary passages ask: experience, not argument
Explain plot structure: exposition, rising action, climax, resolution
Explain narrator and point of view: first person, limited, omniscient
Explain characterisation: speech, thought, action and contrast
Explain setting, imagery and mood
Explain theme versus topic
Explain inference: reading beyond the stated

concepts.term: What literary passages ask: experience, not argument
concepts.statement: Every narrative has a skeleton. The exposition opens the world — who, where, what is ordinary. Rising action introduces and complicates a conflict (against another person, against nature, against society, or against oneself), building tension through choices and setbacks. The climax is the turn: the moment the conflict is decided. The resolution settles the aftermath, sometimes in a deliberate final image. Long passages are rarely complete stories; they are slices of this skeleton, and identifying which slice — before the turn, at the turn, after it — immediately tells you what the questions can ask: motivation before, decision at, consequence after.

concepts.term: Plot structure: exposition, rising action, climax, resolution
concepts.statement: Who tells the story decides what anyone in it can know. A first-person narrator lives inside the text as "I": everything is filtered through one limited, biased consciousness, which is a feature — readers weigh what that narrator admits, hides and misunderstands. A third-person limited narrator rides beside one character, reporting that mind's perceptions while keeping outsiders opaque. A third-person omniscient narrator sees all minds and can editorialise. An unreliable narrator — one whose account the text quietly undermines, by contradictions, by gaps, by other characters' reactions — is the special case that examination passages love, and the antidote is always the same: ask what the text shows that the narrator does not notice.

concepts.term: Narrator and point of view: first person, limited, omniscient
concepts.statement: Character is built from evidence, and the evidence has categories: what characters do (the strongest signal), what they say and how they speak, what they think, how others react to them, and — rarely — what the narrator flatly asserts. Flat characters are built from one or two traits; round characters hold contradictions and change. A foil exists to throw another character into relief by contrast, and a static character who refuses the change everyone else undergoes is often the passage's quiet argument. Questions about motive are answered from the action-thought-reaction evidence, never from adjectives alone.

concepts.term: Characterisation: speech, thought, action and contrast
concepts.statement: Setting is not scenery. Time and place constrain what the characters can want (a harvest, an escape, a marriage) and how fast the conflict can move; weather and light carry mood — the Emotional weather of the scene — and recurring objects gather symbolic weight: the locked door, the untended garden, the river crossing. When a question asks what an image contributes, the honest answers come from the same small set: it establishes mood, characterises a person, foreshadows a turn, or condenses the theme.

Theme is the story's claim about life — ambition hollows, kindness compounds, the past is never past — while topic is merely its subject (love, war, sailing). A theme must be stated as a sentence, and it is inferred from the pattern of the whole: what the conflict costs, what the ending rewards or punishes, what the title points at. Tone is the narrator's attitude toward the material (ironic, wistful, bitter), and mood is the atmosphere raised in the reader; both ride on diction — the specific word choices — which is why vocabulary questions in literary passages are really tone questions in disguise.

Inference is the engine of all the above. Literary texts imply far more than they state, and legitimate inference is disciplined: it moves from textual evidence (a word, a gesture, a silence) plus normal background knowledge (how people usually behave) to the least strong conclusion that explains the evidence. The moment an inference requires inventing facts the text never suggests — a backstory, a country, a motive with no cue — it has stopped being inference and become fan fiction. Answer options in inference questions are built to exploit exactly this gap; the safest option is the modest one fully supported by cues.
The opening that establishes characters, setting and the ordinary state of affairs before conflict disturbs it.
Who tells the story and from where: first person, third limited, third omniscient — each fixing what can be known.
A narrator whose account the text undermines; read what is shown against what is claimed.
A character placed in contrast to another so that qualities become visible by difference.
The atmosphere a passage raises in the reader, built from setting, imagery and diction.
The claim about life the story argues through its pattern — always a sentence, never a single word.
A conclusion drawn from textual cues plus ordinary background knowledge — the least strong explanation that fits.

Narrative reading compresses to a checklist: locate the slice of the arc, fix the point of view and its limits, gather character evidence from action, weigh setting and recurring images for mood and meaning, then infer modestly from cues. Run the checklist twice on any literary passage — once for the story, once for the telling — and the questions have nowhere left to hide.

examples.title: Inferring attitude from diction
examples.problem: Reading Narrative Passages: Plot, Narrator and Inference in Literary Fiction — worked through step by step

steps.label: Excerpt
steps.text: "The ceremony, naturally, was prolonged; the mayor enjoyed, as ever, the sound of his own benevolence."

steps.label: Mark the diction
steps.text: "naturally" (weary expectation), "prolonged" (excess), "as ever" (repetition), "the sound of his own benevolence" (hollow performance).

steps.label: Add the mechanics
steps.text: two commas isolate "naturally" — a spoken aside; "benevolence" is abstract where a sincere writer would be concrete.

steps.label: Infer, minimally
steps.text: the narrator is ironic — outwardly describing a civic ritual, inwardly mocking the mayor's self-regard.

steps.label: Check the rival options
steps.text: "neutral observation" ignores the word choices; "anger" overstates — mockery is cooler than anger. The modest, cue-anchored reading wins.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Pair this lesson with the literary-devices lesson for the technique vocabulary (irony, symbolism, imagery) these passages deploy, the paired-passages lesson for reading two texts against each other, and the verbal-reasoning lesson for claims-and-evidence reading on argumentative text. Background reading: the "How to Analyze Fiction — Elements of Literature" chapter in LibreTexts' Approaches to Literature collection, and any open anthology's introductions to plot and point of view.

quiz.q: A passage opens: "Everyone agreed the ship was seaworthy; Meera counted the lifeboats twice." The narration is…
options: third person, using Meera's contrary action to seed doubt about the collective claim
quiz.explanation: The narrator is outside the story but shows Meera's counting — a gesture the group does not see. The text implies doubt through action while the stated view says the opposite: the classic gap a careful reader tracks.

quiz.q: The climax of a narrative is best described as…
options: the opening that sets the scene
the turn where the central conflict is decided
the final image after everything is over
the moment a new character enters
quiz.explanation: The climax is the decisive turn of the conflict; exposition precedes it and the resolution follows. Entries of new characters usually belong to rising action.

quiz.q: In a story, a careless older brother is constantly paired with a meticulous younger one. The younger brother chiefly functions as…
options: a foil whose contrast sharpens the elder's portrait
quiz.explanation: A foil exists for contrast: the pairing makes each brother's trait legible. Antagonist would require the younger brother to actively oppose the elder's goals.

quiz.q: A question asks what the recurring image of the dried-up well "suggests". The best-grounded answer will…
options: invent a backstory for the well
connect the image to cues about decline and memory elsewhere in the passage
state that wells always symbolise death
complain that the image is decorative
quiz.explanation: Legitimate inference runs from textual cues (what the well touches — scenes of memory, drought, abandonment) to the least strong reading. Universal symbol dictionaries and invented backstories both outrun the evidence.

intro:
Modern legal systems are accumulated answers to one recurring question: how do you make power lawful? Each milestone in this lesson is a step in that argument — a code inscribed so subjects could see the rules; a compilation that outlived its empire; a charter forced on a king at sword-point; a method of reasoning that let judges’ decisions bind their successors; a civil code rewritten in one clean sweep; and, in India, a century of charters, courts and commissions that ended in a constitution of unprecedented length. Reading them in sequence turns a list of dates into a story with a logic — and legal-history questions are almost always that story with one step removed.

**Why this matters.** The examinable skill is three-way matching: a date, an institution or document, and the lasting principle it fixed. 1215 → Magna Carta → the ruler bound by law; 1860 → Indian Penal Code → one criminal law for all; 1804 → Code Napoléon → the civil-law template exported worldwide. When you can run the match in both directions — from date to meaning and from principle to document — the “milestones” format stops being trivia and becomes a map of where today’s doctrines come from, which is exactly what reasoning-based questions reward.
objectives: Explain early written codes: law published for all
Explain roman law and the Corpus Juris Civilis
Explain magna Carta: law above the king
Explain english common law, precedent and equity
Explain codification: the Napoleonic Code and Macaulay’s commissions
Explain indian legal history: charters, courts and the IPC
Explain from the Government of India Acts to the Constitution
Explain seminal legal texts and their authors

concepts.statement: A systematic, authoritative statement of law on a subject, enacted by a legislature — as distinct from case law accumulated by courts. Hammurabi’s stele, Justinian’s compilation and the Indian Penal Code are all codes in this lineage, though built very differently.

The common-law doctrine that earlier decisions of higher courts bind later ones in similar cases: law made vertically through the court hierarchy, case by case, which lets doctrine evolve without fresh legislation.

The parallel body of principles developed by the English Court of Chancery to soften common law’s rigidity — trusts, injunctions, specific performance, maxims such as “he who comes to equity must come with clean hands”. Administered alongside common law since the Judicature Acts of 1873–75.

Justinian’s compilation of Roman law (529–534 CE) in four parts — Institutes (a textbook), Digest (jurists’ opinions), Code (imperial enactments) and Novels (later laws). Rediscovered in medieval Europe, it became the ancestor of the continental civil-law families.

The deliberate restatement of a field of law into one enacted code — the movement Jeremy Bentham championed, Napoleon executed in 1804, and Macaulay’s Law Commissions brought to India in the 1860s–1880s.
A formal grant of rights or powers by the sovereign — the East India Company’s trading charters carried law-making powers, and the great charter of 1215 gave Magna Carta its name.

concepts.term: Early written codes: law published for all
concepts.statement: The first milestone is the idea that law should be visible. Hammurabi’s code, promulgated in Babylon around 1754 BCE and carved on a public stele, listed offences and fixed penalties — including the proportional retaliation of lex talionis — so that any subject could read the rules that bound him. That publicity principle, law published and applying generally rather than decree whispered case by case, is the seed of everything later. Rome systematised it: the Twelve Tables (c. 451–450 BCE) published the early law; centuries of juristic writing refined it; and Justinian’s Corpus Juris Civilis (529–534 CE) gathered statutes and jurists’ opinions into a single authoritative compilation. When Western Europe rediscovered the Digest in the eleventh–twelfth centuries, university lawyers rebuilt continental law on it — the civil-law tradition that still governs most of the world’s jurisdictions.

concepts.term: Roman law and the Corpus Juris Civilis
concepts.statement: England took the other fork — law made by courts — and its constitutional milestone came at Runnymede. On 15 June 1215, King John sealed the charter that became Magna Carta: a peace treaty between a king beaten by failed wars in France and rebellious barons, drafted through Archbishop Stephen Langton’s mediation on the model of Henry I’s older Charter of Liberties. Its clauses promised protection of church rights, freedom from illegal imprisonment, access to swift and impartial justice, and limits on feudal payments — enforced, under the famous security clause (clause 61), by a council of twenty-five barons empowered to seize the king’s castles if he defaulted. Pope Innocent III annulled it within months, the First Barons’ War followed, and the charter survived by being reissued — 1216, 1217 (when it gained the name Magna Carta to distinguish it from the new Charter of the Forest), 1225 and 1297, whose version still has three clauses in force in England and Wales. Its afterlife matters as much as its text: Sir Edward Coke invoked it in the early seventeenth century against the divine right of kings, Parliament carried the argument to the Glorious Revolution, and the colonists carried it into the American constitutions. The honest footnote every examiner loves: the 1215 charter protected free men — above all the barons — not all subjects; the Victorian image of a universal rights declaration was a later construction.

concepts.term: Magna Carta: law above the king
concepts.statement: The common law grew beside the charter. From Henry II’s reign, itinerant royal justices carried uniform procedures across the shires; their decisions, reasoning from one case to the next, hardened into precedent — the stare decisis engine that makes judge-made law consistent yet adaptable. Where the writ system was too rigid, petitioners turned to the king’s chancellor, whose conscience-based rulings accumulated as equity with its own remedies (trusts, injunctions) and maxims; the Judicature Acts of 1873–75 merged the administrations while leaving both bodies of rules alive. The continental answer to legal certainty ran the opposite way: codification. Bentham preached it (reforming “the law’s labyrinth” into a rational code), Napoleon delivered the Code civil of 1804 — clear, secular, property-and-contract centred, and exported by conquest and commerce across Europe, Latin America and beyond — and the codification wave is the hinge on which the civil-law and common-law families still differ.

concepts.term: English common law, precedent and equity
concepts.statement: India’s legal history is the story of that logic arriving by charters and staying as codes. Ancient foundations — the Dharmaśāstras and the statecraft of Kautilya’s Arthashastra (dated around 400 BCE), with the Manusmriti later treated as authoritative guidance — governed through custom and royal courts. The East India Company’s seventeenth-century charters carried power to make laws; Mayor’s Courts appeared in the presidency towns from 1727; and the Regulating Act of 1773 created, at Calcutta in 1774, the first Supreme Court applying English law to Europeans while personal laws (Hindu and Muslim) governed natives in the mofussil — a dual system whose frictions drove reform. Thomas Babington Macaulay arrived as the first Law Member in 1834 and chaired the First Law Commission; the codification wave he set in motion produced the Indian Penal Code (drafted 1837, enacted 1860, in force from 1862) and, through successor commissions, the great procedural and contract codes. The High Courts Act of 1861 merged the Supreme Courts and Sadar Adalats into High Courts at Calcutta, Madras and Bombay from 1862. The Government of India Acts of 1919 and 1935 devolved and federated — the 1935 Act’s administrative skeleton, with its federal scheme and provincial autonomy, carried straight into the Constitution — and the Constituent Assembly (1946–49) finished the arc: the Constitution in force from 26 January 1950, the world’s longest written constitution, administratively rooted in the 1935 Act but anchored in a Preamble the charters never contained.

Reciting the Magna Carta myth: the 1215 charter was a baronial settlement, not a universal bill of rights — historians traced the “ancient liberties” reading to seventeenth-century lawyers such as Coke and later myth-makers. Compressing the IPC timeline: drafted 1837, enacted 1860, in force 1862 — three dates, three events. Treating common law and equity as enemies: they merged administratively in 1873–75 and coexist as rules. Assuming the Constitution of 1950 was written from a blank page: its administrative spine is the 1935 Act; the new element was popular sovereignty. And confusing codification (legislature enacts one systematic code) with precedent (courts bind through decisions) — the defining difference between the civil-law and common-law families, and the axis on which most comparative questions turn.

examples.title: Worked Example — Decode a Legal-History Question in Four Moves
examples.problem: Legal History Milestones: Codes, Charters and the Making of Modern Law — worked through step by step

steps.label: Extract the anchors
steps.text: any date, name, document or court in the stem (“the council of twenty-five barons”, “the first Law Member”, “1861”).

steps.label: Match the date to the event
steps.text: 1215 Runnymede; 1773 Regulating Act; 1774 Supreme Court at Calcutta; 1834 First Law Commission; 1860 IPC enacted; 1861 High Courts Act; 1935 GOI Act; 1950 Constitution.

steps.label: State the principle the event fixed
steps.text: law above the king; a Crown court for the presidency; one criminal code for all; unified High Courts; a federal administrative skeleton for the Constitution.

steps.label: Answer the frame the question asks
steps.text: if it asks “why”, connect the event to its trigger (clause 61 answers “how was the charter enforced?”); if it asks “which”, pick the document whose principle matches — never a merely co-temporal one.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: none; this lesson feeds the doctrinal ones. Follow with the contract-basics and legal-reasoning lessons to see the modern doctrines this history produced, and the Indian Constitution lesson for the institutional end-state. Seminal texts to know by author: Kautilya’s Arthashastra; Blackstone’s Commentaries on the Laws of England (1765–69); Coke’s Institutes; Dicey’s Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885); the Constitution of India — chaired in drafting by B. R. Ambedkar. Primary reading: Wikipedia, “Magna Carta” and “Law of India” (CC BY-SA) for the charter and Indian-arc facts used here, plus NCERT, Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), chapter 1, for the assembly’s work.
Published law begins with Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE); Rome systematises it and Justinian’s Corpus Juris Civilis (529–534 CE) becomes the civil-law ancestor.
Magna Carta, 15 June 1215: barons bind King John; clause 61’s council of twenty-five; reissued 1216–1297; Coke’s invocation makes it the anti-absolutist icon.
England builds law through courts — precedent plus Chancery equity, merged by the Judicature Acts 1873–75; the continent codifies — Code Napoléon 1804.
India: Company charters → Mayor’s Courts 1727 → Regulating Act 1773 and Supreme Court 1774 → Macaulay’s commissions → IPC 1860 → High Courts 1861–62.
GOI Acts 1919 and 1935 federate and devolve; the Constituent Assembly completes the arc with the Constitution, in force 26 January 1950.
The two legal families still divide by method: enacted codes (civil law) versus judge-made precedent (common law), with equity layered on the latter.

quiz.q: Magna Carta was sealed at Runnymede on 15 June 1215 chiefly because…
options: rebel barons forced King John to confirm liberties after his failed wars and heavy taxation
the Pope ordered a new legal code
the barons sought abolition of the monarchy
quiz.explanation: The charter was a peace treaty between John and his rebel barons — church rights, illegal imprisonment, swift justice and limits on feudal payments, enforced by the clause-61 council of twenty-five.

quiz.q: Justinian’s Corpus Juris Civilis is remembered because it…
options: compiled imperial statutes and jurists’ writings into the ancestor of European civil law
codified the law of the East India Company
quiz.explanation: The 529–534 CE compilation (Institutes, Digest, Code, Novels) was rediscovered in medieval Europe and rebuilt continental private law on Roman foundations.

quiz.q: The Indian Penal Code was enacted in 1860 — a product of…
options: the codification programme begun under Macaulay’s First Law Commission of 1834
quiz.explanation: Macaulay, the first Law Member, chaired the First Law Commission; the IPC was drafted in 1837 and enacted in 1860, in force from 1862.

quiz.q: The administrative architecture of the Constitution of 1950 (federation, provinces, services) owes most to…
quiz.explanation: The 1935 Act’s federal scheme and provincial machinery carried into the Constitution; what changed was the source of authority — the people, through the Preamble and Fundamental Rights.

intro:
A warehouse burns the night after the buyer has paid but before the truck is loaded; a man who bought a car in perfect good faith must hand it back because it was stolen. Neither dispute turns on offer or acceptance — the machinery of general contract law — but on a second layer of rules for one thing: the transfer of ownership in movable goods. India carved that layer out of the Indian Contract Act 1872 into the Sale of Goods Act 1930, covering when ownership passes, what the seller silently promises, who bears loss, and what an unpaid seller can still do.

**Why this matters.** Almost every commercial dispute about physical goods runs through this Act: the rejected consignment, the buyer who went insolvent while the goods were on the train, the purchaser who discovers the seller never owned what he sold. It decides whether the buyer may reject outright or only claim damages, whether the seller can stop a shipment in transit, and who bears the loss when goods perish.
objectives: Explain sale versus agreement to sell: when property passes
Explain existing, future and contingent goods
Explain conditions versus warranties and their consequences
Explain implied conditions: title, description, sample, quality, fitness
Explain caveat emptor and its statutory exceptions
Explain transfer of property, risk and the nemo dat rule
Explain the unpaid seller: lien, stoppage in transit, resale

concepts.term: Sale versus agreement to sell: when property passes
concepts.statement: Section 4 defines a contract of sale: the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price. Goods — section 2(7) — means every kind of movable property other than actionable claims and money, including stock and shares, growing crops and things attached to land agreed to be severed. The price is the money consideration; a part-exchange plus cash is still a sale if money forms part of it. Section 9 lets it be fixed by the contract, in an agreed manner or by the course of dealing; section 10 adds that where a third party is to value it and cannot or will not, the agreement is avoided.

Timing of ownership separates the two halves of section 4. Where property passes immediately, the transaction is a sale; where it is to pass later or subject to a condition, it is an agreement to sell, ripening into a sale when the time arrives or the condition is fulfilled — the distinction decides who can sue for the goods and who only for damages. Section 6 sorts the goods by existence: existing goods are either specific — identified and agreed at contracting — or unascertained, defined only by description; future goods are to be manufactured or acquired by the seller afterwards, so a deal for them is only an agreement to sell; contingent goods are future goods whose acquisition depends on an uncertain event. And existence matters: under sections 7 and 8, goods perished before the contract make it void, and goods perishing after an agreement to sell but before it ripens avoid the agreement — nobody pays for what no longer exists.

concepts.term: Conditions versus warranties and their consequences
concepts.statement: Stipulations about the goods come in two grades. Section 12 defines a condition as a stipulation essential to the main purpose, so fundamental that its breach entitles the injured party to repudiate: refuse the goods, treat himself as discharged and claim damages. A warranty is collateral; its breach gives damages only, and the contract survives. Which is which is a question of construction, not labels. Section 13 supplies the safety valves: a buyer may waive a condition, or treat a breached one as a warranty where the breach is so slight that rejection would be unreasonable; and where the contract is not severable and the buyer has accepted the goods, a breach of condition is pursued only as a breach of warranty. Section 11 adds that time of payment is not, merely by agreement, of the essence.

concepts.term: Implied conditions: title, description, sample, quality, fitness
concepts.statement: Most sale disputes are about the promises the Act reads in. Section 14 implies a condition that the seller has a right to sell — in an agreement to sell, that he will have one when the time comes; a buyer who receives no title has been cheated of the whole bargain, which is why the owner of a stolen car recovers it even from an innocent purchaser. Section 15 governs sale by description: in Andrews Bros v. Singer (1934) a “new” machine that had been used failed the description, and in Moore & Co. v. Landauer (1921) fruit packed twenty-four tins to a case against a contract saying thirty was rejected outright though sound. Section 17 governs sale by sample: the bulk must correspond with the sample, the buyer must get a fair chance to compare, and the goods must be free from latent defects making them unmerchantable — Drummond & Sons v. Van Ingen (1887) remains the classic. A sale by sample and description must satisfy both tests at once.

concepts.term: Caveat emptor and its statutory exceptions
concepts.statement: Sections 14 to 17 are the statutory exceptions to caveat emptor — let the buyer beware — which otherwise leaves the buyer to examine and judge for himself. Fitness for purpose, section 16(1): where the buyer makes known, expressly or by implication, the particular purpose required, showing reliance on the seller’s skill and judgment, and the goods are of a description the seller supplies in his business, reasonable fitness is implied — the burst hot-water bottle in Priest v. Last (1903) is the textbook case. Merchantable quality, section 16(2): goods bought by description from a dealer in such goods must be reasonably fit for their ordinary purposes, as the dermatitis-causing wool in Grant v. Australian Knitting Mills (1936) was not. Two provisos bite back: an examination excludes conditions as to defects it ought to have revealed, and no fitness condition arises where the buyer specifies a patent or trade name without relying on the seller. Section 62 lets the parties exclude or vary the implied terms by express agreement, course of dealing or usage — subject to overriding law such as the Consumer Protection Act 2019.

concepts.term: Transfer of property, risk and the nemo dat rule
concepts.statement: Every dispute converges on one question: had property — legal ownership — passed? Section 18: property cannot pass in unascertained goods until ascertained. Section 19 makes intention the master; the rules that follow apply unless a different intention appears. For specific goods in a deliverable state, section 20 passes property the moment the contract is made — the identified bales in the godown are the buyer’s before delivery or payment. Section 21 postpones passage where the seller must first do something to the goods, and section 24 where something remains to fix the price, such as weighing; in both, property passes when the act is done and the buyer notified. Section 22 covers sales on approval — “on sale or return” — passing property on approval signified, on an act adopting the transaction, or on retention beyond a reasonable time; section 23 reserves disposal to the seller until his conditions are met. Then section 26: unless otherwise agreed, the goods are at the seller’s risk until property passes and the buyer’s thereafter — res perit domino, the loss follows the owner — regardless of who holds them or whether the price has been paid.

concepts.term: The unpaid seller: lien, stoppage in transit, resale
concepts.statement: The common law’s nemo dat quod non habet — no one gives what he does not have — is codified in section 27: a buyer acquires no better title than the seller had, unless the owner’s own conduct precludes him from denying the seller’s authority to sell. The Act carves out the pockets commerce demands. Section 28 protects a buyer under a voidable title: where the seller’s title is avoidable for coercion, fraud or the like but unrescinded at the time of sale, a good-faith buyer without notice takes clean title — the principle that saved the innocent purchasers in Phillips v. Brooks (1919) and Lewis v. Averay (1972). Section 29 protects the second buyer from a seller who has sold the goods but remains in possession and resells in the ordinary course; section 30 mirrors it for a buyer in possession with the seller’s consent before property passed. A joint owner’s sale with the others’ consent, and the unpaid seller’s resale under section 54, complete the exceptions.
concepts.detail:
Section 45 defines the unpaid seller: one to whom the whole price is unpaid or untendered, or whose negotiable conditional payment was dishonoured. Section 47 splits the remedies into rights against the goods and rights of action. First, the lien of section 48: while in possession, the unpaid seller may retain the goods until payment where they were sold without credit, where credit has expired, or where the buyer is insolvent; the lien is lost on delivery to a carrier without reserving disposal, when the buyer or his agent lawfully regains possession, or on waiver. Second, stoppage in transit, sections 50 to 53: where the buyer is insolvent and the goods are still with a carrier, the seller may stop them by taking possession or giving notice, before delivery. Third, resale, section 54: perishable goods at once, others after notice, the seller recovering any shortfall and accounting for surplus. Alongside run suits for the price (section 55), damages (section 56), repudiation (section 60) and interest (section 61); the buyer holds damages for non-delivery, specific performance for specific or ascertained goods (section 58) and set-off for breach of warranty (section 59).

Section 64 compresses auction law into a handful of rules. Where goods are put up in lots, each lot is prima facie a separate contract. The sale is complete on the fall of the hammer or another customary announcement, and until then any bidder may retract. Where the sale is notified as subject to a reserve price, the lot may be withdrawn if bidding never reaches it. And where no right to bid on the seller’s behalf is expressly reserved, secret bidding by or for the seller is unlawful, and the buyer may treat the sale as fraudulent.

concepts.statement: A contract in which property in the goods passes to the buyer immediately, for a price.
A contract to pass property later or on a condition; it becomes a sale when that happens.
A stipulation essential to the main purpose; breach permits repudiation plus damages.
A stipulation collateral to the main purpose; breach gives damages only.
Let the buyer beware — the baseline rule, subject to the statutory implied conditions.
No one can transfer a better title than he has; section 27 and its exceptions.
The loss follows the owner — risk passes with property, not possession or payment.
A seller unpaid or untendered, or whose negotiable conditional payment was dishonoured.
The unpaid seller’s right to retake goods from a carrier on the buyer’s insolvency, before delivery.

examples.title: Worked Case: The Twice-Sold Car
examples.problem: The Sale of Goods Act: Conditions, Warranties and the Unpaid Seller — worked through step by step

steps.label: Facts
steps.text: a fraudster pays for a car with a cheque destined to bounce and drives off; within days he resells it at market price to an honest buyer, whom the owner sues for return.

steps.label: Characterise the first sale
steps.text: consent obtained by fraud made the owner’s title voidable, not void.

steps.label: Apply section 28
steps.text: at resale the title was unrescinded, and the second buyer acted in good faith without notice.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.text: the innocent buyer keeps the car — the mirror of Lewis v. Averay (1972); had the car been stolen, nemo dat returns it to the owner.

examples.title: Worked Case: Stopping the Consignment
examples.problem: The Sale of Goods Act: Conditions, Warranties and the Unpaid Seller — worked through step by step

steps.label: Facts
steps.text: a cloth merchant ships 200 bales on seven days’ credit; while they are still with the railways, the buyer is declared insolvent.

steps.label: Check possession
steps.text: parted with, so the section 48 lien is gone — but the goods are still with a carrier, undelivered.

steps.label: Apply sections 50 to 53
steps.text: buyer’s insolvency plus goods in transit and no delivery — stoppage in transit arises.

steps.label: Effect and finish
steps.text: the merchant notifies the railway, which holds the bales for the seller, then resells after notice under section 54, recovering any shortfall and accounting for surplus.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: The Indian Contract Act: Formation, Breach and Remedies, for the general law this Act builds on, and When Consent Fails: Void and Voidable Agreements, which explains the voidable titles section 28 protects. Follow-ons: the partnership and companies lessons in this chapter, and the accounting chapters’ financial-statements lessons on how sales and returns surface in the books.
A sale passes property at once; an agreement to sell passes it later — the divide governs remedies and risk.
Goods are existing (specific or unascertained), future or contingent; perished goods void or avoid the bargain.
A condition permits repudiation on breach; a warranty gives damages only; section 13 lets the buyer downgrade.
Implied conditions — title, description, sample, merchantable quality, fitness — are caveat emptor’s exceptions.
Property passes by intention; risk follows property, not delivery or payment — res perit domino.
Nemo dat yields to voidable titles, possession-based resales and the unpaid seller’s resale.
The unpaid seller’s armoury: lien, stoppage in transit, resale — beside suits for price, damages and interest.

quiz.q: A buyer orders 100 boxes of a stated tea grade, packed 25 bags to the box; the boxes arrive holding only 20. The buyer may:
options: only claim damages, the quality being right
reject the goods and claim damages — breach of a condition
reject only if the seller was fraudulent
not complain, having bought by sample
quiz.explanation: Bought by description, and the packing count is part of it: section 15 makes it a condition — Moore & Co. v. Landauer.

quiz.q: Goods in the seller’s godown are destroyed the night after full payment but before delivery. The buyer bears the loss if:
options: the contract was an agreement to sell
property had already passed to him
the seller still had physical possession
quiz.explanation: Section 26: risk follows property, not possession or payment; once ownership passes, res perit domino — the unpaid price is only a debt.

quiz.q: The unpaid seller’s lien over goods in his possession is LOST when:
options: the credit period expires without payment
he delivers to a carrier without reserving disposal
quiz.explanation: Unreserved carrier delivery ends the possession the lien depends on; insolvency and expired credit are grounds for exercising it, not losing it.

quiz.q: Which purchase carries NO implied condition of fitness for purpose?
options: A customer asks a chemist for something for a cold and takes what is offered
A buyer asks a dealer for a drill suitable for marble, relying on the dealer’s advice
A buyer insists on one patented model, refusing the seller’s alternatives
A farmer buys seed after telling the merchant the crop he intends
quiz.explanation: The proviso to section 16(1) excludes fitness where a patent or trade name is specified without reliance on the seller’s skill.

intro:
Two friends open a hardware shop, share the takings, and sign every cheque either of them writes — until the shop sinks in debt and a supplier asks which of them must pay, and how much. The Partnership Act 1932 answers with one idea: a partnership is a relationship, not a thing, and its defining feature is that each partner acts for all. That single idea — mutual agency — explains why one partner can bind the firm, why every partner is liable for the others’ dealings in the business, and why the death, insolvency or exit of a partner reshapes or ends the relationship. This lesson works through the definition, the relations of partners, registration and dissolution.

**Why this matters.** The Act is the default constitution of every firm that has not drafted one — clinics, law offices, family trading houses, countless informal ventures. It decides who can sign for the firm, whether a lender taking a cut of profits has become a partner, what a minor inherits from an old firm, and what happens when one partner walks out. Because the Act is largely default law, partners can contract around it — but only if they know what the defaults say.
objectives: Explain definition: agreement, business, profits, mutual agency
Explain partnership versus co-ownership, HUF and company
Explain partner as agent: implied authority and holding out
Explain the minor admitted to benefits
Explain registration and section 69 consequences
Explain dissolution modes: agreement, contingency, notice, court
Explain winding up and the order of payment

concepts.term: Definition: agreement, business, profits, mutual agency
concepts.statement: Section 4 defines partnership as “the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.” There must be an agreement — a contract, oral or written, so the general law of agreement supplies the foundation: no free consent, no partnership. There must be a business — an active trade, profession or vocation, not passive co-ownership of a house. There must be sharing of profits — but profit-sharing alone is only evidence, not the test, because profits can be shared as interest on a loan, as rent, or as a caretaker’s wage. The true test is the final element: the business is carried on by all or any of them acting for all — mutual agency. Cox v. Hickman (1860) settled it: trustees for creditors who applied a firm’s profits to repay its debts were not partners, because they were not agents of the trading persons. Sharing profits points to partnership; agency proves it.

concepts.term: Partnership versus co-ownership, HUF and company
concepts.statement: The same logic separates partnership from its neighbours. A co-ownership is ownership of property in common: co-owners may share rent from a building without any of them being able to bind the others, ownership usually arrives by chance (inheritance, joint purchase) rather than agreement, and a co-owner may freely transfer or mortgage his undivided share — a partner may not. A Hindu undivided family is the opposite in its source: membership arrives by birth; the Karta manages with powers no managing partner has by default; and no coparcener is an agent of another. A company, as the companies lesson in this chapter explains, is a separate legal person: its shareholders are not its agents, their liability is capped at their shares, and it survives its members. Partners, by contrast, are personally and jointly liable, and the firm dissolves when the mutual agency dissolves. Size also matters: an association exceeding fifty persons must register as a company, which is why large firms convert.

concepts.term: Partner as agent: implied authority and holding out
concepts.statement: What the firm owns, the Act calls the property of the firm — section 14 sweeps in property originally brought into the common stock, acquired by or for the firm, and property acquired with money belonging to the firm, all held by the partners for the firm. The distinction between firm property and a partner’s private property matters most on insolvency, because section 48 sets the order of application — firm property pays firm debts first, and only the residue reaches partners as individuals; the reverse for private property. Firm property is also the working capital of mutual agency: implied authority to sell extends to the firm’s goods, not to a partner’s personal car.

Externally, section 18 states the keystone: every partner is an agent of the firm and of the other partners for the purposes of the business. Section 19 defines the implied authority that rides on this agency: an act binds the firm if it is done in the firm’s name, is of a kind commonly done in that business, and is done in the usual way — buying stock, selling goods, borrowing money, engaging staff, receiving payments, settling accounts. Section 19(2) lists what implied authority never covers: submitting a dispute to arbitration, opening a bank account other than in the firm’s name, admitting a new partner, acquiring or transferring immovable property, entering into a partnership on behalf of the firm, or renouncing a claim — each needs the other partners’ consent. Internally, the Act polices fiduciary loyalty. Section 16 makes every partner accountable: he must render true accounts, and must account for and indemnify the firm for any personal profit made from the partnership business or any use of the firm’s property, name or business connection. Section 20 extends the duty to competition: a partner who, without consent, carries on a competing business must account to the firm for its profits.

Liability follows agency. Section 25 makes every partner liable jointly with the others, and severally for acts for which he is responsible, for all debts and obligations of the firm incurred while he is a partner. Section 26 fixes the firm with liability for a partner’s wrongs — fraud, conversion, negligence — committed in the ordinary course of the firm’s business or with the authority of co-partners; in Hamlyn v. Houston & Co. (1903) a partner who took a commission for placing orders bound his firm to compensate the supplier. Section 27 similarly makes the firm answer where a partner misapplies money or property received by the firm.
