And section 28 states holding out: anyone who by words, writing or conduct represents himself as a partner — or knowingly suffers himself to be so represented — is liable as a partner to anyone who gave credit on the faith of the representation. A retired partner who lets the old firm letterhead keep circulating can be held out; a landlord whose tenant’s sign says “and Sons” cannot.

concepts.term: Dissolution modes: agreement, contingency, notice, court
concepts.statement: A person who cannot contract cannot be a partner — but the Act makes one deliberate exception. Section 30 lets a minor be admitted to the benefits of a partnership with the consent of all the partners for the time being. The minor is entitled to the agreed share of profits and of property, may inspect the accounts, but is not personally liable for the firm’s acts: his share alone is answerable. The Act then builds an exit ramp around majority: within six months of attaining majority — or of first learning of his admission, whichever is later — the minor must give public notice whether he elects to become a partner; if he does, his liability dates from when he actually became a partner; if he does not, his share is not liable for any act of the firm after the notice.

concepts.term: Winding up and the order of payment
concepts.statement: Registration is optional and can happen at any time — not only at formation — by delivering to the Registrar of Firms a statement in the prescribed form, signed by the partners, with the fee. The price of staying unregistered is section 69: an unregistered firm cannot sue to enforce rights arising from a contract in any court, and a partner cannot sue the firm or his co-partners to enforce rights under the agreement — but third parties are entirely unaffected and can sue the unregistered firm. In practice, non-registration is a litigation trap: the firm that waits until it needs to sue discovers it cannot.
concepts.detail: Dissolution comes in two flavours, and section 39 separates them: dissolution of partnership is any change in the relations of the partners; dissolution of the firm is the termination of partnership among all the partners. The modes travel from consensual to judicial. By agreement, section 40 — all partners may dissolve whenever they consent. Compulsorily, section 41 — if all the partners or all but one are adjudicated insolvent, or the business becomes unlawful. By contingency, section 42 — where constituted for a fixed term, on its expiry; for a single adventure, on its completion; at will, on a partner’s death or insolvency. By notice, section 43 — a partnership at will may be dissolved by any partner giving notice, effective from the date it names or, if none, the date of communication. By court, section 44 — on a partner’s insanity or permanent incapacity, misconduct affecting the business, wilful or persistent breach of the agreement, transfer of his whole interest, business that can only continue at a loss, or any other just and equitable ground. After dissolution, section 47 continues each partner’s authority so far as necessary to wind up, and section 48 orders the proceeds: firm property pays firm debts first, then rateably what is due to the partners, the residue dividing in profit-sharing proportions; each partner’s separate property pays his separate debts first, and only its surplus goes to firm debts.

concepts.statement: The relation between persons agreeing to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.
Each partner is both principal and agent of the others in the business — the true test of partnership.
Common ownership of property without a common business; owners are not agents for one another.
An act done in the firm’s name, of a kind usual for that business, binds the firm without express mandate.
Liability as a partner fastened on one who represented himself as such and let credit be given on that faith.
Section 30 arrangement: the minor shares profits without personal liability, and elects within six months of majority.
Termination of the partnership among all the partners, as against a mere change in relations.
An unregistered firm’s inability to sue on contracts, while third parties remain free to sue it.

examples.title: Worked Case: The Garage That Was a Partnership
examples.problem: The Partnership Act: Nature, Relations and Dissolution — worked through step by step

steps.label: Facts
steps.text: two men owned a garage in shares; one let the upper floor as a flat, the other repaired cars, and the proceeds of parts and repairs were pooled and split. Sued for the parts bill, the repairer argued no partnership existed.

steps.label: Apply the definition
steps.text: a business — car repairs — carried on in common with a view of profit, the takings pooled and shared whatever each believed.

steps.label: Apply the test
steps.text: mutual agency on the facts — each had acted in the repair business as the business of both.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.text: a partnership existed, so both were liable for the parts bought in the ordinary course — the result in Mercantile Credit Co. v. Garrod (1962), where intention not to be partners was irrelevant.

examples.title: Worked Case: The Profit-Sharing Lender
examples.problem: The Partnership Act: Nature, Relations and Dissolution — worked through step by step

steps.label: Facts
steps.text: a struggling firm promises a moneylender a quarter of its profits until his debt is paid; a firm creditor now sues the lender as a “partner.”

steps.label: Identify the trap
steps.text: he shares profits — evidence of partnership, and nothing more.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Apply Cox v. Hickman (1860) and Walker v. Hirsch (1884): profits can be received as interest, so profit-sharing alone creates no relation.

steps.label: Ask the real question
steps.text: was the lender ever an agent of the firm, able to bind it? On the facts, no.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.text: he is a creditor — neither sharing losses nor answerable for debts, and with no right to manage.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: The Indian Contract Act: Formation, Breach and Remedies and When Consent Fails: Void and Voidable Agreements, since a partnership is born from an agreement and dies from a defective one. Follow-ons: the limited liability partnership lesson next in this chapter relaxes the personal-liability price of mutual agency, and the companies lesson completes the spectrum of firm organisation. The accounting chapters’ partnership-accounts lessons take over the numbers — appropriation of profits, guarantee of profit, goodwill and reconstitution on admission, retirement or death — which this lesson deliberately leaves untouched.
Partnership is an agreement to share profits of a business carried on by all or any acting for all — mutual agency is the test, not profit-sharing.
Co-owners, Hindu undivided families and companies are the neighbours: no agency, membership by birth, and separate personality respectively.
Firm property is held for the firm; on insolvency it answers firm debts first, and section 48 orders the winding-up queue.
Every partner is an agent: usual-trade acts bind the firm; arbitration, foreign accounts, new partners and immovable property need consent.
The firm answers for wrongs in the ordinary course of business, and holding out fixes liability on those who let themselves be represented as partners.
A minor may share benefits without personal liability, and must elect by public notice within six months of majority.
Dissolution runs from consent through contingency, notice and court; authority survives only to wind up, and firm property pays firm debts first.

quiz.q: A moneylender receives 20 percent of a firm’s profits as interest on a loan. Regarding the firm’s trade debts, he is:
options: liable as a partner, since he shares profits
a creditor, since profit-sharing without mutual agency does not make a partner
liable only up to his share of the profits received
quiz.explanation: Profits can be payment for capital, labour or debt; only mutual agency creates the relation — Cox v. Hickman, Walker v. Hirsch.

quiz.q: Which act falls OUTSIDE a partner’s implied authority under section 19?
options: buying stock in the firm’s name for its trade
selling the firm’s goods at market
buying an office building for the firm
receiving payment of a debt due to the firm
quiz.explanation: Immovable property, like admitting a partner or opening a foreign bank account, is outside the usual-trade rule and needs the others’ consent.

quiz.q: A minor admitted to the benefits of a partnership attains majority. He:
options: automatically becomes a partner with full liability for past acts
must give public notice within six months whether he elects to become a partner
must repay all profits he received
quiz.explanation: Section 30 gives a six-month election window from majority or from learning of the admission, whichever is later; refusal ends liability for later acts.

quiz.q: A partnership at will with four partners: one partner gives written notice of dissolution. The firm is dissolved:
options: from the date stated in the notice, or the date it is communicated
at the end of the accounting year
quiz.explanation: Section 43: a partnership at will is dissolved by any partner’s notice, from the date it names or its communication.

quiz.q: Which statement about an UNREGISTERED firm is correct?
options: It cannot be sued by third parties
It cannot enforce its contracts in court, but third parties can still sue it
Its partners cannot be made personally liable
It must be wound up immediately
quiz.explanation: Section 69 handicaps the firm as plaintiff, not as defendant — the asymmetry that makes registration the norm in practice.

intro:
A four-partner audit practice loses a negligence claim worth forty times its assets. As a partnership, the shortfall follows every partner home — houses, savings, everything. The same practice organised as a limited liability partnership loses only the firm’s assets and, absent personal wrongdoing, each partner sleeps soundly. The Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008 created this middle form for exactly such firms: professionals and small enterprises who want the internal informality of a partnership — no board, no prospectus, management by mutual agreement — combined with the external personality and liability shield of a company. India followed the United Kingdom’s Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000, itself a response to fears that catastrophic professional-liability claims would otherwise drive firms out of the company-style structures altogether. This lesson covers what the form is, how it is made, how it is run and how it ends.

**Why this matters.** The LLP is now the default choice for consulting outfits, chartered-accountancy and legal practices converting from firms, small startups that want structure without shareholder formality, and family enterprises seeking succession planning with limited liability. Choosing between firm, LLP and company is one of the first structural decisions any enterprise makes — and this lesson supplies the comparison table that decision runs on.
objectives: Explain a hybrid form: partnership flexibility, company shield
Explain body corporate with perpetual succession
Explain incorporation: name, partners and the incorporation document
Explain designated partners and the LLP agreement
Explain the liability shield and its fraud exception
Explain statement of account and solvency
Explain conversion from firm or company

concepts.term: A hybrid form: partnership flexibility, company shield
concepts.statement: Section 3 declares the essentials: an LLP is a body corporate, formed and registered under the Act, with a legal entity separate from that of its partners, and — the phrase that carries the whole design — perpetual succession. A partner’s death, insolvency or retirement changes the LLP’s membership but not its existence; the entity continues as the same person in law until it is wound up and dissolved. Like any body corporate it can own property in its own name, sue and be sued in its own name, enter contracts, and have a common seal if it wants one; unlike a partnership, whose property is held by partners as firm property, the LLP’s assets belong to the LLP itself. The first Indian LLPs were incorporated in 2009, when the Act came into force. For tax, an LLP is treated like a firm — a flat rate on total income, with partners’ profit shares exempt in their hands — which, together with the absence of dividend distribution tax on drawings, long made the form fiscally attractive relative to small companies; the taxation lesson in this chapter picks that thread up.

Set the three forms side by side and the hybrid stands out. A partnership is not a separate person: partners are agents of the firm, personally and jointly liable to the last rupee, governed by the Partnership Act 1932, and dissolved by death or exit unless the partners regroup. A company is a separate person with limited liability, but pays for the shield with formality — memorandum and articles, a board of directors, general meetings, statutory registers, dividend rules, and the Companies Act 2013’s full apparatus. The LLP takes the shield without most of the apparatus.

concepts.term: Incorporation: name, partners and the incorporation document
concepts.statement: Incorporation needs at least two partners — individuals or bodies corporate — and a name. The name must not be identical or too similar to an existing company or LLP, must not be offensive, and must end with “LLP”, with names of for-profit entities also carrying a suffix denoting limited liability; availability is checked and reserved with the Registrar before filing. The substantive filing is the incorporation document under section 7: the proposed name, the nature of the business, the address of the registered office, the particulars of partners, and their consent to act. Two features distinguish it from a plain partnership deed. First, the requirement of designated partners: at least two, each an individual, one of whom must be resident in India; they hold a Director Identification Number-like allotment and carry personal responsibility for the LLP’s statutory compliance, including filings. Second, certification: where the rules require, an advocate, company secretary, chartered accountant or cost accountant in whole-time practice must verify that all incorporation requirements have been met. On satisfaction, the Registrar registers the document and issues the certificate of incorporation under section 11 — conclusive evidence that the Act’s requirements were met. The LLP agreement under section 23 governs the mutual rights and duties of partners, and of the LLP and its partners; where the parties never execute one, the First Schedule to the Act supplies default rules on capital, profits, duties, expulsion and retirement, so the entity can function from day one.

concepts.term: Designated partners and the LLP agreement
concepts.statement: Management is deliberately contractual. There is no board and no articles: the LLP agreement decides who does what, how decisions are made, how profits divide, and how partners join and leave. Any partner can bind the LLP to third parties by acts done in the ordinary course of business, unless the LLP agreement restricts his authority and the third party knows of the restriction — the partnership’s section 19 logic, ported across with a contractual override. The Act polices the boundary of the shield in three moves. Section 25 preserves holding out: one who represents himself as a partner of the LLP, and lets credit be given on that faith, is liable accordingly. Section 26 makes the LLP liable, and the partner liable to the LLP, where a partner is apparently carrying on business in the LLP’s name with the authority of the other partners and causes loss by misapplication of money or property. And section 27 contains the fraud carve-out: where a partner is guilty of fraud in the course of the LLP’s business, the liability of that partner — that partner alone — becomes unlimited. The shield protects partners from each other’s ordinary negligence and commercial error; it never protects the wrongdoer from his own fraud.

concepts.term: The liability shield and its fraud exception
concepts.statement: Ongoing compliance is a sketch rather than a portrait. The LLP must maintain a registered office and notify changes. Each financial year it files with the Registrar an annual return under section 34, giving the partners’ particulars and the state of the LLP’s affairs; and a statement of account and solvency under section 35 — a prescribed statement, signed by designated partners, that the LLP is solvent or, if not, the particulars of insolvency, filed within the time the rules prescribe. Audit is compulsory only for larger LLPs — above modest thresholds of turnover and partner contribution (roughly ₹40 lakh turnover or ₹25 lakh contribution under the rules) — though many LLPs audit anyway for credit and compliance. For winding up, the Act provides both voluntary winding up and winding up by the Tribunal on specified grounds — inability to pay debts among them — with insolvency resolution of LLPs now run through the same Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code machinery as companies, and dissolution following the winding up. Conversion is expressly provided for by schedule: the Second Schedule converts a partnership firm into an LLP, carrying the firm’s property, liabilities and partners across, and the Third Schedule converts a private company, its shareholders becoming partners; in each case the converted entity succeeds to rights and obligations by law.
A body corporate, separate from its partners, with perpetual succession and partner liability capped at contribution.
The entity continues to exist regardless of changes in its partners until wound up and dissolved.
A partner individually answerable for the LLP’s statutory compliance; at least two, one resident in India.
The contract governing mutual rights and duties of the partners; the First Schedule fills its absence.
Section 25 liability fastened on one who represents himself as a partner of the LLP and induces credit.
Section 27: a partner guilty of fraud in the course of business has unlimited personal liability.
The prescribed annual statement, signed by designated partners, declaring the LLP’s solvency.
The conversion route by which a partnership firm becomes an LLP.

examples.title: Worked Case: The Claim Against the Consulting LLP
examples.problem: The LLP Act: Limited Liability Partnerships — worked through step by step

steps.label: Facts
steps.text: three consultants run practice as an LLP with combined contribution of ₹15 lakh. A court awards a client ₹60 lakh for work the LLP botched; the client seeks recovery from each partner’s home and savings.

steps.label: Identify the form
steps.text: the obligation is an obligation of the LLP, incurred in its own name — under the Act it is the LLP’s debt, not the partners’.

steps.label: Apply the shield
steps.text: the client reaches the LLP’s assets, and the partners’ exposure is capped at their agreed contribution; a partner is not personally liable for the LLP’s obligations merely by being a partner.

steps.label: Test the carve-outs
steps.text: the loss arose from negligent work, not fraud — so section 27 unlimited liability does not attach; had one partner forged the client’s documents, that partner alone would answer personally.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.text: the client ranks as an unsecured creditor of the LLP for the shortfall; the partners keep their personal assets — the outcome that would have destroyed them under a partnership.

examples.title: Walkthrough: From Deed to Certificate
examples.problem: The LLP Act: Limited Liability Partnerships — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Two chartered accountants decide to convert their registered firm into an LLP: they first check and reserve the name, ending in LLP, with the Registrar.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: They file the incorporation document — business particulars, registered office, both partners named as designated partners, one being resident in India, with consents.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: The Registrar finds compliance and issues the certificate of incorporation: the LLP exists as a body corporate from the date stated in it.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: They execute the LLP agreement defining capital, profit shares, decision rights and exit; had they not, the First Schedule defaults would govern.

steps.label: Their recurring calendar
steps.text: annual return, statement of account and solvency signed by both designated partners, and audit once turnover crosses the threshold.

keyTakeaways: Legal status — firm: no separate personality; LLP: body corporate with perpetual succession; company: body corporate with perpetual succession.

Liability — firm: every partner personally, jointly liable; LLP: each partner’s liability limited to agreed contribution, except for personal wrongdoing; company: shareholder liability limited to unpaid share value.
Governing instrument — firm: the partnership agreement; LLP: the LLP agreement, with the Act’s First Schedule filling gaps where none exists; company: memorandum and articles.

Management — firm: every partner (or managing partners) with implied authority; LLP: as the LLP agreement provides, with designated partners answerable for compliance; company: the board of directors.

Membership — firm: minimum 2, maximum 50 before company registration is required; LLP: minimum 2 partners, no maximum; company: private minimum 2 and maximum 200 members, public minimum 7, no maximum.

Key compliance — firm: optional registration, no annual filing; LLP: annual return plus statement of account and solvency, audit above thresholds; company: annual return, audited financial statements, board and general meetings.

Where next — Prerequisites: the partnership lesson earlier in this chapter, whose mutual-agency logic the LLP inherits and softens. Follow-ons: the companies lesson completes the organisational spectrum — the LLP skips the board, the memorandum and the prospectus machinery described there. The taxation lesson in this chapter explains the firm-style tax treatment mentioned above, and the accounting chapters’ lessons on financial statements cover the books the statement of account and solvency summarises.
An LLP is a body corporate: separate legal personality and perpetual succession, registered under the LLP Act 2008.
It is a hybrid — partnership-style management by agreement inside, company-style shield outside — as the comparison table shows.
Incorporation needs two partners, a reserved name, and the section 7 incorporation document; the certificate under section 11 is conclusive evidence.
At least two designated partners, one resident in India, carry compliance responsibility; the LLP agreement under section 23 governs, with the First Schedule as default.
The shield: obligations are the LLP’s own; but holding out bites under section 25 and a partner’s own fraud brings unlimited liability under section 27.
Annual compliance is an annual return plus the statement of account and solvency; audit applies above modest thresholds.
Winding up may be voluntary or by the Tribunal; the Second and Third Schedules convert firms and private companies into LLPs.

quiz.q: One of the seven partners of an LLP dies. The LLP:
options: continues to exist because of perpetual succession, though the agreement governs the deceased’s share
must convert to a private company
quiz.explanation: Section 3: an LLP’s existence is independent of its partners’; only winding up and dissolution end it.

quiz.q: A partner of an LLP commits fraud in the course of its business. Liability for that fraud falls on:
options: all partners jointly, like a partnership
quiz.explanation: Section 27 makes the guilty partner’s liability unlimited; the shield never covers the wrongdoer’s own fraud.

quiz.q: The minimum number of partners an LLP must have, and its governing instrument, are:
options: two and a certificate of incorporation
quiz.explanation: At least two partners are required, and section 23 makes the LLP agreement the governing instrument, with the First Schedule as fallback.

quiz.q: A firm of five partners converts to an LLP under the Second Schedule. The firm’s property and liabilities:
options: are divided equally among the partners personally
vest in the LLP by operation of law, and the partners become partners of the LLP
remain with the old firm for five years
quiz.explanation: The conversion schedules carry the entity’s rights and obligations across to the LLP by law — no conveyancing relay is needed.

quiz.q: The statement of account and solvency required of an LLP is:
options: an audited balance sheet in every case
a prescribed annual statement, signed by designated partners, declaring whether the LLP is solvent
filed only when the LLP is wound up
quiz.explanation: Section 35: the solvency declaration is the LLP’s signature annual compliance, alongside the section 34 annual return.

intro:
In 1892 Aron Salomon, a boot manufacturer, turned his sole business into a limited company, sold himself debentures secured over its assets, and when the company collapsed, its unsecured creditors demanded that he stand behind its debts personally — because, they said, the company was merely Salomon wearing a legal costume. The House of Lords disagreed, and that refusal is the foundation of company law: a duly incorporated company is a person in its own right, distinct from the people behind it. The Companies Act 2013, which replaced the 1956 Act, administers everything that flows from that idea — how the artificial person is born, what organs it has, what its ownership instruments are, and which authorities police it. This lesson travels from the certificate of incorporation to the boardroom and closes with the map of Indian corporate regulators.

**Why this matters.** The company is the workhorse of modern business — from one-person startups to listed giants — and every promoter, investor, lender and manager deals with its consequences daily: limited liability, transferable shares, perpetual succession, and a compliance perimeter enforced by a half-dozen regulators. Understanding what the corporate person is (and when courts look through it) is the difference between structuring a business and being structured by it.
objectives: Explain separate legal personality: the Salomon principle
Explain incorporation: name, memorandum, articles, certificate
Explain private, public and one-person companies
Explain lifting the corporate veil
Explain share capital and debentures: ownership versus debt
Explain directors’ duties and company meetings
Explain the regulator map: MCA, SEBI, RBI, IRDAI, CCI, NCLT

concepts.term: Separate legal personality: the Salomon principle
concepts.statement: Separate personality carries five practical consequences. The company owns its property, sues and is sued in its own name, and has perpetual succession — shareholders die, sell or vanish, and the company continues until wound up. Shareholders’ liability is limited to the amount unpaid on their shares: the creditor’s debtor is the company, not the people behind it, exactly as Salomon v. Salomon & Co. (1897) held when it let Salomon rank as a secured creditor of his own failed company. A company can contract with its own members, and in Lee v. Lee’s Air Farming (1961) a man who owned all but one share of his company was nevertheless its employee, so his widow could claim workers’ compensation from it. In exchange for the shield, the law demands incorporation, disclosure and governance — the machinery this lesson sketches. The shield is a privilege of form, and form is what the Act polices.

Birth runs through a defined sequence. First the name: reserved with the Registrar to ensure it is not identical with or too like an existing company’s, is not offensive, and — with limited exceptions — ends with “Limited” or “Private Limited”. Then the two constitutional documents. The memorandum of association is the charter: its clauses state the name, the state of the registered office, the objects for which the company is formed, the liability of members (limited by shares, by guarantee, or unlimited), and the share capital. Acts beyond the objects clause were historically void — Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co. v. Riche (1875) refused to ratify a railway company’s contract to finance a Belgian railway — and though modern law allows objects to be altered and protects outsiders dealing in good faith, the memorandum still defines what the company is. The articles of association are the internal constitution: how directors are appointed and removed, how meetings are called, how shares are transferred, how dividends are declared. Where the articles are silent on internal management, the Act’s model articles in its tables fill the gap. The modern filing is electronic and consolidated: a single integrated form carries the application for the name, the memorandum and articles, the first directors’ particulars and consents, the registered office and the declaration of compliance, supported by professionals. Once the Registrar is satisfied, the certificate of incorporation issues — conclusive evidence that the company exists and has been registered from the date on it, a date no challenge to the antecedent paperwork can erase.

The Act then sorts companies by their accessibility to the public. A private company — section 2(68) — restricts the right to transfer its shares, limits membership to two hundred (excluding employee-members), prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe, and needs at least two members and two directors; since the minimum-capital rules were removed, two people and a modest filing can create one. A public company — section 2(71) — needs at least seven members and three directors, may invite the public through a prospectus, and faces heavier governance: independent directors, stricter audit and, when listed, the market regulator’s continuous obligations. The one-person company — section 2(62) — folds sole proprietorship into corporate form: a single natural-person member who names a nominee in the memorandum to take over on death, and who is relieved of several formalities, including general meetings. Since the 2020 rule changes, an Indian citizen resident for the statutory period can form one, and it can convert to a private or public company at will.

Separate personality is respected, not worshipped: courts lift the corporate veil when the form is abused. The recognised grounds cluster around wrongdoing and public policy — fraud or improper conduct, where the company is a facade for concealing the true actors; revenue evasion; using the form to evade obligations or circumvent statutes; and national emergency, as in Daimler Co. v. Continental Tyre & Rubber Co. (1916), where an English company whose shareholders were German enemies could not be paid during the war because the court looked past the English incorporation to the enemy character of its ownership. In the other direction, Vodafone International Holdings v. Union of India (2012) shows the principle’s strength: the Supreme Court respected the separate existence of an overseas holding company in a chain of share transfers, declining to tax an indirect transfer of Indian assets under the law as it then stood — Parliament’s answer was a retrospective amendment, which itself shows how much the personality principle protects. The routine cases, however, are not constitutional dramas but puppets: where a subsidiary is a mere agent or the alter ego of its parent, or where companies are created to defeat creditors, the veil parts.

concepts.term: Share capital and debentures: ownership versus debt
concepts.statement: Ownership of the artificial person is sliced into shares, and the slice one buys determines one’s rights. Equity shares — section 43 — carry the voting rights and the residual claims: dividends only after everyone else is satisfied, and repayment in winding up last. Preference shares carry preferential rights — a fixed-rate dividend paid before equity holders get anything, and priority on return of capital — usually without votes, and if redeemable they must be redeemed within the twenty years that section 55 allows. The capital architecture runs from authorised capital (the ceiling in the memorandum) through issued, subscribed and paid-up capital — the accounting chapters’ lessons on shares and debentures work through these mechanics and their balance-sheet presentation, and this lesson leaves that machinery to them. Debt enters as debentures: instruments acknowledging a loan. A debenture holder is a creditor, not an owner — paid interest before any dividend, ranking ahead of shareholders in winding up, usually without a vote — and debentures may be secured on the company’s assets, convertible into shares at the holder’s option, or plain paper. The choice between equity and debentures is the choice between sharing control and parting with it, priced by the market.

Governance is the story of two organs. The board of directors manages — the Act vests the company’s powers in the board, exercisable at meetings, at least four a year with no gap beyond the statutory limit. Directors are fiduciaries, and section 166 codifies the core duties: to act in accordance with the articles, in good faith to promote the objects of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole; to exercise due and reasonable care, skill and diligence and independent judgment; to avoid conflicts of interest and situations of undue gain; and to refrain from assignments of office. Breach attracts fines and, for an outright undue gain, disgorgement. The shareholders in general meeting supervise: the annual general meeting must be held within six months of the financial year’s end, and not more than fifteen months may pass between two of them. Resolutions come in two grades — ordinary, carried by a simple majority, and special under section 114, carried by a majority of at least three times the votes cast against — reserved for weightier decisions like altering the articles or varying shareholders’ rights. The default is majority rule: as Foss v. Harbottle (1843) held in the ancestor of the doctrine, a wrong done to the company is the company’s to pursue, and the majority decides whether to pursue it — subject to the Act’s statutory exceptions, chief among them the oppression-and-mismanagement jurisdiction.

concepts.term: The regulator map: MCA, SEBI, RBI, IRDAI, CCI, NCLT
concepts.statement: No company is an island; a constellation of regulators surrounds it. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs administers the Act and runs the electronic registry through which every filing passes. Under it work the Registrars of Companies, one to a region: the registry that registers companies and LLPs, examines filings, maintains the public record and strikes off defunct companies. The Securities and Exchange Board of India — statutory since the SEBI Act 1992 — polices the securities markets: disclosure conditions for public issues under its issue regulations, listing obligations of listed companies, insider trading, takeover bids and investor protection. The Reserve Bank of India governs banking companies, non-banking finance and payments, and runs monetary policy — the inflation lesson in the economics chapters covers that mandate. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority licenses and supervises insurers in the policyholders’ interest. The Competition Commission of India, under the Competition Act 2002, strikes anti-competitive agreements, punishes abuse of dominance and clears combinations — mergers above the thresholds. And adjudication is concentrated in the National Company Law Tribunal and its appellate tribunal: they hear oppression and mismanagement petitions, class actions, schemes of compromise, and — through the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 — corporate insolvency resolution and winding up, with appeals lying upward to the Supreme Court.
A duly incorporated company is a legal person separate from its members — from Salomon v. Salomon (1897).
The charter stating name, objects, liability and capital — the document that defines the company.
The internal constitution governing meetings, directors, transfers and dividends.
The Registrar’s conclusive evidence that the company exists from the date it names.
The separation between company and members; lifted for fraud, facade, revenue evasion or enemy character.
A share with a preferential right to dividend and capital repayment, typically without a vote.
An instrument acknowledging a corporate loan; the holder is a creditor, not an owner.
A resolution carried by at least three times the votes cast against it, for weighty matters.
The adjudicating body for oppression, class actions, schemes and insolvency resolution.

examples.title: Worked Case: Salomon v. Salomon & Co.
examples.problem: The Companies Act and the Regulators: Incorporation to Capital — worked through step by step

steps.label: Facts
steps.text: Aron Salomon incorporated his boot business as a company; he, his wife and five children held the seven shares, and the company issued him debentures secured over its assets in exchange for the purchase price of the business.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: The company failed within a year; the liquidator, acting for unsecured creditors, argued the company was a mere alias for Salomon and that his debentures were a fraud on creditors.

steps.label: Held
steps.text: the company was validly incorporated under the statute; once registered, it is a separate legal person, and the motives of those who formed it are irrelevant.

steps.label: Consequence
steps.text: Salomon was entitled to be repaid as a secured creditor in priority to the unsecured creditors — limited liability worked exactly as the statute promised.

steps.label: Legacy
steps.text: the case is the root of every later rule — including the veil-lifting doctrines that confine it, since the separation it declared was never meant as a licence for fraud.

examples.title: Worked Case: The Enemy Behind the English Company
examples.problem: The Companies Act and the Regulators: Incorporation to Capital — worked through step by step

steps.label: Facts
steps.text: an English-registered company asked a court to restrain a debtor from paying money owed to it; nearly all its shares were held by Germans during the First World War.

steps.label: The question
steps.text: could payment be made to an English company whose beneficial owners were enemy aliens, when trading with the enemy was prohibited?

steps.label: Applied
steps.text: the court looked behind the incorporation to the persons in control, and held the company effectively of enemy character.

steps.label: Result
steps.text: Daimler Co. v. Continental Tyre & Rubber Co. (1916) — the corporate veil lifted for national security, one of the narrow, classic grounds.

steps.label: Contrast
steps.text: Vodafone v. Union of India (2012), where a chain of foreign companies was respected as real persons despite the tax consequences — separation is the rule, piercing the exception.

keyTakeaways: Where next — Prerequisites: the partnership and LLP lessons earlier in this chapter, which supply the two forms the company is contrasted against. Follow-ons: the taxation lesson in this chapter covers corporate tax and MAT, and the accounting chapters’ lessons on shares and debentures take over issue mechanics — prospectus, rights issues, private placement and the entries they generate — which this lesson deliberately only sketches. For how the securities market prices these instruments, pair with the lessons on supply and demand in the economics chapters.
Salomon v. Salomon: a registered company is a separate person — separate property, perpetual succession, limited liability.
Birth is procedural: reserved name, memorandum of objects and capital, articles of internal governance, integrated filing, conclusive certificate.
Private companies cap members at two hundred and restrict transfers; public ones need seven members and face heavier governance; one-person companies wrap sole traders in the shield.
The veil lifts for fraud, facades, revenue evasion and enemy character — Daimler — but held firm in Vodafone.
Equity shares vote and come last; preference shares take dividends first; debenture holders are creditors, not owners.
Directors manage under section 166 fiduciary duties; shareholders meet at AGMs; special resolutions need three-to-one support.

The regulator map: corporate registry under the Ministry, SEBI over markets, RBI over banking, IRDAI over insurance, the Competition Commission over combinations, and the company tribunals for adjudication.

quiz.q: A one-person company differs from a sole proprietorship because:
options: the member’s liability is limited and the company has separate personality, with a nominee named for succession
quiz.explanation: Section 2(62): the OPC wraps the single member in the corporate shield — the proprietorship offers no such separation.

quiz.q: Which instrument creates the debt relationship with a company and priority over shareholders on winding up?
quiz.explanation: A debenture acknowledges a loan; the holder is a creditor with priority over all shareholders on distribution.

quiz.q: A company altering its articles and varying shareholders’ rights generally needs:
options: a special resolution — three times the votes cast against
quiz.explanation: Section 114 reserves weighty matters to the special resolution, the higher grade of shareholder consent.

quiz.q: A listed company making its first public issue of shares is governed, in its disclosure requirements, mainly by:
options: the Securities and Exchange Board of India through its issue regulations
the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority
quiz.explanation: Public-issue disclosure, listing obligations and investor protection are SEBI territory under the SEBI Act 1992; the registry and the tribunal play other roles.

quiz.q: In Daimler Co. v. Continental Tyre, the court lifted the veil because:
options: the shareholders were enemy aliens in wartime, making the company effectively of enemy character
the company was in arrears of tax
its objects clause was ultra vires
quiz.explanation: National security is a classic, narrow ground for looking past incorporation to the persons in control.

intro:
Modern constitutionalism rests on a structural wager: divide the state’s power among a legislature that makes law, an executive that administers it, and a judiciary that adjudicates disputes under it — then give each branch tools to check the others. The lineage runs from Aristotle’s mixed constitution through John Locke’s Two Treatises to Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws (1748), and into the Constitution of the United States of 1787, its clearest implementation. Parliamentary democracies fuse executive and legislature, compensating with different checks, but the underlying problem is universal: how to make power oppose power so that liberty survives.

**Why this matters.** Every headline clash between a president and a parliament, every judicial nomination battle, every veto is this machinery in motion. Reading constitutions structurally — asking who may do what to whom, and who may stop them — turns political news from theatre into mechanism, and it is the basic literacy of citizenship.
objectives: Explain three functions of the state
Explain montesquieu: power checks power
Explain checks and balances as interlock
Explain judicial review
Explain bicameralism as an internal check
Explain parliamentary fusion and its compensations
Explain comparative constitutional designs

concepts.statement: The modern version of an old idea assigns legislation, execution and adjudication to distinct institutions. Locke’s Second Treatise (1689) separated legislative from executive power because those who make laws cannot be trusted to execute them impartially — lawmakers would be tempted to exempt themselves. Aristotle’s classification of governmental functions, and his argument for mixing them, is the ancient root of the whole tradition.

In The Spirit of the Laws, Montesquieu wrote that constant experience shows every person invested with power is apt to abuse it, and that power should be a check to power. His warning was specific: when the legislative and executive powers unite in the same person or body, there can be no liberty; worse still if judging joins them, making the judge a legislator at the same time. His reading of the English constitution was imperfect, but the architecture he extracted from it conquered the world.

Pure separation — each branch sealed off — would leave each branch unsupervised. The American innovation, elaborated in Madison’s Federalist No. 51, was that ambition must be made to counteract ambition: overlapping powers, not hermetic ones. The executive veto, legislative confirmation of appointments, impeachment powers and legislative control of budgets are the interlocking teeth of the machine.

In Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall reasoned that a constitution is law superior to ordinary legislation, and that saying what the law is falls to courts; a statute conflicting with the constitution is therefore void as to that conflict. Neither the constitutional text nor the framers’ debates explicitly granted the power, and debates over its democratic legitimacy — unelected judges striking down popular laws — continue wherever the doctrine exists.

Splitting the legislature into two chambers differently composed is an internal check: a bill must pass both, which slows lawmaking and filters hasty majorities. In federal systems the second chamber typically represents constituent units — states, provinces, cantons — adding territorial balance to the procedural one.

In Westminster-style systems the prime minister and cabinet sit in, and depend on, the legislature — fusion, not separation. The checks migrate: confidence conventions can remove a government between elections, question time exposes it weekly, and backbench rebellion disciplines it. Judicial independence remains, typically strengthened by statutory protections of tenure and salary.

Post-1945 constitutions adapted the model: Germany’s specialised Federal Constitutional Court, operating since 1951, reflects Hans Kelsen’s Austrian idea of concentrated constitutional review, while France’s Fifth Republic mixes a strong presidency with a parliament able to censure the government. Every design trades decisiveness against the diffusion of power.

Students conflate separation of powers — allocating functions to distinct institutions — with checks and balances, the deliberate overlaps that force mutual supervision; the second exists to fix the first’s blind spots. Parliamentary systems are often misdescribed as lacking separation when they redistribute rather than abandon checks. And judicial review is not an appeal: the question there is whether a statute is constitutional, not whether it was wise.
Allocation of legislative, executive and judicial functions to distinct institutions.
Overlapping powers enabling each branch to restrain the others.
Court power to invalidate laws inconsistent with the constitution.
Legislative repassage of a vetoed bill, typically by a supermajority.
Legislative charging and trial process for removing officials.
Parliamentary rule that a government must retain majority support or resign.
A specialised court, in the Kelsen tradition, with jurisdiction over constitutional questions.

examples.title: Worked example — Separation of Powers and Checks and Balances
examples.problem: Trace which checks operate when a legislature passes a bill, the president vetoes it, the legislature overrides by two-thirds, and a court later holds the statute unconstitutional.

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: each branch’s tool is a check on another’s core function — the veto on lawmaking, the override on the veto, judicial review on the enacted text.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: the veto delays and signals; the override clears the higher bar deliberately set to be rare; the ruling exercises judicial review, voiding the statute for conflict with the constitution.

examples.result: the policy survived two filters and failed the third, and at no point did a single actor’s will decide the outcome — exactly the intended architecture.

keyTakeaways: Constitutional drafting in new democracies, where designers allocate and interlock powers with the failures of predecessors in mind.
Judicial appointments politics as a live check in action, since courts are staffed by the branches they check.
Emergency powers: who may declare, who must renew, and who reviews — the classic stress test of the structure.
Rule-of-law indices that score judicial independence and institutional checks comparatively.
Civic education: news literacy about vetoes, confirmations and rulings is applied constitutional structure.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is core-tier constitutional law and general civic literacy. Follow with federalism, the vertical division of power; judicial review doctrine; and comparative constitutional systems. Madison’s Federalist Nos. 10 and 51 are short, readable primary sources.
The legislature makes law, the executive administers it, the judiciary adjudicates under it.
Montesquieu: concentrated power abuses; power must check power.
Checks and balances deliberately overlap branches — ambition counteracting ambition.
Judicial review, from Marbury (1803), lets courts void unconstitutional statutes.
Parliamentary systems fuse executive and legislature, and relocate the checks.

quiz.q: Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws (1748) is cited chiefly for…
options: the argument that liberty requires power to check power
quiz.explanation: His treatment of the English constitution argued that legislative, executive and judicial powers must not be united in the same hands.

quiz.q: Marbury v. Madison (1803) is remembered for establishing…
options: federal judicial review in the United States
quiz.explanation: Marshall held that courts must say what the law is when statutes conflict with the constitution, voiding the conflicting statute.

quiz.q: In parliamentary systems, the executive–legislature relationship is best described as…
options: strictly separated, as in the presidential model
fused, with the cabinet drawn from and responsible to the legislature
controlled by the head of state alone
quiz.explanation: Fusion is checked instead by confidence conventions, question time and the possibility of early elections.

intro:
Treaties are the primary instruments of international law — written agreements between states, governed by international law, running from bilateral border accords to near-universal conventions. Their regime was codified in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties of 1969, itself a treaty about treaties, drafted by the International Law Commission and adopted at the Vienna conference. Its lifecycle logic — negotiate, sign, ratify, enter into force, interpret, and only narrowly terminate — and its enforcement reality, built on reciprocity, reputation and consent to adjudication rather than a world police, are what this topic unpacks.

**Why this matters.** From climate accords to trade law to human rights conventions, most global cooperation is treaty-shaped. Understanding the lifecycle explains real events — why a signature does not bind, why ratification votes matter domestically, and why treaty exit is legally easier than treaty enforcement.
objectives: Explain the VCLT: a treaty about treaties
Explain pacta sunt servanda
Explain signature versus ratification
Explain reservations
Explain interpretation under Articles 31–32
Explain breach, termination and changed circumstances
Explain enforcement without a world police

concepts.term: The VCLT: a treaty about treaties
concepts.statement: The Vienna Convention defines what counts as a treaty, then regulates its making, interpretation, invalidity and termination. It entered into force in 1980, and even states not party — the United States signed in 1970 but has not ratified — accept much of it as codified customary law. For practical purposes, the VCLT is the grammar book of treaty relations.

Article 26 states the regime’s foundation, pacta sunt servanda: every treaty in force binds its parties and must be performed by them in good faith. Article 27 then closes the classic escape: a party cannot invoke internal law — a recalcitrant parliament, a referendum, a change of government — to justify non-performance. International obligation survives domestic politics.

Signature authenticates the text and, under Article 18, creates an interim duty not to defeat the treaty’s object and purpose before ratification — but full consent to be bound comes with ratification, an instrument typically preceded by domestic approval, whether senate assent, a parliamentary vote or a referendum depending on the state. Signature alone usually leaves a state free to walk away, at diplomatic cost.

Article 2 defines a reservation: a unilateral statement, however phrased, excluding or modifying the legal effect of specified provisions for the reserving state. Reservations are allowed unless the treaty forbids them or the reservation is incompatible with its object and purpose, as Article 19 provides; other parties may accept or object, with consequences that vary with their responses.

Article 31 commands interpretation in good faith according to the ordinary meaning of the terms, in their context and in light of the treaty’s object and purpose — the integrated approach that displaced free intent-hunting. Supplementary means, chiefly the negotiating record (travaux préparatoires) and the circumstances of conclusion, enter only under Article 32, to confirm meaning or resolve ambiguity.

A material breach, defined in Article 60, lets injured parties invoke it to suspend or terminate the treaty, in whole or in part. Denunciation is possible only where the treaty provides for it. Article 62’s fundamental change of circumstances — the old rebus sic stantibus idea — is deliberately narrow: it excludes boundary situations and requires a change that was unforeseen and transforms the nature of the obligations.

Compliance runs on reciprocity and reputation, on countermeasures — proportionate, non-forcible responses to breach — on monitoring bodies and reporting, and on consent-based adjudication before the International Court of Justice or treaty-specific systems such as trade panels. The system’s paradox is that binding law depends on voluntary submission and disciplined self-help.

The leading error is assuming a signature binds — it rarely does before ratification, though the object-and-purpose duty constrains sabotage in between. Second, not every reservation is permissible: the object-and-purpose test and the objections of other parties bite. Third, overstating enforcement: there is no global sheriff, and much compliance is managed through dialogue and reporting rather than adjudication. Finally, monist and dualist states bring treaties home differently — forgetting that trips up domestic analysis.
Agreements must be kept in good faith; the baseline norm of treaty law.
The international act confirming consent to be bound, usually after domestic approval.
A unilateral modification of a treaty’s effect for the reserving state, subject to object and purpose.
A serious violation permitting suspension or termination by injured parties.
The negotiating record, a supplementary interpretive aid under Article 32.
A proportionate, non-forcible response to an internationally wrongful act.
Whether treaties apply domestically automatically or require implementing legislation.

examples.title: Worked example — How International Treaties Actually Work
examples.problem: A state signs a climate agreement, and its legislature then refuses the implementing legislation — what are its obligations, exactly?

steps.label: Recall the governing ideas
steps.text: signature creates an Article 18 duty not to defeat the treaty’s object and purpose; ratification is the act that consents to be bound; internal law never excuses breach once bound.

steps.label: Apply it
steps.text: if the state has signed but not ratified, it must refrain from acts that defeat the treaty’s core aims, yet is not fully bound — withdrawal remains legally open, though diplomatically expensive. If it has ratified, the domestic deadlock is irrelevant internationally.

examples.result: the answer turns entirely on the lifecycle stage — which is why ratification votes, not signing ceremonies, are where treaty politics actually bite.

keyTakeaways: Climate law: the architecture of national pledges, ratification thresholds and transparency frameworks.
Trade: binding panel processes in trade agreements, with retaliation authorised at the end of the ladder.
Human rights conventions: state reporting to treaty bodies, and individual complaint mechanisms where accepted.
Arms control: verification regimes that convert paper commitments into monitored ones.
Legal practice: registration under Article 102 of the UN Charter and the use of treaty databases as working tools.

Where next — Prerequisites: a basic sense of what international law is and who its subjects are. Follow with state responsibility, the International Court of Justice, and the formation of customary international law. At the intermediate tier the VCLT itself is unusually readable treaty text.
The VCLT 1969 governs how treaties are made, read and ended.
Pacta sunt servanda: treaties bind in good faith, and domestic law is no excuse.
Signature is interim; ratification is the binding act.
Reservations must respect object and purpose; interpretation starts with text, context and purpose.
Enforcement is decentralised: reciprocity, reputation, countermeasures, consented adjudication.

quiz.q: Under Article 27 of the VCLT, a state that has ratified a treaty…
options: may rely on domestic law to excuse non-performance
cannot invoke internal law to justify breach
may withdraw freely at any time
is bound only if its courts agree
quiz.explanation: Internal law is no defence to breach; the international obligation stands regardless of domestic approval difficulties.

quiz.q: A reservation to a human rights treaty is impermissible if it…
options: is incompatible with the treaty’s object and purpose
is not translated into every language
quiz.explanation: Article 19’s object-and-purpose test, plus objections by other parties, polices the reservation system.

quiz.q: Under Article 31, interpretation of a treaty begins with…
options: the personal intent of the drafters
good faith, ordinary meaning in context, and object and purpose
quiz.explanation: Travaux préparatoires are supplementary under Article 32; the Article 31 starting point is text, context and purpose in good faith.

intro:
Most promises are morally binding; only some are legally binding. Contract law draws the line, and its anatomy has barely changed in centuries: one party offers on definite terms, the other accepts, and each gives the other something of value — the exchange the law will enforce. From a phone app’s terms of service to a shipping charter worth millions, the same skeleton carries the weight. Learn the anatomy once and every agreement you will ever sign becomes readable.

**Why this matters.** You already contract dozens of times a day: every tap of “I agree” accepts terms you have never read. Contract law decides what you actually promised, who bears the risk when performance fails, and what money can mend. It is private law’s engine room, and its default rules quietly allocate billions between parties who never negotiated them.
objectives: Explain offer and acceptance
Explain consideration: the price of a promise
Explain intention to create legal relations
Explain capacity and genuine consent
Explain express, implied and standard-form terms
Explain breach and the menu of remedies
Explain the limits of enforcement

concepts.statement: An offer is a definite proposal, communicated on specified terms, made with intent to be bound the moment it is accepted. An invitation to treat is not an offer — goods in a shop window or prices in a catalogue merely invite the customer to offer, which the seller may decline. Acceptance must mirror the offer exactly: a reply that varies terms is a counter-offer, and it kills the original. Business “battles of the forms”, where purchase orders and confirmations cross with clashing small print, are resolved by working out whose terms fired last.

concepts.term: Consideration: the price of a promise
concepts.statement: Common-law systems demand consideration: each promise must be bought with something of value — money, goods, a return promise, even forbearance from a right. A gratuitous promise to give a nephew 5,000 may be admirable, but unless he gives anything back it is unenforceable, however solemnly made. Civil-law systems generally ask instead for a cause, or simply for agreement, which is why the consideration requirement marks the great divide between the legal families. Note the boundary: consideration must be sufficient, not adequate — courts do not police bad bargains, only empty ones.

Domestic and social arrangements are presumed not to be contracts — the promise to cook Tuesday’s dinner — while commercial dealings are presumed to be. Either presumption flips with evidence: a written agreement between estranged spouses, or the words “binding in honour only” between firms. The test is objective: not what the parties secretly intended, but what a reasonable person would understand them to have intended from what they said and did.

A contract requires parties who can consent, and consent that is genuine. Minors, the intoxicated and those lacking mental capacity may avoid most agreements. Consent is hollow if it was bought with a material misrepresentation, extracted under duress or undue influence, or founded on a mistake so fundamental it hollows out the deal — the classic case of the cow sold as barren that turned out, to both parties’ surprise, to be pregnant. The law asks whether a meeting of minds actually occurred, not merely whether pens touched paper.

Express terms are spoken or written; implied terms are supplied by statute (goods of merchantable quality), by the custom of the trade, or by the obvious unspoken intent of the parties. Standard-form contracts — insurance policies, software licences, tenancies — move the battlefield from negotiation to interpretation, and courts respond: ambiguity is construed against the drafter, unfair terms can be struck under consumer-protection doctrine, and particularly lopsided clauses may simply be refused. The signature on page forty is consent of a kind; the law decides how much weight it can bear.

concepts.term: Breach and the menu of remedies
concepts.statement: Breach triggers a menu, not a punishment. Expectation damages put the innocent party where full performance would have; reliance damages restore what they spent in reliance on the promise. Specific performance orders the breaching party to do what they promised, but it is reserved for unique subject matter — land, a rare painting — since ordinary goods can simply be bought elsewhere. Termination plus damages covers most real disputes, and liquidated damages clauses pre-compute the loss, provided they are a genuine estimate rather than a penalty in costume.

Some promises the law will not touch at all. Agreements to commit crimes or torts are void; contracts that unreasonably restrain trade or exploit one party unconscionably invite refusal or trimming; wagers are unenforceable in many jurisdictions. No court will order specific performance of a personal-services contract, because forcing a reluctant singer to sing is unworkable and inhuman alike. And enforcement fades with time: limitation periods extinguish even good claims, on the logic that stale evidence makes stale justice.
$$D = V_{\text{promised}} - V_{\text{received}}$$
concepts.detail: Damages equal the value of the performance promised minus the value actually received, restoring the innocent party to the position full performance would have produced.

concepts.statement: $$D = P_{\text{cover}} - P_{\text{contract}}$$
concepts.detail: Where the buyer obtains a substitute after breach, damages are typically the cover price minus the contract price — the cheapest route to the same expectation result.

concepts.statement: The first-year error is treating every agreement as a contract: consideration, capacity and genuine consent must each be present, and social promises are presumed outside the law’s reach. Do not confuse remedies with revenge — damages compensate, they do not punish, which is why “penalty” clauses get cut down to genuine pre-estimates of loss. And mind the mirror-image rule: a purported acceptance that tweaks the terms is a counter-offer that destroys the original — a lesson relearned in every battle of the forms.
A definite proposal on stated terms, intended to bind once accepted.
Something of value given by each side; the common-law price of enforceability.
A response varying the terms, which rejects and destroys the original offer.
Money restoring the position full performance would have produced.
A court order compelling performance, reserved mainly for unique subject matter.
A genuine pre-estimate of loss agreed in advance; enforceable where a penalty is not.
A display or advertisement inviting offers rather than making one.

examples.title: Worked example — Contracts: The Anatomy of a Promise the Law Enforces
examples.problem: A buyer contracts to buy a specialised machine for 15,000, the machine being worth 20,000 to the buyer; the seller breaches and the buyer buys an identical machine elsewhere for 17,000 — what damages restore the buyer?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: expectation damages must place the innocent party in the position full performance would have achieved — here, a surplus of 20,000 minus 15,000, that is 5,000.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: after covering at 17,000 the buyer’s surplus is 20,000 minus 17,000, only 3,000; the shortfall equals the cover price minus the contract price — 17,000 minus 15,000 — which is 2,000.

examples.result: damages of 2,000 restore the full promised surplus, since 3,000 plus 2,000 equals 5,000 — and the buyer ends with a working machine rather than a lawsuit about one.

keyTakeaways: Commercial drafting: risk allocation through indemnities, force majeure and liquidated damages clauses happens before disputes, not after.
Consumer protection: unfair-terms doctrine polices the standard forms that dominate mass-market contracting.
Construction and services: substantial-performance and variation rules keep large projects from collapsing over partial default.
Everyday life: employment offers, tenancies, subscriptions and clickwrap all run on offer, acceptance and consideration.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — this is core-tier private law and runs on plain reasoning. Follow with tort law, the other great source of civil obligations, then remedies in depth and commercial drafting. One close reading of a real contract you have signed — a tenancy, an insurance policy, a terms-of-service page — teaches more than a chapter of theory.

quiz.q: A shop misprices a television in its window. Legally, the display is most likely…
quiz.explanation: Displays invite offers; the contract forms only when the seller accepts the customer’s offer at the till.

quiz.q: A grandmother promises in writing to give her grandson 5,000 next year, and he gives nothing in return. In a common-law system the promise is…
quiz.explanation: A gratuitous promise lacks consideration, however formal the writing; the grandson gave nothing to buy it.

quiz.q: Expectation damages aim to put the innocent party…
options: back in the position before the contract
in the position full performance would have produced
quiz.explanation: The goal is the promised position — the surplus the innocent party would have enjoyed had the deal been kept.

quiz.q: A clause fixing damages at 100,000 for a one-day delay is most likely to be…
quiz.explanation: Clauses that punish rather than genuinely pre-estimate loss are penalties, and penalties are unenforceable.

intro:
A trial is not a search for perfect truth; it is a structured contest run under rules about who must prove what, and to what degree. In a criminal case the prosecution must convince the fact-finder of guilt beyond reasonable doubt, while the defendant may sit silent and prove nothing at all. Evidence law — what may be heard, how it may be used, and how it is weighed — is the machinery that keeps that asymmetric contest honest.

**Why this matters.** The burden of proof is where the presumption of innocence actually lives. It decides cases where facts stay murky, shields everyone from having to prove their own innocence, and explains why “not guilty” does not mean innocent — it means not proven. Grasp it, and you grasp why the law sometimes frees the probably guilty rather than convict the possibly innocent.
objectives: Explain who must prove: the burden of proof
Explain standards of proof
Explain direct and circumstantial evidence
Explain relevance, admissibility and exclusion
Explain presumptions and inference
Explain credibility, reliability and corroboration
Explain why wrongful convictions happen

concepts.term: Who must prove: the burden of proof
concepts.statement: Two burdens hide inside the phrase. The legal, or persuasive, burden is the duty to convince the fact-finder of an assertion, and in criminal cases it rests on the prosecution for every element of the offence. The evidential burden is lighter: the duty to point to some evidence before an issue may even be left to the jury. Some defences — insanity in many systems — shift the evidential burden to the accused once raised, but the prosecution’s core burden never travels.

Criminal guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt — not to mathematical certainty, and not beyond any conceivable doubt, but beyond doubts on which a reasonable person would act in their own important affairs. Civil disputes use the balance of probabilities: more likely than not, the scales tipped past fifty per cent. The gap is deliberate. A society that locks people in cages demands more confidence than a society that moves money from one citizen to another.

Direct evidence, if believed, proves a fact outright: the eyewitness who watched the stabbing. Circumstantial evidence proves by inference: fingerprints on the knife, blood on the cuff, a phone pinging towers along the escape route. Circumference is not weakness — a web of circumstantial facts often outperforms a lone eyewitness, whose memory is more editable than juries instinctively believe. DNA, cell-tower data and money trails are all circumstantial, and they convict more reliably than confession ever has.

Relevant evidence makes a material fact more or less probable, but relevance is only a ticket to the door. Admissibility rules then exclude even relevant matter: hearsay — an out-of-court statement offered for its truth — because it cannot be cross-examined; propensity evidence, because “bad person” is not “did it”; and, in some systems, improperly obtained evidence, where courts weigh the justice system’s integrity against the cost of losing the proof. Exclusion protects the trial’s honesty, at the acknowledged price of sometimes blinding it.

A presumption assigns a fact its starting point — innocence, sanity, death after seven years missing — and shifts the evidential burden onto whoever disputes it. Inference reasons from evidence to fact: wet streets imply recent rain. Fact-finders build such chains constantly, and the chains have rules — each link must be reasonable, and speculation dressed as common sense is still speculation. The prosecutor’s fallacy, mistaking “a one-in-a-million random match” for “a one-in-a-million chance of innocence”, is an inference error with wrongful convictions attached.

Weighing testimony is an everyday skill, formalised. Fact-finders audit perception (could the witness actually see?), memory (how much has time edited?), narration (consistent account or coached script?) and sincerity (bias, incentive, fear). Corroboration — independent lines pointing the same way — is the classic safeguard, and some systems require it for notoriously fallible evidence such as accomplice testimony. Demeanour, the cue juries trust most, is the least reliable of the lot; good liars are calm.

Innocence projects have exonerated hundreds, and their case files are evidence law’s failure atlas: mistaken eyewitness identification, false confessions extracted by fatigue and leverage, forensic overstatement, junk science and tunnel-vision investigation — running through them all, confidence mistaken for accuracy. The remedies follow the diagnoses: double-blind identification procedures, recorded interrogations, disclosure duties, post-conviction DNA testing. Every rule in this topic has a face behind it.
$$P(H \mid E) = \dfrac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}$$
concepts.detail: The probability a hypothesis is true given the evidence; combining evidence properly means starting from prior odds, not treating the strength of one item as the final answer.

concepts.statement: $$O_{\text{after}} = O_{\text{before}} \times \dfrac{P(E \mid H)}{P(E \mid \neg H)}$$
concepts.detail: Odds after evidence equal odds before multiplied by the likelihood ratio; the prosecutor’s fallacy is jumping from a large likelihood ratio straight to guilt.

concepts.statement: The prosecutor’s fallacy leads the list: the rarity of a match is not the probability of innocence. Its mirror image, the defence attorney’s fallacy, dismisses weak-but-real evidence entirely. Remember that acquittal means not proven, not innocent; that circumstantial evidence is not second-class evidence; and that a verdict is an authorised conclusion under a standard of proof — deliberately imperfect machinery for a world in which no one witnesses everything.
The duty to persuade the fact-finder; in crime it rests on the prosecution.
The degree of certainty required — beyond reasonable doubt, or balance of probabilities.
Evidence that proves a fact by inference rather than direct perception.
An out-of-court statement offered for its truth, generally excluded because it resists challenge.
The starting allocation of doubt: the accused is innocent unless guilt is proved.
The probability of the evidence if the hypothesis is true, divided by its probability if false.
Independent evidence supporting a witness, guarding against single-source error.

examples.title: Worked example — Evidence and the Burden of Proof
examples.problem: A DNA profile matching the defendant occurs at random in 1 person in 100,000, and the other evidence puts prior odds of his being the source at 1 to 1,000 — how strong is the case once the DNA is in?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: posterior odds equal prior odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio, so the match multiplies the existing case rather than finishing it.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: the likelihood ratio is 100,000 to 1, so posterior odds are 1/1,000 × 100,000 = 100 to 1 — a probability of about 99 per cent that the defendant is the source.

examples.result: the DNA converts weak suspicion into near-proof, but only because the prior was not negligible; treating the 1-in-100,000 match rate as the probability of innocence would be the prosecutor’s fallacy in action.

keyTakeaways: Courtroom advocacy: closing arguments are built around which side bears which burden on each element.
Forensic science: modern standards require match probabilities and likelihood ratios to be reported, not raw certainties.
Journalism and fact-checking: the same logic separates allegation from finding, and evidence from inference.
Medicine: diagnostic testing is Bayesian inference in a white coat — base rates before test results, always.

Where next — Prerequisites: the basics of criminal justice and courts. Follow with criminal procedure, the law of testimony and forensic-science literacy, where the Bayesian logic earns its keep. Watching even one real trial — many courts stream proceedings — makes these abstractions vivid within an afternoon.

quiz.q: In a criminal trial, the legal burden of proving guilt rests…
options: on the prosecution, beyond reasonable doubt
quiz.explanation: The presumption of innocence allocates the persuasive burden to the state for every element of the offence.

quiz.q: Fingerprints, cell-tower records and blood spatter are all…
quiz.explanation: Each proves by inference; a chain of such facts can be stronger than a single eyewitness.

quiz.q: A one-in-a-million random DNA match rate means…
options: a one-in-a-million chance the suspect is innocent
the match is a million times more likely if the suspect is the source than if he is not
the defendant must now disprove the match
quiz.explanation: It states a likelihood ratio, not a probability of guilt or innocence — the prosecutor’s fallacy conflates the two.

quiz.q: The civil standard, balance of probabilities, requires…
options: more likely than not — just past fifty per cent
quiz.explanation: Civil justice tips the scales, and tipping past the midpoint suffices.

intro:
In 1948, with the liberated camps still fresh in memory, the UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: thirty articles, no enforcement machinery, and a claim that still startles — rights belong to every person simply for being human. Everything since, the covenants, the committees, the regional courts, a vocabulary dictators must speak too, grows from that document. Human rights law after 1948 is the story of trying to give the Declaration teeth without a world government to bite with.

**Why this matters.** Human rights are the only legal vocabulary that travels everywhere — invoked in constitutional courts, refugee camps, boardrooms and prison cells. Whether you regard them as humanity’s moral floor, a political project or a language of power, you cannot read the news without them. Their weakness is real: understanding why enforcement fails matters as much as celebrating the idea.
objectives: Explain from the Charter to the Universal Declaration
Explain the treaty pyramid: Covenants and conventions
Explain generations of rights
Explain universality versus cultural relativism
Explain regional systems and their courts
Explain monitoring: treaty bodies, rapporteurs and NGOs
Explain the enforcement gap and its politics

concepts.term: From the Charter to the Universal Declaration
concepts.statement: The UN Charter of 1945 promised human rights but defined none, and the Universal Declaration of 1948 filled the vacuum. Drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, with decisive input from René Cassin, P. C. Chang and Charles Malik, it deliberately fused civil liberties, due process, political participation and social entitlements into one list. It is not a treaty — initially it was dismissed as a non-binding aspiration — yet it outlived most of its critics and became the mother document of the entire field, cited by courts on every continent.
