Land, labour, capital and entrepreneurial talent are finite, so no society — and no household — can have everything. This is the economic problem, and it forces a question that prices, politics and prudence all try to answer: what to produce, how, and for whom? Economics is the study of those choices, and its first lesson is that every choice has a cost measured not in money but in the best alternative forgone. This lesson builds the method economists use to study choice — models, assumptions and a strict distinction between what is and what ought to be — before any markets, curves or policies arrive.

**Why this matters.** Examiners treat this material as the load-bearing wall of the subject: definitions of scarcity, opportunity cost and the frontier reappear inside every later question, from elasticity to development. It is also where the discipline explains itself — why economists use models, why they hold other things equal, and why honest answers so often begin with the phrase "it depends on the assumption".
objectives: Explain scarcity and the economic problem
Explain opportunity cost as the real price
Explain factors of production: land, labour, capital, enterprise
Explain the production possibilities frontier
Explain positive versus normative statements
Explain ceteris paribus and the role of models
Explain marginal analysis and sunk costs
Explain why economists disagree

concepts.statement: The condition that resources are finite while wants are unlimited. Scarcity is not the same as shortage — a shortage is a market outcome at a given price, while scarcity is the permanent starting point of the subject.

The value of the next best alternative sacrificed when a choice is made. The cost of an extra hour of study is the hour of rest given up; the cost of a new motorway is whatever else those funds and crews could have built. Money price is only part of the story.

The scarce inputs every economy combines: land (natural resources, earning rent), labour (human effort and skill, earning wages), capital (produced means of production, earning interest and profit) and enterprise (the risk-bearing that organises the other three, earning profit).

A diagram showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its current resources and technology. Points inside are feasible but wasteful, points on the curve are productively efficient, and points beyond are unreachable without growth.
A claim about what is, testable against evidence: "a rise in the minimum wage reduces teenage employment" can in principle be checked. Positive economics is the territory of data and models.

A claim about what ought to be, carrying a value judgment: "the rich should pay higher taxes" cannot be true or false in the way a fact can. Policy advice mixes both, and spotting the normative residue is a skill examiners explicitly test.

"Other things being equal" — the standing assumption that lets a model isolate one relationship at a time. Demand curves slope down, ceteris paribus; if incomes, tastes and rivals' prices all move at once, no single curve can be read.

The frontier makes the economic problem visible. Moving along the PPF from, say, healthcare to education shows opportunity cost as the slope: the first thousand teachers may cost little, because the resources released are poorly suited to healthcare anyway, but each further transfer costs more as increasingly specialised staff and equipment must be reassigned. That rising cost is the law of increasing opportunity cost, and it explains why the frontier bows outward rather than running straight. A straight-line frontier means resources switch at a constant rate — a useful simplification, an unrealistic description. Economic growth appears as the whole curve shifting outward: more resources, better technology or improved institutions move the boundary itself.

concepts.term: Opportunity cost as the real price
concepts.statement: The frontier also carries two distinct meanings of efficiency. Productive efficiency means operating on the curve — no more output is possible without sacrificing something else. Allocative efficiency means being at the point on the curve that society most values, which requires information about preferences that the diagram itself does not supply. The distinction matters because an economy can be productively efficient and still produce the wrong mix — missiles and no medicine — which is why the choice question "for whom and what" never reduces to the technical question "how".

concepts.term: Factors of production: land, labour, capital, enterprise
concepts.statement: Method is the quiet half of the topic. Economists cannot run laboratory trials on a whole economy, so they build models — deliberately small machines made of assumptions — and test their predictions against data. Marginal analysis is the workhorse: decisions are compared at the margin, asking whether one more unit adds more benefit than cost, and sunk costs are ignored because they are paid whatever happens. A student who abandons a useless course because the fee is already spent is applying the theory better than one who sits through two more years "to get the money's worth". Models are judged not by realism of assumptions but by usefulness of predictions — which is why the same profession can prize a one-factor trade model that no country fits perfectly.

Why do economists disagree? Partly over positive questions — which model fits the data — and partly, more stubbornly, over normative weights: how much to value equality against growth, present against future. Disagreement is not a failure of the discipline but a consequence of its subject matter: human choices under scarcity, where evidence is noisy and values differ. Recognising which half of a disagreement you are watching — facts or weights — is the fastest way to improve any argument about economic policy.

Three errors dominate scripts. First, defining opportunity cost as "money paid" — it is the next best alternative forgone, whether or not money changes hands. Second, calling a point inside the PPF "efficient because it is feasible": inside means idle or misallocated resources. Third, treating "should" statements as testable: mixing normative conclusions into positive analysis is precisely the boundary this topic draws, and examiners set questions to catch it.

examples.title: Reading opportunity cost off a frontier
examples.problem: Economic Methodology: Scarcity, Choice and How Economists Approach the World — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: An economy produces only wheat and cloth. At point A it makes 100 tonnes of wheat and 0 metres of cloth; at point B, 90 tonnes of wheat and 20 metres of cloth.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Moving from A to B, gaining 20 metres of cloth costs 10 tonnes of wheat. The opportunity cost of 1 metre of cloth is therefore 0.5 tonnes of wheat.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Moving from B to a point C at 80 tonnes of wheat and 45 metres of cloth, the next 25 metres of cloth cost 10 tonnes of wheat — opportunity cost per metre has fallen to 0.4, so here the frontier is locally flatter.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Now suppose the economy is producing at 100 wheat and 20 cloth. That bundle lies outside the frontier traced by A–B–C: it is unattainable with current resources, and only growth — immigration, investment, better looms — can reach it.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Finally, a minister argues "we should produce more cloth because cloth employment is fairer". Classify: the employment claim is normative; the statement "moving from A to B costs 10 tonnes of wheat" is positive and checkable.

keyTakeaways: Next: Supply, Demand and Elasticity — how markets answer the what, how and for whom questions this lesson poses.
Then: the comparative-advantage lesson, which reuses the frontier logic across countries rather than goods.
For policy work: When Markets Fail — where allocative efficiency is the measuring stick applied to real-world breakdowns.
Revision cue: practise converting one-sentence news claims into positive and normative parts.
Scarcity makes choice unavoidable; opportunity cost is the real price of every choice.
The PPF turns those costs into geometry: slope = opportunity cost, bow = increasing cost, shift = growth.
Productive efficiency is being on the frontier; allocative efficiency is being at the point society values most.
Positive claims are testable, normative claims are value judgments; good analysis keeps them labelled.
Models isolate with ceteris paribus, decide at the margin and ignore sunk costs.

quiz.q: A student gives up a part-time job paying 200 to attend an extra lecture. The direct cost of attending is 10 in travel. What is the opportunity cost of attending?
quiz.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone plus any direct costs: the 200 in wages given up plus the 10 in travel, totalling 210. The 200 is not "saved" — it is sacrificed.

quiz.q: Which statement is positive rather than normative?
options: Taxes on sugary drinks should be higher.
A 10% rise in the price of a good reduces quantity demanded, other things equal.
The government ought to spend more on railways than on roads.
Inequality is too high in most economies.
quiz.explanation: Only the second is testable against evidence. The others contain "should" and "ought" — value judgments that cannot be confirmed or refuted by data alone.

quiz.q: An economy moves along its bowed-out PPF, producing ever more of one good. Why does opportunity cost rise?
options: Because money wages rise as output grows
Because resources are not equally suited to both goods, so progressively less suitable ones must be switched
Because demand falls as more is produced
quiz.explanation: Increasing opportunity cost reflects heterogeneous resources: the first workers transferred to cloth may be weavers, the last may be farmers whose wheat output is very high, so each extra metre of cloth costs more wheat.

quiz.q: A firm has already paid a non-refundable 5,000 for a project. New information says continuing adds 3,000 of value at 4,000 of extra cost. Rational choice is to:
options: continue, to recover the 5,000 already spent
stop, because total costs 9,000 exceed total value 3,000
stop, because the 5,000 is sunk and the marginal cost 4,000 exceeds the marginal benefit 3,000
continue, because stopping admits a mistake
quiz.explanation: Sunk costs are irrelevant to the decision at the margin. Compare only the additional benefit (3,000) with the additional cost (4,000). Total-loss accounting, the fallacy behind option B, is exactly the error the topic tests.

intro:
Prices coordinate without anyone planning to, but coordination alone is a weak defence of markets. The stronger claim is about welfare: under the right conditions, a competitive equilibrium delivers the largest possible total gain to buyers and sellers combined. This lesson builds that claim from two areas on a diagram. Consumer surplus is what buyers value above what they pay; producer surplus is what sellers receive above what they would have accepted. Where supply meets demand, the sum of the two — community surplus — is maximised, and the marginal buyer values the good exactly at the marginal cost of making it. Every interference with that equilibrium redistributes surplus and usually destroys some of it, and the geometry says precisely how much.

**Why this matters.** Surplus analysis is the welfare toolkit that later topics assume. Market failure is defined as a shortfall from the community-surplus maximum; tax incidence questions are surplus-division questions; the deadweight triangles drawn around tariffs and monopoly are the same triangle computed here. Learn it once as arithmetic on a diagram and the rest of microeconomics reads as applications.
objectives: Explain consumer surplus as the area under demand, above price
Explain producer surplus as the area above supply, below price
Explain community surplus and the maximum-welfare claim
Explain allocative efficiency: price equals marginal cost
Explain productive efficiency at minimum average cost
Explain elasticity and the incidence of a tax
Explain deadweight loss as the measuring rod

concepts.statement: The maximum a buyer will give up for a unit — the height of the demand curve at that quantity. It encodes marginal benefit: the curve is not just a price-quantity relation but a ladder of valuations, tallest for the buyer who wants the good most.

The gap between willingness to pay and the price actually paid, summed over all units bought. On the diagram it is the area between the demand curve and the price line. A price fall raises it twice over: buyers pay less on units they already bought, and new buyers enter the market.

concepts.term: Marginal cost as the supply curve
concepts.statement: Under competition each seller offers units up to the point where price equals marginal cost, so the supply curve is the ladder of marginal costs. Producer surplus — price minus marginal cost, summed — is the area between the price line and the supply curve.

Consumer surplus plus producer surplus. At competitive equilibrium this total is as large as it can be: every unit for which someone's willingness to pay exceeds the marginal cost of production gets produced, and no unit beyond that point is made.

The condition that the last unit produced is worth exactly what it costs society to make: price equals marginal cost. Price measures the marginal buyer's benefit, marginal cost measures the resources absorbed; equality means the mix of goods cannot be improved by making more of one and less of another.

The community surplus destroyed when price departs from marginal cost — the triangle between demand and supply cut off by the interfering price or tax. It is not a transfer: nobody receives it. It is the value of trades that would have benefited both sides but never happen.

concepts.term: Consumer surplus as the area under demand, above price
concepts.statement: Elasticity decides who captures and who loses surplus when price moves. If demand is inelastic, buyers cannot escape a price rise, so they surrender a large slice of their surplus — the classic result that cigarette taxes land on smokers, not sellers. If demand is elastic, buyers defect and sellers absorb the blow. The same logic governs a tax: the side of the market that is relatively less elastic bears the larger share of the burden, whatever the law says about who writes the cheque. Statutory incidence and economic incidence are different animals, and elasticity is the beast that carries the burden between them.

concepts.term: Producer surplus as the area above supply, below price
concepts.statement: The efficiency conditions deserve their own statement, because competitive markets deliver both. Productive efficiency: in the long run, entry and exit drive price to the minimum of average total cost, so output is produced at the lowest possible resource cost per unit — waste is competed away. Allocative efficiency: price equals marginal cost, so the value of the last unit to consumers just covers what society gives up to make it. Both conditions together say the market neither wastes resources nor misdirects them — the two trophies the perfect-competition lesson derives from the firm's decision, restated here from society's ledger.

concepts.term: Community surplus and the maximum-welfare claim
concepts.statement: The claim has conditions, and the conditions are where the honest caveats live. Surplus is maximised only if prices carry all costs and benefits — an externality breaks the link between private and social marginal cost. It assumes no market power — a price setter holds price above marginal cost and parks a triangle for itself. It says nothing about the distribution of the surplus: a market can maximise community surplus while the consumer half goes hungry, which is why efficiency and equity are separate questions requiring separate instruments. The measuring rod is exact; what counts as a good reading is not the rod's job.

Students routinely read the surplus triangles off the wrong curves: consumer surplus runs between demand and price, producer surplus between price and supply — never between the two curves directly. A second trap is treating tax revenue as part of the loss; it is a transfer with its own uses. The third is assuming the side that legally pays a tax bears it — incidence follows elasticity, not the statute, and the exam question is almost always built on that inversion.

examples.title: Surplus arithmetic on a linear market
examples.problem: Competitive Markets: Efficiency, Surplus and Welfare — worked through step by step

steps.label: Demand
steps.text: P = 100 − Q. Supply: P = 20 + Q. Equilibrium: 100 − Q = 20 + Q, so Q = 40 and P = 60.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Consumer surplus is the triangle under demand above the price: base 40, height (100 − 60) = 40, area = ½ × 40 × 40 = 800.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Producer surplus is the triangle above supply below the price: base 40, height (60 − 20) = 40, area = 800. Community surplus = 1,600.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Now a 20-per-unit tax is imposed and, with symmetric elasticities here, splits evenly: buyers pay 70, sellers net 50, quantity falls to 30.

steps.label: New surpluses
steps.text: consumers ½ × 30 × 30 = 450; producers ½ × 30 × 30 = 450; government revenue 20 × 30 = 600. Total = 1,500.

steps.label: Step 6
steps.text: Deadweight loss = 1,600 − 1,500 = 100 — the triangle on the 10 units (30 to 40) whose willingness to pay exceeded marginal cost but which the tax now prices out. Revenue is a transfer; the 100 is the destruction.

keyTakeaways: Before: Supply, Demand and Elasticity — the curves and responsiveness measures used here as tools.
Next: When Markets Fail — what happens to community surplus when prices stop telling the truth.
Then: the tariff lesson, which runs this exact welfare accounting across borders.
Revision cue: redraw the taxed-market diagram from memory and label all four areas plus the triangle.
Demand and supply curves are ladders of marginal benefit and marginal cost.
Consumer plus producer surplus is maximised at competitive equilibrium.
P = MC is allocative efficiency; minimum ATC is productive efficiency.
Elasticity assigns the burden of any price intervention — the inelastic side pays.
Deadweight loss is destroyed surplus, not transferred surplus; it is the cost of the interference.

quiz.q: A buyer would pay 90 for a good priced at 60. What is her consumer surplus on that unit?
quiz.explanation: Consumer surplus is willingness to pay minus price: 90 − 60 = 30. Summing such gaps over all buyers gives the triangular area on the diagram.

quiz.q: A tax is placed on a good with highly inelastic demand. Who bears most of the burden, and why?
options: Sellers, because supply curves are always more elastic
Buyers, because they cannot easily reduce quantity when price rises
The government, because it collects the revenue
It is shared exactly equally regardless of elasticities
quiz.explanation: With inelastic demand, quantity barely falls when the tax raises the price, so buyers keep buying and absorb most of the burden. Elasticity, not the legal assignment of the tax, determines economic incidence.

quiz.q: Deadweight loss from a tax is best described as:
options: revenue the government wastes on administration
a transfer from consumers to producers
the value of mutually beneficial trades prevented by the tax
the difference between consumer and producer surplus
quiz.explanation: The triangle counts units for which willingness to pay exceeded marginal cost but which are no longer traded. Government revenue is a transfer, not a loss; the DWL is the genuinely destroyed part.

quiz.q: Allocative efficiency requires which condition?
quiz.explanation: P = MC aligns the marginal buyer's valuation with the marginal resource cost of production — the social optimum. Price equal to average cost is the break-even condition, a different test.

intro:
The tariff lesson explains why unilateral protection usually hurts the protecting country, and the retaliation analysis shows the trap: each country's best tariff makes both worse off, a prisoner's dilemma that worldwide agreements exist to escape. Regional integration is the halfway house — a group of countries liberalises among themselves faster than the world as a whole. Economists judge the result with a famous pair of concepts due to Jacob Viner: forming a bloc can create trade, replacing costly domestic production with cheaper partner production, or divert it, replacing cheap outside production with dearer partner production. Whether a bloc helps or harms turns on which force dominates, and the answer is empirical, case by case.

**Why this matters.** Exam questions on this topic are almost always evaluative: name the level of integration, apply creation versus diversion, and weigh sovereignty against scale. The concepts also explain the decade's biggest trade story — a large economy renegotiating and then leaving a customs union — so the theory has a live, expensive case study attached.
objectives: Explain the integration ladder: free trade area to economic union
Explain customs unions and the common external tariff
Explain trade creation versus trade diversion
Explain the single market: four freedoms
Explain why blocs form: lock-in, scale and bargaining power
Explain gATT Article XXIV and the WTO exception
Explain evaluating Brexit and the costs of leaving

concepts.statement: Members remove tariffs among themselves but keep their own external tariffs. The weakness is trade deflection: goods enter through the lowest-tariff member and flow freely onward, which is why FTAs need rules of origin documenting where a product was made.

A free trade area plus a common external tariff, so goods circulate internally without origin paperwork on tariffs. Deeper than an FTA but still short of a single market, because non-tariff barriers — different standards, checks, licensing — remain.

A customs union whose members also allow free movement of the factors of production: labour, capital and enterprise. People and firms as well as goods cross borders without restriction, requiring mutual recognition of qualifications and coordinated regulation.

Members harmonise — or in the monetary case surrender — economic policy itself: a common currency, a shared central bank, fiscal rules. The deepest rung short of full political union, and the one that makes integration irreversible enough to hurt when it unravels.

Integration replaces higher-cost domestic output with lower-cost output from a partner. Welfare rises: consumers pay less, the inefficient home industry releases resources, and the gain is genuine because production moves to a lower-cost source.

Integration replaces lower-cost output from outside the bloc with higher-cost output from a partner, simply because the partner now faces no tariff. Welfare falls for the importing country; the outside producer's loss is not offset by anything except the tariff revenue forgone.

concepts.term: The integration ladder: free trade area to economic union
concepts.statement: The World Trade Organization has a paradox at its heart: its most-favoured-nation rule demands that any tariff concession to one member be extended to all, yet it permits customs unions under Article XXIV, provided the bloc covers substantially all trade and does not raise barriers against outsiders. The rationale is political economy — deep liberalisation is easier to sell to domestic industries when it is reciprocal and regional — and the risk is that every exemption seeds a patchwork of preferential agreements, each with its own rules of origin, that quietly re-erects the maze the WTO exists to tear down.

concepts.term: Customs unions and the common external tariff
concepts.statement: Why do countries integrate at all, given the risks? Three motives recur. Lock-in: binding yourself to partners makes backsliding domestically unpopular or impossible — a credible commitment device for reforms governments know are right but cannot defend alone. Scale: a single market of hundreds of millions lets firms spread fixed costs, compete globally and attract investment that a national market could not support. Bargaining power: negotiating as a bloc rebalances leverage against large partners. The European project pressed all three, and its single market's four freedoms — goods, services, capital, people — remain the fullest real-world implementation of the common-market rung.

The costs of exit illuminate the value of membership. An economy leaving a customs union re-acquires its own tariff schedule, its own rules of origin on every exported good, and a border whose checks the single market had abolished; studies of the Brexit divergence consistently find trade below the pre-2016 trend and firms bearing new fixed paperwork costs, while the promised independent trade deals partially offset — slowly, and on terms set by partners who know the exiting country's urgency. The evaluation framework is exactly Viner's: recreating with the world what was surrendered with the bloc, one agreement at a time, against the diversion the split creates.

Do not call trade diversion "more trade" — it is misdirected trade, and the bloc can simultaneously create and divert on different products. Do not assume deeper integration is automatically better: each rung trades policy autonomy for market access, and the optimal depth differs by country. And never evaluate a bloc only by its members' trade volumes; the welfare test compares what was bought, from whom, at what price — including the outside world.

examples.title: Creation or diversion? A three-country arithmetic
examples.problem: Trade Protection and Regional Integration: Blocs, Trade Creation and Diversion — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Country A imports widgets. It can make them domestically at 12 per unit; country B (a prospective partner) produces at 8; the cheapest world producer C sells at 5.

steps.label: Before integration, A charges a tariff of 4
steps.text: the C price lands at 9, undercutting both B (8 + 4 = 12) and domestic production (12). A imports from C and collects 4 per unit.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: A and B now form a customs union with the external tariff unchanged. The B price drops to 8 — imports switch from C to B.

steps.label: Trade creation effect
steps.text: A previously paid 9 to C, now pays 8 to B — consumers gain, and production has moved toward the true low-cost available source within the union.

steps.label: Trade diversion effect
steps.text: production moved away from the true global minimum (C at 5) to B at 8. A also loses the 4 tariff revenue it used to collect per unit.

steps.label: Verdict
steps.text: net effect depends on the quantities. If A switches a large volume from domestic production (12) to B (8), creation dominates and welfare rises; if most imports were already coming from C, diversion dominates and A is worse off — the textbook ambiguity examiners want discussed, not resolved by assertion.

keyTakeaways: Before: Trade Policy: Tariffs, Quotas and Trade Wars — the welfare toolkit and the retaliation dilemma blocs answer.
Next: Exchange Rates and the Balance of Payments — the monetary rung of the ladder and its crises.
Revision cue: write the ladder from memory — FTA, customs union, common market, economic union — with one example at each rung.
Integration deepens by rungs: FTA, customs union, common market, economic union.
Viner's test: weigh trade creation against trade diversion; the net is an empirical question.
Rules of origin are the FTA's price for keeping separate external tariffs.
Article XXIV lets blocs exist inside the WTO's non-discrimination rules under conditions.
Lock-in, scale and bargaining power — not just prices — drive countries to integrate.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a customs union from a free trade area?
options: A customs union removes all internal tariffs; an FTA does not
A customs union adds a common external tariff; an FTA keeps members' external tariffs separate
An FTA allows labour mobility; a customs union does not
There is no difference in practice
quiz.explanation: Both remove internal barriers; the customs union's common external tariff is what eliminates trade deflection and the need for tariff-based rules of origin.

quiz.q: Trade diversion occurs when:
options: a bloc member exports more after integration
imports switch from a lower-cost outside producer to a higher-cost partner because of preferential treatment
a country stops producing a good entirely
tariff revenue replaces income tax revenue
quiz.explanation: Diversion is the welfare-losing switch created by the preference itself: the partner wins the market not by efficiency but by exemption from the external tariff.

quiz.q: Why does the WTO permit customs unions despite the most-favoured-nation principle?
options: Because members of a bloc are exempt from WTO membership
Because the agreements satisfy Article XXIV conditions covering substantially all trade without raising external barriers
Because customs unions abolish all tariffs worldwide
Because the WTO has no jurisdiction over regional agreements
quiz.explanation: Article XXIV is the deliberate exception: deep regional liberalisation is allowed when it is comprehensive and non-discriminatory toward outsiders — the checked conditions, not an absence of jurisdiction.

quiz.q: A country joining a customs union finds its imports switch almost entirely from the cheapest world producer to a partner whose price is slightly higher. The most likely net effect is:
options: unambiguous welfare gain from trade creation
welfare loss dominated by trade diversion
no effect, since total imports are unchanged
a gain equal to the tariff revenue collected
quiz.explanation: When imports were already sourced from the efficient outside producer, preference-driven switching mostly destroys the price advantage and forfeits revenue — the diversion-dominated case.

intro:
On the first day of a financial year a firm pays ₹100,000 for a packaging machine, and the journal entry takes a moment: debit Machinery, credit Bank. The harder question starts the next morning, when the machine has already begun to die. It will run for perhaps ten years before it is worth little more than scrap. Depreciation is the machinery for recognising that slow death — carving the machine's cost into the years that actually consumed it. This lesson builds the concept from the matching principle, works the two classical methods on the same machine, shows the entries for charges and disposal, and then separates provisions (charges against profit) from reserves (appropriations of it).

**Why this matters.** In a capital-heavy business, depreciation is often the largest figure in the profit and loss account after materials and wages. Ignore it and profit is fiction: dividends eat into capital, tax is charged on income that never existed, and replacement day arrives with an empty bank balance. The provision-versus-reserve distinction decides whether a balance-sheet entry is an obligation or a choice — and whether it may lawfully be paid out as dividend.
objectives: Explain depreciation as matching: spreading cost over useful life
Explain wear and tear, effluxion of time, and obsolescence
Explain cost, salvage value, and depreciable amount
Explain straight line versus written down value schedules
Explain recording via the asset account or a provision account
Explain change of method applied prospectively
Explain provisions as charges, reserves as appropriations
Explain provision for doubtful debts and its year-end adjustment

concepts.term: Depreciation as matching: spreading cost over useful life
concepts.statement: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of a fixed asset's cost over its useful life. The wording is deliberate: this is allocation, not valuation — expensing each period's fair share of a cost already incurred, exactly the matching logic of the accounting-cycle lesson, not guessing what the machine would fetch today. Three forces make allocation necessary. Wear and tear is physical: parts abrade, accuracy drifts, output slows. Effluxion of time is calendrical: leases and patents expire by date, used or not. Obsolescence is economic: a healthy machine becomes worthless when a faster one appears. Two consequences follow. Depreciation is a charge, not an option — recorded even in a loss year, because the asset decayed regardless of the firm's fortunes. And land, with no finite life, is the standing exception: not depreciated unless it holds a wasting resource such as a quarry.

concepts.term: Wear and tear, effluxion of time, and obsolescence
concepts.statement: Three inputs drive every computation. Cost is everything spent to bring the asset to working condition: invoice price minus trade discount, plus freight, duties, installation and wiring. Useful life is the expected span of economic service — always the shorter of physical and commercial life; statutes prescribe minimum lives for common asset classes that departures must justify. Salvage (scrap) value is the amount expected on disposal. Cost minus salvage is the depreciable amount, the total to spread. Life and salvage are estimates revisited each year end; a revision changes the current and future years' charges only.
$$D = \frac{C - S}{n} \quad \text{or} \quad D = C \times r$$
concepts.detail: Annual depreciation D equals depreciable amount (cost C minus salvage S) divided by useful life n — equivalently, a fixed percentage r of cost. Every year carries an identical charge, so book value falls in a straight line toward salvage.

concepts.statement: $$D_t = B_{t-1} \times r, \qquad B_n = C\,(1 - r)^n$$
concepts.detail: Each year's charge is a fixed percentage r of the opening book (written down) value B, not of original cost. The charge starts large and shrinks geometrically; book value approaches zero but never lands, so the last stretch is settled by the sale proceeds.

concepts.term: Cost, salvage value, and depreciable amount
concepts.statement: Choosing between them is a judgement about the pattern of benefit. Straight line suits assets that render uniform service — buildings, furniture, pipelines. Written down value suits assets that work hardest when young — vehicles, computers, machinery whose repairs mount as precision fades — because its falling charge offsets the rising repair bill, keeping the annual burden roughly level. Indian tax practice follows written down value for most blocks of assets, one reason it dominates local bookkeeping.

concepts.term: Straight line versus written down value schedules
concepts.statement: The charge can be recorded one of two ways. Under the asset (charging-off) method, depreciation is credited directly to the asset account, so Machinery itself shrinks every year to book value. Under the provision method — mandatory for companies — the asset sits permanently at cost and accumulated depreciation lives in a separate Provision for Depreciation account. The year-end entry has the same shape either way: Depreciation is debited and closed to profit and loss; only the credit target differs. The provision route keeps cost and cumulative charge visible on the ledger's face — machinery at cost, less accumulated depreciation, equals net block.

concepts.term: Recording via the asset account or a provision account
concepts.statement: A change in depreciation method is treated prospectively, as a change in accounting estimate rather than policy: switching methods is new information about how the asset is consumed, not a rewrite of history. The book value on the date of change becomes the de facto cost, spread over the remaining useful life under the new method, with no catch-up restating past years. If the ₹100,000 machine above has reached ₹65,610 after four years on WDV and straight line is now judged more faithful for its remaining six years, the annual charge becomes 65,610 divided by six, or ₹10,935, from this year forward.

Depreciation has two siblings named for their assets. Depletion prices wasting natural resources — mines, wells, quarries — per unit extracted: (cost minus restoration and salvage) divided by estimated total units, times the year's offtake. Amortisation writes off intangible assets — patents, copyrights, software, leasehold premia — normally straight line over the shorter of legal and useful life, with an impairment test whenever value looks wounded. The idea is identical; only the asset's costume changes.

concepts.term: Provisions as charges, reserves as appropriations
concepts.statement: A provision is a charge against profit for a known liability or expected loss whose exact amount is uncertain — the obligation exists, but measuring it needs estimation. Provision for doubtful debts anticipates the receivables that will not pay; provision for taxation estimates the year's tax charge; a warranty provision prices the repairs the law will demand on goods already sold. Being charges, provisions are debited to profit and loss before net profit is struck — made whether the year was profitable or not, and able to push a marginal year into loss.

concepts.term: Provision for doubtful debts and its year-end adjustment
concepts.statement: A reserve is an appropriation of profit — a slice of an already-computed net profit withheld from distribution. Reserves exist only where there are profits and a decision to withhold them. A general reserve bolsters the balance sheet for unnamed needs; a specific reserve earmarks a purpose such as dividend equalisation; a capital reserve (share premium, profit on revaluation) arises from non-operating events and cannot be distributed as dividend, while revenue reserves can. Reserve creation does not reduce the profit and loss account — it happens below that line.

First, do not depreciate land — its life is indefinite. Second, never dress a provision up as a reserve: doubtful-debt provisions are compulsory charges, not prudence piggy banks. Third, secret reserves — deliberately understating assets or overstating liabilities to hide strength — are prohibited for companies because they make accounts untruthful. Fourth, a provision balance is not cash sitting somewhere; it is a deduction or a liability, and no bank account backs it.
Systematic allocation of a fixed asset's cost over its useful life, driven by wear and tear, time or obsolescence.
Cost minus expected salvage value; the total to be spread over the years.
Equal annual depreciation — depreciable amount over useful life, or a fixed percentage of cost.
A fixed percentage of each year's opening book value, giving a declining charge that never reaches zero.
Accumulates depreciation credits while the asset account stays at cost.
Loss of value from becoming outdated rather than worn out.
A charge against profit for a known liability or expected loss whose amount must be estimated.
An appropriation of net profit withheld from distribution to strengthen the firm or earmark a use.
Value deliberately hidden by understating assets or overstating liabilities; prohibited for companies.

examples.title: Worked Example: One Machine, Two Methods
examples.problem: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves — worked through step by step

steps.label: Setup
steps.text: machinery costing ₹100,000, life 10 years, no salvage. Depreciate at 10 per cent — on cost for straight line, on opening book value for written down value — for the first four years.

steps.label: Straight line
steps.text: 10 per cent of ₹100,000 is ₹10,000 every year. After four years the total charged is ₹40,000 and the book value stands at ₹60,000.

steps.label: Written down value
steps.text: year one charges ₹10,000 (10 per cent of 100,000), leaving ₹90,000. Year two charges ₹9,000, leaving ₹81,000. Year three charges ₹8,100, leaving ₹72,900. Year four charges ₹7,290, leaving ₹65,610.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: over the same four years SLM has charged ₹40,000 against WDV's ₹34,390 — WDV shelters early profit and charges more in the tail years.

examples.title: Worked Example: Annual Entries Both Ways
examples.problem: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves — worked through step by step

steps.label: Asset method
steps.text: Depreciation A/c Dr ₹10,000; To Machinery A/c ₹10,000 — the machine account itself drops to ₹90,000. Close it: Profit and Loss A/c Dr ₹10,000; To Depreciation A/c ₹10,000.

steps.label: Provision method
steps.text: Depreciation A/c Dr ₹10,000; To Provision for Depreciation A/c ₹10,000 — Machinery stays at ₹100,000 while the provision accumulates each year.

steps.label: Balance sheet effect
steps.text: either route presents net book value ₹90,000.

examples.title: Worked Example: Selling a Partly Depreciated Machine
examples.problem: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: A machine costing ₹50,000 has run three full years under straight line at 10 per cent: the Provision for Depreciation holds ₹15,000, book value is ₹35,000, and it is sold on 31 March for ₹38,000.

steps.label: Entry
steps.text: Bank A/c Dr ₹38,000; Provision for Depreciation A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Machinery A/c ₹50,000; To Profit on Sale of Machinery ₹3,000.

steps.label: Reading
steps.text: cash plus accumulated provision (₹53,000) retires the ₹50,000 cost, and the ₹3,000 surplus is a gain to profit and loss; a ₹30,000 sale would have produced a loss on sale instead.

examples.title: Worked Example: Provision for Doubtful Debts Across Two Years
examples.problem: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves — worked through step by step

steps.label: Year 1
steps.text: during the year, ₹2,000 owed by a customer is written off — Bad Debts A/c Dr ₹2,000; To Debtors A/c ₹2,000 — and closed to profit and loss. Debtors stand at ₹80,000; the firm carries a 5 per cent provision of ₹4,000.

steps.label: Year 1 creation
steps.text: Profit and Loss A/c Dr ₹4,000; To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c ₹4,000. The balance sheet nets the debtors to ₹76,000.

steps.label: Year 2
steps.text: debtors stand at ₹60,000, so the required provision is ₹3,000 — the existing ₹4,000 is excessive by ₹1,000.

steps.label: Year 2 write-back
steps.text: Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c Dr ₹1,000; To Profit and Loss A/c ₹1,000. Created by debit, released by credit, never left stale.

keyTakeaways: Straight line schedule — Year 1: depreciation ₹10,000, closing book value ₹90,000
Straight line schedule — Year 2: depreciation ₹10,000, closing book value ₹80,000
Straight line schedule — Year 3: depreciation ₹10,000, closing book value ₹70,000
Straight line schedule — Year 4: depreciation ₹10,000, closing book value ₹60,000
Written down value schedule — Year 1: depreciation ₹10,000, closing book value ₹90,000
Written down value schedule — Year 2: depreciation ₹9,000, closing book value ₹81,000
Written down value schedule — Year 3: depreciation ₹8,100, closing book value ₹72,900
Written down value schedule — Year 4: depreciation ₹7,290, closing book value ₹65,610
Nature — a provision is a charge against profit; a reserve is an appropriation of profit.
Timing — provisions are debited before net profit is struck; reserves after it.
Compulsion — provisions are made even in a loss year; reserves only from profits.
Distribution — revenue reserves may fund dividends; provisions cannot.
Purpose — a provision absorbs a known liability or expected loss; a reserve strengthens the financial position.
Examples — doubtful debts, taxation, warranty provisions; general, dividend equalisation and capital reserves.

Where next — This lesson assumes the debit-and-credit fluency of Double-Entry Bookkeeping: The Logic Behind Every Ledger and the accrual matching idea from The Accounting Cycle: Accruals, Adjustments and Closing the Books. Where the numbers land on the balance sheet is shown in Reading Financial Statements, and the revaluation of assets in Partnership Accounts II picks these tools up again when a new partner arrives.
Depreciation allocates cost over useful life to match cost with revenue; a compulsory charge, never an optional appropriation.
Depreciable amount = cost minus salvage; life and salvage are estimates revisited each year end.
Straight line charges an equal sum yearly; written down value charges a fixed percentage of a shrinking base — heavy early, light late.
On the ₹100,000 machine at 10 per cent, four years cost ₹40,000 under SLM but only ₹34,390 under WDV.
Record depreciation straight to the asset account or into a Provision for Depreciation account; companies use the provision route.
On disposal, compare proceeds plus accumulated depreciation with cost: the difference is profit or loss on sale.
A method change is prospective: book value becomes the new cost, spread over the remaining life.
Depletion prices extracted resources per unit; amortisation writes off intangibles over the shorter of legal and useful life.
Provisions are compulsory charges for known-but-uncertain liabilities; reserves are discretionary appropriations, and secret reserves are prohibited for companies.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a cause of depreciation?
options: Fluctuation in the asset's market price
quiz.explanation: Depreciation allocates cost over life; market swings never enter it.

quiz.q: An asset costs ₹200,000 and is depreciated at 10 per cent on the written down value basis. The second year's depreciation is:
quiz.explanation: Year one charges ₹20,000 leaving ₹180,000; year two charges 10 per cent of that — ₹18,000.

quiz.q: Which statement about provisions versus reserves is correct?
options: Both are created only when the firm earns a profit
A provision is a charge against profit while a reserve is an appropriation of profit
Reserves must be created even in a loss year, provisions need not be
A provision can be distributed as dividend but a reserve cannot
quiz.explanation: Provisions are debited before net profit is struck and are compulsory; reserves are carved from profit after it is computed.

quiz.q: A machine costs ₹80,000 with salvage value ₹8,000 and a life of 8 years. Annual straight line depreciation is:
quiz.explanation: Depreciable amount is ₹80,000 minus ₹8,000, or ₹72,000, spread over 8 years — ₹9,000 per year.

quiz.q: A firm switches depreciation methods for a partly used asset. Under the prospective treatment, the new annual charge is computed by:
options: Restating all past years and catching up the cumulative difference
Spreading the current book value over the remaining useful life under the new method
Applying the new rate to the original cost from year one
Ignoring the change until the asset is sold
quiz.explanation: The change is a change in estimate: book value on the switch date becomes the new base for the remaining life, with no rewrite of history.

intro:
Month end. The cash book's bank column says the account holds ₹40,000; the bank statement says ₹33,900. Both figures are right. Nothing has been stolen, no one has blundered, and yet the two records of the same account disagree by ₹6,100 — because they were written by two different people at two different moments, each recording events the other has not yet seen. Bank reconciliation is the discipline of listing, valuing and explaining every one of those differences so that a single question can be answered in minutes: where did the firm's money actually go? This lesson classifies the causes, builds the plus-and-minus logic that drives every statement, works a full reconciliation and its mirror-image overdraft case, and shows when the correct response is not a statement at all but a corrected cash book.

**Why this matters.** Cash is the most liquid asset a firm owns and therefore the most tempting target for fraud and the most common victim of error. A monthly reconciliation is the cheapest audit in existence: it catches forgotten standing orders, bank charges, customer cheques that bounced, deposits credited to the wrong account, and the classic defalcation in which cheques are drawn and the cash book is quietly updated later. Lenders and auditors treat an unreconciled bank account as a red flag on its own.
objectives: Explain cash book versus pass book: mirror-image records
Explain timing differences: cheques in transit in both directions
Explain bank-initiated entries: charges, direct credits, standing orders
Explain plus and minus logic from either starting balance
Explain favourable balance versus overdraft sign flips
Explain amending the cash book before reconciling
Explain dishonoured cheques and their double record

concepts.term: Cash book versus pass book: mirror-image records
concepts.statement: Two books describe one account. The cash book — introduced in the double-entry lesson as the firm's journal of cash and bank movements — records transactions when the firm learns of them. The pass book (bank statement) is the bank's own ledger, written when the bank processes the item. They are mirror images: money deposited is a debit in the cash book's bank column but a credit in the bank's books, because the bank owes the depositor that balance; the same inversion applies to every withdrawal. A favourable balance is therefore a debit in the cash book and a credit on the pass book, while an overdraft — the account running negative — is a credit in the cash book and a debit in the statement. Keep the mirror rule in view and half the confusion of reconciliation dissolves on contact.

concepts.term: Timing differences: cheques in transit in both directions
concepts.statement: Differences arise for three broad reasons. First, timing: a cheque the firm issues today crosses the counter, spends days in the postal system and is presented to the bank only next week — the cash book has moved, the bank has not. The same lag applies to deposits: money paid in late on the last day may not be cleared and credited until the next. Second, knowledge: the bank does things the firm learns about only when the statement arrives — deducting its charges and interest, crediting interest earned, collecting a customer's direct electronic transfer or an outgoing dividend, paying an insurance premium under a standing order, bouncing a customer's cheque marked refer to drawer. The statement knows first; the cash book must catch up. Third, error: either side can mispost, cast wrong, or credit Mr Sharma when it meant Mr Verma — and errors are found precisely because the reconciliation forces a line-by-line comparison.
$$\text{Pass book balance} = \text{Cash book balance} + \text{items the bank recorded first as credits} - \text{items the bank recorded first as debits} \;\pm\; \text{timing adjustments}$$
concepts.detail: Starting from the cash book's favourable (debit) balance, add everything that increases the bank's version of the account and deduct everything that decreases it — items in transit and bank-only entries alike — to arrive at the balance the statement must show. Start from the pass book instead and every sign flips.

concepts.term: Bank-initiated entries: charges, direct credits, standing orders
concepts.statement: The plus-and-minus table is the working heart of the exercise, and it is worth memorising rather than re-deriving under pressure. Starting from a favourable balance as per the cash book, add: cheques issued but not presented (the bank will reduce the balance later, so the true balance is higher than the cash book shows); amounts directly credited by the bank such as interest, dividends and customers' direct transfers; and any bank error that wrongly debited the firm. Deduct: cheques deposited but not yet collected; bank charges and interest debited; payments made under standing orders; dishonoured cheques of customers; and any bank error that wrongly credited the firm. Starting from the pass book balance, every one of these directions reverses — presented-but-unrecorded cheques get deducted, uncollected deposits get added, and so on.

concepts.term: Plus and minus logic from either starting balance
concepts.statement: Overdrafts flip the arithmetic because the starting balance is negative. When the cash book shows a credit balance — an overdraft — its figure is stated as a negative number, so items that would normally be added now make the overdraft smaller and items normally deducted make it larger. Suppose the cash book shows an overdraft of ₹10,000, cheques of ₹4,000 have been issued but not presented, and deposits of ₹2,500 are uncollected: the pass book overdraft is 10,000 minus 4,000 plus 2,500, or ₹8,500. A practical guard: write the opening balance with its sign, treat every adjustment as a signed number, and let the arithmetic produce the answer — never memorise a second table for overdrafts.

concepts.term: Favourable balance versus overdraft sign flips
concepts.statement: A reconciliation statement is the right tool for pure timing differences, but bank-initiated entries are not timing items at all — they are transactions the firm has genuinely failed to record, and the cash book is simply wrong until it records them. The disciplined two-step method handles this. Step one: amend the cash book for every item the statement reveals that the firm should have booked — bank charges, direct credits, standing orders, dishonoured cheques, correcting the firm's own errors — arriving at an adjusted balance. Step two: prepare a reconciliation statement that deals only with the genuine timing items, cheques in transit in both directions. The result must equal the pass book balance exactly, and a mismatch means something was mis-sorted between the two steps.

First, never record timing items in the cash book — a cheque in transit is not an unrecorded transaction, and booking it double-counts the money when it clears. Second, know your starting point: adjustments added from the cash-book side are deducted from the pass-book side, and vice versa. Third, a dishonoured customer cheque is not merely a bank matter — the receivable must be restored by debiting the customer. Fourth, with overdrafts, signs invert; a surprising number of errors trace to adding where the opening balance was negative. Finally, an unreconciled difference that will not resolve is not rounding — chase it to an error or a missing item before signing anything.
The firm's own record of its bank account, written from the firm's knowledge of transactions.
The bank's record of the same account, a mirror image in which deposits are credits and withdrawals are debits.
A cheque issued or deposited that the counterparty bank has not yet processed; the classic timing difference.
An instruction empowering the bank to pay a recurring sum automatically; known to the statement before the cash book.
Money the bank credits on the firm's behalf — interest, dividends, a customer's electronic transfer — before the firm records it.
The bank's refusal to pay a deposited cheque, debiting the account back and reviving the customer's debt.
A positive bank balance: debit in the cash book, credit in the pass book.
A negative balance: credit in the cash book, debit on the statement — the case where every reconciliation sign inverts.

examples.title: Worked Example: A Full Statement from the Cash Book Side
examples.problem: Bank Reconciliation: Explaining Every Difference — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: On 31 March the cash book (bank column) shows a debit balance of ₹40,000. The statement is awaited, and these differences are identified.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Cheques issued to suppliers totalling ₹12,000 have not been presented — add.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Cheques deposited totalling ₹18,000 have not been collected — deduct.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Bank charges of ₹300 appear only in the statement — deduct.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Interest of ₹900 credited by the bank appears only in the statement — add.

steps.label: Step 6
steps.text: A customer paid ₹5,000 directly into the firm's account by electronic transfer; the firm learns of it from the statement — add.

steps.label: Step 7
steps.text: An insurance premium of ₹2,200 was paid by the bank under a standing order; the firm had not recorded it — deduct.

steps.label: Step 8
steps.text: A customer's cheque for ₹3,500 was returned dishonoured and debited by the bank — deduct.

steps.label: Statement
steps.text: 40,000 + 12,000 - 18,000 - 300 + 900 + 5,000 - 2,200 - 3,500 = ₹33,900, the credit balance the pass book must show on 31 March.

examples.title: Worked Example: The Overdraft Case
examples.problem: Bank Reconciliation: Explaining Every Difference — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Cash book shows an overdraft (credit balance) of ₹10,000 on 31 March.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Cheques of ₹4,000 issued but not presented will reduce the overdraft when honoured — treat as plus 4,000.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Cheques of ₹2,500 deposited but not collected will increase the overdraft when processed — treat as minus 2,500.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Pass book overdraft = -10,000 + 4,000 - 2,500 = ₹8,500 overdrawn (a debit balance of ₹8,500 on the statement).

examples.title: Worked Example: Same Data, Amended Cash Book Route
examples.problem: Bank Reconciliation: Explaining Every Difference — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Amend the ₹40,000 cash book balance for the statement-only items: deduct bank charges ₹300; add interest ₹900; add the customer's direct transfer ₹5,000; deduct the standing order ₹2,200; deduct the dishonoured cheque ₹3,500 — the cash book restates the balance at 40,000 - 300 + 900 + 5,000 - 2,200 - 3,500 = ₹39,900.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Note the entry the dishonour requires in the books: Customer A/c Dr ₹3,500; To Bank A/c ₹3,500 — the debt springs back to life, and the bank column absorbs the reversal.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Reconcile the amended balance for timing items only: 39,900 + 12,000 (issued, not presented) - 18,000 (deposited, not collected) = ₹33,900.

steps.label: Cross-check
steps.text: both routes end at the identical ₹33,900 — the statement method in one line, the amended-book method in two, and the agreement of the two is itself the proof of the work.

keyTakeaways: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment — cash book already credited, bank not yet debited.
Cheques deposited but not yet collected or cleared — cash book already debited, bank not yet credited.
Bank charges, interest and fees debited in the pass book only.
Direct credits — interest allowed, dividends and direct deposits from customers — credited in the pass book only.
Cheques received from customers and dishonoured — debited in the pass book, unknown to the cash book until reported.
Standing orders and direct debits — rent, insurance, loan instalments — paid by the bank under prior instruction.
Errors of omission or commission by either the firm or the bank.

Where next — You need the cash book mechanics and the debit-credit mirror from Double-Entry Bookkeeping: The Logic Behind Every Ledger before this lesson, and the adjusting-entry mindset of The Accounting Cycle: Accruals, Adjustments and Closing the Books for the amended cash book step. The provision concept met here resurfaces in Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves, and the reconciled balance flows into the statements covered in Reading Financial Statements.
Cash book and pass book record the same account as mirror images: deposits are debits in one and credits in the other.
Differences come from timing (cheques in transit both ways), knowledge (bank-only entries), and outright error.
From a favourable cash book balance: add unpresented cheques and direct credits; deduct uncollected deposits, charges, standing orders and dishonoured cheques.
From the pass book side, every adjustment direction reverses.
Overdrafts are negative balances — work with signs rather than memorising a second table.
Bank-only items are not timing items: amend the cash book for charges, direct credits, standing orders and dishonours, then reconcile the rest.
A dishonoured customer cheque revives the receivable: debit Customer, credit Bank.
The worked case: ₹40,000 cash book balance reconciles to a ₹33,900 pass book credit, or to an amended book of ₹39,900 plus timing items of +12,000 and -18,000.

quiz.q: Starting from a favourable cash book balance, cheques issued but not yet presented are:
options: Deducted, because the bank has already paid them
Added, because the true bank balance is higher than the cash book shows
Ignored, because the cash book is authoritative
Deducted, because they are the firm's payments
quiz.explanation: The cash book has already credited these cheques; until the bank pays them, the actual account holds more than the cash book records — so they raise the cash book figure toward the statement figure.

quiz.q: A customer's cheque for ₹3,500 is returned dishonoured and appears in the statement only. In the firm's books this requires:
options: No entry until the customer pays again
quiz.explanation: The bank reversal must be taken out of the bank column, and the receivable comes back on the books: debit the customer, credit bank.

quiz.q: Which item belongs in the AMENDED cash book rather than in the reconciliation statement?
options: Bank charges debited by the bank
A cheque posted by the bank to another customer's account in error
quiz.explanation: Bank charges are a real transaction the firm failed to record — the cash book itself must be corrected. The others are timing differences or the bank's error to reverse.

quiz.q: The cash book shows an overdraft of ₹10,000. Cheques of ₹4,000 are unpresented and deposits of ₹2,500 are uncollected. The pass book overdraft is:
quiz.explanation: Unpresented cheques shrink the overdraft (add 4,000); uncollected deposits deepen it (subtract 2,500): -10,000 + 4,000 - 2,500 = -8,500.

quiz.q: In the pass book, a customer's direct deposit into the firm's account appears as a:
options: Debit, because it reduces what the bank owes
Credit, because the bank's debt to the depositor has grown
Debit, because cash has physically entered the bank
quiz.explanation: The pass book is the bank's ledger: money the bank now owes the firm is a credit — the mirror image of the debit the firm will place in its cash book.

intro:
Two friends start a firm. One contributes ₹600,000 of savings; the other contributes clients, working days and a talent for selling. Within a year the firm earns ₹220,000 — and who owns what share of that is answered not by fairness or hours logged but by a document most partners never read closely until money appears: the partnership deed. Partnership accounting is double-entry bookkeeping with a human layer on top — the owners are also managers, so profit is not merely measured but divided, and the rules of division must be recorded as carefully as any sale. This lesson covers the statutory defaults that operate when the deed says nothing, fixed and fluctuating capital accounts, the profit and loss appropriation account that stages the division, interest on capital, salaries and drawings — including the product method — and the guarantee of profit that protects a nervous newcomer.

**Why this matters.** Partnership is among the most common forms of business on earth, and partnership disputes are among the most expensive. Almost every such dispute traces to a silent deed: no interest rate fixed, no salary agreed, no ratio recorded. The accountant's job is to make the division of profit mechanical, transparent and defensible — so that when the profitable year arrives, the ledger answers questions instead of starting arguments.
objectives: Explain statutory defaults when the deed is silent
Explain partnership deed essentials
Explain fixed versus fluctuating capital accounts
Explain the profit and loss appropriation account
Explain interest on capital, salary and commission to partners
Explain product method and average period for interest on drawings
Explain drawings against profits versus against capital
Explain guarantee of profit to a partner

concepts.term: Statutory defaults when the deed is silent
concepts.statement: When the deed is silent, legislation supplies a set of defaults — worth memorising because they surprise people. Absent any agreement to the contrary, profits and losses are shared equally, no matter how unequal the capital contributed. No partner receives interest on capital, and no partner receives salary or other remuneration, however many hours they work. No interest is charged on drawings. But a partner who has lent money to the firm beyond their capital — a loan, not an equity stake — receives interest at 6 per cent per annum, a charge against profit payable even in a loss year. These defaults are the accounting baseline only; the statute that houses them belongs to business-law study.

The partnership deed is the agreement that overrides every default above, and a well-drafted one is specific where the statute is silent. Its accounting-relevant clauses: the capital each partner will contribute and whether those capitals are fixed; the profit-sharing ratio; the rates of interest on capital and on drawings; any salaries, commissions or bonuses to working partners; limits on drawings; and — critically for the second partnership lesson — how goodwill will be valued and how a retiring or deceased partner will be paid out. Where the deed is genuinely silent, the statutory default fills the gap; where the deed speaks, the deed wins.

Partners' capital can be kept one of two ways. Under the fluctuating capital method — the default when the deed says nothing — each partner has a single account that breathes with the business: capital introduced, interest on capital, salary, commission and the share of profit are credited; drawings and interest on drawings are debited; and the closing balance is whatever remains. Under the fixed capital method, the capital account is pinned at the agreed figure and moves only for permanent changes — deliberate fresh capital or a permanent withdrawal. Every recurring item runs instead through a separate Current account: interest, salary and profit share credited there, drawings and their interest debited there. A credit current-account balance is a liability of the firm; a debit balance is an asset, in substance a temporary loan from a partner who drew more than they earned.

concepts.term: The profit and loss appropriation account
concepts.statement: The profit and loss account measures how well the business performed; the appropriation account divides what it earned. The distinction matters because interest on capital, partner salaries and commissions are not expenses of running the business — they are distributions of its result, and charging them above the profit line would understate performance to outsiders. The sequence is fixed by logic: net profit is transferred in; interest on drawings is added (it claws back a benefit partners already enjoyed); interest on capital, salaries and commissions are deducted; and the residue — the divisible profit — is shared in the agreed ratio. If the residue is negative, the appropriations are adjusted per the deed, which is why deeds specify whether interest on capital is payable only out of profits.

concepts.term: Interest on drawings: product method and average period
concepts.statement: $$I = \frac{\sum (\text{amount} \times \text{months outstanding}) \times r}{12} \qquad \text{or} \qquad I = \text{Total drawings} \times r \times \frac{\text{average period}}{12}$$
concepts.detail: Each drawing earns interest from its date to the year end (the product of amount and months outstanding); the sum of products times the monthly rate gives the charge. For equal monthly drawings the shortcut applies: average period is 6.5 months when drawings fall at the beginning of each month and 5.5 months at the end, because the first drawing is outstanding 12 or 11 months and the last one or zero.

concepts.term: Interest on capital, salary and commission to partners
concepts.statement: Drawings come in two flavours and the difference is not cosmetic. Drawings against profits — the ordinary kind — are anticipatory slices of the year's expected result: debited to the drawings or current account during the year, transferred at its close, and charged interest under the deed. Drawings against capital are permanent withdrawals of the capital itself: debited straight to the capital account, and they attract no interest on drawings, because they are not an advance of profit but a reduction of stake.

concepts.term: Product method and average period for interest on drawings
concepts.statement: A guarantee of profit is a promise that a partner will receive at least a stated minimum, whatever the arithmetic of the ratio produces. The guarantee does not create profit; it re-routes it. Compute the divisible profit normally and give the guaranteed partner their share; if the share falls short of the minimum, the shortfall is borne by the guaranteeing partner or partners in their agreed ratio (in the old ratio, if the deed is silent on that too). In the worked example, had A guaranteed B a minimum of ₹50,000, B's ₹41,464 would be topped up by ₹8,536 taken entirely from A, leaving A ₹53,660 and the firm's total distribution unchanged at ₹103,660.

First, do not debit interest on capital or partner salaries to the profit and loss account — they are appropriations, and routing them above the line misstates business performance. Second, interest on drawings is credited to the appropriation account, added to the divisible pot, not deducted as an expense. Third, a deed silent on an item means the statutory default applies — equal shares and no remuneration — however unfair that feels in hindsight. Fourth, under fixed capitals never let recurring items touch the capital account; the moment drawings reduce the capital figure, the method has collapsed into fluctuating by accident.
The written agreement fixing capital, ratio, interest rates, salaries and exit terms; it overrides every statutory default it addresses.
One account per partner absorbing capital, appropriations and drawings alike, so the balance moves each year.
A capital account pinned at the agreed amount, with recurring items routed through a separate current account.
Under fixed capitals, the running account of interest, salary, profit shares, drawings and their interest; a credit balance is a liability, a debit balance an asset.
The account that divides net profit among partners after adding interest on drawings and deducting interest on capital, salaries and commissions.
The charge a deed levies on partners' withdrawals, computed by the product method or the average-period shortcut.
The mean time drawings remain outstanding: 6.5 months for equal monthly drawings at each month's start, 5.5 at each month's end.
A promised minimum share for a partner, with any shortfall made good by the guaranteeing partners in their agreed ratio.

examples.title: Worked Example: A Full Appropriation with Journal Entries
examples.problem: Partnership Accounts I: Formation, Profit Sharing and Capital — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: A and B share profits 3:2 with fixed capitals of ₹600,000 and ₹400,000. The year's net profit before appropriations is ₹220,000. Deed terms: interest on capital 8 per cent per annum; salary to B ₹40,000; interest on drawings 6 per cent per annum. A drew ₹50,000 in one lump on 1 April; B drew ₹2,000 at the end of every month.

steps.label: Interest on capital — A
steps.text: 8 per cent of 600,000 = ₹48,000; B: 8 per cent of 400,000 = ₹32,000. Entry: Interest on Capital A/c Dr ₹80,000; To A's Current A/c ₹48,000; To B's Current A/c ₹32,000.

steps.label: Salary — Entry
steps.text: Partner B's Salary A/c Dr ₹40,000; To B's Current A/c ₹40,000.

steps.label: Interest on drawings — A
steps.text: 50,000 at 6 per cent for a full year = ₹3,000. B: total drawings 24,000; product method gives 2,000 × (11 + 10 + ... + 1 + 0) = 2,000 × 66 = 132,000; interest = 132,000 × 6 per cent ÷ 12 = ₹660 (the average-period shortcut agrees: 24,000 × 6 per cent × 5.5/12 = 660). Entry: A's Current A/c Dr ₹3,000; B's Current A/c Dr ₹660; To Interest on Drawings A/c ₹3,660.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.text: Divisible profit — 220,000 + 3,660 - 80,000 - 40,000 = ₹103,660, shared 3:2 as ₹62,196 to A and ₹41,464 to B. Entry: Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c Dr ₹103,660; To A's Current A/c ₹62,196; To B's Current A/c ₹41,464.

steps.label: Step 6
steps.text: The interest, salary and interest-on-drawings accounts are closed into the Appropriation account, which balances at ₹223,660 on each side.

keyTakeaways: Deed silent on ratio — profits and losses shared equally, irrespective of capital.
Deed silent on interest on capital — none is payable.
Deed silent on salary — no remuneration to any partner for working.
Deed silent on drawings — no interest is charged on them.
Partner's loan to the firm — interest at 6 per cent per annum by default, charged before profit is struck.
Fluctuating — one account per partner; every appropriation and every drawing passes through it; balance moves every year.
Fluctuating — simpler to maintain; the usual method for small firms without a stated preference.
Fixed — capital account frozen at the agreed amount; only fresh injections or agreed permanent withdrawals move it.
Fixed — interest on capital, salary, commission, profit share, drawings and interest on drawings all flow through the Current account.
Fixed — a credit current-account balance is a liability; a debit balance is an asset (a running advance from the partner).
Either way — the total of closing capitals and current balances appears on the liabilities side of the balance sheet (debit balances on the assets side).
Appropriation account, credit side — Net profit transferred in ₹220,000; Interest on drawings ₹3,660; total ₹223,660.
Appropriation account, debit side — Interest on capital ₹80,000; Partner B's salary ₹40,000; A's share of profit ₹62,196; B's share ₹41,464; total ₹223,660.
A's Current account — credits 48,000 + 62,196 = ₹110,196; debits 50,000 + 3,000 = ₹53,000; closing credit balance ₹57,196.
B's Current account — credits 32,000 + 40,000 + 41,464 = ₹113,464; debits 24,000 + 660 = ₹24,660; closing credit balance ₹88,804.

Where next — This lesson builds directly on the journal fluency of Double-Entry Bookkeeping: The Logic Behind Every Ledger and the statement shapes introduced in Reading Financial Statements, since the appropriation account is an extension of the profit and loss account. It is the required foundation for Partnership Accounts II, which adds admission, retirement and dissolution. The law of partnership itself — formation, mutual rights, dissolution by court — is business-law territory and is deliberately not re-taught here.
When the deed is silent: equal shares, no interest on capital, no salary, no interest on drawings — but 6 per cent per annum on a partner's loan to the firm.
The deed overrides every default; its clauses on ratio, interest, salaries and exits are the accountant's instruction set.
Fluctuating capitals put everything in one account per partner; fixed capitals pin the capital and route recurring items through a current account.
The appropriation account divides profit: net profit plus interest on drawings, less interest on capital, salaries and commissions, equals the divisible profit.
Interest on drawings comes from the product method (sum of amount × months outstanding, times monthly rate) or the average-period shortcut (6.5 or 5.5 months).
The worked division: ₹220,000 profit, ₹80,000 interest on capital, ₹40,000 salary, ₹3,660 interest on drawings — ₹103,660 divisible 3:2.
Drawings against profits attract interest and close through the current account; drawings against capital reduce the capital itself and attract none.
A guaranteed minimum tops up the partner's share from the guaranteeing partners' shares, leaving total profit untouched.

quiz.q: A deed fixes capitals of ₹500,000 and ₹100,000 but is silent on the profit-sharing ratio. Profits are shared:
options: As the working partners agree orally
After providing 6 per cent interest on capital
quiz.explanation: Silence on the ratio triggers the statutory default of equal sharing, regardless of how unequal the capitals are.

quiz.q: Under the fixed capital method, a partner's salary is credited to:
quiz.explanation: Fixed capitals move only for permanent injections or withdrawals; salaries, interest and profit shares belong to the current account.

quiz.q: B draws ₹2,000 at the end of each month for a year. At 6 per cent per annum, interest on drawings is:
quiz.explanation: Total drawings ₹24,000; average period 5.5 months; 24,000 × 6 per cent × 5.5/12 = ₹660.

quiz.q: Interest on drawings, when the deed provides for it, appears in the profit and loss appropriation account as:
options: A debit, treated as an expense of the business
A credit, added to the amount available for division
A direct debit to the partners' capital accounts only
An item of the balance sheet
quiz.explanation: It is added on the credit side, increasing the divisible profit — it recovers from partners a benefit already enjoyed.

quiz.q: C is guaranteed a minimum profit of ₹50,000 and the ratio gives C ₹41,464. The shortfall of ₹8,536 is borne by:
options: All partners including C in the new ratio
The guaranteeing partners in their agreed (default: old) ratio
The firm as a business expense
No one — C simply receives the lower figure
quiz.explanation: A guarantee re-routes profit, it does not create it: the guarantors sacrifice in their agreed ratio, defaulting to the old ratio if the deed is silent.

intro:
A partnership is a contract among living, changing people, so the firm's accounts must survive three traumas: a new partner walking in, an old partner walking out, and the whole edifice being taken apart. Each event forces the same question — what is the firm worth at this moment, and who has a claim on that worth? A newcomer must not harvest reserves and reputation earned by others; a leaver must be paid every rupee of goodwill they helped build; a dissolving firm must convert everything to cash and settle everyone in order. Partnership Accounts I built the engine; this lesson drives it through admission, retirement, death and dissolution, with full journal entries for goodwill, revaluation and the realisation account.

**Why this matters.** Changes in composition are when partnerships fight and dissolve badly. The revaluation and realisation machinery replaces sentiment with arithmetic: assets marked to current worth, goodwill priced, gains and losses assigned to exactly those who earned them. Firms that skip these steps hand the incoming partner a claim on profits the old partners already made — and the outgoing partner a stake they no longer hold.
objectives: Explain sacrificing ratio on admission
Explain goodwill: premium method and capital adjustment
Explain revaluation of assets and liabilities
Explain distribution of accumulated reserves
Explain gaining ratio on retirement or death
Explain the deceased partner and the executor account
Explain realisation account on dissolution
Explain insolvency and piecemeal distribution

concepts.statement: On admission the old firm legally ends and a new one begins, so the books must be squared before the newcomer touches them.
