Three adjustments do the squaring: goodwill compensates old partners for sharing the reputation they built; revaluation marks assets and liabilities to their worth on the admission date, so later changes are not misattributed to the new team; and accumulated reserves are credited to the old partners alone, being earned before the new partner existed. Only after this scrubbing does the new capital enter the books.

concepts.term: Goodwill: premium method and capital adjustment
concepts.statement: Two ratios govern every admission. The new profit-sharing ratio divides future profits among all partners; the sacrificing ratio measures what the old partners gave up and is the ratio in which goodwill compensation flows. Suppose A and B share 3:2 and C is admitted, the new ratio being 5:3:2. A's share falls from 6/10 to 5/10 — a sacrifice of 1/10; B's falls from 4/10 to 3/10 — also 1/10. The sacrificing ratio is 1:1, and any premium C pays is split equally between A and B, not in the old 3:2. That asymmetry is the most common admission error, and it is pure arithmetic: sacrifice equals old share minus new share.
$$\text{Sacrifice} = \text{old share} - \text{new share} \qquad \text{Gain} = \text{new share} - \text{old share}$$
concepts.detail: On admission, old partners' sacrifices form the ratio for sharing goodwill brought in. On retirement or death, the continuing partners' gains form the ratio for compensating the outgoing partner — the same subtraction, run backwards.

concepts.statement: Goodwill treatment depends on whether the newcomer pays for it. Under the premium method, C brings their share of goodwill in cash, credited to the sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio and withdrawable or retainable as firm capital. When C brings no premium, the adjustment runs through capital: C's current account is debited and the sacrificing partners' capitals credited, again in the sacrificing ratio. A standards note applies: internally generated goodwill is never recognised — it enters the books only when consideration has changed hands, which is what the premium and adjustment entries record. Valuing the goodwill figure itself (average profit, super profit, capitalisation) is valuation theory, noted here only as an input.

Accumulated profits and reserves are treated the same way — credited to the old partners in the old ratio before the new capital is recorded. For a General Reserve of ₹40,000: General Reserve A/c Dr ₹40,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹24,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹16,000. The logic is identical to revaluation: the past is not for sale to the newcomer.

concepts.term: Gaining ratio on retirement or death
concepts.statement: Retirement and death run the admission machinery backwards. Assets are revalued, reserves distributed, and the outgoing partner's dues assembled: capital, current balance, goodwill share, revaluation share and profits to the date of exit. Goodwill compensation now falls on the continuing partners in the gaining ratio — new share minus old share. If A, B and C share 5:3:2 and B retires, leaving A and C at 3:2, then A gains 1/10 (5/10 to 6/10) and C gains 2/10 (2/10 to 4/10), a gaining ratio of 1:2. When goodwill of ₹200,000 is raised for B's share of ₹60,000, the charging entry is: A's Capital A/c Dr ₹20,000; C's Capital A/c Dr ₹40,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹60,000 — C pays two-thirds, having gained twice as much.

concepts.term: The deceased partner and the executor account
concepts.statement: Death adds one wrinkle: the exit date rarely coincides with the year end, so the deceased's share of profit is computed to the date of death — from the last balance sheet, by sales, by time, or as the deed prescribes — and interest runs on the balance due. Firms commonly hold a joint life policy covering all partners: the proceeds on death provide instant liquidity, and the treatment of premiums and sum assured follows the deed. The total due is transferred to an Executor's Account — Deceased Partner's Capital A/c Dr; To Deceased Partner's Executors' A/c — then paid per the deed, often in instalments with interest at around 6 per cent per annum.

Dissolution ends the firm: assets are sold, liabilities paid, remaining cash divided. The realisation account is the temporary staging ground — every asset except cash (fictitious assets go straight to the partners) is transferred to it at book value; every liability except partners' loans is transferred to it; proceeds, payments to outsiders and expenses flow through it; and the closing balance, profit or loss on realisation, is divided in the profit-sharing ratio. The mirror logic is the whole story: the difference between what the books said the assets were worth and what the world paid belongs to the partners in their agreed ratio.

Insolvency bends the neat ratio arithmetic. If a partner's capital cannot absorb their share of the loss, the deficiency is borne by the solvent partners — not in the profit-sharing ratio but in the ratio of their capitals, the rule carried in the English case Garner v Murray. The working technique is the surplus capital method: compute the notional total loss on the assumption everyone pays, find each solvent partner's surplus capital over their share of that notional loss, and require them to bring in that much cash to fund the insolvent partner's deficiency. When dissolution stretches over time — assets sold piecemeal, creditors pressing — piecemeal distribution applies instead: cash is released so that no partner is paid ahead of the point where all capitals would be equal, commonly via the maximum-loss method, which treats each distribution as the last.

First, goodwill compensation flows in the sacrificing ratio (admission) or gaining ratio (exit) — never the profit-sharing ratio by default. Second, revaluation profit and accumulated reserves belong to old partners only. Third, partners' loans are outside the realisation account, paid per the deed and the law's priority rules. Fourth, cash and fictitious assets never pass through realisation. And remember the case name the right way round: Garner v Murray, capital ratio, deficiency of the insolvent partner.
The ratio among all partners, including the incoming one, from the date of change.
Old share minus new share for each continuing partner; the channel for goodwill compensation on admission.
New share minus old share for each continuing partner; the channel for compensating a retiring or deceased partner.
The incoming partner pays their share of goodwill in cash, credited to sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio.
Marks assets and liabilities to current values on a change in composition; its profit or loss goes to the old partners.
The dissolution staging account: assets and liabilities in, proceeds and payments through, the balance shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
An insolvent partner's capital deficiency is borne by solvent partners in the ratio of their capitals.
Sums due to a deceased partner's estate, usually settled in instalments with interest.
Spreading dissolution proceeds over time so no partner is overpaid before all would be equal, via the maximum-loss method.

examples.title: Worked Example: Goodwill on Admission, Both Routes
examples.problem: Partnership Accounts II: Admission, Retirement and Dissolution — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: A and B share 3:2. C is admitted; the new ratio is 5:3:2 and goodwill is valued at ₹240,000. C's profit share is 2/10, so C's share of goodwill is 2/10 × 240,000 = ₹48,000, owed to A and B in their sacrificing ratio of 1:1 — ₹24,000 each.

steps.label: Premium method — C brings the amount in cash
steps.text: Bank A/c Dr ₹48,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹24,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹24,000. If the deed lets them withdraw it: A's Capital A/c Dr ₹24,000; B's Capital A/c Dr ₹24,000; To Bank A/c ₹48,000.

steps.label: Adjustment via capitals — C pays nothing now
steps.text: C's Current A/c Dr ₹48,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹24,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹24,000. The debt stays on C's current account until the deed says otherwise.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Either route, the sacrificing ratio of 1:1 governs the split — not 3:2, not 5:3:2.

examples.title: Worked Example: The Revaluation Account
examples.problem: Partnership Accounts II: Admission, Retirement and Dissolution — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: On C's admission the books show machinery ₹200,000, stock ₹80,000 and debtors ₹60,000. Current values: machinery ₹240,000 (up ₹40,000), stock ₹68,000 (down ₹12,000); a 5 per cent provision on debtors is needed (₹3,000); and an outstanding repairs liability of ₹2,000 surfaces.

steps.label: Appreciation
steps.text: Machinery A/c Dr ₹40,000; To Revaluation A/c ₹40,000.

steps.label: Depreciation of stock
steps.text: Revaluation A/c Dr ₹12,000; To Stock A/c ₹12,000.

steps.label: Provision
steps.text: Revaluation A/c Dr ₹3,000; To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c ₹3,000.

steps.label: Liability
steps.text: Revaluation A/c Dr ₹2,000; To Outstanding Repairs A/c ₹2,000.

steps.label: Close
steps.text: the net profit of ₹23,000 (40,000 minus 17,000) goes to the old partners in the old ratio — Revaluation A/c Dr ₹23,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹13,800; To B's Capital A/c ₹9,200.

steps.label: Rationale
steps.text: left at ₹200,000, a later sale of the machinery would have produced a profit in which C unfairly shared; revaluation loads it onto A and B now.

examples.title: Worked Example: A Complete Dissolution
examples.problem: Partnership Accounts II: Admission, Retirement and Dissolution — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: A, B and C share 5:3:2. The balance sheet shows creditors ₹60,000, bills payable ₹20,000, and capitals A ₹120,000, B ₹90,000, C ₹70,000 — total ₹360,000 — against cash ₹12,000, debtors ₹80,000, stock ₹88,000, machinery ₹120,000 and building ₹60,000.

steps.label: Transfer the assets at book value
steps.text: Realisation A/c Dr ₹348,000; To Debtors ₹80,000; To Stock ₹88,000; To Machinery ₹120,000; To Building ₹60,000.

steps.label: Transfer the liabilities
steps.text: Creditors A/c Dr ₹60,000; Bills Payable A/c Dr ₹20,000; To Realisation A/c ₹80,000.

steps.label: Sell what sells
steps.text: debtors fetch ₹72,000, stock ₹80,000, machinery ₹100,000 — Cash A/c Dr ₹252,000; To Realisation A/c ₹252,000.

steps.label: Pay the outsiders
steps.text: creditors settle for ₹58,000, bills ₹20,000, expenses ₹3,000 — Realisation A/c Dr ₹81,000; To Cash A/c ₹81,000.

steps.label: Step 6
steps.text: A takes over the building at an agreed ₹66,000: A's Capital A/c Dr ₹66,000; To Realisation A/c ₹66,000 — his claim is reduced, not his cash.

steps.label: Close the account
steps.text: debits ₹429,000 against credits ₹398,000, so a loss of ₹31,000 — A's Capital A/c Dr ₹15,500; B's Capital A/c Dr ₹9,300; C's Capital A/c Dr ₹6,200; To Realisation A/c ₹31,000, in the 5:3:2 ratio.

keyTakeaways: Realisation account, debit side — assets at book value ₹348,000; creditors paid ₹58,000; bills paid ₹20,000; expenses ₹3,000; total ₹429,000.
Realisation account, credit side — cash from debtors, stock, machinery ₹252,000; creditors transferred ₹60,000; bills transferred ₹20,000; building taken by A ₹66,000; total ₹398,000.
Balancing figure — loss on realisation ₹31,000, shared 5:3:2 as ₹15,500, ₹9,300 and ₹6,200.
Cash account flow — opening ₹12,000 + realisations ₹252,000 - outside payments ₹81,000 = ₹183,000 distributed to the partners.

Where next — This lesson assumes Partnership Accounts I: Formation, Profit Sharing and Capital for capitals, current accounts and appropriations, plus the journal fluency of Double-Entry Bookkeeping: The Logic Behind Every Ledger. Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves supplies the revaluation instincts, and Reading Financial Statements shows where revaluation and goodwill balances surface. The statutory side of dissolution — court orders, priorities, insolvency law — belongs to business-law study.
Every change of composition re-prices the firm first: goodwill, revaluation, reserve distribution.
Sacrificing ratio = old share minus new share; it routes goodwill compensation on admission (worked case: 3:2 to 5:3:2 gives 1:1).
Goodwill enters the books only when consideration moves: premium in cash, or an adjustment against the newcomer's current account.
Revaluation marks assets and liabilities to current worth; its profit or loss goes to the old partners in the old ratio (worked profit ₹23,000).
Accumulated reserves are credited to old partners before the incoming capital is booked.
On retirement or death, continuing partners compensate the leaver in the gaining ratio (worked case: 5:3:2 losing B gives 1:2).
The deceased's total due — capital, goodwill, revaluation, profits to date — moves to an executor's account with interest.
Dissolution runs everything through the realisation account; its closing loss (worked: ₹31,000 in 5:3:2) is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
Garner v Murray: an insolvent partner's deficiency is borne by solvent partners in capital ratio; slow wind-ups use piecemeal distribution.

quiz.q: A and B share 3:2; C is admitted and the new ratio is 5:3:2. The sacrificing ratio is:
quiz.explanation: A sacrifices 6/10 - 5/10 = 1/10 and B 4/10 - 3/10 = 1/10 — any goodwill premium is shared equally.

quiz.q: A revaluation profit on a partner's admission is shared by:
options: All partners in the new ratio
The old partners in the old ratio
The old partners in the new ratio
quiz.explanation: Revaluation prices changes that occurred before the newcomer joined — the gain belongs to those who owned the firm then.

quiz.q: A, B and C share 5:3:2. B retires and goodwill of ₹200,000 is to be adjusted, B's share being 3/10. A and C, who now share 3:2, will bear the debit in the ratio:
quiz.explanation: A gains 1/10 while C gains 2/10, so the gaining ratio 1:2 splits B's ₹60,000 as ₹20,000 and ₹40,000.

quiz.q: In dissolution, which item is NOT transferred to the realisation account?
quiz.explanation: Cash never enters realisation — it is the medium of the whole exercise.

quiz.q: Under the rule in Garner v Murray, the capital deficiency of an insolvent partner is borne by the solvent partners in the ratio of:
quiz.explanation: The case settled capital ratio as the measure — each solvent partner loses in proportion to the stake left.

intro:
A company needs ₹120 million for a plant. Rather than beg one banker, it slices the ownership itself into 100,000 pieces of ₹10 each and offers them at ₹12 — and 120,000 people ask for a piece. What follows is a choreography of receipts, promises and contracts that company accountants run every day: money arrives before shares exist, applications exceed allotments, some holders later refuse to pay their calls, and the company must repossess and resell the slices they default on. This lesson walks the whole life of a share issue — the capital hierarchy, premium, the application-allotment-calls sequence with complete journal entries, pro-rata allotment when demand outruns supply, calls in arrears, and the forfeiture and reissue machinery with its capital-reserve payoff.

**Why this matters.** Share capital is the equity cushion every other claim rests on, and the law polices it hard: capital cannot simply be returned to shareholders, premium has restricted uses, and every stage of an issue has prescribed accounts and disclosures. An accountant who cannot build these entries blindfolded cannot work a company ledger — and mis-stating called-up versus paid-up capital misleads every reader of the balance sheet about the firm's real cushion.
objectives: Explain authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up capital
Explain face value, issue price and securities premium
Explain application, allotment and calls in sequence
Explain pro-rata allotment arithmetic
Explain calls in arrears
Explain forfeiture of fully and partly called shares
Explain reissue limits and the capital reserve transfer
Explain share certificates and warrants

concepts.term: Authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up capital
concepts.statement: Share capital wears five shrinking labels, and the order never changes. Authorised (nominal) capital is the maximum the memorandum permits — say 2,000,000 shares of ₹10, or ₹20,000,000. Issued capital is the portion actually offered to the public, perhaps 500,000 shares. Subscribed capital is what takers have committed to — if applications arrive for 600,000 shares but only 500,000 are allotted, subscribed is 500,000. Called-up capital is the part of the face value the company has actually demanded — if ₹8 of each ₹10 has been called, called-up is ₹4,000,000. Paid-up capital is what shareholders have actually paid — with ₹200,000 of calls in arrears, it is ₹3,800,000. Each label is smaller than (or equal to) the one above, and the balance sheet's equity line is built from the last of them.

concepts.term: Face value, issue price and securities premium
concepts.statement: Face value is the ₹10 written on the share; issue price is what the market pays for it. When the price exceeds face value the excess is securities premium, credited not to Share Capital but to a separate Securities Premium account with legally restricted uses — issuing bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses or underwriting commissions, providing the premium payable on redemption of debentures or preference shares, and buying back the company's own shares. Dividends are not on that list: premium is capital, not income. Issuing shares below face value — at a discount — was once common accounting practice but is now prohibited by company law, surviving only as a cautionary entry in old textbooks.

concepts.term: Application, allotment and calls in sequence
concepts.statement: A share is born in three stages, each with its own account. Application: the public sends money before any contract exists; it sits in a Share Application account as a debt the company owes to applicants, because there is not yet a shareholder to credit. Allotment: the company accepts (or rejects) applications, and acceptance is the birth of the contract — application money now becomes part of the share's paid capital, and any balance due is demanded as allotment money. Calls: the company summons the remainder in one or more instalments; each call is due only when formally made, and money unpaid after the due date becomes a call in arrears. One legal guardrail frames the whole sequence: a minimum subscription must be reached — in common practice the large majority of the issue — failing which nothing may be allotted and every rupee of application money must be returned within the prescribed days.
$$\text{Shares allotted} = \text{shares applied} \times \frac{\text{total shares allotted}}{\text{total shares applied}}$$
concepts.detail: When applications exceed the offer, allotment scales every application by the same fraction. In the worked issue, 120,000 applications chase 100,000 shares, so the fraction is 5/6 and an applicant for 24 shares receives 20 — while the excess application money on the 4 unallotted shares is carried forward against that applicant's allotment dues.

concepts.statement: When a shareholder fails to pay calls despite notices, the company can forfeit the shares: membership ends, the name vanishes from the register, and every rupee the defaulter paid on those shares is surrendered to the company. The entries follow a fixed shape. Share Capital is debited with the called-up face value of the shares (never the premium); Calls in Arrears is credited with whatever remains unpaid, clearing the debt that triggered the forfeiture; and the Share Forfeiture account is credited with the amount actually received towards capital — the pool from which any later reissue discount must come. The premium already received stays in Securities Premium untouched; if premium itself was unpaid, Securities Premium is debited for it in the forfeiture entry.

Title to a share is evidenced in one of two instruments. A share certificate is the ordinary one: registered in the holder's name, it proves ownership and moves only by a formal transfer. A share warrant is its negotiable cousin — a bearer instrument transferable by mere delivery, rare today, and held only against fully paid shares. Between the two lies the practical difference between an entry in a register and a piece of paper that can circulate like currency.

First, never debit the reissue discount to profit and loss — it is charged against the forfeiture pool, not against earnings. Second, Share Capital is debited at called-up value on forfeiture, not the full face value of a partly called share. Third, capital reserve is not distributable as dividend; treat it as locked capital. Fourth, premium belongs in Securities Premium from the first receipt — routing it through profit and loss overstates income and breaks the law. Fifth, the pro-rata fraction applies to applicants' money as well as their shares: forgetting the application-money set-off against allotment double-collects from winners and strands the losers' refunds.
The maximum share capital the memorandum permits; every other layer of capital fits inside it.
The portion of face value the company has actually demanded from shareholders so far.
Called-up capital minus calls in arrears; the amount shareholders have actually paid.
The excess of issue price over face value, held in a separate account with legally restricted uses.
Scaling every application by the same fraction when applications exceed the shares offered.
Call money demanded but unpaid by the due date; a debt the shareholder owes the company.
Terminating a defaulting shareholder's membership and absorbing the amounts they paid on the shares.
The unspent balance of a forfeiture pool after reissue; capital in nature and not distributable as dividend.
A negotiable bearer document of title to fully paid shares, transferable by delivery.

examples.title: Worked Example: A Full Issue, Start to Finish
examples.problem: Company Accounts I: Issue and Forfeiture of Shares — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: A company offers 100,000 shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2, payable ₹4 on application, ₹6 on allotment (including the premium) and ₹2 on the first and final call. Applications arrive for 120,000 shares; the directors make a pro-rata allotment.

steps.label: Money in
steps.text: Bank A/c Dr ₹480,000; To Share Application A/c ₹480,000 (120,000 × 4).

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Allotment made — application money becomes capital, and the excess on 20,000 unallotted shares (20,000 × 4 = ₹80,000) is set off against allotment: Share Application A/c Dr ₹480,000; To Share Capital A/c ₹400,000; To Share Allotment A/c ₹80,000.

steps.label: Allotment due
steps.text: Share Allotment A/c Dr ₹520,000 (100,000 × 6, less the ₹80,000 already adjusted); To Share Capital A/c ₹400,000; To Securities Premium A/c ₹200,000. Receipt: Bank A/c Dr ₹520,000; To Share Allotment A/c ₹520,000.

steps.label: Call made
steps.text: First and Final Call A/c Dr ₹200,000; To Share Capital A/c ₹200,000.

steps.label: Step 6
steps.text: Call received on 96,000 shares; a holder of 4,000 shares defaults: Bank A/c Dr ₹192,000; Calls in Arrears A/c Dr ₹8,000; To First and Final Call A/c ₹200,000.

steps.label: Proof
steps.text: Share Capital now totals 400,000 + 400,000 + 200,000 = ₹1,000,000 at face, Securities Premium ₹200,000, and the bank has received 480,000 + 520,000 + 192,000 = ₹1,192,000 — exactly 1,000,000 + 200,000 less the ₹8,000 still owed.

examples.title: Worked Example: Forfeiting Fully and Partly Called Shares
examples.problem: Company Accounts I: Issue and Forfeiture of Shares — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Fully called — the 4,000 defaulting shares above, ₹10 called-up with ₹8 per share received (application ₹4 plus the capital part of allotment ₹4): Share Capital A/c Dr ₹40,000; To Calls in Arrears A/c ₹8,000; To Share Forfeiture A/c ₹32,000. The ₹2-per-share premium received earlier stays in Securities Premium.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Partly called — 1,000 shares of ₹10 on which only ₹7 has been called, the last call of ₹2 being unpaid, so ₹5 per share stands received: Share Capital A/c Dr ₹7,000; To Calls in Arrears A/c ₹2,000; To Share Forfeiture A/c ₹5,000. The capital account is debited only with what was called, not the full face value.

examples.title: Worked Example: Reissue and the Capital Reserve
examples.problem: Company Accounts I: Issue and Forfeiture of Shares — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: All 4,000 forfeited shares (₹10 face, ₹32,000 in the forfeiture pool) are reissued at ₹8 per share — a discount of ₹2 per share, ₹8,000 in all.

steps.label: Entry
steps.text: Bank A/c Dr ₹32,000; Share Forfeiture A/c Dr ₹8,000; To Share Capital A/c ₹40,000 — the new holder pays ₹8, the old partners' surrendered money covers ₹2, and the shares re-enter the books fully paid at face value.

steps.label: The rule enforced here
steps.text: discount on reissue can never exceed the amount forfeited on the shares being reissued — the company cannot fund a discount out of anyone's money but the defaulter's own.

steps.label: Close the pool
steps.text: Share Forfeiture A/c Dr ₹24,000; To Capital Reserve A/c ₹24,000 — the unspent surplus of one defaulter's sacrifice becomes capital, permanently outside the dividend stream.

steps.label: Variant
steps.text: had the shares been reissued at ₹11 instead, the entry would read Bank A/c Dr ₹44,000; To Share Capital A/c ₹40,000; To Securities Premium A/c ₹4,000, and the entire ₹32,000 forfeiture balance would transfer to Capital Reserve.

keyTakeaways: Authorised ₹20,000,000 — 2,000,000 shares of ₹10 permitted by the memorandum.
Issued ₹5,000,000 — 500,000 shares actually offered.
Subscribed ₹5,000,000 — 600,000 applications scaled down to 500,000 allotments.
Called-up ₹4,000,000 — ₹8 of the ₹10 face value demanded by the company.
Paid-up ₹3,800,000 — called-up less ₹200,000 of calls in arrears.

Where next — This lesson leans on the ledger fluency of Double-Entry Bookkeeping: The Logic Behind Every Ledger and on Reading Financial Statements for where these capital layers surface in the equity section. Its mirror is Company Accounts II: Debentures and Borrowings — the same company raising money as debt instead of equity. The accounting-cycle lesson's treatment of closing entries explains why the application and call accounts always wash out to nil.
Capital hierarchy: authorised ≥ issued ≥ subscribed ≥ called-up ≥ paid-up; the balance sheet reports paid-up.
Issue price above face value creates securities premium — restricted-use capital, never dividend income; issues at a discount are prohibited.
Application money is a debt to applicants until allotment creates the contract of shareholding.
Pro-rata: allotment fraction = shares offered / shares applied; excess application money offsets allotment dues (worked: 5/6, so 24 applications yield 20 shares).
The worked issue: 100,000 shares at ₹12 (₹4 / ₹6 incl. premium / ₹2) raises ₹1,000,000 capital plus ₹200,000 premium, less ₹8,000 arrears.
Forfeiture: Share Capital Dr at called-up value; Calls in Arrears Cr for the unpaid; Share Forfeiture Cr for the capital actually received.
Reissue discount may not exceed the amount forfeited on those shares; Bank plus the discount absorbed equals face value restored.
The leftover forfeiture balance becomes Capital Reserve — locked, non-distributable capital.
Certificates prove registered title; warrants are bearer instruments transferable by delivery.

quiz.q: Which layer of share capital can never be smaller than any other?
quiz.explanation: The hierarchy only shrinks downward: authorised contains issued, issued contains subscribed, then called-up, then paid-up.

quiz.q: Securities premium may NOT be used for:
options: Providing the premium on redemption of debentures
quiz.explanation: Premium is capital, and dividends are paid only from distributable profits — the four statutory uses all preserve its capital character.

quiz.q: In the worked issue, applications for 120,000 shares competed for 100,000. An applicant for 24 shares is allotted:
quiz.explanation: The pro-rata fraction is 100,000/120,000 = 5/6, and 24 × 5/6 = 20 shares, with the excess application money on 4 shares carried to allotment.

quiz.q: Shares of ₹10 were called-up in full with ₹8 per share received. On forfeiture, the Share Forfeiture account is credited with:
quiz.explanation: Capital is debited at ₹10 called-up, calls in arrears credited ₹2, and the forfeiture pool holds exactly what the defaulter paid — ₹8.

quiz.q: After forfeited shares are reissued at a discount, the remaining balance of the Share Forfeiture account is transferred to:
quiz.explanation: The unspent surrendered money is capital in nature — it moves to Capital Reserve and can never be paid out as dividend.

intro:
The same company that sliced its ownership into shares can slice its debt instead: 10,000 printed promises to pay ₹100 each, bearing 9 per cent interest and ranking ahead of every shareholder if things go wrong. A debenture is a borrowing under the company's seal — an instrument acknowledging a debt — and the debenture holder is a creditor who lent money, not an owner who bought a stake. That single legal fact drives every accounting difference between the two instruments: interest is a charge that must be paid in good years and bad, redemption is a promise with a date on it, and security can be attached to it that no shareholder can demand. This lesson covers the instrument's anatomy, the entries for issuing at par, premium and discount, the curious loss that appears when redemption promises a premium, debentures as collateral, interest with tax deducted at source, and the three routes to redemption.

**Why this matters.** Debt is the cheaper, faster, riskier way to fund growth — cheaper because interest is deductible and fixed, riskier because it must be paid when due regardless of profits. Reading a balance sheet means knowing whether the debenture stack is secured and when it falls due; writing one means knowing that the interest charge lands in profit and loss even in a loss year, which is precisely how over-leveraged firms tip from slow profit into insolvency.
objectives: Explain debenture holder as creditor, not owner
Explain secured, unsecured, redeemable and convertible types
Explain issue at par, premium and discount
Explain loss on issue when redemption carries a premium
Explain debentures as collateral security
Explain interest as a charge, with tax deducted at source
Explain redemption by lump sum, instalments or conversion

concepts.term: Debenture holder as creditor, not owner
concepts.statement: The contrast with shares runs down every line of the two instruments. A shareholder is an owner; a debenture holder is a creditor. A shareholder's dividend is an appropriation, paid only if profits and directors permit; a debenture holder's interest is a charge, payable whether the year was brilliant or miserable. Shareholders vote and control; debenture holders lend and wait. Share capital is permanent — returnable only through buybacks in narrow legal channels — while debentures carry a redemption date. In liquidation, debenture holders stand with other creditors ahead of every shareholder. And a debenture can be secured against the company's assets, a protection no share enjoys.

concepts.term: Secured, unsecured, redeemable and convertible types
concepts.statement: Debentures sort along three axes. Secured debentures carry a charge on assets — a fixed charge on specific property, or a floating charge over the shifting mass of current assets until crystallised. Unsecured (naked) debentures rest on the company's word alone. Redeemable debentures come home on a fixed date or by instalments; irredeemable ones have no fixed date and ride along as near-permanent debt. Convertible debentures — fully or partly — exchange themselves (or part of themselves) for equity at stated terms, which is why lenders accept coupons below market rates: the conversion option is the sweetener. Registered debentures move by transfer entry; bearer debentures circulate by delivery. Any single instrument combines one choice from each axis, and the prospectus says which.
$$I = F \times r \times t$$
concepts.detail: Annual interest equals the face (nominal) value of the debentures times the coupon rate — never the issue price. A ₹100 debenture pays ₹9 a year whether the subscriber paid ₹95, ₹100 or ₹110 for it; the coupon is fixed to face, and the issue price only changes what the lender actually earns.

concepts.term: Issue at par, premium and discount
concepts.statement: One modern restriction: companies no longer issue debentures at a discount — the entry above survives in practice only where law still permits certain discount structures, and in every textbook written before the prohibition. When a discount is allowed, its accounting is patient: the Discount (or Loss) on Issue account is debited once and then written off systematically, usually in equal annual instalments across the borrowing's term, against securities premium first if available and profit and loss thereafter.

concepts.term: Loss on issue when redemption carries a premium
concepts.statement: Two special situations complete the issue picture. Debentures issued for consideration other than cash — a supplier or a seller of assets paid in paper rather than money — produce the leanest entry imaginable: Assets A/c Dr (or the vendor); To Debentures A/c, at the agreed purchase consideration, with premium or discount recognised the same way as for a cash issue. And debentures issued as collateral security back another borrowing: a bank lends ₹1,000,000 and demands 12,000 debentures of ₹100 as the pledge. No borrowing occurs by that act, so normally no entry is made — the collateral appears as a note to the accounts — though some firms record it with a wash pair (Debentures Suspense A/c Dr; To Debentures A/c) shown as a deduction from the liability, which cancels itself the moment the primary loan is repaid and the debentures return home.

The most mis-booked entry in this chapter is loss on issue of debentures. When debentures are issued at a discount and are redeemable at a premium, the company has promised two losses at once — it received less than face and will repay more than face — and both must be recognised on the day of issue. Suppose the ₹100 debentures above go out at a 5 per cent discount and return at a 10 per cent premium: Bank A/c Dr ₹950,000; Loss on Issue of Debentures A/c Dr ₹150,000; To Debentures A/c ₹1,000,000; To Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c ₹100,000. The loss account blends the ₹50,000 discount given away and the ₹100,000 redemption premium promised, and is written off over the borrowing's life. The Premium on Redemption account sits as a liability until the day it is paid.

concepts.term: Interest as a charge, with tax deducted at source
concepts.statement: Debentures come home by one of three routes. Lump-sum redemption pays the whole issue on the due date; prudent firms build a Debenture Redemption Reserve from divisible profits across the years before the date (a requirement the rules have relaxed for several classes of issuers, but the discipline remains), so the entries run: surplus profits are appropriated — Surplus in Statement of Profit and Loss A/c Dr; To Debenture Redemption Reserve A/c — then the debt is paid — Debentures A/c Dr; To Bank A/c — and once cleared the reserve is freed into General Reserve. Redemption by instalments (drawings) spreads the payments across years, drawing lots each time so that no holder can predict their exit, with the same payment entry repeated per instalment. Redemption by conversion simply changes the paper: convertible debentures become shares at the agreed ratio — Debentures A/c Dr; To Share Capital A/c (and To Securities Premium A/c if the conversion price exceeds face) — and the creditor of yesterday becomes the shareholder of tomorrow with no cash moving at all. Where redemption carries a premium, the extra is paid from the Premium on Redemption account already set up at issue.

First, interest is a charge, not an appropriation: it must be provided for even when profits are negative, unlike a dividend. Second, compute interest on face value, not issue price — a ₹110 purchase price does not raise the ₹9 coupon. Third, do not book the discount twice: the discount and the promised redemption premium are two parts of one loss on issue, recognised together on day one. Fourth, collateral debentures are not new borrowing — booking them as a liability double-counts debt. Fifth, tax deducted at source is a payable to the government, never income and never expense.
An instrument under the company's seal acknowledging a debt; the holder is a creditor, not an owner.
A mortgage on specific identified assets securing debenture holders.
A security over the changing pool of current assets, attaching to specific items only when crystallised.
A debenture exchangeable for equity shares at stated terms, fully or in part.
The combined discount allowed on issue and premium promised on redemption, debited in full at the issue date.
Debentures pledged to a lender to secure another borrowing; usually disclosed rather than entered.
The holder's tax withheld by the paying company and deposited with the government; a liability in between.
An appropriation of profits built up before redemption to protect the repayment of the debt.

examples.title: Worked Example: Three Issues, Three Entries
examples.problem: Company Accounts II: Debentures and Borrowings — worked through step by step

steps.label: At par — 10,000 debentures of ₹100 each
steps.text: Bank A/c Dr ₹1,000,000; To 9 per cent Debentures A/c ₹1,000,000. The liability enters the books at face value.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: At a premium of 10 per cent — the same face, a pricier promise: Bank A/c Dr ₹1,100,000; To 9 per cent Debentures A/c ₹1,000,000; To Premium on Issue of Debentures A/c ₹100,000. The premium is a capital gain of the borrowing itself, not income.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: At a discount of 5 per cent — less cash in for the same promise: Bank A/c Dr ₹950,000; Discount on Issue of Debentures A/c Dr ₹50,000; To 9 per cent Debentures A/c ₹1,000,000. The discount is a capital loss, written off against securities premium, a capital reserve, or profit over the debentures' life.

examples.title: Worked Example: The Interest Charge with Tax Deducted at Source
examples.problem: Company Accounts II: Debentures and Borrowings — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: The 10,000 debentures of ₹100 at 9 per cent accrue ₹90,000 of interest for the year — a charge debited to profit and loss, payable in full year after year regardless of the profit line's mood.

steps.label: Interest becomes due
steps.text: Interest on Debentures A/c Dr ₹90,000; To Debenture Holders A/c ₹90,000 — the holders are creditors now, exactly like any other payee.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: On payment, the company must deduct tax at source where the law requires it (commonly 10 per cent for resident holders): Debenture Holders A/c Dr ₹90,000; To Bank A/c ₹81,000; To Tax Deducted at Source Payable A/c ₹9,000.

steps.label: The ₹9,000 is not the company's money
steps.text: it is the holders' tax, collected by the company and deposited with the government — a liability until it is paid over.

keyTakeaways: Status — shareholder: owner and member; debenture holder: creditor of the company.
Return — dividend: an appropriation of profit, discretionary; interest: a charge, compulsory and date-fixed.
Security — shares: unsecured; debentures: may carry a fixed or floating charge on assets.
Repayment — capital: permanent until buyback; debentures: redeemable on a stated date or in instalments.
Voting — shareholders vote; debenture holders do not (except to protect their debt).
Priority in liquidation — creditors, including debenture holders, rank before equity holders.

Where next — This lesson is the debt-side mirror of Company Accounts I: Issue and Forfeiture of Shares — read them together and the equity-versus-debt contrast becomes mechanical. Double-Entry Bookkeeping: The Logic Behind Every Ledger supplies the ledger fluency, Reading Financial Statements shows where the debenture stack and its interest sit in the reports, and Compound Interest and the Time Value of Money explains why a discount or premium changes the lender's true yield without touching the coupon.
A debenture is borrowed money under seal: creditor status, fixed interest, a redemption date, possible security.
Dividends are discretionary appropriations; debenture interest is a compulsory charge, payable even in loss years.
Issue at par, premium or discount changes the cash raised, never the liability recorded at face value or the coupon.
Issue entries — par: Bank 1,000,000 / Debentures 1,000,000; premium: plus a ₹100,000 credit to Premium on Issue; discount: a ₹50,000 debit for Discount on Issue.
Discount plus promised redemption premium = Loss on Issue of Debentures, debited in full on day one (worked: ₹150,000).
Debentures for consideration other than cash credit the Debentures account directly against the asset acquired.
Collateral debentures usually make no entry at all — they are a note to the accounts.
Interest accrues on face value; tax deducted at source splits the payment between the holder's bank account and a payable to the government.
Redemption comes as a lump sum (with a redemption reserve), by drawn instalments, or by conversion into shares.

quiz.q: A debenture holder differs from a shareholder primarily because the debenture holder is:
options: An owner with limited voting rights
quiz.explanation: A debenture acknowledges a loan: the holder lends and is repaid with fixed interest, holding a creditor's claim and a creditor's priority.

quiz.q: Debentures of ₹1,000,000 face value are issued at a 5 per cent discount and are redeemable at a 10 per cent premium. The Loss on Issue of Debentures account is debited with:
quiz.explanation: The loss blends both promises — ₹50,000 given away as discount plus ₹100,000 that will be overpaid at redemption — recognised together on the issue date.

quiz.q: Interest on debentures is best described as:
options: An appropriation of profit, payable only when profits exist
A charge against profit, payable regardless of results
A contingent liability until the due date
quiz.explanation: Interest is the cost of borrowed money: it is debited to profit and loss every year it accrues, profitable or not.

quiz.q: Debentures issued to a bank purely as collateral security for a loan are normally:
options: Credited to the Debentures account as a liability
Recorded as an asset equal to the loan
Disclosed by note, with no ledger entry
quiz.explanation: The collateral creates no new borrowing; the pledge is a disclosure, with an optional contra entry that cancels itself on repayment.

quiz.q: On payment of ₹90,000 debenture interest with 10 per cent tax deducted at source, the company credits:
options: Bank ₹81,000 and Tax Deducted at Source Payable ₹9,000
quiz.explanation: The holder receives ₹81,000 in cash; the ₹9,000 withheld belongs to the government and sits as a payable until deposited.

intro:
Some transactions refuse to behave like ordinary sales. A trader who accepts a three-month bill has been paid and not paid at once; a manufacturer whose goods sit in an agent's distant warehouse has sold nothing yet owns inventory worth measuring; a firm that ships machinery on approval has recognised no revenue even though the goods have left the building. Each breaks the naive equation goods-out-equals-sale. This lesson assembles the toolkit: the full life of a bill of exchange — drawing, acceptance, discounting, endorsement, dishonour, renewal and retirement, each with its journal entry — then consignment accounting with del credere commission and unsold-stock valuation, closing with sale on approval and ownership in transit.

**Why this matters.** Trade credit still travels largely as negotiable paper. Firms have been financed — and bankrupted — on bills: discount one and you borrow against a customer's promise; let one dishonour and a chain of endorsement unwinds in reverse. Consignment is how manufacturers reach markets they cannot staff — and booking a dispatch as a sale instead of a consignment turns an inventory loan into fictitious revenue.
objectives: Explain bill of exchange: drawer, drawee and payee
Explain discounting, endorsement and days of grace
Explain dishonour, noting charges and renewal
Explain retirement of a bill and rebate
Explain consignor and consignee: agency, not sale
Explain account sales, del credere and commissions
Explain valuing closing stock and abnormal loss on consignment
Explain sale on approval and goods in transit

concepts.term: Bill of exchange: drawer, drawee and payee
concepts.statement: A bill of exchange is an unconditional written order: the drawer tells the drawee to pay a certain sum to a payee, on a fixed date or after a stated period. Sold goods on credit, A draws on B; B signifies acceptance by signing across the bill, becoming the acceptor and primarily liable; the bill is now a bills receivable in A's books and a bills payable in B's. Its cousin, the promissory note, has two parties: the maker unconditionally promises to pay the payee — no acceptance step, because the debtor wrote the instrument itself. A usance bill matures at its due date plus three days of grace — a three-month bill dated 1 April falls due on 4 July — while bills payable on demand take no grace.

concepts.term: Discounting, endorsement and days of grace
concepts.statement: Between acceptance and maturity the holder has three choices. Retain the bill and present it at maturity. Discount it with a bank, which pays face value minus a discount charge for the unexpired period and becomes the holder — the drawer has borrowed against the bill, and if it dishonours the bank reclaims the full amount. Or endorse it — transfer it by signature to a creditor in settlement of a debt, the endorser remaining liable if the bill is dishonoured. Whichever route, the entries live in two sets of books at once: every bills receivable is someone's bills payable.
$$\text{Discount} = F \times r \times \frac{\text{unexpired months}}{12}$$
concepts.detail: The bank's charge equals face value times the discount rate times the fraction of a year still to run. On a ₹30,000 three-month bill discounted immediately at 12 per cent per annum: 30,000 × 12 per cent × 3/12 = ₹900, so the drawer receives ₹29,100 today for a promise worth ₹30,000 in three months.

concepts.statement: Consignment is agency dressed as trade. The consignor ships goods to a consignee who sells them on the consignor's behalf and account: ownership never leaves the consignor until the consignee sells, revenue is recognised only on that sale, and the consignee earns commission — never a trading margin. The paperwork mirrors this: a proforma invoice accompanies the goods (invoice in form, advice in substance — quantity and a nominal price, no sale having happened), and at period ends the consignee sends an account sales — sales, prices, expenses, commission due and the balance to remit. Advances to the consignee are set off before remittance.

concepts.term: Retirement of a bill and rebate
concepts.statement: Commission comes in flavours that shift risk. Ordinary commission is a percentage of sales. Del credere commission is extra pay for a consignee who guarantees collection: once agreed, bad debts on the credit sales the consignee made become the consignee's loss — the consignor has bought credit insurance from its own agent. Over-riding commission rewards agents supervising other agents in a territory. Normal loss — the evaporation, leakage and handling shrinkage inherent in the trade — is not recorded separately: the same total cost simply spreads over fewer surviving units, so unit cost rises. Abnormal loss — fire, theft, abnormal breakage — is a separate misfortune: valued like unsold stock (proportionate cost to the point of loss), set off against any insurance claim, the residue to profit and loss.
$$\text{Stock value} = (\text{cost to consignor} + \text{non-recurring expenses}) \times \frac{\text{unsold units}}{\text{units consigned}}$$
concepts.detail: Unsold goods carry their proportionate share of everything spent to make them sale-ready at the consignee's warehouse: consignor's cost plus freight and insurance, plus the consignee's unloading and cartage (non-recurring). Recurring costs after arrival — godown rent, selling expenses — are excluded; where normal loss exists, the denominator shrinks to the good units.

concepts.term: Consignor and consignee: agency, not sale
concepts.statement: Goods sent on approval (on sale or return) sit in the same ambiguous territory: physically with the customer, legally still the seller's. No revenue is recognised when the goods ship; ownership and recognition pass only on approval, or when the approval period expires without rejection. Until then the goods remain the seller's inventory — at cost or lower net realisable value, even in someone else's showroom — and dispatch entries are at most memorandum. At each period end, bring the unapproved goods back into closing stock at cost.

concepts.term: Account sales, del credere and commissions
concepts.statement: Goods in transit raise the same question at shipment: whose stock is on the truck? The answer is in the delivery terms. Free on board (FOB) at the shipping point transfers ownership and risk to the buyer when the goods are loaded — the goods in transit are the buyer's inventory and purchases. FOB destination, and cost-insurance-freight (CIF) contracts in their usual form, keep ownership with the seller until arrival. The accounting simply follows the contract: find the moment risk changed hands, and book the purchase, the sale and the inventory on the correct side of it.

First, discounting a bill is not realising it — the drawer's contingent liability survives until maturity. Second, noting charges on dishonour are recoverable from the acceptor: debit the acceptor with them, never park them as the holder's expense. Third, a consignment dispatch is never a sale; booking it as one converts inventory into fictitious revenue. Fourth, remember which consignee expenses enter stock valuation — non-recurring yes, recurring no — and shrink the denominator for normal loss. Fifth, on approval goods, possession is not ownership: keep unapproved stock in the seller's inventory at cost.
An unconditional written order by the drawer to the drawee to pay the payee on a fixed date; acceptance creates the acceptor's liability.
A two-party instrument: the maker promises to pay the payee; no acceptance step exists.
The three extra days added to a usance bill's nominal period to fix its due date.
The notary's fee for certifying dishonour; recoverable from the acceptor.
Payment before maturity; the holder allows a rebate equal to interest for the unexpired time.
Advice of dispatch accompanying consigned goods — invoice in form, not in law.
The consignee's periodic statement of sales, expenses, commission due and balance remitted.
Extra commission under which the consignee guarantees collection and absorbs bad debts.
Goods delivered for inspection; ownership and revenue pass only on approval or expiry of the return period.

examples.title: Worked Chain: Draw, Discount, Dishonour — and the Fallout
examples.problem: Bills of Exchange, Consignment and Special Transactions — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: 1 April: A sells goods to B and draws a three-month bill for ₹30,000, which B accepts. A's books: Bills Receivable A/c Dr ₹30,000; To B ₹30,000. (B's books mirror: A A/c Dr ₹30,000; To Bills Payable A/c ₹30,000.)

steps.label: Same day
steps.text: A discounts the bill at its bank at 12 per cent per annum. Bank A/c Dr ₹29,100; Discount A/c Dr ₹900; To Bills Receivable A/c ₹30,000 — the discount is an expense of A.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: 4 July (due date): the bill is dishonoured — B cannot pay. The bank, now the holder, reclaims the full amount plus ₹150 of noting charges paid to have the dishonour certified: B A/c Dr ₹31,150; To Bank A/c ₹31,150. The entire debt revives, larger by the noting charges recoverable from the acceptor.

steps.label: Noting charges exist because proof matters
steps.text: a notary's certificate of dishonour protects every party's recourse rights.

examples.title: Worked Chain Continued: Renewal and Retirement
examples.problem: Bills of Exchange, Consignment and Special Transactions — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: B, unable to pay on 4 July, negotiates a renewal: part payment now, a new two-month bill for ₹20,000, and interest at 12 per cent per annum on the rescheduled portion.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: B pays ₹11,150 cash (₹10,000 of the debt plus ₹150 noting) and interest of ₹400 (20,000 × 12 per cent × 2/12): Bank A/c Dr ₹11,550; To B ₹11,550.

steps.label: The new bill is drawn and accepted
steps.text: Bills Receivable A/c Dr ₹20,000; To B A/c ₹20,000 — due two months later, plus three days of grace.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: One month early, B retires the bill — pays ahead of maturity — earning a rebate, in substance interest for the unexpired month: 20,000 × 12 per cent × 1/12 = ₹200. A's books: Bank A/c Dr ₹19,800; Rebate on Bills A/c Dr ₹200; To Bills Receivable A/c ₹20,000. The rebate is an expense for holder A, income for acceptor B (mirror: Bills Payable Dr ₹20,000; To Bank ₹19,800; To Rebate Received ₹200).

examples.title: The Endorsement Route
examples.problem: Bills of Exchange, Consignment and Special Transactions — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Had A, instead of discounting, endorsed the ₹30,000 bill to its creditor C in settlement of a debt: C A/c Dr ₹30,000; To Bills Receivable A/c ₹30,000.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: On dishonour, liability reverses to the endorser with noting charges: B A/c Dr ₹30,150; To C A/c ₹30,150 — A owes C the amount plus charges, now.

steps.label: The moral
steps.text: the drawer's exposure survives until honour — a discounted or endorsed bill is financing obtained, not risk retired.

examples.title: Worked Example: A Consignment Round Trip
examples.problem: Bills of Exchange, Consignment and Special Transactions — worked through step by step

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: A consigns 100 machines costing ₹500 each (₹50,000) to B, paying ₹4,000 freight. B pays ₹2,000 unloading (non-recurring) and ₹3,000 of godown rent and selling costs (recurring). B sells 75 machines at ₹800 (₹60,000); 5 are destroyed by fire; 20 are unsold. Commission: 5 per cent on sales plus 2 per cent del credere.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Consignor's entries — Consignment A/c Dr ₹50,000; To Goods Sent on Consignment A/c ₹50,000. Consignment A/c Dr ₹4,000; To Bank A/c (freight). Consignee A/c Dr ₹60,000; To Consignment A/c (sales). Consignment A/c Dr ₹9,200; To Consignee A/c (₹5,000 expenses plus ₹4,200 commission).

steps.label: Abnormal loss
steps.text: Abnormal Loss A/c Dr ₹2,800; To Consignment A/c ₹2,800; and with the insurer admitting ₹2,500: Insurance Company A/c Dr ₹2,500; Profit and Loss A/c Dr ₹300; To Abnormal Loss A/c ₹2,800.

steps.label: Closing stock
steps.text: Consignment Stock A/c Dr ₹11,200; To Consignment A/c ₹11,200. Profit on consignment: Consignment A/c Dr ₹10,800; To Profit and Loss A/c ₹10,800.

steps.label: Remittance
steps.text: B sends 60,000 less 5,000 less 4,200 = ₹50,800 — Bank A/c Dr ₹50,800; To Consignee A/c ₹50,800.

keyTakeaways: Consignment account, debit side — goods consigned ₹50,000; freight ₹4,000; consignee's expenses ₹5,000; commission ₹4,200; total ₹63,200.
Consignment account, credit side — sales ₹60,000; abnormal loss ₹2,800; closing stock ₹11,200; total ₹74,000.
Balancing figure — profit on consignment ₹10,800, carried to profit and loss.
Consignee's account — debits ₹60,000 (sales); credits ₹9,200 (expenses and commission) and ₹50,800 (remittance); closes to nil.

Where next — Everything here runs on the journal discipline of Double-Entry Bookkeeping: The Logic Behind Every Ledger, and the revenue-recognition instincts come from The Accounting Cycle: Accruals, Adjustments and Closing the Books — the timing question those lessons pose is exactly what bills and consignments stress-test. Cash discipline for remittances belongs to Bank Reconciliation: Explaining Every Difference; Reading Financial Statements shows where consignment stock and bills receivable surface as current assets.
A bill of exchange is a three-party order — drawer, drawee-acceptor, payee; a promissory note is a two-party promise.
Usance bills mature at nominal period plus three days of grace; a three-month bill dated 1 April falls due 4 July.
The holder may retain, discount (bank pays face minus discount) or endorse a bill; the drawer's exposure survives all three.
Dishonour revives the debt plus noting charges: debit the acceptor with face plus charges.
Renewal settles part of the debt, charges interest on the rest and issues a new bill; retirement pays early and grants a rebate.
Consignment is agency: ownership and revenue stay with the consignor until the consignee sells — the proforma invoice out, the account sales back.
Del credere commission shifts bad-debt risk to the consignee; normal loss raises unit cost, abnormal loss is valued, insured and written off.
Closing stock on consignment carries proportionate cost plus non-recurring expenses only — ₹11,200 in the worked case, inside a ₹10,800 profit.
On-approval goods stay the seller's inventory until approval or expiry; goods in transit belong to whoever bore the risk at shipment.

quiz.q: A bill dated 1 April is drawn payable three months after date. It legally falls due on:
quiz.explanation: Three months after date runs to 1 July, plus three days of grace: 4 July.

quiz.q: When a discounted bill is dishonoured with ₹150 of noting charges, the drawer debits the acceptor with:
quiz.explanation: The full face revives plus noting charges recoverable from the acceptor — the bank collects both from the drawer, who reclaims both from the acceptor.

quiz.q: In the consignment worked example, the value of the 20 unsold machines includes:
options: Cost plus freight and unloading only
Cost plus freight, unloading, godown rent and selling costs
Cost plus the consignee's recurring expenses only
quiz.explanation: Stock carries proportionate cost to sale-ready state — cost, freight, non-recurring unloading (56,000 × 20/100 = ₹11,200); recurring costs are period selling effort, not stock.

quiz.q: A consignee earning del credere commission will, on a customer's bad debt from a credit sale made under the consignment:
options: Reimburse the consignor in full, absorbing the loss
Share the loss with the consignor equally
Pass the loss entirely to the consignor
Recover it from the customer's next purchase only
quiz.explanation: Del credere pay buys a guarantee: credit-sale collection risk sits with the consignee, which is why the commission is higher.

quiz.q: Goods sent to a customer on approval, still within the return period at year end, appear in the seller's closing inventory at:
options: Cost or lower net realisable value
Nil — they have left the premises
Cost plus delivery charges and a normal margin
quiz.explanation: No sale has occurred, so the goods remain the seller's stock — carried at cost or NRV, whichever is lower.

intro:
Economics studies scarcity from two heights. Macroeconomics looks down on the whole economy — national income, aggregate demand, inflation — territory covered by the measuring-the-economy and inflation lessons in the economics chapters. Microeconomics stands at eye level with the decision-makers: a household allocating a salary, a firm choosing an output level, a manager deciding whether to shut a product line. Business decisions are micro decisions almost by definition, and the firm-side half of microeconomics is really the study of one thing — cost. What does the next unit cost? What would we give up by choosing this instead of that? Which numbers in the accounts should change a decision, and which are noise? This lesson assembles the cost concepts every such decision runs on.

**Why this matters.** Pricing, outsourcing, product-line closures, capacity expansion, accepting or rejecting a special order — every one of these decisions is a cost question wearing a business suit. Firms that reason with the wrong cost concept (forgetting implicit costs, honouring sunk ones, allocating head-office rent to products that never caused it) systematically take bad decisions with confident arithmetic. The concepts here are the immune system against that.
objectives: Explain microeconomics: the firm-level lens on choice
Explain explicit and implicit costs; economic versus accounting profit
Explain fixed, variable and semi-variable costs
Explain total, average and marginal cost arithmetic
Explain diminishing returns and the U-shaped cost curve
Explain economies and diseconomies of scale
Explain sunk and opportunity costs as decision filters
Explain break-even and margin of safety

concepts.term: Microeconomics: the firm-level lens on choice
concepts.statement: Start with what a cost actually is. Explicit costs are payments that cross the counter: wages, raw materials, rent, interest, power bills. Implicit costs are the opportunity costs of resources the firm already owns — the owner’s own time, the family building housing the workshop, the savings invested without interest. Accountants, who must verify transactions, deduct only explicit costs; their result is accounting profit. Economists deduct explicit plus implicit costs; their result is economic profit. A shop that clears ₹6 lakh after paying all bills, while the owner could have earned ₹5 lakh in a salaried job and ₹1.2 lakh renting out the premises, is making an accounting profit of ₹6 lakh — and an economic loss of ₹0.2 lakh: the business destroys value relative to the owner’s next best alternative. Related is normal profit: the minimum return just sufficient to keep the entrepreneur’s resources in this business rather than the next best use. Zero economic profit is not failure — it means the firm is doing exactly as well as the best alternative, covering every implicit cost including normal profit.
$$\pi_e = R - (C_{explicit} + C_{implicit})$$
concepts.detail: Revenue minus explicit costs minus implicit costs; positive means the firm beats all alternatives, zero means it just matches them.

concepts.term: Explicit and implicit costs; economic versus accounting profit
concepts.statement: For output decisions, costs sort by how they respond to production. Fixed costs do not move with output in the short run — rent, salaries of permanent staff, insurance, depreciation of machinery — and are incurred even at zero output. Variable costs rise and fall with volume: materials, power, piece-rate wages, freight. Semi-variable costs are hybrids — a telephone bill with a fixed rental plus usage charges, electricity with a demand charge plus a per-unit rate. The distinction defines the short run itself: the period over which at least one input is fixed. In the long run every input can be varied — no cost is truly fixed; the firm can renegotiate leases, resize the plant, exit the industry. Adding the categories, total cost is fixed cost plus variable cost, and dividing by output converts the totals into averages.
$$AC = \frac{TC}{Q} = \frac{FC}{Q} + \frac{VC}{Q}, \qquad MC = \frac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q}$$
concepts.detail: Average cost is total cost per unit of output; marginal cost is the addition to total cost from producing one more unit. Since fixed cost does not change with output, the marginal cost of a unit is driven entirely by its variable cost.

concepts.statement: The arithmetic is worth doing once by hand. Suppose fixed cost is ₹60,000 and variable cost rises with output as in the table below. Reading across each row: total cost is fixed plus variable; average cost is total cost divided by quantity; marginal cost is the step up in total cost from the previous unit.

concepts.term: Total, average and marginal cost arithmetic
concepts.statement: The average-marginal rule explains the shape of the numbers. When marginal cost is below average cost, producing another unit drags the average down; when marginal cost is above average cost, it pulls the average up; marginal cost therefore crosses average cost exactly at average cost’s minimum — output 6 is heading that way in the table. Why does marginal cost fall at first and rise later? The law of diminishing marginal returns. In the short run the firm keeps some factor fixed — the machine, the shop floor — and adds units of a variable factor to it. Early additions specialise and cooperate, so each extra worker adds more output than the last, and the marginal cost of each unit falls. Past a point, the fixed factor becomes crowded: the tenth worker queues for the same machine, each extra worker adds less output than the last, and the marginal cost of each unit rises. The U-shape of short-run average cost is diminishing returns written in rupees. It is a short-run phenomenon: it is caused by a fixed factor, not by the firm being large.

concepts.term: Diminishing returns and the U-shaped cost curve
concepts.statement: Scale is the long-run story, and its logic is different. Moving along the long-run average cost curve, the firm varies every input together. Economies of scale push long-run average cost down as output expands: indivisible machinery used closer to capacity, bulk-purchase discounts, deeper specialisation of management and labour, cheaper finance for larger firms. Beyond some size, diseconomies take over: layers of management thicken, communication slows, coordination costs grow faster than output, and long-run average cost turns upward. The lowest point reachable on the long-run curve defines the minimum efficient scale — the smallest output at which the firm achieves minimum long-run average cost, and a clue to how many firms an industry can support. The classic error here is worth a warning: diminishing returns (short run, one fixed factor) and diseconomies of scale (long run, firm size) are different mechanisms that happen to both bend a cost curve upward.

First, dividing fixed cost by a planned volume and calling the result “the cost of one unit” mixes average and marginal reasoning — pricing that number treats fixed cost as if it varied. Second, sunk costs are not fixed costs: a fixed cost recurs and can be avoided by shutting down; a sunk cost is already spent and unrecoverable, and no decision can change it. Third, “zero economic profit” is not a loss — it includes normal profit, the entrepreneur’s own opportunity cost, fully paid.

That leads to the two great decision filters. A sunk cost — money already spent on a machine, an advertising campaign, a half-built project — is irrelevant to every forward-looking choice precisely because no future action can recover it; only incremental, avoidable costs count. An opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone: occupying the family warehouse for production means forgoing its rent, and that forgone rent is a real cost of production even though no invoice records it. The working distinction is between relevant costs, which differ between the alternatives being compared, and irrelevant costs, which do not — whether that is a sunk cost, an allocated share of common fixed costs, or a cost already committed either way.

concepts.term: Sunk and opportunity costs as decision filters
concepts.statement: Break-even analysis packages the fixed-variable split into planning arithmetic. Each unit sold at price P contributes its price minus its average variable cost toward covering fixed cost; break-even is reached exactly when total contribution equals fixed cost.

concepts.term: Break-even quantity and margin of safety
concepts.statement: $$Q^* = \frac{FC}{P - AVC}, \qquad MoS = \frac{Q_{actual} - Q^*}{Q_{actual}}$$
concepts.detail: Units needed to cover fixed cost: fixed cost divided by contribution per unit. Margin of safety is the fraction by which sales can fall before losses begin.

concepts.statement: An actual payment for a resource — wages, rent, materials — recorded in the books.
The opportunity cost of self-owned, self-employed resources; no invoice, but a real cost.
Revenue minus explicit and implicit costs; zero means matching the best alternative.
A cost with a fixed component and a usage component, like a telephone bill.
The addition to total cost from one more unit of output; driven entirely by variable cost.
The smallest output at which long-run average cost reaches its minimum.
A past, unrecoverable outlay — irrelevant to rational forward decisions.
The value of the best alternative forgone when a choice is made.
The proportional cushion between actual sales and the break-even level.

examples.title: Worked Case: Keep or Close the Product Line
examples.problem: Cost Concepts for Business Decisions — worked through step by step

steps.label: The situation
steps.text: a firm’s mugs line shows a “loss” of ₹40,000 after the accounts allocate it ₹1,50,000 of head-office rent and depreciation on machinery bought two years ago. Mugs revenue is ₹8,00,000; their avoidable costs (materials, labour, power, dedicated supervisor) are ₹7,50,000.

steps.label: Filter the sunk and allocated
steps.text: the rent is paid for the whole building whether or not mugs are made — irrelevant; the machine’s purchase price is spent — sunk and irrelevant. Both exist on one side of each alternative.

steps.label: Compare the alternatives
steps.text: keep mugs and the firm nets ₹8,00,000 − ₹7,50,000 = ₹50,000; close mugs and it nets zero from the line, while the rent and depreciation continue unchanged.

steps.label: Add the opportunity cost check
steps.text: if the vacated space could be sublet for ₹80,000 a year, closing would yield ₹80,000 — better than ₹50,000 — and closing becomes the right call.

steps.label: State the principle
steps.text: only costs that differ between alternatives (the ₹7,50,000 avoidable set, the ₹80,000 sublet) drive the decision; the allocated ₹1,50,000 was noise that made a profitable line look sick.

examples.title: Worked Case: Break-even for a Garment Unit
examples.problem: Cost Concepts for Business Decisions — worked through step by step

steps.label: Inputs
steps.text: fixed costs ₹6,00,000 a year; each shirt sells for ₹1,500 with variable cost ₹900 — materials, trimmings, piece-rate stitching, packaging.

steps.label: Contribution per unit
steps.text: 1,500 − 900 = ₹600, the amount each shirt throws off toward fixed cost.

steps.label: Break-even
steps.text: 6,00,000 ÷ 600 = 1,000 shirts — below that the firm loses money, above it each shirt adds ₹600 of profit.

steps.label: Margin of safety
steps.text: at planned sales of 1,500 shirts, MoS = (1,500 − 1,000) ÷ 1,500 = 33 percent — sales can drop by a third before the unit slips into loss.

keyTakeaways: Output 0 — fixed 60,000, variable 0, total 60,000; average cost undefined at zero output.
Output 1 — variable 20,000, total 80,000, average 80,000, marginal 20,000.
Output 2 — variable 36,000, total 96,000, average 48,000, marginal 16,000.
Output 3 — variable 48,000, total 108,000, average 36,000, marginal 12,000.
Output 4 — variable 60,000, total 120,000, average 30,000, marginal 12,000.
Output 5 — variable 78,000, total 138,000, average 27,600, marginal 18,000.
Output 6 — variable 102,000, total 162,000, average 27,000, marginal 24,000.

Where next — Prerequisites: the lesson on supply, demand and elasticity in the economics chapters, which shows how marginal cost shapes the firm’s supply behaviour — the two lessons meet at the profit-maximising output. Follow-ons: the business-cycles lesson in this chapter shows what fixed costs do to profits when demand swings; the lesson on financial statements in the accounting chapters shows where these costs live in the books; and the macro lessons take the economy-wide view this one deliberately brackets.
Microeconomics is the firm-and-household lens; business decisions are micro decisions, and cost is their common currency.
Economic profit deducts implicit costs alongside explicit ones; zero economic profit means matching the best alternative, normal profit included.
Costs split by behaviour: fixed (unmoved by output), variable (move with it), semi-variable (both).
MC = ΔTC/ΔQ and AC = TC/Q; marginal crosses average at average’s minimum — the U-shape is diminishing returns in rupees.
In the long run all inputs vary: economies of scale then diseconomies set the shape, and minimum efficient scale sizes the efficient plant.
Sunk costs are irrelevant to decisions; opportunity costs are the value of the forgone alternative; only relevant costs — those that differ between alternatives — matter.
Break-even: units = fixed cost ÷ (price − average variable cost); margin of safety measures the cushion above it.

quiz.q: A firm earns ₹2 lakh accounting profit; the owner forgoes a ₹2.4 lakh salary and ₹0.3 lakh interest on invested savings. Economic profit is:
options: zero, because normal profit is included
quiz.explanation: Economic profit deducts implicit costs too: 2.0 − 2.4 − 0.3 = −0.7 lakh; the firm underperforms the owner’s alternatives.

quiz.q: Average cost is falling when:
options: marginal cost is above average cost
marginal cost is below average cost
output is beyond the minimum efficient scale
quiz.explanation: The average-marginal rule: below-average marginals drag the average down; marginal crosses average at its minimum.

quiz.q: A factory paid ₹9 lakh for a machine that now has no resale value. In deciding whether to accept a low-price order that covers materials and labour but nothing more:
options: the order must also cover a share of the ₹9 lakh
the ₹9 lakh is sunk and irrelevant; only incremental costs and forgone alternatives matter
the order must be rejected since fixed costs exist
the decision depends on the depreciation charge
quiz.explanation: A past, unrecoverable outlay cannot be affected by any present choice; only costs that differ between accepting and rejecting count.

quiz.q: Fixed cost ₹4,80,000; price ₹400; average variable cost ₹280. The break-even quantity is:
quiz.explanation: Contribution per unit = 400 − 280 = ₹120; 4,80,000 ÷ 120 = 4,000 units to cover fixed cost.

quiz.q: The U-shape of the SHORT-RUN average cost curve is caused by:
options: the law of diminishing marginal returns to the variable factor
rising input prices as the industry expands
the fall in fixed cost per unit
quiz.explanation: Short-run U-shape is diminishing returns on a fixed factor; scale economies and diseconomies shape the LONG-run curve.

intro:
Market economies do not grow in a straight line. Total output, employment, incomes and trade rise together for a few years, then stall and fall together for a while, then rise again — a rhythm economists have measured since the nineteenth century, when the sunspot-observing William Stanley Jevons first tried to explain it. A business cycle is this sequence of expansions and contractions in aggregate economic activity. The crucial word is recurrence, not periodicity: cycles return, but with no fixed length and no two alike, which is why forecasting them is an art with statistical tools rather than a clock reading. This lesson covers the phases, the measurement apparatus, the competing explanations, and what the cycle does to firms and households — leaving the policy machinery itself to the fiscal and monetary lessons.

**Why this matters.** For a firm, the cycle is the weather: hiring, inventory, capacity and borrowing decisions made at the peak are tested in the trough, and most corporate failures are trough failures. For a household, employment and wage income are the most cyclical things in the economy — recessions destroy jobs years before they destroy capital. For anyone reading economic news, the cycle supplies the frame into which every inflation print, rate decision and budget fits.
objectives: Explain recurrence without periodicity
Explain four phases: expansion, peak, contraction, trough
Explain recession and depression terminology
Explain leading, coincident and lagging indicators
Explain causes: shocks, the accelerator, credit, psychology
Explain procyclical profits and operating leverage
Explain countercyclical policy responses

concepts.statement: The classic definition comes from Wesley Mitchell and Arthur Burns: a business cycle is a type of fluctuation found in the aggregate economic activity of nations that organise their work mainly in business enterprises — a cycle consists of expansion occurring at about the same time in many economic activities, followed by similarly general recessions, contractions and revivals that merge into the expansion of the next cycle. Two features travel with the definition. Comovement: the cycle is not one industry staggering but output, employment, incomes and sales moving together across sectors, which is why a single sector’s boom (a mining discovery) is growth, not a cycle. Pervasive but aperiodic: the same sequence recurs, but intervals vary from a few years to a decade, and no two cycles share an amplitude — the dot-com bust was shallow, the 2008 crisis was deep.

concepts.term: Four phases: expansion, peak, contraction, trough
concepts.statement: The four phases are best read as a story of the economy’s gauges. Expansion: output rises above its previous peak and keeps climbing; employment grows and unemployment falls; capacity utilisation tightens; credit is easy and cheap, so investment in plant, housing and inventories surges; profits rise, stock markets rise with them, and optimism becomes self-reinforcing. Peak: the economy is running hot — labour and raw materials are scarce, wages and input prices accelerate, order books are full but delivery times lengthen, inflation pressure builds, and central banks begin to lean against the boom; confidence surveys register euphoria. Contraction — recession when mild and broad: output falls, firms cut hours first and jobs second, investment in new capacity collapses because existing capacity is idle, inventories are slashed as firms sell from stock, credit tightens as banks grow cautious and defaults rise, profits fall faster than sales. Trough: the low point — idle factories, weak credit demand, pessimism in surveys — from which recovery begins: restocking alone lifts production, borrowing costs are typically at their lows, and expectations, having nowhere lower to go, turn. On terminology: a common rule of thumb calls two consecutive quarters of falling real output a recession, while the American committee that formally dates cycles — and its counterparts elsewhere — defines it more broadly as a significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy, lasting more than a few months, visible in output, income, employment and trade. A depression is simply a recession that is exceptionally deep and prolonged; no formal threshold exists, but the benchmark remains the early 1930s, when output in the United States fell by roughly a quarter to a third and unemployment reached about a quarter of the workforce.
