Percentage is vanity, value per share is sanity — and the check that matters is whether each round’s milestone actually moved the valuation.

keyTakeaways: Crowdfunding platforms enforce the discipline OpenStax preaches: Kickstarter campaigns that budget nothing for reward fulfillment are the canonical way to raise money and still die — the iBackPack raised over $700,000 on Indiegogo and Kickstarter, delivered nothing, and drew an FTC investigation.
Y Combinator standardized the SAFE in 2013; it is now the default instrument for pre-seed rounds precisely because it defers the valuation argument both sides would rather not have yet.
TOMS Shoes’ One-for-One model — a pair donated for every pair sold — is the textbook’s flagship case of social entrepreneurship, where the funding strategy is baked into the revenue model itself.
Accelerators institutionalize the ladder: a fixed seed check on a SAFE, three months of milestones, and a demo day engineered to compress the next round’s diligence into a single afternoon.

Where next — Prerequisite: the lean-startup lesson — unit economics tell you whether the growth you are financing is worth buying. Continue with accounting depth for the three statements in full, the marketing lesson for the CAC side of the runway equation, and the behavioral-economics lesson for how valuation negotiations actually get decided.
Finance raises the money; accounting proves stewardship — investors demand both.
The ladder: bootstrap and no-loan strategies first, angels next, priced venture rounds as milestones unlock them.
Ownership = investment ÷ post-money valuation; the cap table records it in shares.
Dilution compounds each round — judge it by value per share, not percentage.
Runway = cash ÷ monthly burn; the cash-flow statement, not the income statement, is the survival document.

quiz.q: A company has a pre-money valuation of four million and raises one million. What does the new investor own?
quiz.explanation: One million divided by the five-million post-money valuation is twenty percent — the investment, not the pre-money, is the numerator.

quiz.q: According to OpenStax, the structural advantage bootstrapping has over equity funding is:
quiz.explanation: Bootstrapping keeps every share with the founders — the costs are slower growth and full personal exposure to cash shortfalls.

quiz.q: Which financial statement best answers the question "can this startup survive the next six months?"
quiz.explanation: Profitable-on-paper companies die of cash gaps daily; runway comes from cash on hand versus monthly net burn.

quiz.q: A SAFE defers valuation by:
options: Converting into shares at the next priced round, at a cap or discount
Repaying investors in products instead of shares
quiz.explanation: The SAFE buys today’s cash with tomorrow’s equity at a guaranteed discount to whatever valuation the next round sets.

intro:
A factory that runs out of one component stops; a shop that runs out of a bestseller loses the sale to a rival; a warehouse stacked with unsold stock is cash quietly rotting. Operations management — the discipline of turning inputs into outputs reliably, again and again — lives in the gap between those failures, and inventory is its central tension: every unit held is insurance against uncertainty and a cost that never sleeps. Logistics moves the buffers around; lean manufacturing tries to shrink them; and the bullwhip effect explains why, left alone, they scream. This lesson is the machinery behind every shelf you have ever seen empty — and every full one somebody is paying to hold.

**Why this matters.** Supply chains became headline news in 2020–22 when chips, ships and containers all vanished at once, and managers rediscovered what operations researchers had formalised over sixty years: buffers, batching and delays interact in predictable — and fixable — ways. Whether you run a bakery or only read business news, the economic order quantity, safety stock and the bullwhip effect explain the empty shelf, the full warehouse, and the difference between the two.
objectives: Explain inventory as a buffer between rates
Explain the economic order quantity
Explain safety stock and service levels
Explain the bullwhip effect and its four causes
Explain lean manufacturing and the seven wastes
Explain logistics networks and risk pooling

concepts.term: Inventory as a buffer between rates
concepts.statement: Operations management treats a firm as a system of flows — materials, information and money — rather than a box of separate decisions. Inventory comes in four flavours: cycle stock (ordered in batches to exploit economies of scale), safety stock (held against demand and lead-time surprises), pipeline stock (moving on trucks and ships — often half the total), and anticipation stock (built ahead of a known peak, like fireworks before July). Each exists because supply and demand, at some point in the chain, do not arrive at the same rate.

The oldest quantitative answer in the field is the economic order quantity, published by Ford Harris in 1913. Ordering in large batches spreads the fixed cost of an order over more units but piles up holding cost — capital, storage, shrinkage, obsolescence; ordering often does the reverse. The optimum balances the two, and it carries a famous piece of intuition: because the formula takes a square root, doubling your annual demand raises the optimal batch by only about 41 per cent, not 100. Scale rewards bigger batches sublinearly — one reason warehouses grew while delivery windows shrank.

Safety stock answers a different question: how wrong can demand and lead time be before a stockout? A service level — say 95 or 99 per cent — is converted into a statistical buffer over expected lead-time demand. The higher the target, the more expensive the tail: moving from 95 to 99 per cent can nearly double the buffer, because you are insuring against progressively rarer events. Fixing the source — shortening lead times or stabilising demand — is usually cheaper than stacking inventory against it.

concepts.term: The bullwhip effect and its four causes
concepts.statement: The bullwhip effect is the field's signature pathology: small swings in retail demand become violent oscillations in factory orders and raw-material supply. Jay Forrester spotted it in industrial simulations in the late 1950s; Hau Lee and colleagues named its four causes in 1997 — demand-signal processing (each stage forecasts from the orders it sees, not true demand), order batching (lumpy orders look lumpier upstream), price fluctuations (forward buying on promotions), and rationing games (customers inflate orders during shortages, then cancel). MIT's beer-distribution game shows intelligent players generating wild swings from a one-time blip; Procter & Gamble documented it in nappies, where baby consumption was nearly flat yet distributor orders swung wildly. The systems-thinking lesson in Emerging & Interdisciplinary covers the feedback mechanics; the operations cures are shared point-of-sale data, smaller and more frequent batches, everyday-stable pricing, and vendor-managed inventory.

concepts.term: Lean manufacturing and the seven wastes
concepts.statement: Lean manufacturing — the Toyota Production System built by Taiichi Ohno after 1950 — attacks the whole buffer. Ohno catalogued seven wastes: overproduction, waiting, transport, over-processing, excess inventory, unnecessary motion, and defects. His countermeasures were just-in-time flow (produce only what the next station pulls, via kanban cards), jidoka (stop the line the moment something is wrong, rather than passing defects downstream) and kaizen (continuous small improvements). Note the distinction from the lean-startup lesson in this domain: Eric Ries borrowed Toyota's vocabulary, but his build-measure-learn loop searches for a business model; this is the factory-floor original, optimising a process already known to work.

Logistics is the physical network that moves the buffers: modes, routes, warehouses and the trade-off at its heart — fast transport is expensive, slow transport forces bigger inventories. Malcom McLean's container (1956) cut loading costs so far that shipping became nearly free, redrawing global manufacturing maps. One last idea does quiet hero work: risk pooling. Consolidating n warehouses into one cuts total safety stock roughly by the square root of n, because independent demands partially offset each other — the same statistical logic the insurance lesson exploits.
$$Q^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{2 D S}{H}}$$
concepts.detail: D is annual demand, S the fixed cost per order, H the holding cost per unit per year; Q* is the batch size minimising the sum of ordering and holding costs.

concepts.statement: $$TC = \frac{D}{Q} S + \frac{Q}{2} H$$
concepts.detail: Annual ordering cost plus average holding cost; at Q* the two terms are equal — each about half the total.

concepts.statement: $$ROP = \bar{d}\,L + z\,\sigma_{d}\sqrt{L}$$
concepts.detail: Average daily demand times lead time, plus a safety buffer: the z-score for the target service level times daily-demand volatility scaled by the square root of lead time.

concepts.statement: The first error is reading just-in-time as zero inventory: Toyota holds buffers — the discipline is holding the right ones, deliberately. The second is blaming the bullwhip on bad forecasting when its real drivers are batching, promotions and shortage gaming — no forecast fixes incentives. The third is treating EOQ as gospel: it assumes constant demand and instant replenishment, so use it as a heuristic and recompute when the world changes. And safety stock is not a substitute for fixing unreliable lead times; it is a tax you pay for tolerating them.
Inventory ordered in batches to capture economies of scale, drawn down between orders.
Buffer inventory held against variability in demand or lead time, sized to a service level.
The batch size equalising annual ordering and holding costs; grows with the square root of demand.
The inventory level that triggers a new order: expected lead-time demand plus safety stock.
Amplification of demand variability as orders move upstream in a supply chain.
The pull signal — card or digital — authorising production or withdrawal of a container in lean systems.
Consolidating inventory locations so independent demands offset, cutting safety stock by roughly the square root of the number of pools merged.

examples.title: Worked example — Inventory, Logistics and the Bullwhip Effect
examples.problem: A parts distributor sells 12,000 filters a year, each order placed costs 75 in paperwork and freight, and holding a filter for a year costs 4. What should it order, how often, and when should it reorder?

steps.label: Compute the EOQ
steps.text: Q* = sqrt(2 × 12,000 × 75 ÷ 4) = sqrt(450,000) ≈ 671 units — about 18 orders a year, or roughly one every three weeks.

steps.label: Check the balance
steps.text: annual ordering cost = (12,000 ÷ 671) × 75 ≈ 1,342; annual holding cost = (671 ÷ 2) × 4 ≈ 1,342. Equal, as the theory promises — total ≈ 2,684, the cheapest possible.

steps.label: Set the reorder point
steps.text: daily demand = 12,000 ÷ 250 days = 48; lead time 6 days; daily standard deviation 12; for 95 per cent service z = 1.65. ROP = 48 × 6 + 1.65 × 12 × sqrt(6) ≈ 288 + 49 ≈ 337 units.

examples.result: order 671 units whenever stock hits 337. If the supplier offers to hold a consignment stock nearby, lead time effectively falls toward zero — and the safety buffer shrinks with the square root of lead time.

keyTakeaways: Retail replenishment: supermarkets reorder daily from point-of-sale data precisely to starve the bullwhip of order batching.
Automotive supply: car makers kept the Toyota model running for decades, with kanban signals pacing entire supplier networks.
E-commerce fulfilment: Amazon's warehouse placement is risk pooling at national scale, trading delivery speed against inventory consolidation.
Humanitarian logistics: disaster agencies pre-position supplies by expected lead time, because the first week of a crisis has no functioning market.
Chip supply after 2021: firms that had copied just-in-time without Toyota's parallel discipline of strategic buffers learned the difference expensively.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — comfort with square roots helps. Follow with the project-management lesson in this subject, the accounting lessons for how inventory is costed on the balance sheet, and the probability lesson in Everyday Knowledge for the statistics behind safety stock. Exercise: estimate the EOQ for something a campus shop sells, using realistic order and holding costs — the numbers are usually surprising.

quiz.q: A store sells 12,000 units a year; each order costs 75 and each unit costs 4 a year to hold. The economic order quantity is closest to…
quiz.explanation: Q* = sqrt(2 × 12,000 × 75 ÷ 4) = sqrt(450,000) ≈ 671 — ordering and holding costs balance there.

quiz.q: If the annual holding cost per unit doubles, the optimal order quantity…
quiz.explanation: Q* shrinks with 1 over the square root of H: dividing by sqrt(2) ≈ 1.41 leaves about 71 per cent of the original batch.

quiz.q: The bullwhip effect is best described as…
options: random noise in retail sales data
demand variability amplifying upstream as each stage orders from the distorted signal it sees
a sudden rise in transport costs
quiz.explanation: Forecasting from orders rather than demand, batching, promotions and shortage gaming compound at every tier — Lee's four causes.

quiz.q: In lean production, a kanban card is…
options: a quality certificate issued by Toyota
a pull signal authorising production or withdrawal of a specific container
quiz.explanation: Nothing is produced without a kanban authorising it — the downstream station literally pulls work upstream.

intro:
The Sydney Opera House was approved in 1957 as a four-year, 7-million-dollar project; it opened in 1973, ten years late and fourteen times over budget, and remains one of history's most beloved buildings. Projects — temporary endeavours with a defined output, a deadline and a budget — fail in famously predictable ways, and project management is the discipline that grew from their wreckage. Its central insight is structural: scope, time and cost are one constraint wearing three faces, and every methodology, from aerospace flowcharts to software sprints, is a different strategy for keeping them honest.

**Why this matters.** Consultancies, construction firms, software houses, hospitals and film studios all run on projects — the World Bank estimated project-style work at tens of trillions of dollars a year, and independent studies routinely find most large projects finish late and over budget. Knowing the critical path and the difference between waterfall and agile is knowing why your release slipped — and what the honest options for fixing it are.
objectives: Explain projects versus operations
Explain the triple constraint
Explain work breakdown structure
Explain the critical path method
Explain float, crashing and trade-offs
Explain waterfall versus agile delivery

concepts.statement: A project is temporary and unique — build the bridge, launch the app, move the office — while operations repeat a known process, as the inventory lesson in this subject describes. The triple constraint (the iron triangle) binds every project: scope is what is being built, time is the deadline, cost is the budget — and quality sits awkwardly in the middle. Change one corner and the others must give: add features, and time or money must absorb it. Scope creep — requirements arriving after the plan is set — is the quiet killer, because each addition looks small and none of them leave.

Planning starts with the work breakdown structure: decompose the deliverable into work packages small enough to estimate, assign and finish — typically the units that one owner can be accountable for. Two things improve dramatically at this granularity: estimates (big things are estimated by optimism, small things by experience) and accountability. The behavioural lesson in this domain explains the deeper bias at work — the planning fallacy, best countered by consulting how long similar things actually took (the outside view) rather than how this one feels.

The critical path method, developed at DuPont in 1957 by Kelley and Walker (with the Navy's PERT variant arriving a year later for the Polaris programme), turns the task list into a network of dependencies. The longest path through that network — in duration, not in number of tasks — sets the project's length; that chain of tasks is the critical path, and it has zero slack. Every other task has float: how long it can slip without delaying the whole project. This single calculation separates the tasks that matter from the tasks that can wait — the essence of managing anything with dependencies.

Float is also the currency of trade-offs. Crashing means spending money to shorten critical tasks — overtime, more people, faster equipment — and each option has a cost per week saved. The trap is re-criticalisation: shorten one path enough and a formerly slack parallel path becomes the new critical one, after which further crashing of the original tasks buys nothing. Fast-tracking, running tasks in parallel that were planned sequentially, buys time without money but adds rework risk. Both moves say the same thing: once you know which tasks are critical, schedule pressure becomes an engineering decision instead of an atmosphere.

Waterfall is the classic strategy: requirements, design, build, test, deliver — sequential phases, each signed off before the next begins. It suits stable requirements and physical outputs, where late change is ruinous: you cannot iterate a poured foundation. Its weakness is exactly that: if the requirements were wrong, you discover it at the end, when it is most expensive. Winston Royce's 1970 paper, often cited as waterfall's origin, actually presented the model to argue against single-pass use.

Agile inverts the bet. Work ships in short iterations — Scrum, the dominant dialect from 1995, runs one-to-four-week sprints around a prioritised backlog, with daily stand-ups and a retrospective at each cycle. Requirements are expected to emerge, and feedback is the steering wheel; the trade-off is less predictability of final scope and cost. The choice is not fashion but information: waterfall when the destination is known, agile when it is being discovered — which is why the lean-startup lesson reads as agile applied to the business model itself. Most real programmes blend both, shipping increments inside a waterfall-shaped contract.
$$F = LS - ES = LF - EF$$
concepts.detail: Latest start minus earliest start for a task: the slack available before it delays the project's finish (zero on the critical path).
A weighted estimate from optimistic, most-likely and pessimistic durations — the mode counted four times; the spread b − a encodes uncertainty.

concepts.statement: $$s = \frac{\text{crash cost} - \text{normal cost}}{\text{normal time} - \text{crash time}}$$
concepts.detail: The extra money per week (or day) saved by accelerating a task — crash the cheapest critical tasks first.

concepts.statement: The classic diseases are student syndrome (start at the last possible moment, consuming all float) and Parkinson's law (work expands to fill the time available) — together they turn slack into lateness. Managers mistake the critical path for a ranking of importance: it ranks schedule impact, not business value. Agile is not an absence of planning — it is re-planning every sprint, and pretending otherwise produces chaos wearing a board and sticky notes. And multitasking across projects stretches every timeline: queueing effects mean three concurrent projects finish later than three sequential ones.
The interlocked limits of scope, time and cost; changing one corner forces movement in another.
Uncontrolled growth of requirements after the baseline plan is set.
Hierarchical decomposition of a project into estimable, assignable work packages.
The longest duration path through the task network; it fixes the project's minimum length.
Time a task can slip without delaying the project; zero for critical-path tasks.
Spending money to shorten critical tasks, cheapest cost-slope first, watching for path re-criticalisation.
A fixed short iteration in agile methods, ending in reviewable, shipped work.

examples.title: Worked example — Project Management: Scope, Time and Cost
examples.problem: A software release must fit a 12-week deadline. Tasks: A requirements (3 weeks, then everything); B backend build (5 weeks, after A); C interface design (2 weeks, after A, parallel to B); D integration (4 weeks, after B and C); E final testing (2 weeks, after D).

steps.label: Enumerate the paths
steps.text: A–B–D–E = 3 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 14 weeks; A–C–D–E = 3 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 11 weeks. The critical path is A–B–D–E at 14 weeks — the release is 2 weeks late as planned.

steps.label: Compute float
steps.text: the interface design task C sits on an 11-week path, so it has 14 − 11 = 3 weeks of float; it can slip three weeks without moving the release date.

steps.label: Crash the critical path
steps.text: B can be shortened one week for 3,000 and D one week for 4,000 — crash both and the project lands at 12 weeks for 7,000. Note the limit: with B and D shortened, A–B–D–E falls to 12 weeks, exactly equal to the parallel path — A and E are now critical too, and further compression of B alone buys nothing.

examples.result: the deadline is met for 7,000 of acceleration cost, and the manager can articulate the trade — three cheaper alternatives were dropping a feature, moving the date, or accepting the overtime — because the network made the constraint visible.

keyTakeaways: Construction scheduling: critical-path contracts often make the day of completion a liquidated-damages clause — time is literally money.
Software delivery: sprint cadences and burn-down charts are agile's instruments for making progress visible weekly.
Events: an Olympics or a product launch is a fixed-deadline project — scope must flex, because the date cannot.
Pharmaceutical development: stage-gate processes blend waterfall governance with iterative science between gates.
Maintenance turnarounds: refinery shutdowns compress years of planning into weeks of execution, all critical path.

Where next — Prerequisites: none. Follow with the negotiation lesson in the Management & Leadership subject for the politics of scope, the leadership lesson for the people who must actually finish the tasks, and queueing theory in the statistics direction for why multitasking is poison. Exercise: draw the dependency network of a group assignment you have due, find the critical path, and note which deadlines are real and which are theatre.

quiz.q: Total float is best defined as…
options: how long a task can slip without delaying the project finish
the time a worker is idle
quiz.explanation: Float is schedule slack: latest minus earliest start. Critical-path tasks have none.

quiz.q: PERT gives optimistic 2, most-likely 5 and pessimistic 8 weeks. The expected duration is…
quiz.explanation: (2 + 4×5 + 8) ÷ 6 = 30 ÷ 6 = 5 — the most-likely estimate weighted four times.

quiz.q: You crash a critical task until its path is no longer the longest. Project duration is now set by…
options: the parallel path, which is now critical
quiz.explanation: Duration always equals the longest path; compressing one path hands the bottleneck to the next — re-criticalisation.

quiz.q: Agile delivery is the stronger fit when…
options: requirements are stable and fully specified
requirements are uncertain and will emerge through feedback
the deadline must be fixed at any scope
quiz.explanation: Agile trades up-front predictability for steering; discovery is its home ground, as the lean-startup lesson generalises.

intro:
Two identical houses sell on the same street; one fetches fifteen per cent more than the other, and the difference is not the houses. Negotiation — over salaries, cars, mergers, treaties and bedtimes — is where preparation quietly converts into money, and it is a craft with an actual theory. The Harvard Negotiation Project, crystallised in Fisher and Ury's 1981 classic Getting to Yes, replaced the folklore of bluffs and bravado with a small set of load-bearing ideas: interests, alternatives, and the zone of agreement between them. Learn those three and most negotiations stop being contests of nerve.

**Why this matters.** A single negotiated raise early in a career compounds through every subsequent salary, exactly as the compound-interest lesson in this domain predicts — thousands of salary-dollars ride on one conversation. The same toolkit prices mergers, settles lawsuits (the procedure lesson in Law & Governance shows how) and settles family schedules. Nothing else in business pays so reliably per hour of preparation.
objectives: Explain positions versus interests
Explain bATNA: the power to walk away
Explain reservation prices and the ZOPA
Explain creating versus claiming value
Explain anchors and first offers
Explain principled negotiation and ethics

concepts.statement: The founding distinction is positions versus interests. A position is what someone says they want — the orange, the 85,000 salary, the Monday deadline. An interest is why they want it. The parable: two sisters each claim the last orange; they compromise and split it, whereupon one squeezes her half for juice and the other grates her half's peel for a cake. Both could have had whole fruit. Behind most opposed positions lie shared interests and compatible differences; the negotiator's first job is to ask why until the interests surface.

concepts.term: BATNA: the power to walk away
concepts.statement: Your BATNA — best alternative to a negotiated agreement — is your power source. It is not your dream outcome or your budget; it is the concrete course you will take if this deal dies: the other job offer, the other buyer, the courtroom, the status quo. A negotiator with a strong BATNA can walk, and everyone senses it; one who needs this deal pays for the need. Hence the discipline: never negotiate to improve your BATNA — improve your BATNA to negotiate. Get the competing offer, line up the second supplier, before you sit down.

From the BATNA comes the reservation price — the worst terms you will accept before walking — and from two reservation prices comes the ZOPA, the zone of possible agreement between them. If the seller's floor is 9,000 and the buyer's ceiling is 11,500, any price in that band beats both parties' alternatives. If the buyer's ceiling is 8,500, the ZOPA is negative and the correct outcome is no deal — a good walk-away is a success, not a failure. Most bad agreements come from never discovering the zone was empty, or from agreeing inside your own reservation price out of fatigue or need.

Value is created, then claimed. Distributive negotiation divides a fixed pie — one price, one number, my gain your loss. Integrative negotiation grows the pie first: logrolling trades issues the parties value differently (you care about start date, they care about title); contingency agreements bet differences of forecast instead of fighting them (payment scales with performance); and multiple equivalent offers let the other side reveal preferences by choosing. The masters sequence these: create value across many issues, then claim it on the one that matters most. Single-issue negotiations — price only — are where both sides lose the most.

Anchoring is the psychology that prices the room: the first number spoken pulls the final settlement toward it, as the behavioural-economics lesson in this domain documents. When you know the market, make the first offer and make it ambitious-but-defensible; when you are poorly informed, let them anchor, then re-anchor explicitly (“that number is miles from the market — let's start from the data”). A range can soften an anchor's arrogance; a rationale strengthens it. The anchor is not a trick — it is a statement of where you believe the ZOPA sits.

Getting to Yes compresses the ethics into four rules: separate the people from the problem (be soft on persons, hard on issues); focus on interests, not positions; generate options for mutual gain before judging; insist on objective criteria — market comparables, appraisals, precedent — so the standard, not the will, decides. Hardball tactics (good cop/bad cop, the nibble, artificial deadlines) mostly fail against a prepared counterpart who names the tactic and returns to interests. And the legal boundary is real: puffery is ancient, but lying about material facts — the car's accident history, the company's accounts — is fraud, not tactics.
$$\text{ZOPA} = [\,R_{\text{seller}},\; R_{\text{buyer}}\,] \quad \text{nonempty iff} \; R_{\text{buyer}} \ge R_{\text{seller}}$$
concepts.detail: The set of terms better than both parties' reservation prices; a negative zone means walking away is the correct outcome.

concepts.statement: $$P^{*} = \frac{R_{\text{buyer}} + R_{\text{seller}}}{2}$$
concepts.detail: With equal bargaining power and information, surplus tends to split at the midpoint of the zone — which is why anchoring (moving the perceived zone) works.

concepts.statement: Negotiating without a known BATNA is flying blind — you cannot judge an offer you cannot compare. Fixating on one issue (price, salary) forfeits every logroll. Neediness is expensive: the party that must close pays for the urgency. Reflexively splitting the difference rewards whoever anchored most outrageously. Revealing your reservation price invites the deal to land exactly on it. And the agreement bias — accepting anything to be done — quietly signs people up for terms worse than walking away, the one unforced error the whole framework exists to prevent.
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement — the walk-away option that defines negotiating power.
The least favourable terms a party will accept before choosing its BATNA.
Zone of possible agreement: the range between the two reservation prices, when one exists.
Expanding value across multiple issues so both parties gain, before dividing it.
Trading issues the parties value differently — the engine of value creation.
The first number's gravitational pull on the final outcome.
Fisher and Ury's method: people apart from problems, interests over positions, options before judgement, objective criteria.

examples.title: Worked example — Negotiation: Interests, BATNA and the Zone of Agreement
examples.problem: A candidate receives an 80,000 offer. Her best alternative is a competing offer at 76,000 with a slower promotion track — she values that drawback at about 2,000, so her reservation price is 78,000. The employer's budget tops out at 90,000; recruiter fees and a three-month vacancy make it willing to go that high. What should happen?

steps.label: Map the ZOPA
steps.text: 78,000 to 90,000 — a wide zone, which predicts a deal and rewards ambition. The naive acceptance at 80,000 leaves 10,000 a year on the table.

steps.label: Prepare integrative issues
steps.text: the candidate cares about year-one cash (relocation) and title; the employer cares about the start date and internal pay equity — base salary sets precedents.

steps.label: Negotiate
steps.text: she anchors with research at 89,000; the employer counters 84,000. They logroll — a 5,000 signing bonus (cash without touching salary bands) and a start date two weeks earlier — and settle at 85,000 base plus the bonus.

examples.result: year-one cash of 90,000 against a reservation of 78,000 — she captured 12,000 of value at the top of the zone while the employer stayed inside its 90,000 envelope and protected its salary structure. Both sides measure themselves against alternatives, not against each other.

keyTakeaways: Salary and job offers: competing offers are BATNA-building, the single highest-leverage move in a career.
M&A and procurement: due diligence exists to locate the other side's reservation price before anchoring.
Diplomacy: treaties — see the international-law lesson — are integrative negotiation between states with public BATNAs.
House purchases: comparables are the objective criteria; the inspection and financing contingencies are the option value.
Family and shared houses: splitting chores by logrolling preferences is the orange parable with laundry.

Where next — Prerequisites: none. Follow with the game-theory lesson in the Strategy field for the mathematics underneath commitment and credibility, the behavioral-economics lesson for anchoring and loss aversion in the flesh, and the court-procedure lesson in Law & Governance for negotiation's litigation shadow. Exercise: before your next significant negotiation, write down your BATNA, your reservation price, and three questions that will surface the other side's interests.

quiz.q: Your BATNA is…
options: your best course of action if this deal is not reached
quiz.explanation: The alternative, not the aspiration: walk-away power is what a BATNA measures and what preparation strengthens.

quiz.q: A seller will not accept below 200,000; the buyer will not pay above 190,000. The parties should…
options: recognise the negative ZOPA and walk away
keep talking until one side tires
quiz.explanation: No terms beat both alternatives; a good walk-away is the theory working, not failing.

quiz.q: Logrolling refers to…
options: trading issues the parties value differently so both come out ahead
quiz.explanation: Differences in valuation are the raw material of value creation — the orange's peel and juice.

quiz.q: The most reliable source of negotiating power is usually…
options: a genuinely good alternative to this deal
quiz.explanation: Preparation that strengthens your BATNA beats every in-room tactic combined.

intro:
In 2012 Google did what only Google would think to do: it put its best statisticians on its own teams. Project Aristotle studied 180 teams over two years hunting for the composition of greatness — the right mix of geniuses, tenure and degrees. It found nothing of the sort. Who was on a team barely predicted how it performed; how they treated each other predicted almost everything, and the strongest single factor was psychological safety — the shared belief that you can speak up, admit error and ask naive questions without being punished. The finding rewired how serious companies think about management, and it is one pillar of a field — leadership — that most people experience daily and almost nobody studies systematically.

**Why this matters.** Hierarchies decide almost nothing on purpose: plans are proposed in meetings, errors are caught — or hidden — by people deciding whether it is safe to speak, and effort is volunteered or withheld based on motivations no spreadsheet sees. The research on safety and motivation explains why identical teams with identical resources produce wildly different results. For anyone who will ever run a project, a ward round or a study group, this is the highest-return invisible skill there is.
objectives: Explain leadership versus management
Explain styles and situational fit
Explain psychological safety
Explain intrinsic motivation and self-determination
Explain expectancy theory
Explain team stages and social loafing

concepts.statement: Leadership and management are not rival virtues but different jobs. John Kotter's classic distinction: management copes with complexity — planning, budgeting, organising, controlling; leadership copes with change — setting direction, aligning people, inspiring them to move. A function with only management ossifies; one with only leadership thrashes. The recurring failure of organisations is promoting brilliant managers into leadership roles on the assumption that the skills transfer, which is roughly like promoting a great violinist to conductor because the podium is near the stage.

Style theory's honest conclusion is that there is no best style — there is fit. The Blake-Mouton grid (1964) plots concern for people against concern for production and shames the corner that has neither; Hersey and Blanchard's situational model prescribes directing, coaching, supporting or delegating depending on the follower's competence and commitment — telling a novice what to do is kindness, telling an expert what to do is insult. James MacGregor Burns' transformational-versus-transactional distinction separates leaders who elevate followers' goals from those who simply trade rewards for compliance. The durable lesson is diagnostic: read the situation, then choose.

Psychological safety, defined by Amy Edmondson in her 1999 study of hospital teams, is a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking. Her most misunderstood finding: better teams reported more errors, not fewer — because safer climates make reporting honest, while unsafe ones keep the same mistakes in the dark. Google's finding elevated the factor to prime cause: teams where members spoke roughly equally (conversational turn-taking) and were sensitive to each other's cues outperformed teams stacked with individual stars. Safety is built by leaders who model fallibility (“here is what I got wrong”), respond to bad news with curiosity rather than blame, and frame hard work as learning rather than execution.

Motivation research's central divide is intrinsic versus extrinsic. Self-determination theory, by Deci and Ryan, holds that intrinsic motivation — doing something for its own satisfaction — feeds on three nutrients: autonomy (self-direction), competence (visible progress) and relatedness (connection to others). Edward Deci's experiments and later meta-analyses found that contingent external rewards can crowd intrinsic motivation out: pay people to solve puzzles they loved, and when the pay stops, they stop too. The managerial translation is not that money does not matter — unfair pay destroys motivation instantly — but that after pay is fair, the marginal lever is the design of the work itself.

Expectancy theory, Victor Vroom's 1964 account, is the diagnostic toolkit for stalled effort. Motivation is the product of three links: expectancy (effort will achieve performance), instrumentality (performance will be rewarded) and valence (the reward is wanted). A product of three probabilities is brutal: zero anywhere zeroes everything. The unmotivated employee is not a mystery but a triage — unclear goals kill expectancy, a broken appraisal system kills instrumentality, a reward nobody values kills valence. Herzberg's two-factor view adds the asymmetry: hygiene factors like salary and conditions prevent dissatisfaction but do not create satisfaction; only motivators — achievement, growth, recognition — do.

Groups develop, and they loaf. Bruce Tuckman's 1965 stages — forming, storming, norming, performing (adjourning added in 1977) — normalise the conflict phase as the route to norms, not the sign of a broken team. The darker statistical regularity is social loafing: Max Ringelmann's rope-pulling experiments in the 1910s found groups of eight pulling at less than four times one person's force, and later work confirmed effort fades when contributions become anonymous. The cures are structural: make individual contributions visible, keep teams small enough that shirking shows, and make the task matter — people do not loaf on work they find meaningful.

The worst misreading of psychological safety is comfort: safety without standards is a country club, and Edmondson's research is emphatic — the goal is candour plus high expectations, not niceness plus lowered bars. Style-training fails when it teaches one style as personality rather than diagnosis. The intrinsic-versus-extrinsic debate gets caricatured: pay unfairness destroys intrinsic drive faster than any spreadsheet can model. Tuckman's stages are weather, not schedule — teams re-storm when membership changes. And social loafing is not a character flaw; it is a design failure that anonymity guarantees.
Shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — speaking up, admitting error.
Elevating followers' goals and commitment, in Burns' sense, beyond transactional reward-trading.
Matching direction, coaching, support or delegation to the follower's competence and commitment.
Intrinsic motivation grows from autonomy, competence and relatedness.
Vroom: motivation equals expectancy times instrumentality times valence — zero anywhere zeroes it.
Herzberg's conditions that prevent dissatisfaction without creating satisfaction.
Effort falling as individual contributions become invisible in a group.

examples.title: Worked example — Leadership and Team Dynamics
examples.problem: A nine-person product team ships late every quarter; stand-ups are silent except for three voices, and defects surface only in final testing. Diagnose and intervene.

steps.label: Diagnose with the frameworks
steps.text: observe one week of meetings and count airtime — three members produce most of it (no turn-taking), and nobody names a problem until it detonates (low safety). Work is assigned to “the team,” not owners (classic loafing conditions); goals are handed down as fixed specs (no autonomy, low valence).

steps.label: Intervene on the strongest constraint first
steps.text: the lead opens each week by naming her own mistake from the last one, and replaces open stand-ups with a brief written round-robin so every voice arrives before the loudest three set the temperature.

steps.label: Restructure
steps.text: split the team into three trios with named owners per feature — individual contributions become visible; each trio chooses its solution path within the spec (autonomy restored); demos every fortnight make progress visible (competence).

steps.label: Measure after a quarter
steps.text: the same number of defects are found, but two-thirds of them now surface in the first half of the cycle instead of the last — the signature of early reporting rather than more error — and delivery lands on time twice running. The intervention targeted the speaking climate and the visibility of effort, exactly where the diagnosis pointed.

keyTakeaways: Hospital safety rounds and aviation checklists: industries where a silent junior must be able to stop a senior's mistake.
Software teams: blameless postmortems institutionalise safety so failure reports drive learning, not shame.
Schools and universities: project groups fail or succeed on loafing conditions — visibility, size, meaning — before any skill matters.
Boards and committees: the same three voices dominating every discussion is a governance risk, not a personality quirk — the corporate-law lesson shows what it costs.
Military crews: crew resource management was aviation's answer to the cockpit hierarchy that silenced copilots.

Where next — Prerequisites: none. Follow with the negotiation lesson in this subject for the other half of managing relationships, the employment-law lesson in Law & Governance for what may lawfully be asked of the people being led, and the project-management lesson for the structure teams operate inside. Exercise: at your next group meeting, silently count who speaks and who does not — then try one question addressed to the quietest person, phrased as a genuine request for their read.

quiz.q: Google's Project Aristotle found the strongest predictor of team effectiveness was…
options: psychological safety — how members treated risk-taking and each other
quiz.explanation: Composition variables barely predicted anything; conversational turn-taking and safety did.

quiz.q: In Edmondson's hospital study, better teams reported more errors because…
options: safer climates made reporting honest — hidden errors stay hidden elsewhere
quiz.explanation: The reporting rate measured the climate, not the error rate — the study's famous counterintuitive result.

quiz.q: Self-determination theory says intrinsic motivation feeds on…
quiz.explanation: Deci and Ryan's three nutrients — the design of the work, not the decoration around it.

quiz.q: Under expectancy theory, motivation collapses to zero when…
options: any one of the effort-to-performance, performance-to-reward or value links is zero
rewards are delayed by a week
quiz.explanation: Vroom's model is multiplicative — a single broken link zeroes the product, which is what makes it a diagnostic.

intro:
Insurance began in a London coffee house. From 1688, merchants and sea captains at Edward Lloyd's establishment slipped paper among the tables: each scribbled his name under a listed voyage, agreeing to bear a slice of the loss if the ship never came home. “Under-writing” is still the word. The modern industry those slips became — premiums measured in the trillions of dollars annually — does something quietly remarkable: it converts individual catastrophe into a predictable annual cost. The everyday probability lesson in this library covered why buying insurance can be rational despite its negative expected value; this lesson opens the insurer's side of the machine — how a pool prices risk, and the two diseases, adverse selection and moral hazard, that make markets for risk fail.

**Why this matters.** Insurance quietly decides the price of houses, cars, doctors and coastal cities — premiums are the shadow price of risk across the whole economy, and uninsurability is the leading indicator of a risk gone systemic (as flood zones and, in 2020, pandemic business interruption discovered). The pool's arithmetic also explains pension solvency, reinsurance towers and why an insurer can lose money on claims for decades and still thrive.
objectives: Explain risk pooling and the law of large numbers
Explain expected loss and premium loading
Explain float and the combined ratio
Explain adverse selection: the lemons problem
Explain moral hazard after coverage
Explain reinsurance and correlated risk

concepts.term: Risk pooling and the law of large numbers
concepts.statement: The engine is pooling under the law of large numbers. No insurer can say whether your house burns this year; with ten thousand similar houses, the fraction that burns is nearly the expected one, because independent risks partially cancel. The standard deviation of the average loss per policy shrinks with the square root of the pool's size — a hundredfold bigger pool, a tenfold tamer average — which is why insurers grow and why small mutuals buy reinsurance. This is diversification's statistical core, the same logic the inventory lesson exploits when it consolidates warehouses.

Pricing starts from expected loss — probability times severity — but the premium is not the expected loss. Loading covers acquisition commissions, administration, taxes and the cost of holding capital against bad years; a fair premium becomes a loaded one. Then comes the second, less obvious profit engine: float. Premiums arrive years before claims are paid, and the insurer invests the interval — Warren Buffett built much of Berkshire Hathaway's returns on exactly this. The industry's own scoreboard is the combined ratio: claims plus expenses over premiums. A ratio below 100 means underwriting profit; many sound insurers run above 100 and live on float income, which is why judging an insurer without reading both numbers is malpractice.

Adverse selection is the market failure that arrives before the policy does. The insured knows their risk better than the insurer — the asymmetric information of the market-failures lesson, for which George Akerlof's 1970 “lemons” paper is the founding text. If a pool charges one price for mixed risks, the low-risk customers are overcharged; they leave; the average risk worsens; the price must rise; more leave — Rothschild and Stiglitz modelled the resulting death spiral in 1976. The countermeasures are structural: underwriting and risk classification (charging by risk class), mandates that keep the healthy inside the pool (the logic behind the individual mandate in health reform), employer group coverage, and risk-adjustment transfers that pay insurers who enrol sicker members.

Moral hazard is the failure that arrives after the policy does: coverage changes behaviour. The insured lock doors less diligently; the generously reimbursed patient consumes more care; the protected bank takes more risk. Contract architecture is the cure: deductibles put the policyholder's own money at stake in every claim, copays and coinsurance keep marginal consumption costly, exclusions and caps carve out what cannot be priced, and experience rating ties next year's premium to this year's claims. There is even an insurable-interest requirement inherited from history: you may not insure your neighbour's house, because eighteenth-century London discovered that people who could profit from a fire had an alarming tendency to arrange one.

Two boundary conditions discipline the whole machine. First, correlation breaks pooling: the square-root law works only for independent risks, so earthquakes, hurricanes and pandemics — where everyone claims at once — require reinsurance, catastrophe bonds and government backstops, priced by a different and cruder logic. Reinsurance is insurance for insurers: the Munich Res and Swiss Res of the world, and the Lloyd's syndicates that still follow the 1688 model, take slices of primary insurers' books so that a single Florida hurricane does not erase a century of premiums. Second, regulation polices solvency — an insurer's promise is only as good as its capital — which is why supervisors mandate capital buffers and investment limits.
$$E[L] = p \times L$$
concepts.detail: Probability of the loss times its severity — the actuarially fair premium before any loading.

concepts.statement: $$\sigma_{\bar{L}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$
concepts.detail: The standard deviation of the average loss per policy falls with the square root of pool size — the statistical heart of insurance.

concepts.statement: $$P = E[L] \times (1 + \lambda)$$
concepts.detail: Expected loss grossed up by a loading factor for expenses, profit and capital cost.

concepts.statement: $$CR = \frac{\text{claims} + \text{expenses}}{\text{premiums}}$$
concepts.detail: Below 100 is an underwriting profit; above 100 the insurer is betting on float income to carry the year.

concepts.statement: The classic confusions: reading expected loss as the worst case (the tail is the story — that is why reinsurance exists); assuming the premium is the price of risk rather than risk plus loadings plus profit; blaming adverse selection on insurers when it is information asymmetry, cured only by classification or mandates; solving moral hazard with deductibles so large that the poor are effectively uninsured — reintroducing by the back door the variance insurance existed to remove. And whole-life products that mix insurance with investment should be evaluated as two purchases bundled, because that is what they are.
Averaging many independent risks makes the pool's loss fraction converge on its expectation.
The gross-up over expected loss covering expenses, profit and the cost of capital.
Premiums held between collection and claim payment; investable, and often the main profit engine.
Claims plus expenses as a share of premiums; below 100 signals underwriting profit.
High-risk buyers self-selecting into coverage at prices set for average risks — the lemons problem.
Behaviour change after coverage, controlled by deductibles, copays and experience rating.
Insurance bought by insurers to cap losses from large or correlated events.

examples.title: Worked example — Insurance: Pooling Risk and Pricing It
examples.problem: An insurer pools 10,000 houses, each with a 2 per cent annual chance of a 200,000 fire. What premium covers the pool with 95 per cent confidence, and what should be charged?

steps.label: Expected loss per house
steps.text: E[L] = 0.02 × 200,000 = 4,000 — the fair premium.

steps.label: Volatility
steps.text: per-house standard deviation = sqrt(0.02 × 0.98) × 200,000 ≈ 0.14 × 200,000 ≈ 28,000. For the pool's average, divide by sqrt(10,000) = 100 → 280 per house.

steps.label: Confidence
steps.text: the average claim per house is 4,000 ± (1.96 × 280) ≈ 4,000 ± 549 — a 95 per cent band of roughly ±14 per cent. The law of large numbers has done its work: a pool-level gamble has become a bookkeeping entry.

steps.label: Price
steps.text: with a 20 per cent loading for expenses and capital, charge P = 4,000 × 1.2 = 4,800. A 2,500 deductible then fights moral hazard — the homeowner's own money is at stake in the first slice of any loss — and buying reinsurance for the tail beyond, say, three standard deviations caps the pool's worst year.

keyTakeaways: Health-system design: mandates, risk adjustment and open enrolment windows are all adverse-selection engineering.
Auto telematics: pricing by measured driving is classification sharpened to the individual — and privacy's newest battleground.
Crop insurance: government-backed pools for weather risk too correlated for private balance sheets alone.
Cyber insurance: a young market re-learning old lessons about correlated risk every time one vulnerability hits thousands of firms at once.
Climate and coastal property: repricing and retreat from flood zones is insurance acting as the economy's early-warning system.

Where next — Prerequisites: percentages and basic probability — the everyday probability lesson is the warm-up. Follow with the market-failures lesson for the asymmetric-information theory, the banking lesson in this subject for the other great risk-transmuting institution, and the court-procedure lesson in Law & Governance for how coverage disputes are fought. Exercise: pull any insurance policy you hold and find the deductible, the coinsurance clause and one exclusion — then ask of each which failure it was designed against.

quiz.q: An insurer quadruples the size of an independent-risk pool. The standard deviation of the average loss per policy…
quiz.explanation: It falls with one over the square root of n: four times the policies means dividing by two.

quiz.q: A death spiral in an insurance market typically begins when…
options: low-risk customers exit a pooled price, worsening the average risk and forcing prices up
quiz.explanation: Adverse selection in motion — the pool's composition deteriorates exactly as its price rises.

quiz.q: A deductible primarily combats…
options: moral hazard, by putting the policyholder's own money at stake
quiz.explanation: Selection happens before the policy is sold; the deductible reshapes behaviour after it.

quiz.q: An insurer pays 74 in claims and 26 in expenses per 100 of premium, and earns 8 of investment income on float. Its combined ratio and year are…
options: combined ratio 100 — an 8 per cent profit carried by float
quiz.explanation: Claims plus expenses equal premiums (ratio 100), so underwriting breaks even and the float income is the profit.

intro:
Ask most people where money comes from and the folk model appears: somewhere there is a pile of cash, savers deposit it, and banks lend that pile out to borrowers. The mechanics are exactly backwards. When a bank approves your mortgage, no pile is opened; the bank types a loan into existence as an asset and a matching deposit into your seller's account as a liability. New money — broad money, the deposits the whole economy actually spends — is born on bank balance sheets, and it dies there too, extinguished when loans are repaid. The Bank of England said this plainly in a 2014 bulletin; textbooks took years to catch up. The inflation lesson in this domain covers what central banks do with this fact; this lesson is the plumbing underneath.

**Why this matters.** If loans create deposits, then credit booms are money booms and credit crunches are money contractions — the 2008 crisis was, at bottom, the money supply shrinking because banks stopped lending. It also explains the modern policy puzzle of the 2010s: central banks created trillions in reserves and inflation still slept, because reserves are not the fuel of lending. Understanding balance-sheet money is understanding why the economy can be awash in one kind of money and starved of another.
objectives: Explain loans create deposits, not the reverse
Explain the balance-sheet mechanic
Explain reserves and interbank settlement
Explain the money multiplier and its limits
Explain capital as the modern binding constraint
Explain bank runs and deposit insurance

concepts.term: Loans create deposits, not the reverse
concepts.statement: Run the transaction. A bank lends 900,000 for a house: its assets gain a 900,000 loan (the borrower owes it); its liabilities gain a 900,000 deposit (owed to whoever sold the house). No cash moved; both sides of the balance sheet grew. Since bank deposits are what households and firms spend with, the economy's money supply just rose by 900,000. Repayment runs the film in reverse — the deposit is extinguished, the loan disappears, money is destroyed. Money is not a thing that moves around the economy; it is a pair of entries that comes into and out of existence.

Where does cash enter? Reserves are the settlement layer: central-bank money that banks hold to settle with each other. When the house seller banks elsewhere, Bank A transfers reserves to Bank B to settle the deposit it created. Reserves do not constrain lending the way the folk model imagines — banks first lend, then acquire the reserves they need (from other banks, or from the central bank, which supplies them to hit its policy rate). The rate at which reserves trade between banks is the lever the central bank actually holds, which is where the inflation lesson picks up.

The textbook compression of all this is the money multiplier. With a 10 per cent reserve requirement, a 1,000 deposit supports 900 of lending, which becomes a new deposit supporting 810, then 729 — a geometric series converging on 1,000 ÷ 0.10 = 10,000 of deposits from 1,000 of reserves. Every money and banking course teaches it, and the modern literature is blunt: as a description of causality it is a museum piece. Post-2008, jurisdictions flooded with reserves (some abolished reserve requirements outright, as the United States did in 2020) and lending did not explode — because reserves were never the binding constraint.

concepts.term: The money multiplier and its limits
concepts.statement: What actually limits money creation? Capital: the Basel framework requires equity of several per cent of risk-weighted assets, plus buffers, and equity is expensive to raise — a bank with 8 per cent total capital can support roughly 12.5 dollars of lending per dollar of equity. Liquidity regulation: post-crisis rules require liquid asset buffers against deposit flight. Profitability: a loan must clear funding costs, expected losses and administration. And demand: no creditworthy borrower, no loan — money creation needs someone to want to borrow. Modern central banking works on price (the interest rate that clears this demand), not on rationing reserves.

concepts.term: Capital as the modern binding constraint
concepts.statement: The fragility is the mirror of the magic. Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig formalised it in 1983 (work that shared the 2022 Nobel memorial prize): banks fund long, illiquid loans with short, liquid deposits — maturity transformation, valuable to everyone — but that structure has a second equilibrium, the self-fulfilling run. Northern Rock queued around the block in September 2007, Britain's first retail run since 1866. Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023 is the modern textbook: rate rises had driven unrealised losses on its long bonds, and with over 90 per cent of deposits uninsured, depositors coordinated on a phone screen — 42 billion dollars left in one day, roughly 100 billion queued for the next. The fixes are a century old and still load-bearing: deposit insurance (the FDIC dates to 1933, with the standard US cover at 250,000 dollars) to remove the run motive, and the lender of last resort lending freely against good collateral, per Walter Bagehot's 1873 dictum.

One more distinction keeps the whole picture honest. Reserves are central-bank money — the banking system's settlement asset, which the public never touches directly. Deposits are commercial-bank money — promises to pay, whose money-ness depends on each bank staying solvent. “Quantitative easing” creates the first kind by the trillion and only moves the second if banks lend and customers borrow. The decade in which central banks tripled their balance sheets while inflation slept is, in one line, the empirical refutation of the multiplier.
$$\Delta M = \frac{\Delta R}{rr} = \frac{1}{rr} \times \Delta R$$
concepts.detail: With reserve ratio rr, each dollar of reserves supports 1/rr of deposits in the textbook model — an upper bound, not a causal dial.

concepts.statement: $$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Equity}$$
concepts.detail: Every loan created adds equally to assets (the loan) and liabilities (the deposit); the identity never breaks.

concepts.statement: $$\text{Capital ratio} = \frac{\text{Equity}}{\text{Risk-weighted assets}} \ge r^{*} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{Max loans} = \frac{\text{Equity}}{r^{*}}$$
concepts.detail: At an 8 per cent requirement, each dollar of equity supports at most about 12.50 of lending — the modern binding limit.

concepts.statement: Three errors dominate dinner-table economics. “Banks lend out deposits” — no; deposits are created by lending, and this is the single most consequential correction in the field. “The multiplier is a machine” — it is a symptom, describing an equilibrium that capital, liquidity, profitability and loan demand actually set. And “banks create money, therefore they are unconstrained” — the constraints moved, they did not vanish: capital, regulation and creditworthy borrowers bind harder than reserve arithmetic ever did. The corollary matters too: loan repayment destroys money, so an economy deleveraging is an economy whose money supply is quietly shrinking.
The public's spendable money — mostly bank deposits — created when banks lend.
Central-bank money banks hold to settle with one another; not lendable cash, and not the public's money.
The textbook ratio 1/rr linking reserves to deposits — descriptive ceiling, not causal dial.
Equity over risk-weighted assets; the modern binding constraint on bank lending.
Funding long-term loans with demandable deposits — banking's service and its fragility.
Coordinated deposit withdrawal that destroys even a solvent bank; Diamond-Dybvig's bad equilibrium.
The central bank lending freely against good collateral in a panic — Bagehot's rule, since 1873.

examples.title: Worked example — How Banks Create Money
examples.problem: Trace 1,000 of new reserves through a banking system with a 10 per cent reserve requirement, and then ask what limits the same system today.

steps.label: Round 1
steps.text: Bank A receives the 1,000 deposit, holds 100 in reserve, lends 900 — created as a new deposit at Bank B.

steps.label: Round 2 and onward
steps.text: B holds 90, lends 810 to C; C lends 729; and so on down the geometric series.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Sum: total deposits = 1,000 × (1 + 0.9 + 0.81 + …) = 1,000 ÷ 0.10 = 10,000, of which 9,000 is loans created from nothing and 1,000 remains as reserves. Money expanded tenfold; reserves never moved once.

steps.label: Update to the modern balance sheet
steps.text: with reserves abolished as a binding constraint, suppose the system holds 800 of equity and the capital requirement is 8 per cent. Maximum risk-weighted lending = 800 ÷ 0.08 = 10,000 — the same lending ceiling, now set by capital and by borrower demand, which is why a decade of trillion-dollar reserves coexisted with modest credit growth.

keyTakeaways: Mortgage cycles: house-price booms are jointly money booms — each loan is new purchasing power chasing the same stock of homes.
Credit crunches: 2008-09 was a monetary contraction by another name, as banks shrank balance sheets and deposits vanished with the loans.
Quantitative easing: creating reserves to buy bonds swaps one asset for another; the deposit money the public spends only appears if banks then lend.
Bank regulation: stress tests and capital buffers are, functionally, limits on how fast the money supply can grow.
Digital wallets and narrow banks: fintech proposals that hold only reserves are debates about who may create the public's money.

Where next — Prerequisites: none — the double-entry idea is gently introduced by the accounting lessons in this domain. Follow with the inflation and monetary-policy lesson for what central banks do with the policy rate, the insurance lesson for the risk machinery next door, and the fiscal-policy lesson for the government's side of the money system. Exercise: find your own bank's capital ratio in its latest annual report, divide equity by it, and ask what multiple of loans one dollar of your deposits ultimately supports.

quiz.q: A bank approves a 10,000 car loan. The immediate effect on broad money is…
options: it rises by 10,000 — the new deposit created alongside the loan
quiz.explanation: The loan is an asset and the new deposit a liability; deposits are broad money, so it expands on signing.

quiz.q: With a 10 per cent reserve requirement, the textbook deposit multiplier is…
quiz.explanation: 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10 — a geometric series, and in the modern view an upper bound rather than a cause.

quiz.q: Repaying a bank loan…
options: destroys the money the loan originally created
quiz.explanation: Loan and deposit are extinguished together — why economy-wide deleveraging shrinks the money supply.

quiz.q: Silicon Valley Bank's 2023 failure illustrated that runs strike hardest when…
options: deposits are largely uninsured and the balance sheet carries unrealised losses
quiz.explanation: Over 90 per cent uninsured plus paper losses on long bonds — a Diamond-Dybvig run executed at smartphone speed.

intro:
The prisoner’s dilemma — covered in depth in the Social Sciences domain — is game theory’s most famous exhibit, but it is one cell of a much larger map, and by its nature a strange one: both players move at once, in ignorance, once. Real strategic life is mostly not like that. Rivals observe each other, threaten and promise, commit resources before the fight, bid against estimates rather than values, and meet again tomorrow. The wider toolkit — trees instead of matrices, randomisation instead of purity, auction design instead of analysis — is what this lesson adds, and it is the analytical spine of pricing wars, entry battles, M&A bidding and spectrum auctions alike.

**Why this matters.** Business strategy is the management of interdependent decisions: your best move depends on their move, which depends on yours. Backward induction tells you what a threat is worth before you believe it; the winner’s curse tells you why the winning bid in a hot auction is usually a loss; commitment analysis explains why companies pay for capacity they never use. These are not metaphors — they are calculable, and the people bidding against you have done the calculation.
objectives: Explain sequential games and backward induction
Explain credible commitments
Explain mixed strategies and indifference
Explain repetition and reputation
Explain auctions and the winner’s curse
Explain designing the game

concepts.statement: Sequential games replace the matrix with a tree. Players move in turn, later movers observe earlier moves, and the solution concept is backward induction — Zermelo used it on chess in 1913: reason from the last decision node backward, choosing each earlier move as if you had already solved everything after it. The equilibrium this produces has a name and a discipline: subgame-perfect equilibrium, a plan that stays optimal at every node — no empty threats. Reinhard Selten's chain-store paradox (1978) is the classic sting: an incumbent who “will fight every entrant” is bluffing, because when the moment comes, accommodating is cheaper — the threat fails the credibility test that backward induction administers.

The repair for incredible threats is commitment, and Thomas Schelling — whose 1960 The Strategy of Conflict earned a Nobel prize — made it the field's centre of gravity: the power to constrain yourself is often worth more than the freedom you give up. Burning your bridges, sinking capital into capacity, signing long-term supply contracts you cannot exit, publishing a public promise — each visibly changes your own future payoffs so that the response you prefer becomes the one you would actually choose. A threat that is expensive to withdraw is believed; a threat that is merely stated is not. Schelling called it the power to bind; strategy texts call it commitment; boards call it capital expenditure with deterrence value.

Some games have no pure equilibrium at all, and randomisation is not evasion but the answer. In matching pennies — penalty kicks are its highest-paid cousin — if you always go the same way, the opponent exploits you, so the equilibrium is a mixed strategy. The principle is counterintuitive and beautiful: you randomise not to confuse yourself but to make the opponent indifferent — you mix until they cannot profit from predicting you. Ignacio Palacios-Huerta's study of thousands of penalty kicks found professional kickers and goalkeepers mixing close to the theoretical frequencies, exactly as the indifference condition predicts. Random audits, drug tests in sport, and unpredictable patrols are mixed strategies deployed as policy — the tax lesson in Law & Governance is, at bottom, a randomisation device tuned to make evasion not pay on average.

Repetition changes everything the dilemma teaches: the Social Sciences lesson covers how repeated play lets cooperation emerge from self-interest, and reputation is the accounting of that repetition — a brand, a strike history, a payment record all capitalise past conduct into future treatment. The subtlety is the endgame: cooperation in repeated games depends on there being a tomorrow, so finite games unravel from the back (backward induction again) while open-ended relationships sustain it. Businesses spend real money to appear open-ended — flagship stores, durable warranties — because appearing to be a repeat player is worth something only to those planning to stay.

Auctions are game theory with money as the scoreboard. Four formats matter: English ascending (reveal others' prices), Dutch descending, first-price sealed, and second-price sealed — the Vickrey auction, where bidding your true value is dominant because you pay the second-highest bid, not your own. The deeper split is values: in private-value auctions you know what the object is worth to you; in common-value auctions — oil tracts, spectrum, companies — the thing has one true value nobody knows, and everyone estimates it. Then the winner’s curse bites: winning reveals your estimate was the highest, so the expected value of the thing conditional on winning is below your estimate — E. C. Capen's 1971 study of oil-lease bidding showed winners systematically overpaying. The rational bidder shades below their estimate, accepting a lower win probability for a positive expected profit.

The final move is designing the game rather than playing it — mechanism design, the engineering side of the theory (a 2007 Nobel for Hurwicz, Maskin and Myerson; a 2020 one for Milgrom and Wilson's auction work). The US spectrum auctions from 1994 onward are the showcase: a simultaneous ascending format let bidders learn from each other's bids across interdependent licences, raising billions where earlier lottery and beauty-contest methods had misallocated and underpriced. The lesson generalises: when the rules channel self-interest toward the outcome you want, strategy stops being a fight and becomes a design problem — the same spirit as the market-failures lesson's fixes, run in reverse.

concepts.detail: A strategy profile where no single player gains by deviating alone — the baseline test every plan must pass.
Your mixing probability p is chosen so the opponent is indifferent between their options — randomisation to make prediction worthless.

concepts.statement: $$b^{*} < \hat{V} \quad \text{because} \quad E[V \mid \text{winning}] < E[V]$$
concepts.detail: In a common-value auction, the value conditional on having the highest estimate is below your estimate — shade the bid or pay for the privilege of losing.

concepts.statement: First, treating equilibrium as an instant: behavioural evidence — the ultimatum game's rejected “unfair” splits — shows real people punish, and good strategy anticipates it (the behavioural-economics lesson has the details). Second, backward induction is only as honest as the payoffs entered: model the rival's payoffs from their books, not your own. Third, mixed strategies are not coin flips at random intervals — the mix is calibrated to the opponent's indifference, and 50/50 only when symmetric. Fourth, the winner’s curse is not bad luck but selection: the auction does not find who values it most, it finds whose estimate was highest — the most optimistic bidder's signature on a loss. And commitments are not free: the capacity in the example cost 1 even though it never fired.
The extensive-form picture of a sequential game: nodes as decision points, branches as moves.
Solving from the final nodes backward to the start; the engine of subgame-perfect play.
A plan that remains optimal at every node — threats included must be credible.
A costly, visible constraint on your own future options that makes your preferred response believable.
Randomising across actions at calibrated probabilities so the opponent cannot profitably predict you.
In common-value auctions, the systematic overpayment by the most optimistic — and therefore winning — estimate.
Second-price sealed-bid format in which truthful bidding is the dominant strategy.

examples.title: Worked example — Game Theory Beyond the Prisoner’s Dilemma
examples.problem: A monopolist earns 10 if no rival enters. An entrant can enter at no cost; if it enters, the incumbent chooses to fight a price war (entrant −2, incumbent 4) or accommodate and share the market (entrant 3, incumbent 6). What happens, and can the incumbent do better?

steps.label: Draw the tree and solve backward
steps.text: at the fight-or-accommodate node, the incumbent compares 4 with 6 and accommodates. The entrant, anticipating this, compares staying out (0) with entering (3) and enters. Outcome: (3, 6).

steps.label: Test the threat
steps.text: “we will fight” fails credibility — when the moment arrives, fighting is the incumbent's own worst option. A seasoned entrant ignores the press release.

steps.label: Add commitment
steps.text: the incumbent can build excess capacity costing 1, which changes the future payoffs to fight 8, accommodate 4 — the capacity makes fighting genuinely cheaper than sharing.

steps.label: Solve the new game
steps.text: with capacity in place the incumbent now prefers fighting (8 > 4), so the entrant's entry yields −2 and it stays out (0 > −2). The incumbent nets 8 − 1 = 7, beating the 6 of accommodation — one unit of profit sacrificed to buy a threat that never has to be carried out. The entrant's counter, in turn, is its own commitment: a long-term customer contract that makes its entry cost sunk whatever the price war.

keyTakeaways: Entry deterrence: airlines' slot holdings, retailers' flagship leases and excess capacity are commitments priced for deterrence, not throughput.
M&A bidding: competing for a company whose value depends on synergies nobody can verify is the winner’s curse with a memo attached.
Spectrum and bond auctions: governments now engineer billions in revenue and allocation quality through format design.
Deterrence and brinkmanship: Schelling's own application — the Cuban missile crisis as controlled, credible risk, a mixed strategy in policy form.
Anti-doping and tax enforcement: audit probability times penalty must beat the gain from cheating — randomisation is the weapon, indifference the target.

Where next — Prerequisites: the prisoner’s-dilemma lesson in Social Sciences is the natural warm-up. Follow with the network-effects lesson in this field for markets where strategy compounds, the negotiation lesson for the practical craft of commitment at the table, and the market-failures lesson for the design view from the public side. Exercise: find one recent hostile takeover or price war in the news, draw its game tree with your best estimate of the payoffs, and mark the move where someone paid for credibility.

quiz.q: Backward induction solves a sequential game by…
options: playing boldly from the first move
reasoning from the final decision nodes backward to the start
quiz.explanation: Solve what happens last, take that as given for the move before it, and repeat to the root — Zermelo's chess logic.

quiz.q: In a second-price sealed-bid auction with private values, your dominant strategy is to…
options: bid your true value, since you pay the second-highest price anyway
bid above your value to be sure
quiz.explanation: Vickrey's insight: shading gains nothing when the price is set by others, and overbidding risks paying above value.

quiz.q: The winner’s curse arises in common-value auctions because…
options: winning reveals your estimate was among the highest, so value conditional on winning is below your estimate
quiz.explanation: Selection, not chance: the auction finds the most optimistic estimate — the oil-lease lesson from 1971.

quiz.q: An incumbent builds costly spare capacity it never uses, purely so an entrant expects a price war. This is…
options: a commitment device that changes the rival's best response
quiz.explanation: Schelling's point: constraining yourself credibly can be worth more than the constraint costs — deterrence priced as capital expenditure.

intro:
A corn farmer checks the radio for today's price and decides only how many bushels to sell; a pharmaceutical company holding the only patent on a drug decides what the price will be. Same profit motive, opposite powers — and the difference is not the firms' cleverness but the structure of the markets they sit in. Microeconomics names the structures, ranks them from perfect competition through monopolistic competition and oligopoly to monopoly, and shows how structure dictates pricing power, profit durability, efficiency and the case for antitrust. This lesson tours all four, with the marginal arithmetic every firm runs — produce while the next unit adds more to revenue than to cost — as the engine of the tour.

**Why this matters.** Whether a market tips toward one giant or a thousand price takers decides what consumers pay, how fast innovation runs, and what regulators must police. Antitrust cases, utility regulation, merger review and startup strategy are all arguments about which structure a market is in — this lesson is the vocabulary for those arguments. The market-failures lesson in this domain covers where markets go wrong; this one covers how their anatomy differs in the first place.
objectives: Explain the four structures compared
Explain price takers and price makers
Explain profit maximization: MR = MC
Explain shutdown and exit decisions
Explain barriers to entry and monopoly
Explain differentiation and monopolistic competition
Explain oligopoly: collusion versus competition
Explain efficiency and deadweight loss

concepts.statement: Perfect competition is a hypothetical extreme — and the measuring stick for every real market.
