Four conditions define it: many firms selling identical products, many buyers and sellers, full information on both sides, and free entry and exit. Meeting them makes a firm a price taker facing a perfectly elastic demand curve at the market price, because charging a penny more loses every customer and charging less earns nothing extra. Corn is the canonical case: one farmer's output moves the market not at all, so the market price is discovered on the radio, not set at the kitchen table. The single decision left to such a firm is quantity.

The output decision follows one rule: produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Under perfect competition, marginal revenue equals the market price, so the rule collapses to P = MC, and the firm's supply curve is simply its marginal cost curve above minimum average variable cost. Whether the chosen quantity earns money depends on price against average total cost — above it, profit; at it, break-even; below it, loss. Loss triggers a two-stage test. Short run: fixed costs are already sunk — the signed lease, the installed machines — so operate whenever price covers average variable cost and chips away at the fixed bill. Long run: nothing is locked in, so exit whenever price cannot cover average total cost. Entry runs the film in reverse: positive profits attract entrants, market supply shifts right, price falls — and keeps falling until economic profit is zero, with every firm producing at the minimum of average cost. That long-run equilibrium is the source of competitive markets' twin trophies: productive efficiency — producing at the lowest possible average cost — and allocative efficiency — price equal to marginal cost, society's marginal benefit matching its marginal cost.

A monopoly is a single seller of a product without close substitutes — a definition smuggling in a hard question: the market. DuPont had 75 percent of cellophane but under 20 percent of "flexible packaging materials", and the Supreme Court dismissed the case in 1956. Monopolies exist because something blocks entry. Natural monopoly: economies of scale so large relative to demand that one firm serves the whole market cheaper than two — the water utility's pipes, the electric grid, the local cement plant. Resource control: ALCOA's grip on bauxite, DeBeers on rough diamonds. Legal monopoly: the Postal Service on first-class mail, plus patents (twenty years) and copyrights (life plus seventy), which deliberately grant temporary monopoly to reward invention. Intimidation: predatory pricing and advertising walls — the brand budget required to fight Coca-Cola is itself the barrier. Whatever the wall, the monopolist faces the market's downward-sloping demand curve, and that changes the arithmetic: to sell one more unit it must cut the price on all units, so its marginal revenue lies below price. It still produces where MR = MC — then charges the demand curve's price at that quantity, which sits above marginal cost. The result: less output, higher price, and gains from trade that never happen — the deadweight loss the market-failures lesson measures. Hicks's quip that "the best of all monopoly profits is a quiet life" adds the dynamic worry: after AT&T's 1982 breakup, the telephone went from any-color-as-long-as-it's-black to call waiting, caller ID and mobile handsets within a decade.

Most consumer-facing markets are monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products. Differentiation runs four routes — physical attributes, location, intangibles such as guarantees and reputation, and pure perception, which is what advertising manufactures; the golf-ball industry, with thousands of regulation-conforming balls from a hundred-odd makers, is the exhibit for how thin the real differences can be. Each firm holds a mini-monopoly on its own variant and a downward-sloping but elastic demand curve: raise the price and you lose some customers to near-substitutes, not all of them. Price and quantity follow the monopoly recipe — MR = MC, then price from the demand curve — but the ending differs, because entry is free. Short-run profits attract imitators; each entrant shifts every incumbent's demand curve left until it just touches the average cost curve and profit hits zero. The tangency is the tell: long-run equilibrium sits on the downward-sloping part of average cost, not at its minimum, so monopolistic competition runs with excess capacity and a small gap between price and marginal cost — a mild version of monopoly's inefficiency. What the structure buys is variety — the thing a world of identical blue jeans cannot deliver; whether society gets the optimal amount, given an advertising arms race whose rival ads may simply neutralize each other, as Pigou noted a century ago, remains genuinely open.

Oligopoly is a few large firms with most of the sales — autos, cable, air travel — and its defining condition is mutual interdependence: each firm's best move depends on what the others do. The textbook calls them cats in a bag: they can scratch each other to pieces or cuddle up. Compete hard, and the outcome approximates perfect competition with zero profits; collude, and the group acts as a shared monopoly. Collusion — agreeing to hold down output and keep prices up — is illegal in the United States, policed by the Justice Department and the Federal Trade Commission, so formal cartels are rare and tacit coordination is the norm; the lysine cartel of the 1990s, exposed by FBI wiretaps, doubled the price of an animal-feed additive and cost Archer Daniels Midland a 100-million-dollar fine plus prison terms for executives. The economics of the temptation is the prisoner's dilemma, treated at length in the Social Sciences and game-theory lessons: holding output down pays each duopolist 1,000, but expanding is a dominant strategy, and both expanding leaves each with 400. Cartels fight the logic with monitoring, matching-price threats (the kinked demand curve: rivals match cuts, ignore increases, freezing the price in place) and, internationally, agreements no court will enforce — OPEC members cannot sue each other.

The four structures compress into one comparison. Number of firms: astronomical, many, few, one. Product: identical, differentiated, either, unique. Entry: free, free, blocked, blocked. Price control: none (price taker), slight, considerable, maximal (price maker). Efficiency: perfect competition delivers both productive and allocative efficiency; monopolistic competition trades a little of each for variety; oligopoly and monopoly hold price above marginal cost with durable profits — the deadweight triangle — unless the barrier is a patent, in which case the monopoly is the prize that paid for the invention. Public policy runs the whole map: antitrust against cartels and structure-tipping mergers, price regulation of natural monopolies, and patent law tuning innovation's deliberate monopoly.
$$MR = MC \quad (\text{perfect competition: } P = MR = MC)$$
concepts.detail: Produce every unit that adds more to revenue than to cost, and stop where they are equal. Only under perfect competition does price equal marginal revenue — a monopolist's MR lies below its demand curve because it must cut price on all units to sell one more.

concepts.statement: $$\text{Operate if } P \geq \min AVC; \qquad \text{Exit if } P < \min ATC$$
concepts.detail: In the short run fixed costs are sunk, so cover variable costs and limp ahead; in the long run nothing is sunk, so leave unless price covers full average cost.

concepts.statement: Zero economic profit is not zero accounting profit — it means owners earn exactly their opportunity cost, which is why competitive firms persist at "no profit". A large firm is not automatically a monopoly: define the market too narrowly and everything is one, too broadly and nothing is — the DuPont cellophane lesson. Monopoly is not unambiguously evil — natural monopoly is efficient and patents trade short-run deadweight loss for long-run invention (the market-failures lesson weighs the deal). And perfect competition is a benchmark, not a description: it assumes away externalities, information gaps and the income distribution behind willingness to pay.
A firm that must accept the market price — the fate of firms in perfect competition.
Any legal, technological or market force that blocks new competitors from entering a market.
Economies of scale so large relative to demand that one firm serves the market cheapest.
Many firms selling differentiated products — mini-monopolies in open-entry markets.
A few interdependent firms dominating an industry, torn between collusion and competition.
A formal agreement among firms to hold down output and charge the monopoly price.
The price at minimum average variable cost, below which operating loses more than closing.
Making one firm's offering distinct — physically, by location, by intangibles or by perception.

examples.title: Worked Example — Shut Down Now or Limp Ahead?
examples.problem: A yoga studio has signed a 10,000-dollar monthly lease (fixed) and must pay teachers 15,000 (variable) if it opens. Projected revenues run 0, 10,000 or 20,000 for the month. What should it do in each case?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: short-run fixed costs are sunk — the studio pays the lease whether or not it opens — so the test is whether revenue covers the 15,000 of variable cost.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: at zero revenue, opening adds a 15,000 loss to the sunk 10,000 — stay shut and lose 10,000. At 10,000 revenue, opening loses 15,000 (10,000 revenue minus 25,000 total cost) versus 10,000 shut — still stay shut. At 20,000 revenue, opening loses 5,000 (20,000 minus 25,000) versus 10,000 shut — open, because the 20,000 covers all variable cost plus 5,000 of the lease.

examples.result: operate whenever revenue covers variable costs — price at or above minimum average variable cost — and exit the business when the lease expires unless losses have turned to profits.

keyTakeaways: Merger review: competition authorities screen deals by whether they move an industry up the structure spectrum — from many to few, or few to one.
Utility regulation: natural monopolies get regulated prices instead of competitors, because duplicating the water grid wastes the economies of scale.
Patent strategy: the twenty-year monopoly is a deliberate entry barrier — the reward that finances R&D, expiring into generic competition.
Startup moats: founders engineer barriers — brands, network effects, scale — precisely to slow the entry that would compete their profits to zero (the network-effects lesson in this domain).
Competitive strategy: knowing whether you are a price taker (commodity) or a price maker (differentiated) decides whether you fight on cost or on identity.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a condition of perfect competition?
quiz.explanation: A single producer is the definition of the opposite end of the spectrum — monopoly.

quiz.q: A monopolist's marginal revenue lies below its price because…
options: selling one more unit requires cutting the price on all units sold
quiz.explanation: The demand curve is conditional, not sequential — one price applies to every unit, so the extra unit arrives with a discount attached to all the others.

quiz.q: A water utility is the classic natural monopoly because…
options: the pipe network's scale economies make a single provider the cheapest way to serve everyone
quiz.explanation: Once the mains are laid, serving another house costs little — and duplicating the network wastes the economies of scale.

quiz.q: In long-run equilibrium, a monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit with price…
options: above marginal cost and above minimum average cost
quiz.explanation: Entry shifts each firm's demand left until it just touches average cost — but on the downward-sloping part, leaving excess capacity and a small price-cost gap.

quiz.q: Two duopolists could each earn 1,000 by holding output down, but both expand and earn 400 each. This is…
options: the prisoner's dilemma — expansion is each firm's dominant strategy
quiz.explanation: Whatever the other firm does, expanding pays more — so both expand, and the group outcome is worse than cooperation. The game-theory lesson develops the escapes.

quiz.q: A firm should shut down in the short run when…
options: price is below average total cost
price is below minimum average variable cost
quiz.explanation: Below minimum AVC, every unit sold adds more to cost than to revenue; fixed costs are sunk either way, so closing loses least.

intro:
Eight times a year, a committee of twelve decides the price of overnight money — and through a chain of consequences, the pace of hiring, the heat of inflation and the monthly payment on every adjustable mortgage in the land. Central banking looks like a temple and works like a plumbing diagram: a "bank for banks" whose classic tools are simple, whose lags are long and whose independence from the governments it serves is deliberate. This lesson covers the institution — the Federal Reserve's structure and its counterparts abroad — the toolkit of open market operations, reserve requirements and the discount rate, the expansionary-versus-contractionary logic, the regulation that keeps banks solvent, and the pitfalls that make the job genuinely hard.

**Why this matters.** Every recession and every inflation fight of the past fifty years has run through a central-bank decision — the Volcker disinflation, the 2008 rescue, the 2020 dash for liquidity, the post-2021 tightening. You cannot read a financial headline, or a mortgage offer, without the machinery this lesson describes. The inflation lesson in this domain covers what central banks are trying to achieve; this one covers how the machine actually works.
objectives: Explain the central bank as bank for banks
Explain the Fed: Board, districts, FOMC
Explain bank regulation and supervision
Explain open market operations
Explain discount rate and reserve requirements
Explain expansionary versus contractionary policy
Explain transmission to aggregate demand
Explain pitfalls: lags, deflation, velocity

concepts.term: The central bank as bank for banks
concepts.statement: The Federal Reserve is a deliberately hybrid institution: government appointees at the top, private-sector banks inside the system. A Board of Governors — seven members appointed by the president and confirmed by the Senate to staggered fourteen-year terms, one expiring every second January — runs the national level; the long, staggered, single terms are engineered to insulate monetary policy from electoral pressure, and the president cannot dismiss a governor the way a cabinet secretary can be dismissed. One governor serves as Chair — Greenspan, then Bernanke, then Yellen, then Powell — first among equals, setting the agenda and serving as the institution's public voice. Around the Board sit twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks, each serving its district with directors drawn partly from the commercial banks it oversees. The system does three jobs: conduct monetary policy; promote financial stability; and provide banking services — to banks (reserve accounts, check clearing, emergency loans at the discount window) and to the government, alongside keeping currency circulating and enforcing consumer-protection rules on lenders.

The stability job is bank regulation, whose goal is solvency — keeping net worth positive so depositors are safe. The levers: minimum capital requirements (net worth as a percent of assets), restrictions on risky investments (banks may lend and hold Treasuries, not play the stock market with depositors' money) and supervision — on-site examinations. In the American division of labor, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency examines the largest national banks, the NCUA supervises credit unions, and the Fed supervises the holding companies that own banks. Examiners can compel changes or close a bank outright — when they are allowed to: valuing a loan book is genuinely hard, and supervisors face political pressure to go easy, as Japan's decade of tolerated zombie banks showed. The deeper defenses against panic are the two the 1930s taught: deposit insurance — in the United States, the FDIC's 250,000-dollar guarantee, funded by risk-based premiums on banks — and the lender of last resort, the central bank lending freely to solvent-but-illiquid institutions: the role the Fed was invented for after the Panic of 1907 and used again in the 1987 crash.

The classical toolkit assumes a world where reserves are scarce and banks need to borrow them — and it has three instruments. The workhorse since the 1920s is open market operations: the Fed buys or sells Treasury securities to manage the supply of reserves, targeting the federal funds rate — the rate at which banks lend reserves to one another overnight. Buy 20 million of bonds from a bank and the Fed pays with new reserves, created literally with keystrokes; the bank, now holding more reserves than it wants, lends them out, and the deposit multiplier ripples the expansion through the system. Sell bonds and the film runs in reverse: reserves drain, loans contract, the money supply shrinks. The decisions belong to the Federal Open Market Committee — the seven governors plus the New York Fed president and four district presidents rotating annually — meeting about every six weeks. The second tool is the discount rate, the price of borrowing directly from the Fed's window; it is kept deliberately above the federal funds rate so banks borrow from each other first, and its changes are as much signal as mechanics. The third is the reserve requirement, the share of deposits banks must hold back — historically tiered near 10 percent for large banks, too blunt to adjust often, and set to zero in March 2020, when the scarcity assumption itself expired.

Since 2008 the operating environment has been ample reserves rather than scarce. Banks, scarred by the crisis and — by congressional grant — paid interest on their reserve balances, hold trillions at the Fed; the FOMC now steers the federal funds rate administratively rather than by rationing reserves. Raise the interest on reserve balances and banks prefer the Fed's floor; lower it and they lend in the overnight market until the target follows. When the policy rate hit the zero lower bound in 2008 — and again in 2020 — the Fed reached past the toolkit for quantitative easing: massive purchases of long-term Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities to press down long-term rates and unfreeze credit, in successive episodes that swelled its balance sheet from roughly 4 trillion dollars before the pandemic past 8 trillion through it.

The direction of travel is set by the state of the economy, and the logic is countercyclical. Expansionary (loose) policy — buying bonds, supplying reserves — lowers interest rates, stimulates business investment and consumer borrowing on houses and cars, and shifts aggregate demand right: the medicine for a recession with output below potential and unemployment high. Contractionary (tight) policy — selling bonds, draining reserves — raises rates, discourages borrowing and shifts demand left: the medicine for inflation when the economy runs above potential. The history is a list of hard calls. The Fed pushed the federal funds rate from 5.5 percent in 1977 to 16.4 percent in 1981 to break double-digit inflation — and bought back-to-back recessions and 9.7 percent unemployment by 1982 before inflation settled near 3 percent. It slashed rates through the early 1990s, tightened into 2000, slashed again after 2001 and 2008 — reaching the zero bound and staying — and cut to near zero within weeks in March 2020. The federal funds rate leads other rates, a point of it moving mortgages by less than a point, because markets price the long end; expectations do half the work, which is the inflation lesson's territory.

The pitfalls are structural. Lags: policy works through a chain — perceive, meet, decide, transmit through banks, move investment — whose main effects land one to three years out, so the Fed is always steering by forecast. Pushing on a string: in deep downturns banks may hoard excess reserves and borrowers may refuse cheap credit, blunting expansion — Japan held its policy rate at zero and expanded the money supply by half in the early 2000s while the economy barely stirred. Deflation: with nominal rates stuck at zero, expected deflation raises real rates on its own (7 percent nominal minus 2 percent deflation is a 9 percent real rate), defaults and bank losses follow, and policy cannot cut further — the mechanism that deepened 1930–33 in the United States. Velocity: money's turnover ties the money supply to nominal GDP by the identity M × V = P × Y, and V's unpredictability since the 1980s is why Friedman's constant-money-growth rule was abandoned for interest-rate targeting. Add asset bubbles and leverage cycles — the dot-com and housing episodes a narrow inflation mandate can miss — and the case for humility writes itself: the strongest single lever in macroeconomics, with slack built in.
$$\Delta M = \frac{1}{rr}\,\Delta R$$
concepts.detail: In the scarce-reserves model, each dollar of reserves the Fed injects supports 1/rr of deposits — ten times at a 10 percent requirement. The banking lesson in this domain shows why this is a ceiling, not a dial: capital and loan demand bind first.

concepts.statement: $$V = \frac{P \times Y}{M} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; M \times V = P \times Y$$
concepts.detail: Money times its turnover equals nominal GDP — the identity linking monetary policy to prices and output, and the reason unstable velocity makes money-growth targets unreliable.

concepts.statement: The Fed does not "set mortgage rates" — it targets an overnight interbank rate, and longer rates follow imperfectly, priced by markets. "Printing money" is not an instant inflation dial: reserves must become loans and loans become spending, and in a slump that chain can kink. Monetary policy is not fiscal policy — no taxes, no spending, just the price and quantity of money and credit (the fiscal lesson has the other lever). Independence is a design choice with a real democratic critique, not a law of nature. And the zero lower bound is real: with deflation, even a zero nominal rate can be a tight real one.
The institution that conducts monetary policy, regulates banks and safeguards financial stability — the bank for banks.
The Fed's seven presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed governors on staggered fourteen-year terms.
The Federal Open Market Committee — governors plus rotating district-bank presidents — that sets the policy rate.
Central-bank purchases and sales of Treasury securities to manage reserves and steer the federal funds rate.
The interest rate banks pay to borrow directly from the central bank's window.
The central bank's standby lending to solvent banks in a panic — the 1907 lesson institutionalized.
Large-scale purchases of long-term bonds and mortgage securities when the policy rate is at zero.
The overnight rate at which banks lend reserves to one another — the target of policy.

examples.title: Worked Example — Tracing a Disinflation
examples.problem: Inflation runs above 10 percent in 1979–80. What does the central bank do, through what chain, and at what cost?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: contractionary policy drains reserves, raises the federal funds rate, discourages interest-sensitive spending, and shifts aggregate demand left — landing on prices and output with a lag of one to three years.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: the FOMC sells securities; the federal funds rate climbs from 5.5 percent (1977) to 16.4 percent (1981). Borrowing for houses, cars and plant investment collapses, demand contracts, and inflation falls from double digits to 3.2 percent by 1983 — while unemployment rises from 5.8 to 9.7 percent through back-to-back recessions.

examples.result: the disinflation succeeded, and the measured sacrifice of output and jobs while the policy worked its way through the economy is exactly what economists mean when they warn that credibility and lags — not malice — determine how expensive price stability is.

keyTakeaways: Reading FOMC statements: the balance of risk language — inflation versus employment — is the countercyclical dial made public.
Household finance: fixed-versus-floating mortgage choice is a bet on the policy path this lesson describes.
Bank compliance: capital rules, investment restrictions and consumer-protection duties are the regulation half of the central bank's job description.
Dividing the levers: recessions are fought with both monetary and fiscal policy — the fiscal lesson in this domain covers the spending-and-taxing side and the coordination problems.
Business planning: rate-sensitive sectors — housing, autos, construction — read central-bank calendars the way farmers read weather reports.

quiz.q: The Fed's structure — a Board of Governors with staggered fourteen-year terms plus twelve district banks — is designed mainly to…
options: blend public authority with regional input while insulating policy from electoral pressure
quiz.explanation: Long, staggered, single terms and no presidential dismissal are engineering choices for political insulation.

quiz.q: In an open market purchase, the Fed buys bonds from a bank. The immediate effect is…
options: bank reserves rise, and the federal funds rate tends to fall
quiz.explanation: The Fed pays with newly created reserves; more reserves in the overnight market means a cheaper overnight rate.

quiz.q: The discount rate is kept above the federal funds rate so that…
options: banks borrow from each other before coming to the Fed's window
quiz.explanation: The penalty spread makes the discount window a backstop — which is also why discount-rate changes are as much signal as substance.

quiz.q: Facing a recession with output below potential, the countercyclical move is…
options: contractionary policy to shift demand left
expansionary policy — buy bonds, lower rates, shift demand right
quiz.explanation: Loose policy stimulates interest-sensitive spending and moves aggregate demand toward potential output.

quiz.q: With the nominal policy rate at zero and deflation running 5 percent, the real interest rate is…
quiz.explanation: Real = nominal − inflation = 0 − (−5) = +5 percent — the arithmetic trap that makes deflation so hard to fight.

quiz.q: The velocity of money is…
options: nominal GDP divided by the money supply — how often an average dollar turns over
quiz.explanation: In 2009, US nominal GDP of 14.3 trillion against an M1 of 1.7 trillion gave a velocity of 8.4 turns per dollar per year.

intro:
Every exam in macroeconomics begins with the same two questions: how big is the economy, and what happens when demand meets that size? The GDP vital signs lesson introduced the headline numbers; this one goes a level deeper — the full national income accounting ladder from GDP to national income, the three measurement methods, the real-nominal distinction, and the aggregate demand-aggregate supply model that turns the accounts into a theory of booms and slumps. It then applies the whole toolkit to the exam favourite: India's journey from planning (1951) through the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis to liberalisation and the challenges the economy faces now, following NCERT's Introductory Macroeconomics and Indian Economic Development.

**Why this matters.** National income accounting and the AD-AS model are the opening chapters of every Class 12 economics paper (CBSE, CUET, CA Foundation), while the 1951-1991 policy regime and the 1991 reforms anchor UPSC and B.Com syllabi. Division of labour with the rest of this domain: the GDP-inflation-unemployment lesson owns the vital-signs dashboard and its limitations, the fiscal-policy lesson owns the spending-and-taxing response to output gaps, the monetary-policy lesson owns interest rates, and the microeconomics lesson owns single-market supply and demand — which is a different animal from the AD-AS diagram built here.
objectives: Explain gDP, GNP and NNP: the income ladder
Explain factor cost, basic price and market price
Explain three methods of measurement
Explain real versus nominal and the deflator
Explain aD-AS equilibrium and shifts
Explain the Keynesian multiplier
Explain output gaps and unemployment
Explain india 1951-1991: plans, licence and crisis
Explain 1991 reforms and current challenges

concepts.term: GDP, GNP and NNP: the income ladder
concepts.statement: The income ladder starts with gross domestic product — the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year, whoever owns the factors. Add net factor income from abroad (income earned by residents abroad minus income earned by foreigners at home, dominated in India's case by workers' remittances) and you get gross national product, now usually called gross national income. Subtract consumption of fixed capital — depreciation, the machines worn out in the year — and gross becomes net: net national product. NNP at factor cost, the sum of all factor incomes (wages, rent, interest and profit) earned by normal residents, is what Indian statistics officially calls national income; dividing by population gives per capita income. India's GDP in the mid-2020s runs to roughly 3.5-4 trillion US dollars, fifth largest in the world, while per capita income of roughly 2,500-2,800 dollars keeps it firmly middle-income.

concepts.term: Factor cost, basic price and market price
concepts.statement: One more distinction earns marks every year: factor cost versus market price. Market price equals factor cost (what the factors actually earn) plus net indirect taxes (indirect taxes minus subsidies). Between them sits the basic price (factor cost plus production taxes minus production subsidies). A headline GDP series must say which it uses: India's 2011-12 base-year series moved the headline to market prices and made gross value added at basic prices the published sectoral measure — GDP equals GVA plus product taxes minus product subsidies. The 2015 revision that did this, and the accompanying switch of source data for the corporate sector, also produced the famous back-series controversy over whether earlier growth had been understated — a standing lesson in how measurement choices move history.

Three methods measure the same thing, and their agreement is an accounting identity. The product or value-added method sums each sector's gross value added — primary (agriculture), secondary (manufacturing, construction), tertiary (services) — avoiding double counting by counting only value added at each stage. The income method sums the factor incomes plus mixed income (the self-employed farmer-cum-shopkeeper whose earnings cannot be split into wage and profit — large in India). The expenditure method sums final spending: private final consumption + gross domestic capital formation (investment) + government final consumption + net exports — C + I + G + (X − M). Because one agent's spending is another's income, output = income = expenditure identically; in practice the three estimates are reconciled statistically. India's National Statistics Office publishes annual and quarterly estimates, and the informal sector — the overwhelming majority of employment — forces it to use proxies (MCA-21 filings, labour-force indicators), which is why revisions are large and contested.

concepts.term: Real versus nominal and the deflator
concepts.statement: Nominal versus real is the distinction that keeps growth honest. Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP uses constant base-year prices (currently 2011-12), so real growth measures volume, not inflation. The bridge between them is the GDP deflator — the price index that covers everything produced domestically, unlike the consumer price index (a fixed household basket) or the wholesale price index (traded goods at the producer level). If nominal GDP is 300 trillion rupees and real GDP is 200 trillion, the deflator is 150: prices have risen 50 per cent since the base year. A rise in nominal GDP of 11 per cent with 4 per cent inflation is roughly 7 per cent real growth — the arithmetic every exam tests.

The AD-AS model turns the accounts into a theory. Aggregate demand is total planned spending at each price level: C + I + G + NX. It slopes down for three reasons: higher prices shrink real balances (the Pigou effect), raise interest rates and crowd out interest-sensitive spending (the Keynes effect), and make domestic goods dearer for foreigners (the net-export effect). Aggregate supply slopes up in the short run — wages and some prices are sticky, so higher prices raise output — but is vertical in the long run at potential output, the full-employment level an economy can sustain. Where the curves cross sits the equilibrium price level and real GDP; the gap between actual and potential output is the output gap, negative in recession (measured unemployment above its natural rate) and positive in boom. Demand shifts move the economy along the short-run AS curve; supply shocks (an oil spike, a monsoon failure) shift AS itself into stagflation — rising prices with falling output, the hardest case for policy. The classical view assumes flexible prices and self-correction; the Keynesian view assumes sticky prices and demand-driven slumps; the modern synthesis uses each where it works. And note what this diagram is not: it aggregates the whole economy and uses the general price level, not a single market's relative price — the micro supply-demand lesson's curves answer different questions.

Keynes's multiplier is the model's dynamic heart: an initial injection of spending becomes income, part of which is spent again, and again. If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8, each rupee of new income generates 80 paise of spending, so a 100-crore government project ultimately raises income by 500 crore — five times — before leakages into saving, taxes and imports exhaust the rounds. Two implications matter. The multiplier cuts both ways: collapsed confidence shrinks income by a multiple too, which is how a banking crisis becomes a depression. And its size depends on the MPC: poorer households spend more of a marginal rupee, so transfers targeted at them multiply faster than general tax cuts — though leakages (India's high import propensity especially) make real-world multipliers far smaller than the textbook arithmetic.

Now the application. Independent India chose planning: the Planning Commission (1950) ran twelve five-year plans from 1951 to 2017. The First Plan (1951-56) prioritised agriculture and Harrod-Domar saving-investment arithmetic; the Second (1956-61), built on P.C. Mahalanobis's model, swung to heavy industry and import substitution. The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 and the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act of 1951 created the licence-permit raj — capacity expansion, entry and even product mix required state approval — reinforced by the MRTP Act (1969) against large houses and near-complete foreign-investment restrictions. The results were mixed: growth stuck near 3.5 per cent for decades (Raj Krishna's "Hindu rate of growth"), yet the Green Revolution — high-yielding wheat and rice varieties from the mid-1960s, led by M.S. Swaminathan with Norman Borlaug's material, in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, supported by guaranteed procurement prices — ended dependence on imported food, and public investment built IITs, dams and a heavy-industry base.

By 1991 the model was broke. The Gulf War spiked oil prices and squeezed remittances; exports could pay for barely a fortnight of imports, reserves fell to about 1.2 billion dollars, and India airlifted 67 tonnes of RBI gold to London as collateral. The Chandra Shekhar government took an IMF loan; the Narasimha Rao government's finance minister Manmohan Singh presented the 24 July 1991 budget that dismantled the system in one stroke: the rupee devalued about 19 per cent, industrial licensing abolished for most industries, peak import tariffs of well over 100 per cent begun on a path down, public-sector equity disinvestment started, and foreign investment welcomed. Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation — LPG — became the new regime. Growth accelerated from the 3.5-per-cent groove toward 6-8 per cent, poverty rates fell steadily, foreign-exchange reserves grew from two weeks of cover to well over 600 billion dollars by the mid-2020s, and services — above all information technology — became the engine. The critiques are part of the syllabus too: employment growth lagged output (jobless growth), agriculture was left behind investment-wise, inequality widened, and the informal sector still employs the large majority of workers.

The current-challenges file for exams, at survey depth: poverty — methodology battles from Lakdawala through Tendulkar (2009, drew the line at about 29 rupees a day in cities) to Rangarajan, with all series showing a large decline in extreme poverty since 1991 but sensitivity to the line chosen; employment — the Periodic Labour Force Survey shows low headline unemployment (single digits) but low female labour-force participation, high informality, and disguised unemployment crowding agriculture; infrastructure — the persistent gap the capex-heavy budgets of the 2020s target, from highways to logistics; and external balance — a current-account deficit financed increasingly by services exports and remittances, with the 2013 taper episode a reminder of vulnerability. None of these is solved by the multiplier alone — the fiscal and monetary lessons take up the policy instruments.
$$\text{Deflator} = \frac{\text{Nominal GDP}}{\text{Real GDP}} \times 100$$
concepts.detail: The price index covering everything domestically produced. Nominal GDP of 300 with real GDP of 200 gives a deflator of 150 — a 50 per cent rise in prices since the base year.

concepts.statement: $$k = \frac{1}{1 - \text{MPC}} = \frac{1}{\text{MPS}}$$
concepts.detail: The factor by which an initial spending injection raises equilibrium income. At MPC 0.8, k = 5: a 100-crore project ultimately adds 500 crore of income before saving leakages exhaust the rounds.

concepts.statement: Nominal growth is not growth — always ask for the base year. GDP is not welfare: it omits unpaid work and the informal economy's measured part, and says nothing about distribution (the vital-signs lesson owns that critique). GNP differs from GDP only by net factor income from abroad, which for India is now positive — remittances outweigh outflows — so do not automatically write GNP < GDP. The AD curve is not a big demand curve: it plots total spending against the general price level, and its slope runs through real balances, interest rates and trade, not substitution. The textbook multiplier is a ceiling, not an estimate — leakages, capacity and price response shrink it. And the 1991 reforms were a response to a crisis, not an ideological conversion: the sequencing (external first, internal gradually) explains both their speed and their unfinished agenda.
Residents' income earned abroad minus foreigners' income earned domestically; the bridge from GDP to GNP, dominated by remittances in India's case.
NNP at factor cost — the sum of factor incomes earned by normal residents in a year.
Sector output minus intermediate consumption at basic prices; GDP equals GVA plus product taxes minus subsidies.
Nominal GDP over real GDP times 100 — the price index covering all domestic production.
The output an economy can sustain at full employment; actual output below it defines a recessionary gap.
Total planned spending C + I + G + NX at each price level; slopes down through real-balance, interest-rate and trade effects.
The multiple by which an initial spending change raises equilibrium income: 1/(1 − MPC).
The 1951-1991 regime of industrial licensing, import substitution and state allocation of investment.
The 1991 liberalisation-privatisation-globalisation package that followed the balance-of-payments crisis.
concepts.detail: National income accounting tells you how to measure an economy; AD-AS tells you why it fluctuates; India's own seventy-year arc — planning, crisis, reform — shows the stakes of both. The measurement ladder and the multiplier are exam furniture; the deeper skill is knowing which number answers which question, and what each quietly leaves out. From here the domain's remaining lessons supply the levers: fiscal policy for the spending side of aggregate demand, monetary policy for the interest-rate side, and the vital-signs dashboard for reading the results.

examples.title: Worked Example — Deflator and Multiplier in One Problem
examples.problem: An economy reports nominal GDP of 291 trillion rupees for the year and real GDP of 210 trillion at 2011-12 prices; separately, the government spends 40,000 crore on infrastructure and households consume 75 per cent of each marginal rupee. Find inflation since the base year and the ultimate income change.

steps.label: Compute the deflator
steps.text: 291/210 × 100 ≈ 138.6 — prices are about 38.6 per cent above the base year.

steps.label: Extract real growth if needed
steps.text: if last year's real GDP was 199 trillion, real growth is 210/199 − 1 ≈ 5.5 per cent — the honest number, unlike the nominal 12-13 per cent that flatters the headline.

steps.label: Compute the multiplier
steps.text: k = 1/(1 − 0.75) = 4, so the spending injection of 40,000 crore ultimately raises equilibrium income by 1,60,000 crore.

steps.label: State the caveats the markers reward
steps.text: the simple multiplier ignores taxes and imports (India's marginal import propensity trims k well below the arithmetic), assumes spare capacity — at potential output the spending turns into prices instead of output — and requires the money to actually reach high-MPC households to bite.

keyTakeaways: Reading the budget: every "GDP will grow X per cent" claim needs the real-nominal and base-year questions asked before it means anything.
Policy analysis: output-gap estimates are the quiet numbers behind stimulus decisions — the fiscal lesson takes the spending side from here.
India exams: the plans-to-reforms narrative (1951 → 1966 → 1991 → today) is a stock long-answer in UPSC, CUET and B.Com papers.
Business planning: AD components map to the demand forecasts firms actually build — consumption first, investment most volatile.
Data literacy: knowing why GVA differs from GDP explains why one quarter's headlines can disagree with each other.

Where next — Prerequisites: the GDP vital-signs lesson for the dashboard and the micro supply-demand lesson for curve literacy. Follow with fiscal policy and monetary policy — the two levers that move aggregate demand — and the Indian polity lesson for the institutions (Planning Commission to NITI Aayog, Finance Commission) that steer them. NCERT's Introductory Macroeconomics and Indian Economic Development cover this ground exactly.

quiz.q: NNP at factor cost (national income) is derived from GNP by…
quiz.explanation: Gross minus depreciation gives net; the factor-cost valuation then excludes net indirect taxes.

quiz.q: Nominal GDP is 252 trillion rupees and real GDP is 210 trillion. The GDP deflator is…
quiz.explanation: 252/210 × 100 = 120 — prices are 20 per cent above the base year.

quiz.q: With MPC = 0.75, a 20,000-crore rise in government spending ultimately raises income by about…
quiz.explanation: The multiplier is 1/(1 − 0.75) = 4, so income rises by 4 × 20,000 = 80,000 crore.

quiz.q: The immediate trigger of the 1991 reforms was…
options: a balance-of-payments crisis — reserves down to weeks of imports, with gold pledged abroad
the collapse of the Soviet Union only
quiz.explanation: The Gulf War oil spike and remittance slump drained reserves to roughly two weeks of imports; the gold airlift and IMF loan forced the July 1991 budget.

intro:
The four-Ps lesson asked what to deploy — product, price, place, promotion. This lesson asks the prior question, where to aim. Segmentation, targeting and positioning — STP, formalised by Wendell Smith in 1956 — is the systematic playbook modern marketing courses and textbooks (OpenStax’s Principles of Marketing among them) put before the mix decisions: carve a heterogeneous market into meaningful groups, choose the groups worth serving, and stake a position in their minds. Done well, STP turns the four Ps from a generic checklist into a coherent offer aimed at a named customer.

**Why this matters.** Every aisle, app feed and airline fare chart is STP made physical. It is also the analytical core of most marketing case interviews and business-school coursework: given a market, segment it, pick targets, write the positioning statement — then defend the choice.
objectives: Explain why markets are heterogeneous
Explain four segmentation bases: geographic, demographic, psychographic, behavioral
Explain evaluating and choosing target segments
Explain four targeting strategies from mass to micromarketing
Explain perceptual maps and positioning statements
Explain the five-stage buyer decision process
Explain b2B and international segmentation

concepts.statement: Segmentation exists because customers differ, and treating them as an average wastes money on the margins. A usable segment passes five tests: it is measurable (size and purchasing power can be counted), accessible (you can actually reach it), substantial (big enough to be profitable), differentiable (it responds distinctly to a distinct offer) and actionable (your resources can serve it). A segment that fails a test — “left-handed chess players who vape”, say — is trivia, not strategy. Segments are constructed, not discovered: the analyst chooses the basis of division, and the choice is the strategy.

concepts.term: Four segmentation bases: geographic, demographic, psychographic, behavioral
concepts.statement: The four classic bases answer four different questions about the buyer. Geographic segmentation asks where: region, city size, climate, urban density — umbrella sales track rainfall, and cold-chain logistics follow population maps. Demographic segmentation asks who: age, gender, income, occupation, education and family life cycle — the durable workhorse, because demographics are cheap to measure and correlate with needs. Psychographic segmentation asks why: lifestyle, values, personality, often via the AIO inventory (activities, interests, opinions) or the VALS typology that sorts buyers from innovators to survivors. Behavioral segmentation asks how: benefits sought, occasions of use, usage rate and loyalty — the occasion split is why the same airline sells the same seat to a vacationer on Saturday and a deal-chasing executive on Monday.

Business markets segment differently but no less strictly: by end user (a bearing sold to a carmaker is a different market than the same bearing to a wind-farm operator), by company size, by purchasing approach — centralised procurement versus site engineers, tenders versus relationships — and by situational factors like order urgency. International segmentation adds another layer, and a warning: “the Asian market” or “Europe” is rarely one segment; language, regulation, income and culture redraw the map at every border, though genuine intermarket segments — global teenagers, luxury travellers, sustainability-first buyers — do exist across borders.

concepts.term: Four targeting strategies from mass to micromarketing
concepts.statement: Targeting evaluates the segment menu on three axes: segment size and growth, structural attractiveness (competitors, substitutes, buyer and supplier power — Porter’s logic applied to the segment, not the whole market), and fit with the firm’s objectives and resources. Four strategies follow. Undifferentiated marketing serves everyone with one offer — viable for salt and electricity, suicidal for most else. Differentiated marketing runs separate offers for separate segments — the carmaker’s sub-brands, the airline’s cabins. Concentrated (niche) marketing owns one segment deeply — the sports-car boutique, the vegan cheese startup — trading scale for focus. Micromarketing narrows to local neighbourhoods or the individual, enabled by data: the same newsletter, personalised per subscriber, and the ethical debate that follows it.

Positioning is the battle for a slot in the customer’s mental map, and it is engineered, not improvised. A perceptual map plots the competitive set on the two attributes buyers actually trade off — price against performance, convenience against choice — and shows both the crowded centre and the open corners. The written form is the positioning statement: for [target customer] who [need], [product] is the [category] that [key benefit]; unlike [main alternative], ours [point of difference]. The discipline is subtraction — one idea, defended relentlessly. Repositioning is possible but expensive: a brand that spent a decade meaning “cheap” cannot become “premium” by decree, only by a sustained, consistent re-offer.

Underneath it all runs the buyer decision process, five stages a customer traverses: need recognition (something breaks the status quo), information search (ask friends, read reviews, consult the sales engineer), evaluation of alternatives (the criteria set — consciously or not — in stage one decides everything), the purchase decision itself, and post-purchase behaviour, where satisfaction or dissonance writes the next review. High-involvement purchases — a car, an ERP system — walk all five stages slowly; habitual purchases compress them to reflex. STP works because it meets the buyer at a specific stage with a specific message rather than shouting one average message at all stages.
$$\text{For } T \text{ who } N,\; P \text{ is the } C \text{ that } B;\; \text{unlike } A,\; \text{ours } D.$$
concepts.detail: Target T, need N, product P, category C, benefit B, alternative A, differentiator D. If any slot is empty or vague, the positioning — and every campaign built on it — will drift.

concepts.statement: Over-segmentation: a segment too small to serve profitably is a hobby, not a strategy. Demographics describe but rarely explain — “women 25–34” is not a need. Positioning is not a slogan; the slogan is one instrument of the position. Targeting must stay inside law and ethics — segmenting by vulnerability (debt, addiction, health crises) invites regulation and reputational ruin. And VALS-style typologies are heuristics, not laws: they seed hypotheses, which field tests must confirm.
A group of buyers who respond similarly to a distinct offer built for them.
Division by lifestyle, values and personality — the “why” behind purchase behaviour.
Division by benefits sought, occasions, usage rate or loyalty.
Focusing the whole offer on one niche segment — depth over breadth.
Tailoring offers to individuals or hyper-local areas, data-permitting.
A two-axis plot of how buyers perceive competing offers, revealing gaps and clusters.
The one-sentence contract: target, need, category, benefit, differentiator.
Need recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase, post-purchase behaviour.

examples.title: Worked example — Segmentation, Targeting and Positioning: The STP Playbook
examples.problem: A mid-price running-shoe brand entering a market owned at the top by a premium icon and at the bottom by discount labels must segment, target and position.

steps.label: Segment
steps.text: by behavioral benefit — first-time marathoners who want reliable guidance, not race-day glory; demographics (25–40, urban, moderate income) are descriptive, not the basis.

steps.label: Target
steps.text: concentrated strategy — the segment is substantial (growing recreational running), underserved (icons price them out; discounters offer no guidance), and a fit for the firm’s mid-market channel.

steps.label: Position
steps.text: perceptual map axes price versus expert support show the open corner; the statement: for first-time marathoners who want to finish strong, Stride is the running shoe that coaches every step; unlike the prestige racers, ours builds support and pacing for ordinary runners — then every P follows: mid price, coaching content in promotion, specialty-run-store place.

keyTakeaways: Airline cabin architecture: one aircraft, three to four segments, each with its own price logic and positioning.
The cereal and detergent aisle: a shelf is a perceptual map, each row a segment the packager drew.
B2B sales territory design: end-user and purchasing-approach segmentation assign the right seller to the right account.
App freemium tiers: behavioral (usage-rate) segmentation turned into a pricing page.
Political and charity campaigns, which segment audiences by values (psychographics) and tailor messages accordingly.

Where next — Prerequisites: none, but read it beside the four-Ps lesson — STP aims, the mix fires. The psychology of individual choice — biases and nudges — is treated fully in the behavioral lessons; this one stays at strategy altitude. Follow with the entrepreneurship lessons to see STP applied to new ventures. Grounding text: OpenStax Principles of Marketing, chapters on consumer markets and on segmentation, targeting and positioning (2023).
STP precedes the mix: segment, target, position — then the four Ps have a target worth firing at.
Four bases — where, who, why, how: geographic, demographic, psychographic, behavioral; B2B segments by user, size and purchasing approach.
Target on size, structural attractiveness and fit; choose among undifferentiated, differentiated, concentrated and micro strategies.
Position with perceptual maps and a one-sentence statement; defend one idea, and subtract everything else.
Buyers move through five decision stages; effective STP meets them at the right stage with the right message.

quiz.q: Selling the same seat to a price-hunting tourist and a flexibility-buying executive is an example of segmenting by…
quiz.explanation: The trip occasion and the benefit sought differ; the airline prices and restricts each offer accordingly.

quiz.q: A niche startup focusing its entire offer on one underserved segment is using…
quiz.explanation: Concentration trades scale for depth in one segment where the firm can win decisively.

quiz.q: In the five-stage buyer decision process, the evaluation criteria are largely set…
quiz.explanation: Stage three is where criteria are applied — which is why stage-one framing and stage-two search channels shape outcomes before comparison begins.

intro:
Goods, services and capital cross borders, and every crossing demands a currency swap — so the exchange rate, the price of one money in terms of another, is where an economy meets the world. This lesson completes the closed-economy toolkit of the earlier macro lessons (output and inflation, fiscal and monetary policy) with the open economy: how currency prices are set, how the balance-of-payments ledger records every international transaction, and why the choice of exchange-rate regime trades one kind of stability for another.

**Why this matters.** Exchange rates decide the price of your holiday, your imported phone, your country’s exports, and the local-currency value of every foreign asset you or your pension fund holds. Peg collapses — the mechanic behind several historic financial crises — begin as quiet mismatches between a chosen rate and economic fundamentals.
objectives: Explain the exchange rate as a price of currencies
Explain demand and supply shifts in foreign exchange
Explain purchasing power parity as a long-run anchor
Explain balance of payments: current and financial accounts
Explain current-account deficit = net capital inflow
Explain fixed, floating and soft-peg regimes
Explain the impossible trinity of open-economy policy

concepts.term: The exchange rate as a price of currencies
concepts.statement: An exchange rate is just a price, and so it yields to supply and demand. Foreigners need the home currency to buy its exports and assets: that demand, met against residents supplying currency to buy imports and foreign assets, settles the market rate. When the price of a currency in another rises the currency appreciates; when it falls it depreciates. Who wins and who loses flips with the direction: a weaker currency cheers exporters (their goods get cheaper abroad) and overseas earners, while squeezing importers and anyone holding foreign-currency debt; a stronger currency does the reverse. “Strong” is therefore not automatically “good” — it redistributes between sectors.

concepts.term: Demand and supply shifts in foreign exchange
concepts.statement: What moves the curves? Interest-rate differentials: capital chases higher real returns, so a domestic rate hike tends to pull money in and appreciate the currency. Inflation differentials: the country that persistently inflates faster watches its currency slide. Growth prospects, risk sentiment and commodity exposure move rates too. Over the long haul, purchasing power parity anchors the level: a basket costing 100 units at home and 6 units abroad implies a parity rate of about 16.7 home-units per foreign unit; market rates drift far from parity for years — productivity, trade barriers and capital flows see to that — but persistent gaps get punished by inflation differentials eventually. The real exchange rate folds prices back in: nominal rate times domestic price level over foreign price level, the number that actually prices exports against imports.

concepts.term: Purchasing power parity as a long-run anchor
concepts.statement: The balance of payments is the country’s international ledger, kept by double entry: every transaction is recorded twice, once as a credit and once as a debit, so the whole account always sums to zero by construction. The informative split is between the current account — trade in goods and services, primary income from foreign assets and labour, and transfers such as remittances — and the capital-and-financial account, which records purchases and sales of assets: direct investment, portfolio flows, and changes in official reserves. The operative identity: a current-account deficit is matched by a net financial inflow. A country importing more than it exports is, by definition, borrowing from or selling assets to the rest of the world — which is financing investment, not necessarily “losing”. The US runs chronic deficits; Japan and Germany run surpluses; both patterns reflect saving-investment gaps, not virtue or vice.

concepts.term: Balance of payments: current and financial accounts
concepts.statement: Regimes order the spectrum of intervention. Floating: the market sets the rate daily, and the central bank merely watches. Fixed (pegged): the central bank promises a rate and stands behind it, buying or selling its reserves whenever the market leans — credibility priced in reserve holdings. Between sit the soft and crawling pegs, which drift within bands or step by small announced amounts, and the extremes of a currency board or full dollarisation, which surrender monetary policy almost entirely. Floats absorb shocks flexibly but swing; pegs import the anchor country’s stability but invite speculative attack when fundamentals diverge.

The organising theorem is the impossible trinity: a country can have at most two of a fixed exchange rate, free capital movement and an independent monetary policy. A float gives policy independence plus open capital markets; a hard peg gives exchange stability plus open capital markets at the price of importing interest policy; closing capital accounts can preserve both a peg and independence, at the cost of financial openness. Historic peg collapses follow the same script: defend an overvalued rate with reserves, reserves run out, devaluation arrives with a crisis attached — the “first-generation” attack model, played out repeatedly across decades and continents. Depreciation after a collapse passes through to import prices before exports respond — the J-curve dip before the recovery.
$$E_{\text{PPP}} = \frac{P_{\text{domestic}}}{P_{\text{foreign}}}, \quad E_{\text{real}} = E_{\text{nominal}} \times \frac{P_{\text{domestic}}}{P_{\text{foreign}}}$$
concepts.detail: Parity sets the nominal rate that equalises a basket’s price across countries; the real exchange rate — nominal rate times the price ratio — is what prices tradables against each other, and its movements move the trade balance.

concepts.statement: A current-account deficit is not a country “losing money” — it is a saving-investment statement, and sometimes a growth story financed abroad. The balance of payments always sums to zero even when the current account is wildly imbalanced. Depreciation is not always bad news, nor appreciation always good. A fixed rate is a standing policy promise, not a freebie: it costs reserves and, per the trinity, monetary independence. And PPP is a long-run anchor — betting on short-run convergence has bankrupted better traders than any exam candidate.
The price of one currency expressed in another; appreciates or depreciates with market forces.
The long-run rate at which a basket of goods costs the same everywhere.
Nominal rate adjusted by the domestic-to-foreign price ratio; prices tradables against each other.
The BOP record of goods, services, primary income and transfers.
The BOP record of cross-border asset transactions, including reserves.
Central-bank holdings of foreign assets used to defend a rate or smooth a float.
Fixed rate, free capital movement and independent monetary policy — pick any two.
The post-devaluation path where the trade balance worsens before it improves.

examples.title: Worked example — Exchange Rates and the Balance of Payments
examples.problem: A basket costs 100 home-units domestically and 6 foreign-units abroad; the market rate is 20 home-units per foreign-unit. How misaligned is the market rate from parity, and in which direction?

steps.label: Recall the parity rule
steps.text: the PPP rate is the domestic price level divided by the foreign price level.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: E_PPP = 100 ÷ 6 ≈ 16.7 home-units per foreign-unit. The market rate of 20 means foreigners get more home-currency per foreign-unit than parity implies — the home currency is undervalued by roughly (20 − 16.7) ÷ 20 ≈ 17 percent.

examples.result: home goods are about a fifth cheaper than parity predicts — classic conditions for a current-account surplus building over time, exactly the pressure that eventually drags market rates back toward parity.

keyTakeaways: Remittance corridors: migrant families watch the rate the way farmers watch rain.
Corporate hedging: exporters and importers lock forward rates against exactly the volatility this lesson describes.
Reserve management: central banks accumulate foreign assets as insurance for defence of a peg or smoothing of a float.
Travel budgeting and cross-border e-commerce pricing, where PPP gaps show up as “cheaper in” destinations.
Crisis playbooks: rate hikes, reserve deployment, and conditional international-support programmes after peg defence fails.

Where next — Prerequisites: the GDP vital-signs lesson for accounting fluency and the monetary-policy lesson for interest-rate logic; the comparative-advantage lesson explains why trade happens at all — this one explains how it is paid for. Follow with the fiscal-policy lesson to see how open-economy leakages weaken multipliers. Grounding texts: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e, chapters on exchange rates and international capital flows and on open-economy macroeconomic adjustments (2022), and the open-economy unit of any standard macro principles course.
The exchange rate is a price: demand from exports and inflows, supply from imports and outflows.
Interest and inflation differentials move rates; PPP anchors them in the long run.
The BOP always balances; the split between current and financial accounts tells the story.
A current-account deficit equals a net capital inflow — financing, not failure.
The impossible trinity forces a choice among fixed rates, open capital and monetary independence.

quiz.q: A country runs a current-account deficit. By BOP identity, it is simultaneously…
options: printing more of its own currency
quiz.explanation: Double-entry guarantees the gap is financed by net asset sales or borrowing — a financial inflow, not a lost ledger line.

quiz.q: Under an open capital account, a country that fixes its exchange rate must…
quiz.explanation: The impossible trinity: fixing the rate with free capital flows means interest policy must serve the peg, not the domestic cycle.

quiz.q: Immediately after a sharp depreciation, the trade balance often…
options: turns from surplus to deficit by law of one price
quiz.explanation: Import bills repricing beats export response; volumes take months to adjust, so the balance dips first.

intro:
The double-entry lesson explained the logic of the ledger; the financial-statements lesson explained how to read the outputs. This lesson walks the clockwork between them — the accounting cycle, the fixed sequence that turns a shoebox of transactions into trustworthy statements every period. Its centre of gravity is the accrual idea: revenue is recorded when earned and expenses when incurred, not when cash moves. That one decision is why adjusting and closing entries exist, and mastering them is the rite of passage of every accounting course worldwide.

**Why this matters.** The cycle is not bookkeeping trivia: valuation models read accrual numbers, so anyone who reads statements is downstream of these adjustments. Recognising an accrued liability or an unearned revenue in a filing is the difference between seeing a business and seeing its cash timing.
objectives: Explain nine steps from transaction to statements
Explain accrual basis versus cash basis
Explain matching: expenses follow the revenue they earn
Explain four classes of adjusting entries
Explain depreciation as allocation, not valuation
Explain closing entries and temporary accounts
Explain post-closing trial balance

concepts.term: Nine steps from transaction to statements
concepts.statement: The cycle runs nine steps per period: analyse source documents, journalise the transactions, post to the general ledger, prepare an unadjusted trial balance, journalise and post adjusting entries, prepare an adjusted trial balance, build the financial statements, journalise and post closing entries, and finish with a post-closing trial balance. Steps one to four are mechanical bookkeeping; steps five and eight are where judgement lives; the trial balances are the checkpoints that prove debits still equal credits after each layer of entries. The sequence is identical for a corner shop and a listed company — only volume differs.

Accrual accounting answers a timing question: when does the ledger record reality? The revenue-recognition principle says when the earning process is substantially complete, not when the customer pays; the matching principle says expenses attach to the period of the revenue they helped generate, not when they are paid for. Cash-basis accounting — recording only money in and money out — is fine for a lemonade stand and useless for a business that buys inventory in one period and sells it in the next: cash basis would show famine in the buying month and feast in the selling month, misstating both. Accrual smooths the distortion by timing entries to the economic event, at the price of estimates — and estimates are exactly what the adjusting entries carry.

concepts.term: Matching: expenses follow the revenue they earn
concepts.statement: Adjusting entries come in four classic classes. Deferred expenses: cash paid before the benefit is consumed — prepaid insurance recorded as an asset, then expensed month by month as coverage elapses. Deferred revenues: cash received before the obligation is discharged — a year of rent collected up front sits in unearned revenue (a liability) and migrates to revenue as the months deliver. Accrued expenses: cost incurred but not yet paid — the last week of employees’ work in December is December’s wage expense even if payday is January. Accrued revenues: value delivered but not yet billed — the service rendered before month-end that the invoice will chase next week. Each adjustment touches one income-statement account and one balance-sheet account; that symmetry is the diagnostic.

Depreciation is the best-known recurring adjustment and the most misunderstood. It does not value the machine; it allocates its historical cost over the periods that use it, so that matching holds — an estimate of consumption, not a market appraisal. The straight-line method divides cost less salvage value by useful life; accelerated methods front-load the expense for assets that lose productivity early. Depreciation also explains why an income statement is an opinion about timing, not a cash report: a company can be profitable (revenues exceed matched expenses) while cash burns, or cash-rich while reporting losses — the reconciliation lives in the cash-flow statement the statements lesson covers.

Closing entries end the period the way a stage crew resets between shows. Temporary accounts — revenues, expenses, and the owner’s draws or dividends — exist to measure one period; left open, they would blur every year into every other. Closing zeroes them: revenues and expenses are transferred to an income summary (or straight to retained earnings or capital), which then deposits the net result into equity, leaving revenue and expense accounts at zero for the new period. Permanent accounts — assets, liabilities, equity — are never closed; they roll forward, which is why the post-closing trial balance shows only them. Reversing entries are an optional final flourish that unbook accrued items so routine postings do not double-count them — a convenience, not a principle.
$$\text{annual depreciation} = \frac{\text{cost} - \text{salvage value}}{\text{useful life}}$$
concepts.detail: The asset’s depreciable base spreads evenly over its service years — the default allocation when consumption is roughly uniform.

concepts.statement: Treating depreciation as a valuation or a cash reserve — it is an allocation of past cost, and the cash left the building when the asset was bought. Adjusting when cash moves — the whole point is that these entries exist precisely because cash did NOT move (or moved earlier/later than the event). Closing permanent accounts — assets and liabilities never close. And forgetting that every adjustment must pair an income-statement account with a balance-sheet account; an adjustment touching two of the same kind is usually an error.
The period-by-period sequence from transaction analysis through closing and the post-closing trial balance.
Recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash timing.
A period-end entry in one of four classes — deferred expense, deferred revenue, accrued expense, accrued revenue (with depreciation the recurring case).
Cash collected before delivery, carried as a liability until earned.
Cost incurred but unpaid at period end — recorded now, paid later.
Systematic allocation of an asset’s cost over its useful life; an estimate, not a valuation.
Entries that zero the temporary accounts into equity for the new period.
Income-statement accounts reset each period; balance-sheet accounts roll forward.

examples.title: Worked example — The Accounting Cycle: Accruals, Adjustments and Closing the Books
examples.problem: A business pays 2,400 for twelve months of insurance on 1 December. Year-end is 31 December. What adjusting entry closes the year?

steps.label: Recall the class
steps.text: cash left before the benefit was consumed — deferred expense, sitting in the asset account prepaid insurance.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: one month of the twelve has been consumed — 2,400 ÷ 12 = 200 of insurance expense; the remaining 2,200 stays an asset. Entry: debit insurance expense 200, credit prepaid insurance 200.

examples.result: the income statement carries one month’s cost by matching; the balance sheet carries eleven months of unexpired benefit; net income, assets and equity each move by exactly 200 — the adjustment’s symmetry is the proof.

keyTakeaways: Month-end close in every finance department: the same nine steps compressed into a checklist and a deadline.
Audit fieldwork, which tests exactly the adjusting entries — cutoffs, accruals, depreciation estimates.
Reading filings: unearned-revenue balances expose subscription businesses’ backlog; accrued wages expose payroll timing.
Course and certification exams, which drill the four adjustment classes and the closing sequence relentlessly.
Small-business hygiene: knowing why a profitable firm can still run out of cash, and when to distrust a cash-basis spreadsheet.

Where next — Prerequisites: the double-entry lesson for debit/credit logic and the financial-statements lesson for the outputs being assembled. Follow with the finance lessons to see how accrual numbers feed valuation, and the entrepreneurship lessons for how founders live the cash-versus-accrual gap. Grounding texts: OpenStax Principles of Financial Accounting, chapters on the accounting cycle and completing the cycle (adjusting and closing entries), mirrored on the LibreTexts accounting shelves.
Nine steps run each period; adjusting entries (step 5) and closing entries (step 8) carry the judgement.
Accrual basis times entries to economic events: revenue when earned, expenses when incurred, matching as the glue.
Four adjustment classes: deferred expenses, deferred revenues, accrued expenses, accrued revenues.
Depreciation allocates cost — (cost − salvage) ÷ life — it neither values assets nor saves cash.
Closing zeroes temporary accounts into equity; the post-closing trial balance holds only permanents.

quiz.q: A company receives 12,000 on 1 January for a year of services. At 31 January, the adjusting entry is…
options: debit unearned revenue 1,000, credit service revenue 1,000
debit service revenue 1,000, credit unearned revenue 1,000
no entry until the year ends
quiz.explanation: Cash arrived first (deferred revenue, a liability); one month has been earned, so 1,000 migrates from liability to revenue.

quiz.q: December’s wages paid on 5 January are…
quiz.explanation: Accrued expense: the work was December’s, so the expense is December’s and a liability records the unpaid amount.

quiz.q: After closing entries, which accounts appear on the post-closing trial balance?
quiz.explanation: Temporary accounts are zeroed; only permanent accounts — assets, liabilities, equity — survive to the post-closing trial balance.

intro:
The biggest killers are, increasingly, behaviours: smoking, diet, inactivity, alcohol — risks people choose, repeat and can change. That is why the science of health behavior exists: a body of models that predicts when people adopt protective actions (screening, vaccination, exercise, cessation) and designs interventions that actually move them. It pairs with the study of medical care itself — what happens in the consultation, why patients so often do not take the treatment they agreed to, and why access and outcomes differ so sharply across income, race and geography. This lesson covers both halves: the models that explain health behaviour change, and the care context in which advice is given, followed or ignored. The stress-and-coping lesson covers the physiology of pressure; here the subject is behaviour and the system around it.

**Why this matters.** Every professional that touches health — clinicians, public-health planners, insurers, policymakers — works through these models, and exams test them as named constructs: the six Health Belief Model dimensions, the six stages of change, the planned-behaviour trio of attitudes, norms and control. The skill being tested is diagnostic: given a scenario (“he thinks screening is unnecessary because he feels fine”), name the construct (low perceived susceptibility) and the intervention lever (risk communication). Scenario-to-construct-to-leverage is the whole game, and it is learnable.
objectives: Explain health behavior and its preventable burden
Explain health Belief Model: six constructs
Explain transtheoretical stages of change
Explain theory of planned behavior and self-efficacy
Explain doctor–patient interaction and adherence
Explain access, disparities and social determinants

concepts.statement: Any action a person takes that affects health — preventive (screening, vaccination, exercise), risky (smoking, drinking) or sick-role (seeking care, taking medicine). Studied as decision-making under imperfect information, habit and social influence.

The two threat components of the Health Belief Model: how likely a person thinks a condition is to strike them, and how serious its consequences would be. Together they set the perceived threat that motivates (or fails to motivate) action.

The two action-evaluation components: how effective the person believes the recommended behaviour would be, weighed against what it costs — money, time, pain, embarrassment, inconvenience. Action follows when benefits outweigh barriers.

The model’s triggers and confidence terms: cues (symptoms, reminders, campaigns, a doctor’s advice) activate readiness, and self-efficacy — Bandura’s term for belief in one’s own capability — determines whether readiness becomes behaviour.

The Transtheoretical Model’s sequence — precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance (and termination) — with the practical rule that interventions must match the stage: advice pitched at someone in precontemplation bounces off.

The degree to which a patient follows a agreed treatment plan — taking medication as prescribed, attending appointments, keeping lifestyle changes. Non-adherence is one of the largest modifiable causes of treatment failure in modern medicine.

The conditions in which people are born, live, work and age — income, education, housing, neighbourhood, employment — that systematically shape both health behaviour and access to care, producing the disparities the clinical encounter alone cannot fix.

concepts.term: Health behavior and its preventable burden
concepts.statement: The Health Belief Model is the field’s founding framework, built in the 1950s by U.S. Public Health Service researchers studying why people declined free tuberculosis screening — the founding observation being that even free, easy prevention fails when beliefs do not support it. Its logic: the likelihood of a protective action rises with perceived threat (susceptibility × severity) and perceived benefit, falls with perceived barriers, and is triggered by cues to action — with self-efficacy added later as the confidence condition. Every construct is a measurable belief and therefore an intervention target: education raises perceived susceptibility (personalised risk feedback), vividness raises perceived severity (survivor testimony), convenience lowers barriers (clinic hours, transport), reminders act as cues, and skills training builds efficacy.
