Firm pressure on a bleeding wound, applied without lifting to check.
Five sharp strikes between the shoulder blades for severe choking.
Sharp inward-and-upward pulls above the navel to clear a blocked airway.
Chest compressions 100-120 per minute, 5-6 centimetres deep, for absent breathing.
An automated external defibrillator that talks an untrained user through defibrillation.

examples.title: Worked example — First Aid Essentials: Bleeding, Burns, Choking and the Recovery Position
examples.problem: You find a colleague collapsed at the bottom of a stairwell, not obviously responding. Walk through the first sixty seconds.

steps.label: Recall
steps.text: DR ABC orders every action — danger, response, airway, breathing, circulation — and an unconscious person who is breathing normally goes into the recovery position while help is summoned.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: check the stairs for hazards and spillage; squeeze the shoulders and shout — nothing; send a specific bystander to call the emergency services and fetch the first-aid kit; tilt the head, lift the chin; spend no more than ten seconds on look-listen-feel — breathing is normal, so roll into the recovery position and monitor.

examples.result: within a minute the scene is safe, professional help is on its way, and the airway is protected until it arrives — the three interventions that most change outcomes before professionals take over.

keyTakeaways: Workplace first-aid kits and trained first-aiders are a legal requirement in many countries.
CPR courses drill compressions to tempo — any song near 110 beats per minute — until they are muscle memory.
Public defibrillators (AEDs) are built for untrained users and talk the rescuer through every step.
School programmes teaching the recovery position to teenagers measurably improve bystander response.
Emergency dispatchers deliver real-time CPR coaching over the phone, so calling early doubles the help.

Where next — This lesson is education, not certification — take a hands-on course (Red Cross, St John Ambulance or your local equivalent) to practise compressions and the recovery position on a mannequin. Then: CPR in depth, poisoning and overdose response, and wilderness first aid for settings where the ambulance is hours away.

quiz.q: On reaching a collapsed person, your first action is to…
options: check for danger to yourself and others
quiz.explanation: A second casualty doubles the emergency — DR ABC begins with danger before anything else.

quiz.q: The correct first aid for a fresh burn is…
options: cool running water for about twenty minutes
quiz.explanation: Twenty minutes of cool running water reduces burn depth and pain — and still helps hours later. Ice deepens injury.

quiz.q: An adult is choking but can still cough loudly. You should…
options: give five back blows at once
quiz.explanation: An effective cough means a partly open airway — interference can complete the blockage. Blows and thrusts are for the silent, ineffective cough.

quiz.q: The recovery position is used for someone who is…
quiz.explanation: Side-lying with a tilted head keeps the airway open and drains fluids; absent breathing means CPR instead.

intro:
Swallow a tablet and a precisely timed journey begins: through the stomach, across the gut wall, past the liver's chemical filters, out to every tissue, and finally to the kidneys for disposal. Pharmacology, the science of drugs behind this Medicine & Pharmacology topic, divides that journey into two clean questions — pharmacokinetics, what the body does to the drug, and pharmacodynamics, what the drug does to the body. Get those two straight and dosing schedules, pharmacy labels, and the grapefruit-juice warning all turn from folklore into readable engineering.

**Why this matters.** Most adults will take prescription medicines for decades of their lives, yet the instructions read like opaque rules. Pharmacokinetics explains why "every eight hours" is not a suggestion, why some drugs take weeks to reach full effect while others act in minutes, and why stopping suddenly can matter as much as starting.
objectives: Explain pharmacokinetics: what the body does to a drug
Explain pharmacodynamics: what a drug does to the body
Explain aDME: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion
Explain first-pass metabolism and bioavailability
Explain half-life, steady state and washout
Explain agonists and antagonists at receptors
Explain why drug interactions happen

concepts.term: Pharmacokinetics: what the body does to a drug
concepts.statement: Pharmacokinetics is spelled ADME. Absorption gets the drug into the bloodstream; distribution carries it to its targets; metabolism chemically transforms it, mostly in the liver; excretion clears it, mostly through the kidneys into urine. Every dosing decision — how much, how often, by which route — is an attempt to keep the amount of drug at its site of action inside a useful window: enough to work, never quite enough to poison.

concepts.term: Pharmacodynamics: what a drug does to the body
concepts.statement: Absorption depends on the route. Intravenous injection places the drug directly into the blood — 100 percent available by definition. Everything else must cross barriers, and the gut is a gauntlet: stomach acid, digestive enzymes, and the wall of the intestine itself. Bioavailability measures the survivors — the fraction of a swallowed dose that reaches the circulation intact, compared with the same dose injected. Some drugs survive the trip nearly whole; others are mostly destroyed on arrival, which is why doses differ so much between routes.

The gut's blood supply drains straight into the liver before reaching the rest of the body, and the liver takes a cut of everything passing through — the first-pass effect. A drug heavily extracted on that first pass must be swallowed at many times its effective dose, or not swallowed at all: insulin, being a protein, is simply digested like food, which is why it is injected. Tablets dissolved under the tongue and patches stuck on skin exist largely to slip past the liver's toll booth.

Distribution decides where a drug goes once it circulates. Much of it hitches a ride on plasma proteins, and only the unattached fraction is free to act, so anything competing for the same ride can abruptly raise the free portion. Chemistry draws the map: fat-soluble drugs settle into body fat and leak out slowly for days, while the blood-brain barrier excludes all but the smallest, slipperiest molecules from the brain.

The single most useful number in pharmacology is the half-life: the time it takes the body to clear half of whatever remains. Each half-life halves the leftovers — 100 becomes 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25 percent — a tidy exponential decline. Ibuprofen's half-life is about two hours; caffeine's is roughly five, the number behind the sleep lesson's warning about late-afternoon coffee; fluoxetine's stretches for days, which is why it lingers long after the last capsule. Half-life sets the dosing rhythm, the time to full effect, and the time to wash a drug back out.

Pharmacodynamics is the drug meeting its target. Most drugs work by binding receptors or enzymes the body already owns, and they come in two temperaments: agonists switch the receptor on, antagonists occupy it without switching anything on. Salbutamol is an agonist at the airways' beta-2 receptors, relaxing smooth muscle to open constricted airways; beta blockers are antagonists at related receptors in the heart, muting adrenaline's pace-setting. Selectivity is everything — a drug that fits one receptor cleanly has few side effects; one that fits several has a longer warning label.

Bodies differ, and so do outcomes. The liver's CYP enzyme family metabolizes most drugs on the market, and anything that revs or jams those enzymes changes every drug riding the same lane: grapefruit juice inhibits one of them, quietly raising blood levels of certain statins; some antibiotics induce them, weakening contraceptive steroids. Age, kidney function, and genetics move the same dials. And the distance between a helpful dose and a harmful one — the therapeutic index — ranges from generous, as with ibuprofen, to razor-thin, as with warfarin, which is why some drugs demand laboratory monitoring while others sit on supermarket shelves.
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k_e} \approx \frac{0.693}{k_e}$$
concepts.detail: The half-life is the natural log of 2 divided by the elimination rate constant ke — roughly 70 percent of one over the clearance rate.

concepts.statement: $$\frac{C_n}{C_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n}$$
concepts.detail: Concentration halves each half-life: 50 percent after one, 25 after two, 12.5 after three, 6.25 after four.

concepts.statement: $$t_{ss} \approx (4\text{ to }5) \times t_{1/2}$$
concepts.detail: With repeated dosing, levels climb toward a plateau that is effectively reached after four to five half-lives — the same span a full washout takes after stopping.

concepts.statement: The classic error is doubling up after a missed dose — with a long-half-life drug that is a straight overdose. The second is assuming herbal means inert: St John's wort is a powerful liver-enzyme inducer that weakens contraceptives, blood thinners, and antivirals alike. And pain-reliever stacking matters: paracetamol hides in many combined cold remedies, so doubling products can double the dose of the one ingredient with a narrow liver-safety margin.
What the body does to a drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion.
What a drug does to the body, chiefly through receptors and enzymes.
The fraction of a dose reaching circulation intact, measured against intravenous injection.
The liver's extraction of orally absorbed drug before it reaches the rest of the body.
The time for the body to eliminate half of the remaining drug.
A drug that switches a receptor on versus one that merely occupies and blocks it.
The gap between an effective dose and a toxic one; narrow gaps demand monitoring.

examples.title: Worked example — Pharmacology: How Medicines Work
examples.problem: A once-daily blood-pressure medicine has a half-life of 12 hours. When does it reach full effect after starting, and how long after stopping is it effectively gone?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: repeated dosing builds toward a steady state reached after four to five half-lives, and after the last dose the same halving arithmetic runs in reverse.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: four to five half-lives of 12 hours is 48 to 60 hours — about two days of once-daily doses to reach the plateau. After the final dose, 50 percent remains at 12 hours, 25 at 24, 12.5 at 36, and 6.25 at 48 hours: more than 97 percent is gone within roughly two and a half days.

examples.result: the medicine reaches full steady effect in about two days and clears almost completely within two to three days of stopping — which is also why a couple of missed doses can drop levels meaningfully, and why some drugs are tapered rather than stopped cold.

keyTakeaways: Dosing schedules are half-life engineering: amoxicillin, with a half-life near one hour, is prescribed three or four times daily, while once-daily drugs are simply slow to leave.
Hospital loading doses jump straight to steady-state levels when waiting four half-lives is too slow — routine for anticoagulants and anti-seizure medicines.
Kidney-dose adjustments cut or stretch doses when impaired clearance lengthens a half-life, preventing drugs from accumulating to toxic plateaus.
Deprescribing plans sequence washouts: switching between certain antidepressants requires a clearance interval to avoid excess serotonin.
Pharmacy labels carry grapefruit and alcohol warnings precisely because CYP interference is predictable enough to print.

Where next — Pairs naturally with the antibiotic-resistance lesson in Life Sciences for how antimicrobial drugs target bacteria specifically. Next steps: how new drugs are tested in clinical trials, how pain medicines work, and the everyday pharmacology of caffeine and alcohol.

quiz.q: A drug has a half-life of 6 hours. Twenty-four hours after a single dose, roughly what fraction remains?
quiz.explanation: Four half-lives pass in 24 hours, and (1/2)^4 leaves 6.25 percent of the dose behind.

quiz.q: With repeated dosing, drug levels effectively reach their plateau after about:
options: a fixed 24 hours regardless of the drug
quiz.explanation: Accumulation and clearance balance out to a steady state after roughly four to five half-lives of regular dosing.

quiz.q: Insulin is injected rather than swallowed mainly because:
options: it is too large a molecule for the stomach to hold
as a protein it is digested like food before reaching the blood
the liver destroys every trace of it
it would raise stomach acid dangerously
quiz.explanation: Digestive enzymes dismantle proteins — injection bypasses both the gut and the first pass through the liver.

quiz.q: A beta blocker slows the heart by acting as:
quiz.explanation: It occupies the receptor without activating it, so adrenaline's signal cannot get through at full strength.

intro:
Cancer is not one disease but a family of more than a hundred, all sharing a single origin story: one cell that stops obeying the rules of the cooperative. In a body of thirty trillion cells, division, repair, and self-destruction are tightly governed; cancer is what happens when a cell collects mutations that unlock uncontrolled growth. Oncology, the discipline behind this Disease & Treatment topic, has turned that story from fatalism into engineering. The numbers now show it: in high-income countries roughly one in two people will face a cancer diagnosis in their lifetime, and more than half survive it.

**Why this matters.** Cancer remains a leading cause of death worldwide — about one in six of all deaths — yet survival has climbed decade over decade. Understanding the mechanism dissolves both the mystery and the doom: why screening works, why treatments differ so much between patients, and why "caught early" carries so much weight.
objectives: Explain cancer as a disease of accumulated mutations
Explain oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes
Explain the hallmarks of a cancer cell
Explain why tumors stay invisible for years
Explain metastasis: how cancer travels
Explain staging with the TNM system
Explain surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, targeted and immune therapy

concepts.term: Cancer as a disease of accumulated mutations
concepts.statement: Every time a cell divides it must copy three billion DNA letters, and across the trillions of divisions in a lifetime, errors are inevitable. Most are repaired or harmless; a rare cell gathers the wrong combination — mutations that speed division, ignore restraints, or refuse to die — and every descendant inherits them. Mutations come from chance, from carcinogens like tobacco smoke and ultraviolet light, from viruses such as HPV, or from the lottery of inheritance: BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants, passed through families, account for a small minority of cases but a large share of inherited risk.

The key genes fall into two families. Oncogenes are accelerators: growth-promoting genes that, mutated into a permanently active state, drive division — a single damaged copy suffices. Tumor suppressor genes are brakes: p53, the "guardian of the genome," pauses division for repairs or orders a damaged cell to self-destruct, so both copies must fail before the brake releases. Cancer is genuinely multistep — typically several distinct mutations accumulating over years — which is why risk climbs steeply with age and why cancer is a process, not an event.

concepts.term: The hallmarks of a cancer cell
concepts.statement: The mutations converge on a shared playbook, famously catalogued as the hallmarks of cancer. The malignant cell grows without external orders, ignores the signals that say stop, disables its own suicide program, and switches on telomerase so its chromosomes never shorten and division never times out. It recruits new blood vessels to feed itself, digs through surrounding tissue, and — crucially — hides from immune patrols. Each hallmark is also a vulnerability: a process the cell now depends on, which a drug or a retrained immune system can attack.

concepts.term: Why tumors stay invisible for years
concepts.statement: Tumor growth is quietly exponential at first: one cell becomes two, four, eight. Thirty doublings produce about a billion cells — roughly one cubic centimeter, close to the smallest lump a scan can reliably find. Doubling times range from weeks for aggressive lymphomas to years for many prostate and breast tumors, which is why a cancer "discovered suddenly" has usually been developing for a decade or more. That long invisible window is the entire opportunity screening exploits: find it at twenty-nine doublings and it is smaller, contained, and far more curable.

Metastasis — spread to distant organs — is what makes cancer lethal: most cancer deaths involve disease beyond the original site. The sequence is brutal and inefficient: tumor cells push into nearby tissue, squeeze into blood or lymph vessels, survive circulation, lodge in a distant capillary bed, and colonize. The lodging is selective — the "seed and soil" idea — which is why different cancers favor different destinations: bowel cancer to the liver, breast cancer to bone, lung cancer to the brain. Once established, the colonies are every bit the parent's equal in malignancy.

Oncologists describe a cancer's extent with the TNM system: the size and depth of the Tumor, involvement of lymph Nodes, and presence of distant Metastasis, condensed into stages 0 through IV. Broadly, early stage means localized and often curable by surgery alone; stage IV means established spread and shifts the goal toward long-term control. Stage at diagnosis is among the strongest predictors of survival, which is precisely why screening, staging scans, and prompt workups dominate cancer medicine.

concepts.term: Surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, targeted and immune therapy
concepts.statement: Treatment now spans five broad tools, usually in combination. Surgery physically removes localized disease and remains the single best shot at cure when cancer is contained. Radiation therapy aims high-energy beams to shatter DNA in a mapped target while sparing healthy tissue as much as physics allows. Chemotherapy poisons division itself — systemically, which is why fast-dividing marrow, hair roots, and gut lining share the side effects. Targeted therapy exploits a tumor's specific mutation: imatinib blocks the aberrant protein made by the Philadelphia chromosome, converting chronic myeloid leukemia into a disease managed with a daily tablet. Immunotherapy removes the brakes with checkpoint inhibitors, or re-engineers T cells outright, so the immune system — whose patrols were introduced in the Life Sciences immunology lesson — does the killing. Which tools, in what order, is decided by tumor type, stage, and increasingly by the tumor's own molecular profile.

concepts.detail: A tumor doubles its cell count every doubling time Td; from one cell, thirty doublings reach about a billion cells — one cubic centimeter, near the threshold of detection.

concepts.statement: The most damaging misconception is that cancer is automatically a death sentence: five-year survival now exceeds 70 percent for many common cancers when caught early, and childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia has climbed from about 10 percent survival in the 1960s to roughly 90 percent today. Two more: biopsies do not meaningfully "release" cancer — the fear delays diagnosis far more than any procedure spreads disease — and no diet starves a tumor: while healthy weight genuinely lowers the risk of several cancers, internet fasting cures do not shrink established ones.
A growth-promoting gene that drives division when mutated into a permanently active state.
A braking gene, such as p53, that must fail on both copies before control is lost.
Spread of cancer from its origin to distant organs; the cause of most cancer deaths.
A tumor's recruitment of new blood vessels to supply itself.
Describing a cancer's extent by tumor size, node involvement, and metastasis presence.
Systemic drugs that kill rapidly dividing cells, cancerous and healthy alike.
An immunotherapy that releases molecular brakes on T cells so they attack tumors.

examples.title: Worked example — Understanding Cancer: From Mutation to Metastasis
examples.problem: How long does a tumor with a 60-day doubling time take to grow from a single cell to detectable size — and why does that justify screening?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: growth is exponential in doublings, and reliable detection begins near thirty doublings — about one billion cells and one cubic centimeter.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: thirty doublings at sixty days each is 1,800 days, roughly five years of silent growth. Ten further doublings would multiply the burden a thousandfold, from one billion cells toward a trillion; catching the tumor at doubling twenty-five instead of thirty-five means treating a far smaller, better-contained disease.

examples.result: the same arithmetic that makes cancer frightening — silent years of doubling — is what makes screening valuable: colonoscopy programs find pre-cancerous polyps inside the decade-long window before malignancy and remove them before cancer begins.

keyTakeaways: Screening programs — cervical HPV and Pap tests, mammography, colonoscopy and stool tests — are built to catch tumors during their long silent phase.
HPV vaccination prevents cancers at the source, immunizing against the viruses behind most cervical and many throat cancers.
Genetic profiling of tumors now matches patients to targeted drugs and immunotherapies instead of one-size-fits-all chemotherapy.
Staging scans and biopsy results drive the surgery-first versus drug-first decision for every new diagnosis.
Palliative care runs alongside active treatment, managing symptoms and quality of life at every stage — not only at the end.

Where next — Best read alongside the Life Sciences lessons on the immune system (for immunotherapy's machinery) and cell biology. Next steps: how screening tests are evaluated, inherited cancer risk and genetic counseling, and how clinical trials measure survival.

quiz.q: Most cancer deaths are ultimately caused by:
options: the original tumor pressing on nearby tissue
metastatic spread to distant vital organs
quiz.explanation: Localized tumors are often curable; it is established distant spread that turns cancer lethal.

quiz.q: A tumor suppressor gene behaves like:
options: an accelerator with one stuck-on copy
a brake that must fail on both copies before control is lost
a fuel line feeding the tumor
a blood vessel the tumor grows along
quiz.explanation: Both copies of a suppressor like p53 must be damaged before the division brake releases.

quiz.q: Chemotherapy causes hair loss, nausea and infection risk because:
options: the drugs bind receptors in hair and stomach directly
hair roots, gut lining and marrow divide fast and share the vulnerability
tumors pump toxins into those tissues
the drugs lower oxygen delivery everywhere
quiz.explanation: Chemotherapy attacks division itself, so every fast-renewing healthy tissue pays the same toll.

quiz.q: Roughly how many doublings does it take a tumor to reach one billion cells — near the detectable size?
quiz.explanation: Thirty doublings — exponential growth's quiet head start before anything shows on a scan.

intro:
Every cell in the body runs on glucose, and the blood carries it in a band so narrow that a teaspoon too much or too little counts as a medical event. The hormone insulin is the gatekeeper — the anatomy lessons covered how the pancreas senses sugar and releases it in a feedback loop. Diabetes is what happens when that loop breaks. This Disease & Treatment topic explains the two main types, why the damage accumulates silently for years, and how modern management — from a walk after dinner to continuous glucose sensors — keeps the rails back on.

**Why this matters.** Over half a billion adults live with diabetes, and nearly half of them do not yet know it: the disease can simmer for years without symptoms while quietly damaging eyes, kidneys, nerves and arteries. Type 2, which dominates, is largely preventable — and its warning stage, prediabetes, is genuinely reversible.
objectives: Explain how the body normally holds blood glucose steady
Explain type 1: an autoimmune strike on insulin factories
Explain type 2: resistance first, exhaustion later
Explain prediabetes: the reversible warning lane
Explain hbA1c: a three-month memory of blood sugar
Explain small-vessel and large-vessel complications
Explain management: lifestyle, tablets, hormones and technology

concepts.term: How the body normally holds blood glucose steady
concepts.statement: In a healthy system, blood glucose sits near 5 millimoles per liter (about 90 milligrams per deciliter) between meals, rises modestly after eating, and is parked away within two hours. Insulin from the pancreas's beta cells commands muscle and fat tissue to absorb glucose and signals the liver to store it; between meals, glucagon releases it again. Diabetes is defined by numbers: a fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, a two-hour value over 200 after a standard sugar drink, or an HbA1c of 6.5 percent or more.

concepts.term: Type 1: an autoimmune strike on insulin factories
concepts.statement: Type 1 diabetes is friendly fire. The immune system — whose tolerance machinery was unpacked in the immunology lesson — mistakes the pancreatic beta cells for enemies and destroys them, leaving the body with little or no insulin. It can begin at any age but classically surges in childhood and young adulthood, often announcing itself over days to weeks with thirst, floods of urine, and weight loss as the body burns fat in sugar's absence. It is not caused by eating sugar, and it always requires insulin — by pen or pump — to survive.

Type 2 is a slower, quieter story and accounts for about nine cases in ten. Cells respond sluggishly to insulin — resistance — and the beta cells compensate by pumping out more, often for years. Blood sugar stays normal while the system runs hot; by the time it climbs, the beta cells have been overworking for a decade or more, and their capacity slowly erodes. Family history, weight gain, inactivity, and age all raise the risk, and what was once called "adult-onset" now appears in teenagers. Because symptoms arrive late, the diagnosis often lands only through a routine blood test — or when a complication speaks first.

Between normal and diabetes lies prediabetes: an HbA1c of 5.7 to 6.4 percent or fasting glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL. It has no symptoms, which is the point of screening. The landmark Diabetes Prevention Program found that structured lifestyle change — about 150 minutes of weekly activity and a modest 7 percent weight loss — cut progression to diabetes by 58 percent over three years, outperforming metformin, the standard first-line tablet, at 31 percent. The warning lane is not a life sentence; it is a fork in the road.

concepts.term: HbA1c: a three-month memory of blood sugar
concepts.statement: Doctors measure control with HbA1c: glucose permanently gummed onto hemoglobin inside red blood cells. Because those cells live about four months, the test reads like a three-month average of blood sugar — no fasting, no memory of yesterday's cake required. It is the number treatment targets: many adults aim for below 7 percent, with targets individualized upward for the frail and tighter in pregnancy. Daily finger-prick sensors and continuous glucose monitors add the minute-to-minute picture the average hides.

Complications are the disease's long game, and they follow from sugar-coated proteins and damaged vessel walls. Small vessels go first and worst: retinopathy threatens vision (a leading cause of blindness in working-age adults), nephropathy can end in dialysis (diabetes is the top reason for kidney failure worldwide), and neuropathy numbs feet until a blister becomes an ulcer. Large vessels suffer too — heart attack and stroke risk runs two to four times higher — which is why diabetes care is quietly cardiovascular care. The landmark trials of the 1990s proved that tight control slashes these outcomes; the damage is cumulative, and so is the protection.

concepts.term: Management: lifestyle, tablets, hormones and technology
concepts.statement: Management now runs on three engines. Type 1 is an engineering problem: insulin dosed to match food and activity, increasingly guided by continuous sensors and hybrid closed-loop pumps that act almost like an artificial pancreas. Type 2 starts with the pyramid base everyone can act on — activity, weight, sleep, a Mediterranean-style pattern — then adds metformin, and newer drugs that carry independent benefits for heart and kidney disease or weight. Insulin arrives later when needed. Low blood sugar — shakiness, sweating, confusion — is the main hazard of treatment; the rule is fast carbohydrates, recheck in fifteen minutes, and the first-aid lesson's rule that unconscious means emergency, never a drink.
$$eAG \,(\text{mg/dL}) = 28.7 \times \text{A1c} - 46.7$$
concepts.detail: Each percentage point of HbA1c translates to roughly 29 mg/dL of average blood glucose — the arithmetic linking the lab report to daily life.

concepts.statement: "A touch of sugar" is the most dangerous phrase in the vocabulary — prediabetes ignored is diabetes scheduled. The second error is blaming people with type 1 for their disease: it is autoimmune, not a dessert problem. Third, stopping medication when the numbers improve reverses the causality — the numbers improved because of the medication. And beware cure claims: no supplement, berry, or fasting protocol regenerates destroyed beta cells.
The pancreatic hormone that moves glucose out of blood into muscle, fat and liver storage.
Cells answering insulin weakly, forcing beta cells to overproduce to compensate.
Autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells; absolute insulin deficiency.
Insulin resistance combined with gradual beta-cell decline; about 90 percent of cases.
Glucose bound to hemoglobin, reporting the roughly three-month average blood sugar.
The reversible warning zone of 5.7 to 6.4 percent HbA1c before diagnostic thresholds.
Blood glucose low enough to cause shakiness, sweating and confusion; treated with fast carbohydrates.

examples.title: Worked example — Diabetes and Metabolic Health: When Blood Sugar Runs Off the Rails
examples.problem: A lab returns an HbA1c of 7.4 percent. What has the average blood sugar been, and what average corresponds to the common 7 percent target?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: the ADAG study calibrated the formula eAG = 28.7 × A1c − 46.7, converting the three-month memory into daily units.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: at 7.4 percent, eAG = 28.7 × 7.4 − 46.7 ≈ 166 mg/dL. The 7 percent target corresponds to 28.7 × 7 − 46.7 ≈ 154 mg/dL — so roughly a 12 mg/dL average separates the two.

examples.result: the past three months have averaged about 166 mg/dL; reaching the standard target means trimming the average by about a dozen units — the scale of change that losing 5 kilograms or adding a daily walk often achieves in early type 2 diabetes.

keyTakeaways: Continuous glucose monitors and insulin pumps close the feedback loop diabetes breaks, in real time.
Pharmacies and primary-care clinics screen with quick A1c tests, catching the silent years before complications.
Structured lifestyle programs modeled on the Diabetes Prevention Program run at scale in health systems.
Retinal photography in ordinary clinics screens for eye damage without an ophthalmology appointment.
Newer drug classes now protect kidneys and hearts independently of their glucose-lowering effect.

Where next — Read after the Life Sciences lessons on hormones and the kidneys, which set up the feedback loop this topic breaks. Natural pairings: the heart-disease lesson (shared risk machinery), obesity and metabolism, and the technology of glucose sensing. Educational, not diagnostic — numbers belong to clinicians.

quiz.q: Type 1 diabetes results from:
options: eating too much sugar in childhood
autoimmune destruction of the pancreatic beta cells
quiz.explanation: The immune system destroys the insulin-producing cells — an absolute deficiency treated with insulin, not lifestyle alone.

quiz.q: An HbA1c of 7 percent corresponds to an estimated average glucose of about:
quiz.explanation: 28.7 × 7 − 46.7 ≈ 154 mg/dL, the arithmetic behind the standard adult target.

quiz.q: In the Diabetes Prevention Program, structured lifestyle change cut progression to diabetes by:
quiz.explanation: 150 minutes of weekly activity plus modest weight loss outperformed even metformin in the landmark trial.

quiz.q: Which trio is the classic small-vessel (microvascular) complication set of diabetes?
quiz.explanation: Retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy — the small vessels that sugar-coated proteins damage first.

intro:
The heart's plumbing — four chambers, two circuits, valves and all — was unpacked in the Life Sciences anatomy lesson. This Disease & Treatment topic is about what happens when the pipes fail. Cardiovascular disease kills more people than anything else on earth, about a third of all deaths, yet most of it is one process — atherosclerosis — that develops for decades before it speaks. That silence is the whole challenge: the disease is measurable and treatable long before it is feelable.

**Why this matters.** A first heart attack is often the first symptom, because arteries widen outward to hide plaque until late in the process. Prevention therefore runs on numbers — blood pressure, cholesterol, glucose, smoking — rather than on how one feels, and the payoff is enormous: most early cardiovascular disease is avoidable.
objectives: Explain atherosclerosis: plaque built over decades
Explain plaque rupture, not gradual narrowing, causes most heart attacks
Explain fixed versus modifiable risk factors
Explain blood pressure and cholesterol numbers that matter
Explain statins and the arithmetic of prevention
Explain recognizing heart attack and stroke fast
Explain cardiac rehabilitation and living with heart disease

concepts.statement: Atherosclerosis begins when LDL cholesterol particles slip between the endothelial cells lining artery walls and become chemically damaged there. Immune cells called macrophages swallow the damaged cholesterol and turn into lipid-stuffed foam cells; layers of them under the vessel lining form a fatty streak — found in the arteries of most teenagers. Over years the streak becomes a plaque: a cholesterol core under a fibrous cap, wearing the artery wall from inside.

concepts.term: Plaque rupture, not gradual narrowing, causes most heart attacks
concepts.statement: The surprise for most people is that heart attacks are usually not the slow strangulation of an artery by a big plaque — they are ruptures. Inflammation thins the fibrous cap until it tears, and within minutes platelets swarm the wound and build a clot. If the clot seals a coronary artery, heart muscle downstream dies: a myocardial infarction. The same rupture in a brain artery causes the commonest kind of stroke. Stable, heavily narrowed arteries cause predictable effort-chest pain (angina); the modest, unstable plaques that rupture without warning are the killers.

Risk splits cleanly into what cannot be changed and what can. Fixed: age, sex, and family history — including familial hypercholesterolemia, where LDL runs high from birth in about one person in 250 and untreated heart disease arrives early. Modifiable: smoking (the single largest controllable factor), high blood pressure, high LDL, diabetes, inactivity, excess weight, and heavy drinking. Chronic stress amplifies the others — the stress lesson covered its chemistry. Clinicians feed these variables into risk calculators that output a ten-year probability, because treating risk, not isolated numbers, is the modern rule.

concepts.term: Blood pressure and cholesterol numbers that matter
concepts.statement: The numbers worth knowing: normal blood pressure sits below 120/80, with 120-139 systolic counted as elevated-to-stage-1 territory and 140/90 and above as stage 2 hypertension (the anatomy lesson covered how the body regulates the set point; here it is the disease threshold that matters, because sustained pressure above roughly 130/80 quietly scours vessel walls, thickens heart muscle, and strains kidneys). For cholesterol, LDL under 100 mg/dL is optimal for most, with targets set lower as overall risk climbs — the lower the LDL over a lifetime, the fewer the events.

concepts.term: Statins and the arithmetic of prevention
concepts.statement: Statins are the workhorse of prevention. They block the liver's cholesterol-synthesis enzyme, the liver responds by harvesting LDL from the blood with more receptors, and LDL falls 30 to 50 percent. Across the giant trial record that translates to roughly a quarter fewer heart attacks and strokes per millimole of LDL lowered — benefit that compounds with baseline risk, which is why a 65-year-old with prior disease gains far more in absolute terms than a healthy 40-year-old. Blood-pressure medicines earn comparable numbers. Aspirin, famously, does not: its bleeding cost now outweighs routine use in healthy people, and it belongs only where a clinician prescribes it.

concepts.term: Recognizing heart attack and stroke fast
concepts.statement: When disease speaks, speed decides the outcome. A heart attack classically presses rather than stabs — heaviness in the center of the chest, spreading to arm, neck or jaw, with sweat, nausea, breathlessness; women, older adults and people with diabetes often get quieter versions. Stroke is flagged FAST: a drooping Face, weak Arm, slurred Speech — Time to call emergency services. In both cases the motto is the same: muscle and brain die by the minute, and the ambulance is the first ward of the hospital, not a taxi for the stubborn.

concepts.term: Cardiac rehabilitation and living with heart disease
concepts.statement: Survivors enter a second act that medicine keeps improving. Cardiac rehabilitation — supervised exercise, medication tuning, and education — measurably cuts readmissions and death, yet stays under-attended. Stents prop open culprit arteries; bypass grafts rebuild the network; pacemakers and defibrillators manage rhythm; and when the pump itself weakens into heart failure, device therapy and drug sequences extend life for years. The condition becomes chronic, manageable, and very much worth managing.
$$EF = \frac{SV}{EDV} \times 100\%$$
concepts.detail: The stroke volume pumped per beat (SV) divided by the filled ventricle (EDV); normal is 50 to 70 percent, and below 40 percent defines the commonest heart-failure category.

concepts.statement: $$ARR = C_{control} - C_{treated}$$
concepts.detail: The event rate without treatment minus the rate with it — the honest way to size a benefit before dividing it by cost and side effects.

concepts.statement: The deadliest habit is waiting for symptoms — outward-widening arteries hide plaque until rupture day. The second is treating "normal for my age" as safe: pressure that drifts up each decade is damage compounding, not a rite of passage. Third, stopping statins over muscle aches without consulting: switching type or dose usually resolves it, while stopping quietly raises risk. And self-prescribed aspirin is yesterday's advice — bleeding risk now outweighs routine prevention for most healthy people.
Cholesterol-rich plaque accumulating inside artery walls over decades.
Tearing of a plaque's fibrous cap, triggering the clot that causes most heart attacks and strokes.
The lipoprotein fraction that delivers cholesterol into artery walls; the treatment target.
Death of heart muscle from a blocked coronary artery — the heart attack.
A drug blocking liver cholesterol synthesis, lowering LDL and cardiovascular events.
The share of filled ventricle blood pumped per beat; a key heart-failure measure.
Supervised exercise-plus-education program after a cardiac event.

examples.title: Worked example — Heart and Vascular Disease: Atherosclerosis, Risk and Prevention
examples.problem: A 62-year-old smoker with blood pressure 150/90 and total cholesterol 240 mg/dL computes a ten-year cardiovascular risk near 25 percent. What does quitting, pressure control and a statin buy?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: risk multiplies, so removing factors compounds; quitting smoking roughly halves excess risk within about a year, pressure control and statins each shave roughly a quarter of remaining risk.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: from 25 percent, quitting takes the profile toward about 15 percent; blood pressure to target and LDL halved take the estimate toward 8 to 10 percent. The absolute reduction is 25 − 9 ≈ 16 percentage points — 16 fewer events per 100 people over a decade.

examples.result: stacked, modest relative reductions become a four-in-five relative improvement, and the same logic run at a young, low baseline explains why doctors frame statins honestly: the same drug can be transformative for one patient and marginal for another.

keyTakeaways: Ten-year risk calculators turn scattered readings into one number that steers medication decisions.
Stroke units and FAST public campaigns save brain by cutting the door-to-treatment clock.
Cardiac rehabilitation programs cut readmissions, and remain chronically under-used.
Smoking-cessation services roughly double quit rates over willpower alone.
Familial-cholesterol screening finds whole families at inherited risk with one index case.

Where next — Read after the heart-and-circulation anatomy lesson for the plumbing, and pairs with diabetes (shared machinery), the stress lesson (amplifier chemistry), and the first-aid lesson for emergency response. Next: heart rhythm and ECGs, stroke care, and how blood-pressure drugs work. Educational, not diagnostic.

quiz.q: Most heart attacks are triggered by:
options: slow, gradual narrowing until the artery closes
rupture of a plaque followed by rapid clot formation
spasm of a perfectly clean artery
quiz.explanation: The unstable plaque tears, platelets seal the tear, and the clot — not the slow narrowing — blocks the artery.

quiz.q: A ventricle fills with 120 mL and ejects 66 mL per beat. The ejection fraction is:
quiz.explanation: 66/120 = 0.55 — a normal 55 percent; below 40 percent marks reduced pump function.

quiz.q: Which single modifiable factor carries the largest controllable cardiovascular risk?
quiz.explanation: Smoking dwarfs the other modifiable levers — and quitting buys back most of the excess risk within years.

quiz.q: A statin lowers a patient's event risk from 20 percent to 15 percent. The absolute risk reduction is:
quiz.explanation: ARR = 20 − 15 = 5 percentage points; expressed relatively it is 25 percent — both numbers matter.

intro:
A good clinician listens for fifteen minutes, orders two tests, and names a condition that a search engine drowned in possibilities could not. The clinical method — the subject of this Medicine & Pharmacology topic — is not a checklist but a loop: gather evidence, generate hypotheses, test them, and update. Arthur Conan Doyle, a doctor before he was a novelist, modeled Sherlock Holmes on his surgeon teacher Joseph Bell; the deduction is no coincidence. Diagnosis is applied reasoning under uncertainty, and its steps are learnable.

**Why this matters.** Patients who understand the method become better partners in it: they bring a structured story instead of a symptom dump, know why a test was chosen, and can ask the single most useful question — "what are you trying to rule out?" It also explains why "just test everything" backfires: every test has false positives, and untargeted testing produces cascades of follow-up, cost and worry.
objectives: Explain the history: the most powerful diagnostic test
Explain characterizing a symptom systematically
Explain the physical exam as hypothesis testing
Explain differential diagnosis: rank likelihood and danger
Explain sensitivity and specificity of tests
Explain bayesian updating at the bedside
Explain cognitive traps and safety nets

concepts.term: The history: the most powerful diagnostic test
concepts.statement: Everything begins with the history, and the classic teaching is blunt: it alone yields the diagnosis in most encounters. The patient's opening line is recorded verbatim as the chief complaint, then interrogated systematically — pain is characterized by its Onset, what Provokes or relieves it, its Quality (sharp, burning, pressure), its Region and radiation, its Severity, and its Timing. Then the context: past illnesses, medications, allergies, family history, and the social fabric of smoking, alcohol, work and living situation. What looks like small talk is data collection.

The physical examination follows the same discipline in miniature — inspect, touch, percuss, listen — but it is not a routine lap: it is targeted experiment. The clinician who presses the right lower abdomen is testing a hypothesis about appendicitis, watching the face, not just the belly. Vital signs are the dashboard — temperature, pulse, breathing rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation — and any single finding is a data point, interpreted against the story already gathered rather than in isolation.

concepts.term: The physical exam as hypothesis testing
concepts.statement: Before any test is ordered, a good clinician builds the differential diagnosis: a list of plausible explanations ranked by two separate logics — how likely, and how dangerous. A healthy 24-year-old with chest pain probably has a muscle strain, but the list is topped by the must-not-miss causes anyway: the heart attack that is unlikely but lethal outranks the strain that is likely and harmless. Every subsequent test exists to move items up or down that list; "let's just run a panel" is not a differential, it is a coin flip with an invoice.

concepts.term: Differential diagnosis: rank likelihood and danger
concepts.statement: Tests earn their place through two statistics. Sensitivity is the share of people with the disease who test positive — highly sensitive tests, when negative, reliably rule disease out. Specificity is the share of healthy people who test negative — highly specific tests, when positive, confirm. Cutoffs trade the two against each other: lower the threshold and catch more cases at the price of more false alarms; raise it and the reverse. There is no perfect test, only tests matched to a question.

The interpretation step is Bayes' theorem wearing a white coat — the same probability update covered abstractly in the Mathematics library, here deciding who gets sick. A test result does not speak for itself: it must be weighed against the probability before the test, which comes from the history, the exam, and how common the disease is in that population. The same positive result in a symptomatic high-risk patient and in an asymptomatic walk-in means entirely different things, because predictive value rises and falls with prevalence.

Diagnosis also bends around human minds, and medicine has catalogued its own failure modes. Anchoring freezes on the first impression; availability ranks whatever was seen last week too high — the availability heuristic dissected in the Social Sciences lessons, wearing scrubs. The countermeasures are structural: "what else could this be?" asked out loud, second opinions for consequential calls, and safety-netting — explicit instructions to return if things change, plus the decision to re-examine in 48 hours, which turns time itself into a diagnostic test for the self-limiting versus the sinister.

The final discipline is knowing what each result will trigger before ordering. The rule taught to trainees: never order a test unless every possible answer changes the plan. Incidental findings — the scan that shows something unrelated — are the tax on unfocused testing, paid in anxiety, further procedures, and occasional harm. The clinical method closes its loop deliberately: hypothesis, test, update, and a plan for what happens next under each outcome.
$$PPV = \frac{Se \times P}{Se \times P + (1 - Sp)(1 - P)}$$
concepts.detail: The probability that a positive result is truly positive — sensitivity Se and specificity Sp folded with the pre-test probability P of disease in this patient.

concepts.statement: The reflex error is demanding every test "to be thorough" — in a low-risk person that mostly manufactures false positives and their follow-up cascades. The mirror error is dismissing a normal test: taken too early, troponin and some infections test negative while the disease brews, which is why timing and repeat testing exist. And self-diagnosis by search engine reverses the method — it has no differential, no examination, and no way to weigh likelihood against danger.
The ranked list of plausible explanations for a clinical picture.
Share of diseased people who test positive; high sensitivity makes a negative result reassuring.
Share of healthy people who test negative; high specificity makes a positive result convincing.
The chance of disease before testing, estimated from history, exam and prevalence.
The probability that a positive result reflects true disease in this patient.
Sticking with the first impression despite new evidence.
Explicit instructions to return or re-test if the picture changes.

examples.title: Worked example — How Doctors Diagnose: History, Exam and the Differential
examples.problem: A screening test with 99 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity is used in a population where 1 percent has the disease. A person tests positive — what is the chance they actually have it?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: predictive value weighs the test's performance against how rare the disease is; sensitivity and specificity belong to the test, predictive values belong to the patient.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: in 10,000 people, 100 have the disease and 99 of them test positive; of the 9,900 healthy, 5 percent — about 495 — also test positive. PPV = 99/(99 + 495) ≈ 17 percent.

examples.result: roughly five of every six positives are false — which is why screening programs confirm before diagnosing, and why the same positive test in a symptomatic patient (pre-test probability 50 percent) would carry a PPV above 95 percent.

keyTakeaways: Screening programs sequence a sensitive first test with a specific confirmatory one, exploiting exactly the arithmetic above.
Emergency-department triage scores convert history and exam items into tested probability bands.
Hospital handovers and checklists exist to defeat anchoring and attention failure between shifts.
Discharge instructions with explicit safety-netting turn patients into sensors for the evolving diagnosis.
Clinical-decision support embeds pre-test probabilities in the ordering screen itself.

Where next — Pairs with the probability lessons in Mathematics for the underlying updating rule, and with the heuristics lessons in Social Sciences for the biases. Next: how specific tests work — blood counts, ECGs, imaging — and the design of screening programs. Educational, not a license to diagnose.

quiz.q: A test with very high sensitivity and mediocre specificity is most useful for:
options: ruling a disease out when negative
quiz.explanation: High sensitivity means the diseased rarely test negative — a negative result effectively excludes the disease.

quiz.q: In the worked example, the biggest driver of false positives was:
options: the low 1 percent prevalence of disease
quiz.explanation: With rare disease, even excellent specificity leaves many healthy people testing positive — prevalence rules predictive value.

quiz.q: Ranking "unlikely but lethal" causes above "likely but harmless" ones on a differential is the principle of:
quiz.explanation: Must-not-miss diagnoses get tested early because the cost of missing them dwarfs the cost of checking.

quiz.q: The question a clinician should answer before ordering any test is:
options: what will I do with each possible result
is the test covered by insurance
quiz.explanation: A test without a decision attached produces data without value — and incidental findings with consequences.

intro:
The anxiety-and-depression lesson introduced cognitive behavioral therapy's core moves — graded exposure, behavioral activation, testing thoughts against evidence. This Mental Health topic zooms out to the whole landscape: the major schools of psychotherapy, what each assumes about people, and the surprising research on what they share. A hundred brand names reduce to a handful of engines, and knowing them turns "maybe I should talk to someone" into an informed choice about which conversation, with whom, for how long.

**Why this matters.** Roughly a quarter of adults meet criteria for a mental disorder in a given year, and talk therapy stands among medicine's most effective treatments — comparable to medication for many conditions, with lower relapse after it ends. Yet most people could not name two schools of therapy or say what actually happens session to session. Informed clients get better care: they can match method to problem and ask for progress to be measured.
objectives: Explain modern therapy: structured, measured, collaborative
Explain cognitive behavioral therapy deepened
Explain exposure therapy as new learning, not bravery
Explain psychodynamic therapy: patterns from the past
Explain person-centered therapy: the Rogers conditions
Explain third wave: ACT, DBT and mindfulness-based care
Explain common factors: why the alliance predicts outcome

concepts.statement: Forget the couch stereotype. Modern therapy is a structured collaboration: typically fifty-minute weekly sessions, a jointly agreed formulation of the problem, goals with progress tracked on standard scales, and — in most approaches — homework between sessions, because a hour a week cannot outvote the other 167. None of it is advice-giving or passive venting; it is supervised practice at thinking, feeling and behaving differently, and the evidence standards are the same as any other medicine: randomized trials, published outcomes, measured doses.

Cognitive behavioral therapy remains the most widely tested school. Its model is a triangle: thoughts, feelings and behaviors interact, so changing any corner moves the others. The cognitive arm catches automatic thoughts — "I'll fail everything" — and treats them as hypotheses to test against evidence, not facts to obey; the behavioral arm runs experiments: schedule the activity mood insists is pointless, then let the data argue. It is deliberately time-limited, often twelve to twenty sessions, and it teaches a method the client keeps — which is why relapse after CBT runs lower than after medication alone.

concepts.term: Exposure therapy as new learning, not bravery
concepts.statement: Exposure therapy, CBT's most powerful single ingredient for anxiety, deserves its own paragraph because its logic is misunderstood. The modern reading is inhibitory learning: the fear memory is activated, the expected catastrophe fails to arrive, and a competing safety memory is written alongside the fear — so the goal is not white-knuckle bravery but staying long enough for the alarm to quiet and the new learning to consolidate. That is why escape halves the benefit and why therapists now deliberately vary contexts. For obsessive-compulsive disorder the variant is exposure and response prevention: trigger the obsession, refuse the ritual, and let the anxiety decay on its own.

concepts.term: Psychodynamic therapy: patterns from the past
concepts.statement: Psychodynamic therapy — the modern descendant of Freud — targets patterns rather than symptoms: ways of relating, defending and feeling that were learned early and now replay unnoticed, including toward the therapist (transference), where they can be observed live. Where CBT asks "what is the thought," psychodynamic asks "what is the pattern, and where did it start." The stereotype of years of aimless analysis is outdated: short-term formats run to sixteen or thirty sessions, and trials show respectable effects for depression, anxiety and relational difficulties that hold after treatment ends.

Person-centered therapy, built by Carl Rogers in the 1950s, made a radical bet: given the right conditions, people direct their own growth. The therapist's job is to supply those conditions — accurate empathy, unconditional positive regard, and genuineness — and then stay out of the way. As a standalone treatment it has a thinner evidence base than its descendants, but its DNA is everywhere: the non-judgmental stance, the reflective listening, the alliance itself. Half of what every modern therapist does well, Rogers invented.

concepts.term: Third wave: ACT, DBT and mindfulness-based care
concepts.statement: The third wave adapts mindfulness rather than arguing with thoughts. Acceptance and commitment therapy teaches clients to notice thoughts without obeying them — defusion — while committing action to chosen values; dialectical behavior therapy, designed for self-harm and borderline personality disorder, bundles distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness skills, and is the standard of care there; mindfulness-based cognitive therapy roughly halves relapse in people with three or more depressive episodes. The shared move: change the relationship to inner experience, not just its content.

concepts.term: Common factors: why the alliance predicts outcome
concepts.statement: So which therapy wins? Decades of comparative trials produced the famous "Dodo bird verdict" — everybody has won, and all must have prizes — with an asterisk: specific methods do beat generic support for specific problems (exposure for anxiety disorders, response prevention for OCD, DBT for self-harm), and the most robust predictor of outcome across all schools is the therapeutic alliance: the bond plus agreement on goals and tasks. For moderate-to-severe depression, combining therapy with medication outperforms either alone. Choice, then, is a two-step match: method to problem, then person to person.
$$NNT = \frac{1}{ARR} = \frac{1}{C_{control} - C_{treated}}$$
concepts.detail: How many patients must receive a treatment for one extra good outcome; the inverse of the absolute risk reduction between a control and treated group.

concepts.statement: Brand loyalty is the first trap: choosing a therapy by school rather than by problem-method match. The second is expecting insight alone to do the work — understanding why you are anxious changes little without behavioral practice, which is why homework exists. Endless unstructured therapy without goals or review is a third; progress should be measurable. And the gravest: treating self-help as a substitute for care when symptoms are severe — books and apps are supplements, not treatment for an illness that impairs daily life.
The bond plus agreement on goals and tasks; the most robust predictor of therapy outcome.
Treating automatic thoughts as hypotheses and testing them against evidence.
Facing triggers while refusing rituals, letting anxiety decay and new learning consolidate.
Treatment of unconscious relational patterns, including their live appearance toward the therapist.
Rogers' growth-oriented approach built on empathy, regard and genuineness.
A third-wave method of defusing from thoughts and acting on values.
Patients treated per one additional good outcome; the inverse of absolute risk reduction.

examples.title: Worked example — How Psychotherapy Works: The Major Approaches
examples.problem: In a trial, 50 percent of patients receiving CBT for depression respond, versus 28 percent on a waiting list. How effective is that in NNT terms?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: the absolute risk reduction is the difference in response rates, and NNT is its reciprocal.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: ARR = 50 − 28 = 22 percentage points, so NNT = 1/0.22 ≈ 4.5 — call it five patients.

examples.result: for roughly every five patients treated, one additional person recovers who otherwise would not have — comparable to much of general medicine, and better than it first sounds, since the "side effects" are skills the other four keep too.

keyTakeaways: National stepped-care programs deliver guided CBT at scale, with session-by-session outcome measurement now routine.
Digital and blended programs extend evidence-based CBT to people waitlisted, rural, or reluctant to attend in person.
Measurement-based care — brief questionnaires each session — flags stuck cases early enough to adjust.
Schools and workplaces teach third-wave skills outright: mindfulness curricula and stress-inoculation programs.
Trauma services pair exposure-based therapies with phased safety planning for complex presentations.

Where next — Read after the anxiety-and-depression lesson, which covers the conditions this topic treats. Natural next steps: how therapy outcomes are measured, the pharmacology lesson for the medication side of combination treatment, and the stress lesson for the biology both approaches must respect. Educational — therapy choices belong with a qualified professional.

quiz.q: Across therapy schools, the most robust predictor of a good outcome is:
options: the therapist's years of experience alone
the strength of the therapeutic alliance
quiz.explanation: Bond plus agreement on goals and tasks predicts outcomes across CBT, psychodynamic and other approaches.

quiz.q: In the modern reading, exposure therapy works mainly by:
options: writing a competing safety memory alongside the fear
quiz.explanation: Activating the fear while the catastrophe fails to arrive creates inhibitory learning — a new memory, not a deleted one.

quiz.q: A trial shows response rates of 50 percent with therapy versus 30 percent without. The NNT is about:
quiz.explanation: ARR = 20 percentage points, and 1/0.20 = 5 patients per additional responder.

quiz.q: Which therapy is the established standard for self-harm and borderline personality disorder?
quiz.explanation: DBT's skills modules — distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness — were built for exactly these presentations.

intro:
The World Health Organization defines sexual and reproductive health not as the absence of disease but as complete physical, emotional and social well-being in matters of reproduction and sexuality. This Sexual & Reproductive Health topic takes that definition seriously and sticks to the science: how the menstrual cycle actually runs, how each contraceptive method works and fails, what sexually transmitted infections do while nobody is looking, and when fertility deserves medical attention. Clinical, evidence-first, and free of both embarrassment and myth.

**Why this matters.** Contraception is used by most people for decades of their lives; STIs are among the most common infections on earth and frequently silent; and fertility questions dominate the health decisions of a typical adulthood. Yet these topics are learned from folklore more often than from evidence — with predictable consequences in unintended pregnancies, undiagnosed infections, and avoidable infertility.
objectives: Explain the menstrual cycle and its fixed anchor
Explain the fertility window and age-related decline
Explain how each contraception method works
Explain typical versus perfect use effectiveness
Explain sTIs: often silent, mostly treatable
Explain testing windows and screening
Explain hIV today: treatment, prevention and U=U

concepts.term: The menstrual cycle and its fixed anchor
concepts.statement: The menstrual cycle runs 21 to 35 days in adults, orchestrated by the hormone feedback loops the endocrine anatomy lesson introduced. Its counterintuitive feature is which half varies: the follicular phase before ovulation can lengthen or shorten, but the luteal phase after it is close to fixed at fourteen days. Ovulation therefore lands about fourteen days before the next period, not fourteen after the last one — the detail every cycle-tracking misunderstanding flows from. No fertilized egg means the corpus luteum retires, progesterone falls, and the lining sheds: menstruation is the hormone system resetting, not the body "cleansing".

concepts.term: The fertility window and age-related decline
concepts.statement: Fertility is a window, not a switch. An egg survives twelve to twenty-four hours after ovulation; sperm remain viable in the reproductive tract for up to five days. Together they make roughly six fertile days per cycle, ending on ovulation day. For a healthy couple in their mid-twenties the chance of conception per cycle is about one in four — a number that drifts down with age, roughly halving from the twenties to the late thirties, which is why evaluation is suggested after twelve months of trying under 35, and after six months at 35 or older. Smoking, significant over- or underweight, and untreated conditions move the same dial.

Contraception works by three mechanisms, alone or combined: preventing ovulation (hormonal methods), blocking sperm from reaching the egg (barriers and the copper intrauterine device, which also disables sperm chemically), and thinning the uterine lining or thickening cervical mucus so implantation or passage fails. Emergency contraception is not an abortifacient: its main mechanism is delaying ovulation, so it works before fertilization and does nothing to an established pregnancy. Sterilization — blocking or cutting the tubes — is permanent. The method menu is genuinely a menu: effectiveness, side effects and reversibility trade off differently for every user.

Effectiveness comes in two honest versions. Perfect use assumes flawless, consistent use; typical use includes real humans. First-year pregnancy rates tell the story: implant and intrauterine devices under 1 percent either way, the pill about 7 percent in typical use versus near 0.3 in perfect use, condoms about 13 percent typically, withdrawal about 20, and no method about 85. The gap between the columns is a pure measure of adherence — and why long-acting reversible contraception, set once and forgotten, dominates real-world effectiveness rankings.

Sexually transmitted infections share a dangerous talent: silence. Chlamydia, the most reported bacterial infection in many countries, produces no symptoms in most women and about half of men, while quietly inflaming the upper genital tract into pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility — yet it cures with a short antibiotic course (the antibiotics lesson explains why completing it matters). Gonorrhea follows the same pattern and is steadily outgunning drugs, as the antibiotic-resistance lesson documents. Syphilis, resurging after decades of decline, is easily treated early and devastating late. Testing, not symptoms, is the gateway to all three.

The viral infections run on different rules. Human papillomavirus is so common that most sexually active people meet it; most clear it within two years, but persistent high-risk strains cause nearly all cervical cancer and a rising share of throat cancers — which is why the HPV vaccine, covered in the vaccines lesson, is genuinely a cancer vaccine. Herpes is common and manageable with antivirals. HIV has been transformed: antiretroviral therapy restores near-normal life expectancy, and a person on treatment with an undetectable viral load does not transmit the virus — the U=U finding, one of the strongest results in prevention science. Pre-exposure prophylaxis, a daily tablet, prevents over 99 percent of sexual acquisition when taken as prescribed.

concepts.term: HIV today: treatment, prevention and U=U
concepts.statement: Screening ties it together. Guidelines typically recommend annual chlamydia and gonorrhea testing for sexually active people under 25 and risk-based testing after; HIV testing at least once for every adult, and more often with new partners; and cervical screening on the schedule local guidelines set. Modern tests close the window between infection and detection to weeks, and at-home kits have removed most of the remaining excuses. Two clinical footnotes worth knowing: disabling period pain is a treatable condition, not a rite of passage, and new erectile dysfunction can be an early vascular warning — the same endothelium the heart lesson discusses.
$$PI = \frac{\text{pregnancies} \times 12 \times 100}{\text{women} \times \text{months of exposure}}$$
concepts.detail: Pregnancies per 100 women-years of use — the classic measure of contraceptive effectiveness, with lower numbers better.

concepts.statement: Using a cycle app as contraception is the modern classic: ovulation shifts cycle to cycle, and apps predict the past. Assuming "no symptoms" means "no infection" fails silently with chlamydia and HIV alike — testing is the only honest signal. Douching harms the vaginal microbiome the Life Sciences microbiome lesson describes, and does not prevent anything. Emergency contraception neither harms future fertility nor ends a pregnancy. And the STI conversation before a new relationship is a health tool, not an accusation.
Release of an egg, occurring about fourteen days before the next period, not after the last one.
The roughly six days per cycle when intercourse can conceive, ending on ovulation day.
Real-world versus flawless effectiveness of a contraceptive method.
Long-acting reversible contraception — implants and intrauterine devices — set once and effective for years.
A post-intercourse method that works mainly by delaying ovulation before fertilization.
Undetectable equals untransmittable: treated HIV with an undetectable viral load does not transmit sexually.
Pre-exposure prophylaxis: daily medicine preventing over 99 percent of sexual HIV acquisition when taken as prescribed.

examples.title: Worked example — Sexual and Reproductive Health: Cycles, Contraception and STIs
examples.problem: A couple uses the pill with its typical-use failure of 7 percent per year. What is the chance of at least one pregnancy over ten years — and how does the implant compare at 0.1 percent?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: yearly failure compounds across years, so the cumulative probability is one minus the survival probability raised to the number of years.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: for the pill, survival is 0.93 per year, and 0.93 to the tenth power is about 0.48 — so cumulative risk = 1 − 0.48 ≈ 52 percent. For the implant, 0.999 to the tenth is about 0.99, for a cumulative risk near 1 percent.

examples.result: over a decade, typical-use pill users face roughly a coin-flip chance of pregnancy while implant users face one in a hundred — the entire argument for long-acting methods compressed into two numbers.

keyTakeaways: Long-acting contraception access programs have sharply cut unintended pregnancy and abortion rates where deployed.
HPV vaccination is driving cervical cancer toward projected elimination in countries with high coverage.
PrEP rollouts concentrate prevention in the communities carrying the highest HIV incidence.
At-home STI test kits and pharmacy screening normalize testing that clinics historically discouraged.
Comprehensive relationship and sexuality education measurably delays initiation and reduces risk — the evidence runs opposite to common fear.

Where next — Pairs with the endocrine anatomy lesson for the cycle's hormones, the vaccines lesson for HPV, and the antibiotic-resistance lesson for gonorrhea's trajectory. Next: pregnancy and childbirth basics, fertility treatment science, and the public-health design of screening programs. Educational, not medical advice.

quiz.q: In a typical cycle, ovulation occurs:
options: always on day 14 of the cycle
about fourteen days before the NEXT period
exactly at the midpoint between periods
quiz.explanation: The luteal phase is close to fixed at fourteen days, so ovulation is anchored backward — the detail cycle apps routinely get wrong.

quiz.q: The typical-use first-year failure rate of condoms is closest to:
quiz.explanation: About 13 percent with typical use versus about 2 percent with perfect use — the gap is human, not latex.

quiz.q: Emergency contraception primarily works by:
options: killing sperm already in the tract
quiz.explanation: Its main mechanism is postponing the egg's release, so it acts before fertilization — which is why timing matters so much.

quiz.q: U=U means that a person with HIV who maintains an undetectable viral load on treatment:
quiz.explanation: Treatment to undetectable stops sexual transmission — prevention grounded in one of the field's strongest findings.

intro:
Aging is the only condition with total prevalence — and the only one surrounded by an industry worth tens of billions selling its reversal. Geroscience, the discipline behind this Health & Longevity topic, takes a calmer view: aging is the progressive accumulation of molecular damage and the biology is genuinely being mapped, while the interventions that demonstrably lengthen human life remain stubbornly boring. This topic separates the real science — senescent cells, telomeres, mortality curves — from the telomere pills and young-blood clinics, and gives the evidence-based levers their unglamorous due.

**Why this matters.** Life expectancy nearly doubled across the twentieth century — a public-health achievement of clean water, vaccines and safety, not a pharmaceutical one. The unfinished business is the healthspan gap: on average, roughly a decade of extended life is spent in poor health. Aging science asks whether that decade can be compressed, and the honest answers are more useful than any supplement aisle.
objectives: Explain life expectancy, lifespan and healthspan
Explain gompertz law: risk doubling every eight years
Explain why evolution permits aging
Explain hallmarks: senescence, telomeres, mitochondria, inflammation
Explain the levers with real cohort evidence
Explain caloric restriction and the unproven drug pipeline
Explain blue zones and the longevity-hype filter

concepts.statement: Three words get confused constantly. Life expectancy is a population average — it moves with sanitation, medicine and behavior. Lifespan is the ceiling: the oldest verified human, Jeanne Calment, died at 122, and no intervention has moved that ceiling by a day. Healthspan is the years lived in good function, and it is the quantity modern medicine actually wants to extend: a longer life matters little if the extra decade is spent chronically ill. Compression of morbidity — live long, be sick briefly — is the field's explicit goal.

concepts.term: Gompertz law: risk doubling every eight years
concepts.statement: The mathematics of mortality was discovered in 1825, when Benjamin Gompertz noticed that adult death rates rise exponentially: in modern populations, your annual mortality risk roughly doubles every eight years. A quiet exponential explains the shape of every actuarial table and why a 78-year-old and an 86-year-old live in different risk worlds. It also explains longevity outliers statistically rather than mystically: someone at the steep part of the curve who survives a decade has not broken the law, just survived its dice.

Why does the body permit this decline at all? Because natural selection fades with age, as the evolutionary biologists Peter Medawar and George Williams argued: genes that help early reproduction spread even if they cost later, and genes doing maintenance are expensive. Thomas Kirkwood's disposable soma theory framed it as budgeting — an organism allocates energy between reproducing now and repairing forever, and evolution biases the spend toward now. Aging, in this light, is not a programmed countdown but compounding maintenance debt: nothing switches on, things simply stop being fixed.

The maintenance failures themselves have been catalogued as the hallmarks of aging. DNA damage and epigenetic drift accumulate; telomeres — the protective caps whose shortening limits cell division, and whose extension by telomerase tumors hijack (the cancer lesson explains why) — erode; mitochondria run dirtier; proteins misfold and clump; stem cell pools thin. And senescent cells — damaged cells that refuse to die but keep secreting inflammatory signals, earning the nickname zombies — accumulate in tissue, feeding a chronic low-grade inflammation called inflammaging. Multiple intertwined processes, no single switch: the honest headline of modern geroscience.

concepts.term: The levers with real cohort evidence
concepts.statement: What actually moves human survival is documented in giant cohort studies, and the list is unglamorous. Never smoking is worth about ten years of life expectancy compared with continuing; quitting at 40 recovers most of them. Regular physical activity, a Mediterranean-style diet, healthy weight, moderate alcohol at most, adequate sleep, and — the finding that surprises everyone — strong social connection, which large meta-analyses associate with survival odds comparable to quitting smoking. Stacked together, several such habits are associated with over a decade of additional life expectancy at age fifty in cohort after cohort. Association is not proof of a single causal pill, but the consistency across populations is as good as observational evidence gets.

concepts.term: Caloric restriction and the unproven drug pipeline
concepts.statement: Then there is the pipeline. Caloric restriction extends lifespan in nearly every species tested and improves human biomarkers, but no human has been followed long enough to prove added years. Rapamycin reliably extends mouse lifespan; metformin is being trialed explicitly against aging (the TAME trial); senolytic drugs that clear zombie cells are in early human trials. All plausible biology — none yet proven to lengthen human life, which is why none belongs in healthy people's medicine cabinets today. The proper stance is excitement about the science and skepticism about the invoice.

concepts.term: Blue zones and the longevity-hype filter
concepts.statement: The blue zones — Okinawa, Sardinia, Nicoya, Ikaria, Loma Linda — deserve their reputation as lifestyle evidence: natural movement, plant-forward eating, moderate calories, purpose, and dense social ties, all matching the cohort findings. But recent validation work found that some celebrated extreme ages trace partly to record-keeping errors and pension fraud, a reminder that supercentenarian registries are data, not miracles. Take the habits seriously and the geography lightly. Meanwhile, the anti-aging aisle fails the test it most needs to pass: in actual trials, antioxidant supplements did not extend life — beta-carotene even raised lung cancer rates in smokers — while telomere supplements, detoxes and plasma clinics sell biology's vocabulary without its evidence.
$$\mu(t) = \mu_0 \, e^{\alpha t}, \qquad t_{double} = \frac{\ln 2}{\alpha} \approx 8\ \text{years}$$
concepts.detail: Annual mortality risk rises exponentially with age; in modern populations the doubling time for that risk is roughly eight years.

concepts.statement: The most common confusion is lifespan with healthspan — adding years of illness is a Pyrrhic victory, which is why the field aims at compression, not immortality.
