Amber means soon: a steady check-engine light can be anything from a loose fuel cap to a misfire, and a $20 OBD-II reader plugged under the dash will read the code and tell you which. A flashing check engine light is a misfire active enough to destroy the catalytic converter, and it moves you to the red category. The tire-pressure light is amber but deserves same-day attention.

concepts.term: Cost per kilometre: what the car really costs to run
concepts.statement: Split the work honestly. Wiper blades (six to twelve months of life, longer if they streak), washer fluid, cabin and engine air filters, and most bulbs are ten-minute jobs with a video tutorial. Brake work, timing belts, suspension, and anything involving the fuel or safety systems belongs to a professional — not because the fasteners are secret, but because the failure mode of a mistake is severe. Keep every receipt either way: a service history is worth real money at resale.
$$c = \frac{p}{e}$$
concepts.detail: Cost per km equals fuel price p per litre divided by efficiency e in km per litre — the number that makes commuting and road-trip budgets concrete.

concepts.statement: $$C_{yr} = \frac{K}{e} \cdot p + M$$
concepts.detail: Annual cost for K kilometres: fuel plus maintenance M (oil changes, tires amortized, consumables) — the honest line in a household budget.

concepts.statement: Inflating tires to the sidewall number makes them wear in the center and ride harshly — the placard is the answer. Overfilling oil is a real fault: the crankshaft whips it into foam and oil pressure drops, so never guess a whole litre in. Ignoring the tire-pressure light because the car feels fine misses the point — a slow leak is invisible until the sidewall overheats. And never trust a sticker from a shop over the manual: upselling intervals is a business model.
Servicing on a schedule before parts fail, rather than after.
The tire pressure printed on the driver's door jamb — the correct one, unlike the sidewall maximum.
Remaining groove depth; 8 mm new, replace near 3 mm for wet grip, 1.6 mm legal floor.
A metal tab on brake pads that squeals when the friction material is nearly spent.
The standard diagnostic port under the dash; a cheap reader retrieves fault codes.
The shortened maintenance interval for short trips, dust, towing, or heavy city driving.
Fuel price divided by efficiency, plus amortized maintenance — the true price of driving.

examples.title: Worked example — Car Maintenance Basics: Oil, Tires, Brakes and Warning Lights
examples.problem: A driver covering 15,000 km a year in a car averaging 12 km/L, with fuel at 1.70 per litre, wants a realistic running-cost line for fuel and basic maintenance.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: annual fuel spend is distance divided by efficiency times price, and maintenance is estimated from the schedule — two oil changes, tires amortized over their life.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: fuel is 15,000 ÷ 12 = 1,250 litres, costing 1,250 × 1.70 = 2,125 a year. Add two oil changes at 60, and a 640 tire set lasting 60,000 km, which amortizes to 160 a year: roughly 2,345 all-in.

examples.result: about 2,345 per year, or near 0.16 per kilometre before insurance and depreciation — a number that makes a 40-km round trip cost about 6.40 in true wear and fuel, and makes moving closer to work legible as money.

keyTakeaways: Monthly, ten minutes: walk the car, check all lights and wipers, read tire pressures cold against the door placard, pull the oil dipstick, and glance at the coolant tank.
Every oil change interval per the manual: rotate the tires (about every 10,000 km) so they wear evenly, and have the brakes inspected while the wheels are off.
Seasonally: test the battery before winter (batteries live three to five years and cold exposes the weak), top up washer fluid rated for freezing, and re-check pressures after big temperature swings.
When a warning appears: red — stop safely, engine off; amber steady — read the OBD code this week; amber flashing — treat as red.
Keep a folder or app log of every service; hand it to the next buyer and watch their offer rise.

Where next — Natural next step: the used-car buying lesson for the negotiation and inspection side of ownership, and the credit-score lesson if financing is involved. For how engines, transmissions and brakes are engineered, tour the Automobile Engineering subject.

quiz.q: The correct tire pressure for your car is found:
options: On the driver's door jamb placard
Painted inside the fuel door of every car
Whatever the shop sets it to
quiz.explanation: The sidewall shows the tire's maximum, not the car's recommendation — the placard is engineered for the vehicle's weight and handling.

quiz.q: A red warning light (oil pressure, temperature, brake) means:
options: Continue driving but book a service this month
Pull over safely and stop the engine
It can be ignored until the next fuel stop
quiz.explanation: Red lights flag active damage: minutes of driving with no oil pressure or an overheating engine can end in a replacement engine.

quiz.q: A high-pitched squeal from one wheel that stops when you brake lightly is most likely:
options: The wear indicator announcing thin pads
quiz.explanation: The indicator tab rubs the rotor when pads near their limit — you have weeks, not months, to replace them.

quiz.q: Driving 15,000 km a year at 12 km/L with fuel at 1.70 per litre, annual fuel spend is about:
quiz.explanation: 15,000 ÷ 12 = 1,250 litres, and 1,250 × 1.70 = 2,125 — the arithmetic that makes car costs real.

intro:
A used-car sale is a meeting between someone who knows the car and someone who hopes to. Buying well, the practical half of Car & Driving covered in this Everyday Knowledge topic, is about flipping that information gap: verifying history before emotion, inspecting before negotiating, and pricing the next three years of the car rather than the sticker. Do those in order and the used market stops being a casino and becomes a bargain bin — because depreciation is a force working in your favor.

**Why this matters.** A new car can lose 15 to 20 percent of its value the day it leaves the dealer and roughly 40 to 50 percent by year four — while modern vehicles routinely outlast 200,000 km. Buying at three to five years old means someone else paid the steep part of the curve for a machine with most of its life left. The entire skill is verification.
objectives: Explain depreciation: let the first owner pay the curve
Explain total cost of ownership, not sticker price
Explain paperwork first: title, VIN history, liens
Explain the cold-start inspection and the test drive
Explain the pre-purchase inspection is non-negotiable
Explain negotiate the total, never the monthly payment
Explain hidden costs: insurance, transfer, tires, first service

concepts.term: Depreciation: let the first owner pay the curve
concepts.statement: Start with model research, not listings. Reliability varies enormously between models, and owner-survey data surfaces the lemons years before any single seller will. Pick two or three candidate models with a known record, learn their common failure points and their service schedule, and only then start shopping — a buyer who asks about the timing-belt interval reads as a buyer who cannot be fed a story.

concepts.term: Total cost of ownership, not sticker price
concepts.statement: Budget honestly using total cost of ownership, not price. Insurance, registration, fuel at the car's real consumption, tires, and a repair reserve all ride on top of the purchase. A rough guardrail keeps the full transport line — payment plus insurance plus fuel — under about 15 to 20 percent of take-home pay. The Personal Finance lessons in this domain cover the budgeting machinery; the car lesson is simply that the sticker is the entry fee, not the cost.

concepts.term: Paperwork first: title, VIN history, liens
concepts.statement: Paper before feelings. Get the VIN (stamped on the dashboard corner and the door jamb) and buy a vehicle-history report: it lists accidents, title brands, service records, and — critically — whether a bank still holds a lien. The seller must have the title in their own name; a car being sold for a friend, or a title that arrives later, is a walk-away no matter how good the story. A salvage or rebuilt title means an insurer once declared the car economically dead — occasionally fine, never a beginner purchase.

concepts.term: The cold-start inspection and the test drive
concepts.statement: The inspection rewards patience. Arrive to a cold engine and watch the start: blue exhaust is burning oil, persistent white smoke is coolant intruding — often a head-gasket death sentence — and brief white vapor on a cold morning is normal. Then walk the body: paint overspray on rubber trim, uneven panel gaps, or misaligned hood and doors tell of crash repairs; mismatched bolts say something was replaced. Check the tire wear is even across each tire (feathered edges hint at alignment or suspension trouble), look under the mats and the car for rust, and switch on every single electrical thing.

Drive it for at least thirty minutes, highway included. The test is not how it feels on the straight — every car feels fine there. Brake firmly from speed with hands light on the wheel: pulling means caliper or alignment trouble; a pulsing pedal means warped rotors. Listen over bumps for knocks, and note whether the steering wheel sits centered going straight. At the end, turn the engine off, restart it hot, and glance back under the car for fresh drips.

concepts.term: Negotiate the total, never the monthly payment
concepts.statement: The pre-purchase inspection — one to two hundred at an independent mechanic of your choosing — is the cheapest insurance in the whole transaction, and the seller's reaction to the request is itself data. A private seller or dealer who resists a PPI is telling you what the inspection would have found. Ask the shop to scan the OBD codes and put their findings in writing; on a negotiation, that paper is worth its weight in discount.

concepts.term: Hidden costs: insurance, transfer, tires, first service
concepts.statement: Negotiate the total price, never the monthly payment — monthly numbers are where interest and fees hide. Anchor 10 to 20 percent under asking with reasons attached: worn tires at the limit are an 800-line item, the major service is due, the history has a gap. Present the number, then stop talking; silence does more work than persuasion. Have a maximum written down before you arrive, and mean it: the deal you walk away from is tuition, not a loss. Also get an insurance quote on the exact VIN before committing — the premium difference between two similar cars can be surprising.
$$TCO = P + R + I + F - S$$
concepts.detail: Purchase price P, plus repairs R, insurance I and fuel F over the holding period, minus eventual resale S — the number the sticker hides.

concepts.statement: Falling in love before inspecting hands all negotiating power to the seller — decide you are buying a model, not a car, until the PPI clears. Buying at night or in the rain hides paint mismatches, dents and leaks. The monthly-payment question is a trap in any negotiation, and a long loan on an aging car builds negative equity. And an odometer reading far below the wear on the pedals, wheel and driver's seat is the classic rollback signature — walk.
The fall in market value over time — steepest in the first three years, a gift to used buyers.
A VIN-keyed record of accidents, title brands, liens and service; the first thing to buy.
A brand marking a car an insurer wrote off; cheap for experts, hazardous for beginners.
An independent mechanic's assessment of a specific car before you commit — the best money in the deal.
Comparable listings for the same model, trim, year and distance; the factual basis of your offer.
Purchase plus running costs minus resale, over the time you hold the car.
Owing more on a loan than the car is worth — the standard result of long loans on fast-depreciating vehicles.

examples.title: Worked example — How to Buy a Used Car Without Getting Burned
examples.problem: Two identical-model listings — car A at 9,000 with full service records and new tires, car B at 7,500 with tires at 3 mm and no records. Which is cheaper over three years?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: compare total cost of ownership over the holding period, including the work each car needs immediately and a risk premium for unknowns.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: car B needs 800 of tires now and a 600 major service, bringing it to 8,900 — nearly car A's price — before adding a repair reserve for the unknown history, which any prudent buyer sets at several hundred per year. Car A also carries records that support resale.

examples.result: the 1,500 discount shrinks to 100 of hard costs plus an unknown-risk premium, so car A wins. The general law: cheap examples of a model converge upward in cost; good ones do not.

keyTakeaways: Shortlist reliable models, learn their weak points and service intervals, and set a written maximum before viewing anything.
Verify paperwork: title in the seller's name, no liens, history report clean, odometer consistent with pedal and seat wear.
Inspect cold: exhaust colors, panel gaps, even tire wear, rust, every switch and button — then a thirty-minute drive with a firm brake test.
Book the pre-purchase inspection at your own mechanic and read the codes; treat refusal as an answer.
Negotiate total price with comps printed out, anchor low with reasons, then let silence work; confirm insurance on the VIN before signing.
Budget the first month: transfer and registration fees, an immediate fluid-and-filter service, and any tires the inspection flagged.

Where next — Follow with the car-maintenance lesson to protect the purchase, and the credit-score topic before financing anything. The Personal Finance branch of this domain covers budgeting; Behavioral Economics in the Library explains why the walk-away is psychologically hard — and why writing your maximum down works.

quiz.q: The steepest part of a car's depreciation happens:
options: In the first one to three years
quiz.explanation: A new car can drop 15-20 percent immediately and around half by year four — which is why three-to-five-year-old used cars are the value zone.

quiz.q: Persistent white smoke from a warm engine most often signals:
quiz.explanation: Sweet-smelling persistent white smoke is the classic head-gasket symptom — one of the few instant walk-aways on an inspection.

quiz.q: A private seller refuses a pre-purchase inspection at your mechanic. You should:
options: Accept — the car is probably fine
Treat the refusal itself as the finding and walk
Only proceed with a bigger discount
quiz.explanation: The refusal tells you what the inspection would have found; the small discount is not worth the unknown.

quiz.q: In any car-price negotiation you should focus on:
options: The total price of the car
quiz.explanation: Monthly numbers hide interest, fees and term length; negotiate one transparent total, then arrange financing separately.

intro:
Most household repairs are five screw-turns and some confidence, separated from disaster only by owning the right ten tools and knowing which wall you are drilling into. Home repair, the branch of Home & Repair behind this Everyday Knowledge topic, starts with a modest toolkit and three habits: measure twice, match the fastener to the load, and know which jobs belong to a professional. This is the lesson that turns a wobbling shelf or a squeaking door from a landlord's problem into a Saturday morning.

**Why this matters.** A basic toolkit costs about as much as one service-call visit and pays for itself the first time it is used. Every renter eventually hangs something heavy; every homeowner inherits a slow avalanche of small fixes. The people who handle them calmly are not handier by nature — they own a stud finder and a level, and they check before they drill.
objectives: Explain ten hand tools cover most household jobs
Explain the cordless drill: one tool, half the tasks
Explain drywall is weak; studs and anchors carry the load
Explain anchor types matched to weight and wall
Explain measure twice: the V-mark, the level, the story stick
Explain loose hinges, squeaks and nail holes in minutes
Explain knowing the limit: electricity, gas, heights, structure

concepts.term: Ten hand tools cover most household jobs
concepts.statement: The core hand tools: a 5-metre tape measure, a claw hammer, a set of slotted and Phillips screwdrivers (or one handle with interchangeable bits), an adjustable wrench, slip-joint pliers, needle-nose pliers, a utility knife with spare blades, a torpedo level, a magnetic stud finder, and a headlamp. Add duct tape and painter's tape, superglue, wood glue, a tube of spackle, an assortment of screws and wall anchors, and sandpaper from 120 to 220 grit. Mid-range brands from any hardware store last decades; buy the drill used before buying anything cheap twice.

concepts.term: The cordless drill: one tool, half the tasks
concepts.statement: The single most transformative purchase is a cordless drill-driver. It drives screws, bores pilot holes, stirs paint, and with the right bit drills into wood, metal and masonry. A 12-volt model handles apartment life; an 18-to-20-volt one earns its keep for fences, decks and concrete. Learn the clutch: low numbered settings for small screws in soft material, higher for wood, and the drill setting only for making holes. Pilot holes slightly smaller than the screw's shaft stop wood from splitting and keep screws from wandering — and pressing firmly along the screw's axis stops the bit from camming out and stripping the head.

concepts.term: Drywall is weak; studs and anchors carry the load
concepts.statement: Walls decide everything. Drywall (plasterboard) is soft gypsum that a fingernail can dent: fine for a picture nail, hopeless for a shelf. The wooden studs behind it — spaced every 40 to 60 cm (16 to 24 inches) — are the real structure, and a screw driven into a stud can carry tens of kilograms alone. Find them by knocking (a stud sounds dull and solid, the hollow wall rings), with a magnetic finder that snaps to the screws of previous drywall work, or with an electronic finder. Windows and doors are framed with doubled studs called kings and jacks; there is almost always solid wood within a hand's width of an opening.

concepts.term: Anchor types matched to weight and wall
concepts.statement: Between studs, anchors bridge the gap. Lightweight plastic expansion anchors hold a few kilograms in drywall and are what most picture-hanging kits include. Self-drilling threaded anchors bite into the wall like a screw and carry more. For serious weight — a wall-mounted TV, a full bookshelf bracket — toggle bolts fold flat to pass through the hole, then spring open inside the wall, clamping the drywall between wings and screw head. Choose an anchor rated at least three to four times the actual load, and in masonry or brick use proper plastic plugs with a hammer drill. Ceilings follow different physics: a heavy light or a fan must hang from the box or joist, never from drywall anchors.

concepts.term: Measure twice: the V-mark, the level, the story stick
concepts.statement: Measuring is a discipline, not a formality. Mark with a V instead of a dot so the point of the V is exactly where the line crosses; measure with the tape hook hooked on the edge, and burn an extra ten centimetres when measuring inside corners because the tape case lies. Check level on everything — a shelf 2 mm out reads crooked across a wall, and errors compound when pieces stack. For repeated measurements, transfer the dimension to a story stick (any offcut of wood marked once) so every instance shares the same error instead of inventing new ones.

concepts.term: Loose hinges, squeaks and nail holes in minutes
concepts.statement: A dozen common repairs unlock immediately: tightening the screws on loose door hinges and cabinet pulls (the secret is removing one screw, packing the hole with a matchstick and glue, and reinserting), silencing squeaky hinges with a drop of oil or a rub of wax, patching nail holes with spackle and a swipe of sanding, re-securing a wobbling chair by gluing and clamping the loose joint, unsticking a sticky window by waxing its tracks, and replacing the washer in a dripping tap — the plumbing lesson in this branch covers that one in full.

concepts.term: Knowing the limit: electricity, gas, heights, structure
concepts.statement: Respect four limits. Electricity: work on outlets or switches only with the breaker off and verified — and call an electrician for anything beyond swapping like-for-like. Gas lines: never a DIY job in any form. Heights: a ladder tied off, three points of contact, and no overreaching — roof work is a professional's game. Structure: anything touching load-bearing framing, main plumbing, or the service panel is a licensed trade's territory. Before drilling any wall, run the stud finder's AC-detection mode and remember where pipes and wires normally run: up from outlets, down to radiators, horizontally through stud bays at switch and outlet height.

The classic errors are all variations of skipping preparation: drilling blind into a wall and finding a pipe, trusting a plastic anchor with a television, or hanging a heavy mirror from picture wire that frays. Stripped screws come from wrong-size bits and no downward pressure, not bad luck. Duct tape is a temporary patch, never a repair. And the biggest own-goal in home repair is improvising on anything electrical, gas, or structural because it looked simple in a video — the limits in this lesson are cheap to respect.
The vertical wooden framing member behind drywall, spaced 40-60 cm apart; the load-bearer of any wall.
A fitting that grips soft drywall so screws can carry load between studs.
An anchor whose wings spring open inside the wall, clamping the drywall for heavy loads.
A small guide hole that prevents splitting and keeps screws on target.
The drill's torque limiter; set low for delicate screws, high for wood, off for drilling.
Soft filler paste for small holes, sanded flush and painted over.
A marked offcut used to repeat one measurement exactly, avoiding compounding error.

examples.title: Worked example — The Home Toolkit: Screws, Anchors and Your First Real Repairs
examples.problem: Mount a 15-kilogram floating shelf of 120 cm on a plasterboard wall with studs hidden behind, so it safely holds books rather than decorations.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: screws into studs carry the load alone; anchors between studs must be toggle-type and multiply-rated, and the bracket must sit level before anything is committed.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: find the studs with the finder and mark them; the shelf's 120 cm will span roughly two studs 40-60 cm apart — align the bracket so two screws land in studs, each with a pilot hole. Where a bracket hole falls between studs, drill and fit a toggle bolt rated 30 kg. Set the level on the bracket, adjust, then drive everything home snug without crushing the drywall.

examples.result: two stud screws carry the shelf and most of the books directly into framing, the toggle handles the off-center load, and the level guarantees it reads straight from across the room — a mount that holds for decades rather than a dramatic 2 a.m. wall failure.

keyTakeaways: Assemble the core kit first and add specialty tools per project — never buy a 200-piece set to hang one shelf.
Before drilling: identify the wall (knock test), find the studs, scan for wires and pipes, and know what is on the other side.
Match fastener to load: picture nail for a poster, plastic anchor for a mirror, threaded anchor for a small shelf, toggle bolt or stud for anything with books on it.
Pilot hole, drive with pressure, stop at snug — then stop again; overtightening strips heads and cracks anchors.
Fix small things the week they appear: a loose screw today is a stripped hinge and a replaced door in a year.

Where next — This is the entry point of the Around the House branch: continue with the plumbing, electrical-safety and painting lessons in Home & Repair. For how the building itself is put together — foundations to roof — the Construction & the Built Environment subject in the Library covers the engineering view.

quiz.q: You want to hang a 20 kg cabinet on a drywall wall. The best plan is:
options: Long screws straight into the drywall
Screws into studs, with toggle bolts where brackets miss them
Adhesive strips rated for outdoor use
quiz.explanation: Drywall itself carries almost nothing; the studs or proper toggles carry everything, and heavy cabinets should land mostly on studs.

quiz.q: A screw head keeps stripping as you drive it. The usual cause is:
options: Wrong-size bit and too little forward pressure
The pilot hole being too small
quiz.explanation: Cam-out happens when the bit rides out of the head — fix it with the correct bit seated fully and firm axial pressure, or reverse a half-turn and retry.

quiz.q: Before drilling into any wall you should:
options: Find studs and scan for wiring and pipes
Turn off the whole house's electricity
Drill a 10 mm test hole first
quiz.explanation: A stud finder with AC-detection plus knowing that pipes and cables run up from outlets avoids the two expensive surprises inside walls.

quiz.q: Which job is firmly in the call-a-professional category?
options: Work on the main electrical panel
quiz.explanation: The service panel is the point where DIY electrical work becomes genuinely dangerous; the other three are core home-toolkit tasks.

intro:
Plumbing looks intimidating because it hides inside walls, but a home water system is two simple ideas: clean water pushed in under pressure, and dirty water falling out by gravity. Home plumbing, the branch of Home & Repair behind this Everyday Knowledge topic, covers the handful of failures that account for most service calls — the dripping tap, the running toilet, the slow drain — and the one piece of knowledge every occupant should have on day one: where the main shutoff valve is. Respect the two rules of water (it flows downhill, and it will find the hole you missed) and most of this subject de-mystifies.

**Why this matters.** A faucet dripping once per second wastes on the order of 11,000 litres a year — enough to fill hundreds of bathtubs, all quietly added to a metered bill. A running toilet can waste several times that. Meanwhile knowing the main shutoff turns a burst-pipe emergency from a flooded house into a contained ten-minute incident. This is the highest-leverage hour of home knowledge there is.
objectives: Explain supply under pressure, drains by gravity
Explain the main shutoff: know it before you need it
Explain dripping tap: washer or cartridge
Explain running toilet: flapper, chain, fill valve
Explain unclogging in order: plunger, then auger, then chemistry
Explain what never goes down a drain
Explain when to call a licensed plumber

concepts.term: Supply under pressure, drains by gravity
concepts.statement: Find the shutoffs before anything breaks. The main valve sits where the water line enters the house — basement, crawlspace, utility closet or near the meter — and everyone in the home should know where it is and how to turn it (a quarter turn on a lever, several on a round handle). Under every sink and behind every toilet there is a smaller isolation valve for that fixture alone. Tag them, test them annually so they do not seize, and if a pipe bursts: main valve closed first, taps opened second to drain what is left.

concepts.term: The main shutoff: know it before you need it
concepts.statement: Diagnose by system. Supply-side problems leak under pressure — a dripping tap, a hissing fill valve, a wet patch that grows — and they stop when you close the fixture's isolation valve. Drain-side problems are slow, gurgling, or backing up, and they are immune to valve position. Pressure problems announce themselves with banging pipes (water hammer, fixable with a hammer arrestor or recharging air chambers) or a trickle shower (often a clogged showerhead — soak it in vinegar overnight).

A dripping tap is a worn seal. Older compression faucets use a rubber washer at the end of the stem, and the fix is closing the valve, unscrewing the handle and stem, and swapping a washer that costs pocket change. Modern cartridge, ball and ceramic-disc faucets replace as a unit — take a photo, close the valve, pull the old cartridge, and take it to the hardware store to match, because 'universal' is a rumor in plumbing. While it is open, check the O-rings and the seat (the brass ring the washer presses against) for pitting that would eat a new washer.

concepts.term: Running toilet: flapper, chain, fill valve
concepts.statement: A running toilet is almost always the flapper — the rubber seal at the bottom of the tank that lifts when you flush. The ten-second diagnosis: drop a few drops of food coloring into the tank, wait fifteen minutes without flushing, and if color appears in the bowl the flapper is leaking. Chain tension is the other usual suspect: too tight and the flapper cannot seal; too loose or tangled and it cannot rise properly. A fill valve that runs constantly or the water level set above the overflow tube produce the same symptom; the water level should sit about a centimeter below the overflow pipe, set by bending the float arm or adjusting the float clip.

concepts.term: Unclogging in order: plunger, then auger, then chemistry
concepts.statement: Unclog in order of gentleness. First, the plunger — a flanged one for toilets, a cup one for sinks, with enough water in the bowl to cover the cup and a wet rag blocking the overflow so pressure goes down the pipe, not sideways. Second, pull the problem: remove the P-trap (the U under the sink — put a bucket under it) because hair and grease usually live right there; for tubs, a cheap plastic drain snake hooks the hair clog. Third, a closet auger for deep toilet blockages. Chemical drain cleaners are the last resort, not the first — caustic soda formulations generate heat, can damage older pipes, and seriously burn skin; enzymatic cleaners are slower but safe for recurring organic clogs.

concepts.term: What never goes down a drain
concepts.statement: Prevention is mostly about what never goes down. Grease and oil congeal in pipes and bind sediment into wall-thickening sludge — wipe pans with paper first. Coffee grounds, eggshells, pasta and rice (they swell), flour dough, and 'flushable' wipes (they are not) are the recurring drain-killers; hair catchers in showers pay for themselves weekly. In cold climates, know which pipes run through exterior walls: a trickle of water on the coldest night and opened cabinet doors prevent the burst that follows a freeze.

concepts.term: When to call a licensed plumber
concepts.statement: Call a licensed plumber for anything involving the main line, gas water heaters, sewer blockages beyond the fixture (all drains slow at once means the main), hidden leaks you cannot locate, re-piping, and permits-required work. The plumbing code exists for sanitation, and the boundary between DIY and licensed work is a health boundary, not a skill flex. For everything else: close the valve, take a photo before each disassembly, and lay parts out in order on a towel so reassembly is the steps in reverse.
$$V = r \times v_{drip} \times T$$
concepts.detail: Volume wasted equals drip rate r times volume per drip (about 0.25 mL) times time — one drip per second is roughly 11,000 litres in a year.

concepts.statement: Overtightening is the amateur signature: compression fittings and plastic trap threads need snug plus a fraction of a turn, and gorilla force cracks them into instant leaks. Mixing drain chemicals (an acidic cleaner after a caustic one) can generate enough heat and gas to damage pipes and lungs. Closing a stuck isolation valve with full force seizes it permanently — work it gently open-closed instead. And 'flushable' wipes have clogged more sewers than everything else combined; the bin is their home.
The valve that stops all water entering the house; the first thing to know, the first thing to close in a burst.
The small valve serving a single fixture, so one sink can be repaired without drowning the house.
The rubber seal at a toilet tank's bottom; the usual culprit in a running toilet.
The U-shaped pipe under a fixture that holds a water plug against sewer gas — and catches most clogs.
The tower mechanism that refills the tank; its float sets the water level.
A stiff, crank-fed snake designed to reach deep toilet blockages without scratching the bowl.
Banging pipes caused by fast-closing valves stopping moving water abruptly.

examples.title: Worked example — Home Plumbing: Faucets, Toilets and Drains
examples.problem: A toilet that runs intermittently, plus a utility charging about 2 per 1,000 litres for water and sewer together — what is it costing, and what is the fix?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: a leaking flapper silently transfers tank water to the bowl, the fill valve tops the tank up, and every topped-up litre is billed twice — once in, once out as sewer.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: food coloring in the tank confirms the flapper. If the leak is a modest 200 litres a day, that is 73,000 litres a year × 0.002 per litre ≈ 146 of water plus sewer — often 250 to 300 all-in. A replacement flapper costs a few dollars and ten minutes: valve off, flush to empty, unhook the chain, seat the new flapper, adjust the chain to a slight slack, valve on.

examples.result: a repair with a payback measured in weeks, a quieter bathroom, and the diagnostic habit — dye test first, parts-matching second — that generalizes to every fixture in the house.

keyTakeaways: Day one in any home: locate the main shutoff and each fixture's isolation valve; test them so they turn when it matters.
Dripping tap: close the isolation valve, photograph the disassembly at every step, replace washer or matching cartridge, reassemble in reverse.
Running toilet: dye-test for the flapper, check chain slack, set the water level a centimeter below the overflow tube.
Slow drain: plunge with the overflow blocked, then pull and clean the P-trap, then auger — chemicals only as a last resort, never after other cleaners.
Weekly habits: hair catchers in showers, grease into a can and the bin, not the sink.

Where next — Pair this with the home-toolkit lesson for the tools and the electrical-safety lesson for the other hidden household system. The construction subject explains how the whole network of pipes is designed; the environment-domain lessons on water scarcity explain why the 11,000-litre drip matters beyond the bill.

quiz.q: A pipe bursts in the wall. Your first move is:
quiz.explanation: Stop the supply first; opening taps comes second, to drain what remains in the pipes after the pressure is gone.

quiz.q: A toilet runs intermittently. The first diagnostic step is:
options: Dye-test the tank for a leaking flapper
quiz.explanation: Food coloring in the tank appearing in the bowl without a flush proves the flapper is leaking — the fix in the vast majority of cases.

quiz.q: The correct first tool for a blocked sink is:
options: A plunger with the overflow blocked
A garden hose down the vent
quiz.explanation: Mechanical first: pressure from a plunger (or removing the P-trap) resolves most clogs without heat, fumes or pipe damage.

quiz.q: Why should kitchen grease never go down the drain?
options: It congeals in pipes and binds debris into growing blockages
quiz.explanation: Liquid grease solidifies as it cools, coating pipes and catching food particles until the drain chokes — the classic slow-sink story.

intro:
Household electricity is the most dangerous thing most people treat casually, because it usually works and therefore feels safe. This Everyday Knowledge topic in Home & Repair covers the purely practical side — the breaker panel, the outlets in wet rooms, the extension cords under rugs, and the habits that keep a household safe — not circuit theory, which the Library's Electric Circuits subject covers in full. The practical rules are few, old, and written in investigations of house fires.

**Why this matters.** Electrical failures ignite a large share of home fires, and the common culprits are unglamorous: overloaded power strips, cords under carpets, and DIY wiring done confidently and wrongly. Meanwhile a GFCI outlet that trips is not broken — it just did its job of saving a life. Understanding ten mechanisms converts invisible risk into a short checklist.
objectives: Explain the breaker panel: map it and label it
Explain why breakers trip — and why one reset is the limit
Explain gFCI protection where water lives
Explain circuit capacity: add watts, keep headroom
Explain cords, strips and daisy-chains
Explain water, ladders and overhead lines
Explain the bright line: panel work is professional work

concepts.term: The breaker panel: map it and label it
concepts.statement: The breaker panel is the map of the house's electrical system. Each switch controls one circuit — a loop feeding a zone of outlets and fixtures — and typical household circuits are rated 15 or 20 amperes. Spend twenty minutes once: flip each breaker, note what dies, and write it on the panel door in pencil. When a circuit trips at midnight, the difference between a labeled and an unlabeled panel is the difference between a ten-second reset and a flashlight safari. The main breaker at the top kills everything at once.

concepts.term: Why breakers trip — and why one reset is the limit
concepts.statement: A breaker trips because the current exceeded the wire's rating and an overload or a short circuit was building heat. The correct response: unplug what you just added, reset the breaker fully (off, then on), and replug one thing at a time. One trip is an event; repeated trips are a diagnosis. If a circuit trips the moment something specific is plugged in, that device or cord is the fault — stop using it. If a breaker trips instantly with nothing plugged in, or a breaker feels hot, or you smell burning plastic near the panel, that is an electrician today, not this weekend.

GFCI — ground-fault circuit interrupter — is the outlet with TEST and RESET buttons, and it monitors the current going out versus coming back. If as little as 5 milliamperes goes missing (the missing current is leaking through a person or a wet path), it disconnects in a fraction of a second, faster than a heartbeat can be disturbed. Building codes require GFCI protection wherever water and electricity coexist: bathrooms, kitchens near sinks, garages, basements, outdoors. Monthly, press TEST — the outlet should die — then RESET. If it will not test or reset, replace it; they wear out over decades.

concepts.term: Circuit capacity: add watts, keep headroom
concepts.statement: Capacity is arithmetic, not theory. On a 120-volt circuit, a 15-amp breaker carries about 1,800 watts and a 20-amp about 2,400; the safe continuous practice is to stay near 80 percent of that. Space heaters are the classic overload: a single 1,500-watt heater eats most of a 15-amp circuit, and adding a kettle or hair dryer on the same loop finishes it. Any appliance that makes heat draws serious power — heaters, irons, dryers, toasters — and each wants a circuit mostly to itself. If breakers trip whenever the toaster and coffee maker run together, that is the wiring telling you they share a loop, not a defect to workaround.

Cords and strips are where households cheat. Extension cords are temporary tools, not permanent wiring, and they are rated — check the tag — for the load they may carry. Never run them under rugs or through doorways where traffic grinds the insulation; never staple or nail them to walls; never daisy-chain power strips into each other. A power strip is a splitter, not a power source: plugging two heaters into one strip on one outlet still asks the wall's single circuit and the strip's thin wiring for everything. Warm plugs, warm cords, or scorch marks around an outlet are immediate retirement signals. Surge protectors (different job — they clamp voltage spikes) have a joule rating and a finite life; a protector that has absorbed a serious lightning strike has quietly spent itself.

Water and height have their own rules. Never touch electrical anything with wet hands or standing on a wet floor; keep appliances away from sinks and tubs by real distance, not by careful balancing; a hair dryer near a full bath is a cliché of preventable tragedy. Outdoors, treat every overhead line as live forever: keep ladders, poles, kites and tree-trimming equipment at least several metres clear, and never stand a ladder where a fall would land it on the lines. Aluminum ladders are excellent conductors; fiberglass is the electrician's choice for a reason.

concepts.term: The bright line: panel work is professional work
concepts.statement: The bright line: anything inside the panel, anything new-run wiring, and anything permanently installed belongs to a licensed electrician. Swapping a like-for-like outlet or switch with the breaker off and verified is the reasonable DIY ceiling — and in many jurisdictions even that requires a permit. Flickering lights across a room, outlets that only work intermittently, two-prong ungrounded outlets in an old house, aluminum branch wiring in 1960s-70s homes — these are inspection items, not projects. Electricity gives no second chances, and the fatal mistake looks exactly like the safe one until the moment it does not.
$$P = V \times I$$
concepts.detail: Watts carried equal volts times amps: a 120 V, 15 A circuit tops out near 1,800 W — and should cruise below about 80 percent of that.

concepts.statement: Taping a tripping breaker 'on' is the single most dangerous act in a house — the breaker is the only automatic protection the wiring has. The second is the power strip feeding a space heater: strips are splitters, not sources, and heater-plus-strip is a fire drill. Resetting a breaker repeatedly without asking why converts a warning into a schedule. And water-plus-electricity improvisation — radios by the tub, charging phones on beds under pillows — packs real risk into innocent-looking scenes.
The automatic switch that interrupts a circuit when current exceeds its rating; the wiring's heat protection.
An outlet that compares outgoing and returning current and trips within milliseconds when about 5 mA leaks astray.
Volts times amps — the wattage a circuit can carry, with 80 percent as the continuous-practice ceiling.
Plugging power strips into power strips; a classic overload and fire mechanism.
A device that clamps voltage spikes; rated in joules and silently consumed by big strikes.
The large switch that disconnects the whole panel at once.
Electricity jumping a gap in damaged wiring — a fire cause that AFCI breakers are designed to catch.

examples.title: Worked example — Home Electrical Safety: Breakers, Outlets and Cords
examples.problem: Every time a 1,500 W space heater runs in the bedroom, the circuit breaker trips when the desktop computer and monitor also start. Why, and what is the fix?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: everything on one circuit shares its capacity, and a 15 A circuit at 120 V carries about 1,800 W — with 80 percent, about 1,440 W, as the sensible continuous ceiling.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: heater 1,500 W plus computer 200 W plus monitor 40 W is 1,740 W on a circuit whose safe ceiling is about 1,440 W — the breaker is doing precisely its job. Move the heater to an outlet on a different circuit (check the panel map), or run the heater without the office load.

examples.result: the trips stop without any repair, because the problem was never the wiring — it was an arithmetic violation. This is the general habit: when a breaker trips, add up the watts on the loop before touching anything.

keyTakeaways: Map and label the panel once: one person flipping, one person noting what dies; pencil the results on the door.
Test every GFCI monthly: TEST kills it, RESET restores it; replace any that will not play along.
When a breaker trips: unplug recent additions, reset fully, replug one item at a time to find the offender.
Audit cords seasonally: no cords under rugs, no strips chained into strips, no warm plugs — and replace, not tape, damaged insulation.
Give heat-making appliances their own circuit: one heater per outlet loop, and never alongside the kettle.
Before drilling any wall, run the stud finder's live-wire mode; remember that wires rise from outlets and switches.

Where next — For what current, voltage and resistance actually are, start the Electric Circuits subject in the Library — the theory makes every rule here feel inevitable rather than arbitrary. Then finish the Around the House branch with the painting lesson, and read the emergency-preparedness topic for the utilities-shutoff drill that includes the panel's main breaker.

quiz.q: A breaker trips. After one reset it trips again with the same devices plugged in. You should:
options: Reset it again and again until it holds
Tape it in the on position
Unplug the load and investigate — repeated trips are a diagnosis
quiz.explanation: Repeated trips mean a real overload or fault; forcing the breaker on removes the only protection the wiring has.

quiz.q: GFCI outlets exist primarily to:
options: Save people from ground-fault shocks, especially near water
quiz.explanation: They trip on tiny current leaks — the signature of electricity exiting through a body — which is why codes demand them in wet locations.

quiz.q: A 1,500 W heater and a 700 W microwave on one 120 V, 15 A circuit:
options: Slightly exceed the circuit's 1,800 W rating and its safe 80 percent ceiling
Are safe if plugged into different outlets on the same circuit
Only trip the breaker in summer
quiz.explanation: 2,200 W exceeds even the raw 1,800 W rating, and moving to another outlet on the same loop changes nothing — circuits, not outlets, are the unit.

quiz.q: Which of these is safely DIY?
options: Adding a new circuit to the panel
Replacing a like-for-like outlet with the breaker off and verified
quiz.explanation: Panel and new-wiring work is licensed-electrician territory everywhere; a verified-off, like-for-like swap is the reasonable ceiling.

intro:
Nothing transforms a room for less money than paint, and nothing exposes the gap between amateur and professional faster. Painting, the branch of Home & Repair behind this Everyday Knowledge topic, is less about the brush than about the boring two-thirds that happen first: moving furniture, patching, sanding, cleaning, taping. Professionals are not faster painters — they are faster preparers, and their finish looks flat because the wall under it was made flat. This lesson is the full sequence, from bare patch to clean cut line.

**Why this matters.** A painted room is a weekend's work at a tenth of a renovation's cost — but every skip shows forever under side light: ridges of dust in the finish, lap marks where a roller dried mid-wall, and jagged ceiling lines no amount of squinting forgives. The craft is learnable in one honest weekend, and it transfers directly to trim, cabinets and furniture.
objectives: Explain prep is most of the job
Explain patch, sand and clean before anything opens
Explain primer: when it is optional and when it is law
Explain cutting in before rolling
Explain the W pattern and a loaded roller
Explain paint order: ceiling, walls, trim
Explain common mistakes: overworking, dust, cheap nap

concepts.term: Prep is most of the job
concepts.statement: Prepare the room like a hospital, not a crime scene. Furniture to the center under sheets, floor covered with rosin paper or drop cloths (canvas grips and does not slide; plastic does not absorb), switch plates and outlet covers off, hardware removed or taped. Then repair: fill nail holes and small cracks with spackle using a flexible putty knife, let it dry, sand flush with 120-to-220-grit paper, and shine a raking desk lamp across the wall — side light is the lie detector that reveals every bump the overhead light forgives. Glossy existing paint gets a light sanding or a deglosser so the new coat can grip. Finally, wash the wall: dust and kitchen grease films are why paint peels in sheets, and a damp sponge with mild detergent is cheaper than re-doing the room.

concepts.term: Patch, sand and clean before anything opens
concepts.statement: Primer is not a marketing upsell — it is a uniform surface. Bare patches of spackle drink paint differently and will flash (show as dull spots) under the finish coat unless sealed. Prime when covering repairs, when painting new drywall, when going from dark to light colors, and always on water stains (use a stain-blocking primer or the brown ring bleeds back through within weeks). Repainting a similar color over a clean, sound wall is the one case where primer is genuinely optional.

concepts.term: Primer: when it is optional and when it is law
concepts.statement: Buy paint by finish and quantity, not by brand loyalty. Sheens run from flat/matte (hides flaws, hard to clean) through eggshell and satin (the wall sweet spot) to semi-gloss and gloss (durable, scrubbable — the trim and door choice). A rough rule of coverage is 10 to 12 square metres per litre per coat, so measure the wall area and buy for two coats; a second coat is what makes color look intentional rather than inspired. Quality rollers and brushes matter as much as the paint: a cheap nap sheds fibers into the finish forever, and a good angled sash brush is the entire secret of the cut line.

Cut in before you roll: with a 5-centimetre angled brush, paint a 5-to-8-centimetre band along ceilings, corners, trim and around outlets, working the bristles into the junction and feathering outward. Painter's tape helps at trim and baseboards — press it down with a putty knife edge for a sealed line, and remove it while the paint is barely dry, pulling at an angle — but a steady hand and a loaded brush beat tape at the ceiling line, and tape is a sharpness tool, not a skill substitute. One strip of tape reused twice is a smear waiting to happen.

concepts.term: The W pattern and a loaded roller
concepts.statement: Roll with technique, not hope. Load the roller in the tray's ramp until the nap is evenly charged but not dripping, then paint a large W or M about a metre square, and fill it in with overlapping vertical strokes without lifting the roller. Work in sections while the edges stay wet — the 'wet edge' is the whole game: rolling into paint that has begun to set creates visible lap marks, so finish a full wall without a coffee break. Roll top to bottom on the final passes, end each wall at a corner, and resist going back to 'fix' a patch that is merely drying unevenly. Most amateur 'mistakes' are paint being watched too closely while it levels itself.

Sequence the room: ceiling first (splatter insurance), then walls, then trim and baseboards last — so drips from above land on not-yet-finished surfaces and any trim slip-ups get touched up by the wall's own edge. Two thin coats beat one thick one; thick paint sags, curtains and dries into wrinkles. Between coats respect the recoat time on the can (commonly two to four hours), and keep the room ventilated — modern low-VOC paints are gentle, but airflow still speeds a proper cure. Wrap brushes and rollers in plastic wrap or foil between coats rather than washing them; a sealed roller tray overnight is fine.
$$L = \frac{A \times n}{c}$$
concepts.detail: Litres L equal wall area A times number of coats n, divided by coverage c per litre — about 10-12 square metres per litre per coat for typical wall paint.

concepts.statement: Painting over dust and grease is the number-one cause of peeling — wash the wall even when it looks clean. Overworking drying paint (going back for 'one more pass') is the number-one cause of ugly. Painting out of sequence, trim before walls, guarantees repainting the trim. Cheap rollers shed and cheap tape bleeds; the tape must be pressed hard with a blade edge or paint wicks underneath. And never thin wall paint, never stretch a single coat over a color change, and never buy exactly the paint you need — buy a little more, because a half-full matching tin is the cheapest insurance in decorating.
Brush-painting the perimeter band at ceilings, corners and trim before rolling.
The boundary of still-liquid paint; rolling into a wet edge avoids visible lap marks.
A sealing undercoat that equalizes porosity and blocks stains so the finish coat reads even.
The gloss level of paint, from flat (hides flaws) to gloss (scrubbable), chosen per surface.
Dull or shiny patches where paint dried differently over unsealed repairs.
Ridges formed where a roller crossed paint that had already begun to set.
The roller cover's fiber length; 10-13 mm suits smooth interior walls.

examples.title: Worked example — Painting Walls Like a Professional
examples.problem: Paint the walls of a 4-by-5-metre bedroom with a 2.4-m ceiling and one door and one window — how much paint, and in what order over a weekend?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: coverage per litre per coat, two coats for a color change, and the room sequence ceiling-walls-trim.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: perimeter 18 m × 2.4 m ≈ 43 square metres, minus door (about 2) and window (about 2) ≈ 39 m². At 11 m² per litre and two coats: 39 × 2 ÷ 11 ≈ 7 litres — buy 7.5 to 8 to allow for a spare of the same batch, because color matching across batches is never perfect.

examples.result: Saturday is furniture, patching, sanding, washing, taping and cutting in; Sunday is two rolled coats with a lunch break at the recoat interval, trim last — and half a litre sealed in a jar for future touch-ups, labeled with the room and date.

keyTakeaways: Prep day: move and cover, patch and sand everything, wash the walls, remove plates, tape and burnish the edges.
Prime every repair and any stain or dramatic color change; skip primer only on clean, sound, similar-color walls.
Cut in the perimeter with an angled brush first, keeping a wet edge band ahead of the roller.
Roll in W-pattern sections a metre square, working wall by wall without pauses; final strokes top to bottom.
Two thin coats at the can's recoat interval; remove tape while barely dry, pulling at an angle away from the fresh paint.
Finish with the trim in semi-gloss, wrap tools in plastic between coats, and store labeled leftover paint for touch-ups.

Where next — This completes the Around the House branch with the toolkit, plumbing and electrical-safety lessons. Natural extensions: caulk and trim carpentry, furniture refinishing, and color theory from the Visual Design subject for choosing schemes rather than applying them.

quiz.q: The correct order for painting a whole room is:
options: Ceiling and trim together, then walls
quiz.explanation: Drips from above must land on unfinished surfaces: ceiling first, walls second, trim last — the sequence that minimizes rework.

quiz.q: A wall of 40 square metres at 10 m² per litre and two coats needs about:
quiz.explanation: 40 × 2 ÷ 10 = 8 litres — and buying a little extra keeps a labeled, matching tin for touch-ups.

quiz.q: You see dull patches appearing over old nail-hole repairs. The cause is:
options: The porous spackle drinking paint differently — flashing that primer prevents
quiz.explanation: Unsealed repairs change how the finish dries and reflects light; spot-priming equalizes the surface.

quiz.q: Roller lap marks appear when:
options: You roll into paint that has already started to dry
quiz.explanation: The wet edge is everything: pause mid-wall and the boundary between set and fresh paint dries into a visible ridge.

intro:
A tomato from your own balcony tastes better for reasons that are partly chemistry and partly pride, but growing it is a learnable system rather than a green thumb. Home growing, the branch of Garden & Growing behind this Everyday Knowledge topic, comes down to four resources — light, soil, water and timing — and one honest ranking of crops by difficulty. The plant-science background (photosynthesis, soil biology at farm scale) lives in the Library's Botany and Agriculture subjects; this lesson is the practical craft of keeping six pots and one bed alive and productive.

**Why this matters.** A salad garden the size of a doormat produces real food for months from a few dollars of seed. The deeper payoff is calibration: store produce is bred for shipping, picked early and eaten stale, and anyone who grows one basket of real strawberries recalibrates what those words mean. Few skills convert so little space into so much dinner.
objectives: Explain sun is the budget: six hours minimum
Explain soil, drainage and the finger test
Explain containers vs raised beds vs ground
Explain easy wins first: salad, herbs, radishes
Explain frost dates and succession planting
Explain water deep and morning, not daily drizzles
Explain harvest momentum: pick and it keeps producing

concepts.term: Sun is the budget: six hours minimum
concepts.statement: Start with light, because it is the one input you cannot fix later. Vegetables want six to eight hours of direct sun; leafy greens and herbs tolerate four to five; fruiting crops (tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers) compromise badly below six. Track the sun across a candidate spot for one day before committing — a 'sunny balcony' can be a north-facing shade trap, and trees leaf out in late spring to steal the light that March promised. In the southern hemisphere reverse the compass logic; everywhere, the sunniest side is the equator-facing one.

concepts.term: Soil, drainage and the finger test
concepts.statement: Soil is the medium and the pantry. Garden soil plus compost in roughly equal parts makes a raised-bed mix that drains yet holds moisture; straight garden soil in a container compacts into cement, so pots need a proper potting mix (light, with perlite or coco coir). The finger test beats every moisture meter: push a finger 3-4 cm in — if it comes out dry and dusty, water; if it shines wet, wait. Drainage is non-negotiable: every container needs holes, because roots drown in stagnant water faster than they die of thirst, and the classic houseplant funeral is kindness expressed as overwatering.

concepts.term: Containers vs raised beds vs ground
concepts.statement: Match the site to the format. Containers (20-30 cm deep for herbs and salad, 30-40 L for a tomato) suit renters and small spaces; raised beds warm earlier in spring, spare your back, and let you control the soil completely; in-ground beds are cheapest and hold water best once established. Start absurdly smaller than your ambition suggests — two beds or six pots well-kept teach more than a neglected quarter-acre, and the number one first-season failure is scale.

concepts.term: Easy wins first: salad, herbs, radishes
concepts.statement: Rank crops by forgiveness. Tier one: radishes (three weeks from seed), lettuce and salad greens (cut-and-come-again for months), herbs like basil, mint and chives, spring onions, bush beans. Tier two: zucchini (famously prolific), carrots, beets, kale, potatoes in a bucket. Tier three, the ambitious: tomatoes from seed (buy seedlings for year one), peppers, cucumbers, anything in the cabbage family that attracts caterpillars. Nothing in tier one can meaningfully fail, which is exactly what a first season should be made of.

Timing is a local fact. Learn your area's average last spring frost and first autumn frost dates — sowing calendars are written between them. Warm-season crops (tomatoes, beans, zucchini, basil) go out after the last frost, when nights stay reliably above about 10 °C; cool-season crops (lettuce, peas, radishes, spinach) can go in weeks earlier and again in late summer for autumn. Harden off indoor-raised seedlings with a week of gradually longer outdoor visits — a seedling moved straight from windowsill to full sun sunburns like a beach tourist. Succession planting (a short row of lettuce every two weeks) converts one April harvest into a whole season of salads.

concepts.term: Water deep and morning, not daily drizzles
concepts.statement: Water like a professional: deeply and in the morning. A thorough soaking two to four times a week beats a daily sprinkle, because shallow watering grows shallow roots that then depend on you daily; a soak sends roots down after it. Morning watering lets leaves dry by afternoon, starving mildew and fungal spores, and water the soil, not the plant — wet leaves in evening sun-starved hours are how blight epidemics start. Vegetables want roughly 2.5 to 4 cm of water a week, more in pots, which can need daily watering by midsummer. Mulch (straw, shredded leaves, 5 cm deep) cuts evaporation dramatically and suppresses the weeds that would otherwise win July.

concepts.term: Harvest momentum: pick and it keeps producing
concepts.statement: Harvest with greed, because most crops read picking as a signal to produce more. Cut-and-come-again lettuce, beans, zucchini at 15-20 cm (baseball-bat zucchini are starchy testimony to a missed week), and herbs pinched above a leaf pair all respond to harvest by regrowing harder. Let plants bolt (flower and go to seed) and lettuce turns bitter, basil turns tough — frequent picking is literally the pruning strategy. The daily five-minute walk with coffee is where gardening actually happens: spotting the first aphid colony, the first hornworm, the cucumber that appeared overnight, is the entire pest-management program at home scale — pick, squish, and re-check tomorrow.

concepts.detail: Plants N equal bed area A divided by spacing s squared — a 1.2 × 2.4 m bed at 25 cm lettuce spacing holds about 45 heads.

concepts.statement: The rookie scale-up — planting the whole seed catalogue — produces a July of guilt and wasted crops; start small and expand what actually works. Overwatering kills more containers than drought (no drainage holes, saucers left full). Planting warm-season crops too early wastes weeks of stunted growth, because soil temperature, not the calendar, is what a tomato seedling feels. Planting the same crop family in the same spot year after year builds its pests — rotate families if you can. And buying seedlings that are already flowering or rootbound trades a head start for a stunted season.
Harvesting outer leaves so the plant regrows for months of repeat cuts.
The local average end of spring frost; the calendar line warm-season crops wait behind.
Gradually exposing indoor seedlings to sun and wind over about a week before planting out.
Sowing small batches every week or two for a continuous harvest instead of one glut.
A crop prematurely flowering and turning bitter, usually from heat or stress.
A 5 cm blanket of straw or leaves that holds moisture and suppresses weeds.
Checking moisture 3-4 cm under the surface with a finger — the honest moisture meter.

examples.title: Worked example — Growing Food at Home: From Balcony to Garden Bed
examples.problem: Plan a first salad garden on a 1.2 × 2.4 m balcony bed with full sun — what to plant, how many, and on what schedule.

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: tier-one crops only for season one, spacing math for quantities, and succession sowing for a continuous harvest rather than one glut.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: the 2.88 m² bed at 20 cm spacing holds about 70 salad plants — too many at once. Split it: half in cut-and-come-again lettuce and arugula sown now, a quarter in radishes (ready in 25 days), a quarter in herbs and spring onions. Resow the salad third every two weeks; when radishes come out, beans go in after the last frost date.

examples.result: first radishes in under four weeks, first salad cut in five to six, and a rolling harvest that never leaves the bed empty — with every crop chosen so that failure anywhere still leaves a working garden.

keyTakeaways: Audit sun for one full day before choosing a spot; six hours is the working minimum for fruiting crops.
Fill beds with a soil-compost blend and pots with real potting mix; check every container drains.
Plan tier one for the first season: salad, radishes, herbs, beans — resist tomatoes-from-seed until year two.
Sow by frost dates: cool crops early, warm crops after nights hold above 10 °C; harden off seedlings over a week.
Water deeply two to four times a week in the morning, mulch 5 cm deep, and water soil rather than leaves.
Walk the garden daily with coffee: harvest hard, squish aphids and caterpillars by hand, and pull weeds while they are thread-sized.

Where next — Pair with the composting lesson in this branch to close the loop from kitchen to soil. For the underlying science, the Botany subject covers photosynthesis and the Agriculture & Food Systems subject covers soil health and crop breeding at farm scale; the Environment domain explains why local food miles matter.

quiz.q: Fruiting vegetables like tomatoes and peppers need at least about:
options: Constant shade with bright ambient light
quiz.explanation: Six to eight hours of direct sun is the working requirement for fruiting crops; leafy greens can compromise at four to five.

quiz.q: Why water deeply twice a week rather than a little every day?
options: It saves exactly the same water
Deep soakings drive roots downward; daily sprinkles keep roots shallow and dependent
quiz.explanation: Roots grow toward moisture; a deep soak builds a resilient, self-supporting root system instead of a shallow dependent one.

quiz.q: A 1.2 × 2.4 m bed sown at 30 cm spacing holds about:
quiz.explanation: 2.88 m² ÷ (0.3 m)² = 2.88 ÷ 0.09 ≈ 32 plants — the spacing-squared arithmetic that sizes every bed.

quiz.q: Your lettuce has suddenly shot up a flower stalk and turned bitter. This is:
quiz.explanation: Bolting ends the harvest for that plant — sowing in succession and providing some afternoon heat shade delays it.

intro:
Every autumn, forests bury a season of leaves and every spring the soil is richer for it — composting is that process with a steering wheel. Composting, the branch of Garden & Growing behind this Everyday Knowledge topic, is controlled decomposition: feeding a population of microbes the right mix of materials, air and moisture so they convert a year's kitchen scraps and garden waste into dark, crumbly humus that gardeners call black gold. Done right it is odorless, fast and quietly addictive; done wrong it is a slimy smelling liability two habits away from working.

**Why this matters.** Food and garden waste can be a third of what households throw away — material that rots in landfill without oxygen, releasing methane, while the same material in a backyard bin becomes free fertilizer. A household of scraps plus autumn leaves becomes a wheelbarrow of soil life each year. It is the rare habit that cuts waste, saves money and improves a garden simultaneously.
objectives: Explain compost is controlled rot
Explain greens supply nitrogen, browns supply carbon
Explain the roughly 30:1 carbon-to-nitrogen target
Explain air and moisture: turn it, wring-sponge damp
Explain size: a bin at least one cubic metre cooks
Explain troubleshooting by smell and temperature
Explain what never goes in the pile

concepts.statement: Everything you add is either a green or a brown. Greens are moist, nitrogen-rich materials: fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, fresh grass clippings, tea leaves. Browns are dry, carbon-rich ones: autumn leaves, cardboard, shredded paper, straw, wood chips. Microbes building their bodies want roughly 25 to 30 parts carbon for every part nitrogen, and the practical rule of volume is about three parts browns to one part greens — because greens are denser in nitrogen than they look. A pile of pure greens goes anaerobic and sour; a pile of pure browns just sits there for a year, hungry.

concepts.term: Greens supply nitrogen, browns supply carbon
concepts.statement: The workers are bacteria and fungi, and they have two non-negotiables: air and water, in balance. Oxygen enters by diffusion and turning; without it, the aerobic workforce suffocates and anaerobic bacteria take over, producing the sour, rotten smell that gives composting a bad name. Moisture should be like a wrung-out sponge: squeeze a handful and a few drops should come, not a stream. Too dry and nothing happens (the classic 'nothing is happening' pile is almost always thirsty); too wet and air pockets flood shut. Layer browns and greens as you add, and the balance mostly maintains itself.

Size is temperature. A pile needs to be roughly one cubic metre (a meter each way) before its center holds the heat that bacteria generate — a small heap cannot insulate its own metabolism. Hot composting, 55 to 70 °C in the core, is fast (finished in two to three months with turning), kills most weed seeds and plant pathogens, and requires the volume, the balance and the turning. Cold composting — anything smaller, cooler and lazier — still works, in six to twelve months, quietly, with weed seeds surviving. Both end in the same place; one is a slow cooker and the other a pressure cooker.

concepts.term: Air and moisture: turn it, wring-sponge damp
concepts.statement: Chop everything small. Surface area is where microbes eat, and a whole cabbage core can outlast a season while cabbage-core confetti vanishes in weeks. The other accelerators are free: a shovelful of finished compost or garden soil inoculates a new pile with the workforce; urine is a legitimate nitrogen activator for a stalled heap; and turning with a pitchfork — lifting and dropping so the outside becomes the inside — resets both air and evenness. A compost thermometer is the gadget that turns composting from faith into feedback: hot core, sweet earthy smell, and visible shrinkage within weeks mean the machine is running.

concepts.term: Size: a bin at least one cubic metre cooks
concepts.statement: Troubleshooting is a two-question diagnostic, smell and activity. Sour or rotten smell means anaerobic: add browns, turn, and check drainage under the bin. Ammonia smell means too many greens: bury the next scraps under a thick brown layer. Nothing is happening means too dry, too cold, or too much carbon: water it, wait for a bigger mass, or mix in fresh greens. Attracting flies or rodents means exposed food: always bury greens under a brown blanket and never add the attractants below. A healthy pile smells like a forest floor after rain — that smell is the goal state.

Keep the exclusion list firm. Never add meat, fish, dairy, oils or cooked food to a home bin — they rot slowly, smell, and recruit every rat in the district. Avoid pet waste (parasite risk), glossy card stock, treated wood ash in quantity, and diseased plants in a cold pile. Bindweed and other perennial weeds that resprout from fragments go in the municipal green waste (their hot industrial piles kill what yours cannot) or the general waste. Everything else vegetable — including eggshells (mineral, not protein), coffee filters, plain cardboard, hair, wool — is fair game.

concepts.term: What never goes in the pile
concepts.statement: Harvest when the bottom of the pile is dark, crumbly, unrecognizable and earthy-smelling. The simplest method is to lift or open the bin, take finished material from the base, and return the still-woody top third to the new pile as an inoculant. Sift through a coarse screen if you want potting-grade fineness. Use it as a 5 cm mulch on beds, stirred into potting mix at roughly one part in four, or as a handful per planting hole — it is soil structure, microbes and slow-release nutrients in one material, and it is the single best thing you can do for a garden short of the sun.
$$R_{mix} = \frac{w_c C_c + w_b C_b}{w_c N_c + w_b N_b} \approx 30$$
concepts.detail: The blended carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of greens and browns, weighted by mass, targets roughly 30 — in practice, three parts browns to one part greens by volume.

concepts.statement: The single most common failure is the all-greens bin — kitchen scraps added for months with nothing dry — which ends as smelly soup. The second is neglecting the exclusion list: one week of meat scraps can recruit a rat dynasty that no amount of turning evicts. Watering is forgotten in summer heat (a dry pile simply pauses) and drainage ignored in winter (a flooded one goes anaerobic). And expecting finished compost in weeks from a cold, small, unturned pile sets everyone up for disappointment: volume and turning are what make it fast.
Nitrogen-rich moist materials: scraps, coffee grounds, fresh grass.
Carbon-rich dry materials: leaves, cardboard, straw, shredded paper.
Carbon to nitrogen by mass; microbes want roughly 30:1, delivered as 3:1 browns-to-greens by volume.
A large, balanced, turned pile reaching 55-70 °C, finishing in months and killing weed seeds.
The target dampness: a squeezed handful yields a few drops, not a stream.
Oxygen-starved decomposition that sours; the smell that means turn it and add browns.
The stable, dark end-product of decomposition — finished compost itself.

examples.title: Worked example — Composting: Turning Kitchen Scraps into Soil
examples.problem: A three-week-old pile smells sour and is crawling with fungus gnats — what went wrong and what is the rescue?

steps.label: Recall the governing idea
steps.text: a sour smell means the aerobic microbes have lost to anaerobic ones — usually too much green, too much moisture, too little air — and exposed greens recruit flies.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: turn the pile fully with a pitchfork, fluffing in shredded cardboard and dry leaves until the mix reads wrung-sponge damp and reads roughly three browns to one green by the eye. Bury any visible food under a 10 cm brown blanket. Check the bin base drains.

examples.result: within days the smell shifts to earthy, the pile begins shrinking, and a week later the core is warm to the hand — the same pile, converted from liability to composter by browns and air.

keyTakeaways: Site the bin on bare soil (drainage and worm access), in half-sun, one cubic metre or larger if you want it hot.
Keep a browns stash — shredded cardboard and dry leaves — next to the bin all year; every bucket of scraps gets a brown blanket.
Chop additions small, layer greens and browns, and moisten dry layers as you build.
Turn every one to two weeks for hot composting, moving outside material into the center.
Diagnose by nose: sour — turn and add browns; ammonia — more browns next time; nothing — water it and add greens.
Harvest the dark, crumbly base; return coarse unfinished material to the next pile as starter culture.

Where next — This closes the loop with the growing-food lesson — kitchen to compost to bed. Next steps in Garden & Growing: worm composting (vermicomposting) for apartments, and soil testing. For the planetary version of the same chemistry, see the Environment domain's carbon-cycle and landfill-methane lessons.

quiz.q: Coffee grounds and fresh grass clippings are:
quiz.explanation: Both are moist and nitrogen-rich — greens — despite coffee grounds being brown in color; the category is chemistry, not color.

quiz.q: A compost pile smells sour and rotten. The standard fix is:
options: Turn it and mix in browns
Cover it and wait a month
quiz.explanation: Sour means anaerobic: air from turning plus absorbent carbon from browns restores the aerobic workforce.

quiz.q: Why does a compost pile need to be about one cubic metre to get hot?
options: Only that volume insulates the heat its own microbes generate
quiz.explanation: Heat is a by-product of microbial metabolism; below roughly a cubic metre, too much surface area leaks it away and the core never warms.

quiz.q: Which of these should never go in a home compost bin?
quiz.explanation: Meat, fish, dairy and cooked food rot slowly, stink, and attract rodents — the exclusion list exists for them.

intro:
A lost button consigns a perfectly good coat to the back of a closet, and a fallen hem does the same to trousers — the modern wardrobe's small failures are repairs waiting for twenty minutes and four hand stitches. Sewing and mending, the branch of Practical Skills behind this Everyday Knowledge topic, is the oldest textile technology and the most accessible: a needle, thread that matches, and the small set of techniques that keep clothing out of landfill. The cultural meaning of clothes is covered by the Fashion & Identity subject in the Library; this lesson is the craft of keeping them functional.

**Why this matters.** Clothing is among the most discarded consumer goods, and extending a garment's life is one of the simplest sustainability habits there is — the mending movement calls it visible repair with pride, not embarrassment. Beyond the ethics, it is autonomy: a traveler re-securing a strap, a parent fixing a school uniform at 8 p.m., an interview shirt kept alive by a two-minute button. Few skills deliver so much agency for the price of a tin of needles.
objectives: Explain the mending kit: needles, thread, pins, ripper
Explain running, back, whip and ladder stitches
Explain sewing flat and shank buttons properly
Explain hemming by hand with a blind stitch
Explain patches and visible mending
Explain thread matching and fabric behavior
Explain when a sewing machine earns its keep

concepts.term: The mending kit: needles, thread, pins, ripper
concepts.statement: The kit is small and permanent: a pack of sharps (general hand-sewing needles) plus a few betweens (shorter, for fine work), thread in the colors your wardrobe actually is, sharp scissors dedicated to fabric alone (paper blunts them — a law of the household), glass-head pins, a tape measure, a thimble, and the most important tool in the tin: the seam ripper, because half of mending is removing what failed. A needle threader saves ten minutes of squinting, and a tomato-shaped pincushion with a strawberry emery for polishing needles is traditional for a reason.

concepts.term: Running, back, whip and ladder stitches
concepts.statement: Four hand stitches run the whole subject. The running stitch is the straight in-out rhythm — fast, basic, for basting and seams that carry no load. The back stitch doubles back on itself with every stitch and is the strong one: each stitch locks the previous, making a seam nearly as tough as machine work — this is the stitch for seams and straps that must hold. The whip stitch wraps over the fabric edge like a spiral binder, ideal for hemming edges, closing pillows and attaching patches. The ladder (blind) stitch hides inside the fold of a hem so only a thread-width dot shows on the outside — the invisible professional finish.

concepts.term: Sewing flat and shank buttons properly
concepts.statement: Threading and knotting are half the battle. Cut thread with a sharp diagonal point, moisten the needle's eye side, and work with a length no longer than your forearm — long thread tangles, knots itself and frays. Begin and end with a secure fastening: two or three tiny stitches on the same spot, or — the classic — a loop through the last stitch and pull. When a garment's fabric is delicate, anchor knots inside layers, never against the face of the fabric where they pucker it.

concepts.term: Hemming by hand with a blind stitch
concepts.statement: Buttons come in two architectures, and sewing them the right way is the difference between a repair that lasts years and one that pops in a month.
